## Source page 8, section 1

Preface
This dictionary is a modest tribute of my devotion to Canada, whose citizen I am
proud to be, the country in which the spirit of the Bible has dominion from Sea to Sea,
the country in which the Human Rights are a happy, living reality, a reality called upon
to serve as a shining example to mankind.
1 would like to extend my heartfelt thanks to the Canada Council, whose grant made it
possible for me to have the manuscript of my dictionary typed in order to prepare it for
the press. The generosity of this noble institution will continue to serve for me as a
precious stimulus for further scientific work.
Between 1931 and 1944, 1 was Rabbi of the Jewish Congregation in Νονέ Zimky
(Czechoslovakia), whence I was deported by the Nazis to Auschwitz and, from there, to
the concentration camp Allach-Dachau. After the liberation from the latter place by
American troops in 1945, 1 returned home to find only the ruins of what had once been
the flourishing Jewish community of Νονέ Zamky. There I learned that my Father, my
wife, my only child Joseph and two of my three sisters had suffered martyrdom in
Auschwitz. Of my family, my sister Mrs. Paul Horvath (ne'e Elizabeth Klein) and her
husband have survived.
In 1945 I became Chief Rabbi of the Jewish Congregation in Satu Marej Rumania, but
not wishing to remain in that country, I moved together with my sister and brother-in-law
to Budapest,.and from there via Vienna to Paris, where I became Rabbi of the
Congregation Rue de Montevideo.
In 1951 the three of us went to Toronto, Canada, where I began to deliver lectures.
The students who attended these lectures showed their love to me by establishing a
congregation and building a synagogue named Beth Yitshak in memory of my Father. I
have been the rabbi of Congregation Beth Yitshak since 1952.
When I came home from the concentration camp and learned about the whole extent
of the holocaust, I was first near to despair. It was the boundless love and selfless
dedication of my sister Elizabeth that gave me back my interest "in life, in pastoral
activities and in science. She is like a guardian angel who watches over me. When I
discovered several thousand mistakes in the standard etymological dictionaries, I decided
to write my own etymological dictionary. I nevertheless hesitated before commencing the
momentous task. Then my sister's enthusiasm and encouragement were my greatest
inspiration. Without her-urging my etymological dictionary would never have been written.
May this dictionary, which plastically shows the affinity and interrelationship of the
nations of the world in the way in which their languages developed, contribute to
bringing them nearer to one another in the sincere pursuit of peace on earth — which was one
of my cardinal aims in writing this dictionary.
Dr. Ernest Klein

## Source page 10, section 1

Introduction
Since my youth I have devoted myself to philology, with special regard to etymology.
The reasons inducing me to write Ά Comprehensive Etymological Dictionary of the
English Language' may be summed up as follows:
It is a well-known fact that in the course of the last sixty years philology has attained a high
degree of development. It is so much the more to be regretted that modern lexicography has
remained far behind the achievements of philology. As a rule, even the most authoritative
English etymological dictionaries give such etymologies as reflect the level reached by philology
about half a century ago. In most cases etymologies given up by serious science long ago are
still wandering out of one dictionary into another and continue living with tenacity,
apparently ignoring the truths established in the field of philology in the course of the latter decades.
One example may suffice to prove this. Despite the fact that Tocharian (this language extinct
long ago but newly discovered at the end of the Nineteenth Century) occupies a very important
place among the Indo-European languages, Tocharian references appear only quite
exceptionally in the etymological dictionaries of the English language. This is so much the more
striking, because Tocharian may help us understand the development of many a word in the different
Indo-European languages, inasmuch as the words of the Tocharian language often represent
the transitory form — 'the missing link' — between the Old Indian and the other Indo-European
languages. In this dictionary Tocharian words are regularly referred to together with the other
Indo-European equivalents.
English belonging to the great family of the Indo-European languages, it is quite evident
that in tracing any word to its source, an etymological dictionary must take into consideration
all the important cognates of this word in the other Indo-European languages. If we want to
understand the history of an English word, we must compare this word with as many
correspondences as possible.
Most etymological dictionaries do not pay enough attention to this circumstance and
therefore cite equivalents from the kindred languages quite at random, often enumerating the less
important ones but omitting such as had a decisive influence upon the form of the word treated
or upon the development of its meaning. This dictionary tries to be a dependable guide to the
reader in this respect too, by giving him all the necessary information about the origin,
formation and sense development of any word that might interest him.
The scientific value of most etymological dictionaries is much impaired by the circumstance
that their authors are not familiar with the structure of the Semitic languages, a fact thrown
into relief by the inconsistencies of the transliteration of Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic words,
on the one hand, and by the lack of any etymological analysis of these words, on the other. In
tftis dictionary the words of Semitic origin — about 750 in number — are fully analyzed: they
arS traced to their etyma, the cognates are given, the stem is distinguished from the prefixes and
suffixes added to it, etc. In brief: the words of Semitic origin are treated exactly as the Indo-
European words. This is why my dictionary may also serve as a preliminary work for an
etymological dictionary of the Semitic languages themselves.
In all etymological dictionaries we frequently come across such words as are declared to be
'of unknown origin', even in cases when the etymology of such words can be established beyond
any doubt. In many other cases the etymology is not given either, but the origin of the respec-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:11 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:11 COLUMN:1 -->

## Source page 11, section 1

χ
tive word is referred to by such vague terms as 'of uncertain etymology', or 'probably of
Oriental origin', etc., whereas their provenance is very well known. My dictionary contains the
etymology of several hundred such words.
This dictionarv eives also the etvmoloeies of personal names and mythological names.
Some other features of this dictionary:
What the elements are to chemistry, what the sounds are to music, are words to language.
However, words are not only the elements of a language but also of the history of the people
speaking it. They are important milestones along the way leading to the majestic Palace of
Human Knowledge.
One of the basic features of this dictionary is that — in contradistinction to other
etymological dictionaries — its aim is not only to give the history of words, but to give also History in
words. This dictionary is the first attempt to give the history of human civilization and culture
condensed in the etymological data of words. We not only speak but think and even dream
in words. Language is a mirror in which the whole spiritual development of mankind reflects
itself. Therefore, in tracing words to their origin, we are tracing simultaneously civilization
and culture to their real roots.
Another important aim that I set to myself in composing this dictionary was to mirror in it the
history of the humanities and sciences. Since the history of a word is at the same time the history
of the thing denoted or the idea expressed by that word it is obvious that by giving the history
of the technical terms of any branch of science we also give the history of that branch of science
itself. In consideration of this fact one of the goals of an etymological dictionary should be to
deal with the history of scientific technical terms in a manner that would enable the reader to
reconstruct through them the history of the various branches of the humanities and sciences.
This dictionary represents the first attempt to live up to this goal. E.g. in order to know the
important phases of the development of medicine one will only have to look up the medical
terms occurring in this dictionary.
For the illustration of this fact I am quoting here a few entries from this dictionary dealing
with medical terms:

cynanthropy, п., insanity in which the patient believes himself to be a dog (med.) — Formed with suff.

The examples have been taken from among the medical terms beginning with the letter A,
В or C, hence such as are contained in the present (i.e. I) volume of this dictionary.
Similarly, in dealing with the technical terms of the other branches of science in this
dictionary, one of my chief aims was to show the historic development of science in general and of its
various branches in particular, with special regard to biology, zoology, botany, mineralogy,
geography, geology, history, astronomy, physics, chemistry, mathematics, grammar,
philosophy. The entries treating these branches of science in this dictionary, virtually contain the
most important phases of their history.
Two other characteristic features of this dictionary:
HYBRID WORDS
Scientists are rarely also linguists. This is why many scientific terms are inexactly coined and
often erroneous and misleading in sense. Many of these terms are hybrids, i.e. words made up
of elements from different languages. In this dictionary hybrids are not only referred to as such,
but—quite frequently—a new, correctly formed word is suggested instead of the one used
hitherto.
For an example see the entry aureomycin on preceding page.
LOAN TRANSLATIONS
Loan translations are important guideposts on the road on which civilization and culture
traveled in the course of centuries from nation to nation. Through them we learn e.g. that the
chief elements of the science of grammar developed in ancient Greece and reached Western
Europe through the medium of the Romans. (The overwhelming majority of grammatical terms
in the modern languages are loan translations of, or derive directly from, Latin words, which
themselves are loan translations of Greek words. Cp. e.g. the words subject, verb, adverb,
nominative, accusative, genitive, dative in this dictionary.)
In like manner, loan translations are of great importance for the reconstruction of the history
of all the other branches of science as well. This is why, in this dictionary, special attention was
paid to loan translations and their way was traced from language to language.

## Source page 14, section 1

XI11
Transliteration of Semitic Words
The transliteration for Semitic words contained in the etymologies of this dictionary is such
that it renders exactly every consonant, vowel and diacritical sign. It happens Tor the first time
that the Hebrew and Aramaic words quoted in an etymological dictionary are transliterated
according to a system which makes it possible to retransliterate these words into their original
characters, including all the phonetic signs particular to Hebrew and Aramaic. (See the
following Rules for Transliteration.)
As a rule, in this dictionary the accent in Semitic words (with the exception of the Akkadian,
for which the laws of accentuation are not known), is indicated by the usual accent mark ' placed
over the vowel of the accented syllable.

A point in the middle of a consonant, called daghesh hazaq (daghesh forte, 'strong daghesh'),
strengthens (i.e. doubles) the consonant. It is marked by the doubling of the respective
consonant.
The sign daghesh qai (daghesh lene = 'light daghesh'), which is formally identical with the
sign of the daghesh hazaq, is used with the letters Л,0,Э,"Т,Д,Э , to indicate their
original hard pronunciation. In this Dictionary Л , D , Э , ΤΓ, 3 , Э , are transliterated
b, g, d, k, p, t, whereas Л , D , D , Τ , Д , D , are rendered by bh, gh, dh, kh, ph, th.

## Source page 27, section 1

Symbols used in this Dictionary
The asterisk (*) indicates a hypothetical form.
The mark called macron (_) is placed over a vowel to show that it is long.
The mark called breve (~) is placed over a vowel to show that it is short.
In this dictionary the quantity of vowels (esp. in Greek and Latin words) is indicated only
when they are long. The brevity of vowels is indicated only in some special cases (e.g. in Latin
pendere, 'to cause to hang', in contradistinction to pendere, 'to hang' (see pendant). Hence
when there is no mark over a vowel it is to be assumed that it is short.
The mark' after a consonant in the Slavonic languages indicates palatalization.
The mark - after a syllable or a group of syllables (as in ant-, ami-) indicates that this syllable
or group of syllables is a prefix.
The mark - before a syllable or a group of syllables (as in -ate, -ation) indicates that this
syllable or group of syllables is a suffix.

## a
a,indef. article. — Form of an before a consonant.

## a
a, prep, meaning 'of, as in a clock = of the
clock. — ME., fr. OE. of, 'from, off, of. See of.

## a
a, prep, meaning 'on'. — OE. an, on, 'on'. See on.

## a
a, prep, meaning 'to, at, in'. — F., fr. L. ad, 'to,
toward'. See ad- and cp. a-, pref. corresponding
to L. ad-. Cp. also a la.

## a-
a-, pref. meaning 'of, as in akin. — ME. a-,
fr. OE. of. See a, prep, meaning 'of.

## a-
a-, pref. meaning 'on'; used to form adverbs
from nouns as in abroad, ashore. — Fr. OE. an,
on. See a, prep, meaning 'on'.

## a-
a-, intensive pref. — OE. a-, rel. to OS., OFris.
ur-, or-, Du. oor-, OHG., MHG. ur- (unstressed:
OHG. ir-, ar-, MHG., G. -er), Goth. us-. The
orig. meaning of ihese prefixes was 'out, away'.
Cp. the pref. in oakum, ordeal.

## a-
a-, pref. meaning 'away from, from' (occurring
only before v), as in avert. — L. a-, fr. β, short
form of ab, 'away from, from'; rel. lo Oscan
aa-, Umbr. aha-, 'away from, from'. See ab-.

## a-
a-, pref. corresponding to L. ad-, fr. ad, 'to,
toward', either directly or through the medium of
OF. a- or F. a. Cp. the pref. in abandon,
acknowledge, ascend, ascribe, and see ad-. Cp. also a.

## a-
a-, priv. pref. meaning 'not, less, without'. —
Gk. ά-, used before a consonant, the form
before a vowel being άν-. See an- and cp. the priv.
prefixes in- and un-.

## aam
aam, п., a Dutch and German liquid measure. —
Du., fr. L. ama (more exactly hama), 'bucket',
fr. Gk. αμη (prop, άίμη), 'bucket', which is rel.
to άμαοθαι, 'to draw, gather', άμνίον, 'a bowl
in which the blood of victims was caught'. See
amnion.

## aardvark
aardvark, п., a South African burrowing animal.
— Du., lit. 'earth pig', fr. aard, 'earth', and
vark, 'pig'. See earth and farrow.

## aardwolf
aardwolf, п., a South African hyena-like
mammal. — Du., lit. 'earth wolf. See prec. word
and wolf.

## Aaron
Aaron, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the brother of
Moses. — Late L., fr. Gk. 'Ααρών, fr. Heb.
Aharon, which is prob. of Egyptian origin. Arab.
Haran is borrowed from Hebrew.
Derivative: Aaron-ic, adj.

## Aaron's beard
Aaron's beard, name of several plants. — So
called because of their resemblance to a beard
and with allusion to Ps. 133:2.

## Aaron's rod
Aaron's rod, 1) straight molding in architecture;
2) popular name of the common mullein. —
So called with allusion to Nu. 17.

## Ab
Ab, п., name of the fifth Jewish month. — Heb.
abh, fr. Akkad. abu.

## ab-
ab-, pref. in words of Latin origin, denoting
departure, separation. — L. ab-, fr. ab, 'away from,
from; by'. The form ab is regularly used before
all vowels and h; before consonants except h,
ab usually becomes a; before c, q, t, it becomes
abs. L. ab derives fr. orig. *ap (cp. aperio, Ί
open'), and is cogn. with ΟΙ. άρα, 'away from',
Gk. άπό, 'away from, from', Goth, af OE. of,
'away from, from'. See of and cp. a-, 'away
from', apo-, post-.

## aba
aba, п., a form of altazimuth instrument. — So
called after its inventor Antoine Thomson
d'Abbadie.

## aback
aback, adv. — OE. on Ьгес. See a-, 'on', and back.

## abacus
abacus, п., 1) frame with beads for calculation;
2) (archil.) slab at the top of a column. — L.
abacus, fr. Gk. άβαξ, gen. αβακος, 'a square
tablet strewn with dust', fr. Heb. abhuq, 'dust*,
fr. root a-b-q, 'to fly off. The first type of abacus
was a board covered with dust, whence its name.

## Abaddon
Abaddon, п., the bottomless pit. — Heb. ubhad-
ddn, 'destruction', fr. abhadh, 'heperished', which
is rel. to Aram, abhadh, 'he perished', Ugar. 'bd,
'to perish', Ethiop. abada, 'he wandered about',
Arab, abada, 'it (the animal) fled in fright'.

## abaft
abaft, adv., astern, aft; prep., behind. — Formed

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:28 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. a-, 'on', and OE. bexftan, fr. be, 'by, at',
and seflan. 'behind'. See be- and aft.

## abalienate
abalienate, tr. v., 1) to alienate; 2) to remove. —
L. abalienatus, pp. of abalilnure, 'to remove',
lit. 'to make alien from', fr. ab- and aliendre.
See alienate.

## abalienation
abalienation, п., j) alienation; 2) removal. —
L. abalienatio, gen. -onis, fr. abalienatus, pp.
of abalienare. See prec. word and -ion.

## abalone
abalone, п., a mollusk. — Sp., of unknown origin.

## abandon
abandon, tr. v., to leave, forsake. — ME. aban-
donen, fr. OF. abandoner (F. abandonner), fr. a
bandon in (mettre) a bandon, 'to give up to a
public ban', fr. a, 'to' (fr. L. ad) and bandon,
'power, authority, jurisdiction', fr. Late L. ban-
dum, bannum, 'order, decree*, which is of Teut.
origin. See ad- and ban, 'proclamation', and cp.
banish.
Derivatives: abandon, п., abandon-ed, adj., aban-
don-er, п., abandon-ment, n.

## abase
abase, tr. v., to lower. — OF. abaissier (F. abais-
ser), 'to bring low', fr. VL. *adbassiare, which
is formed fr. L. ad- and Late L. bassus, 'thick, fat,
low'. See base, 'low', and cp. the second element
in bouillabaisse.
Derivatives: abas-ed, adj.,abas-ed-ly,adv.,abas-
ed-ness, п., abase-ment, n.

## abash
abash, tr. v., to confuse; to put to shame. — ME.
abassen, abaissen, abashen, fr. OF. esbahiss-,
pres. part, stem of esbahir, 'to astonish',
compounded of pref. es- (fr. L. ex; see 1st ex-) and
a derivative of OF. baer (F. bayer), 'to gape',
the change of conjugation (-ir for -er) being
prob. due to the influence of the OF. adj. half,
'astonished'. The OF. verb baer derives fr. VL.
batare, 'to gape, yawn'. See bay, 'part in the
wall', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: abash-less, adj., abask-less-ly, adv.,
abash-ment, n.

## abasia
abasia, п., inability to walk (med.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. βάσις, 'stepping,
step; base', from the stem of βαίνειν, 'to go'.
See base, п., and -ia.

## abate
abate, tr. and intr. v. — ME. abaten, fr. OF. abatre,
abattre (F. abattre), 'to beat down', fr. VL. *ab-
batere (whence also It. abballere^ Sp. abatir),
fr. ab- and batere (L. baituere), 'to beat, strike'.
See batter, 'to beat, strike', and cp. abatis,
abattoir, bate, 'to reduce'.
Derivative: abate-ment, n.

## abatis
abatis, п., a defense made of felled trees (mil.) —
F., 'things thrown down', fr. abattre, 'to beat
down, throw down'. See prec. word and cp.
abattoir.

## abattoir
abattoir, п., a slaughterhouse. — F., fr. abattre,
'to beat down'. See abate. The subst. suff. -oir
corresponds to L. -orium, whence E. -ory.

## abb
abb, п., the yarn for the woof. — OE. aweb, ab.
See a-, 'on', and web.

## abba
abba, п., title of honor. — L., fr. Gk. άββα, fr.
Aram, abba, 'the falher; my father', emphatic
state of abh, 'father'. See abbot, and cp.
abbacy, abbey.

## abbacy
abbacy, п., the office or jurisdiction of an abbot.
— Eccles. L. abbatia, fr. abbas, gen. abbatis. See
abbot and cp. abba, abbey. Cp. also badia.

## abbe
abbe, п., a title given in France lo a priest. — FI(
fr. Eccles. L. abbatem, ace. of abbas. Cp. It.
abbate, Sp. abaci, 'abbot', which also derive fr.
Eccles. L. abbatem, and see abbot.

## abbess
abbess, n. — ME. abbesse, fr. OF. (= F.) abbesse,
fr. Eccles. L. abbatissa, fern, of abbas, gen. -dtis.
See abbot and cp. It. abbadessa, badessa, and
Sp. abadesa, 'abbess', which also derive fr.
Eccles. L. abbatissa.

## abbey
abbey, п., a convent headed by an abbot or an
abbess. — ME., fr. AF. abbeie, fr. OF. abeie,
abate (F. abbaye), fr. Eccles. L. abbatia, fr. L.
abbas. See abbot and cp. abba, abbacy, abbess.
Cp. also It. abbadia, Sp. abadia, 'abbey', which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:28 COLUMN:3 -->
also derive fr. Eccles. L. abbatia.

## abbot
abbot, n. — OE. abbod, fr. L. abbot-, stem of
abbas, gen. abbatis, fr. Aram, abba, 'the father;
my father', emphatic state of abh, 'father', which
is rel. to Heb. abh, 'father'. See Aboth and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also abba, abbacy,
abbe, abbey, abuna, badia.

## abbreviate
abbreviate, tr. v., to shorten. — L. abbreviatus,
pp. of abbreviare, Ίο shorten', fr. ab- and bre-
vidre, 'toshorten', fr. brevis, 'short'. Seebrief,adj.,
andep. abridge, which is a doublet of abbreviate.
Derivatives: abbreviat-ed, adj., abbreviation, ab·
breviator (qq.v.), abbreviat-ory, adj.

## abbreviatioa
abbreviatioa, n. — F. abrevialion, fr. L. abbrevia-
tionem, ace. of abbreviated, fr. abbreviatus, pp.
of abbreviare. See abbreviate and -ion.
abbreviate!-, n. — L., fr. abbreviatus, pp. of
abbreviare. See abbreviate and agential suff. -or.

## Abderian
Abderian, pertaining to Abdera. — See Abderite
and -ian.

## Abderite
Abderite, п., ι) an inhabitant of Abdera; 2) a
fool. — L. Abderita, fr. Gk. 'Αβδηρίτης,
'inhabitant of Abdera', fr. "Αβδηρα (plj, 'Abdera',
a town proverbial for the stupidity of its
inhabitants. For sense development cp. Gotha-
mite. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## abdest
abdest, п., the Mohammedan rite of washing the
hands before prayer. — Pers. abdasi, lit. 'water
for the hand', fr. ab, 'water', and dast, 'hand'.
Pers. ab, 'water', is rel. to Avestic dp-, OI. apah
(fem. pi.), 'water'; see amide and cp. the first
element in abkari and the second element in
doab and in julep. Pers. dast, 'hand', is rel. to
Aveslic zasta, 'hand', fr. I.-E. base *ghosto-,
whence also OI. hastah, 'hand'. See hasta and
cp. hath.

## abdicate
abdicate, tr. v. — L. abdicatus, pp. of abdicare,
'to renounce, resign, abdicate', fr. ab- and di-
care, 'to proclaim, dedicate, consecrate, devote',
which is related to dicere, 'to say, tell'. See dic-
tioa and verbal suff. -ate and cp. dedicate,
indicate.

## abdication
abdication, n. — L. abdicatio, gen. -onis,
'renunciation, abdication', from abdicatus pp. of
abdicare. See prec. word and -ion.

## abdomen
abdomen, п., the belly. — L. abdomen (later also
abdumen), 'the lower part of the belly, paunch,
abdomen', which prob. meant orig. 'the hidden
part of the body', and stands for *abdgmen, a
derivative of abdo, abdere, 'to hide', which is
formed from ab-, and -dere (used only in
compounds), fr. I.-E. base *dhl-, *dh'-, 'to put,
place'; see do and cp. words there referred to.
See Walde-Hofmann, LEW., Г., р.з.

## abdominal
abdominal, adj., pertaining to the abdomen. —
Medical L. abdOminalis, fr. L. abdomen, gen.
abdominis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: abdominal, п., abdominally, adv.

## abdomino-
abdomino-, combining form denoting the
abdomen. — Fr. L. abdomen, gen. abdominis. See
abdomen.

## abduce
abduce, tr. v., to draw away. — L. abducere, 'to
lead away'. See next word.

## abducent
abducent, adj., drawing back or away (said of the
muscles); the opposite of adducent. — L. abdu-
cins, gen. -entis, pres. part, of abducere, 'to lead
away', fr. ab-, and ducere, Ίο lead'. See duke
and -ent.

## abduct
abduct, tr. v., to kidnap. — L. abductus, pp. of
abducere, 'to lead away'. See prec. word.

## abduction
abduction, n. — L. abduct id, gen. -idnis 'a leading
away', fr. abductus, pp. of abducere, 'to lead
away'. See prec. word and -ion. As a term of
logic, L. abduclio is a loan translation of Gk.
απαγωγή, 'a shifting (of the argument)', lit. 'a
leading away1, used to denote a syllogism whose
major premise is certain, but whose minor
premise is only probable.

## abductor
abductor, n. (anal.) — Medical L., name of a
muscle, lit. 'that which leads away', fr. L. ab-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:29 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ABEAM | 2 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:29 COLUMN:1 -->
ductus, pp. of abducere, 'to lead away'. See
abduct and agential suff. -or.

## abeam
abeam, adv., at right angles to the keel (naul.) —
Lit. 'on the beam', fr. a-, 'on', and beam.

## abecedarian
abecedarian, adj., elementary, rudimentary. —
ML. abecedarius, 'pertaining to the alphabet',
a word formed from the names of the first four
letters of the alphabet. For the ending see suff.
-arian.

## abecedarium
abecedarium, п., an ABC book. — ML., prop,
neut. of the adjective abecedarius, used as a
noun. See prec. word.

## abed
abed, adv., in bed (archaic). — Formed fr. a-,
'on', and bed.

## Abel
Abel, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the second son of
Adam and Eve. — L., fr. Gk. "Αβελ, fr. Heb.
Hibhel, lit. 'breath, vanity'.

## abele
abele, п., the white poplar. — Du. abeel, fr. OF.
aubel, albel, fr. VL. 'albellus, 'whitish', dimin.
of albulus, which itself is dimin. of albus,
'white'. See alb.

## Abelmoschus
Abelmoschus, п., a genus of plants of the mallow
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, habb-al-musk,
in vulgar pronunciation habb-el-mosk, lit. 'grain
of musk'. See bubba and musk.

## abelmosk
abelmosk, п., a plant of the mallow family. —
Fr. prec. word.

## Abeona
Abeona, also Adeona, п., the goddess watching
over the first departure of children from the
house (Roman mythol.) — L. Abeona, Adeona,
formed on analogy of malrona, 'matron', from
the stem of abire, 'to go away', resp. of adire,
'to approach'. See abiturient, resp. adit.

## aberdevine
aberdevine, п., the siskin. — Of unknown origin.

## aberrance
aberrance, aberrancy, n. — L. aberrantia, fr.
aberrant, gen. aberrantis. See aberrant and -ce, resp.
-cy.

## aberrant
aberrant, adj., deviating from what is normal. —
L. aberrans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of aberrare,
'to wander away, go astray', fr. ab- and errdre,
'to wander, stray about'. See err and -ant.

## aberration
aberration, п., — L. aberralio, gen. -dnis, 'a
wandering', fr. aberrul-(um), pp. stem of aberrare.
See prec. word arid -ation.
Derivative: aberraiion-al, adj.

## nbet
nbet, tr. v. — ME. abelten, fr. OF. abeter, 'to
bait', lit. 'to cause to bite', fr. a- (fr. L. ad, 'to')
and OF beter, 'to bait', which is of Teut. origin;
cp. ON. beita, 'to cause to bite', bha, OE. bitan,
'to bite'. See ad- and bait, bite, and cp. bet.
Derivatives: abet-ment, abetl-al, abett-er,
abettor, nouns.

## abeto
abeto, п., the fir tree called Abies religiosa. — Sp.,
fr. L. abies, gen. abietis, 'the silver fir'. See Abies.

## abeyance
abeyance, п., temporary inactivity. — AF. a-
beiance, 'suspension', formed fr. a- (fr. L. ad, 'to',
see ad-), and OF. beer (F. bayer), 'to gape', fr.
L. batare 'to gape'. See bay, 'part in the wall',
and cp. words there referred to.

## abhor
abhor, tr. v. — L. abhorrere, 'to shrink away
' from', fr. ab- and horrere, 'to bristle, shudder*.
See horror.

## abhorrence
abhorrence, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -ce.

## abhorrent
abhorrent, adj. — L. abhonlns, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of abhorrlre, 'to shrink away from'. See
abhor and -ent.
Derivative: abhorrenl-ly, adv.

## abide
abide, intr. and tr. v. — OE. abidan, formed fr.
intensive pref. a- and bidan, 'to remain, await'.
See bide.
Derivatives: abid-ing, adj., abid-ing-ly, adv.

## Abies
Abies, п., a genus of trees, the true fir (bot.) —
L. abies, 'silver fir', cogn. with Gk. άβιν (ace.),
'silver fir', Άβική, name of Southern Russia,
lit. 'a region of firs'. Cp. abeto.

## abietic
abietic, adj., pertaining to the crystalline acid
C20H3o02 (chem.) — Formed with suff. -ic fr.
L. abies, gen. abietis, 'silver fir'. See prec. word.

## Abigail
Abigail, fern. PN.; in the Bible, the wife of Nabal,
later of David. — Heb. Abhigdyil, lit. 'my father
is rejoicing', fr. abh, 'father' and gil, 'to rejoice'.
For the first element see Aboth. The second
element is rel. to Arab. Jala, 'he went round' and
to Heb. galdl, 'he rolled, unfolded'; see gelilah.
The use of the name in the sense of 'waiting
maid' is due to the passage in I Sam. 25:35, where
Abigail calls herself a 'handmaid'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:29 COLUMN:2 -->

## abigeat
abigeat, п., cattle stealing (civil law). — L. abi-
geatus, fr. abigeus, 'cattle stealer", fr. abigere,
'to drive away', fr. ab- and agere, Ίο drive'; see
agent. The change of Latin й (in agere) to ("(in
abigere) is due to the Latin phonetic law according
to which in the unaccented open radical syllable
of the second element of compounds, original
й becomes f. Cp. accident, adhibit, ambiguous,
ancipital, anticipate, artifice, comfit, conceive,
consilient, constitute, contiguous, council,
deceive, deciduous, deficient, delicious, delitescent,
desipient, destine, destitute, difficulty, disciple,
dissilient, efficient, elicit, exhibit, lllicium,
incident, incipient, inhibit, inimical, institute, insipid,
insipient, irritate, 'to make null and void',
navigate, obstinate, Occident, occiput, office,
participate,precipice,prodigal,proficient, prohibit,
prostitute, receive, recidivist, resilient, resipiscence,
restitute, reticent, substitute, superficies,
superstition, supplicate, transilienl.

## ability
ability, n. — ME. abilite, fr. OF. ablete, habilite
(F. habilite), fr. L. habilitatem, ace. of habilitas,
'aptitude, ability', fr. habilis, 'that may be easily
handled or managed, suitable, fit, proper'. See
able and -ity.

## -ability
-ability, subst. suff. expressing ability, capacity,
fitn'.ss. — L. -abililas, forming nouns from
adjectives ending in -abilis. See -able and -ity and
cp. -ibllity.

## abio-
abio-, combining form meaning 'without life'. —
Fr. Gk. ίίβιος, 'without life', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and βίος, 'life'. See bio-.

## abiogenesis
abiogenesis, n. supposed production of living
organisms from unliving matter; spontaneous
generation. — Coined by the English biologist
Thomas Henry Huxley (1825-95) in 1870 fr.
Gk. άβιος, 'without life', and γένεσις, 'origin,
source'. See abio- and genesis and cp.
biogenesis.

## abiogenetic
abiogenetic, adj., pertaining to abiogenesis.—See
prec. word and generic and cp. biogenetic.
Derivative: abiogenetic-al-ly, adv.

## abiogenist
abiogenist, п., one who believes in spontaneous
generation. — See abiogeaesis and -ist.

## abiotrophy
abiotrophy, п., loss of vitality (med.) — Coined
by the English neurologist Sir William Richard
Gowers (1845-1915) fr. Gk. άβιος, 'without
life', and -τροφία, fr. τροφή, 'nourishment'.
See abio- and -trophy.
Derivative: abiotroph-ic, adj.

## abiturient
abiturient, п., one who is preparing for the final
examination of a high school. — G., fr. ModL.
abituriens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of abiturire,
'to wish to leave', a desiderative verb formed fr.
L. abed, abire (neut. pp. abitum), 'to go away,
leave', fr. ab- and eo, ire, 'to go'. See itinerate
and cp. Abeona. For the Latin desiderative suff.
-urire cp. esurient, micturition, parturient,
vomiturition. For the ending see suff. -ent.

## abject
abject, adj., 1) miserable; 2) contemptible. — L.
abjectus, pp. of abicere (less correctly abjicere),
'to throw away', fr. ab- and jacere (pp. jactus),
'to throw'. See jet,'to spirt forth'. For the change
of Latin o(in jactus) to e (in ab-jectus), see accent
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: abjection (q.v.), abject-ly, adv.,
abject-ness, n.

## abjection
abjection, п., the state of being abject (rare). —
F., fr. L. abjectionem, ace. oiabjectio, 'dejection,
despondency', lit. 'a throwing away', fr. abjectus
pp. of abicere. See prec. word and -ion and cp.
dejection, ejection, projection.

## abjuration
abjuration, n. — L. abjuratio, 'a denying on oath',
fr. abjuratus, pp. of abjurare. See next word and
-ation.

## abjure
abjure, tr. v., 1) to renounce on oath; 2) lo
recant. — L. abjurare, 'to deny on oath', fr. ab-
and jus, gen. juris, 'right'. See jury.
Derivatives: abjure-ment, п., abjur-er, n.

## abkari
abkari, п., the sale of intoxicating drinks; the
excise duty on such sale (India). — Pers. abkari,
'business of distilling', fr. abkar, 'a distiller', fr.
ab, 'water', and kar, 'doer, maker'. For the first
element see abdest. The second element is related
to Avestic kar-, 'to make', kfrenaoiti, OI. karSti,
krnati, 'makes', fr. I.-E. base *quer-, 'to make,
form'. See corpus and cp. the second element in
Sanskrit and words there referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:29 COLUMN:3 -->

## ablactate
ablactate, tr. v., to wean. — L. ablactatus, pp. of
ablactare, 'to wean', fr. ab- and lactare. See
lactate,

## ablactation
ablactation, n. — L. ablactdtio, gen. -onis, 'the act
of weaning', fr. ablactatus, pp. of ablactare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## ablation
ablation, п., removal. — L. ablatio, gen. -dnis, 'a
taking away', fr. ablatus (used as pp. of auferre,
Ίο carry or take away'), fr. ab- and lotus (used
as pp. of ferre, 'to bear, carry'), which stands
for *tlatos, fr. *f/-, zero degree of I.-E. base
*tel-, *lol-, 'to bear, carry', whence L. tollere,
'to lift up, raise', tolerare, 'to bear, support'.
See tolerate and cp. collate and words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -ion.

## ablative
ablative, adj. and n. — L. (casus) ablativus,
coined by Quimilian from the pp. ablatus, 'taken
away', to denote the case expressing direction
from a place or time. Cp. F. ablatif and see prec.
word and -ive.
Derivatives: ablativ-al, adj., ablative-ly, adv.

## ablant
ablant, п., vowel gradation. — G. Ablaut, lit.
'off sound', coined by J. P. Zweigel in 1568 fr.
ab, 'off' (which is rel. to OE. of, 'from, of, off'),
and fr. Laut, 'sound, tone' (which is rel. to G.
taut, 'loud'), and popularized by Jacob Grimm.
See of and loud and cp. aalaut, inlaut, auslaut,
umlaut.

## ablaze
ablaze, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. pref- a-, 'on',
and blaze.

## able
able, adj. — ME., fr. OF. able (F. habile), fr. L.
habilis, 'that which may be easily handled or
managed, suitable, fit, proper', fr. habere, 'to
have'. See habit and cp. ability. Cp. also habile,
which is a doublet of able.
Derivatives: able-ness, п., abl-y, adv.

## -able
-able, suff. expressing ability, capacity, fitness. —
F., fr. L. -abilis, fr. a, stem vowel of verbs of the
1st conjugation, and -bill's. See -ble and cp.
-ible. It soon became a living suffix, because of
its supposed connection with the adjective able
(fr. L. habilis, 'handy'), with which it has
nothing to do.

## Ablepharus.n
Ablepharus.n, a genus of lizards (zool.) — ModL.
formed fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. βλέφαρον,
'eyelid'. See blepharo- and cp. next word.

## ablepsia
ablepsia, п., blindness. — L., fr. Gk. αβλεψία,
'blindness', lit. 'lack of sight', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and βλέπειυ, 'to see'. Cp. βλέφαρον,
'eyelid', and see blepharo-. For the ending see
suff. -ia.

## nblet
nblet, п., the bleak (a small water fish). — F.
ablette, dimin. formed fr. able (masc), fr. L.
albulus, 'whitish', dimin. of albus, 'white'. See
alb.

## ablution
ablution, п., a washing, esp. as a ritual. — L.
ablatio, gen. -onis, 'a washing, cleansing', fr.
ablatus, pp. of abluere, 'to wash off', fr. ab- and
lucre, 'to wash', which is rel. to lavare, 'to wash'.
See lave and -ion.
Derivative: ablution-ary, adj.

## abnegate
abnegate, tr. v., to deny, give up. — L. abnegatus,
pp. of abnegdre, 'to refuse, deny', fr. ab- and
negare, 'to say no, deny'. See negate.

## abnegation
abnegation, n. — L. abnegdtio, gen. -onis,
'refusal, denial', fr. L. abnegatus, pp. of abnegdre.
See prec. word and negation.

## Abner
Abner, п., masc. PN.; in the Bible, commander
of Saul. — Heb. Abhnir, lit. 'my father is light',
fr. abh, 'father', and ner, 'light'; cp. the
Babylonian PN. Abunuri. For the first element see
Aboth, for the second see Menorah.

## abnormal
abnormal, adj. — A blend of L. abndrmis and
ML. andrmdlis, this latter itself being a blend
of L. andmalus and ndrmalis. See anomalous and
norm and cp. anormaL
Derivatives: abnormal-ity, п., abnormal-ly, adv.,
abnormal-ness, n.

## abnormity
abnormity, n. — L. abndrmitas, formed with suff.
-itas fr. abndrmis. See prec. word and -ity.

## aboard
aboard, adv. and prep. — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and board.

## Abobra
Abobra, п., a genus of plants of the gourd family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Port, abobara, abobra,
'gourd', fr. L. apopores, apoperes (see Isidorus,
XVII, 10, 16), from a Hispanic language.

## abodah
abodah, п., ])service in the Temple in Jerusalem;
2) liturgy; 3) name of the seventeenth bene-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:30 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 3 | ABSENT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:30 COLUMN:1 -->
diction of the Shemoneh Esreh, containing the
prayer for the restoration of the Temple (Jewish
liturgy). — Heb. 'abhodhd", 'service', fr. 'ab-
hadh, 'he served, worshiped', which is rel. to
Aram.-Syr. 'ubhadh, Arab, 'abada, 'he served,
worshiped', Ugar. 'bd, 'to serve, worship', and
to Heb. 'ebhedh, Aram, 'abhdd, 'slave, servant,
worshiper', Arab, 'abd, 'slave, worshiper'. Cp.
Obadiah, Obed.

## abode
abode, п., dwelling place. — Formed from the
past tense of abide. See next word.

## abode
abode, v., past tense of abide. — ME. abood, fr.
OE. abaci, past tense of abidan. See abide and
cp. prec. word.

## abolish
abolish, tr. v. — F. aboliss-, pres. part, stem of
abolir, 'to abolish, suppress', fr. L. abolire, 'to
destroy, efface, abolish', prob. a back
formation fr. aboliscere, 'to decay gradually, vanish,
cease', which was prob. formed as the antonym
of adolescere, 'to grow up, grow', a verb
dissimilated fr. orig. *ad-aliscere, lit. 'to grow
forward', fr. ad- and aliscere, 'to grow up,
increase', fr. alere, 'to grow'. See ab-, adolescent
and verbal surf. -ish. The change of conjugation
in F. abolir and the related It. abolire, Sp. abolir,
all verbs of the 4th conjugation (fr. L. abolire,
a verb of the 2nd conjugation), is due to the
influence of the noun abolitio, 'abolition' (fr.
abolire), which was mistaken for a derivative of
the (non-extant) Latin verb *abolire. Cp.
abolition.
Derivatives: abolish-er, п., abolish-ment, n.

## aboUtioa
aboUtioa, n. — F., fr. L. abolitionem, ace. of
abolitio, 'abolition', formed with suff. -ion fr. abo-
litus, pp. of abolire, 'to destroy, efface, abolish'.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: abolition-ary, adj., abolition-ism, n,
abolition-ist, n.

## abolla
abolla, п., a thick woolen cloak. — L., of Sicilian
origin. Cp. the Sicilian town Άβόλλα (now
called Avola).

## abomasum
abomasum, п., the fourth stomach of a ruminant
(anat.) — ModL., fr. ab- and L. omasum,
'bullock's tripe'. See omasum.

## abominable
abominable, adj. — F. abominable, fr. L. abomi-
nabilis, 'deserving imprecation, abominable'.
See next word and -able.
Derivatives: abominab-ly, adv., abominable-
ness, n.

## abominate
abominate, tr. v., to loathe, abhor. — L. abomi-
natus, pp. of abominari, 'to deprecate as an ill
omen; to detest, abominate', fr. ab- and omen,
gen. dminis, 'a foreboding, sign, token, omen'.
See omen and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: abominate, abominated, adjs.

## abomination
abomination, n. — F., fr. L. abominationem, ace.
of abominatid, 'abomination', fr. abominatus,
pp. of abominari. See prec. word and -ion.

## aboriginal
aboriginal, adj. and n. — See rjext word.
Derivatives: aboriginal-ly, adv., aboriginal-i-
ty, n.

## Aborigiaes
Aborigiaes, n. pi., the first inhabitants of a
country ; natives. — L. Aborigines, 'ancestors', name
of the primeval Romans; formed from the
words 'ab origine', 'from the origin', fr. ab,
'from' (see ab-), and origine, abl. of origo,
'origin'. See original.

## abort
abort, intr. v., to miscarry. — L. abortare, 'to
miscarry', freq. of aboriri (pp. abortus), 'to
disappear; to miscarry', fr. ab- and oriri, 'to rise,
be born'. See orient.

## abort
abort, п., miscarriage. — L. abortus, 'miscarriage,
abortion', fr. abortus, pp. of aboriri. See abort, v.

## abortifacient
abortifacient, adj. and п., (anything) producing
abortion. — See prec. word and -facient.

## abortion
abortion, п., miscarriage. — L. aborlio, gen. -dnis,
'miscarriage, abortion', fr. abortus, pp. of
aboriri. See abort, v., and -ion.
Derivatives: abortion-al, adj., abortion-ist, n.

## abortive
abortive, adj., 1) born prematurely; 2)unsuccess-
ful. — L. abortivus, 'pertaining to miscarriage',
fr. abortus, pp. of aboriri. See abort, v., and -ive.
Derivatives: abortive-ly, adj., abortive-ness, n.

## Aboth
Aboth,alsoAbot,п., t)the Mishnah treatise also
called Pirke Aboth or The Ethics of the Fathers;
2) name of the first benediction of the Shemoneh
Esreh (Jewish liturgy). — Heb. Abhdth, pi. of
abh, 'father', rel. to Aram, abh (absolute stale),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:30 COLUMN:2 -->
abba (emphatic state), Ugar. 'b, Arab, ab,
Ethiop. ab, 'father'; of uncertain origin, possibly
traceable to *ab(a), a child's word for father.
Cp. the first element in Abraham, Abner,
Absalom, Abigail, and the second element in Joab,
Moab, Barabbas. Cp. also abbot and words
there referred to. Cp. also borage.

## abound
abound, intr. v. — ME. abounden, fr. OF. (= F.)
abonder, fr. L. abundare, 'to overflow; to a-
bound', fr. ab- and unda, 'wave'. See undate and
cp. redound, surround. Derivatives: abound-er,
п., abound-ing, adj., abound-ing-ly, adv.

## about
about, adv. — ME. abuten, abouten, aboute, fr.
OE. abutan, onbutan, 'on the outside of, formed
fr. a-, 'on', and butan, 'outside', which itself is
formed fr. be, 'by', and utan, 'outside', fr. Qt,
'out'. See by and out and cp. but.
Derivative: about, rirerj.

## above
above, adv. — ME. aboven, fr. OE. abufan,
formed fr. a-, 'on', and bufan, 'above', which itself
is formed fr. be, 'by' (see by), and ufan,
'upward, above'; cp. OE. ofer, 'over' which is the
compar. of ufan, and see over. Cp. also about.
Derivatives: above, prep, and adj.

## abracadabra
abracadabra, п., a magic formula. — Late L., fr.
Gk. άβραΰάδαβρα, in which word the letter с =
s was misread for k. It was originally written
as a magic formula on Abraxas Stones, whence
its name. See abraxas.

## abrade
abrade, tr. v., to scrape off. — L. abradere, 'to
scrape off', fr. ab-, and radere, 'to" scrape off,
to shave'. See raze and cp. abrase.

## Abraham
Abraham, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the first of the
patriarchs and father of the Hebrew nation. —
Heb. Abhrahdm, lit. 'father of the multitude',
compounded of abh, 'father', and *raham,
'multitude', which is rel. to Arab, ruhdm, of
s.m.; see Gen. 17:5. See Aboth and cp. next
word.

## Abram
Abram, masc. PN.; in the Bible, former name of
Abraham. — Heb. Abhram, compounded of
abh, 'father', and ram, 'high, exalted', which is
prop. part, of rum, 'to be high, to be exalted'.
For the first element see Aboth and cp.
Abraham. From the second element derive rdmdh,
'height' (prop. fem. part, of rum), romdm,
'extolling, praise; song of praise', marim, 'height',
t'rumd", 'contribution, offering (for sacred
use)', lit. 'something lifted up, something
separated'. Cp. Aram.-Syr. ram, 'was high', Arab.
rdma prop, 'he rose', hence 'he strove for', and,
in Zanzibar and Oman, 'he was able to*. Cp.
the second element in Hiram.

## Abramis
Abramis, п., a genus of fishes (ichthyol.)—ModL.,
fr. Gk. άβραμίς, 'bream', fr. Egyptian rem,
'fish'.

## abranchiate
abranchiate, adj., having no gills. — Formed fr.
priv. pref. a- and branchiate.
Derivative: abranchiate, n.

## abrase
abrase, tr. v., to abrade. — L. abrasus, pp. of
abradere, 'to scrape off'. See abrade.

## nbrasion
nbrasion, n. — Formed with suff. -ioa fr. L.
abrasus, pp. of abradere. See prec. word.

## abrasive
abrasive, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -ive
fr. L. abrasus, pp. of abradere. See abrade.

## abraxas
abraxas, п., a mystical word used as a charm. —
Gk. Άβράξας, according to Irenaeus (in Adver-
sus haereses I, c. 23 and 24) a word formed from
the Greek letters α, β, ρ, cc, ξ, α, σ, whose
numerical value amounts to 365 (a = 1, β = 2,
ρ = loo, к = ι, ξ = 6o, a = ι, σ = 200),
corresponding to the number of aeons in Basilidian
gnosticism and to the number of days in a year.
It is more probable, however, that the word
abraxas is an acrostic formed from the initials
of certain consecutive Hebrew words. Cp.
abracadabra.

## abreast
abreast, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and breast.

## abreuvoir
abreuvoir, п., an interstice between stones
(masonry). —· F., lit. 'a watering trough', fr. abreu-
ver, 'to give drink to (animals)', fr. OF. abevrer,
abrever, fr. VL. *abbiberare, fr. ad- and L.
bibere, 'to drink'. See beverage, and cp. It. abbe-
verare, Proven?., Catal. abeurar, Sp., Port, abre-
var, which all derive fr. VL. *abbiberare.

## abridge
abridge, tr. v. — ME. abregen, fr. OF. abregier,
abreger (F. abreger), 'to shorten', fr. L. abbre-
viare, fr. ad- and breviare, 'to shorten', fr. brevis,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:30 COLUMN:3 -->
'short'. See brief, adj., and cp. abbreviate, which
is a doublet of abridge.
Derivatives: abridg-ed, adj., abridg-ed-ly, adv.,
abridg-er, п., abridgment (q.v.)

## abridgment
abridgment, abridgement, n. — OF. abregement
(F. abregement), fr. abregier. See abridge and
-ment.

## abrin
abrin, п., a toxic albumin (biochem.). — Formed
with chem. suff. -in fr. Abrus; so called because
it is found in the shrub Abrus precatorius.

## abroach
abroach, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and broach.

## abroad
abroad, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and broad.

## abrogate
abrogate, tr. v., to annul, repeal. — L. abrogatus,
pp. of abrogare, 'to annul, to repeal (a law)', fr.
ab- and rogare, 'to ask; to ask the people about
a law, to propose a law'. See rogation and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: abrogation (q.v.), abrogat-tve, adj.,
abragat-or, n.

## abrogation
abrogation, n. — L. abrogatio, gen. -onis, 'repeal
of a law', fr. abrogatus, pp. of abrogare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## Abroma
Abroma, п., a genus of plants of lhe chocolate
family (bot). — ModL., formed fr. priv. pref.
a- and Gk. βρώμα, 'food'. See broma.

## Abronia
Abronia,n., a genus of planls of the four-o'clock
family (bot.) — ModL., for *Habronia, fr. Gk.
αβρές. See Abrus.

## abrotanum
abrotanum, п., southernwood. — ML., fr. L.
abrotonum, fr. Gk. άβρότονον, 'wormwood',
άβρότονον άρρεν, 'southernwood', which is of
unknown origin.

## abrupt
abrupt, adj. — L. abrupt us, pp. of abrumpere, 'to
break off', fr. ab- and rumpere, 'to break'. See
rupture.
Derivatives: abrupl-ed-ly, abrupt-ly, advs.,
abruptness, n.

## Abrus
Abrus, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., for 'Habrus, fr. Gk. αβρός,
'graceful, delicate'. See babro-.

## Absalom
Absalom, masc. PN.; in the Bible, King David's
son; fig. a favorite son. — Heb. Abhshalom, lit.
'father is peace', fr. abh, 'father', and shSIOm,
'peace'. See Aboth and Shalom.

## abscess
abscess, п., a swelling in body tissues (med.). —
L. abscessus, 'a going away, departure, abscess',
fr. abcidere, 'to go away', fr. abs-, ab-, 'away
from, from', and cedere, 'to go'. See ab- and
cede and cp. cease.
Derivative: abscess-ed, adj.

## abscind
abscind, tr. v., to cut off (obsol.) — L. abscindere,
4o cut off', fr. ab- and scindere, perf. scidi, pp.
scissus (for *scid-tos), 'to cut, split'. See shed,
and cp. abscissa, rescind.

## abscissa
abscissa, n. (math.) — L. (lined) abscissa, lit. '(a
line) cut off', fem. pp. of abscindere, 'to tear
away; to cut off'. (The abscissa of a point Ρ is
the portion of the χ axis cut off by the line
drawn through Ρ parallel to the у axis.) See
prec. word.

## abscission
abscission, п., the act of cutting off. — L. ab-
scissio, gen. -onis, 'a cutting off',fr. abscissus, pp.
of abscindere. See abscind and -ion.

## abscond
abscond, intr. v., to depart suddenly and
secretly. — L. abscondere, 'to hide, conceal', fr. abs-,
ab-, 'away from, from' (see ab-) and condere, 'to
put together, hide', fr. con-, 'together' (see con-),
and -dere (used only in compounds), fr. I.-E.
base *dhi-, *dh'-, *dho-, 'to place, put, make',
whence also Gk. τι&έναι, 'to place', L. facere,
'to make, do', OE. don, 'to do'. See do, v., and
cp. fact, theme. Cp. also Consus, recondite,
sconce, 'metal bracket', scoundrel.
Derivative: abscond-er, n.

## absence
absence, n. — F., fr. L. absentia, fr. absens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of abesse, 'to be away from,
be absent'. See absent and -ce.

## absent
absent, adj. — F., fr. L. absentem, ace. of absens,
pres. part, of abesse, 'to be away from, be
absent', fr. ab- and esse, 'to be'. See esse and -ent
and cp. sans, senza. Cp. also present, adj.
Derivatives: absent, v. (q.v.), absent-ly, adv., ab-
sent-ness, п., absent-ation, п., absent-ee, п., ab-
sent-ee-ism п., absenl-er, п., absent-ly, adv.,
absent-ness, n.

## absent
absent, tr. v., to keep (oneself) away. — F. ab-
senter, fr. L. absentare, 'to cause one to be
absent', fr. absens, gen. absent is. See absent, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:31 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ABSINTH | 4 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:31 COLUMN:1 -->

## absinth
absinth, absinthe, п., wormwood. — F. absinthe,
fr. Gk. άψίνθιον, 'wormwood', which is of
OPers. origin; cp. ModPers. Bspand, sipand,
of s.m.

## absolute
absolute, adj. — L. absolutus, pp. of absolvere, 'to
loosen, set free'. See absolve and cp. consolute,
dissolute, resolute.
Derivatives: absolute, п., absolute-ly, adv.,
absoluteness, n.

## absolution
absolution, n. — OF. (= F.) absolution, fr. L. ab-
solutionem, ace. of absolutio, 'an acquittal', fr.
absolutus. See prec. word and -ion.

## absolutism
absolutism, n. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. L.
absolutus. See absolute.

## absolutist
absolutist, n. — Formed with suff. -ist fr. L.
absolutus. See absolute.

## absolve
absolve, tr. v. — L. absolvere, 'to set free', fr.
ab- and solvere, 'to loosen, set free'. See solve
and cp. assoil. Cp. also dissolve, resolve.

## absorb
absorb, tr. v. — L. absorbere, 'to swallow up',
fr. ab- and sorbere, 'to suck in, swallow up',
which is cogn. with Arm. arbi (from. *srbk-),
Ί drank, Gk. £οφεΐν (for *σροφεΐν), 'to sup
up', Alb. gerp (for *serbho-), Ί sip', OSlav.
srubali, Lith. surbiu, sufbti, sribiu, srlbli, 4o
sip'. Mir. srub, 'snout'. Cp. absorption, resorb,
sorb, v., and the second element in Sangui-
sorba.
Derivatives: absorb-ed, adj. absorb-ed-ly, adv.,
absorb-ed-ness, п., absorbent (q.v.), absorb-ing,
adj., absorb-ing-ly, adv.

## nbsorbefaclent
nbsorbefaclent, adj., tending to promote
absorption. — Compounded of L. absorblre, 'to
swallow up', and facilns, gen. -entis, 'to make, do'.
For the first element see absorb, for the second
see -facient, for the ending see suff. -ent. Cp.
sorbefacient.

## absorbency
absorbency, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -cy.

## absorbent
absorbent, adj. — L. absorbens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of absorbere. See absorb and -ent.

## absorption
absorption, n. — L. absorptio, gen. -onis, fr. ab-
sorptus, pp. of absorbere. See absorb and -ion.

## abstain
abstain, intr. v. — ME. absteynen, fr. OF. as-
tenir, fr. VL. *abstentre, corresponding to L.
abstinere, 'to abstain', which is formed fr. abs,
ab, 'away from, from' (see ab-), and tenlre, 'to
hold'. See tenable and cp. appertain, contain,
detain, entertain, maintain, obtain, pertain,
retain, sustain. Cp. also abstention, abstinence.
The ME. and E. forms have been refashioned
after L. abstinere.
Derivatives: abstain-er, п., abstain-ment, n.

## abstemious
abstemious, adj., moderate in eating and
drinking. — L. abslemius, 'sober, temperate', fr. abs,
ab, 'away from, from' (see ab-), and the stem
of temftum, 'intoxicating drink, mead, wine',
which is rel. to temulentus, 'drunken'. See te-
mulent. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see-ous.
Derivatives: abstemious-ly, adv.,
abstemiousness, n.

## abstention
abstention, n. — F., fr. L. abstentionem, ace. of
abstentid, 'the act of retaining', fr. abstenlus, pp.
of abstinere. See abstain and -Ion.

## absterge
absterge, tr. v., 1) to wipe away, cleanse; 2) to
purge. — F. absterger, fr. L. abstergere, 'to wipe
away', fr. abs-, ab-, 'away from, from' (see ab-),
and tergere, 'to rub, wipe off'. See terse and cp.
words there referred to.

## abstergent
abstergent, adj., cleansing; п., a cleansing
substance. — F. abstergent, fr. L. abstergentem, ace.
of abstergens, pres. part, of abstergere. See prec.
word and -ent

## abstersion
abstersion, п., a cleansing. — F. fr. L. abstersus,
pp. of abstergere. See absterge and -ion.

## abstersive
abstersive, adj., cleansing. — F. abstersif (fem.
abstersive), fr. L. abstersus, pp. of abstergere.
See absterge and -ive.
Derivative: abstersive-ness, n.

## abstinence
abstinence, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. abstinentia,
fr. abstinens, gen. -entis. See next word and -ce.

## abstinent
abstinent, adj. and n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. absti-
nentem, ace. of abstinens, pres. part, of
abstinere, 'to refrain from'. See abstain and -ent. The
change of Xatin ё (in tinere) to ί (in abs-tinere)
is due to the Latin phonetic law according to
which in the unaccented open radical syllable of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:31 COLUMN:2 -->
the second element of compounds, original ё
becomes /. Cp. assiduous, continent, continuous,
corrigendum, diligent, dimidiate, eligible,
indigent, insidious, pertinacious, reside.
Derivative: abslinent-ial, adj.

## abstract
abstract, adj. — L. abstractus, pp. of abstrahere,
'to draw away', fr. abs-, ab-, 'away from, from'
(see ab-), and trahere 'to draw'. See tract,
'region'.
Derivative: abstract, n.

## abstract
abstract, tr. and intr. v. — L. abstractus, pp. of
abstrahere. See prec. word and cp. the verbs
contract, detract, distract, protract, subtract.
Derivatives: abstract-ed, adj., abstract-ed-ly,
adv., abstract-ed-ness, п., abstract-er, п.,
abstraction (q.v.)

## abstraction
abstraction, n. — F., fr. L. abstractionem, ace. of
abstractio, fr. abstractus, pp. of abstrahere. See
abstract, adj., and -ion.
Derivative: abstraction-al, adj.

## abstruse
abstruse, adj., difficult, obscure. — L. abstrusus,
pp. of abstrudere, 'to thrust away, conceal', fr.
abs-, ab-, 'away from, from' (see ab-), and tru-
dere, 'to thrust, push, shove', which derives fr.
I.-E. base *treud-, 'to press, push', whence also
Goth, us-priutan, 'to vex', OE. preatian, 'to
press, afflict, threaten'. See threat and cp.
intrude and words there referred to.
Derivatives: abstruse-ly, adv., abstruse-ness, n.

## absurd
absurd, adj. — F. absurde, fr. L. absurdus, 'out
of tune, harsh, rough, incongruous, absurd',
formed fr. ab- and a derivative of the I.-E. base
*swer-, *sur-, 'to sound'. See swarm and cp. surd.
Derivatives: absurdity (q.v.), absurd-ly, adv.,
absurd-ness, n.

## absurdity
absurdity, n. — F. absurdite, fr. L. absurditatem,
ace. of absurditas, 'dissonance, incongruity',
fr. absurdus. See prec. word and -ity.

## abulia
abulia, п., loss of will pov/er(psychol.) — Medical
L., formed fr. priv. pref.. a-, the stem of Gk.
βούλεσ&αι, 'to will', and suff. -ia. See bonle,
'senate', and cp. Gk. αβουλία, 'ill-advisedness'.
апипа, п., the patriarch of the Abyssinian
Church. — Ethiop. abund, 'our father', fr. ab,
'father', which is rel. to Heb. abh, 'father'. See
Aboth and cp. abbot and words there referred to.

## abundance
abundance, also abundancy, n. — ME., fr. OF.
abundance, abundance (F. abundance), fr. L.
abundantia, 'abundance, plenty, fullness', fr.
abundans, gen. amis. See next word and -ce,
resp. -cy.

## abundant
abundant,adj. — ME. fr. OF. abundant, abundant
(F. abondant), fr. L. abundamem, ace. of
abundans, 'abounding', pres. part, of abundare. See
abound and -ant.
Derivative: abundant-ly, adv.

## abuse
abuse, tr. v. — F. abuser, fr. L. abusus, pp. of
abuti, 'to make use of (for any purpose), to
misuse, abuse', fr. ab- and iift, 'to use'. See nse, v.,
and cp. usurp.
Derivatives: abuse-ee, п., abus-er, п., abusive
(qv.)

## abuse
abuse, n. — F. abus, fr. L. abusus, fr. abusus, pp.
of abuti. See prec. word.

## abusive
abusive, adj. — F. abusif (fem. abusive), fr. L.
abusivus, fr. abusus, pp. of abuti. See abuse, v.,
and -ive.
Derivatives: abusive-ly, adv. abusive-ness, n.

## abut
abut, intr. v. — OF. abouter, 'to touch by the
end, border on' (whence F. abouter, 'to join end
to end'), formed fr. a, 'to' (fr. L. ad; see ad-),
and bout, 'end'. See butt, 'the thicker end of
anything'.
Derivatives: abut-ment, п., abutt-al, п., abutt-er,
п., abutt-ing, adj.

## Abutiloa
Abutiloa, п., a genus of plants of the mallow
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Arab. aubutilBn, a
name coined by the Arab philosopher Avicenna
(= Ibn-Sina).

## abysm
abysm, п., poetic for abyss. — OF. abisme (F.
abime), fr. Eccles. L. 'abismus (whence also
OProvenc. abisme, Sp. and Port, abismo),
formed on analogy of words ending in -ismus (fr. Gk.
-ισμός; see -ism), fr. L. abyssus. See abyss.
Derivative: abysm-al, adj.

## abyss
abyss, n. — L. abyssus, 'bottomless pit', fr. Gk
άβυσσος (scil. λίμνη), 'bottomless, unfath-
omed (pool)', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:31 COLUMN:3 -->
βυσσάς, 'depth, bottom', which is related to
βυθός, of s.m. Cp. abysm.
Derivative: abyss-al, adj.

## Abyssinia
Abyssinia, n. — ModL. Abyssinia, Latinized form
of Arab. Hdbasha", 'Abyssinia'. Cp. hubshi.
Derivatives: Abyssini-an, adj. and n.

## ac-
ac-, assimilated form of ad- before с and q.

## -ac
-ac, suff., corresponding in meaning to suff. -ic.
— Fr. F. -aque, or directly fr. L. -acus, fr. Gk.
-ακός.

## acacia
acacia, n. — L. acacia, fr. Gk. ακακία, 'shittah
tree', which, like άκακαλίς, 'gall of the Oriental
tamarisk', is of foreign, prob. Egyptian origin.
Both ακακία and άκακαλίς were prob. influenced
in form by άκανθα, 'thorn, prickle', and other
Greek derivatives of I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp'.

## academe
academe, n. academy (poetic). — See academy.

## academic
academic, adj. — L. academicus, fr. academia.
See academy and -ic.
Derivatives: academic-al, adj., academic-al-ly,
adv.

## academician
academician, п., a member of an academy. — F.
academtcien, fr. academic' See academy and
-ician.

## Academus
Academus, п., name of a hero from whom the
academy near Athens derived its name. — L.
Academus, fr. Gk. 'Ακάδημος, fr. earlier Έκά-
δημος, 'Academus'. Ср. next word.

## academy
academy, n. — F. academic fr. L. academia, fr.
Gk. Άκαδήμεια (or, less correctly, Ακαδημία),
fr. earlier Έκαδήμεια, 'Ihe Academy', a
gymnasium near Athens where Plato taught.
Άκαδήμεια orig. meant 'the olive grove of
Academus'. See prec. word.

## Acadian
Acadian, adj., pertaining to Acadia (Nova
Scotia). — Formed with suff. -aa fr. Acadia,
Latinized form of F. Acadie, former name of Nova
Scotia; prob. so called fr. Micmac akadie,
'fertile land', which occurs in many place names.
Cp. Cajun.

## Acaena
Acaena, п., a genus of plants of the rose family
{bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άκαινα, 'spike, prick,
goad', which is rel. to ακίς, 'point, sting', fr.
I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp, pointed'. See acrid and
cp. words there referred to.

## acajou
acajou, п., the cashew tree. — See cashew,

## acalephe
acalephe, п., jellyfish. — Gk. άκαλήφη (also
άκαλύφη), 'stinging nettle; sea anemone', prob.
a Semitic loan word. Cp. Aram, hil'phd, 'reed',
and Heb. hultphoth or hulaphoth, 'the sharp,
prickly leaves of the spinach', from stem h-l-p,
'to be sharp, cut through, pierce', See H.Lewy,
Die semitischen Fremdworter im Griechischen,
p. 50, and Boisacq, DELG., p. 34. Cp. Acalypha.
Cp. also alfa.

## acalycine
acalycine, adj., without a calyx (bot.). — ModL.
acalycinus, 'having no calyx', formed fr. priv.
pref. a-, Gk. κάλυξ, 'cup, calyx', and L. suff.
-in». See calyx and adj. suff. -ine.

## Acalypha
Acalypha, п., a genus of herbs of the spurge
family (bot.) — ModL. fr. Gk. άκαλύφη,
secondary form of άκαλήφη, 'stinging nettle'. See
acalephe.

## acantha
acantha, п., a prickle (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
άκανθα, 'lhorn prickle', which is rel. to άκή,
'point', ακίς, 'point, sting', fr. I.-E. base *aic-,
'sharp, pointed'. See acrid and cp. acanthus.

## Acanthaceae
Acanthaceae, п., a family of plants (bot.) —·
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. Gk. άκανθα,
'lhorn, prickle*. See prec. word.

## acanthion
acanthion, п., a point at the base of the anterior
nasal spine (craniometry). — Gk. ακάνθων,
'a small thorn', dimin. of άκανθα, 'thorn,
prickle'. See acanthus.

## acantho-
acantho-, combining form meaning 'prickly,
spiny, thorny'. — Gk. άκανθο-, fr. άκανθα,
'thorn, prickle'. See acanthus.

## Acanthocepbala
Acanthocepbala, п., a class of parasitic worms
(helminthol.) — ModL., lit., 'spiny-headed',
compounded of Gk. άκανθα, 'thorn, prickle,
spine*, and κεφαλή, 'head'. See acanthus and
cephalic.

## Acanthopterygii
Acanthopterygii, n.pl., an order of teleost fishes
(ichthyol.) — ModL., lit., 'spiny-winged'. See
acantho- and pterygium.

## Acanthus
Acanthus, п., 1) a genus of plants having large
spiny leaves; (not cap.) any plant of this genus
(bot.); 2) a form of ornament resembling the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:32 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 5 | ACCLAMATION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:32 COLUMN:1 -->
leaves of this plant. — L., fr. Gk. άκανθος,
'bearsfoot, Acanthus mollis', which is rel. to
άκανθα, 'thorn, prickle'. See acantha and cp.
the second element in Diplacanthus, traga-
canth.

## acapnia
acapnia, п., lack of carbon dioxide in the
organism (med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -ia
fr. Gk. άκαπνος, 'smokeless', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and καπνός, 'smoke', which stands for
*κΓαπνός and is cogn. with Lith. kvapas,
'breath, scent, smell, odor', kvipiu, kvipli, 'to
pant, breathe, inhale', and perh. also with OI.
kupyati, 'is agitated', L. cupere, 'to desire'. See
Cupid.

## Acarapis
Acarapis, п., a genus of mites (zool.) — ModL.,
compounded of Acarus and L. apis, 'bee'. See
Apis, 'bee'.

## acardinc
acardinc, adj., having no heart. — Fr. Gk. άκάρ-
διος, 'wanting the heart', fr. ά- (see priv. pref.
a-) and καρδία, 'heart'. See cardiac.

## acariasis
acariasis, п., itch caused by mites. — ModL.,
formed with suff. -iasis fr. Gk. ίίκαρι, 'mite'.
See acarid.

## acariatre
acariatre, adj., bad-tempered. — F., 'contrary,
crabbed, quarrelsome', orig. meaning
'possessed by a demon', formed with pejorative suff.
-aire, from the name of Acharius, bishop of
Noyon in the 7th cent., renowned for curing'
folly. The suff. -aire derives fr. OF. -astre, fr. L.
-aster; see -aster.

## acarid
acarid, п., a mite. — Formed with subst. suff.
-id fr. Gk. ακαρι, 'mite', which is rel. to άκαρής,
'small, tiny', lit. 'too short to be cut', and in
gradational relationship to κείρειν (for *κέριειν),
'to cut'. See shear and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also Acarlna, Acarus, carnal.

## acariform
acariform, adj., of the shape of a mite. — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. ακαρι, 'mite', and L. forma,
'form, shape'. See acarid and form, n.

## Acarlna
Acarlna, n. pi., an order of the Arachnida,
vulgarly called mites. — ModL., formed fr.
Acarus with suff. -ina.

## acaro-
acaro-, combining form, denoting the miles. —
ModL., fr. Acarus (q.v.)

## acarpous
acarpous, adj., unfruitful (hot.) — Gk. άκαρπος,
'without fruit, barren1, fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## Acarus
Acarus, п., a genus of small mites. — ModL. fr.
Gk. άχαρι, 'mite'. See acarid.

## ncatalectic
ncatalectic, adj., having the full number of
syllables or feet (pros.) — Late L. acatalecticus,
fr. Gk. άκατάληκτος, 'incessant; not catalectic',
i.e. 'not allowing of the omission of a syllable
at the end of a line', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
καταλήγειν, 'to leave off'. See catalectic.

## acatalepsy
acatalepsy, п., incomprehensibility (philos.) —
Gk. άκαταληψία, 'inability to comprehend', fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. n-) and καταληψία, 'a seizing,
apprehension' (see catalepsy); first used by
Pyrrho the Sceptic to express the view that
the human mind can know nothing with
certainty.

## acataleptic
acataleptic, adj., incomprehensible. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. ακατάληπτος, 'that
cannot be reached, incomprehensible', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-) and καταληπτός, verbal adj. of
καταλαμβάνειν, 'to seize with the mind,
comprehend'. See cataleptic and cp. prec. word.

## acatharsia
acatharsia, п., filth. — Gk. ακαθαρσία, 'unclean-
ness, foulness, filth', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-),
καθαρός, 'clean, pure', and suff. -ii. See
catharsis and -ia.

## acaudal
acaudal, also acaudate, adj., tailless. — A hybrid

-al, resp. -nte. See caudal.

## ncaulescent
ncaulescent, adj., stemless (hot.) — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
caulescent.

## acauline
acauline, adj., stemless. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ine (representing L. -Inus) fr. ModL. acaulis,
'stemless' (whence also F. acaule, of s.m.), a
hybrid coined fr. Gk. ά- (see priv. pref. n-) and
L. caulis, 'stem'. See caulescent and cp. prec.
word.

## acaulose
acaulose, acaulous, adjs., stemless (bol.) — See
■caulescent and adj. suff. -ose, resp. ous.

## acca
acca, п., medieval fabric of silk mixed with gold

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:32 COLUMN:2 -->
threads. — ML., prob. so called fr. Arab. 'Akka*,
'Akkd, fr. Heb. 'Akkd, 'Acre', in Syria (now in
Israel). Accordingly acca orig. simply meant
'material made in Acco'.
Accadian. — See Akkadian.

## accede
accede, intr. v. — L. accedere, 'to approach, come
near', fr. ad- and cidere, 'to go, yield'. See cede
and cp. access. Cp. also antecede, concede,

Derivative; acced-er, n.

## accelerando
accelerando, adv. and adj., gradually faster
(musical direction). — It., fr. L. accelerando, abl. of

## accelerant
accelerant, l) adj., accelerating; 2) п., that which

## nccelerate
nccelerate, tr. v., to increase the speed of; intr.

Derivatives: accelerat-ed, adj., accelerat-ed-ly,
adv., acceleration (q.v.), acceleral-ive, adj.,
accelerator, п., acceleral-ory, adj.

## acceleration
acceleration, n. — L. acceleratio, gen. -onis, 'a

accelerare. See prec. word and -ion.

## accelerometer
accelerometer, п., an instrument for measuring

accelerare, 'to hasten', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
accelerate and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## accent
accent, n. — F., fr. L. accentus, fr. ad- and can-
tus, 'tone, melody'. See cant and cp. enchant,
incantation. The change of Latin й (in cdnlus)
to ё (in ac-centus) is due to the Latin phonetic
law according to which in the unaccented and
closed radical syllable of the second element of
compounds, original ά becomes ё. Ср. concent,
precentor, succentor. Cp. also abject, accept,
adept, ascend, biceps, biennial, centennial, coerce,
commend, concept, confecl, confection, confess,
congress, conjecture, consecrate, defect,
degression, deject, descend, discerp, disperse, eject,
except, excerpt, execrate, exercise, forceps, im-
petrate, incendiary, incense, incentive, incept,
incest, inept, inerm, inert, infect, inject, integer,
intercept, interject, intersperse, novennial, object,
obsecrate, octennial, percept, peregrine,
perennial, perpetrate, prefect, prince, profess, progress,
project, quadrennial, quadriceps, quinquennial,
refection, regress, septennium, sexennium, solemn,
subreption, surreptitious, susceptible, traject,

accentus is prop, a loan translation of Gk.
προσωδία, fr. προσάδειν, 'to sing to', fr. προς, 'to', and
άδειν, 'to sing' (see prosody).
Derivatives: accent, tr. v., Accentor (q.v.), ac-
centu-able, adj., accentu-al, adj., accentu-al-ly,
adv.

## Accentor
Accentor, п., ι) a genus of small singing birds,
also called Prunella; 2) (not cap.) any bird of

accentor, 'one who sings with another', fr. ad- and

## accentuate
accentuate, tr. v. — ML. accentuatus, pp. of ac-
centuare, fr. L. accentus. See accent and verbal

## accentuation
accentuation, n. — ML. accentuatio, gen. -orris,

## accept
accept, tr. v. — ME. accepten, fr. MF. (= F.)

(in captus) to ё (in ac-ceptus, ac-ceptare) see

## acceptability
acceptability, n. — Late L. acceptabililas, fr. L.

## acceptable
acceptable, adj. — F„ fr. L. acceptubilis, fr.
acceptare. See accept and -able.

## acceptance
acceptance, n. — OF. acceptance, fr. accepter.

acceptancy, n. — See prec. word and -cy.

## acceptation
acceptation, п., ι) acceptance (archaic); 2) the

## acceptation
acceptation, п., formal remission of a debt
(Roman law); remission of sins (theol.) — L.

IStio, 'formal remission of a debt' (from the

I.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence

support'. See tolerate and cp. colinte and words

## acceptor
acceptor, n. — L., fr. acceptus, pp. of accipere.
See accept and agential suff. -or.

## access
access, п., approach. — OF. acces (F. accis), fr.

## accidence
accidence, п., that part of grammar which deals

(pres. part, of accidere), treated as a sing. fern,

## accident
accident, n. — F., fr. L. accidentem, ace. of

cadere, 'to fall'. See cadence. For the change of

## accidental

ial, adj.

## Accipiter
Accipiter, п., a genus of hawks and falcons (prni-

Astur, ostreger.
Derivatives: accipitr-al, adj., accipitr-ary, n. (fr.

## accismus
accismus, п., feigned refusal (rhet.) — ModL.,

meter, άκκώ, 'a vain woman', and cogn. with
OI. akkd, 'mother', L. Acca Larentia, name of
the mother of the 12 Arval brothers. All these
words are of imitative origin.

## acclaim
acclaim, tr. v. — L. acclamare, 'to cry out at',
fr. ad- and clamare, 'to cry out'. See claim and
cp. declaim, exclaim, proclaim, reclaim.

## acclamation
acclamation, n. — L. acclamaiio, gen. -dnis, fr.
acclamat-(um), pp. stem of acclamare, 'to cry

## acclimate
acclimate, tr. and intr. v. — F. acclimater, fr. a

## accolle

## accommodate

Derivatives: accommodat-ing,adj.,accommodat-
ing-ly, adv., accommodation (q.v.),
accommodative, adj., accommodat-or, n.

accommodation, n. — F., fr. L. accommodatio-
nem, ace. of accommodated, fr. accommodatus,

Derivative: accommodation-al, adj.

## accompaniment

## accompany

ad), Ίο4, and compagne, 'companion'. See ad-
and companion.
Derivative: accompan-ist, accompany-ist, n.

accomplice, n.—F., fr. ά (fr. L. ad), 'to', and

## accomplish
accomplish, tr. v. — ME. acomplissen, fr. OF.

-ish. For the change of L. complere, a verb of

complir, a verb of the 4th conjugation, cp. F.

## accomplishment
accomplishment, n. — F. accomplissement, fr. ac-

## accord
accord, intr. v., to agree; tr. v., to grant. — ME.

adv., accord-ing-ly, adv.

## nccord
nccord, п., 1) agreement; 2) harmony. — ME.

accordance, п., ι) agreement; 2) harmony. — OF.

## accordion
accordion, п., a musical instrument. — Formed
from the noun accord in the sense of 'harmony',

with suff. -ion, on analogy of clarion.

## account
account, tr. and intr. v. — ME. acounten, fr. OF.

Ίο count, tell', fr. L. computare. (ModF.

accouter, accoutre, tr. v., to dress, fit out (esp. for

## accouterment
accouterment, accoutrement, п., dress; personal

accnmulable, adj. — See accumulate and -able.

## accumulate

accumulator, n. — L., 'one who, or that which,

## accuracy
accuracy, n. — Formed fr. next word with suff.
