## accurate
accurate, adj., i) exact; 2) precise. — L. accurS-
tus, 'prepared with care', pp. of accurare, 'to
take care of, prepare with care', fr. ad- and
curare, 'to take care of. See cure, v., and adj.
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: accurate-ly, adv., accurate-ness, n.

## accursed
accursed, accurst, adj., cursed. — Prop. pp. of
obsol. accurse, fr. ME. acursien, which is
formed fr. intensive pref. a- and cursien, fr. OE. cur-
sian, 'to curse'. See curse, v., and -ed, resp. pp.
suff. -t.
Derivatives: accursed-ly, adv., accursed-ness, n.

## accusatioa
accusatioa, n. — F., fr. L. accusationem, ace. of
accus&tio, fr. accusatus, pp. of accusare. See
nccuse and -ation.

## accusative
accusative, adj. and n. — L. (casus) accusativus,
fr. Gk. αιτιατική (πτώσις), 'accusative (case)',
lit. '(case) expressing cause', fr. αιτία, 'cause'.
Since αίτίά means not only 'cause', but also
'accusation', αιτιατική πτώσις was
misinterpreted as 'case expressing accusation', and was
rendered accordingly in Latin by (casus)
accusatlvus, fr. accusatlvus, 'pertaining to an
accusation', fr. accusatus, pp. of accusare, 'to call to
account, accuse'. See next word and -ative. The
correct Latin translation would have been casus
causativus. For a mistranslation of another
Greek case name cp. genitive.
Derivatives: accusativ-al,adj., accusalive-ly,adv.

## accuse
accuse, tr. v. — ME. acusen, fr. OF. acuser (F.
accuser), fr. L. accusare, Ίο accuse', fr. ad- and
causa, 'cause, lawsuit', which stands for *caud-
ta-, and is rel. to cudere, 'to strike, beat'. See
cause and cp. excuse, recusant, recuse. The
change of Latin au (in causa) to 0 (in ac-cusare)
is due to the Latin phonetic law, according to
which in the unaccented radical syllable of the
second element of compounds, au becomes й.
Ср. conclude, exclude, occlude.
Derivatives: accus-ed, adj. and п., accus-er, п.,
accus-ing-ly, adv.

## accustom
accustom, tr. v. — OF. acostumer (F. accoutu-
mer), fr. a, 'to', and costume (F. coutume). See a
and custom.
Derivatives: accustom-ed, adj., accustom-ed-ly,
adv., accustom-ed-ness, n.
асе, п., the one in dice, cards, etc. — F. as, 'ace
at cards or dice', fr. L. as, gen. assis, 'unity,
unit'. See as, 'Roman coin', and cp. the second
element in ambsace.

## -acea
-acea, suffix denoting orders and classes in
zoology. — L. -acea, neut. pi. of -aceus, 'belonging
to, of the nature of; see -aceous. The neut. pi.
form of suff. -aceus is used because it refers to
L. animalia ('animals'), pi. of the neuter noun
animal. Cp. -acene.

## -aceae
-aceae, suffix denoting orders and families in
botany. — L. -aceae, fem. pi. of -aceus,
'belonging to, of the nature of; see -aceous. The fem.
pi. form of suff. -aceus is used because it refers
to L. planlae ('plants'), pi. of the feminine noun
planta. Cp. -acea.

## -acean
-acean, adj. suff. used in the sense of -aceous. —
L. -aceanus, compounded of the suffixes -aceus
and -anus. See -acea and -an.

## -acean
-acean, subst. suff. used to denote members of
orders of the animal kingdom. — See -acean,
adj. suff.

## acedia
acedia, п., sloth, lethargy. — Late L., fr. Gk.
άκήδεια, 'carelessness1, which is formed fr. ά-
(see priv. pref. a-) and κήδος (Dor. κάδος),
'care', rel. to κηδεύειν, Ίο take charge of, tend',
κήδιστος (superl. formed fr. κήδος), 'most
worthy of one's care, most cared for', fr. I.-E.
base *kad-, 'ill-humor, hatred', whence also OE.
hele, 'hate', hatian, 'to hate'. See hate and cp.
eplcedium.

## aceituna
aceituna, п., a West Indian tree. — Sp., fr. Arab.
az-zaytuna", 'the olive (tree)', fr. az-, assimilated
form of al-, 'the1, and zaylana", 'olive tree,
olive', nomen unitatis fr. zaytan, 'olive trees,
olives1, fr. zayt, 'olive oil', a word borrowed fr.
Aram, zaythd, zltha, 'olive tree, olive', which is
rel. to Heb. zayith, 'olive tree, olives'.

## Aceldama
Aceldama, п., the potter's field near Jerusalem;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:34 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 7 | ACIDIFY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:34 COLUMN:1 -->
a place of bloodshed. — Gk.' Ακελδαμά, fr. Syr.
haqil d'md, 'the field of blood'.

## acemua
acemua, п., a pack mule. — Sp., 'pack mule', fr.
Arab. az-zamila", fr. az-, assimilated form of
al-, 'the', and zdmila", 'beast of burden'.

## aceology
aceology, п., therapeutics. — Lit. 'the science of
curing', fr. Gk. οίκος, gen. ακεος, 'remedy', and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. Gk. ακος prob. stands for *yakos and
is cogn. with Olr. hlcc, 'cure, payment', icaim,
Ί heal, cure'. For the second element see -logy.
Cp. ecology and the second element in An-
drosace.

## -aceous
-aceous, suff. meaning 'belonging to, of the
nature of. — L. -aceus, enlarged fr. adj. suff. -ax,
gen. -ucis. This suff. corresponds either to L.
-acea (neut. pi. of -Bceus), in which case it means
'pertaining to such and such an order of
animals', or to L. -aceae (fern. pi. of -aceus), in
which case its meaning is 'pertaining to such
and such a family of plants'. See -ous and cp.
-acea, -aceae.

## acephalous
acephalous, adj., headless. — L. acephalus, fr. Gk.
ακέφαλος, 'headless', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and κεφαλή, 'head'. See cephalic. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, L. -us, see -ous.

## Acer
Acer, п., the maple tree. — L., cogn. with Gk.
όίκαο-τος (for *ακαρο-τος), 'maple tree', OHG.,
MHG. ahorn, G. Ahorn, of s.m.

## Aceraceae or Acer'mae
Aceraceae or Acer'mae, n. pi., a family of plants
(order Sapindales). — ModL., formed fr. Acer
with suff. -aceae, resp. -inae.

## Acerntes
Acerntes, п., a genus of plants of the milkweed
family (bot.) — ModL. lit. 'hornless', fr. priv.
pref. a- and Gk. κέρας, gen. κέρατος, 'horn'
(see cerato-); so called because its hoods have
no crest or horn.

## Aceratherlum
Aceratherlum, п., lit. 'hornless animal', a name
given by Каир to some mammiferous fossils
resembling the rhinoceros, but differing from it
in being hornless. — ModL., formed fr. priv.
pref. a-, Gk. κέρας, gen. κέρατος, 'horn', and
θηρίον, 'animal'. See cerato- and therio- and
cp. prec. word.

## acerb
acerb, adj., sour, sharp, bitter. — L. acerbus,
'harsh to the taste, sharp, bitter, sour', fr. Seer,
'sharp'; see acrid. For the formation cp. super-
bus, 'haughty, proud, excellent', fr.super,'above,
over' (see superb).
Derivatives: acerbate (q.v.), acerb-ic, adj.,
acerbity (q.v.)

## acerbate
acerbate, tr. v., to sour, embitter; to aggravate;
to irritate; adj., sour, embittered. — L. acer-
batus, pp. of acerbare, 'to make bitter; to
aggravate', fr. acerbus. See acerb and verbal suff.
-ate and cp. exacerbate.

## acerbity
acerbity, n. — F. acerbite, fr. L. acerbitatem, ace.
of acerbitas, 'harshness, sharpness', fr. acerbus,
'harsh, sharp'. See acerb and -ity.

## acerdol
acerdol, п., calcium permanganate, Ca(Mn04)2
(chem.) — Formed with suff. -ol fr. acerdese,
former name of manganite, fr. Gk. άκερδής,
'bringing no gain, having no value', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-), and κέρδος, 'gain', which is prob.
cogn. with Olr. cerd, 'art, trade, handicraft'.

## aceric
aceric, adj., pertaining to the maple. — ModL.
acericus, fr. L. acer, 'maple'. See Acer and -ic

## acerose
acerose, adj., chaffy. — L. acerosus, 'full of chaff,
chaffy', fr. acus, gen. aceris, 'chaff. See awn and
adj. suff. -ose.

## acervate
acervate, adj., heaped up. — L. acervatus, pp. of
acervare, 'to heap up', fr. acervus, 'heap, pile',
which is of uncertain origin. For the ending see
adj. suff. -ate.

## acescence
acescence, n. — Formed fr. next word with suff.
-ce.

## acescent
acescent, adj., turning sour. — L. aclsclns, gen.
-centis, pres. part, of aciscere, 'to turn sour'
inchoative of acire, 'to be sour'. See acid and
-escent.

## acetabulum
acetabulum, n. 1) a cup for vinegar (Roman an-
tiq.); 2) the cup-shaped socket of the hip bone
(anat.); 3) a sucker of an octopus, a leech, etc.
(zool.) — L. acetabulum, lit. 'a vessel for vinegar',
formed fr. acetum, 'vinegar', with -abulum, a
suffix used to form names of tools and vessels.
See acetum. For the suff. cp. tintinnabulum.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:34 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: acetabul-ar, acetabuli-ferous, aceta-
buli-form, adjs.

## acetanillde
acetanillde, also acetanilid, п., a crystalline
substance, C,HON (chem.). — A hybrid coined fr.
L. acetum, 'vinegar' (see acetam), and anilid(e).

## acetarious
acetarious, adj., used in salad. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. acitaria (pi.), 'vegetables
prepared with vinegar, salad', fr. acetum, 'vinegar*.
See acetum and -ous.

## acetate
acetate, п., salt of acetic acid (chem.) — Formed
with chem. suff. -ate fr. L. acetum, 'vinegar'. See
acetam.

## acetic
acetic, adj. pertaining to vinegar. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. L. acetum, 'vinegar'. See
acetum.

## acetify
acetify, tr. v., to turn into vinegar; intr. v., to
become sour. — Compounded of L. acetum,
'vinegar' (see acetum), and -fy.

## acetone
acetone, п., a colorless volatile liquid, CH3COCH3
(chem.) — A hybrid coined fr. L. acetum,
'vinegar', and the Greek suff. -ώνη. See acetic
and -one and cp. ketone.

## acetous
acetous, adj., pertaining to, or like, vinegar;
sour. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. acetum,
'vinegar'. See next word.

## acetum
acetum, п., vinegar. — L. acetum, 'vinegar', prop.
vinum (acltum), 'wine turned sour, neut. pp. of
acescere, 'to turn sour', fr. acere, 'to be sour*,
which is rel. to acer, 'sharp'. See acrid and cp.
acescent, acetic. For sense development cp. Gk.
βξος, 'winevinegar',which is rel. to οξύς,'sharp'.
Cp. also eisel and the first element in ester.

## acetyl
acetyl, п., the radical of acetic acid, CH3CO
(chem.) — A hybrid coined by the German
chemist Justus von Liebig (1803773) in 1839 fr.
L. acetum, 'vinegar' (see prec. word) and -yl,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## acetylene
acetylene, п., a colorless hydrocarbon (chem.) —
Coined by the French chemist Marcelin-Pierre-
-Eugene Berthelot (1823-1907) fr. acetyl and
suff. -ene.

## achaetous
achaetous, adj., having no bristles or setae. —-
A hybrid coined fr. priv. pref. a-, Gk. χαίτη,
'long flowing hair, mane', and -ous, a suff. of
Latin origin. See chaeto-.

## achar
achar, п., pickles (Angh-Jnd.) — Pers. achar,
'pickles'.

## acharne
acharne, adj., bloodthirsty, furious. — F., pp. of
acharner, 'to madden, embitter, venom*, lit. 'to
flesh', fr. a, 'to', and chair 'flesh, meat', fr. L.
car6, gen. carnis, 'flesh'. See a and carnul.

## acharnemeat
acharnemeat, п., fury. — F., fr. acharner. See
prec. word and -merit.

## Achates
Achates, п., in Virgils Aeneid, the armor-bearer
and faithful friend of Aeneas; hence, a faithful
friend. — L. Achates, fr. Gk. αχάτης, 'agate'.
See agate, n.

## ache
ache, intr. v., to be in pain. — ME. aken, fr. OE.
acan, 'to ache', of uncertain origin. The spelling
ache is due to a confusion of this word with Gk.
αχός, 'pain, distress'.

## ache
ache, п., pain. — ME. ache, fr. OE. &ce, 'pain',
fr. acan, 'to ache'. See ache, v.
Derivatives; ach-ing, adj., ach-ing-ly, adv.

## ache
ache, п., parsley (obsol.) — F., fr. L. apium, of
s.m., prop, 'the plant preferred by bees', fr. apis,
'bee'. See Apis, 'a genus of bees', andep. Apium.

## ache
ache, п., name of the letter h. — See aitch.

## achene
achene, п., a dry carpel containing only one seed
(bot.) — Formed fr. priv. pref. a- and the stem
of Gk. χαίνειν, 'to gape', which is cogn. with
L. Mare, 'to yawn, gape', OE. gSnian, ginian, 'to
yawn'. See yawn and cp. hiatus. Cp. also the
first element in Chaenactis.

## Acheron
Acheron, п., one of the rivers of Hades (Greek
mythology). — L., fr. Gk. Άχέρων. The name
prob. means 'marshlike water' and is rel. to
άχερούσια, 'marshlike water', and cogn. with
OSlav. jezero, 'lake'. The derivation of Gk.
Άχέρων fr. άχος, 'woe*, is folk etymology.

## Acheulean
Acheulean, Acheulian, adj., pertaining to the
paleolithic period preceded by the Chellean and
succeeded by the Mousterian (geology). — F.
Acheulien, from the name of the village St.
Acheul, near Amiens, in France; so called in
allusion to the remains there discovered.

## achieve
achieve, tr. v. — ME. acheven, fr. OF. (= F.)
achever, 'to accomplish, complete', fr. VL. *ac-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:34 COLUMN:3 -->
capare, 'to come to an end', fr. L. ad, 'to', and
*capare, a verb formed from the stem of L.
caput, 'head', Cp. OProvenc. Sp., Port, acabar,
of s.m., and see a and chief.
Derivatives: achievement (q.v.), achiev-er, n.

## achievement
achievement, n. — F. achivemenl, 'completion,
conclusion', fr. achever. See achieve and -ment
and cp. hatchment.

## achili
achili, adv., in a state of chill. — Coined by
William Morris (1834-96) fr. pref. a-, 'on', and
chill.

## Achillea
Achillea, п., a genus of plants of the thistle family
(bot.) — ModL., prop, 'the herb of Achilles',
fr. L. achilleos (scil. herba),(т. Gk. 'Αχίλλειος, 'of
Achilles'; so called because its medicinal
properties are said to have been discovered by
Achilles. See Achilles.

## Achilles
Achilles, п., son of Thetis and Peleus, the bravest
hero in the Trojan war. — L. Achilles, fr. Gk.
Άχιλλεύς, a name of prob. pre-Greek origin.
Achilles' tendon. — So called from the myth of
Achilles being held by the heel when his mother
Thetis dipped him into the river Styx to render
him invulnerable; first used by the Dutch
anatomist Verheyden in 1693 when dissecting his
own amputated leg. See Achilles and tendon.

## achlamydate
achlamydate, adj., having no mantle (zool.) —
Lit. 'not chlamydate', fr. priv. pref. a- and
chlamydate.

## achiamydeons
achiamydeons, adj., having no perianth (bot.) —
Lit. 'not chlamydeous', fr. priv. pref. a- and
chlamydeous.

## Achras
Achras, п., a genus of trees of the sapodilla family
(bot.) — L., fr. Gk. άχράς, gen. άχράδος, 'wild
pear tree', which is prob. rel. to Gk. αχερδος,
'wild pear tree', and cogn. with Alb. darSc,
'pear tree'.

## achromat
achromat, п., an achromatic lens. — See
achromatic.

## nchromat-
nchromat-, form of achromato- before a vowel.

## achromatic
achromatic, adj., colorless; transmitting light
without decomposing it into its component
colors. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk.
«χρώματος, 'colorless', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
χρώμα, gen. χρώματος, 'color'. See chromatic.

## achromaticity
achromaticity, n. — See achromatic and -Ity.

## nchromatism
nchromatism, п., state of being achromatic. —
See achromatic and -ism.

## achromatize
achromatize, tr. v., to deprive of color. —
Formed with suff. -ize fr. Gk. άχρώματος, 'colorless'.
See achromatic.
Derivative: achromatiz-ation, n.

## achromato-
achromato-, before a vowel achromat-, combining
form meaning 'achromatic'. —Gk. άχρωματο-,
άχρωματ-, fr. άχρώματος, 'colorless'. See
achromatic.

## achromatopsia
achromatopsia, achromatopsy, п., color-blindness
(med.) — Lit. 'sight without color', compounded
of achromat- and Gk. -οψία, fr. δψις, 'sight'.
See -opsia.

## nchromatous
nchromatous, adj. having no color. — Gk.
άχρώματος, 'colorless'. See achromatic. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## achroous
achroous, adj., colorless. — Gk. £χροος,
'colorless', formed fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and χρόά,
χροιά (for *χρωΓ-ιά), 'skin, color of the skin,
color', which is rel. to χρώμα, 'color'. See chrome.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## acicula
acicula, п., a spine, prickle. — L., 'a small pin',
dimin. of acus, 'needle, pin', which is rel. to
acuere, 'to sharpen', acer, 'sharp, bitter'. See
acrid.

## acicular
acicular, adj., needle-shaped. — Formed with
suff. -ar fr. L. acicula. See prec. word.
Derivative: acicular-ly, adv.

## aciculate
aciculate, adj., needle-shaped. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ate fr. L. acicula. See acicula.

## acid
acid, adj., sour, sharp to the taste. — Either fr.
F. acide or directly fr. L. acidus, 'sour', fr. acere,
'to be sour*, whence also acetum, 'vinegar' (see
acetum); introduced into English by Francis
Bacon (1561-1626) in 1626.
Derivatives: acid, п., acid-ic, adj.

## Acidaspis
Acidaspis, п., a genus of Trilobites. — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. ακίς, gen. ακίδος, 'pointed
object, point, needle' (fr. άκή, 'point'), and
ασπίς, 'shield'. See acid and aspidistra.

## acidify
acidify, tr. v., to make sour; intr. v., to become

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:35 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ACI DIMETER | 8 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:35 COLUMN:1 -->
sour. — See add and -fy and cp. F. acidifier.
Derivatives: acidif-ic, adj., acidif-ic-ation, п.,
acidifi-er, n.

## acidimeter
acidimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
strength of acids. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
acidus, 'sour' and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
acid and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## acfcUmetry
acfcUmetry, п., the measurement of the strength
of acids. — See prec. word and -merry.

## acidity
acidity, п., the quality of being acid; sourness. —
F. aciditi, fr. L. aciditatem, ace. of acidilas,
'sourness, acidity', fr. acidus. See acid and -ity.

## acidoid
acidoid, adj., resembling acid. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. acidus, 'sour', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See acid and -oid.

## acidophilic
acidophilic, adj., staining easily with acid. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. acidus, 'sour', Gk. φίλος,
'loving', and suff. -ic See acid and -phile.

## acidophilus milk
acidophilus milk, milk that has been fermented
by acidophilic bacteria. — See prec. word.

## acidosis
acidosis, п., a morbid condition, caused by an
accumulation of acids (med.). — A Medical L.
hybrid coined by Bernhard Naunyn of Stras-
burg in 1906 fr. L. acidus, 'sour' (see acid), and
-osis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## acidulate
acidulate, tr. v., to make slightly sour. — Formed
with verbal suff. -ate fr. L. acidulus, dimin. of
acidus. See acidulous.
Derivatives: acidulat-ed, adj., acidulal-ion, n.

## acidulous
acidulous, adj., slightly sour. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L, acidulus, 'slightly sour', dimin.
of acidus, 'sour'. See acid. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us. see -ous.

## acierate
acierate, tr. v., to convert into steel. — A hybrid
coined fr. F. acier, 'steel', and verbal suff. -ate
(fr. L. -atus). F. acier derives fr. Late L. acia-
Hum, fr. L. acies, 'sharp edge, point', acies
ferri, 'steel' (lit. 'point of iron'). Cp. It. acciaio,
Sp. acero, 'steel', which also derive fr. Late L.
aciarium, and see next word.

## acies
acies, п., battle array (Roman antiq.) — L. acies,
'sharp edge, point, the front of an army line
of battle, battle array', rel. to acer, 'sharp,
pointed'. See acrid and cp. prec. word.

## aclform
aclform, adj., needle-shaped. — Compounded of
L. acus, 'needle' and forma, 'form, shape'. See
acus and -form.

## Aclneta
Aclneta, п., a genus of Infusoria (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. ακίνητος, 'immovable', fr. ά-
(see priv. pref. a-) and κινητός, 'moved', verbal
adj. of κΐνεΐν, 'to move'. See kinesis.

## aciniform
aciniform, adj., clustered (bot.) — Lit. 'having
the form of an acinus', fr. L. acinus, 'berry', and
forma, 'form, shape'. See acinus and form, n.

## acinus
acinus, п., drupelet; berry (hot.) — L., 'berry,
stone of a berry', of uncertain origin.
•acious, suff. meaning 'inclined to, abounding
in', as in audacious, tenacious. — Compounded
of L. suff. -ax, gen. Scis (whence also F. -ace)
and -ous.

## -acity
-acity, suff. denoting quality, as in audacity,
tenacity. — F. -acite, fr. L. -acitalem, ace. of -acitas,
compounded of adjectival suff. -ax, gen. -acis,
and subst. suff. -itas. Accordingly this suff.forms
nouns corresponding to adjectives in -acious.
See -acious and -ity and cp. -icily.

## Acipenser
Acipenser, п., a genus of fishes comprising the
sturgeons. — L. aciplnser, name of a fish, prob.
'stuigeon'. The first element of this compound
is prob. rel. to L. acer, 'sharp, pointed' (see
acrid). The second element in aci-penser is of
uncertain origin.

## acknowledge
acknowledge, tr. v. — Fr. earlier aknowledge, a
blend of the ME. hybrid aknowen and ME.
knowlechen. See a-, Ίο', and knowledge.
Derivatives: acknowledg-ed, adj., acknowledge
ed-ly, adv., acknawledg(e)-ment, n.

## aclastic
aclastic, adj., not refracting. — Formed with suff.
-ic fr. Gk. ακλιιστος, 'unbroken', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-) and κλαστός, verbal adj. of κλαν,
'to break'. See clastic.

## aclinic
aclinic, adj., not dipping (said of a magnetic
needle). — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. άκλινής,
'bending to neither side', fr. ά- (see priv. pref.
-a) and κλίνειν, 'to incline'. See clinic.

## acme
acme, п., the highest point. — Gk. ακμή, 'point,
edge; the highest point of anything, the flower,
prime of man's age', rel. to άκή, 'point', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:35 COLUMN:2 -->
cogn. with L. acies, 'point, edge; battle array',
fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp, pointed'. See acrid
and words there referred to, and cp. paracme.
Cp. also acne.

## acmite
acmite, п., a sodium ferrum silicate (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -Ite fr. Gk. ακμή,
'point, edge' (see prec. word); so called in
allusion to the crystal form.

## acne
acne, п., a skin disease caused by the
inflammation of the sebaceous glands (med.) — This word
owes its existence to a clerical error, Gk. ακμή,
'point' (see acme), having been miswritten as
άκνή.

## Acnida
Acnida, п., a genus of plants of the amaranth
family. — ModL., lit. 'without nettles', fr. priv.
pref. a- and Gk. κνίδη, 'nettle', which is rel. to
κνίζειν, 'to scratch'. See cnida.

## acnode
acnode, п., point of a curve, not connected with
real points of the curve (math.) — A hybrid
coined fr. L. acus, 'needle' (see aens), and E. node.

## Acocanthera
Acocanthera, п., a genus of African plants (bot.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. άκωκή, 'point,
sting', and ανθηρός, 'flowery'. The first element
is rel. to άκή, 'point', fr. I.-E. base "ale-, 'sharp,
pointed'; see acrid. For the second element see
anther.

## Acoemeti
Acoemeti, п., pi., name of an order of Eastern
monks. — Eccles. L., fr. Gk. ακοίμητοι, 'the
sleepless ones', from ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
κοιμάν, 'to lull to sleep'. See home and cp.
cemetery.

## ecology
ecology, п., the study of remedies. —
Compounded of Gk. ίίκος, 'remedy', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See aceology.

## acolyte
acolyte, п., ι) an attendant, follower; 2) an altar
attendant. — ML. acolitus, acoluthus, fr. Gk.
ακόλουθος, 'follower', lit. 'having one way', fr.
copul. pref. ά-, 'together with' and κέλευθος,
'way, road, path, track'. Copul. pref. ά- stands
for I.-E. *stn-, a weak gradational form of I.-E.
base *sem-, 'one, together'; see same. Gk.
κέλευθος is cogn. with Lith. kilias, 'way',
keliauju, Ί journey', fr. I.-E. base *qeleu-,
enlargement of *qel-, 'to drive', whence L. celer,
'swift'. See celerity and cp. anacoluthon.

## acomla
acomla, п., baldness. — ModL. formed with suff.
-ia fr. Gk. ίίκομος, 'hairless', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and κόμη, 'hair', whence κομήτης,
'comet'. See coma, 'tuft of hairs' and cp. comet.

## nconite
nconite, п., the monkshood. — L. aconitum, fr.
Gk. άκόνιτον, which prob. derives fr. άκονιτΐ,
'without dust' (scil. of the arena), hence
'without struggle, unconquerable', formed fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-) and κονίειν, 'to cover with dust',
fr. κόνις, 'dust', which is cogn. with L. cinis,
'ashes'; see cinerary. The plant was called
'unconquerable' in allusion to its deadly poison.

## Acontias
Acontias, п., a genus of lizards (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άκοντίας, 'a quick-darting serpent', fr.
άκόντιον, dimin. of άκων, 'dart, javelin'. See next
word.

## acontium
acontium, ri., javelin. — ModL. fr. Gk. άκόντιον,
dimin. of ίίκων, 'dart, javelin', fr. I.-E. base *ak-,
'sharp, pointed', whence also Gk. άκή, 'point', L.
acer, 'sharp, bitter'. See acrid and words there
referred to and cp. esp. prec. word.

## acopic
acopic, adj., removing weariness (med.) —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. δκοπος, 'unwearied', fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. a-), and κόπος, 'striking,
beating, fatigue, weariness', whence κόπτειν, 'to cut,
beat, strike', κόμμα, 'something cut or struck'.
See comma and cp. words there referred to.

## acor
acor, п., acidity (med.) — L. acor, 'a sour taste,
sourness', fr. aclre, 'to be sour'. See acid.

## acorn
acorn, n. — ME. akern, fr. OE. Secern, 'acorn',
reL to ON. akarn, 'acom', Du. aker, LG. ecker
(whence G. Ecker), 'acorn', Goth, akran,
'fruit'. As proved by Goth, akran, the orig.
meaning was 'fruit', esp. 'fruit of the field'.
Accordingly it is very probable that the above
words are rel. to Goth, akrs, etc., 'field'. See
acre. E. acorn was influenced in form by an
association with corn.

## Acorus
Acorus, п., a genus of plants of the arum family
(bot.) — L., an aromatic plant, prob. 'the sweet
flag', fr. Gk. άκορος, which is of uncertain
origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:35 COLUMN:3 -->
acosmism, п., the denial of the independent
reality of the world as distinct from God. — Coined
by Fichte and Hegel fr. Gk. priv. pref. a-,
κόσμος, 'the world' (see cosmos), and suff. -ism.
acosmist, п., one who believes in acosmism. —
See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: acosmist-ical, adj.
acotyledon, п., a plant without cotyledons (bot.)
— See priv. pref. a- and cotyledon,

## acoryledonous
acoryledonous, adj., having no cotyledons. —
Formed fr. acotyledon with suff. -ous.

## acouchy
acouchy, п., a species of agouti. — F. acouchi,
of Tupi origin.

## acoumeter
acoumeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
sense of hearing — Compounded of the stem
of Gk. άκούειν, 'to hear', and μέτρον,
'measure'. See acoustic and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
•ncousia, -acousis, combining forms meaning
'hearing'. — Fr. Gk. ίίκουσις, 'hearing', fr.
άκούειν, 'to hear'. See acoustic,

## acoustic
acoustic, adj. — F. acoustique, fr. Gk. ακουστικός,
'pertaining to hearing', fr. ακουστός, 'heard,
audible', verbal adj. of άκούειν, 'to hear', which
stands for *άκούσιειν, and is prob. formed fr.
copul. pref. a-(see acolyte) and I.-E. base *(s)qeu-,
*(s)qlu-, 'to look at, observe, perceive', whence
also κοεΐν, 'to mark, perceive, hear', Goth.
hausjan, OE. hyran, 'to hear'. See hear and cp.
show. Some scholars explain Gk. άκούειν as
standing for *άκ-ούσ-ιειν, 'to have a sharp
ear', fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp' and "ous, 'ear';
see acrid and ear. See Frisk, GEW., I, 57-58.
Derivatives: acoustic-al, adj., acoustic-al-ly,
adv., acoust-ics, n.

## acquaint
acquaint, tr. v. — ME. acointen, fr. OF. acoin-
tier, acointer, fr. Late L· accognitare, 'to make
known, toacquaint',fr. L. accognitus'a.cxfca.mtsa
with', fr. ad- and cognitus, pp. of cogndscere,
'to know'. See cognition and cp. quaint
Derivatives: acquaintance (q.v.), acquaint-ed,
adj., acquaint-ed-ness, n.

## acqnaintan.ee
acqnaintan.ee, n. — OF. acointance, fr. acointier.
See prec. word and -ance.

## acquiesce
acquiesce, intr. v. — F. acquiescer, fr. L. acqui-
escere, 'to become quiet, to rest', fr. ad- and
quiescere, 'to rest'. See quiesce.

## acquiescence
acquiescence, n. — F., fr. acquiescent. See next
word and -ce.

## acquiescent
acquiescent, adj. — F., fr. L. acquiescentem, ace.
of acquiescgns, pres. part, of acquiiscere. See
acquiesce and -ent.
Derivative: acquiescent-ly, adv.

## acquire
acquire, tr. v. — L. acquirere, 'to seek in addition
to, acquire', fr. ad- and quaerere, 'to seek,
search'. See quaere and cp. acquisition, conquer,
conquest, inquire, require, request. The change
of Latin ae (in quaerere) to ί (in ac-quirere) is
due to the Latin phonetic law according to which
in the unaccented and open radical syllable of
the second part of compounds, ae becomes i. Cp.
-cide, circumcise, collide, concise, conquistador,
decide, elide, excide, excise, 'to cut out*, incise,
iniquity, perquisite, precise, succise.
Derivatives: acquir-ed, adj., acquire-ment, п.,
acquir-er, n.

## acquisition
acquisition, n. — F., fr. L. acquisilionem, ace. of
acquisitio, fr. acquisitus, pp. of acquirere, 'to
acquire'. See prec. word and -ion and cp.
disquisition, inquisition, requisition,

## acquisitive
acquisitive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
acquisitus, pp. of acquirere. See acquisition.
Derivatives: acquisitive-ly, adv.,
acquisitiveness, n.

## acquit
acquit, tr. v. — OF. aquifer (F. acquiuer), fr. VL.
*acquitare, fr. ad- and L. quietare, 'to appease,
settle', fr. quies, gen. quietis, 'rest'. See quiet, п.,
and cp. quit
Derivatives: acquitment (q.v.), acquitt-al, п.,
acquittance (q.v.), acquitt-er, n.

## acquitment
acquitment, n. — OF. aquitement, fr. aquiter. S:e
prec. word and -ment.

## acquittance
acquittance, n. — OF. aquitance, fr. aquiter. See
acquit and -ance.

## aer-
aer-, combining form. — See aero-.

## Acraeinae
Acraeinae, n. pi., a subfamily of butterflies of the
family Nymphalidae (entomology). — ModL.,
formed with suff. -inae fr. Acraeus, Acraea, fr.
Gk.' Ακραίος, 'Ακραία, 'dwelling on the heights',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:36 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 9 | ACTAEON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:36 COLUMN:1 -->

## epithet of Jupiter resp. Juno
epithet of Jupiter resp. Juno, fr. άκρα, 'the end,

## point
point, the highest point, peak, headland", prop,
lem. of άκρος, 'outermost', used as a noun. See

## aero- and cp. acropolis
aero- and cp. acropolis,

## acrasia
acrasia, п., intemperance (med.) — Medical L.,

## prop
prop, a confusion of Gk. άκρασία, 'bad
mixture' (fr. άκρατος, 'unmixed', fr. pref. ά- and
the stem of κεραννύναι, 'to mix') and άκράσία
(= ακράτεια), 'want of power, debility'. See

## priv. pref. a- and crater
priv. pref. a- and crater, resp. acratia.

## Acraspeda
Acraspeda, n. pi., a group of jellyfishes (ichthyol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. άκράσπεδος, 'without
fringes', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and κράσπεδον,
'edge, border, fringe'. See craspedon. The group
is so called in allusion to the lack of a velum.

## acratia
acratia, п., weakness (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. ακράτεια, 'want of power', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-) and κράτος, 'strength, power,
rule', which is cogn. with Goth, hardus, OE.
heard, 'hard'. See hard and cp. -cracy, -crat. For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## acre
acre, n. — ME. aker, fr. OE. secer, rel. to OS.
akkar, ON. akr, Swed. aker, Norw. aaker, Dan.
ager, MLG., MDu. acker, Du. akker, OHG.
achar, MHG., G. acker, OFris. ekker, Goth.
akrs, and cogn. with OI. djrah, Arm. art, Gk.
αγρός, L. ager, 'field, land', which stand for
I.-E. *ag-ro-s and orig. meant 'pasture', i.e. 'a
place where the cattle are driven', fr. I.-E. base
*ag-, 'to drive, lead', whence OI. ujali, 'drives',
Arm. acem, Ί lead, bring', Gk. άγω, Ί lead,
guide', L. ago, Ί drive, lead'. See agent and cp.
agrarian. Cp. also acorn. For sense development
cp. Heb. mighrash, 'common, open land', prop,
'pasture land', i.e. 'a place where the cattle are
driven', fr. garash, 'he drove out'; cp. also G.
Trift, 'pasture, common', which is rel. to trei-
ben, 'to drive'.
Derivative: acre-age, n.

## acrid
acrid, adj. — A blend of L. Seer (fern, ucris, neut.
acre), 'sharp, bitter', and acidus, 'sour', which
are both related to L. acus, 'needle', aciis, 'sharp
edge, point, the front of an army, line of battle,
battle array', acuere, 'to sharpen', fr. I.-E. base
*ak-, *aq-, 'sharp, pointed', whence also Oscan
acrid( = L. acriter), 'sharply', Umbr. per-acri,
'fruitful, fertile', Gk. άκρος, 'at the farthest point,
highest; pointed', άκή, 'a point, edge', ακίς, 'a
point', άκανθα, 'thorn, prickle', άκων, 'a
javelin', άκμων, 'an anvil', OI. aSrth, 'edge', dSman-,
'stone, rock, sky', Avestic, asman-, of s.m. Lith.
akmud, 'stone', aSmuS,'sharpness', OSlav. kamy
(a metathesized form), 'stone', Olr. er (for
*akros), 'high', Arm. as-ein, 'stone' (the force
of the suff. -ein is yet unknown), ON. hamarr,
OE. hamor, hamer, etc., 'hammer'. Cp. Gk.
άκροάομαι, Ί hear, listen', prop, 'have a sharp
hearing', in which the first element is rel. to
άκρος, 'pointed, sharp'. — Cp. the gradational
variant base *oq-, whence Gk. οξύς, 'sharp',
δκρις, 'peak, hilltop', OL. ocris, 'a rugged, stony
mountain', L. mediocris, 'middling, moderate,
indifferent, tolerable' (orig. 'being half-way up
the height of a mountain'), occa, 'a harrow',
OSlav. ostru, Lith. aStrus (for *okro, with
inserted t), 'sharp', MIr. ochar, W. ochr, ochyr,
'edge, corner, border'. Cp. awn, eager, ear of
corn, edge, egg, 'to urge', hammer. Cp. also
Acaena, acantha, acanthion, acantho-, Accipl-
ter, acerb, acescent, acetum, acid, Acipenser,
acme, acne, Acocanthera, acor, Acreinne,
acrimony, aero-, acroama, acrobat, acropolis, Ac-
taea, Actaeon, aculeate, aculeus, acumen, aens,
acute, aglet, ngrito, ague, cute, exacerbate,
eglantine, griotte, paragon, tetrakis, Thrinax, triakis,
vinegar. Cp. also mediocre, ocrea, Ocimum,
Oralis, oxy-, oxygen.
Derivatives: acrid-ity, п., acrid-ly, adv., acrid-
ness, n.

## acrimonious
acrimonious,adj., harsh, bitter. — F. acrimonieux,
fr. ML. acrimoniosus, fr. L. acrimonia. See
acrimony and -ous.
Derivatives: acrimonious-ly, adv., acrimonious-
ness, n.
acrimony, п., harsness, bitterness; asperity. — L.
acrimonia, 'sharpness, pungency', formed fr. L.
acer (fern, ucris, neut. acre), 'sharp', with suff.
-monia. See acrid and -mony and cp. words there

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:36 COLUMN:2 -->
referred to.

## acrisia
acrisia, п., condition of disease with no
symptoms to establish the diagnosis. — Gk. ακρισία,
'want of judgment', fr. άκριτος, 'not judged',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and κριτής, 'separated,
chosen, decided, judged', verbal adj. of κρΐνειν,
'to separate, choose, decide, judge'. See critic.

## acritical
acritical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
Gk. άκριτος, 'not judged'. See prec. word.

## aero-
aero-, acr-, combining form meaning 'pertaining
to the end, extreme'. — Gk. άκρο-, fr. άκρος,
'at the end, at the top, outermost', fr. άκή,
'edge'; cogn. with L. acer, 'sharp', OSlav. ostru,
Lith. astrus, of s.m., Olr. er, 'high'. See acrid
and cp. words there referred to.

## acroama
acroama, п., oral teaching; esoteric teaching. —
L., fr. Gk. ακρόαμα, lit. 'that which is heard
(with pleasure)', fr. άκροάομαι, Ί hear', orig.
Ί have a sharp hearing', fr. *άκρ-ουσά, 'a sharp
hearing', compounded of άκρος, 'pointed,
sharp', and Ion., Att. ους, gen. οΰατος,
corresponding to Gk. ους, gen. ώτός, 'ear'. For
the first element see acrid and cp. acropolis. For
the second element see ear, 'the organ of
hearing', and cp. oto-. For the ending see suff. -ma.

## acroamatic
acroamatic, adj., oral; esoteric. — Gk.
ακροαματικός, 'pertaining to hearing', fr. ακρόαμα,
'that which is heard'. See prec. word and -atic.
Derivative: acroamatic-s, n.

## acrobat
acrobat, n. — F. acrobate, fr. Gk. άκρόβατος,
'walking on tiptoe', fr. άκρος, 'at the end,
outermost, highest', and βατ-, 'going', from the stem
of βαίνειν, 'to go, walk'. (Cp. βατός, 'passable',
verbal adj. of βαίνειν.) For the first element
see aero-, for the second see base, п., and cp.
the second element in aerobatics.
Derivatives: acrobat-ic, adj., acrobat-ic-al-ly,
adv., acrobal-ics, п., acrobat-ism, n.

## acrocarpous
acrocarpous, adj., bearing fruit at the end of the
stalk (bot.) — Gk. άκρόκαρπος, 'bearing fruit
at the top', compounded of άκρος, 'at the end,
outermost, highest', and καρπός, 'fruit'. See
ncro- and carpel. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## acrocephalic
acrocephalic, ncrocephalous, adj., having a
pointed skull. — Compounded of aero- and cephalic

## ncrochordon
ncrochordon, п., a kind of wart (med.) — L., fr.
Gk. άκροχορδών, which is compounded of
άκρος, 'at the end, outermost, highest' and
χορδή, 'chord, string'. See aero- and chord.

## acrodynia
acrodynia, п., disease characterized by pain in
the hands and feet (med.) — Medical L„ coined
by Chardon in 1828, and lit. meaning 'pain in
the extremities', fr. aero- and Gk. οδύνη, 'pain'.
See -odynia.

## ncrogen
ncrogen, п., a plant growing at the apex, as ferns,
mosses, etc. (bot.) — Lit. 'growing at the top'.
See aero- and -gen.
Derivative: acrogen-ous, adj.

## acrolein
acrolein, п., a colorless aldehyde, C3H4O (chem.)
— Compounded of L. acer (fem. acris, neut.
acre), 'sharp', and olere, 'to smell'. See acrid
olfactory, and chem. suff. -ia.

## acrolith
acrolith, п., a statue having the extremities of
stone and the trunk of wood. — L. acrolilhus,
fr. Gk. άκρόλιθος, 'with ends made of stone',
which is compounded of άκρος, 'at the end,
outermost, highest', and λίδος, 'stone'. See
aero- and -lith.

## acromegaly
acromegaly, acromegalia, п., a disease
characterized by an enlargement of the head, thorax and
extremities (med.) — Medical L. acromegalia,
compounded of aero- and Gk. μέγας, fem.
μεγάλη, 'great'. See mega- and the suff. -y,
resp. -ia, which both represent Gk. -Ιά.

## acrominl
acrominl, adj., pertaining to the acromion. — See
next word and adj. suff. -al.

## acromion
acromion, п., the outer end of the shoulderblade
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. άκρωμία, 'point
of the shoulder', which is compounded of άκρος,
'at the end, outermost, highest' and ώμος,
'shoulder'. See aero- and ото-, 'shoulder'.

## acron
acron, n., the foremost segment of the body of an
insect. — Gk. άκρον, 'tip', prop. neut. of the
adjective άκρος, 'at the end, outermost,
highest'. See aero-.

## acronychal
acronychal, acronycal, adj., happening or
occurring at nightfall (astron.) — Formed with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:36 COLUMN:3 -->
adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. άκρόνυχος, 'at nightfall',
fr. άκρος, 'at the end, outermost, highest', and
νύχος = νύξ, 'night'. See aero- and nycti-.
Derivative: acronychal-ly, adv.

## acronym
acronym, п., a word formed from the first letters
of a series of words, as UNO, from United
JVations Organization. — Coined fr. acr- and
Gk. βνυμα, dial, form of βνομα, 'name'. See
name and cp. onomato-.

## acrophobia
acrophobia, п., morbid fear of high places (med.)
— Medical Latin, fr. aero- and Gk. -φοβία, fr.
φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobin.

## acrophony
acrophony, п., the use of the pictorial
representation of an object as the phonetic sign of the
initial sound or syllable with which the name of
that object begins. — Compounded of aero-,
and Gk. -φωνίά, fr. φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See
-phony.

## acropolis
acropolis, п., the fortified upper part of an ancient
Greek city; esp. that of Athens. — Gk.
ακρόπολις, fr. άκρος 'at the end, outermost, highest',
and πόλις, 'city' (see aero- and policy, 'method
of government'). This compound developed
from the older form άκρα πόλις, 'the upper or
higher city'. (Homer still prefers άκρα πόλις to
the compound, which he uses only twice,
Odyssey VIII, 494 and 504.) See Albert
Debrunner, Griechische Wortbildungslehre,
Heidelberg, J917, p.01.

## ncrorhagus
ncrorhagus, п., one of the marginal tubercles of
actinians (zool.) — ModL., compounded of
aero- and Gk. ">άξ, gen. £αγός, 'berry', which
is cogn. with L. racimus, 'the stalk of a cluster
of grapes'. See raceme.

## across
across, adv. and prep. — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and cross.

## acrostic
acrostic, п., a poem in which the initial letters of
the lines form a word or words. — L. acrostichis,
fr. Gk. άκροστιχίς, 'acrostic', which is
compounded of άκρος, 'at the end, outermost', and
στίχος, 'row, line, rank, verse', which is rel.
to στείχειν, 'to go; to march in order'. See
aero- and sty, 'to ascend', and cp. hemistich,
monostich, distich, tetrastich, pentasrich, hexa-
stkh, heptastich, octasrich, decastich, stichich,
orthostichy, stoicbiometry, cadastre.

## Acrostichum
Acrostichum, п., a genus of ferns of the polypody
family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. L.
acrostichis, 'acrostic' (see prec. word); so called from
the position of the sori.

## acroterlum
acroterlum, acroterion, п., pedestal for a statue
or other ornament, placed at the apex or one of
the corners of a pediment (archit.) — L. acrO-
teriurn, fr. Gk. άκρωτήριον, 'extremity,
summit, top', fr. άκρος, 'at the end, outermost*.
See aero-.

## acrotomous
acrotomous, adj., having a cleavage parallel with
the base (mineral) — Gk. άκρότομος, 'cut off,
sharp, abrupt', compounded of άκρος, 'at the
end, outermost', and -τόμος, which is rel. to
τόμος, 'a cut, piece cut off, section', τομός,
'cutting'. See tome and cp. words there

## act
act, n. — F. acte, 'action', partly fr. L. actus, 'a

in motion, drive; to do, act'), partly fr. actum,
'something done' (which is prop. neut. of actus,
pp. of agere). See agent and words there
referred to and cp. esp. entr'acte, interact.
Derivatives: act, tr. and tr. v., act-ing, п., and
adj., active (q.v.)

## Actaea
Actaea, п., a genus of plants, the baneberry

the elder tree', prob. meaning lit. 'the tree with
pointed leaves', fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp,

referred to.

## Actaeon
Actaeon, п., the hunter who, having seen Artemis
bathing, was changed by her into a stag and torn
to pieces by his own dogs (Greek mythol.) —
L. Actaeon, fr. Gk. 'ΑκταΙων, a word of
uncertain etymology. It denoted perh. orig. a
water god and derives fr. ακτή, 'promontory;
beach seashore' (whence also άκταΐος, 'on the
shore'), which is of uncertain origin. It possibly
derives fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp, pointed'. See
acrid and cp. prec. word.

## ad-
ad-, pref. of Latin origin expressing direction
toward or addition to. — Ad- appears in this form
before a'voweland before the consonants d, h,
j, m, v. It is simplified to a- before sc, sp, si.
Before c, f g, I, n, p, q, r, s and t ad- is
assimilated to ac-, resp. af-, ag-, al-, an-, ар-, ас-, ar-,
as-, at-. — L. ad-, etc., fr. ad, 'to, toward', rel.
to Umbr. af-, ars-, Oscan ad-, az (for *ad-s),
'to, toward', and cogn. with Goth, at, OE. жг,
'at'. See at and cp. a, pref. a- (corresponding to
L. ad), and a- in abandon.

## Adam
Adam,п.,name of the first man(Bifc/c); in a

udama", 'ground, earth', and addm, 'man', cp.
L. homo, 'man', humdnus, 'human', which are

ic-al-ly, adv., Adam-ite, п., Adam-it-ism, п.,

## adamant
adamant, п., a very hard stone; adj., very hard,
unyielding. — ME., 'diamond, magnet', fr. OF.

άδάμας, 'adamant, the hardest metal, diamond',
lit. 'unconquerable', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
the verb δαμαν, 'to tame'. See tame and cp.

The sense of 'load stone, magnet', arose from a

## Adam's apple
Adam's apple, the thyroid cartilage. — A name
due to the inexact translation of Heb. tappttah
haadam, lit. 'man's projection (in the neck)', fr.
tappuah, 'anything swollen or protruding;
apple', from the base of laphah, 'it swelled'. The
rendering of this Hebrew term by 'Adam's
apple' is due to two popular beliefs: 1) that the
forbidden fruit eaten by Adam was an apple;
2) that a piece of this apple stuck in Adam's
throat.

For the first element cp. Adein, Adeline, Adolph,
Aline, Athelstan, and allerion, for the second
see -hood, -head. Cp. also Alice.

## Adelia
Adelia, п., a genus of American plants of the
olive family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άδηλος,
'unseen, invisible' (see adelo- and -fa); so called
because of its minute flowers.

## Adeline
Adeline, fem. PN. — F., a word of Teut. origin,
introduced into England through the medium
of the Normans. The name lit. means 'noble'.
See Adelaid and cp. Aline.

## adelite
adelite, п., a calcium and magnesium arsenate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -Ite fr.
Gk. άδηλος, 'unseen, obscure' (see adelo-); so
called in allusion to the lack of transparency.

## adelo-
adelo-, combining form, meaning 'not seen,
concealed'. — Gk. άδηλο-, fr. άδηλος, 'unseen,
invisible', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and δήλος
(Homeric δέελος), 'visible, clear', which is
contracted fr. 'δέιελος, and is rel. to δέατο, 'seemed',
and cogn. with OI. dldeti, 'shines'. See deity and
cp. Adelia.

## adelpho-
adelpho-, combining form meaning 'brother'. —
Gk. άδελφο-, fr. αδελφός, 'brother', lit. 'from
the same womb', fr. copul. pref. ά-, 'together
with', and δελφύς,' 'womb'. Copul. pref. ά-
stands for I.-E. *sm-, a weak gradational form
of I.-E. base *sem-, 'one together"; see same.
For the etymology of δελφύς see calf and cp.
dolphin. Cp. also the second element in Dia-
delphia, Didelphia, monadelphous, Philadelphus.
For the sense development of Gk. αδελφός ср.
Gk. άγάστωρ, 'from the same womb', fr. copul.
pref. ά- and γαστήρ, 'belly, womb'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:38 COLUMN:3 -->
adempted, adj., taken away (law). — Fr. obsol.
adempt, fr. L. ademptus, pp. of adimere, 'to take
away;. See next word and -ed.

## ademption
ademption, п., the act of taking away. — L.
ademptio, gen. -onis, 'a taking away, seizure', fr.
ademptus, pp. of adimere. See adeem and -ion.

## aden-
aden-, form of adeno- before a vowel.

## ndenine
ndenine, п., also adenln, a crystalline base (bio-
chem.) — Coined by the German physiological
chemist Albrecht Kossel (1853-1927) fr. Gk.
άδήν, 'gland' (see adeao-), and chem. suff. -ine,
-in; so called by him because it is derived from
pancreas.

## adenitis
adenitis, п., inflammation of a gland or glands
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr.
Gk. άδήν, gen. άδενος, 'gland'. See adeno-.

## adeno-
adeno-, before a vowel aden-, combining form
denoting 'pertaining to glands, glandular'
(med.) — Gk. άδενο-, άδεν-, fr. άδήν, gen.
άδενος, 'gland', fr. I.-E. '-ng^gn, whence also
L. inguen, 'groin, abdomen'. See inguen and cp.
the second element in Dipladenia.

## adenoid
adenoid, adj., gland-like, glandular. — Medical
L. adenoideus, fr. Gk. άδενοειδής, 'gland-like',
fr. άδήν, gen. άδενος, 'gland', and -οειδής,
'like',fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See adeno-and-oid.
Derivatives: adenoids, n. pi., adenoid-al, adj.,
adenoid-ism, n.

## ndenoma
ndenoma, a benign glandular tumor (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -oina fr. Gk. άδήν,
'gland'. See ndeno-.
Derivative; adenomat-ous, adj.

## Adeona
Adeona, also Abeona, п., the goddess watching
over the first departure of children. — See
Abeona and cp. adit.

## Adephaga
Adephaga, n. pi., an order of beetles (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. αδηφάγα, 'voracious (scil. ζώα,
animals)', neut. pi. of αδηφάγος, which is
compounded of άδην, 'to one's fill', and -φάγος, fr.
φαγεϊν, 'to eat'. Gk. άδην, more correctly άδην
(fr. *sadgn) is rel. to ίίειν (for "saein), 'to
satiate', and cogn. with OE. ssed, 'sated, satisfied*
(whence ME. sad, 'sated, full, satisfied, tired').
See sad and words there referred to and cp. esp.
hadro-. For the second element see -phagous.

## ndepbagoas
ndepbagoas, adj., 1) voracious; 2) pertaining
to the Adephaga. — See prec. word and
-phagous.

## adept
adept, adj., skilled, proficient; п., an expert. —
L. adeptus, 'reached, attained', pp. of adipiscl,
'to arrive at, reach, attain', fr. ad- and apiscl
(pp. aplus), 'to reach, come up with', which is
rel. to OL. *apia, apere, 'to bind, attach', pp.
aptus, 'attached to'. See apt and cp. adapt For
the change of Latin й (in aptus) to ё (in
adeptus) see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: adept-ness, n.

## adequacy
adequacy, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -cy.

## ndequate
ndequate, adj. — L. adaequatus, pp. of adaequare,
'to make equal to', fr. ad- and aequure, 'to make
equal', fr. aequus, 'equal'. See equal and adj.
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: adequate-ly, adv., adequate-ness, n.

## adennia
adennia, п., absence of the skin (med.) — Medical
L., formed fr. priv. pref. a-, Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'
(see derma), and suff. -ia.

## ndevisin
ndevisin, п., the denial of gods. — A hybrid
coined by Max Miiller on analogy of atheism, fr.
priv. pref. a-, OI. devdh, 'god', and -ism, a suff.
of Greek origin. See deity,

## adharma
adharma, п., unrighteousness (Hinduism). — OI.
d-dharmah, formed fr. priv. pref. a- and dhdrmah,
'law, right, justice'. See an- and dharma.

## adhere
adhere, v. — F. adherer, fr. L. adhaergre, 'to stick
to, cling to', fr. nd- and haerere, 'to stick, cling'.
See hesitate and cp. adhesion. Cp. also cohere,
inhere,

## adherence
adherence, n. — F. adherence, fr. ML. adkaeren-
tia, fr. L. adhaerens, gen. -entis. See next word
and -ce.

## adherent
adherent, adj. and n. — F. adherent, fr. L. ad-
haerentem, ace. of adhaerens, pres. part, of ad-
haerere. See adhere and -ent

## adhesion
adhesion, n. — F. adhesion, fr. L. adhaesionem,
ace. of adhaesio, 'a sticking to, adhesion', fr.

## adhaesus
adhaesus, pp. of adhaergre. See adhere and -ion.
Derivative: adhesion-al, adj.

## ndhesive
ndhesive, adj. — F. adhesif (ftm. adhesive), fr. L.
adhaesus, pp. of adhaerere. See adhere and -Ive.
Derivatives: adhesive-ly, adv., adhesive-ness, n.

## adhibit
adhibit, tr. v., to attach, affix. — L. adhibitus, pp.
of adhibere, 'to hold to, apply to', fr. ad- and
habere, 'to have, hold' (see habit). For the
change of Latin & (in habere) to i (in ad-hibere)
see abigeai and cp. words there referred to.

## adhibltion
adhibltion, n. — L. adhibitio, gen. -dnis, fr.
adhibitus, pp. of adhiblre. See prec. word and
-ion.

## adiabatic
adiabatic, adj., impassable. — Formed with suff.
ic- fr. Gk. αδιάβατος, 'not to be passed', fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and διαβατός, 'to be
passed', verbal adj. of διαβϊίνείν, 'to step
across, step over', fr. διά (see dia-) and
βαίνειν, 'to go; to pass'. See base, п., and cp.
diabetes.

## Adiantum
Adiantum, п., a genus of plants, the maidenhair
fern (pot.) — L., fr. Gk. άδίαντον,
'maidenhair', lit. 'unwetted', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and διαίνειν (for *Sifavieiv), 'to wet,
moisten', which is prob. rel. to δεύειν, 'to wet,
moisten'.

## adiaphoretic
adiaphoretic, adj., preventing perspiration (med.)
— Gk. άδιαφορητικός, 'not promoting
perspiration'. See priv. pref. a- and diaphoretic
Derivative: adiaphoretic, п., an adiaphoretic
agent.

## adiaphoresis
adiaphoresis, п., absence of perspiration (med.)—
Medical I,. See priv. pref. a- and diaphoresis.

## adiaphoron
adiaphoron, n. (pi. adiapbora), a thing indifferent
from the ecclesiastical point of view. — Gk.
άοΊάφορον, neut. of αδιάφορος, 'indifferent'. See
next word.

## adiaphorous
adiaphorous, adj., indifferent. — Gk. αδιάφορος,
'not different, indifferent', fr. ά- (see priv. pref.
a-) and διάφορος, 'different', fr. δίά (see dia-)
and φέρειν, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to
carry', and cp. diaphoresis. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## adieu
adieu, interj. and n. — F. a Dieu, which is short
of je vous recommande ά Dieu, Ί commend you
to God', fr. L. ad Deum, 'to God'. See ad- and
deity.

## adipo- before a vowel adip-
adipo- before a vowel adip-, combining form
meaning 'fat, fatty'. — From the stem of L.
adeps, gen. adipis, 'fat'. See adipose.

## adipocere
adipocere, п., a waxy substance into which animal
matter is converted under certain
circumstances. — Coined by the French chemist Count
Antoine-Francois de Fourcroy (1755-1809) fr.
L. adeps, gen. adipis, 'fat', and clra, 'wax'. See
adipose and cere.

## adipose
adipose, adj., fatty. — ModL. adipasus (= L. adi-
patus), 'filled with fat, fatty', fr. L. adeps, gen.
adipis, 'fat of animals', fr. Gk. άλειφα,
'unguent, oil, fat', fr. άλείφειν, 'to anoint'. The
change of / to d is prob. due to Umbrian
influence. Gk. άλείφειν is rel. to Gk. λίπος,
'grease, fat', λιπαρός, 'fat, oily', and is cogn.
with L. lippus, 'blear-eyed', OE. be-lifan, 'to
remain'. See leave v., and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also synaloepha, aliphatic. For the ending
see adj. suff. -ose. Derivative: adipos-ity, n.

## adiposis
adiposis, п., fatness (med.) — A Medical L.
hybrid coined fr. L. adeps, gen. adipis, 'faf (see
adipose), and -osis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## adipsia
adipsia, п., the absence of thirst (med.)— Medical
L., fr. Gk. αδιψος, 'not suffering from thirst',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and 8ίψα, 'thirst', which
is of unknown origin. Cp. dipsomania, Dipso-
saurus, dipsosis. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## adit
adit, п., entrance. — L. adilus, 'approach,
entrance', fr. adit-(um), pp. stem of adire, 'to
approach', which is formed fr. ad- and ire, 'to go',
fr. I.-E. base *ei-, ·ι-, Ίο go', whence also L.
iter, 'a journey.' See Itinerate and cp. aditus.

## Aditi
Aditi, п., the endless heaven, mother of the Adi-
tyas (Vedic mythol.) — OI. dditih,
'boundlessness, infinity'. See Aditya and cp. daitya.

## aditus
aditus, п., an entrance (zool., anal., etc.) — L.
aditus. See adit.

## Aditya
Aditya, п., one of the sons of Aditi (Vedic my-
thol.) — OI. Aditya-, lit. 'the not bound ones',
formed fr. priv. pref. a- (see an·) and dydti,
'binds', fr. I.-E, base *di-, *d'-, 'to bind', whence
also Gk. δέειν, 'to bind'. See desmo- and cp.

prec. word.

## adjacency
adjacency, n. — ML. adjacentia, fr. L. adjaclns,
gen. -entis. See next word and -cy.

## adjacent
adjacent, adj. — L. adjaclns, gen. -entis, 'lying
at*, pres. part, oiadjacere, 'to lie at', fr. ad- and
jacere, 'to lie', which orig. meant 'to cast
oneself down', fr. jacio, jaclre, 'to throw, cast,
hurl'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and -ent and cp.
circumjacent, interjacent, subjacent, superjacent
Derivative: adjacent-ly, adv.

## adjective
adjective, adj. — L. adjectivum (for adjectivum
nOmen), neut. of adjectivus, 'that is added (to the
noun), 'adjective', fr. adjectus, pp. of adicere
(less correctly adjicere), 'to throw or place a
thing near', fr., ad- and jacere (pp. jactus), 'to
throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and -ive and cp.
adjacent. For the change of Latin ά (in jactus)
to i in ad-jlctus see accent and cp. words there
referred to. L. adjectivum is prop, a loan
translation of Gk. έπίθετον, lit. 'something added
to', fr. έπιτι&έναι, 'to add to'.
Derivatives: adjectiv-al, adj., adjectival-ly, adv.,
adjective-ly, adv.

## adjoin
adjoin, tr. and intr. v. — ME. ajoinen fr. OF.
ajoindre fr. L. adjungere, 'to join, add, annex',
fr. ad- and jungere, 'to join, unite'. See join and
cp. adjunct. The insertion of the letter d in
ModF. adjoindre and in E. adjoin is due to the
influence of L. adjungere.
Derivative: adjoin-ing, adj.

## adjourn
adjourn, tr. v., to put off to another day; intr. v.,
to suspend a session. — OF. ajorner (whence
F. ajourner), fr. VL. adjurnare, lit., 'to set a day',
fr. ad- and L. diurnus, 'daily', fr. dies, 'day'. See
diurnal and cp. journal, sojourn. The insertion
of the letter d in E. adjourn is due to the
influence of VL. adjurnare.
Derivatives: adjourn-al, adj., adjourn-ment, n.

## adjudge
adjudge, tr. v. — ME. ajugen, fr. OF. ajugier,
ajuger, fr. L. adjudicare. See next word and cp.
judge. The insertion of the letter d in ModF.
adjuger, and in E. adjudge is due to the influence
of L. adjudicare.
Derivatives: adjudg-er, п., adjudge-ment, n.

## adjudicate
adjudicate, tr. v. — L. adjudicatus, pp. of
adjudicare, 'to adjudge, decide, ascribe', fr. nd- and
judicare, 'to judge'. See judge and cp. judicial,
judicious. Cp. also adjudge. For the ending see
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: adjudication (q.v.), adjudicat-ive,
adj., adjudicat-or, п., adjudicat-ure, n.

## adjudication
adjudication, n. — L. adjudicatid, gen. -dnis, fr.
adjudicatus, pp. of adjudicare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## adjunct
adjunct, adj., added, joined. — L. adjunctus, pp.
of adjungere, 'to join'. See adjoin and cp.
junction,
Derivatives: adjunct, п., adjunction (q.v.), ad-
juncl-ive, adj., adjunct-ive-ly, adv.

## adjunction
adjunction, n. — L. adjunctid, gen. -dnis, 'a
joining to, an addition', fr. adjunctus, pp. of
adjungere. See prec. word and -ion.

## adjuration
adjuration, n. — F., fr. L. adjuratidnem, ace. of
adjuratid, 'a swearing to, adjuration', fr. ad-
juratus, pp. oiadjurare. See next word and -ion.

## adjure
adjure, tr. v., to charge or command solemnly. —
L. adjurare, 'to swear to, to confirm by an oath'
(whence also F. adjurer), fr. ad- and jwrare, 'to
swear', fr. jus, gen. juris, 'law'. See jury, jus.
Derivatives: adjuration (q.v.), adjur-alory, adj.,
adjur-er, п., adjur-or, n.

## adjust
adjust, tr. v., 1) to settle, arrange; 2) to fit
exactly. — Fr. earlier F. adjuster (corresponding to F.
ajuster), fr. ML. adjustare, fr. Late L. adjuxtare,
'to bring near', fr. ad- and L. juxta, 'near'. See
joust, v., and cp. juxta-.
Derivatives: adjust-able, adj., adjust-er, п., ad-
jusl-ive, adj., adjust-ment, n.

## adjutancy
adjutancy, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -cy.

## adjutant
adjutant, п., 1) an officer appointed to assist a
commanding officer; 2) a large stork found in
East India. — L. adjutans, gen. -amis, pres. part,
of adjutare, 'to help, assist', freq. of adjuvare
(pp. adjutus). See next word and -ant

## adjutory
adjutory, adj. and п., helpful.' — L. adjuldrius,
'helping, helpful', fr. adjutus, pp. of adjuvare.
Ίο help, assist'. See aid and -ory and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:39 COLUMN:3 -->
coadjutor.

## adjuvant
adjuvant, adj., helping; п., 1) an assistant; 2) (med.)
a remedial substance. — F., fr. L. adjuvantem,
асе. of adjuvdns, pres. part, of adjuvare. See
prec. word and cp. adjutant.

## Adlumia
Adlumia, п., a genus of plants, the climbing
fumitory (hot.) — ModL., named after the American
gardener Major J. Adlum (1759-1836). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## admeasure
admeasure, tr. v. — OF. amesurer, fr. L. admin-
surare, fr. ad- and mlnsurare, 'to measure', fr.
minsura, 'measure'. See measure. The insertion
of the letter d in E. admeasure is due to the
influence of L. admensurare.
Derivatives: admeasur-er, п., admeasure-ment,n.

## adminicle
adminicle, п., ι) a help; 2) corroborative evidence
(law). — L. adminiculum, 'prop, stay, support',
which prob. derives fr. *adminire, 'to stand out
toward something', fr. ad- and -minire, 'to
stand out'. Cp. l-minire, 'to stand out, project',
and see mount, 'hill, mountain', and -cle.

## adminicular
adminicular, adj., I) helping; 2)corroborative. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. adminiculum. See
prec. word.

## adminiculate
adminiculate, tr. v. — L. adminiculate, pp. of ad-
miniculare, 'to prop', fr. adminiculum. See
adminicle and verbal suff. -ate.

## adminiculum
adminiculum, п., help, support. — L. See
adminicle.
Derivatives: adminicular (q.v.), adminicul-ary,
adj., adminiculate (q.v.)

## administer
administer, tr. v. — OF. aministrer, fr. L. admi-
nistrare, 'to manage, carry out, attend, serve',
fr. ad- and ministrare, 'to serve'. See miuister, v.
The insertion of the letter d in F. administrer
and in E. administer is due to the influence of
L. administrdre.
Derivative: adminisler-ial, adj.

## administrant
administrant, adj. and n. — F., pres. part, of
administrer, fr. L. administrdre. See prec. word
and -ant.

## administrate
administrate, tr. v., to administer. — L.
administratus, pp. of administrdre. See administer and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: administration (q.v.), adminislra-
tion-al, adj., administrative (q.v.),
administrator (q.v.)

## administration
administration, n. — L. administratis, gen. -dnis,
fr. administratus, pp. of administrate. See prec.
word and -ion.
Derivative: administration-al, adj.

## administrative
administrative, adj. — L. administrativus, fr.
administratus, pp. of administrdre. See
administrate and -ive.
Derivative: administrative-ly, adv.

## administrator
administrator, n. — L., fr. administratus, pp. of
administrdre. See administrate and agential suff.
-or.

## administratrix
administratrix, п., a female administrator. —
ModL., fr. L. administrator. See prec. word
and -trix.

## admirable
admirable, adj. — F., fr. L. admirabilis, fr.
admirari, 'to admire'. See admire and -able and
cp. Mirabel.
Derivatives: admirable, п., admirabl-y, adv.

## admiral
admiral, n. — OF. amiral, amiralt (F. amiral),
prob. shortened fr. Arab, amtr-ar-rahl,
'commander of transport, officer commanding a
(transport) fleet', whence also Port, amiralhs,
amiral, It. ammiruglio (It. almiraglio and It., Sp.
and Port, almirante arose from a confusion of
am-, the beginning of the word amir, with the
Arab. art. al-\ It., Sp. and Port, almirante were
transformed after the pres. part. suff. -ante,
fr. L. -anlem; see -ant); influenced in form by
L. admirari, 'to admire'. See ameer, amir.

## admiralty
admiralty, n. — ME., fr. OF. admiralle (whence
MF. amiralte, F. amiraule). See ndmiral and
-ty-

## admiration
admiration, n. — F., fr. L. admlrulianem, ace. of
admiralid, 'a wondering at, admiration', fr. ad-
miralus, pp. of admirari. See admire and -ation.

## admirative
admirative, adj. — F. admirati/'(fern, admirative),
fr. Late L. admirativus, fr. admiralus, pp. of
admirari. See next word and -ative.

## admire
admire, tr. and intr. v. — F. admirer, fr. L.
admirari, 'to wonder at', fr. ad- and mirari, 'to
wonder', fr. mirus, 'marvellous', whence also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:40 -->
