mlraculum, 'a wonderful thing, marvel'. See
miracle and cp. marvel.
Derivatives: admir-ed, adj., admir-ed-ly, adv.,
admir-er, п., admir-ing, adj., admir-lng-ly, adv.

## admissible
admissible, adj. — F., fr. Late L. admissibilis, fr.
L. admissus, pp. of admittere. See admit and -ible.
Derivatives: admissibil-ity, п., admissible-ness,
п., admissibl-y, adv.

## admission
admission, n. — L. admissio, gen. -dnis, 'a letting
in', fr. admissus, pp. of admillere. See admit
and -ion.
admissive. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
admissus, pp. of admittere. See next word.

## admit
admit, tr. v. — L. admittere, 'to allow to enter,
let in', fr. ad- and millere, 'to send'. See
mission and cp. commit, intermit, omit, permit,
submit, transmit
Derivatives: admitt-able, adj., admitt-ance, п.,
admitt-ed, adj., admitt-ed-ly, adv., admilt-ee, n.

## admix
admix, tr. v. — Back formation fr. earlier
admix!, which derives fr. L. admixtus, 'mixed
with', but was mistaken for the pp. of an
English verb (i.e. admix I was supposed to have been
formed from the verb admix and the pp. suff.
-f). L. admixtus is pp. of admiscere, 'to add to
by mingling, mix with', and is formed fr. ad-
and miscere, 'to mix'. See mixed and cp.
commix, intermix.

## admixtion
admixtion, n. — L. admixtid, gen. -6nis, 'a
mingling', fr. admixtus, pp. of admiscere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## admixture
admixture, n. — Formed with suff. -ure, fr. L.
admixtus, pp. of admiscere. See admix.

## admonish
admonish, tr. v. — ME. amonesten, fr. OF. amo-
nester, fr. VL. admonestare, fr. L. admonlre, 'to
remind, suggest, advise, admonish', fr. ad- and
monere, 'to warn'. See monition and cp. next
word. The insertion of the letter d in OF. ad-
monester and E. admonish is due to the influence
of L. admonlre. The use of the suff. -ish is due
to the influence of the numerous English verbs
ending in -ish, in which this suffix corresponds
to OF. and F. -iss and goes back to the Latin
inchoative suff. -tscere. Cp. astonish, distinguish,
extinguish.
Derivatives: admonish-er, m., admonish-ment,n.

## admonition
admonition, n. — F., fr. L. admonitionem, ace. of
admonitio, fr. admonitus, pp. of admonire. See
admonish and -ion.
Derivatives: admonilion-er, n.

## admonitor
admonitor, n. — L., fr. admonitus, pp. of
admonire. See admonish and agential suff. -or.

## admonitory
admonitory, adj. — Late L. admonitorius, fr. L.
admonitus, pp. of admonire. See admonish and
adj. suff. -ory.

## adnate
adnate, adj., attached congenitally (bot.) — L.
adnatus, 'born to', pp. of adnascl, 'to be born
in addition to', fr. ad- and nasci, 'to be born'.
See nascent

## ado
ado, inf. and n. — ME. at do, 'to do', from a
Northern E. dialect, of Scand. origin. In ON.
the prep, at was used before infinitives (cp. the
same function of the prep, to in English). See
at and do. For sense development cp. to-do and
F. affaire (see affair).

## -ado
-ado, suff. occurring in words of Spanish or
Portuguese origin. — Sp. or Port, -ado, fr. L. -atus,
hence related to the suff. -ade (in comrade,
brigade, etc.), which is nothing but a Frenchified
form of Sp.-Port. -ado.

## adobe
adobe, п., brick. — Sp., fr. VArab. at-fdba, 'the
brick', fr. Arab, af-, assimilated form of at-,
'the', and VArab. tdba, corresponding to
classical Arab, tuba", 'a (single) brick', which is a
nomen unitatis fr. fub, 'bricks'(collectively). See
Lokotsch, EW., No. 2083.

## adolescence
adolescence, n. — F., fr. L. adoliscentia, fr.
adolescens, gen. -entis. See adolescent and -ce.

## adolescency
adolescency, n. — L. adoliscentia. See prec. word
and -cy.

## adolescent
adolescent, п., an adolescent person. — F., fr. L.
adolescenlem, ace. of adolescens. See adolescent,
adj.

## adolescent
adolescent, adj., growing up. — L. adolescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of adolescere, 'to grow
up', which stands for *ad-alescere, fr. nd- and
aliscere, 'to grow up', inchoative of alere, 'to
nourish'. See aliment and words there referred

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:40 COLUMN:2 -->
to and cp. esp. adult, soboles. For the ending
see suff. -ent.

## Adolph
Adolph, Adolphus, masc. PN. — L. Adolphus, of
Teut. origin. The name lit means 'noble wolf';
cp. OHG. Alhalwolf, Athaulf, Adulf, Adolf (G.
Adolf), fr. alhal, 'noble', and wolf, 'wolf'. For
the first element see Adelaide and cp. words there
referred to. For the second element see wolf.

## Adonai
Adonai, п., a Hebrew name of God. — Heb.
Adhondy, lit. 'my Lord', the plural of majesty
of Adhdn, 'Lord', with the suff. of the 1st person.
Adhdn prob. meant orig. 'Ruler', and derives
from the base a-d-n = d-w-n, 'to rule, judge'.

## Adonic
Adonic, adj., 1) pertaining to Adonis; 2)
pertaining to a verse called Adonic. — F. adonique,
fr. ML. Adonicus, fr. L. Adonis. See Adonis and
cp. next word.

## Adonic
Adonic, п., a verse consisting of a dactyl and a
spondee or trochee; so called because it was
especially used at the festival of Adonis. — See
prec. word.

## Adonis
Adonis, name of a youth in Greek mythology,
renowned for his beauty and loved by
Aphrodite. — L. Adonis, fr. Gk. "Αδωνίς, fr. Heb.-
Phoen. adhdn, 'lord'. See Adonai.

## Adonis
Adonis, п., name of a genus of plants of the
buttercup family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. Adonis (see
prec. word), who, after his death was changed
by Aphrodite into a plant.

## adopt
adopt, tr. v. — F. adapter, fr. L. adoptare, 'to
choose, select, adopt as a child', fr. ad- and op-
tare, 'to wish, desire'. See option.
Derivatives: adaptable (q.v.), adopt-ed, adj.,
adopt-ee, п., adopt-er, п., adoption (q.v.),
adoptive (q.v.)

## adaptable
adaptable, adj. — Formed fr. ndopt with suff.
-able; first used by Carlyle. Cp. affordable, dis-
likable, forgettable.

## adoption
adoption, n. — F., fr. L. айорЧбпет, ace. of
adoptiO. See ad- and option.

## adoptive
adoptive, adj. — F. adoptif'(fem. adoptive), fr. L.
adoptivus, 'pertaining to adoption', from the
stem of adoptare. See adopt and -ive.
Derivative: adopt ive-ly, adv.

## adorable
adorable, adj. — L. adorubilis, 'worthy of
adoration', fr. adorare. See adore and -able.
Derivatives: adorable-ness, п., adorabl-y, adv.

## adoration
adoration, n. — F., fr. L. adorationem, ace. of
adurSlio, 'worship, adoration', lit., 'a praying
to', fr. addralus, pp. of adorare. See next word
and -ion.

## adore
adore, tr. v. — F. adorer, 'to adore, worship', fr.
L. adorare, 'to speak to, entreat, ask in prayer,
worship', fr. nd- and drdre, 'to speak, pray'.
See oration.
Derivatives: adorable (q.v.), ador-er, п.,
adoring, adj., ador-ing-ly, adv.

## adorn
adorn, tr. v. — ME. adornen, fr. OF. adorner, fr.
L. adornare, 'to furnish, provide, decorate,
adorn, embellish', fr. ad- and бгпйге, 'to deck,
embellish, beautify'. See ornament
Derivatives: adarn-er, п., adornment (q.v.),
adorn-ing-ly, adv.

## adornment
adornment, n. — OF., fr. adorner. See prec. word
and -ment.

## adown
adown, adv., downward. — ME. adoune, adoun,
fr. OE. of-dune, 'from (the) hill', fr. of, 'off',
and dun, 'hill'. See of and down, adv.

## Adoxa
Adoxa, n. a genus of plants, the moschatel (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. άδοξος, 'inglorious, obscure,
insignificant', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and S6%a,
'glory', which is rel. to Soxelv, 'to think,
believe', δήγμα, 'opinion', and cogn. with L. do-
cere, 'to teach', decus, 'honor, ornament'. See
decent and cp. dogma, doxology.

## Adrasten
Adrasten, Adrastia, п., Nemesis. — L. Adrastla,
Adrastia, fr. Gk. 'Αδράστεια, lit. 'she from
whom there is no escape', fr. αδραστος, 'not
running away, not inclined to run away', fr. ά-
(see priv. pref. a-) and the stem of βρασμός, 'a
running away', and of -διδρίσκειν (used only
in compounds, esp. in ά7το-διδράσκειν, Ίο
run away'), fr. I.-E. base *dra-, 'to move
quickly', whence also OI. drdli, 'he runs'. From
"drem-, a collateral form of base *dru-, derive
Gk. δραμεϊν, 'to run', δρόμος, 'course'. See
dromedary.

## adrenal
adrenal, adj., near the kidneys; п., one of the two

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:40 COLUMN:3 -->
ductless glands above the kidneys (anal.) —
Formed fr. ad- and L. renulis, 'pertaining to the
kidneys', fr. ren, 'kidney'. See renal.

## adrenaline
adrenaline, adrenalin, п., a substance secreted by
the suprarenal glands (chem.) — Coined by the
Japanese chemist Jokichi Takamine (1854-1922)
in 1901 fr. nd-, L. remits, and chem. suff. -ine,
-In. See prec. word.

## Adrian
Adrian, adj., Adriatic. — See Adriatic and -an.

## Adrian
Adrian, masc. PN. — L. Adrianus, Hadrianus,
lit. 'of the Adriatic'. See next word.

## Adriatic
Adriatic, adj. — L. Adriaticus, HadriSticus, fr.
Atria, also called Adria, Hadria (now Atri),
a town in Picenum, fr. ater, fem. atra, neut.
atrum, 'black', hence lit. 'the black city' (see
atrabilious and -aric); the town was so called
because it was built on black mud. See Momm-
sen, Inhabitants of Italy, p. 76.

## adrift
adrift, adj. and adv., drifting; floating about
aimlessly. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and drift.

## adroit
adroit, adj., dexterous, skillful. — F., 'dexterous',
orig. 'rightly', fr. a, 'to' (see a), and droit, fr. L.
dirictus, 'right'. See direct, v., and cp. maladroit.
Derivatives: adroit-ly, adv. adrott-ness, n.

## adscititious
adscititious, adj., supplementary, additional. —
Formed fr. L. adscitus, pp. of adsctscere, 'to
take with knowledge, to approve', fr. ad- and
sciscere, 'to seek to know', an inchoative verb
formed fr. scire, 'to know'. See science and -ions.
Derivative: adscititious-ly, adv.

## adscript
adscript, adj., attached to the soil (said of serfs).
— L. adscriptus, ascriptus, 'enrolled', lit.
'written after', pp. of adscrlbere, ascrtbere, 'to add
to a writing, attribute, designate, apply'. See
ascribe and cp. script

## aduana
aduana, п., customhouse. — Arab, ad-diwdn, fr.
ad-, assimilated form of al-, 'the', and diwdn,
fr. Pers. diwan, 'register, office, council,
customhouse'. See divan and cp. douane.

## adsorption
adsorption, п., condensation of gases on the
surfaces of solid bodies. — Formed fr. ad- and L.
sorptio, gen. -dnis, 'a sucking in'. See sorptioa.

## ndularia
ndularia, п., a translucent variety of orthoclase
(mineral.) — Named after the Adula mountains
in Switzerland.

## adulate
adulate, tr. v., to flatter in a servile manner. —
L. adulatus, pp. of adulari, 'to fawn like a dog',
prop, 'to wag the tail', prob. fr. ad- and I.-E.
base "HI-, 'the tail', whence also OI. valah, varah,
'tail', Lith. valai, 'horsehair of the tail'. For
sense development cp. Gk. σαίνειν, προσσαίνειν,
'to wag the tail; to flatter', and E. wheedle,
which derives fr. G. wedeln, 'to wag the tail'.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: adulation (q.v.), adulator (q.v.),
adulat-ory, adj., adulat-ress, n.

## adulation
adulation, n. — OF. adulacion, fr. L. adulationem,
лес. of aduldtio, 'a fawning like that of a dog',
fr. adulatus, pp. of adulari. See prec. word and
-ion.

## aduintor
aduintor, n. — L. adulator, 'a low flatterer', fr.
adulatus, pp. of adulari. See adulate and agential
suff. -or.

## Adullamite
Adullamite, n. name given to the seceders from
the Liberal party in 1866. — Formed with subst.
suff. -ite fr. Heb. 'Adulldm, name of a cave (see
I Sam., 22:1-2). The name was orig. given
by John Bright to Horsman who 'had retired
into what may be called his political cave of
Adullam'.

## adult
adult, adj., and n. — L. adultus, 'grown up', pp.
of adolescere, 'to grow up'. See adolescent

## adulterant
adulterant, adj., adulterating; п., an
adulterating substance — L. adulterant, gen. -amis,
present part, of adulterare, 'to defile, corrupt'.
See adulterate and -nat.

## adulterate
adulterate, tr. v., to make impure by admixture;
to corrupt. — L. adulterants, pp. of adulterare,
'to falsify, corrupt; to corrupt a woman; to
commit adultery', dissimilated fr. *ad-allerare,
lit. 'to change, alter', fr. ad- and alter are, 'to
change, alter'. See alter, v., and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: adulteration (q.v.), adulterat-or, n.

## adulterate
adulterate, adj., guilty of adultery. — L. adul-
teratus, pp. of adulterare. See adulterate, v.

## adulteration
adulteration, n. — L. adulteratio, gen. -onis, fr.
adulter atus, pp. of adulterare. See ndulterate, v.,
and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:41 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ADULTERER | 14 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:41 COLUMN:1 -->

## adulterer
adulterer, η. — Formed with agential suff. -er
from the obsol. verb, adulter, which displaced
ME. avouterer, avoutrer, avowterer, from the
verb avouteren, etc., fr. OF. avoltrer, fr. VL.
*abulterare, a verb formed—with change of
pref.—fr. L. adulterare, 'to commit adultery'.
See adulterate, v.

## adulteress
adulteress, n. — See prec. word and -ess.

## adulterine
adulterine, adj., l) of adultery; 2) spurious. — L.
adultermus, 'bastard, not genuine'. See
adulterer and adj. sufT. -ine.

## adulterous
adulterous, adj. 1) guilty of adultery; 2) relating
to adultery. — See adulterer and -ous.

## adultery
adultery, n. — L. adulterium, displacing ME.
avoutrie, avouterie, avowtrie, fr. OF. avoutre,
fr. avoutre, 'adulterer', fr. VL. *abultrum, ace.
of *abulter, a word formed—with change of
pref.—fr. L. adulter, 'adulterer', which is a back
formation fr. adulterare. See. adulterate and -y
(representing L. -ium).

## ndumbrate
ndumbrate, tr. v., to outline, sketch out. — L.
adumbratus, pp. of adumbrare, 'to cast a
shadow, overshadow, to represent a thing in
outline*, fr. ad- and umbrare, 'to shade,
shadow', fr. umbra, 'shade, shadow'. See umbra
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: adumbration (q.v.), adumbrat-ive,
adj.

## adumbration
adumbration, n. — L. adumbrStio, gen. -onis, 'a
sketch in shadow, sketch, outline', fr.
adumbratus, pp. of adumbrare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## aduncous
aduncous, adj., hooked. — L. aduncus, 'hooked',
fr. ad- and uncus, 'hook'. See uncus. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## adust
adust, adj., burned, parched. — L. adustus, pp.
of adurere, 'to set in a flame, burn, singe', fr.
ad- and wrere, 'to bum'. See combust and cp.
words there referred to.

## advance
advance, tr. and intr. v. —· ME. avancen, fr. OF.
avancier, avancer (F. avancer), fr. VL. 'aban-
tiare (whence also It. avanzare, Sp. avanzar),
fr. Imperial L. abante, 'from before' (prep.);
'before' (adv.), which is compounded of L. ab,
'from' and ante, 'before'; see ab- and ante-. The
d in advance was inserted about the end of the
16th cent., the initial a in avancen having been
mistaken for F. a, 'to' (see a). See avaunt, inlerj.,
and cp. advantage. Cp. also arant-courier,
vanguard and its shortened form van. Cp. also
prance.
Derivatives: advance, n. and adj., advanc-ed,
adj., advancement (q.v.), advanc-er, n„ ad-
vanc-ive, adj.

## advancement
advancement, n. — OF. (= F.) avancement, fr.
avancer. See ndvance and -ment.

## advantage
advantage, n. — ME. avantage, fr. OF (= F.)
avantage, fr. avant, 'before', fr. Imperial L.
abante. See advance and -age and cp. vaatage.

## advantage
advantage, tr. v. — F. avantager, fr. avantage.
See prec. word.

## advantageous
advantageous, adj. — F. avanlageux (fem. avan-
tageuse), fr. avantage. See advantage, n. and -ous.
Derivatives: advantageous-ly, adv., advanta-
geous-ness, n.

## advene
advene, intr. v. to come to. — L. advenlre, 'to
arrive' fr. ad- and venire, 'to come'. See come
and cp. venue 'arrival'. Cp. also advent, avenue,
event.

## adveat
adveat, n. — L. adventus, 'arrival', fr. advent-
(um), pp. stem of advemre. See prec. word.

## adventitious
adventitious, adj., casual. — L. adventictus,
'coming from abroad, extraneous, foreign', fr.
advent-(um), pp. stem of advemre. See advent
and -itious.
Derivatives: adventitious-ly, adv., adventitious-
ness, n.

## adventure
adventure, n. — ME. aventure, fr. OF. (= F.)
aventure, fr. VL. 'adventura, 'a happening', fr.
L. aventHrus, 'that which is going to happen',
fut. part, of advenire, 4o arrive, happen'. The
English word was refashioned after L. advemre,
adventurus. See advent and cp. venture. Cp. also
saunter.
Derivatives: adventure, v. (q.v.), adventurous
(q.v.), adventuresome, п., adventure-some-ly,
adv., adventure-some-ness, n.

## adventure
adventure, tr. and intr. v. — ME. aventuren, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:41 COLUMN:2 -->
OF. aventurer, fr. aventure. See adventure, n.
Derivatives: advemur-er, п., adventur-ess, n.

## adventurous
adventurous, adj. — ME. aventurous, fr. OF. aven-
turos (F. aventureux), fr. aventure. See
adventure, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: adventurous-ly, adv., adventur-ous-
ness, n.

## adverb
adverb, n. — F. adverbe, fr. Late L. adverbium,
'adverb', lit. 'that which is added to the verb',
coined by the grammarian Flavius Sosipater
Charisius fr. ad, 'to', and verbum, 'word; verb'
(see ad- and verb), as a loan translation of Gk.
επίρρημα, 'adverb', lit. 'that which is said
afterward' (see epi- and rhetor).

## adverbial
adverbial, adj. —- Late L. adverbialis, 'pertaining
to an adverb', fr. adverbium. See prec. word
and -ial.
Derivative: adverbial-ly, adv.

## adversaria
adversaria, n. pi., miscellaneous notes. — L.
adversaria (scil. scripta), lit. 'writings turned
toward one', neut. pi. of adversarius. See
adversary.

## adversary
adversary, n. — OF. aversier, adversier, fr. L.
adversarius, 'opponent, adversary, rival', lit.
'turned toward one'. See adverse and subst.
suff. -ary. The insertion of the letter d in F. ad-
versaire, and E. adversary is due to the influence
of L. adversarius.

## adversative
adversative, adj., expressing opposition or
antithesis. — L. adversativus, fr. adversatus, pp. of
adversari, Ίο stand opposite to one', fr. adver-
sus. See next word and -ative.
Derivative: adversative-ly, adv.

## adverse
adverse, adj., opposed; unfavorable. — ME. fr.
OF. avers, later (= F.) adverse, fr. L. adversus,
'turned toward', opposite to; opposed to', pp.
of advertere. See advert.
Derivatives: adverse-ly, adv., adverse-ness, n.

## adversity
adversity, п., misfortune. — OF. aversite, later
adversiie (F. adversite). See prec. word and -ity.

## advert
advert, intr. v., to refer to. — F. avertir, fr. L.
advertere, 'to turn toward', fr. ad- and vertere, 'to
turn'. In English, the word has been
refashioned after L. advertere. See version and cp.
advertise and the second element in animadvert. Cp.
also avert, controvert, convert, covert, culvert,
divert, extrovert, introvert, overt, pervert, subvert.

## advertence
advertence, п., attention. — OF. avertence, later
(= F.) advertence, fr. Late L. advertentia. See
advertent and -ce.

## advertence
advertence, п., advertence. — Late L. advertentia.
See prec. word and -cy.

## advertent
advertent, adj., attentive. — L. advertens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of advertere. See advert and
-ent and cp. inadvertent.
Derivative: advertenl-ly, adv.

## advertise
advertise, tr. and intr.' v. — MF. advertiss-, pres.
part, stem oiadvertir, which corresponds to OF.
avertir, 'to warn, give notice to', fr. VL. *ad-
verlire, formed with change of conjugation, fr.
L. advertere. Cp. It. avvertire, OProvenc.
avertir, Sp., Port, advertir, and see advert.
Derivatives: advertisement (q.v.), advertis-er, п.,
advertis-ing, n.

## advertisement
advertisement, n. — MF. advertissement,
corresponding to OF. and F. avertissement, fr.
advertir, resp. avertir. See advert and -ment.

## advice
advice, n. — ME. avis, 'opinion', fr. OF. (= F.)
avis, formed from a misreading of the OF. term.
ce m'est a vis into ce m'est avis. The former term
itself is an alteration of ce m'est vis, lit. 'this
seems to me', fr. VL. ecce hoc rnihi est visum,
which corresponds to L. hoc mihi viditur, 'this
seems (right) to me'. L. visum is neut. pp. of
videre 4o see'. See ad- and vision and cp.
device. Cp. also next word arid avizandum.

## advise
advise, tr. and intr. v. — ME. avisen, fr. OF.
(= F.) aviser, fr. avis. See prec. word and cp.
devise.
Derivatives: advis-abil-ity, п., advis-able, adj.,
advisable-ness, п., advisabl-y, adv., advis-ed, adj.,
advis-ed-ly, adv., advis-ed-ness, п., advisement
(q.v.), advis-er, advis-or, п., advis-ory, adj.,
advis-ori-ly, adv.

## advisement
advisement, n. — OF. avisement, fr. aviser. See
prec. word and -ment.

## advocacy
advocacy, n. — OF. advocacie, fr. ML. advocatia,
fr. L. advocutus. See advocate and -cy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:41 COLUMN:3 -->

## advocate
advocate, n. — МБ. avocat, fr. OF. avocat, fr. L.
advocutus, 'one called to aid (esp. as a witness
or counsel)', pp. of advocare, 'to call to (esp. 'to
call to a place for counsel')', fr. ad- and vocare,
'to call', fr. vox, gen. vocis, 'voice'. See voice
and verbal suff. -ate and cp. vocation, avouch,
avow.
Derivative: advocate, tr. v.

## advocation
advocation, n. — L. advocatio, gen. -onis, 'a
calling to', fr. advocutus, pp. of advocare. See
advocate and -ion and cp. advowson, which is a
doublet of advocation.

## advowson
advowson, п., the right of presenting a nominee
to a church benefice. — ME. avoweisoun, fr.
OF. avoeson, fr. L. advocationem, ace. of
advocatio. See advocation.

## adynamia
adynamia, п., lack of vital force (med.) — Gk.
αδυναμία, 'want of strength, debility', fr. ά-
(seepriv. pref. a-) and δύναμις,'power,strength'.
See dynamic and -ia.

## adynamic
adynamic, adj., weak. — Formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -ic.

## adytum
adytum, п., ι) the innermost part of a temple;
2) a sanctum. — L., fr. Gk. SSutov, 'innermost
sanctuary', lit. 'a place not to be entered', subst.
use of the neut. of the adj. άδυτος, 'not to be
entered', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and δύειν,
'to sink into, plunge into, penetrate into, dive,
enter'; 'to put on* (lit. 'enter into') clothes; 'to
set' (prop, 'to dive into the sea'; said of the sun
and stars), which is cogn. with OI. upa-du, 'to
put on (clothes)', and perh. also with OI. dosa,
'vespertine, western'. Cp the second element in
Anadyomene, Aptenodytes, ecdysis, Endymion,
endysis, ependyma.

## adz
adz, adze, п., an axlike tool. — OE. adesa, 'ax',
fr. OF. aze, a secondary form of aisse, 'ax' fr.
L. ascia, 'ax, adz', which is metathesized fr.
*acsia and cogn. with Gk. άξ(νη, 'battle ax, ax',
Goth, aqizi, OE. eax. Sex, 'ax'. See ax.
Derivative: adz-er, n.

## Aeacus
Aeacus, п., one of the three judges in Hades,
famous for his piety and prayers {Greek mythol.)
— L„ fr. Gk. Αιακός, a word of uncertain
origin. It is possibly rel. to αίάζειν, 'to wail,
lament', which derives from the interj. αϊ, 'ah'.

## Aechmophonis
Aechmophonis, п., a genus of large grebes (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. αίχμοφόρος, 'spear bearer',
fr. αιχμή, 'spear', and -φόρος, 'bearer'. The
first element stands for 'aiksma and is cogn.
with L. icere, 'to strike'; see ictus. For the
second element see -phore.

## aecidium
aecidium, п., the cup-shaped fruit in certain
parasitic fungi (fcoi.) — ModL. dimin. formed
fr. Gk. αίκίά, 'injury', which is rel. to άεικής,
poetic άΐκής, Att. αίκής, 'unseemly,
shameful', είκών, 'likeness, image, statue'. ϊκελος,
'like'. See icon.

## Aedes
Aedes, п., a genus of mosquitoes (zool.} —
ModL., fr. Gk. αηδής, 'unpleasant, distasteful,
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and ηδύς (for *swadu)
'sweet', which is cogn. with OE. swete, etc.,
'sweet'. See sweet and cp. words there referred to.

## aedile
aedile, п., an official in charge of buildings
(/Сотая antiquity). — L. aedilis, fr. aedes, 'a
building, sanctuary, temple', orig. 'a place with a
hearth', fr. I.-E. base *aidh-, 'to burn', whence
also Gk. αί&ειν, 'to burn', aWpS, 'the clear
sky, fair weather', αίθήρ, 'the upper purer air,
ether'. See edify and cp. ether.

## aegagrus
aegagrus, п., the wild goat. — ModL. fr. Gk.
αίγαγρος, 'wild goat', which is compounded
of αϊξ, gen. αίγός, 'goat*, and άγριος, 'wild'.
See aego- and agrlo-.

## Aegeus
Aegeus, п., the father of Theseus who, believing
his son to be dead, threw himself into the
Aegean sea (said to have been named Aegean after
him) (Greek mythol.)—L. Aegeus, fr. Gk. Αίγεύς,
which prob. derives fr. αίγες, 'waves', a word
of uncertain origin; it is possibly a figurative
use of the pi. of αΐξ, 'goat' (see aegis). Cp.
αιγιαλός, 'seashore', and see Frisk, GEW., I,
p. 42 s.v. αϊξ and p. 31 s.v. αιγιαλός.

## aegicrania
aegicrania, п., representation of goats' heads
(Greek and Roman antiq.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
αϊξ, gen. αίγός, 'goat', and κρανία, pi. of
κράνίον, 'skull'. For the first element see aego-,
for the second see cerebrum.

## aegirite
aegirite, п., a variety of acmite (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite from Aegir, name
of the Icelandic sea-god; so called because it
occurs in Scandinavia.

## aegis
aegis, egis, п., ι) shield used by Zeus, later by
Pallas Athene (Greek mythoi.); i) used
figuratively in the sense of protection. — L. aegis, fr.
Gk. αίγίς, 'goatskin; the skin shield of Zeus',
fr. αίξ, gen. αίγός, .'goat'; see aego-. For this
etymology, suggested already by Herodotus, see
Frisk, GEW., I, p. 32 s.v. αίγίς. Ср. Aegeus.
Ср. also Giles.

## Aegisthus
Aegisthus, п., the lover of Clyterrmestra, with
whom he killed her husband Agamemnon
(Greek mythoi.) — L., fr. Gk. Αίγισθος, a word
of uncertain origin.

## Aegle
Aegle, п., 1) one of the Hesperides; 2) the mother
of the Graces; 3) the fairest of the Naiads
(Greek mythoi.) — L., fr. Gk. Αίγλη, lit.
'radiance, gleam'. The orig. meaning of Gk. αίγλη
was 'quickly moving light'. It is cogn. with OI.
ejati, 'moves about, trembles'.

## Aegle
Aegle, п., a genus of trees of the rue family (boi.)
— Named after the Naiad Aegle. See prec.
word.

## aego-
aego-, combining form meaning 'goat'. — Gk.
αίγο-, fr. αίξ, gen. αίγός, 'goat', which is cogn.
with OI. ajah, 'he-goal', ajinam, 'skin', Avestic
tzaen'm, 'pertaining to skin'. Arm. ate, 'goaf,
Lith. ozys, 'he-goat'. Cp. the first element in
aegicrania.

## Aegopodium
Aegopodium, п., a genus of herbs of the carrot
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. αίγοπόδης,
'goatfooted', fr. αϊξ, gen. αίγός, 'goat', and
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See aego- and podo-j
prob. so called from the shape of i ts small leaves.

## aegrotat
aegrotat, п., a certificate that a student is ill. —
L., 'he is sick', 3 pers. sing, of aegrSture, 'to be
sick', fr. aeger, 'sick', which is prob. cogn. with
Toch. В aik(a)re, A ekro, 'sick'.

## Aello
Aello, п., a harpy (Greek mythoi.) — L., fr. Gk.
'Αελλώ, lit. 'Stormswift', rel. to αελλα, 'tempest,
whirlwind', which stands for *άΓε-λ-ια, fr.
*άτ"ε-λ-ος, 'blowing', and is rel. to ιίημι (for
•αΐημι), Ί blow'. Cp. W. awel, 'wind' and see
atmo-.

## aeluro-
aeluro-, before a vowel aelur-, combining form
meaning 'cat'. — ModL., fr. Gk. αίλουρος, 'cat'.
See Ailurus.

## Aeneas
Aeneas, п., the son of Anchises and Aphrodite,
a Trojan hero and mythical ancestor of the
Romans; the hero of Virgil's Aeneid. — L.
Aeneas, fr. Gk. Αινείας, a name of uncertain
origin. It is possibly rel. to αίνος, 'horrible,
terrible'.

## aeneous
aeneous, adj., bronze-colored. — L. aeneus,
'brazen', fr. aes, gen. aeris, 'brass', which is cogn.
with OI. ayah, Goth, aiz, OE. or, xr, 'brass',
6ra, 'metal'. See ore and cp. words there referred
to. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -oils.

## Aeolian
Aeolian, adj., pertaining to Aeolus, god of the
winds; pertaining to the wind. — See Aeolus
and -ian.

## Aeolian
Aeolian, п., one of a branch of the Greek people
nam-d fr. Aeolus — Formed with suff. -un fr. L.
Aeolius, fr. Gk. Αίόλιος, 'Aeolian', fr. Αίολος,
'Aeolus', after whom the ancient district Αίολίς
(Aeolis) in Asia Minor is said to have been
named.

## Aeolis
Aeolis, п., a genus of mollusks (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. αίόλος, 'quick, quick-moving'. See neon
and cp. Aeolus.

## aeolo-
aeolo-, combining form used to denote musical
wind instruments. — Fr. L. Aeolus, name of the
god of winds. See Aeolian, 'pertaining to
Aeolus'.

## Aeolus
Aeolus, п., the god of the winds in Greek mythoi.
— L. fr. Gk. Αίολος, lit. 'Rapid', fr. αίόλος,
'quick, rapid', which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly stands for 'aifo-λος, and is rel. to
αιών, 'age, eternity'. See next word and cp.
Aeolis.

## aeon
aeon, eon, п., a long and indefinite period of
tim ■. — L. aeon, fr. Gk. αιών, 'age, eternity',
which stands for *αί/ών and is rel. to Gk. αίεί
(for Ίχί/έσι), 'always, ever', and cogn. with
OI. Syu, 'life', Avestic Syu, 'age', L. aevum,
'space of time, eternity', Goth, aim, 'age,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:42 COLUMN:2 -->
eternity', aiw, adv., 'ever', ON. sevi, 'lifetime', OHG.
ewa, 'eternity', Du. eeuw, 'age, century', eeuwig,
OFris. ewich, OS., OHG. Swig, MHG. Iwic,
G. ewig, 'everlasting', OE. a, 'always, ever'. See
aye, 'ever', and cp. words there referred to. See
also age and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also prec. word.

## Aepyornis
Aepyornis, п., a gigantic, extinct bird of
Madagascar. — ModL., lit., 'the tall bird',
compounded of Gk. αίπύς, 'tall, very high', a
word of uncertain origin, and of δρνις, 'bird',
for which see ornitho-.

## aequor
aequor, п., even surface; the sea. — L., 'an even
surface, the even surface of the sea', fr. aequus,
'even, level, flat'; see equal. L. aequor is a loan
translation of Gk. πέλαγος, 'the open sea, the
unbroken surface of the sea', which is cogn.
with L. plaga, 'hunting net, curtain', and planus,
'level, flat' (see pelagian).

## aerarian
aerarian, adj., fiscal. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. aerarius, 'pertaining to copper, pertaining to
money' fr. aes, gen. aeris, 'copper, bronze,
money', which is cogn. with OE. ar, xr, 'brass'.
See ore and cp. aes.

## aerarium
aerarium, п., the public treasury kept in the
temple of Saturn in Rome. — L., prop. neut. of the
adjective aerarius, 'pertaining to money', used
as a noun. See prec. word.

## aerate
aerate, tr. v., to expose to air. — Formed with
verbal suff. -ate fr. L. air, gen. aeris, 'air', fr.
Gk. άήρ. See air and cp. the second element in
saleratus.
Derivatives: aeral-ed, adj., aerat-ion, п.,
aerator, n.

## aerial
aerial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
aerius, fr. Gk. αέριος, 'of air, pertaining to
air', fr. άήρ, 'air'; first used by Shakespeare.
See air.
Derivatives: aerial, п., aerial-ly, adv., aerial-
ness, n.

## aerie
aerie, aery, п., ι) the nest of an eagle or another
bird of prey; 2) the brood of an eagle or
another bird of prey. — ME. aire, fr. OF. (= F.)
aire, fr. Late L. area, nest of a bird of prey'.
(Ducange in Glossarium mediae et infimae
Latinitatis, s.v. area quotes a passage where
area has this meaning; see Skeat s.v.) It is
doubtful whether area in this sense is identical
with L. area, 'vacant piece of ground, open
space' (see area). Cp. eyrie.

## aerification
aerification, п., the act of aerifying, aeration. —
Compounded of L. aer, gen. aeris, 'air' (see
air), and -ficatioa.

## aeriform
aeriform, adj. — Compounded of L. aft-, gen.
aeris, 'air', and forma, 'form, shape'. See air
and form, n.

## aerify
aerify, tr. v. — Compounded of L. aer, gen. aeris,
'air' (see air), and -fy.

## aero-
aero-, before a vowel aer-, combining form
denoting the air. — Gk. άερο-, fr. άήρ gen.
αέρος, 'air'. See air.

## aerobatics
aerobatics, п., acrobatic tricks performed with
aircraft. — Coined on analogy of acrobatics fr.
aero- and the stem of βαίνειν, 'to go'. See
acrobat and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -ics.

## aerobic
aerobic, adj. (biol.), 1) living only in the presence
of oxygen (said of bacteria); 2) produced by
aerobic bacteria (biol.). — Coined by the French
chemist Louis Pasteur (1822-95) ш '863 fr. Gk.
άήρ, 'air', and βίος, 'life'. See aero-, bio- and
-ic and cp. anaerobic. Cp. also the second
element in microbic
Derivative: aerobic-al-ly, adv.

## aerodone
aerodone, п., a gliding machine. — See next word.

## aerodonetics
aerodonetics, п., the science of gliding flight
(aeronautics). — Compounded of Gk. άήρ, 'air', the
stem of δονείν, 'to shake, drive about', and
suff. -ics. For the first element see air. Gk.
δονείν is rel. to δόναξ, Dor. δώναξ, 'reed', and
prob. cogn. with Lett, duonis, 'reed, rush'. The
orig. meaning of these nouns prob. was
'something shaken (by the wind)'.

## aerodrome
aerodrome, п., airpart. — Coined on analogy of
hippodrome fr. nero- and Gk. δρόμος, 'course'.
See dromedary.

## aerodromics
aerodromics, п., the art of flying. — See prec.
word and -ics.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:42 COLUMN:3 -->

## aerodynamics
aerodynamics, п., that branch of dynamics which
deals with the air and other gases. —
Compounded of aero- and dynamics,

## aerography
aerography, п., description of the air. —
Compounded of aero- and Gk. -γραφία, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See graphy.
Derivalives: aerograph-ic, aerograph-ic-al, adjs.

## aerolite
aerolite, п., a stony meteorite. — Compounded
of aero- and -lite,

## aerometer
aerometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
weight of air and other gases. — Compounded
of aero- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## aerometry
aerometry, п., the science of measuring the air,
pneumatics. — Compounded of aero- and Gk.
-μετρία, 'a measuring of, fr. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See -metry.

## aeronaut
aeronaut, n. — Compounded of aero- and Gk.
ναύτης, 'sailor'. See nautical.
Derivatives: aeronaul-ic, aeronaul-ic-al, adjs.,
aeronaut-ic-al-ly, adv., aeronaut-ics, n.

## aerophagia
aerophagia, aerophagy, п., air swallowing (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of aero-and-φαγία,
fr. -φάγος, 'eating'. See -phagy.

## aerophore
aerophore, п., an apparatus carrying air for
breathing as used for miners. — Compounded
of aero- and Gk. -φόρος, 'bearing'. See -phore.

## aerophyte
aerophyte, п., an air plant. — Compounded of
aero- and φυτόν, 'plant'. See -phyte.

## aeroplane
aeroplane, п., an airplane. — F. aeroplane,
compounded of L. aer, 'air', and F. planer, 'to hover,
soar', fr. L. planus, 'level, flat; plain'. See aero-
and plane, 'a flat surface', and cp. nirplane.

## aerostat
aerostat, n. — F. aerostat, compounded of Gk.
άήρ, 'air', and στατός, 'placed; standing'. See
aero- and static and cp. gyrostat, heliostat, hy-
drostat, pyrostat, rheostat, thermostat,

## aerostatic
aerostatic, adj. — F. airostatique, compounded
of Gk. άήρ, 'air', and στατικός, 'causing to
stand'. See aero- and static,

## aerostatics
aerostatics, п., that science which deals with the
equilibrium of gaseous fluids. — See prec. word
and -ics.

## aerostation
aerostation, п., the science of operating flying
machines lighter than the air; opposed te
aviation. — F. aerostation. See aerostat and -Ion.

## aeruginous
aeruginous, also aemginose, adj., pertaining to, or
like, copper rust. — L. aeruginosus, 'full of rust',
fr. aerugo, gen. -ginis, 'rust of copper', fr. aes,
gen. aeris, 'copper'. See ore and -ous and cp. the
first element in esteem. For the formation of L.
aerugo cp. ferrugo, 'iron rust', fr. ferrum, 'iron',
rubigo, 'rust of metals, fr. ruber, 'red', albugo,
'a white spot', fr. albus, 'white' (sou ferruginous,
rubiginous, albugo).

## aery
aery, adj., aerial. — See aerial,

## aery
aery, n. — The same as aerie,

## aes
aes, п., brass, copper (Roman antiq.) — L. aes,
gen. aeris, 'brass'. See ore and cp. aerarium,
aerarian.

## Aeschynomene
Aeschynomene, п., a genus of plants, the sensitive
joint vetch (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. αίσχυνομένη,
'sensitive plant', fem. of αίσχυνόμενος, 'being
ashamed', pass. pres. part, of αίσχΰνειν, to
dishonor, put to shame', fr. αισχύνη, 'shame', fr.
αίσχος, 'shame', which stands for *aigwh-s-kos
and is cogn. with Goth, aiwiski, 'shame,
confusion', MHG. eisch, 'ugly'. For the suff. -μένος
see ulumnus and cp. words there referred to. The
plant was called αίσχυνομένη, 'the ashamed
one', in allusion to the sensitiveness of its
leaflets.

## Aesculaceae
Aesculaceae, n. pi. a family of trees, the horse-
chestnut (hot.) — Formed with suff. -aceae fr.
L. aesculus, 'the Italian oak'. See Aesculus.

## Aesculapian
Aesculapian, adj., 1) pertaining to Aesculapius;
2) medical. — Formed with suff. -an fr.

## Aesculapius
Aesculapius, Latinized from Asclepius, fr. Gk.
'Ασκληπιός, 'the god of medicine'. See Asclepius.

## Aesculus
Aesculus, п., a genus of trees, the horse-chestnut
(bot.) — L. aesculus, 'the Italian oak'. See onk.

## Aesir
Aesir, n. pi., the chief gods of Scandinavian
mythology. — ΟΝ., pi. of ass, 'god', rel. to OE. as,
OS. as-, os-, OHG. ans- (in PN.s), Goth, arts,
'god'; possibly of the same origin as ON. ass,

## Goth
Goth, ans, 'beam'.

## Aesopian
Aesopian, adj., pertaining to, or resembling
Aesop. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Aesopius,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:43 COLUMN:1 -->
'Aesopian', fr. Aesopus, fr. Gk. Αίσωπος, the
Greek fable writer.

## Aestas
Aestas, п., the goddess of summer in Roman
mythology. — L. aestas, 'summer'. See estival.

## aesthete
aesthete, n. — See esthete.

## aesthetic
aesthetic, adj. — See esthetic

## aestival
aestival, adj. — See estival.

## aestivate
aestivate, intr. v. — See estivate.

## aestivation
aestivation, n. — See estivation.

## aether
aether, n. — See ether.

## aethogen
aethogen, п., boric nitrite (chem.) — Lit.
'producing heat', fr. Gk. αΐ&ος, 'burning, heat, fire',
and -γενής, 'produced by' (but used in the
modern sense 'producing'). For the first element
see ether and cp. next word. For the second
element see -gen.

## Aethousa
Aethousa, п., a genus of plants of the carrot family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ρΐΦουσα, 'burning,
fiery', fern. pres. part, of αί&ειν, 'to light up,
kindle, burn', whence αϊ&ος, 'burning heat,
fire', αίθήρ, 'the upper purer air, ether'; see
ether. This genus of plants was prob. called
Aethousa ('the burning or fiery one') in allusion
to the bright leaves.
aetio-. — See etio-.

## aetiology
aetiology, n. — See etiology.
aeto- combining form meaning 'eagle*, as in
Aetosaurus. — Gk. άετο-, fr. αϊετός, αετός,
'eagle', which stands for "άίιετός, lit. 'a large
bird', and is cogn. with L. avis, 'bird'; see aviary.
The suff. -eto-s in *άίιετός prob. has
augmentative force.

## Aetosaurus
Aetosaurus, п., a genus of reptiles of the Triassic
period (paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of
aeto- and Gk. σαϋρος, 'lizard'. See sauro-.

## af-
af-, assimilated form of ad- before /.

## alar
alar, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and far.

## afeard
afeard, afeared, adj., afraid (archaic). — ME.
afered, fr. OE. dfxred, pp. oidfxran, 'to frighten,
terrify', formed from intensivepref. a- and fleran,
'to terrify'. See fear, v. and n.

## affability
affability, n. — F. affabilite, fr. L. affdbilit&tem,
ace. of affdbilitds, 'courtesy, kindness, affability',
fr. affubilis. See affable and -ity.

## affable
affable, adj., easy to speak to; courteous. — F.,
fr. L. affubilis, 'kind, friendly, affable', lit. 'he
who can be (easily) spoken to', fr. affdri, 'to
speak to', fr. ad- and fan, 'to speak'. See fable
and cp. esp. iaeffable.
Derivatives: affable-ness, п., affabl-y, adv.

## affair
affair, n. — ME., fr. OF. afaire (F. affaire),
from the phrase a faire, 'to do', fr. L. ad, 'to',
and facere, 'to do'. See ad- and fact and cp. ado
and to-do.

## affect
affect, tr. v., to act upon. — L. affectus, pp. of af-
ficere, 'to do something to', fr. ad- and facere
(pp. factus), 'to make, do'. See fact and cp.
affettuoso. For the change of Latin d (in factus)
to i (in af-fictus) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: affect-ed, adj., affect-ing, adj., af-
fect-ing-ly, adv., affection (q.v.)

## affect
affect, tr. v., to make a pretence of; to feign. —
F. affecter, fr. L. affectare, 'to strive after, aim
at', freq. of afficere (pp. affectus), 'to do
something to'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: affection (q.v.), affect-ed, adj., af-
fect-ed-ly, adv., affect-er, п., affection (q.v.),
affect-ive, adj. (cp. F. affectif, fern, affective),
affect-ive-ly, adv., affect-iv-Hy, n.

## affectation
affectation, n. — L. affectdtio, gen. -onis, 'a
striving after', fr. affectdtus, pp. of affectare. See
prec. word and -ation.

## affection
affection, п., feeling. — F., fr. L. affectidnem, ace.
of affectio, 'a permanent state of feeling', fr.
affectus, pp. of afficere, 'to do something to'.
See affect, 'to act upon', and affect, 'to make a
pretence of.
Derivatives: affection-al, adj., affection-al-ly,
adv., affect-ion-ate, adj., affecl-ion-ale-ly, adv.

## affection
affection, п., an acting upon. — F., fr. L.
affectidnem, ace. of affectio. See affection, 'feeling'.

## affeer
affeer, tr. v., to confirm (OldEnglish law). — AF.
aferer, corresponding to OF. affeitrer, afeurer,
'to tax', fr. VL. *affordre, fr. ad- and L. forum,
'public place, market', in VL. also 'market price,
tariff' (whence OF. fuer, 'price, tariff, tax). See
forum.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:43 COLUMN:2 -->

## affereat
affereat, adj., bringing inward (physiol.) — L.
afferins, gen. -entis, pres. part, of afferre, 'to
bring or carry to', fr. ad- and ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See bear, 'to carry', and -ent and cp.
efferent.

## affettuoso
affettuoso, adj. and adv., with feeling (mus.) —
It., adj., fr. L. affectuosus, 'full of affection or
love', fr. affectus, 'love, goodwill', fr. afficere
(pp. affectus), 'to do something to, to affect a
person with something'. See affect, 'to act upon'.

## affiance
affiance, п., trust, faith; promise of marriage. —
OF. afiance 'confidence, trust', fr. after, 'to
trust', fr. ML. affiddre, 'to pledge one's faith',
fr. ad- and L. fidare, 'to trust', fr. fides, 'faith',
whence fidelis, 'true, faithful', fidelitas,
'faithfulness, fidelity'. See fidelity and -ance and cp.
faith, affidavit. Cp. also fiaace.

## affiance
affiance, tr. v., to promise in marriage. — OF.
afiancier, fr. afiance. See affiance, n.
Derivative: affianc-er, n.

## affiche
affiche, п., poster. — F., formed fr. d, 'to' (see a),
and ficher, 'to drive in (a stake or a nail), to
stick, fix, fasten', fr. VL. *ffgicdre (contracted
into "ficcdre), freq. of \*.figere, 'to fix, attach'.
Cp. It. ficcare, OProvenc. ficar, Sp. hincar, 'to
thrust, drive in', and see fix. Cp. also affix.

## affidavit
affidavit, п., a sworn statement. — ML. affidavit,
'he has pledged his faith', perf. tense of affiddre;
so called from the first word of a sworn
statement. See affiance, n.

## affiliable
affiliable, adj. — Formed fr. next word with suff.
-able.

## affiliate
affiliate, tr. v. — L. affilidtus, pp. of affilidre, 'to
adopt as a son', fr. ad- and ftlius, 'son'. See

## agent
agent, adj. — L. agens, gen. agentis, pres. part,
of agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead, conduct,
guide, govern; to do, act', whence agmen, 'army,
troop, band, multitude', lit. that which is lead',
fr. I.-E. base *ag-, 'to drive, lead, act, do', whence
also Gk. άγειν, 'to lead, guide, drive, carry
off', άγΐνεΐν, 'to lead, bring', άγων, 'assembly,
contest in the games', «γωνία, 'struggle for
victory, anguish, agony', αγωγός, 'leader', αγωγή,
'a carrying away, a leading', OI. djati, 'drives',
ajirah, 'moving, active', Avestic aza4i, 'drives',
Toch. A ak-, В ak-, 'to travel, lead', Arm. acem,
Ί lead, bring', ON. aka, 'to drive'. Cp. agent,
n. Cp. also ahigeat, acorn, acre, act, action,
activate, actor, actress, actuate, Agelaius, agenda.
agile, agitate, agminate, -agogue, agonist,
agonize, agony, agrarian, agrestic, agriculture, agrio-,
agro-, agronomy, Agrostis, Agyieus, aisle, ala,
ambages, ambagious, ambassador, ambiguous,
ameat, anagogy, antagonist, apagoge, assay,
Auriga, axilla, axiom, axis, axle, cache, chora-
gus, ciarigation, coact, coagalate, cogent,
cogitate, demagogic, deuteragonist, embassy, epact,
essay, exact, examen, exigent, exiguous, exility,
indagate, intransigent, isagoge, paragoge, para-
gonite, pedagogue, pilgrim, prodigal,
protagonist, react, redact, remex, stavesacre, strategy,
synagogue, transact, tritagonist, and the second
element in castigate, ciarigation, fastigiate,
fumigate, fustigate, levigate, litigate, mitigate,
navigate, objurgate, purge, variegate.

## agent
agent, n. — F., in the sense of 'acting force', fr.
ML. agens, in the sense of 'acting person', fr.
It. agente; both these words derive fr. L. agens,
gen. agentis, pres. part, of agere. See agent, adj.

## agential
agential, adj. — Formed fr. agency with suff.
-ial.

## Ageratum
Ageratum, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (hot.) — ModL. ageratum, fr. Gk. άγή-
ρατον, neut. of άγήρατος, 'ageless, everlasting',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and γήρας, 'old age'.
See geronto-.

## ageustia
ageustia, agensia, п., lack of the sense of taste
(med.) — Gk. άγευστία, 'a not-tasting, fasting',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and a derivative of Gk.
γεΰεσθαι, 'to taste', fr. I.-E. base *geus-, *gus-,
'to taste, enjoy by tasting'. See choose and cp.
gust, 'relish'. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## agger
agger, п., mound, rampart (Roman antiq.) — L.,
'heap, pile, dam, dike, mound, rampart', lit.
things brought together', from the stem of ag-
gerere, 'to bring to (a place), bring together',
fr. ad- and gerere, 'to bear, carry'. See gerent
and cp. exaggerate.

## agglomerate
agglomerate, tr. and intr. v., to gather into a
mass. — L. agglomeratus, pp. of agglomerare,
'to wind into or as into a ball', fr. ad- and glo-
merare, 'to form into a ball', fr. glomus, gen.
glomeris, 'a ball of yarn'. See glomerate and cp.
conglomerate.
Derivatives: agglomeration (q.v.), agglomerat-
ive, adj., agghmerat-or, n.

## agglomerate
agglomerate, adj., gathered into a mass. — L.
agglomeratus, pp. of agglomerare, See agglome-
erate, v.
Derivative: agglomerate, n.

## agglomeration
agglomeration, n. — L. agglomeratio, gen. -onis,
fr. agglomeratus, pp. of agglomerare. See
agglomerate, v., and -ion.

## agglutinant
agglutinant, adj. uniting. — L. agglulinans, gen.
-amis. See agglutinate and -ant.
Derivative: agglutinant, n.

## agglutinate
agglutinate, tr. v., to unite with glue or as with
glue; intr. v., to unite. — L. agglutinatus, pp. of
agglutindre, 'to fasten together with glue, to
fasten to', fr. ad- and glutinare, 'to glue', fr.
gluten, gen. glutinis, 'glue'. See gluten, glue and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: agglutin-ated, adj., agglutin-ation,
п., agglutinat-ive, adj., agglutinat-or, n.

## agglutinate
agglutinate, adj., united. — See agglutinate, v.

## agglutinin
agglutinin, п., a substance causing agglutination
(bacteriology). — Coined by the German
bacteriologist Max von Gruber (1853-1927) from
the stem of L. agglutinare, 'to glue on'. See
agglutinate and chem. suff. -in.

## aggrandize
aggrandize, tr. v. to make larger, increase. — F.
agrandiss-, pres. part, stem of agrandir, 'to

enlarge', fr. a, 'to' (see a), and grandir, 'to
increase', fr. L. grandire, 'to make great, increase',
fr. grandis, 'great'. See grand. The spelling with
double g is due to the analogy of Latin words
beginning with agg- (for ad-g).
Derivatives: aggrandizement (q.v.), aggrandiz-
er, n.

## aggrandizement
aggrandizement, n. — F. agrandissement, fr. a-
grandir. See prec. word and -ment.

## aggravate
aggravate, tr. v., to make worse. — L.
aggravate, pp. of aggravare, 'to make heavier, make

load, to make heavy', fr. gravis 'heavy'. See

aggrieve.

vat-ive, adj., aggravat-or, n.

## aggravation
aggravation, n. — Late L. aggravatio, gen. -onis,

word and -ion.

## nggregable
nggregable, adj., that can be aggregated. — See

aggregate, tr. v. to gather into a mass; to amount

aggress, intr. v., to start a quarrel. — F. agresser,

gressus), 'to go to, approach, attack', fr. ad-

pref. a- and OE. gxstan, 'to frighten', fr. gxst,

gust, 'spirit'. See ghost and cp. ghastly. Cp. also

agile, adj., nimble, active. — F., fr. L. agilis,

agio, п., the discount paid to exchange one

lajje, fr. MGk. άλλάγιον, 'exchange', fr. Gk.

agiotage, n. — F., fr. agioter, 'to be a stock

agistor, agister, п., one who agists. — AF. agis-

agitable, adj. — L. agitabilis, 'that can easily be

agitate, tr. and intr. v. — L. agitatus, pp. of

agitation, n. — F., fr. L. agitationem, ace. of agi-

agitato, adj. agitated (musical direction). — It.,

agitator, n. — L., fr. agitatus, pp. of agitare. See

## Agkistrodon
Agkistrodon, п., a genus of pit vipers (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. &γκιστρον,
'fishhook', and οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. The
first element is rel. to άγκος, *a bend, hollow',
άγκών, 'elbow', lit. 'the bend of the arm', and
cogn. with L. angulus, 'angle, corner'; see
angle, 'corner'. For the second element see
odonto-.

## Aglaia
Aglaia, п., one of the Graces in Greek
mythology. — L., fr. Gk. 'Αγλαία, lit. 'splendor,
beauty, brightness', fr. άγλαός, 'splendid, beautiful,
bright', which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly stands for *ά-γλαίός and is formed fr.
copul. pref. ά- and I.-E. base *gl-, zero degree of
base *gel-, 'clear, serene, cheerful, lovely; to
laugh'. Copul. pref. ά- (in *ά-γλα^ός) stands
for I.-E. *sm-, a weak gradational form of I.-E.
base *sem-, 'one, together'; see same. Fr. base
*gel- derive Gk. γαληνός, 'calm, serene', γαλήνη,
'stillness of wind and wave', γελάν, 'to laugh',
γέλως, 'laughter'; see geloto- and cp. words
there referred to.

## Aglaspis
Aglaspis, п., a genus of Cambian Xiphosura
(paleontol.) — ModL., lit. 'with a glittering
shield', contracted fr. Gk. άγλαός, 'splendid,
beautiful, bright', and ασπίς, 'shield'. See
Aglaia and aspidium.

## agleam
agleam, adv. and adj., gleaming. — Formed fr.
a-, 'on', and gleam.

## aglet
aglet, aiglet, п., the metal tag of a lace. — F.
aiguillette, dimin. of aiguille, 'needle', fr. VL.
*acucula, corresponding to L. acicula, dimin. of
acus, 'needle'. Cp. It. agucchia, OProvenc., Port.
agulha, Sp. aguja, 'needle', and see acus,
aiguille. For the ending see suff. -et.

## agley
agley, adv., awry (chiefly Scot.). — Formed fr.
a- 'on', and Scot, gley, 'to squint'.

## Aglossa
Aglossa, n. pi., a suborder of amphibians (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. άγλωσσος, 'tongueless'. See
next word.

## aglossal
aglossal, adj., tongueless. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. Gk. άγλωσσος, 'without a tongue',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. n-) and γλώσσα, 'tongue'.
See gloss, 'note', and cp. prec. word.

## aglow
aglow, adv. and adj., in a glow. — Formed fr.
a-, 'on', and glow,

## agmatine
agmatine, п., name of the base CSH14N4 (biochem.)
— Coined by the German physiological chemist
Albrecht Kossel (1853-1927) fr. Gk. αγμα, gen.
αγματος, 'fragment*, and chem. suff. -ine. Gk.
αγμα is rel. to αγνϋμι (for *5άγνϋμι), Ί break',
and cogn. with Toch. wak-, 'to burst, crack', in
the causative form, 'to cause to split, to
distinguish', wakam, 'peculiarity'. See Frisk,GEW.,
I, p. 13 s.v. αγνυμι.

## agmatology
agmatology, п., the study of fractures in surgery.
— Compounded of Gk. αγμα, gen. &γματος,
'fragment', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See agmatine and -logy.

## agminate
agminate, agmiaated, adj., grouped. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate, resp. also -ed, fr. L. agmen,
gen. -minis, 'multitude in motion, crowd, army',
lit. 'that which moves', fr. agere, 'to set in
motion, drive'; cogn. with OI. djmah, 'path', Gk.
δγμος, 'furrow; path'. See agent, adj., and -men.

## agnail
agnail, п., a hangnail. — OE. angnmgl, 'worn on

the foot', compounded of ang- (used only in
compounds), 'narrow, painful', and nsegl, 'nail'.
The first element is rel. to OE. enge, 'narrow';
see nnger. For the second element see nail. Cp.
anbury,

## agnate
agnate, adj., sprung from the same male
ancestor. — L. agnatus, 'related by the father's side',
lit. 'born to*, pp. of agnascl, 'to be born in
addition to', fr. ad- and OL. gndscl (whence L.
ndsci), 'to be born'. See natal and cp. cognate,

Derivatives: agnate, п., agnal-ic, adj.

## agnation
agnation, п., an agnate relationship. — L. ag-

## agnathous
agnathous, adj., having no jaws. — Formed fr.

## Agnes
Agnes, fem. PN. — L. Agnes, fr. Gk. 'Αγνή, lit.
'pure, chaste', fem. of αγνός. See agnus castus
and cp. Inez. The most frequent ME. forms of
the name Agnes were Annis, Annys. Cp. Nancy.

## Agui
Agui, п., one of the chief gods of the Vedas. —
OI. Agnih, 'the god of fire', fr. agnih, 'fire', which
is cogn. with L. ignis, 'fire'. See igneous,

## agnize
agnize, tr. v., to recognize (archaic). — Formed
fr. L. agnSscere on analogy of recognize (fr. L.
recognoscere).

## agnoiology
agnoiology, п., the doctrine of ignorance (philos)
— Coined by J.-F. Ferrier in 1854 fr. Gk. άγνοια,
'ignorance', and -λογία; fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. Gk. άγνοια is formed
fr. i- (see priv. pref. a-) and the stem of γιγνώ-
σκειν, 'to know'; see gnostic and cp. agnostii.
For.the second element see -logy,

## agnomen
agnomen, п., name added to the surname (Roman
antiq.) — L. agnomen, fr. ad- and OL. gnOmen
(whence L. ndmen), 'name'. See name and cp.
nominal. Cp. also cognomen,

## agnostic
agnostic, п., one who professes that the existence
of a First Cause and the essential nature of
things are not and cannot be known. — Coined
by Thomas Henry Huxley (1S25-95) in 1869 on
analogy of gnostic fr. Gk. άγνωστος, 'unknown,
not to be known'. See priv. pref. a- and gnostic.
Derivative: agnostic, adj.

## agnosticism
agnosticism, п., the doctrine of agnostics. —
Formed fr. prec. word with surf. -ism.

## agnus castus
agnus castus, п., an ornamental tree. — L.; agnus
derives fr. Gk. άγνος, 'a willowlike tree, used
at religious festivals, the chaste tree', which is
of unknown origin. This word was confused
both with L. agnus, 'lamb', and Gk. αγνός,
'sacred, chaste', whence arose the name agnus
castus, prop, 'the chaste lamb', and, as a loan
translation of this latter name, G. Keuschlamm,
and E. chaste tree. For the etymology of castus
see chaste. Cp. the second element in Elaeagnus.

## ago
ago, adv. — Prop. pp. of ME. agon, 'to go away',
fr. OE. agdn, 'to go away, pass by', fr. intensive
pref. a- and gun, 'to go'. See go.

## agog
agog, adverb and adj., in a state of excitement. —
F. en gogues, 'mirthful'. Cp. ilre en goguette(s),
'to be on the spree', goguenard, 'mocking,
bantering'. All these words derive from 'gog-, a
base of imitative origin.

## -agogue
-agogue, combining form meaning 'leading,
guiding', as in demagogue, pedagogue. — Gk.
-αγωγός, fr. αγωγός, 'leader', fr. άγειν, 'to lead'. See

## agomphious
agomphious, adj., toothless. — Coined by the
German naturalist Ch. G. Ehrenberg (1795-1876)
from priv. pref. n- and Gk. γομφίος (scil. 68ών),
'grinder tooth', fr. γόμφος, 'bolt, nail'. Seegom-
phosis and -ous.

## agonic
agonic, adj., not forming an angle. — Formed
with suff. -fc fr. Gk. άγωνος, 'without angles',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and γωνιά, 'angle'. See
-gon.

## agonist
agonist, п., a contender in public games. — Gk.
αγωνιστής, 'combatant; actor', fr. άγωνίζεσ&οα.
See agonize and -ist and cp. antagonist, deutera-
gonist, protagonist, tritagonist.
Derivatives: agonist-ic, adj., agonist-ic-al-ly,
adv., agonistics (q.v.)

## agonistics
agonistics, п., athlelics. — See prec. word and -ics.

## agonize
agonize, intr. v., to suffer extreme pain; tr. v. to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:46 COLUMN:2 -->
cause extreme pain, to torture. — F. agoniser.
Ίο begin death agony', fr. ML. agonizdre, fr.
Gk. άγωνίζεσ&αι, 'to contend for a prize, to
struggle', fr. άγων 'assembly; contest in the
games'. See agony and -ize.
Derivatives: agoniz-er, п., agoniz-ing, adj., ag-
oniz-ing-ly, adv.

## agonothete
agonothete, п., leader of the public games in
ancient Greece. — Gk. άγωνο&έτης, 'judge of the
contest', formed fr. άγων, 'contest', and the
stem of τιθέναι, 'to put, place'. See agony and
theme.

## agony
agony, n„ extreme pain. — OF. (= F.) agonie,
fr. Eccles. L. agonia, fr. Gk. αγωνία, 'struggle',
orig. 'struggle for victory in the games', fr. άγων,
'assembly, contest in the games', fr. αγειν, 'to
lead, guide', which is cogn. with L. agere, 'to
set in motion, drive, lead'. See ageat and -y
(representing Gk. -15) and cp. agonist.

## agora
agora, п., an assembly; the place of assembly;
the market place. — Gk. αγορά, rel. to άγείρειν,
'to assemble', άγυρις, 'assembly', αγύρτης,
'beggar', and cogn. with L. grex, gen. gregis,
'flock'. See gregarious and cp. the second
element in allegory, category, panegyric, paregoric.

## agoranome
agoranome, п., a superintendent of the market
(Greek antiq.) — L. agordnomus, fr. Gk. άγορα-
νόμος, 'clerk of the market', fr. αγορά, 'market'
and the stem of νέμειν, 'to divide, distribute'.
See agora and Nemesis.

## agoraphobia
agoraphobia, п., morbid fear of being in open
spaces (med.) — Coined by Westphal in 1871,
who first described this morbid condition. The
word lit. means 'fear of a public place.' See
agora and -phobia.

## agonti
agonti, aguti, aguty, п., a Central-American and
West-Indian rodent. — F., fr. Sp. aguti, a native
Indian name.

## agraffe
agraffe, п., hook, clasp. — F. agrafe, back
formation fr. agrafer, 'to hook, fasten', fr. a, 'to'
(see a), and OF. grafer, 'to fasten with a hook',
fr. grafe, 'hook', fr. OHG. krdpfo, 'hook'.
See grape.

## agraphia
agraphia, п., inability to write; a form of aphasia
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. priv. pref. a-
and -graphia.

## agrarian
agrarian, adj., 1) of the land; 2) of agriculture. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. agrdrius, 'pertaining
to land', fr. ager, gen. agri, 'field, land', which
is rel. to Umbr. ager and cogn. with Gk. αγρός,
'field', Goth, akrs, OE. secer, 'field'. See acre
and agent and cp. agriculture. Cp. also acorn,
agrestic, agrio-, agro-, Agrostis and the second
element in onager.
Derivative: agrarian, n.

## agree
agree, intr. v. — ME. agreen, fr. OF. agreer (F.
agreer), 'to receive with favor', fr. a (F. a), 'to'
(see a), and gre (F. gre), 'will, pleasure', fr. L.
grdtum, neut. of the adjective gmtus, 'acceptable,
pleasing, agreeable, grateful', used as a noun. See
grateful and cp. the second element in maugre.
Derivatives: agreeable (q.v.), agre-ed, adj., agre-
ed-ly, adv., agvee-ing, adj., agree-ing-ly, adv.,
agreement (q.v.)

## agreeable
agreeable, adj. — ME. agreable, fr. OF. agreable
(F. agreable). See agree and -able.
Derivatives: agreeabil-ity, п., agreeable-ness, п.,
agreeabl-y, adv.

## agreement
agreement, n. — OF. agrement (F. agriment), fr.
agreer. See agree and -ment.

## agrestic
agrestic, adj., rustic, rural. — L. agrestis,
'pertaining to the fields', fr. ager, 'field'; see
agrarian. Agrestis has been dissimilated fr. *agrestris.
(Cp. campestris, 'relating to the field', fr.
campus, 'field', and lerrestris, 'earthly', fr. terra,
'earth'.)

## agricolite
agricolite, п., silicate of bismuth (mineral.) —
Named after the German mineralogist Georg
Agricola (1494-1555). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## agriculturalist
agriculturalist, n„ a farmer. — Formed fr. L.
agricultura (see agriculture) with the suffixes -al
and -ist. Cp. agriculturist.

## agriculture
agriculture, n. — F., fr. L. agricultura, lit.
'cultivation of the land', compounded of ager, gen.
agri, 'field, land', and cultura, 'cultivation'. See
agrarian and culture.
Derivatives: agricultur-al, adj., agriculturalist,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:46 COLUMN:3 -->
agriculturist (qq.v.)

## agriculturist
agriculturist, п., an agriculturalist (rare). —
Formed with suff. -ist fr. L. agricultura. See
prec. word.

## Agrimonia
Agrimonia, п., a genus of herbs (hot.) — ModL.
See next word.

## agrimony
agrimony, n. — L. agrimonia, fr. Glc. άργεμώνη,
'a kind of poppy', which is prob. borrowed fr.
Heb. argaman, 'purple'; influenced in form by
L. ager, gen. agri, 'field'. See Argemone.

## agrimotor
agrimotor, п., a machine used in agriculture. —
Compounded of L. ager, gen. agri, 'field' (see
agrarian), and E. motor.

## agrio-
agrio-, combining form meaning 'wild'. — Gk.
άγριο-, fr. άγριος, 'wild', lit. meaning 'living in
the fields', fr. αγρός, 'field', which is cogn. with
L. ager, 'field'. See agrarian.

## agrlology
agrlology, n. the study of prehistoric human
customs. — Compounded of agrio- and Gk. -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one \vho deals (with a certain topic)'.
See -logy.

## agrito
agrito, п., name of the plant called scientifically
Mahonia trifoliata. — Sp., fr. agrio, 'sour', fr.
VL. dcrus, fr. L. deer, 'sharp', in VL. also 'sour'.
Cp. F. aigre, 'sour', which also derives fr. VL.
actus, and see acrid. Cp. also eager and the
second element in vinegar.

## agro-
agro-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
agriculture'. — Gk. άγρο-, fr. αγρός, 'field',
which is cogn. with L. ager, 'field'. See agrarian.

## agronomy
agronomy, п., the science of crop production;
management of land. — F. agronomic, fr. Gk.
αγρονόμος, 'rural', which is compounded of
αγρός, 'field' and the stem of νέμειν, 'to
assign, manage', 'to drive (cattle) to pasture'. See
agrarian and Nemesis.
Derivatives: agronom-ic, agronom-ic-al, adjs.,
agronom-ics, п., agronom-isl, n.

## Agropyron
Agropyron, п., a genus of perennial grasses (bot.)
— ModL., lit. 'field wheat', fr. Gk. αγρός,
'field', and πυρός, 'corn, wheat'. The first
element is cogn. with L. ager, 'field'; see agrarian.
For the second element see pyrene and cp. words
there referred to.

## Agrostemma
Agrostemma, п., a genus of plants of the pink
family; the corn cockle (bot) — ModL. lit.
'crown of the field', fr. Gk. αγρός, 'field', and
στέμμα, 'wreath'. See agro- and stenuna.

## Agrostis
Agrostis, п., a genus of grasses, the bent grass
(bot.) — L. agrostis, 'couch grass', fr Gk.
άγρωστις, fr. αγρός, 'field'. See agro-.

## agrostology
agrostology, п., that branch of botany which deals
with grasses. —Compounded of Gk. άγρωστις,
'grass', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See Agrostis and -logy.

## aground
aground, adv. (naut.) — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
ground.

## agrypnia
agrypnia, п., sleeplessness (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. αγρυπνία, sleeplessness, wakefulness',
fr. άγρυπνος, 'wakeful', which is compounded
of αγρός, 'field', and ΰπνος, 'sleep'; the orig.
meaning of άγρυπνος was 'sleeping in the field*.
See agro- and hypno-.

## aguardiente
aguardiente, п., spirituous liquor. — Sp., lit.
'burning water', compounded of agua, 'water'
fr. L. aqua, and ardiente, fr. L. ardentem, ace. of
ardens, pres. part, oiardere, '10 burn'. See
aquatic and ardent.

## ague
ague, п., malarial fever. — OF. ague, 'an acute
fever', prop. fem. of the adjective agu (F. aigu),
'sharp, acute (scil. fever)', fr. L. (febris) acuta,
'an acute fever', fem. of acutus, 'sharp, acute'.
See acute.
Derivatives: agu-ish, adj., agu-ish-ly, adv., agu-
ish-ness, п., ague-like, adj.

## agunah
agunah, п., a woman prevented from remarrying
because she has no proof of hei; husband's death
(Jewish religion). — Heb. 'aghHndh, lit. 'restrained
(from marrying)', passive fem. part, of 'dghan,
'he restrained, shut up', which is rel. to Arab.
'a'jama, IV (= causative) form of stem '-/-m, 'to
shut up'.

## Agyieus
Agyieus, п., a name of Apollo (Greek mythol.) —
Gk. Άγυιεΰς, lit. 'guardian of the streets', fr.
άγυια, 'street', lit. 'that through which
something is led or driven', fr. άγειν, 'to drive',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:47 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: AGVNARY | 20 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:47 COLUMN:1 -->
which is cogn. with L. agere, 'to set in motion,
drive; to do, act'. See agent, adj.

## agynary
agynary, adj., having no female organs (hot.) —
Formed fr. priv. pref. a-, Gk. γυνή, 'woman'
(see gyneco-), and adj. suff. -ary.

## ah
ah, interj. — Of imitative origin.

## aha
aha, interj. — Of imitative origin.

## Ahabah Rabbah
Ahabah Rabbah, the second of two benedictions
preceding the Shema in the morning prayer
(Jewish liturgy). — Heb. ahubhdK rabbdH, lit.
'with great love' (so called from the two first
words of the text of the benediction). Ahdbhd",
'love', derives fr. ahabh, 'he loved', which is rel.
to Aram, ahabh, 'he loved', and possibly also
to Arab, hdbba, 'he was moved'. Rabbd" is fem.
of rabh, 'great' (whence Mishnaic Heb. rabh,
'master'). See rabbi and cp. the first element in
Jeroboam.

## Ahabath Olam
Ahabath Olam, the second of the two
benedictions preceding the Shema in the evening prayer
(Jewish liturgy). — Heb. akubhdth 'olam, 'with
everlasting love' (so called from the two first
words of the text of the benediction). Ahabhdth
is the state construct of ahabhah, 'love'; see
prec. word. 'Olam means 'eternity' (in Mishnaic
Hebrew also 'world'); see Olam Habba.

## Ahasnerus
Ahasnerus, п., name of a Persian king (Bible);
identical with Xerxes. — Heb. Ahashwerosh
(also, in the kethib of the Book of Esther ro:i,
Ahashresh), fr. OPers. Xshayarshan- (whence
also Gk. Ξέρξης), 'lit. 'male (i.e. hero) among
kings', fr. xshaya-, 'king', and arshan-, 'male,
man*. The first element derives fr. I.-E. base
*qpe(i)-, *qp!(i)-, 'to rule'; see check, 'a sudden
stop'. The second element is cogn. with Gk.
όίρσην, 'male, masculine', Of. fsabhah, 'bull,
steer', fr. I.-E. base *eras-, *ras~, *eres-, *ers-.
Ίο flow, wet, moisten', whence also L. ros, gen.
roris, 'dew'; see roric and cp. rasa. Cp. Xerxes.

## ahead
ahead, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
head.

## aheap
aheap, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and heap.

## ahem
ahem, interj. — Of imitative origin.

## Ahi
Ahi, a serpent in Vedic mythology, identified
with Vritra. — OI. dhih, 'serpent', rel. to Avestic
azish and cogn. with Gk. £χις, 'viper', L. anguis,
'serpent, snake'. See anguine and cp. echidna.

## ahoy
ahoy, interj. — A natural sound, compounded of
the interjections a, 'ah', and hoy. See ah and hoy.

## Ahriman
Ahriman, п., the spirit of evil in the Zoroaslrian
religion. — Gk. 'Αρειμάνιος (in Aristotle) or
Άρειμάνης (in Agathias), fr. Avestic anra mai-
nyu, 'the evil (lit. hostile) spirit'.

## ahull
ahull, adv. (naut.) — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
hull, 'body of a ship'.

## ahura
ahura, п., a benevolent deity (Persian mythology).
— Avestic ahura-, 'a god, a good spirit', rel. to
OI. dsurah, of same meaning. See asura and cp.
the first element in Ormazd.

## Ahura-Mazda
Ahura-Mazda, n. — See Ormazd.

## ai
ai, п., the three-toed sloth. — Tupi ai, a word
imitative of the cry of the animal.

## aid
aid, tr. v. — OF. aidier, aider (F. aider), fr. L.
adjutdre, 'to help', freq. of adjuvdre (pp. adju-
tus), 'to help', sustain', fr. ad- and juvare, 'to
help', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
adjutant, adjuvant, coadjutor, jocund, jury, adj.
Derivatives: aid-er, п., aid-ful, adj.

## aid
aid, n. — OF. (= F.) aide, back formation fr. aider.
See aid, v.

## aide-de-camp
aide-de-camp, aid-de-camp, n. — F. aide-de-camp,
lit. 'camp assistant'. See aid, п., and camp.

## aigrette
aigrette, п., egret. — F. aigrette. See egret.

## aiguille
aiguille, п., ι) a peak shaped like a needle; 2) a
needlelike borer. — F., 'a needle', fr. VL.
*acucula. See agiet.

## aiguillette
aiguillette, п., an aglet. — F., dimin. of aiguille,
'needle*. See prec. word and -ette.

## aikiaite
aikiaite, п., a sulfobismutite of lead and copper
(mineral.) — Named after the English
mineralogist Arthur Aikin. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## ail
ail, tr. and intr. v. — ME. eilen, ailen, fr. OE.
eglan, 'to molest, trouble', rel. to Goth, agls,
'shameful', agio, 'distress, oppression', us-agljan,
'to oppress'.
Derivatives: ail-ing, adj., ail-ment, n.

## Ailanthns
Ailanthns, more correctly Ailantus, the tree of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:47 COLUMN:2 -->
heaven (bot.) — ModL., fr. Amboyna ailamo,
'tree of the gods', or 'tree of heaven'. The
spelling ailanthus is due to a confusion of the end
of this word with Gk. άνθος, 'flower'.

## aile
aile, winged (her.) — F., 'winged', fr. aile, 'a
wing', fr. L. ala. See aisle and cp. aileron,
alar,

## aileron
aileron, п., hinged flap of the wing of an
airplane. — F., 'little wing', dimin. of aile, fr. OF.
ele, fr. L. ala, 'wing'. See aisle and cp. words
there referred to.

## ailette
ailette, п., a steel plate worn on the shoulders for
protection. — F., 'little wing', dimin. of aile,
'wing', fr. L. ala, 'wing'. See aisle and cp.
preceding word. For the ending see suff. -ette.

## ailurophlle
ailurophlle, allurophil, п., a lover of cats. —
Compounded of Gk. αίλουρος, 'cat', and -φίλος,
'loving'. For the first element see Ailurus, for the
second see -phile.

## nilurophobia
nilurophobia, п., morbid fear of cats. —
Compounded of Gk. αίλουρος, 'cat', and -φοβία,
'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See prec. word and
-phobia.

## AUurus
AUurus, п., the genus consisting of the panda
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. αίλουρος, 'cat', which
is of uncertain origin; its derivation fr. Gk.
αίόλος, 'quick moving, rapid', and ουρά, "tail',
is folk etymology. Cp. aehiro-.

## aim
aim, intr. and tr. v. — ME. aimen, eimen, fr. OF.
aesmer, which is formed fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and
esmer, fr. L. aeslimdre, 'to estimate'. See esteem.
Derivatives: aim, п., aim-less, adj., aim-less-
ly, adv.

## air
air, п., atmosphere. — ME. aire, fr. OF. (= F.)
air, fr. L. air (whence also Rum. aer, OProvenc.,
Catal., Sp. aire. Port, air, 'air'), which derives
fr. Gk. άήρ, gen. ήέρος, Att. gen. αέρος, 'air'
(from the Att. ace. ίέρα is borrowed It. aria,
'air'). Gk. άηρ (ср. the parallel forms Aeol.
αυηρ, Dor. άβήρ) and the rel. αδρά, 'air in
motion, breeze', are of uncertain origin. They
are possibly rel. to άείρειν, 'to lift up, raise',
and lit. mean 'that which rises'. See aorta, and
cp. aerate, aerial, aero-, the first element in
aerostat, and the second element in malaria.
Derivatives: air, v., air-able, adj., air-er, п.,
airing, п., air-less, adj., air-y, adj., air-i-ly, adv.,
air-i-ness, n.

## air
air, п., melody, tune. — F., fr. It. aria, of s.m.,
fr. L. aerea, fem. of the adjective dereus,
'pertaining to the air', fr. Sir, 'air'. See prec. word
and cp. aria.

## airplane
airplane, n. — Compounded of air and plane.
See aeroplane.

## aisle
aisle, n. — ME. He, ele, fr. OF. ele (F. aile),
'wing', fr. L. ala, of s.m., which stands for *ag-
s-la and is rel. to axilla, 'armpit', and cogn. with
OI. aksah, 'collarbone', Avestic ashayi (dual
gen.), 'of both shoulders', Arm. anul' (for *as-
nut'), 'armhole", OHG. ahsala, MHG. ahsel,
G. Achsel, ON. iixl, OS. ahsla, OE. eaxl,
'shoulder'. All these words are formed fr. I.-E.
base *ag-, 'to move, drive', with reference to
the arms moved from the shoulders. See agent,
adj., and cp. aileron, ailette, alar, alate, aliform,
aliped, alula, axil, axilla, axillary, axle, oxter,
and the second element in bezel.
Derivative: aisl-ed, adj.

## aitch
aitch, also ache, п., name of the letter A in
English. — ME. ache, fr. OF. (= F.) ache, which
is of uncertain origin. It possibly
derives—together with It. acca and Port, aga, of s.m.—
from a form "hakka, which would stand for
orig. ha-ka (for h-k, i.e. h and к (as the
consonant following h in the alphabet). The
derivation of the French name of the letter h fr. F.
hache, 'ax' (in allusion to the form of the small
h which resembles an ax) is contradicted by the
fact that whereas the letter h is called acca in It.
and aga in Port., the It., resp. Port, name for
the ax is accia, resp. facha.

## aitchbone
aitchbone, n.— Fr. ME. a nache bone, fr. OF. nache,
pi., 'rump', fr. VL. "natica, fr. L. natis, which is
cogn. with Gk. νώτος, νώταν, 'back'; see nates.
The loss of the initial л is due to a misdivision
of a nache bone into an ache bone. Cp. adder,
apron, auger, ekename, ouch, umble pie, umpire.

## ajar
ajar, adv., on the turn, slightly opened. — ME.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:47 COLUMN:3 -->
on char, 'on the turn', fr. a-, 'on', and ME.
chearr, char, 'a turn', fr. OE. cierr, cyrr. See
char, 'a turn of work', and cp. words there
referred to.

## ajar
ajar, adv., out of harmony. — Compounded of
a- 'on' and jar, 'creak'.

## Ajax
Ajax, п., in the Iliad, the name of two Greek
heroes of the Trojan war: Ajax the Greater, son
of Telamon, and Ajax the Less, son of Olleus.—
L. Ajax, fr. Gk. Αίας. The name Αίας prob.
denoted orig. an earth god and derives fr. Gk.
αϊα, 'earth'. See Kretschmer in Glotta 15,1927,
and Frisk, GEW. I, p. 30.

## ajonjoli
ajonjoli, п., sesame. — Sp. ajonjoll fr. Arab, al-
juljuldn, lit. 'the sesam', altered in Spain into al-
juljultn (cp. the Sp. variant aljonjoli).

## Ajuga
Ajuga, п., a genus of plants of the mint family;
the bugle weed (bot.) — A ModL., hybrid
coined fr. Gk. privative pref. a- and L. jugum,
'joke' (see jugular and yoke); so called from the
seeming absence of the upper lip of the corolla.

## akasa
akasa, п., the name of space in Sankhya
philosophy. — OI. akasa-, 'space', formed fr.
emphatic pref. 5 and kdsate, 'appears, shines', prob.
from I.-E. base *q"ek-, *qv'eg-, whence also
Avestic iashman, 'eye', akasat, 'he beheld', Gk.
τέκμωρ, later form τέκμαρ (prob. for *qaeH-
nwr), 'sign, token', OSlav. kazQ, kazati, 'to
show'. Cp. ukase.

## akerite
akerite, п., a quartz syenite (pelrogr.) — Named
between Άραβάρχης in the sense of 'Ruler of
the Arabs', and άραβάρχης, the assimilated
form of άλαβάρχης, title of the chief magistrate
of the Jewish population in Alexandria, a name
which has nothing to do with the Arabs.

## alabaster
alabaster, п., a translucent whitish kind of
gypsum. — OF. alabastre (whence F. albdtre), fr.
L. alabaster, fr. Gk. αλάβαστρος, άλάβαστρον,
fr. earlier άλάβαστας, fr. Egypt *a-la-baste,
'vessel of the goddess Ehaste (— Bubaste). See
Frisk, GEW., p. 62 s.v. άλάβαστος. Ср. alley
'choice marble'.
Derivatives: alabaster, alabastri-an,
alabastrine, adjs.

## alack
alack, interj. — Prob. formed fr. ME. a, 'ah',
and lak, 'loss, failure'. See ah and lack and cp.
lackaday.

## alacran
alacran, п., scorpion. — Sp. fr. Arab, al-'dqrab,
'the scorpion' fr. al-, 'the', and 'dqrab, 'scorpion',
which is rel. to Heb. 'aqrdbh, Aram, 'aqrabbd,
Syr. 'eqqarba, Ethiop. 'aqrab, 'arqab, Akkad.
aqrabu, 'scorpion'.

## alacrity
alacrity, п., eager readiness. — L. alacritds, gen.
-dtis, 'cheerfulness', fr. alacer, fem. alacris, neut.
alacre, 'cheerful', which stands for "ala-tlis and
is cogn. with Goth, aljan, 'zeal', OE. ellen,
OHG. ellian, ellen, of s.m. Cp. allegro. For the
ending see suff. -ity.
Derivative: alacrit-ous, adj.

## nlalte
nlalte, п., a hydrous vanadium pentoxide
(mineral.) — Named after the Alai Mountains. For
the'ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## alalite
alalite, п., a synonym of diopside (mineral) —
Named after Ala in Tirol. For the ending see
combining form -lite.

## alameda
alameda, п., a public walk with poplar trees
(Sp. American). — Sp., fr. alamo, 'poplar'. See
alamo.

## alamo
alamo, п., poplar (Sp. American). — Sp. dlama,
fr. alno, 'the black poplar', fr. L. alnus, 'alder'.
See alder.

## Alan
Alan, masc. PN. — ML. Alanus, of Celtic origin.

## ulanine
ulanine, alanin, п., aminopropionic acid (chem.)
— Prob. formed from the first syllable of
aldehyde, the syllable -an (inserted for euphonic
reasons), and chem. suff. -ine. The name was
coined by Strecker, the discoverer of this
substance, in 1849, who, however, gives no
explanation for the name.

## alar
alar, adj., 1) pertaining to a wing; 2) winglike;
3) in anatomy, axillary. — L. dl&ris, 'of the
wing', fr. ala, 'wing'. See aisle.

## Alaric
Alaric, masc. PN. — L. Alaricus, a name of Visi-
gothic origin lit. meaning 'all-ruler', fr. Teut.
*ala-, 'all', and *rikja, 'rule'. See all and Reich
and cp. the 2nd element in Roderick, Theodoric.

## alarm
alarm, n. — F. alarme, fr. It. all'arme, 'to arms'
(lit. 'to the arms'), fr. aile (pi. fem.), 'to the',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:48 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 21 | ALCAIDE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:48 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. a (fr. L. ad), 'to', and le, 'the', fr. L. illae,
'those' (fem.) See ad-, ille and arm, 'weapon',
and cp. alarum. For a similar fusion of the
article with the following word cp. alert.
after Aker in Sweden. For the ending see subst.
surf. -ite.

## akimbo
akimbo, adv. and adj. — ME. in kenebowe, prob.
of Scand. origin. Cp. Icel. kengboginn, 'bent into
a curve', and see kiuk and bow, 'a weapon'.

## akin
akin, adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'of, and kin.

## akinesia
akinesia, п., absence of motion in a muscle (med.)
— Medical Latin, fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. xt-
νησις, 'motion', fr. κϊνεΐν, 'to move'. See
kinesis and -ia.

## Akkadian
Akkadian, also Accadian, adj. and n. — Formed
with suff. -ian fr. Heb. Akkad (Gen. lo: 10),
name of a district and city in Babylonia.

## al-
al-, assimilated form of ad- before /.

## -al
-al, suff. forming adjectives, as in royal, or
substantives of adjectival origin, as in rival. —
Either fr. F. -al, -el, or directly fr. L. adj. suff.
-alis. In many cases the suff. -alis was used
already in Latin both adjectivally and substantiv-
ally (cp. L. rivalis, 'pertaining to a brook; one
who uses the same brook; neighbor;
competitor, rival', and see rival). Cp. the suffixes -ial
and -ar.

## -al
-al, suff. forming verbal nouns, as arrival,
avowal. — L. -alia, neut. pi. of -alis, but in Vulgar
Latin mistaken for the fem. sing. suff.; formed
either directly from Latin or through the
medium of OF., F. -aille (as in OF. arrivaille, etc.).

## -al
-al, chem. suff. denoting aldehyde as in brome/,
chlora/. — F., from the first syllable of aldehyde.

## ula
ula, п., a wing or anything similar to a wing (anat.)
— L. See aisle and cp. alar.

## a in
a in, short for ά Ια mode, 'in the fashion or style
of, as ά lafranfaise, 'in the French fashion or
style'. — See a and ille.

## alabamine
alabamine, п., name of a chemical element
discovered in 1931 by the American chemist Fred
Allison (1882- ) and his collaborators and
named by them after the Alabama Polytechnic
Institute; now called astatine. For the ending
see chem. suff. -ine.

## alahaudite
alahaudite, п., manganese sulfide (mineral.) —
Named after Alabanda in Asia Minor. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## ulabarch
ulabarch, п., title of the chief official of the Jews
of Alexandria during the Grecian period. —
Gk. άλαβάρχης, which lit. means 'ink ruler',
and origin, denoted an official in charge of
the 'written' notes or records. — Gk. άλα-
βάρχης, is compounded of £λαβα, 'ink' (He-
sychius), and άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler' (see
-arch). The parallel form άραβάρχης is
secondary and due to assimilation — Most
dictionaries either do not deal with the etymology of
the word alabarch at all, or content themselves
with the stereotypic remark:'origin unknown'.—
In the Addenda et Corrigenda to Liddell and
Scott's Greek-English Lexicon, new (ninth) 'ed.
(reprinted 1951). p. 2053a s.v. Άραβάρχης, the
word Άλαβάρχης is explained as dissimilated
fr. Άραβάρχης, 'ruler of the Arabs, emir'. —
The fact is, however, that we must distinguish
Derivatives: alarm, tr. v., alarm-able, alarm-ed,
adjs., alarm-ed-ly, adv., alarm-ing, adj., alarm-
ing-ly, adv., alarmist (q.v.)

## alarmist
alarmist, п., ι) one who starts alarming rumors;
2) one easily frightened. — A hybrid coined fr.
F. alarme (see prec. word) and -ist, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## alarum
alarum, n. — A poetical variant of alarm.

## alary
alary, adj., pertaining to wings. — L. alarius, fr.
ala, 'wing'. See aisle and -ary and cp. alar.

## alas
alas, interj. — F. helas, composed of he, a word
of imitative origin, and las, 'tired, weary', in OF.
also meaning 'unfortunate', fr. L. lassus, 'tired,
weary'. See lassitade and late. E. alas was prob.
influenced in form by alack (q.v.)

## Alastor
Alastor, п., son of Neleus and brother of Nestor
in Greek mythology; fig. used in the sense of an
avenging spirit. — Gk. 'Αλάστωρ,ΙίΙ. 'wanderer',
a derivative of ibxaSkti, 'to wander, roam'. See
hallucinate and cp. the first element in Aleo-
chara.

## ulastrim
ulastrim, п., a mild form of smallpox (med.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:48 COLUMN:2 -->
Port., fr. alastrar, 'to ballast a ship', fig. to
cover all over, spread, strew', fr. a (fr. L. ad),
'to',and lastro, 'ballast', fr. O.Last, 'load, charge,
burden, weight'. See ad- and last, 'burden'.

## alate
alate, alated, adj., winged. — L. alatus, 'winged',
fr. ala, 'wing'. See aisle and adj. suff. -ate and
cp. words there referred to.

## alatern
alatern, alaternus, п., a buckthorn (Rhamnus ala-
ternus). — L. alaternus, 'buckthorn', of
Etruscan origin.

## Alauda
Alauda, п., a genus of birds, the skylark (orni-
thol.) — ModL., fr. L. alauda, 'lark', of Gaulish
origin, and prob. literally meaning 'tufted'.

## alazor
alazor, п., the safflower. — Sp„ fr. Arab, al-usfBr,
in vulgar pronunciation al-'osfdr, fr. al-, 'the',
and 'usfur, resp. osfOr, 'safflower'.

## alb
alb, a long white vestment. — ML. alba for L.
alba (vestis), 'white (garment)', fem. of albus,
