'white'; cogn. with Gk. άλφος, 'duli-white
leprosy', &λφι, άλφντον, 'barley meal', OHG.
агйн'з, ~е!Ыз. OE. elfel, 'swan', lit. 'the white
bird', OSlav., Russ. lebedi, Serb, labud, Pol.
labedz, Czech labud, 'swan', for orig. *olb-edi,
"olb-edt, *olb-odi, 'the white bird'. Cp. also Arm.
alauni, 'white pigeon, dove', Alb. el'p, еГЫ,
'barley', Hitt. alpash, 'cloud'. Cp. abele, ablet,
albedo, albescent, albino, albite, albo-, Albuca, ul-
bugo, album, albumen, albumin, alburnum, al-
phitomancy, aubade, aube, auburn, danb,

## albacore
albacore, п., a species of tunny (zool.) — Sp. alba-
cora, fr. Arab, albakra", 'the young camel', fr. al-,
'the', and the collective noun bakr, 'young
camels', whence bakra", "young she-camel', rel.
to bikr, 'virgin, woman having first child', from
the stem of the verb bakara, 'he rose early, did
something early', and to Heb. b'khdr, 'first
born', b'khord1*, 'the right of first born', bikh-
rdh, 'young camel', bikkurdh, 'first ripe fig',
bikkurfm, 'first fruits', Ethiop. bakur, 'first
born'.

## ulbatross
ulbatross, n. — Port alcatraz, 'cormorant,
pelican' (whence also F. albatros), a variant of
alcatruz, 'the bucket of a water wheel', fr. Arab.
al-qadus, 'machine for drawing water; jar', fr.
al-, 'the', and Gk. κάδος, 'jar', which is a loan
word from Heb. kadh, of s.m. The name was
orig. applied to the pelican as 'the water carrier',
i.e. the bird that carries water in its pouch. For
sense development cp. Arab, saqqd, 'pelican',
lit. 'water carrier'. The alteration of Port,
alcatraz to E. albatross (after L. albus, 'white') was
prob. suggested by the white color of the
albatross. ModPort. albatroz has been reborrowed
fr. F. albatros. Cp. akatras.

## Alban
Alban, masc. PN. — L. Albanus, lit. 'of Alba', fr.
Alba, name of the mother city of Rome.

## albedo
albedo, п., the ratio of light reflected from a
surface (astron.) — L. albedo, 'whiteness', fr. albus,
'white'. See ulb.

## albeit
albeit, conj. — ME. al be it, 'all through it be',
compounded of all, be and it. Cp. although.

## alberca
alberca, п., a waterhole. — Sp., 'sink, pool', fr.
Arab, al-birka*, fr. al-, 'the', and btrka", 'sink,
pool', which is rel. to Heb. b'rekhd", Aram.
b'rekhtd, 'pool, pond'.

## Albert
Albert, masc. PN. — F., fr. OHG. Adalbert, lit.
'bright through nobility', fr. adal, 'nobility',
and berahl, 'bright'. Cp. Ethelbert, fr. OE. A3del-
bryght, which is the exact equivalent of OHG.
Adalbert. For the first element see atheling and
cp. words there referred to. For the second
element see bright and cp. the second element
in the names Egbert, Gilbert, Herbert, Hubert,
Lambert.

## albert
albert, n. — Shortened from Albert chain; named
after Albert, the Prince Consort (1819-61) of
Queen Victoria.

## Alberta
Alberta, ferft. PN. — Formed fr. Albert.

## albertite
albertite, п., a bituminous mineral. — Named
after Albert County in New Brunswick, where
it is found. For the ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## albescence
albescence, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -ce.

## albescent
albescent, adj., becoming white. — L. albescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of aibescere, 'to become
white', inchoative of alblre, 'to be white', fr.
albus, 'white'. See ulb and -escent.

## Albigenses
Albigenses, n. pi., religious reformers in southern

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:48 COLUMN:3 -->
France between 1020 and 1250. — ML., so
called fr. Albi or Albigia, a town in Languedoc
in France where they resided and where their
tenets were first condemned (in 1176).

## Albin
Albin, masc. PN. — L. Albinus, a Roman
cognomen, fr. albus, 'white'. See alb and cp.
Albina.

## Albinn
Albinn, Albinia, fem. PN. — Fem. of L. Albinus.
See Albin.

## albino
albino, п., man or animal lacking in
pigmentation.—Port., fr. L. albus, 'white', orig. applied
by the Portuguese to African Negroes who were
mottled with white spots. See alb.
Derivatives: albin-ic, adj., albin-ism, n.

## Albion
Albion, ancient name of England. — L., fr. a
non-Aryan base *alb, 'mountain', whence also
Alba, Irish name of Scotland, L. Alpes, 'the
Alps'. See alp, 'high mountain'.

## albite
albite, п., a white feldspar (mineral.) — Formed
with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. albus, 'white'. See alb.

## Albizzia
Albizzia, п., name of a genus of the mimosa
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Albizzi, name of an
Ital. family, one of whom is said to have
introduced it into Italy. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## albo-
albo-, before a vowel alb-, combining form
meaning 'white'. —Fr. L. albus, 'white'. See alb.

## albricias
albricias, п., a gift to the bringer of good news. —
Sp., rel. to Port, alvifaras, Valencian albixeres;
fr. Arab, al-bishdra", fr. al-, 'the', and bishdra",
'tidings, gifl for good tidings', rel. to hashtra,
'he was glad, joyful', bashshara, 'he gladdened
somebody with good tidings', Heb. b'sord",
'tidings, good tidings, reward for good tidings',
bisser, 'he brought tidings, gladdened with good
tidings', Ethiop. absdra, Syr. sabbar (with
metathesis), 'he brought good tidings', Ugar. bshr,
Akkad. bussuru, 'to bring good tidings'.

## Albuca
Albuca, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. albucus, 'the asphodel',
lit. 'the white plant', fr. albus, 'white'. See alb.

## albugo
albugo, п., a white spot on the cornea of the
eye. — L. albugo, 'a white spot, a disease of the
eye, a film', fr. albus, 'white'; see alb. For the
suff. cp.aerugo, 'rust of copper' (see aeruginous).

## album
album, п., a blank book for pictures, stamps,
autographs, etc. — L. album, *a white tablet, on which
various kinds of notices were inscribed'; prop,
neuter of albus, 'white', used as a noun. See alb.

## albumen
albumen, п., the white of an egg. — L. albumen,
gen. albuminis, fr. albus, 'white'. See alb and cp.
cerumen.OeTivauves'.albumen-ize,tT.v.,albumen-
iz-ation, n.

## albumin
albumin, п., one of a class of proteins (biochem.)
— See albumen and chem. suff. -in.

## albumiaoid
albumiaoid," adj., resembling albumin, п.,
protein. — A hybrid coined fr. albumin, a word of
Latin origin, and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## albuminous
albuminous, adj., of, like, or containing albumen
or albumin. — Formed fr. albumen with suff.
-oils (as if fr. L. *albuminosus).

## albuminuria
albuminuria, п., the presence of albumen in the
urine (med.) — Medical L., fr. F. albuminuric
a hybrid coined by the French physician Martin
Solon (1795-1856) in 1838 fr. L. albumen, 'white
of the egg', and Gk. oupov, 'urine'. See albumen,
urine and -ia.

## albumose
albumose, п., proteose formed from albumin
(biochem.) — Coined by Mialhe in 1846 fr.
albumin and subst. suff. -ose.

## alburnum
alburnum, п., sap wood. — L. alburnum (whence
also OF. aubour, and, with change of suff., F.
aubier), prop. neut. of the adjective alburnus,
'white, whitish', fr. albus, 'white'. See alb and
cp. auburn.

## Alca
Alca, п., a genus of birds of the auk family (or-
nithol.) — ModL. See auk and cp. Alcedinidae.

## alcabala
alcabala, п., excise. — Sp., fr. Arab. al-qabdlah,
fr. al-, 'the', and qabdlah, 'act of receiving'.
See cabal.

## Alcaic
Alcaic, adj., pertaining to Alcaeus or to either of
the two meters invented by him. — L. Alcaicus,
fr. Gk. Άλκαΐκός, 'pertaining to or used by
Alcaeus', fr. 'Αλκαίος, Alcaeus, a poet who
lived in Mytileneabout6coB.C.E. For the ending
see suff. -ic.

## alcaide
alcaide, п., commander of a fortress; warden of
a prison. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-qd'id, 'the leader'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:49 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ALCALDE | 22 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:49 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. al-, 'the', and part, oiqada, 'he led (the army)"
Cp. kaid.

## alcalde
alcalde, n. the mayor of a Spanish town. — Sp.,
fr. Arab, al-qadi, 'the judge', formed fr. al-,
'the', and part, of qddd, 'he decided*. See cadi.

## alcatras
alcatras, п., the pelican; the frigate bird. — Port.
alcairaz. See albatross.

## alcazaba
alcazaba, п., fortress. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-qasaba",
'the fortress', from al-, 'the', and qdsabah, 'city,
capital, fortress', fr. qdsaba, 'he cut, chopped
up', which is rel. to Heb. qatzdbh, 'he cut off',
Mishnaic Heb. qatzlzabh, 'butcher', Aram.
qatztzabha, of s.m. (Arab, qassdbh, 'butcher', is
a Hebrew loan word.)

## alcazar
alcazar, п., a castle, a palace. — Sp., fr. Arab.
al-qasr, 'the castle', fr. al-, 'the', and L. castrum,
'fortified place, fort, castle'. See castrameta-
tion and cp. castle.

## Alcedinidae
Alcedinidae, n. pi., a family of birds comprising
the kingfishers (ornilhol.) — ModL., formed
with suff. -idae fr. L. alcedo, 'kingfisher', which
is latinized fr. Gk. άλκυών, on analogy of Latin
words ending in -edd. See halcyon.

## Alces
Alces, п., the genus of the elk (zool.) — L. aids,
'elk', a loan word fr. Teut. *αΙχύ. Ср. ON. elgr,
OHG. elaho, 'elk' and see elk.

## Alcestis
Alcestis, п., wife of Admetus, one of the
Argonauts; she offered her life for her husband but
was rescued from the lower world by Heracles
(Greek mythol.) — L. Alcestis, fr. Gk. "Αλκηστις,
lit. 'valiant, courageous', fr. αλκή, 'protection,
help, strength, power, courage'. See Alexander.

## alchemist
alchemist, n. — OF. alqemisle (F. alchimiste), fr.
alqemie. See alchemy and -ist.

## Alchemilla
Alchemilla, п., a genus of plants of the rose family;
the lady's-mantle (bot.). — ModL., fr. Port.
alchimelech, fr. Arab, iklil al-matik, 'the crown
of the king'. The first element is prob. a loan
word fr. Aram, k'lll, k*lild, 'crown'. For the
second element see nrnlik, Mameluke.

## alchemy
alchemy, n. medieval chemistry. — OF. alquemie
(13th cent.), alchimie (14th cent.) (F. alchimie),
fr. ML. alchemia, fr. Arab, al-kimiyd, fr. al-,
'the', and MGk. χημεία, χημία, prop, 'the art
of the black and (Egypt)', fr. Gk. Χημία, 'Black-
land, Egypt', fr. Egypt, khem, khame, 'black'.
The derivation from Gk. χυμεία, 'pouring',
from the stem of χέειν, 'to pour', is folk
etymology. See W. Muss-Ainolt, Transactions of
the American Philological Association, vol.
XXIII, p. 149. Cp. chemical, chemist, chemistry.
Derivatives: alchem-ic, alchem-ic-al, adjs., al·
chem-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Alcmaeon
Alcmaeon, п., one of the epigones (Greek mythol.)
— L. Alcmaeo(n), fr. Gk. 'Αλκμαίων, prob.
meaning lit. 'valiant, brave'. Cp. Gk. άλκμαΐος
(Hesychius), 'young man', άλκμαρές (neut.)
(ibidem), 'strong, powerful'.

## Alcmene
Alcmene, п., the mother of Hercules (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Αλκμήνη, lit. 'the strong
one', fr. αλκή, 'strength, power'. See Alexaader.

## alcohol
alcohol, n. — ML., fr. Arab, al-kohl, vulgar
pronunciation of al-kuhl, fr. al-, 'the', and kohl,
resp. kuhl, 'antimony (used for painting the
eyelids)', which is rel. to Heb. kahdl (Ezek. 23:40);
'he painted the eyelids with antimony', Aram.-
Syr. k'hal, Ethiop. kahdla, of s.m., Aram.
kuhld, Ethiop. kuhel, 'antimony'. (Akkad. guhlu,
'antimony', is prob. a WSem. loan word.)Its
modern sense ('highly rectified spirits') is due to the
analogy of the fineness of this powder. Cp. kobl.
Derivatives: alcohol-ic, adj., alcohol-lc-ally,
adv., alcohol-ism, п., alcohol-ize, tr. v.

## alcoholometer
alcoholometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the alcoholic strength of liquids. — A hybrid
coined fr. alcohol and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## Alcoran
Alcoran, n. — F. alcoran, fr. Arab, al-qur'dn, 'the
Koran', fr. al·, 'the', and qur'an, lit. 'reading'.
See Koran.

## alcomoque
alcomoque, п., the bark of several trees. — Sp.,
Port, 'cork tree', a hybrid coined fr. Arab, al-,
'the', and L. quercus, 'oak', changed into *quer-
nus. See cork and cp. Quercus.

## nlcove
nlcove, п., ι) a recessed section in a room; 2) any
recess. — F. alcove, fr. Sp. alcoba, fr. Arab, al-
qubba*, fr. al-, 'the', and qubba*, 'arch, vaulted
tent', which is rel. to Arab, qdbba, 'it was bent',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:49 COLUMN:2 -->
and to Heb. qubbd", 'vaulted tent', Syr. q'bhd-
bhd, 'vault, vaulted tent', Akkad. qababut
'shield'. All these words are derivatives of the
Sem. base q-b-b, 'to be bent, crooked, vaulted'.

## aldea
aldea, п., hamlet, villa. — Sp. and Port.,
'hamlet', fr. Arab, al-, 'the', and ddyah, 'farm,
hamlet'. Cp. aldeia.

## Aldebaran
Aldebaran, п., a red star in the constellation
Taurus (astron.) — Arab. Al-Dabaran, lit. 'the
following (star)', fr. ddbara, 'he followed'; so
called in reference to its position with regard to
Pleiades.

## aldehyde
aldehyde, n. (chem) — Coined by the German
chemist Justus von Liebig (1803-73) from the
abbreviation of α/cohol dehydrogenatum,
'alcohol deprived of hydrogen'.

## aldeia
aldeia, п., hamlet. — Port, aldeia. See alden.

## alder
alder, п., tree rel. to the birch. — ME., formed
with excrescent d fr. OE. alor, which is rel. to
OS. elora, ON. Sir, Dan. elle, el, Swed. al,
MDu. else, Du. els, OHG. erila (fr. earlier
elira), G. Erie, fr. Teut. *aliso; cogn. with
Russ. olicha (for *alisa-), 'alder', Pol. olcha, of
s.m., OSlav. jelicha, L. alnus. (for 'alsnos), Lith.
alksnis (with excrescent k), OPruss. alskande.
All these words possibly derive fr. I.-E. base
"el-, *ol-, 'yellow'. Cp. OHG. elo, 'yellow', and
see elk. See also elm and elder, the tree, and cp.
alamo, alameda, allso, Alnus. Cp. also F. alise,
'sorb apple', which is a Frankish loan word.

## alder
alder, п., head of family, chief. — OE. aldor, eal-
dor, fr. aid, eald, 'old'. See old and -or, -er.
Derivatives: alder-dom, п., alderman (q.v.)

## alderman
alderman, n. — OE. (e)aldorman, 'prince, chief,
compounded of (e)aldor, 'chief, and man. See
alder, 'chief, and man. Derivatives: alderman-ic,
adj., alderman-су, п., alderman-ess, п., alderman-
ly, adj., alderman-ry, п., alderman-ship, n.

## Aldine
Aldine, adj., printed by Aldus Manutius (1450-
1515). — Formed with adj. suff. -ine fr. Latin-
ization of It. Aldo, an abbreviated form of Teo-
baldo. See Theobald.

## ale
ale, n. — OE. ealo, alo, rel. to ON. 67, and cogn.
with L. alumen, 'alum', fr. I.-E. base "alu-,
'bitter'. OPruss. alu, 'mead', Lith. aids, OSlav.
olu, 'beer', are Teut. loan words. Cp. alum,
alumina, alnta, alntaceous.

## aleatory
aleatory, adj., depending on chance. — L. alea-
torius, 'pertaining to a gamester', fr. alea, 'die,
game of hazard', prob. meaning orig. 'mere
chance', and derived fr. Gk. άλεός, a collateral
form of ήλεός, 'wandering in mind, distraught,
foolish'. See Aleocbara and the adj. suffixes -ate
and -ory.

## aleberry
aleberry, n. — Compounded of ule and ME. bre,
'brewis, broth', fr. OE. briw. See brew, brewis.

## alec
alec, п., herring; ush pickle. — L. al(J)ec, hal-
(l)ec, also allex, hallix, prob. borrowed fr. Gk.
£λ(λ)ηξ, a var. of £λιξ, 'alec, fish pickle'.

## aleconner
aleconner, п., an old official who tested the
quality of ale (English hisl.) — Compounded of ale,
con, 'to examine', and agential suff. -er.

## alectryomachy
alectryomachy, п., cock-fighting. —
Compounded of Gk. άλεκτρυών, 'cock', and μάχη, 'battle,
fight'. The first element lit. means 'warder off,
fighter', and is rel. to άλέξειν, 'to ward, drive
or keep off, άλεξητήρ, 'fighter', άλκτήρ, of
s.m. See Alexander and cp. the first element in
next word and the second element in hippalec-
tryon. For the second element in alectryomachy
see -machy.

## alectryomancy
alectryomancy, п., divination by means of a cock
and grains of corn. — Compounded of Gk.
άλεκτρυών, 'cock', and μαντεία, 'oracle,
divination'. See prec. word and -mancy.

## alee
alee, adv., on or toward the lee (naut.) — Formed
fr. a-, 'on', and lee. Derivative: alee, adj.

## Alemauni
Alemauni, also Alamanni, n. pi., Suebic tribes,
who settled in Alsace and part of Switzerland.—
L., fr. Teut. Alamann- which prob. means 'the
aliens', lit. 'foreign men'. The al- in Al-e-manm
Al-a-manni lit. means 'other, foreign', and is of
the same origin as al- in L. al-ius, 'the other', in
the tribe name Al-lobrogi (see Allobrogi), and
el- in else (q.v.) Cp. alias and Alsatia. For the
second element in Al-e-manrii, Al-a-mannJ see
man. Cp. F. allemand, 'German', which also
derives fr. Teut. Alamann- (see allemande).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:49 COLUMN:3 -->

## alembic
alembic, n. — ME., fr. OF. ( = F.) alambic, fr.
OSp. (= Sp.) alambique fr. Arab, al-anbfq, 'the
still*, which is formed fr. e/-,'the', and Gk. ίίμβιξ,
'cup, cap of a still, alembic', which is of
uncertain, possibly Semitic origin. Cp. It. lambicco,
which is of the same origin as Sp. alambique.

## Alenu
Alenu, п., concluding prayer (Jewish liturgy). —
Heb. 'alenu, lit. 'upon us', formed fr. 'al, 'on,
upon', with -inu, the pronom. suff. of the ist
person in the plural. The prayer is so called
from the first words 'aUnu leshabbg"h, 'it is
(incumbent) upon us to praise'. Heb. 'al is rel. to
'aid", 'he went up'. See aliyah.

## Aleochara
Aleochara, п., a genus of rove beetles (entomol.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. όίλεός, a
collateral form of ήλεός, 'wandering in mind,
distraught, foolish', and χαρά, 'joy'. The first
element is rel. to άλασθαι, 'to wander, roam*; see
hallucinate and cp. Alastor, aleatory. The second
element is rel. to χαίρειν, 'to rejoice', χάρις,
'grace, kindness'; see Charis.

## aleph
aleph, п., name of the Ist letter of the Heb.
alphabet. — Heb. dleph, pausal form of eleph, 'ox';
so called in allusion to the ancient Hebrew form
of this letter, representing the head of an ox. Cp.
alpha. For the foim cp. daleth, lamedh, samekh.

## alepidote
alepidote, adj., without scales (zool.) — Gk.
άλεπίδωτος,- fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
λεπιδωτός, 'covered with scales', fr. λεπίς, gen.
λεπίδος, 'scale'. See lepido-, leper.
Derivative: alepidote, п., a fish without scales.

## alerce
alerce, alerze, п., the sandarac tree. — Sp., 'the
larch tree', fr. Arab, al-arz, in vulgar
pronunciation al-erz, fr. al-, 'the', and arz, resp. erz,
'coniferous tree, pine tree, cedar', borrowed fr.
Heb. erez, 'cedar'.

## alert
alert, adj., watchful; active, nimble. — F. alerte,
fr. earlier a I'erte, a I'airte, fr. It. all'erta, lit.
'on the height', fr. erta, 'height', prop. fern, of
erto, 'steep, precipitous', pp. oiergere, 'to erect,
raise', used as a noun, fr. L. Irigere. See erect.
Derivatives: alert-ly, adv., alert-ness, n.

## Alethea
Alethea, fem. PN. — Gk. αλήθεια, 'truth', fr.
αληθής, 'true'. See aletho- and cp. Philathea.

## alethiology
alethiology, п., the science of truth. — G. Alethi-
ologie, compounded of Gk. αλήθεια, 'truth' (fr.
αληθής, 'true'), and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See aletho- and -logy.
The word was first used by J. H. Lambert in his
Neues Organon (in 1764).

## aletho-
aletho-, combining form meaning 'true'. —Gk.
άληθο-, fr. άληΰ-ής, 'true', lit. 'not concealing',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and λήθη, 'forgetful-
ness, oblivion', which is cogn. with L. latere,
*to lie hid or concealed, to lurk'. See latent and
cp. Lethe, Alethea.

## Alethopterls
Alethopterls, п., a genus of fossil ferns, found
especially in the coal formation. — ModL., lit.
'having true ferns', coined by Sternberg fr.
aletho- and Gk. πτέρις, 'fern', which is rel. to
πτερόν, 'feather, wing'. See ptero-.

## Aletris
Aletris, п., a genus of plants; the colic root (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. άλετρίς, *a female slave, who
grinds corn', fr. άλεΐν, 'to grind' (see next
word); so called from the mealy appearance of
its blossoms.

## aleurone
aleurone, also aleuron, п., a proteid substance
found in cereals (biochem.) — Gk. α'λευρον,
'wheat flour', fr. άλεΐν, 'to grind', which is
cogn. with Arm. alam, Ί grind, pulverize*, aleur,
'flour', and prob. also with OI. anuh (for *al-
nuh), 'thin, fine'. Cp. prec. word and the first
element in Aleyrodes.

## alevin
alevin, п., a young fish. — F., 'fry, young fish',
fr. OF. alevain, fr. VL. "allevamen, fr. L. alle-
vare, 'to lift up, lighten, alleviate', in VL. also
'to bring up, rear', fr. ad- and levare, 'to raise,
lift up'. Ste lever and cp. elevate. The French
form alevin (fr. OF. alevain) is due to the change
of suff. -ain (fr. L. -amen) to suff. -in (fr. L. -inus).

## Alexander
Alexander, masc. PN. — L. Alexander, fr. Gk.
'Αλέξανδρος, lit., 'defender of men', fr. άλέξειν,
'to ward off, keep off, turn away, defend,
protect, and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man'. Άλέξειν is
desiderative of άλέκειν, 'to ward off', which is
related to αλκή, 'protection, help, strength,
power, courage', όλκιμος, 'strong', and cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:50 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 23 | ALIEN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:50 COLUMN:1 -->
with ΟΙ. rdksati, 'protects', OE. ealgian, 'to
defend', and possibly also with OE. ealh, OS.
alah, Goth, alhs, 'temple', OLith. elkas, alkas,
'sacred wood', Lett, elks, 'idol'. Cp. Alcmene,
alexin, alexipharmic, Alexis, Alexius, Alcestis,
analcite. Cp. also lac, 'one hundred thousand'.
For the 2nd element in Alexander see andro-.

## alexanders
alexanders, the meadow parsnip. — Lit. 'the
flower of Alexander (the Great)'; so called for
its brilliant color suggesting royalty.

## Alexandrine
Alexandrine, п., a verse of six iambic feet, having
the caesura after the third. — F. alexandrin; so
called because first used by the French poet
Alexandre de Paris (de Bernai) in a poem on
Alexander the Great, dating from the 13th cent.

## alexandrite
alexandrite, п., a dark green variety of chryso-
beryl (mineral) — Named after Alexander II
of Russia. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## alexia
alexia, п., inability to read (med.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. λέξις, 'speech',
from the stem of λέγειν, to tell, say, speak'
(see lexicon), but confused in meaning with L.
legcre, 'to read'. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## alexin
alexin, п., a substance which destroys bacteria
(immunology). — Coined by the German
bacteriologist Hans Buchner (1850-1902) in 1888, fr.
Gk. άλέξειν, 'to ward off, keep off, protect'.
See Alexauder and chem. suff. -in.

## alexipharntic
alexipharntic, adj. counteracting poison,
antidotal. — Gk. άλεξιφάρμακος, 'acting as an
antidote', fr. άλέξειν, 'to ward off, keep off,
protect', and φάρμακον, 'drug, poison'. See
Alexander, pharmacy and -ic.
Derivative: alexipharmic, п., an antidote.

## nlexipyrefjc
nlexipyrefjc, adj., keeping off fever. —
Compounded of Gk. άλέξειν, 'to ward off, keep
off, protect', and πυρετός, 'fever', fr. πϋρ, 'fire'.
See Alexander and pyretic.
Derivative: alexipyretic, n.

## Alexis
Alexis, masc. PN. — Gk. "Αλεξις, fr. άλέξειν, 'to
ward off, keep off, protect'. See Alexander and
cp. next word.

## Alexius
Alexius, masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. "Αλέξιος, lit.
'defender, helper', fr. άλέξειν. See prec. word.

## Aleyrodes
Aleyrodes, п., a genus of insects (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. άλευρώδης, 'resembling flour',
compounded of ίίλευρον, 'wheat flour', and
-ώδης, 'like'. See aleuron and -ode, 'like'.

## alezan
alezan, п., a sorrel horse. — Sp. alazan (whence
F. alezan), 'sorrel-colored (horse)', fr. Arab, al-
hisdn, 'the noble and beautiful horse'.

## alfa
alfa, п., the esparto grass. — Arab, halfd', rel.
to Mishnaic Heb. heleph, Aram, hil'phd, 'rush,
reed', from stem b-l-p, 'to be sharp, cut through,
pierce'. Cp. acalephe.

## alfalfa
alfalfa, п., lucerne. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-fdsfasa*.
(Cp. the collateral Sp. form alfalfez, which
represents the intermediate form between Arab.
al-fasfasah and Sp. alfalfa).

## alfaqui
alfaqui, п., a Mohammedan scholar. — Sp., fr.
Arab. al-faqfh, fr. al-, 'the', and faqih, 'learned,
intelligent', fr. fiqk, 'knowledge, intelligence'.

## alfenide
alfenide, п., an alloy of nickel and silver. — So
called after the chemist Halphen, who invented
this alloy in 1850. For the ending see suff. -lde.

## Alfred
Alfred, masc. PN. — OE. ASIfrSd, compounded
of self, 'elf', and rxd, 'counsel'. See elf and read.

## alfresco
alfresco, adv. and adj., in the open air. — It. al
fresco, lit. 'in the fresh (air)'. It. al, lit. 'to the',
is formed fr. a, 'to' (fr. L. ad), and the def. article
il (fr. L. ille, 'that'); see ad- and ille and cp. al
segno. For It. fresco see fresco.

## alga
alga, n. — L., 'sea weed', cogn. with OI. ijisah,
'viscous, sticky', Norw. ulka, 'moldy; slime',
fr. I.-E. base *el-, *ol-, 'to putrefy, rot', whence
also Norw. ul, 'moldy', Swed. ul, 'rancid', L.
ulva, 'sedge'. Cp. Ulva.

## Algae
Algae, n. pi., a division of plants of the Thallo-
phyta (hot.) — L., pi. of alga. See prec. word.

## algalia
algalia, п., the abelmosk. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-
gdliya", 'the civet'; so called in allusion to its
musky seeds.

## algarroba
algarroba, п., ι) the carob tree; 2) the common
mesquite (Prosopis julifiora). — Sp., fr. Arab.
al-kharraba", 'the carob', fr. al-, 'the', and
kharruba*, 'carob tree'. See carob.

## algarrobilla
algarrobilla, п., a yellow dye from the seeds and
pods of Prosopis Julifiora. — Sp., a dimin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:50 COLUMN:2 -->
formed fr. algarroba.

## algebra
algebra, n. — Fr. Arab, al-jabr (in vulgar
pronunciation al-jebr), 'reunion (of broken parts in
equations)', short for al-jabr w'al-muqdbalah,
'reunion and comparison', title of a work written
by Mohammed ibn Miisa al-Khowarizmi,
great mathematician of the 9th cent. The title
refers to, and the work deals with, the solution
of equations, which was the original scope of
algebra. Al-jabr is formed fr. al-, 'the', and jabr,
'reunion', which is rel. to the verb ja'bara, 'he
bound together, united'. Cp. algorism.
Derivatives: algebra-ic, algebra-ic-al, adjs., al-
gebra-ic-al-ly, adv., algebraization (q.v.),
algebraist (q.v.)

## algebraist
algebraist, п., an expert in algebra. — A hybrid
coined fr. algebra and -ist, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## algebraization
algebraization, п., reduction of algebraic
symbols (philos.) — G. Algebraisierung, fr. algebra-
isieren, a hybrid coined by Edmund Husserl
(1859-1938) fr. algebra and suff. -isieren, fr.
Gk. -ίζειν. See -ize and -ation.

## nlgebraize
nlgebraize, tr. v. — See prec. word.

## algedonic
algedonic, adj., characterized by the association
of pain and pleasure. — Compounded of Gk.
&λγος, 'pain, and ηδονικός, 'pleasant', fr. ηδονή,
'pleasure'. See algid and hedonic.

## Algernon
Algernon, masc. PN. — Lit. 'with mustaches', fr.
OF. als gernons. OF. als (F. aux) stands for a
les, lit. 'to the' (pi.), fr. L. ad- (see ad-) and the
plural of the article le, fr. L. ille, 'that one';
see ille and cp. words there referred to. OF. ger-
non is a collateral form of grenon, 'mustache',
fr. VL. 'grandnem, ace. of *grano, a word of
Teuf. origin. Cp. OHG. grana, OE. granu,
'mustache', G. Granne, 'awn, beard', fr. I.-E. base
"gher-, 'to stick out', whence also OSlav. grant,
'point, edge', W. gran, 'eyelid', Mir. grend,
'whiskers'.

## -algia
-algia, suff. denoting 'pain', as in cardialgia,
myalgia, neuralgia (med.) — Gk. -αλγίδ, fr. άλγος,
"pain', whence άλγεϊν, 'to feel pain', άργιιλεος,
(dissimilated fr. *άλγαλέος), 'painful'; of
uncertain origin. Cp. algio-.

## algid
algid, adj., cold; chilly. — F. algide, fr. L. algi-
dus, 'cold', fr. algere, 'to be cold', which is cogn.
with ON. elgiar, Icel. elgur, 'drifting snow'; not
rel. to Gk. άλγεϊν, 'to feel pain'. See E. L. Liden,
Studien zur altindischen und vergleichenden
Sprachgeschichte, Uppsala, 1897, p. 66. Cp.
algor.
Derivatives: algid-ity, п., algid-ness, n.

## algio-
algio-, combining form meaning 'pain' or
'pertaining to pain', as in algiomuscular. — Fr. Gk.
&λγος, 'pain'. See -algia.

## nlgo-
nlgo-, before a vowel alg-, combining form
denoting 'pain', as in algedonic. — Fr. Gk. ίλγος,
'pain'. See -algia.

## algoid
algoid, adj., resembling algae. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. alga and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See alga and -oid.

## algodonite
algodonite, п., a copper arsenide (mineral.) —
Named after the Algodones mine in Chile. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Algol
Algol, п., a fixed star in the constellation
Perseus (astron.) — Lit. 'the Demon Star", fr. Arab.
al-ghul, 'the demon', fr. al-, 'the', and ghul,
'demon'. See ghoul.

## algolagnia) algolagay
algolagnia) algolagay, п., the feeling of pleasure
in causing or suffering pain (psychopathol.) —
ModL. algolagnia, coined by Schrenck-Notzing
fr. Gk. ίίλγος, 'pain', and λάγνος, 'lustful,
lecherous'. For the first element see -algia. Gk.
λάγνος is rel. to λαγαρός, 'slack, loose', λήγειν,
'to stay, leave off, cease', and cogn. with OE.
sleac, 'slow, slack'. See slack, adj., and cp. lack,
languid, lax, adj.

## algology
algology, п., the study of algae. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. alga and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See alga and -logy.
Derivatives: algolog-ical, adj., algolog-isi, n.

## algor
algor, п., cold; chill. — L., fr. algere, 'to be cold'.
See algid and -or. For the mode of formation
cp. terror, 'fright', fr. terrlre, 'to frighten', albor,
'white color', fr. alblre, 'to be white'.

## nlgorism
nlgorism, п., the Arabic system of numerals. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:50 COLUMN:3 -->
ME. algorisme, fr. OF. algorisme (F. algorilh-
me), fr. ML. algorismus, from the inexact
transliteration of Arab. al-Khowarizmi, 'the man of
Khowurizm (the modern Khiva), surname of
Abu Jafar Mohammed ibn MQsa, great
mathematician of the 9th cent. His famous work Al-
jabr w'al muqabala11 ('Reunion and
comparison'), introduced the use of Arabic numerals in
Europe, which denoted a turning point in the
history of mathematics. Cp. algebra.

## ulgous
ulgous, adj., pertaining to algae. — L. algusus,
fr. alga, 'seaweed'. See Alga and -mis.

## alguazil
alguazil, п., peace officer in Spain. — Sp. alguacil,
fr. earlier alguazil, fr. Arab, al-waztr, fr. al-,
'the', and waztr, 'vizier'. See vizier.

## algum
algum, n. — See alroug.

## alhacena
alhacena, п., an alcove. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-khi-
zdnah, 'the store room, the cell', fr. al-, 'the',
and khazana, 'he stored up'. See magazine and
cp. almaccn.

## Alhagi
Alhagi, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, al-haj, 4he camel's
thorn', which is rel. to Talmudic Heb. heghd,
Aram, heghd, hegh'thd, Syr. hagh'thd, of s.m.
The primary meaning of these nouns is 'thorns
formjng a hedge', from the Semitic base b-y-g,
h-w-g, 'to surround, hedge, fence in'. See
H.L.Fleischer in his Contributions to Jacob
Levy'sNeuhebraischesundChaldaischesWorter-
buch iiber die Talmudim und Midraschim, I,
p. 556, and Immanuel Low, Aramaische Pflan-
zennamen, Leipzig, 1881, pp. 145-47.

## Alhambra
Alhambra, п., the palace of the Moorish kings at
Granada. — Sp., fr. Arab, (al-kal'at) al-bamrd',
'the red (castle)', fem. of ahmaru, 'red', rel. to
hammara, 'he dyed red', humrah, 'redness', Heb.
bemar, 'bitumen, asphalt' (so called because of
its reddish color), hamdr, 'he covered or
smeared with asphalt', homer, 'mortar, clay' (so called
from its color), Heb. humor, Arab, himdr,
Aram.-Syr. bamard, Akkad. imiru, 'ass', lit. 'the
reddish brown animal', Heb. yabmur, Aram.
yabmura, Arab, yabmur, 'roebuck' (also named
from its color). The Alhambra was called 'the
red castle', from the color of the sun-dried
bricks of which its outer walls were built.

## Alhambresque
Alhambresque, adj., made in the style of the
Alhambra. — A hybrid coined fr. Alhambra and
suff. -esqne (fr. It. -esco).

## Al Het
Al Het, the longer confession of sin recited on
the day of Atonement (Jewish Religion). —
Heb. 'al bet, 'upon or for the sin'; so called
because each sentence begins with the words 'al
hit, resp. v*al hit ('Forgive us "for the sin" we
have committed by ...').

## alias
alias, adv., otherwise called; п., an assumed
name. — L. alias, 'in another way, at another
time, otherwise', fr. alius, 'another', which is
cogn. with Gk. ίλλος (for *&λιος), 'another',
Goth, aljis, 'other', OE. elles, 'otherwise'. See
else and words there referred to and cp. esp.
alibi, alien.

## alibi
alibi, п., plea that the accused person was
elsewhere than at the place where the crime was
committed (law). — L. alibi, 'elsewhere',
compounded of alius, 'other', and ibi, 'there'. See
prec. word and ibidem.

## alible
alible, adj., nourishing. — L. alibilis, 'nourishing,
nutritious', fr. alere, 'to nourish'. See alimeat
and cp. words there referred to. For the ending
see suff. -ible.
Derivative: alib-il-ily, n.

## Alice
Alice, fem. PN. — OF. Aliz, Aaliz, fr. OHG. Adal-
haid, lit. 'of a noble kind'. See Adelaide and
cp. Alison.
Alice blue. — Named after Mrs. Alice Roosevelt,
wife of President Theodore Roosevelt.

## allcula
allcula, n. a short cloak (Rom. antiq.) — L. 'a
light upper garment', a dimin. formed fr. Thes-
sal. Gk. £λλικοι, ace. of ίλλιξ, 'upper
garment; purple cloak', with suff. -ula (see -ule).
L. alicula is not rel. to L. ula, 'wing'.

## alidade
alidade, п., indicator of an astrolabe. — F., fr.
Sp. alidada, fr. Arab, al-idada", 'the revolving
radius of a circle'.

## alien
alien, adj. and n. — L. alignus, 'belonging to
another', fr. alius, 'another'. See alias.
Derivatives: alien-able, adj. (cp. F. alienable).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:51 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ALIENAGE | 24 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:51 COLUMN:1 -->
alien-abil-ily, п., alienage (q.v.), alienate (q.v.),
alien-ee, п., alienism (q.v.), alienist (q.v.)

## alienage
alienage, п., status of an alien. — F. alienage, ir.
aliener, fr. L. alilnare. See next word and -age.

## alienate
alienate, tr. v. — L. alilnatus, pp. of alilnare, 'to
make something another's, to take away,
remove', fr. alienus. See alien and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: alienation (q.v.), alienat-or, n.

## alienation
alienation, n. — ME., fr. OF. alienation (ΐ.'αΐίέ-
nation), fr. L. aliinalionem, ace. of alilnuM,
'transference or alienation of property', fr.
alienatus, pp. of alienate. See prec. word and -ion.

## alienism
alienism, п., the status of a alien. — Formed fr.
alien with suff. -ism.

## alienist
alienist, п., specialist in mental diseases. — F.
alienisle, a hybrid formed fr. L. alienus, with
suff. -isle. See alien and -ist.

## aliform
aliform, adj., wing-shaded. — Compounded of
L. ala, 'wing', and forma, 'form, shape'. See
aisle and form, n.

## alight
alight, intr. v., to descend, get down. — ME.
alihten, fr. OE. alihtan, fr. a- (see intensive
pref. a-), and lihtan, 'to alight'. See light, 'to
dismount'.

## alight
alight, adj., on fire. — ME. aliht, pp. of alihten,
'to light up'. See a-, 'on', and light, n.

## align
align, tr. v., to range in line; intr. v., to fall into
line. — F. aligner, fr. d, 'to' (see a-), and ligne,
fr. L. linea, 'line'. See line and cp. allineate.
Derivatives: align-er, п., alignment (q.v.)

## alignment
alignment, allgnement, n. — F. alignement, fr.
aligner. See align and -ment.

## alike
alike, adv., adj.—Formed fr. a-,'on', and like, adj.

## aliment
aliment, п., food. — L. alimentum, 'nourishment,
food', fr. alere, 'to rear, nourish, support,
maintain', fr. I.-E. base *al-, 'to grow, nourish'. See
old and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -ment
Derivatives: aliment-al, adj., alimentary (q.v.),
alimentation (q.v.)

## alimentary
alimentary, adj. — ML. alimentarius, 'pertaining
to nourishment', fr. L. alimentum. See aliment
and adj. suff. -ury.

## alimentation
alimentation, n. — ML. alimentutio, gen. -oni's,
fr. L. alimentum. See aliment and -ation.

## alimony
alimony, п., money paid to a wife out of her
husband's income during or after separation or
divorce (law). — L. alimonia, 'nourishment,
sustenance', formed fr. alere, 'to rear, nourish,
support, maintain', with suff. -mania, which is
cogn.with Gk.suff. -μων. See aliment and-mony.

## Aline
Aline, fem. PN. — F., shortened fr. Adeline. See
Adeline.

## aline
aline, tr. and intr. v. — A var. of align.

## aliped
aliped, adj., wing-footed. — Compounded of L.
ala, 'wing', and pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See alar
and pedal.
Derivative: aliped, n.

## aliphatic
aliphatic, adj., fatty. — Formed with suff. -ic
from the stem of Gk. όίλειφαρ, also ίλειφα,
gen. άλείφατος, 'oil, fat', fr. άλείφειν, 'to anoint'.
See adipose and cp. next word.

## aliptes
aliptes, п., the manager in the school for
wrestlers (Roman antiq.)—L.a//V7f£s,fr.Gk.daelTtn^,
lit. 'anointer', fr. άλείφειν, 'to anoint'; see
prec. word. He was so called because it was his
care to annoint the bodies of the wrestlers with
unguents.

## aliquant
aliquant, adj., not dividing without leaving a
remainder. — F. aliquante, fr. L. aliquanlus,
'somewhat, some, moderate', compounded of
alius, 'other', and quantus, 'how great'. See
alias and quantum.
Derivative: aliquant, n.

## aliquot
aliquot, adj., dividing exactly, without leaving a
remainder. — L„ 'some several, a few',
compounded of alius, 'other', and quot, 'how much,
how many'. See alias and quota and cp. the
second element in hidalgo.

## Alisma
Alisma, п., a genus of aquatic plants, the water
plantain (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άλισμα, 'the
water plantain'.
Derivative: alism-al, adj.

## alismoid
alismoid, adj., resembling a water plantain. —
Compounded of Gk. ίλισμα, 'the water

## plantain'
plantain', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'.
See -oid.

## allsu
allsu, п., any of several plants of the genus Alnus

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:51 COLUMN:2 -->
от their wood (bol.) — Sp., 'alder', fr. Goth.
*alisa, 'alder', fr. Teut. 'aliso-. See ulder, the tree.

## Alison
Alison, fem. PN. — F., prop, a dimin. of Alice
(qv.)

## alisonite
alisonite, п., a variety of covellite (mineral.) —
Named after R.E. Alison of Chile. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## aliunde
aliunde, adv., from another place. — L., 'from
another place', compounded of alius, 'another'
(see alias), and unde, 'from which place; from
whatever place', fr. orig. *cunde, rel. to the
pronominal base *qwo-. See who and words there
referred to and cp. esp. ubiety.

## alive
alive, adj. — ME. on live, alive, fr. OE. on life,
'in life*. See on and life, and cp. live.
Derivatives: alive, adv., alive-ness, n.

## aliyab
aliyab, п., 1) the act of being called to the alme-
mar to participate in the reading of the Torah;
2) immigration to Israel. — Heb. 'dtiyyd*, 'a
going up', fr. 'did* 'he went up, ascended', which
is rel. to Ugar. Чу, Arab, 'ala, 'he went up,
ascended', Akkad. elu, 'to go up, ascend', Heb.
'al, Aram.-Syr. 'at, Ugar. 7, Arab, 'ala, 'on,
upon; against', Heb. 'eW, 'leaf, lit. 'that which
springs up', 'old", 'burnt offering' (prop. fem.
part, of the verb 'ala", and lit. meaning 'that
which goes up'), 'elydn, 'high, higher', ma'ald*,
'step, stair', ma'ld*, 'upward'. Cp. Alenu, Eli.

## alizari
alizari, п., madder root. — F., fr. Sp. alizari, fr.
Arab. al-'afira*, 'the juice', fr. al-, 'the', and
asara, 'he squeezed, pressed', which is rel. to
Heb. 'atzar, Aram.-Syr. 'dlzdr, 'he retained'.

## alizarin
alizarin, alizarine, п., a dye (chem.) — F.
alizarine, fr. alizari. See prec. word and chem. suff.
-in, -ine.

## aljamn
aljamn, п., a Jewish congregation in Spain. —
Sp., fr. Arab. al-jamd'ah, fr. al-, 'the', and ja-
mtta", 'assembly', fr. jdma'a, 'he gathered
together, assembled'.

## aljamia
aljamia, п., Moorish name of the Spanish
language. — Sp. aljamia, fr. Arab, al-'ajamtya^,
'the non-Arabic, barbarian (language)', fr. al-,
'the', and fem. oi'ajamt, 'non-Arabic, barbarian'.

## aljofaina
aljofaina, п., wash basin. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-,
jufayna", dimin. of αΐ-jafna* (whence Sp. alja-
fana), fr. al-, 'the', and jafna", 'dish'.

## alkahest
alkahest, п., the universal solvent of the
alchemists. — F. alcahesl, fr. ML. alcahest, a pseudo-
Arabic word prob. coined by Paracelsus.

## alkali
alkali, n. — F. alcalli (now spelled alcali), fr.
Arab, al-qilt, fr. al-, 'the', and qilt, 'charred
ashes of the saltwort', fr. qala, 'he fried,
roasted', which is rel. to Heb. qaldh, 'he roasted,
parched', Aram, q'ld, 'burned', Akkad. qalu,
'to burn'; cp. kali. The word alkali first appears
in the writings of Albertus Magnus (l 206?-1280).

## alkalimeter
alkalimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
strength of alkalis. ·— A hybrid coined fr. alkali
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm*.

## alkaline
alkaline, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. alkali and
-ine, a chem. suff. of Latin origin.

## alkaloid
alkaloid, n. — A hybrid coined fr. alkali and
Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
-oid.

## alkalies
alkalies, n. pi., a series of saturated hydrocarbons;
the methane series (chem.) — Formed fr. e/ftyl
and methanf-i.

## alkanet
alkanet, п., the bugloss. — Sp. alcaneta, dimin.
of alcana, fr. Arab, al-hinnd. See next word.

## Alkanna
Alkanna, п., a genus of plants of the borage
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Sp. alcana, fr. Arab.
al-hinnd', fr. al-, 'the', and hinnd', 'henna'. See
hessia.

## ulkyl
ulkyl, п., any radical of the methane series, as
methyl, ethyl, etc. (chem.) — Formed fr. alkali
with suff. -yl.

## all
all, adj. — ME. all, fr. OE. eall, all, rel. to OS.
OFris., OHG., MHG. al, ON. allr, Dan., Swed.,
G. all, Goth, alls, OHG. ala- (in ala-wari, 'quite
true'), Goth, ala- (in ala-mans, 'mankind', lit.
'all men'), and cogn. with Lith. al- (in al-vlenas,
'every one'). Cp. albeit, withal. Cp. also Alaric,
allodium, alone, Ella.
Derivatives: all, n. and adv., all-ness, n.

## allactite
allactite, п., basic manganese arsenate (mineral.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -Ite fr. Gk. άλλάσ-
σείν, 'to change' (fr. ίίλλος, 'other'); so called

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:51 COLUMN:3 -->
in allusion to its pleochroism. See else and cp.
alio-, alias. Cp. also allagite, cntallactic,
parallactic, trophallai.

## allagite
allagite, п., a carbonated rhodonite (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. αλλαγή,
'change', which derives from the stem of άλλάσ-
<reiv, 'to change'. See prec. word and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also agio, diallage,
hypallage.

## Allah
Allah, п., Mohammedan name of the Supreme
Being. — Arab. Alldhu, contraction of al-ll&hu,
fr. al-, 'the', and Ildh. 'God'. See Elohim.

## allanto-
allanto-, combining form meaning 'sausage'. —
Gk. άλλαντο-, fr. αλλάς, gen. άλλαντος,
'sausage', a loan word fr. L. Шит, allium,
'garlic', the orig. meaning of Gk. άλλος being
'garlicky (sausage)'. Ion. ίλλη, glossed by He-
sychius, and rendered by him with λέχανον
('greens, vegetables'), is of the same origin. See
Allium.

## allantoic
allantoic, adj., pertaining to the allantois. — See
allantois and -ic.

## allantoid
allantoid, adj., resembling a sausage. — Gk.
άλλαντοειδής, 'sausage-shaped', fr. άλλος, gen.
άλλαντος, 'sausage' and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See allanto- and -oid.
Derivative: allantoid-al, adj.

## allantois
allantois, п., a membranous sac in the embryos
of mammals, birds and reptiles (anat.)—ModL.,
fr. Gk. ίίλλαντοειδής, 'sausage-shaped'. See prec.
word.

## allative
allative, adj., pertaining to a case that expresses
motion toward; п., the allative case (gram.) —
Formed with suff. -ive fr. L. allatus, 'brought to'
(used as pp. of adferre, afferre, 'to bring to'),
fr. ad- and lulus, 'borne, carried' (used as pp. of
ferre, 'to bear, carry'), which stands for *tlatos,
fr. *l]-, zero degree of I.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to
bear, carry', whence L. toilere, 'to lift up, raise',
tolerare, 'to bear, support'. See tolerate and cp.
collate and words there referred to.

## allay
allay, tr. v., 1) to quiet; 2) to alleviate. — ME.
alaien, fr. OE. alecgan, *to put down, remit,
give up', fr. a- (see intensive pref. a-) and lecgan,
'to lay'. See lay, 'to place'.
Derivatives: allay-er, п., allay-ment, n.

## allegation
allegation, n. — F. allegation, fr. L. alligationem,
ace. of alllgatio, 'despatching a mission', fr.
alllgalus, pp. of allegare, 'to despatch,
commission, mention, adduce', fr. ad- and legare,
'to send with a commission, despatch'. See
legate and -ion.

## allege
allege, tr. v. — ME. aleggen, 'to bring forward as
evidence', fr. AF alegier, which is formed—
with change of prefix—fr. OF. esligier, 'to free,
disengage, buy, pay, possess', fr. VL. *exBli-
gare, 'to free from a lawsuit', fr. tst ex- and
liligwre, 'to sue, quarrel'. See litigate.
Derivatives: alleg-ed-ly, adv., alleg-er, n.

## allegiance
allegiance, n. — ME. alegeance, formed fr. a (fr.
L. ad), 'to', and OF. ligeaunce, ligeance, fr. lige.
See ad-, liege and -ance and cp. ligeance.

## allegorize
allegorize, tr. and intr. v. — F. allegoriser, fr. L.
allegorizare, fr. alllgoria. See next word and
•ize.
Derivatives: allegoriz-ation, п., allegoriz-er, n.

## allegory
allegory, n. — F. allegoric, fr. L. allegoria, fr.
Gk. αλληγορία, 'figurative language', lit. 'a
speaking about (seemingly) something else';
compounded of ίίλλος, 'other' (see alio-), and
άγορεόειν, 'to speak in the assembly', fr. αγορά,
'assembly', which is rel. to άγείρειν, 'to
assemble', fr. I.-E. base *ger, 'to gather, collect'.
See gregarious and cp. category, panegyric The
word allegory was introduced into English by
Wycliffe.
Derivatives: allegoric (q.v.), allegor-ism, п., al-
legor-ist, п., allegor-ist-er, п., allegorize (q.v.)

## allegretto
allegretto, adj., п., and adv. (music). — It., dimin.
of allegro (q.v.)

## allegro
allegro, adj., п., and adv. (music). — It. allegro,
'cheerful, gay', fr. L. alacer, fem. alacris, neut.
alacre, 'lively, cheerful, brisk'. See alacrity.

## allele-
allele-, combining form, meaning 'one another'.
— Gk. άλληλο-, fr. αλλήλων, Dor. άλλαλων,
'of one another', fr. *άλλϊλλ-, *άλλαλ-,
contraction of "ίλλος-ίλλον (masc.), *«λλα-αλλδν
(fem.), etc., lit. 'the other' (nom.)—'the other'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:52 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 25 | ALLSPICE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:52 COLUMN:1 -->
(ace.), fr. άλλος, 'another, other'. See alio- and
cp. diallelon, parallel,

## alleluia
alleluia, n. and interj. — L., fr. Gk. αλληλούια,
fr. Heb. hall'lH-yak, 'praise ye the Lord'. See
hallelujah,

## allemande
allemande, п., name of various German dances.
— F., prop. fem. of allemand, 'German', fr.
Teut. Alamarm-, stem of L. Alamanni, Alemanni
(pi), name of a Suebic people, applied in
extension to all the Germans. See Alemanni.

## allergology
allergology, п., the study of allergies. — Coined
fr. ModL. allergia and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See allergy and
-logy.
Derivatives: allergolog-ic-al, adj.,
allergologist, a.

## allergy
allergy, п., hypersensitiveness of body cells to
certain substances (immunology). — ModL.
allergia, coined about 1905 by Clemens von Pir-
quet, an Austrian pediatrist (Г874-1910), fr. Gk.
άλλος, 'another' and έργον, 'work'. See alio- and
ergon and cp. energy.
Derivative: allerg-ic, adj.

## allerion
allerion, п., an eagle with expanded wings (her.)
— F. alerion, fr. Frankish *adalaro,
corresponding to MHG. adelar (G. Adler), 'eagle', orig. a
compound meaning 'noble eagle'. The first
element of this compound is rel. to OHG. adal,
'noble family', edili, OE. sedele. 'of noble
descent'. See atheling and cp. words there referred
to. For the second element see erne and cp.
ornitho-.

## alleviate
alleviate, tr. v. — L. alleviatus, pp. of alleviare,
a collateral form of allevare, 'to lighten,
alleviate', fr. ad- and levare, 'to lighten, ease', fr.
levis, 'light'. See levity and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: alleviat-ion, п., allevial-ive, adj.,
alleviat-or, n.

## alley
alley, п., a narrow passage. — OF. alee (F. allee),
'a going, passage', prop. fem. pp. of OF. aler
(F. aller), 'to go', fr. L. ambulare, 'to go, walk'.
See amble and cp. purlieu.
Derivative: alley-ed, adj.

## alley
alley, п., a choice marble. — Abbreviation of
alabaster; so called because it was brig, made
of alabaster.

## alliaceous
alliaceous, adj., belonging to the genus Allium
(bol.) — Formed fr. Allium with suff. -aceous.

## alliance
alliance, n. — ME. aliance, fr. OF. aliance (F.
alliance), fr. OF. alier (F. allier). See ally and
-ance.

## Alliaria
Alliaria, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. L. allium, 'garlic'
(see Allium); so called with reference to its odor.

## allice
allice, allice shad, n. — F. alose, fr. L. alausa,
'shad'. See alose.

## alligation
alligation, п., relation between the prices of the
ingredients of a mixture and the price of the
mixture; 'the rule of mixtures'. — L. alligatid,
gen. -onis, 'a binding to', fr. alligatus, pp. of
alligare, 'to bind something to', fr. ad-, and ligare,
'to bind, tie, fasten'. See ligament and cp.
alloy, ally.

## alligator
alligator, n. — Corruption of Sp. el lagarto,
which is shortened fr. el lagarto de lndias, name
of the cayman, lit. 'the lizard of the (West)
Indies'. Sp. el, 'the', derives fr. L. Hie, 'that one',
lagarto comes fr. L. lacertus, 'lizard'. See ille
and lizard.

## alligator pear
alligator pear, the avocado. — Formed fr. Na-
huatl ahuacatl through the medium of the Мех.
Sp. forms alvacata, alligato. Cp. avocado.

## alliterate
alliterate, intr. v., to use alliteration. — ML. al-
literatus, pp. of alliterare, 'to begin with the
same letter', fr. ad- and L. littera, 'letter'. See
letter and verbal suff -ate.
Derivatives: alliteration (q.v.), alliterat-ive, adj.,
alliterat-ive-ly, adv.

## alliteration
alliteration, п., repetition of the same letter in
several words of a sentence. — ML. alliteratio,
gen. -onis, from alliterutus, pp. of alliterare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## Allium
Allium, п., a genus of herbs of the lily family
(hot.) — L. alium, allium, 'garlic', prob. cogn.
with OI. aluh, alukdm, 'bulb'. Accordingly alium
would lit. mean 'the bulbous plant'. There is
little probability in Vaniiek's suggestion to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:52 COLUMN:2 -->
explain alium as 'the strong-smelling plant', by
deriving it from the base *an-, 'to breathe,
smell'. Cp. alliaceous, Alliaria. Cp. also allanto-.
Cp. also the first element in allyl.

## alio-
alio-, combining form, meaning 'other'. — Gk.
άλλο-, fr. άλλος, 'another, other', which stands
for *άλιος, and is cogn. with L. alius,
'another'. See alias.

## Allobroges
Allobroges, n. pi., a Celtic tribe inhabiting the
north of Gallia Narbonensis (now Savoy). —
L. Allobroges (pi. of Allobrox), lit. meaning 'the
aliens', in allusion to their having driven out the
original inhabitants. The al- in Al-lobroges is
identical both in origin and meaning with al-
in L. al-ius, 'the other', and in ML. Al-satia, and
with el- in E. else (q.v.) See also Alsatia and cp.
Alemanni.

## allocate
allocate, tr. v., to set apart; to allot, assign. —
Late L. allocatus, pp. of allocate, fr. ad-, and
L. locare, 'to place'. See locate and cp. allow,
'to assign', which is a doublet of allocate.

## allocation
allocation, n. — Late L. allocmid, gen. -onis, fr.
allocatus, pp. of allocare. See prec. word and -ion.

## aliochroic
aliochroic, adj., changeable in color. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. άλλάχροος, 'changed in
color, fr. άλλος, 'another* and χοόα, χροιά,
'skin, surface, color of the skin'. See alio- and
chrome.

## allocbroite
allocbroite, п., a sub-variety of andradite. — See
prec. word and subst. suff. -ite.

## allochromatic
allochromatic, adj., changeable in color. —
Compounded of alio- and chromatic

## allochrous
allochrous, adj., changing color. — See
aliochroic and -ous.

## alloclase
alloclase, alioclasite, п., a mineral containing
bismuth, cobalt, arsenic, sulfur and iron. —
Compounded of alio- and Gk. κλάσις, 'a
breaking', fr. κλαν, 'to break'. See clastic and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## allocatioa
allocatioa, п., address. — L. allocutio, gen. -onis,
'address', fr. allocutus, pp. of alloqui, 'to speak
to', fr. ad- and loqui, 'to speak'. See loquacions
and cp. locution.

## allodial
allodial, alodial, adj., pertaining to an allodium.
— ML. allodialis, fr. allodium. See allodium and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: al(l)odial-ism, п., al(l)odial-ist, п.,
al(l)odial-ly, adv.

## allodiality
allodiality, alodiality, п., the quality of being
allodial. — F. allodialile, fr. allodial, fr. ML.
allodialis. See prec. word and -ity.

## allodium
allodium, alodium, п., land held as absolute
property. — ML. allodium. Latinized fr. Frankish
*al-6d (whence also ML. alodis, a word
occurring in the Salic Law), lit. 'entire property',
compounded of "al, 'all' (see all), and* 6d.
'property', which is rel. to OS. od, OHG. *6t, OE. ead,
ON. audr, Goth, auda-, 'possession, property,
wealth', the second element in MHG. klein-61,
G. Klein-od, 'jewel, gem', lit. 'little wealth'. For
the second element in allodium cp. the first
element in Edgar, Edith, Edmund, Edwin. — It. al-
lodio, Sp. alodio, OF. alue, aluef (whence F.
alleu), OProvenc. alo, aloe, 'allodium', are
Frankish loan words.

## allogamy
allogamy, п., cross-fertilization (bot.) —
Compounded of alio- and Gk. -γαμίά, fr. γάμος,
'marriage'. See -gamy.

## allogeneotis
allogeneotis, adj., of a different kind. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. Gk. αλλογενής, 'of another
kind'. See alio- and -gen.

## allogeneity
allogeneity, n. — See prec. word and -ity.

## allograph
allograph, п., a writing made by another person.
— Compounded of alio- and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## allomerism
allomerism, п., variation in chemical
composition without change in crystalline
form.—Compounded of Gk. άλλος, 'other' and μέρος, 'part'.
See alio-, mero- and -ism.

## allomerous
allomerous, adj. — See prec. word and -ous.

## allomorph
allomorph, n. (mineral.) — Gk. άλλόμορφος,
'having another form'. See alio- and -rnorph.
Derivatives: allomorph-ic, adj.,allomorph-ism,n.

## allomorphite
allomorphite, п., a barite with the qualities of
anhydrite. — See allomorph and subst. suff. -ite.

## allonge
allonge, п., a thrust (in fencing) (obsol.) — F., 'a
lengthening', fr. allonger, 'to lengthen', fr. OF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:52 COLUMN:3 -->
alongier, fr. a, 'to' (see a-), and long, 'long'. See
long, adj., and cp. longeron, lunge.

## allonym
allonym, п., the name of another person assumed
by the author of a work. — Compounded of
Gk. άλλος, 'other' and δνυμα, dial, form of
ϋνομϋ, 'name'. See alio- and name and cp. ono-
mato. Cp. also aaonymous, antonym, cryptoaym,
homonym, metonymy, paronymous, patronymic,
synoaym.

## allopath
allopath, n. — Back formation fr. allopathy.

## allopathy
allopathy, п., treatment of disease by remedies
tbat produce effects opposite to those caused

## alloy
alloy, n. — F. aloi, fr. OF. alei, aloi, fr. aleier,
aloier, 'to bind, combine' (whence F. aloyer,
'to alloy'), fr. L. alligare, 'to bind to
(something)', fr. ad- and ligare, 'to bind, tie, fasten'.
See ligament, and cp. alligation.

## alloy
alloy, tr. v. — OF. aleier, aloier, 'to bind,
combine'. See alloy, n.

## alloyage
alloyage, n. — F. aloyage, 'the act of alloying',
fr. aloyer, 'to alloy'. See alloy, and -age.

## allspice
allspice, п., the berry of the pimento (Pimenta
officinalis) and the spice made from it. —·
Compounded of all and spice; so called because it
is supposed to combine the flavors of several
condiments.

## allude
allude, intr. v. — L. alludere, 'to play with; to
refer to', fr. ad- and ludere, 'to play'. See
ludicrous and cp. collnde, delude, elode, illade.

## aUumette
aUumette, п., a match for lighting. — F., fr. al-
lumer, 'to light, kindle', fr. VL. *aUHminare, fr.
ad- and L. liiminure, 'to light up, brighten', fr.
lumen, gen. luminis, 'light'. Cp. It. alluminare,
OProveng. alumenar, Sp. alumbrar, Port, alu-
miar, 'to light, illuminate', and see luminous.

## allure
allure, tr. v., to tempt by a bait. — ME. aluren,
fr. OF. aleurrer, fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and leurrer,
'to lure'. See lure.
Derivatives: allure, п., allure-ment, п., allur-er,
п., allur-ing, adj., allur-ing-ly, adv., allur-ing-
ness, n.

## allusion
allusion, n. — L. allusio, gen. -onis, 'a playing
with, a reference to', fr. allusus, pp. of alludere.
See alinde and -ion, and cp. collusion, delusion,
elusion, illusion.

## allusive
allusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -Ive fr. L. allusus
pp. of alludere. See allude and cp. eollusive,
delusive, elusive, illusive.
Derivalives: allusive-ly, adv., allusive-ness, n.

## alluvial
alluvial, adj. and n. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. alluvius, 'alluvial'. See alluvion.

## alluvion
alluvion, п., i)washing of water against the shore;
2) a flood; 3) alluvium. — F., fr. L. allmiOnem,
ace. of alluvia, 'an overflow, inundation,
alluvial land', lit. 'a washing upon', fr. alluere, 'to
wash upon or against', fr. ad- and lucre, 'to
wash', which is rel. to lavure, 'to wash'. See hive
and -ion and cp. antediluvian, deluge, dilute,
diluvium, elution.

## allnvium
allnvium, п., matter deposited by flowing water.
— L., neut. of alluvius, 'alluvial', fr. alluere.
See alluvion.

## ally
ally, tr., and intr. v. — ME. alien, fr. OF. alter
(F, allier), 'to join, unite', fr. L. alligare, 'to bind
to something', fr. ad- and ligare, 'to bind'. See
ligament and cp. alliance.
Derivative: ally, n.

## nllyl
nllyl, п., a univalent radical, QHj (chem.) —
Formed with suff. -yl fr. allium, 'garlic' (see
Allium); so called because it was first obtained as
a disulfide from garlic (by Wertheim in 1844).

## Alma
Alma, fem. PN. — Lit. 'nourishing', fr. L. alma,
fem. of almus, fr. atere, 4o nourish'. See aliment
and cp. Alma Mater.

## alloy
alloy, n. — F. aloi, fr. OF. alei, aloi, fr. aleier,
aloier, 'to bind, combine' (whence F. aloyer,
'to alloy'), fr. L. alligare, 'to bind to
(something)', fr. ad- and ligare, 'to bind, tie, fasten'.
See ligament, and cp. alligation.

## alloy
alloy, tr. v. — OF. aleier, aloier, 'to bind,
combine'. See alloy, n.

## alloyage
alloyage, n. — F. aloyage, 'the act of alloying',
fr. aloyer, 'to alloy'. See alloy, and -age.

## allspice
allspice, п., the berry of the pimento (Pimenta
officinalis) and the spice made from it. —
Compounded of all and spice; so called because it
is supposed to combine the flavors of several
condiments.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:53 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ALLUDE | 26 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:53 COLUMN:1 -->

## allnde
allnde, intr. v. — L. alludere, 'to play with; to
refer to', fr. ad- and ludere, 'to play'. See
ludicrous and cp. collude, delade, elnde, illude.

## allumette
allumette, п., a match for lighting. — F., fr. al·
lumer, 'to light, kindle', fr. VL. 'alluminSre, fr.
ad- and L. luminare, 'to light up, brighten', fr.
lumen, gen. luminis, 'light'. Cp. It. alluminare,
OProveng. alumenar, Sp. alumbrar, Port, alu-
miar, 'to light, illuminate', and see luminous.

## allure
allure, tr. v., to tempt by a bait. — ME. aluren,
fr. OF. aleurrer, fr. a, 'to' (see a), and leurrer,
'to lure'. See lure.
Derivatives: allure, п., allure-ment, п., allur-er,
п., allur-ing, adj., allur-ing-ly, adv., allur-ing'
ness, n.

## allusion
allusion, n. — L. allusio, gen. -dnis, 'a playing
with, a reference to*, fr. allusus, pp. of alludere.
See allude and -ion, and cp. collusion, delusion,
elusion, illusion.

## allusive
allusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L. allusus
pp. of alludere. See allude and cp. collusive,
delusive, elusive, illusive.
Derivatives: allusive-ly, adv., allusive-ness, n.

## alluvial
alluvial, adj. and n. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. alluvius, 'alluvial'. See alluvion.

## alluvion
alluvion, п., ι) washing of water against the shore;
2) a flood; 3) alluvium. — F., fr. L. alluvionem,
ace. of alluvia, 'an overflow, inundation,
alluvial land', lit. 'a washing upon', fr. alluere, 'to
wash upon or against', fr. ad- and luere, 4o
wash', which is rel. to lavare, 'to wash'. See lave
and -ion and cp. antediluviaa, deluge, dilute,
diluvium, elution.

## alluvium
alluvium, п., matter deposited by flowing water.
— L., neut. of alluvius, 'alluvial', fr. alluere.
See alluvion.

## ally
ally, tr., and intr. v. — ME. alien, fr. OF. alter
(F. alller), 'to join, unite', fr. L. alllgare, 'to bind
to something', fr. ad- and ligare, 'to bind'. See
ligament and cp. alliance.
Derivative: ally, n.

## allyl
allyl, п., a univalent radical, CjHj (cliem.) —
Formed with suff. -yl fr. oKhmi, 'garlic' (see
Allium); so called because it was first obtained as
a disulfide from garlic (by Wertheim in 1844).

## Alma
Alma, fern. PN. — Lit. 'nourishing', fr. L. alma,
fem. of almus, fr. alere, 'to nourish'. See aliment
and cp. Alma Mater.

## almacen
almacen, п., warehouse, magazine. — Sp., fr.
Arab, al-makhzan, fr. al-, 'the', and makhzan,
'storehouse', fr. khazana, 'he stored up'. See
magazine and cp. alhacena.

## almaciga
almaciga, п., the tree Agathis alba. — Sp., a var.
of almastiga, 'mastic', fr. Arab, al-mdstaka*, fr.
al-, 'the', and masiaka11, 'mastic', ult. fr. Gk.
μαστίχη. See mastic.

## almadin
almadin, п., a kind of boat. —- Sp. almadia, fr.
Arab, al-mddtya*, fr. al-, 'the' and maidtyab,
'ferryboat', a derivative of the verb, 'add, 'he
passed by', which is rel. to Heb. 'вяйЛ*, Aram.
'ddht, 'άαηά, Syr. 'udha, Etbiop. 'addwa, 'he
passed by', Heb. 'adh, 'as far as', 'adh, 'eternity'
(lit. 'passing time'), la'ddh, 'for ever'.

## almagest
almagest, п., 1) the treatise of Claudius Ptolemy
of Alexandria on astronomy; hence 2) any
similar medieval work on astronomy or
astrology. — ME., fr. OF. almagesle, fr. Arab, al-
majistt, fr. al-, 'the', and Gk. μεγίστη (scil.
σύνταξις), 'the greatest composition', fem. of
μέγιστος, superlative of μέγας, 'great'; see
mega-. In their admiration for the great work of
Claudius Ptolemy the Arabian translators
changed the title of his work from Μεγάλη
σύνταξις (της αστρονομίας), 'Great work (on
astronomy)', into Μεγίστη σύνταξις, 'the
greatest work'.

## almagra
almagra, п., red ocher. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-
mdghrah, fr. al-, 'the', and mdghra11, 'red ocher'.

## Alma Mater
Alma Mater, one's university or school. — L.,
'fostering mother'. Almus, fem. alma, neut.
airman, 'nourishing, fostering', is related to aid,
alere, 'to nourish', and prob. cogn. with the
second element in Gk. φυτ-άλμιος, 'producing,
nourishing, fostering', epithet of Zeus and of
Poseidon. See aliment and cp. Alma. For the
second element see mater, mother.

## almanac
almanac, п., a calendar giving astronomical data
and other useful information. — F. almanack.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:53 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. ML. almanachus (whence also It. almanacco,
Sp. almanaque, G. Almanack, etc.), fr. Gk.
άλμενιχιακά (pi.), 'calendars', which is prob.
of Coptic origin; prob. influenced in form by a
confusion with Arab, al-manah, 'the gift'. Sp.-
Arab. al-man&kh, 'the almanac', is itself a loan
word fr. ML. almanachus.

## alinandine
alinandine, п., a purple variety of garnet
(mineral.) — F., assimilated fr. earlier alabandine,ft.
L. (gemma) Alabandlna, a precious stone, fr.
Alabanda, a town in Caria, an ancient district
of Asia Minor. For the ending see suff. -ine.

## almemar
almemar, п., platform with reading desk in a
synagogue. — Arab, al-minbar, 'the pulpit', fr.
al-, 'the', and minbar, which orig. denoted 'an
(elevated) seat', and is a loan word fr. Ethiop.
minbar, 'seat'. See mimbar.

## almeriite
almeriite, п., a hydrous basic aluminium sodium
sulfate (mineral) — Named after Almeria in
Spam. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## almighty
almighty, adj. — OE. ealmihtig, selmihtig, fr. call,
'all', and mihtig, 'mighty'. See all and mighty.

## almogavar
almogavar, п., a light-armed Spanish soldier in
the middle ages. — Sp., fr. Ar. al-mughdmr, lit.
'the raider', fr. al-, 'the', and active partic. of
ghawara, 3rd conjugation of ghara, 'he raided,
invaded'.

## Almohades
Almohades, п., pi., members of a Mohammedan
sect, founded by Mohammed ibn Abdallah. —
Lit. 'the unitarians'; shortened fr.* Al-movahides,
from Arab, al-muwahhidan, 'they who profess
the unity of God', fr. al-, 'the', and active part,
of the 2nd conjugation of wahuda, 'he was alone'
whence also wahid, 'solitary'; rel. to Heb. yuhtd,
'only one, solitary', yahad, yahdaw, 'together'.

## almond
almond, n. — ME-, fr. OF. almande (F. amande),
fr. VL. amandula, fr. L. amygdala, fr. Gk.
αμυγδαλή, 'almond', which, according to H.
Lewy, Die semitischen FremdwOrter im Griechi-
schen, pp. 25-26, is borrowed from Heb. me-
ghedh Ё1, 'divine fruit'. [The ending -ula in VL.
amandula, corresponding to the Gk. ending -άλη
in αμυγδαλή, was mistaken for the dimin. suff.
(see -ule) and consequently dropped in OF.
almande, E. almond, etc.] The я before the d is
excrescent. Cp. amygdalate. Cp. also mandorla.

## almoner
almoner, n. — OF. almosnier (F. aumonier), fr.
almosne (F. aumdne), fr. VL. *alemosina, fr.
Eccles. L. eleemosyna. See alms.

## almonry
almonry, n. — OF. almosnerie (F. aumonerie), fr.
almosnier, 'almoner'. See prec. word and -y
(representing OF. -ie).

## Almoravides
Almoravides, n. pi., the members of an African
tribe. — Arab. al-Murabifan, fr. al-, 'the', and
murabifBn, Lit. 'monks living in a fortified
convent', denominated fr. ribaf, 'fortified convent',
fr. rdbafa, 'he applied himself to something,
devoted himself to religious life', 3rd conjugation
of rdbata, 'he bound'. Cp. marabon, marabout,
maravedi.

## almost
almost, adv. — ME. almest, almost, fr. OE. eal-
mSst, xlmSst, lit. 'mostly, all'. See all and most.

## alms
alms, n. — ME. almesse, fr. OE. xlmysse, fr.
Eccles. L. eleemosyna, fr. Gk. ελεημοσύνη,
'pity, mercy', in Eccles. Gk. 'charity, alms', fr.
ελεήμων, 'pitiful, merciful', fr. έλεος, 'pity,
mercy', which is of uncertain, possibly
imitative, origin. Cp. almoner, eleemosynary, the
second element in frankalmoiga, and the second
word in Kyrie eleison.

## almuce
almuce, п., hood, headdress. — OF. almuce, au-
muce (F. aumusse), fr. VL. almucia. See amice,
'hood, headdress', and cp. words there referred
to.

## ahnad
ahnad, almude, п., a dry measure. — Arab, al-
mudd, fr. al-, 'the', and mudd, 'a corn measure',
fr. madda, 'he extended, stretched', which is rel.
to Heb. madad, 'he measured', middd",
'measure, stature, size', Akkad. madadu, 'to measure'.

## almuerzo
almuerzo, п., breakfast. — Sp., fr. almorzar, 'to
breakfast', fr. L. admorsus, pp. of admordire,
'to bite into', fr. ad- and mordlre, 'to bite'. See
mordant

## almug
almug, also algum, п., a tree mentioned in the
Bible, prob. the sandalwood (the first form
occurs I Kings 10:11-12, the second II Chron.
2:7 and 9:10-11). — Heb. almuggtm, resp. al-
gummtm (pi.). The singular of these words must

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:53 COLUMN:3 -->
be almogh, resp. algom, so that [he forms
almug and algum are incorrect. They should be
replaced by almog, resp. algom.

## alnage
alnage, п., measurement by the ell. — OF. aul-
nage (F. aunage), fr. aulne, 'ell', fr. Frankish
*alina, prop, 'forearm', which is rel. to OHG.
elina, OE. eln, 'ell'. See ell and -age.
Derivative: alnag-er. n.

## Alnus
Alnus, п., a genus of plants; the alder (bot.) —
L. alnus, cogn. with ON. obi, OE. alor, 'alder'.
See alder,

## alodial
alodial, alodium, n. — See allodial, allodium,

## uloe
uloe, n. — L. aloe, fr. Gk. αλόη, 'aloe', prob.
borrowed fr. Heb. uhaltm, uhaldth (pi.), which
are perhaps borrowed fr. OI. agaruh, aguruh,
'aloewood', these latter being prob. ofDravid-
ian origin. Cp. agalloch.

## aloetic
aloetic, adj. containing, or of the nature of, aloes;
п., an aloetic medicine. — Formed with suff.
-etic fr. Gk. αλόη, 'aloe!. See aloe,

## aloft
aloft, adv. — ON. a lopt, 'in the air', whence arose
the meaning 'on high'. See a-, 'on', and loft,

## aloin
aloin, п., a bitter crystalline substance (chem.) —
Formed fr. aloe with chem. suff. -in; so called
because it is obtained from the aloe.

## aloisiite
aloisiite, п., a hydrous subsilicate of calcium,
ferrum, magnesium and sodium (mineral.) —,
Named after Prince Luigi (Latinized into Aloi-
sius) Amedeo of Savoy, Duke of the Abruzzi.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## alone
alone, adj. — ME. al one, 'all alone', fr. al, 'all',
and one, fr. OE. an, 'one, alone'. Cp. Du. alleen,
MHG. al-ein, al-eine, G. allein, 'alone', and see
all and one. Cp. also lone,

## along
along, adv. and prep. — ME. anlong, along, fr. OE.
andlang, which is compounded of and-, 'against',
and lang, 'long'. The first element is cogn. with
Gk. αντί, 'against', L. ante, 'before'; see ante-,
anti-. For the second element see loag, adj.

## aloof
aloof, adv. — Originally a nautical term formed
on the analogy of Du. te loef, 'to windward'.
See loof, Inff.

## alopecia
alopecia, n. baldness. — L., fr. Gk. αλωπεκία,
'mange in foxes, bald patches (on the head)',
fr. άλώπηξ, gen. αλώπεκος, 'fox', which is pern,
cognate with L. vulpis, 'fox' See Vulpes and cp.
Alopecurus. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Alopecurus
Alopecurus, п., the genus of foxtails (bot.) —
ModL., lit. 'fox tail', fr. Gk. άλώπηξ, 'fox', and
ούρα, 'tail' (see alopecia and uro-, 'taillike'); so
called from the shape of the spike.

## alose
alose, п., a small fish, the shad. — F., fr. L.
alausa, a word of Gaulish origin. See G.-D.
Dottin, La langue gauloise, Paris 1920, p. 225,
and cp. alike.

## alond
alond, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and loud,

## alow
alow, adv., below (naut.) — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and low, adj.

## Aloysius
Aloysius, masc. PN. — ML. Aloisius, fr. OF.
Loots. See Lonis.

## alp
alp, a high mountain. — L. Alpes, 'the Alps', lit.
'the High Mountains', from non-Aryan base
*alb-, 'high; mountain', whence also Gael, alp,
W. ailp, 'a high mountain' (cp. Albion). The
connection of this word with L. albus, 'white',
is based on folk etymology. See Рокоту in Zeit-
schrift fur Keltische Philologie, 38, 313.

## alp
alp, a demon. — G. Alp, 'elf; rel. to E. elf (q.v.)

## alpaca
alpaca, п., a kind of llama and its wool. — Sp.
alpaca, fr. Quechua alpaca, fr. paco, 'yellowish
red'.

## alpenstock
alpenstock, п., a long iron-pointed staff used for
climbing mountains. — G., lit. 'Alp stick',
compounded of Alpen, 'the Alps', and Stock, 'stick*.
See alp, 'a high mountain', and stock,

## alpha
alpha, п., name of the 1st letter of the Greek
alphabet. — L., fr. Gk. άλφα, fr. Heb.-Phoen.
dleph; see aleph. The final α was added because
a Greek word cannot end with a φ; cp. beta,
gamma, delta, eta, theta, iota, kappa, lambda,
sigma. See Theodor Noldeke, Die semitischen
Buchstabennamen, in Beitrage zur semitischen
Sprachwissenschaft, Strassburg, 1904, pp. 134
and 135, and Eduard Schwyzer, Griechische
Grammatik, MUnchen, 1939, I, 140 γ.

## alphabet
alphabet, n. — L. alphabitum, compounded of
Gk. £λφα and βήτα, names of the first two
letters of the Greek alphabet. See alpha and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:54 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 27 | ALVITE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:54 COLUMN:1 -->
beta.
Derivatives: alphabet, tr. v., alphabet-ar-ian, п.,
atphabet-ic, alphabet-ic-al, adjs., alphabet-ic-al-
ly, adv., alphabel-ics, n. pi., alphabet-ism, п.,
alphabei-ist, n. alphabel-ize, tr. v.,
alphabetization, п., alphabel-iz-er, n.

## alphitomancy
alphitomancy, п., divination from barley meal. —
Compounded of Gk. ίλφιτον, 'barley groats',
and μαντεία, Oracle, divination'. Gk. αλφι,
ίίλφιτον orig. meant 'white (grain)' and are rel.
Ιοάλφός, 'white', and cogn. with L. albus, 'white';
see alb. For the second element see -mancy.

## alphitomorphous
alphitomorphous, adj., of the form of barley meal.
— Compounded of Gk. όίλφιτον, 'barley groats',
and μορφή, 'form, shape'. See prec. word and
-morphous.

## Alphonso
Alphonso, masc. PN. — Sp. Alfonso, fr. OHG.
Adalfuns, which is compounded of adal, 'noble
family, noble descent' (see atheling), and funs,
'ready'.

## alphos
alphos, п., a form of leprosoy (med.) — Gk.
άλφός, 'dull-white leprosy' (whence L. alphas,
of s.m.); cogn. with L. albus, 'white'. See alb.

## Alpine
Alpine, adj., pertaining to the Alps. — L. Al-
p'mus, fr. Alpls, 'the Alps'. See alp and adj.
sufF. -ine.

## Alpinist
Alpinist, п., one who climbs the Alps or other
mountains. See Alpine and -ist

## alraun
alraun, п., the mandrake root. — G. Alraun, fr.
OHG. alruna, fr. AlbrQna, a name given to
seeresses (see Tacitus, Germania, chapter S).
The name Albruna lit. means 'having the secret
power of the Albs'; it is compounded of Alb
and riina, 'secret'. See rune.

## already
already, adj. — Compounded of all and ready.

## alright
alright, adv. — Compounded of all and right/

## Alsatia
Alsatia, n. — ML. Alisutia, Alsatia (whence also
F. Alsace), Latinized fr. OHG. eli-sano
'inhabitant of the other (bank of the Rhine)',
whence G. Elsafi, name of the province. The
first element in OHG. eli-sa330 is rel. to Goth.
aljis, 'other', OE. elles, 'otherwise'; see else. The
second element is rel. to OHG. sissan, OE.
sittan, 'to sil, dwell'; see sit.
Derivatives: Alsatian, adj. and n.

## al segno
al segno, musical direction to go back to the sign.
— It., 'to the sign'. The first word is formed fr.
a, 'to' (fr. L. ad), and the def. article it (fr. L.
ille, 'that one'). See ad- and ille and cp. alfresco.
The second word derives fr. L. signum, 'sign'.
See sign and cp. dal segno.

## alsike
alsike, nlsike clover, (hot.) — Named fr. Alsike,
near "Uppsala, in Sweden.

## Alsine
Alsine, п., a genus of herbs of the chickweed
family (hot.) — L., name of a plant, perh. 'the
chickweed', fr. Gk. άλσίνη.

## Al Sirat
Al Sirat, п., in the Koran, 'the right way' of faith;
the narrow bridge leading over the fire of hell
(Islam). — Arab, al-sirdl, 'the road', fr. al-,
'the', and sirdf, 'road', fr. Aram, isi'rafd, isrdfd,
fr. Late Gk. στράτα, fr. L. strata (scil. via). Hi.
'paved way'. See street.

## also
also, adv. — ME. al so, fr. OE. alswd, selswa,
ealswa, prop, 'all so'. See all, so, and cp. as.

## alt
alt, n. — L. alius, 'high, lofty, tall; high, shrill
(of voice)'. Alius is the pp. of alere, 'to nourish',
and lit. means 'nourished, grown up'. See old
and cp. ailment. Cp. also haughty, hauteur,
hawser, enhance, exalt, the first element in
hautboy, oboe, and the second element in rinlto.

## Altair
Altair, п., a first magnitude star, α Aquilae (as-
tron.) — Arab, al-tdir, shortened fr. al-nasr
altair, 'the flying eagle', fr. al-, 'the', and fair, part,
of fdra, 'it flew'.

## altar
altar, n. — ME. alter, fr. OE. altar, fr. L. altare,
'altar', which is prob. rel. to adoleo, adolere,
'to burn', a verb dissimilated fr. orig. *adaleip;
hence L. altare orig. meant 'a place for burning
(sacrifices)'. It was influenced in form by an
erroneous association with alius, 'high' (as if
altare meant 'a high place'). Cp. ME. auter, St.
OF. alter, auter (F. autel).
Derivative: altar-ed, adj.

## altazimuth
altazimuth, п., an instrument for observing the
altitude and azimuth of a star (astron.) —
Compounded of the abbreviation of altitude and
of azimuth.

## alter
alter, tr. and intr. v. — F. altirer, fr. Late L. al-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:54 COLUMN:2 -->
terdre, 'to change', fr. L. alter, 'the other (of
two)', which stands for 'aliieros, *alitros, 'allros,
and is formed with the compar. suff. -ter fr. base
*ali-, 'there, beyond', whence also alius,
'another'. Hence alter and alius lit. denote 'one
who stands there'; the former—in keeping with
the sense of the compar. suff. -ter—denotes 'the
other of two', the latter means 'another picked
out of many (at least three) persons'. See alias,
else and cp. altercate, altern, alternate,
adulterate, adultery, altruism. For the compar. suff. -ter
see -ther and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: alter-able, adj. alter-abil-ity, п.,
alter-ation, п., alter-al-ive, adj.

## altercate
altercate, intr. v., to dispute, quarrel. — L. al-
tercatus pp. of altercdri, to dispute, wrangle,
quarrel', fr. *altercus, 'disputing', fr. alter,
'another'. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## altercation
altercation, п., dispute, quarrel. — F., fr. L.
altercationem, ace. of altercatio, 'a dispute,
wrangling', fr. altercdtus, pp. of allercdri. See
altercate and -ion.

## altern
altern, adj., alternate. — L. a It emus, 'one after
the other', fr. alter, 'the other (of two)'. See
alter and cp. subaltern.

## alternant
alternant, adj. and n. — L. alterndns, gen. -amis,
pres. part, of alternare. See alternate and -ant.

## alternate
alternate, tr. and intr. v. — L. alternates, pp. of
alternare, 'to do first one thing, then another,
to alternate*, fr. alternus. See altern and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: allernat-ing, adj., alternat-ing-ly,
adv., alternation (q.v.), alternative (q.v.)

## alternate
alternate, adj. — L. alterndtus, pp. of alternare.
See alternate, v.
Derivatives: alternate-ly, adv., alternate-ness, n.

## alternation
alternation, n. — L. alternated, -onis, fr.
alterndtus, pp. of alternare. See alternate, v., and -ion.

## ultemative
ultemative, adj. and n. — ML. alternativus, fr.
L. alterndtus, pp. of alternare. See alternate, v.,
and -ive.
Derivatives: alternative-ly, adv., alternate-
ness, n.

## Althaea
Althaea, п., a genus of plants of the marsh family
(bot.) — L., fr. Gk. άλ&αίϊ, 'marsh mallow',
which is rel. to άλ&αίνειν, 'to heal', αλδη,
'growth', άλδήσκειν, 'to grow', άλδαίνειν, 'to
make to grow, to nourish'; fr. I.-E. base *aldh-,
resp. *ald-, enlarged fr. *al-, 'to nourish, grow'.
See old and words there referred to and cp. esp.
alt.

## although
although, conj. —Compounded of all and though.
Cp. ME. al thagh.

## alti-
alti-, combining form meaning 'high'. — L. alti-,
fr. alius, 'high'. See alt.

## Altica
Altica, a genus of beetles of the family Chryso-
melidae (entomol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άλτικάς,
'good at leaping', from the stem of άλλεσ&αι,
'to leap, jump', which is cogn. with L. satire,
'to leap, jump'. See salient.

## nltigraph
nltigraph, п., an altimeter recording the altitudes
reached. — A hybrid coined fr. L. alius, 'high',
and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
alt and -graph.

## altimeter
altimeter, an instrument for measuring altitudes.
— A hybrid coined fr. L. alius, 'high', and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See alt and meter, 'poetical
rhythm', and cp. ultoineter.

## altissimo
altissimo, adj. and n. (music). — It., superl. of
alio, 'high'. See alto,

## altitude
altitude, п., height. — L. altitude, 'height', fr.
alius, 'high'. See alt and -hide.
Derivatives: altitudin-al, adj., altitudin-arian,
adj. and n.'

## alto
alto, n. (music). — It., fr. L. altus, 'high'. See alt
and cp. contralto,

## altogether
altogether, adv. — ME. altogedere, compounded
of al, 'all', and togedere, 'together'. See all and
together,

## nltometer
nltometer, п., a theodolite. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. altus, 'high' and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See alt and meter, 'poetical rhythm', and cp.
altimeter,

## alto-relievo
alto-relievo, also alto-rilievo, high relief. — It.
altorilievo, 'high relief. See alt and relief,
'projection', and cp. mezzo-relievo,

## altruism
altruism, п., unselfishness,*the opposite of egoism.
— F. altruisme, coined by A.Comte in 1830 fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:54 COLUMN:3 -->
L. alter, 'another', on analogy of OF., F. autrui,
'another', whose ending is due to the influence
of lui, 'he'. See alter and -ism.

## altruist
altruist, п., a person who believes in altruism. —
See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: altruisl-ic,adj.,altruist-ic-al-ly,adv.

## aludel
aludel, n. a pear-shaped pot open at both ends,
so that a series of such pols can be placed one
above another; used for sublimation. — F., fr.
Sp. aludel, fr. Arab, al-uihdl, 'a pot used for
sublimation', fr. al-, 'the', and Gk. αιθάλη,
'sublimed vapor', a derivative of αϊθειν, 'to
burn'. See ether.

## Aludra
Aludra, п., name of a constellation in the zodiac.
— Arab. al-Adhrd', fr. al-, 'the', and WW,
'a virgin', from the stem of 'adharat, 'she was
a virgin'.

## alula
alula, п., the bastard wing of birds (ornithol.) —
ModL., dimin. of L. ala, 'wing'. See aisle and
-nle.

## alum
alum, n. — OF. alum (whence F. alun), fr. L.
alumen, 'alum', lit. 'bitter salt', cogn. with Gk.
άλύδοιμας, 'bitter', OE. ealo, alo, 'ale', ON.
dl, of s.m. See ale and cp. alumina, aluta, alu-
taceous.
Derivative: alum, tr. v.

## alumin-
alumin-, form of alumino- before a vowel.

## alumina
alumina, п., aluminum oxide (chem.) — Fr. L.
alumen, gen. aluminis. See alum.

## aluminite
aluminite, п., a hydrous aluminum sulfate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr.
alumiaum.

## aluminium
aluminium, n. — The same as aluminum (q.v.)

## alumino-
alumino-, before a vowel alumin-, combining form
for aluminum.

## aluminum
aluminum, also aluminium, n. — ModL., coined
by the English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy
(1778-1829) fr. L. alumen, 'alum'. He gave the
new element the name aluminum, but changed
it later to aluminium. See alum and cp. the
second element in duralumin.

## alumnus
