alumnus, п., pupil; graduate of a college or
university. — L. alumnus, 'a nursling, foster-son,
disciple', for *alo-menos, prop. pass. pres. part,
of alere, 'to nourish'; see old and cp. alt. For
the suff. *-menos cp. Gk. -μένος, the suff. of the
med. and pass, part., and L. fe-mina, 'woman',
lit. 'suckling (woman)', and see feminine. Cp.
also the suffixes of the words Aeschynomene,
calumny, catechumea, clement, column,
ecumenic, energumen, hapax legomenon, hegumen,
noumenon, phenomenon, prolegomenon.

## alurgite
alurgite, п., a purplish manganese mica (mineral)
—· Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. άλουργής,
'genuine purple dye', lit. 'wrought in or by the
sea', which is compounded of άλς (fem.), 'sea',
and έργον, 'work'. See halieutic and ergon.

## alushtite
alushtite, п., a hydrous aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after Alushta in the Crimea.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## aluta
aluta, п., a kind of soft leather. — L., for alu-ta,
lit. 'leather prepared by means of alum', rel. to
alumen, 'alum'. See alum.

## alutaceous
alutaceous, adj., resembling aluta. —L. alulacius,
fr. aluta. See prec. word and -aceous.

## alveolar
alveolar, adj., pertaining to alveoli. — Formed
with suff. -ar fr. L. alveolus. See alveolus.

## alveolate
alveolate, adj., pitted with small cavities, as a
honeycomb. — L. alveoldtus, fr. alveolus. See
next word and adj. suff. -ate.

## alveolus
alveolus, п., a small cavity. — L. alveolus, dimin.
of alveus, 'a hollow, cavity', which is rel. to al-
vus, 'belly', and cogn. with Gk. αυλός, 'tube,
pipe', £ν-αυλος, 'channel, riverbed', αυλών,
'hollow way, defile, ravine, glen, channel, strait',
OS1. ufi/i, Lith. aulys, Lett, aulis, 'beehive', lit.
'a trunk hollowed out', OSlav. ulica, 'defile;
courtyard', Lith. aulas, Lett, aule, 'leg of a
boot', OPruss. aulis, 'shinbone', Arm. ul, uli,
'way', yii, 'pregnant'. For the correspondence
of Gk. αυλός and L. alvus, alveus, cp. Gk.
νεϋρον, 'nerve', with L. nervus, of s.m., and
Gk. παϋρος, 'little, small', with L. parvus, of s.m.
For the ending see suff. -ole. Cp. carol,
hydraulic.

## alvite
alvite, п., a hydrous silicate containing yttrium
and other metals (mineral.) — Named after Alve
in Norway. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:55 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ALWAY | 28 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:55 COLUMN:1 -->
ulway, adv., always (archaic or poetic). — ME.,
lit. 'all (the) way'. See all and way.

## always
always, adv. — Formed fr. prec. word with adv.
gen. suff. -s.

## alypin
alypin, alypine, a crystalline compound (pharm.)
— Formed with chem. suff. -in, -ine, fr. Gk.
αλϋπος, 'painless', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
λύπη, 'pain', whence λϋπεϊν, 'to give pain to,
to pain, grieve', λυπηρός, 'painful' (rel. to
λϋπρός, 'wretched, distressed'); so called
because of its anesthetic nature. Ok. λύπη is of
uncertain origin. It is perh. cogn. with OI.
lumpdti, 'breaks, hurts, damages'. See leaf and
cp- library.

## Alyssum
Alyssum, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. αλυσσον, 'mad-
wort', prop. neut. of the adj. αλυσσος, 'curing
madness', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and λύσσα,
Att. λύττα, 'rage, fury, madness, frenzy'. See
lyssa.

## alytarch
alytarch, п., chief of police at the Olympic games.
— L: alytarcha, fr. Gk. αλυτάρχης, fr. άλύτάς,
'police officer (esp. at Olympic games)', and
άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. The first element
stands for *Γαλύ-τάς, lit. 'staff carrier', and is
cogn. with Goth, walus, 'staff', ON. voir, 'a
round stick', fr. I.-E. base *wal-, *wel-, 'to turn,
bend, twist, roll'. See volute and cp. words there
referred to. For the second element see arch-.

## am
am, v. — OE. eom, earn, am, rel. to ON. em,
Goth, im, for I.-E. *esmi, whence also OI. asmi,
Hitt. esmi, Arm. em, Gk. ειμί, Lesbian and
Thessal. έμμί, Dor. ήμί, Alb. jam, L. sum
(formed on the analogy of the plural sumus, 'we
are'), OSlav. jesmi, Lith. esml, OPruss. asmai,
Olr. am, Ί am', fr. I.-E. base *es-, 'to be'. See
esse and cp. are, art, is.

## Amabel
Amabel, fem. PN. — Lit. 'lovable', fr. L. ama-
bilis, fr. amdre, 'to love'. See amatory and cp.
the PN.s Ainandus, Amanda, Amy.

## amadou
amadou, п., a spongy substance.— F.,fr.Provenc.
amadou, lit. 'loving, amorous', fr. L. amdlor,
'lover' (see amatory); so called from the
inflammability of the substance.

## amain
amain, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and main,
'strength'.

## amalgam
amalgam, п., ι) a mixture of mercury with a
metal or metals; 2) a mixture, blend. — F. amal-
game, fr. ML. amalgama, dissimil. fr. Arab, al-
malgham, which is formed fr. Arab, al-, 'the*
and Syr. malagmd, fr. Gk. μάλαγμα, 'a soft
mass*, fr. μαλάσσειν, 'to soften', fr. μαλακός,
'soft'. See malaco- and cp. Amalmaea.
Derivatives: amalgam, v. (q.v.), amalgam-ate,
tr. and intr. v., amalgam-al-ion, п., amalgam-at-
ive, adj., amalgam-at-or, п., amalgam-ist, п.,
amalgam-ize, tr. v., amalgam-iz-at-ion, n.

## amalgam
amalgam, tr. and intr. v., to amalgamate, — F.
amalgamer, fr. amalgame. See amalgam, n.

## Amaithaea
Amaithaea, Amalthea, п., the nurse of Zeus
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Αμάλθεια, which
is prob. rel. to μαλθακός, 'soft, light, weak',
μαλακός, 'soft'. See malaco- and cp. amalgum.

## Amanda
Amanda, fem. PN. — Lit. 'worthy to be loved',
fem. of amandus, gerundive of amdre, 'to love'.
See amntory and cp. Amabel and names there
referred to. For other Latin gerundives used in
English cp. agenda and words there referred to.

## Amandus
Amandus, masc. PN. — L. See prec. word.

## amanuensis
amanuensis, п., a person employed to write from
dictation; secretary. — L. amanuensis, formed
with suff. -ensis from the phrase servus а тапй,
'a servant from the hand', i.e. 'a servant writing
from dictation'. See pref. a-, 'from', and
mmnml.

## Amara
Amara, п., a genus of beetles, the ground beetle
(entomol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. αμάρα, 'trench'
which is prob. rel. to αμη, 'shovel, mattock'
(whence διαμαν, 'to cut through, clear away'),
and cogn. with OSlav. jama, 'a pit'.

## amaranth
amaranth, п., 1) a mythical plant that never fades;
2) any plant of the genus Amaranthus; 3) purple
color. — Gk. αμάραντος, 'unfading; amaranth',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-), and the stem of μαραί-
νειν, 'to put out, quench, extinguish, to make
to waste away', fr. I.-E. base *mer-, 'to rub,
consume, wear away'; see smart, v., and cp.
marasmus. The ending of amaranth (for amarant)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:55 COLUMN:2 -->
is due to the influence of plant names formed
with Gk. άνθος, 'flower'.

## amaranthine
amaranthine, adj., 1) unfading, undying; 2) of
purple color. — Coined by Milton fr. amaranth
and adj. suff. -ine.

## Amaranthus
Amaranthus, п., a genus of plants (bot.)—ModL.,
fr. Gk. αμάραντος. See amaranth.

## amargoso
amargoso, п., the bark of the goatbush. — Sp.,
lit. 'bitter', fr. VL. *amdricdsus, fr. L. amdrus.
See amarine.

## amariUo
amariUo, п., any of several tropical American
trees. — Sp., for *ambarillo, fr. Arab, 'anbarf,
'amber-colored', fr. 'anbar, 'amber'. See amber.

## amarine
amarine, amarin, п., a poisonous compound
(chem.) — Formed with chem. suff. -ine, -in, fr.
L. amdrus, 'bitter', which is cogn. with ON. apr,
'sharp', Swed., Norw., Du. amper, 'sharp,
bitter', OE. ampre, OHG. ampfaro, MHG., G.
ampfer, 'sorrel', OI. amldh, amblah, 'sour';
wood sorrel', Arm. amok', 'sweet, Alb. land's,
'(curdled) milk', emble, 'sweet'; fr. I.-E. *am-ro-,
fr. base *am-, 'bitter', which is rel. to *omo-,
'raw, unripe', in OI. dmah, 'raw, unripe,
uncooked', Gk. ωμός, of s.m. See ото-, 'raw,
unripe', and cp. amargoso, maraschino, nmrgosa,
and the second element in picamar. For the
-reformative element cp. Gk. πικ-ρός, 'bitter' (see
picric).

## amaryllid
amaryllid, п., any plant of the order of Amarylli-
daceae (bot.) — See Amaryllis and -id.

## Amaryllidaceae
Amaryllidaceae, n. pi., an order of plants. —
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae from the PN.
Άμαρυλλίς, gen. Άμαρυλλίδος. See Amaryllis,
a genus of plants.

## Amaryllis
Amaryllis, п., name of a shepherdess in
Theocritus' Idyis. — L., fr. Gk. Αμαρυλλίς.

## Amaryllis
Amaryllis, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — From
prec. word.

## amass
amass, tr. v., to pile up. — F. amasser, 'to
accumulate, heap up', fr. Late L. 'admassdre, fr. ad-
and massdre, 'to heap up', fr. L. massa, 'a lump,
mass'. See mass.
Derivatives: amass-er, п., amass-ment, n.

## amasrJa
amasrJa, n„ absence of the breasts. — Medical
L., fr. Gk. «μαστός, 'without breasts', fr. ά-
(see priv. pref. n-) and μαστός, 'breast'. See
masto- and -la.

## amateur
amateur, n. — F., 'lover of something, amateur',
fr. L. amdtdrem, ace. oiamdtor, 'lover', fr. ama-
tus, pp. of amdre, 'to love'. See amative.
Derivatives: amateur, adj., amaleur-ish, adj.,
amateur-ish-ly, adv., amateur-ish-ness, n.

## Amati
Amati, п., a violin made by a member of the
Amati family at Cremona (16th and 17th cent.)

## amative
amative, adj., pertaining to love, amatory. —
Formed with suff. -lve fr. L. amdtus, pp. of
amdre, 'to love', from the I.-E. infantile imitative
base *ama-, whence also amita, 'father's sister',
amicus, 'friend'. Cp. Gk. άδαμνεΐν, 'to love'
(Hesychius), which is formed fr. Phrygian
intensive, pref. άδ- and 'άμνεΐν, 'to love'. See
aunt and cp. Amabel, amadou, Amanda, Amnn-
dus, amateur, amenity, amiable, amicable, amity,
amorous, amour, emunor, enemy, enmity,
inamorato, inimical.

## amatol
amatol, п., an explosive containing ammonium
nitrate and trinitrotoluene. — Coined fr. the
abbreviations of ammonium and toluene.

## amatory
amatory, adj., pertaining to, or showing, sexual
love. — L. amatorius, 'loving, amorous,
amatory', fr. amdtus, pp. of amdre. See amative and
-ory.
Derivatives: amatory, п., amatori-al, adj., ama-
tori-al-ly, adv., amatori-an, adj.

## amaurosis
amaurosis, п., decay br loss of sight (med.) — Gk.
άμαύρωσίς, 'a darkening', fr. άμαυρός, 'dark,
dim, dull, faint'. See Moor and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -osis.

## amaze
amaze, tr. v. — ME. amasen, fr. OE. dmasian, fr.
intensive pref. a- and -masian. See maze.
Derivatives: amaze, п., bewilderment (poetic),
amaz-ed, adj., amaz-ed-ly, adv., amaz-ed-ness,
п., amaze-ment, n.

## Amazon
Amazon, п., a member of a race of female
warriors in Scythia (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Άμαζών, which prob. derives fr. Heb. ammttz,
'strong'. The form of the word Άμαζών was
prob. influenced by the folk etymology

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:55 COLUMN:3 -->
according to which Άμαζών lit. means 'without
breast', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and μαζός,
'breast' (the Amazons are said to have cut off
their right breasts in order to use the bow with
more ease).
Derivatives: Amazon-ian, adj., and п.,
Amazonism, n.

## Amazon
Amazon, п., name of the largest river in the world
in volume. — Sp. Amazonas, from prec. word;
so called by Francisco Orellana after his battle
with the Tapuyas (in 1541), in allusion to the
circumstance that the women of the tribe
helped the men in their fight. Cp. next word.

## amazonite
amazonite, п., a green variety of microline
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite from the
name of the Amazon River, near which it occurs.

## ambages
ambages, n. pi., a roundabout way. — L.
ambages, 'a roundabout way', lit. 'a going round',
compounded of ambi-, 'about', and dg-,
lengthened form of the stem of agere, 'to move, drive'.
See ambi- and agent, adj., and cp. ambiguous.
Cp. also amt, ambassador, embassy. For dg-,
lengthened form of the stem of agere, cp. L. in-
ddgdre, 'to trace out, investigate', which is
formed fr. ind(u)-, 'in', and dg-, lengthened form of
the stem of agere (see indagate).

## ambagious
ambagious, adj., circuitous. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. ambages. See prec. word.
Derivatives: ambagio'us-ly, adv., ambagious-
. ness, n.

## ambassador
ambassador, п., a diplomat of the highest rank.—
F. ambassadeur, fr. It. ambasciatore, fr. ambas-
ciata, 'embassy'. See embassy.
Derivatives: ambassador-ial, adj., ambassador-
ial-ly, adv.

## ambassadress
ambassadress, n. — Formed fr. ambassador with
suff. -ess.

## ambatoarinite
ambatoarinite, п., a carbonate of the cerium
metals and strontium (mineral.) — Named after
Ambatoarina in Madagascar. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## amber
amber, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) ambre, fr. Arab.
'anbar, 'ambergris'. Cp. It. ambra, Sp., Port.
ambar, alambar, which all derive fr. Arab,
'anbar. Cp. also amariUo. Cp. also ambrosia and
the second element in next word and in Llquld-
ambar, pomander.
Derivatives: amber, adj. and tr. v., amber-y,
adj.

## ambergris
ambergris, adj. — F. ambre gris, 'gray amber'.
For the first word see amber. F. gris is borrowed
fr. Frankish *gris, which is rel. to Du.grijs, 'gray',
OS., OHG., MHG. gris, 'gray', G. Greis, 'old
man', and prob. also to OE. grseg, 'gray'. See
grizzle, 'gray', and cp. gray and words there
referred to.

## amberite
amberite, п., an explosive. — Formed fr. amber
with subst. suff. -ite; so called because it
resembles amber.

## ambi-
ambi-, before a vowel amb-, combining form
meaning'both, on both sides'. — L. ambi-, amb-,
'around, round about', rel. to ambo, 'both', and
cogn. with Gk. άμφί, 'round about', OI. abhi-
(ah, Avestic aiwi-to, 'on both sides', OE. ymbe,
OS., OHG. umbi, ON. umb, urn, MHG. umbe,
iimbe, G. urn, Gaul, ambi-, Olr. imb-, imm-,
imme-, 'round about, about', and with Gk. αμφω,
'both', Toch. A dmpi, атре, В ant-αρί, OI. ub-
hau, Avestic uwa, OSlav. oba, Lith. abu, Lett,
oil, OPruss. abbai, Goth, bai, OE. id, 'both'.
See both and cp. amphi- and the first element in
ambsace, ancile, ancillary, ancipital, umiaut. Cp.
also ember days.

## ambidexter
ambidexter, adj., using both hands with equal
facility. — ML. ambidexter, compounded of
ambi- and L. dexter, 'on the right side, right'.
See dexter.
Derivatives: ambidexter, п., ambidexter-ity, п.,
ambidextrous (q.v.)

## ambidextrons
ambidextrons, adj. — See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: ambidextrous-ly, adv., ambidex-
trous-ness, n.

## ambient
ambient, adj., surrounding. — L. ambiens, gen.
-entis, 'going round', pres. part, of ambire, 'to
go round, surround', compounded of ambi-,
'about, around', and ire, 'to go'. See ambi- and
itinerate and cp. ambition. Cp. also andante.

## ambiguity
ambiguity, n. — F. ambiguiti, fr. L. ambiguitdtem.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:56 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 29 | AMG. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:56 COLUMN:1 -->

## ace. of ambiguitas
ace. of ambiguitas, 'double meaning', fr. ambi-
guus. See ambiguous and -ity.

## ambiguous
ambiguous, adj., unclear; doubtful. — L. ambi-

## guus
guus, 'having double meaning, shifting,
changeable, doubtful*, fr. ambigere, 'to wander about',
which stands for *amb-agere, fr. ambi-, 'about,
around', and agere, 'to set in motion, drive'; see
ambi- and agent. For the change of Latin й (in
agere) to i (in amb-igere) see abigeat and cp.
words there referred to. For E. -ous, as equivalent
to L. -us, see sufT. -ous.
Derivatives: ambiguous-ly, adv., ambiguous-
ness, n.

## ambit
ambit, п., a circuit. — L. ambitus, 'a going round,
circuit', fr. ambitus, pp. of ambire, 'to go round'.
See ambient and cp. ambition.

## ambition
ambition, n. — F., fr. L. ambitione;n, ace. of am-
bitio, 'a going round', esp. 'a going round of
candidates canvassing for office', whence 'a
desire for honor', fr. ambitus, pp. of amblre,
'to go round'. See ambient and -ioa and cp.
ambit.

## ambitious
ambitious, adj. — L. ambitiosus, 'going about in
order to canvass for office', hence 'anxious to
please, ostentatious', fr. ambitio, gen. -onis. See
ambition and -ous.
Derivatives: ambitious-ly, adv.,ambilious-ness, n.

## ambivalence
ambivalence, amblvalency, п., simultaneous
conflicting feelings (psychol.) — Compounded of
ambi- and valence resp. valency; introduced by
Sigmund Freud.

## amble
amble, intr. v., to go at an easy gait. — ME., fr.
OF. ambler, fr. L. ambulare, 'to go about, walk',
which prob. stands for *amb-al-are, fr. amb-
(see amb-) and I.-E. base *Ш-, 'to go', whence
also Gk. &7), 'ceaseless roaming', άλασ!>αι,
άλαίνειν, 'to wander about', αλήτης, 'beggar',
Lett, aluot, Ίο wander about', L. alucin&ri, 'to
wander in mind'. See hallucinate and cp.
ambulance, ambulate, funambulist, noctambulism,
somnambulism. Cp. also Alastor, aleatory, Aleo-
chara, alley, 'a narrow passage', exile, purlieu.
Derivatives: amble, п., amble-ing, adj.

## amble
amble, п., an easy gait. — ME., fr. F. amble, fr.
OF. ambler. See amble, v.

## ambly-
ambly-, combining form meaning 'blunt'. — Gk.
άμβλυ-, fr. αμβλύς, 'dull, blunt, dim', which
prob. stands for *ά-μλ-ύς, and is rel. to
μαλακής, 'soft'. See malaco- and cp. amulgam, Amal-
thea.

## amblyopia
amblyopia, п., weakening of the eyesight, the first
stage of amaurosis (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of ambly- and Gk. -ωπίά, fr. ώψ, gen.
ώπός, 'eye, face'. See -opia.

## ainbo
ainbo, п., a large pulpit in early Christian
churches. — ML., fr. Gk. ίίμβων, 'a ridge', in Middle
Greek also 'pulpit'; of uncertain origin.

## ambos
ambos, incus (anat.) — G. Ambofi, 'anvil'. See
beat, 'to strike', and cp. beetle, 'mallet'.

## ainboyna
ainboyna, amboyna wood. — So called from Am-
boyna Island, one of the Moluccas.

## ambrite
ambrite, п., a fossil resin. — Formed fr. amber
with subst. sufT. -ite; so called because it
resembles amber.

## Ambrose
Ambrose, masc. PN. — L. Ambrosius, fr. Gk. άμ-
βρόσιος, 'immortal, belonging to immortals'. See
ambrosia.

## ambruse
ambruse, п., the wood sage. — ME., fr. F. am-
broise (now ambroisie), fr. L. ambrosia. See
next word.

## ambrosia
ambrosia, п., the food (sometimes the drink) of
the gods in Greek mythology. — Gk. αμβροσία,
fern, of ίιιβρόσιος, a word generally explained
in the sense of 'immortal' and regarded as a
lengthened form of ίίμβροτος, 'immortal'. A. W.
Verrall has proved, however, that the true
meaning of άμβρόσιος is 'fragrant'. (For the
exquisite smell of ambrosia cp. Homer,
Odyssey, 18, 192-3.) 'Αμβρόσιος is prob. a Semitic
loan word, with the original meaning 'as
fragrant as ambergris; pertaining to amber*, and
αμβροσία stands for αμβροσία έδωδή,
'amberlike food'. Cp. Arab, lanbar (pronounced *a/n-
bar'), 'ambergris', and see nmber. See also
nectar.
Derivatives: ambrosi-ac, adj., ambrosial, adj.
(q.v.), ambrosi-an, ambrosi-ate, adjs.

## ambrosial
ambrosial, adj. — Coined by Milton fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:56 COLUMN:2 -->
ambrosius, fr. Gk. άμβρόσιος. See ambrosia and adj.
sufT. -al.

## ambry
ambry, п., cupboard; closet {archaic). — ME. al-
mary, aumbry, fr. OF. almarie, armarie (F. ar-
moire), 'cupboard', fr. L. armarium, 'closet,
chest', lit. 'a place where arms are kept', fr. arma,
gen. armorum, 'arms; tools, instruments,
utensils'. Cp. It. and Sp. armario, OProveng. armari,
and see arm, 'weapon', armory.

## ambsace
ambsace, п., double aces. — OF. ambes as, fr. L.
ambas, fem. ace. of ambo, 'both', and L. as,
'unity, unit'. See ambi- and ace.

## ambulance
ambulance, n. — F., fr. earlier hdpital ambulant
lit. 'a walking hospital', fr. L. ambuluns gen.
-amis. See next word and -ce.

## ambulant
ambulant, adj. — L. ambulansf gen. -antis, pres.
part, of ambulare. See next word and -ant

## ambulate
ambulate, intr. v., to move about, walk. — L. ·
ambulat-(um), pp. stem of ambulare, 'to go
about, walk'. See amble and verbal suff. -ate
and cp. circumambulate, perambulate.

## ambulation
ambulation, n. — L. ambulatio, gen. -onis, fr. am-
bulat-(um), pp. stem of ambulare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## ambulatory
ambulatory, adj. — L. ambulatorius, 'movable',
fr. ambulat-(um) pp. stem of ambulare. See am-
balate and adj. suff. -ory.

## ambulatory
ambulatory, n. — ML. ambulatdrium, a noun
formed fr. L. ambulatorius, 'movable'. See prec.
word and subst. suff. -ory.

## ambory
ambory, n. — See anbury.

## ambuscade
ambuscade, п., ambush. — F. embuscade,
Gallicized fr. It. imboscata (under the influence of
OF. embuscher), lit. 'a hiding in the bush', fr.
imboscare, fr. ML. imboscare, 'to lie in the bush'.
See next word and -ade.
Derivatives: ambuscade, tr. and intr. v., am-
buscad-er, n.

## ambush
ambush, tr. v. — OF. embuscher (F. embucher), fr.
ML. imboscare, 'to lie in the bush', fr. im-, 'in,
within', and boscus, 'bush'. See bush, 'shrub',
and cp. prec. word. Cp. also boscage, bosky.
Derivatives: ambush, n. (q.v.), ambush-er, п.,
ambushment (q.v.)

## umbush
umbush, n. — OF. embusche (F. embuche), back
formation fr. embuscher. See prec. word.

## ambushment
ambushment, n. — OF. embuschement, fr.
embuscher. See ambush, v., and -ment.

## ameen
ameen, п., official, inspector (Anglo-Ind.) —Hind.
amin, fr. Arab, amfn, lit. 'trustworthy', fr. amino,
'he was steady, firm, trustworthy' (whence d'ma-
na, 'he believed'); rel. to Heb. amin, 'verily,
truly'. See amen.

## ameer
ameer, amir, п., a Mohammedan ruler. — Arab.
amir, 'commander, prince', fr. amara, 'he
commanded'. See emir.

## Ameiurus
Ameiurus, п., a genus of catfishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., formed fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. μείου-
ρος, 'curtailed', which is compounded of the
stem of μείων, 'smaller, less', and ουρά, 'tail'.
See meiosis and uro-, 'tail-'.

## umelcorn
umelcorn, n. — G. Amelkorn, compounded of
A met, 'starch', and Korn, 'gram'. The first element
derives fr. L. amylum, fr. Gk. ίίμυλον, 'starch';
see amyl. The second element is rel. to E. com,
'grain' (q.v.) Cp. emmer.

## Amelia
Amelia, fem. PN. — A Teutonic name lit.
meaning 'laborious'. Cp. ON. ama, 'to trouble', and
Amal, name of the ruling family of the
Ostrogoths. The name was confused later with the
name of the Roman gens Aemilia (see Emily).

## ameliorate
ameliorate, tr. v., to make better; intr. v., to
become better. — Formed with verbal suff. -ate
fr. F. ameliorer, which is refashioned after L.
melior, 'better', fr. OF. ameillorer, fr. OF. meil-
lor (whence F. meilleur), 'better', fr. L. melid-
rem, ace. of melior, 'better'. See meliorate.
Derivatives: amelioration (q.v.), amelior-at-ive,
adj., amelior-at-or, n.

## amelioration
amelioration, п., betterment, improvement. — F.
amelioration, St. ameliorer. See prec. word and
•ion.

## amellus
amellus, п., name of a flower. — L., 'the purple
Italian starwort*, a word of Gaulish origin (see
G.-D.Dottin, La langue gauloise, p. 226). The
derivation of this word from the river name
Mella, as suggested by Servius in his
commentary on Virgil 4, 271, is folk etymology.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:56 COLUMN:3 -->

## amen
amen, inter)., п., adv. and tr. v. — OE., fr. Eccles.
L. amin, fr. Eccles. Gk. αμήν, fr. Heb. amin,
'verily, truly, certainly', from stem a-m-n, 'to be
trustworthy, confirm, support*, whence also
Oman, 'he supported, nourished', he'emtn, 'be
believed', gmUna", 'firmness, fidelity', umnam,
omnam, 'verily, truly, emith (for *lminth),
stability, truth'. Cp. the related Syr. ammtn, 'strong,
enduring', Aram. hemanUtha, Syr. haymanutha,
'faithfulness, truth', Arab, dmina, 'he was safe',
amuna, 'he was faithful', a'mana, 'he believed',
amin, 'faithful'. Cp. ameen. Cp. also mammon.

## amenable
amenable, adj., answerable; willing; submissive.
— Formed with suff. -able fr. F. amener, 'to
lead, or bring up, to', fr. d, 4o' (see a), and
mener, 'to lead', fr. VL. minare, 'to drive
(animals) by shouting', fr. L. minari, 'to threaten'.
The orig. meaning of L. minari has survived in
Rum. mana, 'to threaten'. See menace and -able.
Derivatives: amenabil-ity,n., amenable-ness,n.,
amenabl-y, adv.

## ameud
ameud, tr. and intr. v.—OF. (= F.) amender, fr. L.
emendare, 'to correct, emend', with change of
suff. (cp. the same change of suff. in It. ammen-
dare and OProvenc. amendar); fr. ё-, 'out of
(see e-) and menda, 'defect, blemish', which is
cogn. with OI. minda, 'physical blemish' (for
*manda, influenced in form by OI. ninda,
'blame'), Olr. mennar, 'stain, blemish', mind,
'sign, mark', W. mann of s.m. Cp. emend, mend,
mendacious, mendicant.

## amendment
amendment, n. — OF. (= F.) amendement, fr.
amender. See prec. word and -ment.

## ninends
ninends, n. — ME. amendes, fr. OF. amendes, pi.
of amende, fr. amender, 'to amend'. See amend.

## amenity
amenity, п., pleasantness; attractiveness. — F.
aminite, fr. L. amoenitalem, ace. of amoeniISs,
'delightfulness, loveliness', fr. amoenus,
'pleasant, delightful, lovely', which is rel. to amare,
'to love'. See amative and -ity.

## ament
ament, catkin. — L. ammentum, less correctly
amentum, 'strap, thong', so called because of its
resemblance to a strap. Ammentum stands for
*ag-mentum, and prop, means 'something to
lead with', fr. agere, 'to lead'. See agent and
-ment
Derivatives: ament-aceous, ament-al, adjs.

## amentiferous
amentiferous, adj., bearing aments. — See ument
and -ferous.

## amerce
amerce, tr. v., 1) orig., to fine; 2) to punish.—
ME. amercen, 'to fine', fr. AF. amercier, fr. OF.
a merci (F. a merci), 'at somebody's mercy'.
OF. a derives fr. L. ad, 'to'; see ad-. For F.
merci see mercy.
Derivatives: amerce-аЫе, amerci-able, adjs.,
amerce-ment, n.

## Americn
Americn, n. — Named after Americus Vespucius
(Amerigo Vespucci), an Italian merchant (1451-
1512). The name America was first used by the
German cartographer Martin Waldseemuller
(in 1507).
Derivatives: Americ-an, adj. and п., Americ-an-
ism, п., Americ-an-ize, v., Americ-an-iz-ation, n.

## amerlcium
amerlcium, п., name of a radioactive element
(chem.) — ModL., named in 1946 by its
discoverer Glenn Theodore Seaborg (1912- )
after the 2 Americas. For the ending see suff.
-ium.

## Amerind
Amerind, п., an American Indian or Eskimo. —
Abbreviation of American Indian; coined by
Major John Wesley Powell (1834-1902),
director of the bureau of American Ethnology.
Derivatives: Amerindi-an, n. and adj., Amerind-
ic, adj.

## amethyst
amethyst, п., violet quartz, used n jewelry. —
ME. ametist, fr. OF. ametiste (F. amilhyste), fr.
L. ameihystus, fr. Gk. αμέθυστος, 'remedy
against drunkenness', prop, an adjective
meaning 'not intoxicating', fr. ά-, 'not' (see priv. pref.
a-), and μείνύειν, 'to be drunken' (whence
μέθ-υσις, 'drunkenness'), fr. μέθ-υ, 'wine*; see
mead, 'an intoxicating drink', and cp. methyl.
The stone amethyst owes its name to its
supposed power of preventing drunkenness.

## amethystine
amethystine, adj. — L. amelhystinus, fr. ame-
thyslus. See prec. word and adj. suff. -toe
(representing L. -inus).
AMG. — Abbreviation of Allied Military Govern-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:57 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: AMGOT | 30 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:57 COLUMN:1 -->
ment.
AMGOT. — Abbreviation of Allied Military
Government of Occupied Territory.

## Amhaarez
Amhaarez, п., an ignoramus. — Heb. 'am haa-
retz, 'the people of the land'. Heb. 'am, 'people',
derives fr. base '~m-m, 'to join, be united',
whence also 'am, 'kinsman', 'im, 'with'. Cp. the
rel. Aram.-Syr. 'ammd, 'people', Ugar. 'm.'clan',
Arab, 'amm, 'a great crowd', amma", 'rabble',
'dmma, 'it comprised, included', 'amm, 'father's
brother', 'dmma", 'father's sister', Aram, 'im,
Syr. 'am, Ugar. 'm, Arab, md'a, dial, 'am,
'with'. Cp. the first element in Emmanuel and
the second element in Jeroboam. Heb. iretz,
'earth', is rel. to Aram. ura', ar'd, Ugar. 'rf, Arab.
artj, Akkad. irsilu, 'earth'. Cp. Eretz Yisrael.

## amiable
amiable, adj.—OF. (= F.), fr. Late L. amicSbilis,
'friendly', fr. L. amicus, 'friend'. F. amiable was
influenced in form by aimable, 'lovely', fr. L.
amabilis, fr. amare, 'to love'. See amieable.
Derivatives: amiabil-ity, п., amiable-ness, п.,
amiabl-y, adv.

## amianthus
amianthus, п., name of a kind of asbestos. — L.
amiantus, fr. Gk. αμίαντος (sell, λίθος), lit.
"undented (stone)', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-), and
μιαντός, 'stained, defiled', verbal adj. of μιαίνειν,
'to stain, defile'; see miasma. The spelling ih (for
0 is prob. due to the influence of Gk. δνθος,
'flower'.
Derivatives: amianth-ine, amianth-oid, amianth-
otd-al, adjs.

## amicable
amicable, adj., friendly. — L. amicabtlis,
'friendly', fr. amicus, 'friend', fr. amare, 'to love'. See
amative and cp. amiable, which is a doublet of
amicable. Cp. also enemy, inimical. For sense
development cp. Gk. φίλος, 'friend*, from the
base of φιλείν, 'to love', and Heb. ohibh,
'friend', which is prop. part, of dhdbh, 'he
loved'.
Derivatives: amicabil-ity, п., amicable-ness, п.,
amicabl-y, adv.

## amice
amice, п., vestment worn by the celebrant at
Mass. — ME. amyse, fr. OF. amis, amit, fr. L.
amictus, 'mantle, cloak', fr. amiclus pp. of
amido", amictre, 'to wrap, throw around', which
is contracted from *am-jacio, fr. pref. ambi- and
jacio, Ί throw'. See ambi- and jet, 'to spirt forth'.

## amice
amice, п., hood, headdress. — ME. amisse, fr.
OF. aumuce (F. aumusse), fr. VL. almucia,
which is formed fr. Arab, al-, 'the', and mus-
taqah, fr. Pers. mushtS, 'fur cloak'. Cp. Sp. al-
mucio, OProveng. almussa, MDu. almutse, later
mutse, muts, Du. muts, 'cap', MHG. mutze,
miitze, G. Mutze, 'cap', which all derive fr. VL.
almucia. Cp. also almuce, mozzetta, mutch. For
sense development cp. cap.

## amid
amid, prep. — ME. amidde, fr. OE. on middan,
'in the middle', fr. on (see a-, 'on'), and middan,
dat. sing. masc. of midde, adj. See mid and cp.
amidst.

## amide
amide, amid, п., a compound obtained by
replacing one hydrogen atom in ammonia by an
element or radical (chem.) — F. amide, coined
by the French chemist Charles-Adolphe Wurtz
(] 817-84) from the first syllable of ammonia and
sun", -ide, -id.

## amidin
amidin, amidine, п., solution of starch in hot
water (chem.) — Formed fr. F. amidon, 'starch*,
fr. ML. amidum, fr. L. amylum, fr. Gk. δμυλαν,
'starch'. See amyi, 'starch', and chem. sun".
-ine, -in.

## amido-
amido-, combining form meaning 'containing
the radical NH2 and an acid radical* (сЛети.) —
Fr. amide.

## amidogen
amidogen, п., the hypothetical univalent radical
NH2 (chem.) — Coined fr. amido- and -gen.

## amidst
amidst, prep. — Formed with excrescent -t fr.
ME. amiddes (which was formed with adv. gen.
suff. -s fr. amidde, see amid, prep.) For the -t
cp. against, amongst, betwixt, whilst.

## amine
amine, amin, п., a compound obtained by
replacing hydrogen atoms of ammonia by
hydrocarbon radicals (chem.) — Coined from the first
syllable of ammonia and chem. suff. -ine. Cp.
amide and vitamin. Cp. also imine.

## amino-
amino-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to,
or containing, the radical NH2' (chem.) — See
prec. word and cp. deaminate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:57 COLUMN:2 -->

## amir
amir, n. — See ameer.

## amiss
amiss, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
miss, 'failure'.

## amity
amity, п., friendship. — F. amitie, fr. OF. amistie,
fr. VL. 'amicitatem, ace. of *amicitas,
corresponding to L. amicitia, 'friendship', fr. amicus,
'friend', which is rel. to amare, 'to love'. See
amative and cp. enmity.

## ammeter
ammeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
strength of electric currents. — Shortened fr.
ampire-meter. See ampere and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## Ammi
Ammi, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — L. ammi, fr.
Gk. ίίμμι, fr. Aram, ammitha, a secondary form
of hammithd, of s.m.

## ammo-
ammo-, combining form meaning 'sand', as in
ammophilous. — Gk. άμμο-, fr. £μμος, 'sand*,
a blend of δμαθος, 'sand', and ψάμμος, 'sand';
which are both cogn. with E. sand (q.v.)

## nmmonal
nmmonal, п., a high explosive obtained by a
combination of ammonium nitrate and aluminum.
— Formed fr. ammonia and the first two letters
in aluminum.

## ammonia
ammonia, n. — Contraction of sal ammoniac, fr.
L. sal ammoniacum, 'ammoniac salt'. See next
word.

## ammoniac
ammoniac, adj. and n. — F., fr. L. ammoniacum,
fr. Gk. άμμωνιακόν, 'a resinous gum', prob.
fr. orig. Άρμενιακόν, 'Armenian', through the
intermediate form άρμονιακόν, occurring in the
works of ancient authors beside άμμωνιαχόν;
so called because first found in Armenia. See
Pauly-Wissova, Real-Encyclopadie der klas-
sischen Altertumswissenschaft, I, 1861.
Derivative: ammoniac-al, adj.

## ammonite
ammonite, п., a cephalopod mollusk allied to the
nautilus (paleontol.) — Formed with subst. suff.
-ite fr. L. cornu Ammonis, 'the horn of (Zeus)
Amnion; so called from its shape, which
resembles a ram's horn (Zeus Ammon was
represented with ram's horns).

## ammonium
ammonium, п., a basic radical, NH, (chem.) —
ModL., fr. ammonia (q.v.)

## ammophilous
ammophilous, adj., sand-loving (zool. and hot.)
— Compounded of ammo- and Gk. φίλος,
'loving'. See -philous.

## ammotherapy
ammotherapy, п., treatment by means of sand
baths. — Compounded of ammo- and -therapy.

## ammunitioa
ammunitioa, n. — F. amunition, a dialectal form
for munition (see munition). Amunition arose
through a misdivision of la munition imol'amu-
nition.

## amnemonic
amnemonic, adj., characterized by loss of
memory. — Formed fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk.
μνημονικός, 'pertaining to memory'. See
mnemonic.

## amnesia
amnesia, п., loss of .memory (psychiatry). —
Medical L., fr. Gk. αμνησία, 'forgetfulness', fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and μνήσιος, 'pertaining
to memory', which is rel. to μνάομαι, Ί
remember', fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to think, remember*.
See mind and cp. next word. Cp. also
anamnesis, paramnesia. For the ending see suff. -la.

## amnesty
amnesty, п., general pardon. — F. amnestie, fr.
L. amnestia, fr. Gk. αμνηστία, 'forgetfulness,
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and μνηστις,
'remembrance', which is rel. to μνάομαι, Ί remember'.
See prec. word.

## amnic
amnic, adj., pertaining to a river. — L. amnicus,
fr. amnis, 'river', which stands for *ab-nis and
is cogn. with Olr. abann, ab, W. afon, 'river', fr.
I.-E. base *ab-, a collateral form of base *ap-,
'water, river', whence OI. apah, apdh, Avestic
af-sh, 'water', Gk. Άπίά, a name of the
Peloponnesus (so called because surrounded by
water), Μεσσαπία, 'Messapia', a part of Magna
Graecia in Lower Italy comprising Apulia and
Calabria, lit. 'the country between two waters',
L. Αρ-ΰΙία, 'Apulia', lit. 'region abounding in
waters', Lith. upe, Lett, upe, 'water', OPruss.
ape, 'a small river', apus, 'spring, fountain,
well', and prob. also Toch. AB dp-, 'river'. Cp.
the first element in abdest, abkari, Apsaras and
the second element in donb and in Messapian.
For the ending of amnic see suff. -ic.

## amnion
amnion, п., the membrane enclosing the embryos
of mammals, birds and reptiles. — Gk. άμνίον,
'a bowl in which the blood of victims was

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:57 COLUMN:3 -->
caught; membrane round foetus', rel. to άμασ-
βαι, 'to draw, gather', 6ίμη, prop. 4μη (whence
L. hama), 'bucket', and cogn. with Lith. semiu,
semti, 'to draw', samtis, 'scoop, ladle'. These
words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *sem-, 'one,
together', whence also Gk. άμα, 'together with'.
See same and cp. aam.

## amoeba
amoeba, ameba, п., a microscopic one-celled
animal. — Gk. αμοιβή, 'change', rel. to άμείβειν,
'to change*, fr. copul. pref. -ά and l.-E. base
*meigw-, *migw-, 'to change', whence also L.
migrare, 'to wander'; see migrate. Copul. pref.
ά- stands for I.-E. *srn-, a weak gradational form
of I.-E. base *sem-, 'one, together'; see same.

## amoebean
amoebean, amebean, adj., interchanging. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. Gk. αμοιβαίος,
'interchanging, alternate', fr. αμοιβή. See prec.
word.

## amok
amok, adj. and n. — See amuck.

## Amomum
Amomum, п., a genus of plants of the ginger
family (bot.) — L. amomum, 'a spice plant', fr.
Gk. &μωμον, which is of Sem. origin. Cp. Mish-
naic Heb. hamdm, of s.m., and Syr. hamama,
Arab, hamama, *a spice plant*, which prob.
derive from stem h-m-m, 'to be warm'. See Imma-
nuel Low, Aramaische Pftanzennamen, Leipsic,
188 г, andHeinrich Lewy.Diesemitischen Fremd-
worter im Griechischen, Berlin, 1895, p. 37.

## among
among, prep. — ME., fr. OE. on gemang, 'in a
crowd, into a crowd', formed fr. prep, on (see a-,
'on') and a derivative of gemengan, 'to mingle'.
See mingle and cp. words there referred to.

## amongst
amongst, prep. — Formed fr. amoag with adv.
gen. suff. -s and excrescent -t. For this latter cp.
against, amidst, betwixt, whilst.

## amontillado
amontillado, п., a variety of sherry wine. — Sp.,
formed fr. a (fr. L. ad), 'to', and the name of the
town Montilla in the province of Cordova in
Spain. For the pref. see ad-, for the ending see
suff. -ado.

## amoralm
amoralm, n. pi., the teachers who expounded the
Mishna (Jewish literature). — Heb. amora'tm,
pi. of итога, lit. 'speaker', fr. Aram, umar, 'he
said, he spoke', which is rel. to Heb. amor, 'he
said, spoke, commanded', Arab, amara, 'he
ordered, commanded'. Cp. ameer, emir.

## amoral
amoral, adj., non-moral; ethically indifferent. —
A hybrid coined fr. Greek ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and moral, a word of Latin origin; first used by
Robert Louis Balfour Stephenson (1850-94).
Derivatives: amoral-ism, п., amoral-ity, n.

## amorist
amorist, п., a practicer of gallantry, lover. —
Formed fr. L. amor, 'love' (see amorous), with
suff. -ist.

## Amorite
Amorite, п., any of an ancient people inhabiting
Palestine. — Heb. Emdrt, prob. meaning lit.
'mountain dwellers' (sing, used collectively),
and rel. to amir, 'top, summit'. Akkadian Amur-
ru, in mat Amurru, 'land of the West*, is a loan
word whose sense development finds its
explanation in the fact that the Amorites lived to
the west o{ Assyria and Babylonia. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: Amorite, adj., Amorit-ic, adj.

## amorons
amorons, adj. — OF. (whence F. amoureux), fr.
Late L. amorosus, fr. L. amor, 'love', fr. amare,
'to love'. See amative and -ous and cp. enamor,
inamorato, paramour.
Derivatives: amorous-ly, adv., amorous-ness, n.

## Amorpha
Amorpha, п., a genus of American plants (bol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. άμορφος, 'deformed* (see nmor-
phous); so called because of the absence of four
of the petals.

## amorphism
amorphism, п., absence of crystallized form. —
See amorphous and -ism.

## amorpho-
amorpho-, combining form meaning 'shapeless'.
— Gk. άμορφο-, fr. άμορφος. See next word.

## amorphous
amorphous, adj., shapeless. — ModL. amorphus,
fr. Gk. άμορφος, 'without form, shapeless,
deformed', fr. ά- (see priv. pref.-a-) and μορφή,
'form, shape'. See morpho-. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, L. -us, see -ous.

## amortize
amortize, tr. v., to extinguish (a debt) through a
sinking fund. — ME. amortisen, fr. OF. (= F.)
amortiss-, pres. part, stem of amortir, fr. VL.
*admortire, 'to deaden, extinguish', fr. ad- and
VL. morlus (L. morluus), 'dead', fr. L. mors,
gen. mortis, 'death'. Cp. It. ammortire, OProv-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:58 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 31 | AMURCOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:58 COLUMN:1 -->
enc. amortir, Sp., Port, amorlecer, 'to deaden',
and see mortal.
Derivatives: amortiz-able, adj., amorliz-ation,n.,
amortizement (q.v.)

## amortizement
amortizement, n. — F. amortissement, fr.
amortir. See amortize and -ment.

## Amos
Amos, masc. PN; in the Bible 1) the third in the
order of the Twelve Prophets; 2) the Book of
Amos.— Gk. Άμώς, fr. Heb. 'Amos, lit. 'borne
(by God)', fr. '5mas, 'he bore, carried', which is
rel. to Phoen. and Ugar. '-m-s, 'to carry', Aram.
'dmas, 'he compressed', Arab, 'dmisa, '(the day)
was oppressive'.

## amount
amount, intr. v. — ME., fr. OF amonter, 'to raise',
fr. amont, 'upward', lit. 'up hill', fr. a, 'to' (see
4), and том, 'hill, mountain'. See mount and
cp. paramount, tantamount.
Derivative: amount, n.

## amour
amour, п., a love affair. — F., 'love', fr. L. amdrem,
ace. of amor, 'love', fr. amare, 'to love'. See
amative.

## ampangabeite
ampangabeite,n., a complex tantalo-niobate
(mineral.) — Named after Ampangabe in
Madagascar. For the ending see subst. sun", -ite.

## amparo
amparo, п., a certificate issued to the claimant of
land to serve as protection. — Sp., lit.
'protection, help, support', fr. amparar, 'to shelter,
protect, help', fr. VL. *ampardre, which is formed
fr. L. pref. I'm- and parare, 'to prepare'. See im-,
'in', and pare and cp. emperor.

## ampelideous
ampelideous, adj., pertaining to the vine family.—
Compounded of Gk. άμπελος, 'vine', and είδος,
'form, shape'. See ampelo-, -oid and -ous.

## ampelo-
ampelo-, combining form, meaning 'vine'. — Gk.
άμπελο-, fr. άμπελος, 'vine'; of uncertain,
possibly Mediterranean, origin.

## ampelography
ampelography, п., description of the vine. — F.
ampehgraphie, fr. Gk. άμπελος, 'vine', and
-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See ampelo-
and -graphy.

## Ampelopsis
Ampelopsis, п., a genus of plants of the grape
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'looking like vine',
compounded of Gk. άμπελος, 'vine', and δψις,
'appearance'. See ampelo- and -opsis.

## amperage
amperage, п., the strength of an electric current
given in amperes. — Formed fr. ampere with
sun", -age.

## ampere
ampere, п., unit of force of the electric current. —
F.,named after the FrenchphysicistAndre-Marie
Ampere (1775-1836).

## ampersand
ampersand, п., the symbol & (= and). —
Corruption of the partly English, partly Latin
phrase 'and per se and', i.e. 'the sign & by
itself (equals) and'.

## amphi-
amphi-, before a vowel amph-, pref. meaning
'both, on both sides, of both kinds'. — Gk.
άμφι-, άμφ-,Όη both sides, at both ends,around',
fr. άμφί, 'around; round about', which is cogn.
with L. ambi-, amb-, 'around; round about'.
See ambi- and cp. Amphion.

## Amphibia
Amphibia, n. pi., a class of vertebrates. — ModL.
See next word.
Derivatives: amphibian, adj. and n.

## amphibious
amphibious, adj., living both on land and in water.
— Gk. αμφίβιος, 'living a double life', viz. 'on
land and in water', fr. άμφι- (see amphi-)
and βίος, 'life'. See bio-. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## amphibole
amphibole, п., a silicate oT calcium, magnesium,
etc. — F., fr. L. amphibolus, 'ambiguous,
doubtful', fr. Gk. αμφίβολος, of s.m., fr. άμφιβάλλειν,
'to throw around; to doubt', fr. άμφι, 'around',
and βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See amphi- and
ballistic. The name amphibole was given to this
group of minerals by the French mineralogist
Rene-Just Haiiy (1743-1822).
Derivative: amphibol-ic, adj.

## amphibology
amphibology, п., an ambiguous statement. — F.
amphibologie, fr. ML. amphibologta, altered (on
analogy of words ending in -logia), fr. L. amphi-
bolia, fr. Gk. αμφιβολία,, 'ambiguity', fr.
αμφίβολος. See amphibole and -logy.

## amphibolous
amphibolous, adj., ambiguous. — Gk.
αμφίβολος, 'ambiguous, doubtful'. See prec. word. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## amphibrach
amphibrach, п., a metrical foot consisting of three
syllables, the middle one long and the other two
short (pros.) — L. amphibrachys, fr. Gk. άμφί-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:58 COLUMN:2 -->
βραχυς, 'short at both ends', fr. άμφι (see amphi-)
and βραχύς, 'short'. See brachy-.

## Amphicarpa
Amphicarpa, п., a genus of vines (bot.) —ModL.,
fr. Gk. άμφίκαρπος, 'having fruits on both
sides', which is compounded of άμφι- (see
amphi-) and καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous. The genus
was called Amphicarpa because it has two
kinds of pods.

## amphictyonic
amphictyonic, adj., pertaining to an amphicty-
ony. — L. amphictyonicus, fr. Gk. άμφικτυονι-
κός, fr. άμφικτυονίά. See next word and -ic

## amphicryons
amphicryons, n. pi., deputies to an amphictyonic
council.—\u.amphictyones, fr. Gk-άμφικτύονες.
See next word.

## amphictyony
amphictyony, п., confederation of states in
ancient Greece, established around a common
center. — Gk. άμφικτυονίά, 'the Amphictyonic
League', fr. άμφικτύονες, 'amphictyons', fr.
earlier άμφικτίονες, 'they that dwell round
about'. For the first element see amphi-. The
second element is rel. to Gk. κτίζειν, 'to create,
found', κτίσις, 'a founding, settling', κτοίνδ,
κτοϊνα, 'habitation, township', and cogn. with
OI. ksiti, kfiydti, 'abides, dwells', ksitih,
'dwelling place', Arm. shin, 'inhabited' (pp.)

## amphigory
amphigory, amphigouri, п., a nonsense verse. —
F. amphigouri, of unknown origin.
Derivative: amphigor-ic, adj.

## amphimixis
amphimixis, п., union of the germ cells of two
individuals (biol.) — Compounded of amphi-
and Gk. μΐξις, 'mixing, mingling, intercourse'.
See mix.

## Amphion
Amphion, п., son of Zeus and Antiope, king of
Thebes and husband of Niobe (Greek mylhol.)
— L. Amphion, fr. Gk. 'Αμφίων, which is prob.
a derivative of άμφι, 'round about'. See amphi-.

## Ainphioxus
Ainphioxus, п., a genus of marine animals (zool.)
— ModL., coined by the English zoologist Wil-
lianj Yarrell (1784-1856) in 1836 fr. amphi-
and οξύς, ^pointed, sharp'. See oxy-.
Accordingly Amphioxus lit. means 'tapering at both
ends'.

## Amphipoda
Amphipoda, n. pi., an order of the Crustacea with
two kinds of feet for swimming, respectively for
jumping (zool.) — ModL. compounded of
amphi- and Gk. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot' (see -poda).
Accordingly Amphipoda lit. means 'having two
kinds of feet'.
Derivatives: amphipod-an, amphipod-ous, adjs.

## amphishaena
amphishaena, п., a serpent having a head at each
end (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. άμφίσβαινα,
'serpent supposed to be able to go both
forward and backward', which is compounded of
άμφί (see amphi-) and βαίνειν, 'to go'. See base, η.

## Amphisbaena
Amphisbaena, п., a genus of lizards (zool.) — See
prec. word.

## amphiscians
amphiscians, also amphiscu, n. pi., the inhabitants
of the tropic zone. — ML. amphiscii (pi.), fr.
Gr. άμφίσκιος, 'throwing a shadow both ways'
fr. άμφί (see amphi-) and σκιά, 'shade, shadow'
(see skiagraphy); so called because their shadow
falls toward north at one time, toward south at
another. Cp. antiscians.

## amphitheater
amphitheater, amphitheatre, n. — L. amphilhea-
trum, fr. Gk. άμφι&έάτρον, lit. meaning 'having
seats for spectators all round'. See amphi- and
theater.

## Amphitrite
Amphitrite, п., the daughter of Nereus and Doris
and wife of Poseidon (Greek mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. 'Αμφιτρίτη, lit. '(waves of the sea) roaring
round (the earth)', prob. fr. άμφί, 'on both
sides' (see amphi-), and the stem of τρίζειν,
Ίο utter a shrill cry, creak', from the I.-E.
imitative base *(s)trig-; see strident and cp. trismus.
Cp. W. H. Roscher, Ausfuhrliches Lexikon der
griechischen Mythologie, Leipzig, 1884-86, I,
p.318.

## Amphitryon
Amphitryon, п., son of Alceus and husband of
Alcmene in Greek mythology; used
figuratively in the sense of host. — Gk. Άμφιτρύων, a
compound literally meaning 'one who reigns
far and wide'. For the first elemenl of this
compound see amphi-. The second element is prob.
rel. to Gk. τύρ-αννος, 'lord, master, sovereign,
tyrant'; see tyrant. The metaphorical use of this
PN. to denote a host is due to the circumstance
that during Amphitryon's absence his wife

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:58 COLUMN:3 -->
Alcmene was visited and feasted by Zeus in the
shape of her husband. See Pauly-Wissova, Real-
Encyklopadie der klassischen Altertumswissen-
schaft, I, 1967.

## amphodelite
amphodelite, п., a variety of anorthite (mineral.)
— Compounded of amph-, and Gk. όδελός, a
variant of όβελός, 'a spit' (see obelus, obelisk);
so called in allusion to the twin crystals in which
it occurs. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## amphora
amphora, n. — L., 'a vessel with two handles or
ears, a pitcher', fr. Gk. άμφορεύς, of s.m., which
is contracted fr. *άμφι-φορεύς (see haplblogy),
lit. 'two-handled', fr. άμφί (see amphi-) and
φορεύς, 'bearer, carrier', fr. φέρείν, 'to bear'.
See benr, 'to carry', and cp. -phore. Cp. also
ampulla.

## ample
ample, adj., spacious, abundant. — F., fr. L.
amplus, 'large, spacious', which stands for *am-
los and lit. means 'comprehensive', from I.-E.
base *am- 'to seize, hold', whence also L. ampla,
ansa, 'handle', Lith. -qsd, Lett, uosa, 'loop,
knot', OPruss. ansis, 'pot hook, trammel', Gk.
ηνία, Dor. ανία (for *ansia), 'bridle, reins',
ON. ses, MLG. -cese, G. use, 'eye, loop', Mir.
(si (pi.), 'bridle'. Cp. amplify, amplitude.
Derivatives: ample-ness, п., ampl-y, adv.

## amplification
amplification, n. — L. amplificdtio, gen. -dnis, 'a
widening, enlarging, extending', fr. amplificdtus,
pp. of amplificare. See next word and Hon.
amplify, tr. v. — F. amplifier, fr. L. amplificare,
'to widen, enlarge, extend', fr. amplus (see
ample) and -ficdre, (r.facere, 'to make, do'. See -fy.
Derivative: amplifi-er, n.
amplitude, п., spaciousness; abundance; extent.
— F., fr. L. amplitudd, 'wide extent, width', fr.
amplus. See ample and -tilde.
ampulla, п., a flask with two handles. — L.
ampulla (for *ampor-la), 'a globular vessel for
holding liquids', dimin. of amphora, ampora. See
amphora.
Derivatives: ampull-aceous, ampull-ar, ampull-
ar-y, ampull-ate, ampull-at-ed, adjs.

## ampalliform
ampalliform, adj. — Compounded of ampulla
and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## amputate
amputate, tr. v. — L. qmputatus, pp. of amputdre,
'to cut off, to prune', compounded of am-,
shortened form of ambi-, 'around', and putare,
'to trim, prune, lop, clean'. See ambi- and pata-
tive and cp. pave and pit. For the ending see
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: amputation (q.v.), amputat-ive, adj.,
ampulat-or, n.

## amputation
amputation, n. — L. ampututio, gen. -onis, fr.
amputdtus, pp. of amputdre. See amputate and
-ion.

## amrita
amrita, amreeta, п., the drink of immortality
(Hindu mythol.) — OI.am^tah,'immortal; drink
of immortality; immortality', cogn. with Gk.
άμβροτος, 'immortal'. See priv. pref. an- and
mortal.

## amsel
amsel, п., ι) the blackbird; 2) the ring ouzel.—
G. Amsel, fr. MHG. amsel, fr. OHG. amsala,
amusla. See ouzel and cp. words there referred to.

## Amsonia
Amsonia, п., a genus of herbs (bot.) — ModL.,
named in honor of Charles Amson,
physician of Gloucester, Virginia (lSth cent.) For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## amt
amt, п., a territorial division in Denmark and
Norway. — Dan., fr. G. Ami, Office', fr. MHG.
ambeht, ammet, fr. OHG. ambaht, ampaht,
which is of Celtic origin. Cp. Gaulish-Lat.
ambactus, 'servant', and see embassy.

## amnck
amnck, amok, adj., possessed with a murderous
frenzy; adv., in a murderous frenzy. — Malay
amoq, "in a frenzy'.

## amulet
amulet, n. — L. amuletum, 'amulet', prob. orig.
meaning 'food made of amylum (starch flour)',
fr. amulum, amylum, 'starch flour' (see
amylum); influenced in sense by a confusion with
amdlirt, 'to carry away, remove*.
Derivative: amulet-ic, adj.

## amurcous
amurcous, adj., foul. — Formed with suff. -ous
fr. L. amurca, 'the dregs of olives', fr. Gk.
άμόργη, of s.m., fr. άμέργειν, 'to pluck, pull',
which is pern, related to όμοργνύναι, 'to wipe
off', and cogn. with OI. mrjdti, 'wipes off', L.
mergae, 'a two-pronged pitchfork'. For the
change of Gk. γ to c(k) in Latin cp. L. spelunca,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:59 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: AMUSE | 32 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:59 COLUMN:1 -->
'cave', fr. Gk. σπήλυγξ. This change is prob.
due to Etruscan influence; see K.v.Ettmayer,
fndogermanische Forschungen, 45, lof., and
E.Vetter, Glotta, 17, 302.

## amuse
amuse, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) amuser, 'to cause to
muse', lit. 'to cause to gape idly about', fr. a,
'to' (see a), and muser, 'to muse'. See muse.
Derivatives: amus-ed, adj., amus-ed-ly, adv.,
amuse-ment, п., amus-ing, adj., amus-ing-ly, adv.
amus-ing-ness, п., amus-ive, adj., amus-ive-ly,
adv., amus-ive-ness, n.

## amusia
amusia, п., inability for music (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. άμουσίά, 'want of harmony', fr.
£μουσος, 'without song, without harmony', fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and Μούσα, 'Muse; music*.
See Muse and -la.

## Amy
Amy, fern. PN. — OF. Amee, lit. 'beloved', fr.
OF. amee (corresponding to F. aimee), fem.
pp. of amer (F. aimer), 'to love', fr. L. amare,
of s.m. See amative.

## amyelous
amyelous, adj., lacking the spinal chord. — Gk.
άμύελος, 'without marrow', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and μυελός, 'marrow', which stands
for mus-elo-s, and is rel. to μυών (gen. μϋώνος),
'knot of muscles', and to μϋς (gen. μυός),
'muscle'. See myo- and cp. amyous. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## amygdala
amygdala, п., a tonsil (anal.) — L., fr. Gk.
αμυγδαλή, 'almond'; see almond. The use of the
word in its anatomical sense is due to a literal
translation of Arab, al-lauzalani, 'the two
tonsils', lit. 'the two almonds'.

## Amygdalaceae
Amygdalaceae, n. pi., the almond or peach family
(bot.) — ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. L.
amygdala, 'almond'. See amygdala.

## amygdulaceous
amygdulaceous, adj. — Formed fr. amygdala with
suff. -aceous.

## amygdalate
amygdalate, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
almonds. — Formed fr. amygdain with adj.
suff. -ate.

## amygdalic
amygdalic, adj., pertaining to, or designating, the
crystalline acid СмНм013 (chem.) — See next
word and -ic; so called because it is formed by
the decomposition of amygdalin.

## amygdalin
amygdalin, п., a crystalline glucoside QgH]7NO,t
(chem.) — Formed fr. amygdala with chem. suff.
-in; so called because it occurs in bitter almonds.

## amygdaline
amygdaline, adj., 1) pertaining to, or resembling,
an almond or almonds; 2) pertaining to a tonsil
(anal.) — L. amygdalinus, 'of almonds', fr.
amygdala, 'almond'. See amygdala and -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## amyl
amyl, п., starch (obsol.) — L. amylum, fr. Gk.
άμυλον, 'fine meal, starch', prop. neut. of the
adjective ίμυλος, 'not ground at the mill', fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and μύλη, 'mill'. See mid
and cp. aniidm.

## amyl
amyl, п., a hydrocarbon radical CSH,, (chem.) —
Coined from the first two letters of L. amylum
(see prec. word) and suff. -yL

## amyloid
amyloid, adj., starchlike; п., a starchlike
substance. — Compounded of Gk. αμυλον, 'starch',
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
amyl, 'starch', and -oid.

## amyous
amyous, adj., wanting in muscles (med.) — Gk.
£μυος, 'without muscle', fr. ά- (see priv. pref.
a-) and μϋς, gen. μυός, 'muscle*. See myo- and
cp. amyelous.

## Amyris
Amyris, п., a genus of plants of the rue family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. μύρον,
'balsam*. See smear, n.

## nn
nn, indef. art. (before a word beginning with a
vowel), — ME. an, fr. OE. an, 'one', whence also
one (q.v.) Cp. a, indef. article.

## an
an, conj. meaning 'if, and if. — Shortened fr.
aad (q.v.)

## an-
an-, a-, priv. pref. — Gk. άν-, ά-, 'not, without',
rel. to νε-, νη-, ν-, of s.m. (see nepenthe), and
cogn. with OI. an-, a-, L. in-, Goth., OE., etc.
un-, of s.m. See priv. pref. un-.

## an-
an-, form of ana- before a vowel.

## an-
an-, assimilated form of ad- before n.

## -an
-an, suff. meaning 'pertaining to', used in
zoology, chemistry, biology. — Fr. L. -anus, either
directly or through the medium of F. -ain, -en.
Cp. the suffixes -ian and -ain. Cp. also suff. -ana
and ana.

## ana-
ana-, before a vowel an-, pref. meaning: 1) up,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:59 COLUMN:2 -->
upward; 2) back, backward, against; 3) again,
anew; 4) exceedingly; 5) according to. — Gk.
άνα-, άν-, 'up to, upward, up, toward;
exceedingly; back, backward; against', fr. άνά, 'up,
on, upon; throughout; again', rel. to άνω,
'above', and cogn. with Avestic ana, 'on, upon',
L. an- in anhelare, 'to pant, gasp', Goth, ana,
OE. on, an, OSlav. na, Lith. пи, OPruss. no, na,
'on, upon'; fr. I.-E. base *ano-, 'on, upon,
above'. Cp. on and a-, On'. Cp. also the pref.
in anhelation.

## -ana
-ana, pi. suff. meaning 'sayings of, anecdotes of,
as in Johnsoriana. — L. -ana, neut. pi. of -anus,
'pertaining to'. See -an and cp. ana.

## ana
ana, п., collection of memorable sayings of
famous men. — Coined fr. -ana, neut. pi. of
Latin adjectives ending in the masc. sing, into
-anus; abstracted from the ending of names like
Johnsoniana, etc. See -ana.

## Anabaena
Anabaena, п., a genus of algae (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άναβαίνειν, 'to go up', fr. άνά (see ana-)
and βαίνειν, 'to go'. See base, п., and cp. ana-
bas, anabasis.

## anahaptism
anahaptism, п., rebaptism. — ML. anabaptismus,
fr. Late Gk. άναβαπτισμός, 'dipping into water
again, re-immersion', fr. Gk. άνα-, 'again' (see
ana-) and βαπτίζειν, 'to dip, baptize'. See
baptism.

## Anabaptist
Anabaptist, n. — ModL. anabaptisla, 'one who
baptizes again', fr. ana- and Gk. βαπτιστής,
'one that dips, baptizer'. See baptist and cp.
prec. word.
T)eriva.tives:Anabaptist-ic,Anabaplist-ic-al,ad}S.,
Anabaplist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## anahaptize
anahaptize, tr. v., to rebaptize. — ML. anabap-
lizare, fr. Late Gk. άναβαπτίζειν, 'to dip into
water again'. See anahaptism and -ize.

## Anabas
Anabas, п., a genus of fishes (ichthyol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άναβάς, gen. άνάβαντος, aor. part, of
άναβαίνειν, 'to go up, mount, climb' (see next
word); so called by the French naturalist baron
Georges-Leopold-Chretien-Frederic-Dagobert
Cuvier (1769-1832) because the fishes of this
genus are capable of leaving the water and
climbing trees.

## anabasis
anabasis, п., a military expedition, esp. that of
Cyrus the Younger against Artaxerxes,
described by Xenophon in his Anabasis. — Gk.
άνάβασις, 'a going up, an expedition up from
the coast', fr. άναβαίνειν, 'to go up', fr. άνά
(ала-) and βαίνειν, 'to go'. See base, п., and cp.
prec. word and catabasis.

## Anableps
Anableps, п., a genus of S. and Central American
fishes with projecting eyes. — Fr. Gk. άνάβλε-
ψις, 'a looking up', fr. άνά (see ana-) and
βλέπειν, 'to look, see', which is rel. to βλέφαρον,
'eyelid'. See blepharo-.

## anabolic
anabolic, adj., pertaining to anabolism. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. αναβολή, 'that which is
thrown up, mound', fr. άναβάλλειν, 'to throw
up', fr. άνά (see ana-) and βάλλειν, 'to throw'.
See ballistic

## anabolism
anabolism, п., the building up process in the living
protoplasm. — See prec. word and -ism and cp.
catabolism.

## anabrosis
anabrosis, n„ corrosion of soft tissues (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. άνάβρωσις, 'an eating up',
fr. άναβιβρώσκειν, 'to eat up', fr. άνά (see ana-)
and βιβρώσχειν, 'to eat, eat up, devour*. See
broma and -osis.

## anabrotic
anabrotic, adj., corrosive (med.) — Gk. άναβρω-
τικός, 'corrosive*, fr. άνάβρωτος, 'eaten up',
verbal adj. of άναβιβρώσκειν. See prec. word.

## anacatharsis
anacatharsis, п., expectoration (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. άνακάθαρσις, 'a clearing away (of
rubbish), fr. άνά (see ana-) and κάθαρσις, 'a
cleansing', fr. καθαίρείν, 'to cleanse'. See cn-
thnrsis and cp. acatharsin.

## anacnthartic
anacnthartic, adj., emetic, expectorant. — See
prec. word and -ic.

## anachronic
anachronic, adj., marked by anachronism. — See
anachronism and -ic

## anachronism
anachronism, п., an error in chronology. — F.
anachronisme, fr. Gk. αναχρονισμός,
'anachronism*, fr. άναχρονίζειν, 'to refer to a wrong
time', fr. άνά, 'up, against' (see ana-), and χρόνος
'time'. See chronic and -ism.

## anachronistic
anachronistic, adj., marked by anachronism. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:59 COLUMN:3 -->
See prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: anachrdnistic-al, adj., anachro-
nistic-al-ly, adv.

## anaclastic
anaclastic, adj., pertaining to refraction (opt.) —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. άνάκλαστας,
'bent back, broken, reflected' (said of light),
verbal adj. of άνακλαν, 'to bend back, break,
reflect', fr. άνά, 'back' (see ana-), and κλαν, 'to
break'. See clastic.

## anacoluthon
anacoluthon, п., a lack in grammatical sequence.
— Gk. .άνακόλουθον, neut. of ανακόλουθος,
'inconsequent, inconsistent', fr. άν- (see priv.
pref. an-) and ακόλουθος, 'following, attending
on', which is formed fr. copul. pref. ά- and
κέλευθος, 'way, road, path, track'. Copul. pref.
ά- stands for I.-E. *sm-, a weak gradational
form of base *sem-, 'one, together'; see
same. For the etymology of Gk. κέλευθος see
acolyte.

## anaconda
anaconda, п., orig. a name given to a python of
.Ceylon; (zool.) any large snake of the boa
family. — Perhaps of Singhalese origin.

## Anacreontic
Anacreontic, adj., written in the style of Ana-
creon; п., a poem written in the style of Ana-
creon. — L. Anacreonticus, fr. Anacrean, fr. Gk.
'Ανακρέων, a celebrated Greek lyrical poet born
at Teos in Ionia (560-478 B.C.E.).

## anacrusis
anacrusis, п., unstressed syllable before a stressed
syllable at the beginning of a verse. — Gk.
άνάκρουσις, 'a pushing back', fr. άνακρούειν,
'to push back', fr. άνά, 'back' (see ana-), and
κρούειν (for *κροΰσειν), 'to knock, strike,
push', which is rel. to Homeric κροαίνειν (prob.
for *κρουσάν-£ειν), 'to stamp, strike with the
hoof, and cogn. with OSlav. sii-krusp, su-kru-
Siti, Russ. kruSif, Lith. kruSu, kruSti, 'to smash,
shatter', OSlav. kruchu, 'piece, bit of food'.

## anadem
anadem, п., a wreath, garland. — L. anadlma, fr.
Gk. άνάδημα, 'band, headband', fr. άναδεΐν,
'to bind up', fr. άνά (see'ana-) and δεϊν, 'to
bind'. See diadem.

## anadiplosis
anadiplosis, п., repetition of an initial word (rhet.)
— Gk. άναδίπλωσις, 'repetition, duplication',
fr. άναδιπλοΰν, 'to double, fold', fr. άνά, 'again'
(see ana·), and διπλούν, 'to fold, repeat', fr.
διπλόος, διπλοϋς, 'double'. See diplo- and cp.
diploma.

## nnadromous
nnadromous, adj., going up rivers to spawn. —
Gk. ανάδρομος, 'running upward', fr. άνά (see
ana-) and δρόμος, course, race, running'. See
dromedury and cp. catadromous. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## Anadyomene
Anadyomene, п., an epithet of Aphrodite (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Αναδυόμενη, lit. 'she
that emerges (out of the sea)', fem. pres. part, of
άναδυεσθαι, fr. άνά (see ana-) and middle voice
of δύειν, 'to put on (clothes), to enter,
penetrate, dive'. See adytum and cp. ecdysis, en-
dysis.
nnaemia. — See anemia.

## anaerobic
anaerobic, adj., capable of living without oxygen
(bid.) — Coined by the French chemist and
bacteriologist Louis Pasteur (1822-95) in 1863
from priv. pref. an- and aerobic.

## Anagallis
Anagallis, п., a genus of herbs of the primrose
family (bol.) — L. anagallis, 'pimpernel', fr. Gk.
άναγαλλίς, a word of uncertain origin.

## anaglyph
anaglyph, п., an embossed ornament. — Gk.
άνάγλυφον, 'wrought in relief, fr. άναγλύφειν,
'to carve in relief, fr. άνά (see ana-) and γλύφειν,
'to carve', which is cogn. with L. glubere, 'to
peel', and E. cleave, to split (q.v.) Cp. the second
element in hieroglyph, triglypb.

## anaglyptic
anaglyptic, adj., pertaining to anaglyphs. — Gk.
άναγλυπτικός, fr. άνάγλυπτος, 'wrought in
relief, verbal adj. of άναγλύφειν. See prec. word
and -ic

## anagogy
anagogy, п., mystical interpretation of
Scriptures. — Gk. αναγωγή, 'a leading up', fr.
άνάγειν, 'to lead up', fr. άνά (see ana-) and άγειν,
'to lead'; cp. αγωγή, 'a leading'. See agent and
cp. -agogue, npagoge, pedagogne, synagogue.
Derivatives: anagag-ic, anagog-ic-al, adjs., ana-
gog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## anagram
anagram, п., transposition of the letters of a
word or phrase so as to form another. — ModL.
anagramma, fr. Gk. αναγραμματισμός, 'a
transposition of letters', fr. άναγραμματί,ζειν, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:60 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 33 | ANATHEMA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:60 COLUMN:1 -->
transpose the letters of a word', which is
formed fr. άνά, 'back' (see ana-), and γράμμα,
gen. γράμματος, 'written character, letter'. See
-graph and cp. grammar.
Derivatives: anagrammat-ic, anagrammat-ic-al,
adjs., anagrammat-i-cal-ly, adv., anagrammatlsm
(q.v.),anagrammat-ist,n., anagrammatize (q.v.)

## anagrammatism
anagrammatism, п., the making of anagrams. —
ModL. anagrammatismus, fr. Gk.
αναγραμματισμός. See anagram and -ism.

## anagrammatize
anagrammatize, tr. v., to make an anagram of;
intr. v., to make anagrams. — Gk. άναγραμμα-
τίζειν. See anagram and -ize.

## anai
anai, adj., pertaining to, or connected with, the
anus. See anus and adj. suff. -al.

## analcite
analcite, п., a white zeolite (mineral.) — Formed
with subst. sufT. -ite fr. Gk. άναλκής, 'weak,
feeble', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and αλκή,
'protection, help, strength'; so called in allusion
to the weak electricity it acquires when rubbed.
Gk. αλκή is rel. to άλέκειν, 'to ward off',
whence the desiderative verb άλέξειν, 'to ward
off, keep off, turn away, defend, protect'. See
Alexander.

## analectic
analectic, adj., relating to analects. — See next
word and -ic.

## analects
analects, also analecta, n. pi., collected writings;
literary gleanings. — Gk. ανάλεκτα, 'things,
chosen', neut. pi. of άνάλεκτος, 'select, choice*,
verbal adj. of άναλέγειν, 'to pick up, gather
up, collect', fr. ανά (see ana-) and λέγειν, 'to
speak', prop, 'to choose (words)', which is cogn.
with L. legere, 'to read'. See lecture.

## analemma
analemma, п., an orthographical projection of the
sphere on the plane of the meridional (geom.) —
L., 'a sundial showing the meridian and latitude
of a place', fr. Gk. άνάλημμα, 'sundial', fr.
άναλαμβάνειν, 'to receive, take up, restore*,
fr. άνά (see ana-) and λαμβάνειν, 'to receive'.
See lemma and cp. words there referred to.

## analeptic
analeptic, adj., restorative, tonic (said of a
medicine); п., a restorative medicine, a tonic. — Gk.
άναληπτικός, 'restorative', fr. άναλαμβάνειν, 'to
receive', take up, restore', fr. άνά (see ana-) and
λαμβάνειν, 'to take, grasp, seize; to receive'.
See prec. word.

## aaalgesia
aaalgesia, п., absence of pain. — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. αναλγησία,'want of feeling, insensibility',
fr. ανάλγητος, 'without pain'. See next word.
Derivatives: analges-ic, adj., and п.,
analgesics, n.

## analgetic
analgetic, adj., producing analgesia; п., a drug
producing analgesia. — Formed with sufT. -ic
fr. Gk. ανάλγητος, 'without pain', fr. άν- (see
priv. pref. a-) and άλγεΐν, 'to feel pain', fr.
άλγος, 'pain'. See -algla.

## analogical
analogical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. analogicus, fr. Gk. αναλογικός, fr. αναλογία.
See analogy and -ic.
Derivative: analogical-ly, adv.

## analogize
analogize, tr. v., to explain by analogy; intr. v.,
to reason-by analogy or to use analogies. — Gk.
άναλογίζεσθαι, 'to reckon up, sum up', fr.
αναλογία. See analogy and -ize.

## analogous
analogous, adj. — L. analogus, fr. Gk.
ανάλογος, 'according to a due proportion,
proportionate', fr. άνά (see ana-) and λόγος, 'word,
speech, reckoning, proportion'. See logos and
-ous. Derivatives: analogous-ly, adv., analogous-
ness, n.

## analogue
analogue, п., an analogous thing. — F., fr. Gk.
άνάλογον, neut. of ανάλογος. See prec. word.

## analogy
analogy, п., similarity. — F. analogic, fr. L. ana-
logia, fr. Gk. αναλογία, 'proportion, analogy',
fr. ανάλογος. See analogous and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).
Derivatives: analogical (q.v.), analog-isl, п.,
analog-ist-ic, adj., analogize (q.v.)

## analphabetic
analphabetic, adj., not alphabetic. — Formed fr.
privative pref. aa- and alphabetic.

## analysis
analysis, п., separation of a whole into its
component parts. — Gk. άνάλυσις, 'a loosing,
releasing', fr. άναλύειν, 'to unloose, release, set
free', fr. άνά, 'up, on, throughout' (see ana-), and
λύειν, 'to unfasten, loosen, slacken'. See lysis.

## analyste
analyste, п., a person who analyzes. — F., formed
fr. analyser, on analogy of nouns in -isle (E.
-ist) fr. verbs in -iser (E. -ize). See prec. word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:60 COLUMN:2 -->
and cp. analyze,

## analytic
analytic, analytical, adj. -e- ML. analyticus, fr.
Gk. αναλυτικός, 'analytical', fr. άνάλυσις. See
analysis and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: analylic-al-ly, adv.

## analyze
analyze, analyse, tr. v. — F. analyser, formed fr.
analyse, 'analysis', on analogy of verbs in -iser.
See analysis and -ize.
Derivatives: analyz-ation (analys-ation), п.,
analyzed (analys-ed), adj., analyzer (analys-er), n.

## anamnesis
anamnesis, п., recollection, remembrance. — Gk.
άνάμνησις, 'a calling to mind, reminiscence',
fr. άναμιμνήσκειν, 'to remind, recall to
memory', fr. άνά (see ana-) and μιμνήσκειν, 'to
remind', which is rel. to μνάσθαι, 'to
remember', μέμονα, Ί remember', fr. I.-E. base 'men-,
'to think, remember'. See mind and cp. mnesic,
amnesia, paramnesin.

## anamorphosis
anamorphosis, п., a distorted image; a gradual
change in form (biol.) — ModL., fr. άναμόρ-
φωσις, 'a forming anew', fr. άναμορφοϋν, 'to
form anew, transform', fr. άνά, 'again' (see
ana-), and μορφοϋν, 'to give form to, form,
shape', fr. μορφή, 'form, shape'. See morpho-
and cp. metamorphosis, amorphous.

## ananas
ananas, n. — Sp. ananas, fr. Peruv. nanas,
'pineapple'.

## ananda
ananda, п., bliss, one of the three qualities of
Brahma (Hindu mythol.) — OI. ananda-, 'joy,
happiness, bliss', formed from the particle a-
and the stem of nandati, 'he rejoices'. For the
etymology of the particle a- see agama and cp.
words there referred to. OI. nandati is of
uncertain origin.

## anandrous
anandrous, adj., having no stamens. — Gk. αναν
δρος, 'husbandless; unmanly', fr. άν- (see priv.
pref. an-) and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man'. See
•androus.

## Ananke
Ananke, п., the personification of necessity in
Greek mythology. — Gk. ανάγκη, 'necessity',
of uncertain origin; perhaps standing for *an-
ank- and cogn. with Olr. Icen, W. angen,
'necessity, fate', Ir. echt (for *anktu-),
'manslaughter', OE. oht, MDu. aht, OHG. Shta, MHG.
akte, aht, G. Acht, 'hostile persecution', Hitt.
henkan, 'destiny, death'.

## Atlanta
Atlanta, п., the endless, an epithet of the serpent
Shesha in Hindu mythology. — OI. andntah,
'endless', fr. OI. priv. pref. an- (see priv. pref.
an-) and amah- 'end, boundary, edge', which
is rel. to OI. ami, 'opposite', and cogn. with
Gk. αντί, 'over against, opposite, before', L.
ante, 'before, in front of. See ante- and cp.
anti-.

## anapaest
anapaest, п., a metrical foot consisting of two
short syllables followed by a long one, a reversed
dactyl (pros.) — L. anapaestus, fr. Gk.
ανάπαιστος, 'struck back, rebounding', verbal adj.
of άναπαίειν, 'to strike back', fr. άνά, 'back'
(see ana-), and παίειν, 'to strike', which prob.
stands for "πάΓιειν and is cogn. with L. pavire,
'to beat, ram, tread down'. See pave.

## anapaestic
anapaestic, anapaestical, adj. — L. anapaesticus,
fr. Gk. άναπαιστικός, fr. ανάπαιστος* See prec.
word and -Ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: anapaestic-al-ly, adv.

## anapaite
anapaite, п., a hydrous ferrous calcium phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after Anapa on the Black
Sea. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Anaphalls
Anaphalls, п., a genus of plants (hot.) — ModL.,
of uncertain origin.

## Anaphe
Anaphe, п., a genus of moths (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άναφής, 'impalpable', fr. άν- (see priv.
pref. an-) and άφή, 'touch, grip', from the stem
of απτειν, Ίο fasten, usually in the middle
voice απτεσθαι, 'to touch'. See apsis and cp.
words there referred to.

## anaphora
anaphora, п., repetition of the same word or
phrase in successive clauses, (rhet.) — Gk.
αναφορά, 'a carrying back', fr. άναφέρειν, 'to carry
back', fr. άνά, 'back' (see ana-), and φέρειν, 'to
bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry', and cp. -phore.

## anaphrodisiac
anaphrodisiac, adj., that which reduces sexual
desire; п., a drug reducing sexual desire. —
Formed fr. priv. pref. an- and Gk.
αφροδισιακός, 'sexual, venereal'. See aphrodisiac,

## anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis, п., exaggerated susceptibility,
especially to protein (med. and biol.) — Coined

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:60 COLUMN:3 -->
by the French physiologist Charles Richet
(1850-1935) in 1893 on analogy of prophylaxis
(q.v.) Anaphylaxis accordingly means the
opposite of what is expressed by prophylaxis; it is
formed fr. ana- and Gk. φύλαξις, *a watching,
guarding'. See phylaxis.

## anaplasty
anaplasty, п., plastic surgery. — F. anaplastic fr.
Gk. άνάπλαστος, 'made anew', verbal adj. of
άναπλάσσειν, Ίο make anew, remodel', fr. άνά,
'again* (see ana-), and πλάσσειν, 'to mold, form*.
See plnsma.

## anaptotic
anaptotic, adj., of languages: characterized — as
English — by a tendency to lose declensional
forms. — Formed fr. Gk. ανά, 'back' (see ana-),
and πτωτικός, 'pertaining to cases', fr. πτωτός,
'fallen', verbal adj. of πίπτειν, 'to fall', which
stands for *πϊ-πτειν, fr. *pt-, zero degree of
I.-E. base *pet-, 'to fly, to fall'. See fenther and
cp. symptom and words there referred to. For
the ending see suff. -ic.

## anarch
anarch, п., leader in anarchy. — Gk. άναρχος,
'without chief, fr. άνά (see priv. pref. an-) and
άρχος, 'chief, leader, ruler'. See arch-.

## anarchy
anarchy, n. — F. anarchie, fr. Gk. αναρχία, 'lack
of a leader, state of being without any leader',
fr. άναρχος 'without chief'. See anarch and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).
Derivatives: anarch-ic, anarch-ic-al, adjs., an-
arch-ic-al-ly, adv., anarch-ism, п., anarch-ist, п.,
anarch-ize, tr. v.

## annrthria
annrthria, п., inability to articulate words (med.)
— Medical L., coined by the French neurologist
Pierre Marie (1853-1940) fr. Gk. άναρθρος,
'without joints' (see next word). For the ending
see suff. -ia.

## anarthrous
anarthrous, adj., unarticulated. — Gk. άναρθρος,
'without joints', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and
άρθρον, 'joint, limb, organ'. See arthritis. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -«Jus.

## Anas
Anas, п., the genus of ducks (pool.) — L. anas,
'duck', cogn. with Lith. antis, OPruss. amis,
OSlav. Qty, ORuss. urovi, Serb, utva (fr. *<>/-),
ON. and, OF. sened, MDu. sent, OHG. anut,
MHG. ant, G. Erne, and prob. also with Gk.
νήσσα, Att. νήττα, Boeot. νασσα, 'duck', OI.
atlh, 'waterfowl'. Cp. Anatidae, Nesonetta. Cp.
also smew.

## anasarca
anasarca, п., a form of subcutaneous dropsy.
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. άνά σάρκα,
abbreviation of ΰδρωψ άνά σάρκα, 'dropsy
throughout the flesh'; fr. άνά, 'throughout' (see ana-),
and σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'flesh'. See sarco-.

## anaspadias
anaspadias, п., a condition in which the urethra
opens on the upper surface of the penis (med.)
— Medical L., fr. ana- and the stem of σπαν, 'to
draw'. See spasm and cp. words there referred to.

## Anastasin
Anastasin, fern. PN. — Late L., fern, of Anasta-
sius (q.v.).

## anastasis
anastasis, п., convalescence (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. άνάστασις, 'a standing up', fr. άνιστάναι,
'to make to stand up', fr. άνά (see ana-) and
ίστάναι, 'to make to stand'. See state and cp.
apocatastasis, catastasis, hypostasis, metastasis.

## Anastasius
Anastasius, masc. PN. — Late L. Anastasius, fr.
Gk. 'Αναστάσιος, fr. άνάστασις, 'resurrection',
lit. 'a rising up'. See prec. word and cp. Ana-
stasia.

## anastomose
anastomose, tr. v., to communicate by
anastomosis. — F. anastomoser, fr. anastomose, fr. Gk.
άναστόμωσις. See next word.

## anastomosis
anastomosis, п., intercommunication of vessels in
the animal body or of parts in any branching
system (anat.) — Gk. άναστόμωσις, Outlet,
opening', fr. άναστομοϋν, 'to furnish with a
mouth', fr. άνά (see ana-) and στόμα, 'mouth'.
See stoma, stomach.

## anastomotic
anastomotic, adj. — See prec. word and -otic.

## anastrophe
anastrophe, п., inversion of the usual order of
words (rhet.)—L., fr. Gk. αναστροφή, 'a turning
upside down; a turning up or back, inversion',
fr. άναστρέφειν, 'to turn up or back*, fr. άνά
(see ana-) and στρέφειν, 'to turn'. See stropha
and cp. antistrophe, apostrophe, catastropha.

## anathema
anathema, п., curse, malediction; a thing or
person accursed. — L. anathema, fr. Gk. ανάθεμα,
'anything devoted', later used in the sense of
'anything devoted to evil, an accursed thing',
a later variant of ανάθημα, 'an offering', lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:61 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ANATHEMATIZE | 34 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:61 COLUMN:1 -->
'that which is set up', fr. άνατιθέναι, 'to lay
upon', which is formed fr. άνά (see ana·) and
τι&έναι, 'to put, place'. See thesis and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: anathemat-ic, anathetnal-ic-al, adjs.,
anathemat-ic-al-ly, adv., anathemat-ism, п., ana-
themat-ize (q.v.)

## anathematize
anathematize, tr. v. to pronounce an anathema
against; intr. v., to curse. — F. analhematiser,
fr. L. anthematizare, fr. Gk. άναθεματίζειν, 'to
devote to evil', fr. ανάθεμα, gen. -θέματος. See
anathema and -ize.
Derivative: anathemal-iz-ation, п., anathemat-
iz-er, n.

## Anatidae
Anatidae, n. pi., a family of birds, the ducks (or-
nithol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr.
L. anas, gen. analis, 'duck'. See Anas.

## anatocism
anatocism, п., compound interest (law). — L.
anatocismus, fr. Gk. ανατοκισμός,, fr. άνά, 'again'
(see ana-), and τοκίζειν, 'to lend on interest',
which is rel. to τάκος, 'childbirth', τοκεύς,
'father', in pi. 'parents', and in gradational
relationship to τέκνον, 'child', τίκτειν (for *τί-
τκειν), 'to bring forth, bear'. See thane and cp.
tecno-, toco-, atocin. For the ending see suff.
-ism.

## Anatolin
Anatolin, п., ancient name of Asia Minor. — ML.
Anatolia, fr. Gk. ανατολή, 'sunrise, east', lit. 'a
rising above (the horizon)', fr. άνατελλειν, 'to
rise', fr. άνά (see ana-) and τέλλειν, 'to
accomplish, perform; to rise', which is rel. to
τέλος, 'end'. See tele- and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: Anatoli-an, adj. and п., Anatol-ic,
adj.

## anatomic
anatomic, anatomical, adj. — F. anatomique, fr.
L. anatomicus, fr. Gk. ανατομικός, 'relating to
anatomy, skilled in anatomy', fr. ανατομία.
See next word and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: anatomic-al-ly, adv.

## anatomy
anatomy, n. — F. anatomie, fr. L. anatomia, fr.
Gk. ανατομία, ανατομή, 'dissection', which is
related to άνατέμνειν, 'to cut up', fr. άνά (see
ana-) and τέμνειν 'to cut'. See tome and cp.
acrotomous, atom. For the ending see suff. -y
(representing Gk. -lot).
Derivatives: anatom-ism, п., anatom-isl, п., ana-
tom-ize, tr. v., anatom-iz-ation, п., anatom-iz-
er, n.

## anbury
anbury, ambury, п., a soft tumor or wart on the
neck of a horse or an ox. — A compound prob.
meaning lit. 'a painful berrylike tumor'. For the
first element see the first element in agnail. For
the second element see berry.

## -ance
-ance, suff. — Fr. L. -antia, either directly or
through the medium of F. -ance. L. -antia
derives fr. -ans, gen. -antis, pres. part. suff. of the
verbs of the first Latin conjugation, and forms
abstract nouns denoting action, process, state or
quality. See -ant and -ее and cp. -ence. Cp. also
-ancy.

## ancestor
ancestor, n. — A blend of ME. ancestre and an-
cessour. ME. ancestre, derives fr. OF. ancestre
(F. ancetre), fr. L. antecessor, 'predecessor', lit.
'foregoer', fr. antecessus, pp. of antecedere, 'to
go before', fr. ante- and cedere, 'to go'. ME. an-
cessour, 'ancestor', comes fr. OF. ancessor, fr.
L. antecessorem, ace. of antecessor. See cede
and cp. antecessor.

## ancestral
ancestral, adj. — OF. ancestre/, fr. ancestre. See
ancestor and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: ancestral-ly, adv.

## ancestry
ancestry, n. — OF. ancesserie; refashioned after
OF. ancestre. See prec. word and -y
(representing OF. ie).

## Anchises
Anchises, п., the father of Aeneas; see Aeneas. —
L. Anchises, fr. Gk. Άγχίσης, a name of
uncertain origin.

## Anchisten
Anchisten, п., a genus of ferns (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άγχιστεύς, 'next of kin*, fr. αγχιστος,
'nearest', superl. of δγχι, 'near', which is rel. to
αγχειν, 'to squeeze, throttle'. "Αγχι prop,
means 'pressed together'. See anger, anxious.
For the sense development of Gk. αγχι, 'near',
fr. αγχειν, 'to squeeze', cp. F. pres, 'near, by',
fr. L. pressus, 'compressed'. The genus was
called Anchistea to intimate that it is related to
another genus of plants called Woodwardia. For

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:61 COLUMN:2 -->
the Greek superl. suff. -ιστός in £γχιστος see
-est and cp. Callisto and words there referred
to.

## anchor
anchor, n. — ME. anker, fr. OE. ancor, fr. L. an-
cora, fr. Gk. Svxupa, 'anchor', which is rel. to
Gk. αγχών, 'a bend', αγκύλος, 'crooked,
curved'. See angle, 'corner', and cp. ancon,
ankylosis. Cp. also ungora.
Derivatives: anchor, tr. and intr. v., anchor-age,
п., anchor-ed, adj., anchor-er, n.

## anchoress
anchoress, п., a female anchorite. — See next
word and -ess.

## anchorite
anchorite, also anchoret, п., hermit, recluse. —
Anchoret is the earlier form. It is a contraction
of still earlier anachorel,h.\*.anach6re~ta,b.GiV..
αναχωρητής, 'anchorite', lit. 'one who has
retired', fr. άναχωρεΐν, 'to go back, retire', fr.
άνά, 'back' (see ana·), and χωρεΐν, 'to give
place, withdraw', fr. χώρος, 'free space, room'.
See chori-.

## anchovy
anchovy, п., a small, herringlike fish. — Sp. an-
chova, fr. Basque anchu, prop, 'dried fish', fr.
anchua, anchuva, 'dry'.

## Anchusa
Anchusa, п., a genus of plants of the borage
family. — L. anchusa, fr. Gk. δγχουσα, 'alkanet',
which is of uncertain origin.

## anchylose
anchylose, n. — See ankylose.

## anchylosis
anchylosis, n. — See ankylosis.

## anchylotic
anchylotic, adj. — See ankylotic.

## ancient
ancient, adj., old. — F. ancien, fr. VL. *antianus,
