'former', fr. ante, 'before'; see ante-. The -t in
ancient is excrescent and is due to a confusion
of the ending of F. ancien with -ent, the English
equivalent of L. -ins (gen. -entis), the pres. part,
suff. of the II-IV. Latin conjugations. Cp.
pageant, peasant, pheasant, tyrant.
Derivatives: ancient, п., ancient-ly,adv.,ancient-
ness, п., ancient-ry, n.

## ancient
ancient, n. ensign. — Corruption of ensign.

## nnclle
nnclle, п., the sacred shield of Rome. — L. ancile,
'the sacred shield of Rome', said to have fallen
from heaven. — The word prop, means 'cut in
on both sides', and stands for *am(bi)-caid-sli,
from ambi-, 'round about', and caedere, 'to cut,
hew, fell'. See ambi- and cement.

## ancillary
ancillary, adj., pertaining to a maid servant;
secondary, auxiliary. — L. ancillaris, 'relating to
female servants', fr. ancilla, 'a female servant',
dimin. fr. anculus, 'a man servant', which was
misdivided into anc-ulus. In reality, however,
anculus stands for an-culus and is compounded
of pref. am(b)- (see ambi-) and the base of L.
colere, 'to till (the ground), cultivate, dwell,
inhabit'. See colony and -ary. Cp. Gk. άμφίπολος,
'handmaid of gods, priestess, attendant priest',
which is cogn with L. anculus.

## ancipital
ancipital, ancipitous, adj., having two edges. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al, resp. -ous, fr. L. an-
ceps, gen. ancipitis, 'having two heads', fr. an-,
a short form oiambi-, 'on both sides', and caput,
gen. capitis, 'head'. See ambi-, and capital, adj.
For the change of Latin й (in caput) to ί (in
ancipitis) see abigeat and cp. words there referred
to.

## ancon
ancon, п., ]) the elbow (anat.); 2) a projection
supporting a cornice; console (archil.) — L., fr.
Gk. άγκών, 'elbow', lit. 'bend (of the arm)'.
See angle, 'corner', and cp. anchor, aukylosis.

## -ancy
-ancy, suff. denoting quality or state. — Fr. L.
-antia, either directly or through the medium of
F. -ance, hence derivatively identical with -ance
(q.v.) Cp. -ency.

## ancylostomiasis
ancylostomiasis, п., hookworm disease (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of Gk. αγκύλος,
'crooked, curved', and στόμα, 'mouth'. See
ankylosis, stoma and -iasis.

## Ancylns
Ancylns, п., a genus of snails (entomol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. αγκύλος, 'crooked, curved'. See
ankylosis.

## and
and, conj. — ME., fr. OE. and, rel. to OS. endi,
ande, OFris. and(a), ande, MDu. ende,enn, Du.
en, OHG. enti, ami, later unta, unti, MHG. unde,
und, G. und, 'and', ON. enn, en, 'and, but', prob.
fr. I.-E. *ntha-, whence also OI. ath3, 'then,
and'. Cp. an, 'if, and ampersand.

## anadabata
anadabata, п., a Roman gladiator whose helmet
had no opening for the eyes. — L., a word of
Gaulish origin. The first element of this word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:61 COLUMN:3 -->
means 'blind', and is cogn. with OI. andhah,
Avestic anda, of s.m. The second element is of
the same origin and meaning as L. battuere, 'to
beat, strike1. See batter, 'to beat', and cp. words
there referred to.

## Andalusia
Andalusia, п., a former province of southern
Spain. — Andalusia (= Sp. Andalucia), fr. Arab.
Andalus, a name denoting the whole peninsula,
fr. Late L. "Vandalicia, prop, 'the country
occupied by the Vandals'. See Vandal.

## andalusite
andalusite, п., a hard silicate of aluminum (Al2-
SiOj) (mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff.
-ite fr. Andalusia (see prec. word); so called
because it was first found in Andalusia.

## andante
andante, adj., moderately slow; adv., in andante
tempo; п., an andante movement (musical
direction). — It., pres. part, of andare, 'to go',
rel. to Sp. and Port, andar, 'to go'; fr. VL. am-
bitare, 'to go round', fr. L. ambitus, pp. of am-
bire, 'to go round'. See ambient.

## aadantino
aadantino, adj., somewhat quicker (sometimes,
slower) than andante;adv.,in andantino tempo;
n., an andantino movement (musicaldirection).—
It., dimin. of andante.

## aadesine
aadesine, п., a mineral of the group of feldspars.
— Coined by the German geologist Wilhelm
Hermann Abich (1806-86) from the name of the
Andes Mountains. For the ending see chem.
suff. -ine.

## andesite
andesite, п., name of a family of rocks (petrogr.)
— Coined by the German geologist Baron
Christian Leopold von Buch (1774-1853) from the
name of the Andes Mountains. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: andesit-ic, adj.

## andiron
andiron, п., either of a pair of metal supports for
logs in a fireplace. — ME. anderne, aundirne,
aundiren, fr. OF. andier (F. landier), fr. Gaul.
*andero-, 'a young bull' (cp. Ir. ainder, 'a young
woman', W. anner, 'heifer'); so called because
andirons were frequently adorned with the
heads of animals. Andiron was influenced in
form by, but is not related to, iron. Cp. gridiron.

## andouiUe
andouiUe, п., a kind of sausage. — F., fr. VL.
'inductile, neut. of the adjective *inductilis, used
as a noun, fr. L. inductus, pp. of inducere, 'to
introduce'; see induce. AndouiUe must have
denoted originally the filling that was 'introduced'
into the sausage.

## andr-
andr-, form of andro- before a vowel.

## Andrew
Andrew, masc. PN. — OF. Andreu, Andrieu (F.
Andre), fr. L. Andreas, St. Gk. 'Ανδρέας, which
is rel. to ανδρείος, 'manly', fr. άνήρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man'. See andro- and cp. dandy.
'soul, spirit, mind, courage, wish, desire'. See
nnimus.

## anemology
anemology, п., the science of wind. —
Compounded of anemo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy-
Derivative: anemolog-ic-al, adj.

## anemometer
anemometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
velocity of the wind. — Compounded of anemo-
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm.'
Derivatives: anemometr-y, п., anemomelr-ic,
adj.

## anemone
anemone, n. — Gk. ανεμώνη, 'the wind flower*,
which prob. derives fr. Heb. na'amdn in nlfi
na'umantm (Is. 17:10), lit. 'plants of
pleasantness', fr. na'im, 'was pleasant'. See Paul de La-
garde in Abhandlungen der Gesellschaft der
Wissenschaften zu Gottingen, XXXV, p. 205,
and Heinrich Lewy, Die semitischen Fremd-
worter im Griechischen, Berlin, 1895, p. 49. For
the etymology of Heb. паЧт, 'was pleasant', see
Naaman and cp. words there referred to. Gk.
ανεμώνη was influenced in form by άνεμος,
'wind'. For the ending -ώνη in ανεμώνη ср.
άργεμώνη, 'a kind of poppy', fr. Heb. argaman,
'purple' (see Argemone).

## Anemonella
Anemonella, п., a genus of herbs of the family
Ranunculaceae (bot.) — ModL., dimin. of
anemone (q.v.) For the ending see suff. -ella.

## anencephalic
anencephalic, adj., having no brain (zool.) — Gk.
ανεγκέφαλος, coined by Galen from άν- (see
priv. pref. -an) and Gk. εγκέφαλος, 'brain'. See
encephalic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:62 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 35 | ANGINA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:62 COLUMN:1 -->

## anent
anent, prep., concerning, about. — ME. aneni,
arteritis, fr. OE. onefen, onemn, 'near to, close
by', orig. 'on a level with', fr. an-, on-, 'on', and
efen, "even, equal'. Cp. OHG. (MHG., G.) ne-
ben, 'near to, by the side of, shortened fr. in-
eben, fr. in, 'in', and ebani, 'equality'. See on and
even, 'straight'. The final t in anent is excrescent.
Cp. foment
•aneous, adj. suff. — L. -dneus. See -an and -ous.

## energy
energy, п., lack of energy (med.) — Medical L.
anergia, 'lack of energy', formed on analogy of
energy fr. priv. pref. an- and Gk. έργον, 'work'.
See ergon.
Derivative: anerg-ic, adj. ~

## aneroid
aneroid, adj., containing no liquid (said of a kind
of barometer); п., an aneroid barometer.— F.
anerotde, lit. 'without liquid', compounded of
priv. pref. n- and Gk. νϊρός, νηρός, 'flowing,
liquid' (which is rel. to νάειν, 'to flow'), and
-οειδής, 'like',' fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
Nereid and -oid.

## anesthesia
anesthesia, anaesthesin, п., insensibility. — Gk.
αναισθησία, 'lack of sensation', fr. άναισθητεΐν,
'to be without sense of something, lack
sensation', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and αισθητός,
'sensible, perceptible', verbal adj. of αίσθάνεσ-
θαι, 'to perceive'. See esthete and cp. esthesia.

## anesthetic
anesthetic, anaesthetic, adj., producing
insensibility; п., substance producing anesthesia. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. αναίσθητος,
'without feeling', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and
αισθητός, 'sensible, perceptible'. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: anesthet-ist, п., anesthet-ize, tr. v.

## anet
anet, п., dill. — F. anet, aneth, fr. L. anithum,
fr. Gk. ανηθον, 'dill, anise'. Cp. Gk. ανϊσον,
L. anisum, and see anise.

## aneurysm
aneurysm, п., a morbid dilatation of the coat of
an artery (med.) — Gk. ανευρυσμός, 'dilatation',
fr. άνευρύνειν, 'to dilate', fr. άνά (see ana-), and
εύρύνειν, 'to widen', fr. ευρύς, 'wide', which is
cogn. with OI. uruh, 'wide'. The spelling
aneurism (with i instead of y) is due to a
confusion with words ending in -ism.
Derivatives: aneurysm-al, adj., aneurysm-al-ly,
adv., aneurysm-at-ic, adj.

## anfractuosity
anfractuosity, п., circuitousness. — F. anfractu-
osite, fr. L. anfractus. See anfractuous and -ity.

## anfractuous
anfractuous, adj., circuitous. — F. anfractueux
(fern, anfractueuse), fr. L. anfractuosus, fr. am-
fractus,- anfractus, 'a breaking round; a turning,
winding', fr. am-, shortened form of ambi-,
amb-, 'about, around', and fractus, pp. of
frangere, 'to break'. See ambl- and fraction.
Derivatives: anfraciuous-ness, n.

## anew
anew, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'of, and new.

## angaralite
angaralite, п., a magnesium aluminum iron
silicate (mineral.) — Named after Angara River in
Siberia. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## angaria
angaria, п., a system of relays of couriers for
dispatching official letters in ancient Persia, later
also in the Roman empire. — L., 'service to a
lord', fr. Gk. αγγαρεία, 'impressment for the
public service', fr. αγγαρος, 'mounted courier,
messenger*, of Persian, ult. Semitic, origin. See
angel.

## angary
angary, п., the right of a warring nation to use
or destroy the property of neutrals. — F. an-
garie, fr, L. angaria. See prec. word.

## angel
angel, n. — ME., fr. OF. angele (F. ange), fr. L.
angelus, fr. Gk. άγγελος, 'messenger, divine
messenger, angel' (whence the verb άγγέλλειν,
'to bear a message, report, tell'), which is rel. to
ίίγγαρος, 'mounted courier, messenger'; of
Persian, ult. of Sem. origin. Cp. Akkad. agarru,
'hireling, hired laborer', fr. agaru, 'to hire',
which is rel. to Aram, agar, eggar, 'he hired',
(whence Arab, djara, of s.m.), Heb. iggereth,
Aram, igg'ra, iggarld, 'letter', prop, 'message'
Cp. angaria, the first element in Ingram and the
second element in evangel. The sense
development of Glc. αγγαρος, resp. άγγελος, from a
Sem. noun meaning 'hireling', may be illustrated
by the phases: 'hireling, hired messenger,
messenger'. Gk. άγγελος in the sense of 'angel', is
a loan translation of. Heb. mal'akh, 'messenger,
divine messenger, angel', fr. base l-'-k, 'to send'.
Derivatives: angel-ic, adj., angelica (q.v.), angel-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:62 COLUMN:2 -->
ic-al, adj., angel-ic-al-ly, adv., angel-ic-ize, tr. v.,
angel-ize, tr. v,

## andrewsite
andrewsite, п., a hydrous phosphate (mineral.) —
Named after the Irish physicist and chemist
Thomas Andrew (1813-58). For the ending see
subst. suff. -Ite.

## Andrias
Andrias, п., a genus of fossil salamanders (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gr. άνδριάς, 'image of a man',
diminutive formed fr. άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man';
see andro-. For the diminutive character of the
-«/-formative element see Kretschiner in Glotta,
14, 84f.

## andro-
andro-, before a vowel andr-, combining form
meaning 'man'. — Gk. άνδρο-, άνδρ-, fr. άνήρ,
gen. ανδρός, 'man', which is cogn. with OI.
naram (ace.), 'man', naryah, 'virile', Arm. ayr,
gen.-dat. arn, 'man', Alb. n'er, 'man', Umbr.
nerus (pi. ace.), 'men', Sabine-L. Nero, PN., lit.
'strong', W. ner, 'hero', Olr. nert, W., Co. nerth,
'virility'. Cp. Andrew, Andrias, andron, dandy,
'a fop', and the second element in Alexander,
Ardhanari, Dianira, Leander, philander, sundari.
Cp. also the first element in anthropo-.

## androcracy
androcracy, п., rule or supremacy of men. —
Compounded of andro- and -κρατίί, fr. κράτος,
'strength, power, rule'. See -cracy.

## androecium
androecium, п., the stamens of a flower taken
collectively (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
andro- and Gk. οίκίον, dimin. of οίκος, 'house'.
See economy.

## androgen
androgen, п., a male sex hormone (biochem.) —
Coined fr. andro- and -gen.

## androgynous
androgynous, adj., hermaphrodite. — Gk.
ανδρόγυνος, 'man-woman, hermaphrodite', fr. άνήρ,
gen. ανδρός, 'man', and γυνή, 'woman'. See
andro- and gynaeco-, and cp. gynandrous. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see suff.
•ous.

## Andromache
Andromache, п., the wife of Hector (Greek my-
Ihol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Ανδρομάχη, lit. 'whose
husband excells in the fight', fr. άνηρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man', husband', and μάχη, 'fight'. See andro-
and -machy.

## Andromeda
Andromeda, п., 1) the daughter of Cepheus and
Cassiopeia.(Greek mythol.)— Gk. 'Ανδρομέδα,
Ion. Άνδρομέδη, lit. 'mindful of her husband',
compounded of άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man' (see
andro-), and μέδεσθαι, 'to be mindful of, give
heed to, think on', which is rel. to μέδων, μεδέ-
ων, 'guardian, ruler' (prop. pres. part, of the
ancient verb μέδειν, 'to protect, rule over'),
μήδεσθαι, 'to devise, resolve, advise', μήδεα (pi.
neut.), 'counsels, plans, device, cunning', μέδιμ-
νος, 'a measure', fr. I.-E. base *mSd-, 'to measure,
limit, consider', which is a -d-enlargement of
base *mi-, 'to measure'. See meditate and cp.
Medea, Medusa and the second element in aato-
medon, Diomedes, Ganymede. Cp. also medical.

## Andromeda
Andromeda, п., ι) name of a constellation in the
northern hemisphere; 2) name of a genus of
plants of the heath family (bot.) — From prec.
word.

## andron
andron, п., men's apartment in a house (Greek
antiq.) — Gk. ανδρών, a collateral form of
άνδρωνϊτις, 'men's apartment', fr . άνήρ, gen.
ανδρός, 'man'. See andro-.

## androphobia
androphobia, п., morbid dread of the male sex. —
ModL., compounded of Gk. άνήρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man', and -φοβία, fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'.
See andro- and -phobia.

## Andropogon
Andropogon, п., the beard grass (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of andro- and Gk. πώγων, 'beard'.
See Pogonia.

## Androsace
Androsace, п., a genus of herbs of the primrose
family (bot.) — L. androsaces, name of a
zoophyte, fr. Gk. άνδρόσακες, of s.m., lit. 'man's
remedy', compounded of άνήρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man', and ακος, 'remedy'. See andro-, and
aceology.

## androsterone
androsterone, n„ a male sex hormone (biochem.)
— Coined ft. andro-, ster(ol) and -one.

## -androus
-androus, combining form used in botany in the
sense of 'having (a certain number or form) of
stamens (prop, male organs)', as in monandrous,
gynandrous. — Gk. -ανδρός, fr. άνήρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man'. See andro-.

## -ane
-ane, suff., a variant of -an, fr. L. -anus,
generally with differentiation of meaning. Cp. human,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:62 COLUMN:3 -->
humane, and urban, urbane.

## -ane
-ane, suff. used to form names of saturated
hydrocarbons (chem.); derivatively identical with
prec. suff.

## anear
anear, prep, and adv. (poetic). — Formed fr. a-,
'on', and aear.

## anecdote
anecdote, n. — F., fr. Gk. ανέκδοτα (neut. pi. of
ανέκδοτος, 'not published'), used as a noun in
the sense of 'unpublished things', fr. άν- (see
priv. pref. an-) and έκδοτα, 'things given out',
neut. pi. of έκδοτος verbal adj. of έκδίδωμι,
Ί give out' (fr. έκ, 'out', and reduplication of
base *do-, 'to give'). See ec- and date, 'point
of time'.
Derivatives: anecdot-age, п., anecdot-al, anec-
dol-ic, adjs., anecdotic-al-ly, adv., anecdot-ist, n.

## anele
anele, tr. v., to anoint (archaic). — ME. anelien,
'to anoint with oil', fr. OE. an, On', and ME.
ele (fr. OE. ale), 'oil', fr. L. oleum. See a-, 'on',
and oil.

## anemia
anemia, anaemia, п., deficiency of blood (med.)
— Gk. αναιμία, 'want of blood, bloodlessness',
fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and αίμα, 'blood'.
See hemal.
Derivatives: anemi-al (anaemi-al), anem-ic (an-
aem-ic), adjs.

## Anemia
Anemia, п., a genus of plants of the climbing-
fern family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άνείμων,
'unclad', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and είμα,
which corresponds to Dor. .Ρήμα, 'a dress,
garment', and is cogn. with Gk. έσθής (for *5εσθής),
'clothing', έννύναι ('for *5εσνύναι), 'to clothe',
and cogn. with L. vestis, 'covering for the body,
clothes'. See vest and cp. himation.

## anemo-
anemo-, before a vowel anem-, combining form
meaning 'wind'. — Gk. άνεμο-, άνεμ-, fr.
άνεμος, 'wind*, which is cogn. with L. anima,
'breath of air, air, breath, soul, life', animus,

## Angela
Angela, fem. PN. — Fern, of L. angelus, 'angel'.
See prec. word and cp. angelica, Angelina.

## angelfish
angelfish, n. — The name is prob. due to the
misreading of the Dutch name of this fish zeeegel,
lit. 'sea urchin', as zeeengel, 'sea angel' (cp. its
French name ange de mer), a mistake suggested
by the winglike fins of this fish.

## aagellc
aagellc, adj. — F. ang clique, fr. L. angelicus, fr. Gk.
αγγελικός, 'angelic', fr. ΐγγελος. See angel and
-ic.

## Angelica
Angelica, fem. PN. — Fem. of L. angelicus,
'angelic'. See prec. word and cp. Angein, Aagelina.

## Angelica
Angelica, п., a genus of plants (hat.) — ModL.,
lit. 'the angelic (herb)', fr. L. (herba) angelica,
fem. of angelicus (see prec. word); so called
because of its medicinal properties.

## Angelina
Angelina, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Angela (q.v.).

## angelo-
angelo-, combining form meaning 'angel'. See
angel.

## angelolntry
angelolntry, п., the worship of angels. —
Compounded of angelo- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρίά,
fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor, worship'. See -intry.

## angelot
angelot, п., ι) a gold coin; 2) a sort of cheese made
in Normandy; 3) a musical instrument. —
OF., dimin. of angele, 'angel'. See ungel.

## aager
aager, n. — ME., fr. ON. angr, 'sorrow,
affliction', rel. to ON. dngr, OE. enge, 'narrow,
painful', OS. engi, MDu. enghe, Du. eng, OHG. an-
gi, engi, MHG. enge, G. eng, Goth, aggwus,
'narrow', and cogn. with OI. amhu-, 'narrow',
dmhah, 'anguish, need, anxiety', Avestic qzah-,
'distress, oppression', Gk. αγχειν, 'to squeeze'
(esp. the throat), 'strangle, throttle, hang',
αγχόνη, 'strangling, hanging; rope', αγχι,
άγχοϋ, 'near' (lit. 'narrow'), άσσον (for * αγχ-ιον),
'nearer', L. angere, 'to press together, throttle,
torment', angustus, 'narrow', Arm. anjuk,
'narrow', OSlav. qzQ, aziti, 'to narrow, compress',
qzota, 'narrowness', 'qzosti, 'a narrowing,
narrowness', qzuku, 'narrow', Lith. aftkStas,
'narrow', Tr. I.-E. base *angh-, 'to narrow,
compress'; the corresponding Celtic base is *engh-,
*agh-, whence Bret, enk, 'narrow', Ir. cumung,
'narrow', Ir., W. ing, 'distress'. Cp. agnail,
angina, anguish, anxious, and the second element
in cvnanche, quinsy, squinancy, Orobanche.
Derivatives: angr-y, adj., angr-i-ly, adv.

## anger
anger, tr. v. — ON. angra, fr. angr, 'anger'. See
anger, n.

## angina
angina, п., inflammation of the throat; quinsy. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:63 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ANGIO- | 36 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:63 COLUMN:1 -->
L. angina, 'quinsy', prob. a loan word fr. Gk.
αγχόνη, 'a throttling, strangling, hanging'. The
form angina (instead of *ancina) is due to the
influence of angere, 'to throttle', See anger,
п., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: angin-al, adj.

## angio- before a vowel angi-
angio- before a vowel angi-, combining form
meaning 'covered by a seed or blood vessel', as
in angiosperm. — Gk. άγγειο-, fr. άγγεΐον,
'vessel', fr. άγγος, 'vessel', a word of uncertain
origin. Cp. the second element in Hydrangea,
sporangium, synangium.

## anglology
anglology, п., that branch of anatomy which
deals with the blood vessels. — Compounded
of angio-, and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic). See -logy.

## angioma
angioma, п., a tumor consisting of dilated blood
vessels (med.) — Medical L., formed with suff.
-oma fr. Gk. άγγεΐον, 'vessel'. See angio-.

## angiosperm
angiosperm, п., name of a large class of plants
which has its seeds inclosed in an ovary. —
Coined (in the Modern Latin form Angiosper-
mae) by Paul Hermann in 1690 fr. Gk. άγγεΐον,
'vessel, receptacle' and σπέρμα, 'seed'. See
angio- and sperm.
Derivatives: angiosperm-al, angiosperm-atous,
angiosperm-ic, angiosperm-ous, adjs.

## angle
angle, п., corner. — F., fr. L. angulus, 'angle,
corner', which is cogn. with Arm. angiun, anki-
un, OSlav. qg(u)lu, 'corner', OSlav. qkotu,
'hook', Lith. anka, 'loop', OI. dngam, 'limb',
angulift, angurib, 'finger, toe', angusthdh, 'big
toe, thumb', Avestic angushta-, 'toe, finger', OI.
ankdft, 'hook; bent', айсаЧ, 'bends, curves', Gk.
άγκος, 'a bend, hollow', αγχών, 'elbow', αγκύλος,
'crooked, curved', άγκυρα, 'anchor', L. ancus,
'crooked, curved', OE. ancleo, ancliow, 'ankle',
OE. anga, OHG. ango, 'hook'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base *ang-, resp. *anq-, 'to bend'.
Cp. angle, 'fishhook', Angle, anchor, aneon,
angula, angular, ankle, ankylosis, and the second
element in triangle. Cp. also the second element
in sarangousty. The above I.-E. words stand in
gradational relationship to Gk. δγκος, L.
uncus, 'hook', Mir. ecath, 'fishhook'; cp. Uncaria,
unciferous, internal, alternate, uncinus, uncus,
aduncus, Redunca.
angle, п., a fishhook. — OE. angel, fr. anga,
'hook', rel. to ON. ongull, OHG. angul (MHG.,
G. angel), 'fishhook', and cogn. with L. ancus,
'crooked, curved', uncus, 'hook'. See angle,
'corner'.
Derivatives: angle, tr. and intr. v., angl-er, п.,
angl-ing, n.

## Angle
Angle, п., member of a Teutonic tribe that came in
the 5th century from what is now known as
Schleswig-Holsteyi to Britain and conquered it.
— L. Anglus, pi. Angli, of Teut. origin. Cp. OE.
Angle, Engle, prop, 'the people coming from
Angul (= ON. Ongull), 'a hookshaped district
in Schleswig', fr. angul (= ON. JbngulT),
'fishhook, angle', which is rel. to anga, OHG. ango,
'hook'. See angle, 'fishhook', and angle, 'corner',,
and cp. English, Anglican, Anglo-Saxon.

## angleslte
angleslte, п., a mineral containing lead sulfate. —
Coined by the French mineralogist and
physicist Francois Sulpice Beudant in 1832; so called
by him in allusion to the fact that it was
discovered by Withering in Anglesey (in 1783).
For the ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## Anglican
Anglican, adj. and n. — ML. Angltcamis, fr.
Anglicus, 'English', fr. Late L. Anglus. See Angle
and -an.

## anglice
anglice, adv., in English. — ML. Anglice, fr. Ang-
licus. See prec. word.

## Anglicism
Anglicism, anglicism, n. — Formed with suff.
-ism fr. ML. Anglicus. See Anglican.

## Anglicize
Anglicize, anglicize, tr. and intr. v. — Formed
with suff. -ize, fr. ML. Anglicus. See Anglican.
Derivative: angliciz-at'ton, n.

## Anglo-
Anglo-, combining form meaning 'English'. —
Fr. Late L. Angli, 'the English'. See Angle,
Anglo-Saxon.

## Anglomania
Anglomania, n„ a mania for what is English. —
Compounded of Anglo- and Gk. μανία,
'madness, frenzy'. See mania.
Derivative: Anglomani-ac, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:63 COLUMN:2 -->

## Anglophile
Anglophile, Anglophil, п., a friend of England or
the English; adj., friendly to England or the
English. — Compounded of Anglo- and Gk.
φίλος, 'friend'. See -phile, -phil.

## Anglophone
Anglophone, п., one who fears or hates England
or the English. — Compounded of Anglo- and
Gk. -φόβος, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobe.
Derivative: Anglophob-ic, adj.

## Anglophobia
Anglophobia, п., fear or hatred of England or the
English. — Compounded of Anglo- and Gk.
-φοβία, 'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobin.
Derivative: Anglophob-ic, adj.

## Anglo-Saxon
Anglo-Saxon, n. — ML. Anglo-Saxdnls, fr.
earlier Angli Saxonls, 'the English', fr. L. Angli,
'the Angles', in Late L. 'the English', and L.
Saxonls, 'the Saxons', in Late L. 'the English'.
Accordingly the term Anglo-Saxon is
tautological, inasmuch as both elements of this
compound denote 'the English'. See Angle and
Saxon.

## angoin
angoin, n. — Corruption of angora.

## aagorn
aagorn, п., ι) an Angora cat; z) Angora wool or
anything made of it. — Named from the town
Angora (now Ankara) in Asia Minor, fr. L. An-
cyra, fr. Gk."Avxupa, fr. άγκυρα, 'anchor'. See
anchor.

## angosturn
angosturn, п., a bitter aromatic bark. —
Shortened fr. angastura bark, lit. 'bark of the tree
growing at Angostura', now Ciudad Bolivar, in
Venezuela, on the narrows of the Orinoco River;
so called fr. Sp. angostura, 'a narrow pass', fr.
angosto, fr. L. anguslus, 'narrow'. See anguish,
п., and -ure.

## angrite
angrite, п., a meteorite stone. — Named after
Angra dos Reis in Brazil. For the ending see
subst. suff. -Ite.

## angry
angry, adj. — Formed fr. anger with suff. -y
(representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: angri-ly, adv., angrl-ness, n.

## angstrom unit
angstrom unit, aagstrom, п., unit of length equal
to one hundred-millionth of a centimeter; used
to measure the wavelengths of light. — Named
after the Swedish physicist Anders Jonas
Angstrom (1814-1874).

## Anguidae
Anguidae, n. pi., a family of lizards (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. anguis,
'serpent, snake'. See anguine.

## Anguilla
Anguilla, п., a genus of fishes, the common eel
(ichthyol.) — L. anguilla, 'eel', prop, 'the
snakelike fish', fr. anguis, 'snake'; see next word. Cp
the cognate Gk. έγχελυς (see Encelia), OPruss.
angurgis, Lith. ungurys, OSlav. *qgori
(appearing in Russ. Sgori, Pol. wegorz), 'eel', which all
mean derivatively 'the snakelike fish'. It.
anguilla, F. anguille, Sp. anguila, Port, enguia and
prob. also OSlav. qguljajegulja, 'eel', derive fr.
L. anguilla.

## anguine
anguine, adj., pertaining to a serpent. — L. an-
guinus, fr. anguis, 'serpent, snake', which is cogn.
with Arm. auj, oj, Lith. angls, OPruss. angis,
Lett, uodze, Russ. az, Pol. wqz, and prob. also
with OI. ahih, Avestic azish, 'snake', Gk. εχις,
'viper'. See echidna and cp. Anguidae, Anguilla,
Anguis. Cp. also Ahi, Encelia, ask, 'water newt'.
For the ending see suff. -ine (representing L.
-Tnus).

## anguineous
anguineous, adj., serpentlike. — L. anguineus, fr.
anguis, 'serpent'; see prec. word. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see suff. -ous.

## Anguis
Anguis, п., a genus of lizards, the blindwoim
(zool.) — L. anguis, 'serpent, snake'. See
anguine.

## anguish
anguish, n. — ME. anguise, angolse, fr. OF. an-
guisse, angoisse (F. angoisse), fr. L. angustia (in
classical Latin used mostly in the pi.),
'narrowness, deficiency', fr. angustus, 'narrow', fr.
angere, 'to throttle, torment'. See anger and words
there referred to and cp. esp. aagostura.

## aagalsh
aagalsh, tr. and intr. v. — OF. anguissier, an-
goissier (F. angoisser), fr. anguisse, angoisse. See
prec. word.
Derivative: anguish-ed, adj.

## anguishous
anguishous, adj., causing anguish; anguished;
anxious, (obsol.) — OF. angoissos, fr. VL. *an-
gustidsus, fr. L. anguslus, 'narrow'. See
anguish, n.
DemaXive.'anguishous-ly, avd.

## angula
angula, п., a measure in ancient India,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:63 COLUMN:3 -->
corresponding to 1.05 inches, lit., 'finger'. — OI.
angulah, 'finger', rel. to angulib, angurib, 'finger,
toe; angusfbah, 'big toe, thumb', dncati, 'he
bends, curves', and cogn. with Gk. άγκών,
'elbow', L. ancus, 'crooked, curved', angulus,
'angle, corner'. See angle, 'corner'.

## augular
augular, adj. — L. angularis, 'having corners or
angles', fr. angulus. See angle, 'corner', and_ -ar.
Derivatives: angular-ity, п., angular-ly, adv.,
angular-ness, n.

## angulate
angulate, adj. — L. angulatus, pp. of angulare,
'to make angular', fr. angulus. See angle,
'corner', and adj. suff. -ate,

## anguria
anguria,n., the gourd; the watermelon. — ModL.,
fr. Late Gk. άγγούριον, 'watermelon', which
derives fr. Pers. angarah. See gherkin.

## Angus
Angus, masc. PN. — Scot., rel. to Ir. Aonghus,
a compound whose two elements are cognate
with E. one, resp. choice.

## aaheinfion
aaheinfion, п., panting, asthma (archaic). — F.
anhilation, fr. L. anhelatiOnem, ace of anhelatio,
'difficulty of breathing, panting', fr anhelatus,
pp. ofanheldre, 'to breathe with difficulty', which
is prob. compounded of pref. an-, 'up, upward'
(see ana-), and hllare, 'to breathe', which prob.
stands for *anslare, fr. I.-E. base *an-, 'to blow,
breathe'. See animus and cp.'exhale, inhale. For
the ending see suff. -ation.

## anhistous
anhistous, adj., with no recognizable structure
(biol.) — Formed with suff. -ous fr. priv. pref.
an- and Gk. ιστός, 'tissue', which stands for
•σιστάς and lit. means 'that which makes to
stand', from the stem of ϊστημι (for *σίστημι),
Ί make to stand'. See histo- and cp. the second
element in Acrinistia.

## anhydride
anhydride, anhydrid, п., an oxide which is capable
of forming an acid, if added to water (chem.) —
Formed with suff. -ide resp. -Id, fr. Gk. άνυδρος,
'waterless'. See aabydrous.

## anhydrite
anhydrite, п., anhydrous calcium sulfate (mineral.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. άνυδρος,
'waterless'. See next word and cp. prec. word.

## anhydrous
anhydrous, adj., containing no water (chem.) —
Gk. άνυδρος, 'waterless', fr. άν- (see priv. pref.
an-) and ύδωρ, 'water'. See hydro-. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see suff. -ous.

## aid
aid, п., any of certain black birds of the cuckoo
family. — Sp. ant, Port, ani, fr. Tupi ani.

## anicut
anicut, annicut, п., a dam (Anglo-Ind.) — Tamil
anai kalfu, 'dam building'.

## anigh
anigh, adv., new (pseudo-archaic). — Formed
on analogy of afar, etc., fr. a-, 'on', and
nigh.

## anights
anights, adv. (archaic) — Formed fr. OE. on
nihte; see a-, 'on', night, and the adv. suff. -s.

## anil
anil, п., ι) a West Indian shrub, from which
indigo is made; 2) indigo. — Port, anil, fr. Arab.
an-ntl, assimilated fr. al-ntl, fr. al-, 'the', and
nil, 'indigo', fr. Pers. nila, ult. fr. OI. ntli,
'indigo', fr. ntlah, 'dark blue'. Cp. lilac.
Derivatives: anll-ic, adj., anil-ide, п., aniline
(q.v.)

## anile
anile, adj., like an old woman. — L. anilis,
'pertaining to an old woman', fr. anus, gen. anus,
'old woman', from the I.-E. imitative base ·απ-,
whence also Hitt. annash, 'mother', hannash,
'grandmother', Gk. άννίς, 'grandmother',
Lith. anyta, 'mother-in-law', OPruss. one, 'old
mother', OHG. arm, MHG. ane, an,
'grandfather, great grandfather', OHG. ana,
'grandmother, great grandmother', G. Ahnen,
'ancestors', OHG. eninchill (whence MHG. eninkel,
enenkel, G. Enkel), 'grandson', prop, dimin.
of OHG. ano, 'great grandfather'. Cp. the first
element in Olaf.
Derivative: anile-ness, n.

## aniline
aniline, also anilin, п., an oily, poisonous liquid,
CeH5NA2 (chem.) — Coined by C.J.Fritzsche
in 1841 fr. anil and chem. suff. -ine, resp. -in.
Derivative: aniline, anilin, adj.

## anility
anility, п., quality of being anile. — L. anilUas,
'the old age of a woman, anility', fr. anilis. See
anile and -ity.

## nnimadversion
nnimadversion, п., criticism; blame. — L. ani-
madversio, gen. -onis, 'perception, observation,
attention', fr. animadversus, pp. of animadver-
tere. See animadvert and -ion.
Derivative: animadversion-al, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:64 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 37 | ANNOY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:64 COLUMN:1 -->

## animadversive
animadversive, adj., percipient. — Formed with
suff. -ive fr. L. animadversus, pp. of animadver-
lere. See next word.
Derivative: animadversive-ness, n.

## animadvert
animadvert, intr. v., to criticize, blame, censure.
— L. animadvertere, contraction of animum ad-
vertere, 4o direct one's mind, attend', fr.
animum, ace. of animus, ,'mind', and advertere, 'to
turn toward'. See animus and advert.

## animal
animal, n. — L., lit. 'a living being', fr. animate,
neut. of animalis, 'of air, living', fr. anima,
'breath of air, air, breath, soul, life'; see animus
and adj. suff. -al. For sense development cp. Gk.
ζωον, 'animal, which is rel. to ζωή, 'life', and
OE. deor, 'a wild animal', lit. 'a breathing being',
which is cogn. with OSlav. duchu, 'breath,
spirit', dusd, 'soul'. Cp. also Heb. hayyd", 'wild
animal, beast', which is rel. to bayd", 'he lived',
hayytm, 'life'.

## animal
animal, adj. — L. animalis, 'of air, living,
animate'. See animal, n.

## anlmalcular
anlmalcular, adj. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. L.
animalculum. See next word.

## animalcule
animalcule, п., a very small animal, esp. one
perceptible only by a microscope. — Late L.
animalculum, dimin. of L. animal. See animal, п.,
and -cule.

## animalism
animalism, п., animal character; the doctrine that
man is a mere animal. — See animal and -ism.

## animalist
animalist, п., ι) one who believes in animalism;
2) an artist representing animals. — See animal
and -ist.

## annualize
annualize, tr. v., to make like an animal. — See
animal and -ize.
Derivative: animaliz-ation, n.

## animate
animate, tr. v., to give life to, to enliven. — L.
animatus, pp. of animare, 'to fill with air or
breath, to animate', fr. anima. See animus and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: animai-ed, adj. animat-ed-ly, adv.,
animat-er, п., animat-ing, adj., animat-ing-ly,
adv., animation, animalism (qq.v.)

## animate
animate, adj., living. — L. animatus, pp. of
animare. See animate, v.
Derivatives: animate-ly, adv., animaie-ness, n.

## animation
animation, п., life; vivacity. — L. animatio, gen.
-onis, 'an animating', fr. animatus, pp. of
animare. See animate and -ion.

## animatism
animatism, п., the primitive belief that the
inanimate is regarded as if it were animated. —
Coined by Maretti in 1899 in contradistinction
to animism. See animate, adj. and -ism.

## animatistic
animatistic, adj. — See prec. word and -istic

## anime
anime, п., any of various resins. — F., fr. Sp.
αηύηέ, which is a Tupi loan word.

## animism
animism, п., a word of many meanings, but used
esp. in the sense of 'theory of the universal
animation of nature' (Sir Edward Burnett Tylor's
definition in Primitive Culture, chapter 1IJ. —
Coined by the German physicist and chemist
Georg Ernst Stahl (1660-1734) and
re-introduced by E. B. Tylor in 1871. See animus and -ism
and cp. animatism.

## animlst
animlst, п., one who believes in animism. — See,
animism and -ist.
Derivative: animisl-ic, adj.

## nnimosity
nnimosity, п., ill will; enmity. — F. animosili, fr.
L. animosilalem, ace. of animositas, 'boldness,
vehemence', fr. animdsus, 'bold, vehement', fr.
animus. See next word, adj. suff. -ose and suff.
-ity.

## aalmus
aalmus, п., ι) intention; 2) animosity. — L.,
'soul, spirit, mind, courage, wish, desire', rel. to
anima, 'breath of air, air, breath, soul, life', and
cogn. with Gk. άνεμος, 'wind', fr. I.-E. base
*an-, 'to blow, breathe', whence also OI. ani-ti,
άηα-ti, 'breathes', ani-lah, 'breath', Olr. anal, W.
anadl, MBret. (with metathesis) alazn, 'breath',
Olr. animm, Co., Bret, eneff, 'soul', Goth, uz-
anan, 'to exhale', ON. anda, 'to breathe', andi,
and, 'breath, soul, spirit', OE. edian (for *an-
t>jari), 'to breathe', OSlav. vonja, 'smell'. Alb.
Gheg aj, Tosk εη, Ί swell', Toch. A anma, Arm
anjn, 'soul'. Cp. animadvert, animal,
animalcule, animate, animosity, equanimity, exanimate,
exhale, inhale, longanimity, magnanimous,
magnanimity, pusillanimous, pusillanimity,
unanimous, unanimity. Cp. also ahura, anemo-, an-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:64 COLUMN:2 -->
helation, asthma, asura, prana.

## anioa
anioa, п., a negatively charged ion (physical
chem.) — Gk. ανιόν, neut. of ανιών, pres.
part, of άνιένοίΐ, 'to go up', fr. άνά (see ana-)
and ίέναι, 'to go', which is cogn. with L. ire,
'to go'. See itiaerate. The word anion was
introduced into electricity by the English
physicist and chemist Michael Faraday (1791-1867);
cp. ion, cation.
Derivative: anion-ic, adj.

## anis-
anis-, combining form. See aniso-.

## anise
anise, n. — F., fr. L. anisum, fr. Gk. Svioov,
'anise, dill'. Cp. Gk. ανηθον, L. anethum, and
see anet.
Derivative: anis-ic, adj.

## aniseed
aniseed, n. — Contraction of anise-seed.

## anisette
anisette, п., liqueur flavored with aniseed. — F.,
dimin. of anise. For the ending see suff. -ette.

## aniso-
aniso-, anis-, combining form meaning 'a
derivative of anise' (chem.) — Gk. άνΐσ-, άνισο-,
fr. ανΐσον, 'anise'. See anise.

## aniso-
aniso-, anis-, combining form meaning 'unequal,
unsymmetrical'. — Gk. άνισο-, fr. δνισος,
'unequal', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and Ισος,
'equal'. See iso-.

## anisomerous
anisomerous, adj., not isomerous (bot.) — Formed
fr. priv. pref. an- and Isomerous.

## anisotropic
anisotropic, adj., not isotropic
(physics).—Formed fr. priv. pref. an- and isotropic.

## anker
anker, п., a liquid measure. — Du., rel. to G.
Anker, Swed. ankare, fr. ML. anceria, ancheria,
'keg, vat', which is of uncertain origin.

## ankh
ankh, п., a tau cross (T) with an oval at the top,
the Egypt, symbol of life. — Egypt, ankh, 'life'.

## nnklet
nnklet, п., a ring for the ankle. — Contraction of
ankle and dimin. suff. -let.

## ankle
ankle, n. — ME. ancle, ankle, prob. of Scand.
origin; cp. ON. okkla (for *ankula), Dan., Swed.
ankle. The collateral ME. form anclowe derives
fr. OE. anclio, ancllow. Cp. MDu. anclau, enkel,
Du. enkel, OHG. anchlao, anchal, enchil, MHG.,
G. enkel, 'ankle'. All these words are
diminutives formed with suff. -el, -I (see dimin. suff. -le),
from the Teut. stem appearing in MHG. anke,
'joint', G. Enke, 'ankle'. OI. angam, 'limb',
angulih, 'finger', and L. angulus, 'angle, corner',
are cogn. with these Teut. words; see angle,
'corner', and cp. angula.

## ankus
ankus, п., an elephant goad. — Hind., fr. OI.
ankusah, rel. to OI. ancati, 'bends, curves', and
cogn. wilh L. ancus, 'curved, crooked', angulus,
'angle, corner'. See angle, 'corner', and cp.
prec. word.

## ankylo-
ankylo-, before a vowel ankyl-, combining form
meaning 'crooked'. — Gk. άγκυλο-, άγκυλ-,
fr. αγκύλος, 'crooked, curved'. See ankylosis.

## ankylose. anchyluse. tr. v.
ankylose. anchyluse. tr. v., to affect with arJcy-
losis; intr. v., to be affected with ankylosis.—
Back formation fr. ankylosis.

## ankylosis
ankylosis, anchylosis, п., stiffening of the joints.
— Medical L., fr. Gk. άγκϋλωσις, fr. άγκυλοϋν,
'to crook, bend', fr. αγκύλος,'crooked, curved",
which is rel. to άγκος, 'bend, hollow; mountain
glen'. See angle, 'corner', and cp. anchor, ancon,
Ancylus, ankus:

## ankylotic
ankylotic, anchylotic, adj.—See prec. word and -ic.

## nnlace
nnlace, п., a dagger with tapering blade. —
Metathesis of OF. alenas, alesne (F. aline), 'dagger',
fr. OHG. alansa, a derivative of ala, 'awl'.
See awl.

## aalaut
aalaut, п., initial sound. — G. Anlaut, fr. an, 'on,
at', and Laut, 'sound, tone', G. an is rel. to E.
oa (q.v.) G. Laut, 'sound, tone', derives fr. laut,
'loud'; see lond. Cp. ablaut, auslant, iulaut,
umlaut

## Aim
Aim, Anna, Anne, fem. PN. — L. Anna, fr. Gk.
"Αννα, fr. Heb. Hannd", lit. 'grace', from the
base oihanan, 'he was gracious, showed favor'.
See Hannah.

## anaa
anaa, п., an Indian penny. — Hind. ana.

## Annabel
Annabel, Annabella, fem. PN. — The name is
usually interpreted as a compound of Anna and
Belia. It is more probable, however, that it arose
from a misreading of the name Amabel for Ana-
bel. Cp. Arabel, Arabella.

## annahergite
annahergite, n , a hydrous nickel arsenate
(mineral.) — Named after Annaberg in Saxony. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:64 COLUMN:3 -->

## annalist
annalist, п., a writer of annals. — F. annaliste, fr.
annates, 'annals', fr. L. annates. See next word
and -ist.

## annais
annais, n. pi. — L. annates (scil. li'jr't),
'chronicles', lit. 'yearly (books)', pi. of annalis,
'pertaining to a year', fr. annus, 'year'. See aunual.

## annates
annates, n. pi., first fruits of an ecclesiastical
benefice payable to the Pope. — ML. anndta,
'income of a year', fr. L. annus, 'year'. See
annual.

## anneal
anneal, tr. v., to temper by heat; to temper. —
ME. anelen, fr. OE. anxlan, 'to burn, kindle',
fr. an, 'on (see a- 'on'), and Stan, 'to kindle,
burn', which is rel. to OE. al, 'fire', Hied, 'fire,
firebrand'. ME. anelen and E. anneal were
influenced in form by an erroneous association
with OF. neeler (whence F. nieller), fr. VL. *ni-
gellare, 'to blacken', fr. L. nigellus, dimin. of
niger, 'black'.

## aanelid
aanelid, adj., pertaining to the Annelida; п., one
of the Annelida. — See next word.

## Anaellda
Anaellda, n. pi., a phylum of segmented worms
(zool.) — ModL., fr. F. annilide, a hybrid
coined by the French naturalist, J. B. P. Lamarck
(1744-1829), fr. L. anellus, dimin. of anulus, 'a
little ring', and Gk. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
aunular and oid.

## annerodite
annerodite, п., a pyroniobate of uranium, yttrium,
etc. (mineral.) — Named after Annered in
Norway. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## aanex
aanex, tr. v. — F. annexer, fr. L. annexus, pp. of
anneclere, 'to bind to, tie on, annex', fr. ad-
and nectere, 'to bind, join, fasten'. See nexus.
Derivatives: annex-be, adj., annex-ment, n.

## anaex
anaex, n. — F. annexe, fr. L. annexus, pp. of an-
nectere. See annex, v.

## annexation
annexation, n. — ML. annexalid, gen. -onis, 'the
act of annexing*, fr. annexatus, pp. of annexare,
which is formed fr. L. annexus, pp. of annectere.
See annex, v., and -ation.
Derivative: annexation-al, adj.

## annexion
annexion, n. — F., fr. L. annexionem, ace. of an-
nexiS, 'a binding to', fr. annexus, pp. of
annectere. See annex, v., and -Ion.

## annihilate
annihilate, tr. v. — L. annihilatus, pp. of anni-
hilare, 'to bring to nothing, annihilate', fr. ad-
and nihil, 'nothing'. See nihil and verbal suff. -ate.

## annihilation
annihilation, n. — F., fr. annihiler, 'to annihilate',
fr. L. annihilare. See prec. word and -ion.

## annihllationism
annihllationism, п., the doctrine that the wicked
will be annihilated at the end of this life (theol.).
— A hybrid coined by Edward White in
England fr. prec. word and suff. -ism.

## annibilationist
annibilationist, п., a believer in annihllationism.
— Coined fr. annihilation and suff. -ist.

## anniversary
anniversary, n. and adj. — L. anniversarius,
'returning every year', compounded of annus, gen.
anrii, 'year', and versus, pp. of verlere, 4o turn*.
See anaual, version and -ary.

## annona
annona, п., the yearly produce (Roman antiq.) —
L. αηηδηα, fr. annus, 'year'; see annular. For the
suff. ср. рбтдпа, 'fruit trees, fruit', fr. рбтшп,
'fruit', and mulrona, 'a married woman', fr.
mater, 'mother' (see Pomona and matron).

## annotate
annotate, tr. v. — L. annotatus, pp. of annotare,
'to note down', fr. nd- and nature, 'to mark,
note', fr. nota, 'mark, sign'. See note, п., and
verbal suff. -ate and cp. connotate.
Derivatives: annotation (q.v.), annolat-ive, adj.,
annotator (q.v.), annotat-ory, adj.

## annotation
annotation, n. — L. annotdtio, gen. -onis, fr. an-
natalus, pp. of annotare. See prec. word and
-ion and cp. connotation.

## anaotator
anaotator, n. — L., fr. annotatus, pp. of
annotare. See anaotate and agential suff. -or.

## anaounce
anaounce, tr. v. — ME. anounce, fr. OF. anoncer
(F. annoncer), fr. L. annuntiare, 'to announce,
relate*, fr. ad- and nuntiare, 'to relate, report',
fr. nuntius, 'messenger'. See nuncio and cp.
aanunciate.
Derivatives: announce-ment, п., announc-er, n.

## annoy
annoy, n. — ME. anoi, anui, fr. OF. enui (F.
ennui), 'worry', back formation fr. enuier, 'to
worry, vex, annoy'. See annoy, v.

## annoy
annoy, tr. v. — ME. anuien, fr. OF. anoier, en-
noier (F. ennuyer), fr. VL. inodi&re, 'to hate',
fr. L. in odid, 'in hate, in aversion'. See in, prep.,
and odium and cp. ennui, noisome. Cp. also It.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:65 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ANNUAL | 38 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:65 COLUMN:1 -->
annulare, OProvenc. enojar (whence Sp. enojar),
'to vex, annoy', which also derive fr. VL.
inodiare.
Derivatives: annoy-ance, п., annoy-er, п.,
annoying, adj., annoy-ing-ly, adv., annoy-ing-ness, п.,
annoy-ous, adj.

## annual
annual, adj. — OF. annuel, fr. Late L. annualem,
ace. of annualis, corresponding to L. annalis,
'continuing a year, annual', fr. annus, 'year',
which stands for *at-nos and is cogn. with Goth.
apnam (pi. dat.), 'to the years', and with OI.
atati, 'goes, moves on, wanders'; cp. also Osco-
Umbr. akno, 'year, holiday time'. Cp. annalist,
annals, annate, and the second element in
biennial, triennial, quinquennial, septennial,
centennial, millennium, perennial, solemn.
Derivatives: annual, п., annual-ly, adv.

## ananitant
ananitant, п., one who receives an annuity. —
Formed fr. annuity with suff. -ant

## annniry
annniry, n. — F. armuite, fr. ML. annuitatem, ace.
of annuitas, fr. L. annus, 'year'. See anaoal
and -try.

## annul
annul, tr. v. — ME. annullen, fr. OF. a miller (F.
annuler), fr. Late L. annullare, fr. ad- and L.
nullum, 'nothing', neut. of niillus, 'none'. Sec null.
Derivatives: annull-er, п., annul-ment, n.

## annalar
annalar, adj., 1) pertaining to a ring; 2) ring-
shaped. —· L. annularis, correctly anularis,
'pertaining to a ring', fr. annulus, correctly anulus,
'ring', dimin. of anus, 'ring, iron ring for the feet,
anus'. See anus, -ale and -ar and cp. Anaelida.
annular}', adj., annular; п., the ring Anger. — L.
annularius, correctly anularius, 'pertaining to a
ring', fr. anularis. See prec. word and adj. suff.
-ary.

## annulate
annulate, adj., furnished with rings. — L. annu-
latus, correctly anulatus, fr. anulus, 'ring'. See
annular and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: annulat-ed, adj.

## annotation
annotation, п., a ringlike formation. — Formed'
with suff. -ation, fr. L. annulus, correctly anulus,
'ring'. See annular.

## annulet
annulet, п., a little ring. — Formed with dimin.
suff. -et fr. L. annulus, correctly anulus, 'ring'.
See annular.

## anauloid
anauloid, adj., ring-shaped. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. annulus, correctly anulus, 'ring', and Gk.
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
annular and -oid.

## annulose
annulose, adj., ringlike. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ose, fr. L. annulus, correctly anulus, 'ring'. See
annular.

## annunciate
annunciate, tr. v., to announce. — L. annuntialus,
pp. of аппйпЧйге. See announce and verbal
suff. -ate.

## annunciation
annunciation, п., announcement. — F.
annunciation, fr. L. annuntiationem, ace. oiannuntiatid,
fr. annuntiatus, pp. of annuntiare. See announce
and -atioa and cp. prec. word.

## nno-
nno-, combining form meaning 'upward'. — Fr.
Gk. άνω, 'upward', which is rel. to άνά, 'up,
on'. See ana-.

## anode
anode, п., positive electric pole. — Gk. άνοδος,
'way up', fr. άνά (see ana-) and οδός, 'way'.
See odograph and cp. words there referred to.
The term anode was introduced into electricity
by the English physicist and chemist Michael
Faraday (1791-1867); cp. cathode, electrode.
Derivatives: anod-al, anod-ic, adjs., anod-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## Anodonta
Anodonta, п., a genus of mussels (zool.) — ModL.,
lit. 'the toothless ones', formed fr. priv. pref. an-
and Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-.

## anodyne
anodyne, adj., relieving pain (med.) — L. and-
dynus, fr. Gk. ανώδυνος, 'free from pain,
allaying pain', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and
οδύνη, 'pain', which prob. meant orig. 'that
which eats up, devours, bites', and is cogn. with
OI. -advan-, 'eating', Lith. ediioti, 'to devour,
bite', edziolis, 'to suffer pain', Arm. erkn, gen.
erlean (for *edwdn or *edwen), 'labor pains', fr.
I.-E. base *«/-, 'to eat', whence also L. edere,
'to eat'. See eat and cp. odonto-.

## anodyne
anodyne, п., anything that relieves pain. — Gk.
άνώδυνον, neut. of the adjective ανώδυνος. See
anodyne, adj.

## anoetic
anoetic, adj., unthinkable. — Formed with suff.
-ic. fr. Gk. ανόητος, 'not thought on, unheard

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:65 COLUMN:2 -->
of, fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and νοητός,
'perceptible by the mind, mental', verbal adj. of
νοεΐν, 'to perceive', fr. νόος, νους, 'mind'. See
nous and cp. noetic.

## anoint
anoint, tr. v. — OF. enoint, pp. of enoindre, fr. L.
inunguere, 'to anoint', fr. in-, 'in, on', and un-
guere, 'to smear'. See unguent and cp. ointment.
Derivatives: anoint-ed, adj., anoint-er, п.,
anointing, п., anoint-ment, n.

## anomalo-
anomalo-, before a vowel anomal-, combining
form meaning 'anomalous'. — Gk. ανώμαλο-,
άνωμαλ-, fr. ανώμαλος, 'uneven, unequal,
irregular', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and ομαλός,
'even', fr. όμός, 'one and the same', which
derives fr. I.-E. base *sem-, 'one, together'. See
same and cp. words there referred to.

## anomalous
anomalous, adj. — L. anomalus, fr. Gk. ανώμαλος,
'uneven, irregular'. See anomalo-. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous. Derivatives:
anomalous-ly, adv., anomalous-ness, n.

## anomaly
anomaly, n. — L. andmalia, fr. Gk. ανωμαλία,
'inequality', fr. ανώμαλος, 'unequal'. See
anomalo- and -y (representing Gk. -ii).
Derivatives: anomai-ism, п., anomal-isl, п., апо-
mal-ist-ic, anomal-ist-ic-al, adjs., anomal-ist-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## anomo-
anomo-, combining form meaning 'irregular'. —
Fr. Gk. άνομος, 'without law', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-), and νόμος, 'law'. See aomo-.

## anomy
anomy, п., lawlessness. — Gk. ανομία, fr. άνομος.
See anomo- and -y (representing Gk. -Is).

## anon
anon,adv., soon. — ME., fr. OE.on an, ME. anoon,
anon, lit. 'in one (instant)'. See on and one.

## anonym
anonym, n. — F. anonyme, fr. L. anonymus, fr.
Gk. ανώνυμος, 'without a name', fr. άν- (see
priv. pref. nn-) and βνυμα, dial, form of δνομα,
'name'. See name and cp. onomato-, Cp. also
antonym, autoaym, homonym, synonym.
Derivatives: anonym-ity, п., anonymous (q.v.)

## anonymous
anonymous, adj. — Gk. ανώνυμος. See prec.
word. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος,
see -ous. Derivatives: anonymous-ly, adv., anon-
ymous-ness, n.

## Anopheles
Anopheles, п., a genus of mosquitoes (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. ανωφελής, 'useless, hurtful,
harmful', fr. άν- (see priv. pref. an-) and δφελος,
'use, help, advantage', whence όφέλλειν (for
•όφέλιειν), 'to increase, enlarge', οφελμα,
'advantage'. "Οφελος prob. meant orig. 'increase',
and stands for 8-φελος, fr. pref. ό- (see agama)
and *φέλος, which together with OI. phalam,
'gain, success', derives fr. I.-E. base *phel-, 'to
swell'. This base is a collateral form of base
*bhel-, 'to swell', whence L. follis, 'bellows'. See
follicle and cp. Aphelandra, Aphelinus.

## anorexia
anorexia, п., loss of appetite (med.) — Medical
L., formed fr. priv. pref. -an and Gk. δρεξις,
'appetite', from the* stem of όρέγειν, 'to stretch
oneself, reach, reach after, long for, desire',
which is cogn. with L. regere, 'to keep straight,
guide, lead, rule'. See regeat, adj., and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-ia.

## anormal
anormal, adj., not normal. — ML. anormalis.
See abnormal.

## anorthocinse
anorthocinse, п., a triclinic potash-soda
feldspar. — Coined by the German mineralogist
Harry Rosenbusch (1836-1914) in 1885 fr. priv.
pref. -an and orthoclase (q.v.)

## anosmia
anosmia, п., lack of the sense of smell (med.) —
Medical L., fr. priv. pref. an- and Gk. οσμή,
'smell, odor'. See osmium and -ia.

## another
another, adj. and pron. — Formed fr. the indef.
article an and other.

## anoxemia
anoxemia, anoxaemia, п., abnormal condition of
the body due to the lack of oxygen in the blood
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. priv. pref. an-,
the first two letters of oxygen, Gk. αίμα, 'blood'
(see hemal), and suff. -in. Accordingly the word
anoxemia lit. means 'the lack of oxygen in the
blood'. Derivative: anoxem-ic, anoxaemic, adj.

## nnoxia
nnoxia, п., oxygen deficiency. — Medical L.,
coined fr. priv. pref. an-, the first two letters of
oxygen and suff. -ia.

## Anselm
Anselm, Ansel, masc. PN. — L. Anselmus, fr.
OHG. Ansehelm, lit. 'having a divine helmet',
compounded of ansi, 'god', and helm, 'helmet',
For the first element cp. Astrid, for the second

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:65 COLUMN:3 -->
see helmet

## Anser
Anser, п., a genus of birds, the goose (omithol.)
— L. anser, 'goose', for *hanser. See goose and
cp. the second element in merganser.

## anserine
anserine, adj., 1) pertaining to, or resembling, a
goose; z) stupid. — L. dnserlnus, fr. anser. See
prec. word and -ine (representing L. -inus).

## answer
answer, n. — ME. andsware, answere, fr. OE.
andswaru, 'a reply', lit. 'a swearing against', fr.
and-, 'against', and swerian, 'to swear'; cp. OS.
antswOr, ON. andsvar (Dan., Swed. ansvar),
OFris. ondser. The first element is cogn. with
Gk. αντί, 'against', L. ante, 'before'. See ante-
and cp. and-. For the second element see
swear.

## answer
answer, tr. and intr. v. — ME. andswerien, fr. OE.
andswarian, andswerian, fr. andswaru. See
answer, n. Derivatives: answer-able, adj., an-
swer-er, п., answer-ing, adj.

## ant
ant, n. — ME. amete, ante, fr. OE. emete, Smette,
rel. to OHG. ате!за, MHG. ameiy, G. Ameise,
'ant', lit. 'the animal that cuts (i.e. bites) off',
fr. Teut. a, 'off', and *maitan, 'to cut' (whence
Goth, maltan, ON. meila, OHG. mei^an, 'to
cut', ON. meitill, OHG. meiji/, MHG. meigel,
G. Meifiel, 'chisel'). Cp. emmet. Cp. also mite,
'a small arachnid'.

## ant-
ant-, form of and- before a vowel.

## -ant
-ant, adj. and subst. suff. denoting an agent or
an instrument. —- OF. and F. -ant, fr. L. -an-
tem or -enter», ace. of -дам, resp. -ins, pres. part,
suff. of verbs pertaining to the I., resp. II. or Щ.
conjugation. This Latin suffix is cogn. with OI.
-ant, Gk. -ων (fem. -ούσα, neut. -ov). Cp. the
ending of Gk. γέρων, 'old man' (see geronto-).
Cp. also -ent, -ance, -ancy, -ence, -ency, and
pres. part. suff. -ing. Cp. also tooth.

## anta
anta, п., pillar, pilaster (archil.) — Sing, of L.
anlae, gen. -arum, 'pillars, pilasters' (in Latin
the word is used in pi. only); cogn. with OI.
dlab (pi. of ala), 'doorframe, enclosure', ON.
end, 'ante-room', and Arm. dr-and, 'doorpost,
threshold' (see Hubschinann, Armenische Stu-
dien, 1,19).

## antacid
antacid, adj., counteracting an acid (med.) — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. αντί, 'against', and L.
acidus, 'sour'. See ant- and ncid.
Derivative: antacid, n.

## Antaeus
Antaeus, п., a giant of Libya, slain by Heracles
(Greek mythol.) —- L., fr. Gk. 'Ανταίος, fr.
άνταΐος, Opposite, opposed to, hostile', fr. άντα,
'face to face', which is rel. to αντί, Opposite,
against'. See anti-.

## antagonism
antagonism, п., opposition, hostility. — Gk.
ανταγωνισμό, fr. ανταγωνίζεσαι, 'to struggle
against'. See antagonize and -ism.

## antagonist
antagonist, opponent, enemy. — L. anlagonista,
fr. Gk. ανταγωνιστής, 'competitor, opponent,
rival', fr. ανταγωνίζεσαι, 'to struggle against'.
See next word and -ist and cp. deuteragonist,
protagonist
Derivatives: antagonist-ic, antagonist-ic-al, adjs.,
antaganist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## antagonize
antagonize, tr. v., to oppose, bring into opposition.
— Gk. άνταγωνίζεσθαι, 'to struggle against',
ίτ.άντί (seeanti-),and άγωvίζεσ^^αι,'tostruggle',
fr. άγων, 'contest'. See agony and -ize.
Derivatives: antagoniz-ation, п., antaganiz-er, n.

## antalkali
antalkali, п., a substance that neutralizes
alkalinity. — Formed fr. ant- and alkali.
Derivatives: antalkal-ine, adj. and n.

## antaphrodisuic
antaphrodisuic, adj., counteracting sexual desire;
п., a drug counteracting sexual desire. —
Formed fr. ant- and aphrodisiac.

## antarctic
antarctic, adj., pertaining to the South Pole or
regions near the South Pole. — Prop. Opposite
to the north', fr. Gk. αντί, 'opposite' (see anti-),
and άρκτος, 'bear; the constellation of the Great
Bear'. See arctic

## Antares
Antares, п., a large red star, the brightest in the
Constellation Scorpio. — Gk. Άντάρης, lit.
'opposite (the planet) Mars', fr. αντί, 'opposite',
and "Αρης, 'Mars'. See anti- and Ares.

## ante-
ante-, pref. — Fr. L. ante, 'before, in front of,
which is cogn. with OI. anti, 'opposite', Toch.
В ente, 'opposed to', Arm. W, 'opposite', Gk.
αντα, άλιτην, 'opposite', αντί, 'over against,
opposite, before', OLith. anta, Lith. ant, 'on

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:66 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 39 | ANTHROPOMORPHISM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:66 COLUMN:1 -->
to", Goth, and, anda, 'along', ΟΝ., OS., OE.
and- 'against', OHG., MHG., G. ant-, OHG.
int-, MHG., G. ent-, 'along, against', Hitt. hanti,
'opposite', hantezzish, 'the first'. Cp. anti-. Cp.
also Ananta, antiae, enantio-, the first
element in ancestor, antique, antiquity, and the
second element in Rosinante and in Vedanta.
Cp. also end, an-, pref. expressing reversal, and
the first element in along and in answer.

## antecede
antecede, tr. and mtr. v. — L. antecedere, 'to go
before', fr. ante- and cidere, 'to go'. See cede
and cp. precede.

## antecedence
antecedence, n. — L. antecldentia, fr. antecidins,
gen. -entis. See next word and -ce.

## antecedent
antecedent, adj. and n. — F. antecedent, fr. L.
antecedentem, ace. of antecidins pres. part, of
antecedere. See antecede and -ent
Derivative: antecedent-al, adj.

## antecessor
antecessor, п., a predecessor. — L. See ancestor.

## antechamber
antechamber, n. — F. antichambre, formed on
analogy of It. anticamera, which is compounded
of anti, 'before' and camera, 'chamber', fr. L.
ante, 'before', and camera, 'vault, arch'. See
ante- and chamber.

## antechapel
antechapel, n. — Formed fr. ante- and chapel.

## antedate
antedate, n. (rare), — Formed fr. ante- and date,
'point of time'. Derivative: antedate, tr. v.

## antediluvian
antediluvian, adj., relating to the time before the
Deluge. — Coined by the English physician
Sir Thomas Browne (1605-82) fr. ante- and L.
diluvium, 'flood, deluge', fr. diluere, 'to wash
away'. See dilnte and cp. diluvial, deluge. For
the ending see suff. -ian.
Derivative: antediluvian, n.

## antefixa
antefixa, n. pi., small ornaments concealing the
ends of the tiles at the eaves of the roofs (class,
archit.) — L., neut. pi. of antefixus, 'fixed in
front', formally corresponding to the pp. of
*amefigere, fr. ante- and fixus, pp. offtgere,' to
fix'. See fix, 'to attach'.

## antelope
antelope, n. — OF. antelop, fr. ML. ant(h)alopus,
fr. MGk. άνθόλοψ, name of a fabulous
animal, which prob. means 'flower eye', fr.
Gk. άνθος, 'flower', and δψ, 'eye'. See anther
and optic. F. antilope has been reborrowed fr.
E. antelope.

## antemeridian
antemeridian, adj., pertaining to the forenoon.
— L. antemertdianus, 'in the forenoon', fr. ante
meridiem. See next entry and -an.

## ante meridiem
ante meridiem, before noon. — L., fr. ante,
'before', and ace. of meridies, 'midday, noon'. See
ante- and meridian and cp. post meridiem.

## antemandane
antemandane, adj., existing or happening before
the creation of the world. — Formed fr. ante-
and mundane. Cp. premundane.

## antenatal
antenatal, adj., previous to birth. — Formed fr.
ante- and L. natus, 'born', pp. of nascT, 'to be
born'. See natal.

## antenati
antenati, n. pi., persons born before a certain
event (law). — Formed fr. ante- and L. null, pi.
of natus, 'born*. See prec. word.

## antenna
antenna, n. — ModL., feeler or horn of an
insect', fr. L. antemna, antenna, 'snil yard'.which is
of uncertain origin. It is perh. a contraction of
*an(a)tempna, 'that which is stretched,
extended', fr. I.-E. base 'temp-, 'to stretch, extend'. See
temple, 'place of worship', and cp. next word.
Derivative: antenn-al, adj.

## Antennaria
Antennaria, п., a genus of herbs, plants of the
thistle family (bol.) — ModL., fr. antenna; so
called because the pappus resembles the
antennae of insects.

## antenuptial
antenuptial, adj., prior to marriage. — Formed
fr. ante- and nuptial. Cp. postnuptial.

## antepenult
antepenult, n. — Abbreviation of next word.

## antepenulthna
antepenulthna, п., the last syllable but two. —
L. anlepaenultima (scil. syllaba). See ante- and
penultima. Derivative: antepemtllim-ate, adj.

## anteprandial
anteprandial, adj., before dinner. — Formed fr.
ante- and prandial. Cp. postprandial.

## anterior
anterior, adj. — L., 'former*, compar. of ante,
'before'. Cp. F. antirieur and see ante- and -lor.
Derivatives: anterior-ly, adv., anterior-ness, n.

## anteroom
anteroom, п., A hybrid coined fr. L. ante,
'before' (see ante-), and room. The word lit. means
'a room in front'.

## antetype
antetype, п., a prototype. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. ante, 'before' (see ante-), and Gk. τύπος, 'a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:66 COLUMN:2 -->
blow, a stamp'; see type. The correct form is
prototype, in which both elements are of Greek
origin.

## anth-
anth-, form of anti- before an aspirate.

## anthelion
anthelion, п., a kind of halo. — ModL., fr. Gk.
άνθήλιον, neut. of άνθήλιος, 'opposite the sun',
fr. άντι- (see anti-), and ήλιος, 'sun'. See helio-.

## anthelmintic
anthelmintic, adj., destroying or expelling
intestinal worms. — Formed fr. Gk. αντί, 'against'
(see anti-), and 2λμινς, also ϋλμις, gen. έλμιντος,
'worm'. See helminthic

## anthem
anthem, n. — ME. antefne, anient, fr. OE. antefit
(orig. identical in meaning with anttphony), fr.
ML. antiphona, fr. Gk. αντίφωνα, neut. pi. of
άντίφωνος, 'sounding in answer to', which was
mistaken for fern. sing. See antiphon.
Derivative: anthem, tr. v.

## Anthemis
Anthemis, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family; the camomile (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
άνθεμίς, 'a flower resembling the camomile',
fr. άνθος, 'flower'. See next word.

## anther
anther, п., that part of the stamen which contains
the pollen. — F. anthire, fr. ModL. anthera, 'a
medicine extracted from flower', fr. Gk.
ανθηρά, fem. of ανθηρός, 'flowery', fr. άνθος,
'flower', which is cogn. with OI. ananas, 'herb'.
Cp. antho-, Anthus, -anthus, antheridium, Anthyl-
lis, the first element in antelope, Anthemis,
Anthesterion, anthology, Anthrenus, Anthurium,
and the second element in Chrysanthemum,
cllnanthium, coleothar, enanthema, exanthema,
hydranth, isanthous, perianth, polyanthus.

## Antherlcum
Antherlcum, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άνθέρικος, Чпе
asphodel', which is rel. to άνθέριξ, 'blade', αθήρ,
'chaff, barb of a weapon'; of unknown
etymology. Cp. Anthriscus, atherine, atheroma, and
the first element in Atherosperma.

## antheridium
antheridium, п., the male organ in ferns, mosses,
etc. — ModL., formed with the Greek dimin.
suff. -ίδιον fr. ανθηρός, 'flowery', fr. άνθος,
'flower'. See anther and -Idium.

## Anthesterion
Anthesterion, п., name of the 8th month of the
Attic calendar (corresponding to the second
half of February and the first half of March). —
Gk. 'Ανθεστηρίων, lit. 'the month in which
Ανθεστήρια, "the Feast of the Flowers", was
celebrated', fr. άνθος, 'flower'. See anther.

## antho-
antho-, before a vowel anth-, combining form
meaning 'flower'. — Gk. άνθο-, άνθ-, fr. άνθος,
'flower'. See anther.

## anthodium
anthodium, п., the head of a composite plant
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άνθώδης, 'flowerlike',
which is formed fr. άνθος, 'flower', with suff.
-ώδης, 'like'. See anther, -ode, 'like', and 1st
-ium.

## antholite
antholite, п., a fossil flower. — Lit. 'flower stone'.
See antho- and -lite.

## anthology
anthology, n. — Gk. ανθολογία, 'a flower
gathering', fr. ανθολόγος, 'gathering flowers', fr.
άνθος, 'flower', and λέγειν, 'to gather'. See
anther and -logy.
Derivative: antholog-ic-al, adj., antholog-ic-al-
ly, adv., antholog-ist, п., anthalag-ize, tr. v.

## anthophyllite
anthophyllite, п., a magnesium and iron silicate
(mineral) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr.
ModL. anthophyllum, 'clove', fr. Gk. άνθος,
'flower', and φύλλον, 'leaf' (see antho- and
phyllo-); so called in allusion to its clove-brown
color.

## Antboxanthum
Antboxanthum, п., a genus of grasses of the
family Poaceae (hot.) — ModL., lit. 'the yellow
flower', fr. άνθος, 'flower', and ξανθός, 'yellow'.
See antho- and xantho-.

## Anthozoa
Anthozoa, n. pi., a group of Coelenterata (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. άνθος, flower', and ζώα, pi.
of ζωον, 'animal', hence Anthozoa lit. means
'flower animals'. See anther and -zoa and cp.
Zoantbus. Derivatives: anthozo-an, adj. and п.,
anthozo-ic, adj., anthozo-id, n.

## anthracene
anthracene, п., a hydrocarbon C„H10 (chem) —
Formed with suff. -ene fr. Gk. άνθραξ, 'coal'.
See next word.

## anthracite
anthracite, п., a kind of hard coal. — L.
anthracite's, 'a kind of bloodstone', fr. Gk. ανθρακίτης,
'a gem', prop, subst. use of an adj. meaning
'resembling coal', fr. άνθραξ, gen. άνθραχος, 'coal'.
See anthrax and subst. suff. -ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:66 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: anthracite, tr. v., anthracit-ic, adj.,
anthracit-ism, n.

## anthraconite
anthraconite, п., a coal-black marble of limestone
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -Ite fr.
Gk. άνθραξ, 'coal', and χονίά, 'dust, ashes;
lye, soap powder; lime'. For the first element
see anthrax. Gk. xovts derives fr. χόνις, 'dust',
which is cogn. with L. cinis, 'ashes'; see
cinerary.

## anthracosb
anthracosb, п., coal-miner's disease (med.) —
Medical L. lit. 'disease caused by coal', formed
with suff. -osis, fr. Gk. άνθραξ, gen. άνθραχος,
'coal'. See anthrax.

## anthrax
anthrax, п., a malignant disease of cattle and
sheep. — L, fr. Gk. άνθραξ, 'coal; carbuncle,
malignant pustule', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. Arm. ant'et, 'a glowing coal'. — Coal is
first mentioned about 370 B.C.E. by Theo-
phrastus in his treatise 'On Stones', under the
name λίθος άνθραχος (i.e. 'coal stone').

## Anthrenus
Anthrenus, п., a genus of insects (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. άνθρήνη, 'wild bee, hornet',
contraction of *άνθο-θρήνη (see haplology), lit.
'flower bee'. For the first element see antho-.
The second element is rel. to τενθρήνη, 'bee,
wasp*, θρώνδξ, 'drone'. See drone.

## Anthriscus
Anthriscus, п., a genus of plants of the family Am-
miaceae (hot.)—L. anthriscus, 'the wild chervil',
fr. Gk. άνθρίσκος, which is possibly rel. to αθήρ,
'chaff*. See Antherlcum.

## anthrop-
anthrop-, form of anthropo- before a vowel.

## antfaropic
antfaropic, adj., pertaining to man. — Gk. άν-
θρωπιχός, fr. άνθρωπος, 'man'. See anthropo-
and -Ic.

## anthropo-
anthropo-, before a vowel anthrop-, combining
form meaning 'of man, pertaining to man'. —
Gk. άνθρωπο-, άνθρωπ-, fr. άνθρωπος, 'man',
which is perh. a dialectical variant of *άνδρ-
ωπος, a compound of άνήρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man', and ώψ, gen. ώπος, 'eye, face', and lit.
means 'he who has the face of a man'. See
andro- and -ops and cp. the second element in
cynanthropy, Eoanthropus, lycanthrope,
misanthrope, philanthrope, Pithecanthropus, theri-
anthropic.

## anthropocentric
anthropocentric, adj., regarding man as the
center.—Compounded of unthropo- and centric.

## anthropogeography
anthropogeography, п., the study of the
geographical distribution of man. — G. Anthropo-
geographie, coined by the German geographer
Friedrich Ratzel (1844-1904) in 1882 fr.
anthropo- and G. Geographie, fr. L. geographia (see
geography).

## anthropography
anthropography, п., that part of anthropology
which deals with the physical characteristics of
the human race. — Lit. 'the description of man'.
See anthropo- and -graphy.

## anthropoid
anthropoid, adj., manlike; п., an anthropoid ape.
— Gk. άνθροποειδής, 'like a man, resembling
a man', compounded of άνθροπος, 'man', and
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
anthropo- and -oid.
Derivatives: anthropoid-al, anthropoid-an, adjs.

## anthropolatry
anthropolatry, п., the worship of a human being.
— Compounded of Gk. άνθρωπος, 'man', and
-λατρεία, -λατρία, fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor;
worship'. See anthropo- and -latry.

## anthropology
anthropology, п., the science of the natural
history of man. — The word lit. means 'the science
of man'; it is compounded of anthropo- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See anthropo- and -logy.
Derivatives: anthropolog-ic-al, adj., anthropo-
■log-ic-al-ly, adv., anthropolog-ist, n.

## anthropometry
anthropometry, п., measurement of the human
body. — Compounded of anthropo- and Gk.
-μετρία, 'measuring of, fr. μέτρον, 'measure'.
6ee -metry. Derivatives: anthropometr-lc, an-
thropometr-ic-al, adjs., anthropometr-ist, n.

## anthropomorphic
anthropomorphic, adj., pertaining to or having
the nature of anthropomorphism. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. άνθρωπόμορφος, 'of a
human form1. See anthropomorphous.
Derivative: anthropomorphic-al-ly, adv.

## anthropomorphism
anthropomorphism, п., conception of God under
a human form. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk.
άνθρωπόμορφος, 'of a human form'. See anthro-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:67 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ANTHROPDMORPHIST | 40 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:67 COLUMN:1 -->
pomorphous.

## anthropomorphist
anthropomorphist, n. — See prec. word and -1st.

## anthromorphlze
anthromorphlze, tr. and intr. v. — See next word
and -ize.

## anthropomorphous
anthropomorphous, adj., having the form of a
man. — Gk. άνθρωπόμορφος, 'of a human
form', compounded of άνθρωπος, 'man', and
μορφή, form, shape'. See anthropo- and mor-
pho-. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see
suff. -ous.

## anthropopathy
anthropopathy, n., ascription of human feelings to
God. — Gk. άνθρωποπάθεια, 'humanity*, lit.
'human feelings' fr. άνθρωπος, 'man', and
-πάθεια, fr. παθεΐν, Чо suffer'. See anthropo-
and -pathy.
Derivatives: anthropopath-ic, adj. ,anthropapath-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## anthropophagi
anthropophagi, n. pi., cannibals. — L., pi. of
anthrdpophagus, fr. Gk. ανθρωποφάγος, 'man-
eater, cannibal', fr. άνθρωπος, 'man', and the
stem of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See anthropo- and
-phagous.

## anthropophagous
anthropophagous, adj., cannibalistic, Gk.
Ανθρωποφάγος, 'man-eater, cannibal'. See next word.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## anthropophagy
anthropophagy, п., cannibalism. — F. anthropo-
phagie, fr. Gk. ανθρωποφαγία, fr.
ανθρωποφάγος. See prec. word and -y (representing Gk.
-ίά).
Derivatives: anlhropophag-ic, adj., anthropo-
phag-ist, п., anthropophagous (q.v.)

## Anthurium
Anthurium,n., a genus of plants of the arum
family (hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
άνθος, 'flower', and ούρα, 'tail'. See anther and
иго-, 'tail-'.

## Anthus
Anthus, п., a genus of birds, the pipit; the titlark
(ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άνθος, 'flower'.
See anther.

## -anthus
-anthus, suff. used in botany to form generic
names as in Dianthns, Galanihus. — ModL., lit.
'flower', fr. Gk. άνθος. The masculine form of
this suff. is based on the erroneous supposition
that Gk. άνθος is masculine, whereas it is of
the neuter gender. This error was suggested by
the fact that the overwhelming majority of
Greek nouns ending in -ος are masculine.

## AnthylUs
AnthylUs, п., a genus of plants (bol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άνθολλίς, a plant name derived fr.
άνθος, 'flower'; see anther. The name άνθυλλίς
was first used by Dioscorides.

## anthypopbora
anthypopbora, п., reply to a supposed objection
(rhet.) — Gk. άνθυποφορά, formed fr. αντί,
opposite, against' and ύποφορά, 'allegation*,
lit. 'a carrying down' fr. ύποφέρειν, 'to carry
down', fr. ύπό, 'under, below', and φέρειν, 'to
carry'. See anti-, hypo- and -phore.

## and-
and-, before a vowel ant-, pref. meaning
'opposite, against, instead'. — Gk. άντι-, άντ-,
fr. αντί, 'over against, opposite, before,
instead of, which is cogn. with L. ante, 'before,
in front of. See ante-.

## antiae
antiae, n. pi., forelocks (zool.) — L. antiae (gen.
antiarum), rel. to ante, 'before, in front of, and
cogn. with OHG. and!, endi, ON. enni,
'forehead'. See ante- and cp. anti-, end.

## antiar
antiar, п., poison from the resin of the Upas tree.
— Jav. antjar.

## aatiblotic
aatiblotic, adj., tending to destroy life; п., a
substance that inhibits or destroys microorganisms'.
— Medical L. antibioticus, coined fr. anti-, Gk.
βίος, 'life', and suff. -k (see biotk); first used
by the physician Selman Abraham Waksman
(1888- ), the discoverer of streptomycin, in
1941.
Derivative: antibiotic-al-ly, adv.

## antibody
antibody, п., substance developed in the blood as
an antitoxin (jmmunal.) — A hybrid coined fr.
Gk. αντί, 'against (see anti-), and E. body,

## antic
antic, adj., odd, grotesque. — It. antico, 'ancient',
fr. L. antiquus, 'old'. See antiqne.
Derivatives: antic, п., a trick, antic-ly, adv.,
antic-ness, n.

## antichrist
antichrist, n. — Late L. antichristus, fr. Gk.
αντίχριστος, Jfr. αντί, 'against', and Χριστός,
'Christ'. See anti- and Christ

## antichristian
antichristian, adj. — Formed fr. anti- and
Christian,

## anticipant
anticipant, adj. and n. — L. anticipans, gen. -an-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:67 COLUMN:2 -->
tis, pres. part, of anticipare. See next word
and -ant.

## anticipate
anticipate, tr. v. — L. anticipants, pp. of
anticipare, 'to take beforehand, anticipate', fr. ante,
'before', and -cipare, fr. capere, 'to take'. See
ante-, captive and verbal suff. -ate. For the
change of Latin й (in capere) to ί (in anti-cipare)
see abigeat and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: anticipation (q.v.), anticipat-ive,
adj., anticipat-ive-ly, adv., anticipat-or, п., anti-
cipat-ory, adj.

## anticipation
anticipation, n. — L. anticipated, gen. -onis, fr.
anticipants, pp. of anticipare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## nnticlerical
nnticlerical, adj. — Formed fr. anti- and clerical
Derivative: anticlerical-ism, n.

## anticlimax
anticlimax, п., the opposite of climax (rhet.) —
Coined by Alexander Pope (1688-1744) fr- «utt·
and climax.

## anticlinal
anticlinal, adj., leaning in opposite directions. —
Formed fr. anti· and Gk. χλίνειν, Чо cause to
slope'. See clinical.

## anticline
anticline, п., a fold of rock in which the layers
slope down from the axis in opposite directions
(geol.) — See prec. word.

## anticyclone
anticyclone, n. — Coined by the English scientist
Sir Francis Galton (1822-1911) fr. anti- and
cyclone.
Derivative: anticyclon-ic, adj.

## antidote
antidote, п., a remedy counteracting poison. —
L. antidotum, fr. Gk. άντίδοτον, 'a remedy',
lit. 'given against', fr. αντί (see anti-) and δοτόν,
neut. of δοτός, 'given', verbal adj. of διδόναι,
'to give'. See donation and cp. dose. Cp. also
epidote.
Derivatives: antidote, tr. v., antidot-al, adj.,
antidot-al-ly, adv., antidot-ic-al, adj., antidot-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## antifebrile
antifebrile, adj., reducing fever; п., a remedy
reducing fever. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. αντί,
'against' (see anti·), and Late L. febrilis,
'pertaining to fever', fr. L.febris, 'fever' (see febrile).
The correct form is antipyretic (q.v.), in which
both elements are of Greek origin.

## antigen
antigen, п., a substance that causes the
production of anantibody {immunology). — Coined fr.
anti- and Gk. γεννϊν, 'to produce'; see -gen.
Accordingly antigen lit. means 'something
produced against something'.

## Antigone
Antigone, п., daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta
{Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Αντιγόνη, lit.
prob. meaning 'in place of a mother', fr. αντί,
Opposite, in place of (see unti-), and γονή,
'womb'; childbirth, generation', which is rel. to
γονεύς, 'father* (in the pi. γονείς, 'parents'). See
genus.

## antigorite
antigorite, п., a variety of serpentine (mineral.) —
Named after the Antigorio valley in Piedmont.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## antibelix
antibelix, п., the rounded piece of cartilage inside
and in front of the outer rim (helix) of the ear,
(anat.) — Erroneous formation instead of *an-
thelix, for Gk. άνθέλιζ, 'inner curvature of the
ear' (first used by Rufus Ephesius in this sense);
formed fr. αντί, 'before' (see anti-), and έλιξ,
'coil, spiral'. See helix.

## antilobium
antilobium, п., the tragus (anal.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. άντιλόβιον, 'the upper edge of the ear',
fr. αντί, 'opposite, in front of (see anti·), and
λοβός, 'lobe of the ear'. See lobe.

## antilogarithm
antilogarithm, п., the number corresponding to a
logarithm (math.) — Formed fr. anti- and
logarithm.

## antilogous
antilogous, adj., contradictory. — Gk. αντίλογος.
See next word. For E.-out, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see -ous.

## antilogy
antilogy, п., contradiction. — Gk. άντιλογίδ,
'contradiction', fr. αντίλογος, 'contradictory',
fr. άντιλέγειν, 'to contradict', fr. άντι- (see
anti-) and λέγειν, Чо say, tell, speak', which is
cogn. with L. legere, 'to read'. See lecture.

## antimacassar
antimacassar, n.— Orig. 'cloth used for protecting
backs of chairs from macassar oil'. See anti-
arid macassar.

## antimony
antimony, п., a brittle metallic element (chem.) —
ML. antimonium, prob. fr. Arab, al-uthmud,
al-ithmid, from al-, 'the', and uthmud, Ithmid,
'stibium', which prob., derives fr. Gk. στίμμι,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:67 COLUMN:3 -->
'stibium'. See stibium and -y (representing L.
-turn).

## antinomian
antinomian, n. — See next word.

## antiaoinianism
antiaoinianism, n. (Eccles. hist.) —- A term
introduced by Martin Luther. See antinomy, -ian
and -ism.

## antinomy
antinomy, n. — L. antinomia, fr. Gk. αντινομία,
'ambiguity in the law', fr. άντι (see anti-) and
νόμος, 'law*. See nomo- and -y (representing
Gk. -ία).
Derivatives: antinom-ic, antinom-it-al, adjs.

## Antiope
Antiope, п., the mother of Amphion and Zethus
(Greek mythol.) — Gk. 'Αντιόπη, lit.
'opposite, facing', fr. αντί (see anti·) and δψ, gen.
οπός, 'eye, face'. See optical.

## antipathy
antipathy, n. — L. antipathia, fr. Gk. αντιπάθεια,
fr. αντιπαθής, 'having opposite feelings', fr.
αντί (see anti-) and πάθος, 'a feeling,
suffering'. See -pathy and cp. apathy, empathy,
sympathy.
Derivatives: antipath-etic, adj., antipath-etic-al-
ly, adv.

## antiphlogistic
antiphlogistic, adj., tending to counteract
inflammation (med.) — Formed fr. anti- and
phlogistic
Derivative:" antiphlogistic, n.

## antiphon
antiphon, п., a versicle sung responsively. — F.
anliphone, fr. ML. antiphona, fr. Gk. αντίφωνα,
neut. pi. of άντίφωνος, 'sounding in answer
to', mistaken for fern, sing.; fr. άντι, 'over
against, in response to' (see anti-), and φωνή,
'voice, sound'; see phone, n. Cp. anthem, which
is a doublet of antiphon.
Derivatives: antiphon-al, adj., antiphon-al-ly,
adv., antiphonary (q.v.), amiphon-et-ic, adj., an-
tiphon-ic, antiphon-ic-al, adjs., antiphonon (q.v.),
antiphon-y, n.

## antiphonary
antiphonary, n. — A collection of antiphons. —
ML. antiphonarium. See antiphon and subst.
suff. -ary.

## antiphonon
antiphonon, п., an antiphon. — Gk. άντίφωνον,
neut. of άντίφωνος, 'sounding in answer to'.
See antiphon.

## antipodal
antipodal, adj., pertaining to the antipodes. —
Formed fr. antipodes with adj. suff. -al.

## antipodes
antipodes, n. pi., opposite places of the earth. —
L. antipodes, fr. Gk. αντίποδες, pi. of άντίπους,
'having the feet opposite', fr. αντί (see anti-)
and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See foot and cp.
-pod.

## antipope
antipope, n. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. αντί,
'against', and ME. pope, 'pope'. See anti- and
Pope.

## antipyretic
antipyretic, adj., reducing fever; п., a remedy
reducing fever. — Formed fr. anti- and pyretic

## antipyrine
antipyrine, antipyrin, п., a crystalline compound
used as an antipyretic. — G. Antipyrin, coined
by the German chemist Ludwig Knorr (1859-
1921) fr. antipyretic and chem. suff. -in.

## antiquarian
antiquarian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. antiquarius. See next word.

## antiquary
antiquary, n. — L. antiquarius, 'pertaining to
antiquity; an antiquarian', fr. antiquus, 'old'. See
antique and -ary.

## antiquate
antiquate, tr. v., to make old or obsolete. — L.
antlquatus, pp. of antiquare, 'to render
obsolete', fr. antiquus, 'old'. See antiqne and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: antiquat-ed, adj., antiquat-ed-ness,
п., antiquation (q.v.)

## antiquation
antiquation, n. — Late L. antiquatio, gen. -onis,
fr. L. antlquatus, pp. of antiquare. See
antiquate and -ion.

## antiqne
antiqne, adj. — F., fr. L. antiquus, amicus, 'old',
fr. ante, 'before'. See ante·.
Derivatives: antique, n. (q.v.), antique, tr. v.,
anlique-ly, adv., antique-ness, п., antiquity (q.v.)

## antiqne
antiqne, n. — F., fr. antique, adj. See antique,
adj.

## antiquity
antiquity, n. — F. antiqutte, fr. L. antlquitatem.
Sec. of antlquitas, 'ancient times, antiquity', fr.
antiquus. See antiqne and -ity.

## Antirrhinam
Antirrhinam, п., a genus of plants of the figwort
family; the snapdragon (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
άντίρρϊνον, 'snapdragon', fr. αντί, Opposite;
like', and έίς, gen. ρινός, 'nose'. See anti- and
rhino-.

## antiscians
antiscians, also antiscii, n. pi., those who live on

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:68 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 41 | APERIODIC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:68 COLUMN:1 -->
lhe same meridian, but on opposite sides of the
