equator. — L. antiscii, fr. Gk. άντίσκιοι, pi. of
άντίσκιος, 'throwing a shadow the opposite
way', fr. αντί (see anti-) and σκιά, 'shade,
shadow'. See skiagraphy and cp. amphiscians.

## anti-Semitism
anti-Semitism, n. — G. Antisemitismus (see aati-,
Semite and -ism). The word Antisemitismus was
first used by Wilhelm Marr (in 1880).

## antiseptic
antiseptic, adj. and n. — Formed fr. anti- and
septic
Derivatives: antiseptic-al-ly, adv., antiseptic-
ism, п., anliseptic-ist, п., antiseptic-he, tr. v.

## antiserum
antiserum, n. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. αντί,
'against', and L. serum, 'whey'. See anti- and
serum. The correct form would be antiorus, fr.
Gk. αντί, 'against', and ορός, 'whey'.

## antisocial
antisocial, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. αντί,
'against', and L. socialis, fr. socius, 'companion'.
See anti- and social.

## antistrophe
antistrophe, n. — L., fr. Gk. αντιστροφή, 'a
turning* back', fr. άντιστρέφειν 'to turn back or
against', fr. αντί (see anti-) and στρέφειν, 'to
turn'. See strophe.

## antithesis
antithesis, n. — L., fr. Gk. άντίθεσις,
'opposition', lit. 'a placing against', fr. άντιτιθέναι, 'to
set one thing against another, to oppose', fr.
αντί (see anti-) and τιθένοα, 'to place'. See
thesis.

## antithetic
antithetic, antithetical, containing an antithesis.
— Gk. αντιθετικός, 'setting in opposition', fr.
αντίθετος, 'opposed', verbal adj. of άντιτιθέναι.
See prec. word and -etic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: antithetical-ly, adv.

## antitoxic
antitoxic, adj., pertaining to an antitoxin. —
Formed fr. anti- and toxic

## antitoxin
antitoxin, п., a substance neutralizing poisonous
substances (immunology). — Coined by the
German bacteriologist Emil von Behring (1B54-
1917) in 1890 fr. anti- and toxin. Cp. antotoxm.

## antitragus
antitragus, п., the eminence of the external ear
(anal.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. άντίτραγος, lit.
'the part opposite the tragus'. See anti- and
tragus.
Derivatives: antitrag-al, antilrag-ic, adjs.

## antitype
antitype, n. — Gk. άντίτυπος, 'corresponding
in form', lit. 'struck back', fr. αντί (see anti·)
and τύπος, 'a blow, a mark'. See type and cp.
antetype and prototype.

## antler
antler, n. — ME. auntelere, fr. OF. anloillier (F.
andouiller), fr. VL. 'anteoculare, neut. adj. used
as a noun and lit. meaning '(the horn) growing
before the eyes', fr. L. ante oculos, 'before the
eyes'. See ante- and ocular. For sense
development cp. G. Augensprossen, 'antlers', lit. 'eye
sprouts'.
Derivative: antler-ed, adj.

## antierite
antierite, п., a copper sulfate (mineral.) — Named
after the Antler mine in Arizona. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## Antonia
Antonia, fern. PN. — L. Antonia, fern, of An-
tOnius. See Antony.

## antonomasia
antonomasia, п., use of an epithet for a proper
name or vice versa (rhet.) — L., fr. Gk. άντο-
νομασία, fr. άντονομάζειν, 'to name instead, to *
call by a new name', fr. αντί, 'instead of (see
anti-), and όνομάζειν, 'to name', fr. δνομα,
'name'. See antonym.

## Antony
Antony, also Anthony, masc. PN. — L. Antonius,
name of a Roman gens. The spelling Anthony
was suggested by the numerous Greek loan
words beginning with antho-, fr. άνθος, 'flower'.
Cp. Antonia.

## antonym
antonym, п., opposite in meaning to another
word. — Formed fr. Gk. αντωνυμία, 'a word
used for another, a pronoun', fr. αντί, 'instead
of (see anti-), and δνυμα, dialectal form of
δνομα, 'noun'. See name and cp. anonym and
words there referred to.

## antro-
antro-, before a vowel antr-, combining form
meaning 'antrum, cavity' (anat.) — Gk. άντρο-,
άντρ-, fr. άντρον. See next word.

## antrum
antrum, п., a cave or cavity. — L., fr. Gk. άντρον,
'cave, cavern', which is prob. cogn. with Ann.
ayr, 'cave'.

## antrustion
antrustion, п., a voluntary follower of Frankish
princes — F., fr. ML. antrustionem, ace. of an-
trustio, lit. 'in fidelity', which is formed fr. pref.

## -an-
-an-, en, 'in' (see ta-, 'in, on'), OHG. trost,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:68 COLUMN:2 -->
'fidelity', Latinized into trustis, and suff. -ion.
See trast.
Derivative: antrustion-ship, n.

## Anubis
Anubis, п., a jackal god, son of Osiris (Egypt,
mythol.) — L. Anubis, fr. Gk. "Ανουβις, fr.
Egypt. Anepu, Anpu.

## anus
anus, п., inferior opening of the alimentary canal.
— L. anus, 'a ring, an iron ring for the feet;
anus (so called because of its form)'. For sense
development cp. Gk. δακτύλιος, 'ring, signet;
felloe of a wheel; anus', fr. δάκτυλος, 'finger'.
L. anus is cogn. with Olr. unite, dime, 'ring,
rump'. See anaular.

## nnuslm
nnuslm, n. pi., Jews converted to another faith
by force; ipecif. the marranos. — Heb. unustm,
'those compelled (to give up their faith)', pi. of
anus, pass. part, of anas, 'he compelled,
constrained', which is rel. to Aram, anas, Syr. enas,
of s.m.

## anvil
anvil, ME. anveh, anfilt, fr. OE. anfilte, 'anvil',
rel. to MDu. anvilt, anevilte, aenbelt, anebelt,
Du. aanbeeld, aambeeld, OHG. anafalz, Dan.
ambolt, 'anvil', G. fallen, 'to fold' (whence
Falz, 'groove, furrow'), OHG. vilz, OE. felt,
'felt'; see felt L. pellere, 'to strike', is prob. not
cognate with the above Teut. words.
Derivative: anvil, tr. v.

## anxiety
anxiety, n. — L. anxietas, gen. -Oils, 'anguish,
anxiety', fr. anxius. See next word and -Ity.

## anxious
anxious, adj. — L. anxius, 'solicitous, uneasy', fr.
angere, 'to press together, throttle'. See anger and
cp. words there referred to. For E.-ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: anxious-ly, adv., anxious-ness, n.

## nny
nny, adj. and pron. — ME. seniy, sent, any, eny,
ony, fr. OE. inig, which is formed fr. OE. an,
'one', with suff. -ig; rel. to OS. enig, enag (fr. en,
'one'), ON. einigr (fr. einn, 'one'), Du. enig (fr. een,
'one'), OHG. einag, MHG. einec, G. einig (fr.
ein, 'one'). See one and -y (representing OE. -ig).

## Anychia
Anychia, п., a genus of plants of the whitlowwort
family, the forked duckweed (bot.) — ModL.,
aphetic for Gk. παρωνυχίά, 'whitlowwort'. See
paronychia.

## Anzac
Anzac, п., a member of the Australian and New
Zealand Army corps. — Acrostic formed from
the initials of the words Australian (and) New
Zealand Army Corps.
Derivative: Anzac, adj., pertaining to the An-
zacs.

## aorist
aorist, п., a past tense of Greek verbs. — Gk.
αόριστος, 'indefinite' (short for αόριστος χρόνος,
'the aorist, i.e. indefinite tense'), fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. n-) and άριστος, 'limited, defined', verbal
adj. of όρίζειν, 'to limit, define', fr. δρος,
'boundary, limit, border'. See horizon. As a
grammatical term αόριστος was introduced by Dionysius
Thrax.

## aorta
aorta, n. — ModL., fr. Gk. αορτή, 'the grent
artery', fr. άείρειν, 'to lift, raise up, bear',
which is rel. to the second element in μετήορος,
Att. μετέωρος, 'raised from the ground, high',
of uncertain etymology. Cp. artery and the
second element in endaortic and in meteor. Cp.
also air, 'atmosphere'.
Derivatives: aort-al, aort-ic, adjs.

## aortico-
aortico-, combining form meaning 'aortic'. —-
See norm and -ie.

## aosmic
aosmic, adj., having no smell (med.) — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. άοσμος, 'having no smell',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and οσμή, 'smell, odor'.
See osmium.

## Aotus
Aotus, п., a genus of American monkeys, the
night ape (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άωτος,
'earless', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and οδς, gen. ώτάς,
'ear'. See oto-,

## np-
np-, form of apo- before a vowel.

## np-
np-, assimilated form of ad- before p.

## npace
npace, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and pace.

## npache
npache, n„ a Parisian gangster. — F., from the
name of the North American Indian Apaches.

## apagoge
apagoge, п., reductio ad absurdum (logic). — Gk.
απαγωγή, 'a leading away', fr. άπάγειν, 'to
lead away', fr. από (see apo-) and αγειν, 'to
lead', which is cogn. with L. agere, 4o set in
motion, lead'. See agent, adj., and cp. -agogue,
anagogy, pedagogue, synagogue.

## npanage
npanage, n. — See appanage.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:68 COLUMN:3 -->

## aparithmesis
aparithmesis, п., enumeration (rhet.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άπαρίθμησις, fr. άπαριθμεϊν, 'to count
over', fr. άπό (see apo·) and άριθμεΐν, 'to
count', fr. αριθμός, 'number'. See arithmetic.

## apart
apart, adv. — F. ά part, fr. L. ad partem, 'to the
one side or part', fr. ad, 'to' (see ad-) and
partem, ace. of pars, 'part'. See part, п., and cp.
next word and apartment.

## apartheid
apartheid, п., the policy of racial segregation and
discrimination against the native Negroes and
other colored peoples in South Africa. — S.
African Dutch, 'apartness', formed fr. Du. apart,
'separate' [fr. F. ά pan (see apart)], with Du.
suff. -heid, which corresponds to E. -hood (q.v.)

## apartment
apartment, n. — F. appartement, fr. It. apparta-
mento, prop, 'a separated place', fr. appartare,
'to separate', fr. a (fr. L. ad), to', and parte (fr.
L. partem, ace. of pars), 'part'. See npart and
-ment.

## ApateJa
ApateJa, п., a genus of moths (zoal.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. απατηλός, 'illusory', fr. ά-ταταν, 'to
cheat, deceive', fr. άπατη, 'deceit', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. apatite.

## npathic
npathic, adj. — F. apathique, fr. apathie. See next
word and -ic.

## npathy
npathy, n. — F. apathie, fr. L. apathia, fr. Gk.
απάθεια, 'freedom from suffering,
impassibility', fr. απαθής, 'without suffering, impassible',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. n-) and πάθος, 'feeling,
suffering'. See -pathy and cp. antipathy, empathy,
sympathy.
Derivatives: apath-ism, п., apath-ist, п., apath-
ist-ic-al, adj.

## apatite
apatite, п., calcium phosphate fluoride (mineral.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. άπατη,
'deceit' (see Apatein); so called because it has
been mistaken for other minerals.

## ape
ape, n. — ME., fr. OE. ара, rel. to OS. apo, ON.
api, Du. aap, OHG. ago, MHG., G. affe;
according to O. Schrader borrowed fr. OCelt.
άβράνας, a word glossed by Hesychius. It is more
probable, however, that OE. ара, etc., are
Slavonic loan words. Cp. ORuss. opica, Czech
opice, 'ape*.
Derivatives: ape, tr. v., ape-ry, n.

## npeak
npeak, adv., in a vertical position (naut.) — F.
dpic, 'vertically', fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and pic,
'vertex'. See peak, 'sharp point', and cp. peak, 4o
raise vertically'.

## apeiron
apeiron, п., the boundless mass postulated by
Anaximander as the first principle. — Gk.
άπειρον, neut. of άπειρος, 'boundless, infinite',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and πεΐραρ (gen.
πείρατος), 'completion, achievement', which is
rel. to πείρειν, 'to pierce, run through', πόρος,
'ford, ferry', prop, 'means of passing a river',
and is cogn. with L. porta, 'gate', portus,
'harbor'. See port, 'harbor', and cp. words there
referred to.

## apepsia
apepsia, apepsy, п., indigestion (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. άπεψίά, fr. 'undigested',
fr. ά- (see pref. a-) and πεπτός, 'cooked',
verbal adj. of πέπτειν, 'to cook'. See pepsin.

## aper
aper, п., the wild boar. — L., rel. to Umbr. apruf,
abrof, 'the boars' (ace.), and cogn. with OE.
eofor, 'wild boar', OHG. ebur, MHG., G. eber,
of s.m., ON. jofurr, 'prince', and with OSIav.
vepri, Lett, vepris, 'wild boar'. The a in L. aper
(inst. of *eper) is prob. due to dissimilation
under the influence of caper, 'he-goat'. Cp. the
first element in Everard.

## apercu
apercu, п., sketch, rapid survey. — F., prop. pp.
of apercevoir, 4o perceive', used as a noun, fr.
a, 'to' (see a), and percevoir 'to perceive', fr. L.
percipere. See perceive and cp. npperceprJon.

## aperient
aperient, adj., laxative. — L. aperiins, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of aperire, 'to uncover, open', which
stands for *ap-wenre and is rel. to aperire (for
*op-werire), 'to cover, close', and cogn. with
OI. apa-viniti, "uncovers, opens', api-vfniti,
'closes, covers', fr. I.-E. base *wer-, 'to enclose,
cover'. See weir and cp. words there referred to.
The word aperient was first used by Bacon in
1626.
Derivative: aperient, п., a laxative drug.

## aperiodic
aperiodic, adj., not periodic. — Formed fr. priv.
pref. n- and periodic
Derivative: aperiodic-al-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:69 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: APERITIF | 42 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:69 COLUMN:1 -->

## aperitif
aperitif, п., appetizer. — F. See next word.

## aperitive
aperitive, adj. aperient. — F. aperitif (fem.
aperitive), 'opening1 (said of a drug), fr. L. aperi-
tivus, fr. aperire, 'to open'. See nperient and -ive.

## apert
apert, adj., open. — OF., fr. L. apertus, pp. of
aperire, 'to open'. See aperient and cp. pert,
malapert.

## aperture
aperture, п., an opening. — L. apertura, 'an
opening', fr. apertus, pp. of aperire. See aperient and
-ore.
Derivatives: apertur-al, apertur-ed, adjs.

## npetalous
npetalous, adj., having no petals (ЛоГ.) — Formed
fr. priv. pref. a- and Gk. πέταλον, 'thin plate
of metal; leaf'. See petalon and -ous.
Derivative: apetalaus-ness, n.

## apex
apex, п., the highest point of something, top,
summit. — L., 'top, summit, the extreme end of
a thing; the small rod at the flamen's cap', lit.
'something joined or fastened to', formed with
suff. -ex fr. apiO, apere, 'to join, fasten'; see apt
For the formation of apex fr. apere, cp. vertex,
'top, summit', fr. vertere, 'to turn*. Cp.
periapical.

## aph-
aph-, form of про- before an aspirated vowel.

## aphaeresis
aphaeresis, п., loss of a letter or syllable at the
beginning of a word (gram.) — L., fr. Glc.
άφαίρεσις, 'a taking away', fr. άφαιρεΐν, 'to
take away', fr. άπό (see apo-) and αϊρεϊν, 'to
take'. The word aphaeresis was introduced into
English by Sir James Murray (1837-1915). See
heresy and cp. diaeresis, synaeresis.

## Aphanes
Aphanes, п., a genus of plants of the rose family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. αφανής, 'unseen,
unnoticed', fr. i- (see priv. pref. a-) and the base
of φαΐνειν, 'to make visible'. See phantasm.

## aphanite
aphanite, п., name of certain dark rocks (petrogr.)
— lit. 'unseen', fr. Gk. αφανής. See prec. word
and subst. suff. -Ite.
Derivatives: aphanit-lc, adj., aphanil-ism, n.

## aphano-
aphano-, before a vowel aphan-, combining form
meaning 'invisible'. — Fr. Gk. αφανής. See
Aphanes.

## aphasia
aphasia, п., loss of the faculty of speech (med.) —
Medical L., fr. priv. pref. a- and φάσις, 'speech',
from the base of φάναι, 'to speak', which is rel.
to φήμη, 'voice, report, rumor', and cogn. with
L. fama, 'talk, report, rumor'. See fame and
-ia and cp. aphemia.
Derivatives: aphasi-ac, adj. and п., aphas-ic,
adj. and n.

## Aphelandra
Aphelandra, n. 1 genus of plants of the acanthus
family (hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
αφελής, 'even, simple', and the stem of άνήρ,
gen. ανδρός, 'man'. Gk. αφελής prob. means
lit. 'without protuberances' and is formed fr.
ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and *φέλος, 'swelling,
protuberance' (whence also φελλεύς, 'stony
ground'). See Anopheles and cp. next word and
Aphelinus. For the second element in Aphelandra
see andro-. The genus was called Aphelandra in
allusion to the one-celled anthers.

## Apbelenchus
Apbelenchus, п., a genus of nematode worms
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. αφελής,
'even, simple' (see prec word), and έγχος,
'spear', a word of uncertain origin.

## Aphelions
Aphelions, п., a genus of small flies (zool) —
ModL., fr. Gk. αφελής, 'even, simple'. See

## aphelion
aphelion, п., that point of the orbit of a celestial

Grecized fr. ModL. aphllium, which was coined

## apheliotropic
apheliotropic, adj., turning away from the sun
(said of certain plants). — Formed fr. Gk. άπό
(see apo-), ήλιος, 'sun', and τροπικές, 'turning,

## nphemla
nphemla, п., a kind of aphasia (med.) — Medical
L., coined by the French surgeon and
anthropologist Paul Broca (1824-80) in i860 fr. priv.
pref. a- and Gk. φήμη, 'voice', which is rel. to

## nphesis
nphesis, п., gradual aphaeresis (gram.) — Gk.
άφεσις, 'a letting go', fr. άφιέναι, 'to send
forth, let go', fr. άπό (see apo·) and [έναι, 'to
send', which stands for *yi-ye-nai and is cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:69 COLUMN:2 -->
with b.jacire, 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth',

## aphetic
aphetic, adj., pertaining to, or resulting from,
aphesis. — Gk. άφετοίός, 'letting go', fr. αφε-
τος, 'let loose', verbal adj. of άφιέναι, 'to let go*.
See prec. word and -eric.

## -aphia
-aphia, combining form meaning 'touch', and

## aphid
aphid, п., a plant louse. — See next word.

## Aphis
Aphis, п., a genus of plant lice (zool.)— ModL., of

## aphlogistic
aphlogistic, adj., nameless. — Formed with suff.
-ic fr. Gk. άφλόγιστος, 'not inflammable, flame-
less', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-), and φλογιστός,

## aphonia
aphonia, n., the loss of voice (med.) — Medical L.,

'voiceless, speechless', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)

## aphonic
aphonic, adj., having no sound, voiceless. — See

## nphorism
nphorism, п., 1) a short definition; z) a maxim. —

aphorist, п., a writer of aphorisms. — See prec.

aphoristic, aphoristical, adj. — Gk. αφοριστικός,

## npbotic
npbotic, adj., lightless. — Formed with suff. -ic fr.

The name prob. means 'hind'.

## nphrite

aphrizite, n„ a variety of tourmaline. — Formed

## npbrodisia

## nphrodhdac
nphrodhdac, adj., producing or increasing sexual

## Aphrodite
Aphrodite, п., name of the goddess of love in

Roman mythology). — Gk. 'Αφροδίτη, prob.

ρήθη (a change due to the influence ofGk. αφρός,

goddess of love', which is rel. to Akkad. Ashtarte,
Ishtar; cp. Frisk, GEW., I, pp. 196Γ s.v.
'Αφροδίτη. The explanation of the name' Αφροδίτη by
Hesiod as '(the goddess) born of the foam (of
the sea)' is folk etymology. For the change of sh
to φ, ср. Heb. shum, Arab, thum, VArab.
/urn, 'garlic', Heb. gadlsh, Arab, jadath, VArab.
jddaf, 'mound, tumulus', and the Russian PN.
Feodor, which derives fr. Gk. Θεόδωρος (see
Theodore). Cp. Ashtoreth, Astarte, Ishtar. Cp.
aiso April.

## aphtha
aphtha, п., a children's disease, also called

## aphthous
aphthous, adj., caused by aphthae. — See prec.

word and -ous.

## aphyllous
aphyllous, adj. having no leaves (hot.) — Gk.
άφυλλος, 'leafless', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and

## aphthitalite
aphthitalite, п., a potassium sodium sulfate

άφ&ιτος, 'undecaying, imperishable;
unchangeable', and αλς, 'salt'; so called because it is

## apiarian

aplomb, n. — F., 'perpendicularity', whence 'self-

Apluda, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) — L. apluda,

aplustre, п., the curved stern of a ship with its

sfflus, fr. Gk. πάσσαλος, 'bolt', L. Iriumphus,

просоре, п., the omission of the last letter or

Derivative: Apocryph-al, adj.

Derivative: apod(e)ictic-a!-ly, adv.

Apollo, п., one of the most important Olympian

to. The Latin translation of Greek αποπληξία,
'siderutio", lit. 'disease caused by a constellation',
shows that αποπληξία orig. must have denoted
the condition of being struck (άπόπληκτος) by
the stars (cp. sideralion).

## aposiopesis
aposiopesis, п., a sudden breaking off in the
middle of a sentence (rhel.) — L., fr. Gk. άπο-
σιώπησις, 'becoming silent', fr. άπό (see apo-)
and σιωπή, 'silence', which is prob. rel. to Mes-
sapian σίπτα', 'be silent!, and perh. cogn. with
Goth, sweiban, 'to cease', OHG. gi-swiftdn,
'to become quiet'. Cp. swifter, wivel.

## apostasy
apostasy, п., desertion of one's faith, principles,
etc. — ME. apostasie, fr. L. aposlasia, fr. Gk.
αποστασία, a later form of άπόστασις, 'revolt,
defection', lit. 'a standing off', fr. άποστηναι,
'to stand off, revolt', fr. άπό (see apo-) and
στηναι, 'to stand'. See state and -y (representing
Gk. -ία), and cp. stasis. The word apostasy was
introduced into English by Wyclifie.

## apostate
apostate, п., a person guilty of apostasy; adj.,
guilty of apostasy. — ME., fr. OF apostate (F.
apostat), fr. L. apostata, fr. Gk. αποστάτης,
'rebel, deserter', lit. 'a person standing off", fr.
άποστηναι, 'to stand off, revolt'. See prec.
word.

## apostatic
apostatic, apostatical, adj., apostate. — L. apo-
staticus, fr Gk. άποστατικός, 'pertaining to
revolt', fr. αποστάτης. See prec. word and -ic, resp.
also -al.
Derivative: apostatical-ly, adv.

## apostatize
apostatize, intr. v., to become an apostate. —
ML. aposlatizare, fr. L. apostata. See apostate
and -Ize.

## aposteme
aposteme, п., an abscess (med.) — MF„ fr. OF.
aposteme, fr. L. apostema, fr. Gk. απόστημα,
'abscess', lit. 'a standing off', fr. άποστηναι, 'to
stand off". See apostasy and cp. impostume.

## a posteriori
a posteriori, 1) from effect to cause; 2)
inductively; 3) from experience (philos.) — a
posteriori, 'from what comes after', fr. a, 'from' (see
a-, 'from'), and posteriori, abl. of posterior, corn-
par, of posterus, 'coming after'. See posterior.

## apostil
apostil, also npostllie, п., note, esp. on the text
of the Bible. — F. apostille. See postil.

## apostie
apostie, n. — OF. apostle, apostre (F. apotre),
'apostle', fr. Eccles. L. apostolus, fr. Gk.
απόστολος, 'one sent, a messenger, an envoy', fr.
άποστέλλειν, 'to send forth*, fr. άπό (see apo-)
and στέλλειν, 'to set in order, dispatch, send'.
See stall and cp. stele, stole, 'garment', epistle.
Derivative: apostle-snip, n.

## apostolate
apostolate, n. — Eccles. L. aposlolatus, fr.
apostolus, fr. Gk. απόστολος. See prec. word and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:71 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: APOSTOLIC | 44 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:71 COLUMN:1 -->
subst. suff. -ate.

## apostolic
apostolic, apostolical, adj. — F. aposlolique, fr.
Ecclcs. L. apostolicus, fr. apostolus, fr. Glc.
απόστολος. See apostle, -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: apostolic-al-ly, adv.

## apostrophe
apostrophe, п., a sign (') indicating the omission
of a letter or letters. — F., fr. L. apostrophus, fr.
Gk. απόστροφος, 'apostrophe', lit. 'a turning
away', fr. άποστρέφειν, 'to turn away', fr. άπό
(see apo-) and στρέφειν, 'to turn'. See strophe
and cp. next word. Cp. also anastrophe, anti-
strophe, catastrophe, epistrophe.

## apostrophe
apostrophe, п., a turning aside from the subject
(rhel.) — L., fr. Gk. αποστροφή, 'a turning
away', fr. άποστρέφειν. See prec. word.
Derivatives: aposiroph-ic, adj., apostroph-ize,
tr. v.

## apothecary
apothecary, n. — OF. apotecarie (F. apothicaire),
fr. ML. apothecarius, orig. 'storekeeper', fr.
apothgca, 'storehouse', fr. Gk. αποθήκη, lit. 'a
place wherein to lay up a thing', fr. άποτιθέναι,
'to put away', fr. άπό (see apo-) and τιθέναι, 'to
put, place, set down'. See theme and -ary and
cp. next word and apothem. Cp. also bodega,
bottega, boutiqne.

## apothecium
apothecium, п., the ascocarp of lichens (hot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. *άποθήκιον, dimin. of αποθήκη,
'a storehouse'. See apothecary.

## apothegm
apothegm, apophthegm, п., a pithy saying, a
maxim. — Gk. απόφθεγμα, 'a terse saying,
apothegm', lit. 'something uttered', fr. άποφθέγγεσ-
θαι, 'to speak one's opinion plainly', fr. άπό
(see apo-) and φθέγγεσθαι, 'to speak' (whence
φθέγμα, 'voice, speech'), which stands in gra-
dational relationship to φθόγγος, 'a sound, a
voice'. Cp. the second element in inonophthoag,
diphthoag, triphthong.

## apothem
apothem, п., perpendicular drawn from the center
to any of the sides of a regular polygon (geom.)
— Formed fr. apo- and Gk. θέμα, 'that which
is placed', from the stem of τιθέναι, 'to place'.
See theme.

## apotheosis
apotheosis, п., deification. — L., fr. Gk. άποθέω-
σις, 'deification', fr. άποθεοϋν, 'to make
someone a god, to deify', fr. άπό (see apo-) and θεός,
'god'. See thee- and -osis.
Derivative: apotheos-ize, tr. v.

## apotropaion
apotropaion, п., an amulet, a charm, anything
supposed to avert evil. — Gk. άποτρόπαιον,
neut. of αποτρόπαιος, 'that which averts', fr.
άποτρέπείν, 'to turn away, avert', fr. άπό (see
apo-) and τρέπειν, 'to turn'. See trope.

## apozem
apozem, п., a decoction (pharm.) — F. apozime,
fr. L. apozema, fr. Gk. άποζεμα, 'decoction',
fr. άποζεΐν, 'to boil till the scum is thrown off',
fr. άπό» (see про-) and ζεΐν, 'to boil'. See ec-
zema-and cp. words there referred to.

## nppall
nppall, tr. v. — ME. appallen, apallen, 'to make
pale, become pale', fr. OF. apallir, 'to grow
pale', fr. a, 'to' (see a), and pallir,palir (F.palir),
'to grow pale', fr. pale (F. pale). See pallor and
cp. pale, pallid.
Derivatives: apall-ing, adj., apall-ing-ly, adv.

## appalto
appalto, п., a monopoly. — It., 'contract', of
uncertain origin. It stands perh. for *appaclo,
fr. L. *appactum, fr. ad, 'to', and pactum,
'agreement, contract, pact'; see ad- and pact. Rum.
apalt is an Italian loan word. See Meyer-Liibke,
REW., N0.533.

## appanage
appanage, apanage, п., provision made by kings
and princes for their younger children;
perquisite. —F. apanage, fr. OF. apaner, 'to nourish,
support', fr. ML аррвпаге, 'to provide with
bread', fr. ad- and L. panis, 'bread'. Cp. OProv-
enc. apanar, 'to nourish', and see pastor and
-age.
Derivative: appanage, tr. v.

## apparatas
apparatas, п., instruments serving a specific task.
— L. apparatus, 'preparation,' fr. apparatus, pp.
of apparare, 4o make ready', fr. ad- and parare,
'to make ready, prepare'. See pare and cp.
parade, prepare.

## npparel
npparel, n. — ME. appareil, apareil, fr. OF. apa-
reil, (F. appareil), 'preparation', fr. apareillter,
(F. appareiller), fr. VL. *appariculare, fr. L. ap-
parare, 'to prepare', lit. 'to make ready for', fr.
ad- and parare, 'to prepare'. Cp. It. apparecchi-
are, OProvenc. aparelhar, Sp. aparejar, Port.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:71 COLUMN:2 -->
aparelhar, 'to prepare', which all derive fr. VL.
*appariculare, and see pare. Cp. also prec. word.

## apparel
apparel, tr. v. — ME. aparailen, fr. OF. apareil-
lier. See apparel, n.

## apparent
apparent, adj. — OF. aparant (F. apparant), fr.
L. apparentem, ace. of appargns, pres. part, of
apparere, 'to appear*. See appear and -ent.
Derivatives: apparent-ly, adv., appar-ent-ness,n.

## apparition
apparition, n. — F., fr. L. apparitionem, ace. of
appuritid, 'service, attendance' fr. apparit-(um),
pp. stem of apparere, 'to appear'. See appear
and -ition.

## apparitor
apparitor, п., an officer in attendance of a Roman
magistrate (Roman antiq.); an officer who
executes orders. — L., 'an attendant, a public
servant', fr. apparit-(um), pp. stem of apparere. See
prec. word and agential suff. -or.

## appeach
appeach, intr. v. to impeach, accuse (obsol.) —
ME. apechen, formed, with change of suff., from
OF empechier (F. empicher), 'to hinder,
impede'. See impeach.

## appeal
appeal, tr. and intr. v. — ME. appelen, apelen,
fr. OF. apeler (F. appeler), 'to address, entreat,
call', fr. L. appellare, 'to address, accost, appeal
to, apply to, summon, call, name', fr. ad- and
-pellare (found only in compounds), fr. pellere,
'to drive', whence also appellere, 'to drive to'.
The sense development of appellore, 'to
address, accost', etc., fr. pellere, 'to drive', may
be illustrated by the following phases: 'to drive,
push on, incite, warn, admonish, summon, call,
address'. See pulse, 'throb', and cp. repenl. Cp.
also compel, dispel, expel, impel, propel, repel.
Cp. also push. The change from the 3rd
conjugation (pellere, appellere) to the 1st
(appellare) is due to the iterative sense of appellare.
Cp. interpellare, 'to interrupt in speaking', which
is formed fr. inter- and -pellare, and also has an
iterative meaning (see Interpellate). For other
Latin iterative verbs of the 1st conjugation
formed from verbs of other conjugations cp. inter-
polare, 'to give a new form to, to polish,
furbish; to change, vary; to falsify; to insert,
interpolate', fr. inter- and polire, 'to smooth, polish,
furbish' (see interpolate), and occupare, 'to seize,
take possession of, fr. capere, 'to catch, seize,
take' (see occupy).
Derivatives: appeal, n. (q.v.), appeal-able, adj.,
appeal-er, п., appeal-ing, adj., appeal-ing-ly, adv.

## appeal
appeal, n. — ME. appel, apel, fr. OF. apel (F. ap-
pel), back formation fr. OF. apeler. See
appeal, v.

## appear
appear, intr. v. —- ME. apperen, aperen, fr. OF.
aparoir (F. apparoir), 'to appear', fr. L.
apparere, fr. ad- and parere, 'to come forth, appear,
be visible', which is prob. cogn. with Gk. πεπα-
ρεΐν (aorist inf.), 4o display, manifest'. Cp.
peer, 'to appear*. Cp. also apparent, apparition,
apparitor, transparent ·

## appearance
appearance, n. — ME. aparaunce, fr. OF. apa-
rence (F. apparence), fr. L. apparentia, fr.
appargns, gen. -entis, pres. part, of apparere, 'to
appear'. See prec. word and -ance.

## nppease
nppease, tr. v. — ME. apaisen, apesen, appesen,
fr. OF. apeser (F. apaiser), 'to pacify, appease',
fr. OF. pais, a collateral form of paiz (F. paix),
fr. L. pacem, ace. of pax, 'peace'. See peace.
Derivatives: appeas-able, adj., appeas-er, п.,
appeasement (q.v.), appeas-ing, adj., appeas-ing-ly,
adv., appeas-ive, adj.

## appeasement
appeasement, n. — F. apaisement, fr. apaiser. See
appease and -ment.

## appellant
appellant, adj., appealing. — F., fr. L. appellan-
tem, ace. of appellans, pres. part, of appellare,
'to call'. See appeal, v., and -ant
Derivative: appellant, n.

## nppellate
nppellate, adj., pertaining to appeals. — L. appel-
latus, pp. of appellare, 'to address, call'. See
nppeal and adj. suff. -ate.

## appellation
appellation, n. — L: appellutio, gen. -onis, fr. ap-
pellalus, pp. of appellare. See prec. word and
-km.
Derivative: appellation-al, adj.

## appellative
appellative, adj. — L. appellativus, fr. appellaius,
pp. of appellare. See appeal, v., and -ative.

## appellee
appellee, п., a person appealed against (law). —
F. appele, pp. of appeler, 'to call, address'. See
appeal, v., and -ее.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:71 COLUMN:3 -->

## append
append, tr. v., to attach; to join. — OF. apendre
(F. appendre), fr. L. apptndlre, 'to hang
something on', fr. ad- and pendgre, 'to cause to hang*.
See pendant.
Derivatives: appendage, п., appendag-ed, adj.

## appendant
appendant, adj. and n. — F., pres. part, of
appendre. See prec. word and -ant.

## appeadectomy
appeadectomy, п., removal of the appendix
(surgery). — A hybrid coined fr. L. appendix and
Gk. -εκτομία, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a
cutting out'. See appendix and -ectomy.

## appendicitis
appendicitis, п., inflammation of the vermiform
appendix. — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L.
appendix (see next word) and -iris, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## appendix
appendix, n. — L., 'something hung on,
something appended', fr. appendire. See append.
Derivative: appendix, tr. v.

## appercelre
appercelre, tr. v. — ME., fr. OF. aperceivre (F,
apercevoir), fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and perceivre, 'to
perceive', fr. L. percipere. See perceive and cp.
next word. Cp. also npercu.

## apperception
apperception, n. — F. aperception, coined by the
German philosopher Baron Gottfried Wilhelm
von Leibniz (1646-1716) as the noun
corresponding to the verb apercevoir, on analogy of
the noun perception (which corresponds to per-
cevoir). See prec. word and -Ion.

## nppertain
nppertain, intr. v. — ME. aperteinen, apertenen,
fr. apertenen, fr. OF. apartenir (F. appartenir),
fr. L. appertinlre, 'to pertain to', fr. nd- and
pertinire, 'to pertain'. See pertain and cp.
appurtenance.

## appetence
appetence, appetency, п., a strong desire. — F.
appetence, 'longing, covetousness, appetence',
fr. L. appetentia, 'longing after something', fr.
appetgns, gen. -entis, pres. part, of appetere, 'to
seek or long after', fr. nd- and petere, 'to rush at,
seek, request'. See petition and -ence.

## appetent
appetent, adj., eagerly desirous. — L. appetens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of appetere. See prec. word
and -ent Derivative: appetent-ly, adv.

## appetite
appetite, n. — ME., fr. OF. apetit (F. appelil),
fr. L. appetitus, 'appetite', lit. 'a longing after',
fr. appetitus, pp. of appetere. See appetency.
Derivative: appetil-ive, adj.

## appetize
appetize, tr. v. — Irregularly formed fr. L.
appetitus (see prec. word) and suff. -ize.
Derivatives: appetiz-er, п., appetiz-ing, adj. ap-
petiz-ing-ly, adv.
Appian Way. — The road between Rome and
Capua is so called because it was begun by the
consul Appius Claudius Caecus (during his
consulship in 302 B.C.E.).

## applaud
applaud, intr. and tr. v. — L. applaudere, 'to clap
the hands in approbation; fr. ad- and plaudere,
4o clap the hands in approbation, approve,
applaud*. See plaudit and cp. next word.
Derivatives: applaud-able, adj., applaud-abl-y,
adv., applaud-er, п., applaud-ing-ly, adv.

## npplau.se
npplau.se, n. — L. applausus, pp. of applaudere.
See applaud.

## applausive
applausive, adj. — ML. applausivus, fr. L.
applausus. See prec. word and -ive.

## apple
apple, n. — ME. appel, eppel fr. OE. sippel, sept,
rel. to OS., OFris., LG., Du. appel, ON. eple,
epli, Dan. able, Swed. apple, Norw. eple, OHG.
apful, afful, MHG., G. apfel, Crimean Goth.
apel, and cogn. with Gaul, avalio (pi.), 'fruit',
Olr. ubull, 'apple', abatl, 'apple tree', W. afall,
of s.m., afal, Co., Bret, aval, 'apple', Lith.
obalas, obuolas, Lett, abudlis, OPruss. woble,
'apple', OSlav. abluko, jabluko, 'apple'. Cp. L.
Abella (now Avella), name of a town in Cam-
panin, lit. 'Apple town'.
Derivative: apple, intr. V.

## apple pie bed
apple pie bed, a bed in which the sheets are
doubled so as to prevent the user from
stretching his legs. — Apple pie in the above term
is folk etymology and stands for F. nappe pliie,
'folded sheet', pronounced nap-ре pliie. See
napery and ply, 'to bend'.

## appliance
appliance, n. — Formed fr. npply with suff. -ance.

## applicable
applicable, adj. — Formed with suff. -able fr. L.
applicare. See apply.
Derivatives: applicabil-ily, п., applicable-ness,
п., applicabl-y, adv.

## applicancy
applicancy, п., quality of being applicable. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:72 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 45 | APSIS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:72 COLUMN:1 -->
Formed fr. next word with suff. -cy.

## npplicant
npplicant, п., one who applies for something. —
L. applicants, gen. -antis, pres. part, of applicare.
See apply and -ant

## applicate
applicate, adj. l) inclined; 2) applied. — L.
applicants, pp. of applicare. Seeprec. word and adj.
suff. -nte.

## applicntion
applicntion, n. — F. Гг. L. applicdtidnem, ace. of
applicdlio, 'an attaching oneself to', fr. appli-
catus, pp. of applicare. See apply and -ation and
cp. prec. word.

## applicative
applicative, adj., practical. — Formed with suff.
-ive fr. L. applicants, pp. of applicare. See npply.
Derivatives: applicative-ly, adv., applicative-
ness, n.

## applicator
applicator, п., an applier. — Formed as if fr. L.
'applicator, fr. applicare. See apply and agential
suff. -or.

## applicatory
applicatory, adj., applying. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ory. fr. L. applicants, pp. of applicare. See
prec. word.

## applique
applique, adj., applied, attached; п., an applique
work. — F., pp. of appliquer, 'to apply', fr. L.
applicare. See npply.

## apply
apply, tr. and intr. v. — OF. aplier (F. appliquer),
fr. L. applicare, 'to fasten or attach to, to place
near to, to devote oneself to', fr. ad- and pllcdre,
'to fold, bend'. See ply, 'to bend', and cp.
applique.
Derivatives: appli-аЫе, adj., appliable-ness, п.,
appli-аЫ-у, adv., appli-ance, п., appli-anl, adj.

## appoggiatura
appoggiatura, п., a grace note (music). — It., lit.
'a support', fr. appoggiare, 4o lean, rest,
support', fr. VL. *appodiare, 'to support', fr. ad-
and L. podium, 'elevated place, balcony'. See
podium and cp. nppui.

## appoint
appoint, tr. v. — ME. appainlen, fr. OF. apointier,
apoiitteriF. appointer), 'to arrange, settle, place'
fr. VL. appunctdre, 'to bring to a point', fr. ad-
and L. punclum, 'point'. See point.
Derivatives: appoinl-ee, п., appoint-er, п., ap-
point-ive, adj., appointment (q.v.), appoint-or, a.

## appointment
appointment, n. — F. appointement, fr. appointer.
See prec. word and -ment.

## apport
apport, п., an object appearing at a seance
without visible physical agency (spiritualism). — F.,
lit. 'anything brought', back formation fr. ap-
porter, 'to bring', fr. L. apporture, 'to bring,
carry to', fr. ad- and portare, 'to carry'. See
port, 'to carry', and cp. rapport.

## apportion
apportion, tr. v., — OF. apportionner, fr. a, 'to'
(see a), and portionner, 'to divide into portions',
fr. portion, 'share, portion'. See portion, n.
Derivatives: apportion-er, п., apportion-ment, n.

## nppose
nppose, tr. v. — F. apposer, fr. a, 'to' (see a), and
poser, 'to place'. See pose, 'to place', and cp.
words there referred to.

## npposite
npposite, adj., appropriate. — L. apposilus, pp. of
apponere, 'to put near', fr. ad- and ponere, 'to
put, place'. See position and cp. posrJcne.
Derivatives: apposite-ly, adv., apposite-ness, n.

## npposition
npposition, n. — L. appositid, gen. -dnis, 'a placing
before', fr. apposilus, pp. of apponere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## appraisal
appraisal, n. — Formed fr. appraise with subst.
suff. -al.

## appraise
appraise, tr. v. — OF. apreisier, apreiser (F. ap-
pricier), fr. L. appretiare. See nppreciate and cp.
npprize, 'to appraise'.
Derivatives: appraise-ment, п., apprais-er, п.,
apprais-ing, adj., apprais-ing-ly, adv., apprais-
ive, adj.

## appreciable
appreciable, adj. — F. appreciable, fr. apprecter,
'to appreciate*. See next word and -able.
Derivative: appreciabl-y, adv.

## appreciate
appreciate, tr. v. — L. appretiatus, pp. of
appretiare, 'to value, appraise', lit. 'to set a price to',
fr. nd- and prelium, 'price'. See price and cp.
prize. Cp. also appraise, depredate.
Derivatives: appreclat-lng-ly, adv., appreciation
(q.v.), apprecial-ive, adj., appreciat-ive-ly, adv.,
appreciat-ive-ness,n„ арргесЫ-or, п., appreciat-
ory, adj., appreciat-ori-ly, adv.

## nppreciation
nppreciation, n. — F. appreciation, fr. appricier,
'to appreciate', fr. L. appretiare See prec. word
and -ion.

## apprehend
apprehend, tr. v., 1) to arrest; 2) to understand;
3) to fear. — Fr. F. apprehender or directly from

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:72 COLUMN:2 -->
L. apprehendere, 'to seize, take hold of,
apprehend', fr. ad- and prehendere, 'to seize'. See
preheasile and cp. npprentice, apprise.
Derivatives: apprehend-er, п., apprehend-ing-
ly, adv.

## apprehensible
apprehensible, adj. — L. apprehensibilis, 'that can
be seized', fr. apprehensus, pp. of
apprehendere. See apprehend and -ible.
Derivatives: apprehensibil-ity, п., apprehensibl-y,
adv.

## npprehension
npprehension, n. — F. apprehension fr. L. appre-
hensionem, ace. of apprehinsid, fr. apprehensus,
pp. of apprehendere. See prec. word and -ion.

## apprehensive
apprehensive, adj. — ML· apprehensive, whence
also F. apprehensif (fern, apprehensive), fr. L.
apprehensus, pp. of apprehendere. See apprehend
and -ive.
Derivatives: apprehensively, adv., apprehensive·
ness, n.

## apprentice
apprentice, n. — ME. aprenlis, fr. OF. aprentiz
(F. apprenti), fr. aprendre (F. apprendre), 'to
learn, teach', fr. L. apprehendere, 'to seize, take
hold of, grasp, apprehend', whence aiso It. ap-
prendere, OProvenc. aprendre, Catal. apendrer,
Sp., Port, aprender, 'to learn'. See npprehend.
Derivative: apprentice, tr. v.

## appreteur
appreteur, п., dresser. — F. appriteur, lit.
'preparer', fr. appriter, 'to prepare, get ready', fr.
VL. *apprestdre, fr. ad- 'to', and *prestus, fr. L.

ingly lit. meant 'to place into somebody's hand'.

## apprise

pris, fern, apprise, pp. of apprendre, 'to learn'.

## apprize
apprize, also apprise, tr. v., to appraise. — OF.

## approach

Derivatives: approach, п., approach-abil-ity, п.,
approach-able, adj., approach-able-ness, п., ар-
proach-er, п., approach-ing, adj.

## approbate
approbate, tr. v., to approve. — L. approbate,

## approbation
approbation, п., approval. — F., fr. L. approbatus,

## approhative
approhative, adj., approving. — F. approbalif

## approbator
approbator, п., one who approves. — L., 'an

## approbatory

## appropriate
appropriate, adj. — L. appropriate, pp. of appro·
prime, 'to make one's own', fr. ad- and propri-
dre, 'to appropriate', fr. proprius, 'one's own'.

## appropriate

propridre. See appropriate, adj.

ive, adj. appropriat-ive-ness, п., appropriat-or, n.

## appropriation
appropriation, n. — L. appropriate, gen. -6nis, 'a

propridre. See appropriate, adj. and v., and -ion.

## approval
approval, n. — Formed fr. approve with subst.

## npprove
npprove, tr. and intr. v. — ME. aproven, fr. OF.

## approximate
approximate, adj. — L. approximate, pp. of ap-
proximdre, 'to come near, approach', fr. ad- and

## approximate

appube, п., approach, impact. — L. appidsus, fr.

## appurtenance
appurtenance, п., that which appertains;

## appurtenant
appurtenant, adj., appertaining. — ME., fr. AF.

## apricot
apricot, n. — F. abricot, fr. Port, albrlcoque fr.

## April
April, n. — L. (minsis) Aprilis, lit. the month of

a priori, I) from cause to effect; 2) deductively;

## apron

## Apsaras
Apsaras, п., one of the nymphs of India's heaven

apse, п., ι) a semicircular extension at the end of

## apt

Aptenodytes, п., a genus of pinguins (ornithol.) —

aptitude, п., fitness. — F., fr. Late L. aptitude,

aptote, п., an indeclinable noun. — L. aptotum,

## apyretic
apyretic, adj., without fever (med.) — Formed

«pyrexia, apyrexy, п., absence of fever (med.) —

aqna, п., water. — L. See aquatic

## Aqulla

## Aquilo
Aquilo, п., the north wind (Roman antiq.) — L.

east wind', lit. 'the dark one', cogn. with L.

## aquose
aquose, adj., aqueous. — L. aquosus, 'abounding

parched place', fr. I.-E. base *ds-, 'to burn,

Arab, n. — F. Arabe, fr. L. Arabem, ace. ofArabs,

que-ly, adv.

Arabic, adj. — OF., fr. L. Arabicus, 'Arabic', fr.

arachnid, п., any member of the Arachnlda. —

## Arachnida
Arachnida, n. pi., a class of arthropods, the spider

Агапеа, п., a genus of spiders, the garden spider

araneid, п., a member, of the order Araneida. —

## Araneida
