Coined fr. aseptic and suff. -ol (representing L.
oleum, 'oil').

## asexual
asexual, adj., not sexual. — A hybrid coined fr.
Gk. ά-, !nof (see priv. pref. a-), and sexual, a
word of Latin origin.
Derivatives: asexual-ity, п., asexual-ly, adv.

## ash
ash, п., usually in pi. ashes, a powdery substance
that remains after burning anything. — ME.
asche, fr. OE. asce, sesce, rel. to ΟΝ., Swed. aska,
Dan. ask, OHG. asca, MHG., G. asche, Goth.
azgd, 'ashes' (whence Sp. and Port, ascua, 'red
hot coal'), fr. I.-E. *as-gon, *as-ghdn, 'ashes',
fr. I.-E. base *as-, 'to burn, glow', whence also
L. arlre (for *asere), 'to be dry', ardire, 'to
burn'. See ardent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: ash-en, adj., ash-ery, n„ ash-y,
adj.

## ash
ash, п., any tree of the genus Fraxinus. — ME.
asch, esch, fr. OE. sesc, rel. to ON. askr, OS., Dan.
Swed., OHG. ask, MDu. esce, Du. es, MHG.
asch, esche, G. Esche, and cogn with Arm. had,
'ash', Alb. ah, 'beech', Gk. όξύα, όξύη, οξέα,
'beech', and—wilh -л-formative element—with
Russ. jasen', Olr. uinnius, W., OCo. onnen (fr.
base*onna,for*osnu),'ash',L.ornus(for*osinos),
'the wild mountain ash'. The original I.-E. base
*6sis appears in Lith. uosis, Lett, uosis, OPruss.
woasis, 'ash'.
Derivative: ash-en, adj.

## ashamed
ashamed, adj. — Pp. of obsol. ashame, fr. ME.
aschamien, fr. OE. ascamian, 'to put to shame',
which is formed fr. intensive pref. a- and
scamian, 'to put to shame'. See shame.

## Ashamnn
Ashamnn, п., the shorter of the two alphabetical
confessions of sins recited in the liturgy of
Yom Kippur (Jewish religion). — Heb. Asham-
пй, 'we have trespassed', fr. aShdm, 'he has
trespassed', rel. to asham, 'offence, guilt, guilt
offering', and to Arab, athima, 'he has sinned',
ithm, 'offence'.

## Asher
Asher, п., ι) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible: a) a son
of Jacob; b) the tribe descended from him. —
Heb. Asher, lit. 'happy' (see Gen. 30:13), rel. to
ishshir, 'he pronounced happy', Ssher,
'happiness', ashre, 'happy is', and prob. also to Arab.
yasara, 'was gentle, easy, happy'. Cp. the PN.
Felix, fr. L. felix, 'happy'.

## asherah
asherah, п., a Canaanitish and Phoenician god-
ess; a sacred tree or pole. — Heb. ushera*, of
uncertain origin.

## Ashkenaz
Ashkenaz, п., the eldest son of Gomer (Gen.
10:3); also name of a people mentioned in
Jeremiah (51:27); in the Middle Ages applied to
Germany. — Heb. Ashkenaz. Cp. Euxine.

## Ashkenazun
Ashkenazun, n. pi., the Jews of Germany, central
and northern Europe. —- Heb. Ashkenazztm,
pi. formed fr. Ashkenaz. See prec. word.

## ashlar
ashlar,п., l)asquaredbuildingstone; 2)masonry
of squared stones. — ME. ascheler, fr. OF. ais-
selier, fr. L. axillaris, fr. axis, 'board, plank', a
collateral form of assis, of s.m., which is rel. to
asser, 'pole, stake, post'. Axis, 'axle', is not rel. to
axis in the above sense. Cp. as, п., atelier. For
the ending see suff. -ar.
Derivatives: ashlar-ed, adj., ashlar-ing, n.

## ashore
ashore, adv. — Formed fr. a- 'on', and shore.

## ashrafl
ashrafl, п., name of various gold coins, esp. a
gold coin in Persia. — Pers., fr. Arab.
dshraf, lit. 'noble ones', pi. of shartf, 'noble',
fr. shdrafa, 'he was exalted, he was noble'.
See shereef and cp. words there referred to.

## ashrama
ashrama, п., hermitage (Hinduism). — OI. aird-
mah, fr. adnominal pref. a- and sramaft, 'effort,
toil, fatigue', whence iramyali, 'he becomes
tired', which is rel. to OI. klAmyati, klamati, 'he
slackens, languishes' and cogn. with OSlav.
kromiti, 'to tame', chromu, 'lame'.

## Ashtoreth
Ashtoreth, п., a Canaanitish goddess, identical
with Astarte. — Heb. 'Ashttreth, rel. to Ugar.
'sir/, Akkad. Ishtar. Cp. Ishtar, Astarte,
Aphrodite, and the first element in Atargatis. Cp. also
April.

## Ashura
Ashura, п., name of the Mohammedan fast
observed on the 10th day of the month Muhar-
ram. — Arab. 'Ashura', lit. 'the tenth', Arabized
fr. Heb. 'aior, 'the tenth day', which is rel. to
'tUard* (fern.), 'ten'. The Arabic word shows
Aramaic influence; the ending -a represents the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:80 COLUMN:3 -->
Aramaic article. See asor.

## Asia
Asia, n. — L. Asia, fr. Gk. Άοίδ, 'Asia', fr.
Akkad. asu, 'to go out; to rise' (said of the sun),
which is rel. to Heb. yatzA', 'went out; rose'
(said of the sun), Aram. y*'S, 'went forth; burst
forth, bloomed', Ethiop. wadaa, 'went out',
Arab, wadu'a, 'was or became beautiful, neat
or clean'. Accordingly Asia orig. denoted 'the
Region of the Rising Sun', in contradistinction
to Europe, which orig. meant 'the Region of the
Setting Sun' (see Europe). Cp. hamotzl. Cp. also
wudu.

## Asian
Asian, adj. and n. — L. Asianus, fr. Gk. Άσιδνός,
fr. ΆσΙά. See prec. word and cp. next word.
Derivatives: Aslan-ic, adj., Asian-ism, n.

## Asiatic
Asiatic, adj. and n.— L. Asiaticus, fr. Gk.
'Ασιατικός, fr. 'Ante, 'Asia'. See Asia and cp. prec.
word.
Derivatives: Asiatic-al-ly, adv., Asiatic-Ism, п.,
Asialic-ize, tr. v.

## aside
aside, adv., prep., and n. — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and side.

## Asllidae
Asllidae, n. pi., a family of flies (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. L. asllus. See next word and -Idae.

## Asflus
Asflus, п., a genus of flies (zool.) — L. asllus,
'gadfly, horsefly', prob. of Etruscan origin. See
A.Ernout in Bulletin de la societe de linguisti-
que, 30, 1 io*.

## Asimina
Asimina, п., a genus of trees, the North American
papaw (bot.) — ModL., fr. Can. F. assimlnier,
'papaw tree', fr. Illinois Indian rassimina.

## asinego
asinego, п., a little ass, a fool. — Sp. asnico,
dimin. of asno, 'an ass', fr. L. asinus, of s.m. See
next word.

## asinine
asinine, adj., like an ass; stupid. — L. asininus,
fr. asinus, 'ass, dolt, blockhead'. See am and
cp. words there referred to. For the ending see
suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## -asis
-asis, suff. used in medical terminology to
denote a state or condition. — Medical L.
-asis, fr. Gk. -ασις, formed from the aorist
of verbs into -άω, -ω (inf. -άειν, -S\i). Cp. -esis,
-osis, -iasis.

## ask
ask, tr. and intr. v. — ME. asken, axien, fr. OE.
Sscian, acsian, rel. to OS. iscon, Dan. seske,
Swed. aska, OFris. askia, MDu. eiscen, Du.
eisen, 'to ask, demand', OHG. eiscon, heiscon,
'to ask (a question)', MHG. eischen, heischen,
G. heischen, 'to ask, demand', and cogn. with
OI. icchdli (for *is-ske-ti), 'seeks, desires', Arm.
aic (for *ais-sku-\ 'investigation', OSlav. iskati,
'to seek', Lith. ieSkau, ieSkoti, 4o seek', OI.
ismah, 'spring, god of love', prob. also with
Gk. Ιμερος (for* Ισμερος), 'longing, yearning,
desire'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*aish-, 'to wish, desire, seek'.
Derivatives: ask-er, п., ask-ing, п., ask-ing-ly,
adv.

## ask
ask, п., water newt. — ME. aske, corruption of
OE. apexe, which is rel. to OS. egithassa, MDu.
haghedisse, Du. hagedis, OHG. egidehsa, MHG.
egedehse, eidehse, G. Eidechse. The first element
of these words is prob. cogn. with L. unguis,
'serpent, snake', Gk. ϊχις, 'viper'; see anguine
and cp. echidna. The second element is prob.
rel. to MHG. dense, 'spindle'. For sense
development cp. Russ. weretenica, 'lizard', fr. wereleno,
'spindle'. Cp. asker.

## askance
askance, adv. — ME. askaunce; of uncertain
origin.

## askari
askari, п., a native soldier of East Africa. —
Arab. 'aSkart, 'a soldier', fr. 'dskar, "an army',
fr. Late Gk. έξέρκητον, ultim. fr. L. exer-
citus, 'army', fr. exercire, 'to train, drill'. See
exercise and cp. lascar.

## uskew
uskew, adv. — Formed fr. n-, 'on', and skew.

## usker
usker, п., a newt (dial.) — Formed fr. ask, 'newt',
with suff. -er.

## askos
askos, п., a vase resembling a wine skin {Greek
antiq.) — Gk. ασκός, 'leather bag, wine skin'.
See ascus.

## aslant
aslant, adv. — Formed fr. n- 'on', and slant.

## asleep
asleep, adv. and pred. adj. — Formed fr. a-,
'on', and sleep.

## aslope
aslope, adv. and pred. adj. — Formed fr. a-,
'on', and slope.

## Asmodeus
Asmodeus, п., an evil spirit, the prince of the
demons. — L. Asmodaeus, fr. Gk. Άσμοϊαΐος,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:81 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ASOCIAL | 54 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:81 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. Talmudic Heb. Ashm'ddy, fr. Avestic Aesh-
ma-dseva, lit. 'Aeshma, the deceitful'.

## asocial
asocial, adj., not social. — A hybrid coined fr.
Gk. ά-, 'not' (see priv. pref. a-), and social, a
word of Latin origin.

## asoumtic
asoumtic, adj., incorporeal. — Formed with stiff.
-ic fr. L. asdmalus, fr. Gk. ασώματος,
'disembodied, incorporeal', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and Gk. σώμα, 'body'. See somatic.

## asomatous
asomatous, adj., incorporeal. — Gk. ασώματος.
See prec. word. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see -ous.

## asor
asor, п., a Hebrew ten-stringed instrument. —
Heb. 'asor, fr. 'Her (masc.), 'άίάτά" (fern.),
'ten', which is" rel. to Aram, 'dsdr (masc.), 'asrd
(fem.), Ugar. 'shr (masc), 'shrh (fern.), Arab.
'ashr (masc.), 'ashara* (fem.), Ethiop. 'ashru
(masc.), 'ashartu (fem.), Akkad. eshri (masc),
eshertu, esherit (fem.), 'ten'. (The masc.
forms are used with fem. nouns, the fem.
ones with masc. nouns.) In the Sem.
languages the orig. meaning of 'ten' seems to
have been 'gathering, collection, union'. Cp.
Arab, 'dshara, 'he formed a community', 'a-
shtra*, 'a tribe', 'ashtr, 'kinsman', md'shar, 'a
group of men, assembly'. Cp. Ashura.

## asp
asp, п., a snake of the viper family. — OF. aspe,
fr. L. aspidem, ace. of aspis, 'asp', fr. Gk. ασπίς,
gen. άσπίδος, of s.m., which prob. derives fr.
Heb. Izepha', 'basilisk'.
Derivative: asp-ish, adj.

## asp
asp, n. — Poetic form of aspen.
Derivative: asp-en, adj.

## asparagus
asparagus, n. — L., fr. Gk. άσπάραγος, Att
άσφάραγος, 'asparagus,' which prob. means lit.
'a sprout', and is rel. to σπαργδν, 'to swell, be
ripe', fr. I.-E. base *sper(e)g, *spher(e)g-, 'to
sprout, swell, burst', whence also L. spargere,
'to scatter'. See sparse and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also asperges and sparrow-
grass.

## Aspasin
Aspasin, fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk. 'Ασπασία, fem.
of άσπάσιος, 'welcome', which is rel. to άσπά-
ζεσθαι, 'to welcome'; of uncertain origin.

## aspect
aspect, n. — L. aspecius, 'glance, sight,
appearance, countenance', fr. aspecius, pp. of aspicere,
'to look at', fr. ad- and specere, sphere 'to look
at'. See species and cp. coaspectus, iaspect,
introspect, perspective, prospect, respect,
retrospect, suspect.

## aspect
aspect, tr. v. — L. aspect are, free;, formed fr.
aspectus, pp. of aspicere. See aspect, n.

## aspen
aspen, п., a variety of poplar. — Orig. an adj.
formed with suff. -en (cp. ashen, oaken} fr. asp,
'the aspen', fr. ME. aspe, asp, fr. OE. sespe, sesp,
xps, 'aspen, white poplar', which is rel. to ON.
osp, Dan., Swed. asp, MLG., MDu. espe, Du.
esp, OHG. aspa, MHG. aspe, G. Espe,ana cogn.
with Lett, apsa, OPruss. abse, Lith. apuse, Russ.
oslna (for *opsina).

## asperate
asperate, tr. v., to make rough. — L. asperatus,
pp. ofasperdre. See asperity and verbal suff. -ate.

## asperges
asperges, п., the ceremony of sprinkling (R.C.Ch.)
— L. asperges, second person sing. fut. indie,
of aspergere, 'to sprinkle upon'; see asperse. The
ceremony is called asperges from the opening
words of the Vulgate, Ps. 51:9 Asperges me
hyssopo, rendering Heb. fhau'inl bhfizdbh
('purge me with hyssop').

## nspergillum
nspergillum, п., a small brush for sprinkling
(R.CCh.)— ML., 'asmall brush for sprinkling',
a diminutive formed fr. L. aspergere. See prec.
word.

## Aspergillus
Aspergillus, п., a genus of fungi (hot.) — ModL.,
a diminutive formed fr. L. aspergere. See
asperges.

## asperifoliate
asperifoliate, also asperifolious, adj.,having rough
leaves. — Compounded of L. caper, 'rough',
and folium, 'leaf. See next word and foliate.

## asperity
asperity, п., roughness. — F. asperile, fr. L. as-
peritdlem, асе. of asperitds, 'unevenness,
roughness', fr. asper, 'uneven, rough', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. Asperugo, Asperula, Aspredo,
exasperate. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## asperse
asperse, tr. v., 1) to besprinkle (now rare); 2) to
slander. — L. aspersus, pp. of aspergere, 'to
sprinkle upon', fr. ad- and spargere,' to scatter,
sprinkle'. See sparse and cp. asperges, disperse.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:81 COLUMN:2 -->
For the change of Latin ά (in spargere) to l (in
a-spergere) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: aspers-ed, adj., aspers-er, п., aspers-
ive, adj., aspers-ive-ly, adv.

## aspersion
aspersion, n. — L. aspersio, gen. -onis, fr.
aspersus, pp. of aspergere. See prec. word and -Ion.
А$пзгикэ. п.. a genus of plants of the borage
family (hot.) — L. asperugo, 'a plant with
prickly leaves', fr. asper, 'rough'. See asperity.

## Asperula
Asperula, n. a genus of plants of the madder
family (bot.) — ModL., a diminutive formed fr.
L. asper, 'rough'. See asperity.

## asphalt also asphaltum
asphalt also asphaltum, n. — F. asphalte, fr. Late
L. asphaltus, fr. Gk. άσφαλτος, which is of
uncertain, possibly Sem., origin. See Heinrich
Lewy, Die semitischen Fremdw6rter im Grie-
chischen, Berlin, 1895, p.53.
Derivatives: asphalt, tr. v., asphall-ine, asphalt-
ic, adjs.

## asphodsl
asphodsl, n.— L. asphodelus, fr. Gk. άσφάδελος,
a foreign word of uncertain origin. Cp. daffodil,
which is a doublet of asphodel. '

## asphyxia
asphyxia, п.. suspended animation (meJ.) —
Medical L. fr. Gk. ασφυξία, lit. 'pulselessness',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and σφύξις, 'pulsation',
which is rel. to σφυγμάς, 'pulsation', σφύζειν
(for *σφύγ-ιειν), 'to beat, pulsate'. See sphyg-
mus and -in.

## usphyxiant
usphyxiant, adj., asphyxiating; п., an
asphyxiating agent. — See prec. word and -ant

## asphyxiate
asphyxiate, tr. v., to suffocate. — See asphyxia
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: asphyxial-ίοη, n.

## aspic
aspic, п., asp. — OF. (= F.) aspic, which is prob.
a blend of OF. aspe, 'asp* (see asp, 'snake'), and
OF. (= F.) basilic, 'basilisk', fr. L. basiliscus
(see basilisk), two names that are often
associated with each other.

## uspic
uspic, п., a savory meat jelly. — F., the same as
aspic, 'asp'; so called from the varied colors of
this jelly.

## Aspidistra
Aspidistra, п., a genus of plants of the lily-of-the-
valley family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'star shield',
fr. Gk. ασπίς, gen. άσπίδος, 'shield', and αστρον,
'star'. See next word and aster.

## aspidium
aspidium, п., the shield fern (boi.) — ModL., lit.
'little shield', fr. Gk. άσπίδιον, dimin. of ασπίς,
gen. άσπίδος, 'shield', which is of uncertain
origin.

## aspirant
aspirant, adj. — F., fr. L. aspiranlem, ace. of as-
pirdns, pres. part, of asplrare. See aspire and -ant

## aspirate
aspirate, n. — L. aspirutus, pp. of asplrare. See
aspire, and adj. suff. -ate.

## aspirate
aspirate, tr. v. — L. aspirutus, pp. of asplrare.
See aspirate, n.
Derivatives: aspirfit-ed, adj., aspiration (q.v.),
aspiral-or, п., aspirat-ory, adj.

## aspiration
aspiration, n. — L. aspiralio, gen. -onis, fr.
aspirutus, pp. of asplrare. See next word and
-ation.

## aspire
aspire, intr. v. — F. aspirer, fr. L. asplrare, 4o
breathe or blow upon; to aspire', fr. ad- and
spirare, 'to breathe'. See spirit and cp.
conspire, expire, inspire, respire.

## aspirin
aspirin, n. (pharm.) — A hybrid coined by H.
Dreser in Pfliiger's Archiv in 1899. The acetylo-
salicylic acid occurs in the flowers of the plant
Spiraea ulmaria. In order to distinguish from
this natural product the same substance gained
chemically, the word aspirin was formed by
Dreser from priv. pref. a-, the above mentioned
plant Spiraea, and chem. suff. -in. Hence aspirin
prop, means 'acetylo-salicylic acid which is
gained not from the Spiraea ulmaria (but in a
chemical way)'.

## Asplenium
Asplenium, п., a genus of ferns (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. asplenum, 'miltwort, spleenwort', fr. Gk.
ασπληνον, fr. ά- (see priv. pref. n-) and σπλήν,
'spleen'; see spleen. The plant was so called for
its healing qualities. The name ασπληνον lit.
means 'a remedy against (the diseases of) the
spleen'.

## Aspredo
Aspredo, п., a genus of catnshes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., fr. L. aspredo, 'roughness', fr. asper.
See asperity.

## asqulat
asqulat, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and squlat.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:81 COLUMN:3 -->

## ass
ass, n. — ME. asse, fr. OE. assa, fr. Olr. assan,
fr. L. asinus, 'ass, dolt, blockhead', a word
borrowed from a language spoken in the South of
Asia Minor, whence also Gk. ίνρς (for orig.
Osonos), 'ass', Arm. Ish (collective pi. ishan-k'),
of s.m. Cp. asinego, asinine, easel, onager.

## assagai
assagai, assegai, п., a hardwood spear. — Port.
azagaia, fr. Arab.-Berb. az-zaghdyah, fr. az-,
assimilated form of al-, 'the', and zaghiyah, 'a
spear'. Cp. lancegay.
Derivative: assagai, assegai, tr. v.

## assai
assai, adv., very (musical direction). — It., fr. L.
ad, 'to', and satis, 'enough'. See assets.

## assai
assai, п., the assai palm. — Port, assai, fr. Tupi
assahy.

## assaiL
assaiL, tr. v. — ME. assailen, fr. OF. asalir, as-
sailir (F. assailllr), fr. VL. assalire, fr. ad- and
L. satire, 'to leap, spring'. Cp. L. assilire, 'to
leap upon', and see salieut. Cp. also assault
Derivatives: assail-able, adj., assailant (q.v.),
assail-er, п., assail-ment, n.

## assailant
assailant, n. — F. assaillant, pres. part, of as-
saillir. See assail and -ant

## nssart
nssart, п., the act of grubbing up trees, bushes,
etc (Oid English law) — Formed—with change
of prefix—fr. OF. (= F.) essart, 'the grubbing
up of trees', fr. VL. exsarlum, fr. L. ex, 'out of
(see 1st ex-), and the stem of sarire (aiso spelled
sarrire), 'to gruh, hoe', whence also sarculum,
(for *sart-lom), 'hoe'; cogn. with OI. s[nt,
'sickle', srtiib, 'elephant goad'. L. sarire is rel.
to sarpere, 'to cut off, lop, trim*. See sarmentum.

## assart
assart, tr. v. — OF. essarter, 'to grub up trees',
fr. essart. See assart, n.

## assassin
assassin, п., murderer. — F., fr. It. assassino, fr.
Arab, hashshashtn, 'drinkers of hashish', fr.
hashish, 'hemp'; see hashish. The first assassins
were the fanatic followers of the Shaykh-ul-
Jabal (the Old Man of the Mountains), who
committed their murders under the intoxication
of hashish. The plural suff. -in in assassin was
mistaken for part of the word. Cp. Bedouin.
Derivatives: assassin-ate, tr. v.,
assassination, n.

## assault
assault, n. — ME. asaut, fr. OF. asaul (F. as-
saut), fr. VL. *assaltus, fr. ad- and L. salius,
'a leap', fr. satire, 'to leap, spring'. See salient
and cp. assaiL

## assault
assault, tr. v. — OF. assauter, fr. VL. assaltdre,
fr. ad- and L. saltare, freq. of satire. See as-
asult,n.
Derivative: assault-er, n.

## assay
assay, n. — ME., fr. OF. assai, which was
formed—with change of prefix—from OF. essai,
essay (F. essai), fr. L. exagium, 'a weighing',
fr. exigere, 'to weigh, measure, examine', lit.
4o drive out', fr. 1st ex- and agere, 4o drive'.
Cp. It. saggio (with the loss of the initial
syllable) and the verb assaggiare (with the same
change of pref. as in English). See agent, adj.,
and cp. essay. Cp. also exigent, exiguous.

## assay
assay, tr. v. — ME. assayen, fr. OF. assayer, a
collateral form of essaier, essayer, fr. assai,
resp. essai, essay. See assay, n.
Derivatives: assay-able, adj., assay-er, п.,
assaying, n.

## assecuration
assecuration, п., insurance (law). — ML. asse-
curdtid, gen. -dnis, fr. nd- and L. securus, 'free
from care, careless'. See secure.

## assecurator
assecurator, n. (law). — See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.

## assemblage
assemblage, n. — F. assemblage, 'gathering,
assemblage', fr. assembler. See next word and
-age.

## assemble
assemble, tr. and intr. v. — ME. assemble», fr.
OF. (= F.) assembler, 'to gather, assemble', fr.
L. assimulare, 'to make like, think like', in later
sense 'to gather at the same time', fr. nd- and
simulure, 'to make like, imitate', fr. simul,
'together'. See simulate.
Derivative: assembl-er, n.

## assembly
assembly, n. — ME. assemblee, fr. OF. assemblee
(F. assemblee), prop. fem. pp. of assembler, 'to
assemble', used as a noun. See prec. word and
-y (representing OF. -e, -ее).

## assent
assent, intr. v. — ME. assenten, fr. OF. asenter,
assemer, fr. L. assentari, 'to agree with', freq.
formed fr. asseniire, assenliri, fr.ad- and sentire.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:82 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 55 | -ASTER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:82 COLUMN:1 -->
'to feel'. See sense and cp. consent, dissent,
resent.
Derivatives: assentation (q.v.), assent-er, п.,
assent-ive, adj., assent-ive-ness, n.

## assent
assent, n. — ME., fr. OF., back formation fr. as-
senter. See prec. word.'

## nssentatkm
nssentatkm, n. — L. assentatid, gen. -dnis, 'a
flattering assent', fr. assentatus, pp. of assen-
tari. See assent, v., and -anon.

## assentient
assentient, adj., assenting; п., one who assents. —
L. assentiins, gen. -enlis, pres. part, of assentire.
See assent, v., and -ent.

## assert
assert, tr. v. — L. assertus, pp. of asserere, 4o
claim, maintain, affirm', lit. 'to join to oneself',
fr. ad- and serere, 'to join together, connect,
combine'. See series and cp. dissert, insert.
Derivatives: assert-er, п., assertion (q.v.),
assertive, adj., assert-ive-ly, adv., assert-ive-ness, n.

## assertion
assertion, n. — L. assertio, gen. -dnis, fr. assertus,
pp. of asserere. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: assertion-al, adj.

## assertory
assertory, adj. — L. assertdrius, 'pertaining to an
assertion, assertive', fr. assertus, pp. of asserere.
See assert and adj. suff. -ory.
Derivatives: assertori-al, adj., assertori-al-ly,
adv.

## assess
assess, tr. v., to evaluate for taxation. — ME.
assessen, fr. OF. assesser, fr. Late L. assessare,
freq. formed fr. L. assessus, pp. of assidere, 'to
sit by or near; to assist in office', fr. ad- and
sedire, 'to sit'. See sedentary and cp. assiduous,
assize. Cp. also cess, 'tax', which is an aphetic
form of assess.
Derivatives: assess-able, adj., assess-ee, п., as-
sess-ment, п., assessor (q.v.)

## assessor
assessor, h. — ME. assessour, fr. OF. assessour
(F. assesseur), fr. L. assessorem, ace. of assessor,
lit. 'a sitter by', fr. assessus, pp. of assidere. See
prec. word and agential suff. -or.
Derivative: assessor-ial, adj.

## assets
assets, n. — Orig. a singular noun fr. OF. asez
(pronounced asets) (whence F. assez), 'enough',
fr. VL. *ad-satis, 'in sufficiency',fr. L. ad, 'to' (see
ad-), and satis, 'enough'. Cp. OProvenc. assatz,
'enough', It. assai, 'much', which also derive fr.
VL. *ad-satis, and see satis, sad.

## asseverate
asseverate, tr. v., to affirm. — L. asseveratus, pp.
of asseverare, 'to act with earnestness, to assert
strongly' (said of speech), fr. ad- and severus,
'serious, grave, strict, austere'. See severe and
cp. persevere.
Derivatives: asseverat-ive, adj., asseverat-ive-ly,
adv., assever-at-ory, adj.

## asseveration
asseveration, п., affirmation. — L. assevlratio,
gen. -dnis, 'vehement assertion', fr. asseveratus,
pp. of asseverare. See prec. word and -ion.

## assibilate
assibilate, tr. v., to make sibilant. — L. assibi-
latus, pp. of assibilare, fr. ad- and sibilare, 'to
hiss'. See sibilant.
Derivative: assibilat-ion, n.

## assiduity
assiduity, n. — L. assiduitas, gen. -talis,
'continual presence', fr. assiduus. See next word
and -ity.

## assiduous
assiduous, adj., 1) constant in application; 2)
diligent. — L. assiduus, 'busy; incessant, continual,
constant', lit. 'sitting by (one's work)', fr. assi-
dire, 'to sit by', fr. ad- and sedire, 'to sit'. See
ad- and sedentary. For the change of Latin ё
(in sidere) to f (in as-sidere), see abstinent and
cp. words there referred to. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives:aroK/uou£-/y,adv., assiduous-ness, n.

## assiento
assiento, asiento, п., contract or convention. —
Sp. asiento, fr. asentar, 'to adjust, settle,
establish', lit. 'to place on a chair', formed fr. a
(fr. L. ad, 'to'), and senior, 'to place on a chair,
set, set up, establish', fr. L. sedens, gen. -enlis,
pres. part, of sedire, 'to sil'. See ad- and
sedentary.

## assign
assign, tr. v. — ME. assignen, fr. OF. augner, as-
signer, fr. L. assignure, 'to assign, allot,
distribute', lit. 'to mark out', fr. ad- and signare, 'to
mark', fr. signum, 'mark, token, sign'. See slga,
п., and cp. design.
Derivatives: assign-able, adj., assignabl-y, adv.

## assign
assign, п., one assigned. — F. assigne, pp. of as-
signer. See prec. word and cp. amignee.

## assignat
assignat, п., paper money issued by the French

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:82 COLUMN:2 -->
revolutionary government (1789-96). — F., fr. L.
assignatum, neut. pp. of assignore. See a.ssigu, v.

## assignation
assignation, п., appointment to meet; assignment.
— ME. assignacion, fr. OF. assignacion (F.
assignation), fr. L. assignutionem, ace. of assig-
natid, 'allotment', fr. assignatus, pp. of
assignure. See assign, v., and -ntion.

## assignee
assignee, п., an assign. — F. assigne, pp. of as-
signer, fr. L. assigndre. See assign, v., and cp.
assign, n.

## assignment
assignment, n. — ME. assignement, fr. OF.
assignment, fr. assigner. See assign, v., and -ment.

## assimilate
assimilate, tr. and intr. v. — L. assimilStus, pp.
of assimilare, 'to make like, liken', fr. ad- and
similare, 'to make similar to', fr. similis, 'like,
resembling'. See similar and verbal suff. -ate and
cp. assemble.
Derivatives: assimilation (q.v.), assimilat-ive,
adj., assimilat-or, п., assimilat-ory, adj.

## assimilation
assimilation, n. — L. assimilatio, gen. assimila-
tionis, 'likeness, similarity', fr. assimilatus, pp.
of assimilare. See assimilate and -ion.

## assist
assist, tr. and intr. v. — F. assister, 'to stand by,
help, assist', fr. L. assistere, 4o stand by', fr. ad-
and sistere, 'to cause to stand, put, place; to
stand still, stand',.from the reduplicated base of
stare, 'to stand'. Cp. OI. tisthati, Avestic hish-
taiti, 'stands', and Gk. Ιστημι, Ί cause to stand,
place; I stand', which stands for *σί-σττ]μι,
and see state. Cp. also consist, desist, exist,
insist, persist, resist, subsist.

## assistance
assistance, n. — F., fr. assistant. See next word
and -ce.

## assistant
assistant, adj. and n. — F. assistant, adj. and п.,
prop. pres. part, of assister. See assist and -ant.

## assize
assize, n. — ME. assise, fr. OF. asise, 'session'
(whence F. assises, 'the assizes'), prop. fem.
pp. of asseoir, 'to cause to sit, to set', fr. L.
assidere, 'to sit by'. See assess and cp. size.
Derivatives: assize, tr. v., assize-ment, п.,
assizer, n.

## associable
associable, adj. —■ F., fr. associer, fr. L. associare.
See next word and -able.
Derivatives: associabil-ity, п., associable-ness,n.

## associate
associate, tr. and intr. v. — L. associatus, pp. of
associare, 'to join to, unite with', fr. ad- and
sociare, 'to join together, associate', fr. socius,
'companion'. See socinble and verbal suff. -ate
and cp. consociate, dissoemte.
Derivatives: associal-ed, adj., association,
associative (qq.v.)

## associate
associate, adj. — L. associatus, pp. of associare.
See prec. word.
Derivative: associate, n.

## association
association, n. — F., fr. ML. associalidnem, ace.
of associatio, fr. L. associatus, pp. of associare.
See associate, v., and -ion, and cp. consociation,
dissociation. Derivative: association-al, adj.

## associative
associative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive from
the verb associate; first used by Coleridge.
Derivatives: associative-ly, adv., associative-
ness, n.

## assoil
assoil, tr. v., to absolve (archaic). — ME. assoi-
len, fr. OF. assoile, pres. subjunctive oiassoldre
(F. absoudre), 4o absolve'. See absolve, which
is the doublet of assoil.
Derivative: assoil-ment, n.

## assoilzie
assoilzie, tr. v., to acquit {Scot. law). — Formed
fr. prec. word.

## assonance
assonance, n. — F., fr. assonant. See next word
and -ce and cp. sonance and words there
referred to.

## assonant
assonant, adj. — F., fr. L. assonantem, ace. of as-
sonans, pres. part, of assonare, 'to sound to,
respond to'.fr. ad- and sondre, 'to sound'. See sound,
'voice', and cp. sonant and words there referred to.

## assonate
assonate, intr. v. — L. assondtus, pp. of assonare.
See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## assort
assort, tr. and intr. v. — OF. assorter, 4o assort,
match', fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and sorte, 'sort, kind,
species'. See sort, v. and n. The change of
conjugation in F. assortir, of s.m., is due to the
influence of the verb sorlir, 'to go out'.
Derivatives: assort-ative, adj., assort-ed, adj.,
assort-er, п., assort-ive, adj., assort-ment, n.

## assuage
assuage, tr. v., to mitigate; to soothe. — ME.
asuagen, fr. OF. asuager, assouager, assouagier,
fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and L. suavis, 'sweet'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:82 COLUMN:3 -->
'sweet and cp. suave.
Derivatives ·% assuag-er, п., assuagement (q.v.)

## assuagement
assuagement, n. — OF. assouagement, fr.
assouager. See assuage and -ment.

## assuetude
assuetude, п., custom, habit (med.) — L. assui-
tudo, fr. assuetus, pp. of assuescere, 4o
accustom', fr. ad- and suescere, 'to become used or
accustomed', fr. I.-E. base *swedh-, 4o make
one's own'. See custom and cp. consuetude. For
the ending see suff. -fade.

## assume
assume, tr. and intr. v. — L. assumere, 'to take
to (oneself), take up, adopt, usurp', fr. ad- and
sumere, 'to take'; which is compounded of sub-,
'under', and emere, 'to take'. See exempt and
cp. consume, presume, resume, subsume. Cp. also
redeem.
Derivatives: assum-ed, adj., assum-ed-ly, adv.,
assum-ing, adj., assum-ing-ly, adv.

## assumption
assumption, n. — L. assumptio, gen. -dnis, 'a
taking, receiving', fr. assumptus, pp. of assumere.
See prec. word and -ion and cp sumption and
words there referred to.

## assumptive
assumptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
assumptus, pp. of assumere. See assume and cp.
prec. word.

## assurance
assurance, n. — OF. aseiirance (F. assurance),
fr. aseurer. See assure and -ance.

## assure
assure, tr. v. — OF. aseurer (F. assurer), fr. Late
L. assicurdre, fr. ad- and L. sicurus, 'safe'. See
secure, sure.
Derivatives: assur-ed, adj., assur-ed-ly, adv.,
assur-ed-ness, п., assur-er, п., assur-ing, adj., as-
sur-ing-ly, adv.

## assurgent
assurgent, adj., rising. — L. assurgins, gen. -enlis,
pres. part, of assurgere, 'to rise up', fr. ad- and
surgere, 'to rise'. See sarge and cp. insurgent.

## Assyria
Assyria, n. — L. Assyria, fr. Gk. Άσσυρϋ (short
for Άσσυρίϊ γη, 'the Assyrian land'), fem. of
Άσσύριος, 'pertaining to Assyria', fr. Akkad.
Ashshur. Cp. Heb. Ashshar, Gen. 10:10. Cp.
also Syria.
Derivatives: Assyri-an, adj. and п., Assyri-an-
ize, v.

## Assyriology
Assyriology, п., the study of the history and
language of Assyria. — Compounded of As-
syrin and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: Assyriolog-ic-al, adj., Assyriolog-
ist, n.

## -ast
-ast, agential suff., identical in meaning to -ist. —
F. -aste, fr. L. -asm, fr. Gk. -αοτής, which stands
for -ασ-τής and is formed fr. -ασ- (the ending
of the stem of the verbs in -άζειν) and agential
suff. -τής. Ср. -ist.

## Astarte
Astarte, п., a Phoenician goddess, identical with
Greek Aphrodite. — L., fr. Gk. Άστάρτη, fr.
Heb.-Phoen. 'Ashtoreth. See Ashtoreth and cp.
Aphrodite.

## astatic
astatic, adj. (electricity) — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. άστατος, 'not steadfast', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and στατός, 'standing', verbal adj. of
ίστημι (for *σί-στημι), Ί cause to stand, place;
I stand'. See static.

## astatine
astatine, п., name of a radioactive element (chem.)
— Formed with chem. suff. -ine, fr. Gk.
£στατος, 'unstable'. See prec. word.

## asteism
asteism, n„ genteel irony. — Gk. άστεϊσμός,
'wit, witticism', fr. αστείος, 'of the town*, fr.
So-ro, 'town, city', esp. 'the city of Athens', fr.
orig. Γάστυ [ср. Arcadian Γασστυοχω (gen. of
Γασστύοχος), 'protecting the city (of Athens)',
epithet of Pallas Athene], which is cogn. with
OI. vastu, 'dwelling place', vastu, vastu, 'seat,
place, thing', Toch. A wast, 'house', fr. I.-E.
base *wes-, 'to dwell'. See was and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also the first element in
Astyanax. For the ending see suff. -ism.

## Aster
Aster, п., a genus of plants of the thistle family
(bol.) — L. aster, 'star', fr. Gk. αστήρ; so called
from the radiate heads of its flowers .-See star
and cp. asterisk, Astraea, astrology,
astronomy, disaster.

## -aster
-aster, combining form meaning 'star, starlike',
as in Clypeasler. — See prec. word.

## -aster
-aster, suff. expressing incomplete resemblance,
usually of dimin. and depreciative force. — L.
-aster, fr. Gk. -αστήρ, a suff. orig. forming

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:83 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ASTERIA | 56 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:83 COLUMN:1 -->
nouns from verbs ending in -άζειν, later
generalized as a pejorative stiff. Cp. πατραστήρ, 'he
who plays the father', fr. πατήρ, 'father'. The
Gk. suff. -αστήρ was adopted by the Latin,
whence, in the form -astre, -aire, it came into
the Old French, resp. the French. Cp. the words
medicaster, oleaster, pinaster, poetaster. Cp. also
-ster.

## asteria
asteria, п., a gem reflecting a six-rayed light
(Greek anliq.) — L., fr. Gk. αστερία, 'a
precious stone', prop. fern, of άστέριος, 'starred,
starry', used as anoun, fr. αστήρ, 'star'. See Aster.

## asterisk
asterisk, п., the figure of a star (the printing
mark *).—Late L. asteriscus, fr. Gk. αστερίσκος,
dimin. of αστήρ, 'star'. See Aster.

## usterism
usterism, n„ a system of stars, a constellation. —
Gk. αστερισμός, fr. αστήρ, 'star'. See Aster and
-ism.

## astern
astern, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and stern.

## asteroid
asteroid, adj., starlike. — Gk. αστεροειδής,
compounded of αστήρ, 'star', and -οειοής,
'like', fr. είδος,'form, shape'. See Aster and -oid.
Derivative: asteroid, n.

## Asteroidea
Asteroidea, п., a class of echinoderms, the starfish
(zool.) — ModL. See asteroid.

## asthenia
asthenia, п., weakness (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. άσ&ένεια, 'weakness', fr. ασθενής, 'weak',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and σθένος, 'strength'.
See sthenic and cp. sthenia.
■■sthenic, adj., weak (med.) — Gk. ασθενικός, fr.
ασθενής, 'weak'. See prec. word and -ic

## asthma
asthma, п., a chronic disorder characterized by
difficulty in breathing. — Gk. £σθμα, 'hard-
drawn breath', which prob. stands for *άνσθμα
and derives fr. I.-E. base *an-, 'to blow, breathe',
whence also άνεμος, 'wind', L. animus, 'breath
of air, air, breath'; see animus. See Frisk, GEW.,
I, pp. 161-62 s.v. άσθμα.

## asthmatic
asthmatic, adj. — L. aslhmaticus, fr. Gk.
ασθματικός, fr. άσθμα. See asthma and -atic.
Derivative: asthmatic-al-ly, adv.

## astigmatic
astigmatic, adj., pertaining to, or suffering from,
astigmatism (med. and optics). — See next word.

## astigmatism
astigmatism, п., defect of the eye that prevents
the rays of light from converging to a point on
the retina (med. and optics). — Coined by the
English mathematician and philosopher
William Whewell (1794-1866) in 1819 fr. priv. pref.
a- and Gk. στίγμα, gen. στίγματος, 'a prick,
puncture, mark'. See stigmatic and -ism.

## Astilbe
Astilbe, п., a genus of plants of the saxifrage
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'not shining', fr.
priv. pref. a- and στίλβειν, 'to shine'. See stilbite.

## astir
astir, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and stir.

## astomatous
astomatous, adj., having no mouth. — Formed
fr. priv. pref. n- and -stomatous.

## astonish
astonish, tr. v. — Obsol. astony, fr. ME. astonien,
astonen, which is formed with change of pref.
fr. estoner (whence F. etonner), fr. VL. *exto-
nare, lit. 'to strike with thunder', fr. 1st ex·
and L. tonare, 4o thunder'. See thunder and cp.
astound. The verb astonish was influenced in
form by English verbs ending in -ish, in which
this sufMs the equivalent of OF. and F. -iss,
and goes back ultimately to the Latin inchoative
suff. -iscere. Cp. admonish, distinguish,
extinguish.
Derivatives: astonish-ed-ly, adv., astonish-er, п.,
aslonish-ing, adj., astonish-ing-ly, adv., astonish-
ing-ness, n.

## astound
astound, tr. v. — ME. astoned, astouned, pp. of
astonien. See astonish.
Derivatives: astound-ing, adj., astound-ing-ly,
adv., astound-ment, n.

## astraddle
astraddle, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
straddle.

## Astraen
Astraen, п., the goddess of justice in Greek and
Roman mythology. — L., fr. Gk. Άστραίά, lit.
'starry', fern, of άστραΐος, fr. αστήρ, 'star'. See
Aster.

## astragal
astragal, п., a convex molding (archil.) — L.
astragalus, fr. Gk. αστράγαλος, 'one of the
vertebrae of the neck, anklebone, molding',
assimilated fr. *όστράγαλος, which is rel. to δστρα-
hov, 'oyster shell, potsherd', όστέον, 'bone', and
cogn. with L. os, 'bone'. See os.

## astragalus
astragalus, п., the ball of the ankle joint (anat.)
— L. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:83 COLUMN:2 -->

## Astragalus
Astragalus, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — L. See astragal.

## astrakhan
astrakhan, astrachan, п., the fur of still-born or
young lambs from Astrakhan. — From
Astrakhan in Russia. The name of the city lit.
means 'star of the caravanserai'. See astral and
khan, 'caravanserai'.

## astral
astral, adj., pertaining to the stars. — F., fr. L.
astralis, fr. astrum, 'star', fr. Gk. £στρον, which
is rel. to αστήρ, 'star'. See Aster and adj. suff.
-al.
Derivative: astral-ly, adv.

## astrapophobia
astrapophobia, п., morbid fear of lightning (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of Gk. αστραπή,
'lightning1, and -φοβία, 'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'.
Gk. αστραπή is a collateral form of άστεροπή,
στεροττή, and lit. means 'the eye of a star', fr.
αστέρος, αστήρ, 'star', and stem όπ-, 'to look'
(whence also όπή, 'an opening, hole', δψις,
'sight'). See Aster and optic For the second
element see -pbobin.

## astray
astray, adv. and adj. — For on stray, fr. pref. a-,
'on', and the noun stray.

## astrict
astrict, tr. v., 'to bind, constrict. — L. astrictus,
pp. of astringere, 'to draw tight, bind', fr. ad-
and stringere, 'to draw tight'. See stringent.
Derivatives: astriction (q.v.), astrict-ive, adj.

## astriction
astriction, n. — L. astrictio, gen. Snis, 'a drawing
tight', fr. astrictus, pp. of astringere. See prec
word and -Ion.

## Astrid
Astrid, a fem. PN. — A Norse name rel. to
OHG. Ansitruda, which is compounded of ansi,
'god', and trut, drut (whence MHG. trut, G.
traut), 'beloved, dear'. For the first element cp.
Ansehn, for the second see true and cp. the
second element in Ermentrud and in Gertrude.

## astride
astride, adv. and prep. — Formed fr. n-, 'on', and
stride.

## astriage
astriage, tr. v., to bind, constrict. — L.
astringere, 'to draw tight'. See astrict.

## astriagency
astriagency, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -cy. Cp. stringency.

## astringent
astringent, adj., that which contracts, severe. —
L. astringlns, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
astringere, 'to draw close, tighten, contract'. See
astriage and -ent.

## astro-
astro-, before a vowel astr-, combining form
meaning 'star'. — Gk. άστρο-, άστρ-, fr. αστρον,
'star', which is rel. to αστήρ, 'star'. See Aster.

## astrocyte
astrocyte, п., a star-shaped cell (anat.) —
Compounded of astro- and Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow
vessel'. See -cyte.

## astrography
astrography, п., the mapping of the stars. — Lit.
'description of the stars', fr. astro- and Gk.
-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivative: astrograph-ic, adj.

## astrolabe
astrolabe, п., an obsolete astronomical
instrument. — ME., fr. OF. aslrelabe, fr. ML. astro-
labium, fr. Gk. άστρολάβον (scil. δργανον), lit.
'startaking (instrument)', fr. αστρον, 'star', and
the stem of λαμβάνειν, 'to take'. See astro-
and lemma.

## astrologer
astrologer, n. — See astrology and agential suff
-er.

## astrologic
astrologic, astrological, adj. — Gk. αστρολογικός,
fr. αστρολογία. See astrology and -ic, resp.
also -aL

## astrology
astrology, n. — F. astrologie, fr. L. astrologia,
fr. Gk. αστρολογία, 'astronomy', later
'astrology', fr. αστρολόγος, 'astronomer', later
'astrologer', which is compounded of £στρον, 'star',
and -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deais (with a certain topic)'.
See astro- and -logy.

## astrometer
astrometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
brightness of stars. — Compounded of astro-
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## astronant
astronant, п., one who flies through space; one
concerned with space flight. — Compounded
of astro- and Gk. ναύτης, 'sailor, seaman'. See
nautical and cp. cosmoannt.

## astronautics
astronautics, п., the science of space flight. —
Compounded of astro- and nautics. Cp. prec.
word. Cp. also cosmonautics.

## astronomer
astronomer, n. — See astronomy and agential suff.
-er.

## astronomic
astronomic, astronomical, adj.— F. astronomique,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:83 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. L. aslronomicus, fr. Gk. αστρονομικός, fr.
αστρονομία. See next word and -ic, resp. also
-aL
Derivative: aslronomical-y, adv.

## astronomy
astronomy, n. — OF. astronomic, fr. L. astro-
nomia, fr. Gk. αστρονομία, 'astronomy', fr.
αστρονόμος, 'an astronomer', lit. 'star-arranger',
fr. ϊστρον, 'star', and -νόμος, 'arranger', which
is rel. to νέμειν, 'to deal out, distribute'. See
Nemesis and cp. nomo-.

## astrophysics
astrophysics, n. — Lit. 'astronomical physics'.
See astro- and physics.

## astucious
astucious, adj., astute. — F. astucieux (fem.
astucieuse), fr. astuce, 'astuteness', fr. L. astutia,
'dexterity; cunning, subtlety', fr. astutus. See
astute and -ous.

## Astar
Astar, п., the genus of the goshawks (zool.) —
ML., fr. L. acceptor, secondary form of accipiter,
'falcon' (see accipiter), whence also OSp. aztor.
Port, agor, It. astore, OProvenc. austor, OF.
ostoir, oslour, F. autour, 'goshawk'. Cp. ostreger.

## astate
astate, adj., shrewd, cunning, crafty. — L.
astutus, 'artful, drafty, cunning', fr. asms,
'cleverness, craft, cunning', which is of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: astute-ly, adv., astute-ness, n.

## Astyanax
Astyanax, п., the son of Hector and Andromache
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Άστυάναξ, lit.
'king of the city', fr. άστυ, 'city' (see asteism),
and αναξ, orig. *Γάναξ, 'chief, lord, master', a
. name given to him in reference to his father.
Cp. Andromache.

## asunder
asunder, adv. — OE. on sundran. See pref. a-, 'on',
and sander.

## asura
asura, п., a god, a good spirit; later an evil spirit
(Hindu mythol.) — OI. asurah, prob. rel. to OI.
asuh (for *nsu-), 'breath of life', fr. I.-E. base
•ая-, 'to blow, breathe', whence also OI. dni-ti,
άηα-ti, 'breathes', L. jmima, 'breath of air,
breath, soul, life', animus, 'soul, spirit, mind,
courage, wish, derive'. See animus and cp. ahura
and sura, 'spirit, demon'.

## Asrins
Asrins, n. pi., two Vedic gods, twin brothers, the
Dioscuri of Vedic mythology. — OI. Asvinau
(dual), lit. 'horse owners', fr. dsvah, 'horse',
which is rel. to Avestic aspa-, and cogn. with
Gk. ίππος, L. equus, 'horse'. See equine.

## asylum
asylum, n. — L. asylum, fr. Gk. ασϋλον, 'refuge,
sanctuary', prop. neut. of the adjective ασΰλος,
'free from plunder, inviolable*, used as a noun,
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and σόλη, σϋλον, 'the
right of seizure', whence σΟλϊν, 'to strip,
plunder'. Accordingly ασϋλον lit. means 'an
inviolable place'.

## asymmetric
asymmetric, asymmetrical, adj. — Formed with
suff. -ic, resp. also -al, fr. Gk. ασύμμετρος. See
asymmetry.
Derivative: asymmetrlcal-ly, adv.

## asymmetry
asymmetry, n. — Gk. ασυμμετρία,
'incommensurability', fr. ασύμμετρος, 'incommensurate;
disproportionate', fr. 4- (see priv. pref. a-) and
σύμμετρος, 'commensurable'. See symmetry and
cp. dissymmetry.

## asymptote
asymptote, п., a straight line continually
approaching but never meeting a curve (math.) —
Gk. ασύμπτωτος, 'not falling together', formed
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-), σύν, 'with' (see sym-,
syn-), and πτωτός, 'fallen', verbal adj. of πίπτειν,
'to fall', which stands for *πϊ-πτειν, fr. *pl-,
zero degree of I.-E. base *pet-, 'to fly, to fall'.
See fenther and cp. symptom and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: asymptol-ic, asymptot-ic-al, adjs.,
asymptot-ic-al-ly, adv.

## asyndetic
asyndetic, adj., using asyndeton. —See next word
and -ic.
Derivative: asyndetic-al-ly, adv.

## nsyndeton
nsyndeton, п., omission of conjunctions (rhel.) —
Gk. άσύνδετον, neut. of ασύνδετος,
'unconnected', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and σύνδετος,
'connected', verbal adj. of συνδεΐν, 'to bind
together, connect', fr. σύν, 'with' (see syn-), and
δεϊν, 'to bind'. See diadem and cp.
polysyndeton.

## at
at, prep. — OE. set, rel. to ΟΝ., OS., Goth, at,
OFris. et, at, OHG. az, and cogn. with L. ad,
'to, toward', Olr. ad-, W. add-, Phryg. aS-,
αβ-, 'to'. Cp. ad-.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:84 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 57 | ATLANTES -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:84 COLUMN:1 -->

## at-
at-, assimilated form of ad- before t.

## atabal
atabal, п., kettledrum. — Sp., fr. Arab, al-fabl,
'the drum', fr. af-, assimilated form of al-, 'the',
and tabl, 'drum'. Cp. timbal.

## atacamite
atacamite, п., a basic copper chloride (mineral.)
— Named after the province of Atacama, in
Chile. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## atajo
atajo, п., a drove of mules (Amer. Sp.) — Sp.,
'separation', fr. major, 'to separate', fr. a- (fr.
L. ad), 'to', and tajar, 'to cut', fr. VL. 'taliare,
'to cut'. See ad- and tailor.

## Atalanta
Atalanta, п., daughter of King Schoeneus, famous
for her swiftness in running (Greek mythol.) —
L., fr. Gk. 'Αταλάντη (fem. of ατάλαντος),
'having the same value (as a man)', from copul.
pref. ά- and τάλαντον, 'balance, weight, talent,
value'. Copul. pref. ά- stands for I.-E. "sm-, a
weak gradational form of I.-E. base *sem-,
'one, together'; see same. For the etymology
of τάλαντον see talent.

## ataiaya
ataiaya, п., a watchtower. — Sp., fr. Arab, at-
talayi', 'the sentries', fr. af-, assimilated form of
al-, 'the', and faldyi', pi. о!ш11'ал, 'sentinel', but
mistaken for a singular. See Dozy-Engelmann,
Glossaire des mots espagnols et portugais
derives de l'arabe, 2nd edition, pp. 209-10. Arab.
tail·a* derives fr. fata'a, 'he rose'.

## ataman
ataman, п., a Cossack commander. — Russ., fr.
Pol. hetman. See hetman.

## ntaraxin
ntaraxin, п., calmness, impassiveness. — ModL.,
fr. Gk. αταραξία, 'calmness, impassiveness,
calmness', lit. 'imperturbability', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and the stem of ταράσσειν, 'to trouble,
disturb', which is rel. to θράσσειν, of s.m., and
cogn. with ON. dregg, 'dreg'. See dreg.

## Atargatis
Atargatis, п., Syrian goddess of fertility. — Gk.
Άταργάτις, fr. Aram. 'Altar, 'Astarte', which
is rel. to Heb. 'Ashtoretk (see Ashtoreth), and
Palmyrene 'Aihe, name of a goddess (cp. Der-
ceto).

## ataunt
ataunt, adj., fully rigged (naut.) — F. autant, 'so
much, as much as possible', fr. earlier alianl,
which is compounded of the OF. pron. al,
'something else', and mm, 'so much'. The first
element derives fr. VL. *ale, which is shortened
fr. *alid, corresponding to L. aliud, neut. of alius,
'another'; see alias, else. The second element
comes fr. L. tantus, 'so great, so much', for
which see tantamount. Cp. taunt, 'very tall'.

## atavic
atavic, adj., of a remote ancestor. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. L. atavus. See next word.

## atavism
atavism, п., reversion to a remote ancestral type.
— Formed with suff. -ism fr. L. atavus, 'father
of a great-grandfather, ancestor', fr. pref. at-,
'beyond', and avus, 'grandfather'. See uncle and
cp. avuncular.

## atavistic
atavistic, adj., pertaining to atavism; tending to
atavism. — Formed with suff. -istic fr. L. atavus.
See prec. word. See atavism.
Derivative: atavistic-al-ly, adv.

## ataxia
ataxia, п., irregularity of bodily functions (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. αταξία, 'want of order',
fr. &- (see priv. pref. a-) and τάξις,
'arrangement, disposition, order', from the stem of·
τάσσειν, 'to arrange, put in order'. See tactic.

## ataxic
ataxic, adj. — Formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-lc.

## ate
ate, past tense of eat. — ME. ate, formed on the
analogy of brake, spake.

## Ate
Ate, п., the goddess of infatuation and evil in
Greek mythology. — Gk. "Ατη, fr. ίτη,
'infatuation, bane, ruin, mischief, which stands
for *ά5άτη and is rel. to άάω, Ί hurt, damage',
ά-άατος, 'unhurt, uninjured'; of uncertain
etymology.

## -ate
-ate, suff. forming participial adjectives (as in
sedate, ornate) and adjectives (as in chordate,
stellate). — L. Slut, pp. suff. of verbs of the first
conjugation.

## -ate
-ate, verbal suff. — L. pp. suff. -alus, hence
derivatively identical with adj. suff. -ate (q.v.) Its
original use consisted in the formation of verbs
from participial adjectives in -ate. So e.g. from
the participial adj. separate arose the verb to
separate.

## -ate
-ate, subst. suff. expressing office, dignity, rank,
honor. — L. -alus (gen. Stus), a suff. formed
from the participial suff. -atus. Cp. e.g. consulate

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:84 COLUMN:2 -->
and see adj. suff. -ate.

## -ate
-ate, subst. suff. forming names of salts from
acids whose names end in -ic, as nitrate, fr.
nitric acid (chem.) — L. Slum, neut. of pp. suff.
-atus. See adj. suff. -ate.

## atelectasis
atelectasis, п., incomplete expansion of the lungs
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of Gk.
ατελής, 'incomplete', and έκτασις, 'extension,
expansion'. The first element is formed fr. ά-
(see priv. pref. a-) and τέλος, 'end'; see teleo-.
For the second element see ectasis.

## atelier
atelier, п., workshop, studio. — F., fr. OF. aste-
lier, fr. astelle, 'shiver of wood', fr. Late L.
osteite, fr. L. astula, which is prob. a blend of
assula, 'shiver of wood' and has tula, 'a little
spear'. Assula is a dimin. of assis, 'board,plank';
see ashlar. Hastula is a dimin. of hasta, 'spear';
see hastate.

## Athanasius
Athanasius, masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. 'Αθανάσιος,
fr. αθάνατος, 'immortal'. See next word.

## athanasy
athanasy, п., immortality. — Gk. άθανα,σία, fr.
αθάνατος, 'immortal', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and θάνατος, 'death'. See thanato- and cp.
euthanasia. For the ending see -y (representing
Gk. -ία).

## athaaor
athaaor, п., the self feeding furnace of the
alchemists. — F., fr. Arab, at-tannir, 'the oven',
fr. at-, assimilated form of al-, 'the', and tann&r
'oven', borrowed fr. Heb. lannir, which is rel.
to Akkad. tinnuru, 'oven*.

## Atharvan
Atharvan, п., name of a fire priest, the eldest son
of Brahma (Vedic mythol) — OI. atharvan,
'fire priest', rel. to Avestic a&ravan-, 'fire priest',
atarsh, 'fire', atrya-, 'ashes', and cogn. with L.
dler, 'black, dark'. See atrabUiary.

## atheism
atheism, n. — F. athiisme, formed with suff.
-ism fr. Gk. ίίθεος, 'without god', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-) and θεός, 'god'. See theism.

## atheist
atheist, n. — F. atheiste. See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: atheist-ic, athest-ic-al, adjs., athe-
ist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## atheling
atheling, п., a noble, a prince. — OE. zdeling,
'a noble', fr. xdele, 'noble', which is rel. to
OFris. ethele, OS. edili, OHG. edili, MHG.
edele, G. edel, 'noble'. The orig. meaning of
these adjectives was 'noble by birth'. Cp. odal
and the first element in Albert, allerion, Alphon-
so, Atheistan, Audrey, edelweiss, Ethelbert,
Etheldred, Ethelinda, Ulrica.

## Atheistan
Atheistan, masc. PN. — OE. AEdelstane, lit.
'noble stone', fr. sedele, 'noble', and stan, 'stone'.
For the first element see atheling and cp. words
there referred to. For the second element see
stone.

## Athena
Athena, Athene, fem. PN., the goddess of
wisdom in Greek mythology, identified by the
Romans with Minerva. — Gk. Άθήνη, a pre-
Hellenic name of uncertain origin.

## Athenaeum
Athenaeum, п., the temple of Athena at Athens;
whence athenaeum 1) a Roman school of law;
2) a literary club. — L., fr. Gk. 'Αθήναιον, the
temple of the goddess Athene fr. Άθήνη. See
prec. word.

## atherine
atherine, п., any of the fishes of the family Ather-
inidae (ichthyol.) — ModL. ■ atherlna, fr. Gk.
άθερίνη, 'smelt', fr. άθήρη, 'gruel, porridge',
which is rel. to αθήρ, 'awn, chaff, barb of a
weapon', άνθέρικος, 'the asphodel'. See An-
thericum and cp. atheroma.

## Atherinidae
Atherinidae, n. pi., a family of fishes (ichthyol.)
— ModL., fr. atherlna. See prec. word and
-idae.

## athermancy
athermancy, п., impermeability to heat. —
Formed with suff. -cy fr. Gk. ά&έρμαντος, 'not
heated', fr. ά (see priv. pref. a-) and θερμαντός,
'capable of being heated', verbal adj. of
θερμαίνε», 'to warm, heat'. See therm and cp.
diathermancy.

## athermanous
athermanous, adj., not transmitting radiant heat.
— Formed fr. priv. pref. a-, the stem of Greek
θερμαίνείν, 'to warm, heat', and suff. -ous.
See therm and cp. diathermanous. The use of
the suff. -ous is due to the analogy of joyous
and other similar adjectives in which -ous
corresponds to~OF. -ous, -eus (= F. -eux), fr. L.·
Ssus.

## atheroma
atheroma, п., a kind of encysted tumor (med.) —
L., fr. Gk. αθήρωμα, 'a tumor fuil of gruel-like

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:84 COLUMN:3 -->
matter', fr. άθήρη. See atherine and -oma.

## Atherosperma
Atherosperma, п., a genus of trees of the boldo
family (hot.) — ModL., formed fr. Gk. αθήρ,
gen. άθέρος, 'awn, chaff', and σπέρμα, 'seed'.
See atherine and sperm.

## athetize
athetize, tr. v., to reject. — Formed with suff.
-ire fr. Gk. άθετεΐν, 'to deny, disprove, reject',
fr. άθετος, 'not fixed', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-)
and θετός, 'placed, set', verb. adj. of τιθέναι,
'to put, place', fr. I.-E. base *dhe-, 4o place'.
See theme and cp. words there referred to.

## athetosis
athetosis, п., affection of the nervous system
marked by involuntary movements of the fingers
and toes (med.) — Medical L., coined by the
American nerve specialist William Alexander
Hammond (1828-1900) in 1871 fr. Gk. δθετος,
'not fixed', and suff. -osis. See prec. word.

## nthirst
nthirst, adj. — ME. ofthurst, fr. OE. ofpyrsted,
pp. of ofpyrstan, fr. of- (see of) and pyrstan,
'to thirst'. See thirst, v.

## athlete
athlete, n. — L. athleta, fr. Gk. αθλητής,
'combatant, champion', fr. άθλέω, Ι contend for a
prize', fr. άθλος, contracted fr. άεθλος (with
the exception of Odyssey, 8, 160, this latter
form alone is used by Homer), for orig. dtfs-
θλος. The first element of this word is perh.
cogn. with OI. νά-yaii, 'he fatigues himself'; the
second element is of unknown origin. Cp. the
second element in pentathlon, hexathlon,
decathlon.

## athletic
athletic,! adj. — L. athllticus, fr. Gk. αθλητικός,
fr. αθλητής. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: athletic-al-ly, adv., athletic-ism, п.,
athlet-ics, n.

## nthrepsia
nthrepsia, п., debility of children caused by lack
of food (med.) — Medical L., lit. 'condition
caused by the lack of nourishment', fr. Gk.
&θρε7ττος, 'ill-nourished, underfed', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-) and θρεπτός, 'fed, nourished',
verbal adj. of τρέφειν, 'to feed, nourish' (whence
also θρέψις, 'nourishment'). See trophic and cp.
thrombosis. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## athrill
athrill, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and thrill.

## athrob
athrob, adv. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and throb.

## athwart
athwart, adv. and prep. — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and thwart.

## athymy
athymy, also athymia, п., despondency. — Gk.
άθϋμίά, 'faintheartedness, despondency', lit.
'lack of spirit', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
θυμός, 'spirit, mind, soul'. See thio- and cp.
thyme.

## -atic
-atic, adj. suff. of Greek origin, meaning
'pertaining to; of the nature of, as in dramatic,
grammatic. — F. -atique, fr. L. -aticus, fr. Gk.
-ατικός. Ср. -etic.

## -atic
-atic, adj. suff. of Latin origin meaning
'pertaining to; of the nature of, as in erratic,
aquatic. — F. -atique, fr. L. -aticus. This suff.
arose from a misreading of Sl-icus (— pp.
suff. of verbs of the ist conjugation and
suff. -icus) into a-ticus. [Cp. e.g. L. venSt-
icus, 'pertaining to the chase', (fr. venalus, pp.
of venart, 'to chase'), misread into venS-ticus.]
Accordingly suff. -atic is a compound of the
adj. (orig. pp.) suffix -nte and of suff. -Ic.
Later the suff. -atic was also appended to nouns.
Cp. -age.
Derivative: -atic-al.

## -atile
-atile, adj. suff. expressing possibility. — F. -atile,
fr. L. -Stilts, prop. suff. -His added to -atus, pp.
suff. of verbs of the first conjugation. See adj.
suff. -ate and -ile.

## ntilt
ntilt, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
tut.

## -ation
-ation, subst. suff. denoting action, process, state
or condition. — Fr. F. -ation, (or directly) fr. L.
Stionem, ace. of Slid, a suff. forming nouns of
action fr. -atus, pp. suff. of verbs of the first
Latin conjugation. See adj. suff. -ate and cp.
suff. -ition. For the sense of suff. -ation cp. -osis.

## -ative
-ative, adj. suff. meaning 'tending to'. — F. -alif
(fem. -ative), fr. L. Stlvus, prop. suff. -tvus
added to -atus, pp. suff. of verbs of the first Latin
conjugation. Accordingly suff. -alive is a
compound of adj. suff. -nte and suff. -ive.

## atlantes
atlantes, n. pi., figures of men supporting an
entablature (archil.) — L., fr. Gk. "Ατλαντες, pi.
of "Ατλας. See Atlas.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:85 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ATLANTIC | 58 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:85 COLUMN:1 -->

## Atlantic
Atlantic, adj., pertaining to the Atlantic Ocean
or to Mount Atlas. — L. Allanticus, fr. Gk.
'Ατλαντικός, fr. "Ατλας, 'the Atlas mountains'.
See Atlas and -ic.

## Atlas
Atlas, п., one of the Titans, son of Iapetus and
Clymene, supporting the heavens on his
shoulders; later, a king of Mauretania, changed by
Perseus into Mt. Atlas (Greek mythol.) — L.
Alias (gen. Atlantis), fr. Gk. "Ατλας (gen. "Ατ-
λαντος), which stands for "Α-τλας and lit. means
'the Bearer (scil. of Heaven)', fr. copul. pref. ά-
and the stem of τληναι, 'to bear' (cp. πολύ-
τλάς, 'much-enduring'). Copul. pref. ά- stands
for I.-E. *sm-, a weak gradational form of I.-E.
base *sem-, 'one, together'; see same. Gk. τληναι
derives fr. *f/-, zero degree of I.-E. base *tel-,
*tal-, *tol-, 'to bear, lift, suffer', whence τάλδς,
gen. τάλανος and τάλαντος, 'bearing,
suffering', ταλάσσαι (aor.), 'to bear, suffer', L. tol-
lere, Ho lift up, raise', tolerare, 'to bear,
support'. See tolerate and cp. atlas, name of the
first vertebra, atlaates, Atlantic, Atalanta,
talent

## atlas
atlas, п., a collection of maps bound into a book.
— First so called by the geographer Mercator
because the figure of Atlas supporting the world
was frequently put on the front page of such
collections. (The first part of Mercator's Atlas,
sive cosmographicae meditationes defabrica mun-
di appeared in 1585.) See prec. word.

## atlas
atlas, п., name of the first vertebra (anal.) —
From Atlas (q.v.); so called became it bears the
skull. This name was given to the first vertebra
by the Belgian anatomist Andreas Vesalius
(1514-64). See Joseph -Hyrtl, Onomatologia
anatomica, Vienna, 1880, p. 59.

## atlas
atlas, п., silk-satin. — Arab, dflas, lit. 'wiped
smooth', fr. fdlasa, 'he wiped, smoothed away'.

## atie
atie, atlee, п., the tamarisk salt tree. — Arab.
athL·", 'a species of tamarisk', prop, unit name
of athl, rel. to Aram, athla, Heb. ishel,
'tamarisk tree'.

## atman
atman, п., the supreme soul, the principle of life
(Hinduism). — OI. atman, prop, 'breath, soul',
orig. 'cover, body', cogn. with OHG. alum,
MHG. Stem, G. Atem, MDu. идет, OFris.
ilhma, OS. athom, OE. Sum, 'breath'. Cp. the
second element in mahatma.

## atmido-
atmido-, before a vowel atmid-, combining form
meaning 'vapor'. — Gk. άτμιδΌ-, άτμιδ-, fr.
άτμίς, gen. άτμίβος, 'steam, vapor', rel. to ατμός,
of s.m. See anno-.

## atmidometer
atmidometer, п., an atmometer. — Compounded
of atmido- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## anno-
anno-, before a vowel arm-, combining form
meaning 'vapor'. — Gk. άτμο-, άτμ-, fr. ατμός,
'steam, vapor', contraction of άετμός, which
prob. stands for *άίε-τ-μό-ς and is rel. to
αελλα (for *Sf ε-λ-ια), 'tempest, whirlwind', and
to αημι (for '(ΧΤημι), Ί blow', fr. I.-E. base
'we-, to blow', whence also OI. Will, 'blows',
Goth, waian, OE. wawan, 'to blow'. See wind,
'air in motion', and cp. Aello.

## ntinology
ntinology, п., the study of the laws of aqueous
vapor.—Compounded of anno- and Gk.-λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
-logy·
Derivatives: atmolog-lc, atmolog-ic-al, adjs., at-
molog-ist, n.

## atinolysis
atinolysis, п., separation of mixed gases. —
Compounded of anno- and Gk. λύσις, 'a loosing;
dissolution'. See -lysis.

## atmometer
atmometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
rate of evaporation. — Compounded of atino-
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.
Derivatives: atmometr-ic, adj., atmometr-y, n.

## atmosphere
atmosphere, n. — Compounded of Gk. ατμός,
'steam, vapor', and σφαίρα, 'ball, sphere'; see
atmo- and sphere. The word atmosphere was first
used by the English bishop and scientist John
Wilkins (1614-72) in 1638 with reference to the
moon (which in reality has no atmosphere).
Derivatives: almospher-ic, almospher-ic-al, adjs.,
atmospher-ic-al-ly, adv., atmospher-ics, n.pl.

## ntocia
ntocia, п., sterility of the female (med.)—

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:85 COLUMN:2 -->
Medical L., fr. Gk. άτοχίά, 'sterility', fr. άτοκος,
having never yet brought forth', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and τόκος, 'childbirth, parturition',
which is rel. to τοκεύς, 'father', in the pi.,
'parents'. See -tocia, toco-, and cp. anatocism.

## atoll
atoll, п., a coral island. — Malayalam.

## atom
atom, rr. — F. atome, fr. L. atomus, fr. Gk. ατομος,
'atom', prop, 'uncut, indivisible', fr. ά- (see
priv. pref. a-), and -τόμος, fr. τέμνειν, 'to cut'.
See tome and cp. anatomy. The word ατομος
was first used by the Greek philosopher
Leucippus.
Derivatives: atom-ic, adj., atom-ic-ity, п.,
atomism, п., atom-ist, п., atom-lze, tr. v., atom-iz-
ation, п., atom-iz-er, n.

## atomy
atomy, п., skeleton. — From misdivision of
anatomy into an atomy. See anatomy.

## atomy
atomy, п., pygmy. — L. atoml (pi. of atomus,
'atom'), mistaken for a singular. See atom.

## atone
atone, intr. v. — Short for 'to be at one'.
Derivatives: atone-menl, п., aton-ing-ly, adv.

## atonic
atonic, adj. — Formed with sun", -ic fr. Gk.
άτονος, "not stretched, slack; without tone',
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and τόνος, 'tone'. See
tonic and cp. diatonic.

## atony
atony, п., want of tone. — ML. atonla, fr. Gk.
ατονία, 'slackness, debility', fr. άτονος. See prec.
word and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## atopic
atopic, adj., pertaining to atopy (med.)—Formed
with sun", -ic fr. Gk. άτοπος, 'out of place;
unusual', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and τόπος,
'place'. See topic

## atopite
atopite, п., calcium antimonate (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. άτοπος.
See atopic.

## atopy
atopy, п., allergy. — See atopic and -y
(representing Gk. -15).

## -ator
-ator, subst. suff. — L. -ator, forming masculine
agential nouns from verbs of the first
conjugation.' Accordingly the suff. -ator consists of -a-,
the characteristic vowel of the first conjugation,
and suff. -tor (q.v.)

## atrabillary
atrabillary, adj., melancholy, hypochondriac. —
Medical L. atrabiliarius, 'suffering from black
bile', fr. L. atra bills, 'black bile, melancholy',
loan translation of Gk. μέλαινα χολή (see
melancholy). Atra is fern, of ater, 'black, dark', rel.
to Umbr. atru, adro (neut. pi.), 'black', and
prob. cogn. with OI. atharvan-, Avestic S&ra-
van-, 'fire priest', Starsh, 'fire', atrya-, 'ashes',
Arm. airem, Ί light up, kindle'. Cp. atrocious.
Cp. aiso Atharvan. For the etymology of L. bilis
see bile. For the ending of atrabiliary see adj.
suff. -ary.
Derivative: atrabiliari-ous, adj.

## atrabilious
atrabilious, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
atra bilis. See prec. word.
Oemativcs:atribilious-ly,adv.,alrabilious-ness,n.

## Atractaspls
Atractaspls, п., a genus of African burrowing
vipers (zool.) — ModL., lit. 'arrow snake', fr.
Gk. άτρακτος, 'spindle, arrow', arid ασπίς,
'serpent, snake', The first element is cogn. with
L. torquere, 'to twist, bend'; see torque. For the
second element see usp, 'snake'.

## Atragene
Atragene, п., a genus of trees of the buttercup
family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άθραγένη,
'traveler's joy', compounded of ίθρας, 'chariot',
and -γενή, 'of a certain kind'. The first
element stands for *ίά(ν)&ρας and is cogn. with
OI. vandhurah, 'a hamper (made of wicker-
work)', fr. I.-E. base 'wendh-, "wndh-, 'to turn,
twist', whence also ON. vinaa, OE. windan,
'to wind, twist'; see wind, 'to turn'. The
second element is rel. to Gk. γένος, 'race,
descent, gender, kind'; see genus and cp. -gen.

## atresia
atresia, п., occlusion of a natural passage of the
body (pathol.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. ατρητος,
'not perforated', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
τρητός, verbal adj. of τετραίνειν, 'to pierce,
perforate', which is rel. to τείρειν (for "τέριειν),
'to rub, rub away, wear away', fr. I.-E. base
*ter-, Ίο bore, pierce, rub'. See throw and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see
suff. -in.

## Atreus
Atreus, п., a son of Pelops and father of
Agamemnon and Menelaus (Greek mythol.) — L.,
fr. Gk. Άτρεύς, a word of uncertain origin.

## atrip
atrip, adv. (naut.) — Formed fr. a- 'on', and trip.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:85 COLUMN:3 -->

## Atriptex
Atriptex, п., a genus of plants of the goosefoot
family (hot.) — L. atriplex, 'orach', fr. Gk.
άτράφαξυς, which is of unknown origin. Cp.
orach.

## atrium
atrium, п., 1) the central, courtlike room of the
ancient Roman house; 2) (anat.) cavity in the
heart or in the ear. — L. atrium: according to
Varro, De Lingua Latina 5, § 161, a word of
Etruscan origin and rel. to the Etruscan town
Atria, as the place of origin of this kind of
architecture. The connection of atrium with ater,
'black, dark', is folk etymology.

## atrocious
atrocious, adj., extremely cruel or wicked. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. atrox, gen. atrocis,
'cruel, fierce', prop, 'dark-looking, gloomy',
and compounded of ater, 'black, dark', and
-ox, gen. ocis, 'looking'. For the first element see
atrabilious. The second element is cogn. with
Gk. ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye, sight'. See -ops and cp.
the second element in ferocious, velocity.
Derivatives: atrocious-ly, adv., atrocious-ness.

## atrocity
atrocity, п., atrociousness. — F. atrociti, fr. L.
atrScitatem, ace. of alrocitas, 'cruelty', fr. atrox.
See prec. word and -ity.

## Atropa
Atropa, п., a genus of plants of the potato family
(hot) — ModL., fr. Gk. ατροπα, 'the deadly
nightshade', which is rel. to "Ατροπος, name
of one of the Fates. See Atropos.

## atrophy
atrophy, п., a wasting away through lack of
nourishment (med.) — F. atrophie, fr. L.
atrophia, fr. Gk. ατροφία, 'want of food', fr. ίίτρο-
φος, 'not nourished, ill-fed', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and -τροφός, fr. τροφή, 'food,
nourishment'. See trophic and cp. athrepsia. Cp. also
dystrophy, hypertrophy.
Derivatives: atrophy, intr. and tr. v., atroph-ic,
atrophi-ed, adjs.

## atropine
atropine, also atropin, п., an alkaloid poison
extracted from belladonna. — Formed with
chem. suff. -ine, resp. -in, fr. Gk. ατροπα, 'the
deadly nightshade'. See Atropa.

## Atropos
Atropos, п., one of the Fates in Greek
mythology. — Gk. "Ατροπος, lit. 'not to be turned
away, inflexible', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and
the stem of τρέπειν, 'to turn', τρόπος, 'a turn'.
See trope and cp. Atropa, atropine,

## attach
attach, tr. and intr. v. — ME. attachen, fr. OF
atachier, attachier (F. attacher), lit. 'to tack or
fasten to', fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and tache, 'a nail,
hook', a word of Teut. origin. See tack, 'a small
nail', and cp. tache, 'a buckle', detach. Cp. also
attack, which is a doublet of attach. Cp. also
next word.
Derivatives: attach-able, adj., altach-ed, adj.,
attach-ed-ly,adv.,attach-er,n., attachment (q.v.)

## attache
attache, п., a member of the diplomatic staff
attached to an embassy. — F., lit. 'attached', ^p.
of attacher, 'to attach'. See prec. word.

## attachment
attachment, n. — F. attachement, fr. attacher. See
attach and -ment.

## attack
attack, tr. v. — F. attaquer, fr. It. atlaccare, prop,
'to attach, join', whence 'to begin', atlaccare bat-
taglia, 'to begin a battle', whence elliptically
atlaccare, 'to attack'; a doublet of attach (q.v.)
Derivatives: attack, п., attack-able, adj., at-
tack-er, n.

## attacus
attacus, п., a kind of edible locust. — Late L.
(Vulg., Lev. 11:22), fr. Gk. άττακός, mentioned
by Philo (cp. άττάκης, Sept., Lev. 11:22).

## attagen
attagen, п., the Pallas's sand grouse. — L., name
of a kind of bird, possibly the francolin, fr. Gk.
άτταγήν (also άτταγάς, άτταγης); of uncertain,
possibly imitative, origin.

## attain
attain, tr. and intr. v. — ME. atteinen, attainen,
from the stem of OF. ataindre, ateindre (F. al-
teindre), fr. VL. *attangere, corresponding to
L. attingere, 'to touch, to arrive at', fr. ad- and
tangere, 'to touch'. See tangent and cp.
attainder, attaint, attinge.
Derivatives: attain-abil-ity, п., attain-able, adj.

## attainder
attainder, п., the extinction of the civil and legal
rights of a person sentenced to death or
outlawed (law). — OF. infinitive ataindre, ateindre,
'to attain; to accuse, condemn', used as a noun.
For the subst. use of Old French infinitives—
esp. in legal terminology—cp. avoirdupois,
cesser, demurrer, detainer, disclaimer, estovers,
joinder, misnomer, ouster, oyer, rejoinder, re-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:86 COLUMN:1 -->
mainder, retainer, tender, 'offer', terminer, user,
'right of use', waiver.

## attaint
attaint, n. — OF. atainl, pp. of ataindre (see
attain); confused with taint.
Derivatives: attaint, п., attaint-ment, п., attaint-
ure, n.

## attar
attar, п., also otto, volatile oil. — Pers. 'alar, fr.
Arab, 'r'fr, 'perfume'.

## attemper
attemper, tr. v. — OF. atemprer (F. attemprer),
fr. Late L. attemperare, 'to fit, adjust', fr. ad-
and L. temperare, 'to divide duly; to temper'.
See temper, v.
Derivatives; attemper-ed, adj., attemper-ment,n.

## attemperate
attemperate, tr. v.(obsol.)—Late L.allemperatus,
pp. of attemperare. See prec. word and cp.
temperate.
Derivatives: attemperat-ion, п., altemperat-or, n.

## attempt
attempt, tr. v. — OF. atenter, also atempter (F.
attenter), fr. L. attentare, attemptare (whence
also It. attentare, OProven?., Port, attentar, Sp.
atenlar), 'to attempt, try', fr. ad- and tentare,
lemptdre, 'to put to the test, try'. See tempt and
cp. attentat.
Derivatives; attempt, п., attempt-able, adj., at-
tempt-er, n.

## attend
attend, intr. and tr. v. — OF. atendre (F. atten-
dre), 'to expect, wait for', fr. L. attendere (ani-
mum), 'to stretch one's mind to', fr. ad- and
tendere, 'to stretch, extend'. Cp. It. attendere,
OProvenc. atender, which are of the same
origin. See tend, 'to move in a certain direction',
and cp. tend, 'to attend'. Cp. also contend,
intend, portend.
Derivatives: attendance, attendant (qq.v.), at-
lend-er', п., attend-ing-ly, adv.

## attendaace
attendaace, n. — OF. atendance, fr. atendant (F.
attendant), pres. part, of atendre. See next word
and -ce.

## attendant
attendant, adj. — F., pres. part, of attendre. See
attend and -ant.
Derivative: attendant, n.

## attent
attent, adj., attentive (archaic). — L. attentus,
pp. of attendere. See attend.

## attent
attent, п., attention (obsol.) — OF. atente (F. at-
tenle), fr. VL. *attendita, п., prop, subst. use
of the fem. of 'attenditus, pp. formed fr. L.
attendere. See attend.

## attentat(e)
attentat(e), п., ι) a criminal attempt (obsol.); 2) in
law, a proceeding in court of judicature after an
inhibition is decreed. — F. attentat, 'criminal
attempt',fr. L. attentatum, neut. pp. ofattentare,
'to attempt'. See attempt.

## attention
attention, n. — F., fr. L. attentidnem, ace. of at-
tentio, 'attention, attentiveness', fr. attentus, pp.
of attendere. See attead and -ioa.
Derivative: attention-al, adj.

## atteative
atteative, adj. — F. attentif (fem. attentive), fr.
VL. *attenditus. See attent, п., and -ive.
Derivatives: attentive-ly, adv., attentive-ness, n.

## attenuaut
attenuaut, adj., attenuating, diluent; п., an
attenuating substance, a diluent. — L. attenuans,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of attenuare. See next
word and -ant.

## atteauate
atteauate, tr. v., to make thin; to make less; intr.
v., to become thin; to become less. — L.
attenuate, pp. of attenuare, 'to make thin,
attenuate', fr. ad- and tenuare, 'to make thin', fr.
tenuis, 'thin'. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and verbal suff. -ate and cp. tenuis,
thin.

## attenuate
attenuate, adj.,. attenuated. — L. attenuatus pp.
of attenuare. See attenunte, v.

## nttenuation
nttenuation, n. — L. attenuatio, gen. -onis, fr.
attenuatus, pp. of attenuare. See attenuate, v.,
and -ion.

## atter
atter, п., poison. — OE. at(l)or, rel. to OFris.
at(t)er, OS. ettar, ON. eitr, 'poison', Swed., Du.
etter, OHG. eittar, eitar, MHG., G. eiter, 'pus',
and cogn. with Gk. οΐϋμα, οίδος, 'a swelling',
οίδαν, οΕδεΐν, 'to swell'. See edema.
Derivatives: atter-n, atter-y, atlr-y, adjs.

## attest
attest, tr. and intr. v. — F. attester, fr. L.
attestor!, 'to bear witness to, attest', fr. ad- and
testari, 'to bear witness*, fr. testis, 'witness',
See testament and cp. contest, detest. Derivatives:
attestation (q.v.), altest-er, attest-or, n.

## attestation
attestation, n. — F., fr. L. attestatiSnem, ace. of
attestStid, 'an attesting, testimony', fr. attes-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:86 COLUMN:2 -->
tatus, pp. of attestari. See attest and -ation and
cp. contestation, detestation.

## Attic
Attic, adj., of, or pertaining to, Attica. — L. Atti-
cus, fr. Gk. 'Αττικός, 'of Attica'. ,

## attic
attic, n. — F. attique, 'attic', lit. 'Attic (story)'.
See Attic.

## atticism
atticism, п., Attic style, elegant diction. — Gk.
Άττικισμός, fr. 'Αττικός. See Attic and -ism.

## atricize
atricize, tr. v., to adapt to the dialect of Attica;
intr. v., to imitate Attic style. — Gk. Άττικί-
ζειν, fr. 'Αττικός. See Attic and -ize.

## atringe
atringe, tr. v., to touch upon (obsol.) — L. atlin-
gere. See attain.

## attire
attire, tr. v. — ME. atiren, fr. OF. atirier, atirer,
fr. a Here, a tire, 'into a row', fr. a, 'to' (seea), and
Here, 'row, rank, series'. See tier, 'row, series'.
Derivatives: attire, п., atlir-ed, adj., attir-er, n.

## attitude
attitude, n. — F., fr. It. attitudine, 'aptness,
promptitude', fr. ML. aptitudinem, ace. of
aptitude; see aptitade. The word altitude was
introduced into English by the diarist John Evelyn
(1620-1706).
Derivatives: attitudin-al, adj., attitudinarian,
attitudinarianism, attitudinize (qq.v.)

## attitudinarian
attitudinarian, п., one who
attitudinizes.—Formed with suff. -arian fr. It. attitudine. See attitade.
Derivative: attitudinarian-ism, n.

## attitudinize
attitudinize, intr. v., to strike an attitude; to pose.
— Formed fr. It. attitudine (see attitude) with
suff. -ize.

## attorn
attorn, intr. and tr. v., 1) orig., to transfer homage
from one feudal lord to another; 2) to agree to
become a tenant under a new landlord (law). —
OF. atorner, 'to direct, attorn', lit. 'to turn to',
fr. a, 'to' (see 4), and torner (F. tourner), fr. L.
tornare, 'to turn'. See turn, v. and cp. attorney.

## attorney
attorney, п., solicitor. — Lit. 'one authorized to
act for another', fr. OF. atorne, pp. of atorner,
'to turn to'. See prec. word and -ее.

## attornment
attornment, п., ι) a turning over, assignment;
2) acknowledgment of the new landlord. — OF.
atornement, fr. atorner. See attorn and -ment.

## attract
attract, tr. v. — L. attractus, pp. of attrahere, 'to
draw to, attract', fr. ad- and trahere, 'to draw'.
See tract, 'region', and cp. attrahent. Cp. also
contract, detract, protract, subtract
Derivatives: atlract-er, п., attraction,
attractive (qq.v.)

## attraction
attraction, n. — F., fr. L. attractidnem, ace. of
attractio, 'a drawing together', fr. attractus, pp.
of attrahere. See prec. word and -ion.

## attractive
attractive, adj. — F. attractif (fem. attractive),
fr. ML. attractivus, fr. L. attractus, pp. of
attrahere. See attract and -ive.
Derivatives: attraclive-ly, adv., attractive-ness, η.

## attrahent
attrahent, adj., that which attracts. — L. aura-
hens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of attrahere. See
attract and -ent and cp. contrahent, subtrahend.
Derivative: attrahent, n.

## attribute
attribute, tr. v. — L. attributus, pp. of attribuere,
'to add, assign, bestow, give, impute, attribute',
fr. ad- and tribuere 'to assign, allot, bestow,
give, grant'. See tribute.

## attribute
attribute, n. — L. attributum, 'anything
attributed', neut. of attributus, pp. of attribuere.
See attribute, v.

## attribution
attribution, n. — F., fr. L. attributionem, ace. of
altributio, 'assignment, attribution', fr.
attributus, pp. of attribuere. See attribute, adj., and
-ion,

## attribntive
attribntive, adj. — F. aitributif (fem. attributive),
fr. atlribut, 'attribute', fr. L. attributum. See
attribute, п., and -ive.
Derivatives: attributive, п., attributive-ly, adv.,
attributive-ness, n.

## attrite
attrite, adj., worn away by rubbing. — L. allri-
tus, pp. of atterere, 'to wear away', lit. 'to rub
against', fr. ad- and terere, 'to rub'. See trite.

## attrition
attrition, n. — L. attritio, gen. -6nis, lit. 'a rubbing^
against', fr. attritus, pp. of atterere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## attune
attune, tr. v. — Formed fr. at- and time.

## atwain
atwain, adv. (archaic). — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and twain.

## atween
atween, adv. (archaic). — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and -tween (in between).

## auantic
auantic, adj., atrophic. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. αύαντή, 'a wasting, atrophy', fr. αύαί-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:86 COLUMN:3 -->
νειν, 'to wither, be dry', fr. αϋειν, 'to dry', fr.
αδος, 'dry', whjch stands for *sauso-s and
derives fr. I.-E. base *saus-, *sus-, 'dry', whence
also OE. sear, 'dry', OHG. sarin, 'to become
