## auhade
auhade, п., morning serenade. — F., fr. Provenc.
aubada, fr. auba, 'dawn', fr. L. alba, fem. of
albus, 'white', used as a noun. See alb and -ade.

## auhain
auhain, п., alien, foreigner. — F„ orig. written
aubene, fr. Frankish *aliban, lit. 'belonging to
another ban'. The first element of this word is
rel. to Goth, aljis, 'other', and to E. else (q.v.)
The second element is rel. to E. ban, v. (q.v.)
See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 43 s.v. aubain.

## aubergine
aubergine, п., the eggplant. — G., fr. Catal. al-
berginera, alberginia, fr. Arab, al-badinjdn, 'the
eggplant', fr. al-, 'the', and badinjdn, 'eggplant',
fr. Pers. badin-gan, fr. OI. vatin-ganah. Cp.
berengena.

## aubin
aubin, п., canter. — F., fr. earlier hobin, fr. hauby
(15th cent.), fr. E. hobby (q.v.)

## Aubrey
Aubrey, masc. PN. — F. Auberi, fr. G. Alberich,
lit. 'ruler of elfs'. For the first element cp. ON.
alfr, OE. self, 'elf', and see elf. For the second
element see rich and cp. words there referred to.

## Aubrien'a
Aubrien'a, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (bot.) — ModL., named after Claude
Aubriet, painter of flowers and animals (1668-
1743). For the ending see suff. -in.

## auburn
auburn, adj., reddish-brown. — ME. auburne,
'whitish', fr. OF. alborne, auborne, fr. VL. al-
burnus, 'whitish', fr. L. albus, 'white'. The sense
development of the word was influenced by a
confusion with brown. See alb and cp. alburnum.
Derivative: auburn, n.

## auchenium
auchenium, п., part of a bird's neck (ornithol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -ium fr. Gk. αΰχήν,
'neck, throat', which is rel. to Aeol. £μφην, of
s.m., and cogn. with Arm. auj'i-k', 'necklace'.

## auction
auction, n. — L. audio, gen. -onis, 'an increase;
a public sale, auction', fr. auctus, pp. of auglre,
'to increase', fr. I.-E. base *aweg-, *aug-, 'to
grow, increase', whence also Lith. dugu, augti,
Lett, augu, augi, 'to grow', Lith. aukStas, Lett.
augsts, 'high, of superior rank', OPruss. autk-
timmien, 'chief, aucktai-rikyskan, 'authority',
Lett, audiit, 'to bring up', Goth, aukan, 'to
grow, increase', OE. gacian, 'to increase'; see
eke and cp. nugment, augur, august, author. Cp.
the related base *aw(e)ks-, *auks-, *weks-,
*uks-, 'to grow, increase', whence OI. vaksayali,
'causes to grow', uksati, 'grows strong', Gk.
ά5έξειν, άέξείν, αυξειν, αύξάνειν, 'to increase',
L. auxilium, 'help, aid', Goth, wahsjan, OE.
weaxan, 'to grow'. See wax, v., and cp. auxiliary,
anxano-, auxesis, auxetic, auxo-.
Derivatives: auction, tr. v., auction-eer, п., аис-
tion-eer-ing, n.

## aucupate
aucupate, intr. and tr. v., to go fowling. — L.
aucupatus, pp. of aucupdre, later aucuparJ, 'to
go fowling', fr. auceps, 'fowler; spy,
eavesdropper', for *avi-cap-s, fr. avis, 'bird', and
capere, 'to catch, seize, take, receive'. See auspice
and captive.

## aadacious
aadacious, adj., daring, bold. — F. audacieux
(fem. audacieuse), fr. L. audacia, 'daring,
boldness, courage, intrepidity', fr. audax, gen. au-
dacis, 'daring, bold, courageous, intrepid', fr.
audere, 'to dare', which stands for *avide~re, to
be eager', fr. avidus, 'eager'. The meaning 'to
dare' first arose from the negative form: поп
audere orig. meant 'to wish or to have a mind
not to do something', whence it came to denote
'not to risk or dare to do something'. L. avidus
is a derivative of avere, 'to wish, desire, long for,
crave', whence also avarus, 'greedy'. See avid
ajid cp. avarice.
Derivatives: audacious-ly, adv.,
audaciousness, n.

## audacity
audacity, п., daring, boldness. — Formed with
suff. -ity fr. L. audax, gen. -acis, 'bold', fr.
audere, 'to dare'. See prec. word and -ity.

## audible
audible, adj. — ML. audibilis, fr. L. audio, audire,
'to hear', which prob. stands for *awis-d-id, fr,
I.-E. base *awei-, *au-, 'to perceive', whence also
OI. uvlb, Avestic avish, 'openly, evidently', Gk.
αίσ&άνομαι (for *if ισ-θ-άνομω), Ί perceive',
άίω (for ·4Λω), Ί hear' (lit. Ί perceive by the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:87 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: AUDIENCE | 60 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:87 COLUMN:1 -->
ear'), OSlav. avi, javi, 'open, public', avili,
javiti, 'to reveal'. Cp. obedient, obeisance, obey,
oyer, oyez.
Derivatives: audibil-ity, п., audible-ness, п.,
audibl-y, adv.

## audience
audience, n. — F., fr. L. audientia, 'a hearing,
audience', fr. audiens, gen. -entis, pres. part, о
audire. See audible and -ence.

## audient
audient, п., a hearer, listener. — L. audiens, gen.
-entis. See prec. word and -ent.

## audile
audile, adj., auditory. — Formed with suff. -Ue
fr. L. audire, 'to hear'. See andible.
Derivative: audile, п., a person whose imagery
is chiefly auditory (psychol.)

## audiology
audiology, n„ the science of curing defective
hearing. — A hybrid coined fr. L. audire, 'to hear',
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See audible and -logy-
Derivative : audiolog-isl, n.

## nudiometer
nudiometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
intensity of sounds. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
audire, 'to hear', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
audible and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: audiometr-y, п., audiometr-ist, n.

## audipbone
audipbone, п., an instrument for helping the deaf
to hear. —A hybrid coined fr. L. audire, 'to hear',
and Gk. φωνή, 'sound'. See audible and phone.

## nadit
nadit, tr. v. and n. — Back formation fr. auditor
(q.v.)

## audition
audition, n. — L. auditid, gen. -dnis, 'a hearing',
fr. audiius, pp. of audire. See andible and -ion
and cp. auditor.

## auditive
auditive, adj. — F. auditif (fern, auditive), fr. L.
audiius, pp. of audire, 'to hear'. See audible.

## nuditor
nuditor, п., a hearer. — AF. auditour,
corresponding to F. auditeur, fr. L. audilorem, ace. of
auditor, 'a hearer', fr. audiius, pp. of audire. See
audible and agential suff. -or.

## auditorium
auditorium, п., a building or part of a building
assigned to the audience. — L. auditorium,
'lecture room, hall of justice', prop. neut. of the
adjective audiWrius, 'relating to hearing', used
as a noun, and lit. meaning 'the place where
something is heard', fr. auditus, pp. of audire.
See next word and cp. auditory, n.

## auditory
auditory, adj., pertaining to hearing. — L. audi-
tdrius, 'relating to a hearer or hearing', fr.
auditor, 'hearer'. See auditor.and adj. suff. -ory.

## auditary
auditary, п., an audience. — L. auditorium,
'lecture room'. See auditorium and subst. suff.
-ory.

## Audrey
Audrey, fem. PN. — Shortened fr. Etheldreda,
latinization of OE. Cdeldryd, lit. 'noble might',
fr. aedele, 'noble', and dryd, 'strength, might'.
For the first element see atheling. The second
element is rel. to OHG. triuwen, 'to flourish',
trouwen, 'to grow', MHG. druo, 'fruit', ON.
pro-ask, 'to thrive', proskr, 'strong'. Cp. tawdry.

## Augean
Augean, adj., pertaining to Augeas, king of Elis,
whose stable remained uncleaned for thirty
years until Hercules cleaned it in a day (Greek
mythol.) — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Augeas, !
fr. Gk. Αυγείας, 'Augeas'.

## angelite
angelite, п., a hydrous aluminum phosphate
(mineral.) — Lit. 'the bright stone', formed with
combining form-lite fr. Gk. αυγή, 'light of the
sun, brightness'. See augite.

## aager
aager, n. — ME. auger, earlier nauger, fr. OE.
nafugar, which is compounded of nafu, 'nave of
a wheel' and gar, 'spear'; see nave and gore, 'a
triangular piece of land'. The loss of the initial
л is due to a misdivision of ME. a nauger into
an auger. For similar misdivisions cp. adder and
words there referred to.
Derivative: auger-er, n.

## nugfat
nugfat, n. — ME. auhl, fr. OE. awiht, dwihl, lit.
'ever a whit', fr. α, δ, 'ever, always', and wiht,
'creature, thing'. See aye, 'ever', and wight and
cp. naught

## augite
augite, п., a variety of pyroxene (mineral.) — L.
augitis, fr. Gk. αύγίτης, fr. αυγή, 'light of the
sun, ray, brightness;, dawn, daybreak', which is
cogn. with Alb. ago/, 'to dawn', agume, 'dawn',
and prob. also with OSlav. jugu, 'south', lit.
'the place where the sun shines', jutro,
'morning'. Cp. augelite. Cp. also the first element in
Yugoslav.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:87 COLUMN:2 -->

## augment
augment, tr. v., l) to cause to increase; z) to
prefix the augment to (see next word). — F. aug-
menter, fr. L. augmentare, 'to increase', fr. aug-
mentum, 'increase', fr. augere, 'to increase'. See
auction and -ment.
Derivatives: augmenl-ed, adj., augment-ed-ly,
adv., augment-er, n.

## nugment
nugment, n., a prefixed vowel or the lengthening of
the initial vowel to form the past tense in Greek
and Sanskrit (gram.) — F-, fr. L. augmentum,
'increase', fr. augere, 'to increase'. See aag-
ssent, v.

## augmentation
augmentation, n. — F., fr. VL. augmentationem,
ace. of augmentutio, 'an increasing', fr. L. aug-
mentatus, pp. of augmentare, 'to increase'. See
augment, v., and -ion.

## augmentative
augmentative, adj. — F. augmentatif (fem.
augmentative), fr. L. augmentatus, pp. of augmentare.
See augment, v., and -Ive.
Derivative: augmentative-ly, adv.

## augur
augur, п., in ancient Rome, a priest who foretold
events by interpreting omens. — L., 'augur,
diviner, soothsayer; a member of the college of
priests in Rome, who foretold the future',
transformation of OL. *augos, gen. *augeris,
'increase' (with assimilation of the e to the u of
the first syllable), rel. to augere, 'to increase'.
For the change of the neuter gender (in OL.
*augos) to the masculine (in L. augur), cp. L.
vetus, 'old', which derives from the noun *wetos,
'year', and orig. meant 'of (many) years' (see
veteran). The usual derivation fr. *avi-ger (avis,
'bird', and gerere, 'to bear, conduct') is folk
etymology. Cp. inaugurate.

## augur
augur, tr. and intr. v., to foretell; to prophesy. —
L. augurari, 'to perform the functions of an
augur; to foretell by auguries; to foretell; to
prophesy', fr. L. augur. See augur, n.

## augural
augural, adj., pertaining to augurs or augury. —
L. augurdlis, 'belonging to augurs, relating to
soothsaying', fr. augur. See augur, п., and adj.
suff. -al.

## augurate
augurate, п., the office of an augur. — L. augu-
ratus, 'the office of an augur', fr. auguratus,
pp. of augurari. See angur, v., and subst. suff. -ate.

## nugury
nugury, n. — OF. augurie, fr. L. augurium,
'divination; profession of an augur'. See augur, п.,
and -y (representing L. -turn).

## august
august, adj., majestic, venerable. — L. augustus,
'majestic, venerable, august', lit. 'that which is
made to increase', rel. to augere, 'to increase';
cp. Lith. aukStas, Lett, augsts, 'high, of superior
rank'. See aactJon and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: august-ly, adv., august-ness, n.

## August
August, п., name of the eighth month of the
year. — L. Augustus; named after Augustus
Caesar, the first Roman emperor, lit. 'venerable,
august'. See august. For sense development cp.
Sebastian.

## Augusta
Augusta, fem. PN. — L., fem. of Augustus. See
Augustus.

## Augustan
Augustan, adj., l) of, or pertaining to, Augustus
Caesar or his times; 2) of, or pertaining to, any
age resembling that of Augustus Caesar. — L.
Augusldnus, 'of, or relating to, Augustus', fr.
Augustus. See August and -an.

## Augastiae
Augastiae, Augustin, Austin, masc. PN. — L.
Augustinus, lit. 'of, or pertaining to, Augustus',
fr. Augustus. See next word and -ine(representing
L. -inus).

## Augustus
Augustus, masc. PN. — L„ fr. augustus,
'venerable, august'; the name was first applied to
Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus. See august and
cp. August.

## auk
auk, n. — Scand. Cp. ON. alka, Dan. alke,
Swed. alka, which prob. derive from the I.-E.
imitative base *et-, *ol-, 'to shout, cry', whence
also L. olor (for *elor), 'swan', Mir. ela, 'swan',
and possibly also Gk. έλέα, 'a marsh bird',
έλώριος, 'a water bird'. Cp. Alca.

## nuklet
nuklet, п., any of small species of auks. —
Formed fr. prec. word with dimin. suff. -let.

## auksinas
auksinas, п., a money of account in Lithuania. —
Lith., lit. 'gulden', fr. auksas, 'gold', fr. OLith.
ausas, of s.m., which is rel. to OPruss. ausis and
cogn. with L. aurum, of s.m.; see aureate. See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, p. 86 s.v. aurum.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:87 COLUMN:3 -->

## aula
aula, п., a large hall. — L., 'the front court of a
Grecian house', fr. Gk. αυλή, 'open court, court,
hall', fr. I.-E. base *au-, 'to resi', whence also
Arm. ag-anim, Ί pass the night', Gk. ίαύω (for
*!-af -ιω), Ί sleep', and prob. the second element
in Gk. ένιαυτός, 'year'. Cp. oriel.

## aulaco-
aulaco-, before a vowel aulac-, combining form
meaning 'furrow'. — Gk. αύλακο-, αόλακ-,
from the stem of αδλαξ (gen. αΰλαχος),
'furrow', which stands for 'ά-ίλοίκ-ς and is cogn.
with" OSlav. vliko, vUSti, Lith. velku, vilkti, 'to
draw, drag'.

## Aulacomnlum
Aulacomnlum, п., a genus of mosses (hot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. αυλαξ, gen.
αυλικός, 'furrow' (see prec. word), and μνίον, 'moss',
which is cogn. with Lith. mlniava, 'close-mown
turf'.

## aald
aald, adj., old. — OE. aid; a dial, variant of old
(q.v.)

## aallc
aallc, adj., pertaining to a court. — F. aulique, fr.
*L. aulicus, fr. Gk. αυλικός, fr. αυλή, 'court'. See
aula and -ic.
Derivative: aulic-ism, n.

## aumbry
aumbry, aumery, n. — Variants of ambry.

## aumil
aumil, п., a native revenue collector in India. —
Hind, 'dmil, fr. Arab, 'dmil, 'worker, agent',
partic. of 'dmila, 'he worked, labored, made',
which is rel. to 'arnal; 'work, toil*, and to Heb.
'amal, Aram.-Syr. 'amdl, 'he worked', Ethiop.
ma'mal, 'tool', Akkad. riimelu, 'gain, possession'.
Cp. omlah.

## aumiMar
aumiMar, п., a revenue collector in India. —
Hind, 'amaldar, lit. 'one holding an office', a
hybrid coined fr. Arab, 'amal, 'work' (see nu-
mil), and the Persian agential suff. -dar, meaning
'holder, possessor', which is rel. to Avestic
darayeiti, 'holds, supports', OI. dharayati, of
s.m., fr. I.-E. base *dher(e)-, 'to hold, support',
whence also L. firmus, 'firm, steadfast, stable,
strong'. See firm, adj., and cp. the first element
in Darius. Cp. also the second element in baha-
dur, chobdar, cbokidar, dizdar, dufterdar, ea-
amdar, fonjdar, bavildar, jnghiredar, jemadar,
killadar, ressaldar, silladar, sirdar, subahdar,
tahsildar, talakdar, thanadar, zemindar.

## auncel
auncel, п., a weight used in England in the Middle
Ages. — AF. auncelle, fr. It. lancella, dimin. of
lance, 'balance', fr. L. lanx, gen. lands, 'plale,
dish; scale of the weighing machine'. See
balance. The loss of the initial / in E. auncel is due
to the circumstance that the initial / in It.
lancella was mistaken for the It. def. art. /' and
consequently dropped.

## aunt
aunt, n. — AF. aunte, fr. OF. ante (F. tame), fr.
L. amita, 'father's sister', which is formed with
-ita, a suff. of prob. Etruscan origin, from the
infantile imitative base *am(ma), 'mother,
grandmother, nurse'. Cp. Gk. άμμά, άμμάς, άμμίά,
'mother', ON. amma, 'grandmother', OHG.
amma, 'mother, nurse', Mir. ammait, 'old hag'.
The base occurs also in the Semitic languages;
cp. Heb. em, Aram.-Syr. em, Arab, umm, imm,
Ethiop. em, Akkad. ummu, 'mother'. Cp. also
the second element in begum.

## aura
aura, n. emanation; aroma. — L., 'breeze, wind,
air', fr. Gk. aipi, 'air in motion, breeze', which
is rel. to άήρ, 'air'. See air and cp. soar.

## aural
aural, adj., of, or pertaining, to the ear. Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. auris, 'ear'. See auricle.
Derivative: aural-ly, adv.

## aural
aural, adj., pertaining to an aura. — Formed fr.
aura with adj. suff. -al.

## auramine
auramine, aurainin, п., a yellow dyestuff (chem.)
— Coined fr. L. aurum, 'gold' (see aureate), and
amine.

## aureate
aureate, adj., golden (rare). — L. aureatus, fr.
aureus, 'golden', fr. aurum, 'gold', lit. 'the
shining metal', fr. I.-E. base *awes-, 'to shine',
whence also OLith. ausas, Lith. auksas, OPruss.
ausis, 'gold', and possibly also Toch. A was, of
s.m. See aurora and cp. auksinas, auramine, au-
relia, aureole, aurin, dorado, El Dorado, loriot,
moidore, or, 'gold', ore, oriflamme, oriole,
ormolu, oroide, orphrey, orpiment.

## aurelin
aurelin, п., butterfly chrysalis. — ModL., fr. It.
aurelia, prop. fem. of aurelio, 'shining like gold',
fr. L. aurum, 'gold'. See aureate and cp. Aurelia.
Derivative: aureli-an, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:88 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 61 | AUTOBIOGRAPHY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:88 COLUMN:1 -->

## Aurella
Aurella, fem. PN. — L., fern, of Aurelius (q.v.)

## Aurelius
Aurelius, masc. PN. — L., the name of a Roman
gens, rel. to aurum, 'gold'. See aureate.

## Aureobasidium
Aureobasidium, п., a genus of basidiomycetes
(bot.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. L. aureus,
'of gold, golden', and basidium, a word of Greek
origin. The correct form would be Chrysobasi-
dium, in which both elements are of Greek
origin (see chryso- and cp. aureomycin).

## aureole
aureole, п., celestial crown. — L. aureola {corona),
'golden crown', fem. of aureolus, 'golden*, di-
min. of aureus, fr. aurum, 'gold'. See aureate
and cp. oriole,

## aureomycin
aureomycin, п., an antibiotic drug resembling
penicillin (med.) — A hybrid coined fr. L.
aureus, 'golden' (so called from its color), Gk.
μΰκης, 'fungus', and chem. suff. -in; see
aureate and myco-. The correct form would be
chrysomycin, in which both elements are of
Greek origin (see chryso- and cp.
Aureobasidium),

## ami-
ami-, combining form meaning 'gold'. — Fr. L.
aurum, 'gold'. See aureate,

## auri-
auri-, combining form meaning 'ear*. — Fr. L.
auris, 'ear'. See auricie.

## aurichalcite
aurichalcite, п., a basic copper zinc carbonate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. L.
aurichalcum, 'yellow copper ore*, popular
alteration of orichalcum (as if related to aurum,
'gold'), fr. Gk. ορείχαλκος, 'a kind of copper',
later 'brass', lit. 'mountain copper', fr. δρος,
'mountain', and χαλκός, 'copper*. See ого-,
'mountain', and chaico- and cp. orichalc. For
the change of the Greek masculine gender to
Latin neuter cp. Gk. κασσίτερος, 'tin', whence
L. cassiterum (see cassiterite).

## auricle
auricle, п., 1) the external ear; 2) chamber of the
heart. — L. auricula, 'the external ear", dimin.
of auris, 'ear', which stands for *ausis, fr. I.-E.
base *awei-, *au-, 'to perceive'. See ear, 'the
organ of hearing', and cp. aural, 'pertaining to the
ear'. For the ending see suff. -cle.
Derivative: auricl-ed, adj.

## auricula
auricula, п., the Alpine primula (bot.) — Lit. 'a
little ear'. See auricle.
Derivatives: auricular (q.v.), auricul-ale, adj.

## auricular
auricular, adj., I) pertaining to the ear; 2)
pertaining to an auricle. — ML. auricularis, fr. L.
auricula. See auricle and adj. surf. -ar.

## auricalo-
auricalo-, combining form meaning 'auricular'.
— Fr. L. auricula. See auricle,

## auriferous
auriferous, adj., containing gold. — Compounded
of L. aurum, 'gold', and ferre, 'to bear, carry*.
See aureate and -ferous.

## auriform
auriform, adj., earshaped. — Compounded of L.
auris, 'ear', and forma, 'form, shape'. See auricle
and -form,

## aurify
aurify, v., to turn into gold. — See aureate and -fy.

## Auriga
Auriga, п., the Charioteer (astron.) — L. auriga,
'a charioteer, driver', compounded of aureae
(pi.), 'bridle of a horse', and -iga, 'driver'. Aureae
stands for Oreae (pi.), a derivative of 6s, gen. oris,
'mouth'; -iga derives fr. agere, 'to set in motion,
drive, lead'. See oral and agent, adj.

## nurigal
nurigal, adj., pertaining to a charioteer. — L.
aurigalis, fr. auriga. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.

## Aurignacian
Aurignacian, adj. and n. (archaeol.) — Named
from Aurignac, in the department of Haute-
Garonne in France, a place where many
utensils of primeval man were first discovered. For
the ending see suff. -ian.

## aurilave
aurilave, п., earcleaner. — Compounded of L.
auris, 'ear', and lavdre, 'to wash'. See auricle
and lave,

## aurin
aurin, п.; a poisonous red synthetic dye. —
Formed with chem. suff. -in fr. L. aurum, 'gold'.
See aurente.

## aurist
aurist, п., ear specialist, otologist. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. auris, 'ear1 (see aureate), and -ist, a
suff. of Greek origin.

## auro-
auro-, combining form meaning 'gold'. — Fr. L.
aurum, 'gold'. See aureate,

## auro-
auro-, combining form meaning 'wind*. — Fr.
Gk. αΰρά, 'breeze'. See aura,

## aurochs
aurochs, п., the European bison. — G. Auerochs,
fr. MHG. ur(ohse), fr. OHG. ur(ohso), rel. to
ON. Qrr (gen. Qrar), of s.m., ON. Or, 'fine rain,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:88 COLUMN:2 -->
drizzle', ON. urigr, OE. urig, 'wet', and cogn.
with Gk.. ουρον, L. urina, 'urine', but OI.
usrah, 'ox', is not cognate; see urine. For the
second element in aurochs see ox. L. urus,
'aurochs', is a Teut. loan Vord; see urus.

## aurora
aurora, п., the dawn of day; (cap.) the goddess
of dawn in Roman mythology, identified with
the Greek Eos. — L. aurora, 'dawn', for *au-
sosa (for the form cp. L. Flora, 'the goddess of
flowers', fr. flos, gen. floris, 'flower'), fr. I.-E.
base 'awes-, 'to shine', whence also Gk. εως,
Homeric ήώς (for *ausds), 'dawn', Of. usdh,
Lith. ausra, 'dawn*, L. auster, 'south wind', ON.
austr, OE. east, 'east'. See east and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also L. aurum, 'gold',
which also derives fr. I.-E. base *awes-, 'to
shine', and lit. denotes the shining metal (see
aureate and cp. words there referred to). Cp.
also the first element in Ostrogoth.

## aurora australis
aurora australis, the Southern Lights. — L., lit.
'southern dawn'. See aurora and austral.

## aurora borealis
aurora borealis, the Northern Lights. — L., lit.
'northern dawn'. The term was introduced by
Gassendi in 1621. See aurora and boreal.

## aurum
aurum, п., gold (term of chemistry). — L. See
aurente.

## auscultate
auscultate, tr. and intr. v., to examine by
auscultation. — L. auscultatus, pp. of auscultare.
See next word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: auscultation (q.v.), auscult-at-ive,
adj., auscultat-or, п., auscultat-ory, adj.

## auscultation
auscultation, п., a listening to the sounds in the
human body. — L. auscultutio, gen. -onis, fr.
auscultatus, pp. of auscultare, 'to hear with
attention, listen to'. L. auscultare was prob.
formed with metathesis fr. "aus-clutare, fr. "aus-
clutos, 'heard with one's (own) ears', fr. *aus-is
(whence auris), 'ear', and *clutos, 'heard '(cp.
in-clutus, 'celebrated, famous'). See auricle and
loud. Accordingly auscultare lit. means 'to hear
with one's (own) ears*. Cp. Gk. ώτακουστεΐυ, 'to
hearken, listen to', fr. ωτακουστής, 'hearkener,
listener', which is compounded of ους, gen.
ώτός, 'ear', and ακούει, 'to hear', hence is
analogous to L. aus-cultare both in sense and
form. Cp. scout, 'spy'.

## auslaut
auslaut, п., final sound. — G. Auslaut, fr. aus,
'out of, and Laul, 'sound, tone', G. aus derives
fr. MHG. «3, fr. OHG. «3, which is rel. to Goth.,
ΟΝ., OE. ut; see out. G. Laut, 'sound, tone',
comes fr. laut, 'loud'. See loud and cp. ablaut,
aninut, ialaiit, umlaut.

## Ausonia
Ausonia, п., a poetic name for Italy. — L. Au-
sonia, fr. Ausones (Gk. Αΰσονες), 'the Auson-
ians', ancient inhabitants of Middle and Lower

## auspicate
auspicate, tr. v., to predict. — L. ouspicatus, pp.

## auspice

For the first element see aviary and cp. auscul-
tatioa, for the second see species and cp. spy.

## anspicious

Formed with suff. -011s fr. L. auspicium. See prec.

picious-ness, n.

## Auster
Auster, п., the south wind. — L., of uncertain
origin. It is perh. cogn. with ON. austr, п.,
'east*; adv., 'eastward', OHG. ostar, 'to the
east' (whence ostar-rihi, G. Osterreich,
'Austria'), Lett, "austrs, 'eastern' in austrums, 'east',
OSlav. ustru, 'pertaining lo summer', Avestic
ushas-tara, 'eastern*, and with OHG. ostan, OE.
east, 'east'; see aurora and cp. austral; cp. also
east. However, on the basis of this etymology,
it is difficult to explain why L. auster denotes the
'south wind' (and not the 'east wind'). See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, p. 87, where also an
attempt is made to explain the meaning of L.
auster.

## austere
austere, adj., stern, severe; very simple. — OF.
austere (F. austere), fr. L. austina, 'dry, harsh,
sour, tart', fr. Gk. αυστηρός, 'harsh, rough,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:88 COLUMN:3 -->
bitter', fr. αβειν, 'to dry', fr. αδος, 'dry*. See

## austerity
austerity, п., the quality of being austere. — OF.

of austiritas, fr. austirus. See prec. word and -ity.

## Austin
Austin, masc. PN. — Abbreviation of Augustin
(qv.)

## austral
austral, adj. southern; southerly. — L. australis,

## Australia
Australia, n. — Lit. 'southern land', fr. L.

## austro-
austro-, combining form meaning 'south*. — Fr.

## aut-

autarchy, п., absolute sovereignty.—Gk. αύταρ-

autarchy, п., autarky.—See next word; influenced

autarky, п., self-sufficiency. — Gk. αυτάρκεια,

auth-, form of auto- before an aspirate.

## authentic
authentic, adj. authoritative; reliable; genuine. —
OF. autentique (F. authentique), fr. Gk.
αυθεντικός, 'original, genuine, principal', fr. αυθέντης,
αϋτο-έντης, 'absolute master, ruler; murderer',

άνυω, Att. άνΰω, Ί accomplish', and cogn. with

Derivatives: authentic, п., authentic-al-ly, adv.,

## authority
authority, n. — F. autor ite, fr. L. auctoritatem,

Derivatives: authorit-arian, adj. and п.,

ness, n.

## authorize
authorize, tr. v. — OF. autoriser (F. autoriser),

Derivatives: authoriz-able, adj., authoriz-ation,

## autism
autism, п., morbid admiration of oneself

anto, n. (colloq.) — Short for automobile.

autobiography, n. — Compounded of auto- and
biography {first used by the English poet and prose

autocade, п., a procession of automobiles. — A

nntocephalous, adj., having its own head or chief.

autoclave, п., a container used for sterilizing and

ic-at-ly, adv.

antodidact, п., one self-taught. — Gk.

8ι8ακτός, 'taught', verbal adj. of διδάσκειν, 'to

Derivative: autodidact-ic, adj.

autogeny, п., autogenesis. — See autogenesis and

## automation

## antomaton
antomaton, п., 1) any automatic device; 2) any

αΰτόματον, neut. of αυτόματος, 'acting of one's

Automedon, п., a friend and charioteer of

ment of base 'me-, 'to measure'. See meditate

## antomobile

Derivatives: automobile, n. and intr. v., auto-

## autonomic
autonomic, adj. — See autonomous and -ic.

autonomist, n. — Formed with sun", -ist fr. Gk.

## autonomous

For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## autonomy
autonomy, п., self-government. — Gk. αυτονομία,

## autonymous

antoplasty, n. (surg.) — Compounded of anto-

## autumn
autumn, n. — OF. autompne (F. automne), fr. L.

It. autunno, Rum toamna, Provenc. autom, Sp.

otono, OPort. atuno, Port, outono, 'autumn',

## auxanometer
auxanometer, п., an instrument for measuring
, the growth of plants. — Compounded of

## auxesis
auxesis, п., amplificaiion, hyperbole (rhet.) —

## auxetic
auxetic, auxetical, adj., pertaining to auxesis. —

## auxiliary
auxiliary, adj. — L. auxiliaris, 'helpful', fr. auxi-
lium, 'help, aid, assistance, support*, which is

## aval
aval, п., endorsement on a bill. — F., fr. It. avallo,

## avalanche
avalanche, п., mass of snow sliding down a

## avale
avale, tr. v., to cause to descend. — F. avaler, fr.
ά val, 'downhill', lit. 'to the valley', fr. d, 'to'

avaricious, adj., greedy. — F. avaricieux (fern.

Oer\valives:avaria'ous-ly,adv.,avaricious-ness,n.

avast, interj., hold! stop! (naut.) — Prob.

pref. au-, OSlav. и, 'at, with', Olr. 0, Qa, 'down,
from*; cp. the first element in vesania and in

words there referred to.

## avaunr
avaunr, interj., begone. — F. avant, 'forward', fr.
L. ab ante, 'from before', whence also It. avanti,
OSp., Port, avante, Catal. avant, OProvenc.
mans. See advance and cp. ci-devant. Cp. also

of a boot', vamplate, vanguard, vanward.

## ave
ave, interj., i)hail!; 2)farewell!; п., the salutation
ave. — L. ave, in vulgar speech have, 'hail,
farewell', fr. Phoen.-Punic. huwi, corresponding to
Heb. hdyi*, imper. sing. masc. of Phoen.-Punic
hawd, resp. Heb. hayah, 'he lived'. Cp. Plautus,
Poenulus, 994, 998, 1001, and see Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW., I, pp. 80-81. — The identity of the
Semitic bases h-w-h (h-w-) and h-y-h is
illustrated in Gen. 3:20, 'And the man called his wife's
name H4e(Hawwa4'), because she was the mother
of all living (hay)'. See Eve. For sense
development cp. Heb. y*hi adhdnt hammilekh
Dawfdh I'oldm: 'Let my lord king David live for
ever!' (I Kings ]:31; cp. Dan. 2.4 and passim),
E. 'Long live the King!', F. 'Vive le roi', etc.,
all used as formulas of greeting.
(The origin of L. ave being thus'established, we
shall be able to find the exact meaning of the
words with which the gladiators greeted the
emperor: 'Ave, Imperator, morituri te salutant'
(see Suetonius, Claudius 21). The usual rendering
is: 'Hail, Emperor, who are about to die salute
you'. In fact, however, the Latin words express
a perfect antithesis. According to my opinion,
their original meaning was: 'Live, Emperor!
They who are about to die salute you.')

## avellan

## A vena

— L. avina, 'oats', prob. formed fr. orig. *avig-
sna, but influenced in form by the ending of
arena, 'sand'; cogn. with OSlav. ovisu, 'oats',

## avenaceous

## avenalin

## avener

## avenge

(see a), and vengier (F. venger), fr. L. vindicare,
'to lay claim to, avenge, punish'. See vindicate
and cp. veugeance, revenge-
Derivatives: aveng-er, п., avenge-ful, adj., aveng-
ing, adj., aveng-ing-ly, adv.

## avens
avens, п., a plant of the genus Geum (bot.) —
ME. avence, fr. OF. avence.

## aventail
aventail, п., ventail. — Formed—with change of
pref.—fr. OF. esveniail, fr. es- (fr. L. ex), 'out
of (see 1st ex-), and ventail.

## aventurine
aventurine, п., a kind of Venitian glass. — F., fr.
It. avventurino, fr. avvemura, 'chance', fr. VL.
advenlura (see adventure); so called because the
filings used in the fabrication of this glass are
thrown over the melting glass at random.

## avenue
avenue, n. — F., prop. fem. pp. aiavenir, 'to come
to', fr. L. advenire, fr. ad- and venire, 'to come'.
See venue, 'arrival', and cp. advene, advent.

## aver
aver, tr. v. — F. averer, fr. OF. averer, fr. a, 'to'
(see 4), and voire, 'true*, fr. L. virus, 'true'. Cp.
OProveng. averer, aveirar, It. averare, and see
very.

## average
average, п., 1) loss incurred by damage at sea;
2) an equitable division of such loss among all
the parties interested; 3) an arithmetical mean.
— F. avaric, 'damage to ship', fr. It. avaria,
fr. Sp.averia, fr. Arab. 'awartyah, 'merchandise
damaged by sea water', fr. 'awar, 'rent, tear;
flaw; damaged goods'.
Derivatives: average, adj. and tr. v.

## average
average, п., feudal service (Old English lav) —
ME., fr. ML. averagium, fr. ML. avera, fr. OF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:90 COLUMN:2 -->
oevre, ovre (F. auvre), 'work , fr. L. opera. See
opus and cp. opera. ML. avera was prob.
influenced in form by OF. aver, aveir, 'property',
prop. inf. used as a noun, fr. L. habere, 'to have'
(see habit).

## averah
averah, п., transgression, sin (Jewish religion). —
Heb. 'abhirdh, 'transgression', lit. 'a passing
over', fr. 'abhor, 'he passed over'. See Hebrew.

## averment
averment, n. — MF. averement, fr. averer (F.
averer). See aver and -ment.

## Averroism
Averroism, п., the teachings of the Arab
philosopher Averroes (= Ibn Rushd) (1126-98). For
the ending see suff. -ism.

## averruncate
averruncate, tr. v., to avert. — L. averruncatus,
pp. of averruncare, 'to avert, remove', fr. a
'away from', and verruncare, 'to turn', which is
rel. to verrere 'to sweep'. See a-, 'away from',
verricule and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: averruncat-ion, п., averruncat-or, n.

## nverse
nverse, adj. — L. aversus, 'turned away', pp. of
avertere. See avert.
Derivatives: averse-ly, adv., averse-ness, n.

## aversion
aversion, n. — F., fr. L. aversionem, ace. of aver-
sid, 'a turning away', fr. aversus, pp. of
avertere. See next word and -ion.

## avert
avert, tr. v., to prevent, ward off. —· L. avertere,
'to turn away', fr. a, 'away from', and vertere,
'to turn'. See a-, 'away from', and version.
Derivatives: avert-ed, adj., avert-ed-ly, adv.,
avert-ible, adj.

## Aves
Aves, n. pi., the class of birds (zool.) — L. avis
pi. of evii, 'bird'. See aviary.

## Avesta
Avesta, п., the sacred books of the Parsees. —
Pers., earlier form Avistak, lit. 'text'. Cp. Zend-
Avesta.
Derivatives: Avest-an, Avest-ic, adjs.

## aviarist
aviarist, п., one who keeps an aviary. — See next
word and -ist.

## aviary
aviary, n„ a place in which birds are kept. —
L. aviarium, 'a place where birds are kepi, an
aviary', fr. avis, 'bird', which is cogn. with OI.
ν/Λ, vih, Avestic vlsh, 'bird', OI. vayas-, 'fowl,
bird', Gk. αίετός, Att. αετός (for *ά^ετός),
'eagle', and prob. also with Arm. hav, 'bird'.
(For the insertion of the h cp. Arm. hot 'odor',
which is cogn. with L. odor, and hum, 'raw',
which is cogn. with Gk. ωμός.) Ср. aviation,
avion, the first element in aucupate, auspice,
aviculture, bustard, ocarina, ostrich, and the
second element in pettitoes. Cp. also ovum, eta;·

## aviation
aviation, n. — F., coined by G. de la Landelle (in
his Aviation ou Navigation aerienne, Paris, 1863)
fr. L. avis, 'bird' (see prec. word), and suff.
-ntion.

## aviator
aviator, n. — Refashioned after F. aviateur. See
prec. word and agential suff. -or.

## avlatress
avlatress, aviatrix, п., a woman aviator. —
Formed fr. aviator with suff. -ess, resp. -trix.

## Avicennism
Avicennism, п., the teachings of the Arab,
philosopher Avicenna (= Ibn Sina) (980-1037). For
the ending see suff. -ism.

## aviculture
aviculture, n. — Compounded of L. avis, 'bird',
and cultura, 'cultivation, culture'. See aviary
and culture.

## avid
avid, adj., eager. — F. a vide, fr. L. avidus,
'longing eagerly for; desirous, eager", fr. avire, 'to
long eagerly for, to wish, desire', which is prob,
cogn. with Co. awel, awett, 'wish, desire', W.
•ewyll, 'will, volition', OI. dvali, 'wishes, favors,
protects', avitdr, 'protector', Gk. έν-ηής (for
*έν-55ής), 'benevolent, affable'. Cp. nvarice,
audacious.
Derivatives: avid-ly, adv., avid-ious, adj., avid-
ious-ly, adv., avidity (q.v.)

## aridity
aridity, п., eagerness. — F. avidtii, fr. L. avidi-
tatem, ace. of aviditds, 'eagerness, avidity', fr.
avidus. See prec. word and -ity.

## avidya
avidya, п., relative knowledge. — OI. avidya, lit.
'non-knowledge', fr. pref. a-, 'not', and vidya,
'knowledge'. See priv. pref. an- and vldya.

## avifauna
avifauna, п., all the birds of a region, regarded
collectively. — Compounded of L. avis, 'bird'
(see avinry), and fauna.

## avion
avion, п., an airplane. — F., coined by the French
engineer Clement Ader (1841-1925) in 1875 fr.
L. avis, 'bird'. See aviary.

## avltal
avltal, adj., ancestral. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. avilus, 'pertaining to a grandfather,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:90 COLUMN:3 -->
ancestral', fr. avus, 'grandfather', whence
avunculus, 'uncle on the mother's side'. See uncle.

## avitamiaosis
avitamiaosis, П., lack of vitamins in one's food
(biochem.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. priv.
pref. a-, vitamin and suff. -osis.

## avizandum
avizandum, п., consideration (Scot. law). — ML.,
gerundive of avizare. See advise. For other Latin
gerundives used in English cp. agenda and
words there referred to.

## avocado
avocado, п., a tropical pear-shaped fruit. — Sp.,
fr. aguacale, fr. Nahuatl ahuacatl. Cp. alligator
penr.

## avocation
avocation, п., business; occupation; hobby. — L.
uvocatid, gen. -dnis, 'a calling off', fr. dvoedtus,
pp. of dvocdre, 'to call off*, formed fr. a, 'away
from', and vocare, 'to call'. See a-, 'from', and
vocatioa and cp. ndvocate.

## avocet
avocet, avoset, п., a bird with webbed feet (genus
Recurvirostra). — F. avocette, fr. It. avocetta,
which is of unknown origin.

## avogadrlte
avogadrlte, п., fluoborate of potassium and
caesium (mineral.) — Named after the Italian
physicist Amedeo Avogadro (1776-1856). For the
endine see subst. suff. -ite.

## avoid
avoid, tr. v. — ME. avoiden, formed — with
change of pref. — fr. OF. esvuidier, 'to empty',
fr. pref. es- (fr. L. ex), 'out of, and OF. volt,
voide, dial, forms ofvuit, vuide (F. vide), 'empty',
fr. VL. *vocit-(um), for *vacit-(um), for L.
vacat-(um), pp. stem of vacdre, 'to be empty'
See 1st ex- and void, adj.
Derivatives: avoid-аЫе, adj., avold-аЫ-у, adv.,
avoid-once, п., avoid-er, п., avoid-less, adj.,
avoid-ment, n.

## avoirdupois
avoirdupois, п., a system of weights. — Incorrect
for ME. avoir de pots, fr. OF. aveir de pais,
'goods of weight'. OF. aveir, 'goods', is prop,
the inf. aveir (F. avoir), 4o have', used as a
noun, fr. L. habere, 'to bave'; OF. (= F.) de,
from, of, derives fr. L. di, 'from, away from';
OF. peis, pois (F. poids), 'weight', comes fr. L.
pinsum, 'weight', which is prop, the neut. pp.
of pendere, 'to weigh'. See habit, de- and poise.
For the subst. use of the infinitive cp. attainder
and words there referred to.
Derivative: avoirdupois, adj.

## nvouch
nvouch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. avouehen, fr.
OF. avochier, fr. L. ad vocare, 'to summon to a
place', fr. ad- and vocare, 'to call'. See vouch.

## nvone
nvone, п., lawyer, solicitor. — F., 'solicitor', fr.
L. advocaius, 'advocate', prop, 'one called to
aid', pp. of advocdre. See next word.

## avow
avow, tr. v. — OF. avoer, avouer (F. avouer), fr.
L. advocdre, 4o call to; to summon to a place',
fr. ad- and vocare, 'to call', which is rel. to vox,
gen. vOcis, 'voice'. See voice and cp. advocate,
advowee, avoue.
Derivatives: avow-able, adj., avow-al, п.,
avowed, adj., avow-ed-ly, adv., avow-ed-ness, п., avow·
er, п., avowry (q.v.)

## avowry
avowry, n. — ME. avoerie, fr. OF. avoer, avouer.
See prec. word and -ry.

## avulsion
avulsion, п., a pulling away; a part torn off. — L.
avulsiu, gen. -onis, 'a tearing off, a plucking off,
fr. dvulsus, pp. of dvellere, 'to tear off, pluck off,
pull away', fr. d, 'away from', and vellere, 'to
tear, pull, pluck'. See a· 'away from', and velli-
cnte. For the ending see suff. -ion.

## avuncular
avuncular, adj., pertaining to an uncle. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. avunculus, 'uncle
on the mother's side'. See uncle and cp. words
there referred to.

## await
await, tr. v. — ME. awatten, fr. ONF. awaitier,
fr. a, 'to' (see a), and waitier, 'to watch*. See
ad- and wait

## awake
awake, tr. and intr. v. — Partly fr. ME. awaken,
fr. OE. dwacan (fr. a, 'on', and wacan, to arise,
awake*), partly fr. ME. awakien, fr. OE. dwacian
(fr. a, 'on', and wacian, 'to be awake, watch').
See n-, 'on', and wake, v.

## nwake
nwake, adj. — ME. awaken, earlier pp./r. OE.
dwsecnan. See awaken.

## nwaken
nwaken, tr. and intr. v. — OE. awxenan, fr. a-
'on', and wsecnan, 'to waken'. See waken.
Derivatives: awaken-er, п., awaken-ing, adj. and
п., awaken-ing-ly, adv.

## award
award, tr. v. — AF. awarder, formed — with
change of prefix — fr. ONF. eswarder, which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:91 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: AWARD | 64 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:91 COLUMN:1 -->
corresponds to OF. esgarder (MF. igarder), 'to
regard, examine', ft. es- (fr. L. ex), 'out of, and
warder, resp. garder, 'to observe'. See 1st ex-
and ward, v., and cp. guard, v.
Derivatives: award, n. (q.v.), award-er, n.

## award
award, n. — AF. award, fr. ONF. eswarl, which
corresponds to esgart, fr. esgarder. See award,
v.

## aware
aware, adj. — ME. iwar, у war, fr. OE. gewxr,
which is formed fr. pref. ge- (see y-) and wxr,
'aware, cautious*. See ware, 'alert1.
Derivative: aware-ness, n.

## awaruite
awaruite, п., a natural alloy of iron and nickel
(mineral.) — Named after Awarua Bay in New
Zealand. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## awash
awash, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
wash,

## away
away, adv. — ME. away, aweie, fr. OE. on weg,
lit. 'on the way'. See a-, 'on', and way.

## awe
awe, n, — ME. aghe, awe, fr. ON. agi, rel. to OE.
ege, 'fear', OHG. agiso, 'fright, terror', Goth.
agis, 'fear, anguish', prob. also to OHG. z-aggn,
MHG., G. zagen, 'to fear, hesitate', and cogn.
with Gk. £χος, 'pain, grief, ίχομαι, "I am
afflicted', Olr. -agor, Ί fear'.
Derivatives: awe, tr. v., awe-less, adj., aw-ful,
adj., aw-ful-ly, adv., aw-ful-ness, n.

## awsather
awsather, adv. and adj., on the weather side;
toward the wind (паи/.) — Formed fr. a-, 'on',
and weather.

## awhile
awhile, adv. — ME., fr. OE. one hwlle. See a-,
indef. art., and while,

## awkward
awkward, adj. — ME. awkwarde, lit. 'turned the
wrong way', formed fr. auk-, awk-, 'wrong,
contrary', and suff. -warde (see -ward). ME. auk-
is borrowed fr. ON. Ofugr, 'turned backward,
wrong, contrary', which is a derivative of a/,
'of, off. See of, off.
Derivatives: awkward-ly, adv., awkward-ness, n.

## awl
awl, n. — ME. at, alia, alle, fr. OE. xl, rel. to
ON. air, MLG. Ш, Du. aal, OHG. ah, MHG.
ale, G. Ahle, fr. Teut. *el6, corresponding to
I.-E. *ёШ, whence OI. ara, 'awl'. Lith. yla, Lett.
liens, OPruss. ylo, 'awl', are borrowed ft. Goth.
'lla. Cp. aniace.

## awn
awn, n. — ME. awne, agune, fr. ON. dgn, pi.
agnar, which is rel. to OE. egenu, OHG. agana,
MHG. agene, G. Anne, Goth, ahana, and cogn.
with OI. aidni-, 'arrowhead', Gk. £χνη (for
*ak-s-nu), 'husk of wheat, foam, froth', pi.
δχναι, 'chaff, άκοστή, 'barley', lit. 'the awny
one', OL. agna (for 'ac-na), 'ear, straw', L.
acus, gen. aceris, 'chaff, OPruss. ackons, 'awn,
beard', Lith. akuolas, Lett, akudts of s.m., fr.
I.-E. base *ak-, *aq-, 'sharp'. See acrid and cp.
ear, 'corn'. Cp. also acerose.
Derivatives: awn, tr. v., awn-ed, adj., awn-er, п.,
awn-less, awn-y, adjs.

## awning
awning, n. — Of uncertain origin; perhaps formed
with suff. -ing fr. F. auvent, 'shed, pent roof,
which is rel. to OProvenc. amban, anvan, 'a kind
of parapet'.

## awoke
awoke, past tense of awake. — See awake and
woke,

## awry
awry, adv. and adj. — Formed fr. a-, 'on', and
wry.

## ax
ax, axe, n. — OE. eax, sex, rel. to OS. accus,acus,
ON. ex, ox, ex, Dan. ekse, Norw. eks, Swed.
уха, OFris. axe, OHG. ackus, MHG. ackes,
G. Axt, Goth, aqlzi, and cogn. with Gk. άξίνη,
'ax', L. ascia (for *acsia-), 'ax; mason's trowel'.
All these words are prob. of Sem. origin; cp.
Akkad. has(s)innu, Aram.-Syr. batzina, 'ax'. Cp.
axinite, adz.
Derivative: ax, tr. v.

## axial
axial, adj. pertaining to an axis. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. axis. See axis and cp. the
second element in coaxial, uniaxial,

## nxil
nxil, п., upper angle between a leaf, branch, etc.,
and the stem (hot.) — L. axilla, 'armpit'. See
aisle and cp. words there referred to.

## axile
axile, adj., pertaining to an axis (hot.) — Formed
with suff. -De fr. L. axis. See axis,

## axilla
axilla, п., armpit (anal, and zool.) — L. See nxil.
Derivative: axill-ary, adj. and n.

## axialte
axialte, п., a borosilicate of aluminum and
calcium (mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite
fr. Gk. άξίνη, 'ax'. See ax.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:91 COLUMN:2 -->
axiom, n. — F.,axiome, fr. L. axioma, fr. Gk.
αξίωμα, gen. αξιώματος, 'that which is thought
worthy', fr. άξιοϋν, 'to think Worthy', fr. άξιος,
'worthy', prop; 'weighty', from the base of
ίγειν, 'to lead', used in the sense of'to weigh',
which is cogn. with L. agere, 'to set in motion,
drive, lead'. See agent, adj., and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also the second element in
chronaxy. For the ending see suff. -oma.

## axiomatic
axiomatic, axiomatical, adj. — Gk. αξιωματικός,
fr. αξίωμα, gen. αξιώματος. See prec. word and
1st -atic.
Derivative: axiomatical-ly, adv.

## axis
axis, n. — L., axletree, 'axle, chariot, wagon,
axis', cogn. with Gk. άξων, 'axis, axle, wagon*,
Gk. ίμ-αξα, 'carriage', prop, 'that which has
one axle', OI. dksah, 'axis, axle', L. axilla,
'armpit', ala (for *acs-la), 'wing', OSlav. osl, Lith.
aSiz, OPruss. assis, Lett, ass, 'axle', Ir. aiss,
'cart', W. echell, 'axle', OE. eax, OFris. axe,
OS., OHG. ansa, MHG. ahse, G. Achse, ON.
oxull, 'axis, axle'. All these words are
derivatives of I.-E. base ·<#-, 'to lead'. See agent,
adj., and cp. axilla, axle, axon, ala, aisle,
aileron, axial

## axle
axle, n. — ME. axel in the compound axeltre,
fr. ON. Sxul-tre, 'axletree', rel. to ON. oxl, OE.
eaxl, OS. ahsla, OHG. ahsala, G. Achsel,
'shoulder', and cogn. with L. axilla, 'armpit'. See prec.
word and cp. aisle.
Derivative: axl-ed, adj.

## Axmtnster
Axmtnster, п., name of a kind of carpet. —
Named after Axminster, England, where it was
orig. made.

## axo-
axo-, before a vowel ax-, combining form
meaning 'axis'. — Gk. άξο-, άξ-, fr. άξων, 'axis, axle'.
See axon.

## axolotl
axolotl, п., any of several salamanders. — Sp., fr.
Nahuatl, lit. 'servant of the water'.

## axon
axon, п., axis of the vertebrate body. — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άξων, 'axis, axle, vertebra', which is
cogn. with L. axis, 'axis, axle'. See axis.

## Axonopus
Axonopus, п., a genus of plants of the family
Poaceae (bol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
ίξων, 'axis', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See
axon and podo-.

## axunge
axunge, п., lard. — Earlier F. axunge (F. axonge),
fr. L. axungia, 'axletree grease, grease, fat',
which is compounded of axis, 'axletree, axis',
and ungere, 'to grease'. See axis and unguent.

## ay
ay, aye, interj., yes. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: ay, aye, n.

## ayah
ayah, п., a native Hindu nurse. — Hind, aya,
aya, fr. Port, aia, 'nurse, governess', which,
together with Sp. aya, of s.m., derives fr. L. avia,
'grandmother', used in the sense of 'an aged
woman who takes care of the children*. L. avia
derives fr. avus, 'grandfather', whence avunculus,
'uncle on the mother's side'. See uncle and cp.
words there referred to.

## ayah
ayah, п., a verse (in 1he Koran). — Arab, aya",
lit. 'a sign', contraclion of *awayak, rel. to Heb.
oth, Aram.-Syr. at/id, 'sign'.

## aye
aye, ay, adv., ever, always. — ME. ei, ai, ay, fr.
ON. ei, which is rel. to OE. ά, δ, OS. So, 'always,
ever', OHG. eo, later io, MHG. re, G.je, Goth.
aiw, 'ever' and cogn. with Gk. ala, Cyprian,
Phocian, Locrian mife£ (for 'aifeoi), 'always',
Gk. αιών (for *aif ων), 'age, eternity', L. aevum,
'space of time, eternity'. See aeon and cp. each,
ever, the first element in either and the second
element in nay. Cp. also Aeolus, age, eternal.

## nye-aye
nye-aye, п., a small rodent (Daubentonia mada-
gascariensis). — F., fr. Malagasy aiaf, imitative
of the animal's cry.

## ayin
ayin, п., name of the 16th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb. 'ayin, 'eye'; so called in
allusion to the ancient form of this letter. Cp.
Aram, 'ayna, 'end, Syr. 'aynn, Ugar. 'я, Arab.
'ayn, Ethiop. 'ayn, Akkad. emi, 'eye'.

## az-
az-, form of azo- before a vowel.

## Azalea
Azalea, п., a genus of plants of the heath family
(bot.)~ ModL., fr. Gk. άζαλέος, 'dry', fr. άζα,
'dryness, mold', rel. to άζειν, 'to dry up', fr.
I.-E. base *us, 'to be do', to be hot', whence also
Golh. azgo, OE. asce, £sce, 'ashes'. See ash,
'powdery substance', and cp. the first element
in Azolla. This genus of plants was called Azalea

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:91 COLUMN:3 -->
(lit. 'dry plant') because it grows best in a
dry soil.

## azam
azam, п., Persian title of respect. —Arab, a'zam,
'greater', al-a'zam, 'the greatest', elative of
'azim, 'great', fr. 'azuma, 'was great', rel. to 'azm,
Ethiop. adm, 'bones', Hebi 'atzam, 'was
mighty', 'etzem, 'bone', Aram.-Syr. 'atma (in
Babylonian Aram, weakened into atma), 'thigh',
Akkad. e$emtu, 'bones', esenseru, 'backbone,
spine'.

## Azariah
Azariah, masc. PN. (Bible) — Heb. 'Azarydh, lit.
'God has helped'. See Ebenezer and cp. Ezra.

## azarole
azarole, п., fruit of the Neapolitan Medlar
(Crataegus Azarolus); the tree itself. — F. azerole,
fr. Sp. acerola, fr. Arab, az-zu'rara*, 'the
medlar', fr. az-, assimilated form of al-, 'the', and
za'rura", name of unity fr. za'rur, which is rel.
to Mishnaic Heb. 'uzrar, 'medlar'.

## Azazel
Azazel, n„ place to which the scapegoat was sent
(Bible). — Heb. ΆζαζέΙ; in the Talmud
(Yoma 67b) explained as a compound of 'az,
'firm, rough', and el, 'strong'. (Cp. Gesenius-
Buhl, HWAT., p. 576a.)

## azedarach
azedarach, п., the China tree and its bark. —
F. azedarac, fr. Pers. azad dirakhl, 'free (i.e.
noble) tree*.

## Azilian
Azilian, adj., pertaining to one of the transition
periods of lhe Old Stone Age. — From the name
of the village Mas a'Azil in the French
Pyrenees, where remains were found. For the ending
see suff. -Ian.

## azimuth
azimuth, п., distance of a star from the North or
South point of the meridian (astron.) — F.azi-
mut, fr. Arab, as-sumil, pi. oias-samt, 'the way',
fr. as-, assimilated form of al-, 'the', and saml,
'way'. See zenith and cp. altazimnth.

## azo-
azo-, before a vowel az-, combining form
denoting the presence of nitrogen (chem.) —
Shortened fr. azote (q.v.) Cp. diazo-, thiazine.

## azoic
azoic, adj., without life. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. £ζωος, 'without life', fr. ά- (see priv.
pref. a-) and ζωή, 'life'. See zoo- and cp. azote.

## Azolla
Azolla, п., a genus of plants of the salvinia family
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. άζειν. Ίο
dry', and όλλύναι, 'to destroy'. For the first
element see Azalea, for the second see Apollyon.

## azoaic
azoaic, adj., not pertaining to a particular zone.
— Gk. άζωνικός, fr. αζωνος, 'not confined to
a zone', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and ζωνή, 'belt,
zone'. See zone and -ic.

## azorite
azorite, п., a variety of zircon (mineral.) —
Named after the Azores. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## azote
azote, п., nitrogen. — F., lit. 'without life';
coined by the French chemist Antoine-Laurent
de Lavoisier (1743-94) ш '776 ft- P«v. pref. a-
and Gk. ζωή,'life' (see zoo- and cp. azoic); so
called by him because this element is incapable
of supporting life.
Derivatives: azot-ic, adj., azotile (q.v.), azot-ize,
tr. v.

## azote
azote, п., a whip. — Sp., fr. Arab, as-saut, lit.,
'the whip', fr. as-, assimilated form of al-, 'the',
and saut, 'whip', which is rel. to Heb. shot,
Aram, shotd, Syr. shufa, Ethiop. saut, 'whip',
Heb. shut,, 'to rove about', Akkad. shSfu, 'to
drag'.

## azoren
azoren, п., a flat roof. — Sp., fr. Arab, as-satb,
lit. 'the roof, fr. as-, assimilated form of at-,
'the', and sa/h, 'roof, fr. sataha, 'he spread out',
which is rel. to Heb. shatdfi, Aram.-Syr. sh'tah,
'he spread out'.

## azorite
azorite, п., salt of nitrous acid (chem.) — Formed
fr. azote with subst. suff. -ite.

## azulene
azulene, п., blue hydrocarbon (chem.) — Formed
with suff. -ene fr. Sp. azul, 'blue*. See next word.

## nzure
nzure, adj. — ME. asur, fr. OF. azur, fr. Med.
Lat. azura (whence also Ital. azzurro, Sp. azur,
azul, Port, azul), fr. Arab, al-lazaward, fr. Pers.
lajward, 'lapis lazuli'; so called from Lajward,
a place in Turkestan, mentioned in Marco
Polo's Travels. The initial /was mistaken for the
definite article and consequently dropped in the
Romanic languages. Cp. azulene. Cp. also
lapis laznli.

## azurite
azurite, п., hydrous carbonate of copper
(mineral.) — Formed fr. azure with subst. suff. -ite;
so called from its color.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:92 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 65 AZVME -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:92 COLUMN:1 -->

## azygo-
azygo-, combining form meaning 'azygous'.—G k.
άζυγο-, fr. ίίζυγος. See azygous.

## azygous
azygous, adj., odd. — Gk. ίίζυγος, 'odd. not
forming a pair', fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:92 COLUMN:2 -->
ζυγόν, 'yoke'. See zygo-, yoke. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to.Glc. -ος, see suff. -ous.

## azyme
azyme, azym, п., unleavened bread. — Late L.
azymus, fr. Gk. ίίζϋμος, 'unleavened', formed

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:92 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and ζύμη, 'leaven'.
See zyme.
Derivatives: azym-ic, azym-ous, adjs.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:93 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:93 COLUMN:1 -->

## baa
baa, intr. v., to bleat. — Imitative of the cry of
the sheep.
Derivative: baa, n.

## Baal
Baal, п., the name of many deities of the Semitic
peoples. — Heb. Bd'al (pi. B''ailm), lit. 'owner,
master, lord', fr. bd'al, 'he took possession of,
he married', rel. to Akkad. Bilu (whence Heb.
Bel, Gk. Βήλος), name of Marduk (lit. 'Ruler'),
bdlu, 'rule', Arab, bd'ala, 'he possessed (esp. a
wife)', ba'l, 'husband', Ethiop. ba'ala, 'he
married'. Cp. Bel and Betdah and the first element
in Beelzebub.

## Bab
Bab, п., title given to the founder of Babism. —
Pers. bob, 'door, gate', fr. Arab, bub, of s.m.,
fr. Aram, babh, babha, fr. Akkad. babu, 'door,
gate', which is shortened fr. *nebubd, lit. 'hole,
aperture', from Sem. stem n-b-b, 'to make
hollow, to hollow out', whence aiso Heb. n'bhubh,
'hollowed', A ram.-Syr. abbubhd, Akkad. imbubu,
'flute', Arab, anbib, 'part of reed between
knots'. Cp. Babel.
Derivatives: Bab-ism, п., Bab-ist, n.

## habacoote
habacoote, п., a Madagascan lemur (zool.) —
Malagasy.

## Babbitt
Babbitt, babbitt, п., a conventional businessman.
— So called after George Babbitt, the title
character of a novel by Sinclair Lewis (1922).
Derivative: Babbit-ry, babbii-ry, n.
Babbitt metal. — Named after its inventor Isaac
Babbitt (1799-1862).

## babble
babble, intr. and tr. v. — ME. babelen, from the
I.-E. imitative base *bab-, whence also ON.
babha, Swed. babbla, Norw. babble, LG. bab-
beln, Du. babbelen, G. babbeln, 'to prattle', L.
babulus, 'babbler', F. babiller, 'to stutter,
stammer'; cp. babe, baboon, bauble. Cp. the related
imitative base *balb-, whence L. balbus,
'stammerer'; see balbuties, booby. Cp. also the related
imitative base *barb-, 'to stammer', whence Gk.
βάρβαρος, 'foreign, barbarous'; see barbaric,
brave.
Derivatives: babble, п., babbl-er, п., babbl-ing,
n. and adj., babbl-ing-ly, adv., babbl-ish, adj.,
babbl-ish-ly, adv., babbl-ish-ness, п., babbl-y,adj.

## babe
babe, n. — ME., of imitative origin. See prec.
word and cp. baby. Cp. also boy.

## Babel
Babel, п., name of the capital of Babylonia. —
Heb. Babhel, fr. Akkad. Bab-ilu, lit. 'the gate of
God', prop, a literal translation of Sumerian
Ka-dingir. Akkad. Bab-ilu is compounded of
bob, 'gate', and Ни, 'god'. The first element is
rel. to Aram, babh, babha, 'door, gate'; see Bab.
For the second element see EL Cp. the second
element in Zerubhabel. Cp. also Babylon.

## habiroussa
habiroussa, babirussa, п., a species of wild swine.
— Malay, compounded of bdbi, 'hog', and
rusa, 'deer'.

## baboo
baboo, п., Master, Mr. — Hind. babu.

## baboon
baboon, n. — ME. baboin, fr. OF. babuin, ba-
bouin (F. babouiri), a blend of babine, 'the
pendulous lip of certain animals, esp. monkeys' (the
baboon has prominent lips), and baboue, 'wry,
ugly face'; both babine and baboue are of
imitative origin. See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 49
s.v. babouin. MDu. baubijn (whence Du. baviaari)
is an OF. loan word. G. Pavian is borrowed fr.
Du. baviaari.
Derivative: baboon-ery, n.

## babouche
babouche, п., a heelless Oriental slipper. — F.,
fr. Arab, babash, fr. Pers. pdpush, lit. 'foot-
covering', fr. pa, 'foot', and the verb pushiden,
'to cover'. Pers. pa is rel. to Avesticparf-, 'foot';
see foot The change of ρ to b proves that the
word came into Europe through the medium of
the Arabic, which having no p, regularly
changes the ρ of foreigu words into b.

## baby
baby, n. — Dimin. of babe.
Derivatives: baby, adj. and tr. v., baby-hood, п.,
baby-ish, adj., baby-ish-ly, adv., baby-ish-ness,n.

## Babylon
Babylon, п., the capital of Babylonia. — L., fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:93 COLUMN:2 -->
в
Gk. Βαβυλών, fr. Akkad. ВйЬ-ilani, 'the gate
of the gods', fr. bub, 'gate', and Hani, pi. of Ни,
'god*. Compared with Akkad. Bab-ilu (see
Babel), Bab-Hani is a later form, occurring in
texts dating from the Neo-Babylonian period.

## Babylonia
Babylonia, n. — L., fr. Gk. Βαβυλωνία, fr.
Βαβυλών. See prec. word.
Derivatives: Babyloni-an, adj. and n.

## hacalao
hacalao, п., a West Indian fish, Mycteroperca
falcaia. — Sp., 'codfish', fr. L. baculum, 'a stick,
a staff', whence also ODu. bakeljauw. See
bacillus and cp. cabilliau. For sense development
cp. stockfish.

## Bacbuc
Bacbuc, п., name of the Holy Bottle in Rabelais'
Pantagruel. — Heb. baqbuq, 'flask', a word of
imitativeorigin; so called from the gurglingsound
of emptied liquid (cp. Arab, baqbaqa", 'gurgling
noise'). Cp. Syriac buq, 'a two-handled vase or
jug', and see beaker.

## baccalaureate
baccalaureate, п., the academic degree of
bachelor. — ML. baccalauredtus, fr. baccalaureus,
fr. baccalarius, 'the holder of a small farm; a
young man', which is of uncertain origin;
influenced in form by L. bacca, 'berry', and laureus,
'of laurel', fr. laurus, 'laurel'. Cp. bachelor. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ate.

## baccara
baccara, baccarat, п., a gambling card game. —
F., of unknown origin.

## baccate
baccate, adj., bearing berries. — L. bdcatus, bac-
cutus, fr. bdca, bacca, 'berry'. See hacci- and
adj. suff. -ate.

## Bacchae
Bacchae, n. pi., the female attendants of Bacchus.
— L., fr. Gk. Βάκχαι, pi. of Βάκχη, fr. Βάκχος.
See Bacchus.

## bacchanal
bacchanal, adj., pertaining to Bacchus; pertaining
to a reveler. — L. bacchanalis, fr. Bacchus. See
Bacchus and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: bacchanal, п., a reveler.

## Bacchanalia
Bacchanalia, n. pi., the orgies of Bacchus;
revelry. — L., neut. pi. of bacchanalis. See prec.
word.
Derivative: Bacchanali-an, adj.

## bacchant
bacchant, п., a devotee of Bacchus. — L. bacchdns,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of baccharl, 'to celebrate
the festival of Bacchus', fr. Bacchus. See Bacchus
and -ant

## haccharis
haccharis, п., name of an aromatic plant. —
ModL., fr. baccar, 'plant with a fragrant root',
prob. identical with Gnaphalium sanguineum
L., fr. Gk. βάκκαρις, which is a Lydian loan
word. See Scholia Aristoph. Pers., p. 42.

## Bacchic
Bacchic, adj., pertaining to Bacchus. — See
Bacchus and -ic.

## Bacchus
Bacchus, п., the god of wine in Greek mythology.
— L., fr. Gk. Βάκχος, 'the god of wine', orig.
prob. 'the god of grapeberries', and cogn. with
L. baca, bacca, 'berry'. See next word.

## hacci-
hacci-, combining form meaning 'berry'. — L.
bad-, bacci-, fr. baca, bacca, 'berry', which prob.
meant orig. 'grape', and is cogn. with Gk.
Βάκχος. See prec. word and cp. asarabacca,
bagasse, bagatelle, bay, 'the laurel'.

## hacciferous
hacciferous, adj., bearing berries. — Formed
with suff. -ous (as if fr. L. *bacciferus) fr. L.
baccifer, which is compounded of bacca, 'berry',
and ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See bacci- and
-ferous.

## bacciform
bacciform, adj., berry-shaped. — Compounded
of hacci- and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## baccivorous
baccivorous, adj., berry-eating. — Compounded
of bacci- and -vorous.

## bache
bache, п., stream, rivulet (dial. E.) — OE. bsec,
rel. to OS. beki, ON. bekkr, Dan. bsek, Swed.
back, MDu. bike, Du. beek, OHG. bah,
MHC, G. bach, and cogn. with Mir. bual (for
*bhogla), 'flowing water', OI. bhangdh, Lith.
banga, 'wave'. Cp. beck, 'brook'.

## bachelor
bachelor, n. — ME. bachelere, fr. OF. bacheler,
'squire, a young man aspiring to knighthood;
a young man' (whence F. bachelier, 'bachelor'),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:93 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. ML. baccaldris (the usual form is
baccalarius). See baccalaurente.
Derivatives: bachelor-dom, п., bachelor-hood, n.

## bacUlary
bacUlary, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
bacilli. — Formed fr. L. bacillum (see bacillus)
with adj. suff. -ary.

## baciliiform
baciliiform, adj., shaped like a bacillus. —
Compounded of bacillus and L. forma, 'form, shape'.
See form, п., and cp. baculiform.

## bacillus
bacillus, n. — Late L. bacillus, 'a little staff',
dimin. of bacillus, var. ofL. baculum, 'stick, staff',
which stands for *bac-llom and is cogn. with
Gk. βάκτρον, 'staff', βακτήριον, 'a little staff'.
See bacterium and cp. bacillus, baguette, hall,
'crossbar', debacle, imbecile. As a term of
bacteriology the word bacillus was introduced by
the German botanist Ferdinand Cohn (1828-98)
in 1853.

## hack
hack, п., the hinder part of the human body. —
ME. bak, fr. OE. i*c, rel. to OS., ΟΝ., MDu.
bak, OHG. bah, 'back', OHG. bahho, 'ham,
haunch', MHG., G. backe, 'buttock'. Cp. bacon.
Derivatives: back, tr. and intr. v., adj. and adv.,
back-ed, adj., back-er, п., back-ing п., back-ward,
adj., backwardation (q.v.), back-wards, adv.

## hack
hack, п., vat, tub. — Du. bak, fr. F. bac, fr. VL.
bacca, 'water vessel', whence *baccinum, 'basin'.
See basin.
back formation (philol.) — Coined by the English
lexicographer and linguist Dr. (later, Sir James)
Murray (1837-1915).

## backgammon
backgammon, n. — Prop, a game, in which the
pieces are put back; compounded of back, 'the
hinder part of the body', and gammon, 'game'.

## backsheesh
backsheesh, backshish. — Variants of baksheesh.

## backward
backward, backwards, adv. — Formed fr. back,
adv. (see hack, 'the hinder part of the body'),
and -ward, resp. -wards.
Derivative: backward, adj.

## backwardation
backwardation, п., postponement of delivery
(London Stock Exchange). — A hybrid coined
fr. backward and -ation, a suff. of Latin origin.

## bacon
bacon, n. — ME., fr. OF. bacon, bacoun, fr. ML.
baconem, ace. of Ьасб, fr. OHG. bahho, 'ham,
haunch'. See back, 'the hinder part of the body'

## Baconian
Baconian, adj., pertaining to Lord Verulam Bacon
(1561-1626) or his philosophy. For the ending
see suff. -ian.
Васора, п., a genus of plants of the figwort
family; the water hyssop (bot.) — ModL., of
American Indian origin.

## bacteria
bacteria, — The pi. of bacterium.

## Bacteriaceae
Bacteriaceae, n. pi., a family of rod-shaped
bacteria (bacteriol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-aceae fr. L. bacterium. See bacterium.

## bacterial
bacterial, adj., pertaining to bacteria. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. ModL. bacterium. See
bacterium.

## bactericide
bactericide, п., a substance destroying bacteria.
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. βακτήριον and L.
-clda, 'killer', fr. cqedere, 'to kill'. See bacterium
and -cide.

## bacterio-
bacterio-, before a vowel bacteri-, combining form
meaning 'bacteria'. — See bacterium.
bacteriology· п., the study of bacteria. —
Compounded of bacterio- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deais (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: bacteriolog-ical, adj.,
bacteriologist, n.

## hacterioscopy
hacterioscopy, п., investigation of bacteria. —
Compounded of bacterio- and Gk. -σκοπιά, fr.
σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scopy.

## bacterium
bacterium, п., in the pi. bacteria. — ModL.,
coined by the German naturalist Christian
Gottfried Ehrenberg (1795-1876) in 1838 fr. Gk.
βακτήριον, 'a little.staft", which is rel. to
βάκτρον, "staff", fr. I.-E. *bok-, 'staff', whence also
L. baculum, 'rod, staff'. Olr. bacc, 'hook,
crosier*, is prob. a loan word fr. L. baculum and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:94 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 67 | BALANCE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:94 COLUMN:1 -->
derived from it through back formation. See
Frisk, GEW., I, р.-2-и-Г2 s.v. βακτηρία. Ср.
bacalao, cabilliau, Kabbeljaws.

## bacteroid
bacteroid, adj., resembling bacteria. —
Compounded of bacterium andGk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape*. See -oid.
Derivatives: bacteroid, п., bacteroid-al, adj.

## Bactrian
Bactrian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Bactria, lit. 'the Eastern province', fr.
Persian bakhtar, 'the east'. For sense
development cp. Levant.

## Bactris
Bactris, п., a genus of plants of the palm family.
— ModL., fr. Gk. βάκτρον, 'staff'. See
bacterium.

## bacnliform
bacnliform, adj., rod-shaped. — Compounded of
L. baculum, 'a rod', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See next word, and form, п., and cp. bacilliform.

## bacalus
bacalus, п., a rod, esp. as an emblem of authority.
— L. baculus, also baculum. See bacillus.

## bad
bad, adj. — ME. bad, badde, prob. fr. OE. bxddel,
'hermaphrodite'. Ср. ОЕ. bxdling, 'effeminate
person'.
Derivatives: bad, n. and adv., badd-ish, adj.,
badd-ish-ly, adv., badd-ish-ness, п., bad-ly, adv.,
bad-ness, n.

## baddeleyite
baddeleyite, п., zirconium dioxide (mineral.) —
Named after its discoverer Joseph Baddeley. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## bade
bade, v., past tense of bid. ^— ME. bad, bade, fr.
OE. bsed, fr. biddan. The ME. form bade prob.
developed fr. orig. bad, on analogy of spake.

## badge
badge, n. — ME. bage, bagge, of unknown origin.

## badger
badger, п., the animal. — Earlier bageard, prob.
formed fr. badge with the suff. -ard, lit. 'the
animal with a mark', and so called in allusion
to the white mark on its face. For sense
development cp. F. blaireau, 'badger', which derives fr.
OF. bier, 'marked with a spot'.

## badger
badger, tr. v., to worry. — Lit. 'to treat like a
badger"; formed fr. prec. word.

## badger
badger, п., a huckster. — ME. bager, perh.
related to bag.

## badia
badia, monastery, abbey. — It., aphetic fr. Eccles.
L. abbatia, 'abbey', fr. abbas, abbatis, 'abbot'.
See abbacy, abbot.

## badian
badian, п., the Chinese anise. — F. badiane, fr.
Pers. badian, 'anise'.

## badinage
badinage, п., banter. — F., fr. badlner, Ίο jest,
joke', fr. OProvenc. badin, 'simpleton, fool', a
derivative of badar, 'to gape', fr. VL. batare, 'to
gape'. See bay 'part in the wall', and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see suff. -age.
Derivative: badinage, intr. v.

## badminton
badminton, п., name of a game played with
shuttlecocks. — Fr. Badminton, seat of the Duke
of Beaufort in Gloucestershire, England.

## baetulus
baetulus, п., a meteorite (antiq.) — L., fr. Gk.
βαίτυλος, a sacred meteoric stone, fr. Heb.
beth El, 'house of God'; see bethel. The form
βαίτυλος shows that the name came to the
Greeks through the medium of the Phoenicians
who pronounced it bet-ϋΐ. See Muss-Arnolt,
Semitic words in Greek and Latin, in
Transactions of the American Philological
Association, 1892 (volume XX111), pp.51-52, and p.52,
Note r.

## baetyl
baetyl, п., a baetulus. — Gk. βαίτυλος. See prec.
word.
Derivative: baetyi-ic, adj.

## baff
baff, tr. and intr. v., to beat, strike. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. the next two words.

## baffle
baffle, tr. v. — Prob. rel. to OF. beffler, 'to
ridicule, mock at', bafouer, 'to set at nought", dial.
E. baff, 'useless', G. baff in baff machen, '10
astound, flabbergast'. All these words seem to
be derivatives of the I.-E. imitative base *baf.
Cp. prec. and next word.
Derivatives: baffl-er, п., baffi-ing, adj., baffl-ing-
ly, adv., baffl-ing-ness, n.

## baffy
baffy, п., a wooden golf club. — Formed from
the verb baff with suff. -y.

## baft
baft, bafta, п., a course kind of cotton cloth. —
Pers. bafta, 'woven', rel. to Avestic ubdaena,
'woven fabric', OI. urna-vabhih, 'spider', fr.
I.-E. base *webh-, 'to weave'. See weave, and
cp. words there referred lo.

## bag
bag, n. — ME. bagge, fr. ON. baggi, of Celtic
origin. The word was brought to England by

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:94 COLUMN:2 -->
the Normans. See J. M.D. Meiklejohn.The
English language, its grammar, history and
literature, London, 1923, p. 134. Cp. badger,
'huckster', baggage.
Derivatives: bag, tr. v., to inclose in a bag; intr.
v., to swell like a bag, bagg~er, п., bagg-y, adj.,
bagg-i-ly, adv., bagg-i-ness, n.

## bag
bag, tr. v., to cut (grain, weeds). — Of uncertain
origin.

## bagasse
bagasse, п., sugar cane crushed in the mill. —
F., fr. Sp., bagazo, 'dregs', derivative of baga,
'pod, husk', fr. L. idea, 'berry'. See bacci- and
cp. next word. Cp. also megas, megasse.

## bagatelle
bagatelle, п., a trifle.—F., fr. It. bagatella, of s.m.,
dimin. of L. baca, 'berry'. For sense
development cp. It. bagattino, 'a kind of small coin',
which is of the same origin. See bacci- and cp.
prec. word.

## baggage
baggage, n. — F. bagage, fr. OF. bague, 'bundle',
which, together with OProveng. baga, of s.m.,
is prob. borrowed from Teutonic. See bag, п.,
and -age.
Derivative: baggag-er, n.

## bagnio
bagnio, п., a bath. — It. bagno, fr. L. balneum,
whence also F. bain, 'bath'. See balneal and
cp. baignoire.

## baguette
baguette, п., a small molding. — F., prop, 'a
small rod', fr. It. bacchetta, dimin. of bacchio,
'rod', fr. L. baculum. See bacillus,

## bahadur
bahadur, п., a title given to European officers in
India. — Hind, bahadur, 'hero', which
according to Benfey (in Orient und Occident I 137,
quoted in Hobson-Jobson 49a) derives fr. OI.
bhaga-dhara-, 'happiness-possessing'. The first
element is cogn. with Gk. φαγεΐν, 'to eat'; see
-pbagous and cp. baksheesh. For the second
element see aumlldar and cp. words there referred to.

## Bahaism
Bahaism, п., the teaching of the religious sect of
the Bahaists. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Pers.
baha, 'splendor', fr. Arab, baha', of s.m.

## bahar
bahar, п., a weight. — Arab, bahar, a weight used
in India, ultim. fr. OI. bharah, 'load, weight',
which is rel. to bhdrati, bharate, 'carries', and
cogn. with Gk. φέρειν, L. ferre, Ίο bear,
carry'. See benr, 'to carry', and cp. words there
referred to.

## bahur
bahur, п., young man, youth, unmarried man. —
Hebrew bahar, 'young man', rel. to Akkad.
bahulati, 'warriors'.

## bahuvrihi
bahuvrihi, п., name of a class of compounds
(Old Indian gram.) — OI. bahmrihih, 'having
much rice', compounded of bahuh, 'much,
numerous, abundant', and vrihih, 'rice*. The
first element is rel. to Avestic bazah-, 'height,
depth', and cogn. with Gk. παχύς, 'thick'; see
pachy-. For the second element see rice,

## baignoire
baignoire, п., box at a theatre. — F., 'bath,
bathtub; box at a theatre', fr. baigner, 'to bathe', fr.
bain, 'bath', fr. L. balneum. See balneal and cp.
bagnio,

## baikalite
baikalite, п., a dark-green variety of hedenbergite
(mineral.) — Named after Lake Baikal in
Siberia, near which it was first discovered. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## bail
bail, п., security. — OF. bail, 'custody' (whence
F. bail, 'lease'), fr. baillier, 'to seize, carry, give*,
fr. L. bajulare, 'to bear a burden', fr. bajulus,
'porter', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. bail,
'to jlip water', and bailiff.
Derivatives: bail, tr. v., bail-ee, п., bail-er, n.
(law), bail-ie, п., baili-er-y (also baili-ar-y) п.,
bail-ment, n.

## bail
bail, п., fortification; crossbar. — ME., fr. OF.
bail, 'stake; palisade', which prob. derives fr.
L. baculum, 'rod, staff'. See bacillus and cp.
bailey,

## bail
bail, also bale, п., a bucket used to dip water out
of a boat; tr. v., to dip water out of; intr. v., to
dip out water. — F. bailie, 'bucket', fr. ML.
*bajula (aquae) lit. 'porter (of water)', used in
the sense of 'water jar'; *bajula is the fem. of

## bajulus. See bail
bajulus. See bail, 'security'.

## bailey
bailey, п., walls, resp. courts of a feudal castle. —
ME. variant of bail. See bail, 'fortification'.

## bailiff
bailiff, n. — ME. baillif, fr. OF. baillif, 'custodian,

## magistrate'
magistrate', fr. ML. bajulivus, fr. L. bajulus,
'porter'. See bail, 'security', and -ive.
Derivative: bailiff-ry, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:94 COLUMN:3 -->

## bailiwick
bailiwick, п., the district of a bailiff. — ME.
baillifwik, compounded of baillif (see prec.
word) and wick, 'village'.

## baillone
baillone, adj., holding a staff in the mouth (her.)
— F. baillonni, lit. 'gagged', pp. of baillonner,
'to gag', fr. bailler, 'to gape, yawn', fr. VL. bata-
cul&re, fr. batare, to gape, yawn'. Cp.
OProveng. badalhar. It. badigliare, sbadigliare, 'to
yawn', which also derive fr. VL. bataculare, and
see bay, 'part in the wall'.

## bain-marie
bain-marie, n. double pan for holding food. —
F., 'water bath*, fr. ML. balneum Mariae, lit.
'bath of Mary (sister of Moses)', to whom
various works dealing with alchemy were attributed.
See balneal.

## Bairain
Bairain, п., the name of two Mohammedan
festivals following the fast of Ramadan. —Turk.
bairam.

## bairn
bairn, n. (Scot.) — OE. beam, barn, child', rel.
to bear, 'to carry' (q.v.)
Derivative: bairn-ish, adj.

## bait
bait, tr. v. — ME. baiten, beyten, fr. ON. beita,
'to cause to bile', causative of bila, 'to bite'; rel.
to bxtan, 'to bait', OS. bltian, OHG. beizzen,
'to bait'. MHG. beitzen, 'to bait; to hawk', G.
beizen, 'to hawk; to cauterize, etch'. OE.
baton, OS. betian, etc., are causatives of OE. bitan,
resp. OS. bitan, OHG. Ыззап, etc., and lit. mean
'to cause to bite*. See bite and cp. words there
referred to.

## bait
bait, n. — ON. beita, 'food', beit, 'pasture', fr.
beita, 'to cause to bite' (see prec. word); in some
meanings derived directly fr. prec. word.

## baize
baize, п., a coarse woolen cloth. — F. baies, pi. of
baie, prop. fem. of bat, 'bay colored'. See bay,
'reddish'.
Derivative: baize, tr. v.

## bake
bake, tr. and intr. v. — ME. baken, fr. OE. bacan,
rel. to ON. baka, Swed. baka, Dan. bage,
MDu. backen, Du. bakken, OHG. bahhan,
backan, MHG., G. backen, fr. 1-Е. base *bhog-,
'to warm, roast, bake', whence also Gk-φώγειν,
'to roast'. Cp. batch, bate and the second
element in zwieback. Base *bhog- is a -g-enlarge-
ment of base *bhg-, 'to warm'; see bath.
Derivatives: bake, п., bak-ed, adj., baker (q.v.),
bak-ing, п., bak-ing-ly, adv.

## bakelite
bakelite, п., synthetic resin. — Named after its
inventor Leo Hendrik Baekeland (1863-1944).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## baker
baker, n. — ME. bakere, fr. OE. bxcere, fr. bacan,
'to bake'. See bake and agential suff. -er and
cp. baxter.
Derivative: bak-ery, n.

## baksheesh
baksheesh, п., a gratuity; a tip. — Pers. bakhshish,
lit. 'gift', a derivative of the verb bakhshidan, 4o
give', fr. I.-E. base *bhag-, 'to distribute, share
out', whence also OI. bhajati, .'assigns, allots,
apportions, enjoys, loves', bhagah, 'allotter,
distributor, master, lord', Gk. φαγεΐν, 'to eat'.
See -phagous and cp. Bbaga and the first
element in Bhagavadgita, and in bahadur.

## Balaena
Balaena, п., a genus of whales, the Greenland
whale. — L. ballaena, balaena. See baleen.

## balaghat
balaghat, balaghaut, п., tableland above the
passes (Anglo-Ind.) — Formed fr. Pers. bala,
'above', and Hind, ghal, 'a pass'.

## bainlaika
bainlaika, п., a Russian stringed instrument with
a triangular body. — Russ. balalaika, which,
according to Erich Berneker, Etymologisches
Worterbuch der russischen Sprache, I, p. 40,
Heidelberg, 1908-13, is rel. to Russ. balabolit',
'to chatter, babble', from the I.-E. imitative base
*balb-, whence also L. balbus, 'stammering'. See
booby and cp. words there referred to.

## balan-
balan-, form of balano- before a vowel.

## balance
balance, n. — OF. (= F.) balance, fr. L. Ы-,
'two, twice', and VL. 'lancia, fr. L. lanx, gen.
lands, 'plate, dish; scale of weighing machine',
which prob. stands for *llnk-s, fr. I.-E. base
*lliq-, 'to bend', whence prob. also Gk. λέκ,ος,
λεκάνη, 'dish', λέχριος, 'slanting, crosswise',
λοξές, 'slanting, crooked, bent'; see Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., I, p. 761 s.v. lanx. See Ы- and
loxo- and cp. the second element in aimcel. Cp.
also Lecanium, Lecidea, Iekane. The 'first a in
balance is prob. due to an association of this
word with F. bailer, 'to dance', fr. Gk. βάλλειν,
