<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:95 COLUMN:1 -->
'to throw' (see ballistic).
Derivatives: balance, tr. v., balanc-ed, adj.t
balanc-er, п., balanc-ing, adj.

## balaniferous
balaniferous, adj., acorn-bearing. —
Compounded of L. balanus, 'acorn', and L.ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See balano- and -fernus.

## balano-
balano-, before a vowel balan-, combining form
meaning 'acorn'. — Gk. βάλανο-, βαλαν-, fr.
βάλανος, 'acorn', which is cogn. with L. glans,
gen. glandis, 'acorn'. See gland and cp. the
second element in myrobalan.

## balanoid
balanoid, adj., acorn-shaped.— Compounded of
balan- and Gk. -οεΐ8ής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -old.

## halas
halas, п., a variety of spinel ruby. — F. balais,
fr. Arab, balakhsh, fr. Balakhshan, fr. Pers.
Badhakhshan, name of a region in Central Asia
(near Samarkand), where this variety of spinel
ruby is found.

## balatron
balatron, п., jester, buffoon. — L. balatro, gen.
-dnis, of Etruscan origin; not related to L.
blatero, 'babbler'.

## balaustine
balaustine, п., the pomegranate tree. — Formed
with suff. -ine fr. Gk. βαλαύστιον, 'flower of
the wild pomegranate', a word of Sem. origin.
Cp. Aram, baldtz, said of the blossoming of the
pomegranate tree. For the correspondence of
Greek si to Semitic }, Iz, cp. Gk. στύραξ, fr.
Heb. tzdrt (see styrax). Cp. baluster.

## balbriggan
balbriggan, п., a cotton fabric used for hosiery. —
Prop, 'fabric made in Balbriggan (in Ireland)'.

## balbaties
balbaties, п., stammering (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. L. balbutlre, 'to stammer', fr. balbus,
'stammerer', from the I.-E. imitative base *bal-, 'to
stutter'. See booby and cp. words there
referred to.

## balcony
balcony, n. — It. balcone, formed with the
augmentative suff. -one fr. balco, 'scaffold', which
is borrowed fr. OHG. balcho, 'beam' (whence
MHG. balke, G. Balken, 'beam*). See balk,
'beam'.

## bald
bald, adj. — ME. balled, orig. 'white', fr. I.-E.
base *bhel-, 'to shine', whence also OI. bhalam,
'brightness; forehead', Gk. φαλός, 'white',
φαλάρός, 'having a patch of white', φαλάρίς,
'coot' (so called from a white spot on its head),
L. fulica, 'coot', Alb. bale, 'forehead', OSlav.
ЫШ, 'white', Lith. balnas, hallos, Lett. bSls,
'pale', OE. bsl, 'a blazing fire, a funeral pyre',
OHG. belihha, MHG., G. belche, 'coot'. Cp.
balefire, Beltane, beluga, blaze, 'flame', Fulica,
full, 'to thicken cloth', Phalaris, phalarope.
Derivatives: bald-en, tr. and intr. v., bald-ish,
adj., bald-ly, adv., bald-ness, n.

## baldachin
baldachin, п., canopy. — F. baldaquin, fr. It. bal-
dacchino, fr. Baldacco, 'Bagdad', fr. ML. Bal-
dac. It. bdldacchino orig. denoted richly woven
silk stuff brought from Bagdad. Cp. baudekhi.

## balderdash
balderdash, п., 1) nonsense; 2) a poor mixture of
liquors. — The first element is prob. identical
with Dan. balder, 'noise, clatter', the second is
the English word dash. Dan. balder is rel. to
Dan. baldre, dial. Norw. baldra, dial. Swed.
ballra, MLG., earlier Du. balderen, Dan. buldre,
Swed. bullra, 'to make a noise, rattle', MHG.
buldern, G. pollern, 'to knock, rattle, bluster'.
These words derive from a dental enlargement
of I.-E. base *bhel-, 4o sound', whence OE.
bellan, bylgan, 'to bellow'. See bellow, 'to make
a loud noise', and cp. words there referred to.

## baldric
baldric, п., a belt worn over one shoulder. —
ME. baldric, baudric, baudry, fr. OF. baldre,
baldrei, baldroi, (whence F. baudrier and MHG.
balderich), fr. L. balleus, 'belt'. See belt and cp.
words there referred to.

## Baldwin
Baldwin, masc. PN. — OF. Baldoln (F. Bau-
douin), of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. Baldawin, lit.
'bold friend', fr. OHG. baid, 'bold', and wini,
'friend'. For the first element see bold and cp.
the second element in Theobald. OHG. wini,
'friend', is rel. to OE. wine, ON. vinr, 'friend',
and to OE. winnan, 'to strive, struggle, fight'.
See win and wish and cp. the first element
in Winfred and the second element in Edwin.

## bale
bale, п., bundle, package. — ME., fr. OF. bale,
balle (F. balk), fr. OHG. bath, 'ball'. See ball
'a round body'.
Derivatives: bale, tr. v., bal-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:95 COLUMN:2 -->

## bale
bale, п., misfortune.—ME., fr. OE. bealu, bealo,
balu, 'injury, calamity', rel. to OS. balo, 'evil',
ON. Ш, '-misfortune', OFris. bealu, 'evil', OHG.
balo, 'destruction', Goth, balwjan, 'to torment',
balweins, 'pain, torture', balwa-wesei,
'wickedness'.
Derivatives: bale-ful, adj., bale-ful-ly, adv., bale-
ful-ness, n.

## bale
bale, n„ bucket, v., to dip water. — See bail,
'bucket'.

## bale
bale, п., balefire. — OE. bxl. See balefire.

## baleen
baleen, п., whalebone. — ME. balene, baleyne,
'whale, whalebone', fr. OF. baleine, of s.m., fr.
L. baUaena, 'whale', which was borrowed fr. Gk.
φάλλαινα, of s.m., through the medium of the
Illyrian language, a fact which explains the
transition of Gk. φ into L. b (instead of p). Gk.
φάλλαινα is related to φαλλός, 'penis', fr. I.-E.
base *bhel-, 'to swell'. See ball, 'a round body',
and cp. Balaena, balinger.

## balefire
balefire, n. — OE. bzlfpr, 'funeral fire',
compounded of bSl, 'a blazing fire, a funeral pile',
and/pr, 'fire'. The first element is rel. to ON. bal,
'a great fire', fr. I.-E. base *bhel-, 'to shine'; see
bald. For the second element see Are.

## balinger
balinger, п., a whaleship (obsol.) — OF. balen-
gier, 'whaleship', fr. baleine, 'whale'. See baleen.

## balk
balk, also baulk, п., ridge of land left unplowed
between furrows: a beam. — ME. balke, 'beam',
fr. OE. balca, 'ridge between furrows, beam,
rafter', rel. to OS. balko, ON. bjalki, Dan. bjelke,
Swed. bjulke, OFris. balka, OHG. balko, balcho,
MHG. balke, G. Balken, 'beam, rafter' (ср.,
with vowel gradation, OE. bolca, 'wooden
gangway ofaship'), ON. bolt, 'trunk of a tree';
fr. I.-E. base 'bhel'g-, 'beam, plank', whence
also Gk. φάλαγξ, 'trunk, log; line of battle,
battle array', φάλκης, 'beam', L. fulcire, 'to
prop', fulcrum, 'bedpost', Lith. balziena,
'crossbar', Lett, balziita, 'prop, stay'. Cp. balcony.
Cp. also block, bole, 'trunk', bulk, 'projection',
debauch, ebauchoir, fulcrum, phalange, phalanx,
planch, planchet, plancler, plank.
Derivatives: balk v. (q.v.), balk-er, п., balk-ing-
ly, adv., balk-y, adj.

## balk
balk, also baulk, tr. v., to hinder, thwart; intr.
v., to refuse. — Formed fr. prec. word and lit.
meaning 4o put a beam in the way'. Cp. bilk.

## Balkanize
Balkanize, tr. v. — Coined by the English
journalist and editor James Louis Garvin (1868-
1947) in allusion to the political condition in the
Balkans in 1912-13.

## ball
ball, п., a round body; a sphere. — ME. balle,
fr. ON. bdllr, which is rel. to OHG. ballo, balla,
MHG. balle, bal, G. Ball, fr. I.-E. base *bhel-,
'to swell'. See belly and cp. Balaena, bale,
'bundle', baleen, balinger, balloon, ballot,
billow, bulk, 'size', and the first element in blll-
berry and in pall-mall.
Derivatives: ball, tr. v., to form into a ball,
ball-er, n.

## ball
ball, п., a party for social dancing. — F. bal, fr.
OF. bailer, 'to dance', fr. VL. ballare, fr. Gk.
βαλλίζειν, 'to dance', which prob. derives fr.
βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See ballistic and cp. ballad,
bullerina, ballet, bayadere.

## ballad
ballad, п., ι) a sentimental or romantic song; 2) a
narrative song. — ME. balade, prop, 'a song
written for a dance', fr. OF. balade (F. ballade),
fr. OProvenc. balada, lit. 'dance', later used in
the sense of 'dancing song', fr. balar, 'to dance'.
See ball, 'party for dancing'.

## ballade
ballade, n. a poem with three stanzas of eight or,
ten lines each and an envoy of four. — F. See
prec. word.

## balladry
balladry, п., ballad poetry. — Formed fr. ballad
with suff. -ry.

## ballast
ballast, п., henvy material used to steady a ship.
— Dan. and Swed., assimilated fr. earlier bar-
last lit. 'bare load*. The first element of this
compound is rel. to the E. adjective bare; the
second is re], to last, a unit of weight.
Derivatives: ballasl-er, п., ballast-big, n.

## ballerina
ballerina, a woman ballet dancer. — It., fr.
ballare, 'to dance'. See bull, 'party for dancing'.

## ballet
ballet, n. — F., fr. It. ballet to, dimin. of ballo,
'dance'. See ball 'party for dancing', and -et
Derivative: ballet, tr. v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:95 COLUMN:3 -->

## balllsta
balllsta, п., an ancient military engine (Roman
antiq.) — L., lit. 'a throwing machine', fr. Gk.
βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See next word

## ballistic
ballistic, adj., pertaining to projectiles. —Formed
with suff. -istic fr. Gk. βάλλειν, 'to throw',
which stands in gradational relationship to
βολή, βόλος, 'a throw', βέλος, 'bolt, arrow,
dart', lit. 'something thrown', fr. I.-E. base
'g^el-, whence also OI. apa-gurya-, 'swinging',
Avestic ni-yrd-lre, 'they are being hurled down*,
Toch. AB klu-, 'to fall', and perhaps also OI.
galati, 'trickles', OHG. quellan, MHG.,G.quel-
len, 'to well up'. Cp. ball, 'party for dancing',
ballista, amphibole, amphibology, anabolism,
belemnite, Belostoma, bolide, bolometer, boule,
'council', catabolism, devil, diabolic, discobolus,
Eblis, ecbolic, Elaphebolion, emblem, embolism,
emboly, hyperbola, hyperbole, metabolism,
parable, parabola, parlance, parley, parliament,
parlor, parol, parole, periblem, problem, scy-
balum, symbol, Tribolium, Tribulus.

## ballistics
ballistics, п., the study of projectiles. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## ballonet
ballonet, п., an auxiliary gas or air bag in a
balloon or airship. — F. ballonnet, lit. 'a small
balloon', fr.. ballon. See next word and -et.

## balloon
balloon, n. — F. ballon, fr. It. pallone, which is
formed with augment, suff. -one fr. palla, 'a
ball', a word of Teut. origin; see ball, 'a round
body', and -oon. The b in F. ballon (fr. It.
pallone) is due to the influence of F. balle, 'ball'.
Cp. pallone.
Derivatives: balloon, tr. and intr. v., and the
hybrid noun balloon-ist, n.

## ballot
ballot, n. — F. bollotle, fr. It. ballolta, 'little ball',
dimin. of balla, 'ball' (see E. ball, 'a round
body'); so called in allusion to the small balls
formerly dropped into the voting urn.
Derivatives: ballot, intr. and tr. v., ballot-age
(q.v.)

## Ballota
Ballota, п., a genus of plants of the mint family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βαλλωτή, 'the black
horehound'; of unknown origin.

## hallotage
hallotage, n. — F. baliotlage, fr. ballotter, 'to
ballot', fr. ballotte. See prec. word and -age.

## ballyhoo
ballyhoo, п., 1) outcry; 2) noisy advertising
(slang). — Of uncertain origin; possibly fr.
Ballyhooly, a village in County Cork, Ireland.
Derivative: ballyhoo, tr. and intr. v.

## ballyrag
ballyrag, tr. and intr. v. — A variant of bullyrag.

## balm
balm, n. — ME. basme, baume, fr. OF. bausme,
baume (F. baume), fr. L. balsamum, 'gum of the
balsam tree, balsam', fr. Gk. βάλσαμον. See
balsam and cp. embalm.
Derivatives: balm-y, adj., balm-i-ly, adv., balm-
i-ness, n.

## Balmoral
Balmoral, п., name of various objects. — Named
after Balmoral Castle in Scotland.

## balneal
balneal, adj., pertaining to baths. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. balneum, balineum, 'bath', fr.
Gk. βαλανεΐον, of s.m., which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. bagnio, baignoire and the first
element in bain-marie.

## balneo-
balneo-, combining form meaning 'bath'. — Fr.
L. balneum, 'bath'. See balneal.

## balneology
balneology, п., the study of bathing. —
Compounded of balneo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: balneohg-ic-al,adj.,balneolog-ist, n.

## balsam
balsam, n. — L. balsamum, 'gum of the balsam
tree, balsam', fr. Gk. βάλσαμον,fr. Heb. basdm,
which is rel. to Heb. bdiem, Aram, busma, Syr.
besmd, Arab, bashdm, 'balsam, spice, perfume'.
Cp. balm, embalm.
Derivatives: balsam, tr. v., balsam-er, п.,
balsamic, adj. and п., balsam-itic, adj., balsam-ize,
tr. v.

## Balsaminaceae
Balsaminaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL. See next word and -aceae.

## balsamine
balsamine, n. the garden balsam. — F., fr. Gk.
βχλσαμίνη, 'the balsam plant', fr. βάλσαμον. See
balsam and -ine.

## balteus
balteus, п., girdle or belt worn by ecclesiastic
dignitaries. — L., of Etruscan origin. Cp. belt,
baldric.

## Balthasar
Balthasar, masc. PN. — F., fr. L., fr. Gk. Βαλ-
τάσαρ, fr. Heb. Belfshalztzdr (Dan. 10:1), fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:96 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 69 | BANNER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:96 COLUMN:1 -->
Babyl. Balat-shar-usur, lit. 'save the life of the
king'. In Hebrew the name has been assimilated
in form to that of Belshatztzar (see Belshazzar).

## baluster
baluster, п., support for a railing. — F. balustre,
fr. It. balaustro, fr. L. 6aia«ifnim,fr.Gk. βαλαύ-
οτ'.ον, 'flower of the wild pomegranate', a
word of Syrian origin (see balausrine); so called
from the shape of the capital. Cp. next word
and banister.
Derivatives: baluster-ed, adj., balustrade (q.v.)

## balustrade
balustrade, п., a row of balusters. — Prop, 'a set
of balusters', fr. F. balustrade, fr. It. balaustrata,
lit. provided with balusters', fr. balaustro (see
prec. word and -ade); introduced into English
by the diarist John Evelyn (1620-1706).
Derivatives: balustrad-ed, adj., balustrad-ing, n.

## bam
bam, Ir. and intr. v., to bamboozle. — Abrevia-
tion of bamboozle.

## bambino
bambino, п., a little child; an image of the infant
Jesus. — It., 'baby', dimin. of bambo, 'simple',
which is of imitative origin.

## bamboo
bamboo, n. — Malay bambu. Cp. Bambusa.
Derivative: bamboo, tr. v.

## bamboozle
bamboozle, tr. v., 1) to hoax; 2) to confuse, puzzle.
— Of uncertain origin.

## Bambusa
Bambusa, n., a genus of bamboos (hot) — ModL.
See bamboo.

## ban
ban, ir. v., to prohibit; to curse (archaic). — ME.
bannen, fr. OE. bannan, 'to summon, proclaim,
command', rel. to ON. banna, 'to forbid,
prohibit', OHG. bannan, 'to command or forbid
under threat of punishment', MHG., G. bannen,
'to put under the ban, banish, expel, curse';
formed with -я- formative element fr. I.-E. base
*bha-, 'to speak, tell, say', whence also Gk.
φάνοιι, L. fori, 'to say', Arm. ban, 'word', Olr.

## bann
bann, 'law'. See fame and cp. ban, 'edict', banish,
banal, bandit, banns, abandon, aubain, boon, п.,
contraband.

## ban
ban, п., edict. — ME., partly fr. bannen, 'to
summon, proclaim' (cp. ON. bann, 'prohibition',
OHG. ban, 'commandment or prohibition under
threat of punishment, jurisdiction', MHG. ban,
G. Bann, 'public proclamation, jurisdiction, ban,
ostracism, curse', which derive fr. ON. banna,
resp. OHG. bannan, MHG., G. bannen); partly
fr. OF. (= F.) ban, 'public proclamation', fr.
Frankish *ban, which is rel. to OHG. ban
(see above). See ban, v.

## ban
ban, п., a governor of Croatia.—-Serbo-Croatian
ban, 'lord, master, ruler', fr. Pers. ban, 'prince,
lord, chief, governor' (prob. through the medium
of the Avars). As a suff. -ban (var. -wan) means
'keeper, guardian'. Pers. ban, is rel. to OPers.
pa(y)-, 'to guard, protect', OI. pdti, 'guards,
protects', puna-, 'guarding, protecting' (see
P.Horn, GrundriB der neupersischen Etymo-
logie, StraBburg, 1893, N0.176). See food and
cp. banat and the second element in durwaun
and in satrap.

## Bairn
Bairn, п., son of Bali, a thousand armed giant
(Hindu mythol.) — ΟΙ. ΒάηάΊι, lit. 'arrow', prob.
a loan word fr. Austroasiatic.

## banal
banal, adj., trite, commonplace. — OF. banal,
fr. ban, 'proclamation*. See ban, 'edict'. Banal
orig. meant 'compulsory', whence it came to
denote 'common to all, commonplace'.

## banal
banal, adj., pertaining lo a ban or the banat. —
Formed fr. ban, 'governor', with adj. suff. -al.

## banality
banality, п., ι) triteness; 2) a platitude. — F. ba-
nalite, fr. banal. See hannl, 'trite', and -ity.

## banana
banana, n. — Sp. and Port., fr. earlier
Congolese banam.

## hanat
hanat, also banate, п., the district governed by a
ban. — A hybrid coined fr. ban, 'governor' and
suff. -ate (fr. L. -atus). Cp. G., F. banat, which
are of the same meaning and origin.

## banausic
banausic, adj., proper for an artisan; trivial. —
Gk. βαναυσικός, 'relating to artisans', fr. βαναυ-
σίά, 'handicraft', fr. βάναυσος, 'artisan', which
is of uncertain origin. The usual explanation
that βάναυσος is a difsimilated form of *βαΰ-
ναυσος, and compounded of βαΰνος, 'furnace,
forge', and αϋειν, 'to dry', is folk etymology.
Banbury cake. — Named after Banbury in
Oxfordshire.

## baac
baac, п., bench, csp. bench on which judges sit. —
F. See banco.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:96 COLUMN:2 -->

## banco
banco, п., bank.— It., fr. Teut. *banki-. Cp. ME.
banke and see· hank, bench. Cp. also banc and
the last element in charabaac, mountebank,
saltimbanco.

## hand
hand, п., a tie. — ME., fr. ON. band, rel. to OS.,
Swed., Du., G. band, OHG., MHG. bant, Goth.
bandi, lit. 'that which binds', fr. I.-E. base
*bendh-, 'to bind', whence also OI. bandhdft, 'a
tying, fastening; band, bandage', Mir. bainna,
'bracelet'; F.bande, 'band', is a Teut. loan word.
See bind and cp. bend, bond. Cp. also bandage,
bandanna, bandhava, bandhu, bandoleer, and
the second element in ribband, ribboa, roband,
seerband.
Derivatives: band, tr. and intr. v., band-ed, adj.,
band-er, п., band-ing, n.

## band
band, п., troop. — F. bande, fr. OProveng. banda,
fr. Goth, bandwa, bandwo, 'sign, signal'. See
banner and cp. disband. -

## bandage
bandage, n. — F., fr. bande, fr. OF. bende, fr.
ML. benda, 'a band', fr. Goth. *binda, which is
rel. to E. band, 'tie' (q.v.) For the ending see
suff. -nge.
Derivatives: bandage, tr; v., bondag-er, п.,
bandag-ist, n.

## bandanna
bandanna, bandana, п., a colored and spotted
handkerchief. — Hind, bandhnii, 'a mode of
dyeing in which the cloth is tied in various
places to prevent these places from receiving
the dye', rel. to bandhah, 'a tying, fastening;
band, bandage'. See bind and cp. band, 'tie'.
Cp. also bandhu, pandal.

## bandeau
bandeau, п., a narrow band, fillet. — F., fr. earlier
bandel, dimin. of bande, 'band, ribbon', of Teut.
origin. See band, 'tie'.

## banderilla
banderilla, п., a small dart with a streamer thrust
into the bull by the banderiUo. — Sp., dimin. of
bandera, 'banner'. See banner and cp. next word.

## banderole
banderole, banderol, п., a small streamer
attached to a lance. — F. banderole, dimin. of
bandiere, banniere, 'banner'. See banaer and
cp. prec. word.

## bandhava
bandhava, п., a kinsman (Hindu law). — OI.
bdndhavah, rel. to bdndhuh 'relationship,
kinsman'. See next word.

## bandhu
bandhu, п., related through females. — OI.
bdndhuh, 'relationship, kinsman', rel. tobandhah, 'a
binding; band, tie', fr. I.-E. base *bendh-, 'to
bind'. See band, 'tie'.

## bandicoot
bandicoot, п., a kind of a large rat. — Telegu
pandi kokku, lit. 'pig rat'.

## bandit
bandit, n. — F., fr. It. bandito, prop. pp. of ban-
dire, 'to banish', which arose from a blend of
Frankish *bannjan, 'to banish' (whence F. ban-
nir, E. banish), and Goth, bandwa, 'sign, signal'.
See banner.

## banditi
banditi, n. pi., sometimes used as sing., bandits;
bandits collectively. — It., pi. of bandito. See
prec. word.

## baadog
baadog, п., a dog kept tied up as a watchdog or
because of its ferocity; a mastiff or bloodhound.
— Contracted fr. band-dog (see band, 'a tie',
and dog). For sense developmenl cp. F. limier,
'bloodhound; sleuthhound', lit. 'a dog held
with a leash', fr. Hem, ancient form of lien.
'band'.

## baudoleer
baudoleer, also bandolier, п., a shoulder belt. —
F. bandouliire, fr. Sp. bandolera, fr. banda,
'scarf, sash', which is a Teut. loan word. See
band, 'tie'.
Derivative: bandoleer-ed, bandolier-ed, adj.

## baadore
baadore, п., a stringed musical instrument. —
Port, bandurra, fr. L.pandura, fr. Gk. πανδουρχ,
'a musical instrument of three strings'. See
pandora and cp. banjo. Cp. also mandolin.

## bandy
bandy, tr. v., to toss. — F. bander, 'to bind, bend,
bandy', of Teut. origin. See bend, 'to curve', and
cp. next word.

## bandy
bandy, п., 1) a form of hockey; 2) the bent stick
used in this game. — F. bande, pp. of bandei.
See prec. and cp. next word.

## bandy
bandy, adj., bent, crooked, bandy-legged.
—Derivatively identical with prec. word,
andy,п., bullock cart or carriage.—Telugu band:.

## bandy-legged
bandy-legged, adj. — Compounded of bandy,
adj., leg and suff. -ed.

## bane
bane, n. — OE. bona, 'murderer, slayer', rel. to
OE. benn, 'wound', OS. bano, OFris. bona.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:96 COLUMN:3 -->
OHG. bano, 'murderer', OHG. bana, 'murder .
'ON. bani, 'murderer, murder, death', ben.
'wound', Dan., Swed. bane, 'death, murder'.
Goth, banja, 'stroke, wound', and cogn. with
Avestic banta, 'ill', bqnayen, 'they make sick'.
Derivatives: bane-ful, adj., bane-ful-ly, adv..
bane-ful-ness, n.

## bang
bang, tr. and intr. v. — Of. Scand. origin. Cp
ON. banga, 'to hammer', Swed. banga, to make
a noise', Icel. banga, Dan. banke, 'to beat', Cp.
also Lith. bungat, 'to nudge in the ribs', MHG.
bunge, 'drum', G. Bengel, 'cudgel; a clumsy
fellow, a fool', Du. bengel, 'a naughty boy'.
All these words are of imitative origin. Cp.
bungle. Cp. also whang, whiz-bang.
Derivative: bang, n.

## bang
bang, interj. — Of imitative origin. See prec.
word.

## haag
haag, n. — A variant of bhang.

## bang
bang, п., hair cut across the forehead. — Of
uncertain origin.

## bangle
bangle, п., a ring-shaped bracelet. — Hind.
bangrl.

## bangy
bangy, banghy, п., a shoulder yoke for carrying
loads. — Marathi bangi, fr. Hind, bahangi, fr.
OI. vihaAgamd, vihangika. See Yule-Burnell.
Hobson-Jobson, p.6ob.

## banian
banian, п., a Hindu merchant. — Hind, vanija.
'a trader*, fr. OI. vanij, 'merchant'. Cp. bany-
nn tree.

## baaish
baaish, tr.· v. — ME. banishen, fr. OF. baniss-,
pres. part, stem of banir, 'to proclaim; to banish
(F. bannir, 'to banish; to expel'), fr. Frankish
"bannjan, which is rel. to Goth, bandwjan, 'to
make a sign, to signal', whence It. bandire.
OProvenc. bandir, 'to proclaim; to banish'. See
banner and cp. band, 'troop'. For the ending see
verbal suff. -ish. OF. banir, etc., were influenced
in meaning by a confusion with OF. ban, 'public
proclamation' (see ban, 'edict'). See Bloch--
Wartburg, DELF., p. 55 s.v. bannir and Dauzat,
DELF., p. 72 s.v. bannir.

## banister
banister, n. — Corruption of baluster.

## banjo
banjo, п., a musical instrument. — Fr. earlier
banjore, banjer, banshaw, Negro alterations of
bandore (q.v.)
Derivatives: banjo, intr. v., banjo-ist, n.

## bank
bank, п., the edge of a river. — ME. banke, of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. bakki, 'river bank, ridge',
and next word, and see bench, Cp. also bunk,
'sleeping berth'.
Derivative: bank, tr. and intr. v., to pile up in
a bank.

## bank
bank, п., a bench. — ME. banck, prob. fr. OF.
banc, 'a bench', which is of Teut. origin. See
bench and cp. prec. word and banc, banco.

## bank
bank, п., an institution for the custody of money.
— F. banque, fr. It. banco, orig. 'bench, table,
counter' (scil. of a money changer), which is
of Teut. origin. Cp. bank, 'the edge of a river",
bank, 'bench', and see bench. Cp. also bankrupt,
bunco, embankment.
Derivatives: bank, intr. v., to keep a bank; to
keep money in a bank; tr. v., to keep (money)
in a bank; bank-able. adj., bank-er,n.,bank-ing, n.

## banket
banket, п., the conglomerate in the Witwaters-
rand gold district in the Transvaal. — S. Afr.
Du., lit. 'sweetmeat', fr. F. banquet. See banquet.

## bankrupt
bankrupt, n. and.adj. — Refashioned after L.
rupta, fr. F. banqueroute, fr. It. banca rotta, lit.
'a broken bench', fr. banca, 'bench', and rotta
(fr. L. rupta), fem. pp. of rompere, 'to break',
fr. L. rumpere, (see bench and rupture); so called
from the habit of breaking the bench of
bankrupts.
Derivatives: bankrupt, tr. v., bankrupt-су, п.,
bankrupt-ly, adv.

## banksbull
banksbull, п., l) a warehouse; 2) the office of a
harbor master (Anglo-Ind.) — Hind, bangsal,
'store room', prob. fr. OI. bhandasala-,
'storehouse'. See Yule-Burnell, Hobson-Jobson,
p\6ib.

## Banksia
Banksia, п., a genus of Australian evergreen
trees. — Named after the famous English
naturalist and traveler, Sir Joseph Banks (1743-
1820). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## baaner
baaner, n. — ME. banere, fr. OF. baniere (F.
banniere), which is prob. a blend of WTeut. *banda,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:97 COLUMN:1 -->
corresponding to Goth, bandwa, bandwo, 'sign,
signal' (whence also It., OProven?. banda, 'band,
troop', Late L. bandum, 'banner', banderia, ba-
neria, 'place where the banner is set up', OPro-
vcnc. bandiera (whence It. bandiera, F. ban-
diere, Sp. bandera), 'banner', and of OF. ban,
'public proclamation'. Goth, bandwa, prob.
derives fr. I.-E. base *bendh-, 'to bind'. See baad,
'tie', and cp. band, 'troop', banderilla, haaderole,
baaish, pandour. For the etymol. of OF. ban see
ban, 'edict'. MHG. banier(e) (whence G. Banner
and Panier), 'banner', is an OF. loan word.
Derivatives: banner, tr. and intr. v. (obsol.),
banner-ed, adj., bann-er, n. (obsol.), banneret
(q.v.)

## banneret
banneret, п., order of knighthood; orig., a knight
who could lead his men into battle under his
own banner. — ME. banerel, fr. OF. baneret
(F. banneret), a derivative of baniere (F. ban-
mire). See banner.

## banneret
banneret, bannerette, п., small banner. — OF.
banerete, dimin. of baniere (F. banniere). See
banner and -et, -ette.

## bannerol
bannerol, п., banner borne at a funeral and placed
over the tomb. — A variant of banderole.

## bannock
bannock, n„ a thick flat cake. — OE. bannuc,
'cake*, fr. Gael, bonnach, of s.m.

## banns
banns, bans, n. pi., public announcement of a
marriage. — PI. of ban, 'edict'.

## banquet
banquet, n. — F., fr. It. banchelto, dimin. of
banco, 'bench'. See bench and -et and cp. baac,
banco, banket, banquette.
Derivatives: banquet, v., banquet-er, n.

## banquette
banquette, п., the foot bank 'of a trench (fort.) —
F., fr. Languedoc banqueta, dimin. of banc
'bench'. See prec. word and -ette.

## banshee
banshee, n„ a female spirit supposed to warn
families of the death of a member. — From Ir.
bean sidhe, lit. 'woman of the fairies'. Bean
comes fr. OE. ben, which is cognate with E.
quean and queen.

## banstickle
banstickle, п., the stickleback. — Compounded
of ME. ban, 'bone', and stickle (in stickleback),
'prickle'. See bone and stickleback.

## bantam
bantam, п., a kind of small fowl. — Fr. Bantam,
name of a town, west of Jakarta in Java.

## banter
banter, tr. and intr. v. and n. — Of unknown
origin.
Derivatives: banter-er, п., banter-ing-ly, adv.,
banter-y, adj.

## banting
banting, п., a system for reducing weight. —
Named after William Banting (1797-1878), its
inventor and propagator.
Derivatives: banting-ism, п., banting-he, intr. v.

## banding
banding, п., a brat; a bastard. — G. BSnkling,
'bastard', lit. 'conceived on a bench', fr. Bank,
'bench'; see bench and subst. sun", -liag. For
sense development cp. bastard.

## Banta
Banta, п., a group of African languages
comprising most of those spoken south of the
Equator. — Coined by W. H. I. Bleek fr. native
Ba-ntu, fr. plur. pref. ba- and ntu, 'a man, a
person', hence Ba-ntu lit. means 'the men, the
people, mankind'.

## banyan
banyan, n. — See banian.

## banynn tree
banynn tree, also banyan, n. — Orig. 'the tree
under which the banyans (= Hindu merchants)
settled near Gombroon (now called Bandar
Abbas); see banian. See Yule-Burnell, Hobson-
Jobson, p. 65.

## banzai
banzai, interj., form of greeting addressed to the
Emperor of Japan. — Jap. 'may you live ten
thousand years'. Cp. Chin, wan, 'myriad', лиг,
•year'.

## baobab
baobab, п., name of an African tree. — Native
name.

## bap
bap, п., a small roll of bread (Scot.) — Of
uncertain origin.

## Baphia
Baphia, η., a genus of trees and shrubs of the pea
family, (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βαφή, 'a
dipping, a dyeing', which is rel. to βάπτειν, 'to
dip, dye', βαπτίζειν, 'to dip'. See baptism and -la.

## Baptisia
Baptisia, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βάπτισις, 'a dipping',
fr. βαπτίζειν, 'to dip' (see next word); so called
from the use of some species for dyeing. For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## baptism
baptism, n. — ME. bapleme, fr. OE. baptesme

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:97 COLUMN:2 -->
(F. bapleme), fr. Eccles. L. baptisma, fr. Gk.
βάπτισμα, 'a dipping in water', in Eccles. Gk.
'baptism', fr. βαπτίζειν, 'to dip', in Eccles. Gk.
'to baptize', fr. βάπτειν, 'to dip, steep, dye,
color', which is re], to βαφή, 'a dyeing', and
cogn. with ON. kvefja, 'to plunge', OSwed. kvaf,
'a deep place'. For sense development it should
be borne in mind that baptism orig. consisted
in immersion. E. baptism has been refashioned
after Eccles. L. baptisma, Gk. βάπτισμα. For
the ending see suff. -ism. Cp. Baphia, Baptisia,
baptist, baptistery, baptize and the second
element in nbJobaphene.
Derivatives:6apfwm-a/,adj., baptism-al-ly, adv.

## baptist
baptist, n. — OF. (= F.) baptiste, fr. Eccles. L.
baptisia, fr. Gk. βαπτιστής, 'one who dips'. See
baptism and -ist.

## baptistery
baptistery, baptistry, n. — OF. baptislerie (F. bap-
tistire), fr. Eccles. L. baptisterium, fr. Gk. βαπ-
τιστήριον, 'bathing place', in Eccles. Gk.,
baptistery'. See baptist and -cry, resp. -ry.

## baptize
baptize, tr. and intr. v. — ME. baplisen, fr. F.
baptiser, fr. Eccles. L. baptizarc, 'to baptize', fr.
Gk. βαπτίζειν. See baptism and -ize.

## bar
bar, rod of metal or wood. — ME. barre, fr. OF.
(= F.) barre, fr. VL. *barra, a word of Gaulish
origin. See forum and cp. barrier, barrister, bar-
rulet, debar, disbar, embargo, embarrass.

## bar
bar, tr. v. — ME. barren, fr. OF. barrer, fr. barre.
See prec. word and cp. barrage.
Derivatives: barr-ed, adj., barr-er, п., barr-ing,
n. and prep., barr-y, adj.

## bar
bar, п., the maigre (Sciaena aquila). — F. bar, fr.
MDu. ba(e)rse, which is rel. to OS., MHG. bars,
G. Barsch and E. barse (q.v.)

## Barabbas
Barabbas, masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Βαραββας, fr.
Aram, bar abba, 'son of the father, son of the
master', fr. bar, 'son', which is rel. to Heb. ben,
'son', and fr. Aram, abba, 'the father', emphatic
state of abh, which is rel. to Heb. Bbh, 'father'.
For the first element see ben, 'son', and cp. bar
mitzrah and words there referred to. For the
second element see Aboth and cp. Abba, abbot.

## barad
barad, п., the unit of pressure in the centimeter-
gram-second system (physics). — Fr. Gk. βάρος,
'weight'. See baro-.

## barathrum
barathrum, п., 'pit, gulf', esp. that near Athens
into which criminals condemned to death were
thrown. — L., fr. Gk. βάρα&ρον, 'pit, gulf,
cleft', rel. to Homeric βέρεθρον, of s.m., fr. l.-E.
base *g"er-, 'to devour', whence also βοράς,
'voracious', βρώμα, 'food', lit. 'that which is
eaten', L. vorare, 'to devour'. See voracious and
cp. words there referred to.

## barato
barato, п., money given to bystanders by a winner
at the gaming table. — Sp., from the adj. barator
'cheap', fr. baratar, Ίο barter, traffic', which
prob. derives fr. Gk. πράττειν, 'to do, perform*.
See practical.

## barb
barb, п., beard, a beardlike appendage. — OF.
(=F.)barbe, fr. L. barba, 'beard', which is cogn.
with OE. beard. See beard and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: barb, tr. v., to supply with a barb;
barb-ed, adj.

## barb
barb, п., name of a breed of horse. — F. barbe,
shortened fr. Barbaric, prop, 'horse introduced
from Barbary in North Africa'.

## Barbara
Barbara, fem. PN. — L., prop. fem. of barbarus,
'strange, foreign, barbarous', fr. Gk. βάρβαρος.
See barbaric.

## Barbarea
Barbarea, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (bot.) — ModL., named after St. Barbara.

## barbarian
barbarian, n. and adj. — Formed with suff. -ian
fr. Gk. βάρβαρος. See barbaric.

## barbaric
barbaric, adj. — OF. barbarique, fr. L. barbari-
cus, 'foreign, strange, outlandish', fr. G.
βαρβαρικός, fr. βάρβαρος, 'non-Greek, foreign,
barbarous', which is cogn. with OI. barbarah,
'stammering (designation of the non-Aryan
nations), from the I.-E. imitative base *baeb-,
'to stammer, stutter; unintelligible'. Cp. brave.
Cp. also Berber and the second element in rhn-
barb. For *balb-, a collateral base of 'barb-, See
balbaties, booby. For the imitative base 'bob-
set babble.
Derivative: barbaric-al-ly, adv.

## barbarism
barbarism, n. — F. barbarisme, fr. L. barbarismus.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:97 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. Gk. βαρβαρισμός, 'unintelligible speech', fr.
βάρβαρος. See prec. word and -ism.

## barbarity
barbarity, n. — See barbaric and -ity.

## barbarize
barbarize, tr. and intr. v. — Gk. βαρβαρίζειν,
'to speak like a barbarian', fr. βάρβαρος. See
barbaric and -ize.
Derivative: barbariz-ation,n.

## barbarous
barbarous, adj. — L. barbarus, fr. Gk. βάρβαρος.
See barbaric. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see -ous.
Derivatives: barbarous-ly, adv., barbarous-
ness, n.

## Barbary
Barbary, п., the countries in North Africa west
of Egypt. — OF. Barbaric, fr. L. bar bar ia, 'a
foreign country', fr. barbarus, 'strange, foreign,
barbarous'. See barbaric and -y (representing
OF. -ie).
Barbary ape. — Lit. 'ape of North Africa', fr.
Barbary.

## barbasco
barbasco, п., the wild cinnamon. — Sp., fr. L.
verbascum, 'mullein', a word of Ligurian origin.
Cp. Verbascum.

## barbate
barbate, adj., r) bearded; 2) (bot.) having
hairlike tufts or awns. — L. barbatus, 'bearded',
fr. barba, 'beard'. See barb, 'appendage', and
adj. suff. -ate and cp. barbituric.
Derivative: barbat-ed, adj.

## barbecue
barbecue, п., an animal roasted whole; a social
gathering at which animals are roasted whole.
— Sp. barbacoa, orig. 'a framework to sleep on;
a framework for roasting meat", fr. Taino
barbacoa.
Derivative: barbecue, tr. v.

## barbel
barbel, п., a large fish, Barbus fiuviatilis. — OF.
(F. barbeau), fr. VL. 'barbellus, dimin. of Late
L. barbula, which itself is dimin. of L. barbus,
'barbel' (whence OHG. barbo, MHG., G. barbe,
of s.m.), fr. L. barba, 'beard'. See barb, 'beard',

## barber
barber, n. — ME. harbour, fr. OF. barbeor (as
if fr. VL. *barbator), fr. L. barba, 'beard'. Cp.
F. barbier (fr. VL. *barbarius) and see barb,
'beard',

## barberry
barberry, п., any plant of the genus Berberis. —
OF. barbere, barberis, fr. ML. berberis, barbaris,
fr. Arab, barbaris, in vulgar pronunciation ber-
berb, 'barberry'. Cp. Berberis.

## barbet
barbet, n. — F., fr. L. barbatus, 'bearded'. See
bnrbate.

## barbette
barbette, п., mound for mounting guns (fort.) —
F., dimin. of barbe, 'beard' (see barb, 'beard',
and -ette); so called from a fanciful comparison
of the mounted guns with a beard,

## barbican
barbican, п., outer defense of a city or castle. —
ME. barbecan, fr. OF. barbacan, barbican (F.
barbacane), which prob. derives ult. fr. Pers.
bala-khana, 'upper chamber, balcony on the top
of a house', lit. 'a high house', fr. bula, 'high',
and khana, 'house'. The first element is rel. to
Avestic bWzant-, OI. bfhdnt-, 'high'; see
borough. The second element derives fr. stem
khan-, 'to dig'.

## barbicel
barbicel, п., a little process on the barbule of a
feather. — ModL. barbicella, dimin. of barba,
'beard'. See barb, 'beard',

## barbiton
barbiton, п., an ancient many-stringed
instrument resembling a lyre. — Gk. βάρβιτον, earlier
form βάρβιτος, a loan word from a foreign,
prob. the Phrygian, language.

## barbituric
barbituric, adj., designating, or pertaining to, a
crystalline acid, CHjiCO.NH^CO (chem.) —
Coined fr. L. bar bat a (in ML. Usnea barbata,
lit. 'bearded moss'), and uric. L. barbata is fem.
of barbatus, 'bearded'; see barbate. (ML. usnea
derives fr. Arab, ushna", 'moss').

## barbale
barbale, п., a minute barb; a process at the edge
of the barb of a feather. — L. barbula, 'a little
beard', dimin. of barba. See barb 'beard', and
-ule and cp. barbicel.

## barcarole
barcarole, barcarolle, a song sung by Venetian
boatmen. — F. barcarolle, fr. It. barcarola, fr.
barcarolo, 'gondolier', a derivative of barca,
'boat'. Sec bark, 'vessel',

## bard
bard, п., a Celtic minstrel-poet. — С '.el. bard,
fr. Gaul, 'bardo-, 'singer', whence ilso Gk.
βάρδος, L. barSus, 'bard', bardala, 4he copped
lark' (lit. 'the singer').
Derivative: bard-ic, adj.

## bard
bard, also barde, п., armor for the breast and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:98 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 71 | BARROW -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:98 COLUMN:1 -->
flanks of a warhorse. — F. barde, 'armor for
horses', fr. Sp. barda, 'horse armor', albarda,
'packsaddle', fr. Arab. (al-)bdrdaah, '(the) stuffed
packsaddle of an ass'.

## bardasb
bardasb, п., a catamite. — F. bardache, fr. It.
bardascia, fr. Arab, barda}, 'slave', ult. fr. Pers.
bardah, of s.rri.

## bardolater
bardolater, п., a worshiper of the Bard, i.e.
Shakespeare. — Formed fr. bard, 'poet', on analogy of
idolater.

## bardolatry
bardolatry, п., worship of Shakespeare. —
Formed fr. bard, 'poet', on analogy of idolatry.

## Bardolph
Bardolph, masc. PN. — OHG. Berhtolf
compounded oSberaht, 'bright', and wolf, 'wolf. See
bright and wolf.

## bare
bare, adj. — ME. bare, fr. OE. bser, rel. to OS.,
OHG., MHG., G. bar, ON. berr, Du. baar,
(fr. Old Teut. *baza-), and cogn. with Arm. bok
(for *bhos-ko-), 'naked', OSlav. bosu, Lilh. basas,
Lett, bass, 'barefoot'. Cp. the first element in
ballast.
Derivatives: bare, tr. v., bare, п., bare-ly, adv.,
bare-ness, п., bar-er, n.

## barege
barege, barege, п., 1) a gauzelike fabric; 2) a
mineral water from Bareges. — F. barege, so
called fr. Bareges, a village situated in the
department of the Hautes-Pyrenees in France.

## baresark
baresark, adv., without shirt. — Alternation of
berserk (as if deriving from bare sark, i.e. 'bare
shirt'). See berserker.

## baret
baret, n. — A var. of barret.

## bargain
bargain, n. — ME. bargayn, fr. OF. bargaigne,
fr. bargaigner. See bargaia, v.

## bargain
bargain, intr. and tr. v. — OF. bargaignier (F. bar-
guigner), 'to waver, be irresolute', orig. 'to
bargain', prob. fr. Frankish *borganjan, 'to borrow,
to lend', which is rel. to OHG. borgin, OE.
borgian, 'to borrow, to lend'. See borrow.
Derivative: bargain-er, n.

## barge
barge, broad, flat boat. — OF., fr. OProvenc.
barca, fr. L. barca, 'a small boat, bark',
shortened fr. *barica, fr. Gk. βίρις, fr. Copt, bar],
'boat'. Cp. bark, 'sailing ship', and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: barge, intr. v.

## bargeer
bargeer, п., a trooper who is riding another man's
horse (Anglo-Ind.). — Pers. bargir, lit. 'burden
taker', fr. bar, 'burden', and -gir, stem of girif-
tan, 'to seize, take'.

## barite
barite, п., barytes (mineral.) — See barytes.

## baritone
baritone, barytone, п., a male voice between bass
and tenor. — F. baryton or It. bariiono, fr. Gk.
βαρύτονος, 'heavy-toned, low-toned', which is
compounded of βαρύς, 'heavy' (see bary-), and
τόνος, 'tone'. See tone.
Derivative: barytone, baritone, n.

## barium
barium, п., a metallic element (chem.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. βαρύς, 'heavy', which is rel. to βάρος,
'weight'; see baro-. The element was so called
by its discoverer, the English chemist Sir
Humphrey Davy (1778-1829) because of its presence
in barytes or heavy spar.

## bark
bark, п., rind of a tree. — ME. barke, fr. ON.
borker (whence also Dan., Swed. bark), which is
rel. to LG. borke (whence G. Borke). According to
Petersson (in Indogerm. Forschungen 23,403),
these words derive from a -^-enlargement of
1-Е. base *bher-, 'to cut', for which see bore,
'to pierce' and words there referred to. For
sense development cp. L. cortex, 'bark of a
tree', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to cut' (see cortex).
Derivatives: bark, tr. v., bark-en, tr. and intr. v.,
bark-en, adj. (poet.), bark-er, п., bark-er-y, n.

## bark
bark, п., a kind of sailing ship. — F. barque, fr.
It. barca, fr. L. barca, 'a small boat, bark'. See
barge, 'boat', and cp. barkentine, barque,
debark, disembark, embark.

## bark
bark, intr. v., to cry as a dog. — ME. berken, fr.
OE. beorcan, rel. to ON. berkja, 'to bark'; prob.
imitative.
Derivatives; bark-er, п., bark-ing, adj. and n.

## barkentine
barkentine, barquentine, п., a kind of three-
masted vessel. — Formed fr. bark, resp. barque,
"sailing vessel', on analogy of bngantine.

## barkevikite
barkevikite, п., a variety of amphibole (mineral.)
— Named after Barkevik, on the Langesund
fiord, in Norway. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:98 COLUMN:2 -->

## barley
barley, n. — ME. barly, fr. OE. bierlic, orig.
an adjective meaning 'like barley', fr. bere,
barley', and -lie, 'like'. The first element is rel.
to ON. barr, 'barley', Goth, barizeins, 'of
barley', and cogn. with L. far, gen. farris, 'coarse
grain, meal'. See farina, farrage, and cp. barn,
barton. For the second element see adj. suff. -ly
and like, adj.

## barm
barm, п., yeast. — ME. berme, fr. OE. beorma,
rel. to Du. berm, MLG. berm, barm, LG. barme
(whence G. Barme), and cogn. with L. fermen-
turn, 'substance causing fermentation', fr. I.-E.
base *bher-, 'to boil, seethe', whence also OI.
bhurati, 'moves convulsively, quivers', MIr.
berbaim, Ί boil, seethe'. Cp. brand, bread, brew,
broil (in both senses), broth. Cp. also ferment,

## bar mitzvah
bar mitzvah, a male person who has completed
his thirteenth year, when he reaches the age of
religious responsibility (Jewish religion). —
Heb. bar mitzvd1*, lit. 'son of command', fr. bar,
'son', which is rel. to Heb. ben, and mitzvah,
'command, commandment', which is rel. to Iziv-
v<f", 'he commanded'. For the first element see
ben, 'son', and cp. the first element in Barabbas,
Barnabas, Bartholomew. For the second element
see mitzvah.

## barn
barn, n. — ME. bern, fr. OE. bern, shortened fr.
orig. bere-ern, lit. 'barley house', fr. bere,
'barley' and em, sern, 'house'. For the first element
see barley. The second element is a metathesized
form of *ran(n) (for *rasn), 'house', and rel. to
ON. rann, Goth, razn, 'house', and to OE. rest,
rsest, 'resting place'. See rest, 'repose', and cp.
Ihe first element in ransack.

## Barnabas
Barnabas, п., a surname of Joseph, the Levite of
Cyprus (Acts 4:36). — Eccles. L., fr. Gk.
Βαρνάβας, lit. 'son of exhortation', fr. Aram, bar,
'son', and nabha, 'prophecy, exhortation'. For
the first element see bar mitzvah and cp. words
there referred to. The second element is rel. 10
Heb. nabhi, 'prophet', n6bhu'ah, 'prophecy'. See
Nebiim.

## barnacle
barnacle, п., an instrument for pinching a horse's
nose. — ME. bernak, bernacle, bernakile, fr. OF.
bernac, which is of uncertain origin.

## barnacle
barnacle, п., ι) the barnacle goose; 2) shellfish. —
Bret, bernic, 'shellfish' (whence also F. bernicle,
'barnacle goose; shellfish'), prob. fr. Olr. bern,
'cleft, crack, fissure' (according to popular
belief, the goose was supposed to be born from
the shellfish).

## baro-
baro-, before a vowel bar-, combining form
denoting the pressure of the atmosphere. — Gk.
βαρο-, fr. βάρος, 'weight', rel. to βαρύς,
'heavy', fr. I.-E. base 'g^er-, 'heavy', whence also
L. gravis. See grave, 'weighty', and cp. bary-,
Briareus, and the second element in centrobaric,
cbarivari.

## barograph
barograph, п., a recording barometer. —
Compounded of baro- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφε'.ν,
'to write'. See -graph.
Derivative: barograph-ic, adj.

## barology
barology, п., the study of weight or gravity. —

## Compounded of baro-
Compounded of baro-, and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);

## one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## barometer
barometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
pressure of the atmosphere. — Compounded of
baro- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'. The term barometer was prob.
used first by the English chemist and physicist
Robert Boyle (1627-91) in 1665.
Derivatives: barometr-ic, adj., barometr-y, n.

## baron
baron, n. — ME. baron, barun, fr. OF. baron,

## oblique case of ber
oblique case of ber, fr. ML. baro, gen. -onis,
which is of Teut. origin; cp. OHG. baro, 'man',

## prop
prop, 'warrior', which is rel. to ON. berjask,
'to fight', and cogn. with OSlav. borjq, boriii,
'to fight'. All these words prob. derive fr. I.-E.

## base 'bher-
base 'bher-, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry'.
Derivatives: baron-age, п., baron-ess, п., baron-

## el
el, n. and tr. v., baron-et-age, п., baron-et-cy, п.,

## baron-etic-al
baron-etic-al, baron-ial, adjs., barony (q.v.)

## barony
barony, п., ι) a baron's domain; 2) dignity or
rank of a baron. — OF. baronie (F. baronnie),
fr. baron. See prec. word and -y (representing
OF. -ie).

## baroque
baroque, adj., pertaining to an artistic style

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:98 COLUMN:3 -->
characterized by grotesque forms. — F., not fr.
Port, barroco, 'irregularly shaped pearl', as
generally assumed, but from the name of the
founder of the baroque style, Federigo Barocci
(1528-1612).
Derivative: baroque, n.

## baroscope
baroscope, п., an instrument showing the changes
of the pressure of the
atmosphere.—Compounded of baro- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to
look at, examine'. See -scope.
Derivatives: baroscop-ic, baroscop-ical, adjs.

## Barosma
Barosma, п., a genus of plants of the rue family
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'of a heavy smell', fr. baro-
and Gk. 6σμή, 'smell, odor'. See osmium.

## barosmin
barosmin, п., diosmin (pharm.) — Formed fr.
Barosma with chem. suff. -in.

## barouche
barouche, п., a kind of four-wheeled carriage. —
G. Barutsche, fr. It. baroccio, a collateral form
of earlier biroccio, St. VL. 'birrotium, 'a two-
wheeled carriage', fr. L. birotus (for bis-rotus),
'two-wheeled', fr. bis, 'twice', and rota, 'wheel'.
See bi- and rota and cp. britska.

## barque
barque, n. — A variant of bark, 'sailing vessel'.

## barquentine
barquentine, n. — See barkentine.

## barracau
barracau, п., an Oriental fabric, camlet. — F., fr.
Arab, barrakan, 'camlet*, which is of Persian
origin.

## barracks
barracks, n. pi., soldiers' lodgings. — F. baroque,
fr. Sp. barraca, orig. 'hut of bricks', a derivative
of barro, 'clay*, which is prob. of Iberian origin.

## barracuda
barracuda, also barracouta, п., a large sea fish. —
Sp. barracuda, of uncertain origin.

## barrage
barrage, п., dam. — V., fr. barrer, 'to bar,
obstruct'. See bar, v., and -age.

## barrage
barrage, п., curtain fire (mil.) — Fr. F. tir de
barrage, 'curtain fire'. See prec. word.

## barranca
barranca, п., ravine. — Sp., fr. barranco,
'precipice, ravine', fr. VL. barrancus, fr. Gk. φάραγξ,
gen. φάραγγος, 'deep chasm, ravine, gully*,
which is rel. to φάρυγξ, 'throat, chasm, gulf,
φάρειν, 'to cleave, part', and cogn. with L.
forare, 'to bore', OE. borian, 'to bore'. See bore
'to pierce', and cp. pharynx.

## barrandite
barrandite, п., a hydrous phosphate of iron and
aluminum (mineral.) — F., named after' the
French geologist Joachim Barrande (1799-1883).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## barrator
barrator, п., one guilty of barratry. — ME. bara-
tour, 'a quarrelsome person*, fr. OF. barateor,
'deceiver, swindler', fr. barater, 'to deceive,
barter'. See barter.

## barratrous
barratrous, adj., tending to barratry (law). — See
barratry and -ous.
Derivative: barratrous-ly, adv.

## barratry
barratry, п., fraudulent breach of duty (marine).
— See barrator and -ry.

## barrel
barrel, n. — ME. bare!, fr. OF. (= F.) baril,
'barrel, cask', which is of Gaulish origin. The
word came to Britain through the medium of
the Normans; it is not related to F. bane, 'bar'.
Cp. It. barile, OProvenc. and Sp. barril, which
are of the same origin and meaning as OF. baril.
Cp. also barricade, barrico, breaker, 'a small
cask'.

## barren
barren, adj. — ME. barain, barein, fr. OF. bre-
haigne, baraigne, which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: barren-ly, adv., barren-ness, n.

## barret
barret, п., a small cap, esp. a biretta. — F. bar-
rette, St. It. barretta (now berretta). See biretta.

## barricade
barricade, n. — F., fr. MF. barriquer, 'to
barricade', fr. barrique, 'a large barrel', fr. baril,
'barrel'; see barrel. Barricade orig. meant 'an
obstruction made with barrels'. It. barricata,
usually regarded as the etymon of F. barricade,
is in reality a French loan word.

## barricade
barricade, tr. v. — F. barricader, fr. barricade.
.See barricade, n.

## barrico
barrico, п., a keg. — Sp. barrica, fr. barril, 'a
barrel'. See barrel.

## barrier
barrier, n. — ME. barrere, fr. F. barriere,
'obstacle', fr. barre, 'bar'. See bar, 'rod of metal
or wood'.

## barrister
barrister, n. — Formed fr. bar, 'rod of metal or
wood', with suff. -ster.

## barrow
barrow, п., mountain, mound. — ME. barewe,
berewe, fr. OE. beorg, 'mountain*, rel. to OS.,
Swed., Norw., OFris., Du., OHG., G. berg,
'mountain', ON. bjarg, 'rock', Dan. bjerg,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:99 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BARROW | 72 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:99 COLUMN:1 -->
MHG. berc, 'mountain', fr. I.-E. base *bhergh-,
'high'. See borough and cp. the second element
in iceberg,

## barrow
barrow, п., a castrated boar. — OE. bearg, rel. to
OS., OHG. barg, barug, ON.-bHrgr, MDu. barch,
barech, Du. barg, MHG. bare, G. Barch, and
cogn. with OSlav. bravu, fr. earlier borvu,
'castrated young pig; wether', fr. I.-E. base *bher-,
'to cut, bore'. See bore,

## barrow
barrow, п., a handcart. — ME. barewe, fr. OE.
bearwe, 'basket, barrow', fr. beran, 'to carry*.
See bear, 'to carry', and cp. bier.

## barnilet
barnilet, п., a small bar (her.) — Formed with
dimin. suff. -etfr. VL. *barrula, dimin.of'barra.
See bar, 'rod of metal or wood'.

## harry
harry, adj., traversed by an even number of bars
(her.) — F. bane, pp. of barrer, 'to bar', fr.
barre. See bar, 'rod of metal or wood'.

## barse
barse, п., the common perch. — OE. bars, 'perch',
rel. to MDu. ba(e)rse, Du. baars, OS., MHG.
bars, G. Barsch, 'perch', G. barsch, 'rough'; fr.
Teut. base *bars-, 'sharp'. See bristle and cp.
bass, 'perch', bar, 'maigre'.

## barter
barter, intr. and tr. v. — ME. barlren, fr. OF.
barater, 'to deceive, barter', fr. barat, 'cheat,
deception', which is of uncertain, possibly
Celtic, origin. Cp. Ir. brath, 'treachery', Gael.
bratk, 'to betray'. Cp. also barrator.
Derivatives: barter, п., barier-er, n.

## barthite
barthite, п., a hydrous arsenate of zinc and
copper. — Named after Barih, a mining engineer
at Guchab, SW. Africa. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## Bartholomew
Bartholomew, masc. PN. — OF. Barthelemieu (F.
Barthelemy), fr. L. Bartholomaeus, fr. Gk.
Βαρθολομαίος, fr. Aram, bar Talmay, 'son of Tal-
mai". Aram, bar, 'son', is rel. to Heb. ben, of
s.m.; see ben, 'son', and cp. words there referred
to. Talmay, a Heb. name occurring already in
the Bible (e.g. Nu. 13:22), is rel. to Heb. tilem,
'furrow'.
Derivative: Barthohme-an, adj.

## bartizan
bartizan, п., a small tower for defense — First
used by Walter Scott who mistook the real
meaning of Scot, banisene, which is nothing but
the corrupted spelling of brallicing, 'timber-
work', fr. brattice (q.v.)

## barton
barton, п., barn. — ME. berton, fr. OE. beretun,
'threshing floor, barn', lit. 'barley enclosure', fr.
here, 'barley', and tun, 'enclosure'. See barley
and town.

## Bartonla
Bartonla, п., a genus of plants of the gentian
family (bat.) — ModL., named in honor of
Benjamin Smith Barton of Philadelphia (died
in 1815). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## baruria
baruria, п., an abnormal condition in which the
urine has a very high specific gravity (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of Gk. βαρύς,'heavy',
and ουρον, 'urine'. See bary-, uro-, 'of urine',
and -ia.

## bary-
bary-, combining form meaning 'heavy'. — Gk.
βαρύ-, fr. βαρύς, 'heavy', rel. to βαρός, 'weight'.
See baro-.

## barycenter
barycenter, barycentre, п., the center of gravity.
— Compounded of bary- and center.
Derivative: barycentr-ic, adj.

## barysillte
barysillte, п., a lead silicate. — Coined fr. bary-,
silicate and subst. suff. -ite.

## baryta
baryta, п., barium monoxide (chem.) — From
next word.

## barytes
barytes, п., native barium sulfate, BaS04; heavy
spar (mineral.) — Coined by the Swedish
chemist Karl Wilhelm Scheele (1742-86) fr. Gk.
βαρύς, 'heavy', which is rel. to βάρος, 'weight'.
See haro- and cp. barium, barite.

## barythymia
barythymia, п., melancholia (med.) — Medical
L.. compounded of bary- and θυμός, 'spirit,
mind, soul'. See thio- and -in and cp. thyme. Cp.
also the second element in lipothymia,
parathymia.

## harytic
harytic, adj., pertaining to baryta. — Formed fr.
baryta with suff. -ic.

## barytone
barytone, n. — See baritone.

## basal
basal, adj., relating to the base; basic. — Formed

## with adj. suff. -al fr. base
with adj. suff. -al fr. base, n.
Derivative: basal-ly, adv.

## basalt
basalt, n. — L. basaltes, explained by most
lexicographers as a word of African origin. (This

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:99 COLUMN:2 -->
explanation is based on Pliny, Historia 36, 58.)
In Thesaurus Linguae Latinae, s.v. basanites,
several editions are quoted, in which basaltes
stands for basanites. We may, therefore, assume
that the original form is basanites, which was
later shortened into basaltes. L. basanites (lapis)
comes fr. Gk. βασανίτης (λίθος). I tentatively
suggest that βασανίτης derives fr. Βασάν, 'Bash-
an' (Βασάν is the transliteration of Heb.
BSs/ιάη in the LXX), to which the suff. -ίτης
was added (see subst. suff. -ite). Accordingly,
βασανίτης λίθος lit. means 'stone of Bashan'.
This etymology is supported by the fact that
Bashan, this well-known region east of the
Jordan, first mentioned in the Bible as the Kingdom
of Og, is especially rich in basalt. Cp. basanite.

## basan
basan, п., tanned sheepskin. '— F. basane, fr.
OProvenc. basana, fr. Sp. badana, fr. Arab.
bi0nah, lit. 'lining', fr. batana, 'he hid, covered',
fr. bain, 'belly, interior'. See wad, 'soft material'.

## basanite
basanite, п., touchstone. — L. basanites (lapis),
fr. Gk. βάσανος or βασανίτης (λίθος),
'touchstone'. See basalt.

## basaree
basaree, п., a Hindu flageolet (music). — Hind.
basree, fr. OI. vathSah, 'bamboo', which is cogn.
with Mir. feice, Ir. feige (for 'vankia), 'lintel,
rafter'; L. vacerra, 'log, stock, post', however,
is not cognate.

## bascule
bascule, п., an apparatus based on the principle
of the seesaw. — F., 'seesaw', from orig. basse
cute, altered from earlier bacule under the
influence of basse, fem. of bas, 'low'. Bacule is
composed of the imper. of baltre, 'to strike',
and cut, 'posterior'. See batter, 'to beat', and
culet.

## base
base, п., bottom; foundation, pedestal. — F., fr.
L. basis, fr. Gk. βάσις, 'a stepping, step,
pedestal, foot, base', from the stem of βαίνω, Ί go',
which prob. stands for *βάνιω, fr. *βάμ-ιω,
fr. I.-E. base *gwem-, 'to go; to come', whence
also L. venio (prob. for *gwmio), Ί come', Goth.
qiman, OE. cuman, 'to come'. See come and cp.
venue, 'arrival'. Cp. also basis, abasia, acrobat,
aerobatics, amphisbaena, Anabaena, anabas,
anabasis, -bates, bathmism, batophobia, bema, cata-
hasis, diabase, adlabatic, diabetes, ecbatic, gyno-
base, hyperbaton, metabasis, Odobenus, Ori-
batidae, parabasis, presby-, stereobate, stylobate.
As a term of chemistry base was introduced by
the French chemist Guillaume-Francois Rou-
elle (1703-70) in 1754.
Derivatives: base, tr. v., to form a base for;
intr. v., to be based (on or upon something);
base-ment, n.

## base
base, adj. — ME. bas, fr. OF (= F.) bas, 'low',
fr. Late L. bassus, 'thick fat, stumpy' (in classical
L. occurring only as a cognomen); of
uncertain origin. Cp. abase, bass (music), hasset,
basso, bassoon, debase.
Derivatives: base-ly, adv., base-ness, n.

## bash
bash, tr. v., to strike violently. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. Swed. basa, Dan. baske, 'to strike'.

## bashaw
bashaw, n. — A variant of pasha (q.v.)

## bashful
bashful, adj. — Aphetic for abash-ful. See abash
and -ful.
Derivatives: bashful-ly, adv., bashful-ness, n.

## bashi-bazouk
bashi-bazouk, п., a Turkish irregular soldier. —·
Turk, bashi-bdzuq, lit. '(one whose) head is
turned'. Cp. the first element in bashlyk and the
second element in bimbashee.

## bashlyk
bashlyk, also basblik, п., hood covering the ears.
— Turk, bashlyq, 'any kind of headgear'.

## basic
basic, adj. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. base, n.
Cp. the second element in monobasic,
dibasic.
Derivative: basic-al-ly, adv.

## basidium
basidium, п., a form of sporophore characteristic
of the fungi of the class Basidiomycetes (bot.) —

## ModL.
ModL., fr. Gk. βάσις, 'base'. See base, п., and
cp. Aureobasidium.
basiL п., any of a group of aromatic plants of the
mint family. — OF. basile (whence F. basilic),

## fr. Late L. basilicum
fr. Late L. basilicum, fr., Gk. βασιλικόν (scil.
φυτόν), 'basil', neut. of the adjective βασιλικός,
'royal'. See basilica.

## basil
basil, n. — Corruption of basan.

## Basil
Basil, masc. PN. — L. Basilius, fr. Gk. Βασίλειος,

## lit. 'kingly
lit. 'kingly, royal", fr. βασιλεύς, 'king'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:99 COLUMN:3 -->
basilica and cp. basil, the plant.

## basilar
basilar, adj., pertaining to the base; basal, basic,
fundamental.— ModL., irregularly formed fr. L.
basis, fr. Gk. βάσις, 'a stepping, step, pedestal,
foot, base'. See base, 'foundation', and adj.
suff. -ar.
Derivative: basilar-y, adj.

## basilic
basilic, royal. — F. basilique, fr. Gk. βασιλικός.
See next word.

## basilica
basilica, n. — L., 'a public hall with double
colonnades', fr. Gk. βασιλική (scil. στοά), lit.
'royal colonnade', fem. of βασιλικός, 'kingly,
royal', fr. βασιλεύς, 'king', which is of
uncertain origin. It is possibly a loan word from
a language of Asia Minor; cp. Lydian βάττος,
king'. Cp. basil, the plant, basilisk.
basilic vein (anat.) — ML. vena basilica, fr. Arab.
al-bdsiltq, fr. al-, 'the', and basiltq, a word of
uncertain origin, which was confused by the
"translators of Avicenna with Gk. βασιλικός,
'royal' (see prec. word). The term vena basilica
.ippears for the first time in a translation of
Avicenna by Gerardus Cremonensis. See Joseph
Hyrtl, Das Arabische und Hebraische in der
Anatomie, Wien, 1879, PP-74-77-

## basilisk
basilisk,'п., a mythical serpent, cockatrice; a
Central American lizard. — L. basiliscus, fr. Gk.
βασιλίσκος, 'princelet, chieftain, basilisk',
dimin. of βασιλεύς, 'king'; s.o called after Pliny,
Naturalis Historia, 8, 33, from ist 'crown', i.e.
.1 white spot on its head. See basilica and cp.
the second element in aspic, 'asp'.

## basin
basin, n. — ME., fr. OF. bacin, bassin (F. bassiri),
fr. VL. *baccinum, fr. bacchinon (cited by
Gregory of Tours as a vulgar word), fr. *bacca,
'a water vessel' (whence F. bac, 'vat'). See
back, 'vat', and cp. next word.

## basinet
basinet, п., a light steel helmet, later made with
a visor. — ME., fr. OF. bacinet, bassinet (F.
bassinet), dimin. of bacin, bassin (F. bassin), 'basin'.
See prec. word and -et, and cp. bassinet.

## basis
basis, n. — L., fr. Gk. βάσις. See base, n.

## bask
bask, intr. and tr. v. — ME. basken, fr. ON. bada-
sk, a reflexive verb lit. meaning 'to bathe
oneself, fr. bada, 'to bathe' (see bathe), and reflex,
suff. -sk.

## basket
basket, n. — ME., fr. L. bascauda, 'a brazen
vessel', referred to by the Roman poet Martial as an
OBrit. word; cogn. with L. fascis, 'bundle,
faggot' ; see fasces. The orig. meaning of bascauda
was prob. 'wicker basket'.

## bason
bason, n. — A variant of basin.

## Basque
Basque, n. and adj. — F., fr. Sp. vasco, adj., fr.
vascon, п., fr. L. Vasc6nes, name of the ancient
inhabitants of the Pyrenees. According to
Wilhelm von Humboldt, the name Vascdnes orig.
meant 'Foresters'. Cp. Gascon.

## bas-relief
bas-relief, п., low relief. — F., fr. bas, 'low', and
relief, 'raised work', fr. relever, 'to raise'. F. bas-
relief is a loan translation of It. bassorilievo.
See bass, adj., and relief and cp. basso-rilievo.

## bass
bass, п., any of various perchlike fishes. —
Alteration of barse.

## bass
bass, adj. and n. (mus.) — It. basso, fr. Late L.
bassus, 'low'. See base, adj., and cp. bassoon
and the second element in contrabass.

## bassanite
bassanite, п., an anhydrous calcium sulfate
(mineral.) — Named after F. Bassani, professor of
geology in Naples. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## bassarid
bassarid, п., a maenad (Greek mythol.) — Gk.
βασσαρίς, gen. -ιδός, fr. βασσάρα, 'fox', a word
of unknown etymology; so called because their
dresses were made of foxskins.

## basset
basset, п., a variety of small hound. — F., formed

## with dimin. suff. -et fr. bas
with dimin. suff. -et fr. bas, 'low'. See base, adj.

## bassetite
bassetite, п., a phosphate of calcium and uranium
(mineral.) — Named after the Basset mines in
Cornwall.

## bassinet
bassinet, п., cradle. — Usually derived fr. F.

## bassinet
bassinet, 'a little basin', dim. of bassin, fr. OF. bacin
(see basin). This derivation, however, does not
account for the sense of the English word.

## According to my opinion
According to my opinion, E. bassinet is a blend of

## F. barcelonneite
F. barcelonneite, 'a little cradle' (a collateral

## form of bercelonnette
form of bercelonnette, fr. bercer, 'to rock'), and

## F. bassinet
F. bassinet, 'a little basin'.

## basso
basso, п., a bass voice. — It. See bass (mus.).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:100 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 73 | BATTLEDORE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:100 COLUMN:1 -->

## bassoon
bassoon, п., a woodwind instrument. — F. bas-
son, fr. It. bassone, fr. basso. See bass (mus.)
and -oon.

## bassoonist
bassoonist, п., player of a bassoon. — A hybrid
coined fr. bassoon and suff. -ist.

## basso-rilievo
basso-rilievo, п., bas-relief. — It. See bas-relief
and rilievo and cp. cavo-relievo.

## bast
bast, п., the inner bark of the linden tree. — ME.,
fr. OE. bxst, rel. to ΟΝ., OS., MDu., OHG.,
MHG.,G.,'iiMi',OHG.Aesien,,tosew with bast',
and prob. cogn. with L.fascis, 'bundle', see
fasces. OE. bsest, etc., orig. meant'that which serves
for binding'. OF. bastir (whence F. batir), 'to
build', is a loan word fr. Frankish *bast/ati, and
orig. meant 'to sew or bind with bast'. Cp. baste,
'to sew loosely'. Cp. also bastille, bastion, and
the second element in bundobust. For sense
development cp. G. Wandj 'wall', which is rel. to
wenden, 'to turn, twist' (see wand).

## bastard
bastard, m, an illegitimate child. — OF. (F. bd-
lard), identical in meaning with fils de bast,
'acknowledged son of a nobleman, born out of
wedlock', prop, 'son of concubinage', fr. bast,
'concubinage', which prob. derives fr. Teut.
*bansti, 'barn' (cp. Goth, bansts of s.m.);
accordingly, OF. bastard lit. meant 'child born in
a barn'. See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 60 s.v.
balard.
Derivatives: bastard, adj., and the hybrids
bastard-ize, tr. v., bastard-iz-ation, n.

## baste
baste, tr. v., to soak, moisten. — Orig. pp. of a
verb formed fr. OF. basser, 'to soak'; of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: bast-ing, n.

## baste
baste, tr. v., to sew loosely. — OF. bastir (F.
batir), 'to build', fr. Frankish *bastjan 'to sew
or bind with bast', which is rel. to OHG. besten,
of s.m., fr. bast, 'bast'. See bast.
Derivative: bast-ing, n.

## baste
baste, tr. v., to beat. — ON. beysta, 'to beat', rel.
to OE. beatan. See beat.
Derivative: bast-ing, n.

## bastille
bastille, п., a castle or fortress; specif, an ancient
prison of Paris, destroyed by the revolutionaries
July 14, 1789. — F., formed with change of suff.
fr. OProvenc. bastida, fr. bastir, 'to build'. See
baste, 'to sew loosely', and cp. bastion.

## bastinado
bastinado, п., beating with a stick on the soles of
the feet. - - Sp. bastonada, 'a beating, cudgeling,'
fr. baston, 'stick', See baston and -ado.

## bastion
bastion, п., a work projecting outward from a
fortification. — F., variant of bastillon, dimin.
of bastille. It. bastione, is a French loan word,
whereas It. bastia is a back formation fr.
bastione. See bastille.
Derivatives: bastion-ary, bastion-ed, adjs.

## baston
baston, п., a stick, staff. — OF. baston (F. baton),
formed with the augment, suff. -on fr. Late L.
bastum, of s.m. This word is prob. borrowed fr.
Gk. *βάστον or *βάστα, 'support', which is a
back formation fr. Late Gk. *βαστάν (ср. Mod-
Gk. βαστώ), fr. Gk. βαστάζειν, 'to lift up, raise,
carry', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. It. bas-
tone, Sp. baston, and see -oon. Cp. also
bastinado, baton, and batten, 'timber'. Cp. also the
first element in bathorse, batman.

## bat
bat, п., the club used in cricket, clc. — ME. batte,
bat, fr. OE. bait, 'cudgel', prob. rel. to F. batte,
'beater, beetle', back formation fr. battre, 'to
beat'. See batter, v., and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: bat, intr. v., to use a bat, batt-ing, n.

## bat
bat, п., a nocturnal mammal. — A dialectal form
of ME. bakke, a word of Scand. origin. Cp.
Swed. natt-backa, natt-batta, 'bat' (lit. 'night
bat'), Dan. aften-bakke, 'bat' (lit. 'evening bat').
For the change of к (in ME. bakke) to t (in E.
bat) cp. apricot (from orig. apricock), havoc (fr.
OF. havot), and the English words milt and milk,
'milt of fishes'.

## batata
batata, п., the sweet potato. — Sp. See potato.

## batch
batch, n. — ME. bacche, lit, 'a baking', OE. ba-
can, 'to bake'. See bake. Batch stands to bake as
match, 'one of a pair', stands to make.
Derivatives: batch, tr. v., batch-er, n.

## bate
bate, п., a solution used in tanning. — Rel. to
Swed. beta, 'soaking, tanning', and to E. bait,
bite (qq.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:100 COLUMN:2 -->

## bate
bate, v., to reduce. — Aphetic for abate.
Derivative: bat-ed, adj.

## bate
bate, intr. v., to beat the wings, flutter. — F.
battre, 'to beat' (in the term battredesaites, 'to beat
the wings'), fr. L. battuere, battere. See batter, v.

## bate
bate, п., strife (obsol.) — Aphetic for debate.

## -bates
-bates, combining form meaning 'treading on ...
as in Dendrobates, Hylobates. — Fr. Gk. βάτ/;;,
'one that treads', from the stem of βαϊνειν, 'to
go'. See base, n.

## bath
bath, n. — ME. bath, fr. OE. bxd, rel. to OS.
iarA,ON.bo<5,MDu.,MHG.iai,OHG.,G.,Du.
bad. The final dental sound corresponds 10
Teut. -pa (= I.-E. -to) and is added to the Teut.
base appearing in OHG. ba-jan (whence MHG.
bxn, bxjen, G. ba-hen), 'to foment',
corresponding to I.-E. base *bhe~-, 'to warm'. Hence OE.
bxd, etc., orig. meant 'that which warms'. Base
*bhog-, 'to warm, roast, bake', a -^-enlargement
of base bhe-, 'to warm', appears in Gk. φώγε'.ν,
'to roast', and in E. bake (q.v.)
Derivative: bath, tr. v.

## Bath
Bath, brick, chair, etc. — Named after Bath, л
town in Somerset, England.

## bath-
bath-, combining form. — See batho-.

## bathe
bathe, tr. and intr. v. — ME. bathien, fr. OE.
badian, rel. to ON.bada, MDu. baden, Du. baden,
OHG. badon, MHG., G. baden, and lo OE. bxd ,
etc., 'bath'. See bath.
Derivatives: bathe, п., bath-er, п., bath-ing, 11.

## bathkol
bathkol, п., a heavenly voice. — Heb. bath qui,
lit. 'the daughter of a voice"', fr. bath, 'daughter',
and qdl, 'voice'. Bath stands for *banth, fr. orig.
*bint, fern, of ben, 'son'; rel. to Aram, tfrath,
emphatic case blratta, Syr. (emphatic) barta
Arab. bint. Ethiop. bant, 'daughter', See ben,
'son' and cp. the first element in Barhsheba. For
the second element see cowle.

## bathmism
bathmism, п., the growth force (biol.) — A name
coined by the American paleontologist Edward
Drinker Cope (1840-97) fr. Gk. βαθμός, 'step,
threshold', from the stem of βαίνειν, 'to go',
whence also βάσις, 'a stepping, pedestal, foot,
base'. See base, п., and words there referred to.
For the ending see suff. -ism.

## batho-
batho-, bath-, combining form meaning 'depth'.
— Gk. βαθο-, fr. βάθος, 'depth'. See bathos.

## bathometer
bathometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
depth of water. — Compounded of batho- and
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## bathorse
bathorse, п., a horse that carries baggage. —
A hybrid coined fr. F. bat, 'packsaddle' and E.
horse. F. bat derives fr. OProvenc. bast, fr. VL.
*bastum, 'the act of carrying', back formation
fr. *bastare, 'to carry', fr. Late Gk. *βασταν,
'to carry', fr. Gk. βαστάζειν. See baston and cp.
words there referred to.

## bathos
bathos, п., anticlimax, a descent from the sublime
to the ridiculous. — Gr. βάθος, 'depth', rel. to
βαθύς, 'deep', and prob. also to βένθος, 'depth'
—which seems to have been formed on analogy
of πένθος, 'grief—and! to βίασα (for *βάθ-
i=<), 'glen'; prob. cogn. with OI. gdhate, 'dives
into', gahah, 'deep place', Avestic.v/-#ai>,
'ravine', Olr. baidim, Ί cause to sink, drown'. The
word bathos was first used in the above sense
by Pope in his Dunciad. Cp. bathy-, benthos and
the second element in isobath.

## Bathsheba
Bathsheba, fern. PN.; in the Bible, the wife of
King David and mother of Solomon. — Heb.
Bathshebha', lit. 'daughter of the oath'. For the
first element see bathkol. The second element is
rel. to sheva', 'seven'. Cp. nishba' ,'he swore',
orig. 'he bound himself by the sacred number
seven'. See Shabuoth and cp. the second element
in Elizabeth.

## bathy-
bathy-, combining form meaning 'deep' — Gk.
βαθύ-, fr. βαθύς, 'deep', which is rel. to βάθος,
'depth'. See bathos.

## bathybius
bathybius, п., a slimy substance dredged up from
the Atlantic (zool.) — ModL., coined by the
English biologist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825-
95) in 1868 fr. Gk. βαθύς, 'deep' and βίος,
'life'. See bathy- and bio-.

## bathyscaphe
bathyscaphe, п., a diving apparatus for reaching
great depths. — Compounded of bathy- and
Gk. σκάφη, 'boat'. See scapho-.

## bathysphere
bathysphere, п., a spherical diving apparatus for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:100 COLUMN:3 -->
the observation and study of the depths of the
sea. — Compounded of bathy- and Gk. σφαίρα,
'hall, globe, sphere'. See sphere,

## batik
batik, п., a method of coloring designs on cloth.
— Javan. batik, 'spotted, speckled'.
Derivatives: batik, tr. v., batik-er, n.

## batiste
batiste, n. — F., named after its first maker, Bap-
tiste of Cambrai, who lived in the 13th cent.

## batman
batman, п., an officer's servant. — A hybrid
coined fr. F. bat, 'packsad*dle', and E. man. See
batborse.

## batmoney
batmoney, п., allowance to an officer. A hybrid
coined fr. Canarese bhatta, 'rice' (see batta),
and E. money,

## baton
baton, п., a stick, staff. — F. baton. See baston.

## batophobia
batophobia, п., morbid fear of being at great
heights or passing near high objects (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of Gk. βατός,
'passable', verbal adj. of βαίνειν, 'to go', and
-φοβία, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See base, n. and
-phobia. The association of Gk. βατός with height
is due to a connection of this word with the
second element in acrobat. (Acrobats are used
to display their art in the height.) A more
adequate name for this condition is hypsophobta.

## Batrachia
Batrachia,n.,pl.,theamphibians(z00/.)—ModL.,
fr. Gk. βατράχειος, 'pertaining to .a frog', fr.
βάτραχος, 'frog', which is of uncertain origin.
Derivative: batrachi-an, adj.

## batracho-
batracho-, before a vowel batrach-, pertaining to
frogs. — Gk. βάτραχο-, βατραχ-, fr. βάτραχος,
'frog'. See prec. word.

## batta
batta, п., allowance to an officer. — From
Canarese bhatta, 'rice', prob. through the medium of
Port. Cp. batmoney. For sense development cp.
salary, orig. 'salt money'.

## battalion
battalion, n. — F. bataillon, fr. It. battaglione, fr.
battaglia, 'battle'. See battle and -ion and cp.
palton.

## battel
battel, п., college accounts (at the University of
Oxford). — Of uncertain origin.

## batten
batten, intr. v., to grow fat. — The orig. meaning
was 'to become better', fr. ON. balna, which is
rel. to OE. batian, OFris. batia, MLG.,Du. baten,
OHG. Ьазёп, Goth, ga-batnan, 'to become
better, avail, benefit', and to OE. bet, 'better' (adv.),
betera, 'better' (adj.) See better, best,

## batten
batten, п., timber used in flooring. — F. baton,
'stick, staff'. See baton.
Derivative: batten, tr. v., batlen-ing, n.

## hatter
hatter, tr. and intr. v., to beat violently and
rapidly. — ME. bateren, batteren, fr. OF. batre,
battre (F. battre), 'to beat, strike', fr. L.
battuere, later also battere, 'to beat, strike', which
is of Gaulish origin; fr. I.-E. base 'bhat-, 'to
beat, strike', whence also L. con-futare, *to
check, suppress', re-futare, 'to repel, refute', and
prob. also fatuus, 'stupid', lit. 'struck silly'. See
beat and cp. next word, abate, abattis, abattoir,
bascule, bat, 'club', bate, 'to reduce', bate, 'to
flutter', battalion, battle, battledore, combat,
debate and the second element in andabata. Cp.
also confute, refute. Cp. also fade.
Derivatives: batter-ed, adj., batter-er, n.

## batter
batter, п., a mixture of flour, eggs and milk
beaten up together. — ME. bature, batour, fr. OF.
bature, 'a beating', fr. batre, 'to beat'. See prec.
word.

## batter
batter, п., slope of a wall. — Perhaps fr. batter,
'to beat'.
Derivative; batter, intr. v., to slope backward
(said of walls),

## battery
battery, n. — F. batterie, fr. battre, 'to beat'. See
batter, 'to beat', and -y (representing F. -ie).

## battle
battle, n. — ME. bataile, fr. OF. (= F.) bataille,
fr. L. battualia, battalia, 'fighting and fencing
exercises of soldiers and gladiators', fr. battuere,
battere, 'to strike, beat'. See hatter, 'to beat*.

## bathe
bathe, tr. and intr. v., to fight. — ME. batailen,
fr. OF. bataillier, batailler (F. batailler), 'to
fight', fr. bataille. See battle, п., and cp.
embattle, 'to prepare for battle',

## battle
battle, tr. v., to equip with battlements (archaic
or poetic). — OF. bataillier, 'to equip with

## battlements
battlements, fortify', fr. batailles, 'battlements',

## pi. of bataille
pi. of bataille, 'battle'. See battle, n.

## battledore
battledore, п., a wooden instrument with a long
handle and a flat board used to strike a shuttle-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:101 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BATTLEMENT | 74 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:101 COLUMN:1 -->
cock. — ME., prob. fr. OProvenc. batedor, 'an
instrument for beating', fr. L. banuere, battere,
'to beat, strike' (see batter, 'to beat'); influenced
in form by beetle.

## battlement
battlement, n. — ME. batelment, fr. OF. bataille-
ment, fr. bataillier, 'to equip with battlements,
to fortify'. See battle, 'to equip with
battlements', and -ment and cp. embattle, 'to provide
with battlements'.
Derivatives: battlement,tr.v.,battle-ment-ed, adj,

## battology
battology, п., superfluous repetition in speaking
or writing. — Gk. βαττολογίά, 'a speaking
stammeringly', compounded of *βάττος,
'stammerer' (cp.. Βάττος, name of a stammerer in
Herod. 4,155; βαττηιρίζειν, to stutter,
stammer'), and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. The first element is of imitative
origin. For the second element see -logy.
Derivatives: battolog-ical, adj., battolog-ist, n.

## battue
battue, п., ι) beating of woods to drive game out;
2) the game thus shot. — F., 'beating', prop. fern,
pp. of battre, 'to beat'. See batter, 'to beat'.

## hatz
hatz, п., a small coin, formerly current in
Switzerland. — G. Batz, Batzen, orig. meaning 'a
thick piece, lump', rel. to the verb batzen, 'to be
sticky, be adhesive', which is contracted fr.
*backezen, freq. of backen, 'to bake; to stick
together', but influenced in form by G. Batz,
Petz, pet form of Bar, 'bear', the animal
represented in the arms of Bern. See bake and bezzo.

## bauble
bauble, п., jester's stick. — ME. babel, fr. OF.
baubel, babel, 'toy'; related to E. babe, baby.

## band
band, п., (a term in telegraphic signaling) one dot
per second. — Named after the French inventor
Jean Baudot (1845-1903).

## baudekin
baudekin, baudkin, п., baldachin (a kind of
brocade). — ME., fr. OF. baudequin, fr. It. baldac-
chino. See baldachin.

## bauson
bauson,п., badger (archaic). — ME. bausen,
'badger', fr. OF. baugant, 'piebald' (whence also F.
balzan, 'horse with white stockings'), fr. VL.
*balteanus, 'provided with girdles', fr. L. bal-
teus, 'girdle', whence also Rum. bait, 'girdle',
baltat, 'spotted, piebald'. See belt and cp.
bauxite.

## bausond
bausond, adj., having white spots or stripes (dial.
E.) — OF. bauftmt. See prec. word.

## bauxite
bauxite, п., a claylike hydrate of aluminum
(mineral.) — F., fr. Les Baux, near Soles in France,
where this compound was first found. The name
Les Baux, fr. Proveng. Li Baus, lit. means 'the
precipices'. Proven?, baus derives fr. L. balteus,
'girdle', whence also Rum. bait, 'girdle', It. bal-
zo, 'shelf', balzare, 'to spring, jump'. See belt
and subst. suff. -ite and cp. bauson.

## bavenite
bavenite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after Baveno in Italy. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## havette
havette, п., a child's bib. — F., dimin. formed fr.
have, 'drivel, slaver', fr. baver, 'to drivel,
slobber' (whence bavarder, 'to babble, prattle'); of
imitative origin. Bavette lit. means 'slobbering
bib'. For the ending see suff. -ette.

## bawbee
bawbee, п., ι) sixpence; 2) halfpenny. — Named
after the Laird of Siltebawby, a mintmaster of
Scotland in the 16th cent.

## bawd
bawd, п., procurer, procuress. — ME. bawde,
'joyous, merry', prob. fr. OF. baude, baud, 'bold',
which is of Teut. origin. Ср. ОЕ. bald, beald,
'bold', and see bold.
Derivatives: bawdry (q.v.), bawd-y, adj.

## bawdry
bawdry, п., obscenity. — ME. bawdery, prob. fr.
OF. bauderie, 'boldness', fr. baude, baud. See
prec. word and -y (representing OF. -ie).

## bawl
bawl, intr. and tr. v., to howl, bellow. — Prob.
fr. ML. baulare, 'to bark', which is of imitative
origin. Cp. Icel. baula, 'to low', ON. baula,
'cow', lit. 'the lowing animal'. Cp. also bellow.
Derivatives: bawl, п., bawl-er, n.

## baxter
baxter, п., a baker (Scot.) — Orig. 'a female
baker', fr. OE. bxcestre, fem. of bsecere, 'baker'.
See baker and -ster.

## hay
hay, п., inlet. — ME. baye, fr. F. baie, fr. Sp.
bahla, which is prob. of Basque origin. See
Meyer-Lubke in Zeitschrift fur Romanische
Philologie, 32, 492. Cp. embay.

## bay
bay, п., part in the wall. — OF. baee (F. baie),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:101 COLUMN:2 -->
'an opening', prop. fem. pp. of baer (whence
F. bayer, beer, 'to gape'), taken as a noun, fr.
VL. badare or batare, 'to gape, yawn', a word of
imitative origin, whence also It. badare, Prov-
enc. badar, of s.m. Cp. abeyance, abash,
badinage, baillone, bengle, bevel.

## bay
bay, adj., of reddish brown color. —OF. (= F.)
bai, fr. L. badius, 'chestnut-brown', which is
cogn. with Olr. buide, 'yellow'. Cp. baize,
bayard.
Derivative: bay, п., an animal of bay color,
esp. a bay horse.

## hay
hay, intr. and tr. v., to bark. — ME. abayen,
bayen, fr. OF abater, baier (F. aboyer), 'to bark',
which is of imitative origin. Cp. It. abbaiare.
Cp. also Gk. βαύζειν, L. baubart, 'to bark', lit.
'to utter bau\
Derivative: bay, п., barking.

## bay
bay, п., the European laurel tree. — Orig. 'berry',
fr. OF. (= F.) baie, fr. L. baca, bacca, 'berry',
See bacci-,

## baya
baya, п., the weaverbird (Ploceus baya). — Hind.
baia, baya.

## bayadere
bayadere, a female dancer. — F. bayadere, fr.
Port, bailadeira, 'ballet dancer', fr. bailor, 'to
dance', fr. VL. ballare, 'to dance'. See ball,
'party for dancing'.

## baynrd
baynrd, п., a bay horse. — OF., fr. bai. See bay,
adj. and -ard.

## Bayard
Bayard, п., a gentleman of great courage and
integrity. — From the name of Pierre du Terrail,
seigneur de Bayard (1473-1524). the celebrated
'Chevalier sans peur et sans reproche' ('knight
without fear and without reproach').

## bayberry
bayberry, n. — Compounded of bay, 'the laurel',
and berry.

## bayonet
bayonet, n. — F. bayonnette, balonnette, fr.
Bayonne in Southern France; so called because
the first bayonets were made at Bayonne. For
sense development cp. bilbo, Toledo.
Derivatives: bayonet, tr. and intr. v., bayonet-ed,
adj., bayonet-eer, n.

## bayou
bayou, п., a creek. — Amer. F., fr. Chocktaw
bayuk.

## haysalt
haysalt, n. — Fr. Bai, place in France (near
Nantes), renowned as a shipping port for sea salt in
the 15th century. Cp. MDu. bayesout, G. Bai-
salz, which are of the same meaning and origin.

## bazaar
bazaar, п., a market place. — Ult. fr. Pers. bazar.
'market', which is rel. to Pahlavi volar, of s.m.

## bazooka
bazooka, п., a weapon consisting of a metal tube
and used for launching an explosive rocket;
first used in World War II. — Fr. bazooka, name
of a kind of wind instrument invented and
named by the American comedian Bob Burns
(died in 1956).

## bazzite
bazzite, п., a silica'te of scandium, etc. (mineral.)
— Named after the Italian enigineer Alessandro
E. Bazzi (died in 1929). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## bdellium
