Derivative: Biblical-ly, adv.

## biblico-
biblico-, combining form meaning 'Biblical'. —
Fr. ML. biblicus. See prec. word.

## biblio-
biblio-, combining form, meaning 'book'. — Gk.
βιβλίο-, fr. βιβλίον, dimin. of βίβλος, 'book*. See
Bible.

## bibliographer
bibliographer, n. — Formed with agential suff. -er
fr. Gk. βιβλιογράφος, 'writer of books,
transcriber, copyist'. See next word.

## bibliography
bibliography, n. — Gk. βιβλιογραφία, 'writing of
books', compounded of βιβλίον, 'little book',
and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See biblio-
and -graph)'.
Derivatives: bibliograph-ic, bibliograph-ic-al,
adjs., bibliograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## bibliolater
bibliolater, п., a worshiper of books. — See next
word and -later.
Derivative: bibliolatr-ous, adj.

## bibliointry
bibliointry, п., worship of books; worship of the
Bible. — Compounded of biblio- and Gk.
-λατρεία, -λατρίά, fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor,
worship'. See -latry.

## bibliomancy
bibliomancy, п., divination by opening a book,
esp. by opening the Bible. — Compounded of
biblio- and Gk. μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'.
See -mancy.

## biblomania
biblomania, п., book madness. — Compounded
of biblio- and Gk. μανία, 'madness, frenzy'. See
-mania.

## biblomaniac
biblomaniac, adj. — Compounded of biblio- and
ML. maniacus, 'maniac'. See maniac.

## bibliophil
bibliophil, bibliophile, n. a lover of books. — F.
bibliophile, 'lover of books', compounded of
biblio- and Gk. φίλος, 'friend'. See -phiL
Derivatives: bibliophil-ic, adj., bibliophil-ism, п.,
bibliophil-ist, п., bibliophil-y, n.

## bibliopole
bibliopole, п., bookseller. — L. bibliopOla, fr. Gk.
βιβλιοπώλης, 'bookseller', which is compounded
of βιβλίον, 'book' (see biblio-), and πώλης,
'merchant, seller', which derives fr. I.-E. base
*pel-, 'to sell, purchase, barter, gain'. See
monopoly.

## bibliotheca
bibliotheca, п., a library. — L. bibliotheca, fr.
Gk. βιβλιοθήκη, lit. 'a case for books', which
is compounded of βιβλίον, 'book', θήκη, 'case,
chest, sheath'. See biblio- and theca.
Derivative: bibliothec-al, adj.

## bibliothecary
bibliothecary, п., a librarian — L. bibliothecarius,
fr. bibliotheca. See prec. word and subst. suff.
-ary.
Derivative: bibliothecar-ial, adj.

## bibulous
bibulous, adj., fond of drink; spongy. — L. Ы-
bulus, 'drinking readily', fr. bibere 'to drink',
assimilated fr. *pibere, which is cogn., with OI.
plbati, 'drinks', Olr. if, 'drink!', OW. iben, 'we
drink'; from the reduplication of I.-E. base *pi-.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:108 COLUMN:2 -->
*po(i)-, 'to drink', whence ΟΙ. ράιί, 'drinks',

## payayali
payayali, paydte, 'gives to drink', panam,
'beverage', Arm. 'трет, Ί drink', Gk. πίνειν, 'to
drink', πόσις, 'a drink', πότος, *a drinking, a
drinking bout', L. potare, 'to drink', poti'6, 'a
draft, drink', OSlav. pijp, piti, 'to drink'. See
potioa and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
abreuvoir, beverage, bevy, bib, 'to drink', bib,
'piece of cloth', biberon, Imbibe, imbrue. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: bibulous-ly, adv., bibulous-ness, n.

## bicameral
bicameral, adj. having two chambers (said of
legislative bodies). — Formed fr. bi-, camera
and adj. suff. -al.

## bicarbonate
bicarbonate, n. (chem.) — Formed fr. bi- and
carbonate.

## bice
bice, п., blue or green pigment. — F. bis, 'brown,
tawny', rel. to OProvenc. bis. It. bigio; of
unknown origin.

## bicentenary
bicentenary, adj., pertaining to a period of two
hundred years; п., a bicentennial. — Formed
fr. bi- and centenary.

## bicentennial
bicentennial,adj., I) occurring every two hundred
years; 2) lasting for two hundred years; п., the
two hundredth anniversary or its celebration. —
Formed fr. bl- and centennial.

## bicephalous
bicephalous, adj., two-headed. — A hybrid coined
fr. bi-, a pref. of Latin origin, Gk. κεφαλή,
'head' (see cephalic), and -ous, a suff. of Latin
origin.

## biceps
biceps, п., name of various two-headed muscles,
esp. of that on the upper arm (anat.) — L., 'two-
headed', fr. Ы-, 'twice, two' and caput, 'head'.
See bi- and capital, adj. For the change of Latin
й (in caput) to ё (in Ы-cfps) see accent and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. bicipital, triceps,
quadriceps.

## bichir
bichir, п., a fish (Polypterus bichir). — A name of
Arabic origin, introduced into zoolog.
nomenclature by the French naturalist Geoffroy Saint-
Hilaire (1772-1844).

## bichloride
bichloride, n. (chem.) — Formed fr. bi- and
chloride.

## bicho
bicho, п., the chigger. — Sp., 'animal, small
animal', fr. VL. bgstius, fr. L. bestia, 'beast'. See
beast.

## bicipital
bicipital, adj., having two heads (anat.)—Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. biceps, gen. bicipitis.
See biceps.

## bicker
bicker, intr. v., to squabble, quarrel. — ME. Ы-
keren, of uncertain origin; possibly formed with
suff. -er fr. base *bik-, a collateral form of *pik-,
whence the verb pick.

## bicker
bicker, n. — Scot, form of beaker.

## bicuspid
bicuspid, adj., having two points. — Formed fr.
bi- and L. cuspis, gen. cuspidis, 'point*. See cusp
and cp. tricuspid.

## bicycle
bicycle, n. — F., lit. 'two-wheel', a hybrid coined
fr. the L. pref. bi- and Gk. κύκλος, 'a wheel'.
See cycle.
Derivatives: bicycle, intr. v., bicycl-ing, п., bi-
cycl-ism, п., bicycl-ist, n.

## bid
bid, tr. and intr. v. — Prob. a blend of ME.
bidden (fr. OE. biddan), 'to ask', and ME. beden
(fr. OE. biodan) 'to announce, proclaim, offer'.
OE. biddan is rel. to ON. bidja, OS. biddjan,
OHG., MHG., G. bitten, Goth, bidjan, 4o ask',
and to E. bead, and stands in gradational
relationship to OE. bxdan, ON. beida, OHG. beiten,
Goth, baidjan, 'to command, force, compel'. All
thesewordsderivefr.I.-E.base *bheidh-, 'bhidh-,
'topersuade, compel; to trust', whence also Gk.
πείθειν, 'to persuade', πίστις (for *πίθ-στις),
'faith', L. fidere, 'to trust, confide in', foedus,
'compact treaty', Alb. be (for *bhoidha), 'oath',
OSlav. blda (for *bhoidha), 'need', bezdo, bedili.
Ίο compel, incite'. Cp. bide, faith, fidelity, pis-
lology. — OE. biodan is rel. to ON. bjoda, OHG.
biotan, MHG., G. bieten, 'to offer', OE. on-
biodan, OS. an-biodan, OHG. in-biotan, Goth.
ana-biudan, 'to order, command', OE. forbio-
dan, Goth, faur-biudan, 'to forbid', fr. I.-E.
base *bheudh-, 'to offer, present', whence also
OI. bodhati, budhyate, 'is awake, is watchful,
observes, understands', buddhdh, 'awakened,
enlightened', Gk. πεύθεσθαι, πυνθάνεσθαι, 'to
learn by inquiry', OSlav. bljudq, bljusti, 'to
observe', buzdg, budeti, 'to be awake', buzdg, bu-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:108 COLUMN:3 -->
diti, 'to awake', bitdru, 'watchful', Lith. budeti,
"to be awake', Lett, budrus, 'watchful', Lith.
baudiiii, bausti, 'to chastise', Olr. buide,
'contentment, thanks', ro-bud, 'a warning'. Cp.
beadle, bode, forbid, Buddha.
Derivatives: bid, п., bidd-able, adj., bidd-er, п.,
bidd-ing, n.

## bidden
bidden, pp. of bid.

## Biddy
Biddy, fem. PN. — Pet form of Bridget (q.v.)

## biddy
biddy, п., an Irish maid. — From prec. word.

## bide
bide, intr. and tr. v. — ME. biden, fr. OE. bidan,
'to remain, continue, wait', rel. to ON. bida,
OFris. bidia, OHG. bitan, Goth, beidan, 'to
wait' and cogn. with Gk. πείθειν, 'to persuade',
L. fidere, 'to trust, confide in'. See bid and cp.
abide.

## Bldens
Bldens, п., a genus of plants of the thistle family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. L. bidens, 'two-toothed'.
See next word.

## bident
bident, п., an instrument with two prongs. — L.
bidens, gen. -etuis, 'two-pronged', formed fr.
bland dens, gen. dentis, 'tooth'. See dent and cp.
prec. word.

## bidree
bidree, bidry, also blddery, п., an alloy of tin,
zinc and copper. — Hind, bidri, from Bidar, a
town in India.

## Biedermeier
Biedermeier, adj. — After Gottlieb Biedermeier,
the imaginary author of poems written by Lud-
wig Eichrodt (1827-92).

## biennial
biennial, adj., lasting for two years; occurring
every two years; п., a plant living for two years.
— Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. biennium.
'space of two years', fr. bi- and annus, 'year'.
See annual and cp. words there referred to. For
the change of Latin й (in annus) to ё (in
biennium) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.

## bienseance
bienseance, п., propriety. — F., lit. 'well-becom-
ingness', fr. bienseant, 'well-becoming', fr. bien
(fr. L. bene), 'well', and seant, pres. part, of
seoir, 'to sit', fr. L. sedere. See beae-, sedentary
and -ce.

## bier
bier, n. — ME. here, fr. OE. bxr, rel. to OS.,
OHG. bora, ON. barer (pi.), OFris. here, MLG.,
MDu., MHG. bare, Du. baar, G. Bahre, 'bier',
fr. I.-E. *bher-, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to
carry', and words there referred to and cp. esp.
barrow, 'handcart'. E. bier was influenced in
form by F. biire, 'bier'.

## biere
biere, п., beer. — F., fr. Du. bier, which is rel. to
ON. bjdrr, OE. bior. See beer.

## blfarious
blfarious, adj., 1) twofold (rare); 2) arranged in
two rows (bot.) — L. bifurius, 'twofold, double',
prob. orig. meaning 'that which can be
expressed in two ways', and compounded of bi- and
fas in the sense of 'utterance, expression,
manifestation', which is rel. to fart, 'to speak, say'.
See fame and cp. fasti, fate. Cp. also
multifarious, nefarious, omnifarious, trlfarious. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## biff
biff, v., to strike; п., a blow. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. buff, 'a blow'.

## biffin
biffin, also beefui, n. — Variants of orig. beefing,
fr. beef; so called from the color of this variety
of apple.

## bifid
bifid, adj., split into two equal parts. — L. Ы-
fidus, 'split into two parts', fr. Ы- and fid-, the
stem of findere (pp. fissus), 'to split'. See fissile
and cp. trifid, quadrifld, multifld.

## bifocal
bifocal, adj. having two foci. — Formed fr.
bland focal.

## bifoliate
bifoliate, adj., having two leaves (bot.) — Formed
fr. bi- and foliate.

## bifurcate
bifurcate, adj., divided into two branches. — ML.
bifurcalus. See bi- and furcate.

## bifurcate
bifurcate, tr. and intr. v., to divide into two
branches. — See prec. word,.
Derivatives: bifurcat-ed, adj., bifurcat-ion, n.

## big
big, adj. — ME. bigge, big, of uncertain origin.

## big
big, bigg, tr. v., to build. — ME. biggen, fr. ON.
byggja, 'to build; to dwell in', which is rel.
to bua. 'to dwell'. See be and cp. boor, booth.

## biga
biga, п., a two-horsed chariot (Roman antiquities).
— L. bigae (pi.), contraction of *bi-jugae, lit.
'two (horses) yoked together', compounded of
bi-, 'twice' and jugum, 'yoke'. See bi- and yoke
and cp. join.

## bigame
bigame, п., a bigamist (obsol.) — OF., fr. ML. Ы-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:109 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: B1GAMV | 82 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:109 COLUMN:1 -->
gatrnts (corresponding to Gk. δίγαμος), 'twice
married', a hybrid coined fr. L. pref. Ы- and
Gk. -γάμος, fr. γάμος. See next word.

## bigamy
bigamy, п., the state of having two wives or two
husbands at the same time. — OF. (= F.) Ы-
gamie, fr. bigame (see bigame), fr. Eccles. L.
bigamia, a hybrid coined fr. L. Ы- and Gk.
γάμος, 'wedding, marriage', which is rel. to
γαμεΐν, 'to take to wife, to marry', γαμβρός,
'son-in-law, brother-in-law, father-in-law', fr.
I.-E. base *gem(e)-, 'to marry', whence also Of.
jamih, 'brother, sister', jama, 'daughter-in-law',
jama-tar, Avestic zdma-tar,'son-in-law',h.gener
(for *gemer), 'son-in-law' (for the change of m
to л see gener). Cp. Gamelioa, gamete, gamo-,
-gamy. For the difference in meaning between
bigamy and digamy see digamy.
Derivatives: bigam-ist, п., bigam-ous, adj. bi-
gam-ous-ly, adv.

## bigarreau
bigarreau, п., a variety of cherry. — F., fr. bigarre,
'variegated', fr. OF. garre 'variegated', which is
of uncertain origin; so called from its color.

## Big Ben
Big Ben, name of the bell attached to the clock
at Westminster. — Named after Sir Benjamin
Hall, first commissioner of works, under whose
supervision the bell was cast. For Ben, dimin.
of Benjamin, see Ben.

## bigg
bigg, big, п., the four-rowed barley (dial.) — ME.
big, bigge, fr. ON. bygg, 'barley', rel. to OE.
blow, 'grain, barley', OS. beo, bewod, 'harvest'.

## biggin
biggin, п., cap, hood. — F. beguin, fr. beguine,
name of the members of certain lay sisterhoods
(see Beguine); so called from caps originally
worn by them.

## biggin
biggin, п., a coffee percolator. — So called from
the name of its inventor.

## bight
bight, п., ι) a bending; 2) a loop in a rope; 3) a
bay. — ME., fr. OE. byht, 'a bend', rel. to MLG.
bucht (whence G. Bucht, Du. bocht, Dan., Swed.
bught, 'bight,bay'); prop, abstract nouns formed
fr. OE. bugan, resp. MLG. bugen, 'to bend'.
See bow, 'to bend', and cp. obsol. E. bought,
'a bend, turn, curvature'.
Derivative: bight, tr. v.

## Bignonia
Bignonia, п., a genus of vines (bot.) — ModL.,
named by the botanist Tournefort after his friend
the Abbe Jean-Paul Bignon (1662-1723),
librarian at the court of Louis XV. For the
ending see surf. -ia.

## Bignoniaceae
Bignoniaceae, n.pl., the Bignonia family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## bignoniaceous
bignoniaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## bigot
bigot, n. — F. bigot, 'over-devout', of uncertain
origin. It possibly derives fr. Sp. hombre de bi-
gotes, 'a man wearing mustaches', whence 'a
man of a serious, solemn cast of mind'.
Derivatives: bigol-ed, adj., bigot-ry, n.

## bijou
bijou, n. — F., 'jewel, gem', fr. Bret, bizou, 'finger
ring', fr. biz, 'finger'.

## bijouterie
bijouterie, п., articles of jewelry. — See bijou
and -ery.

## bike
bike, n. and v. — Colloq. abbreviation of bicycle,

## bikh
bikh, bish, п., aconite poison (Anglo-lnd.) —
Hind., fr. OI. visam, 'poison', which is cogn.
with Gk. ίός (for Τισός), L. virus (for "vital),
'poison'. See virus,

## bilabial
bilabial, adj., formed with both lips. — Lit. 'made
with both lips', fr. bi- and labial,

## bilabiate
bilabiate, adj., having two lips. — Formed fr.
bi- and inbiate.

## bilateral
bilateral, adj., having two sides. — Formed fr.
bi- and lateral.
Derivatives: bilateral-ity, п., bilaler-al-ly, adv.,
bilateral-ness, n.

## bilberry
bilberry, n. — Dan. bellebser, lit. 'ball berry'. See
ball, 'a round body', and berry,

## bilbo
bilbo, п., a kind of sword. — Sp., fr. Bilbao, town
in Spain. For sense development cp. bayonet.
Toledo.

## bildar
bildar, п., an excavator, digger (Anglo-lnd.) —
Hind., fr. Pers. beldar, 'a spade wielder'.

## bile
bile, n. — F., fr. L. bllis [for *bis(t)-lis], 'gall,
bile', which is cogn. with W. bustl, OCo.
Wife/, Bret, best/, 'gall'. Cp. biliary, bilious, and
the second element in an-abiliary.

## bilge
bilge, n. — A var. of bulge.

## Bilharzia
Bilharzia, п., a genus of worms, parasitic in the
blood (zool.) — ModL., named, at the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:109 COLUMN:2 -->
suggestion of the English biologist T. S. Cobbold, after
the German physician Theodor Bilharz,
discoverer of this parasite. For the ending see
suff. -ia.
Derivatives: bilharzi-al, bilharz-ic, adjs., bil-
harzi-asis, n.
ЬШ-, combining form denoting the bile. — L.
bill·, fr. bilis, 'bile'. See bile.

## biliary
biliary, adj., pertaining to the bile; bilious. —
F. biliaire, 'pertaining to the bile', fr. L. bilis.
See bile and adj. suff. -ary.

## biliate
biliate, tr. v., to treat with bile. — Formed with
verbal suff. -ate fr. L. bilis, 'bile'. See bile.
Derivative: biliat-ion, n.

## bilinear
bilinear, adj., of, or pertaining to, two lines. —
Formed fr. bi- and L. tinea, 'line'. See linear.

## bilingual
bilingual, adj. — Lit. 'of two languages'. See
bland lingual.

## bilious
bilious, adj., 1) related to, or caused by the bile;
2) peevish. — F. bilieux, fr. L. biliosus,
'pertaining to the bile', fr. bilis. See bile and -ous.
Derivatives: bilious-ly, adv., bilious-ness, n.

## bilk
bilk, tr. v., to balk, deceive. — Prob. a var. of
balk, 'to hinder".
Derivatives: bilk, п., a bilking; a swindler,
bilker, п., bitk-ing, n.

## bill
bill, п., an ancient weapon; a halberd. — ME.
bil, fr. OE. bill, 'sword, chopping tool', rel. to
OS. bil, 'sword', MDu. bile, Du. bijl, OHG.
bihat, MHG. bihel, later bil, G. Beil, ON. bilda,
'hatchet', ON. bildr, 'instrument for letting
blood', fr. I.-E. base *bhei-, 'to cut', whence
also Arm. bir, 'cudgel', Gk. φϊτρός, 'block of
wood, log', OSlav. biti, 'to strike', bid, 'whip',
Russ. bllo, 'mallet', Olr. biail, 'ax', benim (for
*bhinami, Ί cut, strike'. Cp. bill, 'beak'. Cp.
also boyar. For *bheid-, a -rf-enlargement of base
*bhei-, see bite and cp. words there referred to.

## bill
bill, п., document. — ME. bille, fr. AF. bilk, fr.
Anglo-L. billa, fr. ML. bulla, 'seal affixed to a
document, sealed document, document', fr. L.
bulla, 'bubble, boss, knob', later 'seal', fr. *bu-l-,
an -/-enlargement of the I.-E. imitative base
*bu-, 'to blow; to swell'. See buccal and cp.
billet, 'note', boil, v., bolas, boule, 'a game',
budge, bulb, bull, 'edict', ballet, bulletia.
Derivative: bill, tr. v., to make out a bill; to
announce by bills.
ЬШ, п., beak. — ME. bille, fr. OE. bile, 'beak',
rel. to OE. bill, 'sword, chopping tool'. See
bill, 'halberd*.
Derivative: bill, intr. v., to touch bills; to caress.

## billet
billet, п., document, note. — F. billet, fr. OF.
billette, which is a blend of bille, 'ball', and OF.
bullette, dimin. of bulle, 'bill', fr. L. bulla. See
bill, 'document'. Cp. also habiliment.
Derivative: billet, tr.-v.

## billet
billet, п., stick, log. — OF. billete (whence, with
change of suff., F. billot), dimin. of bille, 'block
of wood', fr. VL. billa, a word of Gaulish origin.
Cp. Ir. bile, 'tree trunk'. Cp. also billiards,
billon, bullion.

## billet-doux
billet-doux, п., love letter. — F., lit. 'sweet note',
fr. billet, 'document, note', and doux, 'sweet',
fr. L. dulcis, of s.m. See billet, 'document', and
dulcet.

## billiards
billiards, n. — F. billard, first denoting 'a bent
stick', then 'a stick to push balls' (whence its
modern sense), from bille, 'log'. See billet,
'stick, log'.

## billingsgate
billingsgate, п., abusive, blasphemous language.
— Prop, 'the language used at Billingsgate', fish-
market in London.

## billion
billion, п., I) lit. (and still so in England and
Germany) a million millions, (i.e. 1 followed by 12
zeros); 2) in the United States and France, a
thousand millions (i.e. 1 followed by 9 zeros). —
F., a hybrid formed on analogy of million (q.v.)
fr. L. pref. bi-, fr. bis, 'twice'. See bi- and cp.
trillion, quadrillion, quintillion, sextillioa, sep-
tillion, octillloa, nonillion, decillion, centillion.
Derivatives: billionaire (q.v.), billion-th, adj.
and n.

## billionaire
billionaire, n. — Formed fr. billion on analogy of
millionaire.

## billon
billon, п., an alloy of silver with a preponderating
amount of copper. — F., 'lump', fr. bille, 'block
of wood'; prop, a variant of bullion (q.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:109 COLUMN:3 -->

## billow
billow, n. — Fr. ON. bylgja, 'billow', rel. to
MHG. bulge, 'billow, bag', fr. Teut. base *belg-t
'to swell'. Accordingly billow lit. means
'anything swelling', whence 'a swelling wave'. See
belly and cp. bolster.
Derivative: billow-y, adj.

## billy
billy, n. — In all its senses: fr. Billy, pet form of
William.

## billycock
billycock, n. — Altered fr. bully-cocked (hat),
which lit. means 'cocked as hats worn by
bullies'. See bully and cock.

## bilohate
bilohate, adj., having two lobes. — Formed fr.
bi-, Gk. λοβός, 'lobe of the ear' (see lobe), and
adj. suff. -ate.

## biltong
biltong, п., sundried meat (S. African). — S.
African Du., compounded of Du. bil, 'rump',
and tong, 'tongue'(see tongue);so called because
the strips are tongue-shaped.

## bimaual
bimaual, bimanous, adj., having iwo hands (zool.)
— Formed fr. bi-, L. manus, 'hand* (see manual),
and adj. suff. -al, resp. -ous.

## blmastism
blmastism, п., condition of having two mammae
(aaat.) — A hybrid coined fr. L. pref. bi-, Gk.
μαστός, 'mamma', and Gk. suff. -ισμός. See bi-,
masto- and -ism.

## bimbashee
bimbashee, п., a Turkish military officer. — Turk.
bing-bashi, lit. 'head of a thousand'. The second
element of this word forms the first element of
the compound bashi-bazouk (q.v.)

## bimestrial
bimestrial, adj., bimonthly. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. bimenstris, bimestris, 'lasting two
months', fr. bi- and mensis, 'month'. Cp. L.
menstruus, 'pertaining to a month, monthly',
intermenstris, intermestris,' between two months',
and see month. Cp. also menses.

## bimetallic
bimetallic, adj., 1) composed of, or pertaining to,
two metals; 2) pertaining to, or based upon,
bimetallism. — F. bimetallique, coined by the
Italian economist Enrico Cernuschi (1821-96)
in 1869 fr. pref. bi- and metallique, 'metallic'.
See bi-, metal and -ic.

## bimetallism
bimetallism, п., the use of two metals, usually
gold and silver, as standard money. — F. bi-
metallisme, coined by Enrico Cernuschi in 1876.
See prec. word and -ism.

## bimetallist
bimetallist, п., an advocate of bimetallism. — See
prec. word and -ist.

## bimonthly
bimonthly, adj., happening once in two months.
— A hybrid coined fr. the L. pref. bi- (see bi-)
and English monthly (see month).
Derivative: bimonthly, n.

## bin
bin, п., receptacle. — ME. binne, fr. OE. binn,
fr. L benna, 'a two-wheeled cart with a body
of basket work', a word of Celtic (Gaulish)
origin; cp. W. benn, 'cart'. L. benna stands for
*bhenlna and is cogn. with Gk. πά&νη, Att.
φάτνη, 'manger, crib', fr. I.-E. base *bhendh-,
'to bind', whence also E. bind (q.v.) OE. bosig,
'cowstall', and dial. E. boose, 'crib', are prob.
cogn. with W. benn, 'cart'.
Derivative: bin, tr. v., to place in a bin.

## binary
binary, adj., dual. — L. binarius, 'consisting of
two', formed fr. bint, 'two each, two at a time',
which stands for 'dwis-ηϊ, and is rel. to duo,
'two', OL. dvis (whence L. bis), 'twice'. See bi-,
bis, and adj. suff. -ary and cp. combine and the
first element in binocle, binocular.

## binate
binate, adj., double (bot.) — Formed with adj.
suff. -ate fr. L. bini. See prec. word.
Derivative: binary, n.

## bind
bind, tr. and intr. v. — ME. binden, fr. OE.
bindan, rel. to OS., Goth, bindan, ΟΝ., OFris.
binda, OHG. bintan, MHG., G. binden, fr. I.-E.
base *bhendh-, 'to bind', whence also OI. badh-
ndti, later form bandhati, 'binds', bandhuh,
'kinsman', Gk. πεν&ερός, 'father-in-law', prop,
'bound (through marriage)', πείσμα (for "πένθ-
σμα), 'cable', πάθνϊ], Att. φάτνη (for *bhndh-na),
'manger, crib' (lit. 'place where the animal is
tied up'), L. of-fend-ίχ, 'a band', Lith. bendras,
'common, joint', as a noun 'partner', Lett.
biedrs, 'companion, comrade'; see R.Traut-
mann, Baltisch-Slavisches Worterbuch, p. 30.
Cp. band, 'a tie', bandhava, bandhn, bandoleer,
bend, besom, bin, bine, bond, bend, bund, bundle,
bandal, the first element in bundobust and the
second element in cummerbund, sebundy.
Derivatives: bind, п., bind-er, п., bind-er-y, п.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:110 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 83 | BITE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:110 COLUMN:1 -->
bind-ing, η. and adj.

## bine
bine, п., any climbing stem. — A dialectal form
of bind, n. (see prec. word).

## bing
bing, interj. — Imitative.

## binnacle
binnacle, п., case for a compass on a ship. —
Corruption of earlier biltacle, fr. Port, bilacola,
which is formed by aphesis fr. L. habitaculum,
'little dwelling' (whence also F, habitacte), a
derivative of habitare, 'to dwell'; see habitat.
The form of the word binnacle was prob.
influenced by E. bin.

## binocle
binocle, п., a telescope adapted for the use of
both eyes at the same time. — F., fr. L. bint,
'two at a time', and oculus 'eye'. See binary
and ocular.

## binocular
binocular, adj., using both eyes at the same time.
— See prec. word and cp. monocular.
Derivative: binocular, n.

## binomial
binomial, adj., consisting of two terms (alg.) —·
A hybrid coined from the L. pref. Ы- (see bi-) on
analogy of monomial.(q.v.)
Derivative: binomial, n.

## binominal
binominal, adj., having two names. — Formed fr.
bi- and nominal,

## binturong
binturong, п., an animal resembling the civet cat.
— Malay.

## bio-
bio-, combining form meaning 'life'. — Gk. βιο-,
fr. βίος, 'life', dissimilated fr. *β(Γος, fr. I.-E.
*gwiwos; cogn. with Goth, qius, OE. cwicu,
'living'. See qnick, and cp. vital, zoo-. Cp. also
biosis, biotic, and the second element in aerobic,
amphibious, bathybius, cenobite, microbe,
hygiene, Limnobium, Lithobius, macrobiotic,
necrobiosis, Rhizobium, symbion, symbiosis.

## biochemistry
biochemistry, п., chemistry dealing with animal
and plant life. — See bio- and chemistry.

## biogen
biogen, п., a protoplasmic unit (biol.) — Coined
by the German physiologist Max Verworn
(1863-1921) in 1903 fr. bio- and -gen.

## biogenesis
biogenesis, п., the theory that living organisms
can only arise from pre-existing living matter
(610/.)—Coined by the English biologist Thomas
Henry Huxley (1825-95) in 1870 fr. Gk. βίος,
'life', and γένεσις, 'origin, source'. See bio- and
genesis and cp. abiogenesis.

## biogenesist
biogenesist, п., one who believes in the theory of
biogenesis. — See prec. word and -ist

## biogenetic
biogenetic, biogenetical, adj., pertaining to
biogenesis. — See biogeaesis and -etic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: biogenetic-al-ly, adv.

## biogeny
biogeny, п., biogenesis. — Compounded of bio-
and -geny.

## biograph
biograph, п., a cinematograph. — Lit. 'living
description', fr. Gk. βίος, 'life', and -γράφος, fr.
γράφείν, 'to write'. See bio- and -graph and cp.
next word.

## biographer
biographer, n. — See next word and agential suff.
-er.

## biography
biography, n.—Late Gk. βιογραφία, 'description
of life', fr. Gk. βίος, 'life', and -γραφιά, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See bio- and -graphy.
Derivatives: biograph-ic, biograph-ic-al, adjs.,
biograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## biology
biology, n. — Lit. 'the study of life', suggested by
the German naturalist G. Reinhold Treviranus
as a modern coinage fr. Gk. βίος, 'life', and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic) (see bio- and -logy); introduced as a
scientific term by the French biologist Jean-Bap-
tiste-Pierre-Antoine de Monet de Lamarck
(1744-1829) in 1802 (in his Hydrogeohgie).
Derivatives: biolog-ic, biolog-ic-al, adjs., biolog-
ic-al-ly, adv., biolog-ist, n.

## biometry
biometry, п., the calculation of the notable
duration of human life. — Compounded of bio- and
-merry.

## bionomics
bionomics, п., ecology. — Formed fr. bio- on
analogy of economies.

## bioplasm
bioplasm, п., living protoplasm (biol.) —
Compounded of bio- and Gk. πλάσμα, 'something
molded'. See pinsnrn.

## bioplast
bioplast, a particle of bioplasm (biol.) —
Compounded of bio- and Gk. -πλαστός, fr. πλαστός,
'molded, formed'. See -plast.

## bioscope
bioscope, п., a biograph. — Compounded of bio-
and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, Ίο look at,
examine'. See -scope.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:110 COLUMN:2 -->

## biosis
biosis, п., vitality (biol.) — Gk. βίωσις, 'way of
life', fr. βίος, 'life'. See bio- and -osis.

## biosterin
biosterin, n., product from cod-liver oil.—Coined
fr. Gk. βίος, 'life' (see bio-), cholesterol and
chem. suff. -in.

## biotic
biotic, biotical, adj., pertaining to life. — Gk.
βιωτικός, fr. βίος, 'life'. See bio-.

## biparous
biparous, adj., bringing forth two at a birth. —
Formed fr. bi- and L. -parus (in viviparus,
'bringing forth its young alive'). See -parous.

## bipartite
bipartite, adj., divided into two parts (hot.) —
L. biparlitus, pp. of bipartlre, 'to divide into
two parts', fr. bi- and partitus, pp. of partlri,
'to divide'. See partite.

## biped
biped, п., an animal with two feet; a man; adj.,
two-footed. — L. bipes, gen. bipedis, 'two-
footed', fr. bi- and pis, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See
pedal.

## bipinae
bipinae, п., airplane with two planes. — Formed
fr. bi- and plane, 'airplane'.

## Bipontine
Bipontine, adj., relating to the edition of ancient
classics at Zweibriicken. — Lit. 'relating to the
town Zweibriicken (= Town of the 'two
bridges') in Bavaria, whose name was Latinized into
Bipomium. See bi- and pons. For the ending see
adj. suff. -ine.

## biqnadrate
biqnadrate, п., the fourth power, the square of
the square (math.) — Formed fr. bi- and
quadrate.
Derivative: biquadrai-ic, adjl and n.

## birch
birch, n. — ME. birche, fr. OE. bierce, beorc, rel.
to OS. birka, berka, ON. bork, Dan. birk, Swed.
bjork, Norw. bjerk, MOu.berke, Du. berk, OHG.
birihha, birka, MHG. birche, birke, G. Birke,
'birch', and cogn. with Osset. barz, OSlav. brim,
Lith. birias, Lett, beria, OPruss. berse, Russ.
bereza, OCzech bfieza, OI. bhurjah, 'birch', L.
farnus,fraxinus, 'mountain ash'. All these words
lit. mean 'the white (or bright) tree' and derive
fr. I.-E. base *bhereg-, 'to shine, be white'. See
bright and cp. Fraxinus, fraxinella.
Derivatives: birch, adj. and tr. v., birch-en, adj.,
birch-ing, n.

## bird
bird, n. — ME. brid, bird, fr. OE. bridd, 'young
bird', of uncertain origin; possibly in gradational
relationship to breed, brood.

## bireme
bireme, п., a galley having two banks of oars. —
L. birimis, formed fr. bi- and remus (for *res-
mos), 'oar', which is cogn. with Gk. έρέσσειν,
Att. έρέττειν, 'to row*, έρέτης, 'rower', έρετμός,
έρετμόν, 'oar', ΟΙ. aritar-, 'rower', aritrah, 'oar',
OE. rowan, 'to row', rdder, 'rudder'. See row,
'to propel a boat", rudder, and cp. the second
element in unireme, trireme, quadrireme, quln-
quereme. Cp. also remex.

## biretta
biretta, п., a square cap worn by the Roman
Catholic clergy. — It. berrelta, fr. Late L. birrus,
also birrum, 'large cloak with a hood', which is
of Gaulish origin; cp. Mir. berr, W. byrr, 'short'.
Cp. barret, beret, burnous.

## birr
birr, intr. v., to whir. — Of imitative origin.

## birrellism
birrellism, п., style resembling that of Augustine
Birrell (1850-1933). — For the ending see
suff. -ism.

## birtt
birtt, n. — ME. burihe, birthe, fr. ON. byrd, rel.
to OE. gebyrd, OS. giburd, OFris. herd, Du.
geboone,OHG.giburt, MHG., G. geburt.Goth.
gabaiirps. Derivatively these words correspond
exactly to OI. bhriih, 'a bringing, maintenance',
and to L. /«,' gen. Jortis, 'chance', fr. I.-E. base
*bher-, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry', and
cp. berth.

## bis
bis, adv., twice. — L. bis, fr. OL. dvis, cogn. with
OI. dvlh, Avestic bish, Gk. δίς, MHG. zwis,
'twice', Goth. Ms-, 'in two, asunder', ON. tvis-
ira, 'to divide". See bi- and cp. two, twi-, twist.
Cp. also the first element in bevue and the second
element in tite-beche.

## biscuit
biscuit, n. — F. biscuit, fr. L. bis coctus, 'twice
cooked' (whence also It. biscolto), fr. bis,
'twice' (see prec. word), and coctus, pp. of co-
quere, 'to cook'. See cook, п., and cp. bisque.

## bise
bise, п., a dry and cold north wind. — F., fr.
Frankish 'bisa, which is rel. to OHG. bisa, G.
Bise, 'bise', OHG. bison, 'to run about' (said
of cattle attacked by gadflies), OSwed. bisa, 'to
run', Dan. bisse, to run in agitation'; not
related to breeze.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:110 COLUMN:3 -->

## bisect
bisect, tr. v., to cut in two. — Formed fr. bi- and
L. secure, pp. seclus, 'to cut'. See section.
Derivatives: hisect-ion, п., bisect-or, n.

## bisexual
bisexual, adj. — Formed fr. bi- and sexusl.

## bishop
bishop, n. — ME. biscop, bischop, fr. OE. bis-
ceop, biscop, fr. L. episcopus, 'overseer, super-
intendant', in Eccles. L., 'bishop', fr. Gk.
επίσκοπος, 'overseer', fr. έπί, 'on, over', and σκοπός,
'watcher'. See epi- and -scope and cp. episcopal.
Cp. also obispo.
Derivative: bishop, tr. and intr. v.

## bishopric
bishopric, n. — OE. bisceoprice, biscoprice,
compounded of bisceop, biscop, 'bishop', and rice
'dominion'. See prec. word and Reich.

## bismite
bismite, п., bismuth trioxide (mineral.) — Coined
fr. next word and subst. suff. -ite.

## bismuth
bismuth, п., name of a metallic element (chem.) —
G. Bismuth (now spelled Wismut), Latinized by
Georgius Agricola (in 1530) into bisemutum.
The origin of the word is uncertain. It is not
connected with Arab, ithmid, 'antimon', as most
lexicographers would have it.

## bismuto-
bismuto-, bismutho-, combining form meaning
'bismuth'. — See prec. word.

## bisnaga
bisnaga, n. a kind of cactus. — Port, bisnaga (cp.
Sp. biznaga), fr. Arab, bisnaj, secondary form of
bastinaj, fr. L. pastinaca, 'parsnip'. See parsnip.

## bison
bison, п., wild ox. — F., fr. L. bison, fr. OHG.
wisunl (MHG., G. wisent), which is rel. to OE.
wesand, ON. visundr, and cogn. with OPruss.
wis-sambrs, 'aurochs', and with L. vissid,
'stench'. The bison is named after the peculiar
odor of musk emitted by it during the rutting
season. See weasel.

## bisporous
bisporous, adj., having two spores (hot.) — A
hybrid coined fr. L. pref. Ы-, 'twice', and Gk.
σπορά, 'sowing, seed' (see bi- and spore). The
correct form is disporous in which both elements
are of Greek origin. For the ending see suff. -ous.

## bisque
bisque, п., unglazed porcelain (ceramics). —
Corruption of biscuit.

## bissextile
bissextile, adj. and п., intercalary (year). — F.
(аллее) bissextile, fr. Late L. (annus) bissextilis,
'a year containing an intercalary day', fr. (dies)
bissextus, the intercalary day (of the Julian
calendar), lit. 'the twice sixth (day)', i.e. the
sixth day before the calends of March, which
is reckoned twice in a leap year. See bis-, sext
and suff. -ile.

## bister
bister, bistre, п., a dark-brown pigment. — F.
bistre, of unknown origin.

## bistort
bistort, adj., a plant (Polygonum bistorta). — F.
bistorte, lit. 'twice twisted', fr. L. bis, 'twice', and
torta, fem. pp. of torquire, 'to twist' (see bis and
torque). The plant was so called from its twisted
root.

## bistoury
bistoury, п., a small surgical knife. — F. bistouri.
of unknown origin.

## bistro
bistro, п., l) a wine seller; 2) a wine shop (slang).
— F., 'winemerchant, restauramkeeper,
restaurant', fr. bistraud, 'a little shepherd', a word of
the Poitou dialect, fr. biste, 'goat'.

## bit
bit, п., a morsel. — ME., fr. OE. bita, 'a bite,
bit, morsel', lit. 'something bitten off', rel. to
OS. 6ifi", ON. bit, OFris. bite, MDu. bete, Du.
beet, OHG. Ы330, MHG. Ыззе, G. Bissen, 'bit,
morsel', and to OE. bitan, 'to bite'. See bite and
cp. next word.

## bit
bit, п., mouthpiece of the bridle of a horse. —
ME. bit, bitt, fr. OE. bite, 'a biting', rel. to OS.
biti, ON. bit, G. Bifi, and to OE. bitan, 'to bite'.
See bite and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: bit, tr. v.

## bit
bit, past tense of bite. — ME. bit, from the stem
of the OE. pp. biten. See bite and cp. bitten.

## bitartrate
bitartrate, п., an acid tartrate (chem.) — See
bland tartrate.

## Bitch
Bitch, п., female dog.'— ME. bicche, fr. OE. bicce,
rel. to ON. bikkja; of uncertain origin.

## bite
bite, tr. and intr. v. — ME. biten, fr. OE. bitan,
rel. to OS. bitan, ΟΝ., OFris. bita, Swed. bita,
Dan.bide,MLG.,MDu. biten, Du. bijten'OHG.
bissan, MHG. bijen, G. beifien, Goth, beitan, 'to
bite'. The orig. meaning was Ίο cleave, split', fr.
I.-E. base *bheid-, whence also OI. bhinadmi, Ί
cleave', L. findere, 'to cleave, split', and prob.
also Gk. φείδεσ&αι, 'to spare' (orig. 'to cut
oneself off from somebody'). Cp. bit, 'morsel',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:111 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BITT | 84 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:111 COLUMN:1 -->
bit, 'mouthpiece', bait, bate, 'solution used in
tanning', abet, bezzle, embezzle, bitter, adj., vent,
'slit', giblets. Cp. also fissile and words there
referred to. Cp. also bill, 'halberd'.
Derivatives: bile, п., bit-er, п., bit-ing, adj., bit-
ing-ly, adv.

## bitt
bitt, п., timber fastened to the deck of a vessel. —
Prob. fr. ON. biti, 'beam', which is rel. to ON.
beit, 'boat', Du. beeting, 'bitt', MHG. biz'ze,
'wooden wedge'. — F. bitte, 'bitt', is of the same
origin. See boat and cp. bitter, n.

## bitten
bitten, pp. of bite. — ME. bitten, fr. OE. biten,
pp. of bttan. See bite,

## bitter
bitter, adj. — ME. biter, fr. OE. biter, bitor, rel.
to OS. bittar, ON. bitr, Du. bitter, OHG. bittar,
MHG., G. bitter, Goth, baitrs, 'bitter', orig. 'of
a pungent taste' and rel. to OE. bitan, 'to bite'.
See bite and cp. embitter.
Derivatives: bitter-ly, adv., bitter-ness, n.

## bitter
bitter, п., turn of the cable about the bitts (naut.)
— See bitts.

## bitterling
bitterling, п., a small fish (Rhodeus amarus). —
Formed from the adjective bitter with suff.
-ling; so called from its bitter flavor.

## bittern
bittern, п., a heronlike bird. — ME. bitour, fr.
OF. (= F.) butor, fr. VL. *buti-taurus, a
compound of L. buteo, butio, 'a kind of falcon or
hawk', and taurus, 'ox', L. buteo derives fr.
biittre, 'to cry like a bittern', which is of
imitative origin and lit. means 'to utter the sound
bu\ Cp. L. bubere, a synonym of butire and
bubo, 'owl', and see Bnteo, Bubo. For the second
element in VL. "buti-taurus see Taurus. The
reason why in VL. *buti-taurus the bittern is
compared with an ox, may be best explained by
a passage in Pliny (10,42), in which the author
relates that in Gaul the bittern was called taurus
(i.e. 'ox') because of its voice suggestive of the
bellowing of oxen. For the suffixed -n in bittern
cp. marten.

## bittera
bittera, п., the bitter liquid remaining after the
crystallization in saltworks. — A derivative of
bitter, adj.

## bitters
bitters, n. pi., bitter liquors. — The adj. bitter,
used as a noun.

## bitumen
bitumen, п., ι) asphalt; 2) an inflammable mineral
substance. — L. bitumen, 'mineral pitch', an
Osco-Umbrian loan word (the genuine Latin
form would have been *vetumen, fr. *gwetu-
men) of Celtic origin; cogn. with Ol.jdtu, 'lac,
gum', ON. kvada, 'resin', OE. cwidu* cudu,
'mastic, cud'. See cud and cp. beton. Cp. also
Betula.
Derivatives: bitumin-ize, tr. v., bitumin-ous, adj.

## bivalence
bivalence, bivalency, n. (chem.) — Formed from
next .word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## bivaleat
bivaleat, adj. having a valency of two (chem.) —
Formed fr. bi- and L. valens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of valere, 'to have power'. See valiant and
cp. -valent, valence.

## bivalve
bivalve, п., a mollusk with a double shell. —
Formed fr. pref. bi- and valve.

## bivouac
bivouac, n. — F. bivouac, variant bivac, fr. earlier
biwacht, fr. Swiss G. biwacht, which is
equivalent to G. Beiwacht, a collateral form of Bei-
wache, 'a keeping watch', fr. bet, 'at, by', and
Wache, 'watch, guard'. See by and wake, 'to be
awake'. It. bivacco, 'bivouac', is a French loan
word.
Derivative: bivouac, intr. v.

## bixbyite
bixbyite, п., an iron mangenese oxide (mineral.)
— Named after Maynard Bixby of Utah, its
discoverer. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## bizarre
bizarre, adj., strange. — F., fr. It. bizzarro,
'capricious', fr. Sp. bizarro, 'gallant, brave', fr.
Basque bizar, 'beard'. The Sense development
of the word is due to the strange impression
made by the bearded Spanish soldiers upon
the French.

## blab
blab, n. — ME. blabbe, rel. to ME. blaberen.
See blabber.
Derivative: blab, tr. and intr. v.

## blabher
blabher, intr. and tr. v. — ME. blaberen, of
imitative origin. Cp. ON. blabbra, Dan. blabbre,
'babble', OHG. blabbizon, MHG. blepzen, G.
plappern, 'to babble'.
Derivative: blabber, n.

## black
black, adj. — ME. Ыак, Ыакке, fr. OE. blue, rel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:111 COLUMN:2 -->
to ON. Ыаккг, 'dark', OHG. blah, 'black',
Swed. black, 'ink', Du. blaken, '<o burn', fr.
I.-E. base 'bhleg-, 'to shine, gleam', whence
also Gk. φλέγειν, 'to burn, scorch', φλέγμα,
'heat, inflammation', φλόξ, gen. φλογός, 'flame,
blaze', φλογμός, of s.m., L. flamma (fr. 'flag-
ma), 'flame', flagrare 'to blaze, glow, burn',
fulgcre, 'to shine', fulgur, 'lightning', fulmen (fr.
*fulg-men), 'lightning, OI. bhrajate, 'it shines',
bhargah, 'gleam', bhfgavah, 'demi-deities
representing the lightning*, Lith. blagnytis, 'to
brighten' (intr.). Cp. blanc, blank, blink, bream,
'a fish'. Cp. also flagrant, flambeau, flame, flam-
mule, fulgent, fulgara, fulgurant, fulminate,
Phlegethon, phlegm, phlegmon, phlogiston, Phlox.
Derivatives: black, п., and tr. v., Ыаск-ing, п.,
Ыаск-ish, adj., black-ish-ly, adv., black-isb-ness,
п., Ыаск-у, adj. and n.

## blackamoor
blackamoor,n.,aNegro.—Compounded of black
and Moor.

## blackguard
blackguard, n. — Prop, a black guard, a name
orig. given to the lowest menials employed in
the kitchen of a great household.
Derivatives: blackguard, adj. and intr. and tr. v.,
blackguard-ism, п., blackguard-ly, adj. and adv.

## blackjack
blackjack, п., a large leathern vessel. —
Compounded of black and the personal noun Jack.

## blackmail
blackmail, n. — Compounded of black, used
figuratively in the sense 'illegal', and mail, 'rent,
tax'. For this meaning of black cp. the modern
term black market.
Derivatives: blackmail, tr. v., blackmail-er, n.

## bladder
bladder, n. — ME. bladre, bledder, fr. OE. blxdre,
blxddre, 'blister, bladder', rel. to OS. bladara,
ON. Ыабга, Swed. bladdra, OHG. blallara,
MHG. blatere, G. Blatter, Du. blaar; formed
fr. Teut. base *Ыё-, 'to blow, inflate',
corresponding to I.-E. base "bhld-, *bhle- (see blow,
'to puff'), with suff. -dro, which corresponds to
Gk. -τρο, L. -tro (see rostrum). Cp. the second
element in isinglass.
Derivatives: bladder, tr. and intr. v., bladder-y,
adj.

## blade
blade, n. — ME. blad, blade, fr. OE. blssd, 'leaf;
blade (of an ear)', rel. to ON. blad, OS., Dan.,
Swed., Du. blad, OHG., MHG. blat, G. Blatt,
OFris. bled, 'leaf; prop. pp. of OE. blowan, etc.,
'to bloom, flower', fr. I.-E. base *bhlo-, *bhle-,
*bhla-, 'to sprout, bloom; leaf, whence prob.
also Toch. putt, 'leaf'. See blow, 'to bloom', and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: blade, tr. and intr. v., blad-ed, adj.,
blade-let, п., blad-er, п., blad-ing, п., blad-y, adj.

## blae
blae, adj., dark-blue, livid (obsol.) — ME. bio,
bla, fr. ON. blur, which is rel. to OE. blow,
ЬШк>, 'blue'. See blue.

## blaeberry
blaeberry, п., bilberry. — Compounded of blae
and berry.

## blah
blah, interj. and n. (U.S. Slang) — Of imit. origin.

## blain
blain, п., a pustule. — ME. bleine, fr. OE. blegen,
rel. to Dan. blegn, Du. blein, fr. I.-E. base
*bhlei-, 'to swell', an enlargement of base
*bhel-. For other enlargements of base *bhel-
see belly, bloat, bulge, phlebo-.
Derivative: blain, tr. v.

## blake
blake, adj., pale (obsol.) — ME., fr. OE. blae,
'bright, white; pale',rel. to ON. blikja, 'to appear,
shine, glitter'. See bleach and cp. words there
referred to.

## blame
blame, tr. v. — ME. blamen, fr. OF. blasmer (F.
blamer), fr. VL. blastemare, 'to blame', which is
formed—prob. under the influence of L. aesti-
mare.'to estimate'—fr. Late L. blasphemare, 'to
blaspheme, blame', fr. Gk. βλασφημεΐν, 'tospeak
profanely, speak ill'. Cp. Catal. blastemar, Port.
lastimar, Rum. blestema, 'to abuse*, and see
blaspheme.
Derivatives: blame, n. (q.v.), Ыат-аЫе, adj..
Ыат-аЫе-ness, п., blam-abl-y, adv., blam-ed.
adj., Ыат-er, п., Ыат-ing, adj., blam-ing-ly, adv.

## blame
blame, n. — ME., fr. OF. blasme (F. blame),
back formation fr. blasmer. See blame, v.
Derivatives: Ыате-ful, adj., Ыате-ful-ly, adv..
Ыате-ful-ness, п., blame-less, adj., Ыате-less-h,
adv., blame-less-ness, n.

## blanc
blanc, п., a French coin. — Prop, 'a white coin',
fr. F. blanc, 'white'. See blank.

## blanch
blanch, tr. v., to make white; intr. v., to turn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:111 COLUMN:3 -->
pale. — ME. blanchen, fr. OF. (= F.) blanchir
'to make white', fr. blanc, fern, blanche, 'white'.
See blank and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: blanch-er, n.

## Blanch
Blanch, Blanche, fern. PN. — F. Blanche, lit.
'white', fr. blanche, fem. of blanc, 'white'; of
Teut. origin. See blank and cp. blanch. Cp. also
Bianca.

## blancmange
blancmange, п., a kind of dessert. — F. blanc-
manger, lit. 'white food', fr. blanc, 'white', and
manger, 'food', fr. manger, 'to eat'. See blank
and manger.

## bland
bland, adj., 1) gentle, pleasant; 2) mild, soothing.
—L. blandus, 'smooth-tongued, flattering,
pleasant', of uncertain, possibly imitative origin.
Derivatives: bland-ly, adv., bland-ness, n.

## blandish
blandish, tr. v. — ME. blandissen, fr. OF. blan-
diss-, pres. part, stem of blandir, 'to flatter', fr.
L. blandiri, Ίο caress1, fr. blandus. See prec.
ivord and verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: blandish-er, п., blandish-ing, adj.,
blandish-ing-ly, adv.

## blank
blank, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) blanc, fem.
blanche, 'white', fr. Frankish 'blank, 'shining,
bright', which is rel. to OHG. blanc, blanch,
MHG. blanc, G. blank, 'shining, bright', OE.
bianca, ON. blakkr, 'white horse', fr. I.-E. base
*bhleg-, 'to shine, gleam'. See black and cp.
blanc, blanch, Blanch, blanket, Bianca.
Derivatives: blank, п., Ыапк-ly, adv., blank-
ness, n.

## blanket
blanket, n. — OF. blankette, blanquette, dimin.
of blanc, 'white', orig. meaning 'a white cloth'.
See blank, adj., and -et, -ette.
Derivatives: blanket, tr. v., blankei-ing, n.

## blanquilo
blanquilo, п., a fish of the genus Caulolatilus. —
Sp., dimin. of bianco, 'white'; which is a Teut.
loan word. See blank, adj.

## blare
blare, tr. and intr. v., to sound loudly. — ME.
biaren, bloren, 'to cry, weep', of imitative origin.
Cp. MDu. bleren, Du. biaren, bleren, 'to bleat,
cry', MLG. blarren, 'to weep', LG. biaren, 'to
whine', MHG. bleren, G. plarren, 'to bleat; to
bawl, blubber, whine'. Cp. also Gk. βληχή, 'a
bleating', βληχασ&»ι, 'to bleat', L. bdlare,
OSIav. bleju, blejati, Lett, bleju, blit, Russ. ble-
kat', MHG. bleken (G. bldken), 'to bleat', which
are all imitative. Cp. blatant, blent, blurt.
Derivative: blare, n.

## blarney
blarney, п., flattery. — From Blarney, name of a
village and a castle near Cork, Ireland,
containing the Blarney stone, which is said to make
anyone that kisses it a persuasive speaker.
Derivative: blarney, tr. v.

## bias
bias, п., supposed influence of the stars (obsol.) —
Coined by the Flemish physician and chemist
Jan Baptista van Helinont (1577-1644), prob.
after MDu. blses, 'wind', which is rel. to LG.
bias, 'breath', and to E. blast (q.v.) For another
word coined by Helmont see gas.

## blase
blase, adj., surfeited. — F., pp. of blaser, 'to
blunt, cloy, surfeit', fr. Du. blazen, 'to blow",
which is rel. to ON. blasa, OHG. bldsan, 'to
blow', and to E. blast (q.v.) F. blasi orig.
meant 'puffed up under the effect of drinking'.

## blaspheme
blaspheme, tr. v., to speak impiously of; intr. v.,
to utter blasphemy. — ME. blasfemen, fr. OF.
blasfemer (F. blasphemer), fr. Late L.
blasphemare, 'to blaspheme', fr. Gk. βλάσφημε», 'to
speak profanely, to speak ill', fr. βλάσφημος,
'speaking ill'. The first element of this compound
is of uncertain etymology. The second element
is rel. to φήμη, 'report'; see fame.
Derivatives: blasphem-er, п., blasphemous,
blasphemy (qq.v.)

## blasphemous
blasphemous, adj. —■ Late L. blasphemus, fr. Gk.
βλάσφημος, 'speaking ill'. See prec. word. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: blasphemous-ly, adv., blasphemous-
ness, n.

## blasphemy
blasphemy, n. — ME. blasfemie, fr. OF. blas-
femie, fr. Late L. blasphemia, fr. Gk. βλασφημία,
'a speaking ill', fr. βλάσφημος. See prec. word
and -y (representing Gk. -15).

## blast
blast, n. — ME., fr. OE. blxst, 'blowing, blast',
rel. to ON. blastr, OHG. blast, 'a blowing,
blast*, ON. blasa, OHG. blasan, MHG. blasen,
G. blasen, Goth, blisan, 'to blow'; formed —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:112 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 85 | BLITHE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:112 COLUMN:1 -->
with s formative element — fr. I.-E. base *bhla-,
*bhll-, 'to swell'. See blow, 'to puff', and cp.
bias, blase, blaze, 'to make known', blister.
Derivatives: blast, intr. and tr. v., blast-ed, adj.,
blast-er, п., blast-ing, п., blast-ment, п., blast-y,
adj.

## -blast
-blast, combining form denoting an embryonic
cell or a germ layer as in ectoblast, mesoblast
(blot.) — Fr. Gk. βλαστός, 'bud, sprout, shoot',
a word of uncertain origin. Cp. blastema, -bias-
tic, blasto-.

## blastema
blastema, п., the basis from which an organ is
formed (embryol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βλάστημα,
Offspring, offshoot', from the stem of βλασ-
τάνειν, Ίο shoot forth', fr. βλαστός. See -blast.
Derivatives: blastem-al, blastem-atic, blastem-ic,
adjs.

## -blastic
-blastic, combining form meaning 'sprouting', as
in homoblastiCi heteroblastic; connected with
nouns ending in -blast. — Formed with suff. -1c
fr. Gk. -βλαστός, fr. βλαστός. See -blast.

## blasto-
blasto-, before a vowel blast-, combining form
meaning 'bud, germ', as in blastoderm. — Gk.
βλαστό-, βλαστ-, fr. βλαστός. See -blast.

## blastoderm
blastoderm, п., a layer of cells arising from the
segmentation of the ovum (embryol.) —
Compounded of blasto- and Gk. δέρμα 'skin'. See
derma and cp. words there referred to.

## blatant
blatant, adj., offensively noisy. — Coined by
Edmund Spenser (in his 'Faery Queen'); prob.
suggested by L. blattre, 'to babble', which is of
imitative origin; not rel. to E. bleat.
Derivatives: blalan-cy, п., blatant-ly, adv.

## blather
blather, blether, intr. v., to talk nonsense. —
ME., fr. ON. Ыадга, 'to talk nonsense', fr.
bladr, 'nonsense', which is of imitative origin.
Derivatives: blather, blether, п., blather-er,
blether-er, n.

## Blatta
Blatta, п., a genus of cockroaches (enlomol.) —
L. blatta, 'cockroach', of unknown origin.

## blatti
blatti, blatty, п., the plant Sonneralia acida (An-
glo-Ind.) — Hind., lit. 'the foreign plant',
corruption of bilati, bilayati, 'foreign', fr. Arab.
wilayat, 'kingdom, province*. See vilayet and
cp. Blighty, vali.

## blauwbok
blauwbok, bianbok, п., a name given by the Dutch
in South Africa to a large kind of antelope. —
Du. blauwbok, lit. 'blue buck'. See blue and
back.

## blay
blay, п., the bleak. — ME., fr. OE. blxge, rel. to
MLG., MDu. bleie, Du. blei, G. Bleie, Bleihe,
and to E. bleak (q.v.) The litteral meaning is
'shining, white, silvery'.

## blaze
blaze, п., flame. — ME. blase, fr. OE. blsese,
blase, 'torch, Are', rel. to OS. bias, 'white,
whitish*, MHG. bias, 'bald', orig. 'while, shining'
(whence G. blafi, 'pale'), OHG. blas-ros, 'horse
with a white spot', OHG. blassa, MHG. blasse,
MLG. bles, blesse, 'white spot', MDu., Du. bles,
G. Blesse, 'white spot; an animal (esp. a horse
or a cow) with a white spot', ON. bles-ottr,
'marked with a white spot', OE. blysa, 'torch,
flame', blyscan, 'to blush', fr. I.-E. *bhles-, 'to
shine, glitter', enlargement of *bhel-, a base of
the same meaning. See bald, blaze, 'white spot',
and cp. blazon. Cp. also blemish, blizzard, blush.
Derivatives: blaze, intr. v., blaz-y, adj., to burn
with flame, blaz-er, п., blaz-ing, adj., blaz-ing-
ly, adv.

## blaze
blaze, п., a white spot. — Prob. fr. MLG. blase
(in blasenhengst), 'white spot', which is rel. to
MLG. bles, blesse, of s.m. See prec. word.
Derivative: blaze, tr. v., to make a blaze on
(trees).

## blaze
blaze, tr. v., to make known. — The orig.
meaning was 'to blow with a trumpet', fr. ON. blasa,
'to blow'. See blast and cp. blase. Cp. also
emblaze, 'to emblazon'.

## blazer
blazer, п., a light, bright-colored, coat. — Lit.
'that which blazes', so called in allusion to its
color. See blaze, 'flame', and -er.

## blazon
blazon, п., a coat of arms. — ME. blason, fr. OF.
blason, 'shield' (in Mod. French 'coat of arms'),
of uncertain origin; not rel. to OHG. blason,
etc., 'to blow', nor to OE. blsese, blase, 'torch,
fire' (see blaze, 'flame'). It. blasone and Sp.
blason, 'coat of arms', are French loan words. Cp.
emblazon.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:112 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: blazon, tr. v., blazon-ry, n.

## bleach
bleach, tr. v., to whiten. — ME. blechen, fr. OE.
blScan, fr. blac, 'bright, white; pale', rel. to OS.
Ыёк, ON. bleikr, Du. Ыеек, OHG. bleih, MHG.,
G. bleich, 'pale', ON. bleikja, Du. Ыекеп, OHG.
blihhan, MHG. bliken, G. bleichen, 'to bleach',
and perh. cogn. with OSlav. bliskati (for
*bligskati), 'to sparkle, glitter', bliskd, 'gleam,
splendor'. Cp. blake, bleak, adj. and п.,
blight.
Derivatives: bleach, п., bleach-ed, adj.,
bleacher, п., bleach-er-y, п., bleach-ing, n.

## bleak
bleak, adj. — ME. bleke, fr. ON. bleikr, 'pale'.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: Ыеак-ish, adj., Ыеак-ly, adv.,
bleak-ness, п., bleak-y, adj.

## bleak
bleak, п., the blay. — The word lit. means 'the
white, silvery (fish)', and is rel. to Swiss G.
blicke. Swab, blecke, and to E. blay and bleak,
adj.

## blear
blear, adj. and tr. v. — ME. bleren, 'to dim (the
eyes)'. Cp. LG. Ыеег-oged, 'blear-eyed*. Cp.
also hlur.

## bleat
bleat, intr. and tr. v. and n. — ME. bleten, fr. OE.
bUetan, of imitative origin. Cp. Du. blaten, OHG.
bldjan, 'to bleat'. Cp. also ME. blaren, 'to cry,
weep', and see blare.
Derivatives: bleat-er, п., bleating, adj., bleai-
ing-ly, adv.

## bleb
bleb, п., a vesicle, blister; a bubble. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. blob, blnbber, 'the fat of the
whale'.

## bled
bled, past tense and pp. of bleed. — ME. bledde,
resp. (j)bled, fr. OE. bledde, resp. gebledd, ge-
bled, past tense, resp. pp. of bledan. See next
word.

## bleed
bleed, intr. and tr. v. — ME. bleden, fr. OE.
bledan, fr. blod, 'blood'. See blood.
Derivatives: bleed-er, п., bleed-ing, n. and adj.

## blemish
blemish, tr. v. — ME. blemissen, blemisshen, fr.
OF. blemiss-, pres. part, stem oiblemir, blesmir
(F. blimir), which prob. derives fr. Frankish
*blesmjan, 'to make one grow pale', from the
Teut. base seen in G. blass, 'pale'. See blaze,
'flame'.
Derivatives: blemish, п., blemish-er, n.

## blench
blench, tr. v., to make pale; intr. v., to turn pale.
— A var. of blaach.

## blench
blench, intr. v., to shrink. — ME. blenchen, fr.
OE. blencan, 'to deceive', prob. causative of
blink, and orig. meaning 'to make to blink*.
(Blench stands to blink as drench to drink.) Cp.
also OE. cwencan, causative of OE. cwincan, 'to
disappear' (see quench), so that quench prop,
means 'to cause to disappear'.

## blend
blend, tr. and intr. v., to mix. — ME. blenden, fr.
ON. blanda, which is rel. OE., OS., OHG.
blantan, Goth, blandan, MHG. blenden, 'to mix'
(cp. G. Blendling, 'bastard, mongrel'), fr. I.-E.
base *bhlendh-, 'to mix; to confuse', whence
also Lith. blandus, 'troubled, turbid, thick',
OSlav.bledo,blesti, 'to go astray',blqditi, 'toerr',
Lith. blandytis, 'to lower (the eyes)', bl\sti, 'to
become thick, turbid' (said of water). Cp. blend,
'to blind'. Cp. also blond, blunder.

## blead
blead, tr. v., to blind (obsol.) — OE. blendan, rel.
to OFris. blenda, MLG., MHG., G. blenden,
OHG. blentan, 'to blind', and prob. to OE.
blandan, 'to mix'. See blend, 'to mix', and cp.
blind, adj. and v. Cp. also blende.

## blende
blende, п., an ore of zinc, sphalerite. — G. Blende,
back formation fr. blenden, 'to blind; to
deceive'; so called because though it resembles
lead, it yields no lead. Cp. the second element in
pitchblende.
blenheim orange. — Named after Blenheim, seat
of the duke of Marlborough, in Oxfordshire,
England.
blenheim spaniel. — See prec. word; so called
because originally bred at Blenheim.

## blenno-
blenno-, before a vowel blenn-, combining form
meaning 'mucus'. — Fr. Gk. βλέννος or βλέννα,
'slime, mucus', of uncertain etymology; βλέννος
possibly stands for *μλέδ-σ-νος, and is rel. to
μέλδειν, 'to melt', and cogn. with L. mollis (for
*moldwis), 'soft'. See mollify and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also Ыеппу.

## blennorrhea
blennorrhea, blennorrhoea, п., excessive discharge

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:112 COLUMN:3 -->
of mucus (med.) — Medical L., compounded of
blenno- and -rrhea.
Ыеппу, п., a small seafish. — L. blennius, fr. Gk.
βλέννος, name of a fish, fr. βλέννα, 'slime', Ml.
'slime fish'; so called from the mucus which
covers its skin. See blenno-.

## blepharo-
blepharo-, before a vowel blephar-, combining
form meaning 'eyelid'.—Gk. βλέφαρο-, βλεφαρ-,
fr. βλέφαρον (Dor. γλέφαρον), 'eyelid', which is
rel. to βλέπειν (Dor. γλέπειν), 'to look, see'; of
uncertain etymology. Cp. Ablepharus, ablepsia,
anableps.

## blepharospasm
blepharospasm, п., contraction of the eyelids
(med.) — Compounded of blepharo- and Gk.
σπασμός, 'spasm, convulsion'. See spasm.

## Blephilia
Blephilia, п., a genus of plants of the mint family
(bot.) — ModL., contraction of Gk. βλεφαρίς,
'eyelash' (which is rel. to βλέφαρον, 'eyelid'),
and L. cilium, 'eyelid' (see blepharo- and cilia);
so called because of its fringed bracts and calyx ·
teeth.

## bless
bless, tr. v. — ME. blessen, fr. OE. blidsian, blet-
sian, 'to bless, consecrate', rel. to OE. blod,
'blood'; see blood. The orig. meaning of bless
was 'to sprinkle or consecrate with blood' (said
of the sacrificing priest).
Derivatives: bless-ed, adj., bless-ed-ly, adv.,
bless-ed-ness, п., bless-ing, п., bless-ing-ly, adv.

## blew
blew, past tense of blow. — ME., fr. OE. bleow,
past tense of blawan. See blow, Ίο puff'.

## blight
blight, n. — Prob. related to OE. blicettan, 'to
glitter', ME. blickening, 'pallor' (often used as
the English equivalent of L. rubigo, 'mildew'),
and to E. bleach (q.v.) Cp. blitzkrieg.
Derivatives: blight, tr. v., blight-ed, adj.,
blighter, п., blight-ing, adj., blight-ing-ly, adv.

## Bligbty
Bligbty, п., England, home (British army slang).
— Hind, bilaiti, a word used in India to
denote England or Europe, fr. Arab, wildyat,
'kingdom, province', a derivative of waliya; 'he
reigned, governed'. See vilayet and cp. blatti,
vali.

## blimp
blimp, п., a nonrigid (limp) dirigible (colloq.) —
Contraction of В limp, one of the 2 types of the
small nonrigid airship (the other type is called
A limp). See limp, 'relaxed'.

## blind
blind, adj. — ME., fr. OE. blind, rel. to OS., Du.,
G. blind, ON. blindr, OHG., MHG. blint, Goth.
blinds, 'blind', OE. blendan, etc., 'to blind', prob.
fr. I.E. base *bhlendh-, 'to confuse; to mix'.
See blend, 'to mix', blend, 'to blind'.
Derivatives: blind, п., 'screen, cover', blind-ling,
п., blind-ly, adv., blinJ-ness, n.

## blind
blind, tr. v. — The OE. equivalent is blendan, 'to
blind'; see blend, 'to blind'. The E. verb has been
influenced in form by the adj. blind (q.v.)
Derivatives: blind-ed, adj., blind-ed-ly, adv.,
blind-er, п., blind-ing, adj. and n.

## blink
blink, intr. and tr. v. — ME. blinken (rel. to Du.
and G. blinken, 'to gleam, sparkle, twinkle'), a
nasalized variant of the base appearing in OE.
blican, ME. bliken, 'to shine, glitter', OHG.
blihhan, 'to bleach'. See bleach and cp. blench.
Derivatives: blink, п., blink-ard, п., blink-ed,
adj., bltnk-er, n. and tr. v., blink-ing, п., blink-y,
adj.

## bliss
bliss, n. — ME. blis, fr. OE. blis, contraction of
OE. blids, 'joy, happiness', fr. blide, 'gay, happy'.
See blithe. .
Derivatives: bliss-ful, adj., bliss-ful-ly, adv.,
bliss-ful-ness, n.

## blister
blister, n. — ME. blister, blester, fr. OF. blestre,
fr. ON. blastr, 'a swelling', fr. blasa, 'to blow'.
See blast and cp. bluster. ,
Derivatives: blister, intr. and tr. v., blister-y,
adj.

## blite
blite, п., any of various herbs of the goosefoot
family. — L. blitum, fr. Gk. βλίτον, 'a
vegetable used as a salad; orach'; of uncertain
etymology. According to some philologists βλίτον
stands for *μλ-Ιτον and prop, means 'the soft-
leaved'plant', fr. I.-E. base *mel-dft-, whence also
OE. melde, OS. maldia, Swed. mall, Du. melde,
OHG. melta, molta, multa, MHG., G. melde,
'orach'. Base *mel-dh- is an enlargement of
base *mel-, 'to rub, grind'. See meal, 'edible
grain', and cp. Blitum.

## blitbe
blitbe, adj., joyous; cheerful. — ME., fr. OE.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:113 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BLITUM | 86 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:113 COLUMN:1 -->
blide, 'joyful, kind, gentle', rel. to OS. blldi,
'bright, happy', ON. blidr, 'mild, gentle', Du.
blij(de), 'glad', OHG. blldi, 'gay, friendly', Goth.
bleips, 'kind, friendly, merciful'. Cp. bliss.
Derivatives: blithe-ly, adv., blithe-ness, п.,
blithesome, adj., blithe-some-ness, n.

## Blitum
Blitum,n., a genus of herbs of the family Cheno-
podiaceae (the goosefoot family). — L. blitum.
See blite.

## blitz
blitz, п., a sudden overwhelming attack (colloq.)
— Short for blitzkrieg (q.v.)

## blitzkrieg
blitzkrieg, п., a sudden, overwhelming warfare.
— G., lit. 'lightning war'. G. Blitz, 'lightning',
derives fr. MHG. blicze, 'lightning', fr. bliczen,
'to flash, to lighten', rel. to OHG., MHG. blic,
'lightning', G. Blick, 'a glance', and to OE. bli-
cettan, 'to glitter*; see blight. G. Krieg, 'war',
comes fr. MHG. kriec, 'effort, resistance,
combat*, fr. OHG. chreg, 'stubbornness, obstinacy',
which is rel. to MLG. krich, 'combat'.

## blizzard
blizzard, n. — Fr. earlier blizz, 'rain storm', which
is prob. cognate with blaze, 'burst of flame'.
For the ending see suff. -ard.
Derivatives: blizzard-ly, blizzard-y, adjs.

## bloat
bloat, tr. v., to cause to swell; intr. v., to swell. —
OE. *blalian, 'to swell', cogn. with Gk. φλυδαν,
'to swell, overflow with moisture, be ready to
burst', Lett, blldu, blizt, 'to become thick', fr.
I.-E. base *bhlei-d-, enlargement of base 'bhlei-,
'to swell', whence OE. blegen, 'blain'. See blain
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: bloat, п., bloat-ed, adj., bloat-ed-
ness, п., bloater (q.v.)

## bloater
bloater, п., a soaked flat herring or mackerel. —
Formed fr. bloat with agential suff. -er.

## blob
blob, п., a small drop. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
bleb, blubber, babble.
Derivative: blobb-y, adj.

## block
block, n. — ME. blok, fr. OF. (= F.) bloc, 'block,
mass', fr. Du. bloc, 'trunk of a tree' which is rel.
to OHG. bloh, MHG. bloch, G. Block, and
cogn. with Olr. blog, 'fragment'; not rel. to
balk. Cp. en bloc
Derivative: block-ish, adj.

## block
block, tr. and intr. v. — F. bloquer, fr. bloc. See
block, n.
Derivatives: block-ade, n. and tr. v.

## blodite
blodite, also blodite, п., hydrous sulfate of
magnesium and sodium {mineral.) — Named after
the German chemist Carl A. Blode (died in
1820). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## bloke
bloke, п., a man (slang). — Of unknown origin.

## blond
blond, blonde, adj. — F., 'fair of complexion', rel.
to It. biondo, Sp. blondo, OProvenc. blon; of
Teut. origin. Cp. OE. blonden-feax, blanden-feax,
'gray-haired', fr. blondan, blandan, 'to mix', and
see blend, 'to mix'.
Derivatives: blond, п., blond(e)-ness, п., blond-
ine, n. (fr. F. blondine).

## blondine
blondine, n. — F., fr. blonde, fern, of blond. See
prec. word and -iae (representing L. -ϊηα).

## blood
blood, n. — ME. blod, fr. OE. bled, rel. to OS.,
OFris. blod, ON. Ыдд, Dan., Swed. blod, MDu.
bloet, bloed, Du. bloed, OHG., MHG. bluol,
G. В/иг, Goth. Ыбр, blopis, fr. I.-E. 'bhloto-, pp.
of base *bhl6-, 'to bloom'. See blow, 'to bloom',
and cp. bleed. Cp. also bless. The I.-E. bases
denoting 'blood' proper (like L. cruor and sanguis)
were regarded by the Teutons as taboo and
accordingly given up.
Derivatives: blood, tr. v., blood-ed, adj.,
bloodless, adj., blood-less-ly, adv., blood-less-ness, п.,
blood-y, adj., and tr. v., blood-i-ly, adv., blood-
i-ness, n.

## bloodguilry
bloodguilry, adj. — Coined by Miles Coverdale
(1488-1569), English translator of the Bible,
from blood and guilty.
Derivative: bloodguilti-ness, n.

## bloom
bloom, п., flower. — ME. blome, fr. ON. blom,
blomi, which is rel. to OS. blomo, Du. bloem,
OHG. bluoma (fem.), Ыиото (masc.), MHG.
bluome (masc. and fem.), G.BIume (fern.), Goth.
bloma, 'flower, blossom', OE. bloslm, blostma,
'blossom', and cogn. with Olr. blatk, 'bloom,
flower', L. fids, 'flower', florere, 'to blossom,
flourish'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*bhlo-, 'to sprout, bloom'. See blow, 'to bloom,
blossom', and cp. blossom. Cp. also flower.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:113 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: bloom, intr. v., bloom-ing, adj.,
bloom-ing-ly, adv., bloom-ing-ness, п., bloom-y,
adj.

## bloom
bloom, п., rough mass of wrought iron. — OE.
bloma, 'a lump of metal', of uncertain origin.

## bloomer
bloomer, п., a costume for women. — Named
after the inventor Mrs. Amelia Jenks Bloomer of
New York (in 1851).

## bloomer
bloomer, п., a blunder. —· Of uncertain origin.

## blossom
blossom, n. — ME. blosme, blossem, fr. OE.
blostm, blostma, blosma, rel. to MLG. bldsem,
Du. bloesem, MHG. bluest, G. Blust, fr. I.-E.
"bhlos-, enlarged form of base *bhW-, 'to sprout,
bloom'. See bloom, 'flower'.
Derivatives: blossom, intr. v., blossom-ed, adj.,
blossom-ry, п., blossom-y, adj.

## blot
blot, п., a spot. — ME. blot, blotte, fr. MF. blotte,
'a clod or clot of earth', fr. OF. bloste or blostre,
which are of uncertain origin.

## blot
blot, tr. and intr. v., to make spots, to blur. —
MF. blotter, fr. blotte. See prec. word.
Derivatives: blott-er, п., blott-ing, adj., blott-
Ing-ly, adv.

## blot
blot, n., 1) in backgammon, an exposed man; 2) an
exposed point. — Prob. rel. to Dan. blot, Swed.
blott, LG. blutt, MDu., Du. Woof, MHG. Ы03,
G. blofi, 'bare, naked', OHG. Ы03, 'proud', ON.
blautr, 'soft, tender', and possibly cogn. with Gk.
φλυδαν, 'to overflow', φλυδαρός, 'soft, flabby',
L.fluere, 'to flow'. See fluent and cp. words there
referred to.

## blotch
blotch, n. — A blend of blot and botch.
Derivatives: blotch, tr. and intr. v., blotch-y,aaj.

## blouse
blouse, n. — F., fr. ML. pelusia, 'Pelusian
garment' ; so called because during the Middle Ages
blouses were manufactured in Pelusium on a
large scale.
Derivatives: blouse, intr. v., blous-ed, adj.,
blous-ing, n.
blow. intr. and tr. v.. to puff. — ME. blowen, fr.
OE. blawan, rel. to OHG. blaen (for "blajan),
MHG. blsejen, G. blahen, fr. I.-E. base *M/o-,
*bhle-, *bhle-, 'to blow', whence also L. flare,
'to blow'. Cp. bladder, blast, blaze, 'to make
known', blister, bluster. Cp. also flatas and
words there referred to. Cp. also fluent. For a
secondary meaning of base *bhlo- see blow, "10
bloom', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: blow-er, п., blowing, n. and adj.,
blow-y, adj.

## blow
blow, intr. v., to bloom, blossom; tr. v., to cause
to bloom. — ME. blowen, fr. OE. blowan, Ίο
flower, bloom, flourish', rel. to OS. bloian, O-
Fris. bloia, OHG. bluoen (for *bluojan), MHG.
bliien, bliiejen, G. bliihen, fr. I.-E. base *bhlo-,
*bhle-, 'to sprout, bloom', whence also L. flos,
gen. floris, 'flower', Mir. blath, 'bloom, blossom',
W. blawd, of s.m. See flower, and cp. blade, blood,
bloom, blossom. Cp. also folio and words there
referred to. For the original meaning of base
*bhlo- see blow, 'to puff'.
Derivatives: blow, п., blow-er, п., blow-ing, n.

## blow
blow, stroke, n. — ME. blewe, rel. to OS. bleu-
wan, MDu., Du. blouwen, OHG. bliuwan,
MHG. bliuwen, G. bleuen, Golh. bliggwan,' 10
strike', fr. Teut. "bleuwan; of uncertain
etymology.

## blown
blown, pp. and adj. — ME. blowen, fr. OE.
blawen, pp. of blawan. See blow, 'to puff'.

## blubber
blubber, п., the fat of the whale. — The orig.
meaning was 'bubble, foam'; of imitative origin.
Cp. bleb, blob.
Derivatives: blubber-ous, blubber-y, adjs.

## blubber
blubber, intr. v., to weep loudly. — Of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: blubber-er, п., blubber-ing, п., blub-
ber-ing-ly, adv.

## bluchers
bluchers, n. pi., old-fashioned boots. — Named
after the Prussian field marshal Bliicher (1742-
1819). For sense development cp. Wellington.

## bludgeon
bludgeon, п., a short club. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: bludgeon, tr. and intr.
v.,bludgeoned, adj., bludgeon-er, n.

## blue
blue, adj. — ME. blew, fr. OF. (= F.) bleu, fr.
Frankish *blao, which is rel. to OE. blow, blxw,
OS., OHG. Ыао, Dan. Ыаа, Swed. bid, OFris.
blau, MDu. bla, Du. blauw, MHG. Ыа, G. blau,
'blue', ON. blur, 'dark blue, black', and cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:113 COLUMN:3 -->
with Olr. blur, W. blawr, 'gray', L. flatus,
'yellow'. See flavescent and cp. blae, blaeberry,
blauwbok, blnet.
Derivatives: blue, п., blue, tr. v., blu-ing,
blueing, п., Ыи-ish, adj., Ыи-ish-ness, n.

## blnebird
blnebird, n. (ornithol.) — Compounded of blue
and bird.

## blue bird
blue bird, symbolic name of the quest for
happiness. — From the play-romance VOiseau
bleu ('The Blue Bird'), written by the Belgian
dramatist and poet Maurice Maeterlinck (1862-
1949) in 1909, which symbolizes the quest for
happiness.

## bluestocking
bluestocking, п., a pedantic lady boasting of her
erudition. — About 1740 a literary circle used
ι ο assemble at Lady Elizabeth Montague's home
in London. Benjamin Stillingfleet, one of the
leading members of the circle, regularly
attended those meetings, wearing blue stockings, a
circumstance which gave occasion to admiral
Boscawen to deride The blue stocking society;
hence the name bluestocking, and its loan
translations: F. bas-Ыеи, Du. blauwkous, G. Blau-
strumpf, etc.

## bluet
bluet, п., the name of various plants with blue
flowers. — F. bleuet, bluet, dimin. formed fr.
bleu, 'blue'. See blue and -et.

## bluff
bluff, adj., presenting a broad, flattened front. —
Of LG. origin. Cp. MLG. blaff, 'smooth, even',
MDu. blaf, 'fat, broad', blaffaert, 'a man having
a broad face'.
Derivatives: bluff, п., bluff-y, adv., bluff-ness, n.

## bluff
bluff, tr. v., to deceive. — MLG. vorbluffen, 'to
baffle', (whence Du. verbluffen, 'to stun', G. ver-
bluffen, 'to amaze'); prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives: bluff, п., deception, bluff-er, n.

## blnnder
blnnder, intr. and tr. v. — ME. blunderen, 'to
confuse', rel. to blend, 'to mix' (q.v.)
Derivatives/ blunder, п., blunder-er, п.,
blundering, adj., blunder-ing-ly, adv.

## blunderbuss
blunderbuss, п., a short heavy gun with a broad
muzzle. — A blend of Du. donderbus, of s.m.,
lit., 'thunder box', and E. blunder. See thunder
and box, 'case', and cp. blunderhead.

## blunderhead
blunderhead, n. — Alteration of dunderhend. Cp.
prec. word.
Derivatives: blunderhead-ed, adj., blunderhead-
ed-ness, n.

## blunt
blunt, adj. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: blunt, n. and v., blunt-er, п.,
bluntly, adv., blunt-ness, n.

## blur
blur, v. and n. — Prob. in gradational
relationship to blear.
Derivatives: blurr-ed, adj., blurr-ed-ness, п.,
blurr-er, п., blurr-y, adj.

## blurb
blurb, n. — Coined by the American journalist
Frank Gelett Burgess (1866-1951) in 1907.

## blurt
blurt, tr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp. Scot, blirl
and E. blare.
Derivative: blurt, n.

## blush
blush, intr. v. — ME. bluschen, 'to shine; to be
or grow red', fr. OE. blyscan, 'to grow red,
blush', fr. blysa, 'torch, flame, fire', which stands
in gradational relationship to Du. blozen, 'to
blush', andto E. blaze, 'flame'.
Derivatives: blush, п., blush-ing, adj., blush-
ing-ly, adv.

## bluster
bluster, intr. v., to be boisterous. — Rel. to LG.
bliistern, blistern, 'to blow', and to E. blister
Iq.v.)
Derivatives: bluster, п., bluster-er, n., bluster-ing,
adj. bluster-ing-ly, adv.

## B'nai B'rith
B'nai B'rith, a Jewish fraternal organization
founded in New York City in 1843. — Heb.
b'ne b'rth, 'sons of the covenant', fr. b'ni,
state construct of banfm, pi. of ben, 'son', and
b'rith, 'covenant'. See ben and berith and cp.
the first element in Boanerges.

## bo
bo, interj. — Imitative.

## Boa
Boa, п., a genus of snakes, the New World
Constrictor. — L. boa, 'a large serpent', of uncertain
origin. Cp. Boidae.

## Boanerges
Boanerges, п., a name applied to the sons of Ze-
bedee (see Mark 3:17); used figuratively to
denote a clamorous orator. — Galilean dialectal
corruption of Heb. b'ne reghesh, 'sons of
thunder', fr. b'ne (see B'nai B'rith) and reghesh,
'commotion, tumult, throng', frorri the stem of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:114 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 87 | BOLOMETER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:114 COLUMN:1 -->
raghash, 'he was in commotion or in tumult',
which is related to Aram, r'ghash, 'he trembled,
was agitated', and to Arab, rdj'asa, 'he made
a vehement noise'.

## bour
bour, n. — ME. bar, bore, boor, fr. OE. bar, rel.
to OS. Mr, Du. beer, OHG. ber, dial. G. Bar,
'boar' (not to be confused with G. Bar, 'bear').

## board
board, п., table, plank. — ME. bord, 'table,
plank', fr. OE. bord, rel. to ON. bord, 'plank',
Goth, foiu-baurd, 'footstool', lit. 'foot board',
Du. bord, 'board, blackboard', OE., OS. bred,
MLG., OHG., MHG. bret, G. Brett, 'plank';
fr. I.-E. *bhrtom, resp. *bhret-om, fr. base
*bherd-, 'to cut', a -«/-enlargement of base
*bher-, 'to bore, pierce, perforate'. See bore,
'to pierce', and cp. board, 'side of a ship', and
the second element in gar board. Cp. also bord-
age, bordar, bordel, border, berm, breian, brim,
predella.
Derivatives: board, v., to cover with boards,
board-er, п., board-ing, adj. and verbal п.,
board-y, adj.

## board
board, п., side of a ship. — OE. bord, 'border,
edge; side of a ship', rel. to OS. bord, LG.
bo(o)rd (whence G. Bord), Du. board, OHG.
bort, ON. bard, bord, 'border, edge; side of a
ship', and to OE. bord, etc., 'table, plank' (see
prec. word); influenced in sense by F. bord,
'edge, margin, border, shipboard'. See board,
'table, plank', and cp. border and the second
element in larboard.
Derivatives: board, tr. and intr. v., board-er, п.,
board-ing, adj. and n.

## boast
boast, n. — ME. boost, bast. See next word.

## boast
boast, tr. v. — ME. boosten, bosten, fr. boost, host,
п., rel. to OS. bosi, MLG., MDu. base, Du. boos,
'evil, wicked, angry'. OHG. busi, 'worthless,
slanderous', MHG. boese, G. base, 'evil, bad,
angry', Norw. baus, 'proud, bold, daring', fr.
Teut. base *baus-, which lit. means 4o blow up,
puff up, swell'. This base is an enlarged form
of I.-E. *bhou-, *bhu-, 'to swell', for which see
bow, 'anything bent'.
Derivatives: boast-er, п., boast-fid, adj., boast-
ful-ly, adv., boast-fiil-ness, п., boast-ing, adj. and
verbal п., boast-ing-ly, adv.

## boat
boat, n. — ME. boat, fr. OE. bat, 'ship, boat',
whence ON. batr, D. boot, G. Boot, Sp. batel,
F. bateau. It. batto, battello, 'boat'; rel. to ON.
bile, 'beam', hence orig. meaning 'boat made
from one piece of timber, monoxylon'. See bitt.
Derivatives: boat, tr. v., boat-able, adj., boat-
age, п., boat-ing, n.

## bob
bob, п., a knot of hair. — ME. bobbe, bob, 'bunch,
cluster', prob. of imitative origin. Cp. next word.
Derivative: bobb-ed, adj.

## bob
bob, intr. and tr. v., to move rapidly to and fro,
to jerk. — Of imitative origin.
Derivatives: bob, п., a jerky movement,
bobbish, adj.

## bob
bob, tr. v., to cheat, deceive. — ME. bobben, fr.
OF. bober, 'to purse one's lips, pout, deceive',
imitative of the movement of the pursed lips.

## bob
bob, п., trickery. — OF. bobe, fr. bober. See
prec. word.

## bob
bob, п., a shilling (British Slang). — Prob. fr.
Bob, dimin. of Robert. Cp. bobby.

## bobbery
bobbery, п., a squabble (Anglo-lnd.) — Hind.
bapre, Ό father'.

## bobbin
bobbin, reel, spool. — F. bobine, 'a grotesque
figure, a wry face; a reel', from the imitative
base "bob- (see bob, 'to deceive'); so called from
its cylindric form.
Derivative: bobbin, tr. v.

## bobby
bobby, п., a policeman (slang). — Dimin. of Bob,
itself dimin. of Robert; so called after Sir Robert
Peel (1788-1850). Cp. peeler.

## bobolink
bobolink, п., a migratory bird of North America.
— So called from its cry suggestive of boblincoln
(for Bob Lincoln).

## bocaccio
bocaccio, п., the rockfish called scientifically Se-
bastodes paucispinis. — It. boccaccio, fr. boccac-
cia, 'a big mouth', augment, of bocca, 'mouth',
fr. L. bucca, 'mouth'. See buccal.

## Boche
Boche, boche, п., a German. — F. slang,
shortened fr. Aiboche, a slangy alteration of Alle-
mand, 'German', through the intermediary form
AI(le)moche, used in the east of France. The

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:114 COLUMN:2 -->
change of m to b is due to an association with
caboche, 'pate, noodle, nob' (see cabbage).

## bock
bock, bock beer, a kind of beer. — G. Воск,
shortened fr. Ambock, Oambock, Munichian
dialectal words for Einbeck, name of a town in
Germany. Hence bock lit. means '(beer made
at) Einbeck'.

## bocking
bocking, п., a coarse woolen material. — Named
fr. Bocking in England.

## bocking
bocking, smoked herring. — Du. bokking, fr.
MDu. buckinc, a derivative of buc, boc, 'buck'; so
called from its odor. See back and cp. buckling.
For the ending see subst. surf. -ing.

## bode
bode, tr. v. — ME. bodien, fr. OE. bodian, 'to
announce, foretell', fr. boda, 'messenger', which
stands in gradational relationship to OE. biodan,
'to announce, proclaim, command'. Cp. ON.
bodi, OHG. boto, MHG., G. bote, 'messenger',
and see bid.
Derivatives: bode-ful, adj., bod-ing, adj., bod-
ing-ly, adv., bod-er, n.

## bodega
bodega, п., a wineshop. — Sp., fr. L. apotheca,
fr. Gk. αποθήκη, 'any place 'wherein to lay
up something; magazine, storehouse'. See
apothecary and cp. bottega, boutique.

## bodice
bodice, n. — Prop. pi. of body, in 'pair of bodies'.
— For formation cp. stays, pence.
Derivative: bodic-ed, adj.

## bodikin
bodikin, п., an obsolete oath. — Prop, 'a small
body', formed from body with suff. -kin.

## bodkin
bodkin, п., a small dagger. — ME. boydekin,
'dagger', of unknown origin.

## bodle
bodle, п., a small Scottish copper coin. —
Probably corruption of the name of Bothwell, a
Scottish mintmaster.

## body
body, n. — ME. bodi, fr. OE. bodig, rel. to OHG.
botah, of uncertain origin. Cp. bodice, embody.
Derivatives: body, tr. v., bodice (q.v.), bodikin
(q.v.), bodi-ed, adj., bodi-er, п., bodi-less, adj.,
bodi-ly, adj. and adv.

## Boedromion
Boedromion, п., name of the 3rd month of the
Attic Greek calendar (corresponding to August-
September). — Gk. Βοηδρομιών, fr. Βοηδρόμια
(pi.), 'the games in memory of the aid given by
Theseus against the Amazons', fr. βοηδράμος,
'running to aid', lit. 'running on hearing a cry',
fr. βοή, 'a cry, shout', and -δρόμος, 'running',
which is rel. to. δρόμος, 'a running'. For the
first element see reboaat and cp. Boethusian, for
the second see dromedary.

## Boemnerin
Boemnerin, п., a genus of plants of the nettle
family (hot.) — ModL., named after G.R.
Boehmer, professor at Wittenberg (1723-1803).
For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Boer
Boer, n. — Du. boer, 'peasant, farmer'. See boor.

## Boethusian
Boethusian, п., a member of a Jewish sect rel. to
the Sadducees. — Heb. Baytust, 'follower of
Baytas (= Boethus)', fr. Gk. βοηθός (whence
L. Boethus), name of a priest, whose son was
made high priest by Herod the Great. See Jo-
sephus, Antiquitates, 19, 5, § 3. Βοηθός lit.
means 'assisting, helpful'. It is a derivative of
βοή, 'a cry, shout'; see Boedromion.

## bog
bog, n. — Gael, or Ir. bog, 'soft', whence bogach,
'bog'.
Derivative: bog, tr. and intr. v.

## bogey
bogey, bogie, п., ghost, bugbear. — See bogle
and cp. bogy.

## boggle
boggle, intr. ,v. and n. — See bogle.

## bogle
bogle, n. — A. var. of bogey.

## bogle
bogle, n„ a truck. — Of uncertain origin.

## bogle
bogle, boggle, п., — a specter. Scot, bogle, bogill,
'goblin, specter', rel. to bng, 'bugbear', bogey,
bogy.

## bogus
bogus, adj., sham. — Of uncertain origin.

## bogy
bogy, n. — Another spelling for bogey.

## bohea
bohea, п., a kind of Chinese black tea. — Named
after the Wu-i hills in China.

## Bohemia
Bohemia, n. — The word derives from L. Boi-
haemum (see Tacitus, Germ., 28), which lit.
means 'home of the Boii' (a Celtic nation,
expelled from this region by the Marcomans about
the beginning of the 1st cent.) The second
element in Boi-haemum is a Teut. loan word
meaning 'home'. See home.

## Bohemian
Bohemian, adj. and n. — F. bohemien, 'gypsy',
orig. 'inhabitant of Bohemia', where the
gypsies were supposed to come from. See Bohemia

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:114 COLUMN:3 -->
and -an.

## Roidae.n.pl.
Roidae.n.pl., a family of snakes (zool.)— ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. L. boa. See Boa.

## boil
boil, п., inflammation, tumor. — ME. bile, fr. OE.
byle, byl, rel. to OFris. bile, OS., OHG. bulia,
MHG. biule, G. Beule, Goth, ufbauljan, 'to
puff up', Ice!, beyla, 'hump', and cogn. with
Olr. bolach, 'pustule, pimple', Serb, buljiti, 'to
protude one's eyes, to stare'. All these words
derive, with -/-formative element, fr. I.-E. base
"bhou-, *bhu-, 'to swell'. See back, 'the body of a
wagon'.

## boll
boll, intr. and tr. v., to bubble up. — ME. boilen,
fr. OF. boillir (F. bouillir), fr. L. bullire, a
collateral form of bullare, 'to bubble', fr. bulla,
'bubble'. See bill, 'documenl', and words there
referred to and cp. the second element in
parboil.
Derivatives: boil, п., boii-er, п.. boil-ing, п., resp.
adj., boil-ing-ly, adv., boilery (q.v.)

## boilery
boilery, п., a place for boiling, — Formed, on
analogy of F. bouilkrie, fr. boil, v. For the
ending see suff. -ery.

## boisterous
boisterous, adj., rough; noisy. — ME. boistrous,
a var. of boistous, which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: boisterons-iy, adv., boisterous-ness,
n.

## bola
bola, also bolas, п., an implement used by the
