Gauchos. — PI. of Sp. bola, 'ball', fr. L. bulla,
'boss, knob'. See bill, 'document'.

## bold
bold, adj. — ME., fr. OE. bald, beald, rel. to OS.,
OHG. bald, 'bold, swift', OHG. baldo, 'boldly',
MHG. Wife, 'boldly, quickly' (whence G. bald,
'soon'), ODu. baldo, 'with confidence', Goth.
balpei, 'boldness', balpaba, 'boldly', ON. ballr,
'frightful, dangerous', fr. I.-E. base *bbel-, 'to
swell'. It. baldo, OF. and Provenc. haul, 'bold,
daring, fearless', are Teut. loan words. See ball,
'a round object*, and belly and cp. billow. Cp.
also bawd, the first element in Baldwin and the
second element in Leopold and in Theobald.
Cp. also bulk, 'size'.
Derivatives: bold-ly,·adv., bold-ness, n.

## bole
bole, п., trunk of a tree. — ME. bale, fr. ON.
boh; 'trunk of a tree', rel. to MLG. bole' bolle,
G. Bohle, 'plank', MDu. bolle, 'trunk of a tree'.
See balk, п., and cp. words there referred to.

## bole
bole, п., red earthy clay. — L. bolus, 'clay,
morsel', fr. Gk. βώλος, 'lump, clod of earth'. See
bolus.

## bolection
bolection, п., a molding (archit.) — Of unknown
origin.
boleite. п., chloride of lead, copper and silver
(mineral.) — Named after Boleo in Lower
California. For the ending see subsl. suff. -ite.

## bolero
bolero, п., a kind of Spanish dance. — Sp., prob.
fr. bola, 'ball', fr. L. bulla. See bowl, 'a ball'.

## Boletaceae
Boletaceae, n. pi., a family of fungi (hot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Boletus with suff. -aceae.

## boletaceous
boletaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Boletus
Boletus, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — L. boletus.
fr. Gk. βωλίτης, 'mushroom, fungus', which
possibly derives fr. βώλος, 'lump'. See bolus.

## bolide
bolide, п., a brilliant meteor. — F., fr. L. boli*.
gen. bolidis, fr. Gk. βολ(ς, gen. βολίδος, 'a
brilliant meteor', which is rel. to βολή, βολός. a
throw', and in gradational relationship to
βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See ballistic.

## bolivarite
bolivarite, п., a hydrous aluminum phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after the Spanish
entomologist Ignacio Bolivar. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## boll
boll, п., a round seed vessel. — ME. bolle, fr. OE.
holla, 'bowl'. See bowl, 'vessel', and cp. the
second element in thropple.

## bollard
bollard, п., a post, around which a mooring rope
is fastened. — Prob. formed fr. bole, 'trunk of α
tree', with suff. -ard.

## bolo
bolo, п., a kind of large knife. — Sp.

## Bolo
Bolo, also bolo, п., a traitor. — Named after
Paul Bolo, a French traitor, executed fqr treason
in April 1918.
Derivative: Bolo-ism, bolo-ism, n.

## bolometer
bolometer, п., an instrument for measuring
radiant heat.— Compounded of Gk. βολή,'throw,
blow, stroke', and μέτρον, 'measure'. The firs!
element stands in gradational relationship to
βάλλειν, 'to throw'; see ballistic. For the sec-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:115 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BOLSHEVIK | 88 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:115 COLUMN:1 -->
ond clemenl see meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## Bolshevik
Bolshevik, bolshevik, п., 1) orig. (from 1903) a
member of the more radical faction of the
Russian Social Democratic Party; 2) later (since the
revolution of Nov. 7, 1917) a member of the
Russian Communist Party. — Russ., lit. 'one
of the majority' (i.e. bolsheviki), fr. bolshe,
'more, larger'; so called with reference to the
paTty that took over the supreme power in
Russia in Г917, and used in contradistinction to the
mensheviki, i.e. 'those of the minority' (see
Menslievik). Russ. bolshe is rel. to OSlav. bol-
jiji, 'larger', and cogn. with OI. balam, 'strengih.
force", Gk. βελτίων, 'better'. See debile.
Derivative: Bolshevik, bolshevik, adj.

## Bolshevism
Bolshevism, bolshevism, п., the doctrines and
policies of the Bolsheviki. — See prec. word and
-ism.

## Bolshevist
Bolshevist, bolshevist, n. and adj., Bolshevik. —
See Bolshevic and -ist.
Derivative: Bolshevist-ic, bolshevist-ic, adj.

## Bolshevize
Bolshevize, bolshevize, tr. v., to make
Bolshevic. — See Bolshevic and -ize.

## bolster
bolster, n. — ME. bolster, fr. OE. bolster, rel. 10
ON. bolstr, Dan., Swed., MLG., Du. bolster,
OHG. bolstar, MHG., G. polster, fr. Teut.
*bul(h)stra-; formed with suff. -s?n*fr.Teut. base
*belg-, 'to swell', which corresponds to I.-E.
base *bhelgh-\ hence bolster, etc., lit. mean
'something swelled'. The above words are cogn.
with OPruss. balsinis, Lett, pabalsts, Serbo-
Croat, blazina (for 'bolzina), 'pillow'. See belly
and cp. billow, budget, bulge.
Derivatives: bolster, tr. v., bolster-er, n.

## bolt
bolt, п., a bar. — ME., fr. OE. boll, rel. to ON.
bolti, Dan. bolt, Swed. bult, MDu. boute, bout,
Du. bout, OHG., MHG. boh, G. Bolzen, fr. I.-E.
base 'bheld-, 'to knock', whence also Lith. beldu,
baldau, Ί knock, rap', baldas, 'pole for striking'.
Derivatives: bolt, tr. and intr. v., bolt, n. (a
rapid run), boli-er, n.

## bolt
bolt, tr. v., to sift. — ME. bulten, fr. OF. buleler
(F. bluter), fr. MDu. biutelen, 'to bolt, sift',
which is rel. to MDu. bitdel, Du. buidel, 'bag,
pouch'. See bud.

## Boltonia
Boltonia, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., named after James
Bolton, an English botanist of the ]8th cent. For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## bolus
bolus, п., a large pill. — L. bolus, 'clay, morsel',
fr. Gk. βώλος, 'lump, clod of earth', which is
perh. rel. to βολβός, 'onion'. See bulb, and cp.
bole, 'clay', Boletus.

## bomb
bomb, n. — F. bombe, fr. It. bomba, 'explosive
shell', fr. L. bombus, 'a hollow, deep sound, a
humming, a buzzing', fr. Gk. βόμβος, of s.m.,
which is of imitative origin. Cp. bum, bump,
boom. Cp. also Bombus, bound, 'to leap'.
Derivatives: bomb, tr. and intr. v., bombard
(q.v.), bomb-er, n.

## bombard
bombard, п., ι) an early kind of cannon; 2) a
former musical instrument. — F. bombarde, lit.
'that which hums or buzzes', fr. L. bombus. See
prec. word and -ard.

## bombard
bombard, tr. v. — F. bombarder, fr. bombarde.
See bombard, n.
Derivatives: bombard-er, п., bombard-ment, n.

## bombardier
bombardier, n.—F.,lit., 'one who throws bombs'.
See prec. word and -ier.

## bombardon
bombardon, п., a musical instrument. — It. bom-
bardone, augment, of bo/nbardo, fr. bdmbardare.
See bombard, п., and -oon.

## bombasine
bombasine, n. — See bombazine.

## bombast
bombast, п., high-sounding speech. — From
Bombastic, lit.;'in the style of Bombastus
Paracelsus' (1493-154Г). The PN. Bombast comes fr.
ML. bombacium, fr. Gk. βαμβάκιον, 'cotton'.
See Bombyx.
Derivatives: bombast-ic, adj., bombast-ic-al-ly,
adv., bombasl-ry, n.

## bombazine
bombazine, bombasine, п., twilled silk cloth with
worsted or cotton. — F. bombasin, fr. ML.
bombacium, fr. Gk. παμβάκιον, 'cotton'. See
Bombyx.

## bombiccite
bombiccite, п., a hydrocarbon mineral. — Named
after the Italian geologist L. Bombicci. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Bombus
Bombus, п., a genus of insects, the bumblebee

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:115 COLUMN:2 -->
(entomol.) — ModL., fr. L. bombus, 'a
humming or buzzing'. See bomb.

## Bombyx
Bombyx, п., a genus of moths, the silkworm moth
(entomol.) — L. bombyx, 'silkworm', fr. Gk.
βόμβυξ, fr. βαμβάκιον, assimilated form of
παμβάκιον, 'cotton', fr. Pers. panba, 'cotton'.
Cp. bombast, bombazine.

## bona fide
bona fide, in good failh. — L. bona fide, abl. of
bona fides, 'good faith'. See bonus and fidelity
and cp. mala fide.

## bonanza
bonanza, п., a rich vein of ore; hence, colloq., a
source of wealth. — Sp., lit. 'fair weather,
prosperity', fr. VL. *bonacia (whence also It. bo-
naccia, OProvenc. bonassa, F. bonace, 'fair
weather at sea'), alteration of L. malacia, 'calm
at sea', which derives fr. Gk. μαλακιά,
'softness', but was mistaken for a derivative of L.
malm, 'bad', and accordingly changed inio
*bonacia, fr. L. bonus, 'good' (see bonus).

## bonbon
bonbon, п., sweetmeat. — F., reduplication of
bon, 'good', fr. L. bonus, 'good'. See boaus and
cp. bonny.

## bonboaniere
bonboaniere, п., a small box or dish for bonbons.
— F., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -iere;
cp. -ery.

## bond
bond, п., anything that binds. — ME. bond, a
var. of band. See band, 'a tie', and cp. the first
element in bonspiel.
Derivatives: bond, tr. v., bond-ed, adj.

## bond
bond, п., serf (archaic). — ME. bond, 'husband,
householder', fr. OE. bonda, 'householder', fr.
ON. bondi, for buandi, 'householder*, lit.
'dweller', fr. bua, 'to dwell, build'. See be, build, and
cp. Boer, boor, booth, bound, adj., bower,
'arbor', byre, and the second element in husband.

## bondage
bondage, n. — ML. bondagium, fr. OE. bonda,
'householder'. See bond, 'serf', and -age.

## bondman
bondman, n. — Compounded of bond, 'serf', and
man.

## bone
bone, n. — ME. ban, bon, fr. OE. ban, 'bone', rel.
to OS., OFris. ben, ON. bein, Dan., Swed. ben,
MDu., Du. been, OHG., MHG., G. bein, 'bone'.
Cp. the first element in bonfire and in banstickle.
Derivatives: bone, tr. v., ban-ed, bon-y, adjs.

## bonfire
bonfire, n. — ME. bonefire, banefire, orig. 'fire
made of bones'; see bone and fire. — Cp.
Richard Broxton Onians, The Origin of European
Thought, Cambridge, 1951, p.268, Note 1.
Derivative: bonfire, tr. and intr. v.

## bongo
bongo, п., a large antelope. — Native name.

## bonhomie
bonhomie, п., good nature. — F. bonhomie,
compounded of bon, 'good', and homme, 'man'. See
bonus and homage.

## Boniface
Boniface, masc. PN. — L. Bonifacius, Bonifatius,
fr. boni/atus, 'lucky, fortunate', lit. 'of a good
fate',\ fr. bonus, 'good', and fatum, 'fate'. See
bonus and fate and cp. the second element in
mauvais. In the sense of 'innkeeper, hotel
owner', the name Boniface is used in allusion to Will
Boniface, a character in George Farquhar'S play
Beaux' Stratagem (1707).

## bonitarian.adj.
bonitarian.adj., beneficial (Roman law).— Formed
with suff. -arian fr. L. bonitas, 'goodness',
fr. bonus, 'good'. See bonus and -ity.

## bonito
bonito, п., any of various fishes. — Sp. bonito,
prob. lit. 'the good or fine one', and identical
with the adjective bonito, 'pretty good', a
derivative of bueno, 'good', fr. L. bonus, of s.m.
See bonus.

## bonne
bonne, п., a child's nurse. — F., fem. of the
adjective bon, 'good', fr. L. bonus, of s.m. See
bonus.

## bonne Douche
bonne Douche, a titbit. — F., 'a good taste', fr.
fem. of bon, 'good', fr. L. bonus, and bouche,
'mouth', fr. L. bucca, 'cheek'. See bonus and
buccal and cp. bouche.

## boanet
boanet, п., a head covering. — ME. bonet, bonet-
te, fr. OF. bonet, bonnet (F. bonnet), fr. ML.
abonnis, occurring in the Salic Law, a word of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: bonnet, tr .v.

## beany
beany, adj., beautiful; fine. — ME. boni; formed
with suff. -y fr. OF. (= F.) bon, 'good', on
analogy of adjectives like jolly, etc. See bonus.

## bonspiel
bonspiel, п., grand curling match. — Du. bon-
spel. The first element is prob. identical with
Du. bond, abbreviation of verbond, 'league,
alliance' ; see bond, 'anything that binds'. Du. spel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:115 COLUMN:3 -->
'game', is rel. to E. spell, 'to take the place
of (another) at work'; see spiel and cp. the
second element in glockenspiel, kriegspiel.

## bonte
bonte, goodness; civility. -■— F., fr. L. bonitatem,
ace. of bonitas, 'goodness', fr. bonus, 'good'.
See next word and -ity.

## bonus
bonus, n. — L. bonus, 'good', fr. OL. dvenos,
dvonos, rel. to L. bene, 'well', bellus, 'handsome,
charming, fine'. See beauty and cp. bene-,
benediction, benefactor, benefit, benevolent, benign,
bonanza, bonitarian, boaito, bonne, boate, boon,
bounty, bunt, 'to sift', bunting, 'cloth', debonair,
embonpoint, magaum bonum.

## bonze
bonze, п., a Buddhist priest. — F., fr. Port, bonzo,
fr. Jap. bonzo, 'Buddhist priest', fr. Chin, fan-
seng, 'religious person'.

## bonzery
bonzery, п., a Buddhist monastery. — F., fr.
bonze. See prec. word and -ery.

## boo
boo, intr. v. and n. — Imitative of the sound
made by a cow.

## booby
booby, п., an awkward fellow; name of various
seabirds. — Sp. bobo, fr. L. balbits, 'stammering',
from the I.-E. imitative base *balb-, whence also
OI. Balbuthah, a name (lit. 'the stammerer'),
Czech bib, 'booby', blblati, 'to stammer',
Serbian blebitati, 'to blabble', OI. balbala-karoti,
'he stammers', Russ. balaboliti, 'to chatter,
babble', Bulg. ЫаЬоГй, Ί chatter, babble'.
*Barb-, a collateral base of base *balb-,
"appears in OI. barbarah, 'stammering'
(designation of the non-Aryan nations), Gk.
βάρβαρος, 'non-Greek, foreign, barbarous', Slovenic
brbrati, brbljati, Serbian brboljitt, 'to mumble,
mutter', Lith. birbti, 'to buzz, hum'. Cp. babble,
babe, baby, balalaika, balbuties, barbaric, bauble.
Derivative: booby-ish, adj.

## boodle
boodle, п., money (slang). — Prob. fr. Du. boe-
del, 'estate, possession'. Cp. caboodle.

## boohoo
boohoo, intr. v. and n. — Of imitative origin.
Cp. boo.

## book
book, n. — ME. boke, book, fr. OE. hoc (pi. bee),
rel. to OS., ΟΝ., OFris. bdk, Swed. bok, Dan.
bog, Du. boek, OHG. buoh, MHG. buoch, G.
Buch, 'book', Goth, boka 'letter (of the
alphabet)', pi. bokds, 'books', and to OE. boc,
bice, 'beech' (see beech). The connection
between book end beech (cp. G. Buch, 'book',
Buche, 'beech is due to the Teutonic custom
of writing runic letters on thin boards of beech.
Derivatives: book, tr. and intr. v., book-ed, adj.,
book-er, п., book-er-y, п., book-ing, п.,
bookish, adj., book-ish-ly, adv., book-ish-ness, п.,
book-let, п., book-y, adj.

## boom
boom, intr. and tr. v., to hum, buzz. — Of
imitative origin; cp. Du. bommen, 'to drum', ME.
bommen, 'to hum'. Cp. also bomb, bum and
bump.
Derivatives: boom, п., humming, buzzing,
boomer, п., boom-ing, n. and adj.

## boom
boom, п., a long pole (naut.) — Du. boom, 'tree,
beam, pole', rel. to E. beam (q.v.) Cp. the first
element in bumboat.

## boomerang
boomerang, п., Australian throwing stick. —
Native Australian name.

## boon
boon, п., request, favor. — ME. bone, 'petition',
fr. ON. bon, which is rel. to OE. ben, 'prayer,
petition', and in gradational relationship to
OE. bannan, 'to summon', ON. banna, 'to
forbid'. See ban, v., and cp. words there referred
to.

## boon
boon, adj., gay; convivial. — ME. bon, fr. OF.
bon, 'good', fr. L. bonus. See bonus.

## boor
boor, n. — Du. boer, 'peasant, farmer', fr. earlier
geboer, prob. fr. LG. gebur, which is rel. to
OHG. giburo, MHG. gebure, G. Bauer, OE.
gebur, 'peasant', lit. 'one who dwells with others',
fr. ge-, 'with' (see y-, 'with'), and bur, 'a
dwelling', which is геД. to bua, 'to dwell, build'. See
be and cp. Boer. Cp. also bower, 'cottage', and
the second element in neighbor.
Derivatives: boor-ish, adj., boor-ish-ly, adv.,
boor-ish-ness, n.

## boost
boost, tr. v. and n. — Of unknown origin.
Derivative: boost-er, n.

## boot
boot, п., a leather covering for the foot. — ME.
bote, fr. OF. bote (F. botte), which is rel. to F.
bot, 'club-footed'; prob. of Teut. origin.
Derivatives: boot, tr. v., boot-ed, adj., boot-ee.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:116 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 89 | BOSWELL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:116 COLUMN:1 -->
п., boot-er, п., boot-er-y, п., boot-ing, n.

## boot
boot, п., advantage. — ME. hot, bote, fr. OE.
bot, 'remedy, cure, improvement,
compensation', rel. to OS. bot, bota, ON. bot, OFris. bote,
Du. boele, OHG. Ьиоз, Ьиоза, MHG. buoje,
G. Bufie, 'penance, atonement', Goth, bota,
'advantage'. These \yords lit. mean 'a making
better'. See better and cp. bote.

## Boutes
Boutes, п., the Wagoner (a constellation). — L.
Bootes, fr. Gk. βοώτης, 'plowman', fr. βοωτεΐν,
'to plow', fr. βοϋς, gen. βοάς, Όχ', which is
cogn. with L. bos, gen. bovis, 'ox'. See bovine.

## booth
booth, n. — ME. bothe, borrowed fr. ODan.
both; rel. to ON. bud, 'a dwelling', MDu. boede,
MHG. buode, G. Bude, ON. Ьйа, OE., OHG.
buan, 'to dwell', and cognate with Lith. butas,
'house', Olr. both, 'hut'. See be, build and cp.
boor, bothy, bound, 'ready', bower, 'cottage',
busk, 'to prepare', byre, the first element in
bylaw" and the second element in neighbor.

## bootleg
bootleg, tr. and intr. v. — The word orig. meant
'to carry prohibited alcoholic liquor in the leg
of a high boot.
Derivatives: bootleg, adj., bootlegg-er, п., boot-
legg-ing, n.

## booty
booty, n. — F. butin, fr. MLG. bate, 'share,
booty' (whence also Du. buit, MHG. biute,
G. Beute, 'booty'). E. booty was influenced in
form by an association with boot, 'advantage'.
The ending -y (inst. of-in) is due to the analogy
of other nouns in -y, -ty. Cp. the second element
in freebooter, filibuster.

## booze
booze, intr. v., to drink to excess (colloq.) — A
var. of bouse (q.v.)
Derivatives: booz-ed, adj., booz-er, п., booz-y,
adj., booz-i-ly, adv., booz-i-ness, n.

## bo-peep
bo-peep, п., a childish game. — Formed fr. bo
and peep.

## bora
bora, п., a cold northeast wind. — It., a dialectal
form of borea, 'north wind', fr. L. boreas. See
boreal.

## Borachio
Borachio, п., name of a drunkard in Shakespeare's
Much Ado About Nothing. — Sp. borracho,
'drunk, intoxicated', fr. L. burtus, 'red' (see
burro); so called in allusion to the red
complexion of intoxicated people.

## boracic
boracic, adj., boric. — See borax and -ic.

## borage
borage, η , a blue-flowered plant used in salads.
— ME., fr. OF. borrace (cp. its variant burage
and F. bourrache), fr. ML. borrago, ult. fr.
Arab, aba 'arak, lit. 'father of sweat', so called
by the Arab physicians because of its sudorific
effect. See abbot andc p. arrack.

## boraginaceous
boraginaceous, adj. — Formed with suff. -aceous
fr. ML. borrago, gen. borraginis. See prec. word.

## borate
borate, п., salt of boric acid (chem.) — See boron
and chem. suff. -ate.

## borax
borax, п., a white crystalline salt used as a flux
and an antiseptic. — F., fr. Arab, bauraq
(VArab. boraq), fr. Pers. burah.

## bordage
bordage, п., the tenure of a border (Feudal
system). — ML. bordagium. See next word and -age.

## bordar
bordar, п., tenant (Feudal system). — ML. bor-
darius, fr. borda, 'cottage', fr. OF. borde, which
is a Teut. loan word. See board, 'table, plank',
and cp. border.

## Bordenux
Bordenux, bordenux, п., claret. — From
Bordeaux, name of a city and seaport in Southern
France; so called because the wine is shipped
from Bordeaux. The name of the city derives fr.
F. (la ville au) bordd'eaux, '(the city at) the edge
of waters' (see border and Eau de Cologne).

## bordel
bordel, п., a brothel. — F., fr. Provenc., bordel,
•brothel', fr. OF. bordel, 'a poor hut, hovel*,
dimin. of borde, 'hut', fr. Frankish "borda, 'hut
made from planks', fr. *bord, 'plank', which is
rel. to OE. bord, ON. bord, 'plank'. See board,
'table, plank'.

## border
border, n. — OF. (= F.) bordure, fr. border, 'to
border', fr. bord, 'a border', fr. Frankish *bord,
'border, edge; side of a ship', which is orig.
identical with *bord, 'plank'. See board, 'side of
a ship', and cp. bordage, border, bordure. Cp.
also prec. word.
Derivatives: border, v., border-ed, adj.,
borderer, n.

## bordure
bordure, п., a border around a shield (her.) —
F. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:116 COLUMN:2 -->

## bore
bore, tr. and ihtr. v., to pierce. — ME. borien, fr.
OE. borian, rel. to ON. bora, Swed. borra, Dan.
bore, OS., OHG. boron, MDu., Du. boren,
MHG. born, G. bohren, fr. I.-E. base *bher-, 'to
cut with a sharp point; to bore, pierce', whence
also Arm. beran, 'mouth' (prop, 'opening'), Gk.
■ φαράω, φαρόω, Ί plow', φάρος, 'plow', φάραγξ,
'cleft, chasm', φάρυγξ, 'throat, chasm, gulf, L.
ferire, 'to strike, smite', forare, 'to bore, pierce',
OSlav. barjg, brati (for *bor-ti), 'to strike, fight',
Lith. baras, Lett, bars, 'swath', Lith. burna,
'mouth', Russ. borona, 'harrow', Mir. bern,
berna, 'cleft, opening', Alb. brime, 'hole*. Cp.
bark, 'rind of a tree', barranca, barrow, 'castrated
boar', board, 'table, plank', board, 'side of a
ship', Boris, brackish, broom, burin, foralite,
foramen, interfere, perforate, pharynx, and the
second element in Dukhobors.
Derivatives: bore, п., bor-ed, adj., bore-dom, п.,
bor-er, п., bor-ing, adj., bor-ing-ly, adv., bor-
ing-ness, n.

## bore
bore, п., tidal wave. — ME. bore, 'wave, billow',
fr. ON. bara, 'wave*, lit. 'that which is borne
or carried', rel. to ON. bera, 'to bear'. See bear,
'to carry'.

## bore
bore, past tense of bear. — ME. See bear, 'to
carry'.

## Boreades
Boreades, п., pi. the wind gods Zetes and Calais,
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Βορεάδοα, lit. 'the
sons of Boreas', fr. Βορέάς. See Boreas.

## boreal
boreal, adj., pertaining to Boreas; northern. —·
L. boreal is, fr. boreas. See next word and adj.
suff. -al.

## Boreas
Boreas, п., the god of the north wind in Greek
mythology. — L., fr. Gk. Βορέάς, fr. βορέϋς,
'north wind', which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly stands for I.-E. *gmori-yas and orig.
meant 'mountain wind', and is cogn. with OI.
girib, Avestic gairi, 'mountain', Alb. gur, 'rock',
OSlav. gora, 'mountain', Lith. glre, 'forest'. Cp.
bora, Boreades, boreal and the second element
in Hyperborean. Cp. also Croat.

## borecole
borecole, п., kind of cabbage. — Prob. fr. Du.
boerenkool, lit. 'peasant's cabbage'. See boor
and cole.

## boric
boric, adj., pertaining to, or containing, boron
(chem.) — See boron and -ic.

## Boris
Boris, masc. PN. — OSlav., lit. meaning 'fight',
rel. to OSlav. barjg, brati (for 'bor-ti), 'to fight',
and cogn. with L. ferire, 'to strike'. See bore,
'to pierce'.

## born
born, borne, pp. of bear. — ME. boren, fr. OE.
boren, pp. of beran. See bear, 'to carry'.

## borne
borne, adj., narrow-minded. — F., lit. 'limited',
pp. of borner, 'to limit', fr. OF. (= F.) borne,
'limit', fr. earlier bodne, a word of Gaulish
origin. See bourn and bound, 'limit'.

## boron
boron, п., name of a non-metallic element (chem.)
— Originally called by the English chemist Sir
Humphrey Davy (1778-1829) boracium, because
drawn fr. boracic (= boric) acid. See borax.
The ending -on in boron is due to the analogy
of carbon, where, however, the ending -on
belongs to the stem.

## borough
borough, n. — ME. burgh, burwe, fr. OE. burg,
burh, burg, rel. to OS., OFris., burg, 'castle',
ON. borg, 'wall, castle', MDu. burch, borch,
borcht, Du. burcht, burg, OHG. burg, burc,
buruc, 'fortified place, citadel', MHG. burc,
G. Burg, 'castle', Goth, baiirgs, 'city', OE. beorg,
etc., 'mountain'. These words prob. derive fr.
I.-E. base 'bhergh-, 'high', whence also Arm.
berj, 'high place', OSlav. bregu, 'bank (of a
river)', W. bera, 'stack, pyramid', Mir. bri, ace.
brig, 'hill*, Toch. Aparkas, 'long', Hitt. parkush,
'high', OI. brhdnt-, Avestic b'r'zant-, 'high',
OCeltic Brigantes, lit. 'the high ones' (cp. Bur-
gundians, fr. Late L. Burgundiones, lit. 'high-
landers'), prob. also OL. forctus, 'good', L.
fortis (fr. OL. forctis), 'strong', see Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW., Ι,ρρ.535-36, s.v./orii'i.andKluge-
Mitzka, EWDS., p. 67, s.v. Berg. Cp. barrow,
'mountain, mound', bourgeois, burgage, burgess,
burgh, burgrave, Burgundy, canterbury, faubourg,
gaussbergire, ghetto, Hapsburg, hanberk. Cp.
also Brahma, fort, and the second element in bar-
bicane. Cp. also the suff. -bury in English place
names, which comes fr. OE. byrig, the dative

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:116 COLUMN:3 -->
sing of OE. burg. Base 'bhergh- is prob. an
enlarged form of base *bher-, 'to carry, lift'. See
bear, 'to carry'.

## Borrichia
Borrichia, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the Danish
botanist Olof Borrich. For the ending see suff.
-ia.

## borrow
borrow, tr. and intr. v. — ME. borwen, fr. OE.
borgian, 'to lend; to borrow', fr. borg, 'pledge,
security', rel. to ON. borga, 'to become bail for,
to guarantee', MDu. borghen, 'to protect,
guarantee', OHG. boragen, borgen, 'to beware of;
to spare; to remit a debt', G. borgen, 'to
borrow; to lend', biirgen, 'to become bail for, to
guarantee', OE. beorgan, OHG. bergan, 'to hide,
save'. See bury.
Derivatives: borrow-er, п., borrow-ing, n.
Borstal system. — So called fr. Borstal, a town
in Kent, England, in allusion to the reform
system adopted in its prisons.

## borzoi
borzoi, п., the Russian wolfhound. — Russ.
borzoy, lit. 'quick, swift', rel. to Czech brzy,
Serbo-Croat, brzo, 'quickly', and cogn. with
Lilh. bruzdeti, bruzggti, 'to hurry', burzdiis,
'mobile, agile', and cogn. with the first element
in Avestic berez-iachra, 'having fast-moving
wheels'.

## Bos
Bos, п., a genus of quadrupeds (zool.) — L. bos.
gen. bovis, 'ox'. See bovine and cp. the second
element in Ovibos.

## boscage
boscage, h., a thicket. — OF. boscage (F. bocage),
'grove', fr. ML. boscus, 'wood'. See bush and
-age, and cp. bosquet, bouquet.

## Boselaphus
Boselaphus, п., a genus of antelopes, the nilgai
(zool) — ModL., eompounded of L. bos, 'ox',
and Gk. ϊλαφος, 'deer'. See Bos and eland.

## bosh
bosh, п., empty talk, nonsense. — Turk. bosh.

## bosk
bosk, п., a thicket. — ME. bosk, a var. of busk..
See bush, 'shrub', and cp. busk.

## bosky
bosky, adj., bushy. — Formed fr. bosk with adj.
suff. -y.

## bosket
bosket, bosqnet, п., a thicket. — F. bosquet,
'grove, thicket', fr. It. boschetto, dimin. oibosco,
'wood', fr. ML. boscus, of s.m. See bush, 'shrub',
and cp. boscage, bouquet.

## bosom
bosom, n. — ME., fr. OE. bdsm, rel. to OFris.
bosm, OS. bosom, MDu. boesem, Du. boezent,
OHG. buosam, MHG. buosem, buosen, G. Bu-
sen; of uncertain etymology. For the suff. -от
ср. besom. Ср. embosom.
Derivatives: bossom-ed, adj., bossom-er, п.,
bossom-like, bossom-y, adjs.

## bosqnet
bosqnet, n. — See bosket.

## boss
boss, п., a protuberance. — ME. boce, fr. OF.
boce (F. bosse), which is perh. of Teut. origin.
Cp. OHG. Ьоззап, 'to thrust, beat', and see beat.
Cp. also emboss. Cp. also botch, 'a swelling',
eabbage, п., cabochon.

## boss
boss, п., master (colloq.) — Du. baas, 'master',
fr. MDu. baes, rel. to Fris. baes; not rel. to
OHG. basa (whence MHG. base, G. Base), 'aunt'.
Derivative: boss, tr. and intr. v.

## bostangi
bostangi, bostanji, п., a gardener. — Turk, bos-
tanji, formed fr. bostan, 'garden', fr. Pers. bos-
tan, of s.m., with Turk. suff. -ji, which denotes
occupation or trade. Pers. bostan lit. means
'place of fragrance', fr. bo, 'smell, odor,
fragrance', which is "rel. to Avestic baoidi-, of s.m.,
and -stan, a suff. denoting place, which is rel. to
Avestic -stana (in compounds), 'place', lit. "a
place where to stand'. See Hindustani.
boston п., ι) akind of valse; 2)a breed of dog. —
In both senses, named from Boston in
Massachusetts (U.S.A.)

## bostoulte
bostoulte, п., a kind of igneous rock (petrogr.) —
Named fr. Boston in Massachusetts, because
found at Marblehead Neck, near Boston. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Bostrychidae
Bostrychidae, n. pi., a family of beetles (entomol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk.
βόστρυχος, 'lock of hair, curl, foliage; a winged
insect', which is of uncertain origin. It possibly
stands for *gwostruchos and orig. meant
'something twisted', and is cogn. with OSerb. goozd,
'forest', Czech hvozd, 'mountain', MHG., G.
quast, quaste, 'tuft, knot', Alb. ge&, 'foliage,
branch'.

## Boswell
Boswell, п., admirer of a person. — Named after

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: вот | 90 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 COLUMN:1 -->
James Boswell (1740-95), admirer and
biographer of Dr. Johnson.
Derivatives: Boswell-ίαη, adj., Boswell-ism, п.,
Boswell-ize, intr. and tr. v.

## bot
bot, bott, п., an insect larva. — Of unknown
etymology.

## botany
botany, n. — F. botanique, fr. Gk. βοτανική
(επιστήμη), lit. '(knowledge of) botany', prop. fern,
of βοτανικός, 'pertaining to herbs', fr. βοτάνη,
'pasture, fodder', which is re], to βόσις, βοσκή,
'food, fodder', βόσκειν, 'to feed, nourish, tend',
βοσκός, 'herdsman', βόσκημα, 'cattle', lit. 'that
which is fed'; prob. fr. I.-E. base *gw6-, 'to
feed', whence also Lith. giioias, 'herd', gauja,
'herd, flock', gujd, guiti, 'to drive'. Gk.
βοτανική επιστήμη orig. meant 'the science of
fodder'. The ending -y in E. botany is due to the
influence of words like astronomy, etc. Cp. the
second element in Hippoboscidae, proboscis,
syboric.
Derivatives: botan-ist, п., botan-ize, int. v.,
botan-iz-er, n.

## botch
botch, п., a swelling. — ONF. bocke,
corresponding to OF. boce. See boss, 'protuberance'.
Derivatives: botch, tr. v., botch-y, adj., botch-
i-ly, adv., bolch-i-ness, n.

## botch
botch, tr. v., to mend; intr. v., to do mending. —
ME. bocchen, 'to patch, mend', of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: botch, п., botch-ed, adj., botch-er,
п., botch-ery, n.

## botfly
botfly, n. — Compounded of bot and fly, n.

## bote
bote, п., compensation. — ME. form of boot,
'advantage' (q.v.) Cp. the second element in
baybote.

## boterol
boterol, boteroll, n. (her.) — F. bouterolle, fr.
hauler, 'to beat, push' (later 'to put, place'), fr.
Frankish *bdtan, 'to beat, strike', which is rel. to
OHG. Ьдззап and ON. bauta, of s.m. See beat
and -ole.

## both
both, adj., pron. and conj. — ME. bathe, bothe,
fr. ON. bapir, which is rel. to OS. bethia, OFris.
bethe, Du. beide, OHG. beide,bede (masc), beido
(fern.), beidiu (neut.), MHG. beide, bide (masc.
and fern.), beidiu (neut.), G. beide, Goth, bajdps,
'both'; formed fr. Teut. *ba-, 'both', and the
def. article (see the). The first element in both,
etc., is rel. to OE. blgen (masc), ba (fem. and
neut.), Goth. 6ai(masc), ia(neut.), 'both', and
cogn. with the second element, in OI. u-bhau
(masc), u-bhi (fem.), Avestic u-wa (masc), u-be
(fem.), 'both', Toch. A am-pi, am-pe, В ant-api,
Gk. &μ-φω, 'both', άμ-φί, 'round about', L.
am-bo, 'both', am-bi-, 'around', OSlav. o-ba,
Lith. α-bit, Lett, a-bi, OPruss. ab-bai, 'both'. Cp.
ambi-, amphi-.

## bother
bother, tr. and intr. v. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: bother, п., botheration (q.v.),
bother-er, n.

## botheration
botheration, п., bother (colloq.) — A hybrid
coined from the verb bother and -ation, a suff.
of Latin origin.

## bothrio-
bothrio-, combining form for bolhrium. — See
DOthrinm.

## Bothriocephalus
Bothriocephalus, п., a genus of tapeworms (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'having heads resembling little
pits', fr. Gk. βόθριον, 'a little pit', and κεφαλή,
'head'. See next word and cephalic.

## bothrium
bothrium, п., a sucker (esp. on the head of a
tapeworm; zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βόθριον, 'a
little pit', dimin. of βόθρος, 'pit, ditch, trench',
which is prob. cogn. with \-.fodere, 'to dig',/<wso,
'ditch'. See bed and cp. fosse. Cp. also the
second element in Cyclobothra.

## bothy
bothy, п., a hut. — Of Celtic origin. Cp. Olr.
both, 'hut', and see booth.

## botone
botone, botony, adj., having a trefoil at the end
(her.) — F. boulonni, pp. of boutonner, 'to bud;
to button', fr. bouton, 'bud; button'. See bntton.
bo tree. — Singhalese bo, fr. Pali bodhi, shortened
fr. bodhi-taru, 'bo tree', lit. 'tree of wisdom or
enlightenment', fr. bodhi, 'wisdom,
enlightenment', and taru, 'tree'. Pali bodhi is rel. to OI.
buddhah, 'awakened, enlightened'. See Buddha.

## Botrychium
Botrychium, п., a genus of plants, the moonwort
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βότρυχος, 'grapestalk',
which is rel. to βότρυς, 'a cluster of grapes' (see
next word); so called because its sporangia form

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 COLUMN:2 -->
a cluster resembling that of grapes. See next
word.

## botryo-
botryo-, before a vowel botry-, combining form
meaning 'cluster, clusterlike'. — Gk. βοτρυο-,
βοτρυ-, fr. βότρυς, 'a cluster of grapes', of
uncertain origin. Cp. prec. word.

## bottega
bottega, п., shop, workshop. — It., fr. L. apo-
theca, 'storehouse (esp. of wine)', fr. Gk.
αποθήκη, 'any place wherein to lay up
something; magazine, storehouse'. See apothecary
and cp. bodega, boutique.

## bottle
bottle, n. — ME. hotel, fr. OF. botele (F. bou-
teille),fr.VL·. butticula, dimin. of Late L. buttis,
'cask', fr. Gk. πυτίνη, 'flask covered with plaited
osier' (through the medium of Tarent. βυτίνη, of
s.m.). Cp. bntt, 'barrel', butler. For the change of
Gk. π to L. b cp. ML. huxida, fr. Gk. πυξίδα, ace.
of πυξίς, 'box' (see box, 'tree', and box,
'receptacle').
Derivatives: bottle, tr. v., boltl-ed, adj.

## bottom
bottom, n. — ME. botme, boiome, fr. OE. botm,
'lowest part, depth, bottom', rel. to OS. bodom,
ON. botn, OFris. boden, 'soil', Du. bodem,
OHG. bodam, MHG., bodem, G. Boden,
'ground, soil, earth', and cogn. with OI. budh-
nah, Gk. παθμήν, 'foundation, bottom', L.
fundus (metathesis for *fudnos), 'bottom; piece
of land, farm', Olr. bond (metathesis for *bodn),
'sole of the foot'. Cp. found, 'to establish',
founder, v., fund, fundament, profound.
Derivatives: bottom, adj. and v., bottom-less,
adj., bottomry (q.v.)

## bottomry
bottomry, п., bond by which the vessel is
hypothecated for the loan of the money advanced
on the security of the ship. — A blend of
bottom, in the sense of 'ship', and Du. bodemerij,
'bottomry', fr. MLG. bodmen, verbodmen, fr.
bodem, 'bottom; to lend a ship and its cargo',
Cp. F. bomerie, 'bottomry', which also derives
fr. Du. bodemerij.

## botulism
botulism, п., sausage poisoning. — G. Bolulismus,
coined fr. L. botulus, 'sausage', and suff. -ismus.
See bowel and -ism.

## bouche
bouche, п., mouth (obsol.) — F., 'mouth', fr. L.
bucca, 'cheek'. See buccal and cp. boune bouche.

## boucle
boucle, n„ a kind of yarn having small curly
loops. — F., lit. 'buckled, curled', pp. of bou-
cler, 'to buckle, curl', fr. boucle, 'buckle, curl*.
See buckle.

## boudoir
boudoir, п., a woman's private sitting room. —
F., lit. 'sulking or pouting room', fr. bouder,
4o sulk, pout', which is of imitative origin. Cp.
pout.

## Bougainvillaea
Bougainvillaea, п., a small genus of woody vines.
— Named after the French navigator Louis
Bougainville (1729-1811).

## bough
bough, n. — ME. bogh, fr. OE. bog, boh, 'arm,
shoulder, bough', rel. to ON. bogr, 'shoulder;
bow of a ship', OHG. buog, MHG. buoc, G. Bug,
'shoulder, hock, joint', fr. I.-E. 'bhaghus-,
'elbow, arm', whence also OI. banuh, Avestic bazu,
Arm. bazuk, 'arm', Gk. πηχυς, Dor. παχύς,
'elbow', Toch. A poke, В pauke, 'arm'. Cp. bow,
'the fore part of a ship'.

## bought
bought, past tense and pp. of buy. — ME.
boht(e), fr. OE. bohte, resp. (ge)boht. See hay.

## bougie
bougie, п., 1) a wax candle; 2) a surgical
instrument used to dilate a body canal. — F., 'wax
candle*, fr. Bougie, Bugia, a town of Algeria.
The orig. meaning was 'fine wax candles
brought from Bugia', and only at a relatively
later period did the sense of the word develop
into 'candles brought from Algeria', and
'candles' in general.

## bouillabaisse
bouillabaisse, п., a kind of fish stew. — F.,
borrowed fr. Provenc. bouiabaisso, prop, a
compound of the imperatives of two verbs,
corresponding to F. bous-abaisse and to Engl, boil-
abase (this latter taken in its original sense 'to
lower'), expressing, in a joking way, the rapidity
of the cooking. See boil, v., and abase and cp.
bouilli, bouillon.

## bouilli
bouilli, п., boiled meat. — F., prop. pp. atbouil-
lir, 'to boil'. See boil, v., and cp. next word.

## bonillon
bonillon, п., a strong broth. — F., 'broth', fr.
bouillir. Ίο boil'. See boil, v., and cp. prec. word
and the first element in bouillabaisse.

## boulder
boulder, п., a large stone. — Short for boulder

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 COLUMN:3 -->
stone, fr. ME. bulderstan, prob. of Scand.
origin; cp. Dan. buldre, Swed. bullra, 'to roar,
rattle', dial. Swed. bullersten, 'a large stone in
a stream'.

## boale
boale, п., council in ancient Greece. — Gk.
βουλή, 'counsel, deliberation, decree, council',
rel. to βούλεσθαι, 'to will, wish'. The orig.
meaning of this verb was 'to throw oneself upon
something' (in a spiritual sense). It stands in
gradational relationship to βάλλειν, 'to throw';
see ballistic. See Frisk, GEW., I, pp. 258-59 s.v.
βοΰλομαι.

## boule
boule, п., a game. — F., 'ball', fr. L. bulla, 'any
round object, bubble, boss'. See bin, 'document'.

## boulevard
boulevard, n. — F., earlier boloart, boulevert,
balouart, belouart, orig. meaning 'work of
fortification', fr. MDu. bolwerc. See bulwark.

## boulter
boulter, п., a long line for fishing, with hooks
attached. — Of unknown origin.

## bounce
bounce, intr. and tr. v. — ME. bunsen. Cp. LG.
bunsen, Du. bonzen, 'to beat, thump'. Cp. also
jounce.
Derivatives: bounce, п., bounc-er, п., bounc-ing,
adj., bounc-ing-ly, adv.

## bound
bound, п., limit. — ME. bounde, fr. earlier bunne,
fr. OF. bonne, fr. earlier bodne, 'limit,
boundary', fr. ML. bodina, which is prob. of Gaulish
origin. Cp. borne.
Derivatives: bound, tr. v., to set a limit to,
intr. v., to have a boundary, boundary (q.v.),
bound-less, adj., bound-less-ly, adv., bound-less-
ness, n.

## bound
bound, intr. v., to leap. — F. bondir, 'to rebound,
resound, echo', fr. VL. "bombilire, formed—
prob. on the analogy of VL. *tinnitire (whence
OF. tentir, F. retentir), 'to resound'—fr. L.
bombire, 'to resound', fr. bombus, 'a hollow,
deep sound'. Cp. Late L. bombilare, 'to buzz,
hum', another derivative of L. bombire. .See
bomb and cp. bombard, rebound.
Derivatives: bound, a leap, bound-ing, adj.,
bound-ing-ly, adv.

## bound
bound, adj., l) ready (obsol.); 2) ready to go,
going. — ME. boun, bun, 'prepared, ready', fr.
ON. buinn, pp. of bua, 'to dwell, prepare'. See
be and cp. boor, bower, 'cottage', booth, bothy.
The d in bound is excrescent. Cp. pound, 'to
beat', round, 'to whisper', sound, 'noise',
horehound.

## bound
bound, past tense and pp. of bind. — ME. bun-
de(n), past tense, resp. pp. of binden. See bind.

## boundary
boundary, n. — A blend of bound, 'limit', and
ML. bonnarium, 'piece of land with a fixed
limit', fr. OF. bonne, 'limit'. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ary.

## bounden
bounden, adj. — ME. bounden, fr. OE. bunden,
pp. of bindan, 'to bind'. See bind.

## bounder
bounder, п., an ill-bred person. — Formed fr.
bound, 'to leap', with agential suff. -er.

## bounteous
bounteous, adj., 1) generous; 2) abundant. —
ME. bomtevous, formed with suff. -ous fr. OF.
bontif, fem. bontive, fr. bonte (F. bonte). See
bounty. Derivatives: bounteous-ly, adv., boun-
leous-ness, n.

## bountiful
bountiful, adj. — Compounded of bounty and
-fid.
Derivatives: bountiful-ly, adv., bountiful-ness, n.

## bounty
bounty, n. — OF. bonte (F. bonle), fr. L. boni-
tatem, ace. of bonitas, 'goodness', fr. bonus,
'good'. See bonus and cp. It. bonta. Rum. buna-
tare, Engadine bundet, OProvenc., Catal. bon-
tat, Sp. bondad, Port, bondade, 'goodness',
which all derive fr. L. bonitatem. For the ending
see suff. -ty.

## bouqnet
bouqnet, п., ι) a bunch of flowers, nosegay;
2) aroma. — F., orig. meaning 'grove, thicket',
dimin. formed fr. ML. boscus, 'wood', whence
also F. bois, 'wood, forest'; see bush and cp.
bosket. For the original sense of bouquet cp.
bouquet dOrbres, 'group of trees, grove'.

## Bourbon
Bourbon, п., a member of the royal family in
France which reigned 1589-1792 and 1815-
1848. — F., from Bourbon l'Archambault, chief
town of a lordship in central France. The place
name Bourbon is traceable to Borvo, name of a
thermal deity. See burbot.
Derivatives: Bourbon-ism, п., Bourbon-isl, n.

## bourdon
bourdon, п., pilgrim's staff. — F. bourdon, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 91 | BOYCOTT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 COLUMN:1 -->
ML. burdonem, ace. of burdo, fr. L. burdus,
'mule'. For sense development cp. chevron, ram,
sawbuck, sawhorse.

## bourdon
bourdon, п., a drone bass. — F., fr. ML.
burdonem, ace. of burdo. See burden, 'refrain'.

## bourette
bourette, п., a kind of silk linen or cotton yarn
with knots. — F. bourrette, dimin. of bourre,
'flock (for stuffing or padding); floss silk', fr.
Late L. burra, 'a shaggy garment' wich is cogn.
with Gk. βερρόν, 'thick with hair, shaggy'. See
bureau and -ette and cp. burel, burl, burlesque.

## bourgeois
bourgeois, adj., characteristicOf the middle class;
middle-class; п., one of the middle class. —
F., fr. bourg, 'small town', hence prop, meaning
'inhabitant of a bourg'; of Teut. origin. See
borongh and cp. burgess. Cp. also burgee.

## bourgeois
bourgeois, п., a size of printer's type (print). —
Named after Bourgeois, a French type founder.

## bourgeoisie
bourgeoisie, п., middle class. — F., fr. bourgeois.
See bourgeois, 'middle class'.

## bourn
bourn, bourne, also burn, п., a stream. — ME.
burne, borne, fr. OE. brunna, burna, rel. to OS.,
OHG. brunno, ON. brunnr, Norw. brunn, brynn,
Dan. brend, Swed. brunn, OFrls. burna, MLG.,
MDu. borne, Du. bron, MHG. brunne, brun,
G. Brunnen and Born, Goth, 'brunna, 'well,
spring', and cogn. with Gk. φρέάρ, 'well, spring',
Arm. aibeur (gen. aiber), 'source', Russ. brujd,
'current', bruit', 'to stream with force'. For
more cognates see harm, brand, bread, brew,
broil (in both senses), broth, and fervent, phreatic.

## bourn
bourn, bourne, п., a limit. — F. borne, fr. earlier
bodne. See boand, 'limit'.

## bourree
bourree, п., an old lively French dance. — F.,
prop. fem. pp. of bourrer, 'to cram, to stuff (a
chair, etc.)', fr. Late L. burra, 'a shaggy
garment', which is rel. to L. birrus, 'a kind of cloak';
see burnous. The dance was prob. so called from
its rude and uncouth movements.

## bourse
bourse, n. — F„ 'purse, exchange', fr. Late L.
bursa, 'purse' (see purse). The sense
development of the word is due to the following facts.
In the 13th cent, a famous family of merchants
living in Bruges (Belgium) was called Van der
Burse (in allusion to the three purses contained
in their coat of arms). The place before their
house became a celebrated meeting center of
merchants and bankers. This is why the
Exchange of Antwerp built after the pattern of
that in Bruges was called Bourse. Later this word
became the general name denoting exchange.
See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 81. Cp.
bursar, disbourse.

## bouse
bouse, п., a drink. — ME. bous, fr. MDu. buse,
'cup'. See next word.

## bouse
bouse, intr. and tr. v. to carouse. — ME. bousen,
fr. MDu. busen, 'to carouse', rel. to MHG. bus,
'act of swelling, inflation'; of uncertain origin.
Cp. booze.
Derivatives: bous-er, п., bous-y, adj.

## boustrophedon
boustrophedon, п., an old form of writing, in
which lines run alternately from right to left and
from left to right. — Gk. βουστροφηδόν,
'turning as an ox turns in plowing', compounded of
βοΰς, Όχ', and στρέφειν, 'to turn*. See bovine
and strophe.

## bout
bout, п., a contest. — Fr. earlier bought, 'bend',
fromthe base of bow,'to bend',and in gradation-
al relationship to bight.

## boutade
boutade, п., whim, caprice. — F., fr. bouter, 'to
beat, push', fr. Frankish *botan, 'to beat', which
is rel. to OHG. Ьбззап, OE. beatan, of s.m. See
See beat and -ade and cp. boterol, butt, 'to strike'.

## BoutelouB
BoutelouB, п., a genus of grasses (hot.) — ModL.,
named Wter the Spanish botanist Claudio
Bouteloul (1774-1842).

## boutique
boutique, p., a shop. — F., fr. OProvenc. botica
(also botiga), fr. Gk. αποθήκη, 'any place
wherein to lay up something; magazine,
storehouse', whence also L. apothica. See apothecary
and cp. bodega, bottega. The vowel / (for e) is
due to the MGk. pronunciation of η as i.

## bouts-rimes
bouts-rimes, n. pi., rhyming words to which
verses are to be composed. — F., lit. 'rhyming
ends'. See butt, 'the thicker end of anything*
and rhyme.

## bovate
bovate, п., a measure of land (pbsol.) — ML.
bovata, fr. L. bos, gen, bovis, 'ox'. See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 COLUMN:2 -->

## bovine
bovine, adj., pertaining to the ox. — Late L. bo-
vinus, fr. L. bos, gen. bovis, 'ox', which stands for
*g"'6us, and is rel. to Umbr. bum, 'the ox'
(ace.), and cogn. with OHG. chuo, OE. ей,
'cow'. See cow and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see adj. suff. -ine.

## Bovista
Bovista, п., a genus of gasteromycetous fungi. —
ModL., fr. G. Bovist (also Bofist), 'puffbali',
dissimilated fr. earlier vohenfist, fr. MHG. vohe,
'vixen'; see fox. The second -element is cogn.
with OI. picchora, 'pipe, flute', OSlav. piskati,
'to whistle', fr. the I.-E. imitative base *peis-,
'to blow'.

## bow
bow, intr. and tr. v., to bend. — ME. bugen,
bogen, bowen, bugen, fr. OE. bugan, 'to bow
down, stoop, bend, turn; to flee', rel. to OS.
bugan, MLG. bugen, MDu. bughen, Du. buigen,
OHG. biogan, MHG., G. biegen, Goth, biugan,
'to bend', ON. boginn, 'bent', beygja, 'to bend',
Dan. bugne, beie, Swed. buga, bdja, 'to bend*, fr.
I.-E. base *bheug(h)-, 'to bend', whence also OI.
Wm/rfH','bends, thrusts a&tde',bhuktah,'berA' .Base
*bheug(h)-, 'to bend', is identical with base
"bheug-, 'to flee', which prop, meant originally,
'to bend one's course away from a place',
whence Gk. φεύγειν, L. fugere, 'to flee', Lith.
btigstu, bugti, 'to be frightened'. For sense
development cp. OE. bugan, 'to bow down, stoop;
to bend, turn; to flee'. Cp. bow, 'anything bent',
bight, bout, bnxom, akimbo. Cp. also fugitive
and words there referred to.
Derivative: bow, п., inclination of the head.

## bow
bow, п., anything bent; rainbow; weapon. —
ME. bowe, fr. OE. boga, rel. to ON. bogi, OFris.
boga, Du. boog, OHG. bogo, MHG. boge, G.
Bogen, 'bow', and to OE. bugan, etc., 'to bend*,
and cogn. with Ir. fid-bocc, 'wooden bow'. See
bow, 'to bend', and cp. elbow, embow.
Derivatives: bow, intr. v., to use the bow,
bowed, adj., bow-ing, n.

## bow
bow, п., the fore part of a ship. — Of Scand.
origin. Cp. ON. bogr, Dan. bov, Swed. bog,
'shoulder; bow of a ship'. See bough.

## bowdlerize
bowdlerize, tr. v., to expurgate. — Formed with
suff. -ize from the name of Thomas Bowdler,
who in 1818 published The Family Shakespeare,
expurgating from it, according to his own
words, 'whatever is unfit to be read by a
gentleman in a company of ladies'.
Derivative: bowdler-iz-ation, n.

## bowel
bowel, n. — ME. bouel, bouele, fr. OF. boel (F.
boyau), fr. L. botellus, dimin. of botulus,
'sausage', fr. I.-E. base *gwet-, *geut-, 'gut-, 'to
vault', whence also L. gultur, 'throat', Goth.
qipus, OE. cwid, 'belly, womb', ON. kvidr,
'belly', MHG. kutel, G. Kutteln, 'guts, bowels;
tripe; chitterlings'. The above base is a dental
enlargement of base *geu-, 'to bend, curve,
arch'. See 1st cove and cp. botulism, boyau, chit-
terling. Cp. also bitumen, cud, guttural.
Derivatives: bowel, tr. v., bowel(l)-ed, adj.

## bowenite
bowenite, п., a variety of serpentine (mineral.) —
Named after G.T. Bowen, who analyzed it. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
bowe·', п., one who, or that which bows. —
Formed fr. bow, 'to bend', with agential suff. -er.

## bower
bower, п., an anchor carried at the bow of a ship.
— Formed fr. bow, 'the fore part of a ship', with
suff. -er.

## bower
bower, п., cottage. — ME. hour, 'chamber', fr.
OE. bur, rel. to ON. bur, 'chamber', Swed. bur,
'cage', OHG. bur, 'dwelling, chamber', MHG.
bur, 'chamber, cage', G. Bauer, 'cage'. These
words lit. mean 'lodging', and are rel. to ON.
bua, OE. buan, 'to dwell*. See be and cp. boor,
byre. Cp. also next word.
Derivative: bower-y, adj.

## bower
bower, п., the knave in cards. — G. Bauer,
'peasant', fr. MHG. gebure, fr. OHG. giburo,
which is rel. to bur, 'a lodging'. See prec. word.
bowie knife. — Named after its inventor Colonel
James Bowie (1799-1836).

## bowl
bowl, п., a hollow vessel. — ME. bolle, fr. OE.
hol!a,re\. to ON. bolle, OHG. bolla, MHG. bolle,
•a round vessel', G. Bolle, 'bulb', OHG. boldn,
'to roll', fr. I.-E. base *bhel-, 'to swell'. See ball,
'a round body', and cp. boll and the second
element in rocambole.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: bowl-er, п., round felt hat, bowl-y,
adj., bent.

## bowl
bowl, п., a wooden ball. — F. boule, fr. L. bulla,
'bubble*. See bull, 'edict', and cp. bolero.
Derivatives: bowl, tr. v., to roll (bowls); intr. v..
to roll rapidly, bowler (q.v.), bowl-ing, n.

## bowler
bowler, п., one who bowls. — Formed from prec.
word with agential suff. -er.

## bowler
bowler, п., a hard round hat. — Formed with
suff. -er fr. bowl, 'hollow vessel'.

## bowline
bowline, п., a rope used to keep the sail taut
inaut.) — ME. bouline, fr. OF. bouline, which is
of LG. origin. Cp. MDu. boech-llne (whence
Du. boeglijn), 'bowline', and see bow, 'the fore
part of a ship', and line.

## bowls
bowls, n. pi., name of a game. — PI. of bowl, 'a
wooden ball'.

## bowly
bowly, bowry, п., a well with steps leading down
to the water (Anglo-Jnd.) — Hind, 600/1, baort.
'a well'. Cp. OI. vavrah, 'hole, well'.

## bowsprit
bowsprit, п., the spar extending from the bow of
a ship. — ME. bouspret, prob. fr. MLG. bdeh-
sprlt, fr. bach, 'bow' (which is rel. to ON. bogi,
'bow'), and sprit, 'pole' (which is rel. to OE.
spreot, 'pole'). Cp. Du. boegspriet, Dan. bug-
spryd, Swed. bogsprdt, G. Bugspriet. F. beaitpre
is a Dutch loan word. See bow, 'the fore part of
a ship', and sprit.

## bowwow
bowwow, п., and intr. v. — Of imitative origin.

## bowyer
bowyer, п., maker, or seller of bows. — Formed
fr. bow, 'weapon', with suff. -yer.

## box
box, п., the tree. — ME., fr. OE. box, fr. L. buxus
(whence also It. bosso, F. buis), fr. Gk. πυξός,
'box tree', which is perhaps a loan word of
Thraco-Phrygian origin. Cp. next word, bushing,
Buxus, and pyx. Cp. also the second element in
arquebus, blunderbuss. -For the change of Greek
π to b in Latin—which is prob. due to Elruscan
influence—cp. burro, carbasus and sbirro.

## box
box, п., case, chest. — ME., fr. OE. box, orig. 'a
receptacle made of boxwood', fr. L. buxum,
'anything made of boxwood', fr. buxus, 'box
tree'; see prec. word..Cp. MDu. bosse, busse and
OHG. buhsa (whence MHG. buhse, G. Biichse),
which derive fr. VL. *buxcm, contraction of
*buxidem, ace. of buxis, which corresponds to
Classical L. pyxis, 'box of boxwood', fr. Gk.
πυξίς, of s.m., fr. πύξος, 'box tree'. Cp. also
OF. boiste (whence F. boite), which comes fr.
VL. buxida, ace. of buxis. Cp. also Boxing day
and bush, 'metal lining'.

## box
box, a blow. — ME., of uncertain, possibly
imitative, origin.
Derivatives: box, intr. v., boxer (q.v.), boxing, n.

## boxer
boxer, п., a person who fights with his fisls. —
Formed fr. prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## Boxer
Boxer, п., a member of a Chinese secret society.
— Loan translation of Chinese / he ch'iian,
'righteous, uniting fists', a phrase originating in
the misunderstanding of the original name
/ he t'uan, 'righteous harmony band'.

## Boxing day
Boxing day, name given to Dec. 26th. — See box,
'case, chesl'. Dec. 26th was so called from the
custom of distributing on this day the contents
of the Christmas box, i.e. the box (placed in the
church for charity and) opened on Christmas day.

## boxwallah
boxwallah, п., a native peddlar in India (Anglo-
Ind.) — Hind, bakaswalu, a hybrid coined fr.
bakas = English box, 'case', and Hind. suff.
•wala; see wallah. For sense development cp.
Scot, packman, 'peddlar'.
boy.n. — ME. boi, rel. to the OE. PN. Bofa, OFris.
boy, 'a young gentleman', MDu. boeve, Du. boef,
'knave, villain', the OHG. PN. Buobo, MHG.
buobe, G. Bube, 'boy', and in vowel gradationa]
relationship to E. babe, baby (qq.v)
Derivatives: boy, tr. and intr. v.,boy-hood,n.,
boy-ish, adj., boy-ish-ly, adv., boy-ish-ness,n.,
boy-ism, n.

## boyar
boyar, п., a member of an order in Russian
aristocracy. — Russ. boyarin, fr. bojt, 'struggle', in
gradational relationship to OSlav. bijg, biti,
'to strike', bid, 'whip', Russ. 61/0, 'mallet', fr.
I.-E. base *bhei-, 'to cut'. See bill, 'sword'.

## boyau
boyau, п., trench; zigzag. — F., lit. 'gut, bowel',
fr. L. botellus, 'a little sausage', dim. of botulus.
See bowel and cp. botulism,

## boycott
boycott, tr. v., to combine in refusing to deal

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BRAB | 92 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 COLUMN:1 -->
with. — Fr. Captain Charles Boycott, landagent
at Lough-Mask in the county of Mayo, Ireland,
who was the first to be so treated (in 1880).
Derivatives: boycott, п., boycott-age, п., boy-
cott-er, n.

## brab
brab, п., the Palmyra tree. — Corruption of Port.
brava (which is short for palmeira brava, 'wild
palm'), fem. of bravo, 'wild', fr. L. barbarus.
See brave.

## brace
brace, п., clasp, buckle. — ME. brace, fr. OF.
brace, brasse, 'the two arms' (whence F. brasse,
'fathom, armful'), fr. L. brachia, 'the arms', pi.
(of the neut. noun brachium) mistaken for a fem.
sing, noun, fr. Gk. βραχέων, 'arm', which
derives fr. βραχύς, 'short', and prop, means 'that
which is shorter (than the forearm)'. See brachy-
and cp. bracelet, brachial, brassard, braza,
embrace, bretzel, and the second element in vam-
brace.

## brace
brace, tr. v., to encompass. — ME., fr. OF. bra-
cier, 'to embrace', fr. brace, 'the two arms'. See
brace, 'clasp'.
Derivatives: brac-ing, n. and adj.

## brace
brace, п., горе attached to the yard of a vessel
(naut.) — From F. bras in bras de vergue, 'tackle
for trimming a yard', fr. L. brachium, 'arm'. See
brace, 'clasp'.

## bracelet
bracelet, n. — OF. (= F.), formed with the
double dimin. sun", -elet, fr. braz (F. bras),
'arm'. Bracelet lit. means 'a little arm'. See
brace, 'clasp, buckle', -el and -et.
Derivative: bracelet-ed, adj.

## bracer
bracer, п., armor for the arm {archaic). — ME.,
fr. OF. brasseure, formed fr. braz (F. bras),
'arm' (see brace, 'clasp, buckle'), with sun", -cure,
ure, which was changed in English to -er.

## brach
brach, п., a bitch hound (archaic). — ME. brache,
'a scenting hound', fr. OF. brache, which is of
WTeut. origin; cp. MDu. bracke, OHG. brac-
cho, MHG., G. bracke, 'hound, setter'. It.
bracco, Proven?, brae, of s.m., are Teut. loan
words; F. braque is borrowed either fr. Italian
or fr. Provencal. The above Teut. words are
rel. to MHG. brsehen, 'to smell', and cogn.
with L. fragrare, 'to smell sweetly'. See
fragrant.

## brachet
brachet, п., a little brach. — F. bracket, 'scenting
hound', dimin. of OF. brache. See prec. word
and -et.

## brachi-
brachi-, form of brachio- before a vowel.

## brachial
brachial, adj., pertaining to the arm. — L. bra-
chtalis, fr. brachium, 'arm'. See brace, 'clasp',
and adj. suff. -al.

## brachiate
brachiate, adj., having branches arranged in
pairs. — L. brachiatus, 'having branches thai
resemble arms', fr. brachium, 'arm*. See brace,
'clasp', and adj. suff. -ate.

## brachio-
brachio-, before a vowel brachi-, combining form
meaning 'arm' (anal.) — Gk. βραχιο-, βραχι-,
fr. βραχίων, 'arm'. See brace, 'clasp'.

## brachy-
brachy-, combining form meaning 'short'. — Gk.
βραχύ-, fr. βραχύς, 'short', which is cogn. with
L. brevis, 'short'. See brief, adj. and cp. brace,
'clasp'. Cp. also the second element in
amphibrach, tribrach.

## brachycephalic
brachycephalic, also brachycephalous, adj., short-
headed (anthropometry). — Formed fr. brachy-,
Gk. κεφαλή, 'head' and suff. -ic, resp. -ous. See
cephalic. Cp. Gk. βραχυκέφαλος, name of a fish,
lit. 'short-headed'. The word was first used in
anthropometry by the Swedish anthropometrist
Magnus Gustaf Retzius (1842-1919).

## brachylogy
brachylogy, п., a concise phrase or expression,
brevity in speech. — Gk. βραχυλογίδ, 'brevily
in speech', compounded of βραχύς, 'short', and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See brachy- and -logy.

## bracken
bracken, п., a coarse fern. — ME. broken, prob.
of Scand. origin. Cp. Swed. broken, 'fern', and
see brake, 'a fern'.

## bracket
bracket, n. — F. braguetle, 'codpiece', dimin. of
brague, 'breeches', a loan word fr. OProven?.
braga, 'clout', in the pi. bragas, 'breeches', fr.
L. braca, pi. bracae, 'breeches', whence also It.
brache (pi.), 'trousers', Catal., Sp., Port, braga,
'clout', in the pi. bragas, 'breeches', F. braie,
'clout', in the pi. braies, 'breeches'. See breeches'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 COLUMN:2 -->
and cp. brail.
Derivatives: bracket, tr. v., bravkei-ing, n.

## brackish
brackish, adj., salty, fresh. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ish fr. obsol. brack, 'salty", fr. MDu. brae,
'salt water' (whence Du. brak water, G. Brack-
wasser, Swed. brakvatten, Dan. brakvand); fr.
I.-E. base *bher-, 'to cut', whence also E. bore,
'to pierce' (q.v.)
Derivative: brackish-ness, n.

## bract
bract, п., a small leaf at the base of a flower
(bot.) — L. bractea, 'a thin metal plate', of
uncertain origin. The correct form is brattea.

## bracteal
bracteal, adj., pertaining to bracts. — Formed fr.
L. bractea (see prec. word) with adj. suff. -al.

## bracteate
bracteate, adj., having bracts (bot.) — L. brac-
teatus, 'covered with thin plates', fr. bractea. See
bract and adj. suff. -ate.

## brad
brad, п., a small wire nail. — ME. brod, 'spike,
headless nail', fr. ON. broddr, of s.m., which is
rel. to OE. brord, 'point; spire of grass', OHG.
brort, 'point; edge; crown'. Cp. broider, prod.

## bradawl
bradawl, n. — Compounded of brad and awl.

## Bradbury
Bradbury, п., an English treasure note for £ 1
or 10s., signed by John Bradbury, secretary to
the Treasury.

## brady-
brady-, combining form meaning 'slow'. — Gk.
βράδυ-, fr. βραδύς, 'slow', which stands for
*g">rdus and is cogn. with Lith. gurdiis, 'tardy,
negligent', Lett, gufds, 'tired'.

## brae
brae, п., slope, river bank (Scot.) — ON. bra,
'eyelash', rel. to OE. brxw, 'eyelid', OFris. bri,
'eyebrow', OHG. brawa, 'eyebrow', orig.
'eyelash, eyelid', MHG. bra(we), G. Braue,
'eyebrow', Goth, brahaugins, 'moment', fr. I.-E.
base *bherek-, 'to shine', whence also OE. breg-
dan, 'to move quickly, brandish; to weave'. See
braid. E. brow is not related to brae.

## brag
brag, intr. v. — ME. braggen, fr. OF. braguer,
'to brag', fr. brague, 'bragging', which is of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: brag, п., braggart (q.v.),bragg-er,
п., bragg-ing, adj., bragg-ing-ly, adv.

## braggadocio
braggadocio, п., a braggart. — A hybrid coined
by Edmund Spenser (1552-99) in his Faerie
Queen, fr. E. brag, and It. pejorative suff. -occio.

## braggart
braggart, п., a boaster; adj., boastful. — OF.
bragard, fr. braguer. See brag and -ard.

## bragite
bragite, п., a variety of fergusonite (mineral.) —
Named after Brage, the Norse god of poetry.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Brahma
Brahma, Brahamaa, п., ι) the impersonal world
soul; 2) the chief member of the trinity Brahma,
Vishnu and Siva (Hindu religion). — OI.
brahman- (neut.), 'prayer, the universal soul, the
Absolute' (in this last sense exceptionally treated
as masculine), Brahman (masc), 'the chief god
of Hindu religion', of uncertain origin; possibly
related to OI. brhdnt-, 'high', fr. I.-E. base
'bhergh-, 'high'. See borough.
Derivatives: Brahma-hood, п., Brahma-ic, adj.,
Brahman, n. (see next word)

## Brahman
Brahman, п., a member of the highest priestly
caste among the Hindus. — OI. brahmana-, fr.
brahman-, 'prayer'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: Brahman, adj., Brahman-ic, adj.,
Brahman-ism, п., Brahman-ist, п., Brahman-ist- ·
ic, Brahman-y, adjs.

## Brahmanee
Brahmanee, Brahmaul, п., a Brahmin woman. —
OI. brahmani, fem. of brahmana-. See prec. word.

## brahmapootra
brahmapootra, usually shortened to brahma, п.,
name of a large species of fowl. — From
Brahmaputra, name of the great river in India.

## Brahmin
Brahmin, n. — A var. of Brahman.

## braid
braid, tr. v. — ME. breiden, braiden, fr. OE. breg-
dan, 'to move quickly, brandish; to weave', rel.
to ON. bregda, 'to brandish, turn about, braid',
OS. bregdan, 'to weave', Du. breien, 'to knit',
OHG. brettan, MHG. bretten, 'to draw, weave,
braid'. The orig. meaning of these words was
'to move suddenly to and fro'. They ult. derive
fr, I.-E. base *bherek-, 'to shine', whence also
OI. bhrdiate, 'flames, blazes, shines', Gk. φορκός,
'white, gray'. Cp. brae, bream, a fish, bridle,
broider, upbraid. Cp. also bright and words
there referred to.
Derivatives: braid, п., braid-ed, adj., braid-ing,n.

## Braidism
Braidism, п., hypnotism. — Named after
James Braid in Manchester (died in i860). For

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 COLUMN:3 -->
the ending see suff. -ism.

## Braidist
Braidist, п., a hypnotist. — See prec. word and
-1st.

## brail
brail, п., горе used for hauling in a sail before
furling. — ME. brayle, fr. OF. braiel, 'breech
girdle', fr. braie, 'breeches', fr. L. bracale, of
s.m., fr. braca, pi. bracae, 'breeches'. See
breeches and cp. braeket.
Derivative: brail, tr. v., to haul in with the
brails (usually with up).

## Brallie
Brallie, braille, п., system of writing for the
blind. — Named after the inventor Louis Braille
(1809-52), himself blind from the age of three,
and teacher of the blind.
Derivatives: Braille, braille, tr. v., Braill-ist,
braill-ist, n.

## braia
braia, n. — ME., fr. OE. brmgen, rel. to MLG.
bregen, OFris., Du. brein and cogn. with Gk.
βρεχμος (also βρεγμός, βρέγμα, βρέχμα,
βρόχους), the front part of the head'.
Derivatives: brain, tr. v., -brain-ed, combining
form; brain-er, п., brain-less, adj., brain-less-ly,
adv., brain-less-ness, п., brain-y, adj.

## braise
braise, tr. v., to cook (meat) slowly in a covered
dish. — F. braiser, 'to stew', fr. braise, 'glowing
charcoal', fr. WTeut. *brasa; cp. It. bragia,
brace, OProveng. and Sp. brasa, which are of
the same origin. See braze and cp. breeze,
'refuse from charcoal or coke'.

## brake
brake, п., a kind of fern. — ME. brake, 'fern'. See
bracken.

## brake
brake, п., an instrument for breaking fiax. —
ME., fr. MLG. brake, 'instrument for breaking
flax', rel. to Du. braak, G. Breche, of s.m., and
to Du. breken, OE. brecan, 'to break'. See break.

## brake
brake, п., a contrivance for retarding or
stopping the motion of a wheel. — From prec. word.
Derivative: brake-age, n.
Bramah press. — Named after its inventor, the
English mechanician Joseph Bramah.

## bramble
bramble, n. — ME. brembil, fr. OE. brsembel,
brembel, fr. earlier brxmel, bremel (the second
b in brambel, brimbel, is intrusive); rel. to Du.
braam, OHG. brama, bramo, MHG. brume,
'thorny bush, bramble', OE. brdm, 'broom (the
plant)', fr. I.-E. base *bher-, 'point, edge; to cut
with a sharp point; to bore, pierce'. See bore
and cp. broom. For the ending see dimin. suff.
-le.
Derivatives: brambl-ed, adj., brambling (q.v.),
brambl-y, adj.

## brambling
brambling, п., the mountain finch. — Formed fr.
bramble with subst. suff. -ing; cp. G. Bramling,
Branding, of same meaning.

## bran
bran, n. — ME., fr. OF. bren (F. bran), which is
of Celtic origin. Cp. brennage.
Derivative: bran, tr. v.

## brancard
brancard, п., a horse litter. — F., 'stretcher, litter',
a Norman loan word with the original meaning
'thick branch', a derivative of branque, the
Norman equivalent of F. branche. See next word
and -ard.

## branch
branch, n. — ME. branche, braunche, fr. OF.
(= F.) branche, fr. Late L. branca, 'paw, claw',
a Gaulish word, which is cogn., with OSlav.
rqka, Lith. ranka, 'hand'. Cp. orank, brank-
ursine, embranchment.
Derivatives: branch, intr. and tr. v., branch-age,
п., branch-ed, adj., branch-er, п., branch-ing, n.
and adj., branch-y, adj.

## branchia
branchia, п., a gill. — L., fr. Gk. βράγχια (pi.),
'gills' (the sing, βράγχιον means 'fin'), rel. to
βρόγχος, 'tracheal artery'. See bronchi and cp.
branchiate.

## Branchiata
Branchiata, n. pi., a name denoting groups of
animals having gills (zool.) — A ModL. hybrid.
See next word.

## branchiate
branchiate, adj., having gills (zool.) — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. βράγχια (see branchia) and adj.
suff. -ate (representing L. -atus).

## branchiform
branchiform, adj., resembling a gill. — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. βράγχια (see branchia) and L.

## forma
forma, 'form, shape' (see form). The correct form
would be branchiomorph (fr. Gk. βράγχια and
μορφή, 'form, shape').

## brand
brand, n. — ME. brand, brond, fr. OE. brand,
brond, 'firebrand, fire, torch, sword' (the
meaning 'sword' is derived from the flashing of the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 93 | BREAST -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 COLUMN:1 -->
blade), rel. to ON. brandr, 'firebrand, blade of
sword', OHG., MHG. brant, OFris. brond, of
s.m., Dan., Swed., Du., G. brand, 'firebrand,
fire'; formed from the base of OE. beornan, etc.,
'to burn'(seeburn,v.), withsuff.-pa( = I.-E. -to).
Cp. OF. brant, 'blade of a sword, sword', It. bran-
do (poet.), 'sword', F. brandon, 'firebrand, torch',
which are Teut. loan words. Cp. also brandish,
brandy, brindled, the first element in brandreth
and the second element in Hildebrand.

## brandish
brandish, tr. v. — ME. braundisen, fr. OF. bran-
diss-, pres. part, stem of brandir, fr. brant,
'blade of a sword, sword'. See brand and verbal
suff. -ish.
Derivatives: brandish, п., brandish-er, n.

## brandliag
brandliag, п., name of a worm. — Formed fr.
brand with suff. -ling; so called from the red
marking.

## brandreth
brandreth, п..gridiron. — ME., fr. ON. brandreid,
'firegrate', compounded of brandr, 'brand' and
reid, 'vehicle'. See brand and ride.

## brandy
brandy, n. — Shortened fr. earlier brandwine,
brandewine, fr. Du. brandewijn, lit. 'distilled
wine', fr. branden, Ίο burn', whence 'to distil',
and wijn, 'wine'. For the first element see burn,
v., and cp. brand, for the second see wine. Cp.
G. Branntwein, 'brandy'. Cp. also Czech paienka,
'brandy', and its equivalents in the oiher Slavic
languages, fr. ptiliii, etc., 'to burn'.
Derivative: brandi-ed, adj.

## brandypawnee
brandypawnee, п., brandy and water (Anglo-
Ind.) — A hybrid coined fr. E. brandy and Hind.
pani, 'water'.

## brangle
brangle, intr. v., to wrangle (archaic). — Prob.
a var. of wrangle. Cp. embrangle.
Derivative: brangle, n.

## branks
branks, n. pi., a sort of bridle; an instrument used
formerly to punish noisy women. — Norm. F.
branques, the equivalent of F. branches,
'branches'. See branch, brancard.

## brank-ursine
brank-ursine, п., the bear's breech (Acanthus
mollis). — Fr. branche ursine, fr. ML. branca
ursina, lit. 'bear's claw', fr. Lale L. branca,
'claw' and fern, of the L. adjective ursinus,
'belonging to a bear'; so called from the shape of
its leaves. See branch and ursine.

## branle
branle, п., an old French dance. — F., fr. branler,
'to shake, swing' (whence ebranler, of s.m.),
shortened form of brandcler, which is rel. to
brandir, 'to wave'. See brandish.

## brannerite
brannerite, п., a complex uranium titanate
(mineral.) — Named after the American geologist
John Casper Branner (1850-1922). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## brant goose
brant goose, also brend goose, п., — Ср. Swed.
brandgds, G. Brandgans, and see brand and goose;
prob. so called from its dark color.

## Brasenia
Brasenia, п., a genus of plants of the walershield
family (hot.) — ModL., a name of uncertain
origin. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## brash
brash, п., rubbish. — Prob. fr. F. breche, 'breach,
breccia', fr. OHG. brehha, 'breach', fr. brehhan,
'to break'. See break and cp. breccia.
Derivative: brash-y, adj.

## brash
brash, п., eructation. — Prob. identical in origin
with prec. word. For sense development cp. G.
brechen, 'to break; to vomit'.

## brass
brass, n. — ME. bres, bras, fr. OE. bnrs, prob.
borrowed from the same Semitic source as L.
ferrum, 'iron'. See farrier and cp. brassie,
brazen.
Derivatives: brass, adj. and tr. v., brass-y, adj.

## brassage
brassage, п., a charge for coining money. — F.,
fr. brasser, 'to slir up, agitate', fr. OF. bracier,
fr. VL. *braciare, fr. L. braces, quoted by Pliny
as a Gaulish word meaning 'spelt'. Cp. W. brag,
'malt'. Cp. also brassery.

## brassard
brassard, brassart, п., armor for the arm. — F

## brassard
brassard, fr. bras, 'arm', fr. L. brachium. See

## b/ace
b/ace, 'clasp', and -ard.

## brasserie
brasserie, п., brewery. — F., fr. brasser, 'to stir

## up
up, agitate'. See brassage and -ery.

## Brassica
Brassica, п., a genus of plants including the
cabbage, the turnip, the mustard, etc. — L.
brassica, 'cabbage'; cp. Gk. βρίσκη (Hesychius),
'cabbage'; of uncertain etymology.

## Brassicaceae
Brassicaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the
cabbage family (hot.) — ModL., formed fr. prec.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 COLUMN:2 -->
word with suff. -aceae.

## brassie
brassie, brassy, п., a wooden club with a brass
plate. — Formed fr. brass with subst. suff. -ie,
resp. -y.

## brat
brat, п., bib, apron. — OE. bratt, 'a covering,
mantle', fr. Olr. or Gael, bratt, 'cloak, cloth'.

## brat
brat, п., child. — Prob. fr. prec. word.
Derivatives: brat-ling, п., bratt-ish, adj.

## bratstvo
bratstvo, п., brotherhood. — Russ., etc., formed
with suff. -stvo (corresponding in meaning to E.
-hood), fr. Russ., Pol., Slovak, brat, etc.,
'brother', which is cogn. with Goth, bropar,
OE. brodor, 'brother'. See brother.

## brattice
brattice, п., a partition. — ME. bretasce,
'bartizan', fr. OF. bretesche (F. breteche, bretesse),
'brattice', fr. ML. (turn's) brittisca, 'British
tower', fr. OE. Brittisc, 'British'. See British and
cp. bartizan.
Derivatives: brattice, tr. v., bratiic-er, п., brat-
tic-ing, n.

## braunite
braunite, п., a basic manganese silicate (mineral.)
— Named after M. Braun of Gotha. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## bravado
bravado, п., ostentatious show of courage. — Sp.
bravata, bravada, fr. It. bravata, 'boast, bluster',
whence also F. bravade, E. bravado was
influenced in form by the erroneous analogy of
Spanish words ending in -ado, as e.g. renegado.
See next word.
Derivative: bravado, intr. v.

## brave
brave, adj. — F., fr. It. bravo, orig. meaning
'wild, savage', fr. L. barbarus, 'foreigner'
(through the intermediate forms *brabarus,
*brabus); with change of meaning from 'wild'
to 'courageous'. See barbarian and cp. brah.
Derivatives: brave, п., brave, v. (q.v.),
bravery, n.

## brave
brave, tr. v., to defy; intr. v., to boast. — F.
braver, 'to dare, defy', fr. brave. See brave, adj.
Derivatives: braver, п., brav-ing, n.

## bravo
bravo, п., brigand. — It. bravo, fr. L. barbarus.
See brave, adj.

## bravo
bravo, interj., well done!; п., the shout 'bravo'. —
It. bravo, 'the brave man', used in applauding
actors, etc.; the fern, form brava is used in
applauding a woman, the pi. bravi in applauding
several people. See brave, adj.

## bravoitc
bravoitc, п., an iron sulfide containing nickel
(mineral.) — Named after Jose J. Bravo, of
Lima, Peru. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## bravura
bravura, п., ι) boldness, spirit; 2) in music, a
brilliant passage. —It., 'bravery, spirit', formed
fr. bravo, 'courageous, brave', with suff. -ига.
See brave, adj., and -ure.

## brawl
brawl, intr. v. — ME. braulen, 'to scold, quarrel',
fr. braule, 'scold, quarrel', rel. to Du. and LG.
brallen, 'to brag'.
Derivatives: brawl, п., brawl-er, п., brawl-ing, n.

## brawn
brawn, n. — OF. braon, braion, 'piece of flesh*,
which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. bralo, 'tender
meat' (whence—with sense influenced by the
unrelated MHG. braten, G. braten, 'to roast'—
MHG. brute, G. Braten, 'roast'), ON. brad, 'raw
meat', OE. brxd, 'flesh'.
Derivatives: brawn, tr. and intr. v., brawn-ed,
adj., brawn-ed-ness, п., brawn-er,a.,brawn-y, adj.

## braxy
braxy, п., a disease of sheep. — Prob. rel. to OE.
brsec, 'rheum', prop, 'a breach', from the stem
of brekan, 'to break'. See break.

## bray
bray, tr. v., to crush. — ME. braien, fr. OF. breier
(F. broyer), 'to crush, pound', fr. W. Teut. *bre-
can, 'to break', whence also OProvenc. bregar.
See break.

## bray
bray, intr. v., to utter a cry (said esp. of the ass).
— ME. brayen, fr. OF. braire, 'to cry' (whence
F. braire, 'to bray'), fr. VL. 'bragire, 'to whine,
cry' (whence also OProvenc. braire, 'to cry,
sing'), which prob. derives from the Celtic
imitative base *brag-, 'to cry'. Cp. Gael, braigh-,
'to shriek, crack, crackle'.
Derivatives: bray, п., bray-er, n.

## braza
braza, п., a Spanish measure of length, fathom.
— Sp., fr. L. brachia (pi. of brachium, 'arm'),
taken as a fern. sing. Cp. F. brasse, 'fathom', and
see brace, 'clasp'.

## braze
braze, tr. v., to solder. — F. braser, 'to solder,
braze', fr. braise, 'glowing charcoal'. See braise
and cp. brazier, 'a pan for holding hot coals;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 COLUMN:3 -->
brazil, breeze, 'cinders', embracer, 'one who
attempts to corrupt a jury', embrasure.

## braze
braze, tr. v., to cover with brass. — OE. brsesian,
fr. brses, 'brass'; see brass. Cp. the verb glaze,
from the noun glass.

## brazea
brazea, adj. — ME. brasen, fr. OE. brsesen, 'of
brass; bold', fr. brses, 'brass'. See brass and adj.
suff. -en.
Derivative: brazen, tr. v.

## brazier
brazier, п., one who works in brass. — ME. bra-
siere, fr. bras. See brass and -ier.

## brazier
brazier, п., a pan for holding hot coals. — F.
brasier, fr. braise, 'glowing charcoal'. See braze,
'to solder'.

## brazil
brazil, brazilwood, п.,— ME. brasil, fr. Sp. or Port.
brasil, name for a red dye-wood from the East
Indies, fr. F. bresil, of s.m., a derivative of OF.
breze (whence F. braise), 'glowing charcoal',
which is of Teut. origin. See braze, 'to solder'.
The wood was called brasil from its emberlike
color.

## Brazil
Brazil, n. — The country was so called from the
brazilwood found in it.

## brazilite
brazilite, п., a variety of baddeleyite (mineral.) —
So called because found in Brazil. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## breach
breach, n. — ME. breche, partly fr. OE. bryce,
'a breaking', which is rel. to brecan, 'to break',
partly fr. F. breche, fr. OHG. brehha, 'a
breaking', fr. brehhan, 'to break'. See break.
Cp. G. Bresche, 'breach', which was reborrowed
fr. F. breche. Cp. also breccia and brush,
'rubbish'.
Derivatives: breach, v., breach-er, п., breach-y,
adj.

## bread
bread, n. — ME. breed, brede, fr. OE. bread,
'morsel, crumb, bread', rel. to OS. brod, ON.
braud, Dan. bred, Swed. brad, OFris. brad, MDu.
brot, broot, Du. brood, OHG., MHG. brot, G.
Brot, fr. Teut. 'brauda, lit. 'bread leavened with
barm'; cogn. with Thracian Gk. βρϋτος (βρούτος
in Hesychius), βρϋτον, 'fermented liquor made
from barley', L. dg-frutum, 'must boiled down'.
These words are formed with the I.-E. pp. suff.
-to fr. base *bhreu-, *bhru-, 'to boil, ferment',
whence also OE. briowan, ON. brugga, Ίο
brew'. See brew and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: bread, tr. v.

## breadth
breadth, п., — ME. bredethe, formed on the
analogy of ME. lenglhe, etc., fr. OE. brSdu,
'breadth', fr. brad, 'broad'. See broad and subst.
suff. -th.

## break
break, tr. and intr. v. — ME. breken, fr. OE.
brecan, rel. to OS. brecan, OFris. breka, Du.
breken, OHG. brehhan, MHG., G. brechen,
Goth, brikan, and cogn. with L. frangere, past
tense fregi, 'to break', OI. (giri)-bfiraj, 'breaking
forth (out of the mountains)', fr. I.-E. base
*bhreg-, 'to break'. A parallel base *bheg-
appears in OI. bhandkti, 'he breaks'. Arm. be-
kanem, Ί break', bek, 'broken', Olt. com-boing,
'he breaks'. The disappearance of the r in this
secondary base is prob. due to the nasalization
of the base. Cp. brake, 'instrument for breaking
flax', brake, 'contrivance for stopping motion',
brash, braxy, bray, 'to crush', breaeh, breck,
brick, bricole, brioche, brook, n. Cp. also
fraction and words there referred to.
Derivatives: break, п., break-able, adj., break-
agen, п., breaker (q.v.), break-ing, n.

## breaker
breaker, п., one who, or that which, breaks. —
Formed fr. break with agential suff. -er.

## breaker
breaker, п., a small cask. — Sp. barrica, 'cask.
See barrel and cp. barricade.

## breakfast
breakfast, n. — Prop, 'the meal that breaks the
fast. Cp. F. dejeuner, 'to breakfast', fr. L. dis-
jejunare, 'to break the fast' (see dejeuner, dinner).

## bream
bream, п., a fish. — ME. breme, brem, fr. F.
breme, fr. OF. braisme, fr. Frankish 'brahsima,
which is rel. to OHG. brahsima, of s.m.; prob.
fr. Teut. base 'brehwan, 'to shine', which is rel.
to I.-E. *bherek-, 'to shine, be white'. See braid.

## bream
bream, tr. v., to clean a ship's bottom. — Du.
brem, 'furze, broom'. See broom.

## brenst
brenst, n. — ME. brest, fr. OE. briost, rel. to OS.
briost, ON. brjost, OFris. briast, and to OFris.,
OHG., MHG., G. brust, MLG., MDu., Du.
borst, Goth, brusts, 'breast', and cogn. with Mir.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:121 COLUMN:1 -->
bruasach, 'having a broad, strong breast', Olr.
bruinne (for *bhrusm'o-), 'breast', brft (for
*bhrus6-), 'abdomen, belly'; fr. I.-E. base
*bhreus-, 'to swell'. Cp. brisket, browse.
Derivatives: breast, tr. and intr. v., breasi-ed,
adj., breast-er, п., brecist-ing, n.

## breastsummer
breastsummer, п., a large beam. — Compounded

## breath
breath, n. — ME. breeth, breth, fr. OE. brxp, breb,

MHG. bradem, G. Brodem, 'breath, steam', fr.
I.-E. base bher-, 'to boil'. See brew and cp.

Derivatives: breath-less, adj., breath-less-ly,
adv., breath-less-ness, п., breath-y, adj.

## breathe
breathe, intr. and tr. v. —ME. brethen,U. breth.

## breba
breba, п., fig of the first crop. — Sp. breva.

compounded of bis, 'twice', and ferre, 'to bear,

## breccia
breccia, п., a rock composed of angular pieces
(petrogr.) — It., 'a kind of marble consisting of
angular pieces', fr. OHG. brecha, 'a breaking',
whence also F. breche. See breach.

## Brechites
Brechites, п., a genus of mollusks (zool.) —
ModL.,'fr. Gk. βρέχειν, 'to wet', which is cogn.
with Lett, ynerguot, 'to rain softly', merga, "a soft
rain', Russ. rnorosil', 'to rain softly'. Cp.

## breck
breck, п., a breach (obsol.) — Related to break
(qv.)

## bred
bred, past tense and pp. of breed. — ME. bredde,
bred(d), fr. OE. bredde, resp. gebred(tl), past
tense, resp. pp. of bredan, 'to breed'. See breed.

## bredbergite
bredbergite, п., a variety of iron garnet (mineral.)
— Named after E.G.Bredberg, who analyzed
it. For the ending see subst. sufF. -ite.

## brede
brede, tr. v., to roast (obsol.) — OE. brSedan, 'to

there referred to.

## brede
brede, п., breadth (dial.) — OE. brSdu, 'breadth',
rel. to brad, 'broad'. See broad.

## brede
brede, tr. and intr. v., to broaden (dial.) — OE.

OS. brldian, ON. breida, Du. ver-breden, OHG.,
MHG., G. breiien, Goth, braidjan, 'to broaden',
and see broad.

## breeches
breeches, n. pi. — ME. brech, fr. OE. brec, pi. of

Swed., Norw. brok, Du. broek, OHG. bruoh,
MHG. bruoch, G. Brucli, 'breeches'; of
uncertain etymology. L. brdca, pi. bracae, 'breeches',
is a Gaulish word borrowed fr. Teut. Cp.
bracket, brail, brogue, 'shoe'.
Derivatives: breech, tr. v., breech-ed, adj.,
breech-ing, n.

## breed
breed, tr. and intr. v. — ME. breden, fr. OE. bre-
den.'io cherish, keep warm, nourish', rel. to Du.
broeden, OHG. bruoten, MHG. briieten, G. brii-
ten, 'to brood, hatch', fr. I.-E. base *bher-, 'to

Derivatives: breed, п., breed-er, п., breed-ing, п.,
brecd-y, adj.

## breeze
breeze, п., a light wind. — F. brise, prob. fr. Sp.
brisa, 'north-east wind'; not related to F. bise,
'dry and cold north wind' (see bise).
Derivatives: breeze, intr. v., breez-y, adj., breez-
i-ly, adv., breez-i-ness, n.

## breeze
breeze, п., refuse from charcoal or coke. — F.
braise, 'cinders, live coal'. See braise.

## bregma
bregma, п., front part of the head (craniometry).
— Gk. βρέγμα, 'front part of the head', rel. to
βρεχμός, of s.m., and cogn. with OE. brxgen,
'brain'; see brain. The name bregma was
introduced into craniometry by the French surgeon
and anthropologist Paul Broca (1824-80).
Derivatives: bregm-ate, bregm-atic, adjs.

## brehon
brehon, п., one of a class of judges in ancient
Ireland. — Ir. breitheamh, fr. Olr. brithem, gen.
brithemon, 'judge*, fr. breth, 'a bearing;
judgment', which is rel. to biru, Ί bear', and cogn.
with L. ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to
carry'.

## hreislakite
hreislakite, η , a variety of amphibole (mineral.)
— Named after the Italian geologist S.Breislak
(1748-1826). For the ending see subst. sun", -ite.

## breithauptite
breithauptite, n,, nickel antimonide (mineral.) —
Named after the German mineralogist J. F.A.
Breitlmupt (1791-1873). For the ending see
subst. stiff, -ite.

## brelan
brelan, п., name of a gambling game. — F. bre-
lan, fr. OF. brelens, pi. of brelenc, 'table,
gambling lable', whence 'a kind of gambling game',
fr. OHG. bretling, 'small plank', dimin. oibret,
