For the etymology of OHG. bret see board,
'table', for the ending see suff. -ling.

## breloque
breloque, п., a charm for a watch chain. — F.,
a word of imitative origin. Cp. berloque.

## breme
breme, adj., famous (obsol.) — ME., fr. OE.
breiue, "famous'.

## Brengun
Brengun, п., often shortened to brea. — Coined
from the first two letters of Brno, a city in
Czechoslovakia, and the first two letters of
Enfield near London. The patent for the gun was
purchased in Brno; the gun was manufactured
at Enfield.

## brennage
brennage, п., payment made in bran to feed the
lords' hounds (feudal law). — OF. brenage, fr.
bren, 'bran'. See bran and -age.
brent goose. — See brant goose.

## Brenthis
Brenthis, п., a genus of butterflies (entomol.) —
ModL., lit. 'the arrogant (insect)', fr. Gk.
βρενβος, 'pride, arrogance', which is of
uncertain origin.
bressummer. — See breastsummer.

## bretelle
bretelle, п., strap, braces. — F., fr. OHG. brittil,
'bridle', which is rel. to bridel, of s.m. See
bridle.

## brethren
brethren, n. — Archaic pi. of brother.

## Breton
Breton, adj. and n. — F. See Briton and cp. the
first element in next word.

## Bretwalda
Bretwalda, п., a title given to some of the earlier
Anglo-Saxon kings. — OE., lit. 'ruler of the
Britons'. See Breton and wield and cp. the first
element in Walter and the second element in
Oswald.

## breve
breve, п., ι) a writ or brief (law); 2) a curved line
(~) placed over a vowel 10 indicate its shortness
(gram.); 3) a note equal to two whole notes or
the sign for it (|σ|) (mus.) — In the legal sense, fr.
ML. breve, 'letter', prop. neut. of the L. adjective
brevis, 'short'; in the grammatical sense, fr. F.
breve, prop. fern, of bref, 'short', used as a noun,
fr. L. brevis; in the musical sense, fr. It. breve,
which also derives fr. L. brevis. See brief, adj.
and n.
Derivative: breve, tr. v. (obsol.), to write down.

## brevet
brevet, п., a commission giving an army officer
nominal higher rank. — F., dimin. of bref,
'brief, document'. See brief, п., and -et and cp.
prec. word.
Derivative: brevet, tr. v.

## brevi-
brevi-, combining form meaning 'short'. — L.
breve-, fr. brevis, 'short'. See brief, adj.

## breviary
breviary, п., a short prayer book used by priests
in the Roman Catholic Church. — L. brevia-
rium, 'summary*, neut. of the adjective brevi-
arius, 'abridged', used as a noun, fr. breviare,
'to shorten, abbreviate', fr. brevis, 'short'. See
brief, adj., and subst. suff. -ary and cp. brevet,
abbreviate. Cp. also brimborion.

## brevier
brevier, п., a size of small type, between
bourgeois and minion (typogr.) — Lit. 'the breviary
type' (cp. G. Brevier, 'breviary'); so called
because this type was used originally in printing
breviaries.

## breviped
breviped, adj., having short feet. — Compounded
of L. brevis, 'short', and pes, gen. pedis, 'foot*.
See brief, adj., and pedal.

## brevipennate
brevipennate, adj., having short wings. —
Compounded of L. brevis, 'short', and penna, 'wing'.
See brief, adj., and pennate.

## brevity
brevity, п., shortness of time. — L. brevitas,
'shortness', fr. brevis, 'short'. Cp. F. briivete,
of s.m., fr. L. brevitatem, ace. of brevitas. See
brief, adj., and -ity.

brew, tr. and intr. v. — ME. brewen, fr. OE. bre-
owan, rel. to OS. breuwan, ON. brugga, Dan.
brygge, Swed. brygga, Norw. brugga, bryggja,
OFris. briitwa, MDu. brouwen, bruwen, Du.

brouwen, OHG. briuwan, MHG. bruwen,

## brewster
brewster, п., a brewer. — Formed fr. brew with
suff. -ster. The word denoted orig. a female
brewer.

## briar
briar, n. — See brier.

## Briareus
Briareus, п., a hundred-handed giant (Greek

ήπυος, 'loud-shouting'), whence also βρΤ&ύς,

## bribe
bribe, n. — OF. bribe, 'crumb, piece of bread', esp.

brick, n. — F. brique, 'brick', fr. MDu. bricke,

bridegroom, n. — ME. brudgume, bridegome, fr.

OE. brydguma, rel. to OS. brudigumo, ON. Ьгйд-

gumi, OHG. brutigomo, MHG. briutegome, G.

## bridewell

## bridge

## bridge

## Bridget
Bridget, fem. PN. — From Ir. Brighid, name of

## bridle
bridle, n. — ME. bridel, fr. OE. bridel, brigdels,

## bridle

Derivatives: bridl-ed, adj., bridl-er, п.,

## bridoon
bridoon, п., snaffle and reins of a military bridle.
— F. bridon, dimin. of bride, 'bridle'. See bride,
'loop'.

## Brie cheese
Brie cheese, often shortened to brie. — From
Brie, name of a district in the department Seine-
et-Marne in France, renowned for its cheese.

## brief
brief, adj., short in duration. — ME. bref, fr.
OF. (= F.) bref, fr. L. brevis, 'short', which
prob. stands for *mregh-w-i-s, brehvis, and is
cogn. with Sogdian murzak, 'short', the first
element in Avestic merezu-]iti, 'shortlived', Gk.
βραχύς (for I.-E. mrghus), 'short', Goth. *maur-
gus, 'short' (only in the compound gamaurgjan,
'to shorten'), OHG. murg, murgi, 'short', OE.
myrge, 'pleasing, delightful, merry'; see merry,
adj. For sense development cp. G. Kurzweil,
'pastime', lit 'a short time'. Cp. brief, n. Cp.
also brachio-, brachy-, brace, 'clasp', brevet,
brevi-, breviary, brevier, brevity, brnme,
abbreviate, abridge.

## brief
brief, п., a summary. — ME. bref, fr. OF. (= F.)
bref, fr. ML. breve, prop. neut. of L. adj. brevis,
'short', used in the sense of 'short writing, letter,
document'. Cp. It. breve, of s.m., G. Brief,
'letter'. See brief, adj., and cp. breve.
Derivatives: brief, tr. v., brief-less, adj., brief-
less-ly, adv., brief-less-ness, п., briefly, adv.

## brier
brier, briar, п., a prickly plant. — ME. brere, fr.
OE. Ъгэег, brer.

## brier
brier, briar, п., heath. — F. bruyire, 'heather,
heath', fr. VL. *brficaria, 'brugaria, fr. brucus,
'heather', a word of Gaulish origin. Cp. Olr.
fmech (for *vroiko-s), 'heath', which is cogn.
with Gk. έρείκη, έρίκη (for *Γερείκα), 'heath',
Lith. vifzis, Russ. veres, of s.m. Cp. also brisk,
brusque, Erica.

## brig
brig, п., a two-masted square-rigged vessel. —
Abbreviation of brigantine.

## brigade
brigade, n. — F., fr. It. brigata, fr. brigare, 'to
fight', fr. briga, 'strife', which is of Gaulish
origin. Cp. Gael, brigh, W. bri, 'power'. Cp. also
brigand.
Derivatives: brigade, tr. v., brigadier, n. (q.v.)

## brigadier
brigadier, п., an officer commanding a brigade.—
F., fr. brigade. See prec. word.

## brigand
brigand, п., bandit. — F., fr. It. brigante, fr.
brigare, 'to fight'. See brigade.
Derivatives: brigand-age, n. (fr. F. brigandage),
brigander, п., brigandine (q.v.), brigand-ish, adj.,
brigand-ish-ly, adv., brigand-ism, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:122 COLUMN:2 -->

## brigandine
brigandine, п., body armor. — F., fr. It. brigan-
rina, fr. brigare, 'to fight'. See prec. word.

## brigantine
brigantine, п., a two-masted square-rigged ship.
— F. brigantin, fr. It. brigantino, 'piratical (lit.
'fighting') vessel', fr. brigante 'brigand'. See
brigand.

## bright
bright, adj. — ME. briht, fr. OE. beorht, bryht,
rel. to OS. berht, ON. bjartr, Norw. bjerk, OHG.
berafit, MHG. birht, Goth, bairhts, 'bright', fr.
I.-E. base 'bhereg-, 'to shine, be white', whence
also OI. bhrajate, 'shines, glitters', Lith. breksta,
brekiti, 'to dawn', W. berth, 'bright, beautiful'.
Cp. birch. Cp. also Bertha, the first element in
Bardolph, Bertram, and the second element in
Albert, Cuthbert, Egbert, Ethelbert, filbert,
gilbert, Herbert, Hubert, Lambert, Robert. I.-E. base
"bhereg- is rel. to base *bherek-, 'to shine, be
white'; see braid and cp. words there referred to.

## Bright's disease
Bright's disease, chronic nephritis. — So called
after the English physician Richard Bright (17Я9-
1858), who first described this disease (in 1827).

## Brigit
Brigit, fem. PN. — From Ir. Brighid, name of the
Irish fire goddess. See Bridget.

## brill
brill, п., a flat fish allied to the turbot. — Cp. Co.
brilli, 'mackerel', contracted fr. brithelli, lit.
'streaked'.

## brilliance
brilliance, brilliancy, n. — Formed fr. next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## brilliant
brilliant, adj. — F. brillont, lit. 'shining*, pres.
part, of briiler, 'to shine', fr. VL. *beryllare, 'to
shine like a beryl', fr. L. beryllus, fr. Gk. βή-
ρυλλος, 'beryl'. See beryl and -ant.
Derivatives: brilliant, п., brilliant-ly, adv., bril-
liant-ness, n.

## brilliantine
brilliantine, п., an oily liquid used to make the
hair glossy. — F. brillantine, fr. brillant,
'shining'. See prec. word.

## brim
brim, n. — ME. brimme, brim, rel. to ON. barmr,
MHG. brem, 'bordering edging', Late MHG.
verbremen, G. verbrdmen, 'to border, edge',
OHG. bramberi, MHG. bramber, G. Brom-
beere, 'bramble,blackberry',OE. brum,'broom'.
All these words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*bhre-m-, 'edge, point; to bore, pierce', an
enlargement of base *bher-, of s.m., whence berm,
board, 'table', board 'side of a ship', bramble,
broom.

## brimborion
brimborion, п., nonsense. — F., 'knick-knack,
bauble, gewgaw', fr. earlier briborion, breborion,
fr. Eccles. L. breviarium, 'breviary'. See breviary.

## brimmer
brimmer, п., a vessel filled to the brim. — Formed
fr. brim with suff. -er.

## brimstone
brimstone, n. — ME. brinston, brenston, fr. brin-
nen, 'to burn', and ston, 'stone', hence the word
lit. means 'burnstone'; rel. to ON. brennisteinn,
'brimstone'. See burn and stone.
Derivative: brimston-y, adj.

## brindisi
brindisi, п., a rhymed toast. — It., fr. G. (ich)
bring' dir's, lit., '(I) bring it to you', used in the
sense of Ί drink your health'. Cp. G. jemandes
Gesundheit ausbringen, 'to drink one's health'.

## brindled
brindled, adj., streaked with a dark, esp. brown or
tawny, coIot. — Formed—prob. after kindled—
fr. archaic brinded, fr. ME. brended, which is rel.
to brand.

## brine
brine, n. — ME., fr. OE. bryne, rel. to MDu. brine
(whence Du. brijn).
Derivatives: brine, tr. v., brin-er, n.

## bring
bring, tr. v. — MR bringen, fr. OE. bringan, rel.
to OS. brengjan, OFris. brenga, MDu. brenghen,
Du. brengen, OHG. bringan, MHG., G. bringen,
Goth, briggan, fr. Teut. base *bhrenk-. Outside
Teut. cp. W. he-brnwg, 'to send', MCo. hem-
bronk, 'we lead'.
Derivative: bring-er, n.

## brinjarry
brinjarry, also binjarree, п., a dealer in grain and
salt (Anglo-lnd.) — Hind, banjara, lit. 'one who
carries on trade', fr. OI. vanijyi, 'trade, traffic'
(fr. vanij, 'merchant'), and karah, 'doer', which
is rel. to krnoti, 'he does, makes, accomplishes'.
See Sanskrit and cp. Oiatnar. The word brinjarry
was influenced in form by Pers. birinj, 'rice'.

## brink
brink, n. — ME. brink, of Scand. origin. Cp.
Dan. brink, 'steepness, brink, precipice', ON.
brekka, 'projection, slope', which are rel. to
MDu. brink, 'edge, shore'. All these words
derive fr. 1-Е. base 'bhreng-, 'to project', whence

## also Lith. brinkti
also Lith. brinkti, 'to swell'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:122 COLUMN:3 -->

## brio
brio, п., vivacity. — It., of uncertain origin,
perhaps aphetic for L. ebrius, 'drunk, intoxicated'.
See ebrious.

## brioche
brioche, п., a kind of bun. — F., a derivative of
brier, 'to knead the dough', Norman form of
broyer, 'to grind, pound', which comes fr.
WTeut. *brekan, 'to break'. See break,

## briquette
briquette, п., brick made of coal dust. — F.
briquette, dimin. of brique. See brick and -ette.

## brisance
brisance, п., shattering effect of explosives. —
F. brisance, fr. brisant, pres. part, of briser, 'to
break, smash, shatter', fr. VL. brisare, a word of
Gaulish origin; cp. Olr. brissim, Ί break', brisc,
'brittle', Bret, bresk, of s.m.; fr. I.-E. base
*bhres-, 'to break, crush, crumble'. See bruise,
and cp. debris. For the ending see suff. -ance.

## brisk
brisk, adj. — A doublet of brusque (q.v.)
Derivatives: brisk, tr. and intr. v., brisk-en, tr.
and intr. v., brisk-ly, adv., brisk-ness, n.

## brisket
brisket, п., animal's breast. — ME. bruskette, rel.
to MHG. brusche, G. Brausche, 'bruise on the
head', ON. brjosk, Dan. brusk, 'gristle', and to
E. breast (q.v.) F. brechet (fr. earlier brichet,
bruchei) is an English loan word.

## brisling
brisling, bristling, п., a small seafish resembling
sardines. — Of uncertain origin.

## brisqne
brisqne,n., a card game. — F., of uncertain origin.

## bristle
bristle, n. — ME. brustel, brostle, bristel, formed
with dimin. suff. -il, -el, -le, fr. OE. byrst,
'bristle', which is rel. to OS. bursta, ON. burst, Du.
borstel, OHG. burst, MHG., G. borste, 'brush,
bristle', and cogn. with OI. bhrstih, 'point, spike',
and prob. also with h.fastlgium (for *farsllgium),
'top, summit', Lith. barSstis, 'carrot'. Cp. bur.
Cp. also bar, 'maigre', harse, bass, 'perch', beard,
'device for cleaning'. Cp. also fastigiate.
Derivatives: bristle, intr. v., bristl-y, adj.

## brisure
brisure, п., a break in the direction of a parapet
(fort.) — F., fr. briser, 'to break'. See
brisance and -иге.

## brit
brit, п., sing, and pi., the young of the herring. —
Dial. Co., prob. meaning lit. 'speckled', and
rel. to Co. bruit, 'speckled''.

## Brit
Brit, Brett, п., a Briton; adj., British (English
hist.) — OE. Bret (pi. Brettas), of Celtic origin.
Cp. British, Briton, Brython.

## Britain
Britain, n. — ME. Bretayne, Breteyne, fr. OF.
Bretaigne (F. Bretagne), fr. L. Britannia, earlier
Briltania, fr. Britanni, resp. Brittani, 'Britons',
fr. Britto. See Briton.

## Britannic
Britannic, adj. — L. Britannicus. See Britain,
Briton. For the ending see suff. -ic.

## b'rith
b'rith, brith, n. — Variant spellings of berith.

## British
British, adj. — OE. Brettisc, Bryttisc, fr. Bret.
See Brit and adj. suff. -ish.
Derivative: British-er.

## Briton
Briton, n. — ME. Breton, fr. OF. (= F.) Breton,
fr. L. Brittonem, лес. of Britto, a member of the
tribe of the Britons. E. Briton corresponds to
Britd, an erroneous variant of L. Britto. See
Brit and cp. Breton.

## brittle
brittle, adj. — ME. brutel, britel, fr. OE. breotan,
'to break', rel. to ON. brjdta, Swed. bryta, 'to
break', OHG. brodi, 'fragile'.
Derivatives: brittle-ly, adv., brittle-ness, n.

## britska
britska, britzka, п., a long, open carriage. — Pol.
bryczka, prob. fr. It. biroccio. See barouche.

## Briza
Briza, п., a genus of plants of the family Poaceae
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βρίζα, name of a kind
of rye.

## broach
broach, n. — ME. broche, fr. OF. (= F.) broche,
'spit; spindle', fr. VL. brocca, prop. fem. of L.
broccus, 'projecting' (said esp. of teeth) a word of
Celtic origin; cp. Olr. brocc, Co., W.broch,
'badger'. Cp. also brocade, brocatel, broccoli,
brochure, brock, brocket, broker, brooch. Cp.
also bronco.

## broach
broach, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) brocher, fr. broche.
See broach, n.
Derivative: broach-er, n.

## broad
broad, adj. — ME. brod, fr. OE. brad, rel. to QS.,
OFris. bred, ON. breidr, Dan., Swed. bred,
Norw. breid, brei, MDu. breet, breed, Du. breed,
OHG., MHG., G. breit, Goth, braips; of
uncertain origin. Cp. breadth.
Derivatives: broad, п., broad-en, intr. and tr. v.,
broad-ly, adv., broad-ness, n.

## broadloom
broadloom, adj., woven on a wide loom. — Com-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:123 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BROBOINGNAG | 96 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:123 COLUMN:1 -->
pounded of broad and loom.

## Brobdingnag
Brobdingnag, 'the Land of giants'. — Coined by
Jonathan Swift (1667-1745) in his Gulliver's
Travels.
Derivatives: Brobdingnag-lan, adj. and n.

## brocade
brocade, п., a rich figured, woven fabric. — Sp.
brocado, fr. broca, fr. ML. broccare, 'to prick,
emboss', fr. L. broccus, 'projecting' (said esp.
of teeth). Cp. It. broccato, F. brocarl, and see
broach, n. For the ending see suff. -ade.
Derivatives: brocade, tr. v., brocad-ed, adj.

## brocard
brocard, п., a law maxim. — F. brocard, fr. ML.
brocardus, of s.m., fr. Brocardus, fr. Burchardus,
G. Burckard, bishop of Worms, who in the 1st
half of the 1 ith cent, compiled an ecclesiastical
canon.

## brocatel
brocatel, brocatelle, п., a heavy, figured silk used
in upholstery. — F. brocatelle, fr. It. broccatello,
dimin. of broccato, 'brocade'. See brocade.

## broccoli
broccoli, п., a kind of cauliflower. — It., pi. of
broccolo, 'sprout*, dimin. of brocco, 'stalk,
splinter', which is rel. to F. broche, 'spit;
spindle'. See broach.

## broch
broch, п., a prehistoric round tower in the North
of Scotland. — Fr. ON. borg. Sec borough.

## brochantlte
brochantlte, п., a hydrous basic copper sulfate
{mineral.) — Named after the French
mineralogist Brockant de Villiers (1772-Г840). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## brochure
brochure, п., a small pamphlet or tract. — F., 'a
small book stitched and covered with a
wrapper', fr. brocher, 'to stitch (a book, etc.)'. See
broach, v. and п., and -ure.

## brock
brock, п., a badger. — OE. broc, of Celtic origin.
Cp. Gael, and Ir. broc, W., Co., Bret, broch,
'badger', and see broach.

## brocket
brocket, п., a stag two years old. — ME. broke!,
fr. F. brocard, 'fallow deer a year old', a dialectal
word formed from broque, 'tine of an antler'
(corresponding to OF. broche, 'something
pointed; spit; tine of a antler'), with suff. -ard. The
name refers to the small spike of the horn. See
broach, n.

## broggerite
broggerite, п., a crystallized variety of pitchblende
(mineral.) — Named after the Norwegian
mineralogist Waldemar Christofer Brogger (1S5I-
1940). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## brogue
brogue, п., a kind of rough shoe worn by the
Irish. — Gael, and Ir. brog, fr. ON. brok, 'hose'.
See breeches.

## hrogue
hrogue, п., accent. — Prob. fr. Ir. barrog, 'a hold',
esp. 'a hold on the tongue'.

## broider
broider, tr. v., to embroider (archaic). — F. bro-
der, fr. OF. brosder, fr. Frankish *brozdon,
which is rel. to Lombardic *brustan (whence
It. brustare), 'to embroider', and to OE. brord,
'point; spire of grass'. See brad and cp.
embroider.
Derivatives: broider-er, п., broider-y, n.

## broil
broil, tr. and intr. v., to fry. — ME. broilen, fr.
AF. broiller, fr. OF. broueillier (F. brouiller), 'to
mix together, embroil, confuse', which is prob.
a blend oibreu, brou, 'broth' (whence F. brouet,
'thin brolh, brewis'), and fooillier (whence F.
fouiller), 'to rummage, ransack'. OF. breu, brou,
is of Teut. origin. Cp. MLG. broien, MDu.
broeyen, MHG. briieyen, briien, G. bruhen, 'to
scald', ME. breie, MDu. broeye, Du. brut,
MHG. briieje, G. Bruhe, 'broth', fr. I.-E. base
*bheru-, *bhreu-, *bhru-, 'to boil, ferment'. See
brew and cp. brewis, broth. Cp. also broil, 'to
confuse'. F. fouiller derives fr. VL. *fodiculare,
fr. L. fodicare, freq. offodere, 'to dig'. See fosse.
Derivatives: broil, п., broll-er, п., broil-ing, adj.

## broil
broil, tr. v., to confuse (obsol.); intr. v., to
quarrel. — F. brouiller, 'to mix together, confuse'.
See broil, 'to fry', and cp. embroil, imbroglio.
Derivative: broil-er, n.

## broke
broke, past tense of break. — ME. broke, from
the pp. brokein). See broken.

## broke
broke, archaic pp. of break; adj. (slang),
penniless, bankrupt. — See prec. word.

## broke
broke, intr. v., to deal (rare). — Back formation
fr. broker.
Derivative: brok-ing, n.

## broken
broken, pp. of break. — ME. broke(n), fr. OE.
brocen, pp. of brekan, 'to break'. See break.
Derivatives: broken-ly, adv., broken-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:123 COLUMN:2 -->

## brolly
brolly, п., an umbrella (slang). — Corruption of
umbrella.

## brokenhearted
brokenhearted, adj. — Compounded of broken,
pp. of break, and -henrted; first used byTyndale.
Derivatives: brokenhearted-ly, adv., broken-
hearted-ness, n.

## broker
broker, n. — AF. brocour, fr. ONF. brokeor,
Sr. ONF. brokier, 'to broach', lit. 'to open a
cask of wine", fr. ML. broccare, fr. L. broccus,
'projecting' (said esp. of teeth); see broach, n.
The broker was orig. 'a broacher of wine casks',
whence developed the meanings 'wine retailer;
retailer; second-hand dealer; agent'.
Derivatives: broker-age, п., broker-y, n. (obsol.)

## brom-
brom-, form of bromo- before a vowel.

## broma
broma, п., food. — ModL., fr. Gk. βρώμα, 'food',
which is rel. to βορά, 'food', βιβρώσκείν, 'to eat,
eat up, devour', fr. I.-E. base *gwor-, *gwer-,
whence also L. vorax, gen. vorucis, 'hungry,
greedy'. See voracious and cp. Abroma, Bromus,
Broslmum, anabrosis.

## bromal
bromal, п., a colorless, oily fluid, CBr3COH
(chem.) — Abbreviation of bromine and alcohol.

## bromate
bromate, п., a salt of bromic acid (chem.) — See
brom- and chem. suff. -ate.

## brome
brome, п., also brome grass. — Gk. βρόμος, 'wild
oats'. See Bromus.

## Bromelia
Bromelia, п., a genus of American plants {hot.) —
ModL., named after the Swedish botanist Olaf
Bromel (1639-1705). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Bromeliaceae
Bromeliaceae, n. pi., the pineapple family (hot.)
— Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## bromic
bromic, adj., pertaining to, or containing,
bromine (chem.) — Formed fr. bromine with suff.
-ic.

## bromide
bromide, п., a compound of bromine (chem.) —
See bromine and -ide.
Derivatives: bromid-ic, adj.,bromidic-aHy,iA\.

## bromine
bromine, п., name of a nonmetailic element
belonging to the halogen family (chem.)—Formed
with chem. suff. -ine fr. F. brome, 'bromine',
which was coined by its discoverer, the French
chemist Antoine Jerome Balard (1802-76) fr.
Gk. βρωμος, 'noisome smell (see bromo-); so
called by him in allusion to the unpleasant odor
of the fumes.
Derivatives: bromin-ate, tr. v., bromin-ation, п.,
bromin-ism, п., bromism.

## bromism
bromism, п., bromine poisoning (med.) — See
bromine and -ism.

## bromite
bromite, п., salt of bromous acid (chem.) — See
bromine and chem. suff. -ite.

## bromize
bromize, tr. v., to treat with bromine or a
bromide. — See bromine and -ize.
Derivatives: bromiz-ation, п., bromiz-er, n.

## bromo- before a vowel brom-
bromo- before a vowel brom-, combining form
meaning 'containing bromine'. — Gk. βρωμο-,
βρωμ-, fr. βρώμος, more exactly βρόμος,
'noisome smell', identical with βρόμος, 'any loud
noise', which is rel. to βρέμειν, 'to clash, roar',
βροντή (for *βρομ-τϊ), 'thunder', fr. *brem-, a
variant of I.-E. base *bhrem-, whence L. fre-
mere, 'to roar, resound, murmer, W. brefu, 'to
roar', OHG. breman, MHG. bremen, MHG., G.
brummen, 'to growl, buzz', OE. brimsa, OHG.
bremo, brimissa, G. Breme, Bremse, 'horsefly,
gadfly', OI. bhramardh, 'bee'. Cp. Brontes, Bron-
tosaurus. Cp. also fremitus.

## Bromus
Bromus, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. bromos, fr. Gk. βρόμος, 'wild oats', which
is prob. related to βρώμα, 'food', βιβρώσκειν,Ίο
eat, eat up', βορά, 'food'. See broma and cp.
brome.

## bronchia
bronchia, n. pi., the bronchial tubes (anat) —
Late L. bronchia, gen. -drum, fr. Gk. βρόγχια,
fr. βρόγχος, 'windpipe'. See bronchus,

## bronchiole
bronchiole, п., a minute bronchial tube (anat.) —
Medical L. bronchiola, a diminutive coined by
E.Schultz fr. L. bronchia (pi.), 'the bronchial
tubes'; see broachia. Cp. Joseph Hyrtl, Ono-
matologia anatomica, p. 557·
Derivative: bronchiol-ar, adj.

## bronchiolitis
bronchiolitis, п., inflammation of the bronchioles
(med.) — Medical L. formed fr. bronchiola with
suff. -itis. See prec. word.

## bronchitis
bronchitis, п., inflammation of the bronchial tubes
(med.) — Medical L., coined by Charles Bed-
ham in 1808 fr. bronchus and suff. -itis;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:123 COLUMN:3 -->
introduced into medicine by P.Frank in his Inter-
pretationes Clinicae in 1812.

## broncho-
broncho-, before a vowel bronch-, combining form
denoting relation to the bronchi. — Gk. βρόγχο-,
βρογχ-, fr. βρόγχος, 'windpipe'. See next word.

## bronchus
bronchus, п., each of the two forked branches of
the windpipe. — Medical L., fr. Gk. βρόγχος,
'windpipe', which is prob. rel. to βρόχ&ας,
'throat', ϊβροξε (aor.), 'he swallowed up',
βράγχιον, 'gill', and cogn. with Olr. bragae,
'neck', W. breuant, 'throat, gullet', Lith. gur-
klys, 'crop, maw', ME. crave, 'craw'. See craw
and cp. branchia. The above words prob.
derive fr. I.-E. base *g№rogh-, a -^-enlargement
of base *gwer-, 'to devour', whence Gk. βορά,
'food', βρώμα,'food', L. vorare. See voracious
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: bronchi-al, adj., bronchi-al-ly, adv.

## bronco
bronco, п., a rough horse of Western North
America. — Sp. bronco, 'rough', fr. VL. *bruncus,
'block, log, lump', which seems to be a blend
of L. truncus, 'trunk of a tree', and broccus,
'projecting'. See trunk and broach.

## Brontes
Brontes, п., one of the Cyclopes (Greek mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. Βροντής, fr. βροντή, 'thunder'.
See bronto-.

## bronto-
bronto-, before a vowel bront-, combining form
meaning 'thunder'. — Gk. βρόντο-, βροντ-, fr.
βροντή (for *βρομ-τα), 'thunder', which is rel.
to βρόμος, 'any loud noise',· βρέμειν, 'to clash,
roar'. See bromo- and cp. Brontes and the first
element in Brontosnurus.

## Brontosaurus
Brontosaurus, п., a genus of American dinosaurs
(paleontol.) — ModL., coined fr. Gk. βροντή,
'thunder', and σαϋρος, 'lizard'. See bronto- and
saurian.

## bronze
bronze, n. — F., fr. It. bronzo, bronzino, ult. fr.
Persian birinj.
Derivatives: bronze, tr. and intr. v. (cp. F. bron-
zer), bronze, adj., bronz-ify, tr. v. (rare),
bronzing, п., bronz-ite, n. (mineral.), bronz-y, adj.

## brooch
brooch, n. — A var. of broach.
Derivative: brooch, tr. v.

## brood
brood, n. — ME. brod, fr. OE. brad, lit. 'that
which is hatched out by warmth', rel. to Du.
broed, MHG. bruot, G. Brut, 'brood', and to
MLG. broien, MDu. broeyen, MHG. briieyen,
briien, G. bruhen, 'to scald'. See brew and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: brood, v. and adj., brood-er, п.,
brood-ing, adj., brood-ing-ly, adv., brood-y, adj.
and n.

## brook
brook, п., a small stream of water. — ME. broc,
fr. OE. broc, rel. to LG. brok, Du. broek,
OHG. bruoh, MHG. bruoch, G. Bruch, 'marshy
ground', and to E. brenk. Brook orig. denoted
'that which breaks out of the earth'.
Derivative: brook-y, adj.

## brook
brook, tr. v., to endure. — ME. bruken, fr. OE.
brucan, 'to enjoy', rel. to OS. brukan, OFris.
Ьгйка, OHG. bruhhan, MHG. briichen, G. brau-
chen, Goth, brukjan, 'to use', L. fruor, frui, 'to
enjoy', whence fruclus, 'enjoyment, the means
to enjoyment, produce, fruit'. See fruit,

## brookite
brookite,п., titanium dioxide (mineral.)— Named
after the English mineralogist Henry James
Brooke (1771-1857). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## broom
broom, n. — ME. brome, fr. OE. brom, rel. to Du.

## iraam
iraam,'blackberry', OHG. brSma.bramo, MHG.

## brame
brame, 'broom (the plant)', OHG. bramberi,

## MHG. bramber
MHG. bramber, G. Brombeere, 'blackberry';
fr. I.-E. base *bher-, 'point, edge; to cut with a

## sharp point
sharp point, to bore, pierce'. See bore, 'to pierce',

## and cp. bramble
and cp. bramble, bream, v., brim. For the sense

## development of broom cp. brush
development of broom cp. brush, scrub.
Derivatives: broom, tr. v., broom-er, п., broom-

## y
y, adj.

## brose
brose, n. — The same as brewis.
Derivative: bros-y, adj.

## Brosimum
Brosimum, п., a genus of trees of the mulberry
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βρώσιμος,
'edible', rel. to βρώμα, 'food', βιβρώσκειν, 'to

## eat
eat, eat up, devour'. See broma.

## broth
broth, n. — ME., fr. OE. brod, rel. to OHG. brod,
fr. Teut. base *brauda-, lit. 'anything leavened',
cogn. with Thracian Gk. βρϋτος (βροϋτος in

## Hesychius)
Hesychius), βρϋτον, 'fermented liquor made

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:124 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 97 | BUCCAL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:124 COLUMN:1 -->
from barley, beer', L. defrutum, 'must boiled
down', Mir. embruthe, 'broth', bruith, 'to boil',
ModW. brwd, 'hot', ModBret. broud, of s.m.;
fr. I.-E. base *bhreu-, *bhru-, 'to swell', which
is enlarged fr. base *bher-, 4o boil'. See brew
and cp. bread, brood.

## brothel
brothel, n. — ME. brothel, 'worthless person,
prostitute', derived, fr. OE. broden, pp. of
Ьгёодап, 'to destroy'; confused in meaning with
OF. bordel, 'hovel' (for which see bordel).

## brother
brother, n. — ME., fr. OE. brodor, rel. to OS.
brothar, ON. brddir, Dan., Swed. broder, OFris.
brother, MDu., Du. broeder, OHG., MHG. bru-
oder, G. Bruder, Goth, bropar, and cogn. with
OI. bhratar-, Avestic bralar-, Toch. A pracar,
В procer, Arm. eibayr (in Armenian, br became
lb), Gk. φράτηρ, φράτωρ, 'member of a clan',
L. /rater, 'brother', Oscan fratrum, fratrom, 'of
the brothers' (pb gen.), OSlav. bratru, bratu,
'brother', Russ., Pol., Slovak brat, Czech bratr,
OPruss. brati, brote (voc.), 'brother', bratnkai,
'brothers', Lith. broterelis, 'little brother',
whence—through back formation—brolis, Lett.
bralis (voc), 'brother', Olr. brathir, OW.
broder, W. brawd, Bret, brew, 'brother'. Cp.
bratstvo, fraternal, friar, phratry. Cp. also pal.
Derivatives: brother, tr. v., brother-ly, adj. and
adv., brother-li-ness, n.

## Brother Jonathan
Brother Jonathan, a sobriquet for the United
States. — Generally derived fr. Jonathan
Trumbull, governor of Connecticut (1740-1809), to
whom George Washington often referred as
Brother Jonathan.

## brougham
brougham, п., a closed four-wheeled carriage. —
Named after the first Lord Brougham (1778-
1868).

## brought
brought, past tense and pp. of bring. — ME.
brought(e) fr. OE. brohte (past tense), resp. ge-
brdht (pp.), fr. bringan, 'to bring'. See bring.

## brow
brow, n. — ME. browe, fr. OE. bru, rel. to ON.
brun, 'brow', and cogn. with OI. bhrah, Toch.
A parwam (dual), Avestic brvat-, ModPers. abru,
bru, Gk. όφράς, OSlav. bruvl, Lith. bruvis,
'brow', OPruss. wubri (metathesis fr. *brwi),
Olr. bru, 'edge', Mir. bruad, 'brow'. OE. brxw,
'eyelid', is not related to brow (see brae).

## brown
brown, adj. — ME. broun, fr. OE. brun, rel. to
ON. brunn, Dan., Swed. brun, OS., OFris.,
OHG., MHG. brun, MDu. bruun, Du. bruin,
G. braun, 'brown', and cogn. with Russ. bron,
'while, variegated', Gk. φρϋνος, φρδνη, 'toad',
(prop, 'the brown animal'). These words have
been enlarged—with -и-formative element—
from I.-E. base *bher-, 'shining, brown', whence
also Lith. beras, Lett, bfrs, 'brown', OE. bera,
'bear' (prop, 'the brown animal'), OE. be(o)for,
'beaver' (lit. 'the brown animal'). See bear, the
animal, beaver and cp. brnin, brunette, brunis-
sure, Bruno, burnet, burnish, Pruaella.
Derivatives: brown, n. and tr. and intr. v.,
brownie (q.v.), brownish, adj.

## brownie
brownie, п., a good-natured goblin. — Formed
fr. brown with dimin. suff. -ie; so called from its
supposed color.

## Browning
Browning, also browning, n. — Named after its
inventor John M. Browning (1855-1926).

## browse
browse, tr. and intr. v., to feed on; to graze. —
From the obsolete noun browse, 'shoots, twigs'
(often used as cattle food), fr. MF. broust
(whence F. brout), 'sprout, shoot' (whence MF.
brouster, F. brouter, 'to browse'), fr. OF. brost,
of s.m., fr. Teut. *brustjan, 'to bud', lit. 'to swell',
fr. I.-E. base 'bhreus-, 'to swell'. See brenst.
Derivatives: brows-er, п., brows-ing, n.

## brucine
brucine, п., a poisonous alkaloid found in the
seeds of nux vomica (chem.) — Named by the
English naturalist Sir Joseph Banks (1743-1820)
after the Abyssinian traveler James Bruce (1730-
94). For the ending see chem. suff. -iae.

## brucite
brucite, п., magnesium hydroxide (mineral.) —
Named after the American mineralogist A.
Bruce. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## brugnateUite
brugnateUite, п., a hydrous ultrabasic carbonate
of magnesium and iron (mineral.) — Named
after the Italian mineralogist Luigi Brugnatelli
(1859-1928). For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## bruin
bruin, n,, name of the bear in fairy tales. — Du.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:124 COLUMN:2 -->
bruin, 'brown'. See brown. For sense
development see bear, the animal.

## bruise
bruise, tr. and intr. v. — ME. brisen, brusen, a
blend of OE. brysan, 'to crush, bruise', and OF.
bruisier, 'to break'. Both OE. brysan and OF.
bruisier derive fr. I.-E. base 'bhreus-, *bhres-,
'to break, crush, crumble', whence also Olr.
bronnaim (for *bhrusndmi), Ί wrong, hurt', bris-
sim, "I break', brisc, 'brittle', Bret, bresk, of
s.m., brezef, 'war', VL. brisare, 'to break', a
word of Celtic origin (whence F. briser, of s.m.),
Mir. bruim, Ί crush', OE. berstan, OS., OHG.
brestan, etc., Ίο burst', and prob. also L.
frustum (fr. *bhrus-to-), 'piece', Alb. bresen, 'hail'.
Cp. I.-E. 'bhrousmen, whence OS. brosma,
OHG. brosama, brosma, MHG. broseme, bros-
me, G. Brosam, Brosame, 'crumb'. Cp. debris,
debrnise. Cp. also burst. Cp. also frustum.
Derivatives: bruise, п., bruis-er, п., bruis-ing, n.

## bruit
bruit, п., noise; rumor (archaic). — F. 'noise',
orig. pp. of bruire, 'to rustle, rumble', used as a
noun. F. bruire derives fr. VL. *brugere, which
is a blend of L. rugire, 'to roar', wilh VL. "bra-
gere, 'to whine, cry' (whence F. braire, 'to bray'
(see bray, 'to cry'). L. rugire (whence VL. *ru-
gere), 'to roar', is cogn. with Gk. έρυγεΐν, 'to
bellow, roar', ορυμαγδός, 'a loud noise', ρύζειν
(for *ρύγιειν), 'to growl, snarl', OSlav. rykati,
ryknpli, 'to roar, bellow', OE. ryn (for 'ruhjan),
OHG. rohdn, of s.m.
Derivatives: bruit, tr. v., bruit-er, n.

## Brumaire
Brumaire, п., name of the second month of the
French revolutionary calendar (lasting from
October 23rd to November 21st). — F., lit., 'the
foggy month', coined by Fabre d'Eglantine in ,
1793 fr. brume, 'fog', fr. L. bruma. See brume
and -aire.

## brumal
brumal, adj., pertaining to winter. — L. brumulis,
fr. bruma, 'winter'. See brume and adj. suff. -al.

## brume
brume, п., mist, fog. — F., 'mist, fog', fr. L.
bruma, 'winter', lit. 'the shortest day of the year',
contraction of 'brevima, *breuma, superl. of
brevis, 'short'. See brief, adj.

## brummagem
brummagem, adj., counterfeit; cheap and showy;
п., anything cheap and showy. — A vulgar var.
of Birmingham, orig. meaning 'any article made
at Birmingham'.

## brumous
brumous, adj., misty, foggy. — F. brumeux (fem.
brumeuse), fr. brume, 'mist, fog'. See brume
and -ous.

## brunch
brunch, п., breakfast and lunch combined. —
A blend of breakfast and lunch,

## brunette
brunette, п., a woman with dark hair and eyes. —
F., fem. of brunet, 'brownish', dimin. of brun,
'brown', of W. Teut. origin; cp. OHG. bruno,
'brown' and see brown. OProvenc. brun, It.
bruno, 'brown', are of the same origin. For the
ending see suff. -ette. Cp. burnet.

## brunissure
brunissure, п., a plant disease characterized by
the browning of the leaves (plant physiol.) — F.,
lit. 'a browning', formed with suff. -lire fr.
bruniss-, pres. part, stem of brunir, 'to brown',
fr. brun, 'brown' See prec. word.

## Brunnichia
Brunnichia, п., a genus of vines of the buckwheat
family (bot.) — ModL., named after M.T.Brun-
nich, a Norw. naturalist of the 18th cent. For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## Bruno
Bruno, masc. PN. — OHG., lit. 'brown', fr. brun,
'brown'. See brown.

## brunt
brunt, n. — ME., of uncertain origin.
Derivative: brunt, tr.v.

## brush
brush, п., shrubs. — ME. brusche, fr. OF. broche,
broce, brosse, 'brushwood; brush' (whence F.
brosse, 'brush', in the pi. brasses, 'brushwood',
and broussaille, 'brushwood'), fr. VL. *bruscia,
'shoots of a plant', fr. L. bruscum, 'excrescence
of the maple tree', which is prob. cogn. with
Gk. βρύειν, 'to swell', βρύον, 'moss'. See bryo-
and cp. the next three words.

## brush
brush, п., implement used for cleaning. — ME.
brusshe, fr. OF. broisse, brosse (F. brosse),
'brush'; of the same origin as prec. word. The
usual derivation of E. brush in the above sense
fr. Teut. *burstja, 'bristle' (see bristle) cannot
be accepted, owing to the fact that the first
brushes were made not of bristle, but of coach-
grass, brier, and other plants. For sense
development cp. broom, scrub.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:124 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative^brush-y, adj.
'brush, tr. v., to use a brush on. — ME. bruschen,
brusshen, fr. brusche. See prec. word,

## brush
brush, intr. v., to hurry; to rush. — ME. bruschen,
'to rush', prob. fr. MF. brosser, 'to go through
underbrush', fr. brosse, 'brush'. See brush,
'shrubs'.
Derivative: brush, a short, quick fighl.

## brusque
brusque, adj., rough. — F., fr. It. brusco, 'rough,
sharp, not ripe', orig. a noun meaning 'butcher's
broom'; a blend of L. ruscum, of s.m., and VL.
'brucus, 'heath, heather'. See brier, 'heath', and
cp. brisk, which is a doublet of brusque.
Derivatives: brusque, tr. and intr. v., brusque-ly,
adv., brusque-ness, n.

## brut
brut, adj., dry (said of wines, esp. of champagne).
— F., 'raw, crude'. See brute.

## brntal
brntal, adj. — See brute and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: brutal-ity, п., brutal-ize, tr. v.

## brute
brute, n. — F. brut, fem. brute, 'raw, crude', fr.
L. brutus, 'heavy, dull, stupid', which is cogn.
with Lett, griits, 'heavy', OI. guruh, Gk. βαρύς,
L. gravis, 'heavy'. See grave, adj., and cp. baro-,
Briarens.
Derivatives: brute, adj., brutal (q.v.), brut-ish,
adj., brut-ish-ly, adv., brut-ish-ness, n.

## bryo-
bryo-, combining form meaning 'moss'. — Gk.
βρύο-, fr. βρύον, 'moss, catkin', rel. to βρύειν,
'to swell', βρυάζειν, 'to swell, teem', εμβρυον,
'young one, embryo', and prob. cogn. with OS.
krud, MDu. cruut, Du. kruid, OHG., MHG. krut,
G. Kraut, 'herb', Goth, quatru, 'stake, prick,
prickle', perh. also with L. veru, 'spit'. Cp.
embryo. Cp. also brush, 'shrubs', the first element
in verumontaaum and the second element in
choucroute, sauerkraut.

## bryology
bryology, п., the study of mosses. —
Compounded of bryo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: bryolog-ical, adj., bryolog-ist, n.

## Bryonia
Bryonia, п., a genus of vines of the cucumber
family (bot.) — L. bryonia, fr. Gk. βρυωνίδ.
See next word and -ia.

## bryony
bryony, п., any plant of the genus Bryonia. —
Gk. βρυωνίδ, 'bryony', fr. βρύειν, 'to swell',
which is rel. to βρύον, 'moss'. See bryo-.

## Bryophyta
Bryophyta, п., a division of plants including the
mosses and liverworts (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of bryo- and Gk. φυτόν, 'plant'. See
-phyte.

## Bryozoa
Bryozoa, n. pi., a class of aquatic animals (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of bryo- and -zoa.

## Brython
Brython, п., a Briton; a Welshman.—W.Brython,
bf the same origin as L. Britto. See Briton, Brit.
Derivatives: Brython-ic, adj. and n.

## bnbaline
bnbaline, adj., pertaining to a certain group of
antelopes. — L. bubalinus, fr. bubalus, 'anle-
lope' (or 'buffalo'). See buffalo and cp. next
word.

## bubalis
bubalis, п., a large kind of antelope. — ModL.,
fr. Gk. βούβαλις, 'an African antelope', which
is rel. to βούβαλος, 'an African antelope;
buffalo'. See buffalo.

## bubble
bubble, intr. and tr. v. — ME. bobelen, of
imitative origin. Cp. Dan. boble, MLG. bubbeln,
Du. bobbelen, 'to bubble'. Cp. also Dan. boble,
Swed. bubbla, Du. bobbel, 'a bubble', E. blob,
and the second element in hubble-bubble. Cp.
also hurble.
Derivatives: bubble, п., bubbl-ing, adj., bubbl-
ing-ly, adv., bubbl-y, adj.

## Bubo
Bubo, п., a genus of owls (ornithol.) — L. bubo,
'owl, horned owl', from the I.-E. imitative base
*bu-. See Buteo.

## babo
babo, п., a swelling in the groin (med.) — Late L.,
fr. Gk. βουβών, 'groin, swelling in the groin',
which is prob. cogn. with OI. gavint, 'groin'.

## bubonic
bubonic, adj., characterized by swelling in the
groin. — See prec. word and -ic.

## bucca
bucca, п., cheek. — L. See next word.

## buccal
buccal, adj., pertaining to the cheek. —· Formed
with adj. suff. -al, fr. L. bucca, 'cheek', from the
I.-E. imitative base *bu-, 'to blow; to swell'. Cp.
Bubo, buckle, bull, 'edict', debouch, disembogue,
embouchure, pocket, poke, 'a bag', pox, puck.
Cp. also the related base *buq-, 'to roar, bark',
in OI. Ьйк-karab, 'lion's roar', bukkati, 'barks',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:125 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BUCCAN | 98 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:125 COLUMN:1 -->
Gk. βύκτης, 'roaring' (said of the wind). Cp.
also bud.

## buccan
buccan, п., a wooden frame for smoking meat. —
F. boucan, 'frame for smoking meat', fr. Tupi
mocaem (so called in a Port, report fr. 1587);
initial b and m are interchangeable in the Tupi
language. See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p.77.
s.v. boucan.

## buccan
buccan, tr. v., to smoke on a buccan. — F. bou-
caner, fr. boucan. See prec. word.

## buccaneer
buccaneer, п., one who smokes meat; a pirate. —
F. boucanier, fr. boucan. See buccan, n.

## buccinal
buccinal, adj., like a trumpet. — See next word
and adj. sulT. -al.

## buccinator
buccinator, п., a flat thin muscle in the cheek
(anat.) — L. bucinator, buccinator, 'trumpeter',
fr. bucinatus, buccinatus, pp. stem of bucinare,
buccinnare, 'to blow the bucina', fr. biicina, buc-
cina, 'crooked horn, trumpet', which stands for
"bou-cana, lit., 'that which is made from (the
horn of) the ox for blowing', fr. bos, gen. bovis,
'ox' (see bovine), and cano, -ere, 4o sing, sound,
blow' (see cant, 'slang of beggars'). OHG.
buchina (MHG. busine, busune, G. Posaune),
'trumpet, trombone' is a loan word fr. L.
bucina. Cp. Posaune.
Derivative: buccinator-y, adj.

## bucco-
bucco-, combining form meaning 'buccal and'. —
Fr. L. bucca, 'cheek'. See buccal.

## Bucellas
Bucellas, also bucellas, п., a white wine. — Named
after Bucellas, a small town near Lisbon.

## Bucentaur
Bucentaur, п., a fabulous monster, half bull, half
man. — Compounded of Gk. βοϋς, gen. βοός,
'ox', and κένταυρος, 'centaur'. See bovine and
centaur.

## Bucephalus
Bucephalus, п., name of Alexander the Great's
favorite horse. — Gk. Βουκέφαλος, lit. 'oxhead',
fr. βοϋς, gen. βοάς, Όχ', and κεφαλή, 'head'. See
bovine and cepbalic.

## Buceros
Buceros, п., the genus of hornbills (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. βούκερως, 'horned like an ox',
compounded of βοϋς, gen. βοός, Όχ', and κέρας,
'horn'. See bovine and cerate-.

## Buchloe
Buchloe, п., a genus of plants of the family Poa-
ceae (hot.) — ModL., lit. 'buffalo grass',
contracted fr. Gk. βούβαλος, 'buffalo', and χλόη,
'young green shoot'. For the first element see
buffalo. The second is related to χλόος, 'greenish-
yellow color', χλωρός, 'greenish yellow'. See
chlorine.

## buchu
buchu, п., leaves of the plant Barosma betulina
and related species (bot.) — Zulu buchu, bucu,
lit. 'mixture'.

## buck
buck, п., the body of a wagon (dial.) — OE. buc,
'body', rel. to ON. bukr, Swed., Norw. buk,
Dan. bug, OFris. buk, MDu. buuc, Du. buik,
OHG. buh, buhhes, MHG. buch, G. Bauch,
'belly, abdomen', fr. I.-E. base *bhou-, *bhu-,
'to swell', whence also boil, 'inflammation'. Cp.
bucket. Cp. also the second element in sillabub,
trabuco, trebuchet. Cp. also bulk, 'size' buire,
burette.

## buck
buck, t.v., to soak in lye. — ME. bouken, rel. to
MLG. biiken (whence Swed. byka, Norw. bykja,
Dan. byge), G. bauchen, beuchen, and to beech
(q.v.); lye was orig. made of beech ashes.

## buck
buck, п., male deer, stag; dandy. — ME. bucke,
fr. OE. bucca, 'he-goaf, bucc, 'male deer', rel.
to OS. buck, MDu. buc, hoc Du. bok, OHG.,
MHG. hoc, G. Bock, ON. bokkr, bukkr.Oan.
buk, and cogn. with Avestic buza, 'buck', Pers.
buz, 'buck, goat', Arm. buc, 'lamb'. Olr. bocc
and W. bwch are prob. Teut. loan words. Cp.
butcher. Cp. also bocking, 'smoked herring', and
the second element in kleeneboc, gemsbok, grys-
bok, spriagbok.
Derivatives: buck, intr. and tr. v., buck-er, п.,
buck-ish, adj., buck-ish-ly, adv., buck-ish-ness,n.

## buckaroo
buckaroo, also buckayro, п., cowboy (W.
American slang). —Corruption of Sp. vaquero,
'cowboy', fr. часа, 'cow', fr. L. масса. See vaccine.

## buck basket
buck basket, п., a laundry basket. — See buck,
'to soak in lye'.

## buckeen
buckeen, п., an Indian woman (in Guiana). —
Formed fr. buck, 'male deer; dandy', with suff.
-eea.

## bucket
bucket, n. — ME., fr. AF. buket, dimin. formed
fr. OE. buc, 'body, belly, pitcher'. See back,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:125 COLUMN:2 -->
'body of a wagon', and -et.
Derivative: bucket, tr. v.

## buckle
buckle, n. — ME. bokel, fr. OF. boucle, 'boss of a
shield' (whence F. boucle, 'buckle, ring'), fr. L.
buccula, dimin. of bucca, 'cheek'. See buccal
and cp. buckler, boucle.
Derivatives: buckle, v. (q.v.), buckl-ed, adj.
buckl-er, n.

## buckle
buckle, tr. v., to fasten with a buckle. — Fr. prec.
word. Cp. F. boucler, 'to fasten with a buckle',
fr. boucle, 'buckle'.

## buckle
buckle, tr. v., to bend. — F. boucler, 'to buckle;
to bulge' (said of a wall). See prec. word.

## buckler
buckler, п., one who, or that which, buckles. —
Formed fr. buckle, 'to fasten with a buckle',
with agential suff. -er.

## buckler
buckler, п., a large shield. — ME., fr. OF. bocler
(whence F. bouclier), fr. boucle, 'boss of a
shield'. OF. bocler lit. means 'that which is
provided with a boss', fr. VL. *buccularis, fr. L.
buccula. See buckle, n.

## buckling
buckling, п., a smoked herring. — G. Buckling,
alteration of MHG. bucking (owing to a
confusion of suff. -ing with -ling) fr. MDu. buckinc
(whence Du. bokking), fr. buc, boc, 'buck'; so
called from its odor. See buck, 'male deer',
bocking.

## buckram
buckram, п., a coarse linen. — ME. bokeram, fr.
OF. boquerant (F. bougran), fr. Bukhara
(Bokhara), name of a town in Turkestan (now the
chief city of Uzbek, U.S.S.R.) Cp. It. bucherame,
OProvenc. bocaram, Sp. bucaran, 'buckram'.
The orig. meaning of these words was, 'linen
brought from, or manufactured in, Bukhara'.

## buckrams
buckrams, п., ramson. — See buck, 'male deer',
and ramson.

## buckwheat
buckwheat, n. — Compounded of dial. E. buck,
'beech', fr. OE. boc (see beech), and wheat (cp.
Dan. boghvede, Swed. bohvete, MDu. boecweit,
Du. boekweit, G. Buchweizeri); so called
because its seeds resemble the nuts of the beech
tree.

## bucolic
bucolic, adj., pertaining to shepherds, pastoral.
— L. bucolicus, fr. Gk. βουκολικός, 'of
herdsmen', fr. βουκόλος, 'herdsman', which is
compounded of βοΰς, gen βοός, 'ox', and -κόλος,
'keeper'. For the first element see bovine. The
second element stands in gradational
relationship to Gk. πέλειν, 'to be; to become', and is
cogn. with L. colere, 'to till (the ground),
cultivate, dwell, inhabit'; see colony. Cp. Mir. bua-
chaill, W. bugail, 'shepherd', which are the exact
Celtic equivalents of Gk. βουκόλος. Ср. also
Gk. αίπόλος (for *αίγ-πόλος), 'goatherd'.
Derivative: bucolic, n.

## bucranium
bucranium, п., an ornament representing the skull
of an ox. — L., fr. Gk. βουκράνιον, 'oxhead',
fr. βοϋς, gen. βοός,· 'ox', and κρανίον, 'skull'.
See bovine and craninm.

## bud
bud, n. — ME. budde, rel. to Du. bot, 'bud', OS.
budil, 'bag, purse', MDu. budel, Du. buidel,
OHG. bulil, MHG. biutel, G. Beutel, of s.m.,
fr. I.-E. base *b(h)u-, 'to swell'. See bnccal and
cp. bnddy. Cp. also bolt, 'to sift'. Cp. also
boil, 'inflammation'.
Derivatives: bud, intr. and tr. v., budd-er, п.,
budd-ing, n.

## Buddha
Buddha, п., incarnation of deified religious
teachers, esp. of Gautama Siddharta (563-483). —
OI. buddhah, 'awakened, enlightened', pp. of
bodhati, budhyate, 'is awake, observes,
understands', fr. I.-E. base *bheudh-, 'to offer, present'.
See bid and cp. bo tree.
Derivatives: Buddh-ic, adj., Buddh-ism, п.,
Buddh-ist, п., Buddh-ist-ic, Buddhist-ic-al, adjs.

## Buddleia
Buddleia, п., a genus of shrubs (bot.) — Named
after the English botanist Adam Buddie (died
in 1715). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## buddy
buddy, п., chum, companion, former soldier (col-
loq.) — Orig. the noun buddy was an
affectionate term for a child and is etymologicauy
identical with the adj. buddy, 'full of buds, resembling
a bud'. See bud and adj. suff. -y.

## budge
budge, intr. and tr. v., to stir, move. — F. bouger,
fr. VL. *bullicare, 'to bubble, boil up, seethe',
hence 'to be agitated, to be in movement', fr.
L. bullire, 'to bubble'. Cp. It. bulicare, 'to.
bubble, seethe', and OProvenc. bolegar, 'to stir,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:125 COLUMN:3 -->
budge', which are of the same origin as F.
bouger, and see boil, v.

## budge
budge, п., a kind of fur. — ME. bouge, 'bag',.fr.
OF. boge, bouge, 'leather bag, wallet', fr. L.
bulga, 'leather wallet'. See bulge and cp. budget.
Cp. also belly.

## budgereegah
budgereegah, п., the Australian parakeet. —
Native Australian.

## budgerow
budgerow, п., a keelless barge (Anglo-Jnd.) —
Hind, bajra.

## budget
budget, n. — F. bougette, 'a little trunk of wood',
dimin. of boge, bouge, 'leather bag, wallet'. See
budge, 'fur', and -et.
Derivatives: budget, tr. and intr. v., budget-ary,
adj., budget-eer, п., budget-er, n.

## budmash
budmash, п., a worthless fellow, rake (Anglo-
Ind.) — A hybrid coined fr. Pers. bad, 'evil',
and Arab, ma'ash, 'means of livelihood', fr.
'dsha, 'he lived'. Cp. the first element in next
word.

## budzat
budzat, п., an evil fellow. — A hybrid coined fr.
Pers. bad, 'evil', and Arab, dhat, 'essence,
person, individual'. Cp. the first element in prec.
word.

## buff
buff, п., a blow; tr. and intr. v., to strike. —
ME. buffe, fr. OF. buffe, 'blow', which is of
imitative origin. Cp. buffet, puff.

## buff
buff, п., skin of the buffalo. — From earlier buffe,
'buffalo, buff', fr. F. buffle, 'buffalo'. To account
for the loss of the ending -le, I would suggest
that it was mistaken for the diminutive suffix
and accordingly dropped.
Derivative: buff, tr. v., to polish with a buff; to
make as smooth as buff leather.

## buffalo
buffalo, n. — Port, bufalo, fr. L. bufalus, a
collateral form of bubalus, fr. Gk. βούβαλος, 'an
African antelope', later 'buffalo', which is prob.
rel. to βοϋς, Όχ'. See bovine and cp. prec. word
and buffle. Cp. also bubaline, bubalis and the
first element in Buchloe.

## buffer
buffer, п., one who, or that which, buffs or
strikes. — Formed from the verb buff, 'to strike'
(see buff, 'a blow'), with agential suff. -er.

## buffer
buffer, п., a device, esp. at the end of a railroad
car. — Derivatively identical with prec. word.
Cp. Puffer of s.m.

## boffer
boffer, п., a fellow. — Orig. identical with buffer,
'one who buffs'; influenced in meaning by
buffoon.

## buffet
buffet, п., a blow. — OF., dimin. of buffe, 'blow'.
See buff, 'blow', and dimin. suff. -et.
Derivatives: buffet, tr. and intr. v., buffet-er, n.

## buffet
buffet, п., refreshment bar. — F. buffet, of
uncertain origin.

## buffle
buffle, n. (obsol.), 1) buffalo; 2) a bufflehead (ob-
sol.) — F., 'buffalo', fr. Port, bufalo. See buffalo.

## bufflehead
bufflehead, п., a small North American duck. —
Compounded of buffle and head.

## buffoon
buffoon, n. — F. bouffon, buffon, fr. It. buffone,
fr. buffa, 'joke, jest, pleasantry', which is rel. to
buffare, 'to blow'; of imitative origin. Cp. buff,
'to blow*. For the ending see suff. -oon.
Derivatives: buffoon, intr. and tr. v.,
buffoonery, n.

## Bufo
Bufo, п., a genus of toads (zool.) — L. bufo, 'a
toad', an Osco-Umbrian loan word, prob.
standing for *gwobho and cogn. with OPruss.
gabawo, 'toad', OSlav. iaba (for *gl"ibha),
'frog', MLG. kwappe (whence G. Quappe, Kaul-
quappe), 'tadpole'.

## bug
bug, п., an insect. — ME. bugge, 'scarecrow', of
uncertain origin.

## bug
bug, п., a bugbear. — W. bwg, 'ghost, bugbear'.

## bugbear
bugbear, n. — Compounded of prec. word and
the noun bear.

## bugger
bugger, п., ι) a sodomite; 2) a fellow, a chap. —
OF. (= F.) bougre, fr. ML. Bulgarus, 'a
Bulgarian; heretic; sodomite'. See Bulgarian.
Derivative: bugger-y, n.

## buggy
buggy, п., a light vehicle. — Of unknown origin.

## bugle
bugle, п., a buffalo (obsol.); a horn. — OF. 'ox,
buffle', fr. L. buculus, 'young ox', dimin. of tos,
gen. bovis, *ox'; see bovine. F. bugle, 'a wind
instrument', is an English loan word. OF. bugler
(whence F. beugler), 'to blow the horn', derives
fr. OF. bugle. .
Derivatives: bugle, intr. v., to sound a bugle;
tr. v., to summon by blowing a bugle; bugl-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:126 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 99 | BUNOOONT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:126 COLUMN:1 -->

## bugle
bugle, п., an ornament. — Possibly fr. bugle,
'horn', and orig. denoting little horns and
hornlike ornaments.

## bugloss
bugloss, п., name of a plant. — F. bitglosse, fr.
L. buglossa, fr. Gk. βούγλωσσος, *ox-tongued',
fr. βοΰς, gen. βοός, Όχ', and γλώσσα, 'tongue'.
See bovine and gloss, 'interpretation'. The plant
was so called from the shape of the leaves.

## buhl
buhl, n. decoration of furniture inlaid with brass
and tortoise shell. — G., from the name of the
French cabinetmaker Charles-Andre Boulle
(1642-1732).
Derivative: buhl, adj.

## build
build, tr. and inlr. v. — ME. bulden, bilden, fr.
OE. byldan, rel. to OE., OFris. bold, 'a building,
a house', OE., OHG. buan, ON. bua, 'to dwell',
fr. Tcut. base *bfi-, corresponding to I.-E. base
*bhu-, 'to dwell'. See be and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: build, п., buitd-er, п., build-ing, n.

## buire
buire, п., jug, pitcher. — F., 'bottle', a secondary
form of buie, from Frankish buka, alteration of
*buk, 'belly', which is rel. to MDu. buuc, etc.,
'belly'. See buck, 'the body of a wagon', and
cp. burette.

## bulb
bulb, n. — F. bulbe, fr. VL. bulbu,s 'bulb, bulbous
root, onion', fr. Gk. βολβός, of s.m., which
was formed from the reduplication of the I.-E.
imitative base *bol-; prob. not rel. to L. bulla
(seebull, 'edict'). Lith. bulbe, 'potato', is borrowed
fr. Pol. bulba, which is a Latin loan word.
Derivatives: bulb, intr. v., bulb-ar, adj., adj.,
bulb-ed, bulb-ous, bulb-y, adjs.

## bulbul
bulbul, п., a songbird of Persia, prob. the
nightingale. — Pers. bulbul, a word of imitative origin.

## Bulgarian
Bulgarian, adj. and n. — ML. Bulgaria,
'Bulgaria', fr. Bulgari, 'Bulgarians', lit. prob.
meaning 'the men from the Bolg (= Volga)', so called
because they came from the banks of the Volga
where they had lived till the 6th cent. — Volga
is a word of Sarmalian origin and denotes 'the
great river'. For the ending see suff. -an. Cp.
bugger.

## bulge
bulge, n. — OF. boulge, bouge (F.bouge), 'leather
bag, wallet', fr. L. bulga, 'leather knapsack*,
which, according to Festus, is a word of Gaulish
origin. Cp. Olr. bolgaim, *I swell', bolg, 'bag*,
W. bol, bola, boly, 'belly', Bret, bolc'h, 'flax
pod', which derive fr. 1-Е. base *bhelgh-, 'to
swell'. Bulga prop, means 'swelled skin of
animal'. See belly and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: bulge, intr. v., bulg-er, п.,
bulging, adj.

## bulimia
bulimia, п., morbid hunger (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. βουλιμία, 'ravenous hunger', lit. 'ox
hunger', fr. βοϋς, gen. βαός, Όχ', and λιμός,
'hunger'. See bovine, loimic and -ia.

## bulk
bulk, п., size, volume; cargo of a ship. — ME.
bulke, prob. a blend of ON. bulki, 'carge', and
OE. buc, 'body, belly'. ON. bulki, is rel. to ON.
bollr, 'a ball', fr. I.-E. base *bhel-, 'to swell';
see bull, 'the male of a bovine animal', and cp.
ball, 'a round body', bold. For the etymology
of OE. buc see bnck, 'the body of a wagon'.

## bulk
bulk, п., projection from a shop. — ME. balk,
bolk, fr. OE. balca, 'beam'. See balk and cp.
next word.

## bulkhead
bulkhead, n. — Compounded of bulk, 'projection',
and head.
Derivative: bulkhead, tr. v.

## bull
bull, п., the male of a bovine animal. — ME. bule,
bole, fr. OE. bula, 'bull', rel. to ON. boli, MDu.
bul(le), Du. bul, G. Bulle, of s.m., OE. bulluc,
'little bull', bealluc, 'testicle', ON. bollr, 'ball',
fr. I.-E. base *bhel-, 'to swell', whence also Gk.
φαλλός, 'penis', φάλλαινα, φάλλη, 'whale', L.
follis, 'a pair of bellows'. Cp. bullock. Cp. also
baleen, ball, 'a round body', bold, bulk, 'size',
follicle, phallus. For derivatives of base 'bhelgh-,
an enlargement of base *bhel-, see belly,
budget, bulge.
Derivative: bull, intr. and tr. v., bull-ish, adj.

## bull
bull, п., an edict of the pope. — ME. bulle, fr. OF.
bulle, fr. It. bulla, fr. Μ L. bulla, 'seal affixed to a
document, document', fr. L. bulla, 'bubble, boss,
knob*, fr. I.-E. *bu-l-, whence also Lith. bule,
bulls, 'buttock', MDu. puyl, 'bag', MLG. pull.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:126 COLUMN:2 -->
poll, 'pod, husk' (with ρ for b). I.-E. "bu-l- is
an -/-enlargement of base *bu-, 'to blow; to
swell', whence L. bucca, 'cheek'. See buccal and
cp. bill, 'document', bullet, bulletin. Cp. also
poll, 'head'.

## bull
bull, п., a comical blunder. — Of uncertain origin.

## bulla
bulla, п., boss, knob. — L. bulla, 'bubble, boss,
knob'. See bull, 'edict'.

## bullace
bullace, п., a wild plum. — ME. bolace, fr. OF.
beloce, 'sloe', of unknown origin.

## bullate
bullate, adj., blistered. — L. bullatus, fr. bulla,
'bubble'. See bull, 'edict', and adj. suff. -ate.

## bulldog
bulldog, n. — Compounded of bull, male of a
bovine animal', and dog; so called because
originally used for baiting bulls.

## bulldoze
bulldoze, tr. v., to intimidate; to bully (colloq.)
— Of uncertain origin.

## bulldozer
bulldozer, п., l) one who bulldozes; 2) a kind
of tractor.—Formed fr. prec. word with agential
suff. -er.

## bullet
bullet, n. — F. boulel, dimin. of boule, 'ball', fr.
L. bulla, 'bubble'. See bull, 'edict', and -et.
Derivative: bullet-ed, adj.

## bulletin
bulletin, n. — F., fr. It. bullettino,'dimm. of bulla,
'an edict of the pope'. See bull, 'edict'.

## bullion
bullion, п., uncoined gold or silver. — Du. buli-
oen, 'alloy of gold and silver', fr. F. billon, 'lump,
ingot, alloy of silver with a preponderating
amount of copper', fr. bille, 'block of wood'.
See billet, 'a stick'.

## bullock
bullock, n. — OE. bulluc, 'little bull', dimin. of
bull. See bull, 'male of a bovine animal', and
-ock.

## bully
bully, п., adj. and tr. v. — Of uncertain origin.
Cp. billycock.
Derivatives: bullying, adj., bully-ing-ly, adv.

## bulrush
bulrush, n. — ME. bolroysche, bulrysche. See bole,
'trunk of a tree', and rush, the plant.

## bulwark
bulwark, п., I) rampart; 2) protection. — ME.
bulwerk, fr. MLG. (= Du.) bolwerk, which is rel.
to MHG. bolwerk, G.Bollwerk, Swed. bolverk.
These words lit. mean 'bole work'. See bole,
'trunk of a tree', and work and cp. boulevard.
Derivative: bulwark, tr. v.

## bum
bum, intr. v., to make a humming sound. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. boom, bump.
Derivative: bumm-er, n.

## bumbaillff
bumbaillff, п., a bailiff serving writs, making
arrests, etc. —Compounded of obsol. /шт,'rump,
buttocks', and haUifT; so called because he used
to be close behind.

## Bumble
Bumble, п., a self important, petty official. —
From Mr. Bumble, name of a pompous beadle
in Dickens's Oliver Twist.
Derivative: Bumble-dom, bumble-dom, n.

## bumblebee
bumblebee, n. — Compounded of ME. bumlen,
bumblen, 'to hum', and bee. The first element is
of imitative origin; cp. boom, bum, bomb, bump.
Cp. bumblebee,

## bumbo
bumbo, п., a drink made of sugaT, water, spirits
and spice. — It. bombo, a child's word for drink.

## bumboat
bumboat, п., a boat used to convey stores, etc.,
to a ship. — LG. bumboot, lit. 'boat hewn from
a tree trunk', fr. bum, 'tree', and boot, 'boat'.
See beam and boat.

## Bumelia
Bumelia, п., a genus of the family Sapotaceae
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βουμελία, name of a
kind of ash, compounded of βοϋς, gen. βοάς,
Όχ', and μ;λίά, 'ash tree'. See bovine and Melia.

## bnmmalo
bnmmalo, п., the Bombay duck. — Corruption of
Marathi bombil.

## bump
bump, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
boom, bum, bomb. Cp. also bumptious.
Derivatives: bump, n. (q.v.), bump-er, п., bump-
y, adj., bump-i-ness, n.

## bump
bump, n , a blow; swelling, protuberance caused
by a blow. — Fr. prec. word. Cp. bunch,

## bumpkin
bumpkin, п., a rustic, a lout. — Prob. fr. Du.
bommekjjn, 'a little cask'. .For the ending see
suff. -kia.

## bumptions
bumptions, adj., arrogant, obtrusive. — A jocular
word, formed from bump on analogy of
facetious, fractious, etc.
Derivatives: bumptious-ly, adv.,
bumptiousness, n.

## bun
bun, п., a small cake. — ME. bimne, of uncertain
etymology. It is perh. of Celtic origin (cp. Gael.
bonnach) or derives fr. OF. bugne, buigne, bigne,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:126 COLUMN:3 -->
'a swelling; fritter', whence buignet, bignet, F.
beignet, 'fritter'; so called from its swollen shape
Cp. bunion.

## bun
bun, п., the tail of a rabbit. — Of uncertain
origin. Cp. bunny.

## bunch
bunch, n. — Prob. fr. bump, in the sense of
'swelling'. For the connection of bump with bunch
cp. clump and clunch, bump and bunch, lump
and lunch.
Derivatives: bunch, tr. and intr. v., bunch-y, adj.,
bunch-i-ly, adv., bunch-i-ness, n.

## bunco
bunco, bunko, п., swindling at cards; tr. v., to
swindle at cards. — Cp. Sp. banco, 'bank',
banco, 'a game of cards', which are rel. to It.
banco, 'bank'. See bank, 'an institution for the
custody of money'.

## buncombe
buncombe, n. — A spelling var. of bunkum.

## bundle
bundle, n. — ME. bundel, St. MDu. bundel, a
collateral form of bondel, dimin. of MDu. bom
(whence Du. bond), 'bundle', rel. to Du. binden,
'to bind'. Cp. MHG., G. bundel, 'bundle',
dimin. of MHG. bunt, resp. G. Bund, 'bundle',
and OE. byndele', 'a binding', and see bind. For
the ending see dimin. suff. -le. Cp. bunt, n.
Derivatives: bundle, tr. and intr. v., bundl-er, n.

## bundobust
bundobust, п., regulation, settlement (Anglo-
Ind.) — Hind, and Pers. band-o-bast, lit. "tying
and binding'. Hind, band derives fr. OI. band,
'a tying', fr. OI. bandhati, 'he ties up, binds';
see bind. For Pers. bast, 'a binding', see bast.

## bundook
bundook, п., a rifle. — Hind., fr. Arab, bunduq,
'missile', orig. 'weapon made in Venice', fr.
Bunduqtya", the Arabic name of Venice, the city
once so famous for its manufacture of
crossbows and small arms. This etymology is
corroborated by the circumstance that bunduqiya"
means also 'musket, rifle'. Cp. also Al-Bandu-
qdnt, 'the man of the crossbow', a surname of
the caliph Harun-al-Rashid.

## bung
bung, п., a large stopper. — MDu. bonghe, fr. F.
bonde, fr. Gaul, "bunda, whence also OProv-
enc. bonda. Cp. Olr. bonn, Gaelic and Ir. bonn,
W. bon, 'base, sole of the foot". MHG. bunt
punt, spunt (whence. G. Spund), 'bung', are
Romance loan words. See Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 75 s.v. bonde.
Derivative: bung, tr. v.

## bungaloid
bungaloid, adj., resembling bungalows. — A
hybrid coined fr. bungalow and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## bungalow
bungalow, n. — From Hind. Bangla, 'belonging
to Bengal, of Bengal', used elliptically for 'house
of Bengal'.

## bungle
bungle, intr. v., to act clumsily; tr. v., to make
clumsily. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. OSwed.
bunga, 'to strike', bangla, 'to work
ineffectively', which is related to Swed. Mnga, 'to make
a noise', MHG. bunge, 'drum', MDu. benghel,
MHG. bengel, 'cudgel', G. Bengel, 'cudgel; rude
fellow'. All these words are ult. of imitative
origin. See bang.
Derivatives: bungle, п., bungl-er, п., bungl-ing,
adj. and n.

## bunion
bunion, п., a swelling on the first joint of the
great toe. — Fr. MF. bugne, 'a swelling'. See
bun, 'small cake'.

## bunk
bunk, п., a sleeping berth. — Prob. related to
bauk, 'edge of a river', and to bauk, 'bench'.
Cp. buaker.
Derivative: bunk, intr. v.

## bunk
bunk, п., nonsense. — See bunkum.

## buaker
buaker, n. — Scot, bunker, 'bench', prob. rel. to
bench.
Derivative: bunker, tr. v.

## bunkum
bunkum, buncombe, often shortened to bunk, п.,
speechmaking for effect; insincere talk;
humbug. — From Buncombe, name of a county in
North Carolina, one of whose representatives
was said to have spoken frequently in Congress,
merely to impress his constituents.

## bunny
bunny, п., pet name for a rabbit. — Formed fr.
bun, 'rabbit', with dimin. suff. -y.

## bunodont
bunodont, adj., having tubercles in the teeth
(applied to the pig and the hippopotamus). —
Compounded of Gk. βουνός, 'mound, hill', and
οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. The first element is,
according to Herodotus, 4,199, a Cyrenaic loan
word. For the second element see odonto-.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:127 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BUNSEN BURNER | 100 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:127 COLUMN:1 -->
Bunsen burner. — Named after its inventor, the
German chemist Professor Robert Wilhelm
Bunsen (1811-99).

## bunt
bunt, п., a disease of wheat; smut. — Of unknown
origin.

## bunt
bunt, п., the bagging part of a fishing net. — Rel.
to Dan. bundt, Swed. bunt, MDu. bont, MHG.
bunt, G. Bund, Biindel, 'bundle', and to E.
bundle (q.v.)

## bunt
bunt, tr. v., to sift. — ME. bonten,'to sift', formed
— through the medium of OF. — fr. VL. *boni-
tare, 'to make good", fr. L. bonitds, 'the good
quality of a thing, goodness', fr. bonus, 'good'.
See boaus and cp. bunting, 'cloth'.

## bunt
bunt, tr. and intr. v., to strike with the head
or horns, to butt. — Cp. butt, 'to strike'.

## bunting
bunting, п., any of various small birds. — ME.,
of unknown origin.

## bunting
bunting, п., cloth used for patriotic decoration,
— The orig. meaning prob. was 'cloth used for
sifting', fr. ME. bonten, 'to sift'. See bunt, 'to
sift', and subst. suff. -ing.

## bunyip
bunyip, п., a fabulous animal. Hence: a humbug,
an impostor. — Native Australian.

## buoy
buoy, n. — MDu. boeye, boye (Du. boei), fr. OF.
boye (F. bouee), fr. Teut. *baukn, 'signal'. Cp.
OHG. houhhan, OFris. baken, and see beacon.
Derivatives: buoy, tr. v., buoy-age, п., buoy-
ance, п., buoy-ancy, п., buoy-ant, adj., buoy-ant-
ly, adv., buoy-ant-ness, n.

## Bupleurum
Bupleurum, п., a genus of plants of the carrot
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βοϋς, gen. βοός,
'ox', and πλεϋρον, 'rib'. See bovine and pleura.

## Buprestis
Buprestis, п., a genus of beetles (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. βοΰπρηστις, 'a poisonous beetle',
lit. 'burner of cattle', compounded of βοΰς, gen.
βοός, Όχ', and πρή&ειν, 'to blow out, swell out,
blow into flame'; so called because this beetle,
if eaten by cattle, causes them to swell up and
die. For the first element see bovine. The second
element is rel. to πιμπράνοιι, 'to burn, burn up',
and prob. cogn. with Hitt. pardi-, 'to blow into
a flame, to kindle', OSlav. parna, 'smoke,
vapor', Russ. preju, pret', 'to sweat, boil', ON.
fries, 'a blowing'.

## bur
bur, also burr, п., the prickly seed vessel of certain
plants. — Lit. 'the bristly one'; rel. to Dan.
bone, 'burdock', and to E. harse and bristle
(qq.v.) See also fastigiate and cp. the first
element in burdock.
Derivative: bur, burr, tr. v.

## barbie
barbie, intr. v., to make a bubbling sound. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. bubble.
Derivatives: burble, п., burbl-er, п., burbl-y,
adj.

## burbot
burbot, п., a fresh-water fish of the cod family. —
F. bourbolte, fr. bourbe, 'mud, mire', fr. Gaulish
*borva-, a form reconstructed from Borvo, name
of a thermal deity (whence the place name
Bourbon), rel. to Olr. berbaim, Ί boil, seethe',
ft. I.-E. base 'bheru-, 'to boil'. See brew and cp.
F. barbote, 'eelpout', barboter, 'to dabble about
in mud or in muddy water', which are related
to bourbe, 'mud, mire'. Cp. also Bourbon.

## bnrd
bnrd,n., lady. — ME. byrd, burd, prob. metathesis
of OE. bryd, 'bride'. See tst bride.

## burden
burden, п., a load.— ME. burden, btrden, birtken,
fr. OE. byrden, rel. to ON. byrdr, OS. bur-
thinnia, OHG. burdi, MHG., G. burde, Goth.
baurbei; lit. 'that which is borne', fr. I.-E. base
*bher-, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry' and
cp. burthen.
Derivatives: burden, tr. v., burden-er, п.,
burdensome, adj., burden-some-ly, adv., burden-some-
ness, n.

## burden
burden, п., refrain. — F. bourdon, 'drone, drone
bass, humblebee', fr. ML. burdonem, ace. of
burdo, of s.m., which is of imitative origin. Cp.
bourdon, 'drone bass'.

## burdock
burdock, п., the plant Arctium Lappa. —
Compounded of bur, 'prickly seed vessel', and dock,
the plant; so called for its burs and because of
its large leaves resembling those of the dock.
Cp. bardock.

## bnreau
bnreau, n. — F., 'desk, writing table, office', fr.
OF. burel, dimin. of bure (F. bourre), 'coarse
woolen cloth', hence bureau orig. meant 'table
covered with a coarse woolen stuff.' OF. bure,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:127 COLUMN:2 -->
comes fr. VL. *bura, corresponding to Late L.
burra, 'flock of wool', which is eogn. with Gk.
βερράν, βίρροξ, 'thick with hair, hairy'. Cp.
bourette, burel, burl, burlesque.

## bureaucracy
bureaucracy, n. —■ F. bureaucratie, a hybrid coined
by the French economist Jean Claude Marie
Vincent de Gournay (1712-59) fr. bureau and
Gk. -κρατία, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'.
See -eracy.

## bureaucrat
bureaucrat, n. — F. bureaucrate. See prec. word
and -crat.
Derivatives :bureaucrat-ic,bureaucrat-ic-al,SLd}s.,
bureaucrat-ic-at-ly, adv., bureaucrat-ism, п., bu-
reaucrat-ist, п., bureaucrat-ize, tr. v.,
bureaucratization, n.

## burel
burel, п., a kind of woolen cloth {history). — ME.,
fr. OF. burel. See bureau.

## burette
burette, п., a graduated glass tube for measuring
small quantities of liquid. — F., 'cruet, flagon',
dimin. of buire, a secondary form of buie,
'bottle', See buire and -ette.

## burgage
burgage, п., a former form of privileged tenure
of land (law). — F. bourgage, fr. ML. burgdgium,
'municipality', fr. Teut. *burg, 'town'. See
borough and -age.

## burgee
burgee, п., a small pennon used by yachts and
merchant vessels for identification. — Orig.
'owner's pennon', fr. OF. burgcis (F. bourgeois)
in burgeis (F. bourgeois) drun navire, 'owner of
a ship'; see bourgeois. In English, the ί of OF.
burgeis was mistaken for the plural suff. For
other words similarly treated see pea.

## burgeon
burgeon, п., bud. — ME. borjoun, burjon, fr. OF.
burjon (F. bourgeon), fr. VL. *burrionem, ace. of
'burrio, ft. Late L. burra, 'flock of wool' (see
bureau); so called because the buds of many
trees have a hairy, shaggy appearance.

## burgess
burgess, п., citizen of a borough. — OF. burgeis
(F. bourgeois), fr. Late L. burgensis, fr. Teut.
'burg, 'town'. See borough and cp. burgher. Cp.
also bourgeois.

## burgh
burgh, п., I) a borough; 2) in Scotland, an
incorporated town. — A var. of borough (q.v.)
Derivatives: burgh-al, adj., burgher (q.v.)

## burgher
burgher, п., 1) freeman of a burgh; 2) a citizen. —
Prob. fr. Du. burger, 'citizen', fr. MDu. burgher,
fr. MHG. burgxre, burger (whence G. Burger),
fr. OHG. burgdri, fr. OHG. burg, 'castle,
citadel, city'; influenced in form by E. burgh. See
borough and agential suff. -er.

## burglar
burglar, n. — ML. burguldtor, burglator, a
hybrid lit. meaning 'town thief. The first
element is a Teut. loan word (see borough), the
second is traceable to L. latro, gen. -onis, 'thief,
robber'; cp. OF. ler, lerre, ace. laron (whence F.
larron), and see larceny.
Derivatives: burglar-ious, adj., burglar-ious-ly,
adv., burglar-ize, tr. v. (colloq.), burgiar-y, п.,
burgle (q.v.)

## burgle
burgle, intr. v., to commit burglary; tr. v., to
burglarize. — Back formation fr. burglar.

## burgomaster
burgomaster, n. — Formed fr. Du. burgemeester,
with the assimilation of the second element to
E. master (q.v.) For the first element see
borough. Cp. OFris. burgamdsiere, Dan. boig-
mesier, Norw. borgemester, Swed. borgmdsfare,
MHG. biirge-, burge-, burger-, burgermeister,
G. Burgermeister.

## burgonet
burgonet, п., a light helmet. — F. bourguignotte,
prop, 'helmet of Burgundy', fr. Bourguignon,
'man of Burgundy', fr. Bourgogne, fr. ML. Bur-
gundia. See Burgundy.

## burgrave
burgrave, п., in German history, the lord of a
castle. — G. Burggraf, lit. 'count of a castle',
fr. Burg, 'castle', and Graf, 'count'. See borough
and grave, 'count'.

## Burgundy
Burgundy, n. — ML. Burgundia, fr. Late L.
Burgundiones, lit. 'Highlanders'. See borough and
cp. burgonet ar.d burgundy.

## burgundy
burgundy, п., wine of Burgundy.

## burial
burial, n. — ME. buriels, fr. OE. byrgels fr. byr-
gatr, 'to bury', rel. to beorgan, 'to cover'; see
bury. The ending -J in OE. byrgels, ME. buriels,
was mistaken for the pi. suffix and
consequently dropped.

## burin
burin, п., engraver's cutting tool. — F., fr. It.
burino (now bulino), a Teut. loan word. Cp.
OHG. boron, 'to bore', and see bore, v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:127 COLUMN:3 -->

## burke
burke, tr. v., to murder by smothering. — From
the name of William Burk, executed in
Edinburgh in 1829 for murdering several persons in
order to sell their bodies for dissection.
Derivatives: burk-er, burk-iie, n.

## burkundauze
burkundauze, also burkundaz, п., an armed
retainer, an armed policeman (Anglo-tnd.) — A
hybrid coined fr. Arab.-Pers. barq-anddz, 'light-
ning,thrower', fr. Arab, barq, 'lightning' and
Pers. anddz, 'thrower'. Arab, barq is rel. to Heb.
baraq, Aram. beraq, barqd, Akkad. birqu,
'lightning', Arab, baraqa, 'it lightened', Akkad. bardqu,
'to lighten', Aram. bgrdq, Ethiop. baraqa, 'it
lightened'; cp. Egypt, brq, 'to shine, glitter',
Copt, ebreje, 'lightning'.

## burl
burl, п., knot, lump. — OF. burle, dimin. of bure
(F. bourre), 'coarse woolen cloth'. See bureau
and cp. burlesque.

## burlap
burlap, п., a coarse cloth made of hemp, flax or
jute. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: burlap, tr. v., to cover with burlap.

## burlesque
burlesque, adj., comic. — F., fr. It. burlesco, fr.
burla, 'jest', fr. VL. *burrula, "burula, dimin. of
Late L. burra, 'flock of wool', used in the plural
in the sense of 'trifles, nonsense'. For the ety-
mol. of L. burra see bureau.
Derivatives: burlesque, rj. and tr. v., burlrsque-
ly, adv., burlesqu-er, n.

## burly
burly, adj. — ME. borlich, bitrli, 'lofty', prob.
fr. OE. borlice, 'excellency, exactly, very', rel.
to OHG. burlih, 'lofty, exalted', burjan, 'to raise,
lift', prob. fr. I.-E. base bher-, 'to Ьеат, carry';
see bear, 'to carry'. For sense development cp.
Heb. ndsa, 'he lifted, carried'.

## Bnrmannia
Bnrmannia, п., a genus of plants of the burmannia
family (hot.) — ModL., named after the Dutch
botanist Johannes Burmann (1 706-79). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## Burmanniaceae
Burmanniaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## burmanniaceous
burmanniaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## burn
burn, п., a brook, water (Scot, and dial. Engl.) —
ME. burne, fr. OE. brunna, burna. See bourn,
'stream'.

## burn
burn, tr. and intr. v. — ME. birnen, bernen,
brennen, fr. OE. beornan, biernan, brinnan (intr.),
bsernan(tr.), rel. to ON. brenna, brinna (intr.),
brenna (tr.), MDu. bernen, Du. branden, OS.,
OHG. brinnan, MHG. brinnen (intr.), OHG.
brennan, MHG. brennen (tr.), G. brennen, Goth.
brinnan (intr.), brannjan (tr.), 'to burn'; fr. I.-E.
base 'bhreu-, 'to boil'. See brew and words there
referred to and cp. esp. bourn, burn, 'brook',
brand, brindled.
Derivatives: burn, п., burn-able, adj., burn-er, п.,
burn-ing, adj.

## burner
burner, п., any plant of the genus Sanguisorba.
— OF. burnete, metathesis of brunete, brunette,
dimin. of brune. fern, of brun, 'brown'. See
burnish and -et and cp. brunette.

## burneltize
burneltize, tr. v., to impregnate with zinc chloride
solution. — Lit. 'to impregnate according to the
process patented by Sir William Burnett',
physician to the King (1779-Г86Г). For the ending
see suff. -ize.

## burnish
burnish, tr. v., to polish. — ME. burnischen, bur-
nissen, from OF. burniss-, pres. part, stem of
burnir, metathesis of OF. (= F.) brunir, Ίο
make brown', fr. brun, 'brown', fr. WTeut.
*briin-, 'brown'. See brown and cp. brunette,
burnet. For the ending see verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: burnish, п., burnish-er, п.,
burnishing, adj., burnish-ment, n.

## burnous
burnous, п., a long cloak worn by the Arabs. —
Arab, burnus, fr. Gk. βίρρος, 'large cloak with
a hood', fr. Late L. birrus. See biretta and cp.
barret, beret.

## burr
burr, п., prickly seed vessel of certain plants. —
The less usual spelling of bur in the same sense.
Derivatives: burr-er, п., burr-y, adj.

## burr
burr, п., guttural pronunciation of the r. —
Of imitative origin.
Derivatives: burr, intr. and tr. v., burr-ed, adj.

## burra khana
burra khana, a banquet (Anglo-Ind.) — Hind.
bard khana, 'a big dinner'.

## burrito
burrito, п., any of several grunts of America.
(zool.)—Sp., dimin. of burro, 'ass'. See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:128 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 101 | BUTTY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:128 COLUMN:1 -->

## burro
burro, п., a donkey. — Sp., rel. to borrico, of
s.m., fr. Late L. burricus, buricus, 'a small horse',
whence also F. bourrique, 'she-ass; donkey', fr.
burrus, 'red', fr. Gk. πυρρός, 'flame-colored,
yellowish red', assimilated fr. *πυρσός, fr. πϋρ,
gen. πυρός, 'fire*. See fire and cp. words there
referred to.

## burrow
burrow, n. — A var.'of borough, used in the sense
of 'shelter'.
Derivative: burrow, tr. v., lit. 'to make a burrow'.

## bursa
bursa, η., a saclike cavity (anal.) — Late L. bursa,
'bag'. See burse.

## bursar
bursar, п., ι) a college treasurer; 2) in Scotland,
holder of a scholarship. — ML. bursarius, fr.
Late L. bursa. See burse and -ar.
Derivatives: bursar-ial, adj., bursar-y, n.

## bursautee
bursautee, also bursattee, п., a disease of horses
(Anglo-Ind.) — Hind, barsati, 'pertaining to
rain', fr. barsat''the rains'. The word orig.
denoted 'a disease caught in, or owing to, the
rain'.

## bursch
bursch, п., a German university student. — G.,
lit. 'living from the same purse', fr. Late L. bursa,
'purse'. See next word.

## burse
burse, п., ι) a purse; 2) in Scotland, a
scholarship. — F. bourse, fr. Late L. bursa, 'leather-
bag, purse', fr. Gk. βύρσα, 'hide, leather',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. bourse, bursch,
disburse, imburse, reimburse. Cp. also Byrsa.

## bursiform
bursiform, adj., shaped like a purse or poach. —
Compounded of Late L. bursa, 'purse', and
L. forma, 'form, shape'. See burse and form, n.

## bursitis
bursitis, п., inflammation of a bursa (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -itis. fr. Late L.
bursa, 'purse'. See bursa.

## burst
burst, intr. and tr. v. — ME. bersten, bresten, fr.
OE. berstan, rel. to OS., OHG. brestan, ON.
bresta,Swed. brista, OFris. bersta, MDu. barsten,
bersten, borsten, Du. barsten, MHG. bresten,
MHG., G. bersten, 'to burst', and cogn. with
Olr. brissbn (in which ss stands for orig. st),
fr. I.-E. base *bhreus-, *bhres-, 'to break, crush,
crumble'. See bruise and cp. brisance.

## burst
burst, n. — OE. byrst, 'injury, loss', fr. *bursti,
which is rel. to berstan. See burst, v.

## burthen
burthen, n. — A var. of burden, 'load'.

## burton
burton, п., a tackle (naut.) — Of unknown origin.

## bury
bury, tr. v. — ME. burien, berien, fr. OE. byrgan,
'to bury', rel. to OE. beorgan, OS. bergan, ON.
bjarga, Dan. bjerge, Swed. berga, MDu. berghen,
Du. bergen, OHG. bergan. MHG., G. bergen,
Goth, bairgan, 'to save, preserve', fr. I.-E. base
*bhergh-, 'to preserve, save', whence also OSlav.
bregq, Ί preserve, guard'. Cp. the first element
in belfry and the second element in habergeon,
harbor, harbinger, hauberk, scabbard.
Derivatives: burial (q.v.), bury-ing, n.

## bus
bus, n. — Shortened fr. omnibus.

## busby
busby, п., fur hat worn by hussars in full parade.
■— Of unknown origin.

## bush
bush, п., shrub. — ME. bussh, bosck, busk, rel. to
OS., OHG. busc, MLG. busch, busk, Du. bos,
MHG. busch, bosch(e), G. Busch, fr. WTeut.
'busk-, 'bush, thicket'. Dan. busk, Swed. bu'ske,
and ML. boscus (whence It. bosco, OProveng.
bosc, F. bois) are WTeut. loan words. Cp.
boscage, bosket, bouquet, busk, 'strip of steel',
the first element in Bushman and the second
element in ambush, bautboy, tallboy.
Derivatives: bush-y, adj., bush-i-ness, n.

## bush
bush, п., metal lining. — Du. bus, 'box'. See box,
'case, chest'.

## bushel
bushel, η. — Μ Ε. buschel, fr. OF. boissiel (F. bois-
seau), fr. boisse, 'the sixth part of a bushel', fr.
Gaul.-L. 'bostia, 'a handful', fr. Gaul. *bosta,
reconstructed after Ir. bass, boss, Bret, boz, 'the
hollow of the hand'. See Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 74 s.v. boisseau.
Derivatives: bushel, tr. v., bushel(f)-er, n.

## bushido
bushido, п., the code of moral principles in feudal
Japan. — Jap., lit. 'warrior's way'.

## bushing
bushing, п., metal lining. — Formed with subst.
suff. -ing fr. bush, 'metal lining'.

## Bushman
Bushman, n. — Alter, of S. A. Du. Boschjesman
(Du. Bosjesman), lit. 'man of the bush', fr. boschje
(Du. bosje), dimin. of bosch (Du. bos), 'bush,
thicket', and man, 'man'. See bush, 'shrub', and
man.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:128 COLUMN:2 -->

## business
business, n. — Formed fr. busy with suff. -ness.

## busk
busk, п., strfp of steel, formerly of whalebone,
placed in front of a corset. — F. busc, fr. It.
busco, lit. 'a stick of wood', which is of Teut.
origin. Cp. OHG. busc, 'bush', and see bush,
'shrub'.

## busk
busk, tr. and intr. v., to prepare. — ME. busken,
fr. ON. buask, 'to prepare oneself, formed fr.
bua, 'to dwell; to prepare', and -sk, contraction
of the ON. reflexive pron. sik. See be, boor and
suff. -sk and cp. bustle, 'to hurry about'.
Derivative: busk-er, n.

## buskin
buskin, п., a half boot. — Prob. fr. OF. brose-
quin, 'buskin' (whence F. brodequin, under the
influence of F. broder, 'to embroider'), fr. MDu.
