broseken, 'a little shoe', which is of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: buskin-ed, adj.

## buss
buss, п., a small vessel used in herring fishing. —
ME. busse, fr. OF. busse, buce, fr. ML. buza,
bucia, whence also ON. buza, 'man-of-war,
merchantman', OHG. buzo, 'pirate ship*,
MHG. buze, 'man-of-war, merchantman', G.
Buse, 'buss'.

## buss
buss, п., a kiss. — Of imitative origin. Cp. G.
Busserl, dimin. of dial. G. Buss, 'kiss', bussen,
'to kiss', W. and Gael, bus, 'kiss'.

## bust
bust, n. — F. bustle, fr. It. busto, fr. L. bustum,
lit. 'the burned body', prop, neuter pp. of *bu-
rere, for urere, 'to burn'. The initial b in *burere
is due to a misdivision of L. amburere (i.e. amb-
urere), 'to burn around, scorch', into am-burere.
See combust.
bust. — Slang for burst.

## bustard
bustard, п., a large bird related to the crane. —
A blend of OF. bistard and oustarde (whence F.
outarde), both fr. L. avis tarda, lit. 'slow bird'.
Cp. OProvenc. austarda, Sp. avetarda,
'bustard', and see aviary and tardy.

## bustee
bustee, п., a village, slum (Anglo-Ind.). — Hind.
basti, lit. 'an inhabited place', fr. OI. vasati,
'dwells', which is cogn. with Gk. έστιαν, 'to
receive at one's hearth', Goth, wisan, OE., OHG.
wesan, 'to be'. See was and cp. words there
referred to.

## buster
buster, п., something big (slang). — Lit. 'that
which 'busts', formed fr. bust, 'to burst', with
suff. -er.

## bustle
bustle, intr. and tr. v., to hurry about. — Fr. ob-
sol. buskle, freq. of busk, 'to prepare'.
Derivatives: bustle, п., hurry, bustl-ing, adj.,
bustl-tng-ly, adv.

## bustle
bustle, п., framework worn by women to support
the skirt. — Of uncertain origin.

## busy
busy, adj. — ME. busy, bisy, fr. OE. bysig, bisig,
rel. to LG. besig, Du. bezig; of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: busy, v. (q.v.), busy-ness, n.

## busy
busy, tr. v. — OE. bysgian, bisgian, fr. bysig,
bisig. See busy, adj.

## Busycon
Busycon, п., a genus of marine snails (zoof.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. βούσϋκον, 'a large coarse fig';
so called from the fancied resemblance of the
shell to a large fig. Gk. βούσϋκον is formed fr.
augment pref. βου- and oijxov, 'fig'. The pref.
βου- is rel. to βοΰς, Όχ', and orig. meant 'as big
as an ox'. See bovine and Sycon.

## but
but, prep. — ME. butan, buten, bute, fr. OE.
baton, 'without, except, besides', fr. be-utan,
which is compounded of be, 'by', and utan, 'out,
outside, except, without', fr. ut, 'out'. See by
and out and cp. about.
Derivatives: but, conj., adv., п., tr. and intr. v.

## but
but, п., the outer room of a cottage. — Fr. but,
adv. See prec. word.

## butane
butane, п., either of two hydrocarbons in the
methane series (chem.) — Formed with suff.
-ane from the first three letters of L. butyrum,
'butter'. See butter.

## butcher
butcher, n. — ME. bocher, boucher, fr. OF.
bochier bouchier (F. boucher), 'butcher', lit.
'one who slaughters bucks', fr. bouc, 'buck'. See
buck, 'male deer', and -er (representing OF.
-ier).
Derivatives: butcher, tr. v., butcher-ly, adj. and
adv., butcher-li-ness, n.

## butchery
butchery, n. — ME. bocherie, fr. OF. bocherie,
boucherie (F. boucherie), fr. boucher. See
butcher and -y (representing F. -ie).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:128 COLUMN:3 -->

## Buteo
Buteo, п., a genus of hawks, the buzzard. — L.
buteo, 'a kind of falcon or hawk', rel. to buiire,
'to cry like a bittern' (lit. 'to utter the sound
bu'), from the l.-E. imitative base *i«-, whence
also L. biibo, 'owl, horned owl'. Cp. Bubo. Cp.
also bittern, buzzard.

## butler
butler, n. — ME. buteler, fr. AF. butuiller,
corresponding to OF. botillier, bouteillier, fr. botele,
bouteille, 'bottle'. See bottle.
Derivatives: butler-age, п., buttery (q.v.)

## butlery
butlery, n. — ME. botelerie, fr. OF. bouteillerie,
or directly fr. butler.

## Butomaceae
Butomaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —·
.ModL., formed fr. Butomus with suff. -aceae.

## butomaceous
butomaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Butomus
Butomus, п., a genus of plants (йог.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. βούτομος, 'a kind of plant, sedge',
compounded of βοΰς (gen. βοός), Όχ', and τόμος,
'a piece cut off'. See bovine and tome.

## butt
butt, п., a barrel for liquor. — OF. boul (F.
botte), fr. Late L. buttis, 'cask'. See bottle
'vessel'.

## butt
butt, п., the thicker end of anything. — ME. but,
butte, prob. rel. to MDu., Du. bot, LG. butt,
'blunt, dull', and to ON. bauta, OE. beatan, 'to
beat'. See beat and cp. butt, 'aim', butt, 'to
strike', buttock.

## butt
butt, п., aim, goal. — ME., fr. F. o«f,'goal', prob.
fr. Frankish "but, 'stump, stock, block' (cp. ON.
butr, 'log of wood'), taken in the sense of 'mark,
goal'i rel. to butt, 'the thicker end of anything',
and to butte. Cp. debut.

## butt
butt, also but, п., flatfish. — ME. butte, but, fr.
LG. butte or MDu. botte, butte, bot, but (Du.
boi), rel. to G. Butte, Butt, OSwed. tornbut
(whence E. turbot, q.v.), Swed. bulla, Dan. belle
and to MDu. bot, LG. butt, 'blunt'. See butt, 'the
thicker end of anything' and cp. the second
element in halibut.

## butt
butt, tr. v., to strike, thrust. — ME. butten, fr.
OF. boter, buter, 'to strike, push; to put, place'
(whence F. bouter, 'to put, place'; OF. bot,
'a blow; end, extremity', resp. F. bout, 'end,
extremity', are back formations fr. OF. boter,
resp. F. bouter). OF. boter is of Teut. origin;
cp. LG. boten, 'to beat', and see hurt, 'the thicker
end of anything'. OProveng. botar. It. buttare,
Sp. botar, 'to cast, throw', are French loan
words. Cp. boutade, bouts-rimes, buttress, rebut,
sackbut.
Derivative: bittt-er, n.

## butte
butte, п., an isolated hill in the western U.S. —
F.. fr. but, 'goal, target'. See butt, 'aim, goal'.

## butter
butter, n. — OE. butere, buttor-, fr. L. butyrum
(whence also OFris., OHG. butera, Du. boter,
MHG. buter, G. Butter, It. burro, OF. burre,
F. bettrre), fr. Gk. βούτϋρου, 'butter', lit. 'cow
cheese', which is compounded of βοΰς, Όχ,
cow', and τυρός, 'cheese*. See bovine and tyro-.
Derivatives: butter, tr. v., butter-y, adj.

## butterfly
butterfly, n. — ME. btitterflie, fr. OE. buterfleoge.
See butter and fly. Butterfly prop, means 'the
flying buttercolored thing'.

## butteris
butteris, п., an instrument for paring the hoofs
of horses. — A variant of buttress, from which
it is differentiated in meaning.

## buttery
buttery, п., a storeroom for liquor. — Lit. 'a place
where butts or barrels of liquor are stored', fr.
OF. boterie,, 'place for keeping bottles or butts',
fr. bout. See butt, 'barrel', and -y (representing
OF. -ie) and cp. bottle, 'vessel', and butler.

## buttock
buttock, n. — Formed fr. butt, 'thick end', with
the dimin. suff. -ock.

## button
button, n. — OF. baton (F. boutori), 'bud', later
'button', fr. the verb bouter, 'to push', fr.
Frankish *botan, 'to beat'. Cp. LG. boten, of s.m.,
and see butt, 'to strike'.
Derivatives: button, v. (q.v.), button-ry, n.

## button
button, tr. and intr. v. — OF. botoner (F. bou-
tonncr), fr. boton. See button, n.
Derivative: bittton-ed; adj.

## buttress
buttress, п., a structure supporting a wall. —
ME. boterace, butrasse, fr. OF. bouterez (pron.
bouterets), pi. of bouteret, 'support', fr. bouter,
Ίο push; to put, place1. See butt, 'to strike' and
cp. butteris.
Derivative: buttress, tr. v.

## butty
butty, п., a middleman. — Of uncertain origin.

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: BUTYL | 102 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:129 COLUMN:1 -->

## butyl
butyl, п., a hydrocarbon radical, CH, (chem.) —
Formed from the first three letters of L. buty-
rum, 'butter', and fr. Gk. 6λη, 'material, stuff'.
See butter and -yl.

## lmtyractous
lmtyractous, adj., resembling butter. — Formed
with suff. -aceous fr. L. butyrum, 'butter*. See
butter,

## butyrate
butyrate, п., a salt of butyric acid (chem.) —
Formed with chem. suff. -ate fr. L. butyrum,
'butter'. See butter,

## butyric
butyric, adj., pertaining to butter. — Formed fr.
L. butyrum, 'butter' (see butter) and suff. -ic.
butyric acid (chem.) — So called by its discoverer,
the French chemist Michel-Eugene Chevreul
(1786-1889) because it occurs in butter. See
prec. word.

## Buxaceae
Buxaceae, n. pi., the box family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Buxus with suff. -aceae.

## buxom
buxom, adj. — ME. buhsum, buxum, 'pliable,
obedient', rel. to Du. buigzaam, G. biegsam,
'flexible, pliable'; derived fr. OE. bugan, resp.
Du. buigen, G. biegen, 'to bend'. See bow, 'to
bend'. For the ending see 1st -some.
Derivatives: buxom-ly, adv., buxom-ness, n.

## Buxus
Buxus, п., the genus of lhe box tree (bot.) — L.
buxus, 'the box tree'. See box, the tree.

## buy
buy, tr.v. — ME. buggen, biggen, bien, fr. OE.
byegan, rel. to OS. buggian, buggean, ON. bygg-
ja, Goth, bugjan, 'to buy'.
Derivatives: buy, п., buy-able, adj., buy-er, n.

## bnzz
bnzz, intr.v. — Of imitative origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:129 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: buzz, п., buzz-er, n.

## buzzard
buzzard, n. — ME. busard, fr. OF. bus-ard,
formed, with change of suff., fr. OF. buis-on,
bus-on (a regressive derivative of which is F.
base, 'buzzard'), fr. L. buteonem, ace. of bated,
'a kind of falcon or hawk'. See Buteo and cp.
bittern.

## by
by, prep, and adv. — ME. Ы, by, fr. OE. if; the
toneless form is be- (see be-); rel. to OS., OFris.
if, MDu. Ые, Du. bij, OHG., MHG. if, G. bet,
'by, at, near', Goth. if, 'round about, by'. These
words are cogn. with the second element in OI.
a-bhi, 'toward; to', Gk. άμ-φ£, 'around, about',
L. am-bo, 'both'. See ambi-, amphl-, and cp. the
first element in but. Cp. also the second element
in about, above.

## bye
bye, п., something secondary. — Fr. by, prep.

## bye-bye
bye-bye, п., bed; sleep. — A childish word.

## bye-bye
bye-bye, interj., good-by. — A childish word.

## bygoae
bygoae, adj. — Formed from the adv. by and
gone, pp. of go.

## bylaw
bylaw, n. — ME. bihw, prob. meaning lit.
'village law', and derived fr. ON. *bylog, which is
compounded of byr, 'village' (which is rel. to
ilia 'to live'), and log, 'law'. See be and law and
cp. boor, bower, 'cottage', booth, bound, 'ready
for a journey', byre.

## byre
byre, п., a cow shed. — ME., fr. OE. byre, rel.
to i«r, 'dwelling', buan, 'to dwell'. See be and
cp. prec. word and words there referred to.

## Byronic
Byronic, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, Lord

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:129 COLUMN:3 -->
Byron (1788-1824).

## Byronism
Byronism, п., characteristics of Lord Byron. See
prec. word and -ism,

## Byrsa
Byrsa, also Bursa, п., name of the citadel of
Carthage. — Metathesized from Phoen.-Heb. Botz-
ra* (cp. Botzrd" = Gk. Βόσορρηι, later Βόστρα,
name of the capital of Edom), lit. 'enclosure;
citadel', fr. batzar, 'he cut off, made inaccessible
(a technical term of fortification work), but
confused with Gk. βύρσα, 'hide' (see burse), whence
arose the well-known legend concerning the
foundation of the citadel of Carthage.

## byssine
byssine, adj., made of byssus. — L. byssinus,
'made of byssus', fr. Gk. βύσσινος, fr. βύσσος.
See next word and adj. suff. -ine (representing
Gk. -ϊνος).

## byssus
byssus, n. — L., fr. Gk. βύσσος, 'fine white linen',
a Semitic loan word. Cp. Heb. butz, of s.m., fr.
Sem. *b-w-s (*b-w-tz), 'to be white, to surpass
in whiteness', whence Heb. betzah, Arab. baytjah,
'egg'. Cp. W. Muss-Arnolt, Semitic words in
Greek and Latin, in Transactions of the
American Philol. Association, 23, 80, Note 19.
Derivatives: byss-al, adj., byss-in, п., byssine
(q.v.)

## Byzantine
Byzantine, adj., pertaining to Byzantium. -*- L.
Byzantinus, fr. Byzantium, name of the capital
of the Eastern Roman Empire. Cp. bezant. For
the ending see suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).
Derivative: Byzantin-ism, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:130 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:130 COLUMN:1 -->

## cab
cab, п., a Hebrew dry measure. — Heb. qabh.
rel. to Aram.-Syr. qabba, Arab, qabb, name of a
measure of capacity, from the Sem. base *q-b-b,
'to be hollow'.

## cab
cab, п., carriage. — Abbreviation of cabriolet.
Derivative: cab, intr. v.

## cab
cab, tr. v., to crib (slang). — Short for cabbage,
'to pilfer'.

## cabal
cabal, п., a secret intrigue. — F. cabale, fr. Lale
L. cabbala, fr. Mishnaic Heb. qabbald",
'reception; doctrine received', fr. Heb. qibbel, 'he
received, accepted', rel. to Aram. q6bhetl, q°bhdl,
'before', Syr. men q'bhol, 'opposite*, Aram.-
Syr. qabbil, 'he received, accepted', Arab, qdbila,
'was in front of, qabala, 'he received, accepted',
Ethiop. qabala, 'he went to meet, accepted',
Akkad. qablu, 'fight, encounter'. Cp. cabala,
alcabala, gabella, kabyle, kiblah.
Derivative: cabal, intr. v., to conspire.

## cabala
cabala, п., a system of Jewish mystical
interpretation of the scriptures (Jewish literary history).
— Mishnaic Heb. qabbalaK, 'reception', in the
sense of 'teachings received'. See cabal.

## cabalist
cabalist, п., a student of cabala. — A hybrid
formed fr. cabala with surf. -ist.
Derivative: cabalist-ic, adj.

## cabaret
cabaret, n. — F., a loan word fr. MDu.
cabret, denasalized fr. cambrel, camret, fr.
OPicard cambrete, dimin. of cambre, 'chamber,
room', which is rel. to F. chambre, of s.m. See
chamber and -et.

## cabas
cabas, п., a flat basket. — F., 'frail, basket', fr.
OProvenc. cabas, 'basket of sedge', fr. VL. *ca-
pacius, fr. L. capax, gen. capacis, 'that can
contain much, capacious, spacious', fr. capio, ca-
pere, 'to catch, seize, take, hold'. See captive and
cp. cabbage, v.

## cabbage
cabbage, п., plant of the order Brassica. — ME.
caboche, fr. ONF. (— F.) caboche, 'head', fr,
OF. caboce, formed fr. pejorative pref. ca- and
boce (F. basse), 'a swelling'. See boss, 'a
protuberance', and cp. Boche, cabochon.
Derivative: cabbage, intr. and tr. v.

## cabbage
cabbage, tr. and intr. v., to pilfer. — F. cabasser,
'to steal', fr. cabas, 'basket'. See cabas,

## cabby
cabby, п., a cabman (colloq.) — Short for cabman.

## caber
caber, п., a beam. — Gael, cabar, 'pole, beam'.

## cabildo
cabildo, п., the chapter of a cathedral. — Sp.,
metathesized fr. L. capitulum, 'head of a
column', dimin. of caput, 'head'. See capital, adj.,
and cp. chapter.

## cabilliau
cabilliau, п., a codfish. — F. cabillaud, fr. Du.
kabetjauw, fr. MDu. cabbeltau, fr. ML. cabbel-
lauwus, altered fr. Sp. bacallao, 'codfish', fr. L.
baculum, 'stick, staff'. See bacterium and cp.
bacalao. For sense development cp. stockfish.

## cabin
cabin, n. — ME. cabane, fr. F. cabane, fr. Late
L. capanna, which is of Illyric origin. It. capan-
na, Sp. cabana also derive fr. Late L. capanna.
F. cabine and It. cabino are English loan words.
Cp. caboose, Cp. also cuddy, 'cabin in a ship'.
Derivative: cabin, tr. v.

## cabinet
cabinet, n. — It. gabinetto,pioh. dimin. oSgabbia,
'cage', fr. L. cavea. See cage and -et.
Derivative: cabinet-ry, n.

## Cabiri
Cabiri, n. pi., a group of Greek gods (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Κάβειροι, fr. Heb. kabbir,
'great, mighty', fr. base *k-b-r, 'to be great, to
be much, many'. Cp. their title Μεγάλοι θεοί,
'the great gods', which corroborates the above
etymology.

## cable
cable, n. — ME. cable, cabel, kable, fr. F. cable,
fr. Port, cable, which is a blend of Arab, (tabl,
'rope, cable', and VL. cap(u)lum, 'a halter for
cattle', fr. capio, capere, 'to catch, seize, take,
hold'. Arab, habl is rel. to habala, 'he bound',
Heb. hebhel, 'rope, cord', Ethiop. habal, 'rope',
habala, 'he bound', Akkad. nahbalu, 'rope,
snare', Aram, habhld, 'cord, rope'. For the
etymology of L. capere see captive.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:130 COLUMN:2 -->
с
Derivatives: cable, v., cabl-ed, adj., cabl-er, п.,
cabl-ing, п., cabl-et, n.

## cablegram
cablegram, n. — A blend of cable and telegram.

## cabob
cabob, п., roast meat (Anglo-Ind.) — Hind.
kabab, fr. Pers. kabab.
Derivative: cabob, tr. v.

## cabochon
cabochon, п., a polished but uncut precious
stone. — F., fr. caboche, 'head, pate, noddle,
nob'. See cabbage.

## Cabomba
Cabomba, п., a genus of aquatic plants (bot.) —
ModL., a name of American Indian origin.

## caboodle
caboodle, п., group, lot (slang). — Corruption of
kit and boodle. See kit, 'wooden tub', and
boodle.

## cabook
cabook, п., laterite (Ceylon). —Port, cavouco
(also cabouco), short forpedras de cavouco, 'quarry
stones', fr. cavo, 'concave', fr. L. cavus, 'hollow,
concave'. See cave, n.

## caboose
caboose, п., ι) a ship's galley; 2) the trainmen's
car on a goods train. — Du. kabuis, fr. MLG.
kabuse, a compound word, the first element of
which is prob. rel. to cabin. The second element
in MLG. kabuse was perh. orig. identical with
MLG. hits (— Du. huts); see house. Hence
MLG. kabuse and Du. kabuis would prop,
mean 'cabin' house'.

## caboshed
caboshed, adj., showing the animal's head full-
faced (affronte) and without the neck (her.) —
Formed with suff. -ed fr. F. caboche, 'head'. See
cabbage, n.

## cabotage
cabotage, п., coasting trade. — F., fr. caboter,
'to coast', fr. Sp. cabo, 'cape, promontory', fr.
L. caput, 'head*. See capital, adj., and cp. cape,
'promontory'.

## cabrerite
cabrerite, п., a hydrous arsenate of nickel, cobalt
and magnesium (mineral.) — Named after the
Sierra Cabrera in Spain. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## cabrilla
cabrilla, п., any fish of the genus Serranus. —
Sp., dimin. of cabra, 'she-goat', fr. L. capra, of
s.m. See cabriolet.

## cabriole
cabriole, п., a form of leg (furniture). — Prob.
fr. F. cabriole, 'leap of a goat, caper'. See next
word.

## cabriolet
cabriolet, п., a light two-wheeled carriage. — F.,
fr. cabriole, 'leap of a goat, caper', fr. cabrioler,
caprioler, 'to leap like a goat, to caper', fr. It.
capriolare, fr. capriuolo, 'roebuck', fr. L. capre-
olus, dimin. formed fr. caper, 'he goat', whence
capra, 'she-goat', which is rel. to Umbr. kabru,
kaprum (ace.), 'he-goat', and cogn. with" Gk.
κάπρος, 'boar', OE. hsefer, ON. hafr, 'he-goat',
G. Habergeiss, 'goatsucker'; so called from its
easy motion. Cp. caper, v. Cp. also cab, 'carriage',
cabriole, Capella, Caprella, capreol, Capreolus,
capri-, capric, Capricorn, caprification, caprine,
capriole, cheverel, chevron, chevrotain.

## cac-
cac-, form of caco- before a vowel

## Cacalia
Cacalia, п., a genus of plants, the Indian
plantain (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κακαλία, name of
a plant.

## cacao
cacao, n. — Sp., fr. Nahuatl caca-uatl, 'cacao
seed'. See coco.

## cachalot
cachalot, п., the sperm whale. — F., fr. Sp. ca-
chalote, fr. Port, cacholotte, lit. 'thick-headed',
fr. cachola, 'head, pate', which is perh. a dimin.
of cacha, 'handle of a razor', fr. VL. capula,
pi. of capulum, corresponding to L. capulus,
'handle, hilt of a sword', fr. capere, 'to catch,
seize'. See captive.

## cache
cache, п., hiding place. — F., 'hiding place', back
formation fr. cacher, 'to hide', fr. VL. *coacti-
cdre, 'to press together', freq. fr. L. coactare,
itself freq. fr. cogere, pp. coactus, 'to press

## together
together, force'. See со- and act and cp. coact,
cogent. Cp. also cachet.
Derivative: cache, v.

## cachectic
cachectic, adj., pertaining to cachexia. — Gk.
καχεκτικός, fr. καχεκτής, 'in a bad habit of the

## body'
body', fr. κακός, 'bad', and ϊχειν, 'to have'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:130 COLUMN:3 -->
cachexy and -ic.

## cachet
cachet, п., a distinguishing mark of quality or
authenticity. — F., 'seal, stamp', fr. cacher, 'to
hide'. See cache,

## cachexia
cachexia, cachexy, п., bad general state of health
(med.) — L., fr. Gk. καχεξία, lit. 'bad habit', fr.
κακός, 'bad', and 'έξις, 'state, condition, habit'.
For the first element see caco-. The second
element derives fr. ϊχειν (for *εχειν, ср. the fut
έξω), which is cogn. withjOI. sdhate, 'he masters',
sahah, 'victory', Goth, sigis, OE. sige, 'victory'.
See scheme and cp. words there referred to.

## cachinnate
cachinnate, intr.'v., to laugh loudly. —· L. cachin-
nat-(um), pp. stem of cachinnare, 'to laugh
loudly", of imitative origin. Cp. OI. kdkhati,
kakkhali, khakhati, 'laughs', Gk. καχάζειν, later
form κακχάζειν, 'to laugh loudly', OHG. ka-
chazzen, of s.m., Arm. xaxank', 'violent
laughter', which are all imitative.

## cachinnation
cachinnation, п., loud laughter. — L. cachin-
natio, gen. -onis, 'violent laughter', fr. cachinnat-
(um), pp. stem of cachinnare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## cacholong
cacholong, п., an opaque variety of opal. — F.,
fr. a Kalmuck word meaning 'beautiful stone'.

## cachou
cachou, n. — F. See cashew, catechu.

## Cachrys
Cachrys, п., a genus of herbs of the carrot family
(bot.) — Gk. κάχρυς, 'parched barley, catkin',
prob. rel. to κέγχρος, 'millet'. Cp. Cenchrus.

## cachucha
cachucha, п., a Spanish dance. — Sp., lit.
'recipient', fr. cacho, 'saucepan', fr. VL. 'cacculus,
'an earthen pot for cooking'. See cockle, 'stove'.

## cacique
cacique, п., a West Indian chief. — Sp., from a
Haitian language. .

## cachunde
cachunde, п., a pastil (pharm.) — Sp., fr. cachu.
See cashew, catechu,

## cack
cack, intr. v., to void excrement (dial.) — ME.
cakken, fr. L. cacare, which, like Gk. κακκαν,
Russ. kdkat\ Mir. caccaim, etc., derives from
the I.-E. child's word *kakka, 'to void
excrement'. Cp. Cagot.

## cackle
cackle, intr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp. Du.
kakelen, 'to chatter, gabble'. Cp. also quack
and gabble.
Derivatives: cackle, п., cackl-er, п., cacki-ing, n.

## caco
caco, п., a bandit. — Sp., 'thief, fr. L. Cacus =
Gk. Κακός, son of Vulcan; he terrified the
country round about Mount Aventinus by his
robberies and was slain by Hercules.

## caco-
caco-, before a vowel cac-, combining form
meaning 'bad, ill, poor'. — Gk. κακό-, κακ-, fr.
κακός, 'bad, evil', prob. orig. a word from the
child's language. Cp. the first element in
cachexy, kakistocracy, and the second element in
stomacace.

## cacodyl
cacodyl, п., a poisonous, malodorous radical
As(CHj)2 (chem.) — Lit. 'ill smelling matter';
coined by the Swedish chemist Baron Jons
Jakob Berzelius (l 779-1848) from Gk. κακώδης,
'ill smelling', and suff. -yl. Gk. κακώδης is
compounded of κακό- (see caco-) and the stem of
δζειν, 'to smell'. See ozo-, odor,

## cacoepy
cacoepy, п., bad pronunciation. — Gk. κακο-
έπεια, 'bad language', compounded of κακο-
(see caco-) and -έπεια, fr. £πος, 'word'. See
epos and cp. orthoepy.
Derivatives: cacoep-ist, п., cacoep-ist-ic, adj.

## cacoethes
cacoethes, п., a bad habit. — Gk. κακόηθες, neut.
of the adj. κακοήθης, 'of ill habits', used as a
noun; compounded of κακό- (see caco-) and
ήθος, 'habit'. See ethic,

## cacography
cacography, п., bad writing. — Compounded of
caco- and Gk. -γραφία, fr. γράφέιν, 'to write'.

## See -graphy and cp. calligraphy
See -graphy and cp. calligraphy,

## cacology
cacology, п., bad speaking; bad pronunciation.
— Compounded of caco- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);

## one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## caconym
caconym, п., a bad name. — Compounded of
caco- and Gk. όνυμα, dialectal form of 8νομα,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:131 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CACOON | 104 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:131 COLUMN:1 -->
'name'. See name and cp. onomato-.
Derivative: caconym~ic, adj.

## cacoon
cacoon, п., the tropical bean. — Of uncertain
origin.

## cacophonous
cacophonous, adj., ill-sounding. — Gk. κακό-
φώνος, compounded of κακό- (see caco-) and
φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See phone. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see suff. -ous.

## cacophony
cacophony, п., a harsh or discordant sound. —
Gk. κακοφωνία, fr. κακόφωνος. See prec. word
and -y (representing Gk. -Ей).

## Cactaceae
Cactaceae, n. pi., the cactus family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. cactus with suff. aceae.

## cactaceous
cactaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## cactiform
cactiform, adj., resembling a cactus in form. —
Compounded of Cactus and -form.

## cactus
cactus, n. — L., 'a prickly plant', fr. Gk. κάκτος,
of s.m., which is prob. a pre-Hellenic word of
unknown origin.

## cacuminal
cacuminal, adj., 1) pertaining to the top; 2) in
phonetics, pronounced with the tip of the tongne
turned upward; cerebral. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. сасйтеп, 'top, summit', which is
cogn. with OI. kakubh-, 'peak', kakud-, 'peak,
top', kakud-, 'mouth-cavity, palate'; from a
dental enlargement of the reduplication of I.-E.
base *qeu-, 'to bend', for which see cubit, high.
L. сасйтеп prob. developed fr. orig. 'kakud
under the influence of acumen, 'sharpened
point' (see acumen).

## cacuminate
cacuminate, tr. v., to make pointed or sharp. —
L. cacuminatus, pp. of cacuminare, 'to point',
fr. сасйтеп, gen. cacuminis. See prec. word and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: cacumin-alion, n.

## cacuminous
cacuminous, adj., pointed (said 01' the top of
a tree). — See cacuminal and -ous.

## Cacns
Cacns, п., son of Vulcan, a giant, slain by
Hercules in his cave in the Aventine (Roman my-
Ihol.) — L. CScus, of uncertain etymology.

## cad
cad, n. — Shortened fr. caddie, caddy.
Derivatives: cadd-ish, adj., cadd-ish~ly, adv.,
cadd-ish-ness, n.

## cadamba
cadamba, п., an East Indian tree. — Kanarese
kaaamba-. Cp. OI. kadambah, 'Nauclea
cadamba', which is prob. of Dravidian origin (see
Manfred Mayrhofer, A Concise Etymol.
Sanskrit Dictionary I, 144 and 149).

## cadastral
cadastral, adj., pertaining to a cadaster. — F.,
fr. cadastre. See cadastre and adj. suff. -al.

## cadastre
cadastre, cadaster, n. — F. cadastre, 'register of
the survey of lands', fr. OProvenc. cadastre, fr.
It. catastro, catasto, fr. Olt. catastico, fr. Late
Gk. κατάστιχον, 'register', lit. 'by the line',
formed fr. Gk. κατά (see cata-) and στίχος,
'row, line'. See acrostic.

## cadaver
cadaver, п., a dead body, a corpse. — L., 'a dead
body, a corpse', fr. cadere, 'to fall'; see cadence.
For sense development cp. Gk. πτώμα, 'corpse',
which is rel. to -ί-τειν, 'to fall' (perf. ττέ-τωκα\
and Heb. nebhelah, 'carcass, corpse', fr. nabhel,
'it decayed, withered', which is rel. to naphal,
'he fell'. Cp. ptomaine.
Derivatives: cadav-er-ic, adj., cadaverous (q.v.)

## cadaverous
cadaverous, adj., looking like a corpse; pale. —
L. cadaverosus, 'corpselike', fr. cadaver, 'a dead
body, corpse'. See cadaver and -ous.
Derivatives: cadaverous-ly, adv., cadaverous-
ness, n.

## caddie
caddie, caddy, п., a person who carries one's golf
clubs, etc. — F. cadet. See cadet and cp. cad.
Derivative: caddie, caddy, to act as a caddie.

## caddis
caddis, п., ι) worsted yarn (obsol.); 2) lint. —
Prob. fr. OF. cadaz, cadas, also cadarce, fr.
OProvenc. cadarz, which is of uncertain origin;
confused with F. cadis, 'light woolen serge'.
See next word.

## caddis
caddis, п., a kind of cheap serge. — F. cadis,
'light woolen serge', fr. OProvenc. cadis, prob.
fr. Sp. Cadiz, of s.m., which apparently comes
from the name of the city of Cadiz and orig.
meant 'material made at Cadiz'.

## cnddie
cnddie, п., the larva of the caddis fly. — Of
uncertain origin.

## caddy
caddy, п., a small box; orig. used only in the sense
of tea caddy. — Fr. earlier catty, prop, 'a box
containing a catty of tea', fr. Malay kati, a
weight of 1 1/3 lb. Cp. catty.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:131 COLUMN:2 -->

## cade
cade, п., a small barrel. — F., fr. L. cadus, 'bottle,
jar, jug', fr. Gk. κάδος, fr. Heb. kadh, 'pitcher',
prop, 'a rounded vessel', fr. base *k-d-d, 'to be
round'. Cp. cadus.

## cade
cade, п., a juniper (Juniperus oxycedrus). — F„
fr. OProvenc. cade, fr. Late L. calanus, 'cedar
juniper', which is prob. a loan word fr. Sabine
catanus, 'a plant with pointed leaves', fr. Sabine-
L. catus, 'sharp, pointed'. See bone,

## -cade
-cade, suff. denoting a group or the contest of a
group. — Adopted fr. the suff. -cade in
cavalcade (q.v.); accordingly this suff. is the
equivalent of L. -(i)catus. See 2nd -ade and cp.
aquacade, motorcade and subst. suff. -ate.

## cadence
cadence, n. — F., fr. It. cadenza, fr. VL. "cadentia,
a fem. noun, fr. L. cadentia, neut. pi. of cadlns,
gen. -enlis, pres. part, of cadere, 'to fall', which
is cogn. with OI. tad-, 'to fall down', Arm. cac-
num, 'to fall, become low', and possibly also
with It. casair, W. cesair, Co. keser, 'hail'. Cp.
chance, which is a doublet of cadence. Cp. also
accident, cadaver, cadenza, caducity, .cascade,
case, 'condition', casual, cbent, chute, coiacide,
decadence, decay, decheauce, deciduous, escheat,
incident, occasion, Occident, parachute, recidivist.
Derivatives: cadence, tr. v., cadenc-ed, adj.,
cadenc-y, n.

## cadenza
cadenza, п., an ornamental flourish (music). —
It., fr. VL. *cadentia; prop, 'a flourish before
the cadence', whence its name. See cadence,

## cadet
cadet, п., 1) a younger son or brother; 2) a
student at a military or naval school. — F., fr.
Gascon capdet, which corresponds to OProveng.
capdel, 'chief, fr. VL. *capitellus, dimin. formed
fr. L. caput, gen. capitis, 'head'. See capital, adj.,
and cp. cad, caddie,

## cadge
cadge, v., to beg. — Back formation fr. cadger.
For similar back formations cp. peddle, swindle.

## cadger
cadger, п., a hawker. — The word orig. denoted
'one who brought in a cadge or basket eggs,
poultry etc. from the country to the market'.
Cadge derives fr. F. cage in the sense of'basket'.
See cage-

## cadi
cadi, п., a minor Mohammedan judge. — Arab.
qadi, 'judge', prop, partic. oiqadd. 'he decided',
rel. to Heb. qStzln, 'judge, prince, leader'. Cp.
alcalde,

## cadjan
cadjan, п., palm leaves for thatching or matting.
— Malay kajang, 'a matting of palm leaves'.

## Cadmean
Cadmean, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
Cadmus. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Cadmeus,
fr. Gk. Καδμείος, 'Cadmean', fr. Κάδμος,
'Cadmus'. See Cadmus,

## cadmia
cadmia, п., calamine. — L. cadmia. See next
word.

## cadmium
cadmium, п., a white metallic element (chem.) —
ModL., coined by its discoverer, the German
chemist Friedrich Strohmeyer (1776-1835) in
18)7, fr. L. cadmia, 'calamine', fr. Gk. καδμεία,
of s.m., which stands for Καδμεία (scil. γη), lit.
'Cadmean (earth)", fr. Κάδμος, 'Cadmus'. See
next word.
Derivative: cadm-ic, adj.

## Cadmus
Cadmus, п., son of the Phoenician king Agenor
and founder of Thebes (Greek mythol.) — L.,
fr. Gk. Κάδμος, a name of Sem. origin, prop,
denoting 'the man who came from the Easf.
Cp. Heb. qedem (fr. base qadm-), 'East', qiddem,
'he was in front, met', qadmon, 'eastern;
ancient', Ugar. qdm, 'front', Arab, qadama, Ethiop.
qaddma, 'he preceded', Akkad. qudmu, 'front;
former time'. Cp. cadmium, calamine, Camillas.
For other mythological names of Hebrew origin
cp. Danae, Danaus, Niobe.

## cadre
cadre, п., frame, framework; framework of a
regiment. — F., fr. It. quadra, fr. L. quadrus,
'square'. See quadri-.

## caduceus
caduceus, п., the wand of a herald, specif., the
wand of Hermes (Mercury). — L. caduceus,
'herald's staff', fr. Dor. Gk. κδρδκειον
(corresponding Шх Att. κηρΰκειον), of s.m., fr. κάρϋξ
(resp. κήρυξ), 'herald', whence καρΰσσειν (resp.
κηρύσσειν), 'to proclaim' (said of a herald); rel.
to Gk. καρκαίρειν, 'to resound', and cogn. with
OI. carkarti, 'mentions with praise', carkjrtih,
'praise, glory', karuh, 'singer, poet', OHG.
-hruod, -ruod (in compounds), ON. hrodr, OE.

## hred
hred, 'fame; glory'. Cp. kerygma. Cp. also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:131 COLUMN:3 -->
rummer.

## caducity
caducity, п., perishableness. — F. caducite, 'per-
ishableness, frailty', fr. caduc, 'perishable, frail',
fr. L. caducus, 'falling, fallen, inclined to fall',
fr. cadere, 'to fall'. See cadence and -ity.

## cadncous
cadncous, adj., perishable. — L. caducus. See
prec. word. For E. -ous, as equivalenl to L. -us,
see suff. -ous.

## cadus
cadus, п., a large vessel for liquids. — L., fr. Gk.
κάδος. See cade, 'a small barrel'.

## caecal
caecal, adj., pertaining to the caecum (anat.) —
Formed fr. caecum with adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: caecal-ly, adv.

## Caecias
Caecias, п., personification of the northeast
wind. — L. caecias, fr. Gk. καικίας, 'northeast
wind', lit. 'the dark one', cogn. with L. caecus,
'blind'; see next word. For sense development
cp. Aquilo.

## caecum
caecum, п., the blind gut (anat) — L., neut. of
the adj. caecus, 'blind', in ML. colon caecum,
'blind gut', a medical term traceable to the
definition of the blind gut as του έντερου τυφλόν-
Tt (lit. 'some blind part of the intestine'), given
by Aristotle in his work De partibus animalium,
3, 14. L. caecus is cogn. with Gk. καίκίας,
'northeast wind', lit. 'the dark one' (cp. L.
Aquilo, 'north wind', fr. aquilus, 'dark'), OI.
kekarah, 'squinting', Olr. caech, 'one-eyed',
Mir. let-chaech, 'squinting', W. coeg, 'empty',
coeg-ddall, 'one-eyed', Goth, 'haihs, 'one-eyed'.
Cp. Caecias, cecity, and the second element in
pichiciago.

## Caeoma
Caeoma,n.,a form genus of rusts (bot.)— ModL.,
fr. Gk. καίειν, which prob. stands for κά5-ιειν,
'to burn', whence καυστός, 'burnt', καυστικός,
'capable of burning' (see caustic); so called
because of its fiery-red color.

## Caesar
Caesar, masc. PN. — L., of uncertain origin. Cp.
czar, kaiser.
Derivatives: Caesar-ism, п., Caesar-ize, tr. and
intr. v.

## Caesarean
Caesarean, adj., 1) pertaining to Caesar; 2)
pertaining to the Caesarian section. — Formed
with suff. -aa fr. L. Caesareus, fr. Caesar. See
Caesar.

## Caesarean section
Caesarean section, Caesarean operation. — So
called from the belief that Julius Caesar was
thus delivered. This belief is refuted by the fact
that the mother of Caesar was still, alive at
the time of the Gallic wars, whereas, on the
other hand, we know that in antiquity this
operation was never performed on the living
mother.

## Caesarian
Caesarian, adj., Caesarean. — L. Caesarianus,
fr. Caesar. See Caesar, Caesarean.

## Caesarism
Caesarism, caesarism, п., an absolute
government resembling that of Caesar; imperialism. —
F. cisarisme, coined by the French man of
letters and dramatist Auguste Romieu (1800-1855)
fr. Cesar (fr. L. Caesar) and suff. -isme. See
Caesar and -ism.

## caesious
caesious, adj., grayish blue. — L. caesius, 'bluish
gray', of uncertain etymology. It possibly
derives fr. *qaid-to-, or *qait-to-, 'bright, shining',
and is rel. to caelum, 'ceiling'. See celestial and
cp. words there referred to. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## caesium
caesium, n. — See cesium.

## caesura
caesura, п., break in a verse (pros.) — L., 'a
cutting', formed fr. caesus, pp. of caedere, 'to cut'.
See cement and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: caesur-al, caesur-ic, adjs.

## cafard
cafard, п., a hypocrite. — F., 'hypocrite', fr.
Arab, kdfir, 'infidel', part, oikafara, 'he blotted
out, covered; he denied', with substitution of
the French pejorative suff. -ard for the unusual
ending -ir. See Kaffir and -ard.

## cafardise
cafardise, п., hypocrisy. — F., 'hypocrisy',
formed fr. prec. word with suff. -ise.

## cafe
cafe, п., ι) coffee; 2) coffeehouse; restaurant. —
F., fr. It. cage, fr. Turk, qahve, fr. Arab, qahva",
'wine; coffee'. See coffee.

## cafeteria
cafeteria, п., a restaurant at which the patrons
serve themselves from the food displayed at a
counter. — Mexican Sp., meaning 'retail coffee
store'. Cp. F. cafetiere and see prec. word.

## caffeine
caffeine, caffein, п., an alkaloid obtained from
coffee and tea (chem.) — F. cafeine, fr. cafe.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:132 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 105 | CALCIFEROUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:132 COLUMN:1 -->
'coffee'. See coffee and chem. suff. -ine, resp. -in.

## cafila
cafila, п., a convoy of travelers, caravan. — Arab.
qdfila11, fem. used as a collective noun fr. qdfil,
'one who returns from a journey1, part, of qa-
fala, 'he returned from a journey'.

## cafiz
cafiz, п., a measure of capacity. — Sp., fr. Arab.
qaftz, a measure for corn.

## caftan
caftan, п., a long-sleeved garment worn in
Turkey, Egypt, etc.—Turk.ga/rdn.fr. Arab, qaftdn,
fr. Pers. khaftan.

## cage
cage, n. — F., fr. L. cavea, 'an excavated place,
a hollow, cavity; enclosure for animals, cage',
fr. cavus, 'hollow'. Cp. It. gabbia, 'basket for
fowls, coop', gaggia, 'basket', OProvenc. gabia,
'prison', Sp. gavia, 'a place where madmen
are confined', which all derive fr. L. cavea, and
see cave, n. Cp. also cabinet, cadger, cajole,
decoy, gabion, jail.
Derivatives: cage, tr. v., cag-er, n.

## Cagot
Cagot, п., one of an outcast race in southern
France. — F., 'bigot, hypocrite', from cagot,
'leper', a word of the Beam dialect, derived fr.
L. cacdre, 'to stool' (see cack), used in a
pejorative sense to denote the leper, the hypocrite,
the deceiver, etc.

## cahier
cahier, п., a number of sheets of paper stitched
together, a report.—F., fr. OF. quaer, caer, carer,
fr. VL. quaternum, 'four sheets of paper', fr. L.
qualerni, 'four together, four each' See qnire,
'sheets of paper'.

## cahnite
cahnite, п., a hydrous calcium boroarsenate
(mineral.) — Named after L. Cahn, of Colorado
(U.S.A.) For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## caiman
caiman, n. — See cayman.

## Cain
Cain, п., in the Bible, the oldest son of Adam and
Eve. — L., fr. Gk. Κάιν, fr. Heb. Qayin, lit.
'created, creature', from stem q-y-n, 'to form,
fashion', whence also qayin, 'weapon', lit. 'that
which is formed by the craftsman'. The same
base appears in Aram, qena'd, Syr. qenayd,
'worker in metal', and in Arab, qayn, 'craftsman,
worker in steel or another metal, smith'. These
words are rel. to Heb. qandh, 'he created, formed
made' (for this meaning see Gen. 14:19 and 22,
Deut. 32:6, Ps. 139:13, Prov. 8:22), whence
developed the meanings 'he got, acquired; he
bought'. This relationship between the name
Qayin and the verb qandh accounts best for the
fact that in Gen. 4:1 Eve explains the name
Qayin with the word qanilhi. This word is usually
translated, Ί have gotten', but it is more
probable that its sense here is Ί have formed', Ί
have made'. See U. Cassuto, A Commentary on
the Book of Genesis, Part One, From Adam to
Noah, The Hebrew University, Jerusalem, 1961,
pp. 196-202. Cp. Elkanah, kinah.

## caique
caique, п., a light rowing or sailing boat, used
esp. on the Bosporus. — F., fr. It. caicco, fr.
Turk, kayik.

## caird
caird, п., a wandering tinker (Scot.) — Gael., Ir.
ceard, 'tinker', rel. to. Olr. cerd,''smith; poet',
W. cerdd. 'song', and prob. cogn. with Gk.
κέρδος, 'gain, profit'.

## cairn
cairn, п., a heap of stones. — Gael, earn, gen.
cairn, 'heap', rel. to W. and Ir. cam, of s.m. Cp.
the first element in cairngorm.

## cairngorm
cairngorm, п., a yellow crystal. — From the name
of the Scottish mountain Cairngorm, where it is
found. This name is compounded of cairn and
Gael, gorm, 'blue'.

## caisson
caisson, п., box, chest. — F., fr. It. cassone, which
is formed with the augment, suff. -one fr. cassa,
fr. L. capsa, 'chest, box, receptacle'. See case,
'chest', and -oon and cp. capsule.
Derivative: caisson-ed, adj.

## caitiff
caitiff, п., a mean person, a coward; adj., mean,
cowardly. — ME. caitif, 'captive, miserable', fr.
ONF. caitif, which corresponds to OF. chaitif,
'captive; wretched' (whence F. chitif, 'weak,
sickly; miserable, wretched'), fr. L. captivus,
'prisoner' (see captive). Caitiff represents the
early borrowing, its doublet captive is a later
scholarly form; both came into English through
the medium of French.

## caja
caja, п., a cashier's office. — Sp., 'box, chest,
cashier'soffice,fr.L.capia,'box, chest', fr.capere,
'to catch, seize, take, receive, hold'. See case,
'box', and cp. cash,'ready money'. Cp. alsocajeta.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:132 COLUMN:2 -->

## cajaput
cajaput, cajeput, n. — Variants of cajuput.

## cajeta
cajeta, п., a small chest. — Sp., dimin. of caja,
'box, chest'. See caja.

## cajole
cajole, tr. and intr. v. — F. cajoler. The word orig.
meant 'to chatter like a jay in a cage' and is an
alteration of gaioler (a word used in the 16th
cent.), fr. Picard gaiole, 'cage', fr. Late L
caveola, 'cage', dimin. of L. cavea, 'cage'; see
cage. The change of gaioler to cajoler is due
to the influence of F. cage.
Derivatives: cajole, п., cajole-ment, п., cajol-er,
п., cajol-er-y, п., cajol-ing, adj., cajol-ing-ly, adv.

## Cajun
Cajun, п., a native of Louisiana, supposed to be
of Acadian French descent. — Corruption of
Acadian.

## cajuput
cajuput, п., an East Indian tree. — Malay kayu-
putih, lit., 'white tree', fr. kdyu, 'tree', and
putih, 'white'.

## cake
cake, n. — ME., fr. ON. kaka, rel. to MDu. koke,
Du. коек, its dimin. koekje, OHG. chuohho,
kuocho, MHG. kuoche, G. Kuchen; prob. of
imitative origin. The a-o gradation of these
words testifies to their Teut. origin (cp. ON.
taka, 'take', Idk, 'took'). They are not related
to cook. Cp. cooky, kuchen. Cp. also Cockaigne.
Derivatives: cake, v., cak-y, adj.

## Cakile
Cakile, п., a genus of plants of the mustard family
(hot) — F., fr. Arab, qdqulld, also qdqulla11,
name of a plant.
Calabar bean. — Named after Calabar on the
west coast of Africa.

## calabash
calabash, п., a tropical tree of the bignonia
family and its gourdlike fruit. — F. calebasse,
fr. Sp. calabaza, corruption of Arab, qar'a*
ydbisa", 'dry gourd'.

## calaber
calaber, п., a kind of squirrel fur. — Fr. Caiabre,
French name of Calabria, the southeastern
peninsula of Italy.

## calaboose
calaboose, п., a prison (Southern part of the U.S.A.)
— Sp. calabozo, 'prison, cell', prob. fr. VL. *ca-
lafodium, which is compounded of pre-Latin
*calar, 'a protected place, cave', and L. fodere,
'to dig'. See fosse.

## Caladium
Caladium, п., a genus of plants of the arum family
(bot.) — ModL., coined by Rumph in 1750 fr.
Malay kaladi, 'a kind of arum'.

## Calamagrostis
Calamagrostis, п., the reed bent grass (bot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. κάλαμος, 'a reed',
and άγρωστις, 'a grass'. See Calamus and
Agrostis.

## calamanco
calamanco, п., a woolen cloth. — Cp. ML. cala-
macus, calamancus, Sp. calamaco, G. Kalamank,
Kalmank; of uncertain origin.

## calamander wood
calamander wood, calamander, п., wood of a tree
growing in Ceylon. — Corruption of Coroman-
del, name of part of the eastern coast of
southern India.

## calamary
calamary, п., squid. —L. calamdrius, 'pertaining
to a pen', fr. calamus, 'reed, pen', fr. Gk.
κάλαμος, prob. an assimilated form of orig.
'κάλαμος, and, accordingly, cognate with L. culmus,
'stock, stem'. See culm, 'stem of grasses', and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also the first
element in calamint, caramel.

## calamine
calamine, п., a kind of zinc ore. — F., fr. ML.
calamina, fr. L. cadmia, fr. Gk. καδμεία,
'calamine', fr. Κάδμος, 'Cadmus', the founder of
Thebes; so called because this mineral was found
first in the vicinity of Thebes. See Cadmus,
cadmium.

## calamint
calamint, п., an aromatic plant.— ME. calament,
fr. OF. calament, fr. ML. calamentum, fr. L. cala-
minthe.fr. Gk. καλαμΜΗ), which is compounded
of κάλαμος, 'reed', and μίν&η, 'minth'. See
calamary and mint, 'an aromatic herb'. For the
contraction of *καλαμο-μινθη into καλαμίνθη
see haplology.

## calamitous
calamitous, adj., producing calamity, disastrous.
— F. calamiteux (fem. -euse), fr. L. caldmitosus,
haplological contraction of *calumitatSsus, fr.
caldmitas. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: calamitous-ly, adv., calamitous-
ness, n.

## calamity
calamity, п., misery; disaster. — F. catamite, fr.
L. calumitatem, ace. of caldmitds, 'damage,
injury, loss, misfortune', with the primary
meaning 'blow', rel. to in-columis, 'unimpaired,
uninjured', fr. I.-E. base *qel(d)-, *qol(d)-,'to strike,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:132 COLUMN:3 -->
beat', whence also Gk. κλϊν, 'to break', κλήρος,
Dor. κλαρος, prop, 'little piece of wood lopped
off (used for casting lots)', hence 'a casting of
lots'. See holt and cp. words there referred to.

## calamus
calamus, п., reed. — L. See calamary.

## calando
calando, adv. and adj., growing slower (mus.) —
It., fr. calare, 'to let down, lower', fr. L.
colore, chaldre, 'to let down', fr. Gk. χαλάν, 'to
let down, loosen'.

## Calanthe
Calanthe, п., a genus of orchids (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. καλός, 'beautiful', and
αν&ος, 'flower'. See calo- and anther.

## calapite
calapite, п., mass found in coconuts. — Fr. Malay
kaiapa, 'coco tree'.

## calash
calash, п., a kind of carriage. — F. caliche, fr.
Czech kolesa, 'wheels, carriage', pi. of koleso,
'wheel', fr. kolo, 'wheel', which is rel. to OPruss.
kelan, 'wheel', and cogn. with Gk. κύκλος,
'circle', OE. hweogol, hweot, 'wheel'. See wheel
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: calash, tr. v.

## Calathea
Calathea, п., a genus of plants of the arrowroot
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κάλαί^ος,
'basket' (see next word); so called from the shape
of the flowers.

## calathus
calathus, п., a basket (Greek antiq.) — L., fr. Gk.
κάλα&ος, 'basket', prop, meaning 'a plaited
basket', and rel. to κλώθ-ειν, 'to spin'. See Clotho
and cp. Clostridium.

## calcaneum
calcaneum, п., one' of the bones of the tarsus
(anat.) — L. calcaneum (rarely calcaneus),
'heel', a derivative of calx, gen. calcis, of s.m.
See Calceolaria, and cp. calk, 'to stop up the
seams of a ship with oakum'.

## calcaneus
calcaneus, п., one of the bones of the tarsus (anat.)
— See prec. word.

## calcareous
calcareous, adj., pertaining to, or containing,
lime or calcium. — L. calcdrius, 'pertaining to
lime', fr. calx, gen. calcis, 'limestone, lime,
pebble', a loan word fr. Gk. χάλιξ, 'small stone,
pebble', which prob. derives fr. I.-E. *(s)q(h)e-
liq-, enlargement of base "(s)qel-, 'to cut, cleave,
split'. See colter and cp. silica. Cp. also calcine,
calculate, calculus, calx, cauk, causeway, causey,
chalk, chaussee. — The right spelling of the word
would be calcarious (a form now obsolete), the
English correspondence of L. -drius being
-arious (or -ary).
Derivatives: calcareous-ly, adv., calcareous-ness,
n.

## calceate
calceate, adj., shod (said of members of religious
orders). — L. calceatus, pp. of calcedre, 'to
furnish with shoes', fr. calceus. See Calceolaria
and adj. suff. -ate and cp. discalceate.

## calced
calced, adj., calceate. — Formed with suff. -ed
fr. L. calceus, 'shoe'. See next word.

## Calceolaria
Calceolaria, п., a genus of plants of the figwort
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. calceoldrius,
'shoemaker', fr. calceolus, 'a little shoe', dimin. of
calceus, 'shoe', fr. calx, geri. calcis, 'heel', which
is rel. to calcar, 'spur', caliga, 'military shoe or
sandal', inculcare, 'to tread down', calcitrdre,
'to kick, be stubborn', and cogn. with OSIav.
kluka, 'knee', Lith. kulnas, kulnis, 'heel', Lith.
kulse, kulSis, OPruss. eulezi, 'hip', Lith. kul(k)-
sis, kulksnis, 'ankle, hock'. All these words
prob. meant orig. 'something bent' and derive
fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'crooked, bent', whence
also Gk.κωλέά,κωλή, 'thighbone', κώλον,'limb,
member'. See colon, 'punctuation mark', and
cp. calcaneum, caliga, calk, Ίο stop up the
seams of a ship with oakum', calk, 'to copy',
calkin, caltrop, cockatrice, discalceate, iacul-
cate, recalcitrate. This genus of plants was called
Calceolaria from the slipperlike appearance of
the flower.

## Catenas
Catenas, п., son of Thestor, soothsayer of the
Greeks before Troy (Greek mythol.) — L. Cal-
chas, fr. Gk. Κάλχας, a name of uncertain
etymology.

## calci-
calci-, combining form denoting 'lime' or
'calcium'. — L. calci-, stem of calx, gen. calcis,
'lime'. See calcareous.

## calcic
calcic, adj., pertaining to lime or calcium. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. calx, gen. calcis,
'lime'. See calcareous.

## calciferous
calciferous, adj., containing carbonate of lime. —
Lit. 'lime-bearing', compounded of calci- and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:133 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CALCIFICATION | 106 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:133 COLUMN:1 -->
L. ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See -ferous.

## calcification
calcification, п., conversion into chalk;
petrifaction, ossification. — See calci- and -fica-
tion.

## calcify
calcify, tr. v., to make calcareous; intr. v., to
become calcareous. — F. calcifier. See calci-
and -fy.

## calcination
calcination, п., the act qr process of calcining. —
F., fr. calciner, 'to calcine'. See next word and
-ation.

## calcine
calcine, tr. v., ]) to reduce to calx by heat; 2) to
burn to ashes. — F. calciner, fr. ML. calcinare,
'to reduce to lime', fr. L. calx, gen. calcis, 'lime'.
See calcareous.

## calciphylaxis
calciphylaxis, п., increased sensitivity to
calcium (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined by
Dr. Hans Selye (born in 1907), professor of the
University of Montreal, fr. calcium, a word of
Latin origin, and .Gk. φύλαξις, 'a watching,
guarding'. See phylaxis.

## calcite
calcite, п., native calcium carbonate (mineral.) —
G. Calcil, a hybrid coined by the Austrian
mineralogist and geologist Wilhelm Karl von
Haidinger (1795-1871) fr. L. calx, gen. calcis,
'lime', and sun", -it, fr. Gk. -(της. See calcareous
and subst. suff. -ite.

## calcium
calcium, a metallic element (chem.) — ModL.,
coined by the English chemist Sir Humphrey
Davy (1788-1829) fr. L. calx, calcis, 'lime'. See
calx, calcareous.

## calculable
calculable, adj. — F. calculable, St. calculer, 'to
compute, reckon, calculate', fr. L. calculare. See
calculate and -able.
Derivatives: calculabil-ily, п., calculabl-y, adv.

## calculary
calculary, adj., pertaining to calculi (med.) —·
Formed with adj. suff. -ary fr. L. calculus, 'stone,
pebble; stone in the bladder or kidneys'. See
calculns and cp. L. calculdrius, 'pertaining to
calculation'.

## calculate
calculate, tr. v. — L. calculaius, pp. of calculare,
'to reckon, compute, calculate*, fr. calculus, a
small stone, pebble, stone used in reckoning,
reckoning', dimin. of calx, gen. calcis, 'small
stone, pebble, stone used in gaming, counter'.
See calculus and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: calculat-ed, adj., calculat-ing. adj.,
calculation (q.v.), calculat-ive, adj., calculator
(q.v.), calculatory (q.v.)

## calculation
calculation, n. — L. cakuldtio, gen. -onis,
'reckoning, calculation', fr. calculatus, pp. of
calculare. See calculate and -ion.
Derivative: cakulation-al, adj.

## calculator
calculator, п., l) one who calculates; 2) a
calculating machine. — L. calculator, 'a computer',
fr. L. calculatus, pp. of calculare. See calculate
and agential suff. -or.

## calculatory
calculatory, adj. — L. calculatorius, 'pertaining
to reckoning', fr. calculatus, pp. of calculare.
See calculate and adj. suff. -ory and cp. prec.
word.

## calculus
calculus, п., 1) a method in calculation (math.);
2) a stonelike concretion in the body (med.) —
L. calculus, 'small stone, pebble, stone in the
bladder or kidneys; counter used in playing
drafts; stone used in reckoning', dimin. of calx,
gen. calcis, 'small stone, pebble, stone used in
gaming, counter'. See calcareous and cp.
calculate.

## caldarium
caldarium, п., the hot room in the Roman bath. —
L., prop. neut. of the adj. calidarius, caldarius,
'pertaining to warming', used as a noun, fr.
calidus, 'hot'. See next word.

## caldron
caldron, cauldroa, n. — ONF. cauderon, caudron
(corresponding to OF. chauderon, F. chaudron),
formed fr. OF. caudiere (F. chaudiere), fr. Late
L. caldaria, 'caldron', fr. L. calidarius,' caldarius,
'pertaining to warming', fr. calidus, caldus, 'hot',
fr. calere, 'to be warm', which derives fr. I.-E.
base *kel-, 'warm', whence also hith. situ, Silti, 'to
become warm', Siltas, 'warm', situs, more
exactly silius, 'August' (lit. 'the warm month'), W.
clyd, 'warm' (whence MW. claer, clayar,
'warm'), OI. sardd-, 'autumn', Avestic sar'S,
'year', ModPers. sal, of s.m. Cp. It. caldaia.
Rum. culdare, OProvenc. caudera, Catal. cal-
dira, Sp. caldera, Port. caldeira, 'caldron', which
all derive fr. VL. caldaria. Cp. calefacient,
calenture, calescence, callant, calorcscencc,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:133 COLUMN:2 -->
caloric, caudle, chafe, chaldron, chauffeur, chawdron,
chowder, rechauffe, scald, aonchalant. For prob.
derivatives of base *kleu-, enlargement of base
*kel-, 'warm', see lee.

## Caleb
Caleb, п., masculine PN.; in the Bible, one of the
twelve men sent by Moses to spy out the land
of Canaan. — Heb. Kdlebh, prop, 'like a dog',
fr. kelebh, 'dog'. Cp. Noldeke in ZDMG., 40,
p. 164, Note I. Cp. Aram, kalbd, Ugar. klb,
Ethiop. kalb, Akkad. kalbu, 'dog'.

## calefacieat
calefacieat, adj., producing heat, heating (med.)
—. L. calefaciens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of cale-
facere, 'to make warm', compounded of calere,
'to be warm', and facere, 'to make, do'. See
caldron and fact.
Derivative: calefacient, n.

## calefactory
calefactory, adj., making warm. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ory fr. calefactus, pp. oicalefacere, 'to
make warm'. See prec. word.

## calembour
calembour, п., pun. — F., of uncertain origin.

## calendar
calendar, n. — L. calendarium, 'an account book',
fr. calendae, kalendae, 'the first day of the
month' (sea calends). The account book was
called calendarium, because it contained the first
days of the months, on which the accounts were
due.
Derivatives: calendar, tr. v., calendar-er, п.,
calendar-ial, adj., calendar-ian, adj. and п.,
calendar-ic, adj.

## calender
calender, п., a mendicant dervish. — Pers.
qalender.

## calender
calender, п., machine with rollers for pressing
cloth. — F. calandre, 'calender, roller, mangle',
fr. earlier *colandre, fr. VL. 4colendra, fr. Gk.
κύλινδρος, 'roller, cylinder'. See cylinder.

## calender
calender, tr. v. — F. calandrer, fr. calandre. See
prec. word.
Derivative: calender-er, n.

## calends
calends, kalends, n. pi., the first day of the
ancient Roman month. — ME. kalendes, fr. OE.
calend, 'month', fr. L. calendae, kalendae, 'the
first day of the month', fr. calare, 'to call,
proclaim', which is rel. to Umbr. kafetu, kafitu,
carsitu (= L. calato), 'thou shalt (or he shall)
call', and cogn. with Gk. καλέω, Ί call', κέλαδος,
'noise, din', κελαρύζειν, 'to rush, purl', κέλωρ
(Hesychius), 'sound, voice', Lett. ka\uot, 'to
chatter', OHG. halon, 'to call', hellan, 'to
resound', hell, 'resounding', Olr. cailech, W. cei-
liog, Co. chelioc, Bret, kil'ek, 'cock', Lith. kalbd,
'language', kalbdsyti, 'to chatter', Lett, kalada,
'shouting, noise', OPruss. kaltza, kelsai, 'it
sounds', the second element in OI. usa-kalah,
'cock', Toch. В kal(n)-, AB kdl(n)-, 'to resound'.
All these words are derivatives of the I.-E.
imitative base *kel-, *kal-, 'to shout, resound'. Cp.
calendar, Calendula, intercalary, conciliate,
council. Cp. also claim, v., clear, ecclesia. Cp.
also low, 'to make the sound of a cow'.

## Calendula
Calendula, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. calendae, hence
lit. meaning 'the plant blossoming at the time
of calends'. See prec. word and -nle.

## calenture
calenture, п., tropical fever. — Sp. calentura, fr.
L. calens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of calere, 'to be
hot'. See caldroa.
Derivatives: calenture, tr. v., calentur-al, adj.

## calepin
calepin, п., a dictionary. — Named after Am-
brogio Calepino (1435-1511), author of a famous
Latin-Italian dictionary.

## calescence
calescence, п., increasing heat. — See next word
and -ce and cp. calorescence.

## calescent
calescent, adj., growing warm; increasing in
heat. — L. calescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
calescere, 'to grow hot', inchoative of calere,
'to be hot'. See caldron and -ent and cp. in-
calescent, recalescent.

## calf
calf, п., young of a cow, etc. — ME. calf, kalf,
fr. OE. cealf rel. to OS., MDu. calf, ON. kalfr,
Dan. kah, Swed., Du. kalf, OHG. chalp, kalb,
MHG. kalp, G. Kalb, Goth, kalbo, 'calf', OHG.
kilbur (neut.), kilburra (fern.), OE. cilforlamb,
ceolforlamb, 'ewe lamb', fr. I.-E. base *gwelbh-,
*g"Olbh-, 'womb; young of an animal', whence
also OI. gdrbhah, Avestic garewa-, 'womb', Gk.
δελφύς, δολφάς (in Hesychius), 'womb',
αδελφός, 'brother' (lit. 'from the same womb'),
Avestic g'r'bush, 'the young of an animal'. Cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:133 COLUMN:3 -->
adelpho-, dolphin, and the second element in
dagoba. Cp. also chilver.

## calf
calf, п., the fleshy part of the leg. — ON. kalfi,
'calf of the leg', generally supposed to be rel. to
kalfr, 'young of a cow', hence derivatively
identical with prec. word, but prob. not related to
it, but cogn. with OI. gulphds, 'ankle (bone)'.

## Caliban
Caliban, п., a brutal man. — Fr. Caliban, a
character in Shakespeare's Tempest. The name is
prob. a blend of Cariban and cannibal. The
association between these two words is so much
the more natural because the latter is a
derivative of the former.
Derivative: Caliban-ism, n.

## caliber
caliber, calibre, п., the diameter of the bore of a
gun. — F. calibre, fr. It. calibro, fr. Arab, qdlib,
'mold, model', fr. Gk. καλοπόδιον, 'shoemaker's
last*, dimin. of καλόπους, gen. καλόποδος, of
s.m., lit. 'a foot of wood', fr. κάλον, 'wood', esp.
'wood for burning', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot',
Gk. καλόν is contracted fr. 'κάί-ελο-ν or *κά/-
αλο-ν, a derivative of καίειν (for *κά5ιείν), 'to
burn'; see caustic. For the second element see
foot and cp. -pod. Gk. καλοπόδιον came into
Arabic through the medium of the Aramaic.

## calibrate
calibrate, tr. v., to determine the caliber of. —
A hybrid coined fr. caliber and -ate, a suff. of
Latin origin.
Derivative: calibrat-ion, n.

## calicle
calicle, п., a small cup-shaped cavity (zool.) —
L. caliculus, 'a small cup', dimin. of calix, gen.
calicis, 'cup'. See calyx and cp. calycle, calyculus.

## calico
calico, п., cotton cloth. — Named after Calicut in
the East Indies whence it was first imported.
Calico orig. meant 'cotton cloth from India'.

## caliculnr
caliculnr, adj., shaped like a calicle. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. caliculus, 'a small cup'.
See calicle.

## califoraium
califoraium, п., a radioactive element (chem.) —
ModL., named after the University of Califor-.
nia. For the ending see chem. suff. -ium.

## caliga
caliga, п., a heavy military shoe (Roman antiq.)
— L., rel. to calx, gen. calcis, 'heel', calcar,
'spur', calceus, 'shoe'. See Calceolaria.

## caliginous
caliginous, adj., dim, dark. — L. caliginosus, fr.
callgo, gen. cdliginis, 'darkness', fr. I.-E. base
*qal-, 'black, spotted', whence also Gk. κηλίς,
Dor. κάλίς, 'stain, spot, blemish', κηλάς (in
Hesychius), 'cloud wanting water', OSlav. kalu,
'mud, dirt', Olr. caile, 'spot', but OI. kalah,
'black; cuckoo', kali(!em.), 'black color, night',
are not derived from this base (see Albert
Thumb, Handbuch des Sanskrit, II, p. 202). Cp.
the related base *qel-, 'black, spotted', whence
Gk. κελαινός, 'black'. See Celaeno and cp.
Columba, columbine. For the ending sec suff. -ous.
Derivatives: caliginous-ly, adv., caliginous-
ness, n.

## caliginosity
caliginosity, п., dimness, darkness. — Formed
with suff. -iry fr. L. caliginosus. See prec. word.

## caligo
caligo, п., dimness of sight (med.) — L. callgo,
'darkness*. See culiginous.

## caliology
caliology, п., the study of birds' nests. —
Compounded of Gk. καλιά, 'hut, nest', and -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. The
first element is rel. to καλΰβη, 'hut, cabin',
καλύπτειν, 'to cover, hide, conceal', and cogn.
with L. cella, 'storeroom, granary', celdre, 'to
hide, keep secret', occulere, 'to cover, conceal';
see cell and words there referred to and cp. esp.
kalidium. For the second element see -logy.
Derivatives: caliolog-ic-al, adj., caliolog-ist, n.

## calipash
calipash, п., the edible greenish substance found
next 10 the upper shell of a turtle. — Prob.
alter, of carapace.

## calipee
calipee, п., the edible yellowish substance found
next to the lower shell of a turtle. — Prob.
alter, of calipash.

## caliper
caliper, calliper, n. — Variant spellings of
caliber. Derivatives: cal(l)iper, tr. and intr. v.,
cal(l)iper-er, n.

## caliph
caliph, calif, п., title of the successors of
Mohammed. — ME. caliphe, califfe, fr. F. caliphe, fr.
Arab. khalifah, 'successor', fr. khalafa, 'he
succeeded', which is rel. to Heb. haldph, 'he passed
on, passed away, changed', Aram, haldph, of
s.m., Syr. haldph, 'he changed, substituted*,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:134 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 107 | CALUMNIOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:134 COLUMN:1 -->
Ethiop. khalafa, 'he passed by, passed across'.
Cp. Collybia.

## caliphate
caliphate, п., office of a caliph. — Not the
transliteration of Arab, khilafa", bul a hybrid coined
fr. prec. word and -ate, a suff. of Latin origin.

## Calista
Calista, Callista, fem. PN. — Lit. 'most
beautiful', fr. Gk. καλλίστη, fem. of κάλλιστος. See
Callisto.

## calisthenic
calisthenic, callisthenic, adj., pertaining to, or
promoting, calisthenics. — See next word and
-ic.

## calisthenics
calisthenics, callisthenics, n. pi., ι) light
gymnastics tending to promote grace and health; 2)(con-
strued as a singular) the art of such gymnastics.
— Compounded of Gk. κάλλος, 'beauty', and
σθένος, 'strength'. Gk. κάλλος derives fr. καλός,
'beautiful'; see calo-. For the second element
see sthenic and cp. asthenia, neurasthenia. For
the ending of calisthenics see suff. -ics.

## calk
calk, caulk, tr. v., to stop up the seams of a ship
with oakum. — The original meaning was 'to
tread', fr. ME. cauken, fr. ONF. cauquier,
corresponding to OF. cauchier, chauchier (F. edeher),
'to tread', fr. L. calcare, 'to tread', fr. calx, gen.
calcis, 'heel'. See Calceolaria and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: calk, tr. v., calk-er, п., calk-ing, n.

## calk
calk, caique, tr. v., to copy. — F. calquer, 'to
trace, make a drawing', fr. It. calcare, lit. 'to
trample, tread', fr. L. calcare, 'to tread', whence
also OF. cauchier, chauchier. Accordingly calk,
'to copy', is derivatively identical with calk, 'to
stop up with oakum' (q.v.)

## calk
calk, п., projections at the ends of horseshoes to
prevent slipping. — Back formation fr. calkin.

## calkin
calkin, п., calk (in the sense of prec. word). —
OF. calcain, fr. L. calcanepm, 'heel', fr. calx,
gen. calcis, 'heel'. See calcaneum.

## call
call, intr. and tr. v. — ME. callen, fr. OE. ceal-
lian, 'to shout', rel. to ON. к alia, 'to shout,
sing', Du. kallen, 'to talk', OHG. kalian, 'to
call', and cogn. with Mir. gall, 'glory; swan',
W. galw, 'to call', OSlav. glasu (for "golsu),
'voice', Czech and Slovak hlas, of s.m., OSlav.
glasiti, 'to cry, announce', Czech hlasiti,
Slovak hlasii\ of s.m., OSlav. glagolu, 'word',
Czech and Slovak hlahol, 'loud talk', OSlav.
glagolati, 'to speak', Czech hlaholiti, Slovak
hlaholit', 'to sound'. Cp. Glagolitic.
Derivatives: call, п., call-able, adj., caller (q.v.), .
call-ing, n.

## Calla
Calla, п., a genus of plants of the arum family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. calla, calsa, name of a
plant.

## callant
callant, п., boy {Scot.) — Du. kalant (now klant),
'customer', fr. NF. caland, corresponding
to OF. chalant (F. chaland), 'customer', fr. OF.
chaloir, 'to be interested in', fr. L. callre, 'to be
warm', in VL. meaning also 'to be overheated,
become interested' (cp. It. calere, Sp. caler, 'to
import, matter'). See caldron and cp.
nonchalant.

## caller
caller, п., one who calls. — Formed from the
verb call with agential suff. -er.

## caller
caller, adj., fresh {Scot.) — Of uncertain origin.

## Callicarpa
Callicarpa, п., a genus of plants of the vervain
family {bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
κάλλος, 'beauty', and καρπός, 'fruit'. The first
element derives fr. καλός, 'beautiful'; see calo-.
The second element is cogn. with L. carpere, 'to'
pluck'; sec carpel.

## Callicebus
Callicebus, п., a genus of South American
monkeys (zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
κάλλος, 'beauty' (fr. καλός, 'beautiful'), and
κήβος, κήπος, "a long-tailed monkey'. For the
first element see calo-, for the second see
cowhage.

## calllgraph
calllgraph, п., a specimen of calligraphy. — Gk.
καλλιγράφος, 'a calligrapher'. See calligraphy.
Derivative: calligraph-er, n.

## calligraphic
calligraphic, adj. — Gk. καλλιγραφικός,
'pertaining to calligraphy', fr. καλλιγραφία. See next
word and -ic.
Derivatives: calligraphic-al, adj., calligraphic-
al-ly, adv.

## calligraphy
calligraphy, п., beautiful writing. — Gk.
καλλιγραφία, fr. καλλιγράφος, 'a calligrapher', which
is compounded of κάλλος, 'beauty' and -γράφος,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:134 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. The first element derives
fr. καλός, 'beautiful'; see calo-. For the second
element see -graphy.

## Calliope
Calliope, п., the Muse presiding over epic poetry
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Καλλιόπη, lit. 'the
beautiful-voiced one', compounded of κάλλος,
'beauty', and 8ψ, gen. οπός, 'voice'. The first
element derives fr. καλός, 'beautiful'; see cnlo-.
The second element stands for fr. *Яоф, fr. I.-E.
*woqw-s, whence also Gk. επος·(ΰ>τ>ΠοΙεΓέπος),
'word', L. vox, 'voice, sound, tone, call'. See
voice and cp. epic, epos,

## calliper
calliper, n. — See caliper.

## Calllrrhoe
Calllrrhoe, п., I) the wife of Alcmaeon; 2) the
name of a sea nymph (Greek mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. Καλλιρρόη, fem. of καλλίρροος, 'beautifully
flowing', compounded of κάλλος, 'beauty' (fr.
καλός, 'beautiful'), and ροή, 'a flowing stream,
river', which is rel. to ρέειν (for *σρέ/ειν), 'to
flow', fr. I.-E. base *sreu-, 'to flow', whence
also—with inserted t—OE. stream, 'flowing;
river'. See calo- and stream.

## Callirrhoe
Callirrhoe, п., a genus of plants, of the mallow
family (bot.) — Named after the nymph
Callirrhoe. See prec. word.

## callisthenic
callisthenic, adj. — See calisthenic.

## callisthenics
callisthenics, n. — See calisthenics.

## Callisto
Callisto, п., a nymph, mother of Areas by Zeus
(Greek mythol.)— L., fr. Gk. Καλλιστώ, fr.
κάλλιστος, superl. of καλός, 'beautiful'; see calo-.
For the Greek superl. suff. -ιστός ср. αγχιστος,
superl. of αγχι, 'near' (see Anchistea), κάκιστος,
superl. of κακός, 'bad' (see kakistocracy),
πρώτιστος, superl. of πρώτος, 'first' (see protista).
For the cognates of this suff. see superl. suff.
-est.

## Callitriche
Callitriche, п., a genus of aquatic weeds, the water
starwort (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. καλλίτριχος,
'beautiful-haired', which is compounded of
κάλλος, 'beauty', and θρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair'.
The first element derives fr. καλός, 'beautiful',
see calo-. For the second element see tricho-.

## callosity
callosity, п., callousness. — F. callosite,
'hardening of the skin', fr. L. callositatem, ace. of cal-
lositas, fr. callus, callum, 'hardened skin', which
is prob. cogn. with OI. kinah (for *krnah),
'callosity', Olr. and Mir. calath, calad, W. called,
'hard', OSlav. kaliti, 'to cool, harden', Lett.
kalst, kalslu, 'to dry up'. For the ending see
suff. -ity.

## callous
callous, adj., hardened. — L. callosus, 'hard-
skinned', fr. callus, callum, 'hardened skin'. See
prec. word.
Derivatives: callous-ly, adv., callous-ness, n.

## callow
callow, adj., unfledged; immature. — ME. ca-
lowe, fr. OE. calu, 'bare, bald', rel. to MDu. calu,
Du. kaal, OHG. kalo, kalawer, MHG. kal,
kalwer, G. kahl, of s.m., and cogn. with OSlav.
golu, 'naked', OSlav. glava, Lith. galva, OPruss.
gallu, 'head'.
Derivatives: callow, п., callow-er, n.

## Calluna
Calluna, п., a genus of plants of the heath family
(bot.). — ModL., fr. Gk. καλλύνειν, 'to brush,
sweep*, lit. 'to make beautiful', fr. κάλλος,
'beauty', fr. καλός, 'beautiful' (see calo-); so
called because its twigs were used as brooms.

## callus
callus, п., hardened skin (med.) — L. see
callosity,

## calm
calm, n. — F. calme, 'tranquil, quiet', fr. It. cal-
ma, 'absence' of wind, tranquillity', fr. Gk.
καύμα, 'burning heat of the sun', whence arose the
meaning 'tranquillity of the sea during
oppressive heat'. Gk. καϋμα derives fr. *καί-, the stem
of καίειν, 'to burn'. See caustic and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also chomage.
Derivatives: calm, adj. and v., calm-er, п.,
calmly, adv., calm-ness, n.

## calmative
calmative, adj., calming. — F. calmatif (fem.
calmative); see calm and -ative. This is a hybrid
word (a suff. of L. origin having been added to
a word of Gk. origin); it should be superseded
by sedative.

## calo-
calo-, combining form meaning 'beautiful'. —
Gk. κάλο-, fr. καλός, 'beautiful', which is cogn.

## with OI. kalyah
with OI. kalyah, 'healthy'. Cp. calisthenics,
Calista, Callicarpa, Callicebus, calligraphy,
Callisto, Calluna, calomel, caloyer, Hemerocallis,

## Hymenocallis
Hymenocallis, kaleidophone, kaleidoscope.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:134 COLUMN:3 -->

## calomel
calomel, п., mercurous chloride, HgCl (chem.) —
F., prop, 'beautiful (i.e. white) substance
derived from black', fr. Gk. καλός, 'beautiful, fair',
and μέλας, 'black'. See calo- and melancholy.

## Calonyction
Calonyction, п., a genus of plants of the morning-
glory family (bol.) — ModL., compounded of
calo- and Gk. νύκτιος, 'nightly', fr. νύξ, gen.
νυκτός, 'night'. See night and cp. nycti-.

## Calophyllum
Calophyllum, п., a genus of plants of the balsam-
tree family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
calo- and Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo-.

## calorescence
calorescence, п., transference of heat rays into
light rays (phys.) — Coined by the British
physicist John Tyndall (1820-93). The word is
incorrectly formed. The correct form would be
calescence, fr. L. calescens, pres. part, of cale-
scere, 'to grow hot', inchoative of calere, 'to be
hot'. See caldron and -escence and cp.
calescence and calori-.

## calori-
calori-, combining form meaning 'heat*. — L.
calori-, fr. color, 'heat', fr. calere, 'to be hot*.
See caldron.

## caloric
caloric, п., the principle of heat. — F. calorique,
fr. L. color, 'heat'. See calori- and -ic.
Derivative: caloric-ity, n.

## calorie
calorie, also calory, п., unit of heat. — See calori-.

## calorifacieat
calorifacieat, adj., heat-producing. —
Compounded of calori- and -facient.
Derivative: calorifacient, n.

## calorific
calorific, adj., heat-producing. — F. calorifique,
tr. L. calorificus. See calori- and -fie.
Derivative: calorific-ation, n.

## calorifics
calorifics, п., the science of heat. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## calorimeter
calorimeter, п., an apparatus for measuring heat.
— A hybrid coined fr. L. color, 'heat', and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See calori- and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## calotte
calotte, п., a small skullcap. — F., fr. It. callotta,
fr. L. calautica, 'a kind of female headdress
with pendent lappets', a word of foreign origin.
A connection between calotte and Gk. καλύπτρα,
woman's veil', as suggested by many
lexicographers, is impossible for phonetic reasons.
Cp. caul.

## caloyer
caloyer, п., a monk of the Eastern Church. —
F., fr. MF. calogere, fr. ModGk. καλόγερος (γ
being pronounced y), 'a monk', lit. 'a handsome
old man', fr. Gk. καλός, 'beautiful', and γέρων,
'old man'. See calo- and geronto-.

## calpac
calpac, calpack, п., a kind of cap. — Turk, qal-
paq, whence also Hung, kalpag, 'calpac,
headgear', kalap, 'hat'.

## Caltha
Caltha, п., a genus of herbs of ihe crowfoot
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. caltha, 'pot marigold',
fr. supposed Gk. 'κάλθη, prop, 'the yellow
flower', from l.-E. *ghjdha, rel. to *ghelwos,
'yellow', whence L. helvus, 'light bay'. See yellow
and cp. heivite.

## caltrop
caltrop, п., an instrument with four iron spikes
used in medieval warfare. — ME. calketrappe,
fr. ONF. cauketrape, corresponding to OF.
chuueetrape (F. chausse-trape), which is formed
from the imperative of chauchier, 'to tread,
trample', and trape, 'trap, snare'. Accordingly,
OF. chauchetrape lit. means 'tread upon the
trap'. OF. chauchier derives fr. L. calcare, 'to
tread', fr. calx, gen. calcis, 'heel*. See
Calceolaria and cp. the first element in cauchemar. For
the second element see trap, 'snare'.

## calumba
calumba, п., formerly columbo, root of a plant
(phitrm.) — From kolombo, its name in
Mozambique.

## calumet
calumet, п., a pipe with long stem, smoked by
North American Indians, esp. in token of
peace, τ- Can. F., fr. NF., corresponding to
F. ihalumeau (with change of suff.), fr. L.
calamus, 'reed'. Sec calamary.

## calumniate
calumniate, ir. v.·, to slander. — L. calumniatus,
pp. of calumniari, 'to accuse falsely', fr. caluni-
nia. See calumay and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: calunmiat-ion, п., calumniator
(qv.)

## calumniator
calumniator, п., slanderer. — L., fr. calumniatus,
pp. of calumniari. See prec. word and agential
suff. -or.

## calumnious
calumnious, adj., slanderous. — L. calumniosus,
fr. calumnia. See next word and -oils.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:135 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CALUMNY | 108 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:135 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: calumnious-ly, adv., calumnious-
ness, n.

## calumny
calumny, п., slander. — F. calomnie, fr. L.
Columbia, "trickery, artifice, pretense, evasion, false
accusation, false report', for *ca!vomnid, from
*calvomnos, archaic pres. part, of calvi, 'to
devise tricks, deceive', which is prob. cogn. with
Gk. κηλεΐν, 'to bewitch, seduce, beguile', Goth.
holon, 'to deceive', ON. hoi, 'praise, flattery',
OE. hot, 'slander', holian, helian, 'to slander'.
Cp. challenge. Cp. also cavil. For the form of
the pres. part. *calvomnos cp. alumnus.

## Calvary
Calvary, the place of the crucifixion of Jesus;
representation of lhe crucifixion of Jesus. — L.
calvdria, 'skull', translation of Gk. κράνίον in
the Gospels, rendering Aram, gulgultha, 'skull'
(— Heb. gulgoleth), a name given to a hill near
Jerusalem (so called from its shape; see
Golgotha). L. calvdria is a derivative of calvus,
'bald', which is cogn. with the second element
in OI. dti-kulvah, dti-kurvah, 'utterly bare',
Avestic kaurva-, ModPers. kal, 'bare'. Cp.
Calvatia, catvities.

## Calvatia
Calvatia, п., a genus of fungi (hot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. calvus, 'bald'. See Calvary and -ia.

## calve
calve, intr. and tr. v. — ME. calven, fr. OE.
cealfian, fr. cealf, 'calf. See calf, 'young of a
cow'.

## Calvinism
Calvinism, п.,the religious doctrine of John Calvin
(1509-64). Cp. cbauvin. For the ending see suff.
•ism.

## Calvinist
Calvinist, п., a follower of Calvin. — See prec.
word and -ist.
Derivative; Calvinist-ic, adj.

## calviiies
calviiies, п., baldness (med.) — L., 'baldness', fr.
calvus. See Calvary.

## calx
calx, n. (chem.), 1) lime (obsol.); 2) ashy
substance left after a mineral or metal has been
calcined. — L. calx, gen. calcis, 'stone, lime'.
See calcareous.

## Calycaathus
Calycaathus, п., the Carolina allspice (hot.) —
ModL., compounded of κάλυξ, 'cup, calyx', and
άνθος, 'flower'. See calyco- and anther.

## calyci-
calyci-, before a vowel calve-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining 10, or resembling a calyx'.
— Fr. L. calyx, gen. calycis. See calyx.

## calycle
calycle, п., an epicalyx (bot.) — L. calyculus, 'a
small flower bud', dimin. of calyx, gen. calycis.
See calyx and cp. calicle.

## Calycocarpum
Calycocarpum, п., a genus of plants of the moon-
seed family (hot.). — ModL., compounded of
κάλυξ, gen. κάλυκος, 'cup,- calyx', and καρπός,
'fruit'. See calyco- and carpel and cp. the second
element in Callicarpa.

## calyculus
calyculus, п., a small cup-shaped cavity. — L.
Sec calycle.

## Calypso
Calypso, п., a nymph, daughter of Atlas {Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Καλυψώ, from the stem
of καλύπτειν, 'to cover, hide, conceal'. See next
word. For sense development cp. Circe.

## cnlyptra
cnlyptra, п., a covering (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
καλύπτρα, 'a covering, veil', fr. καλύπτειν, 'to
cover, hide, conceal', which is rel. to καλύβη,
'hut, cabin', καλιά, 'hut, nest', and cogn. with
L. cella, 'storeroom, granary', celdre, 'to hide,
keep secret'. See cell and cp. caliology, Calypso,
apocalypse, Eucalyptus, kelyphite.

## calyx
calyx, п., the outer whorl of leaves (bol.) — L.,
fr. Gk. κάλυξ, 'the cup or calyx of a flower',
which stands in gradational relationship to
κύλιξ, 'cup, drinking cup', and is cogn. with L.
calix, 'cup, goblet, drinking vessel', Umbr.
skalce-ta, scalse-to, 'out of the dish or saucer*,
Ol. kaldsah, 'pot, cup', kalikd, 'bud'. OE. celic,
cselic, cxlc, 'cup', is borrowed fr. L. calix. Cp.
chalice, cylix.

## cam
cam, п., a device for changing regular rotary
motion into irregular. — Du. kam, 'comb', fr.
MDu. cam, rel. to OE. comb, whence cumb(q.v.)
Derivative: cam, tr. v.

## enmaieu
enmaieu, п., a cameo. — F., ir. OF. camaheus,
fr. ML. camahuius. See cameo.

## cumail
cumail, п., a piece of chain mail protecting the
neck. — F., fr. OProvenc. capmalh, lit. 'chain
mail for the head', fr. 'capmalhar, 'to cover lhe
head with a chain mail', which is compounded
of cap, 'head' (fr. L. caput, of s.m.), and malhar,
'to put on a coat of mail', fr. malha, 'coat of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:135 COLUMN:2 -->
mail', fr. L. macula, 'spot, mark'. See capital,
adj., and mail, 'armor'.

## camara
camara,п., chamber. — Sp. camara, fr. L. camara,
camera, fr. Gk. καμάρα. See camera, chamber.

## camaraderie
camaraderie, п., comradeship. — F., fr. camara-
de, 'comrade'. See comrade and -ery.

## camarilla
camarilla, п., a small meeting room. — Sp., dimin.
of camara, 'chamber', fr. L. camera, 'vault,
arched roof, arch'; see camara. In its special
sense 'a private audience chamber in the royal
palace; political clique', it was first used in
France about 1S30, to designate the absolutist
party during the reign of Charles X.

## camas
camas, camash, cammas, п., any plant of the
genus Camassia. — Fr. N. American Indian
quamash, 'bulb'.

## Camassia
Camassia, п., a genus of plants with edible bulbs
(bot.) — ModL., from prec. word. For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## Cambarus
Cambarus, п., a genus of crayfishes (zool.) —
ModL., rel. to L. cammarus, fr. Gk. κάμμαρος,
'lobster', which is cogn. with ON. humarr,
'lobster' [whence F. homard and LG. humarr
(whence G. Hummer)], and with Ol. kamathah,
'tortoise'. These words derive fr. l.-E. base
*qam-, 4qem-, 'to vault', and lit. denote an
animal with a vaulted covering. See camera and cp.
Cammarus, Homarus.

## camber
camber, п., a slight convexity. — OF. cambre,
'curved, bent', fr. L. camur, which is rel. to
camera, 'arch, vault*. See camera.

## camber
camber, tr. and intr. v., to curve slightly. — F.
cambrer, 'to curve, bend*, fr. camerdre, of s.m.,
fr. camera. See prec. word.

## cambial
cambial, adj., pertaining to cambium. — Late L.
cambidlis, fr. cambidre, 'to change, exchange'.
See cambinm and adj. suff. -al.

## cambio-
cambio-, combining form for cambium. — See
cambium.

## cambist
cambist, п., an expert in the theory and practice
of exchange. — F. cambiste, 'changer', a hybrid
coined fr. Late L. cambium and -isle, a suff. of
Greek origin. See cambium and -ist.

## cambium
cambium, п.. formative tissue between bark and
wood (bot.) — Late L., 'exchange', fr. cambidre,
'to change, exchange', which is a Gaulish loan
word. See change, v.

## Cambrian
Cambrian, adj., 1) pertaining to Cambria or
Wales; 2) pertaining to the first geological
period in the Paleozoic Era. — Lit. 'of Cambria',
i.e. 'of Wales', fr. L. Cambria, ML. name of
Wales, fr. Celtic, Cymru, 'Wales'. See Cymric
and -an.

## cambric
cambric, п., a fine white linen fabric. — A blend
of Kamerijk, Flemish name of a town in France
(formerly in Flanders), with Cambrai, the
French yiame of the same town; so called
because it was first manufactured in Cambrai.
Cp. chambray.

## came
came, п., a grooved lead bar used to hold
together panes of glass. — Of uncertain origin.

## came
came, past tense of come. — ME. cam (prob. on
the analogy of ME. nam, past tense of niman,
'to take'). See come.

## cameist
cameist, п., I) one who makes or collects cameos;
2) an expert in cameos. — A hybrid coined fr.
.cameo and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## enmel
enmel, n. — ME. camel, cameil, chumel. chamail,
fr. OE. camel, fr. ONF. camel, corresponding to
OF. chamel (whence F. chameau). fr. L. came-
lus, fr. Gk. κάμηλος, fr. Heb. and Phoen. gdinal,
'camel', which is rel. to Arab, jdmal, of s.m.
Cp. gamma, gimel.

## cameleer
cameleer, п., a camel driver. — Formed fr. camel
with suff. -eer.

## Camelidae
Camelidae, п., a family of ruminants (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. camilus.
See camel.

## Camelina
Camelina, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'dwarf flax', fr. Gk.
χαμαί, 'on the ground' (in botany used in the
sense #of 'dwarf'), and λίνον, 'flax'. See chamae-
and line, 'flax'.

## camellia
camellia, n. — Named by lhe Swedish naturalist
Karl von Linne after the Jesuit traveler George
Joseph Kamel (Italianized into Camelli), who
first described this flower. For the ending see
suff. -ia.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:135 COLUMN:3 -->

## camelopard
camelopard, 11,. the giraffe. — Lit. "cainelpard",
fr. L. canielopardus, fr. Gk. καμτλο-άρδοιλίς,
which is compounded of Gk. κάμν,λο:, 'camel',
and πάρδαλις, 'pard'. See camel and pard ;md
cp. leopard.

## camelry
