into flesh. — Compounded of L. card, gen.
carnis, 'flesh, meat' (see carnal), and -Hcation.

## carnify
carnify, tr. v., to turn into, or become, flesh. —
See prec. word and -fy.

## carnival
carnival, n. — F. carnaval, fr. It. carnevale, fr.
ML. carne, vale, Ό flesh, farewell!'. See carnal
and vale, interj.
Derivative: carnival(l)-er, n.

## Carnivore
Carnivore, n. pi., an order of mammals (zool.) —
ModL., neut. pi. of L. carnivorus; see
carnivorous. The term Carnivora was introduced into
zoology bytheFrenchnaturalist,baronGeorges-
Leopold-Chrelien-Frederic-Dagobert Cuvier
(1769-1832).

## carnivore
carnivore, п., a flesh-eating mammal. — F., fr.
L. carnivorus. See next word.

## caraivorous
caraivorous, adj., flesh-eating. — Formed fr. L.
carnivorus, 'feeding on flesh', fr. card, gen.
carnis, 'flesh, meat', and the stem of vorax, gen.
■dcis, 'hungry, greedy' (see carnal and
voracious); first used by Thomas Browne.
Derivatives: carnivorous-ly, adv., carntvorous-
ness, n.

## carob
carob, п., a tree (Ceratonia siliqua); its seed pod.
— F. caroube, fr. ML. carrubia, carrubium, fr.
Arab, kharraba", fr. Aram, harubha, 'carob tree,
carob', which is rel. to Heb. barabh, of s.m. Cp.
algarroba.

## caroche
caroche, п., a kind of carriage used in the 16th
and 17th centuries. — Earlier F. carroche, fr.
It. carroccia, caroccia, a collateral form of car-
rozza, carozza (whence F. carrosse), fr. carro,
'car, carriage'. See car and cp. carrocdo.

## Carol
Carol, masc. PN. — ML. Carolus. See Charles

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:142 COLUMN:2 -->
and cp. Carl·

## Carol
Carol, fern. PN.—Abbreviation of Caroline (q.v.)

## carol
carol, п., a joyful song. — ME. carol, carole, 'a
dance in a ring, a joyful song, fr. OF. carole,
'a dance in a ring', fr. L. choraula, a collateral
form of choraules, 'flute player, who
accompanied with a flute the chorus dance', fr. Gk.
χοραύλης, which is compounded of χορός,
'dance in a ring, chorus', and αύλεϊν, 'to play
on the flute', fr. αυλός, 'flute'. For the first
element see chorus. The second element is rel. to
Gk. αυλών, 'a hollow between hills, a channel',
and cogn. with L. alvus, 'belly', alveus, 'a
hollow, cavity'; see alveolus.

## carol
carol, intr. and tr. v>, to sing joyfully. — F.
caroler, fr. carole. See prec. word.
Derivative: саго!ф-ег, n.

## Caroline
Caroline, adj., belonging to the time of Charles I
or II of England. — Formed fr. ML. Carolus,
'Charles', with suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).
See Charles and cp. Carol.

## Caroline
Caroline, fem. PN. — F., fr. It. Carolina, orig. a
fern. adj. derived fr. ML. Carolus, 'Charles', and
lit. meaning 'of, or pertaining to, Charles'. See
Caroline, adj.

## Carolingian
Carolingian, adj., pertaining to the dynasty of
Charlemagne. — Formed fr. ML. Carolus
(Magnus), 'Charlemagne' (i.e. 'Charles the
Great'). See Charles and -ian and cp. Carlo-
vingian.
Derivative: Carolingian, n.

## carom
carom, п., in billiards, a shot in which the cue
ball hits two other balls. — F. carambole, 'the
red ball (in billiards)', fr. Sp. carambola, 'fruit
of the carambola tree' (which is round and
orange-colored); 'the red ball' (in billiards), ult.
fr. Malay karambil. Cp. cannoa, 'slroke in
billiards', and carambole.

## carotid
carotid, adj., designating either of the two arteries
that conduct the blood from the aorta to the
head; п., a carotid artery (anat.) — Fr. Gk.
καρωτίδες, 'the great arteries of the neck', prop,
'the great arteries of the head', fr. κάρα, 'head',
which is cogn. with L. cerebrum, 'brain'. See
cerebram and cp. cranium. The usual derivation
of καρωτίδες, fr. κάρος, 'heavy sleep, torpor',
which itself is rel. to κάρα, 'head', arose from
the erroneous belief that drowsiness was caused
by the carotids.

## carousal
carousal, п., a carouse. — Formed fr. next word
with adj. suff. -al.

## carouse
carouse, п., a drinking bout. — OF. carous, fr. G.
garaus, 'all out', in the phrase garaus trinken,
'to drink right out', fr. gar, 'altogether', and
aus, 'out'; see yare and out and cp. rouse,
'carousal'. Carouse was orig. an adverb and
used only in phrases like 'to drink carouse', but
it became later a noun.
Derivatives: carouse, intr. v., carous-er, п.,
carous-ing, adj., carous-ing-ly, adv.

## carp
carp, intr. v., to find fault. — ME. carpen, 'to
say, speak', fr. ON. karpa, 4o chatter, boast';
influenced in meaning by L. carpere, 'to pluck'
(see carpel). Derivatives: carp-er, п., carp-ing,
adj., carp-ing-ly, adv.

## carp
carp, п., the fish Cyprinus carpio. — OF. (= F.)
carpe, fr. OProvenc. carpa, fr. Late L. carpa,
which is a Teut. loan word. Cp. MDu. carpe,
carper, Du. karper, OHG. karpfo, MHG. karpfe,
G. Karpfen, 'carp'. Cp. also It. carpa, carpione,
Sp., Port, carpa. Rum. crap, which derive ft.
Late L. carpa. Lith. kdrpis, Lett, karpe, karpa,
Russ. karp and korop are Teut. loan words.

## earp-
earp-, form of carpo- before a vowel.

## carpal
carpal, adj., pertaining to the carpus or wrist. —
Formed ft. carpus with suff. -al.

## carpale
carpale, п., a bone of the carpus (anat.) —
Medical L., fr. carpus.
Carpathian Mountains. — Thracian Gk. Kap-
πάτης δρος, lit. 'the Rocky Mountain', rel. to
Καρποί, name of a Thracian tribe, lit. meaning
'the inhabitants of rocky regions', and cogn.
with Alb. karpe, 'rock'. See next word.

## carpel
carpel, п., a simple pistil (hot.) — ModL. car-
pellum, dimin. formed fr. Gk. καρπός, 'fruit',
lit. 'that which is plucked', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-
(e)p-, 4o cut; to pluck', whence also OI. krpanah,
'sword', Hitt. karp-, karpiyd-, 'to gather, take',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:142 COLUMN:3 -->
Alb. karpe, karme (for *karp-n), 'rock, crag',
Skrep, krep, 'rock, slope', Thracian Gk. Kap-
πάτης δρος, 'Carpathian Mountains' (see prec.
word), Gk. κρώπιο,ι, 'scythe', L. carpere, 'to
pluck, cull, gather', Mir. corrun, 'sickle' cirrim,
Ί beat off, mutilate', Lith. kerpu, kiPpti, 'to cut
with scissors, shear', Lett, cfrpu. cirpt, of s.m.,
dial. Russ. £erp, 'sickle*. For Teut. cognates of
the same base see harrow, harvest, scurf, sharp.
Cp. carp, intr. v., carpet, Carpinus, acarpous,
acrocarpous, amphicarpic, cremocarp, Crepidula,
Crepls, discerp, endocarp, epicarp, excerpt, me-
ricarp, mesocarp, monocarplc, pericarp, scarce,
schizocarp, syncarp, xylocarp. I.-E. *(s)qeiie)p-
is an enlargement of base *(s)qer-, 'to cut',
whence Gk. κείρειν (for *κέριειν), 'to cut, shear',
L. card, 'flesh, meat'. See carnal.

## carpenter
carpenter, n. — ME., fr. ONF. carpentier
(corresponding to F. charpentter), fr. Late L. carnen-
tarius, 'wagonmaker', fr. L. carpentum, 'wagon,
carriage', which is of Gaulish origin. Olr. car-
pat, 'wagon', was re-borrowed fr. L. carpentum,
MW. kerbyt, 'coach', is an Irish loan word.
Derivatives: carpenter, intr. and tr. v.,
carpentry, n.

## carpet
carpet, n. — ME., fr. OF. carpite, fr. ML. carpita,
'a kind of thick cloth', prob. fr. L. carpere, 'to
pluck' (see carpel); so called because the cloth
is made of shreds.
Derivatives: carpet, tr. v., carpet-ing, n.

## Carphophis
Carphophis, п., a genus of snakes (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. κάρφος, 'dry straw,
dry stick', and δφις, 'snake'. The first element
derives fr. I.-E. base *(s)qerebh-, 'to curve,
contract, shrink'. See corf and cp. ramp, v. Cp. also
Crambe, crambo. For the second element see
ophidian.

## Carpinus
Carpinus, п., a genus of trees of the birch family
(bol.) — L., 'the hornbeam'; cogn. with Lith.
skirpstas, 'elm', OPruss. skerptus, of s.m., Lith.
skirpslus, 'copperbeech', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-
(e)p-, 'to cut', whence also L. carpere, 'to pluck,
cull, gather' (see carpel); so dalled from the
double-serrate leaves of the hornbeam.

## carpo-
carpo-, before a vowel carp-, combining form
denoting the carpus (anal.) — Gk. καρπό-, καρπ-,
fr. καρπός, 'wrist'. See carpus.

## carpo-
carpo-, before a vowel carp-, combining form
meaning 'fruit*. — Gk. καρπό-, καρπ-, fr.
καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.

## Carpocapsa
Carpocapsa, п., a genus of moths (enlomol.) —
ModL., compounded of carpo-, 'fruit', and
κάψις, 'a gulping, devouring', from the stem of
κάπτειν, 'to swallow greedily, gulp', which is
cogn. with L. capere 'to catch, seize, hold'. See
captive.

## Carpodacus
Carpodacus, п., a genus of finches (ornilhol.) —
ModL., compounded of carpe-, fruit', and Gk.
δάκος, 'a biting animal', which is rel. to δάκνειν,
'to bite', and cogn. with OI. daiati, 'bites', OE.
tang, lunge, 'tongs' (lit. 'that which bites'). See
tongs.

## carpology
carpology, п., the study of the structure of fruits.
— Compounded of carpo- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)*. See -iogy.

## carpophore
carpophore, п., prolongation of the axis of a
flower (hot.) — Lit. fruit bearer', fr. Gk.
καρπός, 'fruit', and -φόρος, 'bearer'. See carpel
and -phore.

## carpus
carpus, п., the wrist (anal.) — L., ft. Gk. καρπός,
'wrist', which stands for *κΛχρπός and lit.
means that which turns', from I.-E. base
*k"erp-, 'to turn, revolve', whence also OE.
hweorfan, 'to turn about, go, move', hwerf, 'dam,
bank', prop, 'a place for turning about*. See
wharf and cp. the second element in metacarpus.
сатгаск, сагаск, п., a merchant ship. — ME., fr.
OF. car(r)aque, fr. Sp. carraca, fr. Arab, qaraqir,
pi. oiqurqar, 'merchant ship', fr. Gk. κερκοϋρος,
'boat, pinnace', fr. κέρκος, 'tail', and ουρά, 'tail;
stern of a ship'. See cercus and uro-, 'tail-'.

## carrageen
carrageen, п., an edible seaweed. — Short for
carrageenmoss; named from Carragheen in
Ireland, where this seaweed is found.

## carriage
carriage, n. — ONF. cariage, 'that which is
carried', fr. carter, 'to cart, carry' (corresponding to
F: charriage, 'cartage, haulage', fr. charrier, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:143 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CARRICKBEND | 116 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:143 COLUMN:1 -->
cart, carry'), fr. L. carricare, fr. L. carrus,
'wagon, carriage'. See carry and -age.
Derivative: carriage-able, adj.
carrick bend (naut.) — Prob. rel. to carrack.

## carriole
carriole, n. — See cariole.

## carrion
carrion, п., the dead flesh of an animal. — ME.
caroin, carion, fr. ONF. caroigne (corresponding
to OF. charoigne, F. charogne), fr. VL. *caronia,
fr. L. card, gen. carnis, 'flesh, meat' (see
carnal). It. carogna, OProvenc. caronha, Sp. ca-
rroiia, 'carrion', also derive fr. VL. *caronia.
Derivative: carrion, adj.

## carrizo
carrizo, п., reed grass. — Sp., fr. L. carex, gen.
caricis, 'reed grass', whence also It. carice. See
Carex.

## carroccio
carroccio, п., the car on which the standard of an
Italian city was borne into battle during the
Middle Ages. — It., dimin. formed fr. carro,
'car', fr. L. carrus. See car and cp. earache.

## carronade
carronade, п., a kind of short naval gun. —
Named from Carron in Scotland, where this
kind of gun was first made.

## carrot
carrot, n. — F. carotte, fr. L. carota, fr. Gk.
καρωτόν, prob. a derivative of *κάρος, 'head',
and rel. to κάρα, 'head'. See cranium and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: carrot-y, adj., carrot-i-ness, n.

## carrousel
carrousel, also carousel, п., a merry-go-round. —
F. carrousel, fr. It. carosello, prob. fr. Arab.
kurraj, 'a play with wooden horses', fr. Pers.
kurra(k), 'foal'.

## carry
carry, tr. and intr. v. — ME. caricn, fr. ONF.
carter (corresponding to F. charrier), 'to cart,
carry', fr. VL. carricare, fr. L. carrus, 'wagon,
carriage'. See car and cp. carriage.
Derivatives: carry, п., carri-er, n.

## carry-all
carry-all, п., a kind of light carriage (U.S.A.) —
Corruption of F. carriole, 'a light car', based on
folk etymology. See carriole.

## cart
cart, n. — ME. carle, cart, prob. fr. ON. kartr,
which is rel. to OE. crset, 'cart, chariot', MDu.
crane, 'a woven mat, hamper', Du. krat, 'basket',
and to OE. cradol, 'cradle'. See cradle.
Derivatives: cart, tr. and intr. v., cart-age, п.,
cart-er, n.

## carte
carte, quarte, п., a position in fencing. — F.
quarte, prop. fern, of quart, 'a fourth', fr. L.
quartus, 'fourth; a fourth'. See quart.

## carte blanche
carte blanche, blank paper. — F., lit. 'white
paper'. See card, 'a piece of pasteboard', and
blank.

## carte de visite
carte de visite, a portrait mounted on a small
card. — F., lit. 'visiting card'. See card, 'a piece
of pasteboard'.

## cartel
cartel, п., ι) a written challenge; 2) a written
agreement oetween belligerents as to the
treatment and exchange of prisoners; 3) an
association of industrialists. — F., fr. It. cartello,
'placard', whence, 'written challenge', dimin. formed
fr. carta, 'paper, writing', fr. Late L. carta.
See card, 'piece of pasteboard', and cp. chart,
charter. In the sense 'association of
industrialists' cartel derives fr. G. Kartell, which itself
comes fr. F. cartel (see above).

## Cartesian
Cartesian, adj., pertaining to Descartes; п.,
follower of Descartes. — Fr. Canesius, Latinized
form of Descartes. Cp. next word and see -iaa.

## Cartesianism
Cartesianism, п., the philosophy of Rene
Descartes (1596-1650). For the ending see suff. -ism.

## Carthamus
Carthamus, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Arab, qirtim, qurtum,
in vulgar pronunciation qorfom, qdrfam, 'saf-
flower', fr. Aram, qurfma, of s.m.-, literally 'that
which is lopped', fr. Heb. qirtim, 'he lopped',
enlarged form of qatam, of s.m.; so called
because the flowers are plucked off as soon as they
begin to wither.

## Carthusian
Carthusian, п., a monk or nun of the order
founded at Chartreuse. — ML. Cartusianus, from the
place name Chartreuse in France, where the
first monastery of this order was built. Cp.
charterhouse.
Derivative: Carthusian, adj., pertaining to the
Carthusians.

## cartilage
cartilage, n. — F., fr. L. cartilago, which is rel.
to L. crates, 'wickerwork'. See crate and -age,

## cartilaginoid
cartilaginoid, adj., resembling cartilage. — A
hybrid coined fr. cartilage and Gk. -οειδής,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:143 COLUMN:2 -->
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## cartilnginous
cartilnginous, adj. — F. carlilagineux (fern, carti-
lagineuse), fr. L. cartildginosus, 'full of
cartilage', fr. cartilago, gen. -inis, 'cartilage'. See
cartilage and -ous.

## cartograph
cartograph, п., a map. — A hybrid coined fr. F.
carte, 'playing card', and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφει, 'to write'. See card, 'a piece of paste-
board', and -graph.
Derivatives: cartograph-er, п., cartograph-y, n.

## cartomancy
cartomancy, п., divination from cards. — F. car-
tomancie, a hybrid coined fr. F. carte, 'playing
card', and Gk. μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'.
See card, п., 'a piece of pasteboard', and -mnncy.

## carton
carton, п., a cardboard box. — F. See next word.

## cartoon
cartoon, п., ι) a drawing on strong paper; 2) a
comic strip. — F. carton, 'pasteboard', fr. It.
cartone, augment, of carta, 'paper'. See card,
п., 'a piece of pasteboard'.
Derivatives: cartoon, v., cartoonist (q.v.)

## cartooaist
cartooaist, n. — A hybrid coined fr. cartoon and
-1st, a suff. of Greek origin.

## cartouehe
cartouehe, п., ]) a scroll-like ornament; 2) an
oval figure containing the name or title of an
Egyptian deity or king. — F., fr. It. cartoccio,
lit. 'a roll of paper', fr. carta, fr. Late L. carta.
See card, 'a piece of pasteboard', and cp.
next word.

## cartridge
cartridge, n. — Fr. earlier cartrage, corruption of
F. cartouche, 'cartouche, cartridge'. See prec.
word.

## cartulary
cartulary, п., a chartulary. — See chartulary.

## carucate
carucate, п., formerly, a measure of land in
England. — ML. carrucagium, 'tax on plow or
plowland', rel. to carracutium, 'a two-wheeled
coach', fr. L. carruca, 'a four-wheeled coach',
in Gaulish-Latin, 'plow', fr. carrus, 'wagon'.
See car.

## Carum
Carum, п., a genus of plants of the carrot family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κάρον, 'caraway'. See
caraway.

## caruncle
caruncle, п., a fleshy excrescence. — L. caruncula,
'a little piece of flesh', dimin. of card, 'flesh'.
See carnal.

## caruncula
caruncula, п., a caruncle (anat.) — L. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: caruncul-ar, caruncul-ate, caruncul-
at-ed, caruncul-ous, adjs.

## carve
carve, tr. and intr. v. — ME. keruen, fr. OE. ceor-
fan, 'to cut, carve', rel. to OFris. kerva, Du.
kerven, MHG., G. kerben, 'to cut, notch', fr.
I.-E. base *gerbh-, 'to scratch', whence also Gk.
γράφειν, 'to scratch, engrave, write', OSlav.
zribu, zribiji, 'lot' (orig. 'a notched stick'),
OPruss. glrbin, 'number' (lit. 'a notch'). Cp.
graph, -graph, graphic. Cp. also kerf. For the
change of ME. e to E. a cp arbor, 'a shady
retreat', harbor.
Derivatives: carv-er, п., carv-ic, adj.

## Carya
Carya, п., a genus of trees, the hickory (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. καρύά, 'the walnut tree', rel. to
κάρυον, 'nut, walnut', and cogn. with L. carina,
'shell of a nut; keel of a ship'. See careen and
cp. Caryota.

## caryatid
caryatid, п., a draped female figure supporting a
column (archit.) — L. Caryatides, fr. Gk.
Καρυάτιδες, 'priestesses of Artemis (= the Roman
Diana) at Caryae\ sing. Καρυατις; so called fr.
Καρύαι, 'Caryae', a town in Laconia (prob. in
allusion to the dance of the virgins at the festival
held in the temple of Artemis Caryatis at Caryae).

## Caryocar
Caryocar, п., a genus of trees of the family Cary-
ocaraceae (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
κάρυον, 'nut, walnut', and κάρ, 'head'; so
called in allusion to the large fruit. See careen
and cranium and cp. Carya.

## Caryophyllaceae
Caryophyllaceae, п., the pink family (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Caryophyllus, name of the genus, fr.
Gk. καρυόφυλλον, 'clove tree', fr. κάρυον, 'nut,
walnut', and φύλλον, 'leave'. See careen and
phyllo- and cp. prec. word. For the ending see
suff. -acene.

## caryophyllaceous
caryophyllaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## carybpilite
carybpilite, п., a hydrous manganesesilicate(m/n-
eral.) — Compounded of caryo-, Gk. πίλος,
'felt', and λίθος, 'stone' (see pile 'hair', and
-lite); so called in allusion to the felty

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:143 COLUMN:3 -->
appearance.

## Caryota
Caryota, п., a genus of palms of the family Are-
aceae (bot.) — ModL.,fr. Gk. καρυωτός φοίνιξ,
'date palm', lit. 'a palm with walnutlike fruit',
fr. κάρυον, 'nut, walnut'. See careen and cp.
Carya.

## cascabel
cascabel, n. — The same as cascavel.

## cascade
cascade, п., a waterfall. — F., fr. It. cascata, fr.
cascare, 'tofall', fr. VL. *casicare, freq. formed fr.
L. casus, pp. of cadere, 'to fall' (see cadence);
introduced into English by the diarist John
Evelyn (1620-1706).
Derivative: cascade, intr. v.

## cascara sagrada
cascara sagrada, п., a laxative drug. — Sp., lit.
'sacred bark'. Sp. cascara, 'bark', comes from
cascar, 'to break', from VL. quassicare, freq.
of L. quassare, 'to shake violently', itself freq.
of quatere (pp. of quassus). Ίο shake'; see qnash,
'to make void', and cp. casco, cask. Sp. sagrada
is fem. pf sagrado, fr. L. sacratus, 'sacred', pp.
of sacrare, 'to consecrate'; see sacred.

## casco
casco, п., the hull of a ship. — Sp., 'potsherd,
shell, skull, helmet, cask; hull of a ship', fr.
cascar, 'to crack, burst', fr. VL. quassicare. See
prec. word.

## cascavel
cascavel, п., the rattlesnake called scientifically
Crotalus terrificus. —Port., 'rattle, rattlesnake',
fr. Sp. cascabel, of s.m., lit. 'sleigh bell, jingle',
fr. OProvenc. cascavel, fr. ML. cascabellus,
dimin. of cascabus, which is prob. an alteration
of Late L. cac(c)abus, fr. Gk. κάκ(κ)αβος, of
s.m., a word of prob. Sem. origin. Cp. Akkad.
kukubu, 'vessel'.

## case
case, п., condition, instance; a modification in
the inflection of a noun, etc. (gram.) — ME., fr.
OF. (= F.) cas, fr. L. casus, 'fall, occurrence',
fr. cas-(um), pp. stem of cadere, 'to fall, fall out,
happen'. See cadence. In its grammatical sense
L. casus, 'case', is a loan translation of Gk.
πτώσις, 'a falling, fall', which is rel. to πίπτειν,
'to fall'.

## case
case, п., box, chest. — ME. casse, fr. ONF. casse
(F. chasse), 'a box', fr. L. capsa, 'chest, box,
repository', fr. L. capere, 'to catch, seize, hold'.
See captive and cp. capsa, Capsella, Capsicum,
capsule, caisson, cash, 'ready money', casket,
cassone, chassis, encase. See also chase, 'iron
frame', which is a doublet of case.
Derivatives: case, tr. v., cas-er, п., cas-ing, n.

## casein
casein, п., a phosphoprotein that forms the basis
of cheese (chem) — Formed with chem. suff. -in
fr L. edseus, 'cheese'. See cheese.

## casemate
casemate, п., a bomb-proof room (fort.) — F.,
fr. It. casamatta, apparently fr. Gk. χάσματα,
pi. of χάσμα, 'chasm, gap'. See chasm and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivative: casemat-ed, adj.

## casement
casement, п., a hinged window. — Shortened fr.
MF. encassement, a var. of MF. enchassement
(F. enchassement), 'frame', fr. enchasser (F. en-
chasser), 'to enchase'. See enchase and -ment.

## caseose
caseose, п., a soluble product formed during the
digestion of casein (biochem.) — Formed fr.
casein and subst. suff.*-ose.

## caseous
caseous, adj., like cheese. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. caseus, 'cheese'. See cheese and cp.
casein.

## casern
casern, caserne, п., barracks. — F., fr. OProvenc.
cazerna, lit. 'a place for four watchmen', fr. VL.
'quaderna, fr. L. qualernt, 'four each'. See
quarter and cp. quaternion and words there
referred to. It. caserma, 'caserne', has been
influenced in form by L. arma, 'weapons'.

## cash
cash, п., ready money. — F. casse, fr. It. cassa,
'chest, box, money box', fr. L. capsa, 'chest, box,
repository'. See case, 'chest'.
Derivative: cash, tr. v.

## cash
cash, п., a small coin used in East India and
China. — Tamil kasu, 'a small coin'.

## cashew
cashew, п., a tropical American tree yielding
kidney-shaped nuts. — F. acajou, fr. Port, acajt'i,
caju, fr. Tupi acaju. Cp. acajou, cachou, catechu.

## cashier
cashier, п., a person in charge of money. — Not
derived fr. cash but fr. Du. kassier, fr. F. cais-
sier, fr. caisse, 'cashbox'. See cash, 'money'.

## cashier
cashier, tr. v., to dismiss. — MDu. kasseeren, fr.
F. casser, 'to break, annul, set aside'. See quash,
'to make void'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:144 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 117 | CAT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:144 COLUMN:1 -->

## cashmere
cashmere, п., a soft woolen fabric. — From ihe
Vale of Kashmir. Cp. cassimere, kerseymere.

## Casimir
Casimir, masc. PN. — Pol. Kazimir, lit. 'pro-
claimer (or preacher) of peace', fr. kazac, 'to
proclaim, preach', and mir, 'peace'. See ukase
and mir.

## casino
casino, п., г) a small country house; 2) an
amusement hall. — It., lit. 'a little house', dimin. formed
fr. casa, 'house', fr. L. casa, 'hut, cottage'.
See chasuble and cp. cassino.

## cask
cask, n. — Sp. casco, 'potsherd, shell, skull,
helmet, cask', fr. cascar, 'to break', fr. VL. qiias-
sicure, freq. of quassare, 'to shake violently',
itself freq. of L. quatere (pp. quassus), 'to shake'.
See quash, 'to make void', and cp. casco, casque.

## casket
casket, n. — Not a dimin. of cask, but corruption
of F. cassette, dimin. of casse, 'chest, box'. See
case, 'box, chest'.

## Caslon
Caslon, п., a style .of type (print.) — Short for
Caslon type; named after the printer William
Caslon (1692-1766), who designed it.

## casque
casque, п., a helmet. — F., 'helmet', fr. Sp. casco.
See cask.
Derivative: casqu-ed, adj.

## Cassandra
Cassandra, п., daughter of Priam, king of Troy.
Apollo gave her the gift of prophecy, but later
decreed that no one should believe her
prophecies (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Κασσάνδρα, a
word of uncertain etymology.

## cassation
cassation, п., annulment. — F., fr. casser, fr. Late
L. cassare, fr. L. quassare, 'to shake violently'.
See quash, 'to make void', and -ation and cp.
cask, and the second element in fricassee.

## cassava
cassava, п., a West Indian tree. — F. cassave, fr.
Sp. casabe, cazabe, fr. Haiti casavi.

## casserole
casserole, п., ι) a baking dish; 2) a dishlike mold
of rice. — F., 'saucepan', fr. ONF. casse, fr.
OProveng. cassa, fr. VL. cattia, 'trowel, frying
pan', dissimulated fr. *ciattia, fr. Gk. κυάίΗον,
dimin. of κύαθος, 'ladle', fr. κυεΐν, κύειν, 'to
swell', whence also κϋμα, 'anything swelling or
swollen". See cave, п., and cp. cyma. Cp. also
cassolette.
Derivative: casserole, tr. v.

## Cassia
Cassia, п., a genus of plants of the senna family
(bot.) — L. casia, cassia, 'a tree with aromatic
bark', fr. Gk. κασίά, κασσϋ, 'cinnamon, cassia',
fr. Heb. q'tzi'af, 'cassia', which derives from
the base of qatza', 'he scraped off', and is rel.
to Arab, quda', 'fine dust', lit. 'dust scraped
off.

## Cassida
Cassida, п., a genus of tortoise beetles (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. L. cassis, gen. cassidis, 'helmet'.
See Cassis.

## cassimere
cassimere, п., a twilled woolen cloth. — Earlier
form of cashmere (q.v.)

## cassino
cassino, п., a game at cards. — It. casino, 'a little
house', dimin. of casa. See casino.

## Cassiopeia
Cassiopeia, п., the molher of Andromeda; after
her death she was changed into a constellation
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Κασσιόπη, Κασ-
σιέπεια; of uncertain etymology.

## Cassis
Cassis, п., a genus of mollusks (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. L. cassis, 'helmet', which prob. stands for-
*kadh-tis, fr. I.-E. base *kadh-, 'to guard,
watch', whence also OE. hod, 'hood', hxtt, 'hat'.
See hood, hat and cp. Cassida.

## cassiterite
cassiterite, п., native dioxide of tin, Sn02 (chem.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk.
κασσίτερος, 'tin', which is of uncertain origin. It possibly
derives fr. Elamitic *kassi-ti-ra, 'from the land
of the Kassi (i.e. Cosseans)', hence orig.
meaning 'metal occurring in the land of the Kassi'.

## cassock
cassock, п., a long ecclesiastical garment. — F.
casaque, fr. Pers. kazagand, 'a kind of jacket'.
The ending -and of the Persian word was
mistaken for a suff., and consequently dropped.
Cp. F. casaquin, 'jacket', in which the supposed
suff. -and was substituted by suff. -in.
Derivative: cassock, tr. v.

## cassolette
cassolette, п., a box for holding perfumes. —
F., fr. OProvenc. casoleta, dimin. of casola,
itself a dimin. of cassa. See casserole and -ette.

## cassone
cassone, п., a large chest, usually carved and
painted. — It., augment, of cassa, 'chest', fr.
L. capsa. See case, 'box'.

## cassowary
cassowary, п., a large ostrichlike bird of Australia
and New Guinea. — Fr. Malay kasudri, through

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:144 COLUMN:2 -->
the medium of Dutch. See F. Bense, A
Dictionary of the Lew-Dutch Element in the English
Vocabulary, p. 39.

## cast
cast, tr. and intr. v. — ME. casten, fr. ON. kasta,
'to throw', of uncertain origin. There is no'
connection between this word and L. gerere, pp.
gestus, 'to carry' (see gerent).
Derivatives: cast, п., cast-er, п., cast-ing, п.,
castor (q.v.)

## Castalia
Castalia, п., the spring of the Muses on Mount
Parnassus (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Κασταλία.
Derivative: Castali-an, adj.

## Castalia
Castalia, п., the water nymph (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. prec. word.

## Castanet
Castanet, п., usually in the pi., a pair of hollowed
pieces of hard wood or ivory used as an
accompaniment to music. — F. caslagnette, fr.
Sp. castaneta, dimin. of caslana, 'chestnut' (see
chestnut and -et, -ette); so called from its shape.

## caste
caste, п., a distinct social class. — Port, casta,
'race*, prop. fern, of the adj. casto, 'pure, chaste',
used as a noun, fr. L. caslus. See chaste. .

## castelian
castelian, п., governor or warden of a castle. —
ONF. castelain, corresponding to OF. chaste-
lain (F. chalelain), fr. L. castelldnus, 'pertaining
to a castle', fr. castellum, 'castle'. See castle and
cp. chatelain, which is a doublet of castellan.
Cp. also Castilian.

## castellated
castellated, adj., built like a castle. — ML., cas-
tellatus, 'built like, or resembling, a castle', fr.
L. castellum. See castie and the adj. suffixes
-ate and -ed.

## castigate
castigate, tr. v., to punish severely,, chastise. —
L. casttgatus, pp. of castigare, 'to correct,
chastise', prop, 'to induce to moral purity',
compounded of castus, 'clean, chaste, morally pure',
and agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead; to do,
act'. For the first element see chaste and cp.
chasten, chastise. For the second element see
agent and cp. the second element in fastigiate,
fatigue, fumigate, fustigate, levigate.
Derivatives: castigation (q.v.), castigal-ive, adj.,
castigator (q.v.)

## castigation
castigation, п., severe punishment. — L. casti-
gatio, gen. -onis, 'a correcting, chastising', fr.
casttgatus, pp. of castigare. See prec. word and
•-atioa.

## castigator
castigator, п., one who castigates. — L. castigator,
'one who corrects or chastises', fr. casttgatus,
pp. of castigare. See castigate and agential
suff. -or.

## castigatory
castigatory, adj., punitive. — L. castigatorius,
'reproving, censuring', fr. casttgatus, pp. of
castigare. See castigate and adj. suff. -ory.

## castile
castile, п., a fine kind of soap. — Short for
Castile soap; so called from Castile, a province in
Spain, fr. Sp. Castillo. See Castilian.

## Castilian
Castilian, adj. — Sp. castellano, fr. Costilla,
'Castile', a name rel. to Castillo, earlier castlello,
'castle, fort', fr. L. castellum (see castie); so
called from the numerous forts erected on its
frontiers to serve as defense against the Moors.
Cp. castile. For the ending see suff. -an.

## Castilleja
Castilleja, п., a genus of herbs of the flgwort
family (bot.) — ModL, named in 1781 after the
Spanish botanist Domingo Castillejo.

## castle
castle, n. — ME. castel, fr. ONF. castel,
corresponding to OF. chastel (F. chateau), fr. L.
castellum, 'citadel, fortress, stronghold', dimin. of
castrum, 'fortified place, fort, castle', castra
(pi.), 'camp'. See castrametatinn and cp. nlcazar,
castellan, Castilian, chateau.
Derivatives: castle, tr. and intr. v., castl-ed,
adj.

## Castor
Castor, п., one of the Dioscuri (Greek mythol) —
L., fr. Gk. Κάστωρ, lit. 'the Bright one', from the
stem of κέκασμαι, Ί distinguish myself', which
is cogn. with OI. perf. saiaduh (part, sasadanah),
'to distinguish oneself, to shine'.

## castor
castor, п., l) beaver; 2) substance obtained from
the beaver, castoreum. — F., fr. L. castor, fr.
Gk. κάστωρ, of s.m., fr. Κάστωρ (see Castor); so
called because the secretion of the beaver was
used as a remedy for diseases of the womb and
Κάστωρ was known as a preserver (σωτήρ) of
women.

## castor
castor, n. (of pepper, etc.) — Fr. earlier caster.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:144 COLUMN:3 -->
lit. 'thrower', formed fr. cast with agential suff.
-er, resp. -or.

## castor
castor, caster, п., a small wheel fixed below a
chair leg. — Formed fr. cast in the obsolete
sense 'to turn'. See prec. word.

## castor
castor, п., callosity on a horse's leg. — Prob. a
corruption of ME. castane, castanie, fr. ONF.
castaine which corresponds to OF. chastaigne
(F. chataigne), lit. 'chestnut'. See chestaut.

## castoreum
castoreum, п., castor (a secretion of the beaver).
— L. fr. Gk. καστόριον, fr. κάστωρ, gen.
κάστορος, 'beaver'. See castor, 'beaver'.

## Castoridae
Castoridae, n. pi., a family of rodents, the beavers
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -Idae fr.
L. castor, 'beaver'. See castor, 'beavef'.

## castorite
castorite, п., a variety of petalite (mineral.) —
Named after Castor, 'one of the Dioscuri'; cp.
pollucite. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## castral
castral, adj., pertaining to a camp. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. castra, 'camp'. See
next word.

## castrametation
castrametation, п., the laying out of a camp
(mil.) — F. castramitation, fr. ML. castramild-
tidnem, ace. of castrametutid, fr. L. castrameta-
tus, pp. of castrametari, 'to pitch a camp', which
is compounded of castra, 'camp', and metari,
'to measure, mete'. Castra is the plural of
castrum, 'a fortified place, fort, castle', orig. 'that
which has been cut out', fr. *kaslrom, 'a
cutting tool'. See next word and cp. alcazar. L.
metari is rel. to meliri, 'to measure'; see mete,

## castrate
castrate, tr. v., to remove the testicles of. — L.
castratus, pp. of castrare, 'to cut, geld', fr. *kas-
trom, 'a cutting tool'; prob. cogn. with OI.
iusati, iasti, 'cuts', iastram, 'knife*, Gk. κεάζειν,
'to split', and perh. also with OSIav. kosa,
'sickle'. L. castrum, 'a fortified place' (in the pi.
'camp'), carire, 'to be without, be wanting, be
free from, abstain from', castus, 'pure, chaste',
are prob. related to castrare. See chaste and cp.
caret. Cp. also castle and the first element in
castrametation. For the ending see verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: castrat-er, п., castration (q.v.),
caslral-or, n.

## castration
castration, n. — F., fr. L. caslrdlionem, ace. of
castrdtio, fr. castratus, pp. of castrare, 'to cut,
geld'. See prec. word and -ion.

## casual
casual, adj., accidental. — F. casuel, fr. L.casu-
alis, 'accidental, fortuitous', fr. casus, 'case'.
See case, 'condition', and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: casual-ly, adv., casual-ness, п.,
casual-ly, n.

## casuist
casuist, п., a person who resolves questions of
right and wrong. — F. casuiste, fr. Sp. casuista,
orig. 'an expounder of cases of conscience', a
hybrid coined fr. L. casus (in its ML. sense 'case
of conscience') and -ista, a suff. of Greek
origin. See case, 'condition', and -ist.
Derivatives: casuist-ic, casuist-ic-al, adjs., ca-
suist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## casuistry
casuistry, п., the resolving of questions of right
and wrong. — Coined by the English poet
Alexander Pope (1688-1744) fr. casuist and
suff. -ry.

## caswellite
caswellite, п., an altered mica (mineral.) —.
Named after the American mineralogist John H.
Caswell. For the ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## cat
cat, n. — ME., ft. OE. calt, calte, rel. to ON. kSttr
(masc.), ketta (fem.), Du. kat, OHG. kazza,
MHG., G. katze. Cp. Olr., Gael, cat, W. kath,
OCo. kat, Bret, kaz, 'cat'. Both these Teut. and
Celtic words are of uncertain origin. They derive
perh. fr. Late L. cattus (masc.),catta (fem.),
whence It. gatto, Sp. goto, F. chat. Late L. cattus and
catta are possibly loan words from an African
language; cp. Nubian Ααί/Γί, 'cat'. TheBalto-Slavic
names for the cat: OSIav. kotuka, kotel'a, Lith.
katl (whence Finnish katti) are perh. of the
same origin as L. cattus. Cp. Arab, qiff,
'tomcat', qilia", 'cat', which may be from the same
source. Cp. also chatoyant and the first element
in caterpillar, caterwaul. Cp. also kitling,
kitten, kittle, 'to bring forth kittens', kitty, 'kitten',
and the second element in meerkat.
Derivatives: cat, tr. v., catl-ery, п., catt-ish, adj.,
catt-ish-ly, adv., catt-ish-ness, п., catling (q.v.),
catt-y, adj., catt-i-ly, adv., calt-i-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:145 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CATA- | 118 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:145 COLUMN:1 -->

## cata- (before consonants)
cata- (before consonants), cat- (before vowels),
cath- (before aspirated vowels), pref. meaning
'down, downward; against; in accordance with,
entirely, completely'. — Gk. κατά-, κατ-, resp.
καθ-, fr. κατά, 'down from, down to; against;
over,along; according to', cogn. with Hitt. katta,
'down, downward, at, with, under', and prob.
also with Gaul, canta-, OW. cant, Olr. cet-,
'with'.

## eatabasis
eatabasis, п., the decline of a disease (med.) —
ModL., lit. 'a going down', fr. Gk. κατάβασις,
fr. καταβαίνειν, 'to go down', fr. κατά (see cata-)
and βαίνειν, 'to go'. See basis and cp. anabasis.

## eatabolism
eatabolism, п., destructive metabolism (biol. and
physiol.) — Lit. 'a throwing down', fr. Gk.
καταβολή, fr. καταβάλλειν, 'to throw down', fr.
κατά (see cata·) and βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See
ballistic and -ism and cp. anabolism, metabolism.

## catachresis
catachresis, п., incorrect use of a word. — L., fr.
Gk. κατάχρησις, 'excessive use, misuse', which
is compounded of κατά, 'against' (see cata-), and
χρήσις, 'use, employment', from the base of
χρή, 'it is necessary', χράομαι, inf. χρήσ&αι 'to
make use of, to use'. See chrematlstic and cp.
the firs! element in chrestomathy and the second
element in polychrestic.

## catachrestlc
catachrestlc, adj., incorrectly used, misapplied. —
Gk. καταχρηστικός, 'misused, misapplied', fr.
καταχρήσ&αι, 'to misuse', fr. κατά, 'against' and
χρήσ&αι, 'to use'. See prec. word. For the ending
see suff.- -ic.
Derivatives; catachrestic-al, adj., catachrestic-
al-ly, adv.

## cataclasm
cataclasm, п., a breaking down. — Gk. κατάκλασ-
μα, 'a breaking down', fr. κατακλαν, 'to break
down', fr. κατά (see cata-) and κλαν, 'to break',
whence κλάσις, 'a breaking'. See clastic and
cp. words there referred to. For derivatives of
I.-E. "qeiad-, a -(/-enlargement of base "qela-,
see dado-, holt.
Derivative: cataclasm-ic, adj.

## cataclysm
cataclysm, п., a great flood; in geol., a violent
upheaval. — F. cataclysme, fr. Gk.
κατακλυσμός, 'deluge, flood', fr. κατακλύζειν, 'to dash
against, break over, inundate', which is formed
fr. κατά, 'against' (see cata-), and κλύζειν, 'to
wash, dash against, break over', whence also
κλύσμα, 'liquid used for washing out; surf,
κλυστήρ, 'clyster pipe, syringe', κλύδων, 'wave,
surge'. Gk. κλύζειν is cogn. with L. cloaca (fr.
earlier clovaca), 'sewer, drain', OL. cluere, 'to
purge'. See cloaca and cp. clyster.
Derivatives: cataclysm-al, cataclysmat-ic, adjs.,
cataclysm-ist, n.

## catacomb
catacomb, п., an underground cemetery. — F.
catacombe, fr. Late L. catacumba, dissimilated
fr. "cata tumbas, 'beside the tombs' (prob. under
the influence of L. -cumbere, 'to lay oneself
down, to lie'). See cata- and tomb.

## catacumbal
catacumbal, adj., resembling a catacomb. —
Formed fr. Late L. catacumba (see prec. word)
with adj. suff. -al.

## catadioptric
catadioptric, adj., involving both reflection and
refraction (physics). — Formed fr. cata- and
dioptric. Cp. catoptric.

## catadromous
catadromous, adj., going down rivers toward the
sea to spawn. — Formed fr. cata- and Gk.
δρόμος, 'course'. See dromedary and -oils and
cp. anadromous.

## catafnlqne
catafnlqne, п., a temporary structure used at
funerals. — F., fr. It. calafalco, fr. VL. *catafali-
cum (whence also OF. chafaud, F. echafaud,
'scaffold'), which is formed fr. cata- and L. fala,
'a wooden lower (from which missiles were
thrown into a besieged cily); scaffolding', a
word of Etruscan origin. Cp. scaffold.

## Catalan
Catalan, adj., pertaining to Catalonia in Spain or
its language.
Derivative: Catalan, п., the language of
Catalonia.

## catalectic
catalectic, adj., lacking part of the last foot of
the verse (pros.) — Late L. calalicticus, fr. Gk.
καταληκτικός, 'leaving off; having the last foot
of a verse incomplete', fr. καταλήγειν, 'to leave
off, stop', fr. κατά (see cata-), and λήγειν 'to
leave off, cease from', lit., 'to grow tired or
weary', which is related to λαγαρός, 'slack,
hollow, sunken', and cogn. with L. languere, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:145 COLUMN:2 -->
faint, weary', laxus [for '(s)1lg-sos\, 'wide, loose,
open', fr. I.-E. base *(s)leg-, *(s)l*g-, 'to be
slack'. See slack, adj., and cp. lax and words
there referred to.

## catalepsy
catalepsy, п., a condition in which consciousness
is temporarily lost and the muscles become rigid
(med. and psycho!.) — Gk. κατάληψις, 'seizure',
fr. καταλαμβάνειν, 'to seize upon', fr. κατά (see'
cata-) and λαμβάνειν, 'to take, grasp, seize'. See
lemma and cp. words there referred to.

## cataleptic
cataleptic, adj., pertaining to, or having,
catalepsy. — Gk. καταληπτικός fr. καταληπτός,
'capable of being seized', verbal adj. of κατα-
λαμβάνειν. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: cataleptic, п., a person subject to
catalepsy.

## catallactic
catallactic, adj., pertaining to exchange. — Fr.
Gk. καταλλάσσειν, 'to change, exchange', fr.
κατά (see cata-) and άλλάσσειν, 'to change', fr.
ίίλλος, 'other', which is cogn. with L. alius,
'other'. See else and cp. alio-, alias. Cp. also al-
Iactite and words there referred to.
Derivative: catallactic-al-ly, adv.

## catalogue
catalogue, catalog, n. — F. catalogue, fr. Late
L. catalogus, fr. Gk. κατάλογος, 'a counting up,
enrollment', fr. καταλέγειν, 'to count up', lit.
'to count down', fr. κατά (see cata-) and λέγειν,
'to pick out, reckon, count, tell,speak'. See logos.
Derivatives: catalogue, catalog, tr. v.,
cataloguer, catalog-er, n.

## Catalpa
Catalpa, п., a genus of plants of the trumpet-
creeper family (hot.) — ModL., a name of
Carolina Indian origin.

## catalysis
catalysis, п., chemical change caused by an agent
which itself remains unchanged (chem.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. κατάλυσις, 'a dissolving', fr.
καταλΰειν, 'to dissolve' fr. κατά (see cata-) and
λύειν, 'to loose, loosen'. See -lysis.

## catalyst
catalyst, п., a catalytic agent (chem.) — See
prec. word.

## catalytic
catalytic, adj., producing catalysis (chem.) — Gk.
καταλυτικός, 'able to dissolve', fr. καταλΰειν.
See catalysis and -ic.

## catalyze
catalyze, tr. v. — Back formation fr. catalysis.
Derivative: catalyz-er, n.

## catamaran
catamaran, п., ι) a raft of logs; 2) a boat formed
from two parallel hulls. — Tamil katfumaram,
compounded of каци, 'binding', and maram,
'tree, wood'.

## catamenia
catamenia, п., menstruation (physiol.) — ModL,
fr. Gk. τά καταμήνια, which is compounded of
κατά, 'according to' (see cata-), and μήν, gen.
μηνός, 'month'. See meno- and cp. emmenlc.

## catamite
catamite, п., a boy used in pederasty. — L.
Catamitus, a corrupt collateral form of Gany-
medes, fr. Gk. Γανυμήδης, 'Ganymede', name of
Jupiter's cupbearer; see Ganymede. The change
of Greek S to L. f is. due to Etruscan influence.
Cp. sportula.
Derivatives: catamit-ed, catamit-ing, adjs.

## catamountain
catamountain, cat-a-mountain, п., the European
wild cat. — Lit. 'cat of the mountain'.

## catapasm
catapasm, п., a medicinal powder to be sprinkled
upon the skin. — Gk. κατάπασμα, 'powder', fr.
καταπάσσειν, 'to besprinkle with', fr. κατά (see
cata-) and πάσσειν, 'to sprinkle, besprinkle',
which is of uncertain origin.

## cataphora
cataphora, п., lethargy (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. καταφορά, 'lethargic attack', lit. 'a bringing
down', fr. καταφέρεσθ-αι, 'to be brought down',
passive of καταφέρειν, 'to bring down', fr. κατά
(see cata-) and φέρειν, 'to bring'. See bear, 'to
carry', and cp. -phore.

## cataphract
cataphract, п., a coat of mail. — L. cataphractes,
fr. Gk. καταφράκτης, 'coat of mail', fr. κατά-
φρακτος, 'covered up', verbal adj. of κατα-
φράσσειν, 'to fortify', fr. κατά 'down, entirely'
(see cata-), and φράσσειν, 'to fence round,
enclose, defend', which stands for *φράκ-ιειν and
is rel. to φράγμα, 'defence', and prob. cogn.
withL. farcire, 'to fill,stuff\frequens,'crowded'.
See frequent.

## cataphyll
cataphyll, п., a rudimentary leaf (hot.) — Lit.
'down leaf, compounded of cata- and Gk.
φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo- and cp. the second
element in hypsophyll and in sporophyll.
Derivative: cataphyll-ary, adj.

## cataplasm
cataplasm, п., a poultice (med.) — F. cataplasme.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:145 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. L. cataplasma, fr. Gk. κατάπλασμα, 'plaster,
poultice', fr. καταπλάσσειν, 'to plaster over', fr.
κατά (see cata-) and πλάσσειν, 'to form'. See
plasma and cp. words there referred to.

## catapult
catapult, п., an ancient military engine for
hurling stones, spears, etc. — L. catapulta, fr. Gk.
καταπέλτης, 'engine for hurling bolts, catapult',
fr. κατά (see cata-) and the stem of πάλλειν, 'to
hurl', which stands in gradational relationship
to πελεμίζειν, 'to shake, cause to tremble',
πόλεμος, 'war'. See polemic and cp. words there
referred to.

## cataract
cataract, п., a waterfall. — L. cataracta,
'waterfall', fr. Gk. καταράκτης, καταρράκτης, fr. κατα-
ράσσειν, καταρράσσειν, 'to dash down, break in
pieces', fr. κατά (see cata-) and άράσσειν, 'to
smite, break in pieces', which is prob. of imitative
origin; cp. άράγ-δην, 'with a rattle'. The spelling
καταρράκτης (with double p) is prob. due to a
confusion with καταρρηγνύναι, 'to tear in pieces'.
Derivatives: cataract, tr. and intr. v., cataract-
al, n.

## cataract
cataract, п., an eye disease.— L. cataracta,
'waterfall' (see prec. word), substituted for aqua,
'water', which was used as a loan translation
of Arab, ma*, 'water; cataract (the eye disease)'.
See Walt Taylor, Arabic Words in English, in
S.P.E. (= Society for Pure English), Tract
No.XXXVIH, p. 597.

## catarinite
catarinite, п., an iron meteorite (mineral.) —
Named after Santa Catarina, name of a state
and its capita! in southern Brazil. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## catarrh
catarrh, п., inflammation of the mucous
membranes. — F. catarrhe, fr. L. catarrhus, fr. Gk.
κατάρροος, 'cold in the head', lit. 'a running
down', fr. καταρρεΐν, 'to flow down', fr. κατά
(see cata-) and ρεΐν, 'to flow'. See stream and
cp. rheo-.
Derivatives: catarrh-al, adj., catarrh-al-ly, adv.

## Catarrhlna
Catarrhlna, n. pi., a division of the order
Primates, including the gorilla, orangutan .and
chimpanzee (zool.) — ModL., lit. 'with
nostrils downward', fr. cata- and Gk. ρίς, gen.
ρινός, 'nose'. See rhino-.

## catarrhine
catarrhine, adj. and n. — See prec. word.

## Catasetum
Catasetum, п., a genus of orchids (bot.) — A
ModL, hybrid coined fr. cata- and L. saetum,
'bristle'; see seta. The correct form would be
Catachaetum (fr. cata- and Gk. χαίτη, 'long
flowing hair'), in which both elements are of
Greek origin (see chaeto-).

## catastasis
catastasis, п., the part of a drama, in which the
action is at its height. — Gk. κατάστασις,
'settlement, appointment, state, condition', fr. καί>ι-
στάναι, 'to set down, set in order', fr. κατά
(see cata-) and ίστάναι, 'to place'. See state.

## catastrophe
catastrophe, n. — L. catastropha, fr. Gk.
καταστροφή, Overturning, overthrowing', fr. κατα-
στρέφειν, 'to upset, overturn, overthrow', lit.
'to turn down', fr. κατά (see cata-) and στρέφειν,
'to turn'. See strophe.
Derivatives: catastroph-ic, catastroph-ic-al, adjs.,
cataslroph-ic-al-ly, adv., catastroph-ism, п.,
catastroph-ist, n.

## catatonia
catatonia, п., a severe form of dementia praecox
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. κατάτονος, 'a
stretching down; depression', fr. κατατείνειν,
'to stretch down', fr. κατά (see cata-) and τε(-
νειν, 'to stretch', which is cogn. with L. tenuis,
'thin, slight', tendere, 'to stretch'. See tend, 'to
move in a certain direction', and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see suff. -la.

## Catawba
Catawba, п., a kind of grape and wine. — Named
after the Catawba River in the Carolinas.

## catch
catch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. cacchen, fr. ONF.
cachier, corresponding to OF. chacier, F. chas-
ser, 'to hunt', fr. VL. *captiare, fr. L. capture,
'to strive to seize', freq. of L. capere (pp. cap-
tus), 'to catch, seize, hold'. See captive and cp.
chase, which is a doublet of catch. Cp. also
ketch, 'a kind of small vessel'.
Derivatives: catch, п., catch-er, п., catch-ing,
adj., catch-ing-ly, adv., catch-ing-ness, п.,
catchment, п., catch-y, adj.

## catchpole
catchpole, catchpoll, п., a sheriff's officer whose
duty was to make arrests for debt; taxgatherer,
bumbailiff. — ME. cacchepol, from an ONF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:146 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 119 | CAUCASIAN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:146 COLUMN:1 -->
equivalent of OF. chacepol, lit. 'chase-chicken',
fr. ML. cacepullus, chassipullus, fr. *cacere,
*chacere, 'chassere, 'to chase', and L. pullus,.
'chicken' (see catch, chase and pullet, poult);
so called because taxgatherers used to
confiscate poultry.

## catchup
catchup, catsup, n. — See ketchup.

## cate
cate, usually in p]. cates, п., dainties, delicacies.
— Aphetic for acate, fr. ONF. acat, fr. acaier,
'to buy, purchase'. See cater.

## catechesis
catechesis, п., instruction by word of mouth. —
Gk. κατήχησις, 'instruction by word of mouth',
fr. κατηχεΐν. See catechize.

## catechetic
catechetic, catechetical, adj., pertaining to
catechesis or a church catechism. — Gk.
κατηχητικός, 'pertaining to instruction by word of
mouth', fr. κατηχεΐν. See catechize.
Derivatives: catechetical-ly, adv., catechet-ics,n.

## catechism
catechism, п., instruction by questions -and
answers. — F. catechisme, fr. Eccles. L. catlchis-
mus, fr. Gk. κατηχισμός, fr. κατηχίζειν. See
catechize and -ism.

## catechist
catechist, п., one who instructs by questions and
answers. — Eccles. L. catechista, fr. Gk. κατη-
χιστής, fr. κατηχίζειν. See next word and -ist.
Derivatives: catechist-ic, catechist-ic-al, adjs.,
catechist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## catechize
catechize, tr. v., to instruct by questions and
answers. — Eccles. L. catechizare, 'to teach by
word of mouth', fr. Gk. κατηχίζειν, fr.
κατηχεΐν, 'to resound', hence 'to sound (a thing) in
one's ears; to teach by word of mouth', fr. κατά
(see cata-) and ήχεΐν, 'to sound, ring, peal*,
fr. ήχώ, 'sound'. See echo and -ize.
Derivative: catechiz-er, n.
catechu^ п., a stringent substance obtained from
the wood, fruit or leaves of several Asiatic trees.
— Malay kachu (cp. Tamil kasu, Kanarese
каски), fr. Hind, kafh, fr. OI. kvdihati, 'he
decocts', which is cogn. with Goth, hapjan, 'to
foam', hapo, 'foam', OSlav. kvasu, 'leaven',
and L. caseus, 'cheese'. See cheese and cp. F.
cachou (whence E. cashoo, a variant of catechu)
and It. catecu. Cp. also cutch.

## catechumen
catechumen, п., one receiving instruction in the
elements of Christianity. — F. catechumine, fr.
Eccles. L. catechumenus, fr. Gk. κατηχούμενος,
'instructed by word of mouth', pass. pres. part,
of κατηχεΐν, 'to teach by word of mouth'. See
catechize. For the pass. pres. part. suff. -μένος
see alumnus and cp. words there referred to.

## categorematlc
categorematlc, adj., capable of being used alone
(as e.g. the predicate of a sentence). — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. κατηγόρημΛ, gen.
κατηγορήματος, 'accusation, charge; predicate', fr.
κατηγορεΐν. See category.

## categorical
categorical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
Late L. categoricus, fr. Gk. κατηγορικός,
'accusatory, affirmative, categorical', fr.· κατηγορία.
See next word.
Derivatives: categorical-ly, adv., categorical-
ness, n.

## category
category, n. — L. categoria, fr. Gk. κατηγορία,
'accusation, predication, category', fr.
κατηγορεΐν, 'to accuse, signify, indicate, affirm,
predicate', fr. κατήγορος, 'accuser', lit. 'one who
speaks against somebody before an assembly',
fr. κατά, 'against' (see cata·), and the stem of
άγορεύειν, 'to harangue, assert', lit. 'to speak in
the assembly', fr. αγορά, 'assembly', which is rel.
to άγείρειν,Ίο assemble', and cogn. with h.grex,
gen. gregis, 'flock'. See gregnrious and cp. agora,
allegory. Cp. also categorematlc.

## catena
catena, п., a chain. — L., 'chain'. See chain.

## catenarian
catenarian, adj., pertaining lo a chain. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. catlnarius, fr. catena. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ary and cp.
concatenate.

## catenary
catenary, adj. and n. — See prec. word.

## catenate
catenate, tr. v., to link together. — L. catenatus,
pp. of catenare, 'to chain together', fr. catena.
See catena and verbal suff. -ate.

## cater
cater, intr. v., to provide food. — From the ob-
sol. n. catour, 'buyer, caterer', aphetic for aca-
tour, fr. ONF. acatour, corresponding to OF.
achalour (F. acheteur), 'buyer', fr. OF. achater
(cp. the forme acheder, occurring in Jonas,
loth cent.), fr. VL. *accapitare, 'to add to one's

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:146 COLUMN:2 -->
capital', fr. ad, 'to' (see ad-), and a verb formed
from the stem of L. caput, gen. capitis, 'head'
(see capital, adj.). The usual derivation fr. VL.
*accaptare, 'to try to take, seize', cannot be
accepted because of phonetic reasons. The change
of I to d in OF. acheder and OSp. acabdar could
not be accounted for, if it had been preceded
originally by a consonant.

## cater
cater, п., the four at cards or dice. — Orig. 'four',
fr. F. quatre, 'four', fr. L. quattuor. See quart.

## cateran
cateran, п., a highland robber. — Gael, ceathair-
neach, 'marauder', fr. cealhairne, 'common
people, peasantry', rel. to Ir. cealharn, 'a band
of soldiers'. See kera, 'lightarmed foot soldier'.

## caterer
caterer, n. — ME. catour, 'caterer' (whence cater,
v. (q.v.) Accordingly the suff. -er in caterer is
redundant. Cp. fruiterer, poulterer, sorcerer,
upholsterer.

## caterpillar
caterpillar, n. — ONF. catepelose, corresponding
to OF. chalepelose, fr. Late L. catta pildsa,
'hairy cat'. For the etymology of Late L. catta
see cat. L. pildsa is fem. of pilosus, 'hairy', fr.
pilus, 'hair'; see pile, 'hair'. The ending of the
English word was influenced by piller, 'one who
pills' (see pill, 'to rob').
Derivative: caterpillar, intr. v.

## caterwaul
caterwaul, intr. v. — ME. caterwrawen, cater-
wawen, fr. LG. katerwaulen, 'to cry like cats',
fr. kater, 'male cat', and. waulen, 'to cry'. The
first element is rel. to MLG., MDu. katte, 'cat';
see cat. The second element is rel. to E. waul,
a variant of wail (q.v.)
Derivatives: caterwaul, п., caterwaul-er, п.,
caterwaul-ing, n.

## catgut
catgut, n. — Compounded of cat and gnt; so
called although made from the intestines of
sheep.

## Catharist
Catharist, п., a member of any of various sects
aiming at purity (Eccles. hist.) — ML. Catha-
rista, fr. Eccles. Gk. καθαριστής, fr. Gk.
καθαρός, 'pure, clean'; cp. Gk. καθαριστής, Чгее
pruner', and see next word. For the ending see
juff. -ist.

## catharsis
catharsis, п., ι) purgation (med.); 2) purification
of the emotions by art. — ModL., fr. Gk. κάθαρ-
σις, 'cleansing, purification', from the stem of
καθαίρειν, 'to cleanse, purify; to prune (a tree)',
fr. καθαρός, 'clean, pure', which is of uncertain,
origin. Cp. cathartic, Catherine, acatharsia.

## cathartic
cathartic, catbartical, adj., cleansing, purifying.
— Gk. καθαρτικός, 'fit for cleansing', from the
stem of καθαίρειν. See prec. word.
Derivatives: cathartical-ly, adv., cathartical-
ness, n.

## Cathay
Cathay, п., poetic name of China. — ML. Ca-
taya, fr. Khitai, the name of a Tatar kingdom
(the kingdom of the Khitan Tatars). Cp.
Khitan.

## cathedra
cathedra, п., the seat of a bishop. — L., fr. Gk.
καθέδρα. See chair and cp. ex cathedra.

## cathedral
cathedral, n. — ML. cathedrdlis, short for ecclisia
cathedralis, 'church pertaining to the seat of a
bishop', fr. cathedra. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.

## Catherine
Catherine, Catharine, also Katherine, Katharine,
fem. PN. — F. Catherine, fr. L. Ecaterina, Kate-
rina, fr. Gk. Αικατερίνη (whence also Russ.
Ekaterina). The later L. spelling Katharina is
due to a connection with Gk. καθαρός, 'pure',
the supposed origin of the name.
Catherine wheel. — So called from the spiked
wheel with which St. Catherine of Alexandria
was tortured.

## catheter
catheter, п., a surgical instrument used to draw
off fluid from body cavities. — Late L., fr. Gk.
καθετήρ, 'something let down; surgical
instrument for emptying the bladder', from the stem
of καθιέναι, 'to send down', fr. κατά (see cata-)
and Ιέναι, 'to move forward, throw, send',
which stands for 'yi-ye-nai and is cogn. with
L. iacere, 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and
cp. synesis.
Derivatives: catheter-ism, п., catheter-ize, tr. v.,
catheter-iz-athn, n.

## cathode
cathode, kathode, п., negative electric pole
(physics and chem.) — Gk. κάθοδος, 'way down,
descent', fr. κατά (see cata-) and οδός, 'way'.
See odograph and cp. words there referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:146 COLUMN:3 -->
The term cathode was introduced into electricity
by the English physicist and chemist Michael
Faraday "(1791-1867); cp. anode, electrode.
Derivatives: cathod-al, cathod-ic, adjs., cathod-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## catholic
catholic, adj. — F. catholique, fr. Eccles. L. catho-
licus, fr. Gk. καθολικός, 'general, universal', fr.
καθόλου = καθ" όλου, 'on the whole, in general',
fr. κατά, 'according to' (see cata-), and δλος,
'whole', which stands for *δλίος, fr. I.-E. base
*sol-wos, whence also L. salvus, 'saved,
preserved, safe'. See safe and cp. holo-. Cp. also
cathoHcon.
Derivatives: catholic, п., catholic-al, adj., catho-
lic-al-ly, adv., catholic-ism, п., catholic-ize, tr. v.,
catholic-iz-er, п., catholic-ly, adv.

## catholicity
catholicity, п., 1) the quality of being catholic;
2) universality; 3) (usually cap.) Catholicism. —
Coined by Coleridge fr. catholic and suff. -ity
on analogy of F. catholicite which was coined
by Theodore-Agrippa d'Aubigne (1552-1630)
fr. catholique, 'Catholic'.

## catholicon
catholicon, п., a remedy for all diseases. — Gk.
καθολικόν, neut. of καθολικός, 'general,
universal'. See catholic.
Catholicos, п., title of primate of the Armenian
church. — Gk. καθολικός, 'general, universal'.
See catholic,

## cation
cation, п., a positive ion moving toward the
cathode (physics and chem.) — Gk. κατιόν, neut.
of κατιών, pres. part, of κατιέναι, 'to go down,
descend', fr. κατά (see cata-) and Εέναι, 'to go',
which is cogn. with L. ire, 'to go'. See itinerant.
The word cation was introduced into electricity
by Faraday (see cathode),' cp. ion, anion.
Derivative: cation-ic, adj.

## catkin
catkin, п., a tassellike spike of flowers, an ament.
— Du. katleken, dimin. of katte, 'cat', so called
because of its resemblance to a cat's tail. See
cat and -kin.
Derivative: calkin-ate, adj.

## catiiag
catiiag, п., 1) a kitten (rare); 2) catgut (rare);
3) a double-edged k'nife used in amputations. —
Formed fr. cat with suff. -ling.

## catlinite
catlinite, п., a red clay; pipestone (pelr'ogr.) —
Named after the American traveler George
Catlin (1796-1872). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## cato-
cato-, combining form meaning 'down'. — Gk.
κάτω, 'down, downward', rel. to κατά, 'down
from, down to'. See cata-.

## catoptric
catoptric, catoprrical, adj., pertaining to the
reflection of light. — Gk. κατοπτρικός,
'pertaining to a mirror*, fr. κάτοπτρον, 'mirror', fr.
κατά, 'against' (see cata-), and the stem of όπτός,
'seen; visible', οπτικός, 'pertaining to the eyes
or sight'. See optic and cp. dioptric
Derivatives: catoptrical-ly, adv., catoptrics (q.v.)

## catoptrics
catoptrics, п., that part of optics which deals
with the reflection of light. — See catoptric and
-ics and cp. dioptries.

## catoptromancy
catoptromancy, п., divination by a mirror. —
Compounded of Gk. κάτοπτρον, 'mirror', and
μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'. See catoptric and
-mancy.

## Catostomidae
Catostomidae, n. pi., a family of fresh-water
fishes, the suckers (ichthyol.) — ModL., formed
with suff. -idae fr. cato- and Gk. στάμα, 'mouth'.
See stoma.

## cattle
cattle, n. — ME. calel, fr. ONF. catel
(corresponding to OF. chatel), fr. Late L. capttale,
'property*, prop. neut. of the L. adjective capi-
talis, 'pertaining to the head, chief, principal',
from caput, gen. capitis, 'head'.' See capital,
adj., and cp. the noun capital in the sense of
'principal'. Cp. also chattel, which is a doublet
of cattle.

## Cattleyn
Cattleyn, п., a .genus of American orchids. —
ModL., named after the English botanist
William Cattley (died in 1832).

## catty
catty, п., a weight used in China and the East
Indies.— Malay kati, a weight of ij lb. Cp.
caddy.

## Caucasian
Caucasian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -ian
fr. L. Caucasus, fr. Gk. Καύκασις, fr. Scythian
Κρού-κασις, 'Caucasus', a compound meaning
lit. '(the mountain) shining with ice'; see Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., I, pp. 295-96, s.v. crusta. The

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:147 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CAUCHEMAR | 120 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:147 COLUMN:1 -->
first element of this compound is a derivative of
I.-E. base *qreu-, 'to be icy'. For derivatives of
*qrus-, an enlarged form of base *qreu- see
crust, crystal. The second element is rel. to Gk.
καίειν (for "κάίιειν), 'to burn'; see caustic.

## cauchemar
cauchemar, п., incubus. — F., a hybrid coined
from the blend of OF. chaucer and Picard cau-
qiter, 'to trample' (both derived fr. L. calcare,
of s.m., fr. calx, gen. calcis, 'heel'), and fr. MDu.
mare, 'incubus'. See Calceolaria and mare,
'incubus', and cp. the first element in caltrop.

## cancus
cancus, η., private meeting of the leaders of a
political party. — A word of Algonquian origin, lit.
meaning 'counselor'.
Derivative: caucus, intr. and tr. v.

## cauda
cauda, п., tail (zool. and anat.) — L. See next
word.

## caudal
caudal, adj., pertaining to the tail. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. cauda, 'tail', prob. orig.
meaning 'a piece cut, or to be cut, off', and rel.
to caudex, 'a block of wood'; Lith. kuddas,
'tuft', is not cognate with L. cauda (see Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., I, p. 185). See hew and cp.
coda, codetta, coward, cue, queue. Cp. also
candex and words there referred to.

## caudate
caudate, adj., having a tail. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ate fr. L. cauda, 'tail'. See prec. word.

## caudex
caudex, п., the stem of palms and ferns (bot.) —
L. caudex, codex, 'trunk of a tree', lit. 'a tree cut
off', rel. to cudere, 'to strike, beat, pound'. See
bew and cp. codex, code, codicill. Cp. also
caudal, cause and the first element in cockboat.

## caudillo
caudillo, п., commander, chief, leader of an armed
troop; chief, leader. — Sp., a collateral form of
cabdith, fr. L. capiteUum, 'a little head', dimin.
of caput, gen. capitis, 'head'. See capital, adj.,
and cp. capital, 'head of a column'.

## caudle
caudle, п., a hot drink. — ONF. caudel,
corresponding to OF. chaudel (F. chaudeau), fr.
VL. caldellum, dimin. formed from the Latin
adj. calidus, caldus, 'hot', fr. calere, 'to be hot'.
See caldron and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also coddle.
Derivative: caudle, tr. v.

## canght
canght, past tense and pp. of catch. — ME. cauh-
te, formed on the analogy of lauhte, fr. lacchen
(whence E, latch), 'to catch'. See catch.

## cauk
cauk, cawk, п., chalk; barite (dial. E. and Scot.)
— Northern var. of calk.

## cnul
cnul, п., a membrane enclosing the fetus and
sometimes covering the head of a newly born
child. — MF. (= F.) cale; 'cap', back formation
fr. MF. (= F.) calotte. See calotte.

## cauldron
cauldron, n. — See caldroa.

## Caulerpa
Caulerpa, п., a genus of marine green algae (bol.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. καυλός, 'stem,
stalk', and ίρπειν, 'to creep'. See cole and
herpes.

## caulescent
caulescent, adj., having a visible stem. — Formed
fr. L. caulis, 'stalk, stem', with the inchoative
suff. -escent, on analogy of arborescent. See
cole and cp. next word. Cp. also acaulescent.

## cauliflower
cauliflower, n. — Refashioned after L. caulis,
'stem', and E. Bower fr. earlier colyflory, fr. F.
chou-fleuri, chou-fleur, which is formed on
analogy of It. cavolofiore, 'cauliflower', fr. L. caulis,
'stem, stalk', and flos, gen. floris, 'flower'. See
cole.

## cauline
cauline, adj., pertaining to, or growing on, a stem.
— Formed with suff. -ine (representing L. -ma)
fr. L. caulis, 'stem, stalk'. See cole and cp.
acanline.

## cnulis
cnulis, п., the stem or stalk of a plant (бог.) — L.
See cole and cp. prec. word.

## caulk
caulk, v. — A var. of calk.

## caulker
caulker, n. — A var. of calker.

## caulome
caulome, п., the stem of a plant (bot.) — Formed
fr. Gk. καυλός, 'stem, stalk' (see cole), with suff.
-ome, on analogy of rhizome.

## Caulophyllum
Caulophyllum, п., a genus of plants of the
barberry family (bol.) — ModL., lit. 'stem leaf', fr.
Gk. καυλός, 'stem', and φύλλον, 'leaf (see cole
and phyllo-); so called because the stem seems
to form the stalk of the great leaf.

## Caurus
Caurus, п., the northwest wind. — L. caurtts,
corus, cogn. with Lith. siaurys, 'north wind',
Sidure, 'north', Siauriis, 'raging, stormy', OSlav.
severu, 'north wind', Goth, skura (windis).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:147 COLUMN:2 -->
'storm', OE. scur, 'shower'. See shower.

## causalgia
causalgia, п., a burning sensation (med.) —
Medical L., lit. 'a burning pain', coined by the
American physician Silas Weir Mitchell (1829-1914)
fr. Gk. καϋσος, 'burning heat' (which derives fr.
*xaf-, the stem of καίειν, 'to burn'), and άλγος,
'pain'. See caustic and -algia.

## causale
causale, tr. v., to cause. — ML. causatus, pp. of
causure, Ίο cause'. Se2 cause, v. and п., and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: causal-ion, п., causat-ion-al, adj.,
causat-ive, adj., and п., causat-ive-ly, adv., cait-
sat-ive-ness, n.

## cause
cause, n. — F., fr. L. causa, 'cause, reason,
purpose', which is of uncertain origin. It stands
perh. for *caud-ta and orig. meant 'a striking',
hence is rel. to cudere, 'to strike, beat, knock', fr.
I.-E. base *qau-, 'to strike, beat'. See hew and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
accusative, accuse, causerie, coze, excuse, kickshaw,
recusant. For sense development cp. L. decidere,
'to cut off; to decide' (see decide).
Derivatives: caus-al, adj. and п., caus-al-ity, п.,
caus-al-ly, adv., cause-less, adj., cause-less-ly,
adv., cause-less-ness, n.

## cause
cause, tr. v. — F. causer, 'to cause', fr. ML. cau-
sare, 'to cause' (cp. L. causari, 'to plead, to
debate a question'), fr. L. causa, 'cause'. See
cause, n.
Derivative: caus-able, adj.

## causerie
causerie, п., a conversational article in a
periodical or newspaper. — F., 'talk, conversation', fr.
causer, 'to talk', fr. L. causari, 'to plead, dispute,
to discuss a question', fr. causa, 'cause, reason,
purpose' (see cause and -ery); named after
Sainte-Beuve's Causeries du lundi ('Monday
Talks').

## causeway
causeway, п., a raised road. — A blend of
causey and way.
Derivative: causeway, tr. v.

## causey
causey, п., a causeway (dial.) — ME. cauce, fr.
ONF. cauciee, corresponding to F. chaussee,
'causeway', fr. VL. (νια) calciata, lit. 'a road
paved with limestone', fem. pp. of calciare, 'to
pave with limestone', fr.L. calx, gen. calcis, 'lime,
limestone'. See calcareous and cp. cbaussee.

## caustic
caustic, adj., burning, corrosive. — F. caustique,
fr. L. causticus, fr. Gk. καυστικός, 'capable of
burning, corrosive', fr. καυστός, 'burnt', verbal
adj. of καίειν, which stands for *κά5-ιειν, 'to
burn, set on fire', fr. 1-Е. base *кёи-, *кй-, 'to
burn, heat', whence also Lith. kule, 'blight,
mildew', kuliti, 'to become blighted'. Cp. caeoina,
caliber, calm, catacaustic, Caucasian, cautery,
diacaustic, encaustic, holocaust, hypocaust, Ink,
Nausicaa.
Derivatives: caustic, п., caustic-ize, tr. v., caus-
tic-ly, adv., caustic-ness, n.

## cautel
cautel, п., caution; precaution. — OF. cautele
(F. cautele), fr. L. cautela, 'caution', fr. cautus,
'wary, careful, heedful', pp. of cavere, 'to be
on one's guard'. See cave, interj.

## cautelous
cautelous, adj., cautious. — F. cauteleux (fem.
cauteleuse), fr. cautele. See prec. word and -cos.
Derivatives: cautelous-ly, adv., cautelous-ness,n.

## cauter
cauter, п., a hot iron for cauterizing. — F. cau-
tire, fr. L. cauterium, fr. Gk. καυτήριον,
'branding iron', fr. καυτήρ,'burner'. See next word and
cp. cautery.

## canterize
canterize, tr. v., to burn with a hot iron or a
caustic substance. — F. cauteriser, fr. Late L.
caulerizare, fr. Gk. καυτηριάζειν, 'to sear with
a hot iron', fr. καυτήρ, 'burner', rel. to καυστός,
verbal adj. of καίειν, 'to burn'. See caustic and
-ize.
Derivative: cauteriz-ation, n.

## cautery
cautery, п., a cauter. — L. cauterium. See cauter.

## caution
caution, n. — F., fr. L. cautioner», ace. of cautio,
'wariness, carefulness, heedfulness", fr. cautus,
'wary, careful, heedful', pp. of cavere, 'to be on
one's guard, take heed'. See cave, interj.
Derivatives: caution, tr. v., caution-ary, adj. and
п., caution-er, ft.

## cautious
cautious, adj. — Cp. L. cautus, 'careful, heedful',
and see caution and -ous.
Derivatives: cautious-ly, adv., cautious-ness, n.

## cavalcade
cavalcade, п., a procession of horsemen. — F., fr.
It. cavalcata (with the Piemont pronunciation

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:147 COLUMN:3 -->
cavakada), prop. fem. pp. of cavalcare, 'to ride
on horseback', used as a noun, fr. Late L. cabal-
licare, fr. L. caballus. See cavalry.
Derivative: cavalcade, intr. v.

## cavalier
cavalier, п., a horseman; a gentleman serving as
a lady's escort. — F., fr. It. cavaliere, orig.
'horse-soldier', fr. Late L. caballarius (whence
also Provenc. cavalier, Sp. caballero, Port, caval-
leiro), fr. L. caballus. See cavalry and cp.
chevalier, which is a doublet of cavalier.
Derivatives: cavalier, adj., cavalier-ly, adv.

## cavalia
cavalia, п., any of various fishes of the genus
Carangus. — Port, cavalia, rel. to Sp. cabaila,
prop, a feminine form of Port, cavallo, resp. Sp.
caballo, 'horse', fr. L. caballus. See cavalry.

## cavalry
cavalry, n. — F. cavalerie, fr. It. cavalleria, fr.
cavallo, 'horse', fr. L. caballus, 'an inferior
horse, a nag', which is prob. a loan word from
a language of Asia Minor or the Balkan
peninsula. Cp. Gk. καβάλλης, 'horse', the Gaulish
*PN. Caballos and OSlav. kobyla, 'mare', which
also derive prob. from the same language as L.
caballus. MIr. (= Ir.) capall, Bret, caval, W.
ceffyll, 'horse', are Latin loan words. Cp.
chivalry, which is a doublet of cavalry. Cp. also
cavalcade, cavalier, cavalia, cheval-de-frise, cheval
glass, chevalier, capercailzie.

## cavatina
cavatina, п., ashort song or melody (mus.)— It.,fr.
cavata, prop. fem. pp. of cavare, 'to hollow(out),
dig (out)', fr. L. cavare, of.s.m. See next word.

## cave
cave, n. — F., fr. L. cava, fem. of the adjective
cavus, 'hollow, concave', used as a noun. L. cavus
prob. stands for "covvos and is cogn. with Gk.
κόος (Hesychius), 'chasm', κώος, 'prison' (lit.
'a hollow place'), κώδ'εια, 'poppy head', κοίλος
(for 'κόίιλος), 'hollow', κύαρ, 'eye of a needle;
orifice of the ear', Olr. ейа, 'hollow', cuass, 'cave',
Bret, klo, 'cave', OI. svayatl, 'swells', sunah,
'swollen', iavas-, 'strength^ heroism', sdvirah,
surah, 'strong', Gk. κυεΐν, κύειν, 'to become or
be pregnant', κϋμα, 'anything swollen; a wave',
κΰρος, 'authority', κύριος, 'lord, master'. All
these words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *kew(e)-,
*kewa-, *кй-, 'to vault', whence developed the
further meanings 'to bend inward, be hollow or
concave', on the one hand, and 'to bend
outward, swell out, be convex' on the other. See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., 1, pp. 191-92 s.v.
cavus, Boisacq, DELG., p. 481 s.v. καυλός and
Frisk, GEW., p. 38 s.v. κύαρ. Ср. cabinet, ca-
book, cadger, cage, casserole, cavatina, cave ne,
cavity, church and words there referred to, co-
deiae, codon, coelo-, concave, cumulus, cyma,
decoy, excavate, excavation, gabioa, hound
(naut.), jail. Cp. the related base *keu-, 'toswell;
hollow', for the derivatives of which see hole.
Derivatives: cave, tr. and intr. v., cav-ing, n.

## cave
cave, interj., beware! — L. cave, imper. of cavere,
'to be on one's guard, take care, beware', which
stands for *covere and is cogn. with Gk. κοέω
(for ίκοΓέω), Ί mark, perceive', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)qeu-, *(s)qeu-, 'to look at, observe', whence
also OE. sceawian, 'to look, see, behold'. See
show and wo(ds there referred to and cp. esp.
caution. Cp. also next word.

## caveat
caveat, п., 1) notice that no action is to be taken
(law); 2) a warning. — L., 'let him beware', 3rd
p. sing. pres. subj. of cavere. See prec. word.

## caveadish
caveadish, п., tobacco pressed into cakes. — Prob.
so called from the name of the producer or
exporter.

## cavern
cavern, п., a cave. — F. caverne, 'cave', fr. L.
caverna, fr. cavus, 'hollow'. See cave, n. For the
Latin suff. -erna, which is of Etruscan origin,
cp. cistern, tavern.

## cavernous
cavernous, adj., full of caverns or cavities. — L.
cavernosus, fr. caverna. See prec. word and -ous.

## cavesson
cavesson, п., a kind of noseband for a horse. —
F. cavegon, fr. It. cavezzone, 'halter with a
noseband', augment, of cavezza, 'halter', fr. VL.
"capitia, fr. L. capitium, 'a covering for the
head', fr. caput, gen. capitis, 'head'. See capital,
adj.

## Cavia
Cavia, п., the genus of cavies, the guinea pig
(zool.) — ModL., fr. F. cabiai, from a
Caribbean native word. Cp. cavy, capybara.

## caviar
caviar, caviare, n. — F. caviar, fr. It. caviaro (now
caviale), fr. MGk. καβιάριον, fr. Turk, khaviar,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:148 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 121 | CELIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:148 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. Kaffah ( — Theodosia), name of a trading
town on the SE. shore of the Black Sea.

## cavicora
cavicora, adj., hollow-horned. — Compounded
of L. cavus, 'hollow', and cornu, 'horn'. See
cave, п., and horn and cp. corn, 'hardened skin'.

## Cavicoraia
Cavicoraia, n. pi., another name for Bovidae
(zool.) — Lit. 'hollow-horned'. See prec. word.

## cavil
cavil, intr. v., to find trivial faults, to carp. —
OF. caviller, fr. L. cavillari, 'to jest, joke, make
captious objections, to cavil at', fr. cavilla, 'jest,
quibble, trick', dissimilated fr. 'calvilla, and
rel. to calvi, 'to devise tricks, use artifice', calum-
nia, 'false accusation, chicanery'; see calumny
and cp. challenge. For the surf. cp. L. favilla,
'glowing ashes, embers' which is rel. to fovere,
'to warm, keep warm'.
Derivatives: cavil, п., cavillation (q.v.), cavil(l)-
er, п., cavil(l)-ing, adj., cavil(l)-ing-ly, adv., ca-
vil(l)-ing-ness, n.

## cavillation
cavillation, п., a civil, caviling. — F., fr. L. cavil-
lationem, ace. of cavilldtio, 'a jesting, scoffing,
quibbling, shuffling', fr. cavilldtus, pp. of
cavillari. See prec. word and -ation.

## cavity
cavity, n. — F. cavite, fr. L. cavitdtem, ace. of
cavitas, fr. cavus, 'hollow'. See cave, п., and
-ity.

## cavo-relievo
cavo-relievo, п., hollow relief. — It. cavorilievo.
It. cavo derives fr. L. cavus, 'hollow'; see cave,
n. For It. rilievo see rilievo and cp. basso-rilievo.

## cavort
cavort, intr. v., to prance about. — Prob. a blend
of curvet and snort.

## cavy
cavy, п., a guinea pig. — See Cavia.

## cay
cay, п., a small island. — Sp. cayo, fr. Taino
cayo, 'small island'. Cp. key, 'small island'.

## caw
caw, п., the natural cry of the crow and raven;
intr. v., to utter this cry or imitate it. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. chongh.

## cawk
cawk, cauk, п., chalk, barite. — Dialectal
variants of chalk.
Derivative: cawk-y, adj.

## cavraey
cavraey, cavmy, п., a measure of land used in
Madras. — Tamil kdni, 'property , lit. 'that
which is seen or known', fr. кап, 'to see'.
сахоп, п., a wig (archaic). — Prob. fr. tile surname
Caxon.

## Caxton
Caxton, n. — any book printed by William Cax-
ton (died in 1491).

## cayenne
cayenne, п., also cayenne pepper. — Tupi kyinha,
quiynha, 'capsicum', lit. 'of the isle of Cayenne'.

## cayman
cayman, п., any of Central and South American
kinds of alligators. — Sp. caiman, fr. Carrib-
bean acayouman.

## cazimi
cazimi, п., the center of the solar disk (aslrol.) —
Arab, jismjesm, 'body', in the term 'dlajismi'sh-
shantsi, 'on the disk of the sun'. See Devic's
Supplement to Littre's Dictionary, p. 13.

## -ce
-ce, suff. used to form abstract nouns. — Fr. L.
-lia, either directly or through the medium of
F. -ce. See -ance, -eace.

## Ceanothus
Ceanothus, п., a genus of plants of the buckthorn
family (boi.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κεάνω&ος, 'a
kind of thistle'.

## cease
cease, intr. and tr. v. — ME. cassen, fr. OF.
(— F.) cesser, fr. L. cessare, 'to delay, loiter',
freq. of cedere (pp. cessus), 'to withdraw'. See
cede and cp. cessation, decease, incessant.
Derivatives: cease, п., cease-less, adj., cease-
less-ly, adv.

## cebolite
cebolite, п., a hydrous calcium aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after Cebolla Creek in
Colorado. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Cecil
Cecil, masc. PN. — Fr. L. Caecilius, name of a
Roman gens, a derivative of caecus, 'blind'. See
cecity.

## Cecilia
Cecilia, Cecily, also Cicely. — L. Caecilia, fern.
of Caecilius. See prec. word.

## cecity
cecity, п., blindness. — F. cecite, 'blindness', fr.
L. caecttdtem, ace. of caecilds, of s.m., fr.
caecus, 'blind', which is cogn. with OI. klkarah,
'squinting', Goth haihs, 'one-eyed', Olr. caech,
of s.m., MIr. leth-chaech, 'squinting', W. coeg,
'one-eyed'. Gk. καικίκς, 'the northeast wind',
is cogn. with these words and lit. means 'the
dark (wind)'. For sense development cp. L.
aquilo, 'the north wind', which is related to
aquilus, 'dark' (see Aquilo). Cp. caecum, Cae-
clas, Excoecaria. Cp. also Cecil. For the ending
see suff. -ity.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:148 COLUMN:2 -->

## Cecropia
Cecropia, п., a genus of trees of the mulberry
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Cecrops (q.v.) For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## Cecropia moth
Cecropia moth, a large silkworm moth (Samia
cecropia). — ModL. cecropia. See prec. word.

## Cecrops
Cecrops, п., a legendary king of Attica and
founder of Athens. — L., fr. Gk. Κέκροψ. The name
Κέρφοψ is prob. metathesized fr. *κέρκοψ and
lit. means 'face with a tail', fr. κέρκος, 'tail',
and δψ, gen. δπός, 'eye, face'. For the first
element see cercus. The second element is rel. to
Gk. <5ψις, 'sight', ότττός, 'seen, visible', οπτικός,
'pertaining to the eyes or sight'; see optic

## cedar
cedar, n. — ME. cedre, fr. OF. cedre (F. cedre),
fr. L. cedrus, fr. Gk. κέδρος, 'cedar', which prob.
denoted orig. 'a tree whose wood was used for
burning sacrifices', and derives fr. Heb. qdfdr,
'it exhaled odor, smoked'; see Heinrich Lewy,
Die semitischen Fremdworter im Griechischen,
Berlin, 189,5, p. 35. For sense development cp.
Gk. βυίκ, name of an African tree, prop, 'a tree
whose wood was burnt for sacrificial purposes',
fr. θύειν, 'to sacrifice', prop, 'to cause to smoke'
(see Thuja). Heb. qatar [whence q'fdrelh, 'odor
(of burning sacrifice), smoke, incense'] is rel. to
Arab, qatara, 'it exhaled odor, smoked', qular,
'exhalation, smoke', etc. Cp. Cedrela, cedrine,
Cedrus. Cp. also citron.
Derivatives: cedar, cedar-ed, cedar-η, adjs.

## cede
cede, tr. v. — L. cedere (pp. cessus), 'to go, go
away, yield, give up, withdraw', prob. for *ce-
zdere, from the demonstr. particle ce- and
I.-E. base *sed-, 'to go', whence also Gk. οδός,
'way', OSlav. chodu, 'a walking, going', choditi,
'to walk, go', OI. α-sad-, 'to go, approach', ut-
sad-, 'to step aside, disappear'. See he and odo-
grnph and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also '
abscess, accede, access, ancestor, antecede, cease,
cession, cesspool, concede, concession, decease,
exceed, excess, intercede, intercession, necessary,
precede, predecessor, procedure, proceed,
process, procession, recede, retrocede, secede,
succeed, success. — I.-E. base *sed-, 'to go', is prob.
identical with *sed-, 'to sit', the original sense of
the base having been~4o place (either the seat in
order to sit down, or the foot upon the ground
in order to go'). See sedentary.

## cedilla
cedilla, п., a graphic symbol put under the letter
с in some French and Spanish words. — Sp.,
spelled also zedilla, lit. 'a little z\ from the name
of the Greek letter zeta (ζ); so called because
orig. the letter z was added to с (e.g. F. leczon =
lecon), to indicate that it has not the usual sound
of k, but that of ρ (in Spanish), resp. that of s
(in French). See zeta.

## Cedrela
Cedrela, п., a genus of trees of the mahogany
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Sp. cedrelo, dimin. of
cedro, 'cedar'. See cedar.

## cedrine
cedrine, adj., pertaining to cedar. — L. cedrinus,
fr. Gk. κέδρινος, fr. κέδρος, 'cedar'. See cedar
and -ine (representing Gk. -ΐνος).

## Cedric
Cedric, masc. PN. — This name, which was first
used by Walter Scott ('Cedric the Saxon' is one
of the characters in Ivanhoe) prob. stands for
OE. Cerdic and owes its form to a mistake of
Scott's.

## Cedrus
Cedrus, п., a genus of trees of the pine family
(bol.) — L., 'cedar'. See cedar.

## ceduln
ceduln, п., in Spanish countries; order,
certificate, security. — Sp. cedilla, fr. L. schedula.
See schedule.

## cell
cell, tr. v., to overlay, cover. — F. ciel, 'sky,
canopy', fr. L. caelum, 'sky'. See celestial.
Derivatives: ceil-er, п., ceil-ing, n.

## celadon
celadon, п., pale green color. — F. celadon, fr.
Celadon, Astree's lover in Honore d'Urfe's
novel Astree. Honore d'Urfe formed this name
from the Latin PN. Celadon occurring in Ovid's
Metamorphoses.

## celadonite
celadonite, п., a green silicate of iron, magnesium
and potassium (mineral.) — Formed with subst.
pref. -ite fr. celadon (q.v.); so called in allusion
to its color.

## Celaeno
Celaeno, п., one of the Harpies (Greek mylhol.) —
L., fr. Gk. Κελοιινώ, lit. 'the Black one', fr.
κβλαινος, 'black', fr. I.-E. base *qel-, *qol-,
'black, spotted', which is rel. to base *qal-, of
s.m., whence L. cdligd, 'darkness'. See caliginous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:148 COLUMN:3 -->

## celandine
celandine, п., the swallowwort. — ME. celydoine,
fr. OF. celidoine (F. chelidoine), fr. L. chelido-
nium, fr. Gk. χελιδόνων, fr. χελϊδών, gen.
χελιδόνος, 'the swallow', which is rel. to κίχλη,
'the thrush', and cogn. with OE. gellan, '10 yell,
