shriek', galan, 'to sing'. See yell and alghtingale
and cp. chelidonium.

## Cclastrnceae.n.pl.
Cclastrnceae.n.pl., the staff-tree family (Лог) —
Formed fr. Celastrus with suff. -aceae.

## celastraceous
celastraceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Celastrus
Celastrus, п., a genus of trees, the staff-tree (hot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. κήλαστρος, 'a kind of
evergreen', a loan word from an Aegean language,
whence also Basque gorostri.

## -cele
-cele, suff. meaning 'tumor, hernia', as in
hydrocele, variocele (med.) — Fr. Gk. κήλη (Art. κάλη),
'tumor, hernia', which is cogn. with OSlav. kyla,
ON. haull, OE. hiala, OHG. hula, 'hernia'.

## celebrant
celebrant, п., one who celebrates. — L. celebrans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of celebrare. See next
word and -ant.

## celebrate
celebrate, tr. v., to perform (a rite) in a public
and solemn manner; to observe,
commemorate; intr. v., to observe a holiday, anniversary,
etc. — L. celebrdtus, pp. of celebrare, 'to
frequent, repeat, praise, honor, celebrate', fr. cele-
ber (masc), Celebris (fem.), celebre (neut),
'crowded, much frequented, renowned', which
prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *qel-, 'to drive', whence
also Gk. κέλλειν, 'to drive on, push', L. celer,
'swift'. See celerity and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: celebrat-ed, adj., celebrat-ed-ness,
п., celebration (q.v.), celebrat-ive, adj., celebra-
lor (q.v.), celebrat-ory, adj.

## celebration
celebration, n. — L. celebrdtid, gen. -6nis,
'concourse, festal celebration', fr. celebrdtus, pp. of
celebrare. See prec. word and -ion.

## celebrator
celebrator, n. — L., fr. celebrdtus, pp. of
celebrare. See celebrate and agential suff. -or.

## celebrity
celebrity, п., fame, a famous person. — L. cele-
britds, 'multitude, festal celebration', fr. celeber.
See celebrate and -ity.

## celeriac
celeriac, п., a variety of celery. — Formed fr.
celery.

## celerity
celerity, п., speed. — F. celer ite, fr. L. celer ita-
tem, ace. of celeritas, 'swiftness', fr. celer,
'swift', fr. I.-E. base *qel-, 'to drive', whence
also κέλλειν, 'to drive on, push; to run (a ship)
to land', κέλεσ!>οα, 'to urge on, exhort', κελεύειν,
'to urge on, exhon, order', κέλης, 'race horse;
small fast boat', OI. kaldyati, 'he urges on', and
prob. also Goth, haldan, 'to tend (orig. prob.
to drive on) the sheep', OE haldan, 'to hold'.
See hold and cp. acolyte, anacoluthoa, celebrate,
clonus, proceleusmatic. For the ending see Suff.
-ity.

## celery
celery, п., a plant with edible leafstalks. — F.
celeri, fr. Lombardic It. seller/, pi. of sellero
(corresponding to li. sedano), fr. L. seltnuin, fr.
Gk. σέλΐνον,' parsley". See parsley and cp. words
there referred to.

## celesta
celesta, п., a musical instrument. — F. celesta,
fr. celeste, 'heavenly', fr. L. caelestis. See
celestial.

## celeste
celeste, п., sky-blue color. — F. celeste, fr. L.
caelestis, 'heavenly', fr. caelum. See celestial.

## Celeste
Celeste, fem. PN. — F. Celeste, fr. L. caelestis,
'heavenly'. See prec. word.

## celestial
celestial, adj. — OF. celestial, celestiei, fr. L.
caelestis, 'pertaining to the sky, heavenly, divine',
fr. caelum, which is of uncertain origin. It
stands perhaps for *caid-(s)hm, and derives fr.
I.-E. base *(s)qdit-, *sqdid-, 'bright', whence also
OI. ketiili, 'brightness, light', citrah, 'bright,
apparent, obvious'. Litli. skaidnts, 'shining, clear',
skdistas, skaistiis, 'shining'. Lett, skaidrs, of
s.m., ON. Iieid, 'clear sky', OE. hador, OHG.
heitar, MHG., G. heiier, 'clear, shining,
cloudless'. Cp. caesious, ceil, ceiling, cerulean, Selina.
Cp. also -hood and words there referred to. —
The suff. -stis in L. caeie-stis is related to stare.
'to stand'. See state. Derivatives: celestial, п.,
celestial-ity, п., celestial-ly, adv.

## celi-
celi-, combining form. — A variant spelling of
coeli-.

## Celia
Celia, fem. PN. — It., fr. L. Caelia, fem. of
Caeliits, name of a Roman gens. Cp. F. Celie
and Sheila.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:149 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CELIAC | 122 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:149 COLUMN:1 -->
celiac. — See coeliac.

## celibacy
celibacy, п., unmarried state. — Formed with
suff. -ce fr. L. caelibntus. See celibate.

## celibatarian
celibatarian, adj., advocating celibacy; п., one
who advocates celibacy. — Formed with suff.
-arian fr. L. caelibatus. See next word.

## celibate
celibate, adj., unmarried; п., an unmarried
person. — Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. caelebs,
'unmarried, single', which is of uncertain
origin. It perh. meant orig. 'living alone', and is
formed fr. 1-Е. "qaiwclo-, 'alone' (whence also
OI. kevalah, 'belonging exclusively to a single
person, alone', see kevalin), and *lib(h)-, 'living',
which is prob. traceable funher to base *Ieip-, 'to
stick, adhere; .to remain, persevere, continue,
live' (whence Goth, liban, OE. libban, lifian, etc.,
'to live'). 1-Е. 'qaiwelo- is an enlargement of
*qai-wo-, which is rel. to 'qai-lo, appearing in
Lett, kails, OE. Hal, 'whole, uninjured, healthy'.
See whole and cp. words there referred to. For
derivatives of I.-E. *leip- see leave, v., and cp.
esp. life, live. Derivative: celibat-ic, adj.

## celio-
celio-, combining form. — A variant spelling of
coelio-.

## cell
cell, n. — ME. celle, fr. OF. celle, fr. L. cella,
'storeroom, granary, bee's cell, hut, cot', fr.
I.-E. base *Hel-, 'to hide, conceal', whence also
L. celare, 'to hide, conceal', oc-culere, 'to cover,
conceal', OI. sdla, 'hut, house, hall, stable",
salah, 'hedge, enclosure, wall', Gk. καλϊά, 'hut,
nest', καλύβη, 'hut, cabin', καλύπτειν, 'to cover,
hide, conceal', κέλυφος, 'sheath, case', κολεός,
'sheath', Mir. cut, 'defence, shelter', culaid,
'cover', Olr. cuile, 'cellar, magazine', OE. heall,
half, 'hall', hel, hell, helle, 'hell', helan, 'to cover,
hide', Goth, huljan, of s.m., hulistr, 'covering,
veil', huhmdi, 'cave', OE. heolstor, 'that which
veils, hiding place, darkness*. Cp. cella, cellar,
cellule and the second element in Paludicella.
Cp. also caliology, calyptra, cilia, clandestine,
color, conceal, dharmsala, Eucalyptus, hall, hell,
helmet, holster, hull, kalidium, kelyphite, kil-,
occult, superciliary, Valhalla.
Derivatives: cell, tr. and intr. v., cell-ed, adj.

## cella
cella, п., the inner part of a temple in ancient
Greece or Rome (archit.) — L. See prec. word.

## cellar
cellar, n. — ME. celler, fr. OF. celier (F. cellier),
fr. L. cellarium, 'a receptacle for food, pantry',
prop. neut. of the adjective cellarius, 'pertaining
to a storeroom', used as a noun, fr. cella. Cp. It.
cellaio, OProveng. celier, Catal. celler, Sp. cillero
and Port, celleiro, 'storeroom', and see cell.
Derivatives: cellar,tr.v.,cellar-age,n.,cellar-er,n.

## cellaret
cellaret, n. — Diminutive formed fr. cellar with
suff. -et.

## ceUiform
ceUiform, adj., having the form of a cell. —
Compounded of L. cella and forma, 'form, shape'.
See cell and -form.

## cello
cello, n. — Short for violoncello.

## celloidin
celloidin, п., a solution of pyroxylin used for
embedding. — Formed from celi, -oid and chem.
suff. -ia.

## cellophane
cellophane, п., a flexible transparent material.—A
hybrid coined by the Swiss chemist Jacques
E. Brandenberger (born in 1872) from the
first syllable of cellulose and the stem of Gk.
φαίνειν, 'to show'; see phantasm.

## cellular
cellular, adj. — F. cellulaire, fr. cellule. See next
word and -ar.
Derivative: cellular-ity, n.

## cellule
cellule, n. — F., lit. 'a small cell', fr. L. cellula,
'a small storeroom', dimin. of cella. See cell
and -ule. Derivatives: cellular (q.v.), cellul-ate,
cellul-ated, adjs.

## celluloid
celluloid, n. and adj. — A hybrid coined by the
American inventor John Wesley Hyatt (1837-
1900) fr. cellulose and -oid, a suff. of Greek origin.

## cellulose
cellulose, n. (chem.) — F., coined by the French
chemist Anselme Payen (1795-1871) fr. L.
cellula (see cellule) and suff. -ose, which was soon
taken over to form many other chemical terms
(see subst. suff. -ose).

## cellulose
cellulose, adj., containing cells. — Formed fr. L.
cellula (see cellule) with adj. suff. -ose.

## Celosla
Celosla, п., a genus of plants of the amaranth
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κήλεος,
'burning', contracted fr. 'κη^άλεος, fr. *καί-, the
stem of καίειν, 'to burn*, whence also καυστός,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:149 COLUMN:2 -->
'burned', καυστικός, 'capable of burning'; see
caustic and cp. words there referred to. The
name Celosia, 'burning', was suggested by the
color of the leaves.

## celt
celt, п., a chisel of stone. — Late L. celtis, a loan
word of unknown origin.

## Celt
Celt, Kelt, n. — F. Celte, fr. L. Celtae, 'Celts', fr.
Gk. Κέλται, earlier Κελτοί. Ср. celtium.

## Celtic
Celtic, Keltic, adj. — L. Celticus, fr. Celtae. See
prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: Celtic-ism, п., Celtic-ize, tr. and
intr. v.

## Celtis
Celtis, п., a genus of plants of the elm family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. celtis, name of an African
species of lotus, a loan word of uncertain origin.

## celtium
celtium, п., a supposed chemical element. —
ModL. celtium, lit. 'the Celtic (element)', fr. L.
Celtae. See Celt and chem. suff. -ium.

## Celtologist
Celtologist, п., a student of the Celtic languages
or of the history of the Celts. — Compounded
of Celt and -logist.

## Celtomaniac
Celtomaniac, n. — Compounded of Celt and
maniac.

## cement
cement, n. — ME. cyment, ciment, fr. OF. (= F.)
ciment, fr. L. caementum, 'rough stone, stone
chippings', for *caia\s)mentom, fr. caedo, cae-
dere, 'to cut, hew, lop', whence also caelum [for
*caid-(s)lom\, 'chisel', which is cogn. with OI.
khidati, skhiddti, 'thrusts, tears', khida,
'hammer, mallet', khedayati, 'molests, tires, fatigues',
MHG., G. heie, 'mallet, rammer'. Cp. ancile,
caesura, cespitose, cestus, 'cover for the hand',
chisel, -cide, circumcise, concise, - decide,
decision, excide, excise, 'to cut out', exeision,
incise, precis, precise, sallet, scissors, succise. For
the ending see suff. -ment.
Derivatives: cement, tr. v., cement-ation, п., ce-
ment-er, n.

## cemetery
cemetery, n. — Late L. coemitlrium, fr. Gk.
κοιμητήριον, 'sleeping room, burial place*, fr.
κοιμαν, 'to put to sleep', which is rel. to κοίτη,
'place to lie down in, bed', κοΐτος, 'place to lie
down in, bed; sleeping, sleep', κοιτών,
'bedchamber', κεΐμαι, "I lie down, lie asleep', κώμη,
'village', fr. I.-E. base *kei-, 'to lie, rest', whence
also Goth, haims, 'village', OE. ham, 'home,
house, dwelling'. See home and cp. city, civil.
Cp. also the second element in neossine.

## cenacle
cenacle, п., a dining room. — F. cenacle, fr. L.
cenaculum, 'dining room', fr. cena, 'dinner*,
which stands for *qert-sna (cp. Oscan kersnu,
of s.m.), lit. 'portion', fr. I.-E. base *qert-, 4o
cut', whence also OI. kjntati, 'cuts', Lith. kertu,
kifsti, 'to hew', Arm. k'erfem, Ί skin, flay', and
prob. Hitt. karsh-, 'to cut off'. Base *qerl- is
an enlargement of base *qer-, 'to cut*, for which
see carnal.

## Ceitchrus
Ceitchrus, п., a genus of grasses, 'the sandbur,
the burgrass' (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κέγχρος,
'millet'. See Cachrys.

## -cene
-cene, combining form denoting certain periods
in geology, as in Eocene. — Introduced by the
British geologist Sir Charles Lyell (1797-1875)
fr. Gk. καινός, 'new', which is cogn. with L.
recins, gen. -entis, 'new'. See reeent and kainite.

## cenoblte
cenoblte, coenobite, п., a member of a religious
order living in a community. — Eccles. L. coe-
nobita, 'a cloister brother', fr. coenobium, 'a
convent', fr. Gk. κοινόβιον, 'life in community,
monastery', fr. κοινός, 'common', and βίος,
'life'. For the first element see coeno-, for the
second see bio-.
Derivatives: cenobit-ic, cenobil-ic-al, adjs., ceno-
bit-ic-al-ly, adv., cenobit-ism, n.

## cenoby
cenoby, n. — See coenobium.

## -cenosls
-cenosls, combining form meaning 'discharge'
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. κένωσις, 'an
emptying', fr. κενές, 'empty'. See cenotaph.

## cenosite
cenosite, п., a hydrous silicate and carbonate of
calcium, yttrium, etc. (mineral.} — Formed with
subst. suff. -lte fr. Gk. καινός, 'new, novel,
unusual' (see -cene); so called in allusion to its
composition.

## cenotaph
cenotaph, п., an empty tomb in honor of a dead
person who is buried elsewhere. — F. ceno-
laphe, fr. L. cenotaphium, fr. Gk. κενοτάφιον,
'an empty tomb', compounded of κενός,
'empty', and τάφιον, neut. of τάφιος, 'pertaining to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:149 COLUMN:3 -->
a grave', fr. τάφος, 'burial, grave, tomb'. The
first element is cogn. with Arm. sin, 'empty'; cp.
keno-, kenosis. The second element is rel. to Gk.
θάπτειν, 'to bury', τάφρος, 'ditch', and cogn.
with Arm. damban, dambaran, 'grave, tomb'.
Cp. Taphrina and the second element in epitaph,
tritaph.

## Cenozoic
Cenozoic, adj., designating the geological period
extending from the beginning of the Tertiary to
the present. — Compounded of Gk. καινές,
'new, recent', ζωή, 'life', and suff. -ic. See -cene
and zoo-,

## cense
cense, tr. and intr. v. — Aphetic for iacense.

## censer
censer, n. — Aphetic for incenser, fr. OF. en-
censier (F. encensoir), fr. Eccles. L. incensarium,
fr. incensum, 'incense', lit. 'that which is burnt',
neut. pp. of L. incendere, 'to set fire to, burn'.
See Incense, 'smoke of burning spices'.

## censor
censor, n. — L. censor, fr. censere, 'to reckon,
assess, estimate, value, deem, judge', cogn. with
OI. sdmsati, 'recites, praises', iamsayati,
'announces', sdsa, 'song of praise', Toch. В сап-
maya, 'he has been proclaimed'. Cp. census,
excise, 'duty', recension.
Derivatives: censor, tr. v., censor-ial, adj.,
censorious (q.v.)

## ceasorious
ceasorious, adj., inclined to censure; critical. —
L. censorius, 'pertaining to a censor', fr. censor.
See prec. word and -orious.
Derivatives: censorious-ly, adv., censorious-
ness, n.

## censure
censure, n. — F. censure, fr. L. censura,
'judgment, criticism', fr. census, pp. of censere. See
censor and -ure.

## censure
censure, tr. and intr. v. — F. censurer, fr. censure.
See censure, n.
Derivatives: censur-аЫе, adj., censur-er, n.

## census
census, n. — L. census, 'rating of property,
registration of citizens and their property', fr.
census, pp. of censere. See censor.
Derivative: census, tr. v.

## cent
cent, п., a hundred (used in certain phrases only).
— F., 'a hundred', fr. L. centum, 'a hundred'.
See hundred and cp. next word, centenarian,
centner, century, percentage.

## ceat
ceat, п., the hundredth part of a dollar. —
Abbreviation of L. centisima (scil. pars), 'the
hundredth part*, fern, of centesimus, 'the hundredth',
fr. centum, 'a hundred'. See prec. word and cp.
mill.

## cental
cental, п., a unit of weight, hundredweight. —
Formed fr. L. centum, 'a hundred', with adj.
suff. -al, on analogy of quintal.

## centaur
centaur, п., 1) one of a mythical race in ancient
Thessaly, conceived as monsters, half man, half
horse (Greek mythol); 2) (cap.) = Centaurus
(astron.) — L. Centaurus, fr. Gk. Κένταυρος,
which is of uncertain origin-

## Centaurea
Centaurea, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. centaureum or
centaurium. See centaury.

## Centaurium
Centaurium, п., a genus of plants of the gentian
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. centaurium or
centaurium. See centaury and -ium.

## Centaurus
Centaurus, п., a southern constellation between
Hydra and Cross (astron.) — L., 'centaur'.
See centaur.

## centaury
centaury, п., any of a group of plants of the
gentian family. — ME., fr. ML. centauria, fr.
L. centaureum, centaurium, fr. Gk. κενταύρειον,
κενταύριον, lit. 'Centaur's plant', fr. Κένταυρος,
'centaur'. According to Pliny (see Nat. Hist. 25,
66) the Centaur Chiron, wounded by an arrow
shot by Heracles, heals his wound with this plant,
whence its name κενταύρειον or κενταύριον,
'Centaur's plant' (see centaur). In Latin, folk
etymology altered the foreign word into the
compound of the Latin words centum, 'hundred',
and aurum, 'gold*. As a loan translation of L.
centaureum in this mistaken sense, arose G.
Tausendguldenkraut, 'centaury', lit. 'thousand-
golden-herb'.

## centenarian
centenarian, adj., pertaining to a period of a
hundred years; п., a person one hundred years
old. — L. centenarius, 'relating to a hundred*, fr.
centlni, 'a hundred each', fr. centum, 'a
hundred'. See cent, 'a hundred', and -arlan and cp.
centner, kantar.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:150 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 123 | CERATDDUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:150 COLUMN:1 -->

## ceatenary
ceatenary, r) adj., pertaining to a century;
pertaining to a period of a hundred years; 2) п.,
a century; a period of a hundred years. — L.
centenarius, 'relating to a hundred'. See prec.
word and adj. sun", -ary.

## centeanial
centeanial, adj., of a hundred years; happening
once in a hundred years; one hundred years old;
п., the hundredth anniversary; the celebration
of'the hundredth anniversary. — Formed, on
the analogy of Ы-ennial, fr. L. centum, 'a
hundred', and annus, 'year'. See mutual, biennial.
Derivative: centennial-ly, adv.

## center
center, ceatre, n. — F. centre, fr. L. centrum, fr.
Gk. κέντρον, 'point, prickle, spike, ox goad,
point round which a circle is described', from the
stem of κέντειν, 'to prick, goad', whence also
κέντωρ, 'a goader, driver', κεστός (for *κεντ-
τάς), 'embroidered', κέστρά, 'pickax', κοντός,
'pole', fr. I.-E. base *kent-, 'to prick', whence
also Bret, kentr, Olr. ctnteir, 'a spur', OHG.
hantag, 'sharp, pointed', Lett, sits, 'hunter's
spear*, situ, sist, 'to strike', W. cethr, 'nail'. Cp.
centrifugal, centripetal, concentrate, eccentric,
Dicentra, paracentesis. Cp. also oestrum, cestus,
'girdle', kent, 'a pole', quant, 'a pole'.
Derivatives: center, centre, intr. and tr. v., cen-
ter-ing, cenlr-ing, centre-ing, n.

## centesimal
centesimal, adj., counting by hundredths. —
Formed with adj. sun", -al fr. L. centesima(pars),
'a hundredth (part)', fr. centum, 'a hundred'.
See cent (in both senses).

## centi-
centi-, combining form meaning 'one hundred',
or 'a hundredth part*. — L. centi-, fr. centum,
'a hundred', See cent, 'a hundred'.

## centigrade
centigrade, adj. — Compounded of centi- and
gradus, 'degree'. See -grade.

## centigram
centigram, centigramme, n. — F. centigramme,
compounded of centi- and gramme, fr. Gk.
γράμμα, 'that which is written'. See centi- and
-gram.

## centiliter
centiliter, centilitre, n. — F. centilitre,
compounded of centi- and litre. See centi- and liter.

## centUlion
centUlion, n. — Formed fr. centi- on the analogy
of millloa (q.v.) See also billion.

## centime
centime, n. — F., formed fr. cent, 'a hundred', on
the analogy of decime, One tenth (of a franc)',
fr. L. decima (pars), 'tenth (part)', fr. decern,
'ten'. See cent, 'a hundred', and decimal.

## centimeter
centimeter, centimetre, n. — F. centimitre,
compounded of centi- and metre. See centi- and
-meter.

## centipede
centipede, n. — F. centipede, fr. L. centipeda,
'centipede, many-footed insect', compounded
of centum, *a hundred', and pes, gen. pedis,
'foot'. See centi- and pedal.

## centner
centner, п., commercial hundredweight. — G.,
fr. L. centenarius, 'relating to a hundred'. See
centenarian and cp. kantur.

## cento
cento, п., a composition made up of selections
from different works. — L. cento, 'patchwork',
cogn. with OI. kanlhS, 'patched garment', OHG.
hadara, MHG., G. hader, 'rag' [ср., with -/-
formative element, MHG. hadel (whence F.
haitlon), 'rag']. Gk. κέντρων, 'piece of
patchwork', is a loan word fr. L. cento, and was
influenced in form by κέντρων, 'one that deserves
the goad (= κέντρον)'. Cp Centunculus.

## central
central, adj. — L. centralis, 'pertaining to a
center', fr. centrum; first used by the philosopher
of the Cambridge Platonist school, Henry More
(1614-87), in 1647. See center and adj. sun", -al.
Derivatives: central, п., central-ism, п.,
centralist, п., central-ist-ic, adj., central-ity, п.,
centralize, tr. and intr. v., central-iz-ation, п., centrai-ly,
adv., central-ness, n.

## centric
centric, centrical, adj. — Gk. κεντρικές, fr.
κέντρον. See center and -lc and cp. anlhropocentric,
egocentric, geocentric, heliocentric, paracentric.
Derivatives: centrical-ly, adv., cenlric-ity, n.

## centrifugal
centrifugal, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
ModL. centrifugus, 'fleeing from the center*,
which was coined by Sir Isaac Newton from L.
centrum, 'center', and fugere, 'to flee from'. See
center and fugacious and cp. centripetal.
Derivatives: centrifugal, п., centrifugal-ize, tr.v.,
centrifug-al-ly, adv.

## centrifuge
centrifuge, п., a rotary machine. — F., fr.

## centrifuge
centrifuge, 'centrifugal', fr. ModL. centrifugus. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:150 COLUMN:2 -->
pre», word.

## centripetal
centripetal, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
ModL. centripetus, 'tending toward the center',
which was coined by Sir Isaac Newton fr. L.
centrum, 'center', and petere, 4o fall upon,
move toward, seek'. See center, petition and cp.
centrifugal.
Derivative: centripetal-ly, adv.

## centre-
centre-, combining form meaning 'center,
central'. — L„ fr. Gk. κέντρο-, fr. κέντρον,
'center'. See eenter.

## centrobaric
centrobaric, adj., relating to the center of gravity.
— Fr. Gk. τά κεντροβαρικά, title of a treatise
of Archimedes on the center of gravity,
compounded of κέντρον, 'center', and βάρος,
'weight'. See center, baro- and -lc.

## Centrosema
Centrosema, п., name of a genus of the family
Fabaceae (bol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
κέντρον, 'spur', and σήμα, 'sign, standard'. See
center and semantics.

## ceatrosome
ceatrosome, п., a minute body occurring in the
cytoplasm (biol.)—Coined by the German
zoologist Theodor Boveri (1862-1915) in 1888 from
Gk. κέντρον, 'center', and σώμα, 'body'. See
ceatro- and soma, 'body'.

## centumvir
centumvir, п., one of a court of one hundred
judges or jurors (Roman hist.) — L., compounded
of centum, 'a hundred', and v/r, 'man'. See cent,
'a hundred', and virile.

## Centunculus
Centunculus,.п., a genus of the primrose family
(hot.) — L. centunculus, 'bindweed, knotweed,
patch', formed fr. cento, 'patchwork', with di-
min. suff. -unculus. See cento and -uncle.

## ceataple
ceataple, adj., a hundred times as much, a
hundredfold. — F., fr. L. centuplus, 'a
hundredfold', lit. 'folded a hundred times', formed fr.
centum, 'a hundred', with suff. -plus, 'fold', on
analogy of du-plus, 'double', fr. duo, 'two'. See
double.
Derivatives: centuple, tr. v., centupl-y, adv.

## centapticate
centapticate, tr. v., to make a hundredfold. —
L. centuplicalus, pp. of centuplicare, 'to increase
a hundredfold', fr. cenluplex, gen. centuplicis,
'a hundredfold', which is compounded of
centum, 'a hundred', and -plex, gen. -plicis, '-fold',
from the stem of plicare, 'to fold, bend'. See
ply, 4o bend', and cp. plicate.
Derivative: centuplical-ion, n.

## ceatuplicate
ceatuplicate, adj. and п., a hundredfold. — L.
centuplicatus. See prec. word.

## eenturion
eenturion, п., a captain commanding a hundred
men in the Roman army. — L. centurio, gen.
-dnis, 'commander of a century', fr. cenluria.
See next word and cp. deeurion.

## centary
centary, n. — L. centuria, 'a parcel or division
of a hundred things of one kind'; formed fr.
centum, 'a hundred', on the analogy of decu-
ria, 'a company of ten' (fr. decern, 'ten'). See
ceat, 'a hundred', and cp. decury.

## ceorl
ceorl, п., a churl. — OE. See churl.

## cephal-
cephal-, form of cephalo- before a vowel.

## cephalalgia
cephalalgia, cephalalgy, п., headache (med.) —
L., fr. Gk. κεφαλαλγία, which is compounded
of κεφαλή, 'head', and άλγος, 'pain'. See cephalic
and -algia.

## Cephalanthus
Cephalanthus, п., a genus of plants of the madder
family (bol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
κεφαλή, 'head', and άνθος, 'flower'. See cephalic
and anther.

## cephalate
cephalate, adj., having a head. — See cephalic
and adj. suff. -ate.

## cephalic
cephalic, adj., pertaining to the head. — F. сё-
phalique, fr. L. cephalicus, fr. Gk. κεφαλικός,
'pertaining to the head', fr. κεφαλή, 'head', dis-
similated fr. 'χεφαλή, fr. I.-E. base *gheb'l-,
whence also Toch. A ipal-, 'head', Goth, gibla,
ON. gafl, 'gable', OE. gafol, 'fork'. See gable
and -ic and cp. Acanthocephala, acephalous,
acrocephalic, anencephaljc, nutocephalous,
bicephalous, Bucephalus, dolichocephalic, Draco-
cephalum, encephalic, encephahm, Enchelyce-
phali, hydrocephalus, fsocephalic, umcrocephalic,
megacephalk, mesocephalic, microcephalous,
ortbocephalic
cephalic vein (anat.) —- ML. vena cephalica, fr.
Arab, al-αϊβΙ, fr. al-, 'the', and qlfal, a word of
uncertain origin, which was confused by the
translators of A vicenna with Gk. κεφαλή, 'head' ■

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:150 COLUMN:3 -->
(whence κεφαλικός, 'pertaining to the head, see
prec. word). The word cephalic in its above
sense appears' first in a translation of A vicenna
by Armegandus Blasius de Montepessulano in
1564. See Joseph Hyrtl, Das Arabische und
HebraischeinderAnatomie,Wien, i879,p. 96-98.

## cephalo-
cephalo-, before a vowel cephal-, combining form
meaning 'head, with reference to the head'. —
Gk. κεφαλο-, κεφαλ-, fr. κεφαλή, 'head'. See
cephalic

## cephaloid
cephaloid, adj., shaped like a head. — Gk. κεφα-
λοειδής, fr. κεφαλή, 'head', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See cephalic and -«id.

## cephalopod
cephalopod, п., one of the Cephalopoda. — See
next word. _

## Cephalopoda
Cephalopoda, n. pi., a class of mollusks, including
the cuttlefish, squid, octopus, etc. (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of κεφαλή, 'head', and
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See cephalic and -pod.

## cephalothorax
cephalothorax, п., the united head and thorax
(of spiders and crustaceans) (zool.) — See
cephalo- and thorax.'

## Cephalotus
Cephalotus, п., a genus of Australian plants (hot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. κεφαλωτός, 'having a head,
headed', fr. κεφαλή, 'head'. See cephalic.

## cephalous
cephalous, adj., having a head. — See -cepbalous.

## -cephalous
-cephalous, combining form meaning 'having
(such and such) a head'. — Gk. -κέφαλος (as in
μακροκέφαλος, 'long-headed'), fr. κεφαλή,'head'.
See cephalic. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see -qus.

## cer-
cer-, form of сего- before a vowel.

## ceraceous
ceraceous, adj., waxy. — Formed with suff.
-aceous fr. L. cera, 'wax'. See cere, n.

## cerago
cerago, п., beebread. — Formed fr. L. cera, 'wax'.
See cere, n.

## ceral
ceral, adj., pertaining to wax. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. cera, 'wax'. See cere, n.

## Ceraroiaceae
Ceraroiaceae, n. pi., a family of algae (bot.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. Ceramium.

## ceramiaceous
ceramiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## ceramic
ceramic, adj., 1) of pottery; 2) of ceramics. —
Gk. κεραμικός, 'of pottery, made of
earthenware', fr. κέραμος, 'earthen vessel, jar, potter's
clay, pottery', a pre-Hellenic word derived from
a language of Asia Minor and not cognate with
L. cremdre, 'to burn'. See Kretschmer, Glotta,
.11, 284, and Schrader, Reallexikon der indo-
germanischen Altertumskunde II2, 694. Cp.
Ceramium, and the second element in Inoce-
ramus.

## ceramics
ceramics, п., ι) the art of making pottery,
earthenware, of porcelain, etc.; 2) objects made of
any of these materials.—See prec. word and -ics.

## Ceramium
Ceramium, п., a genus of red algae (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. κεράμιον, dimin. of κέραμος,
'earthen vessel, jar'. See ceramic.

## cerargyrite
cerargyrite, п., a synonym of hornsilver. —
Compounded of Gk. κέρας, 'horn' (see cerato-),
άργυρος, 'silver' (see argyro-), and subst. suff.
-ite.

## cerastes
cerastes, п., the horned viper (zool.)—L. cerastes,
'a homed serpent', fr. Gk. κεραστής, 'horned;
a horned serpent', fr. κέρας, 'horn'. See cerato-.

## Cerastium
Cerastium, п., a genus of plants of the chickweed
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κεραστής,
'horned' (see prec. word); so called from the
shape of the pod.

## cerate
cerate, п., a kind of ointment consisting of wax,
lard, oil and other ingredients. — L. ciratum,
prop. neut. pp. of cerare, 'to cover with wax',
fr. cera. See cere, п., and adj. suff. -ate.

## cerated
cerated, adj., waxed. — Formed with suff. -ed fr.
L. ceratus, pp. of cerare, 'to wax', fr. cera. See
cere, n.

## cernto-
cernto-, kerato-, before a vowel cenrt-, kerat-,
combining form meaning 'horn, horny'. — Gk.
κέρατο-, κερατ-, fr..κέρας, gen. κέρατος, 'horn',
which is cogn. with L. cornu, 'horn', fr. I.-E.
base *her-, 4he uppermost part of the body,
head, horn, top, summit'. See horn, and cp.
carat, cervine, crio-, keratin. Cp. also Acera-
terium, Acerates and the second element in
Dicruridae, Dinoceras, Megnceros, rhinoceros,
Triceratops.

## Ceratodus
Ceratodus, п., a genus of fishes, the barramunda
(ichlhyol.)—ModL., compounded of Gk. κέρας,
gen. κέρατος, 'horn', and -οδούς, '-toothed*,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:151 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CERATOPHYLLACEAE | 124 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:151 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. οδών, 'tooth'. See cerato- and odonto-.

## Ceratophyllaceae
Ceratophyllaceae, n. pi., the hornwort family
(bot.) — Formed fr. Ceratophyllum with suff.
-aceae.

## ceratopbyllaceous
ceratopbyllaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Ceratophyllum
Ceratophyllum, п., a genus of plants, the horn-
wort (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'with hornlike leaves',
fr. Gk. κέρας, gen. κέρατος, 'horn*, and φύλλον,
'a leaf (see cerato- and phyllo-); so called
because the sessile leaves are divided into hard,
threadlike, parts.

## cerauno-
cerauno-, kerauno-, a combining form meaning
'thunderbolt'. — Gk. κεραυνό-, fr. κεραυνός,
'thunderbolt, lightning', which stands for *κερα-
Γ(ε)νός, lit. 'smasher, crusher', rel. to κεραΐζειν
(for *κεραίίζειν), 'to lay waste', and cogn.
with L. caries, 'decay, rottenness'. See carles
and cp. the second element in sincere.

## ceraunograph
ceraunograph, keraimograpb, п., an instrument
for recording thunderstorms and lightnings. —
Compounded of cerauno- and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write*. See -graph.

## Cerberus
Cerberus, n. (Greek mylhot.) — L., fr. Gk.
Κέρβερος, which is prob. cogn. with OI. karbardh,
sdrvarah, sabalah, 'spotted, speckled' (whence
Sabalah, name of one of the two dogs of Yama).

## cercaria
cercaria, п., a larval stage of trematode worms
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κέρκος, 'tail'. See
cercus and -aria and cp. next word.

## Cercis
Cercis, п., a genus of shrubs and trees, the red-
bud, the Judas tree (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
κερκ(ς, 'weaver's shuttle; the Judas tree', which
is prob. a dimin. of κέρκος, 'tail'. See cercus.

## Cercopithecus
Cercopithecus, п., a genus of long-tailed
monkeys (zool.) — L. cercopithecus, fr. Gk. κερκο-
πίθη-..ος, 'a long-tailed monkey', which is
compounded of κέρκος, 'tail', and πίθηκος,
'monkey'. See cercus and Pithecanthropus.

## cercus
cercus, п., either of a pair of anal appendages
found in many insects (entomol.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. κέρκος, 'tail', which is of unknown origin.
Cp. cercaria, Cercis, the first element in carrack
and in Cercopithecus, and the second element in.
cysticercus. Cp. also the first element in Cecrops.

## cere
cere, п., a waxlike protuberance at the base of the
bill of some birds. — F. cire, fr. L. cera, 'wax',
which is a loan word fr. Gk. κηράς, 'beeswax,
wax', whence κηρίον, 'honeycomb'. Gk. κηρός
is of uncertain etymology. It is perh. cogn. with
Lith. korps, 'honeycomb', Lett, kare, 'honey in
the comb'. Cp. cere, v., cerement, Cereus, Ce-
rinthe, Cerion, cerumen, ceruse, cierge, cirueia,
Kerite, and the second element in adipoceres,
mellceris, ozocerite, tricerion.

## cere
cere, tr. v., to wrap in a cerecloth. — F. cirer, 'to
cover with wax', fr. cire, 'wax', fr. L. cera. See
cere, n.
Derivative: cer-ed, adj.

## cerenl
cerenl, adj. and n. — L. Cerealis, dissimil. fr.
'Cereralis, 'pertaining to Ceres', fr. Ceres, gen.
Cereris, 'Ceres', name of the Italian goddess of
agriculture, prop, 'goddess of growth', fr. I.-E.
base *ker-, *kere-, 'to grow', whence also L. cri-
scere, 'to grow', creare, 'to create', Oscan. carta,
'bread', Gk. κορεννΰναι, 'to satisfy, fill with a
thing' (whence κόρος, 'one's All, satiety'), Arm.
serm, sermn, 'seed, shoot, sprout', serein, Ί
produce', Alb. β-jer, 'acorn', bjeft, 'lentil' (lit.
'food'), Lith. Seriu, Sirti, 'to feed', OPruss. ser-
men, 'funeral repast', OHG. hirst, hirso, 'millet'.
Cp. herd. Cp. also Ceres, accrue, create,
denture, Creole, crescendo, crescent, decrease,
excrescent, increase, increment, procreate, recreate,
recruit. Cp. also cerium. For the ending see adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: cereal-tan, cereal-ic, adjs., cereal-
ism, п., cereal-isi, n.

## cerebellum
cerebellum, п., the hinder part of the brain (anal.
and zool.) — L., dimin. of cerebrum. See
cerebrum.

## cerehr-
cerehr-, form of cerebro- before a vowel.

## cerebral
cerebral, adj., pertaining to the brain. — F.
cerebral, fr. L. cerebrum. See cerebrum and adj. suff.
-al.

## cerebrate
cerebrate, intr. v., to use one's brain; to think. —
See cerebrum and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: cerebral-ton, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:151 COLUMN:2 -->

## cerebric
cerebric, adj., pertaining to the brain. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. L. cerebrum. See cerebrum.

## cerebrc-
cerebrc-, before a vowel cerebr-, combining form
denoting the brain. — Fr. L. cerebrum. See
cerebrum.

## cerebrose
cerebrose, п., galactose obtained from cerebro-
sides (biochem.) — Formed fr. cerebrum with
subst. suff. -ose.

## cerebroside
cerebroside, п., glucoside occurring in brain and
nerve tissue (biochem.) — Formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -ide.

## cerebrum
cerebrum, п., the main part of the brain (anal, and
zool) — L. cerebrum, 'brain' (prob. for *keris-
rom), fr. I.-E. base *ker-, 'the uppermost part
of the body, head, horn, top, summit', whence
also OI. slras, 'head, summit', sirsdm, 'head',
Avestic sarah-, ModPers. sar, 'head', Arm. jar,
'top', Homeric Gk. καρ, 'head', Ion. κάρη, Att.
κάρα, κράς (poetic form for κάρα), Ion. κάρηνον,
Att. and Dor. χάρανον, 'head', Gk. κράνίον,
'skull', ON. hjarni, Du. hersenen, OHG. hirni,
MHG. hirne, G. Him, Gehirn, 'brain'. Cp.
cranium and words there referred to. Cp. also
cernuous, cervical, cheer, coryphaeus, the first
element in cerveiat, charivari, sarangousty,
saveloy, seerband, seerpaw, serang, seraskier,
sircar and the second element in mahseer. Cp.
also horn and words there referred to.

## cerecloth
cerecloth, n. — Compounded of cere, v., and
cloth.

## cerement
cerement, п., a shroud. — Orig. 'waxed shroud',
fr. F. cirement, 'a waxing', fr. cirer, 'to wax',
fr. cire, 'wax'. See cere and -ment.

## ceremonious
ceremonious, adj. — F. ceremonieux (fern, сёгё-
monieuse), fr. Late L. caerimoniosus, fr. L.
caerimonia. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: ceremonious-ly, adv., ceremoniotts-
ness, n.

## ceremony
ceremony, n. — OF. ceremonie (F. ceiimonie), fr.
L. caerimonia, 'sacred usage, ceremony', prob.
orig. meaning 'the rites performed by the
Etruscan pontiffs at Caere (near Rome)'. See Sexti
Pompei Festi de verborum significatu quae su-
persunt cum Pauli epitome, Lipsiae, 1880. For
the ending see suff. -mony and cp. words there
referred to. The word ceremony was introduced
into English by Wycliffe.
Derivatives: ceremoni-al, adj. and п.,
ceremonial-ism, п., ceremoni-al-ist, п., ceremoni-al-ize,
tr. v., ceremonious (q.v.)

## Ceres
Ceres, п., Italian goddess of agriculture,
identified with the Greek goddess Demeter (Roman
mylhol.) — L. Ceres. See cereal.

## Cereus
Cereus, п., a genus of cacti (bot.) — L. cereus,
'wax candle', fr. cera, 'wax' (see cere, п.); so
called.from the shape suggestive of awaxcandle.

## cerevis
cerevis, п., a small cap worn by German students.
— G., fr. L. cervisia., cervisia, 'beer', a word
of Gaulish origin. See cervisia.

## cerlc
cerlc, adj., containing cerium (chem.) — Formed
fr. cerium with suff. -ic.

## Cerinthe
Cerinthe, п., a genus of plants of the borage
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. cerintha, cerinthe,
'the waxflower', fr. Gk. κήριν&ος, 'beebread',
which was prob. formed fr. κηρός, 'wax', with
suff. -ινθος. See cere, n.

## Cerion
Cerion, п., a genus of snails (zool.) — Gk. κηρίον,
'honeycomb', fr. κηρός, 'beeswax'. See cere, n.

## ceriph
ceriph, serif, п., a horizontal line at the top or
bottom of a capital letter. — Prob. fr. Du.
schreef, 'stroke, dash', which is rel. to schrijven,
'to write', fr. L. scribere. See scribe and cp.
sanserif.

## cerise
cerise, п., cherry color. — F. cerise, 'cherry'. See
cherry.

## cerite
cerite, п., a hydrous silicate of cerium (chem.) —
Formed fr. cerium with subst. suff. -ite.

## cerium
cerium, п., a metallic element. — ModL.,
contracted fr. cererium, a name coined by the
Swedish chemist Baron Jdns Jakob Berzelius (1779-
1848) after the asteroid Ceres, discovered in
1801, which was called after the Roman goddess
Ceres. See Ceres. For the ending of cerium
see chem. suff. -ium.

## cernuous
cernuous, adj., bowing downward (said of the
bell or cup of flowers) — L. cernuus, 'with the
face toward the earth', standing for *kers-n-
owos and rel. to cerebrum, 'brain'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:151 COLUMN:3 -->
cerebrum. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
suff. -ous.
сего, п., a fish of the mackerel family. —
Corruption of Sp. sierra, 'saw, sawfish', fr. L. serra,
'saw'. See serra.

## cero-
cero-, before a! vowel cer-, combining form
meaning 'wax, wa?4y'. — Gk. κηρο-, κηρ-, fr. κηρός,
'beeswax, wax,'. See cere, n.

## cerograph
cerograph, п., a writing or painting on wax. —
See next word.

## cerography
cerography, п., the art of making cerographs on
wax. — Gk. κηρογραφία, fr. κηρογραφεΐν, *tO
write or paint on wax', fr. κηρός, 'wax', and
γράφειν., 'to write'. See cere, п., and -graphy.
Derivatives: cerograph-ic, cerograph-ic-al, adjs.,
cerograph-isl, n.

## cerolite
cerolite, п., a hydrous magnesium silicate
(mineral.) — Compounded of cero- and -lite; so
called in allusion to its waxy appearance.

## ceroplastic
ceroplastic, adj., pertaining to modeling in wax.
— Gk. κηροπλαστικός, 'pertaining to molding in
wax', fr. κηρόπλαστος, 'molded in wax', fr.
κηρός, 'wax', and πλάσσειν, 'to mold'. See cero-
and plastic.

## ceroplastics
ceroplastics, п., the art of modeling in wax. —
See prec. word and -ics.

## cerous
cerous, adj., containing cerium (chem)—Formed
fr. cerium with suff. -ous.

## cerrero
cerrero, adj., wild (said of horses). — Sp., fr.
cerro, 'neck of an animal', fr. L. cirrus, 'curl,
lock, the hair on the forehead of a horse'. See
cirrus.

## cerris
cerris, п., a kind of oak, the Turkey oak. —
ModL., fr. L. cerrus, a word of Hamitic origin.
See Schuchardt, Sitzungsberichte der Akademie
der Wissenschaften in Wien, 188, 4. Abhand-
lung, lSf.

## certain
certain, aaj. — ME., fr. OF. certain, certein (F.
certain), fr. VL. *cerlSnus ч (whence also Olt.,
OSp. certano, OProvenc. certan), fr. L. certus,
'determined, resolved, sure, certain' (whence
OF., OProvenc. cert, It. certo, Sp. cierto,
'certain'), which stands for *cri-los and is rel.
to cerno (= *crtno), cernere, pp. cretus, 'to
separate, sift, distinguish, discern, understand,
decide', and cogn. with Gk. κρίνειν (*for κρΐ-
v;eiv), 'to separate, pick out, decide, judge',
κριτός, 'picked out, chosen, excellent' (prop,
verbal adj. of κρίνειν), κριτής, 'judge', κρ(σις,
'a separating, putting apart, a decision', L.
cribrttm (for *qrei-dhron\), 'sieve', discrtmen,
'distinction, difference, interval', excrlmentum,
'what is sifted out, refuse', W. gogrynu, 'to
sift', gogr, gwagr, 'sieve', Mir. cr'tth, 'division',
crtch, 'border, boundary', OE. hridder, hriddel,
'sieve', Goth, hrains, OHG. hreini, MHG. reine,
G. rein, ON. hreinn, OS. hrini, 'clean, pure'.
All these words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*(s)q(e)re(i)-, 'to separate'. See riddle, 'sieve',
and cp. acrisia, ascertaia, certify, certitude,
concern,- crayon, cribriform, crisis, criterion, critic,
decern, decree, decretal, dincritical, discern,
discriminate, eccrinology, endocrine, excrement,
excrete, garble, hypocrisy, hypocrite, recrement,
secern, secret Base *(s)q(e)re(t)-, is an
enlargement of base *(s)qer-, 'to cut', whence Gk. κεί-
ρειν (for *κέρ-$ειν), 'to cut', L. card, 'flesh, meat',
orig. 'a piece'. See carnal.
Derivatives: certain, п., certain-ly, adv.

## certainty
certainty, n. — OF. certainete, fr. certain. See
prec. word and -ty.

## certes
certes, adv. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) certes, fr.
VL. certus, corresponding to L. certo,
'certainly', fr. certus. See certain.

## certificate
certificate, n. — F. certifical, fr. ML. certificatum,
neut. of certificatus, pp. of certificare. See certify
and adj. suff. -ate.

## certificate
certificate, tr. v. — ML. certificatus, pp. of
certificare. See prec. word.

## certification
certification, n. — F., fr. ML. certificationem,
ace. of certificatid, fr. certificatus, pp. of
certificare. See certify and -ation.

## certify
certify, tr. v. — F. certifier, fr. ML. certificare,
'to certify', lit. 'to make certain', compounded
of L. certus, 'sure, certain', and -ficare, ft.facere,
'to make, do'. See certaia, and -fy.
Derivatives: certifi-able, adj., certifi-able-ness,
п., certifi-abl-y, adv., certifi-ed, adj., certifi-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:152 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 125 | CHAIN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:152 COLUMN:1 -->

## certiorari
certiorari, п., a writ from a superior to an
inferior court, calling up the records of a case
(law). — L. certiorari, pass. pres. infin. of cer-
tiorare, 'to certify, inform', lit. 'to make more
certain', fr. cerlior, compar. of certus, 'sure,
certain' (see certain and -ior); so called from
the word certiorari occurring in the Latin text
of the writ (certiorari volumus, 'we wish to be
certified').

## certiorate
certiorate, tr. v., to certify. — L. certiuratus, pp.
of certiorare. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## certitude
certitude, n. — F., fr. Late L. certitudinem, ace.
of certitude, fr. L. certus, 'sure, certain'. Cp. It.
certitudine, OProvenc. sertelut, Catal. certilut,
Sp. cerlidumbre, and see certain and -rude.
The word certitude was introduced into French
by Nicole Oresme, bishop of Lisieux (about
1330-1382).

## cerulean
cerulean, adj., sky-blue. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. caeruleus, 'dark blue, azure', prob. dis-
similated fr. *caeluleus and lit. meaning 'sky-
color', fr. caelulum, dimin. of caelum, 'sky'. See
celestial.

## cerumen
cerumen, п., earwax (physiol.) — Medical L.,
coined by the Swiss anatomist Gaspard Bauhin
(1560-1624) fr. L. cira, 'wax' (see cere, п.), on
analogy of albumen, 'white of the egg' (see
albumen). Cp. J. Hyrtl, Onomatologia ana-
tomica, p. 104.
Derivative: cerumin-ous, adv.

## cerumini-
cerumini-, combining form meaning earwax. —
See prec. word.

## ceruse
ceruse, п., white lead. — F. ceruse, fr. L. cerussa,
which is of uncertain origin. It is perh.
borrowed fr. Gk. "κηρόεσσα (fem.), 'waxen', taken
in the sense of 'white-colored', fr. κηρός,
'beeswax'. See cere, n.

## cerussite
cerussite, п., lead carbonate (mineral.) — Formed
fr. L. cerussa (see prec. word) with subst. suff. -ite.

## cervantite
cervantite, п., an antimony oxide (mineral.) —
Named after Cervantes, a town in Spain. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## cervelat
cervelat, п., a saveloy sausage. — Fr. earlier F.
cervelal (F. cervelas), fr. It. cervellato. See
saveloy.

## cervical
cervical, adj., pertaining to the neck. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. cervix, gen. -ids, 'neck'.
The first element of this word is prob. rel. to
cerebrum, 'brain', and the second, to the base of
vincire, 'to bind'. Accordingly L. cervix lit.
means 'that which binds or fixes the head'. See
cerebrum and vincalum.

## cervicitis
cervicitis, п., inflammation of the cervix uteri
(med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L.
cervix (see prec. word) and -itis, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## cervico-
cervico-, before a vowel cervic-, combining form
meaning 'cervical'. — Fr. L. cervix, gen. cervi-
cis, 'neck'. See cervical.

## cervid
cervid, adj., pertaining to the Cervidae. — See
next word.

## Cervidae
Cervidae, n. pi., a family of mammals, the deer
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L·.
cervus, 'deer'. See next word.

## cervine
cervine, adj., pertaining to the deer family (zool.)
— L. cervinus, 'pertaining to the deer', fr. cervus,
'deer', prop, 'the horned animal'. Cp. Gk. κέρας,
L. cornu, 'horn', and see Isidorus, Etymologiae,
12, I, IS: cervi dicti άπο των κέρατων ('called
cervifrom their κέρατα, i.e.'antlers'). See cerato-
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also serval
and the second element in Rncervine. Cp. also
hart. For the ending of cervine see -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## cervisia
cervisia, п., beer. —L. cervisia, cervesia, 'beer', of
Gaulish origin; cp. MIr. coirm, cuirm, 'beer*.
Cp. cereris.
Derivative: cervisi-al, adj.

## Cervus
Cervus, п., the genus of deers (zool.) — L. cervus,
'deer'. See cervine.

## cesarevitch
cesarevitch, п., title of the eldest son of the czar,
or of the heir to the Russian throne. — Russ.
tsesarevitch, fr. tsesar, earlier form of tsar,
'czar'. See czar and cp. czarevitch.

## cesium
cesium, also caesium, п., a rare alkaline metal
(chem.) — ModL. caesium, coined by Robert
Wilhelm Bunsen (1811-99) and Gustav Robert
Kirchhoff (1824-87) in i860 fr. L. caesius,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:152 COLUMN:2 -->
'bluish gray' (see caesious); so called by them
in allusion to the two blue lines of its spectrum.

## cespitose
cespitose, adj., turfy. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ose from L. caespes, gen. caespitis, 'turf,
sod cut out, knot, knob; clump'. The orig.
meaning seems to have been 'something cut off',
which makes a connection between caespes and
L. caedere, 'to cut', very likely; see cement. See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, p. 134.

## cess
cess, п., a tax. — Fr. earlier sess, which is aphetic
for assess.
Derivatives: cess, tr. v., cess-er, n.

## cessation
cessation, п., a ceasing. — F., fr. L. cessationem,
ace. of cessatio, 'a tarrying, delaying', fr. ces-
satus, pp. of cessare, 'to tarry, delay'. See cease
and -ation.

## cesser
cesser, п., a ceasing of liability (law.) — OF.
cesser, infin. used as a noun, fr. L. cessare, 'to
cease'. See cease. For the subst. use of the
infinitive cp. attainder and words there referred to.

## cession
cession, п., a ceding. — F., fr. L. cessio, gen.
-dnis, 'a giving up, surrendering', fr. cess-(um),
pp. stem of ceaere, 'to go away, yield, give up'.
See cede and -ion.

## cessionary
cessionary, п., an assignee. — ML. cessionarius,
fr. L. cessio, gen. -onis. See cession and -ary.

## cesspool
cesspool, п., a receptacle for
refuse.—Compounded of cess (which is prob. aphetic for recess)
and pool.

## cesta
cesta, п., a basket. — Sp., fr. L. cesta, 'chest, box',
fr. Gk. κίστη, of s.m. See chest.

## Cestoda
Cestoda, n. pi., a class of worms, the tapeworms
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κεστός, 'girdle', and
-ώδης, 'like'. See next word.

## cestode
cestode, cestoid, п., tapeworm. — Formed with
suff. -ode, resp. -oid, fr. Gk. κεστός, 'girdle'. See
cestas, 'girdle'.

## cestrum
cestrum, п., a graving tool. — L., fr. Gk. κέστρον,
which stands for *κέντ-τρον, from the stem of
κέντειν, 'to prick, goad'. See center.

## Cestrum
Cestrum, п., a genus of plants of the potato
family (Solanaceae) (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
κέστρον, 'betony'.

## cestui
cestui, pron., 'he, the one', used in legal phrases
(as in cestui qne trust or cestui qui trust, the
beneficiary of a trust). — AF. and OF. cestui,
'that one', fr. VL. *ecce istui, 'behold this one'.
For the etymology of ecce see ecce homo. VL.
*istui corresponds to L. isti, dat. of iste, 'this
one', which is compounded of is, 'he, the same'
(see idem), and the pronominal base *le-,

## cestus
cestus, п., a covering for the hand used by Roman
boxers (Roman antiq.) — L. caesius, for *caed-
stus, lit. 'strap for striking', fr. caedere, 'to
strike'. See cement.

## cestus
cestus, п., a girdle (Greek and Roman antiq.) —
L., fr. Gk. κεστός, 'embroidered; girdle', which
stands for *κεντ-τός, from the stem of κέντειν,
'to prick, goad'. See center and cp. next word.

## Cestus
Cestus, п., a genus of ribbon-shaped jelly fishes
(ichthyoid) — ModL., fr. prec. word.

## Cetacea
Cetacea, п., pi., an order of aquatic mammals,
the whale, porpoise, etc. (zool.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -acea fr. L. cetus, 'whale', fr. Gk.
κήτος, which is of uncertain origin. Cp. the
second element in spermaceti.

## cetacenn
cetacenn, cetaceous, adj., pertaining to the order
of Cetacea; п., an animal pertaining to this
order. — Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -an,
resp. -ous.

## cetene
cetene, п., unsaturated hydrocarbon (chem.) —
Formed with suff. -ene fr. L. cetus, 'whale'. See
Cetacea.

## cetin
cetin, п., a crystalline fat forming the chief
component in spermaceti (chem.) — Formed with
chem. suff. -in fr. L. cetus, 'whale'. See Cetacen.

## cetology
cetology, п., that part of zoology which deals
with the whales. — Compounded of Gk. κήτος,
'whale' (see ceto-), and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## ceryl
ceryl, п., a univalent radical, С,бН3з, occurring
in spermaceti, beeswax (chem.) — Formed with
suff. -yl fr. L. cetus, 'whale'. See Cetacea.

## chabazite
chabazite, chabasite, п., a hydrous silicate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk.
χαβάζιε (occurring in the poem Περί λίθων
ascribed to Orpheus), an erroneous reading for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:152 COLUMN:3 -->
,χαλάζιε, vocative of χαλάζιος, name of a
precious stone, lit. 'resembling hailstone', fr. χάλαζα,
'hail, hailstone'. See chalaza.

## chablis
chablis, п., light, white Burgundy wine. — Named
from Chablis, a town in the Department of
Yonne in France.

## chabot
chabot, п., the fish called miller's thumb (her.) —
F., 'miller's thumb', also 'bullhead', fr. earlier
cabot, fr. OProveng. cabotz, 'a large-headed
(fish)', fr. VL. *capoceus, fr. L. caput, 'head'. See
capital, adj., and cp. Capito.

## chabouk
chabouk, chabuk, п., a long whip. — Pers. chabug,
'a whip'. Cp. chawbuck, sjambok.

## cha-cha
cha-cha, also cha-cha-cha, п., a dance in 3-beat
rhythm. — Amer. Sp. cha-cha-cha.

## chacma
chacma, п., a South African baboon. —
Hottentot.

## chnconne
chnconne, п., a slow Spanish dance. — F., fr. Sp.
chacona, a kind of Spanish dance, prob. fr.
Basque chucun, 'pretty'.

## Chaenactis
Chaenactis, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
χαίνειν, 'to gape, yawn' and άκτίς, 'ray'. The
first element is cogn. with L. hiare, 'to gape,
yawn', OE. ganian, 'to yawn'; see yawn and cp.
achene, chama. For the second element see
actinic.

## Chaenolobus
Chaenolobus, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
χαίνειν, 'to gape, yawn', and λοβός, 'lobe'. See
prec. word and lobe.

## Chaenomeles
Chaenomeles, п., a genus of plants of the apple
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
χαίνειν, 'to gape, yawn', and μήλον, 'apple'.
See Chaenactis and Malus.

## chaeto-
chaeto-, before a vowel chaet-, combining form
meaning 'spine' or 'bristle'. — Fr. Gk. χαίτη,
'long flowing hair, mane', which is cogn. with
Avestic gaisa-, 'curly hair', Ir. gaoisideach,
'hair'. Cp. achaetous and the second element in
spirochete, Coleochaete, Oligochaeta.

## Chaetodon
Chaetodon, п., a genus of fishes having spiny fins
(ichthyoL) — ModL., compounded of chaet-
and Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-.

## chaeropod
chaeropod, adj., pertaining to the Chaetopoda;
п., a chaetopod worm. — See next word.

## Chaetopoda
Chaetopoda, n. pi., a class of annelids or
segmented worms (zool.) — ModL., compounded
of chaeto- and Gk. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See
-poda.

## chafe
chafe, tr. v., 1) to warm by rubbing; 2) to irritate
by rubbing; 3) to irritate; intr. v., 1) to rub;
2) to become or be irritated. — ME. chaufer,
fr. OF. chaufer (F. chauffer), fr. VL. 'calefare
(whence also OProvenc. calfar), fr. L. calefacere,
'to make warm, to heat', which is compounded
of calere, 'to be warm' and facere, 'to make, do*.
See caldron and fact and cp. ealefacieat,
calorific. Cp. also chaff, 'to banter', chauffeur,
rechauffe.
Derivatives: chafe, п., chafer (q.v.)

## chafer
chafer, п., a vessel for heating. — Formed fr.
chafe with agential suff. -er. Cp. chauffer.

## chafer
chafer, п., a beetle. — ME., fr. OE. ceafor, rel.
to OS. kevera, Du. kever, OHG. chevar, MHG.
kever, G. Kafer, lit, 'gnawer'. Cp. MHG. kiven,
Du. keveren, 'to gnaw*, OE. ceafl, ME. chavel,
G. Kiefer, 'jaw', and see jowl, 'jaw'.

## chaff
chaff, п., husk of grain. — ME. chaf, fr. OE. ceaf,
rel. to MDu., Du. kaf, G. Kaff, and prob. also
to OHG. cheva, MHG. keve, 'husk'.
Derivatives: chaff, tr. v., chaff-y, adj.

## chaff
chaff, tr. v., to banter. — Prob. a var. of chafe.

## chaffer
chaffer, п., a bargain. — ME. cheapfare, chapfare,
chaffare, fr. OE. сёар, 'price, bargain' and faru,
'going, journey, proceeding'. For the first
element see chapman, cheap, for the second see
fare.

## chaffer
chaffer, intr. v., to bargain. — ME. chaffaren,
fr. chaffare, 'bargain'. See prec. word.
Derivative: chaffer-er, n.

## chaffinch
chaffinch, n. — OE. ceaffinc. See chaff and flach.

## chagrin
chagrin, п., mortification. — F., 'grief, sorrow,
affliction', of uncertain origin.
Derivative: chagrin, tr. v.

## chain
chain, n. — OF. chaeine (F. chaine), fr. L. catena,
'chain, fetter', which is of uncertain origin. It
stands perh. for 'cates-ηά, from base *qat-, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:153 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CHAIR | 126 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:153 COLUMN:1 -->
twist together', whence also L. cassis
(assimilated fr. *cat-sis), 'hunter's net, snare'. Cp.
catena, catenary, concatinate, chignon.
Derivatives: chain, tr. v., chain-ed, adj., chain-er,
п., chain-less, adj.

## chair
chair, п., seat. — ME. chaiere, chaere, chaire, fr.
OF. chaiere, chaere, 'chair' (whence F. chaire,
'pulpit, throne'), fr. L. cathedra, fr. Gk. καθέδρα,
'seat, chair, pulpit', formed fr. κατά, 'down' (see
cata-), and eSpa, 'seat', which is rel. Ιο £ζεσθαι,
'to sit', fr. Gk. base *έδ-, corresponding to
I.-E. base *sed-, 'to sit', whence L. sedere,
'to sit'. See sedentary and cp. cathedra,
cathedral. Cp. also chaise, which is a doublet of chair.
Derivative: chair, tr. v.

## chair
chair, п., flesh color. — F. chair, 'flesh', fr. OF.
charn, char, fr. L. carnem, ace. of caro, 'flesh',
for which see carnal.

## chaise
chaise, п., a light carriage. — F. chaise, 'chair',
orig. a dialectal variant of chaire, fr. L. cathedra.
In French chaire and chaise were differentiated in
meaning {chaire — 'pulpit', chaise — 'chair*).
See chair, 'seat'.

## chakra
chakra, п., a metal disk. — OI. cakrah, 'circle,
wheel', cogn. with Gk. κύκλος, 'circle'. See
cycle.

## chalana
chalana, п., a kind of barge. — Sp., fr. VL. che-
landium, fr. Late Gk. χελάνδιον.

## chalaza
chalaza, п., ι) the part of an ovule where the
integuments are united to the nucellus (bot.);
2) one of the two spiral albuminous chords in
the white of an egg (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
χάλαζα, 'hail, hailstone, lump', which stands for
*χάλαδ-ια and is cogn. with OSlav. ilidica,
'frozen rain'. Cp. next w<5rd. Cp. also chabazite.

## chalazion
chalazion, п., a small tumor in the eyelid (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. χαλάζιον, dimin. of
χάλαζα, 'hail; pimple, small tubercle'. See
chalaza.

## chalc-
chalc-, form of chalco- before a vowel.

## chalcedony
chalcedony, п., a variety of quartz. — So called
from the ancient town Chalcedon in Asia Minor.

## chalcid
chalcid, adj., pertaining to the Chalcidae. — See
next word.

## Chalcididae
Chalcididae, n. pi., a family of flies (entomol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Chalcis, gen.
Chalcidis, name of the type genus, fr. Gk.
χαλκός, 'copper' (see chalco-); so called from
their copperlike color.

## chalco-
chalco-, combining form meaning 'copper'. —
Gk. χαλκό-, fr. χαλκός, 'copper', dissimulated fr.
*χαλχός; cogn. with Lith. gelzis, gelezls, OSlav.
zelizo, 'iron'. Cp. the first element in colcothar
and the second element in aurichalcite, orichalc.

## chalcography
chalcography, п., the act of engraving on copper.
— Compounded of chalco- and Gk. -γραφιά,
fr. γράφειν, 'to scratch, write'. See -graphy.

## chalcostibite
chalcostibite, п., an antimony copper sulfide
(mineral.) — Compounded of chalco-, stibium
and subst. suff. -ite.

## Chaldean
Chaldean, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Chaldaeus, fr. Gk. Χαλδαΐος, fr. Aram.
Kalda'S, fr. Akkad. (mat)Kaldu, dissimilated fr.
(mat)Kashdu, '(the land of) the Chaldeans', rel.
to Kaidtm, of s.m. According to some
authorities the original meaning of the name is
'descendants of Kesed', the nephew of Abraham
(see Gen. 22; 22). According to others, Akkad.
Kashdu and Heb. Kasdtm lit. mean
'Conquerors', and are connected with Akkad. kashadu,
'to conquer'. The change of shd, id (in Akkad.
Kashdu, resp. Heb. Kasdtm) to Id (in Aram.
Kalda'e*) is due to dissimilation.

## chaldron
chaldron, п., a measure for coals, 32-36 bushels.
— OF. chauderon (F. chaudron), 'kettle'. Prop,
a doublet of caldron.

## chalet
chalet, п., 1) a herdsman's hut in the Swiss Alps;
2) a Swiss cottage. — F., formed with dimin.
suff. -et fr. pre-Latin *cala-, 'shelter', in a
widened sense: 'dwelling place', found as part of
many place names. The original meaning of
*cala- must have been 'a shelter of stone', cp.
F. caillou, 'pebble'. See A.Dauzat, DELF.,
p. r 57 s.v. chalet.

## chalice
chalice, п., a cup. — OF. chalice, a collateral
form of calice (F. calice), fr. L. calicem, ace. of
calix, 'cup, goblet', which is cogn. with Gk.
κάλυξ, 'the cup of a flower', κΰλιξ, 'cup,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:153 COLUMN:2 -->
drinking cup'. See calyx.
Derivatives: chalice, tr. v., chalic-ed, adj.

## chalk
chalk, n. — ME., fr. OE. cealc, 'chalk, lime', fr.
L. calx, gen. calcis, 'stone, chalk, lime', fr. Gk.
χάλιξ. See calcareous and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: chalk, v., chalk-y, adj.

## challah
challah, n. — See hallah.

## challenge
challenge, n. — ME. chalenge, 'claim,
accusation', fr. AF. chalenge (corresponding to OF.
chalonge), 'accusation; dispute', fr. AF. chalen-
gier (resp. OF. chalongier), 'to accuse; to dis-
pute','fr. VL. calumniare, which corresponds to
L. calumniari, 'to accuse falsely', fr. calumnia,
'false accusation'. See calumny.

## challenge
challenge, tr. v. — ME. chalengen, 'to claim,
accuse', fr. AF. chalengier. See prec. word.
Derivatives: challenge-able, adj., challeng-er, n.

## challis
challis, п., a fabric of wool and silk. — Of
unknown origin.

## chalumeau
chalumeau, п., a wind instrument. — F., 'reed,
pipe, flute', fr. Late.L. calamellus, dimin. of L.
calamus, 'reed'. See calamary.

## chalukkah
chalukkah, n. — See halukkah.

## chalutz
chalutz, n. — See halutz.

## Chalybean
Chalybean, adj., pertaining to the Chalybes, an
ancient people inhabiting Pontus in Asia
Minor. — Formed with suff. -ean fr. L. Chalybes,
fr. Gk. Χάλυβες, pi. of Χάλυψ. Ср. next word.

## chalybeate
chalybeate, adj., impregnated with iron. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. Gk. χάλυψ, gen.
χάλυβος, 'steel', fr. Χάλυβες, 'the Chalybes' (see
prec. word), a people famous fer their skill in
working iron and steel. (Cp. the attribute σιδη-
ροτέκτονες, 'workers in iron', given them by
Aeschylus in Prometheus, 715.)

## Chama
Chama, п., a genus of bivalve mollusks (zool.) —
L. chama, chema, 'cockle', fr. Gk. χήμη,
'yawning, gaping; clam', which is rel. to χαίνειν,
'to gape, yawn', and cogn. with L. hiare, OE.
ganian, of s.m. See yawn and cp. the first
element in Chaenactis, Chaenolobus, Chaeno-
meles.

## chamade
chamade, п., a signal by drum or trumpet for a
parley. — F., fr. Piedmontese ciamada, prop,
fem. pp. of ciama, 'to call', fr. L. clamare. See
claim, v.

## chamae-
chamae-, combining form lit. meaning 'on the
ground', used in the sense of 'low' (bot. and
zool.) — Gk. χαμαι-, fr. χαμαί, 'on the ground',
cogn. with L. humus, 'earth', humilis, 'low, base,
humble'. See humble and cp. the first element in.
Camelina, camomile and in germander.

## Chamaecyparis
Chamaecyparis, п., a genus of trees of the pine
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'ground cypress', fr.
chamae- and κυπάρισσος, 'cypress'. See cypress.

## Chamaedaphne
Chamaedaphne, п., a £enus of plants of the heath
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. χαμαιδάφνη,
'periwinkle', lit. 'ground laurel', fr. χαμαί, 'on
the ground', and δάφνη, 'laurel'. See chamae-
and Daphne.

## Chamaelirium
Chamaelirium, п., a genus of plants, the devil's
bit (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'ground lily', fr. chamae-
and λείριον, 'a lily'. See lily.

## Chamar
Chamar, Chumar, п., 1) an important caste in
India; 2) (not cap.) a leather worker. — Hind.
chamar, fr. OI. carma-karah, 'a leather worker'.
For the first element see shear and cp. corium.
The second element is related to OI. karoti,
krnoti, 'makes', fr. I.-E. base *q™er-, 'to make,
form, shape'. See Sanskrit, and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also churrus.

## chamber
chamber, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) chambre,
'room, chamber', fr. L. camera, 'vault, arched
roof, arch'. See camera and cp. antichamber,
cabaret, cbambranle. Cp. also next word and
fille de chambre.

## chamberlain
chamberlain, n. — OF. chamberlenc (F. cham-
bellan), fr. Frankish *kamerling (cp. OHG. cha-
marling, G. Kammerling), formed with suff.
-ling fr. *kamer, a loan word fr. L. camera,
'vault, arched roof, arch'. See camera and cp.
chamber. Cp. also camerleago.

## chamberlet
chamberlet, п., a small chamber. — Diminutive
formed fr. chamber with suff. -let.

## Chambertin
Chambertin, п., red Burgundy wine. — Named
from a vineyard near Dijon, where this vine
is grown.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:153 COLUMN:3 -->

## chambranle
chambranle, п., doorframe, windowframe,
mantelpiece. — F., a blend of branler, 'to shake,
brandish', and OF. chambrande, 'vault*. F.
branler is a shortened form of OF. brandeler, 'to
shake', which is rel. to OF. (= F.) brandir, 'to
brandish', fr. brand, 'sword'; see brandish. OF.
chambrande derives fr. L. cameranda, prop. fem.
of the gerundive of camerare, 'to vault', fr.
camera, 'vault, arched roof, arch'. See camera.

## chambray
chambray, п., a kind of gingham. — Fr. Cambrai,
a town in France (formerly in Flanders). Cp.
cambric.

## chameleon
chameleon, п., a lizard that can change the color
of its skin. — Lit. 'ground lion', fr. Gk. χαμαί,
'on the ground', and λέων, 'lion'. See chamae-
and lion.

## chametz
chametz, n. — See hantetz.

## chamfer
chamfer, п., a small groove; bevel.—F. chanfrein,
fr. OF. chanfraint, pp. of chanfraindre, 'to bevel
off', fr. chant, 'edge' and fraindre, 'to break', fr.
L. frangere, of s.m. See cant, 'slope', and fraction.
Derivatives: chamfer, tr. v., chamfer-er, n.

## chamois
chamois, п., a small kind of antelope. — F., fr.
L. camox. See gemsboc and cp. It. camoscio,
OProvenc. camos, Sp. camuza, gamuza, Catal.
gamussa. Port, camurca, Rhaeto-Romanic cha-
molsch, OHG. gamiza (whence MHG. gamz,
gamze, G. Gemse), which all derive fr. L.
camox. Cp. also shammy.

## chamois leather
chamois leather, chamois, n. — Orig. 'leather
made of the skin of chamois'. See prec. word.
Derivative: chamois, tr. v.

## Chamomila
Chamomila, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.
See camomile.

## champ
champ, tr. and intr. v., to chew noisily. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. jam, 'to press tightly'.
Derivatives: champ, п., champ-er, n.

## champac
champac, champak, п., an East-Indian tree. —
Malay tshampaka, fr. OI. campakah, which is
prob. an Austric loan word.

## champagne
champagne, n. — F., abbreviation of vin de
Champagne, 'wine made in the province of
Champagne', a name derived fr. Late L. Campania,
'plain, open country'. See campaign and cp.
champaiga.
Derivative: champagne, intr. v.

## champaign
champaign, п., open country, plain. — OF. cham-
paigne, fr. L. campania. See campagna,
campaign, and cp. champion, scamp.

## champak
champak, n. — See champac.

## champertor
champertor, п., a person who commits the act
known as champerty (law). — F. champarteur,
fr. champart. See champerty and agential suff.
-or.

## champertous
champertous, adj., pertaining to champerty (law).
— See next word and -ous.

## champerty
champerty, п., an illegal act by which a person
makes a bargain with the litigants, in order to
share in the gains in case of success (law). —
F. champart, 'division of land (rent)', fr. L.
campl pars, 'part of the field', fr. campus, gen.
campl, 'field', and pars, gen. partis, 'part'. See
camp and part.

## champignon
champignon, п., fungus, mushroom.—F., formed,
with, change of suffix, fr. OF. champegnuel,
fr. VL. *campaniolus, 'that which grows in the
field', fr. Late L. campaneus, 'pertaining to the
fields', fr. campus, 'field'. See camp.

## champion
champion, n. — ME., fr. OF. champion, fr. Late
L. campiSnem, ace. of campid, 'fighter', lit. 'one
who takes the field', fr. L. campus, 'field'. See
camp and cp. champaign.
Derivatives: champion, tr. and intr. v.,
champion-ship, n.

## champleve
champleve, adj., grooved (said of enameled work).
— F., lit. 'raised field', fr. champ, 'field', and
levi, pp. of lever, 'to raise'. F. champ derives fr.
L. campus, 'field', F. lever, fr. L. levare, 'to
raise, lift'. See camp and le»er.

## chance
chance, n. — ME. cheaunce, cheance, chance, fr.
OF. cheance, chance (F. chance), fr. VL. "caden-
tia, 'a falling', esp. 'a falling of dice', fr. L.
cadentia, neut. pi. of cadens, pres. part, of ca-
dere, 'to fall'. See cadence.
Derivatives: chance, adj. and intr. and tr. v.,
chanc-y, adj.

## chancel
chancel, п., the part of a church around the altar.
— OF., fr. L. cancellT (pi.), 'lattice, enclosure,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:154 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 127 | CHARGE D'AFFAIRES -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:154 COLUMN:1 -->
crossbars, railings'. The chancel was orig.
separated from the altar by a lattice or crossbars.
See cancel. Cp. chancellor.

## chancellery
chancellery, n. —■ OF. (= F.) ckancellerie, fr.
chancelier. See next word and -y (representing
OF. -ie) and cp. chancery.

## chancellor
chancellor, n. — ME. chanceler, fr. OF. (= F.)
chancelier, fr. Late L. cancellarius, 'chancellor',
fr. L. cancelti (see chancel); so called because his
place was near the lattice that surrounded the
judge's seat.

## chance-medley
chance-medley, п., accidental homicide,
manslaughter (law). — AF. chance medlee, lit.
'mixed chance'. See cbance and medley.

## chancery
chancery, n. — ME. chancerie, shortened fr.
chancelerie, fr. OF. chancellerie. See chancellery.

## chnncre
chnncre, a venereal ulcer (med.) — F., fr. L. cancer,
'crab, ulcer, cancer'. See caacer and cp. canker.
Derivative: chancr-ous, adj.

## chancroid
chancroid, п., a sore resembling chancre; soft
chancre (med.) — A hybrid lit. meaning 'like
chancre', coined fr. F. chancre and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See chancre and
-oid and cp. cancroid.

## chandaul
chandaul, chandal, п., an outcast (Anglo-Ind.) —
Hind, chandal, fr. OI. candalah, which is of
uncertain, prob; non-Aryan, origin.

## chandelier
chandelier, n. — F., 'candlestick', fr. VL. *can-
delarium, which is formed, with change of suff.,
fr. L. candelabrum. See candelabrum.

## chandler
chandler, n. — ME. chandeler, fr. OF. chandelier,
'maker or seller of candles', fr. Late L. cande-
larius, of s.m., fr. L. candela, 'candle'. See candle.

## change
change, tr. and intr. v. — ME. chaungen, changen,
fr. OF. (= F.) changer, fr. Late L. cambiare,
'to change, exchange', which is a Gaulish loan
word derived fr. I.-E. base *(s)qamb-, *(s)qemb-,
'to bend', whence also Olr. camm, 'crooked,
curved', Mir. cimb, 'tribute', cimbid, 'prisoner',
Gk. σκαμβός, 'crooked, bent", Swed. skumpa,
'to limp', skimpa, 'to skip'. The original
meaning of Late L. cambiare must have been 'to
bend', whence arose the following phases of
meaning: 'to turn, to change, to barter'. Cp.
Gaulish *camb-ita, 'felloe' (whence F. Jante,
'felloe'), and see cambium. Cp. also excambion,
exchange, gombeen. Cp. also camp and words
there referred to.
Derivatives: change-able, adj., change-abil-tty,n.
change-able-ness, п., change-ling, n.

## change
change, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. changer. See
change, v.

## chank
chank, also chunk, п., a large shell (Turbinella
rapa) (Anglo-Ind.) — OI. sankhah, cogn. with
Gk. κόγχη, κόγχος, 'shell'. See conch.

## channel
channel, n. — ME. chanel, chanelle, fr. OF. chanel,
fr. L. canalis, 'waterpipe, channel, canal'. F.
canal, 'channel', is a learned word, borrowed
directly fr. L. canalis. See canal.
Derivatives: channel, tr. v., channel(t)-er, п.,
channel(l)-ing, n.

## chanson
chanson, п., a song. — F., fr. L. cantidnem, ace.
of cantio, 'song', fr. cant-(um), pp. stem of
canere, 'to sing'. See cant, 'slang of beggars',
and cp. canzone.

## chant
chant, п., a song. — F., fr. L. cantus, fr. cant-(um),
pp. stem of canere, 'to sing'. See prec. word.

## chant
chant, tr. and intr. v., to sing. — F. chanter, 4o
sing', fr. L. cantare, freq. of canere [pp. stem
cant-(um)], 'to sing'. See chant, n.
Derivatives: chanter (q.v.), chant-ing, adj. and
п., chant-ing-ly, adv.

## chantage
chantage, п., extortion of hush money,
blackmail. — F., prop, 'the action of causing a person
to sing', fr. faire chanter quelqu'un, 'to
blackmail somebody', lit. 'to make somebody sing',
fr. chanter, 'to sing', fr. L. cantare, 'to sing';
see chant, v., and -age.

## chanter
chanter, п., l) one who chants; 2) the fingerpipe
of a bagpipe. — ME. chauntour, fr. OF. chanleor
(F. chantew), fr. L. cantorem, ace. of cantor,
'singer'. See cantor.

## chanterelle
chanterelle, п., a species of edible mushroom. —
F., fr. Cantharellus (q.v.)

## chantey
chantey, chanty also shanty, п., sailors' rhythmical
song. — Fr. F. chanlez, imper. pi. of chanter,
'to sing', fr. L. cantare. See chant, v.

## chanticleer
chanticleer, п., a cock. — ME. Chantecleer, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:154 COLUMN:2 -->
OF. Chanlecler (F. Chanleclair), name of the
cock in Reynard the Fox; compounded of
chanter, 'to sing', and cler (F. clair), 'clear'. See
chant, v., and clear.

## chantier
chantier, п., hut, shanty. — Can. F., fr. F. chart-
tier, 'timber yard', fr. L. canthlrius, 'a gelding;
rafter; trellis', fr. Gk. κανθήλιος, 'pack ass', a
word of non-Aryan origin. Cp. gantry and
shanty, 'hut'.

## chantress
chantress, п., songstress. — F. chanteresse, fr.
chanter, 'to sing'. See chant, v., and cp. chanter.

## chantry
chantry, п., an endowment for the chanting of
masses. — Orig. *a singing', fr. OF. chanterie,
fr. chanter, 'to sing'. See chant, v.

## Chanukkah
Chanukkah, n. — See Hanukkah.

## chaos
chaos, п., disorder, confusion. — L. chaos, fr. Gk.
χάος (for *χάτ"ος), 'gulf, chasm, abyss, the rude
unformed mass', which is rel. to χαϋι/ος,' gaping;
flaccid, loose', and cogn. with OE. goma,
'palate', pi. 'jaws', fr. I.-E. base *iho(u)-, *gheu-,
*g¥u-, 'to gape'; see gum, 'flesh in which the
teeth are set', and cp. Chauna. This base is rel.
to base *ghe(i)-, *ghi-, *g¥-, 'to gape, yawn',
whence Gk. χαΕνειν, 'to yawn, gape', χάσμα, 'a
yawning hollow, gulf', χή-μη, 'a yawning,
gaping', χη-λή, 'fork, claw', OE. gunian, 'to
yawn'; see yawn and cp. chasm, chori-.

## chaotic
chaotic, adj. — Coined fr. prec. word on analogy
of demotic (fr. demos) and other adjectives of
Greek origin ending in -olic (fr. Gk. -οτικός).
Derivatives: chaotic-al, adj., chaotic-al-ly, adv.

## chap
chap, tr. and intr. v., to chop, split, crack. —
ME. chappen, 'to cut', rel. to MDu. kappen, 'to
chop, cut'. Dan kappe, Swed. kappa, 'to cut'.
Cp. chop, 'to cut'.
Derivatives: chap, п., a crack, chapp-ed, adj.,
chapp-ing, n.

## chap
chap, also chop, п., one of the jaws. — Of
uncertain origin.

## chap
chap, n. — Short for chapman.

## chaparajos
chaparajos, n. pi., overalls used to protect the
legs from the thorns of the chaparral. — Мех.
Sp., fr.- Sp. chaparral. See chaparral.

## chaparral
chaparral, п., a thicket of shrubs. — Sp., fr.
chaparro, 'evergreen oak', fr. Basque txapar,
dimin. of sapar, 'heath, thicket'.

## chapbook
chapbook, п., one of a class of popular books
formerly sold by chapmen. — Compounded of
chap, 'chapman', and book.

## chape
chape, п., I) the metal mounting of a scabbard;
2) the piece by which a buckle is fastened to a
strap. — F., 'cope, cap, chape', fr. OF., fr. Late
L. cappa, 'hood, cap, mantle'. See cape,'cloak',
and cp. chapeau, chaperon.

## chapeau
chapeau, п., a hat. — F., fr. VL. *cappellus, a
dimin. formed fr. Late L. cappa. See prec. word
and cp. chaplet.

## chapel
chapel, n. — ME., fr. OF. chapele (whence F.
chapelle), fr. VL. cappella, 'cloak', later used in
the sense of 'a sanctuary containing relics', orig.
'the shrine containing the cloak of St. Martin
of Tours'. VL. cappella is the dimin. of Late L.
cappa, 'hood, mantle'. See cape, 'cloak', and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also chaplain
and the first' element in kapellmeister.
Derivatives: chapel, tr. v., chapel-et (F.), chapel·
ry, n. (fr. OF. chapelerie).

## chaperon
chaperon, п., a person, esp. an older woman,
who, for propriety, accompanies a young
unmarried woman. — F., 'a hood', fr. OF. chape,
'a churchman's cope, a cover, a chape', whence
arose its figurative use in modern French to
denote 'a protector', esp. 'the protector of a
young lady'. See chape.
Derivatives: chaperon, tr. v., chaperon-age, n.

## chapiter
chapiter, п., the capital of a column (archaic). —
OF. chapitre, 'capital, chapter'. See chnpter.

## chaplain
chaplain, n. — ME., fr. OF. chapelein (F. chape-
lain), fr. Eccles. L. cappellanus, fr. VL. cappella.
See chapel and cp. capelia.
Derivatives: chaplain-су, п., chaplain-ry, n.

## chaplet
chaplet, п., a wreath, rosary. — ME. chapelet, fr.
OF. (= F.) chapelet, 'garland, rosary', prop,
'a small hat', dimin. of OF. chapel (F. chapeau),
'hat'. See chapeau and -et.

## chapman
chapman, п., an itinerant dealer, peddler. — ME.
chapman, chepman, fr. OE. сёартап, 'trades-,
man', compounded of ceap, 'trade, bargain,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:154 COLUMN:3 -->
price', and man, 'man'. See cheap, п., and man
and cp. Du. kaopman, G. Kaufmann, 'merchant'.
Cp. also chap, 'chapman'.

## chaps
chaps, n. pi. — Abbreviation of chaparajos.

## chapter
chapter, n. — ME. chapitre, fr. OF. (= F.)
chapitre, fr. earlier chapitle, fr. L. capitulum, dimin.
of caput, gen. capitis, 'head; chapter'. See
capital, adj., and cp. cabildo.
Derivatives: chapter, tr. v., chapter-al, adj.

## char
char, п., an odd job. — See chare, 'turn of work'.

## char
char, п., a species of trout.—Prob. fr. Gael, ceara,
'blood-colored, red', fr. cear, 'blood'; so called
from the color of its belly.

## char
char, tr. and intr. v., to reduce to charcoal. —
Back formation fr. charcoal.

## Chara
Chara, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL., fr.
L. chara, name of an unidentified plant, of
unknown origin.

## charabanc
charabanc, char-a-banc, п., a long open car with
several benches. — F. char ά bancs, 'a long car
with benches', fr. char, 'car', a, 'to, at, for' (fr.
L. ad, 'to, toward'), and bancs, pi. of banc,
'bench'. See car, ad- and banc, bench.

## Characeae
Characeae, n. pi., a family of plants (bar.) —
ModL., formed fr. Chara with suff. -aceae.

## characeous
characeous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## character
character, n. — ME. caracter, caractere, fr. OF-
caraclere (F. caractere), fr. L. character, fr. Gk.
χαρακτήρ, 'graying tool, mark engraved,
impress, character', from the stem of χαράσσειν,
'to engrave', which is of Semitic, prob. Hebrew,
origin. Cp. Heb. hardsh, 'he engraved, plowed',
harath, 'he engraved', Aram, hurath, 'he
plowed', Ugar. firs, 'to plow'. Arab, haratha, Ethiop.
harasa, 'he plowed', Akkad. erishu, 'to till the
ground'. See D.H.Miiller in Wiener Zeitschrift
zur Kunde des Morgenlandes, I, 25. Lith. ieriu,
zerti, 'to scrape, scratch', is not cogn. with Gk.
χαράσσειν. Ср. gash.
Derivatives: character, tr. v., characterism (q.v.),
character-ist, п., characteristic (q.v.),
characterize (q.v.), character-less, adj.,
characterlessness, n.

## characterism
characterism, n. — L. charactlrismus, fr. 6k.
χαρακτηρισμός, 'characterization', fr. χαρακτη-
ρίζειν. See characterize and -ism.

## characteristic
characteristic, adj. — Gk. χαρακτηριστικός,
'characteristic', Λ-.χαρακτηρίζειν. See next word.
Derivatives: characteristic, п., characteristic-al,
adj., characteristic-al-ly, adv.

## characterize
characterize, tr. v. — ML. characterizare (whence
also F. caracteriser), fr. Gk. χαρακτηρίζειν, 'to
characterize', fr. χαρακτήρ. See character and
-ize.
Derivatives: character-iz-ation, п., character-
iz-er, n.

## charade
charade, п., a riddle based on the syllables of a
word. — F., fr. Proven?, charrado, 'talk, chat',
fr. charra, 'to talk, chat', which is of imitative
origin. Cp. It. ciarlare, Sp. charlar, 'to talk,
prattle'.

## charcoal
charcoal, n. — ME. char cole, prop, '(wood)
turned to coal', fr. charren, 'to turn' (fr. char,
'a turning'), and cole, 'coal'. See chare, 'turn
of work', and coal.
Derivatives: charcoal, tr.v., charcoal-y, adj.

## chard
chard, п., the blanched leafstalks of the
artichoke. — From earlier card, fr. F. carde, 'chard',
fr. OProvenc. cardo, fr. L. carduus, 'thistle'. See
card, 'machine for combing woo]', and cp. car-
doncillo, cardoon, Carduus.

## chare
chare, also char, п., ι) a turn of work, occasion
(obsol.); 2) an odd job. — ME. cherr, chearr,
char, 'a turn, turning, time', fr. OE. cierr, cyrr,
'a turn, time, occasion', fr. cierran,.'to turn*,
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. ajar, charcoal,
charwoman, chore.
Derivative: chare, intr. v.

## charge
charge, tr. and intr. v. — ME., fr. OF. chargier,
charger, fr. VL. *carricare, 'to put a load on', fr.
L. carrus, 'car'. See car and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: charge, п., charge-able, adj., charge-
abl-v, adv., charge-able-ness, п., charger, n.
(q.v.)

## charge d'affaires
charge d'affaires, п., ι) deputy to an ambassador;
2) representative of a country sent to another,
smaller country. — F., lit. 'charged with affairs'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:155 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CHARGER | 128 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:155 COLUMN:1 -->

## charger
charger, п., a large dish (archaic.) — ME. char-
geour, fr. 'utensil for loading or carrying on it',
fr. VL. *carricatorium, fr. *carricatus, pp. of
*carricare. See charge.
charger n„ anything that charges; a war horse. —
See charge and agential suff. -er.

## chariot
chariot, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), augment, of
char, fr. L. carrus, 'car'. See car and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: chariot, tr. and intr. v., charioteer,
n. and v., chariot-ry, n.

## Charis
Charis, п., Grace, one of the three attendants of
Aphrodite = Venus (Greek and Roman mylhol.)
— Gk. Χάρις, fr. χάρις, 'grace', rel. to χαίρειν,
(for *χάρ-ιειν), 'to rejoice', fr. I.-E. base *gher-,
'to desire', whence also OE. georn, 'desirous'.
See yearn and cp. charism and the second
element in Elcocbaris, Eucharist, Hydrocharis. Cp.
also Charon.

## charism
charism, п., a divine favor or gift. — Gk. χάρισμα,
'grace, favor, gift', fr. χαρίζεσ&αι, 'to show
favor', fr. χάρις. See prec. word and -ism.

## Charissa
Charissa, fem. PN. — MGk., fr. Gk. χάρις,
'grace'. See Charis.

## charitable
charitable, adj. —OF. ( — F.) See charity and -able.
Derivatives: charitable-ness, п., charitabl-y, adv.

## charity
charity, n. — F. chariti, fr. L. caritatem, ace. of
caritas, 'deamess, affection, love', fr. carus,
'dear, precious, esteemed, loved', which is cogn.
with Olr. carae, 'friend', caraim, W., Co.
car, 'friend', W. caraf, Ί love', Lett, kurs,
'greedy', kare, 'desire', kSruot, 'to desire', ON.
hdra, OE. hore, 'whore'. All these words derive
fr. I.-E. base *qa-, 'to desire', whence also OI.
kdmah, 'desire', kayamanah, 'loving', Toch. В
kawan, 'desire', Lith. kamaros, 'lasciviousness',
Lett, kumel, 'to hunger'. Cp. caress, cherish,
Kama, whore. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## charivari
charivari, п., a mock serenade, rough music. —
F., fr. Late L. caribaria, fr. Gk. καρηβαρία,
'heaviness in the head, topheaviness',compound-
ed of κάρα, 'head', and βάρος, 'weight'; see
cerebrum and baro-. The sense development of
the French word is explained easily by the effect
of a deafening noise ('charivari') upon the head.
Cp. shivaree.
Derivative: iharivari, tr. and intr. v.

## chark
chark, п., charcoal. — Shortened fr. charcoal.
Derivative: chark, tr. v.
