<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CHUBBV | 136 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:163 COLUMN:1 -->
chubbe, of unknown origin.

## chnbby
chnbby, adj., plump. — Lit. 'resembling a chub";
formed fr. chub with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: chubb-i-ly, adv., chubb-i-ness, n.

## chuck
chuck, tr. v., to throw. — Fr. earlier chock, fr. F.
choquer, 'to shock', which is prob. borrowed
fr. Du. schokken, a word of imitative origin.
Cp. shock, 'to collide'.

## chnck
chnck, intr. v., to cluck. — Of imitative origin.
Derivative: chuck, n.

## chnck
chnck, п., a chock. — Prob. a var. of chock,
'block'. Cp. chunk.
Derivatives: chuck, tr. v., to put into a chuck,
chuck-er, n.

## chuckle
chuckle, intr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp. chuck,
'to cluck'.

## chucklehead
chucklehead, п., a blockhead.—The first element
derives fr. obsolete chuckle, 'stupid', fr. chuck,
n. For sense development cp. blockhead.

## chudder
chudder, also chuddar, п., a sheet of cloth (Anglo-
lnd.) — Hind, chadar, fr. Pers. chadar, 'tent,
pavilion; mantle; scarf, veil; sheet; table cloth'.

## Chueta
Chueta, п., name of a descendant of a
christianized Jew on the Balearic Islands. — Sp., fr.
Majorcan jueuet, dimin. of juiu, 'Jew', fr. L.
Judaeus, whence also Sp. judio. See Jew.

## chub
chub, п., a sedge, Cyperus esadentus. — Sp., fr.
L. typhi, 'an Egyptian compound incense', fr.
Gk. κϋφι.

## chuff
chuff, п., a churl. — Of uncertain origin.

## chnkker
chnkker, also chucker, п., a wheel; a circ\e(India).
— Hind, chakwr, chakkar, fr. OI. cakrdh, 'wheel,
circle', which is cogn. with Gk. κύκλος, 'a ring,
circle'. See cycle and cp. hackery, jack, 'an East
Indian tree'.

## cham
cham, n. — Abbreviation of chamber fellow or
chamber mate.
Derivatives: chum, intr. v. (colloq.), chumm-y,
adj., chum-ship, n.

## Chumar
Chumar, n. — A var. of Chamar.

## chump
chump, n. — A blend of chunk and lump.

## chunk
chunk, п., a thick block. — A nasalized var. of
chuck, 'block'.
Derivatives: chunk-ing, chunk-y, adjs.

## chnpatty
chnpatty, also chapatty, п., a thin unleavened
cake (Anglo-Indian). — Hind, chapali, fr. OI.
carpafi, 'a flat cake', fr. carpatah, 'flat', which is
possibly of Dravidian origin.

## chuppah
chuppah, n. — See hnppah.

## chuprassy
chuprassy, п., a messenger wearing a badge
(Anglo-Ind.) — Hind, chaprasi, fr. chaprds.
'badge plate', a word of uncertain origin. The
usual derivation of chapras fr. Pers. chap-u-
rast, 'left and right', is folk etymology.

## church
church, n. — ME. chirche, churche, fr. OE. cirice,
cyrlce (whence ON. kirkja), fr. MGk. κϋρικόν,
fr. Gk. κϋριακόν (scil. $ωμα), 'the Lord's house'.
OS. kirika, ON. kirkia (Dan. kirke, Swed.
kyrka), OFris. kerke, MDu. kerke (Du. kerk),
OHG. kirihha, chirihha (MHG., G. kirche),
'church', also derive fr. MGk. κϋρικόν. OSlav.
cruky (Russ. cerkov') is prob. a Teut. loan word.
Gk. κϋριακόν is prop, the neut. of the adjective
κϋριακός, 'belonging to the Lord', fr. χδρίος,
'lord, master', from the adj. κόριος, 'having
power, having authority', fr. χϋρος, 'authority',
which is cogn. with OI. idvirah, iuraft, 'strong,
brave, courageous', Avestic sura-, sura-, 'strong,
mighty', Gaul. Καύαρος, ΟΙτ. сайг, 'hero', Co.
caur, W. cawr, 'giant, hero'. These words prob.
derive fr. I.-E. base *kew(e)-, *kewa-, *ku-, 'to
swell out', whence also Gk. κυεΐν, also κύειν,
'to become or be pregnant', L. cavus, 'hollow'.
See cave, п., and cp. kirk, kermess, 'fair'. Cp.
also curiologic, Cyril, Kyrie elelson, acyrology.
Derivatives: church, tr. v., church-ing,n.,church-
ly, adj., church-li-ness, п., church-y, adj.

## churchite
churchite, п., a hydrous cerium calcium
phosphate (mineral) — Named after the English
chemist Arthur H.Church (1834-1915). For the
ending see subst. suff. -Me.

## churl
churl, п., ι) a peasant; 2) a boor. — ME. cheorl,
cherl, churl, fr. OE. ceorl, 'a freeman of low
degree, man, husband, male', rel. to MLG.
kerle, Du. kerel, 'freeman of low degree', G.
Kerl, 'fellow", ON. karl, 'old man, man, servant'
(whence OE. carl, 'manO, Norw. kar, 'man',
kail, 'an old man', OHG. karal, 'man, husband,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:163 COLUMN:2 -->
lover' [whence MHG. karl, of a.m., and the
ML. PN. Carolus, the G. PN. Karl; cp. also Lith.
karSlius, OSlav. kralji (Russ. korof, Pol. krol,
Czech kraJ), 'king', which go back to Carolus =
Charles I (Charlemagne), long of the Franks];
fr. I.-E. base *ger(e)-, 'to become ripe, grow
old', whence also OI. jarati, 'grows old', Gk.
γέρων, Old man', γηραιός, γηραλέος, Old*, Goth.
kaurn, OE. corn, 'grain'. See com, 'grain',
and cp. next word. Cp. also Carl, carting,
Caroline, Caroline, 'old woman', Carolus,
Charles, Charles's Wain, housecarl. Cp. alsogeronto-
and words there referred to.
Derivatives: churl-ed, churl-ish, adjs., churl-ish-
ly, adv., churl-ish-ness, п., churl-y, adj.

## chura
chura, п., a machine for making butter. — ME.
chirne, chyrne, cherne, fr. OE. cyrin, rel. to ON.
kirna, Swed. karna, Dan. kjerne, Du. karn,
MHG. kern, dial. G. Kirn, Kern, 'a churn',
fr. Teut. 'kerna-, 'cream', prop, 'the kernel of
the milk'; rel. also to OE. cyrnel, ON. kjarni,
'kernel', and to OE. corn, ΟΝ., OHG. korn,
'corn'. See corn, 'grain', and cp. kernel. Cp.
also kirn. Cp. also prec. word.

## churn
churn, tr. v., to make (butter) in a churn; intr.
v., to use a churn in making butter. — ME.
chirnen, chyrnen, chernen, rel. to Swed. karna,
Dan. kjerne, Du. karnen, G. kernen, 'to churn',
and to ME. chirne, 'churn'. See churn, n.
Derivatives: churn-er, п., chum-ing, n.

## churr
churr, intr. v., to make a whirring sound (as that
made by some birds or insects); tr. v., to utter
with a churr. — Of imitative origin. Cp. chirr.
Derivative: churr, n.

## churrus
churrus, п., an apparatus for drawing water
(India). — Hind, char as, fr. charsa, 'hide', fr.
OI. carman-, 'hide, leather'. See corlum and cp.
Chamar.

## chate
chate, п., waterfall; shoot. — F. chute, 'fall',
refashioned after the pp. chu, fr. OF. cheoite, fern,
pp. of cheoir used as a noun fr. VL. 'cadectus,
formed on analogy of L. collectus, pp. of colli-
gere, 'to gather', fr. *cadere (L. cadere), 'to
fall'. See cadence. In sense development, E.
chute was partly influenced by the word shoot.
Cp. parachute.
Derivatives: chute, tr. and intr. v., chut-er, n.

## chntney
chntney, п., a strong pickle. — Hind, charm.

## chyle
chyle, п., fluid formed from the chyme in the
small intestine(physiol.)—Late L. chplus, fr. Gk.
χυλός, 'juice', from the stem of χείν, 'to pour',
whence also χυμός, 'juice', χύσις, 'effusion',
χύτρα, χύτρος, 'earthen pot', χύτλον, 'a liquid'
(lit. 'anything that may be poured'), χύδην, 'in
a stream', χοή, 'a pouring out', χοάνη, 'funnel',
χωννύναι, 'to throw up, heap up', fr. base χυ-,
corresponding to I.-E. base *ghu-, *gheu-, 'to
pour', whence OI. ju-hSti, ju-huti, 'pours into
the Are, sacrifices', hatar, 'sacrificer, priest',
hotrah. Offering, oblation', Arm. joyl, 'poured',
jew, 'form, figure', L.futis, 'a water vessel,
pitcher', futilis, 'that pours out easily; vain, futile'.
Cp. chyme. Cp. also choana, chonolith, chytra,
chytridium, diachylon, ecchymosis, synchytrium,
urachas. For base *ghu-d-, *gheu-d-, a
-(/-enlargement of the above base, see found, 'to cast',
and cp. words there referred to.

## chyll-
chyll-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
chyle'. — See chylo-.

## chyliflcation
chyliflcation, п., the formation of chyle (physiol!)
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. χυλός, 'juice', and
the Latin suff. -ficatio (see -fication). The
correct form would be chylosis, fr. Gk. χυλωσις,
'a converting into chyle', fr. χυλός. See chyle
and cp. chymification.

## chylify
chylify, tr. v., to convert into chyle; intr. v., to
be converted into chyle (physiol.) — See prec.
word and -fy.

## chylo-
chylo-, chyli-, combining form meaning
'pertaining to chyle'. — Gk. χϋλο-, χϋλι-, fr. χυλός,
'juice'. See chyle.

## chyme
chyme, п., the semiliquid food passing from the
stomach into the small intestine, (physiol.) —
Late L. chymus, fr. Gk. χυμός, 'juice', which is
rel. to χυλός, 'juice'. See chyle and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also euchyma and words
there referred to.

## chymiferous
chymiferous, adj., containing chyme. — See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:163 COLUMN:3 -->
chyme and -ferous.

## chymification
chymification, п., the conversion of food into
chyme (physiol.) — A hybrid coined fr. Gk.
χυμός, 'juice', and the Latin suff. -ficatio (see
-fication). The correct form would be chymosis,
fr. Gk. χόμωσις, 'a converting into chyme', fr.
χυμός. See chyme and cp. chyliflcation.

## chymify
chymify, tr. v., to convert into chyme (physiol.) —
See prec. word and -fy.

## chymous
chymous, adj., pertaining to chyme. — See chyme
and -ous.

## chytra
chytra, п., an earthen pot (Greek anliq.) — Gk.
χύτρα, fr. χυ-, the stem of χεΐν, 'to pour',
whence also χυλός, 'juice'. See chyle and cp.
next word.

## Chytridium
Chytridium, п., a genus of fungi (hot.)—A ModL.
dimin. formed fr. Gk. χύτρα, 'earthen pot'. See
prec. word and -idium.

## cibol
cibol, п., the Welsh onion. — F. ciboule, fr.
OProvenc. cebula, fr. L. caepulla, dimin. of cae-
pa, clpa, 'onion', fr. Gk. *κήπη or *κήπια; ср.
Gk. χάπια, rendered in Hesychius by σκόροδα
('garlic'). Cp. chive, cipolin.

## cibophobia
cibophobia, п., morbid aversion to food (med.) —
A hybrid coined fr. L. cibus, 'food', and Gk.
φόβος, fear'. L. cibus is of uncertain origin. For
the etymology of Gk. φόβος see -phobe. The
correct form is sitophobin (q.v.), in which both
elements are of Greek origin.

## ciborium
ciborium, п., ι) a canopy, esp. one covering an
altar; 2) a covered cup for keeping the
consecrated Eucharistic wafers (R.C.Ch). — L.
ciborium, 'a drinking cup resembling in form
the leaves of the Egyptian bean'.fr. Gk. χιβώριον,
'fruit of the Egyptian bean', a word of foreign,
prob. Sem., origin.

## Cicada
Cicada, п., a genus of insects (entomol.) — L.
cicada, 'tree cricket', perh. a loan word from a
Mediterranean language. Cp. cigala, Cp. also
Ciconia.

## cicatrice
cicatrice, п., a scar. — F., fr. L. cicatricem, ace.
of cicatrix. See cicatrix.

## cicatricial
cicatricial, adj., relating to, or resembling, a
cicatrice. — See prec. word and -ial.

## cicatrlcle
cicatrlcle, also cicatrlcule, п., 1) a small cicatrix;
2) the germinating point in the yolk of an egg
(embryol.) — L. cicatrlcula, dimin. of cicatrix,
gen. cicatricis, 'scar'. See cicatrix.

## cicatricose
cicatricose, adj., marked by cicatrices. — L. ci-
cSlricosus, 'marked with scars', fr. cicatrix, gen.
cicatricis. See next word and adj. suff. -ose.

## cicatrix
cicatrix, п., a scar (med. and bot.) — L. cicatrix,
'scar', of uncertain origin.

## cicatrize
cicatrize, tr. and intr. v., to heal by the formation
of a cicatrix. — ModL. cicatrizare, formed fr.
L. cicatrix, with suff. -izare. Cp. L. cicatricSri,
'to be cicatrized'. See prec. word and -ize.
Derivative: cicatriz-ation, n.

## cicely
cicely, also cecily, n. — L., fr. Gk. σέσελις, 'hart-
wort', which is prob. of Egyptian origin;
influenced in form by the PN. Cecily, Cicely.

## Cicely
Cicely, fem. PN. — A var. of Cecily (q.v.)

## cicerone
cicerone, п., guide. — It., fr. L. Cicero, the great
Roman orator (106-43 B.C.E.); so called in
allusion to the talkativeness of guides.
Derivatives: cicerone, tr. v., ciceron-age, п.,
cicerone-ship, п., ciceron-ize, tr. and intr. v.

## Ciceronian
Ciceronian, adj., resembling Cicero, eloquent. —
Formed fr. L. Cicero (see prec. word) with suff.
-ian.
Derivative: Ciceronian-ism, n.

## Cichoriaceae
Cichoriaceae, n. pi., the chicory family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Cichorium with suff. -aceae.

## cichoriaceous
cichoriaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Cicborium
Cicborium, п., a genus of plants, the succory or
chicory (bot.) — ModL., see chicory.

## Cicindelidae
Cicindelidae, n. pi., a family of beetles, the tiger
beetles (entomol) — ModL., fr. L. cicindela,
'glowworm', formed with reduplication—
through the medium of the forms *cecande~la,
*cecendela—fr. candere, 'to glow'. See candid
and cp. words there referred to. For the ending
see suff. -Idae.

## clcisbeo
clcisbeo, n„ the recognized lover of a married
woman. — It., pliob. of imitative origin. Cp.
Venetian cici, 'chattering of women', used in
this sense in the lSth century.

## ciclatoun
ciclatoun, п., a medieval fabric of precious ma-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:164 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 137 | CIRCAETUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:164 COLUMN:1 -->
terial (obsol.) — OF. ciclaton, fr. Arab, siqillaf,
'tissue adorned with seals'. See scarlet.

## Clcoala
Clcoala, п., a genus of birds, the stork (orniihol.)
— L. ciconia, 'stork'; of uncertain origin. It is
possibly, like cicada, 'tree cricket' (see Cicada),
a loan word from a Mediterranean language.

## Cicuta
Cicuta, п., a genus of herbs of the carrot family
(hot.) — L. cicuta, 'hemlock', of uncertain
origin. Cp. kex.

## -cide
-cide, sun", meaning 'killer, murderer', as in
fratricide, regicide, suicide. — F. -cide, fr. L.
•cida, fr. -cldere, used in compounds for caedere,
'to strike down, slay', whence caementum, 'rough
stone, stone chippings'. See cement and cp.
words there referred to. For the change of ae (in
L. caedere) lo I (in -cidere) see acquire and cp.
words there referred to.

## -cide
-cide, sun", meaning 'killing, murder', as in
fratricide, regicide, suicide. — F. -cide, fr. L. -ci-
dium, fr. -cidere. See prec. word and cp. words
there referred to, most of which are used
according to both senses of the sun", -cide (e.g. regicide
can mean both 'the killing of a king', and 'the
killer of a king', etc.)

## cider
cider, n. — ME. sidre, fr. OF. sidre (F. cidre),
fr. Late L. sicera, fr. Septuagint Gk. σίκερα, fr.
Heb. shekhar, 'strong drink', fr. shakhar, 'he
drank his fill, became drunk', which is rel. to
Arab. sOkira, Ethiop. sakdra, 'he was drunk',
Ugar. shkr, Akkad. shakaru, 'to be drunk',
Aram, shikhra, Syr. shafchra, Arab, sakar,
'strong drink'.

## ci-devant
ci-devant, adj., former. — F., 'formerly,
previously', compounded of ci-, 'here', and devant,
'before, in front of. The first element derives fr.
L. ecce hie, 'behold here' (see ecce). The second
element is formed fr. de, 'from' (fr. L. de, 'from,
away from'), and avant, 'before' (see de- and
avannt).

## cienagn
cienagn, п., marsh, moor. —Sp. cienaga,
formed fr. L. caenum, 'dirt, filth, mud, mire'. See
obscene.

## cierge
cierge, п., a wax candle. — F., fr. L. clreus, 'of
wax', used as a noun, fr. cera, 'wax'. See cere, n.

## cignla
cignla, cigale,n.,acicada.— F. cigale, fr. OProv-
enc. cigala, fr. VL. "cicala (whence also It.
cicala, Sp. cigarra), fr. L. cicada, 'tree cricket'.
See cicada.

## cigar
cigar, n. — Sp. cigarro, fr. Maya siqar, 'to smoke
tobacco', fr. siq, 'tobacco'. Connection with Sp.
cigarra, 'grasshopper' (see cicada), is due to
popular etymology.

## cigarette
cigarette, cigaret, n. — F. cigarette, dimin. of
cigare, 'cigar', fr. Sp. cigarro. See prec. word
and -ette, resp. -et.

## cilia
cilia, n. pi., I) eyelashes (anat.); 2) fine hairs
resembling eyelashes (hot. and zool.) — L. cilia,
pi. of cilium, 'eyelid', prob. back formation fr.
supercilium, 'eyebrow', so that cilium would lit.
mean 'that which is under the eyebrows', i.e.
'the eyelid'. (Cilium means also 'eyebrow'. This
meaning is secondary, and prob. taken over fr.
supercilium.) Supercilium, 'eyebrow', stands for
*superkeliom and prop, means 'the covering
above', fr. super- and -cilium, which is rel. to
celdre, 'to hide'. See cell and words there
referred to, and cp. superciliary. Cp. also seel, 'to
blind', and the second element in Blephilia.
Derivatives: cili-ary, cili-ate, cili-ated, adjs.

## cilice
cilice, п., a coarse cloth. — F., fr. L. cilicium, 'a
covering', orig. 'cloth made of Cilician goats'
hair', prop. neut. of the adjective Cilicius,
'Cilician', fr. Gk. Κιλίκιος, of s.m., whence also
Κιλικία (scil. γη), 'Cilicia', lit. 'Cilician earth'.

## clliosis
clliosis, п., a spasmdBic trembling of the eyelid
(med.) — A Medical L. hybrid formed fr. L.
cilium, 'eyelid', with the Greek sun", -ωσις. See
cilia and -osis.

## clmelln
clmelln, n. pi., treasures.— ML., fr. Gk.κειμήλια,
pi. of κειμήλιον, 'treasure', lit. 'anything stored
up', from the stem of κεΐμαι, Ί lie down, rest'.
See home and cp. civil.

## cimex
cimex, п., bedbug. — L. cimex, 'a bug', lit. 'the
dark-brown insect', cogn. with OI. syamah,
'black, blackish', Avestic soma-, 'black', Lith.
Slmas, 'bluish grey, grey'. Cp. chinch and the
first element in syagash.

## Cimicifuga
Cimicifuga, п., a genus of plants of the crowfoot

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:164 COLUMN:2 -->
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'driving away the
bugs', fr. L. cimex, gen. cimicis, 'bug', and
-fugus, 'flying from', in modern usage, 'putting
to flight'. See cimex and -fuge.
Cimmeriaa, adj. and n. — Formed with sun", -an
fr. L. Cimmerii, fr. Gk. Κιμμέριοι.
cimolite, п., a hydrous aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. sun", -ite fr. L. Ci-
molia, fr. Gk. Κιμωλία (scil. γη), 'Cimolian
earth', fr. Κίμωλος, 'Cimolus', an island of the
Cyclades, well known for its chalky soil.

## cinch
cinch, п., ι) a saddle girth; 2) a firm hold (colloq.)
— Sp. cincha, 'girth', fr. cincho, 'girdle, belt',
fr. L. cinctum, neut. pp. of cingere, 'to gird'.
See cincture.
Derivative: cinch, tr. v.

## Cinchona
Cinchona, п., 1) a genus of trees of the madder
family (bot.); z) (r.ot cap.) the dried bark of
various species of Cinchona and the drug
made from it. — ModL., coined by Linnaeus
from the name of the countess of Chinchon,
who introduced the drug into Spain in 163S.
(The formation of the name is erroneous. The
exact form should have been Chinchonia.)

## cinchoaism
cinchoaism, п., the effect of cinchona or its
alkaloids (med.) — Formed fr. prec. word with sun".
-ism.

## cinclls
cinclls, п., an orifice for the protrusion of the
acontia of sea anemones (zool.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. κιγκλίς, 'a latticed gate'. See cincture,

## cinct
cinct, adj., girt, girdled. — L. cinctus, pp. of
cingere, 'to gird'. See next word.

## cincture
cincture, п., a belt, girdle. — L. cinctura, 'a girdle',
fr. L. cinctus, pp. of cingere, 'to gird, bind
round', prob. cogn. with OI. kancatl, 'binds',
kanct, 'girdle', Lith. kinkau, kinkyti, 'to harness
horses', and perh. also with Gk. κιγκλίς, 'a
latticed gate'. For the ending see sun", -иге. Ср.
cinch, cingnlum, cinter, precinct, succinct,
surcingle, shiagles, enceinte, adj. and n.
Derivative: cincture, tr. v.

## cinder
cinder, n. — OE. sinder, 'impurity of metal,
dross', rel. to OS. sinder, ON. sindr, Dan sinder,
MLG., MDu. sinder, Du. sintel, OHG. sintar,
MHG. sinter, sinder, G. Sinter, and cogn with
OSlav. sedra, 'sinter', Czech sadra (for *sen-
dhra), 'gypsum'. Cp. sinter. The spelling of sinder
was influenced by F. cendre, 'ashes', with which
it has nothing in common.
Derivatives: cinder, tr. v., cinder-y, adj.

## Cinderella
Cinderella, n. — Formed with dimin. suff. -ella
fr. cinder on analogy of F. Cendrillon,
'Cinderella', fr. cendre, 'ashes', which derives fr. L.
cinerem, ace. of cinis, 'ashes'. See cinerary and
cp. G. Aschenbredel, 'Cinderella' (fr. Asche,
'ashes', and brodeln, 'to boil').

## cinema
cinema, п., a motion picture. — Short for clae-
matograph.

## cinematograph
cinematograph, kinematograph. — Coined by the
brothers Lumiere in 1896 fr. Gk. κίνημα, gen.
κινήματος, 'motion', and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write' See kinematic and -graph.
Derivatives: cinematograph, tr. and intr. v. and
ad}.,cinematograph-ic,cinematograph-ic-al,ad)S.,
cinematograph-ic-al-ly, adv., cinemalograph-y,n.

## cinerama
cinerama, п., a modern motion-picture system
employing a wide screen to simulate panoramic
vision. — Formed fr. Gk. κϊνεϊν, 'to move'
(see kinematic), on analogy of panorama; see
-rama. The word cinerama is incorrectly formed.
The correct form would be cinorama.

## Cineraria
Cineraria, п., a genus of plants of the aster family
(bot.) — ModL-, fr. L. cinerarius, 'of ashes', fr.
cinis, gen. cineris, 'ashes' (see cinerary); so called
from the color of the down on the leaves.

## cinerarium
cinerarium, п., a place to keep the ashes of the
cremated dead. — L., prop. neut. of the
adjective cinerarius, 'pertaining to ashes', used as a
noun, fr. cinis, gen. cineris, 'ashes'. See next
word.

## cinerary
cinerary, adj., pertaining to ashes. — L.

## cinerarius
cinerarius, 'pertaining to ashes', fr. cinis, gen. cineris,
'ashes', which is cogn. with Gk. κόνις, 'dust'.
For the ending see adj. suff. -ary. Cp.

## incinerate. Cp. also aconite
incinerate. Cp. also aconite, conio-, conidium, and the

## second element in Cycioconium
second element in Cycioconium, Gymnoconia,

## pneumoconiosis
pneumoconiosis,

## cinereous
cinereous, adj., of the color of ashes. — L. cine-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:164 COLUMN:3 -->
reus, 'ashen, ashy', fr. cinis, gen. cineris, 'ashes'.
See cinerary. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L.
-us, see suff. -ous.

## Cingalese
Cingalese, n. and adj., Singhalese. — See
Singhalese,

## cingulum
cingulum, п., belt, girdle (anat. and zool.) — L.,
'girdle', fr. cingere, 'to gird'. See cincture and
cp. surcingle.

## cinnabar
cinnabar, п., HgS, mercuric sulfide, a bright red
mineral. — F. cinabre, fr. OF. cenobre, fr. L.
cinnabaris, fr. Gk. κιννάβαρι, which prob.
derives fr. Pers. shungttrf 'red lead, cinnabar'.
Derivatives: cinnabar-ic, cinnabar-ine, adjs.

## Cinnamomum
Cinnamomum, п., a genus of plants of the laurel
family (bot.) — L., 'cinnamon'. See next word.

## cinnamon
cinnamon, n. — L. cinnamomum, cinnamon, fr.
Gk. κιννάμωμον, κίνναμον, fr. Heb. qinnamdn.
The Greek word has been altered fr. orig.
*κιννάμωνον, prob. under the influence of Gk.
άμωμον, 'a spice plant'.

## cinq(ue)
cinq(ue), п., the five in dice or cards. — F. cinq,
dissimilated fr. L. quinqae, 'five'. See quinque-.

## cinquecentist
cinquecentist, п., an Italian artist or poet of the
16th century. — It. cinquecentista, 'an artist of
the cinquecento', a hybrid coined fr. It. cinque-
cento (see next word) and -ist, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## cinquecento
cinquecento, п., the 16th century in Italian art and
literature. — It., shortened from mil cinquecento,
'one thousand and five hundred'. See cinque
and cent, 'a hundred'.

## cinquefoil
cinquefoil, п., a plant of the rose family, with
leaves compounded of five leaflets. — ME. cinc-
foille, fr. L. quinquefolium (whence also It. cinque-
foglie, cinquefoglio), which is compounded of
quinque, 'five', and folium, 'leaf; cp. F. quinte-
feuille, 'cinquefoil', and see cinque and 1st
foil. L. quinquefolium is a loan translation of
Gk. πεντάφυλλον, which is compounded of
πέντε, 'five', and φύλλον, 'leaf.

## cinque-pace
cinque-pace, п., a dance whose rhythm was
regulated by the number five. — Compounded of
cinqne and pace, n.

## Cinq Ports
Cinq Ports, a group of towns (orig. five) on the
southeast coast of England. — F., 'five (sea)
ports'. See ciaq(ue) and port, 'harbor'.

## ciater
ciater, cintre, п., the centering of an arch or
bridge. — F. cintre, 'curve, bend',fr. cintrer, 'to.
curve, bend', fr. VL. *cincturare, fr. L. cinctura,
'cincture, girdle', fr. cinctus, pp. of cingere, 'to
gird'. See cincture andep. words there referred to.

## don
don, п., the uvula. — Gk. κίων, 'pillar; uvula',
cogn. with Arm. siun, 'pillar'.

## cipher
cipher, n. — ME. cyphre, fr. OF. cifre, 'zero', fr.
Sp. cifra, fr. Arab, sifr, 'empty; zero' (ir.safara,
'was empty'), which is a loan translation of OI.
sunyah, 'empty; cipher with no real value; zero'
(F. chiffre, 'cipher', derives fr. It. cifra, of s.m.,
fr. ML. cifra, which is also borrowed fr. Arab.
sifr). Cp. MHG. cifre, 'zero' (whence G. Ziffer,
'cipher'), which derives fr. OF. cifre. Cp.
decipher. Cp. also zero, which is a doublet of cipher.
Derivatives: cipher, tr. and intr. v., cipher-er, n.

## cipolin
cipolin, п., a green Italian marble. — F., fr. It.
cipollino, 'a little onion', dimin. formed fr. ci-
polla, 'onion', fr. L. caepulla, dimin. of caepa,
сера, ш 'onion'; so called because the foliated
form of this marble resembles the coats of an
onion. See cibol and cp. chive.

## eippus
eippus, п., post, inscribed column used as a
landmark (Roman antiq.) — L., 'post, stake, pillar,
gravestone, boundary stone, landmark', of
uncertain origin. It is possibly rel. to L. scipio,
'staff, and cogn. with Gk. σχίπων, 'staff,
stick', ON. skifa, OS. skiHa, etc., 'disk, slice'.
See sbenve, n.

## circa
circa, adv. and prep. — L., 'round about, nearly'.
See circus and cp. clrcum-.

## Circaea
Circaea, п., a genus of plants, the enchanter's
nightshade (bot.)—ModL., named after L.Circe,
the enchantress. See Circe.

## Circaerus
Circaerus, п., a genus of large hawks (ornithol.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. κίρκος, 'hawk',
and αετός, 'eagle'. The first element, together
with κρέξ, κερκάς, κέρκνος, 'hawk', prob.
derives from the I.-E. imitative base *qer-q-,
whence also OI. krkarah, 'partridge', Alb.
sk'irake, 'hen', skireze, 'partridge', Gk. κέρχνος,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:165 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CIRCAR | 138 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:165 COLUMN:1 -->
'hoarseness'. Ср. croak, grackle. For the
imitative base *qer-, 'to crow', see raven and cp.
words there referred to. For the second element
in Circaetas see aeto-,

## circar
circar, n. — A var. of sircar.

## Circe
Circe, п., name of a sorceress in the Odyssey. —
L. Circe, fr. Gk. Κίρκη, which prob. means lit.
'wrapping up, covering', and derives fr. Heb.-
Phoenician karakh, 'he wrapped up'. For sense
development cp. Calypso, fr. Gk. καλύπτειν, 'to
cover'.

## Circean
Circean, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, Circe.
— Formed with sun", -an fr. L. Circaeus, fr.
Circe. See Dree. word.

## circinate
circinate, adj., ring-shaped. — L. circinatus, pp.
of circinare, 'to make round', fr. circinus, 'a pair
of compasses', fr. Gk. κίρκινος, fr. κίρκος,
'circle'. See circus and adj. surf, -ate and cp.
circle. Cp. also next word.

## Circinus
Circinus, п., the Compasses, a southern
constellation (aslron.) — L., 'a pair of compasses',
fr. Gk. κίρκινος. See prec. word.

## circle
circle, n. — ME. cercle, fr. F. cercle, fr. L. cir-
culus (whence also OProvenc. cercle, celcle,
Catal. cercle, It. cerchio), dimin. of circus, 'ring'.
See circus and cp. circuit, circular.
Derivatives: circle, tr. and intr. v., circl-ed, adj.,
circl-er, п., circl-et, n.

## circuit
circuit, n. — F., fr. L. circuitus, fr. circuire, cir-
cumire, 'to go round', fr. circum, 'round', and
ire, 'to go'. See circum- and itinerate.
Derivatives: circuit, tr. and intr. v., circuit-al,
adj., circuit-er, n.

## circuitous
circuitous, adj., roundabout. — ML. circuilosus,
fr. L. circuitus, also circumitus, 'a going round',
fr. circuitus, pp. of circuire, circumire, 'to go
round*; see prec. word and -ous. The word
circuitous was first used by Henry More (1614-
87), philosopher of the Cambridge Platonist
school, in 1664.
Derivatives: circuitous-ly, adv., circuitous-ness,
n.

## circular
circular, adj. — L. circularis, fr. circulus. See
circle and -ar.
Derivatives: circular, п., circularity (q.v.), cir-
cular-ize, tr. v., circular-iz-alion, п., circular-iz-
er, п., circular-ly, adv., circular-ness, n.

## circularity
circularity, n. — ML. circularitas, fr. L.
circularis. See prec. word and -ity.

## circulate
circulate, intr. and tr. v. — L. circuldtus, pp. of
circulari, 'to form a circle', fr. circulus. See
circle and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: circulation (q.v.), circulat-ive, adj.,
circulator, circulatory (qq.v.)

## circulator
circulator,n. — L.,'peddler, mountebank, quack',
fr. circulatus, pp. of circular!. See prec. word
and agential suff. -or.

## circulatory
circulatory, adj. — L. circulutorius, fr. circulatus,
pp. of circulart. See circulate and adj. suff.
-ory.

## circum-
circum-, pref. meaning 'around, all around,
about'. — L., 'around, about', lit. "in a circle',
adv. ace. of circus, 'ring'. See circus.

## circumambience
circumambience, circumambiency, n. — Formed
fr. next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## circumambient
circumambient, adj., going round, surrounding.
— Compounded of circum-, and ambient

## circumambulate
circumambulate, tr. and intr. v. — L. circum-
ambulatus, pp. of circumambulare, 'to walk
around', fr. circum- and ambulare, 'to walk'.
See ambulate, amble.
Derivatives: circumambulat-ion, п., circumambu-
lat-or, п., circumambulat-ory, adj.

## circumbendibus
circumbendibus, п., a roundabout way. —
Facetiously formed fr. circum-, bend and -ibus, the
Latin abl. pi. suff. of the 3rd declension.

## circumcise
circumcise, tr. v. — L. circumcisus, pp. of circum-
cidere, 'to cut around', fr. circum- and caedere,
'to cut'. See cement. For the change of caedere
to -cidere (in circum-cidere) see acquire and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: circumcis-er, п., circumcision (q.v.)

## circumcision
circumcision, n. — L. circumcisio, gen. -onis, 'a
cutting around', fr. circumcisus, pp. of circum-
cidere. See prec. word and -ion.

## circumference
circumference, n. — L. circumferentia, fr. L. cir-
cumferens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of circumferre,
4o carry round', fr. circum- and ferre, 'to bear.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:165 COLUMN:2 -->
carry'. See bear, 'to carry'. L. circumferentia
is a loan translation of Gk. περιφέρεια, lit.
'a carrying round', fr. περιφέρειν, 'to carry
round' (see periphery).
circumferential, adj. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. circumferentia. See prec. word.
circumflex, adj. — L. circumflexus, 'bent round',
pp. of circumflectere, 'to bend round', fr.
circum and flectere, 'to bend'. See flex, 'to bend'.
Derivatives: circumflex, tr. v., circumflex-ion, n.
circumflex, п., the mark \ ", or " placed over
long vowels in Greek to indicate a composite
(i.e. rising and then falling) tone. — L. (accen-
tus) circumflexus, lit. '(accent) bent round' (see
prec. word), is a loan translation of Gk.
(προσωδία) περισπωμένη, lit. 'accent drawn round'
(see perispomenon); so called in allusion to its
shape.

## circumfluence
circumfluence, п., a flowing round. — L. *cir-
cumfluentia, fr. circumflulns, gen. -entis. See next
word and -ce.

## circumflneat
circumflneat, adj., flowing round. — L. circum-
fluens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of circumfluere,
'to flow round*, fr. circam- and fluere, 'to flow'.
See fluent,

## circumfuse
circumfuse, tr. v., 1) to pour round; 2) to
surround. — L. circumfusus, pp. of circumfundere,
'to pour around', fr. circum- and fundere, 'to
pour'. See found, 'to cast'.

## circumfusion
circumfusion, n. — L. circumfusio, gen. -onis, fr.
circumfusus, pp. of circumfundere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## circumgyrate
circumgyrate, intr. v., to revolve, rotate. — Late
L. circumgyratus, pp. of circumgyrare, 'to turn
round, revolve', fr. circum- and L. gyrare, 'to
turn'. See gyrate.
Derivatives: circumgyrat-ion, п., circumgyrat-
ory, adj.

## circumjacence
circumjacence, circumjacency, n. — Formed fr.
next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## circumjacent
circumjacent, adj., lying around. — L. circum-

## jacens
jacens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of circumjacere,
'to lie around, border upon', fr. circum- and ja-
cere, 'to lie', which orig. meant 'to cast oneself
down', fr. jacio, jacere, 'to throw, cast, hurl'.
See jet, 'to spirt forth' and -ent and cp. adjacent
and words there referred to.

## circumlittoral
circumlittoral, adj., lying along the shore. —
Formed fr. circum- and littoral,

## circumlocution
circumlocution, п., a roundabout expression. —
L. circumlocutid, gen. -onis, 'circumlocution', fr.
circumlocutus, pp. of circumloqui, 'to make use
of circumlocution', lit. 'to talk round', fr.
circum- and loqui, 'to speak'. See locution.
Derivatives: circumlocution-α], circumlocution-
ary, adjs., circumlocution-ist, п.,
circumlocutory, adj.

## circumnavignble
circumnavignble, adj. — See next word and -able
and cp. navigable,

## circumnavigate
circumnavigate, tr. v., to sail round. — L. circum-
navigatus, pp. of circumnavigare, 'to sail round',
fr. circum- and navigare, 'to sail'. See navigate.
Derivatives: circumnavigat-ion, п., circumnavi-
gat-or, п., circumnavigat-ory, adj.

## circumnutate
circumnutate, intr. v., to move around in an
irregular spiral or elliptical path (said of growing
parts of a plant). — Formed fr. circum- and
nntate.
Derivatives: circumnutat-ion, п., circumnutat-
ory, adj.

## circumpolar
circumpolar, adj., around or near a pole. —
Formed fr. circum- and polar,

## circumscissile
circumscissile, adj., opening by a transverse
circular line. — Formed with suff. -ilefr. L. circum-

## scissus
scissus, pp. of circumscindere, 'to strip off a-

## round'
round', fr. circum- and scindere, 'to cut, split,
cleave'. See scissile.

## circumscribe
circumscribe, tr. v., i) to encircle; 2) to limit. —

## L. circumscribere
L. circumscribere, 'to draw a line round,

## enclose'
enclose', fr. circum- and scribere, 'to write'. See
scribe.
Derivative: circumscrib-er, n.

## circumscript
circumscript, adj. — L. circumscripta,
'circumscribed', pp. of circumscribere. See prec. word.
Derivatives: circumscriptive, adv., circumscript-

## ive-ly
ive-ly, adv.

## circumscription
circumscription, n. — L. circumscriptio, gen. -onis,

## fr. circumscripta
fr. circumscripta, pp. of circumscribere. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:165 COLUMN:3 -->
circumscribe and -ion.

## circumspect
circumspect, adj., cautious. — L. circumspeclus,
pp. of circumspicere, 'to look about', fr. specere,
spicere, 'to look'. See species.
Derivatives: circumspection (q.v.),
circumspective, adj., circumspect-ly, adv.

## circumspection
circumspection, n. — L. circumspeclio, gen. -onis,
fr. circumspectus, pp. of circumspicere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## circumstance
circumstance, n. — ME., fr. OF. circumstance,
circonstance (F. circonstance), fr. L. circumstan-
tia, 'a surrounding, condition, attribute,
circumstance', lit. 'a standing around', fr. circumstans,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of circunvsture, 'to
surround', fr. circum- and stare, 'to stand', see
state. L. circumstantia is a loan translation of
Gk. περίστασις, 'circumstance', lit. 'a standing
around'.
Derivatives: circumstance, tr. v., circumstance-
ed, adj.

## circumstantial
circumstantial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. circumstantia. See prec. word.
Derivatives: circumstantial, п.,
circumstantiality, п., circumstantial-ly, adv.

## circumstantiate
circumstantiate, tr. v., to give a detailed proof
of. — Formed with verbal suff. -ate fr. L.
circumstantia. See circumstance.
Derivative: circumstantiat-ion, n.

## circumvallate
circumvallate, tr. v., to surround with a rampart.
— L. circumvallatus, pp. of circumvallare, 'to
surround with a wall', fr. circum- and vallare,
'to entrench with a wall, to wall', fr. vallum,
'wall, rampart*. See vallum.
Derivative: circumvallat-ion, n.

## circumvent
circumvent, tr. v., to go around; to outwit. —
L. circumventus, pp. of circumvenire, 'to come
around (something), to surround in a hostile
manner, to oppress', fr. circum- and venire, 'to
come'. See venue, 'arrival'.
Derivatives: circumvention (q.v.), circumvent-
ive, adj.

## circumvention
circumvention, n. — L. circumventio, gen. -onis,
fr. circumventis, pp. of circumvenire. See prec.
word and -ion.

## circumvolution
circumvolution, п., a rolling around. — Formed
with suff. -ion fr. L. circumvolutus, pp. of cir-
cumvolvere, 'to roll round', fr. circum- and vol-
vere, 'to roll'. See volute and -ion.

## circumvolve
circumvolve, tr. and intr. v., to revolve. — L.
circumvolvere. See prec. word.

## circus
circus, n. — L. circus, 'a circle, ring, a round
enclosure for games', more prob. borrowed
from, than cogn. with Gk. κίρκος, κρίκος, 'a
ring*, fr. I.-E. base *qri-q-, enlargement of base
"qer-, 'in turn, twist', whence L. curvus, 'bent,
curved'. See curve and cp. cirque, search, cricoid.

## cirque
cirque, п., circus. — F„ fr. L. circus. See prec.
word.

## cirrhosis
cirrhosis, п., a disease of the liver (ma/.) —
Medical L., coined by the French physician Rene-
Theophile-Hyacinthe Laennec (1781-1826) fr.
Gk. κιρρός, Orange tawny*, which is of
uncertain origin; so called in allusion to the
yellowish color of the diseased liver. For the
ending see suff. -osis.

## cirri-
cirri-, combining form meaning 'curl, ringlet'. —
Fr. L. cirrus, gen. cirri. See cirrus.

## cirriferous
cirriferous, adj., having tendrils (bot.) —
Compounded of cirri- and -ferous.

## cirriform
cirriform, adj., having the shape of a curl or
tendril. — Compounded of cirri- and L. forma,
'form, shape'. See -form.

## cirriped
cirriped, adj., pertaining to the Cimpedia. —
See next word.

## Cimpedia
Cimpedia, n. pl„ an order of crustaceans (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of L. cirrus, 'curl', and
pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See cirrus and pedal.
cirro-. — See cirri-.

## cirrose
cirrose, adj., resembling a curl or curls (bot. and
zool.) — Formed fr. cirrus with adj. suff. -ose.

## cirrous
cirrous, adj., cirrose. — Formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -ous.

## cirrus
cirrus, п., ι) a tendril (bot.); 2) appendage (zool.);
3) a kind of cloud (meteorol.) — L., 'lock,
curl, ringlet, tuft of hair', of uncertain origin.
Cp. cerrero. _

## cirs-
cirs-, form of cirso- before a vowel.

## Cirsium
Cirsium, п., a genus of plants of the thistle family

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:166 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 139 | CLAIM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:166 COLUMN:1 -->
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κίρσιον, 'thistle', fr.
κιρσός, 'varix, enlargement of a vein', which is
of uncertain origin. The plant was called
κίρσιον for its alleged healing qualities; κίρσιον
prop, means 'remedy for dilated veins'.

## cirso-
cirso-, before a vowel cirs-, combining form
meaning 'varix, dilated vein'. — Gk. κιρσό-,
κιρσ-, fr. κιρσός. See prec. word.

## ciruela
ciruela, п., any plumlike fruit. — Sp., 'plum',
fr. L. areola (pruna), 'wax-colored plume',
neut. pi. of cereolus, 'of the color of wax',
mistaken for fem. sing; L. cereolus is dimin.
of clreus, 'of wax, waxen', fr. clra, 'wax'. See
cere, n.

## cis-
cis-, pref. meaning 'on this side'. — L. cis-, fr.
cis, 'on this side', rel. to citra, 'on this side of,
from the I.-E. pron. base *£/-, 'this', whence also
OSlav. ίί, Lith. Sis, Hitt. ki, 'this', Teut. *hi- in
Goth, hidrl, OE. hider, 'hither', Goth, hi-mma
daga, 'on this day, today'. See he, her, here,
hither, and cp. citra-.

## cisalpine
cisalpine, adj., on this side of the Alps (from the
point of view of Italy). — L. Cisalplnus, fr. cis,
'on this side of' (see prec. word), and Alplnus,
'Alpine'; see Alpine and cp. transalpine.

## cisatlantic
cisatlantic, adj., on this side of the Atlantic. —
Formed fr. cis- and Atlantic. Cp. transatlantic.

## Cisco
Cisco, п., any of whitefishes of the genus Argyroso-
mus. — Abbreviation of Can. F. ciscoette, a
word of Algonquian origin. Cp. siscowet.

## cisium
cisium, п., a light two-wheeled vehicle (Rom.
archaeology). — L., 'a light two-wheeled vehicle,
cabriolet', a word of Gaulish origin; cp. Olr.
cess, 'basket', and see chest. The spelling of L.
cisium with one s is prob. due to Etruscan
influence. See Vendryes, Memoires de la societe
de linguistique, Paris, 19, 6off.

## cismontane
cismontane, adj., on this side of the mountains;
esp. on this side of the Alps, cisalpine. — L. cis-
monldnus, fr. cis- and montanus, 'pertaining to
a mountain', fr. mons, gen. montis, 'mountain'.
See montane and cp. citramoatane. Cp. also
tramontane, ultramontane.

## cispadaae
cispadaae, adj., on this (the south) side of the
river Po. — Formed fr. cis- and L. Paddnus,
'pertaining to the Po', fr. Padus, 'Po'.

## cispontine
cispontine, adj., on this side of the bridge. —
Formed fr. cis- and L. pons, gen. pontis, 'bridge'.
See poas and adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus)
and cp. transpontine.

## cisrhenane
cisrhenane, adj., on this (the western) side of the
Rhine. — L. Cisrhenanus, fr. cis- and Rhenanus,
'pertaining to the Rhine', fr. Rhenusx 'Rhine'.
See Rhenish.

## cissoid
cissoid, п., a curve invented by the geometer
Diodes (geom.) — Gk. κισσοειδής, 'like ivy',
compounded of κισσός, 'ivy', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See next word and -oid.

## Cissus
Cissus, п., a genus of plants of the family Vita-
ceae (bot.) — L., fr. Gk. κισσός, 'ivy', which is
a foreign word of unknown origin. Cp. cissoid.

## cist
cist, п., a chest, esp. one used for sacred utensils.
— L. cista, 'chest, box of wood'. See chest and
cp. kist.

## cist
cist, п., a sepulchral stone chest. — W., fr. L.
cisla. See prec. word and cp. cistvaen.

## Cistaceae
Cistaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the rockrose
family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Cisrus with
suff. -aceae.

## cistaceous
cistaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Cistercian
Cistercian, п., a monk of the Cistercian order. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. ML. Cisiercium (F.Cf-
leaux), a place near Dijon, where this order was
founded (in 1098).
Derivative: Cistercian, adj.

## cistern
cistern, n. — ME. cisterne, fr. OF. cisterne (F. ci-
terne), fr. L. cisterna, 'a reservoir for water,
cistern', formed fr. cista, 'chest', with suff. -erna.
See chest. For the suff. see cavern.
Derivative: cislern-al, adj.

## cisterna
cisterna, п., cistern (anat.) — See prec. word.

## Cisrus
Cisrus, п., the genus of rockroses (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. κίστος, κίσθος, 'rockrose', which is of
unknown origin.

## cistvaen
cistvaen, kistvnen, п., a stone coffin. — W. cist-

## faen
faen, lit. 'stone chest', fr. cist, 'chest' (see cist,
'stone chest'), and faen, aspirated form of maen,
'stone'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:166 COLUMN:2 -->

## cit
cit, n. — Contraction of citizen,

## citadel
citadel, n. — F. citadelle, fr. It. cittadella, dimin.
of Olt. citlade (It. citta), fr. L. civitatem, ace. of
civitas, 'city'. Cp. Port, citadella, Sp. ciudadela,
and see city,

## citation
citation, п., ι) summons; 2) quotation. — ME.,
fr. L. citatidnem, ace. of citatio, fr. citatus, pp.
of citare. See cite and -ation.

## cltatory
cltatory, adj. — L. citatorius, fr. citatus, pp. of
citare. See next word and the adj. suffixes -ate
and -ory.

## cite
cite, tr. v., l) to summon; 2) to quote. — F. citer,
fr. L. citare, 'to put into quick motion, excite,
provoke, call urgently', freq. of ciere (pp. citus),
'to set in motion', fr. base *qi-, whence also Gk.
κίειν, 'to go'. This base is rel. to base *qi-,
whence Gk. κΐνεΐν, 'to move', and to base
*qieu-, whence OI. cyavate, 'moves, goes away',
Gk. σεύειν, 'to hunt, chase, drive away'. Cp.
excite, incite, kinetic, oscitancy, recite, solicit,
suscitate. Cp. also hight and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: cit-able, adj., citation(q.v.), cit-er,n.

## cithnra
cithnra, п., an ancient musical instrument
resembling a lyre. — L., fr. Gk. κιθάρα. See
next word.

## cither
cither, also cithern, a stringed musical
instrument. — F. cilhare, fr. L. cithara, fr. Gk. κιθάρα,
fr. Pers. sihtar. Cp. cithara, citole, cittern, git-
tern, guitar, kit, 'a small fiddle', zither.

## citizen
citizen, n. — ME. citezein, formed—prob. under
the influence of denizen—fr. OF. citeain (F.
citoyen), which was formed fr. cite (F. cite) with
suff. -ain. See city and -aa.
Derivatives: citizen-ess, п., citizen-ry, п.,
citizenship, n.

## citizen of the world
citizen of the world, a cosmopolitan. — Loan
translation of Gk. κοσμοπολίτης, 'a
cosmopolitan', lit. 'a citizen of the world'.

## citole
citole, п., a kind of dulcimer (obsol.) — OF., fr.
L. cithara, fr. Gk. κιθάρα; see cither. The ending
of L. cithara was mistaken for a suff. and this
alleged suff. was changed into suff. -ole.

## citra-
citra-, pref. meaning 'on this side of. — L. citra,
rel. to cis, 'on this side'. See cis-.

## citramontane
citramontane, adj., on this side of the
mountain. — Formed fr. citra- and montane. See
cismontane.

## citrate
citrate, п., salt of citric acid, (chem.) — Formed
fr. citr(ic) with chem. suff. -ate.

## citrine
citrine, adj., lemon-colored. — F. citrin, fem. ci-
trine, fr. L. citrus, 'citron tree'. See next word
and adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## citron
citron, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. citrus,
'citron tree,' fr. Gk. κέδρος, 'cedar'; see cedar.
(Gk. κίτρον, 'citron', is borrowed fr. L. citrus.)
The change of tr into dr shows that the word
came from Greek into Latin through the
medium of the Etruscans. — Cp. Citrus.
Derivatives: citron-ade, п., citron-in, n.

## citronella
citronella, п., ι) citronella grass; 2) the horse
balm. — ModL. See prec. word and -ella.

## citrul
citrul, п., the watermelon; the pumpkin (bot.) —
OF. cilrole (earlier form of citrouille), fr. Olt.
citruolo (It. cetriolo), a diminutive formed fr.
Late L. citrium, 'a kind of gourd', fr. L. citrus.
See Citrus and cp. next word.

## Citrallus
Citrallus, п., a genus of plants of the cucumber
family (bot.) — ModL., a diminutive formed fr.
L. citrus. See Citrus and cp. prec. word.

## Citrus
Citrus, п., genus of shrubs and trees, including
citrons, lemons, etc. — L. citrus, 'citron tree',
fr. Gk. κέδρος. See citron.

## citric
citric, adj. — Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -ic.

## cittern
cittern, n. — A var. of cither(n).

## city
city, n. — ME. cite, fr. OF. cite (F. cile~), fr. L.
civitatem, ace. of civitas, 'citizens of a
community, citizenship, state', (r..civis, 'member of a
community, citizen'. See civil and -ty and cp.
Olt. cittade (whence It. citta), OProvenc. and
Catal. ciutat, Sp. ciudad, Port, cidade, 'city,
town', Rum. cetate, 'castle, fortress', which all
derive fr. L. civitatem.
Derivative: citi-ed, adj.

## civet
civet, п., 1) a musklike substance obtained from
the anal glands of the civet cat; 2) the civet cat.
— F. civette, fr. It. zibetto, fr. Arab, zabad,
'civet', which is rel. to zabad, 'foam, froth',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:166 COLUMN:3 -->
zubd, 'cream'. Cp. zibet,
civic, adj. — L. civicus, 'pertaining to citizens,'
fr. ctvis. See "civil.

## civics
civics, п., the science dealing with the duties and
rights of citizens. — See prec. word and -Ics.

## civil
civil, adj. — F., fr. L. civilis, 'pertaining to a
citizen, pertaining to public life; polite', fr. civis,
'member of a community, citizen', fr. I.-E. base
*kei-, 'to lie, settle down', whence also Gk.
κεΐσθαι, 'to lie, to lie asleep', κειμήλιον,
'treasure', lit. 'anything stored up', κοιμάν, 'to put
to sleep', κοιμητήριον, 'a sleeping room, a burial
place', κοίτη, 'place to lie down in, bed', κοΐτος,
'place to lie down in, bed; sleeping, sleep*, κώμη,
'village', the second element in νεοσσός (for
•vefo-κιό-ς), 'a young bird', and in περισσός
(for* περι-κιό-ς), 'beyond the regular number,
odd', lit. 'lying beyond', OSlav. simija, 'family,
domestic servants', Lith. Seima, Seimyna, Lett.
saime, OPruss. seimins, 'domestic servants',
Lett, sieva, 'wife', OSlav. po-sivu, 'able, fit',
Goth, haims, 'village', OE. ham, 'home, house,
dwelling', Olr. cOim, coem, 'dear, beloved', ОW.
cum, ModW. cu, of s.m., and prob. also OI.
sivah, sivdh, 'kind, friendly, gracious'. All these
words denote relationship or love to the family
or clan. See home and cp. city, citizen. Cp.
also cemetery, cimelia, coma, 'insensibility',
iacunabula, neossine, neossology, perissad, Peris-
sodacryla, quiet, Siva.

## civility
civility, n. — OF. civilite (F. civilite), fr. L. civili-
tatem, ace. of civilitas, 'the art of governing,
politics; courteousness, politeness', fr. civilis.
See prec. word and -ity.

## civilize
civilize, tr. v. — F. civiliser, fr. civil. See civil
and -ize.
Derivatives: civiliz-ation, п., civilrz-er, n.

## civism
civism, п., good citizenship. — F. civisme, formed
fr. L. civis, 'citizen', with suff. -isme. See civil
and -ism.

## clachan
clachan, п., a small village (Scot, and Irish) —
Gael., fr. clach, 'stone', which is rel. to Olr.
cloch, 'stone', and prob. cogn. with Arm. sal,
'stone slab', OI. itld, 'stone, rock', possibly also
with ON. hallr, Goth, hallus, 'stone', ON. bella
(fr. 'haljon), 'flat stone'. All these words
possibly derive fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'to cut,
cleave, split'. See colter.

## clack
clack, intr. and tr. v. — ME. clacken, clakken,
of imitative origin. Cp. Du. klak, 'a crack',
klakken, 'to clack, crack', F. claquer, 'to clap,
crack', and MHG. Mac, 'crack', which all are
imitative. Cp. also clap and clatter.
Derivatives: clack, п., clack-er, n.

## clad
clad, adj. — ME. cladde, clad, fr. OE. cladod,
pp. of cladian, 'to clothe'. See clothe.

## clado-
clado-, combining form denoting 'branch, shoot'.
— Gk. κλάδο-, fr. κλάδος, 'young branch or
shoot', lit. 'branch lopped off, fr. I.-E. base
*qelad-, a -rf-enlargement of base mqel(a)-,
*qol(a)-, 'to strike, beat, break'. See holt and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also the next
three words.

## cladode
cladode, п., a cladophyll (bot.). — Gk. κλαδώδης,
'having many shoots', compounded of κλάδος,
'sprout, shoot', and -ώδης, 'like'. See dado- and
-ode, 'like'.

## cladophyll
cladophyll, п., a branch assuming the form of a
leaf (bot.) — Compounded of clado- and Gk.
φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo-.

## Cladrastis
Cladrastis, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., shortened fr. Gk. κλάδος,
'branch' (see clado-), and θραυστός, 'brittle',
verbal adj. of θροιύειν, 'to break in pieces',
which is prob. rel. to θρύπτειν, 'to break in

## pieces
pieces, soften', τρυφή, 'softness, delicacy*. See
, drop.

## claim
claim, tr. and intr. v. — ME. claimen, fr. OF.

## claim-
claim-, accented stem of clamer, 'to call, cry out,

## claim'
claim', fr. L. clumare, 'to shout, cry aloud, call,

fr. I.-E. base *kla-, var. of *kal-, 'to shout,

resound'. See calends and cp. clear. Cp. also low,
'to make the sound of a cow'. Crj. also acclnhn,

chamade, clamant, clamor, clarity, class and

the second element in council, declaim,

declamation, disclaim, exclaim, exclamation, no-

menclator, nomenclature, paraclete, proclaim,

proclamation, reclaim, reclamation.
Derivatives: claim, n. (q.v.), claim-able, adj.,
