## claim
claim, n. — ME., fr. OF. claime, fr. clamer, 4o
call, cry out, claim'. See claim, v.

## claimant
claimant, n. — OF., pres. part, of clamer. See
claim, v. and -ant, and cp. clamant

## clairaudience
clairaudience, п., the ability to hear something
not present to the ear. — Lit. 'a clear hearing',
compounded of F. clair, 'clear', and audience,
'hearing'. See denr and audience.

## clairvoyance
clairvoyance, п., the ability to see objects not
actually present; 'second sight'. — F., lit. 'a
clear sight', formed fr. next word with sun", -ce.

## clairvoyant
clairvoyant, adj., 1) related to clairvoyance; 2)
having clairvoyance; п., a person having
clairvoyance. — F., lit. 'seeing clearly', compounded
of clair, 'clear', and voyant, pres. part, of voir,
'to see', fr. L. vidire. See clear, vision and -ant.

## clam
clam, п., a bivalve mollusk. — Short for clam-
shell. The first element of this compound derives
fr. OE. clamm, 'bond, fetter'. See clamp, 'a
device for fastening', and cp. clem.

## clam
clam, tr. v., to smear (now dial.), intr. v., to be
sticky (now dial.) — Cp. OE. clam, 'mud',
clSman, 'to smear, plaster', and E. clammy, clay.
Derivatives: clamm-i-ly, adv., clamm-i-ness, n.

## clamant
clamant, adj., loud; insistent. — L. damans, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of clamare, 'to shout, cry
aloud'. See claim, v., and -ant and cp. claimant.

## ciamber
ciamber, intr. v. — ME. clambren, clameren, 'to
climb', rel. to MHG. klemberen, 'to climb', and
to ME. climben, of s.m. See climb and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivative: clamber-er, n.

## clamor
clamor, clamour, п., a loud cry. — ME. clamour,
fr. OF. clamur, clamour, fr. L. clamorem, ace.
of clamor, 'a loud cry', fr. clamare, 'to shout, cry
aloud'. See ciaim, v. and cp. acclamation.
Derivatives: clamo(u)r, v., clamo(u)r-er, n.

## clamorous
clamorous, adj., loud. — ML. clSmorasus, fr. L.
clamor. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: clamorous-ly, adv., clamorous-
ness, n.

## clamp
clamp, п., a device for fastening. — ME. prob.
fr. MDu. *clampe (Du. klamp), 'a clamp', which
is rel. to OE. tlamm, 'bond, fetter, chain; grasp',
OE. beclemman, 'to bind, enclose, fetter', OHG.
biklemmen, 'to squeeze in', Du., MHG., G.
klemmen, 'to squeeze', MHG., G. klemme,
'clamp', fr. I.-E. base *glem-, 'to embrace,
compress, squeeze', whence also L. glomus,
gen. glomeris, 'ball, sphere', Lith. glomoti, 'to
embrace', Lith. glemziu, glemzti, Lett, glemzt,
'to compress, crush'. I.-E. *glem- is an
enlargement of base *gel-, 'to roll up into a ball,
compress'. See glebe and cp. glomerate. Cp. also
next word. Cp. also dam, 'bivalve', clasp,
clem, clip, 'to embrace', dub, dump, clumsy.
Derivatives: clamp, to fasten with clamps,
clamp-er, n.

## clamp
clamp, п., a heap. — Prob. fr. Du. klamp, 'heap',
which is prob. related to damp, 'a device for
fastening'.
Derivative: clamp, tr. v., to heap.

## clan
clan, n. — Gael, clann, 'offspring, children,
descendants', fr. L. plania, 'sprout, shoot, twig',
whence also Olr. eland, clann, 'children,
descendants', chndaim, Ί plant', MW. plant, 'children,
descendants', Mir. plannda, 'plant, twig'. See
plant.
Derivatives: clarm-ish, adj., clann-ish-ly, adv.,
clann-ish-ness, п., clan-ship, n.

## clandestine
clandestine, adj., secret. — L. clandeslinus, 'secret,
clandestine', formed on analogy of intestlnus,
'inward, internal', fr. *clam-de, *clan-de, a
derivative of clam, 'secretly', which stands for cl-am,
and is formed from zero degree of base *kel-,
'to hide, conceal' (whence L. celare, 'to hide,
conceal'), with the adverbial suff. -am. See cell
and words there referred to. For the suff. -am
cp. L. cdr-am, 'in the presence of, pal-am,
'publicly'.
Derivatives: clandestine-ly, adv., clandestine-
ness, n.

## clang
clang, intr. v. — L. clangere, 'to resound, clang',
of imitative origin. Cp. Gk. κλαγγή, 'a sharp,
quick sound, twang', κλάζειν (for *κλάγ-ιειν),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:167 COLUMN:2 -->
'to make a sharp, quick sound', Lith. klagiti,
Lett, kladzit, 'to cackle', Goth, hlahjan, OE.
hleahhan, 'to laugh'. See laugh, and cp. Klaxon.

## clangor
clangor, п., a clang. — L., 'a sound, clang', fr.
clangere, 'to resound, clang'. See prec. word.
Derivative: clangor, intr. v.

## clangorous
clangorous, adj. — ML. clangorosus, fr. L.
clangor. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivative: clangorous-ly, adv.

## clank
clank, intr. and tr. v. and n. — Of imitative origin
and related to clink. For the thinning of a to ι
cp. the verbs clack and click,

## clap
clap, intr. v., to make an explosive noise; tr. v.,
to strike together. — ME. clappen, fr. OE. chep-
pan, 'to clap, beat, throb'; of imitative origin.
Cp. ON. klappa, 'to clap, beat', Du., G. klappen,
'to clap'. Cp. also clack, clatter.
Derivatives: clao, п., clapp-er, n.

## clap
clap, п., gonorrhea. — So called from le Clapier,
name of a district of Paris in the Middle Ages,
ill-famed for its many brothels (whence also F.
clapise, 'brothel'). Clap orig. meant 'disease
contracted in a brothel'.

## clapboard
clapboard, n. — Formed on analogy of clap-
holt.

## clapholt
clapholt, п., clapboard (obsol.) — LG. klappholt,
rel. to G. Klappholz, which is compounded of
klappen, 'to clap, beat, tally, fit together', and
Holz, 'wood'. See clap, 'to strike together', and
holt

## clapperclaw
clapperclaw, tr. v., to claw with the hand and
nails. — Compounded of clapper and claw.

## claque
claque, п., hired applauders in theaters. — F., fr.
claquer, 'to clap', a word of imitative origin.

## daqneur
daqneur, п., a hired applauder. — F., fr. claquer,
'to clap'. See prec. word.

## Clara
Clara, Clare, fern. PN. — L. Clara, fr. clara,
fern, of clarus, 'bright, shining, clear'. See clear
and cp. Clarice, Clarinda.

## clarabella
clarabella, п., an organ stop with a soft tone
(mus.) — Formed from the fem. of L. clarus,
'bright,' and bellus, 'beautiful'. See clear and
beauty.

## Clarence
Clarence, masc. PN. — From ML. Clarencia,
name of Ihe dukedom created for Lionel, the
third son of Edward III; so called from the
name of the town Clare (in Suffolk), whose
heiress Lionel married.

## clarence
clarence, п., a closed four-wheeled carriage. —
From the name of the Duke of Clarence (later
William IV).

## Clarendeux
Clarendeux, Clarenceux, п., title of the second
king-of-arms at the Heralds' College.— Formed
from the name of the dukedom Clarencia.

## clarendon
clarendon, п., a kind of heavy-faced type (typogr.)
— From a printer of the name Clarendon, who
lived in the 19th cent.

## claret
claret, п., a red wine. — ME., prop, 'a clarified
wine*, fr. OF, claret, used as a noun for vin
claret, lit. 'clear wine', whence F. (v«i) clairet;
dimin. of OF. cler (F. clair), fr. L. clarus. See
clear and -et

## Claribcl
Claribcl, fem. PN. — A name coined by
Tennyson on analogy of Christabel. See Clara and
Bell.

## Clarice
Clarice, Clarisse, fem. PN. — Derived fr. Clara
(q.v.)

## clarification
clarification, n. — F., fr. Late L. ciarificalidnem,
ace. of clarificdlio, 'glorification', fr. clarificatus,
pp. of cldrificdre. See next word and -atJon.

## clarify
clarify, tr. and intr. v. — OF. clarifier, fr. Late
L. clarificare, 'to glorify', fr. L. clarus, 'bright,
shining, clear, glorious', and -ficare, fr. facere,
'to make, do'. See clear and -fy.
Derivative: clarifi-er, n.

## clarigation
clarigation, п., a solemn demand of redress
before the declaration of war by the Fetiales
(Roman antiq.) — L. clarigatio, gen. -onis, fr.
clarigat-(um), pp. stem of clarigare, 'to demand
redress', prob. formed on analogy of OL. puri-
gdre = L. purgdre, 'to cleanse, purify';
compounded of clarus, 'bright, shining, clear', and
agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead, do, act'.
See clear and agent, adj. For the ending see
suff. -atioa.

## clarin
clarin, п., trumpet, clarion. — Sp. clarin, fr. claro,
'clear', fr. L. clarus. See clear and cp. clarioa,
clarinet.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:167 COLUMN:3 -->

## Clarinda
Clarinda, fem. PN. — A derivative of Ciara (q.v.)

## clarinet
clarinet, п., a woodwind instrument. — F. clari-
nette, dimin. formed fr. clarine, 'bell', orig. fem.
of the OF. adj. clarin, 'clear*, fr. L. clarus. See
clear and -et, -ette and cp. darin, clarion.
Derivative: clarinett-ist, n.

## clarion
clarion, п., a kind of trumpet. — OF. damn,
cleron (F. .clairon), fr. ML. cldrionem, ace. of
clario, fr. L. clarus, 'clear'. See clear and cp.
clarin, clarinet.

## clarionet
clarionet, п., a clarinet. — Formed from prec.
word with dimin. suff. -et.

## Clarkia
Clarkia, п., a genus of herbs allied to the fuchsia
(boi.) — ModL., named after its discoverer
William Clark, an American explorer (1770-
1838). For the ending see suff. -la.

## clary
clary, п., name of several plants. — F. sclarie,
fr. ML. schirea.

## clash
clash, intr. and tr. v. and n. — Prob. a blend of
clap and crash.

## clasp
clasp, tr. and intr. v. — ME. claspen, metathe-
sized fr. ME. clapsen and rel. to clamp, 'device
for fastening' (q.v.)
Derivatives: clasp-er, п., clasp-mg, adj.

## clasp
clasp, n. — ME. claspe, fr. claspen. See clasp, v.

## class
class, n. — F. classe, fr. L. classis, 'army fleet,
class, division', esp. 'one of the six classes of the
Roman people', which prob. stands for *qlad-
t-is, and is related to colore, 'to call, proclaim'.
See claim, v., and cp. calends.
Derivative: class, tr. v.

## classic
classic, adj. — F. classique, fr. L. classicus,
'relating to the classes of the Roman people', esp.
'relating to the first class'. See prec. word and
-ic.
Derivatives: classic, п., classic-al, adj.,
classically, adv., classic-at-ness, п., classic-ism, п.,
classic-isi, п., classic-ize, tr. and intr. v.

## classification
classification, n. — See classify and -ation.

## classificatory
classificatory, adj. — See next word and adj.
suff. -ory.

## classify
classify, tr. v. — F. classifier, fr. fictitious L.
classificare, fr. L. classis, 'class', and -ficare, fr.
facere, 'to make, do'. See class and -fy.
Derivatives: classifi-able, adj., dassifi-er, n.

## classy
classy, adj., pertaining to a higher class (slang.)—
Formed fr. class with suff. -y.

## clastic
clastic, adj., refracting. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. κλαστός, 'broken in pieces', verbal adj.
of nX5v, 'to break, break in pieces', fr. I.-E. base
*qel(d)-, *qol(d)-, 'to strike, beat'. See calamity
and cp. adastic, anaclsstic, cataclasm, icono-
clasm, oligoclase, orthoclase, periclase. Cp. also
clergy, cleric, clerk.

## dathrnte
dathrnte, adj., resembling a lattice (hot.) .—
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. clathri(p\.),
'lattice', fr. Dor. Gk. κλί&ρον, which is rel. to
Gk. κλϊΐ&ρον, Ion. κλήϊ&ρον, Old Att. κλη&ρον,
'bar for closing a door', fr. κλείε'.ν (for *y\iF-
teiv), 'to shut, close, bar'. See cleldo- and cp.
cleithrnl.

## clatter
clatter, intr. and tr. v. — ME. clateren, a verb of
imitative origin; related to clack and clap (qq.v.)
Derivatives: clatter, п., clatter-er, п., clatler-
ing-ly, adv., clatter-y, adj.
Claude. — See Claudius.

## claudetite
claudetite, п., arsenic trioxide (mineral.)—Named
after its discoverer F. Claude I. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## Claudia
Claudia, fem. PN. — L., fem. of Claudius. See
Claudius and cp. Gladys.

## claudicant
claudicant, adj., limping. — L. claudicdns, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of claudicare, 'to limp'. See
next word and -ant

## claudicate
claudicate, intr. v., to limp. — L. claudicat-(um),
pp. stem of claudicare, 'to limp, halt, be lame',
fr. claudus, 'lame,' which is of uncertain origin.
It was influenced in form by a popular
connection of this word with claudere, 'to shut,
enclose' (see close, adj.).

## Claudins
Claudins, Claude, masc. PN. — L. Claudius,
name of two Roman gentes, rel. to claudus,
'lame'. See prec. word and cp. Claudia.

## clausal
clausal, adj., pertaining to a clause. — Formed
fr. next word with adj. suff. -al.

## clause
clause, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) clause, fr. ML.
clausa, used in the sense of L. clausula, 'the
close of a rhetorical period.', fr. L. ciausus, pp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:168 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 141 | CLENCH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:168 COLUMN:1 -->
of claudere, 'to shut, enclose'. See close, adj.,
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: clause, tr. v.

## claustral
claustral, adj., pertaining to a cloister. — ML.
claustralis, fr. L. claustrum, 'bolt, bar', in its
ML. sense 'cloister'. L. claustrum stands for
"claud-trom and literally means 'that by which
anything is shut up', and is formed fr. claudere,
'to shut', with instrumental stiff. *-trom. See
close, adj., and cp. cloister. For the suff. see
rostrum. Cp. also next word and the first
element in claustrophobia.

## claustration
claustration, п., the act of shutting up in, or as
in, a cloister. — Fictitious L. claustratio, fr.
claustratus, pp. of daustrare, fr. L. claustrum.
See prec. word and -ation.

## claustrophobia
claustrophobia, п., morbid fear of being shut up
in a confined place (med.) — A Medical L.
hybrid coined fr. L. claustrum, 'bolt, bar, a
confined place', and Gk. -φοβία, fr. φόβος, 'fear'.
See claustral and -phobia.

## clava
clava, п., the clublike end of the antennae of
certain insects (entomol.) — L. clava, 'club'. See
claviform and cp. next word.

## clavate
clavate, adj., club-shaped (bot.) — Formed with
adj. suff. -ate fr. L. clava, 'club'. See claviform.

## clavecin
clavecin, п., a harpsichord. — F., formerly spelled
clavcssin, shortened fr. earlier clavycimbale, fr.
ML. clavicymbalum. See clavicembalo.
Derivative: ciavecin-ist, n.

## clavelizatiun
clavelizatiun, п., inoculation with sheep pox
virus (med.) — F. clavilisation, fr. clavelie,
'sheep pox', fr. Late L. clavellus, 'sheep pox',
dimin. of L. clavus, 'nail', which is rel. to clavis,
'key'; see clavicle and -ization. The disease is
so called because the pustules caused by it
resemble nailheads.

## clavicembalo
clavicembalo, п., a harpsichord. — It., lit. 'cymbal
with a keyboard', compounded of L. clavis,
'key', and cymbalum, 'cymbal'. See clavicle and
cymbal.

## Qaviceps
Qaviceps, п., a genus of sac fungi (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of L. clava, 'club', and -ceps,
'-headed', fr. L. caput, 'head'. See clava and
capital, adj. For the change of Latin ά (in caput)
to б (in -ceps) see biceps.

## clavichord
clavichord, п., an early keyboard instrument. —
ML. clavichordium, compounded of L. clavis,
'key', and chorda, 'string'. See clavicie and chord.

## clavicle
clavicle, п., the collarbone. — F. clavicule, fr. Late
L. clavicula, 'a little key, bar, bolt, tendril', dimin.
of L. clavis, 'key', which is rel. to clavus, 'nail',
claudere, 'to shut'. In its anatomical sense Late
L. clavicula was first used by the translators
of Avicenna about the year 980. See close, adj.,
and cp. chiave, clavelization, clavier, clavis, clef,
antoclave, conclave, enclave, kevel, laticlave,
subclavian. Cp. also lot.

## clavicular
clavicular, adj., pertaining to the collarbone. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr. Late L. clavicula.
See prec. word.

## clavier
clavier, п., keyboard. — F., lit. 'keybearer', fr.
L. clavis, 'key'. See clavicle. In the sense of
'piano', clavier is borrowed fr. G. Klavier, which
itself derives fr. F. clavier, 'keybearer'.

## claviform
claviform, adj., club-shaped. — Compounded of
L. clava, 'knotty stick, cudgel, club', and forma,
'form, shape'. The first element is rel. to clavus,
'nail'; see clavicle and cp. clava, clavate. For the
Second element see -form.

## claviger
claviger, п., one who carries a club. —· L. cldviger,
'club bearer' (epithet of Hercules), compounded
of clava, 'club', and the stem of gerere, 'to
carry'. See prec. word and gerent.

## clavis
clavis, п., a key (used also figuratively). — L.
clavis, 'key', whence clavicula, 'a little key'. See
clavicle.

## claw
claw, n. — OE. clawu, var. of clea, rel. to ON.
Ы6, OFris. klawe, kit, MLG. klouwe, Du. klauw,
OHG. klawa, Ш, MHG. klawe, G. Klaue,
'claw', and to OE. cleowe, cleowen, cliwen, 'ball
of thread'. See clew and cp. cloot, Clootie.
Derivatives: claw, tr. and intr. v., claw-ed, adj.

## clay
clay, n. — ME. clei, clai, fr. OE. clxg, rel. to OS.
klei, Dan. klxg, MDu. clei, Du. klei, LG.
klei (whence G. Klei), 'clay', OE. сШтап,
ON. kleima, OHG. kleimen, 'to cover with clay,
besmear', OHG. kliwa, klta, MHG. klige, kite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:168 COLUMN:2 -->
G. Kleie, 'bran', fr. I.-E. base *glei-, *gli-, 'to
glue, paste*, stick together', whence also Gk. γλία,
γλοίϋ, 'glue', γλοιός, 'anything sticky', γλίνη,
of s.m., OSlav. glenu, 'slime, mucus', glina,
'clay', Russ. glej, 'clay', Lett, glive, 'slime,
mucus', Olr. glenim, Ί cleave, adhere'. Cp. clam,
'to smear', clammy, cleave, 'to stick,' clever,
clevis, cliff, climb, clote. Cp. also glioma, and
the second element in neuroglia. For derivatives
of I.-E. *gleit-, a -r-enlargement of base *glei-,
see glue. Derivatives: clay, tr. v., clay-ey, adj.

## claymore
claymore, п., a large double-edged sword
formerly used by the Scottish Highlanders. — Gael.
claidheam mdr, lit. 'a big sword, fr. claidheamh,
'sword', and mdr, 'great'. The first word is
rel. to W. cleddyf, Olr. claideb, and cogn. with
Gk. κλάδος, 'young branch or shoot', L. eludes,
'disaster', fr. I.-E. *qelad-, a -rf-en'argement of
base "qela-, *qola-, 'to strike, beat, break'. See
holt and cp. clado-. Gael, mdr, 'great', is rel. to
W. mawr, 'great', and cogn. with OE. mxre,
OHG. mart, 'famous'. See more.

## Claytonia
Claytonia, п., a genus of plants of the purslane
family (hot.) — ModL., named by Gronovius
after the American botanist John Clayton
(] 693-1773). For the ending see suff. -in.

## -cle
-cle, dimin. subst. suff. — Fr. L. -cuius (masc),
■cula (fern.), or -culum (neut.), either directly
or through the medium of F. -cle. See -cule.

## clean
clean, adj. — ME. dene, fr. OE. clsene, 'clear,
clean, pure', rel. to OS. kleni, 'dainty, graceful',
OHG. kleini, 'shining, neat, elegant' (whence
MHG. kleine, 'nice, graceful, small', G. klein,
'small'; in G. Kleinod, 'jewel, gem', prop,
'something neat or fine', the orig. meaning of
klein survives), and prob. cogn. with Gk. γλαινοί
(Hesychius), 'star-shaped ornaments', γελάν,
'to laugh'. See geloto- and cp. the first clement
in kleeneboc. Derivatives: clean, adv. (q.v.),clean-
er, п., clean-ing, п., clean-ly, adv.

## dean
dean, adv. — OE. clxne, 'entirely', fr. cliene
'clear, clean, pure'. See clean, adj.

## cleanly
cleanly, adj. — ME. clenly, St. OE. dxnlic, fr.
clsene. See clean, adj., and adj. suff. -ly.
Derivatives: clean-li-ly, adv., clean-li-ness, n.

## cleanness
cleanness, n. — ME. clennesse, fr. OE. clxnnes,
fr. clsene. See clean, adj., and -ness.

## cleanse
cleanse, tr. v. — ME. clensien, clensen, fr. OE.
clxnsian, fr. сШпе. See clean, adj.
Derivatives: cleanser (q.v.), cleans-ing, n.

## cleanser
cleanser, n. — OE. clSnsere, fr. clxnsian. See
prec. word and agential suff. -er.

## clear
clear, adj. — ME. cler, cleer, fr. OF. cler, clier
(F. clair), fr. L. clarus, 'bright, shining, clear,
plain, manifest, illustrious, famous, glorious',
which stands for cla-rus, and is rel. to cla-mare,
'to call, cry out, shout, declare', fr. I.-E. base
*кШ-, var. of *kal-, 'to shout, resound'. See
calends, and cp. claim. Cp. also claret, clarify,
Clara, clarin, clarinet, clarion, clarity, declare,
eclair, glair, the first element in clairaudience,
clairvoyance, chiaroscuro and the second element
in chanticleer.
Derivatives: clear, tr. and intr. v. and adv.,
clear-age, п., clear-ance, п., clear-ing, п.,
clearly, adv., clear-ness, n.

## clearstory
clearstory, n. — See clerestory.

## cleat
cleat, п., a piece of wood or metal. — ME. clete,
elite, 'wedge', fr. OE. cleat, rel. to MLG. klot,
klute, MDu. cloot, Du. Moot, OHG., MHG.
kldj, G. ΚΙοβ, 'clod, dumpling*, and cogn. with
Ok. γλουτός, 'rump', lit. 'something round';
see glutaeus and cp. clod, clot, clond, ciout. All
these words are -/-enlargements of I.-E. base
"gleu-, 'to form into a ball', whence OI. glaiih,
'ball', and E. claw, clew (qq.v.)
Derivative: deal, tr. v.

## clenve
clenve, intr. v., to stick, adhere. — ME. eleven,
clevien, cliven, fr. OE. cleofian, clifian, rel. to
OS. kliban, OHG. kliban, Du. kleven, OHG.
kleben (intr. v.), MHG., G. kleben, 'to stick,
adhere', OHG. kliban, 'to stick', prob. also to
ON. klifa, 'to repeat over and over again', fr
I.-E. base *glei-, *gli-, 'to stick, glue, paste'.
See clay and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also clover.

## cleave
cleave, tr. and intr. v., to divide, split. — ME.
eleven, cliven, fr. OE. cieofan, rel. to OS. kli&ban.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:168 COLUMN:3 -->
ON. kljiifa, Dan. kluve, Du. kloven, OHG.
klioban, MHG., G. klieben, 'to cleave, split',
and cogn. with Gk. γλύφειν, 'to hollow out,
carve', γλύπτης, 'carver, sculptor', L. glubere,
'to peel, strip', gluma (for *glubh-ma), 'hull,
husk'. Cp. cleft, clove, 'bulb'. Cp. also glyph,
glume, glyptic
Derivatives: cleav-er, п., cleav-ing, n.

## cleavers
cleavers, n.pl., catchweed. — Lit. 'that which
sticks', fr. cleave, 'to stick'.

## cledonism
cledonism, п., the avoidance of words deemed
unlucky. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk.
κλτ)8ων, 'omen, presage, calling, rumor,
report', which stands for 'κλεί-η-δών and is rel.
to κλέος (Phocian xJif ος), 'fame, report, rumor',
κλέω (for *κλέΓω), Ί celebrate, glorify', κλυτός,
'famous, renowned, glorious', and cogn. with
OFris., OS., OE. hlud, etc., 'loud'. See loud and
cp. words there referred to.

## cleek
cleek, п., a large hook. — ME. cleken, clechen,
'to seize firmly', rel. to clutch,' v.

## clef
clef, п., sign of pitch (mus.) — F., 'key', fr. L.
clavis, whence also It. chiave. Rum. cheie, Pro-
νεης., Catal. clou, Sp. Have, Port, chare, 'key'.
See clavicle and cp. encinve.

## cleft
cleft, n. — ME. clifl, fr. OE. geclyfl, rel. to
OHG., MHG., G. kluft, MLG. kluft, klucht,
and to OE. cieofan, 'to cleave'. See cleave, 'to
divide, split'.

## eieft
eieft, past tense and pp. of cleave. — ME. clefl(e),
newly formed fr. eleven. See clenve, 'to divide,
split*.

## cieido-
cieido-, before a vowel cieid-, combining form
meaning'key'or'clavicle'.—Gk. κλειδΌ-,κλειθ-,
fr. κλείς (for *κλτ)ΐς, fr. "κλάΐις, ср. Ion. κλτ^ς,
Dor. κλδίς, Old Att. κλής), 'bar, bolt, key',
whence κλείειν (for *κλέ^ειν), 'to shut, close,
bar', κλεΐθρον, 'bar for closing a door"; cogn.
with L. clavis, 'key', clavus, 'nail', claudere, 'to
shut'. See close, adj., and cp. cleisto-, cleithral
and the first element in cleoid. Cp. also clathrate.

## cieisto-
cieisto-, before a vowel deist-, combining form
meaning 'closed', as in cleistogamy. — Gk.
κλειστός, 'shut', verbal adj. of κλείειν. See
cieido-.

## cleistogamy
cleistogamy, п., self fertilization of certain closed
flowers (hot.) — Compounded of cleisto- and
Gk. -γαμίϋ, fr. γάμος, 'marriage'. See -gamy.
Derivatives: cleistogam-ic, adj., cleistogam-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## cleithral
cleithral, adj., having a roof (said of a temple). —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. κλεΐϋρον, 'bar
for closing a door'. See cieido- and cp. clathrate.

## clem
clem, tr. v., to pinch or starve (with hunger or
thirst). — Cp. Du. and-G. klemmen, 'to pinch',
and see clamp, 'device for fastening'.

## Clematis
Clematis, п., a genus of plants of the crowfoot
family (hot.) — L.,fr. Gk. κληματίς, 'brushwood,
bag of wood', dimin. of κλήμα, gen. κλήματος,
'shoot or twig broken off (for grafting)', fr.
κλαν, 'to break'. See clastic.

## Clemence
Clemence, Clemency, fem. PN. — Fr. L.
dementia, 'mildness, mercy'. See next word and cp.
Ciement

## demency
demency, n. — L. dementia, 'calmness,
mildness, forbearance, clemency', fr. clemens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -cy.

## clement
clement, adj. — L. clemens, gen. -entis, 'mild,
calm, soft, gentle, merciful, forbearing,
indulgent', for *kUyomenos, lit. 'inclined', a
participial form of base *klei-, 'to lean, incline',
whence also 01. srdyate, 'leans', srayamttnah,
'leaning', Gk. κλίνειν, 'to cause to slope, slant',
L. -clinare (found only in compounds), 'to bend,
turn'. See clinical and cp. words there referred
to. For the participial suff. -menos see alumnus.
For the sense development of L. cllmens (fr.
base *klei-, 'to lean, incline'), cp. the E. adj.
inclined, in the sense 'disposed favorably'.

## Clement
Clement, masc. PN. — Lit. 'mild, merciful', fr.
L. clemens. See prec. word and cp. Ciemence,
Clemency.

## dench
dench, tr. v. — ME. clenchen, fr. OE. -clencan
(in beclencan) 'to hold fast', lit. 'to cause to
cling', causative of clingan, 'tocling' (seeding);
rel. to Dan. klinke, Swed., Norw. klinka, MDu.
cllnken, Du. klinken, OHG. klenken, 'to clench,
rivet', Dan., Norw. klinke, Swed. klinka, Du.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:169 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CLEOIO | 142 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:169 COLUMN:1 -->
klink, G. Klinke, 'latch', G. klinken, 'to press
the latch'. Cp. clinch.
Derivative: clench, n.
cleold, п., an instrument used to excavate teeth
(dent.) — Lit. 'key-shaped', irregularly formed
fr. Gk. κλείς, gen. κλειδός, 'key', and -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See cleldo- and
-oid.
Cieome, п., a genus of the caper family (bot.) —
ModL., of uncertain origin,
clepe, tr. v., I) to call (obsol.); z) to name
(archaic). — ME. clepen, fr. OE. cleopian, clipian,
'to call (out)', prob. related to clap, v. (q.v.)
Cp. yclept.

## clepsydra
clepsydra, п., a device for measuring time by the
gradual flow of water; waterclock. — L., fr.
Gk. κλεψύδρα, 'waterclock', which is
compounded ofthestemofitX£7rreiv, 'to steal', and ύδωρ,
'water'; so called in allusion to the circumstance
that the water is flowing stealthily from it (cp.
κλεψίρρυτος, 'flowing secretly', lit. 'flowing
stealthily'). For the first element see klepto- and cp.
klepht and the first element in kleptomania. For
the second element see hydro-.

## clepto-
clepto-, before a vowel clept-. — See klepto-,
klept-.

## clerestory
clerestory, clearstory, п., the upper part of the
nave, transepts and choir of a large church. —
Compounded of clear and story, 'section of a
house, floor'.

## clergy
clergy, n. — ME., fr. OF. clergie (F. clerge),
'clerkship, clergy', fr. Eccles. L. clericatus, fr.
clericus. See next word.
Derivative: clergy-able, adj.

## cleric
cleric, n. a clergyman; adj., clerical. —Eccles.
L. clericus, fr. Eccles. Gk. κληρικός, 'belonging
to the clergy, clerical'. See clerk.

## clerical
clerical, adj. — Eccles. L. clericalis, 'belonging
to the clergy', fr. clericus. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ai. Derivatives: clerical, п.,
clericalism, п., clerical-ist, n.

## clerk
clerk, п., — OE. cleric, clerec, clerk, fr. Eccles.
L. cllricus, fr. Eccles. Gk. κληρικός, 'belonging
to the clergy, clerical', fr. Gk. κλήρος (Dor.
κλϊρος), 'little piece of wood lopped off (used
for casting lots)', hence 'a casting of lots,
allotment, portion', in Eccles. L. 'clergy', rel. to Gk.
κλαν, 'to break', and cogn. with Olr. clar, W.
clawr, claur, 'board, plank', fr. I.-E. base
*qeHSy, *qol(a)-, 'to strike, beat, break'; see
culamity and cp. clergy and the first element in
cieruch. For a -(/-enlargement of base *qel(a)-,
see holt, 'small wood', and cp. words there
referred to. For the sense development of Eccles.
Gk. κλήρος, 'clergy', cp. the LXX version of
Deut. 18,2: κύριος αύτος κλήρος αύτοΰ, 'the
Lord is his (= Levi's) inheritance'. Derivatives:
clerk, intr. v., clerk dom, п., clerk-ly, adv.

## cieruch
cieruch, п., a citizen who received an allotment
of land in conquered territory, but retained his
citizenship (Greek anliq.) — Gk. κληροϋχος,
compounded of κλήρος, 'lot, allotment', and
the stem of έχειν, 'to hold'. See clerk and hectic.

## Ciethra
Ciethra, п., a genus of plants, the white alder
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κλήθρά, 'alder', which
is possibly cogn. with dial. G. lutter, ludere,
'alpine alder'.

## clevelte
clevelte, п., a variety of uraninite (mineral.) —
Named after the Swedish chemist Per Teodor
Cleve (1840-1905). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## clever
clever, adj. — ME. diver, 'skilled, expert', prob.
rel. to ME. clivers, 'claws' (hence orig. meaning
'quick at seizing'), and to OE. clifian, 'to cleave'.
See cleave, 'to stick, adhere'.
Derivatives: clever-ly, adv., clever-ness, п.,
clever-ish, adj., clever-ish-ly, adv.

## clevis
clevis, п., a U-shaped piece of iron used as a
securing device. — Related to cleave, 'to stick,
adhere'.

## clew
clew, clue, n. — ME. clewe, clue, fr. OE. cllowe,
cleowen, cliwen, 'ball of thread, anything in the
shape of a ball', rel. to OS. cleuwin, Du. ktuwen,
OHG. kliuwa, chliwa, MHG. kliuwe, dimin.
kliuwel, dissimilated into kniuwel, kniul (whence
G. Knuuel), 'clue, ball', OE. clla, 'claw', fr.
I.-E. base *gleu-, 'to form into a ball', whence
also OI. glduh, 'ball', Olr. glo-snathe, 'clue, ball'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:169 COLUMN:2 -->
The same base—with -/-enlargement—appears
in Gk. γλουτός, 'rump', OE. clud, 'cloud'. Cp.
claw, cleat, clod, clot, cloud, clout, knawel.
Derivative: clew, clue, tr. v.

## Qianthus
Qianthus, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., irregularly formed fr. Gk.
κλέειν, 'to make famous' (fr. κλέος, 'fame,
glory'), and άνθος, 'flower'. For the first
element see lond and cp. cledonism, Clio. For the
second element see anther.

## cliche
cliche, п., a trite phrase. — F., prop. pp. of
clicher, 'to stereotype', which is of imitative
origin. Cp. click.

## click
click, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
East Fris., Du. klikken, and E. clack and clink.
For the thinning of a to i, cp. the verbs clank
and clink. Cp. cliche, clique.
Derivatives: click, п., click-er, п., click-y, adj.

## client
client, n. — F., fr. L. clientem, ace. of cliins,
'retainer, follower, dependent', lit. 'one who
leans on another', fr. I.-E. base "klei-, 'to lean,
incline', whence also L. -clinare, 'to bend, turn'.
See clinical and cp. words there referred to. The
usual derivation of L. cliins from the stem of
cluire, 'to be named', is erroneous.
Derivatives: client-age, п., client-al, adj., client-
ed, adj., client-ry, n.

## clientele
clientele, п., the clients of a lawyer, doctor, etc. —
F. clientele, fr. L. clientila, formed from the
stem of cliins, gen. clientis (see prec. word) on
analogy of tut-ela, 'guardianship' (see tutelage).

## cliff
cliff, п., a steep rock. — ME. clif, fr. OE. clif, rel.
to OS. clif, ON. klif, OHG. klep, MDu. klippe
(whence Du. klip and MHG., G. klippe), 'cliff,
steep rock', and to OE. cliofan, 'to cleave'. See
cieave, to stick, adhere', and cp. klippe, kloof and
the first element in klipspringer. For the
relationship between OE. clif and cliofan cp. L. rupis,
'rock', which is rel. to L. rumpere, 'to break,
burst, tear, rend' (see rupestrian and cp. words
there referred to).
Derivatives: cliff-ed, adj., cliff-y, adj.

## cKinacteric
cKinacteric, п., a critical period in human life. —
L. cltmactericus, 'pertaining to a dangerous
period in life', fr. Gk. κλΐμακτηρικός, fr.
κλΐμακτήρ, 'rung of the ladder; critical point in
human life', fr. κλιμαξ, gen. κλίμχκος, 'ladder'.
See climax and -ic.

## climacteric
climacteric, adj., pertaining to a climacteric. —
From prec. word.

## climacterinm
climacterinm, п., a critical period in human life.
— ModL., fr. L. climactlr, 'a critical period in
human life', fr. Gk. κλΐμακτήρ. See climacteric,
п., and -ium.

## climactic
climactic, adj., pertaining to a climax. —
Irregularly formed fr. Gk. κλιμαξ, gen. κλίμακος,
'ladder'. See climax and -ic.

## climate
climate, n. — F. climat, fr. L. cllma, gen. -atis,
'region, climate', fr. Gk. κλίμα, gen. κλίματος,
'inclination, slope, region', from the stem of
κλίνειν, 'to cause to slope, bend'. See clinical
and cp. clime, which is a doublet of climate. Cp.
also climax, acclimate, acclimatize.
Derivatives: climate, intr. v., climat-ic, climat-
ic-al, adjs., climat-ic-al-ly, adv.

## cllmatography
cllmatography, п., description of climates. —
Compounded of Gk. κλίμα, gen. κλίματος,
'climate', and -γραφίάϊ, fr. γράφειν, 'to write*.
See climate and -graphy.
Derivative: climatograph-ical, adj.

## climatology
climatology, п., the scientific study of climates. —
Compounded of Gk. κλίμα, gen. κλίματος,
'climate', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one whospeaks
(in a certain manner); one who deais (with a
certain topic)'. See climate and -logy.
Derivative: climatolog-ist, n.

## climax
climax, n. — L., fr. Gk. κλιμαξ, 'ladder', lit.
'something sloping, something leading up by
degrees', from the stem of κλίνειν, 'to cause to
slope, bend'. See clinical and cp. ladder.
Derivative: climax, intr. and tr. v.

## climb
climb, intr. and tr. v. — ME. climben, fr. OE.
climban, rel. to OHG. klimban, MHG. klimben,
klimmen, G. klimmen, MLG. klimmen, klim-
meren, and in gradational relationship to ME.
clambren, clameren, 'to climb'. The original
meaning of these words was 4o stick on to'.
They are rel. to clam, 'to smear', clammy, cienve,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:169 COLUMN:3 -->
'to stick', and further to clay (qq.v.)
Derivatives: climb, п.,climb-able, adj. (a hybrid),
climb-er, n.

## clime
clime, п., 1) a region; 2) climate. — L. clima. See
climate.

## clin-
clin-, form of clino- before a vowel.

## clinamen
clinamen, п., inclination; bias. — L. clinamen,
fr. -clinare.'to bend, turn', which is cogn. with Gk.
κλίνειν, 'to cause to slope, bend'. See clinical,

## clinandrium
clinandrium, п., a cavity in the top of the column
of certain orchids, in which the anther rests
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. κλίνη,
'bed', and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man', used in its
modern botanic sense 'stamen'. See clinical and
andro-.

## clinanthium
clinanthium, п., the receptacle in the florets of
composite plants (bot.) — ModL., compounded
of Gk. κλίνη, 'bed', and άνθος, 'flower'. See
clinical, anther and -ium.
clinch, tr. v. — ME. clenchen; a var. of clench.
Derivatives: clinch, п., clinch-er, п., clinch-ing-
ly, adv., clinch-ing-ness, n.

## cliag
cliag, intr. v. — ME. clingen, fr. OE. clingan, 'to
shrink, shrivel, contract', rel. to Dan. klynge,
'to cluster', klynge, 'cluster'. Cp. Clench, clinch,
which are causatives of cling. Cp. also dutch, v.
Derivatives: cling, п., cling-er, п., cling-ing, adj.,
cling-ing-ly, adv., cling-ing-ness, п., cling-y, adj.

## clinic
clinic, n. — F. clinique, fr. L. clinicus. See next
word.

## clinical
clinical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
clinicus, fr. Gk. κλινικός, 'a physician who
attends patients in their beds', from the adjective
κλινικός, 'pertaining to a bed', fr. κλίνη, 'bed',
which is rel. to κλίνειν, 'to cause to slope, slant,
incline', κλίμα, 'inclination, slope, region',
κλιμαξ, 'ladder', κλΤμακτήρ, 'rung of a ladder',
κλιτός, κλειτής, 'slope, hillside', fr. I.-E. base
*klei-, 'to incline, lean', whence also L. -clinare
(with the exception of the pp. clinatus,
occurring only in compounds), 'to bend, turn', clivus,
'slope, hill', clitellae (dimin. of 'clitra, for
'kleitra), 'a packsaddle', Umbr. kletram (ace.),
'litter, bier', OI. irayati, 'leans', sritdh, 'leaning',
Lith. Slyti, 'to slope', sliiti, 'to lean', Slaltas,
'declivity,' sleivas, 'bandy-legged', Olr.. cloin,
'crooked, wrong', Mir. clithar, 'hedge', W.
cledren, 'enclosure', Mir. ell, W. cledd, Co.
cledh, Bret, kleiz, 'left', lit. 'slanting, oblique',
Mir. fo-chla, W. go-gledd, 'north', lit. 'left' (for
sense development cp. Heb. s'mol, Arab.
sham'al, shimdl, 'left; north'), Arm. learn (gen.
leriri), 'mountain', Goth, hlaiw, 'grave, tomb',
OE. hlxw, hlaw, 'mound, hill; cave', OE. hlinian,
'to lean'. See lenn, 'to incline', and cp. words
there referred to. Cp also acclivity, aclinic,
anticlinal, clement, client, climacterinm, climate,
climax, clinamen, clmo-, cliteUum, clirion, clirus,
declension, decline, declivity, diclinous, enclitic,
heteroclite, incline, isoclinlc, microcline, mono-
cllnal, pericUne, recline, synclinal, triclinium.
I.-E. base *klei- is an enlargement of base *kel-,
for the derivatives of which see heel, 'to lean'
Derivative: clinical-ly, adv

## clink
clink, intr. and tr v. — Prob. fr. MDu. clinken
(Du. klinken), 'to sound, tinkle', which is rel. to
MLG. klingen[whenceON. klingia,Oan.klinge,
Swed. klinga], OHG.klingan,MHG.,G.klingen,
'to sound, tinkle'; of imitative origin. Clink is
related to clank; for the thinning of a to 1 cp.
click and clack. Cp. dough.
Derivatives: clink, п., clink-er, п., clink-ing, adj.

## clmo-
clmo-, before a vowel clin-, combining form
denoting bed, or slope, slant, incline, decline. —
Gk. κλΐνο-, κλΐν-, fr. κλίνη, 'bed', respectively
fr. κλίνειν, 'to cause to slope, slant'. See clinical,

## clinometer
clinometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
angles of slopes. — Compounded of clino- and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm', and cp. inclinometer.
Derivatives: clinometr-y, п., clinometr-ic, adj.

## Clintonia
Clintonia, п., a genus of plants of the lily-of-the-
valley family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
American statesman De Witt Clinton (1769-
1S2S). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Clio
Clio, п., the Muse of history (Greek mythol.) —
L. СПб, fr. Gk. Κλειώ, lit. 'the proclaimer', fr.
κλείειν, κλέειν, 'to tell of, celebrate, make

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:170 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 143 | CLOVE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:170 COLUMN:1 -->
famous', fr. κλέος, 'fame, flory'. See loud and
cp. cledonism, and the first element in Clianthus.

## clip
clip, tr. and intr. v., to embrace (archaic.) —
ME. clippen, cluppen, fr. OE. clyppan, 'to
embrace, love', rel. to OFris. kleppa, of s.m.,
OHG. klaftra, MHG. klafter, G. Klafier, MLG.
klachier, 'fathom', lit. 'the outstretched arms',
and cogn. with Lith. glibys, 'armful', globiu,
globii, 'to embrace, support', Lett, glabt, glibt,
'to protect', L. gllba, 'clod', globus, 'ball, sphere'.
See clamp, 'a device for fastening', and cp. words
there referred to.

## clip
clip, п., a term for mechanical devices. — OE.
clypp, 'embrace', fr. OE. clyppan, 'to embrace'.
See prec. word.

## clip
clip, tr. v., to cut off; intr. v., to cut something. —
ME. clippen, fr. ON. klippa, which is of
imitative origin. Derivatives: clip, п., clipp-er, п.,
clipp-ing, n. and adj.

## clipcus
clipcus, clupeus, clypeus, a large shield. — L.,
possibly of Etruscan origin. Cp. Clupen.

## clique
clique, п., a small, exclusive group of persons. —
F., fr. OF. cliquer, 'to make a noise', which
is of imitative origin. Cp. click.
Derivatives: clique, intr. v., cliqu(e)-y, cliqu-ish,
adjs., cliqu-ish-ly, adv., cliqu-ish-ness, п., cliqu-
ism, n.

## cliteUum
cliteUum, п., the raised band of earthworms and
leeches (zool.) — ModL., fr. L. clitellae, 'pack-
saddle', dimin. of *clitra (for *kleitra), which
is rel. to Umbr. kletram (ace.), 'bier, litter';
formed fr. I.-E. base *klei-, 'to lean, incline',
with instrumental suff. -tra, fem. of -tro. See
clinical. For the suff. see rostrum.

## clithridiate
clithridiate, adj., having the form of a keyhole
(zool.) — Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. Gk.
κλειθρίδιον, dimin. of κλειθρίϊ, 'keyhole', fr.
κλεΐθρον, 'bar for closing'. See cieithral.

## clition
clition, п., the center of the anterior part of the
clivus (cranial.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. κλιτής,
'slope'. See clinical.

## Clitoria
Clitoria, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., of uncertain origin. For the
■ ending see sufT. -ia.

## clitoris
clitoris, п., a small, penislike organ of the female.
— Medical L., fr. Gk. κλειτορίς, lit. 4hat which
is shut up (scil. by the labia minora)', fr. κλείειν,
'to shut, close, bar', which is cogn. with L. clau-
dere, 'to shut'. See close, adj., and cp. cleido-,
cleisto-, cieithral, clithridiate.

## clitorism
clitorism, п., hypertrophy of the clitoris (med.) —
Formed fr. clitoris with suff. -ism.

## clitoriris
clitoriris, п., inflammation of the clitoris (med.)
— Medical L., formed fr. clitoris with suff. -itis.

## clivus
clivus, п., the slanting surface of the body of the
sphenoid bone (anat.) — L. clivus, 'slope, hill',
fr. *kloi-wos (rather than fr. *klei-wos); cogn.
with Goth, hlaiw, 'grave, tomb', OE. hlSw,
hlaw, 'mound, hill; cave', fr. I.-E. base *klei-,
'to incline, lean', whence also L. -clinare, 'to
bend, turn', Gk. κλίνειν, 'to cause to slope,
slant, incline'. See clinical and cp. acclivity,
declivity, proclivity.

## clonca
clonca, п., a sewer; a watercloset. — L., 'an
artificial canal in Rome, which carried the sewage
into the Tiber, sewer, dram', fr. earlier clovuca,
fr. OL. cluere, 4o purge', which is cogn. with
Gk. κλύζειν, 'to dash against, break over,
inundate, wash away, drench with a clyster',
κλύσμα, 'liquid used for washing out', κλύδων,
'wave, surge', κλυστήρ, 'clyster pipe, syringe',
Tech. В klyauccan, "broth, bubble', W. clir,
'clear', Lith. Sttoju, Sluoti, 'to sweep', Sluota,

## Lett
Lett, sluota, 'broom', Goth, hlutrs, OHG. ЫШ-
(l)ar, MHG. luter, G. lauler, OE. hlut(t)or, 'pure,
clear'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*Ши-, resp. *kleu-d-, 'to wash up, rinse'. Cp.

## clysis
clysis, ciysma, clyster and cataclysm.
Derivative: cloac-al, adj.

## cioak
cioak, n. — ME. cloke, fr. OF. cloke, cloque,

## clache (F. cloche)
clache (F. cloche), 'bell', fr. Late L. clocca,
'bell', also 'cloak' (so called from its bell-like

## appearance). See dock
appearance). See dock, which is a doublet
of cloak.
Derivatives: cloak, tr. v., cloak-ed, adj., cloak-

## ed-ly
ed-ly, adv., cloak-ing, n.

## cloche
cloche, п., a bell-shaped protection of glass for
plants. — F., 'bell'. See next word.

## clock
clock, п., a device for measuring time. — ME.
clok, clokke, fr. MDu. clocke (Du. klok), fr.
OF. cloke, cloque, cloche (F. cloche), fr. Late L.
clocca, fr. Celtic *klokka (whence Olr. clocc,
W. cloch, cloc'h, 'bell'), which is of imitative
origin. Cp. cloak, cloche, and the first element
in glockenspiel.
Derivatives: clock, intr. and tr. v., clock-ing, n.

## clock
clock, п., ornament on a stocking. — Prob.
identical with prec. word and orig. meaning 'bell-
shaped ornament*. Derivative: clock-ed, adj.

## clod
clod, n. — ME. clodde, fr. OE. clod- (used only
in compounds), a collateral form of OE. clott,
'lump'. See dot
Derivatives: clod, tr. and intr. v., clodd-ish, adj.,
clodd-ish-ly, adv., clodd-ish-ness, п., clodd-y,
adj., clodd-i-ly, adv., clodd-i-ness, a.

## clog
clog, п., ι) obstruction; 2) a wooden shoe. —
ME. klogge, 'log of wood'. Cp. Norw. klugu,
'a knotty log of wood'.
Derivatives: clog, tr. and intr. v., clogg-y, adj.,
clogg-i-ly, adv., clogg-i-ness, n.

## clolson
clolson, п., a partition, division. — F., fr. VL.
*clausi6nem, ace. of *clausio~, *a closing', fr. L.
clausus, pp. of claudere, 'to shut*. See close, adj.,
and cp. words there referred to.

## cloisonne
cloisonne, п., divided into compartments. — F.,
'partitioned, divided into compartments', pp.
of cloisonner, 'to partition', fr. cloison. See
prec. word.

## cloister
cloister, n. — ME. cloislre, cloister, fr. OF.
cloistre (F. clattre), a blend of OF. closlre, of
s.m., and of cloison. OF. closlre derives fr. L.
claustrum, 'bar, bolt, place shut up'; see clau-
stral. For the etymology of F. cloison see cloison.
Derivatives: cloister, tr. v., cloister-al, adj.,
cloister-ed, adj.

## Clonorchis
Clonorchis, п., a genus of flukes (zool.) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. κλών, 'branch, twig, slip'.
and δρχις, 'testicle'. The first element stands for
•κλάων and is rel. to κλαν, 'to break', fr. I.-E.
base *qel(a)-, *qol(a)-, 'to strike, beat, break';
see calamity. For the second element see orchid.

## Cionothrix
Cionothrix, п., a genus of bacteria (bacteriol.) —
ModL., compounded of κλών, 'branch, twig,
slip', and θρίξ, 'hair'. See prec. word and -thrix.

## clonns
clonns, also clones, п., a series of violent muscular
spasms (med) — Medical L., fr. Gk. κλόνος,
'a violent motion, confusion, tumult', prob. a
derivative of I.-E. base *kel-, 'to move violently',
whence κέλεσθαι, 'to urge on, exhort', κελεύειν,
'to urge on, exhort, order', L. celer, 'swift'. See
celerity.

## cloot
cloot, п., hoof, division of a hoof. — ON. kid,
'claw'. See claw and cp. next word.

## Clootie
Clootie, п., the devil. — Lit., 'hoofed'. See prec.
word.

## close
close, adj. — ME. clos, fr. OF. (= F.) clos, fr.
L. clausus, pp. of claudere, 'to shut, close*,
which is rel. to clavis, 'key', clavus, *nail', clma,
'a knotty stick, staff, club', and cogn. with Gk.
κλείς, gen. κλειδός, 'bar, bolt, key' [whence
κλείειν (for *κλέ\τ"ιειν), 'to shut, close, bar',
κλεΐθρον, 'bar for closing a door'], Olr. eld, 'nail',

OSlav. kljuci, 'key', Russ. kljui, of s.m., OSlav.

kljuiiti, 'to shut up', Serb, kljuka, 'hook', Lith.

## kliuti
kliuti, 'to catch, be caught on', kliduties, Lett.

## klauties
klauties, 'to rely upon', OFris. sluta, MLG.,

## sliesen
sliesen, G. schliefien, 'to shut, close, lock', OS.

## slutil
slutil, OFris. sletel, MDu. slotel, Du. sleulel,

## OHG. slu33il
OHG. slu33il, MHG. slUjsel, G. Schliissel,
'key'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *qlau-,
*(s)qleu-, 'hook, forked branch, key; to close,

shut'. Cp. autoclave, chlave, clathrate, claustral,

clava, davate, clavelization, davide, davier,

claviform, clavis, cleido-, cleisto-, cieithral,

clove, 'a former weight', cloy, coaclave,

sloal, slot, 'bolt', subclavian. Cp. also lot.

close,п., enclosure, space. — OF. (= ¥.)clos,
'enclosure', pp. used as a noun. See next word.

## close
close, п., completion. — Fr. prec. word.

## closet
closet, n. — OF., dimin. of clos, 'enclosure'. See
close, 'enclosure', and -et.
Derivatives: closet, tr. v., closet-ed, adj.

## Clostridium
Clostridium, п., a genus of bacteria (bacteriol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idium, fr. Gk. κλωσ-
τήρ, 'thread, spindle', fr. κλώθειν, 'to spin'.
See Ciotho.

## closure
closure, n. — OF., fr. L. clausura (whence also
It. chiusura), fr. clausus, pp. of claudere, 'to
shut'. See dose, adj., and -ure. F. cloture,
'closure', has been refashioned fr. OF. closure on
analogy of nouns ending in -lure. Cp. cloture.
Derivative: closure, tr. and intr. v.

## clot
clot, n. — ME., fr. OE. clott, clot, 'lump', rel.
to MHG. kloz, klotzes, G. Klotz, 'lump', block',
and to ME. dele, elite, 'wedge'. See cleat and
cp. clod. Cp. also dout, cluster, clutter.
Derivatives: clot, tr. and intr. v., cloll-ed, clott-
y, adjs.

## clote
clote, п., the burdock. — ME., fr. OE. elate, rel.
to OS. cledthe, OHG. cletha, cletto, delta,
MHG., G. klette, fr. Teut. base *kleip-,
corresponding to I.-E. base 'gleil-, -/-enlargement
of *glei-, 'to cleave, stick to', whence L. gluten,
'glue'. See clay, and cp. glne, gluten.

## doth
doth, n. — ME., fr. OE. clap, 'cloth', rel. to
OFris. klath, MDu. cleet, Du. kleed, MHG. kleil,
G. Kleid, 'garment' (ON. klxdi is possibly
borrowed fr. OE. сШр, a collateral form of clap).
These words prob. stand in gradational
relationship to OE. clidan, 'to adhere to', clida, 'plaster',
elide, 'bur'. See glne.
Derivatives: clothes, n. pi., cloth-ier, п., cloth-y,
adj.

## clothe
clothe, tr. v. — ME. clothen, clathen, fr. OE.
cladian, 'to clothe', fr.c/a/>,'cloth'.Seeprec. word.
Derivative: cloth-ing, adj. and n.

## Ciothilda
Ciothilda, Clothilde, fem. PN. — F. Clotilde, fr.
G. Klothilde, a compound lit. meaning 'famous
in battle', fr. OHG. *klod, 'famous', and hildl,
'battle'. For the first element cp. OHG. hint,
OE. hlud, 'loud', and see loud. For the second
element see Hilda.

## Ciotho
Ciotho, п., one of the Fates in Greek
mythology. — L. Ciotho, fr. Gk. Κλωθώ, lit. 'the
spinner', fr. κλώθειν, 'to spin', which is prob. rel. to
κάλαθος, 'basket'. See calathus and cp.
Clostridium.

## cloture
cloture, п., closure of a debate in parliament. —
F. cloture, 'closing, close, cloture*. See closure.
Derivative: cloture, tr. and intr. v.

clou, п., object of chief attraction. — F., 'nail;

chief attraction', fr. L. clavus, 'nail', which is
rel. to clOvis, 'key'. Cp. It. chiodo, chiovo, OProv-
enc., Glial, clau, Sp. clavo, Port, cravo, 'nail',
which all derive fr. L. clavus. See clavide and

cp. clove, 'spice', clove, 'a former weight', cloy.

cloud, n. — ME. clud, cloud, 'rock, cloud', fr. OE.

clud, 'mass of rock, rock', which meant orig.

cloud-less-ness, п., cloud-y, adj., cloud-i-ly, adv.,

G. Klinge, 'clough'; prob. of imitative origin.

dout, п., a patch. — ME., fr. OE. clut, 'piece of

cloth or metal, patch', rel. to ON. klutr,

and to OE. clou, clot, 'lump'. See dot.

clout, tr. v., to patch, mend. — ME. clouten, fr.

OE. clutian, 'to patch', fr. clut, 'a patch'. See

## clout
clout, п., a stupid person. — ME. clute, fr. Du.

kluit, 'clod'. See dout, 'a patch'.

## clove
clove, п., a spice. — ME. claw, fr. MF. (= F.)

## clou
clou, short for clou de girofte, lit. 'nail of clove';
so called from its resemblance to a nail. F. clou

## dove
dove, n„ a small bulb of garlic, etc. — OE. с/и/и,
rel. to OS. cluf- in clufloc, MLG. klof-, in klof-
iok, MDu. clof-, cluf- in cloflooc, cluflooc
(whence, with dissimilation, Du. knoflook),

## clove
clove, п., a former weight. — AF. clou, fr. Anglo-
L. clavus, name of a weight, fr. L. clavus, 'nail'.

## clove
clove, past tense of cleave, 'to divide'. — Formed
on analogy of cloven. See cleave, 'to divide'.

## clove
clove, past tense of cleave, 'to stick'. — Formed
on analogy of prec. word. See cleave, 'to stick'.

## cloven
cloven, adj. — ME. cloven, fr. OE. clofen,
'divided', pp. of cleofan. See cleave, 'to divide'.

## clover
clover, n. — ME. claver, clover, fr. OE. clafre,
clMfre, rel. to MLG. klever, MDu. claver, Du.
klaver, OS. kli, OHG. kleo, MHG. Ш, G.
Klee, 'clover', and prob. also to OE. cleofian,
'to stick, adhere' (see clenve, 'to stick'), so that
clover lit. means 'the plant with the sticky
sap'.
Derivative: clover-ed, adj.

## clown
clown, n. — Of uncertain origin. Perh. rel. to
Icel. klurmi, 'a clumsy, boorish fellow', North
Fris. kldnne, 'clown', Du. kloen, 'hoyden', dial.
Swed. kluns, 'a hard knob; a clumsy fellow',
klunn, "log', Dan. klunt, 'log, block', and to
Dan., Swed. klump, 'lump'. See dump.
Derivatives: clown, intr. v., clown-ade, п., down-
age, п., clown-ery, п., clown-ish, adj., clown-ish-
ly, adv., clown-ish-ness, n.

## cloy
cloy, tr. v., to satiate; to surfeit; to weary with
excess. — Aphetic for obsol. accloy, which is
formed (with change of prefix) fr. F. enclouer,
'to prick (horses) in shoeing, to spike (a gun)',
lit. 'to nail up', fr. en, 'in' (see 1st en-) and clou,
'nail', fr. L. clavus. See clou and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: cloy-er, п., cloy-ing, adj., cloy-ing-
ly, adv., cloy-ing-ness, n.

## dub
dub, n. — ME. clubba, fr. ON. klubba, klumba,
'a thick stick, ciub'. See clump and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: club, tr. and intr. v., clubb-able,
adj. (a hybrid), clubb-ed, adj., clubb-er, п., clubb-
ish, clubb-y, adjs.

## clock
clock, intr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp. OE.
cloccian, Dan. klukke, Du. klokken, MHG.
klucken, MHG., G. glucken, Gk. κλώζειν,
χλώσσειν, L. glocire, 'to cluck', which all are
imitative. Cp. also clutch, 'brood'.
Derivative: cluck, n.

## clue
clue, n. — The same word as clew.

## clumber spaniel
clumber spaniel, clumber, n. — Named after one
of the estates of the 1st Duke of Newcastle.

## dump
dump, п., a heap, mass. — MLG. klumpe, klom-
pe, 'clog, wooden shoe', prop, 'shoe formed
from a lump of wood', rel. to LG. klump
(whence G. Klumpe, Klumpen), 'clump, lump',
MDu. clampe, 'lump, mass', Du. klomp, 'lump;
wooden shoe', Dan., Swed. klump, 'lump', OE.
clympre, 'lump of metal, metal', and to ON.
klumba, klubba, 'a thick stick, club'. See clamp
'device for fastening', and cp. clnb. Cp. also
chinch. Cp. also clown.
Derivatives: clump, intr. and tr. v., clump-y, adj.

## clumsy
clumsy, adj. — ME. clumsed, pp. of clumsen, 'to
benumb', rel. to dial. Swed. klummsen,
'benumbed with cold', OE. be-clemman, 'to bind,
enclose, fetter', and to E. clamp, 'a device for
fastening (q.v.). For the insertion of s before the
suff. -y cp. flimsy.
Derivatives: clumsi-ly, adv., clumsi-ness, n.

## chinch
chinch, п., a kind of limestone. — Cp. Du. klont,
klomp, of s.m., 'lump', and see dump. For the
connection between clump and clunch cp. bump
and bunch, hump and hunch, lump and lunch.

## dung
dung, past tense and pp. of cling. — ME. pp.
clungeiri), fr. OE. clungen, fr. clingan, 'to shrivel,
contract'. See ding.

Chrniac, п., a monk of the order of Benedictines

## Ciupea
Ciupea, п., the genus of herrings (ichthyol.) —
L. ciupea, 'a kind of very small river fish', of
uncertain origin; possibly rel. to clupeus, a
collateral form of clipeus, 'a round shield'. See
clipeus.

## Clupeidae
Clupeidae, n. pi., a family of fishes, the herrings,
sardines, etc. (ichthyol.) — ModL., formed with
suff. -idae, fr. Ciupen.

## duster
duster, n. — OE. cluster, clyster, prob. rel. to OE.

Derivatives: cluster, intr. v., cluster-ed, adj.,

## dutch
dutch, tr. and intr. v., to seize with the hands. —

cling (q.v.)

## dutch
dutch, п., claw, grip, grasp. — ME. clucche, fr.
clucchen. See prec. word.

## clutch
clutch, п., a brood. — Fr. earlier cletch, fr. ON.
klekja, which is prob. of imitative origin. Cp.
cluck,

## clnrter
clnrter, п., confusion, disorder; intr. v., to run
in disorder; tr. v., to put into disorder, to litter;
— A var. of obsol. clatter, freq. of the verb clot.
See clot and freq. suff. -er.
Derivative: clutter-er, n.

## Clydesdale
Clydesdale, п., a heavy breed of cart horse. —
Named fr. Clydesdale, the valley of the River
Clyde in Scotland.

## Clydesdale terrier
Clydesdale terrier, a breed of Scotch terrier. —
See prec. word.

## clyer
clyer, п., a scrofulous tumor, a wen. — Du. klier,
'gland, scrofula'.

## Clypeaster
Clypeaster, п., a genus of sea urchins (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. L. clypeus, 'a round shield',
and aster, 'star'. See clipeus and Aster,

## clypeate
clypeate, adj., shaped like a round shield. — L.
clypeatus, pp. of clypeare, 'to provide with a
round shield', fr. clypeus. See clipeus and adj.
suff. -ate.

## clypeus
clypeus, n. — See clipeus.

## clysis
clysis, п., a washing out by a clyster (med.) —
Gk. κλύσις, fr. κλύζειν, 'to wash away, to drench
with a clyster', which is cogn. with OL. cluere,
'to purge', L. cloaca, 'sewer, drain*. See cloaca,

## clysma
clysma, п., an enema (med.) — Gk. κλύσμα,
'liquid used for washing out', fr. κλύζειν. See
prec. word and cp. cataclysm.

## clysmic
clysmic, adj., washing, cleansing. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. κλυσμός, 'liquid used for
washing out', fr. κλύζειν. See clysis.

## ciyster
ciyster, п., an enema. — F. clystire, fr. L. clyster,
fr. Gk. κλυστήρ, 'clyster pipe, syringe', fr.
κλύζειν. See clysis and cp. cataclysm.
Derivatives: clyster, tr. v., clyster-ize, tr. v.

## Ciytemaestra
Ciytemaestra, Ciytaemnestra, п., the wife of
Agamemnon. With the aid of her lover Aegisthus
she murdered her husband on his return from
Troy (Greek mythol.) — L. Ciytaemnestra, fr.
Gk. Κλυταιμνήστρα, a word compounded of
κλυτός, 'heard of, celebrated', and μνηστήρ,
'willing to mind; mindful of; wooer, suitor',
which is rel. to μνασθαι, 'to remember', μνησις,
'memory, remembrance'. For the first element

sic, mnestic.

## Cnicus
Cnicus, п., a genus of plants of the thistle family

κνηκος, 'safflower', whence Gk. κνηκός, Dor.
κνάκάς, 'pale, yellow, tawny'; cogn. with OE.
hunig, 'honey'. See hoaey.

## cnida
cnida, п., a nematocyst (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
κνίδη, 'nettle', from the stem of κνίζείν, 'to
scratch, scrape', rel. to Homeric Gk. κνίση,
Att. κνίσα, 'smell of a burnt sacrifice, steam,
savor', and cogn. with L. nidor (for *cnldos),
'smell of burnt things, savor'. See nidor.

coacervate, tr. v., to heap up (obsol.) — L. co-

acervatus, pp. of coacervare, 'to heap together.

coacervation, n. — L. coacervatio, gen. -dnis, 'a

See prec. word and -ion.

## coach
coach, n. — F. coche, fr. G. Kutsche, fr.
Hungarian kocsi, short for orig. kocsi szekir,

Derivatives: coach, tr. and intr. v., coach-ee, п.,

## coact
coact, tr. v., to force, compel (obsol.) — L. code-

Derivatives: coaction (q.v.), coact-ive, adj.

and act

coadjutor, n. — OF. coadjuteur, fr. L. coadju-
tdrem, ace. of coadjutor, fr. со- and adjutor,

'to help, assist'. See aid and cp. adjutant,

## coadunate
coadunate, tr. v., to unite. — Late L. coadunatus,
pp. of coadunare, 'to unite', fr. со- and L. ad-
unare, 'to make one, unite', which is formed fr.

## coadunate
coadunate, adj., united. — Late L. coadunatus,
pp. of coadunare. See condanate, v.

## coadunation
coadunation, п., union. — Late L. coadunatid,
gen. -dnis, fr. coadunatus, pp. of coadunare. See

## coagulate
coagulate, intr. and tr. v., to curdle. — L. coagu-
latus, pp. of coaguldre, fr. coBgulum, 'means of
coagulation', fr. *co-agere, 'to drive or press

-ate. For sense development cp. curd. Cp. quail,
'to lose heart'.

## coagnlntion
coagnlntion, n. — L. codgul&tid, gen. -dnis, fr.
coagulatiO, gen. -dnis, fr. coagulatus, pp. of
coagulare. See prec. word and -ion.

## coaita
coaita, п., the spider monkey. — A Tupi name.

## coal
coal, n. — ME. cole, fr. OE. col, rel. to ΟΝ.,
Norw., Swed. kol, Dan. kul, OFris., MDu. kole,
Du. kool, OHG. koto, kol, MHG. kol, G. Kohle,
'coal', and cogn. with Olr. glial, 'coal'. Cp.

Derivatives: coal, tr. and intr. v., coal-er, п.,
coal-ing, п., coal-y, adj.

## coalesce
coalesce, intr. v., to grow together, unite. — L.
coalescere, 'to grow together, unite', fr. co-
and alescere, 'to grow up', inchoative of alere,
'to nourish'. See aliment and cp. adolescent.
Derivatives: coalesc-ence, n.,'coalescent (q.v.)

## coalescence
coalescence, n. — Formed with suff. -ce, fr. L.
coalescens, gen. -entis. See next word.

## coalescent
coalescent, adj. — L. coalescens, gen. -entis, pres.

## coalite
coalite, intr. and tr. v., to unite (obsol.) — L. co-
alitus, pp. of coalescere. See coalesce and next

Derivatives: coalition-al, adj., coalition-ist, n.

## coalmouse
coalmouse, п., the European titmouse. — OE.

## conmlng
conmlng, п., a raised edge around an opening. —
Of uncertain origin.

## Coan
Coan, adj., of, or pertaining to the island of Cos.
— Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Cos, fr. Gk. Κως,

Derivative: Coan, n.

## coarctation
coarctation, п., tightening of the aorta, an
orifice, etc. (med.) — L. coarctdlid, gen. -dnis, 'a
crowding or pressing together*, fr. coarctdtus,
a collateral form of coartatus, pp. of coarctdre,
resp. coartare, 'to crowd or press together',
fr. со- and arclSre, artdre, 'to press together',

related to ars, gen. artis, 'art', arma, 'armor';

is due to folk etymology, which associated this
word with L. arcere, 'to hold off, keep off'.

## coarse
coarse, adj. — Earlier also course, of uncertain
origin; possibly adjectival use of the noun
course in the term 'of course', taken in the sense
of 'common, ordinary, rude'.
Derivatives: coarse-ly, adv., coars-en, tr. and
intr. v., coarse-ness, n.

## coast
coast, n. — ME. cost, fr. OF. coste (F. cote),

with OSlav. kosti, 'bone'. Cp. Rum. coastu. It.,
OProvenc. costa, 'rib, coast', Sp. cuesta, 'hill,
mount, slope', costilla, 'rib', which all derive
fr. L. costa. Cp. accost, costal, costalgia,
costard, costermonger, costrel, cuesta, cutlet,
intercostal.
Derivative: coastal (q.v.)

## coast
coast, intr. and tr. v. — ME. costeyen, costien,
fr. OF. costeier, costoier (F. cotoyer), fr. OF.
coste (F. cote), 'coast'. See coast, n.
Derivatives: coast-er, п., coast-ing, n.

## coastal
coastal, adj., pertaining to, or bordering on, a
coast. — A hybrid formed fr. E. coast with -al,
a suff. of Latin origin. The proper form is costal
(fr. L. costa), which, however, is used only in
the sense 'pertaining to a rib or ribs'.

## coat
coat, n. — ME. cote, fr. OF. cote (F. cotte).
'coat, petticoat', fr. Frankish *kotta, which is
rel. to OHG. chozza, chozzo, MHG., G. kotze,

OProvenc., Sp., Port, corn, It. cotta, 'coat', ML.
cotta, 'cowl', areTeut. loan words. Cp. cotillion,
cotise, cotta, and the second element in hausse-
col.
Derivatives: coat, tr. v., coai-ed, adj., coatee
(q.v.), coat-ing, n.

## coatee
coatee, п., a short coat. — Formed fr. coat with

## coati
coati, п., a small Brazilian raccoon. — Port., fr.
Tupi coati, which is compounded of cua,
'cincture, belt', and tim, 'nose'.

## coax
coax, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. earlier cokes, 'a fool,
dupe', which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: coax, п., coax-er, п., coax-ing, п..
coax-y, adj.

## coaxal
coaxal, coaxial, adj., having a common axis
(math.) — Formed fr. со-, axis and adj. suff. -al.

## cob
cob, п., a heap, lump. — Prob. rel. to cub. Cp.

Derivative: cobb-y, adj.

## cob
cob, п., a gull. — Rel. to Du. kobbe, of uncertain
origin; possibly orig. denoting a plump,
roundish bird and rel. to cob, 'heap, lump'.

## cob
cob, п., a spider (rare). — See cobweb.

## cobalt
cobalt, п., a silver-white metallic element (chem.)

malicious sprite', and Gk. καβάλος, 'rogue,
knave; an evil spirit'. See kobold and goblin.
For sense development cp. nickel and wolfram.
Derivative: cobalt-ic, adj.

## cobble
cobble, п., a rounded stone. — Formed with suff.
-le fr. cob, 'heap, lump'.
Derivatives: cobble, tr. v., to pave with cobbles,
cobbl-ing, п., cobbl-y, adj.

## cobble
cobble, tr. v., to patch. — Of uncertain origin.
Perhaps rel. to cob, 'heap, lump', hence
derivatively identical with cobble, 'to pave with
rounded stones' (see prec. word).
Derivatives: cobbl-er, п., cobbl-ing, n.

## Cobdenism
Cobdenism, п., the doctrine of the English
economist Richard Cobden (1804-65). — For the
ending see suff. -ism.

## Cobdenite
Cobdenite, п., an adherent of Cobdenism. — See
prec. word and subst. suff. -ite.

## coble
coble, п., a kind of fishing boat. — Bret, canbal.
fr. L. caupulus, 'a kind of small ship', which is
of uncertain origin.

## cobnut
cobnut, n. — L. 'nut in heaps or clusters',
compounded of cob, 'heap, lump', and nut.

## cobra
cobra, п., a poisonous snake of Asia and Africa.
— Port, cobra de capello, 'serpent with a hood'
(so called because it expands its neck so as to
resemble a hood). Cobra derives fr. VL. *colo-
bra (whence also F. couleuvre, 'adder'), formed
with vowel assimilation fr. L. colubra, 'female

## coca
coca, п., a South American plant. — Sp., fr.
Peruvian coca. Cp. cocaine.
Coca Cola. — A trade name; so called in allusion

## cocaine
cocaine, cocain, п., a drug obtained from coca
leaves, used as a local anesthetic. — A hybrid
coined by Niemann in 1859 fr. coca and chem.
suff. -ine, resp. -in, which is of Latin origin.

## cocainize

A double hybrid coined fr. cocaine and -tee. a

## cocco-
cocco-, before a vowel cocc-, combining form
meaning 'berry, seed'. — Gk. κόκκο-, κοκκ-,

## coccoid
coccoid, adj., resembling a coccus (bacteriol.) —
Compounded of cocc- and Gk. -οεώής, 'like',

## Cocculus
Cocculus, п., a genus of plants of the family
Menispermaceae (hot.) — ModL., dimin. of

## coccns
coccns, п., ι) one of the carpels of a dry fruit
(hot.); 2) a spherical cell (bacteriol.) — ModL.,

berry', which is prob. a foreign word. Cp. the
second element in gonococcus and in Chiococca.
Cp. also cocoon. Cp. also scotch, 'to make an
incision'. The word coccus was introduced into
bacteriology by the German surgeon Albert
Christian Theodor Billroth (1829-94).

## Coccus
Coccus, п., a genus of insects of the family Coc-
cidae. — See prec. word.

coccyg-, form of coccygo- before a vowel,

## coccygo-
coccygo-, before a vowel coccyg-, combining form
denoting the coccyx (med.) — Fr. Gk. κοκκυξ,
gen. κόκκΰγος. See next word.

## coccyx
coccyx, п., the end of the vertebral column in
man and in some apes; the rudiment of a tail
(anal.) — Gk. κοκκυξ, gen. κόκκΰγος, 'cuckoo;

was so called from its supposed resemblance to

## Cochin
Cochin, п., a breed of large domestic fowl. —
Named fr. Cochin China.

## cochineal
cochineal, п., a scarlet dye. — Fr. F. cachenille,

Both Sp. cochina and F. cochon prob. are of

## cochlen
cochlen, п., the spiral part of the inner ear (anat.)

with a spiral shell', fr. κόχλος, 'shellfish with a
spiral shell', which is rel. to Gk. κόγχος, 'shell*.
See conch and cp. cockle, 'bivalve'.
Derivative: cochle-ar, adj.

## cochleare
cochleare, п., a spoonful (med.) — L., 'a spoon,
whose pointed end was used to extract snails
from the shell', dissimilated fr. 'cocleale, fr.
coclea, cochlea, 'snail', fr. Gk. κοχλίίς. See cochien.

## cochleate
cochleate, adj., shaped like a snail shell. —
Formed fr. cochlea with adj. suff. -ate.

## cochleated
cochleated, adj., cochleate. — See prec. word
and -ed.

## cock
cock, п., the male of the domestic fowl. — ME.

• сок, fr. OE. cocc, сое, кок, imitative of the cry
of the bird. Cp. ON. kokr. Late L. coccus, OF.

kutdh, 'cock', which all are imitative. Cp. also
chicken, cockade, cockney, coquet, coquette,

Derivatives: cock, tr. v., cock, п., the act of

## cock
cock, п., a small pile of hay. — ME. cokke. Cp.
Dan. kok, 'pile of hay', ON. кбккг, 'lump, ball".

## cock
cock, п., a cockboat. — See cockbout.

## cockade
cockade, n. — F. cocarde, fr. OF. coquarl, co-
guard, 'vain', fr. coq, 'cock'. See cock, 'the male
of the domestic fowl'. In English the word was
assimilated in form to the numerous nouns
ending in -ade.
Derivative: cockad-ed, adj.

## cock-a-doodle-doo
cock-a-doodle-doo, n. — Childish imitation of
the cry of a cock.

## Cockaigne
Cockaigne, п., an imaginary land .of luxury. —
ME. cocaygne, fr. OF. quoquaigne (F. cocagne)
in pais de quoquaigne (F. pays de cocagne), 'land
of plenty', which is prob. a Teut. loan word and
lit. means 'land of cake'. See cake and cp. It.
cuccagna, Sp. cucana, Port, cucanha, which are
of the same origin and meaning, as OF.

## cockalorum
cockalorum, п., a conceited little man. — Formed

## cockatoo
cockatoo, п., a large parrot of Australia. — Du.

contraction of kakak luwa, 'old sister'. See Yule-
Burnell, Hobson Jobson, p. 227. For sense
development ср. Е. poll, 'parrot', fr. the PN. Poll,
a shortened form of Polly, 'Mary' (see Polly).

## cockatrice
cockatrice, п., a fabulous serpent. — ME. coca-
tryse, cocatrice, fr. OF. cocatris (F. cocalrix),
'a fabulous serpent', fr. Late L. calcalrix,
'treader, tracker', fr. calcare, 'to tread'; see
calk, 'to stop with oaKum'. OF. cotalris was
influenced in form by OF. coc, 'cock'. Late L.
calcairix is a loan translation of Gk. Εχνεύμων,
'ichneumon', lit. 'tracker', fr. Ιχνος, 'track'.

## cockboat
cockboat, п., a small boat, esp. one used as a
tender. — ME. cokbote, fr. сок, 'cockboat', and
bote, 'boat'. The first element derives fr. OF.
coque, cogue (F. coche), 'a kind of boat', fr. Late
L. caudica, 'a kind of boat', lit. 'a boat made
from the trunk of a tree', fr. L. caudex, gen.
caudicis, 'trunk of a tree'. See caudex. OF. coque,
cogue, were influenced in form by MDu. cogghe.
Cp. coxswain. Cp. also cog, 'a small fishing boat'.
For the second element in ME. cokbote see boat.

## cockchafer
cockchafer, n. — Compounded of cock, the bird,
and chafer; so called from its large size.

## cocker
cocker, tr. v., to pamper. — Formed with suff.
-er fr. obsol. cock, 'to make a nestle cock of.
See cock, the bird. For sense development cp.
OF. coqueliner, 'to pamper', fr. coq, 'cock'.

## cocker
cocker, п., quiver (obsol.) — ME. coker, 'quiver,
boot', fr. OE. cocur, cocer, rel. to ODu. cocar,
MDu. coker, Du. koker, OHG. kochar, kochari,
MHG. kocher, kochere, G. Kocher, 'quiver'.
These Teut. words are connected with ML. cu-
curum, MGk. κούκουρον, whence Russ. kukor,
'cartridge box'. Cp. quiver, 'a case for arrows'.

## cocker
cocker, п., also cocker spaniel. — Formed fr.
cock, the bird; so called because originally used
for hunting woodcocir.

## cockerel
cockerel, п., a young cock. — Dimin. of cock,
the bird. For the suff. cp. dotterel (fr. dote),
pickerel (fr. pike):

## cocket
cocket, seal of the king's customhouse. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: cocket, tr. v.

## cockle
cockle, п., the corn cockle. — ME. cokel, cokille,
fr. OE. coccel, 'corn cockle, darnel; tares'; of
uncertain origin.

## cockle
cockle, п., a stove. — Du. kachel, short for kachel-
oven, fr. MHG. kacheloven (whence also G.
Kachelofen), 'stove of Dutch tiles', fr. VL. *cac-
culus, 'an earthen pot for cooking', a collateral
form of L. caccabus, fr. Gk. κάκκαβος, κακκάβη,
'a three-legged pot', which is of Sem. origin;
cp. Akkad. kukubu, 'a pot'. — Cp. cachucha.

## cockle
cockle, п., bivalve mollusk of the genus Cardium.
— ME. cokel, fr. OF. (= F.) coquille, 'shell', fr.
VL. *conchilia, neut. pi. taken for fern, sing-,

fir. L. conchylium, fr. Gk. κογχύλιον, dimin. of
κογχύλη, 'shell', fr. κόγχη, 'shell'. See conch and
cp. cochlea, cochleare, coquma, and the second
element in caracole.

## cockle
cockle, intr. v., to wrinkle, pucker; tr. v., to саше
to wrinkle or pucker. — F. coquiller, 'to swell,
form blisters', fr. coquille, 'shell'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: cockle, п., a wrinkle, pucker, cockl-
У, adj.

## cockney
cockney, п., ι) a native of the East End of
London ; 2) a resident of London; 3) his
pronunciation. — ME. cockeney, prob. from a NF.
dial, form of OF. acoquine (F. acoquine),
'greatly attached to', pp. of acoquiner, 'to make
fond of', formed fr. a, 'to' (see a), and coquiner,
'to play the knave', fr. coquin, 'knave, rascal,
rogue', which prob. derives fr. coq, 'cock' (cp.
F. coquard,'ridiculous old beau', and other
derivatives of coq with a depreciatory sense). See

Derivatives: cockney-dom, п., cockney-ism, n.
cockroach n. — Alteration of Sp. cucaracha,
'wood louse', fr. сисо, 'a sort of caterpillar;
cuckoo', possibly derived fr. L. cucus, 'daw',
which is of imitalive origin. Cp. Gk. κόκκυξ,
L. cuculus, 'cuckoo', and see cuckoo. The change
of Sp. cucaracha to E. cockroach is due to a folk-
etymological association with E. cock and roach.

## cockscomb
cockscomb, n. — Lit. 'the comb of a cock'. See
cock and comb and cp. coxcomb.
Derivative: cockscomb-ed, adj.

## cocky
cocky, adj., conceited. — Formed with adj. sun".
-y fr. cock, the bird. Cp. coxy.
Derivatives: cock-i-ly, adv., cock-i-ness, n.

## coco
coco, cocoa, п., palm tree. — Fr. Port, coco,
'grimace', so called from the monkeylike face at
the base of the nut. Cp. coqnito.

## cocoa
cocoa, n. — Sp. cacas. See cacao.

## cocoon
cocoon, п., the silky case spun by the larvae of
certain insects. — F. cocon, fr. Proven?, cou-
coun, 'shell of eggs; cocoon', fr. L. coccum,
'excrescence on a plant; kernel, berry', whence also
F. coque, 'shell of eggs'. L. coccum is a loan
word fr. Gk. κόκκος, 'grain of the kermes,
kernel, berry'. See coccus.

## coction
coction, п., a cooking, boiling. — L. coelio, gen.
