## Cocytus
Cocytus, п., one of the five rivers of Hades (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Κωκϋτός, 'the River of
Lamentation', fr. κωκϋτός, 'lamentation', fr.
κωκδειν, 'to cry, lament', dissimilated fr. *κϋ-
κυειν, and rel. to καύαξ, Homeric Gk. κήξ,
κηϋξ, 'a sea bird'. Cp. OI. kduli, 'shouts', kokah,
'goose', Arm. k'uk', 'sighing, groaning'. All these
words are of imitative origin.

## cod
cod, п., a large sea fish. — ME. cod, prob. fr.
cod, 'bag' (see next word), and orig. meaning
'bag fish'. Cp. cuttlefish.

## cod
cod, п., a small bag; a pillow. — ME., fr. OE.
codd, 'bag, shell, husk', rel. to ON. koddi,
'pillow', Du. kodde, 'bag', fr. I.-E. base *geu-d-,
*gu-d-, -(/-enlargement of base *geu-, 'to bend,
curve, arch'. See cove and cp. peasecod. Cp. also
coddle, 'to pamper'.

## coda
coda, п., a concluding passage in a musical
composition. — It. coda, fr. L. coda, secondary form
of cauda, 'tail'. See caudal and cp. words there
referred to.

## coddle
coddle, tr. v., to pamper. — Formed with freq.
surf, -le fr. cod, 'pillow'.
Derivative: coddl-er, n.

## coddle
coddle, tr. v., to cook slowly. — Prob. a var.
form of caudle.

## code
code, n. — F., fr. L. codex, later spelling far
caudex, 'the trunk of a tree; a writing tablet;
an account book, a code of laws'. See caudex
and cp. codex.
Derivative: code, tr. v.

## codeine
codeine, п., an alkaloid obtained fr. opium (chem.)
— Formed with chem. sun", -ine fr. Gk. κώδεια,
'poppy head', which is rel. to κωος, 'prison'
(lit. 'a hollow place'), κώδων, 'bell, mouth of
a trumpet, trumpet', κοίλος (for *κόΛλος),
'hollow', fr. I.-E. base *kew-, *кй-, 'vault; to
be hollow; to swell', whence also L. cavus,
'hollow'. See cave, п., and cp. codon.

## codetta
codetta, п., a short coda (mus.) — It., dimin. of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:173 COLUMN:2 -->
coda (q.v.)

## codex
codex, n. — L. See code and cp. codicil.

## codger
codger, n. — A var. of cadger.

## codicil
codicil, п., an addition to a will. — L. codicillus,
'a small writing tablet; an appendix to a will',
dimin. of codex, gen. codicis. See codex.

## codicillary
codicillary, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature
of, a codicil. — Late L. codicillaris, fr. L.
codicillus. See prec. word and adj. sun", -ary.

## codification
codification, n. — See next word and -fication.

## codify
codify, tr. v., to reduce to a code; to
systematize. — Formed fr. code with suff. -fy.
Derivative: codifi-er,n.

## codllle
codllle, п., a term at omber, used when the game
is lost by the challenging player. — Sp. codillo,
lit. 'elbow, bend, knee of quadrupeds', dimin.
of codo, 'elbow, cubit', fr. L. cubitus. See cubit.

## codling
codling, п., a young cod. — Formed fr. cod, 'a
large fish', with the dimin. suff. -ling.

## codling
codling, п., a variety of apple. — ME. querdling,
corruption of F. cotur de lion, 'heart of lion'.
F. caur derives fr. L. cor, de fr. L. de, 'from,
away from', lion fr. L. leonem, ace. of leo, 'lion'
(see cordate, de- and Hon); influenced in form
by E. coddle, 'to cook slowly', and by nouns
ending in -ing.

## codon
codon, п., a small bell, mouth of a trumpet. —
Gk. κώδων, rel. to κώδεια, 'poppy head'. See
codeine and cp. the second element in Poly-
codium.

## codpiece
codpiece, п., formerly, a bag worn in the front of
the breeches. — Compounded of cod, 'bag', and
piece.

## coed
coed, co-ed, п., a female student in a
coeducational college (slang). — Abbreviation of next
word.

## coeducation
coeducation, n. — Formed fr. со- and education.
Derivative: coeducation-al, adj.

## coefficient
coefficient, adj. and n. — Formed fr. со- and
efficient. The term coefficient was introduced
into mathematics by the French mathematician
Francois Viete (Vieta) (1540-1603).

## coehorn
coehorn, п., an obsolete weapon for throwing
shells. — Named after its inventor, the Baron
Menno van Coehoorn (1641-1704).

## coel-
coel-, form of coelo- before a vowel.

## Coeleaterata
Coeleaterata, п., a phylum of invertebrate
animals (zool.) — ModL., lit. '(animals) with empty
intestines', coined by the German zoologist
Rudolf Leuckart (1822-98) fr. Gk. κοίλος,
'hollow', and έντερον, 'intestine'. See coelo-,
enteric, and adj. suff. -ate.

## coelenternte
coelenternte, adj. and n. — See prec. word.

## coelenteric
coelenteric, adj. — See Coelenterata and -ic

## coeli-
coeli-, form of coelio- before a vowel.

## coelin
coelin, п., cavity (anat.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κοιλία,
'cavity in the body'. See next word.

## coeliac
coeliac, celiac, adj., pertaining to the cavity of
the abdomen (anat.) — L. coeliacus, fr. Gk.
κοιλιακός, 'pertaining to the cavity of the body',
fr. κοιλία, 'cavity of the body, abdomen', a
word coined by Aristotle fr. κοίλος, 'hollow'.
See coelo- and cp. coelio-.

## coelio-
coelio-, before a vowel coeli-, also spelled celio-,
celi-, pertaining to the abdomen (anat.) — Gk.
κοιλιο-, κοιλι-, fr. κοιλία, 'abdomen', fr. κοίλος,
'hollow'. See coelia, coelinc, and cp. next word.

## coelo-
coelo-, before a vowel coel-, combining form
meaning 'hollow'. — Gk. κοίλο-, κοιλ-, fr.
κοίλος, 'hollow', which stands for *κόΓιλος and
is cogn. with L. cavus, 'hollow'. See cave, п.,
and cp. coelia, coeliac, coelio-, and the second
element in Odocoileus.

## coelom
coelom, п., the body cavity of Metazoa (zool.) —
Coined by the German biologist Ernst Heinrich
Haeckel (1834-1919) fr. Gk. κοίλωμα, 'a hollow,
cavity', fr. κοίλος, 'hollow'. See coelo-.

## Coelopleunim
Coelopleunim, п., a genus of plants. — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. κοίλος, 'hollow', and πλευ-
ρόν, 'rib'. See coelo- and pleura.

## coen-
coen-, form of coeno- before a vowel.

## coenesthesis
coenesthesis, coenaestbesis, п., organic sensation
(in contradistinction to external sensation, as
hearing, seeing, etc.) (psychol.) — Fr. Gk. κοινή
αίσθησις, 'common sensation'. See coeno- and
esthesis.

## coeno-
coeno-, before a vowel coen-, combining form
meaning 'common'. — Gk. κοινό-, κοιν-, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:173 COLUMN:3 -->
κοινός, 'common, public, general', which prob.
stands for *κομ-ιός, a compound prob. formed
fr. ·κομ-, 'with', which is cogn. with L. com-, cum,
'with' (see com-), and from a derivative of I.-E.
base yo-, 'going' (see itinerate). Accordingly
κοινός lit. means 'that which goes together'.
For the formation of the word cp. Gk. ξΰνός,
of s.m., which stands for *ξυν-ι^ός, fr. ξΰν,
'with', and *-ιος, 'that which goes'. Cp. L.
comes, 'companion', for com-e-s, lit. 'he who
goes with somebody', fr. com-, 'with, together',
and the stem of ire, 'to go'. Cp. epicene.

## coenobite
coenobite, n. — See cenobite.

## coenobium
coenobium, п., a religious community. — Eccles.
L. coenobium, 'a convent', fr. Gk. κοινόβιον,
'life in community, monastery', fr. κοινός,
'common', and βίος, 'life'. For the first element
see coeno-, for the second see bio-. Cp. cenoby.

## coeaosarc
coeaosarc, п., the common soft tissue that unites
the polyps of a compound zoophyte (zool.) —
Compounded of coeao- and Gk. σαρξ, gen.
σαρκός, 'flesh'. See sarco-.

## coenurus
coenurus, п., the larva of a tapeworm (Taenia coe-
nurus). — ModL., compounded of coen- and
Gk. ουρά, 'tail'. See uro-, 'tail-'.

## coequal
coequal, adj. — Formed fr. со- and equal. Cp.
L. coaequSlis, 'of equal age, equal'.
Derivatives: coequal, intr. and· tr. v., coequal-
ity, п., coequal-ly, adv., coequal-ness, n.

## coequate
coequate, tr. v. — L. coaequatus, pp. of coaequare,
'to make equal to (something else)', fr. со- and
aequare, 'to make equal'. See equate and cp.
adequate.
Derivatives: coequat-ed, adj., coequat-ion, n.

## coerce
coerce, to force, constrain. — L. coercere, 'to shut
up together, confine, restrain, limit', fr. co-
and arcere, 'to shut up, enclose, hold', fr. area,
'chest, box'; see ark and cp. exercise. For the
change of Latin a (in arcere) to £ (in co-irclre)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: coerc-er, п., coerc-ible, adj., coerc-
ibil-ity, п., coerc-ible-ness, п., coerc-ibl-y, adv.,
coercion (q.v.)

## coercion
coercion, п., a coercing. — MF. (= F), fr. L.
coerctio, coercid, shortened fr. coercitio, fr.
coercitus, pp. of coercere; partly through the
medium of OF. cohercion (F. coercion), a form
less frequently used than OF. (= F.) coercition,
which derives fr. L. coercitionem, ace. of coer-
citio. See coerce and -ion.
Derivatives: coercion-ary, adj., coercion-ist, n.

## coessenrial
coessenrial, adj., having one essence. — Formed
fr. со- and essential.
Derivatives: coessential-ily, п., coessential-ly,
adv., coessential-ness, n.

## coetaneous
coetaneous, adj., having the same age. — Late L.
coaetaneus, formed fr. pref. со-, L. aetds, 'age',
and suff. -dneus. See со-, age and -aneous.

## coeternal
coeternal, adj., equally eternal. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. Eccles. L. coaeternus, fr. со- and
L. aeternus, 'eternal'. See eternal.
Derivative: coeternal-ly, adv.

## coetus
coetus, п., an ecclesiastical meeting. — L., fr.
coitus, 'coming together, assembly', fr. coitus,
pp. of coire, 'to come together'. See coition,
coitas.

## coeval
coeval, adj., having the same age. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. Late L. coaevus, fr. со- and
L. aevum, 'age'. See aeon and cp. the second
element in longevity, primeval.
Derivatives: coeval-ity, п., coeval-ly, adv.

## coexist
coexist, intr. v. — Formed fr. со- and exist.
Derivatives: coexist-ent, adj., coexist-ence,
coexist-ency, n.

## coffee
coffee, n. — It. caffe, fr. Turk, qahve, fr. Arab.
qahwa", 'wine; coffee', fr. Kaffa, Kafa, a district
in the southwestern part of Ethiopia. Arab.
qa/iwa* orig. meant 'the plant or drink coming
from Kaffa'. In Kaffa itself the coffee is called
bund and the Arabs borrowed this word in the
form bunn, naming by it the raw coffee. Cp.
cafe, caffeine.

## coffer
coffer, n. — ME. cofre, cofer, fr. OF. cofre (F.
coffre), fr. L. cophinus. See next word.
Derivatives: coffer, tr. v., coffer-er, п.,
coffering, n.

## coffin
coffin, n. — ME., fr. OF. cofin, fr. L. cophinus
(whence also It. cofano, Sp. cuebano, cuevano,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:174 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 147 | COLO-SHORT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:174 COLUMN:1 -->
'basket'), fr. Gk. κάφινος, 'basket', a word of
foreign origin.
Derivative: coffin, tr. v.

## raffle
raffle, п., a slave caravan. — Arab. qdfilah,
'caravan'.

## coffret
coffret, п., a little coffer. — F., formed with di-
min. stiff, -et fr. F. coffre. See coffer.

## cog
cog, п., tooth on a wheel. — Of Scand. origin.
Cp. Swed. kugge, Norw. kug, 'cog', and see
cudgel.
Derivatives: cog, tr. v., cogg-ed, adj., cogg-er, п.,
cogg-ing, n.

## cog
cog, tr. and intr. v., to cheat. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: cogg-ed, adj.

## cog
cog, п., a small fishing boat. — OF. cogue, a
collateral form of coque, 'a kind of boat'. See
cockboat.

## cogency
cogency, n. — Formed fr. next word with suff. -cy.

## cogent
cogent, adj., forcible; convincing. — L. cogens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of cogere, 'to drive
together; to compel', fr. со- and agere, 'to set in
motion, drive, lead'. See agent and cp. cache,
coact, squat.
Derivative: cogent-ly, adv.

## cogitable
cogitable, adj., thinkable. — L. cogitabilis,
'conceivable, imaginable, thinkable', fr. cogitare, 'to
ponder, weigh, reflect, think'. See next word
and -able.

## cogitate
cogitate, intr. v., to think; to ponder. — L. cdgi-
tatus, pp. of cogitare, 'to ponder, weigh,
reflect, think', fr. со- and agitare, 'to put in
constant motion, drive, impel', freq. of agere, 'to
set in motion, drive, lead'. See agitate and cp.
excogitate.

## cogitatioa
cogitatioa, n. — F., fr. L. cogitationem, ace. of
cogitatio, 'thinking, considering, meditation,
resolution', fr. cogitdtus, pp. of cogitare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## cogitative
cogitative, adj., pertaining to thinking;
meditative. — F. cogitatif (fem. cogitative), fr. ML.
cogitativus, fr. L. cogit&tus, pp. of cogitare. See
cogitate and -ive.
Derivatives: cogitative-ly,adv.,cogitative-ness,n.

## cognac
cognac, п., French brandy. — Prop, brandy made
from wine produced at Cognac, Department of
Charente, in France.

## cognate
cognate, adj. — L. cogndtus, 'related by blood,
kindred', fr. со- and OL. gnat us, L. natus, 'born',
pp. of nasci, 'to be born'. See natal and adj.
suff. -ate and cp. connate.
Derivative: cognate, n.

## cognation
cognation, n. — L. cognatio, -onis, 'relationship,
connection', fr. cognatus. See prec. word and
-ion.

## cognition
cognition, п., knowledge; perception. — L. co-
gnitio, gen. -onis, 'a becoming acquainted with,
acquiring knowledge, knowledge, conception,
notion', fr. cognitus, pp. ofcognoscere, 'to become
acquainted with, perceive, understand, know',
fr. со- and OL. gnoscere, L. noscere,'to know'. See
can, aux. v., and -ition and cp. quaint, acquaint.
Cp. also cognizance, cognoscente, cognoscible,
cognovit, conaoisseur, incognito.

## cognitive
cognitive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
cognitus, pp. of cognoscere. See prec. word.
Derivative: cognitive-ly, adv.

## cognizable
cognizable, adj., recognizable. — Formed fr.
cognize with suff. -able.
Derivatives: cognizable-ness, п., cognizabl-y, adv.

## cognizance
cognizance, п., knowledge, notice. — ME. coni-
saunce, fr. OF. conoissance (F. connaissance),
'knowledge', fr. conoistre (F. connattre), 'to
know', fr. L. cognoscere; see cognition and
-ance. E. cognizance was refashioned after L.
cognoscentia.

## cognize
cognize, tr. v. — Back formation fr. cognizance.
Derivatives: cogniz-ant, adj., cogniz-er, n.

## cognomen
cognomen, п., the family name of an ancient
Roman. — L. cognomen, 'a Roman family
name, surname', formed fr. nomen on analogy
of cogndscere, 'to know', which derives fr.
noscere, 'to know' (i.e. cognomen stands to nomen,
as cognoscere to noscere). See nomiual and cp.
cognition.

## cognominal
cognominal, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. cognomen, gen. cognominis. See prec. word.

## cognoscente
cognoscente, п., a connoisseur. — It. cognoscente,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:174 COLUMN:2 -->
conoscente, lit. 'one who knows', fr. L. co-
gnoscentem, ace. of cognoscSns, pres. part, of
cognoscere, 'to know'. See cognition and cp.
next word.

## cognoscible
cognoscible, adj., that which can be known or
perceived. — Late L. cogndscibilis,
'recognizable, discernible, knowable', fr. L. cognoscere. See
cognition and -ible.

## cognovit
cognovit, п., a document in which the defendant
acknowledges liability (law). — L. cognovit, 'he
has acknowledged' (short for cognovit actionem,
'he has acknowledged the action'), 3rd pers.
sing, of the perf. of cognoscere. See cognition.

## cogon
cogon, п., a coarse grass, Imperataarundinacea.—
Sp. cogon, from a Philippine native word.

## cohabit
cohabit, intr. v., 1) to live together (archaic);
2) to live together as husband and wife. — Late
L. cohabiture, 'to dwell together', fr. со- and
L. habitare, 'to have frequently, have possession
of, inhabit', freq. of habere (pp. habitus), 'to
have'. See habit.

## cohabitation
cohabitation, n. — Late L. cohabitatid, gen. -onis,
fr. L. cohabitants, pp. of cohabiture. See prec.
word and -atioa.

## coheir
coheir, п., a joint heir. — Formed fr. со- and heir.

## coheiress
coheiress, п., a joint heiress. — Formed fr. co-
and heiress.

## Cohen
Cohen, п., ι) a priest; 2) a Jewish surname
indicating.priestly descent. — Heb. kshin, 'priest'.
See Kohen.

## cohere
cohere, intr. v., to stick together. — L. cohaerlre,
'to stick or cling together', fr. со- and haerlre,
'to stick, cleave, cling'. See hesitate and cp.
cohesion. Cp. also adhere, inhere.

## coherence
coherence, coherency, n. — F. coherence, fr. L.
cohaerentia, 'a sticking together, coherence', fr.
cohaerlns, gen. -entis. See next word and -ce
resp. -cy.

## coherent
coherent, adj. — F. coherent, fr. L. cohaerlns,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of cohaerlre, 'to stick
together'. See cohere and -ent.
Derivative: coherent-ly, adv.

## coherer
coherer, n. — Formed fr. cohere with agential
suff. -er.

## cohesion
cohesion, n. — F. cohesion, fr. L. cohaesionem,
ace. of cohaesio, 'a sticking together', fr. co-
haesus, pp. of cohaerlre. See cohere and -ion.

## cohesive
cohesive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. co-
haesus, pp. of cohaerlre. See cohere.
Derivatives: cohesive-ly, adv., cohesive-ness, n.

## cohort
cohort, п., a company of soldiers. — F. cohorte,
fr. L. cohortem, ace. of cohars, 'an enclosed
place, yard; a company of soldiers, the tenth
part of a legion'. See court, which is a doublet
of cohort.

## Cohosh
Cohosh, п., name of several N. American
medicinal plants. — Of Algonquian origin.

## cohne
cohne, п., rout, mob, tumult. — F., orig. 'hall',
fr. MBret. cochuy.

## coif
coif, п., cap, headdress. — ME. coif, coife, fr.
OF. coife, coiffe (F. coiffe), fr. VL. cofia, cofea,
cuphia, 'a cap* (whence also It. cuffia, scuffia.
Sp. cofia, escofia, of s.m. ), fr. OHG. kupphia,
'cap, coif'.
Derivative: coif, tr. v.

## coiffeur
coiffeur, п., a hairdresser. — F., fr. coiffer, 'to
dress the hair of, fr. coiffe. See prec. word.

## coiffure
coiffure, п., headdress. — F., fr. coiffer. See prec
word and -ure.

## coign
coign, n. — An old spelling of coin.

## coil
coil, tr. and intr. v., to wind. — OF. coittir, 'to
collect' (whence F. cueillir, 'to gather, pluck'),
fr. L. colligere, 'to gather, collect'. See collect
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also coil,
'tumult'.
Derivatives: coil, п., coil-er, n.

## coll
coll, п., tumult. — Prob. fr. OF. acueil (F. ac-
cueil), 'reception, encounter', fr. acueillir (F.
accueillir), 'to receive', fr. VL. 'accolligere, fr.
ad- and L. colligere, 'to gather'. See coll, 'to
wind'.

## coin
coin, n. — F., 'wedge, coin, stamp', fr. L. cuneus,
'wedge', which possibly derives fr. I.-E. *kun-,
enlargement of base *кй-, 'pointed', whence
perh. also L. culex, 'gnat'. See Culex and cp.
cuneate, cuneiform, quoin. Cp. also Olt. cogno,
'die', OProvenc. conk, 'wedge, die', Catal. cony,
Sp. curio, Port, cunho, 'die', Sp. cuua. Port.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:174 COLUMN:3 -->
cunha, 'wedge', Rum. cidu, 'nail', which all
derive fr. L. cuneus.

## coin
coin, tr. and intr. v., to make coins. — OF. coi-
gnier (F. cogner), fr. coin. See coin, n.
Derivatives: coinage(<l.v.), coin-er, n.,coin-ing,n.

## coinage
coinage, n. — OF. coignaige, fr. coignter. See
prec. word and -age.

## coincide
coincide, intr. v., 1) to agree exactly; 2) to occupy
the same place; 3) to occur at the same time. —
ML. coincidere, lit. 'to fall upon together", fr.
со- and L. incidere, 'to fall upon, light upon',
fr. in-, 'in', and cadere, 'to fall'. See incident,

## coincidence
coincidence, n. — F. coincidence, fr. MF. cofn-
cidance, fr. colncidant, pres. part of colncider,
fr. ML. coincidere. See prec. word and -ence.

## coincident
coincident, adj. — F. coincident. See prec. word
and -ent.
Derivatives: colncident-al, adj.,
coincident-ally, adv.

## colustantaneous
colustantaneous, adj., happening at the same
moment. — Formed fr. со- and instantaneous.
Derivatives: coinstantaneous-ly, adv., coinslan-
taneous-ness, п..

## coir
coir, п., fiber made from the husk of the
coconut. — Malayalam kayar, 'cord', fr. kayaru,
'to be twisted'.

## coition
coition, п., sexual intercourse. — L. coitio, gen.
-onis, 'a coming together', fr. coitus, pp. of coire,
4o come together', fr. со- and ire, 'to go'. See
itinerate and -ition and cp. next word.

## coitus
coitus, п., sexual intercourse. — L., 'a coming
together', fr. coitus, pp. of coire. See prec. word
and cp. coetas.

## coke
coke, п., charred coal. — ME. colke, 'a core", in
gradational relationship to ME. kelkes, 'spawn',
Swed. kalk, 'pith', and cogn. with Gk. γέλγϊς
(for *γέλ-γλις), 'clove of garlic', αγλΐς, 'clove
of garlic' (in the pi. 'head of garlic'). Cp. kelk.
Derivatives: cok-er, п., сок-егу, п., cok-y, adj.

## coke
coke, п., cocaine (slang). — Short for cocaine,

## col
col, п., a pass between mountain peaks. — F. col,
'neck', fr. L. collum, of s.m. See collar and cp.
words there referred to.

## col-
col-, assimilated form of com- before /.

## col-
col-, form of colo- before a vowel.

## Cola
Cola, п., a genus of trees of the chocolate family
(bol.) — ModL., from a W. African native
word meaning 'kola nut'. Cp. kola, kola nnt.

## colander
colander, also cullender, п., a large strainer. —
VL. *cdlutor, corresponding to L. cdlutorium,
'a strainer', fr. colore, 'to strain', fr. cdlum,
'strainer', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.

## Colchian
Colchian, adj., of, or pertaining to Colchis. —
Formed with suff. -ian fr. L. Colchis, fr. Gk.

Colchicum, п., a genus of herbs (bot.) — L. col-

χιχός, of s.m., fr. ΚολχΙς, 'Colchis'. Cp. prec.

colcomar, п., red oxide of iron. — F. and Sp.

See chalco- and anther,

## cole
cole, n„ cabbage. — ME. col, fr. OE. cat, cowl,

## Colemanite
Colemanite, п., a calcium borate (mineral.} —
Named after William Tell Coleman of San
Francisco (1824-93). For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## eoleo-
eoleo-, before a vowel eole-, combining form
meaning 'sheath', as in Cofeoptera. — Gk.
κολεο-, κολε-, fr. κολεός, 'sheath', of uncertain

Coleus.

## Coleochaete
Coleochaete, п., a genus of green algae (hot.) —
ModL., compounded of coleo- and Gk. χαίτη,
'long flowing hair, mane'. See coleo- and
chaeto-.

## Coleoptera
Coleoptera, n. pi., an order of insects (= Beetles).
— ModL., lit. 'sheath winged', fr. Gk. κολεά-
ΐΓτερος, fr. κολεός, 'sheath', and πτερόν, 'wing'.
See enleo- and ptero-.

## eoIeopteraL coleopteran
eoIeopteraL coleopteran, coleopterous, adj.,
pertaining to the Coleoptera (bot.) — See prec.
word and adj. suff. -al, resp. -an, -ous.

## coteorbiza
coteorbiza, п., the sheath that envelops the
radicle in some plants (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of coleo- and Gk. ρίζα, 'root'. See
rhizo-.

## coleslaw
coleslaw, п., sliced cabbage salad. — Du. kool-
sla, fr. kool, .'cabbage', and sla, 'salad'. See cole
and slaw and cp. the first element in colza.

## Coleus
Coleus, п., a genus of plants of the mint family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κολεός, 'sheath' (see
coleo-); so called in reference to the union of
the filaments.

## colibri
colibri, п., a hummingbird. — F. colibri, fr. Sp.
colibri, which is prob. of Caribbean origin.

## colic
colic, adj., pertaining to the colon. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. κόλον, 'large intestine,
colon'. See colon, 'part of the larger intestine'.

## colic
colic, п., a sharp pain in the intestines. — F. coli-
que, fr. L. colicus, 'pertaining to the colic; sick
with the colic', fr. Gk. κωλικός, 'sick with the
colic', fr. κώλον, incorrect form for κόλον, 'large
intestine, colon'. See colon, 'part of the larger
intestine', and -ic.
Derivatives: colic-al, colick-y, adjs.

## Colin
Colin, п., in pastoral verse, a name denoting a
shepherd. — F., prop, a dimin. of Col, itself a
dimin. of Nicolas. See Nicholas and cp. collie.

## coliseum
coliseum, п., a music hall. — ModL., a blend of
It. coliseo and L. Colosseum. See Colosseum.

## colitis
colitis, п., inflammation of the colon. — Medical
L., formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk. κόλον, 'large
intestine'. See colon.

## coll-
coll-, from of collo- before a vowel.

## collaborate
collaborate, intr. v. — L. collaborat-'um), pp.
stem of collaborare, 'to work together'. See com-,
labor, v., and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: coflaborat-ion, п., collaborat-ive,
adj., collaborator, n.

## collagen
collagen, п., a gelatinous substance occurring in
the animal body (pliysiol.) — Compounded of
Gk. κόλλα, 'glue', and -γενής, 'born of, of the
nature of, See collo- and -gen.

## collapse
collapse, intr. v. — L. collapsus, pp. of collSbi,
to fall in ruins, fall together', fr. col- and Mb;,
'to fall'. See lapse and cp. words there
referred 10.
Derivatives: collapse, п., coflaps-ible, adj.

## collar
collar, n. — ME., fr. AF. coler, corresponding
to OF. colter (F. collier), 'necklace, collar', fr.
L. collare, "a chain for the neck', fr. collum (for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:175 COLUMN:2 -->
*colsoin), 'neck', which is cogn. with Goth.,
OHG., OFris., ΟΝ., OS. hals, OE. heals, 'neck'.
These words prob. meant orig. 'that which
turns the head', and derive fr. I.-E. base mq"el-,
'to turn, turn round', whence also L. colere, 'to
till (the ground); to dwell, inhabit', colonus,
'tiller of the ground, husbandman, farmer'.
See colony and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also Lith. kaklas, Lett, kakls, 'neck', fr.
*q"oq"'lo-, reduplication of base *q"el-, 'to turn'
(see above and cp. cycle, wheel). Cp. col,
collaret, collet, accolade, cuddle, decollate,
decollete, hauberk, hausse-col, hawse. For sense
development cp. Gk. τράχηλος, 'neck', which prob.
means lit. 'turner', and is rel. to τροχός, 'wheel'
(see trachelo-), and OSlav. vratu, 'neck', fr.
vratiti, 'to turn'.
Derivatives: collar, tr. v., collar-ed, adj.

## collaret
collaret, collarette, п., a small collar. — F. colle-
rette, formed fr. collier, 'necklace, collar', with
dimin. suff. -ette. See collar and -et, -ette.

## collate
collate, tr. v., to compare. — L. collatus, 'brought
together' (used as pp. of conferre, 'to bring
together'), fr. com- and lotus, 'borne, carried' (used
as pp. of ferre, 'to bear, carry'), which stands
for "tlatos, fr. *;/-, zero degree of I.-E. base *tel-,
*tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence L. tollere, 'to lift
up, raise', tolerare, 'to bear, support'. See foler-
nte and cp. ablation, ablative, acceptation, al-
lative, delate, dilatory, elate,' illation, legislnte,
oblate, prelate, relate, correlate, sublate,
superlative, translate. The word collate was
introduced into English by Bacon.
Derivatives: collat-ing, adj., collat-or, n.

## collateral
collateral, adj., 1) placed side by side; 2)
secondary. — ML. collateralis, 'alongside of, fr.
col- and L. latus, gen. lateris, 'side'. See lateral.
Derivatives: collateral, п., collateral-ly, adv.,
collateral-ity, п., collareral-ness, n.

## collatioa
collatioa, п., ι) the act of collating; 2)
contribution; 3) a light meal. — OF. collacion (F.
collation), fr. L. collationem, ace. of collatio, 'a

together'. See collate and -ion.

## collative
collative, adj., having the power to confer. —
L. collativus, 'brought together', fr. collatus,
'brought together'. See collate and -ive.

## collator
collator, п., one who collates. — L., 'one who

## colleague
colleague, intr. v., to enter into an alliance (ob-

## colleague
colleague, п., an associate in work, office, etc. —
F. collegue, fr. L. collega, 'one who is chosen

## collect
collect, n. — F. collecte, fr. L. collecta, 'a
gathering together', fern. pp. used as a noun, fr.
colligere. See collect, v.

## collect
collect, tr. and intr. v. — L. collectus, pp. of

collect*, fr. com- and legere, 'to gather, collect,
pick out, choose, read'. See lecture and cp. coil,
'to wind', and cull, which are doublets of collect.
Derivatives: collect-ed, adj., collect-ed-ly, adv.,
collect-ed-ness, п., collection (q.v.), collective
(q.v.), collector (q.v.)

## collectanea
collectanea, n. pi., a collection of writings from
works of one author or of several authors. —
L., neut. pi. of collectaneiis, 'gathered or
collected together', formed fr. collectus, pp. of
colligere, Ίο gather', with suff. -uncus. See prec.

## collection
collection, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. collectionem,
ace. of collectio, 'a collecting, bringing
together', fr. collectus, pp. of colligere. See collect,
v., and -ion.
Derivative: collection-al, adj.

## collective
collective, adj. — F. collectif (fem. collective), fr.
L. collectivus, 'gathered together, collected', fr.

Derivatives: collective, п., collective-ly, adv.,
collective-ness, п., collectiv-ism, п., collectiv-ist,
п., collectiv-ist-ic, adj., collectiv-ity, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:175 COLUMN:3 -->

ace. of collector, fr. L. collectus, pp. of colligere.
See collect, v., and agential suff. -or. Cp. OProv-
enc. collector, Sp. colector, It. collettore, which
all derive fr. ML. coilectorem.
colleen, п., a girl. — Ir. cailin, dimin. of caile,
'girl'. For the dimin. Suff. cp. smithereens.
college, n. — OF. college (F. college), fr. L.
collegium, 'persons united by the same office,

## collegial

Derivatives: collegiate-ly, adv. ,collegiate-ness, n.

## Collembola
Collembola, п., an order of insects, including the

## collenchyma

collet, п., a metal band. — F., 'little collar',

## Colletotrichum
Colletotrichum, п., a form genus of imperfect

κολλητός, 'glued', and θ-ρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair*.
See prec. word.and tricho-.

## colliculus
colliculus, п., a prominence (anat. and 200I.) —·
L., 'a little hill', dimin. of collis, which stands

## collide
collide, intr. v. — L. colliderc, 'to dash together',

## coUidine
coUidine, п., an alkaloid, QHuN (chem.) — Lit.

-ine fr. Gk. κόλλα, 'glue', and είδος, 'form,

## collie

## collier
collier, п., 1) a ship for carrying coal; 2) coal

## colliery
colliery, п., a coal mine. — Formed fr. collier

## colligate
colligate, tr. v., to bind together. — L. colligatus,

## colligation

See prec. word and -ion.

## collimate
collimate, tr. v., to make parallel to a given line.

Derivatives: collimat-ion, п., collimat-or, n.

## colline
colline, п., a small hill (obsol.) — F., fr. Late L.

collina, prop. fern, of L. collinus, 'pertaining

## collinear
collinear, adj., lying in the same line. — Formed

## Collins
Collins, п., a bread-and-butter letter. — So called

## Collinsia
Collinsia, п., a genus of plants of the figwort

For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Collinsonia
Collinsonia, п., a genus of herbs of the mint

## collision
collision, n. — L. collisio, gen. -onis, 'a dashing

dere. See collide and -ion and cp. elision.

## collo-
collo-, before a vowel coll-, combining form
meaning 'glue'. — Gk. κολλο-, κολλ-, fr. κόλλα,
'glue', which stands for "κόλια and is prob.
cogn. with OSlav. kleji, kleji, 'glue', MLG. helen,

## collocate
collocate, tr. v., to place side by side; to arrange.
— L. collocutus, pp. of collocare, 'to place

See locate and cp. couch, which is a doublet of
collocate.

## collocation
collocation, n. — L. collocatio, gen. -onis, fr.
collocutus, pp. of collocare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## collocution
collocution, п., a speaking together. — L. collo-

-ion and cp. colloquy.

## collocutor
collocutor, n. — Late L. collocutor, 'he who talks

See prec. word and agential suff. -or.

## collodion
collodion, п., a solution of nitrated cellulose

Derivative: collodion-ize, tr. v.

## collogue
collogue, intr. v., to converse confidentially. —
A blend of F. colloque, 'conversation' (fr. L.

## colloid
colloid, adj., 1) gluelike; of the nature of a colloid
2) п., a gelatinous substance. — Compounded
of coll- and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: colloid-al, adj.

## collop
collop, п., a slice of meat. ■*- ME. colhoppe,
coloppe, compounded of col, 'coal' (see coal),
and hoppe, a word of uncertain origin. Cp. dial.
Swed. gISdhoppa, 'baked over gleeds (i.e.
glowing coals)'.

## coUophore
coUophore, п., a suckerlike organ in the abdomen
of insects (enlomol.) — Compounded of collo-
and Gk. -φόρος, 'bearing'. See -phore.
couoqniaL adj. — Formed fr. colloquy with adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: colloquial-ism, п., colloquial-isl, п.,
colloquial-ize, tr. v. colloquial-ly, adv.

## colloquy
colloquy, п., conversation. — L. colloquium,
'conversation', fr. com- and loqui, 'to speak'. See
loquacious.
Derivative: colloquial (q.v.)

## collotype
collotype, п., a photographic print made from a
gelatin plate. — Compounded of collo- and
-type,

## collude
collude, intr. v., to cooperate in a fraud. — L.
colludere, 'to play together', fr. com- and ludere,
4o play'. See ludicrous, and cp. allude and words
there referred to.

## coUusinn
coUusinn, п., cooperation in a fraud. — F., fr. L.

## collusionem
collusionem, ace. of collusio, 'a playing together',

## fr. collus-(um)
fr. collus-(um), pp. stem of colludere. See prec.
word and -Ion and cp. allusion and words there
referred to.

## collusive
collusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.

## collus-(um)
collus-(um), pp. stem of colludere. See collude
and cp. allusive and words there referred to.
Derivatives: collusive-ly, adv., collusive-ness, n.

## Collybin
Collybin, п., a genus of agarics (bot.) — ModL.,·
fr. Gk. κόλλυβας, 'coin', orig. '(small) change',
which stands for *χόλλυφος, and derives fr. Heb.
haloph, fr. haldph, 'he changed'. Mishnaic
Hebrew qolbdn, 'rate of exchange', has been
reborrowed fr. Gk. κόλλυβος. Ср. caliph.

## collyrium
collyrium, п., an eye salve (med.) — L., fr. Gk.
κολλδριον, 'poultice, eye salve', dimin. of
κολλδρα, 'a loaf of coarse bread', which is rel.
to κόλλΐξ, of s.m.; of unknown origin. The eye
salve was called κολλόριον ('a little loaf'),
because it was made up in small loaves.

## colo-
colo-, before a vowel col-, combining form
denoting the colon (med.) — Fr. Gk. κόλον. See
colon, 'part of the larger intestine'.

## colobium
colobium, п., a sleeveless or short-sleeved tunic,
formerly used by the clergy. — Late L., fr. Gk.
κολόβιον, fr. κολοβός, 'docked, curtailed,
mutilated', fr. κόλος, of s.m., whence also κολούειν,
'to cut short, curtail'; rel. to κλαν, 'to break',
fr. I.-E. base *qel(Sy, *qol(a)-, 'to strike, beat'.
See clastic and cp. the next two words and the
first element in colure.

## coloboma
coloboma, n., a defect of the eye (med.)—Medical
L., fr. Gk. κολόβωμα, 'the part taken away in
mutilation', fr. κολοβοϋν, 'to mutilate', fr.
κολοβός, 'mutilated'. See colobium.

## Colobus
Colobus, п., a genus of African monkeys (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. κολοβός, 'docked, curtailed,
mutilated' (see colobium); so called in allusion

## colocynth
colocynth, n. — L. colocynthis, fr. Gk. κολοκυνίΚς,
'the wild gourd', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. coloqumrida.

## cologne
cologne, п., perfumed liquid. — Shortened fr.
eau de Cologne, lit. "water of Cologne', fr.
Cologne, French name of Koto in Germany,
orig. called Coldnia Agrippina ('colony of
Agrippa'), after Agrippa, wife of the Roman
emperor Claudius. Cp. Eau de Cologne.

## colon
colon, п., that part of the larger intestine, which
extends from the caecum to the rectum (anal.)
— L., fr. Gk. κόλον, 'large intestine', which is
of uncertain origin.

## colon
colon, п., the punctuation mark: — L. colon, fr.
Gk. κώλον,'limb, member; member of a clause
or a sentence', which is rel. to κωλέά, κωλή,
'thighbone', and cogn. with OSlav. kollno, 'knee',
*Иёпй (fr. *fetou), 'limb, member' (whence
Russ., Czech ilea, of s.m.), Lith. kelps, Lett, celts,
'knee', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'crooked, bent',
whence also Gk. σκαληνός, 'limping, halting,
uneven', σκέλος, 'leg', σκόλιες, 'crooked, bent'.
See scaleae and cp. semicolon. Cp. aiso cylinder.

## colon
colon, п., the monetary unit of Costa Rica. —
Sp. colon, named after Christopher Columbus
(Cristobal Colon), the discoverer of America.

## colonel
colonel, n. — Earlier also spelled coronet, fr. F.
colonel, earlier also coronel, fr. It. colonnello, fr.
colonna, 'column'. Cp. Sp. coronel (with
dissimilation of the first / to r) and see column. It.
colonnello orig. meant 'the leader of a column
of soldiers'.
Derivative: colonel-су, n.

## colonial
colonial, adj. — Coined by the British statesman
Edmund Burke (1729-97) fr. L. coldnia. See
colony and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: colonial, п., colonial-ism, п., colo-
nial-ist, n.

## colonization
colonization, n. — Formed fr. colonize with suff.
-ation; first used by Edmund Burke. See prec.
word.
Derivative: colonization-ist, n.

## colonize
colonize, tr. and intr. v., 1) to settle with colonists;
2) to form a colony or colonies. — In the first
sense formed fr. L. colonus, 'tiller of the
ground, farmer'; in the second sense derived fr.
colony (q.v.) For the ending see suff. -ize.
Derivatives: colonization (q.v.), coloniz-er, n,

## colonnade
colonnade, п., a series of columns. — F., fr. earlier
colonnate, fr. It. colonnato, 'colonnade*, fr.
colonna, 'column'. See column.
Derivative: colonnad-ed, adj.

## colonnette
colonnette, п., a small column. — F., dimin.

## formed with suff. -ette fr. colonne
formed with suff. -ette fr. colonne, 'column'. See
column.

## colony
colony, n. — ME. colonie, fr. L. coldnia, 'landed

## estate
estate, farm, settlement, colony', fr. colonus.

'tiller of the ground, husbandman, farmer', fr.
colere, 'to till (the ground), cultivate, dwell,
inhabit', rel. to incola, 'inhabitant', inquilinus,
'inhabitant of a place'which is not his own, lodger',
fr. I.-E. base *qwel-, 'to turn, turn round,
move about', whence also OI. cdrati, 'moves
about, wanders, drives', carah, 'walk, motion',

OI. cakrab, Toch. A kukal, В kokale, Gk.
κύκλος, OE. hweogol, hwiol, wheel', Lith.

ker, collar, cologne, cycle, domicile, fallow,
'plowed land', inqniline, Limicolae, paleo-, Pa-

talisman, tele-, telegnosis, telegraph, teleology,
telephone, telescope, telesterion, terricolous, Tri-
teleia, wheel,

## colopexy
colopexy, also colopexia, п., the suturing of the
sigmoid flexure to the abdominal wall (surg.) —
Medical L. colopexia, compounded of κόλον,
'large intestine, colon', and πηξις, 'a fixing'. See
colon, 'part of the larger intestine', and -pexy.

## colophane
colophane, п., a resin. — F. colophane, fr. OF.
colofonie, cotafoine, fr. L. colophonia (see
colophony); influenced in form by F. diaphane,
'transparent' (see diaphanous).

## colophon
colophon, п., inscription at the end of a book,
corresponding to the title page of modern
books. — Gk. κολοφών, 'top, summit, finishing

## touch'
touch', for I.-E. *qol-n-bho-\ rel. to κολωνός,
κολώνη, 'hill', and cogn. with L. collis, 'hill'.
See colliculus.

## colophony
colophony, п., a resin. — L. colophonia, fr. Gk.
(*>ητίνη) Κολοφώνια, 'resin from Colophon', fr.
Κολοφών, name of a town in Lydia, lit.

## meaning 'summit'. See colophon
meaning 'summit'. See colophon,

## coloquintida
coloquintida, п., colocynth. — Med. L., fr.
Gk. κολοκυνίΚδα, ace. of κολοκυνίΗς. See
colocynth.

## color
color, colour, n. — ME., fr. OF. culour, colour
(F. couleur), fr. L. colorem, ace. of color, 'color

## of the skin
of the skin, color in general, appearance'. L.

## color prop
color prop, means Outward show, covering',

## and is rel. to L. cilare
and is rel. to L. cilare, 'to hide'; see conceal.

## Cp. It. colore
Cp. It. colore, OProven?. and Sp. color. Port.

## cor
cor, 'color', which all derive fr. L. coldrem. For

## the sense development of L. color cp. OI. varnah
the sense development of L. color cp. OI. varnah,
'covering, color', rel. to νχηόίί, 'covers', and
Gk. χρώμα, 'surface of the body, skin, color of

## the skin
the skin, color', χρως, of s.m. Cp. tricolor.
Derivatives: colo(u)r, v. (q.v.), colo(u)r-ful, adj.,

## colo(u)r-ful-ly
colo(u)r-ful-ly, adv., colo(u)r-ful-ness, п., col(u)r-

## less
less, adj., colo(u)r-less-ly, adv., colo(u)r-less-ness,
п., colo(u)r-y, adj.

## color
color, colour, tr. and intr. v. — F. colorer, fr. L.

## colorare 'to color'
colorare 'to color', fr. color, 'color'. See color,
п., and cp. discolur.
Derivatives: colo(u)r-able, adj., colo(u)r-abil-ity,
п., colo(u)r-able-ness, п., colo(u)r-abl-y, adv.,
•colo(u)r-er, п., colo(u)r-mg, n.

## Colorado
Colorado, adj., of medium color (said of cigars).
— Sp., 'ruddy, reddish', lit. 'colored', pp. of

## colorar
colorar, 'to color, dye, paint, stain', fr. L.

## colorare. See color
colorare. See color, v.

## colorant
colorant, п., a dye. — F., prop. pres. part, of

## colorer
colorer, 'to color', fr. L. colorare. See color, v.,
and -ant.

## coloration
coloration, colouration, п., a coloring. — L.

## Colorado
Colorado, gen. -onis, fr. coloratus, pp. of colorare.

## See color
See color, v., and -ation. /

## coloratura
coloratura, п., florid ornaments (mus.) — 1Ц lit.
'a coloring,' fr. colorare, fr. L. colorare. See

## color
color, v.

## colorific
colorific, adj., producing color. — F. color ifique,

## fr
fr, L. color, gen. color is, 'color', and the stem

## of L. -ficere
of L. -ficere, unstressed form otfacere, 'to make,

## do'. See color
do'. See color, п., and -fie.

## colorimeter
colorimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
strength of colors.—A hybrid coined fr. L. color,

## gen. colons
gen. colons, 'color', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.

## See color
See color, п., and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## colossal
colossal, adj., huge. — F. colossal, formed with
suff. -al (fr. L. -alls) fr. L. colossus. See colossus
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: colossal-ly, adj., colossal-ily, n.

## colossean
colossean, adj., colossal. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. colossius, fr. Gk. κολοσσαΐος, 'colossal',
fr. κολοσσός. See colossus and cp. Colosseum.

## Colosseum
Colosseum, less correctly Coliseum, п., the great
amphitheater in Rome built by Vespasian and
Titus. — Neut. of the adj. colosseus, used as a
noun. See prec. word.

## Colossochelys
Colossochelys, п., a genus of Pliocene tortoises
(paleonlol.) — ModL., lit. 'gigantic tortoise', fr.
Gk. κολοσσός, 'colossus', and χέλΰς, 'tortoise'.
See colossus and Chelonia.

## colossus
colossus, п., τ) a gigantic statue; 2) anything
huge. — L., fr. Gk. κολοσσός, 'a gigantic statue,
colossus', a word borrowed from an Aegean
language.

## colostrum
colostrum, п., the first milk after pregnancy (med.)
— L. colostra, colostrum, 'beestings', of
uncertain origin.

## colpo-
colpo-, before a vowel colp-, combining form
meaning 'in relation to the womb' (med.) —
Gk. κόλπο-, κολπ-, fr. κόλπος, 'womb'. See gulf.

## colporteur
colporteur, п., a hawker. — F., 'hawker, peddler',
fr. colporter, 'to hawk about, peddle', lit. 'to
carry on one's neck' (fr. col, сои, 'neck', and
porter, 'to carry', see con and collet), a folk-
etymological alteration of OF. comporter, 'to
carry, convey, transport', fr. L. comportare, 'to
bring together'. See comport.

## colt
colt, п., a young horse. — ME., fr. OE. colt,
'young ass or camel' (for the meaning 'young
camel' cp. the Authorized Version to Gen.
32:15). Cp. dial. Swed. kult, 'a boy', Dan. kuld,
'brood'.
Derivatives: colt-ish, adj., colt-ish-ly, adv.

## Colt
Colt, п., a revolver. — Named after the American
Samuel Colt (1814-62), who invented it in 1836.

## colter
colter, coulter, п., a knife or blade attached to a
plow. — ME. culter, colter, fr. OE. culter, fr. L.
culter, 'plowshare, knife' (whence also OF.
coltre, F. coutre), fr. I.-E. base *(s)aet-, 'to cut,
cleave, split', whence also Hitt. ishkalla, ish-
kallai, 'to break', Arm. celum, Ί cleave, split',
Gk. σκάλλειν, 'to hoe, dig', σκαλίς, 'hoe,
mattock', σκάλμτ), 'knife, sword', σκιιλμός, 'pin or
thole (to which the oar was fastened)', σκάλοψ,
'mole' (lit. 'the digger'), σκόλοψ, 'pale, stake',
σκώλος, 'a pointed stake', OSlav. skolika,
'oyster', skala, 'rock, stone', Ir. scelec, 'rock',
Mir. scailim, Ί scatter, disperse', ON. skalm,
'a short sword, knife', OHG. scala, 'drinking
cup', OE. scalu, 'shell, scale of a balance'. See
scale, 'weighing instrument', and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also coutel, caltrate, cul-
triform, cutlass, cutler, cntiery. Cp. also
calcareous.

## Coluber
Coluber, п., a genus of snakes (zool.) — L.
coluber, 'serpent, snake', of uncertain origin. Cp.
colubriae. Cp. also cobra, culverin.

## Colubridae
Colubridae, n. pi., a family of snakes (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -Idae.

## coinbrine
coinbrine, adj., 1) pertaining to, or like, a snake;
cunning; 2) pertaining to the subfamily of snakes
called Colubrinae, of the family Colubridae
(zool.) — L. colubrlnus, 'like a snake, cunning',
fr. coluber, 'serpent, snake'. See Coluber and
adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## Columba
Columba, п., a genus of birds, the pigeon (or-
nithol.) — L., 'dove, pigeon', cogn. with Gk.
κόλυμβος, κολυμβίς, 'diver' (name of a bird),
OSlav. golgbl, 'dove', lit. 'the blue bird', Russ.
goluboj, OPruss. golimban, 'blue', Lith. gelumbe",
'blue cloth'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*qel-, *qol-, 'of a dark color', whence also Gk.
κελαινός, 'black'. Cp. columbine, Colymbus. This
base is related to base *qal-, whence L. caligd,
'darkness'. See caliginous and cp. Celaeno.

## columbaceous
columbaceous, adj., dovelike; pertaining to the
pigeons. — Formed with suff. -aceous fr. L.
columba, 'dove'. See Columba.

## columbarium
columbarium, п., a dovecot. — L. columbarium,
prop. neut. of the adjective columbarius,
'pertaining to doves', used as a noun, fr. columba.
See Columba and -arium.

## columbate
columbate, п., a salt of columbic acid (chem.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:177 COLUMN:2 -->
See columbium and chem. suff. -ate.

## Columbella
Columbella, п., a genus of gastropods (zool.) —
ModL., dimin. of columba, 'dove'. See Columba
and -ella.

## columbiad
columbiad, п., a kind of heavy gun used in the
American Civil War. — From next word.

## Columbiad
Columbiad, п., an epic of America. — Formed
with suff. -ad fr. Columbia, poeticname of North
America, which was so called from its
discoverer Christopher Columbus.

## columbine
columbine, adj., pertaining to a dove or doves;
dovelike. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) colombin, fr.
L. columblnus, fr. columba, 'dove'. See Columba
and adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## columbine
columbine, п., any plant of the genus Aquilegfa.
— F. colombine, fr. ML. columbina, fem. of
L. columblnus, 'dovelike' (see prec. word); so
called from the resemblance of the inverted
flower to a group of doves.

## Columbine
Columbine, fem. PN. — Lit. 'dovelike', fr. L.
columbina, fem. of columblnus. See columbine,
adj.

## Columbine
Columbine, п., a female character in comedy and
pantomime, the sweetheart of Harlequin. — It.
Colombina, fr. L. columbina, 'dovelike'. See
Columbine, adj.

## columbite
columbite, п., a columbate of iron, Fe(CbO,)2
(mineral.) — Formed fr. next word with subst.
suff. -ite.

## columbium
columbium, п., a metallic element (chem.) — The
original name given to niobium by its discoverer
Charles Hatchett(I765-l847)in 1801; he named
it so because he signalized it first in the ore
called columbite (q.v.) For the ending of
columbium see -ium.

## columella
columella, п., a part resembling a column (anat.,
zool. and bot.) — L., dimin. of columna. See
next word and -ella.

## column
column, n. — L. columna, 'pillar, column', prob.
standing for *qelom(e)na, 'that which rises',
fem. passive part, formed fr. I.-E. base *qel-, 'to
rise, be elevated', whence also columen, culmen,
'top,summit,gable',cetei, 'high, lofty, elevated',
excellere, 'to rise, excel', collis (for*col-n-is), 'a
hill', OI. кЩат (for kultam), 'top, skull' (orig.
'elevation'), Gk. κολωνός, κολώνη, 'hill', κο-
λοφών, 'top, end', Lith. kalnas, Lett, kalns,
'mountain', Lith. kalva, Lett, kalva, 'hill', Lith.
keliit, kelti, Lett, celu, celt, 'to raise, lift', OSlav.
celo, 'forehead', (elesinU, 'particular, peculiar'.
OS. holm, 'hill', OE. holm, 'island, wave, sea'.
Cp. hill, holm. Cp. also coUiculus, colline,
colonel, colonnade, colophon, culminate, excel.
For the participial suff. in L. columna (for
*qelo-mena~) see alumnus and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: columnar (q.v.), column-ed, adj.

## columnar
columnar, adj., formed in columns. — L. colum-
naris, 'rising in the form of a pillar', fr. columna.
See prec. word and -ar.

## columniform
columniform, adj. — See column and -form.

## colure
colure, п., one of the two celestial circles
intersecting each other at the poles (aslron.) — Late L.
coluri (pi.), fr. Gk. at κόλουροι (scil. γραμμαί),
'the colures', lit. 'the truncated (lines)', pi. of
κόλουρος, 'dock-tailed', which is compounded
of κόλος, 'docked, mutilated, curtailed', and
ουρί, 'tail' (see colobium and uro-, 'tail-'); so
called because in Greece their lower part is
always 'cut off' (i.e. beneath the horizon).

## Colutea
Colutea, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κολουτέά, κολοιτέά,
κολωτέα, name of a tree.

## Colymbus
Colymbus, п., a genus of birds (omithol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. κόλυμβος, 'diver (the bird)',
which is cogn. with L. columba, 'dove, pigeon'.
See Columba.

## colza
colza, п., coleseed; rapeseed. — F., fr. Du. kool-
zaad, lit. 'cabbage seed', fr. kool, 'cabbage', and
zaad, 'seed'. See cole and seed.

## com-
com-, pref. meaning 'with, together'. — L. com-,
fr. OL. com (whence L. cum), 'with', rel. to
Oscan com, con, 'with', com-, кит-, Umbr. com-,
со-, ku- — L. com-, con-, and to L. contra (for
*com-tro-), 'against', and cogn. with Olr., Mir.
com-, con-, 'with', Alb. ke-, 'con-', the Teut.
perfective prefixes: Goth, ga-, OE. ge-, etc.,
and prob. also with Gk. κοινός, 'common, public,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:177 COLUMN:3 -->
general' (see coeno-). Cp. 1st con-, contra-,
count, 'title of nobility'. Cp. also y-.

## coma
coma, п., a state of insensibility. — ModL., fr.
Gk. κώμα, 'a deep sleep, lethargy', which is prob.
rel. to κοιμαν, 'to put to sleep', κεΐσθαι, 'tolie', fr.
I.-E. base kei-, 'to lie, settle down', whence also
L. civis, 'member of a community, citizen'. See
civil and cp. acomia.

## coma
coma, п., 1) a tuft of hairs (bot.); 2) a nebulous
mass (astron.) — L., fr. Gk. κόμη, 'hair of the
head', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. next
word, comet, comose, pyrone.

## Comandra
Comandra, п., a genus of plants of the
sandalwood family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
Gk. κόμη, 'hair' and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man'
(see coma, 'tuft of hair', and andro-); so called
because the hairs on the calyx lobes are attached
to the anthers.

## Comarum
Comarum, п., a genus of plants of the rose family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κόμαρος, 'the arbutus',
a pre-Hellenic word.

## comatose
comatose, adj., in a state of coma. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ose fr. Gk. κώμα, gen. κώματος,
'a deep sleep'. See coma, 'insensibility'.

## comb
comb, n. — ME., fr. OE. camb, rel. to OS. camb,
ON. kambr, Du., Dan. and Swed. kam, OHG.
champ, kamb, MHG. kamp, kam, G. Kamm,
'comb', lit. 'something tooth-shaped', fr. I.-E.
base "gembh-, 'to bite'; to cut to pieces', whence
also OI. jambhah, 'tooth', Toch. A kam, В кете,
'tooth', Gk. γόμφος, 'bolt, nail', γομφίος (scil.
οδών), 'grinder tooth, tooth of a key', γαμφαί,
γαμφηλαί, 'jaws of animals, beak or bill of
birds'. Alb. demp, Gheg 6qm, 'tooth', OSlav.
zpbu, Lett, zuobs, 'tooth', Lith. zathbas, 'edge of a
beam', Lith. gembe, 'peg', OSlav. zebg (for
*gembh-), Ί tear to pieces'. See gemma and
cp. cam, п., kemb, unkempt, oakum. Cp. also
gomphosis.
Derivatives: comb, tr. and intr. v., comb-ed,
adj., comb-er, n.

## combat
combat, intr. v., to fight; tr. v., to fight with. —
F. combattre, 'to fight', fr. VL. *combatlere, fr.
com- and L. battuere, battere, 'to beat, strike'.
See batter, 'to beat violently', and cp. abate,
debate, hors de combat.
Derivatives: combat, п., combat-ive, adj., com-
bat-ive-ly, adv., combat-ive-ness, n.

## combat
combat, п., fight. — F., back formation fr.
combattre. See prec. word.

## combatant
combatant, 1) adj., fighting; ready to fight; 2) п.,
fighter. — F. combattant, pres. part, of
combattre. See combat, v., and -ant.

## combe
combe, п., a deep valley. — OE. cumb, of Celtic
origin; cp. Bret, komb, 'small valley', W. cwmm,
'dale, valley', MIr. comm, Ir. and Gael, cum,
'vessel', which are cogn. with Gk. κύμβη, 'the
hollow of a vessel, cup, boat'. See cymbal and
cp. 2nd coomb.

## combinant
combinant, adj. and n. (math.) — Late L. com-
binans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of combinare. See
combine and -ant.

## combination
combination, n. — OF. combination (F. combi-
naison), fr. Late L. combindtionem, ace. of com-
binatio, fr. combinatus, pp. of combinare. See
combine and -ation.

## combinative
combinative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive from
Late L. combinatus, pp. of combinare, fr. com-
and bint, 'two each, two at a time'. See binary.
Derivatives: combine, п., combin-ed, adj., com-
Ып-ed-ly, adv., combin-ed-ness, п., combin-er,n.

## Combretum
Combretum, п., a genus of plants of the myro-
balan family (bot.) — L. combretum, 'a kind of
rush', of uncertain origin. It stands perh. for
*kwendhro-, and is cogn. with Lith. SveHdrai
(pi.), 'a kind of rash', Faroeish Dan. qvander,
the plant 'Angelica silvestris'. See Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW., I. p. 253 s.v. combretum.

## combust
combust, adj., burnt. — L. combustus, pp. of com-
biirere, 'to burn up', fr. *co(m)-urere, with
inserted b on analogy of ambiirere, 'to burn
round', which stands for amb-urere, 'to burn
round', but was misdivided into am-burere.
(Owing to this misdivision the new verb 'burere
was formed, with the pp. bustum; see bust.) L.
*com-urere is formed fr. com- and wrere, 'to
burn', which is cogn. with OI. Osali, 'burns',
usnah, 'hot', ustah, 'burnt, hot', Gk. εϋειν (for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:178 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 151 | COMMENOATOR -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:178 COLUMN:1 -->
•εΰσειν), 'to singe', OHG. usil-far, 'yellow' (lit.
'ash-colored'), ON. ysja, 'fire', usll, OE. ysle,
'glowing ashes, embers', ON. eimyrja, OE.
xmerge, 'embers'. All these words derive fr.
I.-E. base *eus-, 'to burn'. See ember, 'live
coal', and cp. Eurns, uredo, Urtica, urticaria, ur-
ticate, Ustilago, ustulate.

## combustible
combustible, adj. — F., fr. Late L. combustibilis,
fr. L. combuslus, pp. of comburere. See
combust and -ible.
Derivatives: combustible, п., combustibil-lty, п.,
combustible-ness, п., combuslibl-y, adv.

## combustion

bustidnem, ace. of combuslio, 'a burning', fr.

## come
come, intr. v. — ME. cumen, comen, fr. OE. cu-
man, rel. to OS. cuman, ON. кота, OFris. cuma,
Du. komen, OHG. queman, koman, MHG. ko-
men, G. kommen, Goth, qiman, 'to Come', fr.
I.-E. base *gwem-, 'to go; to come', whence also
OI. gamati, gacchati, 'he goes', gatdh, 'gone',
Avestic jamaiti, 'goes', Toch. A kakmu, В ке-
kamu, 'come' (pp.), A kumnds, 'comes', В kdm-
naskem, 'they come', Arm. ekn (for *e-gwem-t),
'he came', Gk. βαίνω (prob. for *βάνιω fr.
•βάμιω), Ί go', L. venio (prob. for *g«>mi6), Ί
come', Mir. beim for *ben-smeri), 'pace, step',
Lith. gemii, gimti, 'to be born', lit. 'to come'.
Cp. the collateral base *gwd- in OI. agam (aor.),
Gk. ίβην (aor.), Ί went', Gk. βήμα, 'pace, step',
βώμος, 'altar', Lett, gaju, Ί went', gatwa,
'passage', Alb. ngd, Ί run'. Cp. welcome. Cp. also
base, п., and words there referred to. Cp. also
venue, 'arrival', and words there referred to.
Cp. also agama, jngat.

## come-at-able
come-at-able, adj., accessible. — Formed fr.
come, at, and -able.

## comedian
comedian, n. — F. comedien, fr. comedie, 'com-
medy*. See comedy and -an.

## comedieune
comedieune, n. — F. comedienne, 'an actress in

## comedietta
comedietta, п., a short comedy. — It. (now

## comedo
comedo, п., blackhead (med.) — L. comedo, 'a

## comedy
comedy, n. — F. comedie, fr. L. comoedia, fr. Gk.
κωμωδία, 'comedy', fr. κωμωδός, 'comic actor'
(orig. 'singer in the κώμος or comic chorus'),
contraction of κωμαοιδός, which is
compounded of κώμος, 'revel, carousal, merry-making,
j)mic chorus', and αοιδός, 'singer'. The first
element is of uncertain origin; it is perh. rel.
to Gk. κώμη, 'village'. See home and cp. comic,
Comus, encomium, afikoman. The second element
is rel. to Gk. άείδειν, 'to sing', άοιδή, ωδή,
'song*; see ode and words there referred to and
cp. esp. tragedy.

## comely
comely, adj. — ME. cumelich, cumlich, comeiiche,
comlich, fr. OE. cymllc, formed with suff. -lie
(see Kke, adj.), fr. cyme, 'fine, beautiful,
splendid', orig. 'frail, delicate, tender', which is rel.
to ME. kime, 'weak, delicate', OHG. chumo,
кйтб, MHG. ките, 'with difficulty', OHG.
chumig, kumig, 'weak, delicate', G. kaum,
'hardly, scarcely'. The original meaning of ME.
kime and OHG. chumig was 'lamentable,
pitiable'; cp. OHG. chuma, 'sorrow', OHG. chu-
твп, 'to mourn', OS. kumian, 'to lament,
deplore'. All these words are derivatives of the
I.-E. imitative base *gou-, *gow-, 'to shout, cry'
whence also OE. ciegan (for orig. *kaujan), 'to
call', cyla, 'kite', OI. gdvate, 'sounds, resounds',
Gk. γοαν, 'to wail, groan, weep', MLG. kuten,
'to chatter, babble, prate', Lith. gaudziii, gausti,
'to howV, gaudas, 'lamentation', OSlav. govoriti,
'to make a noise', Russ. govorit', Serb, and
Croat iangovoriti, Czech hovoriti, Slovak hovorit',
'to speak', Olr. gulh, 'voice'. Cp. kite. The word
comely was influenced in meaning by an
association with come.
Derivatives: comeli-ly, adv., comeli-ness, n.

## comestible
comestible, adj., eatable. — F., formed with suff.
-Ible fr. L. comestus, a collateral form of сотё-
sus, pp. of comedere, 'to eat up, consume', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:178 COLUMN:2 -->
com- and edere, 'to eat'. See edible and cp.
comedo.

## comet
comet, n. — L. comltes, fr. Gk. κομήτης (scil.
αστήρ), 'comet', lit. 'a long-haired (star)', fr.
κομδν, 'to wear long hair', fr. κόμη, 'hair'. See

Derivatives: comet-ic, adj., comel-ary, adj.

## cometoid
cometoid, adj., resembling a comet. —
Compounded of comet and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## comfit

i (in con-flcere) see abigeal and cp. words there
referred to.

## comfort
comfort, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) conforler, fr. Late
L. confortare, 'to strengthen', fr. con- and L.
fortis, 'strong'. See fort.

## comfort
comfort, n. — OF. (= F.) confori, back
formation fr. conforter. See prec. word.
Derivatives: comfort-less, adj., comforl-less-ly,
adv., comfort-less-ness, n.

## comfortable
comfortable, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) con-
fortable, fr. conforter. See comfort, v., and -able.
Derivatives: comfortable-ness, п., comfortabl-y,
adv.

## comforter
comforter, n. — OF. conforteor, fr. conforter. See

## comfrey
comfrey, п., a plant of the borage family — ME.

## comic
comic, adj. — L. cdmicus, fr. Gk. κωμικός,

Derivatives: comic, п., comic-al, adj., comic-al-
ity, п., comic-al-ly, adv., comic-al-ness, n.

## Comintern
Comintern, п., the Third International. — Coined

## comitia
comitia, n. pi., assembly of the Roman people
(Roman antiq.) — L., pi. of comitium, 'place of

fr. com- and the stem of Hum, pp. of ire, 'to go'.
See itinerate.

## comity
comity, п., courtesy. — F. comite, fr. L. comita-
lem, ace. of cdmitds, 'courtesy, kindness,
affability*, from cdmis, 'courteous, kind, affable',
fr. OL. cosmis, which prob. stands for co-smi-s
and lit. means 'he who smiles with', and is
formed fr. со- and the I.-E. base of *smei-, 'to
smile, wonder'; see mirror, smile. OL. cosmis
became L. cdmis in the sense of the Latin
phonetic law, according to which ί disappeared
before d, I, m or я. Cp. L. IQbricus (for *slubri-
cos), 'slippery', mirus (for *smeiros),
'wonderful', nidus (for *nizdos), 'nest', pdnere (for
'posnere, fr. *po-si-nere), 'to place', primus (for
'prismas), 'first*; see lubricate, miracle, nest,
position, prime.

## comma
comma, n. — L., 'division of a period; comma',

L. capo, 'castrated cock'. See capon, and cp.
acopic, Coptis, pericope, syncope.
Derivative: comma, tr. v.

## command
command, tr. and intr. v. — OF. comander, (F.

manddre, refashioned after manddre fr. L.
commenddre, 'to commit to one's charge', fr. com-
and manddre, to commit to one's charge*, lit:

Latin d (in manddre) to ί (in com-minddre) see
accent and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
commend, which is a doublet of command.
Derivatives: command, n. (q.v.), commandant
(q.v.), command-er, п., command-er-ship, п.,
commandery (q.v.), command-ing, adj., com-
numd-ing-ly, adv., commandment (q.v.)

## command
command, n. — F. commande, fr. commander. See

commandant, n. — F., 'the one commanding',
prop. pres. part, of commander. See commaud,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:178 COLUMN:3 -->
v., and -ant.

ral-ive-ly, adv., commemorat-ive-ness, п., сот-

## commendator

mentum*. See comment, п., and subst. suff. -ary.

commiserationem, ace. of commiserulid, 'part of

commode, п., ι) a chest of drawers; 2) a movable

commodity, п., ι) convenience; 2) an article of

commodore, п., ι) in the United States Navy, an

common, adj. — ME. commun, comun, fr. OF.

common,п., ι)common land; 2)common people;

adj. Cp. discommon.

## commonalty
commonalty, п., l) the common people; 2) the

nalle, fr. OF. comunaulte (F. communauti), fr.

## communal
communal, adj. — Late L. communalts, fr. com-
тйпа, 'a commune'. See commune, 'a small

The first element prob. stands for *kwonqw-m-

ML., fr. L. compurgatus, pp. of compurgare. See

γεΐν ('to work, be active'), fr. Greco-L. base

κονεΐν, 'to be quick and active, to hasten', and

coacatenate, adj., linked together. — Late L. con-

## concert
concert, n. — F., fr. It. concerto. Most
lexicographers derive this word fr. L. concertare, 'to
dispute, contend'. This etymology cannot be
accepted because of the great discrepancy in
meaning. The origin of It. concerto and concertare
must be sought in another Latin word. It.
concertare prob. comes fr. L. concentare, 'to sing
together' (whence concentus, 'symphony,
harmony, harmonious music, concert'), fr. con- and
can/are, 'to sing'. See cant, 'slang of beggars',
and cp. concent. For the change of Latin й (in
caniare) to ё (in con-centare) see accent. For the
change of -nt- to -rt-, which is due to
dissimilation, cp. L. carmen, 'song', dissimilated fr.
*camncn (fr, canere,' to sing'), and germen, 'bud,
sprout', dissimilated fr. * gen-men (see charm and
germ).

## concert
concert, tr. v. — F. concerter, fr. It. concertare.

Derivatives: concert-ed, adj., concert-ed-ly, adv.
