confnsion, n. — OF. (= F), fr. L. confusionem,
ace. of confisid, fr. confusus, pp. of confundere.
See prec. word and -ion.

## confutation
confutation, n. — L. confitatio, gen. -onis, fr. con-
futatus, pp. of confiture. See next word and
-ation.

## confute
confute, tr. v., to prove to be wrong. — F. con-
futer, fr. L. confiture, 'to repress a boiling liquid;
to check, suppress, disprove', fr. coa- and *fu-
tare, which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *bhit-,
'to strike down', whence also OE. beatan, 'to
strike'. See beat, 'to strike', and cp. refute. Cp.
also footy.
Derivative: confit-er, n.

## congf
congf, п., leave to depart, dismissal; 2) a formal
farewell. — F., 'permission, leave of absence,
dismissal', fr. OF. congie, fr. L. commeatus, 'a
going to and fro, a going at will', fr. com- and
meatus, 'a going, passing', fr. medt-(um), pp.
stem of meare, 'to go, pass'. See meatus and cp.
congee, 'dismissal'.

## congeal
congeal, tr. and intr. v. — F. congeler, fr. L. con-
geldre, 'to cause to freeze', fr. con- and geldre,
'to freeze', fr. gelu, 'frost, cold'. See gelid.
Derivatives: congeal-able, adj., congeal-er, п.,
congeal-menl, n.

## congee
congee, п., leave to depart, dismissal. — OF.
congie. See conge.

## congee
congee, п., water in which rice has been boiled
(Angh-Ind.) — Tamil kanji, 'boilings'.

## congelation
congelation, n. — F. congelation, fr. L. congeld-
tionem, ace. of congelatio, fr. congeldtus, pp. of
congelare. See congeal and -ation.

## congener
congener, п., a person or thing of the same kind.
— L. congener, 'of the same race or kind', fr.
con- and genus, gen. generis, 'race, kind,
species'. See genus.
Derivatives: congener-ic, congener-ic-al, con-
gener-ous, adjs.

## coagenial
coagenial, adj., of the same nature. — Formed
fr. con- and genial.
Derivatives: congenial-ity, п., congenial-ly, adv.,
congenial-ness, n.

## congenital
congenital, adj., existing from birth. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. congenitus, 'born
together with', fr. con- and genitus, pp. of gignere,
'to beget'. See genital.
Derivatives: congenital-ly, adv., congenital-ness,
n.

## conger
conger, п., a kind of large marine eel. — ME., fr.
OF. congre, fr. L. congrum, ace. of conger, fr.
Gk. γάγγρος, 'sea eel, conger;tubercular growth
on trees', prob. meaning lit. 'something round',
and rel. to γογγύλος, 'round, rounded'. Cp.
gingiva.

## coageries
coageries, п., a heap, pile. — L., lit. 'that which
is brought together', fr. conger^, e, 'to bring or
carry together', fr. con- and gerere, 'to bear,
carry'. See gerent and cp. congest.

## congest
congest, tr. v., to overcrowd. — L. congestus, pp.
of congerere. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:185 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: congest-ed, adj., congestion (q.v.),
congest-ive, adj.

## congestion
congestion, п., overcrowding. — F., fr. L. con-
gestidnem, ace. of congestio, 'a heaping up', fr.
congestus, pp. of congerere. See congeries and
-ion.

## conglus
conglus, п., ]) a liquid measure containing about
three quarts; 2) in pharmacy, a gallon. — L.,
name of a liquid measure, cogn. with Gk. κόγ-
χος, κόγχη, 'shell; a liquid measure' (whence L.
concha, 'shell'). See conch and cp. words there
referred to.

## conglobate
conglobate, adj., formed into a ball or rounded
mass. — L. conghbatus, pp. of conglobdre, 'to
gather into a ball', fr. coa- and globdre, 'to make
into a ball', fr. globus, 'ball'. See globe and adj.
suff. -ate.

## conglobate
conglobate, tr. v., to form into a ball or rounded
mass. — L. conghbatus, pp. of conglobdre. See
conglobate, adj.

## conglobation
conglobation, n. — L. conglobdtid, gen. -onis, 'a
heaping together', fr. conghbatus, pp. of
conglobdre. See conglobate, v., and -ion.

## conglobe
conglobe, tr. and intr. v., to conglobate. — F.
conglobcr, fr. L. conglobdre. See conglobate, v.

## conglomerate
conglomerate, adj., formed into a ball or rounded
mass; п., something conglomerate; tr. and intr.'
v., to form into a ball or rounded mass. — L.
conglomerate, pp. of conglomerate, 'to roll
together', fr. con- and glomerare, 4o form into a
ball', fr. glomus, gen. glomeris, 'ball'. See
glomerate and cp. agglomerate.

## conglomeration
conglomeration, n. — Late L. conglomeratio, gen.
-onis, fr. L. conglomerate, pp. of conglomerdre.
See prec. word and -ion.

## conglutinant
conglutinant, adj., gluing; healing. — L. con-
glutindns, gen. -antis, pres. part, of conglutinare.
See next word and -ant.

## conglutlnate
conglutlnate, tr. and intr. v., to glue together. —
L. conglutinatus, pp. of conglutinare, 'to glue
together', fr. con- and gltitinare, 'to glue', fr.
gluten, gen. glutinis, 'glue'. See gluten, glue.

## conglutination
conglutination, n. — L. congliitinatio, gen. -onis,
'a gluing together', fr. conglutinatus, pp. of
conglutinare. See prec. word and -ion.

## congou
congou, also Congo, п., a kind of black China tea.
— Chin, kung-fu, 'labor'.

## congratulaat
congratulaat, adj. — L. congrdtulans, gen. -antis,
pres. part, of congratulari. See next word and
-ant.

## congratulate
congratulate, tr. v. — Fr. L. congratulatus, pp. of
congratulari, 'to wish joy warmly, congratulate',
fr. con- and gratulari, 'to wish joy', fr. gratus,
'pleasing'. See grace, п., and cp grateful.
Derivatives: congratulation (q.v.), congratulat-
or, п., congratulat-ory, adj.

## congratulation
congratulation, n. — F-, fr. L. congrdtuldtionem,
ace. of congratulatio, fr. congratulatus, pp. of
congratulari. See prec. word and -ion.

## coagregant
coagregant, п., a member of a congregation. —
L. congregans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of congre-
gore. See next word and -ant.

## congregate
congregate, adj., assembled. — L. congregatus,
'flocking together', pp. of congregdre, 'to flock
together', fr. con- and gregare, 'to gather into
a flock', from grex, gen. gregis, 'flock'. See
gregarious and adj. suff. -ate.

## congregate
congregate, tr. and intr. v., to gather into a crowd;
to assemble. — L. congregatus, pp. of
congregdre. See prec. word.

## congregation
congregation, n. — F. congregation, fr. L. con-
gregationem, ace. of congregatio, fr.
congregatus, pp. of congregdre. See congregate, adj., and
-ation.
Derivatives: congregation-al, adj.,
congregational-ism, п., congregational-ist, n.

## congress
congress, n. — L. congressus, 'a coming together,
a friendly meeting', fr. congressus, pp. of con-
gredt, 'to come or go together', fr. con- and
gradi, pp. gressus, 'to step, walk, go'. See grade,
'step', and cp. gradus and retrograde. The change
of Latin d (in gradi) to e (in con-gressus) is due
to the Latin linguistic law according to which,
in the second element of compounds, d in a
closed radical syllable regularly became ё. See
accent and cp. words there referred to. (The pp.
of gradi should be *grassus. The form gressus
is due to the influence of the past participles of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:185 COLUMN:3 -->
the compounds: con-gressus, pro-gressus, etc.)
Derivatives: congress-er, п., congress/on (q.v.),
congress-ive, adj.

## congressional
congressional, adj., 1) pertaining to a congress;
2) (cap.) pertaining to Congress. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. congressio, gen. -onis, 'a
coming together', fr. congressus, pp. of con-
gredi, 'to come or go together'. See congress
and -ion.
Derivatives: congression-al, adj., congresshn-
alist (q.v.), congression-al-ly, adv.

## congressionalist
congressionalist, п., an adherent of a congress. —
Formed fr. congression with adj. suff. -al and
iuff. -ist.

## congressist
congressist, п., a member of a congress. —
Formed fr. congress with suff. -ist.

## Congreve rocket
Congreve rocket, Coagreve match. — Both named
after their inventor Sir William Congreve
(1772-1828).

## congruence
congruence, congruency, n. — L. congruentia,
'agreement, harmony', fr. congruins, gen. -entis,
'agreeing'. See congruent and -ce, resp. -cy.

## congruent
congruent, adj., agreeing,
corresponding,-coinciding. — L. congruens, gen. -entis, pres. part.
oicongruere, 'to come together, coincide, agree',
fr. con- and *-gruere, which occurs also in L.
ingruere, 'to rush or break into', and is of
uncertain etymology. L. ruere, 'to fall violently',
is not rel. to congruere, ingruere.
Derivative: congruent-ly, adv.

## congruity
congruity, п., agreement, correspondence,
coincidence. — F. congruite, fr. Late L. congrui-
tdtem, ace. of congruitds, fr. congruus. See
congruous and -ity.

## congruous
congruous, adj., congruent, fitting, suitable. —-
L. congruus, 'fit, suitable, congruous', fr.
congruere. See congruent. For E. -ous, as equivalent
to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: congruous-ly, adv., congruous-
ness, n.

## conic
conic, adj., i) pertaining to a cone; 2) cone-
shaped or resembling a cone. — F. conique, fr.
Gk. κωνικός, 'pertaining to a cone', fr. κώνος,
'cone'. See cone and -ic.
Derivatives: conic-al, adj., conic-al-ly, adv.,
conic-al-ness, п., conic-ity, n.

## conidium
conidium, п., an asexual cell occurring in certain
fungi. — ModL., formed with the ModL. di-
min. suff. -idium fr. Gk. κόνις, 'dust'. See conio-.

## conifer
conifer, п., a cone-bearing tree (bot.) — L.,
compounded of cdnus, 'cone', and ferre, 'to bear*.
See cone and -fer.

## coniferous
coniferous, adj., cone-bearing. — See prec. word
and -ferous.

## coniform
coniform, adj., having the form of a cone. — See
cone and -form.

## conine
conine, п., a poisonous alkaloid, C,H17N, found
in hemlock (chem.) — Formed fr. Conium with
chem. suff. -ine.

## conio-
conio-, combining'form meaning 'dust'. — Gk.
κονιο-, fr. κάνις, 'dust', which is cogn. with L.
cinis, 'ashes'. See cinerary and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also the second element in
anthraconite.

## Conioselinum
Conioselinum, п., a genus of plants of the carrot
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Conium
and Gk σέλινον, 'celery'. See celery.

## Conium
Conium, п., a genus of poisonous plants of the
carrot family (bot.) — L. conium, 'hemlock', fr.
Gk. κώνειον, of s.m., which is prob. rel. to
κώνος, 'pine cone, fir cone'. See cone.

## conjecture
conjecture, п., i) guesswork; 2) guess. — L.
conjee tura, 'inference, conclusion' (whence also F.
conjecture), fr. conjectus, pp. of conicere (less
correctly conjicere), 'to throw together; to infer,
conclude', fr. con- and jacere, 'to throw'. See
jet, 'to spirt forth', and -ure. For the change of
Latin a (in jacere) to ё (in con-jectus) see accent
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: conjecture, tr. and intr. v., con-
jectur-able, adj., conjectur-abl-y, adv.,
conjectural, adj., conjectur-al-ly, adv.

## conjoin
conjoin, tr. v. — ME. conjoinen, fr. F. conjoindre,
fr. L. conjungere, 'to join together' (whence also
It. congiungere, Proveng. conjonher), fr. con- and
jungere, 'to join'. See join and cp. conjoint,
conjugnte.
Derivatives: conjoin-ed, adj., conjoin-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:186 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 159 | CONSECRATE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:186 COLUMN:1 -->

## conjoint
conjoint, adj. — F. conjoint, pp. of conjoindre.
See prec. word and conjunct and cp. disjoint.
Derivatives: conjoint-ly, adv., conjoint-ness, n.

## conjugal
conjugal, adj., of marriage. — L. conjugate,
'relating to marriage' (whence also F. conjugal),
fr. L. conjux (later form conjunx), gen. conjugis,
'spouse', which is rel. to conjungere, 'to join
together'. See conjoin and adj. sun", -al.
Derivatives: conjugality (q.v.), conjugal-ly, adv.

## conjugality
conjugality, n. — Coined by Milton fr. prec. word
and stiff, -ity.

## conjugate
conjugate, tr. and intr. v. — L. conjugatus, pp. of
conjugare, 'to join together, unite', fr. con- and
jugare, 'to join; to yoke; to marry', which is
rel. to jugum, 'yoke', jungere, 'to join'. See join
and verbal stiff, -ate and cp. jugate. Cp. also
conjoin.

## conjugate
conjugate, adj. — L. conjugatus, pp. of conjugare.
See conjugate, v.
Derivative: conjugate-ly, adv.

## conjugation
conjugation, n. — L. conjugatio, gen. -onis, 'a
combining, connecting, conjugation', fr.
conjugatus, pp. of conjugare. See conjugate, v., and
-ion. In its grammatical sense, L. conjugatio is
a loan translation of Gk. συζυγία, lit. 'a yoking,
or binding, together'.
Derivatives: conjugation-al, adj.,
conjugation-ally, adv.

## conjunct
conjunct, adj., joined together, united (archaic).
— L. conjunctus, pp. of conjungere, 'to join
together'. See conjoin and cp. conjoint.
Derivatives: conjunct, п., conjunct-ly, adv.

## conjunction
conjunction, n. — ME., fr. OF. ( = F.)
conjunction, fr. L. conjunctionem, ace. of conjunctio, fr.
conjunctus, pp. of conjungere. See conjunct and
-ioa. Cp. It. congiunzione, OProvenc. conjunctio,
Sp. conjuncidn, which all derive fr. L.
conjunctionem. In its grammatical sense L.
conjunctio is a loan translation of Gk. σύνδεσμος
(fr. συνδεϊν, 'to bind together').
Derivatives: conjunction-al, adj.,
conjunction-ally, adv.

## conjuactiva
conjuactiva, п., the mucous membrane which
covers the inner surface of the eyelids (anat.) —
Medical L. (short for membrana conjunctiva),
fern, of L. conjunctiva, 'serving to connect,
connective'. See next word.
Derivative: conjunctiv-al, adj.

## conjunctive
conjunctive, adj. — L. conjunctiva, 'serving to
connect, connective', fr. conjunctus, pp. of
conjungere. See conjunct and -ive and cp.
disjunctive, subjunctive.
Derivatives: conjunctive, п., conjunctive-ly, auv.,
conjunctive-ness, n.

## conjunctivitis
conjunctivitis, п., inflammation of the conjunctiva
(med.) — A Medical L. hybrid formed fr.
Medical L. conjunctiva (fern, of L. conjunctivus), with
-ids, a suff. of Greek origin. See conjunctiva.

## conjuration
conjuration, n. — ME., fr. OF. (— F.)
conjuration, fr. L. conjurationem, ace. of conjuratio, lit.
'a swearing together, conspiracy', fr. conjuratus,
pp. of conjurare; cp. It. congiurazione and Sp.
conjuracian, which are of the same origin. See
conjure and -ation.

## coajure
coajure, tr. v. — ME. conjuren, fr. OF. (= F.)
conjurer, fr. L. conjurare, 'to swear together,
conspire', fr. con- and jurare, 'to swear an oath'.
See jury.
Derivatives: conjur-er, conjur-or, conjur-ing,
nouns.

## conk
conk, п., nose (slang). — The same as conch.

## conn
conn, tr. v., to direct the steering of a ship. —
Fr. obsol. cond, fr. ME. conduen, 'to lead,
guide', fr. MF. (— F.) conduire, fr. L. conducere.
See conduce and cp. conning tower.
Derivative: conn-er, n.

## connate
connate, adj., born with. — Late L. connatus, pp.
of connascl, 'to be born with, to be born at the
same time', fr. con- and ndsci, 'to be born'. See
natal and cp. cognate.

## connatnral
connatnral, adj., i) innate; 2) born at the same
time. — ML. conndturalis, 'of the same nature;
inborn'. See con- and natural.

## connect
connect, tr. and intr. v. — L. connectere, 'to bii:d
or join together', fr. con- and nectere, 'to tie,
bind, join', fr. I.-E. base *ned-, 'to twist, knot';
see net and cp. nexus, annex. L. nectere was
influenced in form by pectere, 'to comb, dress,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:186 COLUMN:2 -->
weed'.
Derivatives: connect-ed, adj., connected-ly, adv.,
connect-ed-ness, п., connect-ive, adj., connect-
ive-ly, adv., connect-iv-ity, n.

## connection
connection, connexion, n. — L. connexid, gen.
-onis, 'a binding or joining together, connection',
fr. connexus, pp. of connectere. See prec. word
and -ion. The spelling connection is due to the
influence of the many English nouns in -Hon
(fr. L. -tidnem).
Derivative: connection-al, connexion-al, adj.

## connellite
connellite, п., copper chloride with copper sulfate
(mineral.) — Named after A. Connel, who
analyzed it. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
conning tower (naut.) — The first word is the pres.
part, of conn (q.v.)

## conniption
conniption, п., a fit of hysteria (U.S. Slang). —
Of unknown origin.

## connivance
connivance, n. — F. connivence, fr. L. coniventia,
conniventia, fr. conivens, connivens, gen. -entis.
See conniveat and -ance.

## connive
connive, intr. v., to pretend ignorance. — L. conl-
ved, conivere, less exactly spelled connived, con-
nivere, 'to close the eyes, blink, wink at,
overlook (errors), connive at', which stands for
*con-cni(g)ued and is formed fr. con- and I.-E.
base 'kneigMfi-, 'to bend', whence also L. nictd,
niclare, 'to wink, blink', riitor, nlti [for *nlvitor
(fr. *kneig"hetor) or *nivitor (fr. *knigwhetdr)\
'to strive, make an effort, exert oneself, Goth.
hneiwan, 'to bend toward', OE., OS., OHG. hni-
gan, ON. hniga, MHG. nigen, G. neigen, 'to
bend, bow'. Cp. nictitate, nisus, realtent.
Derivatives: connivent (q.v.), conniv-er, n.

## connivent
connivent, adj. — L. conivens, connivens, gen.
■entis, pres. part, of conivere, connivere. See
prec. word and -enf.

## connoisseur
connoisseur, п., a critical judge. — OF. conois-
seor, conoisseur (F. connoisseur), fr. conoistre
(F. connaltre), 'to know', fr. L. cognoscere, 'to
become acquainted with, perceive, understand,
know'. See cognition.

## connotate
connotate, tr. v. — ML. connotatus, pp. of
connotare. See connote and verbal suff. -ate and cp.
annotate.
Derivatives: connotation (q.v.), connotat-ive,
adj., connotat-ive-ly, adv.

## connotation
connotation, n. —- ML. connolatid, gen. -onis, fr.
connotatus, pp. of connotare. See next word and
-ion and cp. annotation.

## coanote
coanote, tr. v. —■ ML. connotare, 'to mark
together', fr. con-, and L. notare, 'to mark', fr.
nota, 'a mark'. See note.
Derivatives: connot-ive, adj., connot-ive-ly, adv.

## connubial
connubial, adj., pertaining to marriage. — L.
conubialis (later connubialis), 'pertaining to
marriage', fr. cambium (later connubium),
'marriage', fr. со- and the stem oinubere (pp. nuptus),
'to marry'. See nuptial and cp. nubile.
Derivatives: connubial-ity, п., connubial-ly, adv.

## cono-
cono-, before a vowel con-, combining form
denoting the cone. — Gk. κώνο-, κων-, fr. κώνος,
'cone'. See cone.

## conodont
conodont, п., any of certain minute fossils of a
toothlike shape. — Compounded of Gk. κώνος,
'cone', and οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See
cono- and odonto-.

## conoid
conoid, adj., cone-shaped. — Gk. κωνοειδής,
'conical, cone-shaped', compounded of κώνος,
'cone', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'.
See cone and -oid.
Derivative: conoid, n.

## Conopholis
Conopholis, п., a genus of plants of the broom-
rape family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
Gk. κώνος, 'cone' (see cone), and φολίς, 'scale*,
which is cogn. with φελλός, 'cork tree, cork' (see
phello- and cp. words there referred to); so
called because the upper scales form bracts to
the flowers, resembling those of the fir cone.

## Conopophagidae
Conopophagidae, n. pi., a genus of birds, the ant
pipit (ornithol.) — ModL., lit. 'gnat eaters',
formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk. κώνωψ, 'gnat,
mosquito', and the stem of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See
canopy and phago-.

## conquer
conquer, tr. and intr. v. — ME. conqueren, fr. OF.
conquerre, St. VL. 'conquaerere. 'to seek with
care, conquer' (remodeled after L. quaerere, *to
seek'), for L. conquirere, 'to seek for' (whence

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:186 COLUMN:3 -->
Olt. conquidere; F. conquerir, 'to conquer', is a
new formation after quirir, 'to seek', fr. VL.
'quaerire, which corresponds to L. quaerere).
L. conquirere is formed fr. con- and quaerere,
'to seek'. See quaere and cp. conquest. Cp. also
acquire, inquire, require.
Derivatives: conquer-able, adj., conquerable-
ness, п., conquer-ing, adj., conquer-ing-ly, adv.,
conqueror (q.v.)

## conqueror
conqueror, n. — ME. conquereour, fr. OF. con-
quereor, fr. conquerre, 'to conquer'. See prec.
word and agential suff. -or.

## conquest
conquest, n. — ME., partly fr. OF. conquest (F.
conquel), 'acquisition', partly fr. OF. conqueste
(F. conquite), 'acquisition, conquest'. These
words prop, are the masc, resp. fern. pp. of OF.
conquerre, and derive fr. VL. 'conquaesitus,
resp. "conquaesila (corresponding to L. con-
quisitus, conquisila), pp. of *conquaerere. See
conquer and cp. conquistador.

## conquian
conquian, п., a card game with two players. —
Fr. Sp. icon quieni, 'with whom?' Sp. con derives
fr. L. cum, 'with'; see ] st eon-. Sp. quien comes fr.
L. quern, ace. oiquis, 'who'; see who. Cp. cooncan.

## conquistador
conquistador, п., a conqueror, applied esp. to the
Spanish conquerors of Mexico and Peru. — Sp.,
fr. conquistar, 'to conquer', fr. VL. conquistare,
St. L. conquisitus, pp. of conquirere, 'toseek for';
see conquer. L. conquisitus stands for *con-
quaesltus. For the change of Latin ae (in quae-
situs) to ί (in con-qulsitus) see acquire and cp.
words there referred to.

## Conrad
Conrad, masc. PN. — G. Konrad or F. Conrade,
fr. OHG. Kuonrat, which is compounded of
kuon, 'bold', and rat, 'counsel'; hence Conrad
lit. means 'bold in counsel'. See keen and rede.

## consanguine
consanguine, adj., consanguineous. — F. con-
sanguin, fr. L. cdnsanguineus. See next word.

## consangniaeous
consangniaeous, adj., of the same blood; having
the same ancestor. — L. cdnsanguineus, 'of the
same blood, related by blood', fr. con- and
sanguineus, 'of blood', fr. sanguis, gen. sanguinis,
'blood'. See sangnine and cp. sanguineous.. For
E. -ous, as corresponding to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivative: consanguineous-ly, adv.

## consanguinity

contra-, pref. meaning 'against, opposite to'. —

to, opposed to', prop. abl. fem. sing, of *com-
tro, which was formed fr. OL. com, 'with,
together with' and -tr, zero degree of the compar.
suff. -ter-, which appears in L. alter, 'lhe other
(of two)'. Contra orig. denoted the being
together of two things compared with each other.
For the first element see com-. For the second
see -ther and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also counter, adv., contrary, country, and the first
element in contrast.

ion-ary, adj., convolut-ive, adj.

## convolve
convolve, tr. v., to roll up together; intr. v., to
revolve together. — L. convolvere, 'to roll
together, roll round, roll up', fr. con- and volvere,
'to roll'. See volute and cp. prec. word.

## Coavolvulaceae
Coavolvulaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the
morning-glory family (бог.) — ModL., formed
fr. Convolvulus with sun*, -aceae.

## convolvulaceous
convolvulaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Convolvulus
Convolvulus, п., a genus of plants, the bindweed
(бол) — L. convolvulus, 'the bindweed', a
diminutive noun formed fr. convolvere, 'to roll
together'. See coavolve and -ule.

## convoy
convoy, tr. v., to escort for protection. — OF.
convoier (F. convoyer), 'to escort', fr. VL. con-
viare, lit. 'to go together with somebody'. Соя-
voy is the doublet of convey (q.v.)

## convoy
convoy, п., a protecting escort. — OF. (= F.)
convoi, fr. convoier, 'to convoy'. See convoy, v.

## convulse
convulse, tr. v., to shake violently. — L.
convulsus, pp. of convellere, 'to tear up, pull up, shake,
destroy, overthrow', fr. con- and vellere, 'to
pluck, pull, twitch'. See vellicate and cp. words
there referred to.

## convulsion
convulsion, n. — L. convulsio, gen. -onis, 'cramp,
convulsion', fr. convulsus, pp. of convellere. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: convulsion-al, convulsion-ary, adjs.

## convulsive
convulsive, adj. — F. convulsif (fem. convulsive),
fr. L. convulsus, pp. of convellere. See convulse
and -ive.
Derivatives: convulsive-ly, adv., convulsive-
ness, n.

## coay
coay, coney, п., a rabbit. — ME. coning, coni, fr.
OF. conin, fr. L. cumculus, 'rabbit', a word of
Sp.-Iberian origin. Cp. Basque unchi, 'rabbit'.
Cp. also cunlcnlus. The alteration of OF. -in
to ME. -ing is due to a change of suff.; cp.
pudding, fr. F. boudin.

## coo
coo, intr. and tr. v., to utter the sound
characteristic of doves and pigeons. — Of imitative
origin; coined by John Dryden (1631-1700).
Derivatives: coo, п., coo-er, п., coo-ing, adj.,
coo-ing-ly, adv.

## cooee
cooee, cooey, interj. and п., cry used as a signal
by the Australian aborigines and adopted by
the Australian colonists. — Of imitative origin.

## cooja
cooja, п., an earthenware jar {India). — Hind.
kiiju, fr. Pers. kuza, which is rel. to Avestic

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:192 COLUMN:2 -->
xawza-, 'pot'.

## cook
cook, n. — ME. coc, fr. OE. coc, fr. VL. cocus,
fr. L. coquus, 'cook', fr. coquere, 'to cook'
(whence L. coquina, culina, 'kitchen', rel. to Os-
can popina, of s.m.), cogn. with OI. pacati,
'cooks' .pacyati, 'ripens' (intr.), pakvah, 'cooked,
ripe', Toch. В pepaksu, 'cooked', A p(u)kalune,
'ripening', Arm. ephem, 'cook', hac, 'bread', Gk.
πέσο-etv, πέπτειν, 'to soften, ripen, boil, cook',
πέπων, 'cooked by the sun, ripe, soft, sweet', the
second element in άρτο-κόπος (for *άρτο-πόκος)>
'baker', lit. 'bread baker', Alb. pjek, Ί bake',
Lith. kepii, kipti (metathesis for *peku, *pikti),
'to bake, roast', OSlav. *pekp, 'peSti, 'to bake',
pelenu, 'roasted', реки, 'heat', pelt, 'oven', OE.
a-figen, 'roasted', W. pobl, Co. pobas, 'to bake',
W. poeth, 'cooked, baked, hot', Bret, pobet,
'baked'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*peqw- (in Latin and in the Celtic languages
assimilated into *qweqw-), 'to cook'. Cp. apricot,
biscuit, concoct, cotta, culinary, decoct, dyspepsia,
kiln, kitchen, melon, pepo, pepsin, peptic,
precocious, pucka, pumpkin, quittor, terra cotta, and
the second element in crumpet, drnpe.
Derivatives: cook, tr. and intr. v., cook-er, п.,
cook-ery, n.

## cooky
cooky, also cookie, п., a small cake.—Du. koekje,
dimin. of коек, 'cake'. See cake and dimin.
suff. -y.

## cool
cool, adj. — ME. cole, fr. OE. col, rel. to MDu.
coel, Du. koel, OHG. kuoli, MHG. kiiele, G.
kiihl, 'cool', ON. kola, OE. colon, 'to be cold,
freeze', fr. I.-E. base *gel-, 'cold, to freeze',
whence also L. gelu, 'frost, cold', gelare, 'to
freeze', gelidus, 'icy, frosty', glacils, 'ice'. Cp.
cold, chill, keel, 'to keep cool', Cp. alsocongeal,
gelatin, gelid, glacier, jelly.
Derivatives: cool, п., cool, v. (q.v.), cool-ly, adv.,
cool-ness, n.

## cool
cool, intr. and tr. v. — OE. colian, 'to grow cold,
to cool', fr. col, 'cool'. Cp. OE. cllan, 'to make
cold', fr. earlier 'koljan, hence derivatively
identical with OE. culian. See cool, adj.
Derivatives: cool-er, п., cool-ing, adj., cool-ing-
ly, adv., cool-ing-ness, n.

## coolie
coolie, cooly, п., an unskilled laborer in Asia. —
Hind, quli, prob. fr. Kull, Koli, name of an
aboriginal tribe of Gujarat, India.

## coolth
coolth, n. — Formed fr. cool with suff. -th (on
analogy of warmth, fr. warm). Cp. tilth, formed
on the analogy of wealth.

## coomb
coomb, coom, п., a measure of grain. — ME.
combe, fr. OE. cumb, 'vessel, a measure', rel. to
MLG. kump, MHG., G. kumpf, 'a deep basin,
bowl, trough', G. Kumme, 'a deep bowl'.

## coomb
coomb, combe, п., a deep valley. — OE. cumb, of
Celtic origin. See combe.

## coon
coon, п., ι) a raccoon; 2) a Negro. — Shortened
from raccoon (q.v.)

## cooncan
cooncan, п., a card game. — Corruption of
conquian.

## coop
coop, n. — ME. cope, 'a basket', corresponding
to OE. *сйре (cp. OE. cype, 'cask'), fr. L. сира,
'cask, tub'. See cup.
Derivative: cooper (q.v.)

## cooper
cooper, п., one who makes barrels. — ME. cou-
per, prob. fr. MLG. kuper (cp. Du. kuiper, G.
Kiifer, of s.m.), fr. L. сира. See prec. word and
agential suff. -er.
Derivatives: cooper-age, п., cooper-y, n.

## cooper
cooper, also coper, п., a kind of vessel. — Du.
koper, 'trading vessel', fr. kopen, 'to buy,
trade', fr. koop, 'purchase'. See cheap, n.

## co-operant
co-operant, adj. and n. — Late L. cooperans, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of cooperari. See co-operate
and -ant.

## co-operate
co-operate, intr. v. — Fr. Late L. cooperatus,
pp. of cooperari, 'to work together with', fr. co-
and L. operari, 'to work, labor'. See opernte.
Derivatives: co-operation (q.v.), co-operat-ive,
adj. and п., co-operat-ive-ly, adv., cooperat-ive-
ness, n.

## co-operation
co-operation, n. — Late L. cooperatio, 'a working
together', fr. cooperatus, pp. of cooperari. See
prec. word and -ion.

## Cooperla
Cooperla, п., a genus of plants of the amaryllis
family (hot.) — ModL., named after Daniel
Cooper, an English botanist of the 19th cent.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:192 COLUMN:3 -->
•For the ending see suff. -ia.

## co-opt
co-opt, tr. v. — L. cooptare, 'to choose, elect', fr.
со- and optare, 'to wish, desire, require, demand,
choose'. See option and cp. adopt

## co-optation
co-optation, n. — L. cooptatio, gen. -onis, fr.
cooptatus, pp. of cooptare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## co-optative
co-optative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
cooptatus, pp. of cooptare. See co-opt and cp.
optative.

## co-ordinate
co-ordinate, adj. — Formed fr. со- and ordinate
(fr. L. ordinatus).
Derivatives: co-ordinate, n. and tr. v.,
co-ordination nw co-ordinat-ive, adj., co-ordinat-or, п.,
co-ordinat-ory, adj.

## coot
coot, п., a web-footed water bird. — ME. cote,
coote, rel. to Du. koet; of uncertain origin.

## cop
cop, п., the top of anything; a mound. — ME.
cop, coppe, fr. OE. cop, copp, 'summit', rel, to
OE. cuppe, 'cup', ON. koppr, 'cup-shaped
vessel', MLG. kopp, OHG. chuph, kopf, 'cup',
MHG. kopf, 'drinking vessel; skull', G. Kopf,
'head', Du. kop, 'head; cup'. All these words
are traceable to Late L. cuppa, 'cup'. See cup
and cp. kopje. For the sense development of the
Teut. words cp. corrie and tete-a-tete.

## cop
cop, tr. v., to catch, arrest (slang). — A dial. var.
of obsol. cap, 'to seize', which derives fr. OF.
caper, 'to seize', fr. L. capere. See captive and
cp. copper, 'policeman'.

## cop
cop, п., a policeman (slang). — Shortened fr.
copper, 'policeman'.

## copaiba
copaiba, п., an oily resin obtained from trees of
the genus Copaiva (pharm.) — Sp. and Port.
copaiba, fr. Tupi copaiba.

## Copaifera
Copaifera, also Copaiva, п., a genus of trees of
the senna family (bot.) — ModL. See prec. word
and -ferous.

## copal
copal, п., a resin. — Sp. copal, fr. Nahuatl
copalli, 'resin'.

## coparcenary
coparcenary, п., joint heirship. — Formed fr. co-
and parcenary.

## coparcener
coparcener, п., a joint heir. — Formed fr. со- and
parcener.

## copartner
copartner, n. — Formed fr. со- and partner.
Derivatives: copartner-y, п., copartner-ship, n.

## cope
cope, п., a long mantle worn by ecclesiastics. —
ME. cope, fr. earlier cape, fr. Late L. cappa,
'hood, mantle'. See cape, 'a sleeveless cloak',
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: cope, tr. v., to dress in, or furnish
with, a cope, coping (q.v.)

## cope
cope, intr. v., to struggle, deal with. — ME. cou-
pen, fr. OF. colper, couper, 4o strike' (whence
also F. couper, 'to cut'), fr. colp, coup (F. coup),
'stroke, blow'. See coup and cp. words there
referred to. Derivative: cop-ing, n.

## cope
cope, tr. and intr. v., formerly 10 buy; now, to
barter (dial. Eng.) — ME. copen, fr. MDu. copen
(Du. kopen), 'to buy', which is related to OE.
ce~apian, of s.m. See cheap, v.

## copeck
copeck, n. — A var. spelling of kopeck.

## copepod
copepod, п., a minute crustacean pertaining to
the order Copepoda. — See next word.

## Copepodn
Copepodn, n. pi., an order of minute crustaceans
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. κώπη,
'handle of an oar, oar', and πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. Gk. κώπη is rel. to κάπτειν, 'to swallow
greedily*, and cogn. with L. capere, 'to catch,
seize, hold'. See captive. For the second element
see -poda-

## coper
coper, п., a barterer, dealer. — Formed fr. cope,
'to barter', with agential suff. -er.

## coper
coper, п., a kind of vessel. — See cooper.

## Copemican
Copemican, adj., pertaining to Copernicus (1473-
'543) or his system. For the ending see suff. -nn.

## copestone
copestone, п., a coping stone. — See cope,
'mantle', and cp: coping.

## cophosis
cophosis, п., deafness (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
κώφωσις, fr. κωφός, 'deaf, dull', which stands
in gradational relationship to κηφήν 'dull, lazy;
drone'. For the ending see suff. -osis.

## copier
copier, n. — Formed from the verb copy with
agential suff. -er.

## coping
coping, п., course of a wall, sloped to carry off
water (archil) — Formed fr. cope, 'to furnish
with a mantle' (see cope, 'mantle'), with subst.
suff. -Ing.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:193 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: COPIOUS | 166 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:193 COLUMN:1 -->

## copious
copious, adj. — L. cdpiosus, 'well supplied,
plentiful, abounding, copious', fr. cdpia, 'plenty,
abundance', contraction of *co-opia, fr. со- and
ops, gen. opis, 'power, might, abundance, wealth,
riches, treasure'. See opalent, and cp. copy and
the second element in cornucopia. For the ending
see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: copious-ly, adv., copious-ness, n.

## copped
copped, adj., rising to a point. — Formed fr. cop,
'top', with suff. -ed.

## copper
copper, п., a reddish metal. — ME. coper, fr. OE.
copor, coper, fr. Late L. cuper, fr. L. cuprum,
'copper', fr. earlier cyprum, fr. aes Cyprium, lit.
'Cyprian brass', fr. Gk. κύπριον, 'Cyprian
(brass)', neut. of Κύπριος, 'of Cyprus', fr.
Κύπρος, 'Cyprus'; so called because Cyprus was the
place par excellence from which the ancients
obtained copper. For the etymology of Cyprus
see Cyprian, adj. Cp. cupreous. Cp. also kipper
and the first element in copperas.
Derivatives: copper, tr. v., to cover with copper,
copper-y, adj.

## copper
copper, п., policeman (slang). — Prob. formed fr.
cop, 'to catch', with agential suff. -er and lit.
meaning 'catcher'.

## copperas
copperas, п., ι) green vitriol; 2) sulfate of iron. —
ME. coperose, fr. OF. couperose, fr. ML. cupri
rosa, 'rose of copper', fr. gen. of cuprum, 'copper',
and rosa, 'rose'; see copper and rose. Cp. It.
copparosa, Sp. caparrosa, which are of the same
origin.

## coppice
coppice, п., a wood of small trees. — OF. colpeis,
copeiz, 'cut wood, brushwood', fr. colper, cou-
per (F. couper), 'to strike', fr. colp, coup, 'stroke,
blow'. See conp and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: coppice, tr. v., coppic-ed, adj.

## copple
copple, п., a crest on a bird's head. — Formed fr.
cop, 'top', with the dimin. suff. -le.
Derivative: coppl-ed, adj.

## coppy
coppy, п., a dialectal form of coppice. — This
word owes its existence to a double error. The
noun coppice (q.v.) was misspelled coppies, and
this latter was mistaken for a plural, from which
the singular coppy was reconstructed.
сорт-, form of сорго- before a vowei.

## copra
copra, п., the dried kernel of the coconut. —
Port., fr. Malayalam koppara, fr. Hind, khoprd,
rel. to Hind, khoprl and khappar, 'skull', fr. OI.
kharparah, 'skull'. See Yule-Burnill, Hobson-
Jobson, p. 254.
сорго-, before a vowel сорт-, combining form
meaning 'dung'. — Fr. Gk. κόπρος, 'dung,
excrement, filth, dirt', which is cogn. with OI.
Sdkrt, 'dung', and prob. also with Lith. Siku,
Sikli, 'to go to stool'.

## coprolith
coprolith, п., fossil dung. — Compounded of
сорго- and Gk. λίθος, 'stone'. See -11th.

## coprology
coprology, п., the study of obscene literature. —
Compounded of сорго- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## cqprophagous
cqprophagous, adj., dung eating. — Compounded
of сорго- and Gk. -φάγος, 'eater of, from the
stem of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

## Coprosma
Coprosma, п., a genus of plants of the madder
family (hot.) — ModL., lit. 'of a filthy smell',
compounded of сорго- and Gk. οσμή, 'smell';
see osmium. The genus is so called in allusion
to the unpleasant odor of some species.

## copse
copse, n. — Short for coppice.
Derivatives: copse, tr. v., cops-y, adj.

## Copt
Copt, п., ι) a native Egyptian descended from
the ancient Egyptians; 2) a member of the
Coptic church. — ModL. Coptus, fr. Arab. Quft,
Qift, fr. Coptic Kuplios, Kuplaios, fr. Gk.
Αιγύπτιος, 'Egyptian'. See Egyptian.

## Coptic
Coptic, adj. — ModL. Copticus, fr. Coplus. See
prec. word and -ic
Derivative: Coptic, n.

## Coptis
Coptis, п., a genus of plants of the crowfoot
family (bot.) — ModL., from the stem of Gk.
κόπτειν, 'to cut', whence aiso κόμμα, 'something
cut off' (see comma); so called with reference
to its divided leaves.

## copula
copula, n. — L. copula, 'that which binds
together, band, bond', which stands for *co-
apula, and is formed fr. со- and a dimin. from
the stem of apio, apere, 'to join, fasten'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:193 COLUMN:2 -->
apt and cp. couple.

## copulate
copulate, intr. v. — L. copulalus, pp. of copulare,
'to bind together, copulate', fr. copulare. See
copula and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: copulation, copulative (qq.v.), co-
pulat-ory, adj.

## copulation
copulation, n. — F., fr. L. copuldtionem, ace.
of сбриШЧб, 'a binding together', fr. copulalus,
pp. of copulare. See prec. word and -ion.

## copulative
copulative, adj. — F. copulatif (fern, copulative},
fr. L. copulativus, fr. copulalus, pp. of copulare.
See copulate and -ive.
Derivatives: copulative, п., copulative-ly, adv.

## copy
copy, n. — ME. copie, fr. MF..(= F.) copie,
'abundance; copy', fr. L. copia, 'plenty, abundance';
see copions. For sen se development see next word.

## copy
copy, tr. and intr. v. — F. copier, fr. ML. capture,
'to transcribe', orig. 'to write in plenty' (fr.
L. copia, 'plenty, abundance'), whence arose the
particular meaning 'to write the original text
many times'. See prec. word.

## copyist
copyist, n. — A hybrid coined fr. copy and -ist,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## coqnellcot
coqnellcot, п., red poppy. — F., fr. earlier coque-
licoq, 'cock', a word of imitative origin. The
name was given later to the flower, because its
color resembles that of the cockscomb. Cp.
cock.

## coquet
coquet, adj., coquettish. — F., 'coquettish', lit. 'a
little cock', dimin. of coq, 'cock'. See cock and
-et.
Derivatives: coquett-ish, adj., coquelt-ish-ly,
adv., coquetl-ish-ness, n.

## coquet
coquet, intr. v., to flirt. — F. coqueter, lit. 'to
behave like a cock', fr. coquet. See coquet, adj.

## coquetry
coquetry, n. — F. coauetterie, 'coquettishness,
flirtation, coquetry', fr. coquet, 'coquettish'.
See coquet, adj., and -ry.

## coquette
coquette, n. — F., fern, of coquet, 'coquettish'.
See coquet, adj.
coquin п., rogue, rascal. — F., prob. a derivative
of coq, 'cock'. See cock.

## coqnina
coqnina, п., a whitish rock consisting of
fragments of marine shells. — Sp., 'cockle,
shellfish', fr. OSp. coca, fr. VL. *cocca, fr. L. concha,
'mussel, shell'. See conch.

## coquito
coquito, п., a kind of South American palm tree.
— Sp., dimin. of coco. See cocoa, 'palm tree'.

## cor-
cor-, assimilated form of com- before r.

## Cora
Cora, fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Κόρη, orig. epithet
of Persephone, daughter of Demeter, fr. κόρη,
'maiden', rel. to κόρος, 'child, youth', which
prob. stand for *xopfa, resp. *κόρίος, fr. I.-E.
base 'iter-, 'to grow', whence also L. creare, 'to
create', crescere, 'to grow'. See create, crescent
and cp. core-. Corinna, Curetes and the second
element in Dioscuri, Halicore, hypocoristic

## Coracias
Coracias, п., a genus of birds, the common roller
(ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κορακίας, 'chough',
fr. κόραξ, gen. κόρακος, 'crow, raven'. See
coracoid.

## coracine
coracine, п., a perchlike Nile fish. — L. coracinus,
fr. Gk. κορακΐνος, 'a Nile fish', fr. κόραξ, gen.
κόρακος, 'crow, raven' [see coracoid and adj.
suff. -ine (representing L. -inus)]; so called from
its black color, Cp. crucian carp.

## coracie
coracie, п., a wicker boat. — W. corwgl, cwrwgl,
'coracle', dimin. of corwg, cwrwg, 'anything
round, the trunk of the body, carcass, boat', rel.
to Gael, curachan, 'coracle-1, dimin. of curach,
'boat, little ship,' fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to cut,
separate', whence also OI. krntdti, 'cuts', Gk.
κειρειν (for *κέρ-ιειν), 'to cut off', L. corium,
'hide, leather'. See corium and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also currach.

## coraco-
coraco-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
the coracoid process' (anat.) — Short for
coracoid. See next word.

## coracoid
coracoid, adj., pertaining to a process or bone
of the shoulder girdle (anal.) — Lit. 'resembling
a crow's beak', fr. Gk. κορακοειδής, which is
compounded of κόραξ, gen. κόρακος, 'crow',
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. For
the first element see raven and cp. corvine, for
the second see -oid.

## coral
coral, n. — ME., fr. OF. coral (F. corail), fr. L.
corallum, corallium (poet, curalium), fr. Gk.
κοράλλιον, prob. formed with the dimin. suff.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:193 COLUMN:3 -->
-ιόν fr. Heb. gordl, 'lot', which prob. meant
originally 'a small stone, pebble; a small stone for
casting lots', and is rel. to Arab, jural, jaural,
'stones, pebbles'. For the change of Heb. g to
Gk κ ср. Gk. κάμηλος, 'camel', fr. Heb.-Phoen.
gamal. For the sense development of Heb. goral
cp. Gk. ψήφος, 'pebble; vote', andκύαμος, 'bean;
lot'. The usual derivation of Gk. κοράλλιον fr.
κούρα αλός, 'puppet of the sea', is folk
etymology.

## coralline
coralline, adj. — Late L. corallinus, 'coral-red',
fr. L. corallum. See prec. word and adject,
suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## coralline
coralline, п., seaweed of the coral family (bot.) —
Fr. It. corallina, dimin. of corallo, 'coral', fr.
L. corallum. See coralline, adj.
corallite п., a fossil coral. — Formed fr. L.
corallum, 'red coral' (see coral), with subst. suff. -ite.

## coralloid
coralloid, adj., resembling coral. — Compounded
of coral and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -oid.

## Corallorhiza
Corallorhiza, n , a genus of orchids (bot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. κοράλλιον, 'coral'
and ρίζα, 'root'. See coral and rhizo-.

## coram
coram, prep., in the face of, in the presence of,
before. — L., fr. co(m)- (see com-, со-) and
"-Oram, which is formed (on analogy of clam,
'secretly', palam, 'openly'), fr. L. os, gen. -oris,
'mouth, face'. See oral.
coranto п., a lively dance. — Fr. F. (danse) cou-
rante, 'running (dance).' but assimil. to Sp.
words ending in -o. See current.

## corban
corban, п., an offering to God (Bible). — Heb.
qorbdn, 'offering, oblation' (whence Arab, qur-
bdn, Ethiop. qerban, of s.m.), lit. 'something
brought near', fr. Heb. qdrdbh, 'he came near',
which is rel. to Aram.-Syr. q'rebh, Arab, qdriba,
qdruba, Ethiop. qardba, 'he came near', Akkad.
qarabu, 'to come near'.

## corbeau
corbeau, п., a dark green color. — F. corbeau,
'raven', dimin. formed fr. OF. corp, fr. L. corvus,
'raven'. See raven and cp. the next two words,
Corvus and the first element in cormorant.

## corbel
corbel, п., a projection jutting out from the wall
(arch.) — OF. corbel (— F. corbeau), prop,
'raven', dimin. of OF. corp. See prec. word.
Derivatives: corbel, tr. and intr. v.,
corbelling, n.

## corbie
corbie, п., a raven; a carrion crow (Scot.) — OF.
corp, 'raven'. See corbean.

## corcopali
corcopali, п., the fruit of the Garcinia Indica
(India). — Compounded of Malayalam kodukka,
name of the fruit, and puli, 'acid'.

## cord
cord, n. — ME. corde, fr. OF. (= F.) corde,
'rope, string, twist, cord', fr. L. chorda, fr. Gk.
χορδή, 'intestine, string of gut'. See chord.
Derivatives: cord, tr. and inlr. v., cord-ed, adj.

## cordage
cordage, n. — F., fr. corde, 'rope, cord'. See prec.
word and -age.

## cordate
cordate, adj., heart-shaped. — L. cordatus, 'wise,
prudent' (in ModL. 'heart-shaped'), from cor,
gen. cordis, 'heart', which is cogn. with Goth.
hairto, OE. heorte, 'heart'. See heart and adj.
suff. -ate.
Derivative: cordate-ly, adv.

## Cordelier
Cordelier, п., a Franciscan friar. — F., formed
with suff. -ier, fr. OF. cordele (F. cordelle),
dimin. of corde, 'rope' (see cord and cp. cordelle);
so called in allusion to the girdle of knotted
cord worn by Franciscan friars.

## cordelle
cordelle, п., a towline. — I7., dimin. of corde. See
cord and cp. prec. word.

## cordial
cordial, adj. — Late L. cordialis, fr. L. cor, gen.
cordis, 'heart'. See cordate and -inl.
Derivatives: cordial, п., cordial-ity, п.,
cordially, adv., cordial-ness, n.

## cordiform
cordiform, adj., heart-shaped. — Compounded
of L. cor, gen. cordis, 'heart' and forma, 'form,
shape'. See cordate and form, n.

## Cordillera
Cordillera, п., one of several parallel mountain
ranges. — Sp., fr; cordilla, dimin. of cuerda,
'rope, cord', fr. L. chorda (see cord); hence the
name Cordilleras (pi.) given by the Spaniards
to the parallel ranges of the Andes.

## cordite
cordite, п., a smokeless explosive. — Formed fr.
cord with subst. suff. -ite.

## cordoba
cordoba, п., the monetary unit of Nicaragua. —
Sp. cordoba, named after Francisco de Cordoba

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:194 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 167 | CORNIFEROUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:194 COLUMN:1 -->
(died in 1526). Cp. Cordovas.

## cordoa
cordoa, η., ι) a guarded line; 2) an honorary cord
or ribbon. — F., fr. corde, 'lwist, cord, cordon,
ribbon (of an order)'. See cord.
cordon bleu. — Orig. the blue ribbon worn by the
knights of the Holy Ghost, the highest order in
France under the Bourbons; later used to
denote a distinguished person and, facetiously, a
first-rank cook. — F., 'blue ribbon'. See cordon
and blue.

## Cordovan
Cordovan, adj., of Cordova; n. (not cap).
Cordovan leather. — Sp. cordobdn, lit. 'Cordovan',
fr. Cordoba, name of the famous city of Spain,
fr. L. Corduba, fr. Gk. Κορδύβη. Ср. Cordoba,
cordwain, cordwalaer.

## corduroy
corduroy, п., a ribbed cotton fabric. — Perh. fr.
F. corde du roi, 'the king's cord'. See cord and
royal.
Derivatives: corduroy, adj., corduroy, tr. v.,
corduroy-ed, adj.

## cordwain
cordwain, п., Cordovan leather (archaic). — ME.
cordewane, 'leather of Cordova', fr. OF. cordoan,
cordouan. See next word.

## cordwainer
cordwainer, п., shoemaker. — ME. cordwaner,
fr. OF. cordoanier (F. cordonnier), 'shoemaker',
lit. 'a worker in Cordovan leather', fr. cordoan,
cordouan, 'Cordovan leather', fr. OProvenc.
cordoan, fr. Sp. cordobdn, 'Cordovan (leather)',
fr. Cordoba, 'Cordova'. See Cordovan. F.
cordonnier was influenced in form by F. cordon,
'cord, cordon'.

## Cordyline
Cordyline, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.xopSuXr), 'club' (seecor-
dylo-); so called in allusion to the thick caudex.

## cordylo-
cordylo-, before a vowel cordyl-, combining form
meaning 'club'. — Gk. κορδϋλο-, κορδϋλ-, fr.
κορδΰλη, 'club, cudgel, swelling, headdress',
which is of uncertain origin. See Frisk, GEW.,
I, p. 918 s.v. κορδΰλη.

## core
core, п., hard center of a fruit, etc. — Prob. fr.
L. cor, 'heart'; see cordate. For sense
development cp. Avestic zeredaya, 'middle', OSlav.
srudice, 'heart', sreda, 'middle', Russ. serdce,
'heart', sereaa, 'middle'; Wednesday (i.e. middle
of the week)', Lith. sirdis, 'heart', W. craidd,
'heart; center', Bret, kreiz, 'middle'; all these
words are cogn. with L. cor, 'heart'. Cp. also
Heb. lebh, 'heart', and lebk yam, 'the midst (lit.
the heart) of the sea', lebk ha'lla", 'the midst of
the terebinth', Akkad. libbu, 'heart; middle'.
Derivative: core, tr. v.

## core-
core-, combining form denoting the pupil of the
eye. — Gk. κόρη, 'girl; pupil of the eye'. See
Cora.

## Coregonus
Coregonus, п., a genus of salmonid fishes (ich-
thyol.) — ModL., compounded of core- and
Gk. γωνία, 'angle'. See -gon.

## coreligionist
coreligionist, n. — See со-, religion and -1st.

## Corema
Corema, п., a genus of plants of the crowberry
family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κόρημα, 'a
broom', a derivative of κορεϊν, 'to sweep out',
fr. κόρος, 'broom, besom', which is of unknown
etymology; so called from its bushy aspect.
For the ending see suff. -ma.

## Coreopsis
Coreopsis, п., a genus of yellow colored plants. —
ModL., compounded of Gk. κόρις, 'bug' and
βψις, 'sight, appearance'; see coriander and -op-
sis. The name Coreopsis was given to this genus
in allusion to the seeds which look like bugs.

## corespondent
corespondent, п., a joint respondent, esp. in a
divorce suit (law). — Formed fr. со- and
respondent.

## corf
corf, п., a basket. — MLG. korf, prob. fr. L.
corbis, 'basket', which prob. meant orig.
'something twisted or plaited', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qe-
reb(h)-, 'to twist, curve, contract, shrink', whence
ce also Gk. κάρφος, 'dry twigs, chips', κάρφειν,
'to dry up, wither', καρφαλέος, 'dry, parched',
Lith. skribti, 'to be dry', ON. herpask, 'to
contract convulsively'. Cp. the first element in Car-
phophis. it. corba 'wicker basket', derives fr. L.
corbis, whence also ON. korf, OHG. chorp, korb
(MHG. korp, korb, G. Korb), 'basket'. F. cor-
beille, 'basket', comes fr. L. corbicula, dimin. of
corbis; cp. corvette. — For derivatives of
*qremb-, a nasalized enlargement of base *qe-
reb-, see rumple. — Base *qereb(h)- is an
enlargement of base *(s)qer-, 'to turn, twist'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:194 COLUMN:2 -->
curve and cp. words there referred to.

## coriaceous
coriaceous, adj., leathery. — L. coriaceus, 'of
leather', fr. corium. See corium and -aceous.

## coriander
coriander, п., I) a plant of the carrot family (Co-
riandrum sativum); 2) its fruit. — F. coriandre,
fr. L. coriandrum, fr. Gk. κορίαννον, κορίαν-
δρον, which is of uncertain origin. It possibly
derives fr. κόρις, 'bedbug', which stands in gra-
dational relationship to άκαρής, 'small, tiny' (lit.
'too short to be cui'), άκαρι, 'mite'; fr. I.-E.
base *(s)qer-, 'to cut' (see shear and cp. corium);
the plant would have been so called from its
odor reminding that of the bedbug. Cp. the first
element in Coreopsis, Corimelaena.

## Coriandrum
Coriandrum, п., a genus of plants of the carrot
family (bot.) — L. See prec. word.

## Corimelaena
Corimelaena, п., a genus of insects, the negro bug
(entomol.)— ModL., lit.'black bug', fr.Gk. κόρις,
'bug', and μέλαινϋ, fern, of μέλας, 'black'. See
coriander and melano-.

## Corinna
Corinna, fern. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Kopiwm, prop,
dimin. of κόρη, 'maiden*. See Cora.

## Corinthian
Corinthian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -en
fr. L. Corinlhius, 'of Corinth', fr. Gk. Κορίνθιος,
fr. Κόρινθος, 'Corinth'. Cp. currant.

## corium
corium, п., vascular layer of the skin, the derma.
— L., 'hide, skin, leather', lit. 'the hide stripped
off', rel. to cortex, 'bark', scortum, 'skin, hide',
fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to cut, separate', whence
also OI. kftib, 'hide', carman-, Avestic iareman-,
'hide, skin', Russ. skora, 'hide', кого, 'bark,
rind', Gk. κορμός, 'trunk of a tree', OHG. scerm,
scirm, 'shield, defence, cover' (orig. 'the hide
covering the shield'), OHG. herdo, 'fleece', OE.
heorda, ON. horundr, 'skin', Mir. scairt,
'midriff, heart', W. corwg, cwrwg, 'trunk of the body,
carcass, boat', OE. sceran, sciran, 'to cut, shear'.
See shear and cp. words there referred to.

## Corixa
Corixa, п., a genus of insects (entomol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. κόρις, 'bug'. See coriander.

## cork
cork, n. — Sp. alcorque, 'corkwood soles', fr.
Mozarabic al-qurq, al-qorq, fr. Arab, al-, 'the',
and qurq, 'alcorque', which prob. derives
fr. L. quercus, 'oak*. See Quercus and cp. al-
comoqne.
Derivatives: cork, tr. V/, cork-age, п., cork-ed,
adj., cork-er, п., cork-y, adj., cork-i-ness, n.

## corm
corm, п., a subterranean bulb (bol.)—Gk. κορμός,
'trunk of a tree (with the boughs lopped off)'. See
corium.

## conno-
conno-, combining form denoting the trunk of a
tree. — Gk. κορμό-, fr. κορμός. See prec. word.

## cormophyte
cormophyte, п., any plant having a stem and a
root (bol.) — ModL. Cormophyta, pi., coined
by the Hungarian botanist Stephan Ladislaus
Endlicher (1S04-49) fr. Gk. κορμός, 'trunk of a
tree', and φυτόν, 'plant'. See conno- and -phyte.

## cormorant
cormorant, п., a large voracious sea bird. — F.
cormoran, fr. OF. cormaran, fr. earlier corma-
re(n)g, a word compounded of OF. corp,
'raven', fr. L. corvus (see corvine and cp. cor-
beau, corbel), and of marenc, 'pertaining to the
sea', fr. L. mare, 'sea' (see marine), and the Teut.
suff. -enc. The t in cormorant is due to a
confusion of the suff. -an (= Teut. -enc) with -ant
(fr. L. -ans, gen. -amis, the pres. part. suff. of
the verbs of the 1st conj.) Cp. ML. corvus ma-
rinus, whence Provenc. corpmari(n), Port, corvo
marinho.

## cormus
cormus, п., corm. — ModL., fr. Gk. κορμός. See
corm.

## corn
corn, п., grain. — ME., fr. OE. corn, rel. to OS.,
ΟΝ., OFris., OHG., MHG., G. .korn, MDu.
coren, corn, Du. koren, Goth, кайт, 'grain',
and cogn. with L. granum, 'grain, seed, small
kernel', Gk. γίγαρτον, 'grapestone, olivestone',
OSlav. zrino, zruno, 'grain', OPruss. syrne,
'kernel', Lith. ilrnis, Lett, zifnis, 'pea', W. grown,
pi., Olr. gran, 'granule', fr. I.-E. base *ger(i\-,
'to become ripe, grow old', whence also OI.
jdrati, jfryati, 'makes old, grows old', jdran,
'old', jariman-, 'old age', jdrab.^growing old',
jiryati, 'grows old' Jtrndh, 'old', Avestic zaur-
van-, 'old age', Pers. zar, 'old man', Ossetic
zarond, 'old man', Arm. cer, of s.m., Gk.
γέρων, 'old man', γηραλέος, 'old', γήρας, 'old
age', OSlav. zirlti, zreti, 'to ripen'. Cp. geronto-,
grain. Cp. also kernel. Cp. also churl and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:194 COLUMN:3 -->
words there referred to. Derivative: corn, tr. v.,
to granulate; to sprinkle with salt in grains; to
pickle with salt; intr. v., to form grains.

## corn
corn, п., a horny induration. — OF. corn (F.
cor), fr. L. согяй, 'horn'. F. corne, 'horn',
derives fr. VL. *corna (fr. L. cornua), pi. of L.
cornu, but was mistaken for a fem. sing. noun.
See horn and cp. cerato-. Cp. also the second
element in Capricorn, longicorn, unicorn.

## Comaceae
Comaceae, n. pi., a family of trees, the dogwood
family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Cornus with
suff. -aceae.

## cornaceous
cornaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## cornbrash
cornbrash, n. (geol.) — Compounded of corn,
'grain', and brash.

## cornea
cornea, п., the transparent portion of the external
coat of the eye (anat.) — L. cornea (short for
cornea tunica, lit. 'a horny coating'), fem. of
corneus, 'horny', fr. согяй, 'horn'. See horn and
cp. corn, 'a horny induration'.

## corneal
corneal, adj., pertaining to the cornea. — See
prec. word and adj. suff. -al.

## cornel
cornel, n. — MDui kornelle (Du. kornoelje), fr.
OF. corneille, cornille (F. cornouille), fr. Late L.
cornicula, dimin. of L. cornus, 'cornel tree',
which is cogn. with Gk. κρίνον, κράνεια, 'cornel
cherry', Lith. Kirnis, 'god of the cherry trees'.
Cp. cornelian.
Derivative: cornel-ian, adj. (in cornelian cherry).

## Cornelia
Cornelia, fem. PN. — L. Cornelia, fem. of
Cornelius. See Cornelius.

## cornelian
cornelian, п., a variety of chalcedony. — Formed
with change of suff. fr. ME. corneline, fr. OF.
comeline (F. cornaline), fr. OF. corne, 'cornel
cherry', fr. VL. *corna, pi. of L. cornum, of s.m.,
but mistaken for a fem. sing, noun; so called
because its color resembles that of the cornel
cherry. See cornel and cp. carnelian.

## Cornelius
Cornelius, masc. PN. — L. Cornelius, name of a
Roman gens. Cp. Cornelia. Cp. the first element
in keeshond.

## cornemuse
cornemuse, п., bagpipe. — F., fr. cornemuser, 'to
pipe', compounded of corner, 'to blow the horn',
and muser, 'to play the bagpipe'. The first
element derives fr. F. corne, 'horn'; see corn, 'horny
induration'. The second element comes fr. OF.
muse (F. musette), 'bagpipe'; see musette.

## coraeo-
coraeo-, combining form meaning 'horny'. — L.
corneus, 'horny'. See corneous.

## corneo-
corneo-, combining form meaning 'corneal' (anat.)
— See cornea.

## corneous
corneous, adj., horny. — L. corneus, 'horny', fr.
cornu, 'horn'. See corn, 'a horny induration'.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## corner
corner, n. — ME., fr. AF. cornere, corresponding
to OF. corniere, fr. ML. corneria, 'angle,
corner', fr. VL. *corna, which corresponds to L.
cornua, pi. of L. cornu, 'horn', but was mistaken
for a fem. sing. See horn and cp. corn, 'a horny
induration'.
Derivatives: corner, tr. and intr. v., corner-ed,
adj.

## cornet
cornet, п., a musical wind instrument. — F.
cornet, 'a small horn, trumpet', dimin. of cor, 'horn',
fr. OF. согя, fr. L. согяй. See horn and -et and
cp. corn, 'a horny induration'. Cp. also prec.
word.

## cornet
cornet, п., a headdress worn formerly by women.
— F. cornette, rel. to cornet, 'a small horn'. See
prec. word.

## cornice
cornice, п., a horizontal projection at the top of
a wall, etc. — F. cornice (now corniche), fr. It.
cornice, fr. L. coronis, fr. Gk. κορωνίς, 'anything
curved, a curved line', which is rel. to κορωνός,
'curved', κορώνη, 'ring, crown' (see crown);
influenced in form by It. cornice, 'crow', fr. L.
cornlcem, ace. of comix. Cp. the French
architectonic term corbeau (whence E. corbel), lit.
'raven'.
Derivatives: cornice, tr. v., cornic-ed, adj.

## cornicle
cornicle, п., a little horn. — L. corniculum, dimin.
of cornu, 'horn'. See corn, 'a horny induration',
and -cle.

## Corniferous
Corniferous, adj., pertaining to the Middle
Devonian system containing hornstone (geol.) —
Compounded of L. cornu, 'horn*, and ferre, 'to
bear, carry'. See corn, 'horny induration', and
•ferous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:195 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CORNISH | 168 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:195 COLUMN:1 -->

## Cornish
Cornish, adj. and n. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ish from the first element in Cornwall (fr. OE.
Cornweallas, lit. 'Cornish-Welsh').

## cornopean
cornopean, п., an early form of cornet (mus.) —
Invented word suggested by cornet, 'a wind
instrument'.

## cornucopia
cornucopia, п., ι) the horn of the goat Amaltha,
which suckled Zeus; 2) a horn of plenty; 3) a-
bundance; 4) a horn-shaped receptacle {Greek
mythot.) — Late L. cornucopia, for L. cornu
copiae, 'horn of plenty', fr. cornu, 'horn', and
copiae, gen. of cdpia, 'plenty'. See corn, 'horny
induration', and copious.

## cornucopiate
cornucopiate, adj., resembling a cornucopia. —
Formed fr. prec. word with adj. suff. -ate.

## Cornus
Cornus, п., a genus of plants, the dogwood and
the cornel (bot.) — L., 'cornel tree*. See corael.

## cornute
cornute, comuted, adj. — L. cornutus, 'horned',
fr. cornu, 'horn'. See corn, 'a horny induration'.

## cornwallite
cornwallite, п., a basic copper arsenate {mineral.)
— Named after Cornwall in England. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## coroa
coroa, п., a former Portuguese gold coin. —
Port., lit. 'a crown', fr. L. corona. See crown.

## corody
corody, corrody, п., an allowance of food {old
law). — ML. corrodium, corredium, 'provision'.
See cnrry.

## corolla
corolla, п., the whole of the petals of a flower
{bot.) — L. corolla, 'little crown, garland', di-
min. of corona, 'crown'. See crown.
Derivatives: coroll-ate, adj., coroll-at-ed, adj.

## corollary
corollary, п., ι) a proposition proved from
another that has been proved; 2) an inference;
3) a result. — L. corollarium, 'garland given as
a present', fr. corolla, 'little crown, garland;
gift, present, gratuity'. See prec. word and subsl.
suff. -ary.
Derivatives: corollari-al, adj., corollari-al-ly,
adv.

## corona
corona, п., a crown. — L. corona, 'garland,
wreath, crown', fr.Gk.xopcuVTj, 'anything curved;
a wreath, garland'. See crown.

## coronach
coronach, п., a dirge. — Gael, corranach, fr. Mir.
com-, 'with' (see com-), and ranach, 'a roaring,
weeping', fr. ran, 'to roar, weep'.

## coronal
coronal, adj., pertaining to a crown. — L. cord-
nalis, 'pertaining to a crown', fr. corona. See
corona and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: coronal-ly, adv.

## coroaal
coroaal, п., circlet, diadem. — L. coronalts,
'pertaining to a crown'. See coronal, adj.

## coronary
coronary, adj., 1) pertaining to a crown; 2)
encircling ; 3) pertaining to either of the two
arteries supplying the heart tissues. — L. coro-
narius, 'pertaining to a crown', fr. corona. See
corona and adj. suff. -ary.

## coronate
coronate, tr. v., to crown. — L. coronatus, pp. of
coronare, 'to crown', fr. corona. See corona and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: coronat-ed, adj., coronation (q.v.)

## coronation
coronation, n. — OF. coronacion, coronation, fr.
coroner, 'to crown', fr. L. coronare. See coronate
and -ion.

## coroner
coroner, п., an official whose chief duty is to
inquire into the causes of deaths not obviously
due to natural causes. — AF. corouner, fr. co-
roune, fr. OF. corone, 'crown', fr. L. corona,
'garland, crown' (see crown and agential suff.
-er); so called because his original task was to
watch over crown property.
Derivative: coroner-ship, n.

## coronet
coronet, п., a small crown. — OF. coronete, coro-
nette, dimin. of corone, 'crown', fr. L. cordna.
See corona and -et and cp. croner, crownet.
Derivatives: coronet{t)-ed, coronett-y, adjs.

## Coronilla
Coronilla, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
{bot.) — ModL., dimin. of L. corona, 'crown'
(see corona); so called in allusion to its
inflorescence.

## Coronis
Coronis, п., mother of Asclepius and consort of
Apollo in Greek mythol. — L., fr. Gk. Κορωνίς,
which is rel. to κορώνη, 'crow', from the I.-E.
imitative base *qer-, *qor-, 'to cry, shout',
whence also κόραξ, 'crow'. See coracoid.

## coronium
coronium, п., an element supposed to be in the
solar corona {astrophysics). — ModL., formed
fr. L. corona, 'crown'. See corona and chem.
suff. -ium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:195 COLUMN:2 -->

## coronoid
coronoid, adj., curved (anat.) — Lit. 'resembling
the tip of a bow', fr. Gk. κορώνη, 'anything
hooked or curved; crow; tip of a bow', and
-οειδής,' 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'; see
corona and -oid. The usual translation of
coronoid as 'shaped like a crow's beak', is erroneous.
See Joseph Hyrtl, Onomatologia anatomica,
pp. 150-51.

## Coronopus
Coronopus, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family {bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κορωνόπους, 'the
hartshorn', which is compounded of κορώνη,
'crow', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. The first
element is rel. to Gk. κόραξ, 'raven', and cogn.
with L. corvus, 'raven', comix, 'crow'; see
coracoid. For the second element see -pod.

## corozo
corozo, п., the name of several S. American palms.
— Sp. (now spelled corojo), from a S. American
native word.

## corporal
corporal, adj., of the body; bodily. — OF.
corporal (F. corporel), fr. L. corporalis, 'pertaining
to the body', fr. corpus, gen. corporis, 'body'.
See corpus and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: corporaiity (q.v.), corporal-ly, adv.

## corporal
corporal, п., a linen cloth covering the
consecrated element at the Eucharist {eccles.) — Ec-
cles. L. corporalis (scil. palla), 'body cloth', fr.
L. corporalis, 'pertaining to the body'. See
corporal, adj.

## corporal
corporal, п., the lowest noncommissioned officer
(mil.) — Earlier F. corporal, an alteration—due
to corps, 'body'—of F. caporal, fr. It. caporale,
lit. 'chief, which derives fr. capo, 'head', fr. L.
caput. See capital, adj., and cp. caporal. The
ending of It. cap-orale shows the influence of
It. pettorale.

## corporaiity
corporaiity, n. — Late L. corporalitas, fr. L.
corporalis. See corporal, adj., and -ity.

## corporate
corporate, adj. — L. corporatus, pp. of corporare,
'to make into a body, incorporate, incarnate',
fr. corpus, gen. corporis, 'body'. See corpus and
adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: corporate-ly, adv., corporate-ness, n.

## corporation
corporation, n. — Late L. corporatio, gen. -onis,
'incorporation, incarnation', fr. L. corporatus,
pp. of corporare. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: corporation-al, adj., corporation-
er, n.

## corporative
corporative, adj. — Late L. corpordtlvus,
'pertaining to the forming of a body', fr. L. corporatus,
pp. of corporare. See corporate and -ive.

## corporator
corporator, п., member of a corporation. —
Formed with agential suff. -or fr. L. corporatus,
pp. of corporare. See corporate.

## corporeal
corporeal, adj., of the body; bodily. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. corpus, gen. corporis,
'body'. See corpus and cp. corporal, adj.
Derivatives: corporeal-ity, п., corporeal-ly, adv.

## corporeity
corporeity, п., corporeality. — ML. corporeitas,
fr. L. corporeus, 'pertaining to the body', fr.
corpus, gen. corporis, 'body'. See corpus and
-ity.

## corposant
corposant, п., an electric light seen sometimes in
stormy weather; called also St. Elmo's fire. —
Fr. Port, corpo santo, 'holy body', fr. L. corpus
sanctum. See corpus and sanctus.

## corps
corps, п., г) a group of persons; 2) a military unit.
— F., fr. L. corpus. See corpus and cp. corpse
and corse.

## corpse
corpse, n. — ME. corse, corps, 'body', fr. OF.
cors, fr. L. corpus. See prec. word. The MF. and
modern F. spelling corps is due to the influence
of L. corpus.

## corpulence
corpulence, corpulency, п., fatness. — L. corpu-
lentia, 'grossness or fleshiness of body', fr. cor-
pulentus. See next word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## corpulent
corpulent, adj., fat. — F., fr. L. corpulentus,
'fleshy, fat, stout'. See corpus and -ulent.
Derivatives: corpulent-ly, adv., corpulent-ness,n.

## corpus
corpus, п., body. — L. corpus, gen. corporis,
'body', prob. cogn. with OI. kfp-, 'form, beauty',
Avestic k'r'fsh, gen. k'hrpo-, 'form, body', OE.
hrif, OHG. href, 'womb, belly, abdomen', OFris.
hrif, href, 'belly'; prob. fr. I.-E. base *qwrep-,
*q"TP-, enlargement of *q"er-, 'to make, form',
whence Oi. kfnoti, karoti, 'makes', Avestic kar-,
'to make', k'r'naoiti, 'makes', OPers. kar-, 'to
make', kara-, 'maker', Lilh. kuriu, kurti, 'to
build', OPruss. kura, 'he built', Olr. cruth,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:195 COLUMN:3 -->
'figure, shape', W. pryd, 'appearance, look'. Cp.
corporal, corporate, corporation, corporeal,
corporeity, corposant, corps, corpse, corpulent,
corse, incorporate. Cp. also Sanskrit and words
there referred to. Cp. also the second element in
midriff.

## corpus callosum
corpus callosum, a mass of white fibers connecting
the cerebral hemispheres (anat.) — L., 'callous
body', in its modern, anatomical sense, a loan
translation of σώμα πώς τυλώδες (lit. 'callous
body'), which is the name given to the corpus
callosum by Galen. See corpus and callous.

## corpuscle
corpuscle, п., a small particle. — Formed fr. L.
corpusculum, 'a little body', dimin. of corpus
(see corpus and -cle and cp. corpuscule);
introduced into English by the physicist and chemist
Robert Boyle (1627-91).

## corpuscule
corpuscule, п., a corpuscle. — L. corpusculum.
See corpuscle and -cule.
Derivatives: corpuscul-ar, adj., corpuscui-ar-ity,
п., corpuscul-ated, corpuscul-ous, adjs.

## corrade
corrade, tr. and intr. v., to wear by scraping (geol.)
— L. corradere, '10 scrape together', fr. com-
and radere, 'scrape'. See raze and cp. corrasion.

## corral
corral, п., a pen for horses. — Sp., fr. corro,
'ring', fr. correr, 'to run', fr. L. currere, 'to run'.
See courier and course and cp. corridor. Sp. corral
is rel. to Port, curral, 'pen, enclosure', whence
kraal (q.v,)
Derivative: corral, tr. v.

## corrasion
corrasion, п., the process of corrading. — L. cor-
rasio, gen. -onis, fr. corrasus, pp. of corradere.
See corrade and -ion.

## correal
correal, adj., under joint obligation (law). —
Formed with adj. suff. -al ff. L. correus, 'under
joint obligation', fr. cor- and reus, 'defendant',
lit. 'a party to an action', fr. res, 'thing, matter,
affair, action'. See res and cp. reus, reatus.

## correct
correct, adj. — L. corrlctus, pp. of corrigere, 'to
make straight, set right, correct', fr. cor-and
revere, 'to make straight, lead, guide, conduct'.
See regent, adj., and cp. corregidor, corrigendum,
escort.
Derivatives: correct-ly, adv., correct-ness, n.

## correct
correct, tr. v. — L. correctus, pp. of corrigere.
See correct, adj.
Derivatives: correct-ed, adj., correct-ed-ly, adv.,
correct-ed-ness, п., correction (q.v.)

## correction
correction, n. — F., fr. L. corrSctidnem, ace. of
corrictid, 'a making straight, improvement', fr.
correctus, pp. of corrigere. See correct, adj.,
and -ion.
Derivatives: correction-al, adj. and п.,
corrections, n.

## correctitude
correctitude, n. — Formed fr. correct on analogy
of rectitude.

## corrective
corrective, adj. — F. correctif (fem. corrective),
fr. L. correctus, pp. of corrigere. See correct and
-i»e.
Derivatives: corrective, п., corrective-ly, adv.,
corrective-ness, n.

## corrector
corrector, n. — L. corrector, 'improver,
corrector', fr. correctus, pp. of corrigere. See correct
and agential suff. -or.

## corregidor
corregidor, п., a Spanish magistrate, mayor of a
town. — Sp., lit. 'corrector', fr. corregir, 'to
correct', fr. VL. *corregire, which corresponds to
L. corrigere, 'to correct'. See correct, adj.

## correlate
correlate, intr. and tr. v., to relate mutually. —
Formed fr. cor- and L. relatus, used as pp. of
referre, 'to carry back, bring back, relate'. See
relate.
Derivatives: correlate, п., correlat-ion,
correlative, adj. and п., correlat-ive-ly, adv.

## conception
conception, п., a shortening in pronunciation. —
L. correptio, gen. -onis, 'a shortening,
decreasing', fr. correptus, pp. of corripere, 'to shorten,
abridge, diminish; to chide', lit. 'to seize upon',
fr. com- and rapere,*to seize* (seerapid and -ion).
For the change of Latin й (in ruptus) to ё (in
cor-reptus) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.

## correspond
correspond, intr. v. — F. corresponds, fr. ML.
correspondere, fr. cor- and L. respondere, 'to
answer'. See respoud.
Derivatives: correspond-ence, п.,
correspondency, п., correspond-ent, adj., correspond-ent-ly,
adv., correspond-ing, adj., correspond-ing-ly,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:196 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 169 | COSHER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:196 COLUMN:1 -->
adv.

## corresponsive
corresponsive, adj., corresponding. — Formed fir.
com- and responsive.
Derivative: corresponsive-ly, adv.

## corridor
corridor, n. — F., fr. It. corridore, lit. 'a place for
running', fr. correre, 'to run', fr. L. currere. Cp.
OProveng. courradour and Sp. corrector, which
are of the same origin .and meaning.

## corrie
corrie, п., a circular hollow in the side of a
mountain (Scot.) — Gael, coire, 'caldron, kettle', rel.
to Olr. coire, W. pair, of s.m., and cogn. with
OE. hwer, ON. hverr, OHG. hwer, wer, 'kettle',
Goth, hairnei, 'skull', OI. carub, 'kettle, pot',
karankas, 'skull'. For sense development cp. F.
tite, 'head', fr. L. testa, 'postherd' (see tester,
'canopy'), and G. Kopf, 'head', fr. MHG. kopf,
'drinking vessel, skull' (see cop, 'the top of
anything', and cup).

## corrigendum
corrigendum, п., something to be corrected. —
L., neut. gerundive of corrigere, 'to make
straight, correct', fr. com- and regere, 'to make
straight, lead, guide, conduct; see correct. For
the change of Latin i (in rigere) to ί (in
corrigere) see abstinence and cp. words there
referred to. For other Latin gerundives used in
English cp. agenda and words there referred to.

## corrigible
corrigible, adj. — F., fr. ML. corrigibilis, 'that
which can be corrected', fr. L. corrigere, 'to
correct'. See prec. word and -ible.
Derivatives: corrigibil-ity, п., corrigible-ness, п.,
corrigibl-y, adv.

## corrival
corrival, п., a rival, competitor. — L. corrivttlis,
fr. cor- and rivalis, 'rival'. See rival.

## corroborant
corroborant, adj. and n. — L. corroborans, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of corrobare, 'to strengthen'.
See next word and -ant.

## corroborate
corroborate, tr. v. — L. corroborate, pp. of
corroborare, 'to strengthen', fr. com- and robur, gen.
rOboris, 'strength'. See robust and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: corroboration, corroborative (qq.v.),
corroboral-or, п., corroborat-ory, adj.

## corroboration
corroboration, n. — F., fr. corroborer, 'to
strengthen, corroborate', fr. L. corroborare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## corroborative
corroborative, adj. — F. corroborate/(fem.
corroborative), fr. L. corroboratus, pp. of corroborare.
See corroborate and -ive.
Derivative: corroborative-ly, adv.

## corroboree
corroboree, п., a festivity of Australian
aborigines. — A native name.
Derivative: corroboree, intr. v.

## corrode
corrode, tr. v., to eat away gradually; intr. v.,
to become corroded. — F. corroder, fr. L. cor-
rddere, 'to gnaw to pieces', fr. com- and rodere,
'to gnaw'. See rodent and cp. erode.
Derivatives: corrod-er, п., corrod-ing, adj.

## corrody
corrody, n. — See corody.

## corrosion
corrosion, n. — F., fr. L. corrosionem, ace. oicor-
rosio, 'a gnawing to pieces', fr. corrosus, pp. of
corrodere. See corrode and -ion.

## corrosive
corrosive, adj. — F. corrosif (fem. corrosive), fr.
L. corrosus, pp. of corrodere. See corrode and
-ive.
Derivatives: corrosive-ly, adv., corrosive-ness,
п., corrosiv-ily, n.

## corrugate
corrugate, tr. and intr. v., to wrinkle. — L.
corrugatus, pp. of configure, 'to make full of wrinkles,
to wrinkle', fr. com- and rugare, 'to wrinkle', fr.
ruga, 'wrinkle'. See ruga and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: corrugal-ed, adj., corrugat-ion, cor-
rugator (q.v.)

## corrugate
corrugate, adj., wrinkled. — L. corrugatus, pp. of
corrugare. See corrugate, v.

## comigator
comigator, п., either of the two muscles that
contract the brows {anal.) — Medical L., lit.
'that which wrinkles', fr. L. corrugatus, pp. of
corrugare. See corrugate and agential suff. -or.

## corrupt
corrupt, adj. — L. corruplus, pp. of corrumpere,
'to destroy, ruin, corrupt', fr. com- and rumpere,
'to break'. See rupture.
Derivatives: corrupt, tr. and intr.v.; corrupt-ly,
adv., corrupt-ness, п.; corrupt-ed, adj., corrupt-
ed-ly, adv., corrupt-ed-ness, п., corrupt-er, п.,
corrupt-ing, adj., corrupt-ingly, adv.

## corruptible
corruptible, adj. — Late L. corruptibilis (whence
also F. corruptible), 'liable to decay,
corruptible', fr. L. corruptus, pp. of corrumpere. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:196 COLUMN:2 -->
corrupt, v., and -ible.
Derivatives: co'rruptibil-ity, п., corruptible-ness,
п., corruptibl-y, adv.

## corruption
corruption, n. — F., fr. L. corruptionem, ace. of
corruplio, 'a corrupting, spoiling', fr. corruptus,
pp. of corrumpere. See corrupt and -ion.

## corruptive
corruptive, adj. — Eccles. L. corruptivus, fr. L.
corruptus, pp. of corrumpere. See corrupt and
-ive.
Derivative: corruptive-ly, adv.

## corsac
corsac, п., a small yellowish fox (Vulpes corsac)
of Central Asia. — Russ. korsak, fr. Kirghiz
karsak.

## corsage
corsage, n. — F., formed with suff. -age fr. OF.
cors (F. corps), 'body'. See corps and cp. corse,
corset.

## corsair
corsair, п., a pirate. — F. corsaire, fr. It. corsaro,
'pirate', lit. 'runner', fr. ML. cursarius, fr. L.
cursus, 'a running, course, voyage'. See current,
adj., and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
hussar.

## corse
corse, n. {poet.) — A var. of corpse.

## corselet
corselet, corslet, п., armor for the body. — F.
corselet, lit., 'little body', dimin. of OF. cors(f.
corps), 'body'. See corps and cp. next word.

## corset
corset, п., a close-fitting undergarment; stays. —
F. corset, lit. 'a little body', dimin. of OF. cors (F.
corps), fr. L. corpus, 'body'. See corpus and -et
and cp. corps.
Derivatives: corset, tr. v., corset-ing, п., corset-
ry, n.

## cortege
cortege, cortege, п., a train of attendants;
retinue. — F. cortege, fr. It. corteggio, 'retinue',
fr. corteggiare, 'to court', fr. cone, 'court', fr. L.
cohortem, cortem, ace. of cohors, cors, 'enclosed
place, yard'. See court and cp. next word.

## Cortes
Cortes, п., the two chambers of the legislative
assembly in Spain and Portugal. — Sp. and
Port., lit. 'courts', pi. of corte, 'court', fr. L.
cohortem, cortem. See prec. word.

## cortex
cortex, п., the bark of a tree (hot.) — L., 'bark,
rind', lit. 'that which is stripped off', fr. I.-E.
base *(s)qer-, 'to cut, separate', whence also L.
corium, 'hide, leather'. See corium, and cp.
Corticium, excorticate, scorch, scortation. For
sense development cp. bark, 'rind of a tree', fr.
I.-E. base *bher-, 'to cut'.

## cortical
cortical, adj., pertaining to a cortex. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. cortex, gen. corticis,
'bark'. See prec. word.

## corticate
corticate, corticated, adj., provided with a cortex.
— L. corticatus, 'covered with a bark', fr.
cortex, gen. corticis. See cortex and verbal suff. -ate.

## Corticium
Corticium, п., a genus of fungi (hot) — ModL.,
fr. L. cortex, gen. corticis, 'bark'. See cortex
and 1st -ium.

## cortico-
cortico-, combining form denoting the cortex. —
Fr. L. cortex, gen. corticis, 'bark'. See cortex.

## corticosterone
corticosterone, n. (biochem.) — Coined fr. cortico·
and sterone, which is formed fr. sterol and
suff. -one.

## cortisone
cortisone, п., an adrenal cortex hormone
(biochem.) — Coined by Edward С Kendall, its
discoverer, and Philip S. Hench, of the Mayo
Clinic, in 1936 through the abbreviation of prec.
word.

## corundum
corundum, п., a very hard mineral. — Tamil
kurundam, fr. OI. kuruvinda-, 'ruby', which is of
uncertain etymology.

## comscant
comscant, adj., sparkling, Hashing. — L. corus-
cans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of coruscare. See
next word and -aat.

## coruscate
coruscate, intr. v., to sparkle, flash. — L. corus-
catus, pp. of coruscare, 'to thrust with the horns;
to shake, vibrate, wave; to flash, glitter', fr.
coruscus, 'vibrating, waving, glittering', which
is of uncertain origin. It possibly stands for
*coroscos, and orig. meant 'leaping, jumping',
and is cogn. with Gk. σκαίρειν, 'to leap, skip,
bound', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to jump, leap,
bound'. See cardinal, adj., and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## coruscation
coruscation, n. — Late L. coruscatio, gen. -dnis,
fr. L. coruscatus, pp. of coruscare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## corvee
corvee, п., unpaid labor. — F., 'forced labor,
statute labor', fr. VL. corrogala (opera), '(work) in
which people are asked to participate', fem. pp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:196 COLUMN:3 -->
of L. corrogare, 'to bring together by entreaty',
fr. cor- and rogare, 'to entreat'. See rogation.

## corvette
corvette, п., a small fast war vessel (naut.) — F.,
dimin. formed fr. corve (a word occurring only
in a text of the year 1700), which was prob.
borrowed fr. MLG. korf, 'basket; a kind of ship';
see corf and -ette. It. corvetla and Sp. corbeta
are French loan words.

## Corvidae
Corvidae, n. pi., a family of birds including the
ravens, crows, etc. — ModL., formed with suff.
-idae fr. L. corvus, 'raven'. See corvine.

## corvine
corvine, adj., pertaining to the raven or crow. —
L. corvinus, fr. corvus, 'raven', from the I.-E.
imitative base *qer-, *qor-, *qr-, 'to cry, shout'.
See raven and -lne (representing L. -inus) and cp.
coracoid.

## Corvus
Corvus, п., a genus of birds, the crow (ornithol.)
— L. corvus, 'raven'. See prec. word.

## Corybant
Corybant, п., one of the attendants of Cybele
(Greek mythol.) — F. Corybante, fr. L. Cory-
bantem, ace. of Corybas, fr. Gk. Κορύβάς, gen.
Κορύβαντος, a word of uncertain, possibly
Phrygian, origin.
Derivatives: Corybant-ian, Corybant-ic, adjs.

## Corydalis
Corydalis, п., a genus of plants of the fumewort
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κορυδαλλίς,
'crested lark', fr. κόρυδος, of s.m., fr. κόρυς,
'helmet', which is rel. to κορύνη, 'club, mace',
κορυφή, 'head, top, summit'. See coryphaeus' and
cp. words there referred to.

## Corydon
Corydon, п., the traditional name for a shepherd
or a rustic swain in pastoral poetry. — L.
Corydon, fr. Gk. ΚορυδώΦ, лате of a shepherd
in the idylls of Theocritus and in Virgil's
Eclogues.

## Corylus
Corylus, п., a genus of trees, the hazel (bot.) —
L. coryfus, corulus, 'the hazel', cogn. with ON.
has/, OE. hsesel, of s.m. See hazel.

## corymb
corymb, п., a broad cluster of flowers (bot.) —
L. corymbus, 'cluster of flowers', fr. Gk. κό-
ρυμβος, 'uppermost point, cluster of flowers',
which is rel. to κορυφή, 'head, top, summit'. See
coryphaeus and cp. next word.
Derivatives: cotynib-ed, adj., corymbi-ate, co-
rymbi-at-ed, corymb-ose, adjs., corymb-ose-ly,
adv., corymb-ous, adj.

## Coryneum
Coryneum, п., a form genus of imperfect fungi
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κορύνη. 'club, mace',
which is rel. to κορυφή, 'head, top, summit'. See
next word and cp. corymb.

## coryphaeus
coryphaeus, п., ι) the leader of the chorus in the
Greek drama; hence 2) a leader. — L., fr. Gk.
κορυφαίος,'leader, chief, fr. κορυφή,'head, top,
summit, the highest point', which is rel. to
κόρυς. 'helmet', κάρυμβος, 'uppermost point,
cluster of flowers', κορύνη, 'club', and prob.
stands in gradational relationship to Att. Gk.
κάρα, Att. and Dor. κάράνον, Ion. κάρηνον,
'head', and to Gk. κράνίον, 'skull'. See cranium
and cp. Corydalis, corymb, Coryneum. Cp. also
next word.

## coryphee
coryphee, п., a ballet dancer. — F. coryphee, fr. L.
coryphaeus. See prec. word.

## Coryphodon
Coryphodon, п., a genus of extinct mammals
(paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of κορυφή,
'head, top, summit', and οδών, gen. οδόντος,
'tooth'. See coryphaeus and odonto-.

## coryza
