coryza, п., nasal catarrh (ined.) — L. coryza, fr.
Gk. κόρυζα, 'a cold in the head, nasal catarrh',
which is prob. cogn. with OE. hroi, 'thick fluid,
scum', OHG. hroz, roz, 'nasal mucus', MHG.,
G. rotz, 'nasal mucus', OE. hrutan, 'to snore;
to resound', ON. hrjuta, OS. hrutan, ON.
Itrjota, OHG. Игйззап, 'to rattle in one's throat'.

## cos
cos, cos lettuce, n. — Prop, 'lettuce introduced
from Cos', fr. L. Cos, fr. Gk. Κως, one of the
Aegean islands, now called Stanchio. Cp. Coan.

## cos
cos, n. — Abbreviation of cosine.

## cosecant
cosecant, п., the secant of the complement of an
angle (trigon.) — Formed on analogy of cosine
and cotangent fr. ModL. compiementi secans.
See со- and secant.

## coseismal
coseismal, coseismic, adj., noting points where
an earthquake arrives simultaneously. —
Formed fr. со- and seismal.

## cosher
cosher, intr. v.. to feast. — Ir. coisir, 'a feast'.

## cosher
cosher, tr. v., to pamper. — Of uncertain origir.

## cosher
cosher, adj. — A var. spelling of kosher.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:197 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: COSIGNATORV | 170 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:197 COLUMN:1 -->

## cosiguatory
cosiguatory, adj., signing jointly with another
or others. — Formed fr. со- and signatory.

## cosine
cosine, п., the sine of the complement of an angle
(trigon.) — Fr. со. sinus, abbreviation of ModL.
complement! sinus, 'the sine of the complement'.
This name and its abbreviation into со. sinus
were first used by Edmund Gunter, a
mathematician of the early 17th cent. See complement
and sine and cp. cotangent, cosecant.

## cosmetic
cosmetic, adj., serving to beautify. — Gk.
κοσμητικής, 'skilled in arranging', fr. κοσμητός,
'well-ordered', verbal adj. of κοσμάν, 'to order,
arrange, adorn', fr. κόσμος, 'order, ornament,
decoration, set form; world, universe'. See
cosmos and -ic.
Derivatives: cosmetic, п., a preparation for
beautifying the skin, cosmetic-al-ly, adv.,
cosmetic-tan, п., one who makes or applies
cosmetics.

## cosmetology
cosmetology, п., the study of cosmetics. —
Compounded of Gk. κοσμητός, 'well-ordered' (see
prec. word), and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## cosmic
cosmic, adj., pertaining lo the cosmos; vast. —
Gk. κοσμικός, 'of, or connected with, the world',
fr. κόσμος, 'world'. See cosmos and -ic.
Derivatives: cosmic-al, adj., cosmic-al-ity, п.,
cosmic-al-ly, adv.

## cosmo-
cosmo-, combining word denoting the world. —
Gk. κόσμο-, fr. κόσμος, 'world'. See cosmos.

## cosmogony
cosmogony, п., the origination of the universe. —
Gk. κοσμογονία (whence also F. cosmogonie),
compounded of κόσμος, 'world', and -γονίά, fr.
γόνος, 'race, offspring'. See cosmos and -gony.
Derivatives: cosmogon-ic, cosmogon-ic-al, adjs.,
cosmogon-ist, n.

## cosmography
cosmography, п., description of the universe. —
Gk. κοσμογραφία, compounded of κόσμος,
'world', and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
cosmos and -graphy.
Derivatives: cosmograph-ic, cosmograph-ic-al,
adjs.

## cosmology
cosmology, п., that part of metaphysics which
deals with the universe. — Compounded of
cosmo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: cosmolog-ic, cosmolog-ic-al, adjs.,
cosmotog-ic-al-ly, adv., cosmohg-ist, n.

## cosmonaut
cosmonaut, п., an astronaut. — Compounded of
cosmo- and Gk. ναύτης, 'sailor, seaman'. See
nautical and cp. astronaut.

## cosmonautics
cosmonautics, п., astronautics. — Compounded
of cosmo- and nautics. Cp. prec. word. Cp. also
astronautics.

## cosmoplastic
cosmoplastic, adj., pertaining to the plastic force
that forms the world. — Compounded of
cosmo- and plastic.

## cosmopolitan
cosmopolitan, adj., belonging to the whole world;
п., a citizen of the world. — Formed with suff.
-an, fr. Gk. κοσμοπολίτης, 'citizen of the world',
fr. κόσμος, 'world,' and πολίτης, 'citizen' (fr.
πόλις, 'cily'). See cosmo- and politic.
Derivatives: cosmopolitan-ism, п., cosmopolitan-
ize, v.

## cosmopolite
cosmopolite, п., a cosmopolitan person. — Gk.
κοσμοπολίτης. See prec. word.
Derivatives: cosmopoUt-ic, cosmopolit-ic-al,
adjs., cosmopolit-ism, n.

## cosmorama
cosmorama, п., an exhibition of views of different
parts of the world. — Compounded of Gk.
κόσμος, 'world', and δράμα, 'that which is seen,
view, sight', fr. όράν, 'to see'. For the first
element see cosmos. The second element is cogn.
with L. verlri, 'to observe with aWe, revere,
respect, fear', OE. wxr, 'cautious, aware'. See
ware, 'alert', and cp. the second element in
diorama, myriorama, panorama. Cp. also -rama.
Derivative: cosmoram-ic, adj.

## cosmos
cosmos, п., the world conceived as an ordered
whole. — Gk. κόσμος, 'order, ornament,
decoration, set form; world, universe', whence
κοσμαν, 'to order, arrange, adorn', κοσμητός
(verbal adj.), 'well-ordered, regular'; of
uncertain origin. Cp. cosmetic, the first element in
cosmetology and the second element in
macrocosm, microcosm.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:197 COLUMN:2 -->

## coss
coss, n. — A variant spelling of kos.

## cossack
cossack, n., one of a people of the southern Soviet
union in Europe and near-by parts of Asia,
noted- as horsemen. — Russ. kozak, kazak, fr.
Turk, qazaq, qazaq, 'nomad, vagabond'.

## cosset
cosset, п., a lamb reared by hand, a pet lamb. —
Prob. fr. OE. cot-sxta, 'cottage dweller, house
dweller', fr. cot, 'cot, house', and sseta, 'dweller',
fr. sittan, 'to sit, to dwell'. See cot, 'cottage', and
sit. For sense development cp. G. Hauslamm,
'pet lamb', fr. Haus, 'house', and Lamm, 'lamb',
and It. casiccio, 'pet lamb', fr. casa, 'house'.
Derivative: cosset, tr. v., to treat as a pet.

## cost
cost, intr. v. — ME. costen, fr. OF. coster (F.
couter), 'to cost', fr. L. constare, 'to stand
together, to be established, settled,·certain,
evident', which is formed fr. coa- and stare, 'to
stand'; cp. It. constare, OProvenc. Cat., Sp.
costar, Port, custar, 'to cost', Rum. custa, 'to
live', which all derive fr. L. constare. See state
and cp. constant

## cost
cost, n. — OF. (F. cout), back formation fr.
coster (F. couter). Cp. It., Sp. costo, Sp. costa.
Port, custa, 'cost, price', Rum. cust, 'duration
of life', and see cost, v.
Derivatives: cost-less, adj., cost-less-ness, п.,
cost-ly, adv., cost-li-ness, n.

## costal
costal, adj., pertaining to a rib or ribs. — F., fr.
ML. costalis, fr. L. costa, 'rib, side, coast'. See
coast and adj. suff. -al and cp. coastal. Cp. also
costard, costate, coteau.
Derivative: costal-ly, adv.

## costard
costard, п., a variety of apple. — Lit. 'ribbed', fr.
OF. coste (F. cote), 'rib', fr. L. costa (see coast
and -ard); so called with reference to the ribs
on its surface. Cp. costermonger.

## costate
costate, adj., having ribs, ribbed. — L. costatus,
'having ribs', fr. costa. See costal and adj. suff.
-ate.

## costean
costean, intr. v., to bore through the soil down
to the rock to find out the course of a mineral
deposit. — Co. costen, prob. contracted fr.
cothas stln, 'dropped tin'. Co. sten is rel. to
Gael., Ir. stun, 'tin'. See stannary.

## coster
coster, n. — Short for costermonger.

## costermonger
costermonger, п., an apple seller. — From orig.
costardmonger, lit. 'apple seller'. See costard
and monger.

## costive
costive, adj., constipated. — MF. costive, fr. L.
constipatus, pp. of constipare, 'to press closely
together'. See constipate. For the loss of the
French pp. suff. -i in English cp. defile, 'a
narrow valley', signal, 'noticeable', trove.
Derivative: costive-jtess, n.

## costmary
costmary, п., a plant with fragrant leaves
(Chrysanthemum balsamita) — ME. costmarye,
compounded of OE. cost, 'costmary', and Mary.
OE. cost derives fr. L. cosius, fr. Gk. κόστος, fr.
Heb. qoshf, 'an oriental aromatic plant', which,
together with Arab, qusf, of s.m., is borrowed
fr. OI. kusthah.

## costo-
costo-, combining form meaning 'rib'. — Fr. L.
costa, 'rib'. See costal.

## costotome
costotome, п., an instrument for the dissection
of ribs. — A hybrid coined fr. L. costa, 'rib',
and Gk. -τόμος, 'cutting'. See coast and -tome.

## costotomy
costotomy, п., division of a rib (med.) — A hybrid
coined fr. L. costa, 'rib', and Gk. -τομία, 'a
cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See coast and -tomy.

## costume
costume, п., — F., 'costume, dress', fr. It.
costume, 'custom, fashion, customary dress, dress',
fr. L. cdnsuetudinem, ace. of consuetude,
'custom'. See custom.
Derivatives: costume, tr. v., costum-er, п., cos-
tum-ery, п., costum-ing, n.

## costumier
costumier, п., a costumer. — F., 'dealer in
costumes', fr. costume. See prec. word and -ier.

## cosy
cosy, adj. — A var. spelling of cozy.
Derivatives: cosi-ly, adv., cosi-ness, n.

## cot
cot, п., hut, cottage. — ME. cot, cole, fr. OE. cot,
cote, 'cottage, house, dwelling', rel. to ON. kot,
'hut', MDu. cot, cole, Du. kot, 'hovel, cot'. Cp.
cote, coterie, cottage, cotter, 'cottager', cottier.
Derivative: cot, to put in a cot.

## cot
cot, п., bedstead; bed (паи?.) (Anglo-Ind.) —
Hind, khat, khafva, fr. OI. khafva, borrowed
from Dravidian; cp. Tamil kattil, 'beadstead'.

## cot
cot, n. — Abbreviation of cotangent.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:197 COLUMN:3 -->

## cotangent
cotangent, п., the tangent of the complement of
an angle (trigon.) — Fr. со. tangens, abbrevation
of ModL. complement! tangens, 'the tangent of
the complement'. This name and its abbreviation
into со. tangens were first used by Edmund
Gunter, a mathematician of the early 17th
century. See complement and tangent and cp.
cosecant, cosine.

## cotarnlne
cotarnlne, also cotarnin, п., a nonpoisonous
alkaloid, Ci2HlsN04 (chem.) — Anagram of nar-
cotine; so called in allusion to the circumstance
that cotarnine is obtained by the oxidation of
narcotine.

## cote
cote, п., a shelter for pigeons, sheep, etc. — ME.
cote, cot. See cot, 'hut, cottage'.

## coteau
coteau, п., an upland (Canada and U.S.A.) — F.,
'a hill', fr. OF. costel, orig. 'side', fr. coste (F.
cote), 'rib, side, hillside', fr. L. costa. See coast.

## cotemporary
cotemporary, adj. — The same as contemporary.

## cotenant
cotenant, п., a joint tenant. — Formed fr. Co- and
tenant.

## coterie
coterie, п., an exclusive group of persons. — F.,
'association of country people, set, circle', fr.
OF. cotier, 'cottager, cotter'. See cot, 'hut', and
-ery.

## cothurnus
cothurnus, п., the buskin worn by the Greek and
Roman tragic actors; tragedy; tragic style. —
L., fr. Gk. κό&ορνος, which is of foreign,
possibly Lydian, origin.

## cotillion
cotillion, п., a lively dance. — F. cotillon, name
of a dance, lit., 'petticoat', dimin. of cone,
'coat', fr. OF. cote, fr. Frankish *kotta, 'coat'.
See coat and cp. cotta.

## cotise
cotise, п., the fourth part of a band, used in pairs
(her.) — F. cotice, fr. ML. coticium, fr. cota,
cotta, 'tunic', which is of Teut. origin. See cont
and cp. cotillion, cotta.
Derivative: cotise, tr. v.

## Cotoneaster
Cotoneaster, п., a genus of plants of the apple
family (hot.) — ModL., formed with the
pejorative suff. -aster fr. L. cotonea, 'quince'. See
quince.

## cotrustee
cotrustee, п., a joint trustee. — Formed fr. co-
and trustee.

## cotta
cotta, п., a short surplice (eccles.) — ML. cotta,
'tunic', of Teut. origin. See coat and cp. words
there referred to.

## cottabus
cottabus, п., a game in vogue at drinking parties
in ancient Athens. — L., fr. Gk. κότταβος, 'a
Sicilian game of throwing the wine left in one's
cup into a metal basin', which stands perh. for
•κότίαβος and is rel. to κοτύλη, 'cup'. See
cotyledon.

## cottage
cottage, n. — AF. cotage, a hybrid coined fr. OF.
cole, a Frankish loan word (see cot, 'hut,
cottage'), and -age, a suff. of Latin origin.
Derivatives: cottag-ed, adj., cottag-er, n.

## cotter
cotter, cottar, п., a cottager. — ML. cotarius, cot-
larius, fr. cota, cotta. See cot, 'hut, cottage'.

## cotter
cotter, п., a wedge, bolt. — Of unknown origin.

## cotterite
cotterite, п., a variety of quartz (mineral.) —
Named after its discoverer Miss Cotter, of Rock-
forest, Ireland. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## Cottidae
Cottidae, n. pi., a family of fishes, the sculpins,
etc. (ichthyol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-idae fr. Cottus (q.v.)

## cottier
cottier, п., a cottager. — OF. cotier, fr. cote. See
cote and -ier.

## cotton
cotton, n. — ME. coton,Jr. F. colon, fr. Sp. colon,

## fr. Arab
fr. Arab, qujun, whence also It. cotone,

## OProvenc. colon. Port
OProvenc. colon. Port, coluo, Du. katoen, and
(through the medium of Dutch) G. Katlun,
'cotton'. Cp. acton, kittel.
Derivatives: cotton, adj., cotton, v. (q.v.), cot-

## ton-y
ton-y, adj.

## cotton
cotton, intr. v., to agree. — Fr. cotton, n. The
orig. meaning of the verb was 'to stick together
like cotton'.

## cotula
cotula, п., an ancient Greek measure (Greek an-
liq.) — L. cotula, cotyla, 'a small vessel; a

## measure of capacity'
measure of capacity', fr. Gk. κοτύλη. See
cotyledon.

## Coturnix
Coturnix, п., a genus of birds, the Old World
quail (ornithol.) — L. coturnix, 'a quail', dissi-

## milated from earlier cocturnlx
milated from earlier cocturnlx, quocturntx, fr.
base *qwok-, imitative of the quail's cry. For a

## similar
similar, but not related, imitative base cp. quail,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:198 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 171 | COUPE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:198 COLUMN:1 -->
the bird.

## cotwal
cotwal, n. — A var. spelling of kohval.

## cotyledon
cotyledon, п., a seed leaf (hot.) — L., 'navelwort',
fr. Gk. κοτυληδών, 'any cup-shaped hollow,
navelwort', fr. κοτύλη, 'anything hollow, a cup,
socket of a joint', which is possibly rel. to
κότταβος, 'cottabus' (name of a game), and
cogn. with L. catinus, 'deep vessel for cooking,
or serving up, food' (whence dimin. catillus);
cp. ON. ketill, OHG. кеззИ, 'kettle', which are
borrowed fr. L. catillus, and see kettle. Cp.
acotyledon, cotyliscus, cotala. Cp. also cottabus.

## cotyledonous
cotyledonous, adj., having cotyledons. — Formed
from prec. word with suff. -ous.

## cotyliscus
cotyliscus, п., a small cup (Greek and Roman an·
tiq.) — L., fr. Gk. κοτυλίσκος, 'a little cup',
dimin. of κοτύλη. See cotyledon.

## cotyloid
cotyloid, adj., cup-shaped. — Compounded of
κοτύλη, 'cup', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See cotyledon and -oid.

## couch
couch, п., a bed. — F., fr. coucher, 'to lay down*.
See couch, v.

## couch
couch, tr. and intr. v. — F. coucher, 'to lay down,
put to bed', fr. OF. colchier, couchier, coucher,
of s.m., fr. L. collocare, 'to place, station,
arrange', whence also It. collocare, Proven?, colcar,
colgar, 'to lay, place', Sp. colgar, 'to hang up,
suspend', It. colcare, coricare. Rum. culca, 'to
lay down, put to bed'. See collocate and cp.
accouchement
Derivatives: couch-er, п., couch-ing, n.

## couch
couch, п., couch grass. — See couch grass.
Derivative: couch-y, adj.

## couchant
couchant, adj., lying down with the head up (her.)
— F., pres. part, of coucher. See couch, v., and
-ant.
couch grass. — A var. of qnitch grass.

## congar
congar, n. — F. couguar, a name coined byBuffon
on analogy of jaguar fr. cuguacuarana, supposed
to be a Brazilian word. In reality, however, this
latter is due to an erroneous reading. Tupi susu-
arana was transliterated by the Portuguese into
cucuarana. Through the negligent omission of
the cedillas from under the letters с arose the
word from which Buffon coined F. couguar.

## cough
cough, intr. v. — ME. cowhen, coughen, fr. OE.
"cohhian (whence OE. cohhetan, 'to make a
noise'), rel. to MDu. cochen, Du. kuchen, 'to
cough', MHG. kuchen, 'to breathe'. Cp. G.
keuchen, 'to pant, gasp', which is a blend of
MHG. kuchen, 'to breathe', and klchen, 'to
pant'. For this latter see chincough.
Derivatives: cough, п., cough-er, n.

## could
could, aux. v. — Past tense of can, fr. ME. coude,
fr. OE. сйре. The / in could is etymologically
incorrect and due to the analogy of should and
would.

## coulee
coulee, п., a stream of solidified lava. — F., fem.
pp. of couler, 'to flow', used as a noun. See
next word.

## coulisse
coulisse, п., back stage place. — F., prop. fem.
of the adj. coulis, 'that which glides' (in vent
coulis, 'a wind that comes through crevices'),
fr. OF. colels, coulefs, fr. VL. 'colSticius, 'that
which pertains to gliding', fr. L. colore, 'to
strain, filter', in VL. 'to flow; to glide', fr. colum,
'strainer'. See colander and cp. words there
referred to.

## couloir
couloir, п., a mountain gully, gorge. — F.,
'strainer; corridor, passage way', fr. couler, 'to flow,
run, strain', fr. L. colore. See prec. word.

## coulomb
coulomb, п., the unit of quantity in electricity. —
Named after the French physicist Charles-
Augustin de Coulomb (1736-1806).

## coumarin
coumarin, п., a crystalline substance (chem.) —
F. coumarine, fr. coumarou, 'the Tonka-bean
tree', fr. Tupi cumaru.

## council
council, n. — OF. cuncile, fr. L. concilium, 'a
gathering, meeting, assembly', which stands for
*con-caliom, and prop, means 'a calling
together', fr. coa- and calare, 'to call, proclaim'.
See calends and cp. conciliar, conciliate. For the
change of Latin ά (in *con-culiom) to I (in
concilium) see abigeat and cp. words there referred
to. Council was often confused with counsel.

## councilor
councilor, councillor, n. — Formed from prec.
word with agential suff. -or.

## counsel
counsel, n. — ME. conseil, counseil, fr. OF. con-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:198 COLUMN:2 -->
seil, counseil (F. conseil), fr. L. consilium,
'deliberative assembly; consultation, deliberation,
plan, design, advice, counsel', which is prob.
rel. to consulere, 'to take counsel, deliberate'.
See consult, v.

## counsel
counsel, tr. v. —· ME. conseillen, fr. F. conseiller,
'to advise, counsel, recommend', fr. L. con-
siliari, 'to take counsel; to give counsel', fr.
consilium. See couusel, n.

## counselor
counselor, counsellor, n. — ME. counseiller, fr.
OF. conseilleor, conseillere (F. conseiller), fr. L.
cdnsiliatdrem, ace. of constitutor, 'counselor','
fr. cdnsilidri. See counsel, v., and agential suff.
-or.

## count
count, tr. and intr. v. — ME. counten, fr. OF.
confer (F. compter), 'to count, reckon', fr. L.
computare, 'to sum up, reckon'. See compete
and cp. conte. Cp. also account, discount,
recount. Modern French differentiates between
compter, 'to count', and center, 'to narrate',
although the two words are etymologically
identical.
Derivatives: count-able, adj. and п., count-able-
ness, п., countabl-y, adv.

## count
count, п., the act of reckoning. — Late L.
computus, fr. L. computare. See count, v., and cp.
computes.

## count
count, п., a title of nobility. — AF. counte, fr.
OF. conte (F. comte), fr. L. comitem, ace. of
comes, 'companion' (in Late L. also 'one
belonging to the imperial court'), fr. 'com-i-t-, lit.
'one who goes with another', fr. com- and the
stem of ire, 'to go'; see itinerate. Cp. It. conte,
OProvenc. comte, Catal., Sp. and Port, conde,
'count', which all derive fr. L. comitem. Cp. also
countess, county, contessa, concomitant, the first
element in constable, and the second element in
viscount.

## countenance
countenance, n. — OF. (= F.) contenance,
'demeanor, bearing', fr. L. continentia, 'a holding
together; self control', fr. contingns, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of continere, 'to hold together'. See
contain and -ance and cp. continence, which is
a doublet of countenance.
Derivatives: countenance, tr. v., countenanc-er,n.

## counter
counter, п., one who counts. — ME. countour,
fr. OF. conteor (F. compteur), fr. Late L. com-
putaWrem, ace. of computator, 'computer,
reckoner', fr. L. computatus, pp. of computare.
See count, 'to reckon', and agential suff. -er.

## counter
counter, п., a table on which money is counted.
— ME. countour, fr. OF. conteoir (F. comptoir),
fr. ML. computatorium, prop, 'a place for
counting', fr. L. computare. See count, 'to reckon'.

## counter
counter, adv., in the opposite way or direction. —
F. contre, fr. L. contra, 'against, opposite'. See
contra-.

## connter
connter, adj., contrary. — Fr. prec. word.

## counter
counter, п., that which is opposite or contrary
to something. — Fr. counter, adj.

## counter
counter, tr. v., to go or act counter to; intr. v., to
make a counter move; to oppose. — Fr.
counter, adv. Cp. encounter.

## counter-
counter-, combining form expressing opposition,
contrast, correspondence, reciprocity. — F.
contre-, fr. contre, 'against', fr. L. contra. See
counter, adv.

## counterfeit
counterfeit, adj. — OF. contrefait, contrefet (F.
contrefaii), pp. of contrefaire, 'to counterfeit',
fr. contre, 'against', and /aire (fr. L. facere), 'to
make, do'. See counter- and fact.
Derivatives: counterfeit, n. and v., counterfeit-er,
п., counterfeit-ly, adv., counterfeil-ment, п.,
counterfeil-ness, n.

## counterfoil
counterfoil, п., a stub. — Formed fr. counter- and
foil, 'a thin leaf of metal'.

## counterfort
counterfort, п., a buttress. — F. contrefort, lit., 'a
strong support placed against the wall', fr.
contre, 'against', and fort, 'strong'. Seecounter-
and fort.

## countermark
countermark, n. — F. contremarque, fr. contre,
'against', and marque, 'mark'. See counter- and
mark.

## countermark
countermark, tr. v. — F. contremarquer, fr.
contremarque. See countermark, n.

## counterpaly
counterpaly, adj., paly and divided fesswise (her.)
— F. conlrepale, fr. contre, 'against', and pale,
'provided with pales', fr. pal, 'a stake'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:198 COLUMN:3 -->
counter- and pale, 'stake', and cp. paly.

## connterpane
connterpane, п., a coverlet. —: Fr. earlier
counterpoint, 'coverlet', fr. earlier F. contrepointe,
which is a blend of contre, 'against', and OF.
coite-pointe, lit. 'quilt stitched through', fr. L.
culcita piincta, fr. cuicita, 'quilt', and puncta,
fem. pp. of pungere, 'to prick, pierce, point'.
See quilt and point, п., and cp. counterpoint,
'counterpane'. F. courtepointe, 'counterpane', is

## - a blend of court
- a blend of court, 'short', and contrepointe. The
second element in E. counterpane is due to a
confusion of OF. pointe, 'stitched through',
with pan, 'cloth', fr. L. pannus, 'piece of cloth'
(see pane).

## counterpoint
counterpoint, п., combination of melodies (mus.)
— OF. contrepoint, fr. ML. cantus contrapunctus
(whence also It. contrappunto), from the term
punctus contra pQnctum, 'note against note' (lit.
'point against point'). The former practice was
to write the notes for the accompanying voice
against (i.e. over or under) the notes for the first
voice. See counter- and point, п., and cp.
contrapuntal.

## counterpolat
counterpolat, п., a counterpane (obsol.) — Fr.
earlier F. contrepointe, 'coverlet'. See
counterpane.

## counterpoise
counterpoise, п., a counterweight. — ME. coun-
trepeis, fr. OF. contrepois (F. contrepoids), fr.
contre, 'against', and pois (F. polds), 'weight'.
See counter- and poise, n.

## counterpoise
counterpoise, tr. v., to counterbalance. — ME.
countrepesen, countrepeisen, fr. OF. contrepeis-,
contrepois-, pres. sing, stem of contrepeser. See
counter- and poise, v., and cp. counterpoise, n.

## counterscarp
counterscarp, п., the outer slope of a ditch (fort.)
— F. contrescarpe, fr. It. contrascarpa, fr.
contra, 'against' (fr. L. contra), and Scarpa, 'scarp'.
See counter- and scarp.

## counterslga
counterslga, tr. v. — F. contresigner, fr. MF., fr.
contre, 'against', and signer, 'to sign' (fr. L.
signare). See counter- and siga, v. and n.

## countersign
countersign, n.— MF. contresigne, fr. contresigner.
See countersign, tr. v.

## countertenor
countertenor, п., a high tenor voice (mus.) — MF.
contreleneur, fr. It. contratenore, fr. contra,
'against', and tenore, *a tenor'. See counter and
tenor.

## countervail
countervail, tr. and intr. v., 1) to compensate;
2) to counteract. — ME. countrevailen, fr. OF.
contrevaloir, 'to be effective against', fr. contre,
'against', and talovr, 'to be worth' (fr. L. valere,
'to be strong, be well, be worth'). See counter-
and valiant.

## countess
countess, n. — OF. contesse (F. comtesse), fem.
of conte (F. comte), 'count'. See count, 'title of
nobility', and -ess.

## countless
countless, adj. — Formed fr. count, 'number',
with suff. -less; first used by Shakespeare.

## countrified
countrified, adj. — Pp. of obsol. countrify,
arbitrarily formed fr. country and suff. -fy.

## country
country, n. — ME. contree, fr. OF. cuntree, con-
tree (F. contree), fr. Late L. contrata, 'land lying
opposite', fr. L. contra, 'against, opposite'. See
contra- and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
It., OProvenc. Catal., Sp. and Port, contrada,
which also derive fr. Late L. contrata.

## county
county, n. — OF. cunte, conte, contee (F. comte),
fr. L. comitatus, 'escort, retinue', lit. 'a
company', fr. comitatus, pp. of comitari, 'to
accompany', fr. comes, gen. comitis, 'companion'. See
count, 'title of nobility', and cp. contadino and
posse comitatus.
Derivative: county, adj.

## coup
coup, п., a successful stroke of business. — F.,
'stroke, blow', fr. VL. colpus (occurring in the
text of the Salic law), fr. L. colaphus, 'a blow
with the fist, a box on the ear', fr. Gk. κόλαφος,
of e.m., which is rel. to κολάπτειν, 'to hew, cut',
fr. I.-E. base *qola-, 'to strike, cut', whence also
κολούειν, 'to cut short, curtail', κόλος, 'docked,
curtailed, stunted; short-horned, hornless',
κολοβός, 'docked, curtailed, stunted, mutilated'.
See calamity and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also cope, 'to struggle with', coppice, copse,
coupe, coupee, coupon, recoup, calpable and the
second element in Dendrocolaptidae.

## coupe
coupe, п., ι) a half-compartment in a European
railway car; 2) a closed carriage seating two

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:199 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: COUPEE | 172 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:199 COLUMN:1 -->
persons with an outside seat for the driver; 3) a
closed two-door automobile. — F., prop. pp. of
couper, 'to cut', used as a noun, fr. coup, 'stroke,
blow'. See prec. word and cp. next word.

## coupee
coupee, п., a term of dancing. — F., prop. fern,
pp. of couper, 'to cut', used as a noun. See
coup and cp. preceding word.

## couple
couple, n. — OF. cople, cuple, couple (F. couple),
fr. L. copula, 'that which binds together, band,
bond'. See copula and cp. couplet.

## couple
couple, tr. and intr. v. — OF. copier, cupler,
coupler (F. coupler), fr. L. copulare, 'to bind
together, couple', fr. copula. See prec. word.
Derivatives: coupl-ed, adj., coupl-er, п.,
coupling, n.

## couplet
couplet, п., a pair of usually rhyming lines. —
F., dimin. of couple. See couple, п., and -et.
Derivative: couplei-eer, n.

## coupon
coupon, п., a detachable part of a ticket or a
certificate. — F., lit. 'a piece cut off', fr. couper, 'to
cut', fr. coup, 'stroke, blow'. See coup.

## courage
courage, n. — ME. corage, fr. OF. corage, curage,
courage (F. courage), fr. VL. 'coraticum (whence
also It. coraggio, OProvenc. coraige, Sp. coraje,
Port, coragem), fr. L. cor, 'heart'. See cordate
and -age and cp. encourage, discourage.

## courageous
courageous, adj. — AF., fr. OF. corageus (F.
courageux), fr. corage. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: courageous-ly, adv., courageous-
ness, n.

## courant
courant, п., a newspaper (now used only in the
names of newspapers). — F., 'running', pres.
part, of courir, 'to run'. See current, adj., and
-ant and cp. next word.

## courante
courante, п., a dance characterized by running
steps. — F. courante, fern, of courant. See prec.
word.

## courier
courier, п., a messenger. — F. courrier, fr. It. cor-
riere, fr. ML. currerius, 'a professional runner',
fr. L. currere, 'to run'. See current, adj.

## courlan
courlan, п., a bird of the genus Aramus. — F.,
changed fr. courliri, fr. Galibi kurliri, which is
of imitative origin.

## course
course, n. — Partly fr. F. cours, fr. L. cursus, 'a
running, course', partly fr. F. course, fr. It. corsa,
'a course', which also derives fr. L. cursus, fr.
curs-(um), pp. stem of currere, 'to run'. See
current, adj., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: course, tr. and intr. v., courser
(q.v.), cours-ing, n.

## courser
courser, п., a swift horse. — F. coursier, fr. ML.
cursarius, fr. L. cursus, 'a running, course'. See
course.

## courser
courser, п., a bird of the genus Cursorius (orni-
thol.) — Late L. cursorius, 'pertaining to
running', fr. L. cursus, 'a running, course'. See
course and cp. prec. word.

## court
court, n. — ME. court, curt, fr. OF. court, curt
(F. cour), 'court, yard', fr. L. cdrtem, ace. of
cors, contracted form of cohors, 'yard, enclosure;
company; crowd, cohort', which is formed fr. co-
and l.-E. *gkftis, 'enclosure', fr. base "gherdh-,
'to enclose', whence also L. hortus, 'garden', lit.
'an enclosed place', Gk. χόρτος,'enclosed place;
cattle farm'. Goth, gards, 'house', OE. geard,
'piece of land, garden, yard'. Cp. Rum. curte,
It., Sp., Port, corte, OProvenc., Catal. cort, which
all derive fr. L. cdrtem. See yard, 'enclosure',
and cp. cohort, which is a doublet of court. Cp.
also cortege, curtain, curtilage.
Derivatives: court, tr. v., courteous, courtesy
(qq.v.), court-ier, п., court-ier-ly, adj., court-ling,
п., court-ly, adj. and adv., court-li-ness, n.

## courtcard
courtcard, п., a king, queen or knave of playing
cards. — Folk-etymological alteration of
original coat-card.

## courteous
courteous, adj. — ME. cortais, corteis, cortois, fr.
OF. curteis, corteis (F. courtois). See court and
-ous and cp. courtesy.
Derivatives: courteous-ly,adv.,courteous-ness, n.

## courtesan
courtesan, courtezan, n. — F. courtisane, fem.
of courtisan, 'courtier', fr. It. cortigiano, fr.
corte, 'court'. See court.

## courtesy
courtesy, n. — ME. cortaisie, corteisie, cortesie,
courtesie, fr. OF. cortesie, corteisie (F. cour-
toisie), fr. corteis (F. courtois). See courteous
and -y (representing OF. -ie) and cp. curtesy,
curtsy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:199 COLUMN:2 -->

## couscous
couscous, п., an African dish of meat and steamed
flour. — F., fr. Arab, kuskus, fr. kdskasa, 'he
pounded', which is rel. to Heb. kiskes, of s.m.
These verbs are prop. Pilpel forms of Arab.
kassa, resp. Heb. kasds, 'he chewed'. Cp. Ak-
kad. kasasu, 'to cut small', Aram.-Syr. kiss'tha,
Akkad. kissatu, 'fodder'.

## cousin
cousin, ri. — F. cousin, rel. to OProvenc. cozin;
fr. L. consobrinus, 'cousin-german', orig.
denoting only 'the child of a mother's sister', fr.
con- and sobrinus, 'a cousin by the mother's
side', contraction of sororinus, from soror,
'sister' (hence prop, meaning 'sister's child'), which
is cogn. with Goth, swistar, OE. sweostor,
'sister'. See sister and cp. cozen.
Derivatives: cousin-ly, adj. and adv., cousin-
hood, п., cousin-ship, n.

## coutel
coutel, п., a kind of knife (hist.) — OF. coutel
(whence F. couteau), fr. L. cultellus, dimin. of
cutter, 'plowshare, knife'. See colter,

## coutil
coutil, coutllle, п., a close-woven canvas fabric. —
F. coutil, 'drill, twill, ticking', fr. OF. coute
(now couetie, coite), 'featherbed', fr. L. cukita,
'sack filled with feathers, cushion', which is
cogn. with OI. kurcah, 'bundle, bunch, tuft'.
Cp. quilt and words there referred to.

## couvade
couvade, п., a practice among some primitive
peoples according to which, when a child is
born, the father also takes 10 bed and takes care
of the child. — F., 'a brood', fr. couver, 'to
brood', fr. L. cubare, 'to lie down'. See covey
and -ade and cp. concubine,

## cove
cove, п., a small bay; a sheltered nook. — ME.,
fr. OE. cofa, 'chamber', rel. to ON. kofi, 'hut',
MHG. kobe, G. Koben, 'pigsty', and cogn. with
Gk. γύ7τη, 'cave, den, hole', γόψ, gen. γϋπός,
'vulture', fr. I.-E. *geu-p-, a -p-enlargement of
base *geu-, 'to bend, curve, arch', whence Gk.
γύης, 'the curved piece of a wood in a plow',
γυΐον, 'limb' (chiefly used in the pi. γυΐα), and
*γύα, 'hand', which prob. appears in έγγύη,
'surety, security, bail', prop, 'pledge put into
one's hand', and in εγγύς, 'near'. Cp. base
*g(u)wel-, an -/-enlargement of base *geu-,
whence OI. golah, gulah, 'sphere', Gk. γύαλου,
'a hollow', Megarian γυάλας, 'cup', Gk. γυλιός
(also γύλιος), 'long-shaped wallet', OHG. kiol,
'vessel', kiulla, 'pocket, wallet'. Cp. bowel
and words there referred to, cod, 'a small bag',
endyscope, Gyps, gyre. For derivatives of I.-E.
*qeu-p-, a collateral form of base *geu-p-, see
cup and words there referred to.
Derivatives: cove, tr. and intr. v., cov-ed, adj.

## cove
cove, п., fellow, chap (slang). — Gypsy kova,
'that man'.

## covellite
covellite, п., indigo copper (mineral.) — Named
after the Italian chemist Niccolo Covelli (1790-
1829), who discovered it in the lava of Mount
Vesuvius. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## coven
coven, covine, п., an assembly of witches. — OF.
covent, 'assembly'. See convent and cp. covin,

## covenant
covenant, n. — OF. covenant, 'a coming together,
assembly', prop. pres. part, of covenir, 'to come
together, assemble', whence F. convenir, 'to
agree; to suit, fit'. See convene and -ant and
cp. convenieat.
Derivatives: covenant, v., covenant-ed, adj.,

## covenant-er
covenant-er, n.

## cover
cover, tr. v. — OF. covrir, cuvrir (F. couvrir), fr.

## L. cooperire
L. cooperire, 'to cover wholly, cover', fr. co-

## and operire
and operire, 'to cover', for *op-werire, which is

## formed fr. ob
formed fr. ob, 'toward', and I.-E. base *wer-,
'to enclose, cover'. See ob- and weir and cp.

## aperient
aperient, operculum. Cp. also the first element
in curfew.
Derivatives: cover, п., cover-age, п., cover-ed,

## adj.
adj., cover-er, п., cover-ing, adj. and n.

## coverlet
coverlet, п., a bedcover. — ME. coverlyle, fr. AF.

## coverlit (cp. F. couvre-lit)
coverlit (cp. F. couvre-lit), fr. OF. covrir, cuvrir
(F. couvrir), 'to cover', and lit, 'bed', fr. L. lectus.

## See cover and lie
See cover and lie, 'to recline'.

## covert
covert, adj., 1) covered, hidden, sheltered; 2) (law)

## married (said of a woman)
married (said of a woman), lit. 'covered (i.e.
protected) by her husband'. — ME., fr. OF.

## covert (F. couveri)
covert (F. couveri), pp. of covrir. See cover and
cp. overt. Cp. also feme covert and discovert.
Derivatives: covert, п., coverl-ly, adv., coverl-

## ness
ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:199 COLUMN:3 -->

## covertare
covertare, п., the status of a married woman (law).
— OF. (F. couverture), fr. covert, pp. of covrir.
See prec. word and -ure.

## covet
covet, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. OF. coveitier, fr. VL.
*cupidietare, fr. *cupidietas, altered fr. L. cupi-
ditas, 'desire', fr. cupere, 'to desire'; see Cnpid.
OF. coveitier soon became conveitier (F. con-
voiter) on analogy of the numerous words
beginning with con-.
Derivatives: covet-able, adj., covel-er, п.,
coveting, adj., covet-ing-ly, adv., covetise (q.v.), covet-
ive-ness, п., covetous (q.v.)

## covetise
covetise, п., covetousness (obsol.) — OF. coveitise
(F. convoitise), fr. VL. *cupiditia, fr. L. cupidus,
'desirous', fr. cupere, 'to desire'. See covet and
-ise.

## covetous
covetous, adj. — OF. coveitos (F. convoiteux),
from the stem of coveitier, 'to covet'. See covet
and -ous.
Derivatives: covetous-ly, adv., covetous-ness, n.

## covey
covey, п., a brood of partridges. — OF. covee
(F. couvee), prop. fem. pp. of cover (F. couver),
'to sit on, hatch', fr. L. cubare, 'to lie down',
which is cogn. with Gk. κύβος, 'hollow above
the hip of cattle'. See cubicle.

## covid
covid, п., a varying measure of length. — Indo-
Port., fr. Port, covado, 'ell, cubit', fr. L. cubilum,
cubit us, .'elbow, ell, cubit', whence also Sp. coda,
Catal. colde, colze, Proven?, coide, F. coude,
Tosc. goviio, Olt. gombito, It. gomito. Rum. cot,
'elbow'. See cubit.

## covil
covil, n. — A var. spelling of kovil.

## covin
covin, п., an unlawful agreement (law). — OF.
covin, covine, lit. 'a coming together', fr. covenir.
See covenant and cp. coven.

## covine
covine, n. — See coven.

## coving
coving, п., a cove or series of coves (archit.) —
Formed fr. cove, 'arch,' with subst. suff. -tag.

## cow
cow, n. — ME. ky, kye, fr. OE. ей, rel. to OS. кб,
OFris. кй, MDu. сое, Du. кое, OHG. chuo,
kuo, MHG. kuo, G. Kuh, Dan. and Swed. ко,
ON. kyr, Norw. kyr, ко, 'cow', and cogn. with
Olr. bo, W. buw, 'cow', L. bos, Gk. βοϋς (for
*gwaus-), 'ox', Lett, guovs, 'cow', OSlav. *gov-
edo, Czech hevado, Slovak hovado, 'ox', OI.
gduh, Avestic gaush, 'ox, bull, cow', Toch. A
ко, ki, В keu, 'cow', Arm. hov, 'cow', kogi,
'butter'. All these words ult. derive fr. Sumeric
gu (fr. earlier gud), 'bull, ox', a word of
imitative origin. Chinese ngo, ngu, 'ox', is a Sumeric
loan word (possibly through the medium of an
Indo-European language). Cp. kiite. Cp. also
Bos, boustrophedon, bovine, Bucentaur, Bnce-
phalus, Buceros, bucolic, buffalo, bagle, bngloss,
Bapleurnm, Buprestis, Busycon, butter, Gaek-
nar, gaur, Gautama, gopura, hecatomb, nilgai,
priest, sang-de-boeuf.
Derivatives: cow-ish, adj., cow-like, adj.

## cow
cow, tr. v., to frighten. — ON. kuga (whence
Dan. кие), 'to tyrannize over'.

## coward
coward, adj. — OF. coart, coard, couard (F. cou-
ard), fr. OF. сое (F. queue), 'tail', prop, 'one
who turns tail', fr. L. coda, secondary form of
cauda, 'tail', prob. orig. meaning 'stump,
anything cut off', and related to caudex, 'trunk of
a tree, block of wood'. See caudal and -ard.
Derivatives: coward, п., cowardice (q.v.), co-
ward-ly, adv., coward-li-ness, n.

## cownrdice
cownrdice, n. — ME. cowardise, fr. OF. (= F.)
couardise, fr. couard. See prec. word and -ice.

## cower
cower, intr. v., to crouch in fear. — ME. couren,
of Scand. origin. Ср. ОН кйга, 'to doze, lie
quiet', Dan. kure, Swed. kura, 'to squat', which
are rel. to MLG. kuren, G. kauern, 'to squat,
cower', and cogn. with Gk. γϋρος, 'circle',
γϋρος, 'rounded, curved'. See gyre.

## cowhnge
cowhnge, also cowitch, п., the Indian climbing
plant Mucuna pruriens, the hairs of which
cause itching. — Anglicized fr. Hind, kewanch,
fr. OI. kapikacchnh, lit. 'monkey itch', fr. kapib,
'monkey', and kacchuh, 'itch'. OI. kapib is ety-
mologically connected with Akkad. uqupu, Heb.
qoph, Gk. κήπος, κήβος, and with Egypt, qephi,
'monkey', however, the ultimate origin of these
words has not yet been established. See Manfred
Mayrhofer, A Concise Etymological Sanskrit
Dictionary, I, 156 s.v. kaplh, 'monkey'. OI.
kacchuh, 'itch', and the related kharjuh, 'itching,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:200 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 173 | CRANIO- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:200 COLUMN:1 -->
scratching', are Dravidian loan words; cp.
Kanarese касс и, karcu, 'to bite, sting, ail'.

## cowl
cowl, п., a hood. — ME. cowle, fr. OE. cugele,
cule, fr. L. cucullus, 'hood', which is prob. of
Gaulish origin; cp. L. bardacucullus, 'a Gaulish
overcoat with a cowl of wool', prop, meaning
'the cowl of a bard', fr. *bardus, 'bard', and
cucullus, 'cowl'. Ir. cochull, 'a veil covering the
head and the shoulders'-, has been reborrowed
fr. L. cucullus. Cp. cucullate.
Derivative: cowl, tr. v.

## cowl
cowl, п., a large tub for water. — ME. covel, coul,
fr. OF. cuvele, fr. Late L. cupella, dimin. of
L. сира, 'tub, cask'. See cup and cp. words there
referred to.

## cowle
cowle, п., a grant in writing (Anglo-lnd.) — Hind.
qawl, fr. Arab, qaul, 'sound, voice, saying,
word', from the base of gala, 'he spoke', rel. to
Heb. qol, 'sound, voice', Ugar. ql, Aram, qal,
quia, Syr. quia, Ethiop. qal, of s.m., Akkad.
qulu, 'shouting' and to Heb. qahal, 'assembly,
congregation', hiqhfl, 'he assembled', qehillah,
'assembly, congregation'. Cp. kchillah, Ko-
heleth and the second element in bathkol.

## cowrie
cowrie, cowry, п., a small shell of the genus Cy-
praea, used as money in parts of S. Asia. —
Hind, kauri, kaudl, fr. Mahrati kavadt, fr. OI.
kapardab, kapardika-, derived—through the
medium of the forms "kavatu, kapafu, *kapar-
du—fr. Tamil kofu, 'shell', orig. meaning
'crookedness'.

## cowslip
cowslip, п., a plant with yellow flowers. — OE.
сй-slyppe, fr. ей, 'cow', and slyppe, 'slime'. See
cow and slip and cp. oxlip.
Derivative: cowslipp-ed, adj.

## cox
cox, n. and tr. v. (colloq.) — Short for coxswain,

## coxa
coxa, п., the hip (anat.) — L., 'hip', cogn. with
OI. kaksab, kaksa, 'armpit', OE. huh, 'heel', and
with the first element in OE. hoh-sinu, 'hock
sinew'. See hock, 'joint in the hind leg of a
horse', and cp. cuisse, cushion, Quixotic.
Derivative: cox-al, adj.

## coxalgia
coxalgia, п., pain in the hip (med.) — A Medical
Latin hybrid coined fr. L. coxa, 'hip', and Gk.
-αλγία, fr. άλγος, 'pain'. See prec. word and
-algia.
Derivative: coxalg-ic, adj.

## coxcomb
coxcomb, n. — For cock's comb. The word orig.
meant 'a cap resembling a cock's comb'.
Derivatives: coxcomb-ess, п., coxcomb-ic, cox-
comb-ic-al, adjs., coxcomb-ic-al-ly, adv., cox-
comb-ry, п., coxcomb-y, adj.

## coxitis
coxitis, п., inflammation of the hip (med) — A
Medical Latin hybrid coined fr. L. coxa, 'hip'
(see coxa) and -itis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## coxswain
coxswain, п., a steersman. — From earlier
cockswain, which is compounded of cock, 'cockboat',
and swaia.
Derivative: coxswain, tr. and intr. v.

## coxy
coxy, adj., cheeky (schoolboy's slang). — A var.
of cocky.

## coy
coy, adj., shy. — ME., 'quiet', fr. OF. coi, coy,
fr. earlier quel, fr. L. quietus. See quiet, adj.
Derivatives: coy, v., coy-ly, adv., coy-ness, n.

## coyote
coyote, п., prairie wolf of North America. — Sp.,
fr. Nahuati koyoll.

## coypu
coypu, п., a South American water rodent. —
Sp., from native name.

## coz
coz, n. — Abbreviation of cozen.

## coze
coze, intr. v., to talk in a friendly way, to chat. —
Prob. fr. F. causer, 'to talk', fr. L. causari, 4o
plead, dispute, to discuss a question', fr. causa,
'cause, reason, purpose'. See cause and cp.
causerie.

## cozen
cozen, tr. v., to cheat, deceive; intr. v., to act
deceitfully. — Orig. 'to pretend to be a cousin;
to deceive by pretending to be a cousin', fr. F.
cousiner, 'to call cousin, be related to; to
sponge, live on others', fr. cousin. See cousin.
Derivatives: cozen-age, n. (cp. F. cousinage),
cozen-er, п., cozen-ing, adj. and verbal п., cozen-
ing-ly, adv.

## cozy
cozy, also cosy, adj., comfortable. — Prob. fr.
Norw. koselig, 'cosy', fr. kose sig, 'to make
oneself comfortable'.
Derivatives: cozi-ly, adv., cozi-ness, n.

## crab
crab, п., a crustacean. — ME. crabbc, fr. OE.
crabba, rel. to ON. krabbi, MLG. krabbe, MDu.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:200 COLUMN:2 -->
crabbe, Du. krab, 'crab', OHG. кгеЫз, MHG.
krebes, G. Krebs, 'crayfish'. These* words lit.
mean 'the scratcrier', and are rel. to Du. krab-
belen, 'to scratch'. See crawl and cp. crab, 'crab
apple'. Cp. also OF. crevice, escrevice (F.
ecrevisse), 'crayfish', which derive fr. OHG.
krebij (see crayfish).
Derivatives: crab, intr. v., to fish for crabs;
tr. v., to drift sidewise (nam. and aviation),
crabb-y, adj.

## crab
crab, п., crab apple. — ME. crabbe, prob. fr.
crab, the animal. For sense development cp.
crabbed.

## crab apple
crab apple, a small, sour wild apple. — See prec.
word and cp. Swed. krabapple.

## crabbed
crabbed, adj., peevish, morose. — Lit. 'resembling
a crab'. Formed fr. crab, the animal, with suff.
-ed.
Derivatives: crabb-ed-ly, adv., crubb-ed-ness, n.

## crachoir
crachoir, п., spittoon. — F., fr. cracker, 'to spit',
fr. VL. *craccare, of s.m. (whence also It. scrac-
chiare, scaracchiare, OProvenc. escracar); of
imitative origin.

## crack
crack, intr. and tr. v. — ME. cracken, fr. OE.
cracian, 'to resound', rel. to MDu. craken, Du.
kraken, OHG. krahhon, MHG., G. krachen, 'to
crack', OE. cearcian, 'to creak, to gnash (the
teeth)', F. craquer, 'to crack', from the I.-E.
imitative base *ger-, 'to make a noise', whence
also Lith. girgzdeti, 'to creak', Arm. karkaS,
'to make noise', OI. garjati, 'roars', Cp.
cracknel.
Derivatives: crack, n. and adj., crack-ed, adj.,
crack-er, п., crackle (q.v.), crack-y, adj.

## crackle
crackle, intr. v. — Formed fr. crack with freq.
suff. -le.
Derivatives: crackle, п., crackl-ed, adj.,
crackling, n.

## cracknel
cracknel, п., a kind of hard, brittle biscuit. —
Fr. earlier crakenel, metathesis of F. craquelin,
'cracknel', fr. MDu. crakelinc (Du. krakeling),
fr. craken, 'to crack'. See crack.

## cracovienne
cracovienne, п., a Polish dance. — F. (short for
danse cracovienne, lit. 'a Cracow danse'), fem.
of cracovien, 'of Cracow', fr. Cracovie, 'Cracow'.

## -cracy
-cracy, combining form meaning a certain type
of'rule' or 'government', as in monocracy. — OF.
-cracie (F. -cratie), fr. Gk. -κρατίά, 'rule', fr.
κράτος, 'strength, might, power, rule, sway,
dominion' (whence κρατειν, 'to be strong, rule
over', κρατύς, 'strong, mighty'), which is cogn.
with Goth, hardus, 'hard', OE. heard, 'hard,
brave'. See hard and cp. acrasia, acratia and the
first element in Crataegus.

## cradge
cradge, п., a small bank raised to prevent
overflow of water. — F. creche, 'crib, cradle', fr.
Frankish *kripja, which is rel. to OHG. krippa,
OE. cribb, 'crib'. See crib and cp. cratch, creche.
Derivative: cradge, tr. and intr. v.

## cradle
cradle, n. — ME. cradel, fr. OE. cradel, cradol,
rel. to OE. crxt, 'cart', and to OHG. kratto,
'basket', OHG. chrezzo, MHG. krezze, of s.m.,
G. Kratze, 'basket carried on the back', and
cogn. with OI. grathnali, granthayati, 'twists,
ties', granthah, 'knot'. Cp. cart.
Derivatives: cradle, tr. \.,cradl-er, п., cradl-ing,n.

## craft
craft, п., skill. — ME. craft, fr. OE. crseft,
'strength, power, skill, cunning; trade,
profession', re], to OS., Dan., Swed., OHG., MHG.,
G. kraft, ON. kraptr, OFris. kreft, MDu. craft,
cracht, Du. kracht, 'strength, power', and
perhaps also to ON. krefja, 'to crave, demand',
and to E. crave.

## craft
craft, п., a boat, vessel. — Shortened from the
phrase a vessel of small craft, in which craft is
used in its original sense (i.e. 'power'). See
prec. word.

## crafty
crafty, adj. — ME., fr. OE. crxftig, fr. crxft. See
craft and -y (representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: crafti-ly, adv., crafti-ness, n.

## crag
crag, п., a steep rock. — Of Celtic origin. Cp.
W. craig, Gael, creag, Ir. carraig, 'cliff, rock'.
Derivatives: cragg-ed, cragg-y, adjs., cragg-i-
ness, n.

## crag
crag, п., neck (dial.) — MDu. craghe (Du. kraag),
'neck, gullet; collar'. See craw.

## crake
crake, п., the corn crake. — ME., of imitative
origin. Cp. ON. kraka, 'crow', krakr, 'raven',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:200 COLUMN:3 -->
and E. croak. Cp. also next word.

## crake
crake, intr. v., to utter a harsh cry. — ME. craken,
'to shriek', of imitative origin, and rel. to prec.
word.

## cram
cram, tr. and intr. v. — ME. crammen, fr. OE.
crammian, 'to cram, stuff', fr. crimman, 'to cram,
insert', which is rel. to ON. kremia, 'to press,
squeeze', fr. I.-E. base *grem-, 'to press, squeeze',
whence also OI. grumah, 'heap, troop, village',
OSIav. gramota, 'a heap' ,gromada, 'a large heap',
L. gremium, 'bosom, lap'. Base *grem- is an
enlargement of base *ger-, 'to gather together'.
See gregarious and cp. gremial.
Derivatives: cram, п., cramm-er, n.

## Crambe
Crambe, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (hot.) — L. crambe, fr. Gk. κράμβη,
'cabbage', which is rel. to κράμβος,'dry,
shriveling', κρομβοΰν (assimilated fr. *κραμβοΰν), 'to
roast', and cogn. with OHG. hrimfan, rimfan,
'to contract, wrinkle', OE. hrympel, 'wrinkle'.
See rumple and cp. next word and the second
element in Cynocrambe.

## crambo
crambo, п., a game in which one player gives a
word, to which another has to find a rhyme. —
Fr. Gk. κράμβη, 'cabbage', prob. in allusion to
the Latin expression crambe repetita, 'an old
story', lit. 'cabbage warmed over'. See prec.
word.

## cramoisy
cramoisy, adj., crimson. — F. cramoisi, whence
ME. crimosine. See crimson.

## cramp
cramp, п., spasmodic muscular contraction (med.)
— ME. crampe, 'spasm', fr. OF. (= F.) crampe,
fr. Frankish *krampa, 'cramp, spasm,
convulsion'. Cp. OS., Du. kramp, OHG. kramph(o),
MHG., G. krampf, 'cramp, spasm, convulsion',
and see next word.
Derivative: cramp, tr. v.

## cramp
cramp, п., a bent piece of iron. — MDu. crampe,
cramp, rel. to OHG. kramph, 'bent, crooked',
ON. krappr (for *krampr), 'strait, narrow', and
in gradational relationship to Du. and LG.
krimpen, OHG. krimphan, 'to curve, shrink'.
Cp. prec. word. Cp. also crimp, v., crumple and
grape, grapple, grapnel.
Derivatives: cramp, tr. v., cramp-ed, adj.

## crampon
crampon, п., a grappling iron; climbing iron. —
F., fr. Frankish *kramp-, 'bent, crooked', which
is rel. to OHG. kramph, of s.m. See cramp, 'a
bent piece of iron'.
сгап, п., a measure for herrings, 37^ gallons. —
Gael, crann, 'tree, lot, a measure', rel. to Olr.
crann, 'tree', W. prenn, 'tree stump', and
possibly cogn. with Gk. πρέμνον, 'tree stump'. Cp.
crannog.

## cranage
cranage, п., ι) the use of a crane; 2) the charge
for the use of a crane. — Formed fr. crane with
suff. -age.

## cranberry
cranberry, n. — LG. kranbere, rel. to G. Kranich-
beere, of s.m. See crane and berry.

## crandallite
crandallite, п., a hydrous calcium-aluminum
phosphate (mineral.) — Named after its
discoverer M. L. Crandall, mining engineer of
Provo, Utah. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## crane
crane, n. — ME. crane, crone, fr. OE. cran, rel.
to OS., OHG. krano, Du. kraan, MHG. krone,
OE. cranoc, сотое, MLG. kranek, OHG. chra-
nuh, MHG. kranech, G. Kranich, 'crane', and
cogn. with Arm. kfunk, Gk. γερανός, Co., W.,
Bret, garan, 'crane', Lilh. garnys, 'heron, stork',
gerve, Lett, dzefve, OPruss. gerwe, OSIav. zeravl,
'crane', L. grus, 'crane'. All these words derive
from the I.-E. imitative base *ger-, 'to utter a
hoarse cry'. Cp. the first element in cranberry.
Cp. also Geranium, the first element in Grui-
formes, and the last element in pedigree. For the
sense development of crane, which denotes also
'a machine for raising weights' (so called from
the long neck of the instrument), cp. Gk.
γερανός, 'crane' (in both senses of the English
word).
Derivatives: crane, tr. v., cran-er, п., crane-y,
adj.

## cranial
cranial, adj., pertaining to the skull. — Formed
with adj. suff. -a] fr. ML. cranium. See cranium.
Derivative: cranial-iy, adv.

## cranio-
cranio-, combining form denoting the skull (anat.)
— Gk. κρανίο-, fr. κρανίον, 'skull'. See era-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:201 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CRANIOLOGV | 174 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:201 COLUMN:1 -->
nium.

## craniology
craniology, п., the science dealing with the shape,
size and other characteristics of the human skull.
— Lit. 'lhe study of the skull', fr. cranio-, and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives*, craniolog-ical, adj., craniolog-ical-
ly, adv., craniolog-ist, n.

## craniometer
craniometer, п., an instrument for measuring
skulls. — Compounded of cranio and Gk. μέ-
τρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## craniometry
craniometry, п., the science of measuring skulls.
— Compounded of cranio- and Gk. -μετρία,
'measure of. See -metry.

## cranium
cranium, п., the skull (anal.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. κρανίον, 'the skull', which is rel. to, and
prob. derives from, κράς, gen. κρδτός (a poetic
form), 'head', hence rel. also to Ion. κάρη, Att.
κάρα, Homeric κάρ, 'head', Att., Dor. κάράυον,
Ion. κάρηνον, 'head', the first element in Gk.
κράσ-ιτεδον, 'edge, border, skirt', lit. 'place of
the head', and cogn. with L. cerebrum, 'brain'.
See cerebrum and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also bias, bucranium, carrot, charivari,
coryphaeus, craspedon, hemicrania, megrim, mi-
graiae, pericranium.

## crank
crank, п., a turn, twist; part of a machine. — ME.
cranke, rel. to OE. cringan, crincan, 'to bend,
sink down in a battle'. See crank, adj.

## crank
crank, adj., bent; sick; cranky. — G. krank,
'sick', fr. MHG. kranc, 'narrow, slender, weak',
which is rel. to MDu. crane, Du. krank, 'sick',
OE. crane, 'brittle, tender', cringan, 'to sink
down in battle, to perish', and to crank, п.,
MHG. krangel, 'circle', is of the same base.
Outside Teut. cp. Lith. greziu, grezti, 'to turn,
twist', OPruss. granstis, 'borer'. Cp. cringe,
crinkle.
Derivatives: crank, tr. and intr. v., crank-ed,
adj., crank-er, п., crank-er-y, п., crank-le, tr.
and intr. v. and п., crank-y (sickly), adj., crank-
i-ly, adv., crank-i-ness, n.

## crannog
crannog, п., an ancient lake dwelling in Scotland
or Ireland. — Ir. crannog, fr. crann, 'tree, beam'.
See cran.

## cranny
cranny, п., a small cleft. — ME. crany, 'chink',
fr. F. cran, 'notch', a collateral form of cren,
of s.m., fr. crlner, 'to notch', fr. VL. *crlnare,
fr. Late L. crlna, 'notch'. See crenel and cp.
crenate.

## crape
crape, n. — Anglicized spelling of F. crepe, fr.
OF. crespe, 'curled', fr. L. crispus. See crisp
and cp. crepe.

## crape
crape, tr. v. — F. crlper, fr. crepe. See crape, n.

## crappie
crappie, п., name of a fish found in the
Mississippi (Pomoxis annularis). — Of uncertain
origin.

## crapulence
crapulence, crapulency, n. — Formed fr. next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## crapulent
crapulent, adj., sick from excess in eating' or
drinking. — L. crapulentus, 'very much
intoxicated', fr. crapula, 'drinking bout,
intoxication, debauch', fr. Gk. κραιπάλη, of s.m., which
is possibly rel. to. κραιπνός, 'swift, rushing'.
For the change of Greek α to и in Latin cp. L.
aplustre fr. Gk. αφλαστον, 'the curved stern of a
ship', L. pessulus, fr. Gk. πάσσαλος, 'bolt', L.
triumphus, 'triumph', fr. Gk. θρίαμβος, 'a
procession (made in honor of Bacchus)'; see
aplustre, pessulus, triumph.

## crapulous
crapulous, adj., crapulent. — VL. crapulosus, fr.
L. crapula, 'intoxication'. See prec. word and
-ous.
Derivatives: crapulous-ly, adv.,crapulous-ness,n.

## crash
crash, intr. v., to fall with a noise; tr. v., to cause
to crash. — ME. craschen, of imitative
origin; related to craze and to crack (qq.v.) Cp.
clash.
Derivatives: crash, п., a loud, sudden noise,
crash-er, n.

## crash
crash, п., a coarse linen fabric. — Short for Russ.
krashenina, 'colored linen', fr. krashenie, 'a
dyeing', fr. krasit', 'to color, paint, dye', fr.
krasa, 'beauty' (whence also krasnyj, 'red'),
which is rel. to Lith. grozis, 'beauty', grazus,
'beautiful'.

## crasis
crasis, п., contraction of two vowels. — Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:201 COLUMN:2 -->
κράσις, 'a mixing, blending', rel. to κρατήρ, 'a
large bowl for mixing wine and water'. See
crater and cp. dyscrasia, idiosyncrasy.

## craspedon
craspedon, also craspedum, п., the velum of a
jellyfish (zool.) — Gk. κράσπεδον, 'edge,
border, skirt', for κράσ-πεδον, lit. 'place of the
head', fr. κράς, 'head', and πέδον, 'ground,
earth'. See cranium and pedal and cp. next word.
Derivative: crasped-al, adj.

## Craspedota
Craspedota, n. p]., a group of coelenterates {zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. κρασπεδωτά, neut. pi. of
κρασπεδωτός, verbal adj. of κρασπεδοϋσθαι, 'to
be edged, bordered', fr. κράσιτεδον. See prec.
word.

## crass
crass, adj. — L. crassus, 'thick, solid, dense, fat',
for *qrtt-tos, fr. I.-E. base *qerat-, *qert-, 'to roll
or twist together', whence also L. cratis, 'wicker-
work, hurdle'. See crate and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also Crassula, cresset, incras-
sate. Cp. also degras, grease, and lhe first
element in grampus.
Derivatives: crass-ly, adv., crass-ness, n.

## crassitude
crassitude, п., grossness. — L. crassitudo,
'thickness, density, fatness', fr. crassus. See crass and
-tude.

## Crassula
Crassula, п., a genus of herbs (hot.) — ModL.,
a dimin. noun formed fr. L. crassus, 'thick'. See
crass and -ule.

## Crassnlaceae
Crassnlaceae, n. pi., a family of herbs (hot.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## crassulaceous
crassulaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## -crat
-crat, combining form denoting 'a supporter' or
'member' of a certain type of government, as in
democrat. — F. -crate, fr. Gk. -κράτης, fr.
κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'. See -cracy.

## Crataegus
Crataegus, п., a genus of plants of the apple family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κράταιγος, 'thorn',
which is compounded of κρατύς, 'strong', and
-αιγος, 'tree, oak'. The first element is cogn.
with Goth, hardus, OE. heard; see hard. The
second element is cogn. with L. aesculus, 'the
Italian oak', OE. ac, 'oak'; see oak and cp.
Aesculus.

## cratch
cratch, п., crib, rack. — ME. crecche, fr. OF.
creche (F. creche), fr. Frankish *kripja, which is
related to OHG. krippa, OE. cribb. See crib and
cp. cradge, creche.

## cratch
cratch, tr. and intr. v., to scratch (pbsol.) — MDu.
cratsen, rel. to OHG. krazidn, 'to scratch'. See
scratch.

## crate
crate, n. — L. cratis, 'wickerwork, hurdle', fr.
I.-E. base *qeral-, *qert-, 'to roll or twist
together', whence also L. crassus, 'thick, solid,
dense, fat', OI. krtsnah, 'complete, whole',
Russ.-Church Slav, iristvu, iirstvu, 'firm, solid
genuine', Russ. krutu, 'firm, thick', OE. hyrd,
'door' (orig. 'door of wickerwork'), hyrdel,
'hurdle'. See hurdle and cp. cartilage, crass,
creel. The above base is a -r-enlargement
of base *qer-, 'to turn, twist', whence L. curvus,
'bent, crooked'. See curve and cp. words there
referred to.

## crater
crater, n. — L. crater, 'a large bowl for mixing
wine and water', fr. Gk. κρατήρ, which is rel. to
κρασις, 'a mixing, blending', κεραννύναι, 'to
mix, mingle, blend, temper", άκέραστος,
άκρατος. Ion. ακρητος, 'unmixed, pure', fr. I.-E.
base *kerai-, *tcer-, 'to mix, blend', whence also
OI. srayati, 'cooks', Srinati, 'mixes, cooks', OE.
hrlran, 'to move, stir, shake', hrlr, 'underdone'.
See rare, 'underdone', and cp. krater. Cp. also
acrasia, dyscrasia, grail, 'chalice', syncretism.
Derivatives: crater, intr. v., crater-al, adj.,
crater-ed, adj.

## craterUorm
craterUorm, adj., crater-shaped. — Compounded
of crater and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## cratometer
cratometer, п., an instrument for measuring
power. — Compounded of κράτος, 'strength,
might, power', and μέτρον, 'measure'. See
-cracy and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: cratometr-ic, adj., cratometr-y, n.

## crnunch
crnunch, tr. and intr. v., to crunch. — An earlier
form of crunch.

## cravat
cravat, n. — F. cravate, fr. Cravate, 'Croat,
Croatian', and lit. meaning 'neckcloth worn by
the Croats', fr. Serbo-Crotian Hrvat, 'Croat', fr.
OSlav. Churiatinu; originally meaning'necktie
after the Croatian fashion'. See Croat.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:201 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: cravat, tr. and intr. v.

## crave
crave, tr. and intr. v. — ME. craven, fr. OE.
crafian, 'to demand one's right, ask', rel. to ON.
krefja, 'to crave, demand', krafa, 'a demand',
Swed. krafva, 'to demand', and perhaps also
to E. craft (q.v.)
Derivatives: crav-er, п., crav-ing, adj. and п.,
crav-ing-ly, adv., crav-ing-ness, n.

## craven
craven, adj., cowardly. — ME. cravant, 'beaten,
vanquished, overcome', fr. OF. cravant, pres.
part, of craver, crever (F. crever), 'to crack,
break, burst', fr. L. crepdre, 'to rattle, crack,
break with a crack, burst*. See crepitate and cp.
words there referred to.
Berivatives: craven, n. and tr. v., craven-ly, adv.,
craven-ness, n.

## craw
craw, п., the crop of a bird. — ME. crawe, rel. to
MLG. krage, MDu. craghe, Du. kraag, 'neck,
gullet; collar', MHG. krage, of s.m., G. Kragen,
'collar', and prob. cogn. with Gk. βρόχ&ος,
'throat', έβροξε (aor.), 'he swallowed up',
βρόγχος, 'windpipe', Olr. bragae, 'neck', W.
breuanl, 'throat, gullet', fr. I.-E. base *gwr6gh-,
a -^-enlargement of base *gwer-, 'to swallow',
whence L. vorare, 'to devour'. See voracious and
cp. crag, 'neck'. Cp. also bronchus.

## crawfish
crawfish, n. — A var. of crayfish.

## crawl
crawl, intr. v. — ME. crawlen, fr. ON. krafla,
'to paw, crawl', rel. to Dan. kravle, 'to crawl',
Du. krabbelen, 'to scratch', LG. krabben, 'to
scratch, claw' (whence G. krabbeln, 'to grope,
crawl'), and to crab, 'crustacean' (q.v.) Cp.
scrawl.
Derivatives: crawl, п., crawl-er, п., crawl-ing,
adj. and п., crawl-ing-ly, adv.

## crawl
crawl, п., an enclosure in water for turtles. — Du.
kraal. See kraal and cp. corral.

## crayfish
crayfish, also crawfish, n. —· ME. crevise, crevis,
fr. OF. crevice (also escrevice, whence F. ecre-
visse), fr. Frankish *krabitja, *krebilja, dimin.
forms rel. to OS. krebit, MDu. crevet, Du.
kreeft, OHG. кгеЫз, MHG. кгеЬез, G. Krebs,
and to LG. krabbe, Du. krab, ON. krabbi, OE.
crabba, 'crab'. See crab, 'crustacean'.

## crayon
crayon, п., a stick of colored chalk. — F.,
'pencil', orig. 'a chalk pencil', derived fr. craie,
'chalk', fr. L. crlta, lit. 'sifted earth', fr. (terra)
crlta, fem. pp. of cernere, 'to sift' (see certain).
The usual derivation of Latin crlta, 'chalk',
from Crlta, the Latin name of the isle of Crete,
is erroneous. Any Latin derivative of the island
name Crlta must needs have a Latin suff. If
crlta, 'chalk', were really a derivative of the
island name Crlta, its form should be crltica or
crltlnsis, etc. (for terra Crltica or Crltlnsis, lit.
'earth of Crete'). Confusion with the isle of
Crete is prob. due to the fact that Cimolus (Gk.
Κίμωλος), one of the islands of the Cretan Sea,
was famous for the chalk produced there (see
cimolite). For the sense development of L. crlta,
'chalk', lit. 'sifted earth', cp. OSlav. mllu,
'lime', and Russ. mllu, 'chalk', fr. OSlav. meljp,
mllli, 'to grind'. Cp. It. creta, OProvenc., Catal.,
Sp., Port, greda, MLG. krile, MDu. (= Du.)
krijt, OS. krida, MHG. kride (G. Kreide), Bret.
creiz, etc., which all derive fr. L. crlta. The word
crayon was introduced into English by the
English diarist John Evelyn (1620-1706).

## crayoa
crayoa, tr. v., to draw with a crayon. — F. cray-
onner, 'to draw with a pencil', fr. crayon,
'pencil'. See crayon, n.

## crayonist
crayonist, n. — F. crayonniste, 'one who draws
with a pencil', a hybrid coined fr. F. crayon
(see crayon, п., 1), and suff. -iste (fr. Gk. -ιστής,
see -ist).

## craze
craze, tr. and intr. v. — ME. crasen, 'to break,
crack', of Scand. origin. Cp. Swed. krasa, 'to
crackle'. F. ecraser (fr. earlier acraser), is from
the same source. Swed. krasa is of imitative
origin and related to E. crush and crack (qq.v.)
Derivatives: craze, п., craz-ed, adj., crazy (q.v.)

## crasy
crasy, adj. — Formed fr. craze with suff. -y
(corresponding to OE. -ig).
Derivatives: crazi-ly, adv., crazi-ness, n.

## creak
creak, intr. and tr. v. — ME. creken, 'to croak',
of imitative origin. Cp. cricket, the insect, and
croak.
Derivatives: creak, п., creak-y, adj., creak-i-ly,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:202 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 175 | CREOLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:202 COLUMN:1 -->
adv., creak-i-ness, n.

## crenm
crenm, n. — ME. creme, fr. OF. cresme (F.
crime), which is a blend of Gaulish crama and
Eccles. L. chrtsma, fr. Gk. χρίσμα. See chrism.
Derivatives: cream, tr. and intr. v., cream-er, п.,
creamery (q.v.), cream-y, adj.

## crenmery
crenmery, n. — F. cremerie, fr. crime. See cream
and -ery.

## crease
crease, п., a fold, ridge. — Fr. earlier creast, 'a
ridge', a var. of crest
Derivatives: crease, tr. and intr. v., creas-ed,
adj., creas-er, п., creas-ing, п., crau-j>, adj.

## crease
crease, creese, п., a dagger. — Var. spellings of
kris (q.v.)

## create
create, tr. v.' — L. creatus, pp. of creare, 4o
make, produce, create', lit. 'to cause to grow',
fr. I.-E. base *ker-, *kere-, *lo grow', whence
also crescere, 'to grow', creber, 'thick, close,
frequent, numerous', lit. 'densely grown', Ceres,
gen. Cereris, Italian corn goddess, lit. 'goddess
of growth', pro-cerus, 'high, tall', prop, 'high
grown*, Gk. κορεννύναι, 'to fill with a thing,
satisfy', κόρος, 'one's fill, satiety', κόρος,
'stripling, child', κόρη, 'maiden', lit. 'grown up', Arm.
serm, sermn, 'seed, shoot, sprout', serem, Ί
produce', Alb. djer, 'acorn', &jeH, 'lentil', lit. 'food',
Lith. seriu, serti, 'to feed', OPruss. sermen,
'funeral repast', and prob. also OHG. hirsi,
hirso, 'millet'. Cp. I.-E. base *ker-dh-, 'row,
herd', a -dft-enlargement of base *ker-, whenoe
OI. sardhah, 'herd', Goth, hairdo, OE. heord,
'herd'. See cereal, crescent, herd and cp.
creature, procreate, recrente. Cp. also accrescent,
concrescence, concrete, Cora, core-, Coriiuia, cre-
bri-, Creole, crescendo, decrease, decrement,
Dioscuri, excrescent, hypocoristic, increase,
increment, procerity, recrudesce, recruit. For the
ending of create see verbal sun", -ate.
Derivatives: creation, creative, creator (qq.v.)

## creatine
creatine, creatin, п., a white crystalline substance
occurring in the muscles of vertebrates (bio-
chem.) — F. creatine, coined by the French
chemist Michel-Eugene Chevreul (1786-1889),
the discoverer of this substance in 1835, fr. Gk.
κρέας, 'flesh', which is cogn. with L. crudus,
'raw', cruor, 'thick blood, gore'. See crude and
chem. surf, -ine, -in, and cp. the first element in
creosote and the second element in Pancreas.

## creation
creation, n. — F. creation, fr. L. creationem, ace.
of creatio, *a creating, producing', fr. creatus,
pp. of credtre. See create and -ion.
Derivatives: creation-ism, п., creation-ist, n.

## creative
creative, adj. — Coined by the English
philosopher Ralph Cudworth (1617-88) in 1678 (see
his The True Intellectual System of the Universe,
published in that year) fr. L. creatus, pp. of
creare (see create) and sun", -ive.
Derivatives: creative-ly, adv., creat-ive-ness, п.,
creativ-ity, n.

## creator
creator, n. — L. creator, 'creator, author,
founder', fr. creatus, pp. of creare. See create and
agential stiff, -or.

## creature
creature, n. — OF. creature (F. creature), fr. Late
L. creatura, 'a thing created', fr. L. creatus,
pp. of creare. See create and -иге.
Derivatives: creatur-al, creature-ly, adjs., crea-
tur?.-li-ness, n.

## crebri-
crebri-, combining form meaning 'closely set'. —
Fr. L. creber, fern, crebra, neut. cribrum, 'thick,
close, frequent, numerous', which stands for
"кгё-dhro-s and lit. means 'growing densely',
fr. I.-E. base *кег-, *кегё-, 'to grow', whence
also L. crescere, 'to grow', creare, 'to create'. See
create.

## creche
creche, п., a day nursery. — F., 'crib, cradle', fr.
Frankish 'kripja, which is rel. to OHG. krippa,
OE. cribb, 'crib, manger'. See crib and cp. crad-
ge, crntcfa.

## credence
credence, п., belief. — OF., fr. ML. credenlia,
'belief, fr. L. crldlns, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
credere, 'to believe'. See creed and -ence and
cp. credent.

## credenda
credenda, n. pi., articles of faith. — L. credenda,
lit. 'those things which must be believed', neut.
pi. of cridendus, gerundive of credere, 'to
believe'. See creed. For other Latin gerundives
used in English see agenda and words there
referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:202 COLUMN:2 -->

## credent
credent, adj., believing. — L. credens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of credere, 'to believe'. See creed
and -ent.

## credential
credential, adj., that which entitles to credit. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. ML. credenlia. See
credence.
Derivatives: credential, tr. v., credentials, n. pi.

## credibility
credibility, n. — ML. credibilitas, fr. L. credi-
bitis. See next word and -ity.

## credible
credible, adj. — L. credibilis, 'worthy of belief,
credible", fr. credere. See creed and -ible.
Derivatives: credible-ness, п., credibl-y, adv.

## credit
credit, n. — F. credit, fr. It. credito, fr. L. ere-
dilum, 'that which is believed; a loan', pp. of
credere, 'to believe', used as a noun. See creed.
Derivatives: credit, tr. v., credit-able, adj., cre-
dit-abiUity, п., creditable-ness, п., creditabl-y,
adv.

## creditor
creditor, n. — L. creditor, 'truster, lender', fr.
creditus, pp. of credere, 'to believe, trust'. See
creed and agential suff. -or.

## crednerite
crednerite, п., an oxide of cuprum and manganese
(mineral.) — Named after lhe German
geologist Karl Friedrich Heinrich Credner (1809-76).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## credo
credo, п., a creed. — L. credo, Ί believe'. See
creed.

## credulity
credulity, n.— ME., fr. L. credulitatem, ace. of
credulitas, 'easiness of belief, fr. cridulus. See
next word and -ity.

## credulous
credulous, adj. — L. cridulus, 'easy of belief, fr.
credere, 'to believe'. See creed. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -mi, see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: credulous-ly, adv.,credulous-ness,n.

## creed
creed, п., a formula of belief. — ME. crede, fr. OE.
creda, fr. L. credere, 'to believe', which is cogn.
with OI. srad-dadhati, 'trusts, believes', Avestic
zrazda- (assimilated fr. *sraz-da), 'to believe',
Olr. cretim, W. credu, Ί believe', prob. fr. I.-E.
base *kred-dhe-, 'to attribute magic power to
somebody', i.e. 'to believe somebody', fr. *kred-,
'magic power' (whence OI. srdd, 'magic power'),
and *dhe-, 'to place' (whence OI. dddhati, 'he
places', Gk. τιθέναι, 'to place'). See do an cp.
words there referred to. The usual connection
of L. credere, etc., with L. cor, gen. cordis, Gk.
καρδιά, 'heart', etc., is due to folk etymology.
Cp. accredit, credence, credential, credible,
credit, creditor, credulity, credulous, grant, in-
croyable, miscreant, recreant, sraddha.

## creedite
creedite, п., a hydrous fluoride and sulfate of
calcium and aluminum (mineral.) — Named after
the Creede quadrangle of the U.S. Geol. Survey,
Colorado. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## creek
creek, п., г) a brook; 2) a narrow inlet. — ME.
creke, crike, fr. ON. kriki, 'bay' (whence also
F. crique, 'creek'), which is rel. to MDu. creke,
Du. kreek, 'creek'. The orig. meaning of these
words was 'a bend, turn, angle'. They are rel. to
the second element in dial. Swed. armkrik, 'bend
of the arm', and to ON. krokr, 'hook*. See
crutch.

## creel
creel, п., a wicker basket. — OF. creit, 'wicker-
work', fr. Late L. craticulum, a var. of L. crati-
cula, 'fine hurdle work', dimin. of cratis, 'wicker-
work . See crate and cp. grill, 'gridiron'.
Derivative: creel, tr. v.

## creep
creep, intr. v. — ME. creopert, crepe», fr. OE. cre-
opan, rel. to ON. krjupa, Swed. krypa, Dan.
krybe, OFris. kriapa, MLG. кгёреп, кгйреп,
MDu. crupen, Du. kruipen, 'to creep'. These
words prob. meant orig. 'to go bent down', and
derive fr. I.-E. base *greub-, whence also Gk.
γρυπός, 'curved, hook-nosed', γρύπτειν, γρΰ-
ποΰσ!>αι, γρυμπάνειν, "to become bent or
wrinkled'. Cp. cripple, croft, crop, crumple. Cp. also
grovel. Base *greub- is an enlargement of base
*greu-, which itself is. an enlargement of base
*ger-, 'to turn, twisf, whence Gk. γέρρον,
'anything made of wickerwork', esp. 'an oblong
shield', γυργα^ός, 'a wicker basket'.
Derivatives: creep, п., creep-er, п., creep-ing, n.
and adj., creep-ing-ly, adv., creep-y, adj.

## creeper
creeper, п., a climbing plant. — Formed fr. prec.
word with agential suff. -er; first used in this
sense by Bacon.

## creese
creese, n. — See kris.

## cremaster
cremaster, п., the muscle by which the testicle is

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:202 COLUMN:3 -->
suspended (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. κρε-
μαστήρ, 'suspender'; in the pi.: 'muscles by
which the testicles are suspended', fr. κρεμαστός,
'hung, suspended', verbal adj. of κρεμάννΰμι,
Ί hang up, suspend', which is rel. to κρήμνημι,
of s.m., κρημνός, 'precipice', and perh. cogn.
with Goth, hramjan, Ίο crucify'. Cp. the first
element in cremnopbobia, cremocarp.

## cremate
cremate, tr. v., to burn to ashes. — L. crematus,
pp. of cremare, 'to consume by fire, burn', rel.
to Umbr. krematra, 'an instrument for burning
the intestines', fr. I.-E. *ker-em, an -m-en-
largement of base *ker-, 'to singe, burn, glow',
whence also L. carbo, 'coal', OE. heorp, 'hearth'.
See carbon, hearth and verbal suff. -ate. Gk.
κέραμος, 'potter's clay', is not cogn. with L.
cremare (see ceramic).

## cremation
cremation, n. — L. crematio, gen. -onis, 'a
burning', fr. crematus, pp. of cremare, 'to burn'. See
prec. word and -ion.

## cremationist
cremationist, п., one who advocates the cremation
of dead human bodies instead of burying them.
— See cremation and -ist.

## cremator
cremator, n. — Eccles. L. cremator, 'a burner', fr.
L. crematus, pp. of cremare. See cremate and
agential suff. -or.

## crematorium
crematorium, n. — A Modern Latin word. See
crematory, n.

## crematory
crematory, adj. — ModL. crematorius,
'pertaining to cremation', fr. L. crematus, pp. of
cremare. See cremate and adj. suff. -ory.

## crematory
crematory, n. — ModL. crematorium, 'a place
for burning corpses', fr. L. crematus, pp. of
cremare. See cremate and subst. suff. -ory.

## crembalum
crembalum, п., a Jew's harp. — ModL., fr. Gk.
κρέμβαλον, 'castanet'. See crepitate.

## cremnopbobia
cremnopbobia, п., a morbid fear of precipices
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of Gk.
κρημνός, 'an overhanging bank, precipice, cliff,
crag', and -φοβία, 'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. The
first element is rel. to Gk. κρήμνημι, Ί hang up,
suspend'; see cremaster. For the second element
see -phobia.

## cremocarp
cremocarp, п., a form of fructification, in which
the fruit is split into two indehiscent o'ne-seeded
carpels called mericarps, which hang from the
summit of the central axis called carpophore
(hot.) — Lit. 'hanging fruit', fr. Gk. κρέμα-,
stem of κρεμαννύναι, 'to hang', and καρπός,
'fruit'. See cremaster and carpel and cp. the
first element in carpophore and the second
element in mericarp.

## Cremona
Cremona, п., a violin made at Cremona in Italy.

## cren-
cren-, form of creno- before a vowel.

## crenate
crenate, crenated, adj., notched, scalloped. — VL.
'crinalus, pp. of 'crenare, 'to notch'. See crenel
and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also -ed.
Derivatives: crenat-ion, п., crenat-ure, n.

## crenel
crenel, crenelle, п., one of the indentations in a
battlement. — OF. crenel (F. creneau), dimin.
of OF. cren, cran (F. cran), 'a notch', fr. crener,
'to notch', fr. VL. *сгёпйгг, fr. Late L. crena,
'notch', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. cranny,
crenate.

## crenelate
crenelate, crenellate, tr. v. — F. creneler, fr. OF.
creneler, fr. crenel, See prec. word and verbal
suff. -ate. Derivatives: crenel(l)-at-ed, adj.,
crenel(l)-at-ion, n.

## crenic
crenic, adj., pertaining to an acid occurring in
humus and in deposits (chem.) — Formed with
suff. -ic fr. Gk. κρήνη, 'spring, fountain', which
prob. stands for *κράσν5 and is rel. to κρουνός
(for *κρουσνός), 'spring, well head'. Cp. the
second element in Hippocrene.

## creno-
creno-, before a vowel cren-, combining form
used in the sense of 'mineral spring'. — Fr. Gk.
κρήνη. See prec. word.

## crenulate
crenulate, adj., minutely crenate. — ModL. cri-
nulatus, fr. crinula, dimin. of VL. crena. See
crenate.
Derivatives: crenulat-ed, adj., crenulat-ion, n.

## Creole
Creole, п., a native of the West Indies, of
European descent. — Fr. Creole, earlier criole, fr.

## Sp. criollo
Sp. criollo, fr. Port, crioulo, orig. 'brought up
(in one's house)', fr. criar, 'to nourish, bring

## up'
up', fr. L. creare, 'to make, produce, create'.
See create and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: Creole, adj.

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CREON | 176 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:203 COLUMN:1 -->

## Creon
Creon, п., brother of Jocasta and brother-in-law
of Oedipus; he was king of Thebes (Greek my-
thol.) — Gk. Κρέων, fr. κρέων, a var. of κρείων,
'ruler, lord, master', which is cogn. with OI.
sriyas-, Avestic srayah-, 'better'.

## creophagous
creophagous, adj., flesh-eating. — Gk. κρεοφάγος,
compounded of κρέας, 'flesh', and -φάγος,
'eating'. See creosote and -phagous.

## creosote
creosote, п., an oily liquid obtained from tar. —
G. Kreosot, coined by the German natural
philosopher, Baron Karl von Reichenbach (1788-
1869) in 1832 fr. Gk. κρέας, gen. κρέως, 'flesh',
and σώζειν, 'to save'. The first element is cogn.
with L. crudus, 'raw', cruor, 'gore, thick blood';
see crude. The second element is rel. to Gk.
σάος, 'safe', σωτήρ, 'savior'; see soter.

## crepe
crepe, п., a light crinkled cloth of silk. — F.,
'crape', fr. OF. crespe, fr. L. crispus, 'curled'.
See crisp and cp. crape.
Derivative: crepe, tr. and intr. v.

## Crepidula
Crepidula, п., a genus of gastropods (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. crepidula, 'a small sandal', dimin.
of crepida, 'sandal', fr. Gk. κρηπΐδα, ace. of
κρηπίς, of s.m., which is cogn. with L. carpiscu-
lum, 'a kind of footwear'. For the ending see
suff. -ule.

## Crepis
Crepis, п., a genus of plants of the chicory family
(hot.) — L. crepis, fr. Gk. κρηπίς, 'sandal; name
of a plant'. See prec. word.

## crepitant
crepitant, adj., making repeated cracklingsounds.
— L. crepitans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of crepi-
tare. See crepitate and -ant.

## crepitate
crepitate, intr. v., to make repeated crackling
sounds. — L. crepitdt-(um), pp. stem of crepi-
tare, 'to rattle, creak, crackle, clatter', freq. of
crepare, 'to rattle, crack, break with a crack,
burst', which is cogn. with O]. kfpate, 'laments',
from the I.-E. imitative base *(s)krep-; cp.
craven, crevasse, crevice, decrepit, decrepitate,
discrepant, quebracho. Cp. base *(s)qreb-,
whence Gk. κρέμβαλα (pi.), 'castanets', OSlav. skro-
botu, 'noise', Lith. skrebu, skrebeti, 'to rustle',
and see crembalum, roup, 'to sell by auction'.
Bases *(s)qreb- and *(s)krep- are enlargements
of the imitative base *qer-, *qr-, *ker-, *kr-; see
raven, n.
Derivative: crepitat-ion, n.

## crepitus
crepitus, п., a sound made by a sudden discharge
of wind from the bowels (med.) — L. (short for
crepitus venlris, lit. 'sound made by the belly*),
fr. crepare. See prec. word.

## crepon
crepon, п., crepe of firm texture — F., fr. crepe,
'crape'. See crepe.

## crept
crept, past tense and pp. of creep. — ME. crepte,
a newjormation. See creep.

## crepascle
crepascle, п., twilight. — L. crepusculuni, fr.
creper, 'dusky', which is of uncertain origin.

## crepuscular
crepuscular, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
twilight. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. crepus-
culum. See prec. word.

## crepuscule
crepuscule, п., twilight. — F. crepuscule, fr. L.
crepusculum. See crepuscle.

## crescendo
crescendo, adj. and adv., gradually increasing in
loudness; п., a gradual increase in loudness. —
It., lit. 'increasing', fr. crescere, 'to increase,
grow', fr. L. crescere. See next word.

## crescent
crescent, п., the waxing moon. — ME. cressant,
fr. OF. creissant (F. croissant), prop. pres. part,
of creistre (F. croitre), 'to grow', fr. L. crescere,
of s.m., fr. I.-E. base *icer-, 'to grow', whence
also L. creare, 'to create'. See create and -ent
and cp. decrement, increase, increment.

## crescent
crescent, adj., increasing in size. — L. crescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of crescere. See prec.
word.

## cresol
cresol, п., a caustic liquid (chem.) — Formed fr.
creosote with suff. -ol.

## cress
cress, п., plant of the mustard family. — ME.
cresse, fr. OE. cxrse, cerse, cresse, rel. to MDu.
kersse, Du. kers, OHG. kresso (masc), cressa
(fern.), MHG., G. kresse, 'cress', and cogn.
with Gk. γράσιις, 'grass, green fodder', γράειν,
'to gnaw, eat', OI. grasati, 'eats'. Cp. gastro-.
Cress orig. meant 'the edible plant'. See Kluge-
Mitzka, EWDS., p.403 s.v. Kresse. F. cresson
and It. crescione, 'cress', are Teut. loan words.

## cresset
cresset, п., an iron vessel for holding oil or grease.
— ME., fr. OF. craisset, fr. craisse, graisse.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:203 COLUMN:2 -->
'grease', fr. VL. *crassia, fr. L. crassus, 'thick'.
See crass,

## crest
crest, n. — ME., fr. OF. creste (F. crete), fr. L.
crista, 'tuft on the head of animals, cock's comb',
which is cogn. with Mir. cressaim, Ί shake,
swing', ON. hrista, 'to shake', OHG. risla,
MHG. riste, G. Reiste, 'bundle'. These words
derive from a -f-enlargemenl of I.-E. base
*qreis-, whence OPruss. craysi, 'blade, stalk',
crays (pi.), 'hay', Goth, af-hrisjan, us-hrisjan, 'to
shake off', OE. hrisian, OS. hrissan, 'to rattle,
creak', OE., OS., ΟΝ., OFris., OHG. hrls, later
ris, MHG. ris, G. Reis, Dan., Swed. ris, MDu.,
Du. rijs, 'twig, sprig', L. crispus, 'curly', crinis
(for crisnis), 'hair of the head'. Cp. crinite, crisp,
crease, 'a fold', and kestrel. Base *qreis- is an
enlargement of base *(s)qer-, 'to bend, turn,
twist'. See curve and cp. words there referred to.

## cresyl
cresyl, п., 1) a univalent radical, C,H70; 2)
another name for tolyl (chem.) — Formed fr.
cresol with suff. -yl.
Derivative: cresyl-ic, adj.

## cretaceous
cretaceous, adj., chalky. — L. crituceus,
'chalklike', fr. creta, 'chalk'. See crayon and -aceous.
Derivative: cretaceous-ly, adv.

## cretic
cretic, п., name of a metrical foot. — Fr. L. (pes)
Creticus, fr. Gk. (πους) Κρητικός, lit. 'Cretan
