(foot)', fr. Κρήτ/j, 'Crete'. For the ending see
suff. -ic.
Derivative: cretic, adj.

## cretincation
cretincation, n. — See next word and -flcation.

## cretify
cretify, tr. v., to convert into chalk. — Formed
fr. L. creta, 'chalk' (see crayon), with suff. -fy.

## cretin
cretin, п., ι) a person suffering from cretinism;
2) an idiot. — F. cretin, fr. cretin, a word of the
dial, of Valais, fr. F. Chretien, 'Christian', fr. L.
Christianus (see Christian). The different stages
of sense development were prob. 1) Christian;
2) human being; 3) wretched human being;
4) idiot.
Derivatives: cretinism (q.v.), cretin-oid, adj.,
cretin-ous, adj.

## cretinism
cretinism, п., a disease caused by the deficiency
of the thyroid gland (med.) — F. cretinisme,
formed fr. cretin with suff. -isme. See cretin
and -ism.

## Cretism
Cretism, п., Cretan behavior; lying. — Gk. Κρη-
τισμός, fr. Κρητίζειν, 'to behave like a Cretan',
i.e. 'to lie', fr. Κρής, gen. Κρητός, 'Cretan'. For
the ending see suff. -ism.

## cretonne
cretonne, п., a kind of cotton cloth. — F., fr.
Creton, a village in Normandy, where it was
originally made.

## crevasse
crevasse, п., a deep cleft, gap, rift, crack. — F.,
fr. crever. See next word.

## crevice
crevice, п., a narrow opening. — ME. crevasse,
crevice, fr. OF. (= F.) crevasse, 'gap, rift, crack,
crevasse', fr. VL. *crepdtia (whence also OProv-
enc. crebassa), fr. L. crepare, 'to rattle, crack,
break with a crack, burst'. See crepitate.
Derivatives: crevice, tr. v., crevic-ed, adj.

## crew
crew, n. — Formerly spelled crue, aphetic for
accrue, 'a reinforcement', fr. OF. accreue, accrue,
'an increase', prop. fern. pp. of accroistre (F.
accroilre), 'to increase', fr. L. accrescere, 'to
increase', fr. ad- and crescere, 'to grow'. See
crescent, adj., and cp. accrue.

## crewel
crewel, п., worsted yarn. — Fr. earlier crule,
crewle, which is of uncertain origin.

## crib
crib, n. — ME. cribb, fr. OE. cribb, rel. to OS.
kribbia, Dan. krybbe, OFris., MDu. kribbe, Du.
krib, kribbe, OHG. kripia, krippa, MHG., G.
krippe, 'crib, manger', MHG. krebe, 'basket'.
The orig. meaning of these words seems to have
been 'wickerwork'. It. greppia, OProvenc.
crepcha and F. creche 'manger, crib', are Teut.
loan words. Cp. cradge, cratch, creche.
Derivatives: crib, tr. and intr. v., cribb-age, п.,
cribb-ing, n.

## cribble
cribble, п., a coarse sieve. — F. crible, fr. Late L.
cribellum, 'a small sieve', dimin. of cribrum. See
next word.

## cribriform
cribriform, adj., sievelike, perforated like a sieve.
— Formed fr. L. cribrum, 'a sieve', and forma,
'form, shape'. L. cribrum stands for *qreidhrom
Pit. 'an instrument for sifting', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)qerei-, 'to sift, separate', and instrumental
suff. *-dhro-] and is cogn. with Olr. criathar.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:203 COLUMN:3 -->
OW. cruitr, OCo. croider, MBret. croezr, 'sieve',
OE. hrldder, OHG. ritera, 'a sieve'. See riddle,
'sieve', and cp. garble. Cp. also certain and
words there referred to. For the second element
in cribriform see -form.

## crick
crick, п., a painful spasmodic affection of the
muscles. — ME. crykke, of uncertain origin.
Derivative: crick, tr. v.

## cricket
cricket, п., an insect of the order Orthoptera.—
OF. (= F.) criquet, rel. to criquer, 'to crack'; of
imitative origin. Cp. creak, grig.
Derivative: cricket-y, adj.

## cricket
cricket, п., the game. — OF. criquet, 'stick, stake
used as goal in the game of bowls', fr. MDu.
cricke, 'stick', which stands in gradational
relationship to OE. cryce, 'crutch'. See crutch.
Derivatives: cricket-er, п., bricket-ing, n.

## crico-
crico-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
the cricoid cartilage' (anat.) — See next word.

## cricoid (anat.)
cricoid (anat.), adj., pertaining to the cartilage
of the larynx; п., the cricoid cartilage. — Gk.
κρικοειδής, 'ring-shaped', compounded of
κρίκος, 'ring', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape. See circus and -oid.

## cried
cried, past tense and pp. of cry. — ME. cride,
cried, fr. crien, 'to cry'. See cry and -ed.

## crier
crier, n. — ME. criere, fr. OF. criere, nom. of
crieur, fr. crier, 'to cry'. See cry and agential
suff. -er.

## crime
crime, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) crime, fr. L.
crimen, 'judicial decision, judgment, charge,
crime', which stands for cri-men and orig. meant
'cry of distress' (see Brugmann, in Indoger-
manische Forschungen, 9, 353Γ, Porzig, ibid.
42, 265). It derives fr. I.-E. base "(s)qrei-,
enlargement of the imitative base *qer-, 'to shout,
cry', whence also OHG. scrian, 'to cry', ON.
hreimr, 'to squeak', hrina, 'to squeal, squeak'.
See scream. For further derivatives of base *qer-
see raven and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also criminal, criminology, incriminate,
recriminate. There is no connection between L.
crimen and cernere, 'to sift'.
Derivatives: crime, tr. v., crime-less, adj., crime-
less-ness,'n.

## criminal
criminal, adj. — F. criminel, fr. L. criminalis,
'pertaining to crime, criminal', fr. crimen, gen.
crtminis. See crime and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: criminal п., criminal-ism, п., cri-
minal-ist, п., criminality (q.v.)

## criminality
criminality, n. — F. criminalite, fr. ML. crimi-
nalitatem, ace. of crimindlitas, fr. L. criminalis.
See prec. word and -ity.

## criminate
criminate, tr. v., 1) to accuse of a crime; 2) to
incriminate; 3) to censure. — L. crimindtus, pp.
of crtminari, 'to accuse somebody of a crime,
to charge with', fr. crimen, gen. criminis. See
crime and verbal suff. -ate and cp. discriminate,
incriminate, recriminate.
Derivatives: crimination (q.v.), criminat-ive, adj.,
criminator (q.v.), criminat-ory, adj.

## crimination
crimination, n. — L. criminatio, gen. -onis,
'accusation', fr. crimindtus, pp. of crtminari. See
prec. word and -ioa

## criminator
criminator, n. — L., 'accuser', fr. crimindtus, pp.
of crtminari. See criminate and agential suff.
-or.

## criminology
criminology, п., the study of crime. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. crimen, gen. criminis, 'charge,
crime' and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See crime and -logy.
Derivatives: criminolog-ic, criminolog-ic-al,
adjs., criminolog-ist, n.

## criminous
criminous, adj., criminal. — L. criminosus,
'slanderous, faulty, blameworthy', fr. crimen, gen.
crtminis, 'charge, crime'. See crime and -ous.
Derivatives: criminous-ly, adv.,criminous-ness,n.

## crimp
crimp, tr. v., to wrinkle. — Du. and LG. krimpen,
'to curve, shrink', rel. to OHG. krimphan, of
s.m., and to E. cramp and crumple (qq.v.)
Derivatives: crimp, п., crimp-er, п., crimp-ing,
п., crimp-y, adj.

## crimp
crimp, п., one who procures seamen by
entrapping them. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: crimp, tr. v., to entrap (seamen).

## crimson
crimson, п., deep red. — Sp. cremesin, St. Arab.
qirmiz, ult. fr. OI. *kfmi-ja-, 'produced by a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:204 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 177 | CROP -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:204 COLUMN:1 -->
worm'. ΟΙ. kfmih, 'worm', is cogn. with Lith.
kirmis, kirmele, Olr. cruim, Alb. krimp, 'worm'.
Cp. Iterates, carmine.
Derivatives: crimson, adj. and tr. v., crimson-ly,
adv., crimson-ness, n.

## crinal
crinal, adj., pertaining to the hair. — L. crinalis,
fr. crinis, 'hair'. See crinite and adj. suff. -al.

## cringe
cringe, intr. v. — ME. crengen, fr. OE. cringan,
'to fall in battle, yield', lit. 'to be bent', rel. to
ON. kringr, LG., Du. kring, MHG. krinc, G.
Kring, 'circle, ring', and to crank, crinkle (qq.v.)
Derivatives: cringe, п., cring-ing, п., cring-ing-
ly, adv., cring-ing-ness, n.

## cringle
cringle, п., a small ring. — LG. kringel, dimin.
of kring, 'circle, ring'. See prec. word and dimin.
suff. -le and cp. degringolade.

## crini-
crini-, combining form meaning 'hair*. — Fr. L.
crinis, 'hair'. See crinite.

## crinite
crinite, adj., hairy. — L. crinltus, pp. of crinire,
'to provide or cover with hair*, fr. crinis, 'hair*,
which stands for *cris-nis and is rel. to crispus,
'curly', crista, 'tuft on the head of animals,
cock's comb'. See crest and adj. suff. -ite and
cp. crisp. Cp. also crinal, crino- and the first
element in crinoline.

## crinkle
crinkle, intr. and tr. v., to wrinkle. — ME. (in
the participle crinkled), freq. formed fr. OE.
crincan, a collateral form of cringan, 'to yield*.
See cringe and freq. suff. -le.
Derivatives: crinkle, п., crinkl-y, adj.

## criakum-crankum
criakum-crankum, adj., full of twists and turns
(colloq.) — See crinkle and crank; jocosely
formed in imitation of Latin words ending in -um.

## crinoid
crinoid, adj., lily-shaped. — Gk. κρικοειδής,
compounded of κρίνον, 'lily', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See Crinum and -oid
and cp. encrinite.

## Crinoidea
Crinoidea, n. pi., a class of echinoderms (zooi) —
ModL. See prec. word.

## crinoline
crinoline, π., ι) a stiff cloth; 2) a petticoat made
of stiff cloth; 3) a hoop skirt. — F., fr. It.
crinoline, which is compounded of crino, 'hair' (fr.
L. crinis), and lino, 'flax' (fr. L. Unum). It. crino·
lino prop, denotes a fabric whose woof is made
of hair and whose warp is made of linen. See
crinite and linen.
Derivative: crinoline, tr. v.

## Crinum
Crinum, п., a genus of plants of the amaryllis
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κρίνον, 'lily*,
which is a foreign word of unknown origin. Cp.
the first element in crinoid.

## crio-
crio-, combining form meaning 'ram-headed*. —
Gk. κρΐο-, fr. κριός,'ram, battering ram', which
prob. stands for *κρΐ5ός and is rel. to κεραός,
'horned*, fr. κέρας, 'horn*, and cogn. with ON.
hreinn, 'reindeer'. See horn and cp. cerato-,
cervine. Cp. also the first element in reindeer.

## criosphinx
criosphinx, п., a sphinx with the head of a ram. —
Compounded of Gk. κριός, 'ram', and σφίγξ,
'sphinx*. See prec word and sphinx.

## cripple
cripple, n. — ME. cripel, crepel, crupel, fr. OE.
crypel, rel. to ON. kryppill, OFris. kreppel, MDu.
cropel, crepel, Du. kreupele, 'cripple', MHG.,
G. kruppel, lit. 'bent, twisted', and to OE.
creopan, 'to creep*. See creep and cp. croft, crop.
Derivatives: cripple, tr. v., crippl-ed, adj., crip-
ple-ness, п., crippl-er, п., crippf-ing, adj. and п.,
crippl-ing-ly, adv., crippl-y, adj.

## crisis
crisis, n. — L., fr. Gk. κρίσις, 'a separating,
putting apart, a decision', rel. to κριτής, 'judge,'
κρίνείν, 'to separate, pick out, decide, judge*,
fr. I.-E. base *(s)q(e)re(i)-, to separate*, whence
also L. cernere, 'to separate, sifl, distinguish,
discern, understand, decide*. See certain and cp.
critic and words there referred to. Cp. also
acrisia, eccrinology, endocrine, hypocrisy.

## crisp
crisp, adj., 1) brittle; 2) lively; 3) fresh; 4) curly.
— OE., fr. L. crispus, 'curly', which is cogn.
with W. crych, Bret, crecli, of s.m., fr. I.-E. base
*(s)qreis-, whence also L. crinis (for *crisnis),
'hair', and crista, 'tuft on the head of animals,
cock's comb'. See crest and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also Crispin.
Derivatives: crisp, tr. and intr. v., crispate, adj.
(q.v.), crisp-ly, adv., crisp-ness, п., crisp-y, adj.

## crispate
crispate, adj., of a curly appearance. — L. cris-
paiits, pp. of crispare, 'to curl, wave', fr. crispus.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:204 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: crispat-ion, n.

## Crispin
Crispin, masc. PN. — L. CrispTnus, a Roman
cognomen derived fr. crispus, 'curled'. See
crisp, adj., and -in (representing L. -tnus).

## criss-cross
criss-cross, п., a mark made with two crossing
lines. — Fr. earlier Christ-cross.
Derivatives: criss-cross, adj., tr. v., adv.

## cristate
cristate, adj., crested (said esp. of birds and other
animals). — L. cristatus, 'having a crest or tuft',
fr. crista. See crest and adj. suff. -ate.

## criterion
criterion, n. — Gk. κριτηρίου, 'a means
forjudging", fr. κριτής, 'judge', fr. κρίνείν, 'to
separate, decide, judge'. See critic.

## crith
crith, п., a unit of weight for gases. — Coined by
Hoffmann fr. Gk. κρΖθή, 'barleycorn', which is
prob. cogn. with L. hordeum, 'barley*. See
Hordeum.

## critic
critic, n. — L. criticus, fr. Gk. κρι,τικός, 'capable
of judging', fr. κριτής, 'judge', fr. κρίνειν, 'to
separate, decide, judge1, which is cogn. with L.
cernere, 'to sieve, distinguish, discern,
understand, decide'. See certain and cp. crisis,
criterion, diacritical, hypocrite, oneirocritic.
Derivatives: critic-ai, adj., critical-ly, adv.,
critical-ness, п., critic-ism, п., critic-ize,
criticise, intr. and tr. v., critic-iz-er, critic-is-er, п.,
critic-iz-ing-ly, critic-is-ing-ly, adv.

## critiqne
critiqne, n. — F., fr. Gk. κριτική (short for
κριτική τέ/w], 'the critical art'), fern, of κριτικός,
'of, or for, judging, capable of judging'. See
critic.

## croak
croak, intr. and tr. v. — From the stem of OE.
crac-ettan, 4o croak', which is re], to OE. cra-
cian, '10 resound', OE. crawan, 'to crow', ME.
croken, 'to croak'. All these words are of imita-
live origin. See raven and cp. Circaetus. Cp. also
crack, crake, creak, crow, grackle.
Derivatives: croak, п., croak-er, п., croak-ing,
adj. and п., croak-y, adj.

## Croat
Croat, n. — Fr. earlier Chorwat, fr. Serbo-
Croatian Hrvat, fr. OSIav. Churvatinu, 'Croat',
lit. 'mountaineer, highlander', fr. churva,
'mountain', which is rel. to OSIav., Serb, and
Croatian gora, Russ. gora, Pol. gora, Czech and
Slovak hora, and cogn. with OI. girth, Avestic
gairi, 'mountain', Alb. gur, 'rock', Lith. gire,
'forest' and prob. also with Gk. βορέας, 'north
wind*, lit. 'a mountain wind'. See Boreas and
cp. cravat.
Derivatives: Croat-ian, adj. and n.

## crocein
crocein, croceine, п., any of several yellow and
red dyes (chem.) — Formed with chem. suff. -in,
resp. -ine fr. L. croceus, 'saffron-colored', fr.
crocus, 'saffron'. See Crocus.

## crochet
crochet, п., a kind of knitting done with a small
hook. — F., 'a small hook', dimin. of croc,
'hook', which is a Teut. loan word. Cp. ON.
krokr, 'hook' and see crook. Cp. also crotchet,
crocket, and accroach, encroach.
Derivatives: crochet, tr. and intr. v., crochet-er,
п., crochet-ing, n.

## croc idol ite
croc idol ite, п., a blue or green fibrous mineral,
consisting of silicate of iron and solium
{mineral.) — Compounded of Gk. κροκΰς, gen. κρο-
κύδος, 'a nap of woolen cloth', and λίθ-ος,
'stone'. The first element is rel. to Gk. κρόκη,
'woof, thread', stands in gradational
relationship to κρέκειν, 'to weave*, and is cogn. with
OE. hreol, 'reef, hrxg(e)l, 'garment5, ON. hrxll,
'a weaver's sley', fr. I.-E. base *qrek-, 'to strike'.
See rail, 'garment', reel, 'a revolvable
instrument', and cp. next word. For the second
element see -lite.

## Croc i dura
Croc i dura, п., a genus of shrews {zooi) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. κροκύς, gen. κροκύδος, 'a
nap of woolen cloth*, and ούρα, 'tail'. See prec.
word and uro-, 'tail-'.

## crock
crock, п., an earthen pot. — OE. crocca, rel. to
OS. kruka, MDu. cruke (Du. kruik), MHG.
kruche, OHG. krog, kruog (MHG. kruoc, G.
Krug), 'pitcher, jug'. Cp. Mir. crocan, 'pot', Gk.
κρωσσός, 'pitcher', OSIav. krugla, 'cup*. All
these words are prob. borrowed from the same
unknown language.
Derivatives: crock, tr. v., to put into a crock,
crock~ery, n.

## crock
crock, п., an old, worn-out horse. — Rel. to
Swed. krake, LG. krakke, 'a worn-out horse',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:204 COLUMN:3 -->
and to E. crack (q.v.)
Derivative: crock, tr. v., to break down (a
horse).

## crocket
crocket, п., an ornament placed on the sides of
pinnacles, gables, spires, etc. (archit.) — AF.
croquet, corresponding to OF. crochet. See
crochet.
Derivatives: crocket-ed, adj., crocket-ing, n.

## crocodile
crocodile, n. — ME. cocodrille, fr. OF. cocodrille,
metathesized fr. L. crocodilus, fr. Gk. κροκόδϊλος,
'lizard; crocodile', dissimilated fr. *κροκό-δρΐλος,
lit. 'stone worm*, fr. κρόκη, 'pebble', and δρΐλος,
'worm'. Gk. κρόκη is cogn. with OI. sarkarah,
sark-ara, 'gravel, pebble, sugar'; see sugar and
words there referred to. The etymology of Gk.
δρΐλος is unknown.
Derivatives: crocodil-ian, adj. and n.

## crocoite
crocoite, п., native lead chromate, PbCrO+
{mineral.) — Fr. earlier crocoisite, which was formed
with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. κροκόεις,
'saffron colored*, fr. κρόκος, 'saffron'. See next
word.

## Crocus
Crocus, п., a genus of plants of the iris family
(bot.) — L., fr. Gk. κρόκος, 'saffron', a word
of Sem. origin. Cp. Heb. karkom, Arab, kur-
kum, 'saffron*, Aram.-Syr. kurkema, Akkad.
kurkanu, 'saffron'. OI. kunkumam, 'saffron', is
prob. a Sem. loan word; cp. Manfred Mayr-
hofer, A Concise Etymological Sanskrit
Dictionary, Heidelberg, 1956, I, p.219s.v. kunkumam.
Derivative: crocus-ed, adj.

## Croesus
Croesus, п., name of a king of Lydia renowned
for his great riches. — L*., fr. Gk. Κροίσος.

## croft
croft, n. — OE., 'a small field', rel. to MDu.
krocht, Du. kroft, 'hillock', lit. 'something
curved*, from the base appearing also in MDu.
criipen, OE. creopan, 'to creep'. See creep and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: croft-er, п., croft-ing, n.

## Cro-Magnon
Cro-Magnon, also cro-magnon, adj. (anthropol.)
— So called from the name of a cave in the
Department of Dordogne in France, where remains
of this race of men have been found.

## cromlech
cromlech, п., 1) a dolmen; 2) a circle of
monoliths. — W., fr. crom, fem. of crwm, 'bent'
(which is prob. cogn. with MDu. rompelen,
'to wrinkle', see rumple, v.), and llech, 'a flat
stone'.

## cromorna
cromorna, п., an organ reed stop (mus.) — F.
cromorne, corruption of krummhorn (q.v.)

## crone
crone, п., a withered old woman. — ME., fr.
MDu. kronje, karonjer 'an old ewe', fr. ONF.
carogne (corresponding to OF. charogne),
'carcass*. See carrion. For sense development cp. F.
carogne, 'hag, jade*.
Derivative: cron-ish, adj.

## Cronian
Cronian, adj., Satumian. — Formed with suff.
-aa fr. Κρόνιος, 'of Cronus', fr. Κρόνος. See
next word.

## Cronus
Cronus, п., a Titan, son of Uranus and Gaea and
father of Zeus in Greek mythol.; identified by
the Romans with Saturn. — L., fr. Gk. Κρόνος;
of unknown etymology. Cp. the second element
in geocronite.

## crouy
crouy, п., a close friend. — Fr. earlier chrony,
fr. Gk. χρόνιος, 'lasting', fr. χρόνος, 'time*. See
chronic.
Derivative: crony, intr. v.

## crook
crook, n. — ME. crok, fr. ON. krokr, 'hook,
bend', which is rel. to OE. cryce, 'crutch, staff,
crozier*. See crutch and cp. crosier. Cp. also
crochet and words there referred to.
Derivatives: crooky tr. and intr. v., crook-ed,
adj., crook-ed-ly, adv., crook-ed-ness, n.

## crookesite
crookesite, п., selenide of copper, thallium and
silver (mineral.) — Named after the English
chemist Sir William Crookes (1832-1919). For
the ending see *subst. suff. -ite.

## croon
croon, intr. and tr. v., to sing softly; to hum. —
MDu. cronen (Du. kreunen), 'to groan,
whimper'; prob. of imitative origin.
Derivative: croon, n.

## crop
crop, n. — ME. croppe, fr. OE. crop, cropp,
'sprout, bunch of flowers or berries; the top of a
plant; ear of corn; crop of a bird; kidney', rel.
to ON. kroppr, 'trunk of a body', Dan. krop,
Swed. kropp, 'trunk of the body', MDu. crop,
Du. krop, 'the craw of a bird*, OHG., kropf,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:205 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CROQUET | 178 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:205 COLUMN:1 -->
'growth on human body; craw', MHG., G.
kropf, 'craw'. The original meaning of these
words was 'protuberance'. They derive fr. I.-E.
base *greub-, 'curved, rough, uneven', whence
also Gk. γρυπός, 'curved, hook-nosed'. See
creep and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
croup (of a horse), crupper, group.
Derivatives: crop, tr. v., to cut off (esp. the
tops of plants); to pluck off, reap; intr. v.,
to yield a crop, cropp-er, п., cropp-y, adj.

## croquet
croquet, п., a game played by driving wooden
balls with wooden mallets through a series of
iron hoops. — From a northern dial. var. of
F. crochet, dimin. of croc, 'hook'. See crochet.
Derivative: croquet, tr. v.

## croquette
croquette, п., a ball of minced meat, fish, or of
rice or potato. — F., formed with dimin. suff.
-ette fr. croquer, 'to crunch', which is of
imitative origin.

## crore
crore, п., ten million rupees, i.e. one hundred
lakhs (Anglo-Indian). — Hind, karor, rel. to
Prakrit krodi, fr. OI. kotih, 'end', which is prob.
a Dravidian loan word.

## crosier
crosier, crozier, п., the staff of a bishop. — The
word orig. meant 'staff-bearer', and derives fr.
OF. crocier, crossier, fr. crosse, 'crosier', fr.
WTeut. *krukja, 'crutch'. See crutch and cp
words there referred to. Cp. also crosse, crossette,
lacrosse.

## cross
cross, n. — ME. cros, fr. OE. cros, fr. ON. kross,
fr. Olr. cros, fr. L. crucem, ace. of crux, 'cross',
which is of uncertain, perh. Punic, origin. Cp.
It. croce, OProvenc. crotz, F. croix, Sp., Port.
cruz, Catal. creu, OS. kruzi, MDu. cruce (Du.
kruis), OHG. kruzi (MHG. kriuze, G. Kreuz),
which all derive fr. L. crucem. Cp. across,
crucial, Crncianella, crucible, crucify, cruise,
cruiser, crusade, crusily, crux, cruzeiro,
excruciate, kreutzer and the second element in haken-
kreuz. Cp. also ridge, rung.
Derivatives: cross, tr. and intr. v., cross-ing, n.

## cross
cross, adj., l) placed across, transverse; 2)
contrary ; 3) ill-humored. — Fr. cross, n.
Derivatives: cross-ly, adv., cross-ness, n.

## cross-country
cross-country, adj. — Aphetic for across-country.

## crosse
crosse, п., the racket used in the game lacrosse. —
See Incrosse and cp. next word.

## crossette
crossette, n. (archaic). — F., dimin. of crosse,
'crosier, stock.' See prec. word and -ette.

## crossite
crossite, п., a variety of amphibole (mineral.) —
Named after the American geologist Whitman
Cross (1854-1949). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## crosso-
crosso-, combining form meaning 'provided with
a fringe'. — Gk. κροσσό-, fr. κροσσοί (pi.),
'tassels, a fringe', rel. to κρόσσαι (pi.),
'battlements, copings of parapets', which prob. stands
for *qroqyd-, and is cogn. with Czech and Russ.
krokva, 'spar, rafter', OE. hrxgan, MHG., G.
ragen, 'to jut out'. See rake, 'to project'.

## Crotalaria
Crotalaria, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κρόταλον, 'rattle', fr.
κρότος. See next word.

## Crotalus
Crotalus, п., the genus consisting of the
rattlesnakes (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κρόταλον,
'rattle', fr.κρότος, 'the sound of rattling, beating,
striking or clapping' (whence also κροτεϊν, 'to
cause to rattle; to knock, beat, strike, clap'), fr.
I.-E. base *kret-, 'to make a noise, to rattle',
whose nasalized form appears in ON. hrinda, OE.
hrindan, 'to thrust'. Cp. next word, Crotaphytus,
and the second element in dicrotic, rricrotism.

## crotaphion
crotaphion, п., the point at the posterior
extremity of the sphenoid (anat.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. κρατάφιον, neut. of κροτάφιος, 'of the
temples', fr. κρόταφος, 'side of the forehead',
in the pi. 'temples', prop, meaning 'the place of
beating', and rel. to κρότος, 'the sound of
beating'. See prec. word.

## crotaphite
crotaphite, adj., temporal (anat.) — Formed with
subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. κρόταφοι (pi.), 'temples'.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: crotaphite, п., the temporal fossa,
crotaphit-ic, adj., temporal.

## Crotaphytus
Crotaphytus, п., a genus of lizards (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. κροταφίτης, 'pertaining to the
temples, temporal', fr. κρόταφοι (pi.), 'the
temples'. See crotaphion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:205 COLUMN:2 -->

## crotch
crotch, п., a forked part. — F. croche, fr. croc,
'hook'. See next word.
Derivative: crotch, tr. and intr. v.

## crotchet
crotchet, п., ι) a small hook; 2) a hooklike part.
— ME., fr. OF. crochet (pronounced crotchet),
fr. croc, 'hook', a var. of crochet (q.v.) See also
crocket.
Derivatives: crotchet, tr. and intr. v.,
crotcheteer, п., crochet-y, adj., crotchet-i-ness, n.

## Croton
Croton, п., a genus of plants of the spurge family
(hot.)— ModL., fr. Gk. κρότων, 'a tick; castor-
oil tree', a word of unknown origin.

## crouch
crouch, intr. v. — ME. crouchen; prob. a blend
of cringe and couch.
Derivatives: crouch, п., crouch-er, n.

## croup
croup, п., an inflammatory disease. — Scot.
croup, 'to croak', of imitative origin.
Derivatives: croup-y, adj., croup-i-ly, adv.,
croup-i-ness, n.

## croup
croup, п., the hind part of quadrupeds, esp. of a
horse. — ME., fr. F. croupe, fr. Frankish *krup-
pa, which orig. meant 'protuberance', and is rel.
to crop (q.v.) See also next word and crupper.

## croupier
croupier, п., a person in charge of a gaming table,
collecting stakes. — F., lit. 'rider on the croup',
hence 'assistant', fr. croupir, 'to ride on the
croup*, fr. croupe. See prec. word.

## crouton
crouton, п., a small piece of toasted bread used
in soups, etc. — F., lit. 'a little crust', dimin. of
croute. See crust.

## crow
crow, intr. v. — ME. crowen, fr. OE. crawan, 'to
crow', rel. to MLG. kreien, MDu. crayen, Du.
kraaien, OHG. kruen, MHG. krsejen, G. krahen,
'to crow', of imitative origin. Cp. OSlav. grajg,
grajati, 'to crow, caw', which is also imitative.
Cp. also next word and croak.
Derivatives: crow, п., crow-ing, п., crow-er, n.

## crow
crow, п., the bird. — ME. crowe, fr. OE. crawe,
rel. to OS. krdja, MDu. crate, Du. kraai, OHG.
kra, krawa, kraja, kraha, MHG. kra, krseje,
G. Krone, 'a crow', and to OE. crawan, etc.,
to crow'; see crow, v. These nouns lit. mean
'the crowing (bird)'. Cp. next word.

## crowbar
crowbar, n. — Lit. 'a bar with a pointed end
resembling a crow's beak'.

## crowd
crowd, п., an ancient Celtic stringed instrument.
— ME. crowde, fr. W. crwth, 'anything swelling,
bulging', which is rel. to Olr. crot, 'harp', Gael.
cruit, 'harp, violin', Ir. cruit, 'violin', and to
OW. crunn, Gael, cruinn, 'round, curved'. See
crown, п., and cp. rote, 'a musical instrument'.

## crowd
crowd, intr. and tr. v., to press. — ME. cruden,
crouden, fr. OE. crudan, 'to press, push', rel.
to MDu. cruden, later kruyden, kruyen, Du.
kruien, 'to push', MHG. kroten, 'to press,
oppress'. Cp. curd.
Derivatives: crowd, п., multitude, crowd-ed, adj.,
crowd-ed-ly, adv., crowd-ed-ness, п., crowder
(q-v.)

## crowder
crowder, п., one who or that which crowds. —
Formed fr. prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## crowder
crowder, п., one who plays on a crowd (archaic).
— Formed fr. crowd, 'a musical instrument',
with agential suff. -er.

## crown
crown, n. — ME. croune, fr. earlier coroune, co-
rune, fr. OF. corone (F. couronne), fr. L. corona,
'garland, wreath, crown', fr. Gk. κορώνη,
'anything curved; crown', fr. κορωνός, 'curved,
crooked', which is cogn. with Mir. cruind, OW.
crunn, W., MW. crwnn, Gael, cruinn, 'round',
curved', L. curvus, 'bent, crooked'. Cp. It., Sp.
corona, Port, coroa, OFris., MLG. krone (Du.
kroon, kruin), OHG. corona (MHG krone, G.
Krone), ON. kruna, which all derive fr. L.
corona. See curve and cp. corona. Cp. also
cornice, coroa, corollary, crowd, 'a musical
instrument'.

## crown
crown, tr. v. — ME. crounen, fr. earlier corunen,
fr. OF. coroner (F. couronner), fr. L. coronare,
'to crown', fr. согбпа. See crown, n. Cp. Rum.
cununa, 'to crown, wreathe; to unite in
wedlock', It. coronare, OProvenc., Catal., Sp. coro-
nar, Port, coroar, 'to crown', which all derive
fr. L. coronare.
Derivative: crown-er, n.

## crozier
crozier, n. — See crosier.

## crucial
crucial, adj., 1) cross-shaped; 2) decisive, critical.
— F., fr. L. сгих, gen. crucis, 'cross'. See cross

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:205 COLUMN:3 -->
and adj. suff. -al. In' its second sense, the word
crucial derives from Bacon's phrase inslantia
crucis (see Novum Organum II, XXXVI).
Derivative: crucial-ly,adv.

## crucian carp
crucian carp, п., a species of a carp. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. MLG. karusse (whence also
Dan. karuds), which prob. derives fr. Lith.
karusis (whence also G. Karausche). Lith.
karusis is a collateral form of karosas, which,
together with Czech karas, Pol. karas, Russ.
karas', 'crucian carp', is borrowed fr. L. cora-
cinus, 'a Nile fish' (whence also F. corassin;
carassin, 'crucian carp'), fr. Gk._ κορακΐνος, of
s.m., lit. 'a fish or ravenlike color', fr. κόραξ,
gen. κόρακος, 'raven'; see coracine. MG. кагаз,
of s.m., is a Slavic loan word.

## Crucianella
Crucianella, п., a genus of plants of the madder
family (bot.) — ModL. formed with the dimin.
suff. -ella fr. L. crux, gen. crucis, 'cross'. See
cross, n.

## cruciate
cruciate, adj., cross-shaped. — ModL. cruciatus,
'cross-shaped', fr. crux, gen. crucis, 'cross'. See
cross and adj. suff. -ate and cp. excruciate. In
the now obsolete sense, 'tortured, tormented',
cruciate derives fr. L. cruciatus, pp. of cruciare,
'to crucify, torture, torment', fr. crux (see
above).

## crucible
crucible, п., a vessel for melting metals. — ML.
crucibulum, 'night lamp, melting pot, crucible',
formed fr. L. crux, gen. crucis, 'cross* (see
cross, п.), and the instrumental suff. -bulum.
The lamp was so called from its shape suggestive
of a cross.
Derivalive: crucible, tr. v.

## cruciferous
cruciferous, adj., 1) bearing a cross; 2) pertaining
to the mustard family (bot.) — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. crucifer, 'cross bearer', fr. crux,
gen. crucis, 'cross', and ferre, 'to bear, carry'.
See cross and -ferous. The mustard family is
called cruciferous because the four petals of the
flowers are arranged crosswise.

## crucifix
crucifix, n. — ME., fr. OF. crucefix (F. crucifix),
fr. L. crucifixus, One fixed to the cross*, orig.
spelled in two words: crucifixus, from the dative
of crux, 'a cross', and pp. of figere, 'to fix'. See
cross, п., and fix, adj., and cp. crncify.

## crucifixion
crucifixion, n. — Eccles. L. crucifixio, gen. -onis,
fr. L. crucifixus. See prec. word and -ion.

## cruciform
cruciform, adj., cross-shaped. — Compounded of
L. crux, gen. crucis, and forma, 'form, shape'.
See cross and form, n.

## crucify
crucify, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) crucifier, fr. L. cruci-
figere, orig. spelled in two words: cruel figere,
'to fix to the cross'; see crucifix. OF. crucifier was
influenced in form by the many verbs ending
in -fier, a suff. corresponding to L. -ficare.
Derivatives: crucifi-ed, adj., crucifi-er, n.

## crude
crude, adj., 1) raw; not refined; 2) not finished.
— L. crudus, 'raw, crude, not cooked', lit.
'trickling with blood, bleeding', rel. to cruor, 'blood
(flowing from a wound)', cruentus, 'stained
with blood, bloody', fr. I.-E. base *qrew'-,
*qreu-, 'coagulated, congealed, bloody', whence
also OI. kravih, 'raw flesh', kravyam, 'blood',
krurah, 'raw, bloody, cruel', Avestic хгйт(асс),
'a piece of bloody flesh', xrura-, 'bloody, cruel',
xruma-, xruta-, 'dreadful, horrible', Gk. κρέας
(for *κρέίας), 'flesh', OPol. kry, OSlav. kruvi,
OPruss. krawian, Lith. kraiijas, 'blood', Lett.
kreve, 'clotted blood', Mir. cru, W. crau, Co.
crow, 'blood', Olr. cruaid, 'firm, hard', OE.
hreaw, 'raw'. Cp. raw. Cp. also creosote, cruel,
cruentation, crust, crystal, ecru, recrudesce.
Derivatives: crude-ly, adv., crude-ness, n.

## crudity
crudity, n. — F. erudite, fr. L. crUditdtem, ace. of
crOditas, fr. crudus. See crude and -ity.

## cruel
cruel, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) cruel, fr. L.
crOdelis, 'hard, unmerciful, cruel, fierce', fr.
crudus: see crude. For the formation of crudelis, fr.
crudus, cp. L. fidelis, 'true, faithful', fr. fidus,
of s.m.
Derivatives: cruel-ly, adv., cruel-ness, п., cruelty
(qv.)

## cruelty
cruelty, n. — OF. cruelte (F. cruaute), fr. L. cru-
delitatem, ace. of crudelUas, 'cruelty*. See prec.
word and -ty.

## cruentation
cruentation, п., oozing of blood, esp. from a dead
body after incision. — L. cruentatio, gen. -onis,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:206 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 179 | CRVPTOGRAMMA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:206 COLUMN:1 -->
'a staining with blood', fr. cruentutus, pp. of
cruentare, 'to stain with blood', fr. cruentus,
'bloody', fr. cruor, 'blood', which is rel. to
crudus. See crnde and -ation.

## cruet
cruet, п., a small glass bottle for vinegar, oil,
etc. — AF., dimin. of OF. crue, cruie, 'an
earthen pot', fr. Frankish *kruka (whence also
OProvenc. cruga, and F. cruche, 'pitcher'), which
is rel. to MHG. kriiche, 'pitcher, jug', and to
OHG. kruog, of s.m. See crock, 'earthen pot'.

## cruise
cruise, intr. and tr. v. — Du. kruisen, 'to cross;
to cruise', fr. kruis, 'cross', fr. L. crucem, ace.
of crux, 'cross'. See cross, n.
Derivatives: cruise, п., cruiser (q.v.)

## cruiser
cruiser, n. — Lit. 'a cruising vessel', formed fr.
cruise with agential sun", -er.

## cruller
cruller, п., a small sweet cake. — Du. kruller, lit.
'a curled cake', fr. krullen, 'to curl'. See curl.

## crumb
crumb, n. — ME. crume, crumme, fr. OE. cruma,
rel. to ON. krumr, Dan. krumme, MLG., MDu.
crome, Du. kruim, MHG. кгйте, G. Krume,
'crumb', and cogn. with Gk. γρΰμέα, γρϋμεί,α,
'bag, trash, trumpery; fish remnants', γρό-τη,
'frippery', γρ5, 'dirt under the nail', L. grumus,
'a little heap'. All these words prob. mean lit.
'something scraped together', and derive fr. I.-E.
base "greu-, 'to scrape together'. Cp. crumple.
Cp. also crumen, grume.
Derivatives: crumb, tr. and intr. v., crumble, v.
(q.v.), crumb-y, crumm-y, adjs.

## crumble
crumble, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. crumb with
freq. suff. -le.
Derivative: crumbl-y, adj.

## crumen
crumen, п., the name of the suborbital gland in
deer and antelopes. — L. crumlna, crumena,
'purse, bag', fr. Gk. γρΰμέα, γρΰμείά. See crumb.

## crump
crump, tr. and intr. v., to crunch. — Of imitative
origin.
Derivative: crump, п., ι) a crunching sound;
2) a heavy shell.

## crumpet
crumpet, п., a kind of sticky cake. — ME. crom-
pid cake (Wycliffe's rendering of Heb. raqtq,
Ex. 29:23). ME. crompid prob. derives fr. OE.
cron peht, 'a thin flat cake', which is, indeed,
the most exact rendering of Heb. raqtq, fr. Heb.
raq, 'thin'. OE. cron peht is of Celtic origin.
Cp. Bret, krampoez, 'a thin flat cake', in which
the second element is rel. to W. poeth, 'cooked',
and cogn. with OI. paktah, Gk. πεπτός, L. coc-
tus, 'cooked' Lith. keptas, 'baked'. See cook.

## crumple
crumple, tr. and intr. v. — Freq. formed with
suff. -le from obsol. OE. crump, crumb, 'crooked',
which is rel. to OS. crumb, Du. krom, OHG.,
MHG. krump, G. krumm, 'crooked', and cogn.
with Gk. γρυπός, 'curved, hook-nosed'. See
creep and cp. cripple. Cp. also the first element
in krummhorn.
Derivatives: crumple, п., crumpl-ed, adj., crumpl-
er, п., crumpl-ing, п., crumpl-y, adj.

## crunch
crunch, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
craunch and scrunch.
Derivatives: crunch, п., crunch-ing, n. and adj.,
crunch-ing-ly, adv., crunch-ing-ness, п., crunch-y,
adj., crurich-i-ly, adv., crunch-i-ness, n.

## crunode
crunode, п., a point at which a curve crosses
itself (geom.) — Irregularly formed fr. L. crux,
'cross', and nodus, 'knot'. See cross and node.
Derivative: crunod-al, adj.

## crnpper
crnpper, п., l) the rump of a horse, croup; 2) a
leather strap attached to a saddle. — ME. cro-
pere, fr. OF. cropiere (F. croupiere), 'crupper,
saddle tie', fr. crope (F. croupe), 'croupe, rump'.
See croup, 'the hind part of a horse'.
Derivative: crupper, tr. v.

## crural
crural, adj., pertaining to the leg (anat. and zool.)
— L. cruralis, fr. crus, gen. cruris, 'leg'. See
next word and adj. suff. -al.

## crus
crus, п., the leg; the shank (anat.) — L. crus, gen.
cruris, 'leg, shank, shin', of uncertain origin;
possibly cogn. with Arm. srun-k' (pi.), 'shin-
bones, calves of the leg'; not related to L. cruor,
'blood', crudus, 'raw'. Cp. crural.

## crusade
crusade, n. —A blend of Sp. cruzada and F. croi-
sade, fr. Sp. cruzar, resp. F. croiser, 'to cross,
to take the cross', fr. Sp. cruz, resp. F. croix,
fr. L. crucem, ace. of crux. See cross, п., and
-ade (representing Sp. -add) and cp. next word.
Derivatives: crusade, intr. v., crusad-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:206 COLUMN:2 -->

## crusado
crusado, cruzado, п., name of a Portuguese coin.
— Port, cruzado, lit. 'marked with a cross', fr.
cruzar, 'to cross, mark with a cross', rel. to
Catal. crusar, Olt. crociare, OProvenc. crozar,
F. croiser, fr. L. crux, 'cross'. See cross, п., and
cp. prec. word.

## cruse
cruse, п., a small earthen vessel. — ME. cruse,
cruce, prob. fr. MDu. cruese (Du. kroes), 'cup,
pot, mug', which is rel. to MLG. krus, ON. krus,
Dan. krus, 'mug, jug', Swed. krus, 'mug',
MHG. kruse, G. Krause, 'jug, mug'.

## crush
crush, tr. and intr. v. — ME. cruschen, fr. OF.
cruissir, a var. of croissir, 'to break', fr.
Frankish *krostjan, 'to gnash the teeth', which is rel.
to Goth, kriuslan, 'to gnash the teeth', krusts,
'the gnashing of teeth', ON. kreista, 'to press,
squeeze', OSwed. krusa, krosa, 'to crush*. Cp.
It. crosciare (fr. OF. croissir), and OProvenc.
croisir, cruisir, Catal. cruxir (whence Sp. crujir),
'to crack', which are Teut. loan words.
Derivatives: crush, п., crush-ed, adj., crush-er,
п., crush-ing, adj., crush-ing-ly, adv.

## cruslly
cruslly, crusile, adj., sprinkled with small crosses
(her.) — OF. croisillie, croisille, crusillie, fr.
croisille, 'a small cross', dimin. of OF. croiz (F.
croix), fr. L. crucem, ace. of crux, 'cross'. See
cross.

## crust
crust, n. — ME., fr. OF. crousle (F. croute), fr.
L. crusia, 'the hard surface of a body, rind,
crust, shell*, which stands for *crus-ta, and lit.
means 'that which has been hardened by
freezing', and is cogn. with Gk. κρύος (prob. for
*κρύσος), 'icy cold, frost', κρυερός,'icy, chilling',
κρΰμός (for *κρυσμός), 'frost', κρύσταλλος, 'ice,
crystal', Toch. A kuras, В krost, 'cold', Lett.
kruvesis, 'mud frozen in the field; roughness of
the soil', Lith. at-krusti, 'to revive' (said of
frozen people), OHG. (h)rosa, (h)roso,' ice, crust',
ON. hriosa, 'to shudder', OE. hruse, 'earth,
ground*. All these words derive fr. I.-E. *qreus-,
*qrus-, *qruwes-, enlarged forms of base *qreu-,
'icy, solid, coagulated, congealed', whence also
L. crudus, 'raw'. See crude and cp. Crustacea,
encrust. Cp. also crouton, crystal, custard and
the first element in Caucasian.
Derivatives: crust, v. (q.v.), crust-y, adj., crust-
i-ly, adv., crust-i-ness, n.

## crust
crust, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. crust, п., on
analogy of OF. crouster (F. crouter), fr. crousle.
Derivatives: crust-ed, adj., crust-ed-ly, adv.

## Crustacen
Crustacen, n. pi., a large class of animals
characterized by a hard outer shell; including crabs,
lobsters, shrimps, crayfish, etc. (zool.) — Neut.
pi. of ModL. cruslaceus, lit. 'pertaining to the
crust or shell', fr. L. crusta. See crust, n.

## crustacean
crustacean, adj., pertaining to the Crustacea. —
See prec. word and -an.
Derivative: crustacean, n.

## crustaceology
crustaceology, п., the study of crustaceans. — A
hybrid coined fr. Crustacea and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## crustaceous
crustaceous, adj., 1) pertaining to crust; 2) the
same as crustacean. — ModL. crustaceus. See
Crustacea and -ous.

## crutch
crutch, n. — ME. crucche, fr. OE. cryce^ 'crutch,
staff, crozier", rel. to OS. krukka, Dan. krykke,
Swed. krycka, MDu. crucke, Du. kruk, OHG.
krucka, MHG. krucke, G. Krucke, 'crutch'.
These words stand in gradational relationship
to ON. krdkr, 'hook', kraki, 'a stick with a hook
at its end'. They are related also to E. cricket,
the game, creek, crook and crosier. Dial. It.
croccia, It. gruccia, 'crutch', and crocco, 'hook',
are Teut. loan words.
Derivatives: crutch, tr. and intr. v., crutch-ed, adj.

## crux
crux, п., something difficult to explain, a hard
puzzle. — L. crux, 'cross', used also in the sense
of 'torture, trouble'. Cp. crux interpretum, 'a
crux of interpreters'. Cp. also crucial, excruciate
and see cross.

## cruzado
cruzado, n. — See crusado.

## cruzeiro
cruzeiro, п., the monetary unit of Brazil. — Port.,
fr. cruz, 'cross', fr. L. crucem, ace. of crux,
'cross'. See crucial.

## cry
cry, intr. and tr. v. — OF. (= F.) crier, fr. VL.
'critare, corruption of L. quiritare. Ίο cry, wail,
scream', denominated fr. Quiritgs, 'Roman

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:206 COLUMN:3 -->
citizens' ; see Quirites. Accordingly quiritare orig.
meant 'to address the Romans', whence arose
the meanings 'to implore somebody's help; to
raise a plaintive cry; to cry aloud'. Cp. It. gri-
dare, OProvenc., OSp. cridar, Sp., Port, gritar,
which all derive from L. quiritare. Cp. also
decry, descry.
Derivatives: cry, п., cry-ing, adj., cry-ing-ly, adv.

## cry-
cry-, form of cryo- before a vowel.

## crymodynia
crymodynia, п., pain caused by cold weather
(med.) — Medical L., lit. 'pain caused by frost',
fr. κρΰμός (for *κρυσμός), 'frost', and oSuwj,
'pain'. Gk. κρϋμός is cogn. with L. crusia,
'crust'; see crust, п., and cp. the second element
in isocryme. For the second element see -odynia.

## crymotherapy
crymotherapy, п., the therapeutic application of
cold (med.) — Compounded of Gk. κρϋμός,
'frost', and θεραπεία, 'a waiting on, service,
attendance'. See prec. word and -therapy.

## cryo-
cryo-, before a vowel cry-, combining form
meaning 'cold, freezing'. — Gk. κρύο-, κρυ-, fr. κρύος
(for *κρύσος), 'icy cold, frost', which is cogn.
with L. crusta, 'crust'. See crust.

## cryogea
cryogea, п., a refrigerant. — Compounded of
cryo- and -gen.

## cryolite
cryolite, п., a fluoride of sodium and aluminum
(mineral.) — Orig. kryolith, coined by Peter
Christian Abilgaard (1740-180Г), director of the
Veterinary College in Copenhagen, fr. Gk.
κρύος, 'icy cold, frost', and λ(9-ος, 'stone'. See
cryo- and -lite; so called by him from its trans-
lucency. See J.R.Partington, A History of
Chemistry, Volume III, London, 1962, p. 554.

## cryometer
cryometer, п., a thermometer for measuring very
low temperatures. — Compounded of cryo- and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## cryophorus
cryophorus, п., an instrument for showing the
freezing of water by its own evaporation. —
Compounded of cryo- and Gk. -φόρος, 'bearer',
fr. φέρειν, 'to bear'. See -phore.

## crypt
crypt, п., an underground chamber. — L. crypta,
'vault, cave, crypt', fr. Gk. κρυπτή, of s.m., short
for κρυπτή καμάρα, 'a hidden vault'. Κρυπτή
is fern, of κρυπτός, 'hidden, concealed', verbal
adj. of κρυπτειν, 'to hide, conceal', fr. I.-E. base
*qru-bh-, enlargement of base *qru-, 'to hide',
whence OSlav. kryjp, kryti, 'to hide'. Cp.
krypton. Cp. also grot, grotto, which are doublets of
crypt. Cp. also Apocryphn. undercroft.

## crypt-
crypt-, form of crypto- before a vowel.

## cryptic
cryptic, adj., secret. — L. crypticus, 'covered,
concealed', fr. Gk. κρυπτικός, fr. κρυπτός, verbal
adj. of κρυπτειν, 'to hide, conceal'. See crypt
and -ic.
Derivative: cryptic-al-ly, adv.

## crypto-
crypto-, before a vowel crypt-, combining form
meaning 'hidden, secret'. — Gk. κρυπτό-, κρυπτ-,
fr. κρυπτός, verbal adj. of κρυπτειν. See crypt.

## cryptocrystalline
cryptocrystalline, adj., indistinctly crystalline
(petrogr.) — Compounded of crypto- and
crystalline.

## Cryptodira
Cryptodira, n. pi., a suborder of tortoises (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'having a concealed neck',
compounded of crypto- and Ion. Gk. δειρή, 'neck',
which is rel. to Gk. δέρη, Lesbian δέρρα, Dor.
δήρϊ, Arcad. δερίά, of s.m. (I.-E. *gwer-wa), and
is cogn. with OI. griva (for 'g^ri-wa), 'nape',
OSlav griva, 'mane', fr. I.-E. base *gmer-, 'to
swallow', whence also Gk. βορά, βρώμα, 'food',
L. vorare, 'to devour'. See voracious.
Derivatives: cryptodir-an, cryptodir-ous, adjs.

## cryptogam
cryptogam, п., one of the group of plants which
have no external flowers and seeds. — F. cryp-
logame, fr. Gk. κρυπτός, 'hidden', and γάμος,
'marriage'. See crypto- and -gamy.
Derivatives: cryptogam-ian, cryptogam-ic, adjs.,
cryptogam-y, п., cryptogam-isl, п., cryptogam-
ous, adj.

## Cryptogamia
Cryptogamia, n. pi., the group of cryptogams
(hot.) — ModL., formed fr. prec. word with
suff. -ia.

## cryptogram
cryptogram, п., something written in cipher. —
Compounded of crypto- and γράμμα, 'something
written'. See -gram.
Derivatives: cryptogram-ic, cryplogrammal-ic,
adjs.

## Cryptogramma
Cryptogramma, п., a genus of plants of the poly-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:207 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CRYPTOGRAPH | 180 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:207 COLUMN:1 -->
pody family (hot,) — ModL., compounded of
crypto- and Gk. γράμμη, 'a line', which is rel. to
γράμμα, 'something written' (see -gram and cp.
cryptogram); so called in allusion to the lines
of sporangia at first hidden by the margin.

## cryptograph
cryptograph, п., a cryptogram. — Compounded
of crypto- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, Чо
write'. See -graph and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: cryptograph-er, п., cryptograph-ic,
adj., cryptograph-y, n.

## cryptology
cryptology, п., a secret language. — Compounded
of crypto- and Gk. -λογίδ, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## cryptorchid
cryptorchid, п., one with undescended testicles
(anat.) — Medical. L. cryptorchis, corrupted fr.
Gk. κρύψορχις, 'undescended testicles', a word
coined by Galen fr. κρύψις, 'hiding, concealment'
(fr. κρύπτειν, 'to hide'), and ίίρχις, 'testicle'.
See crypt- and orchid.
Derivative: cryptorchid-ism, also cryptorch-ism,
n.

## Cryptostegia
Cryptostegia, п., a genus of woody vines of the
milkweed family (hot.) — ModL., compounded
of crypto- and Gk. στέγη, 'roof, which is rel. to
στέγος, 'roof, fr. στέγειν, 'to cover'. See ste-
gano-.

## Cryptotaenia
Cryptotaenia, п., a genus of plants containing
the honewort (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
crypto- and Gk. ταινία, 'fillet'. See taenia.

## crystal
crystal, n. — ME. cristal, fr. OF. crista! (F.
crystal), fr. L. crystallum, fr. Gk. κρύσταλλος, 'ice;
crystal', which is rel. to κρυσταίνειν, 'to
congeal, freeze'. Both these words derive fr. κρύος
(for "κρύσος), 'frost', which is cogn. with L.
crusta, 'crust*. See crust and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also crymodynia, cryogen,
cryolite.
Derivatives: crystal, adj. and tr. v., crystalline
(q.v.), crystall-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
crystallization, п., crystalliz-ed, adj., crystalliz-er, n.

## crystall-
crystall-, form of crystallo- before a vowel.

## crystalline
crystalline, adj. — F. crysiallin, fr. L.
crystalline, fr. Gk. κρυστάλλινος, 'of crystal', fr.
κρύσταλλος. See crystal and -ine (representing Gk.
-ΐνος.
Derivatives: crystalline п., crystallin-ity, n.

## crystallo-
crystallo-, before a vowel crystall-, combining
form meaning 'crystal'. — Gk. κρύσταλλο-,
κρυσταλλ-, fr. κρύσταλλος. See crystal.

## crystallographer
crystallographer, n. — See crystallography and
agential suff. -er.

## crystallography
crystallography, п., the study of the formation of
crystals. — Compounded of crystallo- and Gk.
-γραφίδ, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.

## crystalloid
crystalloid, adj., resembling a crystal. —
Compounded of crystallo- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## crystallomaacy
crystallomaacy, п., divination by crystal gazing.
— Compounded of crystallo- and Gk. μαντεία,
'oracle, divination'. See -mancy.

## csardas
csardas, п., a Hungarian national dance. —
Hung, csdrdds.

## ctea-
ctea-, form of cteno- before a vowel.

## ctenidium
ctenidium, п., the gill of a mollusk (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idium fr. Gk. κτείς,
gen. κτενός, 'comb*. See cteno-,

## cteno-
cteno-, before a vowel ctea-, combining form
meaning 'comblike' (zool.) — Gk. κτενο-, κτεν-,
fr. κτείς, gen. κτενός, 'comb', which stands for
*pkten, and is rel. to πέκειν, *to comb', and
cogn. with L. pecten, 'comb', pectere, 'to comb'.
See pecten.

## ctenoid
ctenoid, adj., comblike. — Compounded of
ctea- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -oid.

## Ctenophora
Ctenophora, n. pi., a phylum of Coelenterata
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of cteno- and
neuL.pl. of Gk. -φόρος, 'bearer', fr. φέρειν, 'to
bear'. See -phore.

## cuarenta
cuarenta, п., a silver coin of Cuba. — Sp., 'forty',
fr. L. quadraginta. See quadragenarian and cp.
quarantine.

## cub
cub, п., the young of the fox, bear, wolf, lion,
tiger etc. — Of uncertain origin; perhaps rel.
to ON. and Icelandic kobbi, Norw. kobbe, 'seal',
which is prob. so called from its heavy and
clumsy form, to Norw. kubbe, kub, 'stump,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:207 COLUMN:2 -->
block', and to E. cob, 'heap, lump', and further to
Norw. kop, 'cup', earlier Dan. kop, 'head', Dan.
kop, 'cup', OHG. chupk, kopf, 'cup', MHG. kopf,
'drinking vessel; head', G. Kopf, 'head'. See cup.
Derivatives: cub, tr. and intr. v., to bring forth
cubs, cubb-ing, п., cubb-ish, adj., cubb-ish-ly,
adv., cubb-ish-ness, п., cub-hood, n.

## cub
cub, п., a stall, shed. — MDu. cubbe (Du. kub,
kubbe), 'stall, shed', rel. to cove (q.v.) See also
cubby.

## cubage
cubage, п., cubic content. — See cube and -age.

## cuhature
cuhature, п., cubic content. — F., irregularly
formed fr. L. cubus, 'cube', on analogy of
quadrature. See cube and -ure.

## cubby
cubby, п., a small space. — Derived fr. cub,
'stall, shed'.

## cube
cube, n. — F., fr. L. cubus, fr. Gk. κύβος, 'cube,
cubical die', prob. of Sem. origin. Cp. Arab.
ka'b, 'cube', and see Kaaba. The u in Gk. κύβος
is equivalent to Sem. ayin (represented by the
sign '). See W. Muss-Arnolt in Transactions of
the American Philological Association, p. 147.
Gk. κύβος in the sense 'hollow above the hip',
is not related to κύβος, 'cube'.
Derivatives: cube, tr. v., cub-er, п., cubic (q.v.)

## cubeb
cubeb, п., a small aromatic berry used in
medicine. — F. cubibe, fr. ML. cubeba, fr. VArab.
kubaba, corresponding to Arab., kababa", of
s.m.

## cubelet
cubelet, п., a little cube. — A double dimin.
formed fr. cube with the suffixes -el and -et.

## cubic
cubic, adj. — F. cubique, fr. L. cubicus, fr. Gk.
κυβικός, fr. κύβος, 'cube*. See cube and -ic.
Derivatives: cubic, п., cubic-at, adj., cubic-al-ly,
cubic-ly, advs.

## cubicle
cubicle, п., г) a small sleeping room; 2) any small
room. — L. cubiculum, 'an apartment for
reclining or resting', for cubi-clom, lit. 'a place for
reclining', formed from the stem of cubare, 'to
lie down, recline', with -clom, a suff. denoting
place. L. cubare derives fr. I.-E. base *qeu-b-,
'to bend, curve, arch', whence also L. cubitum,
'elbow', Gk. κύβος, 'hollow above the hip of
cattle' (but κύβος in the sense of 'cube, die',
is a Semitic loan word), Goth, hups, OE. hype,
'hip'. See hip and cp. accumbent, concubine, cou-
vade, covey, cubit, incubate, incubus, incumbeat,
procumbent, recumbent, succubus, succumb. Cp.
also coomb, 'a deep valley'. Base *qeub- is a
-ύ-enlargement of base *qeu-, 'to bend', curve,
arch', whence — with reduplication — L. ca-
cumen (prob. fr. orig. *kakud), 'top, summit'.
See high and cp. cacuminal. For a -^-enlargement
of this base see cup and cp. words there
referred to.

## cubiculum
cubiculum, п., a cubicle. — L. See cnbicle.

## cubiform
cubiform, adj., having the form of a cube. —
Compounded of L. cubus, 'cube', and forma,
'form, shape'. See cube and form, n.

## cnbism
cnbism, п., a school of modern art characterized
by the use of cubes and other geometric solids.
— F. cubisme, fr. cube, 'cube'; see cube and
-ism. The word cubisme was coined by the
French art critic Louis Vauxcelles on the basis
of a remark made by the French painter Henri
Matisse (1869-1954) before a landscape
exhibited by Georges Braque (1882-1963) in the
Autumn Salon of 1908. On that occasion
Matisse spoke of the 'small cubes' (peiits cubes)
characterizing the painting of Braque. This
remark induced Vauxcelles to form the word
cubisme.

## cubist
cubist, п., an adherent of cubism. — F. cubiste,
fr. cube, 'cube'. See prec. word and -ist
Derivative: cubist, adj.

## cubit
cubit, n. — L. cubitum (also cubitus), 'elbow', fr.
I.-E. base *qeu-b-, 'to bend, curve', whence also
cubare, 'to lie down'. See cubicle and cp. cubitus.
Cp. also codilli.

## cubital
cubital, adj., pertaining to the cubitus or cubit. —
L. cubitalis, fr. cubitum (cubitus). See cubit and
adj. suff. -al.

## cubitus
cubitus, п., the ulna (anat.) — L. 'elbow'. See
cubit.

## cuboid
cuboid, adj., resembling a cube in shape. — Gk.
κυβοειδής, 'like a cube, cubical', compounded
of κύβος, 'cube', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See cube and -oid.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:207 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: cuboid, n.

## cuckold
cuckold, п., the husband of an unfaithful wife. —
ME. cocold, kokewoid, kokeweld, fr. OF. cucu-
ault, 'cuckold', a hybrid coined fr. OF. соси
(whence F. coucou), 'cuckoo', and -ault, -alt,
a suff. of Teut. origin. See next word. OF. соси
unites the senses of'cuckoo' and 'cuckold'. The
sense development of OF. соси, cucuault, 'finds
its explanation in the fact that the female of the
cuckoo never remains with the same male for
a longer time. Modern French distinguishes
between coucou, 'cuckoo', and соси, 'cuckold'.
Derivatives: cuckold, tr. v., cuckold-ry, n.

## cuckoo
cuckoo, n. — F. coucou, fr. OF. соси, a word
imitative of the bird's cry. Cp. Gk. κόκκΰξ, L.
cucuius, 'cuckoo', OI. kokildh, 'the Indian
cuckoo', kdkah, 'goose', Mir. cuach, W. cog, 'cuckoo',
which all are of imitative origin. Cp. cuckold,
coccyx, koel. Cp. also cock.

## cuculiform
cuculiform, adj., resembling, or pertaining to,
the cuckoos. — Compounded of L. cucuius,
'cuckoo', and forma, 'form, shape'. See cuckoo
and form, n,

## cucullaris
cucullaris, п., the trapezius muscle (anat.) —
Medical L. cucullaris, lit. 'resembling a cap', fr.
L. cucullus, 'cap, hood'. See cowl and cp.
next word.

## cucullate
cucullate, cucullated, adj., hooded; hood-shaped
(bot. and zool.) — Late L. cucullatus, 'hooded',
pp. of cucullare, 'to cover with a hood', fr. L.
cucullus, 'cap, hood'. See cowl and cp. prec.
word.
Derivative: cucullate-ly, adv.

## cuculliform
cuculliform, adj., hood-shaped. — Compounded
of L. cucullus, 'cap, hood', and forma, 'form,
shape'. See cowl and form, n.

## cuculoid
cuculoid, adj., resembling, or pertaining, to the
cuckoos. — A hybrid coined fr. L. cucuius,
'cuckoo', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See cuckoo and -oid. The correct
form is cuculiform, in which both elements are
of Latin origin.

## cucumber
cucumber, n. — ME. cucumer, fr. OF. cocombre,
cucombre (F. concombre), fr. OProvenc. cogom-
bre, fr. L. cucumerem, ace. of cucumis,
'cucumber', fr. Gk. κύκυος, assimilated fr. σίκυος,
'cucumber', a collateral form of σικύη, of s.m.,
which was prob. formed through metathesis fr.
Heb. qishshu'ah, 'cucumber'. See Sicyos and
cp. It. cocomero, Sp. cohombro, Port, cogombro,
which also derive fr. L. cucumerem. Cp. also
Cucumis.

## cucumiform
cucumiform, adj., having the form of a
cucumber. — Compounded of L. cucumis, 'cucumber',
and forma, 'form, shape'. See encumber and
form, n.

## Cucumis
Cucumis, п., a genus of plants of the cucumber
family (bot.) — L., 'cucumber'. See cucumber.

## cucurbit
cucurbit, п., 1) a gourd; 2) a gourd-shaped flask. —
F. cucurbite, fr. L. cucurbim, 'a gourd', which
is cogn. with OI. carbhatah, 'gourd'. The
reduplication in L. cu-cur-bita is prob. due to the
influence of L. cu-cu-mis, 'cucumber'. Cp. Rum.
cucurbetd, OProvenc. cogorda, OF. coorde
(whence F. courge and gourde), 'gourd,
pumpkin', OE. cyrfet, OHG. kurbis, MHG. кигЫз,
G. Kurbis), 'gourd', which all derive from L. cu-
curbita. Cp. gourd.

## Cucurbita
Cucurbita, п., a genus of vines (bot.) — L.,
'gourd'. See prec. word.

## Cucurbitaceae
Cucurbitaceae, n. pi., a family of vines (bot.) —
Formed fr. Cucurbita with suff. -aceae.

## cucurbitaceous
cucurbitaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## cud
cud, n. — ME., fr. OE. cwidu, cudu, 'mastic, cud',
rel. to ME. code, 'pitch', ON. kvada, 'resin',
OHG. quiti, kuti, 'glue' (whence MHG. kiite,
kiit, G. Kitt, 'putty'), and cogn. with Ol.jdtu-,
lac, gum', and with L. bitumen (an Osco-
Umbrian dial, word; the genuine Latin form
would have been *vetumen, fr. *gwetumeri),
'mineral pitch'. All these words are derivatives
of I.-E. *gwet-, *geut-, *gut; dental enlargements
of base *geu-, 'to bend, curve, arch'. See cove,
*a small bay', and cp. quid for chewing. Cp. also
bitumen, bowel, guttural.

## cudbear
cudbear, п., a dye made from lichens. — Coined
from the name of Culhbert Gordon (in 1766)
who patented this dye.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:208 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 181 | CUMULATE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:208 COLUMN:1 -->

## cuddie
cuddie, tr. and intr. v. — Prob. formed fr. dial.
cull, coll, 'to hug, embrace', fr. ME. collen, fr.
OF. coler, 'to embrace', fr. col, 'neck*, fr. L. col-
lum. See collar.
Derivatives: cuddle, п., cuddle-some, cuddl-y,
adjs,

## cuddy
cuddy, п., a donkey. —.From the Scot, name
Cuddy, dimin. of Cuthberf.

## cuddy
cuddy, п., a cabin in a ship. — Du. kajuit, fr. F.
cahutc, 'cabin', which is a blend of cabane, 'hut,
shanty, cabin', and hutte, 'hut'. Cp. G. Kajiite,
Dan. kahytt Swed. kajuta, 'cabin*, which all are
borrowed fr. F. cahute, and see cabin and hut.

## cudgel
cudgel, n. — ME. kttggel, fr. OE. cycgel, rel. to
MDu. koghele, 'club with a round end', Du.
kogel, MHG. kugele, kugel, G. Kugel, 'ball,
globe', OHG. coccho, 'rounded ship', MHG.
kiule, kule, G. Keule, 'club with a round end',
Swed. kugge, Norw. kug, 'cog', and cogn. with
Lith. guga, 'pommel of a saddle, hump, hillock',
gaugaras, 'summit', Russ. guglja, 'tumor,
swelling'. Cp. cog, 'tooth on a wheel'.
Derivatives: cudgel, tr. v., cudgel{l)-er, n.

## cue
cue, п., tail; billiard rod. — F. queue, 'tail', fr.
L. coda, of s.m. See caudal and words there
referred to and cp. esp. queue.

## cue
cue, п., direction for an actor's appearance. -—
Prob. name of the letter q, used as the
abbreviation of L. quando/when (the actor has to come
in)'.

## cueist
cueist, п., a billiard player (slang). — A hybrid
coined fr. cue, 'tail; billiard rod', a word of
Latin origin, and suff. -ist (fr. Gk. -ιστής).

## cuesta
cuesta, п.. a hill, slope (Southwestern U.S.A.)-—
Sp., fr. L. costa, 'rib, side*. See coast.

## cuff
cuff, п., the lower part of the sleeve. — ME. cuffe,
coffe, 'glove, mitten', of uncertain origin; not
related to coif.
Derivatives*, cuff, tr. v., to put cuffs on, cuff-er,n.

## cuff
cuff, tr. v., to strike. — ME., prob. fr. ME. cuffe,
'glove', and orig. meaning 'to strike with a
glove'. See cuff, n.

## cuirass
cuirass, п., armor protecting the breast and back.
— F. cuirasse, orig. 'a leather breastplate', fr.
cuir, 'hide, leather', fr. L. corium. Cp. It. coraz-
za, OProvenQ. coirassa, cuirassa, Sp. coraza,
Port, coura$a, 'cuirass', and see corium.
Derivatives: cuirass, tr. v., cuirass-ed, adj.

## cuirassier
cuirassier, п., a soldier wearing a cuirass. — F.,
formed with suff. -ier fr. cuirasse. See prec. word.

## cuisine
cuisine, п., the kitchen; style of cooking. — F.,
'kitchen', fr. Late L. cocina, a var. of coqulna,
'kitchen', fr. coquere, 'to cook'. See cook and
cp. kitchen.

## cuisse
cuisse, cuish, п., usually in the pi., armor for
protecting the thigh. — ME. a/issues, fr. OF. cuis-
seaux, pi. of cuissel, fr. cuisse, 'thigh', fr. L.
coxa, 'hip', whence also It. coscia, 'thigh'. Rum.
coapsd, 'hip, thigh', OProvenc\ coissa, cueisa,
'thigh', Catal. cuxa, OSp., Port, coxa, of s.m.
See coxa and cp. cushion.

## -cula
-cula, L. fern, dimin. suff., corresponding to
masc. -cuius, neut. -culum. — See -cule.

## cul-de-sac
cul-de-sac, п., a blind alley. — F., lit. 'bottom
of a bag'. For the etymology of F. cul see culet.
F. de, 'of, from', derives fr. L. de, 'from, away
from'; see de-. For the origin of F. sac see sac.

## -cule
-cule, dimin. subst. suff. — F. -cule, fr. L. -cuius
(masc), -cula (fern.), or -culum (neut.) Cp. -cle.

## culet
culet, п., ι) the facet forming the bottom of a
brilliant; 2) armor covering the hinder part of
the body.— F., dimin. οι cul, 'backside,
posterior, bottom', fr. L. cuius, 'posterior, fundament',
which is cogn. with Olr. cul, W. cil, 'back'. Cp.
culot, culotte, bascule, recoil and the first
element in cul-de-sac. For the ending see suff. -et.

## Culex
Culex, п., a genus of mosquitoes. — L. culex,
'gnat', cogn. with Olr. cuil (for *ku-li) 'gnat',
W. cylionen, 'gnat, fly', Co. kelionen, 'fly' and
prob. also with Ol. s'ufa-, 'spear, spit'. These
words possibly derive fr. I.-E. *kul-, enlargement
of base *кй-, 'pointed', whence also L. cuneus,
'wedge'. See coin.

## culici-
culici-, combining form meaning 'gnat'. — L.,
stem of culex, gen. culicis, 'gnat'. See Culex.

## Culicidae
Culicidae, n. pi., a family of insects, the
mosquitoes (entomoL) — ModL., formed with suff.
-idae fr. L. culex, gen. culicis, 'gnat'. See Culex.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:208 COLUMN:2 -->

## culinary
culinary, adj., pertaining to the kitchen; fit for
cooking — L. culinarius, 'pertaining to the
kitchen', fr. cultna, 'kitchen*, which is rel. to
coquere, 'to cook'. For the suff. Ana in culina cp.
Late L. coquina, 'kitchen', dial, h.popina, 'cook-
shop, eating-house1. See cook and adj. suff. -ary
and cp. cuisine. Cp. also kiln,

## cull
cull, tr. v., to select. — ME. cullen, fr. OF. cuillir,
coillir (F. cueillir), 'to collect, gather, pluck', fr.
L. coWgere, 'to collect'. See collect and cp. coil,
'to wind'.
Derivatives: cull, п., cull-age, п., cull-er, п.,
cull-ing, n.

## cullender
cullender, n. — A var. of colander,

## cullet
cullet, п., broken or refuse glass. — F. collet, 'a
little neck' (see collet); so called in allusion to
the small pieces of glass at the neck of the bottle
detached in blowing the glass.

## cull ion
cull ion, п., abase fellow. — The original meaning
is 'testicle', fr. couillon, 'testicle; base fellow',
fr. VL. *coleonem, ace. of *coleo, fr. L. coleus,
'testicles', lit. 'straining bag*, which prob.
derives fr. cofum, 'strainer, colander*, and lit.
means 'that which perlains to the strainer'. See
colander and cp. cullis.

## cull is
cull is, п., a strong broth of meat. — OF. coleis,
couleis (F. coulis), fr. VL. *cofdticius, 'that which
pertains to straining', fr. L. colore, 'to strain'.
See colander and cp. coulisse, cullion.

## cully
cully, п., a dupe. — Perhaps abbreviation of
cullion,

## culm
culm, п., stalk, stem. — L. culmus, 'stalk, stem',
cogn. with Gk. κάλαμος, καλάμη, 'reed', OSlav.
sfama, Russ. soloma, 'straw', OPruss. salme,
Lett, salms, 'blade of straw'. Cp. calamary,
Calumet, chalumeau, haulm, shawm,

## culm
culm, п., coal dust. — ME. cofme, perhaps rel. to
col, 'coal'. See coal.
Derivative: culm-y, adj.

## culminant
culminant, adj., culminating. — L. culminans,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of culminare. See next
word and -ant.

## culminate
culminate, intr. v., to reach the highest point. —
Late L. culminatus, pp. of culminare, 'to top, to
crown', fr. L. culmen, gen. culminis, contracted
form of columen, gen. columinis, 'the top of an
object, summit', which is rel. to columna, 'pillar,
column'. See column and verbal suff. -ate and
cp. hill.
Derivative: culminatAon, n.

## culot
culot, п., a small sheet iron cup inserted into the
base of projectiles. — F., 'bottom of lamps or
crucibles, metal end of crucibles', dimin. of cul,
'bottom*. See culet and cp. next word.

## culotte
culotte, п., breeches. — F., fr. cul, 'bottom'. See
culet and cp. prec. word. Cp. also sansculotte,

## culottic
culottic, adj., wearing breeches. — Formed with
suff. -ic fr. F. culotte, 'breeches*. See prec. word.

## calpability
calpability, n. — Late L. culpabilims, 'guilt,
culpability', fr. L. culpabilis. See next word and -ity.

## culpable
culpable, adj. — ME. culpable, coupable, fr. OF.
culpable, coupable (F. coupable), fr. L.
culpabilis, 'worthy of blame, culpable', fr. culpa,
'blame, fault', which is rel. to Oscan kulupu,
of s.m. It is possible that the original meaning
of L. culpa was 'blow', in which case it is quite
probably cogn. with Gk. κόλαφος (whence L.
colaphus), 'a blow with the fist, a box on the
ear', fr. I.-E. base *qola-, 'to strike, hew*. See
coup, and -able and cp. culprit and disculpate,
exculpate, inculpate.
Derivatives: culpable-ness, п., culpabl-y, adv.

## culprit
culprit, n. — The first element is shortened fr.
culpable, the second is identical with AF. prist,

## prit
prit, fr. OF. prest (F. pret), 'ready*, fr. Vh.praes-
tus, fr. L. adv. praesio, 'at hand, ready, present'.
See culpable and presto. The word culprit arose
from the abbreviation culpable: prest (or prist),
which is the shortening of culpable: prest d'a-
verrer ('he is guilty. I am ready to prove it*),
words with which the clerk of the court
expressed his readiness to prove the guilt of the
accused,

## cult
cult, n. — F. cuite, fr. L. cultus, 'care, cultivation,
culture*, fr. cultus, pp. of colere, 'to till (the
ground), cultivate, dwell, inhabit'. See colony,

## cultivable
cultivable, adj. — F., fr. cultiver, 4o cultivate'.
See next word and -able.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:208 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: cultivabilAty, п., cultivabl-y, adv.

## cultivate
cultivate, tr. v. — ML. cultlvatus, pp. of cultivare,
fr. cultivus, 'fit for tilling/the ground)', fr. L.
cultus, pp. of colere. See cult, -ive and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivalives: cultivat-ed, adj., cultivation, п.,
cultivat-or, n.

## cultrate
cultrate, adj., shaped like a pruning knife. — L.
cultratus, 'knife-shaped', fr. culter, gen. cultri,
'plowshare, knife'. See colter and adj. suff. -ate.

## cul triform
cul triform, adj., cultrate. — Compounded of L.
culter, gen. cultri, 'plowshare, knife', and forma,
'form, shape'. See colter and form, n.

## culture
culture, n. — F., fr. L. cultura, 'a cultivating,
culture, agriculture', fr. cultus, pp. of colere. See
cult and -ure and cp. agriculture, floriculture,
horticulture. Cp. also kultur, Kulturkampf.
Derivatives: cultur-al, cultur-ed, adjs.

## -culum
-culum, L. neut. dimin. suff., corresponding to
masc. -cuius, fern. -cula. — See next-word.
•cuius, L. masc. dimin. suff. — See -cule.

## culver
culver, п., a dove, a pigeon. — ME. culver, colver,
fr. OE. culfre, fr. VL. *columbra, contraction of
columbula, dimin. of columba, 'dove*. See
columbine.

## culveria
culveria, п., a kind of heavy cannon. — F. coule-
vrine, lit. 'adderlike', fr. couleuvre, 'adder', fr.
VL. *colobra, corresponding to L. colubra,t 'a
female snake, a snake*; so called in allusion to
the very long and thin form of this kind of
cannon. For the etymology of L. colubra see cobra
and cp. colubrine,

## culvert
culvert, п., a drain crossing,*a conduit. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: culvert, tr. v.

## cum
cum, prep., with, together with. — L. See com-
and cp. the second word in vade mecum.

## cumber
cumber, tr. v. — ME. combren, fr. OF. combrer,
'to hinder', fr. VL. combrus, 'barrier, bank of
earth, ruins', fr. Gallo-Latin *comboros, whence
also MHG. kumber, 'ruins, rubbish', and G.
Kummer, 'grief, lit. 'that which weighs heavily
upon somebody'. Gallo-Latin *comboros lit.
means 'that which is carried together', and is
formed fr. com- and I.-E. base *bher-, 'to carry*,
whence also Gk. φέρειν, L. ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See bear, 'to carry', and cp. encumber.
Derivatives: cumber, п., cumber-er, п.,
cumbersome, adj., cumber-some-ly, adv., cumber-some-
ness, п., cumbr-ous, adj., cumbrous-ly, adv., cum-
brous-ness, n.

## cumbly
cumbly, also cumly, п., a woolen blanket (Indie).
— Hind, kamli, fr. OL kambalah, 'woolen
blanket', which prob. stands for "ka-mbal-a
and is rel. to Austroasiatic bal, 'hair*. See
Manfred Mayrhofer, A Concise Etymological
Sanskrit Dictionary, I, 161.

## cumin
cumin, also cummin, n. — ME. cumin, comin, fr.
OE. cymen, cymyn, fr. L. curninum, fr. Gk. κύ-
μϊνον, which is of Semitic origin. Cp. Heb.
kammon, of s.m., Aram, kammona, Syr. kam-
mund, Ugar. kmn, Akkad. катйпи, Punic χαμάν,
'cumin*. Cp. also cymene, kitmmel. — Κύμϊνον
entered into Mycenaean Greek as early as the
15th cenlury. See Michael Ventris and John
Chadwick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek
(CambridgeUniversity Press), Index, s.v. Semitic
Loanwords. Cp. the words chiton, chrysalis,
sesam.

## cummer
cummer, п., a woman companion (Scot.) — F.
commire, 'godmother', fr. Eccles. L. commuter,
lit. 'a joint mother', fr. со- and L. mater,
'mother'. See mater, mother and cp. godmother,
the English equivalent of F. commire. Cp. also
It. comare, OProvenc\ comaire, Catal. comare,
Sp., Port, comadre, 'godmother*.

## cummerbund
cummerbund, п., waistband (Anglo-ind.) — Hind.-
Pers. kamar-band, fr. Pers. kamar, 'waist, loins*,
and band, 'band, bandage'. See bind and cp.
band.

## cumquat
cumquat, n. — A var. spelling of kumquat.

## cum shaw
cum shaw, п., present, tip. — Amoy pronunciation

## of Chin
of Chin, кап hsieh, 'grateful thanks'.

## cumulate
cumulate, tr. and intr. v., to accumulate. — L.

## cumulatus
cumulatus, pp. of cumulare, *to heap'. See
cumulus and verbal suff. -ate and cp. accumulnte.
Derivatives: cumulat-edy adj., cumulat-ion, п.,

## cumulat-ive
cumulat-ive, adj., cumulat-ive-ly, adv., cumulat-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:209 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CUMULO- | 182 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:209 COLUMN:1 -->
ive-ness, η.

## cumulo-
cumulo-, combining form meaning 'a heap*. —
Fr. L. cumulus. See next word.

## cumulus
cumulus, п., 1) a heap; 2) rounded mass of cloud
with a flat base. — L., 'a heap', prob. standing
for *ku-me-los, *a swelling*, and derived fr.
I.-E. base *kew(e)-, *кй-, 'to swell', whence also
Gk. κυεΐν, κύειν, 'to become or be pregnant',
κΰμα, 'a wave', lit. 'something swelling', κοίλος,
L. cdvus, 'hollow'. See cave, п., and cp. words
there referred to. For the formation of cumulus
cp. L. tumulus, 'a raised heap of earth'.

## cunabula
cunabula, п., a cradle. — L. cunabula (pi.), dimin.
formed fr. сйпае, 'cradle'. See incunabula.

## cunctation
cunctation, п., delay. — L. cunctdtio, gen. -onis,
fr. cunctdtus, pp. of cunctdrt, 'to delay', fr.
I.-E. base *kcnq-, *konq-, 'to waver*, whence
also Goth, hdhan, OE. hdn, 'to hang'. See
hang and -ation.

## cunctator
cunctator, п., a delayer. — L. cunctdtor, fr. cunc-
tatus, pp. of cunctdri. See prec. word and
agential sun", -or.

## cuneal
cuneal, adj., wedge-shaped. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. cuneus, 'wedge*. See coin.

## cuneate
cuneate, adj., wedge-shaped. — L. cunedtus, pp.
of cunedre, 'to furnish with wedges, drive into
a wedge', fr. cuneus, 'wedge'. See coin and adj.
suff. -ate.

## coneiform
coneiform, adj. — Lit. 'wedge-shaped',
compounded of L. cuneus, 'wedge', and forma,
'form, shape'. See coin and form, n. The name
cuneiform was first applied to the characters of
the ancient inscriptions of Assyria and Persia
by the explorer Engelbert Kampfer (1651-1716).
Derivative: cuneiform, n.

## cuniculus
cuniculus, п., an underground passage. — L.,
'rabbit, rabbit burrowing, underground
passage, hole, pit, cavity'. See cony and -cuius.

## Cunila
Cunila, п., a genus of plants of the mint family
(bot.) — L. cunila, 'name of a plant, a species
of origanum', fr. Gk. κονίλτ), which is of
uncertain origin. OE. cunele, 'thyme', OS. que-
neia, Du. kwendel, OHG. chonela, quenela (G.
Quendel), of s.m., are Latin loan words.

## cunner
cunner, п., either of two fishes of the family of
wrasses. — Of uncertain origin.

## cunniag
cunniag, adj. — ME., 'knowing', pres. part, of
cunnen, 'to know'. See the verbs con and can
and cp. canny, uncouth.
Derivatives: cunning-ly, adv., cunnlng-ness, n.

## cunniag
cunniag, n. — ME. cunning, conning, 'skill,
knowledge', fr. cunnen, 4o know'. See cunning, adj.

## cup
cup, n. — ME., fr. OE. cuppe, rel. to MLG. kopp,
OHG. chuph, kopf, 'cup', chupfa, 'cap', MHG.
kopf, 'drinking vessel; skull', G. Kopf, 'head',
Norw. kop, 'cup', earlier Dan. kop, 'head', Dan.
kop, 'cup', fr. Late L. cuppa, 'cup' (whence also
It. coppa, OProvenc., Catal., Sp., Port, сора,
F. coupe, 'cup', OProvenc. cop, cobs, 'skull',
OF. cope, 'summit', Sp., Port, copo, 'flax put
on the distaff for spinning, flock of wool'). Late
L. cuppa derives fr. L. сира, 'tub, cask, tun,
vat', which is cogn. with OI. kttpah, 'hollow,
pit, cave', Gk. κύπη, 'a kind of ship', κύπελλον,
'cup', OE. hyf, 'hive', ON. hufr, 'the hull of a
ship', Lith. kiiopa, 'heap', kiipstas, 'hill', OSlav.
кирй, Lith. kaiipas, OE. heap, 'heap', OHG.
hubil, OS. huvil, 'hill'. All these words derive
fr. I.-E. base *qeu-p-, 'to bend, arch, vault', -p-
enlargement of base *qeu-, 'to bend'. Cp. coop,
cop, 'top', cowl, 'tub', cupel, cupola, cupula,
cupale. Cp. also cub, 'the young of an animal'.
Cp. also heap, hive, keeve. For the sense
development of the above mentioned Teut. words cp. F.
lite, 'head', fr. L. testa, 'potsherd' (see tester,
'canopy'). For the derivatives of base *qeu-b-,
a -i-enlargement of base *qeu-, 'to bend', see
cubicle and cp. words there referred to. From
base *qeu-bh-, a collateral form of base *qeu-b-,
derive OI. kubhrah, 'humpbacked', Gk. κϋφος,
'hump', κϋφός, 'bent, curved, crooked', κύφελλα
(pi), 'the hollows of the ears'. Cp. cyphella,
cypho-, cypsela. For derivatives of I.-E. base
*geu-p-, a collateral form of base *qeu-p-, see
cove and words there referred to.
Derivatives: cup, tr. and intr. v., cupp-er, п.,
cupp-ing, п., cupp-y, adj.

## cnpboard
cnpboard, n. — Orig. 'a board for holding cups*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:209 COLUMN:2 -->

## capel
capel, п., a vessel used in assaying metals. — F.
coupelle, fr. ML. cupella, dimin. of L. сира,
'tub, cask, vat'. See cup and cp. cupola.
Derivative: cupell-ation, n.

## Cupid
Cupid, п., the god of love in Roman mythology.
— L. Cupido, personification of cupido, 'desire,
love', fr. cupidus, 'longing, desirous, eager', fr.
cupio, cupere, 'to desire', which is prob. cogn.
with OI. kupyati, 'bubbles up,becomes agitated',
OSlav. kypljo, kypeti, 'to boil', Lith. кари, kupeli,
'to boil over', Lett, кйри, kupit, 'to smoke,
steam', Lith. kvepiu, kvipti, 'to breathe, exhale
fragrance', kupiioti, 'to breathe with difficulty',
Gk. καπνός (for *κ^απνος), 'smoke, vapor',
Goth, af-hapjan, 'to put out, extinguish', af-
tvapnan, 'to go out, be extinguished'. Cp.
concupiscence, covet. Cp. also acapnia. Cp. also vapor.

## cupidity
cupidity, n. — F. cupidite, fr. L. cupiditdtem, ace.
of cupiditds, desire, longing', fr. cupidus. See
Cupid and -ity.

## cnpola
cnpola, п., a small dome. — It., fr. Late L. cupula,
'a little tub', dimin. of L. сира. See enp and
cp. cupel,

## cupreous
cupreous, adj., containing, or resembling, copper.
— Late L. cupreus, 'of cupper', fr. cuprum. See
copper. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## cupric
cupric, adj., containing copper as a bivalent
element (chem.) — Late L. cupricus, 'of copper',
fr. cuprum. See copper and -ic

## enpriferous
enpriferous, adj., containing copper (chem.) —
Compounded of Late L. cuprum, 'copper', and
the stem of L. /его, ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See
copper and -ferous.

## enprite
enprite, п., a red oxide of copper (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Late L. cuprum,
'copper'. See copper.

## cuprous
cuprous, adj., containing copper as a univalent
element (chem.) — Formed with suff. -ous fr.
Late L. cuprum, 'copper'. See copper.

## cupula
cupula, п., a cupule (anat.) — Medical L., fr. L.
cupula, 'a little tub or cask', dimin. of сира,
'tub'. See cupule.
Derivatives: cupul-ar, cupul-ate, adjs.

## cupule
cupule, п., a little cuplike structure (bot. and
zool.) — L. cupula, 'a little tub or cask', dimin.
of сира, 'tub, cask, vat'. See cup and -ale and
cp. cupel, cupola.

## cur
cur, п., — ME. curre, fr. earlier kurdogge, prob. fr.
MDu. corre, 'a house dog', lit. 'the grumbling
animal', and rel. to ON. terra, 'to grumble,
murmur'; prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives: curr-ish, adj., curr-ish-ly, adv.,
curr-ish-ness, n.

## curable
curable, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. curSbilis, fr. L.
curare, 'to care for'. See cure, v., and -nble.
Derivatives: curabil-ity, п., curable-ness, п.,
сигаЫ-у, adv.

## curacao
curacao, curacoa, п., a liqueur made from the
dried peel of the Curacao orange. — Named
from Curacao, an island in the Caribbean Sea.
Cp. curassow.

## curacy
curacy, n. — Formed fr. curate with suff. -cy.

## curare
curare, curari, п., a blackish resinous substance '
used by the Indians as arrow poison. — Fr.
Tupi urari, lit. 'he to whom it comes falls'. Cp.
ourali, woorali.

## curarine
curarine, curarin, n., an alkaloid obtained from
curare, С1!(Нм^20 (chem.) — A hybrid coined
fr. curare and chem. suff. -ine, -in, which is of
Latin origin.

## curarize
curarize, tr. v., to poison with curare. — A hybrid
coined fr. curare and -ize, a suff. of Greek origin.

## curassow
curassow, п., large crested bird. — Phonetic
spelling of Curacao; so called, fr. Curacao
island, its place of origin. Cp. curacao.

## enrate
enrate, п., a clergyman who assists a rector or
vicar. — ML. curdtus, lit. One who is charged
with the care of the souls', fr. L. сига, 'care'.
See cure, п., and adj. suff. -ate.

## curative
curative, adj. — F. curatif(fern, curative), formed
with suff. -ive fr. L. curdtus, pp. of curare, 'to
care for'. See cure, v., and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: curative-ly, adv., curative-ness, n.

## curator
curator, n. — Formed (partly through the medium
of AF. curatour, equivalent to F. curateur) fr.
L. curator, 'manager, overseer, superintendent',
lit. one who has the care of, fr. curdtus, pp. of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:209 COLUMN:3 -->
curdre. See curate and agential suff. -or.

## curb
curb, п., 1) a strap for restraining a horse; 2) a
restraint; 3) a stone or concrete edge of a
sidewalk. — F. courbe, 'curve', from the adjective
courbe, 'curved, bent, crooked', fr. L. curvus.
See curve and cp. kerb.
Derivatives: curb, tr. v., curb-er, п., curb-ing, n.

## curbstone
curbstone, n. — See kerb, kerbstone.

## Curculio
Curculio, п., a genus of weevils (entomof.) — L.
curculio, 'a grain weevil', lit. 'a winding,
twisting (beetle)', fr. I.-E. base "qer-, 'to turn, twist',
whence also L. curvus, 'bent, curved'. See curve.

## Curcuma
Curcuma, п., a genus of plants of the ginger
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, kurkum,
'saffron, curcuma'. See Crocus and cp. turmeric.

## carcumin
carcumin, п., the coloring substance of curcuma
root (C21H20O6) (chem.) — Formed fr. prec.
word with chem. suff. -in.

## curd
curd, n. — ME. curd, metathesized fr. ME. crud,
fr. OE. crudan, 'to crowd, press together'. See
crowd, 'to press', and cp. curdle. For the
metathesis of ME. crud to curd cp. curl. For sense
development cp. L. coagulum, 'curd', fr. *co-
agere, co-gere, 'to drive or press together' (see
coagulate).
Derivatives: curd, tr. and intr. v., curd-y, adj.,
curd-i-ness, n.

## curdle
curdle, intr. and tr. v. — Formed from the verb
curd (see prec. word) with freq. suff. -le.
Derivatives: curdl-er, п., curdl-y, adj.

## cure
cure, п., care. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) сиге, 'care',
fr. L. cura, 'care, solicitude, concern', fr. OL.
coira, which is of uncertain origin. Cp. curnte,
curative, cure, curette, curious, accurate, assure,
manicure, pedicure, pococurante, proctor,
procure, scour, 'to clean', secure, sinecure, sure,
Kursaal.
Derivative: cure-less, adj.

## cure
cure, tr. and intr. v. — OF. curer, 'to take care
of, to heal' (whence F. curer, 'to cleanse)', fr.
L. curare, 'to care for, take care of, heal', fr.
cura. See prec. word.
Derivative: cur-er, n.

## cure
cure, п., a strange, queer person (slang). —
Abbreviation of curious. Cp. curio.

## cure
cure, п., a parish priest. — F., fr. ML. curdtus,
whence also E. curate (q.v.)

## Curates
Curates, n. pi., divinities worshiped on the island
of Crete (Greek mythol.) — L. Curetes, fr. Gk.
Κουρήτες, pi. of Κουρής,. lit. meaning 'youthful',
and rel. to κόρος, 'child, youth'. See Cora and
cp. words there referred to.

## Curetonian Syriac
Curetonian Syriac, name of an ancient version
of the Gospels in Syriac. — So called from
William Cureton, who published it in London
in 185S.

## curette
curette, п., name of a surgical instrument. — F.,
fr. curer, 'to cleanse'. See cure, v., and -ette.
Derivative: curette, tr. v.

## curfew
curfew, п., evening signal. — ME. courfew, cor-

## few
few, fr. AF. caverfu, covrefeu, corresponding to
OF. covrefeu, lit. 'cover the fire', fr. covre, im-
per. of OF. covrir (F. couvrir), 'to cover', and

## feu
feu, fr. L. focus, 'hearth, fireside', in Late L.>
also 'fire'. See cover and focus and cp. the first
element in kerchief.

## enria
enria, п., 1) the Roman senate; 2) a court; 3) the
papal court. — L. curia, 'one of the thirty parts,
into which the Roman people was divided (ten
for each of the three tribes); the senate house;
the senate', in ML., 'court', prob. for *co-"iria,
