hence literally meaning 'community of men', fr.
со- and vir, 'men'. See virile and cp. Quirites,cry.

## curial
curial, adj., pertaining to a curia. — L. curialis,
'pertaining to a curia', fr. curia. See curia and
adj. suff. -al.

## curie
curie, п., the unit of radioactivity (physical chem)
— Called after Mme Marie Curie (1867-1934),
discoverer (with her husbandPierre Curie, 1859-
1906) of radium.

## curio
curio, n. — Abbreviation of curiosity.

## curiologic
curiologic, adj., pertaining to that form of
hieroglyphics in which objects are represented by
pictures (not by symbols, as in symbolic
hieroglyphics). — Gk. κΰριολογικός, 'speaking
literally', fr. κϋριολογία, 'use of literal expressions',
fr. κύριος, 'lord, master' and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who

deals (with a certain topic)'. See church and
-logy. Curiologic is an inexact transliteration

## curiosity
curiosity, n. — ME. euriosite, fr. OF. curiosete,
curiosite (F. euriosite), fr. L. curiositatem, ace.
of ciiriositds, 'desire of knowledge, curiosity',
fr. curiosus. See curious and -ity.

## curious
curious, adj. — ME., fr. OF. curios, curius (F.
curieux), fr. L. curiosus, 'careful, diligent,
thoughtful, inquisitive, curious', fr. cura. See
cure, 'care', and -ous.
Derivatives: curious-ly, adv., curious-ness, n.

## curlte
curlte, п., a radioactive mineral. — Named after
the French chemisi Pierre Curie (1859-1906).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## curium
curium, п., name of a radioactive element (chem.)
— ModL; named in 1946 by its discoverer,
the American chemisi Glenn Theodore Seaborg
(born in 1912) in honor of the two Curies (Pierre
and his wife Marie), for their pioneering work
on radioactivity. Cp. curie and prec. word. For
ihe ending of curium see chem. suff. -ium.

## curl
curl, tr. and intr. v. — ME. curlen, metathesized
fr. ME. crullen, fr. crul, 'curly', which is rel. to
Norw. krull, Dan. krelle, E. Fris. krul, krulle,
MDu. crulle, crolle, crul, Du. krul, 'curl', Norw.
krulla, Dan. krelle, MDu. crullen, crollen, Du.
krullen, 'to curl', MHG. krol, 'curly', E. Fris.
krillen, 'to bend, twist'. Cp. cruller. For the
metathesis of ME. crullen to curlen cp. curd.
Derivatives: curl, п., curl-ed, adj., curl-ed-ly,
adv., curl-ed-ness, п., curl-er, п., curl-ing, n. and
adj., curl-y, curl-i-ness, n.

## curlew
curlew, п., any of several kinds of wading birds.
— OF. corlieu, courlieu (F. courlis), of imitative
origin.

## curmudgeon
curmudgeon, п., a churlish, surly, ill-tempered
person. — Of unknown origin.
Derivatives: curmudgeon-ish, curmudgeon-ly,
adjs.

## curr
curr, intr. v., to make a murmuring sound, to
purr. — Of imitative origin.

## currach
currach, curragh, п., a coracle. — Ir. currach,
'boat, little ship', rel. to Gael, curach, of s.m.,
W. corwgl, cwrwgl, 'coracle'. See coracle.

## currant
currant, п., ι) a small seedless raisin; 2) the acid
berry of certain species of Ribes. — AF. raysyns
of Coraunlz = F. raisins de Corinthe, 'dried
grapes of Corinth', fr. L. Corinlhus, fr. Gk.
Κόριν&ας, 'Corinth', a city of Greece. Cp.
Corinthiaa.

## currency
currency, n. — ME. currenlia, fr. L. currens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of currere, 'to run'. See
current, adj., and -cy.

## current
current, adj. — ME. currant, fr. OF. coram, cu-
rant (F couram), pres. part, of corre, curre
(whence, with change of conjugation, F. courir),
'to run', fr. L. currere (pp. stem curs-um), 'to
run', which is cosn. with Gk. -κούρος (for *-κορ-
σας) in έπί-κουρος, 'running to aid, an ally',
Olr., MW. can, 'cart, waggon', Bret, karr,
'chariot', MW. carrawc, W. carrog, 'torrent'.
Cp. currency. Cp. also coranto, corral, corridor,
corsair, courant, courante, courier, course,
curricle, curricutnm, cursive, cursor, cursory,
concourse, concur, concurrant, decurrent, decursive,
discourse, discursive, excurrent, excursion,
excursus, incur, intercourse, kraal, occur,
occurence, precursor, recourse, recur, snecor, suc-
cursal. Cp. also car and words there referred to.
ON. hross, OE. hros, hors, 'horse', are prob. not
cogn. with L. currere, but derivatives of I.-E.
base *(s)qcrd-, a -rf-en'argement of *(s)qer-, 'to
leap, jump' (sa. horse). Derivatives: current, n.
(q.v.), current-ly, adv., current-ness, n.

## current
current, n. — ME. coram, fr. OF. corant, curant
(F. courant), pres. part, of curre, 'to run', used
as a noun. See enrrent, adj.

## curricle
curricle, п., a light two-wheeled carriage. — L.
curriculum, 'a running, a course; a chariot for
racing-, fr. currere, 'to run'. See current, adj.,
and -cle and cp. curriculum.
Derivative: curricle, intr. v.

## curricular
curricular, adj., 1) pertaining to carriages; 2)
pertaining to the curriculum. — Formed with suff.
-ar fr. L. curriculum. See next word.

## curriculum
curriculum, п., course of study. — L., 'a course'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:210 COLUMN:2 -->
See curricle,

## currier
currier, п., ι) one who dresses leather; 2) one who
curries horses. — ME. corier, fr. OF. corier, fr.
L. coriarius, 'tanner, currier', fr. corium,
'leather; see corium. E. currier was influenced in form
by next word.

## curry
curry, tr. v., to dress leather. — ME. curreien, fr.
OF. carreer, correier, fr. earlier conreer, 'to
prepare, equip, furnish' (whence F. corroyer, 'to
curry leather'), fr. VL. *conredare, a hybrid
coined fr. L. con-, 'with' (see con-) and Teut.
*raidjan, Ίο place in order', whence Goth, gare-
dan, 'to attend to, provide for', garaips, 'fixed,
appointed, ordained', OE. gerxde, rxde, 'ready,
mounted', gerxdu, 'armor, trappings'. See
ready and cp. array,

## curry
curry, п., a kind of seasoned dish. — Tamil kari,
'sauce'.
Derivative: curry, tr. v., to flavor with curry.

## enrse
enrse, n. — OE. curs, of uncertain origin;
perhaps connected with Olr. cursagim, Ί
reprehend'. Cp. accursed,

## curse
curse, tr. and intr. v. — OE. cursian, fr. curs. See
curse, n.
Derivatives: curs-ed, adj., curs-ed-ly, adv., curs-
ed-ness, n.

## cursive
cursive, adj. — ML. cursivus, 'running', fr. L. curs-
(um), pp. stem of currere, 'to run'. See current,
adj., and -ive.
Derivatives: cursive-ly, adv., cursive-ness, n.

## cursor
cursor, п., the sliding part of a mathematical
instrument. — L., 'runner', fr. curs-'um), pp. stem
of currere. See prec. word and agential suff.
-or.

## Cursores
Cursores, n. pi., 1) an order of birds (ornithol.);
2) a group of spiders (zool) — L., 'runners', pi.
of cursor. See prec. word.

## cursory
cursory, adj., hastily or superficially done. —
Late L. cursorius, 'hasty', fr. L. curs-(um), pp.
stem of currere, 'to run'. See course and adj.
suff. -ory.
Derivatives: cursori-ly, adv., cursori-ness, n.

## curt
curt, adj., short, brief. — L. curtus, 'mutilated,
broken, short', rel. to cordus, 'late born', orig.
'stunted (in one's growth)*, fr. I.-E. base
*(s)qer-, 'to cut', whence also OHG. scurz, OE.
sceort, 'short'. See short and cp. curtail, curtal,
Curtana, curtate. OHG. (MHG., G.) kurz, OS.,
OFris. kurt, ON. kortr, Du. kort, 'short', are
borrowed fr. L. curtus.
Derivatives: curt-ly, adv., curt-ness, n.
irtail, tr. v., to cut short. — Fr. curtal;
influenced in form by a folk-etymological association
with the noun tail.
Derivatives: curtail-ed, adj., curtail-er, п., cur-
tail-ment, n.

## enrtain
enrtain, n. — ME. cortin, fr. OF. cortine, curtine,

fr. Eccles. L. cortina, 'curtain', rendering of Heb.
y'rVa" (Ex. 26:1 and passim) by the Vulgate.
Eccles. L. cortina derives fr. L. cohors, cors,
'court' (see court), and is prop, a loan translation
of Gk. αυλαία, 'curtain' (= the Septuagint
rendering of Heb. y*rVah, see above), fr. Gk. αυλή,
'court, courtyard'.
Derivatives: curtain, tr. v., curtain-ing, n.

## curtal
curtal, п., having the tail docked, curtailed (ob-
sol.) — OF. cortald, courtald (F. courtaud),
'docked, thick-set', a hybrid formed with the

## Teut. suff. -aid fr. L. curtus
Teut. suff. -aid fr. L. curtus, 'short'. See curt

## and cp. curtail. Cp. also It. cortaldo
and cp. curtail. Cp. also It. cortaldo, which is
of the same origin and meaning as OF. cortald.

## Curtana
Curtana, п., the pointless sword borne before
English sovereigns at their coronation. — ML.

## curtana (scil. spada)
curtana (scil. spada), 'a short sword', fr. L.

## curtus
curtus, 'short'. See curt,

## curtate
curtate, adj., shortened. — L. curtatus, pp. of

curtare, 'to shorten', fr. curtus, 'short'. See curt
and adj. suff. -ate.

## curtesy
curtesy, n. — A var. of courtesy,

## curtilage
curtilage, п., a courtyard surrounding a dwelling
house (law). — OF. cortillage, curtillage, fr. cor-

## til
til, curtil, 'a small courtyard', fr. cort (F. cour),
'courtyard, court'. See court and -age.

## curtle axe
curtle axe, curtal axe, (archaic) — Alteration of
cutlass. Folk etymology explained cutlass as

## curtle axe
curtle axe, i.e. 'a short axe' (see curtail).

## curtsy
curtsy, curtsey, n. — Variants of courtesy.

## curale
curale,adj., designating a chair used by the highest
magistrates in ancient Rome. — L. curulis (in
sella curulis,' 'the curule chair*), fr. *currulis,
'pertaining to a chariot or car', fr. currus,
'chariot, car, triumphal car'. See current, adj., and
cp. curricle. The shortening of rr (in currus) to
r (in curulis) is due to the shifting of the accent.
Cp. canal and mammilla.

## curvate
curvate, curvated, adj., bent, curved. — L. cur-
vatus, 'crooked, bent, curved', pp. of curvare,
'to crook, bend, curve', fr. curvus. See curve and

## enrvature
enrvature, п., a curving. — L. curvatura, 'a

## curve
curve, п., a ben] line. — L. curvus, 'crooked, bent,
curved', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to bend, turn,
twist*, whence also Gk. κορωνός, 'curved, bent',
κορώνη, 'anything curved; crown', κρίκος,
κίρκος, 'ring', κυρτός, 'curved, bent, arched', Mir.
cor, W. cor, 'circle', Russ. krivu, Czech kfivy,

krails, 'bent, crooked', kreilis, 'left hand', Mir.
cruind, OW. crunn, MW. crwnn, Gael, cruinn,
'round*. Cp. crown, п., and words there
referred to. Cp. also cartilage, circus, corf,
crass, crate, crease, 'a fold', creel, cresset, crest,
cricoid, crowd, 'a musical instrument', curb,
Curcnlio, curvet, cyrto-, incurvate, kestrel, re-
enrve, rote, 'a musical instrument', Scorzonera.
scrinium, shrine, Tricyrtis.

## curve
curve, tr. v. — L. curvare, 'to crook, bend, twist',
fr. curvus. See curve, n.
Derivatives: curv-ed, adj., curv-ed-ly, adv., curv-
ed-ness, п., curv-er, n.

## curvet
curvet, п., a leap. — It. corvetta, dimin. of corvo
(now curvo), 'a curve', fr. L. curvus. See curve,
п., and cp. cavort.

## curvet
curvet, intr. and tr. v., to leap, bound. — It. cor-
vcttare, fr. corvetta. See curvet, n.

## curvi-
curvi-, combining form meaning 'curved, bent'.
— Fr. L. curvus. See curve, n.

## curvilineal
curvilineal, curvilinear, adj., consisting of,
bounded by, curved lines. — Compounded of curvi-
and L. linea, 'line'. See line.

## curvometer
curvometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
length of a curve. — A hybrid coined fr. L
curvus, 'curved, bent', and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure*. See curve and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
The correct form would be cyrtometer (fr. Gk.
κυρτός, 'curved, bent'), in which both elements
are of Greek origin. The form cyrtometer is
actually used, but only as a medical term.

## cuscus
cuscus, n. — A var. of cous-cous.

## cuscus
cuscus, п., the aromatic root of an Indian grass,
used for making fans, screens, etc. — Pers.
khas-khas.

## Cuscus
Cuscus, n. — A genus of marsupials, the Pha-
langer (zool.) — ModL., from the Moluccan
native name.

## Cuscuta
Cuscuta, п., a genus of parasitic plants, the
dodder (bot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, kushath, kas-
huthd fr. Pers. kushalh, 'dodder', whence also
Mishnaic Heb. kashuth, 'dodder; fine hair1.

## cusbat
cusbat, п., the wood pigeon or ringdove. — OE.
cuscote, cusceote, of uncertain origin.

## cushion
cushion, n. — ME. quisshin, cusshin, fr. OF. cois-
sin, cussin (F. coussin), fr. ML. *coxinus, fr. L.
coxa, 'hip'; see coxa and cp. cuisse. Cp. also
It. cuscino and Sp. cojin, which are French loan
words. The orig. meaning of OF. coissin was
'hip cushion'.
Derivatives: cushion, tr. v., cushion-ed, adj.,
cushion-y, adj.

## cushy
cushy, adj., easy, pleasant (slang). — Hind, khashi,
.'pleasant', fr. Pers. khush, 'pleasant'.

## casp
casp, п., a sharp point. — L. cuspis, 'point,
pointed end', of uncertain origin. Cp. cuspid,
bicuspid, tricuspid.

## cuspate
cuspate, adj., 1) having a cusp; 2) shaped like a
cusp. — Formed fr. cusp with adj. suff. -ate.

## cuspated
cuspated, adj. etispate. — Formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -ed.

## cuspid
cuspid, adj., a canine tooth. — L. cuspis, gen.
cuspidis, 'point, pointed end'. See cusp.

## cuspidal
cuspidal, adj., 1) pertaining to a cusp; 2) like a
cusp; 3) having a cusp. — Formed with adj.

suff. -al fr. L. cuspis, gen. cuspidis. See cusp.

## cuspidate
cuspidate, cuspidated, adj., having a cusp. —
L. cuspidatus, pp. oicuspiddre, 'to make pointed',
fr. cuspis, gen. cuspidis. See cusp and adj. suff. -ate.

## cuspidor
cuspidor, п., a spittoon. — Port, cuspideira,
fr. cuspir, 'to spit', fr. L. conspuere, 'to spit
upon', fr. con- and spuere, 'to spit', which is of
imitative origin. See spew and cp. conspue.

## cuss
cuss, п., a curse. — A colloquial corruption of
curse.
Derivatives: cuss-ed, adj., cuss-ed-ness, n.

## cuss
cuss, п., a fellow. — A colloquial abbreviation
of customer.

## custard
custard, п., a cooked dish of eggs, milk and sugar.
— ME. crustad, fr. OF. (= F.) croustade, fr. It.
croslata, 'fruit tart', lit. 'something covered with
a crust', fr. L. crustata, fern, of crustalus, pp. of
crustdre, 'to cover with a crust', fr. crusta. See
crust. The change of ME. crusiad to E. custard
is due to the influence of mustard.

## custodial
custodial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. custddia. See custody.

## custodian
custodian, n. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L.
custddia. See next word.

## custody
custody, n. — L. custodia, 'watching, guard, care,
protection', fr. custos, gen. custddis, 'watch,
guard, preserver, keeper, overseer, protector',
fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeudh-, 'to cover', whence also
L. cudo, 'helmet made of skin', OI. kuharam,
'cave', kuhBfi, 'new moon', lit. 'that which is
hidden', Gk. κεύθειν, 'to cover, hide, conceal',
W. cudd, 'a hiding', cuddio, 'to hide', Mir. codal,
'skin'. Cp. custos. For derivatives of the related
base *(s)qeut- see hide, 'skin'. The bases
*(s)qeu-dh- and *(s)qeu-t- are denial enlarge
ments of base *(s)qeu-, 'to cover, hide'. See sky
and cp. words there referred to.

## custom
custom, n. — ME. custume, custome, fr. OF.
costume, custume (F. coutume), fr. L. consuetu-
dinem, асе. of consuetudo, 'custom, habit, use,
usage', fr. consuetus, pp. of consuescere, 'to
accustom', fr. con- and suescere, 'to become
used or accustomed', fr. I.-E. base *swedh-,
whence also Gk. £θος, ήθος, 'custom, usage',
έθνος, 'race'. Base *swedh- is compounded of
*swe-, 'his, her, its, one's own', and *dhi-, 'to
put, place; to do, make', hence lit. means 'to
make one's own'. See sui- and the verb do and
cp. consuetude, costume, which are doublets of
custom. Cp. also assuetude, de suetude, man-
suete, mastiff, sodality. Cp. also ethical, ethnic,
hetaira.

## customable
customable, adj. — OF. costumable, fr. costume,
'custom'. See prec. word and -able.

## enstomary
enstomary, adj. — OF. costumier (F. coutumier),
fr. costume, 'custom'. See custom and adj. suff.
-ary.
Derivatives :customari-ly,adv.,customari-ness,n.

## customer
customer, n. — Formed with agential suff. -er
fr. custom, partly through the medium of AF.
custumer. Cp. cuss, 'fellow'.

## custos
custos, п., keeper, guardian. — L. custos, gen.
custddis. See custody.

## custumal
custumal, п., a written collection of the customs
of a city, a province etc. — ML. costumalis
(scil. liber), 'a book of customs', fr. OF.
custumal, fr. custume. See custom and adj. suff. -al.

## cut
cut, tr. and intr. v. — ME. cutten, kutten, kitten,
prob. rel. to dial. Swed. kuta, kota, Icel. kuta,
'to cut with a knife, dial. Swed. kuta, kytti, Icel.
kuti, 'knife'.
Derivatives: cut, pp. and п., cutt-er, п., cutt-ing,
n. and adj., cutt-ing-ly, adv., cutty (q.v.)

## cutaneous
cutaneous, adj., pertaining to the skin. — ML.
cutdneus, fr. L. cutis, 'skin'. See cutis and
-aneous.

## cutch
cutch, п., black catechu. — Malay kachu. See

## cutcherry
cutcherry, cutchery, п., office of administration
(Anglo-India). — Hind, kachahrl.

## cute
cute, adj., clever; sharp. — Aphetic for acute.
Derivatives: cute-ly, adv., cute-ness, n.

## Cuterebra
Cuterebra, n. — See Cutiterebra.

## Cuthbert
Cuthbert, masc. PN. — Compounded of OE. cud,
'known, famous', and beorht, 'bright'. For the
first element see uncouth. For the second element
see bright and cp. Albert, Bardolph, Bertha,
Bertram.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:211 COLUMN:2 -->

## cuticle
cuticle, п., the epidermis. — L. cuticulum, dimin.
of cutis, 'skin'. See cutis and -cle.

## cuticular
cuticular, adj., pertaining to the cuticle. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. cuticulum. See prec.
word.

## cutis
cutis, п., the skin beneath the epidermis, the
derma (anat.) — L. cutis, 'skin', lit. 'that which
covers', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeut-, 'to cover',
whence also OE. hyd, 'skin'. See hide, 'skin', and
cp. cutaneous, cuticle. Cp. also cyst, -cyte, ecu,
escutcheon, esquire, scudo, scum, Scutellaria,
scutellum, scnttle, 'receptacle', scutum,
syncytium, zuchetto. Base *(s)qeut- is rel. to base
*(s)qeudh-, 'to cover'; see custody.

## Cutiterebra
Cutiterebra, Cuterebra, п., a genus of botflies (en-
tomol.) — ModL., compounded of L. cutis,
'skin', and terebra, 'borer'. See cutis and terebra.

## cutlass
cutlass, cutlas, п., a short curving sword. — F.

is formed with augment, suff. -accio fr. coltello,
'knife', fr. L. cultellus (whence also OF. coutel,
F. couteau), dimin. of culler, 'knife'. See colter.

## cutler
cutler, n. — ME. cotelere, coteler, fr. OF. cote-
lier (whence F. coutelier), 'a knife maker', fr.
Late L. cultellarius, fr. L. cultellus. See prec.
word.

## cutlery
cutlery, n. — OF. cotelerie (F. coutellerie), fr.
cotelier. See prec. word and -y (representing
OF. -ie).

## cutlet
cutlet, n. — F. cdtelette, lit. 'a little rib', a double
dimin. of cote, 'rib', fr. OF. coste, fr. L. costa,
'rib, side'. See coast and cp. costal. Cutlet was
prob. influenced in form by cut.

## cuttlefish
cuttlefish, cuttle, n. — ME. cotul, codul, fr. OE.
cudele, 'cuttlefish', rel. to dial. Norw. kaule (for
*kodle), lit. 'pouch fish', and to OE. codd, 'bag,
shell, husk'. See cod, 'a small bag'.

## cutty
cutty, adj., short (Scot, and dial.) — Formed fr.
cnt with adj. suff. -y.

## -cy
-cy, suff. used to form abstract nouns denoting
quality or rank, corresponding in meaning to
the suffixes -ship and -hood. — L. -cia, -lia, or
Gk. -κεία, -κίά, -τείά, -τία. Suff. -cy occurs
chiefly as the termination of the suffixes -асу,
-ancy, -ency, -cracy, -mancy (qq.v.)

## cyan-
cyan-, form of cyano- before a vowel.

## cyanate
cyanate, п., a salt of cyanic acid (chem.) — See
cyanic and chem. suff. -ate.

## Cyanea
Cyanea, п., a genus of jelly fishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. κυάνεος, 'dark blue', fr. κύανος,
'the dark blue color'. See next word.

## cyanic
cyanic, adj., i) of blue color; 2) pertaining to, or
containing, cyanogen. — Formed with suff. -1c
fr. Gk. κύανος, 'dark blue enamel, lapis lazuli,
the dark blue color', a foreign word connected
with Hitt. kuwanna(n)-, 'copper, copperblue;

## cyanide
cyanide, cyanid, п., a compound of cyanogen
with an element or a radical (chem.) — See prec.
word and chem. suff. -ide, resp. -id.
Derivative: cyanide, tr. v.

## cyanite
cyanite, п., an aluminum silicate, Al2SiOs
(mineral.) — G. Cyanit, coined by the German
geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner (1750-Г817) in
1794 fr. cyan- and suff. -it, which goes back to
Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## cyaao-
cyaao-, before a vowel cyan-, combining form
meaning 'dark blue*. — Gk. κυανό-, κυαν-, fr.
κύανος, 'the dark blue color'. See cyanic.

## Cyanocitta
Cyanocitta, п., a genus of birds, the American
blue jay (ornithol.) — ModL., lit. 'blue jay', fr.
Gk. κύανος, 'the dark blue color', and κίσσα,
κίττα (for *κίκια), 'jay'. For the first element
see cyanic. The second element is of imitative
origin. Cp. OI. kikih, 'the blue jay', OHG. he-
hara (MHG. heher, G. Haher), 'jay', which all
are imitative of the cry of the bird.

## cyanogen
cyanogen, п., t) the radical CN (carbon and
nitrogen); 2) a poisonous gas (CN)j (chem.) —
Compounded of cyano- and -gen.

## cyanometer
cyanometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
degrees of blueness. — Compounded of cyano-
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.
Derivative: cyanometr-y, n.

## cyanopathy
cyanopathy, п., another name for cyanosis (med.)
— Compounded of cyaao- and Gk. -πάθεια,
fr. πάθος, 'suffering'. See -pathy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:211 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: cyanopath-ic, adj.

## cyanosis
cyanosis, п., pathological condition in which the
surface of the body becomes blue for lack of
aeration (med.) — Medical L., formed fr.
cyano- and suff. -osis.

## cyathus
cyathus, п., a cup or ladle for drawing wine out
of the crater (mixing-bowl) into the drinking-
cup (Greek aniiq.) — L., fr. Gk. κύαθος, 'cup',
which is prob. rel. to κυεΐν, κύε'.ν, 'to become
pregnant', κύαρ, 'eye of a needle; orifice of the
ear', κϋμα, 'anything swollen; a wave'. See
cyma and cp. cyesis.

## Cybele
Cybele, п., goddess of the earth and mother of
the gods in Greek mythology. — L., fr. Gk.
Κυβέλη, a name of uncertain origin.

## cybernetics
cybernetics, п., the comparative study of complex
electronic calculating machines and the human
nervous system. — Coined by the Jewish
mathematician of the U.S. A .,Norbert Wiener (1894-
1964), fr. Gk. κυβερνήτης, 'steersman, pilot' (fr.
κυβερνάν, 'to steer, guide, govern', whence L.
guberndre, of s.m., see govern), and suff. -ics.

## Cybister
Cybister, п., a genus of diving beetles (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. κυβιστητήρ, 'tumbler', fr.
κυβιστάν, "to tumble head foremost', which is of
uncertain origin. It is perh. cogn. with OI. kub-
hanyuh, 'dancing', OE. hoppian, 'to hop, dance'.
See hop, 'to leap'.

## cycad
cycad, п., any of the plants of the family Cyca-
daceae. — See Cycas.

## Cycadaceae
Cycadaceae, n. pi. (bot.) — ModL., formed fr.
next word with suff. -aceae.

## Cycas
Cycas, п., a genus of trees (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. κύκας, erroneously written for κόϊκας,
ace. pi. of κόϊξ, 'the doom palm', which is a
foreign word of unknown origin.

## cycl-
cycl-, form of cyclo- before a vowel.

## cyclamen
cyclamen, n. — ML. and ModL., fr. Gk. κυκλά-
μΐνος, fr. κύκλος, 'circle'. See cycle.

## Cyclanthus
Cyclanthus, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
coined by Poiteau fr. Gk. κύκλος, 'circle', and
άνθος, 'flower'. See cyclo- and anther.

## cyclas
cyclas, п., a kind of tunic worn by Roman
women. — L., fr..Gk. κυκλάς, 'state robe of
women', short for κυκλάς έσθής, 'a circular
garment', from the adjective κυκλάς, 'encircling',
fr. κύκλος, 'circle'. See next word.

## cycle
cycle, n. — F., fr. Late L. cyclus, fr. Gk. κύκλος,
'ring, circle, wheel', which is cogn. with OI.
cakrah, OE. hweol, hweogol, 'wheel'. See wheel
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
cyclamen, cyclas, and the second element in hemi-
cycle, monocycle, multicycle, pericycle, tricycle.
Cp. also chukker, hackery, jack, 'an East Indian
tree', Ku Mux Klan.
Derivatives: cycle, intr. v., cycl-er, п., cyclic
(q.v.), cycl-ing, п., cycl-ism, п., cycl-ist, n.

## cyclic
cyclic, adj. — F. cyclique, fr. L. cyclicus, fr. Gk.
κυκλικός, 'circular, moving in a circle', fr.
κύκλος. See cycle and -ic, and cp. acyclic,
monocyclic.
Derivatives: cyclic-al, adj., cyclical-ly, adv.

## cyclist
cyclist, ii., 1) one who rides a bicycle, tricycle,
etc.; 2) one who reckons by cycles. — Formed
fr. cycle with suff. -ist.
Derivative: cyclist-ic, adj.
yclo-, before a vowel cycl-, combining form
meaning 'circular'. — Gk. κύκλο-, κυκλ-, fr.
κύκλος, 'circle'. See cycle.

## Cyctobofhra
Cyctobofhra, п., a genus of plants of the lily
family; called also Calochortus (bot.) —
Compounded of cyclo- and Gk. βόθρος, 'pit' (see
bothrium); so called in allusion to the nectar'es.

## Cycloconium
Cycloconium, п., a genus of imperfect fungi (bot.)
— ModL., compounded of cyclo- and Gk.
κόνις, 'dust', which is cogn. with L. cinis,
'ashes'. See cinerary and cp. words there
referred to.

## cycloid
cycloid, adj., circular; п., a curve described by
a point in the circumference of a circle that rolls
along a straight line. — Gk. κυκλοειδής,
'circular', compounded of κύκλος, 'circle', and
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. Seecyclo-
and -oid.
Derivatives: cycloid-al, adj., cycloid-al-ly, adv.

## Cycloloma
Cycloloma, п., a genus of plants of the goosefoot
family (bot.). — ModL., compounded of cyclo-
and Gk. λώμα, 'fringe, border' (see loma); so

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:212 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 185 | CYNO- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:212 COLUMN:1 -->
called in allusion to the wing of the calyx
encircling it.

## cyclometer
cyclometer, п., an instrument for measuring
circles. — Compounded of cyclo- and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## cyclone
cyclone, n. — Irregularly formed fr. Gk. κύκλος,
'circle', or fr. κψ<λών, 'whirling round', pres.
part, of κυκλοΰν, 'to move in a circle, whirl
round4, which is a derivative of κύκλος (see
cycle); coined by H.Piddington in 1848.
Derivative: cyclon-ic, adj.

## cyclonology
cyclonology, п., the science dealing with cyclones.
— Compounded of cyclone and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: cyclonolog-ist, n.

## Cyclopean
Cyclopean, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, the
Cyclopes. — Formed with surf, -an fr. L.
Cyclopeus, fr. Gk. Κυκλώπειος, fr. Κύκλωψ. See
Cyclops.

## cyclopedia
cyclopedia, cyclopaedia, n. — ModL.,
abbreviation of encyclopedia (q.v.)
Derivatives: cychp{a)ed-ic, adj., cychp(a)ecl-
ist, n.

## Cyclops
Cyclops, п., one of a race of one-eyed giants in
Greek mythology. — L., fw-Gk. Κύκλωψ, gen.
Κύκλωπος, lit. 'round-eyed', fr. κύκλος, 'circle',
and ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye', fr. I.-E. base *okw-, a
collateral form of base *ok"'-, 'eye'. See cyclo-
and -opia.
cyclo га пш, п., a pictorial representation of a
landscape on the inner wall of a cylindrical room,
the spectators standing in the middle. —
Compounded of Gk. κύκλος, 'circle', and όραμα,
'view', fr. όραν, 'to see'. For the first element see
cycle. The second element is cogn. with L.
vereri, 4o observe with awe, revere, respect,
fear', OE. wxr, 'cautious, aware'. See ware,
'alert*, and cp. the second element in cos-
morama and words there referred to.

## cyclosis
cyclosis, п., circulation of protoplasm within a
cell (plant physiol.)— ModL., coined by C.H.
Schultz in 1835 fr. Gk. κύκλωσις, 'circulation', fr.
κυκλοΰν, 'to move in a circle', fr. κύκλος. See
cycle and -osis.

## Cyclostomata
Cyclostomata, n. pi., a class of eel-like
vertebrates, the lampreys and hagfishes (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'round-mouthed', fr. Gk. κύκλος,
'circle', and στόμα, gen. στόματος, 'mouth'. See.
cycle and stoma.

## cyclostome
cyclostome, adj., pertaining to the
Cyclostomata; п., a cyclostome vertebrate. — See prec.
word.

## cyclostyle
cyclostyle, п., a device for printing copies. —
Compounded of cyclo- and style.

## cyclotron
cyclotron, п., an apparatus used for splitting
atoms; an atom smasher. — Coined fr. cyclo-
with the ending of electron.

## cyder
cyder, n. — A var. of cider.

## Cydonia
Cydonia, п., a genus of trees of the apple family.
— L. cydonia (scil. mala), pi., 'quince apple'.
See quince.

## cyesis
cyesis, п., pregnancy. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
κύησις, 'conception, pregnancy', fr. κυεΐν, κύειν,
'to be pregnant', whence also κύμα, 'anything
swollen; a wave'. See cyma and cp. cyathus.

## cygnet
cygnet, п., a young swan. — Dimin. of F. cygne,
'swan' (refashioned after L. cygnus, a variant
of eyenus), fr. OF. cisne, fr. VL. cicinus (which
occurs in the Salic law), fr. L. eyenus, fr. Gk.
κύκνος, 'swan', which is prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. Russ. кукй, 'swan's cry*. Cp. also
Cygnus.

## Cygnus
Cygnus,п., i)theSwan (name ofaconstellation);
2) the genus of swans (ornithol.) — L. cygnus,
'swan*. See cygnet.

## cylinder
cylinder, n. — F. cylindre, fr. L. cylindrus, fr. Gk.
κύλινδροσ, 'roller, roll, cylinder', fr. κυλίν8ειν,
'to roll', which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base
*(s)qel-, 'to bend, twist*, whence also Gk.
κυλλός (for *κυλ-νός, *κελνός), 'crooked,
crippled*, κώλον, 'limb, member; member of a clause

## or a sentence'. See colon
or a sentence'. See colon, 'punctuation mark',
and cp. calender. Base *qwe-qwlos, reduplication
of base *qef-, 'to bend, twist*, appears in OI.

## cakrah
cakrah, Gk. κύκλος, "cycle*. OE. hweogol, hweol,
'wheel'. See wheel and cp. cycle.
Derivatives: cylinder, tr. v., cylinder-ed, adj.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:212 COLUMN:2 -->
cylinder-er, n.

## cylindr-
cylindr-, form of cylindro- before a vowel.

## cylindrical
cylindrical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
ModL. cylindricus, fr. Gk. κυλινδρικός, fr.
κύλινδρος. See cylinder.

## cylindro-
cylindro-, before a vowel cylindr-, combining
form meaning, 'cylindrical'. — Gk. κύλινδρο-,
κυλινδρ-, fr. κύλινδρος. See cylinder.

## cylindroid
cylindroid, adj. and n. — Compounded of Gk.
κύλινδρος, 'cylinder', and-οειδής,'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See cylinder and -oid.

## cylix
cylix, п., an ancient drinking cup {Greek antiq.)
— Gk. κύλιξ, 'drinking cup', in gradational
relationship to κάλυξ, 'cup, calyx of a flower'.
See calyx.

## cyllosis
cyllosis, п., clubfool (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. κύλλωσις, 'clubfoot*, fr. κυλλός (for *κυλ-
νός, *κελ-νός), 'crooked, crippled*, which is
prob. rel. to κυλίνδειν, 'to roll', κύλινδρος,
'roller, roll, cylinder'. See cylinder.

## cym-
cym-, form of cymo- before a vowel.

## cyma
cyma, п., molding of a cornice, with an ogee
profile (arch.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κΰμα, 'anything
swollen, a wave, billow, surge', fr. κυεΐν, κύειν,
Чо be pregnant', whence also κύησις,
'conception, pregnancy', fr. I.-E. base *kew-, *kewa-,
'to swell out', whence also OI. svayate, 'swells',
surah, 'strong', L. inciens (for *en-fcw~yent-s),
'pregnant'. See cave, п., and cp. cyme,cymatium,
cyathus, cyesis, kymatology, acyrology, church.
Cp. also casserole, coelo-, maroon, One of a
class of Negroes'.

## cymar
cymar, п., a robe. — F. cimarre, fr. It. simarra.
See chimere.

## cymatium
cymatium, п., i)a molding; 2) a cyma (archit.) —
L., fr. Gk. κϋμάτιον, dimin. of κΰμα. See cyma.

## cymba
cymba,n., l) a boat-shaped sponge spicule (zoo/.);
2) the upper part of the concha of the ear (anat.)
— L. cymba, fr. Gk. κύμβη, 'the hollow of a
vessel, cup, boat*. See next word and cp. Cym-
bella, Cymbidium.

## cymbal
cymbal, п., either of a pair of brass plates used
in orchestras. — ME. cimbal, symbol, fr. OE.
cymbal and MF. (= F.) cymbale, which both
derive fr. L. cymbalum, fr. Gk. κύμβαλον, fr.
κύμβη, 'the hollow of a vessel, cup, boat', fr.
I.-E. base *qumb-, 'to bend, curve', whence also
OI. kumbhdk, 'pot, jar', Avestic xumba, of
s.m., Toch. A kumpac, 'drum', W. cwmm,
'valley', Bret, komb, 'small valley', Mir. comm,
'vessel', cummal, 'cup', and E. hump, 'swelling,
protuberance' (q.v.) Cp. cymba, chime, n. Cp.
also combe.
Derivatives: cymbal-er, cymbal-eer, п.,
cymbalist, n.

## Cymbella
Cymbella, п., a genus of diatoms (hot.) — ModL.,
formed with dimin. suff. -ella fr. L. cymba, 'boat'
(see cymba); so called in allusion to their
boatlike shape.

## Cymbidium
Cymbidium, п., a genus of orchids (bot.) —
ModL., formed with dimin. suff. -idium fr. Gk.
κύμβη, 'cup*. See cymba.

## cymbiform
cymbiform, adj., shaped like a boat. —
Compounded of L. cymba, fr. Gk. κύμβη, 'boat', and
L. forma, 'form, shape'. See cymba and form.

## Cymbium
Cymbium, п., a genus of marine snails (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. cymbium, 'a small cup', fr. Gk.
κυμβίον, dimin. of κύμβη, 'cup'. See cymbe.

## cymbocephalic
cymbocephalic, adj., having a boat-shaped skull
(craniol.) — Lit. *boat-headed', compounded of
Gk. κύμβη, 'boat', and κεφαλή, 'head'. See cymba
and cephalic.

## cymbocephaly
cymbocephaly, п., the condition of having a
boatshaped head (craniol.) — See prec. word
aлd -y (representing Gk. id.).

## Cymbopogon
Cymbopogon, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) - -
ModL., compounded of Gk. κύμβη, 'boat' and
ττώγων, 'beard'. See cymba and Pogonia.

## cyme
cyme, п., a mode of inflorescence in which the
primary and the secondary axes bear a single
terminal flower (bot.) — L. cyma, 'young sprout
of a cabbage', fr. Gk. κΰμα, 'anything swollen'.
See cyma.

## cymene
cymene, п., a hydrocarbon (chem.) — Gk. κύ-
μϊνον, 'cumin'. See cumia.

## cymling
cymling, п., a kind of squash. — A var. of simnel
(with change of suff.).

## cymo-
cymo-, before a vowel cym-, combining form

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:212 COLUMN:3 -->
meaning 'wave' or 'sprout'. — Fr. Gk. κΰμα,
'anything swollen'. See cyma.
Cyniodoce, п., one of the Nereids (Greek mythol.)
— L. Cymodoce, fr. Gk, Κϋμοδόκη, lit. 'she who
receives the waves', fr. κΰμα. 'wave*, and Se-
κεσθ-αι, δέχεσ&αι, 'to receive'. See cyma and
decent.

## cymograph
cymograph, п., an instrument for tracing graphs
representing electric waves. — Lit. 'tracer of
waves', fr. Gk. κϋμα,'wave', and -γραφυς, fr.
γροίφειν, 'to write'. See cyme and -graph.
Derivative: cymograph-k, adj.

## cymometer
cymometer, п., formerly an instrument for
measuring etheric waves. — Compounded of
Gk. κΰμα, 'wave*, and μέτρον, 'measure'. See
cyma and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## cymophane
cymophane, п., a wavy variety of chrysoberyl
(mineral.) — Compounded of Gk. κΰμα,'wave',
and the stem of φαίνειν, 'to show*, φαίνεσθαι,
'to appear'. See cyma and phantasm.

## cymoscope
cymoscope, п., a device for detecting electric
waves. — Compounded of Gk. κΰμα, 'wave',
and -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπειν, 'to look at, examine*.
See cyma and -scope.

## cymotrichy
cymotrichy, п., wavy hair. — Compounded of
Gk. κΰμα, 'wave', and θρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair'.
See cyma and tricho-.

## Cymric
Cymric, Kymric, adj., Welsh. — Formed with
suff. -ic fr. W. Cymry, 'the Welsh1, pi. of Cymro,
'Welshman', which prob. derives fr. OW. *com-
brog, 'compatriot*, fr. com-, 'with', and *brog
(whence W. bro), 'region', which is rel. to Olr.
bruig, mruig, 'boundary, region*, and cogn.
with OE. mearc, 'boundary, sign, mark'. See
com- and mark, 'sign*. Cp. L. Allobroges, name
of a warlike people in Gallia Narbonensis, lit.
'those from another land'. Cp. also Cambrian.
суп-, form of cyno- before a vowel.

## cynanche
cynanche, п., a medical term for diseases of the
thToat. — Gk. κυνάγχη, 'sore throat', lit. 'dog
quinsy', formed fr. κύων, gen. κυνός, 'dog', and
όίγχειν, 'to throttle, strangle'. See quinsy.

## Cynaachum
Cynaachum, п., a genus of plants of the milkweed
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κυνάγχη, 'dog
quinsy*. See prec. word.

## cynanthropy
cynanthropy, п., insanity in which the patient
believes himself to be a dog (med.) — Formed
with suff. -y (representing Gk. -ία), fr. Gk.
κυνάνθρωττος, 'of a dog-man*, which is
compounded of κύων, gen. κυνός, 'dog*, and
άνθρωπος, 'man'. See cyno- and anthropo-. The name
cynanthropy prop, derives fr. Gk. νόσος κυνάν-
θρωπος, lit. 'dog-man's disease', a name given
to this mania by Galen (see Galen 19, 719).

## cynegetics
cynegetics, п., hunting. — Gk. κυνηγετική (scil.
τέχνη), '(the art of) hunting', fr. κυνηγέτης,
'huntsman, hunter', (whence κυνηγετεϊν, 'to
hunt'), which is compounded of κύων, gen.
κυνός, 'dog', and ήγεϊσθ-αι, 'to lead'. See cyno-,
seek and -ics.

## Cynias
Cynias, п., a genus of Carchariidae, the smooth
dogfish (ichthyol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κύων, gen.
κυνός, 'dog'. See cyno-.

## cyniatrics
cyniatrics, п., that branch of veterinary medicine
which deals with diseases of dogs. —
Compounded of суп- and -iatrics.

## cynic
cynic, n. — L. cynicus, 'a cynic', fr. Gk. κυνικός,
an adjective formed fr. Κυνόσαργες, 'Cyno-
sarges', a gymnasium near Athens. It was in this
gymnasium that Antisthenes taught, whence
his disciples were called κυνικοί, lit. Of Cyno-
sarges'. (For sense development cp. stoic and
academician, which are also formed from place-
names.) The usual derivation of Gk. κυνικός,
'a cynic', fr. κύων, gen. κυνός, 'dog', and the
explanation that κυνικός orig. denoted a 'dog-
like' philosopher, is erroneous. The only
connection between a cynic and a dog is given by
the quite incidental fact that the first element in
the name Κυνόσαργες comes fr. κύων, gen.
κυνός, 'dog' (see cyno-).
Derivatives: cynic, cynic-al, adjs., cynic-al-lyt
adv., cynic-ism, п., cynic-ist, n.

## cyno-
cyno-, before a vowel суп-, combining form
meaning 'dog-'. — Gk. κυνο-, κυν-, fr. κύων,
gen. κυνός, 'dog', which is cogn. with L. canisy
Goth, hunds, OE. hund, 'dog*. See hound and
cp. canine. Cp. also cynanche, Cynias, cynosure,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:213 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: CYNOCEPHALIC | 186 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:213 COLUMN:1 -->
quinsy, squinancy.

## cynocephalic
cynocephalic, п., cynocephalous. — See next
word and -ic.

## cynocephalous
cynocephalous, adj., dog-headed. — Gk. κυνο-
κέφαλος, 'dog-headed*, compounded of κύων,
gen. κυνός, 'dog', and κεφαλή, 'head'. See cyno-
and cephalic. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see -ous.

## Cynocrambaeeae
Cynocrambaeeae, n. pi., a family of plants (hot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Cynocrambe with suff.
-nceae.

## cynocrambaceous
cynocrambaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Cynocrambe
Cynocrambe, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — Mod-
L., fr. Gk. κυνοκράμβη, 'dog cabbage', which is
compounded of κύων, gen. κυνός, 'dog', and
κράμβη, 'cabbage'. See cyno- and Crambe.

## Cynodon
Cynodon, п., a genus of plants of the family Poa-
ceae (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κυνόδων, 'the
canine tooth', compounded of κύων, gen. κυνός,
'dog' and δδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See cyno-
and odonto-.

## Cynoglossum
Cynoglossum, п., a genus of the borage family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κυνόγλωσσον, 'hound's-
tongue', which is compounded of κύων, gen.
κυνός, 'dog' and γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See cyno- and
gloss, 'explanation'.

## cynoid
cynoid,adj.. I) doglike; 2) pertaining to the dog
family. — Gk. κυνοειδής, 'doglike',
compounded of κύων, gen. κυνός,'dog', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See cyno- and -oid.

## cynorrfaodon
cynorrfaodon, п., the dogrose. — L., fr. Gk. κυνό-
ροδον, 'dogrose', which is compounded of κύων,
gen. κυνός, 'dog', and ρόδον, 'rose'. See cyno-
and rhodo-,

## Cynoscion
Cynoscion, п., a genus of fishes, the weakfish
(ichthyol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. κύων,
gen. κυνός, 'dog', and σχ(.αινα, a seafish, prob.
'the grayling', fr. σκιά, 'shade, shadow'. See
cyno- and skiagraphy and cp. Sciaenidae.

## cynosure
cynosure, п., the Lesser Bear (constellation). —
F., fr. L. Cynosura, fr. Gk. κυνόσουρα, 'dog's
tail; the Lesser Bear', compounded of κύων,
gen. κυνός, 'dog', and ούρα, 'tail'. See cyno- and
uro-, 'tail-'.

## Cynthia
Cynthia, 1) Artemis, goddess of the moon, whence:
the moon personified; 2) fern. PN. — L„ fr.
Gk. Κυνθία, epithet of the goddess Artemis,
lit. '(the goddess) of Cynthus', fern, of Κύν&ιος,
'of Cynthus, Cynthian', fr. Κύν&ος, 'Cynthus',
a mountain in Delos, birthplace of Apollo and
Artemis.

## Cynthian
Cynthian, adj., pertaining to Mt. Cynthus in
Delos. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Cynthius,
fr. Gk. Κύν&ιος, 'of Cynthus, Cynthian'.

## Cyperaceae
Cyperaceae, n. pi., the sedge family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Cyperus with suff. -aceae.

## cypernceous
cypernceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Cyperus
Cyperus, п., a genus of plants of the family
Cyperaceae (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κύπειρος,
'sedge', a word prob. rel. to κύπρος, 'the henna
plant' (Lawsonia inermis Linn.), which is of
Sem. origin; cp. Heb. kopher, Aram, k'phora,
Syr. kuphrd, 'the henna plant'. Cp. Cyprinus.

## cyphella
cyphella, п., a cuplike depression on the lower
surface of the thallus of lichens (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. κύφελλα (pi.), 'the hollows of the ears',
fr. κϋφός, 'bent, crooked', which is rel. to κϋφος,
'hump, hunch', and cogn. with OI. kubhrdh,
'humpbacked', fr. I.-E. base "qeu-bh-, 'to bend',
which is rel. to base *qeu-p-, whence L. сира,
'tub, cask, vat'. See cup and cp. cypho-, cypsela,
kyphosis.

## cypher
cypher, n. — A var. spelling of cipher.

## cypho-
cypho-, before a vowel cyph-, combining form
meaning 'bent, humpbacked'. — Fr. Gk. κϋφός,
'bent, crooked', or fr. κϋφος, 'hump, hunch'.
See cyphella.

## cyphosis
cyphosis, n. — A var. spelling of kyphosis.

## cy-pres
cy-pres, cypres, adv. and adj., as nearly as
possible in agreement with the testator's intentions
(law). — F. si-pris, 'so near, as near', fr. VL. sic

## presse
presse, 'from so near', fr. L. sic, 'so', and presse,
adv. of pressus, 'pressed', pp. of premere, 'to
press'. See sic and press, v.

## cypress
cypress, n. — ME. cipres, cypres, fr. OF. cipres
(F. cypresse), fr. Late L. cypressus, fr. Gk.
κυπάρισσος, which prob. derives fr. Heb. gopher,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:213 COLUMN:2 -->
name of the tree of whose wood the ark was
made (see Gen. 6:14). Cp. gopher and see Hehn-
Schrader, Kulturpftanzen und Haustiere in
ihrem Ubergang aus Asien nach Griechenland
und Italien, 5th edition, p. 23 r. Cp. Cyprian.
Derivatives: cypress, adj., cypress-ed, adj.

## cypress
cypress, п., cypress lawn. — ME. cipres, 'gauze,
cloth of gold', fr. OF. Cipre, Cypre, 'the island
of Cyprus'; so called because orig. brought
from Cyprus.

## Cyprian
Cyprian, adj. and n. — L. Cyprianus, 'of Cyprus,
Cyprian', formed with suff. -an fr. L. Cyprius,
fr. Gk. Κύπριος, of s.m., fr. Κύπρος, 'Cyprus',
lit. 'the island of cypress trees'. See cypress arid
cp. copper. For sense development cp. Pityuses,
lit. 'the islands covered with pines', fr. Gk.
πίτυς, 'pine', and Port. Madeira, 'the island
of timber', fr. madeira, 'timber', fr. L. materia,
'stuff', matter, timber'.

## cyprinid
cyprinid, adj., pertaining to the family Cyprini-
dae. — See next word.

## Cyprinidae
Cyprinidae, n. pi., a family of soft-finned fishes
(ichthyol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -Idae fr.
L. cyprinus. See next word.

## Cyprinus
Cyprinus, п., the typical genus of the family
Cyprinidae (ichtyol.). — L. cyprinus, 'carp', fr. Gk.
κυπρίνος, 'carp', fr. κύπρος, 'the henna plant'
(see Cyperus); so called in allusion to its color.

## Cypriote
Cypriote, adj. and п., Cyprian. — Fr. L. Cyprius,
'Cyprian'. See Cyprian and -ote.

## Cypripedium
Cypripedium, п., a genus of orchids (bot.) —
ModL., 'the lady's slipper', coined by Linnaeus
fr. Gk. Κύπρις, 'Aphrodite' (see next word), and
πέδΐλον, 'shoe, slipper', which is rel. to πέδη,
'fetter', and stands in gradational relationship to
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'; see foot. The correct
form of the word would be Cypripedilum.

## Cypris
Cypris, п., a name of Aphrodite. — L., fr. Gk.
Κύπρις, lit. 'the Cyprian (goddess)', fr. Κύπρος,
'Cyprus'. See Cyprian and cp. the first element
in prec. word.

## Cypris
Cypris, п., a genus of crustaceans (zool.) — Fr.
prec. word.

## cypsela
cypsela, п., an achene with an adherent calyx
tube (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κυψέλη, 'a hollow
vessel', which is rel. to κϋφός, 'bent, crooked'.
See cyphella.

## Cyrenaic
Cyrenaic, adj., l) pertaining to the Cyrenaica;
2) pertaining to the hedonistic school of
philosophy founded by Aristippus of Cyrene.
Derivative: Cyrenaic-ism, n.

## Cyril
Cyril, masc. PN. — Late L. Cyrillus, fr. Gk.
Κύριλλος, lit. 'lordly, masterly', rel. to κύριος,
'lord, master'. See church and cp. words there
referred to.

## Cyrffla
Cyrffla, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after Domenico Cyrillo, professor of
medicine at Naples.

## Cyrillaceae
Cyrillaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## cyrillaceous
cyrillaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Cyrillic
Cyrillic, adj., pertaining to the alphabet ascribed
to Cyril, apostle of the Slavs. — Lit. 'of, or
pertaining to, Cyril'; so called because his name is
associated with the invention of the Slavic
alphabet. For the origin of this name see Cyril,
for the ending see suff. -ic.

## cyrto-
cyrto-, before a vowel cyrt-, combining form
meaning 'curved', — Gk. κυρτό-, κυρτ-, fr.
κυρτός, 'curved, bent, arched', rel. to κορωνός,
'curved, bent', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to bend,
turn, twist', whence also L. curvus, 'crooked,
bent, curved'. See curve п., and cp. the second
element in Tricyrtis.

## cyrtometer
cyrtometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
curves of parts of the body
(med.)—Compounded of cyrto- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## cyrtosis
cyrtosis, n., curvature of the spinal column (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. κύρτωσις, 'being
humpbacked', fr. κυρτός, 'curved, bent'. See cyrto-
and -osis.

## Cyrus
Cyrus, masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Κύρος, fr. OPers.
Kurush, whence Akkad. Kurash, Heb. KOresh,
Egypt. Kawarusha.

## cyst
cyst, п., a closed membranous pouch or sac
containing fluid (med.) — Medical L. cystis, fr. Gk.
κύστις,'bladder, bag, pouch', which is prob. cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:213 COLUMN:3 -->
with OI. svdsati, svdsiti, 'blows, breathes, sighs'.
L. queri, 'to complain'. See quarrel, 'dispute'.

## cyst-
cyst-, form of cysto- before a vowel.

## -cyst
-cyst, combining form meaning 'pouch, sac', as
in cholecyst. — Fr. Gk. κύστις, 'bladder, bag,
pouch'. See prec. word.

## cysti-
cysti-, combining form. — See cysto-,

## cystic
cystic, adj., pertaining to a cyst; esp., pertaining
to the urinary bladder. — F. cystique, fr.
Medical L. cysticus, fr. cystis. See cyst and -ic.

## cysticercus
cysticercus, п., the larval form of tapeworms
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of cysti- and
Gk. κέρκος, 'tail'. See cercus and cp. words
there referred to.

## cystiform
cystiform, adj., having the form of a cyst. — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. κύστις, 'bladder, bag,
pouch', and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See cyst
and form, n.

## cystitis
cystitis, п., inflammation of the bladder (med.)
— Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk.
κύστις. See cyst.

## cysto-
cysto-, cysti-, before a vowel cyst-, combining
form meaning 'pertaining to, or resembling, a
bladder (esp. the urinary bladder)'. — Fr. Gk.
κύστις, 'bladder, bag, pouch'. See cyst.

## cystoid
cystoid, adj., resembling a cyst or bladder. —
Compounded of Gk. κύστις, 'bladder, bag,
pouch', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See cyst and -oid.

## cystotomy
cystotomy, п., incision of the uninary bladder
(med.) — Compounded of cysto-and Gk. -τομίά,
'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.

## cyt-
cyt-, form of cyto- before a vowel.

## -cyte
-cyte, combining form denoting a cell, as in hema-
tocyte, leucocyte. — Fr. Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow,
hollow vessel, vault, body, skin', fr. I.-E. base
*qeu-t-, 'to cover, hide*, whence also L. cutis,
OE. hyd, 'skin'. See hide, 'skin', and cp.
cyto-.

## Cytherea
Cytherea, п., a name of Aphrodite or Venus. —
L., fr. Gk. ΚυΟέρεια, lit. 'of Cythera', fr.
Κύθηρα (pi.), name of an island in the Aegean Sea
(now called Cerigo), celebrated for the worship
of Aphrodite. Cp. next word.
Derivatives: Cythere-an, adj., pertaining to
Aphrodite.

## Cytherella
Cytherella, п., a genus of crustaceans (zool) —
ModL., formed with dimin. suff. -ella fr. L.
Cythera, a var. of Cytherea, 'Aphrodite'. See
prec. word.

## Cytinus
Cytinus, п., a genus of plants of the family
Rafflesiaceae (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. κύτινος,
'flower of the pomegranate', wich derives perh.
fr. κύτος, 'a hollow vessel'. See -cyte and -ine
(representing Gk. -ινος).

## Cytisus
Cytisus, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — L. cytisus, 'a kind of clover', fr. Gk.
κύτισος, of s.m., a foreign word of unknown
origin.

## cytitis
cytitis, п., inflammation of the skin (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk. κύτος,
'skin'. See -cyte.

## cyto-
cyto-, before a vowel cyt-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining to a cell or cells'. — Gk. κυτο-,
κυτ-, fr. κύτος, 'a hollow vessel'. See -cyte.

## cytology
cytology, п., study of the structure, functions and
life history of cells (biol.) — Lit. 'study of cells',
compounded of cyto- and -λογίδ, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: cytolog-ic-al, adj., cytologic-al-ly,
adv.

## cytoplasm
cytoplasm, п., the protoplasm of the cells (biol.
— Compounded of cyto- and Gk. πλάσμα,
'something molded'. See plasma.
Derivative: cytoplasm-ic, adj.

## czar
czar, tsar, n. — Russ. tsar, fr. earlier tsesar\ fr.
OSlav. cesari, fr. Goth, kaisar (which is rel. to
OE. casere, OHG. keisar, OFris., MHG. keiser,
G. Kaiser), 'emperor', fr. L. Caesar, title adopted
by Augustus and the succeeding Roman
emperors from the cognomen of Caius Julius
Caesar. Cp. Caesar, kaiser. For sense
development cp. Lith. karalius, OSlav. kralji, 'king', fr.
L. Carolus, 'Charles' in Carolus Magnus, i.e.
'Charlemagne* (see churl).

## czardas
czardas, п., a Hungarian national dance. — See
csardas.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:214 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 187 | CZECHOSLOVAKIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:214 COLUMN:1 -->

## czarevitch
czarevitch, tsarevitch, п., a son of the czar (in
contradistinction to cesarevitch, which denotes
the eldest son of the czar). — Russ. tsarevitch,
fr. tsar. See czar,

## czarina
czarina, tsarina, п., title of an empress of Russia.
— G. Zarin (formerly spelled Czarin), fr. Zar,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:214 COLUMN:2 -->
'czar-. The Russian equivalent is tsaritsa. See
next word.

## czaritza
czaritza, п., czarina. — Russ. tsaritsa, fr. tsar,
'czar'. See czar and cp. prec. word.

## Czech
Czech, п., a Slavic native of Bohemia. — Polish
spelling of Czech Cech, inhabitant of Cechy,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:214 COLUMN:3 -->
'Bohemia'.

## Czechoslovak
Czechoslovak, n. — Back formation fr.
Czechoslovakia.

## Czechoslovakia
Czechoslovakia, n. — Lit. 'the land of the Czechs
and the Slovaks'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:215 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:215 COLUMN:1 -->

## dab
dab, tr. and intr. v., to touch or strike lightly. —
ME. dabben, prob. fr. MDu. dabben, Ίο pinch,
dabble', which is prob. of imitative origin. Cp.
dabble, dap, dib, 'knucklebone', and tap, 'to
strike lightly'.
Derivatives: dab, n. (q.v.), dabb-er, n.

## dab
dab, п., a light blow; a soft or flattish mass. —
Fr. prec. word.

## dab
dab, п., any small flatfish. — Fr. dab, 'a soft or
flattish mass'.

## dab
dab, п., a skillful person (colloq.) — Prob. fr.
dab, 'to strike lightly'.

## dabb
dabb, also dab, п., a large Arabian lizard (Uro-
mastix spinipes). — Arab, dabb, 'the thorn-
tailed lizard', rel. to Heb. Izabh, Aram, tzabba,
Syr. 'abba, 'abha, of s.m.

## dabble
dabble, tr. and intr. v. — Freq. formed with suff.
-le fr. dab, 'to strike lightly'.
Derivatives: dabbl-er, п., dabbl-ing, adj., dabbl-
ing-Iy, adv., dabbl-ing-ness, n.

## dabchick
dabchick, п., I) the little grebe of Europe; 2) the
pied-billed grebe of America. — Fr. earlier dap-
chick, lit. 'dipping chick'. See dap and chick
and cp. didapper.

## da capo
da capo, from the beginning (mus.) — It., 'from
the head, from the beginning'. The first word
is a contraction of L. de, 'from, away from',
and a, 'away from, from; by'; see de- and a-,
'from'. The second word derives fr. L. caput,
'head'; see capital, adj., and cp. the first word
in dal segno.

## dace
dace, п., a small cyprinoid fish. — ME. darce,
fr. OF. dan, dars, fr. ML. darsus, a word of
Gaulish origin. F. dard, 'dace', was influenced
in form by a confusion with F. dard, 'dart'
(see dart).

## dachshund
dachshund, п., a small dog of German breed. —
G., compounded of Dachs, 'badger' and Hund,
'dog'. The first element is rel. to Du. das and
to the second element in Dan. and Norw. svin-
toks, and lit. means 'the builder'; it is cogn.
with Ol. tdksati, 'fashions, constructs', Gk.
τέκτων, 'carpenter', τέχνη, 'handicraft, art', L.
texere, 'to weave'. ML. taxus, taxo, F. taisson,
Sp. texon, later tejon, It. tasso, 'badger', are
Teut. loan words. See technic and cp. text. Cp.
also Taxidea and the second element in ratel.
For the second element see hound,

## Dacian
Dacian, adj., pertaining to Dacia. — Formed
with suff. -anfr. L. Dacia, 'Dacia', fr. Gk.Aaxti.
Cp. next word.

## dacite
dacite, п., an igneous rock (petrogr.) — Formed
with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. Dacia. See prec.
word.

## dacoit
dacoit, п., one of an armed gang of robbers. —
Hind, dakait, daka, 'gang robbery'.
Derivative: dacoit, tr. and intr. v.

## dacoity
dacoity, п., robbery by dacoits. — Hind, dakaiti
'gang robbery', fr. dakait. See prec. word.

## dacron
dacron, п., a washable synthetic fabric; (cap.) a
trademark.
dacry-. — See dacryo-.

## Dacrydium
Dacrydium, п., a genus of plants of the yew
family (bot.) — ModL·., fr. Gk. δάκρυ, δάκρυον,
'tear' (see dncryo-); so called in allusion to the
resinous exudations.

## dacryo-
dacryo-, before a vowel dacry-, combining form
meaning 'tear; lachrymal'. — Gk. δάκρυο-,
δάκρυ-, fr. δάκρυον, 'tear'. See tear, п., and cp.
lachrymal,

## dacryoa
dacryoa, п., the point of junction of the
lachrymal and the frontal bone (craniometry). —
ModL., fr. Gk. δάκρυον, 'tear'; see dacryo-.
The name dacryon was introduced into
craniometry by the French surgeon and
anthropologist Paul Broca (1824-80).

## dactyl
dactyl, п., a metrical foot consisting of one long
syllable followed by two short syllables or one
accented followed by two unaccented (pros.) —

## L. dactylus
L. dactylus, fr. Gk. δάκτυλος, 'finger; dactyl'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:215 COLUMN:2 -->
D
(so called in allusion to the three joints of the
finger); of uncertain etymology. Gk. δάκτυλος
in this sense is not related to δάκτυλος, 'date'
(see date, the fruit), nor is it cogn. with L. digitus,
'finger'. Cp. next word and Dactylis. Cp. also
adactylous, and the second element in lepto-
dactyl, monodactylous, tridactyl, pentadactyl.

## Dactyl
Dactyl, п., one of the priests of Cybele (Greek
mylhol.) — L. Daclyli, 'the Dactyls', fr. Gk.
Δάκτυλοι, lit. 'Fingers', pi. of δάκτυλος (see
prec. word); so called because they were ten
in number.

## dactylic
dactylic, adj., pertaining to, or consisting of,
dactyls. — L. dactylicus, fr. Gk. δακτυλικός,
'pertaining to a dactyl', fr. δάκτυλος. See dactyl
and -ic.
Derivative: dactylic, п., a dactylic verse.

## dactylio-
dactylio-, combining form meaning 'finger ring'.
— Gk. δακτύλιο-, fr. δακτύλιος, 'finger ring,
signet', fr. δάκτυλος. See dactyl.

## dactylioglyph
dactylioglyph, п., an engraver of rings. — Gk.
δακτυλιογλύφος, 'an engraver of gems for finger
rings', fr. δακτύλιος, 'finger ring', and -γλύφος,
fr. γλύφειν, 'to carve, engrave'. Sec dactylio- and
glyph,

## dactyliography
dactyliography, п., the study of gem engraving. —
Compounded of dactylio- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: dactyliograph-er, п., dactyliograpk·
ic, adj.

## dactyliomancy
dactyliomancy, п., divination by means of a finger
ring. — Compounded of dactylio- and Gk.
μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'. See -mancy.

## Dactylis
Dactylis, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. δάκτυλος, 'finger' (see dactyl); so called
from the digitate spikes.

## dactylo-
dactylo-, before a vowel dactyl-, combining form
meaning 'finger' or 'toe'. — Gk. δάκτυλο-,
δακτυλ-, fr. δάκτυλος, 'finger; toe'. See dactyl,

## dactylogram
dactylogram, п., fingerprint. — Compounded of
dactylo- and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written'.
See -gram,

## dactylography
dactylography, п., l) dactylology; 2) the study of
fingerprints. — Compounded of dactylo- and
Gk.-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν,'to write'. See-graphy.

## dactyloid
dactyloid, adj., resembling a finger. — Gk.
δακτυλοειδής, 'fingerlike', fr. δάκτυλος, 'finger',
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
dactyl- and -oid.

## dactylology
dactylology, п., the art of communicating ideas
by signs made with the fingers. — Lit. 'the study
of the fingers', fr. dactylo- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## dactyloscopy
dactyloscopy, п., identification by means of
fingerprints. — Compounded of dactylo- and
Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκο7τεϊν, 'to look at, examine'.
See -scopy.

## Dacus
Dacus, п., a genus of flies, the olive fly (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. δάκος, 'any animal, the bite
of which is dangerous', lit. 'a biting animal',
rel. to δάκνειν, 'to bite', δάξ, 'biting', δήγμα, 'a
biting', δήκτης, 'biter', fr. I.-E. base *denk-,
'to bite', whence also OL ddsali (for 'dnketi),
'bites', ON. tong, OE. tang, tange, 'tongs'. See
tongs and cp. the second element in carpodacus,
Tridacna, Demodex, Mixodectes.

## dad
dad, daddy, п., father. — A child's word. Cp.
W. lad, dad, Ir. daid, Co. tat, 'father', hendal,
'grandfather', Czech lata, Russ. tata, Lith.
litis, tele, 'father', OPruss. tketis, 'father, old
man', lr. daid, Co. tat, W., Bret, tad, tat, 'father',
Alb. tats, 'father', L. tata, 'father', Gk. τάτα,
'father', τατα, τέττα, Ό father, daddy', τατα-
λίζειν, 'to flatter', ModGk. δάδας, 'father', OL
tatah, 'father, son', which all are of childish
origin.

## Dada
Dada, п., an artistic movement characterized by
incoherence and the love of paradoxes (art and
lit.) — F. dada, prop, a child's word meaning

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:215 COLUMN:3 -->
'horse, hobby horse, hobby'. This word was
chosen in 1916 by Tristan Tzara, a Rumanian-
born poet and editor in Paris (1896-1963), to
designate this artistic movement.

## Dadaism
Dadaism, п., Dada. — F. dadaisme, formed from
prec. word with suff. -isme (see -ism).

## Dadaist
Dadaist, п., an adherent of Dada::m. — F. dada-
iste, formed fr. Dada with suff. -iste (see -ist).

## dado
dado, п., a part of the pedestal. — It. dado, 'die,
cube, pedestal', fr. L. datus, 'given', pp. of dare,
'to give'. See date, 'point of time', and cp.
die, 'cube'.
Derivative: dado, tr. v.

## daduchus
daduchus, dadouchos, п., torchbearer in the Eleu-
sian mysteries. - L. daduchus, fr. Gk. δαδοΰχος,
'torchbearer', which stands for *δαδο-όχος and
is compounded of δαίς, δάς (gen. δαίδος, resp.
δαδός), 'torch', and ϊχειν, 'to hold, have'. The
first element is rel. to δαίειν (for *δά^ειν), 'to
blaze, burn', and cogn. with OL dundti, 'burns',
davdh, 'conflagration', Olr. doim, Ί singe, burn'.
Cp. the first element in Deianira. For the second
element see hectic.

## daedal
daedal, adj., ingenious, skillful. — L. daedalus, fr.
Gk. δαίδαλος, 'cunningly made', fr. δαιδάλλειν,
'to work cunningly or skillfully', which stands
for *δαι-δάλιειν and is formed with
reduplication of I.-E. base "del-, *dol-, 'to split, cut,
carve', which appears in OL dalati, 'splits,
bursts', dalayati, 'causes to burst, splits open',
dalam, 'part, piece', L. dolare, 'to hew with an
ax', dolium, 'a very large jar'. See dole, 'grief,
and cp. Daedalus, dal and the second element in
logodaedaly. Cp. also tale. The word daedal was
first used in«English by Spenser.

## daedalian
daedalian, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, the
work of Daedalus. — See Daedalus and -ian.

## Daedalus
Daedalus, п., the mythical artist, father of Icarus
and builder of the Cretan labyrinth. — L., fr. Gk.
Δαίδαλος, lit. 'the cunning worker'. See daedal.

## daemon
daemon, n. — L., fr. Gk. δαίμων. See demon.

## daemonic
daemonic, adj. — Late L. daemonicus, fr. L.
daemon. See daemon and -ic.

## daffodil
daffodil, n. — Du. de affodil, 'the asphodel', fr.
OF. affrodile, a var. of asfodile, fr. L. aspho-
delus. See the, def. art. and asphodel.

## daffodilly
daffodilly, daffodilly, daffadowndilly, daffy do wn-
dilly, п., a daffodil. — Poelic and dial, variants
of prec. word.

## daft
daft, adj., foolish (dial.) — ME. dafte, 'meek;
stupid', fr. OE. (ge)dxfte, 'mild, gentle', rel. to
gedafen, gedefe, 'suitable', Goth, gadaban, 'to
be fit'. See deft. For sense development cp. silly,
simple.
Derivatives: daft-ly, adv., daft-ness, n.

## dag
dag, п., a kind of long pistol formerly used. —
Of uncertain origin.

## dagesh
dagesh, n. — See daghcsh.

## dagger
dagger, n. — F. dague (whence also MDu. dagge,
Dan. daggert, G. Degen), fr. OProvenc. daga,
a word of Celtic origin. Cp. Gael, dag, dager,
'dagger'.
Derivatives: dagger, tr. v., dagger-ed, adj.

## daggle
daggle, tr. v., to make wet by sprinkling; to
draggle. — Formed with frequent, suff. -le from
dial. E. dag, 'to sprinkle with water, to wet',
fr. dial. E. dag, 'mist, drizzling rain', which is a
Scand. loan word. Cp. ON. dbgg, *dew', and
see dew.

## daghesh
daghesh, dagesh, п., dot in a letter denoting the
reduplication of a consonant or the harder
pronunciation of the consonants b, g, d, k, p, t
(Hebrew and Aram, gram.) — Medieval
Heb., fr. Syriac daghesh, active participle of
d'ghash, 'he pricked, pointed'.
Derivative: daghesh, dagesh, tr. v.

## dago
dago, п., a name given contemptuously to
Spaniards, Portuguese and Italians. — From
corruption of the Sp. PN. Diego, equivalent to
E. James.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:216 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 189 | DAMN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:216 COLUMN:1 -->

## dagoba
dagoba, п., a Buddhist shrine. — Singhal. dagaba,
fr. Pali dhatugabbha, fr. OI. dhdtugarbhah, which
is compounded of dhdtuh, 'layer, ingredient',
and garbhah, 'womb, interior'. OI. dhdtuh,
derives from the stem of dadhati, 'he puts,
places', fr. I.-E. base *dhe-, 'to place'; see do, v.
OI. garbhah is a derivative of I.-E. base *gwelbh-
*gwolbh-, 'womb; young of an animal', whence
also Gk. δελφύς, δολφός, 'womb', Goth kalbo,
OE. cealf, 'calf; see calf.

## Dagon
Dagon, п., the main god of the Philistines. — L.,
fr. Gk. Δαγών, fr. Heb. Dagon, which prob.
derives fr. Heb. dag, 'fish'.
daguerreotype» n., an early kind of photograph. —
F. daguerreotype, a hybrid coined fr. the name
of (Louis) Daguerre (1789-1851), inventor of the
process, and F. type, fr. Gk. τύπος, 'blow,
mark, impression1. See type, -type.
Derivatives: daguerreotype, tr. v., daguerreotyp-
er, п., daguerreotyp-ist, п., daguerreo-typ-y, n.

## dah
dah, п., a large hewing knife {India). — Hind.
duo, fr. OI. ddtram, 'sickle', from the stem of
ddti, dyati, 'cuts, separates, divides', da-yate,
'divides, participates, destroys', fr. I.-E. base
*da-, *dai-, *dt-, *de-, 'to cut off, separate,
divide, distribute', whence also datar-, 'reaper,
mower', ditih, 'division', Gk. δΛεσθ-αι, 'to
divide, distribute; to feed on', δαίμων, 'god,
goddess', lit. 'divider, distributor (of men's
destinies)'. See demon and words there referred
to.

## dahabiah
dahabiah, dahabeah, п., a sailing boat used on
the Nile. — Arab. dkckcbtyah, lit. 'the golden
one', fern, of dhakabt, fr. dhakab, 'gold', which
is rel. to Heb. zahdbh, Aram.-Syr. dehabh,
dakabka, 'gold', Heb. tzahobk, 'gleaming,
yellow', Arab. sdhiba, 'was reddish yellow', ashabu,
'reddish yellow'.

## Dahlia
Dahlia, п., name of a genus of Mexican plants
of the family Compositae. — ModL., named
by the Spanish botanist Antonio Jose Cavanilles
(1745-1804) in 1791 after the Swedish botanist,
Anders Dahl, a pupil of Linnaeus. For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## Dail Eireann
Dail Eireann, п., the lower house of the
Parliament of the Irish Free State. — Lit. 'assembly
of Ireland', fr. Ir. dail, 'assembly*, and Eireann,
gen. of Eire, 'Ireland'. Cp. Erin.

## daily
daily, adj. — ME. daili, fr. OE. dxglic, fr. dxg,
'day'. See day and adj. suff. -ly.
Derivatives: daily, n. and adv., daili-ness, n.

## daimio
daimio, daimyo, п., a feudal prince of Japan. —
Jap., lit. 'a great name', fr. Chin, dai, 'great',
and mio, myo, 'name'.

## dainty
dainty, n. — ME. deintee, fr. OF. daintie, deintie,
'pleasure, delicacy', fr. L. dignitatem, ace. of
dignitas, 'greatness, rank, dignity'. See dignity,
which is a doublet of dainty.
Derivatives: dainty, adj., dainti-ly, adv.,
daintiness, n.

## da'ira
da'ira, п., formerly, estates of the Egyptian khe-
dive. — Arab. dd4rah (in vulgar pronunciation
dayra), 'circle, enclosure', prop. fern, partic.
of dura, 'he moved in a circle, went about',
which is rel. to dar, 'house', orig. 'buildings
surrounding a court*, daur, 'circumference*, dahr,
'long time, age', Heb. dar (п.), 'circle, ball', dur
(v.), 'to dwell', orig. 'to move in a circle', dor,
'generation', Mishnaic Heb. madhor, 'dwelling
place', Aram, dur, 4o dwell*, madhor, medhary
'dwelling place*, dar, 'generation', Akkad. duru,
'wall, fortress', also 'duration, eternity*, daru,
'everlasting'. Cp. next word.

## daira
daira, п., a large kind of Oriental tambourine. —
Fr. dayra, vulgar Arab pronunciation of dayirah,
'circle, tambourine'. See prec. word.

## dairy
dairy, n. — ME. deierie, formed with suff. -erie
fr. deie, 'dairymaid', fr. OE. dsege '(female)
breadmaker', lit. 'kneader of dough', fr. dag,
'dough'. Cp. ON. deigja, Swed. dej'a,
'dairymaid', which derive fr. ON. deig, resp. Swed.
deg, 'dough', and see dough. Cp. also the second
element in lady. For the ending see -ery.
Derivative: dairy-ing, n.

## dais
dais, п., a raised platform in a hall. — ME. deis,
deys, fr. OF. deis, dots, 'table; platform' (whence
F. dais, 'canopy'), fr. VL. discus, 'table', fr. L.
discus, 'quoit, dish, disc*. See dish, disk and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:216 COLUMN:2 -->
cp. desk.

## daisy
daisy, n. — ME. daies eie, fr. OE. dxges ege,
dxges eage, lit. 'day's eye' (see day and eye); so
called because it opens its flower in the morning.

## Daisy
Daisy, fern. PN. — Orig. used as a pet name for
Margaret, F. marguerite being identical in
meaning with E. daisy.

## daitya
daitya, п., a demon {Hindu mythoi.) — OI. dai-
tya-, lit. 'a daughter of Diti', a metronymic
formed fr. Diti, an aphetic form of Aditi. See
Aditi.

## daiva
daiva, п., the second form of marriage {India). —
OI. daivah, 'marriage rite', lit. 'peculiar to the
gods, divine', fr. devah, 'god'. See deva and
cp. Devi.

## dak
dak, n. — A var. of dawk.

## Daksha
Daksha, п., one of the Prajapatis, a son of
Brahma {Hindu mythoi.) — OI. Daksah, lit. 'able,
apt, clever, competent, intelligent', rel. to dak-
sinah, daksinah, 'the able one' (i.e. 'the milch
cow'), and cogn. with Gk. δεξι,ός, Όη the right
hand', L. dexter, of s.m. See dexter.

## dai
dai, also dhal, dhall, п., split pea {India). — Hind.
dai, fr. OI. dalati, 'bursts, splits', rel. to OI.
dalam, 'piece', fr. I.-E. base "del-, *dol-, 'to
split, cut, carve*, whence L. dolare, 'to chip, cut
out', ddlium, 'a large jar, vessel'. See dole,
'grief, and cp. words there referred to. For the
sense development of Hind, dai, 'split pea', fr.
OI. dalati, 'bursts, splits', ср. Е. split pea.

## Dalai Lama
Dalai Lama, the Grand Lama of Tibet. — Lit.
'the Ocean Lama', fr. Mongolian dalai, 'ocean',
and Tibetan blama, lama, 'lama'. See Lama.

## Dalbergia
Dalbergia, п., a genus of trees of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., named after the Swedish
physician Nils Da/berg (1736-1820). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## dale
dale, п., valley. — ME., fr. OE. dsel, rel. to OS.,
Du., Goth, dai, ON. dalr, OHG., MHG., G. tai,
'valley', and cogn. with OSlav. dotit, 'pit' (do)
dolii, 'down, downward', Russ. do/. Valley', Gk.
ί>άλαμος, "inner room', θόλος, 'dome, round
chamber, circular vault", and the second
element in αφ-ί>αλμός, 'eye', lit. 'vault of the eye'.
All these words are traceable to l.-E. *dhol-,
'something bent', 'convex or concave surface'.
Cp. dell, dollar. Cp. also thalamus, ophthalmo-.

## dale
dale, п., spout, trough. — Fr. ON. die la, 'gutter',
prob. through the medium of MF. (— F.) dalie,
'gutter: slab (of marble)1. Cp. dalle.

## dalesman
dalesman, п., one who lives in a valley. —
Compounded of dale, 'valley', and man.

## daleth
daleth, п., name of the 4th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb. daleth, pausal form of deleth,
'door', which is rel. to Ugar. dl, Akkad. daliu,
'door'; so called in allusion to the ancient
Hebrew form of this letter. Cp. delta. For the form
cp. afeph, lamedh, samekh.

## Dalibardia
Dalibardia, п., a genus of American plants (bot.)
— ModL., named after the French botanist
Thomas-FranQois Dalibard (1703-79). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## dalle
dalle, п., a slab. — F., fr. ON. dsela, 'gutler'. Cp.
dale, 'spout, trough4.

## dalliance
dalliance, n. — ME. daliance, fr. dalien, 'to chat'.
See nest word and -ance.

## dally
dally, intr. v., 1) to sport; 2) to trifle; 3) to waste
lime. — ME. dalien, 'to chat*, fr. OF. dalier, 'to
converse, talk, chat', which is of uncertain
origin. Derivatives: dalliance (q.v.), dally-ing,
adj., dally-ing-ly, adv.

## Dalmatian
Dalmatian, adj., pertaining to Dalmatia; п., one
of the inhabitants of Dalmatia. — Formed with
suff. -an fr. L. Dalmatia, name of the country
on the eastern coast of the Adriatic. Cp.
dalmatic.

## Dalmatian
Dalmatian, п., a large white colored dog with
black spots. — Short for Dalmatian dog; so
called from its alleged place of origin.

## dalmatic
dalmatic, adj., a vestment worn by deacons,
bishops, etc. — Fr. L, Dalmatica (scil. tunica or
vestis), 'garment made of Dalmatian wool'. See
Dalmatian, adj., and -ic.

## dai segno
dai segno, musical direction to return to the sign.
— It., lit. 'from the sign'. The first word is
contracted from da, 'from', and the def. article il
(fr. L. Шит, асе. of ilk, 'that one1). Sec-da capo
and ille. The second word derives fr. L^signum,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:216 COLUMN:3 -->
'sign'. See sign and cp. al segno.

## daltonism
daltonism, п., color blindness. — Named after
the English chemist and physicist John Da/ton
(1766-1844), who first described it in 1794. For
the ending see suff. -ism.

## dam
dam, п., an earth bank built to obstruct the water
of a river. — ME. dam, fr. MDu. dam, damm
(Du. dam), which is rel. to ON. dammr, 'dam',
MHG. tarn, G. Damm, and to OE. for-demman,
Goth, faur-dammjan, 'to stop up', and prob.
cogn. with Gk. (τα.) ί>έμεί>λα, 'foundations,
lowest part', fr. l.-E. base *dhe-, 'to place'. See
do, v., and cp. theme.
Derivative: dam, tr. v., to obstruct by a dam,
damm-er, n.

## dam
dam, п., a female parent. — ME. dam, dame, fr.
OF. dame. See dame.

## dam
dam, п., the name of a former copper coin in
India. — Hind. dam.

## Dama
Dama, п., the genus of the fallow deer. — L.
dama, damma, 'fallow deer', prob. a Celtic loan
word. Cp. Olr. dam, 'ox', dam a/laid, 'stag'
(prop, 'wild ox'), W. dafad, 'sheep', and see doe.

## damage
damage, n. — ME., fr. OF. damage (F. dommage),
fr. VL. *damnaticum, fr. L. damnum, 'harm,
loss'. See damn and subst. suff. -age. F.
dommage was prob. influenced in form by a
confusion with L. dominus, 'lord, master'.
Derivatives: damage, tr. and intr. v., damag-er,
п., damage-able, adj., damage-abl-y, adv., dam-
age-able-ness, n.

## daman
daman, п., a small rabbillike mammal (Procavia
syriaca), the cony of the, English version of the
Bible (see e.g. Lev. 11 -.5). — Arab, daman Is-
rd'il, 'sheep of Israel'.

## damascene
damascene, п., damson plum. — Lit. 'plum of
Damascus', fr. L. Damascena (scil. pruna),
'plums of Damascus', neut. pi. of Damascenus,
'of Damascus', fr. Damascus. See damask and
-ene and cp. damson.

## damascene
damascene, tr. v., to ornament metals with inlaid
patterns in gold or silver. — Fr. L. Damascenus,
'of Damascus'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: damascen-ed, adj., damascen-er, n.

## damask
damask, п., a woven figured fabric. — Orig.
'textile manufactured in Damascus', fr. It. da-
masco, fr. L. Damascus, fr. Heb. Dammeseq,
name of the ancient city situated on the river
Amanah (= Gk. Χρΰσορρόας, now called Nahr
Barada). Cp. damascene, damaskeen, damase,
damassin.
Derivative: damask, adj. and tr. v.

## damaskeen
damaskeen, tr. v., to damascene. — F. damasqui-
ner, from the early French adjective damasquin,
'of Damascus', fr. It. damasco. See prec. word.

## damasse
damasse, adj., woven like damask; п., a da-
masse fabric. — F., prop. pp. of damasser, 'to
damask', fr. damas, 'damask*, fr. Damas,
French name of Damascus, fr. L. Damascus.
See damask.

## damassin
damassin, п., a kind of damask. — F., fr. damas,
'damask'. See prec. word.

## dame
dame, п., a noble lady. — ME. dame, ir. OF.
(== p.) dame, fr. L. domina, 'the mistress of a
household', fern, of dominus, 'lord', prop,
'owner of Ihe house', and rel. to domus, 'house'. For
the form cp. tribunus, fr. tribus, 'tribe'. Dominus
is only indirectly rel. to domare, 'to tame' (see
dome and cp. dominate); but was directly
influenced in meaning by it. See Walde-Pokorny,
VWIS., I, 787. Cp. dam, 'female parent', bel-
dam(e), belladonna, duenna, madam, madame,
demijohn, grandam.

## dammar
dammar, п., a resin used for making varnish. —·
Malay damar.

## dama
dama, tr. v., to condemn; intr. v., to say 'damn',
to swear. — ME. damnen, fr. OF. damner, damp-
ner (F. damner), fr. L. damnare, 'to injure, cause
loss, condemn', fr. damnum, 'harm, loss', which
stands for *dap-nom and orig. meant
'expenditure', and is rel. to daps, 'sacrificial feast,
banquet', and cogn, with Gk. δαπάνη, 'cost,
expenditure*, δάπτει,ν, 'to devour', OI. dapayatey 'he
shares', and prob. also with Toch. A tap-, 'to
eat'. All these words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base
*dap-, a -^-enlargement of I.-E. base "da-,
*dai-, *dt-, *de-, 'to cut off, separate, divide,
distribute', whence OI. ddti, dyati, 'cuts, sepa-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:217 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DAMNABLE | 190 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:217 COLUMN:1 -->
rates, divides', da-yate, 'divides', Gk. δαίεσθ-at,
'to divide, distribute; to feed on', δαίμων, 'god,
goddess', lit. 'divider, distributor (of men's
destinies)'. See demon and cp. damage, condemn,
indemnify. Cp. also the first element in dapifer.
Derivatives: damn, п., damnable (q.v.),
damnation (q.v.), damnatory (q.v.), damn-ed, adj.,
damn-er, п., damn-ing, adj., damn-ing-ly, adv.,
damn-ing-ness, n.

## damnable
damnable, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. damnabilis,
'worthy of condemnation, damnable', fr.
damnare. See dama and -able.
Derivatives: damnabil-ity, п., damnable-ness, п.,
damnabl-y, adv.

## damnation
damnation, п., condemnation. — OF. (= F.), fr.
L. damnationem, ace. of damnatio,
'condemnation', fr. damnaius, pp. of damnare. See damn
and -ation and cp. condemnation.

## damnatory
damnatory, adj., condemnatory. — L. damnato-
rius, fr. damnatus, pp. of damnare. See prec.
word and adj. stiff, -ory and cp. condemnatory.

## damnify
damnify, tr. v., to cause damage. — OF. dam-
nifier, fr. Late L. darrmificare, fr. L. damnificus,
'injurious, hurtful', which is compounded of
damnum, 'harm, loss', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to
make do'. See damn and -fy and cp. indemnify.
Derivative: daminific-ation, n.

## Damocles
Damocles, п., a courtier of Dionysius I, tyrant of
Syracuse.— Dor. Gk. Δαμοκλής, corresponding
to Ion. Δημοκλής. The name lit. means 'fame of
the people', and is compounded of δήμος (Dor.
δαμος), 'people', and κλέος (Dor. κλέίος), 'fame'
(see demos and loud). — Sword of Damocles is
used to denote an imminent danger, in allusion
to the banquet at which Dionysius seated
Damocles so that a sword was suspended over his
head by a single hair.

## damoiseau
damoiseau, п., a young nobleman who has not
yet been made a knight. — OF., fr. earlier da-
moisel, fr. VL. 'dominicellus, dimin. of L. do-
minus, 'lord'. See damsel and words there
referred to.

## damosel
damosel, n. — An archaic var. of damsel.

## damourite
damourite, п., hydromica (mineral.) — Named
after the French chemist A. Damour (1808-1902).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## damp
damp, n. — MDu. (= Du.), 'vapor', rel. to Dan.
damp, OHG., MHG. dampk, tamph, G. Damp/,
of s.m., ON. dampi, 'dust', and in gradationa]
relationship to MHG. dimpfen, 'to smoke', OE.
dimme, dim, 'dark, obscure'. See dim and cp.
dump, 'sadness'. Cp. also dank.
Derivatives: damp, adj. and tr. v., damp-en, tr.
and intr. v., damp-er, п., damp-ish, adj., damp-ly,
adv., damp-ness, n.

## damsel
damsel, п., a girl. — ME. dameisele, fr. OF. da-
meisele, damoiselle, 'a woman of noble birth'
(whence F. demoiselle, 'young lady'), fr. VL.
*dominicella, dimin. of L. domina, 'mistress'
(see dame), fern, of dominus, 'master, lord'. See
dominus, dome, 'building', and cp. damoisean,
demoiselle, doncella, donzella, mademoiselle. For
the ending see suff. -el.

## damson
damson, п., a small, purple plum. — ME. dama-
sin (plumme), prop, '(plum) of Damascus'. Cp.
L. Damascena pruna, 'plums of Damascus', and
see damascene, n.

## Dan
Dan, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible: a) son of
Jacob and Bilhah; b) the tribe descended from
him. — Heb. Dan, lit. 'he who judges', rel. to
Heb. din, 'to judge', Aram, dun, din, Syr. din,
Ugar. dn, Akkad, danu, of s.m., Heb. and Aram.
din, 'judgment', dayyan, Akkad. dayanu, 'judge',
Aram, mfdhina", 'district, province' (whence
Heb. rrfdhina11, Syr. m'dhitta, of s.m., Arab, ma-
dtnak, 'city'), orig. 'district of jurisdiction*, Heb.
madhdn, 'strife, contention'. Cp. Daniel, Dinah.
Cp. also Danails.

## Daa
Daa, п., a title of honor equivalent to Master. —
OF. dan, fr. L. dominus, 'lord, master'. F. dom
(an ecclesiastic title) also derives fr. L. dominus
(through the medium of It. don, short form of
donno). See dominus, dome, 'building', and cp.
Dom, domiue, dominie, domino, donna.

## Danae
Danae, п., daughter of Acrisius and mother of
Perseus (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Δανάη,
lit. prob. meaning 'she who judges', and rel. to
Δαναός. See Daaaiis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:217 COLUMN:2 -->

## Danaid
Danaid, п., one of the Danaides. — See Danaides.

## Danaidean
Danaidean, adj., pertaining to the Danaides. —
Formed fr. Danaides with suff. -an.

## Danaides
Danaides, Danaids, n. pi., the fifty daughters of
Danaus, king of Argos, who—with the
exception of Hypermnestra—killed their
husbands, at their father's command. For this
crime they were condemned to draw water
perpetually with vessels that had no bottoms
(Greek mythol.) — L. Danaides, fr. Gk. Δαναίδες,
'daughters of Danaus', fr. Δαναός 'Danaus*.
See DanaOs.

## danaite
danaite, п., a cobaltic arsenopyrite (mineral.) —
Named after the chemist J. Freeman Dana, of
Boston (died in 1827). For the ending see subst.
sufT. -ite.

## danalite
danalite, п., a reddish mineral. — Named after
the American mineralogist James Dwight Dana
(1813-95). For the ending see combining form
-lite.

## Danaus
Danaus, п., a king of Argos, who commanded his
fifty daughters, the Danaides, to murder their
husbands on the wedding night (Greek mythol.)
— L. Danaus, fr. Gk. Δαναός (whence the pi.
Δαναοί,'theDanaans', i.e. 'descendants or
subjects of Danaus', whence 'the Greeks', in
general), which prob. derives fr. Heb.-Phoen. Dan,
and lit. means 'one who judges'; see Dan, PN.,
and cp. Danae, Danaides. This etymol. is
corroborated by the fact that the myth of Belus
and the Danaides "records the early arrival in
Greece of Helladic colonists from Palestine"
(quoted from Robert Graves, 'The Greek
Myths', I, p. 203, Penguin Books). For other
Greek mythological names of Hebrew origin
cp. Cadmus, Niobe. — According to Kretsch-
mer, Glotta 24, 15 ff., the Danaans are idenlical
with the men of Tanaus, king of the Scythians,
who allegedly came to Argos in the 15th cent.
B.C.E. and became blended with the Greeks.
Kretschmer also assumes that there is a
relationship between Tanaus and the river names Tanais
and L. Danubius (whence F. and E. Danube),
and Danu-, name of an Indo-Iranian people.
See Frisk, GEW., I, p. 347 s.v. Δαναοί and cp.
Albert Carnoy, Dictionnaire etymologique de
la mythologie greco-romaine, p. 42 s.v. *Da-
naos. — Cp. Danae, Danaides.

## dance
dance, intr. and tr. v. — ME. dancen, dauncen,
fr. OF. dancer (F. danser), prob. borrowed fr.
Frankish *dintjan, 'to move to and fro', which
is rel. to Du. deinzen; cp. danseuse. Cp. It. dan-
zare, OProvenc. dansar, Sp. danzar, Port, dan·
far, Du. dansen, G. tanzen, 'to dance', which
derive fr. OF. dander.
Derivatives: danc-er, п., danc-er-ess, п.,
dancing, n.

## dance
dance, n. — ME. daunce, fr. OF. dance, fr.
dander. See dance, v.

## dancetty
dancetty, dancette. adj., indented (her.) — Fr. F.
danche, 'indented', pp. of dancher, fr. OF. den-
chier, fr. VL. *demiare, 'to provide with teeth',
fr. L. dens, gen. dentis, 'tooth'. See denti-.

## dandelion
dandelion, п., a weed with yellow flowers. — F.
