dent de lion, 'lion's tooth', fr. L. dentem, ace. of
dens, 'tooth', de, 'from, away from', and leonem,
ace. of led, 'lion'; see denti-, de- and lion. The
plant was so called from its indented leaves. Cp.
Leontodon.

## daoder
daoder, intr. v., to stroll, wander about. —Cp.
dandle.

## dander
dander, п., temper, anger. — Of uncertain origin.

## dandiacal
dandiacal, adj., resembling a dandy. — Formed
fr. dandy on analogy of hypochondriacal and
other adjectives ending in -iacal.

## Dandie Dinmont terrier
Dandie Dinmont terrier, n. — Named after Dandy
Dinmont, a farmer in Scott's Guy Mannering,
who possessed a special breed of terriers.

## dandify
dandify, tr. v., to cause to resemble a dandy; to
dress up. — Compounded of dandy and -fy.
Derivative: dandific-ation, n.

## dandle
dandle, tr. and intr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
It.·dondolare, 'to dandle, swing', which is also
imitative, and F. dandiner, of s.m., which derives
fr. OF. dandin, "small bell', a word of imitative
origin.
Derivative: dandier, n.

## dandruff
dandruff, dandriff, n. — The first element of this

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:217 COLUMN:3 -->
compound is of uncertain origin. The second
derives fr. ON. hrufa, 'scab', which is rel. to.
OHG. An//, ruf, G. Rufe, MDu. rove, of s.m.,
ON. hrjufr, OE. hreof, 'rough, scabby, leprous',
and cogn. with W. crawen, 'crust', Lith. krau-
piis, 'rough', Lett, kraupa, 'scab'.
Derivative: dandruff-y, adj.

## dandy
dandy, п., a fop. — Fr. Dandy, a var. of St.
Andrews. The name Andrews ult. derives fr. the
Greek PN. 'Ανδρέας, which is rel. to ανδρείος,
'manly', both being derivatives of άνήρ, gen.
ανδρός, 'man'. See andro-.
Derivatives: dandy, adj , and the hybrids
dandyish, adj., dandy-ism, n.

## dandy
dandy, dandi, п., l) a boatman; 2) a hammock
(Anglo-Ind.) — Hind, dandi, dandi, fr. dand,
dand, 'staff, stick, wand, oar', fr, OI. dandah,
of s.m., which is of uncertain etymology.

## dandy
dandy, dandi, п., a Sivaitic mendicant. — Of the
same origin as prec. word; so called from the
small wand carried by him.

## dandy
dandy, n. — Corruption of dengue.

## Dane
Dane, п., a native of Denmark. — ME. Dan, fr.
ON. Danir (pi.), lit. 'Lowlanders', which is rel.
to MLG. denne, 'lowland, wooded vale, den',
OE. denn, 'lair of a wild beast, den'. See den.
Tor sense development cp. Pole.
Derivatives: Dan-ish, adj. and n.

## Danegeld
Danegeld, п., an annual land tax (English hist.) —
ME., lit. 'tribute paid to the Danes', fr. Dane,
gen. pi. of Dan, 'Dane', and geld, 'payment,
tribute', fr. OE. gield, of s.m. See Dane and yield.

## Danelaw
Danelaw, also Danelagh, п., Danish law
prevailing in the northeastern pari of England held
by the Danes during the Danish Conquest. —
OE. Dena lagu, 'Danes' law'. See Dane and law.

## danger
danger, n. ~- ME. danger, 'power, difficulty,
resistance, jurisdiction', fr. OF. danger, 'power,
domination' (whence F. danger, 'danger'), fr.
VL. *dominiarium, 'power', which derives fr.
dominus, 'master, lord'. The change of L. о to a
in OF. danger is due to the influence of L.
damnum, 'damage'. See dominate and dome,
'building', and cp. dominion, dungeon.
Derivatives: danger-ous, adj., danger-ous-ly,
adv., danger-ous-ness, n.

## dangle
dangle, intr. v., to hang loosely. — Of Scand.
origin. Cp. Dan. dangle, Swed. dangla, 'to swing
about, dangle', which stand in gradational
relationship to Dan dingle, Swed. and Norw.
dingla, of s.m. Cp. also adangle.
Derivatives: dangle, п., dangl-er, п., dangl-ing,
adj., dangl-ing-ly, adv.

## Daniel
Daniel, masc. PN., the hero of the Book of
Daniel (Bible). — Heb. Darii'il, lit. 'God is my
judge', rel. to Akkad. Danilu. For the first
element see Dan, PN., for the second see El.

## dank
dank, adj., moist, damp. — ME. danke, of Scand.
origin; cp. Swed. dank, 'moist place', danka,
'to moisten', which are rel. to OS. dunkar,
OFris. diunk, 'dark', ON. dokkr, Du. donker,
OHG. tunkal, dunkal, MHG. tunkel, G. dunkel,
of s.m., and to OHG., MHG. damph, MDu.,
Du. damp, 'vapor'. See damp.
Derivatives: dank-ish, adj., dank-ish-ness, п.,
dank-ly, adv., dank-ness, n.

## danseuse
danseuse, п., a femaledancer. — F., fem. of dan-
seur, 'dancer', fr. danser, 'to dance'. See dance, v.

## danta
danta, п., a tapir. — Sp. and Port, danta, 'tapir',
fr. Sp. de anta, short for piel de anta, '(of)
buckskin', fr. de, 'of, from', and anta, 'elk, tapir,
buckskin', fr. Arab, lamt, 'antelope', the I of
which was mistaken for the article and
consequently dropped.

## Dantesque
Dantesque, adj., resembling Dante or his style. —
Formed with suff. -esque from the name of the
poet Dante (1265-1321).

## Danthonia
Danthonia, п., a genus of plants, the wild oat
grass (hot.) — ModL., named after the French
botanist Etienne Danthoine. For the ending see
suff. -ia.

## dap
dap, intr. and tr. v., to fish by allowing the bait
to dip into the water. — Prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. dab, 'to strike gently'.
Derivative: dap, n.

## Dnphne
Dnphne, п., a nymph (who was turned into a
laurel) (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Δάφνη, fr.
δάφνη, 'laurel'. See next word and cp. Daphnis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:218 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 191 | DATE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:218 COLUMN:1 -->

## Daphae
Daphae, п., a genus of plants of the mezereon
family (bot.) — Gk. δάφνη, 'laurel', rel. to Per-
gamene λάφνη, Thessalian δαύχνα, of s.m.;
borrowed—together with L. founts, 'laurel'—from
a language of Asia Minor. Cp. prec. word and
laurel, Cp. -also Daucns.

## Daphnean
Daphnean, adj., pertaining to Daphne. — Formed
fr. Daphne with suff. -an.

## Daphnis
Daphnis, п., a shepherd in Sicily, the inventor of
pastoral songs (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Δάφνις, which is rel. to δάφνις, 'bayberry', fr.
δάφνη, 'laurel'. See Daphne.

## dapifer
dapifer, п., a servant waiting at table. — L., 'a
bringer of meat', compounded of daps, gen.
dapis, 'sacrificial feast, banquet', lit. 'expense',
and fero,ferre, 'to bear, carry'. The first element
is rel. lo L. damnum (for *dap-nom), 'harm,
loss', orig. 'expenditure', and cogn. with Gk.
δαπάνη, 'cost, expenditure'. See damn. For the
second element in dapifer see -fer.

## dapper
dapper, adj., neat; smart. — ME. daper, 'agile,
strong', fr. MDu. (= Du.) dapper, 'strong,
valiant, brave', which is rel. to ON. dapr,
'dejected, sad', Dan. tapper, 'brave', OHG. tapfar,
'heavy, weighty', MHG. tap fer, dapfer, 'thick,
weighty', Late MHG. and G. tapfer, 'brave', fr.
I.-E. base *dheb-, 'thick, heavy, strong', whence
also Toch. A tappo, 'worth, force', OSlav. dobru,
Russ. dobry), dobry, Czech and Slovak dobry,
'good', OSlav. debelu, 'thick', dial. Russ. debolyj,
'strong, powerful', OPruss. deblkan, 'large, great'.
Derivatives: dapper-ly, adv. dapper-ness, n.

## dapple
dapple, п., a spot on the skin of an animal. —
Prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. depill, 'a spot,
dot, a dog with spots above the eyes'.
Derivatives: dapple, adj. and tr. and intr. v.,
dappl-ed, adj.

## dapple-gray
dapple-gray, dapple-grey, adj. — A blend of
apple-gray and dapple.

## darbies
darbies, n. pi., handcuffs (slang).- — Prob.
shortened fr. Father Darby's bands, in which phrase
Darby (prop, phonetic spelling of Derby) refers
to a usurer of this name.

## Darby and Joan
Darby and Joan, an old, happy married couple.
— First referred to in the Gentleman's
Magazine of 1735,V. 153.

## dare
dare, intr. and tr. v. — ME. dor, Ί dare' (in the
past tense dorste, durste), fr. OE. ic dearr, Ί
dare' (in the past tense dorste), rel. to OHG. tar,
Ί dare', Goth, ga-daursan, 'to dare', preterite
ga-dars, 'dared', fr. I.-E. base 'dhars-, "dhers-,
'to dare, be courageous', whence also OI.
dhdrsati, 'dares', dh[suk, 'courageous', Avestic
darshi-, darshita-, 'bold', Gk. θ-άρσος, θ-ράσος,
Att. θ-άρρος,'courage, audacity', θ-αρσύς, θ-ρασύς,
'bold, audacious', θ-αρσεΐν, Att. 8-αρρεϊν, 'to be,
bold', Lith. dresii, dr{stii, dr{sti, 'to dare', drqsiis,
'courageous', and possibly also L. in-fesius,
'disturbed, molested, infested, unquiet', and
Toch. В tsir, A tsrasi, 'strong, powerful'. Cp.
thersitical, thrasonical, infest, manifest.
Derivatives: dare, п., dar-ing, n. and adj., dar-
ing-ly, adv.

## dargah
dargah, also dnrgah, п., the shrine of a
Mohammedan saint in India. — Hind, dargah, fr. Pers.
dargah, lit. 'royal gate'. Pers. dar, 'door, gate',
is rel. to Avestic dvar'm (ace. sing.) ,'gate,
court', OPers. duvaraya-, 'at the door', and to
OI. dvurah, 'door'. See door and cp. the first
element in durbar and in durwaun.

## daric
daric, п., an ancient Persian gold coin. — Fr. Gk.
Δάρείκός, also written Δαρικός, Δαριχός, fr.
Δαρείος, 'Darius', hence lit. meaning 'of, or
pertaining to, Darius'. See next word and -ic.

## Darius
Darius, masc. PN. — L. Darius, fr. Gk. Δαρείος,
fr. OPers. Darayava(h)ush (whence also Heb.
Daryawesh), a compound lit. meaning 'he who
holds firm the good'. The first element of this
compound derives from the stem of OPers.
ddrayamiy, Ί hold', fr. I.-E. base *dher(e)-, 'to
hold'; see firm, adj., and cp. the second element
in aumildar and in words there referred to. The
second element in OPers. Daraya-va(h)ush
means 'the good', and is related to Avestic
vanhu, vohu, OI. vasuh, 'good'. Cp. prec. word.

## dark
dark, adj. — ME. deork, derk, darke, fr. OE.
deorc, rel. to OHG. tarchanjan, 'to hide,
conceal', MHG. terken, 'to make dark, soil', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:218 COLUMN:2 -->
cogn. with Lith. darga, 'rainy weather', and
prob. also with Olr. derg, 'red'.
Derivatives: dark, п., dark-en, tr. and intr. v.,
dark-en-er, п., dark-en-ing, п., dark-ish, adj.,
dark-ish-ness, п., dark-ly, adv., dark-ness, п.,
dark-some, adj., dark-some-ness, n.

## darkle
darkle,intr. v., 1) to appear dark; 2) to grow dark;
tr. v., to obscure. — Back formation fr.
darkling, which was mistaken for a pres. part.

## darkling
darkling, adv., in the dark. — Formed fr. dark
with suff. -ling. Cp. darkle.
Derivative: darkling, adj.

## darky
darky, darkey, п., a Negro (colloq.) — Formed
fr. dark with suff. -y.

## darling
darling, n. and adj. — ME. derling, fr. OE. deor-
ling, formed fr. deore, 'dear', with suff. -ling.
See dear and -ling.
Derivatives: darling-ly, adv., darling-ness, n.

## darn
darn, tr. v, — From earlier dern, fr. dial. F. der-
ner, darner, 'to patch', fr. OF. derne, 'a piece',
fr. Bret, darn, of s.m. (whence F. darne, 'a slice of
fish'), fr. I.-E. base *dere-, *der-, 'to tear, divide,
flay', whence also OI. drnati, 'cleaves, bursts',
Gk. δέρειν, 'to flay', δέρμα, δορά, 'skin', δάρσις,
'tearing, flaying, separation', OE. teran, 'to
tear'. See tear, 'to rend', and cp. derma, dartars.
Derivatives: darn, п., darn-er, п., darn-ing, n.

## darn
darn, tr. v. — Euphemism for damn.

## darnel
darnel, п., a poisonous weed; called also rye
grass. — ME. dernel, darnel, fr. dial. F. darnelle,
a word compounded of an unknown first
element and OF. neelle (F. nielle), 'cockle', fr. VL.
nigella, 'a black-seeded plant', prop. fern, of L.
nigellus, 'blackish', fr. niger, 'black'. See Negro
and cp. niello.

## daroga
daroga, darogha, п., governor (Anglo-Ind.) —
Hind, daroghah, fr. Pers. daroghah, 'super-
intendant'; which is prob. of Mongolian origin.

## darrein
darrein, adj., last (law). — OF. darrein, derrain,
fr. earlier dererain, fr. VL. 'deretranus, fr. L.
deretro, 'from behind' (whence also F. derriere,
'behind'), fr. di, 'from, away from', and retro,
'back'. See de- and retro- and cp. dernier
ressort.

## darshana
darshana, п., any of the six schools of Hindu
philosophy. — OI. darsanah, lit. 'demonstration',
rel. to dadarsa, Ί have seen', djrs-, 'sight, view',
dfs'ya-, 'visible', fr. I.-E. base *derk-, 'dfk-, 'to
see, look at', whence also Gk. δέρκεσ&χι, 'to
look at', δράκων, 'dragon', lit. 'the sharp-sighted
one'. See dragon and cp. words there referred to.

## darso
darso, п., a hybrid grain sorghum. — Formed
from the initials of dwarf red and sorghum.

## dart
dart, п., a pointed weapon. — ME. dart, fr. OF.
dan, dard (F. dard), fr. Frankish *darop, 'dart',
which is rel. to OE. darop, OHG. tart, ON. dar-
rapr, 'darl'. OProveng. dart is of the same origin
as OF. dan, ]t. and Sp. dardo are OProveng.
loan words.
Derivatives: darl, intr. and tr. v., darter (q.v.),
dart-ing, adj., dart-ing-ly, adv., dart-ing-ness, n.

## dartars
dartars, п., a kind of mange affecting esp. the
chin of lambs. — F. dartre, 'eruption of the
skin, blotch, herpes, tetter', fr. Gaulish L. der-
bita, 'tetter', which is rel. to W. darwyden,
MBret. daroueden, ModBret. dervoeden, of
s.m. See tetter and cp. dartre. Cp. also darn.

## darter
darter, п., 1) one who, or that which, darts; 2) the
name of various fishes. — Formed from the verb
dart (see dart, n.) with agential suff. -er.

## dartle
dartle, intr. v. — Formed from the verb dart (see
dart, n.) with freq. suff. -le.

## dartos
dartos, п., the contractile layer beneath the skin
of the scrotum (anal.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
δαρτός, 'flayed', in anatomy: 'separated by
avulsion' [first used by Rufus (cca. too C.E.)
for a tunica surrounding the testicles]. Gk. δαρτός
is verbal adj. of δέρειν, 'to flay', in anatomy:
'to separate by avulsion'; which is cogn. with
Goth, dis-tairan, OE. teran, 'to tear'. See tear,
'to rend', and cp. darn, dartars, derma.
Derivatives: darto-ic, dart-oid, adjs.

## dartre
dartre, п., a name for various skin diseases. —
F. See dartars.

## dartrous
dartrous, adj., pertaining to dartre. — A hybrid
coined fr. dartre and -ous, a suff. of Latin origin.

## darwan
darwan, n. — See durwaun.

## Darwinian
Darwinian, adj., pertaining to Charles Robert

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:218 COLUMN:3 -->
Darwin (1809-82) or his theories. For the ending
see suff. -ian.

## Darwinism
Darwinism, п., the theory of the origin of species
propounded by Charles Robert Darwin. — See
prec. word and -ism.

## darzee
darzee, п., a tailor. — Hind, darzi, 'tailor'. See
Druse.

## dash
dash, tr. and intr. v. — ME. dasshen, of Scand.
origin. Cp. Swed. daska, Dan. daske, 'to beat,
strike', Swed., Dan. dask, 'a blow'.
Derivatives: dash, п., dash-er, п., dash-ing, adj.,
dash-ing-ly, adv., dash-y, adj.

## Dashahara
Dashahara, п., the 'ten days festival' (Hindu
religion). — OI. dasahara, lit. 'that which takes away
ten (sins)', fr. ddsa, 'ten', and hard, fern, of hara,,
'that which takes away', from the stem of harati,
'brings, carries, takes away, robs'. OI. daia is
cogn. with Gk. δέκα, L. decern, Goth, taihun,
OE. tien, ten, 'ten'; see ten. OI. harati derives
fr. I.-E. base *gher-, 'to seize, take', whence also
Gk. χείρ, 'hand'; see chiro- and cp. the second
element in vihara.

## dasi
dasi, п., a female-slave; a concubine (Hinduism).
— Hind., fr. OI. dasi-, 'female slave', which is
rel. to dasah, 'demon, enemy, barbarian, slave,
servant', and prob. also to dasyuh, 'demon,
enemy of the gods, barbarian', dasyuh,
'bondage, servitude'. Cp. the second element in
devadasi.

## Dasiphora
Dasiphora, п., a genus of plants of the family
Rosaceae (bot.)— ModL., irregularly formed fr.
Gk. δασύς, 'thick with hair, hairy, bushy', and
-φάρος, 'bearing', which is rel. to φέρειν, 'to
bear*. See dasy- and -phore. The exact form of
the word should have been Dasyphora.

## dastard
dastard, п., a coward. — ME., prob. formed
with the pejorative suff. -ard fr. dost, which is
equivalent to dased, pp. of dasen, 'to daze'. See
daze and cp. ON. dxstr, 'out of breath,
exhausted'.
Derivatives: dastard-ly, adj., dastard-li-ness, n.

## dasy-
dasy-, combining form meaning 'thick, hairy,
rough'. — Gk. δασύ-, fr. δασύς, 'thick with hair,
hairy, bushy, thick, dense, rough'; which stands
for *dnsus and is cogn. with L. densus,
'crowded, dense'. See dense and cp. the first element
in Dasiphora.

## Dasylirion
Dasylirion, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of dasy- and Gk.
λείριον, 'lily'. See lily and cp. words there
referred to.

## dasymeter
dasymeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
density of gases. — Compounded of dasy- and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## Dasypus
Dasypus, п., a genus of armadillos (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. δασύπους, 'a hare', lit. 'the
hairy-footed animal', fr. dasy- and πους, gen.
ποδός, 'foot'. See dasy- and -pod.

## Dasystephana
Dasystephana, п., a genus of plants of the gentian
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of dasy-
and Gk. στέφανος, 'crown'. See Stephanos.

## dasyure
dasyure, п., any of small marsupial mammals of
Australia. — Compounded of dasy- and Gk.
ουρά, 'tail'. See uro-, 'tail-'.

## data
data, n. — PI. of datum (q.v.)

## date
date, п., a given point of time. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) date, fr. ML. data (scil. littera) (whence
also It., Provenc., Sp. data), lit. '(letter) given',
prop. fern. pp. of L. dare, 'to give'. This term
derived fr. L. datum (neut. pp. of dare), the first
word used in letters to indicate the place and
time of writing as e.g. datum Romae pridie
Kalendas Maids, 'given (i.e. written) at Rome
on the last day of April'. L. dare is rel. to dos,
'marriage portion, dowry', do-пит, 'gift', done,
donare, 'to give as a present', fr. I.-E. base "do-,
*d'-, 'to give', whence also OI. da-du-ti, 'gives',
Avestic dadaiti, of s.m., OI. da-tar-, da-tar-,
'giver', da-tram, 'gift', Gk. δί-δω-μί, Ί give',
δώ-τωρ, δω-τήρ, δο-τήρ, 'giver', δώ-ρον, δω-
τίνη, δώς, 'gift', δό-σις, 'a giving; gift', δο-τός
(verbal adj. of δΐ-δω-μι), 'given', OSlav. dati, 'to
give', da-ru, 'gift', da-ni, 'tax', dami, Ί shall give',
Lith. duomi, Ί give', OPruss. dast, 'give's'. Arm.
ta-m, Ί give', tu-r, 'gift', Alb. δα-ίε, Ί gave'.
Ср. add, addendum, anecdote, antedate,
antidote, apodosis, condone, dado, dation, dative,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:219 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DATE | 192 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:219 COLUMN:1 -->
die, 'cube', donation and words there referred
to, dose, dosimeter, dosology, dot, 'marriage
portion', dower, dowry, edit, irredenta,
postdate, reddendum, reddition, render, rendition,
sacerdotal, subdititious, surrender, tradition,
traitor, treason. Cp. also mandate, command,
commend, countermand, demand. Cp. also the
second element in vend.
Derivatives: date, tr. and intr. v., dat-ableradj.,
dat-er, п., dat-ing, n.

## date
date, п., fruit of the palm tree. — OF. dale (F.
datte). fr. OProvenc. datil (or fr. It. dallero), fr.
L. daaylus, fr. Gk. δάκτυλος, 'date', which is
of Sem. origin. Cp. Heb. deqel, Aram, diqtd,
Syr. deqla, Arab, daqal, 'date palm', and Heb.
Diqldh, name of a region in Arabia, rich in date
palms (see Gen.ro:27 and I Chron.i:2i). The
form of Gk. δάκτυλος, 'date', was influenced
by a folk-etymological association with
δάκτυλος, 'finger', suggested by the fingerlike shape
of the date.

## dation
dation, п., the act of giving (law). — L. datio,
gen. -onis, 'a giving', fr. datus, pp. of dare, 'to
give'. See date, 'point of time', and -ion.

## Datisca
Datisca, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL., of
unknown origin.

## dative
dative, adj. and n. — L. dativus (casus), loan
translation of Gk. δοτική (πτώσις), 'the dative
case'; fr. dativus, 'pertaining to the act of
giving', fr. datus, pp. of dare, 'to give'. See date,
'point of time', and -ive.
Derivatives: dativ-al, adj., dative-ly, adv.

## datolite
datolite, п., a translucent calcium borosilicate
(mineral.) — Formed from the stem of Gk.
δατεΐσ&αι, 'to cut in two, divide, distribute',
and λί&ος, 'stone'. Gk. δατεΐσθ-αι prob. derives
fr. 1-Е. base *dl-t-, a -f-enlargement of base
*dai-, *dl-, *de-, 'to cut off, separate, divide,
distribute', whence O]. ddli, dyali, 'cuts,
separates, divides', da-yate, 'divides', Gk. δαίεσθ-αι,
'to divide, distribute; to feed on', δαίμων, 'god,
goddess', lit. 'divider, distributor (of men's
destinies)'. See demon and -lite.

## datum
datum, п., something given or assumed. — L.
datum, neut. pp. of dare, 'to give'. See date,
'point of time', and cp. data.

## Datura
Datura, п., a genus of plants of the potato family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Hind, dhatura, fr. OI. dhat-
tiirah, dhusturah, 'thorn apple', which is cogn.
with the secondelement in OE. dweorge-dwostle,
'penny royal*, and possibly also with L. festuca,
'stalk, stem, straw'. See festuca.

## daub
daub, lr. and intr. v. — ME. dauben, fr. OF.
(= F.) dauber, 'to plaster', fr. L. dealbare, 'to
whiten, whitewash, plaster', fr. de- and albare,
'to whiten', fr. albus, 'white'. See alb.
Derivatives: daub, п., daub-er, п., daub-ery, п.,
daub-ing, п., daubster, п., daub-y, adj.

## dauberite
dauberite, п., basic uranium sulfate (mineral.) —
Named after H. Dauber, who analyzed it. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## daubreeite
daubreeite, daubreite, п., a hydrous bismuth oxy-
chloride (mineral.) — Named after the French
mineralogist Gabriel-Auguste Daubree (1814-
96). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## daubreelite
daubreelite, п., a chromium iron sulfide (mineral.)
— Named after Daubree. See prec. word and
the combining form -lite.

## Daucus
Daucus, п., a genus of plants, the carrot (bot.) —
L. daucus, daucum, fr. Gk. δαΰκος, δαΰκον, 'a
kind of parsnip', which is rel. to Thessalian Gk.
δαύχνα, Gk. δάφνη, 'laurel'. See Daphne.

## daughter
daughter, n. — ME doghter, dohter, fr. OE. doh-
tor, dohter, rel. to OS. dohtar, ON. ddm'r,
OFris., Du. dochter, OHG., MHG. tohter, G.
Tochter, Goth, dauhtar, 'daughter', and cogn.
with Ol. duhita, Avestic dugeda-, duydar-, Toch.
A ckacar, В tkacer, Arm. dustr, Gk. θυγάτηρ,
OSlav. dusti, OPruss. duckti, Lith. dukte,
'daughter'.
Derivatives: daughter-hood, п., daughter-ly, adj.,
daughter-li-ness, n.

## daunt
daunt, tr. v. — ME. daunten, fr. OF. danter, don-
ter (F. dompter), fr. L. domitare, 'to tame,
subdue', freq. of domare (pp. domitus), 'to tame,
subdue, vanquish, conquer', lit. 'to accustom
to the house', fr. domus, 'house'. See dome,
'building', and cp. indomitable. Cp. also tame.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:219 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: daunt-er, п., daunt-ing, adj.,
daunting-ly, adv., daunt-ing-ness, п., dauntless (q.v.).

## dauntless
dauntless, adj. — Formed fr. the ME. noun daunt,
fr. daunten (see daunt) with suff. -less; first used
by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: dauntless-Iy, adv., dauntless-ness, n.

## dauphin
dauphin, п., the title of the eldest son of the king
of France. — F., lit. 'dolphin', translation of
L. Delphlnus, lit. 'dolphin', orig. a name borne
by Guigo IV, count of Vienne (died in 1142)
and by his successors. The name Delphinus was
chosen in allusion to the three dolphins
represented in the coat of arms of the lords above
mentioned. Hence the province owned by them
came to be known as Delphinatus in Latin
(whence F. Dauphine). See dolphin.

## dauphine
dauphine, п., a dauphiness. — F. dauphine, fern,
of dauphin. See dauphin.

## dauphiness
dauphiness, п., the wife of a dauphin. — Formed
fr. dauphin with suff. -ess.

## davenport
davenport, п., a kind of writing desk. — So called
from the name of its first maker.

## David
David, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the second king
of Israel and Judah, the writer of the Psalms.
— Heb. Dawtdh, lit. 'beloved,friend', rel. to dodh,
'beloved, uncle', and to dudha'tm, 'mandrake',
prop, 'love-exciting (plant)'. Cp. dudaim.

## daviesite
daviesite, п., a lead oxychloride (mineral.) —
Named after Thomas Davies, of the Minera-
logical Dept. of the British Museum (1837-91).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## davit
davit, п., a projecling piece of vessel for
suspending or lowering a boat. — OF. daviet, daviot
(whence F. davier, with change of suff.), dimin.
of the PN. David, so called in allusion to the
slaying of Goliath. See David and cp. -et.

## davy
davy, п., safety lamp. — Shortened fr. Davy lamp;
named after its inventor, the English chemist
Sir Humphrey Davy (1778-1829).

## davy
davy, n. (slang). — Short for affidavit.
Davy lamp. — See davy, 'safety lamp'.

## daw
daw, п., a kind of crow, a jackdaw. — ME. dawe,
rel. to OHG. taha, MHG. tahe, also tahele,
tale, tale (diminutives of tahe), G. Dohle; cp.
OPruss. doacke, 'starling', ML. tacula, It. tac-
cola, 'jackdaw', which are German loan words.

## dawdle
dawdle, intr. and tr. v., to waste (time). — Perhaps
a var. of dial. E. daddle, 'to walk unsteadily'.
Derivatives: dawdl-er, п., dawdl-ing, n.

## dawk
dawk, dak, п., transport by relays of men and
horses, mail (Anglo-lnd.) — Hind, dak, 'post,
mail*.

## dawn
dawn, intr. v. — ME. dawening, of Norse origin;
cp. Swed. and Dan. dagning, 'a dawning', fr.
dag, 'day'. Cp. also OE. dagian, 'to dawn', fr.
dxg, 'day', Du. dagen, 'to dawn', fr. dag, 'day',
G. tagen, 'to dawn', fr. Tag, 'day', and see day.
Derivatives: dawn, п., dawning (q.v.)

## dawning
dawning, n. — ME. dawening. See prec. word
and subst. -iag.

## dawsonite
dawsonite, п., a basic aluminum sodium
carbonate (mineral.) — Named after the Canadian
geologist Sir John William Dawson (1865-
1951). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## day
day, n. — ME. dai, dei, fr. OE. dxg, rel. to
ON. dagr, OS.,Dan., Swed., Du. dag, Goth, dags,
OHG. tag, MHG. tac, G. Tag, 'day', orig.
'burning heat', fr. I.-E. base *dhegwh-, *dhogwh-,
'to burn', whence also OI. dahati, 'burns', ni-
daghah, 'heat, summer', Avestic dazaiti, 'burns',
Toch. A tsak-, В isak-, 'to burn', tsak-, 'to shine,
glow', L. fovea (for *dhog"heyo), fovire, 'to
warm, keep warm', favilla (for *fovilla), 'embers'.
Gk. τέφρα (for *dheg"hra), 'ashes', OPruss.
dagis, 'summer', Lith. dagas, 'burning, harvest',
daga, 'harvest', degit, degti, OSlav. zego, zeSti,
'to burn', Alb. djek, Ί burn', Mir. daig (gen.
dega), 'fire, pain, disease'. Cp. also Arm. dag,
'impressive' (orig. sense prob. 'fiery'), W. deifio,
Bret, devi, 'to burn'. L. dies, 'day', is not
cognate. Cp. daisy, dawn, and the second
element in landtag, Reichstag, Rigsdag, Riksdag.
Cp. also favor, febrile, fever, foment, fomes,
tephrite.

## daydream
daydream, п., a reverie. — Coined by John Dry-
den (1631-1700).
Derivatives: daydream, intr. v., daydream-er, п.,
daydream-y, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:219 COLUMN:3 -->

## daze
daze, tr. v. — ME. dasen, 'to stupefy', fr. ON.
dasa in dasa-sk, 'to become weary', lit. 'to
weary oneself (-sk being the ON. reflexive suff.,
cp. bask, busk), which is rel. to dasa, 'to lie idle',
dasi, 'an idle man'. Cp. dazzle, dastard.
Derivatives: daze, п., daz-ed, adj., daz-ed-ly,
adv., daz-ed-ness, n.

## dazzle
dazzle, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. daze with
freq. suff. -le.
Derivatives: dazzle, п., dazzl-er, п., dazzl-ing-
ly, adv.

## DDT
DDT, п., a very strong insecticide.— Formed from
the initials of the chemical name rfichloro-rfi-
phenyl-rrichloro-ethane.

## de
de, prep, meaning 'from'. — See pref. de-.

## de-
de-, pref. meaning: 1) down; 2) away from; 3)
utterly, completely; 4) the negation or reversal
of the notion expressed in the primary word. —
Fr. L. de, 'from, away from, down from, out of,
on account of, concerning, according to', either
directly or through the medium of OF. de-, F.
de-. L. de derives fr. I.-E. *de, whence also Olr.
di, de, OW. di, ModW. y, Co. the, 'down from',
'away from'. For derivatives of rel. I.-E. *dezx\d
*dSscc to and cp. words there referred to. Cp. the
first elemt in deteriorate, dupe and the second
element in ci-devant, ibidem, tandem. —
Sometimes E. de- comes fr. F. de-, fr. OF. des-,
fr. L. dis-; see dis-.

## deacon
deacon, n. — ME. deken, diacne, fr. OE. diacon, fr.
Late L. diaconus, fr. Gk. διάκονος, 'servant,
minister of a church', which is rel. to έγ-κονεϊν, 'to
be quick and active, to hasten', ά-κονϊτί,
'without effort', fr. Greco-L. base *ken-, 'to toil,strive,
exert oneself, whence also L. conari, 'to
attempt, try, endeavour'. See conation and cp.
diaconal and the second element in ratiocinate,
larceny, tirocinium, vaticinate.
Derivatives: the hybrid words deacon-ess, п.,
deacon-hood, п., deacon-ry, п., deacon-ship, n.

## dead
dead, adj. — ME. dede, deade, deed, fr. OE. dead,
'dead', rel. to OS. dod, Dan. ded, Swed. dod,
OFris. dad, MDu. doot, Du. dood, OHG. tot,
tod, MHG, tot, G. tot, ON. daudr, Goth, daups,
'dead', fr. Teut. participial base "dau-pa, *dau-
da, 'dead', formed with participial suff. -pa, -da
(= I.-E. suff. -*to), fr. Teut. base *dau-, 'to die',
which corresponds to I.-E. base *dhew-, *dheu-,
*dhow-, *dhou-, 'to pine away, die'. Fr. *dhwei-
an enlargement of this base, derive Arm. di,
'dead body, corpse', Olr. dith, 'end, death',
OSlav. daviti, Russ. davit', 'to choke, suffocate'.
Cp. death, die, dwindle. Cp. also funeral. For
the formation of Teut. adjectives from past
participles cp. cold, loud, old, sad.
Derivatives: dead, adv. and п., dead-en, tr. and
intr. v., dead-en-er, п., dead-en-ing, п., deadly
(q.v.), dead-ness, n.

## deadly
deadly, adj. — ME. deedlich, fr. OE. deadlic,
formed fr. dead, 'dead' with suff. -lie. See dead
and' adj. suff. -ly.
Derivative: deadli-ness, n.

## deadly
deadly, adv. — ME. deedliche, fr. OE. dgadlice,
formed fr. dead, 'dead', with suff. -lice. See
dead and adv. suff. -ly.

## deaf
deaf, adj. — ME. dee/, def, fr. OE. deaf, rel. to
OS. do/, ON. daufr, OFris. daf, Du. doof 'deaf,
OHG. toub, MHG. toup, 'deaf, stupid', G. taub,
Goth, daufs, 'deaf, insensate', and cogn. with
Gk. τυφ-λός (dissimil. fr. "8-υφ-λός), 'blind',
Olr. dub, dubh (for "dhubu), 'black; ink', fr. I.-E.
base *dheu-bh-, 'to fill with smoke, to cloud,
darken; to be dull, dumb or deaf. Cp. dove. Cp.
also dumb, which derives from a nasalized form
of base *dheu-bh-. Cp. base *dheu-p-, which
appears in OI. dhupah, 'smoke'. The bases
*dheu-bh-, *dheu-p-, are enlargements of base
*dheu-, 'to fly about like dust, to smoke'. See
thio- and cp. duffer. Cp. also stove.
Derivatives: deaf-en, tr. and intr. v.,
deafening, adj. and п., deaf-ish, adj., deaf-ly, adv.,
deaf-ness, n.

## deal
deal, п., part, share. — ME. deel, fr. OE. dxl,
rel. to ON. deild, OS., OFris. del, Du.
deel, OHG., MHG., G. teil, Goth, dails,
part, share', and cogn. with OSlav. delu, of
s.m., dlliti, 'to share, divide'. Cp. dole, 'a small
portion', and the second element in ordeal and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:220 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 193 | DECAMERDUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:220 COLUMN:1 -->
in fardel.
Derivative: deal, v. (q.v.)

## deal
deal, tr. and intr. v., to distribute. — ME. dehn,
fr. OE. dielan, 'to share, divide', fr. dsel, 'part,
share'. Cp. OS. delian, ON. deila, OFris. dela,
Du. delen, OHG. teilan, MHG., G. teilen,
Goth, dailjan, 'to share, divide', which derive
from tae respective nouns, and see prec. word.
Derivatives: deal-er, п., deal-ing, n.

## deal
deal, п., a plank of fir. — MDu. dele, 'board,
plank*. See thill.
Derivative: deal, adj., made of deal.

## dealt
dealt, past tense and pp. of deal.

## deaminate
deaminate, tr. v., to remove the amino radical
(NH2) (chem.) — Formed fr. de-, amino- and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: deaminat-ion, n.

## dean
dean, n. — ME. deen, dene, fr. OF. deien (F.
doyen), fr. L. decanus, 'one set over ten persons',
in Eccles. L. 'a superior set over ten monks', fr.
decern, 'ten*. See ten and cp. decimal. Cp. also
doyen, which is a doublet of dean.
Derivatives: dean, intr. v., dean-ery, п., dean-
ess, п., deanship, n.

## dean
dean, п., a valley. — A var. of dene, 'valley'.

## dear
dear, adj. — ME. dere, fr. OE. deore, diere, rel.
to OS. diuri, ON. dyrr, OFris. afore, MDu. dure,
Du. duur, OHG. tiuri, MHG. tiure, G. teuer,
'dear'. Cp. darling, dearth, endear.
Derivatives: dear, п., adv. and interj., dear-ly,
adv., dear-ness, п., dear-y, dear-ie, n. (colloq.).

## dearborn
dearborn, п., a kind of four-wheeled carriage. —
Named afier its inventor, either the American
Henry Dearborn (l 751-1829) or one of his sons.

## dearth
dearth, n. — ME. derih, derthe, 'dearness', fr.
dere, 'dear'. See dear and subst. suff. -th.

## death
death, n. — ME. deeth, deth, fr. OE. dead, rel.
to OS. doth, ON. daudi, Dan. dod, Swed. dod,
OFris. dath, ODU. dot, dod, Du. dood, OHG.
tod, MHG. tot, tod, G. Tod, Goth, daupus,
'death', fr. Teut. *dau-, 'to die'. See die, dead.
Derivatives: death-less, adj., death-less-ly, adv.,
death-less-ness, п., death-like, adj., death-fy, adj.

## debacle
debacle, debacle, п., a complete rout. — F.
debacle, 'a breaking up (of ice); downfall, collapse,
disaster', fr. debacler, 'to break up' (said of ice);
'to unfasten, unbar (a door)', formed fr. pref.
de- (see de-) and bacler, 'to bar, fasien', fr.
OProveng. baclar, fr. VL. *baccularey lit. 'to bar
with a staff', fr. VL. *bacculum, corresponding
to L. baculum, 'a staff*. See bacuius, bacillus.

## debar
debar, tr. v. — F. debarrer, 'to unbar', fr. OF.
desbarer, formed fr. des- (see de-) and barrer,
'to bar*. See bar and cp. disbar.

## debark
debark, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. de- and
bark, 'a kind of sailing ship1. Cp. disembark.
Derivatives: debark-ation, п., debark-ment, n.

## debarrass
debarrass, tr. v., to disembarrass. — F. debar-
rasser, for *desembarrasser. See de- and
embarrass and cp. disembarrass.

## debase
debase, tr. v. — Formed fr. de- and the obsolete
verb base, 'to abase'. See base, adj., and cp. abase.
Derivatives: debas-ed, adj., debase-ment, п.,
debas-er, п., debas-ingr adj.

## debatable
debatable, adj. — OF. debattabfe, debatable
(F. debatable), fr. debatre (F. debattre). See
debate and -able.

## debate
debate, tr. and intr. v. — ME. debaten, fr. OF.
debatre, 4o fight, combat* (whence F. debattre,
'to discuss, debate, agree'), formed fr. de- and
batre (F. battre), 'to beat, strike', fr. Late L.
batlere, fr. L. battuere, of s.m. See batter, 'to
beat violently*, and cp. combat.
Derivatives: debate, n. (q.v.), debat-er, п.,
debating, n. and adj., debat-ing-ly, adv.

## debate
debate, n. — ME. debat, fr. MF. (= F.)debat,
'dispute, strife, debate', ΐτ. debattre. See debate, v.

## debauch
debauch, tr. v., to lead astray, corrupt. — OF.
debaucher, 'to leave work, be idle' (whence F.
debaucher,\ό turn somebody away from his work;
to entice away, lead astray'). The orig. meaning
of OF. debaucher was 'to rough down timber'.
11 is a hybrid coined fr. de-, a pref. of Latin
origin (see de-), and OF. bale, bauch, bau (F.
bau), 'beam', fr. Frankish *balk, which is rel.
10 OHG. balko, OE. baica, ridge between
furrows' ; see balk and cp. ebauchoir. The sense of
OF. debaucher underwent the followi ng phases of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:220 COLUMN:2 -->
development^'to rough down timber; to split,
cleave; to separate; to turn somebody away
from his work or from his duty; to entice away;
to lead astray*.
Derivatives: debauch, п., debauch-ed, adj., de·
bauch-ed-ly, adv., debauch-ed-ness, п., debauchee
(q.v.), debauch-er, п., debauch-ery, п.,
debouchment, n.

## debauchee
debauchee, п., a debauched person. — F. de-
bauche, pp. of debaucher, Ίο entice away, to
lead astray'. See debauch and -ее.

## debenture
debenture, п., certificate of indebtedness. — L.
debenfur, 'they are owing", passive pres. 3rd
person pi. of debere, 'to owe'; see debt. The
certificate was so called because its text originally
began with the words debe/ttur mihi ('there are
owing to me').
Derivative: (iebenlur-ed, adj.

## debile
debile, adj., weak. — F. debile, fr. L. debilis,
'weak, infirm, disabled', which stands for *de-
bel-is, lit. 'without strength', fr. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix) and a derivative of
base *bel-, 'strong; strength', whence also OI.
balam, 'strength, force', baliyan, 'stronger/
bdlisfhah, 'the strongest', Gk. βελτίων, βέλτερος,
'better', βέλτιστος, βέλτατος, 'best'. (The τ in
these adjectives arose from earlier *βελ£ων etc.
on analogy of the comparatives and
superlatives of other synonymous adjectives ending in
-τέρας, resp. -τατος, as e.g. φέρτερος, 'better,
braver', φέρτατος, 'best, bravest'.) OSlav. bol-
/Ϊ/Ϊ (for *bolji), 'greater', bolje (adv.), 'more,
rather', bolshe, 'more, larger', derive from the
same base; see Bolshevik.

## debilitate
debilitate, tr. v., to render weak. — L. debilitatus,
pp. of debiiitare, 'to lame, cripple, maim,
weaken', fr. debilis. See prec. word and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: debilitat-ed, adj.

## debilitation
debilitation, n. — F. debilitation, fr. L. debili-
tationem, ace. of debilitas. See debility and -ation.

## debility
debility, п., weakness. — F. debilite, fr. L. debili-
tatem, ace. of debilitas, 'a laming, crippling,
weakening', fr. debilis. See debile and -ity.

## debit
debit, п., an entry of debt in an account. — L.
debitum, 'that which is owing', neut. pp. of
debere, 'to owe*. See debt.
Derivative: debit, tr. v.

## debonair
debonair, also debonnaire, adj., genial, affable;
gay. — ME. debonaire, fr. OF. de bon aire (F.
debonnaire), 'of good race', fr. de-, bon, 'good'
and aire, 'place, exlraction*, fr. L. area, 'a vacant
piece of ground, an open space'. See bonus
and area.
Derivatives: debonair-ity, п., debonairly, adv.,
debonair-ness, n.

## Deborah
Deborah, fern. PN.; in the Bible, a prophetess
and judge in Israel. — Heb. Debhorah, lit. 'bee',
rel. to Syr. debbora, 'wasp', debboritha, 'bee',
Aram, dibborithd, Arab, zunbur, dabbar, 'bee',
from the Sem. base d-b-r-, meaning 'to hum,
buzz', whence also dibber, 'he spoke', dabhar,
'word, thing'.

## debouch
debouch, intr. v., to flow out, emerge. — F. de-
boucher, 'to uncork, open; to empty itself (said
of rivers), formed fr. de- and bouche, 'mouth',
fr. L. buccat 'cheek'. See buccal and cp.
disembogue, embouchure.

## debouchment
debouchment, n. — F. debouckement, fr. debou-
cher. See prec. word and -ment

## debridement
debridement, п., the excision of damaged tissue.
— F., lit. 'unbridling', fr. debrider, 'to unbridle',
fr. de- (see de-) and bride, 'bridle', fr. MHG.
bridel. See bridle and -ment.

## debris
debris, debris, п., rubbish. — F. debris, 'remains:
waste, rubbish', fr. OF. debriser, 'to break
down, shatter', fr. de- (see de-) and briser, 'to
break', fr. VL. brisare, 'to break', a word of
Gaulish origin; cp. Ir. brissim, Ί break'. See
bruise and cp. frustum. Cp. also next word.

## debruise
debruise, tr. v., to cross a charge with an ordinary
(her.) — OF. debruisier, 'to shatter'. See de- and
bruise and cp. debris.
Derivative: debruis-ed, adj.

## debt
debt, n. — ME. dette, fr. OF. (= F.) dette, fr. L.
debita, neut. pi.—but mistaken for fern. sing.
—of debitus, pp. of debere, 'to owe, be under
obligation1, contracted fr. *de-habere, fr. de-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:220 COLUMN:3 -->
and habere, 'to have'. See babit and cp. debit,
debenture, debtor, devoir, due, duty, endeavor.
The insertion of the letter b in debt is due to the
imitation of the spelling of the Latin etymon.
In ME. the word is spelled correctly without b.
Cp. doubt.

## debtor
debtor, n. — ME. dettur, fr. OF. detor, dettor,
detur, dettur, fr. L. debitorem, ace. of debitor,
fr. debitus, pp. of debere. See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.

## debunk
debunk, tr. v., to expose the false claims of (U.S.
slang). — Coined by the American writer
William E. Woodward (1874-L950), fr. de- and
bunk.
Derivatives: debunk-er, п., debunk-ing, п., de-
bunk-ment, n.

## debut
debut, debut, п., first appearance in public. —
F, debut, fr. debuter, 'to play first; to make one's
first appearance', fr. de- (see de-) and F. but,
'aim, goal', used in the sense of 'playground'
(see butt, 'aim'); introduced into English by
Lord Chesterfield (1694-1773).
Derivatives: debut, intr. v., debutantie), (q.v.).

## debutant(e)
debutant(e), debutant(e), п., one who makes a
debut. — F. debutant, fern, debutante, pres. part,
of debuter. See prec. word.

## deca-
deca-, before a vowel dec-, pref. meaning 'ten'. —
Gk. δέκα-, fr. δέκα, 'ten', cogn. with OI. dasat
L. decern, Goth, taihun, OE. tien, ten-, 'ten*.
See ten and cp. decade, decern-.

## decachord
decachord, п., a harp with ten strings. — Gk.
δεκάχορδος, 'ten-stringed', fr. δέκα, 'ten\ and
χορδή, 'string'. See chord.

## decad
decad, п., the number ten. — See decade.

## decadal
decadal, adj., pertaining to ten; consisting of
groups of ten. — See decade and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: decadal-ly, adv.

## decade
decade, п., ι) a group of ten things; 2) a period
of ten years. — F. decade, fr. L. decas, gen.
decadis, fr. Gk. δεκάς, gen. δεκάδος, 'the number
ten; a group often', fr. δέκα. See deca-.

## decadence
decadence, decadency, п., deterioration, decay.
— F. decadence, fr. ML, decadentia, 'a falling
down', fr. *decadere, 'to fall down*, fr. de- and
L. cadere, 'to fall'. See cadence and cp. deche-
ance. For the ending see suff. -ence, resp. -ency.
Cp. also decay, deciduous.
Derivative: decadent-ly, adv.

## decadent
decadent, adj., r) deteriorating; 2) pertaining to
the decadents. — Back formation from prec.
word; coined by Thomas Carlyle (1795-1881).
For the ending see suff. -ent.
Derivative: decadent-ly, adv.

## decadeat
decadeat, п., one of a French literary .school
about the end of the 19th cent. — F. decadent\
back formation fr. decadence (see decadence);
so called after the verse of Verlaine; "Je suis
l'empire a la fin de la decadence" ("I am the
empire established at the end of decadence").
See prec. word.

## decagon
decagon, п., a ten-sided plane figure (geom.) —
Ult. fr. Gk. δεκάγωνον, 'decagon', lit. 'having
ten angles', fr. δέκα, *ten\ and -γωνος, neut.
-γωνον, from the stem of γωνία, 'angle'. See
deca- and -gon and cp. undecagon, adj.
Derivative: decagon-aly adj.

## decagram
decagram, decagramme, n. — F. decagramme, lit.
'ten grams'. See deca- and -gram,

## decalcification
decalcification, п., the process of removing lime.
— Formed fr. de- and calcification,

## decalcify
decalcify, tr. v., to remove lime from bones and
other substances. — Formed fr. de- and calcify,

## decaliter
decaliter, decalitre, n. — F. decalitre, lit. 'ten
liters'. See deca- and liter.

## Decalog
Decalog, Decalogue, п., the Ten Commandments.
— Gk. δεκάλογος, prop, ή δεκάλογος (scil.
βίβλος), '(the book) consisting of ten words*,
fr. earlier qI δέκα λόγοι, 'the ten words', fr.
δέκα, 'ten', and λόγος, 'word'. See deca- and
logos.

## Decameron
Decameron, п., a collection of 100 tales by
Boccaccio, supposed to be told during ten days. —
It. Decamerone, fr. Gk. δέκα, 'ten', and ήμερα,
'day'. See deca- and hemero- and cp. ephemere.
Derivative: Decameron-ic, adj.

## decamerous
decamerous, adj., having ten parts (said of a
flower). — Compounded of Gk. δέκα, 'ten',
and μέρος, 'part*. See deca-, mero- and -ous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:221 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DECAMETER | 194 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:221 COLUMN:1 -->

## decameter
decameter, decametre, n. — Lit. 'ten meters'. See
deca- and meter, 'unit of length'.

## decamp
decamp, intr. v., to break up a camp; to run
away. — F. decumper, 'to break up a camp; to
run away', fr. de- (see de-) and camp, 'camp', fr.
L. campus. See camp. For sense development
cp. scamper,

## decampment
decampment, n. — F. decampement, fr. decamper.
See prec. word and -ment.

## decan
decan, п., the ruler of ten parts of a zodiacal sign
(astrol.) — L. decanus, 'one set over ten', fr.
decern, 'ten'. See decimal and cp. dean, doyen.
Derivative: decan-ate, n.

## decanal
decanal, adj., pertaining to a dean. — Formed
fr. Eccles. L. decanus, with adj. suff. -al. See
dean and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: decanal-ly, adv.

## decanate
decanate, п., deanery. — Eccles. L. decanatus, fr.
decanus. See prec. word and subst. suff. -ate.

## decangular
decangular, adj., having ten angles (geom.) —
A hybrid coined fr. Gk. δέκα, 'ten', and L. an-
gulus, 'angle, corner'. See deca- and angular,

## decani
decani, п., decanal; said of the south side of the
choir where the dean sits. — Gen. of Eccles. L.
decanus, hence lit. Of the dean'. See decanal,

## decant
decant, tr. v., to pour off gently. — F. decanter,
fr. ML. decanthare, 'to pour from the edge of a
vessel', fr. de- and ML. canthus, 'edge of a ves:
sel', fr. L. cantus, canthus, 'the iron ring round
a carriage wheel'. See cant, 'a slope'.
Derivatives: decantat-ion, п., decant-er, n.

## decapitate
decapitate, tr. v., to behead. — Late L. dlcapi-
tatus pp. of decapitare, 'to cut off the head', fr.
de- and L. caput, gen. capitis, 'head'. See capital,
adj.

## decapitation
decapitation, n. — Late L. decapitatio, gen. -onis,
fr. dicapitalus, pp. of decapitare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## decapod
decapod, adj., pertaining to the Decapoda; п.,
a member of the Decapoda. — See next word.

## Decapoda
Decapoda, n. pi., an order of crustaceans (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'having ten feet', fr. Gk. δέκα,
'ten', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See deca-
and -poda.

## decapodal
decapodal, decapodous, adj., having ten feet. —
Formed fr. Gk. δέκα, 'ten', πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot', and adj. suff. -al, resp. -ous.

## decarbonate
decarbonate, tr. v., to deprive of carbon dioxide
or carbonic acid. — Formed fr. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix), carbon and verbal
suff. -ate.

## decarbonize
decarbonize, v., to deprive of carbon. — Formed
fr. de- (in the privative sense of this prefix),
carbon- and -ize.
Derivatives: decarboniz-ation, п.,
decarbonizer, n.

## decarch
decarch, п., a commander often men; a decurion.
— Gk. δεκάρχης, compounded of δέκα, 'ten',
and -άρχης, fr. αρχός, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See
deca- and -arch.

## decarchy
decarchy, п., a government often. — Gk. δεκαρ-
χίδ, fr. δεκάρχης. See prec. word and -archy.

## decastich
decastich, п., a poem of ten lines. — Gk. δεκά-
στιχος, 'containing ten lines', fr. δέκα, 'ten', and
στίχος, 'row, line, rank'. See deca- and stlchic.

## decastyle
decastyle, п., a portico with ten columns (arch.)
— Compounded of deca- and Gk. στϋλος, 'pillar'.
See style, 'gnomon'.

## decasyllabic
decasyllabic, adj., having ten syllables. — See
deca- and syllabic.
Derivative: decasyllabic, п., a line of ten
syllables.

## decasyllable
decasyllable, п., a line of ten syllables. —
Compounded of deca- and syllable.

## decathlon
decathlon, п., an athletic contest consisting of ten
different events. — Compounded of Gk. δέκα,
'ten', and άθλος, ά&λον, 'contest'. See deca- and
athletic and cp. pentathlon.

## decatize
decatize, tr. v., to cause to uncurl by means of hot
water or steam. — A hybrid formed with -ize,
a suff. of Greek origin, fr. F.decatir, 'to take the
gloss off (a woolen cloth), to sponge', fr. de- (see
de-) and catir, 'to press, gloss', fr. VL. *coac-
tire, a derivative of L. coactus, pp. of cogere,
'to press', prop, 'to drive together'. See cogent
and -ize.
Derivative: decatiz-er, n.

## decay
decay, intr. v. — ONF. decair, corresponding to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:221 COLUMN:2 -->
OF. dechair, decheeir (F. dechoir), 'to fall off,
decay', fr. VL. *decadere, refashioned (after VL.
'cadere) fr. L. decidere, 'to fall off, fall down'.
See de- and cadence and cp. deciduous, escheat.
Derivatives: decay, п., decay-ed, adj.

## decease
decease, n. — ME. deces, fr. OF. deces (F. deces),
'decease, death', fr. L. decessus, 'departure,
death', fr. decess-(um), pp. stem of decidere, 'to
go away, depart'. See de- and cease and cp.
predecessor.
Derivatives: decease, intr. v., deceas-ed, adj.

## deceit
deceit, n. — ME. deceite, fr. OF. deceite, prop,
fern, of deceit, pp. of degeveir. See next word
and cp. receipt.
Derivatives: deceit-ful, adj., deceit-ful-ly, adv.,
deceit-ful-ness. n.

## deceive
deceive, tr. and intr. v. — OF. deceivre, a
collateral form of deceveir (F. decevoir), 'to
deceive', fr. L. decipere, 'to beguile, deceive, elude',
fr. de- and capere, 'to catch, seize, take, hold'.
See captive and cp. apperceive and words there
referred to. For the change of Latin ά (in
capere) to i (in de-cipere) see abigeat and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: deceiv-abil-ity, п., deceiv-able, adj.,
deceiv-able-ness, п., deceiv-abl-y, adv.,
deceiver, п., deceiv-ing, adj., deceiv-ing-ly, adv.

## decelerate
decelerate, tr. v., to decrease the velocity of;
intr. v., to decrease in velocity. — Formed on
analogy of accelerate fr. de- (in the privative
sense of this pref.) and celeratus, pp. of celerare,
'to hasten'.
Derivatives: decelerat-ion, п., decelerat-or, n.

## decern-
decern-, combining form meaning 'ten'. — L.
decern-, fr. decern, 'ten', which is cogn. with
Gk. δέκα, 'ten'. See deca- and cp. December,
decemvir. Cp. also deci-.

## December
December, n. — L. December, 'the tenth month',
fr. decern, 'ten' (see decern-); so called because
the Roman year began with March.
Derivatives: December-ish, adj., December-ly,
adj., Decembr-ist, n. (Russ. hist.)

## decemvir
decemvir, n., ι) a member of a council of ten men
(Roman hist.); 2) a member of an authoritative
body of ten men. — L., back formation fr. the
pi. decern viri, 'ten men.' See decern- and virile
and cp. duumvir, triumvir, cenrumvir.

## decemviral
decemviral, adj. — L. decemviralis, 'pertaining to
the decemvir(s)', fr. decern virl. See prec. word
and adj. suff. -al.

## decemvirate
decemvirate, п., ι) office of the decemvirs; 2) an
authoritative body of ten men. — L. decem-
viratus, 'the office of a decemvir'. See decemvir
and subst. suff. -ate.

## decency
decency, n. — L. decentia, fr. decens, gen. -entis,
'becoming, seemly, decent'. See decent and -cy.

## decennary
decennary, п., a period of ten years. — Formed
with subst. suff. -ary fr. L. decennis, 'of ten
years'. See decennium.

## decenniad
decenniad, п., a period of ten years. — See
decennium and -ad.

## decennial
decennial, adj. —Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
decennis, 'of ten years'. See next word and cp.
undecennial.

## decennium
decennium, п., a period of ten years. — L„ 'a
period of ten years', fr. decennis, 'of ten years',
fr. decern, 'ten', and annus, 'year'. See decem-
and annual and cp. decennary, decenniad. For
the change of Latin й (in annus) to i (in
decennis, dec-lnnium) see accent and cp. biennial.

## decent
decent, adj. — L. decens, gen. -entis, becoming,
seemly, fitting, proper, decent', pres. part, of
decet, declre, 'to be seemly or fitting', rel. to
decus, gen. decoris, 'ornament, grace, splendor,
glory, honor, dignity', dignus (for *dec-nos),
'suitable, becoming, proper' (lit. 'decorated,
splendid'), dexter (for *dexi-leros), 'on the right
side' (lit. 'on the becoming or fitting side'), do-
cere, 'to teach' (orig. 'to cause somebody to
receive something'), discere, 'to learn'; fr. I.-E.
base *dek-, *dok-, 'to take, receive, accept;
acceptable, becoming, good', whence also OI.
daksati, 'is apt, proper, pleasing', daksah, 'able,
apt, clever; competent, intelligent', daksinah,
daksinah, 'on the right hand; southern', dasfi,
'he honors', Gk. δέκεο-ftai, Att. δέχεσ»οα, 'to
take, accept, receive, receive hospitably, hold',
δοκεΐν, 'to seem good, to seem, think, believe',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:221 COLUMN:3 -->
δοκεύειν, 'to watch closely', δόξα (for *δόκ-σα),
'notion; opinion; honor, glory', δόγμα, 'that
which one thinks true, opinion, doctrine, decree',
δόκιμος, 'tried, assayed, genuine', δόκος, a
wooden beam' (lit. 'that which holdsthe roof), δεξιός,
'on the right', διδάσκειν, 'to teach', Mir. dech,
the best'. Cp. Adoxa, choledoch, condign, Cymo-
doce, dainty, Daksha, decorate, decorous, deign,
dexter, diadoche, Diadochi, didactic, dignify,
dignity, diksha, Diplodocus, disdain, docent,
Docetism, docile, docimasy, docimology, Doco-
glossa, doctor, doctriae, document, dogma, doxa-
stic, doxology, heterodox, orthodox, pandect,
paradox, synecdoche.
Derivatives: decent-ly, adv., decent-ness, n.

## decentralize
decentralize, tr. v. — Formed fr. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix) and centralize.
Derivative: decentraliz-ation, n.

## deception
deception, n. — F. deception, fr. Late L. decep-
tionem, ace. of deceptio, 'a deceiving,
deception', fr. L. deceptus, pp. of decipere, 'to deceive'.
See deceive and -tion.

## deceptive
deceptive, adj. — F. deceptif (fern, deceptive), fr.
ML. deceptivus, fr. L. deceptus, pp. of decipere,
'to deceive'. See deceive and -ive.
Derivatives: deceptive-ly, adv., deceptive-ness,n.

## decera
decera, tr. v., to decree. — F. decerner, fr. L. de-
cernere, 'to decide, determine', pp. decretus.
See decree and cp. concern, discern, secern.

## decheance
decheance, п., forfeiture. — F., 'fall, downfall,
forfeiture', fr. ML. decadentia, 'a falling down'.
See decadence.

## dechristiaaize
dechristiaaize, tr. v., to deprive of its Christian
character. — Formed fr. de- (in the privative
sense of this prefix) and christianize.
Derivative: dechristianiz-ation, n.

## deci-
deci-, combining form used in the metric system
to denote one tenth of a given unit, in
contradistinction to deca-, which is used to mean 'ten
times as much' (as the given unit). — F. deci-,
arbitrarily formed fr. L. decimus, the tenth', fr.
decern, 'ten'. See decimal and cp. deca-,

## decibel
decibel, п., a unit for measuring the loudness of
sounds. — Compounded of deci- and bel and
lit. meaning 'the tenth part of a bel'.

## decide
decide, tr. and intr. v. — F. decider, fr. L.
dlcidere, 'to decide, determine, settle', prop, 'to cut
off', fr. de- and caedere, 'to cut, hew, lop',
whence caemenlum (for *caid(s)mentom), 'rough
stone, stone clippings'. See cement. For the
change of Latin ae (in caedere) to Г (in de-cidere)
see acquire and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: decid-ed, adj., decid-ed-ly, adv.,
decid-ed-ness, п., decid-er, п., decid-ing-ly, adv.
decidua п., that part of the mucous membrane
of the uterus, which is cast off at parturition
(anat.) — Medical L., short for membrana
decidua, 'the membrane that falls off', fern, of
L. deciduus, 'falling off'. See next word.

## deciduous
deciduous, adj., 1) falling off at a certain season
or stage of growth, etc.; 2) shedding leaves
annually (said of trees). — L. deciduus, 'falling
off', fr. decldere, 'to fall off', fr. de- and cadere,
'to fall'. See cadence and cp. decadent. For the
change of Latin й (in cadere) to Г (in de-cidere)
see abigeat and cp. words there referred to. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: deciduous-ly, adv., deciduous-ness,
n.

## decigram
decigram, decigramme, n. — F. decigramme, 'the
tenth part of a gram', a hybrid coined fr. deci-,
and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written'. See
-gram.

## decile
decile, decil, п., the aspect of two planets when
distant from each other 36 degrees (i.e. one
tenth of the zodiac). — F. decile, formed fr. L.
decern, 'ten', with the suff. -He (on analogy of
the Latin neut. adjectives qu'mtile, sextile). See
decern and -ile.

## deciliter
deciliter, decilitre, n. — F. decilitre, 'the tenth
part of a liter', a hybrid coined fr. deci- and
Gk. λίτρα, 'a pound'. See liter.

## decillioa
decillioa, п., ι) in the United States and France,
a thousand raised to the eleventh power (i.e.
1 followed by 33 zeros); 2) in England and
Germany, a million raised to the tenth power (i.e. 1
followed by 60 zeros). — Formed fr. L. decern,
'ten' (see decern-), on analogy of million (q.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:222 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 195 | DECREASE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:222 COLUMN:1 -->
Ср. billion and words there referred to.
Derivatives: dea'Uion-th, adj. and n.

## Decima
Decima, fem. PN. — L., fem. of decimus, 'tenth'.
See Decimus.
decima], adj. — ML. decimalis, 'pertaining to a
tenth part\ fr. L. decimus, earlier form decu-
mus, 'the tenth', fr. I.-E. *dekemos, whence also
OI. dasamah, Avestic daslma-, Olr. dechmad,
'the tenth'. Cp. also I.-E. *dekm-tos, whence
Gk. δέκατος, Goth, tai-hunda, OHG. zehando,
ON. tiundi, OE. teogoda, teoda, OSIav. desetu,
Lith. desimtas, Lett, desmitais, OPruss. dessimts,
Toch. A skant, В skante, skance, 'the tenth*.
For the corresponding cardinal numbers, from
which these ordinal numbers derive, see ten.
Cp. tithe. Cp. also dean, demean, Decimus,
decuman, Decumaria, dime, doyen, and the second
element in dozen, duodecimo.
Derivatives: decimal, п., decimalism (q.v.), de-
cimalist (q.v.), decimalize (q.v.), decimal-ly, adv.

## decimalism
decimalism, п., the use of the decimal system. —
A hybrid coined fr. decimal and -ism, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## declmalist
declmalist, п., an advocate of the decimal system.
— A hybrid coined fr. decimal and -ist, a suff.
of Greek origin.

## decimalize
decimalize, tr. v., to reduce to the decimal system.
— A hybrid coined fr. decimal and -ize, a suff. of
Greek origin. Derivative; decimaliz-ation, n.

## decimate
decimate, tr. v. — L. decimatus, pp. of decimare,
'to select by lot every tenth man for punishment,
to decimate*, fr. decimus, 'tenth'. See decimal
and verbal suff. -ate.

## decimation
decimation, n. — L. decimatio, gen. -onis, fr.
decimatus, pp. of decimare^ 'to decimate'. See
prec. word and -ion.

## decimeter
decimeter, decimetre, n. — F. decimetre, lit. 'ten
meters', a hybrid coined fr. deci- and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See meter, 'unit of length'.

## Decimus
Decimus, masc. PN. — L., 'the tenth', a name
given to the tenth child in a family, fr. decern,
'ten*. See decimal and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also Decima. For sense cp. Sextus, Septimus.

## decipher
decipher, tr. v. — Formed fr. de- and cipher on
analogy of F. dechiffrer. Derivatives:
decipherable, adj., decipher-er, п., decipher-ment, n.

## decisioa
decisioa, n. — F. decision, fr. L. decisionem, ace.
of decisid, 'decision, settlement', fr. decisus, pp.
of decidere, 'to decide, determine, settle*. See
decide and -ion. Derivative: decision-al, adj.

## decisive
decisive, adj. — ML. decisivus, fr. L. decisus, pp.
of decidere. See decide and -ive.
Derivatives: decisive-ly, adv., decisive-ness, n.

## deck
deck, tr. v., r) to cover (obsol.); 2) to cover with
ornaments, to adorn. — MDu. decken (Du. dek-
ken), 'to cover'. See thatch.

## deck
deck, п., covering (obsol.) — MDu. decke, dek,
(Du. dek), 'roof, covering', fr. decken, 'to cover'.
See deck, v., and cp. next word.

## deck
deck, п., covering of a ship. — Shortened fr. G.
verdeck (whence also Du. overdek, later dek),
lit. 'covering* (see for- and thatch and cp. deck,
v.), and prop, a loan translation of OIL (= It.)
coperta or MF. couverte. That E. deck is not a
LG. or Du. loan word, as suggested by most
lexicographers, is proved by the fact that the E.
word appears first in 1513, whereas Du.
overdek and dek occur for the first time in 1599,
resp. 1675. See Friedrich Kluge, Seemanns-
sprache, Halle, 1911, p. I77.

## deckle
deckle, п., in papermaking, 1) a wooden frame
serving to keep the paperpulp from spreading
beyond a desired size; 2) a deckle edge. — G.
Deckel* 'lid, cover', dimin. of Decket 'cover',
which is rel. to E. (batch (q.v.) See also dimin.
suff. -le.

## declaim
declaim, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. earlier declame, fr.
L. declamare, 'to practice speaking aloud,
declaim*, fr. de- and clamare, 'to call, cry out'.
See claim and cp. next word.
Derivative: declaim-ery n.

## declamation
declamation, n. — F. declamation, fr. L. decla-
mationem, ace. of declamatio, "practice in
speaking, declamation', fr. declamatus, pp. of
declamare. See prec. word and -ion.

## declamatory
declamatory, adj. — L. declamatorius, 'pertaining
to the practice of speaking, declamatory,
rhetorical', fr. declamatus, pp. of declamare. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:222 COLUMN:2 -->
prec. word and adj. suff. -ory.

## declarant
declarant, п., one who makes a declaration {law).
— F. declarant, fr. L. declarantem, ace. of de-
clarans, pres. part, of declarare. See declare
and -ant.

## declaration
declaration, n. — F. declaration, fr. L. diclara-
tionem, ace. of declaratio, 'an exposition,
declaration', fr. declaratus, pp. of declarare. See
declare and -ation.

## declarative
declarative, adj. — L. declarative, 'serving for
explanation', fr. declaratus, pp. of declarare. See
declare and -ative.
Derivative: declarative-ly, adv.

## declaratory
declaratory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory
fr. L. declaratus, pp. of declarare. See declare.

## declare
declare, tr. and intr. v. — F. declarer, fr. L.
declarare, 'to make clear, to make evident, to
manifest, declare', fr. de- and clarare, 'to make
clear*, fr. clams, 'clear*. See clear.
Derivatives: declar-able, adj., declar-ed, adj.,
declar-ed-ly, adv., declar-ed-ness, п., declar-er, n.

## declass
declass, tr. v., to degrade from one's class. —
Formed on analogy of F. declasser. See next
word.

## declasse
declasse, adj., declassed. — F., pp. of declasser,
'to degrade', fr. de- (in the privative sense of
this prefix) and classer, 'to class'. See de- and
class and cp. prec. word.

## declension
declension, n, — OF. declinaison (F. declinaison),
fr. L. declinationem, ace. of decllnatid, *a
bending aside', fr. decimatus, pp. of declinare, 'to
bend aside, decline*. See decline and cp.
declination, which is a doublet of declension.
Derivative: declension-al, adj.

## declinable
declinable, adj. — F. declinable, fr. L. decllna-
bilis, 'that which can be declined', fr. decimare.
See decline, v., and -able.

## declination
declination, n. — OF. declinacion (F. declinaison),
fr. L. declinationem, ace, of declinatio. See
declension and -ation.

## declinator
declinator, п., an instrument for measuring
declination. — Formed with agential suff. -or fr.
L. declinatus, pp. of declinare. See decline.

## declinatory
declinatory, adj., pertaining to declination. —
ML. decflnatoriuSy.fT. L. decimatus, pp. of
declinare. See decline, v., and the adj. suffiy.es -ate
and -ory and cp. declivity.

## decline
decline, intr. and tr. v. — ME. declinen, fr. MF.
(= F.) decliner, fr. L. declinare, fr. de- and
-clinare. See clinical and cp. incline, recline.
Derivatives: declin-ed, adj., declin-er, n.

## decline
decline, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) diclin, back
formation fr. decliner. See decline, v.

## declinometer
declinometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
declination of the magnetic needle (jthys.) —
A hybrid coined fr. L. declinare, 'to decline',
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See declination and
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## declivitous
declivitous, adj., having a downward slope. —
See next word and -ous and cp. declivous.

## declivity
declivity, п., a downward slope. — F. declivite,
fr. L. declivitatem, ace. of decllvitds, 'a sloping
place, declivity', fr. declivis, 'sloping
downward', fr. de- and clivus, 'slope, hill'. See clivus
and -ity.

## declivous
declivous, adj., having a downward slope. — See
prec. word and -ous and cp. declivitous.

## declutch
declutch, intr. v., to disengage a clutch. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and clutch.

## decoct
decoct, tr. v., to prepare or extract by boiling. —
L. decoctus, pp. of decoquere, 'to boil down',
fr. de- and coquere, 'to cook, boil'. See cook
and cp. concoct.

## decoction
decoction, n. — F. decoction, fr. L. decoctionem,
ace. of decoctio, *a boiling down', fr. decoctus,
pp. of decoquere. See prec. word and -ion and.
cp. concoction.

## decode
decode, v., to translate from a code into ordinary
language. — See de- and code.

## Decodon
Decodon, п., a genus of plants, the swamp
loosestrife (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'having ten teeth*,
compounded of Gk. δέκα, 'ten*, and οδών, gen.
οδόντος, 'tooth'; so called in allusion to the
ten-toothed calyx. See deca- and odonto-.

## decollate
decollate, tr. v., to behead. — L. decoHatus, pp.
of decollare, 'to behead', lit. 'to cut off from
the neck', fr. de- and collum, 'neck'. See collar

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:222 COLUMN:3 -->
and verbal suff. -ate and cp. collet. Cp. also
decollete.
Derivatives: decollat-ed, adj., decollation (q.v.)

## decollation
decollation, п., the act of beheading. — F.
decollation, fr. L. decollationem, ace. of decollatio,
fr. decollatus, pp. of decollare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## decollete
decollete, adj., leaving the neck and shoulders
bare. — F., pp. of decolleter, 'to uncover the
neck and shoulders*, fr. de- (see de-) and collet,
dimin. of col, сои, 'neck'. See collet and cp.
decollate.

## decolor
decolor, decolour, tr. v., to decolorize. — Formed
fr. de- (in the privative sense of this prefix) and
color, v.

## decoloraat
decoloraat, п., a substance that removes color. —
L. decolorans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of deco-
lorare. See next word and -ant.

## decoloration
decoloration, п., removal of color. — L. de-
cotoratio, 'a discoloring,' fr. decoloratus, pp. of
decolordre, 'to deprive of color, discolor', fr.
de- and colorare, 'to color'. See color, v., and
-ation.

## decolorize
decolorize, decolourize, tr. v., to remove the color
of, to bleach. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
decoldrare (see decolor) and -ize, a suff. of Greek
origin. The correct form is decolor.
Derivatives: decolo{u)r\z-ation, п., decolo(u)riz-
er, n.

## decompose
decompose, tr. and intr. v., to'separate into
components; to rot. — F. decomposer, 'to
decompose, rot, decay*, fr. de- (in the privative sense
of this prefix) and composer. See de- and
compose.
Derivatives: decompos-ed, adj., decompos-er, n.

## decomposite
decomposite, adj., compounded more than once.
— Late L. decomposing, 'formed from a
compound*, fr. de- (with intensive force) and L. com-
positus, pp. of componere, 'to put together'. See
composite and cp. decompound.
Derivative: decomposite, n.

## decomposition
decomposition, п., the act of decomposing. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and composition. Cp. decompose.

## decompound
decompound, tr. v., to compound more than
once; adj., compounded more than once; п.,
a decomposite. — Formed fr. de- (with intensive
force) and compound.

## decorate
decorate, tr. v. — L. decoratus, pp. of decorare,
'to decorate, adorn, embellish; to honor,
distinguish', fr. decus, gen. decoris, 'ornament,
grace, splendor'. See decent and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: decorat-ed, adj., decoration (q.v.),
decoral-ive, adj., decorat-ive-fy, adv., decorat-
ive-ness, п., decorat-or, n.

## decoration
decoration, n. — Late L. decoraiio, gen. -onis, fr.
L. decoratus, pp. of decorare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## decorous
decorous, adj., proper, dignified. — L. decorus,
'becoming, fitting, seemly', fr. decus, gen.
decoris, 'ornament, dignity'. See decent and cp.
decorate, decorum. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
L. -us, see -ous. The word decorous was
introduced into English by Henry More (Г614-87),
philosopher of the Cambridge Platonist school.
Derivatives: decorous-ly, adv., decorous-ness, n.

## decorticate
decorticate, tr. v., to strip off the bark, to flay. —
L. decorticatus, pp. of decorticare, 'to bark', fr.
de- (in the privative sense of this prefix), and
cortex, gen. corticis, 'rind, bark'. See cortex and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: decorticat-ion, п., decorticat-or, n.

## decorum
decorum, n.f that which is proper. — L. decorum,
'that which is seemly', prop. neut. of the adj.
decorus. See decorons.

## decoy
decoy, п., a lure; a bait. — Formed from Du. de,
def. article, and kooi, 'cage', fr. L. cavea.
'excavated place, cavity, enclosure.' See the, def.
art., and cage.
Derivative: decoy, v.

## decrease
decrease, intr. and tr. v. — Fr. AF. decreiss-,
pres. part, stem of decreistre, corresponding to
OF. descreistre, descroistre (F. decroiire), fr.
VL. discrescere, for L. decrescere, 'to grow less,
grow shorter, decrease, diminish'. See de- and
crescent.
Derivatives: decrease, п., decreas-ing-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:223 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DECREE | 196 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:223 COLUMN:1 -->

## decree
decree, η. — ME. decree, fr. OF. decre, decret
(F. decret), fr. L. decretum, 'decision, decree,
ordinance', prop, neut.'of decretus, pp. of de·
cernere, 'to pronounce a decision, decide,
determine', fr. de- and cernere, 'to separate, sift,
distinguish, discern, understand, decide'. See
certain and cp. decretal, decern, discern, secern.
Derivatives: decree, intr. and tr. v., decre-er, n.

## decrement
decrement, п., decrease; diminution. — L. decre-
mentum, 'diminution, decrease', fr. decrescere.
See decrease and cp. increment. For the ending
see suff. -ment.

## decremeter
decremeter, п., an instrument for measuring
the dampening of electric waves. — Shortened
for decrement meter. See prec. word and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## decrepit
decrepit, adj., feebled by age. — F. decrepit, fr.
L. decrepitus, 'very old, infirm, decrepit', lit.
'noiseless*, fr. de- and crepitus, 'a rattling,
creaking» clattering, a noise', fr. crepare [pp. stem
crepit-(um)], 'to rattle, crack, burst\ which is of
imitative origin. See crepitate and cp. craven.
Derivatives: decrepit-ly, adv., decrepit-ness, n.

## decrepitate
decrepitate, tr. v., to heat salt or mineral so as
to cause crackling; intr. v., to crackle. — ML.
decrepitatus, pp. of decrepitare, which is prob.
formed fr. de- (in the priv. sense of this prefix)
3nd L. crepitare, 'to rattle, creak, crackle', freq.
of crepare. See crepitate and cp. decrepit.
Derivative: decrepitat-ion, n.

## decrepitude
decrepitude, п., the state of being decrepit. —
F. decrepitude, fr. L. decrepitus, 'very old, in-
.firm, decrepit'. See decrepit and -ude.

## decrescendo
decrescendo, adj., and adv., gradually decreasing
in loudness; п., a gradual decrease in loudness.
— It., compounded of de- and crescendo.

## decrescent
decrescent, adj., growing smaller. —
Compounded ot de- and crescent.

## decretal
decretal, adj., pertaining to a decree. — Late L.
decretalis, 'pertaining to a decree', fr. L. decre-
turn. See decree and adj. suff. -al.

## decretal
decretal, п., a papal decree. — F. decretale, fr.
ML. decretale, prop. neut. of Late L. decretalis,
used as a noun. See decretal, adj.

## decretalist
decretalist, п., one learned in the decretals. —
See prec. word and -ist and cp. next word.

## decretist
decretist, п., the same as decretalist. — See prec.
word.

## decretive
decretive, adj., having the force of a decree. —
Formed with suff. -ive fr. L. decretum. See
decree.

## decretory
decretory, adj. — L. decretorius, 'pertaining to a
decree or decision', fr. decritum. See decree and
adj. suff. -ory.

## decrial
decrial, n. — Formed fr. decry with subst. suff. -al.

## decrustation
decrustation, п., the act of removing a crust. —
Formed with suff. -ion fr. L. decrustatus, pp. of
decrustare, 'to peel off, split off', fr. de- and
crustare, 'to cover with a crust', fr. crusta,
'crust'. See crust

## decry
decry, tr. v. — See de- and cry, v., and cp. descry.

## decuman
decuman, adj., large, immense (said of waves). —
L. decumanus, also decimanus, 'of, or pertain- '
ing to, the tenth', fr. decumus, decimus, 'the
tenth' (see decimal and -an); so called from
the idea that every tenth wave was large.

## Decumaria
Decumaria, п., a genus of vines (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. decumarius, also decimarius, 'pertaining
to the tenth part', fr. decumus, decimus, 'tenth,
a tenth part*, fr. decern, 'ten' (see decimal and
cp. decuman); so called in allusion to its often
10-merous flowers.

## decumbence
decumbence, decumbency, n. — Formed fr. next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## decumbent
decumbent, adj., lying down; lying on the ground
{bot.) — L. decumbens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
dicumbere, 'to lie down', fr. de- and -cumbere
(found only in compounds), nasalized form of
cubdre, 'to lie down, recline'. See cubicle and
cp. accumbent and words there referred to.
Derivative: decumbent-ly, adv.

## decuple
decuple, adj., tenfold. — F. decuple, fr. L. de-
cuplus, 'tenfold', formed fr. decern, 'ten', on
analogy of dupfus, 'double' (lit. 'twofold'), fr.
duo, 'two'. See decern- and -fold and cp. ply,
'to bend', and words there referred to.
Derivatives: decuple, n. and tr. v.

## decurion
decurion, п., an officer in the Roman army,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:223 COLUMN:2 -->
commanding a company of ten men. — L. decurio,
gen. -onis, 'chief of a company of ten*, fr. de-
curia, 'a company of ten men'. See decury.

## decurrence
decurrence, decurrency, n. — Formed fr. decur-
rent with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## decurrent
decurrent, adj., running downward. — L. de-
currens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of decurrere, 'to
run down', fr. de- and currere, 'to run'. See
current, adj., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: decurrent-ly, adv.

## de curs ive
de curs ive, adj., running downward. — ModL.
decursivus, fr. L. decursus, pp. of decurrere. See
prec. word and -ive.
Derivative: decursive-ly, adv.

## decury
decury, п., a division or company of ten men. —
L. decuria, fr. decern, 'ten'. See decern- and cp.
decurion. Cp. also dicker, 'a set of ten', and
century.

## decussate
decussate, lr. and intr. v., to cross or divide in
the form of an X. — L. decussatus, pp. of de-
cussare, 'to divide crosswise (in the form of an
X)', fr. decussis (for decern asses), 'ten asses;
the number ten; the symbol X, as representing
ten4. See decern- and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: decussat-ed, adj.

## decussate
decussate, adj., crossed, shaped like an X. — L.
decussatus. See decussate, v.

## decussation
decussation, n. — L. decussatio, gen. -6nis,
'intersecting of two lines crosswise', fr. decussatus,
See decussate, v., and -ion.

## dedicate
dedicate, tr. v. — L. dedicatus, pp. of dedicare,
'to affirm, declare, announce, dedicate,
consecrate', fr. de- and dtcare, 'to proclaim, dedicate',
which is rel. to dicere, 'to say, tell'. See diction
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: dedicat-ee, adj., dedication, dedica-
tive (qq.v.), dedicat-ory, adj., dedicat-ori-ly, adv.

## dedicate
dedicate, adj., dedicated. — L. dedicatus, pp. of
dedicare. See dedicate, v., and adj. suff. -ate.

## dedication
dedication, n. — OF. dedication (F. dedication),
fr. L. dedicationem, ace. of dedicatio,
'dedication, consecration', fr. dedicatus, pp. oidedicare.
See dedicate, v., and -ion.
Derivative: dedication-al, adj.

## dedicative
dedicative, adj. — Late L. dedicativus, fr. L.
dedicatus, pp. of dedicare. See dedicate, v., and -ive.

## deduce
deduce, tr. v. — L. deducere, 'to lead or bring
down, deduct, derive, trace down', fr. de- and
ducere, 'to lead'. See duke and cp. deduct.
Derivatives: deduc-ible, adj., deduc-ibil-ity, п.,
deduc-ible-ness, п., deduc-ibl-y, adv.

## deduct
deduct, tr. v. — L. deductus, pp. of deducere. See
prec. word.

## deduction
deduction, n. — L. diductio, gen. -onis, 'a leading
away; deduction, diminution; reasoning', fr.
deductus, pp. of deducere; see deduce and -ion.
As a term of philosophy, L, deductio was first
used by Anicius Manlius Severinus (cca. 480-
524) as a loan translation of Aristotle's
αναγωγή, lit. 'a leading away*, fr. άπάγει,ν, 'to lead
away*.

## deductive
deductive, adj. — L. deductivus, 'derivative', fr.
deductus, pp. of deducere. See deduce and -ive.
Derivative: deductive-ly, adv.

## deed
deed, n. — ME. dede, fr. OE. dxd, rel. to OS. dad,
ON. dad, OFris. dede, ded, Du. daad, OHG.,
MHG. tat, G. Tat, 'deed, act', Goth, ga-deps,
'a putting, placing, adoption', fr. I.-E. *dke-ti-,
whence also Lith. detis, 'load, burden', and the
second element in OSlav. blago-deti, 'good
deed, favor'; cp. I.-E. *dhe-ti-, whence Ol.
-(d)hitik (only in compounds), 'a placing', Gk.
θ-έσις, 'a placing, setting', Late L. con-diti-ό, 'a
founding' (fr. L. conditus, pp. of condere). I.-E.
*dhe-ti- and *dhe-ti- are derivatives of bas.e
*dhi-, *dhe-, 'to put, place; to do, make'. See
do, v., and cp. thesis.
deem. tr. v. — ME. demen,. fr. OE. deman, 'to
judge, condemn, think, believe', rel. to ON.
doema, OFris. dema, OS. adomian, Du. doemen,
OHG. tuomen, Goth, -domjan (only in
compounds). Cp. doom and -dom.

## deemer
deemer, п., one who deems. — OE. demere, fr.
demon. See prec. word and agential suff. -er.

## deemster
deemster, п., judge. — ME. demestre, 'judge', fr.
demen. See deem and -ster- and cp. doomster,
dempster.
Derivative: deemster-ship, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:223 COLUMN:3 -->

## deep
deep, adj. — ME. deop, dep, deep, fr, OE. deop,
rel. to OS. diop, OFris. diap, Du. dlep, OHG.
tiof, tiuf, MHG., G. tie/, ON. djupr, Dan. dyb,
Swed. djup, Goth, diups, 'deep', fr. Teut. base
*deupa-, 'deep', corresponding to I.-E. base
*dheubh-, *dkubh-, whence Luh. dubus, 'deep,
hollow', duobe, 'pit', Lett, dubens, 'bottom',
OSlav. duno (for *dkubno), Czech, Slov., etc.
dno, 'bottom*, Olr. domain (for *dhubni-), 'deep',
domun (for *dhubno-), 'world*, W. dwfn, 'deep'.
Cp. depth, dip, dive, dope, dopper.
Derivatives: deep, n. deep, adv. (q.v.), deep-en,
v., deep-en-er, п., deep-en-ing, adj. deep-en-ing-
fy, adv.

## deep
deep, adv. — ME. depe, fr. OE. deope, 'deep'
(adv.), 'deeply', fr. deop, 'deep'. See deep, adj.

## deer
deer, n. — ME. dere, deer, fr. OE. deor, 'a wild
animal·, rel. to OS. dior, ON. dyr, OFris. diar,
Du. dier, OHG. tior, MHG., G. tier, 'animal,
Goth, dius, 'wild animal'; orig. 'a breathing
being', and cogn. with OSlav. duckii, 'breath,
spirit', duSa, 'soul*, Lith. dvasas (masc), dvasia,
(fern.), 'spirit', Lett, dvasa, 'breath, odor',
dvesele, 'breath, soul, life'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. *dheus-, *dkous-, *dhwos-, *dhe-
wes-, *dhwes-, 'to breathe', which are
enlargements of base *dheu-, 'to fly about like dust,
to smoke'. See thio- and cp. words there
referred to. For sense development cp. L. animal,
'animal', lit. 'a living being', fr. anima, 'air,
breath of life, soul', Gk. ζωον, 'animal', lit. 'a
living being', Heb. hayyah, *animal, beast', lit.
'a living being'; cp. animal, zoo-.

## deface
deface, tr. v., to mar. — ME. defacen, fr. OF.
desfacier, 'to disfigure', fr. L. dis- and VL. facia
(for L. fades), 'face'. See dis- and face and cp.
efface.
Derivatives: deface-able, adj., deface-ment, п.,
defac-er, п., defac-ing, adj., defac-ing-ly, adv.

## de facto
de facto, in actual fact, the opposite of de jure. —
L. de facto, 'in fact', fr. de, 'from, down from,
according to', and abl. of factum, 'deed, act,
fact*. See de- and fact.

## defalcate
defalcate, intr. v., to embezzle. — ML.
defalcate, pp. of defalcare, 'to cut off with a sickle'.
whence fig. 'to deduct', fr. de- and L. falx, gen.
falcis, 'sickle'. See falchion and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: defalcation (q.v.), defalcat-or, n.

## defalcation
defalcation, п., embezzlement. — ML.
defalcate, gen. -onis, fr. defalcatus. See prec. word
and -ion.

## defamation
defamation, п., calumny, aspersion. — ME. dif-
famacioun, fr. OF. dijfamation, fr. L. diffama-
tionem, ace. of diffamatio, fr. diffamatus, pp. of
diffamare. See defame and -ation.

## defamatory
defamatory, adj., tending to defame. — ML. dif-
famatorius, 'tending to defame', fr. L.
diffamatus, pp. of diffamare. See next word and adj.
suff. -ory.
Derivative: defamatori-ly, adv.

## defame
defame, tr. v., to calumniate, asperse. — ME.
defamen, diffamen, fr. OF. diffamer, fr. L.
diffamare, 'to spread an evil report, defame*, fr.
dis- and fama, 'report, rumor'. See fame.
Derivatives: defam-ed, adj., defam-er, n. de-
fam-ing-ly, adv.

## default
default, n. — ME. defaulte, defaute, fr. VL. *de-
faffita, pp. of *defallere (whence F. defaillir, 'to
be wanting'), used as a noun, fr. de- and L. fal-
lere, 'to deceive*. See fail and cp. fault. Cp.
OProven$. defauta, defaulta, which are the exact
equivalents of OF. defaute. In MF. and ModF.,
defaut, 'default, blemish', a collateral form,
superseded the ancient form defaute. (Cp. also*
OProvenc. defaut, a collateral form of defauta.

## default
default, intr. and tr. v. — ME. defaulen, fr.
defaute. See default, n.
Derivatives: default-ant, adj., defauft-er, n.

## defeasance
defeasance, п., the act of making null and void
{law). — OF. defesance, 'undoing', fr. defesant,
desfesant, pres. part, of defaire, desfaire, 'to
undo'. See defeat, v., and -ance.

## defeasible
defeasible, adj., capable of being made null and
void. — AF., 'capable of being annulled', fr.
AF. defaire, which corresponds to OF. defaire,
desfaire, 'to undo'. See defeat, v., and -ible and
cp. feasible.
Derivatives: defeasibil-ity, п., defeasible-ness, n.

## defeat

*di.sfacere (corresponding to L. deficere), fr. dis-
and L. facere, 'to make, do'. See fact and cp.
defect.

## defeat
defeat, n. - Formed fr. defeat, v., on analogy
of F. defaite^ 'defeat', which derives fr. defaire,
'to undo'.
defeatism» n. — Formed on analogy of F. de-
faitisme, which derives fr. defaite. See defeat,

## defeatist

## defecation
defecation, n. — Late L. defaecatio, gen. -onis,

## defect
defect, n. — L. defectus, 'a failing, failure', fr.

(q-v.)

## defection
defection, n. —- L. Uefectio, gen. -onis, 'failure,

## defective

Derivatives: defective, п., defective-ly, adv.,

## defector

## defence
defence, n. — The British spelling of defense.
