fense-less-ly, defence-less-Jy, adv., defense-less-
ness, defence-less-ness, n,

## defensible

defensive, 'to defend diligently*, freq. of defendere
(pp. defensus), 'to defend*. See defend and -ible

Derivatives: defensibil-ity, п., defensible-ness.

п., defensibi-y, adv.

## defensive
defensive, adj. — F. defensif (fem. defensive), fr.

-ory.

## defer

## defer
defer, intr. v., to submit. — F. deferer, 'to yield,

or bring down, grant, allot, offer', fr. de- and
ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, Ίο carry', and
cp. confer and words there referred to.

## deference
deference, n. — F. deference, fr. deferer. See

## deferent
deferent, adj., ι) carrying away or down; 2)
pertaining to the ductus deferens (anat.) — L.
deferens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of defcrre. See

## deferential
deferential, adj. - Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. deferens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of deferre.
See defer, Ίο submit'.
Derivative: deferential-ly, adv.

## defervescence
defervescence, п., ι) a cooling down; 2)

-ce fr. L. defervescens, gen. -entis. See next
word and cp. effervescence.

defervescent, adj., pertaining 10 defervescence;

## defeudalize
defeudalize, tr. v., to deprive of feudal character.
— Compounded of de- (in the privative sense

## defiance

Derivatives: defiant-ly, adv., defiant-ness, n.

## deficiency
deficiency, n. — Late L. deficientia, 4he warning,

and -cy.

## deficient
deficient, adj. — L. deficiens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of deficere, 'to be wanting', fr. de- and

Derivatives: deficient, п., deficient-ly, adv.

## deficit

## defilade

Formed fr. prec. word with subst. suff. -ing.

foler, defouler, of s.m., fr. de- (see de-) and foler,

file-ment, п., defil-er, п., defil-ing-ly, adv.

Cp. OProven?. and OSp. desfilar, Sp. deshilar.
Port, desfiar, 'to march in files', and see file,
'thread'.

## defile
defile, п., a narrow passage. — F. defile, 'a

narrow passage*, prop, 'a passage in which troops

## define

ation, п., definitor, n. (q.v.)

## deflagrate

Ίο burn'. See flagrant and verbal suff. -ate.

## deflection

deform, tr. v. — F. deformer, fr. L. deformare.
Ίο deform, disfigure', fr. de- and formare, Ίο

deformation, n. — F. deformation, fr. L. deforma-
tionem, ace. of deformatio, 'a deforming, dis-

## degression

## degressive

## degringolade

## degust

## deha
deha, п., the body (Hinduism). — OI. dehah,

*I smear, anoint', dehf, 'rampart, dam, dike',
Avestic daeza, 'wall', pairi-daeza, 'enclosure',

## dehisce

hlscere, 'to split open, gape, yawn', fr. de-
and hlscere, inchoative of hiare, 'to yawn'.

## dehors

## dehort

Ίο dissuade', fr. de- and horxarl, 'to urge,

## dehortation

## dehumanize

## dehydrate

## dehypnotize

## Deianira

Δηιάνειρα, lit. 'destroyer of her husband', fr. δήϊος,

element is rel. to Gk. δηϊόω, Ί cut down, slay',
δαΐ, 'in battle', δαΐ-φρων, 'proved in battle',
δαίειν, 'to blaze, burn up', δάος, 'torch', δανός,

## deicide
deicide, п., the killer of a god. — Late L. deicida,

## deicide

cidium, compounded of L. deus, 'god', and
-cldium, 'killing'. See deity and -cide, 'killing*.

## deictic
deictic, adj., demonstrating, proving directly. —
Gk. δεικτίκός, 'able to show', fr. δεικτός,
'shown', verbal adj. of δεικνύναι., 'to show*,
which is cogn. with L. dlcere, 'to say, tell'. See
diction and -ic and cp. apodictic, epideictic. Cp.
also hygrodeik.

## deific
deific, adj., deifying. — F. deiftque, fr. L. dei-

## ftcus
ftcus, 'who makes one a god', which is
compounded of deus, 'god', and -ficus, fr. -ficere,
unstressed form of facere, 'to make, do*. See fact
and -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:225 COLUMN:3 -->

## deification
deification, п., the act of making a god; the state
of being made a god. — See deify and -ation.

## deiform
deiform, adj., having the form of a god. — ML.
deiformis, compounded of L. deus, 'god', and
forma, 'form, shape*. See deity and form, n.

## deify
deify, tr. v., to make a god of. — F. deifier, fr.
Late L. deificdre, which is compounded of L.
deus, 'god', and -ficare, 'to make', fr. -ficus, fr.
facere, 'to make, do'. See deity and -fy.

## deign
deign, intr. and tr. v., to condescend. — ME.
deinen, deignen, fr. OF. degnier, deignier (F.
daigner), fr. VL. *dignare, fr. L. digndrl, 'to
deem worthy', fr. dignus, 'worthy*. Cp. It. deg-
nare, ■ OProveng. denhar, Catal. denyar, Sp.
denar, which all derive fr. VL. *dignare, and see
dignity. Cp. also dainty, condign, dignify,
disdain.

## deipno-
deipno-, combining form meaning 'dining'. —
Gk. δείπνο-, fr. δεΐπνον, 'dinner', of unknown
origin.

## deipnosophist
deipnosophist, п., one learned in the art of
dining. — Gk. δειπνοσοφίστής, compounded of
δεΐττνον, 'dinner', and σοφιστής, 'a learned
man', fr. σοφός, 'skilled, clever, wise'. See
deipno- and sophist. Δειτυνοσοφίσταί (pi.) is the title
of a work by Athenaeus.
Derivative: deipnosophist-ic, adj.

## deism
deism, п., the belief that God has created the
world but has no immediate relation with it. —
F. deisme, a hybrid coined by Pascal (1623-62)
fr. L. Deus, 'God', and -isme, a suff. of Greek
origin. See deity and -ism.

## deist
deist, п., an adherent of deism. — F. deiste, a
hybrid word. See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: deist-ic, deist-ic-al, adjs., deist-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## deity
deity, n. — ME. deite, Гг. OF. deite (F. deite),
fr. Late L. deitdtem, ace. of deitds, 'divine
nature*, which was coined by Augustine on
analogy of Gk. θ-εότης, 'divine nature*, fr. L. deus,
'god', fr. OL. deivos (whence also L. dlvus,
'divine'), which is cogn. with OI. devak, 'god',
devt, 'goddess', Avestic daeva-, 'demon', Lith.
dievas, Lett, dievs, OPruss. deiwas, deiws, Olr.
dia (gen. de), OW. duiu, MW. duw, OCo. duy,
MCo. dew, 'God', OHG. Zio, Zio, ON. Tyr,
OE. Tlw, name of the Teutonic war god, Gk.
δΐος, 'divine', Ζευς, gen. Atf ός, Διός, 'Zeus', OI.
dyauh, 'heaven, god of Heaven*, Dyauspita,
'heavenly father', L. Diespiter, Jupiter. 'Jupiter'.
All these words come fr. *deyew(o)-, 'shining*,
which derives fr. I.-E. base *dei-, *deya-, *di-,
dyd-, 'to shine', whence also OI. df-de-ii, 'shines,
diva, 'by day', di-vasah, 'heaven; day', Arm. tiv,
'day', Gk.SdfXTo,'seemed', δήλος, Homeric δέελος
(for *δέι.-ελος), 'visible, clear', L. dies, Olr. die,
W. rfyuCday', Olr. in-diu, W. he-ddyw, 'today*. Cp.
Adelia, adelo-, adieu, adjourn, Bhumi Devi, daiva,
deiform, deify, deodand, deodar, devadasi, Dewali,
dial, Diana, diary, dies поп, diet, 'assembly', Dios-
ma, Dis, dismal, diurnal, diuturnal, diva, Dives,
divine, Dorothea, Dya us, eudiometer, joss, journey,
Jove, jovial, Jnpiter, Lent, meridian, prie-dieu,
quotidien, sojourn, Tuesday, Zenobia, Zeus.

## deject
deject, tr. v., to cast down. — L. dejectus, pp. of
dejicere, 'to throw down, drive off, lower, let
down; lo humble', fr. de- and jacere (pp. jac-
tus), 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and cp.
words there referred to. For the change of Latin
a (in jdctus) to ё (in de-jectus) see accent and cp.
words ihere referred to.

## dejecta
dejecta, n. pi., excrements. — L., neut. pi. of de-
jectus, pp. of dejicere. See prec. word.

## dejection
dejection, n. — OF. (F. dejection), fr. L. dejec-
tionem, ace. of dejectio, fr. dejectus, pp. of
dejicere. See deject and -ion.

## dejeuner
dejeuner, п., breakfast. — F. dejeuner,
'breakfast', from the verb dejeuner, 'to break the fast',
fr. OF. desjuner, shortened form of desjejuner
(see haphlogy), which derives fr. VL. disjejundre,
'to break the fast', fr. dis- and L.jejunus,
'fasting'. See jejuae and tp. dine, dinner. For sense
development ср. Е. to breakfast, lit. 'to break
the fast'.
Derivative: dejeuner, intr. v.

## de jure
de jure, by right, rightfully; the opposite of de
facto. — L. de jure, "by right*, fr. de, 'from,
down from, according to*, and abl. of jus,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:226 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 199 | DELLACRUSCAN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:226 COLUMN:1 -->
'right'. See de- and jus.

## delaine
delaine, п., a material made of wool, or of wool
and cotton. — F. de laine, 'of wool', fr. L. de,
'from', and lana, 'wool*. See de- and lanate.

## delate
delate, tr. v., to inform against. — L. delatus,
'brought or carried do\vn' (used as pp. of de-
ferre, 'to bring or carry down, to indict, inform
against'), formed fr. de- and laws, 'born,
carried' (used as pp. offerre, 'to bear, carry'),which_
siands for *tlatos, fr. *//-, zero degree of I.-E.
base *tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence L. tol-
lere, 'to lift up, raise', tolerare, 'to bear,
support'. See tolerate and cp. collate and words
there referred to.

## delation
delation, п., information against a person. — L.
delatio, gen. -onis, 'denunciation, accusation',
fr. delatus, 'brought or carried down'. See prec.
word and -ion.

## delator
delator, п., an informer. — L. delator, fr. delatus,
'brought or carried down*. See delate and
agential sufF. -or.

## delay
delay, tr. and intr. v., to defer, postpone. — ME.
delai?n, fr. OF. delaier, fr. de- and laier, 'to let,
leave'. Originally Ihe verb later occurred only
in those forms of the present, in which the
radical was stressed, and in the future. These forms
prob. derive from the respective forms of OF.
laissier, 'to let, leave', and were influenced in
their conjugation by that of /aire, 'to do'. (See
Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. Г76 s.v. delai.) OF.
laissier (whence F. laisser) derives fr. L. laxare,
'to unloose, relax', fr. laxus, 'loose'. See lax
and cp. relay.
Derivatives: delay, п., delay-age, п., delay-er, п.,
delay-ing-ly, adv.

## del credere
del credere, a phrase expressing the obligation of
an agent who guarantees the solvency of a buyer
(law), — It., lit. 'of trust*. Del is contracted from
the prep, de, 'of (fr. L. de), and the def. art.
il (fr. L. ilium, ace. of We, 'that one'). See de-
and ille. It. credere derives fr. L. credere, 'to
believe'. See creed.

## dele
dele, v., typographic direction to blot out a letter,
a word, etc. — L. dele, imper. sing, of delere,
'to destroy; wipe out, blot out, efface'. See
delete. ,

## delectable
delectable, adj., delightful. — OF. (F. delectable),
fr. L. delectabilis, 'delightful', fr. delectare, 'to
delight1. See next word and -able.
Derivatives: delectabil-ity4 п., delectable-ness,
п., delectabl-y, adv.

## delectation
delectation, п., delight, enjoyment. — OF.
delectation (F. delectation), fr. L. delectationem, ace.
of delectatio, 'a delighting, pleasure,
amusement', fr. delectatus, pp. οι delectare, 'to delight,
charm, amuse', freq. of delicere, 'to entice',fr.
de- and lacere, 'to entice', which is cogn. with
laqueus, 'noose snare*. See lace, п., and cp.
words there referred to.

## delectus
delectus, п., a collection of passages for translation.
— L. delectus, 'choice, selection', fr. delectus,
pp. of deligere, 'to pick out, choose, select', fr.
de- and legere, 'to choose; to re£d'. See lecture.

## delegacy
delegacy, n. — Formed fr. delegate, п., with
suff. -cy.

## delegate
delegate, n. — L. delegatus, pp. of delegare, 'to
send, assign, delegate, transfer', fr. de- and le-
gare, 'to send with a commission, appoint as a
deputy'. See legate.

## delegate
delegate, adj., delegated. — L. delegatus, pp. of
delegare. See delegate, n.

## delegate
delegate, tr. v. — L. delegatus, pp. of delegare.
See delegate, n.

## delegation
delegation, n. — L. delegatio, gen. -onis,
'assignment, delegation', fr. delegatus, pp. of delegare.
See delegate, п., and -ion.

## delete
delete, tr. v., to erase. — L. defetus, pp. of delere,
'to efface, abolish, obliterate, destroy', which is
prob. a back formation from de-levi
(misinterpreted as dele-vi), perf. oide-linere, 'to besmear',
fr. de- and linere, 'to daub, smear' (applied esp.
to the wax on the writing table). Accordingly
the orig. meaning of delere prob. was 'to wipe
out'. See liniment and cp. slime. Cp. also dele,
delible.

## deleterious
deleterious, adj., harmful, — ML. deletertus, fr.
Gk. δηλητήριος, 'noxious', fr. δηλητήρ,
'destroyer', fr. δηλεΐσϊ>αι, Ίο hurt, damage', which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:226 COLUMN:2 -->
is cogn. with Toch. A talo, В tallawo, 'miserable,
wretched', Lett, delit, 'to wear out, worry,
harass'. These words prob. meant orig. 'to cut,
split', whence 'to hurt by cutting', and derive
fr. I.-E. base *def-, *dol-, 'to split, cut, carve',
whence also L. dolare 'to hew with an ax'. See
dole, 'grief, and words there referred to. For
the ending see suff. -ous. The word deleterious
was introduced into English by the physician
Sir Thomas Browne (1605-82).
Derivatives; deleterious-ly, adv., deletcrious-
ness, n.

## deletion
deletion, n. — L. deletio, gen. -onis, fr. deletus,
pp. of delere. See delete and -ion.

## delft
delft, also delf, п., glazed earthenware. — Prop,
earthenware of Delft (formerly Delf), name of
a town in Holland. The name lit. means 'canal'
and is cogn. with E. delve (q.v.)

## Delia
Delia, fern. PN. — L. Delia, orig. epithet of the
goddess Artemis, lit. 'Delian', from her
birthplace Delos. See Delian,

## Delian
Delian, adj., pertaining to the island of Delos
in the Aegean Sea. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Defius, fr. Gk. Δήλιος, fr. Δήλος, 'Delos'.
Cp. prec. word.

## deliberate
deliberate, adj. — L. deliberatus, pp. of deliberure,
'to think over, take counsel about, reflect,
determine', which prob. means lit. 'to weigh in
one's mind', and derives fr. original *de-librare,
which is formed fr. de- and libra, 'scales; that
which is weighed; a pound'. See libra and adj.
suff. -ate and cp. equilibrium. L. deltberare was
influenced in form by liberare, 'to make free'.
Derivatives: deliberate-ly, adv., deliberate-
ness, n.

## deliberate
deliberate, intr. and tr. v. — L. deliberatus, pp.
of deltberare. See deliberate, adj., and verbal
suff. -ate.

## deliberation
deliberation, n. — ME. deliberacioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) deliberation, fr. L. deliberationem, ace. of
deliberation 'deliberation, consideration', fr.
deliberatus, pp. of deliberure. See deliberate, v. and
adj., and -ioa.

## deliberative
deliberative, adj. — L. deliberative, 'pertaining
to deliberation', fr. deliberatus, pp. of deltberare.
See deliberate, adj., and -ive.
Derivatives: deliberative-ly, adv., deliberative-
ness, n.

## delible
delible, adj., capable of being deleted. — Fr.
earlier deleble, fr. L. defebifis, 'that which can be
blotted out', fr. delere. See delete. Delible was
influenced in form by the many adjectives ending
in -ibfe (fr. L. ibilis).

## delicate
delicate, adj., l) dainty; 2) fine. — L. delicatus,
'delightful, charming, voluptuous', pp. of * deli-
сйге, rel. to delicere, 'to allure, entice, delight'
(whence the freq. delectare) and to deliciae,
'allurement, charm, delight'. See lace and cp.
delectation, delicious, delight. The derivation of
deli-:atus, fr. *de~ficiatus, a supposed derivative
of deliciae, is erroneous. See Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., I, p. 336.
Derivatives: delicate, п., delicate-ly, adv., deli-
cate-ness, п., delica-cy, п., delicatessen (q.v.)

## delicatessen
delicatessen, n. pi., cooked foods. — G. Delika-
tessen (p|.), fr. F. delicatesse, 'delicacy', fr. deli-
cat, 'delicate', fr. L. delicatus. See prec, word.

## delicious
delicious, adj. — OF. delicieus (F. delicieux), fr.
VL. deliciosus, fr. L. deliciae (gen. -arum),
'allurement, charm, delight, pleasure', fr. *de~-
laquiae, which is formed fr. de- and laqueus,
'noose, snare'. See lace and cp. delicate and
words there referred to. Cp. also luscious. For
the change of Latin a in laqueus 10 ί in de-ficiae
see abigeat and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: delicious-ly, adv., delicious-ness, n.

## delict
delict, п., an offense against the law. — L.
delictum, 'fault, offense, transgression', prop. neut.
pp. of dilinquere, 'to fail, be wanting,
transgress, offend', fr. de- and linquere, 'to leave'.

See relinquish and cp. delinquent, relict, derelict,

delight, tr. and inir. v. — ME. deliten, fr. OF.

## defiter
defiter, 'to delight', fr. L. delectare, 'to delight,

## charm
charm, amuse'. See delectation and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: delight-ed, adj., delight-ed-ly, adv.,

## delighi-ed-ness
delighi-ed-ness, п., delighi-er, п., delight-ing,

## adj.
adj., delight-ing-ly, adv.

## delight
delight, n. — ME. delit, fr. OF. delit, fr. deliter,
'to delight'. See delight, v.
Derivatives: delight-ful, adj., delight-ful-ly, adv.,
delight-ful-ness, п., delight-some, adj.

## Delilah
Delilah, п., the mistress of Samson, who
betrayed Samson (Judges, chapter 16). — Heb.
D4ilah, lit. 'delicate, languishing, amorous',
from the base of d-l-l, 'to hang down, to
languish', whence also dal, 'low, poor, thin', dalluh,
'hair; thrum' (lit. 'that which hangs down');
rel. to Akkad. dafalu, 'to be weak or humble',
Arab, dalla, 'he was low or pliant', tadaldala,
'it hung down, dandled', Ethiop. dalul,
'hanging curls'.

## delimit
delimit, tr. v., to mark the limits of. — F.
delimiter, fr. L. delimitare, 'to mark out, limit', fr.
de- and Umitare, 'to limit'. See limit, v., and cp.
next word.

## delimitate
delimitate, tr. v., to delimit. — L. delimitatus,
pp. of delimitare. See prec. word and verbal
suff. -ate.

## delimitation
delimitation, n. — L. delimitaiio, gen. -onis, fr.
delimitatus, pp. of delimitare. See delimitate
and -ion.

## delineate
delineate, tr. v., to sketch. — L. deltneatus, pp. of
deltneare, 'to sketch out', formed fr. de- and
linea, 'line'. See line and verbal suff. -ate.

## delineation
delineation, n. — Late L. delineatio, gen. -onis,
'a sketch', fr. L. delineatus, pp. of delineare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## delinquency
delinquency, n. — L. delinquentia, 'a fault, crime,
delinquency', fr. delinquens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of dilinquere, 'to fail, be wanting,
transgress, offend'. See delict and -ency.

## delinquent
delinquent, adj. — L. delinquens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of delinquere. See prec. word and -ent.
Derivatives: delinquent, п., delinquent-ly, adv.

## deliquesce
deliquesce, intr. v., to become liquid. — L. de-
liquescere, 'to melt away, dissolve', fr. de- and
liquescere, 'to become liquid'. See liquescent.

## deliquescence
deliquescence, n. — Formed with suff. -ce fr. L.
deliquescens, gen. -entis. See next word.

## deliquescent
deliquescent, adj., deliquescing. — L.
deliquescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of deliquescere. See
deliquesce and -ent.

## delirious
delirious, adj. — Formed fr. delirium with suff.
-ous.
Derivatives: delirious-ly, adv., delirious-ness, n.

## delirium
delirium, п., a violent mental excitement. — L.
delirium, 'madness, delirium', fr. delirare, 'to
turn aside from the furrow', whence arose the
meanings 'to deviate, to become deranged,
crazy or delirious', fr. de- and lira, 'the earth
thrown up between two furrows, furrow'. L.
lira stands for *leisa and is cogn. with Goth.,
OHG. leisa (in wagenleisa), 'track of carriage
wheels', MHG. leise, gefeis, G. Geleise, Gteis,
'track', and also with Goth, lais, Ί know*,
laisjan, OE. Шгап, 'to leach', OE. leornian, 'to
learn' (fr. Teut. base *lais-, 'to learn, know,
teach', orig. 'to follow or find the track'). See
learn and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
lirella.

## delitescence
delitescence, delitescency, n. — Formed fr. next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## delitescent
delitescent, adj., latent (said of symptoms of a
disease). — L. delitescens, gen. -entis, pres. part.
of delitescere, 'to lie hidden, be concealed', fr.
de- and latescere, 'to hide oneself, lie hidden',
inchoative of latere, 'to lie hidden'. See latent.
For the change of Latin a (in latescere) to Ϊ
(in de-fitescere) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

## deliver
deliver, tr. v. — OF. defivrer (F. defivrer), 'to set
free', fr. VL. deltberare, of s.m., fr. de- and
liberare, 'to set free', fr. liber, 'free'. See liberal and
cp. liberate.

## deliverance
deliverance, n. — OF. delivrance (F. delivrance),
fr. delivrer. See prec. word and -ance.

## delivery
delivery, n. — OF. delivree, prop. fern. pp. of
delivrer, 'to set free, to deliver', used as a noun.
See deliver and cp. livery.

## dell
dell, a small valley. — OE., rel. to MLG., MDu.
defle, MHG., G. delle, telle and to E. daie,
'valley' (q.v.)
Delia < ruscan, i) adj., pertaining to the Acca-
demia delta Crusca (established in 1582 for the
sake of purifying the Italian language); 2) п., а
