member of the Accademia della Crusca.

## Delia Robbia
Delia Robbia, also Delia Robbia ware, a kind of
terra-cotta ware made in Florence by Luca della
Robbia (died in 1482), his family or his pupils.

## Delphian
Delphian, adj., Delphic. — See next word and
-ian.

## Delphic
Delphic, adj., l) pertaining to Delphi; pertaining
to the oracle in Delphi. — L. Delpkicus, fr. Gk.
Δελφικός, 'of, or pertaining to, Delphi*, fr.
Δέλφοι, 'Delphi'.

## Delphinidae
Delphinidae, n.pl., a family of toothed whales
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L.
defpkinus, 'dolphin'. See dolphin.

## Delphinium
Delphinium, п., a genus of plants, the larkspur
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δελφίνι,ον, 'larkspur*,
fr. δελφίς, gen. δελφίνος, 'dolphin* (see
dolphin); so called from the shape of its flowers,
which resemble a dolphin.

## delta
delta, п., ι) name of the 4th letter of the Greek
alphabet; 2) triangular area formed at the mouth
of some rivers, as of the Danube. — Gk. δέλτα,
fr. Heb.-Phoen. duleth; see daleth. The α was
added because a Greek word cannot end with
a τ; ср. alpha and words there referred to.

## deltafication
deltafication, п., the formation of a delta. —
Formed fr. delta and -fication.

## deltaic
deltaic, adj., forming a delta. — Formed fr. delta
with sufF. -ic.

## deltoid
deltoid, adj., delta-shaped, triangular. — Gk.
δελτοειδής, compounded of δέλτα and -οειδής
'like*, fr. είδος 'form, shape*. See delta and -oid.

## deltoid
deltoid, п., the large muscle covering the shoulder
joint (anat.) — From deltoid, adj.; so called
from its triangular shape.

## delubrum
delubrum, п., a shrine, a sanctuary (Roman an-
tiq.) — L. delubrum, 'temple, shrine, sanctuary*,
a derivative of deluere, 'to wash off, cleanse',
originally meaning 'place for washing (near the
sanctuary)'. Delubrum prob. stands for *de-
lu-dhlom or *de-lu-dhrom, fr. de, 'away from*,
the stem of luere, 'to wash', and a suff. denoting
place (cp. pollubrum, polubrum, 'wash basin',
for *pd~Iu-dhlom or *po-lu-dhrom). See de- and
lave.

## delude
delude, tr. v., to deceive, beguile. — L. deludere,
'to mock, deceive, play false', fr. de- and ludere,
4o play*. See ludicrous and cp. delusion. Cp. also
allude and words there referred to.
Derivatives: delud-ingy adj., delud-ing-ly, adv.

## deluge
deluge, п., the great flood, flood. — F. deluge, fr.
L. diluvium, 'a flood, inundation', fr. diluere, 'to
wash away', fr. di- 'apart', and lucre, 'to wash,
lave, cleanse'. See lave and cp. diluvium.
Derivative: deluge, tr. v.

## delundung
delundung, п., a mammal of the Malay
Archipelago, pertaining to the civet family. — Native
name.

## delusion
delusion, п., the act of deluding; a mistaken
belief. — L. delusio, gen. -onis, 'a deceiving', fr.
delusus, pp. of deludere. See delude and -ion and
cp. allusioa and words there referred to.

## delusive
delusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
delusus, pp. of deludere. See delude and cp.
allusive and words there referred to.
Derivatives: defusive-ly, adv., delusive-ness, n.

## delve
delve, tr. and intr. v., to dig {archaic). — ME.
delven, fr. OE. delfan, 'to dig, burrow*, rel. to
OS. delfian, Du. delven, MHG. telben, 'to dig',
and cogn. with Lith. delba, 'crowbar', Russ.
dolbif, Czech dlabati, Pol. dlubac, 'to chisel',
Russ. doloto, Czech dlato, Pol. dloto (for *dolb-
to), 'chisel'. Cp. delft.

## delve
delve, п., a hollow. — OE. gedelf, 'ditch, trench*,
rel. to delfan. See delve, v.

## dem-
dem-, form of demo- before a vowel.

## demagaetize
demagaetize, tr. v. — Formed fr. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix) and magnetize.
Derivatives: demagnetiz-ation, п., demagnetiz-
er, n.

## demagogic
demagogic, demagogical, adj. — Gk.
δημαγωγικός, 'fit for a popular leader', fr. δημαγωγός, 'a
popular leader'. See next word and suff. -ic,
resp. also -al.
Derivative: demagogical-ly, adv.

## demagogue
demagogue, n. — Gk. δημαγωγός, *a popular
leader, leader of the mob', compounded of
δήμος, 'district, country, land, people', and
αγωγός, 'leading'. Gk. δήμος, Dor. δαμος stand

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:227 COLUMN:2 -->
for *da-mos and,are cogn. with Olr. dam,
'followers, troop'. Both Gk. δήμος, δαμος, and Olr.
dam orig. meant 'part, division', and are
derivatives of I.-E. base da-m-, an -^-enlargement
of base *da-, *dai-, 'to divide', whence Gk.
δαίεσ&αΛ, 'to divide, distribute', δαίμων, 'god,
goddess', lit. 'divider, distributor (of men's
destinies)*. See demon and cp. words there
referred to. Gk. αγωγός, 'leading*, derives fr.
#γεΐν, 'to lead*; see -agogue.
Derivatives: demagogic (q.v.), demagog-ism, п.,
demagogu-ery, п., demagogy (q.v.)

## demagogy
demagogy, n. — Gk. δημαγωγία, 'leadership of
the people', fr. δημαγωγός. See demagogue and
-y (representing Gk. -ία).

## demand
demand, tr. v. — F. demander, 'to ask, request',
fr. L. demandare, 'to give in charge, entrust,
commit', in VL., 'to ask, request, demand', fr.
de- and mandare, 4o give in charge, enjoin'.
Cp. It. domandare, OProvenc., Catal., Sp. de-
mandar, 'to ask, request', and see mandate.
Derivatives: demand-er, п., demand-ing, adj.,
demand-ing-ly, adv.

## demand
demand, n. — F. demande, fr. demander. See
demand, v.

## demandant
demandant, п., plaintiff (law). — F., 'asking,
requesting', pres. part of demander. See demand,
v., and -ant.

## demarcate
demarcate, tr. v. — Back formation fr.
demarcation.

## demarcation
demarcation, n. — F. demarcation, fr. Sp.
demarcation, fr. demarcar, 'to mark out the
boundary*, fr. de- and marcar, 'to mark', fr. marcat
'mark', fr. MHG. marke. See mark, 'sign', and
-ation. The word was first used of the linea de
demarcacion ('demarcation line*) established in
M93 by Pope Alexander VI, in order to divide
the New World between the Spaniards and the
Portuguese.

## demarch
demarch,n., i) (in ancient Greece) a ruler of a
deme; 2) (in modern Greece) a mayor. — Gk.
δήμαρχος, lit. 'chief of the people', fr. δήμος,
'people', and άρχος, 'chief, ruler'. See deme and
-arch.

## demarche
demarche, п., proceeding, course of action. —
F., lit. 'gait, walk, bearing', fr. de- (see de-) and
marcher, 'to walk'. See march, 'walk, advance'.

## dematerialize
dematerialize, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. de-
fin the privative sense of this prefix) and mate-
rislize.
Derivative: dematerializ-ation, n.

## deme
deme, п., a township in ancient Greece. — Gk.
δήμος, 'district, country, land, people'. See
demos.

## demean
demean, tr. v., to conduct (oneself). — ME. de-
meinen, demenen, fr. OF. demener, 'to guide,
conduct' (whence F. se demener, 'to struggle'),
fr. de- and mener, 'to lead', fr. VL. minare,
'to drive (cattle)', prop, 'to drive by threatening*
(whence also It. menare, 'to lead'), fr. L. minarl,
'to threaten' (whence Rum. типа, 'to threaten').
See miaatory and cp. menace, promenade.

## demean
demean, tr. v., to debase. — Formed fr. de- and
mean, 'low'.

## demeanor
demeanor, demeanour, n. — Formed fr. ME. de-
meanure, 'behavior', with change of suff. due
to the influence of nouns ending in -or, -our.
See demean, 'to behave', and -or (representing
OF. -our, -or).

## dement
dement, tr. v., to cause to become mad. — L. de·
mentdre, 'to drive mad, craze', fr. demens, gen.
dementis, 'mad, raving, crazy*, lit. 'out of one's
mind*, fr. de- and mens, gen. mentis, 'mind'.
See mental, 'pertaining to the mind', and cp.
dementia.
Derivatives: dement-ed, adj., dement-ed-ly, adv.

## dementi
dementi, п., an official denial. — F., prop. pp. of
dementir, 'to give the He to, contradict', used
as a noun, fr. de- (see de-) and mentir (fr. L.
mentiri), 'to lie*. See mendacious.

## dementia
dementia, п., a form of insanity. — L, dementia^
'insanity, madness*, lit. 'a being out of one's
mind*, fr. demens, gen. -entis, 'mad, raving,
crazy'. See dement.

## demerit
demerit, п., want of merit, ill desert. — OF.
demerge (F. demerite), 'blame, demerit', fr. VL.
demeritum, 'fault', fr. pref. de-, taken in a
privative sense (see de-), and meritum, 'desert,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:227 COLUMN:3 -->
reward, merit'; see merit. In contradistinction to
VL. demeritum, 'fault', classical L. demeritum
means 'merit, desert'. This contrast of meaning
finds its explanation in fhe fact that classical
L. demeritum prop, is the neut. pp. of dimerere,
demereri, 'to merit, deserve*, in which the pref.
de has intensive force; cp. next word.

## demerit
demerit, tr. v., to merit, deserve (archaic). — F.
demeriter, 'to deserve ill', fr. demerite. See prec.
word.

## demeritorious
demeritorious, adj., blameworthy. — Formed
with suff. -orious fr. VL. demeritum, 'fault'. See
demerit, п., and cp. meritorious.

## demersal
demersal, adj., sunk to the bottom (said of the
eggs offish). — Formed with adj. suff. -al from
the obsolete verb demerse, 'to immerse', fr. L.
demersus, pp. oidemergere, 'to submerge*, fr. de-
and mergere, 'to plunge, immerse'. See merge.

## demesne
demesne, п., ι) possession (of land) as one's own
(law); 2) an estate kept by the owner for his
own use. — ME. demein, fr. AF. demeine,
demesne (with silent s), fr. OF. demaine, demeine
(whence also F. domaine, 'domain, estate'), fr.
L. dominicus, 'pertaining to the lord', fr. domi-
nus, 'lord, master'. See domain. The 5 in demesne
is prob. due to an erroneous association of this
word with OF. maisniee, mesnee, 'household',
fr. VL. *mansionata, fr. L. mansio, gen. -onis,
'habitation' (see mansion).

## Demeter
Demeter, п., the goddess of agriculture in Greek
mythology. —Gk. Δημήτηρ,ΟοΓ.Ο^Δαμάτηρ,
lit. 'earth-mother', fr. δα, Doric equivalent of
Gk. γη, 'earth', and μάτηρ\ Doric equivalent of
Gk. μήτηρ, 'mother'. See geo- and mother and
cp. next word.

## Demetrius
Demetrius, masc. PN. — L. Demetrius, fr. Gk.
Δημήτριος, lit. 'son of Demeter', fr. Δημήτηρ.
See Demeter.

## demi-
demi-, pref. meaning 'half. — F. demi, 'half, fr.
VL. dimedius, a blend of L. medius, 'middle',
and dimidius, 'half. This latter is a back
formation fr. dimidiatus, 'halved', pp. of dimidiare,
'to halve', fr. dis-, di-, and medius, 'middle'.
OProvenc. demeg, 'half, also derives fr. VL.
dimedius. See di-, 'apart', and cp. medium.Cp.
also dimidiate, demy and talmi gold.

## demigod
demigod, п., a deified hero. — Lit. 'half god', a
hybrid coined fr. demi- and god.

## demijohn
demijohn, п., a large botlle covered with wicker-
work. — Alteration of¥.dame-jeanne, for Dame
Jeanne, 'Lady Jane', a name used humorously
to denote a bottle; see dame and Jane. The
alteration of F. dame to demi in English demijohn
is due to a confusion with F. demi, 'half (see
demi-).

## demilune
demilune, п., ι) a half-moon, crescent; 2) a
crescent-shaped outwork. — F. demi-fune, 'half-
moon', fr. demi, 'half, and lune (fr. L. luna),
'moon'. See demi- and lune.

## demimonde
demimonde, п., a class of women of doubtful
social standing. — F. demi-monde, lit. 'half-
world', coined by Alexandre Dumas fils in
1855, who used it as the title of one of his most
successful social comedies. For the etymology
of F. demi see demi-. F. monde derives fr. L.
mundus, 'world'. See mundane.

## demirep
demirep, п., a woman of doubtful reputation
(slang). — Shortened fr. demi-reputation, in
which demi is used in the sense given to it in F.
demi-monde. See prec. word and reputation.

## demise
demise, п., ι) transference of an estate by death;
hence also 2) death. — AF., prop. fern. pp. of
OF. — AF. demetre (whence F. demettre, pp.
demis, fern, demise). Ίο send away, dismiss'.
See demit.
Derivatives: demise, tr. and intr. v., demis-able,
adj.

## demisemlquaver
demisemlquaver, п., an English term for a thirty-
second note (music). — Lit. 'the half of a
semiquaver'. See demi- and semiquaver.

## demission
demission, n. — F. demission, fr. L. demissionem,
ace. of demissio, 'a sending down or away', fr.
demissus, pp. of demittere. See next word and
-ion.

## demit
demit, tr. and intr. v., to resign. — Orig. Ίο
dismiss', fr. L. demittere 'to send down or away',
fr. de- and mittere (pp. missus), 'to send'. See
mission and cp. demise, dismiss.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:228 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 201 | DENDRITE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:228 COLUMN:1 -->

## demiurge
demiurge, п., ι) in some ancient Greek states, a
magistrate; 2) in Platonic philosophy, the
Maker of the world. — Gk. δημιουργός, 'one
who works for the people, skilled workman,
maker, creator, the Creator of the visible world',
compounded of δήμιος, 'pertaining to the
people', and έργον, 'work'. Gk. δήμιος derives
fr. δήμος, 'people'; see demos. For the second
element see ergon.

## deminrgic
deminrgic, deminrgical, adj., pertaining to a
demiurge; creative. — Gk. δημιουργικός, fr.
δημιουργός. See prec. word and -ic, resp. also -al.

## demivolt
demivolt, п., a half turn with the forelegs raised
(manege). — F. demi-volte, fr. demi, 'half, and
volte, *a leap'. See demi- and vault, 'to leap1,
and cp. volt, 'a turning movement'.

## demo-
demo-, before a vowel dem-, combining form
meaning 'people, population, deme'. — Gk.
δήμο-, δημ-, fr. δήμος, "district, country, land,
people'. See demos.

## demobilize
demobilize, tr. v. — Formed fr. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix) and mobilize.
Derivative: demobiliz-ation, n.

## democracy
democracy, n. — F. democratic, fr. ML. demo-
cratia, fr. Gk. δημοκρατία, 'democracy, popular
government', lit. 'rule of the people', fr. δήμος,
'people', and -κρατία, fr. κράτος, 'strength,
power, rule'. See demos and -cracy.

## democrat
democrat, n. — F. democrate, back formation fr.
democratic. See prec. word.

## democratic
democratic, adj. — F. democratique, fr. ML. de~
mocraticus, fr. Gk. δημοκρατικός, 'pertaining
to democracy', fr. δημοκράτη. See democracy
and -ic.
Derivative: democrat ic-al-ly, adv.

## democratism
democratism, n. — See next word and -ism.

## democratize
democratize, tr. v. — F. democratiser, fr.
democratic. Cp. Gk. δημοκρατίζειν, 'to be on the
democratic side', and see democrat and -ize.
Derivative: democratiz-ation, n.

## Demodex
Demodex, п., a genus of arachnids, the face mite
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. δημός,
'fat', and δήξ, 'worm'. The first element is cogn.
with Alb. djame, 'fat, bacon', and prob. also
with Arm. tam-uk, 'moist, wet'. The second
element lit. means 'biter', and is rel. to δάξ,
'biting'. See Dacus.

## Demogorgoa
Demogorgoa, п., a terrible deity {Greek mythoi.)
— Late L., first mentioned by Lactantius (or
Lutaiius) Placidus on Statius. The first element
in the name of this deity is of uncertain origin.
The second element certainly derives fr. Gk.
γοργός, 'terrible'. See Gorgon.

## demography
demography, п., statistics of births, marriages,
diseases, deaths, etc. — Coined fr. demo- and
Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See demo-
and -graphy.
Derivatives: demograph-ic, demograph-ic-al,
adjs., demograph-ic-al-ly, adv., demograph-ist, n.

## demoiselle
demoiselle, п., ι) a damsel {archaic); 2) a small
crane of N. Africa; the Numidian crane. — F.
fr. OF. dameiselfe, damoiselle, fr. VL. *domini-
cella, dimin. of domina, 'mistress, lady', fern.
of L. dominus, 'lord', fr. domus, 'house*. See
dome and cp. dame. Cp. also damsel, damoiseau,
doncella, donzella; cp. also Don.

## demolish
demolish, tr. v. — Fr. OF, demoliss-, pres. part,
stem of demolir (F. demolir), 'to pull down,
overthrow, destroy, demolish*, fr. L. demolirX,
'to throw or pull down, overthrow, demolish',
fr. de- and molirlt 'to construct', fr. moles, 'mass,
heap'. See mole, 'mound', and verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: demolish-er, п., demolish~mentt n.

## demolition
demolition, n. — F. demolition, fr. L. demolitio-
nem, ace. of demolttio, 'a pulling down', fr. de-
molitus, pp. oidemoliri. See prec. word and -ion.

## demon
demon, n. — L. daemon, 'a spirit', in Eccles. L.!
'an evil spirit', fr. Gk. δαίμων, *god, goddess',
lit. 'a divider, distributor (of men's destinies)',
which is rel. to δαίεσθαι, *to divide, distribute;
to feed on', δαίς, δαίτη, δαιτός, 'meal,
banquet', Soclvuvou, 'to give a banquet or feast',
δαΐζειν, 'to cleave asunder, rend, divide', δήμος,
'district, country, land, people', fr. I.-E. base
*da-, *dai-, *dt-, *de-, 'to cut off, separate,
divide, distribute', whence also OE. tld, 'time',
ttma, 'time, date', prop, 'division of time*. See
tide and cp. demagogue, deme, democracy,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:228 COLUMN:2 -->
demos. Cp. also eudaemonic, pandemonium,
geodesy. Cp. also dah. For a derivative of *di-t-,
a -f-enlargement of base *de-, see datolite.

## demoa-
demoa-, form of demono- before a vowel.

## demonetization
demonetization, n. — F. demonetisation, fr. de-
monetiser. See next word and -ation.

## demonetize
demonetize, tr. v,, to deprive of monetary value.
— F. demonetiser, fr. de- (used in the privative
sense of this prefix), and monetiser. See de- and
moaetize.

## demoniac
demoniac, demoniacal, adj., possessed by a
demon. — Late L. daemoniacus, fr. Gk. δαιμονια-
κός, 'possessed by a demon', fr. δαιμόνιος, 'of, or
pertaining to, a demon', fr. δαίμων. See demon.
Derivative: demoniacal-ly, adv.

## demonic
demonic, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
a demon. — Late L. daemonicus, fr. Gk.
δαιμονικός, 'possessed by a demon', fr. δαίμων.
See demon and -ic.

## demoa ism
demoa ism, п., belief in demons. — Gk.
δαιμονισμός, *a being possessed by a demon', fr.
δαίμων. See demon and -ism.

## demonist
demonist, п., an adherent of demon ism. — See
prec. word and -ist

## demonize
demonize, tr. v., 1) to convert inlo a demon;
2) to subject to the influence of a demon. —
ML. daemonizare, fr. L. daemon, fr. Gk. δαίμων.
See demon and -ize.

## demono-
demono-, demon-, combining form from Gk.
δαίμων, gen. δαίμονος, 'demon*. — See demon.

## demonolatry
demonolatry, п., the worship of ghosts. —
Compounded of demono- and -λατρεία, -λατρία,
fr, λατρεία, 'hired labor, worship'. See -latry.

## demono logy
demono logy, п., the study of popular beliefs in
demons. — Compounded of demono- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a cer-
lain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: demonolog-ic, adj., demonolog-ic-
al-ly, adv., demono fog-ist, n.

## demonstrable
demonstrable, adj. — L. demonstrabilis, 'that
which can be pointed out or demonstrated', fr.
demonstrare. See demonstrate and -able.
Derivatives: demonstrabil-ityt п., demonstrable-
ness, п., demonstrabl-y, adv.

## demonstrate
demonstrate, tr. and intr. v. — L. demonstratus,
pp. of demonstrare, 'to point out, indicate, show,
demonstrate', fr. de- and monstrare, 'to show,
point out'. See monster and verbal suff. -ate.

## demonstration
demonstration, n. — L, demonstratio, gen. -onis,
'a pointing out, showing, demonstration', fr,
demonstratus, pp. of demonstrare. See prec.
word and -ion.
Derivatives: demonstration-al, adj.,
demonstrationist (q.v.)

## demonstrationist
demonstrationist, п., one who takes part in a
demonstration. — See prec. word and -ist.

## demonstrative
demonstrative, adj. — F. demonstratij'(fern,
demonstrative), fr. L. demonstrative, 'pointing out,
demonstrating', fr. demonstratus, pp. of
demonstrare. See demonstrate and -ive.
Derivatives: demonstrative-ly, adv., demonstra-
tive-ness, n.

## demonstrator
demonstrator, n. — L. demonstrator, 'one who
points out or demonstrates', fr. demonstratus, pp.
of demonstrare. See demonstrate and agential
suff. -or.

## demoralize
demoralize, tr. v. — F. demoraliser, fr. de (in the
privative sense of this pref.) and moraliser, 'to
moralize'. See de- and moralize.
Derivatives: demoraliz-ation, п., demoraliz-er, n.

## demos
demos, п., the common people; the mob. — L.,
fr. Gk. δήμος, 'district, country, land, people',
which stands for *damos, lit. 'a division of the
people', and is cogn. with Olr. dam, 'followers',
fr. I.-E. base *da-, *dai-, 'to cut off, separate,
divide', whence also Gk. δαίμων, 'god, goddess',
lit. 'divider, distributor (of men's destinies)'. See
demon and cp. deme, demo-, demotic, endemic,
epidemic, paademic, and the first element in
Damocles, demagogue, democracy.

## Demosthenic
Demosthenic, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
Demosthenes (384-322); eloquent. — L. Demos-
thenicus, fr. Gk. Δημοσθενικός, fr. Δημοσθένης,
'Demosthenes',

## demotic
demotic, adj., 1) popular; 2) specif, designating
the popular form of the ancient Egyptian
writing, as distinguished from hieratic. — Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:228 COLUMN:3 -->
δημοτικός, 'pertaining to the people, popular',
fr. δήμος, 'people'. See demos and -ic.

## dempster
dempster, п., a judge. — ME. demestre, formally
fern, of demere, 'deemer, fr. demen, 'to judge'.
See deem and cp. deemster, doomster.

## demulcent
demulcent, adj., soothing; п., a soothing
substance. — L. demulcens, gen. -entis, pres. part,
of demulcere, 'to stroke down, to soften', fr.
de- and mulcire, 'to soften, appease', fr. I.-E.
base *melk-, which is rel. to *melg-, 'to milk*
(the original meaning of both bases was 'to
stroke, rub, squeeze'). See milk and cp. emul-
gent, emulsify, Mulciber. For the ending see
suff. -ent.

## flemur
flemur, intr. v., to object. — OF. demorer,
demurer, demourer, 'to linger, tarry' (whence F.
demeurer, 'to remain, stay, reside, live'), fr. L.
demorari, 'to linger, loiter, tarry', fr. de- and
morari, 'to delay', fr. mora, 'hesitation, delay'.
See moratory.
Derivatives: demur, п., demurrage (qq.v.),
demurrable, adj., demurrer (q.v.), demurr-ing-ly,
adv.

## demur
demur, п., objection. — OF. demor, fr. demorer.
See demur, v.

## demure
demure, adj., 1) sober; 2) affectedly modest. —
Fr. OF. de {bons) murs, 'of (good) manners', fr.
de, 'of, from' (fr. L. de) and murs (whence F.
maurs), 'manners', fr. L. mores, pi. of mos,
'manner, custom, conduct, behavior'. See
dean d moral.
Derivatives: demure-ly, adv., demure-ness, n.

## demurrage
demurrage, п., undue delay of a ship, a railroad
car, etc. — OF. demorage, demurage, demou-
rage, 'delay', fr. demorer. See demur, v., and
-age.

## demurrer
demurrer, п., a pleading by a party that the
opposite party should not be allowed to proceed
(law). — OF. demorer, 'to linger, tarry'; see
demur, n. For the subst. use of the infinitive
in legal terminology cp. attainder and words
there referred to.

## demy
demy, п., a size of paper. — Elliptical use of demy
paper, lit. 'paper folded in half*, fr. F. demi,
'half*. See demi·.

## demyship
demyship, п., a scholarship at Magdalen College,
Oxford, which had originally half the value of
a fellowship. — A hybrid coined fr. F. demi,
'half (see'demi-), and suff. -ship (fr. OE. -scipe).

## den
den, n. — ME., fr. OE. denn, 'lair of a wild
beast', rel. to MLG. denne, 'lowland, wooded
vale, den', OE. denu, 'valley', OFris. dene,
'down', OHG. tenni, MHG., G. tenne,
'threshing floor', and to ON. Danir, 'the Danes', lit.
'lowlanders' (see Danes), and prob. cogn. with
OI. dhanuh, 'sandbank'. Cp. dene, 'valley', dene-
hole. Cp. also thenar.

## denarius
denarius, п., an ancient Roman silver coin. —
L. denarius, short for denarius nummus, *the
coin containing ten (asses)', from denarius,
'containing ten', and nummus, 'coin*. Denarius
derives fr. dim, 'ten each*, which stands for
*dec-noi, fr. decern, 'ten'. (Cp. senl, 'six each*,
fr. *sex-noi.) The denarius was so called because
it originally contained ten asses. See ten and
cp. decern-, decimal. Cp. also denary, deaier,
dinar.

## denary
denary, п., tenfold. — L. denarius, 'containing
ten*. See prec. word and -ary.

## denationalize
denationalize, tr. v. — F. denationaliser, fr. de-
(used in the privative sense of this prefix) and
nationaliser. See de- and aationalize.
Derivative: denationaliz-ation, n.

## denaturalize
denaturalize, tr. v. — Formed fr. de- (used in the
privative sense of this prefix) and naturalize.
Derivative: denaturaliz-ation, n.

## denature
denature, tr. v. — F. denaturer, fr. de- (used in the
privative sense of this prefix) and nature. See
de- and nature.
Derivative: denatur-ation, n,

## dendr-
dendr-, form of dendro- before a vowel.

## deadriform
deadriform, adj., shaped like a tree. — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. δένδρον, 'tree', and L. forma,
'form, shape'. See dendro- and form, n. The
correct form is arborlform, in which both
elements are of Latin origin.

## dendrite
dendrite, п., a mineral with markings resembling
a tree (mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ke

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:229 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DENDRITIC | 202 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:229 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. Gk. δένδρον, 'tree'. See dendro-.

## dendritic
dendritic, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
dendrite. — See prec. word and -ic.

## Dendrinm
Dendrinm, п., a genus of plants of the heath
family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δενδρίον, di-
min. of δένδρον, 'tree'. See dendro- and -ium.

## dendro-
dendro-, dendri-, before a vowel dendr-,
combining form meaning 'tree'. — Gk. δένδρο-,
δενορι-, δενδρ-, fr. δένδρον, 'tree', for *S£vSpefov,
which is dissimilated fr. *δέρ8ρείον, and is cogn.
with δρυς, 'an oak; a tree', δρυμός, 'forest', δόρυ,
'stem, tree, beam, spear', fr. I.-E. base *derew(o)-,
*drew(p)-t 'tree, wood', whence also Goth, triu,
OE. trio, treow, 'tree'. See tree and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also the second element
in Epidendrum, Liriodendron* Oxydendrum,
Phoradeadron, rhododendron.

## Dendrobates
Dendrobates, п., a genus of American frogs of
the family Ranidae (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
δενδροβατεϊν, 'to climb trees', which is
compounded of δένδρον, 'tree', and βατός,
'accessible', verbal adj. of βαίνειν, 'to go'. See
dendro- and -bates.

## Dendrobium
Dendrobium, п., a genus of orchids (hot.) —
ModL., compounded of dendro- and Gk. βίος,
'life'. See bio-.

## Dendrocolaptidae
Dendrocolaptidae, n.pl., a family of South
American birds (ornithol.) — ModL., formed with
suff. -idae fr. dendro- and Gk. κολάπτειν, 'to
hew, cut, peck', which is rel. to κόλαφος, 'a
blow with the fist', fr. base *qold-, 'to strike,
cut'. See coup and cp. words there referred to.

## dendroid
dendroid, adj., shaped like a tree. — Gk.
δενδροειδής, 'treelike', compounded of δένδρον,
'tree', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form shape'.
See dendro- and -oid.

## dendrolite
dendrolite, п., a fossil plant. — Lit. 'tree stone'.
See dendro- and -lite.

## deadrology
deadrology, п., the study of trees. —
Compounded of dendro- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: dendrolog-ic, dendrolog-ic-al, adjs.,
dendrolog-ist, n.

## dendrometer
dendrometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
height and diameter of trees. — Compounded
of dendro- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## dene
dene, п., a small valley. — ME. dene, fr. OE.
denu, 'valley', rel. to OE. denn, 'lair of a wild
beast'. See den and cp. denebole.

## dene
dene, п., a sandy tract of land. — Prob. in gra-
dational relationship to OE. dun, 'hill'. See
down, 'hill'.

## Deneb
Deneb, п., the star χ in the constellation Cygnus.
— Arab, dhanab (in vulgar pronunciation dhe-
neb), short for dhanab ad-dajajah, 'the tail of the
hen'. Arab, dhanab is rel. to Heb. zanubh, Aram.
dunba, dinbd, Ethiop. zanb, Akkack.. zibbatu,
'tail'.

## Deaebola
Deaebola, п., the star β in the constellation Leo.
— Arab, dhanab al-(asad), 'the tail of the (lion)'.
See prec. word.

## denegate
denegate, tr. v.. to deny (obsol.) — L. dinegdtus,
pp. of dinegare, 'to deny'. See deny and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: denegat-ion, n.

## denehole
denehole, п., one of the ancient caves found in
Kent and Essex. — Compounded of dene,
'valley', and hole.

## dengue
dengue, п., an infectious tropical disease
characterized by high fever, rash and severe pains
in the head, back and joints. — Sp., lit.
'stiffness', fr. Swahili dinga, 'cramplike seizure';
influenced in form by Sp. dengue, 'prudery'. The
Negroes of the West Indies altered this word
into dandy, whence dandy fever.

## denial
denial, n. — Formed fr. deny with subst. suff. -al.

## denier
denier, п., one who denies. — Formed fr. deny
with agential suff. -er.

## denier
denier, п., a French coin. — F., fr. L. denarius,
whence also Olt. danaio, It. danaro, dendro,
Provenc. denier, dinier, Sp. dinero, Port, di-
nheiro. See denarius.

## denigrate
denigrate, tr. v., to blacken; to sully; to defame.
— L. denigratus, pp. of denigrdre, 'to blacken
thoroughly; to defame', fr. de- and nigrdre, 'to
be black, to blacken', fr. niger, 'black'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:229 COLUMN:2 -->
Negro and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: denigrai-ion, п., denigrat-or, n.

## denim
denim, п., a coarse cotton drill. — Fr. F. de Ni-
mes, 'of Nimes', in serge de Nimes, 'serge of
Nimes'; so called after Nimes, a city in southern
France, where it was first made.

## Denis
Denis, masc. PN. — F. Denis, fr. L. Dionysius,
fr. Gk. Διονύσιος, 'of Dionysos'. See
Dionysius.

## Denise
Denise, fem. PN. — F., fem. of Denis. See prec.
word.

## denitrate
denitrate, tr. v., to remove nitric acid from. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and nitrate.
Derivatives: denitrat-ion, п., denitrat-or, n.

## denitrify
denitrify, tr. v., to remove nitrogen or nitrates
from. — Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense
of this prefix) and nitrify.

## denizen
denizen, п., an alien admitted to certain rights
of citizenship, a naturalized citizen. — AF.
deinzein (corresponding to OF. denzein, dein-
zein), lit. 'one living within', fr. AF. deinz
(corresponding to OF. deenz, deeinz, F. dans),
'within; in', fr. Late L. deintus, 'within', fr. L.
de, 'from', and intus, 'within', which is formed
fr. in, 'in', with adv. suff. -lus, and suff. -ein, fr.
L. -aneus. Cp. Gk. εντός, 'within', fr. t), 'in',
and see in, prep., and -aneous.
Derivative: denizen, tr. v.

## denomiaate
denomiaate, tr. v. — L. denominatus, pp. of
denominare, 'to name specifically, denominate',
fr. de- and nominare, 'to give a name to, to
name', from nomen, gen. nominis, 'name'. See
nominate.

## denomination
denomination, n. — OF. denominacion (F.
denomination), fr. L. denomindtionem, ace. ofdenomi-
natio (in classical L. used only in the sense of
'metonymy'), fr. denominatus, pp. of
denominare. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: denomination-al, adj., denomina-
lion-al-ly, adv., denomination-al-ism, п., deno-
mination-al-ize, tr. v.

## denominative
denominative, adj. — Late L. denominate us, fr.
L. denominatus, pp. of denominare. See
denominate and -ive.
Derivatives: denominative, п., denominative-ly,
adv.

## denominator
denominator, n. — ML., fr. L. denominatus, pp. of
denominare. See denominate and agential suff. -or.

## denotation
denotation, n. — Late L. denotdtio, gen.'-o/ш, 'a
marking or pointing out', fr. L. denotatus, pp. of
denotare. See denote and -arion.

## deaotative
deaotative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
denotatus, pp. of denotare. See next word.
Derivatives: denotative-ly, adv., denotative-
ness, n.

## denote
denote, tr. v. — F. denoter, fr. L. denotare, 'to
mark or point out, indicate', fr. de- and notare,
'to mark, note, observe'. See note, v.

## denouement
denouement, п., unraveling of a plot; final
revelation in a play, etc. — F., lit. 'an unknotting,
untying', fr. denouer, 'to untie, unravel', fr. de-
(see de-) and nouer, fr. L. noddre, 'to fill or
furnish with knots', fr. nodus, 'knot'. See node
and -ment.

## denounce
denounce, tr. v. — OF. denoncier, denoncer (F.
denoncer), fr. L. dinuntidre, 'to make an official
announcement of, announce, declare; to
threaten, denounce', fr. de- and nuntiare, 'to
announce, declare, report, narrate; to inform against,
denounce', fr. nuntius, 'messenger, envoy'. See
nuncio and cp. denunciate.

## denouncement
denouncement, n. — OF. denoncement, fr.
denoncer. See prec. word and -ment.

## dense
dense, adj. — L. densus (whence also F. dense),
'thick, thickly set, crowded, dense', cogn.'with
Gk. δασύς (for *dnsus), 'thick, with hair, hairy,
bushy, thick, dense'. Cp. dasy-.Cp. also condense.
Derivatives: dense-ly, adv., dense-ness, n.

## densimeter
densimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
density of a substance. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. densus, 'dense", and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See dense and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## density
density, n. — F. densite, fr. L. densitatem, ace.
of dinsitas, 'thickness, density', fr. dinsus. See
dense and -iry.

## dent
dent, п., depression. — A dialectal var. of diat.

## deat
deat, п., a toothlike projection; an indentation.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:229 COLUMN:3 -->
— F., fr. L. dentem, ace. of dens, 'tooth'. See
denti- and cp. indentation.

## dentagra
dentagra, п., г) toothache; 2) a tooth forceps. —
A Medical Latin hybrid coined fr. L. dens, gen.
dentis, 'tooth', and Gk. άγρα, 'a catching,
seizure'. For the first element see denti-, for the
second see chiragra. The correct· word would be
odontagra, fr. Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth',
and άγρα.

## dental
dental, adj. — ML. dentalis, 'pertaining to a
tooth or teeth', fr. L. dins, gen. dentis, 'tooth'.
See denti- and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: dental, п., a dental sound, dentalize
(q.v.), dentai-iy, adv.

## dentalize
dentalize, tr. v., to make dental. — A hybrid
coined fr. ML. dentalis (see prec. word) and
-ize, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivative; dentaliz-ation, n.

## Dentaria
Dentaria, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Late L. denlarius,
'pertaining to the teeth', fr. L. dens, gen. dentis,
'tooth'. See denti-,

## deatate
deatate, adj., having a toothlike projection. —
L. dentdtus, 'toothed, dentate', fr. dens, gen.
dentis, 'tooth'. See denti- and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: dentat-ed, adj., dentat-ion, n.

## deatato-
deatato-, combining form meaning 'dentate'. —
Fr. L. dentatus. See prec. word.

## dentelle
dentelle, п., lace. — F„ lit. 'a little tooth', dimin.
of dent, 'tooth', fr. L. deptem, ace. of dens,
'tooth'. See denti- and cp. dentil.

## denti-
denti-, before a vowel dent-, combining form
meaning 'tooth'. — L. denti-, dent-, fr. dens, gen.
dentis, 'tooth; point, spike', which is cogn.
with Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, Goth, tunpus, OE.
top, 'tooth'. See tooth and cp. words there
referred to.

## denticle
denticle,п., 1) a small tooth; 2) a small
projection; 3) a dentil. — L. denliculus, 'a small tooth',
dimin. of dens, gen. dentis, 'tooth'. See denti-
and -cle.

## denticular
denticular, adj., resembling a small tooth. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. denticulus. See
denticle.

## denticulate
denticulate, adj., having small toothlike
projections. — L. denticuldtus, 'furnished with small
teeth', fr. denticulus. See denticle and adj. suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: denticulat-ed, adj., denticulat-ion, n.

## dentiform
dentiform, adj., tooth-shaped. — Compounded
of denti- and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See
form, n.

## dentifrice
dentifrice, п., toothpowder. — F. dentifrice, fr.
L. dentifricium, 'powder for rubbing the teeth',
fr. dens, gen. dentis, 'tooth', and the stem of
fricare, 'to rub'; see denti- and friction. L.
dentifricium was coined by Pliny. The word
dentifrice was introduced into French by the surgeon
Ambroise Pari (15177-1590).

## dentigerous
dentigerous, adj., having teeth. — Lit. 'bearing
teeth', compounded of denti-, the stem ofgerere.
Ίο bear', and suff. -ous. See gerent.

## dentil
dentil, п., one of a series of square blocks
projecting like teeth (archil.) — ME. dentille, fr.
OF. dentille, lit. 'a small looth', dimin. of dent,
fr. L dentem, ace. of dens, 'tooth'. See denti- and
cp. dentelle.

## deatilingual
deatilingual, adj., pronounced with the point of
the tongue against the teeth (said of consonants,
esp. of the sounds of th in thin and this). — See
denti- and lingual.

## dentimeter
dentimeter, п., an instrument for measuring
teeth. — A hybrid coined fr. L. dens, gen. dentis,
'tooth', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See denti-
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'. The correct form
would be odontometer, fr. Gk. οδών, gen. όδόν-
,τος, 'tooth', and μέτρον, 'meter'.

## dentine
dentine, also dentin, п., a calcareous substance
forming the chief mass of a tooth (anat.) —
Formed with suff. -ine, -in, fr. L. dens, gen.
dentis, 'tooth'. See denti-.

## dentipbone
dentipbone, п., an instrument placed against the
teeth to enable the deaf to hear. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. dins, gen. dentis, 'tooth', and Gk.
φωνή, 'sound'. See denti- and phone. The correct
form would be odontophone, fr. Gk. οδών, gen.
οδόντος, 'tooth', and φωνή, 'sound'.

## dentist
dentist, n. — F. dentiste, a hybrid coined fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:230 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 203 | DEPOSITOR -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:230 COLUMN:1 -->
dens, gen. dentis, 'tooth', and Gk. suff. -ιστής.
See denti- and suff. -ist.
Derivative: dentist-ry, n.

## dentition
dentition, п., the cutting of teeth; teething. — L.
dentitio, gen. -onis, 'teething', fr. dentit-(um),
pp. stem of dentire, 'to cut teeth, to teethe*. See
denti- and -ion.

## dentoid
dentoid, adj., tooth-shaped. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. dens, gen. dent is, 'tooth', and Gk. -οει&ής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, Shape*. See denti- and
-oid. The correct form is either odontoid or
dentiform. (In the former both elements are of
Greek, in the latter, of Lalin origin).

## denture
denture, п., a set of teeth, esp. a set of false teeth.
— F,, fr. dent, 'tooth'. Sec dent, 'toothlike
projection', and -ure.

## denudation
denudation, n. — F. denudation, fr, L. dinuda-
tionem, ace. of denudatio, 'a laying bare*, fr.
denfidatus, pp. of denudare. See denude and
-ation.

## denodative
denodative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
denudatus, pp. of denudare. See next word.

## denude
denude, tr. v., to lay bare. — L. denudare, 'to lay
bare, strip; to uncover, expose', fr. de- and nu-
dare, 'to make naked; to expose', fr. nudus,
'naked'. See nude.

## denunciate
denunciate, tr. v., to denounce. — L. deniintiatus,
pp. of dem'mtiare. See denounce and verbal suff,
-ate.

## denunciation
denunciation, n. — L. denuntiatio, gen. -onis, fr.
deniintiatus, pp. of denuntiare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## denunciative
denunciative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr.
L. deniintiatus, pp. of denuntiare. See denunciate.
Derivative: denunciative-ly, adv.

## denunciatory
denunciatory, adj. — Formed wiih adj. suff. -ory
fr. L. denuntidtus, pp. of denuntiare. See
denunciate.

## deny
deny, tr. v. — M£. denien, fr. F. denier, fr. L. de-
negare, 'to deny, reject, refuse' (whence also It.
dinegare. Proven?., Sp., Port, denegar), fr. de-
and negare, 'to say no, to deny, refuse'. See
negate.

## deodand
deodand, п., a thing that had caused the death of
a human being and was therefore forfeited to
the Crown, to be used for pious purposes
{English law). ~ ML. deodandum, fr. L. Deo dandum,
'to be given to God', from the dative of Deus
and the neut. gerundive of dare, 'to give'. See
deity and date, 'point of time'. For the use of
Latin gerundives in English cp. agenda and
words there referred to.

## deodar
deodar, п., a kind of cedar. — Hind., lit. 'divine
tree*, fr. OI. devadaru, fr. devah, 'divine' and
daru, 'wood, tree'. See deity and tree.

## deodorant
deodorant, adj. and n. — See deodorize and -ant.

## deodorize
deodorize, tr. v., to remove the odor of. — Formed
fr. de- (used in the privative sense of this
prefix), L. odor, 'smell\ and -ize, a suff. of Greek
origin. See odor.
Derivatives: deodoriz-ation, п., deodoriz-er, n.

## deontology
deontology, п., the science of moral duty. —
Coined by the English philosopher Jeremy Bent-
ham (1748-1832) in 1826 fr. Gk. δέον, gen.
δέοντος, 'that which is needful', neut. pres.
part, of δεΐ, 'it is necessary, it behoves one4,
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. Gk. δεΐ is the third person of δέω, Ί am
in need of, ] need', which prob. stands for
*δεύσω, and is rel. to δεύω, δεύομαι, Ί am
wanting, 1 am deficient', and cogn. with OI.
ddsah, 'want, need'. Cp. deutero-. For the second
element see -logy.
Derivatives: deontolog-ical, adj., deontolog-ist, n.

## deoxidize
deoxidize, tr. v., 1) to remove oxygen from; 2) to
reduce from the state of an oxide (ckem.) —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and oxidize.
Derivatives: deoxidiz-ation, п., deoxidiz-er, n.

## deoxygenate
deoxygenate, tr. v., to remove oxygen from
{ckem.) — Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense
of this prefix), oxygea and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: deoxygenat-iony n.

## depart
depart, intr. and tr. v. — ME. departen, 'to
depart; to go away', fr. OF. departir (F. departir),
'to divide, distribute', se departir, *to separate
oneself, fr. de- (see de-) and partir, 'to divide,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:230 COLUMN:2 -->
separate4, se partir, 'to separate oneself, leave*,
fr. L. partlre, 'to divide', fr. pars, gen. partis,
'part'. See part, n, and v., and cp. OProveng.
d?partir, and Sp. despartir, It. spartire, 'to
divide, distribute' (these latter derive fr. L. dis-
partire, of s.m.).

## department
department, n. — ME., fr. OF. departement (F.
departement), fr. departir. See depart and -ment.
Derivatives: department-al, adj.,
departmentalism, departmental-ize, tr. v., department-al-ly,
adv., departure (q.v.)

## departure
departure, n. —- OF. departeure, fr. departir. See
depart and -ure.

## depasture
depasture, tr. v., to pasture. — Formed fr.
dean d pasture.
Derivatives: depastur-age, п., departur-ation, n.

## depauperate
depauperate, tr. v., to make poor. — ML. depau-
peratus, pp. of depauperare, 'to make poor', fr.
de- and L. pauper, 'poor'. See pauper and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: depauperat-ion, n.

## depauperate
depauperate, adj., depauperaied. — ML. depaupe-
ratus, pp. of depauperare. See depauperate, v.

## depauperize
depauperize, tr. v., to free from paupers or from
poverty. — Formed fr. de- (in the privative
sense of this prefix) and pauperize.
Derivative: depauperiz-ation, n.

## depeche
depeche, п., a dispatch. — F., fr. depecher, 'to
dispatch', fr. OF. despeechier (shortened fr. *des-
empechier), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and -peechier
(F. -pecker) in empeechier (F. empecher), 'to
hinder', fr. L. impedicare, 'to catch in a trap',
fr. ped/ca, 'shackle, fetter', fr. pes, gen. pedis,
'foot'. See dis- and pedal and cp. impeach. E.
dispatch (q.v.) is not related to depeche.

## depend
depend, intr. v. — OF. dependre (F. dependre),
fr. VL. dependere, corresponding to L. depen-
dere, 'to hang from, hang down; be dependent
on', which is formed fr. de- and pendere, 'to
hang, be suspended, float, hover, depend on'.
See pendant.
Derivatives: depend-able, adj., depend-abil-ity,
п., depend-able-ness, п., depend-abl-y, adv.,
dependence (q.v,), dependent (q.v.), depend-er, п.,
depend-ing, adj., depend-ing-ly, adv.

## dependence
dependence, also dependance, n. — F. depen-
dance, fr. dependant, pres. part, of dependre. See
prec. word and -ence.

## dependency
dependency, n. — See prec. word and -cy.

## dependent
dependent, adj. — F. dependant, pres. part, of
dependre, 'to depend'. See depend and -ent.

## dependent
dependent, dependant, n. — Fr. prec. word.

## dephlogistlcate
dephlogistlcate, tr. v., to deprive of phlogiston.
— Formed fr. de- (in ths privative sense of this
prefix), phlogistic and verbal suff. -ate.
dephlogisticated air. — A name given to oxygen
by its discoverer, the English clergyman and
chemist Joseph Priestley (1733-1804).

## dephosphorize
dephosphorize, tr. v., to remove phosphorus from.
— Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix), phosphorus and suff. -ize.
Derivative: de phosphor iz-at ion, n.

## depict
depict, tr. v., to portray; to describe. — L. de-
pictus, pp. of depingere, 'to portray, paint,
sketch, describe', fr. de- and pingere, 'to paint,
color, decorate, embellish, embroider'. See
picture.
Derivatives: depict-er, depict-or, п., depiction
(q.v.), depicture (q.v.).

## depiction
depiction, n. — Late L. depictio, gen. -onis,
'painting, description', fr. L. depictus, pp. of
depingere. See prec. word and -ion.

## depicture
depicture, tr. v., to depict. — Formed with suff.
-ure fr. L. depictus, pp. of depingere. See depict,
picture.

## deplenish
deplenish, tr. v., to remove the furniture from, —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and OF. pleniss-, pres. part, stem of
plenir, 'to fill', fr. L. plenus, 'full'. See full, adj.,
and verbal suff. -ish, and cp. plenum, replenish.
Cp. also next word.

## deplete
deplete, tr. v., to empty. — L. depletus, pp. of
deplere, 'to empty out, draw off, exhaust', fr.
de- and ρ fere, 'to fill', whence plenus, 'full*. See
Full, adj., and cp. prec. word. Cp. also complete,
replete.
Derivatives: deplet-ion, п., deplet-ive, deplet-ory,
adjs.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:230 COLUMN:3 -->

## deplorable
deplorable, adj. — F. deplorable, fr. deplorer, 'to
deplore', fr. L. deplorare. See next word and -able.
Derivatives: deplorabil-ity, п., deplorable-ness,
п., deplorabl-y, adv.

## deplore
deplore, tr. v. — F. deplorer, fr. L. deplorare, 'to
weep bitterly, moan, bewail, lament', fr. de-
andplorare, 'to cry out; to wail, lament', which
is of imitative origin. Cp. explore, implore.
Derivative: deplor-er, n.

## deploy
deploy, tr. and intr. v., to spread out, extend
{mil.) — F. deployer, 'to unfold', fr. L. displicare,
'to unfold'. See display, which is a doublet of
deploy.
Derivative: deploy, n.

## deployment
deployment, n. — F. deploiement, 'unfolding', fr.
deployer. See prec. word and -ment.

## deplume
deplume, tr. v., to pull the feathers of, to un-
plume. — F. depfumer, pluck, unplume', fr.
ML. deplumare, fr. de- and L. pluma, 'feather,
down'. See plume and cp. unplume.

## depolarize
depolarize, tr. v., to deprive of polarity. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and polarize.
Derivative: de polar iz-ation^ n.

## depolish
depolish, tr. v., to destroy the polish of. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and polish.

## depone
depone, tr. and intr. v., to depose. — L. deponere,
'to lay down, put aside, deposit', in ML. also
'to testify', fr. de- and ponere, 'to put, place,
set up; to appoint; to propose'. See position and
cp. words there referred to.

## deponent
deponent, adj., said of verbs that are passive in
form but active in meaning (Latin and Greek
grammar). — L. deponens, gen. -entis, lit.
'putting down or aside', pres. part, of deponere; see
prec. word and -ent. These verbs are called
deponent, because they have 'put aside', part of
their conjugation, i.e. the active voice. L.
deponens is prop, a loan translation of Gk.
άττοθετίκός, fr. άττοτιθ-έναι., 'to put away*.
Derivative: deponent, п., a deponent verb.

## deponent
deponent, п., one who makes a deposition under
oath. — See depone and deponent, adj.

## depopulate
depopulate, tr. and intr. v. — L. depopulate, pp.
of depopulari, 'to lay waste, ravage, destroy*,
fr. de- and popular!, 'to lay waste, destroy', lit.
'to overrun with an army', fr. populus, 'people',
also used in the sense of 'army'. See people,
populate. For the sense development of L. popu-
larl, 'to lay waste', fr. populus, 'people', cp. G.
verheeren, 'to lay waste', fr. Heer, 'army*.

## depopulation
depopulation, n. — L. depopulation gen. -onis, 'a
laying waste*, fr. depopulatus, pp. of depopulari.
See prec. word and -ion,

## deport
deport, tr. v., to expel, exile. — F. deporter, fr.
L. diportare, 'to carry off or away', fr. de- (see
de-) and portare, 'to carry'. See port, 'to carry'.

## deport
deport, reflexive v., to behave. — OF. deporter
(F. deporter), 'to behave', fr. de- (see de-) and
porfer, 'to carry*, fr. L. portare. See port, 'to
carry*.

## deportment
deportment, п., behavior. — OF. deportement, fr.
deporter. See deport, 'to behave', and -ment.

## depose
depose, tr. v. — F. deposer, fr. de- (see de-) and
poser, 'to place*. See pose, 'to place', and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: depos-able, adj., depos-al, п., de-
pos-er, n.

## deposit
deposit, tr. v. — L. depositus, pp. of deponere,
'to lay down, entrust*, fr. de- and ponere, 'to
place'. See depone.
Derivatives: deposit-ation, п., deposit-ee, n.

## deposit
deposit, n. — L. depositum, 'something laid
down*, neuter of depositus, pp. of deponere. See
prec. word and cp. depot, which is "a doublet
of deposit.

## depositary
depositary, п., ι) a person with whom something
is left for safekeeping; 2) a depository. — Late
L. depositarius, One who receives a deposit*,
fr. L. depositus, 'laid down, deposited'. See
deposit, v., and subst. suff. -ary.

## deposition
deposition, n. — OF., fr. L. depositionem, ace. of
depositio, 'a laying down, depositing*, fr.
depositus, pp. of deponere, 'to lay down'. See
deposit and -ion.
Derivative: deposition-al, adj.

## depositor
depositor, n. — Late L. depositor, 'one who de-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:231 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DEPOSITORY | 204 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:231 COLUMN:1 -->
posits*, fr. L. depositus, pp. of deponere. See
deposit and agential suff. -or.

## depository
depository, п., a place where something is
deposited. — ML. depositorium, 'a place where
something is deposited', fr. L. depositus, pp. of
deponere. See deposit, v., and subst. suff. -ory.

## depot
depot, п., ι) a storehouse; 2) a railroad station. —
F. depot, fr. OF. depost, lit. 'a place where
something is deposited*, fr. L. deposition. See
deposit, n.

## depravation
depravation, п., corruption. — F. depravation, fr.
L. depravationem, ace. of depravatid, 'a
perverting, distorting* fr. depravatus, pp. of dipra-
vdre. See next word and -ion.

## deprave
deprave, tr. v., to corrupt. — L. depravare, 'to
pervert, corrupt, distort, disfigure', fr. de- and
pravus, 'crooked, perverted, vicious, wicked'.
See pravity.
Derivatives: deprav-ed, adj., deprav-ed-ly, adv.,
deprav-ed-ness, п., deprav-er, n.

## depravity
depravity, n. — Formed fr. deprave on analogy
of pravity.

## deprecate
deprecate, tr. v., i) to seek to avert by prayer
{archaic); 2) to disapprove of. — L. deprecatus,
pp. of deprecari, 'to avert by prayer, to pray
for, intercede for', fr. de- and щесаг'х, 'to ask,
beg, pray, request'. See pray and verbal suff.
-ate and cp. imprecate.
Derivatives: deprecating-ly, adv., deprecation,
deprecative, deprecatory (qq.v.).

## deprecation
deprecation, п., disapproval — F. deprecation,
fr. L. deprecationem, ace. of deprecatio, 'an
averting by prayer, intercession', fr. deprecatus,
pp. of deprecari. See prec. word and -ion.

## deprecative
deprecative, adj., deprecatory. — F. deprecatif
(fern, deprecative), fr. Late L. deprecativus, fr.
L. deprecatus, pp. of deprecari. See deprecate
and -ive. Derivative: deprecative-ly, adv.

## deprecatory
deprecatory, adj., deprecating. — Late L. depre-
catorius, fr. L. deprecatus, pp. of deprecari. See
deprecate and adj. suff. -ory.
Derivatives: deprecatori-iy, adv., deprecatori-
ness, n.

## depreciable
depreciable, adj. — See next word and -able.

## depreciate
depreciate, tr. and intr. v., i) to lower the price
of; 2) to belittle, disparage. — L. depretiatus,
pp. of depretiare, 'to lower the price of,
undervalue, depreciate', fr. de- and pretiare, 'to prize,
value*, fr. pretium, 'price, value*. See price and
cp. appreciate. Cp. also dispraise, disprize.
Derivatives: depreciat-ing-ly, adv.,
depreciation, п., depreciat-ive, adj., depreciat-ive-ly, adv.,
depreciat-or, п., depreciat-ory, adj., depreciat-
ori-ness, n.

## depredate
depredate, tr. and intr. v., to plunder. — L.
depraedatus, pp. of depraedari, 'to plunder,
pillage', fr. de- and praedarit 'to plunder', fr.
praeda, 'booty, plunder*. See prey and verbal
suff. -ate.

## depredation
depredation, п., plundering. — F. depredation, fr.
L. depraedationem, ace. of depraedatio, 'a
plundering', fr. depraedatus, pp. of depraedari. See
prec. word and -ion.

## depredator
depredator,n., a plunderer. — Late L. depraedator,
'plunderer', fr. depraedatus, pp. of depraedari.
See depredate and agential suff. -or.

## depress
depress, tr. v. — OF. depresser, fr. Late L. *de-
pressare, freq. of L. deprimere (pp. depressus),
'to press down, weigh down, plant deep, dig
deep, depress*, fr. de- and premere, 'to press'.
See press, v., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: depress-ant, adj. and п., depress-ed,
adj., depress-ible, adj., depress-ing, adj., depress-
ing-ly, adv., depress-ing~ness, п., depression
(q.v.), depress-ive, adj., depress-ive-Iy, adv., de-
press-ive-ness, п., depress-or, n.

## depression
depression, n. — L. depressio, gen. -Onis, 'a
pressing down', fr. depressus, pp. of deprimere. See
prec. word and -ion.

## deprivable
deprivable, adj. — See deprive and -able.

## deprivation
deprivation, n. — ML. deprhmio, gen. -onis, fr.
deprivare. See deprive and -ion.

## deprive
deprive, tr. v. — OF. depr'iver, fr. ML. deprivare,
fr. de- and L. privare, 'to bereave, deprive, rob'.
See private.
Derivatives: deprive-ment, п., depriv-er, n.

## de profundis
de profundis, name of the 130th psalm. — L.,
Out of the depths'; so called from the first

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:231 COLUMN:2 -->
words of the Latin version, rendering Heb. mim-
ma'amaqqim. See de- and profound.

## depside
depside, also depsid, п., any of a group of
compounds formed by the condensation of two
molecules of a phenolic acid (chem.) — G. Depsid,
coined by the German chemist Emil Fischer
(1852-1929) fr. Gk. δέψειν, 'to tan', an j-en-
largement of δέφειν, 'to knead, soften', which is
prob. cogn. with. Arm. top'em, Ί strike, beat.',
Serbo-Croatian depam, depati, 'to thrust, strike*,
Pol. deptac, 'to tread1. For the ending see chem.
suff. -id.

## depth
depth, n. — Formed fr. deep on analogy of length.
Cp. ON. dypt, dypd, Du. diepte, Goth, diupipa,
'depth*.

## depurate
depurate, tr. v., to free from impurities. — ML.
depuratus, pp. of depurare, 'to purify
thoroughly', fr. de- and purare, 'to purify', fr. pftrus,
'clean, pure*. See pure and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: depurai-ion, п., depurat-ive, adj..
depurat-or, п., depurat-ory, adj.

## deputation
deputation, n. — See next word and -ation.

## depute
depute, tr. v. — F. deputer, fr. L. deputare, 'to
cut off, prune; to esteem, consider', in Late L.,
'to destine, allot', fr. de- and putare, 'to trim,
prune, lop, clean, cleanse; to think over,
consider, reckon, count*. See putamen and cp.
putative and words there referred to.

## deputize
deputize, tr. v., to appoint as a deputy; intr. v.,
to act as a deputy. — Formed fr. deputy with
suff. -ize.

## deputy
deputy, n. — F. depute, prop. pp. of deputer, used
as a noun. — See depute and -y (representing
OF. -e, F. -έ).

## deracinate
deracinate, tr. v., to tear out by the roots. — Fr.
F. deraciner, fr. de- (see de-) and racine, 'root*, fr.
Late L. radicina, dimin. of L. radix, gen. radicis,
'root' (see radix and verbal suff. -ate);
introduced into English by Shakespeare. Cp. Rum.
radicina, 'root*, which also derives from Laie
L. radicina. Derivative: deracinat-ion, n.

## deraign
deraign, tr. v., to vindicate. — OF. deraisnier,
'to tell, teach; to vindicate, justify', fr. de- and
raisnier, 4o speak, plead, instruct', fr. VL.
*rationare, "to reason', fr. L. ratio, 'reckoning,
calculation, reason'. See reason and cp.
arraign, "to call to account'.

## derail
derail, tr. v., to cause to run off the rails;
intr. v., to run off the rails. — F. deraiiler, fr.
de- (see de-) and rail, 'rail'. See rail, 'bar'.

## derailment
derailment, n. — F. de rail!erne nt, fr. deraiiler.
See prec. word and -ment.

## derange
derange, tr. v., t) to disarrange; 2) to make
insane. — F. deranger, fr. OF. desrengier, a
hybrid coined fr. des- (fr. L. rf/.v, 'apart, asunder')
and OF. rengier, rangier (F. ranger), 'to put
into line', a word of Teut. origin. See dis- and
range and cp. arrange.

## derangement
derangement, n. — F. derangement, fr. deranger.
See prec. word and -ment.

## derate
derate, tr. v., to reduce the rates of. — Formed
fr. de- (in the privative sense of this prefix) and
rate, 'amount'.

## Derby
Derby, п., a horse race held annually at Epsom.--
Named after the 12th Earl of Derby.

## derby
derby, п., a bowler hat. — Of uncertain origin.

## Derceto
Derceto, п., the same as Atargatis. — L. Der-
ceto, fr. Gk. Δερκετώ, shortened fr. Άταργάτις.
See Atargatis.

## derelict
derelict, adj., abandoned; п., something
abandoned. — L. derelictus, 'wholly forsaken', pp.
of derelinquere, 'to forsake wholly, resign,
relinquish'. See de- and relinquish and cp. relict.
Derivatives: dereliction (q.v.), derelict-ly, adv.,
derelict-ness.

## dereliction
dereliction, п., the act of abandoning. — L. de-
relictio, gen. -onis, 'an abandoning, forsaking',
fr. derelictus, pp. of derelinqu°,re. See prec. word
and -ion.

## deride
deride, tr. v., to mock. — L. deridere, 'to laugh
at, scorn, mock', fr. de- and ridere, 4o laugh'.
See risible and cp. next word.
Derivative: derid-er, n.

## derision
derision, п., the act of deriding; contempt. — F.
derision, fr. L. derisidnem, ace. of derisio, fr.
derisus, pp. οι deridere. See prec. word and -ion.

## derisive
derisive, adj., expressing derision. — Formed
with suff. -ive fr. L. derisus, pp. of deridere. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:231 COLUMN:3 -->
deride.
Derivatives: derisive-ly, adv., derisive-ness, n.

## derivate
derivate, adj. — L. derivatus, pp. of derivare. See
derive and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: derivate, п., derivate-ly, adv.

## derivation
derivation, n. — F. derivation, fr. L. derivationem,
ace. of derivatio, 'a leading off, turning off;
etymology, derivation'. See derive and -ation.
Derivatives: derivaiion-al, adj., derivation-ist, n.

## derivative
derivative, adj. and n. — F. derivatif (fern,
derivative), fr. Laie L. derivativus, fr. L. der'watus.
See derivate and -ive.

## derive
derive, tr. and intr. v. — OF. deriver (F. deriver),
fr. L. derivare, 'to change the course of a river',
in Late L. used also in the sense of 'to derive';
fr. de- and rivus, 'a small stream*. Accordingly
the word prop, means 'to draw away a word
from its source'. See rivulet.
Derivatives: deriv-able, adj., deriv-ahi-y, adv.,
deriv-abii-ity\ п., deriv-αί, п., derivate (q.v.),
derivation (q.v.), derivative (q.v.), deriv-ed, adj.,
deriv-ed-ly, adv., deriv-ed-ness, п., deriv-er, n.

## -derm
-derm, suff. meaning 'skin, covering', as in
blastoderm. — Fr. Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma and
cp. pachyderm.

## derma
derma, also derm, п., skin, esp. the layer of the
skin below the epidermis (anat.) — ML. derma,
fr. Gk. δέρμα, 'skin', formed with suff. -μα (see
-m), from the stem of δέρει/ν, δείρειν, 'to flay'
(whence also δέρας, δέρος, δέρρι,ς, δορά, 'skin',
δάρσις, 'tearing, flaying, separation*), which is
cogn. with Goth, dis-tairan, 'to tear to pieces',
OE. teran, 'to tear'. See tear, 'to rend', and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also adermia, ec-
deron, endermic, epidermis, exodermis, hypo-
dermis, leucoderma, pachyderm, taxidermy,
xeroderma.

## dermal
dermal, adj., pertaining to the skin. — A hybrid
formed fr. Gk. δέρμα, 'skin' (see prec. word),
with -al, a suff. of Latin origin.

## dermal-
dermal-, form of derma to- before a vowel.

## dermatalgia
dermatalgia, п., pain in the skin (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of dermat- and -αλγία, fr.
άλγος, 'pain'. See -algia.

## dermatic
dermatic, adj., pertaining to the skin. — Gk.
δερματικός, fr. δέρμα, gen. δέρματος, 'skin'. See
derma and -ic.

## dermatitis
dermatitis, п., inflammation of the skin below the
epidermis (med.) — Medical L., formed with
suff. -itis fr. Gk. δέρμα, gen. δέρματος, 'skin'.
See derma.

## derma to-
derma to-, before a vowel dermat-, combining
form meaning 'of, or pertaining to, the skin*. —
Gk. δερματο-, Sep ματ-, fr. δέρμα, gen. δέρματος,
'skin'. See derma.

## Dermatobia
Dermatobia, п., a genus of botflies (entomof.) —
ModL., lit. 'living under the skin', compounded
of derma to- and Gk. βίος, 'life' (see bio-); so
called because the larvae of this genus live
under the skin of animals and man.

## dermatography
dermatography, п., anatomical description of the
skin. — Compounded of dermato- and Gk.
-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, *to write*. See -graphy.

## derma to id
derma to id, adj., resembling skin. — Compounded
of dermat- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like*, fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## dermatology
dermatology, п., the study of the skin. —
Compounded of dermato- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
One who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: dermatofog-ical, adj.,
dermatologist, n.

## dermatosis
dermatosis, п., any disease of the skin {med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -osis fr. Gk. δέρμα,
gen. δέρματος, 'skin'. See derma.

## Dermestes
Dermestes, п.. a genus of voracious beetles
{entomol.) — ModL.. fr. Gk. δερμηστής, 'a worm
that eats skin', which is compounded of Gk.
δέρμα, 'skin', and the stem of έσθίειν, 'to eat'.
For the first element see derma. Gk. έσθίείν is
a back formation fr. Έσ&ι, 'eat!', imper. of
ϋδειν, 'to eat', which is cogn. with Goth, itan,
OE. etan, 'to eat'. See eat and cp. words there
referred to.

## dermic
dermic, adj., pertaining to the skin. — Irregularly
formed fr. Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'; see derma. The
regular form is dermatic.

## dermis
dermis, п., the derma. — Medical L., back form-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:232 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 20S | DESMAN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:232 COLUMN:1 -->
ation fr. epidermis (q.v.)

## dermo-
dermo-, combining form, of the same meaning as
dermato- (anat.) — Gk. δερμο- (as in δερμό-
πτερος, 'with membranous wings', δερμόπτυλον,
'leather cushion'), a short form for δερματο-.
See dermato-.

## Dermochelys
Dermochelys, п., a genus of turtles (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of dermo- and Gk. χελΰς,
'tortoise'. See Chelonia.

## dern
dern, adj., hidden, secret (archaic). — ME. derne,
fr. OE. derne, dierne, 'concealed, secret, dark',
rel. to OS. dernl, OFris. dern. OHG. tarni, of
s.m., OHG. larnjan, MHG. tarnen, 'to conceal,
hide' (whence G. Tarnkappe, 'cloak of
invisibility'). F. ternir, 'to tarnish, to dull', is a Teut. loan
word; see tarnish.

## dernier ressort
dernier ressort, last expedient. — F., lit. 'last
resort', F. dernier, 'last', is a contraction of OF.
derrenier, which is formed on analogy oipre-
mier, 'first', fr. OF. derrain, 'last'. See darreia.
For the etymology of F. ressort, 'resort', see
ressort, n.

## derogate
derogate, tr. v., to reduce the value of, detract
from; intr. v., to detract. — L. derogatus, pp. of
dirogdre, Ίο take away, detract from, diminish;
to disparage', fr. de- and rogdre, 'to ask, beg,
entreat'. See rogation and cp. abrogate.

## derogation
derogation, n. — F. derogation, fr. L. dirogdtio-
nem, ace. of dirogdtid, fr. derogatus, pp. of
dirogdre. See prec. word and -ion.

## derogatory
derogatory, adj. — Late L. dirogdtorius, fr. L.
derogatus, pp. of dirogare. See derogate and adj.
suff. -ory.
Derivatives: derogatori-ly, adv., derogatori-
ness, n.

## derrick
derrick, п., a device for lifting weights. — Named
after Derrick, a hangman at Tyburn Prison in
London, who lived about the beginning of the
17th cent.
Derivative: derrick, tr. and intr. v.

## derring-do
derring-do, п., desperate courage. — This noun
owes its existence to an error. Spenser mistook
the words dorryng don in Chaucer's Troilus,
v. 834, for a noun. The equivalents of these two
words are in reality daring do (i.e. 'daring
to do').

## derringer
derringer, п., a short-barreled pistol. — Named
after its inventor Henry Derringer, an American.

## Derris
Derris, п., a genus of vines of the pea family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δέρρις, 'skin; leather
covering', which is rel. to δέρμα, 'skin'. See
derma.

## dervish
dervish, п., a Mohammedan mendicant monk. —
Turk, derwish, fr. Pers. ddrwish, 'beggar; poor'.
Cp. Avestic driyu-, fern, driwi-, 'poor'.

## descant
descant, п., song, melody (music). — ONF.
descant, descaunt, corresponding to OF. deschant
(F. dechant), fr. ML. discantus, fr. dis- and L.
cantus, 'song, melody'. See cant, 'slang of
beggars'.

## descant
descant, intr. v., 1) to play or sing a descant; to
sing; 2) to comment (on or upon). — Partly fr.
descant, п., partly fr. ONF. descanter
[corresponding to OF. deschanter (F. dechanter)], fr.
ONF. descant.
Derivative: descant-er, n.

## descend
descend, intr. and tr. v. — F. descendre, fr. L. di-
scendere, 'to come down, descend, sink*, fr. de-
and scandere, 'to climb'. See scan and cp.
ascend, condescend. For the change of Latin й
(in scandere) to έ (in di-sefndere) see accent and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: descendant, descendenl (qq.v.),
descend-er, п., descendible (q.v.), descend-ing,
adj., descend-ing-ly, adv.

## descendant
descendant, adj., descending (rare). — F.
descendant, pres. part of descendre: See prec. word and
-ant.
Derivative: descendant, п., an offspring.

## descendent
descendent, adj., descending. — L. discendins,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of descendere. See
descend and -ent.

## descension
descension, n. — OF., fr. L. discinsionem, ace.
of descinsio, 'a going down, descending*, fr.
descensus, pp. of descendere. See descend and
-ion and cp. ascension.

## descensive
descensive, adj. — Formed with suff. -he fr. L.
descensus, pp. of descendere. See descend and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:232 COLUMN:2 -->
-ive and cp. ascensive.

## descent
descent, n. — F. descente, formed fr. descendre.
Ίο descend', on analogy of nouns like OF.
pente, 'slope' (fr. pendre, 'to hang'), vente,
'sale' (fr. vendre, 'to sell'). See descend and cp.
ascent.

## Deschampsia
Deschampsia, п., a genus of plants (hot.) —
ModL., named after the French botanist Loise-
leur Deslongchamps (1774-1849). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## describe
describe, tr. v. — L. discribere, 'to write down,
copy; to sketch, represent, describe', fr. de- and
scrtbere, 'to write'. See scribe and cp. words

Derivatives: describ-able, adj., describ-abil-ity,
п., describ-abl-y, adv.

## description

discriptio, 'representation, description, copy',
fr. descriptus, pp. of discribere. See describe
and -ion.

## descriptive
descriptive, adj. — Late L. discriplivus,
'containing a description', fr. L. descriptus, pp. of
discribere. See describe and -ive.
Derivatives: descriptive-ly, adv., descript-rive-
ness, n.

## descry
descry, tr. v., to discern. — OF. deserter (F. de-
crier), 'to proclaim, decry*, fr. des- (fr. L. dis-)
and crier (fr. L. quiritdre), 'to cry'. See dis- and
cry and cp. decry.

## desecrate
desecrate, tr. v., to deprive of sacredness. — A
blend of de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and consecrate (q.v.) (L. disacrdre, dise-
crare means 'to consecrate'.) Cp. OF. dessacrer,
'to desecrate', which is formed fr. pref. des- (fr.
L. dis-) and sacrer (fr. L. sacrdre), 'to
consecrate'.
Derivative: desecrat-ion, n.

## desensitize
desensitize, tr. v. —· Formed fr. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix) and sensitize.
Derivatives: desentiz-ation, п., desensitiz-er, n.

## desert
desert, intr. v., to leave one's duty. — OF.
deserter (F. deserter), fr. VL. disertdre, freq. of
diserere (pp. disertus), 'to put down', hence 'to
leave, forsake, abandon, desert', lit. 'to put
down', fr. de- and serere, 'to put in a row, join
together'. See series.
Derivatives: desert-ed, adj., desert-ed-ly, adv.,
desert-ed-ness, п., desert-er, п., desertion (q.v.)

## desert
desert, adj., uninhabited, waste. — OF. desert
(F. desert), fr. L. disertus, 'deserted; desert,
waste' (whence also It. diserto, OProvenc. dezert,
Sp. desierto), pp. of diserere. See desert, v.
Derivative: desert-ness, n.

## desert
desert, п., wilderness. — OF. desert (F. desert),
fr. Late L. disertum, 'a desert place, desert' (cp.
the classical L. pi. diserta, 'deserted places,
deserts'), neut. of L. disertus, pp. of diserere, used
as a noun; the It., OProveng. and Sp.
correspondences are identical in form with the
respective adjectives. See desert, adj.

## desert
desert, п., merit. — ME. deserte, fr. OF. deserte,
prop. fern. pp. of deservir, used as a noun,
fr. VL. "diservtta, corresponding to L. diser-
vila, fern. pp. of disermre. See deserve.

## desertion
desertion, n. — F. desertion, fr. L. disertionem,
ace. of disertio, 'a forsaking, abandoning,
deserting', fr. disertus, pp. of diserere. See
desert, 'to leave', and -ion.

## deserve
deserve, tr. and intr. v. — OF. deservir (F. des-
servir), fr. L. deservire, 'to serve diligently, take
care of, be devoted to', fr. de- and servlre, 'to
serve'. See serve and cp. desert, 'merit'.
Derivatives: deserv-ed, adj., deserv-ed-ly, adv.,
deserv-ing, adj., deserv-ing-ly, adv.
deshabille. — See dishabille.

## desiccate
desiccate, tr. v., to dry up; intr. v., to become

dry up completely', fr. de- and siccare, 'to make
dry, drain', fr. siccus, 'dry'. See siccative and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: desiccat-ion, п., desiccat-ive, adj.,
desiccat-or, n.

## desiderate
desiderate, tr. v., to feel a desire for. — L. disi-
deratus, pp. of disiderdre, 'to feel the want of,
wish for, long for, desire'. See desire and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: desideration (q.v.), desiderat-ive,
adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:232 COLUMN:3 -->

## desideration
desideration, n. — L. desideratio, gen. -onis, fr.
disiderdtus, pp. of disiderdre. See prec. word
and -ion.
desiderative. п., a desiderative verb (gram.) —
Short for desiderative verb. See desiderate.

## desideratum
desideratum, п., something lacking. — L., lit.
'something desired', neut. pp. of disiderdre. See
desiderate.

## design
design, tr. and intr. v. — F. designer, fr. L.
disigndre, 'to mark out, trace out, designate, point
out, appoint', fr. de- and signdre, 'to mark'.
See sign, v.
Derivatives: design-ed, adj., design-ed-iy, adv.,
design-ed-ness, п., design-er, п., design-ing, n.
and adj., design-ing-ly, adv.

## design
design, n. — Earlier F. desseing (now spelled
dessein), fr. desseigner (now dessiner), fr. It.
disegnare, 'to draw, sketch; to plan', fr. L. de-
signdre. See design, v. Modern French
differentiates between dessein, 'design, plan, scheme',
and dessin, 'drawing, sketch'.

## designate
designate, tr. v. — L. disigndtus, pp. of disigndre.
See desiga, v., and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: designation (q.v.), designat-ive, adj.,
designat-or, п., designat-ory, adj.

## designate
designate, adj. — L. disigndtus, pp. οι disigndre.
See designate, v.

## designation
designation, n. — L. disigndtio, gen. -onis, 'a
marking out, designating', fr. disigndtus, pp. of
disigndre. See design, v., and -ation and cp.

## desilverize
desilverize, tr. v., to remove silver from. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and silverize.

## desinence
desinence, п., ending, suffix. — F. desinence, fr.

-entis, pres. part, of disinere, 'to cease, end,

## desipience
desipience, п., folly. — L. disipientia. fr. disi-
piins, gen. -entis. See next word and -ce.

## desipient
desipient, adj., foolish. — L. disipiins, gen. -entis,

For the change of Latin d (in sdpiins) to i (in
di-sipiins) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

## desirable
desirable, adj. — F. desirable, formed fr. disirer

Derivatives: desirabil-ity, п., desirabie-ness, п.,
desirabl-y, adv.

## desire
desire, tr. v. — F. disirer, 'to wish for, long for,
desire', fr. L. disiderdre, 'to feel the want of,
wish for, long for, desire' (whence also It. desi-
derare, OProveng. dezirar), orig. 'to expect

Derivatives: desire n. (q.v.), desir-ed, adj., desir-
ed-ly, adv., desir-ed-ness, п., desir-er, п., desirous
(q.v.)

## desire
desire, n. — OF. desir (F. desir), fr. desirer. See

## desirous
desirous, adj. — OF. desiros, desireus (F. desi-

Derivatives: desirous-ly, adv., desirous-ness, n.

## desist
desist, intr. v., to stop. — OF. desister (F.

referred to.

## desistance
desistance, п., the state of desisting. — Formed

## des'ition

Formed with suff -ioa fr. L. disitus, 'a ceasing',

## desk

## desm-
desm-, form of desmo- before a vowel.

desma, п., a sponge spicule (zool.) — ModL., fr.

## desman
desman, п., either of two molelike mammals
(Myogale moschata, resp. Myogale pyrenaica).

## Desmanthus
Desmanthus, п., a genus of plants of the mimosa

δέσμη, 'bundle', and άνθ-ος, 'flower'. See desmo-
and anther and cp. the first element in Desmo-
dium and the second element in Teleodesmacea.

## desmid
desmid, п., an alga of the family Desmidiaceae
{bot.) — ModL. Desmidium (name of the genus)
as if fr. Gk. *δεσμίδίον, dimin. of δεσμός,
'band, bond, chain' (see desmo-); so called

## Desmidiaceae
Desmidiaceae, n. pi., a family of algae {bot.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. ModL.

## desmo-
desmo-, before a vowel desm-, combining form
meaning 'bond*. — Gk. δεσμό-, δεσμ-, fr.
δεσμός, 'band, bond', rel, to δέσμα, of s.m.,
δέσμη, 'bundle*, δέσις, 'a binding', fr. δέειν, 'to
bind', whence also δετή, 'torch', lit. 'sticks,
bound together' (prop. fern, verbal adj. of δέειν,
'to bind'), the second element in κρή-δε-μνον,
'headdress', δ tot- δη μα, 'band or fillet*, ύττό-δημα,
*a sandal' (lit. 'that which is bound under*), fr.
l.-E. base *de{i)-, *df-, 'to bind. See diadem and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also desma,
desmid, syndesmo-.

## Desmodium
Desmodium, п., a genus of plants, the tick trefoil

and suff. -ώδης, 'like' (see desmo- and -ode); so

## desmoid
desmoid, adj., ligamentous. — Compounded of
Gk. δεσμός, 'band, bond', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See desmo- and -oid.

## Desmoncns
Desmoncns, п., a genus of trees of the palm family
{bot.) — Compounded of Gk. δεσμός, 'band,
bond*, and δγκος, 'bend, curve, hook, barb'.
See desmo- and onco-, 'barb, hook'.

## Desmoscolex
Desmoscolex, n,, a genus of marine worms {kef-
minthology). — ModL., compounded of δεσμός,

and scolex); so called from the globular head.

## desolate
desolate, adj., l) lonely; 2) deserted; 3) laid waste.

Derivatives: desolat-ing, adj., desofat-ing-fy,

## desolation

## despair

despair*, fr. de- and sperare, 'to hope', fr. spes,

spelt, 'to be successful', spechu, 'endeavor,
aspiration*, Lith. spiju, speti, 'to have time; to be

I.-E. base *spe{i)-, *spe-, 'to draw, stretch,
spread, extend, swell; to be successful'. See
prosperous and cp. desperado, desperate,
Esperanto.
Derivatives: despair, п., despair-er, п.,
despairing, adj., despair-ing-ly, adv., despair-ing-ness, n.

## despatch
despatch, tr. v. — A var. of dispatch. The spelling

Johnson.

## desperado

## desperate
desperate, adj. — L. desperaius, pp. of desperare.
See despair and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: desperate-fу,adv.,desperate-ness,n.

## desperation
desperation, n —ME. desperacioun, fr. MF.

## despicable
despicable, adj. — Late L. despicabilis, 'contempl-
ible, despicable', fr. L. despicari, 'to despise,
disdain', rel. to dispicere, 'to look down upon;
to despise, disdain', fr. de- and specere, spicere,

word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:233 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: despicabil-ity, п., despicable-ness,

## despise
despise, tr. v. — ME. despisen, fr. OF. despis-,
pres. part, stem of despire, 'to despise', fr. L.

disdain', fr. de- and specere, spicere, Ίο look al\

## despite
despite, n. — ME. despit, fr. OF. despit (F. depit),

spite-ful-ly, adv., despite-ful-ness, n.

## despite
despite, adj. — Shortened fr. orig. 'in despite of.

## despoil
despoil, tr. v., to plunder, — ME. despoilen, fr.

an enemy; prey, booty'. See spoil, п., and cp.

Derivatives: despoif-er, п., despoil-ment, n.

## despond
despond, intr. v., to lose hope and courage. — L.

lose courage, despond', fr. de- and spondere, 'to
engage oneself, promise'. See spouse.
Derivatives: despond-ence, п., despond-ency, п.,

## despondent
despondent, adj. — L. despondens, gen. -entis,

## despot
despot, п., tyrant. — OF. despot (F. despote), fr.

L. domus, 'house'; see dome, 'building'. The
second element is rel. toGk. πόσις (for *πότι.ς),
'husband', and cogn. with Ol. patih, 'master,
husband', L. polis, 'able, powerful', potens,
'able, mighty, powerful'. See potent and cp.

Derivatives: despotic (q.v.), despot-ism, п., des-
pot-ist, n.

## despotic
despotic, despotical, adj., pertaining to a despot;

Derivatives: despotically, adv., despotical-ness,
n.

## desquamate
desquamate, intr. v., to peel off {rned.) — L. de-

adj., desquamat-ory, adj.

## dessert
dessert, п., a course of fruit, sweets,'etc., served

remove what has been served', fr. des~ (fr. L. dis-,

servire). See dis- and serve.

## destination
destination, n. — L. destinatio, gen. -onis,

See next word and -ation.

## destine
destine, tr. v. — ME. destenen, fr. OF. (= F.)

L. destinare, 'to make firm, fasten; to intend,
devote, destine', which stands for *de-stun-are,
fr. de- and *sta~n, -w-enlargement of I.-E. base

(in *stanare) to ί (in de-sitnare) see abigeat and

## destiny
destiny, n. — ME. destinee, fr. OF. destinee (F.

## destitute
destitute, adj., needy, deprived. — L. destitutus,
pp. of destitueret 'to set down; to forsake,

abandon, desert; to disappoint', fr. de- and
statuere, 'to cause to stand, place, set up'. See

referred to. For the change of Latin a (in statuere)
to Γ (in de-stituere) see abigeat and cp. words
there referred to.

## destitution
destitution, n. — F. destitution, fr. L. destitutio-
nem, ace. of destitutio, 'a forsaking, deserting*,
fr. destiiutus, pp. of destituere. See prec. word
and -ion.

## destour
destour, destoor, dustoor, п., a Parsee high priest.
— Pers. dastur, 'ruler, rule, custom', fr. Pahlavi
dastobar, 'ruler, minister, a Parsee high priest*,

## destrier
destrier, п., a war horse (archaic). — OF., fr. VL.

trare, 'to lead by the right hand, to lead, guide*,
fr. L. dextra (short for dextra manus, 'right
hand'), fern, of dexter, 'right, on the right hand'.

## destroy
destroy, tr. v. — ME. destroien, destruien, fr. OF.

(whence also It. distruggere), refashioned fr. L.
destruxi{= destruc-si)and destruc-tus,past tense

destroy-ing-ly, adv. '

## destructible
destructible, adj. — Late L. destructibilis, fr. L.

Derivali ves: destructibil-ity, n., destructible-
ness, n.

## destruction
destruction, n. — L. destructio, gen. -onis, 'a

destruere. See destroy and -tion and cp.
construction,

## destructive
destructive, adj. — OF. (= F.) destructif (fern.

## destructor
destructor, n. —- L. destructor, 'a destroyer', fr,

## desuetude
desuetude, п., disuse. — F. desuetude, fr. L. de-
suetiido, 'disuse, discontinuance of a habit', fr.
desuitus, pp. of desuescere, 'to give up the use

## desulfurize
desulfurize, tr. v., to remove sulfur from. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this

Derivatives: desulfuriz-ation, п., desulfuriz-er,

## desultory
desultory, adj., jumping from one thing to
another; unmethodical. — L. desultorius,

another), which stands for *de-saltor and is rel.
to desi/tre, 'to leap down', fr. de- and satire, 'to
leap, spring, jump', whence the freq. saltare,
'to leap, jump, dance'. See salient and adj. suff.
-ory. The change of a (in saltare) to й (in
de-suitor) is due to the Latin phonetic law
according to which in the unaccented and closed
radical syllable of the second element of
compounds, d, followed by / and another
consonant, becomes w. Cp. exult, insult, result, sub-

sultory, inculcate.

desynonymize, tr. v., to deprive of synonymous
character. — Formed fr. de- (in the privative

Derivative: desynonymiz-ation, n.

detach, tr. v. — F. detacher, 'to detach, untie',

## fr. OF. destachier
fr. OF. destachier, lit. Ίο untack, disjoin', fr.

des- (fr. L. dis-, 'apart, asunder') and tache,

with suff. -able; first used by Jeremy Bentham
(1748-1832).
Derivatives: detachabil-ity, п., detachable-ness.
