<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 207 | OEVA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:234 COLUMN:1 -->
п., detachabl-y, adv.

## detachment
detachment, n. — F. detachement, fr. detacher.
See detach and -ment.

## detail
detail, tr. v. — F. detailler, 'to cut in pieces, divide
up; to relate in detail', fr. de- and miller, 'to
cut', fr. L. taliare, 'to split, cut'. See tailor.

## detail
detail, n. — F. detail, lit. 'a cutting in pieces, a
dividing up', fr. detailler. See detail, v.
Derivatives: detail-ed, adj., detail-er, n.

## detain
detain, tr. v. — Late ME. deteyuen, fr. OF. de-
tenir (F. detenir), fr. L. detinere, 'to hold off,
keep back, retain*, fr. de- and tenere, 4o hold,
keep', OF. detenir was influenced in form by
tenir (fr. VL. *tenire). Cp. Proveng., Sp. de-
tener, Catal. detenir and see tenable. Cp. also
detention, detinue. Cp. also abstain and words
there referred to.

## detainer
detainer, п., one who deiains. -- Formed from
prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## detainer
detainer, п., a detaining in one's possession (law).
— AF. detener (corresponding to OF. detem'f),
'to detain'. For the subst. use of the infinitive—
esp. in legal terminology—cp. attainder and
words there referred to.

## detect
detect, tr. v. — L. delectus, pp. of detegere, 'to
uncover, discover, disclose, reveal, detect', fr.
de- and tegere, 'to cover1. See tegument.

## detection
detection, n. — L. detectio, gen. -onis, 'an
uncovering, detecting', fr. detectus, pp. of de~-
tegere. See prec. word and -ion.

## detective
detective, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
detectus, pp. of de'tegere. See prec. word.

## detective
detective, n. — Shortened fr. detective policeman.
See detective, adj.

## detector
detector, n. — L. detector, 'uncoverer, revealer',
fr. detectus, pp. of de tegere. See detect and
agential suff. -or.

## detent
detent, п., a catch. — F. detente, lit. 'a loosening,
slackening, relaxation,' and prop, subst. use of
the fern. pp. of detendre, 'to loosen, slacken,
relax', fr. OF. destendre (fr. L. dis-, 'apart,
asunder') and tendre, 'to stretch' (fr. L. tendere).
See dis- and tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and cp. distend. Cp. also next word.

## detente
detente, л., a relaxing in the political situation.
— F. See prec. word.

## detention
detention, n. — L. detentio, gen. -Onis, 'a holding
off, keeping back', fr. detentus, pp. of detinere.
See detain and -ion.

## deter
deter, tr. v., to frighten, discourage. — L. deter-
rere, 'to frighten from, discourage from,
prevent', fr. de- and terrere, 'to frighten*. See
terrible and cp. deterrent.
Derivative: deter-ment, n.

## deterge
deterge, ir. v., to cleanse. — F. deterger, fr. L.
detergere, 'to wipe off, wipe away, cleanse', fr.
de- and tergere, 'to rub, wipe off'. See terse
and cp. deters ion.

## detergence
detergence, detergency, n. — Formed fr. next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## detergent
detergent, adj., cleansing; п., a cleansing agent.
— F. detergent, fr. L. detergentem, ace. of dc-
tergens, pres. part, of detergere. See deterge and
-ent.

## deteriorate
deteriorate, tr. v., to make worse; intr. v., to
become worse. — Late L. deterioratus, pp. of
deter iorare, "to make worse', fr. L. deterior, 'lower,
inferior, worse, meaner', fr. *de-ier, 'lower',
comparaiive of de, 'down from'. See de-, -ther
and verbal suff. -ate.

## deterioration
deterioration, n. — F. deterioration, fr. dett'iioicr,
fr. Late L. deteriorate. See prec. word and -ion.

## deteriorative
deteriorative, adj. — Coined by Jeremy Bentham
(1748-1832) fr. deteriorate and suff. -ive.

## determinable
determinable, adj. — Late L. determinabilis, 4hat
which has an end', fr. L. determinare. See
determine and -able.
Derivatives: detcrminable-ness, adj., detcrmin-
ahl-y, adv.

## determinant
determinant, adj. — L. dvtermincms, gen. -antis,
pres. part, of determinate. See determine and -ant.
Derivative: determinam, n.

## determinate
determinate, adj., 1) definite; 2) decided; 3)
resolute. — L. determinants, pp. of determinare. See
determine and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: determinate, п., determinate-ly,
adv., determin-ate-ness, n.

## determination
determination, n. — L. determination gen. -onis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:234 COLUMN:2 -->
'conclusion, boundary', fr. determinatus, pp. of
determinare. See determine and -ation.

## determinative
determinative, adj. — F. determinatif (fem.
determinative)^ fr. L. determinatus, pp. of
determinare. See next word and -ive.
Derivatives: determinative, п., determinative-ly,
adv., deter minative-ness, n.

## determine
determine, tr. v. — OF. determiner (F.
determiner), fr. L. determinare, 'to bound, limit,
prescribe, determine*, fr. de- and terminare, 'to mark
off by boundaries, mark, limit, define,
terminate*, fr. terminus, 'boundary, limit*. See term.
Derivatives: determin-ed, adj., determin-ed-ly,
adv., determin-ed-ness, п., determin-er, n.

## determinism
determinism, п., the doctrine that the action of
a man is determined by motives independent of
his will. —- F. determinisme, fr. G. Determinis-
mus, which is prob. a back formation of Prae-
determinismus, 'predeterminism'; introduced
into English by Sir William Hamilton (1788-
1856), who applied it to the doctrine of Hob-
bes. See prec. word and -ism.

## determinist
determinist, п., a believer in determinism, — See
prec. word and-ist. Deri vative :determinist-ic,ad}.

## deterrence
deterrence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## deterrent
deterrent, adj. — L, deterrens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of deterrere. See deter and -eat.
Derivative: deterrent, n.

## detersion
detersion, п., the act of cleansing. — L. detersio,
gen. -onis, 'a wiping off, a cleansing', fr. deter-
sus, pp. of detergere. See deterge and -ion.

## detersive
detersive, adj., cleansing, detergent. — F. deter-
sif (fem. detersive), fr. L. detersus, pp. of
detergere. See deterge and -ive.
Derivatives: detersive, п., a detergent, deter-
sive-ly, adv., detersive-ness, n.

## detest
detest, tr. v., to hate. — F. ditester, fr. L.
detestari, 'to curse while calling a deity to
witness; to execrate, abominate; to ward off', fr.
de- and testari, 'to be a witness, bear witness,
testify', fr. testis^ 'witness'. See testa meat and
cp. attest, contest.

## detestable
detestable, adj. — F. detestable, fr. L. detesta-
bitis, 'execrable, abominable', fr. detestari. See
detest and -able.
Derivatives: detestabil-ity, п., detestable-ness, п.,
detesiabl-y, adv.

## detestation
detestation, n. — F. detestation, fr. L. detes-
tationem, ace. of detestatio, 'execration,
detestation', fr. detestatus, pp. of detestari. See detest
and -ation.

## dethroae
dethroae, tr. v. — Formed fr. pref. de- (in the
privative sense of this prefix) and throae. Cp. F.
detroner, fr. de- (fr. L. de) and trone, 'throne'.
Derivative: dethrone-mem, n.

## detinue
detinue, п., wrongful detention of personal
property {law). — OF. detenue, 'detention*, prop.
fem. pp. of detenir, Ίο detain', used as a noun.
See detain and cp. continue, retinue.

## detonate
detonate, intr. and tr. v. — L. detonat-(um), pp.
stem of detonare, 'to thunder down, thunder
forth*, fr. de- and tonare, 'to thunder'. See
thunder, п., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: detonat-ing, adj., detonat-ive, adj.,
detonat-or, n.

## detour
detour, detour, п., a degression. — F. detour, 'a
turning away, shift, evasion', fr. detourner, 'to
turn away', fr. de- (fr. L. de) and toumer, 'to
turn'. See de- and tour.
Derivative: detour, intr. v.

## detract
detract, tr. and intr. v., to take away. — L. de-
tractus, pp. of detrahere, 'to draw off, draw a-
way, pull down', fr. de- and trahere, 'to pull,
draw*. See tract.

## detraction
detraction, n. —- F. detraction, fr. L. detractid-
nem, ace. of detractio, 'a drawing off1, fr. de-
tractus, pp. of detrahere. See prec. word and -ion.

## detractive
detractive, adj. — OF. detractif(fem. detractive),
fr. L. detractus, pp. of detrahere. See detract and
-ive.
Derivatives: detractive-ly, adv., detractive-ness,
n.

## detrain
detrain, tr. v., to set down from a railroad train;
intr. v., to alight from a railroad train. —
Formed fr. de- and the noun train.

## detriment
detriment, п., loss, harm, damage. — F.
detriment, fr. L. detrimentum, 'a rubbing off; a loss,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:234 COLUMN:3 -->
damage, defeat, detriment', fr. detritus, pp. of
deterere, 'to rub down, rub away, wear away',
fr. de- and terere, 'to rub, grind, wear away'.
See throw and -ment and cp. trite, detritus,
intertrigo.
Derivatives: detriment, tr. v., detriment-al, adj.,
detriment-al-ity, п., detriment-al-ly, adv., de-
triment-al-ness, n,

## detrital
detrital, adj., composed of detritus. — See
detritus and adj. suff. -al.

## detrited
detrited, adj., worn away. — See detritus and -ed.

## detrition
detrition, п., wearing down by friction. —Formed
with suff. -ion fr. L. detritus, pp. of deterere. See
detriment.

## detritus
detritus, п., fragments of rocks, etc., worn away
by friction, — L. detritus, 'a rubbing away*, fr.
detritus, pp. of deterere. See detriment.

## de trop
de trop, too many, too much. — F. See de- and
troppo.

## detrude
detrude, tr. v., to thrust away. — L. detrudere, 'to
thrust down, thrust away', fr. de- and trudere,
'to thrust, push', fr. I.-E. base treud-, 'to press,
push', whence also Goth, us-priutan, 'to vex',
OE. preotan, 'to weary, vex, annoy'. See threat
and cp. intrude and words there referred to.

## detruncate
detruncate, tr. v., to shorten by cutting off a part.
— L. detruncatus, pp. of detruncare, 'to lop,
cut off', fr. de- and truncare, 'to cut off'. See
truncate, v.

## detruncation
detruncation, n. — L. detruncatio, gen. -onis, 'a
cutting off', fr. detruncatus, pp. of detruncare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## detmsioa
detmsioa, п.. the act of thrusting away. — Late
L. detrusio, gen. -onis, 'a thrusting away', fr.
detrusus, pp. of detrudere. See detrude and -ion
and cp. intrusion and words there referred to.

## deuce
deuce, п., a card or die with two spots. — Fr. F.
deux, fr. OF. deus, fr. L. duos, ace. of duo, 'two*;
see dual. Since two is the lowest, hence the
losing, throw at dice, the word deuce in a
figurative sense denotes also 'ill-luck; devil'.
Derivatives: deuc-ed, adj. and adv., deuc~ed-ly,
adv.

## deuter-
deuter-, form of deutero- before a vowel.

## deuteragonist
deuteragonist, п., an actor taking the second part
in a drama. — Gk. δευτερ αγωνιστή ς,
compounded of δεύτερος, 'second', and αγωνιστής,
'combatant; actor'. For the first element see
deutero-, for the second see agonist and cp. words
there referred to.

## deuterium
deuterium, п., the isotope of hydrogen of atomic
weight or mass 2; heavy hydrogen (chem.) —
ModL., coined fr. deuter- and suff. -ium.

## deutero-
deutero-, before a vowel deuter-, combining form
meaning 'second'. — Gk. δεύτερο-, δευτερ-, fr.
δεύτερος, 'second', orig. 'that which falls short
of something', formed with the comparative
suff. -τερος from the stem of δεύειυ, δεύεσθαι,
'to be wanting, be deficient*, which is rel. to
δεΐν, 'to be in need of, to need'; see deontology.
For the etymology of the Greek comparative
suff. -τερος see -ther and cp. words there
referred to.

## deuteron
deuteron, п., also deuton, the nucleus of an atom
of deuterium. — ModL., coined fr. deuterium,
resp. deuterium.

## Deuteronomy
Deuteronomy, п., name of the 5th book of the
Pentateuch. — Late L. Deuteronomium, fr. Gk.
Δευτερονόμιον, 'second law', a name due to the
erroneous rendering of Heb. mishni*1 hattorah
kazzoth (Deut. 17:18) by the Septuagint into
δευτερονόμιον тоито, lit. 'this second law'. The
real meaning of the Hebrew words quoted is
'a copy of this law'. Δευτερονόμιον is
compounded of δεύτερος, 'second', and νόμος, 'law'.
See deutero- and nomo-.

## deuto-
deuto-, before a vowel deut-, shortened form of
deutero- resp. deuter-.

## deuton
deuton, n. — See deuteron.

## deutoplasm
deutoplasm, п., yolk (biol.) — Coined from deuto-

## and plasm
and plasm, on analogy of protoplasm.

## Deutzia
Deutzia, п., a genus of shrubs (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Dutchman Johann van der
Deutz (1743-84)- For the ending see suff. -ia.

## deva
deva, п., a deity (Hinduism). — OI. devah, 'god',

## rel. to devi
rel. to devi, 'goddess*, Avestic daeva-, 'demon',
and cogn. with Gk. δϊος, 'divine', Ζευς, gen.
Διός, 'Zeus*, OL. deivos (whence L. deus), 'god'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:235 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OEVADASI | 208 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:235 COLUMN:1 -->
See deity and cp. next word, daiva, Devi and
the second word in Bhumi Devi.

## devadasi
devadasi, п., a dancing girl in a Hindu temple. —
Hind., fr. OI. devadasi, 'slave girl of a god', fr.
devah 'deity', and dasi, 'slave girl'. See deva and
dasi. For sense development cp. Gk. ίερόδου-
λος, 'temple slave* (see hierodule).

## devaluate
devaluate, tr. v. —'See de- and valuation.
Derivative: devaluat-ion, n.

## Devanagari
Devanagari, п., the Old Indian alphabet. — OI.
devanagari, lit. 'the divine city script'. See deva
and Nagari.

## devastate
devastate, tr. v., to lay waste. — L. devastatus,
pp. of devustare, 'to lay waste, devastate', fr.
de- and vastare, 'to make empty, lay waste', fr.
vastus, 'empty, waste, desert'. See waste, adj.
and v., and verbal suff. -ate. Derivatives: dev-
astat-ing-ly, adv., devastat-ive, adj.

## devastation
devastation, n. — F. devastation, fr. L. devasta-
tus, pp. of devustare. See prec. word and -ion.

## develop
develop, tr. and intr. v. — F. developper, fr. OF.
desveloper, which is prob. formed fr. pref. des-
(fr. L. dis-, 'apart, asunder'), and a blend of
ML. faluppa, 'fiber, straw, ball of corn', and L.
volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and cp. envelop.
Derivatives: devehp-able, adj., develop-er, п.,
develop-ment, п., develop-ment-al, adj.

## devest
devest, tr. v., to deprive of a right (law). — OF.
devestir (F. devetir), fr. VL. divestlre, fr. de- and
L. vestire, 'to clothe', fr. vestis, 'garment'. See
vest and cp. divest.

## Devi
Devi, п., ι) any goddess; 2) the mother goddess,
the goddess par excellence (Hindu mythol.) —
OI. devt, 'goddess', rel. to devah, 'god', Avestic
daeva-, 'demon'. See deva and cp.-the second
word in Bhumi Devi.

## deviate
deviate, intr. and tr. v. — Late L. divial-(um),
pp. stem of deviare, 'to turn from the straight
road, go aside', fr. de- and L. via, 'way'. See
devious. Derivative: deviat-ion, n.

## device
device, n. — A blend of ME. devis, 'intention,
invention', and ME. devise, 'design, plan', which
derive fr. OF. devis, 'division, intention, plan;
coat of arms, emblem; last will, testament*
(whence F. devis, 'estimate'), resp. fr. OF. devise,
of s.m. (whence F. devise, 'device, emblem'),
which both derive fr. OF. deviser, 'to divide,
distri- bute; to put in order'. See devise.
Derivatives: device-ful, adj., device-ful-ly, adv.,
device-ful-ness, n.

## devil
devil, n. — ME. devel, It. OE. deofol, deoful, fr.
Eccles. L. diabolus, fr. Eccles. Gk. διάβολος,
'devil', fr. Gk. διάβολος, 'slanderer', fr. Sta-
βάλλειν, 'to throw across; to attack; to
calumniate, slander', fr. διά (see dia-) and βάλλειν,
'to throw'. See ballistic and cp. diablerie,
diabolic, Eblis. Cp. also It. diavolo, Provenc., F.,
Catal. diable, Sp. diablo. Port, diabo, Goth.
diabaiilus, which all derive fr. Eccles. L.
diabolus. OHG. tiufal (whence MHG. liuvel, G.
Teufel, prob. also MDu. duvel, Du. duivel, OS.
dtubal, ON. djofull, Dan. djxvel, Swed. djavul)
is a Goth, loan word.
Derivatives: devil-dom, п., devil-ish, adj., devil-
tsh-ly, adv., devit-ish-ness, devil-ism, п.,
devilment, п., devil-ry, n.

## devious
devious, adj., roundabout, circuitous. — L. de-
vius, 'off the high road, out of the way, devious',
fr. de- and via, 'way'. See via and cp. deviate.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: deviotts-ly, adv., devious-ness, n.

## devise
devise, tr. v. — OF. deviser, 'to divide,
distribute ; to put in order; to chat' (F., 'to chat,
gossip'), fr. VL. *devisare, formed with vowel
dissimilation fr. *dlvtsare, freq. of L. dlvidere, 'to
divide'. See divide and ep. device.
Derivatives: devise, n. (q.v.), devis-able, adj.,
devis-al, п., devis-ee, п., devis-er, п., devis-or, n.
(law).

## devise
devise, п., the act of devising; a will (law). —OF.
devise, 'division; will, testament', fr. deviser, 'to
divide, distribute'. See devise, v.

## devitalize
devitalize, tr. v., to deprive of vitality. — Formed
fr. de- (in the privative sense of this prefix) and
vitalize. Derivative: devita/iz-ation, n.

## devitaminize
devitaminize, tr. v., to deprive of vitamins. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix), vitamin and suff. -ize.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:235 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: devilaminiz-ation, n.

## devitrification
devitrification, n. — See next word and -fication.

## devitrify
devitrify, tr. v., to deprive of glassy character. —
Formed fr. de- (in the privative sense of this
prefix) and vitrify.

## devoid
devoid, adj., completely void. — ME., short form
of devoided, pp. of devoiden (whence the obsolete
E. verb devoid), fr. OF. desvuidier, desvoidier,
'to empty out' (whence F. devider), fr. des- (fr.
L. dis-, 'apart, asunder') and vuidier, voidier, 'to
empty'. See dis- and void.

## devoir
devoir, п., task, duty. — F., prop, subst. use of
the infinitive devoir, Ίο owe', fr. OF. deveir, 'to
owe', fr. L. debere. See debt and cp. endeavor.

## devolute
devolute, tr. v., to devolve. — L. devolutus, pp.
of devolvere. See devolve.

## devolution
devolution, n. — ML. devoifitio, gen. -onis, fr. L.
devolutus,.pp. οι devolvere. See next word and-ion.

## devolve
devolve, tr. and intr. v. — L. devolvere, 'to roll
down, tumble down; to have recourse to', fr.
de- and volvere, 'to roll, roll along, turn about'.
See volute.

## Devon
Devon, п., one of a breed of cattle, orig. raised
in Devon, a county in England.

## Devonian
Devonian, t) adj., of Devonshire in England;
pertaining to, or designating, a geological period;
2) п., an inhabitant or native of Devonshire. —
Formed with suff. -ian fr. Devon, shortened form
of Devonshire.

## devote
devote, tr. v. — L. devotus, pp. of devovere, 'to
vow, to devote (to a deity), to sacrifice oneself,
to promise solemnly', fr. de- and vovere, 'to
vow'. See vote, vow and cp. devout.
Derivatives: devot-ed, adj., devoted-iy, adv.,
devoted-ness, п., devot-ee, devote-ment, п.,
devot-er, п., devotion (q.v.)

## devotion
devotion, n. — OF. (F. devotion), fr. L. tievolio-
nem, ace. of devotio, 'a devoting, consecrating;
devotion', fr. devotus, pp. of devovere. See
devote and -ion.
Derivatives: devotion-al, adj., devotion-al-ly,
adv., devotion-al-ity, п., devotion-ate, adj., and
the hybrids devotion-al-ism, п., devotion-al-ist, n.

## devour
devour, tr. v. — ME. devouren, fr. OF. devorer (F.
devorer), fr. L. devorare, 'to swallow, gulp down,
devour; to read eagerly', fr. de- and vor&re, 'to
swallow greedily, swallow up, devour'. See
voracious and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: devour-er, п., devour-ing, adj., de-
vour-ing-ly, adv.

## devout
devout, adj. — ME. devot, devout, fr. OF. devot
(fern, devote), fr. L. devotus, pp. of devovere, 'to
vow, devote'. See devote.
Derivatives: devout-ly, adv., devout-ness, n.

## dew
dew, n. — ME. deu, deau, dew, fr. OE: deaw, rel.
to OS. dou, OFris. daw, MDu. dau, OHG.,
MHG. tou, G. Таи, ON. ddgg, 'dew', and cogn.
with OI. dhdvate, dhavati, 'runs, flows', dhautlh,
'a spring, a stream', Gk. θέειν (for *&έΓειν),
'to run, flow; to move quickly, whirl', θοός (for
*&οΓός), 'quick, active', θοάζειν, "to move
quickly. Cp. daggle, dhobl.
Derivatives: dew, tr. v., dew-less, adj., dew-y,
adj., dew-i-ly, adv., dew-i-ness, n.

## Dewali
Dewali, п., a Hindu autumnal festival. — Hind.
divali, fr. OI. dipavali, dipalt, lit. 'row of lamps,
illumination', fr. dipah, 'lamp', and avail, all,
'row'. The first element derives from a -p-en-
largement of I.-E. base *dei-, *deyd-, *di-, *dya-,
'to shine', whence OI. divdm, 'heaven; day'. See
deity.

## dewan
dewan, п., minister of finance, chief officer in
India. — Arab, and Pers. diwan; see divan. The
orig. sense of Pers. diwan was 'register', whence
developed the senses 'register of accounts;
department of accounts; ministry of finance;
minister of finance'.

## dewanee
dewanee, dewany, п., the office of a dewan. —
Hind, diwani, fr. Pers. diwani, fr. diwan. See
prec. word.

## Dewitt
Dewitt, dewitt, tr. v., to lynch. — After the
brothers Cornells and Jan De Witt, Dutch
statesmen, murdered by a mob in 1672.

## dexiocardia
dexiocardia, п., an abnormal condition in which
the heart is on the right side (anal.) —· Medical
L., compounded of Gk. δεξιός, 'on the right
hand', and καρδίϊ, 'heart". See dexter and
cardiac.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:235 COLUMN:3 -->

## dexter
dexter, adj., on the right-hand side. — L. dexter,
'on the right hand', whence arose the meanings
'skillful, favorable, Dropitious, fortunate'; cogn.
with Gk. δεξιτερός,'οη the right hand', and with
OI. daksinah, daksinah, 'on the right hand,
southern, skillful', Avestic dashina-, 'on the
right hand', Gk. δεξιός, Όη the right hand,
fortunate, clever', OSlav. desnu, Lith. dlsinas,
'on the right hand', Lith. deSine, 'the right
hand', Goth, taihswa, OHG. zeso, 'on the right
hand', Olr. dess, 'on the right hand, southern',
W. deheu, Co. dyghow, 'on the right hand', Gaul.
Dexsiva, 'goddess of fortune', Alb. dja^-te, 'on
the right hand'. All these words are prob.
derivatives of I.-E. base *dek-, 'to take, receive,
accept; acceptable, becoming, good', whence
also L. dlcere, 'to be fitting or seemly*. See
decent and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
ambidexter. L. dexter and Gk. δεξιτερός were
formed fr. base *dek- with the compar. suff.
-ter, -terus, resp. -τερος, and orig. meant 'that
which is in the better or more favorable
direction'. For the compar. suff. see -ther and cp.
words there referred to. For the sense
development of L. dexter, Gk. δεξιτερός, δεξιός, etc.,
ср. Heb. yamtn, 'right hand, south', Arab.
yaman, 'right hand, south', yamana, 'he was
happy' (see Yemen).

## Dexter
Dexter, masc. PN. — L., 'on the right hand,
fortunate'. See prec. word. For sense development
cp. Benjamin.

## dexterity
dexterity, п., 1) skill; 2) cleverness. — F. dexte-
rile, fr. L. dexleritatem, ace. of dexteritas,
'readiness, skillfumess, prosperity', fr. dexter.
See dexter and -ity.

## dexterous
dexterous, dextrous, adj., skillful, adroit, quick. —
Formed with suff. ous- fr. L. dexter. See dexter.
Derivatives: dexi(e)rous-ly, adv., dext(e)rous-
ness, n.

## dextrad
dextrad, adv., to the right side. — A hybrid
Coined fr. L. dextra, 'right hand', fem. of dexter
(see dexter), and -ad, a suff. of Greek origin.

## dextral
dextral, adj., pertaining to the right hand. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. dextra (short
for dextra manus), 'right hand', fem. of dexter.
See dexter.
Derivatives: dextral-ity, п., dextral-ly, adv.

## dextrin
dextrin, dextrine, п., a soluble gummy substance
made from starch (chem.) — F. dextrine, coined
by the French physicist Jean Baptiste (1774-
1862) and the French chemist and pharmacist
Jean-Francois Persoz (1805-68) in 1833 (in
Annates de Chimie et de Physique) fr. L. dexter,
'on the right hand' (see dexter), with chem. suff.
-ine; so called by them because it turns the plane
of polarization of light to the right.

## dextro-
dextro-, combining form meaning 'to the right'.
— Fr. L. dexter, 'to the right hand'. See dexter,

## dextrocardia
dextrocardia, п., the same as dexiocardia. — A
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. dexter, 'right',
and Gk. καρδία, 'heart'. The correct form is
dexiocardia (q.v.), in which both elements are of
Greek origin.

## dextrorse
dextrorse, adj., twining from left to right (bot.)
— L. dextrorsus, 'toward the right side, to the
right', contraction of dextrovorsus, dextro-
versus, lit. 'turned toward the right', fr. dexter,
right', and vorsus, versus, pp. of vortere, ver-
tere, 'to turn'. See dexter and version and cp.
sinistrorse.

## dextrose
dextrose, п., starch sugar (chem.) — See dextrin
and subst. suff. -ose.

## dextrous
dextrous, adj. — See dexterous.

## dey
dey, п., the governor of Algiers (before the French
conquest in 1830). — Turk, dot, prop,
'maternal uncle'.

## dhak
dhak, dhawk, п., an East Indian bushy tree
(Butea froridosa). — Hind. dhak.

## dhal
dhal, n. — A var. spelling of dal.

## dhan
dhan, п., property, wealth, treasure, price, gain.
— Hind., fr. OI. dhanam, 'booty, possession,
property', rel. to dddhati, 'puts, places'. See do,
v., and cp. the second element in stridhana.

## Dhanvantari
Dhanvantari, п., the physician of the gods in
Hindu mythology. — OI., Dhanvantarih, lit.
'passing through the bow of dhanvanah, a
circle', compounded of dhanva(n)-, 'bow', and
tarati, 'passes through, crosses over*. The first

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:236 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 209 | DIALIST -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:236 COLUMN:1 -->
element is perh. cogn. with OS. danna, OHG.
lanna, MHC, G. lanne, "fir', OS. dennia, Du.
den, 'pine'. The second element derives fr. I.-E.
base *ier-, 'to pass beyond, cross over', whence
also Gk. τέρμα, 'boundary, end limit', L.
terminus, 'boundary line, boundary, limit'. See
term and cp. words there referred to.

## dharma
dharma, п., law, right, justice (Hinduism). — O].
dharma, dharmah, rel. to dharayati, 'holds', and
to Avestic darayeili, of s.m., and cogn. with L.
firmus, 'firm, steadfast, stable, strong'. See firm,
adj., and cp. adharma, dharna.

## dharmashastra
dharmashastra, dharmasastra, п., book of laws
(India). — OI. dharmasdstrah, compounded of
dharma, 'law' (see dharma), and sastrah,
'teaching, precept, instruction, textbook'. See shastra.

## dharmsala
dharmsala, dhurmsala, п., a resting place (India).
— Hind, dharmsaia, fr. OI dharmasala, lit. 'a
pious building'. See dharma, and cell.

## dharna
dharna, dhurna, п., a mode of demanding justice
by fasting while sitting at the debtor's dooi
(India). — Hind, dharna, fr. OI. dharayati,
'holds'. See dharma.

## dhobi
dhobi, dhoby, dobyie, п., a washerman (Angio-
Ind) — Hind, dhobi, fr. OI. dhdvaii, 'washes
off, washes', which is prob. orig. identical with
dhdvati, 'runs, flows'. See dew.

## dhole
dhole, п., the wild dog of India (Cuon javanicus).
— Of uncertain origin.

## dhoni
dhoni, dhoay, п., a small fishing vessel (India). —
Hind, doni, fr. OI. droni, 'a trough', which is rel.
to dm, 'wood', drumah, 'tree'. See dinghy.

## dhoti
dhoti, dhotee, dhoty, п., a loincloth worn by
Hindus. — Hind, dhoti.

## dhow
dhow, п., an Arabian kind of vessel. — Prob. rel.
to Persian dav, 'running', which is rel. to OI.
dhavate, dhdvati, 'runs, flows', and cogn. with
Gk. »έειν (for *&έίειν), 'to run', ON. dogg,
OE. dew», 'dew'. See dew and cp. dhobi. Arab.
daw ('a kind of vessel') is an Indian loan word.

## dhurrie
dhurrie, dhurry, п., an Indian cotton fabric. —
Hind. dari.

## dhyana
dhyana, п., meditation (Hinduism). — OI. dhya-
nab, 'thought', rel. to dhyati, dhydyati, 'thinks,
meditates, fancies', Avestic day-, 'to see', OI.
dhyaman-, 'thought', and cogn. with Gk. σήμα,
'sign'. See semantics.

## di-
di-, pref. meaning 'apart, asunder'. — L., form
of dis- before b, d, g, I, m, n, r, v.

## di-
di-, pref. meaning 'two, double, twice', used esp.
in chemistry to denote two atoms, molecules,
radicals, equivalents, as the case may be. —
Gk. Si-, fr. δίς, 'twice', which stands for *dwis
and is rel. to OL. dvis (whence L. bis), and cogn.
with OI. dvih, Avestic bish, MHG. zwis, 'twice',
Goth, twis-, 'in two, asunder', ON. tvistra, 'to
divide'. See dis- and cp. two, twi-. Cp. also bi-,
bis, dia-, dicho-, disso-, dvaita, dvandva, dys-
and the second element in sapsago.

## di-
di-, form of dia- before a vowel.

## dia-
dia-, before a vowel di-, pref. meaning 'through;
thoroughly, entirely, utterly'. — Gk. δια-, fr. δια,
'through, throughout', which prob. stands for
*δισά and was formed (on analogy of μετά,
'after') fr. δίς, 'twice', hence orig. meant "divided
in the middle'. See di-, 'two, double, twice'.

## diabase
diabase, n. (petrogr.) — F., coined by the French
mineralogist Alexandre Brogniard (1770-1847)
in 1807 to name what is now called diorite. The
name was meant to signify 'a rock with two
bases', and should really have been dibase (fr.
di-, 'two', and base, n.) — In the above sense
the name was given up by Brogniard himself.
It is now applied to an igneous rock consisting
of augite and feldspar, in the sense of Gk. διά-
βασις, 'a crossing over, passage through', fr. δια
(see dia-) and βάσις, 'base' (see base, п.); so
called in allusion to the line of cleavage.

## diabetes
diabetes, п., a disease characterized by excessive
discharge of urine (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
διαβήτης, lit. 'that which causes a going
through', fr. διά (see dia-) and -βήτης, 'that
which goes, moves or flows', from the stem of
βαίνειν, 'to go'. See base, n. and cp. adiabatic.
The disease was called διαβήτης by Aretaeus
the Cappadocian, a physician, who lived in
Alexandria in the second century C.E., in
allusion to the excessive urination.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:236 COLUMN:2 -->

## diabetic
diabetic, adj., pertaining to, or having, diabetes.
— See prec. word and -ic.

## diablerie
diablerie, п., devilry. — F., fr. diable, 'devil', fr.
Eccles. L. diabolus, fr. Eccles. Gk. οΊίβολος,'άενΐΓ.
See devil. For the etymology of F. -erie see -ery.

## diabol-
diabol-, form of diabolo- before a vowel.

## diabolic
diabolic, diabolical, adj., pertaining to devils,
devilish. — F. diabolique, fr. Eccles. L. diabolicus,
fr. Eccles. Gk. διαβολικός, 'devilish', fr.·
διάβολος, 'devil'. See devil and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: diabolicai-ly, adv.

## diabolism
diabolism, п., devil worship; devilishness. —
Formed with suff. -ism.fr. Eccles. Gk. διάβολος,
'devil'. See devil.

## diabolize
diabolize, tr. v., to render diabolical. — Formed
with suff. -ize fr. Eccles. Gk. διάβολος, 'devil'.
See devil and cp. prec. word.

## diabolo-
diabolo-, before a vowel diabol-, combining form
denoting the devil. — Fr. Eccles. Gk. διάβολος,
'devil'. See devil.

## diacaustic
diacaustic, adj., pertaining to a caustic curve
caused by refraction. — Formed fr. dia- and
caustic.
Derivative: diacaustic, п., a diacaustic curve.

## diachylon
diachylon, п., a plaster made of olive oil and lead
oxide. — ModL., fr. Gk. διάχΰλον, neut. of
διάχδλος, 'juicy', fr. διά (see dia-) and χυλός,
'juice'. See chyle.

## diacid
diacid, adj., able of combining with two
molecules of a monobasic acid (chem.) — A hybrid
coined fr. di-, 'two' (fr. Gk. δι-), and acid (fr.
L. acidus, 'sour').

## disconal
disconal, adj., pertaining to a deacon or deacons.
— Late L. diaconalis, fr. diaconus. See deacon
and adj. suff. -al.

## diaconate
diaconate, п., the office of a deacon. — Eccles.
L. diaconatus, fr. Late L. diaconus. See deacon
and subst. suff. -ate.

## diacoustic
diacoustic, adj., pertaining to the refraction of
sounds. — Formed fr. di- (form of dia- before
a vowel) and acoustic.

## diacoustics
diacoustics, п., that part of acoustics which deals
with the refraction of sounds. — Formed fr.
di- (form of dia- before vowels) and acoustics.

## diacritic
diacritic, adj., distinguishing; п., a diacritical
mark. — Gk. διακριτικός, fr. διακρίνειν, 'to
separate one from another', fr. διά (see dia-)
and κρίνειν, 'to separate, decide, judge'. See
critic.
Derivatives: diacritic-al, adj., diacritical-ly, adv.

## diactinic
diactinic, adj., capable of transmitting the actinic
rays of light. — Formed fr. di- (form of dia-
before vowels) and actinic,

## Diadelphia
Diadelphia, п., a class of plants in the Linnaean
system (bol.) — ModL., prop, 'plants, the
stamens of which are united into two bundles',
lit. 'like two brothers', fr. di-, 'two', and Gk.
αδελφός, 'brother'. See adelpho- and -ia.

## diadelpbous
diadelpbous, adj., 1) having filaments united by
two bundles; 2) pertaining to the class
Diadelphia. — Formed fr. di-, 'two', Gk. αδελφός,
'brother', and suff. -ous. See prec. word.

## diadem
diadem, п., crown; fillet. — OF. diademe (F. dia-
deme), fr. L. diadema, fr. Gk. διάδημα, 'band,
fillet, royal headband', fr. διαδεϊν, 'to bind
on either side', fr. διά (see dia-) and δεΐν, 'to
bind', fr. I.-E. base *de(i)-, *d'-, 'to bind',
whence also OI. dy-ati, 'binds', da-man, 'band,
bond', Alb. del, 'sinew, tendon', dual, 'sheaf.
See desmo- and -ma and cp. anadem. Cp. also
Aditi, Aditya.
Derivatives: diadem, tr. v., diadem-ed, adj.

## diadoche
diadoche, п., succession. — Gk. διαδοχή,
'succession', rel. to διάδοχος, 'succeeding, successor',
in gradational relationship to διαδέχεσθ-αι, 'to
succeed', lit. 'to receive one from another', fr.
διά (see dia-) and δέχεσ&αι, 'to take, accept,
receive', fr. I.-E. base *dek-, *dok-, 'to take,
receive, accept; acceptable, becoming, good',
whence also L. decere, 'to be seemly or fitting'.
See decent and cp. words there referred to.

## Diadochi
Diadochi, n.pl., the successors of Alexander the
Great; hence also successors (in general). —
ModL. Diadochi, fr. Gk. διάδοχοι, pi. of
διάδοχος, successor'. See prec. word.

## diadochokinesia
diadochokinesia, diadochokinesis, п., the normal
power of performing alternating movements
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:236 COLUMN:3 -->
διάδοχος, 'succeeding', and κίνησις, 'motion'.
See prec. word and kinesis.

## diadochokinetic
diadochokinetic, adj., pertaining to
diadochokinesia. — See prec. word and kinetic.

## diaeresis
diaeresis, dieresis, п., 1) the division of one
syllable into two; 2) a mark (usually two dots)
placed over the second of two consecutive
vowels to indicate that they are to be pronounced
separately. — Late L. diaeresis, fr. Gk. δί-
αίρεσις, 'division into parts, separation of. a
diphthong into two syllables', fr. διαίρειν, 'to
divide', fr. Si- (see di-, form of dia- before a
vowel) and αίρεϊν, 'to take'. See heresy and cp.
aphaeresis, synaeresis.

## diagnose
diagnose, tr. v. — Back formation fr. diagnosis.

## diagnosis
diagnosis, п., determination of the nature of a
disease. — Medical L., fr. Gk. διάγνωσις, 'a
distinguishing, discerning, determining,
decision', lit. 'a knowing thoroughly', from the stem
of διαγιγνώσκειν, 'to distinguish, discern,
determine', lit. 'to know thoroughly', fr. διά (see dia-)
and γιγνώσκειν, 'to learn, know'. See gnome,
'maxim', and cp. gnosis.

## diagnostic
diagnostic, adj., pertaining to diagnosis. — Gk.
διαγνωστικός, 'able to distinguish', fr. διαγνωσ-
τός, 'to be distinguished', verbal adj. of
διαγιγνώσκειν. See diagnosis and -ic.
Derivatives: diagnostic п., diagnosticate (q.v.),
diagnostic-ian, n.

## diagnosticate
diagnosticate, tr. v., to diagnose. — A hybrid
formed fr. Gk. διαγνωστικός (see prec. word)
and -ate, a suff. of Latin origin.
Derivative: diagnosticai-ion, n.

## diagonal
diagonal, adj. — L. diagonaiis, fr. Gk. διαγώνιος,
'from angle to angle', fr. διά (see dia-) and
γωνία, 'an angle'. See gon- and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: diagonal, п., diagonal-ly, adv.

## diagram
diagram, п., ι) a sketch, plan; 2) a chart. — F.
diagramme, fr. L. diagramma, fr. Gk. διάγραμμα,
'something marked out by lines, a geometrical
figure', fr. διαγράφειν, 'to mark out by lines,
draw out'. See diagraph and -gram.

## diagrammatic
diagrammatic, adj., pertaining to a diagram. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. διάγραμμα, gen.
διαγράμματος. See prec. word.
Derivative: diagrammatic-al-ly, adv.

## diagrammatize
diagrammatize, tr. v., to make a diagram of, to
diagram. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. Gk.
διάγραμμα, gen. διαγράμματος. See diagram.

## diagraph
diagraph, п., an instrument for drawing plans,
maps, etc. — F. diagraphe, fr. Gk. διαγράφειν,
'to mark out by lines, draw out', fr. διά (see
dia-) and γράφειν, 'to scratch, draw, write'. See
-graph and cp. diagram.

## dial
dial, n. — ME., fr. ML. dialis, 'daily', fr. L. dies,
'day'. See dies поп and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: dial, tr.v., dial(l)-er, п., dial(l)-ing,
п., dialist (q.v.).

## dialect
dialect, n. — F. diaiecte, fr. L. dialectus, fr. Gk.
διάλεκτος, 'talk, discourse, conversation, speech,
language; the language of a country, dialect', fr.
διαλέγεσ&αι, 'to converse, talk with, discuss',
middle voice of διαλέγειν, 'to pick out, choose',
fr. διά (see dia-) and λέγειν, 'to pick out,
reckon, count, tell, say, speak', which stands in
gradational relationship to λόγος, 'word, speech,
discourse, account'. See logos and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: dialect-al, adj., dialect-al-ly, adv.,
dialectic (q.v.), dialectician (q.v.)

## dialectic
dialectic, adj. — L. diaiecticus, fr. Gk.
διαλεκτικός, 'skilled in discourse', fr. διάλεκτος. See
dialect and -ic.

## dialectic
dialectic, п., the art of discussion. — OF. (= F.)
dialectique, fr. L. dialectica (scil. ars), fr. Gk.
διαλεκτική (scil. τέχνη), 'the art of discussion
by question and answer', fern, of διαλεκτικός,
'skilled in discourse'. See dialectic, adj.
Derivatives: dialectic-ai, adj., dialectic-al-ly, n.

## dialectician
dialectician, n. — F. dialecticien, fr. diaiecte. See
dialect and -ician.

## dialectology
dialectology, п., the study of dialects. — See
dialect and -logy.
Derivatives: dialectolog-icai, adj., dialectolog-
ist, n.

## dialist
dialist, п., a maker of dials. — A hybrid coined
fr. dial, a word of Latin origin, and suff. -ist (fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:237 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OIALISTER | 210 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:237 COLUMN:1 -->
Gk. -ιστής).

## Dialister
Dialister, п., a genus of parasitic bacteria (bac-
teriol.) — ModL., formed fr. dia- and Gk. υλισ-
τήρ, 'filter', which is rel. to υλη, 'slime, mud*,
and cogn. with OI. surah, 'intoxicating drink',
sura, 'brandy', Lith. suld, Lett, sula, 'sap',
OPruss. sub, 'curdled milk', OHG. sullen,
MHG. siiln, G. suhlen, OE. syljan, sylian, 'to
make muddy or dirty'. All these words derive
fr. I.-E. base *su-l-, enlargement of base *seu-,
'to rain; sap', whence Gk. Sslv, 'to rain', υετός,
'rain'. See hyeto-.

## diallage
diallage, п., a dark green laminated variety of
pyroxene (mineral.) — F., fr. Gk. διαλλαγή,
'change', from the stem of διαλλάσσειν, 'to
change', which is formed fr. διά (see dia-) and
άλλάσσειν, 'to change', fr. άλλος, 'another'.
See else, and cp. alio-, alias. Cp. also hypallage,
allagite. The mineral was so called in allusion
to the irregular planes of fracture.

## dialleloa
dialleloa, п., definition in a circle (logic). — Gk.
δι' αλλήλων, 'through one another'. See dia- and
allelo-.

## dialogic
dialogic, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
a dialogue. — ML. dialogicus, 'pertaining to a
dialogue', fr. Gk. διάλογος. See dialogue and -ic.
Derivative: dialogic-al-ly, adv.

## dialogist
dialogist, п., ι) speaker in a dialogue; 2) a writer
of a dialogue. — Formed with suff. -ist fr. Gk.
διάλογος. See next word.

## dialogue
dialogue, also dialog, п., — F., fr. L. dialogus, fr.
Gk. διάλογος, 'conversation, dialogue', fr. δια-
λέγεσθαι, 'to converse'. See dialect and cp. the
second element in monologue.
Derivatives: dialogue, dialog, intr. and tr. v.,
dialogu-er, n.

## dialyse
dialyse, v. — See dialyze.

## dialysis
dialysis, п., separation of crystalloids from
colloids (chem.) — L., 'separation', fr. Gk. διά-
λυσις, 'separation, dissolution', fr. διαλύειν, 'to
part asunder, break off, dissolve', fr. διά (see
dia-) and λύειν, 'to loose, loosen'; see -lysis.
The word dialysis was introduced into chemistry
by the Scottish chemist Thomas Graham (1805-
69), the discoverer of this process, in 1861.

## dialytic
dialytic, adj., pertaining to dialysis. — Gk.
διαλυτικός, 'able to dissolve', fr. διαλυτός,
'dissolved', verbal adj. of διαλύειν, 'to dissolve'.
See prec. word and -ic.

## dialyze
dialyze, also dialyse, tr. v. (chem.) — Back
formation fr. dialysis.
Derivative: dialyz-er, dialys-er, n.

## diamagnetic
diamagnetic, adj., tending to take a position at
right angles to the direction of the magnetic
current. — Formed fr. dia- and magnetic.
Derivative: diamagnetic-al-ly, adv.

## dia magnetism
dia magnetism, n. — Formed fr. dia- and
magnetism. See prec. word.

## diamantiferous
diamantiferous, adj., yielding diamonds. — F.
diamantifere. See diamond and -fenms and cp.
diamondiferous.

## diameter
diameter, n. — OF. diametre (F. diamitre), fr.
L. diametros, fr. Gk. διάμετρος (scil. γραμμή),
lit. 'a diametral line*. See dia- and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: diametr-al, adj., diametrical (q.v.)

## diametric
diametric, diametrical, adj. — Gk. διαμετρικός,
'diametrical', fr. διάμετρος. See diameter and
-ic.
Derivative: diametrical-ly, adv.

## diamine
diamine, also diamin, п., a double amine (chem.)
— Formed fr. di-, 'double', and amine,

## diamond
diamond, n. — ME. diamant, diamaunt, fr. OF.
diamante fr. Late L. diamantem, ace. of diamas,
which is a blend of Gk. άδάμάς, 'adamant,
diamond', lit. 'unconquerable' and διαφανής,
'transparent'. See adament and diaphanous.
Derivatives: diamond, adj. and tr. v., diamond-
edy adj., diamondize (q.v.)

## diamondiferous
diamondiferous, adj., yielding diamonds. — A
hybrid coined fr. diamond and L. ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See diamond and -ferous and cp. dia-
maatlferous.

## diamondize
diamondize, tr. v., to ornament with diamonds.
— A hybrid coined fr. diamond and -ize, a suff.
of Greek origin.

## Diana
Diana, п., the goddess of the moon and of
hunting in Roman mythology; identified with the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:237 COLUMN:2 -->
Greek Artemis. — L., earlier Diviana.
According to Kretschmer the name means 'belonging
to *Divia, the goddess of the moon' (lit. 'she
who illuminates*), fr. dlus, 'divine', which stands
for *diwios and is rel. to dlvus, 'god, divine*,
deus, 'god'. See deity.

## Diantbera
Diantbera, п., a genus of plants, the water willow
(hot.) — ModL., lit. 'having two anthers', fr.
di-, 'two', and Gk. ανθηρός, 'flowery', fr. άνθος,
'fiower'. See anther.

## Dianthus
Dianthus, п., a large genus of herbs, the pink and
the carnation (bot.) — ModL., coined by
Linnaeus fr. Gk. Διός, gen. of Ζευς, 'Zeus', and
άνθος, 'flower'. Accordingly the word lit. means
'flower of Zeus'. See Zeus and anther.

## diapason
diapason, п., the total range of a voice or
instrument (music). — L. diapason, 'the whole
octave', fr. Gk. διαπασών, for δια πασών (short for
δια πασών χορδών συμφωνία),'concord through
all of the notes, the octave', fr. διά, 'through',
and fern. pi. gen. of πας, 'а|Г. See dia- and pan-.

## diapedesis
diapedesis, п., the oozing of blood from the
unruptured vessel walls into the tissues (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. διαπήδησις, 'a leaping
through', fr. διαπηδάν, 'to leap through', fr. διά
(see dia-) and πηδαν, 'to leap'. See pedes is.

## diaper
diaper, n. — ME. diaper, diapery, fr. OF. diapre,
fr. earlier diaspre (whence F. diapre, 'diapered,
variegated'), fr. ML. diasprum (whence also It.
diaspro, OProveng. diaspre, Sp. diaspero, Port.
diaspero, diaspro), 'jasper', fr. L. iaspis, fr. Gk.
ΐασπις, 'jasper', ult. fr. Heb. yaskepkeh (see
jasper). ML. and Romance di- (in diasprum etc.)
is merely an inexact transliteration of J in L.
jaspis (for L. iaspis). Cp. obsolete E. diasper =
E. jasper.

## diaper
diaper, tr. v. — Partly fr. OF. diasprer (F. dia·
prer), fr. diaspre, 'diaper', partly fr. diaper, n.
(q.v.)
Derivative: diaper-ing, n.

## diaphanous
diaphanous, adj., transparent. — ML. diaphanus,
fr. Gk. διαφανής,'transparent', fr. διαφαίνειν,'ίο
show through', fr. διά (see dia-) and φαίνειν, 'to
show*. See phantasm and suff. -ous.
Derivatives: diaphanous-ly, adv., diaphanous-
ness, n.

## diaphoresis
diaphoresis, п., perspiration (med) — Late L., fr.
Gk. διαφόρησις, 'evaporation, perspiration', fr.
διαφορεΐν, 'to spread abroad, disperse, to
dissipate by evaporation or perspiration', prop, 'to
carry through', fr. διά (see dia-) and φορεΐν, freq.
of φέρειν, 'to bear, carry*. See bear, 'to carry',
and cp. -phore. Cp. also adiaphorous.

## diaphoretic
diaphoretic, adj., promoting perspiration. — Late
L. diaphoreticus, fr. Gk. διαφορετικός, fr. δι<*-
φορεΤν. See prec. word and -ic

## diaphragm
diaphragm, п., ι) muscular partition between the
thorax and abdomen; 2) a vibrating membrane.
— Late L. diaphragma, fr. Gk. διάφραγμα,
'partition, barrier; muscle which divides the thorax
from the abdomen', fr. διαφραγνύναι, δια-
φράσσειν, 'to divide off, barricade', fr. διά (see
din-) and φραγνύναι, φράσσειν, 'to enclose,
fence round', which is cogn. with L. farclre, 'to
stuff*, frequens, gen. -entis, 'thronged, pressed
together'. See farce, 'to stuff, cram', and cp.
frequent.
Derivatives: diaphragm, tr. v., diaphragm-al,
adj.

## diaphragmatic
diaphragmatic, adj., pertainins to the diaphragm.
— Formed with sufT. -ic fr. διάφραγμα, gen.
διαφράγματος. See prec. word.
Derivative: diaphragmatic-al-ly, adv.

## diaphysis
diaphysis, п., l) the shaft of a long bone (бол);
2) an abnormal prolongation of the axis of
inflorescence (bot.)— ModL., fr. Gk. *&ι£φυσις,
'germination; division; point of separation;-
spinous process of theshinbone', lit. 'a growing
between', fr. διαφύεσθαι, 'to grow between*, fr.
διά (see dia-) and φύειν, 'to bring forth,
produce, make to grow*. See physio-and words there
referred to and cp. esp. apophysis, epiphysis.
Derivative: diaphysi-al, adj.

## Diaporthe
Diaporthe, п., a genus of sac fungi (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. διαπορθεΐν, freq. of διαπέρθειν,
'to destroy utterly', fr. διά (see dia-) and πέρθειν,
'to destroy', which is of uncertain origin.

## diarchy
diarchy, п., governmenl by two rulers. — Formed

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:237 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. di-, two', and -archy. Cp. triarchy, tetrarchy,
heptarchy.

## diarial
diarial, adj., pertaining to a diary. — Formed fr.
diary with adj. suff. -al.

## diarist
diarist, п., one who keeps a diary. — A hybrid
coined fr. diary, a word of Latin origin, and
suff. -ist (fr. Gk. -ίστής).
Derivative: diarist-ic, adj.

## diarrhea
diarrhea, diarrhoea, п., excessive evacuation of
the bowels. — Late L. diarrhoea, fr. Gk.
διάρροια, fr. διαρρεΐν, 'to flow through', fr. διά (see
dia-) and ρεΐν, 'to flow'. See rheo- and cp.
-rrhea.
Derivatives: diarrke-al, diarrhoe-af, diarrke-ic,
diarrhoe-ic, adjs.

## diarthrosis
diarthrosis, п., articulation (anai.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. διάρθρωσις, 'articulation', fr. διαρθροϋν,
'to divide by joints, articulate', fr, διά (see dia-)
and άρθροϋν, 'to connect byajoinf, fr. άρθρον,
'joint'. See arthro- and -osis.

## diary
diary, п., a daily record. — L. diarium, 'a daily
allowance', later used also in the sense 'diary',
fr. dies, 'day*. See dial and subst. suff. -ary.

## Diasia
Diasia, п., an annual festival in honor of Zeus
Meilichios at Athens (Greek religion). — Gk.
Διάσια (pi.), lit. 'festival of Zeus', fr, Διός, gen.
of Ζευς. See Zeus.

## diaskeuasis
diaskeuasis, п., revision, recension. — ModL., fr.
Gk. διασκευάζει, 'to prepare for oneself,
revise, edit', fr. διά (see dia-) and σκευάζειν. Ίο
prepare, make ready, to furnish wiih something',
fr. σκεύος, 'a-vessel, an implement', which is of
uncertain etymology. Cp. parasceve. For the
ending see suff. -asis.

## diaskeuast
diaskeuast, п., a reviser. — Gk. διασκευαστής,
'a reviser, editor', fr. διασκευάζειν. See prec.
word and -ast.

## Diaspora
Diaspora, п., the Dispersion, the Jews scattered
among the Gentiles after the Babylonian
captivity. — Gk. διασπορά, 'a scattering about,
dispersion', fr. δίασπείρειν, 'to scatter about,
distribute', fr. διά (see dia-) and σπείρειν, 'to
scatter'. See spore and cp. next word.

## dia spore
dia spore, п., native aluminum hydroxide(HA102)
(chem.) — Gk. διασπορά, 'a scattering about'
(see prec. word); so called in allusion to its
strong decrepitation before the blowpipe.

## diastaltic
diastaltic, adj., extended (said of intervals) (Greek
music). — Gk. διασταλτικός, 'serving to
distinguish', fr. διαστέλλειν, 'to put asunder,
separate, divide, expand, dilate; to distinguish,
define', fr. διά (see dia-) and στέλλειν, 'to make
ready, set in order, arrange, equip, dispatch,
send', which stands in gradational relationship
to στολή,'equipment, garment'. See stole, *a long
garment', and cp. diastole.

## diastase
diastase, п., ι) an amylase; 2) an enzyme
(biochemistry). — F., fr. Gk. διάστασις,
'separation', fr. διϊστάναι, 'to separate', lit. 'to stand
apart', fr. διά (see dia-) and στάναί, 'to stand';
see state. Diastase lit. means 'a separating
substance'. It was introduced into French in this
sense by Payen and Persoz in 1833.

## diastatic
diastatic, adj., having the properties of diastase.
— Gk. διαστατικός, 'separating,
disintegrating', fr. διάστατος, 'divisible', verbal adj. of
διιστάναι, 'to separate'. See prec. word and -ic.

## diastole
diastole, п., dilatation of the heart (med.) — Gk.
διαστολή, 'drawing asunder, dilatation;
distinction, difference', fr. διαστέλλειν. See
diastaltic and cp. systole.

## diastyle
diastyle, п., a colonnade in which the interval
between each pair of columns equals three times
the diameter of one column (archit.) — L. dia-
stylos, fr. Gk. διάστϋλος, 'having the space of
three diameters between the columns', fr. διά
(see dia-) and στϋλος, 'a pillar'. See style,
'gnomon', and cp. words there referred to.

## diatessaron
diatessaron, п., a harmony of the four gospels.
— Gk. δια τεσσάρων, 'by four', fr. διά,'through,
by means of, by1, and gen. of τέσσαρες, 'four'.
See dia- and tessera.

## diathermancy
diathermancy, п., the property of transmitting
radiant heat. — F. diathermansie, formed with
suff. -cy from the stem of Gk. διαθερμαινειν, 'to
warm through', fr. διά (see dia-) and θερμαΐνειν,
'to warm, heat1. See therm and cp. athermancy.

## diathermanous
diathermanous, adj., transmitting radiant heat. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:238 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 211 | DIDACTIC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:238 COLUMN:1 -->
Formed fr. dia- the stem of Gk. θερμαίνειν, 'to
warm, heat' (fr. θ-έρμη, 'heat', see therm) and
-ous.

## diathermic
diathermic, adj., diathermanous. — Formed with
stiff, -ic fr. Gk. διά&ερμος, 'thoroughly warm',
fr. dia- and θέρμη, 'heat'. See therm.

## diathermy
diathermy, п., application of heat in the tissues
of the body by means of high-frequency electric
currents. — Medical L. diaxkermia, coined by
Nagelschmidt in ige8 fr. dia,- and -thermy.

## diathesis
diathesis, п., bodily constitution which makes
susceptible to disease (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
διάθ-εσις, 'a placing in order, arrangement,
disposition, physical condition', fr. διατι&έναι, 'to
place separately, arrange, manage', fr. 8ii (see
dia-) and τιθέναι, 'to put, place'. See theme and
cp. thesis and words there referred to.

## diatom
diatom, п., any of microscopic unicellular algae
(bot.) — Gk. διάτομος, 'cut through', verbal
adj. of διατέμνειν, 'to cut through', fr. διά (see
dia-) and τέμνειν, 'to cut'. See tome and cp.
'words there referred to.

## diatomaceous
diatomaceous, adj., pertaining to, or containing,
diatoms. — Formed fr. Gk. διάτομος, 'cut
through' (see prec. word), and suff. -aceous.

## diatomic
diatomic, adj., consisting of two atoms (chem.)
— Compounded of di-, 'two', atom, and -ic.

## diatonic
diatonic, adj., pertaining to, or consisting of, the
standard major or minor scale, without
chromatic variations (music). — F. diatonique, fr. L.
diatonicus, fr. Gk. διατονικός, fr. διάτονος,
'extending; pertaining to the diatonic scale', fr.
. διατείνειν, 'to stretch out', which is formed
fr. διά (see dia-) and τείνειν, 'to stretch'. See
tonic.

## diatribe
diatribe, п., a bitter criticism. — F. diatribe, fr.
L. diatriba, 'a learned disputation', fr. Gk.
διατριβή, 'a wearing away', esp. 'a wearing away
of time, amusement, pastime, occupation,
labor', fr. διατρΐβειν, 'to rub or wear away, to
wear away time, to spend time', fr. διά (see
dia-) and τρίβειν, 'to rub'. See tribulation.
Derivative: diatribe, intr. v.

## dlazo-
dlazo-, before a vowel diaz-, combining form
denoting compounds in which two nitrogen atoms
are united with one hydrocarbon radical (chem.)
— Coined fr. di-, 'two', and azo-,

## dib
dib, п., knucklebone; a game with knucklebones.
— Prob. fr. obsol. dib, a weakened form of dab,
'to strike lightly'.

## dibasic
dibasic, adj., having two atoms of hydrogen
replaceable by bases (chem.) — Formed fr. di-,
'two', and basic.

## dibber
dibber, n. — See next word.

## dibble
dibble, also dibber, п., a pointed implement for
making holes. — Formed with instrumental
suff. -le fr. obsolete dib, 'to strike lightly'. See
dib, 'knucklebone'.
Derivative: dibble, tr. v.

## dibbuk
dibbuk, п., the soul of a dead sinner that attaches
itself to the body of a living man (Jewish
folklore). — Mishnaic Heb. dibbttq, 'a joining,
attachment', fr. dibbiq, 'he joined together', fr.
Heb. dabhdq, 'he clung, cleaved, kept close to,
attached himself, which is rel. to Aram.-Syriac
d'bhaq, d'bhiq, Arab, dabiqa, of s.m.

## dlcast
dlcast, п., a judge (Greek antiq.) — Gk. δικαστής,
'a judge', fr. δικάζειν, 'to judge', fr. δίκη,
custom, usage, order right', which is rel. to δεικ-
νύναι, 'to show', fr. I.-E. base *deik-, 'to show,
point out', whence also L. d'icere, "to say, tell".
See dictioa and cp. the second element in
Enrydice.

## dicastery
dicastery, п., the body of dleasts (Greek antiq.) —
Gk. δικαστήριον, 'a court of justice, the court',
fr. δικαστής. See prec. word.

## dice
dice, n. — PI. of die.
Derivatives: dice, tr. v., dic-er, п., dic-ing, n.

## DIcentra
DIcentra, п., a genus of plants of the family Fu-
' mariaceae (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'having two
spurs', fr. di-, 'two', and Gk. κέντρον, 'spur'.
See center.

## dich-
dich-, form dieho- befote a vowel.

## dichlamydeous
dichlamydeous, adj., having calyx and corolla
(bot.) — Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. χλαμύς,
gen. χλαμύδος, 'mantle, cloak'. See chlamys.

## dicho-
dicho-, before a vowel dich-, combining form
meaning 'in two, asunder'. — Gk. διχο-, διχ-,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:238 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. δίχα, 'in two, asunder, apart from,
separately', which is rel. to δίς, 'twice'. See di-, 'two',
and cp. disso- and the first element in dittography.

## dichogamous
dichogamous, adj., characterized by dichogamy
(bot.) — See next word and -ous.

## dichogamy
dichogamy, п., maturation of the stamens and
pistils at different times (bot.) — Compounded
of Gk. δίχα, 'in two, apart', and γάμος,
'marriage'. See dicbo- and -gamy.

## dichotomous
dichotomous, adj., branching in pairs (bot.) —
See next word and -ous.
Derivative: dichotomous-Iy, adv.

## dichotomy
dichotomy, п., division into two parts; branching
in pairs (bot.) — Compounded of dicho- and
Gk. -τομίδ, 'a cutting of. See -tomy.
Derivative: dichoiom-ic, adj.

## dichroic
dichroic, adj. characterized by dichroism. — See
next word and -ic.

## dichroism
dichroism, п., the property of certain crystals to
exhibit different colors when viewed from
different angles (crystaiiogr.) — Formed with suff.
-ism fr. Gk. δίχροος, 'two-colored', fr. δι- (see
di-, 'two') and χρως, gen. χρωτός (Ion. χροός),
'skin; color of the skin, color'. See chrome.

## dichromatic
dichromatic, adj., having two colors. — Formed
fr. di-, 'two', and chromatic.

## dichromic
dichromic, adj., able to distinguish only two of
the three primary colors. — Formed with suff.
-ic fr. Gk. δίχρωμος, 'two-colored', fr. δι- (see
di-, 'two') and χρώμα, 'color'. See chrome.

## dick
dick, п., fellow. — Fr. Dick, short for Dickon,
Dickens, popular forms of Richard. Cp.
dickens.

## dick
dick, n. (in the phrase to take one's dick) (slang).
— Short for declaration.

## dickens
dickens, п., the devil. — From the name Dickens,
alteration of Dickon, apopularformofRiciiard.
Cp. dick, 'fellow'.

## dicker
dicker, п., the number ten; esp. ten hides; a set
of ten things. — Rel. to MLG. deker, MHG.
techer, decher, G. Decher, 'set of ten things'; fr.
L. decuria, 'a company of ten', which was fr.
decern, 'ten', on the analogy of centuria, 'a
division of a hundred things of one kind' (from
centum, 'a hundred'). See decern-, deca- and
cp. decury.

## dicker
dicker, intr. and tr. v., to haggle. — Fr. prec.
word. The original meaning of the verb was 'to
haggle about the price of ten hides'.

## Dicksonia
Dicksonia, п., name of a genus of ferns of the
polypody family (bot.) — ModL., named after
the English botanist James Dickson (1738-
1822). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## dicky
dicky, dickey, п., ι) a donkey; 2) a small bird;
3) a false shirt front. — Fr. the PN. Dick. See
dick, 'fellow'.

## dicky
dicky, adj., shaky (slang). — Prob. of the same
origin as prec. word.

## diclinous
diclinous, adj., having the androecium and the
gynoecium in separate flowers (bot.) — Lit.
'having two beds', fr. Gk. δι-, 'two', and κλίνη,
'bed'. See di- 'two', clinic and -ous.

## dicotyledon
dicotyledon, п., a plant with two cotyledons (bot.)
— Formed fr. di-, 'two', and cotyledon.

## Dicotyledones
Dicotyledones, n. pi., one of the two subclasses of
angiospermous plants (bot.) — ModL. See prec.
word.

## dicotyledonous
dicotyledonous, adj., 1) having two cotyledons;
2) pertaining to the Dicotyledones (bot.) — See
di-, 'two', cotyledon and -ous.

## dicoumarin
dicoumarin, also dicoumarol, п., a white
crystalline compound used as an anticoagulant (med.)
— Formed fr. di-, 'two, double', and coumarin.
For the ending of dicoumarol see suff. -ol.

## dlerotic
dlerotic, adj., doubly pulsating (so that two beats
of the artery correspond to one of the pulse
(med.) — Formed with suff. -Ic fr. Gk. δίκροτος,
'double beating', fr. δι- (see di-, 'two, double'),
and the stem of κροτεΐν, 'to beat, strike'. See
Crotalus.

## dicrotism
dicrotism, п., dicrotic condition.— See dicrotic
and -ism.

## DIcruridae
DIcruridae, n. pi., a family of birds, the drongo
(ornithol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr.
Gk. δίκροος, δίκρους, 'forked', and ουρά, 'tail'.
The first element prob. meant orig.
'two-horned', and stands for *δί-κροί"-ος, a compound
formed fr. δι- (see di-, 'two') and a word rel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:238 COLUMN:3 -->
to κέρας, 'horn' (see cerato-). For the seond
element see uro-, ktaiF.

## DictamnuS
DictamnuS, п., a genus of plants of the rue family
(bot.) — L. dictamnus. See dittany.

## dictaphone
dictaphone, п., a phonographic instrument for
recording and reproducing. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. dictare, 'to dictate', and Gk. φωνή, 'sound,
voice'. See dictate and phone, 'speech, sound'.

## dictate
dictate, tr. and intr. v. — L. dictatus, pp. of die-
tare, 'to say often, pronounce repeatedly,
dictate (for writing)', freq. of dicere (pp. dictus),
'to say'. See diction and verbal suff. -ate and cp.
dictum, dight, ditty, indict.

## dictate
dictate, n. — L. diclatum, 'something dictated',
neut. pp. of dictare. See dictate, v.

## dictation
dictation, n. — ML. dictatio, gen. -onis, fr. L.
dictatus, pp. of dictare. See dictate, v., and -ion.
Derivative: dictation-al, adj.

## dictator
dictator, n. — L. dictator, fr. dictatus, pp. οι die-
tare. See dictate and agential suff. -or.

## dictatorial
dictatorial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. dictatorius, fr. dictator. See prec. word.
Derivatives: dictatoriai-iy, adv., dictatorial-
ness, n.

## diction
diction, n. — L. dictio, gen. -onis, 'a saying,
speaking, speech, diction', fr. dictus, pp. of
dicere, 'to say, tell, mention, relate, affirm', orig.
Ίο show', rel. to dicare, 'to proclaim, dedicate,
consecrate, devote', and to Oscan deikum,
deicum, 'to speak', fr. I.-E. base *deik-, *dik-,
'to show, point out', whence also L. digitus,
'finger' (lit. 'pointer'), the second element in L.
ju-dex, 'judge' (lit. 'he who shows or teaches
justice'), in-dex, forefinger, index' (lit. 'pointer'),
and OI. disati, 'shows', disa, 'direction', desah,
'region', Hitt. tekkushami, Ί show', Gk.
δεικνύναι, 'to show', δίκη, 'custom, usage,
order, right', Goth, ga-teihan, 'to announce', OE.
teon (for *tih-an), 'to accuse', tacen, tacn, 'sign,
token', txcan, 'to show, teach'. Cp. teach and
words there referred to. Cp. also abdicate, addict,
apodictic, benediction, benison, condition,
contradict, dedicate, deictic, dicast, dictate,
dictionary, dictum, dight, digit, ditto, edict, endeictic,
epidictic, fatidic, index, indicate, indicia, indict,
indite, interdict, judge, judicial, juridical,
jurisdiction, malediction, malison, paradigm, policy,
'document', preach, preconize, predicate, predict,
soi-disant, swadeshi, syndic, valediction, verdict,
veridical, vindicate.

## dictionary
dictionary, n. — ML. dictionarium (whence also
F. dictionnaire), prop, 'a book of sayings', fr. L.
dictio, gen. -onis, 'a saying'. See prec, word and
subst. suff. -ary.

## dictograph
dictograph, п., a telephonic instrument, used for
transmitting conversations, etc. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. dictum, 'a saying, word', and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See next word
and -graph.

## dictum
dictum, п., a saying, maxim, proverb. — L., lit.
^something said', neut. pp. of dicere, 'to say'.
See diction.

## dicty-
dicty-, form of dictyo- before a vowel.

## Dictynidae
Dictynidae, n. pi., a family of spiders (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk. δίκτυον,
'net', lit. 'that which is thrown or cast', fr.
δικεϊν, 'to throw, cast', whence also δίσκος (dis-
similated fr. *δίκ-σκος), 'quoit, dish'. See dish
and cp. next word. Cp. also the second element
in Eriodicytion.

## Dictynna
Dictynna, п., a Cretan goddess (Greek mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. Δίκτυννα, lit. 'she who is
associated with a nef, fr. δίκτυον (see prec. word); so
called because when, being pursued by Minos,
she had thrown herself into the sea, fishermen
rescued her in a net.

## dictyo-
dictyo-, before a vowel dicty-, combining form
meaning 'net'. —· Gk. δίκτυο-, δικτυ-, fr.
δίκτυον, 'net'. See Dictynidae.

## did
did, past tense of do. — ME. dude, dide, fr. OE.
dyde, fr. don. See do.

## Didache
Didache, п., a Christian treatise of the second
century (eccles.) — Gk. διδαχή, 'teaching', from
the stem of διδάσκειν, 'to learn'. See didactic.

## didactic
didactic, adj., used for teaching; instructive. —
Gk. διδακτικός, 'skilled in teaching', fr.
διδακτός, 'taught', pp. of διδάσκειν, 'to teach', prob.
dissimilated fr. *δι-δακ-σκειν and cogn. with L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:239 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OIDAPPER | 212 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:239 COLUMN:1 -->
discere (for *didfc~skere), 'to learn', fr. 1-Е. base
*dek-, 'to take, receive, accept; acceptable,
becoming good', whence also L. decere. 'to be
fitting or seemly'. See decent and cp. docite. Cp.
also autodidact.

## didapper
didapper, п., the small grebe or dabchick. — Late
ME. dydoppar, for dive dapper (which occurs in
Shakespeare). Ср. OE. di/fedoppa, 'pelican', and
see dive and dip. Cp. also dap, dabchick.

## diddle
diddle, ir. v., to swindle. — Back formation from
Jeremy Diddler, name of a swindling character
ir.JamesKenney'sfarce Raising the Wind (1803).
Elymologically, the name Diddler is prob.
connected wiih OE. dydrian, 'to deceive'.

## diddle
diddle, intr. v., to move up and down, or to and
fro. — Prob. of imitative origin. Cp. dial. E.
didder, 'to tremble'.

## Didelphia
Didelphia, п., the group of marsupials (zool.) —
ModL., lit. "having a double uterus', fr. di- 'two,
double', and Cik. δελψύς, 'womb, uterus', which
is rel. to αδελφός, 'brother', lit. 'from the same
womb'. See adelpho- and -ia.

## Dido
Dido, п., foundress and queen of Carthage. —
L. Dido, fr. Gk. Διδώ, of Phoen.-Heb. origin.
The name prob. means 'beloved'. Cp. Heb. dodh,
'beloved, father's brother', dqfi/ifm, 'love'. Cp.
also David.

## dido
dido, п., a trick; a caper (U.S., collaq.) — Of
uncertain origin.

## didrachma
didrachma, didrachm, п., an ancient Greek silver
coin, a two-drachma piece*. — Late L.
didrachma, fr. Gk. δίδραχμον, 'a two-drachma piece',
fr. δι- (see di-,'two') and δραχμή, 'drachm'. See
drachma.

## didymium
didymium, п., name of a rare metal (chem.) —
ModL., coined by its discoverer, the Swedish
chemist Carl Gustav Mosander (1797-1858), fr.
Gk. δίδυμος, 'twin', which is formed fr. δι-,
(rel. to δις, 'twice'), and -δυμος (rel. to δύο,
'two'); see di- and dual. Mosander thought that
this metal consisted of one single element and
called this alleged element didymium, 'the twin
element', because it is always found associated
with another element, the lanthanum. Cp. neo-
dymium, praseodymium, tetrad у mite, tridymite,
Cp. also epididymis.

## die
die, n, cube. — ME. dee, fr. OF. de (F. de), fr. L.
datus, pp. οι dare, 'to give', used as a noun. Cp.
It., Sp., Port, dado, OProvenc. dat, 'die', and see
date, 'point of time'. Cp. also dado.

## die
die, intr. v. -- ME. dien, deyen, fr. ON. deyja,
rel. to Dan. de, Swed. do, 'to die', OFris. deja,
'to kill', OS. doian, OHG. touwe/t, Goth, diwans,
'mortal', fr. Teut. base *dau-, 'to die'. See dead
and cp. words there referred to.

## dielectric adj.
dielectric adj., nonconducting (efectr.) —
Formed fr. di- (form of dia- before a vowel) and
electric.
Derivative: dielectric, n.

## Diervilla
Diervilla, п., a genus of planis, the bush
honeysuckles (hot.) — ModL., named by the botanist
Tourneville in honor of N. Diercvillc, a
surgeon, who brought this plant from Canada to
Tourneville in 1699.

## Diesel engine
Diesel engine, also diesel, n. — Named after its
inventor Kudolf Diesel (1858-1913).
Derivatives: dieselize, tr. v., diesel-iz-ation, n.

## Dies irae
Dies irae, name of a Medieval Latin hymn,
ascribed to Thomas of Celano, who lived in the first
half of the thirteenth cent. — Lit. 'the day of
wrath'; so called from the first two words of the
hymn. See dies поп and ire.

## diesis
diesis, п., ι) the Pythagorean semitone in ancient
Greek music; 2) the difference between a major
and a minor semitone (ratio 125:128); 3) the
sign sharp (4Ф) (music). — L., fr. Gk. δίεσις, 'a
quarter tone', lit. 'a letting through', fr. διιέ-
ναι, 'to send through', fr. δι-, form of δια
before a vowel (see dia-) and ίέναι, 'to send',
which stands for *yi-ye-nai, and is cogn. with
\,.jacere, 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and
cp. aphesis.

## dies noa
dies noa, a day on which no legal business is
carried on. — L. dies поп (juridicus), lit. 'a not
juridical day'. L. dies, 'day', derives fr. I.-E.
base *dei-r *deya-, *dl-, *dya-, 'to shine'. See
deity and cp. dial, diary, diet, assembly',
diurnal, diuturnal, journal, and the second element

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:239 COLUMN:2 -->
in hodiernal, meridian, Midi, quotidian. For L.
поп, 'not', see поп-.

## diet
diet, п., a parliamentary assembly. — ML. dieta,
'an appointed day' (whence also F. diete,
'parliamentary assembly), fr. L. dies, 'day' (see dies
поп); prop, a loan translation of G. Tag, 'day',
in the sense of 'parliamentary assembly'. For
sense development cp. landtag and words there
referred to.

## diet
diet, п., fare, food. — ME. diete, fr. OF. diete
(F. diete), fr. L. diaeta, 'mode of living', fr. Gk.
δία'-τα, 'the office of an arbiter; mode of living;
dwelling, abode', back formation fr. διαιταν,
Чо maintain, support', which is formed fr. St-
(Torm of διά before a vowel') and αΐσα (for
*αΐτια), 'share, lot, destiny'. See dia- and etio-.
Derivatives: diet, tr. v., to prescribe a diet,
dietary, adj., diet-er, n.

## dietetic
dietetic, also dictetical, adj., pertaining to diet. —
— Gk. διαιτητικός, 'of, or pertaining to, diet',
fr. δίαιτα. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: dieteticaf-ly, adv., dietet-ics, n.

## dietician
dietician, dietitian, п., an expert in dietetics. —
Formed fr. diet, 'fare, food', on analogy of
phys-ician.

## dif-
dif-, assimilaied form of dis- before /.

## differ
differ, intr. v. — F. differer, fr. L. differre, 'to
carry away, scatier, disperse, protract, delay,
differ', fr. dis- and ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See
bear, 'to carry'.

## difference
difference, n. — F. difference, fr. L. differentia,
'diversity, difference', fr. differem, gen. -entis.
See next word and -ce.
Derivative; difference, tr. v.

## different
different, adj. — F. different, fr. L. differentem,
ace. of diffcens, pres. part, of differre. See differ
and -ent.
Derivatives: different-ly, adv., different-ness, n.

## differentia
differentia, п., a distinguishing attribute or
characteristic (logic). — L. See difference.

## differential
differential, adj. — ML. differentialis, fr. L.
differentia. See difference and adj. suff. al.
Derivatives: differential, п., differential-ly, adv.

## differentiate
differentiate, tr. and intr. v. — ML. differentia'
tus, pp. of differential, which was formed fr.
L. differentia. See difference and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: differential-ion, n.

## difficile
difficile, adj., difficult. — F., fr. L. difficilis,
'difficult'. See difficult, difficulty.

## difficult
difficult, adj. — Back formation fr. difficulty.

## difficulty
difficulty, n. — ME. difficultee, fr. OF. difficulte
(F. difficulte), fr. L. difficultatem, ace. of
difficulties, 'difficulty, distress, poverty', formed fr.
difficilis, 'difficult', on analogy of facultas,
'capability, power'. Difficilis is formed fr. dis- and
facilis, 'easy'; see facile and cp. faculty. For the
change of Latin a (in facilis) to f (in difficilis)
see abigeat and cp. words there referred to.

## diffidence
diffidence, n. — L. diffident ia, 'want of
confidence, distrust, diffidence', fr. diffidens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -ce.

## diffident
diffident, adj. — L. diffidens, gen. -entis, pres.
part of diffldere, 'to distrust, be diffident,
despair', fr. dis- and ftdere, 'to trust*. See fidelity
and -ent.
Derivatives: diffident-ly, adv., diffident-ness, n.

## diffiuence
diffiuence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## difflnent
difflnent, adj., tending to melt or dissolve, liquid.
— L. difftuens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of difftu-
ere, 'to flow away, melt away', fr. dis- 2J\ufluere,
'to flow*. See fluent and cp. words there
referred to.

## diftorm
diftorm, adj., l) differing in form; 2) of irregular
form. — ML. difformis, fr. dis- and L. forma,
'form, shape'. See form, п., and cp. deform.
Derivatives; difform-ed, adj., difformity (q.v.)

## difformity
difformity, n. — F. difformite, fr. ML. difformi-
tatem, ace. of difformitas, fr. difformis. See prec.
word and -ity.

## diffract
diffract, tr. v., to break into parts. — L. dif-
fractus, pp. oidiffringere, 'to break in pieces, to
shatter', fr. dis- and frangere, 'to break*. See
fraction.
Derivatives: diffraction (q.v.), diffract-ive, adj.,
diffract-ive-ly, adv., diffract-ive-ness, n.

## diffraction
diffraction, n. — ModL. diffractio, gen. -onis,
fr. L. diffractus, pp. of diffringere. See prec.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:239 COLUMN:3 -->
word and -ion.

## diffuse
diffuse, adj., spread, scattered. — L. diffusus, pp.
of diffundere. See diffuse, v.
Derivatives: diffuse-ly, adv., diffuse-ness, n.

## diffuse
diffuse, tr. and intr. v., to spread, scatter. — L.
diffusus, pp. of diffundere, 'to pour forth, spread
about', fr. dis- and fundere, 'to pour, melt'. See
fuse, 'to melt'.
Derivatives: diffus-ed, adj., diffus-ed-ly, adv.,
diffus-ed-ness, п., diffus-er, п., diffus-ible, adj.,
diffus-ibif-ity, п., diffus-ible-ness, п., diffusion
(q-v.)

## diffusiometer
diffusiometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the rate of diffusion of liquids or gases. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. diffusio and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See diffusion and meter, 'poetical
rhythm*.

## diffusion
diffusion, n. — L. diffusio, gen. -onis, 'a pouring
forth, spreading about', fr. diffusus, pp. of
diffundere. See diffuse, v., and -ion.

## dig
dig, tr. and intr. v. — ME. diggen, fr. F. diguer,
'to make a dike, to dam, excavate; to spur (a
horse)', fr. digue, 'dike, dam*. See digue.
Derivatives: dig, п., digg-er, п., digg-ing, n.

## digamist
digamist, п., one who marries for the second time
(in contradistinction to bigamist, which denotes
a man who has two wives or a woman who has
two husbands at the same time). — See digumy
and -ist.

## digamma
digamma, п., the lelter F, sixth letter of the
original Greek alphabet, corresponding to, and
pronounced like, the Semitic waw (i.e.
approximately like an English w). The letter digamma
was later disused. — Gk. δίγαμμα, formed fr.
δι- and γάμμα, lit. 'two gammas' (see di-, 'two',
and gamma); so called from its shape (f), which
resembles two gammas set one above the other.

## digamous
digamous, adj., married for a second time. —-
Late L. digamus, fr. Gk. δίγαμος, fr. δι- (seedi-,
'two') and γάμος, 'marriage*. See -gamy and
-ous.

## digamy
digamy, п., second marriage (in contradistinction
to bigamy, which denotes the state of having
two wives or husbands at the same time). — Late
L. digamia, fr. Gk. δίγαμία, 'a second marriage',
fr. Si- (see di-, 'two') and γάμος, 'marriage*.
See -gamy and cp. monogamy, bigamy,
polygamy.

## digastric
digastric, adj., having two swollen ends (said of
muscles) (anat.) — Lit. 'having two bellies', fr.
di- 'two', and γαστήρ, gen. γαστρός, 'belly'.
See gastric.

## digest
digest, tr. v., 1) to arrange systematically; 2) to
prepare (food in the stomach) for assimilation;
intr. v., to be digested. — L. digestus, pp. of di-
gerere, 'to carry apart, distribute, divide, spread
about', fr. di-, 'apart', and gerere, 'to carry'.
See gerent.
Derivatives: digest, n. (q.v.), digest-ed, adj.,
digest-ed-ly, adv., digest-ed-ness, п., digest-ertn.,
digestible (q.v.), digestion (q.v.), digestive (q.v.)

## digest
digest, п., a collection; a summary. — L. digesta,
'a digested collection of writings', lit. 'digested
things', pi. neut. of digestus, pp. of digerere.
See digest, v.

## digestible
digestible, adj. — F., fr. Late L. digestibilis, fr.
digestus, pp. of digerere. See digest, v., and -ible.
Derivatives: digestibil-ity, п., digestible-ness, п.,
digestibl-y, adv.

## digestioa
digestioa, n. — F., fr. L. digestionem, ace. of
digestio, 'a dividing of food, digestion*, fr.
digestus, pp. of digerere. See digest, v., and -ion.
Derivative: digestion-al, adj.

## digestive
digestive, adj. pertaining to digestion. — F.
digestif (fern, digestive), fr. Late L. digestivus,
'pertaining to digestion', fr. L. digestus, pp. of
digerere. See digest, v., and -ive.
Derivatives: digestive-ly, adv., digestive-ness, n.

## dight
dight, tr. v., to adorn (poetic). — ME. dihten, fr.
OE. dihtan, 'to dictate, guide, compose, set in
order', fr. L. dictare, Чо dictate' (whence also
OHG. dihton, tihton, 'to write, compose', MHG.
tihten,G.dichten, 'to write poetry'). Seedictate, v.

## digit
digit, п., ι) a finger or toe; 2) any figure from о to
9. — L. digitus, 'finger, toe', prob. dissimilated
fr. orig. *dic-itus, prop, 'pointer', fr. I.-E. base
*deik-, 'to show', whence also OE. take, td, 'toe'.
See diction and cp. toe. Cp. also interdigitate,
