dital, and the second element in hallnx.

## digital
digital, adj., pertaining to the fingers. — L.
digitalis, fr. digitus. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.

## digitalin
digitalin, п., an extract obtained from the foxglove
(chem.) — See next word and chem. suff. -in.

## Digitalis
Digitalis, п., ι) a genus of plants of the figwort
family, the foxglove (bot.); 2) (not cap.) a
medicine obtained from the purple foxglove. —
ModL., coined by the German botanist Leon-
hard Fuchs ([501-66) in 1542 fr. L. digitalis,
'pertaining to the fingers' (see digital), as a loan
translation of G. Fingerkut, 'thimble; foxglove'
(so called in allusion to the finger-shaped
corollas).

## Digitaria
Digitaria, п., a genus of plants, the finger grass
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. digitus, 'finger'. See digit
and the suffixes -ar and -ia.

## digitate
digitate, adj., having separate fingers or toes. —
L. digitatus, 'having fingers or toes', coined by
Pliny fr. digitus, 'finger'. See digit and adj. suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: digitat-ed, adj., digitation (q.v.)

## digitation
digitation, п., a fingerlike process. — Medical
L., formed fr. L. digitatus. See prec. word and
-ion,

## digitigrade
digitigrade, adj., walking on the toes (zool.) —
F., compounded of L. digitus, 'finger, toe', and
gradi, 'to walk', which is rel. to gradus, 'step'.
See digit and grade,

## diglot
diglot, adj., bilingual. — Gk. δίγλωττος, fr. δι-
(see di-, 'two') and γλώττα, γλώσσα, 'tongue'.
See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## diglyph
diglyph, п., a projecting tablet with two grooves
(archit.) — Gk. δίγλυφος, 'doubly indented',
fr. δι,- (see di-, 'two') and γλύφειυ, 'to carve'.
See glyph and cp. triglyph.

## digniflcation
digniflcation, n. — ML. dignificatio, gen. -onis,
fr. dignificatus, pp. of dignificdre. See next word
and -ation.

## dignify
dignify, tr. v., — OF. dignifier, fr. ML.
dignificdre, formed fr. L. dignus, 'worthy', and -ficare,
fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See dignity and -fy.
Derivatives: dignifi-ed, adj., dignifi-ed-ly, adv.,
dignifi-ed-ness, n.

## dignitary
dignitary, n. — Formed with suff. -ary. fr. L.
dignitas. See next word.

## dignity
dignity, n. — OF. dignete (F. dignite), fr. L.
dignitatem, ace. of dignitas, 'worth, merit, desert,
authority, rank, power', fr. dignus, 'suitable, fit,
becoming, proper, worthy', which stands for
'dec-nos and is rel. to L. decere, 'to be fitting
or seemly'. See decent and -ity and cp. dainty,
deign, condign, indign.

## digraph
digraph, п., a group of two letters representing
a single sound. — Formed fr. di-, 'two', and
γραφή, 'a writing', fr. γράφειν, Ίο write'. See
-graph,

## digress
digress, intr. v. — L. digressus, pp. of digredi,
'to step aside, depart, deviate, digress', fr. di-,
'apart', and gradi, 'to step, walk', which is rel.
to gradus, 'step'. See grade. For the change of
Latin ά (in gradi) to ё (in di-gressus) see congress.
Derivatives: digression (q.v.), digress-ive, adj.,
digress-ive-ly, adv., digress-ive-ness, п., digress-
ory, adj.

## digression
digression, n. — L. dlgressio, gen. -onis, 'a going
away, departing', fr. digressus, pp. of digredi.
See prec. word and -ion and cp. degression.
Derivatives: digression-al, digression-ary, adjs.

## digue
digue, п., a dike. — F., 'dike, dam' (whence also
It. diga, Sp., Port, digue), fr. MDu. dijc (Du.
dijk), 'dike'. See dike and cp. dig.

## dihedral
dihedral, adj., having two plane faces. — Formed
fr. di- 'two', and Gk. έδρα, 'seat; base, side,
face'. See sedentary and cp. -hedral.
Derivative: dihedral, n.

## dik-dik
dik-dik, п., a small antelope of North East Africa.
— Abyssinian native name.

## dike
dike, also dyke, n. — ME. dik, fr. OE. die. See

## ditch
ditch, which is a doublet of dike.

## dike
dike, dyke, tr. v. — Fr. dike, dyke, n. Ср. ОЕ.
dician.
Derivative: dik-er, dyk-er, n.

## diksha
diksha, п., initiation preceding certain
ceremonies (Hinduism). — Ol. diksa (for *didk-sa),
'initiation', rel. to ddksab, 'apt, clever', ddsti, 'he

## honors'
honors', fr. I.-E. base "dek-, *dok-, '10 take,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:240 COLUMN:2 -->
receive, accept; acceptable, becoming, good',
whence also L. decere, 'to be seemly or fitting'.
See decent and cp. words there referred to.

## dilacerate
dilacerate, tr. v., to tear to pieces. — L. dllace-
ratus, pp. of dilacerare, fr. di-, 'asunder', and
lacerare, 'to tear to pieces, to rend'. See
lacerate.

## dilaceration
dilaceration, n. — L. dilacerdtio, gen. -onis, 'a
tearing to pieces', fr. dilacerdtits, pp. of
dilacerare. See prec. word and -ion.

## dilantin
dilantin, п., a drug used in the treatment of
epilepsy. — Short for i//pheny/-hydtf/iroin-so-
dium.

## dilapidate
dilapidate, tr. v., to ruin partially, squander,
waste; intr. v., to fall into decay. — L. dilapi-
ddtus, pp. of dilapiddre, 'to throw away,
squander, waste', lit. 'to scatter like stones', fr. di-,
'apart, asunder', and lapidare, 'to throw stones
at', fr. lapis, gen. lapidis, 'stone'. See lapidary
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: dilapidat-ed, adj. dilapidation (q.v.).

## dilapidation
dilapidation, n. — L. dilapiddtio, gen. -onis, 'a
squandering, wasting', fr. dilapidatus, pp. of
dilapidare. See prec. word and -ion.

## dilatable
dilatable, adj. — Formed witlj suff. -able fr. L.
dilatare. See dilate.
Derivatives: dilatabil-ity, п., dilatable-ness, п.,
dilatabl-y, adv.

## dilatate
dilatate, adj., dilated, enlarged. — L. dtlatalus,
pp. of dilatare. See dilate, 'to become wider',
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: dilatation (q.v.), dilatat-ive, adj.

## dilatatioa
dilatatioa, n. — OF. dilatation, fr. Late L. di-
latationem, ace. of dilatatio, 'a widening,
enlargement, extending', fr. L. dilatatus, pp. of
dilatare. See next word and -ion.

## dilate
dilate, intr. v., to become wider; tr. v., to make
wider. — F. dilater, fr. L. dilatare, 'to widen,
enlarge, extend', fr. di-, 'apart', and latus,
'broad'. See latitude.
Derivatives: dilate, adj., dilat-ant, adj. and п.,
dilat-ancy, п., dilatate (q.v.), dilat-ed, adj.,
dilat-er, п., dilat-ion, п., dilat-ive, adj., dilator
(q.v.), dilatory (q.v.)

## dilate
dilate, tr. v., to delay (obsol.) — F. dilater, fr.
Late L. dilatare. See dilatory.
Derivative: dilat-ion, n.

## dilatometer
dilatometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
dilatation of a substance. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. dilatare, 'to widen, enlarge', and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See dilate, 'to become wider',
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## dilator
dilator, п., a delayer. — L. dilator, fr. dilatus, pp.
of differre. See next word and agential suff. -or.

## dilatory
dilatory, adj., causing delay. — Late L. dilatdrius,
'dilatory', fr. L. dilator, 'a delayer', fr. dilatus
(used as pp. of differre,'io defer, delay'), fr. di- and
latus (used as pp. of ferre, 'to bear, carry'),
which stands for *tlatos, fr. *tf-, zero degree of
I.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence
L. tollere, 'to lift up, raise', toler&re, 'to bear,
support'. See tolerate and cp. collate and words
there referred to.
Derivatives: dilatori-ly, adv., dilatori-ness, n.

## dilemma
dilemma, п., a choice between two unpleasant
alternatives; a quandary. — Late L., fr. Gk.
δίλημμα, 'a double proposition, dilemma', fr.
δι- (see di-, 'two') and λήμμα, 'assumption', lit.
'something received, something taken for
granted'. See lemma and cp. trilemma.

## dilemmatic
dilemmatic, dilemmatical, adj., pertaining to a
dilemma. — Formed with suff. -ic, resp. -ic and
-al, fr. Gk. δίλημμα, gen. διλήμματος. See next
word.

## dilettante
dilettante, п., a superficial amateur. — It., pres.
part, of dilettarsi, 'to take delight in', reflexive
of dilettare, 'to delight', fr. L. dclectare, 'to
delight'. See delight and cp. delectation.
Derivatives: dilettante, n. and intr. v.,
dilettantism, п., dilettant-ist, n.

## diligence
diligence, п., assiduity. — F., 'diligence,
application; haste, speed; dispatch', fr. L. diligentia,
'attentiveness, carefulness, diligence', fr. diligens,
gen. -entis. See diligent and -ce.

## diligence
diligence, п., a public stagecoach. — F., short for
earlier carrosse de diligence, 'coach of speeds'.
See prec. word.

## diligent
diligent, adj. — F., fr. L. diligens, gen. -entis,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:240 COLUMN:3 -->
pres. part, of diligere, 'to value highly, love',
which stands for *dislegere and orig. meant 'to
pick out, select', fr. dis- and legere, 'to pick
out, choose; to read'. See lecture and -ent and
cp. predilection. For the change of Latin ё (in
legere) to / (in di-ligere) see abstinence and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: diligent-ly, adv., diligent-ness, n.

## dill
dill, n. — ME. dile, dilk; fr. OE. dile, rel. to OS.
dilli, MDu., Du. dille, Swed. dill, Dan. diid,
OHG. tilli, tilla, MHG. title, dille, G. Dill.

## dilly
dilly, п., a small tree, Mimusops sieberi. — Aphe-
tic for sapodilla.

## dillydally
dillydally, intr. v. — Antiphonic reduplication
of dally,

## diluent
diluent, adj., diluting. — L. diluens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of dilitere. See next word and -ent.
Derivative: diluent, п., a diluting agent.

## dilute
dilute, tr. v., to thin, weaken. — L. diluius, pp.
of diluere. Ίο wash away, dissolve, dilute', fr.
di-, 'apart, asunder', and luere, 4o wash'. See
lave and cp. deluge, diluvian.
Derivatives: dilut-ed, adj., dilut-ed-ly, adv.,
dilut-ed-ness, п., di/ut-ion, n.

## dilute
dilute, adj., diluted. — L. dilatus, pp. of diluere.
See dilute, v.
Derivatives: dilutv-ly, adv., dilute-ness, n.

## diluvial
diluvial, adj., pertaining to the flood. — Late L.
diluvialis, fr. L. diluvium. See diluvium and adj.
suff. -al.

## diluvialist
diluvialist, п., an adherent of diluvianism. —
Formed with suff. -ist fr. Late L. diluvialis. See
prec. word.

## diluvian
diluvian, adj., pertaining to the flood. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. diluvium. See diluvium,

## diluvianism
diluvianism, п., the theory that many geological
phenomena are due to the Deluge. — Formed
with suff. -ism fr. L. diluvium. See next word

## diluvium
diluvium, п., an accumulation of sand and gravel
(geol.) — L. diluvium, 'flood, deluge', fr. diluere,
'to wash away' fr. di-, 'apart', and luere, '10
wash, lave, cleanse'. See lave and cp. deluge.
The accumulation of sand was formerly
attributed to the Deluge, whence its name diluvium.

## dim
dim, adj. — ME. dimm, dim, fr. OE. dimme,
dimm, 'dark, obscure; unknown; wicked', rel.
to ON. dimmr, OFris. dim, OHG., MHG.
timber, 'dark, black, somber', and prob. cogn.
with Gk. Э-έμερος, 'grave, austere', &εμερωπις,
'of grave countenance', Mir. dent, 'black, dark'.
Cp. damp, dump,

## dime
dime, п., the tenth part of a dollar. — ME. dime,
fr. OF. disme, dime (F. dime), 'a tenth part,
tithe', fr. L. decima, fem. of decintus, 'the tenth',
fr. decern, 'ten'. Cp. It. decima, OProvenc. des-
ma, 'a tenth part', which derive fr. L. decima, and
OProvenc. desmo, Sp. diezmo, of same meaning,
which come fr. L. decimus. See decern-, decimal,

## dimension
dimension, n. — F., fr. L. dimensionem, ace. of

## dimensio
dimensio, 'a measuring', fr. dimensus, pp. of

## dimetiri
dimetiri, '10 measure out', fr. di-, 'apart', and

## metiri
metiri, 'to measure'. See measnre and -ion.
Derivatives: dimension-al, adj., dimension-al-

## ity
ity, п., dimension-al-ly, adv.

## dimensionless
dimensionless, adj. — Formed fr. dimension and
-less; first used by Milton,

## dimerous
dimerous, adj., having two parts. — Formed fr.

## di-
di-, 'two', Gk. μέρος, 'part' (see mero-), and suff.
-ous (fr. L. -osus). See mero-.

## dimeter
dimeter, п., a verse consisting of two measures
(prosody). — Late L. dimeter, fr. Gk. δίμετρος,
'(a verse) having two measures', fr. δι- (seedi-,
'two') and μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,'poetical
rhythm'.

## dimidiate
dimidiate, adj., divided into halves. — L. dimi-
dicitus, 'halved', pp. of dimidiare, 'to divide
into two equal parts', which stands for *dis-
medidie and lit. means 'to go through the
middle', fr. dis- and medium, 'middle', neut. of
medius, 'middle'. L. dimidius, 'half, is back
formation fr. dimidiare. See medium and adj.
suff. -ate and cp. demi-. For ihe change of Latin
e" (in medius) to / (in di-midiare) see abstinent
and cp. words there referred to.

## dimidiation
dimidiation, п., division into halves. — Late L.
diinidiatio, gen. -onis, 'a halving', fr. L. dimi-
diatus, pp. of dimidiare. See prec. word and
-ion.

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DIMINISH | 214 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:241 COLUMN:1 -->

## diminish
diminish, ir. and intr. v. — A blend of earlier E.
dimitnie (fr. OF. diniinuer, fr. L. diminuere), 'to
reduce', and E. minish (q.v.) For the pref. see
di-, 'арап'. Ср. diminution.
Derivatives: diminish-ed, adj., diminish-er, п.,
diminish-ing-ly, adv.

## diminuendo
diminuendo, adj. and adv., diminishing, growing
softer (music). — It., fr. pres. part, of diminuire,
which is formed—with change of conjugation—
fr. L. diminuere, earlier dcminuere, 'to diminish'.
See next word.

## diminution
diminution, n. — F., fr. L. diminuiionem, ace. of
dimiiuttio, 'a decrease, lessening, diminishing',
fr. earlier deminutid, fr. deminCitus, pp. of de-
minuere, 4o lessen, diminish', fr. de- and mi-
nuere, 'to make smaller, to lessen, diminish'.
See minute, п., and -ion and cp. diminish.

## diminutive
diminutive, adj. — OF. (= F.) diminutif'((em.
diminutive), fr. L. diminittivtis, fr. earlier deminu-
livus, 'diminutive', fr. dentinutus, pp. of demi-
nuere. See prec. word and -ive.
Derivatives: diminmiv-al, adj., diminulive-ly,
adv., diminutive-ness, n.

## dimissory
dimissory, adj. — Late L. dimissorius, 'pertaining
to sending away', fr. dimissus, pp. of dimitlere,
Ίο send away, dismiss', fr. di-, 'apart', and mit-
tere. Ίο send'. See dismiss and adj. suff. -ory.

## dimity
dimity, п., a thin cotton fabric. — It. dimiti, pi. of
dimito, 'a kind of strong cotton', fr. ML. dimi-
rum, fr. Gk. δίμιτος, 'of double thread;
dimity', fr. δι- (see di-, 'apart'), and μίτος, 'warp
thread, thread', which is of uncertain etvmo-
logy. It is perh. cogn. with Hitt. mitish, 'string,
chord'. Cp. mitosis, samite.

## dimorph
dimorph, п., one of the two forms of a
dimorphous substance. — Back formation fr.
dimorphous.

## dimorphic
dimorphic, adj., dimorphous. — See dimorphous
and -ic.

## dimorphism
dimorphism, п., the property of existing in two
distinct forms. — See next word and -ism,

## dimorphous
dimorphous, adj., existing in two distinct forms.
— Gk. δίμορφος, 'two-formed', fr. δι- and
μορφή, 'form, shape'. See di-, 'double', and
morpho-.

## dimple
dimple, n. — ME. dympull, rel. to OHG. шт-
philo, 'a whirlpool' (whence MHG. tiimpfel, G.
Tiimpel, 'pool'), and to MLG. diimpelen, Du.
dompelen,4o plunge'; prob. from the nasalized
form of the Teut. base *dup-, 'to be deep'. Cp.
Lith. dumbii, diipti, 'to sink', and see deep.
Derivatives: dimple, v., dimpl-y, adj.

## din
din, n. — ME. dine, fr. OE. dyne, 'noise, a loud
sound', rel. to ON. dynr, OS. done, Dan. don,
Swed. dan, MLG., MHG. don, 'noise', from the
I.-E. imitative base *dhwen-, *dhun-, 'to sound,
roar', whence also OI. dhunih, 'roaring', dhva-
naii, 'roars, resounds'.

## din
din, tr. and intr. v. — ME. dinien, fr. OE. dynnan,
dynian, rel. to ON. dynja, OS. dunian, 'to make
a loud noise', and to OE. dyne, 'noise, a loud
sound'. See din, n.

## Diaah
Diaah, fern. PN.; in the Bible, Jacob's daughter
by Leah. — Heb. Dtnah, lit. 'judgment', fr. din,
'to judge'. See Dan, PN.

## dinanderie
dinanderie, п., decorated articles of brass. — MF.
(— F.) fr. OF. dinandier, 'worker in brass',
formed with -ier, a suff. denoting trade or
occupation, fr. Dinand (now Dinant), a town in
Belgium, famous for its brasswork. For the
ending see the suffixes -ier and -ery.

## dinar
dinar, n. — Arab, dinar, fr. Late Gk. δηνάριον, fr.
L. denarius. See denarius and cp. denier.

## dine
dine, intr. and tr. v. — ME. dinen, fr. OF disner
(F. diner), 'to djne', orig. 'to breakfast', fr.
*desjuner, shortened form of desjejuner (see
haplology), which derives fr. VL. *disjejundre,
'to break the fast', fr. dis- and L. jejunus,
'fasting'. See jejune and cp. dinner, dejeuner.
Derivatives: din-er, п., din-ing, n.

## ding
ding, tr. v., to beat. — ME. dingen, dengen, fr.
ON. dengja, 'to hammer, beat', which is rel. to
OHG. langol, 'hammer', MHG. tengeln, G. den-
geln, 'to hammer, beat'; prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. next word. Cp. also dangle, dint.

## diag
diag, intr. and tr. v., to sound. — Of imitative
origin.
Derivative: ding, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:241 COLUMN:2 -->

## ding-dong
ding-dong, п., adj., v. and adv. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. prec. word.

## dinghy
dinghy, п., a small boat. — Hind, dengi, 'a rowing
boat', a collateral form of dongi, prob. fr. OI.
dronam, 'a trough', which is rel. to dm-, 'wood',
drumdh, 'tree', and cogn. with Gk. δρυς, gen.
δρυός, 'an oak; a tree', Goth, triu, OE. trio,
treow, 'tree'. See tree and cp. dryad. Cp. also
dhoni.

## dingle
dingle, п., a small valley. — ME. dingel, 'a
hollow', of uncertain origin.

## dingle-dangle
dingle-dangle, adv. and n. — A blend of diag-
dong and dangle,

## dingo
dingo, п., the Australian wild dog, Cams dingo.
— Native name.

## diagy
diagy, adj., dirty; dark. — Prob. related to dung.
For the softening of the hard g cp. stingy.
Derivatives: dingi-ly, adv., dingi-ness, n.

## dinic
dinic, dinical, adj., pertaining to vertigo (med.) —
Formed with suff. -ic, resp. also -al, fr. Gk.
δΐνος, 'a whirling, vertigo'. See dinus.

## dinky
dinky, adj., dainty. — Cp. Scot, and Northern
dial, dink, denk, 'neat'; of uncertain origin.

## dinner
dinner, n. — ME. diner, fr. F. diner, 'dinner',
prop, the infinitive diner, 'to dine', used as a
noun. See dine.
Derivatives: dinner-y, dinner-less, adjs.

## dino-
dino-, combining form meaning 'fearful'. — Gk.
δεινό-, fr. δεινός (for *δίει-νός), 'fearful', rel.
to δείδω (for *δέ-δίοι-α), Ί fear', δέος (for
*δ^εΐ-ος), 'fearful, terrible, powerful, mighty,
marvelous', δειλός (for * δΓει-λός),'cowardly, and
possibly cogn. with L. dims, 'fearful'. See dire.

## Dinobryon
Dinobryon, п., a genus of flagellates (biol.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. δΐνος, 'a
whirling', and βρύον, 'moss'. See dinus and bryo-.

## Dinoceras
Dinoceras, п., a genus of extinct ungulates (pale-
ontol.) — ModL., compounded of dino- and
Gk. κέρας, 'horn'. See cerato-.

## Dinoflagellata
Dinoflagellata, n. pi., an order of flagellates
(biol.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk. δΐνος,
'a whirling', and L. flagellum, 'whip'. See dinus
and flagellum.

## Dlnornis
Dlnornis, п., a genus of recently extinct birds
resembling an ostrich. The New Zealand Moa
belonged to this genus (paleontol.)— ModL., lit.
'a frightful bird', compounded of dino- and
Gk. Ορνις, 'bird'. See ornitho-.

## dinosaur
dinosaur, n. any member of the Dinosauria. —
See next word.

## Dinosauria
Dinosauria, n. pi., a group of extinct Saurian
reptiles (paleontol.) — ModL., lit. 'frightful
lizards', compounded of dino- and Gk. σαύρα,
σαϋρος, 'lizard'. See sauro-.
Derivatives: dinosaurian, adj. and n.

## dinothere
dinothere, п., any member of the genus Dino-
therium. — See next word.

## Dinotherium
Dinotherium, п., a genus of extinct elephantlike
animals (paleontol.) — ModL., lit. 'the frightful
animal', compounded of dino- and Gk. &ήρ,
θηρίον, 'wild beast, animal'. See therio-.

## dint
dint, п., a force. — The original meaning was
'blow, stroke'; ME. dint, dunt, dent, fr. OE.
dynt, which is rel. to ON. dyntr, dyttr, and to
E. ding, 'to beat' (q.v.) Cp. dent, 'depression'.

## dint
dint, tr. v., to mark with a dint. — ME, dinien,
fr. OE. dyntan, 'to beat, strike', fr. dynt, 'blow,
stroke'. See prec. word.

## dinus
dinus, п., vertigo (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
δΐνος, 'a whirling, rotation, vertigo', which is
rel. to δίνη, 'a whirling', δΐνέω, δΐνεύω, Ί make
whirl or spin round', δίνευμα, 'a whirling
round', δίεμαι, Ί hasten away', and prob. cogn.
with OI. diyati, 'flies, hovers', Lett, diet, 'to
dance', Olr. dian, 'swift, rapid'. Cp. dinic and
the second element in scotodinia.

## diocesan
diocesan, adj., pertaining to a diocese. — F. dio-
cesain, fr. diocese. See next "word and -an.
Derivative: diocesan, n.

## diocese
diocese, п., district under a bishop's jurisdiction.
— ME. diocise, fr. OF. diocise (F. diocese), fr.
ML. diocesis, dissimilated fr. L. dioecesis, fr.
Gk. διοίκησις, 'administration, control', fr. διά
(see dia-) and οίκειν, 'to inhabit, possess; to
manage, govern', fr. οίκος, 'house'. See
economy and cp. next word. Cp. also L. parochia,
dissimilated fr. L. paroecia, fr. Gk. παροικία
(see parish).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:241 COLUMN:3 -->

## Diodia
Diodia, п., a genus of plants of the madder family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δίοδος, 'a
thoroughfare', fr. διά, 'through', and οδός, 'way' (see
dia- and odograph). The name prop, denotes
plants growing by the wayside.

## dioecious
dioecious, adj., having the male and female
reproductive organs in separate individuals (biol.)
— A hybrid formed fr. di-, 'two', Gk. οίκία,
'house' (see diocese), and suff. -ous (fr. L. -osus).

## Diomedes
Diomedes, п., son of Tydeus and Deipyle, one
of the Grecian chiefs in the Trojan war (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Διομήδης, lit. 'advised by
Zeus', fr. Διός, gen. of Ζευς, 'Zeus', and μήδος,
'counsel, plan, device, cunning'. For the first
element see Zeus. The second element is rel. to
μήδεσθ-αι, 'to devise, resolve, advise', μέδεσθ-αι,
'to be mindful of, give heed to, think on', μέδων,
μεδέων, 'guardian, ruler' (prop. pres. part of
the ancient verb μέδειν, 'to protect, rule over'),
μέδιμνος, 'a measure', fr. l.-E. base mid-, 'to
measure, limit, consider', which is a -rf-enlarge-
ment of base 'me-, 'to measure'. See meditate
and cp. Andromeda and words there referred
to.

## Dion
Dion, masc. PN. — Short for Dionysius.

## Dionaea
Dionaea, п., a genus of insectivorous plants of
the sundew family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
Διώνη, a name of Aphrodite. See next word.

## Dione
Dione, п., 1) the mother of Aphrodite; 2)
Aphrodite (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Διώνη, lit.
'pertaining to Zeus', fr. Διός, gen. of Ζευς. See
Zeus and cp. prec. word and the first element in
Diomedes.

## dionise
dionise, п., a kind of precious stone. — OF., fr.
ML. dionysia, fr. L. dionysias, fr. Gk. διονΰσιάς,
fr. Διόνυσος, 'Dionysus', the name of the god
of wine in Greek mythology; see Dionysus. The
stone was supposed to have the power of
preventing intoxication, whence its name. Cp.
amethyst.

## Dionysia
Dionysia, n. pi., festivals held in honor of
Dionysus (Greek religion). — L„ fr. Gk. Διονυσία,
(scil. ιερά), fr. Διόνυσος, 'Dionysus'. See Dio-
aysus.

## Dionysiac
Dionysiac, adj., pertaining to Dionysus or the
Dionysia. — L. Dionysiacus, fr. Gk.
Διονυσιακός, fr. Διόνυσος, resp. Διονυσία. See Dionysus,
resp. Dionysia.

## Dionysian
Dionysian, adj., pertaining to Dionysus. — See
Dyonysus and -ian.

## Dionysius
Dionysius, masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Διονύσιος,
lit. 'pertaining to Dionysus', fr. Διόνυσος. See
Dionysus and cp. Denis, Dion.

## Dionysus
Dionysus, Dionysos, п., son of Zeus and Semele,
the god of wine, orig. the god of vegetation
(Greek mythol.); identified with the Roman
god Bacchus. — L., fr. Gk. Διόνυσος, a name
of uncertain origin. Cp. Dionysius and dionise.

## Dioon
Dioon, п., a genus of plants of the family Cyca-
daceae (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. di- and
Gk. ωον, 'egg'. See 00-.

## diopside
diopside, п., a variety of pyroxene (mineral.) —
Formed fr. di-, 'two', and όψις, 'sight,
appearance'. See -opsis.

## dioptase
dioptase, п., a mineral consisting of hydrous
copper silicate. — Formed fr. di- (form of dia-
before a vowel) and thestem of όπτάζειν,'Ιοβεβ',
which is rel. to όπτός, 'seen; visible'. See next
word.

## dioptric
dioptric, adj., pertaining to the refraction of
light. — Gk. διοπτρικός, 'pertaining to the use
of the optical instrument called δίοπτρα, fr. δι-,
form of δια- before a vowel (see dia-), and the
stem of όπτός, 'seen; visible', οπτικός,
'pertaining to sight'. See optic and cp. catadioptric,
catoptric, scioptric.
Derivative: dioptric-al-ly, adv.

## dioptrics
dioptrics, п., that part of optics which deals with
the refraction of light. — See prec. word and
-ics and cp. catoptrics.

## diorama
diorama, п., a scenic representation in which a
picture is seen through an aperture. — Formed
fr. di- (form of dia- before a vowel) and Gk.
όραμα, 'that which is seen, view, sight', fr. όραν,
'to see'. See cosmorama and cp. words there
referred to.

## diorite
diorite, п., an igneous rock (petrogr.) — F.,
formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. διορίζειν, 'to

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 215 | DIRECT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:242 COLUMN:1 -->

## divide by limits
divide by limits, separate', fr. δι-, form of δια-

## before a vowel (see dia-)
before a vowel (see dia-), and όρίζειν, "to mark

## by boundaries
by boundaries, to limit'. See horizon.

## Dioscorea
Dioscorea, п., a genus of plants, the yam (hot.)
— ModL., named after the Greek naturalist
Dioscorides.

## Dioscoreaceae
Dioscoreaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## dioscoreaceous
dioscoreaceous, adj — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Dioscuri
Dioscuri, n. pi., Castor and Pollux, the twin sons
of Zeus (Greek mylhol.) — Gk. Διόσκουροι, Att.
and poetic Διόσκοροι, lit. 'the sons of Zeus',
fr. Διός, gen. of Ζευς, 'Zeus', and κούροι, κόροι,
pi. of κούρος, κόρος, 'boy, son'. Foi the first
element see Zeus. The second element derives
fr. I.-E. base 'iter-, 'to grow'; see Cora, create.

## Diosma
Diosma, п., a genus of plants of the rue family
(bol.) — ModL., irregularly formed fr. δΐος,
'divine', and οσμή, 'odor'. For the first element
see deity, for the second see osmium.

## Diospyros
Diospyros, п., a genus of plants of the ebony
family (hot.) — L., name of a plant, fr. Gk.
Διόσπϋρος, lit. 'wheat of Zeus', fr. Διός, gen.
of Ζευς, 'Zeus', and πυρός, 'wheat'. For the
first element see Zeus, for the second see
pyrene and cp. words there referred to.

## diota
diota, п., a vessel with two ears (Greek and Roman
antiq.) — L., fr. Gk. δίωτος, 'two-eared', fr. δι-
(see di-, 'two') and ους, gen. ώτός, 'ear'. See
oto-,

## dioxide
dioxide, also dioxid, п., a compound containing
two atoms of oxygen and one of a metal (chem.)
— Formed fr. di-, 'two', and oxide,

## dip
dip, tr. and intr. v. — ME. dippen, duppen, fr.
OE. dyppan, 'to dip, immerse: to baptize', rel.
to ON. deypa, 'to dip', Dan. dyppe, 'to dip',
dgbe, 'to baptize', Swed. doppa, 'to dip,
immerse', dopa, 'to baptize', OS. ddpian, OFris.
depa, MLG. dopen, MDu. ddpen, Du. dopen,
OHG. toufan, toufen, MHG. toufen, toufen, G.
laufen, Goth, daupjan, 'to baptize', lit. 'to dip',
prop, a loan translation of Gk. βαπτίζειν, 'to
dip, plunge'; in Eccles. Gk., 'to baptize'; rel.
alSb to OE. deop, 'deep', and prob. also to
OHG. tupfen, MHG. tupfen, tupfen. G. tiipfen,
'to dab', orig. prob. 'to dip'.
Derivatives: dip, п., dipp-er, п., dipp-ing, n.

## diphtheria
diphtheria, п., an infectious disease
characterized by the formation of a false membrane in
the air passages. — Medical L., fr. F.
diphtheric, coined by the French physician Pierre
Bretonneau (1778-1862) fr. Gk. διφθέρα,
'prepared hide, leather, membrane', which is of
uncertain origin; it is possibly rel. to Gk. δέφειν,
δέψειν, 'to soften'. The disease was so called
by Bretonneau because it is characterized by
the formation of a false membrane. For the
ending of diphtheria see 1st suff. -ia. Cp. dufter.
Derivatives: diphlheri-al, diphther-ic, diphther-
it-ic, adjs.

## diphtheroid
diphtheroid, adj., of the nature of diphtheria. —
Compounded of diphthera and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## diphthong
diphthong, п., union of two vowels pronounced
in one syllable. — F. diphthongue, fr. Late L.
diphthongus, fr. Gk. δίφθογγος, 'having two
sounds', fr. δι- (see di-, 'two'), and φθόγγος,
'sound, voice, vowel', which is rel. to φθέγμα,
'sound, voice, speech', φθέγγεσθαι, 'to speak
loud; to praise, sing'. Cp. moaophthong,
triphthong.
Derivatives: diphthong, tr. and intr. v., diph-
lhong-al, adj., diphlhong-al-ly, adv.,
diphthongize, tr. and intr. v., diphthong-iz-ation, n.

## diphy-
diphy-, combining form meaning 'double'. — Gk.
διφυής, 'twofold, double', lit. 'of double
nature', fr. δι- (see di-, 'two') and the stem of
φύειν, 'to bring forth, produce, make to grow',
whence also φύσις, 'nature'. See physio- and
cp. Diphyes.

## Diphyes
Diphyes, п., a genus of hydrozoans (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. διφυής, 'twofold'. See diphy-.

## Diphylleia
Diphylleia, п., a genus of plants of the barberry
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'having double
leaves', fr. di-, 'double', and Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf.
See phyllo-. For the ending see 2nd suff. -ia

## diphyllous
diphyllous, adj., having two leaves (bot.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:242 COLUMN:2 -->
Formed fr. di-, 'two', and Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf.
See -phyllous and cp. prec. word.

## dipl-
dipl-,- form of diplo- before a vowel.

## Diplacanthus
Diplacanthus, п., a genus of fishes (paleontol.) —
ModL., lit. 'having two spines', fr. dipl- and
άκανθα, 'spine (see acantho-); so called in
allusion to the two spines between the pectoral
fins.

## Dipladenia
Dipladenia, п., a genus of plants of the dogbane
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'having two glands',
fr. dipl- and αδην, 'gland' (see adenoid); so called
in allusion to the two nectar glands. For the
ending see 2nd suff. -ia.

## diplegia
diplegia, п., paralysis of both arms and both
legs (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. di-,
'double', and Gk. πληγή, 'stroke', from the
stem of πλήσσειν, 'to strike', which is cogn.
with L. plaga, 'stroke, injury, plague'. See
plague and cp. monoplegia.

## diplex
diplex, adj., pertaining to sending two messages
simultaneously over the same line (radio). —
A hybrid coined fr. Gk. δι- (see di-, 'two') and
L. suff. -plex, '-fold' (see plicate). The word
diplex has been arbitrarily coined to differentiate
it from duplex (q.v.)

## diplo-
diplo-, before a vowel dipl-, combining form
meaning 'double'. — Gk. διπλό-, διπλ-, fr.
διπλόος, διπλοϋς, 'twofold, double', formed fr.
δι- (see di-, 'two') and *pl-, zero degree of base
*pel-, '-fold'. Cp. Gk. δι-πλάσιος, 'double', and
see ply, 'to bend'. Cp. also diplomn, nna-
diplosis. Cp. also double.

## diploblastic
diploblastic, adj., having two germ layers (biol.)
— Compounded of diplo- and Gk. βλαστός,
'bud, sprout, shoot'. See -blastic.

## diplocardlac
diplocardlac, adj., having the heart double (as
birds and mammals). — Compounded of
diplo- and cardiac.

## Diplodocus
Diplodocus, п., a genus of gigantic dinosaurs
(paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of diplo-
and Gk. δοκός, 'beam, bar', lit. 'that which
holds the roof, fr. I.-E. base 'dele-, dole-, 'to
take, receive, accept'. See decent and cp. words
there referred to.

## diploe
diploe, п., the cancellous bony tissue between the
tables of the skull (anat.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
διπλόη, 'fold, doubling; cancellous substance
between the double plates in the bones in the
skull', prop. fern, of the adj. διπλόος, διπλοϋς,
'twofold, double'. See diplo-.

## diploic
diploic, adj., pertaining to diploe. — Formed fr.
prec. word with suff. -ic. Cp. diploetic.

## diploetic
diploetic, adj., diploic (anat.) — An incorrect
var. of diploic. The Greek adjectival suff.
-ητικός derives from nouns ending in -ησις
(see e.g. exegesis and exegetic); since, however,
there is no such Greek word as διπλόησις,
there can be no Greek adjective of the form
διπλοητικός either. See diploic.

## diploma
diploma, n. — L. diploma, fr. Gk. δίπλωμα,
'anything double, folded paper, license', fr.
διπλούν, 'to bend double, to double', fr. διπλόος,
διπλούς, 'double'. See diplo- and -oma and cp.
double.
Derivatives: diploma, tr. v., diplomacy (q.v.),
diplomat (q.v.), diplomatic (q.v), diplomat-ist,
п., diplom-at-ize, intr. v.

## diplomacy
diplomacy, n. — F. diplomatie, fr. diplomate;
introduced into English by Edmund Burke (1729-
97). See diplomatic and -cy.

## diplomat
diplomat, diplomate. — F. diplomate, back
formation fr. diplomatique in agent diplomatique,
'diplomatic agent'. See next word.
Derivative: diplomate, tr. v.

## diplomatic
diplomatic,-adj. — F. diplomatique, fr. ModL. di-
pWmalicus, formed with suff. -icus fr. diploma,
fr. Gk. δίπλωμα. See diploma and -atic.
Derivatives: diplomatic-ai, adj.,
diplomatic-ally, adv., diplomat-ics, n.

## diplopia
diplopia, п., double vision (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of διπλόος, διπλούς, 'double', and
-ωπίϋ, from ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye'. See diplo-
and -opia.
Derivative: diplop-ic, adj.

## Diplotaxis
Diplotaxis, п., a genus of plants of the family
Brassicaceae (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'doubly
arranged' (see diplo- and taxis); so called in
allusion to the biserrate seeds.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:242 COLUMN:3 -->

## dipnoan 1) adj.
dipnoan 1) adj., pertaining to the Dipnoi, 2) п.,
a dipnoan fish. — See next word and -an.

## Dipuoi
Dipuoi, n. pi., a group of fishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. δίπνοι, pi. of δίπνοος, 'doubly
breathing", fr. Si-(see di-, 'two') and -πνοος, fr.
πνοή, 'breath', which is rel. to πνέειν, 'to breathe',
whence also πνεύμα, 'breath'. See pneuma.

## dipolar
dipolar, adj., having two poles (as a magnet, elc.)
— Formed fr. dl- 'two', and polar.

## Dipsacaceae
Dipsacaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Dipsacus with suff. -aceae.

## dipsacaceous
dipsacaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Dipsacus
Dipsacus, п., a genus of plants, the teasels (hoi.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. δίψακος, 'teasel', rel. to δίψα,
'thirst', διψήν, 'to thirst'; so called in allusion
to the water contained in the cup-shaped bases
of the leaves. See dipsosis.

## dipsomania
dipsomania, п., a morbid periodic craving for
alcoholic liqueurs (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of Gk. δίψα, 'thirst', and μανία,
'madness'. See next word and -mania.
Derivative: dipsoman-iac, adj.

## dipsosis
dipsosis, п., excessive thirst caused by disease
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -osis fr.
Gk. δίψα, 'thirst', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. prec. word and adipsia.

## Diptera
Diptera, n. pi., an order of insects, the flies (en-
tomol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δίπτερα, neut. pi. of
δίπτερος, 'having two wings', fr. δι- (see di-,
'two') and πτεράν, 'feather, wing'. See ptero-
and cp. next word.

## dipteral
dipteral, adj., 1) having two wings (said of
insects); having two peristyles (archit.) — Formed
wilh adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. δίπτερος, 'having two
•wings; having a double peristyle'. See prec.
word.

## dipterous
dipterous, adj., 1) belonging to the order Diptera
(entemol.); 2) two-winged (bot.) — Gk. δίπτερος.
See Diptera. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see suff. -ous.

## Dipteryx
Dipteryx, п., a genus of trees of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. di-, 'two', and Gk. πτέρυξ,
'wing', which is rel. to πτερόν, 'feather, wing'.
See ptero-.

## diptote
diptote, п., a noun having only two cases (gram.)
— Late L. diptota (pi.), fr. Gk. δίπτωτα, pi. of
δίπτωτον, prop, the neut. of the adj. δίπτωτος,
'having only two cases', fr. δι- (see di-, 'two')
and πτωχός, 'fallen', verbal adj. of πίπτειν, 'to
fall', which stands for πί-πτειν, fr. *pt-, zero
degree of I.-E. base "pet-, 'to fly, to fall'. See
feather and cp. symptom and words there
referred to.

## diptych
diptych, п., l) a two-leaved tablet used by the
ancients for writing; 2) picture or carving on two
panels hinged together. — Late L. diptycha, fr.
Gk. δίπτυχα, neut. pi. of δίπτυχος, 'double-
folded, doubled', fr. δι- (see di-, 'two') and
*πτύξ, gen. πτυχός, 'fold', layer', which is rel.
to πτύσσειν, 'to fold'. Cp. triptych, polyptych.

## Dirca
Dirca, п., a genus of plants of the mezereon
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. Dirce, fr. Gk. Δίρκη,
name of a fountain near Thebes.

## Dircaean
Dircaean, adj., pertaining to the fountain Dirce;
poetic. — Formed with suff. -aean fr. L. Dirce.
See prec. word.

## dire
dire, adj., dreadful. — L. dims, 'fearful, awful,
ill-omened, horrible, terrible', of uncertain
origin. It possibly derives fr. I.-E. base *dwei-, 'to
be afraid, fear', whence also Gk. δείδω (for
*Se-Sfoi-a), 'fear', δέος (for *δίεΐ-ος),
'fearful, terrible, powerful, mighty, marvelous',
δειλός (for ·δίει-λός), 'cowardly', δεινός (for
*δίει-νός), 'fearful', Ol. dvesti, 'hates', dvisah,
'hatred', Avestic dvaeba-, 'threat, menace', and
prob. also Arm. erkniim, Ί fear'. Cp. dino-,
diaosaur.
Derivatives: direful (q.v.), dire-ly, adv.

## direct
direct, tr. and intr. v. — L. dlrectus, pp. of diri-
gere, Ίο put into a straight line, sel in order,
draw up, aim, direct, guide', fr. di-, 'apart', and
regere, 'to keep straight, direct'. See regeat and
cp. dress, which is a doublet of direct. Cp. also
dirge, dirigible, droit, adroit, maladroit.

## direct
direct, adj. — ME., fr. F. direct, fr. L. dirictus,
'straight, direel', pp. of dirigere. See direct, v.
Derivatives: direct, adv., direct-ly, adv.,
directness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:243 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DIRECTION | 216 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:243 COLUMN:1 -->

## direction
direction, η. — F., fr. L. directionem, ace. of
directid, 'a making straight, aiming, directiruj',
fr. directus, pp. of dlrigere. See direct, v., and
-ion.
Derivatives: direction-al, adj., directional-ly,
adv.

## directive
directive, adj. — ML. directivus, fr. L. directus,
pp. of dlrigere. See direct, v., and -ive.
Derivatives: directive, п., directive-ly, adv.,
direct ive-ness, n.

## directoire
directoire, п., the French Revolutionary
Government of 1795-99. — F., fr. ML. directdrium. See
directory, n.

## director
director, n. — AF. directour, equivalent to F.
directeur, fr. Late L. directorem, ace. of director,
fr. directus, pp. of dirigere. See direct, v. and
agential sun", -or.
Derivatives: director-ial, adj., director-iai-ly,
adv.

## directorate
directorate, n. — Formed fr. prec. word with
subst. sun", -ate.

## directory
directory, adj. — Late L. directorius, 'that which
directs', fr. L. directus, pp. of dirigere. See
direct, v. and adj. sun", -ory.

## directory
directory, n. — ML. directdrium, prop. neut. of
Late L. directorius, used as a noun. See prec.
word and subst. suff. -ory.

## directress
directress, n. — See director and -ess.

## directrix
directrix, n. — ModL., formed with suff. -trix
fr. director, on analogy of L. victrix, 'victress'
(fr. victor).

## direful
direful, adj., dire. — Formed on analogy of
dreadful. See dire and -ful.
Derivatives: direful-ly, adv., direful-ness, n.

## dirge
dirge, п., lament. — Fr. L. dirige, 'direct', the
first word of the antiphon sung in the Roman
Catholic Office of the dead, adopted from the
Vulgate rendering of Ps. 5:9, which begins with
dirige, a word translating Heb. hayshar (lit.
'make even'). L. dirige is the imper. of dirigere,
'to direct, guide'. See direct, v.
Derivative: dirge, tr. and intr. v.

## dirhem
dirhem, п., a weight and a silver coin used in
various Mohammedan countries. — Arab, dir-
ham. fr. Gk. δρηιχμή. See drachma.

## dirigible
dirigible, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -ible
fr. L. dirigere, 'to direct, guide'. See direct, v.

## dirimeat
dirimeat, adj., rendering null and void (law). —
L. dirimens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of dirimere,
'to separate, divide, interrupt, destroy', fr. di-,
'apart', and emere, 'to buy', orig. meaning 'to
take, receive'. Accordingly dirimere lit. means
'to take away'. The form of the verb should
properly be *disimere (fr. dis- and emere)', the
change of s to r is due to rhotacism. See exempt
and -ent.

## dirk
dirk, п., a short dagger. — Fr. earlier durk, dork,
rel. to G. Dolck, 'dagger'; of uncertain origin.
The spelling dirk is arbitrary. It is based on
Johnson's authority. Du., Dan., Swed. dolk are
German loan words.
Derivative: dirk, tr. v.

## dirndl
dirndl, п., a kind of dress. — G. Dirndl, short
for Dirndlkleid, fr. Dirndl, dimin. formed fr.
Dime, 'girl' (now meaning 'low woman, wench,
hussy'), and Kleid, 'dress'. Dime derives fr.
MHG. dierne, 'maid' fr. OHG. thiorna, which
is rel. to OS. thiorna, ON. perna, Dan. terne,
MLG. derne, MDu. dierne, 'maidservant', Du.
deern(e), 'girl, wench, huSsy', and to OE pegn,
'thane, man, servant'. See thane.

## dirt
dirt, n. — Metathesized fr. ME. dril, fr. ON.
drilr, 'excrement', which is rel. to ON. dr'tto, OE.
dritan, 'to void excrement', and cogn. with
Serb, driskati, dial. Russ. dristat', 'to have
diarrhea', Maced. Gk. δαρδαίνειν, 'to soil, defile'.
Derivatives: dirt, tr. v., dirt-y, adj. and tr. v.,
dirt-i-ly, adv., dirt-i-ness, n.

## Dis
Dis, also Dis pater, a Roman underworld god,
equivalent to Greek Pluto. — L. Dis, fr. dis,
contracted form of dives, 'rich', prop, loan
translation of Gk. Πλούτων, 'Pluto', which lit.
means 'rich, wealthy' (fr. πλοΰτος, 'riches'). L.
dives is rel. to divus, 'divine, god', and orig.
meant 'favored by the gods'. For sense
development cp. OSlav. bogatu, 'rich', fr. bogu, 'God'.
See deity and cp. Dives.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:243 COLUMN:2 -->

## dis-
dis-, pref. of Latin origin denoting t) separation:
2) removal; 3) negation, deprivation, undoing,
reversal. — L. dis-, meaning 1) 'apart, asunder';
2) 'away from'; 3) 'utterly, completely'; 4) 'un-'
(in the privative sense of this prefix), derived
fr. I.-E. *dis-, 'apart, asunder', whence also Alb.
ts-, a privative pref. (e.g. in tik'ep, 'to rip,
undo'), OE. te-, OS, ti-, to-, OHG. zi-, ze- [later
zir- (a compound of the prefixes zi- and -ir),
whence MHG., G. zer-, 'asunder']. I.-E. *dis-
is a secondary form of "dwis-, which appears in
OI. dvih, Avestic bish, Gk. δίς (for *dwis), OL.
dvis (whence L. bis), MHG. zwis, 'twice', Goth.
twis-, 'in two, asunder', ON. tvistra, 'to divide'.
Cp. di-, 'apart, asunder'. Cp. also di-, 'two', and
words there referred to. Cp. also de-.

## disability
disability, n. — Formed with suff. -ity from the
obsolete adj. disable, fr. dis- and ahle.

## disable
disable, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and the adjective
able.
Derivatives: disabl-ed, adj., disable-ment, n.

## disabuse
disabuse, tr. v., to undeceive. — Formed fr. dis-
and abuse.

## disaccord
disaccord, n. — Formed fr. dis- and accord, n.

## disaccord
disaccord, intr. v. — ME. disacorden, fr. OF. des-
acorder, desaccorder (F. desaccorder), fr. des-
(fr. L. dis-) and acorder, accorder. See dis- and
accord, v.

## disaccustom
disaccustom, tr. v. — OF. desacostumer (F. des-
accoutumer), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and acostumer
(F. accoutumer). See dis- and accustom.

## disadvantage
disadvantage, n. — ME. disavauntage, fr. F. des-
avantage, fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and avamage. See
dis- and advantage.
Derivatives: disadvantage, tr. v.,
disadvantageous, adj., disadvantage-ous-ly, adv., disadvan-
tage-ous-ness, n.

## disaffect
disaffect, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and affect, v.
Derivatives: disaffect-ed, adj., disaffect-ed-ly,
adv., disaffect-ed-ness, п., disaffect-ion, n.

## disaffirm
disaffirm, tr. v., to reverse (law). — Formed fr.
dis- and affirm.
Derivatives: disaffirm-ance, п., disaffirm-ation,n.

## disafforest
disafforest, tr. v. — ML. disafforestare. See dis-
and afforest and cp. deforest, disforest.
Derivatives: disafforest-ation, n.

## disagree
disagree, intr. v. — F. desagreer, fr. des- (fr. L.
dis-) and agreer. See dis- and agree.
Derivatives: disagreeable(q.v.),disagree-menttn.

## disagreeable
disagreeable, adj. — F. desagreable, fr. des- (fr.
L. dis-) and agreable. See dis- and agreeable.
Derivatives: disagreeabl-y, adv., disagreeable-
ness, n.

## disallow
disallow, tr. v. — OF. desaiouer, 'to blame', fr.
des- (fr. L. dis·) and alouer, 'to allow'. See dis-
and albw.
Derivative: disallow-ance, n.

## disannul
disannul, tr. v., to annul completely. — Formed
fr. dis-, in the sense 'utterly, completely', and
annul.
Derivatives: disannuli-er, п., disannul-ment, n.

## disappear
disappear, intr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and appear.
Derivatives: disappear-ance, п., disappear-er, n.

## disappoint
disappoint, tr. v. — OF. desapointier (F. desap-
pointer), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and apointier (F.
appointer), 'to appoint'. See dis- and appoint.
Derivatives: disappoint-ed, adj.,
disappointedly, adv., disappoint-er, п., disappoint-ing, adj.,
disappoint-ing-ly, adv., disappoint-ing-ness, п.,
disappoint-ment, n.

## disapprobation
disapprobation, n. — Formed fr. dis- and
approbation.

## disapprobative
disapprobative, adj. — Formed fr. dis- and appro-
bative.

## disapprobatory
disapprobatory, adj. — Formed fr. dis- and
approbatory.

## disapprove
disapprove, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and
approve.
Derivatives: disapprov-al, п., disapprov-er, п.,
disapprov-ing-ly, adv.

## disarm
disarm, tr. and intr. v. — ME. desarmen, fr. MF.
(= F.) desarmer, fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and armer,
'to arm'. See dis- and arm, v.

## disarmament
disarmament, n. — Formed fr. prec. word on
analogy of armament.

## disarrange
disarrange, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and arrange.
Derivative: disarrange-ment, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:243 COLUMN:3 -->

## disarray
disarray, tr. v. — Formed on analogy of OF.
desareer, fr. dis- and array, v.
Derivative: disarray, n.

## disarticulate
disarticulate, tr..v., to disjoint. — Formed fr. dis-
and articulate, v.
Derivative: disarticulat-ion, n.

## disassociate
disassociate, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and

## associate
associate, v. Cp. dissociate.
Derivative: disassociat-ion, n.

## disaster
disaster, п., misfortune, calamity. — F. desastre,
fr. It. disastro (but with the substitution of the
F. prefix des- for It. dis-). It. disastro is a back
formation from disastrato, 'born under an ill
star', from the pejorative pref. dis-, fr. L. dis-
(see dis-), and L. astrum, 'star'. See Aster.

## disastrous
disastrous, adj. — F. disastreux (fern, desastreu-
se), fr. It. disastroso, 'ill-starred', fr. disastro.
See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: disastrous-ly, adv., disastrous-
ness, n.

## disavow
disavow, tr. v. — ME. disdvouen, fr. OF. desavou-
er (F. desavouer). fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and avouer,
'to own, acknowledge, avow'. See dis- and avow.
Derivatives: disavow-al, п., disavow-er, п., dis-
avow-ment, n.

## disband
disband, tr. v. — Earlier F. desbander (F. deban-
der), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and band, 'band'. See
dis- and band, 'troop'.
Derivative: disband-ment, n.

## disbar
disbar, tr. v., to expel from the bar. — Formed
fr. dis- and bar, 'rod of metal'. Cp. debar.
Derivative: disbar-ment, n.

## disbelief
disbelief, n. — ,Α hybrid coined fr. dis-, a pref.
of Latin origin, and the Teut. word belief.

## disbelieve
disbelieve, tr. and intr. v. — A hybrid coined fr.
dis- and the Teut. word believe. See prec. word.
Derivatives: disbeliev-er, п., disbeliev-ing-ly,
adv.

## disbench
disbench, tr. v., t) to deprive of a bench; 2) to
deprive a bencher of the membership of an Inn
of Court. — Formed fr. dis- and bench. Cp.
bencher.

## disbranch
disbranch, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and branch.

## disbud
disbud, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and bud.

## disburden
disburden, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and burden.

## disburse
disburse, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. earlier disbourse,
fr. OF. desbourser, which is formed fr. des- (fr.
L. dis-) and bourse. See dis- and bonrse. E.
disburse was assimilated in form to Late I., bursa.
Derivatives: disburse-ment, п., disburs-er, n.

## disc
disc, n. — See disk. The spelling disc is used esp.
in zoology.

## discalceate
discalceate, adj., unshod, barefooted (said of
members of religious orders). — L. discalceatus,
'unshod, barefooted', fr. dis-, and calceatus, pp.
of calceare, 'to furnish with shoes', fr. calceus,
'shoe'. See Calceolaria and adj. suff. -ate and cp.
calceate.

## discalced
discalced, adj., discalceate. — Formed fr. dis- and
calced. Cp. prec. word.

## discard
discard, tr. v. — Lit. 'to throw a card away', fr.
dis- and card.
Derivatives: discard, п., discard-er, n.

## discern
discern, tr. v., to distinguish. — F. discemer, fr.
L. discemere, 'to separate, set apart, divide,
distribute; to distinguish, perceive, discern,
understand, decide, judge', fr. dis- and cemere, 'to
separate, sift, distinguish, discern, understand,
decide'. See certain and cp. concern, decern,
secern. Cp. also discreet.
Derivatives: discern-er, п., discernible (q.v.),
discern-ing, adj., discem-ing-ly, adv.,
discernment, n.

## discernible
discernible, adj. — F. discernable, fr. discemer.
The English word was refashioned after L. dis-
cernibilis. See discera and -ible.
Derivatives: discernible-ness, п., discemibl-y,
adv.

## discerp
discerp, tr. v., to tear to pieces. — L. discerpere,
'to tear to pieces, rend', fr. dis- and carpere, 'to
pluck, gather'; see carpel. For the change of
Latin ά (in carpere) to ё (in dis-cirpere) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.

## discerptible
discerptible, adj. — Formed with sufT. -ible fr.
L. discerptus, pp. of discerpere. See prec. word.
Derivatives: discerplibil-ity, п., discerpiible-ness,
п., discerptibl-y, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:244 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 217 | DISCURSION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:244 COLUMN:1 -->

## discerption
discerption, η. — L. discerptio, gen. -0/1/5, *a
tearing to pieces, rending', fr, discerptus, pp. of dis-
cerpere. See discerp and -ion.

## discharge
discharge, tr. and intr. v. — ME. dischargen, des-
chargen, fr. OF. deschargier, descharger (F. de-
charger), 'to unload, unlade, discharge', fr. VL.
*discarricdre, fr. dis- and *carricdre, 'to put
a load on'. See charge, v.
Derivatives: discharge, п., discharg-er, п.,
discharging, n.

## disciple
disciple, n. — ME., fr. OE. discipui, fr. L.
discipulus, 'pupil, disciple*, fr. *dis-cipere, 'to seize
mentally', fr. dis- and capere, 'to catch, seize,
take hold of, take, receive'. See captive. For the
change of Latin a (in capere) to ϊ (in dis-cipulus)
see abigeat and cp. words there referred to.
Folk etymology has associated L. discipulus
with discere, 'to learn*, although derivatively the
two words are not related.

## disciplinable
disciplinable, adj. — Late L. disciplindbilis, fr.
L. disciplina. See discipline and -able.
Derivatives: disciplinabil-ity, п., disciplinable-
ness, n.

## disciplinary
disciplinary, adj. — ML. disciplindrius (whence
also F. disciplinaire), fr. L. disciplina. See next
word and -ary.
Derivatives: disciplinar-ian, adj. and n.

## discipline
discipline, n. — ME., fr. F., fr. L. disciplina,
instruction, teaching, learning, knowledge,
science', fr. discipulus. See disciple and subst.
suff. -ine.
Derivative: disciplin-al, adj.

## discipline
discipline, tr. v. — F. discipliner, fr. ML. disci-
pltnare, 'to teach*, fr. L. disciplina. See
discipline, n.

## discipular
discipular, adj., pertaining to a disciple. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. discipulus. See
disciple.

## disclaim
disclaim, tr. and intr. v. — AF.-OF. disclamer,
desclamer, fr. dis-, des- (fr. L. dis-) and clamer,
'to call, cry out, claim*. See dis- and claim and
cp. declaim.

## disclaimer
disclaimer, п., one who disclaims. — Formed fr.
prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## disclaimer
disclaimer, п., denial of a claim (law). — AF.
disclamer, desclamer, inf. used as a noun; see
disclaim. For the subst. use of the infinitive in
legal terminology see attainder and cp. words
there referred to.

## disclamation
disclamation, п., the act of disclaiming. - ML.
discldmdtio, fr. discldmdtus, pp. of discldmdre.
See disclaim and -ation.

## disclose
disclose, tr. v. — ME. desclosen, disclosen, fr. OF.
desclos- pres. stem of desclore (F. declare), fr.
des- (fr. L. dis) and clore, 'to shut, close* (fr. L.
claudere). See dis- and close, adj.
Derivatives: disclos-ed, adj., disclos-er, п.,
disclosure (q.v.)

## disco-
disco-, before a vowel disc-, combining form
meaning 'disk'. — Gk. δ;σκο-, Stent-, fr. δίσκος,
"quoit, disk'. See disk.

## discobolus
discobolus, п., a discus thrower. — L., fr. Gk.
δισκοβόλος, *a quoit thrower*, fr. δίσκος, 'quoit,
discus', and-βόλος, 'thrower of, which stands
in gradational relationship to βάλλειν, 'to throw*.
See disco- and ballistic.

## discoid
discoid, adj., having the form of a disk. — Gk.
λσκοεώής, 'resembling a quoit', fr. δίσκος,
'quoit, disk*, and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See disco- and -oid.

## discolor
discolor, discolour, tr. and intr. v. — OF. des-
colorer (F. decolorer), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and
colordre, 'to color'. See dis- and color, v.
Derivatives: discolo(u)r, п., discolo(u)r-ation, n.

## discomfit
discomfit, tr. v. — ME. discomfiten, fr. OF. des-
confit, 'defeated', pp. oidesconfire(F. deconfire),
4o defeat', fr. VL. disconficere, fr. dis- and L.
conficere, 'to put together, make ready, prepare,
bring about, accomplish, produce, consume*.
See confect and cp. comfit.

## discomfiture
discomfiture, n. — OF. descomfiture (F. deconfi-
ture), fr. desconfire. See prec. word and -ure.

## discomfort
discomfort, tr. v. — OF. desconforter (F. decon-
forter), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and conforter. See
dis- and comfort, v.

## discomfort
discomfort, n. — OF. desconfort (F. deconfort),
fr. desconforter. See discomfort, v.

## discomfortable
discomfortable, adj. — OF. desconfortable. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:244 COLUMN:2 -->
discomfort and -able and cp. comfortable.

## discommode
discommode, tr. v., to inconvenience. — Formed
fr. dis- and L. commodore, 'to make fit,
accomodate', fr. commodus, 'fit, suitable, convenient'.
See dis- and commode.

## discommodity
discommodity, п., inconvenience. — Formed fr.
dis- and commodity.

## discommon
discommon, tr. v., to deprive of the character of
a common. — Formed fr. dis- and common, n.

## discompose
discompose, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and compose.
Derivatives: discompos-ed, adj., discompos-ed-
ly, adv., discompos-ing, adj., discompos-ing-ly,
adv., discompos-ure, n.

## disconcert
disconcert, tr. v. — Obsol. F. disconcerted
(corresponding to F. deconcerter). See dis- and
concert.
Derivatives: disconcert-ed, adj., disconcert-ed-
ly, adv., disconcert-ed-ness, п., disconcert-ing,
adj., disconcert-ing-fy, adv., dfsconcert-ing-ness,
п., disconcert-ion, п., disconcert-ment, n.

## disconnect
disconnect, tr. v., to disjoin, separate. — Formed
fr. dis- and connect.
Derivatives: disconnect-ed, adj.,
disconnectedly, adv., disconnect-ed-ness, п., disconnection
(q.v.), disconnect-ive, adj., disconnect-or, n.

## disconnection
disconnection, disconnexion, n. — Formed fr.
dis- and connection, connexion.

## disconsolate
disconsolate, adj., inconsolable, sad. — ML. dis·
consoldtus, fr. dis- and L. consoldtus, pp. of cdn-
soldri, 'to console, comfort*. See console, v., and
adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: disconsolate-ly, adv., disconsolate-
ness, n.

## discontent
discontent, п., want of content. — Formed fr.
dis- and content, n.

## discontent
discontent, tr. v., 10 dissatisfy. — Formed fr. dis-
and content, v.
Derivatives: discontented, adj.,
discontentedly, adv., discontent-ed-ness, п., discontent-ing,
adj., discontent-ment, n.

## discontinuance
discontinuance, n. — AF., fr. OF. (= F.)
discontinues See discontinue and -ance.

## diseontiauation
diseontiauation, n. — F., fr. discontinuer. See next
word and -ation.

## discontiaue
discontiaue, tr. and intr, v. — F. discontinuer, fr.
ML. discontinuare, fr. dis- and L. continudre, 'to
join together, unite, continue'. See continne.
Derivatives: discontinu-er, n.,discontinu-ity,n.,
discontinu-ous, adj., discontinu-ous-ly, adv., dis-
continu-ous-ness, n.

## discord
discord, n. — ME, descord, discord, fr. OF. des-
corder, discorder. Cp. OF. discorde, sometimes
descorde (F. discorde), fr. L. discordia,
'discord*, fr. discors, gen. discordis. See discord, v.

## discord
discord, intr. v. — ME. descorden, discorden, fr.
OF. descorder, discorder (F. discorder) (the form
discorder was refashioned after the Latin), fr.
L. discorddre, 'to be at variapce, differ,
disagree' (whence also It. discordare, OProvenp.
descordar), fr. discors, gen. discordis,
discordant, disagreeing, at variance', fr. dis- and cors,
gen. cordis, 'heart'. See cordate and cp. scor-
dato. Cp. also accord, concord.

## discordaace
discordaace, n. — OF. descordance (F.
discordance), fr. descordant. See next word and -ce and
cp. concordance.

## discordant
discordant, adj. — OF. descordant<F. discordant),
pres. part, of descorder (F. discorder). See
discord, v., and -ant.
Derivatives: discordant-ly, adv., discordant-
ness, n.

## discouat
discouat, n. — 16th cent. F. descompte, fr. ML.
discomputus (whence also It. disconto), fr. dis-
and L. computare, 'to count*. See count, v.

## discount
discount, tr. and intr. v. — OF. descompter, des-
conter(F. decompter), fr. 16th cent. F. descompte.
See discount, n.
Derivative: discount-able, adj.

## discountenance
discountenance, tr. v., to discourage, disapprove.
— Formed fr. dis- and countenaace. Cp. F. de-
contenancer.

## discourage
discourage, tr. v. — OF. descoragier, descoura-
gier (F. decourager), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and
corage (F. courage). See dis- and courage and
cp. encourage.
Derivatives: discouragement (q.v.), discourag-er,
п., discourag-ing, adj., discourag-ing-ly, adv.

## discouragement
discouragement, n. — OF. descouragement (F. de-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:244 COLUMN:3 -->
couragement), fr. descouragier. See prec. word
and -ment.

## discourse
discourse, n. — F. discours, fr. L. discursus, 'a
running to and fro', in Late L., 'a conversation,
discourse', fr. discurs-(um), pp. stem of discur-
rere, 4o run to and fro*, fr. dis- and currere, 'to
run'. See conrse.
Derivatives: discourse, intr. and tr. v., discours-
er, п., discoursive (q.v.).

## discoursive
discoursive,adj., 1) pertaining to discourse; 2)
rational; 3) discursive. — Formed from prec.
word with surT. -ive. Cp. discursive.
Derivatives: discoursive-ly, adv., discoursive-
ness, n.

## discourteous
discourteous, adj., impolite, rude. — Formed fr.
dis- and courteous. Cp. F. discourtois.
Derivatives: discourteous-ly, adv., discourteous-
ness, n.

## discourtesy
discourtesy, n. — Formed fr. dis- and courtesy.
Cp. F. drscourioisie.

## discover
discover, tr. v. — OF. descovrir, descouvrir (F. de-
couvrir), fr. Late L. discooperlre, fr. dis- and L.
cooperire, 'to cover wholly*. See cover.
Derivatives: discover-able, adj., discover-abil-
ity, п., discover-abl-y, adv., discover-er, п.,
discovert (q.v.), discovery (q.v.)

## discovert
discovert, adj., not covert, unmarried (prop, not
protected by a husband) (law). — OF. descovert,
descouvert (F. decouveri), 'uncovered', prop. pp.
of descovrir, descouvrir. See prec. word and cp,
covert.

## discovery
discovery, n. — Formed fr. discover on analogy
of recovery.

## discredit
discredit, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and credit.
Derivatives: discredit, п., discredit-able, adj.,
discredit-abl-y, adv.

## discreet
discreet, adj., prudent. — OF. (= F.) discret, fr.
L. discretus, pp. of discernere, 'to separate, set
apart, discern'. See discern and cp. discrete. Cp.
also decera, secern.

## discrepancy
discrepancy, п., difference. — OF. discrepance,
fr. L. discrepantia, 'discordance, discrepancy',
fr. discrepdns, gen. -antis. See next word and -cy.

## discrepant
discrepant, adj., different. — L. discrepdns, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of discrepdre, 'to sound
differently, differ, vary', fr. dis- and crepare, 'to
rattle, crack, break with a crack, burst'. See
crepitate and -ant.
Derivative: discrepant-ly, adv.

## discrete
discrete, adj., separate. — L. discreius, pp. of
discernere. See discreet, which is a doublet of
discrete.
Derivatives: discrete-ly, adv., discrete-ness, n.

## discretion
discretion, n. — OF. descrecion, discrecion (F.
discretion), fr. L. discretionem, ace. of discreiio,
'separation, discrimination, discernment*, fr.
discretus, pp. of discernere. See discreet and -ion.
Derivatives: discretion-al, adj., discretion-al-ly,
adv., discretion-ary, adj., discretion-ari-ly, adv.

## discriminant
discriminant, adj., discriminating. — L. discri-
mindns, gen. -antis, pres. part, of discriminate.
See next word and -ant.

## discriminate
discriminate, intr. and tr. v. — L. discrimindtus,
pp. of discrimindre, 'to divide, separate,
distinguish, distribute, apportion', fr. discrlmen, gen.
discriminis, 'interval, distinction, difference,
turning point, critical moment, decision', from
the stem of discernere (pp. discretus), 'to
separate, set apart, discern*. See discern and cp.
crime, criminate, incriminate, recriminate.
Derivatives: discriminat-ing, adj.,
discriminatingly, adv., discrimination (q.v.),
discriminative, adj., discriminat-ive-ly, adv., discriminat-ory,
adj.

## discrimination
discrimination, n. — Late L. discrimindtio, gen.
-onis, 'the contrasting of opposite thoughts', fr.
L. discrimindtus, pp. of discrimindre. See prec.
word and -ion.

## discrown
discrown, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and crown.

## disculpate
disculpate, tr. v., to exculpate. — ML. disculpa-
tus, pp. of disculpdre, 'to free from blame', fr.
dis- and L. culpdre, 'to reproach, blame', fr.
culpa, 'fault, blame'. See culpable and verbal
suff. -ate and cp. exculpate.
Derivatives: disculpat-ion, п., disculpat-ory, adj.

## discursion
discursion, n. — Late L. discursio, gen. -onis, 'a
running to and fro', fr. L. discurs-(um), pp. stem
of discurrere. See next word and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:245 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DISCURSIVE | 218 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:245 COLUMN:1 -->

## discursive
discursive, adj., l) running to and fro (rare);
2) rambling. — F. discursif (fem. discursive), fr.
discurs-(um), pp. stem of discurrere, 'to run to
and fro'. See discourse and -ive and cp. dis-
coursive.
Derivatives: discursive-ly, adv., discursive-ness,
n.

## discus
discus, п., a disk. — L., fr. Gk. δίσκος, 'quoit,
disk'. See disk.

## discuss
discuss, tr. and intr. v. — L. discussus, pp. of dis-
cutere, 'to shake violently, shatter, dash to
pieces, scatter, disperse', in Late L. 'to discuss',
fr. dis- and quatere, 'to shake, wield, brandish,
strike, shatter'. See quash, 'to annul', and cp.
concuss, concussion, percuss, percussion.
Derivatives: discuss-erjn., discuss-ible, adj.,
discussion (q.v.), discuss-ive, adj.

## discussion
discussion, n. — OF. (— F.), fr. L. discussionem,
ace. of discussio, 'a shaking', in Late L.
'discussion', fr. discussus, pp. of discutere. See prec.
word and -ion.
Derivative: discussion-al, adj.

## disdain
disdain, tr. v. — ME. disdaynen, fr. OF. des-
deignier, desdeigner (F. dedaigner), fr. VL. *dis-
dignare, corresponding to L. dedignari, 'to
disdain', prop, 'to reject as unworthy'. Cp. It.
sdegnare, OProveng. desdenhar, Sp. desdenar,
'to disdain', and see dis- and deign.
Derivative: disdain-er, n.

## disdain
disdain, n. — ME. disdayn, fr. OF. desdeign, des-
dain (F. dedain), fr. desdeignier. See disdain, v.
Derivatives: disdain-ful, adj., disdain-ful-ly,adv.,
disdain-ful-ness, n.

## disease
disease, n. — ME. disese, desese, fr. OF. desaise,
lit. 'lack of ease', fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and aise,
'ease'. See dis- and ease.

## disease
disease, tr. v. — ME. disesen, fr. OF. desaaisier,
fr. desaise, 'disease'. See disease, n.
Derivative: diseas-ed, adj.

## disembark
disembark, tr. and intr. v. — F. desembarquer, fr.
des- (fr. L. dis-) and embarquer, 'to embark'. See
dis- and embark.
Derivative: disembark-ation, n.

## disembarrass
disembarrass, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and
embarrass, on analogy of F. desembarrasser. Cp.
debarrass. Derivative: disembarrass-ment, n.

## disembody
disembody, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and embody.
Derivative: disembodi-ment, n.

## disembogue
disembogue, tr. and intr. v., to flow into the sea,
lake, etc.; to empty. — Sp. desembacar, fr. des-
(fr. L. dis-) and embocar, 'to put or enter into
the mouth', fr. em-, assimilated form of en-, 'in',
and boca, 'mouth', fr. L. bucca, 'cheek'. See in-,
'in', and buccal, and cp. debouch.

## disembosom
disembosom, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. dis-
and embosom and lit. meaning to cast from
the bosom'.

## disembowel
disembowel, tr. v., to remove the bowels from. —
Formed fr. dis- and embowel.

## dlseme
dlseme, п., a syllable of two times (pros.) — See
next word.

## dlsemic
dlsemic, adj., having the length of two times
(pros.) — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Late L.
disemus, 'dissyllabic', fr. Gk. δίσημος, fr. 54-
(see di-, 'two'), and σήμα, 'sign'. See semantics
and cp. words there referred to.

## disenchant
disenchant, tr. v. — F. desenchanter, fr. des- (fr. L.
dis-) and enchanter, 'to enchant, bewitch'. See
dis- and enchant.
Derivatives: disenchant-er, п., disenchant-ment,
n.

## disencumber
disencumber, tr. v. — F. desencombrer, fr. des-
(fr. L. dis-) and encombrer, 'to obstruct,
encumber'. See dis- and encumber.

## disenfranchise
disenfranchise, tr. v., to disfranchise. — Formed
fr. dis- and enfranchise. Cp. disfranchise.
Derivative: disenfranchise-ment, n.

## disengage
disengage, tr. v. — Formed fr. dis- and engage.
Derivatives: disengag-ed, adj., disengage-ment, n.

## disfavor
disfavor, disfavour, n. — Formed fr. dis- and
favor, favour.
Derivative: disfavo(u)r, tr. v.

## disfigure
disfigure, tr. v. — OF. desfigurer (F. defigurer),
fr. VL. 'disfigurdre, fr. dis- and L. figurare, 'to
form, fashion', fr. figura, 'form, shape'. See
figure, n.
Derivatives: disfigur-ation, п., disfigure-ment,
п., disfigur-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:245 COLUMN:2 -->

## disforest
disforest, tr. v., to disafforest. — Formed fr. dis-
and forest. Cp. deforest, disafforest.

## disfranchise
disfranchise, tr. v., to deprive of a franchise. —
Formed fr. dis- and franchise. Cp.
disenfranchise.
Derivative: disfranchise-ment, n.

## disgorge
disgorge, tr. v., to throw out from the throat. —
OF. desgorger (F. degorger), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-)
and gorge, 'throat'. See dis- and gorge.

## disgrace
disgrace, n. — F. disgrace, fr. It. disgrazia, fr.
dis- (fr. L. dis-) and grazia, 'grace', fr. L. gratia,
'favor, kindness, charm'. See dis- and grace, v.
Derivatives: disgrace-ful, adj., disgrace-ful-ly,
adv., disgrace-ful-ness, n.

## disgrace
disgrace, tr. v. — F. disgracier, fr. disgrace. See
disgrace, n.

## disgruntle
disgruntle, tr. v., to make discontented. —
Formed fr. dis- and gruntle, freq. of grunt.
Derivatives: disgrunll-ed, adj. ,disgruntle-ment,n.

## dlsgnise
dlsgnise, tr. v. — ME. desguisen, desgisen, degisen,
fr. OF. desguisier, desguiser (F. deguiser), fr.
des- (fr. L. dis-) and OF. (= F.) guise. See dis-
and gnise.
Derivatives: disguise, п., disguis-ed, adj., dis-
guis-ed-ly, adv., disguis-ed-ness, п., disguis-er, n.

## disgust
disgust, tr. v. — Earlier F. desgouster (F. de-
gouter), 'to disgust', fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and
gouster (F. gouter), 'to taste', fr. L. gustare, of
s.m. See gust, 'relish', and cp. degust.
Derivatives: disgust-ed, adj., disgust-ed-ty, adv.,
disgust-ed-ness, п., disgust-er, п., disgust-ing,
adj., disgust-ing-ly, adv., disgust-ing-ness, n.

## disgust
disgust, n. — Earlier F. desgoust (F. degout), fr.
desgouster. See disgust, v.
Derivatives: disgust-ful, adj., disgust-ful-ly, adv.,
disgust-ful-ness, n.

## disb
disb, n. — ME. disch, fr. OE. disc, 'dish, plate,
bowl', rel. to ON. diskr, 'dish', OS. disk, 'table',
OHG. tisc, 'dish; table', MHG., G. tisch,
'table', fr. L. discus, 'quoit', in Late L. 'dish'
(so called because of its shape), fr. Gk. δίσκος,
'quoit, disk', which is dissimilated fr. *δίκ-σκος
and prop, means 'that which is thrown', from
the stem of δικεΐν, 'to throw, cast', whence also
δίκτυον, 'net'. Cp. dais, desk, disc, discus and
the second element in oftish. Cp. also Dictynidae,
Dictynna, dictyo-.
Derivatives: dish, tr. and intr. v., dish-ed, adj.,
dish-er, n.

## dishabille
dishabille, also deshabille, п., negligee, undress.
— F. deshabille, prop. pp. of deshabiller, 'to
undress', used as a noun, fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and
habiller, 'to dress". See dis- and habiliment. For
the loss of the French pp. suff. -e in E. deshabille
cp. costive and words there referred to.

## disherison
disherison, п., the aci of disinheriting (archaic).
— Fr. earlier disheriteson, fr. OF. desheriteison,
fr. desheriter, 'to disinherit', fr. des- (fr. L. dis-)
and heriter, 'to inherit', fr. L. hereditare, 'to
inherit'. See heredity and cp. disinherit.

## dishevel
dishevel, tr. v. — Back formation fr. disheveled.

## disheveled
disheveled, dishevelled, adj., disarranged; untidy;
tousled. — Formed with suff.-ed fr. OF.descheve-
le, 'disheveled', fr. ML. discapillatus, 'stripped
of hair', fr. dis- and L. capillus, 'hair'. In F.
echevele, 'disheveled', the pref. des- has been
replaced by the pref. e- (fr. L. ex-, 'out of, from';
see 1st ex-). See capillary.

## dishonest
dishonest, adj. — ME. dishoneste, fr. OF. des-
honeste (F. deshonnite), fr. VL. dishonestus
(corresponding to L. dehonestus), fr. dis- and L.
honestus. See honest.
Derivative: dishonest-ly, adv.

## dishonesty
dishonesty, n. — OF. deshoneste(F. deshonnetete),
fr. deshoneste, adj. See prec. word and cp.
honesty.

## dishonor
dishonor, dishonour, n. — OF. deshonor (E. des-
honneur), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and honor. See dis-
and honor, n.

## dishonor
dishonor, dishonour, tr. v. — OF. deshonorer (F.
deshonorer), fr. Late L. dishonorare, 'to
dishonor', fr. dis- and L. honorare. Ίο honor'. See
honor, v.
Derivatives: dishono(u)r-able, adj., dishono(u)r-
able-ness, п., dishono(u)r-abl-y, adv.

## dishorse
dishorse, tr. and intr. v. — A hybrid coined fr.
dis-, a pref. of Latin origin, and the Teut. word
horse.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:245 COLUMN:3 -->

## disinherit
disinherit, tr. v., to deprive of the right to
inherit. — Formed fr. dis- and inherit, in the now
obsolete sense 'to make one's heir'. Cp.
disherison.
Derivative: disinherit-ance, n.

## disject
disject, tr. v., to scatter, disperse. — L. disjectus,
pp. of disicere (less correctly disjicere), 'to throw
asunder, scatter', fr. dis- and jdcere, 'to throw'.
See jet, 'to spirt forth*. For the change of Latin
ά (in jacere) to ё (in dis-jectus) see accent and
cp. words there referred to.

## disjecta membra
disjecta membra, scattered members. — See
disject and member.

## disjoin
disjoin, tr. v. — OF. desjoindre (F. disjoindre, de-
joindre), fr. L. disjungere, 'to disjoin, disunite,
separate', fr. dis- and jungere, 'to join*. See join
and cp. disjoint, disjunct, disjunction.

## disjoint
disjoint, adj. — OF. desjoint (fr. L. disjunctus),
pp. of desjoindre. See prec. word and cp.
disjunct, conjoint.
Derivatives: disjoint-ed, adj., disjoint-ed-ly,adv.,
disjoint-ed-ness, n.

## disjunct
disjunct, adj. — L. disjunctus, pp. of disjungere.
See disjoin.

## disjunction
disjunction, n. — L. disjunctio, gen. -onis,
'separation', fr. disjunctus, pp. of disjungere. See
disjunct and -ion and cp. junction, conjunction.

## disjunctive
disjunctive, adj. — L. disjunctivus, 'placed in
opposition', fr. disjunctus; pp. of disjungere. See
disjoin and -ive and cp. conjunctive, subjunctive.
Derivatives: disjunctive, п., disjunctivc-ly, adv.

## disk
disk, also disc, n. (the latter spelling is used
especially in zoology). — L. discus, 'quoit, disk',
fr. Gk. δίσκος. See dish and cp. words there
referred to.

## dislikable
dislikable, adj. — Formed from the verb dislike
with suff. -able; first used by Carlyle. Cp.
adaptable, affordable, forgettable.

## dislike
dislike, tr. v. — A hybrid coined fr. dis- (fr. L.
dis-) and like, 'to be fond of (fr. OE. gelician).
Cp. the verb mislike, in which both elements
are Teutonic.
Derivative: dislike, n.

## dislocate
dislocate, tr. v., t) to put out of joint; 2) to upset.
— ML. dislocatus, pp. of dislocafe, 'to put out
of place', fr. dis- and locdre, 'to put, place', fr.
locus, 'place'. See locate.

## dislocation
dislocation, n. — ML. dislocatio, gen. -onis, fr.
dislocatus, pp. of dislocare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## dislodge
dislodge, tr. v. — OF. deslogier, desloger (F. de-
loger), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and logier, loger, 'to
lodge'. See dis- and lodge, v.
Derivative: dislodg-ment, n.

## disloyal
disloyal, adj. — OF. desloial (F. deloyai), fr. des-
(fr. L. dis-) and loial (F. loyal). — See dis-and
loyal.
Derivatives: disloyal-ly, adv., disloyalty (q.v.),
and the hybrid noun disloyal-ist, n.

## disloyalty
disloyalty, n. — OF. desloiaute (F. deloyaute), fr.
OF. desloial. See disloyal and -ty and cp.
loyalty.

## dismal
dismal, п., a period of dies mall, or 'unlucky
days'; adj., ι) gloomy; dreary; 2) miserable. —
ME. dysmal, fr. OF. dis mal, 'evil, or unlucky,
day', fr. L. dies mail, 'evil, unfortunate days'.
See deity and mal-.
Derivatives: dismal-ly, adv., dismal-ness, n.

## dismantle
dismantle, tr. v. — OF. desmanteler (F. deman-
teler), fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and manteler, 'to cover
with a mantle', fr. mantel, 'mantle'. See dis- and
mantle.
Derivatives: dismantle-ment, п., dismantl-er, n.

## dismay
dismay, tr. v., to discourage. — ME. dismayen,
fr. OF. *desmayer, *dismayer (occurring only in
the form of the pp. dismaye), a collateral form of
esmayer, 'to trouble, disturb, frighten* (whence
OF. esmais, esmoi, F. emoi, 'anxiety'), fr. VL.
*exmagare, 'to remove the power from', a
hybrid coined fr. L. pref. ex-, 'out of, from', and
Teut. "magan, 'to be able'. See dis- and the
auxiliary verb may. Cp. It. smagare, 'to weaken,
dismay, discourage', smagarsi, 'to be
discouraged', OProvenc. esmagar, esmaiar, 'to trouble*,
Port, esmagar, 'to crash', which all derive fr.
VL. 'exmagare. Sp. desmayar, 'to be dispirited',
is an OF. loan word.
Derivatives: dismay, п., loss of courage, dismay-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:246 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 219 | DISS- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:246 COLUMN:1 -->
ed, adj., dismay-ed-ness, n.

## dismember
dismember, tr. v. — OF. desmembrer (F. demem-
brer), fr. VL. dismembrare (corresponding to L.
demembrare), 'to dismember', fr. dls- and mem-
brum, 'member'. See member.
Derivatives: dismember-ed, adj., dismember-er,
п., dismemberment (q.v.)

## dismemberment
dismemberment, n. — OF. desmembremenl (F.
demembrement), fr. desmembrer. See prec. word

## dismiss
dismiss, tr. v. — Formed, with change of suffix

lere, 'to send'. See mission.
Derivatives: dismiss-al, п., dismiss-ible, adj.,
dismiss-ion, п., dismiss-ive, adj.

## disnature
disnature, tr. v. — OF. desnaturer (F. denaturer),
fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and nature. See dis- and
nature.

## disobedience
disobedience, n. — OF. desobedience, fr. VL.
*disoboedientia (corresponding to L. inoboe-
dientia), fr. *disoboediins, gen; -entis. See dis-
and obedience.

## disobedient
disobedient, adj. — OF. desobedient, fr. VL. *dis-
oboedientem, ace. of "disoboediens, which
corresponds to L. inoboediens, 'disobedient'. See
dis- and obedient and cp. next word.
Derivative: disobedient-ly, adv.

## disobey
disobey, tr. and intr. v. — F. desobeir, fr. VL.
'disoboedire, corresponding to L. inoboedire,
'to disobey'. See dis- and obey.

## disoblige
disoblige, tr. v. — F. desobliger, fr. des- (fr. L.
dis-) and obliger, 'to oblige'. See dis- and oblige.
Derivatives: disoblig-er, п., disoblig-ing, adj.,

## disorder
disorder, n. — Formed fr. dls- and order, on

Derivatives: disorder, tr. v., disorder-ed, adj.,

disorderly, adj., n. and adv., disorder-li-ness, n.

## disorganization
disorganization, n. — F. desorganisation, fr. rfes-
organiser. See next word and -ation.

## disorganize
disorganize, tr. v. — Coined by Edmund Burke

## disparage

See dls-, pair and verbal suff. -age.
Derivatives: disparag-er, п., disparag-ing, adj.,
disparag-ing-ly, adv.

## disparagement
disparagement, n. — OF. desparagement, fr.
desparagier. See prec. word and -ment.

## disparate
disparate, adj., unequal. — L. disparatus, pp. of
disparare, 'to part, separate', fr. dis- and parare,
'to prepare'. See pare and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: disparate-ly, adv., disparate-ness,n.

## disparity
disparity, п., inequality. — F. disparile. See dls-
and parity.

## dispart
dispart, tr. and intr. v., to divide, separate. —
OF. despartir (F. depariir), fr. L. dispartire, a
collateral form of dispertire, 'to divide,
distribute', fr. dis- and partire, 'to divide', fr. pars,
gen. partis, 'part'. See part, v., and cp. depart

## dispart
dispart, п., the difference between the semidia-
meters at the breech of a gun and at its muzzle.
— Fr. prec. word.

## dispatch
dispatch, despatch, tr. v. — Sp.-Port. despachar,
'to hasten, speed', fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and VL.
"pactare, 'to fasten, fix', freq. of L. pangere (pp.
pactus), 'to rhake firm, fasten', which is rel. to
pacisci, 'to make a treaty', pax, gen. pads,
'peace'. See dis- and pact and cp. words there
referred to. The correct spelling is dispatch. The
spelling despatch is due to an error in Johnson's
Dictionary. Cp. It. dispacciare, 'to dispatch',
which is formed fr. dls- and VL. *pactiare, fr.
L. pactus, pp. of pangere (see above). F. di-
pecher, 'to dispatch', is not related to Sp.-Port.
despachar, but derives fr. dis- and L. -pedicure
(in impedicare), 'to catch in a trap', fr. pedka,
'shackle, fetter' (see depiche).
Derivatives: dispatch, n. (q.v.), dispatch-er, n.

## dispatch
dispatch, despatch, n. — Sp.-Port. despacho, fr.
despachar. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:246 COLUMN:2 -->

## dispel
dispel, tr. v. — L. dispellere, 'to drive away,
scatter', fr. dis- and pellere, 'to push, drive'. See
pulse, 'throb', and cp. appeal and words there
referred to.
Derivative: dispell-er, n.

## dispensable
dispensable, adj. — ML. dispensabilis, fr. L. dis-

Derivaiives: dispensabil-ity, п., dispensable-
ness, n.

Derivative: dispensation-αί, adj.

## dispense

manage, regulate, control, impart', freq. of dis-
pendere (pp. displnsus), 'to weigh out', fr. dis-
and pendere, 'to weigh out, pay out; to consider,
ponder'. See pension and cp. spend. Cp. also
spence.
Derivatives: dispensable (q.v.), dispens-er, n.

## dispeople
dispeople, tr. v. — OF. despeupler (F. depeupler),

## disperse
disperse, tr. and intr. v. — F. disperser, fr. L.
dispersus, pp. of dispergere, 'to scatter,
disperse', fr. dis- and spargere, 'to sprinkle, scatter,
disperse, divide'. See sparse and cp. asperse.
For the change of Latin ά (in spargere) to e
(in di-spergere, di-spersus) see accent and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: dispers-al, п., dispers-ed-ly, adv.,
dispers-ible, adj., dispers-ibil-ily, п., dispersion
(q.v.), dispers-ive, adj., dispers-ive-ly, adv.,

## dispersion
dispersion, n. — F., fr. L. dispersionem, ace. of

## dispirit
dispirit, tr. v., to discourage. — Formed fr. dis-

Derivatives: dispirit-ed-Iy, adv., dispirit-ed-
ness, n.

## displace
displace, tr. v. — OF. desplacer (F. deplacer), fr.

displacency, n. — ML. displacentia (for L. dis-
plicentia), 'dissatisfaction', fr. dis-, L. placere,

## display
display, tr. v. — OF. despleier (F. deployer), 'to

play-er, n.

## displease
displease, tr. v. — OF. desplaisir, fr. VL. *dis-
placere, corresponding to L. dispiicere, 'to
displease', fr. dis- and pfacere, 'to please'. See
please.
Derivatives: displeas-ed, adj., displeas-ed-ly,
adv., displeas-ing, adj., displeas-ing-ly, adv.

## displeasure
displeasure, n. — OF. desplaisir (F. deplaisir),
infinitive used as a noun. See prec. word and
cp. pleasure.
Derivative: displeasure, tr. v.

## displume
displume, tr. v., to deprive of feathers. — OF.

## disport
disport, п., diversion; amusement {archaic). —

## disport

carry oneself in the opposite direction', fr. des-
(fr. L. dis-) and porter (fr. L. portare), 'to carry'.
See port, 'to carry', and cp. sport, which is a
doublet of disport.

## Disporum
Disporum, п., a genus of plants of the lily-of-the-
valley family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. di-,
'two', and σπορά, 'seed' (see spore); so called
in allusion to the two ovules in each cell.

## dispose
dispose, tr. and intr. v. — OF. (= F.) disposer,
fr. L. disponere (pp. dispositus), 'to dispose',

which was Gallicized after F. poser, 'to put,
place'. See next'word and cp. compose and words
there referred to. See also pose, 'to place'.
Derivatives: dtspos-able, adj., dispos-abil-ity, п.,
dispos-abfe-ness, п., dispos-al, п., dispos-ed, adj.,
dispos-ed-ly, adv., dispos-ed-ness, п.,
disposer, n.

## disposition
disposition, n. — ME.,fr. MF. (= F .)disposition,fr.
L. dispositionem, ace. ofdispositio, 'arrangement,
management disposition', fr. dispositus, pp. of
disponere, 'to place here and there, arrange,

dispositive, adj. — F. dispositif (fem. dispositive),
