dispossess, tr. v. — OF. despossessier, desposses-

dispraise, tr. v., to disparage; to blame. — OF.

pretiare, corresponding to L. depretiare, 'to

## disprize
disprize, tr. v., not 10 prize, to despise. — OF.
despriser. See prec. word.

## disproof
disproof, n. — Formed fr. dis- and proof, on

disproportion. — F. See dis- and proportion.

af, adj., disproportion-al-ity, п., disproportion-
al-ly, adv., disproportion-ate, adj., disproportion-
ate-Iy, adv., disproportion-ate-ness, n.

## disputable
disputable, adj. — L. disputabilis, fr. disputare.

Derivatives: disputabil-ity, п., disputable-ness,

## disputant
disputant, adj. and n. — L. dispuians, gen. -antis,

## disputation

## disputatious
disputatious, adj. — See prec. word and -ous.

nesSi n.

## disputative
disputative, adj. — Late L. disputativus,

Derivatives: disputative-Iy, adv., disputative-

## dispute
dispute, tr. and intr. v. — ME. desputen, disputen,
fr. OF. despmer, dispufer (F. disputer), fr. L.
disputare, 'to reckon up, calculate, examine,

cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: dispute, п., disput-er, n.

## disquisition
disquisition, п., inquisition; examination. — L.

Derivative: disquisition-al, adj.

## disrate.
disrate., tr. v., to reduce to a lower rating. —
Formed fr. dis- and rate, 'amount'.

## disrupt
disrupt, tr. v. — Back formation fr. disruption.

## disruption
disruption, n. — L. disruptio, diruptio, gen. -onis,
'a breaking asunder', fr. disruptus, diruptus, pp.
of disrumpere, dirumpere, 'to break to pieces,

and rumpere, 'to break, burst, tear'. See rupture
and -ion.

## disruptive
disruptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
disruptus, pp. of disrumpere. See prec. word.
Derivaiives: disruptive-ly, adv., disruptive-ness,
n.

## diss-
diss-, form of disso- before a vowel.

## dissect
dissect, tr. v., to cut apart. — L. dissectus, pp. of

## dissecare
dissecare, 'to cut to pieces', fr. dis- and secure,
'to cut; to cut off'. See section.
Derivatives: dissect-ed, adj., dissect-ing, adj.,
dissection (q.v.), dissect-ive, adj., dissect-or, n.

## dissection
dissection, n. — L. dissectio, gen. -onis, 'a cutting
to pieces', fr. dissectus, pp. o(dissecare;seeprec.
word and -ion. .The term dissection was
introduced by the English philosopher, Baron Veru-
lam Francis Bacon (1561-1626).

## disseize
disseize, disseise, tr. v., to deprive of seizing or

dis-) and saisir, 'to seize'. See dis- and seize and

## disseizin
disseizin, disseisin, п., the act of disseizing (law).
— Formed fr. dis- and seizin. Cp. prec. word.

## dissemble
dissemble, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. earlier dissimule,

## disseminate

## dissemination
dissemination, n. — L. disseminatio, gen. -onis, 'a

## disseminator
disseminator, n. — Late L. disseminator, 'one who

disseminare. See disseminate and agential suff. -or.

## dissension
dissension, п., disagreement. — F., fr. L. dis-
sensionem, ace. of dissensio, 'difference of

sus, pp. of dissentire. See dissent and -ion.

## dissent
dissent, intr. v., to disagree. — L. dissentire, 'to

and sentire, 'to perceive by the senses, to feel'.
See sense and cp. assent, consent, resent.
Derivatives: dissent, п., dissent-er, п.,
dissenting, adj., dissent-ing-ly, adv.

## dissentient
dissentient, adj., dissenting. — L. dissentilns,

and -lent and cp. sentient.

## dissepiment
dissepiment, п., a partition, enclosure. — L. dis-
saepimentum, 'a partition', lit. 'that which
separates', fr. dissaepire, 'to part off, separate,
divide*, fr. dis- and saepire, Ίο hedge in, fence in,
enclose'. See septum and -meat.

## dissert
dissert, tr. v., to dissertate (rare). — L. dissertus,
pp. of disserere, 'to examine, argue, discuss,

## dissertate
dissertate, intr. v., to discourse, discuss. — L.
dissertatus, pp. of dissertare, 'to discuss, argue,
debate', freq. of disserere (pp. dissertus). See
prec. word and verbal suf. -ate.

## dissertation
dissertation, n. — L. dissertdtio, gen. -onis, fr.
dissertatus, pp. of dissertare. See prec. word and
-Ion.

## disserve
disserve, tr. v., to serve ill. — Formed fr. dis- and
serve, on analogy of F. desservir.

## disservice
disservice, п., ill service. — Formed fr. dis- and
service, on analogy of F. desservice.

## dissever
dissever, tr. v., to sever, separate. — AF. dese-
verer, corresponding to OF. dessevrer, desseve-
rer, fr. des- (fr. L. dis-) and severer, 'to
separate'. See dis- and sever,

## disseverance
disseverance, n. — OF. dessevrance, fr. dessevrer.
See dissever and -ance and cp. severance.

## dissideace
dissideace, п., dissent. — L. dissidentia,
'diversity, contrariety', fr. dissidens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of dissidere. See next word and -ce.

## dissident
dissident, adj., dissenting; п., a dissenter. — L.
dissidens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of dissidere, 'to
sit apart, be remote from, be divided, be at
variance, be unlike', fr. dis- and sedere, 'to sit'.
See sedentary. For the change of Latin ё (in
sedere) to i (in dis-sidere) see abstinent and cp.
words there referred to.

## dissilient
dissilient, adj., bursting open (hot.) — L. dissi-
liens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of dissilire, 'to leap
asunder, burst asunder', fr. dis- and satire, 'to
leap'. See salient and cp. resilient, transilient.
For the change of Latin a (in satire) to /" (in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:247 COLUMN:2 -->
dissilire) see abigeat and cp. words there referred
to.

## dissimilar
dissimilar, adj. — Formed fr. dis- and similar,
on analogy of F. dissimilaire.
Derivatives: dissimilar-ity, п., dissimilar-ly, adv.

## dissimilate
dissimilate, tr. v. — Formed with verbal suff.
-ate fr. L. dissimitis, 'unlike, different', on
analogy of assimilate. See dis- and similar.
Derivatives: dissimilat-ion, п., dissimilat-ive, adj.

## dissimilitude
dissimilitude, n. — L. dissimilitude), 'unlikeness',
fr. dissimitis, 'unlike', fr. dis- and similis, 'like'.
See similar and -tude and cp. prec. word.

## dissimulate
dissimulate, tr. v., to conceal, dissemble. — L.
dissimulatus, pp. of dissimuiare, 'to disguise,
hide, conceal, keep secret', lit. 'to pretend that
a thing is not such as it really is', fr. dis- and
simulare, 'to imitate, assume, pretend'. See
simulate and cp. dissemble.

## dissimulation
dissimulation, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. dissimula-
tionem, ace. of dissimUldtid, 'a concealing,
disguising, dissimulation', fr. dissimulatus, pp. of
dissimuiare. See prec. word and -ion.

## dissipate
dissipate, tr. v., r) to scatter; 2) to squander; intr.
v., 1) to disappear; 2) to engage in frivolous
pleasures. — L. dissipatus, pp. of dissipare, 'to
scatter, disperse; to destroy; to squander', fr.
dis- and -sipare, -supdre, 'to throw', fr. I.-E.
base *sup-, *swep-, 'to throw, swing, shake',
whence also Lith. supu (supaff), siipti, 'to swing,
rock', OSlav. supo, suti, 'to strew', and its
iterative sypati, 'to shale', ra-sypati, 'to scatter',
svepiti se, 'to be shaken about, be tossed,
agitated'. For the ending see verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: dissipat-ed, adj., dissipat-ed-ly,adv.,
dissipat-ed-ness, п., dissipat-er, п., dissipation
(q.v.), dissipat-ive, adj., dissipator (q.v.)

## dissipation
dissipation, n. — L. dissipatio, gen. -onis,
'dispersion, destruction', fr. dissipatus, pp. of
dissipare. See prec. word and -Ion.

## dissipator
dissipator, n. — L. dissipator, 'a disperser,
destroyer', fr. dissipatus, pp. of dissipare. See
dissipate and agential suff. -or.

## disso-
disso-, before a vowel diss-, combining form
meaning 'double'. — Gk. δισσο-, δισσ-, fr. δισ-
σός, corresponding to Att. διττός, 'double',
which stand for *διχ-ιός, and are rel, to δίχα,
'in two, asunder', δις, 'twice'. Seedi-, 'two', and
cp. dicho- and the first element in dittography.

## dissociable
dissociable, adj. — L. dissocidbilis, 'separating,
dividing, incompatible', fr. dissociare. See
dissociate and -able.
Derivatives: dissociabil-ity, п., dissociable-
ness, n.

## dissocial
dissocial, adj., unsocial. — Formed fr. dis- and
social.

## dissociate
dissociate, tr. v., to separate. — L. dissociatus,
pp. of dissociare, 'to disjoin, disunite, to set at
variance', fr. dis- and socidre, 'to associate,
unite', fr. socius, 'companion'. See dis- and
sociable and cp. disassociate.
Derivatives: dissociation (q.v.), dissociat-ive,a.d\.

## dissociatioa
dissociatioa, n. — L. dissociatio, gen. -onis,
'separation', fr. dissociatus, pp. of dissociare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## dissogeny
dissogeny, п., reproduction in two different
periods of maturity in the same individual (zool.)
— Lit. 'double reproduction'. See disso- and
-geny.

## dissoluble
dissoluble, adj. — L. dissolubilis, 'that whic' can
be dissolved', from the stem of dissolvere. See
dissolve and cp. solnble.
Derivatives: dissolubil-ity, п., dissoluble-ness, n.

## dissolute
dissolute, adj. — L. dissolutus, pp. of dissolvere.
See dissolve.
Derivatives: dissolute-ly, adv., dissolute-ness, n.

## dissolution
dissolution, n. — L. dissolutio, gen. -onis, 'a
dissolving, destroying, interruption, dissolution',
fr. dissolutus, pp. of dissolvere. See dissolve and
-tion.
Derivative: dissolutton-al, adj.

## dissolvable
dissolvable, adj. — Formed fr. dissolve with suff.
-able. Cp. dissoluble.
Derivatives: dissolvabil-ity, п., dissolvable-ness,
n.

## dissolve
dissolve, tr. and intr. v. — L. dissolvere (pp.
dissolutus), 'to loosen, disunite, dissolve, separate,
abolish, destroy', fr. dis- and solvere, 'to loosen,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:247 COLUMN:3 -->
unlie, dissolve'. See solve and cp. absolve,
resolve.
Derivatives: dissolv-er, п., dissolv-ing, adj.

## dissolveat
dissolveat, adj. and'n. — L. dissolvens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of dissolvere. See prec. word and -ent.

## dissonance
dissonance, n. — F., fr. Late L. dissonantia,
'dissonance', fr. L. dissonans, gen. -amis, pres. part,
of dissonare. See dissonant and -ce and cp. so-
nance and words there referred to.

## dissonant
dissonant, adj. — F., fr. L. dissonantem, асе. of
dissonans, pres. part, of dissonare, 'to disagree in
sound; to disagree, differ', fr. dis- and sondre,
'to sound'. See sonant and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivative: dissonant-ly, adv.

## dissuade
dissuade, tr. v. — L. dissuadere, 'to advise against,
oppose by argument, dissuade', fr. dis- and
suadire, 'to advise, recommend, persuade'. See
suasion and cp. assuage, persuade.

## dissuasion
dissuasion, n. — L. dissuasion gen. -onis, 'an
advice to the contrary', fr. dissuasus, pp. of
dissuadere. See prec. word and -ion.

## dissuasive
dissuasive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
dissuasus, pp. of dissuadere. See dissuade.
Derivatives: dissuasive-ty, adv., dissuasive-
ness, n.

## dissyllabic
dissyllabic, adj., having two syllables. — F. dis-
syllabique, formed with suff. -que fr. L. disyl-
labus, 'dissyllabic', fr. Gk. δισύλλαβος, fr. δι-
(see di-, 'two'), and συλλαβή, 'syllable*. See
syllable and cp. syllabic. Cp. also disyllabic, which
is the etymologically correct spelling.
Derivative: dissyllbbic-al-ly, adv.

## dissyllable
dissyllable, п., a word consisting of two
syllables. — Formed fr. di-, 'two', and syllable.
See prec. word.

## dissymmetric
dissymmetric, dissymmetrical, adj., 1)
asymmetrical; 2) symmetrical in opposite directions. —
Formed fr. dis- and symmetric, resp. symmetrical.

## dissymmetry
dissymmetry, п., I) absence of symmetry,
asymmetry; 2) symmetry in opposite directions. —
Formed fr. dis- and symmetry.

## distaff
distaff, n. — ME. distaf, dysestaf, fr. OE. distxf,
a compound lit. meaning 'a bedizened staff.*
The first element of this compound is rel. to
MLG. dise, LG. diesse, 'a bunch of flax on a
distaff', and to E. dizen, bedizen. The second
element is identical with OE. stxf, 'staff'. See
staff.

## distain
distain, tr. v. — ME. disteinen, fr. OF. disteindre
(F. deteindre), 'to take the color out of, fr. VL.
*disiingere, fr. dis- and L. lingere, '10 dye'. Cp.
It. stingere, Sp. destenir, and see tinge. Cp. also
stain, which is a doublet of distain.

## distal
distal, adj., remote from the center of the body
(anat.) — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. di-
stare, 'to stand apart', on analogy of words like
central, proximal, etc. See distant.
Derivative: distal-ly, adv.

## distance
distance, n. — F., fr. L. distantia, 'distance,
remoteness', fr. distorts, gen. -aittis. See distant
and -ce.
Derivative: distance, tr. v.

## distant
distant, adj. — F., fr. L. distantem, ace. of distdns,
pres. part, of distare, 'to stand apart, be remote,
separate or distant', fr. di- 'apart', and stare,
'to stand'. See state and -ant and cp. distal,
equidistant
Derivatives: distant-ly, adv., distant-ness, n.

## distemper
distemper, tr. v., to disturb. — OF. destemprer,
'to put out of order*, fr. ML. distemperare, of
s.m., fr. dis- (in the privative sense of this
prefix), and L. temperare, 'to mingle in due
proportion, combine properly, moderate, regulate',
fr. tempus, gen. temporis, 'time'. See temper and
cp. distemper, 'to coat with distemper'.
Derivative: distemper, п., disorder.

## distemper
distemper, tr. v., to coat with distemper
(painting). — OF. destemprer, later, with metathesis,
destremperr 'to mix' (whence F. detremper, 'to
dilute, dissolve, moisten, weaken, soften'), fr.
ML. distemperare, 'to mingle in exact
proportion', fr. dis- (in the sense 'completely') and L.
temperare. See distemper, 'to disturb', and cp.
tempera. Cp. also distemper, 'to disturb'.
Derivatives: distemper, a method of painting,
tempera, distemper-er, n.

## distend
distend, tr. v., to expand. — L. distendere, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:248 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 221 | D1TT0L0GY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:248 COLUMN:1 -->
stretch out, swell out, extend', fr. dis- and ten-
dere, 'to stretch'. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: distend-er, n.

## distensible
distensible, adj. — Formed with suff. -ible fr.
Late L. distinsus, a collateral form of L. dis-
tenlus, pp. of distendere. See prec. word.
Derivative: deslensibil-ily, n.

## distension
distension, п., the same as distention. — Late L.
dislensio, gen. -onis, fr. distgnsus, collateral form
of L. distentus, pp. of distendere. See distention
and cp. distensible.

## distention
distention, п., expansion. — L. distentio, gen.
-onis, 'a stretching out', fr. distentus, pp. of
distendere. See distend and -ion and cp. distension.

## disthene
disthene, п., cyanite (mineral.) — F. disthine, lit.
'having two forces', fr. Gk. Si- (see di-, 'two')
and σθένος, 'strength' (see sthenin); so called in
allusion to its different electrical properties in
two different directions.

## distich
distich, п., a group of two lines (pros.) — L. di-
stichon, fr. Gk. 81στιχον, neut. of δίστιχος, 'of
two rows, two-ranked', fr. Si- (see di-, 'two')
and στίχος, 'order, row, line, rank; verse',
which is rel. to στείχειν, 'to go, march in order'.
See acrostic and cp. words there referred to.

## Distichlis
Distichlis, п., a genus of grasses, the spike grass
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δίστιχος, 'of two
rows, two-ranked'. See prec. word.

## distichous
distichous, adj., arranged in two rows (hot.) — L.
distichus, fr. Gk. δίστιχος, 'of two rows*. See
distich. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος,
L. -us, see -ous.
Derivative: distichous-ly, adv.

## distill
distill, distil, tr. and intr. v. — OF. (= F.)
distiller, fr. L. distillSre, later distlllare, 'to drip,
trickle down, distill', fr. de-, resp. di-, 'apart'
and stillare, 'to drop, trickle', fr. slilla, 'drop'.
See still, 'to distill', and cp. still, 'vessel'. Cp.
also instill.
Derivatives: dislill-able, adj., distillate (q.v.),
distillation (q.v.), distill-atory, adj., distill-ed,
adj., distill-er, п., distill-ery, п., distill-ing, n.

## distillate
distillate, п., a product of distillation. — L.
distillatus, distillatus, pp. of destillare, distillare, 'to
drip down'. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.

## distillation
distillation, n. — F., fr. Late L. distillationem,
ace. of distillatio, fr. L. distillatus, pp. of
distillare. See distill and -ation.

## distinct
distinct, adj. — L. distinctus, 'separate, distinct,
decorated, adorned', pp. of distinguere. See
distinguish and cp. contradistinct. Cp. also F.
distinct, which also derives fr. L. distinctus.
Derivatives: distinct-ive, adj., distinct-ive-ly,
adv., distinct-ive-ness, п., distinct-ly, adv.,
distinctness, n.

## distinction
distinction, n. — F., fr. L. distinctionem, ace. of
distinctio, 'separation, division, distinction,
discrimination', fr. distinctus, pp. of distinguere.
See prec. word and -ion.

## distingue
distingue, adj., having an air of distinction. — F.,
'distinguished', pp. of distinguer, fr. L.
distinguere. See distinguish.

## distinguish
distinguish, tr. and intr. v. — Formed with verbal
suff. -ish fr. L. distinguere, 'to separate,
distinguish, discriminate; 10 decorate, adorn; to mark
by pauses, punctuate' (gram.), fr. dis- and I.-E.
base *steig-, 'to prick, stick, pierce', whence
also L. instinguere, 'to incite, impel', Instigare,
'to goad'. See stick, v., and cp. words there
referred to. The suff. -ish in the verb distinguish
(as well as in extinguish, admonish, astonish) is
due to the influence of the numerous verbs in
which this suff. is the equivalent of OF. and
F. -iss-, and ultimately goes back to the Latin
inchoative suff. -fscere; see verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: distinguish-able, adj., distinguish-
abU-ity, п., dislinguish-able-ness, п., dislinguish-
abl-y, adv., distinguish-ed, adj., distinguish-ed-
ly, adv., distinguish-er, п., distinguish-ing, adj.,
distinguish-ing-ly, adv.

## distort
distort, tr. v. — L. distortus, pp. of distorqulre,
'to turn different ways, twist, distort', fr. dis-
and torquire, 'to turn, twist, bend'. See torque
and cp. contort, extort, retort.
Derivatives: dislorl-ed, adj., distort-ed-ly, adv.,
dislorl-ed-ness, п., distort-er, n.

## distortion
distortion, n. — L. distortio, gen. -onis, 'a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:248 COLUMN:2 -->
distorting, distortion', fr. distonus, pp. of distorquire.
See distort and -ion.
Derivatives: dislortion-al, adj., distortionist(q.v.)

## distortionist
distortionist, п., an acrobat who twists his body.
— See distortion and -ist and cp. contortionist.

## distract
distract, tr. v. — L. distractus, pp. of distrahere,
'to pull apart, separate by force, tear to pieces;
to perplex, distract', fr. dis- and trahere, 'to
draw, pull'. See tract, 'region', and words there
referred to and cp. esp. distrait, distraught,
stress, 'refuse of silk'.
Derivatives: distract-ed, adj., dislract-ed-ly,
adv., distract-er, n.,distract-ible, adj., distract-
ibil-ity, п., distract-ing-ly, adv., distraction (cp.v.),
distract-ive, adj., distract-ive-ly, adv.

## distraction
distraction, n. — L. distractio, gen. -onis, 'a
pulling apart, separating', fr. distractus, pp. of
distrahere. See distract and -ion.

## distrain
distrain, intr. v., to levy a distress upon (law). —
ME. distreinen, fr. OF. destraindre, fr. L. di-
stringere, 'to draw asunder, stretch out; engage,
detain', fr. di-, 'apart', and stringere, 'to draw
tight, to draw, bind or press together'. See
stringent and cp. strain, v. Cp. also distress,
district.
Derivatives: distrain-ee, п., distrain-ment, п.,
distrain-or, п., distraint (q.v.)

## distraint
distraint, п., the act of distraining. — OF. des-
trainte, prop. fern. pp. of destraindre. See prec.
word.

## distrait
distrait, adj., absent-minded. — F., fr. L.
distractus, pp. of distrahere. See distract and cp.
next word.

## distraught
distraught, adj., perplexed, bewildered: — ME.
distrauhte, altered fr. distract, fr. L. distractus.
See prec. word.

## distress
distress, n. — ME. destress, distresse, fr. OF. de-
strece, destrecce (F. detresse), fr. VL. "districtia,
'narrowness, distress*, fr. L. districtus, pp. of
distringere. See distrain, and cp. district. Cp. also
OProvenc. destreissa, 'distress', which is of the
same origin.
Derivatives: disiress-fui, adj., distress-ful-ly,
adv., distress-ful-ness, n.

## distress
distress, tr. v. — OF. destresser, fr. VL. *distric-
tiare, fr. *districtia, 'distress'. See distress, n.
Derivatives: distress-ed, adj., distress-ed-ly, adv.
distress-ed-ness, n.

## distributable
distributable, adj. — Irregularly formed fr. L.
distributus, pp. of distribuere. (The suff. -able
should be added to the Latin present stem—
and not to the past participle stem—of the
respective verb.) See next word.

## distribute
distribute, tr. and intr. v. — L. distributus, pp. of
distribuere, 'to divide, distribute', fr. dis- and
tribuere, 'to assign, allot, bestow, give, grant'.
See tribute and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: distributable (q.v.)' distribut-ed,
adj., distribut-ed-ly, adv., distribut-er, п.,
distribution (q.v.), distributive (q.v.)

## distribution
distribution, n. — F„ fr. L. distributionem, ace. of
distributio, 'a division, distribution*, fr.
distributus, pp. of distribuere. See prec. word and
-ion.
Derivative: distribution-al, adj.

## distributive
distributive, adj. — F. distributif (fern,
distributive), fr. Late L. distributive, 'apportioning,
distributive', fr. L. distributus, pp. of distribuere.
See distribnte and -ive.
Derivatives: distributive-ly, adv., distributive-
ness, n.

## distributor
distributor, n. — L., fr. distributus, pp. of
distribuere. See distribnte and agential suff. -or,

## district
district, n. — ML. districtus, prop. pp. of L. di-
«/vn£ere,'to draw asunder, stretchout ;toengage,
detain', fr. di-, 'apart', and stringere, 'to draw'.
See distrain and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: district, tr. v.

## distrophy
distrophy, п., defective nutrition (med.) —
Medical L. dislrophia, fr. dys- and Gk. τροφή,
'nourishment'. See -trophy.

## distrust
distrust, n. — A hybrid coined fr. L. dis-, 'apart'
(see dis-) and trust, a word of Scand. origin.
The etymologically correct form is mistrust, in
which both elements are Teutonic.
Derivatives: distrust, tr. v., distrust-ful, adj.,
distrust-ful-ly, adv., distrust-ful-ness, n.

## disturb
disturb, tr. v. — ME. destorben, destourben, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:248 COLUMN:3 -->
OF. destorber, desturber, destourber, fr. L. dis-
turbare. Ίο drive asunder, separate by violence,
disturb, frustrate', fr. dis- and turbare, 'to
confuse, bewilder', fr. turba, 'uproar, confusion,
crowd'. See turbid and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: disturbance (q.v.), disturb-er, п.,
disturb- ing-ly, adv.

## disturbance
disturbance, n. — OF. destorbance, desturbance,
fr. destorber, desturber. See prec. word and
-aace.

## disulfate
disulfate, also spelled disulphate, п., ι) a salt ol
disulfuric acid; 2) a bisulfate (chem.) — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. Si- fsee di-, 'two') and L.
sulpur, sulphur, sulfur. See sulfate.

## disulfide
disulfide, also spelled disulphide, п., a compound
in which two atoms of sulfur are united with
another element or radical (chem.) — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. Si-, (see di-, 'two') and L. sulpur,
sulphur, sulfur. See di-, 'two', and sulfide.

## disuse
disuse, tr. v. — Formed on analogy of OF. des-
user, fr. dis- and the verb use. Cp. misuse, v.

## disuse
disuse, n. — Formed fr. dis- and the noun use.
Cp. misuse, n.

## disyllabic
disyllabic, adj. — The etymologically correct
spelling for dissyllabic (q.v.)

## disyllable
disyllable, n. —The etymologically correct
spelling for dissyllable (q.v.)

## dital
dital, п., a fingerkey by which, in a harp guitar,
the pitch can be raised a semitone (music). —
Formed with suff. -al fr. It. dito, 'finger', fr. L.
digitus. See digit and cp. digital.

## ditch
ditch, n. — ME. dich, fr. OE. die, rel. to ON.
diki, 'dike, ditch', OS., OFris., MLG, dik, MDu.
dijc, Du. dijk, MHG. dich, G. Deich, 'dike',
MHG. tich, G. Teich, 'pond' (F. digue, 'dike,
dam', is a Dutch loan word). These words prob.
meant orig. 'something cut out', and derive fr.
I.-E. base *dheig-, 'to cut out', whence also L.
fTgere, 'to fix, fasten, drive in', Lith. diegiu,
diegti, Lett, diegt, 'to prick, sting', Lith. dygstu,
dygti, Lett, digt, 'to sprout, germ', Lith. dygiis,
'pointed', dyglys, 'thorn', OPruss. deicktas,
'place', orig. 'point' (for sense development cp.
point) See dike, which is a doublet of ditch.
See also dig, finis, fix.
Derivatives: ditch, tr. and intr. v., ditch-er, п.,
ditch-ing, n.

## ditheism
ditheism, п., belief in the existence of two gods.
— Formed fr. di-, 'two', and theism.

## dithionic
dithionic, adj., pertaining to a compound that
contains two atoms of sulfur (chem.) — Formed
fr. di-, 'two', and Gk. θείον, 'sulfur'. See thio-
and -ic and cp. thionlc.

## dithyramb
dithyramb, п., ι) in ancient Greece, a song in
honor of Bacchus; 2) any wildly emotional
song. — L. dithyrambus, fr. Gk. δϊ&ύραμβος,
'poem in honor of Bacchus', a loan word of
pre-Hellenic origin. Cp. triumph. Cp. also iamb.
Derivative: dithyramb-ic, adj.

## ditriglyph
ditriglyph, п., a space between two columns of
the Doric style (archit.) — Formed fr. di-, 'two',
and triglyph.

## ditrochee
ditrochee, п., a double trochee (pros.) — L. dt-
trochaeus, fr. Gk. 8ιτροχαιος, 'a double
trochee', fr. Si- (see di-, 'double') and τροχαίος,
'trochee'. See trochee.

## dittamy
dittamy, n. — The same as dittany (q.v.)

## dittander
dittander, п., I) the Cretan dittany; 2) the
European pepperwort. — See next word.

## dittany
dittany, п., an aromatic plant (bot.) — ME. de-
tane, detany, fr. OF. ditain, ditame, dictam(m)e
(F.dictame), fr. L. dictamnum, fr. Gk. 8ίκταμνον,
which derives perh. fr. Δίκτη, name of a
mountain in Crete. Cp. Dictamnus, dittamy,
dittander.

## ditto
ditto, п., the same (lit. the foresaid). — It., form
used in Tuscany for literary It. detto, 'that which
has been said (before)', pp. of dire, 'to say', fr.
L. dicere, 'to say'. See diction and cp. dictum.

## dittography
dittography, п., the unintentional repetition of a
letter or letters in writing. — Compounded of
Gk. Si-ιτος, Att. var. of 8ισσός, 'double,
twofold', and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. For
the first element see disso- and cp. words there
referred to, for the second see -graphy.
Derivative: dittograph-ic, adj.

## dittology
dittology, п., a twofold reading or interpretation.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:249 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DITTY | 222 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:249 COLUMN:1 -->
— Compounded of Gk. διττός, 'double,
twofold', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See prec. word and -logy.

## ditty
ditty, п., a short song. — ME. dite, ditee, fr. OF.
ditie, dite, fr. L. dictatum, 'anything dictated',
prop. neut. pp. of dictare, 'to say often,
pronounce repeatedly', freq. of dicere (pp. dictus),
'to say'. See diction and cp. dictate, dight.
Derivative: ditty, tr. and intr. v.

## diuresis
diuresis, п., excessive excretion of urine (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. *διουρησις, 'urination', fr.
διουρεΐν, 'to pass urine', fr. δ4ά, 'through', and
ούρεΐν, 'to make water', fr. ουρον, 'urine'. See
dia-, uriue and -esis, and cp. next word.

## diuretic
diuretic, adj., increasing, or tending to increase
the secretion of urine. — Late L. dureticus, fr.
Gk. διουρητικός, 'pertaining to urine', fr.
διουρεΰν, 'to pass urine'. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: diuretic, п., a diuretic drug, diu-
retic-al-ly, adv., diuretic-al-ness, n.

## diurnal
diurnal, adj., daily. — L. diurnalis, 'diurnal', fr.
diurnus, 'daily', which is formed fr. di-(es), 'day',
with -urnus, an adj. suff. denoting time. This
suffix is a contraction of orig. 'ri-nos, which
derives fr. Gk. -ρινός, a suff. of the same
meaning. (Cp. e.g. Gk. χειμερινός = L. hibernus,
'wintry'.) See dies поп and adj. suff. -al and cp.
next word. Cp. also journal, which is a doublet
of diurnal. Cp. also journey, adjourn, sojourn.
For the suff. cp. nocturnal, modern.
Derivatives: diurnal-ly, adv., diurnal-ness, n.

## diutuntal
diutuntal, adj., of long duration. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. diuturnus, 'of long duration,
lasting' (on analogy of diurnus, 'daily'), fr. diu,
'by day; a long time, a long while', which is rel.
to dies, 'day'. See dies поп. For the suff. see
prec. word.

## diuturnity
diuturnity, п., long duration. — L. diuturnitas, fr.
diuturnus. See prec. word and -ity.

## diva
diva, п., a prima donna. — It., fr. L. diva, 'a
goddess', fern, of divus, 'divine'. See divine.

## divagate
divagate, intr. v., to wander about. — L. diva-
gatus, pp. oidivagari, 'to wander about', fr. di-,
'apart', and vagari, 'to wander, ramble'. See
vagary and verbal suff. -ate.

## divagation
divagation, п., a wandering about. — L. diva-
gatus, pp. of divagdri. See prec. word and -ion.

## divalence
divalence, п., bivalence (chem.) — Formed from
next word with suff. -ce.

## divalent
divalent, adj., bivalent (chem.) — A hybrid coined
fr. Gk. Si-, 'two, double', and L. vallns, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of valere, 'to have power'. See
di-, 'two', and -valent. The correct form of the
word is bivalent, in which both elements are of
Latin origin.

## divan
divan, п., ι) in Oriental countries, a council of
state; 2) a court of justice; 3) a large low sofa.
— Turk, diwan, fr. Pers. diwan, 'a royal court;
a council of state*, whence on the one hand, 'a
convenient seat, couch', and on the other 'a
register, an account book; a col lection of poems'
(whence also Arab, diwan. It. divano, F. divan,
etc.); rel. to Pers. debir, dibir, 'writer'. Cp. de-
wan, dewanee, diwaa, douane, aduana.

## divaricate
divaricate, intr. and tr. v., to branch, diverge. —
L. divaricatus, pp. of divaricare, 'to stretch
apart, spread asunder', fr. di-, 'apart', and vari-
care, 'to spread the legs apart, to straddle', fr.
varicus, 'with bent feet, with feet spread apart,
straddling', fr. varus, 'bent, knock-kneed', fr.
I.-E. base *wS-, 'to bend, turn, twist', whe;._e
also L. varius, 'different, changing, varying,
various'. See various and verbal suff. -ate and
cp. prevaricate.

## divaricate
divaricate, adj., divergent. — L. divaricatus, pp.
of divaricare. See divaricate, v.
Derivatives: divaricate-ly, adv., divaricate-ness,
п., divaricat-ion, п., divaricat-or, n.

## dive
dive, intr. v. — ME. diven, duven, fr. OE. dyfan,
'to immerse', a weak transitive verb, causative
of OE. diifan, a strong intransitive verb meaning
'to sink, plunge, dive'; rel. to ON. dyfa, 'to dip',
and to E. dip, deep, dove (qq.v.)
Derivatives: dive, п., div-er, n.

## diverge
diverge, intr. v., to move or be in different
directions. — ModL. divergere, 'to go in different
directions, to separate', fr. di- and L. vergere.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:249 COLUMN:2 -->
'to bend, incline, turn'. See verge, 'to bend',
and cp. converge.
Derivatives: divergence, divergent (qq.v.),
diverging, adj., diverg-ing-iy, adv.

## divergence
divergence, divergency, n. — ModL. divergentia,
fr. divergent, gen. -eniis. See next word and -ce
resp. -cy.

## divergent
divergent, adj. — ModL. divergens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of divergere. See diverge and -ent and
cp. F. divergent.
Derivative: divergent-ly, adv.

## divers
divers, adj. — ME. divers, diverse, fr. OF (= F.)
divers, fr. L. diversus, 'different, opposite,
contrary, various', pp. of divertere, 'to turn or go
in different ways'. See divert.

## diverse
diverse, adj. — A var. of prec. word.
Derivatives: diverse-ly, adv., diverse-ness, n.

## diversification
diversification, n. — See diversify and -ation.

## diversiform
diversiform, adj., differing in form. — Formed
fr. L. diversus, 'different', and forma, 'form,
shape'. See diverse and form, n.

## diversify
diversify, tr. v., to give variety to. — F. diversifier,
lit. 'to make diverse', fr. ML. diversificare,
which was formed fr. L. diversus, 'different' and
-ficSre, fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See diverse
and -fy.
Derivatives: diversifi-ed, adj., diversifi-er, n.

## diversion
diversion, n. — ML. dhersio, gen. -onis, fr. L.
diversus, pp. of divertere. See divert and -ion.
Derivative: diversion-al, adj.

## diversity
diversity, n. — OF. diversite (F. diversite), fr. L.
diversitatem, ace. of diversitas, 'difference,
contrariety, contradiction', fr. diversus, 'different'.
See diverse and -ity.

## divert
divert, tr. v. — ME. divenen, fr. OF. (= F.) di-
vertir, fr. L. divertere, 'to turn or go in different
ways, part, separate', fr. di-, 'apart', and vertere,
'to turn'. See version and cp. divorce.
Derivatives: divert-ing, adj., divert-ing-ly, adv.,
divert-ing-ness, n.

## diverticulum
diverticulum, п., a blind process of the intestinal
Canal (anat.) — L. diverticulum, diverticulum,
'byroad, bypass', fr. devertere, divertere, 'to turn
away, turn aside (something)', fr. de-, resp. di-,
'apart', and vertere, 'to turn'. See divert.
Derivatives: diverticul-ar, diverticui-ate, di-
verticul-ated, adjs.

## Dives
Dives, п., the rich man in the parable Luke
16: [9-31. — L. dives, 'rich', rel. to divus,
'divine'. Dives orig. meant 'favored by the gods'.
For sense development cp. OSlav. bogatu,
'rich', fr. bogu, 'god'. See divine and cp. Dis.

## divest
divest, tr. v., to deprive. — Fr. earlier devest, fr.
OF. desvestir (F. devetir), fr. ML. disvestire, di-
vestire, fr. dis-, and L. vestire, 'to clothe', fr.
vestis, 'garment'. See vest and cp. devest, invest.
Derivatives: divestiture (q.v.), divest-'ment, n.

## divestiture
divestiture, n. — Formed fr. divest on analogy of
investiture.

## divide
divide, tr. and intr. v. — ME. deviden, dividen,
fr. L. dividere, 'to force apart, separate, divide',
fr. di-, 'apart', and I.-E. base *widh-, 'to
separate', whence also L. vidua, Goth, widuwo, OE.
widewe, 'widow'. See widow and cp. divisi,
division; device, devise, individual. I.-E. base *widh-
is probably compounded of base *wi-, 'apart,
asunder', and base *dhl-, 'to place7. Accordingly
base *widh-, lit. means 'to place apart'. See
with and do, v.
Derivatives: divide, п., divid-ed, adj., divid-ed-
ly, adv., divid-ed-ness, п., dividend (q.v.),
divider, п., divid-ing-ly, adv.

## dividend
dividend, n. — F. dividende, fr. L. dividendum,
'that which is to be divided', neut. of dividendus,
gerundive of dividere, 'to divide'. See divide. For
other Latin gerundives used in English cp.
agenda and words there referred to.

## divi-divi
divi-divi, п., a small tree of S. America and W7
India (Caesalpinia coridria). — Sp. dividivi, from
native name.

## dividual
dividual, adj., separate, divisible. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. dividuus, 'separate, divisible',
fr. dividere, 'to divide'. See divide and cp.
individual.
Derivative: dividual-ly, adv.

## divination
divination, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. divinatidnem,
ace. of divinatid, 'the power of foreseeing,
divination, prediction', fr. divinatus, pp. oidivinare.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:249 COLUMN:3 -->
See divine, v., and -ation.

## divine
divine, adj. — ME. devine, divine^ fr. OF. devin,
fr. L. divinus, 'pertaining to a deity' (whence
also It., Sp. divino, Provenc. devin. Port, adi-
vinho), fr. OL. deivinus, fr. deivos (whence L.
deus), 'a god'. See deity.
Derivatives: divine, n. (q.v.), divine-ly, adv.,
divine-ness, n.

## divine
divine, n. — OF. (= F.) devin, soothsayer', fr.
VL. 'divinus, dissimilated fr. L. divinus,
'divine'. See divine, adj.

## divine
divine, tr. and intr. v. — ME. divinen, devinen,
fr. OF. (= F.) deviner, fr. VL. "devinare,
dissimilated fr. VL. divinare, 'to foresee, foretell,
divine', lit. 'to be inspired by a god', fr. L. divinus,
'divine'. Cp. OProven?. devinar, endevinar, It.
indovinare, Sp. adivinar, 'to foretell, divine,
guess', and see divine, adj.
Derivatives: diviner (q.v), divin-ing, n.

## diviner
diviner, n. — ME. devinour, fr. OF. devineor, fr.
L. divinatdrem, ace. of divinator, 'soothsayer,
diviner', fr. divinatus, pp. oidivinare. See divine,
v., and agential suff. -or.

## divinity
divinity, n. — OF. devinite (F. divinite), fr. VL.
*devinitatem, ace. of *devinitas, formed with
vowel dissimilation fr. L. divinitas, 'godhead,
divinity', fr. divinus. See divine, adj., and -irj
and cp. deity.

## divinize
divinize, tr. v., to deify. — F. dmniser, fr. L.
divinus, 'divine'. See divine, adj., and -ize.
Derivative: diviniz-ation, n.

## divisi
divisi, adj., a direction for the players to divide
themselves into two groups (music). — It., pi.
of diviso, 'divided', fr. L. divisus, pp. of dividere.
See divide.

## divisible
divisible, adj. — Late L. divisibilis, fr. L. divisus,
pp. of dividere. See divide and -ible.
Derivatives: divisibil-ity, п., divisible, п., divis-
ible-ness, п., divisibl-y, adv.

## division
division, n. — ME. devisioun, divisioun, fr. OF.
devisiun, division (F. division), fr. L. divisionem,
ace. of divisio, 'a division, separation', fr.
divisus, pp. of dividere. See divide and -ion.
Derivatives: division-al, adj., division-al-ly, adv.,
division-ary, adj.

## divisive
divisive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
divisus, pp. of dividere. See divide.
Derivatives: divisive-ly, adv., divisive-ness, n.

## divisor
divisor, n. — L. divisor, 'divider', fr. divisus, pp.
of dividere. See divide and agential suff. -or.

## divorce
divorce, n. — ME., fr. F. divorce, fr. L. divortium,
'a separation, dissolution of marriage, divorce',
fr. divortere, divertere, 'to turn different ways'.
See divert.

## divorce
divorce, tr. v. — F. divorcer, fr. divorce. See
divorce, n.
Derivatives: divorce-able, adj., divorc-ee, п.,
divorce-ment, п., divorc-er, п., divorc-ive, adj.

## divot
divot, п., a piece of turf cut out with the club
in making a stroke. — Of uncertain origin.

## divulgate
divulgate, tr. v., to make public. — L. divulgatus,
pp. of divulgare. See divulge and verbal suff.
-ate.

## divulgation
divulgation, n. — Late L. dlvulgatio, gen. -unis,
'a publishing', fr. L. divulgatus, pp. of divulgare.
See next word and -ation.

## divalge
divalge, tr. v., to make known; to disclose. — L.
divulgare, 'to spread among the people, publish,
make known', formed fr. di-, 'apart, asunder',
and vulgare, 'to make known, spread abroad',
fr. vulgus, 'the great mass, the multitude,
people'. See vulgus.
Derivatives: divulge-ment, п., divulg-ence, п.,
divulg-er, n.

## diwan
diwan, n. — A var. of dewan.

## diwaai
diwaai, n. — A var. of dewaaee.

## dixie
dixie, also dixy, п., a kind of mess tin (slang). —
Hind, degchi, 'a small kettle', fr. Pers. degcha,
dimin. of deg, 'pot', which is rel. to Pahlavi dig,
'pot', Arm. dez, 'heap', and to OI. dihmi, Ί
smear, anoint', fr. I.-E. base *dheigh-, *dhoigh-,
*dhigh-, 'to form out of clay, to knead, form'.
See dough and cp. next word.

## dizdar
dizdar, disdar, п., the warden of a castle. — Pers.
dizdar, 'holder of a castle', fr. diz, 'castle', and
-dar, 'holder, possessor'. The first element is
rel. to OPers. dida, 'castle', Avestic daeza,
'wall', Arm. dez, 'heap'; see prec. word and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:250 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 223 | DOG -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:250 COLUMN:1 -->
the second element in paradise. For the second
element see numUdar and ср.- words there
referred to.

## dizen
dizen, tr. v., 1) to put flax on a distaff (obsoh);
2) to bedizen. — ME. disen, fr. MLG. dise, 'a
bunch of flax on a distaff'. See distaff and cp.
bedizen.

## dizzy
dizzy, adj. — ME. dust, disi, fr. OE. dysig,
'foolish', rel. to LG. dlisig, 'dizzy', dusel, 'dizziness',
Du. duizelen, 'to be dizzy', duizelig, 'dizzy',
OHG. dusig, tusig, MHG. dusec, 'foolish',
MLG. dare, MDu. dor, MHG. tore, 'fool, deaf
person', G. Tor, 'fool', OE. dwxs, MLG. dwas,
Du. dwaas, 'foolish'. All these words prob.
derive fr. I.-E. base "dhewis-, *dhwis-, 'to breathe,
smoke', whence also L.furere, 'to rage, be mad'.
See fury and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also doze.
Derivatives: dizzy, tr. v., dizzi-ly, adv.,
dizziness, n.

## dp
dp, tr., intr. and auxil. v. — ME. don, fr. OE. don,
rel. to OS. duan, OFris. dua, ODu. duon, Oa.doen,
OHG., MHG. won, G. tun, 'to do", fr. WTeut.
base *do-,tto do', orig. 'to put, place',
corresponding to I.-E. base *dho-, *dhe-, *dh'-, 'to put,
place; to do, make', whence also OI. dadhati,
'puts, places', dhitih, 'the act of placing', dha-
tar-, 'creator', dhatar-, 'founder, originator',
Tech. A ?a-, tas-, tits-, В tes-, 'to place', Hitt.
dai-, te-, 'to place', tehhi, Ί place', Arm. dnem,
"I place', aor. ed, 'he placed', Gk. τι&έναι, 'to
put, place, set', θέσις, 'a placing, setting', δήκη,
'case in which to put something', Э-έμα, 'that
which is placed', θέμις, 'right, decree', 8-εσμός,
'law, rule, precept', lit. 'that which is laid down',
θημών, θωμός, 'heap', θέμεθλα (pi.), Homeric
θεμείλια (pi.), 'foundation', L. facere, 'to make,
do', -dere in ab-dere, 'to hide, conceal', con-dere,
'to found, establish', per-dere, 'to lose, throw
away, ruin', OSlav. dejp, deti, 'to place, lay',
Lith. deti, Lett, del, 'to place, put', OSlav.
o-dinu, 'clothed, dressed', Gael, dede, 'placed'.
Cp. ado, deed, deem, doff, -dom, don, v., doom,
dout, dup. Cp. also theme and words there
referred to. Cp. also fact and words there
referred to. Cp. also abdomen, abscond, condiment,
Census, dagoba, dam, 'an earthbank', family,
fetinl, hoard, perdition, recondite, sacerdotal,
samadh, samadhi, sconce, 'a metal bracket',
stridhann. Cp. also the second element in creed
and in jubilate, and the third element in divide
and in Ormazd.
Derivatives: do, п., do-able, adj., do-er, п.,
doing, n.

## do
do, п., a syllable used in solmization to denote
the first tone of the diatonic scale (mus.).

## doab
doab, п., a track of land between two rivers in
India. — Pers.-Hind. doab, lit. 'two waters', fr.
do, 'two', and ab, 'water'. The first element is
rel. to OI. dvau, dva, Avestic dva, 'two'; see
two. The second element is rel. to OI. dpah,
apah, Avestic dp-, 'water'; see amnlc.

## doat
doat, v. — See dote.

## dobbin
dobbin, п., name for a farm horse. — Fr. PN.
Dobbin, dimin. of Dob, a variant of Rob, which
is a dimin. of Robert (q.v.)

## doblon
doblon, п., an obsolete Spanish gold coin. — Sp.
doblon. See doubloon.

## dobra
dobra, п., any of several former Portuguese coins.
— Port, dobra, lit. 'double', fr. dobrar, 'to
double', fr. L. dupldre, 'to double' (see
double, v.); so called because it was orig. the double
of the Johannes,

## dobson
dobson, п., the hellgrammite. — Of uncertain
origin.

## docent
docent, adj., teaching. — L. docens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, oidocire, 'to teach'. See docile and -ent.

## docent
docent, π., ι) short for privatdocent; 2) lecturer
■ in general. — See prec. word and cp. privnt-
docent.

## Docetae
Docetae, n. pi., a heretical sect (Eccles. hist.) —
Eccles. L., fr. Gk. Δοκηταί. See next word.

## Docetism
Docetism, п., heresy of the Docetae, who held
that the body of Jesus was a phantom (Eccles.
hist.) — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Eccles. L.
Docetae, fr. Gk. Δοκηταί, lit. 'believers', fr.
δοκεΐν, 'to seem, have the appearance of, think,
believe', whence δόξα (for δόκ-σα), 'opinion,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:250 COLUMN:2 -->
glory', δόγμα, 'thai which one thinks true,
opinion, decree'. See dogma.

## doch-an-doris
doch-an-doris, п., a stirrup cup. — Gael, deock-
an-doruis, lil. 'drink of the door', fr. deoch,
'drink', an, 'the', doruis, gen. of dorus, 'door'.
Gael, dorus derives fr. OCelt. *dvorestu-, which
is cogn. with Gk. θύρα, L. fores (pi.), 'door',
OE. dor, 'door, gate'. See door.

## dochmiac
dochmiac, adj., pertaining to the dochmius. —
Gk. δοχμιακός, fr. δόχμιος. See next word.
Derivative: dochmiac-al, adj.

## dochmius
dochmius, п., a foot of five syllables (pros.) —
L., fr. Gk. δάχμιος, lit. 'across, aslant', fr.
δοχμός (prob. assimilated fr. *δαχμός),
'slantwise, sideways'; cogn. with OI. jihmah,
'slanting, slantwise', which prob. stands for zizhma-,
a form assimilated fr. orig. *dizhma-.

## docile
docile, adj. — F., fr. L. docilis, 'easily taught,
docile', fr. docere, 'to teach, inform', orig. 'to
cause somebody to receive something', fr. I.-E.
base *dek-, *dok-, 'to take, receive, accept;
acceptable, becoming, good', whence also L.
decere, 'to be seemly or fitting'. See decent and
words there referred to and cp. esp. docent. For
the ending see suff. -ile.
Derivative: docile-ly, adv.

## docility
docility, n. — F. docilite, fr. L. docilitatem, ace.
of docilitas, fr. docilis. See prec. word and -ity.

## docimasy
docimasy, п., a judicial inquiry into the character
of aspirants for office or citizenship (Greek an-
tiq.) — Gk. δοκιμασία, 'assay, proving,
examination', from the stem of δοκιμάζειν, 'to assay,
prove, test', fr. δόκιμος, 'assayed, proved,
genuine', prop, 'accepted', in gradational
relationship to δέχεσθοιι, 'to take, accept, to receive
hospitably', and cogn. with L. decere, 'to be
seemly or fitting'. See decent and cp. words there
referred to.

## docimology
docimology, п., a treatise on the art of assaying
metals, etc. — Compounded of Gk. δοκιμή, 'a
test' (fr. δόκιμος, 'assayed, proved, genuine'),
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See prec. word and -logy.

## dock
dock, п., enclosure for the repairing and loading
of ships. — MLG. and MDu. docke (whence
Du., Norw. dok, G. Dock). Prob. borrowed fr.
Late 1.. *ductia, 'aqueduct', fr. L. ducere, 'to lead,
conduct'. See duct and cp. douche, conduit.
Derivative: dock, tr. v., to bring (a ship) into
a dock, dock-age, п., dock-er, п., dockize (q.v.)

## dock
dock, п., place for prisoner at his trial in a
criminal court. — Flem. dok, docke, 'cage'.

## dock
dock, п., the common name of various species
of the genus Rumex. — OE. docce, rel. to MDu.
docke-blaederen, G. Dockenblatter, 'dock (the
plant)', and to E. dock, 'fleshy part of a tail'
(q.v.) Cp. the second element in burdock,
hardock.

## dock
dock, п., solid, fleshy part of an animal's tail. —
From an imitative, expressive base, appearing
also in ON. dokkr, 'tail', dokka, 'bundle; girl',
Fris. dok, 'bundle, knot', MLG. docker, Swed.
docka, Dan. dukke, 'doll', OHG. tocka, toccha,
MHG. tocke, of s.m., G. Docke, 'small column,
bundle, skein, doll, smart girl'. Cp. dock, the
plant.

## dock
dock, tr. v., to cut off, curtail. — Fr. prec. word.

## docket
docket, п., a memorandum. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: docket, tr. v.

## dockize
dockize, tr. v., to build docks (in a river or in a
harbor). — A hybrid coined fr. dock, 'enclosure
for ships', and -ize, a suff. of Greek origin.

## Docoglossa
Docoglossa, п., a suborder of marine gastropods,
the limpets (zool.) — ModL., compounded of
Gk. δοκός, 'beam', and γλώσσα, 'longue'; so
called in allusion to the beamlike teeth,
appearing on the lingual ribbon. The first element
is rel. to Gk. δέκεσ&αι, Att. δέχεσ&αι, 'to
take, receive', fr. i.-E. base *dek-, *dok-, 'to
take, receive, accept; acceptable, becoming,
good', whence also L. decere, 'to be seemly or
fitting'; see decent and cp. words there referred
to. For the second element see gloss,
interpretation'.

## doctor
doctor, n. — L. doctor, 'teacher, instructor', fr.
doctus, pp. of docere, 'to teach'. See docile and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:250 COLUMN:3 -->
agential suff. -or and cp. doctrine, document.
Derivatives: doctor, tr. and intr. v., doctor-al,
adj., doctorate (q.v.), doctor-ess, п., doctor-iai,
adj., doctor-ly, adj.

## doctorate
doctorate, n. — ML. doctoralus, fr. L. doctor.
See doctor and subst. suff. -ate.

## doctrinaire
doctrinaire, п., an impractical person; adj.,
impractical. — F., orig. 'adherent of doctrines',
formed fr. doctrine with suff. -aire. See doctrine
and adj. suff. -ary.

## doctrine
doctrine, n. — F., fr. L. doctrina, 'teaching,
instruction', fr. doctor, 'teacher'. See doctor and
subst. suff. -ine (representing L. -Tna). Cp.
indoctrinate.
Derivatives: doctrinaire (q.v.), doctrin-al, adj.,
doctrin-al-ly, adv., doctrin-ar-ian, adj., doctrin-
ar-ian-ism, п., doctrin-ar-ian-ist, п., doctrin-ary,
adj., doctrin-ari-ly, adv., doctrinar-ity, п., doc-
trin-ism, п., doctrin-ist, n.

## document
document, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. documentum,
'lesson, example, pattern, proof, fr. docere, 'to
teach'. See docile and -ment and cp. doctor,
doctriae.
Derivatives: documeni-al, adj., document-ary,
adj., document-ari-ly, adv., documentation (q.v.)

## documentation
documentation, n. — Late L. documentatio, gen.
-onis, fr. L. documentum. See prec. word and
-ation.

## dodder
dodder, п., any of the parasitic plants of the
genus Cuscuta. — ME. doder, rel. to MLG.
doder, dodder, 'dodder', OS. dodro, 'yolk', OE.
dydring, Du. dooier, OHG. totoro, MHG. toter,
tuter, G. Doner, 'yolk', and prob. also to next
word. The dodder was prob. named from the
color of its flower clusters which resembles that
of yolk.

## dodder
dodder, intr. v., to shake, quaver. — Rel. to dial.
Norw. dudra, 'to quaver'. Cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: dodder-er, п., dodder-y, adj.

## doddered
doddered, adj., having lost the branches through
age or decay. — Prob. from dial, dod, 'to poll',
fr. ME. dodden.

## dodeca-
dodeca-, before a vowel dodec-, pref. meaning
'twelve'. — Fr. Gk. δώδεκα, 'twelve', shortened
fr. δυώδεκα, fr. δύο, 'two', and δέκα, 'ten'; cp.
OI. dvadasa, Avestic dvadasa-, L. duodecim,
Umbr. desenduf, 'twelve'. See dual and deca-
and cp. duodecim-.

## dodecagon
dodecagon, п., a plane figure with twelve angles
and twelve sides (geom.) — Gk. δωδεκαγωνον,
lit. 'having twelve angles', fr. δώδεκα, 'twelve',
and γωνιά, 'corner, angle'. See dodeca- and
-gon.

## dodecahedron
dodecahedron, п., a solid figure with twelve faces
(geom.) — Gk. δωδεκάεδρον, lit. 'having twelve
faces', fr. δώδεκα, 'twelve', and εδρδ, 'seat,
chair, bench; side, face'. See dodeca- and
-hedral.

## dodecasyllabic
dodecasyllabic, adj., having twelve syllables. —
See dodeca- and syllabic.

## dodecasyllable
dodecasyllable, п., a word of twelve syllables. —
See dodeca- and syllable.

## Dodecatheon
Dodecatheon, п., a genus of plants of the
primrose family (bot.) — L. dodecatheon, 'primrose',
fr. Gk. δωδεκά&εον, a name coined by Pliny fr.
δώδεκα, 'twelve', and θεός, 'god'; see dodeca-
and theo-. Dodecatheon prop, denotes the plant
that is under the care of the twelve greater gods.

## dodge
dodge, intr. v., to move to and fro; tr. v., to
elude. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: dodge, п., dodg-er, п., dodg-ery, п.,
dodg-y, adj., dodg-i-ly, adv., dodg-i-ness, n.

## dodo
dodo, п., an extinct large bird. — Port, doudo,
lit., 'stupid'.

## doe
doe, п., femaleof the fallow deer. — ME.rfo.fr. OE.
da (whence Dan. daa), prob. a Celtic loan word;
cp. Co. da, 'fallow deer', Olr. dam, 'ox', dam
allaid, 'stag' (prop, 'wild ox'), W. dafad, 'sheep*,
which are prob. cogn. with Gk. δαμάλης, 'young
steer', δαμάλη, δάμαλις, 'young cow, heifer' (L.
damma, dama, 'fallow deer, buck, doe', is prob.
borrowed fr. Celtic); cp. Dama. These animal
names are prob. connected with I.-E. base
*doma-, 'to tame' and orig. denoted 'tamed
animals'; see tame,

## doff
doff, tr. v. — Contracted fr. do and off. Cp. don,

## v. dont
v. dont, dup.

## dog
dog, n. — ME. dogge, fr. OE. docga, of uncertain

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:251 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OOGANA | 224 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:251 COLUMN:1 -->
origin; F. dogue, Du. dog, Dan. dogge, Swed.
dogg, 'mastiff', are E. loan words. Cp. doggerel.
Derivatives: dog, tr. v., dogg-ed, adj., dogg-ed-
ly, adv., dogg-ed-ness, п., dogg-ery, п., dogg-y,
adj., dogg-i-ly, adv., dogg-i-ness, п., dogg-ish,
adj., dogg-ish-ly, adv., dogg-ish-ness, n.

## dogana
dogana, п., a customhouse in Italy. — It., fr.
Arab, diwan, fr. .Pers. diwan, 'register, office;
council; customhouse; collection of books'. See
divan and cp. aduana, douaae.

## dogaressa
dogaressa, п., wife of the doge. — It., formed fr.
doge with suff. -essa. See doge and -esse.

## dogate
dogate, п., the office of a doge. — F. dogai, fr. It.
dogato, fr. L. ducatus, 'military leadership,
command', fr. dux, gen. ducis, 'leader'. See
doge and subst. suff. -ate.

## dogbane
dogbane, п., also dog's bane, a perennial plant. —
So called because it was supposed to be
poisonous to dogs.

## dogbcrry
dogbcrry, n. — Compounded of dog and berry,
prop, 'berry fit for dogs'.

## Dogberry
Dogberry, п., a blundering constable or official.
—Fr. Dogberry, a self-satisfied, blundering
constable in Shakepeare's Much Ado About Nothing.
Derivatives: Dogberry-dom, п., Dogberry-ism, n.

## doge
doge, п., the chief magistrate of the republics of
Venice and Genoa. — F., frTVenetian It. doge,
fr. L. ducem, ace. of dux, 'leader'; see duke. In
literary Italian L. ducem became duce. Cp.
dogaressa, dogate,

## dogger
dogger, п., a kind of fishing boat. — ME. doggere,
of uncertain origin.

## doggerel
doggerel, п., bad poetry. — Prob. a derivative of
dog, used contemptuously. Cp. dog rime, dog
Latin.
Derivative; doggerel, adj.

## dogma
dogma, п., a tenet. — L., fr. Gk. δόγμα, gen.
δόγματος, 'that which one thinks true, opinion,
doctrine, decree', fr. δοκεΐν, 'to seem, have the
appearance of, think, believe', whence also
δόξα (for δόκ-σα), 'opinion, glory', fr. I.-E. base
*dek-, *dok-, 'to take, receive, accept;
acceptable, becoming, good', whence also L. decere,
'to be seemly or fitting'. See decent and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-ma.

## dogmatic
dogmatic, also dogmatical, adj., 1) pertaining to a
dogma; 2) opinionated. — Late L. dogmaticus,
fr. Gk. δογματικός, 'pertaining to doctrines', fr.
Gk. δόγμα, gen. δόγματος. See dogma and -ic,
resp. also -al.
Derivatives: dogmatic-al-ly, adv., dogmat-ics, n„
dogmatism, dogmatist, п., dogmatize (qq. v.)

## dogmatism
dogmatism, п., dogmatic assertion of opinion. —
F. dogmatisme, fr. ML. dogmatismus, fr. L.
dogma, gen. -atis, fr. Gk. δόγμα, gen. -ατός. See
dogma and -ism.

## dogmatist
dogmatist, n„ a dogmatic person. — F. dogma-
lisle, fr. ML. dogmatisla, fr. Gk. δογματιστής,
from the stem of δογματίζειν. See dogmatize
and -ist.

## dogmatize
dogmatize, intr. v., to speak or write dogmatically;
tr.v., to express dogmatically. — F. dogmatiser,
fr. ML. dogmatizdre, fr. Gk. δογματίζειν, 'to
lay down an opinion', fr. δόγμα, gen. δόγματος.
See dogma and -ize.
Derivatives: dogmatiz-ation, п., dogmatiz-er, n.

## doily
doily, also dolley, doyly, п., an ornamental
napkin. — Named after Doily or Doyley, a London
draper, who flourished in the early years of the
18th cent.

## doit
doit, п., a coin of trifling value. — MDu. duit,
deyt, doyt (Du. duit), rel. to G. Deut, Dan. dejt,
ON. pveit(i), 'a coin of trifling value'. The orig.
meaning of these words was 'a piece cut off'.
They are rel. to ON. pveita, 'to hew*. See
thwaite and cp. whittle.

## doited
doited, adj., stupid (Scot.) — Of uncertain origin.

## dolabriform
dolabriform, adj., shaped like an axe (hot. and
zool.) — Formed fr. L. dolabra, 'mattock,
pickax', and forma, 'form, shape'. The first
element lit. means 'an instrument for hewing', and
is formed fr. L. dolare, 'to hew' (with I.-E.
instrumental suff. *dhro-)\ see dole, grief. For
the second element see form, n.

## dolce
dolce, adj., sweetly (musical direction). — It., fr.
L. dulcis, 'sweet'. See dulcet,

## dolce far niente
dolce far niente, delightful idleness. — It., lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:251 COLUMN:2 -->
'sweet doing nothing'. For the first word see ·

## dolce. It. fare
dolce. It. fare, far, 'to do', derives fr. L. facere,
whence also F. faire; see fact. It. niente,
'nothing', comes fr. Late L. nee entem, lit. 'not a

## being'
being', fr. L. nee, 'neither, nor', and entem, ace.

## oiens
oiens, 'being', pres. part, oiesse, 'tobe'. See ens,

## entity. Cp. OProveng. nien
entity. Cp. OProveng. nien, OF. neient, noient,

## nient (F. neant)
nient (F. neant), 'nothing', which also derive fr.
Late L. nee entem.

## doldrums
doldrums, n.pl., dullness. — Perh. rel. to dall.

## dole
dole, п., a small portion. — ME. dot, fr. OE. dal,
'part, portion', rel. to dxl, of s.m. See deal,
'part'.

## dole
dole, usually dole out, tr. v., to deal out. — Fr.
prec. word.

## dole
dole, п., grief (archaic and poet.) — ME., fr. OF.

## dol
dol, doel, deol (F. deuil), 'sorrow, grief,

## mourning'
mourning', fr. Late L. dolus, 'sorrow (whence also It.

## duolo
duolo, OProvenc. dol, 'sorrow, grief', Sp. duelo,
'sorrow, grief; mourning'), fr. L. dolere, 'to

## suffer pain
suffer pain, grieve, be afflicted, deplore, lament',

## fr. I.-E. base 'del-
fr. I.-E. base 'del-, *dol-, 'to split, cut, carve',

## whence also OI. dalati
whence also OI. dalati, splits, bursts', dalayati,
'causes to burst', dalam, 'part, piece', Arm. tai,
'impression, sign', Gk. δαίδαλος, 'cunningly

## made'
made', δαιδάλλειν, 'to work cunningly or

## skillfully'
skillfully', L. ddlium, 'a very large jar, vessel', dolare,
'to hew with an ax', Russ. dolja, 'part', Lith. dalis,
'part, destiny', Lith. daliju, dalyti, Lett, daltt,
'to divide', ON. tai, OE. talu, 'number' (prop.
'incision in the tally'), Olr. delb, 'figure, form',

## Toch. A talo
Toch. A talo, В tallawo, 'miserable, wretched'.
The original meaning of L. dolere was 'to be
torn'. For sense development ср. Е.

## heartrending. Cp. condole
heartrending. Cp. condole, dolabriform, dole, 'guile',

## dolent
dolent, dolente, Doliolum, dolium, dolor,
dolorous, indolent. Cp. also daedal, dal, deleterious,
taal, tale, talk, toll, Zoll.
Derivatives: dole-ful, adj., dole-ful-ly, adv., dole-

## ful-ness
ful-ness, n.

## dole
dole, п., guile. — L. dolus, 'guile, deceipt,
deception', cogn. with or borrowed fr. Gk. δόλος,
of s.m.; fr. I.-E. base 'del-, 'to aim at', which
is prob. identical with base 'del-, 'to split, cut,
carve'. See dole, 'grief, and cp. dolerite, dolose,
sedulous, subdolous.

## dolent
dolent, adj., sorrowful. — F., fr. L. dolentem, ace.
of dolens, pres. part, of dolere, 'to suffer pain'.
See dole, 'grief, and -ent.
Derivative: dolent-ly, adv.

## dolente
dolente, adj., sorrowful (musical direction). —
It., pres. part, of dolere, fr. L. dolere. See prec.
word.

## dolerite
dolerite, п., a coarse form of basalt (petrogr.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. δολερός,
'deceptive', fr. δόλος, 'deceipt' (see dole,
'guile'); so called because easily confused with
diorite. Cp. dolose,

## dolicho-
dolicho-, before a vowel dolich-, combining form
meaning 'long'. — Gk. δόλιχο-, δολιχ-, fr.
δόλιχος, 'long', rel. to έν-δελεχής, 'continued;
constant', and cogn. with OI. dirghah, 'long',
Avcsticdarega-,Hitt. daluga-, 'long', Hitt. dalu-
gashli, 'length', L. in-dulgire, 'to indulge', lit., 'to
be long-suffering', Goth, tulgus, 'firm, steadfast',
OE. lulge, 'firmly', OS. lulgo, 'very, much',
OSlav. diugu, 'long', Lith. ilgas, Lett, ilgs,
OPruss. ilgi, of s.m. Cp. indulge. For connection
with L. longus see long, adj.

## dolichocephalic
dolichocephalic, also dolichocephalous, adj.,
having a relatively long head. — Lit., 'long-headed',
fr. Gk. δόλιχος, 'long', and κεφαλή, 'head'; see
dolicho- and cephalic, resp. -cephalous. The term
dolichocephalic was introduced into
anthropology by the Swedish anatomist and
anthropologist Anders Adolf Retzius (1796-1S60).

## Dollcholus
Dollcholus, п., the same as Rhynchosia (bol.) —
A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk. δόλιχος, 'long'
(see dolicho-), and the Latin dimin. suff. -olus
(see -ole). The correct form is Dolichidium,
which is formed fr. δόλιχος with the Greek
dimin. suff. -ίδιον (see -idium).

## Dollcbos
Dollcbos, п., a genus of vines (hot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. δόλιχος, 'long; name of a kind of pulse'.
See dolicho-.

## Doliidae
Doliidae, n. pi., a family of mollusks (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. Dolium with suff. -idae.

## Doliolum
Doliolum, п., a genus of tunicates (zool.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:251 COLUMN:3 -->
ModL., fr. L. doliolum, 'a small cask', dimin. of
dolium. See dolium.

## dolium
dolium, п., a very large cask or jar. — L. dolium,
rel. to dolare, 'to hew', fr. I.-E. base 'del-, 'dol-,
'to split, cut, carve'. See dole, 'grief, and cp.
the first element is dolabriform.

## Dolium
Dolium, п., a genus of large mollusks (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. dolium. See prec. word.

## Doll
Doll, fem. PN. — A shortened form of Dorothy,

## doll
doll, п., a child's toy. — Fr. prec. word.
Derivatives: doll-ish, adj., doll-ish-ly, adv., doll-
ish-ness, п., dolly (q.v.)

## dollar
dollar, n. — LG. daler, fr. G. Taler, abbreviation
of Joachimstaler, fr. Joachimstal (lit. 'Valley of
Joachim') in Bohemia; so called from the piece
of money first coined there in 1519. Cp. Du.
daalder, Dan., Swed. daler. It. tallero (whence
Hung, taller), which all are German loan words,
and see taler. For the etymology of G. Tai see
dale,

## dollop
dollop, п., a coarse lump. — Of unknown origin.

## dolly
dolly, п., ι) pet name for a doll; 2) name for
various devices suggestive of a doll. — Formed
fr. doll with dimin. suff. -y.
Derivative: dolly, tr. v.

## dolly
dolly, п., an offering of fruit, flowers, etc. (India).
— Hind, dali, lit. 'branch, basket, tray, that
which is offered on a tray', fr. OI. daru-f 'piece of
wood, wood, wooden implement', which is rel.
to dru-, 'wood', drumah, 'tree'. See tree and cp.
dryad. Cp. also dinghy.

## Dolly Varden
Dolly Varden, a fantastic style of woman's dress.
— From a character in Dickens's Barnaby
Rudge (1841).

## dolman
dolman, п., a long Turkish robe; a kind of jacket
worn by hussars. — F., fr. G. Dolman, fr. Hung.
dolmany, fr. Turk, dolaman, the red cloak of the
Janizaries.

## dolmen
dolmen, п., a large flat monumental stone. — F.,
lit. 'a table of stone', fr. Bret, tool, tul, 'table',
a loan word fr. L. tabula, 'board, plank' (see
table), and Bret, maen, тёп, 'stone', which is
rel. to W. maen, Co. men, 'stone'. Cp. the first
element in menhir.

## dolomite
dolomite, п., a kind of rock (mineral, andpetrogr.).
— Named after the French geologist and
mineralogist Deodat de Dolomieu (1750-1801). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: dolomit-ic, adj., dolomit-ize, tr. v.,
dohmit-iz-ation, n.

## dolor
dolor, dolour, п., grief, mourning. — OF. dolor,
dolur, dolour (F. douleur), fr. L. doldrem, ace. of
dolor, 'pain, distress, grief, affliction', fr. dolere,
'to suffer pain'. See dole, 'grief.

## doloroso
doloroso, adj., sorrowful (musical direction). —
It., fr. L. dolorosus. See dolorous.

## Dolores
Dolores, fem. PN. — Sp., shortened fr. Maria de
los Dolores, lit. 'Mary of the sorrows', pi. of
dolor, fr. L. dolor, 'pain, sorrow'. See dolor and
cp. Mercedes.

## dolorous
dolorous, adj. — OF. dolorous, doleros, doloreus
(F. douloureux), fr. Late L. dolorosus, 'painful,
sorrowful', fr. L. dolor. See dolor and -ous.
Derivatives: dolorous-ly, adv., dolorous-ness, n.

## dolose
dolose, adj., with evil intent (law). — L. dolosus,
'deceitful', fr. dolus. See dole, 'guile', and cp.
dolerite.

## dolphin
dolphin, n. — ME. delphin, delfyn, fr. OF. daul-
phin, dalfin (F. dauphin), fr. ML. dalfinus, fr. L.
delphinus, delphin,fr. Gk. δελφίς, gen. δελφίνος,
'dolphin', which is rel. to δελφύς, 'womb'; the
animal is so called in allusion to the womb of
the female. For the etymology of δελφύς see
adelpho-, Cp. dauphin, Delphinium.

## dolt
dolt, п., a stupid fellow. — ME. duit, lit. 'dulled',
fr. dul, 'dull'. See dull and verbal suff. -t.
Derivatives: doll-ish, adj., dolt-ish-ly, adv., dolt-
ish-ness, n.

## dom
dom, п., 1) a title once given to certain Roman
Catholic dignitaries; 2) a Portuguese title
equivalent to the Spanish title don. — Port, dom,
which, like Sp. don, It. donno, derives fr. L.
dominus, 'master, lord', orig. 'master of a house',
fr. domus, 'house'. See dome, 'building', and cp.
dominns and words there referred to.

## -dom
-dom, suff. denoting 1) dignity, rank or position,
as in kingdom, earldom; 2) state or condition,
as in freedom; 3) members of a group collect-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:252 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 225 | DOOR -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:252 COLUMN:1 -->
ively, as in officialdom. — ME., fr. OE. -dom,
fr. dam, 'judgment, authority'; rel. to OS. -dom,
ON. ddmr, MDu. -doem, Du. -dom, OHG.,
MHG. -tuom, G. -turn. See doom.

## domain
domain, n. — F. domaine, 'domain, estate*, fr.
OF. demaine, fr. L. dominium, 'property, right
of ownership', fr. dominus, 'master, lord'. See
dome, 'building', and cp. domiaus and words
there referred to. F. domaine was influenced in
form by ML. domanium, 'domain, estate',
which itself derives fr. OF. demaine.

## domaaial
domaaial, adj., pertaining to a domain. — F., fr.
ML. domanium. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ai.

## dome
dome, п., a building, palace. — F. dome, fr. It.
duomo, 'a cathedral church', fr. L. domus,
'house' (in domus Del, 'house of God'), whence
dominus, 'master, lord', lit. 'master of the house',
domdre, 'to tame', lit. 'to accustom to the house'.
L. domus is eogn. with Gk. δήμος, ΟΙ. damah,
'house', Gk. δώμα (prob. for *dom-m), "house,
chief room, housetop', OSlav. domu, 'house',
doma, 'at home', domov, 'home*, Arm. tun prob.
for *dd(m)-m, 'house*, the first element in Gk.
δεσ-πάτης (for *dems-pold), 'despot', lit. 'lord
of the house', δά-πεδον (for *dm-pedom),
'ground about a house', and in Lith. dim-slis
(for *dm-sto-), 'estate, yard', and the second
element in Gk. έν-δον (fr. ev, 'in', and *dom),
'within', lit. 'in the house'; fr. I.-E. 'dim-,
*dSm-, *dm-, 'dm-, 'house'. These words
possibly meant orig. 'building', and are cogn. with
Gk. δέμειν, 'to build'. Cp. tame, timber. Cp.
also adamant, belladonna, dam, 'a female
parent', dama, dame, damoiseau, damsel, dan, title,
danger, daunt, demesne, demijohn, despot, din-
mond, doe, dom, domain, domestic, Domicella,
domicile, dominate, domineer, Dominic,
dominion, domino, dominus, don, 'title', donjon, duenna,
dungeon, endo-, duomo, Hippodamia,
indomitable, madam, madame, major-domo, vidame.
Cp. also toft.
Derivatives: dome, tr. and intr.'v., dom-ed, adj.

## dome
dome, п., cupola. — F. dome, fr. OProvenc. doma,
fr. Gk. δώμα, 'house, chief room, housetop'. See
dome, 'building'.

## domesday
domesday, n. — Ancient form of doomsday.

## Domesday (Book)
Domesday (Book), the record of the Great
Inquest of the lands of England made by the order
of William the Conqueror in 1086. — OE.
ddmesdxg, lit. 'day of judgment'. See doomsday.

## domestic
domestic, adj. — F. domestique, fr. L. domesticus,
'pertaining to the house, private', fr. domus,
'house, home'; see dome, 'building'. The form
domesticus is enlarged fr. 'domestis, which was
formed on analogy of agreslis, 'pertaining to
land' (fr. ager, 'land').
Derivatives: domestic, п., domestic-al-ly, adv.,
domestic-ity, n.

## domesticable
domesticable, adj. — ML. domesticdbilis, fr.
domesticare. See next word and -able.

## domesticate
domesticate, tr. v., to tame. — ML. domesticdtus,
pp. of domesticare, 'to tame', lit. 'to make
domestic', fr. L. domesticus. See domestic and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: domesticat-ion, n.

## domett
domett, п., a kind of cloth, of which the warp is
cotton and the weft woolen. — Of unknown
origin.

## domic
domic, domical, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
a dome. — Formed fr. dome with suff. -ic, resp.
also -al.

## Domicella
Domicella, п., a genus of parrots (prnithol.) —
ModL., dimin. of L. domus, 'house'. See dome,
'building'.

## domicile
domicile, п., home. — F., fr. L. domicilium,
'dwelling, abode', prob. formed fr. *domi-coliom,
lit. 'house to dwell in', fr. domus, 'house', and
the stem of colere, 'to till (the ground), to dwell,
inhabit'. See dome, 'building', and colony.
Derivatives: domicile, v., domiciliary (q.v.),
domicili-ate, v., domiciliat-ion, n.

## domicilinry
domicilinry, adj. — ML. domicilidrius (whence
also F. domiciliaire), fr. L. domicilium. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ary.

## dominance
dominance, domiaancy, n. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## dominant
dominant, adj. and n. — F., fr. L. dominans, gen.
■antis, pres. part, of dominari. See next word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:252 COLUMN:2 -->
and -ant.
Derivative: dominant-ly, adv.

## dominate
dominate, tr. and intr. v. — L. dominatus, pp. of
dominari, 'to rule, reign, dominate', fr. dominus,
'master, lord'. See dominus and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: domination (q.v.), dominat-ive, adj.,
dominator (q.v.)

## domination
domination, n. — F., fr. L. domindlionem, ace. of
domindtid, 'lordship, dominion, domination',
fr. dominatus, pp. of dominari. See prec. word
and -ion.

## dominator
dominator, n. — F. dominaleur, fr. L. dominato-
rem, ace. of dominator, 'ruler', fr. dominatus, pp.
of dominari. See dominate and agential suff. -or.

## domineer
domineer, intr. v. — Du. domineren, fr. F. domi-
ner, fr. L. dominari, 'to rule' (see dominate);
first used by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: domineer-ing, adj., domineer-ing-
ly, adv.

## Dominic
Dominic, masc. PN. — L. dominicus, 'pertaining
to a lord', fr. dominus. See dominus.

## dominical
dominical, adj. — ML. dominicalis, 'pertaining
to a master or lord', fr. L. dominicus, of s.m.,
fr. dominus. See dominus and adj. suff. -al.

## Dominican
Dominican, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. ML. Dominicanus, fr. Dominicus, Latinized
name of Domingo de Guzman (Santo Domingo),
the founder of this order of monks. For the
origin of the Latin name Dominicus see Dominic.

## dominie
dominie, п., ι) a schoolmaster (Scot.); 2) a
clergyman. — L. domine, voc. of dominus, 'master,
lord'. See dominus.

## dominion
dominion, n. — Obsol. F. dominion, fr. ML. domi-
nionem, ace. of dominio, corresponding to L.
dominium. See next word and -ion.

## dominium
dominium, п., ownership (law). — L., 'property,
right of ownership, domain', fr. dominus. See
dominus and cp. coadominium. Cp. also danger,
dungeon.

## domino
domino, п., a robe with hood. — F., fr. VL.
domino, dat. or abl. of dominus, 'lord, master'.
See dominus.
Derivative: domino-ed, adj.

## domiao
domiao, п., name of the game played with 28
pieces of bone or ivory. — F., fr. It. domino,
'master, lord', fr. L. dominus (see next word);
prob. so called because he who has first
disposed his pieces becomes 'the master'. Cp.
prec. word.

## dominus
dominus, п., master. — L., 'master, lord', lit.
'master of the house', formed with -nus (for
I.-E. *-no-), a suff. denoting ownership or
relation, fr. domus, 'house'. See dome, 'building', and
cp. dame, damoisenu, demoiselle, dom, dominate,
domineer, Dominic, dominie, dominion, domino,
don, 'a title', Dona, Dona, donzella, duenna, Suff.
*«o- appears also in Gk. κοίρανος, 'ruler,
commander' (fr. "κοίρά, 'army'). For the suff. cp.
also tribune.

## don
don, п., a Spanish title. — Sp., fr. L. dominus,
'lord'. See dominus and cp. dom.
Derivative: donnish (q.v.)

## don
don, tr. v. — Contracted fr. do and on. Cp. doff,
dout, dup.

## Donn
Donn, п., a Portuguese title corresponding to Sp.
Dona. — Port., fr. L. domina. See next word.

## Donn
Donn, п., a Spanish title given to a married
woman. — Sp., 'lady, madam', fr. L. domina,
'mistress', fem. of dominus, 'master, lord'. See
dominus and cp. dame and words there
referred to.

## Donnld
Donnld, masc. PN. — Prob. fr. Gael. Domhnall,
lit. 'world ruler'.

## donate
donate, tr. v. — Back formation fr. donation.
Cp. orate.

## donation
donation, n. — F., fr. L. ddnationem, ace. of
donatio, 'a presenting, giving', fr. dondtus, pp.
of donare, 'to present, bestow, donate', fr.
ddnum, 'gift, present, offering, sacrifice', which
is rel. to Umbr. dunu(m), and cogn. with OI.
ddnam, of s.m., OSlav. dani, 'tribute', Lith.
duonis, 'gift', Olr. dan, 'gift, endowment, talent',
W. dawn, 'gift', fr. I.-E. base "dd-nom, 'gift, a
collateral form of *dd-rom, whence Arm. tur,
Gk. δώρον, OS. daru, 'gift', darovati,'to present'.
All these words ultimately derive fr. I.-E. base
*dd-, *d'-, 'to give'. See date, 'point of time',
and cp. donee, donor. Cp. also Doras, the first

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:252 COLUMN:3 -->
element in Dorothea and the second element in
pardon and in Eudora, Fedora, Fructidor,
Isidore, Messidor, Theodore. For the ending see
suff. -ion.

## Donatist
Donatist, п., an adherent of a sect which arose in
the Christian Church of N. Africa in the 4th
century. — ML. Ddndtista, formed with suff.
-ista (see -ist) from the name of Dondtus of
Casae Nigrae, leader of this sect. For the
etymology of the name Ddnatus see prec. word.
Derivatives: Donatist, Donatistic, adjs.

## donative
donative, п., an official gift, donation. — L. ddnd-
tivum, 'official gift, gratuity', fr. dondtus, pp. of
donare. See donation and -ive.

## donatory
donatory, п., a donee. —- ML. ddndtdrius, 'one
who receives a gift', fr. L. ddnatus, pp. of donare.
See doaation and -ory.

## doncella
doncella, п., l) a wrasslike fish; 2) name of
timber trees in W. Indies. — Sp., lit. 'damsel',
fr. VL. 'dominicella, dimin. of L. domina,
'mistress'. See damsel and cp. words there referred
to.

## done
done, adj. — ME. doon, fr. OE. geddn, pp. of don.
See do, v.

## donee
donee, п., he who receives a gift. — OF. done
(F. donne), pp. of doner (F. donner), 'to give',
fr. L. donare, 'to present, beslow, donate'. See
donation and -ее.

## donga
donga, п., a ravine. — A Zulu word.

## donjon
donjon, п., the keep of a castle. — OF. (= F.),
fr. VL.1 'dominidnem, ace. of 'dominio, fr. L.
dominium, 'domain'. See dungeon, which is a
doublet of donjon.

## donkey
donkey, n. — A double diminutive, formed fr.
the adj. dun, 'dark, brown', with the suffixes -k
and -(e)y, but influenced in form by the word
monkey.
donkey's years. — Corrupted fr. donkey's ears,
with reference to the long ears of this animal.

## donnish
donnish, adj., resembling a university don;
pedantic. — Formed from the noun don with adj.
suff. -ish.
Derivative: donnish-ness, n.

## donor
donor, n. — AF. donour, corresponding to OF.
doneur (F. donneur), fr. L. ddndtorem, ace. of
ddndtor, 'giver, donor*, fr. ddnatus, pp. ofddndre.
See donation and agential suff. -or..

## donna
donna, п., an Italian title given to a lady. — It.,
' fr. L. domina. See dame and cp. Madonna. Cp.
also Dona, duenna.

## donzel
donzel, п., squire, page (archaic). — It. donzello,
fr. VL. 'dominicelio, dimin. of L. dominus,
'master, lord*. See damoiseau and cp. next word.

## donzella
donzella, п., damsel. — It., fr. VL. *dominicella,
dimin. of L. domina, 'mistress'. See doncella.

## doob
doob, п., a creeping grass (Cynodon dactyion)
(India). — Hind, dub, fr. Ol. dfirvd, 'a kind of
millet grass', which is cogn. with MLG. tarwe,
ME. tare, 'vetch, darnel'. See tare.'vetch, darnel'.

## doolie
doolie, dooly, dhooly, п., a covered litter (East
Indies). — Hind, doll, fr. dolnd, 'to swing', fr.
OI. dold, 'swinging' which is rel. to andoldyati,
'swings, seesaws', a word derived fr. *an-dola,
'swing, seesaw, litter'; of Austroasiatic origin.
Cp. landau.

## doom
doom, n. — ME. dom, fr. OE. dom, rel. to OS.,
OFris. dom, ON. ddmr, OHG. tuom, Goth.
doms, 'judgment, decree', fr. I.-E. base *dhom-,
whence also Ol. dhiman-, 'law', Gk. θωμός,
'heap', 8-έμις, 'law', Lith. dome, 'attention'. I.-E.
*dhdm- is an enlargement of base *dho-, *dhe-,
*dhe-, 'to put, place'. See do, v., and cp. deem
and -dom. Cp. also duma, theme.
Derivative: doom, tr. v.
doom palm. — F. doum, fr. Arab, dawm, daum,
dum, 'a large Egyptian palm tree'.

## doomsday
doomsday, п., the day of the Last Judgment. —
OE. ddmesdxg, 'day of judgment', fr. domes,
gen. of ddm, 'doom, judgment', and dxg, 'day'.
See doom and day and cp. Domesday (Book).
Doomsday Book. — See Domesday (Book).

## doomster
doomster, п., judge. — A var. of deemster, demp-
ster; influenced in form by doom.

## door
door, n. — ME. dore, dure, fr. OE. dor, 'door,
gate', duru, 'door', rel. to OS. duru, ON. dyrr,
Dan. der, Swed. dorr, OFris. dure, dore, OHG.
turi, MHG., G. tur, 'door', OHG., MHG., G.
tor, Goth, daur, 'gate', and cogn. with OI.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:253 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DOPATTA | 226 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:253 COLUMN:1 -->
dvarah (nom. pi), durah, durah (ace. pi.),
'door', durona-, 'dwelling, home', Avestic dvar'm
(ace. sing.), 'gate, court', OPers. duvaraya-,
'at the door', Toch. В twere, Arm. durk' (pi.),
durn (sing.), Gk. θύρα, 'door', Э-υρίς, 'window',
παράθυρα, 'side door, wicket', πράθυρον, 'front
door, doorway, porch', Alb.dere, p\.duer,'door,
house', L. fores (pi.), 'door', foras, 'out of doors,
out', /oris, 'out at the doors, out of doors',
OSlav. dvtri, 'door', dvoru, 'courtyard', Lith.
durys, Lett, duris, diirvis, OPruss. dauris, 'door',
W., Co., OBret. dor, Olr. dorus, OCo. darat,
'door'. Cp. dargah, dehors, doch-an-doris,
durbar, durwaun, foreclose, foreign, forisfamiliate,
forjudge, hors de combat, hors d'oeuvre, Thyri-
didae, thyroid,

## dopatta
dopatta, also dooputty, п., a garment for women.
— Hind, do-patta, lit. 'of double breadth'.

## dope
dope, п., a thick liquid. — Fr. Du. doop, 'a
dipping, liquid, sauce', fr. dopen, 'to dip'. See
dip and cp. dopper.
Derivatives: dope, tr. v. ,dop-er, n. dop-ing-ly, adv.

## Doppelgaager
Doppelgaager, п., the phantasm or counlerpart
of a living person, a double ganger. — G., lit.
'a double walker'. See double, gang and agential
suff. -er and cp. doublegaager.

## dopper
dopper, п., a S. African Dutch baptist. — Du.
doper, lit. 'dipper', fr. dopen, 'to dip'. See dip
and cp. dope,

## dopplerite
dopplerite, n. — G. Dopplerit; named in 1849
after the German physicist Christian Johann
Doppler (1803-53). The G. suff. -// represents
Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## dor
dor, п., a droning insect, the dorbeetle. — ME.
dore, fr. OE. dora, 'humblebee', rel. to MLG.
dorte, 'drone', from the I.-E. imitative base
*dher-, 'to hum, buzz, murmur'. See drone.

## Dora
Dora, fern. PN. — A shortened form of Doro-
then, Dorothy,

## dorado
dorado, п., a large fish of the genus Coryphaena.
— Sp., prop. pp. of dorar, fr. L. deaurare, 'to
gild', fr. de- and aurare, 'to gild', fr. aurum,
'gold'. See aureate and cp. El Dorado and dory,
'a seafish'.

## Dorcas society
Dorcas society, meeting of ladies to make
garments for the poor. — From Dorcas, name of a
woman (mentioned in Acts IX, 36-41). The
name derives from Gk. δορκάς, 'gazelle', which
is rel. to δόρξ, gen. δορκός, of s.m., and was
altered (owing to a popular connection with
δέρκομαι, Ί see, regard', see dracon), fr. orig.
ζορκάς, resp. ζόρξ, which is cogn. with W.
iwrch, Co. yorch, 'roebuck'.

## dorian
dorian, n. — See durian.

## Dorian
Dorian, adj., pertaining to Doris or the ancient
inhabitants of Doris. — Formed with suff. -aa,
fr. L. Dorius, fr. Gk. Δώριος, fr. Δωρίς, 'Doris',
name of a district in Central Greece, named
after Δώρος, 'Dorus', the ancestor of the
Dorians. See Dorus.
Derivative: Dorian, n.

## Doric
Doric, adj., pertaining to Doris or the Dorians.
— L. Doricus, fr. Gk. Δωρικός, fr. Δωρίς. See
prec. word.

## Dorize
Dorize, tr. and intr. v., to make or become Doric
or Dorian. — Gk. Δωρίζειν, 'to imitate the
Dorians, to speak Doric Greek', fr. Δωρίς,
'Doris'. See Dorian and -ize.

## Dorking
Dorking, n. — Short for Dorking fowl, from
Dorking, name of a market town in Surrey,
England.

## dormancy
dormancy, n. — Formed fr. next word with suff.
-cy.

## dormaat
dormaat, adj., 1) sleeping; 2) inactive. — ME.,
fr. OF. (= F.) dormant, pres. part, of dormir,
'to sleep', fr. L. dormire, of s.m., which is cogn.
with OSlav. drimati, 'to sleep, doze', and with
Gk. εδραθον (II aor.), Ί slept', later form
έδαρθον, whence the new formation δαρθάνω,
Ί sleep', ΟΙ. drati, drayati, drayati, 'sleeps'. Cp.
dormer, dormitory, dormouse, dormy, dorter. For
the ending see suff. -ant.
Derivative: dormant, n.

## dormer
dormer, п., dormer window. — OF. dormeor, fr. L.
dormitorium, 'sleeping room', fr. dormJt-(um),
pp. stem of dormire, 'to sleep'. See prec. word
and subst. suff. -ory and cp. next word.

## dormitory
dormitory, n. — L. dormitorium. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:253 COLUMN:2 -->

## dormouse
dormouse, п., a small rodent. — Perh. meaning lit.
'sleeping mouse', and formed fr. OF. dorm-, stem
of dormir, 'to sleep' (see dormer), and E. mouse.

## dormy
dormy, adj., being ahead as many holes as there
remain to be played (golf). — F. dormi, pp. of
dormir, 'to sleep'. See dormant.

## Doronicum
Doronicum, п., a genus of plants. — ModL., fr.
Arab, daranaj, daranaj.

## Dorothea
Dorothea, Dorothy, fern. PN. — L. Dorothea, fr.
Gk. Δωροθέα, fern, of Δωρόθεος, lit. 'gift of
God', fr. δώρον, 'gift', and θεός, 'God'. See
donation and 1st theism and cp. doll, dolly. Cp.
also Theodora, and the second element in Eu-
dora, Isidore. In the form Dorothy, the name was
