taken over from Latin through the medium of
F. Dorothee.

## dors-
dors-, form of dorso- before a vowel.

## dorsal
dorsal, adj., pertaining to, or situated on or near,
the back. — F., fr. ML. dorsalis, corresponding
to L. dorsualis, 'of the back', fr. dorsum, 'the
back'. See dorsum.

## dorsi-
dorsi-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
the back', or 'on the back'. — L. dorsi-, fr.
dorsum, 'back'. See dorsum.

## dorso-
dorso-, before a vowel dors-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining to the back'. — L. dorso-,
dors-, fr. dorsum, 'back'. See next word.

## dorsnm
dorsnm, п., the back. — L., of uncertain origin.
The derivation of this word by the ancients fr.
L. "dlvorsum, 'that which is turned away', is
folk etymology. Cp. dorsal, doss, dosser, dossier,
endorse, extrados, parados, reredos. The L. word
dorsum was introduced into anatomy by the
Belgian anatomist Andreas Vesalius (1514-64).

## dorter
dorter, dortour, п., the dormitory of a monastery.
— OF. dortour, fr. L. dormitorium. See
dormitory.

## Dorus
Dorus, п., the legendary ancestor of the Dorians.
— L. Dorus, fr. Gk. Δώρος, a word rel. to δώρον,
'gift', which is cogn. with OS1. daru, 'gift', daro-
vati, 'to present', and with L. dOnum, 'gift'. See
donation and cp. Dorothy, Eudora.

## dory
dory, п., a seafish, Zeus faber. — F. doree, 'dory',
lit. 'the gilded one', fern, of dore, fr. L. deaurdtus,
'gilded'. See dorado.

## dory
dory, п., a light kind of boat. — From Honduran
native name.

## dory-
dory-, combining form meaning 'spear'. — Fr.
Gk. δόρυ (gen. δόρατος), 'stem, tree, beam, shaft
of a spear, spear*, rel. to δρυς, gen. δρυός, 'oak,
tree', and cogn. with OI. daru, wood, piece of
wood, spear', and cogn. with OE. trio, treow,
'tree, wood'. See tree and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also dryad and the second element
in Echinodorus.

## dosage
dosage, п., administration of medicine in doses.
— Formed fr. dose with suff. -age.

## dose
dose, п., amount of medicine taken at one time.
— F„ fr. ML. dosis, fr. Gk. δόσις, 'a gift', from
the stem of διδόναι, 'to give', fr. I.-E. base *do-,
*de-, 'to give', whence also L. dare, 'to give'.
See date, 'point of time', and cp. donation, dot,
'marriage portion'. Cp. also apodosis, dosimeter,
dosology.
Derivatives: dose, tr. and intr. v., dos-er, n.

## dosimeter
dosimeter, п., an instrument for measuring doses.
— Compounded of Gk. δόσις, 'a gift', and
μέτρον, 'measure'. See dose and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## dosimetry
dosimetry, п., the measurement of doses. — See
prec. word and -metry.
Derivatives: dosimetr-ic, adj., dosimetr-ic-ian,
п., dosimetr-ist, n.

## dosology
dosology,п., the science of doses.—Compounded
of Gk. δόσις, 'gift', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See dose and -logy.

## doss
doss, п., a bed(slang). — Prob. fr. F.dos, 'back',
fr. VL. dossum, fr. L. dorsum. See dorsum.
Derivative: doss, intr. v., to go to bed.

## dossal
dossal, п., a cloth for the back of a chancel. —
Eccles. L. dossale, assimilated fr. L. dorsale,
prop. neut. of the adj. dorsalis, 'pertaining to the
back', used as a noun. See dorsum.

## dosser
dosser,п., i)adossal; 2)apannier. — Οι.dossier,
fr. VL. 'dossiarium, fr. VL. dossum, 'back',
assimilated fr. L. dorsum. See dorsal and cp.
dossier.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:253 COLUMN:3 -->

## doss house
doss house, a cheap lodging house. — See doss,
'bed', and house.

## dossier
dossier, п., a collection of documents. — F., fr.
dos, 'back', fr. VL. dossum. See dosser.

## dot
dot, п., a spot. — OE. dott, 'head of a boil, speck,'
rel. to Norw. dot, 'lump, small knot', Du. dot,
'knot, small bunch, wisp', OHG. tutta, 'nipple',
MHG. tiilel, 'point', OE. dyttan, 'to shut, stop'
(whence dial. E. dit, 'to shut, stop'). Cp. dottle.
Derivatives: dot, tr. v., to mark with a dot,
dotted, adj., dott-er, п., dott-y, adj.

## dot
dot, п., marriage portion. — F., fr. L. dotem, ace.
of dos, 'marriage portion', from the base of do,
dare, 'to give'. See date, 'point of time', and
cp. dower.

## dotard
dotard, п., a foolish old person. — ME., formed
fr. doten (see dote, v.) with suff. -ard.

## dote
dote, п., marriage portion. — F. dote, a var. of
dot. See dot, 'marriage portion'.

## dote
dote, doat, intr. v., to be foolish. — ME. doten,
dotien, fr. MLG. doten, 'to be foolish rave',
which is rel. to MDu. doten, 'to doze, be
childish' [whence OF. re-doter, later ra-doter (F.
radoter), 'to drivel']. Cp. dotterel.
Derivatives: dot-age, п., dot-ard, п., dot-ing,
adj., dot-ing-ly, adv.

## dotterel
dotterel, п., a kind of plover. — Formed fr. dote,
'to be foolish', with dimin. suff. -erel. For the
suff. cp. cockerel (fr. cock), pickerel (fr. pike).

## dottle
dottle, п., plug of tobacco remaining in the pipe.
— Formed fr. dot, 'a spot', with dimin. suff.
-le.

## douane
douane, п., a customhouse. — F., fr. Arab, dlwan,
fr. Pers. diwan, 'register,
office;council;customhouse; collection of books'. See divan and cp.
aduana, dogana.

## double
double, adj. — ME., fr. OF. double, fr. L. duplus,
'twofold, double', lit. 'twice folded', formed fr.
du- (fr. duo), 'two', and *pl-, zero degree of base
"pel-, '-fold', and cogn. with Gk. δι-πλόος,
διπλούς, 'double'. See dual and ply, 'to bend', and
cp. plicate. Cp. also decuple, diploma, doblon,
dobra, Doppelganger, doubloon, duple, duplex,
duplicity, and the second element in centuple,
multiple, simple, treble, triple, triplex, quaflruple,
quadruplex, quintuple, sextuple, septuple. Cp.
also fold, -fold.
Derivatives: double, adv., п., double, v. (q.v.),
double-ness, п., doubl-y, adv.

## double
double, tr. and intr. v. — ME. doublen, fr. OF.
(= F.) doubter, fr. L. duplare, 'to double', fr.
duplus. See double, adj.
Derivatives: doubl-er, п., doubl-ing, n.

## double-enteadre
double-enteadre, п., a word of double meaning.
— Obsol. F. (for F. double entente), lit. 'a
twofold meaning', fr. double, 'double', and entendre,
'to hear; to understand, mean'. See double, adj.,
and entente.

## doubleganger
doubleganger, п., a counterpart of a living person.
— Anglicized form of Doppelganger.

## doublet
doublet, n. — ME. dobbelet, 'a garment', fr. OF.
doublet, lit. 'something doubled', formed fr.
double with the dimin. suff. -et. See double, adj.

## doubloon
doubloon, п., an obsolete Spanish gold coin. —
F. doublon, fr. Sp. doblon, augment, of dobla,
name of an ancient Spanish gold coin, lit.
'double', fr. L. dupla, fem. of duplus, 'double'. See
double, adj., and -oon and cp. doblon, dobra.

## doublure
doublure, п., lining. — F., 'lining', lit. 'doubling',
fr. doubier, 'to double'. See double, adj., and
-иге.

## doubt
doubt, intr. and tr. v. — ME. duten, douten, fr.
OF. duler, douter (F. douter), fr. dubitare, 'to
be uncertain in opinion, to doubt', freq. formed
fr. OL. dubdre, of s.m., fr. dubius, 'doubting,
uncertain, doubtful'; a derivative of duo, 'two'.
See dual and cp. dubious, redoubtable. The b in
E. doubt was inserted later owing to an
'etymological' spelling. L. dubitare orig. meant 'to
have to choose between two things'. For sense
development cp.'G. Zweifel, 'doubt', fr. zwei,
'two'.
Derivatives: doubt, n. (q.v.), doubt-ful, adj.,
doubt-ful-ly, adv., doubt-ful-ness, п., doubl-ing,
adj., doubt-ing-ly, adv., doubt-less, adj.

## doabt
doabt, n. — ME., fr. OF. dute, dome (F. doute),
fr. douter, 'to doubt'. See doubt, v.

## donee
donee, adj., sober, gentle (Scot.) — The orig.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:254 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 227 | ORACONTIUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:254 COLUMN:1 -->
now obsolete, meaning is 'sweet'. It is borrowed
fir. F. douce, fem. of doux, 'sweet, gentle', fr. L.
dulcis. See dulcet and cp. next word and dolce.

## donceur
donceur, п., gentleness; tip; bribe. — F. douceur,
'sweetness; favor', fr. doux, fem. douce, 'sweet';
see prec. word. The word douceur was
introduced into English by Horace Walpole.

## douche
douche, п., a jet of water. — F., fr. It. doccia,
'douche', fr. It. doccione, 'conduit, lead-pipe,
tube', fr. L. ductionAn, асе. of duetto, 'a
leading', fr. ducere, 'to lead'. See duct, duke.
Derivative: douche, tr. and intr. v.

## dough
dough, n. — ME. dog, dogh, dah, fr. OE. dag,
rel. to ON. deig, Dan deig, Swed. deg, MLG.
deck, MDu. deech, Du. deeg, OHG., MHG.
teic, G. Teig, Goth, daigs, dough', digan, 'to
knead', fr. I.-E. base "dheigh-, "dhoigh-, 'dhigh-,
'to form out of clay, to knead, form', whence
also OI. dihmi, Ί smear, anoint', dehah, 'body',
lit. 'that which is formed', deht, 'rampart, dam,
dike', Avestic daeza, 'wall', pairi-daeza,
'enclosure' (whence Gk. παράδεισος, 'enclosed
park'), OPers. dida, 'castle', Toch. A Isek-,
tsaik-, В tsik-, 'to form', tseke, 'statue'. Arm.
dez, 'heap, pile', dizanem, Ί heap up, pile up',
Gk. τείχος, τοίχος (dissimulated fr. *θεΐχος,
*θ·οΐχος), 'wall' (orig. 'clay wall'), ίΗγγάνειν, 'to
touch', Thracian -δΕζα, 'castle', L. fingere, 'to
form, shape, fashion', figura, form, shape', fi-
gulus, 'potter', Oscanfeihuss, 'the walls', ORuss.
deza, 'baker's trough', Lith. diezti, dyzti, 'to
cudgel, thrash' (lit. 'to knead thoroughly'), Olr.
digen, 'firm, solid' (orig. 'kneaded into a
compact mass'). Cp. also the metathesized forms:
Lith. ziedziii, zilsti, 'to form, build', OSIav.
zizdo, zidati, 'to build', zidu, 'wall'. Cp. dairy,
duff, 'pudding', and the second element in lady.
Cp. also deha, dixla, dizdar, effigy, faint, feiga,
fictile, fiction, fictitious, figure, thigmo-, the first
element in Tichodroma, thixotropy and the
second element in paradise.
Derivatives: dough, tr. and intr. v., dough-y,
adj., dough-i-ness, n.

## doughty
doughty, adj. — ME. dohti, duhti, fr. OE. dohtig,
fr. earlier dyhtig, 'able, fit, useful, valiant', rel.
lo MHG. tuhtec, G. tiichtig, of s.m., OE. dugan,
'to avail, be of use, be strong', ΟΝ., OFris. duga,
Du. deugen, OHG. tugan, MHG. tugen, G. tau-
gen, Goth, dugan, of s.m., OE. dugup, 'power,
rule, majesty; virtue, happiness', OHG. tu-
gundi, 'ability', MHG. tugenl, 'skill, worthiness,
virtue', G. Tugend, 'virtue', and cogn. with Gk.
τεύχειν, 'to make ready', τυγχάνει, 'to
happen, be at a place', τεϋχος, 'tool, implement',
later 'book', τύχη, 'fortune, fate, providence',
Hitt. tukka-, 'to fall to a person's share', lr.
dual (for "dhughlo-), 'becoming, fit', duan (for
*dhughna), 'poem', Lith. daug, 'much', Russ.
duzij, d'uzij, 'strong, robust'. All these words
prob. derive fr. I.-E. base "dheugh-, 'to be fit,
be of use, prosper'. Cp. dow, 'to be able', Tyche,
and the second element in Pentateuch.
Derivatives: dought-y, adj., dought-i-ly, adv.,
dought-i-ness, n.

## Douglas
Douglas, masc. PN. — Orig. only a river name,
fr. Gael. dub(h)glas, 'dark blue'.

## Douglas spruce
Douglas spruce, a N. American coniferous tree.
— Named after the Scottish botanist David
Douglas (1798-1834).

## Doukhobors
Doukhobors, n. pi. — See Dukhobors.
doum palm. — See doom palm.

## dour
dour, adj., hard, stern (Scot.) — L. durus, 'hard'.
See dure.
Derivatives: dour-ly, adv., dour-ness, n.

## douse
douse, dowse, tr. v., to plunge into water. — Prob.
fr. obsol. douse, 'to strike', which is prob. of
LG. origin. Cp. MDu. dossen, Du. doesen, 'to
strike'.
Derivative: dous-er, n.

## dout
dout, tr. v., to put out, extinguish. — Contracted
fr. do and out. Cp. doff, don, v., dup.

## dove
dove, n. — ME. dove, douve, duve, fr. OE. dufe-
(only in compounds), rel. to OS. duba, ON.
dufa, Swed. duva, Dan. due, MLG., MDu. duve,
Du. duif, OHG. tuba, MHG. tube, G. Taube,
Goth, -dubo (only in compounds), 'dove', orig.
'the dark-colored bird', fr. 1-Е. base 'dheubh-,
*dhubh-, 'to fill with smoke, to darken*, whence

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:254 COLUMN:2 -->
also U"· $иЬ, lr. dubh, 'dark-colored'. See deaf
and ci,. mtmb, typhlo-. Cp. also Taube. For sense
development cp. Gk. πέλεια, 'wood pigeon',
fr. πελιός, 'grayish black'.

## dovetail
dovetail, п., a joint made to fit a tenon into a
corresponding mortise. — Lit. 'that which
resembles a dove's tail'; so called in allusion to
the shape of the tenon.
Derivatives: dovetail, tr. and intr. v.,
dovetailed, adj., dove-tail-er, n.

## dow
dow, п., a dah (India). — A var. of dah.

## dow
dow, intr. v., to be able. — OE. dugan, 'to avail,
be of use, be strong'. See doughty.

## dowager
dowager, п., a widow holding a jointure. — OF.
douagiere, douagere (F. douairiere), fem. of dou-
agier (earlier F. douairier), 'pertaining to a
dower', fr. douage (F. douaire), 'dower'. The
word lit. means 'a woman who has received a
dower'. See dower and the suffixes -age and -er
and cp. endow.

## dowdy
dowdy, adj., not fashionable. — Lit. 'ill-dressed',
fr. earlier dowd, of s.m.; rel. to dnds (q.v.)
Derivatives: dowd-i-ly, adv., dowd-i-ness, п.,
dowdy-ish, adj.

## dowel
dowel, п., a headless pin or peg for fastening
together pieces of wood, etc. — ME. dowle, prob.
fr. MLG. dovel, which is rel. to OHG. (gi)tubili,
MHG. tiibel, G. Dobel, 'peg, pin, plug'; formed
with instrumental suff. -/ from Teut. base *dub-,
'to strike' (whence also LG. dubben, 'to strike'),
corresponding to I.-E. base 'dheubh-, "dhubh-,
'to strike', whence Gk. τύφος (dissimilated fr.
*θύφος), 'wedge, peg'. Lith. dubelis, 'peg', is a
Teut. loan word. Cp. dub, 'to make a knight'.
Derivative: dowel, tr. v.

## dower
dower, п., an endowment. — ME. dowere, fr.
OF. (= F.) douaire, fr. ML. dotarium, fr. L.
dotare, 'to endow, portion', which derives fr.
dos, gen. dotis, 'marriage portion', from the
base of do, dare, 'to give'. See date, 'point of
time', and cp. dot, 'marriage portion'. Cp. also
dowager, dowry.
Derivatives: dower, tr. v., dower-less, n.

## dowitcher
dowitcher, п., the gray snipe. — Of N. American
Indian origin.

## dowlas
dowlas, п., a coarse kind of calico. — From Da-
oulas (also spelled Doulas), a town near Brest
in Brittany.

## down
down, п., soft plumage. — ME. downe, doun, fr.
ON. dunn, which is rel. to MLG. dune (whence
G. Daune), fr. I.-E. base *dheu-, 'to fly about
like dust, whirl, shake', whence also ON. dyja,
'to shake', Lith. du/e, 'down', du/a, 'particle of
dust; very fine flour; fine rain, drizzle', and
OI. dhunoli, 'shakes, moves'. See thio- and cp.
down, 'hill'.
Derivative: downy (q.v.)

## down
down, п., hill. — ME. doun, fr. OE. dun, 'hill'
rel. to MDu. dunen, Du. duin (G. Dune, F. dune.
It. and Sp. duna are Dutch loan words), fr.
I.-E. base *dheu-, 'to shake'; hence down orig.
meant 'something cast up'. See down, 'soft
plumage'. See also dun, 'hill', and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: down, adv. (q.v.), downy (q.v.)

## down
down, adv., to, or in, a lower place. — Aphetic
for adown, fr. OE. of-dune, α-dune, prop,
meaning 'from the hill, downhill', fr. of-, a-, 'off,
from', and dune, dat. of dim, 'Ы1Г. See down,
'hill'.
Derivatives: down, adj., prep. tr. v. and n.

## downward
downward, adv. — OE. adunweard. See down,
adv., and -ward.
Derivative: downward, adj.

## downwards
downwards, adv. — Formed fr. prec. word with
adv. gen. suff. -es, -s. See -wards.

## downy
downy, adj., covered with, or resembling, down.
— Formed fr. down, 'plumage', with adj.
suff. -y.
Derivatives: downi-ly, adv., downi-ness, n.

## downy
downy, adj., resembling downs, undulating. —
Formed fr. down, 'hill', with adj. suff. -y.
Derivative: downi-ness, n.

## dowry
dowry, n. — ME. dowerie, fr. OF. douaire. See
dower.

## dowse
dowse, v. — See douse.

## dowse
dowse, intr. v., to seek water by the aid of a
divining rod. — The word prob. meant

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:254 COLUMN:3 -->
originally 'to dip or plunge into water', and is identical
with douse.
Derivative: dows-er, n.

## doxastic
doxastic, adj., pertaining to opinion. — Gk.
δοξαστικός, 'forming an opinion, conjecturing',
from the verbal adj. stem of δοξάζειν, 'to think,
imagine, to form an opinion', fr. δόξα, 'notion;
opinion; honor, glory', which stands ίΟΓδόκ-σα
and derives fr. δοκεΐν, 'to seem good, to seem,
think, believe' (whence also δόγμα, 'that which
one thinks true, opinion, doctrine, decree'), fr.
I.-E. base *dek-, *dok-, 'to take, receive, accept;
acceptable, becoming, good', whence also L.
decere, 'to be seemly or fitting'. See decent and
cp. dogma, the first element in doxology and the
second element in heterodox, orthodox, paradox.

## doxology
doxology, п., a hymn of praise. — Eccles. L.
doxologia, fr. Eccles. Gk. δοξολογία, 'praise,
laudation', which is compounded of Gk. δόξα,
'glory', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See prec. word and -logy. Cp.
also next word.

## doxy
doxy, п., opinion, doctrine (colloq.) — Back
formation from words ending in -doxy (as
heterodoxy, orthodoxy, etc..) See prec. word.

## doxy
doxy, п., a wench; a mistress (slang). — Of
unknown origin.

## doyen
doyen, п., senior member. — F., fr. OF. deien,
fr. L. decanus, 'one set over ten persons'. See
dean.

## doze
doze, intr. and tr. v. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. ON.
dusa, 'to doze', Dan. dese, 'to make drowsy',
dos, 'drowsiness', desig, 'drowsy', which are rel.
to OE. dysig, 'foolish'. See dizzy.
Derivatives: doze, п., doz-y, adj., doz-i-ly, adv.,
doz-i-ness, n.

## dozen
dozen, n. — OF. dozaine, dosaine, douzaine (F.
douzaine), fr. douze, 'twelve', fr. L. duodecim,
'twelve', fr. duo, 'two', and decern, 'ten'. See
duodecim-,

## drab
drab, п., a dirty woman; a slattern. — Of
uncertain origin. Cp. Ir. drobog, Gael, drabag, 'a
dirty woman'.
Derivative: drab, intr. v., to associate with
drabs.

## drab
drab, п., 1) a kind of cloth of brownish-yellow
color; 2) a brownish-yellow color. — F. drop,
'cloth', fr. Late L. drappus, fr. Gaulish *drappo-.
See drape and cp. drabbet.
Derivatives: drab, adj., drab-ly, adv., drab-
ness, п., drabb-ish, drabb-y, adjs.

## Draba
Draba, п., a genus of plants of the family Bras-
sicaceae (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δράβη, name
of a kind of cress.

## drabbet
drabbet, п., a coarse linen material. — Formed
fr. drab, 'cloth', with suff. -et.

## drabble
drabble, tr. v., to make wet and dirty; to draggle;
intr. v., to become draggled. — ME. drabelen,
drablen, fr. LG. drabbeln, 'to splash in water';
prob. of imitative origin.

## Dracaena
Dracaena, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δράκαινα, 'she-dragon',
fem. of δράκων. See dragon.

## drachm
drachm, п., a drachma. — See dram.

## drachma
drachma, п., ι) an ancient Greek coin; 2) an
ancient Greek weight. — L., fr. Gk. δραχμή.
See dram and cp. didrachma.

## Draco
Draco, п., name of a constellation between the
Great and Little Bear. — L. draco, 'dragon'.
See dragon.

## Dracocephalum
Dracocephalum, п., a genus of plants, the dragon
head (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
δράκων, 'a dragon', and κεφαλή, 'head' (see
dragon,and cephalic); so called in allusion to
the form of the corolla.

## dracoaian
dracoaian, adj., also dracouic, 'pertaining to a
dragon'. — See Draco and -ian, resp. -ic.

## Draconian
Draconian, Draconic, also draconian, draconic,
adj., severe, harsh. — Lit. 'in the manner of
Draco', fr. L. Draco, fr. Gk. Δράκων, the
Athenian legislator, who codified his laws in 621
B.C.E. For the meaning of this name in Greek
see dragon.

## Dracontium
Dracontium, п., a genus of plants of the arum
family (bot.)—-ModL., fr. L. dracontium, 'a kind
of plant, the dragon wort', fr. Gk. δρακόντιον,
of s.m., fr. δράκων, gen. δράκοντος, 'dragon'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:255 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DRACUNCULUS | 228 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:255 COLUMN:1 -->
See dragon.

## dracunculus
dracunculus, п., 1) the Guinea worm; 2) a fish;
3) (cap.) a genus of plants of the arum family
(hot.) — L., 'a small serpent; a kind of fish;
the plant tarragon', dimin. of draco, 'dragon'.
See dragon and -cuius.

## draff
draff, п., dregs. — ME. draf, 'dregs', rel. to ON.
draf, 'refuse', Dan.,.Norw. drat, Swed., MLG.,
MDu., Du. draf, OHG. trebir, MHG., G. treber,
'draff', and possibly also to OHG. truobi,
MHG. iriiebe, G. Iriib, 'dull, sad'; fr. I.-E. base
*dhrebh-, 'to make firm, curdle', whence also
Russ. drob, droba, 'dregs, lees', Lilh. drimbii,
dribti, 'to fall in clots', drebiii, drebti, 'to blot,
blur', drebnus, 'fat', Gk. τρέφειν, *to make solid,
thicken, congeal, curdle; to nourish' (lit. 'to
make thick'), θρόμβος (a nasalized enlargement
of base *dhrebh-), 'lump, clot', θρόμβωσις,
'coagulation'. Cp. drivel. Cp. also thrematology,
threpsology, threptic, thrombo-, thrombosis,
trophic.
Derivative: draff-y, adj.

## draft
draft, n. — ME. drahl, draught, fr. OE. dragon,
'to draw'. See drag, draw, and cp. draught.
Derivatives: draft, draught, tr. v. and adj.,
drafter, draught-er, п., draft-ing, draugkt-ing, п.,
draft-y, draught-y, adj.

## drag
drag, tr. and intr. v. — ME. draggen, fr. OE.
dragon or ON. draga, 'to draw'. See draw and
cp. draggle. Cp. also droshky.
Derivatives: drag, n. (q.v.), dragg-er, п.,
dragging, adj., dragg-ing-ly, adv., dragg-y, adj., dragg-
i-ly, adv., dragg-i-ness, n.

## drag
drag, n. — Fr. prec. word. The various meanings
of this noun are all traceable to the original
meaning, 'that which drags or is dragged'. Cp.
drogue.

## draggle
draggle, tr. and intr. v. — Formed from the verb
drag with freq. suff. -le. Cp. drawl.
Derivative: dragg-ly, adv.

## dragoman
dragoman, п., guide and interpreter. — F.
dragoman, drogman, fr. It. dragomano, fr. MGk.
δραγούμανος, fr. targumdn, Egypt,
pronunciation of Arab, tarjumdn, fr. Aram, turgh'mana, ult.
fr. Akkad. targumanu, 'interpreter'. See Targum.

## dragon
dragon, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. draconem, ace.
of draco, 'a kind of a serpent; dragon', fr. Gk.
δράκων, which prob. means lit. 'the sharp-
sighted one', and is rel. to δέρκεσθαι, 'to look
at', fr. I.-E. base *derk-, *drk-, 'to see, look at',
whence also OI. dars-, 'to see', da-daria, Ί have
seen', darsatdh, 'visible', drs-, 'seeing, sight',
Avestic darshti-, 'sight', Alb. drite (for *drkta-),
'light', Goth. (ga)tarhjan, 'to make distinct',
OE. torht, 'bright', OHG. zoraht, 'clear', Olr.
derc, 'eye', W. drych, 'aspect', drem, Bret.
dremm (for *d[k-sma), 'face'. Cp. darshana,
Dracaena, Dracontium, dracuncalus, dragoon,
drake, 'dragon', rancle, tarragon.
Derivatives: dragon-ess, п., dragonet (q.v.), dra-
gonnade (q.v.)

## dragonet
dragonet, п., ι) a little dragon; 2) a small marine
fish. — OF., dimin. of dragon. See dragon'
and -et.

## dragonnade
dragonnade, п., persecution of the French pro-
testants during Louis XIV; military attack on
the civil population. — F., fr. dragon, 'dragoon'.
See dragon and -ade.

## dragoon
dragoon, n. — F. dragon, 'dragon, diagoon,
carbine' ; so called from its resemblance to the fire
breathing dragon of the fable. See dragon.
Derivatives: dragoon, tr. v., dragoon-age, п.,
dragoon-er, n.

## drall
drall, tr. and intr. v., to drag or trail; to draggle.
— A blend of drag and trail.
Derivative: drail, n.

## drain
drain, tr. and intr. v. — ME. draynen, fr. OE.
drehnigean, dreahnian, drehnian, 'to strain', lii.
'to dry out', and rel. to OE. dryge, 'dry'. See dry.
Derivatives: drain, п., drain-age, п., drain-ed,
adj., drain-er, n.

## draisine
draisine, п., a dandy horse. — F. draisine, drai-
sienne, fr. G. Draisine, named after its inventor,
Baron Karl von Drais of Saverbrun near
Mannheim (died in 1851).

## drake
drake, п., the male of the duck. — ME. drake,
rel. to LG. drake and to the second element in
OHG. anutrehho. (This latter stands for *anut-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:255 COLUMN:2 -->
trahho, a compound, the first element of which
is cogn. with L. anas, 'duck'; see Anas.) ME.
and LG. drake and the second element in OHG.
*anut-trahho are of imitative origin and mean
'drake'. (Cp. Alamannic ratsch, ratscher, 'drake',
from the verb ratschen, 'to rattle'.) Accordingly
OHG. anutrehho (whence MHG. antrech, G.
Enterich) is tautological and lit. means 'duck-
duck'.

## drake
drake, п., dragon. — ME., fr. OE. draca, fr. L.
draco, 'dragon'. See dragon.

## dram
dram, п., a weight. — OF. drame (F. drachme),
fr. L. drachma, 'drachma', fr. Gk. δραχμή, 'an
Attic weight; a silver coin', lit. 'a handful', rel.
to δραγμή, 'handful', δράγμα, 'a sheaf, lit. 'as
much as one can grasp, a handful', from the
stem of δράσσεσ&αι (for *8ράχ-σεσίΚίί), 'to
clutch, grasp, seize'; cogn. with Arm. trcak,
'faggot', perh. also with OSlav„ po-dragu,
'border', OHG. zarga, 'border, edge, frame',
ON. targa, OE. targe, 'shield, buckler'. Cp.
drachma, Drassidae. Cp. also targe, 'shield'.

## drama
drama, n. — Late L., fr. Gk. δράμα, 'deed, act,
action represented on the stage, drama', fr.
δρ5ν,4ο do, accomplish', which is rel. Ιοδραίνειν,

dramatis personae, the characters in a play. — L.

## dramatist

## dramatize

## dramaturge

δραματουργός, 'a maker of plays, dramatist', which
is compounded of δράμα, gen. δράματος,'drama',
and έργον, 'work'. See drama and work and cp.
ergon and words there referred to. The word
dramaturge was introduced into French in 1668
by the poet Jean Chapelain (1595-1674).

## dramaturgy
dramaturgy, п., composition and production of

## drank

## drape
drape, tr. v. — F. draper, 'to cover with cloth,

derives fr. 1-Е. *dre-p-, 'to tear off, whence also
OI. drapih, 'mantle, garment'. Lith. drapanos
(pi.), 'linen, women's linen, undergarment' (the
original meaning prob. was 'a piece torn off),
Gk. δρέπειν, 'to pluck', Russ. drdpati, drjdpati,
Pol. drapat, Serbo-Croat, drapati, 'to scratch,
tear'. I.-E. *dre-p- is a -p-enlargement of base
*der-, 'to flay*, whence Gk. δέρειν, 'to flay*,
δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma and cp. drab, 'a kind
of cloth', trap, 'clothes'. Cp. also the first
element in drepanoid.

drape, n. — Partly fr. F. drop, partly fr. drape, v.

## draper
draper, n. — ME., fr. AF. draper, which

## drapery
drapery, n. — OF. (= F.) draperie, fr. draper, 'to

## Drassidae

See dromedary,
dromedary, n. — OF. dromedaire (F. dromadaire),

δέδρομα, Ί ran', δρόμος, 'a running, course,
race, racecourse', fr. l.-E. base *drem-, 'to run',
whence also OI. dmmati, 'runs'. Base *drem- is a
collateral form of base *dra-, 'to move q uickly, to
run', whence ОI. drdli, 'runs, hastens', Gk. άποδι-
δράσκειν, 'to run away' (with reduplication of
base *δρϊ-), δρϊσμός, 'a running away, flight',

'Αδράστεια, 'Nemesis', lit. 'from whom there is no
escape', and prob. also ON. titra, OHG. zit-
tardn, 'to tremble'. Cp. Adrastea, -drome,
Dromiacea, Dromiceius, dromond, and the
second element in anadromous, Boedromion,
catadromous, hippodrome, lampadedromy, loxo-
dromic, palindrome, prodrome, syudrome. Cp.
also teeter. — The change of a to e in Late L.

words ending in -edarius, as essedarius, 'a fighter
in a British or a Gallic war chariot' (see esse-
dum), veredarius, 'post boy, courier' (fr. veredus,
'a swift horse'). F. dromadaire—with a
instead of e—has been refashioned after Gk.
δρομάς.

droop, intr. v., to sink, hang down; to fail; tr.v.,
to let sink or hang down. — ME. droupen, fr.

ON. drupa, 'to droop, sink', which is rel. to

## ON. dropi
ON. dropi, OE. dropa, 'drop'. See next word.

## ing-ly
ing-ly, adv., droop-ing-ness, n.

## drop
drop, n. — ME. drope, fr. OE. dropa, 'drop', rel.

## to OS. dropo
to OS. dropo, ON. dropi, MLG. troppe, Du.

## drop
drop, OHG. tropfo, MHG. tropfe, G. Tropfen,
'drop', OE. dreopan, OS. driopan, ON. drjiipa,

## OFris. driapa
OFris. driapa, Du. druipen, OHG. triofan,

## MHG.
MHG., G. triefen, 'to drop, drip'. All- these

formative element—Lett, drupul drupl, 'to
crumble to pieces'. Cp. drip. Cp. also the second
element in Cladrastis and in lithontriptic.

## drop
drop, tr. and intr. v. — OE. dropian, fr. dropa,
'drop'. See drop, n.
Derivatives: dropp-er, п., dropp-tng, n.

## droplet
droplet, n. — Formed fr. drop, п., with dimin.
suff. -let.

## dropsy
dropsy, n. — ME. dropsie, aphetic for ME. idrop-
sie, ydropsie, fr. OF. idropisie (F. hydropisie),
fr. L. hydropisis, fr. Gk. ΰδρω^|ι, 'dropsy', which
is formed from ϋδωρ, 'water', and suff. -ωψ, lit.
'-eyed'. See hydro- and -ops and cp. hydropsy,
which is a doublet of dropsy.
Derivatives: drops-ical, adj., drops-ical-ly, adv.

## Drosera
Drosera, п., a genus of plants, the sundew (hot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. δροσερός, 'dewy', fr. δρόσος,
'dew', which is of uncertain origin; so called
because the glands of the leaves exude drops
of a fluid resembling dewdrops.

## Droseraceae
Droseraceae, n.pl., the sundew family (hot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## droseraceous
droseraceous, adj. — See prec. word and -accous.

## droshky
droshky, also drosky, n. — Russ. drozki (pl.\
dimin. of drogi (pi.), 'wagon', rel. to doroga,
(which corresponds to Pol. draga, Czech draha),
'way', and cogn. with Norw. drag, 'drawing
rope', and with ON. draga, 'to draw'; see drag,
draw. For the relationship between Russ. drogi,
'wagon', and doroga, 'way', ср. Е. wain and
wagon, which are related to way.

## drosometer
drosometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
quantity of dew. — Compounded of Gk.
δρόσος, 'dew', and μέτρον, 'measure'. See
Drosera and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## dross
dross, п., refuse. — ME. drosse, fr. OE. dross,
'dregs, dirt', rel. to drosna (pi.), 'dregs', MDu.
droesen(e), Du. droesem, OHG. truosana,
MHG. drusene, G. Drusen, 'husks, dregs', and
to E. dreg (q.v.) Cp. druse.
Derivatives: dross, tr. v., dross-er, п., dross-y,
adj., dross-i-ness, n.

## drought
drought, n. — ME. drougth, drugthe, fr. OE.
drugad, drugod, rel. to OE. drugian, 'to dry,
wither', dryge, 'dry', and to Du. droogte,
'drought'. See dry.
Derivative: drought-y, adj.

## drove
drove, п., a number of cattle, or other animals,
driven; a herd. — ME. drof, drove, fr. OE. draf,
drxf, 'drove, herd, crowd, band', rel. to drifan,
'to drive'. See drive.
Dirivative: dro-ver, n.

## drove
drove, past tense of drive. — ME. drof, fr. OE.
draf, 'drove', fr. drifan, 'to drive'. See drive.

## drown
drown, intr. and tr. v. — ME. drunen, drounen,
corresponding to OE. "drunian. Cp. ME. drunk-
nen, fr. OE. druncnian, 'to become intoxicated;
to be drowned'. Cp. also ON. drukna, 'to be
drowned', G. ertranken, 'to drown', ertrinken,
'to be drowned', and see drink.
Derivatives: drown-er, п., drown-ing-ly, adv.

## drowse
drowse, intr. and tr. v. — OE. drusian, drusan,
'to become languid, to be slow or sluggish', rel.
to driosan, 'to fall, sink'. See dreary.
Derivatives: drowse, п., drows-y, adj., drows-i-
ly, adv., drows-i-ness, n.

## drub
drub, tr. v., to beat with a stick; intr. v., to stamp.
— The orig. meaning was 'to bastinado'; prob.
fr. Arab, darb, 'a beating (with a stick)', fr.
daraba, 'he beat, struck'.
Derivatives: drub, п., drubb-er, п., drubb-ing, n.

## drudge
drudge, intr. and tr. v. — ME. druggen, prob. fr.
OE. dreogan, 'to work, suffer, endure'. See dree.
Derivatives: drudge, п., drudg-ery, п., drudg-
ing-ly, adv.

## drug
drug, n. — ME. drogge, drugge, fr. F. drogue, fr.
MLG. droge fate, 'dry casks', i.e. 'goods in
packing cases', in which phrase droge was
mistaken to be the name of the contents. See E.
Gamillscheg, Etymologisches Worterbuch der
franzosischen Sprache, 1918, p.327. For the
etymology of MLG. droge see dry.
Derivatives: drug, tr. and intr. v. drugg-er, п.,
druggery (q.v.), drugget (q.v.), druggist (q.v.),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:257 COLUMN:2 -->
drugg-y, adj.

## druggery
druggery, п., l) drugs; 2) a place for selling drugs.
— F. droguerie, fr. drogue. See drug and -ery.

## drugget
drugget, п., a coarse woolen fabric. — F. droguet,
fr. drogue, 'drug; worthless stuff, trash'. See drug,

## druggist
druggist, n. — F. droguiste, a hybrid coined fr.
drogue and -iste, a suff. of Greek origin. See
drug and -ist.

## druid
druid, п., an ancient Celtic priest or soothsayer.
— F. druide, fr. L. pi. druides (Caesar), druidae
(Cicero), fr. OCelt. druid, which stands for
*dru-wid, and is compounded of *daru-, *dru-,
'oak', and *wid-, 'know', hence lit. meaning
'they Who know the oak'; so called in allusion
to their practices with the mistletoe. Cp. Pliny,
16, 249. For the first element see tree and cp.
dryas, Drusilla, for the second see vision.
Derivatives: the hybrids druid-ess, п., druid-ic,
druid-ic-al, adjs., druid-ism, п., druid-ry, n.

## drum
drum, n. — Prob. fr. LG. trumme or MDu. trom-
me, 'drum'; cp. Du. trom, trommel, Dan. trom-
me, MHG. trunte, trumme, trumbe, G. Trommel,
Dan. tromme, Swed. trumma, 'drum'; of
imitative origin. Cp. trombone, trommel, trump,
'trumpet'.
Derivatives: drum, intr. and tr. v., drumm-er, п.,
drumm-y, adj.

## drum
drum, n. — See drumlin.

## drumble
drumble, п., a sluggish person. — A var. of
dumble, which itself is a dial. var. of dummel.
Derivative: drumble, intr. v., drumbl-er, n.

## drumiin
drumiin, п., a small hill consisting of glacial drift
(geol.) — Fr. drumling, dimin. of drum, 'ridge'
(cp. 2nd drum), fr. Gael, and Ir. druim, 'back,
ridge', which is rel. to Olr. druimm, W. Irum,
of s.m.
Drnmmond light. — Named after the Scottish
engineer Thorns Drummond(L797-1840).

## drunk
drunk, adj. — ME. drunke, alter, of drunken, fr.
OE. druncen, 'drunk', fr. drincan, 'to drink';
prop. pp. of drink.
Derivatives: drunk, п., drunk-ard, п., drunken
(q.v.), drunk-ery, n.

## drunken
drunken, adj. — ME., fr. OE. druncen, 'one who
has drunk, intoxicated'; prop, old pp. of drink.
Cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: drunken-ly, adv., drunken-ness, n.

## drupe
drupe, п., stone fruit (bot.) — F., fr. L. drupa,

δρύππά, which is shortened fr. δρυ-ττεπής,
'ripened on the tree', said especially of olives. See

Derivatives: drup-aceous, adj., drupel (q.v.),

## drupel
drupel, drupelet, п., a little drupe. — Formed fr.

## druse

## Druse
Druse, п., member of a Mohammedan sect. —
Arab. durBz, pi. of darazl, 'Druse'. Named after
the founder of the sect, Ismail ad-Darazi, 'the
tailor' (11th cent.) Cp. darzee, 'tailor'.

## Drusilla
Drusilla, fern. PN. — L. Drusilla, fern, dimin. of
L. Drusus, a surname frequently occurring in
the Livian gens, for earlier Drausus, which is
prob. a Celtic word and lit. means 'strong'. Cp.
OCelt. *daru-, *dru-, 'oak; strong', and see druid.

## dry
dry, adj. — ME. dry, drie, fr. OE. dryge, 'dry',

Du. droog, OHG. trucchan, MHG. trucken,
trocken, G. trocken, 'dry', ON. draugr, 'dry
wood', OE. drugad, drugod, 'drought'. Cp.
drain, drogher, drought, drug.
Derivatives: dry, п., dry-ish, adj., dry-ly, adv.,
dry-ness, n.

## dry
dry, tr. and intr. v. — ME. dryen, drien, fr. OE.

Derivative: dry-er, n.

## dryad
dryad, п., a forest nymph. — L. dryas (pi. drya-
dis), fr. Gk. δρυάς (pi. δρυάδες), fr. δρυς, gen.
δρυός, 'oak; tree', which is rel. to δρυμός, 'oak-
wood; wood', δόρυ, 'stem, tree, beam, shaft of
a spear, spear', δένδρεον, δένδρον (dissimilated
fr. *δέρ-δρεί-ον), 'tree', fr. I.-E. base *derew-
(o)-, *d<-ew(o)-, 'tree, wood', whence also OE.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:257 COLUMN:3 -->
treo, triow, 'tree, wood'. See tree and cp. dendro-,

Compounded of the words dry as dust.
Derivative: dryasdust, adj., dry and pedantic.

## dual
dual, adj., composed of two. — L. dualis,

## dualin

## duality
duality, п., the quality of being dual. — F. dua-

## dualize

## dub

OF. adober (also spelled aduber, adouber), 'to

## dub
dub, п., a pool, a puddle. — Of uncertain origin.

dubash, dobash, п., an Indian interpreter. —
Hind, dubhaskiya, dobashi, lit. 'a man of two

## dubber

## dubious
dubious, adj. — L. dubiosus, 'doubtful', fr. dubius,

prob. appears also in the second element of L.
probus, 'good, serviceable', and superbus,

διφυής, 'of double nature or form', which is
formally the exact equivalent of L. dubius.

## dnbitable
dnbitable, adj. — L. dubitabilis, 'doubtful', fr.

## dubitative

## ducal
ducal, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a duke.

Derivative: ducal-ly, adv.

## ducat
ducat, п., name Qf several coins. — OF. (= F.),

Empire (1059-67), which was impressed upon the
gold coins struck during his reign. This name
was confused later with It. ducato, 'duchy,
dukedom', fr. duce, 'duke', fr. L. ducem, ace. of dux,
'leader' (see duke).

## duchy

## ducker

duckling, п., a young duck. — Formed fr. duck,

dictil-ity, n.

Named after ils discoverer, the Danish

## ductor

## dud
dud, п., a shell that fails to explode. — Prob. fr.

dudaim, п., a variety of melon. — Heb. dudha'tm
(pi.) (Gen. 30:14), 'mandrake', prop, 'love-
exciting (plant)', fr. sing. *duday, rel. to dodh,
'beloved, uncle'. Cp. David,

## dude
dude, п., a dandy (U.S. Slang). — Of uncertain

## dudeen
dudeen, dudheen, п., a small tobacco pipe. — Ir.

## duidin
duidin, dimin. of dud, 'pipe'. For the ending see

## Dndelsack
Dndelsack, п., bagpipe. — G„ fr. Czech dudy,

## duduq
duduq, 'pipe', which is prob. of imitative origin.

For the second element in Dudelsack see sack,

## dudgeon
dudgeon, п., 1) a wood, prob. boxwood, used for

## dudgeon
dudgeon, п., anger. — Of unknown origin.

## duds
duds, n. (pi.), cast-off clothes, rags. — ME. dudde,
'clothes', rel. to ON. dudi, 'swaddling clothes',

## duda
duda, 'to wrap up'. Cp. dud. Cp. also dowdy.

due, adj. — ME., fr. OF. deii (F. du), fr. VL.

## duel
duel, n. — F., fr. L. duellum, archaic form of

duenna, п., an elderly woman; a chaperon. —

duet, n. — F., fr. II. duetto, 'duet', dimin. of due,

quartet, quintet, sextet.

## duffer

dufrenoysite, п., a lead arsenic sulfur compound

dug. — Past tense and pp. of dig.

## dug
dug, pap, teat. — Rel. to Dan. dxgge, Swed.

## diigga
diigga, 'to suckle', fr. I.-E. base *dhe(i)-, 'to
suckle'. See fecund and cp. words there
referred to.

## dugong
dugong, п., a cetaceous mamma]. — Malay

## duyung
duyung, Javanese duyung.

## duiker
duiker, п., a small horned antelope of S. Africa.
— S. Afr. Du., lit. 'diver', fr. Du. duiken, 'to

## dive'. See duck
dive'. See duck, 'to dive'.

## dukan
dukan, п., priestly blessing; prop, the platform
in the Temple on which the priests pronounced
the blessing (Jewish religion). — Mishnaic Heb.

## dukhdn
dukhdn, 'platform', lit. 'place to stand on', rel.

## to Arm. dukh (masc)
to Arm. dukh (masc), dukhtd (fern.), 'place'.

## Cp. Arab
Cp. Arab, dukkdn, 'platform'.

## duke
duke, n. — ME. due, duk, fr. F. due, fr. OF. due,

## ace. of dues
ace. of dues, fr. L. dux, gen. ducis, 'leader,

## conductor
conductor, chief, commander', fr. ducere, 'to lead,

## conduct
conduct, guide, draw', fr. OL. doucere, fr. I.-E.
base *douk-, *deuk-, 'to pull, draw', whence
also Gk. δαιδύσσεσθαι (for *δαι-δΰκιεσθαι), 'to

## drag'
drag', Alb. nduk, Ί pluck*, MW. dygaf Ί draw',

## OE. teon
OE. teon, 'to draw', and prob. also Hitt. tuh-

## hushzi
hushzi, 'he takes*, tuhkantish, 'first leader'. See

## tow
tow, 'to draw', and cp. words there referred to.

## Cp. also abducent
Cp. also abducent, abduct, adduce, adduct, an-

## douille
douille, aquaduct, conduce, conduct, conn,

## deduce
deduce, deduct, endue, dock for ships, dogaressa,

## dogate
dogate, doge, douche, ducat, ducatooa, duchess,

## duchy
duchy, duct, educate, educe, ednct, ednction,

## induce
induce, induction, introdnce, introduction, produce,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:258 COLUMN:3 -->
product, production, redoubt, reduce, reduction,
redirit, ridotto, seduce, seduction, subduce,
subduct, subdue, snperinduce, tradnce, traducinn,
tradnction, ventidnct, vindnct.

## Dukhobors
Dukhobors, n. pi., the name given by the
Russian Orthodox Church to a nonconformist
sect. —Russ. duchobortsy, lit. 'spirit fighters', fr.
duch, 'spirit', and bortsy, pi. of borets, 'wrestler,
fighter'. The first element is rel. to OSlav. duchu,
'spirit, breath', duSa, 'soul', andcogn. withLith.
dvasia, 'spirit', Lett, dvasa, 'breath, odor', Goth.
dius, 'wild animal', orig. 'a breathing being',
OE. deor, 'a wild animal'; see deer. The second
element is rel. to borot'sja, 'to wrestle', borba,
'wrestling', and cogn. with L. ferire, 'to strike',
forare, 'to bore, pierce', fr. I.-E. base "bher-,
'to cut, bore', whence also OE. borian, 'to bore';
see bore, v., and cp. words there referred to.

## dulcet
dulcet, adj., sweet. — Refashioned after L. dul-
cis It. OF. doucet, 'sweetish, sweet' (whence F.
doucel, 'demure, mild'), formed with dimin.
suff. -et fr. L. dulcis, 'sweet; pleasant,
charming', which stands for *dfkwis and is cogn. with
Gk. γλυκύς (for *δλυκ-ύς), 'sweet'. Cp. billet-
doux, dolce, dolce far niente, douce, Dulcie,
dulcify, dulcimer, Dulcinea, glucinum, edulcorate,
glucose, glyceria, glycerine, glyco-, licorice,
Polydeuces.

## Dulcie
Dulcie, fern. PN. — Lit. 'sweet', fr. L. dulcis. See
prec. word.

## dulciflcation
dulciflcation, n. — See next word and -ation.

## dulcify
dulcify, tr. v., to sweeten. — L. dulcificare, fr.
dulcis, 'sweet', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to make,
do'. See dulcet and -fy.

## dulcimer
dulcimer, п., an old musical instrument. — OF.
doulcemele, also (with dissimilation) doulcemer,
fr. L. dulce melos, 'a sweet tune'. See dulcet and
melody.

## Dulcinea
Dulcinea, п., sweetheart, worshiped by her lover.
— From the name of Don Quijote's mistress in
Cervantes' celebrated work. The name lit.
means 'sweet', fr. L. dulcis. See dulcet.

## dull
dull, adj. — ME. dulle, dull, fr. OE. dyl, an
unrecorded parallel form of OE. dot, 'foolish,
presumptuous', rel. to OE. dwellan, 'to lead
astray', dwala, dwela, gedwola, 'error', gedwelan,
'to err', OE. dwolma, 'chaos', OS., OFris.,
MLG., MDu., Du. dol, OHG., MHG., lot, G.
toll, 'mad, furious', OHG. gitwelan, 'to be
perplexed', MLG. dwal, Goth, dwals, 'foolish', Du.
dwalen, 'to roam, wander, err', and cogn. with
Olr. OCo., W., Bret, dall (for *dh"alno-),
'blind', Olr. cluas-dall, deaf, lit. 'troubled with
regard to one's sight, resp. hearing', Lith. du-
lineti, 'to fool around', Lett, duls, 'half-mad',
Gk. Э-ολός (for "θίολός, 'mud; the dark juice
of the cuttle fish', ftoXtav, 'to make muddy',
8-ολερός, 'muddy, dirty; troubled'. All these
words are derivatives of I.-E. base *dhwel-,
'muddy, gloomy, dim, dull'. Cp. doldrums, dolt,
dwale, dwell. Base *dhwel- is an -/-enlargement
of base *dheu-, 'to fly about like dust'. See thio-
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: dull, tr. and intr. v., dull-ard, п.,
duii-ish, adj., dull-ness, п., dul-ly, adv.

## dulocracy
dulocracy, also doulocracy, rule of slaves. —
Compounded of Gk. δοΰλος, 'slave', and -κρατία,
'rule'. The first element stands for *δόελος and
derives fr. Aegean doerq, 'slave'. The second
element comes fr. Gk. κράτος, 'strength, power,
rule'. See -cracy and cp. the second element in
hierodule.

## dulse
dulse, п., an edible seaweed. — Ir. and Gael.
duileasg.

## duma
duma, n.r the former Russian national assembly.
— Russ., lit. 'thought', of Teut. origin. Cp.
Goth, doms, 'judgment', and see doom.

## dumb
dumb, adj. — OE. and ME., rel. to ON. dumbr,
'dumb', Dan., Swed. dum, 'dull, stupid', Du.
dom, 'stupid', OHG. tumb, 'dumb, stupid',
MHG. tump, G. dumm, 'stupid', Goth, dumbs,
'dumb'. The orig. meaning of all these words
was 'dumb'. They derive fr. I.-E. base "dhumbh-,
a nasalized form of base 'dhubh-, 'to fill with
smoke, to cloud, darken; to be dull, dumb or
deaf. See deaf and cp. dummy. Cp. also stove.

## dumbcow
dumbcow, tr. v., to browbeat (Anglo-Ind.) —
Hind. dhamkanH, 'to chide, threaten'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:259 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: DUMBFOUND | 232 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:259 COLUMN:1 -->

## dumbfound
dumbfound, tr. v. — A blend of dumb and
confound.

## dumdum
dumdum, п., bullet with soft nose, expanding on
contact. — From the place name Dumdum (near
Calcutta); the name lit. means 'hill, mound,
battery', and is cogn. with Pers. damdama,
of s.m.

## dummy
dummy, п., a model. — For dumb-y. See dumb
and adj. surf. -y. The orig. meaning of dummy
was 'a dumb creature'. For primitive sense and
formation cp. blacky, whity.
Derivative, dummy, v.

## dummy
dummy, adj., silent. — For dumb-y. See prec.
word.

## dumontite
dumontite, п., a hydrated phosphate of uranium
and lead {mineral.) — Named after the Belgian
geologist Andre-Hubert Dumont (1809-57). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## dnmose
dnmose, dumous, adj., bushy. — L. dumosus, 'full
of thornbushes', fr. dumus, 'thornbush,
bramble', fr. OL. dusmus, which prob. stands for
*dus-mos and is cogn. with MHG. zus-ach,
'bush', OHG. zir-zuson, 'to tug, pull, dishevel',
ME. -tousen, -tusen (in compounds), of s.m. See
touse and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending see adj. sufT. -ose, resp. -ous.
Derivative: dumos-ity, n.

## dump
dump, п., a thick ill-shaped lump. — Back
formation fr. dumpy.

## dump
dump, tr. and intr. v., to let fall, to plunge. —
A Scand. loan word; cp. Dan. dumpe, Norw.
dumpa, 'to fall down suddenly', which are of
imitative origin.
Derivatives: dump, п., dump-er, п., dump-ing, n.

## dump
dump, п., sadness, melancholy. — Rel. to G.
Damp/, 'steam, vapor', dump/, 'hollow, gloomy,
musty', Dan. dump, 'dull', and to E. damp (q.v.)
Derivatives: dump-ish, adj., dump-ish-ly, adv.,
dump-ish-ness, n.

## dumpling
dumpling, п., a round pudding. — Formed fr.
dump, 'a lump', with the double dimin. suff. -ling.

## dumpy
dumpy, adj., short and thick. — Prob. of
imitative origin. Cp. dnmp, 'a lump'.
Derivatives: dumpi-ly, adv., dumpi-ness, n.

## dumpy
dumpy, adj., sulky. — Formed fr. dump,
'sadness', with adj. suff. -y.

## dun
dun, adj., dark brown. — ME. dunn, donn, fr. OE.
dunn, rel. to OS. dosan, OE. dosen, 'chestnut-
brown' (said of the color of a horse), OHG.
dosan, tusin, 'pale yellow', and cogn. with Mir.
dunn, Gael, donn, 'brown, dark', W. dwnn,
'brownish'; formed fr. I.-E. base *dhus- with
suff. *-no. For other enlargements of the same
base cp. L. fuscus, 'dark', furvus, 'dark, brown,
swarthy', and OE. dose, dox, 'dusk'. See dusk
and fuscous and cp. donkey. Cp. also the first
element in Duncan.
Derivatives: dun-ness, п., dunn-ish, adj., dunn-y,
adj.

## dun
dun, tr. v., to demand with insistence the
payment of a debt. — Denominated from the name
of Joe Dun, a London bailiff famous for
catching defaulters.
Derivative: dun, п., a creditor who demands the
payment of a debt.

## dun
dun, п., a hill; a hill fortress. — Ir. and Gael, dun,
'hill, hill fort, fortress'. See town and cp. down,
'hill', dune, and the second element in Merlin.

## Duncan
Duncan, masc. PN. — A name of Gaelic origin,
compounded of donn, 'brown' (see dun, 'dark
brown'), and ceann, 'head'.

## dunce
dunce, п., a stupid person. — A contemptuous
appellative formed from the name of John Duns
Scotus by the followers of St. Thomas Aquinas
in ridicule of the disciples of the former. John
Duns Scotus was born in the village of Duns in
Scotland, whence his name. According to my
opinion, the sense development of the word
dunce from Duns, 'of Duns', is prob. due to an
awkward pun made on the word Scorns
('Scotchman'), which was interpreted as Sottus
('stupid, foolish'; see sot).

## dundasite
dundasite, п., a lead aluminum carbonate
{mineral.) — Named after Dundas in Tasmania. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## dunder
dunder, п., the lees or dregs of cane juice (W.
Indies). — Corrupted fr. Sp. redundar, 'to
overflow', fr. L. redundare. See redundant.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:259 COLUMN:2 -->

## dunderhead
dunderhead, п., a stupid person. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: dunderhead-ed, adj.

## Dundreary whiskers
Dundreary whiskers, often shortened to dun-
drearies, n. pi. — So called from the form of
whiskers worn by E. A.Sothern (1826-81) in the
role of Lord Dundreary in Tom Taylor's Our
American Cousin.

## dune
dune, п., sand hill formed by the wind. — F., fr.
ML. duna, fr. MDu. dunen. See down, 'hill'.
Derivative: dun-al, adj.

## dnng
dnng, n. — ME. dunge, fr. OE. dung, rel. to
OFris. dung ,OHG. tunga, MHG. tunge,G.Dung,
and to ON. dyngja, 'dung, heap, women's
apartment'. These words are traceable to I.-E. base
'dhengh-, 'to cover', whence also Lith. dengti,
'to cover', OI. dingim, Ί press'. For sense
development it should be considered that
according to Tacitus (in Germania, Chapter 16), the
Germans used to cover their houses with mud
to protect them against the cold.
Derivatives: dung, intr. and tr. v., dung-er, п.,
dung-y, adj.

## dungaree
dungaree, п., a coarse kind of cotton fabric. —
Hind, dungr'i, from the name of a village now
forming one of the quarters of Bombay.

## dungeon
dungeon, n. — ME. donjon, dongeon, fr. OF.
(= F.) donjon, 'keep of a lord's castle', fr. VL.
*dominionem, ace. of *dominio, fr. L. dominium,
'domain'. See dominion and cp. donjon, which
are both doublets of dungeon.
Derivatives: dungeon, tr. v., dungeon-er, n.

## dnniwassal
dnniwassal, п., a gentleman among the high-
landers in Scotland. — Gael, duine uasal, lit.
'a noble man', fr. duine, 'man', and uasal,
'noble', lit. 'high, exalted'. For the first element
see chthonian. The second element is rel. to Olr.
uasal, W. uchel (for *oup-selo-), 'high, noble',
Gael, os, Olr. os, Has (for *oup-su-), 'above,
over'; see hypsi-.

## dunk
dunk, v., to dip. — G. tunken, fr. MHG. tunken,
dunken, fr. OHG. dunkon, fr. earlier thunkon,
'to dip'; cogn. with L. tinguere, tingere, Gk.
τέγγειν, 'to moisten'. See tinge and cp. Dunker.

## Dunker
Dunker, п., one of a sect of German Baptists in
America who administer baptism only by triple
immersion, also called Dippers. — G. Tunker,
lit. 'dipper', fr. tunken, 'to dip'. See prec. word
and agential suff. -er.

## dunlin
dunlin, п., a kind of sandpiper. — Formed fr. dun,
'dark brown', with the double dimin. suff. -ling.

## dunnage
dunnage, п., loose packing of material to protect
cargo (naut.) — Of unknown origin.

## dunstable
dunstable, п., a straw hat or its plait. — From
Dunstable in Bedfordshire, England, where such
hats were made originally.

## dunstable
dunstable, adj., plain, direct. — So called from
Dunstable Road, an even road leading from
Dunstable to London.

## duo
duo, п., a duet {music). — It. duo, lit. 'two',
archaic form of due, fr. L. duo, 'two'. See dual
and cp. duo-,

## duo-
duo-, combining form meaning 'two'. — Fr. L.
duo, 'two'. See dual.

## duodecim-
duodecim-, combining form meaning 'twelve'. —
L. duodecim, 'twelve', fr. duo, 'two', and decern,
'ten'. See duo- and decern- and cp. dozen. Cp.
also dodeca-.

## duodecimal
duodecimal, adj., pertaining to twelve; pertaining
to a system of numbers the base of which is
twelve. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
duodecim, 'twelve'. See duodecim-.
Derivative: duodecimal, n.

## duodecimo
duodecimo, the size of a book in which each page
is the twelfth part of the printer's sheet,
abbreviated into 12mo. — L., abl. of duodecimus,
'twelfth', fr. duodecim. See duodecim- and cp.
twelvemo, sixteenmo.

## dnodenary
dnodenary, adj., in twelves; increasing by twelves.
— L. duodenarius, 'containing twelve', fr. duo-
deni, 'each twelve'. See duodenum and adj. suff.
-ary.

## duodenitis
duodenitis, п., inflammation of the duodenum
(med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr.
duodenum and -itis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## duodeno-
duodeno-, combining form, meaning 'referring to
the duodenum'. — See next word.

## duodenum
duodenum, п., the first part of the small intestine

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:259 COLUMN:3 -->
leading from the stomach to the jejunum
(anatomy). — ML. duodenum, coined by Gerard of
Cremona (died in 1187), the translator of the
Canon Avicennai, fr. L. duodini, 'twelve each',
fr. duo, 'two', and deni, 'ten each" which is rel. to
decern, 'ten' (see duodecim-, dozea); prop, loan
translation οίΰ^δωδεκαδάκτυλον, 'duodenum',
lit. 'twelve fingers long'; so called by the Greek
physician Herophilus (cca. 353-cca 280. B.C.E.)
from its alleged length of 12 fingers breadth.
The rendering of Gk. δωδεκαδάκτυλον into ML.
duodenum (see above) is incorrect. The correct
Latin rendering would be duodecim digitorum,
'of twelve fingers; twelve ringers long'.

## duologue
duologue, п., a dialogue between two persons. —
A hybrid coined fr. L. duo, 'two', and Gk. λόγος,
'word, speech, discourse'. See dual and -logue.

## duomo
duomo, п., a cathedral in Italy. — It., fr. L. do-
mus, 'house'. See dome.

## dup
dup, tr. v., to open. — Contracted of do and up.
Cp. doff, don, v., dout.

## dupe
dupe, п., a person who is easily misled. — F. dupe,
fr. de huppe, i.e. the agglutination of the prep, de
(see de-) with huppe, 'hoopoe', fr. L. upupa,
'hoopoe', a word of imitative origin. See hoopoe.
Derivatives: dupe, tr.v., dup-able, adj., dup-abil-
ity, п., dup-ery,

## dnple
dnple, adj. — L. duplus, 'double'. See double and
cp. next word.

## duplex
duplex, adj., twofold, double. — L., 'twofold,
double', cogn. with Gk. &ίπλιχξ, 'twofold,
double'; compounded of L. duo, 'two' (resp.
Gk. Si-, 'twice, double'), and -plex (resp. Gk.
-πλαξ), '-fold'. See double, adj., and cp. triplex.
Derivatives: duplex, n. and tr. v.

## duplicate
duplicate, adj., 1) double; 2) corresponding
exactly. — L. duplicatus, 'doubled', pp. of
duplicare, 'to double; to enlarge', fr. duplex, gen.
duplicis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate and
cp. conduplicate.
Derivative: duplicate, п., an exact copy.

## duplicate
duplicate, tr. v., 1) to double; 2) to make an exact
copy of. — L. duplicatus, pp. of duplicare. See
duplicate, adj.
Derivatives: duplication (q.v.), duplicat-ive, adj.,
duplicator (q.v.)

## duplication
duplication, n. — F., fr. L. duplicationem, ace. of
duplicatid, *a doubling', fr. duplicatus, pp. of
duplicare. See duplicate, v., and -ion.

## duplicator
duplicator, n. — L., 'a doubler', fr. duplicatus,
pp. of duplicare. See duplicate, v., and agential
suff. -or.

## duplicity
duplicity, п., double-dealing. — F. duplicite, fr.
Late L. duplicitatem, ace. of duplicitas, 'double-
ness', fr. L. duplex, gen. duplicis. See duplex and
-Ity and cp. trlplicity.

## durability
durability, n. — F. durabihte, fr. Late L. dura-
bilitaiem, ace. of durubiliias, fr. L. durSbilis. See
next word and -Ity.

## durable
durable, adj., enduring. — F. durable, fr. L.
durSbilis, 'lasting', fr. durare, 'to harden; to continue,
last', fr. durus, 'hard'. See dure, 'hard', and -able.
Derivatives: durable-ness, п., durabl-y, adv.

## durain
durain, п., a constituent of coal. — Formed fr.
L. durus, 'hard' (see dure, adj.), with suff. -ain,
on analogy of fusain.

## duralumin
duralumin, п., a strong alloy of aluminum with
copper, manganese and magnesium. — Prop,
name of an aluminum alloy first made at Diiren
in Germany. The word duralumin is a compound
of Durum in Marcodurum, ancient name of
Diiren, and of aluminum (q.v.)

## dura mater
dura mater, the tough outer membrane, which
surrounds the brain and the spinal chord (anal.)
— ML., shortened fr. dura mater cerebri, 'hard
mother of the brain', loan translation of Arab.
umm al-dimAgh as-$afya", 'it- 'thick mother of
the brain'. (In Arabic, the words 'father',
'mother' and 'son' are often used to denote
relationship between things). See dure, 'hard',
and mater, mother, and cp. pia mater.

## duramen
duramen, п., the hard wood in the center of the
tree trunk, the heartwood (bot.) — L. duramen,
'hardness; a hardened vinebranch', from the
stem of durare, 'to harden'. See dure, v., and
-men.

## durance
durance,п., ι)duration; 2) imprisonment. — OF.
durance, 'duration', fr. durer, 'to endure', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:260 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 233 | DVSACOUSIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:260 COLUMN:1 -->
L. durare, 'to harden; to continue, last', fr.
durus, 'hard'. See dure, adj., and -ance.

## durangtte
durangtte, п., a sodium aluminum fluoarsenate
(mineral.) — Named after Durango in Mexico.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## duration
duration, n. — Obsol. F., fr. Late L. durationem,
ace. of dfiratio, 'a hardening; duration', fr. L.
duratus, pp. of durare. See dure, v., and -atioa.

## durbar
durbar, п., a state levee; government of a native
state (India). — Hind, darbar, fr. Pers. darbar,
fr. dar, 'door, gate', and bar, 'court'. Pers. dar
is rel. to Avestic dvarem (ace. sing.), 'gate,
court', OPers. duvaraya-, 'at the door', and to
OI. dvarah (nom. pi.), 'door'. See door and cp.
the first element in dargah and in durwaun.

## durdenite
durdenite, п., a hydrous ferric tellurite (mineral.)
— Named after H. S. Durden, of San Francisco.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## dure
dure, adj., hard; severe (archaic). — F. dm, fern.
dure, fr. L. durus, 'hard, rough, rude', prob.
dissimilated fr. *dru-ros, for 'dreu-ros, and lit.
meaning 'as hard as wood', fr. I.-E. base *de-
rew(o)-, *drew(o)-, *dru-, 'tree, wood', whence
also Gk. δρυς, 'oak, tree', δήρυ, 'stem, tree, beam,
shaft of a spear, spear', OI. dru-, 'wood, wooden
vessel', daru, 'wood', OE. tree·, treow, 'tree,
wood'. See tree and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also doar, durable, durain, duralumin, dura
mater, duramen, durance, duration, duress,
during, endure, Indurate, obdurate, perdure.

## dure
dure, intr. v., to last (obsol. or poetic). — F. durer,
fr. L. durare, 'to harden; to continue, last', fr.
durus, 'hard'. See durej adj.

## duress
duress, п., ι) imprisonment; 2) compulsion. —
ME. duresse, fr. obsol. F. duresse, fr. L. durilia,
'hardness, severity, austerity', fr. durus. See
dure, adj., and -ess.

## durgah
durgah, n. — See dargah.

## durum
durum, dorinn, п., fruit of the tree Durio zibelh-
inus. — Malay durian, fr. dun, 'thorn'; so
called from its prickly rind. — Cp. Durio.

## during
during, prep. — Prop. pres. part, of the verb
dure; used in imitation of the Latin ablative
absolute.

## Durio
Durio, п., a genus of trees in Asia. — Fr. Malay
durian. See duriaa.

## durmast
durmast, п., a European oak (quercus sessili-
flora). — A compound, the first element of
which is of unknown origin. For its second
element see mast, 'acorns'.

## durra
durra, п., the Indian millet. — Arab. dhurah.

## durst
durst, past tense of dare. — OE. and ME. dorsie.
See dare.

## durwaun
durwaun, darwan, п., a doorkeeper (Anglo-Ind.)
— Pers. darban, darwan, compounded of dar,
'door, gate', and -ban, resp. -wan, 'keeper,
guardian'. For the first element see durbar, for
the second see ban, 'governor'.

## dusk
dusk, adj. — ME. dusk, dosk, fr. OE. dose, dox,
'dusk', rel. to Swed. duska, 'to be misty', OS.
dosan, 'chestnut brown', OHG. lusin, 'yellow',
and cogn. with L. fuscus (for *dhus-qo-), 'dark',
furvus (for *dhus-wo-), 'dark, brown, swarthy',
OI. dhusarah, 'dust-colored'. Cp. dun, 'dark
brown', fuscous.
Derivatives: dusk, n. and tr. and intr. v., dusk'
ish, adj., dusk-ish-iy, adv., dusk-ish-ness* п.,
dusk-y, adj., dusk-i-ly, adv., dusk-i-ness, n.

## dust
dust, n. — ME., fr. OE. dust, rel. to ON. dust,
'dust', Dan. dyst, 'milldust', OHG. tunst, tunisl,
'storm, breath', MHG. tunst, G. Dunst, 'vapor',
fr. I.-E. base *dhewes-, *dhwens-, *dhus-, 'to fly
about like dust', whence also OI. dhvamsati,
'falls to dust', Toch. В taur, A tor, 'dust', A twe,
В tweye, of s.m. For other derivatives of the
above base see thio- and words there referred to.
Derivatives: dust, tr. and intr. v., dust-er, п.,
dust-ing, verbal п., dust-less, adj., dust-y, adj.,
dust-i-ly, adv., dust-i-ness, n.

## dustoor
dustoor, n. — A var. of destour.

## Dutch
Dutch, adj. and n. — MDu. duutsc, dutsch, 'Hol-
landish, Dutch' (whence Du. duits, 'German'),
rel. to OS. thiudisk, OHG. diutisc, 'belonging to
the people' (whence MHG. tiutsch, G. deutsch,
'German'), Goth, piudisko, 'in a heathen way'.
OS. thiudisk, OHG. diutisc, and Goth, piudisko
derive fr. OS. thioda, resp. OHG. dial, Goth.
piuda, 'people', which are rel. to OFris. thidde.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:260 COLUMN:2 -->
ON. pjod, OE. plod, 'people'; fr. Teut. base
*peudo-, corresponding to I.-E. base *leuta-,
'people', whence Olr. tuoth, 'people', W. tud,
'country', Bret, tud, 'people', OLith. and Lett.
tauta, 'people', OPruss. tauto, 'country', Lith.
Tauta, 'Germany', Oscan touto, 'community',
Umbrian tuta, tota,oi s.m. Cp. Teuton, Theobald,
Theodoric and the second element in Platt-
deutsch. For sense development cp. Lett.

## duteous
duteous, adj., dutiful. — Formed with suff. -ous
fr. OF. duete, 'duty' (see duty); first used by
Shakespeare.
Derivatives: duteous-ly, adv., duleous-ness, n.

## dutiable
dutiable, adj. — Formed fr. duty with suff. -able.

## dnty
dnty, n. — ME. dueje. fr. AF. duete, fr. du,
corresponding to OF. deu, F. du, fr. VL. "debiitus
(for L. debitus), pp. of L. debere, 'to owe'. See
due and -ty.
Derivatives: dutiable (q.v.), duti-ful, adj., duti-
ful-ly, adv., duti-fitt-ness, n.

## duumvir
duumvir, п., one of two officials having the same
public function. — L., name of various
magistrates; back formation from the archaic gen.
pi. duum virum, '(one) of the two men'. See dual
and virile and cp. triumvir, decemvir.

## duumviral
duumviral, adj. — L. duumviralis, 'pertaining to
the duumvirs', formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-alts (see adj. suff. -al).

## duumvirate
duumvirate, n. — L. duumviratus, 'the office of a
duumvir'. See prec. word and subst. suff. -ate.

## dvaita
dvaita, п., dualism (Hindu philos.) — OI. dvaita-,
fr. dvi-, 'two' (in compounds), which is rel. to
Avestic bi-, and cogn. with Gk. δι-, OL. dvi-,
L. bi-, OE. iwi-. See di-, 'two', and cp. next
word.

## dvandva
dvandva, п., a copulative compound; dualism. —
OI. dvamdvd-, lit. 'pair, couple', reduplication
of dvd, 'two', which is rel. to Avestic dva and
cogn. with Gk. δύο, L. duo, 'two'. See dual and
cp. prec. word.

## dwale
dwale, п., the deadly nightshade. — Of Scand.
origin. Cp. Dan. dvale, Swed. dvala, 'stupor,
deep sleep', which are rel. to dwala, dwela, ge-
dwola, 'error', dwelian, 'to lead astray'. See
dwell.

## dwarf
dwarf, n. — ME. dwergh, dwerf, fr. OE. dweorh,
rel. to OS. gidwerg, ON. dvergr, Swed. dvdrg,
Dan., Du. dwerg, OFris. dwerch, OHG. getwerg,
twerg, MHG. getwerc, twerc, zwerc, G. Zwerg;
of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: dwarf, adj. and tr. and intr. v.,
dwarf-ish-ly, adv., dwarf-ish-ness, п., dwarf-y,
adj.

## dwell
dwell, intr. v. — ME. dwelien, fr. OE. dwelian,
'to lead astray, deceive; to hinder; to wander,
go astray; to tarry', rel. lo ON. dvelja, 'to delay;
to tarry', OHG. twaljan, 'to hinder, delay', OE.
dwolian, 'to stray, err', dwala, dwela, gedwola,
'error*, gedwelan, 'to err', and to E. dull, dnale
(qq.v.) For the sense development of E. dwell
(fr. OE. dwelian, 'to tarry'), cp. F. demeurer, 'to
remain, stay, lodge, reside, live'.
Derivatives: dwell, п., dwell-er, п., dwell-ing, n.

## dwindle
dwindle, intr. v. — Dimin. of next word. The
verb dwindle was first used by Shakespeare.

## dwine
dwine, intr. v., to waste away (archaic and dial.
Brit.) — ME. dwinen, fr. OE. dwinan, 'to
languish, waste away, vanish', rel. to ON. dvina,
MDu. dvinen, Dan. nine, of s.m., Du. verdwij-
nen, 'to waste away, vanish', and cogn. with
Arm. di, 'dead body, corpse', Olr. dith, 'end,
death'; fr. I.-E. nase "dhwei-, enlargement of
base *dhew-, *dheu-, 'to pine away, die', whence
Goth, diwans, 'mortal', and, with vowel
gradation, OS. doian, ON. deyja, 'to die', Goth.
daups, 'dead'. See dead and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: dwindl-er, n.

## dy-
dy-, combining form meaning 'two'. — Gk. δυ-,
fr. δύο, 'two', which is cogn. with L. duo, 'two'.
See dual.

## dyad
dyad, п., two units regarded as one. — Late L.
dyas, gen. dyadis, fr. Gk. δυάς, gen. δυάδος, 'the
number two', fr. δύο, 'two'. See dy- and -ad.

## dyadic
dyadic, adj., pertaining to a dyad. — Gk.
δυαδικής, 'pertaining to two', fr. δυάς, gen. δυάδος.
See prec. word and -ic

## Dyak
Dyak, п., one of the aborigines of Borneo. —
Malay, lit. 'savage'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:260 COLUMN:3 -->

## dyarchy
dyarchy, n. — See diarchy.

## dye
dye, n. — ME. deh, deih, die, fr. OE. dedg, deah,
'dye, color'; prob. cogn. with Lett, dukans,
'dark-colored*.

## dye
dye, tr. and intr. v. — ME. deyen, dyen, fr. OE.
deagian, fr. deag. See dye, n.
Derivatives: dy-er, п., dye-ing, n.

## dying
dying, adj. and n. — Formed from the verb die
with suff. -ing.
Derivative: dying-ness, n.

## dyke
dyke, n. — See dike.

## dyna-
dyna-, combining form meaning 'power'. —
Shortened fr. Gk. δύναμις, 'power'. See
dynamic.

## dynameter
dynameter, п., an instrument for measuring the
magnifying power of telescopes. —
Compounded of dyna- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: dynametr-ic, dynametr-ic-al, adjs.

## dynamic
dynamic, adj. — F. dynamique, coined by the
German philosopher and mathematician, Baron
Gottfried Wilhelm von Leibniz (1646-1716) fr.
Gk. δυναμικός, 'powerful', fr. δύναμις, 'might,
power*, which is rel. to δύναμαι, Ί am able,
I am worth', δυνατής, 'strong, able'; of
uncertain origin. Cp. dyna-, dynamite, dynamo-,
dynasty. For the ending see suff. -lc. The word
dynamic was introduced into English by Jeremy
Bentham (1748-1832).
Derivatives: dynamic, п., dynamic-al, adj., dy-
namic-al-ly, adv., dynamics (q.v.), dynam-ism,
п., dynam-ist, п., dynamite (q.v.)

## dynamics
dynamics, n„ that branch of physics which deals
with the action of force on bodies. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## dynamite
dynamite, n. — A name given by the Swedish
chemist Alfred Bernhard Nobel (1833-96) in
1867 to the explosive invented by him, fr. Gk.
δύναμις, 'power'. See dynamic and Subst. suff.
-ite.
Derivatives: dynamite, tr. v., dynamit-er, п.,
dynamit-ic, dynamit-ic-al, adjs., dynamit-ic-al-
ly, adv., dynamit-ism, п., dyniamil-ist, n.
dynamo- combining form meaning 'power'
(electr.) — Formed fr. Gk. δύναμις, 'power'
(see dynamic). The -o in dynamo- (for dynami-)
is due to the analogy of combining forms like
baro-, thermo-, etc., in which the о represents
Greek 0.

## dyaamo
dyaamo, п., a machine that converts mechanical
energy into electrical energy. — Orig. called
by its inventor, the German engineer Werner
von Siemens (1816-92), Dynamo-elektrische
Maschine ('dynamo-electric machine'). This
name was later shortened by him into Dynamo-
Maschine ('dynamo-machine'). The name
dynamo-machine was shortened in England (in
1882) into dynamo. See dynamo-.

## dynamometer
dynamometer, п., an instrument for measuring
power. — Compounded of dynamo- and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: dynamometr-y, п., dynamometr-ic,
dynamometr-ic-al, adjs.

## dynast
dynast, п., a ruler. — L. dynastes, fr. Gk.
δυνάστης, 'ruler', from the stem of δύναμαι, Ί am
able, I am worth'. See dynamic.

## dynastic
dynastic, adj. — Gk. δυναστικής, 'pertaining to
a ruler', fr. δυνάστης. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: dynastic-al-ly, adv.

## dynasty
dynasty, n. — F. dynastie, fr. Gk. δυναστεία,
'power, lordship', fr. δυνάστης. See dyaast and
-y (representing Gk. -cti).

## dyne
dyne, п., unit of force in the C.G.S. system (phys.)
— F., fr. Gk. δύναμις, 'power'. See dynamic
and cp. neutrodyne.

## dys-
dys-, pejorative suff. used esp. in the senses 'hard
to, difficult at, slow of';-the opposite of the pref.
eu-, — Gk. δυσ-, meaning 'hard, bad, ill', cogn.
with the suffixes OI. dus-, Avestic dusk-, duz-,
of s.m., Arm. I- (negative pref.), Goth, tuz-,
OHG. za-, zi-, zu-, zar-, zir-, zur-, MHG., G.
zer-, 'apart, asunder', ON. tor-, 'difficult, hard',
Olr. do-, du-, 'bad, ill', OS. to-, te-, ti-, OE. to-,
te-, tor-, 'apart, asunder', and perh. also with
OL. dvis (whence L. bis), 'twice'. See dls-.

## dysacousia
dysacousia, dysacousis, dysacusia, п., a condition
in which sounds cause discomfort (med.) —
Medical L., fr. dys- and Gk. ίίκουσις, 'a hearing',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:261 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OVSCHROA | 234 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:261 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. ακούω (for 'άκούσ^), Ί hear'. See acoustic
and cp. words there referred to.

## dyschroa
dyschroa, dyischrola, п., discoloration of the skin
(meet.) — Medical L., formed fr. dys- and Gk.
χράά, resp. χροιά, 'color'. See -chroin.

## dyscrasia
dyscrasia, п., an ill state of the body (meet.) —
Medical L., formed fr. dys- and κράσις, 'a
mixing, blending'. See crater and cp. crasis.
For the ending see suff. -ia.

## dysenteric
dysenteric, adj., i) pertaining to dysentery; 2)
having dysentery. — L. dysentericus, fr. Gk.
δυσεντερικός, 'pertaining to dysentery', fr.
δυσεντερία. See next word and -ic.

## dysentery
dysentery, п., inflammation of the large intestine.
— OF. elissenterie (F. etysenterie), fr. Medical
L. etysenteria, fr. Gk. δυσεντερία, 'dysentery',
which lit. means 'bad intestines', and was coined
by the Greek physician Hippocrates fr. δυσ-
(see dys·) and έντερα, 'intestines'. See enteric,

## dysgeaic
dysgeaic, adj., detrimental to the hereditary
constitution of the race; opposite to eugenic. —
Formed fr. dys- and -genie Cp. engenic.

## dyslogistic
dyslogistic, adj., unfavorable. — A blend of dys-
and eulogistic.
Derivative: dyshgislic-al-ly, adv.

## dyspepsia
dyspepsia, п., disturbed digestion (med.) — L.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:261 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. Gk. δυσπεψία, 'indigestion', lit. 'bad
digestion*, fr. δύσπεπτος, 'hard to digest', fr. δυσ- (see
dys-) and πεπτός, 'cooked', verbal adj. of
πέσσειν, πέπτειν, 'to cook, to digest'. See
pepsin and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## dyspeptic
dyspeptic, adj., pertaining to, or suffering from,
dyspepsia. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk.
δύσπεπτος, 'hard to digest'. See prec. word and
-ic and cp. peptic and words there referred to.

## dysphoria
dysphoria, п., mental anxiety; a general feeling
of indisposition. — Formed with suff. -ia fr.
Gk. δύσφορος,'hard to bear', fr. δυσ- (seedys-)·
and the stem of φέρειν, 'to bear, carry'. See
bear, 'to carry', and cp. euphoria. For the ending
see suff. -Ia.

## dyspnea
dyspnea, dyspaoea, п., difficult breathing (med.)
— L. dyspnoea, fr. Gk. δύσπνοια, 'difficulty in
breathing', fr. δύσπνοος, 'breathing with
difficulty', fr. δυσ- (see dys-) and πνοή, πνοιή,
'breath'. See pneuma and cp. eupnea.

## dysprosia
dysprosia, п., dysprosium oxide (chem.) — See
next word.

## dysprosium
dysprosium, п., name of an element (chem.) —
ModL., coined fr. Gk. δυσπρόσιτος, 'hard to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:261 COLUMN:3 -->
get at', fr. δυσ- (see dys-) and προσιτός, verbal
adj. of πρόσειμι, Ί go in*, fr. προς, 'toward, to*
(see pros-), and είμι, Ί go', which is cogn. with
OI. imi, L. еб, Ί go'. See itinerate and cp. words
there referred to. This element was so called,
because it was hard to reach.

## Dyssodla
Dyssodla, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δυσωδίά, 'an ill
smell', fr. δυσώδης, 'ill-smelling', fr. δυσ- (see
dys-) and βζειν, 'to smell', whence οσμή, 'smell,
odor' (see osmium and cp. hyposmin, parosmia);
so called from the ill smell of the leaves. For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## dystocia
dystocia, п., difficult parturition (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. δυστοκία, 'painful delivery', fr.
δυσ- (see dys-) and τάκος, 'childbirth,
parturition'. See -tocin.

## dystrophy
dystrophy, dystrophia, n,, defective nutrition
(med.) — Medical L. dystrophia, fr. dys- and
Gk. τροφή, 'nourishment'. See trophic and cp.
atrophy, hypertrophy.

## dysuria
dysuria, п., painful urination (med.) — Late L.,
fr. Gk. δυσουρία, fr. δυσ- (see dys-) and οΰρον,
'urine'. See urine and -ia.
Derivative: dysur-ic, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:262 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:262 COLUMN:1 -->
е-, form of L. σχ- before voiced consonants.
— See ist ex-.

## each
each, adj. — ME. зек, elc, eche, fr. ОЕ- ж/с, which
is short for a-geUc, 'ever alike', and is rel. to
OFris. elllK elk, Du. elk, OHG. iogilih, MHG.
iegelTch, G.jeglich, 'each, every'. See aye, 'ever',
and like, adj. and adv., and cp. ilk,

## eager
eager, adj. — ME. eger, egre, 'sharp, eager', fr.
AF. egre, corresponding to OF. (— F.) aigre,
'sour, acid; harsh, bitter, rough', fr. L. acrem,
ace. of deer, 'sharp, pointed, piercing; acute,
ardent, zealous'. See acrid and cp. agrito and
the second element in vinegar. Cp. also ear
of corn. Derivatives: eager-ty, adv., eager-ness, n.

## eagle
eagle, n. — ME. egle, fr. OF. egle, aigle (F.
aigle), fr. L. aquila, 'eagle', whence also It.
aquila, Rum. acera, Provenc. aigla, Sp. aguila,
Port, aguia, of s.m. See aquiline.
Derivative: eaglet (q.v.)

## eaglet
eaglet, п., a young eagle. — Formed fr. eagle
on analogy of F. aiglette, dimin. of aigle,
'eagle'. See prec. word and -et, -ette.

## eaglewood
eaglewood, п., agalloch. — Loan translation of
F. bois d'aigle, fr. Port, aguila, 'aloewood', fr.
Gk. άγάλλοχον, 'aloe, aloewood'; see agalloch.
French bois d'aigle arose from a confusion of
Port, aguila, 'aloewood', with Port, aguia, Sp.
aguila, 'eagle' (see eagle).

## eagre
eagre, п., a tidal wave; a bore. — Lit. 'water
borer', fr. OE. ёа, 'water', and gar, 'spear'. See
aquatic and gore, 'to pierce'.

## ean
ean, tr. and intr. v. — A var. of yean (q.v.)
Derivative: ean-ling (cp. yeanling).

## ear
ear, п., the organ of hearing. — ME. ere, fr. OE.
eare, rel. to ON. eyra, Swed. ora, Dan. ere,
OS., ODu., OHG. ora, OFris. are, Du. oor,
MHG. ore, G. Ohr, Goth, auso, and cogn. with
Gk. ους, gen. ώτός (for *ουσος, resp. *οϋσατος),
L. auris (for *ausis), Avestic ushi, 'both ears',
OSIav. ucho (gen. uSese, dual uii), Lith. ausis,
Lett, auss, OPruss. ausins (ace. pi.), Olr. au, δ,
'ear', Arm. unkn (for *uson-qo-m), Alb. ves,
'ear'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *au-,
'ear'. Cp. aural, 'pertaining to the ear', auricle,
auscultation, orillion, ormer, oto-, oyer, oyez.
Cp. also acroama.
Derivatives: ear-ed, adj., earing (q.v.)

## ear of corn
ear of corn, n. — ME. ere, ear, fr. OE. eare, rel.
to Du. aar, OHG. ehir, ahir, MHG. eher, G.
Ahre, ON. ax, Goth, ahs, 'ear of corn', fr. Teut.
*ahiz, corresponding to l.-E. 'altos-, whence L.
acus, 'chaff, husk', Gk. άκοστή, 'barley', lit. 'the
awny one', fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'to be sharp or
pointed', whence also L. acer, 'sharp, pointed'.
See acrid and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: ear-ed, adj.

## ear
ear, tr. v., to plow (archaic or obsol.) — ME.
erien, fr. OE. erian, rel. to OS. erian, ON. erja,
OFris. era, OHG. erien, Goth, arjan, fr. I.-E.
base *ara-, 'to plow', whence also L. arare, 'to
plow'. See arable,

## earing
earing, п., горе by which the upper corners of
a sail are fastened to the yard (naut.) — For
ear-ring. See ear, 'organ of hearing', and ring, n.

## earl
earl, п., a title of nobility. — ME. erl, fr. OE.
eorl, 'man, warrior, chief, nobleman', rel. to
ON. jarl, 'chief, nobleman', OS., OHG. erl,
'man'. Cp. jarl.

## earl
earl, tr. v., to pledge (Scot.) — Rel. to ME. erles,
erres, 'earnest money', fr. OF. erres, fr. L. arra.
See earnest, 'pledge', and cp. words there
referred to.

## earldom
earldom, n. — ME. erldom, fr. OE. eorldom, fr.
eorl. See prec. word and -dom.

## early
early, adv. — ME. erliche, erli, fr. OE. xrlice,
'early', compounded of жг, 'before', and suff.
■lice. See ere and adv. suff. -ly.
Derivatives: early, adj., earli-ness, n.

## earn
earn, tr. v. — ME. ernien, ernen, fr. OE. earnian,
'to deserve, earn', rel. to OHG. атёп, агпбп.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:262 COLUMN:2 -->
Ε
'to reap', OE. ern, OHG. aran, am, G. Ernte,
'harvest', Goth, asans, 'harvest, summer', ON.
onn (for *aznu), 'work in the field', and cogn.
with OSIav. jeseni, Russ. osen', OPruss. assanis,
'autumn'.
Derivatives: earn-er, п., earning, n. (q.v.)

## earnest
earnest, п., seriousness. — ME. ernest, fr. OE.
eornost, rel. to OS., OHG., ernust, 'struggle',
MHG. ernest, 'struggle; earnest', G. Ernst,
'earnest, seriousness', Goth, arniba, 'safely', ON.
jarna, 'fight, combat', ern, 'able, fit, vigorous',
orig. 'able to fight'. Cp. Ernest.
Derivatives: earnest, adj., earnest-ly, adv., ear-
nest-ness, n.

## earnest
earnest, п., pledge. — ME. ernest, ernes,
apparently fr. OF. erres, 'earnest money', fr. L. arra,
arrha, 'pledge', shortened fr. arrabo, arrhabo,
fr. Gk. άρραβών, 'earnest money', fr. Heb.
'erabhon, 'pledge, surety', fr. 'arabh, 'he
pledged'. Cp. arras, arrha, arles, earl, 'to pledge'.

## earning
earning, n. — OE. earnung, fr. earnian, 'to
deserve, earn'. See earn and subst. suff. -ing.

## earth
earth, n. — ME. eorthe, erthe, fr. OE. eorde, rel.
to OS. ertha, ON./dVd, Dan., Swed.^'oi-rf, OFris.
erthe, MDu. eerde, aerde, Du. aarde, OHG.
erda, MHG., G. erde, Goth, airpa, and cogn.
with Mir. -ert (in compounds), 'earth'; fr.
I.-E. base *er-t, a -(-enlargement of base *er-,
'earth', whence OHG. его, 'earth', Gk. ερϋ,
'earth', έρδζε (for *epSff-8e, cp. Dor. εράσδε),
'to earth', £ράς (prop. gen. of Spa), 'of earth'.
Fr. base *er-w-, a -^-enlargement of base *er-,
derive ON. jdrvi, 'sandbank', W., Co. erw,
'strip of land', OBret. его, 'furrow'. Cp. the
first element in aardvark, aardwolf.
Derivatives: earth, tr. and intr. v., earth-ed,
adj., earthian (q.v.), earth-less, adj., earth-like,
adj., earth-ly, adj., earth-li-ness, п., earth-y,

## adj.
adj., earth-i-ness, n.

## earthian
earthian, п., an inhabitant of the earth. — A
hybrid coined fr. E. earth and suff. -ian (fr. L.
-ianus).

## em-wig
em-wig, n. — ME. erwigge, fr. OE. earwicga,
'earwig', fr. eare (see ear, organ of hearing) and
wicga, 'insect, beetle', lit. 'the runner', rel. to

Eau de Cologne, cologne. — F., lit. 'water of

## eaves
eaves, n. pi., the edge of a roof. — ME. evese
(pi. eveses), fr. OE. efes, 'eaves, brim, border',
rel. to ON. ups, upse, OHG. obasa, obisa, 'porch,
hall, roof, MHG. obese, obse, 'eaves', dial.
G. Obsen, Obsten, 'porch', Goth, ubizwa,
'porch', OHG. obana, 'from above', G. oben,
'above', and to E. over, up. Derivatively, eaves
is a singular. It was mistaken for a plural
because of Ihe confusion of the final s in OE. efes
with the plural suffix. From the alleged plural
eaves the singular eave was formed. — Cp.
next word.

## envesdrop
envesdrop, intr. v. — Formerly eavesdrip, fr. OE.
yfesdrype, 'drip from eaves'. See eaves and drip.
To eavesdrop orig. meant 'to stand under
droppings from the eaves of a house', whence
arose the meaning 'to listen to a conversation
secretly' (lit. 'under the eaves', i.e. 'near the
window or door'.
Derivatives: eavesdropp-er, п., eavesdropp-ing,n.

## ebauchoir

— F. ibauchoir, fr. ebaucher, 'to rough out,

bauch, bale, 'beam', fr. Frankish 'balk; cp.
OHG. balko, 'beam', OE. balca, 'ridge between

ebb, n. — ME. ebbe, fr. OE. ebba, rel. to OS.

ebb, intr. v. — ME. ebben, fr. OE. ebbian, fr.

## ebba

## Eblis
Eblis, п., the prince of the fallen angels (Arabian

mistaken for the Syriac genitive particle di and

## ebon
ebon, п., ebony (poetic}. — ME. ebon, fr. L.

## ebonite
ebonite, п., vulcanite. — Forrned fr. ebony with

## ebonize

## ebony
ebony, n. — OF. ebaine (F. ebene), fr. L. ebenus
(whence also OHG., MHG. ebenus, G. Eben-
holz), fr. Gk. ίβενος (whence also Arabo-
Persian abnQs), fr. Egypt, hebni (whence also

ebriety, п., drunkenness. — F. ebriete, fr. L.

## ebullience
ebullience, ebulliency, n. — Formed fr. next word

## ebullient
ebullient, adj., boiling up, exuberant. — Lit.

## ebullioscope

## ebullition

## Eburna
Eburna, п., a genus of marine gastropods, the

ebumine, adj., eburnean. — Formed with suff.

ecbolic, adj., causing abortion (med.) — Formed

abortion'ч fr. έκβάλλειν, 'to throw out', fr. έκ ·

ecce homo,' 'behdtd-the man' (see John 19:5). —

eccentric, adj. — F. excentrique, fr. ML. excen-

Out of the centre', fr. έκ (see ec-) and κέντρον,

ecchymosis, п., extravasation of blood (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. έκχόμωσις, 'bruise,

## ecclesin
ecclesin, п., ι) assembly of citizens in ancient
Athens; 2) a church. — L. ecclesia, 'assembly

εκκλησία, 'an assembly of citizens', in Eccles.

## ecclesiast

## Ecclesiastes
Ecclesiastes, п., name of one of the 5 Scrolls of
the Hagiographa, corresponding to Heb. Qohe-
leth (Bible). — L. ecclesiastes, fr. Gk.
εκκλησιαστής, 'speaker in an assembly', fr. εκκλησία,
'assembly'; see ecclesia and -ast. (For the
meaning of εκκλησιαστής ср. Plato, Gorgias, 452e;
the usual rendering as 'preacher', is erroneous.)
Accordingly, εκκλησιαστής, the translation of
qdheleth in the LXX, is the exact rendering of
this Hebrew word, which derives fr. qahal,
'assembly'.

## ecclesiastic
ecclesiastic, adj., pertaining to the churcb;

clesiaslicus, fr. Gk. εκκλησιαστικές, 'pertaining
to the assembly or the ecclesia', fr. εκκλησία.
See ecciesia and -ic and cp. Ecclesiastes.
Derivatives: ecclesiastic, п., ecciesiastic-al, adj.,
ecclesiaslic-al-ly, adv., ecclesiastic-ism, n.

## Ecclesiasticus
Ecclesiasticus, п., name of the Jewish apocryphal

Jesus, the son of Sirach. — Eccles..L.
Ecclesiasticus, lit. 'pertaining to the church', fr. Gk.
