-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ecclesiolog-ic, ecclesiolag-ic-al,
adjs., ecclesiolog-ic-al-ly, adv., ecclesiolog-ist, n.

## eccrinology
eccrinology, п., the study of secretions (phy-
siol.) — Compounded of Gk. έκκρΐνειν, 'to

(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. The first element is formed fr.
έκ (see ec-), and κρίνειν, 'to separate'. See

## ecderon

Coined by Huxley fr. ec- and Gk. δέρος, 'skin',

## ecdysis

έκδυσις, 'getting out, putting off, shedding',

## echelon
echelon, п., sleplike formation of troops (mil.)
— F. echelon, fr. ichelle, 'ladder', fr. L. scala,

Echenels, п., a genus of fishes, the remora (ich-
thyol.) — ModL., fr. L. echeniis, 'remora', fr.

Gk. έχενηΐς, lit. 'ship-detaining', compounded
of εχειν, 'to have, hold', and ναϋς, gen. νηός,
'ship'(see hectic and naval); so called in allusion
to its alleged power of detaining a ship.

## echidna
echidna, п., an Australian egg-laying mammal.
— L., 'adder, viper', fr. Gk. ίχιδνα, prop. fern,

## ecbino-
ecbino-, combining form meaning 'prickly, spiny'.

## Echinochion
Echinochion, п., a genus of grasses (bol.) —
ModL., lit. 'hedgehog grass', fr. ecbino- and
Gk. χλόη. Dor. χλόά, 'grass', which is rel. to

## Echinocystis
Echinocystis, п., a genus of plants, the wild

## Echinodermata
Echinodermata, n. pi., a phylum of sea animals

spiny skin', compounded of echino- "and Gk.
δέρματα, pi. of δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma.

Echinodorus, п., a genus of herbs (bot.)—ModL.,

dory-.

## Echinops
Echinops, п., a genus of plants, the globe thistle
(bol.) — ModL., lit. 'resembling a hedgehog',
fr. echino- and Gk. -ωψ, lit. '-eyed', fr. ώψ, gen.
ώπός, 'eye'. See -ops.

## echinus
echinus, п., sea urchin, pi. echini. — L., fr. Gk.
έχϊνος, 'hedgehog, sea urchin', prob. formed
fr. ίχις, 'viper' (see echidna), with suff. -ΐνος;

Lett, ezis, OE. igel, ME. II, OS., OHG., MHG.,
G. igel, Du. egel, 'hedgehog'.

## Echinm
Echinm, п., a genus of plants, the viper's bugloss
(bot.) — ModL., fr; Gk. ^χιον, lit. 'viper's
plant', fr. έχις, Viper'. See echidna.

## echo
echo, n. — L. echo, fr. Gk. ήχώ, 'sound, noise;
echo', rel. to ήχή, 'noise', ήχεΐν, 'to resound',
fr. Gk. base *ίαχ- (whence also ίάχειν, 'to
resound'), corresponding to I.-E. 'wag-, 'to
sound', whence OI. vagnufi, 'sound', L. vagire,
'to cry'. Cp. catechize, vagitus.
Derivatives: echo, tr. and intr. v., echo-er, п.,
echo-ic, adj., echo-ism, п., echo-ist, п., echo-ize,
intr. v.

## eclair
eclair, п., a kind of light long cake filled with
cream. — F„ lit. 'lightning', back formation fr.
iclairer, 'to light, illuminate', fr. VL. 'excla-
riare (whence also OProvenc. esclairar),
corresponding to L. exclarare, 'to light up, illumine',

## eclampsia

Medical L., fr. Gk. Εκλαμψις, 'a shining forth', fr.
έκλάμπειν, 'to shine forth', fr: έκ (see ec-) and
λάμπειν, 'to shine'. See lamp and -la. The word
eclampsia was introduced into medical
terminology by the French pathologist Francois-
Boissier de la Croix de Sauvages (1706-67).

## eclamptic
eclamptic, adj., pertaining to eclampsia. — See
prec. word and -ic.

## eciat
eciat, п., brilliancy, applause. — F., 'burst, crash,
clap; shiver, splinter; brightness', back
formation fr. F. iclater, 'to burst, split, shiver; to
explode; to cry out, exclaim; to shine, sparkle,
flash', fr. OF. esclaler, 'to break, burst', prob. fr.
Frankish 'station, 'to rend, tear', which is rel.
to OHG. sti^an, OE. slitan, of s.m. See slit and
cp. slate, 'piece of rock', and slate, 'to censure'.

## eclectic
eclectic, adj., selecting doctrines from various
philosophic systems. — Gk. εκλεκτικές,
'picking out, selecting', fr. εκλεκτός, verbal adj. of
εκλέγειν, 'to pick out, select', fr. έκ (see ec-),
and λέγειν, 'to pick out, choose; to tell, say,
speak'. See lecture and -lc and cp. eclogue.
Derivalives: eclectic, п., an eclectic philosopher,
eclectic-al-ly, adv., eclectic-ism, n.

## eclipse
eclipse, η. — OF. eclipse (F. eclipse), fr. L. eclip-
sis, fr. Gk. εκλειψις, 'a leaving out, forsaking,
failure; eclipse', fr. έκλείπειν, 'to leave out,
forsake, cease; to be eclipsed', Jr. έκ (see ec-)
and λείπειν, 'to leave', which is cogn. with L.
linquere, 'to leave'. See relinquish and cp. ellipse.
Derivatives: eclipse, tr. v., eclips-er, n.

## ecliptic
ecliptic, adj., l) pertaining to an eclipse; 2)
pertaining to an ecliptic. — L. eclipiicus,
'pertaining to an eclipse', fr. Gk. έκλειπτικός, fr.
έκλείπειν. See prec. word and -ic.

## ecliptic
ecliptic, п., apparent annual path of the sun. —
Fr. L. linea ecliptica, 'the ecliptic', fr. eclipiicus,
'pertaining to an eclipse'. The ecliptic was so
called because it was supposed that eclipses of
the sun and moon take place on the great circle
forming the apparent annual path of the sun.

## eclogue
eclogue, п., a short poem of pastoral character.
— F. eclogue, eglogue, fr. L. ecloga, fr. Gk.
εκλογή, 'a choice, selection', fr. εκλέγειν, 'to
pick out, select'. See eclectic

## eclosion
eclosion, п., the process of hatching of a chicken
from an egg, or of an insect from a pupa case
(zool.) — F. eclosion, 'a breaking forth,
hatching', lit. 'an opening', fr. iclos, pp. of eclore, 'to
be hatched, to open' (said of an egg), fr. VL.
'exclaudere, 'to shut out, exclude, drive out';
'to hatch out' (tr.), refashioned (after L. clau-
dere, 'to shut, close'), fr. L. excludere, of s.m.
See exclude and -Ion.

## eco-
eco-, oeco-, combining form meaning
'environment'. — Gk. οίκο-, fr. οίκος, 'house'. See
economy,

## ecology
ecology, oecology, п., that branch of science which
deals with animals and plants in relation to their
environment. — G. Okologie, coined by the
German biologist Ernst Heinrich Haeckel
(1834-1919) fr. Gk. οίκο- (see eco-) and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ecolog-ic, ecolog-ic-al, adjs., ecolog-
ic-al-ly, adv., ecolog-isl, n.

## economic
economic, adj. — F. economique, fr. L. oecono-
micus, 'pertaining to economy; orderly,
methodical', fr. Gk. οικονομικός, 'economical', fr.
οικονομία. See next word and -ic.
Derivatives: economic-al, adj., economic-al-ly,
adv., econom-ics, n.

## economy
economy, n. — L. oeconomia, 'the management of
a household', fr. Gk. οικονομία, of s.m., fr.
οικονόμος, 'the manager of a household,
steward', which is compounded of οίκος, 'house,
dwelling, place to live in', and -νόμος,
'managing'. Gk. οίκος (dial, ίοϊκος), is rel. to οίκίά,
Gortynic Gk. foutii, 'house', and cogn. with
L. vicus, 'district', vicinus, 'near, neighboring',
Goth, weihs, OE. улс, 'dwelling, village'. See
vicinage, wick, 'village', and cp. androecium,
nutooecious, diocese, dioecious, ecumenical,
monoecious, oecist, oecus, parish; paroecious, peri-
oeci. Gk. -νόμος stands in gradational
relationship to νέμειν, 'to deal out, distribute,
allot'. See Nemesis and cp. nomud,

## ecru
ecru, adj., of the yellowish color of unbleached
linen. — F. ecru, formed with pref. i- fr. L.

## crudus
crudus, 'raw' (whence also It., Sp. crudo,

## OProvenc. cru
OProvenc. cru, crut). See crude. The pref. e- in
ecru derives fr. L. ё, 'out of (see e-), but has
here only intensive force.

## ecstasy
ecstasy, n. — OF. extasie (F. extase), fr. Late
L. ecstasis, fr. Gk. ϊκστασις, 'removal from

## the proper place
the proper place, displacement', lit. 'a standing
outside oneself, from the stem of έξιστάναί,
'to put out of place, derange; to stand aside
from', fr. έξ, 'out of (see 2nd ex-) and ίστάναι,
'to place; to stand'. See state,

## ecstasy
ecstasy, tr. v. — F. extasier, fr. extase. See
ecstasy, n.

## ecstatic
ecstatic, adj., pertaining to, or causing, ecstasy.
— Gk. εκστατικός, 'unstable', fr. ϊκστασις. See
prec. word and -Ic. Derivative: ecslatic-al-ly, adv.

## ect-
ect-, form of ecto- before a vowel.

## ectasia
ectasia, п., the same as ectasis. — Medical L.
See next word.

## ectasis
ectasis, п., dilation of a tubular vessel (med.) —

## Late L. ectasis
Late L. ectasis, 'a stretching out', fr. Gk. έκ-
τασις, fr. έκτείνειν, 'to stretch out', fr. έκ (see
ec-) and τείνειν, 'to stretch'. See tasimeter and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:264 COLUMN:2 -->
cp. atelectasis, entasia, entasis, epjtasis, protasis,
ecthlipsis, п., the suppression of a consonant. —
Late L., fr. Gk. έκ&λΐψις, 'a squeezing out', fr.
έκϋλίβειν, 'to squeeze out', fr. εκ (see ec-) and
θλίβειν, 'to press, crush*. See thlipsis.
ecto-, before a vowel ect-, combining form
meaning 'outside, external'. — Att. and Ion.
Gk. έκτο-, έκτ-, fr. εκτός, 'outside', formed fr.
έκ, 'out of, with suff. -τός, on analogy of εντός,
'inside' (fr. έν, 'in'). The regular form should
have been "έχ&ός. Ср. Locrian έχθάς = Att.
and Ion. έκτος, and see ec-.
ectoblast, п., the outer membrane of a cell (biol.)
— Compounded of ecto- and Gk. βλαστός,
'sprout'. See -blast,
ectoderm, п., the outer investing membrance of
a cell (biol.) — Lit. 'outer skin', coined by the
German physician Robert Remak(l8l5-65)fr.
ecto- and Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma and
cp. endoderm, mesoderm,

## -ectomy
-ectomy, combining form denoting 'surgical
removal', as in appendectomy, gastrectomy. — Gk.
-εκτομία, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting
out, excision', fr. έκτέμνειν, 'to cut out', fr.
έκ (see ec-) and τέμνειν, 'to cut'. See -tomy.

## ectopia
ectopia, п., morbid displacement of an organ or
another part of the body (med.) — Medical L.,
formed with suff. -ia fr. Gk. έκτοπος, 'away
from a place', fr. έκ (see ec-) and τόπος, 'place'.
See topic. Derivative: ectop-ic, adj., out of place.

## Ectopistes
Ectopistes, п., a genus of pigeons, the wandering
pigeon (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έκτοπίζειν,
'to remove from a place', fr. έκτοπος. See prec.
word and -ist.

## ectoplasm
ectoplasm, п., the external layer of a protoplasm
in a cell (biol.) — Compounded of ecto- and
piasm. Cp. endoplasm.

## ectro-
ectro-, combining form denoting congenital
absence (med.) — Fr. Gk. έκτρωσις, 'miscarriage',
fr. έκτιτρώσκειν, 'to miscarry', fr. έκ (see ec-)
and τιτρώσκειν, 'to wound, hurt, injure'. See
throw and cp. words there referred to.

## ecu
ecu, п., an old French silver coin. — F., fr. OF.
escu, fr. L. scutum, 'shield'. See scutum and cp.
escudo. The coin was called ecu ('shield') from
the coins issued under Louis IX, which had the
shield of France as device.

## ecumenic
ecumenic, ecumenical, adj., general, universal. —
Late L. oecumenicus, fr. Gk. οικουμενικός, 'open
to the whole world', fr. οικουμένη (scil. γη),
'the inhabited world', fem. of the pass. pres.
part, of οίκεΐν, 'to inhabit', fr. οίκος, 'house,
abode, dwelling'. See ecoaomy and -ic. For the
use and force of the passive suff. "-menos in
English words of Greek and Latin origin see
alumnus and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: ecumenical-ly, adv., ecumenic-ity, n.

## eczema
eczema, п., inflammatory disease of- the skin
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. έκζεμα, prop,
'something thrown out by heat', fr. έκ (see ec-)
and ζέμα, 'that which is boiled', fr. I.-E. base
"yes-, 'to boil, seethe'. See yeast and cp. the
first element in zeolite and the second element
in apozem.

## eczematous
eczematous, adj., of the nature of ec2ema. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. έκζεμα, gen.
εκζέματος. See prec. word.

## -ed
-ed, 1) pp. suff. of weak verbs in English; 2) used
also to form adjectives: a) from nouns, as in
cultured; b) from other adjectives ending in -ate
(derived from L. pp.s in -alus), as in foliated,
demoted. — ME. -ed, fr. OE. -ed, -od, -ad,

## formed from the thematic vowel -e-
formed from the thematic vowel -e-, resp. -o-

## or -a-
or -a-, and -t, the pp. ending of weak verbs,

## which is rel. to ON. -pr
which is rel. to ON. -pr, G. -t, Goth, -bs, Teut.
*-do, corresponding to I.-E. *-to, whence OI.

## -tdh
-tdh, Gk. -τός, L. -tus. Cp. the final -d in cold,

## dead
dead, loud, old, sad and suff. -t. Cp. also adj.
suff. -ate.

## -ed
-ed, suff. of the past tense of weak verbs in
English. — ME. -ede-, -de, fr. OE. -ede, -ode, -ade,

## formed from the thematic vowel -e-
formed from the thematic vowel -e-, resp. -o-

## or -a-
or -a-, and -de, past ending of the 1st pers. of

## weak verbs
weak verbs, which is rel. to the corresponding

## endings ON. -pa
endings ON. -pa, OHG. -la, G. -te, and prob.

## also to OE. -ie)d
also to OE. -ie)d, pp. ending of weak verbs. See

## -ed
-ed, pp. suff.

## -ed
-ed, suff. forming adjectives from nouns, with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:264 COLUMN:3 -->
the sense 'possessed of, characterized by', as in
bearded, toothed. — OE. -ede, rel. to OS. ~odi.
edacious, adj., devouring, voracious. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. L. edax, gen. edacis,
'voracious, gluttonous', fr. edere, 'to eat'. See eat.
Derivatives: edacious-ly, adv., edacious-ness, n.
edacity, п., voracity. — L. edacitas, 'voracity,
gluttony', fr. edax, gen. edacis. See prec. word
and -ity.
Edam cheese, often shortened to Edam, edam, n.
— From Edam, name of a village in Holland,
where this cheese was originally made.
edaphic, adj., pertaining to the condition of the
soil rather than to climate {plant ecology). —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. έδαφος, 'soil;
floor', which was probably dissimilated fr.
•έδαφος and is rel. to έδος, 'seat, base,
foundation', fr. stem *έδ- (= I.-E. *sed-), 'to sit',
and cogn. with L. sedlre, 'to sit'. See sedentary
and cp. next word.
edaphology, п., the study of soils. —
Compounded of Gk. 6&αφος, 'soil', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See edaphic and
-logy.

## Edda
Edda, п., orig. name of the book written by
Snorri Sturluson (died in 1241); later used to
denote ancient Icelandic poems in general. — ΟΝ.,
fr. 6dr, 'spirit, mind; passion, song, poetry', rel.
to OE. w6p, 'sound, melody, song', and cogn.
with Olr. faith, 'poet', W. gwawd, 'poem', L.
votes, soothsayer, prophet, seer'. See vales and
cp. words there referred to.

## eddy
eddy, п., whirlpool; current of air. — ME. ydy,
prob. fr. ON. ida, 'whirlpool', lit. meaning 'that
which rebounds or flows back', fr. ON. pref.
id-, 'again', which is rel. to OE., OS. ed-, OHG.
et-, it-, Goth, ip, 'and, but, however', and cogn.
with L. et, 'and'. See et. Derivative: eddy, inlr. v.

## ede-
ede-, form of edea- before a vowel.

## eden
eden, n. pi., the external genitals. — Fr. Gk.
αιδοία, 'privy parts, pudenda', prop. neut. pi.
of αίδοΐος, 'bashful, shamefaced', lit. 'having
a claim to regard', fr. αιδώς, 'shame, bash-
fulness, reverence', fr. the stem of α?δεσ&αι,
'to be ashamed, fear, show a sense of regard,
respect', which prob. stands for *αΙσδεσθαι, fr.
I.-E. *aiz-d-, whence also OI. i$i (for *izdi), Ί
honor', Goth, aistan, 'to fear'. I.-E. *aiz-d- is
a-i/-enlargementofbase*a/i-,'tohonor,respect',
whence OHG. era, MHG. ire, G. Ehre, 'honor',
ON. eir, 'grace', OE. Sr, 'honor, dignity, benefice,
prosperity, help, kindness, mercy'. Cp. the first
element in Eric.

## edelweiss
edelweiss, п., а small Alpine plant bearing white
flowers. — G. Edelweifi, compounded of edel,
'noble', and weifi, 'white'. For the first element
see atheling, for the second see white,

## edema
edema, oedema, a swelling (med.) — Medical L„
fr. Gk. οίδημα, 'a swelling', fr. οίδϊν, οίδεΐν, 'to
swell', which is cogn. with Arm. aitnum, Ί
swell', aitumn, 'a swelling', L. aemidus (for
*aidmo-dos or *aidsmo-dos), 'swelling', ON.
eisla (for *oid-s-to-), 'testicle', eitill, 'swelling',
eitr, 'poison', OE. ator, at tor, p( s.m., and prob.
also with OSlav. jadu, 'poison', jadra (pi.),
'bosom'. See atter and cp. the first element in
Oedipus and the second element in myxedema.
Derivatives: edem-ic, oedem-ic, edemat-ous,
oedemat-ous, also edemat-ose, oedemat-ose, adjs.

## Eden
Eden, п., in the Bible, the garden in which Adam
and Eve first lived; Paradise. — Heb. 'ndhen,
name of the region in which lay the Paradise
(see Gen. 2:8, 10, 15, etc.) The name is usually
explained as 'the place of delight', and derived
fr. Heb. 'idhen, 'dainty, delight'; cp. Edna. U.
Cassuto in his Commentary on the Book of
Genesis, Part One, From Adam to Noah, The
Hebrew University, Jersusalem, 1961, pp. 107-
108, explains the name Eden—with reference
to the meaning of the base 'dn in Ugaritic—
as 'a place that is well watered throughout'.
Derivative: Eden-ic, adj.

## edenite
edenite, п., a variety of aluminous amphibole
(mineral.) — Named after Edenvilh, New York.
For the ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## Edentata
Edentata, n. pi., a group of placental mammals

## including the armadillo
including the armadillo, sloth, anteater, etc.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:265 COLUMN:1 -->
(zool.) — ModL., neut. pi. of L. edentatus,
'toothless', pp. of edentare, 'to render

## edentate
edentate, adj., l) toothless; 2) pertaining to the
Edentata. — L. edentatus, 'toothless'. See prec.
word.
Derivative: edentate, п., one of the Edentata.

## edeo-
edeo-, before a vowel ede-, combining form

## edestin
edestin, п., formerly, a globulin found in various

fr. Gk. έδεστός, 'eatable', fr. ίδειν, 'toeat'. See eat.

## Edgar
Edgar, masc. PN. — OE. Eadgar, compounded
of lad, 'wealth, prosperity, happiness', and gar,
'spear'. The first element is rel. to OS. od, OHG.
*oi, the second element in MHG. kleindt
(whence G. Kleinod, 'jewel, gem', lit. 'little
wealth'), ON. audr, Goth, auda-, 'possession,
property, prosperity, wealth', OE. eadig, OS.
odag, ON. audigr, OHG. itag, Goth, audags,
'rich'. Cp. the first element in Edith, Edmund,
Edward, Edwin, and the second element in
allodium. For the second element in Edgar see
gar and cp. words there referred to.

## edge
edge, n. — ME. egge, fr. OE. ecg, 'edge; sword',
rel. to OS. eggia, ON. egg, Dan. eg, OS. eggia,
MDu. egghe, Du. eg, egge, OHG. ecka, egga,
MHG. ecke, egge, G. Eck, Ecke, 'edge, point',
ON. eggja, 'to provoke', fr. I.-E. base *ak-,

Gk. άκή, 'point', ίίκρος, 'sharp', L. deer, 'sharp,
bitter'. See acrid and words there referred to
and cp. esp. egg, 'to urge'. Cp. also the first
element in Egbert.
Derivatives: edge, tr. v., edg-ing, п., edg-ing-ly,
adv., edg-y, adj., edg-i-ness, n.

## edible
edible, adj. — Late L. edibilis, 'eatable', fr. L.

Derivatives: edibil-ity, п., edible-ness, n.

## edict
edict, n. — L. edictum, 'proclamation, ordinance,
edict', prop. neut. pp. of edicere, 'to declare,

Derivatives: edict-al, adj., edicl-al-ly, adv.

## edification
edification, n. — L. aedificatio, gen. -onis, 'a

aedificare. See edify and -ation.

## edifice
edifice, п., a building. — F. edifice, fr. L. aedi-
ficium, 'a building', from the stem of aedificare.
See next word.

## edify
edify, tr. v. — ME. edifien, fr. F. edifier, fr. L.
aedificare, 'to erect a building, to build', fr.
aedls (or aedis), 'a building, sanctuary, temple',
orig. 'a place with a hearth', and -ficare, fr.
facere, 'to make, do'. L. aedes derives fr. I.-E.
base 'aidh-, 'to burn', whence also Gk. αϊθειν,
'to burn', αί&ρά, 'the clear sky, fair weather',
«1%, 'the upper, purer air, ether', ίδαρός,
'clean, pure, clear', OI. inddhi, 'bursts into
'flame', idhah, idhmah, 'wood for burning',
OE. ad, OHG. eit, 'funeral pile, fire', Olr. aed,
'fire', W. aidd, 'heat, zeal'. Cp. aedile, Aethusa,
Aludel, estival, estuary, ether, Ethiop, oast. For
the second element in edify see -fy.
Derivatives: edifi-er, п., edify-ing, adj., edify-
ing-ly, adv., edify-ing-ness, n.

## edtngtonite
edtngtonite, п., a hydrous aluminum barium

Mr. Edington of Glasgow. For the ending see
subst. surf. -ite.

## edisonite
edisonite, п., a variant of rutile (mineral.) —
Named after the American inventor Thomas
Alva Edison (1847-1931). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## edit
edit, tr. v. — Back formation fr. editor (q.v.)

## Edith
Edith, fern. PN. — OE. Eadgyth, compounded
of ead, 'wealth, prosperity, happiness', and gud,
'war'. For the first element see Edgar and cp.
words there referred to. OE. gud is rel. to OHG.
gund-, ON. gunnr, guar, 'war', and cogn. with
Gk. θείνειν, 'to strike', φόνος, 'murder', L.
-fendere, 'to thrust, strike'. See defend and cp.
the words there referred to.

## edition
edition, n. — F. edition, fr. L. editionem, ace. of

editio, 'a bringing forth, publishing', fr. edere,
'to give out, bring forth, publish', formed fr. e-

## editor
editor, n. — L., 'one who brings forth, publishes',

agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: editor-ial, adj., and п.,
editor-tally, adv.

## editress
editress, п., a female editor. — See prec. word

## Edmond
Edmond, Edmund, masc. PN. — OE. Eadmund,
lit. 'rich protector', compounded of iad,

For the first element see Edgar. The second

## Edna
Edna, fem. PN. — Gk. Έδνά, fr. Heb. 'ednd\

## education
education, n. — L. iducatio, gen. -onis, 'a

## educator

## educe
educe, tr. v., to infer, deduce; to separate from

## educible

## eduction

edulcorate, tr. v., to render sweet; to free from

## Edward
Edward, masc. PN. — OE. Eadweard,

Edwin, masc. PN. — OE. Eadwine, compounded

For the first element see Edgar. The second
element is rel. to OE. wine, ON. vinr, 'friend', and
to OE. winnan, 'to strive, struggle, fight'; see
wia and wish and cp. the first element in Win-
fred and the second element in Baldwin.
-ее, suff. formed fr. AF. (= F.) pp. suff.' -ё, fr.

## eel
eel, n. — ME. ele, fr. OE. xl, rel. to ON. all, OS.,

## eelfare
eelfare, п., the passage of young eels up a river.

## eelpout
eelpout, п., 1) any of a group of blennylike fishes;
2) the burbot. — OE. xlepute. See eel and pout,

e'en, n. — Contraction of the noun even,

## -een
-een, dimin. suff. of Irish origin as in dudeen. —
Ir. -in.

## e'er
e'er, adv. — Contraction of ever.

## -eer
-eer, agential suff. — Fr. -ier, fr. L. Srius. Cp.
the subst. suffixes -ary, -er, -ier, -yer,

## eerie
eerie, eery, adj., 1) timid; 2) weird. — ME. eri,
'timid', fr. OE. earg, earh, xrg, 'inert, cowardly,
miserable', rel. to ON. argr (also metathesized
into ragr); 'unmanly, voluptuous', Dan. arrig,
org, Swed. arg, 'malicious', OFris. erg, MDu.
arch, erch, Du. erg, 'bad', OHG. arag, arg,
MHG. arc, arg, 'cowardly, avaricious', G. arg,
'bad, wicked'. Finn, arka, 'cowardly', is a Teut.
loan word.
Derivatives: eeri-ly, adv., eeri-ness, n.

## ef-
ef-, pref. — Assimilated form of 1st ex- before/.

## effnee
effnee, tr. v. — F. effacer, fr. OF. esfacier, 'to
wipe out, destroy', lit. 'to remove the face', fr.
es- (F. e-), 'out', and VL. facia (for L. fades),
'face'. See e- and face and cp. deface.
Derivatives: efface-able, adj., efface-ment, n.

## efTect
efTect, n. — OF. effect (F. effel), fr. L. effectus,
'accomplishment, performance', fr. effectus, pp.
of efficere, 'to execute, accomplish, produce',
fr. tst ex- and facere (pp. factus), 'to make, do*.
See fact and cp. feckless. For the change of
Latin й (in factus) to ё (in ef-fectus) see accent
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: effect, tr. v., effective (q.v.),
effectual (q.v.), effectuate (q.v.)

## effective
effective, adj. — F. effectif (lem. effective), fr. L.
effectivus, 'productive, effective', fr. effectus, pp.
of efficere. See effect and -ive.
Derivatives: effective, п., effective-ly, adv.,
effective-ness, n.

## effectual
effectual, adj. — F. effectuel, fr. Late L. effec-
tualis, fr. L. effectus. See effect and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: effectual-ly, adv., effectual-ness, n.

## effectuate
effectuate, tr. v. —· Formed on analogy of F.
effectuer fr. L. effectus. See effect and verbal
suff. -ate. Derivative: effectual-ion, n.

## effeminacy
effeminacy, n. — Formed fr. next word with
suff. -cy.

## effeminate
effeminate, adj. — L. effemindtus, 'womanish,
effeminate', pp. of effeminare, 'to make
womanish, to enervate', formed fr. 1st ex- and femina,
'woman'. See feminine and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: effeminate, п., effeminale-ly, adv.,
effeminale-ness, n.

## effeminate
effeminate, tr. and intr. v. — L. effeminatus, pp.
of effeminare. See prec. word and verbal suff.
•nte.

## effendi
effendi, п., a Turkish title of respect; sir. —
Turk, efendi, 'master', fr. MGk. αφέντη (read
afendi), voc. of αφέντης (read afendis), fr. Gk.
αΰθέντης, 'an absolute master or ruler*. See
authentic.

## efferent
efferent, adj., conveying outward (physiol.) — L.
efferens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of efferre, 'to
carry out or away; to spread abroad', fr. 1st
ex- and ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to
carry', and -ent and cp. afferent.

## effervesce
effervesce, intr. v., to give off bubbles of gas. —
L. effervescere, 'to boil over, effervesce,
ferment', fr. 1st ex- and fervescere, 'to begin to
boil, to bubble', inchoative of fervere, 'to be
hot'. See ferveat and -esce.

## effervescence
effervescence, effervescency, n. — Formed from
next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## effervescent
effervescent, adj. — L. effervescens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of effervescere. See effervesce and -ent.

## efTervescive
efTervescive, adj., tending to effervesce. — See
effervesce and -ive.

## effete
effete, adj., exhausted, worn out. — L. ef-
fitus, 'that has brought forth young; exhausted,
worn out', fr. 1st ex- and fetus, 'that has brought
forth', fr. L. base *fe-, corresponding to I.-E.
*dhe(i)-, 'to suckle'. See fecund and cp. fetus.
Derivative: effete-ness, n.

## efficacious
efficacious, adj., effective. — Formed with suff.
-ous from L. efficax, gen. -acis, 'powerful,
efficacious', fr. efficere, 'to execute, accomplish,
produce'. See effect.
Derivatives: efficacious-ly, adv.,
efficaciousness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:266 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 239 | EIRENICON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:266 COLUMN:1 -->

## efficacy
efficacy, п., effectiveness. — L. efficacia, "efficacy,
efficiency', fr. efficax, gen. efficacis. See prec.
word and y- (representing L. -ia).

## efficiency
efficiency, n. — Formed from next word with
stiff, -cy.

## efficient
efficient, adj. — F., fr. L. efjicientem, ace. of ef-
ftciens, pres. part, of efficere, 'to execute,
accomplish, produce'. See effect and -ent. For
the change of Latin ά (in fucere) to Ϊ (in ef-
fYcere) see abigeat and cp\ words there referred to.
Derivative: efficient-ly, adv.

## effigy
effigy, п., portrait, image. — F. effigie, fr. L.
effigies, 'likeness, portrait, image', fr. effingere,
'to form, fashion; to portray', fr. 1st ex- and
fingere, 'to shape, form'. See figure and cp.
words there referred to. Derivative: effigy, tr. v.

## effloresce
effloresce, intr. v., to come into flower. — L. ef-
florescere, 'to blossom, spring up', fr. 1st ex-
and florescere, 'to begin to blossom', fr. fids,
gen.floris, 'flower'. See flower and cp. florescent.

## efflorescence
efflorescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce. See florescence.

## efflorescent
efflorescent, adj. — L. efflorescens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, oiefflorescere. See effloresce and -ent.

## effluence
effluence, п., a flowing out. — Formed fr. effluent
with suff. -ce.

## effluent
effluent, adj., flowing out. — L. effluins, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of effluere, 'to flow out', fr.
1st ex- and fiuere, 'to flow'. See fluent and cp.
affluent. Cp. also the next two words.
Derivative: effluent, n.

## effluvium
effluvium, п., exhalation, emanation. — L„ 'a
flowing out, outlet', fr. effluere, 'to flow out', fr.
ist ex- and fluere, 'to flow'. See fluent and cp.
effluent, efflux.

## efflux
efflux, п., the process of flowing out. — L. ef-
fluxus, pp. of effluere. See prec. word.
Derivative: efflux-ion, n.

## effort
effort, n. — F., fr. OF. esforz, back formation fr.
esforcier, esforcer, 'to force, reinforce' (whence
F. s'efforcer, 'to exert oneself), fr. VL. *ex-
fortiare, prop, 'to show strength', fr. 1st ex- and
L. fortis, 'strong'. See fort and cp. sforzando.
Derivatives: effort-less, adj., effort-less-ly, adv.

## effrontery
effrontery, n. impudence. — F. effronierie, fr. ef-
fronte, 'shameless, bold', fr. VL. *effroniatus, fr.
1st ex- and L. from, gen. fronlis, 'forehead,
brow; front'. See front and -ery.

## effulge
effulge, tr. and intr. v., to shine forth. — L. ef-
fulgere, 'to shine forth', fr. 1st ex- and fulgire,
'to shine'. See fulgent.

## effulgence
effulgence, п., radiance; brightness. — Formed
from next word with suff. -ce.

## effulgent
effulgent, adj., radiant; brilliant. — L. effulgens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of effulggre. See effulge.
Derivative: effulgent-ly, adv.

## effuse
effuse, tr. and intr. v., 1) to pour forth; 2) to
spread. — L. effusus, pp. of effundere, 'to pour
forth, spread abroad', from Ist ex- and fundere,
'to pour forth, shed'. See fuse, 'to melt'.
Derivatives: effusion (q.v.), effus-ive, adj., effus-
ive-ly, adv., effus-ive-ness, n.

## effuse
effuse, adj., 1) poured out; 2) spread out (said of
a flower). — L. effusus, pp. of effundere. See
effuse, v.

## effusion
effusion, n. — L. effusio, gen. -onis, 'a pouring
forth; profusion', fr. effusus, pp. of effundere.
See effuse, v., and -ion.

## eft
eft, п., a newt (archaic.) — ME. evete, efle, fr.
OE. efeta, 'lizard', a word of uncertain origin.
Cp. newt

## eft
eft, adv., again (archaic). — ME., fr. OE. left, eft,
'afterward, a second time, again', rel. to seftan,
'behind'. See aft.

## eftsoons
eftsoons, eftsoon, adv., forthwith, soon
afterward (archaic). — ME. eftsone(s), fr. OE. eft-
sona, which is compounded of eft (see prec.
word) and sona, 'immediately'. See soon.

## Egbert
Egbert, masc. PN. — OE. Ecgbeorht,
compounded of ecg, 'edge, sword', and beorht, 'bright'.
For the first element see edge, for the second
see bright.

## egeran
egeran, п., a var. of vesuvianite (mineral.) —
Named after Eger (now Cheb) in Bohemia.

## Egeria
Egeria, п., a fountain nymph, adviser of Numa
Pompilius, the second king of Rome (Roman
mythol.) — L. Egeria, a name of Etruscan
origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:266 COLUMN:2 -->

## egest
egest, tr.v., to discharge from the body. — L.
egestus, pp. of egerere, 'to bring out, carry out',
fr. e- and gerere, 'to carry'. See gerent and words
there referred to and cp. esp. ingest.
Derivatives: egestion (q.v.), egest-ive, adj.

## egestion
egestion, n. — L. egestio, gen. -onis, 'a carrying
out', fr. egestus, pp. of igerere. See prec. word
and -ion.

## egg
egg, n. — ME. egg, egge, fr. ON. egg (Dan. xg,
Swed. agg), rel. to OE. xg, ME. ei, Crimean
Goth, ada(for "addja), OS., MLC, MDu.,Du„
OHG., MHG., G. ei, and cogn. with OSlav.
aje, Jaje, ajlce, ajice, 'egg', Russ. jajco, W. wy,
OCo. uy, Bret, ш, Агт.уи (gen.juoj), Gk. ώον, L.
ovum, of s.m. All these words prob. mean lit. 'that
which pertains to the bird', and are cogn. with
OI. vih, L. avis, 'bird'. Cp. the second element
in kidney. Cp. also augur, auspice, aviary,
aviation, 00-, oval, ovary, ovum, the first element in
ostrich and the second element in pettitoes.
Derivatives: egg, tr. v., egg-er, п., egg-ler, n.

## egg
egg, tr. v., to incite, urge on. — ME. eggen, fr.
ON. eggja, 'to goad on, incite', fr. egg, 'edge'.
See edge.

## egger
egger, п., one who incites. — Formed fr. egg, v.,
with agential suff. -er.

## egger
egger, п., one who collects eggs. — Formed fr.
egg, п., with agential suff. -er.

## egger
egger, п., any of various moths. — Prob. formed
fr. egg, п., with suff. -er.

## eglantine
eglantine, п., the sweetbrier. — F. eglantine, 'dog
rose' (the flower), fr. eglanlier, 'dog rose' (the
bush), fr. OF. aiglent, 'dog rose' (the bush), fr.
fr. VL. 'aquilentus, 'rich in prickles', irregularly
formed fr. L. aculeus, 'spine, prickle', dimin.
of acus, 'needle'. See acus and -ine
(representing L. -ϊηά).

## eglestonite
eglestonite, п., a mercury oxychloride (mineral.)
— Named after the mineralogist Prof. Thomas
Egleston, of Columbia University in New York
(1832-1900). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## ego
ego, n. — L., T, cogn. with OE. ic, T. See I,
personal pron.

## egoism
egoism, п., self-interest; selfishness. — F. egots-
me, formed with suff. -isme fr. L. ego. See prec.
word and -ism.

## egoist
egoist, n. — F. egotste, formed with suff. -iste
fr. L. ego. See ego and -ist.
Derivatives: egoist-ic, egoisl-ic-al, adjs., egoist-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## egotism
egotism, п., I) excessive use of the pronoun I;
speaking much of oneself; 2) self-conceit. —
Formed fr. L. ego, Τ (see ego), with suff. -ism;
first used by the English poet Joseph Addison
(1672-1719). The intrusive t is due to the
analogy of nepotism, in which word the t is organic
(fr. L. nepos, gen. nepotis, 'grandson').

## egotist
egotist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: egotist-ic, egotist-ic-al, adjs., ego*
tist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## egotize
egotize, intr. v., to exhibit egotism (rare). — See
egotism and -ize.

## egregious
egregious, adj., 1) orig. prominent, distinguished;
2) flagrant; infamous. — L. egregius,
'distinguished, excellent', lit. 'chosen out of a herd',
fr. e~, 'out of, and grex, gen. gregis, 'herd, flock'.
See gregurious and cp. aggregnte. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to L. -us, see -oiis.
Derivatives: egregious-ly, adv., egregious-ness, n.

## egress
egress, п., г) the act of going out; 2) exit. — L.
egressus, 'a going out', fr. egressus, pp. of egredi,
'to go out, come forth, digress; to surpass,
exceed', fr. e- and gradi, 'to step, walk, go'. See
grade, congress.

## egression
egression, n. — L. Sgressio, gen. -Onis, 'a going
out', fr. egressus, pp. of egredi. See prec. word
and -Ion.

## egret
egret, п., any of various herons. — ME. egrete,
fr. F. aigrette, fr. OProvenc. aigreta, 'heron',
fr. aigron, of s.m., which is of Teut. origin. See
heron and cp. aigrette.

## Egretta
Egretta, п., a genus of herons (ornithol.) —
ModL. See prec. word.

## egueiite
egueiite, п., a hydrous iron phosphate containing
calcium and aluminum (mineral.) — Named
after Eguet, in French Sudan. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## Egyptian
Egyptian, adj. — F. igyptien, fr. Egypte, fr. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:266 COLUMN:3 -->
Αίγυπτος, 'the river Nile, Egypt', fr. Amarna
Hikuptah, corresponding to Egyptian ffa(l)-ka·
ptah, one of the names of Memphis, the
ancient city of Egypt. Cp. Copt. Cp. also gitano,
gypsy-

## Egyptology
Egyptology, п., the study of Egyptian antiquities.
— Compounded of Gk. Αίγυπτος, 'Egypt', and
-λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See Egypt and -logy. Derivative: Egyptolog-ist, n.

## eh
eh, interj. — Imitative. Cp. F. eh, G. ei.

## eider
eider, п., duck of lhe genus Somateria. — Fr.
Icel. xdar (pron. aidar), gen. of xdr, whence also
OSwed. eider (Swed. ejder), Du. eider, G. Eider.

## eidetic
eidetic, adj., pertaining to the faculty of
projecting images; vivid (psychol.) — G. eidetisch,
coined by the German psychologist Erich
Jaensch (1883-1940) fr. Gk. είδητικός,
'pertaining to images, pertaining to knowledge*, fr.
είδηοις, 'knowledge', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'.
See eido- and -Ic.

## eido-
eido-, combining form meaning 'image, figure'.
— Gk. είδο-, fr. είδος, 'form, shape', which
stands for *5εΐδος and lit. means 'that which
is seen', from the stem of ίδεϊν, 'to see'. See
idea and words there referred to and cp. esp.
kaleidophone, kaleidoscope.

## eidograph
eidograph, п., an instrument for the copying of
drawings on the same or on a larger or smaller
scale. — Compounded of eido- and Gk. -γράφος,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## eidolon
eidolon, п., a phantom. — Gk. είδωλον, 'image,
phantom'. See idol.

## eight
eight, adj. and n. — ME. eighte, eihte, fr. OE.
■ eahta, rel. to OS. ahto, ON. atta, Swed. atta,
Dan. otte, OFris. ahta, Du. acht, OHG. ahto,
MHG. ahte, G. acht, Goth, ahtau, 'eight', and
cogn. with OI. asfd, asfdu, Avestic ashta, Toch.
A okal, В okt. Arm. ut' (for *opto), Gk. οκτώ,
Alb. tete (for *okto-t), L. octo, OSlav. osmi
(refashioned after the ordinal number osmu, 'the
eighth'), Lith. aStuoni, Olr. ocht n-, W. wyth,
Bret, eiz, 'eight'. All these words prob. derive fr.
I.-E. *okto\u), an old dual form, orig. meaning
'lwice four' (Tetradic system of reckoning!).
The π in Elian Gk. όπτώ, and the form of
Arm. ut' (for *οριδ·) is due to the analogy of
I.-E. 'seplm- (whence Gk. επτά, etc.), 'seven'.
Cp. also Rum. opt, 'eighl' (fr. L. octo),
influenced in form by sapte, 'seven'. The я in Olr.
ocht n- is due to the analogy of secht n-, 'seven'.
Cp. octa-, octant, octave, octet, octillioa, octo-,
October, octopus, octoroon, octuple, utas.

## eighteea
eighteea, adj. and n. — ME. eightetene, eightene,
eihtene, fr. OE. eahtatyne, eahtatlne, fr. eahta,
'eight', and -tyne, -tene, '-teen' (see eight and
-teen); rel. to OS. ahtotian, Du. achttien, OHG.
ahtozehan, MHG. ahtzehen, G. achtzehn, ON.
uttj&n, atjan, Swed. adertan, Dan. atten,
'eighteen'.

## eighteenth
eighteenth, adj. and n. — Formed fr. eighteen
with numeral suff. -th on analogy of tenth. Cp.
OE. eahtateoda, which was formed fr. eahtatyne,
'eighteen', after teoda, 'tenlh'; see tithe. Cp. also
ON. atljandi, atjandi, 'eighteenth'.

## eighth
eighth, adj. and n. — ME. eightethe, eihtithe, fr.
OE. eahtoda, rel. to OS., OHG. ahtodo, OFris.
achta, MHG. ahtode, ahtede, ahte, G. achte,
Goth, ahtuda, ON. atti, 'eighth'. See eight and
numeral suff. -th. Derivative: eighth-ly, adv.

## eightieth
eightieth, adj. and n. — Formed fr. eighty with
numeral suff. -th on the analogy of tenlh.

## eighty
eighty, adj. and n. — ME. eigteti, fr. OE. (hund)-
eahtatig, rel. to OHG. ahtozug, G. achtzig,
'eighty'. See hundred, eight and -ty, suff. denoting
multiples of ten.

## eikoa
eikoa, n. — See icon.

## Eileen
Eileen, fem. PN. — A name of Celtic origin (cp.
Ir. Eibhlin); influenced in form by the name
Helen.

## Einsteinian
Einsteinian, adj., pertaining to the Jewish
physicist Albert Einstein (1879-1955) or his theory
of relativity. For the ending see -Ian.

## einsteinium
einsteinium, п., a radioactive element produced
espec. by bombardment of Plutonium with
neutrons (chem.) — ModL., named after Albert
Einstein. See prec. word and chem. suff. -ium.

## eirenicon
eirenicon, n. — See irenicon.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:267 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: EISEL | 240 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:267 COLUMN:1 -->

## eisel
eisel, eisell, п., vinegar (archaic). — OF. aissil,
aisil, fr. VL. acetulum, dimin. of L. acetum,
'vinegar'. See acetum.

## eisteddfod
eisteddfod, п., annual assembly of Welsh bards.
— W., 'session', fr. eistedd, 'to sit' (fr. sedd,
'seat'), and bod, 'to be'. The first element is
cogn. with L. sedire, 'to sit'; see sedentary. The
second element is rel. to Olr. builh, 'to be',
and cogn. with OE. bion, 'to be'; see be.

## either
either, adj., pron., conj. and adv. — ME. aither,
either, fr. OE. Sghwseder, xgder, 'each of two,
both', for *a-gi-hwxder, which is formed fr. a,
'ever', pref. gi- (for ge-) and hwxder, 'whether*.
See aye, 'ever', pref. y- and whether and cp.
neither. Cp. also Du. ieder, OHG. eogiwedar,
iowedar, MHG. iegeweder, ieweder, ieder, G.
jeder, 'either, each, every'.

## ejaculate
ejaculate, tr. v., to exclaim. — L. ejaculatus, pp.
of ejacularl, 'to throw out, shoot out*, fr. e- and
jaculari, 'to throw, hurl, cast', fr. jaculum, 'dart,
javelin', from the stem oijacire, 'to throw'. See
jet, 'to spirt forth'.
Derivatives: ejaculat-ion, п., ejaculal-ory, adj.

## eject
eject, tr. v·. — L. ejecius, pp. of eicere (less
correctly Sjicere), 'to throw out, cast out', fr. e-
and jacire, 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth'.
For the change of Latin i"(in jdctus) to f (in
i-jectus) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: eject, n. (q.v.), ejection (q.v.),ejecl-
ive, adj., ejeclive-ly, adv., eject-ment, п.,
ejector, n.

## eject
eject, п., representation of another's mind as a
copy of one's own (jjsychol.) — L. 'something
thrown out', fr. L. ejecius, pp. of eicere. See
eject, v.

## ejectamenta
ejectamenta, n. pi., things thrown out from a
volcano in eruption. — L., 'things thrown out',
neut. pi. of ejecius, pp. of eicere. See eject, v.

## ejection
ejection, n. — L. ejectio, gen. -onis, 'a throwing
out', fr. ejecius, pp. of eicere. See eject, v., and
-loa.

## eka-
eka-, combining form used in chemistry to
denote next in order (said of a chemical element).
— OI. ikah, 'one', rel. to Avestic aeva-, OPers.
aiva-, and cogu. with Cypr. Gk. olfo?, Gk. οίος,
'alone*, fr. I.-E. *oi-wos-, 'one*; cp.—with suff.
-nos—Gk. οίνος, οίνή, 'the ace (on dice)', L.
Onus, 'one', OE. an, 'one'. See one and cp. unl-.

## eke
eke, adv., also (arch.) — ME. ec, eke, fr. OE.
lac, rel. to OS., ODu. 5k, ΟΝ., Goth, auk,
OFris. ak, OHG. ouh, MHG. ouch, G. auch,
'also', and to the verb eke (q.v.)

## eke
eke, tr. v., to increase. — ME. eken, fr. OE.
iacian, icon, iecart, 'to increase', rel. to OS.
dkian, ON. auka, OFris. aka, OHG. ouhhdn,
Goth, aukan, fr. I.-E. base *aweg-, *aug-, 'to
grow, increase', whence also L. augere, 'to
increase'. See auction and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also eke, adv. and ekename.

## ekebergite
ekebergite, п., a variety of wernerite (mineral.) —
Named after the Swedish traveler A.G.Eke-
berg, who analyzed it. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## ekename
ekename, п., a nickname (obsol.) — Compounded
of eke, v., and name. Cp. nickname.

## El
El, п., Hebrew name for God. — Heb. El, 'God',
of uncertain etymology; possibly related to el,
'strong' (cp. e.g. Gen. 31:29 yesh I'il yudt, 'it
is in my power'). Cp. Elohim. Cp. also the first
element in the PN.s Eleazar, Ellezer, Elihu,
Elijah, Elishah, Elizabeth, and the second
element in Battel, bethel and in the PN.s Daniel,
Emmanuel, Ezekiel, Gnbrlel, Gamaliel, Ishmael,
Israel, Joel, Michael, Nathaniel, Raphael,
Samuel.

## -el
-el, suff., as in hovel. — OE. -el, -ela, -ele. Cp.
-le, suff. representing OE. -el, -ela, -ele.

## -el
-el, dimin. suff. of French origin. — 1) OF. -el
(F. -eau), fr. L. -ellus (as in tunnel); OF. -ele,
-elle (F. -elle), fr. L. -ella (as in chapel). See -le,
suff. of French origin.

## -eL suff. representing OF.
-eL suff. representing OF., F. -el, fr. L. -alls, as
in vowel (fr. L. vocalis). Cp. adj. suff. -al.

## elaborate
elaborate, adj., worked out in detail. — L. ela-
bordtus, pp. of elaborate, 'to exert oneself, lit.
'to work out', fr. e- and laborare, 'to work'. See
labor, v., and adj. suff. -ate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:267 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: elaborate-ly, adv.;elaborate-ness,ri.

## elaborate
elaborate, tr. v., to work out in detail. — L. ila-
borutus, pp. of elaborare. See elaborate, adj.
Derivatives: elaborat-ive, adj., elaboral-or, n.

## elnboration
elnboration, n. — L. elabdratio, gen. -onis,
'persevering labor', fr. elaboratus, pp. of elaborare.
See elaborate, adj., and -ion.

## Elaeagaaceae
Elaeagaaceae, n. pi., the oleaster family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Eleagnus with suff. -aceae.

## elaeaguaceous
elaeaguaceous,adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Elaeagnus
Elaeagnus, a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. έλαίαγνος, name of a Boeotian plant,
compounded of έλαια, 'olive tree', and αγνός, 'the
agnus castus'. See elaio- and agnus castus.

## Elaeis
Elaeis, п., a genus of palms (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. έλαια, 'olive tree'. See elaio-.

## elaec-
elaec-, latinized form of elaio-.

## elaio-
elaio-, combining form meaning 'olive oil'. —
Fr. Gk. £λαιον, 'olive oil, oil', for *£Xaifov, rel.
to έλαια (for *έλαίία), 'olive tree'; prob. of
Cretan origin. See oil and cp. olive. Cp. also the
second element in Thymelaeaceae.

## elan
elan, п., impetuosity, vigor. — F., 'spring, bound,
impetus', fr. earlier elans, fr. elancer, 'to throw',
fr. e- (for earlier es-, fr. L. ex, 'out of) and ML.
lanceare, 'to throw*, orig. 'to throw a lance',
fr. L. lancea, 'lance'. See 1st ex- and laace and
cp. launch, v.

## elance
elance, tr. and intr. v., to throw; to lance (poetic).
— F. elancer. See prec. word.

## eland
eland, п., a large S. African antelope. — S. Afr.
Du. eland, 'elk, eland', fr. Du. eland, 'elk', fr.
early G. elend, elen (= G. Elentier), fr. Lith.
elnis, 'hind; elk', fr. OLith. ellenis, which is rel.
to OSlav. jeleni, 'stag, hart', lani (for *olnia),
'hind', and cogn. with W. elain, 'hind', Arm. ein,
of s.m., Gk. έλλός (for *έλνός), 'young deer,
fawn', and possibly also with Toch. A yttl,
'antelope, gazelle'. All these words derive fr.
I.-E. base *eln-, -я-enlargement of base *el-,
'brown'. A -^-enlargement of the same base
appears in elk (q.v.) See also lamb and cp. next
word. Cp. also elaphlne.

## Elaphebollon
Elaphebollon, п., name of the 9th month of the
Attic Greek calendar (corresponding to the
second half of March and first half of April). —
Gk. Έλαφηβολιών, lit. 'month in which the Ela-
phebolia were held', fr. Έλαφηβόλια (scil. ιερά),
lit. 'feast of the shooting of deer', fr. έλαφηβόλος,
'shooting deer', a compound of ϊλαφος, 'deer',
and -βόλος, 'throwing, shooting', which stands
in gradational relationship to βάλλειν,Ίο throw'.
See next word and ballistic.

## elaphine
elaphine, adj., pertaining to the red deer. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ine fr. Gk. ελαφος,
'deer', which stands for *el-n-bhos and is rel.
to έλλός, 'young deer, fawn'. See eland, the first
element in next word and the second element in
Boselaphus, tragelaphus.

## Elaphodus
Elaphodus, п., a genus of small deer in China
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έλαφώδης, 'deerlike',
formed fr. ϋλαφος, 'deer', with suff. -ώδης, 'like'.
See elaphine and -ode, 'like'.

## Elaplnae
Elaplnae, n. pi., a sub-family of venomous snakes
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -inae fr.
ModL. Elaps, the type genus, fr. Gk. έλοψ, a
var. of ίλλοψ. See ellops and cp. elops.

## elapse
elapse, intr. v., to pass (said of time). — L. llap-
sus, pp. of elabi, 'to slip away, glide away, pass,
disappear', fr. e- and labi, 'to slide, glide'. See
lapse.

## elasmo-
elasmo-, combining form meaning 'lamelliform'.
— Gk. έλασμο-, fr. έλασμός, 'a metal plate', fr.
έλαν, 'to drive, strike'. See next word and cp.
the second element in xanthelasma.

## elastic
elastic, adj., springy. — ModL. elaslicus, fr. Gk.
ελαστικός, fr. έλαν, 'to drive', strike', which is
rel. to έλαύνειν, of s.m., and to ήλθον, Ί came,
arrived' (used as the aor. of έρχομαι, Ί come,
arrive'), and possibly cogn. with Arm. elanem,
Ί go forth'. Cp. elnsmo-, elater, elaterium and
the second element in Oestrelata and xenelasia.
Derivatives: elastic, п., elastic-ian, п., elasl-ic-
ity, п., elast-ic-ize, tr. v., elast-ic-iz-er, n.

## elastin
elastin, п., an albuminoid forming the basic
constituent of elastic tissue (biochem.) — See prec.
word and chem. suff. -in.

## elastometer
elastometer, п., an instrument for measuring

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:267 COLUMN:3 -->
elasticity. — See elastic and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## elate
elate, tr. v., to uplift. — L. ilatus, 'uplifted,
exalted' (used as pp. of efferre, 'to bring out, carry
out; to raise, lift up'), fr. e- and latus (used as
pp. of ferre, 'to bear, carry'), which stands for
'llatos, fr. *f/-, zero degree of I.-E. base *lel-,
*tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence L. tollere, 'to lift
up, raise', tolerare, 'to bear, support'. See
tolerate and cp. collate and words there referred to.
Derivatives: elat-ed, adj., elat-ed-ly, adv., elat-
ed-ness, n.

## elate
elate, adj., elated. — L. Ilatus. See prec. word.

## elater
elater, n„ an elastic filament serving to disperse
the ripe spores (bot.) — Gk. έλατήρ, 'driver',
fr. έλαν, 'to drive'. See elastic.

## elaterite
elaterite, п., an elastic bitumen (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. έλατήρ,
'driver* (see prec. word); so called because of
its elasticity.

## elaterium
elaterium, п., a purgative substance obtained
from the squirting cucumber. — L., fr. Gk.
έλατήριον, 'squirting cucumber; drug prepared
from the squirting cucumber', prop. neut. of
the adjective έλατήριος, 'driving', used as a noun,
fr. έλαν, 'to drive'. See elastic and cp. eiater.

## Elatinaceae
Elatinaceae, n. pi., the waterwort family (bot.) —
Formed fr. next word with suff. -aceae.

## elatinaceous
elatinaceous, adj. — See prec, word and -aceous.

## Elatine
Elatine, п., a genus of plants, the waterwort (bot.)
— L. elatine, name of a plant, fr. Gk. έλατίνη,
prop. fern, of έλάτινος, 'pertaining to the fir',
used as a noun, fr. ελάτη, 'fir', which prob.
stands for *el-n-ta and is cogn. with Arm. eievin,
cedar', Russ. jalovec, 'gin'.

## elation
elation, п., elatedness. — L. elatio, gen. -onis, 'a
lifting up; transport, passion; exaltation', fr.
Ilatus, 'uplifted, exalted'. See elate and -Ion.

## elbow
elbow, n. — Prop, 'bend of the ell'; ME. elbowe,
fr. OE. elnboga, 'elbow', rel. to ON. olnbogi,
MDu. ellenboghe, Du. elleboog, OHG. elinbogo,
ellinbogo, MHG. ellenboge, G. Ellenbogen, Ell-
bogen. See ell and bow, 'anything bent'.
Derivatives: elbow, tr. v., elbow-ed, adj., elbow-
er, п., elbow-y, adj.

## elchee
elchee, п., an ambassador. — Turk, ilchi, prop,
'representative of a tribe*, fr. V, 'tribe'.

## eld
eld, п., old age (archaic.) — ME. elde, fr. OE.
yldo, eldo, 'old age', fr. aid, eaid, 'old'. Cp.
OHG. alii, elti, ON. elli, 'old age', and see old.

## elder
elder, п., a shrub or a tree of the genus Sambucus.
— ME. eldre, eller, ellerne, fr. OE. ellern, ellen,
rel. to OS. elora, MLG. elre, aire, OHG. elira
(whence G. Eller), erila (whence G. Erie), and
to E. alder and elm (q.v.)

## elder
elder, adj., older; п., an older person. — ME.
elder, fr. OE. eldra (fem. and neut. eldre), corn-
par, of aid, eald, 'old'. See old.
Derivatives: elder-ly, adj., elder-ll-ness, п.,
eldership, n.

## eldest
eldest, adj. — ME. eldest, fr. OE. eldest(a), iel-
dest(a), superl. of aid, eald, 'old'. See old and -est.

## El Dorado
El Dorado, an imaginary country or city
abounding in gold. — Sp. el dorado (pais), lit. 'the
gilded land', fr. el, masc. def. article (fr. L. ille,
'that'), and dorado, pp. of dorar, 'to gild', fr. L.
deaurare, 'to gild'. See ille and dorado.

## Eldred
Eldred, masc. PN. — OE. Ealdred, lit. 'great in
counsel', fr. eald, 'old; great', and rxd, 'counsel'.
See old and rend.

## eldritch
eldritch, adj., uncanny. — A collateral form of
Scot, elphrish, which prob. derives fr. elph, 'elf.
See elf.

## Eleanor
Eleanor, Elinor, fem. PN. — OF. Elienor, Alienor,
fr. OProvenc. Alienor, a var. of Leonore (q.v.)
Cp. Ella.

## Eleatic
Eleatic, adj., pertaining to the philosophers Xeno-
phanes, Parmenides and Zeno, who lived in
Elea. — L. Eleaticus, fr. Elea, ft. Gk. 'Ελέα,
name of an ancient Greek colony in Italy (now
called Velia). For the ending see suff. -Ic
Eleazar 1) masc. PN.; z) in the Bible, Aaron's
son and successor as high priest. — Late L.,
fr. Gk. 'Ελεάζαρ, Έλεάζαρος, fr. Heb. El'azdr,
lit. 'God has helped'. For the first element see
El, for the second see Ebenezer. Cp. Lazarus.

## elecampane
elecampane, п., name of a plant. — OF. enule
сатрапе, fr. ML. enula сатрапа. The first word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:268 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 241 | ELFIN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:268 COLUMN:1 -->
derives fr. L. inula, 'elecampane'; see Inula.
The second word is prob. a later form for L.
campanea, fem of campaneus, 'pertaining to the
field', fr. campus, 'field'; see camp.

## elect
elect, tr. and intr. v. — L. eliclus, pp. of eligere,
'to pick out, choose', fr. e- and legere, 'to gather,
collect, pick out, choose, read'. See lecture and
words there referred to and cp. esp. elegant.

## elect
elect, adj. — L. electus, pp. of eligere. See elect, v.
Derivative: elect, n.

## election
election, n. — OF. (F. election), fr. L. ilictionem,
ace. of elecliO, 'choice, selection', fr. electus, pp.
of eligere. See elect, v., and -ion.
Derivatives: eleclion-ary, adj., electioneer (q.v.)

## electioneer
electioneer, intr. v., to work for the success of a
candidate in an election. — Coined fr. election
by the British statesman Edmund Burke (1729-
97). For the ending see suff. -eer.
Derivatives-" electioneer, п., electioneer-er, п.,
electioneer-ing, n.

## elective
elective, adj. — F. electif (fem. elective), fr. L.
electus, pp. of eligere. See elect, v., and -ive.
Derivatives: elective-ly, adv., eleclive-ness, п.,
electiv-ity, n.

## elector
elector, n. — L. elector, 'chooser, selecter', fr.
eliclus, pp. of eligere. See elect, v., and agential
suff. -or. Derivatives: elector-al, elector-ial, adjs.,
elector-ate, n.

## Electra
Electra, п., daughter of Agamemnon (Greek
mythol.) — L. Electra, fr. Gk. 'Ηλέκτρα, which
lit. means 'shining, brilliant', and is rel. to
ήλέκτωρ, 'the beaming sun1. See electric

## electress
electress, n. — See elector and -ess.

## electric
electric, adj. — ModL. electricus, lit. 'resembling
amber'; coined by the English physicist William
Gilbert (1540-1603) in 1600 to denote
substances which share the quality of amber
(inasmuch as they attract other substances when
rubbed), fr. L. eleclrum, 'amber', fr. Gk. ήλεκ-
τρον, of s.m., which is rel. to ήλέκτωρ, 'the
beaming sun', and possibly cogn. with OI. ulka
'firebrand, meteor'. Cp. Electra.
Derivatives: electric, п., electric-al, adj., electric-
al-ly, adv., electric-ian, п., electric-ity, п., elec-
tri-fy, tr. v., electri-fi-er, п., electri-fic-ation, п.,
electr-ize, tr. ν„electr-iz-alion, n.,electr-iz-er, a.

## electricity
electricity, n. — Formed fr. electric with suff.
-ity; first used by the English physician Sir
Thomas Browne (Г605-1682) in 1646.

## electro-
electro-, combining form meaning 'electric;
electricity'. — Fr. Gk. ήλεκτρον, 'amber'. See
electric.

## electrocute
electrocute, tr. v. — Formed fr. electro- on
analogy of execute, the ending of which was
mistaken for a suff. Derivative: eleclrocut-ion, n.
electrode; п., a conductor by which an electric
current enters or leaves another medium (phys.)
— Coined by the English physicist and chemist
Michael Faraday (1791-1867) fr. electro- and
Gk. όδος, 'way'. See odograph and cp. anode
and cathode.

## electrolier
electrolier, п., a support for electric lamps,
resembling a chandelier. — Formed fr. electric
on analogy of chande-lier. Cp. gaselier.

## electrolysis
electrolysis, п., decomposition by electricity (phys.
and chem.) — Compounded of electro- and Gk.
λύσις, 'a loosing, loosening, setting free;
dissolution', fr. λύειν, 'to loose, loosen, set free; to
dissolve'. See -lysis. The word electrolysis was
introduced by Faraday (see electrode) at the
suggestion of Rev. William Whewell.

## electrolyte
electrolyte, п., substance decomposed by
electrolysis. — Compounded of electro- and -lyte.
Like the preceding word, this one was also
introduced by Faraday at the suggestion of
William Whewell.
Derivatives: electrolyt-ic, electrolyt-ic-al, adjs.,
electrolytic-al-ly, adv.

## electrolyze
electrolyze, tr. v., to decompose by electricity. —
Back formation fr. electrolysis.
Derivatives: electrolyz-ation, п., electrolyz-er, n.

## electromotion
electromotion, п., motion by electricity. — A
hybrid coined fr. electro- and motion (fr. L.
motio).

## electromotive
electromotive, adj., pertaining to electromotion.
— See prec. word and -ive.

## electron
electron, п., ι) electrum; 2) unit of negative
electricity. — ModL., fr. Gk. ήλεκτρον, 'amber'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:268 COLUMN:2 -->
See electric and cp. next word.

## electrum
electrum, п., an alloy of gold and silver. — L.
eleclrum, 'amber', fr. Gk. ήλεκτρον. See electron,

## electuary
electuary, п., a medicine formed into a pasty mass
by a combination with honey or sirup. — Late
L. ilecluarium, fr. Gk. έκλεικτόν, neut. verbal
adj. of έκλείχειν, 'to lick out', fr. έκ (see ec-) and
λείχειν, 'to lick'. See lick and subst. suff. -ary.
•eleemosynary, adj., 1) charitable; 2) dependent
on charity. — ML. eleimosynarium, fr. L. elei-
mosyna, 'alms', fr. Gk. ελεημοσύνη, 'pily,
mercy'. See alms.
Derivatives: eleemosynary, п., eleemosynari-ly,
adv., eleemosynari-ne'ss, n. t

## elegance
elegance, n. — F. elegance, fr. L. clegantia, fr.
elegans. gen. -amis. See elegant and -ce.

## elegancy
elegancy, n. — See prec. word and -cy.

## elegant
elegant, adj. — F. elegant, fr. L. elegantem, ace.
of elegans, 'choice, tasteful, elegant', a collateral
form oieligens, pres. part, of eligere, 'to choose,
pick out'. See elect, v., and -ant.

## elegiac
elegiac, adj., 1) pertaining to the elegiac meter;
2) used for elegies; 3) mournful. — Late L. ele-
giacus, fr. Gk. ελεγειακός, 'elegiac', fr. ελεγεία.
See elegy,

## elegize
elegize, tr. v., to lament in an elegy; intr. v., to
compose an elegy. — See next word and -ize.

## elegy
elegy, n. — F. iligie, fr. L. elegia, fr. Gk. ελεγεία,
'elegy', which is short for ελεγεία ωδή, 'an
elegiac song', ελεγεία being the fem. of έλεγεΐος,
'elegiac', fr. έλεγος, 'song of lament', which is
prob. of Phrygian origin. Cp. elogium.

## element
element, n. — OF (F. element), fr, L. elementum,
'first principle, element'. Of the many
etymologies suggested, the most probable is that
which derives the word elementum fr. *elepan-
tum, 'ivory letter', an ancient Latin loan word
fr. Gk. ελέφαντα, ace. of έλέφδς, 'elephant;
ivory'. The change of *elepantum to elementum
is prob. due to Etruscan influence. See elephant.
Derivatives: element-al, adj. and п., element-ary,
adj., element-ari-ly, adv., element-ari-ness, n.

## elemi
elemi, п., a fragrant raisin. — Sp. elemi, fr. VArab.
elemt, corresponding to Arab, al-lamt.

## elenchus
elenchus, п., a refutation. — L., fr. Gk. έ"λεγχος
(masc.), 'disproof, argument by refutation',
which is rel. to ϊλεγχος (neut.), 'blame, disgrace',
έλέγχειν, 'to disprove; to disgrace', and possibly
cogn. with Lett, langdt, 'to disgrace, abuse'. Cp.
next word.

## elenctic
elenctic, adj., serving to disprove. — Gk.
ελεγκτικός, 'fond of cross-questioning, critical', fr.
έλέγχειν. See prec. word and -ic.

## Eleocharis
Eleocharis, п., a genus of plants, the spike rush
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'delight of the marsh',
compounded of Gk. έλος, 'marsh', and χάρις,
'grace, delight'. The first element is cogn. with
OI. saras-, 'pond'. For the second element see
Charis.

## elephant
elephant, n. — ME. elifaunt, olifaunl, fr. OF. oli-
fant (F. elephant), fr. L. elephantus, fr. Gk.
έλέφας (gen. -αντος). The first element of Gk.
έλ-έφάς appears also in Hamitic e[u, 'elephant',
whence prob. Pers. p-il, Arab, ph-il, Mishnaic
Heb. p-il, of s.m. The second element is an
Egyptian loan word. Cp. MEgypt. yb,
'elephant', whence Yebu (Heb. Yebh), original
name of the island Elephantine; cp. also the
second element in Heb. shen-habbfm, 'ivory',
lit. 'tooth of the elephant', and OI. tbhah,
'elephant'. See ivory and cp. Eburna. Cp. also
element.
Derivatives: elephantiac (q.v.), elephantiasis
(q.v.), elephant-ic, adj., elephantine (q.v.), ele-

## phantOid
phantOid, elephant-ous, adjs.

## elephantine
elephantine, adj., one who has elephantiasis. — L.
elephantiacus, rel. to elephantiasis. See next
word.

## elephantiasis
elephantiasis, п., a chronic disease of the skin
characterized by the thickening of certain parts

## of the body
of the body, esp. the legs. — L., fr. Gk. έλε-
φαντίασις, fr. έλέφας, gen. -αντος, 'elephant'.
See elephant and -lasis. According to Aretaeus
έλεφαντίασις prop, means 'disease characterized
by a skin resembling that of an elephant'.

## elephantine
elephantine, adj., 1) of an elephant; 2) like an

## elephant
elephant, clumsy. — L. elephantinus,
'pertaining to the elephant', fr. elephantus, 'elephant',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:268 COLUMN:3 -->
cp. Gk. έλεφάντινος, 'of ivory', fr. έλέφάς, gen.
-αντος, 'elephant'. See elephant and -ine
(representing Gk. -ϊνος).

## Elephantopas
Elephantopas, п., a genus of plants (bot.) —
ModL., lit. 'the elephant's foot', compounded
of Gk. έλέφας, gen. -αντος, 'elephant', and πους,
'foot'. See elephant and -pod.

## Elephas
Elephas, п., the genus of elephants. — L. ele-
phas, a secondary form of elephantus, fr. Gk.
έλέφας. See elephant.

## Eleusine
Eleusine, п., a genus of grasses, the goose grass,
the yard grass (bot.)— ModL., fr. Gk. Έλευσίς,
gen. -ΐνος, 'the town of the cult of Demeter'.
See next word.

## Eleusinian
Eleusinian, adj., pertaining to Eleusis. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. Eleusinius, fr. Gk.
'Ελευσίνιος, 'pertaining to Eleusis', fr. Έλευσίς, gen.
-ΐνος, town of the cult of Demeter, the goddess
of harvests. Cp. prec. word.

## eleutber-
eleutber-, form of eleuthero- before a vowel.

## eleutherarcb
eleutherarcb, п., chief of an (imaginary) society
(lit. 'chief of the free'). — Compounded of
eleuthero- and Gk. -άρχης, 'leader of. See
-arch.

## Eleutherian
Eleutherian, adj., delivering (epithet of Zeus). —
Formed with suff. -an fr. Gk. ελευθέριος,
'releaser, deliverer', fr. ελεύθερος, 'free'. See
eleuthero-.

## eleuthero-
eleuthero-, before a vowel eleuther-, combining
form meaning 'free'. — Gk. ελεύθερο-, έλευ-
θερ-, fr. ελεύθερος, 'free', fr. I.-E. base *leu-
dheros, whence also L. liber, 'free'. This base
derives fr. base *leudho-, *leudhi-, 'people';
accordingly Gk. ελεύθερος and L. liber orig.
meant 'belonging to the people', hence 'of legal
descent'. See liberal and cp. words there
referred to.

## eleutheromania
eleutheromania, п., a frantic zeal for freedom. —
Compounded of eleuthero- and mania.
Derivative: eleutheromani-ac, adj.

## eleutheropetalous
eleutheropetalous, adj., having free petals (hoi.) —
Compounded of eleuthero- and -petalous.

## eleutherophyllous
eleutherophyllous, adj., having free leaves (bot.)
— Compounded of eleuthero- and -phyllons.

## eleutherosepalous
eleutherosepalous, adj., having free sepals (bot.)
— Compounded of eleuthero- and -sepalous.

## elevnte

## eleven
eleven, adj. and n. — ME. elevyn, enleven, fr. OE.

ϋαη; ON. ellifu, Dan. elve, Swed. elva, OFris.
andlova, elleva, Du. eif, OHG. einlif, MHG.

These words are formed fr. Teut. 'ain-, 'one',

## elf

Derivatives: elfin (q.v.), elf-ish, adj., elf-ish-ly,

## elk

Ellen, fem. PN. — An earlier form of Helen,

## ellipse
ellipse, п., one of the three conic sections (geom.)
— Back formation fr. L. ellipses, pi. of ellipsis,
'want, defect, omission, ellipse', fr. Gk. ϊλλειψις,
'a falling short, defect', fr. έλλείπειν, 'to fall
short of, fail, omit', fr. έν (see en-) and λείπειν,
'to leave, forsake, be behind', which is cogn.
with L. linquere, 'to leave'; see relinquish and
cp. eclipse. The Pythagoreans used the word
ελλειψις if the base of a figure, that was to be
constructed so that it should be equal in area
to a given figure of different shape, fell short of
the base of the original figure. Apollonius of
Perga, 'the Great Geometer', who lived in the
3rd cent. B.C.E., applied the term ελλειψις for
the first time to denote the ellipse (in his Conica,
113), in reference to the circumstance that the
square on the ordinate is equal to a rectangle
whose height is equal tp the abscissa, applied
to the parameter, but falling short of it; see
parabola and cp. hyperbola.

## ellipsis

— L., fr. Gk. ελλειψις, 'a falling short, defect'.
See prec. word.

elliptoid.
Derivative: ellipsoid-al, adj.

Elvira, fem. PN. — Sp., of Teut. origin.

Elymus, п., a genus of plants, the wild rye, the

Elysia, п., a genus of sea slugs (zool.) — ModL.,
