free and independent, to give from under one's
own authority into that of another', fr. e- and
mancipare, 'to make over as property, to
transfer property', fr. manceps, gen. -ipis, 'purchaser,
contractor, owner', which stands for *man-
cap-s, lit. 'one who takes by hand', fr. manus,
'hand', and capere, 'to catch, seize, take, hold'.
See manual and captive and verbal suff. -ate and
cp. mancipate.
Derivatives: emancipat-ive, adj., emancipal-or,
п., emancipatory, adj., emancipat-ress, n.(rare).

## emancipation
emancipation, n. — L. emancipulid, gen. -onis,
'the releasing of a son from paternal authority',
fr. emancipatus, pp. of emancipare. See prec.
word and -km and cp. mancipation.

## emancipationist
emancipationist, п., an advocate of
emancipation. — A hybrid coined fr. prec. word and -ist,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## emasculate
emasculate, tr. v. 1) to castrate; 2) to weaken. —
L. emasculatus, pp. of Imasculare, 'to
emasculate, castrate', fr. e- and masculus, 'male; manly'.
See masculine and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: emasculat-ion, п., emasculat-ive,
emasculat-ory, adjs.

## emasculnte
emasculnte,adj., 1)emasculated; 2)effeminate.—
L. emasculatus, pp. of emasculare. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ate.

## embalm
embalm, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) embaumer, fr. em-,
en-, 'in', and baume, 'balm'. See em- and balm.
Derivatives: embalm-er, п., embalm-ment, n.

## embank
embank, tr. v. — Formed fr. еш- and bank, 'edge
of a river'.
Derivative: embank-ment, n.

## embargo
embargo, n. — Sp., 'seizure, embargo', fr. em-
bargar, 'to impede, restrain, seize, embargo', fr.
VL. * imbarricare, 'to impede', formed fr. 1st
im- and *barra, 'bar, barrier'. See bar, 'rod of
metal', and cp. embarrass.
Derivative: embargo, tr. v.

## embark
embark, tr. and intr. v. — F. embarquer, fr. VL.
'imbarcare, fr. im- and L. barca, 'a small boat,
bark'. See em- and bark, 'a kind of ship', and
cp. disembark.
Derivatives: embark-ation, п., embark-ment, n.

## embarras de richesse
embarras de richesse, embarrassment caused by a
surplus of riches. — F.; see next word. The
phrase is now replaced in French by embarras
du choix (lit. 'embarrassment of choice').

## embarrass
embarrass, tr. v. — F. embarrasser, fr. Sp. em-
barazar, fr. It. imbarazzare, a derivative of im-
barrare, 'to impede, bar, embarrass', fr. im- and
barra, 'bar'. See em- and bar, 'rod of metal', and
cp. embargo. Cp. also disembarrass, debarrass.
Derivatives: embarrass-ing-ly, adv.,
embarrassment (q.v.)

## embarrassment
embarrassment, n. — F. embarrassement, fr.
embarrasser. See prec. word and -ment.

## embassage
embassage, п., embassy (archaic). — See next
word and -age.

## embassy
embassy, n. — OF. ambassee, fr. It. ambasciata,
'embassy' (whence also F. ambassaae), fr.
OProvenc. ambaissada (whence also Sp. em-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:270 COLUMN:3 -->
bajaJa), fr. ©Proven?, 'ambaissa, 'service',
which is a Teut. loan" word. Cp. Goth, andbahti,
OE. ambiht, OS. ambaht, ON. embxtti, OHG.
ambaht(i), MHG. ambeht, 'service, office', G.
Ami, 'office'. The Teut. words themselves are of
Celtic origin, and lit. mean 'a going or driving
around'; cp. Gaul.-L. ambactus, 'servant', lit.
'one going around'. See ambages and cp.
ambassador, amt.

## embattle
embattle, tr. v., to prepare for battle. — OF. em-
bataillier, fr. em-, 'in', and bataille, 'battle'.
See em- and battle.
Derivative: embattl-ed, adj.

## embattle
embattle, tr. v., to provide with battlements. —
See em- and battlement.

## embay
embay, tr. v., l) to shelter as in a bay; 2)toform
into bays. — Formed fr. em- and bay, 'inlet'.
Derivatives: embay-ed, adj., embay-ment, n.

## embed
embed, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and bed.

## embellish
embellish, tr. v., to adorn. — ME. embellisshen,
fr. OF. (= F.) embelliss-, pres. part, stem of
embellir, 'to beautify', fr. em- and bet,
'beautiful'. See beauty and verbal suff. -ish and cp.
beau, belle.
Derivatives: embellish-er, п., embellish-ment, n.

## ember
ember, n. — ME. emer, aymer, fr. OE. xmerge,
'embers, ashes', rel. to ON. eimyrja, OHG. ei-
muria, MHG. eimer, G. Ammern, 'embers', ON.
ysja, 'fire', usli, OE. ysle, 'glowing ashes,
embers', fr. I.-E. base *eus-, 'to burn', whence also
L. mere, 'to burn'. See combust and cp. words
there referred to.

## ember days
ember days, twelve days of the year, three in each
season, set aside for fasting and prayers (Roman
Catholic and Anglican Church). — ME. ymber,
fr. OE. ymbren, prop, 'recurring days', fr. ym-
bryne, 'a circuit', lit. 'a running around',
compounded of ymb, 'round', and ryne, 'a running,
course'. OE. ymb is cogn. with Gk. άμφί, 'round
about', L. ambd, 'both'; see ambi-. OE. ryne
is rel. to OE. rinnan, 'to run'; see run.

## embergoose
embergoose, п., the loon. — Norw. imbre, 'loon',
prob. fr. imbredage, name of the days in the week
before Christmas; so called because the bird
appears on the coast in the days before
Christmas. Norw. imbredage derives fr. ON. imbru-
dagar, ymbrudagar, 'ember days', fr. OE.
ymbren, of s.m. See ember days.

## Emberiza
Emberiza, п., a genus of birds, the bunting (orni-
thol.) — ModL., fr. Swiss G. Emmeritz, which
is rel. to dial G. Emmerling and to G. Ammer,
'bunting'. See yellowbammer.

## embezzle
embezzle, tr. v., to appropriate by fraud. — OF.
embesillier, 'to ill-treat', fr. em-, 'in' (see em-)
and besillier, 'to torment', which is derived by
Skeat from the OF. pref. bes- (fr. L. bis-, used
in a pejorative sense). — I suggest that OF.
beser derives fr. OHG. ifjjan, equivalent of
OE. bitan, 'to bite, sting'. See bite and cp. bezzle.
Derivatives', embezzle-ment, п., embezzl-er, n.

## embitter
embitter, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and bitter.
Derivatives: embilter-er, п., embitler-ment, n.

## emblaze
emblaze, tr. v., to emblazon, embellish. —
Formed fr. em- and blaze, 'to make known'.

## emblaze
emblaze, tr. v., to set ablaze. — Formed fr. em-
and blaze, 'to burn with flame'.

## emblazon
emblazon, tr. v., to adorn with heraldic devices,
etc. — Formed fr. em- and blazon.
Derivatives: emblazon-ment, п., emblazon-ry, n.

## emblem
emblem, п., a visible symbol. — L. emblima, fr.
Gk. έμβλημα, 'insertion', lit. 'something thrown
in', fr. έμβάλλειν, 'to throw in, insert', fr. έν
(see 2nd en-) and βάλλειν, Ίο throw'. See
ballistic and cp. periblem, problem, symbol.
Derivatives: emblem, tr. v., emblemat-ic, em-
blemat-ic-al, adjs., emblemat-ic-al-ly, adv., em-
blemat-ic-al-ness, п., emblem-at-ist, п.,
emblematize, tr. v.

## emblemeat
emblemeat, п., usually in the pi.: emblements,
crop; profits of a crop (law). — OF.
emblement, emblavement, 'land sown with wheat', fr.
emblaer (F. emblaver), 'to sow with wheat', fr.
ML. imbladare, fr. im- (see im-,'in') and blada,'the
yield of a land', fr. Frankish *ЫМ- (whence also
F. bU, 'wheat, corn'), which is rel. to OE. bhed,
'flower, fruit, harvest*. See blade and -ment.

## emblic
emblic, п., name of an East Indian tree. — ML.
emblica, fr. amleg, Egyptian pronunciation of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:271 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: EMBODY | 244 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:271 COLUMN:1 -->
Arab, amlaj, fr. Pers. dmleh, ultimately fr. OI.
amlak, whence also Malay malaka, 'emblic',
which latter, according to Malay tradition,
appears also in the name of the peninsula Malakka.
See Devic's Supplement to Littre's Dictionary.
P-33-

## embody
embody, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. em- and
body.
Derivative: embodi-ment, n.

## embog
embog, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and bog.

## embolden
embolden, tr. v. — Formed fr. em-, bold and
verbal suff. -en,

## embolic
embolic, adj., pertaining to an embolus or an
embolism (med.) — See embolus, embolism,
and -ic

## embolism
embolism, η., ι) intercalation of a day or days in
the calendar, as in a leap year; 2) the time
intercalated; 3) in med., obstruction of a blood vessel
by an embolus. — Late L. embolismus, 'insertion,
interposition*, fr. Gk. εμβολισμός, fr. έμβάλλειν,
'to throw in, insert'. See emblem and -ism.
Derivatives: embolism-al, embolism-ic, embo-
lism-ic-al, adjs.

## embolus
embolus, п., something inserted (calendar, mech.
and med.) — L., fr. Gk. ϊμβολος, 'stopper,
wedge', fr. έμβάλλειν. See prec. word and cp.
next word.

## emboly
emboly, п., invagination (embryol.) — Gk.
εμβολή, 'a throwing in, putting in, insertion', fr.
έμβάλλειν, 'to throw into'. See emblem and cp.
embolism.

## embonpoint
embonpoint, п., stoutness. — F., fr. en bon point,
'in good condition', euphemism for 'stoutness*.
See 1st en-, bonus and point, n.

## embosom
embosom, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and bosom.

## emboss
emboss, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and boss,
'protuberance'.
Derivatives: emboss-er, п., emboss-ment, n.

## embonchure
embonchure, п., mouth of a river; mouthpiece.
— F„ fr. emboucher, 'to put to one's mouth; to
sound (a wind instrument)', fr. em- and bouche,
'mouth'. See buccal and -иге and cp. debouch.

## embow
embow, tr. v., to bend into a bow; to vault. —
Formed fr. em- and bow, 'anything bent'.
Derivative: embow-ed, adj.

## embowel
embowel, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and bowel. In
the sense 'to disembowel', the pref. em- has
been confused with OF. as- (fr. L. ex), 'out of.

## essbower
essbower, tr. v., to enclose in, or as in, a bower.
— Formed fr. em- and bower, 'cottage'.

## embrace
embrace, tr. v. —· ME. embracen, fr. OF.
embracer (F. embrasser), lit. 'to take into one's
arms', fr. em- and OF. braz (F. bras), 'arm', fr.
L. brachium. See brace, 'clasp*.

## embracer
embracer, п., one who embraces. — Formed fr.
prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## embracer
embracer, also embraceor, п., one who attempts
to corrupt a jury (law). — OF. embraseor, em-
braceur, 'instigator, corrupter', fr. embraser, 'to
set on fire, instigate', fr. em- and breze (F.
braise), 'wood embers, live coals'. See braze,
'to solder', and cp. embrasure.

## embracery
embracery, n„ the attempt to corrupt a jury (law).
— Formed from prec. word with suff. -y
(representing OF. -ie).

## embranchment
embranchment, п., a branching off. — Formed
fr. em-, branch and -ment

## embrangle
embrangle, tr. v., to confuse. — A blend of
embroil and brangle.

## embrasure
embrasure, п., window opening, splay (archil.) —
F., fr. embraser, 'to splay', prop, the same word
as embraser, 'to fire, set on fire'; see embracer,
'one who attempts to corrupt the jury', and
-ure. For the sense development of F. embrasure
it should be borne in mind that this word orig.
denoted an opening from which the gun was
pointed.
Derivative: embrasure, tr. v.

## embrocate
embrocate, tr. v., to moisten with a lotion (med.)
— ML. embrocatus, pp. of embrocare, 'to
moisten', fr. Gk. έμβροχή, 'lotion, fomentation', fr.
έμβρέχειν, 'to steep, foment', fr. έν (see 2nd
en-) and βρέχειν, 'to water, wet', which is rel.
to βροχή, βροχετός, 'rain'. See Brechites and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: embrocat-ion, n.

## embroider
embroider, tr. and intr. v. — ME., fr. em- and
brolder.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:271 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: embroider-er, п., embroider-y, n.

## embroil
embroil, tr. v., to confuse. — F. embrouiller, 'to
embroil, confuse, confound'. See em- and broil,
'to confuse', and cp. imbroglio. Cp. also
embrangle.
Derivatives: embroil, п., embroil-er, п.,
embroilment, n.

## embrown
embrown, tr. v., to make brown. — Coined by
Milton fr. em- and brown. Cp. empurple.

## embryo
embryo, n. (biol.) — Medical L„ fr. Gk. ϊμβρυον,
'a new-born lamb; embryo, fetus', lit. 'that
which grows in the body', fr. έν (see 2nd en-)
and βρύειν, 'to be full, to swell'. See bryo-.
Derivatives: embryon-al, adj., embryon-ic, adj.,
embryon-ic-al-ly, adv., embryon-y, a.

## embryo-
embryo-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
an embryo'. See prec. word.

## embryogeny
embryogeny, п., formation and development of
an embryo. — Compounded of embryo- and
-geny.

## embryology
embryology, п., the science of the formation and
development of the embryo. — Compounded
of embryo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'.

## emcee
emcee, n„ master of ceremonies; tr. v., to act as
master of ceremonies for (colloq.) — Coined
fr. M.C., abbreviation of Master of Ceremonies.

## eme
eme, п., uncle (dial.) — ME., fr. OE. earn, rel. to
OFris. em, MLG. Bme, Du. 00m, OHG., MHG.
dheim, G. Oheim, Ohm, 'uncle', which stand for
W. Teut. "awahaim-, lit. 'he who dwells with the
grandfather'. The first element is cogn. with L·
avus, 'grandfather', avunculus, 'the mother's
brother, maternal uncle'; see uncle. For the
second element see home. Cp. 00m.

## emeer
emeer, n. — A var. of emir.

## emend
emend, tr. v., to correct. — L. Imendare, 'to
correct, improve, emend', fr. e- and menda, 'defect,
blemish'. See amend.

## emendation
emendation, n.— L. emendatio, 'correction,
emendation', fr. Imendatus, pp. of Imendare. See
prec. word and -ation.

## emendatory
emendatory, adj., pertaining to emendation. —
Late L. emendatdrius, fr. L. Imendatus, pp. of
emendare. See emend and -atory.

## emerald
emerald, п., a bright-green precious stone. —
ME. emeraude, fr. OF. esmeralde, esmeraude (F.
emeraude), fr. L. smaragdus (whence also It.
smeraldo, Sp. esmeralda), fr. Gk. σμάραγδος,
μάραγδος, 'emerald', which is of Sem. origin.
Cp. Heb. bareqeth, Akkad. barraqtu, 'emerald',
lit. 'something flashing', a derivative of Heb.
bardq, resp. Akkad. birqu, 'lightning', which are
rel. to Aram, b'raq, barqa, Arab, barq,
'lightning', Heb. baraq, Aram, b'raq, Arab, bdraqa,
Ethiop. baraqa, 'it flashed, glistened', Akkad.
baraqu, 'to flash'. Cp. OI. marakatam, Pers.
zumurrud (whence Turk, ziimriid, whence Russ.
izumrud), 'emerald', which are also Sem. loan
words. Cp. also smaragd, which is a doublet of
emerald. Cp. also Esmeralda.
Derivative: emerald, adj.

## emeraldine
emeraldine, п., a dark green dye. — Formed fr.
prec. word with suff. -ine (representing Gk. -ϊνος).

## emerge
emerge, intr. v., to rise from a fluid, to appear. —
L. emergere, 'to come forth, come up, rise,
extricate oneself, fr. e- and mergere, 'to dip,
immerse, plunge'. See merge and words there
referred to and cp. esp. emersion.

## emergence
emergence, n. — Late L. emergentia, fr. L.
emergens, gen. -etuis. See emergent and -ce.

## emergency
emergency, n. — Late L. emergentia. See prec.
word and -cy.

## emergent
emergent, adj., emerging. — L. emergens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of emergere. See emerge and
-ent.
Derivatives: emergent, п., emergent-ly, adv.

## emeritus
emeritus, adj., retired, but retaining one's title. —
L. emeritus, 'a veteran; a soldier who has
served his time', prop. pp. of emereri, 'to obtain
by service, earn, deserve', fr. e- and merer!, 'to
earn, gain, acquire, deserve'. See merit.

## emerods
emerods, п., hemorrhoids (archaic.) — OF. em-
meroides. See hemorrhoids.

## emersion
emersion, n. — L. emersus, pp. of emergere. See
emerge and -ion.

## emery
emery, п., a hard variety of corundum. — OF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:271 COLUMN:3 -->
emeril (F. emeri), fr. It. smeriglio, fr. MGk.
σμηρι, fr. Gk. σμύρις, 'emery powder', which is
prob. borrowed fr. Heb. shSmtr, 'adamant;
emery'; see Jer.i7:f, Ezek.3:o, Zech. 7:12. See
Encyclopaedia Biblica by Cheyne and Black,
I, 63-64. Cp. Amyris, moray, Muraena. — E.
smear is not cognate.
Derivative: emery, tr. v., to cover, or rub, with
emery.

## Emery
Emery, also spelled Emmery, masc. PN. — Prob.
fr. OF. Aimeri, fr. OHG. Amalrlc, Amelric
(whence also G. Emmerich), lit. 'work ruler', fr.
amal, 'work', and Teut. *rik-, 'ruler'. For the
first element cp. the first element in Milicent.
The second element is related to OHG. rihhi,
'powerful, rich'. See rich and cp. words there
referred to.

## emesis
emesis, п., vomiting (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. ϊμεσις, *vomiting\ fr. έμεϊν. See next word.

## emet-
emet-, form of emeto- before a.vowel.

## emetic
emetic, adj., causing vomiting. — L. emelicus,
fr. Gk. εμετικός, 'provoking sickness', fr.
έμετος, 'vomiting', fr. έμεϊν, 'to vomit, throw
up', which stands for *Fεμεϊv, fr. I.-E. base
*wem-, 'to spit, vomit', whence also L. vomere,
'to vomit'. See vomit and cp. Emys.
Derivative: emetic, п., a substance that causes
vomiting.

## emeto-
emeto-, before a vowel emet-, combining form
meaning 1) vomiting; 2) emetic (med.) — Fr.
Gk. Εμετός, 'vomiting'. See emetic

## eineute
eineute, п., a riot. — F., 'riot', fr. VL. "exmovita,
fem. pp. of 'exmovere, 'to set in motion', used
as a noun, fr. 1st ex- and movere, 'to move'.
See move.

## -emia
-emia, -aemia, suff. denoting a certain, usually
diseased, condition of the blood, as in hydremia,
leukemia (med.) — Gk. -αιμίί, fr. αίμα, gen.
αίματος, 'blood'. See hemal and -la.

## emiction
emiction, п., urination. — Formed fr. e- and
mlctus, pp. of mingere, 'to make water'. See
micturition.

## emigrant
emigrant, adj. — L. gmigrans, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of emigrare. See next word and -ant.
Derivative: emigrant, n.

## emigrate
emigrate, intr. v. — L. emigratus, pp. of
emigrare, 'to move away, remove, emigrate', fr. e-
and migrare, 'to move, migrate'. See migrate.
Derivatives: emigration (q.v.), emigrat-ive,
emigratory, adjs.

## emigration
emigration, n. — Late L. emigrutid, gen. -onis,
fr. L. emigratus, pp. of emigrare. See prec. word
and -Ion.

## emigre
emigre, п., an emigrant; specif., a person
compelled to leave France during the French
Revolution. — F., pp. of emigrer, 'to emigrate', fr.
L. emigrare. See emigrate.

## Emil
Emil, Emfle, masc. PN. — G. Emit, fr. F. Emile,
fr. L. Aemilius, name of a Roman gens, fr. ae-
mulus, 'imitating, rivaling', fr. aemularl, 'to
strive to equal'. See emulate and cp. Emilia.

## Emilia
Emilia, Emily, fem. PN. — F. Emilie, fr. L. Ae-
milia, fem. of Aemilius. See prec. word.

## eminence
eminence, n. — L. Sminentia, 'prominence,
eminence', fr. iminlns, gen. -entis. See next word
and -ce.

## emineat
emineat, adj., 1) high; 2) exalted. — L. eminens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of iminere, 'to stand out,
project; to be eminent', fr. e- and I.-E. base
*men-, 'to stand out, project'. See mount, 'hill,
mountain' and -ent and cp. imminent, prominent.
Derivative: eminent-ly, adv.

## emir
emir, п., ι) an Arabian prince; 2) a title given
Mohammed's descendants through his daughter
Fatima. — Arab, amir, 'commander', fr. dmara,
'he commanded'. See amoraim and cp. ameer,
admiral, omrah.

## emissary
emissary, n. and adj. — L. emissarius, 'one sent
out', fr. emissus, pp. of emittere. See emit and
-ary.

## emission
emission, n. — L. emissio, gen. -onis, *a sending
out1, fr. emissus, pp. of emittere. See emit and
-ion.

## emissive
emissive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
emissus, pp. of emittere. See next word.
Derivative: emissiv-ity, n.

## emit
emit, tr. v., 1) to send out; 2) to utter; 3) to
issue. — L. emittere, 'to send out, send forth, let

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:272 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 245 | EN- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:272 COLUMN:1 -->
out, emit', fr. e- and mittere, 'to send'. See
mission.
Emma*, fem. PN. — G., fr. Erma, contracted
from names beginning with Erm- (e.g. Ermen-
trud, q.v.) Cp. Irma.

## Emmaauel
Emmaauel, masc. PN. — Gk. 'Εμμανουήλ, fr.
Heb. 'Immanffil, lit. 'God is with us*. See Im-
manuel.

## emmenic
emmenic, adj., capable of menstruation (med.)
Formed with stiff, -ic fr. Gk. έμμηνα, 'the
menses', fr. έν (see 2nd en-), and μήν, gen. μηνός,
'month'. See meao-, and cp. catamenia.

## emmenology
emmenology, п., that part of medicine which
treats of menstruation. — Compounded of Gk.
έμμηνα, 'the menses', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See emmenic and
-logy.

## Emmentaler cheese
Emmentaler cheese, often shortened to emmen-
taler, n. — G. Emmentaler Kiise, 'Emmentaler
cheese', prop, 'cheese of the valley of the Great
Emmen, in Switzerland'. The second element in
Emmentaler derives fr. G. Tal, 'valley'; see dale,

## emmer
emmer, п., amelcorn. — DiaL G. Emmer, a var.
of Amelkorn. See amelcorn.

## emmet
emmet, п., an ant (archaic). — ME. emete, emte,
fr. OE. xmete, 'ant'. See ant.

## emmetropia
emmetropia, п., the normal refractive condition
of the eye (meet.) — Medical L., compounded
of Gk. έμμετρος, 'in measure', and ώψ, gen.
ώπός, 'eye'. The first element is formed fr.
έ«, 'in' (see 2nd en-), and μέτρον, 'measure';
see meter, 'poetical rhythm'. For the second
element see -opia.
Derivative: emmetrop-ic, adj.

## emodin
emodin, п., a compound obtained from rhubarb
(chem.) — Formed with chem. suff. -in fr. ModL.
(Rheum) imodl, 'Turkey rhubarb', lit. 'rhubarb
of the Himalaya', fr. Gk. Ήμωδός, 'the
Himalaya'.

## emollient
emollient, adj., softening, soothing. — L. emol-
liens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of ётоШге, 'to
soften, soothe', fr. e- and mollire, 'to soften',
fr. mollis, 'soft'. See mollify and -ent.
Derivative: emollient, п., a soothing medicine.

## emolument
emolument, п., gain; salary, fees. — L. emolu-
mentum, 'gain, profit, advantage', orig. 'miller's
fee for grinding', fr. emolere, 'to grind out', fr.
e- and molere, 'to grind'. See meal, 'edible
grain', and -meat,

## emotion
emotion, n. — F. emotion, formed fr. emouvoir,
'to move, stir up (a passion), to affect, touch',
orig. 'to set in motion', after the relation of F.
motion (see motion) to mouvoir, 'to move'. F.
emouvoir derives fr. OF. esmovoir, fr. VL. *ex-
movere, which corresponds to L. emovSre, 'to
move out, move away; to stir up, agitate'. See
e-, resp. ist ex-, and move.
Derivatives: emotion-al, adj., emotion-al-ism,
п., emotion-al-ist, п., emotion-al-ily, п., emotion-
al-ize, tr. v., emotional-ly, adv.

## emotive
emotive, adj., causing emotion. — Formed with
suff. -ive fr. L. emotus, pp. of emovere, 'to move
out, remove'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: emotive-ly, adv., emotive-ness, п.,
emotiv-ity, n.

## empanel
empanel, impanel, tr. v. — OF. empaneller. See
em- and panel.
Derivative: empanel-ment, n.

## empathy
empathy, п., sympathetic understanding of
another person or an object (psychol.) — Gk.
έμπάθ-εια, 'affection, passion', fr. εμπαθής, 'in

## a state of emotion
a state of emotion, much affected', fr. έν (see
2nd en-) and πάθος, 'feeling' (see -pathy); used

## as a loan translation of G. Einfiihlung
as a loan translation of G. Einfiihlung, which
was coined by the German philosopher Rudolf
Hermann Lotze (1817-81) in Mikrokosmus
(1858), fr. ein, 'in, into', and Fiihlung' 'feeling'.

## emperor
emperor, n. — OF. empereor (F. empereur), fr.

## L. imperatorem
L. imperatorem, ace. of imperdtor, 'ruler, com-

## mandor
mandor, emperor', fr. imperatus, pp. of im-

## perare
perare, 'to command', fr. 1st im- and parare,
'to prepare'. See pare and cp. imperative,

## imperalor
imperalor, empire, empress.

## Empetraceae
Empetraceae, n. pi., the crowberry family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Empetnun with suff.
-aceae.

## empetrnceous
empetrnceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceons.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:272 COLUMN:2 -->

## Empetrum
Empetrum, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. έμπετρον, 'sea heath', prop. fem. of
the adj. έμπετρος, 'growing on rocks', used
as a noun, fr. έν, 'in' (see 2nd en-), and πέτρα,
'rock'. See petro-.

## emphasis
emphasis, п., stress. — L., fr. Gk. έμφασης,
'outward appearance; reflection; significance,
emphasis', fr. έμφαίνειν, 'to exhibit, display,
indicate', which is formed fr. έν, 'in' (see 2nd
en-), and φαίνειν, 'to show'. See phantasm and
cp. phase. Cp. also emphatic.
Derivative: emphas-ize, tr. v.

## emphatic
emphatic, adj., 1) expressed wilh emphasis;
2) clear, definite. — Gk. εμφατικός, 'expres,
sive, forcible', prop, 'exhibited, displayed*, fr.
έμφαίνειν. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: emphatic-al-ly, adv.

## emphysema
emphysema, п., a condition caused by the
abnormal presence of air in the lungs or of gas
in the body tissues (meet.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. εμφύσημα, 'inflation', fr. έμφΰσαν, 'to blow
in', fr. έν (see 2nd en-), and φϋσαν, 'to blow',
fr. φϋσα, 'wind, blast, bladder', from the. I.-E.
imitative base *pu-, *phi>-, 'to blow, swell'
whence also L. pustula, 'blister, pimple, pustule'.
See pustule and cp. Physalia, Physeter. For the
ending see suff. -ma.

## empire
empire, n. — F., fr. OF. empirie, fr. L. imperium,
'command, authority; sovereignty, dominion,
empire', which is rel. to imperare, 'to command'.
See emperor,

## empiric
empiric, 1) adj., derived from, or guided by,
experience or experiment; 2) п., one of an ancient
Greek sect of physicians who relied only upon
experience. — L. empiricus, fr. Gk. εμπειρικός,
'experienced', fr. έμπειρος, 'experienced', fr. έν
(see 2nd en-) and πείρα, 'trial, experiment'. See
pirate and -ic and cp. metempiric.
Derivatives: empiric-al, adj., empiric-al-ly, adv.,
empiric-ism, n„ empiricist, n.

## emplacement
emplacement, n. 1) a placing in position; 2) (mil.)
a platform for guns. — F. emplacement, 'place,
situation', formed fr. en, 'in', and placer, 'to
place', fr. place, 'place'. See em-, place and
-ment.

## emplane
emplane, tr. v., to embark on an airplane. —
Formed fr. em- and plane, 'airplane'.

## employ
employ, tr. v. — F. employer, fr. L. implicare, 'to
infold, involve, include'. See imply, which is a
doublet of employ. Derivatives: employ-ed, adj.,
employee (q.v.), employer, п., employ-ment, n.

## employ
employ, n. — F. emploi, 'employ, employment',
back formation fr. employer. See employ, v.

## employee
employee, employe, n. — F. employe, 'employed,
pp. of employer. See employ, v., and -ее.

## empoisoa
empoisoa, tr. v. — F. empoisonner. See em- and
poison,

## emporium
emporium, п., a trading place; a center of trade.
— L., fr. Gk. έμπόριον, 'a trading place,
market*, prop. neut. of έμπόριος, 'pertaining
to trade', used as a noun, fr. έμπορος, 'traveler;
trader, merchant', fr. έν (see 2nd en-), and πόρος,
'passage, way, road', which stands in gradational
relationship to πείρειν (for *πέρ-ιειν), 'to pierce,

## cross
cross, traverse, go through'. See fare, 'to
prosper', and cp. words there referred to.

## empower
empower, tr. v. — Formed fr. em- and power,

## empress
empress, n. — ME. emperesse, fr. OF. emperesse,

## fem. of empereor
fem. of empereor, 'emperor'. See emperor and
-ess.

## empressement
empressement, п., zeal, eagerness. — F., fr. s'em-

## presser
presser, 'to be eager, be ardent', fr. em- and

## presser
presser, 'to press'. See press, v., and -ment.

## emprise
emprise, emprize, п., enterprise, adventure
(archaic). — OF. emprise, prop. fem. pp. of em·

## prendre
prendre, used as a noun, fr. VL. 'imprendere,
'to undertake', fr. L. im-, 'in', and prehendere,

## prendere
prendere, 'to take'. See em- and prehensile and

## cp. enterprise
cp. enterprise, Impress. The word emprise was
first used in English by Spenser.

## emprion
emprion, п., purchase. — L. emptio, gen. -onis,
'a buying, purchase', fr. emptus, pp. of emere,
''to buy'. See exempt and -ion and cp.

## preemption
preemption, redemption,

## empty
empty, adj. — ME. emtie, empti, fr. OE. xmetig,

## xmtig
xmtig, 'vacant, free, idle', formed with suff. -ig
(whence E. -y) fr. xmetta, 'leisure'. This latter
is formed fr. priv. x- and the stem of (ge)mut.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:272 COLUMN:3 -->
'meeting'. See moot, meet. For the excrescent ρ
ср. glimpse, sempstress, etc.
Derivatives: empty, n. and tr. and intr. v., emp-
li-er, п., empti-ness, n.

## empurple
empurple, to make purple. — Coined by Spenser
fr. em- and purple. Cp. embrown.

## empyema
empyema, n„ accumulation of pus in a cavity of
the body (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
εμπύημα, 'suppuration', fr. έμπυεΐν, 'to suppurate',
fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and πϋον (for *πυσον),
'matter'. See pus and -ma.
Derivative: empyem-ic, adj.

## empyrenl
empyrenl, adj., 1) heavenly, sublime; 2) formed
from pure fire. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
ML. empyrius, empyreus, fr. Gk. έμπύριος,
έμπυρος, 'fiery', fr. έν, (see 2nd en-) and πΰρ,
gen. πυρός, 'fire'. See pyre and cp. empyreuma.

## empyrean
empyrean, adj., empyreal. — See prec. word
and -an.
Derivative: empyrean, п., the highest heaven.

## empyreuma
empyreuma, п., the odor of organic substances
burned in close vessels' (chem.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. έμπύρευμα, 'a live coal covered with ashes',
fr. έμπυρεύειν, 'to set on fire', fr. έμπορος. See
empyreal and -ma.

## empyreumatic
empyreumatic, adj. — Formed with suff. -ic fr.
Gk. εμπόρευμα, gen. έμπυρεύματος. See prec.
word.

## emu
emu, п., a large bird of Australia. — Shortened
fr. Port, ema di gei, 'crane of the ground'; so
called because the emu cannot fly. Port, ema is
a loan word fr. Moluccan erne.

## emulate
emulate, tr. v., to try to equal or surpass. — L.
aemulatus, pp. of aemulari, 'to strive to equal,
vie with, emulate,' fr. aemulus, 'striving to
equal, rivaling', which stands in gradational
relationship to imitart, 'to copy, imitate', imago,
'representation, likeness, image'. See image,
imitate and verbal suff. -ate and cp. emulous,
Emll, Emilia. Cp. also even, adj.
Derivatives: emulation (q.v.), emulat-ive, adj.,
emulative-ly, adv., emulator (q.v.), emulat-ory,
adj.
emulation n. — L. aemulatio, gen. -onis, fr.
aemulatus, pp. of aemulari. See prec. word and
-Ion.

## emulator
emulator, n. — L. aemulator, fr. aemulatus, pp.
ot aemulari. See prec. word and agential suff. -or.

## emulgent
emulgent, adj., draining, purifying (applied to
renal vessels). — L. imulgens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of emulggre, 'to milk out, drain out'. See
milk and -ent and cp. emulsify, emulsion.
Derivative: emulgent, п., 1) renal vessel; 2)
(pharm.) a medicine exciting the flow of bile.

## emulous
emulous, adj., trying to equal or surpass another.
— L. aemulus. See emulate. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: emulous-ly, adv., temulous-ness, n.

## emalslfy
emalslfy, tr. v., to convert into an emulsion. —
L. emulsus, pp. of imulgere. See emalgent and
-fy. Derivatives: emulsifi-able, adj., emulsifi-abil·
ity, п., emulsifi-er, n.

## emulsioa
emulsioa, п., a milky fluid. — ModL. ётиЫб,
gen. -onis, fr. L. emulsus, pp. of Imulgere. See
emalgent and -ion and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: emulsion-ize, tr. v.

## emuislve
emuislve, adj. — Formed fr. L. emulsus, pp. of
Imulgere. See emulgent and -ive.

## emunctory
emunctory, adj., excretory; п., any organ of the
body carrying off waste. — Late L. emunctd-
rium, 'a pair of snuffers', fr. L. emunctus, pp. of
emungere. 'to blow the nose', fr. e- and тип·
gere, 'to blow the nose*. See mucus and -ory.

## Emys
Emys, п., a genus of turtles (zool.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. έμύς, gen. έμύδος, 'fresh water turtle',
which is of uncertain origin. It possibly stands
for */εμΰς and is a derivative fr. I.-E. base
"wem-, to spit, vomit', whence also Gk. έμεΐν,
'to vomit', and is so called from the bubbles
emitted by the animal under the water. See
emetic and cp. the second element in Chry-
semys.

## en
en, п., ι) the letter n; 2) anything resembling the
letter n.

## en- (em- before p
en- (em- before p, b, m), pref. meaning 'in, into".
— OF., F. en-, em-, fr. L. in-, -im;; see 1st In-.
This pref. is often used to form verbs from
English nouns, in which case the pref. en- means

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:273 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: EN- | 24G -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:273 COLUMN:1 -->
'to put into' (cp. embay, embed, enshrine). It
is also added to English adjectives and nouns
to form causative verbs (cp. embitter, enable,
ennoble, enslave).

## en- (em- before p
en- (em- before p, b, m; el- before /; er- before
r), pref. meaning 'near, at, in'. — Fr. Gk. έν,
'in', which is cogn. with L. in. See 1st in- and
cp. prec. pref. Cp. also Gk. ές, εις (for *ένς),
'into', ϊσω, Ion. είσω (for *ένσω), 'in, within',
and see eso-, esoteric.

## -en
-en, suff. forming the plural of some nouns, as
in brethren, children, oxen. — ME. -en, fr.
OE. -ал.

## -en
-en, the pp. ending of many strong verbs, as in
broken, spoken, written. — ME., fr. OE. -en,
cogn. with OI. -na.

## -en
-en, old fem. surf. — OE. -ел as in wylfen, 'she-
wolf, fyxen, 'she-fox'; rel. to G. -in. Cp. vixen.

## -en
-en, suff. forming adjectives from nouns,
meaning 'made of, as in golden, woolen, oaken. —
ME., fr. OE., rel. to OS., ON. -in, OHG. -in, G.
-en, Goth, -eins, and cogn. with L. -inus, Gk.
-ίνος. Ср. adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus,
resp. Gk. -ϊνος).

## -en
-en, suff. forming verbs from adjectives and
nouns, as deepen, darken; lengthen, strengthen.
— ME. -en, -ten, fr. OE. -nian.

## enable
enable, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and able.
Derivatives: enabl-er, п., enabl-ing, adj.

## enact
enact, tr. v., to make into an act. — Formed fr.
1st en- and act. Derivatives: enact-ion, п., enacl-
ive, adj., enact-ment, п., enact-or, n.

## Eualiosauria
Eualiosauria, n. pi., a group of extinct gigantic
marine reptiles (paleontol.) — ModL., lit.
'marine lizards', compounded of Gk. ενάλιος,
'of the sea', and γαύρος, 'lizard'. The first
element is formed fr. έν (see 2nd -en) and αλς,
gen. αλός (fem.), 'sea'. See halieutic. For the
second element see sauro-.

## enam
enam, п., land exempt from rent or with
favorable rent (Hindu law). — Hind. Mam,
borrowed, through the medium of Persian, fr.
Arab, in'am, 'benefit, favor', inf. of an'ama, 'he
granted a favor, favored', IV (i.e. causative)
form of na'ima, 'was easy or pleasant', which is
rel. to Heb. na'im, 'was pleasant or lovely',
na'fm, 'pleasant, lovely'. Cp. the Hebrew PN.s
Na'ama", Na'uman, No'dmt, which all derive
from the stem of the verb na'im, and see
Naanrnn, Naomi.

## enamdar
enamdar, п., holder of an enam (India). — "Hind.
in'amdar, fr. Pers. inamddr, a hybrid coined fr.
Arab, in'am (see prec. word) and Pers. -dar,
'holder, possessor'. See aumildar and cp. words
there referred to.

## enamel
enamel, tr. v. — ME. enamelen, fr. AF. ena-
mayller, fr. 1st en- and amayl, fr. OF. esmail (F.
email), which is a Teut. loan word. Cp. OHG.
smelzen, OE. meltan, 'to melt', and see melt,
smelt.
Derivatives: enamel, п., enamal(l)-er, п.,
enamelling, verbal n.

## enamor
enamor, enamour, tr. v. — OF. enamourer, fr. ι st
en- and amour, 'love', fr. L. amdrem, ace. of
amor. See amorous.
Derivatives: enamo(u)r-ed, adj., enamo(u)r-ed-
ness, n.

## enanthema
enanthema, п., an eruption on a mucous
membrane (med.) — Medical L., fr. 2nd ea- and
Gk. £ν*ημα, 'efflorescence', fr. άνθος, 'flower'.
See anther and cp. exanthema.

## enantio-
enantio-, combining form meaning 'opposite'. —
Gk. ενάντιο-, fr. έναντίος, 'opposite', fr. έν (see
2nd en-), and άντίος, 'opposite', fr. αντί, 'over
against, opposite'. See anti-.

## enantiopathy
enantiopathy, п., allopathy. — Fr. Gk. έναν-
τιοπαθής, 'of contrary properties', fr. έναντίος,
'opposite', and πάθος, 'suffering'. See enantio-
and -pathy and cp. allopathy, homeopathy.

## enarthrosis
enarthrosis, п., a ball-and-socket joint (anat.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -osis fr. Gk.
έναρθρος, 'jointed', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
άρθρον, 'joint'. See arthro-, and cp. arthritis.

## en bloc
en bloc, in a lump. — F., fr. en, 'in', and bloc,
'block, lump'. See 1st en- and block.

## encaenia
encaenia, п., annual ceremony of the dedication
of a church; also annual ceremony at the
University of Oxford, in commemoration of the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:273 COLUMN:2 -->
founders and benefactors. — L., 'a dedication',
fr. Gk. εγκαίνια, 'feast of dedication', lit. 'feast
of renovation', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and καινός,
'new'. See recent and cp. kainite and words
there referred to.

## encage
encage, tr. v., to shut up in, or as in, a cage. —
Formed fr. ist en- and cage.

## encamp
encamp, intr. and tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and
camp. Derivative: encamp-ment, n.

## encase
encase, lr. v., to put into a case. — Formed fr.
ist ea- and case, 'chest'. Cp. enchase.
Derivative: encase-ment, n.

## encash
encash, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and cash.
Derivative: encash-menl, n.

## encarpus
encarpus, п., an ornament consisting of a festoon
of fruits, leaves, flowers, etc. — ModL., fr. Gk.
εγκαρπος, 'containing fruit*, fr. έν (see 2nd
en-) and καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.

## encaustic
encaustic, adj., burnt in; prepared by heat. —
Lit., 'burnt in'; fr. Gk. έγκαυοτικός, fr. £γ-
καυστος, verbal adj. of έγκαίειν, 'to burn in', fr.
έν (see 2nd en-) and καίειν, 'to burn'. See caustic.

## encaustic
encaustic, n. — L. encaustica, fr. Gk. έγκαυστική
(scil. τέχνη), 'encaustic art', fem. of έγκαυστικός.
See caustic, adj.

## -ence
-ence, suff. forming abstract nouns denoting
action, process, state, or quality. — L. -entia,
either directly or through the medium of F.
-ence. L. -entia derives fr. -ens, gen. -entis, pres.
part. suff. of the verbs of the second and third
conjugaiions. See -ent and -ce and cp. -ance.
Cp. also -ency.

## enceinte
enceinte, adj., pregnant (said of a woman). —
F., fr. Late L. incincta (whence also It. incinta,
OProvenc. encencha), lit. 'without a girdle', fr.
L. priv. pref. in- and cincta, fem. of cinctus, pp.
of cingere, 'to gird'. See ia-, 'not', and cincture.

## eaceinte
eaceinte, п., enclosure of a fortress. — F., fem.
pp. of enceindre, 'to gird, surround', fr. L. in-
cingere, of s.m., which is formed fr. in-, 'in', and
cingere, 'to gird'. See cincture and cp. prec. word.

## Enceladus
Enceladus, п., a hundred-armed giant, who fought
against the gods; Zeus hurled Mount Etna upon
him (Greek mylhol.) — L., fr. Gk. Έγκέλαδος.

## Encelia
Encelia, п., a genus of plants, the brittlebush
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έγχέλειον, 'a little eel',
dimin. of έγχελυς, 'eel'; so called in allusion
to the shape of the seeds. Gk. ϊγχελυς is of
uncertain origin. It possibly means, 'the
snakelike fish', and is a blend of Gk. έχις, 'viper',
and the I.-E. base appearing in L. anguis,
'snake'. See angnine and cp. the first element in
Enchelycephali, For sense development cp. L.
anguilla, 'eel', prop, 'the snakelike fish', fr.
anguis, 'snake' (see Anguilla).

## eacephalic
eacephalic, adj., pertaining to the brain. —
Formed wilh suff. -ic fr. Gk. εγκέφαλος, 'brain',
which is short for ό μυελός εγκέφαλος, lit. 'the
marrow within the head', from the adj.
εγκέφαλος, 'that which is within the head', fr. έν
(see 2nd ea-) and κεφαλή, 'head'. See cephalic
and cp. encephalon, anencephalic.

## encephalitis
encephalitis, п., inflammation of the brain (med.)
— Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk.
εγκέφαλος, 'brain'. See prec. word and cp.
next word.

## encephalon
encephalon, п., the brain (anat.) -r- Medical L.,
fr. Gk. εγκέφαλος, 'brain'. See encephalic and
cp. metencephaton, rhinencephalon.

## enchain
enchain, tr. v. — OF. enchainer (F. enchainer),
VL. *incatenare, fr. 1st in- and "L. catenare, 'to
chain', fr. catena, 'chain'. See chain.
Derivative: enchain-ment, n.

## eacbaat
eacbaat, tr. v., to bewitch; trj charm. — OF.
(= F.) enchanter, fr. L. incantare, 'to chant a
magic formula, bewitch, enchant', fr,. ist en-
and chanter, 'to sing, fr. L. canlare. See cant,
'slang-of beggars', and cp. accent, chaat, dis.
enchaat, incantation.
Derivatives: enchant-er, п., enchant-ing, adj.,
enchant-ing-ly, adv., enchantment (q.v.),
enchantress, n.

## enchantment
enchantment, n. — OF. (= F.) enchantement, fr.
enchanter. See enchant and -ment.

## enchase
enchase, tr. v. — F. enchasser, fr. 1st en- and
chasse, 'box, case, frame'. See chase, 'frame',
and cp. encase, casement.

## Enchelycephali
Enchelycephali, n. pi., an order of Apodes, the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:273 COLUMN:3 -->
common eels (ichthyol.) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. εγχελυς, 'eel', and κεφαλή,
'head'. See Encelia and cephalic,

## enchiridioa
enchiridioa, п., a handbook. — Late L., fr. Gk.
έγχειρίδιον, 'handbook', prop. neut. of έγχει-
ρίδιος, 'that which is held in the hand', used as
a noun, fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and χειρ, 'hand'. See
chiro-.

## enchoadroma
enchoadroma, п., a cartilaginous tumor (med.) —
Medical L., coined by the German physiologist
and anatomist John MUller (1801-58) fr. Gk.
εγχονδρος, 'cartilaginous', and suff. -oma. Gk.
εγχονδρος is formed fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
χόνδρος, 'corn, grain, groat; cartilage'. See
chondro-.

## enchorial
enchorial, adj., pertaining to a country; native;
said esp. of demotic writing. — A hybrid formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. εγχώριος, 'of the
country, domestic, native', fr. έν (see 2nd en-)
and χώρα, 'place, land, country'. See chori-.

## enchymatous
enchymatous, adj., distended by infusion (biol.)
— Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. ίγχυμα, gen.
έγχύματος, 'filling (of a vessel), infusion', fr.
έγχεϊν, 'to pour in', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and χεΐν,
'to pour'. See chyme and -ma and cp. collen-
chyma, mesenchyme, parenchyma, proseachyma,
sclerenchyma.

## eacina
eacina, п., a species of live oak (Quercus agri-
folia). — Sp., fr. Late L. Xlicina, 'holm oak'
(whence also It. elcina, Catal. alsina. Port, en-
zinha), prop. fem. of tlicinus, 'of a holm oak',
used as a noun, fr. L. ilex, gen. -ilia's, 'holm
oak'. See ilex.

## encircle
encircle, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and circle.
Derivatives: encircle-ment, п., encircl-er, n.

## eaclasp
eaclasp, tr. v. — Lit. 'to take into one's clasp',
fr. 1st en- and clasp.

## enclave
enclave, tr. v., to enclose within alien territory. —
F. enclaver, fr. VL. *inclavare, 'to lock with a
key' (whence also OProveng. enciavar, 'to put
in, enclave', Rum. incheia, 'to close'), fr. L. in
(see in-, 'in') and Claris, 'key'. See clavicle and
cp. cief.
Derivatives: enclave, n. (q.v.), enclave-ment, n.

## enclave
enclave, п., a territory enclosed by the. territory
of a foreign country. — F., fr. enclaver. See
enclave, v. and cp. exclave.

## enclitic
enclitic, adj., dependent on the preceding word
(said of a word whicb has no accent but forms
a mere suffix to the preceding word). — Late
L. encliticus, fr. Gk. εγκλιτικός, 'throwing its
accent back', lit. 'leaning on*, from the verbal
adj. stem of έγκλίνειν, 'to bend, lean on', fr.
έν (see 2nd en-) and κλίνειν, 'to lean'. See
Clinical and cp. proclitic.
Derivative: enclitic-al-ly, adv.

## eaclose
eaclose, inclose, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) enclos,
fem. enclose, pp. of enclore, 'to enclose', fr. VL.
*inclaudere, refashioned (after claudere, 'to shut,
close') fr. L. includere, 'to shut in, enclose'. See
Include.

## enclosure
enclosure, n. — OF., fr. enclos, pp. of enclore. See
prec. word and -иге.

## encloud
encloud, tr. v., to envelop in a cloud. -1- Formed
fr. 1st en- and clond.

## encomiast
encomiast, п., one who writes or utters an
encomium. — Gk. εγκωμιαστής, 'one who
praises', fr. έγκωμιάζειν, 'to praise', fr. έγκώμιον,
'panegyric, encomium'. See encomium.

## encomiastic
encomiastic, adj., pertaining to an encomium or
encomiast. — Gk. εγκωμιαστικός, fr.
εγκωμιαστής. See prec. word and -ic.

## encomium
encomium, п., panegyric, eulogy; praise. — L„
fr. Gk. έγκώμιον, 'panegyric, eulogy', fr. έν
(see 2nd en-) and κώμος, 'banquet, revelry; an
ode sung at festivities'. See comedy.

## encompass
encompass, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and
compass.
Derivatives: encompass-er,n., encompass-ment, n.

## encore
encore, interj. used in the sense 'again'. — F.,
'again, still, yet', fr. L. hanc ad horam, 'to this
hour'. L. hanc is ace. of haec, fem. of hie, 'this*;
see hodiernal and cp. haecceity. For L. ad, 'to,
toward', see nd-. L. horam is ace. of hdra,
'hour'; see hour. It. ancora, 'again, still, yet',
'S a French loan word.
Derivative: encore, n. and tr. v.

## encounter
encounter, tr. and intr. v. — OF. encontrer, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:274 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 247 | ENDYMION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:274 COLUMN:1 -->
meet', fr. VL. 'incontrdre, fr. L. in (see in-, 'in')
and contra, 'against, opposite'. See contra- and
cp. counter, v.

## encounter
encounter, n. — OF. encontre, fr. enconlrer. See
encounter, v.

## encourage
encourage, tr. v. — OF. encoragier (F. encou-
rager), fr. 1st en-, and courage, 'courage'. See
courage and cp. discourage.
Derivatives: encourage-ment, п., encourag-er,
п., encourag-ing, adj., encoumg-ing-ly, adv.

## encrimson
encrimson, tr. v., to make crimson. — Formed
fr. ist en- and crimson.

## encriaite
encriaite, п., a fossil crinoid (paleonl.) — Formed
fr. 2nd en- and Gk. κρίνον, 'lily'. See crinoid.

## eacroach
eacroach, intr. v., to trespass. — ME. encrochen,
fr. OF. encrochier, 'to catch in a hook', fr. 1st
en- and croc, 'hook'. See crochet and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: encroack-er, п., encroach-ment, n.

## encrust
encrust, Incrust, tr. v. — F. incruster, fr. L. in-
crustare, 'to cover with a crust', fr. in-, 'in' and
crusta, 'crust'. See crust and cp. F. encrouter,
'to incrust; to plaster (walls)', which is a doublet
of incruster.
Derivative: encrust-ment, n.

## encumber
encumber, tr. v., I) to hinder; 2) to burden. —
OF. (= F.) encombrer, 'to block up, obstruct',
fr. 1st en- and combre, 'things thrown down,
abatis', fr. VL. combrus. See cumber.
Derivatives: encumber-er, п., encumber-ment, n.

## eacumbrance
eacumbrance, n. — OF. encombrance, fr.
encombrer. See prec. word and -ance.
Derivative: encumbranc-er, n.

## -ency
-ency, suff. denoting quality or state. — Fr. L.
-entia (either directly, or through the medium
of F. -ence), hence derivatively identical with
-ence (q.v.) Cp. -ancy.

## encyclic
encyclic, encyclical, adj., circular, general. —
Late L. encyclicus, for L. encyclius, fr. Gk.
εγκύκλιος, 'in a circle, circular', fr. έν (see 2nd
en-) and κύκλος, 'circle'. See cycle and -Ic,
resp. also -al.

## encyclic
encyclic, encyclical, п., an encyclical letter, esp.
one sent by the Pope to all the bishops. — See
encyclic, adj.

## encyclopedia
encyclopedia, encyclopaedia, n. — Late L.
encyclopaedia, fr. inexact Gk. εγκυκλοπαίδεια, for
εγκύκλιος παιδεία, 'circular education, general
education', lit. 'training in a circle'. See en-
cycilc and pedo- and cp. cyclopedin.
Derivatives: encyclop(a)edi-ac, encyclop(a)edi-
ac-al, encyclop(a)edi-al, encyclop{a)edi-an, en-
cyclop(a)ed-ic, encyclop(a)ed-ic-al, adjs., ency-
clop(a)ed-tc-al-ly, adv., encyclop(a)ed-ism, п.,
encyclop(a)ed-isl, п., encyclop(a)ed-ize, tr. v.

## encyst
encyst, tr. v., to enclose in a cyst. — Formed fr.
2nd .en- and cyst.
Derivatives: encyst-alion, п., encyst-ment, n.

## end
end, n. — ME. ende, fr. OE, ende, rel. to OS.
endi, OFris. enda, ODu. ende, Du. einde, ON.
endir, endi, 'end', OHG. ami, enti, 'top,
forehead, end', MHG., G. ende, Goth, andeis, 'end'.
All these words orig. meant 'the opposite side',
fr. I.-E. base *anla-, *anti-, Opposite, in front
of, before', whence also OI. antah, 'end, border,
boundary', Tech. A antus, 'end', Hitt. hantl,
'opposite', hantezzi, 'the first', Olr. etan (for
*ant-ono-), 'forehead', L. antiae, 'the hair
growing on the forehead, forelocks', ante, 'in front
of, before', Gk. αντί, 'against'. See aate-, anti-
and cp. antiae and the second element in
Vedanta.
Derivatives: end-er, п., end-ing, п., endless (q.v.)

## end
end, intr. and tr. v. — OE. endian, fr. ende, 'end'.
See end, n.

## end-
end-, form of eado- before a vowel.

## Entamoeba
Entamoeba, п., a genus of parasitic amoebae
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of end- and
amoeba.

## endanger
endanger, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and danger.

## endaortic
endaortic, adj., pertaining to the interior of the
aorta. — Compounded of end-, aorta and -ic

## endear
endear, tr. v. — Formed fr. ist en- and dear.
Derivatives: endear-ing, adj.,endear-ing-ly,aav„
endear-ment, n.

## endeavor
endeavor, endeavour, intr. v. — ME. endever, fr.
1st en- and clever, 'duty'; see devoir. Accordingly
ME. endever lit. means 'in duty', and is used

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:274 COLUMN:2 -->
elliptically for 'to be in duty, to do one's duty'.
Cp. F. se mettre en devoir defaire quelque chose,
'to set about doing something'.
Derivatives: endeavo(u)r, п., endeavo(u)r-er, n.

## endeictic
endeictic, adj., serving to demonstrate. — Gk,
ενδεικτικός, fr. ένδεικνύναι, 'to show, point
out, demonstrate', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
δεικνύναι, 'to show', which is cogn. with L. di-
cere, 'to say, tell'. See diction and -ic and cp.
apodictk.

## endemic
endemic, adj., prevalent in a particular region or
group. — Formed with suff. -Ic fr. Gk. ένδήμιος,
ένδημος, dwelling in a place, native', fr. έν (see
2nd en-) and δήμος, 'people'. See demos and cpT
epidemic.
Derivatives: endemic, п., endemic-al-ly, adv.,
endemic-ily, п., endem-ism, n.

## endemiology
endemiology, п., the study of endemic diseases.
— Compounded of Gk. ένδήμιος (see prec.
word) and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See -logy. Cp. epidemiology.

## endermlc
endermlc, adj., acting through the skin (med.) —
Formed fr. 2nd en- and Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'. See
derma and -Ic and cp. epidermic.

## endive
endive, п., a kind of chicory used in salads. —
F., fr. ML. endivia, fr. MGk. έντυβον
(pronounce endibo), fr. Gk. έντύβιοι (pi.), ult. fr.
Egypt, tybi, 'January*; so called because this
plant grows in Egypt in the month of January.
L. intubus and intybum, 'endive', also derive fr.
Gk. έντύβιοι.

## endiess
endiess, adj. — ME. endelees, fr. OE. endeleas,
which is compounded of ende, 'end', and leas,
'devoid of. See end, п., and -less.
Derivatives: endless-ly, adv., endless-ness, n.

## endo-
endo-, before a vowel also end-, combining form
meaning 'within'. — Gk. ένδο-, ένδ-, fr. ένδον,
'within', lit. 'in the house', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
the base of δόμος, 'house'. See dome, 'a building'.

## endocardial
endocardial, adj., 1) situated within the heart;
2) pertaining to the endocardium (anat.) — Lit.
'within the heart', fr. endo- and Gk. καρδία,
'heart'. See cardio-.

## endocarditis
endocarditis, п., inflammation of the
endocardium (med.) — Medical L., coined by the French
physician Jean Bouillaud (1796-1881) about
1835 from next word and suff. -Iris.

## endocardium
endocardium, п., the serous membrane lining the
cavities of the heart (anat.) — Medical L. See
endocardial and cp. epicardium, pericardium.

## endocarp
endocarp, n„ the inner wall of the pericarp (hot.)
— See eado- and carpel and cp. eplcarp,
pericarp.

## endocrine
endocrine, adj., secreting internally (said of
certain glands (physiol) — Compounded of endo-
and Gk. κρίνειν, 'to separate'. See critic.

## endoderm
endoderm, п., the epithelium lining the alimentary
canal. — Lit. 'inner skin*, coined by the German
physician Robert Remak (1815-65) fr. endo- and
derm. Cp. ectoderm, mesoderm.
Derivative: endoderm-ic, adj.

## endodontitis
endodontitis, п., inflammation of the pulp of a
tooth called also pulpitis (med.) — Medical L.,
coined fr. end-, odont- and suff. -iris.

## endogamy
endogamy, п., marriage within the tribe or clan
(anthropol.) — Lit. 'in-marriage'; compounded
of eado- and -gamy. Cp. exogamy.
Derivatives: endogam-ic, endogam-ous, adjs.

## Endogenae
Endogenae, n. pi., an obsolete name of the Mono-
cotyledones (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'growing
within' (see endo- and -gen); so called because the
stems were erroneously supposed to grow from
within. Cp. Ezogenae.

## endogenous
endogenous, adj., growing from within (biol.) —
See prec. word and -genous and cp. exogenous.

## endolymph
endolymph, п., the fluid in the labyrinth of the
ear (anat.) — Compounded of endo- and lymph.

## endomorph
endomorph, п., a crystal enclosed in another
(mineral.) — Compounded of endo- and Gk.
μορφή, 'form, shape'. See morpho-.
Derivative: endomorph-ic, adj.

## endoparasite
endoparasite, п., an internal parasite (as e.g. a
tapeworm): — Compounded of endo- and
parasite.

## endoplasm
endoplasm, п., the inner layer of protoplasm in
a cell (biol.) — Compounded of endo- and
plasm. Cp. ectoplasm.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:274 COLUMN:3 -->

## endoplast
endoplast, п., the nucleus of a protozoan (biol.) —
Compounded of endo- and -plast. Cp. ectoplast.

## endopleura
endopleura, п., the inner integument of a seed
(bot.) — Compounded of endo- and pleura.

## endorse
endorse, indorse, tr. v. — Fr. earlier endosse, fr.
OF. (= F.) endosser, lit. 'to put on the back of,
fr. en- (see 1st en-) and VL. dossum, assimilated
form of L. dorsum, 'back'; see dorsal and cp.
dosser, dossier. E. endorse was assimilated in
form to ML. indorsare.
Derivatives: endors-ee, п., endorse-ment, п.,
endorser, n.

## endosarc
endosarc, п., the endoplasm (zool.) —
Compounded of endo- and Gk. σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'flesh'.
See sarco-.

## endoscope
endoscope, n„ an instrument for examining the
interior of cavities in the body (med.) — Coined
by its inventor Desormeaux in 1852 fr. endo-
and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at,
examine'. See -scope.

## endoskeleton
endoskeleton, п., the internal skeleton of
vertebrates, in contradistinction to the exoskeleton
of invertebrates, crustaceans, etc. (zool.) —
Compounded of endo- and skeleton. The term
endoskeleton was introduced into science by the
English anatomist Sir Richard Owen (1804-92).
Cp. exoskeleton, splanchnoskeleton.
Derivative: endoskelet-al, adj.

## endosmosis
endosmosis, п., inward osmosis (physiol.) —
Compounded of end- and osmosis. Cp. exos-
mosis.

## endosperm
endosperm, п., nutritive matter formed in the
embryo sac of seed plants (bot.) — Compounded
of endo- and sperm.

## endospore
endospore, п., the inner layer of a spore (bot.,
zool. and bacteriol.) — Compounded of endo-
and spore.

## endosteum
endosteum, п., the lining of the medullary cavity
in bones (anat.) — Medical L., compounded of
ead- and Gk. όστέον, 'bone'. See osteo-.

## endostosis
endostosis, п., bone formation beginning in the
substance of a cartilage (anat.) — Medical L.,
lit. 'bone increase from within', compounded of
endo- and -ostosis. Cp. exostosis.

## endotheclum
endotheclum, п., the inner lining of the cavity of
an anther (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'inner case', fr.
endo- and Gk. θήκη, 'case'. See theca and cp.
exothecium.

## endothelium
endothelium, п., a tissue which lines internal
cavities of the body (anal.) — Medical L.,
compounded of endo- and Gk. θηλή, 'teat, nipple'.
See thely- and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: endotheli-al, adj.

## endow
endow, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) endouer, fr. 1st en-
and douer, 'to bestow, endow', fr. L. dotare, 'to
endow', prop, 'to provide with a dowry', fr. dds,
gen. dotis, 'marriage portion, dowry'. See dower,
dowry.
Derivatives: endow-er, п., endow-ment, n.

## Endromis
Endromis, п., a genus of moths, the Kentish glory
(entomol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ένδρομίς, gen.
ένδρομίδος, 'a thick cloak worn by runners' fr.
έν (see 2nd en-) and δρόμος, 'running course,
race'; see dromedary. The genus was called
Endromis in allusion to the hairy body.

## endue
endue, indne, tr. v., 1) to put on (a garment); 2) to
invest; 3) to endow. — ME. endewen, fr. OF.
enduire, fr. L. inducere, 'to lead into*, fr. in,
'in', and ducere, 'to lead' (see in-, 'in', and duke);
influenced both in form and sense by a
confusion with L. induere, 'to put on' and with E.
endow.

## endure
endure, tr. and intr. v. — OF. endurer, fr. L. «1-
durare, 'to make hard, harden', fr. in-, 'in', and
durare, 'to make hard, harden', fr. durus, 'hard'.
See dure, adj., and cp. indurate.
Derivatives: endur-able, adj., endur-abil-ity, п.,
endur-able-ness, п., endur-abl-y, adv.,
endurance, п., endur-ant, adj., endur-er, п., endur-ing,
adj., endur-ing-ly, adv., endur-ing-ness, n.

## Eadymlon
Eadymlon, п., a beautiful youth loved by the
Greek moon goddess Selene (Greek mythol.) —·
L., fr. Gk. Ένδυμίων, lit. prob. 'Diver, Plunger',
fr. ένδύειν, 'to enter into, sink into', fr. έν (see
2nd en-) and δύειν, 'to enter into, sink into,
plunge into, dive; to set' (prop, 'to dive into
the sea'; said of the sun and stars). According
to the opinion of several scholars Endymion was

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:275 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ENDVSIS | 248 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:275 COLUMN:1 -->
orig. worshiped as a solar deity and his name
is a personification of the Setting Sun Sinking
into the Sea. See adytum and cp. Anadyomene.

## endysis
endysis, п., the act of developing a new coat of
hair, etc. (biol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ενδυσις, 'a
putting on', fr. evSuciv, 'to enter into; to put
on', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and δύειν, 'to enter;
to put on' (lit. 'to enter into'). See adytum and
cp. ecdysls, ependyma. Cp. also prec. word.

## -ene
-ene, sufT. used to form names of unsaturated
hydrocarbons (chem.) — Gk. -ήνη, fem.
patronymic sun".

## Eneas
Eneas, masc. PN. — L. Aeneas, fr. Gk. Αινείας,
lit. 'praiseworthy', fr. αίνος, 'tale, story, saying;
praise'. See enigma.

## enema
enema, п., injection of a fluid into the rectum
(med.) — Late L., fr. Gk. ένεμα, 'injection,
clyster', fr. ένιέναι, 'to throw in, send in', fr. έν
(see 2nd en·) and ίέναι, 'to send, throw,
project', which stands for 'yi-ye-nai and is cogn.
with L. jacire, 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt
forth', and cp. words there referred to.

## enemy
enemy, n. — OF. enemi (F. ennemi), fr. L. ini-
mlcus, 'hostile, unfriendly; an enemy', fr. in-,
'not', and amicus, 'friend'. Cp. It. nemico, Prov-
enc. enemic, Catal. enamic, Sp. enemigo, Port.
inimigo, which all derive fj. L. inimicus, and
see amicable. Cp. also enmity, inimical.

## energetic
energetic, adj. — Gk. ενεργητικός, 'able to act
upon', fr. ένεργεΐν, 'to work, be strenuous, act
upon', fr. ενεργής, later form of ενεργός, 'at
work, active'. See energy and -ic.
Derivatives: energetics, n. pi., energetic-al-ly,
adv., energet-ic-isl, п., energet-ist-ic, adj.

## energumen
energumen, п., a demoniac; a fanatic. — Late L.
energumenos, 'one possessed of the devil', fr.
Gk. ενεργούμενος, pass. pres. part, of ένεργεΐν,
'to act upon'. See energy. For the sufT. see
alumnus and cp. words there referred to.

## energy
energy, n. — Late L. energia, fr. Gk. ενέργεια,
'energy, efficiency', which was formed by
Aristotle fr. ενεργής, later form of ενεργός, 'at
work, active', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and έργον,
'work'. See ergon and cp. allergy, anergy.
Derivatives: energ-ic, adj. (rare), energ-ize, tr.
and intr. v., energ-iz-er, n.

## enervate
enervate, tr. v. — L. enervatus, pp. of enervare,
'to enervate, weaken', fr. e- and nervus, 'nerve,
sinew'. See aerve and verbal sufT. -ate.

## enervate
enervate, adj. — L. enervatus, pp. of enervare. See
enervate, v.

## enervation
enervation, n. — L. enervalio, gen. -onis, fr.
enervatus, pp. of enervare. See enervate, v., and -ion.

## enface
enface, tr. v., to write (print, etc.) on the face (of
a document). — Formed fr. 1st en- and face.

## eufeeble
eufeeble, tr. v. — OF. enfeblir, fr. 1st en- and
feble, 'feeble'. See feeble.

## enfeoff
enfeoff, tr. v., to invest with a fief. — AF. enfe-
offer, corresponding to OF. enfeffer, enfieffer.
See 1st en- and feoff, fief.
Derivative: enfeoff-ment, n.
Enfield rifle. — So called from the factory in
Enfield in Middlesex, England, where it was first
manufactured.

## enfilade
enfilade, п., gunfire sweeping from flank to flank.
— F., fr. enfiler, 'to thread (a needle); to
enfilade', fr. 1st en- and fit, 'thread'. See file,
'collection of papers', and -ade and cp. filament,
profile.
Derivative: enfilade, tr. v.

## enfold
enfold, tr. v. — Formed fr. ι st en- and fold.

## enforce
enforce, tr. v. — OF. enforcier, enforcer (F. en-

## forcir)
forcir), 'to strengthen', fr. VL. *infortldre, 'to
make strong', fr. in- 'in', and fortis, 'strong'.
See force. Derivatives: enforce-able, adj.,
enforc-ed-ly, adv., enforcement (q.v.), enforc-er, n.

## enforcement
enforcement, n. — OF., fr. enforcer. See prec.
word and -ment.

## enfraachise
enfraachise, tr. v., to admit to citizenship. — OF.
enfranchiss-, pres. part, stem of enfranchir, fr.
ι st en- and franchir, 'to set free', fr. franc, fem.
tranche, 'free'. See franchise.
Derivatives: enfranchis-er, п., enfranchise-ment,
n.

## engage
engage, tr. and intr. v. — F. engager, fr. 1st en-
and gage, 'pledge'. See gage.
Derivatives: engag-ed, adj., engage-ment, п.,
engag-er, п., engag-ing, adj., engag-ing-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:275 COLUMN:2 -->

## engender
engender, tr. v. — F. engenJrer, fr. L. ingenerare,
"to implant, produce, engender', fr. in-, 'in*, and
generare, 'to produce, engender'. See ingener-
ate, v.
Derivatives: engender-er, п., engender-ment, n.

## engine
engine, n. — OF. engin, 'skill; invention;
machine, engine', fr. L. ingenium, 'nature, natural
disposition, talent, ability', fr. in-, 'in', and the
stem of gignere (perf. genui), 'to beget'. See
genus and cp. genius, ingenious.
Derivatives: engineer (q.v.), engin-ery, n.

## eagine
eagine, tr. v. — Partly fr. OF. enginier, 'to con-
. irive, invent', fr. ML. ingenidre, fr. L. ingenium,
partly directly fr. engine, n.

## engineer
engineer, n. — Formed fr. engine with suff. -eer.
Derivatives: engineer, tr. and intr. v.,
engineering, n.

## England
England, n. — OE. Engla land, lit. 'land of the
Angles'; see next word and land: For the
contraction of OE. Engla land into England see
haplology.
Derivative: England-er, n.

## English
English, adj. and n. — OE. Englisc, Aenglisc,
'English', fr. Engle, Angle, name of a Teutonic
tribe that settled in Britain, prop, 'the people
coming from AnguV. See Angle and adj. suff. -isb.
Derivatives: English, tr. v., English-ry, n.

## engorge
engorge, tr. v. — F. engorger, 'to obstruct, block;
to congest' (med.) See ist en- and gorge.
Derivative: engorge-ment, n.

## engrail
engrail, tr. v., 1) to indent (her.); 2) to adorn. —
ME. engrailen, fr. OF. engresler (F. engreler),
fr. 1st en- and gresle (F. grele), 'hail', fr. greler,
'to hail', which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: engrail-ed, adj., engrail-ment, n.

## engrain
engrain, tr. v., 1) to ingrain; 2) to grain in
imitation of wood. — ME. engreynen, lit. 'to dye
in grain', fr, OF. (= F.) en graine, 'in grain',
fr. en, 'in' (see 1 st en-), and graine, 'seed of plants;
cochineal; scarlet grain', fr. L. grana, pi. of gra-
num, 'grain, seed', which was mistaken for a fem.
singular. The French language differentiates
between grain (fr. L. grdnum), 'grain, berry'
and graine (fr. L. grana), 'seed of plants'.
Cp. also It. and Sp. grano, 'grain', grana, 'seed
of plants; cochineal; scarlet grain', and see
grain, Cp. also ingrain, which is a var. of
engrain.

## engrave
engrave, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and grave,
'to carve'.
Derivatives: engrav-ed, adj., engrave-ment, п.,
engrav-er, п., engrav-ing, n.

## engross
engross, tr. v., to write in large letters. — AF.
engrosser, fr. F. en grosse, 'in large letter', fr. en,
'in' (see 1st en-), and grosse, 'large writing',
prop, fem of gros, 'big, bulky, thick', fr. Late
L. grossus. See gross.
Derivatives: engross-ed, adj. engross-ment, n.

## engross
engross, tr. v., to monopolize, absorb. — The
orig. meaning was 'to buy up the whole of a
commodity'; fr. F. acheter en gros, 'to buy
wholesale', fr. en gros, 'in a bulk; wholesale', fr. en,
'in' (see 1st en-), and gros, 'big, bulky, thick', fr.
Late L. grossus. See gross and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: engross-ed, adj., engross-ed-ly, adv.,
engross-ing, adj., engross-ing-ly, adv., engross-
ing-ness, п., engross-ment, n.

## engulf
engulf, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and gulf.
Derivative: engulf-ment, n.

## engyscope
engyscope, п., a kind of microscope (optics). —
Compounded of Gk. εγγύς,'near', and-σκόπιον,
fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine'. The first
element is prob. formed fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
*γύ5, 'hand', and lit. means 'that which is at
hand'. Cp. έγγύη, 'surety, security, bail', prop,
'pledge put into one's hand', which is prob.
also formed fr. έν and *γύ5. Gk. *γύδ is cogn.
with Avestic gava, 'both hands'. Both these
words derive fr. I.-E. base *geu-, 'to bend, curve,
arch'; see cove and cp. words there referred to.
For the sense development of Gk. εγγύς, 'near',
lit. 'at hand', cp. L. comminus, 'close at hand',
which is formed fr. OL. com (= L. cum), 'with',
and manus, 'hand'; cp. also E. at hand, G. vor-
handen, "existing', lit. 'before the hands', and
Heb. 'al yad, 'next to, near', lit. 'on, or by, the
hand'. For the second element in engyscope see
-scope. Cp. telengyscope.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:275 COLUMN:3 -->

## enhance
enhance, tr. v., to raise, increase. — ME. en-
hauncen, fr. AF. enhauncer. Drob. a eormntinn
of OF. enhaucer, fr. VL. *inaltiare, 'to raise',
fr. in-, 'in, upon', and "airfare, 'to raise', fr. L.
alius, 'high'. See 1st ea- and alt and cp. haace,
hawser.
Derivatives: enhanc-ed, adj., enhance-menl, п.,
ennanc-er, n.

## enharmonic
enharmonic, п., pertaining to tones derived from
different degrees, but practically of the same
pitch (mus.) — Late L. enkarmonicus, fr. Gk.
έναρμονικάς, έναρμονιάς, 'musical, harmonious,
enharmonic', fr. έν (see 2nd ea-) and αρμονία,
'harmony'. See harmony.
Derivatives: enharmonic, п., enharmonic-al-ly,
adv.

## Enid
Enid, fem. PN. — W., lit. 'soul' or 'purity'.

## enigma
enigma, п., a riddle, puzzle. — L. aenigma, fr.
Gk. αίνιγμα, gen. αινίγματος, 'dark saying,
riddle', fr. αΙνίσσεσ!>αι, 'to speak darkly, speak
in riddles', fr. αίνος, 'tale, story, saying; praise;
proverb; riddle', which is of unknown origin.
Cp. Enens.
Derivatives: enigmatical) (q.v.), enigmat-ist, п.,
enigmat-ize, tr. v.

## enigmatic
enigmatic, enigmatical, adj., 1) pertaining to an
enigma; 2) puzzling. — Late L. aenigmaticus
(whence also F. enigmatique), fr. aenigma, geh.
aenigmatis, fr. Gk. αίνιγμα. See prec. word and
-1c, resp. also -al.

## enigmatographer
enigmatographer, п., a maker of enigmas. — See
next word and agential suff. -er.

## enigniatography
enigniatography, п., the art of making
enigmas. — Compounded of Gk. αίνιγμα, gen.
αινίγματος, 'riddle', and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See enigma and -graph}'.

## enisle
enisle, tr. v., 1) to place on an island; 2) to make
an island of. — Formed fr. ist en- and isle.

## enjambment
enjambment, п., the running over of a sentence
into the next verse. — F. enjambement, fr. en-
jamber, 'to skip over', fr. 1st en- and jambe, 'leg'.
See jamb and -ment.

## enjoin
enjoin, tr. v., 1) to command; 2) to prohibit. —
ME. enjoignen, fr. F. enjoign-, stem of enjoindre,
'to enjoin, charge, direct', fr. L. injungere, 'to
join, attach; to charge, impose upon', fr. in-,
'in' and jungere, 'to join'. See join and cp. in-
junctioa.
Derivatives: enjoin-er, п., enjoin-ment, n.

## enjoy
enjoy, tr. v. — ME. enjoyen, fr. OF. enjolr, 'to
enjoy', fr. 1st en- unajolr (f.jouir), fr. VL. *gau-
dire, formed (with change of conjugation) fr. L.
gaudlre, 'to rejoice, be glad'. Cp. OProvenc.
jauzir (fr. VL. 'gaudire), It. godere (fr. L.
gaudlre), 'to rejoice', and see joy.
Derivatives: enjoy-able, adj., enjoy-able-ness, п.,
enjoy-abl-y, adv., enjoy-er, п., enjoy-ment, n.

## ealace
ealace, tr. v. — F. enlacer, fr. L. inlaqueare, il-
laqueare, 'to ensnare, entangle', fr. ia-, 'in' and
L. laqueus, 'noose, snare'. See lace.
Derivative: enlace-ment, n.

## enlarge
enlarge, v. — ME. enlargen, fr. OF. enlargier, en-
larger, fr. ist en- and large, 'broad, wide'. See
large.
Derivatives: enlarg-ed, adj., enlarg-ed-ly, adv..
enlarg-ed-ness, п., enlarge-ment,'n., enlarg-er, п.,
enlarg-ing-ly, adv.

## enlighten
enlighten, tr. v. — Formed fr. ist en-and lighten.
Derivatives: enlighten-ed, adj., enlighlen-ed-ly,
adv., enlighten-ed-ness, п., enlighten-ing, adj.,
enlighten-ing-ly, adv., enlighten-ment, n.

## enlist
enlist, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. ist en- and
list, 'roll, catalogue'.
Derivatives: enlist-er, п., enlist-ment, n.

## enliven
enliven, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en-, life (cp. the
plural lives) and verbal suff. -en.
Derivatives: enliven-er, п., enliven-ing, adj., en-
liven-ing-ly, adv.

## en masse
en masse, in a mass, by the bulk, as a whole. —
F., fr. en, 'in*, and masse, 'mass'. See 1st en-
and mass, 'quantity, size'.

## enmesh
enmesh, tr. v. ■— Formed fr. 1 st en- and mesh (q.v.)
Derivative: enmesh-ment, n.

## enmity
enmity, n. — ME. enemyte, fr. OF. enemistie, fr.
VL. *inimicitatem, ace. of 'inimicitas,
corresponding to L. inimicitia, 'enmity, hostility',
fr. inimicus, 'enemy'. See enemy and -ity and
cp. amity.
