емка-, combining form meaning *nine\ — Fr.
Gk. εννέα, 'nine', which stands for *έννέ5α,
*ένΓα-, and is cogn. with ΟΙ. πάνα, L. novem,
Goth, niun, OE. nigon, 'nine'. See nine and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also eunead.

## enneacontahedron
enneacontahedron, п., a polyhedron with ninety
faces. — Compounded of Gk. *έννεάκοντα.
'ninety', and έδρα, 'side, face'. *Έννεάκοντα is
erroneously formed fr. εννέα, 'nine'; the correct
form is ένενήκοντα. See eunea- and -hedron.
For the suff. -κοντά (in *έννεάκοντα,
ένενήκοντα) see penteconta-.

## ennead
ennead, п., a group of nine things. — From Gk.
έννεάς, gen. έννεάδος, 'a group of nine', fr. εννέα.
See eunea- and -nd.
Derivative: ennead-ic, adj.

## ennoble
ennoble, tr. v. — F. ennoblir. See 1st en- and noble.
Derivatives: ennoble-ment, п., ennobl-er, п., en-
nobl-ing, adj., ennobl-ing-Iy, adv.

## ennui
ennui, п., weariness, boredom. — F., fr. OF.
enui, back formation fr. enuier (F. ermuyer). See
anaoy, v. and n.

## Enoch
Enoch, masc. PN.; l) the eldest son of Cain;
2) the father of Methuselah (Bible). — Late L.
Enoch, fr. Gk. Ένώχ, fr. Heb. Hunikh, lit.
'dedicated, consecrated', fr. hanakh, 'he dedicated,
consecrated*, whence also hanukkdl·,
'dedication', consecration'. See Hanukkah.

## enorm
enorm, adj., l) abnormal (obsol.); 2) enormous;
outrageous (archaic). — F. enorme, fr. L. ёпбг-
mis, 'irregular, unusual, enormous, immense', fr.
ё norma, 'out of rule*, fr. ё, 'out of (see e-), and
norma, abl. of norma, 'rule, pattern'. See norm.

## enormity
enormity, n. — F. enormite, fr. L. endrmitatem,
ace. of enormitas, 'hugeness, vastness', fr. ёпбг-
mis. See prec. word and -ity.

## enormous
enormous, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
inormis. See enorm.
Derivatives: enormous-ly, adv., enormous-ness, n,

## Euos
Euos, masc. PN.; in the Bible, son of Seth. —
Gk. Ένώς, fr. Heb. Entsh, lit. 'man', rel. to Heb.
nashfm, 'women', ish (for insh), 'man', Arab.
ins (coll.), 'men, people', and prob. also to
Arab, anisa, 'he joined, was friendly', Akkad.
eneshu, to unite, join (intr.)

## enough
enough, adj. — ME. inogh, enogh, enouh, fr. OE.
genoh, rel. to OS. ginog, ON. gnogr, Swed. nog,
Dan. nok, OFris. enoch, Du. genoeg, OHG. ginu-
og(i), MHG. genuoc, G. genug, Goth, ganohs,
'enough', OE. geneah, OHG. ginah, Goth.ganah,
'it suffices', fr. I.-E. base *enek-, *nek-, *nk-, 'to
reach, attain, carry', whence also OI. aSnati,
Avestic ashnaoiti, 'reaches, arrives at', ΟΙ. ηά-
iati, Avestic nasaiti, 'reaches', OI. amsah,
'portion, part', Avestic qsa-, 'party', Hitt. nakish,
'heavy', nikzi, 'rises', ninikzi, 'lifts, raises', Gk.
έν-εγκεΐν, 'to bear, carry', διηνεκής, Att. διανε-
κής, 'continuous, unbroken' (which are prob. a
contraction of *δια-τ)νεκής and lit. mean
'capable of being carried through', fr. 8ιά, 'through',
and ένεγχεΐν, 'to carry'), 8γκος, 'bulk, size, mass,
body', L. nanclsci (for na-n-c-isci), perf. naclus
sum, 'to reach, obtain', OSlav. nesg, nesli, Lith.
neSu, niSti, Lett, nesu, nest, 'to bear, carry',
Lith. naSta, 'burden', and perh. also Toch- A
ents-, В enk-, 'to seize, take'. Cp. onco-, 'bulk,
size'.
Derivatives: enough, n. and adv.

## enounce
enounce, tr. v., t) to state publicly; 2) to utter. —
F. enoncer, fr. L. enuntiare, 'to divulge, disclose,
report, say, declare', fr. e- and nuntiare, 'to
announce, declare', fr. nuntius, 'messenger'. See
nuncio and cp. enunciate. Cp. also announce
and words there referred to.
Derivative: enounce-ment, n.

## enow
enow, adj. n. and adv., enough. — ME. inowe;
an archaic var. of enough.

## en passant
en passant, by the way. — F.", lit. 'in passing', fr.
en, 'in' and passant, pres. part, of passer, 'to
pass*. See 1st en-, pass and -ant

## enquire
enquire, enquiry. — See inquire, inquiry,

## enrage
enrage, tr. and intr. v. — OF. (= F.) enrager,
formed fr. 1st en- and rage, 'rage, fury'. See
rage.
Derivatives: enrag-ed, adj., enrag-ed-ly, adv.,
enrag-ed-ness, n.

## enrapt
enrapt, adj., enraptured. — Formed fr. 1st en-
and rapt; introduced by Shakespeare-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:276 COLUMN:2 -->

## enrapture
enrapture, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and rapture.
Derivative: enraplur-er, n.

## enravish
enravish, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and ravish.

## enregister
enregister, tr. v. — F. enregtstrer, 'to enter into a
register', fr. 1st en- and registre. See register.
Derivatives: enregistr-ation, п., enregistr-y, n.

## enrich
enrich, tr. v. — F. enrichir, formed fr. 1st en-
and riche, 'rich'. See rich.
Derivatives: enrich-er, п., enrich-ing, adj., en-
rkh-ing-ly, adv., enrich-ment, n.

## enroll
enroll, enrol, tr. v. — ME. enrollen, fr. OF. en-
roller (F. enrdler), 'to enter into a roll, enroll',
which is formed fr.-ist en- and OF. rolle (F.
role). See roll, v. and п., and cp. role.
Derivatives: enroll-ed, adj., enroll-er, п.,
enrollment (q.v.)

## enrollment
enrollment, enrolment, n. — F. enrolement, fr.
enrdler, to enroll'. See enrol and -ment.

## en route
en route, on the way. — F., fr. en, 'in, on', and
route, 'road, way, route'. See 1st en- and ronte.

## ens
ens, п., being; entity (philos.) — Late L. ens (gen.
entis), back formation fr. est, 'is'. See esse and
cp. entity and the third word in dolce far niente.

## ensample
ensample, п., an example (archaic.) — ME. en-
sample, fr. OF. ensample, a var. of essample,
fr. orig. example, exemple. See exnmple and
cp. sample.

## ensanguine
ensanguine, tr. v., to stain with blood. — Formed
fr. 1st en- and L, sanguis, gen. sanguinis, 'blood'.
See asnguine.

## ensconce
ensconce, tr. v., to conceal. — The original
meaning was 'to cover with a fort'. See 1st en- and
sconce.

## ensemble
ensemble, п., the whole. — F., 'together', fr. L.
insimul, 'at the same time', which is formed fr.
in-, 'in', and simul, 'at the same time, together'.
See simultaneous and cp. assemble.

## enshrine
enshrine, tr. v. — Formed fr. ist ea- and shrine.

## ensiform
ensiform, adj., sword-shaped. — Compounded
of L. ensis, 'sword', and forma, 'form, shape'.
The first element stands for *nsis and is cogn.
with OI. <u/A, 'sword, butcher's knife*. For the
second element see form, n.

## ensign
ensign, п., ι) a flag; 2) in the United States Navy,
a commissioned officer of the lowest rank. —
OF. (= F.) enseigne, fr. L. insignia, pi. of In-
signe, 'mark, sign, badge of office', prop. neut.
of insignis, 'remarkable, noted, distinguished',
but mistaken in Vulgar Latin for a fern. sing,
noun. L. insignis is formed fr. in- 'in", and sig-
num, 'mark, sign'; see sign and cp. insignia. Cp.
also It. insegna, OProvenc. ensenha and OSp.
ensena, which all derive fr. L. insignia.
Derivative: ensign-су, n.

## ensign
ensign, tr. v., to distinguish. — OF. ensignier, en-
seignier, 'to point out, indicate, teach' (whence
F. enseigner, 'to teach'), fr. VL. *lnsignwre,
corresponding to L. insigntre, 'to "mark,
distinguish', fr. in-, 'in' and signum, 'mark, sign'.
See siga, п., and cp. prec. word.

## ensilage
ensilage, п., the preservation of food in a silo. —
F. See next word and -age and cp. silage.
Derivative: ensilage, v.

## ensile
ensile, tr. v., to preserve (food) in a silo. — F. en-
siler, fr. 1st en- and silo, fr. L. sirus. See silo.

## enslave
enslave, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and slave.
Derivatives: enslave-ment, п., enslav-er, n.

## ensnnre
ensnnre, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and snare.
Derivatives: ensnare-ment, п., ensnar-er, п.,
ensnar-ing-ly, adv.

## enstatite
enstatite, п., a magnesium silicate (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. ένστάτης,
'adversary'; so called in allusion to its
refractory nature. Gk. ένστάτης derives from the stem
of ένίστημί, Ί stand in; I oppose', fr. έν (see
2nd en-) and Ιοτημι, Ί cause to stand; I stand',
fr. I.-E. base *sta-, 'to stand', whence also L.
stare, 'to stand'. See state and cp. histo-.

## ensue
ensue, tr. and intr. v. — OF. enseu, pp. of en-
suivre, 'to follow, ensue*, fr. VL. *insequere,
corresponding to L. insequi, 'to follow, strive after',
fr. in-, 'in', and sequi, 'to follow*. See sequel and
cp. sue, suit, suite.
Derivatives: ensu-ing, adj., ensu-ing-ly, adv.

## ensure
ensure, tr. v. — AF. enseurer, formed fr. 1st
en- and OF. seur (whence F. sur), 'sure'. See
sure and cp. insure.
Derivative: ensur-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:276 COLUMN:3 -->

## -ent
-ent, adj. and subst. suff. denoting an agent or
an instrument. — OF. and F. -ent, fr. L. -en-
tern, ace. of -ens, pres. part. suff. of verbs
pertaining to the II and III conjugation. See -ant
and cp. -ence, -ency.

## entablature
entablature, п., a horizontal structure composed
of cornice, frieze and architrave and supported
by columns (archit.)'— MF., fr. It. intavolatura,
fr. intavolare, fr. in- (fr. L. in) and tavola (fr. L.
tabula, 'board, plank, table'). See in-, 'in', table
and -ure.
Derivative: entablatur-ed, adj.

## entablement
entablement, п., platform -on which a statue
stands. — F., fr. VL. intabulamentum, fr. In-,
'in', and L. tabulamentum, 'boarding, flooring',
fr. tabula, 'table'. See table and -ment.

## entail
entail, tr. v., 1) to bestow as a heritage; 2) to
involve. — Formed fr. 1st en- and AF. tail,
'limitation, limit of ownership', fr. OF. taillier (F.
tailler), 'to cut'. See tail, tailor.
Derivatives: entail,n.; entail-er, п., entail-ment, n.

## entangle
entangle, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and tangle
(q-v.)
Derivatives: entangl-ed, adj., entangl-ed-ly, adv.,
enlangl-ed-ness, п., entangl-er, п., entangl-ing,
adj., entangl-ing-ly, adv.

## entasla
entasla, п., tonic spasm (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. εντασις, 'a stretching, straining'. See
next word and -ia.

## entasis
entasis, п., convexity in the shaft of a column
(archit.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έντασις, 'a
stretching', fr. έντεΐνειν, 'to stretch or strain tight',
fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and τείνειν, 'to stretch,
strain'. See tasimeter and cp. ectasis and words
there referred to.

## entelechy
entelechy, п., actuality as opposed to potentiality
(philos.) — L. entelechia, fr. Gk. εντελέχεια,
'full reality', coined by Aristotle fr. εντελής,
'complete', and έχειν, 'to have'. The first
element is formed fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
τέλος, 'end, perfection'; see tele-. For the
etymology of έχειν see hectic.

## entellus
entellus, п., name of the long-tailed monkey of
the East-Indies. — Named after Entellus, a
Sicilian hero, a pugilist, mentioned in the Ae-
neid (V, 387 foil.). The name is prob. related to
Entella, a town in Sicily (now called Rocca
d'Entella).

## entelodoat
entelodoat, п., any animal that pertained to the
extinct genus Elotherium. — Compounded of
Gk. εντελής, 'complete, fullgrown', and οδών,
gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See entelechy and -odont.

## entente
entente, п., an understanding. — F.,
'understanding, agreement, skill, judgment*, prop. fem. pp.
of entendre, 'to hear, understand, intend, mean',
used as a noun. F. entendre orig. meant 'to
direct one's attention'. It derives fr. L. intendere,
'to stretch out, extend; to direct'. See intend.

## enter
enter, tr. and intr. v. — ME. entren, fr. OF. (= F.)
entrer, fr. L. intrare, 'to enter' (whence also Rum.
intra. It. entrare, OProvenc. entrar, intrar, Catal.,
Sp,, Port, entrar), formed fr. intra, 'within'; see
intra- and cp. enter-, entre-, entrance, entrant,
eatree, entry. For sense development cp. OE.
innian, 'to enter', fr. inne, 'therein'. — There is
no connection between L. intrare and trans,
'across, over'.

## enter-
enter-, combining form in words of French
origin, corresponding to F. entre-, fr. L. inter,
'among, between'. — See inter, prep., and cp.
entre-.

## eater-
eater-, form of entero- before a vowel.

## enteric
enteric, adj., pertaining to the intestines. — Gk.
εντερικός, 'intestinal', first used by Aristotle;
formed fr. έντερα (pi.), 'intestines', fr. I.-E.
*enter-, compar. of *en-, 'in', whence also L.
inter, 'among, between'. See inter, prep., and
-ic and cp. entero- and the second element in
archenteron, Coelenterata, dysentery, exeaterate,
lientery, mesentery, parenteric

## enteritis
enteritis, п., inflammation of the intestines (med.)
— Medical L., coined by the French
pathologist Francois-Boissier de la Croix de Sauvages
(1706-67) about 1750 fr. Gk. έντερα, 'intestines'.
See prec. word and -itis and cp. peritonitis.

## entero-
entero-, before a vowel sometimes enter-,
combining form denoting the intestines. — Gk.
έντερο-, έντερ, fr. έντερα, 'intestines'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:277 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ENTEROTOMV | 250 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:277 COLUMN:1 -->

## enterotomy
enterotomy, п., incision of the intestines. —
Compounded of entero- and Gk. -τομία, 'a Gutting
of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.

## enterprise
enterprise, n. — OF. (= F.) entreprise, 'an
undertaking', prop. fern. pp. of entreprendre, 'to
undertake', used as a noun, fr. VL. *inter-
prendere, fr. inter- and L. prehendere, prendere,
'to take, seize'. See prehensile and cp.
entrepreneur.
Derivatives: enterpris-er, п., enterpris-ing, adj.,
enterpris-ing-ly, adv.

## entertain
entertain, tr. and intr. v. — F. enireienir, fr. entre-
(see entre-, enter-) and tenir, 'to hold', fr. L.
tenlre. Cp. OProvenc. enireienir, Sp. enlretener,
It. intrattenere, 'to entertain', and see tenable.
Derivatives: entertain-ed, adj., entertain-ing,
adj., entertain-ing-ly, adv., enlerlain-ing-ness, п.,
enter lain-ment, n.

## enthetic
enthetic, adj., introduced from without (said of
diseases).— Gk. ένθετικός,ΐι for implanting',
fr. ένθετος, 'that which can be introduced or
implanted', verbal adj. of έντιθέναι, 'to put in,
introduce, implant', which is formed fr. έν (see
2nd en-) and τιθέναι, 'to put, place'. See theme
and -ic and cp. epenthetic, hypothetic,
parenthetic, prosthetic, synthetic.

## enthrall
enthrall, enthral, tr. v., to enslave. — Lit. 'to hold
in bondage', fr. 1st en- and thrall.
Derivatives: enihrall-er, п., enlhrall-ing, adj.,
enlhrall-ing-ly, adv., enthral(J)-ment, n.

## enthrone
enthrone, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st ea- and throne.
Derivatives: enthrone-ment, п., enthron-ize, tr.
v., enthron-iz-ation, n.

## enthuse
enthuse, tr. v., to make enthusiastic; intr. v., to
become enthusiastic^coZ/Oi?.) — Back formation
fr. enthusiasm.

## enthusiasm
enthusiasm, п., ι) inspiration; 2) zeal, fervor.—
Gk. ενθουσιασμός, 'divine inspiration', fr. έν-
θουσιάζειν, 'to be divinely inspired', fr. εν-θεος,
'divinely inspired', fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and θεός,
'god'. See theo-.

## enthusiast
enthusiast, n. — Gk. ενθουσιαστής, 'a person
inspired', fr. ένθουσιάζειν, 'to be divinely inspired'.
See prec. word.

## enthusiastic
enthusiastic, adj. — Gk. ενθουσιαστικός,
'inspired', fr. ενθουσιαστής, *a person inspired'. See
prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: enthusiastic-al, adj., enthusiastic-
al-ly, adv.

## enthymeme
enthymeme, п., a syllogism in which one premise
is omitted (logic). — L. enthymema, fr. Gk.
ενθύμημα, 'thought, argument', lit. 'a keeping in
mind', fr. ένθϋμεϊσθαι, 'to keep in mind,
consider, reflect', which is formed fr. έν (see 2nd en-)
and θυμός, 'spirit, mind, soul'. See thyme, thio-.

## enthymematic
enthymematic, enthymematical, adj., pertaining
to an enthymeme. — Gk. ένθΰμηματικός, fr.
ενθύμημα, gen. ενθυμήματος. See prec. word
and -ic.

## entice
entice, tr. v. — ME. entisen, fr. OF. enticier, 'to
stir up (fire); to excite, incite', fr. \\*.*intitiare,
'to stir up (fire)', fr. in-, 'in', and L. titio, gen.
-onis, 'a burning brand, a firebrand'. L. Ιΐϋδ
is of uncertain origin. Cp. F. tison, 'a firebrand'
(fr. L. titionem, ace. of titio), and attiser, 'to stir
up a fire, provoke' (fr. VL. *ad-titiare).
Derivatives: enticement (q.v.), enlic-er, п., en-
tic-ing, adj., entic-ing-ly, adv., entic-ing-ness, n.

## enticement
enticement, n. — OF. enticement, fr. enticier. See
prec. word and -ment.

## entire
entire, adj. — ME. enter, fr. OF. (= F.) entier,
fr. L. integrum, ace. of integer, 'whole,
undiminished, entire', lit. 'untouched'; see
integer. The OF. form entier (beside the regular
form entir) is due to the substitution of the
suff. -ier for the ending of this word, which was
mistaken for a suff.
Derivatives: entire-ly, adv., enlire-ness, п.,
entirety (q.v.)

## entirety
entirety, n.—AF. entiertie, corresponding to OF.
entierete, fr. L. integritutem, ace. of integritas,
'completeness, soundness, integrity'. See
integrity and cp. prec. word.

## entitle
entitle, tr. v. — AF. entiller, corresponding to
OF. entiteler, entituler (F. intituler), fr. 1st en-
and L. tilulus, 'title'. See title and cp. intitule,
which is a doublet of entitle.

## entity
entity, n. (philos.), l) being, existence, 2) the real

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:277 COLUMN:2 -->
thing. — ML. entitas (whence also F. entile), fr.
Late L. ens, gen. entis, 'a thing', prop, back
formation fr. L. esse, 'to be', and serving as
pres. part, of this verb. The formation of a pres.
part, of L. esse was esp. necessary to render the
Greek philosophical term τό fiv, 'that which is'
(8v is neut. of ών, pres. part, of είναι, 'to be').
See esse and cp. essence. Cp. also ens and the
third word in dolce far niente.

## ento-
ento-, combining form meaning 'within, inside,
inner'. — Gk. έντο-, fr. εντός, 'within, inside',
cogn. with L. intus, 'within', fr. I.-E. *en-tos,
fr. *en, 'in' and adverbial suff. -tos, denoting
the origin. For the first element see 2nd en-.
For the second element cp. OI. i-tdh, 'from
here', L. cael-itus, divin-itus, 'from heaven'.

## entomb
entomb, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st ea- and tomb.
Derivative: entomb-ment, n.

## entomlc
entomlc, adj., pertaining to insects. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. έντομα, 'insects'. See en-
tomo-.

## entomo-
entomo-, combining form meaning 'insect, in-
secti-', Gk. έντομο-, fr. έντομος, 'cut up, cut in
pieces', used in pi. neut. (= έντομα, scil. ζωα)
in the sense of 'insects', lit. 'animals cut in');
so called by Aristotle, Historia animalium,
487" 33 because their body is divided inio
segments; έντομος derives from έντέμνειν, to
cut in', which is formed fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and
τέμνειν, 'to cut'; see tome. Cp. L. insecta,
'insects' (fr. insecure, 'to cut into'), which is a loan
translation of Gk. έντομα (see insect).

## entomology
entomology, п., the study of insects. — F. ento-
mologie, which is compounded of entomo- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.

## entomophagous
entomophagous, adj., feeding on insects. —
Compounded of entomo- and Gk. -φάγος, 'eater of.
See -phagous.

## entomophilous
entomophilous, adj., fertilized by insects. —
Compounded of entomo- and Gk. φίλος, 'loved,
beloved'. See -phllous.

## Entoinostraca
Entoinostraca, n. pl„ a subclass of crustaceans
(zool.) — Compounded of entomo- and Gk.
80-τρακον, 'oyster shell'. See entomo- and os-
tracon.

## entomotomy
entomotomy, п., dissection of insects. —
Compounded of entomo- and Gk. -τομίά, 'a cutting
of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.
Derivative: entomotom-isl, n.

## entophyte
entophyte, п., a vegetable parasite living within
the body of an animal or another plant (hot.)
— Compounded of ento- and Gk. φυτόν, 'plant'.
See -phyte.
Derivative: entophyt-ic, adj.

## entotic
entotic, adj., pertaining to the interior of the ear.
— Compounded of Gk. εντός, 'within', and
ώτικός, 'pertaining to the ear'. See ento- and otic.

## entourage
entourage, п., ι) surroundings; 2) circle of
followers. — F., fr. entourer, 'to surround', fr. 1st
en- and tour, 'turn, circuit'. See tour and -age
and cp. tournure, detour.

## entozoa
entozoa, n. pi., internal parasites, esp. intestinal
worms. — ModL., compounded of ento- and
ζωα, pi. of ζωον, 'animal'. See zoo-i
Derivatives: entozo-al, adj., entozo-an, adj. and
п., entozo-ic, adj.

## entr'acte
entr'acte, п., interval between two acts;
interlude. — F., formed fr. entre, 'between', and
acte, 'act'. See entre- and act and cp. interact.

## entrails
entrails, n. pi., the internal organs; specif., the
intestines. — ME. entraille, fr. OF. entraille (in
F. only in pi.), fr. VL. intralia (occurring in the
Reichenau Glosses, dating from the end pf the
8th cent.), which is formed—with change of
suff.—fr. L. interanea, neut. pi. of interaneus,
'that which is within'," fr. inter, 'between,
among'. See inter, prep., and cp. enteric, entero-,

## entrain
entrain, tr. and intr. v., to put or go aboard a
train. — Formed fr. 1st en- and the noun train.

## entrain
entrain, tr. v., to draw on or along. — F. en-
trainer, fr. 1st en- and trainer, 'to draw'. See
train, v.

## entrammel
entrammel, tr. v., to put into trammels. —
Formed fr. 1st en- and trammel.

## entrance
entrance, п., the act of entering. — OF., fr. en-
trer. See enter and -ance.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:277 COLUMN:3 -->

## entrance
entrance, tr. v., to put into a trance. — Formed
fr. 1st en- and trance.
Derivatives: entrance-ment, п., entranc-ing, adj.,
entranc-ing-ly, adv.

## entrant
entrant, adj., entering; п., one who enters. — F.
entrant, pres. part, of entrer, 'to enter'. See
eater and -ant.

## entrap
entrap, tr. v. — OF. enlraper, 'to catch'. See 1st
en- and trap, 'mechanical device for catching
animals'. Derivative: entrapp-er, n.

## entre-
entre-, combining form in French loan words,
corresponding to English enter-, — Fr. F. entre,
'between, among', fr. L. inter, of s.m. See 1st
enter-,

## entreat
entreat, tr. and intr. v. — ME. entreten, fr. OF.
entrailer, 'to treat', fr. 1st en- and trailer, 'to
treat'. See treat.
Derivatives: entreat-ing, adj., entreat-ing-ly, adv.

## entreaty
entreaty, n. — Formed fr. entreat on analogy of
treaty.

## entree
entree, entree, п., 1) entrance, right to enter;
2) a course of meal. — F. entree. See entry.

## entremets
entremets, п., side dish, extra dish. — F„ fr. entre
mets, 'between dishes'. See 1st entre- and mess.

## entrench
entrench, intrench, tr. v. — Lit. 'to surround
with entrenchments'; formed fr. 1st en- (resp.
in-, 'in') and trench.
Derivatives: enlrench-er, п., enlrench-ment, n.

## entrepot
entrepot, п., a warehouse. — F.? fr. L. interposi-
tum, 'that which is placed between', neut. pp. of
interpOnere. See inter- and positioa and cp. depot.

## entrepreneur
entrepreneur, п., one who manages an
undertaking. — F., fr. entreprendre, 'to undertake', fr.
VL. *interprendere. See eatreprise.

## entresol
entresol, п., a story between the ground floor and
the first floor. — F., formed fr. 1st entre- and
sol, 'ground, earth', fr. L. solum, 'the lowest
part of a thing; the floor of a room', whence

## entropy
entropy, п., measure of the waste thermal energy
(phys.) — G. Entropie, formed on analogy of G.
Energie, 'energy', fr. 2nd en- and τροπή, 'a
turning, turn, change', first used in 1850 by the
German physicist Rudolf Julius Emmanuel
Clausius (1822-88). See trope and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## entrust
entrust, intrast, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- (resp.
in-, 'in') and trust.

## entry
entry, n. — F. entree, prop. fem. pp. of entrer,
'to enter', fr. L. intrare. Cp. It. entrata (fem. pp.
of enlrare), OProvenc. intrada (fem. pp. of in-
trar), Sp. entrada (fem. pp. of entrar) and see
enter. Cp. also entree.

## entwine
entwine, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and twine.

## entwist
entwist, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and twist.

## Enryloma
Enryloma, п., a genus of parasitic fungi (bot.) —
ModL., fr. 2nd en- and Gk. τύλωμα, 'callus', fr.
τύλος, 'a swelling'. See tyloma.

## enucleate
enucleate, tr. v., 1) to remove the kernel from the
husk; 2) to make clear; 3) (surg.) to remove (a
tumor, etc.) from its sac. — L. enucleatus, pp. of
enucleare, 'to take out the kernel, clear from
the husk, enucleate', fr. e- and nucleus, 'nut,

Derivative: enucleat-ion, n.

## enucleate
enucleate, adj., having no nucleus. — L.
enucleatus, pp. of enucleare. See enucieate, v.

## enumerate
enumerate, tr. v. — L. enumeratus, pp. of enu-
merare, 'to reckon up, count over, enumerate',
fr. e- and numerare, 'to count, number*, fr.
numerus, 'number'. See number and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: enumeration (q.v.), enumerat-ive,
adj., enumeral-or, n.

## enumeration
enumeration, n. — F. enumeration, fr. L. inume-
rationem, ace. of inumeratio, 'a counting up',
fr. enumeratus, pp. aienumerare. See prec. word
and -ion,

## enunciate
enunciate, tr. v., 1) to announce; 2) to pronounce.
— L. enHntidtus, pp. of enuntiare, 'to divulge,
disclose, report, say, declare', fr. e- and пйп-
tiare, 'to announce, declare'. See enounce.

## enunciation
enunciation, n. — L. enuntidtio, gen. -dnis,
'enunciation, declaration', fr. enuntialus, pp. of ёпйп-
tiare. See prec. word and -Ion and cp.
annunciation, denunciation, pronunciation.

## enuresis
enuresis, п., incontinence of urine (jned.) —

Medical L., fr. Gk. ένουρεΐν, 'to make water in',
fr. έν (see 2nd en-) and οΰρεΐν, 'to make water'.
See urhie.

## envelop
envelop, tr. v. — ME. envelupen, fr. OF. enve·
loper (F. envelopper), which is prob. formed fr.
1st en- and a blend of ML. faluppa, 'straw, ball
of corn', and L. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and
cp. develop.
Derivative: envelop-ment, n.

## envelope
envelope, n. — F. enveloppe, back formation fr.
envelopper. See prec. word.

## envenom
envenom, tr. v., l) to put poison on or in; 2) to
embitter. — ME. envenimen, fr. OF. envenimer,
fr. 1st en- and venim, 'venom'. See venom.

## enviable
enviable, adj. — Formed fr. envy with suff. -able.
Derivatives: enviable-ness, п., enviabl-y, adv.

## envious
envious, adj. — OF. envieus, fr. L. invidiosus,
'full of envy, envious', fr. invidia, 'envy'. See
envy, п., and -ous and cp. invidious, which is a
doublet of envious.
Derivative: envious-ly, adv., envious-ness, n.

## environ
environ, tr. v., to surround. — F. environner, 'to
surround', fr. environ, 'round about*, fr. 1st en-
and viron, 'a going round, circuit', fr. virer, 'to
turn round'. See veer.

## environment
environment, п., surroundings. — Formed fr.
environ with suff. -ment; introduced by Thomas
Carlyle (1795-1881) to render G. Umgebung.
Derivative: environment-al, adj.

## environs
environs, n. pi., outskirts. — F., fr. environ,
'round about'. See enviroa.

## envisage
envisage, tr. v., ]) to face; 2) to visualize. —F.
envisager, 'to face, consider, contemplate', fr.
1st en- and visage, 'face' (see visage); prob.
introduced into English by John Keats (1795-
1821).

## envoy
envoy, п., a postscript to a poem or to a prose
composition. — OF. envoy (F. envoi), 'a
sending', back formation fr. OF. envoiier (F. en-
voyer), 'to send', fr. VL. *invidre, of s.m., lit.
'to put on the way', fr. in-, 'in' and L. via, 'way'.
See via and cp. voyage, invoice.

## envoy
envoy, п., a messenger. —· F. envoye, pp. of en-
voyer, 'to send'. See prec. word.

## envy
envy, n. -»- OF. (= F.) envie, fr. L. invidia, 'envy,
jealousy', fr. invidere, 'to look askance at, look
maliciously at, cast an evil eye upon, to envy,
grudge', fr. in-, 'in', and vidire, 'to see'. See
vision and cp. envious. For sense development
cp. Avestic nipashnaka-, 'envious' (cogn. with
L. specid, Ί look at, behold'), OSlav. zavideti,
'to envy' (fr. viditi, 'to see') and Lith. pa-vydeli,
'to envy* (rel. to veizditi, 'to see, to look at*).

## envy
envy, tr. v. — F. envier, fr. VL. invidiare, 'to
envy', fr. L. invidia. See envy, n.

## enwind
enwind, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and wind,
'to turn' (q.v.)

## enwomb
enwomb,'tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and womb
(q.v.)

## enwrap
enwrap, tr. v. — Formed fr. 1st en- and wrap
(q.v.)

## enzootic
enzootic, adj., prevailing in a certain area (said
of diseases affecting animals) and
corresponding to endemic diseases in man. — F. enzoo-
tique, fr. 2nd en- and Gk. ζωον, 'animal'. See
zoo- and -ic and cp. epizootic.
Derivative: enzootic, п., an enzootic disease.

## enzyme
enzyme, п., a chemical ferment (biochem.) —
G. Enzym, coined by the German physiologist
Wilhelm Kuhne (1837-1900) in 1878 fr. MGk.
ένζυμος, 'leavened', fr. Gk. έν (see 2nd en-) and
ζόμη, 'leaven'. See zymosis.
Derivatives: enzym-atlc, enzym-ic, adjs.

## eo-
eo-, combining form meaning 'dawn'. — Gk.
ήω-, fr. ήώς, 'dawn', which stands for 'ausds
and is cogn. with OE. east, 'in the east'. See
enst and cp. words there referred to.

## eoan
eoan, adj., pertaining to the dawn. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. Sous, fr. Gk. ήφος, 'of the
dawn, pertaining to the dawn', fr. ήώς. See eo-
and -an.

## Eoanthropus
Eoanthropus, п., a prehistoric type of man, the
Piltdown man (anthropol.) — ModL., lit. 'man
of the dawn', compounded of eo- and Gk.
ίνθρωπος, 'man'. See anthropo-.

## Eocene
Eocene, adj., pertaining to the earliest division
of the Tertiary period (geol.) — Compounded
of eo- and Gk. καινές, 'new'. See kainite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:278 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: Eocene, п., the Eocene period.

## Eohlppus
Eohlppus, п., the progenitor of the horse (pale-
ontol.) — ModL., lit. 'horse of the dawn
(period)'; compounded of eo- and Gk. Ιππος,
'horse'. See hippo-,

## eolith
eolith, n„ a rude stone implement. — See next
word.

## eolithic
eolithic, adj., pertaining to the age preceding the
paleolithic Age (geol.) — Compounded of eo-
and Gk. λίθος, 'stone'. See lltbo-,

## Eomecon
Eomecon, п., a genus of Chinese plants of the
poppy family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
eo- and Gk. μήχων, 'poppy'. See meconium,

## eon
eon, n. — A variant of aeon.

## Eos
Eos, п., the goddess of dawn in Greek
mythology; identified with the Roman Aurora. — L.
Eos, also Eos, fr. Gk. Ήώς, lit. 'dawn'. See eo-.

## eosin
eosin, eosine, п., a rose-colored dye (chem.) —
Formed with chem. suff. -in, -ine fr. Gk. ήώς,
'dawn'. See eo-.

## -eous
-eous, adjectival suff. meaning 'of the nature of*.
— L. -eus as in ligneus, 'of wood, wooden' (fr.
lignum, 'wood', see ligneous). Cp. -ous.

## ep-
ep-, form of epi- before a vowel.

## epact
epact, п., the excess of the solar year over 12
lunar months (chronol.) — F. ipacte, fr. Late
L. epacta, 'an intercalary day', fr. Gk. έπακταί
(scil. ήμέραι), 'intercalary days', fern. pi. of
έπακτές, 'added, intercalated', verbal adj. of
έπάγειν, 'to bring forward, add, intercalate', fr.
έπί (see epi-) and αγειν, 'to lead', which is cogn.
with L. agere, 'to drive, set in motion, lead'. See
agent, adj., and cp. words there referred to.

## eparch
eparch, п., ι) governor of an eparchy; 2) bishop
of an eparchy. — Gk. ϊπαρχος, 'commander,
governor', fr. έπί (see epi) and άρχος, 'leader,
chief, ruler'. See -arch.

## eparchy
eparchy, п., subdivision of a province in modern
Greece. — Gk. επαρχία, 'office of an eparch,
province', fr. έπαρχος. See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. 45).

## epaulement
epaulement, п., breastwork serving as protection

'shoulder piece, breastwork', fr. ipauler, 'to
support with the shoulder, to make an
epaulement', fr. epaule, 'shoulder'. See next word and
-ment.

## epaulet
epaulet, also epaulette, n„ a shoulder ornament.
— F. epaulette, dimin. of epaule, 'shoulder', fr.
OF. espalle, espalde, fr. L. spatula, spathula, 'a
broad piece' (later 'shoulder'), dimin. of spatha,
'a broad wooden instrument, a broad, two-
edged sword', fr. Gk. σπάθη, 'a broad flat
sword'. See spade and cp. epauliere, epee,
espalier, pauldron, pawl, 'bar'. For the ending see
the suffixes -et, -ette.

## epauliere
epauliere, n„ shoulder piece worn on uniforms.
— F., 'shoulder strap; shoulder plate (armor)',
fr. epaule, 'shoulder', fr. OF. espauliere. See
prec. word.

## epee
epee, п., sword. — F„ fr. L. spatha. See epaulet.

## epeiric
epeiric, adj., covering continents or parts of
them — said of seas (geol.) — Formed with
suff. -ic fr. Gk. ήπεφος, 'mainland', which
stands for *απερ-ιος (ср. Dor. άπειρος, Aeol.
ίπερρος, of s.m.), and is cogn. with OE. ofer,
OFris. over, Du. oever, MHG. uover, G. Ufer,
'shore'.

## ependyma
ependyma, n„ the lining membrane of the
ventricles of the brain and the canal of the spinal
cord (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. έπένδυμα,
'upper garment', fr. έπεν8ύειν, 'to put on
over', fr. έπί (see epi-) and ένδύειν, 'to put on
(clothes)' (whence ένδυμα, 'garment'); see en-
dysis. Considering the fact that this membrane
consists of a single layer (= 'garment'), endyma
would be a more befitting name than ependyma,
since this latter lit. denotes a garment worn over
another garment.
Derivative: ependym-al, adj.

## ependymitis
ependymitis, п., inflammation of the ependyma
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -iris.

## ependymoma
ependymoma, п.; diseased condition of the
ependyma (jned.) — Medical L., formed fr.
ependyma with suff. -oma.

## epenfhesis
epenfhesis, п., insertion of a letter or a syllable
in a word (gramm.) — Late L., fr. Gk. έπέν-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:278 COLUMN:3 -->
θεσις, 'insertion*, fr. έπεντιθέναι, 'to insert',
fr. έπί (see epi-) and έντι*έναι, 'to put in', fr.
έν (see 2nd en-) and τιθέναί, 'to put, place'.
See theme and cp. thesis and words there
referred to.

## epenthetic
epenthetic, adj., of the nature of, or pertaining
to, epenfhesis. — Gk. έπενθετίκός, fr. έπεντι-
θέναι, 'to insert'. See prec. word and -ic.

## epergne
epergne, п., an ornamental centerpiece. — F.
epargne, 'a saving', fr. epargner, 'to save', fr.
OF. espargnier, a word of Teut. origin. Cp. OS.
sparon, OHG. spardn, sparen, 'to save, spare',
and see spare. OProvenc. esparnhar and It.
risparmiare, 'to save', are also Teut. loan words.

## epexegesis
epexegesis, п., an added explanation. — Gk.
έπεξήγησις, 'a detailed account, explanation',
fr. έπεξηγεΐσ1>αι, 'to recount in detail', fr. έπί
(see epi-) and έξηγεΐσ&αι, 'to explain'. See
exegesis,

## epexegetic
epexegetic, epexegetical, adj., explanatory. — See
prec. word and exegetic, exegetical.

## eph-
eph-, form of epi- before an aspirated vowel.

## ephah
ephah, epha, п., a Hebrew grain measure. — Heb.
epha", prob. fr. Egypt, 'pt (whence Coptic
uoipe, oipe, LXX Greek οίφεί, οίφί).

## ephebe
ephebe, п., an ephebus. — See ephebus.

## epheblc
epheblc, adj., pertaining to the ephebi. — Gk.
εφηβικός, fr. ϊφηβος. See next word and -lc.

## ephebus
ephebus, п., a citizen between 18 and 20 years
(Greek hist.) — L., fr. Gk. έφηβος, 'a youth', fr.
έπί (see epi-) and ήβη, 'youth, early manhood'.
See Hebe.

## Ephedra
Ephedra, п., a genus of desert shrubs of the joint-
fir family (bot.) — L. ephedra, 'horsetail', fr.
Gk. έφεδρα, prop. fern, of έφεδρος, 'sitting
upon', used as a noun, fr. έπί (see epi·) and
SSpS, 'seat*. See -hedron.

## ephelis
ephelis, п., a freckle. — Gk. ϊφηλις (in the pi.
έφήλιδες), 'freckle', fr. έπί (see epi-) and ήλιος,
'sun'. See helio- and cp. words there referred to.

## Ephemera
Ephemera, п., the genus of the Ephemerida (en-
tomol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έφήμερον, 'dayfly',
prop. neut. of εφήμερος, 'lasting but a day,
short-lived', used as a noun, fr. έπί (see epi-)
and ήμερα, 'day*. See hemero-.

## ephemeral
ephemeral, adj., living only for a day;
shortlived, fleeting. — Lit. meaning 'of one day';
formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. εφήμερος. See
prec. word.
Derivatives: ephemeral-ity, п., ephemeral-ly,
adj., ephemeral-ness, n.

## ephemerid
ephemerid, п., any of the Ephemeridae. — See
next word.

## Ephemeridae
Ephemeridae, n. pi., an order of insects, the May
fly (entomol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-idae fr. Gk. έφήμερον, 'dayfly'. See Ephemera,

## ephemeris
ephemeris, п., ι) a diary (obsol.); 2) an
astronomical calendar. — Gk. έφημερίς, 'diary; calendar',
fr. εφήμερος, 'lasting but a day'. See Ephemera,

## ephemeron
ephemeron, п., l) an ephemerid; 2) anything
transitory. — Gk. έφήμερον, neut. of εφήμερος,
'lasting but a day'. See Ephemera,

## ephetae
ephetae, n. pi, a court of si members, which
tried cases of homicide in ancient Athens. —
ModL., fr. Gk. έφέται, pi. of εφέτης, from the
stem of έφιέναι, 'to send to, send against,
impose upon', fr. έπί (see epi-) and Ιέναι, 'to send,
throw', which stands for *yi-ye-nai and is cogn.
with L.jacere, 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt forth',
and cp. words there referred to.

## Ephialtes
Ephialtes, п., a giant slain by Apollo (Greek my-
thol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Εφιάλτης, of uncertain
origin. The explanation of the ancients that the
name derives from the verb έφάλλεσ&αι, 'to
leap upon', is prob. folk etymology. See Frisk,
GEW., pp. 508-509.

## ephialtes
ephialtes, п., a nightmare. — Orig. (cap.)
denoting a demon supposed to cause nightmares, and
identical with prec. word.

## ephippium
ephippium, п., the pituitary fossa (anat.) — L.
'saddle cloth, caparison', fr. Gk. έφίππιον, prop,
neut. of the adj. έφίππιος, 'for putting on a horse',
fr. έπί (seeepi-) and ίππος, 'horse' (see hippo-);
so called from its shape.

## ephod
ephod, п., a Jewish priestly garment. — Heb.
iphodh, whence aphadh, 'he girded on the
ephod'. Cp. Akkad. gpattum, pi. epadatum,
'garment'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:279 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: EPHOR | 252 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:279 COLUMN:1 -->

## ephor
ephor, п., one of a body of magistrates in various
ancient Dorian states, esp. in Sparta, where a
body of five ephors was annually chosen. — L.
ephorus, fr. Gk. έφορος, Overseer, guardian',
the same as έπίουρος, fr. έπί (see epi-) and
οδρος, 'watcher, guard', prop, 'seer, overseer',
which is rel. to όράν, 'to see', and cogn. with
OE. wxr, 'aware, cautious'. See ware, 'alert'.
Derivatives: ephor-al, adj., ephor-al-ty, п.,
ephor-ate, п., ephor-ic, adj.

## ephphatha
ephphatha, interj., lit. 'be opened' (see Mark
7:34). — Gk. έφφα&ά, corrupt transliteration of
Aram, ethpattdh, 'be opened!', imper. Elhpa'al
of p'lah, 'he opened', which is rel. to Heb.
pdtkdh, Arab, fdtaha, 'he opened', Akkad. pittt,
patu, 'to open'.

## Ephraim
Ephraim, l) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible: a) the
younger son of Joseph; b) the tribe descended
from him, whence c) the Kingdom of Israel. —
Late L., fr. Gk. Έφραΐμ, fr. Heb. Ephrdyim,
a derivative of pardh, 'was fruitful', which is rel.
to Heb. and Aram. plri, Атат.-Syi.perd, 'fruit'.
See Gen.41:52 and cp. Hos. 13:25.

## Ephydra
Ephydra, п., a genus of brine flies (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. έφύδρα, fern, of ΙΊρυδρος, 'living
on the water', fr. έπί (see epi-) and ΰδωρ,
'water'. See hydro-,

## epi-
epi-, before a vowel ep-, before an aspirate eph-,
pref. meaning 'on, beside, among, above,
anterior'. In chemistry this pref. denotes relation
of some kind to a specified compound. — Gk.
έπι-, έττ-, έφ-, fr. έπί, Όη, upon; up to, over,
after; at; beyond, besides', cogn. with OI. dpi,
'also, besides', Avestic aipi, 'also; to, toward',
Toch. -pi, Arm. ev, 'also, and', and in gradat-
ional relationship to Gk. όπι- in 6πιθε(ν), Ion.
and Att. £πισθε(ν), 'after, behind', L. ob,
'toward, against, in the way of; about; before; on
account of; instead of. Cp. ob- and words there
referred to. Cp. also the first element in bias,
bishop. For Teut. cognates see even, 'evening*.

## epiblast
epiblast, п., the outer layer of the embryo (biol.)
— Compounded of epi- and Gk. βλαστός, 'bud,
sprout, shoot'. See -blast.
Derivative: epiblast-ic, adj.

## epic
epic, adj. — L. epicus, fr. Gk. επικός, 'epic', fr.
έπος, 'word, song*, in pi., 'epic poetry'. See
epos and -ic and cp. epopee.
Derivatives: epic, п., epic-al, ad\.,epic-al-ly,stdv.

## epicardinm
epicardinm, п., the viscera] layer of the
pericardium (anal.) — Medical L., fr. epi- and Gk.
καρδία, 'heart'. See cardio- and cp. eadocar-
dium, pericardium.

## Epicarides
Epicarides, n. pi., a group of small crustaceans
parasitic on shrimp (zool.) — ModL., lit. 'those
(living) on shrimps', fr. epi- and Gk. καρίς, gen.
καρίδος, 'shrimp, prawn'. See Caridea.

## epicarp
epicarp, п., the outermost layer of a pericarp
(hot.) — See epi- and carpel and cp. eadocarp,
pericarp.

## epicedium
epicedium, п., a funeral hymn, dirge. — L. epi-
cldium, fr. Gk. έπικήδειον, 'a dirge, elegy', prop,
neut. of the adjective επικήδειος, 'funeral', used
as a noun, fr. έπί (see epi-) and κήδος, 'sorrow*,
which is rel. to Dor. κάδος, of s.m., and cogn.
with Goth, hatis, OE. hete, 'hatred'. See hate
and cp. acedia.

## epicene
epicene, adj., of common gender (gramm.) — L.
epicoenus, fr. Gk. έπίκοινος, 'common,
promiscuous', fr. έπι (see epi-) and κοινός,
'common'. See coeno-,

## epicenter
epicenter, epicentre, п., the area of the earth's
surface immediately above the center of an
earthquake (seismol.) — Gk. έπίκεντρος, 'on
the center', fr. έπί (see epi-) and κέντρον,
'center'. See center.

## epicentrum
epicentrum, п., an epicenter. — ModL. See prec.
word.

## epichorial
epichorial, adj., pertaining, or restricted, to a
country or a district. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. Gk. έπιχώριος, 'in, or of, the country',
fr. έπί (see epi-) and χώρα, 'country'. See
enchorial.

## epicondyle
epicondyle, п., a surface or process above a
condyle (anal.) — Orig. used to denote 'the lateral
epicondyle of the humerus'. The name is
erroneous. It was coined by the French anatomist
and surgeon Francois Chaussier (1746-1828) fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:279 COLUMN:2 -->
epi- and condyle. The correct form should have
been paracondyle (in accordance with the
meaning of Gk. παρά, 'beside', in contradistinction
to έπί, which means 'on, upon'). See Joseph
Hyrtl, Onomaiologia anatomica, pp. 200-201.
A similar erroneous anatomical term (also
coined by Chaussier) is epitrochlea (q.v.)

## Epicrates
Epicrates, п., a genus of nonpoisonous boas
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έπικρατής, .'having
mastery, superior', fr. έπί (see epi-) and κράτος,
'strength, power'. See -cracy.

## epicure
epicure, п., one given up to sensual enjoyment.
— L. Epicurus, fr. Gk. 'Επίκουρος, Greek
philosopher said to have regarded sensual enjoyment
as the highest good.

## Epicurean
Epicurean, adj., pertaining to Epicurus; п., а
follower of Epicurus. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Epicureus, fr. Gk. 'Επικούρειος,
'pertaining to Epicurus', fr. Έπίκουρος..8εε prec. word.

## Epicureanism
Epicureanism, п., ι) the doctrine of Epicurus;
2) epicurism. — See epicure and· -ism.

## epicurism
epicurism, п., addiction to sensual enjoyment. —
See epicure and -ism.

## epicycle
epicycle, п., a circle whose center moves along
the circumference of another and larger circle.
— Late L. epicyclus, fr. Gk. έπίκυκλος, fr. έπί
(see epi-) and κύκλος, 'circle'. See cycle.
Derivative: epicycl-ic, adj.

## epicycloid
epicycloid, п., the curve traced by a point on the
circumference of a circle that rolls upon the
outside of the circumference of another circle.
— Compounded of epicycle and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: epicycioid-al, adj.

## epldeictic
epldeictic, adj..serving to display or exhibit. — Gk.
επιδεικτικός, 'for displaying', fr. έπιδεικνύναι,
'to show off, display', fr. έπί (see epi-) and
δεικνύναι, 'to show'. See deictic and cp. apo-
dictic.

## epidemic
epidemic, epidemical, adj., prevalent among many
people in a community at the same time. — F.
epidemique, fr. epidemie, 'epidemic (n.)', fr. ML.
epidemia, fr. Gk. επιδημία [for επιδημία (νόσος),
'(disease) prevalent among the people'], fern, of
έπιδήμιος, 'among the people', fr. έπίδημος, 'at
home, current, prevalent', fr. έπί, 'among' (see
epi-), and δήμος, 'people'. See demos and -ic,
resp. also -al, and cp. endemic.
Derivatives: epidemic, п., epidemic-al-ly, adv.,
epidemic-al-ness, п., epidemic-ity, n.

## epidemiology
epidemiology, п., the study of epidemics. —
Compounded of Gk. έπιδήμιος, 'prevalent among
the people', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See epidemic and -logy
and cp. endemiology.
Derivatives: epidemiolog-ic-al, adj., epidemio-
log-ist, n.

## epidemy
epidemy, п., an epidemic (rare). — F. epidemie,
fr. ML. epidemia. See epidemic.

## Epidendrum
Epidendrum, also Epidendron, п., a genus of
American orchids (hot.) — ModL., formed fr.
epi- and Gk. δένδρον, 'tree'. See dendro-.

## epidermal
epidermal, epidermic, adj., pertaining to the skin.
— See epidermis and -al, resp. -ic.

## epidermis
epidermis, п., lhe outer skin (a/iat.) — Late L.,
fr. Gk. έπίδερμίς, 'the outer skin', lit. (that
which is) on the skin', fr. έπί (see epi-) and
δέρμα, 'skin' (see derma); first used by the
English philosopher Francis Bacon (1561-1626).

## epididym-
epididym-, form of epididymo- before a vowel.

## epididymis
epididymis, п., mass at the back of the testicle
(anat.) — ModL., lit. 'that which is on the
testicle', fr. Gk. έπιδιδυμίς, a name prob.
coined by the Greek anatomist Herophilus
(about 300 B.C.E.) fr. έπί (see epi-) and δίδυμος,
'testicle', prop, an adjective meaning 'double,
twofold, twin'. See didymium.
Derivative: epididym-al, adj.

## epididymectomy
epididymectomy, п., removal of the epididymis.
— Compounded of the prec. word and Gk.
-εκτομίά, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a
cutting out'. See -ectomy.

## epididymitis
epididymitis, п., inflammation of the epididymis
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. epididymis with
suff. -itis.

## epididymo-
epididymo-, before a vowel epididym-, combining
form meaning 'pertaining to the epididymis. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:279 COLUMN:3 -->
See epididymis,

## epidote
epidote, п., a complex silicate of calcium,
aluminum and iron, of a yellowish-green color
(mineral.) — F. .epidote, a name coined by the
French mineralogist Rend-Just Haiiy (I743-
1822), from the stem of Gk. έπιδιδόναι, 'to
give besides, increase', fr. έπί,. 'besides' (see
epi-) and διδόναι, 'to give' (verbal adj. δοτός,
'given*, see antidote); so called by him because
two of the sides of the parallelogram serving
asthe base of this mineral are much longer than
the other two sides. Derivative: epidot-ic, adj.

## Epigaea
Epigaea, п., a genus of plants of the heath family
(bol.) — ModL., lit. 'growing on the ground',
fr. epi- and Gk. γαία, γη, 'earth'. See Gaea.

## epigastric
epigastric, adj., on or above the stomach (anat.)
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. έπιγάστριος,
'above the belly', fr. έπί (see epi-) and γαστήρ,
'belly'. See gastro- and cp. hypogastric, meso-
gastric.

## epigastrium
epigastrium, п., the epigastric region of the body
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. έπιγάστριον, 'that
which is above the belly', prop. neut. of έπι-
γάστριος, 'above the belly', used as a noun. See
prec. word and cp. hypogastrium, mesogastrium.

## epigene
epigene, adj., 1) growing on the surface of the
earth (geol.); 2) foreign (said of crystals). — F.
epigene, fr. Gk. έπιγενής, 'growing on or after'.
See epi- and -gene.

## epigenesis
epigenesis, п., the theory that each germ or
embryo is an entirely new creation (biol.) —
Formed fr. epi- and genesis.

## epigeous
epigeous, adj., 1) growing on or near the ground;
borne above ground after germination (said of
cotyledons). — Gk. επίγειος, 'on or of the earth',
fr. έπί (see epi-), and γη, 'earth'. See Gaea. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## epiglottic
epiglottic, adj., pertaining to the epiglottis. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. έπιγλωττίς. See
next word.

## epiglottis
epiglottis, п., the triangular cartilage at the base
of the tongue, which closes the opening of the
windpipe during swallowing (anat.) — Gk.
έπιγλωττίς, "valve which covers the larvnx,
epiglottis', lit. '(that which is) upon the tongue',
fr. έπί (see epi-), and γλώττα, 'tongue'. See
glottis.

## epigone
epigone, п., г) one of the succeeding generation;
esp. applied to the sons of the 'Seven against
Thebes' in Greek mythology; whence 2) an
inferior imitator of a great man. — h.Epigoni, 'the
son of the Seven who went against Thebes', fr.
Gk. 'Επίγονοι, lit. 'born after', pi. of επίγονος,
fr. έπιγίγνεσ&αι, 'to be born after', fr. έπί (see
epi-) and γίγνεσθαι,- 'to be born'. See genus.

## epigram
epigram, п., a terse, witty statement in prose or
verse. — F. epigramme, fr. L. epigvamma, fr.
Gk. επίγραμμα, gen. -γράμματος, 'inscription;
epigram', lit. 'something written on', fr. έπι-
γράφειν, 'to write upon', fr. έπί (see epi-) and
γράφειν, 'to write'. See gramme and cp. epigraph.

## epigrammatic
epigrammatic, adj. — Late L. epigrammaticus, fr.
L. epigramma, gen. -grammatis, 'epigram'. See
prec. word and -atic.
Derivatives: epigrammalic-al, adj., epigramma-
tic-al-ly, adv.

## epigrammatism
epigrammatism, п., the use of epigrams. —
Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk. επίγραμμα, gen.
-γράμματος. See epigram.

## epigrammatist
epigrammatist, п., a maker of epigrams. — Late
L. epigrammatista, fr. Gk. έπιγραμματιστής,
'writer of epigrams, epigrammatist', fr. έπι-
γραμματίζειν, 'to write epigrams', fr. επίγραμμα.
See epigram and -ist and cp. next word.

## epigrammatize
epigrammatize, tr. v., to express in an
epigrammatic form; intr. v., to write epigrams. — Gk.
έπιγραμματίζειν, 'to write epigrams', fr.
επίγραμμα. See epigram and -ize.

## epigraph
epigraph, п., an inscription. — Gk. επιγραφή,
'inscription', fr. έπιγράφειν. See epigram.
Derivatives: epigraph, tr. v., epigraph-er, п.,
epigraph-ic, epigraph-ic-al, adjs., epigraph-ic-

## al-ly
al-ly, adv., epigraph-ist, п., epigraph-y, n.

## epilepsy
epilepsy, п., a chronic nervous disease
characterized by convulsions. — OF. epilepsie (F. epi-

## lepsie)
lepsie), fr. Late L. epilepsia, fr. Gk. επιληψία,
'liability to seizure, epilepsy', rel. to έπιλαμ-
βάνειν, 'to lay hold of, seize, attack', fr. έπί (see

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:280 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 253 | EP1TRITE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:280 COLUMN:1 -->
epi-) and the future stem of λαμβάνειν, 'to take,
grasp, seize'. See lemma and cp. words there
referred to.

## epileptic
epileptic, adj. l) pertaining to epilepsy; 2)
affected with epilepsy. — F. epileptique, fr. Late
L. epilepticus, fr. Gk. επιληπτικής, 'subject to
epilepsy, epileptic', fr. έπίληπτος, 'suffering
from epilepsy', verbal adj. of έπιλαμβάνεΐν. See
prec. word and -ic Derivative: epileptic, n.

## epilogist
epilogist, п., writer or speaker of an epilogue. —
See next word and -1st.

## epilogue
epilogue, epilog, п., speech at the end of a play. —
F. epilogue, fr. L. epilogus, fr. Gk. επίλογος,
'peroration; concluding part of a play', lit. 'a
saying in addition', fr. έπιλέγειν, 'to say in
addition' fr. έπί (see epi-) and λέγειν, 'to say,
speak'. See lecture and cp. logos.
Derivative: epilogue, tr. v.

## Epimedium
Epimedium, п., a genus of plants of the barberry
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. epimedion, fr. Gk.
έπιμήδιον, name of a plant, possibly 'barren-
wort', fr. έπί (see epi-) and μήδιον, name of a
plant (Campanula); so called because of its
resemblance to the plant μήδιον.

## Epimetheus
Epimetheus, п., the brother of Prometheus {Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Έπιμη&εύς, lit. 'after-
thinker', fr. έπί (see epi-) and ·μήθος,
corresponding to Dor. ·μί&ος, 'care', fr. I.-E.
*madh-, a var. of *men-dh, enlargement of base
*men-, 'to think'. See mathematical and cp.
Prometheus.

## epinasty
epinasty, adj., increased growth of the upper
surface of an organ, causing that organ or part of
it to bend downward (plant physiol.) — G. Epi-
nastie, formed fr. epi- and Gk. ναστός, 'pressed
close, compact', verbal adj. of νάσσειν, 'to press
close', which is of uncertain origin.
Derivative: epinast-ic, adj.

## epinicion
epinicion, п., an ode in honor of a victor. —
ModL., fr. Gk. έπινίκιον, 'song of victory'
(short for $σμα έπινίκιον), neut. of έπινΐκιος,
'of victory', fr. έπί (see epi-) and νίκη, 'victory'.
See Nicholas.

## epiotic
epiotic, adj., pertaining to the upper ear. —
Formed fr. epi- and Gk. ώτικος, 'of, or
pertaining to, the ear'. See otic.

## epipnstic
epipnstic, adj., having the qualities of, or serving
as, a dusting powder (med.) — Formed with
suff. -lc fr. Gk. έπίπαστος, 'sprinkled over',
verbal adj. of έπιπάσσειν, 'to sprinkle over', fr.
έπί (see epi-) and πάσσειν, 'to besprinkle', which
is of uncertain origin.

## Epiphany
Epiphany, п., a festival held January 6,
commemorating the first manifestation of Jesus to the
Gentiles (eccles.) — OF. epiphanie, fr. Late L.
epipkania, neut. pi., fr. Late Gk. επιφάνια,
prop. neut. pi. of the adj. έπιφάνιος, 'appearing,
manifest', used as a noun, fr. επιφανής, of s.m.,
fr. έπιφαίνειν, 'to show forth, display, make
manifest', which is formed fr. έπ( (see epi-) and
φαίνειν, 'to bring to light, show'. See
phantasm and cp. theophany, tiffany.

## epipbany
epipbany, п., manifestation of a divine being. —
Gk. επιφάνεια (neut. pi.), 'coming into light,
appearance, manifestation', fr. επιφανής. See
prec. word.

## Epiphegus
Epiphegus, п., a genus of parasitic herbs of the
broomrape family (bot.) — ModL., lit. '(that
which grows) on the oak', fr. epi- and Gk. φηγός,
Dor. φαγός, 'oak'. See beech and cp. the first
element in Phegopteris.

## epiphora
epiphora, п., an overflow of tears (med.) — L.,
fr. Gk. έπιφορά, 'persistent flow of tears', lit.
'a bringing upon', fr. έπιφέρειν, 'to bring upon',
fr. έπί (see epi-) and φέρειν, 'to bear, carry'.
See bear, 'to carry', and cp. -phore.

## epiphysis
epiphysis, п., process on a bone (anat.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. έπίφυσις, 'outgrowth, excrescence;
epiphysis', fr. έπιφύεσθαι, 'to grow on', fr. έπί
(see epi-) and φύεσθαι, 'to grow', pass, of φύειν,
'to bring forth, produce, make to grow'. See
physio- and cp. apophysis, diaphysis.

## epiphyte
epiphyte, п., any non-parasitic plant growing on
another plant (bot.) — Lit. 'growing on a
plant', fr. epi- and -phyte. Cp. prec. word.

## epiphytic
epiphytic, adj., of the nature of an epiphyte (bot.)
— See prec. word and -ic

## epiploltis
epiploltis, п., inflammation of the epiploon (med.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:280 COLUMN:2 -->
— Medical L., formed fr. next word with suff.-itis.
epiploon, п., the great omentum (anat.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. έπίπλοον, 'omentum', which
stands for *έπί-πλο5ον. For the prefix see epi-.
Gk. -πλοίον in *έπί-πλοΓον derives fr. I.-E.
base *pel-, 'skin', whence also Gk. πέλμα, 'sole
of foot 01 shoe', L. pellis, 'hide, skin', OE. fil-
men, 'membrane'. See fell, 'hide', and cp. words
there referred to. The explanation of Galen and
Oribasius that έπίπλοον derives fr. έπιπλείν,
"to swim or sail against' (quoted by Joseph
Hyrtl, Onomatologia Anatomica, p. 204), and
that the omentum is so called because it seems
'to swim over the intestines', is folk etymology.

## episcopacy
episcopacy, п., church government by bishops. —
Formed with suff. -асу fr. Eccles. L. episcopus.
See next word.

## episcopal
episcopal, adj., pertaining to, or governed by,
bishops. — Eccles. L. episcopalis, 'episcopal', fr.
L. episcopus, 'an overseer', in Eccles. L.,
'bishop'. See bishop.
Derivative: episcopal-ly, adv.

## episcopalian
episcopalian, adj., pertaining to bishops or to
episcopacy. — See prec. word and -Ian.
Derivative: episcopalian-ism, n.

## episcopallsm
episcopallsm, п., the doctrine that authority
resides in a body of bishops and not in any
individual. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Eccles.
L. episcopalis. See episcopal,

## episcopate
episcopate, п., t) the office or dignity of a bishop;
2) the whole body of bishops. — Eccles. L.
episcopatus, 'dignity of a bishop', fr. episcopus,
'bishop'. See episcopal and subst. suff. -ate.

## episio-
episio-, combining form denoting 'relation to
the vulva'. — Fr. Gk. έπίσιον, έπίσειον, 'public
region', which is of unknown origin.

## episiotomy
episiotomy, п., the cutting of the tissues of the
pudenda (obstetrics). — Coined by Braun in
1857 fr. episio- and Gk. -τομίδ, 'a cutting of,
fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.

## episode
episode, n. — Gk. έπεισόδιον, 'addition,
episode', prop. neut. of the adjective έπεισόδιος,
'coming in besides, adventitious', fr. έπί, 'at,
on, in addition to' (see epi-), εις, ές (for *ένς,
'into', rel. to έν, 'in'; see 2nd en-) and οδός,
'way' (see odograph).
Derivatives: episod-ic, episod-ic-al, adjs., episod-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## epispastic
epispastic, adj., causing blistering of the skin
(med.) — Gk. έπισπαστικός, 'drawing in', fr.
έπίσποιστος, 'drawn in', verbal adj. of έπισπδν,
'to draw in', fr. έπί (see epi-) and σπδν, 'to
draw'. See spasm and cp. spastic.
Derivative: epispastic, п., an epispastic agent,

## epistaxis
epistaxis, п., bleeding of the nose (med.) —
Medical L., lit. 'dropping', fr. Gk. έπιστάζειν,
'to let fall in drops upon', fr. έπί (see epi-) and
στάζειν, 'to drop'. See stacte.

## epistemic
epistemic, adj., pertaining to knowledge. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. επιστήμη,
'knowledge, understanding', fr. έπίσταμαι, Ί
understand, know', lit. Ί stand upon', fr. έπί (see
epi-) and ίσταμιχι, Ί stand'. See state. For sense
development ср. Е. understand.

## epistemology
epistemology, п., the theory of knowledge. —
Coined by the Scottis hphilosopher James
Frederick Ferrier (1808-64) in his Institutes of

## Metaphysics (1854)
Metaphysics (1854), fr. Gk. επιστήμη, 'knowledge,
understanding', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See epistemic and -logy.
Derivatives: epistemolog-ic-al, adj., epistemolog-
ic-al-ly, adv., epistemolog-ist, n.

## episternum
episternum, п., the interclavicle (zool.) — ModL.,
lit. '(bone) upon the chest', formed fr. epi- and
sternum,

## epistle
epistle, п., letter. — OF. epistle, epistre (F. epitre),
fr. L. epistola, fr. Gk. επιστολή, 'a letter', lit.-
'something sent, message', fr. έπιστέλλειν, 'to
send to; to order, command', fr. έπί, 'upon, to'
(see epi-), and στέλλειν, 'to set in order,
arrange, equip, make ready, Send out'. See stall
and cp. stele. For the sense development of Gk.
επιστολή, 'something sent, letter', cp. Akkad.

## shipru
shipru, shipir, 'message, letter, document', fr.

## shaparu
shaparu, 'to send'.

## epistler
epistler, п., epistoler. — Foimed fr. epistle with
agential suff. -er.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:280 COLUMN:3 -->

## epistolary
epistolary, adj., pertaining to epistles. — F. epis-
tolaire, fr. L. epistolaris, 'epistolary', fr. epistola.
See epistle and adj. suff. -ary.

## epistoler
epistoler, п., the priest who reads the Epistle at
the Eucharistic service (eccles.) — F. epistolier,
fr. L. epistolaris, 'one celebrated for his letters',
fr. epistola, 'letter'. See epistle and agential
suff. -er.

## epistrophe
epistrophe, п., repetition of the same word at the
end of successive clauses or sentences (rhet.) —
Late L., fr. Gk. επιστροφή, 'a turning about',
fr. έπιστρέφειν, 'to turn about', fr. έπί, 'upon,
to' (see epi-), and στρέφειν, 'to turn'. See
strophe and cp. apostrophe and words there
referred to.

## epistropheus
epistropheus, п., name of the second vertebra
(anat.) — Gk. έπιστροφεύς, 'that which causes
to turn', fr. έπιστρέφειν, 'to cause to turn, to
turn about'. See epistrophe. The name is
inexact, because it is the first cervical vertebra that
turns about the alveolar process of the second
vertebra, and indeed, originally epistropheus was
the name of the first vertebra. See Joseph Hyrtl,
Onomatologia anatomica, pp. 59-6].
Derivative: epistrophe-al, adj.

## epistyle
epistyle, п., an architrave (archit.) — L. episty-
lium, fr. Gk. έπιστόλιον, fr. έπί (see epi-) and
στύλος, 'pillar, column'. See style, 'gnomon',
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also next
word.

## Epistylis
Epistylis, п., a genus of protozoans (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. epi- and Gk. στύλος, 'pillar,
column'. See prec. word.

## epitaph
epitaph, п., inscription of a tomb. — L. epi-
taphium, fr. Gk. έπιτάφιον, 'a funeral oration',
prop. neut. of the adj. επιτάφιος, 'over a tomb',
used as a noun, fr. έπί (see epi-) and τάφος,
'tomb'. See cenotaph.
Derivatives: epitaph, tr. and intr. v., epitaph-er,
п., epitaph-ic, adj., epitaph-ist, n.

## epltasis
epltasis, п., that part of the play in which the
main action is developed, leading to the
catastrophe. — ModL., fr. Gk. έπίτασις, *a
stretching upon or over', fr. έπιτείνειν, 'to stretch
upon or over', fr. έπί (see epi-) and τείνειν, 'to
streich'. See tasimeter and cp. ectasis and
words there referred to.

## epithalamium
epithalamium, п., a bridal song. — L., fr. Gk·
έπιθαλάμιον, 'a bridal.song', fr. έπί, 'at' (see epi-),
and θάλαμος, 'bridal chamber'. See thalamus.
Derivatives: epithalami-al, epithalam-ic, adjs.

## epithelio-
epithelio-, before a vowel epitheli-, combining
form, meaning 'pertaining to the epithelium'. —
See next word.

## epithelium
epithelium, п., cellular tissue forming the outer
layer of the mucous membrane in animals (anat.)
— Medical L., coined by the Dutch anatomist
Fredrik Ruysch (1638-1731). The word lit.
means 'that which is above the nipple', fr. epi-
and Gk. &ηλή, 'nipple'. See thely- and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: epitheli-al, adj., epithel-ize, tr. v.,
epithel-iz-ation, п., epithel-oid, adj.

## epithet
epithet, п., a descriptive name for a person or
thing. — L. epitheton, fr. Gk. έπίθετον,
'something added', neut. verbal adj. of έπιτιθ-έναι,
'to add something to', fr. έπί, 'on, to' (see epi-),
and τιίΚνοα, 'to put, place'. See theme and cp.
words there referred to.

## epithetic
epithetic, epithetical, adj., 1) pertaining to an
epithet: 2) full of epithets. — Gk. έπιθ-ετικός,
'added', fr. έπίθ-ετος, verbal adj. of έπιτιθ-έναι.
See prec. word and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: epiihetic-al-ly, adv.

## epitomator
epitomator, п., an epitomist. — ML., fr. L. epi-
tomaius, pp. of epitomare, 'to abridge,
epitomize', fr. epitome. See next word and -ator.
Derivative: epitomator-y, adj.

## epitome
epitome, п., a summary. — L. epitome,
'abridgment, fr. Gk. επιτομή, 'abridgment', lit. 'a
cutting into', fr. έπιτέμνειν, 'to make incisions
inio, cut into, cut short, abridge', fr. έπί (see
epi-) and τέμνειν, 'to cut'. See tome.
Derivatives: epitom-ist, п., epitom-ize, tr. v.

## epitrite
epitrite, п., a foot consisting of three long
syllables and one short (pros.) — L. epitritos, fr.
Gk. έπίτριτος, 'containing an integer and one
third; in the ratio of four to three (tj = $ =

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:281 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: EPITROCHLEA | 254 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:281 COLUMN:1 -->
4:3)'; formed fr. έπί (see epi-) and τρίτος,
'third'. See trito-.

## epitrochlea
epitrochlea, п., the medial condyle of the
humerus (anat.)— ModL., fr. F. epitrochlee, a name
formed erroneously by the French anatomist and
surgeon Francois Chaussier (1746-1828), fr.
epi- and trochlea. In this name the meaning of
Gk. έπί, Όη', is confused with that of παρά,
'beside'. The same confusion of the meanings
of Gk. επί and παρά led to Chaussier's coining
the word eprcondyle (q.v.)
Derivative: epitrockle-ar, adj.

## epizeuxis
epizeuxis, п., repetition of a word or words for
the sake of emphasis (rhet.) — Late L., fr. Gk.
έπίζευξις, lit. 'a joining or fastening together',
fr. έπιζευγνύνοα, 'to join to', fr. έπί (see epi-)
and ζευγνύναι, 'to joke, join'. See zygo- and cp.
zeuxite.

## epizoon
epizoon, n, an external parasite (zoo!.) — ModL.,
formed fr. epi- and ζωον, 'animal'. See zoo-.

## epizootic
epizootic, adj., 1) parasitic on other animals;
2) (of diseases) prevalent temporarily among
animals (corresponding to epidemic diseases in
man). — See prec. word and cp. enzootic.

## epoch
epoch, n. — Late L. epocha, fr. Gk. εποχή,'check,
cessation, stoppage, pause; epoch of a star;
fixed point in time, epoch', fr. έπέχειν, 'to keep
back, withhold, stop, pause', fr. έπί (see epi-)
and έχειν, 'to hold, have, possess'. See hectic
and cp. apocha.
Derivatives: epoch-al, adj., epoch-al-ly, adv.,
epoch-ism, n.

## epode
epode, п., a kind of lyric poem. — L. epodos, fr.
Gk. επωδός, 'part of an ode sung after the strophe
and amistrophe; burden, refrain', prop, the
adjective επωδός, 'singing to or over', used as a
noun, which is rel. to έπάδειν, 'to sing to',
a word formed fr. έπί, 'upon, to' (epi-), and
φδείΛΐ, 'to sing'. See ode and cp. words there
referred to.

## eponym
eponym, п., a real or mythical person from whom
a family, tribe or nation derives its name. —
Gk. επώνυμος. See next word.

## eponymous
eponymous, adj., giving name to a family, tribe
or nation. — Gk. επώνυμος, 'given as a name,
giving one's name to (a thing or person)', fr.
έπί, 'upon, to' (see epi-) and βνυμα, dialectal
form of ΰνομα, 'name'. See name and cp. words
there referred to. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
Gk. -ος, see suff. -ous.

## epopee
epopee, п., an epic poem. — F. epopee, fr. Gk.
εποποιία, 'an epic poem; epic poetry', fr. έπο-
ποιός, 'an epic poet', which is compounded of
έπος, 'word; poetry*, and ποιεΐν, 'to make,
produce, create'. See epos and poet.

## epoophoron
epoophoron, п., parovarium (anat.) — Medical
L., compounded of ep-, Gk. ώόν, 'egg*, and the
stem of φέρειν, 'to bear, carry'. See 00- and
-phore and cp. parovarium.

## epopt
epopt, п., one initiated into the Eleusinian
mysteries; one initiated into any secret system. —
Gk. επόπτης, 'seer, beholder', formed fr. έπί
(see epi-) and the stem όπ-, 'to see', whence also
όπτός, 'seen; visible', οπτικός, 'pertaining to
the eyes or sight'. See optic and cp. words there
referred to.

## epos
epos, п., a primitive epic poem. — L., fr. Gk. έπος,
'word, speech, tale, song, heroic poetry', rel.
to Cypr. Gk. /έπος, of s.m., Gk. βψ (for *Щ),
'voice*, δσσα (for *f όκια), 'voice, tale', έν-οπή,
'crying, shouting, voice', εΤπον (for *έΤειπον,
fr. *έ-^ε-υπ-ον), Ί spoke', and cogn. with L.
vox, gen. vocis, 'voice'. See voice and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also epyllion and the
second element in cacoepy, orthoepy.

## epris (fem. eprise)
epris (fem. eprise), adj., enamored. — F., pp.
of eprendre, fr. OF. esprendre, 'to seize, kindle',
fr. es- (fr. L. ex) and prendre, 'to take', fr. L.
prehendere, piendere, 'to grasp'. See 1st ex- and
prehensile.

## epsilon
epsilon, п., the fifth letter of the Greek alphabet
(e, E). — Gk. ί ψϊλόν, 'a mere or bare e'\ so
called in contradistinction to the diphthong αι,
which is pronounced in Medieval and Modern
Greek exactly like ε (= e). See psilo- and cp.
upsilon.

## Epsom salts
Epsom salts, hydrated magnesium sulfate. — So
called because it was first prepared from the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:281 COLUMN:2 -->
water of the mineral springs of Epsom, Surrey,
England.

## epalis
epalis, п., any tumor of the gum (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. έποιιλίς, 'gum boil', fr. έπί
(see epi-) and ουλον, 'gum'. See alitis.

## epyllioa
epyllioa, п., a short epic. — Gk. έπύλλιον, dimin.
of έπος. See epos.

## equability
equability, n. — L. aequabilitas, 'equality,
equability', fr. aequabilis. See next word and -ity.

## equable
equable, adj., 1) uniform; 2) even; serene. — L.
aequabilis, 'equal, uniform, equable', fr. aequare,
'to make equal', fr. aequus, 'equal'. See next
word and -able.
Derivatives: eq'uable-ness, п., equabl-y, adv.

## equal
equal, adj. — L. aequalis, 'even, level, smooth,
equal, like', fr. aequus, 'level, equal, like', which
is of uncertain origin. Cp. adequate, aequor,
coequate, equation, equator, equilibrium, equinox,
equitable, equity, equivocal, iniqnity.
Derivatives -..equal, tr. and intr. v., equality (q.v.),
equal-ize, tr. v., equal-iz-ation, п., equal-iz-er, n.

## equality
equality, n. — OF. equalite (F. igalite), fr. L.
aequalitatem, ace. of aequalitas, 'equality,
uniformity', fr. aequalis, 'equal'. See equal and -ity.

## equanimity
equanimity, п., calmness. — F. iquanimite, fr. L.
aequanimitatem, ace. of aequanimitas,
'evenness of mind, calmness', fr. aequanimus, 'even-
minded, calm', which is compounded of aequus,
'even, level', and animus, 'soul, spirit, mind*.
See equal, animus and -ity.

## equate
equate, tr. and intr. v. — L. aequatus, pp. of
aequare, 'to make level or equal', fr. aequus. See
equal and verbal suff. -ate.

## equation
equation, n. — L. aequatio, gen. -dnis, 'an
equalizing', fr. aequatus, pp. of aequare. See prec.
word and -ion.
Derivatives: equation-al, adj., equation-al-ly, adv.

## equator
equator, n. — Late L. aequator, 'one who or that
which equalizes', used in the sense of (circulus)
aequator diei el metis, 'equalizer of day and
night', fr. L. aequatus, pp. of aequare. See
equate and agential suff. -or.
Derivative: equator-ial, adj. and n.

## equerry
equerry, п., ι) originally, an officer in charge of
the horses of a prince; 2) esp. in England, a
personal attendant of the king, queen or
another member of the Royal family. — F. icurie,
'stable', fr. OF. escuerie, escuyrie, orig. Office
of a squire', later 'place for the squires and their
horses', fr. escuyer (F. ecuyer), 'squire, riding
master', orig. 'shield bearer*, fr. VL. scutarius
(but classical L. scutarius means 'shield maker'),
fr. L. scutum, 'shield'. See escutcheon and -y
(representing OF. -ie) and cp. esquire. E. equerry
was influenced in form by an association with
L. equus, 'horse', to which, however, it is not
related.

## equestrinn
equestrinn, adj., 0 pertaining to horsemen or
horsemanship; 2) п., horseman. — Formed with
suff. -Ian fr. L. equester (fem. equestris, neut.
equestre), 'pertaining to a horseman', from
equus, 'horse'. See eqnine.

## equestrienne
equestrienne, п., a horsewoman; a female
performer on horseback. — Formed from prec.
word with the F.fem. suff. -ienne.

## equi-
equi-, combining form meaning 'equal'. — L.
aequi-, fr. aequus, 'equal'. See equal.

## equiangular
equiangular, adj., having only equal angles. —
Compounded of equi- and angular.
Derivative: equiangular-ity, n.

## Eqnidae
Eqnidae, n. pl„ the horse family (zool.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. L. equus, 'horse'. See
equine·

## equidistance
equidistance, п., equal distance. — F.
equidistance, fr. equidistant. See next word and -ce.

## eqnidistant
eqnidistant, adj., equally distant. — F.
equidistant, fr. Late L. aequidistantem, ace. of aequi-
distans, which is compounded of L. aequus,
'equal', and distans, 'distant'. See equal and
distant. Derivative: equidistant-ly, adv.

## equilateral
equilateral, adj., having all sides equal. — Late L.
aequilateralis, compounded of L. aequus, 'equal',
and latus, gen. laleris, 'side'. See equi- and
lateral.

## equilibrate
equilibrate, tr. and intr. v., to balance. — Late L.
aequilibratus, pp. of aequilibrare, 'to balance',
compounded of L. aequus, 'equal', and libra,
'balance'. See equilibrium and verbal suff. -ate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:281 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: equilibrat-ion, п., equilibrat-ive, adj.

## equilibrist
equilibrist, п., one skilled in balancing, esp. a
ropedancer. — F. equilibriste, a hybrid coined
fr. equilibre, 'equilibrium, balance' (fr. L. aequi-
librium) and suff. -iste (fr. Gk. -ιστής). See next
word and -ist.

## equilibrium
equilibrium, п., balance. — L., 'even balance',
compounded of aequus, 'equal', and libra,
'balance'. See equi- and libra.

## equimultiple
equimultiple, n„ one of the products obtained
by multiplying two or more numbers by the
same number. — Compounded of equi- and
multiple.

## equine
equine, adj., pertaining to a horse. — L. equlnus,
'pertaining to horses', fr. equus, 'horse' (whence
equa, 'mare'), fr. I.-E. *ekwos, 'horse', whence
also OI. aSvah, Avestic aspa-, Toch. A yuk,
Byakwe, Osset. jdfs, Gk. ίππος, dial. Gk. Ικκος,
Gael, epo-, Olr. ech, 'horse', OLith. eiva, Lith.
aSva, 'mare', OE. eoh (for *ehv), OS. ehu- (in
ehuscalc), ON. jor, 'horse', Goth, aiha-tundi,
'thorn', lit. 'horse tooth'. Cp. Asvins, hippo- and
the first element in Equisetum. For the ending
see suff. -Jne (representing L. -inus).

## equinoctial
equinoctial, adj. and n. — L. aequinoctidlis, fr.
aequinoctium. See equinox and -lal.

## equinox
equinox, n. — F. equinoxe, fr. L. aequinoctium,
'the time of equal days and nights', lit. 'equal
night', fr. aequus, 'equal', and nox, gen. noctis,
'night'. See eqnal and night and cp. nocti-,
nocturnal.

## equip
equip, tr. v., to furnish, fit out, provide. — F.
iquiper, 'to fit out, furnish, equip', orig. 'to fit
out a ship', fr. OF. esquiper, which is of Teut.
origin. Cp. ON. skipa, 'to fit out a ship', fr.
skip, 'ship', and see ship.
Derivatives: equipage (q.v.), equip-ment, n.

## equipage
equipage, n. — F. equipage, fr. iquiper. See prec.
word and -age.

## equipoise
equipoise, п., balance, equilibrium. — A hybrid
coined fr. equi- and poise. Derivative: tr. v.

## equipollence
equipollence, n„ equality of force. — Formed
from next word and suff. -ce.

## equipollent
equipollent, adj., equal in force. — F. equipollent,
fr. L. aequipollentem, ace. of aequipollens, 'of
equal value or force', compounded of aequus,
'equal' (see equi-), and pollens, gen. pallentis,
pres. part, of pollere, 'to be powerful, to be able'.

## equiponderant
equiponderant, adj., of equal weight. — See next
- word and -nat.

## equiponderate
equiponderate, tr. v., to counterbalance. — ML.
aequiponderatus, pp. of aequiponderare. See
equi-, ponder and verbal suff. -ate.

## equipotential
equipotential, adj., having equal potential force.
— Compounded of equi- and potential.

## Equisetum
Equisetum, п., the horsetail (hot.) — L. equi-
saetum, equisetum, 'the horsetail', fr. equus,
'horse', and saetum, 'bristle'. See equine and
seta and cp. the second element in Catasetum,
Trisetam.

## eqnitable
eqnitable, adj., just; fair. — F. equitable, fr. iqui-
ti. See equity and -able.
Derivatives: equitable-ness, п., equitabl-y, adv.

## eqnitant
eqnitant, adj., having bases which overlap each
other (said of leaves). — L. equitans, gen. -antis,
'riding'-, pres. part, of equitare, 'to ride', fr.
eques, gen. equitis, 'horseman', fr. equus,
'horse'. See equine and -ant.

## equitation
equitation, n„ horsemanship. — F. equitation, fr.
L. equilSlidnem, ace. of equitatio, 'riding', fr.
equitat(-um), pp. stem of equitare. See prec.
word and -Ion.

## eqalty
eqalty, n. — OF. equite (F. iquiti), fr. L. aequi-
tStem, ace. of aequitas, 'equality, conformity,
symmetry, fairness*, fr. aequus, 'level, equal'.
See equal and -ity.

## equivalence
equivalence, n. — F. equivalence, fr. ML. aequi-
valentta, fr. Late L. aequivalens, gen. -entis.
See next word and -ce.

## equivalent
equivalent, adj., 1) equal; 2) having the same
valence (chem.) — F. equivalent, fr. Late L. aequi-
valentem, ace. of aequivalens, pres. part, of
aequivalere, 'to have equal force of value',
which is compounded of L. aequus, 'equal',
and valere, 'to be well, to be strong'. See equal
and valiant and cp. -valent.
Derivative: equivalent, п., l) something
equivalent; 2) (chem.) equivalent weight.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:282 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 255 | ERIN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:282 COLUMN:1 -->

## equivocal
equivocal, adj., dubious, ambiguous. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. Late L. aequtvocus, 'of
equal voice, of equal significance, ambiguous,
equivocal', which is compounded of L. aequus,
'equal', and the stem of vox, gen. vdcis, 'voice'.
See equal and vocal and cp. equivoque. Late L.
aequtvocus is prop, a loan translation of Gk.
ομώνυμος, 'having the same name; equivocal,
ambiguous'.
Derivatives: equivocal, п., equivocal-ly, adv.,
equivocal-ness, n.

## equivocate
equivocate, intr. v., to use ambiguous terms. —
ML. aequivocdlus, pp. of aequivocare, 'to call
by the same name', fr. Late L. aequtvocus. See
prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: equivocation (q.v.), equivocat-or, n.

## equivocation
equivocation, n. — ML. aequivocatio, gen. -onis,
fr. aequivocatus, pp. of aequivocare. See prec.
word and -km.

## equivoque
equivoque, п., an equivocal term, a pun. — Late
L. aequtvocus, 'of equal voice, ambiguous'
(whence also F. equivoque, adj., 'ambiguous',
equivoque, п., 'ambiguity'). See equivocal.

## equold
equold, adj., resembling a horse (zool.) — A
hybrid coined fr. L. equus, 'horse', and Gk.
-οει&ής-, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
equine and -old. The correct form is hippoid, in
which both elements are of Greek origin.

## Equus
Equus, п., the typical genus of the horse family
(zool.) — L. equus, 'horse', whence equinus,
'pertaining to horses'. See equine.

## -er
-er, suff. used to form nouns denoting an agent
as in hatter, ruler, teacher. —· ME. -ere, -er, fr.
OE. -ere, rel. to OS. -eri, ON. -ari, Dan., Du. -er,
OHG. -art, ari, -eri, MHG. -ere, G. -er, Goth.
-areis; fr. OTeut. *-arjo-z, which derives fr. L.
-arius. See adj. suff. -ary and cp. -yar. Cp. also
agential suff. -or. In some cases ME. -ere, -er
comes fr. MF. -ere, ft. L. -Шдгет, асе. of -ator;
see -ator and cp. agential suff. -or.

## -er
-er, a suff. denoting a person or a thing connected
with something. — OF. -er, -ier, fr. L; -arius (if
connected with persons as in butler, grocer);
or -arium (if connected with things as in laver).
See adj. suff. -ary and cp. prec. suff.

## -er
-er, suff. meaning 'receptacle for', as in garner,
larder. — ME. -er, fr. AF. -er (corresponding to
OF., F. -ier), fr. L. -arium. See -ary,'a place for'.

## -er
-er, suff. forming the comparative degree of
adjectives and adverbs. — ME, -er, -ere, fr. OE.
-ra (in adjectives), -or (in adverbs), rel. to ON.
-ri, -ari (in adjectives), -r, -ar (in adverbs), Du.
-er, OHG. -iro, -dro (in adjectives), -or (in
adverbs), MHG., G. -er, Goth, -iza, -oza (in
adjectives), -is, -os (in adverbs), and cogn. with
L. -ior, Gk. -Ιων, ΟΙ. -iyas. Ср.' -ior. Ср. also
superl. suff. -est.

## -er
-er, a suff. forming French infinitives, used in
English (esp. in law terms) to express the action
denoted by the verb. — OF. -er or -re, fr. L.
•are, resp. -ere, pres. inf. suff. of the first, resp.
the third conjugation. Cp. e.g. attainder,
disclaimer, rejoinder.

## -er
-er, suff. forming frequentative verbs as flicker,
glimmer, patter. — ME. -гея, -rien, fr. OE. -rian.

## era
era, n. — Late L. aera, 'era', fr. L. aera,
'counters; items of calculation, money', pi. of aes,
'brass'. See ore.

## eradiate
eradiate, intr. and tr. v., to emit light. — Formed
fr. e- and radiate.

## eradiation
eradiation, п., emission of light. — Formed fr. e-
and radiation.

## eradicable
eradicable, adj. — See next word and -nble.

## eradicate
eradicate, tr. v., to root out. — L. erudicatus, pp.
of eradicure, 'to root out', fr. e- and radix, gen.
radicis, 'root'. See radix and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: eradicat-ion, п., eradicat-ive, adj.,
eradicat-or, n.

## Eragrostis
Eragrostis, п., a genus of plants (pot.) — ModL.,
compounded of έραν, 'to love', and αγρωστις,
'grass'. For the first element see erotic, for the
second see Agrostis.

## Eranthemum
Eranthemum, п., a genus of plants of the family
Acanthaceae (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ήράνθε-
μον, 'a camomile-like plant', which is
compounded of ήρ, 'spring', and ίίνθεμον, 'flower'.
The first element is a contraction of έαρ, fr.
orig. *f έσαρ, and is cogn. with L. vir, 'spring';

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:282 COLUMN:2 -->
see vernal and cp. Erynglum. For the second
element see anther.

## Eranthis
Eranthis, п., a genus of plants, the winter aconite
(ior.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. ήρ,
'spring', and £νθος, 'flower'. See prec. word.

## erase
erase, tr. v., to rub out. — L. erasus, pp. of era-
dere, 'to scratch out, scrape off', fr. e- and
rasus, pp. of radere, 'to scrape, scratch'. See
raze.
Derivatives: eras-ed, adj., eras-er, п., eras-ion,
п., eras-иге, n.

## Erasmus
Erasmus, masc. PN. — L., lit. 'beloved', rel. to
Gk. εράσμιος, 'lovely, pleasant', fr. έράν, 'to
love', See erotic and cp. Erastus.

## Erastian
Erastian, adj., pertaining to, or in accordance
with, the teachings of Thomas Erastus, a Swiss
physician (1524-83), follower of Zwingli. For
the ending see suff. -ian.
Derivative: Erastian-ism, n.

## Erastus
Erastus, masc. PN. — L., lit. 'beloved', fr. Gk.
έραστ&ς, verbal adj. of έραν, 'to love'. See erotic
and cp. Erasmus.

## Erato
Erato, п., the Muse that presided over lyric
poetry (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Ερατώ, fr.
έρατός, 'loved, beloved', verbal adj. of έράν, 'to
love'. See erotic and cp. Erasmus, Erastus.

## erbium
erbium, п., a rare metallic element (chem.) —
ModL., coined by the Swedish chemist Karl
Gustaf Mosander (1797-1858), the discoverer
of this element (in 1843), from the name of the
Swedish town Ytterby, on analogy of many
other element names ending in -him. Cp.
terbium, ytterbium, yttrium.

## ere
ere, adv., prep, and conj. — ME. er, fr. OE. xr,
'soon, before (in time)', adv., prep, and conj.;
prop, an adv. in the compar.; rel. to OS.,
OFris., OHG., MHG. er, Du. eer, G. eher,
'earlier', ON. or, 'early', Goth, air, 'early', compar.
airis, 'earlier', and cogn. with Avestic ayar',
'day', Gk. ήρι [for *α(ι)ερι], 'early, in the
morning', Homeric ήέριος, 'early, at daybreak',
Gk. άριστον, 'breakfast'. Cp. early, erst, or,
