'before'. Cp. also the first element in Erigenia,
Erigeron, nristology.

## Erebus
Erebus, п., a place of nether darkness leading
from Earth to Hades (Greek mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. Έρεβος, fr. Heb. 'irebh, 'sunset, evening'.
See maarib and cp. Europe.
Derivative: Ereb-ian, adj.

## Erechthenm
Erechthenm, Erechtheion, п., a temple on the
acropolis of Athens. — L. Erechtheum, fr. Gk.
Έρέχθειον, called after Έρεχθεύς, 'Erechtheus',
the legendary founder of Athens. See next word.

## Erechtheus
Erechtheus, п., a king said to have founded
Athens (Greek mythol.) — L„ fr. Gk. Έρεχθεύς,
lit. 'the Shaker (of the Earth)', fr. έρέχθειν,
'to rend, break, shatter, shake', fr. I.-E. base
*rekp-, 'to pull, tug, drag, pester', whence also
OI. raksas-, 'goblin, evil spirit', lit. 'damage,
causer of damage', Avestic rashah, 'damage',
rashayeiti, 'damages'. Cp. prec. word. Cp. also
rakshasa.

## Erechtites
Erechtites, п., a genus of plants, the fireweed
(hot.)— ModL., fr. Gk. έρεχθϊτις,'groundsel'.

## erect
erect, adj., upright. — L. erectus, 'upright, lofty,
elevated', pp. of erigere, 'to set up, put straight,
erect, raise', fr. e- and regere, 'to keep straight,
lead, direct, rule, govern'. See regent and cp.
direct, v., and words there referred to.

## erect
erect, tr. v., to raise, set up. — Back formation
fr. erect, adj.
Derivatives: erect-er, п., erect-ive, adj.,
erector, n.

## erectile
erectile, adj. — F. irectile, fr. erectus, pp. of
erigere, 'to set up, erect'. See erect, adj.; and -ile.

## erectility
erectility, n. — F. erectilite. See prec. word and
-iry.

## erection
erection, n. — L. erictid, gen. -onis, 'a setting up,
erecting', fr. erectus, pp. of erigere. See erect,
adj., and -ion.

## erem-
erem-, form of eremo- before a vowel.

## eremite
eremite, п., hermit. — ME. eremite, fr. Eccles.
L. eremita.See hermit.

## eremitic
eremitic, eremitical, adj., pertaining to an
eremite. — See prec. word and -ic, resp. also -al.

## eremo-
eremo-, before a vowel erem-, combining form
meaning 'lonely, solitary'. — Gk. έρημο-, έρημ-,
fr. έρημος. See hermit and cp. eremite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:282 COLUMN:3 -->

## erepsin
erepsin, п., an enzyme in the small intestine (bio-
chem.) — Coined by the German pathologist
Julius Friedrich Cohnheim (1839-1884), on
analogy of pepsin, fr. Gk; έρέπτεσθαι, 'to feed upon',
which is cogn. with L. rapere, 'to seize'. See
rapid and chem. suff. -in.

## erethism
erethism, п., irritability (physiol.) — F. erilhisme,
fr. Gk. ερεθισμός, 'irritation', fr. έρεθίζείν,
έρέθειν, 'to rouse, stir, irritate', formed with
-ί/Λ-enlargement from I.-E. base *er-, *or-, 'to
set in motion, stir up, raise', whence also Gk.
όρνύναι, 'to rouse, start, chase', L. oriri, 'to
rise'. See orient, n. and -ism.

## Eretz Yisrael
Eretz Yisrael, the Land of Israel. — Heb. Eretz
Yisra'el, 'the land of Israel'. See Amhaarez and
Israel.

## erg
erg, п., the unit of energy in the C.G.S. system
(physics). — Fr. Gk. έργον, 'work'. See ergon.

## ergasin
ergasin, п., the total functions of an individual.
— ModL., fr.. Gk. εργασία, 'work', fr. έργά-
ζεσθαι, 'to be busy, to work', fr. ϊργον, 'work';
see ergon. The word ergasia was introduced into
psychiatry by the American psychiatrist Adolf
Meyer (1866-1950).

## ergo
ergo, adv., therefore. — L. ergo, prob. standing
for *e rego, 'from the direction', fr. ё, 'out of
(see e-), and *regum, a noun formed from the
stem of regere, 'to direct', and meaning
'direction'. Cp. erga, Opposite, toward', and see regent.

## ergon
ergon, п., work (in terms of heat). — ModL., fr.
Gk. έργον (dial, ίέργον), 'work'. See work and
cp. erg. Cp. also allergy, alurgite, anergy, argon,
chirurgeon, demiurge, dramaturge, dramaturgy,
energumen, energy, ergasia, exergue, George,
georgic, liturgy, metallurgy, Panurge, surgeon,
synergetic, telergy, thaumaturge, theurgy. Cp.
also organ, orgy.

## ergosterol
ergosterol, п., an alcohol, C28H4jO, occurring esp.
in ergot and yeast (biochem.) — Compounded
of ergot and sterol.

## ergot
ergot, п., a disease of cereals caused by a fungus
(pathol.) — F., fr. OF. argos, argot, lit. 'a cock's
spur'; of unknown origin.

## ergoted
ergoted, adj., infected with ergot. — Formed fr.
ergot with suff. -ed.

## ergotin
ergotin, ergotine, п., an extract of ergot (pharm.)
— Formed fr. ergot with chem. suff. -in.

## ergotism
ergotism, n„ disease contracted by eating ergoted
grain. — A hybrid coined ft. ergot and -ism,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## ergotize
ergotize, tr. v., to infect with ergot. — A hybrid
coined fr. ergot and -ize, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivative: ergotiz-ation, n.

## Erianthus
Erianthus, п., a genus of plants, the woolly bear
grass (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'wool grass', fr. Gk.
έριον, 'wool', and άνθος, 'flower'. See erio- and
anther.

## Eric
Eric, masc. PN. — ON. Eirikr. Cp. Dan. and
Swed. Erik, G. Erich, lit. 'honored ruler',
compounded of Teut. "aiza-, 'honor' and *rik-,
'ruler'. Teut. *aiza- derives fr. I.-E. base *ais-,
'to honor'; see eden. For the second element see
rich and cp. words there referred to.

## Erica
Erica, п., the genus of heaths (bol.)— ModL., fr.
L. trice, 'heath', fr. Gk. έρείκη, έρίκη, of s.m.,
which prob. stands for "^ερείκα and is cogn.
with Olr. froech (for *vroiko-s), 'heath', Lith.
vifiis, Russ. veres, of s.m. Cp. brier, 'heath .
Cp. also Hypericum.

## Ericaceae
Ericaceae, n.pl., the heath family (hot.)— ModL.,
formed fr. Erica with suff. -aceae.

## ericaceous
ericaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Erigenia
Erigenia, п., a genus of plants of the carrot
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ήριγένεια (fern.),
'early-born', compounded of ήρι, 'early, in the
morning', and -γένεια, fr. γεν-, stem of
γίγνεσθαι, 'to become, be born', <5ee ere and genns.

## Erigeron
Erigeron, п., a genus of plants, the daisy fleabane
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ήριγέρων, 'groundsel',
which is compounded of ήρι, 'early' and γέρων,
'an old man' (see Erigenia and geronto-); so
called in allusion to the hoariness of some
species.

## erikite
erikite, п., a silicate and phosphate of cerium,
lanthanum, etc. (mineral.) — Named after Erik
the Red, discoverer of Greenland: For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Erin
Erin, п., ancient (now poetic) name of Ireland. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:283 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ERINITE | 256 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:283 COLUMN:1 -->
OE. Erirm, dat. of Eriu (whence Ir. Eire),
'Ireland'. Cp. Dai] Eireann, Erse, Irish, Hibernian.

## erinite
erinite, п., a basic copper arsenate of emerald-
green color (mineral.) — Named after Erin,
'Ireland'. See prec. word and subst. suff. -ite.

## Erinys
Erinys, п., one of the three avenging spirits,
Alecto, Tisiphone and Megaera (Greek mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. 'Ερΐνΰς, which is of uncertain
origin. It possibly means lit. 'the angry spirit'f
and is rel. to Arcadian έρ(νειν, 'to be angry',
and to Gk. όρΐνειν, 'to raise, stir, excite', ε*ρις,
'strife, discord', fr. I.-E. *erei-, enlargement
of base *er-, 'to set in motion, stir up', whence
Gk. όρνύναι, L. orirl, 'to rise'. See orient, п.,
and cp. erethism, Eris, eristic.

## erio-
erio-, combining form meaning 'wool'. — Gk.
έριο-, fr. ϊριον, 'wool', rel. to Homeric and Ion.
εϊρος, 'wool' (fr. "Spfo?, which was prob.
dissimulated fr. *f έρ^ος), Gk. άρήν, Gortyn. ίαρήν,
'ram', and cogn. with OI. ura, 'sheep', uranah,
'ram, lamb', ura-bhrah, 'ram', Arm. gafn,
'lamb', L. vervex, 'wether' (prop, 'wool
bearer'). Cp. Iresine. Cp. also berger and the first
element in Arnoseris.

## Eriocaalaceae
Eriocaalaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the pipe-
wort family (hot.) — ModL., formed fr. Erio-
caalon with suff. -aceae.

## eriocaulaceous
eriocaulaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Eriocaulon
Eriocaulon, п., a genus of plants, the pipewort
(hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. ϊριον,
'wool' (see erio-), and καυλός, 'stalk' (see can-
line); so called from the wool at the base of
the stalk.

## Eriodictyon
Eriodictyon, п., a genus of the waterleaf family
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'woolen net', fr. erio- and
Gk. βίκτυον, 'net'. See Dictynidae.

## Eriogonum
Eriogonum, п., a genus of plants, of the
buckwheat family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
erio- and Gk. γόνυ, 'knee'. See -gon and cp.
words there referred to.

## erionlte
erionlte, n.,a zeolitic silicate (mineral.)— Formed
with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. ϊρίον, 'wool' (see
erio-); so called from its woolly appearance.

## Eriophornm
Eriophornm, п., a genus of plants, the cotton
grass (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. έριοφέρος, 'wool-
bearing', fr. Sptov, 'wool', and -φόρος, 'bearing,
carrying'. See erio- and -phore.

## Eris
Eris, п., the goddess of discord in Greek
mythology. — L., fr. Gk. Έρις, lit. 'strife, discord',
fr. I.-E. *erei-, enlargement of base *er-, 'to set
in motion, stir up'. See Erinys and cp. next word.

## eristic
eristic, adj., controversial. — Gk. εριστικός,
'connected with strife', fr. ερις, 'strife, debate,
discord'. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: eristic, п., a controversialist.

## erlking
erlking, п., a spirit who does mischief, esp. to
children (German and Scandinavian mythology).
— G. Erlkonig, coined by Herder as translation
of Dan. elle(r)konge, fr. elve(r)konge; see elf and
king. The word ellerkonge lit. means 'king of
the elves', but was mistaken by Herder and by
Goethe for 'king of the alder' (cp. G. Eller,
Erie, 'alder', and see elder, aider).

## Ermentrud
Ermentrud, Ermentrude, Ermyatrude, fern. PN.
— OHG. Ermentrudis, Irmintrud, compounded
of ermin, 'whole, universal', and trut, drut
(whence MHG. trut, G. tram), 'beloved, dear'.
For the first element cp. Irma. For the second
element see true and cp. the second element in
Astrid, Gertrude.

## ermine
ermine, п., a kind of weasel. — OF. ermine (F.
hermine), femin. of OF. ermin, hermin, which
prob. derives fr. L. Armenius, 'Armenian', used
in the sense of Armenius mus, lit. 'Armenian
mouse', fr. Armenia, fr. G k. 'Αρμενία, 'Armenia'.
Derivatives: ermine, adj. and tr.v., ermin-ed,
adj., ermines, n.pl. (her.), ermin-ois, n. (her.)

## -ern
-ern, suff. denoting direction. — OE. -erne, rel.
to OHG. -гая/ (in nordaroni, 'northern').

## erne
erne, also em, п., a sea eagle. — ME. ern, am, fr.
OE. earn, 'eagle', rel. to ON. от, MDu. arent,
OHG., aro, am. MHG. am, G. Aar, Goth, are,
'eagle', and cogn. with Gk. δρνις, 'bird',
OSIav. orilu, Lith. erelis, Bret., Co. er, W. eryr,
Olr. ilar, 'eagle' (dissimil. fr. *erir-), Hitt.
harash, haranash, 'eagle'; cp. Akkad. агй, егй,
'eagle'. See ornitho- and cp. arend, the first
element in Arnold and the second element in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:283 COLUMN:2 -->
allerion.

## Ernest
Ernest, masc. PN. — F. Ernest, of G. origin.
Cp. OHG. Ernusl, whence G. Ernst. The name
lit. means 'earnestness'. See earnest,
'earnestness', and cp. next word.

## Ernestine
Ernestine, fem. PN. — Formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -Ine.

## erode
erode, tr. v., to eat into, wear away. — F. eroder,
fr. L. erodere (pp. erosus), 'to gnaw away,
consume', fr. e- and rodere, 'to gnaw'. See rodent
and cp. corrode. Derivative: erod-ed, adj.

## erodent
erodent, adj., causing erosion. — L. erodens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of erodere. See prec. word
and -ent

## Erodium
Erodium, п., a genus of plants of the geranium
family (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ερωδιός, 'heron',
so called in allusion to the shape of the fruit
resembling the beak of the heron. Gk. ερωδιός
stands in gradational relationship to L. ardea,
'heron', ON. arta, 'creek duck' (whence the
dimin. ertla, 'wagtail'), Serb, and Croat, roda,
'stork'. Cp. Ardea.

## erogenous
erogenous, adj., productive of sexual desire. —
Compounded of Gk. ε*ρως, 'love, desire', and
γεν-, the stem of γεννϊν, 'to beget, bring forth,
generate, produce'. See erotic and -genous.

## Eros
Eros, п., the god of love in Greek mythology. —
L., fr. Gk. Έρως, personification of ε*ρως, 'love',
which is rel. to έραν, 'to love'. See erotic.

## erosion
erosion, n. — F. erosion, fr. L. erosionem, ace. of
erosio, 'a gnawing away', fr. erosus, pp. of
erodere. See erode and -ion.

## erosive
erosive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
erosus, pp. of erodere. See erode.

## erotic
erotic, adj., of sexual love. — Gk. ερωτικός,
'caused by love; referring to love', fr. ϋρως, gen.
ε'ρωτος, 'love, sexual desire', rel. to έραν, έρϊσ-
θαι, 'to love', which is of uncertain etymology.
Cp. Erasmus, Erastus, Erato, Eros, the first
element in Eragrostis and the second element in
pederasty. For the ending see suff. -ic.
Derivatives: erotic, п., erotica, n.pl. (ModL.),
erotic-al, adj., erot-ic-ai-Iy. adv., erot-ic-ism, п.,
erot-ism, n.

## eroto-
eroto-, combining form, used in the sense of
erotic. — See prec. word.

## erotomania
erotomania, n. — ModL., fr. Gk. έρωτομανίά,
έρωμανίά, 'mad love', which is formed fr. έρως,
'love', and μανίχ, 'madness, frenzy'. See erotic
and mania.

## err
err, intr. v. — ME. erren, fr. F. errer, 'to wander',
fr. L. errare (for *ersare), 'to wander, stray
about, miss the right way, wander from the truth,
err, mistake', which is cogn. with Golh. airzeis,
'astray, going astray', airzjan, 'to lead astray,
deceive', OHG. irron, MHG., G. irren, 'to err.'
Cp. erratic, error, aberration, inerrable. Cp. also
It. errare, OProvenc., Catal., Sp. and Port.
error, which all derive fr. L. errare.
Derivative: err-ing, adj.

## erraad
erraad, n. — ME. erande, fr. earlier arende, fr.
OE. xrende, 'a message', rel. to OS. arundi, ON.
erendi, Dan. xrende, Swed. arende, OFris.
erende, OHG. arunti, 'message'.

## errant
errant, adj., wandering, roving. — F., pres. part,
of OF. errer, 'to journey, march, wander', fr.
VL. "iterare, fr. L. iter, 'journey'. See itinerate
and cp. arrant. Cp. also eyre. OF. errer in the
above sense was confused with OF. and F. errer,
'to err', fr. L. errare', see err.

## erratic
erratic, adj., irregular. — F. erratique, fr. L. er-
raticus, 'wandering, straying about, roving', fr.
errdtus, pp. of errare, 'to wander, stray about,
rove'. See err and -ic. Derivative: erratic, n.

## erratum
erratum, n. (pi. errata), an error in writing or
printing. — L., neut. pp. of errare, 'to err'.
See err.

## erroneous
erroneous, adj. — L. erroneus, 'wandering,
straying, roving'. See err. For E. -ous, as equivalent
to L. -us, see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: erroneous-ly, adv. ,erroneous-ness, n.

## error
error, n. — L. error, 'a wandering, straying about,
missing the right way, wandering from the
truth, error', rel. to errare, 'to wander, stray
about'. See err.

## ersatz
ersatz, п., a substitute. — G., lit. 'replacement',
fr. ersetzen, 'to replace', fr. OHG. irsezzen, fr.
pref. ir-, unaccented equivalent of pref. -ur, and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:283 COLUMN:3 -->
setzen, 'to set'. See a-, intensive pref., and set, v.

## Erse
Erse, п., pertaining to Scottish or Irish Gaelic. —
A var. of Irish.
Derivative: Erse, п., Scottish or Irish Gaelic

## erst
erst, adv., formerly (archaic). — ME. erest, erste,
fr. OE. xresl, 'soonest, earliest' (rel. to OS.
and OHG. erist, MHG. irst, G. erst); superl.
of яг, 'soon, before (in time)'. See ere and cp.
early. Compound: erst-while, adv.

## erubescence
erubescence, п., process of becoming red. — L.
Irubescentia, 'a blushing', fr. Irublsclns, gen.
entis. See next word and -ce.

## erubesceat
erubesceat, adj., reddening, blushing. — L. tru-
bescens, gen. -entis, pres part, of irubiscere,
'to grow red, blush', fr. e- and rubescere, 'to
grow red', inchoative of rubere, 'to be red'.
See rubric and -escent and cp. rubescent.

## eruct
eruct, tr. and intr. v., to belch. — F. erucier, fr.
L. gructare, 'to belch forth'. See next word.

## eructate
eructate, intr. v., to belch. — L. Iructatus, pp. of
eruclare, 'to belch forth', fr. e- and ructare, 'to
belch', frequentative formed fr. (e)ruclus, pp. of
(e)rugere, to belch', from the I.-E. imitative
base *reug-, 'to belch*, whence also Lith. rugiu,
rugli, 'to belch', Gk. έρυγή, 'eructation', Arm.
orcam, Ί belch'. The letter о in Arm. orcam (for
*o-rucam) and ε in Gk. έρυγή are prosthetic
and due to the influence of the initial r; cp. Gk.
έ-ρυθρός, 'red', which is cogu. with L. ruber,
'red', and see erysipelas.

## eructation
eructation, n. — L. gruclatio, gen. -onis, 'a
belching forth', fr. Iructatus, pp. of eruclare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## erudite
erudite, adj., learned. — L. irudtius, pp. of em-
dire, 'to polish, instruct', lit. 'to bring out of
the rough', fr. e- and rudis, 'rough'. See rude.
Derivatives: erudite-ly, adv., erudite-ness, n.

## erudition
erudition, n. — L. Iruditid, gen. -onis,
'instruction, education', fr. eruditus, pp. of erudire. See
prec. word and -ion.

## erupt
erupt, intr. v. — L. eruptus, pp. of erumpere, 'to
break out, burst', fr. e- and rumpere, 'to break
forth'. See rupture.

## eruptioa
eruptioa, n. — L. erupiio, gen. -6nis, 'a breaking
out*, fr. eruptus, pp. of erumpere. See prec. word
and -ion.

## eruptive
eruptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -Ive fr. L.
eruptus, pp. of erumpere. See ernpt.
Derivatives: eruptive, п., eruplive-ly, adv.

## Ervum
Ervum, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bol.) — L. ervum, 'the bitter vetch', which,
together with Gk. δροβος, 'the bitter vetch',
έρέβινθος, 'chick-pea', OS. eriwii, erit, MDu.
erwete. OHG. araweis (MHG. arwis, arwis,
G. Erbse), 'pea', of s.m., prob. derives from an
unknown, perh. non-Indo-European, language.
Cp. arvejon, Orobanche.

## -ery
-ery, suff. denoting 1) things collectively, as in
finery; 2) place where something is produced,
as in bakery; 3) business, trade, occupation, as
in archery, surgery; 4) behavior, conduct, as in
foolery. — OF. or F. -erie, a suff. compounded
of OF. or F. -ier (fr. L. -alius) and OF. or F. -ie
(fr. L. -ia). See -er, suff. denoting connectedness,
and -y (representing OF. or F. -ie) and ср. -ту.

## Eryngium
Eryngium, п., a genus of plants (bol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. ήρύγγιον, dimin. of ήρυγγος (fem.),
'sea holly, eryngo', rel. to ήρυγγος (masc.),
'goatsbeard'; prob. derived fr. ήρ, contracted
form of έαρ, 'spring', and lit. meaning 'spring
flower'; see Frisk, GEW„ p.644. See Eran-
themum and cp. Aruncus.

## eryngo
eryngo, п., a plant of the genus Eryngium. —
Gk. ήρυγγος, 'sea holly, eryngo'. See prec. word.

## Erysibe
Erysibe, п., a genus of powdery mildews (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. έρυσίβη, 'mildew', which is
prob. rel. to ερυθρός, 'red', ερυσίπελας,
'erysipelas'. See erysipelas.

## Erysimum
Erysimum, п., a genus of plants of the mustard
family (bot.) — L., fr. Gk. έρύσιμον, 'hedge-
mustard', fr. έρύειν, 'to draw, drag', fr. base
*Fepu-, 'to draw*, whence also Ερυμα, 'fence,
guard', ρϋτήρ, 'one who draws'.

## erysipelas
erysipelas, п., an acute inflammatory disease of
the skin. — Gk. ερυσίπελας, lit. 'red skin', fr.
ερυθρός, 'red', and -πελας, 'skin' (used only in
compounds), which is cogn. with L.pellis, 'skin'.
Gk. ερυθρός is cogn. with L. ruber, rufus, 'red',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:284 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 257 | ESPERANTO -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:284 COLUMN:1 -->
rublre, 'to be red', Goth, roups, OE. read, 'red'.
The initial έ in ερυθρές is prosthetic and due
to the circumstance that the Greek never begins
a word with r. (Initial ρ in Greek words is the
equivalent of I.-E. *sr- or *wr-.) See red and cp.
Erysibe, Erysiphe, Erythronium. For the second
element in erysipelas see fell, 'hide'.

## Erysiphe
Erysiphe, п., a synonym of Erysibe (hot.) —
ModL., short for *Erysisiphe (see haplology);
compounded of έρυσι- (for ερυθρός), 'red', and
σίφων, 'tube'. See prec. word and siphon.

## erythema
erythema, п., redness of the skin (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. ερύθημα, 'redness of the skin',
fr. έρυθαίνειν, 'to make red', dye red', fr. έρεύ-
θειν, of s.m., which is rel. to ερυθρός, 'red'.
See erysipelas and -ma.

## erythro-
erythro-, before a vowel erythr-, combining form
meaning 'red'. — Gk. έρυθρο-, έρυθρ-, fr.
ερυθρός, 'red'. See erysipelas.

## erythrocyte
erythrocyte, п., a red blood cell. — Compounded
of erythro- and -cyte.

## Erythronium
Erythronium, п., a genus of plants, the dog's-
tooth violet (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ερυθρός,
'red'. See erythro-,

## Esan
Esan, п., the son of Isaac and Rebecca (Bible). —
Late L. Esau, fr. Gk.' Ησαϋ, fr. Heb. 'Esaw, prob.
meaning lit. 'hairy', and rel. to Arab, d'tha,
'hairy'. See Gen. 25:25.

## escadrille
escadrille, п., a small naval squadron. — F., fr.
Sp. escuadrilla, dimin. of escuadra, 'square,
squad, squadron', fr. escuadrar, 'to square', fr.
VL. *exquadrare. See square and cp. squad,
squadron.

## escainde
escainde, п., the act of scaling the walls of a
fortified place by means of ladders. — F., fr. It.
scalata, prop. fem. pp. of scalare, 'to climb by
means of a ladder', fr. scala, 'ladder'. See scale,
'measure', and -ade.
Derivatives: escalade, tr. v., escalad-er, n.

## escalator
escalator, п., a moving staircase. — ModL. See
escalade and agential suff. -or.

## Escallonia
Escallonia, п., a genus of South American shrubs
(hot.) — ModL., named after its discoverer, the
18th cent. Spanish traveler Escallon. For the
ending see suff. -la.

## Escalloniaceae
Escalloniaceae, n. pi., a family of shrubs. —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## escalloniaceous
escalloniaceous, adj. — Formed fr. Escallonia
with suff. -aceous.

## escalop
escalop, escallop, п., scallop shell; scallop. — OF.
escalope, 'shell'. See scallop.
Derivative: excal(l)op-ed, adj. (her.)

## escapade
escapade, п., a wild prank. — F., fr. Sp. esca-
pada, 'escape', prop. fem. pp. of escapar, 'to
escape', See next word and -nde,

## escape
escape, intr. and tr. v. — ME. escapen, fr. ONF.
escaper, which corresponds to OF. eschaper (F.
echapper), 'to escape', orig. 'to throw off the
cowl', fr. VL. *excappare (whence also Ruman.
scupd, It. scappare, OProvenc., Catal., Sp.
escapar, Port, escappar), formed fr. 1st ex- and Late
L. cappa, 'hood, mantle'. See cape, 'cloak'.
Derivatives: escape, п., escapement (q.v.),
escap-er, n.

## escapement
escapement, n. — Formed on analogy of F.
echappement from escape with suff. -ment.

## escarbuncle
escarbuncle, n. (her.) — OF. (F. escarboucle), fr.
L. carbunculus, 'a small coal; a bright, reddish
kind of precious stone', dimin. of сагЬб, gen.
-Onis 'coal'. See carbon and cp. carbuncle.

## escarp
escarp, п., a steep slope. — F. escarpe, fr. It.
Scarpa, prob. derived fr. Goth, 'skrapa, which
is rel. to MHG. schrof, 'crag'. Cp. scarp, n.

## escarp
escarp, tr. v., to make into an escarp. — F. es-
carper, fr. escarpe. See escarp, n.

## escarpment
escarpment, п., wide ground formed into an
escarp. — F. escarpement, fr. escarper. See prec.
word and -ment

## -esce
-esce, suff. forming inchoative verbs. — L. -isco,
•iscere, cogn. with Gk. -ακ-ω, -σκ-είν, ΟΙ. -ccha,
Avestic -sa-\ cp. OI. gacchati, Avestic jasaiti,
'goes', Gk. βάσκω, Ί go'; OI. prcchati, Avestic
p'r'saili, 'asks', corresp. to L. poscere (for
*porc-scere), 'to demand, desire', OHG. forscdn
(MHG. vorschen, G. forschen), 'to search,
inquire'. Cp. verbal suff. -Jsh. Cp. also -escency,
-escent

## -escence
-escence, suff. forming abstract nouns from

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:284 COLUMN:2 -->
adjectives ending in -escent. — See -escent and -ce.

## -escency
-escency, suff. denoting incipiency. — See the
suffixes -escent and -cy.

## -escent
-escent, suff. forming adjectives and nouns from
verbs and meaning 'beginning to; beginning to
be in the condition expressed by the verb'. —
L. -iscins, gen. -entis, pres. part. suff. of verbs
into -iscere; meaning 'to begin to ...'. See
-esce and -eat.

## eschalot
eschalot, n. — See shallot.

## eschar
eschar, п., a dry crust on a burn (med.) — Late
L. eschara, fr. Gk. έσχάρά, 'hearth; scar from
a burn'. See scar, 'mark on the skin'.

## escharotic
escharotic, adj., causing an eschar; caustic. —
Late L. escharolicus, fr. Gk. έσχαρωτικός, fr.
έσχάρϋ. See prec. word and -ic.

## eschatology
eschatology, п., the doctrine of the last things. —
Lit. 'the study of the last things', fr. Gk. εοχατος,
'furthest, remotest, last', and -λογία, fr, -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one
who deals (with a certain topic)'. Gk. έσχατος
is a derivative of έξ (Boeotian ές), 'out of'; see
2nd ex-. For the second element see -logy.
Derivatives: eschatolog-ical, adj., eschatolog-
isl, n.

## escheat
escheat, п., the reverting of the land to the king
or another lord of the fee. — ME. eschete, fr.
OF. escheoite, prop. fem. pp. of escheoir (F.
echoir), fr. VL. *excadere, 'to fall out', fr. 1st
ex and *cadlre, corresponding to L. cadire, 'to
fall'. See cadence and cp. chent, decay.
Derivative: escheat, intr. and tr. v.

## eschew
eschew, tr. v., to shun, avoid. — ME. eschewen,
eschuen, fr. OF. eschiuver, eschiver, eschever,
'to shun', fr. Frankish *skiuhan, which is rel.
to OHG. sciuhen, 'to avoid, escape', MHG.
schiuhen, G. scheuen, 'to fear, shun, shrink from',
MHG. schiech, G. scheu, 'shy, timid'. It. schivare,
'to avoid, shun, protect from' (whence F. esquiver,
'to avoid, dodge'), derives fr. It. schivo, 'shy,
bashful', which is a loan word fr. WTeut. *skiu,
'shy'. See shy and cp. skew, which is a doublet
of eschew.
Derivatives: eschew-al, п., eschew-er, n.

## Eschscbolrzin
Eschscbolrzin, п., a genus of herbs of the Pa-
paveraceae. — ModL., named after the German
botanist Johann Friedrich von Eschscholtz
(1793-1831). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## esciandre
esciandre, п., a scandal, scandalous scene. — F.,
fr. OF. escandle, fr. earlier escandele, fr. L. scan-
dalum. See scandal and cp. slander.

## esclavage
esclavage, n„ necklace. — F., lit. 'slavery', fr.
esclave, 'slave'. See slave and -age.

## escoba
escoba, п., tropical American mallow. — Sp.,
'broom," fr. L. scupa, 'twig, shoot; broom,
besom,' which is rel. to scapus, 'shaft, beam',
fr. I.-E. base *skap-, *skop-, 'shaft, thin branch',
whence also shaft, 'stem, stock', and scepter
(qq.v.) Cp. also scopa.

## esconson
esconson, a..(archil.) — OF. escoinson (F. ecoin-
ςοη, ecoinson), 'jamb of doors or windows'. See
sconcheon, which is a doublet of esconson.

## Escorial
Escorial, п., a palace built in the 16th century
by Philip II of Spain, NW. of Madrid. — Sp.,
prop, 'a place where a mine has been exhausted',
fr. escoria, "dross, scoria', fr, L. scoria, of s.m.
See scoria and adj. suff. -al.

## escort
escort, п., a person or persons accompanying
another or others for protection, courtesy, etc. —
F. escorte, fr. It. scorta, fr. scorgere, 'to show,
to guide', fr. VL. "excorrigere, fr. 1st ex- and
L. corrigere, 'to make straight, set right'. See
correct, adj.
Derivative: escort, tr. v.

## escritoire
escritoire, п., a writing desk. — OF. (F. ecritoire),
fr. Late L. scriptorium, 'place for writing', prop.,
neut. of the Latin adjective scriptorius,
'pertaining to writing', fr. scriptus, pp. of scribere,
'to write'. See scribe and cp. scriptorium, which
is a doublet of escritoire.

## escrow
escrow, п., a written engagement (law). — OF.
escroe, escroue, 'roll of papers'. See scroll.

## escudo
escudo, п., 1) name of various Spanish and
Portuguese gold and silver coins; 2) the gold
monetary unit of Portugal. — Sp. and Port, escudo,
fr. L. scutum, 'shield'. See scutum and cp.
escutcheon.

## esculent
esculent, adj., eatable; edible. — L. esculenlus,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:284 COLUMN:3 -->
'good to eat, eatable', fr. esca, 'food', fr. *eds-
qa (cp. Lith. eska, 'appelite'), fr. I.-E. base *ed-,
'to eat'. See eat.

## escutcheon
escutcheon, п., a shield on which a coat of arms
is depicled (her.) — ONF. escuchon,
corresponding to OF. escuson, F. ecusson, fr. VL.
*scutionem, ace. of "scutio, fr. L. scutum, 'shield'.
See scutum and cp. scutcheon, escudo. For the
collateral forms escutcheon and scutcheon cp.
espy, spy; esquire, squire; estate, state.

## Esdras
Esdras, п., either of two apocryphal books
ascribed to Ezra. — Gk. Έσδράς, fr. Heb. 'Ezra.
See Ezra.

## -ese
-ese, suff. used to form adjectives or nouns
denoting 'names of nations or their language' (cp.
Portuguese, Chinese, etc.) — OF. -eis (F. -ois)
fr. L. -ensis.

## -ese
-ese, suff. used in chemistry to denote an
enzyme that accelerates synthetic action. —
Suggested as a collateral form of -ase (q.v.)

## -esis
-esis, suff. denoting process of action. — ModL.,
fr. Gk. -ησις, formed fr. ε-stem verbs. Cp. -asis,
-osis, -iasis.

## eskar
eskar, esker, п., deposit left by a subglacia]
stream (geol.) — Ir. eiscir, 'a ridge'.

## Eskimo
Eskimo, n. and adj. — N. American Indian
eskimantsik, 'eaters of raw flesh', a name given
by the Algonquians to the N. American Indian
tribes living in the Arctic and Greenland. Cp.
Husky.

## Esmeralda
Esmeralda, fem. PN. — Sp., lit. 'emerald'. See
emerald.

## eso-
eso-, combining form meaning 'within'. — Fr.
Gk. έσω (Ion. εϊσω), 'in, within', which
stand for *ευσω and are rel. to ές, εις (for
*ένς), 'into', and to έν, 'in'. See 2nd en-.

## Esocidae
Esocidae, n. pi., a family of fishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. esox, gen.
esocis, 'a kind of fish' (prob. 'salmon'), a word
of Gaulish origin. Cp. OCo., MBret. ehoc, Ir.
lo (gen. iach), 'salmon'.

## esophag-
esophag-, form of esophago- before a vowel.

## esophageal
esophageal, oesophageal, adj., pertaining to the
esophagus. — See esophagus and adj. suff. -al.

## esophago-
esophago-, before a vowel esophag-, pertaining
to the esophagus. — Fr. Gk. οισοφάγος. See
next word.

## esophagus
esophagus, п., the gullet (anat.) — Medical L„
fr. Gk. οισοφάγος, 'the gullet', which prob.
means lit. 'bearer of food', and is compounded
of οίσω, "I shall carry' (used as future of φέρειν,
'to bear, carry'), a word of unknown etymology,
and φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

## esoteric
esoteric, adj., intended for the initiated only,
secret. — Gk. εσωτερικός, lit. 'pertaining to
those within', fr. έσωτέρω, 'more within', corn-
par, of ίσω, 'within'. See eso- and cp. exoteric.
For the etymology of the compar. suff. -ter see
-ther and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: esoteric, п., esoteric-al-ly, adv.,
esoteric-ism, n.

## espadon
espadon, п., a long two-handed sword. — F., fr.
It. spadone, augment, of spada, 'sword', fr. L.
spada. See spade and cp. words there referred to.
For the It. augment, suff. -one see -oon.

## espagaolette
espagaolette, п., bolt for a casement window. —
F., fr. espagnol, 'Spanish' (fr. Espagne, 'Spain'),
and dimin. suff. -ette.

## espalier
espalier, п., a trellis or framework on which fruit
trees are trained flat. — F., fr. It. spalliera, fr.
spalla, 'shoulder', fr. L. spatula, 'broad piece',
whence also F. epaule, 'shoulder'. See epaulet
and cp. epauliere.
Derivative: espalier, tr. v.

## esparto
esparto, п., also esparto grass. — Sp. esparto, fr.
L. spartum, fr. Gk. σπάρτον, 'rope, cable;
Spanish broom; esparto', which is rel. to
σπαρτός, 'Spanish broom; esparto', and to
σπείρα, 'coil, twist', and prob. cogn. with Lith.
spartas, 'band'. See spire, 'spiral', and cp.
Spartina, Spartium.

## especial
especial, adj. — ME., fr. OF. especial (F. special),
fr. L. specialis. See special, which is a doublet
of especial.
Derivatives: especial-ly, adv., especial-ness, n.

## Esperanto
Esperanto, n. — Fr. Esperanto, pseudonym of
Dr. Lazarus Ludwig Zamenhof (1859-1917),
inventor of this language, fr. Sp. esperanza, 'hope',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:285 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ESPIAL | 258 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:285 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. esperar, 'to hope', fr. L. sperdre. See despair
and -ance.
Derivatives: Espcrant-ic, adj., Esperant-i.\m, п.,
Esperant-ist, n. and adj.

## espial
espial, n. — OF. espiaille, St. espier, "to spy'. See
espy and subst. sun*, -al.

## espionage
espionage, n. — F. espionnage, 'spying', fr. espion,
'spy', fr. It. spione. See espy and -age.

## esplanade
esplanade, п., a level place; esp. one serving as a
promenade. — F., fr. It. spiaiiata, "leveling;
esplanade', prop, subst. use of the fem. pp. of
spianare, 4o level', fr. L. explanare, 'to flatten,
level', whence also explain (q.v.)

## espousal
espousal, n. — OF. espousailles (F. epousailles),
fr. L. sponsalia, 'betrothal, espousal' (whence
also OProvenc. espozalha, OSp. esposayas, Sp.
esponsales), prop. neut. pi. of the adjective spon-
salis, 'pertaining to betrothal', fr. sponsus, pp.
of spondlre, 'to engage oneself, promise'. See
spouse and subst. suff. -nl and cp. spousal.

## espouse
espouse, tr. v. — OF. espouser (F. epouser), fr.
L. sponsare, 'to betroth, espouse', freq. of
spondlre (pp. sponsus), 'to engage oneself, promise'.
See prec. word and cp. spouse.
Derivative: espous-er, n.

## espressivo
espressivo, adv., with expression (musical
direction). — It., 'expressive', fr. espresso, fr. L. ex-
pressus, 'distinct', lit. 'expressed', pp. of expri-
mere. See express, adj., and -ive.

## esprit
esprit, п., spirit, wit. — F., fr. L. spiritus. See
spirit.

## esprit de corps
esprit de corps,spirit of attachedness and devotion
to a body of persons associated. — F„ lit.
'spirit of the body'. See prec. word, de- and corps.

## espy
espy, tr. v. — ME. espien, fr. OF. espier (F. epier),
fr. Frankish *spehon, which is rel. to OHG.
spehon, 'to spy'. See spy, v.

## esquamate
esquamate, adj., having no scales (zool. and hot.)
— Formed fr. e- and L. squamatus, 'scaly', fr.
squama, 'scale'. See squama and cp. desquamate.

## -esque
-esque, suff. — F., fr. It. -esco, borrowed fr. Teut.
-isk. See adj. suff. -ish.

## esquire
esquire, n. — ME. esquier, fr. OF. escuyer, es-
quier (F. ecuyer), 'squire, equerry', orig. 'shield-
bearer', fr. VL. sculSrius, 'shield bearer' (but
classical L. scQtarius means 'shield maker'), fr.
L. scutum, 'shield'. See equerry and cp. squire.

## esqnisse
esqnisse, п., first sketch. — F., fr. It. schizzo. See
sketch.

## ess
ess, п., ι) the letter s; z) anything shaped like
the letter s.

## -ess
-ess, suff. forming feminine nouns, as in countess,
hostess. — ME. -esse, St. OF. (= F.) -esse, fr.
Late L. -issa (whence also It. -ezza, Sp., Port.
-esa). Si. Gk. -ισσα, which—in classical Greek—
occurs only in βασίλισσα, 'queen' (fr. βασιλεύς,
'king'). However, in later Greek, several other
nouns were formed on analogy of βασίλισσα
(ср. e.g. πανδόκισσα, 'female innkeeper', fr.
πανδοκεύς, 'innkeeper').

## -ess
-ess, suff. forming nouns of quality from
adjectives, as in duress. — ME. -esse, fr. OF. (= F.)
-esse, fr. L. -itia, whence also It. -ezza, Proven?.,
Sp., Port. -eza. Cp. the subst. suffixes -ice, -ise.

## essay
essay, tr. and intr. v. — OF. essaier (F. essayer),
St. VL. 'exagiare, 'to weigh', fr. L. exagium, 'a
weighing', fr. exigere, 'to weigh, measure,
examine', lit. 'to drive out', fr. 1st ex- and agere, 'to
drive'. See agent and cp. assay.

## essay
essay, n. — OF. (= F.) essai, fr. essaier. See
essay, v.

## essayist
essayist, п., a writer of essays. — A hybrid coined
fr. essay, п., and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivatives: essayisl-ic, essayist-ic-al, adjs., es-
sayist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## esse
esse, п., being, actual existence. — L. esse, 'to
be', fr. I.-E. base *es-, 'to be', whence also L.
es-t, 'is', OI. dsmi, Hitt. esmi. Arm. em, Gk.
ε[μί, Lesb. and Thessal. έμμί, Dor. ήμί. Alb.
jam, OSlav. jesmt, Lith. esmi, Olr. am, Goth, im,
OE. eom, earn, am, Ί am', OI. smah, Gk. έσμέν,
Ion. είμέν, Dor. είμές, Lith. esme, OSlav.jesmu,
L. sumus, 'we are' (L. sum, Ί am', has been
formed on analogy of the pi. sumus). Cp.
absence, absent, -ent, entity, essence, essential,
interest, presence, present, prosit. Cp. also am, art,
are, is, sin, 'transgression', sooth. Cp. also
etymology, etymon, heteroousian, homoiouslan,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:285 COLUMN:2 -->
bomoousian, onto-, sattwa, suttee, swastika,
essence, n. — F., fr. L. essentia, 'being or essence
of a thing', fr. essent-, pres. part, stem of esse,
'to be'; prop, loan translation of Gk. ουσία,
'essence'. See esse and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending see suff. -ence.

## Essene
Essene, п., a member of an ancient Jewish sect of
ascetics, first appearing in history in the 2nd
century B.C.E. — L. Esseni (pL), 'the Essenes',
fr. Gk. Έσσηνοί. Most scholars derive this word
from Heb. tzfyu'fm, 'the modest ones', or from
Heb. hashSim, 'the silent ones'. It is more
probable, however, that Gk. Έσσηνοί derives fr.
Syr. husin, pi. absolute state of huse, 'pious'; cp.
the pi. emphatic state hasayya, whence the parallel
Greek form Έσσαΐοι. This etymology gains in
probability by the fact that Philo (in Quod om-
nis probus liber sit, § 13) identifies the Essenes
with the 'Pious' (των Έσσαίων ή οσίων = 'of
the Essenes or the Pious').
Derivatives: Essen-ian, adj., Essen-ian-ism, п.,
Essen-ic, Essen-ic-al, adjs., Essen-ism, п., Essen-
ize, tr. v.

## essential
essential, adj. — ML. essentialis, 'essential', fr.
L. essentia. See essence and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: essential-ity, п., essential-ly, adv.

## essonfte
essonfte, also, more correctly, hessonite, п.,
cinnamon stone (mineral.) — Formed with subst.
suff. -ite fr. Gk. ήσσων, 'inferior to', compar. of
3)κα, 'slightly, a little, slowly, faintly'; which is
prob. cogn. with L. segnis, 'slow, tardy,
sluggish'. The cinnamon stone was so called in
allusion to its being less hard than true hyacinth
and some other minerals.

## -est
-est, suff. forming the superlative degree of
adjectives and adverbs. — ME., fr. OE. -ost, -est,
rel. to ON. -astr, -str, OHG. -isto, -dsto, G. -est,
Goth, -ists, -osts, and cogn. with Gk. -ιστός,
OI. -isfha; formed orig. from the compar. suff.
through the addition of a suff. beginning with t.
See compar. suff. -er and cp. Anchistea, Calista,
Callisto, kakistocracy, protista.

## -est
-est, -st, suff. of the second person singular
indicative of English verbs (as in doest, dost, did-
dest, didst, etc.) — ME., fr. OE. -ast, -est, -st,
rel. to OHG. -1st, -ost, -est, G. -est, -st, Goth, -is,
-os -ais, ON. -r, -ar, -ir, and cogn. with Gk. -ς, L.
-s, OI. -si, second person sing, endings of verbs.

## establish
establish, tr. v. — ME. establissen, ir. OF. esta-
bliss-, pres. part, stem of establir (F. itablir), fr.
L. stabilire, 'to make firm or stable', fr. stabilis,
'firm, stable*. See stable, adj., and verbal suff.
-ist and cp. stablish.
Derivatives: eslablish-ed, adj.,establish-ment,n.,
establishmentarian (q.v.)

## establishmentarian
establishmentarian, п., adherent of the principle
of an established church. — Formed fr.
establishment (see prec. word) with suff. -arian.

## estacade
estacade, п., a dike of stakes in the sea or river.
— F., fr. Sp. estacada, ir. estaca, 'stake', which
is of Teut. origin. See stake, and -ade and cp.
stockade.

## estafette
estafette, п., a courier, esp. a mounted one. —
F., fr. It. staffetta, 'small stirrup; courier', dimin.
of staffa, 'stirrup*, which is of Teut. origin.
Cp. G. Stapfe, 'footstep', and see E. step. For
the ending see suff. -ette.

## estate
estate, n. — ME. eslal, Si. OF. eslal (F. elat), fr.
L. status, 'condition, state'. See state.

## esteem
esteem, tr. v. — ME. estemen, fr. OF. (= F.) es-
timer, fr. L. aeslimare, fr. OL. aeslumare, *to
value, appraise', which is denominated fr. *ais-
temos, lit. 'one who cuts the ore', fr. aes, gen.
aeris, 'ore', and I.-E. base *tem-, 'to cut', whence
also Gk. τέμνείν, 'to cut'. For the first element
see ore, for the second see tome.
Derivative: esteem, n.

## Estella
Estella, fem. PN. — Sp.-, lit. 'star', fr. L. Stella.
See star and cp. Stella, stellar.

## ester
ester, п., any compound ether (chem.) — G.
Ester, coined by the German chemist Leopold
Gmelin (1788-1853) in 1848 from the
abbreviation of Essiguther, which is compounded of
Essig, 'vinegar*, and Ather 'ether'. Essig derives
fr. MHG. esiich, St. OHG. ejjiA, fr. "alecum,
metathetized form of L. acltum, 'vinegar'
(whence Goth, akeil); see acetum. For the
second element see ether.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:285 COLUMN:3 -->

## Esther
Esther, 1) fem. PN.; 2) in the Bible, wife of the
Persian king Ahasuerus. — Gk. Έσθήρ, fr. Heb.
Ester, fr. Pers. sitareh, 'star', which is rel. to
Avestic and OI. star-, and cogn. with Gk. αστήρ,
L. stella, 'star'. See star.

## Estherin
Estherin, п., a genus of brancbiopod crustaceans.
— Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -la.

## esthesia
esthesia, aesthesia, п., sensibility. — ModL. aes-
thesia, fr. Gk. αϊσθησις, 'perception, sensation*,
from the stem of αισθάνομαι. See esthete and
-ia and cp. anesthesia.

## esthesio-
esthesio-, aesthesio-, combining form meaning
'pertaining to perception'. — Fr. Gk. αίσθησις.
See prec. word and cp. kinesthesia, pallesthesia.

## esthete
esthete, also aesthete, n. — Gk. αισθητής, 'one
who perceives', from the stem of αισθάνομαι
(for *ά^ισ-θ-άνομαΐ), Ί perceive', aor. αίσ-
θέσθαι, shortened fr. *άτ"ισ-θ-έσθαι, rel. to άίω
(for *af ίω), Ί hear', lit. Ί perceive by the ear',
and cogn. with L. audio (for *awis-d-io), Ί hear',
fr. I.-E. base *awei-, 'to perceive'. See audible
and cp. esthesia, anesthesia, anesthetic, coen-
esthesis.

## esthetic
esthetic, aesthetic, adj. — Gk. αίσθητικός,
'perceptive', fr. αισθητός, 'sensible, perceptible',
verbal adj. of αισθάνομαι. See esthete and cp.
kinesthetic.
Derivatives: (a)esthetic-al-ly, adv., (a)esthetic-
ism, n.

## esthetics
esthetics, aesthetics, n. — G. Asthetik, coined
by A. G. Alexander Baumgarten (1714-62) about
1750 fr. Gk. αισθητικός, 'perceptive' (see prec.
word), to denote that branch of science which
deals with beauty.

## estimable
estimable, adj. — F., fr. L. aestimabilis, 'valuable,
estimable', fr. aeslimare. See esteem and -able.
Derivatives: estimab-ly, adv., estimable-ness, n.

## estimate
estimate, tr. and intr. v. — L. aestimatus, pp. of
aestimare, 'to value, appraise*, see esteem, v.,
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: estimate, п., estimating-ly, adv.,
estimation (q.v.), estimat-ive, adj., estimator (q.v.)

## estimation
estimation, n. — OF. (= F.) estimation, fr. L.
aestimationem, ace. of aestimatio, 'money value
of a thing, valuation', fr. aestimatus, pp. of
aeslimare. See prec. word and -ion.

## estimator
estimator, n. — L. aestimdtor, 'valuer, appraiser',
fr. aestimatus, pp. of aeslimare. See estimate and
agential suff. -or.

## estival
estival, aestival,* adj., pertaining to summer. —
F. estival, fr. L. aestivalis, 'pertaining to
summer', fr. aestivus, of s.m., fr. aeslus, 'heat',
which is rel. to aestas, gen. aestatis,
'summer', lit. 'hot season', fr. I.-E. base *aidh-, 'to
burn', whence also L. aedes, 'a building,
sanctuary, temple'. See edify and words there
referred to and cp. esp. estuary.

## estivate
estivate, aestivate, intr. v., 1) to spend the
summer; 2) to spend the summer in a dormant
condition. — L. aestlvatus, pp. of aestivare, 'to
spend the summer', fr. aestivus. See prec. word
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: (a)estivat-ion, n.

## estoile
estoile, n„ a star with six or eight points (her.) —
OF. estoile (F. etoile), fr. L. stella, 'star'. See
stellar.

## estop
estop, tr. v., to bar; (law), to bar by estoppel. —
AF. and OF. esloper (F. etouper), 'to stop', fr.
L. *stuppare, 'to stop with flax or tow' (whence
also It. stoppare, OProveng. estopar), Fr. L.
stuppa, stupa, 'the coarse part of flax, tow'. See
stop.

## estoppel
estoppel, п., preclusion of a statement or claim
because it is contrary to a previous statement
or claim (law). — OF. estoupail, 'stopper, bung',
fr. estoper. See prec. word and subst. suff. -el,

## estovers
estovers, n. pi., necessaries granted by law;
specif, wood for a tenant, alimony for a wife. —
OF. inf. estover, estovoir, 'to be necessary', used
as a noun; of uncertain origin; cp. stover. For the
subst. use of the infinitive in law terms see
attainder and cp. words there referred to.

## estrade
estrade, п., a platform. — F„ fr. Sp. estrado, fr.
L. stratum, 'something spread out', neut. pp. of
sternere, 'to spread out, cover'. See stratum and
cp. words there referred to.

## estradiol
estradiol, п., a crystalline estrogenic hormone
СцНгчО- (biochem.) — Coined fr. estrus, pref.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:286 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 259 | ETHNIC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:286 COLUMN:1 -->
di-, and -ol, a suff. denoting alcohol.

## estrange
estrange, tr. v. — OF. eslrangier, estranger, 'to
alienate', fr. VL. *extraneare, 'to treat as a
stranger', fr. L. extraneus, 'stranger'. See
strange.
Derivatives: estrang-ed-ness, п., estrange-ment,
п., estrang-er, n.

## estrangelo
estrangelo, n„ a type of Syriac cursive writing
characterized by rounded letters. — Syr.
es(rangelo, fr. Gk. στρογγυλός, 'twisted, round'.
See stringent and cp. words there referred to.

## estray
estray, п., a strayed animal (law). — AF. estray,
fr. OF. estraier, 'wandering, stray, lost*. See
stray, n.

## estreat
estreat, п., true extract, copy. — AF. estrete, fr.
OF. estraile, fr. L. extracta, prop. fem. of ex-
Iraclus, pp. of extrahere, 'to draw out'. See
extract.

## estrepement
estrepement, п., waste committed by a tenant for
life in lands, woods or houses to the damage of
the reversioner (law). — OF., 'waste, ravage',
fr. estreper, 'to waste', fr. L. exstirpare, 'to
pluck out by the stem or root, extirpate*. See
extirpate and -ment.

## estrlol
estrlol, n„ a crystalline estrogenic hormone
CnHMOj (biochem.) — Coined fr. estrus and
-ol, a suff. denoting alcohol.

## estrogen
estrogen, n.t a substance producing estrus
(biochem.) — Coined fr. estrus and -gen.

## estrogenic
estrogenic, adj., producing estrus (biochem.) —
Coined fr. estrus and -genie.

## estrone
estrone, п., a female sex hormone; theelin
(biochem.) — Coined fr. estrus and suff. -one.

## estrus
estrus, oestrus, п., ι) a vehement desire, frenzy;
2) the sexual heat of female mammals. — L.
oestrus, 'gadfly; frenzy', fr. Gk. οίστρος,
'gadfly; sting; frenzy', which is cogn. with Lith.
aisira, 'violent passion', and prob. also with
L. fra, 'anger'. See ire and cp. the first element
in Oestrelata.

## estuary
estuary, п., broad mouth of a river. — L. aestu-
arium, 'a tideplace, an estuary', fr. aestus, 'heat,
fire, the ebb and flow of the sen, tide', rel. to
aestus, 'heat*. See estival.

## esurience
esurience, esuriency, n. — Formed fr. next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## esurient
esurient, adj., hungry; greedy. — L. iswilns,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of esurire, 'to desire, to
eat, be hungry', a desiderative verb formed fr.
esus, pp. of edere, 'to eat*. See ent. For the
desiderative suff. -wire cp. Abiturient and words
there referred to.
Derivative: esurtent-ly, adv.

## et
et, conj. meaning 'and'. — L.; cogn. with Ol.
dti, Avestic aiti, 'over, beyond', Gk. Ιτι, 'yet,
still, besides, moreover', Gaul, eti, 'also,
moreover', Goth, ip, 'and, but, however', OE., OS.
ed-, ON. id-, OHG. et-, it-, 'again'. Cp. eddy.

## -et
-et, subst. suff. of orig. diminutive force. — OF.
and F. -et, prob. of Etruscan origin. In French,
the suff. always had and still has diminutive
force. For the feminine form of this suff. see
-ette. Cp. -let

## -et
-et, an infix used in chemistry (as in phen-et-
idine), to denote the presence of the ethyl radical.
— Short for rthyl.

## eta
eta, п., name of the seventh letter of the Greek
alphabet. — Gk. ήτα, fr. earlier ήτα (see Theo-
dor Noldcke, Beitrage zur semitischen Sprach-
wissenschaft, Strassburg, 1904, p. 124), fr. Heb.
hlth; see cheth. The α was added because a
Greek word cannot end with a τ; cp. alpha and
words there referred to.

## etacism
etacism, п., the pronunciation of Gk. eta (i.e. the
letter η) as e i.e. like a in English ale; called the
Erasmian pronunciation. — Formed fr. eta
with suff. -ism. Cp. itacism.

## etage
etage,п., stage. — F., 'abode, stage; story, floor',
also 'rank', fr. VL. *staticum, for L. stolid,
'station, post, residence', lit. 'a standing', fr. stare,
'to stand'. See state and cp. stage, 'platform'.

## etagere
etagere, п., cabinet. — F„ fr. etage, 'shelf. See
prec. word.

## etamine
etamine, п., a dress fabric of cotton, worsted or
silk. — F. etamine, fr. OF. eslamine, fr. VL.
'slSminea, fem. of the Latin adj. stamineus,
'made of threads', fr. stamen, gen. slaminis
'warp in the upright loom, thread'. See stamen.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:286 COLUMN:2 -->

## etape
etape, п., ι) a halting place for troops; 2) a day's
march. — F., 'stage of journey, halting place,
distance between two halting places', fr. OF.
estaple; fr. MDu. staple, 'storehouse'. See staple.

## etat
etat, п., state. — F„ fr. L. status, prop, 'mode of
standing'. See state and cp. words there
referred to.

## etatism
etatism, п., state socialism. — F. etatisme, formed
fr. etat, 'state', with suff. -isme. See prec. word
and -ism.

## Etat Major
Etat Major, the staff of the army. — F. etal-
major, fr. etat, 'state', and L. major, 'greater'.
See etat and major, adj.

## et cetera
et cetera, 'and other things'. — L„ fr. et, 'and'
(see et), and neut. of ceteri, 'the others', which
is formed fr. I.-E. pron. pref. *ce-, 'there; behold'
(see he), and I.-E. *etero-, 'the other', whence
also Umbr. etro-, 'another', Avestic a-tura-,
'one of the two, this'. Alb. jdtere, jatrt, 'the
other*, OSlav. jeteru, iteru, 'some, one*.

## etch
etch, tr. and intr. v., to engrave with acid. — Du.
etsen, 'to etch', fr. G. atzen, 'to corrode', fr.
MHG. atzen, etzen, fr. OHG. αζζδη, prop, 'to
feed, bait', causative of ejjo/i, 'to eat'. See eat.
Derivatives: etch, п., elch-er, п., etch-ing,
verbal n.

## Eteocles
Eteocles, п., son of Oedipus and Jocasta, and
king of Thebes (Greek mythology). — L., fr.
Gk. 'Ετεοκλής, lit. 'of true fame', compounded
of έτεός, 'true, real, genuine', and κλέος, 'fame'.
The first element is rel. to ϊτυμος, 'true'; see
etymon. The second element is rel. to κλοτός,
'famous', and cogn. with L. in-clutus, in-clytus,
of s.m„ OE., OS. hlud, 'loud'. See loud.

## eternal
eternal, adj. — L. aeternulis, fr. aeternus,
'everlasting, eternal', contracted fr. OL. aeviternus,
fr. *aeviter, an adverb formed fr. aevum, 'age*.
See aeon and adj. suff. -al and cp. age and words
there referred to. Cp. also next word.
Derivatives: eternal-ly, adv., eternal-ness, n.

## eterne
eterne, adj., eternal (poetic). — OF., fr. L.
aeternus. See eternal.

## eternity
eternity, n. — ME. eternite, fr. F. eternite, fr. L.
aetemitatem, ace. of aeternitas, fr. aeternus.
See eternal and -ity.

## eternize
eternize, tr. v., to render eternal. — F. eterniser,
a hybrid coined fr. L. aeternus (see eternal) and
-ize, a suff. of Greek origin.

## etesian
etesian, adj., annual (said of periodical winds). —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. etlsiae, fr. Gk. έτη-
σίαι, 'periodic winds that prevail in the Aegean',
lit.'annual (winds)', fr. ετήσιος, 'annual',fr. έτος
(dial. Γέτος), 'year', which is cogn. with L. vetus,
'old'. See veteran and cp. the second element in
brieteric.

## -eth
-eth, archaic ending of the third person singular
of the present indicative, as knoweth. — ME.
-eth, -th, fr. OE. -ер, -ap, -p, rel. to ON. -id, -ёд,
do-, OHG. -it, -el, -dt, G. -t, Goth, -ip, -aip-,
-eip-, -op-, and cogn. with L. -I, Gk. -τι, ΟΙ. -li,
third person sing. pres. indie, endings.

## -eth
-eth, suff. forming ordinal numbers, as in
fortieth. — See -th, suff. forming ordinal numbers.

## Ethan
Ethan, masc. PN. — Heb. Ethan, fr. eth&n,
'strong, permanent, perennial, ever-flowing'
(said of a river), which is rel. to Arab, watana,
'was perpetual*, wdtin, 'anything permanent'.

## Ethel
Ethel, fem. PN. — Not directly fr. OE. /Edelu,
which is rel. to xdele, 'noble', but back
formation fr. names like Etheldred, Ethelinda (qq.v)

## Ethelbert
Ethelbert, masc. PN. — OE. Mdelbryht, lit.
'bright through nobility', fr. xdele, 'noble', and
beorht, 'bright'. For the first element see athel-
ing, for the second see bright. Cp. Albert, which
derives — through the medium of French — fr.
OHG. Adalbert, the exact equivalent of OE.
Abdelbryhl, and cp. words there referred to.

## Etheldred
Etheldred, fem. PN. — OE. AEdeldryd, lit. 'of
noble strength', compounded of xdele, 'noble',
and dryd, 'strength'. For the first element see
atheling. The second element is rel. to ON.
prudr, 'strength', ON. pro-ask, 'to thrive',
proskr, 'strong', OHG. triuwen, 'to blossom,
flourish', trouwen, 'to grow', MHG. druo, 'fruit'.

## Ethelinda
Ethelinda, fem. PN. — Formed fr. OE. xdele,
'noble', and lindi, 'a serpent'. For the first
element see atheling and cp. the two prec. words.
The second element is rel. to OHG. lind, lint.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:286 COLUMN:3 -->
'serpent*, OHG. lindwurm, MHG. lintwurm
(renewed in G. Lindwurm), 'dragon', ON. linnr
(for *lmpr), 'serpent', lit. 'the lithe animal', fr.
I.-E. base 'lent-, 'flexible', whence also ΟΝ.,
OE. lind, 'linden tree', lit. 'the tree with pliant
bast', OE. tide, OHG. lindi, 'soft, mild, gentle'.
See lithe and cp. linden.

## ether
ether, also nether, п., 1) the upper regions of
space; 2) (chem.), a colorless liquid used as an
anesthetic. — L. aether, fr. Gk. αίθήρ, 'the
upper, purer air, ether', which, together with
αϊθράϊ, 'the clean sky, fair weather', derives fr.
αίθειν, 'to burn', fr. I.-E. base *aidh-, 'to burn',
whence also L. aedes, 'a building, sanctuary,
temple'. See edify and words there referred to
and cp. esp. Aethusa, Ethiop; cp. also hypae-
thral. As a chemical term, the word aether was
coined by August Sigmund Frobenius (in 1730),
the discoverer of this liquid.

## ethereal
ethereal, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. aethereus, fr. Gk. αιθέριος, 'pertaining to
ether', fr. αίβήρ. See prec. word.
Derivatives: ethereal-ity, п., ethereat-ize, tr. v.,
ethereal-iz-ation, п., ethereal-ly, adv., ethereal-
ness, n.

## etherification
etherification, n. — See ether and -ficatlon.

## emerify
emerify, tr. v., to change into ether. — See ether
and -fy.

## ethic
ethic, п., ethics. — F. ilhique, fr. L. ilhica, fr.
Gk. ηθική (scil. τέχνη), 'moral art', fem. of
ηθικός, 'moral'. See ethical.

## ethic
ethic, adj., ethical (now rare). — See ethical.

## ethical
ethical, adj., relating to morality; moral. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. ηθικής,
'pertaining to morals, moral*, fr. ήθος, 'habit ,cus-
tom, usage, disposition, character, moral*, rel.
to έθος (for *σ5έθος), 'custom, usage', έθίζειν,
'to accustom', εΐωθα, (for *σέ-σ^ωθ-α), Ί
am accustomed', and cogn. with Ol. svadha,
'custom, peculiarity', L. sodalis (for *swedhalis),
'fellow, companion', suescere, 'to become
accustomed', Goth, sidus, OHG. situ, MHG. site,
G. Sitte, MDu. sede, Du. zede, ON. sidr, Dan.
sxd, OS. sidu, 'custom, habit, usage'. The orig.
meaning of all these words was 'property,
peculiarity'. They are traceable to I.-E. 'swedh-,
'a compound base lit. meaning 'to make one's
own', formed from the reflexive base *swe-, 'his,
her, its, one's', and *dhi-, 'to make, do'. See
sui- and theme and cp. ethos, cacoethes, ethnic.
Cp. also custom and words there referred to.
Derivatives: ethical-ily, п., ethical-ly, adv., ethi-
cal-ness, n.

## ethicize
ethicize, tr. v., to make ethical. — See ethic, adj.,
and -ize.

## ethico-
ethico-, combining form expressing relation to
ethics. — Fr. Gk. ηθικός, 'pertaining to morals'.
See ethical.

## ethics
ethics, п., the science of morality. — See ethic, п.,
and -ics.

## Ethiop
Ethiop, n„ an Ethiopian. — L. Aethiops, fr. Gk.
Αίθίοψ, which prob. means lit. 'burnt face', fr.
αίθείν, 'to burn' and ίψ, 'eye, face'. See ether
and optic. Cp. Gk. αίθοψ, ■fiery-looking'.

## Ethiopia
Ethiopia, n. — L. Aethiopia, fr. Gk. ΑΙθιοπΙά,
'Ethiopia', fr. Αίθίοψ. See prec. word and ist-ia.
Derivatives: Ethiopi-an, adj. and n.

## ethmoid
ethmoid, ethmoidal, adj., sievelike; pertaining to
a bone or bones forming part of the septum and
walls of the nasal cavity (anat. and zool.) — Gk.
ήθμοειδής, 'like a sieve', compounded of ηθμός,
'sieve* and -οειδής, 'like*, fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. The first element derives fr. ήθεΐν, 'to
sifl', which is cogn. with Lith. sietas, OSlav.
sito (for *sil-to-), 'sieve', W. hidl, ON. said (for
*se-tlo), 'sieve', Alb. SoS, Ί sift'. For the second
element see -oid.
Derivative: ethmoid, п., and ethmoid bone.

## ethnarch
ethnarch, п., governor of a nation or province. —
Gk. εθνάρχης, 'ruler of the people',
compounded of έθνος, 'people' and -άρχης, 'leader'.
See ethnic and -arch.

## ethnarchy
ethnarchy, п., the office of an ethnarch. — Gk.
έθνχρχία, fr. εθνάρχης. See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ίδ).

## ethnic
ethnic, adj., related to a race. — L. ethnicus, fr.
Gk. εθνικός, fr. έθνος, 'nation, race' (in Eccles.
Greek the plural £θνη means 'the heathens,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:287 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ETHNO- | 260 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:287 COLUMN:1 -->
gentiles')· Gk. έθνος prob. stands for *σ5έθνος
and orig. meant 'one's own'. It is rel. to εθος
(for *σίέθος), 'custom, usage'. See ethical and
cp. ethnos.
Derivatives: etknic-al-ly, adv., ethnic-ism, n.

## ethno-
ethno-, combining form meaning 'race'. — Fr.
Gk. έθνος, 'nation, race'. See ethnic.

## ethnography
ethnography, п.. the description of races.
—Compounded of ethno- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν,
to write'. See -graphy.

## ethnology
ethnology, п., the study of races. — Compounded
of ethno- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ethnolog-ic, ethnotog-ic-al, adjs.,
ethnolog-ic-al-iy, adv., ethnolog-ist, n.

## ethology
ethology, π., ι) the science of character; 2) the
study of customs. — L. Sthologia, fr. Gk.
ηθολογία, 'description of character', which is
compounded of ήθος, 'custom', and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'; see next
word and -logy. In the sense 'science of
character' the word ethology was introduced by the
English philosopher John Stuart Mill (1806-73).
Derivatives: etholog-ic, etholog-ic-al, adjs.

## ethos
ethos, п., the moral atmosphere of a people or a
community. — Gk. ήθος, 'habit, custom, usage,
disposition, character, moral'. See ethical.

## ethrog
ethrog, п., the citron (Citrus medico), one of the
'Four Species' of plants used in the celebration
of the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkoth). — Mish-
naic Hebrew ethrog, fr. Pers. turitnj (whence also
Arab, turunj, ittrunj. Cp. toronja.

## ethyl
ethyl, п., a hydrocarbon radical, C2H5 (chem.) —
Coined by the Swedish chemist Jons Jakob
Berzelius (1779-1848) in 1840 fr. Gk. αίθήρ, 'the
upper air', and 6λη, 'stuff'. See ether and -yl.

## -etic
-etic, adj. suff. meaning 'pertaining to; of the
nature of. — Gk. -ετικός, formed from stems
ending in -ετ- through addition of suff. -ικός;
see -ic. Gk. adj. suff. -ετικός corresponds to
nouns ending in -εσις. Ср. e.g. Gk. θετικός
(see thetic), which is rel. to θέσις (see thesis).

## etio-
etio-, also aetio-, aitio-, combining form denoting
cause or causation. — Gk. αίτιο-, fr. αιτία,
"cause, origin; occasion', which derives either
fr. αίτιος, 'causing, occasioning', or — like
αίτιος — directly fr. *αϊτος, 'share, lot'
(whence also αίτέω, Ί ask for, demand'), which is rel.
to αΐσα (for αίτια), 'share, lot, destiny', αίνυμαι,
Ί take', εξαιτος, 'picked, choice', αίσιος,
'auspicious, opportune', and cogn. with Avestic aeta-,
'share, lot, due', Oscan aeteis (gen.), 'of
somebody's part', Toch. В ai-, 'to give' (lit. 'to allot').
Cp. diet, 'fare'.

## etiolate
etiolate, tr. and intr. v., to blanch, esp. through
the absence of light (bot.) — Fr. F. etiole, pp.
of etioler, 'to blanch', which prob. derives fr.
eteule, *a stalk', fr. OF. esteule, fr. L. stipula%
'stubble'; see stipule and verbal suff. -ate.
Accordingly the orig. meaning of F. etioler seems
to have been 'to become like straw'.
Derivatives: etiolat-ed, adj., etiolat-ion, n.

## etiology
etiology, aetiology, п., the science of causes. —
Late L. aetiologia, fr. Gk. αιτιολογία, 'an
inquiring into causes', fr. αίτιολογειν, 'to inquire
into causes', fr. αίτια, 'cause' and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner):
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See etio-
and -logy.
Derivatives: (a)etiolog-ic-al, adj., (a)etiolog-ic-
al-lyy adv., (a)etiolog-ist, n.

## etiquette
etiquette, п., conventional rules of social
behavior. — F. etiquette, fr. OF. estiqtiier, esiiquer,
'to stick on, attach', fr. Du. sttkken, 'to stitch',
which is rel. 10 G. sticken, 'to embroider', stechen,
'to stab, prick, puncture'. See stitch and cp.
ticket, which is a doublet of etiquette.

## etna
etna, п., a device for boiling water. — Fr. Mt.
Etna, fr. Phoen. attiinu, 'furnace', which prob.
derives fr. Akkad. atunu, utimu, whence also
Aram, attftn, attima, Syr. attonia, of s.m.; cp.
Arab, attftn, Ethiop. etSn, of s.m., which are
Syriac loan words. Cp. Etnean.

## Etnean
Etnean, adj., pertaining to Etna. — Formed with
suff. -an fr. L. Aetneus, fr. Gk. Αίτναΐος, fr.
Αίτνη, 'Etna', fr. Phoen. attima, 'furnace'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:287 COLUMN:2 -->
prec. word.

## Etonian
Etonian, п., a student of Eton College (i.e. the
college at Eton, England). For the ending see
suff. -ian.

## Etrurian
Etrurian, adj. and п., Etruscan. — Formed wiih
suff. -an fr. L. Etruria, a name of uncertain
etymology.

## Etruscan
Etruscan, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Etruscus, 'Etruscan', fr. Etruria. See prec.
word.

## Etta
Etta, fern. PN. — Orig. used only as dimin. of
Henrietta.

## -ette
-ette, suff. used to form nouns which may or may
not have diminutive force. — F. -cite, fern, of
-et. See -et.

## etude
etude, п., study (music). — F., fr. L. studium.
See study.

## etui
etui, п., a small case. — F. etui, fr. OF. estui, back
formation fr. estuier, estoier, 'put in, put aside,
spare', fr. VL. *estudiare, fr. L. studere, 'to
study; to care for'; see Meyer-Liibke, REW.,
N0.8325. See study and cp. prec. word. Cp.
also tweezers.

## etymologic
etymologic, etymological, adj. — L. etymologicus,
fr. Gk. ετυμολογικός, 'pertaining to etymology',
fr. ετυμολογία. See etymology and -ic, resp.
also -al. Derivative: elymological-ly, adv.

## etymologicon
etymologicon, п., an etymological dictionary. —
Gk. έτυμολογικόν, neut. of ετυμολογικός, used
as a noun. See prec. word.

## etymology
etymology, n. — F. etymologie, fr. L. etymotogiay
fr. Gk. ετυμολογία, 'etymology', prop, 'the
study of the true sense of a word', compounded
of έτυμον, 'the true sense of a word according
to its origin' (prop. neut. of ετυμος, 'true') and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See next word and -logy.
Derivatives: etymohg-ist, п., etymohg-ize, intr.
v., etymohg-iz-ation, n.

## etymon
etymon, п., primitive word. — Gk. ϊτυμον, 'the true
sense of a word', neut. of έ'τυμος, 'true, real,
actual', enlarged fr. έτεός (for "έτεΓός), 'true'.
This latter derives fr. έτος, 'true' (whence also
έ^άΓειν, 'to examine, test', prop, 'to establish
as true'), which prob. stands for *έτός, fr. I.-E.
*se-to-s), hence lit. means 'that which is', and
is cogn. with OI. satyah (for *snt-yo-), Goth.
sunjis, OE. sod, 'true'. See sooth and words
there referred to.

## eu-
eu-, combining form meaning 'good, well'. — Fr.
Gk. e5, 'well', prop. neut. of έύς, 'good', which
is cogn. either with Hitt. ashshush, 'good', or—
more probably—with OI. vdsuh, Avestic vohu-,
'good', Ir. feb (fr. I.-E. *wesw-a), 'excellence'.
Eu- is the opposite of dys-,

## eucaine
eucaine, п., name of two synthetic alkaloids
called alpha-eucaine and beta-eucaine. — Coined
fr. eu- and the second and third syllable of
cocaine.

## eucairite
eucairite, п., a copper silver selenide {mineral.) —
Swed. eukairil, formed with suff. -if
(representing Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite) fr. Gk.
εύκαίρως, adv. of εύκαιρος, 'seasonable,
opportune', fr. εΰ, 'well' (see eu-), and καιρός, 'the
right season, the right time' (see kairme). The
mineral was so called because it was found by
theSwedish chemist Baron Jons Jakob Berzelius
(1779-1848) soon after the discovery of selenium.

## Eucalyptus
Eucalyptus, п., a genus of plants of the myrtle
family (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'well covered',
coined by the French botanist L'Heritier de
Brutelle (1746-1800) in 1788 fr. eu- and Gk.
καλυτττός, 'covered', verbal adj. of καλύπτειν,
'to cover, conceal' (see calyptra); so called in
allusion to the cap covering the bud.

## Eucharis
Eucharis, п., a genus of the plants of the amar-
yllis family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. εύχαρις,
'pleasant, agreeable', fr. εύ, 'well', and χάρις,
'favor, grace'. See next word.

## Eucharist
Eucharist, n. (eccles.), 1) communion; 2) its
consecrated elements. — OF. eucariste (F, eucha-
rislie), fr. Eccles. L. eucharistia, fr. Gk.
ευχαριστία, 'thankfulness, gratitude', fr. ευχάριστος,
'pleasant, agreeable', fr. εύχαρίζειν, 'to render
thanks', fr. ευ (see eu-) and χάρις, 'favor, grace'.
See Charts and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: eucharist-ic, eucharist-ic-al, adjs.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:287 COLUMN:3 -->
eucharist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Euchite
Euchite, п., one of a medieval sect that flourished
in the 4th cent., whose members believed in the
saving power of perpetual prayer; applied also
to various other sects that shared this belief. —
Eccles. L. euchita, fr. Gk. ευχή, *vow, wish,
prayer', which is cogn. with OI. vaghdt-, 'one
who offers a sacrifice', L. vovere, 'to vow'. See
vote and cp. next word.

## enchology
enchology, п., prayer book. — Eccles. Gk. εϋχο-
λόγιον, compounded of Gk. ευχή, 'prayer', and
-λόγιον, fr. λέγειν, 'to tell, say, speak'. See
prec. word and -logy.

## euchre
euchre, п., a card game. — Of unknown origin.
Derivative: euchre, tr. v.

## euclase
euclase, п., a brittle green silicate of beryllium
and aluminum (mineral.) — Lit. 'that which
breaks easily'; formed fr. eu- and Gk. κλάσις,
'a breaking', from the stem of κλαν, 'to break'.
See clastic and cp. words there referred to.

## Euclea
Euclea, п., a genus of plants of the ebony family
(bot.)—ModL., lit. 'glorious', fr. εΰκλεια, 'glory',
fr. εύκλεής, 'famous, glorious', which is formed
fr. εύ (see eu-) and κλέος, 'fame' (see Eteocles);
so called in allusion to the beautiful foliage.

## Euclid
Euclid, euclid, n. — Short for Euclid's geometry,
i.e. geometry based on the treatise of Euclid,
the great Greek mathematician who lived about
300 B.C.E. (The name lit. means 'renowned',
and is rel. to εύκλεής, 'renowned', prop, 'of
good report', fr. ε5, 'well', and κλέος, 'fame';
see prec. word.)
Derivative: Euclid-ean, Euclid-ian, adj.

## endaemonic
endaemonic, endaemonical, adj., producing
happiness. — Gk. εύδαιμονικός, 'conducive to
happiness', fr. ευδαίμων, 'fortunate, happy', lit.
'blessed with a good genius', fr. ευ (see eu-) and
δαίμων 'god'. See demon and cp. pandemonium.

## eudaemonics
eudaemonics, п., that branch of ethics which deals
with happiness. — See prec. word and -ics.

## eudaemoaism
eudaemoaism, п., that system of ethics which
makes the moral value of actions dependent
upon their relation to happiness. — Gk.
ευδαιμονισμός, 'a thinking happy', fr. εύδαιμονίζειν,
'to think happy', fr. ευδαίμων. See eudaemoaic
and -ism.

## eudiometer
eudiometer, п., an instrument for the volumetric
measuring of gases. — Coined by the English
clergyman and chemist Joseph Priestley (1733-
1804) fr. Gk. εΰδιος, 'fine, dear' (said esp. of air
and weather), and μέτρον, 'measure'. The first
element stands for *ευ-διίος and lit. means
'having a good day', fr. εδ, 'well', and δΐος
(for *δίίιος), 'divine'. Cp. OI. su-divah, 'having
a fine day', which is the equivalent of Gk. εδδίος.
See eu- and deity. For the second element see
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: eudiometr-ic, eudiometr-ic-al, adjs.,
eudiometr-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Eudora
Eudora, fern. PN. -— L., fr. Gk. Ευδώρά, lit.
'generous', fern, of εΰδωρος, fr. ευ (see eu-) and
δώρον, 'gift'. See donation.

## Eudorina
Eudorina, п., a genus of flagellates (biol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -ina fr. Gk. ευδωρος,
'generous'. See prec. word.

## Eugene
Eugene, masc. PN. — F. Eugene, fr. L. Eugenius,
fr. Gk. Ευγένιος, fr. ευγενής, 'well born'. See
eugenic and cp. Eugenia.

## Eugeuia
Eugeuia, fern. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Ευγενία, lit.
'nobility of birth', rel. to Ευγένιος. See prec. word.

## eugenic
eugenic, adj., improving the human race;
pertaining to the improvement of the human race.
— Gk. ευγενής, 'well bora', fr. εΰ (see eu-) and
γένος 'race, descent, gender, kind', See genus
and cp. Eugene, Eugenia.

## eugenics
eugenics, п., the study of the improvement of the
human race by selection of the parents. —
Coined by Sir Francis Galton (1822-1911) in
1883 from the adjective eugenic. For the ending
see -ics.

## Euglandma
Euglandma, п., a genus of snails (zool.) — A
ModL. hybrid coined fr. eu-, L. glans, gen.
glandis, 'acorn' (see gland), and suff. -ina.

## euhemerism
euhemerism, п., theory of Eubemerus, a Sicilian
Greek philosopher of about 300 B.C.E. —
Formed with suff. -ism fr. L. Euhemerus, fr.
Gk. Εύήμερος (a name lit. meaning 'bright,
happy', fr. εδ, 'well' and ήμερα, 'day').

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:288 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 261 | EUSTACE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:288 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: euhemerist-ic, adj., euhemerist-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## euhemerist
euhemerist, п., one who believes in the theory of
Euhemerus. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: euhemerist-ic, adj., euhemerist-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## euhemerize
euhemerize, tr. v., to interpret (myths) according
to euhemerism. — See euhemerism and -ize,

## Ealalia
Ealalia, fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Εύλαλία, fr.
εδλαλος, 'sweetly speaking', fr. εδ (see eu-) and
λαλίά, 'talk, chat, speech', fr. λαλάς, 'talkative,
loquacious'. See Lalage and cp. the second
element in mogilalia, paralalia, Cp. also lull.

## eulogium
eulogium, п., eulogy. — Late L., fr. Gk. ευλογιά.
See next word.

## eulogy
eulogy, п., high praise. — Gk. ευλογία, 'good
language; praise, eulogy', lit. 'a speaking well',
fr. εδ (see eu-) and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy and cp. elogium.
Derivatives: eulogi-ous, adj., eulog-ism, п.,
eulogist, п., eulog-isl-ic, eulog-isl-ic-a!, adjs.,
eulogize, tr. v., eulog-iz-ation, п., eulog-iz-er, n.

## eulysite
eulysite, п., a granular kind of peridotite
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk.
εύλυσίά, 'dissolubility', fr. εβλυτος, 'easily
dissolved, soluble', fr. εδ (see eu-) and λυτός,
'loosened, solved; dissolved', verbal adj. of
λύειν, 'to loose, loosen, set free; to dissolve'.
See -lysis and cp. words there referred to.

## Eumenides
Eumenides, n. pi., the Erinyes (Greek mythology}.
— L., fr. Gk. Ευμενίδες, lit. 'the Well-Minded
Ones', a euphemistic name of the Erinyes, fr.
ευμενής, 'well-minded, kind', fr. εύ (see eu-)
and μένος, 'life, soul, spirit', which is cogn.
with OI. manyate, 'thinks', L. mens, 'mind,
reason, thought', monere. Ίο remind'. See mind
and cp. mental, 'pertaining to the mind'.

## Eunectes
Eunectes, п., a genus of snakes, the anaconda
(zool.) — ModL., lit. 'the good swimmer', fr.
εδ (see eu-) and Gk. νήκτης, 'swimmer', fr.
νήχειν, 'to swim', which is cogn. with Gk. νάειν,
L. nitre, 'to swim'. See natation.

## Eunice
Eunice, fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Ευνίκη, lit.
'victorious*, fr. εδ (see eu-) and νίκη, 'victory'.
See Nike and cp. Nicholas.

## eunomy
eunomy, п., the condition of being governed by
good laws. — Gk. ευνομία, 'good order', fr.
ευνομος, 'under good laws, well ordered', which
is compounded of εδ (see eu-) and νόμος, 'law'.
See -nomy.

## eunuch
eunuch, n. — L. eunuchus, fr. Gk. ευνούχος, lit.
'guardian of the bed', fr. εύνή, 'couch, bed',
which is of uncertain etymology, and the base
of ίχειν, 'to hold, have'. See hectic and cp.
the second element in Ophiuchus.

## Euonymus
Euonymus, n. — See Evonymus.

## euosmlte
euosmlte, п., a fossil resin. — Formed with subst.
suff. -ite fr. Gk. εύοσμος, 'sweet-smelling', fr.
εδ (see eu-) and δσμή, 'smell,odor'- (see osmium);
so called because it yields an aromatic odor
when burned.

## Eupatorinm
Eupatorinm, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. εύπατόριον,
Agrimonia Eupatorinm, named after Eupator
Mithridates, who first used it for medicinal
purposes.

## eupepsia
eupepsia, п., good digestion (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. εύπεψίά, fr. εύπεπτος, 'easy of
digestion', fr. εδ (see eu-) and πεπτός, 'cooked',
verbal adj. of πέσσειν, πέπτειν, 'to cook'. See
pepsin and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -in.

## eupeptic
eupeptic, adj., having good digestion; promoting
digestion. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk.
εύπεπτος. See prec. word and cp. peptic and
words there referred to.

## Euphemia
Euphemia, fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Ευφημία, lit.
'speech of good omen, good repute', fr. εδ (see
eu-) and φήμη, 'prophetic saying, saying, speech'.
See next word.

## euphemism
euphemism, п., substitution of a mild word or
expression for a harsh or vulgar one (rhel.) —
Gk. ευφημισμός, 'use of an auspicious word for
an inauspicious one', fr. εύφημίζεσθαι, 'to use
auspicious words', fr. ευφημία, 'use of words
of good omen', fr, εδ (see eu-) and φήμη,
'prophetic saying, saying, speech' which is cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:288 COLUMN:2 -->
with L. fama, 'talk, report'. See fame and -ism
and cp. prec. word.

## euphemist
euphemist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: euphemist-ic, euphemist-ic-al, adjs.,
euphemist-ic-ai-ly, adv.

## eupbemize
eupbemize, tr. v., to express euphemistically;
intr. v., to use euphemisms.—Gk. εύφημ'.ζεσθαι,
to use auspicious words'. See euphemism and
-ize.
Derivative: euphemiz-er, n.

## euphoae
euphoae, п., a free-reed organ stop giving a sweet
tone (music). — Gk. εΰφωνος, 'sweet-voiced'.
See euphony,

## euphonium
euphonium, п., a small brass instrument (music).
— ModL., fr. Gk. ευφωνος, 'sweet-voiced'. See
next word.

## euphony
euphony, п., pleasantness of sound. — F.
euphonic, fr. L. euphonia, fr. Gk. εύφωνίδ, 'sweetness
of voice', fr. εΰφωνος, 'sweet-voiced', fr. εδ (see
eu-) and φωνή, 'sound, tone, voice'. See phone
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: euphon-ic, euphon-ic-al, adjs.,
euphon-ic-al-ly, adv., euphon-ic-ai-ness, п., еи-
phoni-ous, adj., euphoni-ous-ly, adv., euphoni-
ous-ness, n.

## Euphorbia
Euphorbia, п., a genus of African plants. —
ModL., fr. L. euphorbeum, name of an African
plant. See euphorbium.

## Enphorbiaceae
Enphorbiaceae, n. pi., a family of African plants.
— Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## euphorbiaceous
euphorbiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## euphorbium
euphorbium, п., a gum resin derived from
Euphorbia resinifera. — ModL., fr. L. euphorbeum, fr.
Gk. εύφόρβιον, named after Εΰφορβος, Euphor-
bus, a Greek physician. (The name lit. means
'well nourished', fr. eu, 'well' and φορβή, 'pas-
lure, nourishment', which is rel. to φέρβείν,
to feed'.)

## euphoria
euphoria, п., the sense of well-being (psychol.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. ευφορία, 'well-being', lit. 'a
bearing well', fr. εύφορος, 'easy to bear, easily
born', fr. εδ (see eu-) and the stem of φέρειν,
Ίο bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry' and cp.
dysphoria. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Euphrasia
Euphrasia, п., a genus of plants of the figwort
family (bot.) — ModL. See next word.

## euphrasy
euphrasy, п., name of a plant. — ML. euphrasia,
fr. Gk. εύφρασίά, 'delight', fr. εΰφραίνειν, 'to
delight', fr. ευ (see eu-) and φρήν, gen. φρενός,
'mind'. See phrenetic and -y (representing Gk.
-:s).

## euphroe
euphroe, also uphroe, п., a block of wood
perforated to receive the cords of an awning. — Du.
juffromi, 'young woman; pulley', rel. to OFris.
jungfrouwe, OHG. jungfrouwa, MHG.juncvrou
(we), 'young woman, girl', G. Jungfrau, 'maid,
virgin; spinster'. See yonng and frow,

## Euphrosyne
Euphrosyne, п., I) one of the three Graces (Greek
mythol.); 2) fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Ευφροσύνη,
lit. 'mirth, merriment', fr. εΰφρων, 'cheerful,
merry', lit. 'of a good mind', fr. εδ (see eu-) and
φρήν, gen. φρενός, 'mind'. See phrenetic and cp.
Sophronia. Cp. also prec. word.

## euphuism
euphuism, п., the affected style used by John Lyly
in his Euphues. — Formed with suff. -ism fr.
Euphues, a name coined by the English writer
John Lyly (i554?-i6o6) in 1578 fr. Gk. ευφυής,
'well-grown, excellent', fr. eu (see eu-) and the
stem of φύειν, 'to bring forth, produce, make
to grow'. See physio- and cp. words there
referred to.

## euphuist
euphuist, п., one characterized by euphuism. —
See euphuism and -ist.
Derivatives: euphuist-ic, euphuist-ic-al, adjs..
euphuist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## enpnea
enpnea, eupnoea, п., normal breathing (med.) —
Medical L. eupnoea, fr. Gk. εΰπνοια, 'easy
breathing', fr. εΰπνοος, 'breathing well', fr. εΰ
(see eu-) and πνοή, πνοιή, 'breath'. See pneuma
and cp. dyspnea.

## Eurafrica
Eurafrica, п., Europe and Africa taken together.
— A blend of Europe and Africa.
Derivative: Eurafric-an, adj. and n.

## Eurasia
Eurasia, п., Europe and Asia taken together. —
A blend of Europe and Asia.
Derivative: Eurasi-an, adj. and n.

## eureka
eureka, interj., the exclamation attributed to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:288 COLUMN:3 -->
Archimedes when he discovered a method to
determine the purity of the gold in King Hiero's
crown; hence exclamation of triumph. — Gk.
εΰρηκα, Ί have found', perf. of εύρίσκείν, Ίο
find'. See heuristic.

## eurythmic
eurythmic, adj. — See eurhythmic.

## euripus
euripus, п., a strait. — L., fr. Gk. εϋρϊπος, 'strait',
fr. εδ (see eu-) and ριπή, 'rush, impetus', which
is rel. to ρίπτειν, Ίο throw, hurl', and cogn.
with Fris. wriwwe, MLG., MDu. wriven, OHG.
riban, MHG: riben, G. reiben 'to rub'; see
Hofmann, EWG., p. 299 s.v. ρίπτω. Cp. ribald.

## Euroclydon
Euroclydon, п., a stormy wind. — New Testament
Gk. εύροκλύδων (Acts 27: Г4) fr. Εδρος,
'southeast wind', and κλΰδων, 'wave' (from the stem
of κλύζειν, Ίο dash against, break over,
inundate') ; prob. a false reading for εύρακύλων,
Grecization of Late L. Euraquilo, 'northeast
wind', fr. L. Eurus, 'eastwind', and Aquilo.
'north wind'. See Eurus and Aquilo.

## Europu
Europu, п., a daughter of Agenor, king of
Phoenicia (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Ευρώπη.
See Europe.

## Enrope
Enrope, n. — L. Europa, fr. Gk. Ευρώπη, 'Europa;
Europe', which is prob. of Semitic origin. Cp.
Akkad. erebu, Ίο enter, go in; to go down, set'
(said of the sun), erlb shamshi, 'sunset', Heb.
'erebh, 'sunset, evening'; see Heinrich Lewy.
Die semitischen Fremdworter im Griechischen.
Berlin, 1895, pp. 139-140. Accordingly Ευρώπη
orig. meant 'the Region of the Setting Sun'. Cp.
Hesychius, who renders Ευρώπη with the words
χώρα της δύσεως (— 'the Land of the Setting
Sun'). Cp. also Gk. "Ερεβος, 'place of nether
darkness', which derives fr. Heb. 'erebh. See
maarib and cp. Erebus. The form Ευρώπη (as if
the name meant εύρ-ώπη, 'broad face') is due
to the natural tendency of the Greeks to Grecize
words foreign to their language. For the sense
development of Gk. Ευρώπη from a Semitic
word meaning 'sunset, evenine'. cd. Asia.

## European
European, adj. and n. — F. europien, fr. L. Euro-
paeus, fr. Gk. Ευρωπαίος, 'European', fr.
Ευρώπη, 'Europe'. See prec. word and -an.
Derivatives: European-ism, п., European-ize,
tr. v., European-iz-ation, n.

## europium
europium, п., name of a rare metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., named by its discoverer, the
French chemist Eugene Demarcay (1852-1903)
in 1896 after the continent Europe. For the
ending of europium see suff. -mm.

## Eurus
Eurus, п., I) the god of the southeast wind (Greek
mythol.); 2) hence the southeast wind. —
L., fr. Gk. Εύρος, which possibly stands for
*Εδσ-ρος and orig. meant 'the singeing wind',
fr. εδειν (for ·ευσειν), Ίο singe', which derives
fr. I.-E. base *eus-, 'to burn'; see combust. The
change of the rough spirit (in εΰειν) to the
smooth one (in Εδρος) is prob. due to the
influence of αυρά, 'air'. Cp. the first element in
Euroclydon.

## eury-
eury-, combining form meaning 'wide'. — Gk.
εύρυ-, fr. εδρύς, 'wide', which is cogn. with OI.
uruh, 'broad, wide', vdras-, 'breadth, width'. Cp.
the first element in next word.

## Eurydice
Eurydice, п., the wife of Orpheus (Greek mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. Ευρυδίκη, lit. 'wide justice', fr.
ευρύς, 'wide', and δίκη, 'right, custom, usage,
law; justice'. For the first element see eury-,
for the second see dicast.

## eurythmic
eurythmic, eurhythmic, adj.,
harmonious.—Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. ευρυθμία, 'rhythmical
order', fr. εύρυθμος, 'rhythmical', fr. εδ (see eu-)
