and ρυθμός, 'rhythm'. See rhythm.

## eurythmics
eurythmics, eurhythmies, п., the art of expressing
musical harmony by bodily movements. — See
prec. word and -ics.

## eurythmy
eurythmy, eurhythmy, п., harmonious proportion.
— L. eurythmia, fr. Gk. ευρυθμία. See
eurythmic and -y (representing Gk. -lot).

## eusol
eusol, п., an antiseptic solution for wounds.
(pharm.) — Lit. 'a good solution'; coined fr. en-
and the first three letters of the word solution.

## Eustace
Eustace, masc. PN. — OF. Eustace (F. Eustache),
fr. Late L. Euslachius, fr. Gk. Εύστάχιος, lit.
'fruitful', fr. εδ (see en-) and στάχυς, 'ear (of
grain)', which is a derivative of I.-E. base
*stengh-, Ίο be pointed', whence also E. sting

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:289 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: EUSTACHIAN | 262 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:289 COLUMN:1 -->
(q.v.) Ср. Stacfays. The name Eustachius should
not be confused with Eustatkius, which comes
fr. Gk. ευσταθής, 'stable'.

## Eustachian
Eustachian, adj., pertaining to Eustachio or to
the Eustachian tube. — Formed with suff. -an
from the name of the Italian physician Barto-
lomeo Eustachio (15247-1574), the discoverer
of the air passage connecting the eardrum
cavity with the pharynx.

## eutectic
eutectic, adj., of the greatest fusibility. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. εβτηκτος, 'easily melted',
fr. ей (see ей-) and τηκτός, 'melted', verbal adj.
of τήκειν, 'to melt', which is cogn. with L. tabes,
'a wasting away'. See tabes and cp. eutexin.
Derivative: eutectic, п., a eutectic substance.

## Euterpe
Euterpe, п., the Muse of music (Greek mythology),
— L., fr. Gk. Εύτέρττη, lit. 'pleasing well', fr
ευ (see en-) and τέρπειν, 'to delight, please'.
See Terpsichore.

## eutexia
eutexia, п., the quality of melting at a low
temperature (physics). — ModL., fr. Gk. εΰτηξία,
'fusibility', which is rel. to εΰτηκτος, 'easily
melted'. See eutectic

## Euthamia
Euthamia, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. εϋθήμων,
'harmonious, pretty', lit. 'well placed', fr. εύ (see
eu-) and the base of τιθέναι, 'to put, place'. See
theme and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## euthanasin
euthanasin, п., an easy and painless death. —
Gk. ευθανασία, 'easy death', fr. eu (see eu-)
and θάνατος, 'death'. See thanato- and -ia and
cp. athanasy.

## Enxine
Enxine, adj., pertaining to the Euxine (= Black
Sea). — L. Pontus Euxinus, fr. Gk. Πόντος
Εύξεινος, 'the hospitable sea', euphemized fr.
Πόντος "Αξεινος, 'the Axine', lit. 'the
inhospitable sea', in which name "Αξεινος is pern, a
popular alteration of a name like *Αξενάζ,
metathesis of Άσχενάζ,' Ασχανάζ, Septuagintal
rendering of Heb. Ashk'naz, a people mentioned
in Gen. 10:3 and I Chr. 1:6. Accordingly
Axine orig. would have meant 'the Ashkenaz
Sea'. See Ashkenaz.

## Eva
Eva, feni. PN. (Bible). — See Eve.

## evacuant
evacuant, adj., promoting evacuation, purgative
(med.) — L. gvacuans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of
evacuare. See next word and -ant.
Derivative: evacuant, п., a purgative agent.

## evacuate
evacuate, tr. v., ]) to withdraw troops from a
place; 2) to promote evacuation (med.) — L.
evacuatus, pp. of evacuare, 'to empty out, purge',
formed fr. e- and vacuus, 'empty'. See vacant
and verbal suff. -ate.

## evacuation
evacuation, n. — F. evacuation, fr. Late L. eva-
cuationem, ace. of evacuatio, 'an evacuating', fr.
L. evacuatus, pp. of evacuare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## evade
evade, tr. v., to avoid. — L. evadere, 'to go out;
to escape*, fr. e- and vsdere, 'to go', which is
rel. to vadum, 'a shallow', and cogn. with OE.
wadan, 'to wade'. See wade and cp. vade mecum.
Cp. also evasion, invade, invasion, pervade,
pervasion.

## Evadne
Evadne, 1) the wife of Capaneus, one of 'the
Seven before Thebes' (Greek mythoi); 2) fern.
PN. — L., fr. Gk. Εύάδνη, a word of uncertain
origin.

## evaginate
evaginate, tr. v., to turn (a tube) inside out. —
L. evaginatus, pp. of evagindre, 'to unsheathe',
fr. e- and vagina, 'sheath'. See vagina and verbal
suff. -ate.

## evaglnation
evaglnation, n. — Late L. gvagindtio, gen. -onis,
'a spreading out, extending', fr. L. evaginatus,
pp. of evagware. See prec. word and -ion.

## evaluate
evaluate, tr. v. — F. evaluer. See e-, value and
verbal suff. -ate, and cp. valuation.
Derivative: evalual-ion, n.

## Evan
Evan, masc. PN. — W., lit. 'young'. Cp. W. iau,
'young', ieuanc, 'young man', ieuaf, 'youngest',
MW. ieu, 'younger*, Olr. δα, 6am, 'younger,
youngest'. These words are cogn. with L.

## juvenis
juvenis, 'young, young man*, Goth, juggs, OE.
geong, 'young'. See young and cp. juvenile.

## evanesce
evanesce, intr. v., to vanish. — L. evanescere, 'to
pass away, vanish', fr. e- and vanescere, 'to pass
away', which is an inchoative verb formed from
the adjective vdnus, 'vain'. See vahi and -esce.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:289 COLUMN:2 -->

## evanescence
evanescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## evanescent
evanescent, adj. — L. evaniscens, gen. -entis,
pres. part of evunslscere. See evanesce and -ent
Derivative: evanescenl-ly, adv.

## evangel
evangel, п., the gospel. — ME. evangile, fr. OF.
evangile (F. evangile), fr. Eccles. L. evangelium,
'gospel', fr. Gk. εΰαγγέλιον, 'reward of good
tidings; gospel', fr. εύάγγελος, 'bringing good
news', fr. ευ (see eu-) and άγγελος, 'messenger'.
See angel.
Derivatives: evangelic (q.v.), evangel-ic-ity, п.,
evangelist (q.v.), evangelize (q.v.)

## evungel
evungel, п., evangelist. — Gk. εόάγγελος,
'bringing good news'. See prec. word.

## evungelic
evungelic, evangelical, adj. — Eccles. L. evange-
licus, fr. Gk. ευαγγελικός, fr. εΰαγγέλιον. See
evangel, 'gospel', and -ic, resp. also -al.

## Evangeline
Evangeline, fem. PN. — F. Evangeline, ult. fr.
Gk. εΰαγγέλιον, 'good news'. See evangel,
'gospel', and -ine (representing L. -Ina).

## evangelist
evangelist, n. — F. ivangelisle, fr. Eccles. L.
evangelista, fr. Gk. ευαγγελιστής, fr. εύαγγε-
λίζεσθαι. See next word and -ist.
Derivatives: evangelist-ic, adj.

## evangelize
evangelize, tr. and intr, v. — OF. evangeliser, fr.
Eccles. L. evangelizare, fr. Gk. εύαγγελίζεσθαι,
'to bring good news, to preach glad tidings', fr.
εΰαγγέλιον. See evangel, 'gospel', and -ize.
Derivatives: evangeliz-ation, п., evangeliz-er, n.

## evanish
evanish, intr. v., to vanish. — OF. esvanir (F.
evanouir). See e- and vanish.
Derivative: evanish-ment, n.

## evansite
evansite, n„ a basic aluminum phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after Brooke Evans, of
England, who brought it from Hungary. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## evaporate
evaporate, intr. and tr. v. — L. evaporatus, pp. of
evaporare, 'to disperse in vapor', fr. e- and vapor,
'steam, vapor'. See vapor and verbal suff. -ate.

## evaporation
evaporation, n. — F. evaporation, fr. L. evapd-
rdlionem, ace. of evaporatio, 'an evaporating', fr.
evaporatus, pp. of evapdrare. See prec. word
and -Ion.

## evaporative
evaporative, adj. — Late L. evapdrativus, 'tending
or apt to evaporate', fr. L. evaporatus, pp. of
evaporare. See evaporate and -ive.

## evasion
evasion, n. — F. evasion, fr. L. evasidnem, ace. of
evasio, 'a going out; escape', fr. ivasus, pp. of
evadere. See evade and -ion and cp. invasion,
pervasion.

## evasive
evasive, adj. — F. ivasiflfem. evasive), fr. L.
Ivasus, pp. of evadere. See evade and -ive.
Derivatives: evasive-ly, adv., evasive-ness, n.

## eve
eve, п., 1) evening; 2) time immediately preceding
an event. — ME. eve; a variant of even,
'evening*.

## Eve
Eve, 1) fem. PN; 2) in the Bible, the wife of
Adam. — Late L. Eva, fr. Heb. Hawwak, lit.
'a living being', from the base of bawa = haya,
'he lived'. See Gen. 3:20. Heb. haya*, 'he lived',
is rel. to Aram.-Syr. baya, 'he lived', Ugar. hwy
(hyy), 'to live', Arab, hdyya, 'he lived'. Heb.
hayytm, Aram, hayytn, hayyi, Arab, haya*,
'life'. Cp. Eva. Cp. also ave.

## evection
evection, п., irregularity of the moon's motion
in its orbit (aslron.) — L. evectid, gen. -onis, 'a
going upward', fr. evectus, pp. of evehere, 'to
carry out', fr. e- and vehere, 'to carry, convey'.
See vehicle and -ion.

## Evelina
Evelina, Evelyn, fem. PN. — 1) Dimin. of Eve;
2) fr. OHG. Avelina, ir.Avi.

## Evelyn
Evelyn, masc. PN. — Prob. fr. prec. word.

## evea
evea, п., evening (poet.) — ME. eve, even, fr. OE.
ifen, rel. to OS. Sband, ON. aptann, Dan.
often, OFris. evend, Du. avond, OHG. a band,
MHG. abend, G. Abend, and cogn. with Gk.
όπι- in δπιθε(ν), I°n· aD^ Att. βπισθε(ν),
'after, behind', όψέ, 'late in the day, at even',
έπί, 'upon, after'; hence evening) lit. means
'the hinder' (= latter) part of the day'. See epi-
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also the
second element in Halloween.

## even
even, adj. — ME. even, fr. OE. efen, efn, 'level,
even', rel. to OS. eban, OFris. even, Du. even,
effen, OHG. eban, MHG., G. eben, ON. jafn,
Dan. jsevn, Goth, ibns, fr. Teut. base *ebna-,
which possibly corresponds to I.-E. *im-no-,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:289 COLUMN:3 -->
enlargement of base *im-, whence L. im-ituri, 'to
represent, copy, imitate'. See imitate and cp.
anent.
Derivatives: even, п., adv. and tr. v., even-ег, п.,
even-ly, adv., even-ness, n.

## evening
evening, n. — ME., fr. OE. aefnung, 'evening',
prop, verbal n. fr. aefnian, 'to become evening',
fr. ifen, 'evening'. See even, 'evening', and -ing,
suff. forming verbal nouns, and cp. morning
(fr. morn).

## evensong
evensong, n.—ME.,fr. OE. ifensang,
compounded of xfen, 'evening', and sang, 'song'. See
even, 'evening', and song.

## event
event, n. — OF. event, fr. L. iventus, 'occurrence,
event', fr. event-(um), pp. stem of evenire, 'to
come forth, happen, occur', fr. e- and venire,
'to come'. See come and cp. venue, 'arrival'.

## eventful
eventful, adj. — Compounded of event and -fid;
first used by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: eventful-ly, adv., eventful-ness, n.

## eventide
eventide, n. — ME., fr. OE. xfentid, compounded
of xfen, 'evening', and lid, 'time'. See even,
'evening', and tide.

## eventration
eventration, п., protrusion of the abdominal
viscera (med.) — F. eventration, formed fr. e-
(see e-), L. venter, gen. ventris, 'belly' (see venter,
'abdominal cavity'), and suff. -ation.

## eventual
eventual, adj. — Fictive L. 'eventudlis (whence
also F. iventuel), fr. L. eventus. See event and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: eventual-ity, п., eventual-ly, adv.

## eventante
eventante, intr. v., to turn out, result. — Formed
fr. event with verbal suff. -ate.

## ever
ever, adv. — ME. ever, fr. OE. xfre, prob. rel.
to OE. a, 'always, ever'. See aye, 'ever', and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the first
element in every and the second element in never.

## Everard
Everard, masc. PN. — OF. Everart, of Teut.
origin. Cp. OHG. Eburhard (= G. Eberhard,
Ebert), lit. 'strong as a boar', fr. ebur, 'boar',
and hart, 'hard'. See aper and hard.

## Evernia
Evernia, п., a genus of lichens of the family Us-
neaceae (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. εύερνής,
'sprouting well', fr. ευ (see eu-) and ίρνος,
'young sprout, twig, shoot', which is cogn. with
Norw. runne, rune, 'branch', ON. renna, 'to
shoot up', fr. I.-E. base *er-, *or-, 'to stir, move',
whence also L. oriri, 'to rise'. See orient and cp.
words there referred to.

## eversion
eversion, n. — F. aversion, fr. L. eversionem, ace.
of Sversio, 'a turning out, overthrowing', fr.
eversus, pp. of Svertere, 'to turn out, twist,
overthrow', fr. e- and vertere, 'to turn'. See version.

## evert
evert, tr. v., 1) to overthrow (archaic); 2) to turn
inside out. — L. Ivertere. See prec. word.

## every
every, adj. — ME. everilk, everich, evert, lit. 'ever
each', fr. OE. ifre, 'always, ever', and Sic,
'each'. See ever and each.

## evict
evict, tr. v., to dispossess by law. — L. evictus,
pp. of Svincere, 'to overcome completely,
vanquish; to recover one's property'. See evince.

## eviction
eviction, n. — Late L. evictio, gen. -onis, 'recovery
of one's property', fr. L. evictus, pp. of evincere.
See prec. word and -ion.

## evidence
evidence, n. — F. evidence, fr. L. evidentia,
'clearness, distinctness', fr. evidlns, gen. -entis. See
next word and -ce.

## evident
evident, adj. — F. evident, fr. L. evidentem, ace.
of evidlns, 'apparent, visible, clear, evident',
formed fr. e- and vidlre, 'to see'. See vision
and -ent
Derivatives: evident-ial, adj., evident-ial-ly, adv.,
evidenli-ary, adj., evident-ly, adv.

## evil
evil, adj. — ME. evil, eve/, ive/, uvel, fr. OE. yfel,
yfil, rel. to OS. uVil, OFris., MDu. eve/, Du.
euvel, OHG. ubil, MHG., G. iibel, Goth, ubils,
ievil'. These words are prob. rel. to up, nbove,
over (qq.v.) Accordingly, the orig. meaning of
OE. yfel, etc., seems to have been 'going
upward', hence 'going beyond, transgressing'.
Derivatives: evil, n. and adv., evil-ly, adv.

## evil-starred
evil-starred, adj. — Coined by the English poet
Alfred Tennyson (1809-92) fr. evil, star and adj.
suff. -ed. Cp. ill-starred.

## evince
evince, tr. v., 1) to show; 2) to exhibit. — L.
evincere, 'to overcame completely, vanquish; to
succeed in proving, demonstrate', fr. e- and
vincere, 'to vanquish'. See vincible and cp. evict.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:290 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: evinc-ible, adj., envinc-ibl-y, adv.,
envinc-ive, adj.

## evirate
evirate, tr. v., to castrate. — L. eviratus, pp. of
evirare, 'to deprive of manhood', fr. e- and vir,
'man'. See virile and verbal suff. -ate.

## eviration
eviration, п., castration. — L. iviratio, gen. -onis,
'a depriving of manhood', fr. eviratus, pp. of
evirare. See prec. word and -ion.

## eviscerate
eviscerate, tr. v., to disembowel. — L. eviscerutus,
pp. of eviscerdre, 'to disembowel', lit. 'to remove
the viscera from', fr. e- and viscera, 'the inner
parts of the body'. See viscera and cp. viscerate.
Derivative: eviscerat-ion, n.

## evitable
evitable, adj., avoidable. — L. evUdbilis,
'avoidable*; fr. evltdre, 'to avoid', fr. e- and vttdre,
'to seek to escape, to avoid', which seems to be
a contraction of *vi-itare, 'to go out of the
way', fr. via, 'way', and itdre, freq. of eo, Ire,
'to go'; see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, p.805
s.v. vitd. See vin and Itinerate.

## evocation
evocation, п., an evoking. — L. evocutid, gen.
-onis, 'a calling out, summoning', fr. evocdtus,
pp. of evocare. See evoke and -ation.

## evocative
evocative, adj., tending to evoke. — Late L. evo-
cathus, 'pertaining to summoning', fr. L.
evocdtus, pp. of evocare. See evoke and -ative and
cp. vocative.

## Evodin
Evodin, п., a genus of plants of the rue family
(bot.) —· ModL., fr. Gk. εύωδία, 'sweet smell,
fragrance', fr. ευώδης, 'sweet smelling, fragrant',
formed fr. εύ (see ей-) and the stem of δζειν,
'to smell', whence also οσμή, 'smell, odor'. See
odor and cp. osmium. For the ending see suff.
-ia.

## evoke
evoke, tr. v., to call forth. — F. evoquer, fr. L.
evocare, 'to call out, summon', fr. e- and vocdre,
'to call', from vox, gen. vocis, 'voice'. See voice.

## evolnte
evolnte, п., a curve which is the locus of the
center of curvatures of another curve (geom.) —
L. evolulus, pp. of evolvere. See next word and
cp. involute.

## evolution
evolution, n. — L. IvolQtio, gen. -onis, 'an
unrolling (of a scroll), an opening (of a book)', fr.
evolulus, pp. of evolvere, 'to unroll, unfold', fr.
e- and volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: evolution-al, adj., evolution-al-ly,
adv., evoluiion-ary, adj., evolutionism (q.v.),
evolutionist (q.v.)

## evolutionism
evolutionism, п., the theory of evolution. —
Formed with suff. -ism fr. L. ivolHtio, gen. -onis.
See prec. word.

## evolntionist
evolntionist, п., one who believes in the theory of
evolution, -s- Formed with suff. -ist fr. L. ivo-
tatid, gen. -onis. See evolution.

## evolve
evolve, tr. v., 1) to unfold; z) to develop gradually.
— L. evolvere. See evolution.

## Evonymus
Evonymus, п., a genus of plants, the spindle tree
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'of good name', fr. Gk. εδ
(see eu·) and βνυμα dialectal form of άνομα,
'name'; see onomato-. The name is euphemistic,
in allusion to the poisoning quality of this
genus.

## evulsion
evulsion, п., the act of plucking out. — L. evul-
sid, gen. -dnis, 'a pulling or plucking out', fr.
Ivulsus, pp. of evellere, 'to pull out, pluck out',
fr. e- and vellere, 'to pull off, pluck off'. See
vellkate and -ion and cp. convalse, revulsion,
vulsellum.

## ewe
ewe, n. — ME. ewe, fr. OE. Sowu, fern, of low,
'sheep', rel. to MDu. ooye, ooy, Du. 001", OHG.
ouwi, ou, 'sheep', OE. eowestre, OHG. awist,
Goth, awistr, 'shcepfold', OE. iowde, OHG.
ewit, Goth, awepi, 'flock of sheep', and cogn.
with OI. avih, Gk. ίΐς, Att. οϊς, Argive δΤις, L.
ovis, Lith. avis, Lett, avs, 'sheep', Lith. dvinas,
Lett, duns, OPruss. awins, 'ram', OSlav. ovinu,
'ram', ovica, 'ewe', Olr. oi, 'sheep', W. ewig,
'hind', and possibly cogn. with Arm. hoviv,
'shepherd'. Cp. ovine.

## ewer
ewer, п., a wide-mouthed water pitcher. — ME.,
fr. AF. ewiere, ewer, corresponding to OF.
aiguiere (F. aiguHre), ft. OProvenc. aiguiera,
'water vessel', fr. VL. aquaria, lit. 'pertaining to,
or containing, water' (cp. L. vai aquarium,
'water vessel'), fr. L. aqua, 'water'. See aquatic
and cp. aquarium. Cp. also sewer.

## ex
ex, prep, meaning 'out of and used in various

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:290 COLUMN:2 -->
phrases of Latin origin. See 1st ex-.
ex- pref. occurring in words of Latin origin used
in the senses: 1) out of, from; 2) upward;
3) completely, entirely; 4) to remove from,
deprive of; 5) without; 6) former (said of previous
holders of office or dignity). Before f, ex-
becomes ef-\ before all voiced consonants (as
b, d, g, etc.) ex- becomes g-. — L. ex-, from the
prep, ex, 'out of, from', which is cogn. with
Gk. έξ, έκ, 'out of (see 2nd ex-), Arm. 1, 'from',
pref. y- (as in y-atnem, *I rise'), Gaul, ex, Olr.
«*-, ass-, OPruss. esse, Lith. iS, OSlav. is-, iz-
(pref.), iz (prep.) Cp. extraneous, strange.
ex- pref. occurring in words of Greek origin and
meaning 'out of. — Gk. έξ, έκ, 'out of. The
former is used before vowels and is rendered
in English by ex-; the latter appears before
consonants and is transliterated ec-. For the
etymology of Gk. έξ, έκ see 1st ex-. Cp. ec-, ecto-
and the first element in eschatology.
ex-, form of exo- before a vowel.

## exacerbate
exacerbate, tr. v., to render worse, aggravate. —
L. exacerbdtus, pp. of exacerbare, 'to
exasperate, irritate, grieve, afflict', fr. 1st ex- and acer-
bdre, 'to make harsh or bitter; to aggravate',
fr. acerbus, 'harsh to the taste, bitter; sour'. See
acerb and verba] pref. -ate and cp. acerbate.

## exacerbation
exacerbation, n. — Late L. exacerbdtid, gen.
-Onis, 'exasperation', fr. L. exacerbdtus, pp. of
exacerbare. See prec. word and -ion.

## exact
exact, adj., 1) accurate; 2) precise. — L. exactus,
■precise, accurate', pp. of exigere, 'to demand,
require', lit. 'to drive out or forth', fr. 1st ex-
and agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead; to do,
act'. See agent, adj., and cp. act. Cp.also assay
essay, examen, examine, exigent, exiguous,
exility.
Derivatives: exacl-ly, adv., exact-ness, n.

## exact
exact, tr. v., to demand. — L. exactus, pp. of
exigere. See exact, adj.
Derivatives: exact-ing, adj., exact-ing-ly, adv.,
exact-ing-ness, п., exaction (q.v.), exactitude
(q.v.)

## exaction
exaction, n. — ME. exaccioun, fr. MF. (= F.)
exaction, fr. L. exactionem, ace. of exdetid, 'a
demanding, requisition', fr. exactus, pp. of
exigere. See exact, adj., and -ioa.

## exactitude
exactitude, n. — F„ fr. exact, fr. L. exactus, pp.
of exigere. See exact, adj., and -ude.

## exactor
exactor, n. — L., 'a demander', fr. exactus, pp.
of exigere. See exact, adj., and agential suff. -or.

## exaggerate
exaggerate, tr. and intr. v. — L. exaggeralus,
pp. of exaggerdre, 'to heap up; to magnify,
exaggerate', formed fr. 1st ex- and agger, 'heap,
pile, dam, dike, mound, rampart'. See agger
and verbal suff. -nte.
Derivatives: exaggerat-ed, adj., exaggerat-ed-ly,
adv., exaggerat-ing, adj., exaggerat-ing-ly, adv.,
exaggeration (q.v.), exaggeral-ive, adj., exagger-
at-ive-ly, adv., exaggerat-ive-ness, n.,exaggerat-
or (q.v.), exaggerat-ory, adj.

## exaggeration
exaggeration, n. — L. exaggerated, gen. -onis, 'a
heaping up; an exaggeration', fr. exaggeralus,
pp. of exaggerare. See prec. word and -ion.

## exaggerator
exaggerator, n. — L., fr. exaggeratus, pp. of
exaggerare. See exaggerate and agential suff. -or.

## exalt
exalt, tr. v., to raise, lift up; 2) to praise, extol. —
OF. (= F.) exalter, fr. L. exaltdre, 'to raise,
exalt', fr. ist ex- and alms, 'high'. See alt and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: exalt-ation, п., exalt-ed, adj.,
exalted-ly, adv., exalted-ness, п., exalt-er, n.

## exam
exam, n. — Colloq. abbreviation of examination.

## examen
examen, п., examination. — L. examen. See
examine.

## examinant
examinant, adj. and n. — L. exdminans, gen.
•antis, pres. part, of examinure. See examine
and -ant.

## examination
examination, n. — F., fr. L. exdmmdlidnem, ace.
of examinStiS, 'a weighing, examination', fr.
exdmindtus, pp. of exdmindre. See next word
and -ation.
Derivative: examinalion-al, adj.

## examine
examine, tr. v. — OF. (= F.) examiner, fr. L.
examinare, 'to weigh; to consider, ponder; to
test, examine', fr. examen (gen. exdminis), 'the
tongue of a balance; a weighing examination',
which stands for 'ex-ags-men, and is formed fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:290 COLUMN:3 -->
1st ex- and ago, agere, 'to drive; to act'; the
orig. meaning of examen was 'driving of the
balance out of its equilibrium'. See agent, adj.,
and cp. exact, adj., and words there referred to.
Derivatives: examin-ative, adj., examin-atory,
examin-atori-al, adjs., examin-ee, п., examin-er,
п., examin-ing, adj., examin-ing-ly, adv.
example, n. — OF. example (F. exemple), fr. L.
exemplum, lit. 'something taken out of a larger
quantity', fr. 1st ex- and emere, 'to take'. See
exempt and cp. words there referred Ю. Cp.
also exemplar, exemplify, sample, easample. For
the inserted -p- in exemplum (for *ex-em-lom)
cp. L. amplus, 'large' (see ample).
Derivative: example, tr. v.

## exanimate
exanimate, adj., 1) inanimate; 2) spiritless. — L.
exanimatus, pp. of exanimare, 'to deprive of air
or breath; to deprive of life; to terrify', fr. tst
ex- and anima, 'breath of air, air, breath, soul,
life'. See animus and adj. suff. -ate.

## exanthema
exanthema, п., an eruption, esp. one
accompanied by fever (med.) — Late L., fr. Gk.
εξάνθημα (gen. εξανθήματος), 'eruption', lit. 'a
bursting forth into flower', fr. έξανθεΐν, 'to
burst forth into flower', fr. έξ (see 2nd ex-) and
άνθείν, 'to bloom', fr. δίν&ος, 'flower'. See
anther and -ma.
Derivatives: exanthemat-ic, exanthemat-ous,
adjs. (this latter is a hybrid).

## exarch
exarch, п., l) the governor of a province in the
Byzantine Empire; 2) a bishop of the Eastern
Church, standing in rank below a patriarch and
above a metropolitan. — Late L. exarchus, fr.
Gk. εξαρχος, fr. έξ (see 2nd ex-) and άρχος,
'leader, chief, ruler'. See -arch and cp. words
there referred to.

## exarchate
exarchate, п., the office or dignity of an exarch.
— ML. axarchdtus, fr. Late L. exarchus. See
prec. word and subst. suff. -ate.

## exasperate
exasperate, tr. v., to make angry; to provoke. —
L. exasperatus, pp. of exasperare, 'to make
rough, irritate, provoke', fr. 1st ex- and asper-
dre, 'to make rough, to excite', fr. asper,
'uneven, rough'. See asperity and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: exasperat-ed, adj., exasperat-ed-ly,
adv., exasperat-ing, adj., exasperat-ing-ly, adv.,
exasperation (q.v.)

## exasperation
exasperation, n. — L. exasperdtio, gen. -onis,
'exasperation, bitterness', fr. exasperatus, pp. of
exasperare. See prec. word and -ion.

## excambion
excambion, п., exchange of land (Scot, law) —
ML. excambium. See Ist ex- and cambium and
cp. exchange.

## ex cathedra
ex cathedra, with authority. — L., lit. 'from the
chair'. See ex and cathedra.
Derivative: ex cathedra, adj., authoritative.

## excavate
excavate, tr. v., to dig oul. — L. excavatus, pp.
of excavare, 'to hollow out', fr. 1st ex- and
cavdre, 'to hollow, hollow out', fr. cavus,
'hollow'. See cpve, 'hollow space', and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: excavation (q.v.), excav-ator, п.,
excav-ator-ial, adj.

## excavation
excavation, n. — L. excavdtio, gen. -onis, 'a
hollowing out', fr. excavatus, pp. of excavare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## exceed
exceed, tr. and intr. v. — ME. exceden, fr. MF.
(= F.) excider, fr. L. excidere, 'to go away, go
beyond, depart; surpass, excel', fr. 1st ex- and
cedere, 'to go, go away, yield, withdraw*. See
cede and cp. excess.
Derivatives: exceed-er, п., exceed-ing, adj. and

## adv.
adv., exceed-ing-ly, adv.

excel, tr. and intr. v. — F. exceller, fr. L. excel-

lere, 'to rise, raise oneself, distinguish oneself,

celsus, 'high'), fr. I.-E. base *qel-, 'to rise, be

## excellence
excellence, n. — F., fr. L. excellentia,
'superiority, excellence', fr. excellens, gen. -entis. See
excellent and -ce.

## excellency
excellency, n. — F. excellence. See prec. word
and -cy.

## excellent
excellent, adj. — F., fr. L. excellentem, ace. of

excellens, pres. part, of excellere. See excel

Derivatives: exceltent-ly, adv., excellent-ness.

## excelsior
excelsior, adj. and interj., higher (used as a
motto). — L., 'higher', compar. of excelsus,
'high', which is prop, the pp. of excellere. See
excel and compar. suff. -ior.

## except
except, tr. v., to exclude; intr. v., to object. —
ME. excepten, fr. MF. (= F.) excepter, fr. L.
exceptare, 'to take out, take up', freq. of excipere
(pp. exceptus), 'to take out', fr. rst ex- and
capere (pp. capitis), 'to take*. See captive and
cp. excipient. For the change of Latin a (in
capitis) to e (in ex-ceptus, ex-ceptare) see accent
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: except, prep, (q.v.), excepting, prep,
(q.v.), exception (q.v.), except-ive, adj., except-
ive-ly, adv., except-ive-ness, n.

## except
except, prep., excluding. — L. excepto, ablative
of exceptus (followed by a subst. in the
ablative ; the so called ablative absolute construction).
See except, v.
Derivative: except, conj.

## excepting
excepting, prep., except. — Prop. pres. part, of
the verb except.

## exception
exception, n. — ME., fr. AF. excepcioun,
corresponding to OF. excepcion, exception (F.
exception), fr. L. exceptionem, ace. of exceptio.
'an exception, restriction', fr. exceptus, pp. of
excipere. See except, v., and -ion.
Derivatives: exception-able, adj., exception-
able-ness, п., exception-abl-y, adv., exception-al'.
adj., exception-al-ity, п., exception-al-ly, adv..
exception-al-ness, n.

## excerpt
excerpt, tr. v., to pick out, select. — L. excerptus.
pp. of excerpere, 'to pick out, choose, seleci,
extract', fr. 1st ex- and carpere, 'to pick, pluck,
gather'. See carpel and cp. scarce. For the change
of Latin й (in carpere) to e" (in ex-cirpere) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: excerpt-ible, adj., excerption (q.v.),
excerpt-ive, adj., excerpt-or, n.

## excerpt
excerpt, п., something excerpted; a passage from
a book, etc. — L. excerptum, 'an extract,
selection, excerpt', prop. neut. pp. of excerpere, used
as a noun. See excerpt, v.

## excerption
excerption, n. — L. excerptio, gen. -dnis, 'an
extract*, fr. excerptus, pp. of excerpere. See
excerpt, v., and -ion.

## excess
excess, n. — ME. exces, fr. OF. exces (F. exces),
fr. L. excessus, 'a going beyond, departure', fr.
excessus, pp. of excedere. See exceed.
Derivatives: excess-ive, adj., excess-ive-ly, adv.,
excess-ive-ness, n.

## exchange
exchange, n. — ME. eschaunge, eschange, fr. AF.
eschaunge, which corresponds to OF. eschange,
(F. echange), fr. eschangier. See exchange, v.

## exchange
exchange, tr. and intr. v. — OF. eschangier (F.
echanger), 'to exchange', ft. VL. *excambiare,
'to exchange' (whence also It. scambiare, Rum.
schimba, OProvenc. escambiar), fr. 1st ex- and
Late L. cambiare, 'to exchange'. See cambium
and cp. change. Cp. also excambion.
Derivatives: exchange-able, adj.,
exchange-ability, п., exchange-abl-y, adv., exekang-er, n.

## exhilarate
exhilarate, tr. v., to cheer; to stimulate. — L. ex-
hilaratus, pp. of exhilarare, 'to gladden, make
merry, exhilarate*, fr. 1st ex- and hilarare, 'to
make cheerful, make merry', fr. hilaris,
'cheerful, merry'. See hilarious and verbal stiff, -ate.
Derivatives: exhilarat-ed, adj., exhilarat-ing,
adj., exhilarat-ing-ly, adv., exhilaration (q.v.),
exhilarat-ive, exhilarat-ory, adjs.

## exhilaration
exhilaration, n. — Late L. exhilaratio, gen. -onis,
'a gladdening', fr. L. exhilaratus, pp. of
exhilarare. See prec. word and -ion.

## exhort
exhort, tr. and intr. v., to advise earnestly. —
ME. exhorten, fr. L. exhortari, 'to exhort,
encourage, stimulate', fr. 1st ex- and hortart, 'to
incite, encourage, urge'. See hortation and cp.
words there referred to.

## exhortation
exhortation, n. — L. exhortatio, gen. -onis,
'encouraging, exhortation', fr. exhortdlus, pp. of
exhortari. See prec. word and -ation.

## exhortative
exhortative, adj. — L. exhortattvus, 'pertaining
to or containing exhortation', fr. exhortatus,
pp. of exhortari. See exhort and -ive and cp.
hortative.

## exhortatory
exhortatory, adj. — Late L. exhortatorius,
'pertaining to exhortation', fr. L. exhortatus, pp. of
exhortari. See exhortation and adj. suff. -ory.

## exhumation
exhumation, η. — ML. exhumdtio, gen. -onis,
'unearthing', fr. exhumalus, pp. of exhumare.
See next word and -ation.

## exhume
exhume, tr. v., to dig out of the earth, disinter. —
F. exhumer, fr. ML. exhumare, 'to unearth', fr.
1st ex- and L. humus, 'earth'. See humus and
cp. words there referred to.

## exigennt
exigennt, adj., exacting, demanding. — F., pres.
part, ofexiger, 'to exact, demand', fr. L. exigere.
See exigent and -ant.

## exigence
exigence, п., exigency. — F. See next word and
-ce.

## exigency
exigency, п., state of urgency. — ML. exigenlia,
'urgency*, fr. L. exigens, gen. -entis. See next
word and -cy.

## exigent
exigent, adj., requiring immediate action,
urgent. — L. exigens, gen. -enlis, pres. part, of
exigere, 'to demand, require; to weigh,
measure', lit. 'to drive out or forth', fr. 1st ex- and
agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead; to do, act'.
See agent, adj., and -ent and cp. exigcant, exi-
gaous, exact, examine, assay, essay.
Derivative: exigent-ly,stdv.

## exigible
exigible, adj., capable of being exacted. —
Formed with suff. -ible fr. L. exigere (see prec.
word), whence also F. exigible, of s.m. See
exigeat

## exiguity
exiguity, п., scantiness. — L. exiguitas, 'small-
ness, scantiness', fr. exiguus. See next word and
-ity.

## exiguous
exiguous, adj., scanty. — L. exiguus, 'small,
scanty, petty', fr. exigere. See exigent and cp.
exility. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
suff. -ous.
Derivatives: exiguous-ly, adv., exiguous-ness, n.

## exilarch
exilarch, п., head of the Jewish exiles in
Babylonia (Jewish hisl.) — A hybrid coined fr. L.
exilium, 'exile', and Gk. αρχάς, 'leader, chief,
ruler'. See next word and -arch.

## exile
exile, п., banishment. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.),
exil, fr. L. exilium, exsilium, 'banishment, exile',
fr. exul, exsul, 'a banished person, wanderer',
which is of uncertain origin. It possibly stands
for *eks-al-s and is formed fr. 1st ex- and I.-E.
base *&l-, 'to wander about', whence also Gk.
άλασθαι, 'to wander about', L. al-ucinari, 'to
wander in mind' (see hallucinate). The spelling
exsul, exsilium is due to a confusion with L.
solum, 'soil', from which the ancients derived
exilium and exul, but with which these words
have nothing in common. Nor is there any
connection between L. exilium and exsilire, 'to
spring forth'.

## exile
exile, п., a banished person. — Fr. prec. word.

## exile
exile, tr. v., to banish. — OF. exilier (F. exiler),
fr. L. exiliare, exsiliare, fr. exilium, exsilium. See
exile, 'banishment'.

## exilian
exilian, exilic, adj., pertaining to the exile of the
Jews in Babylonia. — Formed with suff. -Ian,
resp. -ic, fr. L. exilium. See exile, 'banishment'.

## exility
exility, п., slenderness. — L. exilitas, 'smallness,
thinness, meagerrjess, slenderness', fr. exilis,
'small, thin, meager, slender*, which prob.
stands for *ex-ag-slis and is rel. to exiguus,
'small, scanty, petty'. See exiguous and -lty.

## eximious
eximious, adj., choice, excellent. — L. eximius,
'select, choice', lit. 'taken out', fr. eximere, 'to
take out, take away', fr. 1st ex- and emere, 'to
take, buy'. See exempt, v. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: eximious-ly, adv., exlmlous-ness, n.

## exlnanite
exlnanite, tr. v., to make empty (obsol.) — L.
exinaniius, pp. of exinamre, 'to empty, make
empty', fr. 1st ex- and inunis, 'empty'. See inane.

## exinanition
exinanition, п., ι) the action of emptying; z)
exhaustion. — L. ехтйпШб, gen. -dnis, 'an
emptying, exhausting', fr. exinaniius, pp. of exinamre.
See prec. word and -Ion.

## exist
exist, intr. v. — F. exister, fr. L. exsistere, exis-
tere, 'to stand forth, appear, exist', fr. 1st ex-
and sistere, 'to cause to stand still, to put, place;
to stand still, stand', from the reduplicated base
of stare, 'to stand'. See nssist and cp. words
there referred to.

## existence
existence, n. — OF. (= F.) existence, fr. ML.
existentia, fr. L. existens, gen. -entis. See next
word and -ce.

## existent
existent, adj., existing. — L. existens, gen. -entis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:293 COLUMN:2 -->
pres. part, of existere. See exist and -ent.

## existential
existential, adj., pertaining to existence. — ML.
existeniidlis, fr. existentia. See existence and -ial.
Derivatives: existential-ly, adv., existentialism
(q.v.)

## existentialism
existentialism, п., a system of philosophy based
on the tenet that everybody in general exists as
an individual. — Orig. used to translate G.
Exislenzphilosophie, lit. 'philosophy of
existence' ; see prec. word and -ism. The term
'existence' is used here in the special sense given to
it by the Danish philosopher Saren Aabye
Kierkegaard (1813-55), who is the originator of
existentialism.

## existentialist
existentialist, п., an adherent of existentialism.
— See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: existentialist, existentialist-ic, adjs.

## exit
exit, v., he goes out (of the stage). — L., 3rd
pers. pres. indicative of exire, 'to go out', which
is formed fr. 1st ex- and ire, 'to go'. See
itinerate and cp. exeat, exeunt.

## exit
exit, п., a going out, departure. — L. exitus, 'a
going out, egress, departure', fr. exitus, pp. of
exire, 'to go out'. See prec. word.

## ex-llbris
ex-llbris, п., a bookplate giving the name of the
owner of the book. — L„ 'from the books of...',
fr. ex, 'out of, from', and abl. pi. of liber,
'book'. See Ist ex- and library.

## exo-
exo-, before a vowel ex-, pref. meaning 'outer,
outside'. — Gk. ϊξω, 'outside', fr. έξ, 'out of.
See 2nd ex-.

## exoderm
exoderm, n. — The same as exodermis.

## exodermis
exodermis, п., the outer layer in roots (hot.) —
ModL. exodermis, formed fr. exo- and Gk.
δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma and cp. words there
referred to.

## exodus
exodus, п., going out, departure. — L., fr. Gk.
Εξοδος, lit. 'way out', fr. έξ (see 2nd ex- and
οδός, 'way'. See odograph and cp, words there
referred to.
ex officio. — L„ 'by virtue of an office', formed
fr. ex, 'out of, and abl. of officium, 'service;
office'. See ist ex- and office.

## exogamy
exogamy, n„ marriage outside the tribe or clan
(anthropoid — Lit. 'outside marriage';
compounded of exo- and -gamy. Cp. endogamy.
Derivatives: exogam-ic, exogam-ous, adjs.

## Exogenae
Exogenae, n.pl., the Dicotyledones (hot.) —
ModL., lit. 'growing outside' (see exo- and
-gen); so called in allusion to the annual rings
of the stem. Cp. Endogenae.

## exogenous
exogenous, adj., growing from outside (biol.) -*-
See prec. word and -genous and cp. endogenous.

## exomis
exomis, п., a garment worn by the poor classes
and slaves (Greek antiq.) — Gk. έξωμίς, 'a
garment without sleeves or with one sleeve', lit.
'that which leaves the shoulder bare', fr. έξ (see
2nd ex-) and ώμος, 'shoulder'. See ото-,
'shoulder-'.

## exomphalos
exomphalos, п., umbilical hernia (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. έξόμφαλος, 'a prominent navel',
fr. έξ (see 2nd ex-) and ομφαλός, 'navel*. See
omphalo-.

## exon
exon, п., one of four officers commanding the
Yeomen of the Guard. — Corruption of F.
exempt, 'an underofficer', lit. 'free'. See exempt,
adj. and v.

## exonerate
exonerate, tr. v., to free from blame. — L.
exonerate, pp. of exonerare, 'to unload, free from
a burden, lighten', fr. ist ex- and onerare, 'to
load, freight, overload, oppress', fr. onus, gen.
oneris, 'load, burden, weight'. See onus and
verbal suff. -ate and cp. onerous. Derivatives:
exoneration (q.v.), exonerat-ive, adj.

## exoneration
exoneration, n. — Late L. exoneratio, gen. -onis,
'an unloading, lightening', fr. L. exoneralus,
pp. of exonerare. See prec. word and -ion.

## exophthalmic
exophthalmic, adj., pertaining to, or affected
with, exophthalmos. — See next word and -ic

## exophthalmos-
exophthalmos-, exophthalmus, n. abnormal
protrusion of the eyeball (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. εξόφθαλμος, 'with prominent eyes', fr. έξ
(see 2nd ex-) and οφθαλμός, 'eye'. See ophthal-
mo- and cp. iagophthaimos.

## exorable
exorable, adj., susceptible of being moved by
entreaty. — L. exorabilis, 'easily moved by
entreaty', fr. ехбгйге, 'to move by entreaty,
persuade', fr. 1st ex- and or are, 'to pray'. See oration

and -able and cp. inexorable.

## exorbitance
exorbitance, exorbitancy, n. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy,

## exorbitant
exorbitant, adj., excessive; extravagant. — Late
L. exorbitans, gen. -amis, lit. 'out of the track',
pres. part, of exorbitare, 'to go out of the track,
deviate', fr. ist ex- and orbita, 'wheel track, rut'.
See orbit and -ant. Derivative: exorbitant-ly, adv.

## exorcise
exorcise, exorcize, tr. v., to drive out an evil spirit
by ritual charms. — F. exorciser, fr. Late L.
exorcizare, fr. Gk. εξόρκιζε», 'to bind by an
oath; to banish an evil spirit', fr. έξ (see 2nd
ex-) and όρκίζειν, 'to make to swear', fr. δρκος
(for *σόρκος), 'an oath', lit. 'a limitation,
binding, obligation', in gradational relationship to
6ρκος (for *σέρκος), 'enclosure, hedge, fence',
and prob. cogn. with L. sarcire, 'to patch,
mend'. See sartorial and -ise, ize.

## exorcism
exorcism, n. — Late L. exorcismus, fr. Gk.
εξορκισμός, 'binding by an oath; banishment of an
evil spirit', fr. έξορκίζειν. See prec. word and
-Ism.

## exorcist
exorcist, n. — Late L. exorcista, fr. Gk.
εξορκιστής, 'exorcist', fr. έξορκίζειν. See exorcise and
-ist.

## exordium
exordium, п., beginning. — L. exordium,
'beginning of a web, beginning of a speech, beginning

warp, begin', which is rel. to 6rdo, 'a straight
row, order'. See order and cp. ornament

## exoskeleton
exoskeleton, п., the skeleton of invertebrates in
contradistinction to the skeleton of vertebrates
(zool.) — Compounded of exo- and skeletoa.
The term exoskeleton was introduced into science
by the English anatomist Sir Richard Owen
(1804-92). Cp. endoskeleton, splanchnoskeleton.
Derivative: exoskelel-al, adj.

## exosmosis
exosmosis, also exosmose, п., outward osmosis.
— Compounded of 3rd ex- and osmosis. Cp.

## exosmotic
exosmotic, adj. — See prec. word and -otic.

## exosphere
exosphere, п., the outermost part of the earth's
atmosphere. — Compounded of exo- and sphere.

## exostosis
exostosis, п., a bony outgrowth from the surface

τωσις, lit. 'bone increase from without', fr. ϊξω
(see exo-) and -όστωσις (see -ostosis). Cp. en-
dostosis.

## exoteric
exoteric, also exoterical, adj., external. — Late

έξωτέρω, 'more outward', compar. of ϊξω,

Derivatives: exolerical-ly, adv., exoteric-ism, n.

## exothecium

## exotic
exotic, adj., foreign. — L. exuticus, fr. Gk.

## expand
expand, tr. and intr. v., to spread out. — L. ex-

ist ex- and pandere, 'to spread out, extend',
which is rel. to L. palere, 'to be open', patulus,
'extended'. See fathom and cp. expause,
expansion, spandrel, spawn. Derivatives:
expanded, adj., expand-ed-ly, adv., expand-ed-ness, п.,
expand-er, п., expand-ing-ly, adv.

## expanse
expanse, п., an extended space. — L. expansum,
neut. pp. of expandere, 'to spread out', used as

## expansible
expansible, adj. — Formed with suff. -Ible fr. L.

Derivatives: expans-ibil-ily, п., expans-ible-
ness, п., expans-ibl-y, adv.

## expansile
expansile, adj. — Formed with suff. -ile fr. L.
expansus, pp. of expandere. See expand.

## expansion
expansion, n. — Late L. expansio, gen. -onis, 'a
spreading out, expansion', fr. L. expansus, pp.
of expandere. See expand and -ioa. Derivatives:
expansion-al, expansion-ary, adjs.,
expansionism, п., expanshn-ist, п., expansion-ist-ic, adj.

## expansive
expansive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
expansus, pp. of expandere. See expand.
Derivatives: expansive-ly, adv., expansive-ness,

## ex parte
ex parte, from one side only. — L., formed fr. ex,

expatiate, intr. v., to speak or write at length. —
L. exspatidtus, expatiates, pp. of exspatidri,
expatidri, 'to spread out, extend; to digress,

Derivatives: expatiat-ion, п., expaiial-ory, adj.

expatriate, intr. v., to exile. — ML. expatriates,

Derivative: expatriat-ion, n.

## expatriate
expatriate, adj., exiled; п., an exile. — ML.
expatriate. See expatriate, v.

## expect
expect, tr. and intr. v. — L. exspectare, expectare,
'to look out for, await; to desire, hope', fr. ist
ex- and spectare, freq. of specere, spicere, 'to

expectance, expectancy, n. — Formed from next

expectant, adj., expecting. — F., fr. L. exspec-
tantem, expectantem, ace. of exspectdns, ex-
pectdns, pres. part, of exspectare, expectare. See

expectation, n. — L. exspecldtio, expectdtio, gen.

tdtus, expectatus, pp. of exspectare, expectare.
See expect and -ation.

expectative, adj. — ML. expeclativus, fr. L. ex-
spectdlus, expectatus, pp. of exspectare,

## expectorant
expectorant, adj., causing expectoration; п., an

## expectorate

## expedience
expedience, n. — F. expedience. See expedient

## expediency
expediency, n. — Formed from next word with

## expedient
expedient, adj., suitable; convenient. — OF.

pediens, pres. part, of expedire, lit. 'to free the
feet from fetters', hence 'to extricate,
disengage, set free; to make ready', fr. ex, 'out of
(see 1st ex-), and *pedis, 'fetter', prop, 'chain
for the feet', which is rel. to pedica, 'shackle,
fetter', compes, 'fetter', and cogn. with Gk.
πέδη, 'fetter', fr. I.-E. *pid-, *pdd-, 'foot'. See
foot and cp. fetter. Cp. also pedal, impede,
impend].

expedienl-ial-ly, adv., expedient-ist, п.,
expediently, adv.

## expedite
expedite, tr. v., to speed up. — L. expedites, pp.

## expedite
expedite, adj., 1) unimpeded, free; 2) prompt. —

Derivatives: expedite-ly, adv., expedite-ness, n.

expeditionist, a.

## expeditious
expeditious, adj., speedy, prompt. — Formed fr.

Derivatives: expeditious-ly, adv., expeditious-
ness, Ώ.

## expel
expel, tr. v. — L. expellere, 'to drive out or

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:294 COLUMN:2 -->

## expeliant

## expend

'to cause to hang down, suspend; to weigh'.

## expenditure
expenditure, n. — Coined by the Brilish

## expense
expense, n. — ME., fr. AF., fr. L. expensa, fern,

## expensive

## experience
experience, n. — F. experience, fr. L. experientia,

## experiential
experiential, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. experientia. See prec. word.
Derivatives: experiential-ism, п., experiential-
ist, п., experiential-ly, adv.

## experiment
experiment, n. — OF., fr. L. experimentum, 'trial,
proof, test', fr. experiri. See experience and

adj., experiment-al-ism, experiment-al-ist, п.,
experiment-al-ize, intr. v., experiment-al-ly, adv.
experiment-ation, п., experiment-ative, adj., ex-
periment-ed, adj., experiment-ee, п.,
experimenter, п., experiment-ize, intr. v.

## expert
expert, n. — F. expert, п., fr. OF. expert, adj.
See prec. word.

## explable
explable, adj. — F., fr. expier, fr. L. expidre.

## expiate
expiate, tr. v., to atone for. — L. expiates, pp. of

## expiation
expiation, n. — L. expiatio, gen. -onis,

## expiatory
expiatory, adj. — Late L. expidtorius, fr. L.
expidtus, pp. of expiare. See expiate and adj.

## expiration
expiration, n. — L. exspirdtio, expiratio, gen.
-onis, fr. exspiratus, expirdtus, pp. of exspirdre,

## expiratory
expiratory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory

## expire
expire, intr. and tr. v. — F. expirer, fr. L.

## expound

beside expoune, the form expounde, derived
from the inf., also appears quite early. Finally
expounde prevailed, whence the English form
expound. On the analogy of expound, fr. L.
exponere, ME. compoune, compone (fr. L. com-
рбпеге) became E. compound, and ME. propone
(fr. L. proponere) became E. propound. Cp. F.

## extract

pp. of extrahere, 'to draw out'; see extract, v.
As a legal term, E. extract represents L. extrac-
ia, the fem. of extractus (see above). Cp.
estreat.

## extraction
extraction, n. — F., fr. ML. extractionem, ace. of
extractio, 'the act of extracting', fr. L. extractus,
pp. of extrahere. See extract, v., and -Ion.

## extradite
extradite, tr. v. — Back formation fr. extra-
dttian.

## extradition
extradition, n. — F, fr. L. ex, 'out of, and
traditid, gen. -onis, 'a delivering up, surrender'.
See ist ex- and tradition.

## extrados
extrados, п., the exterior surface of an arch
(archit.) — F., a hybrid coined by the French
dramatist and journalist Thomas Corneille
(1625-1709) in 1694 fr. extra and F. dos, 'back',
fr. L. dorsum. See dorsal and cp. intrados.

## extramundane
extramundane, adj., beyond the material world.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:296 COLUMN:2 -->
— Formed fr. extra- and mundane.

## extrainnral
extrainnral, adj., outside the walls. — Formed
fr. extra- and mural.

## extraneous
extraneous, adj., external, foreign.—L. extraneus,
'external, strange'. See extra- and cp. strange.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ons.
Derivatives: extraneous-ly, adv., extraneous-
ness, n.

## extraordinary
extraordinary, adj. — L. extraordinarius, 'out of
the common order, extraordinary', fr. extra 5r-
dinem. Outside the (common) order', fr. extra
(see extra) and grdinem, ace. of drdd, 'order'.
See ordinary.
Derivatives: extraordinari-ly, adv., extraordi-
nari-ness, n.

## extraterritorial
extraterritorial, adj., exterritorial. — Formed fr.
extra- and territorial. Cp. exterritorial.
Derivative: extraterritorial-ity, n.

## extravagance
extravagance, extravagancy, n. — F.
extravagance, fr. extravagant. See next word and -ce,
resp. -cy, and cp. extravaganza.

## extravagant
extravagant, adj., prodigal, wasteful., п., an
extravagant person. — F., fr. ML. extravagan-
tem, ace. of extravagans, pres. part, of extra-
vagarl, 'to wander outside (the limits)', fr.
extra- and L. vagari, 'to wander, ramble, roam
about'. See vagary and -ant.
Derivatives: extravagance (q.v.), extravagant-ly,
adv., extravagant-ness, n.

## extravagnnza
extravagnnza, п., a fantastic musical or non-
musical composition. — It. estravaganza, slra-
vaganza, lit. 'extravagance', fr. estravagante,
stravagante, 'extravagant*, fr. ML. extravagan-
tem (see prec. word); influenced in form by
extravngance (q.v.)

## extravagate
extravagate, intr. v., to rove. — ML. extra-
vagatus, pp. of extravagurl. See extravngaat and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: extravagat-ion, n. (obsol.)

## extravnsate
extravnsate, tr. v., to force out of the proper
vessels, as blood; intr. v., to ooze out into
surrounding tissues, as blood (pathol.) — Formed
fr. extra- and L. vas, 'vessel'. See vase and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: extravasat-ion, n.

## extreme
extreme, adj. — OF. (F. extreme), fr. L. extremus,
'outermost, utmost, extreme', superl. of exter,
exterus, 'on the outside, outward, external,
foreign, strange'. See exterior.
Derivatives: extreme, п., extreme-ly, adv.,
extremeness, п., exlrem-ism, п., extrem-ist, n.

## extremity
extremity, n. — OF. extremite (F. extremite), fr.
L. exlremitatem, ace. of extremitas, 'the end of
a thing', fr. extremus. See extreme and -ity. In
the sense of 'hands or feet', L. extremitas was
first used by the translator Gerard of Cremona
(died in 1187).

## extrfcable
extrfcable, adj. — See next word and -able.

## extricate
extricate, tr. v. — L. extricatus, pp. of extrlcure,
'to disentangle, extricate', formed fr. ist ex- and
trlcae (pi.), 'trifles, stuff; perplexities, wiles,
tricks', which is of uncertain origin. It meant
perh. orig. 'twisted ways', and derives fr^I.-E.
base *lreik-, 'to turn, twist', which is rel. to
base "tereq-, of s.m., whence lorqulre, 'to turn,
twist'. See torque and verbal suff. -ate and cp.
trlca, intricate.
Derivative: extricat-ion, n.

## extrinsic
extrinsic, adj., external. — F. extrinsique, fr. L.
exlrinsecus, 'from without, from abroad',
formed fr. exter, 'outer', and secus, 'beside, by,
along'. For the first element see extra-, exterior.
L. secus orig. meant 'following'; and is rel. to
sequi, 'to follow'. See sequel and cp. second.
Cp. also intrinsic.
Derivatives: extrinsic-al, adj., extrinsical-ity, п.,
extrinsical-ness, п., exlrinsical-ly, adv.

## extra-
extra-, pref. formed fr. extra-, on the analogy
of the pref. intro-,

## extrorse
extrorse, adj., turned outward (hot.) — F., fr.
Late L. extrorsus, 'in an outward direction',
contraction of extra, 'on the outside', and
versus, 'turned', pp. of vertere, 'to turn'. See extra-
and version and cp. introrse, retrorse, intro-
verse, prose.
Derivative: extrorse-ly, adv.

## extroversion
extroversion, п., 1) the condition of being turned
inside out (med.); 2) also extroversion, interest

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:296 COLUMN:3 -->
directed to external things; the opposite of
introversion (psychol.) — Formed fr. extro- (resp.
extra-) and version.

## extroversive
extroversive, also extraversive, adj., pertaining or
tending to extroversion; the opposite of intro-
versive (psychol.) — Formed with suff. -ive fr.
extro- (resp. extra-) and L. versus, pp. of
vertere, 'to turn'. See version.

## extrovert
extrovert, tr.. v., 1) to turn outward; 2) also
extravert; intr. v., to turn one's interest toward
external things; the opposite of introvert
(psychol.) — Formed fr. extro- (resp. extra-)
and L. vertere, 'to turn'. See version. The term
extrovert was introduced into psychology by
the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Gustav Jung (1875-
1961). Cp. introvert, v.

## extrovert
extrovert, also extravert, п., one characterized by
extroversion; the opposite of introvert (psychol.)
— Fr. extrovert, v.

## extrude
extrude, tr. v., to push out; intr. v., to protrude. —
L. extrudere, 'to thrust out, drive away', fr. 1st
ex- and trudere, 'to thrust, push, shove', which
derives fr. I.-E. base *treud-, 'to press, push',
whence also Goth, us-priutan, 'to vex', OE.
preotan, 'to. weary, vex, annoy', Creation, 'to
press, afflict, threaten'. See threat and cp. thrust
Cp. also intrude and words there referred to.

## extrusion
extrusion, n. — ML. extrusio, gen. -onis, fr. L.
extrusus, pp. of extrudere. See prec. word and
-ion and cp. intrusion and words there referred to.

## extrusive
extrusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
extrusus, pp. of extrudere. See extrude and cp.
intrusive, obtrusive, protrusive,

## exuberance
exuberance, exuberancy, п., luxuriance. — F.
exuberance, fr. L. exuberantia, 'superabundance,
exuberance', fr. exuberans, gen. -amis. See next
word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## exuberant
exuberant, adj., lavish, luxuriant. — F. exuberant,
fr. L. exuberantem, ace. of exuberans, pres. part,
of exuberare, 'to come forth in abundance,
grow luxuriantly', fr. ist ex- and Qberare, 'to be
fruitful', from the adjective uber, 'fruitful'.which
derives from the noun uber, 'udder'. See
uberous.
Derivatives: exuberant-ly, adv.,exuberant-ness,n.

## exuberate
exuberate, intr. v., to be exuberant; to abound.
— L. exuberatus, pp. of exuberare. See prec.
word and verbal suff. -ate.

## exudate
exudate, п., exuded substance. — L. exsudutum,
exudalum, neut. pp. of exsudare, exudare. See
exnde and adj. suff. -ate.

## exudation
exudation, n. — Formed with suff. -ion fr. L.
exsiidatus, exudatus, pp. of exsudare, exudare.
See next word.

## exude
exude, intr. and tr. v., to ooze. — L. exsudare,
exudare, 'to sweat out', fr. 1st ex- and siidare,
'to sweat', fr. sudor, 'sweat', which is cogn. with
OE. swat, 'sweat', sw&tan, 'to sweat'. See swent
and cp. sudation.

## exalt
exalt, intr. v., to rejoice greatly. — F. exulter,
fr. L. exsultare, exultare, 'to leap about, leap
for joy, triumph', which stands for *ex-saltare
and is freq. of exsilire, 'to leap out, spring out,
leap up, start up', fr. ist ex- and satire, 'to leap,
spring, jump', whence the freq. saltare, 'to leap,
jump, dance'. See salient and cp. saltant. For
the change of Latin й (in saltare) to й (in
exsultare, ex-Шаге) see desultory and cp. words
there referred to.

## exultancy
exultancy, n. — L. exsultantia, exultantia, fr. ex-
sultans, exultans, gen. -antis. See next word
and -cy.

## exultant
exultant, adj. — L. exsultans, exultans, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of exsultare, exultare. See exult
and -ant Derivative: exultant-ly, adv.

## exultation
exultation, n. — F., fr. L. exsultutidnem, exul-
tatidnem-, ace. of exsultatid, exultatio, 'a leaping
about', fr. exsultat-(um), exultat-(um), pp. stem
of exsultare, exultare. See prec. word and -ion.

## exuviae
exuviae, n. pi., cast skins of animals. — L., 'that
which is stripped off, clothing, equipments',
from the stem of exuere, which stands for *exo-
were, 'to pull or strip off', fr. 1st ex- and
*-owere, earlier *-ewere, fr. I.-E. base *ew-, 'to
put on', whence also OSIav. ob-ujg, ob-uti, 'to
put on shoes', Lith. aunu, auti, 'to put on
shoes', aviu, aviti, 'to wear shoes', Arm. ag-
anim, Ί put on something', Avestic ao&ra-.

derivatives of base *w-es, 'to clothe', an

## eyalet
eyalet, п., formerly, a province of the Ottoman
Empire; now called viyalet. — Turk., fr. Arab.
lydlah, 'government', prop. inf. of the verb Ah,
'was at the head of, whence dwwal, 'first'.

## eyas
eyas, п., a nestling; a young hawk taken from
the nest. — F. niais, 'nestling' (the modern
French meaning is 'silly, simple'), fr. VL.
*nidacem, ace. of *mdax, 'nestling', fr. nidus.
'nest'; see nidus. The English form arose from
a misdivision of a nias into an eyas. For similar
misdivisions cp. adder and words there
referred to.

## eye
eye, n. — ME. eige, eye, eie, fr. OE. eage, rel. to
OS. dga, OFris. age, ON. auga, Swed. Sga, Dan.
eie, OFris. age, MDu. dghe, Du. oog, OHG.
ouga, MHG. ouge, G. Auge, Goth, augo, 'eye',
fr. I.-E. base *oqw-, 'to see; eye', whence also
OI. dksi, gen. aksnah, 'eye', aksdh, 'die', tksaie.

'sees', Toch. A ak, В ек, 'eye', Arm. akn, gen,
akan, 'eye, opening, hole*, Gk. δκκος, 'eye',
βσσε (for oqwi·), 'the two eyes', δσσεσ&αι, 'to
see, look at, presage', 6πή, Opening, hole',
δψομαι, Ί shall see', όπτός, 'seen; visible',
βπτικός, 'pertaining to sight', Alb. sli, 'eye', L.

mo- and the second element in antler. Cp. also
the second element in atrocious, ferocious,
velocity. Derivatives: eye, tr. v., ey-ed, adj.

## eyelet
eyelet, n. — ME. oilet, fr. MF. (= F.) aittet,
dimin. of ail, 'eye', fr. L. oculus; influenced in
spelling by eye (q.v.)

## eyot
eyot, п., a small island. — ME. eyt, fr. OE. igeod,
dimin. of eg, ig, leg, 'island'. See island and cp.
the second element in Scandinavin. The ending
of the word eyot was influenced by the French

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:297 COLUMN:3 -->
dimin. suff. -or.

## eyre
eyre, п., journey, circuit; circuit court. — ME.,
fr. OF. eire, 'journey, way', fr. L. iter, of s.m.
See Itinerate and cp. errant.

## eyrie
eyrie, eyry, n. — Variants of aerie, aery.

## Ezekiel
Ezekiel, I) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible: a) name
of one of the great prophets of Israel; b) the
Book of Ezekiel. — Late L. Ezechill, fr. Gk.
ΊΕζεκιήλ, fr. Heb. Y'hezqil, lit. 'God strength-
ens'. The first element derives fr. hazaq, 'he
was strong; he strengthened', whence hazaq,
'strong', hizeq, hezqa41, hizeq, hozqa", 'strength*,
Mishnaic Heb. huzuqa", 'taking hold of;
presumption; usucaption*. Heb. hazaq is rel. to
Aram.-Syr. hazaq, 'he was strong', Arab, hd-
zaqa, 'he bound, squeezed', Akkad. eshqu,
'strong', isqu, 'possession'. Cp. Hezeklah. For
the second element in the name Ezekiel see El.

## Ezra
Ezra, l) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible: a) name of
a celebrated scribe of the 5th century B.C.E.:
b) the Book of Ezra. — Late L., fr. Heb. 'Ezra,
abbrevation of 'Azarydh(u), lit. 'God has
helped'. See Azariah and cp. Esdras. For similar
abbreviations cp. Jesse and Micah.

## fa
fa, п., a syllable used in solmization to denote
the fourth tone of the diatonic scale (mus.)

## Fabaceae
Fabaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the pea
family (hot.) — Formed with stiff, -aceae fr.
ModL. Faba, the type genus, fr. L. faba, 'bean',
from the I.-E. child's word "bhabha, 'bean', lit.
'something swelling', prop, reduplication of the
child's word *bha-, 'something swelling'. See
bean and cp. Fabian.

## fabaceous
fabaceous, adj., pertaining to the Fabaceae (bot.)
— L. fabdceus, 'consisting of beans', fr. faba.
See prec. word and -ous.

## Fnbian
Fnbian, adj., dilatory, cautious. — L. Fabianus,
from the name of the Roman general Quintus
Fabius Maximus, surnamed Cunctator (=
'Delayer'). — (The Latin name Fabius is rel. to faba,
'bean', for whose etymology see Fabaceae). For
the ending see suff. -an.

## Fabian
Fabian, masc. PN. — L. Fabianus, a derivative
of Fabius. See Fabian, adj.

## fable
fable, п., a story. — OF. (= F.), 'fable, story,
tale', fr. L. fabula, 'narrative, account, tale,
story', lit. 'that which is told', rel. to fori, 'to
speak, tell, foretell', fama, 'talk, report, rumor,
saying, tradition, reputation', jacundus,
'eloquent', fateri, 'to confess', fr. I.-E. base *bhd-,
'to speak'. See fame and words there referred
to and cp. esp. fabulous, confabalate, affable,
fib, ineffable.

## fable
fable, intr. v., to write or tell fables; tr. v., to
invent. — OF. fabler, fr. L. fdbulari, 'to speak,
talk', fr. fabula. See fable, n.
Derivatives: fabl-ed, adj., fable-ist, п., fabl-er,
п., fabl-ing, n.

## fabllnn
fabllnn, п., a short medieval French metrical
story. — F., fr. Picard fabliau, fr. OF. fablel,
fableau, masc. dimin. offable, 'fable, story, tale'.
See fable, n.

## fabric
fabric, n. — F. fabrique, fr. L. fabrica, 'workshop
of an artisan, building, fabric', fr. faber, gen.
fabrl, 'workman, artisan, artificer, forger,
smith', from L. base *fab-, corresponding to
I.-E. base *dhabh-, 'to become or be suitable',
whence Arm. darbin, 'smith', OSlav. dobru,
'fine, good', doba, 'opportunity', Lith. dablnti,
'to adorn', dabniis, 'graceful'. Cp. daft, deft,
forge.

## fabricate
fabricate, tr. v. — L. fabricdtus, pp. of fabricdri,
'to frame, construct, build', fr. fabrica. See
prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## fabrication
fabrication, n. — L. fabricdtio, gen. -onis, 'a
framing', fr. fabricdlus, pp. of fabricdri. See
fabric and -ion.

## fabulist
fabulist, n. — F. fabulisie, fr. L. fabula. See fable
and -ist.

## fabalosiry
fabalosiry, n. — F. fabuhsite, fr. L. fabulosl-
latem, ace. of fdbuWsilas, 'fabulous invention,
fabulosity', fr. fabuldsus. See next word and -ity.

## fabulous
fabulous, adj. — L. fabuldsus, 'fabulous', fr.
fabula. See fable and -«us.
Derivatives: fabulous-ly, adv., fabulous-ness, n.

## facade
facade, п., the front of a building. — F., fr.
earlier facciale, fr. It. facclata, lit. 'face (of a
building)', fr. faccia, 'face', fr. VL. facia, fr. L.
fades. See next word and -ade.

## face
face, n. — F., fr. VL. facia (whence also It. faccia,
OProvenc. fossa), fr. L. faciis (whence also Sp.
haz), 'face', orig. 'a making, shaping', fr. facere,
'to make, do', See fact and cp. facade, facet,
facetious, deface, efface, superficies, surface,
volta-face. For the formation of L. faciis, 'face',
fr. facere, 'to make', cp. L. species, 'sight,
appearance', fr. specere, 'to look at'; for the sense
development of facies, 'face', fr. facere, 'to
make', cp. F. figure, 'face', fr. L. figura, 'figure,
appearance'. The orig. meaning of L. facies
may easily be derived from the meaning of the
compound superficies, 'surface', which lit.
means 'superstructure'.
Derivatives: face, tr. and intr. v., fac-ed, adj..

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:298 COLUMN:2 -->
F
fac-ing, adj. and п., fac-ing-ly, adv.

## facet
facet, п., 1) surface of a cut gem; 2) aspect. —F.
facette, dimin. of face. See face and -et, -ette.
Derivatives: facet, tr. v., facet-ed, adj.

## facetiae
facetiae, n. pi., l) witticisms; 2) books of a
coarse character. — L., pi. of facetia. See next
word.

## facetious
facetious, adj., joking. — F. facetieux (fern, fa-
cetieuse), fr. facetie, fr. L. facetia, 'jest,
witticism' (pi. facetiae, 'witty sayings, witticisms,
pleasantry'), fr. facltus, 'elegant, fine, facetious',
which is of uncertain origin. It is perh. rel. to
fax, gen. facis, 'torch', whence the dimin. facula,
'torch'. See facula and -ous.
Derivatives: facelious-ly, adv., facetious-ness, n.

## facia
facia, n. — See fascia.

## facial
facial, adj., of, or pertaining to, the face. — F.,
fr. ML. facialis, fr. L. facies. See face and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivative: facial-ly, adv.

## facient
facient, п., an agent. — Lit. 'a maker, doer', fr.
L. faciens, gen. -entis, pres. part. of.facere, 'to
make, do'. See fact.

## -facient
-facient, suff. meaning 'making, causing to
become' (as calorifacienl, 'making heat', lique-
facient, 'causing to become liquefied'). — L.
-faciens, fr. faciens, pres. part of facere. See
prec. word.

## facile
facile, adj., easy. — F., fr. L. facilis, 'easy', lit.
'feasible', fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See fact
and -lie.
Derivatives: facile-ly, adv., facile-ness, n.

## facilitate
facilitate, tr. v., to make easy. — F. faciliter, fr.
It. facilitare, fr. facilita, 'facility', fr. L. facili-
tatem. See next word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: facilitat-ion, n.

## facility
facility, n. — F. facilite, fr. L. facilitdlem (whence
also It. facilita, OProvenc. facilitat, Sp. facili-
dad), ace. of facilitds, 'easiness, ease, fluency,
willingness, readiness', fr. facilis. See facile
and -ity.

## facinorous
facinorous, adj., wicked, criminal (rare). — L.
facinorosus, 'criminal, atrocious', fr. facinus,
gen. facinoris, 'deed', esp. 'wicked deed, crime,
villainy', fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See fact. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## facio-
facio-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
the face, facial'. — Fr. L. facies, 'face'. See face.

## facsimile
facsimile, п., an exact copy. — L. fac simile,
'make like', (т. fac, imper. of facere, 'to make',
and neut. of similis, 'like'. See fact and similar.
Derivatives: facsimile, adj. and tr. v., facsimil-
ist, п., facsimil-ize, tr. v.

## fact
fact, n. — L. factum, 'deed, act', lit. 'something
done', neut. pp. of facere, 'to make, do; to
perform, accomplish; to act', fr. I.-E. base *dho-,
*dhe-, *dhl-, 'to put, place; to do, make,
construct'. See do and theme and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also feat (which is a doublet of
fact) and the words facade, facient, facile,
facilitate, facility, facinorous, facsimile, faction,
-faction, factor, factory, factotum, factual, affair,
affect, affettuoso, artifact, artifice, benefaction,
benefactor, benefice, benefit, calefaclent, comfit,
confect, confection, counterfeit, defaced, defeat,
defect, deficient, deficit, deific, difficult,
discomfit, dolce far niente, efface, effect, efficacious,
efficient, face, fashion, feasance, feasible,
feature, fecit, feckless, fetish, -fy, infect,
labefaction, maguificent, malefic, maleficence,
malfeasance, manufacture, misfeasance, munificent,
office, orifice, perfect, pontiff, prefect, proficient,
refection, rifaclmento, satisfaction, savoir-faire,
somnifacient, Spinlfex, suffice, sufficient,
superficial, surface, surfeit.

## faction
faction, п., a party or clique. — F., fr. L. fac-
tionem, ace. of foetid, 'a making, doing; party'
(lit. 'persons acting together'), fr. foetus, pp.
of facere, 'to make, do, act'. See fact and -ion
and cp. fashion, which is a doublet of faction.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:298 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: faction-al, adj.

## -faction
-faction, suff. forming nouns meaning 'a making
into something' and corresponding to verbs in
-fy (fr. L. facere). — Fr. L. factio, 'a making,
doing; party'. See prec. word and cp. -ficatlon.
factious, adj., addicted to faction; seditious. — L.
factiosus, fr. factio, 'faction'. See faction and -ous.
Derivatives: factious-ly^ adv., factious-ness, n.
factitioes, adj., artificial. — L. facticius, 'made
by art, artificial', fr. factus, pp. of facere, 'to
make, do'; introduced into English by Sir
Thomas Browne (1605-82) in 1646. See fact
and -ous and cp. fetish, which is a doublet of
factitious.
Derivatives: factitious-ly, adv., faclitious-ness, η.
factitive, adj. — ModL. factitims, fr. L. factus,
pp. of facere, 'to make, do'. See fact and -ive.
Derivative: factitive-ly, adv.

## factor
factor, n. — F. facteur, 'maker, agent', fr. L. fac-
tdrem, ace. of factor, 'maker, doer, performer',
fr. factus, pp. of facere, 'to make, do'. See fact
and agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: factor, tr. v., factor-tal, adj. and п.,
factor-ial-ly, adv.

## factory
factory, n. — ML. factoria, fr. L. factor. See prec.
word and -y (representing L. -ia).

## factotum
factotum, п., a man hired to do all kinds of work;
handy man. — ML., lit. 'one who does
everything', fr. L. fac totum, 'do everything', fr. fac,
imper. of facere, 'to do', and tdtum, neut. of
tolas, 'all'. See fact and total,

## factual
factual, adj., pertaining to facts. — Formed fr.
fact on analogy of actual.
Derivatives: factual-ly, adv., factual-ness, n.

## factum
factum, п., a statement of facts, a fact (law). —
L., prop. neut. pp. of facere. See fact,

## facula
facula, п., one of the bright spots on the disk of
the sun. — L. facula, 'a little torch', dimin. of
fax (OL. faces), 'torch', which is of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: facul-ar, facul-ous, adjs.

## facultative
facultative, adj. — F.facultatif (fem. facultative),
Optional, facultative', fr. faculte, 'option,
faculty'. See next word and -Ive.

## faculty
faculty, n. — OF. faculte (F. faculte), fr. L. facul-
tatem, ace. of facultas, 'capability, power', fr.
*fakli-tds, fr. L. facilis, 'easy'. See facile and
-ty and cp. difficulty,

## fad
fad, п., a whim, craze. — Perh. a back formation
fr. F. fadaise, 'trifle, nonsense, stuff', fr.
OProvenc. fadeza, 'stupidity, foolishness', fr. fat,
'stupid', fr. L. fatuus. See next word.
Derivatives: fadd-ish, adj., fadd-ish-ness, п.,
fadd-y, adj., fadd-i-ness, п., fadd-ism, п.,
faddist, n.

## fade
fade, adj., 1) pale, wan (archaic); 2) insipid. —
F., 'insipid, tasteless, dull', fr. OF. fade, fr.
VL. 'fatidus, a blend of L. fatuus, 'tasteless;
stupid, foolish', and vapidus, 'that has lost its
vapor, flat, flavorless, insipid'. L. fatuus prob.
meant orig. 'blunt, obtuse', and is a derivative
of the I.-E. base *bhat-, 'to beat, strike'. See
natter, 'to beat', and cp. bent and words there
referred to. Cp. also fad, fatuous, infatuate. For
the etymology of vapidus see vapid.
Derivatives: fade-less, adj., fade-less-ly, adv.,

## fad-y
fad-y, adj.

## fade
fade, intr. v., 1) to lose freshness; to languish;
2) to disappear gradually; tr. v., to cause to
fade. — OF. fader, fr. fade. See fade, adj.
Derivatives: fad-ed, adj., fad-ed-ly, adv.,
fading, adj., fad-ing-ly, adv., fad-ing-ness, n.

## faecal
faecal, faeces. — See fecal, feces,

## faerie
faerie, faery, п., fairyland. — Former spellings
of fairy.

## fag
fag, tr. v., to weary, exhaust; intr. v., to labor,
toil. — According to Skeat, possibly a

## corruption of flag
corruption of flag, 'to droop'.

## fag
fag, п., the loose end of anything, esp. of a cloth.
— Of uncertain origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:299 COLUMN:1 -->

## fag
fag, п., cigarette (slang). — Back formation fr.
fag end.

## Fagncene
Fagncene, n. pi., the beech family (hot.) —
Formed fr. Fagus with suff. -nceae.

## fogaceous
fogaceous, adj. (hot.) — See prec. word and
-accous.
fag ead. — Fr. fag, 'the loose end of anything'.

## Fagopyrum
Fagopyrum, п., a genus of plants of the buck-
wheatjamily (bot.) — A ModL., hybrid coined
fr. L. fagus, 'beech' (see beech), and Gk. πυρός,
'wheat' (see pyrene and cp. words there
referred to). The correct form would be Phego-
pyrus, fr. Gk. φηγός, 'oak' (see beech) and πυρός,
'wheat'. Cp. Nothofagns.

## fagot
fagot, faggot, п., a bundle of sticks used for fuel.
— F. fagot, prob. fr. VL. *facus, a back
formation fr. Gk. φάκελος, 'bundle', a word of
uncertain origin, the ending of this word having
been mistaken for the Latin dimin. suff. -ellus.
Cp. It. fagotto, OProvenc. fagot, which also
derive fr. Gk. φάκελος. Ср. fagotto.
Derivatives: fag(g)ot, tr. and intr. v., fag(g)oi-
ing, n.

## fagotto
fagotto, п., bassoon {music). — It., 'bassoon',
prop, 'bundle'. See faggot.

## Fagas
Fagas, п., a genus of trees, the beech (pot.) —
L. fagus, 'beech'. See beech and cp. words there
referred to.

## Fahrenheit
Fahrenheit, п., a type of thermometer. — Named
after the inventor of the mercurial thermometer,
the German physicist Gabriel Daniel Fahrenheit
(1686-1736).

## faience
faience, п., a fine kind of painted and glazed
porcelain. — F. faience, shortened fr. original
vaisselle de Faience ('vessel of Faenza'), fr.
Faenza, name of a town in Italy,

## foil
foil, п., failure. — ME. faille, faile, fr. OF.
faille, faile, fr. faillir. See faa, v.

## fail
fail, intr. and tr. v. — ME. faillen, fatten, fr. OF.
(= F.) faillir, fr. VL. *falltre, corresponding to
L. fallere, 'to deceive'. See folse and cp. faucet,
fault.
Derivatives: fail-ing, п., failing, prep, (q.v.)

## failing
failing, prep. — Prop. pres. part, of the verb foiL

## failure
failure, n. — Orig. failer, fr. AF. failer, which
corresponds to F. faillir; infinitive used as a
noun. See fail, v.

## fain
fain, adj., 1)glad; 2)compelled; 3) willing, eager.
— ME. fain, 'joyful', fr. OE. fxgen, 'glad,
rejoicing', rel. to OS. fagan ON. feginn, 'glad',
OS., OHG. faginSn, Goth, faginon, 'to rejoice',
OE. geflon, OHG. gifehan, 'to rejoice', ON.
faga, 'to adorn'. Cp. fawn, 'to act in a servile
manner'.
Derivatives: fain, adv., gladly, fain, v. (q.v.)

## fain
fain, intr. v., to rejoice. — OE. fiegnian, 'to
rejoice', fr. fxgen. See foin, adj.

## falnaigue
falnaigue, intr. v., to revoke at cards. — Of
uncertain origin.

## faineant
faineant, adj., idle; п., an idler. — F. faineant,
'idler', altered by popular etymol. fr. OF. faig-
nant, feignant, pres. part, of faindre, feindre, 'to
feign', often used in OF. in the sense 'to be
idle'. Faignant was changed by folk etymology
to faineant as though it denoted one who 'does
nothing', fr. faire, 'to do', and neant, 'nothing'.
See feign.

## faint
faint, adj. — ME. faint, feint, 'weak', fr. OF.
feint, 'soft, weak, sluggish', prop. pp. of feindre,
'to feign'. See feign.
Derivatives: faint, intr. v., faint, п., fainl-ish,
adj., faint-ly, adv., faint-ness, п., faints (q.v.)

## faints
faints, also feints, n. pi., the impure spirit which
comes last in the distillation of whisky. — From
prec. word.

## fair
fair, п., a gathering of buyers. — ME. faire, fr.
OF. faire (F. foire), fr. VL. feria (whence also
It. fiera, OProvenc. feira, fiera), fr. L. feriae,
'holidays, festivals', fr. OL. fesiae, which is rel.
to L. fistus, 'solemn, festive, joyous'. See feast
and cp. fane, ferinl.

## fair
fair, adj., beautiful. — ME. fair, fayer, faiger,
fr. OE. fxger, rel. to OS. fagar, ON. fagr, OHG.
fagar, 'beautiful', Goth, fagrs, 'fit', ON. faga,
'to adorn', MLG., Du., MHG. vegen, 'to
sweeep', and cogn. with Lith. puoiiu, Ί
decorate'. Cp. feague.
Derivatives: fair, adv., fair-ly, adv., fair-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:299 COLUMN:2 -->
(airy, n. — ME. faierie, 'enchantment, fairy', fr.
OF. faerie (F. feerie), 'enchantment', fr. foe
(F. fee), 'fairy'. See By, 'fairy'.
Derivatives: fairy, adj., fairy-dom, п., fairy-
hood, п., fairy-ism, п., fairy-like, adj.
fairy tale. — Loan translation of F. conte de fe.

## foith
foith, n. — ME. feith, fr. OF. feid, fei (F. foi),
fr. L.fidem, ace. of fides, 'trust, belief. See bid
and cp. fidelity and words there referred to.
Derivatives: faith-ful, adj., faith-ful-ly, adv.,
faith-ful-ness, п., faith-less, adj., faith-less-ly,
adv., faith-less-ness, n.

## Faith
Faith, fem. PN. — From prec. word.

## fake
fake, tr. v., 1) to counterfeit; 2) to alter, to tamper
with; intr. v., to practice faking (colloq.) —
Perh. a var. of feagne.
Derivatives: fake, п., fak-er, п., fak-er-y, n.

## fakir
fakir, п., a Moslem or Hindu ascetic beggar. —
Arab, faqtr, fr. faqura, 'he was poor'.

## Falange
Falange, п., the Fascist party in Spain. — Sp.
Falange (EspaHola), '(Spanish) Phalanx', fr.
falange, 'phalanx', fr. L. phalanx, gen. phalangis,
fr. Gk. φάλαγξ, gen. φάλαγγος. See phalanx.

## Falangista
Falangista, п., a member of the Falange. — Sp.
Falangista, formed fr. Falange (see prec. word)
with -ista, fr. L. -ista (see -ist). The formation
of the name is erroneous. It should be Falangita,
fr. Gk. φαλαγγίτης, 'soldier in a phalanx', fr.
φάλαγξ.

## Fulasha
Fulasha, п., one of a tribe of dark-skinned Jews
in Abyssinia. — Ethiop., lit. 'exiled, wanderer,
immigrant', fr. falasa, 'he wandered', which is
rel. to Syr. p4ash, 'he broke through', Akkad.
palashu, 'to dig a hole'.

## falbala
falbala, п., flounce, frill. — F., prob. an
alteration of Franco-Provenc. farbella, 'fringe, lace',
which is prob. of imit. origin. Cp. furbelow.

## falcate
falcate, adj., curved like a sickle. — L. falcatus,
'sickle-shaped, curved', fr. falx, gen. falcis,
'sickle', prob. a back formation fr. falcula, 'a
sickle' (which, however, was mistaken for the
dimin. oifalx), fr. Ligurian *dalkla, whence also
Sicil. Ζάγκλη, the ancient name of Messina, lit.
'the hook-shaped town' (rel. to ζάγκλον,
'sickle'). See M. N. Niedermann, Essais d'etymologie
et de critique verbale latines, Neuchatel, 1918,
pp. 17 ft. Cp. falchion, falcon, falcula, falx. For
the ending see verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: falcat-ed, adj.

## falchion
falchion, п., ι) a short curved sword; (poet.) any
sword. — ME.fauchoun, fr. OF.fauchon, fr. VL.
*falcionem, ace. of *falcio, dimin. of L. falx,
gen. falcis, 'sickle'. See prec. word and suff. -ion.

## falciform
falciform, adj., sickle-shaped. — Formed fr.
L. falx, gen. falcis, 'sickle', and forma, 'form,
shape'. See falcate and -form.

## folcon
folcon, n. — ME. faucoun fr. OF. (= F.)faucon,
fr. Late L. falconem, ace. of falcd, prop, 'the
bow-legged (animal)', and identical with L.
falco, -dnis, 'bow-legged', fr. falx, gen. falcis,
'sickle', for which see falcate. For sense
development cp. Gk. 4ρπη, 'sickle; kite'. OHG. falcho
(MHG. mike, G. Falke), MDu. valke (Du. valk),
ON: falki, are Latin loan words. Cp. gerfalcon.
Derivatives: falcon, intr. v., falconer, n. (q.v.)

## Falcoa
Falcoa, п., the typical genus of falcons (ornithol.)
— L. falcd. See falcon.

## falconer
falconer, n. — ME. fauconer, fr. OF. falconier,
fauconier (F. fauconnier), fr. faucon. See falcon.

## falcula
falcula, п., a sharp-pointed claw (zool.) — L.,
'sickle'. See falcate.
Derivatives: falcul-ar, falcul-ate, adjs.

## falderal
falderal, also folderol, п., ι) a refrain in old
songs; 2) a trifle. — Perh. of imitative origin.

## faldstool
faldstool, п., a folding stool. — OE. faldestoel,
fr. ML. faldistolium, fr. OHG. faldstuol, which
is compounded of faldan, 'to fold', and stuol,
'stool, chair'. See fold and stool and cp. fanteuil.

## Falernian
Falernian, adj., pertaining to the ager Falernus
('Falernian field') in Italy, or to the wine grown
in it. — Formed with suff. -Ian fr. L. Falernus,
'Falernian', fr. Falerii, name of the capita] of
the Falisci. Cp. next word.

## Faliscan
Faliscan, adj., pertaining to the Falisci, a people
of ancient Etruria. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Falisci, 'the Faliscans', which is rel. to
Falerii, name of the capital of the Falisci. Cp.
prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:299 COLUMN:3 -->

fall, intr. v. — ME. fallen, fr. OE. feallan, rel. to
ΟΝ., Swed. falla, Du. vallen, OHG. fallan,
MHG. vallen, vain, G. fallen, Dan. falde and
prob. cogn. with Arm. p'ul, 'downfall', p'lanim,
Ί fall down', Lith. puolu, pulti, Lett, piiolu, pull,
'to fall', OPruss. aupallai, 'finds' (orig. 'falls
upon'). All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
'phol-, 'to fall'. Cp. fell, tr. v.
Derivatives: fall, n. (q.v.), fall-ing, verbal n.
and adj.

## fall
fall, n. — Fr. fall, v. In the sense of 'autumn',
fall is short for 'the season of the falling leaves'.

## fnllacions
fnllacions, adj. — L. fallacidsus, 'deceitful,
deceptive, fallacious', fr. fallax, gen. falldcis,
'deceitful'; fr. fallere, pp. falsus, 'to deceive'.
See false and -acious.
Derivatives: fallacious-ly, adv. ,fallacious-ness, n.

## fallacy
fallacy, n. — L. fallacia, 'deceit, artifice,
stratagem', fr. fallax, gen. falldcis. See prec. word
and -y (representing L. -ία).

## fallal
fallal, п., a bit of finery. — An invented word.

## fallalery
fallalery, п., valueless finery. — Formed from
prec. word with suff. -ery.

## fallen
fallen, pp. of fall. — ME. fallen, fr. OE. feallen,
'fallen', fr. feallan, 'to fall'. See fall, v.

## fallible
fallible, adj. — Late L. fallibilis, fr. L. fallere,
'to deceive'. See false and -ible.
Derivatives: fallibil-ity, п., fallible-ness, n.fal-
libl-y, adv.

## Fallopian
Fallopian, adj., discovered or described by
Gabriel Fallopius (in Italian Gabriele Fallopio),
the celebrated Italian anatomist (1523-62).

## Fallopian tubes
Fallopian tubes, the oviducts of mammals. — So
called because they were discovered and first
described by Fallopius. See prec. word.
(allow, adj., brownish yellow. —· OE. fealo, gen.
fealwes, 'dull-colored, yellow, yellowish red,
brown', rel. to OS. falu, ON. fair, MDu. valu,
vale, Du. vaal, OHG. falo, MHG. vai, vaiwer,
G. fahl, falb, fr. I.-E. base *pel-, 'dark-colored,
gray', whence also OI. palilah, 'gray', panduh
(for *paln-du-), 'whitish, pale', Arm. alik',
'waves; white beard', alevor, 'gray', Gk. πελιός
(prob. for *πελι-^ός), 'livid', πελιτνός, Ion.
πελιδνός, 'gray', πελλός, (for *πελιός or *πελ-
νός), 'dark-colored, dusky', πελαργός, 'stork*
(for *πελα^-αργός), 'stork', lit. 'the blackish
white bird', πέλεια, 'pigeon', lit. 'the dark-
colored bird', πολιός (prob. for *πολι-/ός),

pullus, 'dark-colored, blackish gray, dusky',
palumbes, 'wood pigeon', lit. 'the dark-colored
bird', OSIav. plavu, Lith. palvas, 'sallow', pil-
kas, 'grey', pilvi, 'mud, mire', pell, 'mouse',
OPruss. poalis, 'pigeon', Mir. Hath, W. Ilwyd,
'gray'. Cp. appall, favel, pale, adj., pall, v.,
pallid, pallor, Pelargonium, Pellaean, peristeronlc,
Pleind, polyomyelitis.

## fallow
fallow, п., land plowed, but left unsown. — ME.
falwe,falow, fr. OE.fealg,fealh, 'harrow', rel. to
OHG. felga, of s.m., MHG. valgen, velgen, 'to
plow up', and cogn. with Gaul, olka (for
"polka-), whence Late L. oka, 'land fit for plowing'.
I.-E. *polkd- lit. means 'something turned', and
derives fr. base *pel-, 'to turn', whence also Gk.
πόλος, 'pivot (on which something turns)'. For
other derivatives of base "pel- see colony. Cp.
felly.
Derivatives: fallow, adj. and tr. v.

## folse
folse, adj. — ME. fats, ft. OF. fab, fem. false
(F. faux, fem. fausse), fr. L. falsus, pp. of'fallere,
'to deceive', which is of uncertain etymology.
It is perh. cogn.^with Gk. φηλός or φηλος,
'deceitful', φηλόω, Dor. φαλόω, Ί deceive',
φήλωμα, 'deception', φήλωσις, 'deceit'. Ср. fail,
fallncy, faucet, fault.
Derivatives: false, adv., false-hood, п., false-ly,
adv., false-ness, п., falsify (q.v.), fals-ity, n.
falsetto п., an artificial voice (mus.) — It.,
dimm. of falso, 'false', fr. L. fabus. See prec.
word.

## falsiflcate
falsiflcate, n. — Late L. falsificatus, pp. of falsi·
ficare. See falsify and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: falsification (q.v.), falsificat-or, n.

## falsification
falsification, n. — F., fr. Late L. falsificationem,
ace. of falsificatid, fr. falsificatus, pp. of falsi-
ficare. See next word and -ion.

## falsify
falsify, tr. v. —F. falsifier, fr. Late L. falsificare,
