<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:300 COLUMN:1 -->
'to falsify'. See false and -fy.
Derivative: falsifi-er, n.

## falsity
falsity, n. — OF. falsete (F. faussete), fr. Late
L. falsitatem, ace. offalsitds, 'falsity, falsehood*,
fr. L. falsus. See false and -ity.

## fnlter
fnlter, intr. v., to waver. — ME. falieren, of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: falter, п., falter-ing, adj., faller-
ing-ly, adv.

## falx
falx, п., a sickle-shaped structure (anat.) — L.
falx, 'sickle'. See falcate.

## Fama
Fama, п., the personification of rumor in Roman
mythology. — L. See fame.

## lame
lame, n. — F. fame, fr. L. fama, 'talk, report,
rumor, tradition, reputation, lit. 'saying', from
the stem αϊ for, farl, pp. fatus, 'to speak', rel. to
fateri, 'to confess', fdbula, 'narrative, account,
tale, story', fas, 'divine law' (lit. 'utterance'), fr.
I.-E. base *bha-, 'to speak, tell, say', whence
also OI. bhanati, 'speaks', Arm. bay, gen. bayi,
'word, term', bay, 'he said', ban, gen. bani,
'word, speech, judgment', Gk. φημί, Ί say',
φήμη, Dor. φαμά, 'voice, report, rumor', φάτις,
'saying, speech, report', OSlav. bajg, bajaii, 'to
talk, tell', basnl, 'fable, tale, charm', OE. boian,
'to boast', ON. ban, OE. ben, 'prayer, request'.
Cp. phone, 'speech sound'. Cp. also abandon,
affable, aphasia, aphemia, apophasis, ban, 'to
prohibit', ban, 'edict', bandit, banish, bifarious,
blame, blaspheme, boon, confabulate, confess,
defamation, defame, euphemism, fabulous,
famous, fascinate, fate, infamous, infamy,
infant, infantry, maltifarious, nefarious, -phasia,
-phemia, Polyphemus, preface, prefntory,
profess, prophet, trlfarious.
Derivatives: fame, tr. v., fam-ed, adj.

## familiar
familiar, adj. — OF. (= F.) familier, fr. L./ami-
liaris, 'pertaining to a household, domestic',
dissimilated fr. "familid-lis, fr. familia,
'household'. See family and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: familiar, п., familiar-ism, п.,
familiarity (q.v.), familiar-ize, tr. v., familiar-iz-
alion, п., familiar-iz-er, п., familiar-ly, adv.

## familiarity
familiarity, n. — F. familiarite, fr. L. familiari-
talem, ace. of familiaritas, fr. familiaris. See
familiar and -ity.

## family
family, n. — L. familia, fr. famulus, fr. OL. famul,
'servant', which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly means lit. 'belonging to the house', and
derives fr. I.-E. base *dh'-mo-, 'house', whence
also OI. dhaman, 'seat, house', Gk. θαιμός
(Hesychius), 'house'. Base *dh'-mo- is an
enlargement of base *dhi-, 'to put, place; to do,
make'. See do and fact and cp. famulus and the
second element in forisfamiliate.
Derivatives: famili-at, ad}., familiar (q.v.)

## famine
famine, n. — F., fr. VL. *famino, fr. L. fames,
'hunger', which is of uncertain origin. For the
ending see -be (representing L. -ina). Cp.
next word.

## famish
famish, tr. and intr. v. — Formed on analogy of
synonymous verbs in -ish fr. L. fames, 'hunger'.
See prec. word.
Derivative: famish-ing, adj.

## famous
famous, adj. — OF. fameus (F. fameux), fr. L.
fumosus, 'much talked of, renowned', fr. fama.
See lame and -ous.
Derivatives: famous-ly, adv., famous-ness, n.

## famulus
famulus, п., attendant, esp. on a magician. —
L., 'servant'. See family.

## fan
fan, п., an instrument for winnowing. — ME., fr.
OE. fann, fr. L. vannus, 'winnowing fan'. See
van, 'winnowing fan'.
Derivatives: fan, tr. and intr. v., to winnow,
fann-er, п., fann-ing, n.

## fan
fan, п., an enthusiastic supporter of any sport,
esp. of base-ball (U.S. Slang). — Shortened fr.
fanatic.

## fana
fana, п., nullification of the will of the individual
before the divine will (an important principle
of Sufism). — Arab, fana', 'disappearance', inf.
of faniya, 'he passed away, disappeared', rel. to

furrier, п., ι) one who shoes horses; ablacksmith;

fat, adj. — ME. fait, fat, fr. OE. fiett, contraction

feilr, OFris. fatt, fit, MLG., MDu., Du. vet,
OHG. fei3it, MHG. vet3(e)t, G. feist, 'fat' (G.
fett, 'fat', is a LG. loan word). These adjectives
are prop. pps. of Teut. "faitian, 'to feed, fatten'
(appearing in ON. feita, OHG. feiseri), fr. I.-E.
base *poid-, *pld-, 'to abound in water, milk,
fat, etc.', whence also Gk. πίδύειν, 'to gush
forth', πΐδαξ, 'spring, fountain', πΐδήεις, 'rich
in springs'. Base *poid-, *pld-, is a
-(/-enlargement of base "pot-, *pt-, 'sap, juice; to abound
in sap or juice, etc.', whence OI. payate, 'swells,
exuberates', payas-, 'water, milk', Lith. pienas,
'milk'. Cp. OI. pituh, 'juice, sap, resin, drink',
ptvan, 'fat, fatty', pfvah 'fat, grease', Gk. πίτυς,
'the pine tree', πίων, 'fat, wealthy', πϊαρ, 'fat,
tallow', πϊμελή, 'fat', πίσσα (for *πίκια), 'pitch',
L. pinguis, 'fat', pituita, 'slime, phlegm, viscous
moisture', L. pix, 'pitch', opimus, 'fat, fertile,
rich', which also derive from enlargements of
base 'poi-, *pt-. Cp. pay, 'to coat with pitch',
pimelosis, pinguid, pip, pitch, 'a resinous sub-

stance', pituitary and the second element in
propionic Cp. also pine, the tree, and words

fat-ling, п., fat-ness,n.,fatt-en,tT.v.,fatt-ish,SLd)„

## fat
fat, tr. and intr. v. — ME. fatten, fr. OE. fxttian,
'to grow fat', it. fsett, 'fat'. See fat, adj.

## fat
fat, п., vessel. — ME. fat, fr. OE. fset; a var. of
vat (q.v.) Cp. fettle.

## fatal
fatal, adj., — OF. (= F.) fatal, it. L.fStalis,
'ordained by fate', fr. fatum, 'fate'. See fate and
adj. surf. -al.
Derivatives: fatal-ism, п., fatal-ist, п., fatal-ist-
ic, adj., fatal-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., fatality (q.v.)

## fatality
fatality, n. — F. fatalite, fr. VL. fatdlitStem, ace.
of fatalitas, 'fatal necessity', fr. L. fatalis. See
prec. word and -ity.

## fata morgana
fata morgana, mirage. — It.; a name orig. given
to the mirages that are often to be seen in the
streets of Messina. The name lit. means 'the
fairy Morgana*; Morgana itself derives fr. Arab.
marjan, 'pearl', used also as a female name, and
is to be explained from the Arabic popular
belief which ascribes mirages to the work of the
sorceress Marjan. See fairy and margaric,
marguerite.

## fate
fate, n. — ME., fr. OF. fate, fr. L. fatum, Oracle,
fate, destiny', lit. 'that which is spoken', neut.
pp. of for, fan, 'to speak; to foretell', used as
a noun, rel. to fama, 'report, rumor, tradition,
reputation'. See feme and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also fandango and the second
element in Boniface, mauvais.
Derivative: fat-ed, adj.

## fatefal
fatefal, adj. — Coined by the English poet
Alexander Pope (1688-1744) fr. fate and -fid.
Derivatives: fateful-ly, adv., fateful-ness, n.

## father
father, n. — ME. fader, fr. OE. fseder, rel. to OS.
fadar, ON. fadir, Dan., Swed. fader, OFris.
feder, Du. vader, OHG. fater, MHG., G. rater,
Goth, fadar (occurring only once), and cogn.
with OI. pilar-, Toch. А рйсаг, В pacer. Arm.
hayr, Gk. πατήρ, L. pater, Olr. athir, 'father'.
All these words are traceable to pa, a child's
word for 'father'. Cp. pater, 'father'. Cp. also
expatriate, impetrate, Jupiter, padre, parricide,
patriarch, Patrician, patrimony, patron, pattern,
pere, perpetrate, repair, 'to resort', repatriate.
Derivatives .father, tr. ν „father-hood, a.,
fatherland (q.v.), father-less, adj., father-ly, adj.,
father-li-ness, n.

## fatherland
fatherland, n. — Loan translation of G.
Valeriana, which itself is a loan translation of L.
patria (scil. terra), 'native land', lit. 'father's
land'.

## fathom
fathom, n. — ME. fadme, fathme, 'fathom, the
outstretched arms', fr. OE. fiedm, 'the
outstretched arms, embrace, bosom, fathom', rel.
to OH.fadmr, 'embrace, bosom', OFris. fethem,
'thread', OS. fathmos (pi.), 'the outstretched
arms, fathom', OHG. fadum,- fadam, MHG.
vadem, raden, G. Faden, 'thread', Dan. favn,
Norw., Swed. farm, 'fathom', fr. Teut. "fap-ma,
'embrace', corresponding to I.-E. *pet-lma,
whence—with the regular loss ot the initial ρ—
OW.etem, W. edaf, 'thread'; fr. I.-E.base*pet-,
'to spread', which occurs also in Gk. πεταννύνοα,
"to spread out', πέταλον, 'leaf, L.patere, 'to
be open', patera, 'a broad flat dish used in
offerings', patulus, 'extended, open', passus (for
*pat-tus), "step, pace', pandere, 'to spread out',
Lith. petys, OPruss. pen is, 'shoulder'. Cp. fotner,
'a weight'. Cp. also expand, expanse, pace,
pan, 'a broad vessel', pandiculation, pandy,
passage, passim, passport, paten, patent, patera,
patibulary, patina, patio, patulous, petal, petalon,
Petasites, petasns, sur- pass, trespass.
Derivatives: fathom, tr. v. (q.v.), fathom-age, п.,
fathom-er, п., fathom-less, adj., fathom-less-ly,
adv., fathom-less-ness, n.

## fathom
fathom, tr. v. — ME. fadmen, fathmen, fr. OE.
fxdmian, 'to embrace, surround, envelop', fr.
fsedm. See fathom, n.

## fatidic
fatidic, fatidical, adj., prophetic. — L. fatidicus,
'predicting future events, prophetic,
prophesying', compounded ot fatum, 'prophecy, fate,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:302 COLUMN:2 -->
destiny', and dicere, 'to say, tell'. See fate and
diction.

## fatigue
fatigue, n. — F„ back formation fr. fatiguer, 'to
fatigue', fr. L. fatigare, 'to weary, tire, vex,
worry', fr. *fati-agos, *faii-igos, 'driving toward
exhaustion', fr. *fati, 'exhaustion, weariness',
and agere, 'to drive'. *Fa-ti, the first element of
this compound is rel. to affatim (whence with
back formation fatim), 'sufficiently' (lit. 'to
weariness'). For the second element see agent,
adj., and cp. the second element incastigate and
in words there referred to. Cp. also indefatigable.

## fatigue
fatigue, tr. v. — F. fatiguer. See fatigue, n.
Derivatives: fatigue-less, adj., fatigu-ing, adj.,
fatigu-ing-ly, adv.

## fatuity
fatuity, п., silliness, foolishness. — F. fatuile, fr.
L. fatuitatem, ace. of fatuitas, 'foolishness,
folly', fr. fatuus. See next word and -ity.

## fatuous
fatuous, adj., silly, foolish. — L. fatuus, 'foolish,
silly, simple; tasteless'. See fade and cp. in-
fatnate. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.
Derivatives: fatuous-ly, adv., fatuous-ness, n.

## faubourg
faubourg, п., outskirts, suburb. —ME. faubourg,
fabour, fr. MF. faux bourg (F. faubourg), fr.
OF. forsbourc, lit. 'that which is outside of the
town', fr. OF. pref. fors, 'outside' (fr. L. forts)
and bourc, 'town'; see forum and borough. The
change of OF. forsbourc to F. faubourg (MF.
faux bourg), lit. 'a false town', is due to folk
etymology; the suburb was looked upon as a
not genuine town.

## faucal
faucal, adj., pertaining to the upper part of the
throat. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
fauces, 'the upper part of the throat', which is
of uncertain origin. Cp. suffocate.

## fauces
fauces, n. pi., the cavity at the back of the mouth,
leading to the pharynx (anat.) — L. See prec.
word.

## faucet
faucet, п., a tap for drawing liquid. — F.fausset,
'vent plug', fr. fausser, 'to make false, to falsify',
fr. Late L. falsare, fr. L. falsus. See false and -et.

## faucitis
faucitis, п., inflammation of the fauces (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. fauces and -itis,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## faugh
faugh, interj.; an exclami.;ion of disgust or
abhorrence. — Imitative.

## faujasite
faujasite, п., a nau.dm, calcium and aluminum
silicate (mineral.) — Named after the French
geologist Barthelemy Faujas de Saint-Fond
(1741-1819). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## fault
fault, n. — ME. faute, fr. OF. (= F.) faute, fr.
VL. 'fallita, fem. pp. of fallere, 'to deceive,
disappoint; to fail'; see fail, v., and cp. default
The / in fault is intrusive and was originally
mute in pronunciation; its insertion into the
word is due to the influence of L. fallere. For
the insertion of the / cp. vault.
Derivatives: fault, intr. v., fault-ful, adj., fault-
ful-ly, adv., fault-ing, п., fault-less, adj., fault-
less-ly, adv., fault-y, adj., faulti-ly, adv., fault-
i-ness, n.

## faun
faun, п., one of a class of deities represented with
horns, pointed ears and goat's feet. — L. Fau-
nus. See fauna.

## Fauna
Fauna, п., sister of Faunus (Greek mythol.) —
See next word.

## fauna
fauna, п., a collective name for the animals of a
certain region or time. — ModL., fr. L. Fauna,
goddess of fruitfulness in Roman mythology,
sister of Faunus. These names are of uncertain
origin. They are perh. cogn. with Gk. θαϋνος
(Hesychius), 'wild beast', Illyr. Δαϋνος, Daunus
(name of a fabulous king said to have reigned
in a part of Apulia), fr. I.-E. *dhau-no-, 'wild
beast, strangled, enlargement of base *dhau-, 'to
strangle', whence OSlav. davljg, daviti, 'to
strangle', Goth, af-dau-ips, 'maltreated'. Cp.
faun, Faunus, Fauna. Cp. also avifauna. Cp. also
Thos. The name fauna was introduced into
zoology by the Swedish botanist Carolus
Linnaeus (Karl von Linne (1707-78); cp. flora.
Derivatives: faun-al, adj., pertaining to the
fauna; faun-isl, п., a student of fauna, faun-ist-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## faunology
faunology, п., zoogeography. — A hybrid coined
fr. fauaa and Gk. -XoyCS, fr. -λύγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:302 COLUMN:3 -->
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## Faunus
Faunus, п., an Italian deity of agriculture;
identified later with Pan. — L. See Fauna, fauna,

## fauteuil
fauteuil, п., an armchair. — F., fr. OF. falde-
stoel, faldestueil, faudeteuil, fr. Frankish *faldi-
stol, which is rel. to OHG. faldstuol. See
faldstool. It. faldistorio, 'faldstool', OProvenc. falde-
stol, 'armchair, chorister's desk, lectern', and
Sp. facistol, 'chorister's desk, lectern', are also
Teut. loan words.

## feint pas
feint pas, a mistake, blunder. — F., lit. 'false
step'. See false and pace,

## favel
favel, adj., fallow (said of a horse). — OF. favel,
fauvel, fr. WTeut. 'falwa, whence also OF.
falve (F. fame), OProvenc. falp, It. falbo,
'fallow, tawny'. Cp. OHG. falo, 'fallow, tawny,
pale', and see fallow, adj.
Derivative: favel, a.

## favonian
favonian, adj., pertaining to the west wind. —
L. Favonianus, fr. Favdnius, 'west wind'. See next
word.

## Favonius
Favonius, п., personification of the west wind
(Roman mythol.) — L. Favonius, 'west wind', dis-
similated fr. *fovdnius, lit. 'the warming wind',
h.fovere, 'to warm'. Cp. favilla, 'glowing ashes',
which stands for *fovilla, hence is of the same
base. See foment and cp. Foehn. Favonius is not
rel. to L. favere, 'to favor'.

## favor
favor, favour, n. — ME. favor, favour, fr. OF.
favor, favour (F. faveur), fr. L. favdrem, ace. of
favor, 'good will, inclination, favor', coined by
Cicero from the stem of L. favere, 'to be
inclined toward, be favorable, befriend', which is
prob. cogn. with OSlav. govejQ, goveti, Czech.
hoveti, 'to indulge, spare'.

## favor
favor, favour, tr. v. — OF. favorer, fr. favor,
favour, 'favor'. See favor, n.
Derivatives: favo(u)r-ed, adj., favo(u)r-ed-ty,
adv.,favo(u)r-ed-ness, n.,favo(u)r-er,
a.,favouring, adj., favo(u)r-ing-ty, adv.

## favorable
favorable, favourable, adj. — F. favorable, fr.
L. favorabilis, 'favored, in favor', fr. favor. See

Derivatives: favo(u)rable-ness, п., favo(u)rabl-y,
adv.

## favorite
favorite, favourite, adj. — F. favori (fem.

Derivative: favo(u)rit-ism, n.

## favose
favose, adj., resembling a honeycomb. — L.
favosus, fr. favus, 'honeycomb'. See next word

## favus
favus, п., a skin disease caused by a parasitic
fungus (med.) — L. favus, 'honeycomb', of
uncertain origin; so called in allusion to the
depressions left on the scalp.

## fawn
fawn, п., a young deer. — ME. foun, fr. OF.

## feon
feon, faon, 'the young of an animal', esp. 'a

Derivatives: fawn, adj., fawn-colored; fawn,
intr. and tr. v., to give birth (to a fawn).

nian, fagnian, fahnian, collateral forms of OE.

fxgenian, flegnian, 'to rejoice', fr. fagen, resp.

fiegen, 'glad'. See fain.

ly, adv., fawn-ing-ness, n.

pacisci, 'to covenant, make a treaty, agree,

fay, fairy. — OF. fae (F.fee), fr. VL. fata,

feague, tr. v., to whip, beat (jahsot.) — Prob. fr.

## Teal
Teal, adj., faithful. — OF. feal, a collateral form

## fealty
fealty, n. — OF. fealte, feelte, fr. L. fidelitatem,

## fear
fear, n. — ME. fere, feer, fr. OE. fxr, 'sudden
danger, calamity', rel. to OS. far, 'ambush', ON.
far, 'harm, distress, deception', Du. gevaar,

fear, tr. and intr. v. — ME. feren, 'to frighten;

Derivatives: fear-er, п., fear-ing-ly, adv.

## feasance
feasance, п., the doing of a condition, duty (law).
— AF. fesance, corresponding to OF. (= F.)
faisance, which derives fr. OF., F. faisant, pres.
part, of faire, Ίο make, do', fr. L. facere. See

## feasible
feasible, adj., that can be done. — ME. faisibte, fr.
OF. faisible, ix.fais-, imperf. stem of faire, 'to
make, do', fr. L. facere. See prec. word and
-ible.
Derivatives: feasibil-ity, п., feastbl-y, adv.

## feast
feast, n. — OF. fesle (F. fete), 'festival, feast',
fr. VL. festa (scil. dies), 'festival, feast, holiday',
fern, of the Latin adjective fistus, 'solemn,
festive, joyous'; which is rel. to OL. fesiae (whence
L. feriae), 'holidays, festivals', fanum (for *fas-
nom), 'a consecrated place'. Cp. It. festa, OPro-
venc., Catal., Port, festa, Sp. fiesta, 'feast,
holiday', and see fane, feria. Cp. also festival,
festive, festoon, Festus, fete. The above Latin
words derive fr. I.-E. base "dhes- (= L. "fes-,
*/as-), 'holy', whence also Gk. θεός, 'god', OI.
dhisnyah, 'pious, devoted'. See ist theism and
cp. words there referred to.

## feast
feast, intr. and tr. v. — ME. festen, fr. OF. fester
(F. filer), fr. feste, 'festival, feast'. See feast, n.

## feat
feat, п., a deed. — ME. fait, fet, fr. OF. fait, fet
(F. fait), fr. L. factum, 'deed', neut. pp. of
facere, 'to make, do', used as a noun. See fact,
which is a doublet of feat, and cp. feat, adj.,
and featare.

## feat
feat, adj., neat, dexterous (archaic). — ME. fete,
fr. OF. fait, fet, 'made', fr. L. factus, pp. of
facere. See feat, n.
Derivative: feat-ly, adv.

fj0r, Dan. fjxr, MLG., MDu. vedere, veder

corresponding to I.-E. *petra-, zero degree *ptera-,
'wing; feather', whence OI. putram, 'wing,

OE. gefiderian, it. feder, 'feather'. See feather, n.

## feature
feature, n. — ME. feture, 'shape, form, feature',

fr. OF. failure, feture, 'fashion, shape, form',

## febri-
febri-, combining form meaning 'fever'. — L.

## febri-
febri-, fr. febris, 'fever'. See fever.

## febrifugal
febrifugal, adj., dispelling fever. — See next word
and adj. suff. -al.

## febrifuge
febrifuge, п., a remedy for allaying or removing
fever (med.) — F. febrifuge, lit. 'driving fever
away', fr. L. febris, 'fever', and fug-are, 'to put

## febrile
febrile, adj., l)pertaining to fever; 2) feverish;
3) caused by fever. — F. febrile, fr. Late L. fe-

See fever and -He.
Derivative: febril-ily, n.

## February
February, n. — L. Februarius, 'the month of
purification', fr. februare, 'to purify, expiate', fr. fe-
bruum, 'means of purification', which is of
uncertain origin. For the ending see suff. -ary.

## fecal
fecal, faecal, adj., pertaining to feces. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. faeces. See feces.

## feces
feces, faeces, n. pi., excrement. — L. faeces, pi.
of faex, 'dregs, sediment'; of uncertain origin.
Cp. fecula, feculent, defecate,

## fecit
fecit, v., he (or she) made (it). — L., 3rd pers.
sing. perf. of facere, 'to make'. See fact,

## feckless
feckless, adj., 1) ineffective; 2) thoughtless. —
Scot., short for effectless. See effect and -less.
Derivatives: feckless-ly, adv., feckless-ness, n.

## fecula
fecula, п., starch. — L. faecula, 'burnt tartar,
salt of tartar', dimin. formed fr. faex, gen. fae-
cis, 'dregs'. See feces. For the ending see suff.
-tile.
feculence, n. — F. feculence, fr. L. faeculentia,
'dregs, lees', fr. faeculentus. See next word and
-ce.

## feculent
feculent, adj., muddy; foul. — F. feculent, fr.
L. faeculentus, 'abounding in dregs', fr. faeces.
See feces and -ent.

## fecund
fecund, adj., fruitful. — F. fecond, fr. L. fe-
cundus, 'fruitful, fertile', which is rel. to fl-nus,
'proceeds, increase', lit. 'that which is produced',
fe-lare, 'to suck', fe-mina, 'a woman', fi-lius,
(for *fe-lios), 'son', fr. Latin base *fe-,
corresponding to I.-E. base *dhe(i)-, *dh'(i)-,
*dht-, 'to suck, suckle'. See filial and cp. words
there referred to. For the suff. -cundus in L. fe-
cundus cp. fa-cundus, 'eloquent' (fr. fart, 'to
speak'), ira-cundus, 'irascible' (fr. ira, 'anger'),
ju-cundus, 'pleasant' (fr. juvare, 'to help, aid,
delight'), rubi-cundtis, 'reddish' (fr. rubere, 'to
be red'), vere-cundus, 'shamefaced' (fr. vereri,
'to observe with awe, revere'). Cp. Jocund,
rubicund, verecund.

## fecundate
fecundate, tr. v., to make fecund; to impregnate.
— L. fecundatus, pp. of flcundare, 'to make
fruitful, fertilize', fr. fecundus. See prec. word
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: fecundat-ion, п., fecundat-ive, adj.,
fecundator (q.v.), fecundat-ory, adj.

## fecundity
fecundity, п., fruitfulness. — L. fecunditas, 'fruit-
fulness, fertility', fr. fecundas. See fecund and
-ity.

## federal
federal, adj. — F. federal, from L. foedus, gen.
foederis, 'league, treaty, covenant', which stands
in gradational relationship to fidere, 'to trust',
fidelis, 'true, faithful, sincere'. See fidelity and
cp. federate, confederate. For the ending see
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: federal, п., federalism (q.v.),
federalist (q.v.),federal-ize, tr. v., federal-iz-alion, п.,
federal-ly, adv., federal-ness, n.

## federalism
federalism, п., the principle of federal union. —
Coined by the English statesman and author
Edmund Burke (1729-97) fr. federal and suff.
-ism.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:303 COLUMN:3 -->

## federalist
federalist, п., an adherent of federalism. —
Coined by Edmund Burke fr. federal and suff.
-ist. See prec. word.

## federate
federate, tr. v., to unite into a league or
federation. — L. foederatus, pp. of foederare, 'to
establish by treaty', fr. foedus, gen. foederis,
'treaty'. See federal and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: feaerat-ion, п., federation-ist, п.,

## federat-ive
federat-ive, adj., federat-ive-ly, adv.

## federate
federate, adj., leagued; confederate. — L.
foederatus, 'leagued together, allied', pp. of foederare.
See federate, v.

## Fedora
Fedora, fem. PN. — F. Fedora, fern, of Russ.
Fedor, fr. Gk. Θεόδωρος, lit. 'gift of God', which
is compounded of θεός, 'god', and δώρον, 'gift'.
See Theodore.

## fedora
fedora, п., a kind of soft felt hat. — So called
from Fedora, a play written by Victorien Sardou
in 1882. For sense development cp. trilby.

## fee
fee, п., cattle; property; money (obsol.) — ME.
feoh, fr. OE. feoh, 'cattle, money, property,
wealth', rel. to OS. fehu, ON. ft, Dan. fie,
Swed. fa, OFris. fia, Du. vee, OHG. feho, fihu,
MHG. vihe, vich, G. Vieh, 'cattle', Goth, faihu,
'money, fortune', and cogn. with OI. pasu,
pasu, pasuh, Avestic pasu-, L. реей, 'cattle',
pecus, gen. pecoris, 'cattle', pecus, gen. pecudis,
'a single head of cattle', pecunia, 'money,
property', Umbr. pequo, Lith. pekus, OPruss. pecku,
'cattle', fr. I.-E. base *peku-, 'the woolly
animal', whence 'sheep, cattle, property, money'.
This base is an enlargement of base *pek-, 'to
pluck (wool or hair); hairy, woolly', whence
OI. paksman, 'eyebrows, hair', Pers. pashm,
'wool', Arm. asr, gen. asu, 'sheep's wool, fleece',
Gk. πέκος, πόκος, Aeol. πέκκος, 'uncombed
wool, fleece', Gk. πέκειν, Att. πεκτεΐν, 'to
comb, shear', Gk. κτείς, gen. κτενός (for
*pfcten-), 'comb', L. pexus, 'woolly', pectere,
'to comb, shear', pecten, 'comb', pectus, gen.
pectoris, 'breast*, Toch. A passam, В pascane
(dual.), 'the breasts' (prop, 'the hairy part of
the body'), OE. feax, OS., OHG. fahs, 'hair',
ON. fax, 'mane', OE. feohtan, 'to fight' (orig.
'to pluck, pull, scuffle'). Cp. fee, 'estate', flght,
and the first element in fellow. Cp. also cteno·,'
pashm, paxwax, Pecora, pecten, pectinate,
pectoral, peculate, pecuniary, impecunious, peignoir,
pekin, 'a civilian', petto, poitrel, and the second
element in parapet.
Derivative: fee, tr. v., to pay a fee to.

## fee
fee, п., estate. — AF. fee, fie, fr. OF. feu, fieu,
fiu, fr. ML. feum, fevum, a word of Teut.
origin; cp. Goth, faihu, 'property', OHG. fihu,
'cattle'. See fee, 'cattle, money', and cp. feu,
feud, 'estate', fief, feodary, feoffee.

## feeble
feeble, adj. — ME. feble, fr. OF. feble (F. faible),
formed, with dissimilation, fr. L. flebilis,
'lamentable, doleful, mournful', lit. 'to be wept
over', fr. flere, 'to weep', which is of imitative
origin. Cp. It. fievole, OProvenc. feble, 'weak',
which also derive fr. L. flebilis. Cp. also foible.
Derivatives: feeble-ness, п., feebl-ish, adj.,
feebl-y, adv.

## feed
feed, tr. and intr. v. — ME. feden, fr. OE. Sedan,
rel. to OS. fddjan, ON. fada, OFris. ftda,
OHG. fuotan, Goth, fddjan, 'to feed', Goth.
fodeins, OE. foda, 'food'. See food.
Derivatives: feed, п., feed-er, п., feed-ing, adj.,
feed-y, adj.

## feel
feel, tr. and intr. v. — ME. felen, fr. OE. ftlan,
rel. to OS. gi-folian, OFris. ftla, MDu., Du.
voelen, OHG. fuolen, MHG. viielen, G. fiihlen,
'to feel', ON. falma, 'to grope', and prob. cogn.
with OI. a-sphalayati, 'he causes to collide,
strikes', Gk. ψάλλειν, 'to pluck, twitch the harp,
play on a stringed instrument', ψάλμα, 'tune
played on a musical instrument', ψαλμός, 'a
plucking, twitching of the harp', later 'song,
psalm', ψαλτήρ, 'harper', ψαλτήριον, 'stringed
instrument, harp', ψαλμωδία, 'a singing to the
harp', ψηλαφάω, Ί feel or grope about'
(compounded of *ψαλα, 'a twitching', and άφάω, Ί
touch'), L. palpare, 'to touch softly, stroke', pal-
pitare, 'to move quickly', palpebra, 'eyelid', lit.
'that which moves quickly'. All these words
prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *(s)phel-, *(s)phal-,
'to strike softly'. Cp. palp, palpable, palpebra.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:304 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 277 | FENIAN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:304 COLUMN:1 -->
psalm, psalter, psaltery, and the first element in
Pselaphidae.
Derivatives: feel, п., feel-er, п., feel-ing, n. and
adj., feel-ing-ly, adv.

## fehmgericht
fehmgericht, n. — See vehmgericht.

## feign
feign, tr. and intr. v. — ME. feinen, fr. OF.
(= F.) feign-, pres. part, stem of feindre, fr. L.
fingere, 'to form, shape, invent', fr. I.-E. base
'dheigh-, 'to form, shape'. See dough and cp.
words there refeneu to.
Derivatives: feign-ed, adj., feign-ed-ly, adv.,
feign-ed-ness, n.

## feint
feint, п., something feigned; pretence. — F. fein-
te, fem. of feint, 'something feigned', pp. of
feindre. See prec. word.

## feint
feint, adj., feigned (obsol.) — F. feint, pp. of
feindre. See feint, п., and cp. faint, which is a
doublet of feint, adj.

## feint
feint, intr. v., to make a feint. — F. feint, pp. of
feindre. See feint, n.

## feldspar
feldspar, п., any of a group of crystalline
minerals. — G. Feldspat, compounded of Feld, 'field*,
and Spat, 'spar'. See field and spathic and cp.
next word. The form feldspar is due to the
influence of spar, 'a nonmetallic element'.

## feldspathic
feldspathic, adj., pertaining to, or consisting of,
feldspar. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. G. Feld-
spath, now spelled Feldspat. See prec. word.

## Felicia
Felicia, fem. PN. — L., from fllix, gen. fllicis,
'happy'. See felicity and cp. Felicity, Felix.

## feticide
feticide, п., the killing of a cat. —Compounded
of files, 'cat', and -cldium, 'a killing', fr. caedere,
'to kill'. See felid and -cide, 'killing'.

## felicific
felicific, adj., making happy. — L. fllicificus,
'making happy', fr. fllix, gen. fllicis, 'fruitful;
auspicious, happy', and -ficus, from the stem
of -ficere, unstressed form of facere, 'to make,
do'. See felicity and -flc and cp. next word.

## felicify
felicify, tr. v., to make happy (rare). — Formed fr.
L.felix, gen. fllicis, 'fruitful; happy', and -ficare,
fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See prec. word and -fy.

## felicitate
felicitate, tr. v. — VL. fllicitatus, pp. of fllicitare,
'to render happy, felicitate', fr. L.felicitas, gen.
fllicitatis, 'fruitfulness, happiness', fr. felix,
gen. -ids. See felicity and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: felicitat-ion, п., felicitat-or, n.

## felicitous
felicitous, adj., happy (rare). — Formed fr.
felicity with suff. -ous.
Derivative: felicitous-ly, adv.

## felicity
felicity, п., happiness, blissfulness. — OF. felicite
(F. felicite), fr. L. fllicitatem, ace. of fllicitas,
'fruitfulness; happiness, felicity', fr. fllix, gen.
fllicis, 'fruitful; auspicious, happy', which is
rel. to fe-cundus, 'fruitful, fertile', fi-lius (for
*fl-lios), 'son', fr. L. base *fl-, corresponding
to I.-E. base 'dhl(i)-, *dhl(i)-, *dhl-, 'to suck,
suckle'. See filial and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## Felicity
Felicity, fem. PN. — Fr. L. fllicitas, 'happiness'.
See prec. word.

## felid
felid, п., an animal pertaining to the cat family.
— See next word.

## Felidae
Felidae, n. pi., the cat family (zool.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -ldae fr. L. fills, 'cat', which
is of uncertain etymology. It is perh. cogn.
with W. bete, 'marten'. Cp. feticide.

## feline
feline, adj., pertaining to the cai family (zool.) —
L, felinus, fr. fells, 'cat'. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -ine.

## felinity
felinity, п., the quality of being feline. — See
feline and -ity.

## Felix
Felix, masc. PN. — L., lit. 'happy'. See felicity
and cp. Felicia, Felicity. For sense development
cp. Asher

## fell
fell, п., hide, skin. — OE., rel. loON.fjall, 'skin',
OHG. fel, MHG. vel, G. Fell, 'hide, skin',
Goth, fill (only in derivatives and compounds,
as e.g. filleins, 'leathern', faura-filli, 'foreskin'),
L. pellis (for *pel-nis), 'hide, skin, leather', fr.
I.-E. base 'pel-, 'skin', whence also Gk. πέλμα,
'sole of foot or shoe', πέλλα (prob. for *πέλ-να),
'wooden bow], milk pail' (the orig. meaning
prob. was 'a vessel made of skin'), and the
second element in έρυσί-πελας, 'erysipelas', and
Liih. pleve, 'a fine, thin layer of skin'. Cp. film
and the first element in veldtshoen. Cp. also
epiploon, erysipelas, paillasse, pall, 'claok',
pelisse, pell, pellagra, pellicle, pelta, Peltandra,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:304 COLUMN:2 -->
peltry, pitch, pillion, plaid, surplice, Uropeltidae.

## fell
fell, п., rocky hill. — ME. fell, fr. ON. fiall,
'mountain,' which is rel. to OHG. felis (masc),
felisa (fem.), MHG. vets, G. Fels, 'stone, rock',
and cogn. with Gk. πέλλα (for *πέλσ«), 'stone',
OI. pasmiah, 'stone, rock', Olr. all (for *pals-
os), 'stone'. Cp. felstone.

## fell
fell, tr. v., to cause to fall. — ME. fellen, fr. OE.
fellan, rel. to ON. fella, Swed. falla, Dan. fxlde,
OFris. falla, MDu., Du. vellen, OHG. fellan,
MHG. vellen, G. fallen; causative of OE. feal-
lan, etc., 'to fall'. See fall, v.
Derivatives: fell-er, п., fell-ing, n.

## fell
fell, adj., cruel. — ME. fel, fr. OE. fel, 'fierce,
cruel', fr. OF. fel (nom.), fr. VL. fella, 'felon'.
See felon.

## fell
fell, past tense of fall. — ME. fell, fr. OE. floll,
'fell', fr. feallan, 'to fall'. See fall, v.

## feliah
feliah, n. pi. fellahin, an Egyptian peasant or
laborer. — Arab, fallah, in vulgar pronunciation
fellah, 'plowman', fr. falaha, 'he cleft, tilled the
ground' (in this latter sense, borrowed fr.
Aramaic); rel. to Heb. palah, 'he cleft', Aram.-Syr.
pelah, 'he tilled the ground; he served' (whence
the noun polkan, 'work, service', esp. 'divine
service'), Heb. pelah, 'cleavage' (whence the
meanings 'millstone, slice of fruit').

## felloe
felloe, n. — See felly.

## fellow
fellow, n. — ME. felaghe, felawe, fr. OE. flolaga,
fr. ON. fllagi, 'partner, companion', from
fllag, 'companionship', lit. 'laying down of
money', fr. fl, 'cattle, money', and lag, 'a
laying'. See fee, 'money', and lay, 'to place'.
Derivatives :/ё//ои', tr. v., and яау, fellowship,^

## felly
felly, felloe, п., the rim of a spoked wheel. —
ME. feli, felwe, felow, fr. OE. felg, felge, rel. to
OS. felga, MLG., MDu. velge, Du. velg, OHG.
felga, felaga, MHG. velge, G. Felge. These
words are -^-enlargements of I.-E. base *qwel-,
'to turn'. See wheel and cp. cycle. Cp. also
fallow, n.

## felo-de-se
felo-de-se, п., one who commits suicide. —
Anglo-Latin fel(l)o-dl si, lit. One guilty
concerning himself. See next word de- and sui.

## felon
felon, adj., cruel, criminal; п., a criminal. —
ME., fr. OF. felon (F. felon), fr. Carolingian L.
fellonem, ace. of felid (the pi. fellonls occurs in
the Capitularies of Charles the Bald), prob. of
Teut. origin and lit. meaning 'whipper (of
slaves)'; cp. OHG. fillen, 'to whip', Cp. prec.
and next word.

## felon
felon, п., a painful swelling of the finger. — The
same word as the preceding.

## felonry
felonry, п., the class of felons. — Formed fr.
feion, 'criminal', with suff. -ry.

## felony
felony, n. (law). — F. felonie, fr. felon. See felon,
'criminal', and suff. -y (representing OF. and
F. -ie).
Derivatives: feloni-ous, adj., felonious-ly, adv.,
felonious-ness, n.

## felsite
felsite, n. (petrogr.) — A hybrid var. of felstone.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: felsit-ic, adj.

## felstone
felstone, п., an igneous rock containing quartz
and feldspar (petrogr.) — Altered fr. G. Fels-
stein, lit. 'stone of a rock', fr. Fels, 'rock', and
Stein, 'stone'. See fell, 'rocky hill', and stone.

## felt
felt, n. — OE. rel. to OS. fill, OHG. filz, MHG.
vilz, G. Filz, fr. Teut. *felti-, 'something beaten'.
The same base appears in the second element
of OE. an-filte, OHG. ana-falz; see anvil. The
base is prob. not cognate with L. pellere, 'to
strike' (see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, p. 277).
Cp. felter, filter.
Derivatives: felt, tr. and intr. v., felt-ed, adj.,
felt-er, п., fell-ing, п., felt-y, adj.

## felter
felter, tr. v. — OF. feltrer (F. feutrer), fr. feltre
(F. feutre), 'felt', fr. ML. feltrum, filtrum,'felt,
strainer of felt', See filter.

## felucca
felucca, п., a small coasting vessel used in the
Mediterranean. — It. feluca, fr. Arab. /и/А,
'ship', rel. to falak, 'circle', from the base of
fdlaka, 'was round'; rel. also to Heb. pelekh,
'spindle'. See S.Fraenkel, Die aramaischen
FremdwSrter im Arabischen, p. 212.

## female
female, n. and adj. — ME. femele, femelle,
assimilated in ending to male, fr. OF. femelle, fr.
L. flmella, dimio. of flmina, 'woman; female

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:304 COLUMN:3 -->
animal'. See feminine and cp. fimble.
Derivatives: femal-ity, п., female-ly, adv., fe-
male-ness, n.

## feme
feme, п., wife. — ME., fr. OF. feme (F. femme),
fr. L. flmina, 'woman'. See feminine.

## feme covert
feme covert, a married woman (law). — OF.
feme coverte. For the first word see prec. word.
OF. coverte (F. couverte) is the feminine of
covert (couvert), 'covered'. See covert.

## feme sole
feme sole, an unmarried woman (law). — For
the first word see feme; the second comes fr.
OF. sole, 'alone', fr. L. sola, fem. of solus,
'alone'. See sole, 'alone'.

## feminality
feminality, п., the quality or state of being
female. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. the rare
adjective feminal, fr. OF. feminal, 'female'. See
feminine and adj. suff. -al.

## feniineity
feniineity, п., the quality or state of being
feminine; womanliness. — Formed with suff. -Ity
fr. L. flmineus, 'pertaining to a woman,
womanish', fr. flmina. See next word.

## feminiae
feminiae, adj. — OF. feminin (F. flminin), fr. L.
flmininus, 'feminine', fr. flmina, 'woman', orig.
a middle pres. part, meaning 'she who suckles',
fr. L. base "fl-, corresponding to I.-E. base
*dhe(iy, *dhl(i)-, *dht-, 'to suck, suckle',
whence also L. fl-cundus, 'fruitful', fl-lare, 'to
suck', fl-lix, 'fruitful; auspicious, happy',
filius (for *fl-lios), 'son'. See filial and adj. suff.
-ine and cp. effeminate. For the middle and
passive part. suff. -meno- see alumnus and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: feminine-ly, adv.,feminine-ness, п.,
feminin-ism, п., feminin-ity, п., femin-ism,n.,
femin-ist, п., feminity (q.v.)

## feminity
feminity, п., the quality or state of being
feminine. — OF. feminite, fr. L. flmina, 'woman'.
See feminine and -ity.

## feminize
feminize, tr. v., to render feminine; intr. v., to
become feminine. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
flmina, 'woman' (see femiaine), and -ize, a suff.
of Greek origin.
Derivative: feminizat-ion, n.

## femme de chambre
femme de chambre, 1) a lady's maid; 2) a
chambermaid. — See feme, de- and chamber.

## femoral
femoral, adj., pertaining to the thigh. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. femur, gen. femoris. See
next word.

## femur
femur, п., ι) the thighbone; 2) the thigh (anat.) —
L., 'thigh', of uncertain origin.

## fen
fen, п., flat marshy land. — ME. fen, fr. OE.
fenn, rel. to OS. feni, OR/eit, OFris. fenne,fene,
Du. veen, OHG. fenna, G. Fenn, 'marsh', Goth.
fani, 'mud', and cogn. with Gaul, anam, Mir.
an, 'water', OI. pdnkah, 'bog, marsh, mud'.
Derivative: fenn-y, adj,

## fence
fence, n. — Aphetic for defence.
Derivatives: fence, intr. and tr. v., fence-less,
adj., fenc-er, п., fenc-ing, n.

## fencible
fencible, п., soldier enlisted for home service
only (hist.) — Aphetic for defencible.

## fend
fend, tr. and intr. v. — Aphetic for defend. Cp.
forfend.
Derivatives: fend-er, п., fend-er-less, adj.

## fenestclla
fenestclla, п., a small window. — L. dimin. of
fenestra, 'window'. See next word and -ella.

## fenestra
fenestra, п., a small opening in a bone (anat.) —
L., 'window', prob. fr. Etruscan *fnes-tra;
-(s)tra is an Etruscan suff. (cp. the L. words
aplustre, 'the carved stern of a ship with its
ornaments', genista, 'the plant broom', and
lanista, 'trainer of gladiators'; see aplustre,
Genista, lanista). L. fenestra is not cogn. with
Gk. ipaCveiv, 'to shine' (see phantasm), as
suggested by most lexicographers.
Derivatives: fenestr-al, adj., fenestr-ate, adj.,
fenestr-at-ed, adj., fenestration (q.v.), fenestrule
(q.v.)

## fenestration
fenestration, n„ 1) arrangement of windows in a
building (archit.); 2) the state of being
perforated (zool. and йог.) — See fenestra and
-ation and cp. defenestration.

## fenestrule
fenestrule, п., a small opening (zool.) — L.
fenestrula, dimin. of fenestra, 'window'. See
fenestra and -ule.

## Fenian
Fenian, n. and adj. — A blend of Olr. flinne, pi.
cSfiann, name of a band of Irish warriors, and
Olr. Fine, name of the ancient inhabitants of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:305 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: FENKS | 278 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:305 COLUMN:1 -->
Ireland.
Derivative: Fenian-ism, n.

## fenks
fenks, п., refuse of whale's blubber. — Of
unknown origin.

## fennec
fennec, п., a small African fox. — Arab, fdnak,
in vulgar pronunciation fenek.

## fennel
fennel, п., a plant of the parsley family (Foeni-
culum vulgare). — OE. fenol, finul, fr. OF. fenoil.
(F. fenouil), fr. VL. *fenuc(u)lum, fr. L. feni-
culum, dimin. of flnum, 'hay', which prob.
means lit. 'produce, yield', fr. Latin base *fl-,
'to suck, suckle, produce, yield', whence also
fe-nus, 'proceeds, increase', fe-mina, 'woman';
see feminine. The fennel was so called in allusion
to its smell which reminds that of hay. Cp. next
word.

## fenugreek
fenugreek, п., a leguminous plant. — ME. fenu-
grek, fr. MF. (= F.) fenugrec, fr. L. fenu-
graecum, for fenum Graecum, lit. 'Greek hay'.
See fennel and Greek and cp. flnochio and the
second element in sainfoin.

## feoff
feoff, tr. v., to invest with a fee. — ME. feoffen,
fr. AF. feoffer, corresponding to OF. feffer,
fieffer (F. fieffer), fr. OF. fieu, fief (F. fief),
'fee'. See fee, 'estate*, and cp. fief, enfeoff.
Derivatives: feoff-ment, п., feoffor (q.v.)

## feoffee
feoffee, п., a person to whom a feoffment is
granted. — ME. feoffe, fr. AF. feoffe, pp. of
feoffer. See prec. word and -ее.

## feoffor
feoffor, feoffer, n. — ME. feoffor, fr. AF. feoffour,
fr. feoffer. See feoff and agential suff. -or, resp.
-er.

## -fer
-fer, Latin subst. suff. denoting the agent, as in
conifer. — From the stem of L. ferre, 'to bear,
carry', which is cogn. with OE. beran, 'to bear'.
See bear, 'to carry', and cp. -ferous (which is the
adj. suff. corresponding to the subst. suff. -fer).

## feral
feral, adj., wild, savage, untamed. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. fera (scil. bislia), 'a wild
animal', fern, of ferus, 'wild'. See fierce and cp.
ferocious.

## feral
feral, adj., funereal, deadly. — L. ferSlis,
'funereal, deadly, fatal', prob. meaning lit.
'pertaining to the feast of the souls', fr. *dhwgsa, 'soul,
spirit, ghost', and rel. to Lith. dvSse, 'spirit',
dvasid, 'breath, soul'. See deer and adj. suff. -al.

## ferash
ferash, farash, п., a menial servant. — Hind, far-
rash, fr. Arab, farr&sh, prop, 'one who spreads
carpets', fr. farsh, 'rug, carpet', from the stem
of farasha, 'he spread out', which is cogn. with
Heb. paraS, Aram.-Syr. p'ras, 'he spread out',
Akkad. parashu, 'to fly', lit. 'to spread one's
wings'.

## ferberite
ferberite, п., a basic ferrous tungstate (mineral.)
— Named after Rudolph Ferber, of Gera,
Germany. For the ending see subst. suff. -fie.

## fer de lance
fer de lance, a large poisonous snake of South
America and Mexico (Bothrops alrox). — F.,
'iron of a lance, lance head' fr. fer (fr. L.
ferrum), 'iron', de (fr. L. de), 'from', and lancea,
'lance' (see ferro-, de- and lance); so called in
allusion to its shape.

## Ferdinand
Ferdinand, masc. PN. — F., a compound of Teut.
origin. The first element is prob. a derivative
of Teut. *fardi, an abstract noun formed from
base 'far-, 'to fare, travel'; see fare, 'to
prosper'. The second element is rel. to Goth, -nanp-
jan, in ana-nanpjan, 'to risk, venture', OE. пёдап,
OS. nadian, OHG. nendan, 'to risk, venture'.

## fere
fere, n. (archaic) i) a companion; 2) a husband
or wife. — ME. fere, aphetized fr. OE. gefera,
which is formed fr. ge- (see y-) and -fera, from
the base oifaran, 'to go, travel'. Cp. OHG. gi-
ferto (whence MHG. geverte, G. Gefihrte),
'companion', formed fr. gi- and faran, 'to go,
travel', and see fare, v.

## feretory
feretory, п., a shrine, reliquary. — ME. fertre,
'shrine, bier', fr. OF. fiertre, fr. L. feretrum, 'a
litter, bier', fr. Gk. φέρετρον, a derivative of
φέρειν, 'to carry', fr. I.-E. base *bher-, 'to bear,
carry", whence also OE. beran, 'to bear, carry',
bSr, 'bier'. See bear, 'to carry', and cp. bier.

## fergantte
fergantte, п., a hydrated uranium vanadate
(mineral.) — Named after Fergana in Turkestan.
For the ending see subst. suff. -tte.

## Fergus
Fergus, masc. PN. — Olr. Fer-gus, lit. 'man's
ability', fr. fer, 'man', and gas, 'ability, excellency,
strength, inclination'. The first element is cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:305 COLUMN:2 -->
with L. vir, 'man'; see virile. The second element
derives fr. Celtic *gustu-, 'choice', fr. I.-E. base
*§eus-, *ius-, 'to taste'; see choose.

## fergusonite
fergusonite, п., a niobate and tantalate of
yttrium, erbium etc. (mineral.) — Named after
Robert Ferguson (1799-1865), of Raith
(Scotland). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## feria
feria, n. (pi. feriae), 1) pi., feast days, holidays;
2) (eccles.) a weekday. — Late L. feriae (pi.),
'days of rest, holidays, festivals', fr. OL. fesiae
(see rhotacism), rel. to festus, 'solemn, festive,
festal', /Злит, 'temple'. See fair, п., and cp.
words there referred to.

## ferial
ferial, adj., 1) pertaining to holidays; 2) (eccles.)
pertaining to weekdays. — OF., fr. ML. feri-
dalis, fr. L. feriae. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.

## ferine
ferine, adj., wild. — L. ferinus, 'pertaining to
wild animals', fr. ferus, 'wild'. See fierce and
adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -fnus).

## Feringhee
Feringhee, п., a name used in India for the
European. — Pers. Farangi, fr. Arab. Faranjf, which
was formed with the ethnic suff. -/fr. OF. Franc,
'Frank'. See Frank.

## fermata
fermata, п., a pause (mus.)—It., 'stop, pause;
halting place', fr. fermare, 'to fasten; to stop; to
resolve', fr. fermo, 'strong, fastened', fr. L.
firmus, 'firm, steadfast, stable, strong'. See
firm, 'solid'.

## ferment
ferment, n. — F.s fr. L. fermentum, 'substance
causing fermentation', fr. I.-E. base *bher-,
'to boil up, seethe'. See barm and cp. fervent.
Cp. also fry, 'to cook in fat'. For the ending
see suff. -ment.

## ferment
ferment, tr. and intr. V. — F'. fermenter, fr. L.fer-
mentare, 'to ferment', fr. fermentum. See
ferment, n.
Derivatives: ferment-able, adj., ferment-abil-ily,
п., ferment-arian, п., fermentation (q.v.),
ferment-alive, adj., ferment-ative-ly, adv., ferment-
ative-ness, п., ferment-er, п., ferment-itious, adj.,
ferment-ive, adj., fermenl-or, n.

## fermentation
fermentation, n. — L. fermentatio, gen. -ionis, fr.
fermentare, 'to ferment'. See ferment, v. and п.,
and -ation.

## fenahim
fenahim, п., a radioactive element produced by
nuclear bombardment in a cyclotron (chem.) —
ModL., named after the Italian physicist Enrico
Fermi (1901-54). For the ending of fermium
see chem suff. -ium.

## fennorite
fennorite, п., an arsenate, phosphate and fluoride
of calcium and strontium (mineral.) — Named
after Lewis Leigh Fermor (died in 1954),
director of the Geological Survey of India. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## fern
fern, n. — ME. fern, fr. OE. fearn, rel. to OS.
farn, MDu. varn, varen, Du. varen, OHG. farn,
MHG. varn, G. Farn, Farnkraut, and cogn.
with OI. ρατηά-m, 'feather', Lith. papartis, 'fern',
Lett, paparnite, Russ. paporoC, Gaul, ratis (for
*pratis), Olr. raith, of s.m., Gk. πτέρις, 'fern',
πτερίν, 'feather'. See feather.
Derivatives: fern-ed, adj., fern-ery, п.,
fernlike, adj.

## femandinite
femandinite, п., a hydrous calcium vanadyl
vanadate (mineral.) — Named after Eulagio E. Fer-
nandini, from whose vanadium deposit it was
first obtained. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## ferocious
ferocious, adj., fierce. — Formed with suff. -ons
fr. L. ferox, gen. ferucis, 'wild, savage, un-
tameable, bold', prop, 'wild-looking', fr. ferus,
'wild', and -ox, gen. -ocis, 'looking'. For the
etymology of L. ferus see fierce. The second
element in L. fer-дх, 'wild', is cogn. with Gk.
ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye, sight'. See eye and cp. -ops.
Cp. also the second element in atrocious,
velocity.
Derivatives: ferocious-ly, adv., ferocious-ness, n.

## ferocity
ferocity, п., fierceness. — F. ferociti, fr. L. ferd-
citatem, ace. of ferocitas, 'fierceness', fr. ferox,
gen. ferdcis. See ferocious and -ity.

## Feronia
Feronia, п., an ancient Italian goddess identified
later with Juno. — L. Feronia, of Etruscan
origin.

## Feronia
Feronia, п., a genus of trees of the famiiy Ruta-
ceae (= the rue family). — ModL., from
preceding word.

## -ferous
-ferous, adj. suff. meaning 'bearing, having,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:305 COLUMN:3 -->
containing, producing, yielding', as in coniferous,
ferriferous. — Prop, formed fr. L. -fer, 'bearing,
producing' (see -fer), and suff. -ous.

## ferrate
ferrate, п., a salt of ferric acid (chem.) — See
ferro- and chem. suff. -ate.

## ferreous
ferreous, adj., pertaining to, or containing, iron.
— L. ferreus, 'made of iron, iron', fr. ferrum,
'iron'. See ferro-. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
L. -us, see -ous.

## ferret
ferret, п., a small animal of the weasel family. —
ME. feret, foret, fr. OF. *fuiret, *furet, fr. VL.
"furittus (whence also It. furetto), lit. 'a little
thief, fr. L. fur, 'thief. (Cp. OF. fuiron, furon,
'ferret', fr. VL. 'furidnem, ace. of 'fwrid,
enlarged fr. Late L. furd, 'thief, fr. L. fur.) See
furtive.
Derivatives: ferret, tr. and intr. v., to hunt
(rabbits) with ferrets, ferret-y, adj.

## ferret
ferret, п., a kind of ribbon. — It. fioretti, 'floss
silk', pi. of fioretto, dimin. of fiore, 'flower', fr.
L. florem, ace. of fids, 'flower'. See flora and
cp. floret.

## ferret
ferret, п., the iron used to try the molten glass. —
F., dimin. offer, 'iron', fr. L. ferrum. See ferro-.

## ferri-
ferri-, combining form meaning 'iron'. — L.
ferri-, fr. ferrum, gen. ferri, 'iron'. See ferro-,

## ferric
ferric, adj., of iron. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. L. ferrum, 'iron'. See ferro-.

## ferriferous
ferriferous, adj., yielding iron. — Compounded
of ferri- and -ferous.

## ferro-
ferro-, combining form meaning 'iron'. — L.
ferro-, fr. ferrum, 'iron'. See farrier and cp.
ferret, 'iron used for trying', ferruginous.

## ferrotype
ferrotype, п., a photograph taken on a thin iron
piate. — Compounded of ferro- and type.

## ferrous
ferrous, adj., pertaining to, or containing, iron.
— Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. ferrum, 'iron'.
See ferro-.

## ferruginous
ferruginous, adj., 1) containing iron; 2) rust-
colored. — L. ferrugineus, ferruginus, fr. fer-
rugd, gen. -ginis, 'rust; rust color', fr. ferrum
'iron'. See ferro- and -ous.

## ferrule
ferrule, п., a metal ring or cap on the end of
a stick, etc. — A blend of L. ferrum, 'iron' (see
ferro-), and earlier E. verrel, which derives fr.
OF. virelle, virol, fr. L. viriola, 'a little bracelet',
dimin. of viriae, 'bracelet', a word of Celtic
origin. Cp. Olt.fiar, 'bent, crooked', and see wire.
Derivative: ferrul-ed, adj.

## ferry
ferry, tr. and intr. v. — ME. ferien, 'to carry,
transport', fr. OE. ferian, rel. to ON. ferja, 'to
pass over, to ferry', and to OE. faran, 'to go,
travel'. See fare, 'to prosper', and cp. words
there referred to.

## ferry
ferry, n. — Fr. ferry, v. Cp. ON. ferja, Swed.
fSrja, Dan. fierge, MDu. vere, Du. veer, MHG.
vere, ver, vere, G. Fahre, 'a ferry'.

## fertile
fertile, adj. — OF. fertil, fr. L. fertilis, 'fruitful,
fertile', fr. ferre, 'to bear, carry, produce', which
is cogn. with OE. beran, 'to bear'. See bear, 'to
carry', and -ile.
Derivatives: fertile-ly, adv., fertile-ness, п.,
fertility (q.v.), fertit-ize, tr. v., fertil-iz-able, adj.,
fertil-iz-ation, п., fertil-iz-er, n.

## Fertile Crescent
Fertile Crescent, a semicircle of fertile land
extending from Palestine and Phoenicia around
the Euphrates-Tigris valley to the Persian Gulf
(Ancient hist.) — Coined by the American
archaeologist and historian James H. Breasted
(1865-1935)..

## fertility
fertility, n. — F. fertiliti, fr. L. fertililatem, ace.
of fertilitas, 'fruitfulness, fertility', fr. fertilis.
See fertile and -ity.

## ferula
ferula, п., the giant fennel. — L., 'the giant
fennel ; branch, staff, rod', which prob. stands for
*fes-ola and is rel. to festuca (for fes-tuca)
'stalk, straw, rod'. Cp. ferule, fescue, Festaca;
cp. also furl. The association of L. ferula with
ferlre, 'to strike, smite', is folk etymology.

## ferule
ferule, п., a rod for punishing children. — L.
fetula, 'the giant fennel; branch, staff, rod'. See
prec. word.
Derivative: ferule, tr. v.

## fervency
fervency, n. — OF. fervence, fr. L. fervire. See
next word and -cy.

## fervent
fervent, adj., i)Tiot; 2) deeply earnest; ardent. —
L. fervlns, gen. -emis, pres. part. (A fervire, 'to
boil, glow, foam', fr. I.-E. base *bheru-, en-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:306 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 279 | FIACRE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:306 COLUMN:1 -->
Urged form of *bher-, 'to boil, seethe', whence
also L. defrutum, 'must'. See barm and -ent and
cp. ferment
Derivatives: fervent-ly, adv., fervent-ness, n.

## fervescence
fervescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## fervescent
fervescent, adj., growing hot. — L. fervescins,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of fervlscere, 'to become
hot', inchoative of fervere. See fervent and
-escent.

## fervid
fervid, adj., i) very hot; 2) vehement. — L. fer-
villus, 'glowing, burning, fiery, vehement,
impetuous, violent', fr. fervere. See fervent and
adj. suff. -id. Derivatives: fervid-ity, п.,
fervidly, adv., fervid-ness, n.

## fervor
fervor, fervour, п., ι) intense heat; 2) ardor. —
OF. fervor (F. ferveur), 'fervor', fr. L. fervorem,
ace. of fervor, 'violent heat', fr. fervere. See
fervent and -or.

## Fescennine
Fescennine, also fescennine, adj., scurrilous,
obscene. — L. Fescenninus, 'of Fescennia', fr.
Fescennia, a city in ancient Etruria.
Derivative: fescennin-ity, n.

## fescue
fescue, п., ι) teacher's pointer (rare); 2) a kind
of tall meadow grass used as pasture. — ME.
festu, 'bit of straw', fr. OF. festu (F. fetu), fr.
VL. feslucum, fr. L. festuca, 'stalk, straw, rod',
which prob. stands for *fes-tuca and is rel. to
ferula, 'the giant fennel; branch, staff, rod'. See
feruia and cp. Festuca.

## fess
fess, fesse, п., a white horizontal band drawn
across the center of an escutcheon (her.) —
ME. fesse, fr. OF. faisce, fesse, fr. L. fascia, 'a
band'. (F. fasce is formed directly from L.
fascia.) See fascia, fasces.

## festal
festal, adj., of a feast. — OF., formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. fesle (F. file), 'feast'. See feast.
Derivative: festal-ly, adv.

## fester
fester, п., a small sore discharging pus; a pustule.
— ME. festre, fr. OF. festre, fr. L. fistula, 'pipe,
tube; sort of ulcer, fistula'. See fistula.

## fester
fester, intr. v., to form pus; to suppurate. —
ME. festren, fr. festre, n. See fester, n.

## festival
festival, adj. — ME., fr. OF. festival, fr. ML.
festivdlis, fr. L. festivus. See next word and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: festival, п., festival-ty, adv.

## festive
festive, adj. — L. festivus, 'festive, joyous, gay',
fr. flstum, 'holiday, festival', fr. flstum, neut. of
the adj. festus, 'festive'. See feast and -ive.
Derivatives: festive-ly, adv., festive-ness, n.

## festivity
festivity, n. — OF. festivite, fr. L. flstivitatem,
ace. of festivitas, 'festivity, joy, merriment', fr.
festivus. See prec. word and -ity.

## festoon
festoon, п., a garland. — F. feston, fr. It. festone,
lit. 'a festive ornament', fr. festa, 'feast', fr. VL.
fesla (scil. dies), 'festival, feast, holiday'. See
feast and -oon. Derivatives: festoon, п., festoon-
ery,ti.,festoon-y, adj.

## Festuca
Festuca, п., a genus of plants, the fescue grass
(hot.) — L. festuca, 'stalk, straw'. See fescne.

## Festus
Festus, masc. PN. — L., lit. 'solemn, festive,
joyous'. See feast and cp. festive.

## fetal
fetal, foetal, adj., pertaining to a fetus. — See
fetus and adj. suff. -al.

## fetation
fetation, foetation, п., formation of a fetus. —
Formed with suff. -ion fr. L. fetatus, pp. of
/etare, 'to produce offspring', fr. fetus, 'a
bringing forth; offspring'. See fetus.

## fetch
fetch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. fecchen, fr. OE.
feccan, earlier fetian, 'to fetch, bring', rel. to
OE.fatian, of s.m., obsol. E.fet, 'to fetch', ON.
/ere, 'to find one's way', OHG. sih fa33dn, 'to
mount, climb', MHG. sih vauen, 'to go, travel',
OE. fat, 'foot'. See foot and cp. fetlock, fetter.
Derivatives -.fetch, n.,fetch-er, a„fetch-ing, adj.,
fetch-ing-ly, adv.

## fetch
fetch, п., an apparition, specter; a double. —
Of unknown origin.

## fete
fete, п., a festival. — F., fr. OF. feste, 'festival,
feast'. See feast and cp. words there referred to.
The word file was introduced into English by
Horace Walpole (1717-97).

## fete
fete, tr. v. — F. feter, 'to celebrate; to entertain,
feast', fr. fete. See fete, n.

## fetial
fetial, adj., pertaining to the fetiales; pertaining
to declarations of war or treatises of peace. —
L. fltialis. See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:306 COLUMN:2 -->

## fetial
fetial, п., one of a college of twenty priests whose
duty it was to act as heralds and maintain the
laws of war. — L. fetidlis, 'pertaining to the
fetiales', fr. *fgtis, fr. I.-E. 'dhg-ti-s, 'statute,
treaty', fr. base *dhe-, *d¥-, 'to put, place;
to do, make', whence also L. facere, 'to make,
do'. See fact and -ial.

## fetialis
fetialis, п., a fetial. — See prec. word.

## feticide
feticide, foeticide, п., the act of destroying a fetus.
— Compounded of L. fetus, 'S bringing forth;
offspring', and -cidium, 'killing', fr. caedere, 'to
kill'. See fetus and -cide, 'killing'.

## fetid
fetid, foetid, adj., having a bad smell. — L. feti-
dus, written also foetidus, 'having an ill smell',
fr. fitlre, foetire, 'to have an ill smell, to stink',
which is prob. rel. to fi-mus, 'dung', suf-fire, 'to
fumigate', and possibly also to fumus, 'smoke'.
See fume and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also the second element in asafetida.
Derivatives: fetid-ity, п., fetid-ly, adv.,
fetidness, a.

## fetish
fetish, п., an object worshiped. — F. fetiche, fr.
Port, feitico, fr. L. facticius, 'made by art', fr.
facia, facere, 'to make'. See fact and cp.
factitious. Derivatives: fetish-ism, п., fetish-ist, п.,
fetish-ist-ic, adj.

## fetlock
fetlock, п., ι) part of a horse's leg where a tuft
of hair grows; 2) the tuft. — ME.fetlakJytlok,
lit. 'lock of the foot', rel. to MHG. wjje/ocA,
G. Fifiloch, and to ON. fit, 'the webbed foot
of a water bird', fel, 'pace, step', ON. fotr, OE.
fat, 'foot'. See foot and lock and cp. fetch, fetter.
Derivative: fetlock-ed, adj.

## feto-
feto-, foeto-, combining form meaning 'fetus*. —
See fetus,

## fetor
fetor, foetor, п., an offensive smell. — L. foetor,
fetor, 'offensive smell, stench', fr. foetere, fitere.
See fetid and -or.

## fetter
fetter, п., a shackle. — ME. feter, fr. OE. fetor,
rel. to OS. feteros (pi.), MDu. veter, OHG. /ej-
зага, fe33era, MHG. veiier, ON.fjoturr, Swed.
fjdtter, and cogn. with Gk. πέδη, 'fetter', πεδαν,
'to bind with fetters', L. peda, 'footstep', pedica,
'shackle, fetter', impedire, 'to entangle, ensnare,
hinder, detain', expedire,'to extricate, disengage'.
AH these words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*ped-, 'foot'. See foot and cp. fret, 'ornament'.
Cp. also expedient, impede.
Derivatives: fetter, tr. v., fetter-er, п.,
fetterless, adj.

## fettle
fettle, tr. v., to put in order, arrange. — ME.

## fetlen
fetlen, 'to gird up', fr. OE. fetel, 'girdle, belt',
rel. to ON. fetill, 'strap, brace', MLG. vetel,
OHG. /ejji/, MHG. ve33el, G. Fessel, 'fetter,
chain', to OE. fatian, OHG. /aj3<jn, 'to seize,
hold', and to E. vat (q.v.); confused with OE.

## fetor
fetor, OS. feteros, etc. 'fetter' (see prec. word).
Derivatives: fettle, п., fettl-er, п., fettl-ing,
verb. n.

## fetus
fetus, foetus, п., unborn offspring. — L. fetus,

## foetus
foetus, 'a bringing forth, offspring', rel. to fl-
mina, *a woman', lit., 'she who suckles*, fe-lare,
'to suck', fe-cundus, 'fruitful, fertile', fl-nus,
'proceeds, increase', lit. 'that which is

## produced'
produced', fi-lius (for *fe-lios), 'son', lit. 'a
suckling', fr. Latin base *fl-, corresponding to
I.-E. base *dhe(i)-, *d¥(i>, *dht-, 'to suck,
suckle'. See filial and cp. words there referred to.

## fetwa
fetwa, n. — See futwa.

## feu
feu, п., a fief. — OF. feu, fieu, fiu, fr. ML. feum,

## fevum
fevum, a word of Teut. origin. See fee, 'estate',

## and cp. feud
and cp. feud, 'fief.
Derivatives: feu, tr. v.,feuar (q.v.)

## feuar
feuar, п., a person holding a feu (Scot. law). —

## A hybrid coined fr. feu and -ar
A hybrid coined fr. feu and -ar, a suff. of Latin
origin. Cp. fiar.

## feud
feud, п., enmity. — ME. fede, feide, fr. OF. fede,

## fr. OHG. flhida (MHG. vide
fr. OHG. flhida (MHG. vide, G. Fehde),
'contention,· quarrel, feud', which is rel. to OE.
fxho\o), 'feud, enmity', MDu. vide, vete, (Du.

## vete)
vete), of s.m., OE. /ah, 'hostile'. See foe.
Derivative: feud-al, adj.

## fend
fend, п., a fief. — ML. feudum, fr. feum, a word
of Teut. origin; cp. Goth, faihu, 'property',

## OHG. fihu
OHG. fihu, 'cattle', and see fee (in both senses)
and cp. infeudation. The б/ in ML. feudum tc
prob. due to the influence of the word
allodium (q.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:306 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: feudal (q.v.), feudatory (q.v.)

## feudal
feudal, adj., 1) pertaining to land held in feud;
2) pertaining to feudalism. — OF., fr. ML. feu-
dalis, fr. feudum. See feud, 'fief, and adj. suff.
-al.
Derivatives: feudal-ism, п., feudal-ist, a.,feudal-
ist-ic, &aj.,feudal-ity, n.,feudal-ize, tr. v.,feudal-
iz-ation, п., feudal-ly, adv.

## feudatory
feudatory, adj. and n. — A collateral form of
obsolete feudatory, fr. ML. feudatarius, fr. feudum,

-ory. Derivatives: feudatori-al, adj.

## feu de joie
feu de joie, public bonfire. — F., lit. 'fire of joy'.
F. feu derives fr. L. focus, de, 'of, from', comes
fr. L. de, 'from, away from', joie derives fr. L.
gaudia, pi. of gaudium, 'joy'. See focus, de-
and joy.

## fenille morte
fenille morte, adj. and п., filemot. — F. feuille
morte, 'dead leaf. See filemot.

## feuilleton
feuilleton, п., 1) part of a French newspaper
devoted to criticism, etc.; 2) installment of a serial
story printed in a newspaper. — F., orig. a
'leaflet added to the newspaper', dimin. of feuille,
'leaf, fr. L. folium, of s.m. See foil, 'leaf of
metal'.
Derivatives: feuilleton-ism, п., feuilleton-ist, п.,
feuilleton-ist-ic, adj.

## fever
fever, n. — ME. fevre, fevere, fr. OE. fefor,flfer,
rel. to MLG. vever (whence Dan. and Swed.
feber), OHG. fiebar (whence MHG., vieber, G.
Fieber), fr. L. febris, 'fever' (whence also It.
febbre, Rum. febra, OProvenc febre, F. fiivre,
OSp. hiebre, Sp. fiebre. Port, febre), which is
rel. to L. fovere, 'to warm, keep warm', /avilla
(for *fovilla), 'embers', fr. I.-E. base *ddgwh-,
*degmh-, 'to burn', whence also Goth, dags, OE.
dxg, 'day', orig. 'burning heat'. See day and
cp. next word and febrifuge, febrile. Cp. also
foment.
Derivatives: fever, tr. and intr. v., fever- ed, adj.,
fever-ish, adj., fever-ish-ly, adv., fever-ish-ness,
п., fever-ous, adj., fever-ous-ly, adv.

## feverfew
feverfew, п., a plant of the aster family. — OE.
feferfuge, fr. Late L. febrifuga, fr. L. febrifugia,
lit. 'driving fever away', fr. febris, 'fever', and
fug-are, 'to put to flight', fr. fug-ere, 'to flee';
so called for its alleged medicinal properties.
See prec. word and fugitive and cp. febrifuge.

## few
few, adj. — ME. fewe, fr. OE. flawe, pi. of /la,

'few, little', παις, gen. παιδός, 'child', πώλος,

'a young animal', Oscan pu-klu, 'child', OI.
potah, 'a young animal', putrah, 'son', Avestic
pu&ra-, 'son, child', OSlav. puta, putica, 'bird',
Lith. putytis, 'young animal, young bird', Lett.
putns, 'bird', Alb. pel's, 'mare', OE. fola, Goth.

## fula
fula, 'foal'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*pSu-, *peu-, *рй-, 'small, little, few, young'.

orthopedic, parvi-, paucity, Paul, paulo-post-
future, pauper, polecat, poltroon, pony, pool (in
gambling), poor, poult, ponlter, poultry, poverty,
puberty, pubes, pubescent, pubis, pucelle, puerile,

'scholar', pupil of the eye, puppet, puppy,
pusillanimous, putti and the second element in

## fey
fey, adj., fated; doomed to die. — ME. feie, fr.
OB.fxge, rel. to OS.flgi, fig, ΟΉ./eigr, OFris.

## fai
fai, OHG. feigi, 'doomed to die', MDu. vige,
Du. veeg, 'about to die', MHG. veige, 'doomed
to die; timid, coward', Dan. feig, Swed. feg,
G. feig, 'cowardly', and to OE. fah, 'hostile',
fr. I.-E. base *peik-, 'evil-minded, treacherous,
hostile'. See foe and cp. feud, 'enmity'.

## fez
fez, п., a red felt cap with a long black tassel. —
Fr. Fez, a town in Morocco.

## fincre
fincre, п., a French hackney cab. — F., fr. the
Hdtel St. Fiacre, rue St. Antoine, Paris, where

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:307 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: FIANCE | 280 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:307 COLUMN:1 -->
carriages were first hired (since 1640). Fiacre is
the French form of the name of the Celtic saint
Fiachra.

## fiance
fiance, fem. fiancee, п., a betrothed person. —
F., pp. of fiancer, *to affiance, betroth*. See
affiance.

## fiar
fiar, п., a person in whom a fee simple is vested
(Scot. law). — See feuar.'

## fiars
fiars, n. pi., prices of grain, fixed every February
for the coming year (Scot.) — OF. fuar, fuer,
'price' (whence F. fur, 'proportion'), fr. Late
L. forum, 'price', fr. L. forum, 'market, public
place'. See forum.

## fiasco
fiasco, п., a complete failure. — It., lit. 'bottle',
in the phrase far fiasco, 'to make a bottle; to
fail'. This sense development is prob. due to
the fact that the Venetian glass-makers used
only perfectly flawless material for the articles
manufactured by them. If in the course of their
work the glass showed any flaw, they set it aside
to make of it a fiasco, a common bottle or
flask. Accordingly far fiasco came to denote
not only 'to make a bottle', but 'to fail in one's
work or plans'. For the etymol. of It. fiasco
see flask.

## flat
flat, п., an authoritative command. — L. fiat,
'let it he done', 3rd person sing. subj. pres. of
fieri, 'to be done, to become', rel. to L. fui,
Ί have been'. See be and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also the second element in ratafia.

## fib
fib, п., a mild lie. — Prob. fr. earlier fibble-fable,
antiphonic reduplication of fable.
Derivatives: fib, intr. v., fibb-er, п., fibb-ery, n.

## fiber
fiber, fibre, n. — F. fibre, fr. L. fibra, 'fiber', which
is of uncertain origin. It stands perh. for I.-E.
*g"'his-ra and is rel. to filum, 'thread', which
stands for "g^his-lom. See file, 'a collection
of papers.
Derivatives: fibril (q.v.), fibritta (q.v.), fibrin
(q.v.), fibro-, combining iorm,fibroid(q.v.),fibro-
in, п., fibroma (q.v.), fibrosis (q.v.), fibr-ous, adj.,
fibr-ous-ly, adv., fibr-ous-ness, n.

## fibriform
fibriform, adj., fiberlike. — Compounded of L.
fibra, 'fiber', and forma, 'shape, form1. See
fiber and form, n.

## fibril
fibril, п., a small fiber. — Back formation fr.
ModL. fibrilla. See next word.

## flbrilla
flbrilla, п., a fibril. — ModL., 'fibril', dimin. of
L. fibra, 'fiber'. See fiber.
Derivatives :fibrill-ar,fibrill-ary, ad)s.,fibrill-ate,
intr. v., fibrill-at-ed, adj., fibrill-ation, o.,fibrill-
ed, fibrill-ose, fibrill-ous, adjs.

## fibrin
fibrin, п., a coagulable fibrous protein found in
blood (biochem.) — Coined fr. L. fibra (see
fiber) and chem. suff. -in. The term fibrin was
introduced by the Swiss anatomist and
physiologist Albrecht von Haller (1708-77) and
adopted by Alexander Schmidt (1831-94) about 1870.

## fibrinogen
fibrinogen, п., a protein in the blood, which
produces fibrin (biochem.) — A hybrid coined by
Alexander Schmidt (see prec. word) fr. fibrin
and Gk. -γενής, 'born of, produced by'. See -gen.
Derivatives: fibrinogen-ic, fibrinogen-ous, adjs.

## fibroid
fibroid, adj. and n. — A hybrid coined fr. L. fibra
(see fiber) andGk. -οειδής,'Μβ',ιϊ.είδος,'form,
shape'. See -oid.

## fibroin
fibroin, п., an albuminoid, forming the chief
constituent in natural silk. — F. fibroine, formed
fr. L. fibra (see fiber) with suff. -ine (see chem.
suff. -ine, -in).

## fibroma
fibroma, п., a benign fibrous tumor (med.) — A
Medical L. hybrid coined by Verneuil fr. L. fibra
(see fiber) and -опта, a suff. of Greek origin.

## fibrosis
fibrosis, п., abnormal formation of fibrous tissue
(med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. fibra
(see fiber) and -osis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## fibula
fibula, п., ι) a clasp; 2) the outer bone of the leg
(anat.) — L. fibula, 'clasp, buckle, brooch',
haplologic contraction of VL. "fivibula, for
'fig^e-bula, fr. VL. "fivere, a collateral form of
L.figere, 'to stick, fasten, fix'. See ditch and cp.
fix. Cp. also infibulate.
Derivative: fibul-ar, adj.

## -fie

-ficus (mostly through the medium of F. -fique),
formed from the stem of -ficere, unstressed form
of facere, 'to make, do'. See fact and cp. -ficate,
-fy. The suff. -fie is connected with the primary

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:307 COLUMN:2 -->
word by the thematic vowel -i- (cp. e.g. aur-i-

## fic
fic, color-i-fic).

## -ficate
-ficate, verbal suff. meaning 'to make, cause'. —
L. -ficalus, pp. suff. of verbs in -ficare. See -fie
and verbal suff. -ate and cp. -fy.

## -fication
-fication, subst. suff. denoting a making or
causing. — F. -fication, fr. L. -ficationem, ace. of

## fickle
fickle, adj. — ME. fikel, fr. OE. ficol, 'deceitful',

flkan, OHG. feihhan, 'deceit, fraud, treachery',
OE. fan, 'hostile', OHG. fenan, 'to hate', fr. I.-E.
base *peig-, 'evil-minded, treacherous, hostile',
whence also L. piget, 'it irks, troubles,

collateral base *peik-, whose derivatives see
under feud, 'enmity', fey and foe.
Derivatives: fickle-ness, п., fickl-y, adv. (rare).

## flcoid
flcoid, adj., resembling a fig. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. ficus, 'fig', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See Ficus and -oid.

## fictile
fictile, adj., capable of being molded, plastic. —
L. fictilis, 'made of clay, earthen', fr. fictus, pp.

word and -ile.

## fiction
fiction, n. — F., fr. L. fictldnem, ace. of fictid, 'a
forming, shaping', fr. fictus, pp. of fingere, 'to
form, shape'. The original meaning of this verb
was 'to knead'. It derives fr. I.-E. base *dheigh-,
*dhoigh-, *dhigh-, 'to knead, form out of clay,
form, shape', whence also OE. dag, 'dough'; see
dough and -ion. For the change of the concrete
meaning to the abstract cp. L. comprehendere,
'to seize, grasp; to comprehend, understand'
(see comprehend).
Derivatives: fictionist (q.v.), fiction-al, adj.,
fiction-al-ly, adv.

## fictionist
fictionist, п., a writer of fiction. — A hybrid

origin.
Derivative: ficlionist-ic, adj.

## fictitious
fictitious, adj., 1) imaginary; 2) false. — L.
ficticius, 'counterfeit, feigned, not genuine',
f r. fictus, pp. of fingere. See fiction and -itious.
Derivatives: fictitious-Iy, adv., fictitious-ness, a.

## Active
Active, adj., imaginary; feigned. — F. fictif
(fem. fictile), fr. L. fictus, pp. of fingere. See
fiction and -ive.
Derivative: fictive-ly, adv.

## Ficus
Ficus, п., a genus of trees, the fig. — L. ficus,
'fig tree, fig.' See fig.

## fid
fid, п., a bar of wood used as support (naut.) —
Of uncertain origin.

## fiddle
fiddle, n. — ME. fithele, fr. OE. fidele, rel. to
ON. fidla, MDu. vedel(e) [Du. ve(d)el\, OHG.
fidula (MHG. videle, G. Fiedel). These words
probably derive fr. VL. vitula, name of a
stringed instrument, which is of uncertain
origin. It is possibly a back formation fr. L.
vitulari, 'to exult, be joyful', which prob. stands
for vi-tulari and orig. meant 'to lift up one's
voice in joy', fr. *vi, exclamation of joy (cp.
Gk. εύαϊ, exclamation used in the cult of
Dionysus) and tulo, a secondary form of tolls, Ί
raise'. See tolerate and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also viol.
Derivatives: fiddle, v., fiddler (q.v.),fiddl-ing, adj.

## fiddle-faddle
fiddle-faddle, intr. v., to trifle. — Antiphonic

## fiddler
fiddler, n. — OE. fidelere, fr. fidele. See fiddle and

## fiddley
fiddley, п., the iron framework round the deck
opening that leads to the stokehole of a
steamship (naut.) — Of uncertain origin.

## fldeicommissnm

and neut. pp. of committere, 'to join together;
to entrust'. See faith and commit

## fidelity
fidelity, n. — F. fidelite, fr. L. fidelilalem ace. of

fidelitas, 'faithfulness, fidelity', fr. fidelis, 'true,
faithful', fr. fides, 'faith, confidence, belief,
which is rel. to foedus, 'compact, treaty', and
cogn. with OE. biddan, 'to ask'. See bid and

-ity and cp. affidavit, auto-da-fe, beadle, bona

## fide
fide, confederate, confide, defy, diffident, feal,

## fidget
fidget, intr. v., to move restlessly; tr. v., to cause

## fidibus
fidibus, п., a paper spill for lighting pipes. — G.,
prob. from facetious interpretation of the word

## fidibus in Horace
fidibus in Horace, Odes I 36: Et Hire et fidibus
juvat placare ... deds ('It pleases to appease
the gods with incense and lyre'); lure abl. of
tils, 'smoke', was taken humorously, in the
sense of 'tobacco-smoke', and fidibus was
accordingly explained as 'spill for lighting the
pipe'. Fidibus is the pi. ablative of L. fides, 'gut
string, stringed instrument, lyre', which is cogn.
with Gk. σφίδες (Hesychius), 'sausage'. The
word fidibus was introduced into English by
the American poet Henry Wadsworth
Longfellow (1807-82) in 1829.

## fiducial
fiducial, adj., 1) based on faith; 2) like a trust. —
L. fiducialis, 'reliable', fr. fiducia, 'trust, faith',
it.fidere, 'to trust'. See fidelity and adj. suff. -al.

## fiduciary
fiduciary, adj., 1) of a trustee; 2) held in trust; п.,
a trustee. — L. fiduciarius, 'relating to a thing
held in trust', fr. fiducia. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ary.

## fie
fie, interj. — ME. fi, fr. OF. fi; imitative. Cp.
L.fi.

## fief
fief, also feoff, п., land held in fee. — OF. feof
fief, fr. feudum, 'fief. See feud, 'a fief.

## field
field, n. — ME. field, fild, fr. OE. feld, rel. to OS.,
OFris., OHG. feld, MHG. wit, G. Feld, Du.
veld, 'field', and to ON. fold, 'earth', OE. folde,
OS. folda, of s.m. Cognates outside Teut. are
Lett, plain, 'to flatten', Olr. lathar,
'distribution', Mir. lathair, 'surface'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. *peld-to, enlargement of
base *pela-, 'flat, plain', whence L. planus, 'flat,
level', OSlav. polje, 'field'. See plain, adj., and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also veld and
the first element in feldspar. Cp. also Pole.
Derivatives: field, tr. and intr. v., field-er, n.

## fieldfare
fieldfare, п., a kind of thrush. — ME. feldefare,
fr. OE. feldefare, lit. 'field goer'. See field and
fare, 'to prosper'.

## fiend
fiend, n. — ME., fr. OE. feond, 'enemy, foe', lit.
'hater', rel. to ON. fjandi, OHG. fiant (MHG.
vient, G. Feind), Goth.fi/ands; prop. pres.
participles of OE. flon, flogan, resp. ON. fja,
OHG. fieri, Goth, fijan, 'to hate'; fr. I.-E. base
*pei-, *pi-, 'to blame, revile', whence also Goth.
faian, 'to blame', OI. ptjati, 'reviles, scorns'.
For mode of formation cp. friend.
Derivatives: fiend-ful, adj., fiend-ful-ly, adv.,
fiend-ish, adj., fiend-ish-ly, adv., fiend-ish-ness,
п., fiend-like, fiend-ly, adjs., fiend-U-ness, n.

## fierce
fierce, adj. — ME. fers, fiers, fr. OF. fers, fiers,
nom. of fer, fier, 'wild, ferocious' (whence F.

*gwer-, 'wild, wild animal', also Gk. *ήρ, whence
Lesbian φήρ, Thessal. φείρ, 'wild beast', OSlav.
zviri, Lith. zveris, 'wild beast', OPruss. swirins
(ace. pi), 'wild beasts'. Cp. feral, 'wild',
ferocious. Cp. also theralite, theriac, therio-, treacle,
Derivatives: fierce-ly, adv., fierce-ness, n.

## fieri facias
fieri facias, name of writ issued by a sheriff

## fiery
fiery, adj. — Formed fr. fire with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: fieri-ly, adv., fieri-ness, n.

## fife
fife, n. — F. fifre, 'fife, fifer', fr. Swiss G. pfifer,

*pipare, 'to pipe'. See pipe and cp. peep,'tochirp'.
Derivatives; fife, intr. and tr. v., fif-er, n.

## fifteen

fifteenth, adj. and n. — Formed fr. fifteen with

## fifth
fifth, adj. and n. — ME. fifihe, formed—on the

ftmfto, funflo, MHG. viinfte, G. flinfte, Goth.

## fiftieth
fiftieth, adj. and n. — Formed fr. fifty with
numeral suff. -th on analogy of tenth. Cp. OE. fif-
tigoda, fr. fiflig, 'fifty'. Cp. also ON. fimm-

## fifty
fifty, adj. and n. — ME., fr. OE.fiftig, which is

## fig
fig, п., the fruit. — OF. (= F.) figue, fr. OProv-
εης. ftga, fr. VL. *fica, fr. L. ficus, 'fig tree,

## fig
fig, tr. v., to dress. — A var. of feague.
Derivative: fig, п., dress; condition.

## fight
fight, tr. and intr. v. — ME. fehten, fr. OE. feoh-
tan, rel. to OFris. fiuhta, OS., OHG. fehtan,
Du. vechten, MHG. vehten, G. fechten, fr. I.-E.
base *pek-, 'to pluck out (wool or hair)', whence

Derivatives: fight, n. (q.v.),fight-er, n.,fight-ing,

## fight

fig tree', Hind, pargai, 'the evergreen oak', L.
quercus, 'oak'. Cp. alcornoque, cork, Quercus.
I.-E. *perq"(o)-, 'oak', developed over 'oak
forest' into 'wooded mountain', in Goth, fair-
guni, 'mountain', OE. fiergen-, 'wooded
mountain', OCelt. "Perkunia, whence Gk. Άρκύνια
8pr],' Ορκύνιος δρυμός, L. Hercynia silva, Her-
cynius saltus, 'Hercynian forest'. See Hercynia.
Derivative: firr-y, adj.

## fire
fire, n. — MM. fire, fir, fur, fyr, fr. OE. fyr, rel. to
OS., OFris. fiur, ON. fun, fyrr, MDu., Du.
vuur, OHG. fiur, MHG. viur, viuwer, G. Feuer,

-r, Goth, fan, gen. funins, ON. funi, and OPruss.
panno, 'fire*. Cp. also, with -r in the nom. and
-n in the gen., Hitt. pahhur, gen. pahhuenash,
'fire'. Cp. also pyre.
Derivatives: fire, tr. and intr. v., fire-less, adj.,
fir-ing, n.

## firkin
firkin, п., a small cask. — Fr. earlier ferdekyn,

was so called because it orig. contained a
quarter of a barrel.

## firm
firm, adj. — ME.ferme, fr. OF. (= F.)ferme, fr.
L. firmus, 'firm, steadfast, stable, strong', rel.
to fere, ferme, 'nearly', prob. also to fritus,

thorax, dharma, dharna, the first element in
Darius and the second element in aumildar and
in words there referred to.
Derivatives: firm, adv. and tr. and intr. v.,
firm-ly, adv., firm-ness, n.

## firm
firm, п., partnership. — It. firma, 'confirmation,

## firmament

## firman

## firn
firn, п., last year's snow, neve (phys. geogr.) —

Of last year', fr. MHG. virne. Old', fr. OHG.
firni, of s.m., which is rel. to OE. fyrn, 'old',
Goth, fairns, 'of last year, old', and cogn. with
Lith. pernai, 'last year", Lett, perns, 'old', Gk.
πέρυσι, 'a year ago, last year', OI. parut, 'of
last year', pura, 'before, formerly', puranah.

πίθος (dissimilated fr. ·φί9ος), 'winejar', ON.

fish, п., an aquatic animal. — ME. fisch, fr. OE.

adj., fish-i-ly, adv.,fisfi-i-ness, n.

fish, п., a counter used in games. — F. fiche, 'peg,

fissur-y, adjs.
