G. flackern, 'to flare, flicker'. These verbs prob.
meant orig. 'to beat with the wings', and are
rel. to dial. E. flack, 'to flap, strike'. See prec.
word.
Derivative: flicker, п., the act of fluttering.

## flicker
flicker, п., one who or that which Hicks. —
Formed fr. flick with agential suff. -er.

## flicker
flicker, п., a woodpecker of N. America. — Lit.
'the striking bird', hence prop, identical with
prec. word.

## flier
flier, flyer, n. — Formed fr. fly, v., with agential
suff. -er.

## flight
flight, п., the act of flying. — ME. fliht, fr. OE.
flyht, rel. to OE. fleogan, 'to fly'. Cp. LG. flugt
(whence G. Flucht), MLG., Du. vlucht, 'flight
of birds', OE. flyge, OS. fllugi, ON. flugr,
OHG. flug, MHG. vluc, G. Flug, 'flight', and
see fly, v. Cp. also next word. For the ending
see subst. suff. -t.
Derivatives: flight-y, adj., flight-i-ly, adv., flight-
i-ness, n.

## flight
flight, п., the act of fleeing. — ME. fluht, fliht,
fr. OE. fleoh-, stem of fleon (for "fleohan), 'to
flee', rel. to OS., OHG. fluht, OFris. flecht, Du.
vlucht, MHG. vluht, G. Flucht, 'the act of
fleeing- (see flee); confused with prec. word.

## flight
flight, intr. v., to fly in a flock; tr. v., to shoot
birds flying in a flock. — Fr. flight, 'the act
of flying'.

## flimflam
flimflam, п., humbug. — Antiphonic
reduplication of flam, 'sham, trick', fr. obsol. flamfew,
'gewgaw, trifle', fr. OF.fanfelue (F.fanfreluche),
'trifle, bauble', fr. ML. famfaluca, corruption
of Gk. πομφόλυξ,'βΐΓ bladder', lit.'water bubble'.
See pompholyx. Cp. It. fanfaluca, 'trifle', which
also derives fr. ML. fanfaluca.

## flimmer
flimmer, intr. v., to glitter, glimmer. — Prob. a
blend of flame and glimmer. Cp. G. flimmern.

## flimsy
flimsy, adj., 1) thin; 2) weak. — Formed with
metathesis fr. film. For the insertion of the
letter s before the suff. -y cp. clumsy.
Derivatives: flimsi-ly, adv., flimsi-ness, n.

## flinch
flinch, intr. v., to shrink back. — OF. flainchir,
flenchir, 'to turn, bend', prob. of Teut. origin.
Cp. MHG. linken, G. lenken, 'to bend, turn,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:313 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: FLINCH | 286 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:313 COLUMN:1 -->
lead', and see dank, lank, link, 'ring of a chain'.
Derivatives: flinch, п., flinch-er, n„ flinch-ing-
ly, adv.

## flinch
flinch, v. — A var. of flench.

## flinders
flinders, n. pi., fragments. — ME. flenderis, prob.
of Scand. origin. Cp. Norw. flindra, 'a thin piece,
splinter', which is rel. to Norw. flinter, 'a little
piece', and to Du. flenter, 'piece, fragment', and
prob. also to OE. flint, 'flint, rock'. See flint.

## Flindersia
Flindersia, п., a genus of Australian timber trees.
— ModL., named after the English navigator
Matthew Flinders (1774-1814). For the ending
see sufT. -ia.

## fling
fling, tr. and intr. v. — ME. flingen, flengen, 'to
rush', of Scand. origin. Cp. QN.flengja, 'to flog',
Dan. flenge, dial. Sv/ed.flanga, 'to slash', which
are of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: fling, п., fling-er, п., fling-y, adj.

## flinkite
flinkite, п., a basic manganese arsenate (mineral.)
— Named after the Swedish mineralogist
Gustaf Flink (1849-1931). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## flint
flint, n. — ME., fr. OE. flint, cogn. with Gk.
πλίνθος, 'brick', Olr. slind, 'brick', fr. I.-E. base
'splind-, *splid-, 'to split, cleave', OSlav. plinuta,
plita, Lith. plyta, Lett, plite 'brick', are Greek
loan words. Cp. plinth. Cp. also flinders. Cp.
also splint, splinter, split.
Derivatives :./?inr, adj.,flint-y, adj.,flint-i-ness,a.

## flip
flip, tr. and intr. v., to move with a jerk, tap, whip.
—Of imitative origin. Cp.flap.fillip, flippant, flop.
Derivative: flip, п., the act of flipping.

## flip
flip, п., a drink consisting of beer, egg, sugar. —
Lit. 'beaten up; whipped', derived fr. flip, v.

## flippancy
flippancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## flippant
flippant, adj., frivolous; disrespectful. — Coined
from the verb flip in imitation of French present
participles and adjectives in -ant. For a similar
formation cp. blatant.
Derivatives: flippant-ly, adv., flippant-ness, n.

## flipper
flipper, п., a broad flat limb adapted for
swimming. — Formed from the verb flip with agential
suff. -er.

## flirt
flirt, tr. and intr. v. — OF.fleureter (= F. comer
des fleurettes), 'to talk sweet nonsense, to flirt',
fr. OF.fleurete (F.fleurette), 'little flower;
courteous flattery', dimin. of fleur, 'flower', fr. L.
fldrem, ace. oiflds, of s.m. See flower.
Derivatives: flirt, п., flirt-ation, п., flirt-ation-al,
adj., flirt-atious, adj., flirt-atious-ly, adv., flirt-
atious-ness, п., flirt-ish, adj., flirl-ish-ness, п.,
flirt-y, adj.

## flit
flit, intr. v., 1) to move rapidly; 2) to flutter. —
ME. flitten, flatten, 'to carry away, go away',
fr. ON. flytja, 'to cause to flit', which is the
weak grade of fljota, 'to float'. See fleet, v., and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: ./fir, n.

## flitch
flitch, п., side of bacon. — ME. flicche, fr. OE.
flicce, 'flitch of bacon', rel. to ON. flikki, Norw.
flika, MLG. vlicke, 'piece of flesh', ON. fllk,
'tip, patch rag', and cogn. with Lith. plySti, 'to
tear', plaiSinti, 'to cause to burst', Lett, plaisa,
'cleft, gap'; not rel. to flesh.
Derivative: flitch, tr. v.

## flite
flite, flyte, intr. v., to quarrel; tr. v., to quarrel
with, to scold. — ME. fliten, fr. OE. flitan, 'to
contend, struggle, quarrel', rel. to OHG. /Пзап,
'to strive', OHG., MHG. flia, 'contest, diligence',
G. Fleifi, Du. vli/t, 'diligence, industry'.

## fliting
fliting, flyting, п., ι) a scolding; 2) an abusive
speech. — ME. fliting. See prec. word and -ing,
suff. forming verbal nouns.

## flitter
flitter, intr. v., to flutter. — Freq. of flit. Cp.
flutter.

## flittermouse
flittermouse, п., bat (dial.) — Lit. 'a fluttering
mouse'. See prec. word and mouse and cp.
OHG. fledarmus (MHG. fledermus, G. F/eder-
maus), 'bat*, which is compounded of fledaron,
*to flutter', and mus, 'mouse'. Cp. the equivalent
Du. vledermuis, vleermuis.

## flivver
flivver, п., a small and cheap motorcar (U.S.
Slang). — An invented word.

## flix
flix, п., down; fur. — Of uncertain origin.

## float
float, intr. and tr. v. — ME. floten, flotien, fr. OE.

## flotian
flotian, rel. to ON.flota, MDu. vloten, Du. vlot-
ten, and to OE. fleotan, 'to float'; OE. flotian

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:313 COLUMN:2 -->
was influenced in form by OF. floter (F. flotter),
'to float'. See fleet, v., and cp. float, ή.
Derivatives: float, n. (q.v.),float-er, п., float-ing,
n. and adj., float-ing-ly, adv., float-y, adj.,
floatation (q.v.)

## float
float, n. — ME. flote, 'ship, fleet', fr. OE. flota,
lit. 'that which floats', rel. to ON. floti, Dan.
flaade, MDu. vldte, Du. viol, OHG.,MHG.v/£j,
G. Flofi, 'float, raft', and to OE. flotian, 'to
float'. F. flotte, It. flotta, 'fleet', are Teut. loan
words. G. Flotte, 'fleet', has been reborrowed fr.
F. flotte. See float, v., and cp. flotilla, flotsam.
Derivatives: floatage (q.v.)

## floatage
floatage, п., flotage. — Formed fr. float, п., with
suff. -age. Cp. flotage.

## floatation
floatation, п., flotation. — Formed fr. float, v.,
with suff. -ation. Cp. flotation,

## flocciliation
flocciliation, п., picking at bedclothes in delirium
(med.) — Formed with suff. -ation fr. L.floccus,
'flock of wool". See flock of wool.

## floccose
floccose, adj., woolly. — L. floccosus, fr. floccus,
'flock of wool'. See flock of wool, and adj.
suff. -ose.
Derivative: floccose-ly, adv.

## fioccule
fioccule, п., detached mass of wool. — See
flocculus,

## flocculence
flocculence, n. — Formed fr. flocculent with suff.
-ce.

## flocculent
flocculent, adj., resembling wool, flocky. —
Formed fr. flocculus with suff. -ent.
Derivative: flocculent-ly, adv.

## flocculose
flocculose, adj., minutely floccose. — See
flocculus and adj. suff. -ose.

## flocculous
flocculous, adj., flocculose. — See next word and
•ous.

## flocculus
flocculus, п., ι) a small tuft of wool or woolly
substance; 2) a small lobe on the lower side of
the cerebellum (anal.); 3) cloudlike mass of
vapors in the solar atmosphere. — ModL.,
dimin. of L. floccus, 'flock of wool'. See next
word.

## floccus
floccus, п., tuft of wool or hair. — L., 'lock or
flock of wool', which prob. stands for "bhlokos
and is cogn. with OHG. blaha, MHG. btahe,
G. Blahe (dial. Blache), OSwed. blan, bla,
earlier Dan. blaa, Dan. blaar, 'tow, hards', ON.
blxja, Dan. ble, 'sheet'. Cp. flock of wool,
fioccule, floss.
flock of wool. — ME. flocke, fr. OF. floe, fr. L.
floccus. See prec. word.
Derivatives: flock, tr. v., to fill with flocks,
flock-y, adj.

## flock of sheep
flock of sheep, n. — ME., fr. OE. flocc, rel. to
ON. flokkr, 'crowd, troop, band', Dan. flok,
Swed. flock, MLG. vlocke, 'crowd, flock', of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: flock, intr. v., to crowd together;
tr. v., to bring together (rare).

## floe
floe, п., a field of floating ice. — Norw./fo, 'layer',
fr. ON. fid; rel. to flag, 'stone' (q.v.)

## Floerkea
Floerkea, п., a genus of plants, the false
mermaid (hot.) — ModL., named after the German
botanist Heinrich Gustav Florke (1764-1835).

## flog
flog, tr. v., to beat; to whip. — Prob. corruption
of L. flagellare, 'to scourge'. See flagelluin.
Derivatives: flogg-ing, п., flogg-ing-ly, adv.

## flood
flood, n. — ME. flod, fr. OE. flod, 'a flowing,
flow, stream, flow of tide, tide', rel. to OS.,
OFris. flod, ON. flod, Dan., Swed. flod, MDu.
vloet, vloed, Du. vloed, OHG., MHG. fluot, G.
Flut, Goth, flodus and to ON. floa, 'to flood',
and cogn. with Gk. πλώειν, 'to float, swim',
πλωτός, 'floating, navigable'. These words
derive fr. I.-E. base *pldu-, a gradational variant
of *pleu-, 'to flow, swim'. See flow and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: flood, tr. and intr. v.,flood-ed, adj.,

## flood-ing
flood-ing, n.

## floodometer
floodometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
height of floods. — A hybrid coined fr. flood
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## floor
floor, n. — ME. flor, fr. OE. flor, rel. to MDu.,
Du. vloer, ON. flor, fldrr, Norw. flor, 'floor of
a cow stall', MHG. vluor, G. Flur, 'field,
meadow, plain, floor', fr. I.-E. base *plaros, "plara,
whence also Olr. lar (for *pldr), W. llawr, Bret.
leur, 'ground, floor'. This base is an

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:313 COLUMN:3 -->
enlargement of base *p(e)/e-, 'spread out, broad, flat',
whence L. planus, 'level, flat'. See plain, adj.,
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: floor, tr. v„floor-er, п., floor-ing, n.

## flop
flop, intr. v., to fall down suddenly; tr. v., to
throw with a sudden thud. — Orig. an anti-
phonic variant of flap (q.v.) Cp. flump.
Derivatives: flop, n. and adv.,flopp-y, nd\.,flopp-
i-ly, adv., flopp-i-ness, n.

## Flora
Flora, 1) Roman goddess of flowers; 2) fern. PN.
— L. Flora. See next word.

## flora
flora, п., plants of a region or period. — L. Flora,
name of the goddess of flowers, fr. flSs, gen.
fldris, 'flower'. See flower and cp. floral, Floreal.
The name flora was introduced into botany by
Linnaeus; cp. fauna.

## floral
floral, adj., 1) pertaining to a flora; pertaining
to flowers. — L. Floralis, 'pertaining to Flora',
fr. Flora. See Flora and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: floral-ly, adv.

## Floreal
Floreal, п., name of the 8th month of the French
revolutionary calendar (lasting from April 20th
to May 19th). — F. Floreal, lit. 'the month of
flower'; a word coined by Fabre d'Eglantine in
1793 from L. floreSiis, 'pertaining to flowers', fr.
flos, gen. floris, 'flower'. See flower and adj. suff.
-al.

## Florence
Florence, fern. PN. — L. Florentia,fem. of Floren-
tius, lit. 'blooming', fr. florins, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of flOrere, 'to flower, flourish', fr. flos,
gen. flur is, 'flower'. See flower and -ence and
cp. florence.

## florence
florence, п., a kind of woven material (esp. of
silk). — Orig. 'anything made in Florence
(Italy)', fr. L. Florentia, 'Florence', lit. 'bloom'
(whence It. Fiorenze, later contracted into Fi-
renze, and F. Florence), fr. florins, gen. -entis.
See prec. word and cp. Florentine.

## Florentine
Florentine, adj., pertaining to the city of
Florence, Italy. — L. Florentinus, 'of Florence', fr.
Florentia. See florence and adj. suff. -ine.

## florescence
florescence, п., a blooming, blossoming. —
Formed from next word with stiff, -ce. Cp.
efflorescence, inflorescence.

## florescent
florescent, adj., blooming, blossoming. *- L.
fldrescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of florescere,
'to begin to flower', inchoative of florere, 'to
flower, flourish*, from flos, gen. floris, 'flower*.
See flower and -escent and cp. efflorescent, in-
florescent.

## floriculture
floriculture, п., the cultivation of flowers. —
Formed on analogy of agriculture, fr. L. flos,
gen. floris, 'flower', and cultura, 'a cultivating,
culture'. See flower and culture.
Derivatives: floricultur-al, adj., floricultur-al-ly,
adv., floricultur-isl, n.

## floret
floret, п., a small flower. — OF. florete (F. fleu-
rette), dimin. of OF. flor (F. fleur), fr. L. fldrem,
ace. of flos, 'flower'. See flower and -et and cp.
fleuret.
Derivative: floret-ed, adj.

## donate
donate, floriated, adj., decorated with floral
ornaments. — Formed with adj. suff. -ate (resp.
also -ed), fr. L. flos, gen. floris, 'flower*. See
flower.
Derivative: floriat-ion, n.

## florid
florid, adj., full of flowers. — L.floridus,
'abounding in flowers', fr. flos, gen. floris, 'flower'. See
flower and adj. suff. -id.
Derivatives:florid-ity, п., florid-ly, adv., florid-
ness, n.

## Florideae
Florideae, n. pi., an order of algae (hot.) —
ModL., fr. L. floridus, 'abounding in flowers'.
See prec. word and -idae.

## floriferous
floriferous, adj., bearing flowers. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. florifer, 'bearing flowers', from

## fids
fids, gen. floris, 'flower', and ferd, ferre, 'to
bear, carry'. See flower and -ferous.

## florilegium
florilegium, п., ι) a collection of flowers; 2) an
anthology. — ModL., formed on analogy of
Gk. ανθολογία (ср. anthology) fr. L. florilegus,
'flower-culling', fr. flos, gen. floris, 'flower', and
legere, 'to gather, collect'. See flower and lecture.

## florin
florin, п., ι) orig. a gold coin issued in Florence
in 1252; 2) name of various European gold and
silver coins. — ME., fr. OF., fr. It. fiorino, fr.

## fiore
fiore, 'flower', fr. L. fldrem, ace. of flos, 'flower';
so called because gold coins issued at Florence

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:314 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 287 | FLURRY | Derivatives: fluid, п., fluid-al, adj., fluid-al-ly. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:314 COLUMN:1 -->
had originally the figure of a lily (the badge of
the city) stamped upon them; see Bower, n. OF.
florin was influenced in form by Latin florem.

## florist
florist, n. — Formed on analogy of F. fleurisie,
from L. fids, gen. fldris, 'flower'. See flower
and -ist.

## -florous
-florous, combining form meaning 'having (a
certain number of) flowers, as uniflorous,
multiflorous. — Formed fr. L. fids, gen. fldris,
'flower' (see flower), and -ous.

## floruit
floruit, п., period at which a person flourished. —
L., 'he flourished', pret. of fldrere, 'to flower,
flourish', tr.flds, gea. fldris, 'flower'. See flower,

## flory
flory, adj. — A variant of fleury.

## floscule
floscule, п., a floret. — F., fr. L. fldsculus, 'a little
flower', dimin. of fids, gen. fldris, 'a flower'.
See flower and -cule.
Derivatives: floscul-ar, floscul-ous, adjs.

## floss
floss, п., i)the rough outside silk of a silkworm's
cocoon; 2) waste fiber of silk; 3) soft silk used
in embroidery. — Orig. used as an adj. in floss
silk, translation of the Old French phrase soye
flosche (F. soiefloche), lit. 'soft silk'. OF.flosche
derives fr. OF. floe, 'a small tuft of wool', fr.
L. floccus. See floccus.
Derivative: floss-y, adj.

## flotage
flotage, п., ι) the act of floating; 2) anything that
floats. — See floatage,

## fiotant
fiotant, adj., floating in water; flying (her.) —
OF. flotant (F. floliant), pres. part, of floter
(F. flotter), 'to float'. See float, v., and -ant.

## flotation
flotation, п., ι) the act of floating; 2) the act of
starting a business. — Altered fr. floatation
under the influence of F. flotation, 'floating',
flottaison, 'water line'. Cp. flotsam,

## flotilla
flotilla, п., a small fleet. — Sp., dimin. of flota,
'fleet', which is of Teut. origin. See float, п.,
and cp. words there referred to.

## flotsam
flotsam, п., floating wreckage. — AF. floteson,
'flotsam', corresponding to OF. flotaison, 'a
floating' (whence F. flottaison, 'water line'), fr.
floter (F. flotter), "to float'; see Boat, v., and cp.
flotation. The ending of flotsam was influenced
by the Scand. surf. -sam. Cp. jetsam.

## flounce
flounce, intr. v., to move jerkily; to plunge; to
flounder. — Prob. borrowed from Scand. Cp.
dial. Swed. flunsa, 'to plunge', Norw. flunsa,
'to hurry', which are of imitative origin; prob.
influenced in form by bounce.
Derivative: flounc-ing, n.

## flounder
flounder, п., one of several edible flatfishes. —
OF. flondre, of Scand. origin. Cp. Swed., Norw.

## flundra
flundra, Dan. flynder, ON. flydra, 'flatfish',
which are rel. to MLG. vlundere, MHG. vluo-
der, 'flounder' (G. Flunder, of s.m., is a LG.
loan word), and cogn. with Gk. πλατύς, 'flat,
wide, broad', L. planta, 'sole of the foot'. See
place and cp. plaice. Cp. also flat,

## flounder
flounder, intr. v., to struggle in an awkward
manner. — Prob. a blend of founder and blunder.
Derivatives: flounder, п., flounder-ing, adj.,

## flounder-ing-ly
flounder-ing-ly, adv.

## flour
flour, n. — A var. of flower, orig. identical also
in meaning with it, but later used only in the
figurative sense as 'flower (i.e. the finest part)
of the meal'.
Derivatives: flour, tr. v., flour-y, adj.

## flourish
flourish, intr. and tr. v. — ME. florisshen, fturis-
shen, fr. OF. floriss-, pres. part, stem of florir,
fr. VL. "florlre, corresponding to fldrere, 'to
blossom, flourish', flos, gen. fldris, 'flower'. See
flower, п., and verbal suff. -ish and cp. fleury.
Derivatives: flourish, п., flourish-ing, adj.,

## flourish-y
flourish-y, adj.

## flout
flout, tr. and intr. v., to mock, jeer. — Fr.
ME. flouten, 'to play the flute'. For sense
development cp. the related MDu. fluyten, Du.

## fluiten
fluiten, 'to play the flute; to jeer'. See flute.
Derivatives: flout, n.,flout-er, n.,flout-ing-ly, adv.

## flow
flow, intr. v. — ME. flowen, fr. OE. fldwan, rel.
to Du. vloeien, 'to flow', ON. flda, 'to deluge',
flood', OHG. flouwen, 'to rinse, wash', fr. I.-E.
base *pleu-, 'to flow, swim', whence also OI.

## plavati
plavati, 'navigates, swims', plavayati, 'causes to
swim, overflows', Toch. В plewe, 'ship', Arm.
luanam, Ί wash', hetum, Ί pour', Gk. πλόνω,
Ί wash', πλέω (for 'πλέίω), Ί sail, go by sea,
swim', L. pluere, 'to rain', pluvia, 'rain', OSIav.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:314 COLUMN:2 -->
piovo, pluti, 'to flow, navigate', Lith. pilu, pilti,
'to pour out', plau/u, plauti, 'to swim, rinse'.
See pluvial and cp. fleet, v., adj. and п., flit,
float, flood, flutter, fly, v. and n. Cp. also paludal,
Plynteria, paeumo-, pulmo-, pyelo-. I.-E. base
'pleu-, 'to flow', is ult. identical with base
'pete-, "pie-, 'to fill'. See full, adj., and words
there referred to and cp. esp. plutocracy.
Derivatives: flow, п., flow-ing, adj., flow-ing-Iy,
adv.

## flower
flower, n. — ME. flour, it. OF. flour, flur, flor
(F. fleur), fr. L. florem, ace. of flos, 'flower', fr.
I.-E. base *bhld-, *bhle-, *bhla-, 'to blossom,
flourish', whence also Mir. blath, W. blawd,
'bloom, flower', OE. bldwan, 'to flower, bloom'.
See blow, 'to flower', and cp. blade, blood,
bioom, blossom. Cp. also cauliflower, defloration,
deflower, effloresce, ferret, 'ribbon', fleuret,
fleur-de-lis, flirt, Flora, flora, floral, Floreal,
Florence, Florentine, florescent, floret, florid,
florin, flour, flourish, milleflori, Phyllis, phyllo-.
The meaning 'to blossom, flourish', denoted by
base 'bhld-, *bhle-, 'bhld-, is secondary. The
orig. meaning of this base is 'to blow, to swell'.
See blow, 'to puff', and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: flower, v.,flower-ed, adj., flower-er,
п., flower-ing, adj., flower-y, adj.

## flower-de-luce
flower-de-luce, п., iris. —Corruption of fleur-de-
lis (q.v.)

## floweret
floweret, п., a little flower. — Dimin. of flower.
Cp. fleuret, floret.

## flown
flown, pp. of fly.

## flu
flu, n„ influenza (colloq.) — Shortened fr.
Influenza.

## flucti-
flucti-, combining form meaning 'wave'. — L.
flucti-, fr. fluctus, 'wave', fr. fluct-ium), arctiaic

## fluctuant
fluctuant, adj., undulating (rare). — L. fluctuant,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of fluctuare. See next

## fluctuate
fluctuate, intr. v., to move like a wave; to

## fluctuation
fluctuation, n. — L. fluctudlio, gen. -dnis, 'a
wavering motion, fluctuation', fr. fluctudt-(um),
archaic pp. stem of fluctuare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## flue
flue, п., formerly, a chimney; now, a channel for
the passage of smoke, etc. — Of uncertain
origin.

## flue
flue, п., fluff. — ME. fluwe, fr. Flemish vluwe, fr.
F. velu, 'hairy, shaggy', fr. Late L. villutus,
corresponding to L. vittdsus, 'hairy'. See velours
and cp. flue, 'fishing net', which is derivatively
identical with/7ие, 'fluff'. Cp. also fluff.
Derivative: flue-y, adj.

## flue
flue, п., the fluke of an anchor or a harpoon. —
Cp. fluke, 'broad end of the arm of an anchor'.

## flue
flue, п., a kind of fishing net. — ME., fr. Flem.
vluwe. See flue, 'fluff'.

## fluellite
fluellite, п., aluminum fluoride (mineral.) — A
blend of flu(orine) and (wavjellite.

## fluency
fluency, n. — Formed from next word with suff.

## fluent
fluent, adj. — L. fluins, gen. -entis, pres. part,
of fluere, 'to flow', whence flumen, 'river'; cogn.
with Gk. φλύειν, 'to boil over, bubble up',
φλεϊν, 'to abound', fr. I.-E. 'bhleu-,
enlargement of base *bhel-, *bhle~-, 'to blow, swell'.
See blow, 'to puff', and -ent and cp. affluent,
afflux, circumfluent, confluent, defiuent, diffluent,
flimflam, floss, fluid, flume, fluor, fluorescence,
fluorine, flush, 'number of cards', Fiustra,
flnvial, flux, Influence, influenza, influx,
mellifluent, reflux, superfluous. Cp. also phello- and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: fluent-Iy, adv.,fluent-ness, a.

## fluff
fluff, п., soft down. — Prob. rel. to flue, 'fluff'.
Derivatives: fluff, tr. and intr. v., fluff-y, adj.,
fluff-i-ly, adv., fluff-i-ness, n.

## flugelman
flugelman, n. fugleman. — G. Fliigelmann, 'file

## fluid
fluid, adj. — F. fluide, fr. L. fluidus, 'flowing,
fluid', fr. fluere. See fluent and adj. suff. -id.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:314 COLUMN:3 -->
adv., fluid-ty, adv., fluid-ness, п., fluidity (q.v.),
fluidize (q.v.)

## fluidify
fluidify, tr. v., to make fluid. — See fluid and -fy.

## fluidity
fluidity, п., fluid state or quality. — See fluid and
-ity and cp. F. fluidity.

## fluidize
fluidize, tr. v., to make fluid. — A hybrid coined

## fluke
fluke, п., ι) flounder, flatfish; 2) a flat parasitic
worm. — ME. floke, fluke, fr. OE. fldc,
'flatfish', rel. to ON. fldki, of s.m., and in gradat-
ional relationship to Norw. flak, 'disk, floe'. See

## fluke
fluke, п., part of an anchor. — Prob. figurative

arm of an anchor was compared with a flatfish.

## fluke
fluke, п., a lucky accidental stroke at billiards
or other games. — Of unknown origin.

## fluky
fluky, adj., infested with flukes. — Formed with

worm'.

## fluky
fluky, adj., lucky. — Formed with adj. suff. -y
fr. fluke, 'accidental stroke'.
Derivatives: fluki-ly, adv., fluki-ness, n.
Нише, п., artificial water course. — ME., fr.
OF. flum, 'river', fr. L. flumen, 'river', from the
stem of fluere, 'to flow'. See fluent.

## flummery
flummery, п., ι) a soft jellylike food made from
the husks of oats; 2) empty compliments;
nonsense. — W. Ilymru, 'sour oatmeal jelly boiled
with the husks'.

## flummox
flummox, tr. v., to confound (slang). — Prob. rel.
to OE. flummocks, 'to maul, mangle', and,

## flump
flump, tr. v., to move or fall heavily, to plump;

flop and plump.

## flung
flung, past tense and pp. of fling. — ME. flungen,

## flunky
flunky, flunkey, п., a lackey. — Prob. meaning

F. flanquer, 'to be at the side of, to flank', fr.

Derivatives: flunkey-dom, п., flunkey-ish, adj.,
flunkey-ism, n.

## duo-
duo-, combining form indicating the presence of

See next word.

## fluor
fluor, п., a mineral containing fluorine, fluorite.
— ModL., fr. L. fluor, 'a flowing', ft. fluere, Ίο
flow'. See fluent and -or and cp. fluorine.

## fluoresce
fluoresce, intr. v. — Back formation fr.
fluorescence.

## fluorescence
fluorescence, n. (physics). — Formed with suff.
-escence (on analogy of opalescence,
phosphorescence) fr. fluor(spar). The word fluorescence
was coined by the English mathematician and
physicist, Sir George Gabriel Stokes (1819-1903)
in 1852 in allusion to the circumstance that he
noticed this phenomenon first in fluorspar.

## fluorescent
fluorescent, adj. — See prec. word and -ent.

## fluoric
fluoric, adj., pertaining to fluorine (chem.) —
Formed with suff. -1c fr. fluor.

## fluorine
fluorine, п., name of a nonmetallic element
belonging to the halogen family (chem.) — Coined
by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy
(1778-1829) fr. fluor with chem. suff. -ine (on
analogy of brom-ine, chlor-ine. iod-ine). Tho
element was so called by him because it was
found first in fluorspar.

## fluorite
fluorite, п., fluorspar (mineral.) — Formed fr.
fluor with subst. suff. -He.

## fiuoro-
fiuoro-, combining form denoting either 1)
fluorine or 2) fluorescence. — See fluor.

## fluoroscope
fluoroscope, п., an instrument for observing
fluorescence. — A hybrid coined fr. L. fluor and
Gk. -σκότηον, fr. σκοττεΐν, 'to look at,
examine'. See fluor and -scope.
Derivative: fiuoroscop-y, n.

## fluorspar
fluorspar, п., fluorite. — Lit. 'fluor used as a
spar'. See fluor and spar, and cp. G. Flufispat.
Cp. also feldspar, feldspathic.

## flurry
flurry, п., 1) a gust of wind; 2) agitation. — Prob.
a blend of obsol. flurr, 'to whir' (which is of
imitative origin), and hurry.
Derivative: flurry, tr. v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:315 COLUMN:1 -->

## flush
flush, intr. and tr. v., to start up suddenly. —
ME. fluschen, of imitative origin.

## flnsh
flnsh, п., a flock of flushed birds. — Fr. prec. word.

## flush
flush, intr. v., i) to rush (said of blood); to flow
suddenly; 2) to blush; tr. v., i) to cleanse with
a sudden flow of water; 2) to make red; 3) to
excite. — A blend of flash and blush.

## flush
flush, adj. and adv., full to overflowing. — Fr.
prec. word.
Derivatives: flush, tr. v., to fill up, flush-ness, n.

## flush
flush, adj., even, level. — Prob. identical with
prec. word and orig. applied to a river running
full, hence level with its banks.

## flush
flush, п., a number of cards of the same suit. —
F. flux, lit. 'flux, flow', fr. L. fluxus. See flux.
Derivative: flush, adj., consisting of cards of
the same flush.

## flushing
flushing, п., a kind of coarse cloth. — From

## fluster
fluster, tr. v., to confuse with drink; to confuse;

Derivatives: fluster, п., flusler-y, adj.

## Flustra
Flustra, п., a genus of marine Polyzoa (zool.) —
ModL., coined by Linnaeus fr. L. flustra (pi.),

for "flugs-tra and derives fr. fluere, 'to flow'.
See fluent.

## flute
flute, n. — ME. floute, floite, fr. OF. flaute,

loan words. Cp. flout.

## flute
flute, intr. v. — ME. flouten, flatten, fr. OF. flau-

Derivatives: flut-ed, adj., flut-er, a.,flut-ing, п.,
flut-y, adj.

## flutist
flutist, n. — A hybrid coined fr. flute and -ist,

## flutter
flutter, intr. v., to flap the wings; tr. v., to move

Derivatives: flutter, п., flutter-er, п., flutter-ing,
adj., flutter-ing-ly, adv., flutter-y, adj.

## fluvial

## fluviatic

## fluviatile
fluviatile, adj., fluvial. — F., fr. L. fluviatilis,

## finvio-
finvio-, combining form meaning 'river'. — Fr.

## flux
flux, п., ι) a flowing; 2) a continuous change. —
ME., fr. MF. (= F.)flux, fr. L. fluxus, 'a

flow'. See fluent and cp. flush, 'a number of
cards', afflux, conflux, efflux, influx, reflux.
Derivatives '.flux, v.,fluxible (q.v.),flux-ibil-ity, n.

## fluxible

— OF., fr. Late L. fluxibilis, 'fluid', fr. L. fluxus,

## fluxion
fluxion, п., ι) a flowing; 2) a continuous change.
— F., fr. L. fluxidnem, ace. of fluxio, 'a
flowing', fr. fluxus, pp. of fluere. See flux and -ion.
Derivatives: fluxion-al, fluxion-ary, adjs.

## fly
fly, intr. and tr. v. — ME. flegen,flien, fr. OE.fleo-
gan, rel. to OS., OHG.fliogan, ON.fljuga.Swed.

fliaga, MDu. vlieghen, Du. vliegen, MHG.
vliegen, G. fliegen, 'to fly*, Goth, us-flaugjan, 'to

and cp. fledge, flight, 'the act of flying', fowl.
Derivatives: fly, п., the act of flying, fly, adj.
(q.v.), fly-ing, adj. and n.

## fly
fly, п., a two-winged insect. — ME. flege, flie,
fr. OE. flioge, flyge, rel. to OS. fliega, ΟΝ.,
Swed. fluga, Norw. fljuge, earlier Dan. fluge,
Dun. flue, MDu. vtieghe, Du. vlieg, OHG. flioga,
fliuga, MHG. vliuge, vliege, G. Fliege, 'fly', lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:315 COLUMN:2 -->
'the flying (scil. insect)', fr. OE. fliogan etc.,
'to fly'. See fly, v.

## fly
fly, adj., agile; knowing, sharp (slang). — Fr. fly, v.

## flyte
flyte, flyting. — See flite, fliting.

foal, n. — ME./ofe, fr. OE.fola, rel. to OS., OHG,
folo, ON. foil, OFris. fola, MHG. vole, G.
■Fohlen, Goth, /и/а, and cogn. with Gk. πώλος,

## foam
foam, n. — ME. fame, fome, fr. OE. fam, rel. to

OI. phenah, L. рйтех, 'pumice', spitma, 'foam',

## foam
foam, intr. v. — ME. famien, fomen, fr. fame,

Derivative: foam-er, n.

fob, tr. v., to cheat (archaic). — Prob. fr. G. fop-

focal, adj. — Formed fr. focus with adj. suff. -al.

fochneter, п., an instrument for measuring the

## focus
focus, п., a point at which rays of light, heat,

Derivatives: focus, tr. and intr. v., focus-er, n.

## fodder
fodder, n. — ME. foder, fr. OE. fddor, from the

Swed. foder, MDu. voeder, Du. voe(de)r, OHG.

Derivatives: fodder-er, п., fodder-less, adj.

## foe
foe, n. — ME. fo, fa, fr. OE. fag, /ah, 'hostile',
rel. to OHG. fehan, 'to hate', gi-flh, MHG. ge-
vech, 'hostile', Goth, faih, 'deception', bi-faih,

Foehn, Fohn, п., a warm dry wind blowing down

## foeman
foeman, п., foe, enemy. — ME. fomon, fr. OE.

## Focniculum
Focniculum, п., a genus of plants of the carrot

## foetal
foetal, adj. — See fetal.

## foetathm
foetathm, n. — See fetation.

## foeticide
foeticide, n. — See feticide.

## foetus
foetus, n. — See fetus.

## fog
fog, п., coarse grass, aftermath. — ME. fogge,

OS. fuht, MLG., MDu. vucht, Du. vocht,
OHG. fiiht(i), MHG. viuhte, G. feucht, 'moist,
damp', and cogn. with OI. pankah, 'mud, mire',

and prob. also with Arm. zanganem (for "z-han-
ganem), 'to knead'.
Derivative: fog, tr. v., to leave the grass

## fog
fog, п., mist. — Dan. fog, 'spray, shower, drift

Derivative: fog, tr. v., to envelop into a fog,

foggage, п., the right of pasturing cattle on fog

## foggy

## fogy
fogy, fogey, adj., an old dull fellow. — Of

## foible
foible, п., a weak point in one's character. —
OF., 'weak' (F. faible), dissimil. fr. L. flebilis,

of a sword blade', in contradistinction to its
strongest part, called forte.

## foil
foil, п., ι) a leaflike space in the tracery of a
window ; 2) a leaf of metal. — OF. foil, fuil, fr. L.

## foil

## foil

## foiling
foiling, п., decoration with foils. — Formed with

## foiling
foiling, п., trail of a deer. — Formed with subst.

## foin

## foison

## foist
foist, tr. v., to palm off; to put in surreptitiously.

## fold
fold, tr. and intr. v., to double. — ME. falden,

Dan. folde, Swed. falla, MLG. volden, MDu.
vouden, Du. vouwen, OHG. faldan, MHG. val-
den, valten, G. fatten, Goth, falpan, and cogn.

I.-E. *pel-to-, enlargement of base *pel-, 'to

## fold
fold, п., a folding; anything folded. — ME. feald,

fold, п., pen for sheep. — ME. fold, fr. OE. falod,

-fold, suff. — ME., fr. OE. -feald, rel. to OS. -/ей/,

and cogn. with Gk. -παλτος, -πλάσιος, and -πλός,
-ττλόος, Att. -πλους (in ά-ττλός, ά-ττλόος, resp.

resp. Att.· δι-πλοϋς, 'double', etc.), and L. -plus
(in simrplus, 'simple, single', du-plus, 'double',
etc.) See fold, v., and cp. haplo-. Cp. also simple,

## folding
folding, п., the act of folding. — Formed fr. fold,

nouns.

## folding
folding, adj., that which folds or is folded. —

## folding

## foliaceous

See folio and -aceous.

## folinge
folinge, n. — Altered fr. F. feuillage, fr. feuille,
'leaf, fr. L. folia, 'leaves', pi. of folium, but
mistaken for a fern. sing. E. foliage was
influenced in form by L. folium. See folio and -age
and cp. foil, 'space in the tracery of a window'.

## foliar
foliar, adj., pertaining to leaves. — Formed with
suff. -ar fr. L. folium, 'leaf. See folio.

## foliate
foliate, adj., i) having leaves; z) resembling
leaves. — L. foliatus, 'leafy', fr. folium, 'leaf.
See folio and adj. suff. -ate and cp. defoliate,
exfoliate, perfoliate.

## folinte
folinte, tr. v., ι) to beat into a leaf; z) to furnish
with foils; intr. v., to split into laminae or
leaves. — L. foliatus. See prec. word.
Derivatives: foliat-ed, adj., foliat-ion, n.

## foliature
foliature, п., foliage. — L. foliatUra, fr. foliatus,
'leafy'. See foliate, adj., and -иге.

## folio
folio, п., ι) a leaf of a book; z) a sheet of paper
once folded. — АЫ. of L. folium, 'leaf, which
prob. stands for I.-E. 'bholrom, and is cogn. with
Gk. φύλλον (for *ЬЫ1Уот), 'leaf, Gael, bile (for
*Ьке1Уот), 'leaflet, blossom'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base *bhl6-, *bhle-, 'to blossom',
properly 'to swell'. See blow, 'to flower', blow,
'to puff, and cp. foliage, foil, 'leaf of me1 .1',
feuilleton, filemot, and asperifoliate, bifolinte,
Caprifolinceae, defoliate, exfolinte, perfolinte,
portfolio, Trifolium. Cp. also phyllo-. Cp also
blade.
Derivatives: folio, adj. and tr. v.

## folioie
folioie, п., leaflet (oof.); a small organ resembling
a leaf (zool.) — F., fr. L. foliolum, dimin. of
folium, 'leaf. See folio and dimin. suff. -ole.

## foliose
foliose, adj., leafy. — L. foliosus, fr. folium. See
folio- and adj. suff. -ose

## folium
folium, п., ι) a leaf; г) a thin layer. — L. See
folio-.

## folk
folk, n. — ME., fr. OE. folc, 'people, crowd', rel.
to ΟΝ., Dan., Swed., OFris. folk, MLG., MDu.
vole, Du. voile, OHG. folc, MHG. vole, G.
Volk, 'people', fr. Teut. "fulka-, which prob.
meant orig. 'host of warriors'. The above words
are rel. to OE. ge-fylce, OH.fylki, 'troop, army',
and prob. cogn. with Alb. plogu, 'heap, crowd'.
For the orig. meaning of Teut. 'fulka- cp. Lith.
pulkas, 'heap, troop', OSlav. pluku (for *pulkii),
'host of warriors', which are traceable to Teut.
*fulka-. The orig. meaning of the above Teut.
words shows that they cannot be connected
etymologically with Gk. πλήθος, 'multitude', L.
plebs, 'people; mob', populus, 'people', as is
done by most linguists. Cp. the first element in
Volkslied, Volksraad.

## folkland
folkland, п., land held by customary right (Engl.
Hist.) — OE. folcland. See folk and land.

## folklore
folklore, п., the traditional customs, beliefs and
tales of a people. — Coined by the English
antiquary William John Thomas (1803-85) in 1846
for earlier popular antiquities. See folk and lore.

## folklorist
folklorist, п., an expert in folklore. — A hybrid
coined fr. folklore and -ist, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## folkmote
folkmote, folkmoot, п., general assembly of a
town or shire in Anglo-Saxon England. —
Modern rendering of OE. folcmdt, folcgemdt,
lit. 'people's meeting*. See folk and moot.

## follicle
follicle, п., ι) a small sac, cavity or gland (anal.);
2) a seed vessel (bot.) — F. follicule, 'a little
bag', fr. L. folliculus, of s.m., dimin. of follis,
'a leather sack; a pair of bellows, moneybag,
wind cushion, stomach'. L. follis stands for
*bhol-nis or *bh]-nis and is a derivative of base
*bhel-, 'to swell'. See bull, 'male of the ox', and
cp. belly and words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -cle.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:316 COLUMN:2 -->

## follicular
follicular, adj., pertaining to a follicle.— L.fol-'
licularis, "pertaining to a little bag', tr. folliculus.
See follicle and adj. suff. -ar.

## follicubite
follicubite, adj., consisting of a follicle or
follicles. — Formed fr. L. folliculus (see follicle)
with adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: folliculat-ed, adj.

## folliculitis
folliculitis, п., inflammation of follicles (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. folliculus (see
follicle) and -itis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## folliculosis
folliculosis, п., abnormal development of the
lymph follicles (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid
coined fr. L. folliculus (see follicle) and -osis,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## follow
follow, tr. and intr. v. — ME. folewe/ι, foluwen,
folwen, folgen, fr OE. folgian, also fylgan, rel.
to OS. folgon, OFris. folgia, fulgia, ΟΝ., Norw.
fylgja, Swed. fbtja, Dan. felge, MDu. volghen,
Du. volgen, OHG. folgen, MHG. volgen, G.
folgen, 'to follow', and perh. cogn. with W.,
Co. ol (for 1-Е. "polgh-), 'track of the foot',
W. ar ol, 'behind, after', olafiad, 'successor'.
Derivatives: follow, п., follower (q.v.), follow
ing, adj. and n.

## follower
follower, n. — ME. folwere, fr. OE. folgere, fr.
folgian, 'to follow'. See prec. word and agential
suff. -er.
folly, n. — ME. folie, fr. OF. (= F.), folic fr.
OF. fol (F. fou, fol), 'fool'. See fooi and -y
(representing OF. -ie).

## foment
foment, tr. v., 1) to treat with warm water; 2) ic
stir up, stimulate. — F. fomenter, fr. L. fomen-
tare, 'to fornent', fr. fomentum, contraction
of *fovimentum, 'a warm application, poultice',
fr. fovere, 'to warm, keep warm', which stands
for *dhogweyo, prop, a causative form lit.
meaning Ί cause to burn', fr. 1-Е. base *dhegwh-,
*dhog"h-, 'to burn'. See day and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -ment.
Derivatives: foment, п., foment-er,
fomentation, n.

## fomes
fomes, п., a porous substance capable of
absorbing contagious germs. — I., fomes, 'kindling

'a warm application, poultice'. See foment.

## fond
fond, п., foundation. — F. fond (now fonds), fr.

element in plafond.

## fond
fond, adj., infatuated; loving. — ME. fonned,

fr. fon, fonne, 'fool, foolish', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. fondle, fun. Derivatives:
fondle (q.v.), fond-ly, adv., fond-ness, n.

## fonda
fonda, п., hotel, inn. — Sp., fr. Arab, funduq. See

## fondaco
fondaco, п., inn. — It., fr. Arab, funduq. See

## fondant
fondant, п., a kind of sweetmeat that melts easily
in the mouth. — F., prop. pres. part, of fondre,
'to melt*, fr. L. fundere, 'to pour'. See found,
'to establish', and -ant and cp. fondue.

## fondle
fondle, tr. and intr. v. — Formed with freq. suff.
-Ie fr. obsol. fond, 'to be fond of, fr. fond, adj.
Derivative: fondl-ing, n.

## fondne
fondne, п., a dish made of melted cheese, eggs,
butter, etc. — F„ prop. fern, of fondu, pp. of
fondre, 'to melt'. See fondant.

## fonduk
fonduk, п., ι) a warehouse, also an inn, in N.
Africa. — Arab, funduq, fr. Mishnaic Heb. pun-
daq, or Aram, pund'qa, it. Gk. πανδοκεϊον, 'inn',
lit. 'a place for the reception of everybody', fr.
πάνδοκος, 'all-receiving', compounded of παν,
'all, everything', and the stem of δέχεσθαι, 'to
receive hospitably, entertain'. Cp. Sp. alfondega,
which derives fr. Arab, al-, 'the', and funduq,
'inn', and see pandect. Cp. also fonda, fondaco.

## font
font, п., receptacle for baptismal water — ME.,
fr. OE. font, 'baptismal font', fr. L. fons, gen.

## font
font, п., set of type of one size (fypogr.) — F.
fonte, 'a casting', prop, the fern. pp. of fondre,
'to cast, melt', used as a noun. See found, 'to
cast', and cp. fount, 'font'.

## fontal
fontal, adj., 1) pertaining to a fountain; 2)
baptismal. — Late L. fontalis, fr. L. fons, gen.
fontis, 'fountain'. See ist fount and adj. suff. -al.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:316 COLUMN:3 -->

## fontanel
fontanel, fontanelle, п., membranous space
between the bones of the skull of a baby or a
young animal (anat.) — F. fontanelle,
transformation of OF. fontenelle, fr. Medical L. fon-
tanella, prop, the latinized form of the dimin.

dimin. suff. -el, resp. -elle.

## food
food, n. — ME. fode, fr. OE. foda (whence

πατεϊσθαι, 'to feed', fr. I.-E. *pat-, *pll-,

sHo), pasti, 'to feed, tend (ihe flock)', Toch. A
pas-, В pask-, 'to feed, tend (the flock)', Hitt.

ποιμήν, 'shepherd', πώί), 'flock of sheep', πώμα,

## fool
fool, п., a jester, ; dupe. — ME. fol, fr. OF. fol

ball filled with air', in VL. 'empty-headed
person, fool'. See follicle. Derivatives: fool, intr.
and tr. \.,fool-ery, n.,fool-ing, п., foot-ish, adj.,
fool-ish-ly, adv., fool-ish-ness, n.

## fool
fool, п., dish consisting of crushed fruit, milk and
cream. — Fr. prec. word in its colloquial sense

## foolhardy

Derivatives: foolhardi-ly, adv., foolhardi-ness, n.

## foolscap
foolscap, п., a size of writing paper. — So called

watermark.

## foot
foot, n. — ME. fot, fr. OE. fit, rel. to QS. fol,
ON. fotr, Swed. fot, Dan. fod, Du. voet, OHG.
fuo3, MHG. VU03, G. Fufi, Goth, fdtus, 'foot', and

pad-, 'foot', Toch. Ape, Βραι, 'foot', Арет, В

Dor. Gk. πώς, Att. πους (formed on analogy of
οδς, 'ear'), gen. ποδός, L. pes, gen.pedis, 'foot',
Ol. padam, 'step, track', Arm. het, gen. hetoy,
'track, footmark', Gk. πέδη, 'fetter', πεδϊν, 'to

'footstep', pedica, 'shackle, fetter', impedire,

impeach, impede, impedimenta, Lycopodlum,

footeite, п., a hydrous copper oxychloride

footfall, n. — First used by Shakespeare.

## footie
footie, intr. v., to trifle. — Formed with suff. -Ie
fr. dial. E. footer, 'to trifle', which is rel. to

footpad, п., a highway robber on foot. —

## footy
footy, adj., mean; paltry (dial. English). — F.

## fop
fop, n„ a dandy. — ME. fop, foppe, 'fool', fr.

Derivatives: fop-ling, п., fopp-ery, п., fopp-ish,
adj., fiopp-ish-ly, adv., fopp-ish-ness, n.

## for
for, prep. — ME., fr. OE. for, fore, 'before (prep,
and adv.), for, on account of, rel. to OS. fur,
furl, 'before', Du. voor, 'for, before', OHG. fora,

for, 'for', far, 'before' (prep, and adv.), Swed.
for, 'for', fore, 'before', Goth, faiir, 'for', faiira,

for-, pref. — OE., replacing earlier fxr-, fer-, rel.

## forage
forage, п., fodder. — ME., fr. OF. forage, for-
rage, fourage (F. fourrage), fr. OF. forre, fuerre
(F. feurre), 'fodder, straw', fr. Frankish "fddr,

also fore].

## forage
forage, tr. and intr. v. — F. fourrager, fr. four-
rage. See forage, n.

## forager
forager, n. — ME., fr. OF. foragier, forragier,

rageur), 'forager'. See forage, n. and v., and

## foralite
foralite, n„ marking found in rocks (geol.)
— A hybrid coined from the stem of L. forare,

## foramen
foramen, п., a small orifice, aperture. — L.

## foraminate
foraminate, adj., perforated. — L. foraminatus,

## Foraminifera
Foraminifera, n. pi., an order of rhizopods (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'bearing holes', compounded of
L. foramen, gen. foraminis, 'hole, opening', and
ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See foramen and -fer.

## foraminifera)
foraminifera), foraminiferous, adj., containing
Foraminifera; pertaining to the Foraminifera.
— See prec. word and adj. suff. -al, resp. -ous.

## foraminous
foraminous, adj., having foramina. — L.forami-
nosus, 'full of holes', fr. foramen, gen. foraminis,
'hole, opening'. See foramen and -ous.

## foray
foray, tr. and intr. v., to raid, ravage. — ME. for-
rayen, back formation fr. forreier, 'forayer'. See
forayer.

## foray
foray, п., a raid. — ME. forrai, fr. forrayen. See
foray, v.

## forayer
forayer, n. — ME. forreier, 'forager', fr. OF. for-
rier, fr. forrer, forer, 'to forage', fr. forre, fuerre,
'fodder'. See forage, v., and agential suff. -er.

## forbade
forbade, forbad, past tense of forbid,

## forbear
forbear, n. — See forebear,

## forbear
forbear, tr. and intr. v., to refrain from. — ME.
forberen, fr. OE. forberan, 'to endure, suffer;

## to restrain from'
to restrain from', formed fr. for- and beran, 'to

## bear'. See bear
bear'. See bear, 'to carry'.
Derivatives: forbear-ance, п., forbear-er, п.,

## forbear-ing
forbear-ing, adj., forbear-ing-ly, adv.

## forbesite
forbesite, п., a hydrous nickel cobalt arsenate
(mineral) — Named after the English geologist

David Forbes (1828-76), who first analyzed it.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## forbid
forbid, tr. v. — ME. forbeden, fr. OE. forbeodan,
rel. to Du. verbieden, OHG. farbiotan, MHG.,
G. verbieten, Goth, faurbiudan, 'to forbid'. See
for- and bid.
Derivatives: forbidd-ance, п., and forbidd-en,
adj., forbidden-Iy, adv., forbidden-ness, п., for-
bidd-er, п., forbidd-ing, adj., forbidd-ing-ly, adv.,
forbidd-ing-ness, n.

## forbore
forbore, past tense of forbear.

## forby
forby, forbye, prep., near, next to; adv. 1) aside;
2) past; 3) besides. — ME. forbi, fr. for-, fore-,
'fore-', and by, 'by'. Cp. G. vorbei, 'along, by,

## force
force, п., strength. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) force,

neut. pi. of L. fortis, 'strong', but mistaken for

Derivatives: force-ful, adj., force-ful-ly, adv.,
force-ful-ness, п., force-less, adj.

## force
force, tr. v., to compel. — F. forcer, fr. VL. *for-
tiare, fr. fortia. See force, n.
Derivatives: forc-ed, adj., forc-ed-ly, adv., forc-
ed-ness, п., forc-er, п., forcible (q.v.), forc-ing, n.

## force
force, п., waterfall. — ON. fors, foss, whence
Swed. fors, Dan. fos, of s.m., Swed. forsa, frusa,
'to gush forth'.

## force
force, tr. v., to stuff, farce. — A var. of farce.

## force majeure
force majeure, irresistible force. — F., lit.
'superior strength'. See force, 'strength', and
major, adj.

## forcemeat
forcemeat, п., minced meat. — Compounded of
force, 'to stuff', and meat.

## forceps
forceps, п., a pair of pincers used in surgery. —
L., 'pair of tongs, pincers', contracted fr.
*formi-caps, fr. formus, 'hot', and capere, 'to
catch, seize, take, hold'. See warm and captive
and cp. forfex. For the change of Latin й (in
capere) to ё (in for-cips) see accent and cp.
words there referred to.

## forcible
forcible, adj.—OF., ir. force. See force,'strength',
and -ibie.
Derivative: forcibl-y, adv.

## forcipate
forcipate, adj., resembling a forceps. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. forceps, gen. forcipis,

## forcipated
forcipated, adj., forcipate. — Formed fr. prec.
word with suff. -ed.

## Forcipulata
Forcipulata, n. pi., an order of starfishes (ich-
thyol.) — ModL., lit. 'resembling a small
forceps'. See next word.

## forcipulate
forcipulate, adj., resembling a small forceps. —
ModL. forcipulatus, fr. forcipulus, dimin. of
L. forceps, gen. forcipis. See forceps and cp.
prec. word.

## ford
ford, n. — ME., fr. OE. ford, rel. to OS. ford,

ritum, lit. 'Ford of Augustus), and to OE. faran,

firth, frith. Cp. also port, 'harbor'.
Derivatives: ford, tr. v., ford-ing, n.

## fordo
fordo, tr. v., to undo (archaic). — ME. for don,
fr. OE. fordon, fr. for- and don, 'to do'. See do, v.

## fore
fore, adv. — ME. fore, fr. OE. fore, 'before (prep,
and adv.), for, on account of, rel. to OS.,
OHG. fora, OFris. fara, fore, 'before' (adv. and
prep.), MLG., MHG. vore, vor, G. vor (prep,
and adv.), 'before', Goth, faura, 'before' (adv.
and prep.), ON. fyrr, 'before' (adv.), fyrir,
'before' (prep.), and cogn. with OI. purd, 'before,
formerly', purah, 'in front, before', Avesticpara,
paro, 'before', para, 'beyond', pra-, 'before,
forward, forth', Hitt. para-, 'on, forth', Gk. πάρος,
'before', παρά, 'from beside, against, beyond',

place name Armorica, which stands for Are-
mor-ica and lit. means 'before the sea'. All these

## forensic

## forest
forest, n. — ME., fr. OF. forest (F. forel), fr.

Formica, п., the genus of ants (entomol.) — L.;

of fortificare. See fortify and -ion.

## fortify
fortify, tr. v. — F. fortifier, fr. Late L. fortificare,
'to strengthen', lit. 'to make strong', formed fr.
L. fortis, 'strong', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to
make, do'. See fort and -fy.
Derivatives: fortifi-er, п., fortify-ing, adj., forti-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:319 COLUMN:2 -->
fy-ing-ly, adv.

## fortissimo
fortissimo, adj. and adv., very loud (mus.) —
It., superl. of forte, 'loud', lit. 'strong'. See
forte, adj.
Derivative: fortissimo, п., a very loud passage.

## fortitude
fortitude, п., courage in endurance. — F., fr. L.
fortitftdinem, ace. of fortitfidd, 'strength,
courage', fr. fortis, 'strong'. See fort and -tude.

## fortnight
fortnight, n. — Shortened fr. fourteen nights. Cp.
sennight, which is coniracted fr. seven nights.
Derivative: fortnight-iy, adv.

## fortress
fortress, n. — ME. fortresse, fr. OF. (= F.)
forteresse, 'strong place, stronghold', fr. VL.
*fortaricia, fr. L. fortis, 'strong'. See fort and
cp. fortalice.
Derivative: fortress, tr. v.

## fortuitism
fortuitism, п., the doctrine that natural
phenomena are the result of chance. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. fortuitus (see fortuitous) and -ism,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## fortuitist
fortuitist, п., an adherent of fortuitism. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. fortuitus (see next word)
and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## fortuitous
fortuitous, adj., happening by chance; accidental.
— L. fortuitus, 'casual, accidental', prob. a blend
of *fortutus and *fortJtus, fr. *fortii = forte, 'by
chance', prop. abl. of fors, 'chance', which is
rel. to fortuna, 'chance, fate'. See fortune. For
E, -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous. The
word fortuitous was introduced into English by
Henry More (1614-1687), philosopher of the
English Platonist school.
Derivatives: fortuitous-ly adv.,fortuitous-ness, n.

## fortuity
fortuity, п., chance. — Contraction of 'fortuit-
ity; formed with suff. -ity fr. L. fortuitus. See
fortuitous. For the contraction of "fortuit-ity
into fortuity see haplology.

## fortunate
fortunate, adj. — L. fortundtus, pp. of fortunare,
'to make prosperous', fr. fortuna. See next word
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: fortunate, п., fortunate-ly, adv.,
fortunate-ness, n.

## fortune
fortune, n. — ME., fr. F. fortune, fr. L. fortuna,
'chance, fate, good luck', fr. fors, gen. fortis,
'chance', which stands in gradational
relationship loferre, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry'
and cp. fortuitous.
Derivative: fortune-less, adj.

## fortune
fortune, tr. v. — ME. fortunen, fr. OF. fortuner,
fr. L. fortunare, 'to make fortunate', fr. fortuna.
See fortune, n.

## forty
forty, adj. and n. — MB. fourti, fr. OE. feowertig,
which is formed fr. OE. feower, 'four', with -tig,
'-ty' (see four and -ty, suff. denoting multiples
of ten); rel. to OS. fiwartig, fiartig, OFris. fiu-
wertich, fiortig, Du. veertig, OHG. fiorzug,
MHG. vierzic, G. vierzig, ON. fjdrir tigir,
Swed. fyratio, fyrtio, Norw. fyrti, Dan. fyrre-
tyve, Goth, fldwor tigjus, 'forty'.

## forum
forum, п., ι) a market place, esp. the market
place in Rome; 2) a law court; 3) an assembly
for public discussion.—L., 'public place, market
place, market', prob. meaning lit. 'a place
fenced by planks', and rel. to forus, 'plank,
board' (fr. I.-E. *bhoros, 'something cut,
section'), and to VL. *barra, 'beam, rafter', a word
of Gaulish origin. See bar, 'rod', and cp.
forensic, affeer, flars, triforium.

## forward
forward, adv. — ME. foreword, forward, fr. OE.
foreweard, forweard, formed fr. fore, for,
'before', and -weard, '-ward'. See fore, adv. and
-ward.
Derivatives: forward, adj., n. and tr. v.,
forwarder, п., forward-ing, п., forward-ness, n.

## forwards
forwards, adv. — ME. forewardes. See prec.
word. For suff. -es in ME. foreward-es, see adv.
suff. -s.

## forwenried
forwenried, adj., tired out, exhausted (obsol. or
archaic). — ME. forweried, pp. of forwerien, 'to
weary out', fr. for- and weri, 'weary'. See weary
and -ed, pp. suff.

## forwhy
forwhy, adv., why; conj., because (archaic). —
ME. forwhi, fr. OE. for hwy, 'because', fr. for,
'for', and hwy, instrumental of hwset, 'what'. See
for and what.

## forworn
forworn, adj., worn out (archaic). — Formed fr.
for- and worn, pp. of wear, 'to carry on the
body; to last'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:319 COLUMN:3 -->

## fossa
fossa, п., pit, cavity (anat.) — L., 'ditch'. See
next word.

## fosse
fosse, п., ditch, moat. — F., fr. L. fossa, 'ditch',
prop, short for fossa terra, 'earth dug', fr. fossa,
'dug', fern. pp. oifodere, 'to dig', fr. I.-E. base
'bhedh-, *bhod-, 'to dig, pierce'. See bed and
cp. fossette, fossil and the second element in
calaboose.

## fossette
fossette, п., a dimple. — F., dimin. of fosse. See
prec. word and -ette.

## fossick
fossick, intr. v., to search for gold in old
workings; tr. v., to dig out. — Prob. fr. dial. E.fus-
sock, fossick, 'to bustle about', fossick, 'a
troublesome person'.
Derivative: fossick-er, n.

## fossil
fossil, п., petrified Temains of an animal or plant
dug out of the earth; adj., pertaining to, or of
the nature of, a fossil. — F. fossile, fr. L. fossilis,
'dug out, dug up', fr, fossus, pp. of fodere. See
fosse and -ile.

## fossiliferous
fossiliferous, adj., containing fossils. — See prec.
word and -ferous.

## fossilize
fossilize, tr. v., to change into a fossil; intr. v.,
to become fossilized. — See fossil and -ize.
Derivative: fossiliz-ation, n.

## fossilology
fossilology, п., former name of paleontology. —
A hybrid coined fr. L. fossilis, 'dug out, dug up',
and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See fossil and -logy.

## fossorial
fossorial, adj., digging. — Formed with adj. suff.
-a] fr. L. fossdrius, 'fit for digging', fr. fossus,
pp. οι fodere. See fosse.

## foster
foster, п., food, nourishment (obsol.) — ME., fr.
OE. fdstor, foster, 'feeding; food', rel. to ON.
fdstr, 'the bringing up (of a child)', and to OE.
fdda, 'food'. See food.

## foster
foster, tr. v., to nourish. — ME. fostren, fr. OE.
fdstrian, 'to nourish', fr. fdstor, foster, 'feeding;
food'. See foster, n.
Derivatives: foster-age, п., foster-er, п.,
fosterling (q.v.)

## foster
foster, п., forester. — Contraction of forster,
forester. See forest and agential suff. -er.

## foster brother
foster brother, n. — OE. fdstorbrddor. See foster,
'food', and brother.

## foster father
foster father,—OE. fdstorfxder. See foster, 'food',
and father.

## fosterling
fosterling, η. — OE. fdstorling. See foster,'food',
and -ling.

## foster mother
foster mother, n. — OE. fdstormodor. See foster,
'food', and mother.

## foster sister
foster sister, n. — OE. fdstorsweostor. See foster,
'food', and sister.

## fostress
fostress, n. — See foster, 'food', and -ess.

## fother
fother, п., a load, weight. — OE. fddor, 'a
cartload', rel. to OS. father, MDu. voeder, Du. voer,
OHG. fuodar, MHG. vuoder, G. Fuder [whence
F. foudre (masc.), 'tun, hogshead'], and in
gradational relationship to OE. fiedm, 'the
outstretched arms, embrace, bosom, fathom'. See
fathom.

## fother
fother, tr. v., to cover (a sail) with oakum, rope
yarn, etc. — MDu. voederen (Du. voeren), rel.
to OHG. fdlar, fuotar, 'a cover, coverlet', MHG.
vuoter, 'lining, case, sheath', G. Futter, 'lining',
Goth, fddr, 'sheath of a sword', and cogn. with
OI. pdtram, 'receptacle, container', Hitt. paddar,
'basket', fr. I.-E. *pdt-, *pdt-, 'a
-(-enlargement of base "pa-, *pd-, 'to protect'. See food
and cp. fur.

## Fothergilla
Fothergilla, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the English physician Dr.John
Fothergill (1712-80).

## foudroyant
foudroyant, adj., stunning, dazzling. — F., pres.
part, of foudroyer, 'to thunderstrike', fr. foudre
(fern.), 'lightning, thunder, thunderbolt', fr. L.
fulgur. See fnlgurant.

## fougasse
fougasse, п., a small mine (mil.) — F., formed,
with change of suffix, fr. fougade, fr. It. fogata,
prop, subst. use of fern. pp. of fogare, 'to put
to flight, chase', fr. foga, 'Hight', fr. L. fuga,
of s.m. See fugitive.

## fonght
fonght, past tense and pp. of fight. — ME. fauht,
fr. OE. feaht, 'fought', past tense oifeohtan, 'to
fight'. See fignt, v.

## foughten
foughten, oW pp. of fight. — ME. foughten, fr.
OE. fohten, pp. oifeohtan, 'to fight'. See fight,v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:320 COLUMN:1 -->

## foujdar
foujdar, п., an officer; a criminal judge (.India). —
Hind, fawjdar, it. Pers. fawjdar, a hybrid lit.
meaning 'a holder of military force', coined fr.
Arab, fauj, 'band, troop, military force', and the
Pers. suff. -dar, 'holder, possessor'. See aumildar
and cp. words there referred to.

## foujdary
foujdary, also foujdarry, п., a criminal court. —
Hind, fawjdari, fr. fawjdar. See prec. word.

## foul
foul, adj. — ME. foul, fr. OE. ful, rel. to OS.,
OFris., MLG., OHG., MHG. ful, ON. full,
Dan., Swed., Norw. ful, MDu. vuul, Du. vuil,
G. foul, Goth, fuls; formed with suff. -la fr.
Teut. base *fu- (whence also ON. fuinn, 'foul,
rotten'), corresponding to l.-E. base *p«-,
whence OI. payati, 'rots, stinks', p&tih, 'foul,
rotten'. Arm. Ли, 'purulent blood', Gk. πϋός,
'first milk after the birth', πΰον or πύον,
'discharge from a sore; matter', πυθειν, 'to cause
to rot', L. pus, 'matter', putere, 'to stink', puter,
putridus, 'foul, rotten', Lith. puviu, puti, 'to rot',
pidial, 'matter', Mir. othrach, 'dung'. Cp. filth,
defile, 'to pollute', foumart. Cp. also empyema,
purulent, pus, pustule, putanism, putois, Pu-
torins, putrid, pyaemia, pyo-, Pythium,
suppurate.
Derivatives: foul, adv. and п., foul, v. (q.v.),
foully (q.v.), foulness (q.v.).

## foul
foul, intr. and tr. v. — OE. fulian, 'to become
foul, to rot', fr. ful. See foul, adj.

## foulard
foulard, п., ι) a thin textile of silk; 2) a
handkerchief made of this material. — F., prob.
formed, with change of suff., fr. OProveng.
foulat, 'fulled', fr. VL. 'fullare, 'to full'. See full,
'to thicken (cloth)'.

## foully
foully, adv. — ME., fr. OE. fullice, 'in a foul
manner'. See foul, adj., and adv. suff. -ly.

## foulmouthed
foulmouthed, adj., speaking foully or obscenely. —
Formed fr. foul, 'filthy', and pp. of mouth, v.
(see mouth); first used by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: foulmouthed-ly, adv., foulmouthed-
ness, n.

## foulness
foulness, n. — ME. foulnesse, fr. OE. fulness, fr.
ful, 'foul'. See foul, adj., and -ness.

## foumart
foumart, п., polecat. — ME. fulmart, fulmard.
fr. OE. ful, 'foul', and meard, 'marten'. See foul,
adj., and marten. E. foumart was influenced in
form by F. marie, 'marten'.

## found
found, tr. and intr. v., to establish. — ME. foun-
den, fr. OF .funder, fonder (F.fonder),'to found',
fr. L. fundare, 'to found', lit. 'to lay the bottom
of, fr. fundus, 'bottom'. See fund and cp. fond,
'foundation'.

## found
found, tr. v., to cast. — F. fondre, fr. L. fundere,
'to pour, melt', fr. I.-E. base *ghu-d-, 'to pour',
whence also Goth, giutan, OS. giotan, OFris.
giala, OE. geotan, OHG. giotan, MHG. giejen,
G. giefien, ON. gjota, Swed. gjuta, Dan. gyde, 'to
pour': cp. ingot, and gut. Base *ghu-d-, is a -d-
enlargement of base *ghu-, 'to pour', for the
derivatives of which see chyle. Cp. circumfuse,
confound, confuse, diffuse, effuse, funnel, fusel oil,
fusibie, fusion, futile, infundibulum, infuse,
infusion, interfuse, profuse, refound, refund, refuse,
ruse, rush, v., transfuse. Cp. also geyser.

## found
found, adj., provided, equipped, with. — Prop,
pp. of find.

## foundation
foundation, n. — F. fondation, fr. L. funduMnem,
ace. of fundaiio, 'a founding', fr. fundatus, pp.
of fundare. See found, 'to establish', and -ation.
Derivatives: foundation-al, adj.,
foundation-ally, adv., foundation-ary, adj., foundation-er, п.,
foundation-less, adj.

## founder
founder, п., one who founds something. —
Formed fr. found, 'to establish', with agential suff. -er.

## founder
founder, п., one who casts metal or glass. —
Formed fr. found, 'to cast', with agential suff.
-er. Cp. F. fondeur.

## founder
founder, intr. and tr. v., to sink. — OF. fondrer,
'to fall to the bottom', fr. fond, 'bottom', fr. L.
fundus. Cp. F. effondrer, 'to dig deeply', s'ef-
fondrer, 'to break in', fr. OF. fondrer, 'to sink
to the bottom', and see found, 'to establish'.

## founder
founder, п., inflammation in the foot of a horse.
— Fr. founder, 'to sink'.

## foundling
foundling, n. — ME. foundling, fundling, fr. fun-
den, pp. of finden, 'to find'. Cp. Du. vondeling,
G. Findling, and see find and -ling.

## foundress
foundress, п., a female founder. — Fern, of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:320 COLUMN:2 -->
founder. For the ending see suff. -ess.

## foundry
foundry, n. — F. fonderie, fr. fondre, 'to cast'
See found, 'to cast', and -ry.

## fount
fount, п., fountain. — F. font, fr. L. fontem, ace.
οι fans, 'spring, fountain', which is cogn. with
OI. dhdnvati, 'flows, runs', dhanu-tar-, 'running,
flowing'. Cp. next word and font, 'receptacle for
baptismal water'.

## fount
fount, п., the British equivalent of font. — F.
fonte. See font, 'set of type of one size'.

## fountain
fountain, n. — OF. (= F.) fontaine, fr. Late L.
fontana, prop. fern, of fontanus, 'pertaining to
a spring', used as a noun, fr. L. fons, gen. fontis,
'spring'. See font, 'receptacle', and cp. fontanel.

## four
four, adj. and n. — ME. feower, fower, foure,
four, fr. OE. flower, rel. to OS. fiuwar, fiwar,
OFris. fiuwer,fior, Du. vier, OHG. fior, MHG.,
G. vier, ON. fjdrir, Oaa. fire, Swed. fyra, Norw.
fire, Goth, fidwar, 'four', and cogn. with OI. cat-
vurah, Avestic ca&waro, Pers. Hatvar, Toch. A
stwar, В itwer, Arm. (ork\ Gk. τέσσαρες, Att.
τένπχρες, Ion. τέσσερες, Aeol. πίσυρες, πέσυ-
ρες, L. quattuor, Oscan petora, Umbr. petur-,
OSlav. letyre, Lith. keturi, Olr. cethir, W. pet-
guar, pedwar, 'four'. (Alb. kater is a loan word
fr. L. quattuor.) All these words derive fr. I.-E.
base *qwetwdr-, 'four'. Cp. fardel, 'fourth part',
farthing, firkin, forty. Cp. also cadre, cahier,
carfax, carillon, cater, 'four at cards or dice',
charpoy, quadrant, quadrate, quadri-, quadrille,
quadroon, quarantine, quarrel, 'arrow, bolt',
quarry, 'a place for excavating stones', quart,
quatrain, quaternion, quire of paper, squad,
square, tessara-, tetarto-, terra-, tetrakis-, te-
trarch, trapezium, trocar.

## fourchee
fourchee, fourche, adj., forked, divided (her.) —
V.fourchee, fern, of fourche, 'forked*, fr. fourche,
'fork'. See fork. Since the adj. mostly refers to
a cross (F. croix, a fern, noun), the fern, form
of the adjective is preferred to the masculine.

## fourchette
fourchette, п., a fork or something resembling a
fork. — F., dimin. of fourche, 'fork'. See fork
and -ette.

## fourfold
fourfold, adj. and adv. — ME. fourfold, fr. OE.
flowerfeald, fr. flower, 'four', and -feald, '-fold'.
See four and -fold.

## fourgon
fourgon, п., a baggage waggon. — F., of
uncertain origin.

## Fourierism
Fourierism, п., a system for the reorganization of
society. — Named after the French socialist
Francois-Marie-Charles Fourier (1772-1837).
For the ending see suff. -ism.

## fourteen
fourteen, adj. and n. — ME. fourtene, fr. OE.
flowertyne, flowertene, which is formed fr.
flower, 'four', with suff. -tyne, -tine, '-teen' (see
four and -teen); rel. to OS. fiertein, ON.//oVian,
Dan. fjorten, Swed. fjorton, OFris. fiuwertine,
Du. veertien, OHG. fiorzehan, MHG. vierzehen,
G. vierzehn, Goth, fidwortaihun, 'fourteen'.

## fourteenth
fourteenth, adj. and n. — Formed fr. fourteen
with numeral, suff. -th on the analogy of tenth.Cp.
ME. fourtethe, fr. OE. flowerteoda, 'fourteenth',
which was formed fr. flowertyne, 'fourteen', on
the analogy of teoda, 'tenth'; see tiflie, n. Cp.
ON. fjortandi, Dan. fjortende, Swed. fjortonde,
Du. veertiende, G. vierzehnte, 'fourteenth'.

## fourth
fourth, adj. — ME. fourthe, formed—under the
influence of ME foure, four, 'four'—fr. OE.
florda, 'fourth', which is rel. to OS. fiortho,
Oti. fiorde, Dan., Swed. fjerde, Du. vierde, OHG.
fiordo, MHG., G. vierte, 'fourth', and cogn. with
OI. caturthdh, Toch. A start, Gk. τέταρτος,
τέτρατος, L. quartus, OSlav. ietvritu. Olr. ce-
thramad, MW. pedweryd, 'fourth'. See four and
numeral suff. -th and cp. fardel, 'fourth part',
and firkin. Cp. also quart.
Derivatives: fourth, п., fourth-ly, adv.

## fovea
fovea, п., a small pit (anat. and hot.) — L., rel.
to favissae, 'underground reservoirs'; of
uncertain, possibly Etruscan, origin.

## foveola
foveola, п., a small fovea. — ModL., dimin. of
L. fovea. See prec. word and -ole.

## fowl
fowl, n. -r- ME. foghel, fugel, fowel, foule, it. OE.

## fugol
fugol, 'bird', rel. to OS. fugal, ΟΝ., Oa.a~.fugl,
Swed. fugel, OFris. fugel, MDu. voghel, Du.
vogel, OHG. fogal, MHG., G. wgel, Goth.

## fugls
fugls, 'bird, fowl', prob. fr. Teut. "fug-la-, dis-
similated fr. *flug-la-, and lit. meaning 'flyer',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:320 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. Teut. base *flug-, 'to fly', corresponding to
I.-E. base "pleuq-, 'to move forward (by
swimming, running or flying)'. See fly, v.

## fowi
fowi, intr. v. — ME. foulen, fr. OE. fuglian, 'to
catch birds', fr. fugol. See fowl, n.

## fowler
fowler, n. — ME. fugelere, fr. OE. fugelere, fr.
fugol, 'bird'. See fowl, п., and agential suff. -er.
fowlerite п., a variant of rhodonite (mineral)
— Named after Samuel Fowler (1779-1844) of
New Jersey. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## fowling
fowling, n. — ME. foulinge, fr. foulen. See fowl,
v., and -ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## fox
fox, n. — ME., fr. OE. fox, rel. to OS. vohs,
MLG., MDu., Du. vos, OHG., MHG. fuhs,
G. Fuchs, 'fox', ΟΝ./όβ, MLG. vohe, νδ, OHG.
foha, MHG. vohe, G. Fohe, Goth, fauho,
'vixen'; prob. fr. I.-E. base *pSq-, *peuq-,
'bushy, shaggy', whence also OI. pucchah, 'tail',
Russ. and Pol. puch, 'woolly hair'. Accordingly
fox prob. means lit. '{he bushy-tailed animal'.
For sense development cp. Lith. uodegis, 'fox',
lit. 'tailed', fr. uodega, 'tail'. Cp. vixen. Cp. also
the first element in Bovista.
Derivatives: fox, v., fox-y, adj., fox-i-ly, adv.,
fox-i-ness, n.

## foxglove
foxglove, n. — ME. foxes glove, fr. OE. foxes
glofa. See fox and glove.

## foyer
foyer, п., lobby in a theater. — F., orig.
'fireplace', fr. L. focarium, 'fireplace', prop. neut.
of the adj. focarius, 'pertaining to a fireplace',
used as a noun, fr. focus, 'hearth, fireplace'. See
focus and subst. suff. -ary.

## fra
fra, п., title of a friar. — It., abbreviation oifrate,
'brother'. See frate.

## fracas
fracas, п., noisy dispute; brawl. — F., fr. It.
fracasso, 'a crash', back formation fr. fracas-
sare, 'to break in pieces', fr. fra-, 'among', which
is aphetic for L. infra, 'below', and It. cassare,
'to break', fr. L. quassare, 'to shake'. See infra
and quash, 'to make void'.

## fracted
fracted, adj., having a part displaced as if broken
(her.) — Formed with suff. -ed fr. L. fractus,
'broken', pp. of frangere. See fraction.

## fractile
fractile, adj., fragile. — Formed with suff. -ile
fr. L. fractus, 'broken', pp. of frangere. See next
word and -ile.

## fraction
fraction, n. — ME., fr. OF. fraccion, fraction (F.
fraction), fr. L. fractidnem, ace. of fractio, 'a
breaking', fr. L. fractus, pp. of frangere, 'to
break', fr. I.-E. base "bhreg-, 'to break', whence
also Goth, brikan, OE. brecan, 'to break'. See
break and -ion and cp. fractile, fractious,
fracture, fragile, fragment, frail, frangible, diffract,
fritter, 'a fragment', infract, infringe,
irrefragable, refract, refractory, refrain, п., suffrage,
and the second element in chamfer, naufragous,
ossifrage, osprey, septifragal.
Derivatives: fraction-al, adj., fracttonal-ly, adv.,
fraction-ary, adj., fractionate (q.v.), fractionize
(q.v.)

## fractionate
fractionate, tr. v., to separate into fractions
(chem.) — See fraction and verbal suff. -ate.

## fractionize
fractionize, tr. v., to separate into fractions. —
See fraction and -ize.
Derivative: fractioniz-ation, n.

## fractious
fractious, adj., peevish, irritable. — A blend of
fraction (in the now obsolete sense 'dissension')
and factious.

frank, adj. — OF. (= F.) franc, 'free', fr. ML.

viousness', Pol. pragnqf, 'to crave for'. Cp.

## free
free, adj. — ME. freo, fre, fr. OE. freo, fri, rel.
to OS., OHG., MHG. vri, G. frei, Du. vrij,
Goth, frets, 'free', OE. freogan, frion, Goth.
frijdn, 'to love', OE. friod, 'affection,
friendship', friga, 'love', freodryhten, 'noble lord',
OE. fridu, OS. /rftA«,ON. fridr, OFris. frethu,
OHG. fridu, MHG. fride, G. Friede, 'peace',
OE. freo, OS. fri, 'wife', ON. Frigg, name of the
wife of Odin (lit. = 'beloved, loving; wife'),
MLG. men, 'to take to wife', Du. vrijen, G.
freien, 'to woo'. The primary sense of all these
words was 'beloved, friend; to love'. In English
freo, etc., this sense developed into 'free'. (The
terms 'beloved' and 'friend', were applied, as a
rule, to the free members of the clan and in
contradistinction to slaves.) For sense development
cp. L. liberi, which unites the meanings 'free'
(pi.) and 'children'. The above Teut. words are
cogn. with OI. priyah, 'own, dear, beloved',
priyale, 'loves', OSlav. prijati, 'to help', prya-
lelji, 'friend', W. rhydd (for *prijos), 'free'. Cp.
affray, defray, fray, 'tumult', fresh, 'obtrusive',
friend, Frigg, frith, 'brushwood', the first
element in filibuster, Frederic, Friday, and the
second element in belfry, Geoffrey, Godfrey,
Humphrey, Winfred. Derivatives: free, adv.,
free, v. (q.v.), free-ly, adv., free-ness, n.

## free
free, tr. v. — ME. freen, fr. OE. freogan, freon,

free owing to a confusion with F. frere, 'brother'

frenum, also, less exactly, fraenum, п., a small
ligament supporting or checking the movements of
any organ. — L. frenum, fraenum, 'bridle, curb,
bit', prob. standing for *fre-nom, 'something
to hold with', fr. I.-E. base *dher(e)-, 'to hold,
support', whence also L. firmus, 'firm, strong'.
See firm, adj., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: fren-al, adj., frenate (q.v.)

## frenzy
frenzy, п., wild excitement. — ME. frenesye, fr.
OF. frenesie, fr. ML. phrenesia, fr. Late L.
phrenesis, fr. pseudo-Gk. φρένησις (back
formation from the Late L. adj. phreniticus,
corruption of Gk. φρενϊτικός, 'suffering from the
inflammation of the brain'), corresponding to
Gk. φρενϊτις, 'inflammation of the brain', fr.
φρήν, gen. φρεϋός, 'midriff, heart, mind'. See
phrenetic.
Derivatives: frenzi-ed, adj., frenzi-ed-ly, adv.

## frequence
frequence, n. — F. frequence, fr. L. frequentia.
See next word and -ce.

## frequency
frequency, n. — L. frequentia, 'a crowding,
crowd', fr. frequens. See frequent, adj., and -cy.

## frequent
frequent, adj. — p. frequent, fr. L. frequentem,
ace. of frequens, 'crowded, repeated, constant',
which is rel. to farcere, 'to stuff, cram'. See
farce, and -ent.
Derivatives .frequent, v. (q.v.),frequent-ly, adv.,
frequem-ness, n.

## frequent
frequent, tr. v. — F. frequenter, fr. L. frequentSre,
'to resort to frequently, to frequent', ft. frequens.
See frequent, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:322 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: frequent-able, adj., frequentation
(qv)> frequent-er, n.

## frequentation
frequentation, n. — F. frequentation, fr. L. fre-
quentationem, ace. of frequentatio, fr. frequen-
tatus, pp. of frequentare. See frequent, v., and
-ation.

## frequentative
frequentative, adj. — F. frequentatif (fern, -ive),
fr. Late L. frequentativus, 'that which denotes
the repetition of an act', fr. L. frequematus, pp.
of frequentare. See frequent, v., and -ive.

## fresco
fresco, n. — It., lit. 'fresh'. See fresh, 'newly
made', and cp. alfresco.

## fresh
fresh, adj., newly made; cool. — ME. fresch, fr.
OF. fres, freis, fern, fresche (whence F. frais,
fern, fraiche), 'fresh', fr. Teut. 'frisk- (whence
also It., Sp., Port, fresco, OProvenc. fresc); cp.
OE. fersc [whence ON. ferskr (Dan. fersk, Swed.
farsk)], OFris. fersk, MLG. versch, Du. vers
(Dan., Swed., Norw. frisk are MLG. loan
words), OHG. frisc, MHG. vrisch, G. frisch,
'fresh' [MLG., MDu. vrisch (Du. fris), are
borrowed fr. MHG. vrisch]. These Teut. words are
prob. cogn. with OSlav.presinu (for 'praisicino-),
'fresh' (whence Lith. preskas, 'sweet;
unleavened'). Cp. afresh, refresh. Cp. also fresco, frisk.
Derivatives: fresh, п., fresh-en, tr. and intr. v.,
fresh-en-er, п., fresh-ly, adv., fresh-ness, n.

## fresh
fresh, adj., obtrusive, impudent (slang). — G.
frech, 'impudent', fr. OHG. freh, 'covetous,
avaricious', rel. to OE. free, 'gluttonous, greedy,
bold' (see freak, 'whim'); influenced in form,
but different in origin, from fresh, 'new'.

## freshet
freshet, п., a stream of fresh water; a flood. —
Formed fr. fresh, 'newly made', with suff. -et.

## fret
fret, tr. v., to eat away; intr. v., to gnaw (into,
on or upon); to be worn away. — ME. fre ten,
fr. OE. fretan, 'to eat up, devour'; which stands
for fr-etan, fr. pref. fr- (fr. Teut. *fra-) and OE.
etan, 'to eat'; rel. to Du. vreten, OHG. fre33an,
MHG. vre33en, G. fressen, Goth, fra-itan, of
s.m. See for- and eat and cp. frass.
Derivatives: fret, п., the act of fretting; worry,
anxiety; fretful (q.v.)

## fret
fret, п., ornament. — ME. frete, fret, fr. MF.
frete, freite (F. frette), 'interlaced work, iron
hoop, ferrule', fr. OF. frete, frette, prob. derived
fr. Frankish "fetur, which is rel. to OE. fetor,
OHG. fe33ara, 'fetter'. See fetter.

## fret
fret, tr. v., to ornament. — ME. fretten, fretien,
fr. MF. freter, fretter (F. fretter), 'to decorate
with interlaced designs, to bind with a ring or
with a ferrule', fr. OF. freter, fr. frete. See prec.
word.
Derivative: frett-ed, adj.

## fretful
fretful, adj. — Formed fr. fret, 'the act of
fretting' (see fret, 'to eat away' and -fill); first used
by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: fretful-ly, adv., fretful-ness, n.

## fretty
fretty, adj., interlaced (her.) — ME. frette, fr.
MF. frete, frette pp. of freter, fretter. See fret,
'to ornament', and -y (representing OF. -e, MF.,
F. -έ).

## Freudian
Freudian, adj., pertaining to, or agreeing with,
the theories of Sigmund Freud (1856-1939). For
the ending see suff. -ian.

## Frey
Frey, п., the god of the crops and fertility in

## Frcya
Frcya, п., the goddess of love and beauty in
Norse mythology. — ON. Freyja, rel. to Freyr,
and to OE. fria, 'lord', OS. frua, MDu. vrouwe,
'woman, wife*. See frow.

## freyalite
freyalite, п., a radioactive silicate of thorium,

goddess of love in Norse mythology. See prec.
word and -lite.

## friable
friable, adj. — F., fr. L. friabi/is, 'crumbling', fr.

friare, 'to crumble, rub away', which is prob.
cogn. with OI. bhrinanti, 'they hurt, damage',
Avestic pairi-brin*nti, 'they cut round about',
OSlav. britva, 'razor', Russ.-Church Slav, briju,
briti, 'to shear'. L. friare is rel. to fricare, 'to
rub'. See friction and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also frivolous. For the ending see suff. -able.
Derivative: friabil-ity, п., friable-ness, n.

## friar
friar, n. — ME. frere, fr. OF. frere, freire (F.

## frere)
frere), fr. L. fratrcm, ace. of frater, 'brother'.
See fraternal.

fribble, inir. v., ю irifle. — Prob. of imitative

Derivatives: fribble, n.,fribbl-er, n.,fribbl-ery,n.

## fricandeau
fricandeau, п., stew of veal. — F., back formation

## fricassee
fricassee, п., a dish made of meat stewed in

and quash, 'to make void', and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: fricassee, tr. v.

## fricative
fricative, adj., produced by forcing the breath

teeth, etc. (said of a consonant). — ModL.

Derivative: fricative, п., a fricative consonant.

## friction
friction, n. — F., fr. L. frictionem, ace. offrictio,

Derivatives: friction-al, adj., friction-al-ly, adv.,

## Friday
Friday, n. — ME. fridai, fr. OE. frigedxg, lit.
'the day of the goddess Frig', fr. Frige, gen. of
Frig, which corresponds to ON. Frigg, name
of the wife of Odin (sec Frigg), and dxg, 'day',
re], to ON. frijadagr, Dan., Swed. Fredag,
OFris. frigendei, friadei, fredei, MLC, MDu.
vridach, Du. vrijdag, OHG. friatag, MHG. vri-
tac, G. Freitag; prop, a loan translation of L.
Veneris dies, 'the day of Venus, Friday' (whence
It. venerdi, Rum. virteri, OF. vendresdi, F. ven-
dredi, Provenc. divenres, Sp. viernes), itself a
loan translation of Gk. 'Αφροδίτης ήμέρί, 'the
day of Aphrodite'; ON. Frigg, was considered
as the goddess of love. For the second element
in OE. frigedxg see day.

## friedelite
friedelite, п., a manganese silicate {mineral.) —
Named after the French mineralogist Charles
Friedel (1832-99). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## friend
friend, n. — ME. freond, frend, fr. OE. freond,
'friend, lover', rel. to ON. frxndi, OS., OFris.
friund, Du. vriend, OHG., MHG. friunt, G.
Freund, Goth, frijonds, 'friend'. All these nouns
are prop. pres. participles and orig. meant
'loving' (so e.g. OE. freond is the pres. part, of
OE. freogan,freon, 'to love', and Goth, frijonds
the pres. part, of Goth, fryon, 'to love'). They
are rel. to OE. frfo, 'free'. See free, adj., and
cp. words there referred to. For the participial
origin of the noun friend cp. fiend.
Derivatives: friend, tr. v. (rare), friend-less, adj.,

## friend-less-ness
friend-less-ness, п., friendly (q.v.)

friendly, adj. — ME. frendly, fr. OE. friondlic.

## friendly
friendly, adv. (rare). — ME. frendly, fr. OE.
freondlice. See friend and adv. suff. -Iy.

## friendship
friendship, n. — ME. frendship, fr. OE. freond-
scipe. See friend and -ship.

## frieseite
frieseite, п., a silver iron sulfide (mineral.) —

## Friesian
Friesian, adj. and n. — A var. spelling of Frisian.

## Friesic
Friesic, adj., Frisian. — See Frisian and -ic.

## Friesish
Friesish, adj. — See Frisian and adj. suff. -ish.

## frieze
frieze, п., a kind of woolen cloth. — F. frise, rel.
to friser, Ίο cur], friz/. See frizz, 'to curl'.

## frieze
frieze, tr. v., to cover with a nap, to trim. —
F. friser, Ίο curl, frizz'. See prec. word.

## frieze
frieze, п., an ornamented band (archit.) — F.

## frise
frise, fr. ML. frisium, a collateral form of fri-

## gium
gium, phrygium, 'fringe', lit. 'Phrygian, related

frigate, п., a fast sailing vessel. — F.fregate, fr.

It. fregata, fr. Neapolitan fregate, prob. fr. Gk.

ships), fr. ά- (see priv. pref. a-) and φράσσειν,

## Frigg
Frigg, п., the wife of Odin, the goddess of heaven

## fright
fright, n. — ME. fryght, fryhte, fyrhte, fr. OE.

Derivaiives: fright, v. (q.v.), fright-en, tr. v.,

ed-ness, п.,"fright-en-er, п., fright-en-ing, adj.,

fright-fully, adv., fright-ful-ness, n.

## fright
fright, tr. v., to frighten. — ME. frigten, fr. OE.

fear', OS. forahtian, OFris. fruhtia, OHG. forah-
tan,furihten, MHG. viirhten, G.fiirchten, Goth.
faurhtjan, 'to fear', OE. forht, OS., OHG. foraht,

## frigid
frigid, adj., very cold. — L. frigidus, 'cold', fr.

and the first element in rhigolene. Cp. also

sang-froid.
Derivatives: frigidity (q.v), frigid-ly, adv.,
frigid-ness, n.

## frigidity
frigidity, n. — F. frigidite, fr. Late L. frigiditatem,

## frlgorific
frlgorific, adj., causing cold. — F'. frigorifique, fr.
Late L. frigorificus, 'cooling', which is
compounded of L. frigus, gen. frigoris, 'cold', and
-ficus, 'making', from the stem of -ficere,
unstressed form of facere, 'to .nake, do'. See

## frijole

## Frimaire

French revolutionary calendar (lasting from
November 21st to December 20th). — F., lit.

d'Eglantine in 1793 fr°m F.frimas, 'frost,

(fr. L. -drius). See rime, 'hoarfrost', and adj.
suff. -ary.

## fringe
fringe, п., a border of loose threads. — ME.
frenge, fr. OF. fringe, frenge, fr. VL. 'frimbia,
metathesis of L. fimbriae (pi.), 'border, edge,

Derivatives: fringe, tr. v., fring-ed, fring-y,
adjs.

## Fringilla
Fringilla, п., a genus of birds of the finch family

'to squeak, squeal', which is of imit. origin. Cp.
Gk. φρυγίλος (a metathesized form of orig.
•φριγύλος), a kind of bird, dial. Russ. berglez',

bhfnga, 'a large black bee', is not related.

## Fringiilidae
Fringiilidae, n.pl., the finch and sparrow family

## frippery
frippery, п., tawdry finery. — F. friperie, fr. OF.
freperie, fr. frepe, ferpe, felpe, 'fringe, old
garment', ult. fr. ML. faluppa, 'fiber, trifle'.

## frisette
frisette, п., a fringe of curled hair worn on the
forehead. — F., 'little curl', fr. friser, 'to curl'.
See frizz, Ίο curl', and -ette.

## friseur
friseur, п., a hairdresser. — F., fr. friser. Ίο curl'.
See prec. word.

## Frisian
Frisian, adj. and п., belonging to the tribe Frisii.
— Fr. L. Frisii, a name of Teut. origin, lit.
meaning 'curly-headed'. Cp. OFris. frisk, 'curly

## hair'
hair', and see frizz, 'to curl'. For the ending see
suff. -ian. Cp. Friesian.

## frisk
frisk, adj., lively. — OF. (= F.)frisque, fr. MDu.

## vrisch
vrisch, 'fresh', which is rel. to OHG. frise, OE.

## fersc
fersc, 'fresh'. See fresh, 'newly made'.

## frisket
frisket, п., a light frame of iron attached to the

## frit
frit, п., material for glass-making. — F. fritte,
