## frit fly
frit fly, a small fly. — Of uncertain origin.

## frith
frith, п., a narrow arm of the sea, inlet; a firth. —

## frith
frith, п., enclosure; wooded land, brushwood. —

## Fritillaria
Fritillaria, п., a genus of plants of the lily family

called from the markings on the petals), which
is rel. to fritinnire, 'to twitter'; of imitative

## frltillary
frltillary, п., ι) any plant of the genus Fritillaria;
2) any butterfly of the genus Argynnis. — See

fritter, п., a slice of fruit fried in butter. — F.

## fritter
fritter, п., a fragment. — OF. fraiture, freture, 'a

## fritter
fritter, tr. v., to waste. — Fr. prec. word.

## frivoi
frivoi, intr. and tr. v. — Back formation fr.

## frivolous
frivolous, adj., trifling. — L. frivolus, 'brittle,

## frizz
frizz, friz, tr. and intr. v., to curl. — F. friser, Ίο
curl, dress the hair', a word of Frisian origin.
Cp. OFris. frisle, 'curly hair', and the name

## frizz

## frizzle
frizzle, tr. and intr. v., to curl. — Formed fr. frizz,

## frizzle

## fro

OE. rocc, OFris. rokk, OS., Du. rok, OHG. roc,
roch, MHG. roc, G. Rock, 'coat'. These words

## froe
froe, п., a wedge-shaped cleaving tool. — Prob.

## frog
frog, п., a small tailless amphibian. — ME.

hopper, Alemanic hopzger, 'frog', lit. 'hopper'.

## frog
frog, п., a loop on a belt for receiving a sword,
etc. — Of uncertain origin.

## frog
frog, п., a horny pad in a horse's hoof. — Of

from, prep. — ME., fr. OE. from, from, rel. to

forma, Goth, fruma, 'first', OHG. fruma,

## frond
frond, п., a leaflike organ, foliage. — L. from,

## Fronde
Fronde, п., name of a party in France during the

'sling; casting net; purse', which is of uncertain
origin. It is perh. cogn. with, or derived from,
Gk. σφενδόνη, 'sling'; seesphendone. L. funda was
influenced in form by L.fundere, 'to pour, shed'.

## frondesce
frondesce, intr. v., to put forth leaves. — L. fron-
descere, inchoative of frondere, 'to put forth
leaves', fr. frons, gen. frondis, 'leafy branch,
foliage'. See frond and -esce.

## frondescence
frondescence, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce.

## frondescent
frondescent, adj. — L. frondescens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of frondescere. See frondesce and
-ent.

## frondiferous
frondiferous, adj., bearing fronds. — L.frondifer,
'bearing leaves', compounded of frons, gen.
frondis, 'leafy branch, foliage', and ferre, 'to
bear, carry'. See frond and -ferous.

## frondose
frondose, adj., bearing fronds. — L. frondosus,
'leafy', fr. frons, gen. frondis. See frond and adj.
suff. -ose.

## front
front, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) front, fr. L.
frontem, ace. of frons, 'forehead, brow,
countenance; the forepart of anything', prob.
meaning lit. 'that which projects', and standing
for I.-E. *bhron-t-, fr. base "bhren-, 'to project,
stand out', whence also Mir. broine, 'prow of
a ship', Ir. brainech, Co. brenniat, 'watchman
at the prow of a ship'. For the sense
development of L.' frons, 'forehead*, from a base
meaning 'to project', cp. OSlav. ielo, 'forehead',
which is cogn. with L. excellere, 'to rise, stand
out'. Cp. affront, confront, effrontery,
frontispiece.
Derivatives: front, adj. and tr. and intr. v.,
front-age, п., front-ag-er, п., frontal (q.v.),
fronting, п., front-less, adj., front-less-ly, adv., front-
less-ness, n.

## frontal
frontal, п., a band worn on the forehead. — OF.
frontel (F. fronteau), fr. Late L. frontale, 'an
ornament for the forehead', fr. L. frons, gen.
frontis. See front.

## frontal
frontal, adj., pertaining to the front; pertaining
to the forehead. — ModL. frontalis, fr. L. frons,
gen. frontis. See front and adj. suff. -al and cp.
prec. word.

## frontier
frontier, п., — OF. frontier (F. frontiire), from
the adjective frontier, 'facing, neighboring', fr.
front, 'forehead, forepart'. Cp. It. frontiera, Sp.
frontera, and see front.

## Frontignac
Frontignac, п., a kind of muscat grape and wine
made from it. — A blend of Frontignan in the
Department of Herault, and coguac.

## frontispiece
frontispiece, п., an illustration facing the title
page of a book. — F. frontispice, fr. ML. fron-
tispicium, 'a front view', fr. L. frons, gen. frontis,
'forehead, forepart', and specere, spicere, 'to
look at'. See front and species. The spelling
frontispiece is due to a confusion with piece.

## frontiet
frontiet, п., a band worn on the forehead. — OF.
frontelet, dimin. of frontel (F. fronteau). See
front and -let.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:324 COLUMN:2 -->

## fronto-
fronto-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
the forehead, frontal'. — Fr. L. frons, gen.
frontis, 'forehead, forepart'. See front.

## fronton
fronton, п., a pediment (.archil.) — F., fr. It.
frontone, which is formed fr. fronte, 'front,
forepart', with augment, suff. -one. See front and
cp. -oon.

## frore
frore, adj., frosty; frozen (archaic). — ME. frozen,
fr. OE. froren, pp. o(fre~osan,'to freeze'. See freeze.

## frost
frost, n. — ME. forst, frost, fr. OE. forst, frost,
rel. to OS., OHG. frost, MHG. vrost, ON. frost,
Du. vorst, fr. Teut. *frus-ta, an abstract noun
formed with -l-formative element fr. Teut. base
*freus-, 'to freeze'. See freeze.
Derivatives: frost, tr. and intr. v., frost-ed, adj.,
frost-er, п., frost-ing, п., frost-y, adj., frosti-ly,
adv., frosti-ness, n.

## froth
froth, n. — ME. frothe, fr. ON. froda, rel. to OE.
afreodan, 'to froth up', and cogn. with OI.
prdthati, 'pants, snorts'.
Derivatives: froth, intr. and tr. v.,froth-y, adj.,
froth-i-ly, adv., froth-t-ness, n.

## frou-frou
frou-frou, п., a rustling. — F., of imitative origin.

## frounce
frounce, tr. and intr. v., to wrinkle, curl. — ME.
frouncen, 'to wrinkle', fr. OF. froncier (F. fron-
cer), fr. fronce, 'a wrinkle', fr. Frankish *hrunkja,
'wrinkle', which is rel. to ON. hrukka, OHG.
runza, 'wrinkle'. See ruck, 'crease', wrinkle, and
cp. flounce, 'strip of material'.

## frounce
frounce, п., a wrinkle, curl. — OF. (= F.) fronce,
fr. OF. froncier. See fronnce, v.

## frow
frow, п., a Dutch woman; a woman. — ME.
frowe, fr. MDu. vrouwe (Du. vrouw), rel, to
OHG. frouwa, MHG. vrouwe, G. Frau, OS.
frua, 'woman, wife', ON. Frevja, name of the
goddess of love in Norse mythology, OE. frea,
OHG. fro, Goth, frauja, 'lord'. See province
and cp. Frau, Fraulein, Frey, Freya. Cp. also
the second element in euphroe.

## froward
froward, adj., perverse. — Lit. 'turned away';
formed fr. fro, with suff. -ward. Cp. froe.
Derivatives: froward-ly, adv., froward-ness, n.

## frown
frown, intr. and tr. v. — ME. frounen, fr. OF.
froignier, 'to knit one's brows' (whence F. ren-
frogner, of s.m.), fr. Gaulish *frogna, 'nostril'.
Cp. W. ffroen, 'nose'.
Derivatives: frown, п., frown-ing, adj., frown-
ing-ly, adv.

## frowsty
frowsty, adj., musty (dial. English). — See frowzy.
Derivatives: frowsti-ly, adv., frowsti-ness, n.

## frowzy
frowzy, also fronsy, adj., musty. — Of uncertain
origin; prob. rel. to frowsty.
Derivatives: frowzi-ly, adv., frowzi-ness, a.

## froze
froze, past tense of freeze.

## frozen
frozen, pp. of freeze.

## Fructidor
Fructidor, п., name of the izth month of the
French revolutionary calendar (lasting from
August 18th to Sept. 16th). — F., lit. 'the month
of fruit'; a hybrid coined by Fabre d'Eglan-
tine in 1793 from L. fructus, 'fruit', and Gk.
δώρον, 'gift'. See fruit and donation and cp. the
second element in Messidor, Thermidor.

## fructiferous
fructiferous, adj., bearing fruit. — Formed with
suff. -oils fr. L. fructifer, 'fruit-bearing', which
is compounded of fructus, 'fruit', and ferre, *to
bear, carry'. See fruit and -ferous.

## fructification
fructification, n. — L. fructificatiu, gen. -dnis,
'bearing of fruit', fr. fructificatus, pp. of friicti-
ficdre. See next word and -ation.

## fructify
fructify, intr, v., to bear fruit; tr. v., to make
productive. — F. fruclifier, fr. L. friictificare,
'to bear fruit', which is compounded of fructus,
'fruit', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See
fruit and -fy.

## fructose
fructose, п., fruit sugar (chem.) — Formed with
subst. suff. -ose fr. L. fructus, 'fruit'. See fruit.

## fructuous
fructuous, adj., fruitful. — OF., fr. L. fructuosus,
'abounding in fruit, fruitful', fr. fructus. See
fruit and -ous.
Derivatives: fructuous-ly, adv.,fructuous-ness, n.

## frugal
frugal, adj., thrifty. — L. frugatis, 'pertaining to
fruit; thrifty, temperate, frugal', fr. frugi,
'useful, fit, proper', prop. dat. oifrux, 'fruit', which
is rel. to frui, 'to enjoy', fructus, 'fruit'. See
fruit and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: frugality (q.v.% frugal-ly, adv.,

## frugal-ness
frugal-ness, n.

## frugality
frugality, п., frugalness, thrift. — F. frugalite, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:324 COLUMN:3 -->
L. frugSlitatem, ace. of frugalitas, 'thriftiness,
temperance, frugality', fr. frugatis. See prec.
word and -ity.

## fruit
fruit, n. — ME. fruit, fr. OF. fruit, fr. L. fructus,
'enjoyment, the means to enjoyment, produce,
fruit', fr. fruor, Ί enjoy', which stands for
*friigwor, *fruwor, for *frugor, and is cogn.
with OE. brucan, 'to enjoy'. See brook, v., and
cp. Fructidor, fructify, frugal, frumentaceous,
and the second element in tutti-frutti, usufruct.
Derivatives:/™/'!, intr. and tr. v., fruit-age, п.,
fruit-ari-an, n. and adj., fruit-ari-an-ism, fruit-ed,
adjs., fruiterer (q.v.), fruitery (q.v.), fruil-ful,
adj., fruit-ful-ly, adv., fruit-ful-ness, п., fruit-y,
adj., fruit-i-ness, п., fruit-ing, п., fruit-ist, п.,
fruit-ive, adj., fruit-less, adj., fruit-less-ly, adv.,
fruit-less-ness, п., fruit-let, n.

## fruiterer
fruiterer, п., one who deals in fruit. — Formed
with agential suff. -er fr. obsol. fruiter, a loan
word fr. F. fruitier, 'fruiterer', fr. fruit, 'fruit'.
See fruit. Accordingly the suff. -er in fruiterer
is redundant. Cp. caterer, poulterer, sorcerer,
upholsterer.

## fruitery
fruitery, n. — F. fruiterie, 'fruit loft'. See fruit
and -ery.

## frumentaceous
frumentaceous, adj., made of, or resembling,
wheat or other grain. — Late L. frumeniaceus,
'of com or grain', fr. L. frumentum (for "friig-
mentum or *frug-smentum), 'corn, grain', which
is formed from the stem of frugi, 'useful, fit.
proper'. See frugal and -aceous.

## frumenty
frumenty, п., a kind of food made of wheat
boiled in milk. — OF. frumentee, fr. L.
frumentum, 'corn, grain'. See prec. word.

## frump
frump, tr. and intr. v., to flout. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: frump, п., frump-ery, п., frump-ish,
adj., frump-ish-ly, adv., frump-ish-ness, п.,
frump-y, adj., frump-i-ly, adv., frump-i-ness, n.

## frush
frush, п., a horny pad in a horse's foot. — See
frog, 'a horny pad'.

## frustrate
frustrate, adj., frustrated (archaic). — L. frus-
tratus, pp. oifrustrari, 'to deceive, disappoint',
fr. frustra, 'uselessly, in vain', which prob.
derives fr. *fraud-trom, fr. fraus, gen. fraudis,
'deceit, guile'. See fraud and adj. suff. -ate. For
the change of dtr to sir cp. L. claustrum, 'bolt,
bar', which stands for "claud-trom (see claus-
tral).

## frustrate
frustrate, tr. v., to make vain, to thwart —
L. friistrutus, pp. oifrustrari. See frustrate, adj.
Derivatives: frustrat-er, п., frustration (q.v.),
frustrat-ive, frustrat-ory, adjs.

## frustration
frustration, n. — L. frustratio, gen. -onis,
'deception, disappointment', fr. friistrutus, pp. of
frustrSri. See frustrate, adj., and -ion.

## frustule
frustule, п., the shell of a diatom (bot.)*— F., fr.
L. frustulum, 'a small piece', dimin. of frustum.
See next word and -ule.

## frustum
frustum, п., the lower part of a solid figure formed
when the top of a cone is cut off parallel to the
base. — L., 'piece', fr. I.-E. 'bhrus-to-, fr. base
"bhreus-, 'to break, crush, crumble', whence
also OE. brysan, 'to bruise'. See bruise.

## frutescent
frutescent, adj., shrubby. — Incorrectly formed
for 'fruticescent, fr. L. frutex, gen. fruticis, 'a
bush'. See next word and -cscent.

## frutex
frutex, п., a shrub. — L., 'shrub, bush'; of
uncertain origin. Cp. frutescent, frutieose. L. Frutis,
name of Venus, is not related to L. frutex (see
bride).

## fraticose
fraticose, adj., bushy, shrubby. — L. fruticosus,
'full of shrubs or bushes', fr. frutex, gen. fruticis.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ose.

## fry
fry, tr. v., to cook in fat; intr. v., to be cooked
in fat. — ME. frien, fr. frire, fr. L. frigere, 'to
roast, parch, fry', which is cogn. with OI.
bhfjjati, 'roasts', bharjanah, 'roasting' (part.);
ModPers. birishtan, 'to roast', Gk. φρόγειν, 'to
roast, bake', Lith. blrgelas, 'small beer', Lett.
bifga, 'vapor, smoke', OPruss. au-birgo, 'owner
of a cook shop'. All these words derive fr. I.-E.
*bher(e)g-, *bhrtg-, *bhrug-, enlargements of
base *bher-, 'to boil, seethe'. See brew and cp.
fervent. Cp. also fricandeau, fricassee, frit,
fritter, 'piece of fruit'.
Derivatives: fry, п., 'fried food', fry-er (also
fri-er), n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:325 COLUMN:1 -->

## fry
fry, п., I) young fish; 2) young, offspring. — ME.
fri, 'seed, offspring', prob. fr. AF. frie, fry,
which corresponds to OF. froi (F. frai), 'spawn',
fr. freier, froier, 'to rub, spawn', fr. L. fricare,
'to rub'. See friction.

## fub
fub, tr. v., to cheat. — G. foppen, 'to jeer at,
make a fool of. See fob.

## fubsy
fubsy, adj., plump, squat (Colloq. Engl.) — Of
uncertain origin.

## Fuchsia
Fuchsia, п., a genus of plants of the evening
primrose family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
German botanist Leonhart Fuchs (1501-1566).
For the ending see suff. -ia.

## fuchsin
fuchsin, fuchsine, п., a variety of rosaniline
(mineralogy). — Formed fr. Fuchsia with suff.
-in, resp. -Ine; so called in allusion to its color,
which resembles that of fuchsia.

## fucoid
fucoid, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
seaweed; п., a seaweed. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. fucus, 'rock lichen', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like*,
fr. είδος, 'form, shape' (see Fucus and -oid).
The correct form would be phycoid (fr. Gk.
φϋχος, 'seaweed', and -οει8ής, 'like').

## Fucus
Fucus, п., ι) a genus of algae; 2) (not cap.) any
plant of this genus (bot.) — L. fucus, 'rock
lichen', fr. Gk. φΰκος, 'seaweed; red paint,
rouge', fr. Heb. pukh, .'antimony, stibium, lye,
paint'. Cp. the second element in Zygophyceae.

## fuddle
fuddle, tr. v., to render confused. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: fuddle, п., fuddle-ment, n.

## fudge
fudge, tr. v., to fake. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: fudge, n.

## fuel
fuel, n. — OF. fouaille,fuaille, fr. Late L./ocd/ia,
neut. pi. of focalis, 'pertaining to the hearth',
fr. L. focus, 'hearth'. See focus and cp. focal.
Derivatives: fuel, tr. and intr. v., fuel(l)-er, п.,
fuel(l)-ing, n.

## fugacious
fugacious, adj., fleeting. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. fugdx, gen. fugacis, 'apt to flee,
transitory', fr. fugere. See fugitive and cp.
fougasse.
Derivatives: fugacious-ly, adv., jugacious-ness,a.

## fugacity
fugacity, n. — Late L. fugacitas, fr. L. fugax,
gen. fugacis, 'apt to flee, transitory'. See prec.
word and -ity.

## fuga)
fuga), adj., pertaining to a fugue (mus.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. It. fuga. See fugue.
Derivative: fugal-ly, adv.

## -fuge
-fuge, combining form meaning 'that which
drives away (something)', as in febrifuge,
vermifuge. — F„ fr. L. fugus, 'fleeing away' (used
in Modern Latin in the sense 'causing to flee,
putting to flight'), fr. L. fugere. See fugitive.

## fugient
fugient, adj., fleeing. — L. fugiens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of fugere, 'to flee'. See fugitive and
-ent.

## fugitive
fugitive, adj. — OF. (= F.)fugitif(iem. fugitive),
fr. L. fugitivus, 'running away, fleeing, fugitive',
fr. fugit-(um), pp. stem of fugere, 'to flee', which
is cogn. with Gk. φεύγειν, 'to flee', Lith. bugstu,
bagti, 'to be frightened', fr. I.-E. base *bheug-,
'to flee', which prop, meant originally 'to bend
one's course away from a place", and is identical
with base *bheug(h)-, 'to bend', whence OI.
bhujati, 'bends, thrusts aside', Goth, biugan,
'to bend', OE. bugan, 'to bow down, stoop;
to bend, turn; to flee'. See bow, 'to bend', and
cp. fougasse, fugacious, fugue, centrifugal, Cimi-
fuga, feverfew, heliofiigal, iucifugous, refuge,
refugee, subterfuge. Cp. also apophyge, hypo-
phyge, phygoid.
Derivatives: fugitive, п., fugitive-ly, adv., fugi-
tive-ness, a.

## fngle
fngle, intr. v. — Back formation fr. fugleman,

## fugleman
fugleman, also fugeiman, п., ι) a well-drilled
soldier placed in front of a company to serve as a
model; hence 2) a leader, guide. — Dissiniilated

## fr. G. Fliigeunann
fr. G. Fliigeunann, 'file leader, fugleman', lit.,
'man on the wing' (of a regiment), fr. Fliigel,
'wing' and Mann, 'man'. G. Fliigel is rel. to

## ftiegen
ftiegen, 'to fly'; see fly, v. For the second element
in fugleman see man.

## fugue
fugue, n. (mus.) — F., fr. It. fuga, 'flight, escape;

## ardor'
ardor', fr. L. fuga, 'a fleeing, flight; swiftness,

## speed'
speed', from the stem of fugere, 'to flee'. See

fugitive,

## fuguist
fuguist, п., a composer of fugues. — A hybrid

coined fr. It. fuga (see prec. word) and -ist, a
suff. of Greek origin.
fiihrcr, fuehrer, п., a title applied chiefly to the
leader of the German nazis. — G. Fiihrer,
'leader', fr. fiihren, 'to lead', fr. MHG. viieien,
'to lead, drive', fr. OHG. fuoren, 'to set in
motion, lead', prop, a causative of OHG. faran,
'to go, travel', which is rel. to OE. faran, of

## Fuirena
Fuirena, п., a genus of plants, the umbrella grass
(bot.) — ModL., named after the Danish
physician and botanist Jergen Fuiren (1581-
1628).

## -fill
-fill, adj. suff. meaning 'full of. — See full, adj.

## fulcrum
fulcrum, п., the support on which a lever turns.
— L., 'bedpost', fr. fulcire, 'to prop', which is
cogn. with Gk. φάλκης, 'beam', φάλαγξ, 'trunk,
log, line of battle, battle array', OE. balca,
'ridge'. See balk, п., and cp. words there
referred to.

## fulfill
fulfill, fulfil, tr. v. — ME. fulfillen, fr. OE. full-
fyllan, Ίο fulfill', lit. 'to fill full', fr. ful, 'full',
and fyllan, 'to fill'. See full, adj., and fill.
Derivatives: fulfill-er, п., fulfillment, n.

## fulgent
fulgent, adj., shining. — L. fulgins, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of fulgere, 'to shine', rel. to fulgur,
'lightning', fulmen (for *fu]g-men), of s.m.,
flagrare, 'to blaze, glow, burn'. See black, and
cp. effulgent, refulgent, fulminate. Cp. also
flagrant. For the ending see suff. -ent.
Derivatives: fulgent-ly, adv., fulgent-ness, n.

## fulgid
fulgid, adj., glittering, shining. — L. fulgidus, fr.
fulgere, 'to shine'. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -id.

## Fulgora
Fulgora, п., a genus of insects, the lantern fly
(entomol.) — L., name of the goddess of
lightning, rel. to fulgus, gen. fulguris, 'lightning'. See
fulgent and cp. next word.

## fulgurant
fulgurant, adj., flashing. — L. fulgurans, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of fulgurare, 'to lighten', fr.

## fulgur
fulgur, 'lightning', which is rel. to fulgere, 'to
shine'. See fuigent and -ant and cp. foudroyant.

## fulgurite
fulgurite, п., glassy substance produced by the
passage of lightning (geol.) — A hybrid coined
fr. L. fulgur, 'lightning' (see fulgent), and -ite,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## fuiham
fuiham, also fullam, fuliom, п., a loaded die. —
From Fuiham in London, formerly a resort of
crooks.

## Fulica
Fulica, п., a genus of birds, the true coot (or-
nithol.) — L. fulica, 'coot', lit. meaning 'having
a white spot (scil. on the head)', and cogn. with
Gk. φάλός, 'white'. See full, 'to thicken'.

## fuliginous
fuliginous, adj., sooty, — Late L. fuliginosus, fr.
L. fuligo, gen. fuligim's, 'soot'; cogn. with Ol.
dhiilili, 'dust', dhulika, 'fog', Lith. dulis, Tog,
vapor', fern. pi. dulkes, 'dust', Lith. dulsvas,
'smoke-colored'.
Derivatives: fuliginous-ly, adv., fuliginous-
ness, n.

## full
full, adj. — ME., fr. OE. full, rel. to OS. full,
OFris. ful, ON. fullr, Swed. full, Dan. fuld.
OHG. fol, MHG. vol, G. roll, Goth, fulls, 'full',
and cogn. with OSlav. pluiiu, Lith. pilnas, Olr.
Ian, W. llawn, Brei. leun, L. plenus, OI. pmnuh,
'full', Avestic p'r'na-, 'full', fr. I.-E. base 'ρ/ηό-,
'filled, full'. This base is a participial derivative
of base *peli-, *ple-, 'to fill', whence Gk. πλή-
θειν, 'to be full', πίμπλάναι, Ίο fill', πλήρης,
'full', L. plere, 'to fill'. Cp. also OE. felajeala,

## feola
feola, OFris. felo, fel, OS., OHG. filu, MHG.

## vil
vil, G. viel, Goth, filu, 'much', OI. puruh, Gk.
πολύς, 'much', L. plus, 'more', Lith. pilus, Olr.

## it
it, 'plenty'. E. folk is not cognate. Cp. fill. Cp.

also flow. Cp. also accomplish, complement,

## complete
complete, comply, deplete, expletive, implement,

## maniple
maniple, manipulate, plebeian, pleio-,

## Pleistocene
Pleistocene, plenary, plenty, plenum, pleonasm, ple-

## rome
rome, plethora, plethysmograph, plural, plus,

## piutarchy
piutarchy, plutocracy, poly-, replenish, replete,

## replum
replum, supplement, supply, terreplein.
Derivatives: full, п., tr. and intr. v. and adv.,

## ful-ly
ful-ly, zav.,ful(l)-ness, n.

## fuli
fuli, tr. v., to thicken (cloth). — ME. fullen, fr.

## OE.ful/ian
OE.ful/ian, 'to whiten, full', fr. OF. foler, fouler
(F. fouler), 'to tread, trample on, to full', fr. VL.
'fullare, fr. L. fullo, 'fuller', which is of
uncertain origin. It is perh. cogn. with Gk. ιραλός,

'white', ME. balled, 'bald', orig. 'white'. See
bald and cp. words there referred to. Proveng.,
Catal. folar, Sp. hollar, 'to full', also derive fr.
VL. 'fullare. Cp. foil, 'to baffle', foulard.
Derivative: full-ing, n.

## fuller
fuller, п., one who fulls. — ME., fr. fultere, fr.
L. fullo, 'a fuller'. See full, 'to thicken (cloth)'.

## fuller
fuller, п., a grooving tool. — Formed fr. full, 'to
make full' (see full, adj.), with agential suff. -er.

## fulmar
fulmar, п., an arctic sea bird resembling a gull.
— Compounded of ON. full, 'foul', and mar,
'sea mew'. See foul, adj., and mew.

## fulminant
fulminant, adj., fulminating. — L. fulminans, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of fulmindre. See next word
and -ant.

## fulminate
fulminate, intr. v., to explode; tr. v., to cause to
explode; to denounce. — L. fulminatus, pp. of
fulminate, 'to lighten, to hurl lightnings', fr.
fulmen, gen. fulminis, 'lightning', which stands
for *fulg-men and is rel. to fulgere, 'to shine'. See
fulgent and verbal suff. -ate and cp. fulinine.
Derivatives: fulminat-ing, a.dj.,fulmination (q.v.),
fulminatory (q.v.)

## fulminate
fulminate, п., a salt of fulminic acid (chem.) —
See fulminic and chem. suff. -ate.

## fulmination
fulmination, n. — L. fulminatio, gen. -6nis, fr.

## fulminatus
fulminatus, pp. of fulminBre. See fulminate v.,
and -ion.

## fulminatory
fulminatory, adj. — F. fulminatoire, fr. fulminer.
Ίο fulminate', fr. L. fulm/nare. See fulminate
and adj. suff. -ory.

## fnlmine
fnlmine, intr. and tr. v., to fulminate (rare). —
F. fulminer, fr. L. fulmindre. See fulminate, v.

## fulminic
fulminic, adj., pertaining- to the acid CNOH
(chem.) — Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. fulmen,
gen. fulminis, 'lightning' (see fulminate); so
called in allusion to its forming highly explosive
salts.

## fulminous
fulminous, adj., resembling lightning. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. L. fulmen, gen. fulminis,
'lightning'. See fulminate, adj.

## fulsome
fulsome, adj., cloying; disgusting; offensive. —
Formed fr. full, adj., and -some; influenced in
meaning by ME. ful, 'foul'.
Derivatives: fulsome-ly, adv., futsome-ness, n.

## fulvous
fulvous, adj., reddish yellow, tawny. — L. fulvus,
cogn. with L. fiavus, 'yellow'. See flavescent.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## fumade
fumade, funrado, п., a smoked and salted
pilchard. — Sp. fumado, 'smoked', fr. L. fumatus,
pp. of fumare. Ίο smoke'. See fume.

## fumarole
fumarole, п., a hole in a volcano whence fumes
issue. — F. fumerole, Frenchified fr. It. fuma-
ruolo, fr. Late L. fumariolum, 'a smoke hole',
fr. L. fumarium, 'a smoke chamber for aging
wine', fr. fumus. 'smoke'. See fume.

## fumatorium
fumatorium, п., a place for smoking or
fumigating. — ModL., fr. L. fumatus, pp. of fumare, 'to
smoke'. See fume and -orium.

## fumatory
fumatory, adj., pertaining to smoking; п.,
fumatorium. — See prec. word and adj., resp. subst.,
suff. -ory.

## fumble
fumble, intr. v., to grope about; tr. v., to handle
awkwardly. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. Swed. and
dial. Norw. fumla, which are rel. to Du. fomme-
len, 'to grope'. The orig. meaning of these words
was 'to rub'. They are prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives: fumble, п., fumbl-er, п., fumbl-ing,
n. and adj., fumbl-ing-ly, adv.

## fume
fume, n. — OF. fum, fr. L. fumus, 'smoke, steam,
vapor', whence also It. fumo, OProvenc. fum,
Sp. humo. L. fumus is cogn. with OI. dhumah,
'smoke', OSlav. dymu, Lith. damai, Lett. dUmi
(pi.), OPruss. dumis, 'smoke', Mir. dumacha,
'fog', ir. dumhach, 'foggy', Gk. θυμός, 'spirit,
mind, soul'; these words derive fr. I.-E. *dhu-
mo-s, fr. base *dheu-, 'to. fly about like dust',
whence also OI. dhiinoti, 'shakes'. See thio- and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also fumigate,
perfume, sfumato.

## fume
fume, intr. and tr. v. — F. fumer, fr. L. fumare,
'to smoke', fr. fumus. See fume, n.
Derivatives: fum-ed, adj., fum-er, п., fum-ing,
adj., fum-ing-ty, adv.

## fumigate
fumigate, tr. v., to disinfect with fumes. — L.
fumigatus, pp. of fumigare, 'to smoke,
fumigate', lit. 'to cause to smoke', compounded of
fumus, 'smoke, steam, vapor', and agere, 'to set

## in motion
in motion, drive, lead; to do, act'. See fnme, п.,

## and agent
and agent, adj., and cp. the second element in
castigute and in words there referred to.
Derivatives: fumigation (q.v.), fumigat-or, п.,

## fumigat-ory
fumigat-ory, adj.

## fumigation
fumigation, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. fiimigationem,

## ace. of fumigatio
ace. of fumigatio, 'a smoking', (i.fitmigatus, pp.
of fumigare. See prec. word and -ion.

## fumitory
fumitory, п., a plant formerly used as an
antiscorbutic. — ME., fr. OF. fumeterre, lit. 'smoke

## of the earth'
of the earth', compounded of fume, 'smoke',

## and terre
and terre, 'earth', fr. L. terra. See fnme, п., and
terra.

## fumous
fumous, adj., smoky. — L. fiimosus, 'full of

## smoke
smoke, smoky', fr. fumus. See fume, п., and -ous.
Derivative: fumous-ly, adv.

## fumy
fumy, adj., full of fumes; vaporous. — Formed
fr. fume, п., with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: fumil-y, adv., fumi-ness, n.

## fun
fun, n. — Fr. obsol. E. fun, 'to trick', fr. ME.

## fon
fon, fonne, 'a fool', fr. fonnen, 'to make a fool
of. See fond, adj.
Derivatives: fun, intr. v., to cause fun, funny
(q.v.)

## funambulist
funambulist, п., a ropewalker. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. funis, 'rope', and ambulare, 'to walk', and
Gk. suff. -ιστής. See funicular, amble and -ist.

## Funaria
Funaria, п., a genus of mosses (hot.) — ModL.,
fr. Late L. funarius, 'pertaining to a rope', fr. L.
funis. See funicle and cp. prec. word.

## function
function, n. — OF. function (F. fonction), fr. L.
functionem, ace. of functio, 'performance,
execution', fr. functus, pp. of fungi, 'to perform,
execute, discharge', which is cogn. with OI.
bhunakti, bhunjaii, 'enjoys, consumes', bhogah,
'enjoyment'. Cp. fungible, defunct, perfunctory.
For the ending see suff. -ion.
Derivatives: function, intr. v., funclion-al, adj.,
function-al-ly, adv., function-ary, adj.,
functionate, intr. v.

## fuud
fuud, п., stock of money. — F. fond, 'bottom,
foundation, basis', fr. L. fundus, 'bottom piece
of land, farm', which is metathesized f r. *fudnos
and cogn. with OI. budhnah, Gk. πυθμήν,
'foundation, bottom', OE. botm, 'lowest part, depth,
bottom'. See bottom and cp. found, 'toestablish',
fond, 'foundation', founder, 'to sink', profound,
fundament, latifundium.
Derivatives. fund,lr.v.,fund-ed,adj.,fund-ing,n.

## fundament
fundament, n. — ME. fondement, fr. OF. (= F.)
'fondement, fr. L. funddmentum, 'foundation',
fr.funddre, 'to lay the bottom, found'. See fund
and -ment.
Derivatives: fundament-al, adj. and п.,
fundamental-ism, п., fundamental-ist, п.,
fundamentally, adv.

## funebrial
funebrial, adj., funereal. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. funebris, 'pertaining to a funeral',
which stands ioc*funesris, fr. funus, gen. funeris,
'funeral'. See funerai, n.

## funeral
funeral, adj., pertaining to a funeral. — ML.
funeratis, fr. L.funus, gen. funeris. See funeral, n.

## funeral
funeral, п., a burial. — OF. funeraille (F. fune-
railles), fr. ML. funeralia, 'funeral rites', fr. L.
funus, gen. funeris, 'burial, funeral', which
prob. stands for *dhewenos, 'that which pertains
to death', fr. I.-E. base "dhew-, *dheu-, 'to die',
whence also Goth, daups, 'dead', divans,.
'mortal'. See dead and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also funebrial.

## funerary
funerary, adj., pertaining to a funeral. — L.
funerarius, fr. funus, gen. funeris, 'burial,
funeral'. See funeral, п., and adj. suff. -ary.

## funereal
funereal, adj., pertaining to a funeral; mournful.
— Coined by Pope fr. L. funereus, fr. funus, gen.
funeris. See funeral, n.
Derivative: funereal-ly, adv.

## fungible
fungible, adj., capable of being used in place of
another (law). — ML. fungibilis, fr. L. fungi,
'to perform, execute, discharge'. See function,
and -ibie.
Derivative: fungible, п., a fungible thing.

## fungicide
fungicide, п., a substance that kills fungi. —
Compounded of fungus and L. -cida, 'killer', fr.
caedere, 'to kill'. See -cide, 'killer'.

## fungiform
fungiform, adj., having the form of a fungus. —
Compounded of fungus and forma, 'form,
shape'. See form, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:326 COLUMN:2 -->

## fungoid
fungoid, adj., resembling a fungus. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. fungus, 'mushroom', and Gk.
-οειδής, 'like", fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
fungus and -okl.

## fungosity
fungosity, п., a fungoid excrescence. — Formed
fr. fungus with suff. -ity.

## fungous
fungous, adj., spongy. — L. fungosus, 'spongy,
fungous', fr. fungus. See fungus and -ous.

## fungus
fungus, п., ι) any of a group of plants including
mushrooms, molds, mildews, etc.; 2) (med.) a
spongy morbid growth. — L., 'mushroom', fr.
Att. Gk. σφόγγος, corresponding to Gk. σττόγ-·
γος, 'sponge'. For the change of Gk. σφ to/in
Latin cp. L. fides, 'gut string; lyre, lute' (if it
derives fr. Gk. σφίδες, 'sausage'). Cp. sponge.
Derivative: fungus-y, adj.

## funicle
funicle, п., a small cord. — L. funiculus, dimin.
of funis, 'rope', which prob. stands for *dhu-
nis and is cogn. with Gk. θώμιγξ, θώμιξ, 'rope,
cord'. Cp. Funaria and the first element in
funambulist. For the ending see suff. -cle.

## funicular
funicular, adj., pertaining to a rope or cord. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. funiculus, 'a
small rope'. See prec. word.

## funk
funk, п., cowardice, panic (colloq.) — Perh. fr.
Flemish fonck, 'perturbation'.
Derivatives: funk, intr. and tr. v.,funk-y, adj.,
funk-i-ness, n.

## funnel
funnel, n. — ME. fonel, fr. OProvenc. founhil,
enfounhil, fr. Late L. fundibulum, short for L.
infundibulum, 'funnel', lit. 'instrument for
pouring into', fr. infundere, 'to pour into', fr. ia-,
'in', and fundere, 'to pour'. See found, 'to cast',
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: funnel, intr. and tr. v.

## funny
funny, adj., amusing. — Formed with adj. suff.
-y from the noun fun.
Derivatives: funni-ly, adv., funni-ment, a.,funni-
ness, n.

## funny
funny, п., a small rowboat. — Prob. fr. prec.
word.

## fur
fur, n. — ME. forre, furre, 'fur', orig. 'covering',
fr. furren, 'to cover'. See fur, v.

## fur
fur, tr. v. — ME. furren, fr. OF. forrer (F. four-
rer), 'to cover', fr. OF. fuerre, forre, 'sheath,
case, covering' (whence OF. furrel, F. fourreau,
of s.m.), fr. Frankish "fddr, which corresponds
to OHG. fotar, fuotar, 'a cover, coverlet'. Cp.
It. fodera, 'covering, lining, sheathing', which
is also a Teut. loan word, and see fother.
Derivatives: furr-ed, adj., furri-er, п., furri-er-ed,
adj., furri-ery, п., furr-ing, п., furr-y, adj., furr-
i-ly, adv., furr-i-ness, n.

## furan
furan, furane, furfnran, furfurane, п., a colorless
liquid, C4H40 (chem.) — Formed fr. L. furfur,
'bran' (see furfur), with suff. -an, resp. -ane.

## furbelow
furbelow, п., a flounce. — Folk-etymological
corruption of Franco-Provenc. farbella, 'fringe,
lace' (whence also F. falbala), which is of
imitative origin. Cp. falbala.
Derivative: furbelow-ed, adj.

## furbish
furbish, tr. v., to polish. — ME. forbischen, fr.OF.
forbiss-, furbiss- (F. fourbiss-), pres. part, stem
of forbir (F. fourbir), 'to polish, burnish,
furbish', which is of Teut. origin; cp. OHG.furban,
MHG. furben, 'to polish'. It. forbire and
OProvenc. forbir are of the same origin and
meaning as OF. forbir.

## furca
furca, п., a fork; a process resembling a fork
(zool.) — L. See fork and cp. next word.

## furcate
furcate, adj., forked. —ML.furcatus, fr. L.furca,
'fork'. See fork and adj. suff. -ate and ср. Ы-
furcate.
Derivatives: furcate, intr. v., furcat-ion, n.

## furcula
furcula, п., the clavicular bone of a bird, the
wishbone (zool.) — L„ 'a forked prop', dimin. of
furca, 'fork' (see fork); so called from its
forked shape.

## furfur
furfur, п., dandruff, scurf. — L., 'bran, scurf,
of uncertain origin. It stands perh. for *for-for,
and was formed by reduplication and vowel
gradation fr. I.-E. base *gher-, 'to rub', whence
Gk. χόνδρος (dissimilated fr. orig. "χρόνδρος),
'corn, grain, groat', OE. grindan, 'to grind'. See
grind and cp. chondro-.

## fnrfuraceous
fnrfuraceous, adj., scurfy. — Late L.furfurdceus,
'resembling bran', fr. L. furfur. See furfnr and
-aceous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:326 COLUMN:3 -->

## furfural
furfural, n. — The same as furfurol.

## furfuran
furfuran,furfurane,n.—The same as furan, furane.

## furfurol
furfurol, п., a volatile oil, CsH,Oi (chem.) —
Compounded of L. furfur, 'bran', and oleum,
'oil' (see furfur and -ol, 'oil'); so called because
it is easily obtained by distilling bran.

## furibund
furibund, adj., furious (rare). — L. furibundus,
'raging, furious', fr. furere, 'to rage, be mad'.
See fury.

## Furies
Furies, n. pi., the three avenging spirits Alecto,
Tisiphone and Megaera; the Erinyes (Greek and
Roman mythol.) — L. Furiae, pi. of Furia,
personification oifuria, 'fury'. See fury.

## furious
furious, adj. — OF. furieus (F. furieux), fr. L.
furiosus, 'full of rage or madness', fr. furia. See
fury and -ous.
Derivatives: furious-ly, adv., furious-ness, n.

## furl
furl, tr. v., to roll up. — F. ferler, 'to furl', of
uncertain origin. It derives perh. fr. OF. ferle,
•branch, staff, rod', fr. L. ferula. See ferule.
Derivatives: furl, п., furl-er, n,

## furlong
furlong, п., a measure of distance equal to 220
yards. — ME. furlang, furlong, fr. OE. furtang,
length of a furrow', compounded of furh,
'furrow', and long, 'long'. See furrow and long, adj.

## furlough
furlough, п., leave of absence. — Earlier E. fur-
loff. fr. Du. verlof which is formed fr. ver-,
'for-' and lof, 'leave, permission', and is rel.
10 MLG. vorlof 'leave, permission', Late MHG.
verlouben, 'to permit', G. Verlaub, 'leave,
permission'. See for- and leave.
Derivatives: furlough, tr. v., furlough-ed, adj.

## furmety
furmety, n. — See frumenty.

## furnace
furnace, n. — ME. forneis, fornais, fr. OF. fornais
(a collateral form of fornaise, whence F. four-
naise), fr. L. fornacem, ace. of forndx, 'furnace,
oven', fr. fornus (also furnus), 'oven', which is
rel. to L. formus and cogn. with Gk. θερμός,
OE. wearm, 'warm'. See warm and cp. Fornax,
fornicate, Funiarius, hornito. Cp. also therm.
Derivatives '.furnace, tr. v., furnac-er, n.

## furnacite
furnacite, п., a lead copper chrom-arsenate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. furnax,
erroneous form for L. for/tax, 'furnace' (see
furnace); so called after the colonial governor
Lucien Fourneau (fr. fourneau, 'furnace').

## Furnariidae
Furnariidae, n. p]., a family of South American
birds, the ovenbirds (ornithol.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. Furnarius (q.v.)

## Fnrnarius
Fnrnarius, п., the type genus of birds of the family
Furnariidae (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. L.
furnarius, 'baker', fr. furnus. "oven'. See furnace
and 2nd -ary.

## furnish
furnish, tr. and intr. v. — OF. forniss-, furniss-
(F. fourniss-), pres. part, stem of fornir, furnir
(F. fournir), fr. orig. *furmir (cp. AF. furmir),
1Ϊ. OHG. frumjan, 'to do, execute, provide',
which is rel. to OE. fremman. Ίο funher'. See
from, frame and verbal suff. -ish and cp. veneer.
Cp. also perform.
Derivatives: furnish, u.,furnish-ed, adj.,
furnisher, п., furnish-ing, n..furnish-ment, n.

## furniture
furniture, n. — F. fowniture, fr. fournir, 'to
furnish'. See prec. word and -ure.

## furor
furor, п., ι) craze, rage; 2) general enthusiasm. —
L. furor, 'rage, madness', fr. furere, '10 rage,
be mad'. See fury.

## furore
furore, п., furor (2nd sense). — It., fr. L.furorem,
ace. of furor. See prec. word.

## fnrrow
fnrrow, n. — ME. forow, forgh, furgh, fr. OE.
furh, rel. to ON. for, 'furrow, drainage ditch',
Dan. fure, Swed. fura, MDu. vore, Du. voor,
OFris. furch, OHG. furuh, furh, MHG. furch,
G. Furche, 'furrow*, fr. I.-E. base *ρ$-, whence
also L. porca, 'ridge between two furrows'
(whence porculetum, 'a field divided into beds'),
Gaul.-L. *rica, 'furrow' (whence F. raie,
OProvenc. rega), Olr. -rech (in compounds), W. rhych,
'furrow', OBret. rec, Ί plow'. Cp. furlong. Cp.
also porcate.
Derivatives: furrow, tr. v., furrow-ing, n.

## further
further, adj. — ME. farther, further, fr. OE.
furdra, fr. furdor, 'further', adv.; rel. to OS.
further, 'further', adv., OHG. furdir, MHG.
viirder, G. flirder, 'further', adv., and to OHG.
fordar, MHG-, G. vorder, 'forward, foremost',
and cogn. with Gk. πρότερος, 'former'. See forth
and -ther and cp. furthest. Cp. also farther.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:327 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: FURTHER | 300 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:327 COLUMN:1 -->

## further
further, adv. — ME. forthere, furthere, fr. OE.
furdor, fordor, compar. of/on). See further, adj.

## further
further, tr. v. — ME. forthren, furthren, fr. OE.
fyrdrati, 'to advance, further, promote1, rel. to
MLG. vorderen, OHG. furdiran, MHG. vurdern,
G.fordern, of s.m., and to OE.furdra, 'further'.
See further, adj., and cp. afford.
Derivatives: furtker-ance, п., further-er, n.

## furthest
furthest, adj. and adv. — Superl. formed on
analogy of the comparative further. Cp. far,
farthest.

## furtive
furtive, adj., stealthy. — F. furtif (fem. furtive),
fr. L. furtivus, 'stolen; concealed, secret', rel. to
furtum, 'theft', fr. fur, 'thief, which is cogn.
with Gk. φώρ, 'thief, prop, 'he who carries
(things) away', and stands in gradational
relationship to L. ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See bear,
'to carry', and -ive, and cp. ferret, 'the animal',
furuncle, and the first element in Phoradendron.
For sense development cp. OI. bharah, 'robbery',
and MPers. burl, 'stolen', which are from the
same base.
Derivaiives:/M/7/ve-/y, SLdv.,furtive-ness, a.

## furuncle
furuncle, п., a boil. — L. furunculus, 'a petty thief;
a boil, furuncle', dimin. of fur, 'thief. See prec.
word and -cle.

## furuncular
furuncular, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr.
L. furunculus. See prec. word.

## furunculosis
furunculosis, п., condition marked by being
affected with furuncles (med.) — A hybrid coined
fr. L. furunculus (see furuncle) and -osis, a sufT.
of Greek origin.

## furunculous
furunculous, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr.
L. furunculus. See furuncle.

## fury
fury, n. — F. furie, fr. L. furia, 'rage, madness',
fr. furo, furere, 'to rage, be mad', which prob.
stands for 'dhuso and is cogn. with Gk. &6ει\ι,
Lesb. θύιειν, Gk. θυιάζειν, 'to rage', θυΐα, θυιάς,
'bacchante', Gk. θυειν, 'to sacrifice', prop, 'to
cause to smoke*. See thio- and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also Furies, furor.

## furze
furze, п., a spiny evergreen plant; also called
whin or gorse. — ME. firse, fr. OE. fyrs, cogn.
with Gk. πυρός, 'corn, wheal', OSlav. pyro,
'spelt', Russ. pyrej, Czech pyr, 'couch grass',
Lith. purai (pi.), 'wheat'. Cp. pyrene, 'stone of
a drupelet'.
Derivatives: furz-ed, adj., furz-ery, п., furz-y,
adj.

## fusain
fusain, п., fine charcoal used in drawing. — F„
'the spindle tree, charcoal made from spindle
wood', fr. L. fusus, 'spindle'. See fuse, 'tube'.

## Fusarium
Fusarium, п., a genus of imperfect fungi (bot.) —
ModL., fr. L. fusus, 'spindle*. See fuse, 'tube'.

## fuscous
fuscous, adj., dark-colored. — L.fuscus (fr. *dhus-
qo-), 'dark, swarthy', rel. to L. furvus (fr. *dhus-
wo-), 'dark, brown, swarthy', and cogn. with
OI. dhiisarah, 'dust-colored', OE. dose, dox,
'dusk'. See dusk and cp. infuscate, obfuscate.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## fuse
fuse, tr. and intr. v., to melt, dissolve. — L. fusus,
pp. of fundere, 'to pour, melt'. See found, 'to
cast', and cp. infuse, profuse, refuse, transfuse.
Cp. also fuse, 'tube', and words there referred to.
Derivatives: fusible (q.v.), fus-ing, n.

## fuse
fuse, п., a tube filled with explosive material. —
It. fuso, 'spindle', fr. L. fusus, of s.m., which
prob. derives fr. fusus, pp. of fundere, 'to pour'.
See fose, v., and cp. fusain, Fusaria, fusee,
fuselage, fusil (her.), Fusus. For sense development
cp. Gk. σφόνδυλος, 'spindle, circular whorl,
vertebra', which is rel. to σφενδόνη, 'sling'.

## fusee
fusee, п., i) a kind of wooden match; 2) a conical

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:327 COLUMN:2 -->
wheel of a clock or watch, on which the chain
is wound; 3) a flare used as a railroad signal;
4) a bony growth on a horse's leg. — F. fusie,
'spindleful', fr. ML. fiisata, fr. L·. fusus, 'spindle'.
See prec. word.

## fuselage
fuselage, п., the body of an airplane. — F., fr.
fusil, 'spindle', fr. OF. fusel (F. fuseau). See
fusil (her.) and -age.

## fusel oil
fusel oil, an oily liquid of unpleasant odor (chem.)
— G. Fusel, 'a bad liquor', fr. L.fusilis, 'molten,
liquid', fr. fusus, pp. of fundere, 'to pour'. See
found, 'to cast'.

## fusibility
fusibility, n. — F. fusibilite, fr. fusible. See next
word and -ity.

## fusible
fusible, adj., that which can be fused. — F., fr.
L. fusus, pp. of fundere, 'to pour'. See fuse, 'to
melt', and -ible.
Derivatives: fusible-ness, a.,fusibl-y, adv.

## fusiform
fusiform, adj., spindle-shaped. — Compounded
of L. fusus, 'spindle', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See fuse, 'tube', and form, n.

## fusil
fusil, п., a flintlock musket. — F., 'musket, gun,
rifle', orig. 'steel for striking sparks', fr. OF.
foisil, fuisil, fr. VL. 'focilis (scil. pelra), '(stone)
producing fire' (whence also It. fucile, OPro-
venc\ fozil, 'musket, gun, rifle'), fr. L. focus,
'hearth'. See focus.
Derivative: fusil-ly, adv.

## fusil
fusil, п., a lozengelike figure (her.) — OF. fusel
(F. fuseau), 'spindle', dimin. formed fr. L. fusus,
'spindle'. See fuse, 'tube'.

## fusil
fusil, fusile, adj., molten, fluid. — L. fusllis, fr.
fusus, pp. of fundere, 'to pour'. See found, 'to
cast', and -He and cp. fuse, 'to melt'.

## fusilier
fusilier, fusileer, п., a soldier belonging to one
of those British regiments that were formerly
armed with fusils. — Orig. 'a soldier armed
with a fusil'; F. fusilier, fr. fusil. See fusil,
'musket', and -ier, -eer.

## fusillade
fusillade, п., rapid and continuous fire from many
firearms. — F., fr. fusilier, 'to shoot', fr. fusil.
See fusil, 'musket', and -ade.
Derivative: fusillade, tr. v.

## fusion
fusion, n. — L. filsio, gen. -onis, 'a pouring out',
fr. fusus, pp. of fundere, 'to pour'. See found,
'to cast', and cp. fuse, 'to melt'. Cp. also foison,
which is a doublet of fusion.
Derivatives: fusion-al, adj., fusion-ism, п.,
fusion-ist, n.

## fum
fum, п., bustle. — Prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives: fuss, intr. and tr. v., fuss-y, adj.,
fuss-i-ly, adv., fuss-i-ness, a.

## fust
fust, п., ι) the shaft of a column (archit.); 2) a
strong moldy smell. — OF. fust (F.fut), "shaft,
cask', fr. L. fastis, 'stick, staff, cudgel, club',
whence also It. fusto, 'stem, stalk, trunk',
OProvenc. fust, 'staff, cask'. L. fastis
corresponds to Gaul. *bustis, 'trunk of a tree'
(whence OProvenc\ bust, of s.m.). For Teut.
cognates of L. fustis see bush and cp. words
there referred to. E. beat is not cognate. Cp.
fustian, fustigate.
Derivatives: fust-y, adj., moldy, fust-i-ness, n.

## fustanella
fustanella, п., a short skirt of stiffened linen. — F.
fustanelle, fr. It. fustanella, dimin. of fustagno,
fr. ModGk. φουστάνι, fr. ML. fustaneum. See
next word and -ella.

## fustian
fustian, п., thick cloth of cotton. — Orig. 'a coarse
cioth of cotton', fr. ME. fustyane, fr. OF. fus-
taigne, Justaine (F. futaine), fr. ML. fiistaneum,
translation of Septuagint Greek λίνα ξύλινα,
'cotton of wood', i.e. 'tissue of cotton coming
from a tree'. Fustaneum is prop, an adjective

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:327 COLUMN:3 -->
formed from L. fustis, 'stick, staff; see fust.
For sense development cp. G. Baumwolle,
'cotton', lit. 'wool of a tree', and the explanation of
ML. xylinum (= Gk. ξύλινον) as lana de lignd,
'wool coming from wood'. Arabic fushtan is a
Romance loan word. The usual derivation of
fustian fr. Fostat, name of a suburb of Cairo, is
untenable. Cp. fustanella.
Derivative: fustian, adj.

## fustic
fustic, п., the wood of a Mexican tree (Chloro-
phora tinctoria) and the yellow dye it yields. —
Sp. fustoc, fr. Arab, fiistuq, fr. Pers. pistah. See
pistachio.

## fustigate
fustigate, tr. v., to cudgel. — L. fustigatus, pp.
of fistigdre, 'to cudgel', which is formed on
analogy of castigare, 'to chastise', fr. fustis,
'staff, cudgel', and agere, 'to set in motion,
drive, lead; to do, act'. See fust and agent and
cp. castlgnte and the compound words there
referred to.
Derivatives: fustigat-ion, п., fustigat-or, п.,
fustigat-ory, adj.

## Fusus
Fusus, п., a genus of marine snails (zool.) — L.
fusus, 'a spindle' (see fuse, 'tube'); so called in
allusion to the spindle-shaped shell.

## futchel
futchel, futchell, п., a timber supporting the shafts
of a carriage. — Of unknown origin.

## futharc
futharc, futhorc, п., the runic alphabet. — So
called from the first six letters /, u, ρ (= th), a
(or о), г, с

## futile
futile,adj., 1) vain; 2) trifling. — F., fr. L.futilis,
'that which easily pours out; brittle; worthless',
rel. to fulis, 'pitcher*, fr. base *ghu-, 'to pour'.
See found, 'to cast', and -ile.
Derivatives: futile-ly, adv., futile-ness, n.

## futility
futility, n. — F. futilite, fr. L. futilitatem, ace. of
futilitas, 'worthlessness', fr. futilis. See futile
and -ity.

## futtock
futtock, п., one of the crooked timbers of a ship.
— Prob. corrupted fr. foot hook.

## future
future, adj. — OF. (= F.) futur, fem. future, fr.
L. futurus, 'about to be', used as fut. part, of
esse, 'to be*. See be and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: future, п., future-less, adj.,
futurity, a.

## futurism
futurism, n„ a modern movement in art, literature
and music, emphasizing originality. — It.
futurism), lit. 'the movement considering the future';
coined by its founder, the Italian poet and
writer Filippo Tommaso Marinetti (1876-1944)
in 1909 fr. L. futurus, 'future', and suff. -ismo
(fr. L. -ismus). See future and -ism.

## futurist
futurist, п., an adherent of futurism; adj.,
pertaining to futurism or futurists. — See prec.
word and -ist.

## futwa
futwa, also fetwa, п., a judicial sentence
pronounced by a mufti. — Arab, fatwd, fr. fata,
'he decided, declared'. Cp. mufti.

## fuzz
fuzz, п., light particles or fibers. — Prob. back
formation fr. fuzzy.

## fuzzy
fuzzy, adj., covered with fuzz; fluffy. — LG.
fussig, 'weak, loose, spongy'; re], to Du. voos,
'spongy'.
Derivatives: fuzzi-ly, adv.,fuzzi-ness, n.

## -fy
-fy, suff. meaning 'to make into'. — F. -fier, fr.
L. -ficare, fr. -ficus, it. -ficere, unstressed form
of facere, 'to make, do'. See -Be, -flcation.

## fylfot
fylfot, п., the swastika. — Prob. for fill - foot and
orig. denoting the device that fills the foot of
a painted window.

## fytte
fytte, n. — A var. of fit, 'division of a song'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:328 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:328 COLUMN:1 -->

## gab
gab, intr. v., to chatter. — Of imitative origin.
Cp. gabble.
Derivative: gab, п., idle talk.

## gabardine
gabardine, n. — See gaberdine.

## gabble
gabble, intr, v,, to chatter, talk rapidly; tr. v.,
to utter rapidly. — Freq. of gab. Cp. gobble, 'to
make the noise of a turkey'.
Derivatives: gabble, п., gabbl-er, n.

## gabbro
gabbro, п., a basic igneous rock (geol.) — It.
(Tuscan), fr. L. glaber, 'bare, smooth, bald'.
See glabrous.

## gabelle
gabelle, п., ι) a tax levied in certain countries;
2) specif, a tax on salt levied in France before
the Revolution of 1789. — F., 'tax on salt', fr.
It. gabella, fr. Arab, qabala", 'tax', lit. 'receipt',
fr. qabala, 'he received, accepted', which is rel.
to Heb. qibbel, 'he received, accepted'. See
cabal.

## gaberdine
gaberdine, gabardine, п., a long, loose gown;
specif, a gown worn esp. by Jews in the Middle
Ages. — Sp. gabardina, lit. 'pilgrims frock', fr.
MHG. wallevart (G. Wallfahrt), 'pilgrimage',
which is compounded of MHG. wallen (fr.
OHG. wallon), 'to roam, wander', and OHG.,
MHG. vart, 'journey', fr. OHG. faran, 'to go'.
The first element is rel. to OE. weallian, 'to
wander', OHG. wadal, wadol, MLG. wadel, OE.
wadol, 'full moon', and prob. also to OHG.
wadal, MHG. wadel, wedel, G. Wedel, 'tail,
duster, fan'. For the second element see fare, v.

## gubion
gubion, п., a basket of wickerwork. — F., fr. It.
gabbione, augment, of gabbia, fr. L. cavea, 'an
excavated place, cavity, cage'. See cage.
Derivatives: gabion, tr. v., gabion-ed, adj.

## gubionade
gubionade, п., embankment made with gabions
(fori.) — F. gabionnade, fr. gabionner, 'to cover
with gabions', fr. gabion. See prec. word
and -ade.

## gabionage
gabionage, п., gabions (taken in a collective
sense). — F. gabionnage, fr. gabionner. See prec.
word and -age.

## gable
gable, п., the triangular upper part of a wall at
the end of a ridged roof. — ME., fr. OF. gable,
fr. ON. gaft, which is rel. to MDu. ghevel, Du.
gevel, OHG. gibil, MHG. gibel, G. Giebel,
Goth, gibla, 'gable', OHG. gibilla, OS. gibillia,
'skull', OE. gafol, OS. gafala, Du. gaffel, OHG.
gabala, MHG. gabele, gabel, 'pitchfork', G.
Gabel, 'fork', for I.-E. *ghebh'l, whence also
Olr. gabul, 'forked twig, fork', W. gafl, 'fork',
Toch. A Spill-, 'head', Gk. κεφαλή, 'head'. See
cephalic and cp. gafHe.
Derivatives: gabl-ed, adj., gable! (q.v.)

## gablet
gablet, п., a small gable-shaped ornament. —
Formed fr. gable with dimin. sufT. -er.

## Gabriel
Gabriel, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, name of an
angel. — Heb. GabhrVel, lit. 'man of God', fr.
gebher, 'man', and El, 'God'. Heb. gebher
derives from the base of the verb gabhdr, 'was
strong', whence also gibbor, 'strong, mighty;
hero', g'bhfr, 'lord', g'bhird", g'bhereth, 'lady,
queen', glbhHrah, 'strength, might'. Cp. the
related words: Aram.-Syr.g'bhar,'was mighty',
g'bhar, gabhra, 'man', Syr. gabbdr, 'hero',
Arab, jabr, 'a strong, young man', jabbdr,
'tyrant', Akkad. gapru, 'strong', Ethiop. gabdra,
'he acted'. For the first element cp. gibbar, for
the second see El.

## gaby
gaby, п., a foolish person. — Prob. related to
gape and assimilated in form to baby.

## gad
gad, interj. — Used as a var. of God.

## Gad
Gad, п., in the Bible: 1) son of Jacob and Zilpah;
2) the tribe descended from him. — Heb. Gadh,
fr. gadh, 'fortune', which is rel. to Aram.-Syr.
gadda, Arab, jadd, of s.m. See the explanation
of the name in Gen. 30:11.

## gad
gad, intr. v., to rove about. — Perh. back
formation fr. obsol. gadling, 'companion', fr. ME.
gadeling, fr. OE. gxdeling. See gather.

## gad
gad, п., a bar, rod. — ME. gad, gadd, 'a goad',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:328 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. ON. gaddr, 'spike, sting, nail'. See yard,
'unit of length', and cp. gadfly.

## gaddi
gaddi, guddy, guddee, п., a cushion serving as a
throne, a throne (India). — Hind, gaddi.

## gadfly
gadfly, n. — Lit. 'a goading fly', compounded of
gad, 'bar', and fiy, n.

## gadget
gadget, п., any small ingenious device. — Of
uncertain origin.

## Gadidae
Gadidae, n. pi., a family of fishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. gadus, 'cod'.
See Gadus.

## gudoid
gudoid, adj., pertaining to the family Gadidae. —
A hybrid coined fr. ModL. gadus, 'cod', and
Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
Gadns and -oid and cp. prec. word.

## gadolinia
gadolinia, п., gadolinium oxide (chem.) — ModL.,
named by the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq
de Boisbaudran (1838-1912); so called by him
because it was discovered in the mineral gado-
linite. For the ending of gadolinia see -ia.

## gadolinite
gadolinite, п., a silicate of iron, yttrium, cerium,
erbium, beryllium, etc. (mineral.) — Named
after its discoverer, the Finnish mineralogist
Johan Gadolin (1760-1852). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## gadolinium
gadolinium, п., a rare metallic element (chem.)
— ModL. See gadolinia. For the ending of
gadolinium see suff. -ium.
Derivative: gadolin-ic, adj.

## gadroon
gadroon, also spelled godroon, п., a kind of fluting;
a notched molding. — F. godron, 'gadroon',
orig. written goderon, formed with dimin. suff.
-eron, fr. godet, 'bowl, cup, mug; fold, crease',
which derives fr. MDu. corfife.'cylindriform piece
of wood'. For change of meaning cp. G. Hum-
pen, 'piece of wood', later used in the sense of
'goblet, hanap'.

## Gadus
Gadus, п., the genus of codfishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., 'cod', fr. Gk. γάδος, 'a kind of fish',
which is of uncertain origin.

## Gaea
Gaea, Gaia, п., the earth as a goddess (Greek
myihol.) — Gk. Γαία, personification of γαία,
'earth', a collateral form of γη, Dor. γα, Cypr.
ζα, 'earth'; of uncertain origin. Cp. geo-, Epi-
gaea, epigeous.

## Gaekwar
Gaekwar, Gaikwar, п., title of the Marathi rulers
of Baroda, India. — Marathi Gaekvad, lit.
'cowherd', fr. OI. gauh, gen. goh, 'ox'. See cow and
cp. gnur, Gautama, the first element in gopura
and the second element in nilgai.

## Gael
Gael, п., a Scottish or Irish Celt. — Gael. Gaid-
heal, corresponding to Ir. Gaedheal. Cp. L.
Gallus, 'a Gaul' (see Gallic). Cp. also Goidelic.
Derivatives: Gael-ic, adj. and n.

## gaff
gaff, n:, a Ashing hook. — F. gaffe, fr. OProvenc.
gaf, which is prob. of Gothic origin.
Derivative: gaff, tr. v., to strike with a gaff.

## gaff
gaff, п., place of amusement for the lowest classes
(English Slang). — Prob. fr. prec. word and
orig. denoting a place where fish are gaffed.

## gaffer
gaffer, п., an old man, esp. an old rustic. —
Corrupted fr. grandfather. Cp. gammer.

## gaffle
gaffle, п., a lever for bending a crossbow. — Du.
gaffel, 'fork', rel. to OE. gafol, 'pitchfork'. See
gable.

## gag
gag, tr. and intr. v. — ME. gaggen, 'to choke,
strangle', imitative of the sound of choking.
Derivatives: gag, п., gagg-er, п., gagg-ery, n.

## gage
gage, п., pledge, security.— ME., fr. OF. guage,
gage (F. gage), fr. Frankish *wadi, 'pledge',
which is rel. to Goth, wadi, OE. wedd, 'pledge'.
It. gaggio and Sp. and Port, gage are French
loan words. See wage and cp. wed. Cp. also the
second element in mortgage.

## gage
gage, tr. v., to offer as pledge. — F. gager, fr.
gcge. See gage, 'pledge', and cp. engage.
<>ige, п., a variety of plum. — See greengage.

## gage
gage, n. — See gauge.

## gagelte
gagelte, п., a hydrous silicate of magnesium,
manganese and zinc (mineral.) — Named after

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:328 COLUMN:3 -->
R. B. Gage of Trenton, New Jersey. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## gaggle
gaggle, intr. v., to cackle. — Of imitative origin.
Cp. Du. gagelen, gaggelen, 'to cackle, chatter',
G. gackern, 'to gaggle'; cp. also ON. gaggl,
'flock of geese', and E. giggle.
Derivative: gaggle, п., a flock of geese.

## guhnite
guhnite, п., a pure zinc aluminate, ZnAl204
(mineral.) — Named after the Swedish chemist and
mineralogist Johan Gottlieb Gahn (1745-1818).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Gaia
Gaia, n. — See Gaen.

## gaiety
gaiety, n. — F. gaiete, fr. gai, 'gay'. See gay
and -ty.

## Gaillardia
Gaillardia, п., a genus of plants of the family
Carduaceae (bot.) — ModL., named after the
French botanist Gaillard de Charontonneau
in 1788. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## gaily
gaily, also spelt gayly, adv. — Formed fr. gay
with adv. suff. -ly,

## gain
gain, tr. v., to earn; to win; intr. v., to profit. —
F. gagner, fr. OF. gaaignier, 'to win', fr.
Frankish *waidanjan, 'to provide oneself with food',
which is rel. to OHG. weida, 'pasture, grazing,
food; pasture land', weidanon, 'to search for
food, to hunt', OE. wap, 'hunting', ON. veidr,
'hunting; catch of fish', fr. I.-E. base *wei-,
'to strive after', whence also L. yenari, 'to hunt'.
See venery, 'hunting'.
Derivatives: gain-er, п., gain-ing, n.

## guin
guin, п., profit. — F., fr. OF. gaain, fr. gaaignier.
See gain, v.
Derivatives: gain-ful, gain-less, adjs.

## guinly
guinly, adj., shapely; comely. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ly fr. obsol. E.gain, 'graceful, suitable,
kindly', fr. ME. gayn, geyn, 'direct, ready,
convenient', fr. ON. gegn, of s.m. See again.

## gainsay
gainsay, tr. v., to contradict. — ME. geinseien,
lit. 'to say against', fr. ON. gegn, 'against'
(which is rel. to OE. gegn-, gean-, 'against'), and
ME. seggen, seien, 'to say'. See again and say, v.

## gainst
gainst, prep. — Aphetic for agninst.

## gait
gait, п., manner of walking. — ME. gate, 'a way'.
See gate, 'passage'.
Derivatives: gait, tr. v., gait-ed, adj.

## gaiter
gaiter, п., covering for the lower leg. — F. guelre,
prob. fr. Frankish "wrist, 'instep', which is rel.
to MHG. riste, 'back of the hand; instep', and
to OE. wrist. See wrist.
Derivative: gaiter-ed, adj.

## gala
gala, п., festival; celebration. — F., fr. Sp. gala
(in vestido de gala, 'robe of state'), fr. Arab.
кШГа", 'robe of honor presented by oriental
rulers to their favorites'. Cp. gallant and words
there referred to.
Derivative: gala, adj., festive.

## galact-
galact-, form of galacto- before a vowel.

## galactagogue
galactagogue, adj., promoting the secretion of
milk. — Lit. 'leading milk'; compounded of
galact- and Gk. αγωγός, 'leading*, fr. άγαν, 'to
lead'. See -agogue.

## Galactia
Galactia, п., a genus of plants, the milk pea
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γάλα, gen. γάλακτος,
'milk'. See next word.

## galactic
galactic, adj., pertaining to the Milky Way
(astron.) — Gk. γαλακτικός, 'milky', fr. γάλα,
gen. γάλαχτος, 'milk', which is cogn. with L.
lac (for *glac-t), 'milk'. See lactenl, adj., and
-Ic and cp. galaxy and the second element ίο
Ornithogalum. Cp. also lactic, lettuce.

## galacto-
galacto-, before a vowel galact-, combining form
meaning 'milk*. — Fr. Gk. γάλα, gen. γάλακτος,
'milk'. See prec. word.

## galactometer
galactometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the purity of milk. — Compounded of galacto-
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm', and cp. lactometer.

## galactonic
galactonic, adj., pertaining to a crystalline acid
CH2OH(CHOH)4C02H (chem.) — Coined fr.
combining form galact- and suff. -onic. Cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:329 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GALACTOPHOROUS | 302 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:329 COLUMN:1 -->
talose.

## galactophorons
galactophorons, adj., conveying milk. —
Compounded of galacto- and Gk. -φόρος, 'bearing'.
See -phorous.

## galactopoietic
galactopoietic, adj., producing milk. —
Compounded of galacto- and Gk. ποιητικός,
'capable of making, productive'. See -poietic.

## galactorrhea
galactorrhea, galactorrhoea, п., an excessive flow
of milk. — Compounded of galacto- and Gk.
-ρροίά, 'flow, flowing'. See -rrhea.

## galactose
galactose, п., a crystalline sugar (chem.) —
Formed fr. galact- with subst. suff. -ose. Cp.
tagatose.

## Galago
Galago, п., a genus of African lemurs (zool.) —
ModL., from native African name.

## galangale
galangale, n. — See galingale.

## Galanthus
Galanthus, п., a genus of plants, the snowdrop
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'milk flower', fr. Gk. γάλα,
'milk", and άνθος, 'flower'. See galactic and
anther.

## galantine
galantine, п., veal, chicken or other meat, boned
and served cold, — F., fr. ML. galatlna, assimil.
fr. gelatlna, fr. L. geldtus, 'frozen', pp. of gelare,
'to cause to freeze', fr. gelu, 'frost'. See jelly.

## galanty show
galanty show, pantomime produced by throwing
shadows of puppets on a wall or screen. — it.
galante, 'gallant'. See gallant.

## Galatea
Galatea, п., a sea nymph in Greek mythology. —
L., fr. Gk. Γαλάτεια.

## galatea
galatea, п., a cotton fabric of superior quality
used for children's sailor suits. — So called
from Galatea, name of a British warship. For
the origin of this name see prec. word.

## Galatian
Galatian, adj., pertaining to Galatia, in Asia
Minor. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Galatia,
fr. Gk. Γαλατία, 'Galatia'.

## Galax
Galax, п., a genus of plants of the family Dia-
pensiaceae(bot.) — ModL.,fr. Gk. γίίλα, 'milk'.
See galactic and cp. Galactia, galaxy.

## galaxy
galaxy, п., the Milky Way. — F. galaxie, fr. L.
galaxias, fr. Gk. γαλαξίας (scil. κύκλος), 'the
Milky Way' (lit. 'the Milky Circle'), fr. γάλα,
gen. γάλακτος, 'milk'. See galactic.

## galbanum
galbanum, п., a bad-smelling gum resin. — L.,
fr. Gk. χαλβάνη, fr. Aram, halban, fr. Heb.
Iielb'nah, 'galbanum', fr. helebh, 'fat', which is
rel. to Aram.-Syr. helba, Arab, hilb, 'fat'. Cp.
jaundice.

## gale
gale, п., an aromatic shrub. — ME. gawel, fr.
OE. gagel, 'sweet gale', rel. to Du., MHG., G.
gagel, 'sweet gale'; of uncertain origin.

## gale
gale, п., a strong wind. — Of uncertain origin.
It is perh. rel. to Dan. gal, 'furious', and to Nprw.
galen, of s.m. (ihis latter is often used of the
weather), and also to OE. galan, 'to sing', gietlan,
'to scream, cry'. See yell and cp. the last element
in nightingale.

## gale
gale, п., a periodical payment of rent (rare). —
Contraction of gavel, 'tribute'.

## galea
galea, п., a helmet-shaped structure (zool. and
bot.) — L., 'helmet', borrowed fr. Gk. γαλέη,
Att. γαλή, 'weasel, polecat, marten'. The phases
of sense development seem to have been:
l) weasel; 2) weasel's skin or hide; 3) leather;
4) helmet made of leather. Gk. γαλέη is prob.
cogn. with OI. girili, girika, 'mouse', L. glis,
'dormouse'. Cp. galley. Cp. also Glires, loir.

## galeated
galeated, adj., covered with a helmet-shaped
structure. — L. galeatus, pp. of galeare, 'to
cover with a helmet', fr. galea. See galea and
adj. suff. -ate and -ed.

## galeeny
galeeny, п., a guinea fowl (dial. E.) — Sp.gallina
(Morisca), '(Moorish) hen', fr. L. gallina, 'hen'.
See gallinaceous.

## galeiform
galeiform, adj., helmet-shaped. — Compounded
of L. galea, 'helmet', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See galea and form, n.

## Galen
Galen, п., a physician (facet.) — See Galenic.

## galena
galena, п., native lead sulfide. — L., first
mentioned by Pliny. Galena is a foreign, prob.
Etruscan, word, and has nothing in common
with Gk. γαλήνη, 'calmness of ihe sea'. See
A.E. Ernoui in Bulletin de la societe de lin-
guistique 30, 92.

## galenic
galenic, galenical, adj., pertaining to galena. —
See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative; galenic-al, adj.

## Galenic
Galenic, Galenical, adj., pertaining to Galen (L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:329 COLUMN:2 -->
Galenus, fr. Gk. Γαληνός), the celebrated Greek
physician (lived about 130-200).

## Galeopsis
Galeopsis, п., a genus of plants, ihe hemp neitle
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γαλίοψις, which is
compounded of γάλιον, 'bedstraw', and δψις,
'appearance'. See Galium and -opsis.

## gali
gali, galee, п., abuse (India). — Hind, gali, fr.
Ol. gali(i, 'execration', which is of uncertain
origin.

## Galilean
Galilean, п., adj., of Galilee. — Formed with
suff. -an fr. L. Galilaeus, 'Galilean', fr. Galilaea,
'Galilee'. See next word.

## Galilee
Galilee, name of the northern province of
western Palestine. — L. Galilaea, fr. Gk. Γαλιλαία,
fr. Heb. Haggalil, lit. 'ihe district', shortened fr.
G'HI haggoyi'm, 'the District of nations' (Is.
8:23). Haggalil was the name of a district in the
hill country of Naphtali (see Josh. 20:7 and
21:32), and it was only at a relatively later period
that it began to denote the territory of Palestine
north of ihe Emek Jezreel (Esdraelon). For the
etymology of Heb. galil, 'district', see gelilah.

## galimatias
galimatias, n, jargon. — F., 'nonsense, gibberish',
prob. a deformation of Late L. ballUnathia,
'indecent songs'. For the etymology of this latter
word see Du Cange, Glossarium mediae et in-
fimae latinitatis, s.v. balare.

## galingale
galingale, п., an aromatic root of the ginger
family. — OF. galingal, formed—through the
medium of MGk. γαλάγγα and ML. galanga—
fr. Arab, khalanjan, fr. Pers., ult. fr. Chin. Ko-
leung-keung, lit. 'mild ginger from the region
of Kao'.

## Galinsoga
Galinsoga, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Spanish botanist Mariano
Martinez de Galinsoga (died in 1797).

## galiot
galiot, galliot, п., a small swift galley. — F.
galiote, fr. OF. galie. See galley.

## galipot
galipot, gallipot, п., resinous substance of certain
pines. — F. galipot, of unknown origin.

## Galium
Galium, п., a genus of plants, the bedstraw (hot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. γάλιον,'bedstraw', coined by
Dioscorides fr. γάλα, 'milk' (see galactic); so
called by him because used in place of rennet.
For the ending see suff. -inm.

## gall
gall, п., bile. — ME. galle, gawle, fr. OE. gealla,
galla, rel. to ON. gall, OS., OHG. galla, MHG.,
G. galle, and cogn. with Gk. χολή, L. fel, fr. I.-E.
base "ghel-, 'to shine; yellow, yellowish green,
green'. See choler and cp. words there referred to.

## gall
gall, п., gallnut. — F. galle, fr. L. galla, 'gallnut',
prop, 'a globulous excrescence', fr. I.-E. base
*gel-, 'to form into a ball'. See glebe, globe,
and cp. ellagic.

## gall
gall, п., sore (esp. on horse). — ME. galle, fr.
OE. gealla, 'sore place', fr. L. galla, 'gallnut',
whence also Du. gal, MLG., MHG., G. galle,
'a sore place'. See gall, 'gallnut'.
Derivatives :gall,tc.v., to make sore, to abrade,
gall-ing, adj., gall-ing-ly, adv., gall-ing-ness, n.

## gallant
gallant, adj., brave; noble. — F. galant, fr. Sp.
galante, fr. galan, shortened form of galano,
'gallant', fr. gala. See gala and cp. galanty show,
gallimaufry, gallivant, galloon, regale, 'feast*.
Derivatives: gallant, n. and tr. and intr. v.,
gqllant-ly, adv.

## gallantry
gallantry, n. — F. galanterie, fr. galant. See
gallant and -ry.

## galleass
galleass, п., a large three-masted galley. — F.
galeasse (also galeace), fr. It. galeazza, augment,
of galea, 'galley'. See galley.

## galleon
galleon, п., a large ship formerly used esp. by
the Spaniards. — Sp. galeon, formed fr. ML.
galea, 'galley', with augment, suff. -on. See
galley and -oon.

## gallery
gallery, n, — F. galerie, fr. It. galleria, which is
of uncertain origin.
Derivative: galleri-ed, adj.

## galley
galley, n. — ME. gale i,' gale ie, fr. OF. galie, fr.
ML. galea, fr. Byzant. Gk. γαλέα, which derives
fr. Late Gk. γαλίά, name of a seafish, and ult.
fr. Gk. γαλέη, 'weasel'. See galea and cp. galiot,
galleass, galleon, gallipot.

## galliambic
galliambic, п., name of a meter in Greek and
Roman prosody. — Formed with suff. -ic fr.
L. galliambus, 'a song of the priests of Cybele',
fr. Gk. γαλλίαμβος, which is compounded of
Γάλλος, 'priest of Cybele' (a name related to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:329 COLUMN:3 -->
Γάλλος, a river of Phrygia, whose water caused
madness), and ίαμβος, 'iambus'. See iambus.
Derivative: galliambic, adj.

## galliard
galliard, adj., gay. — OF. (= ¥.)gaillard, 'strong,
vigorous, merry', of uncertain origin.

## galliard
galliard, п., a lively dance of the 16th cent. —
Fr. prec. word,

## gallic
gallic, adj., pertaining to, or obtained from, galls.
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. galla, 'gallnut'.
See gall, 'gallnut'.

## gallic
gallic, adj., pertaining to, or containing, gallium.
— See gallium and -ic.

## Gallic
Gallic, adj., pertaining to Gaul or the Gauls. —
L. Gallicus, fr. Galtus, 'a Gaul'. Cp. Gael, galosh.

## Galilean
Galilean, adj., pertaining to the Roman Catholic
Church in France. — L. Gallicanus, 'pertaining
to Gaul', fr. Gallicus. See Gallic and -an.
Derivatives: Gallican-ism, п., Gallican-ist, n.

## Gallice
Gallice, adv., in French. — L., 'in Gallic', adv.
of Gallicus. See Gallic.

## Gallicism
Gallicism, also spelled gallicism, п., a French
idiom (used in another language). — See Gallic
and -ism.

## Gallicize
Gallicize, also spelled gallicize, tr. and intr. v., to
make French, to Frenchify. — See Gallic and
-ize.

## Galliformes
Galliformes, n. pi., an order of birds including
the common domestic fowl (ornithol.) — ModL.,
compounded of gal/us, 'cock', and forma,
'form, shape'. See gallinaceous and form, n.

## galligaskins
galligaskins, n. pi., loose breeches. — OF. gar-
guesque, metathesis of greguesque, fr. It. gre-
chesca, prop. fern, of grechesco, 'Grecian', fr.
Greco, 'Greek'; influenced in form by galley and
Gascony. See Greek and -esque.

## gallimaufry
gallimaufry, п., a medley. — F. galimafrie, 'hash,
ragout', a compound, whose first element is
related to OF. galer, 'to make merry, to live
well', which is of uncertain origin; the second
element is identical with Picard mafrer, 'to eat
much', which is borrowed fr. MDu. maffelen,
of s.m.

## gallinacean
gallinacean, adj., gallinaceous. — See next word
and -acean.

## gallinaceous
gallinaceous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
the domestic fowls. — L. gallinaceus, 'of
domestic fowls', fr. gallina, 'hen', fr. gallus,
'cock', which is prob. a loan word from a
language of Asia Minor. Cp. galeeny, gallinazo, gal-
linule, Gallus. For the ending see suff. -aceous.

## gallinazo
gallinazo, п., a vulture. — Sp. gallinaza,
'vulture', formed with augment, suff. -aza fr.
gallina, 'hen', fr. L. gallina. See prec. word.

## gallinule
gallinule, п., water hen, moor hen. — L. gallinula,
'chicken', dimin. of gallina. See gallinaceous
and -ule.

## Gallio
Gallio, п., a careless official; an easy-going
person. — From Gallio, name of a Roman
proconsul (mentioned in Acts, XVIII, 17).

## galliot
galliot, n. — A var. spelling of galiot.

## gallipot
gallipot, п., a pot for holding medicines. —
Compounded of galley and pot. The orig. meaning
was 'pot shipped in a galley'.

## gallipot
gallipot, n. — A var. spelling of galipot.

## gallium
gallium, п., a rare metallic element (chem.) —
ModL., coined by the French chemist Paul-
Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran (1838-1912), the
discoverer of this element, from L. Gallia, the
former name of France (cp. Gallic, Gaul). The
name gallium may also be an allusion to his
name Lecoq (lit. 'the cock' = L. gallus). For the
ending of gallium see -ium.

## gallivant
gallivant, intr. v., to gad about. — A playful
derivative of gallant.
galinut. — See gall, 'gallnut'.

## Gallo-
Gallo-, combining form meaning, 1) Gallic;
2) French. — Fr. L. Gallus, 'a Gaul'. Cp. Gallic.

## galloglass
galloglass, gallowglass, п., a heavily armed
retainer of an Irish chief. — Ir. galloglach, lit. 'a
foreign soldier', fr. gall, 'foreigner', and oglach,
'servant, soldier', fr. Olr. Sclach, 'youth', which
derives fr. Olr. бас, 'young'. See young.

## gallon
gallon, п., a measure equal to 4 quarts. — ME.
galoun, fr. AF. galon, corresponding to OF.
jalon, 'a liquid measure', and rel. to OF. jale, 'a
bowl', which is of uncertain origin. F. gallon,
'gallon', is an English loan word.

## galloon
galloon, п., a braid used for trimming. — F.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:330 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 303 | GANGLION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:330 COLUMN:1 -->
galon, fr. galonner, 'to lace, braid the hair',
which is prob. rel. to F. gala, 'festivity'. See gala
and cp. gallant.

## gallop
gallop, intr. and tr. v. — F. galoper, fr. Frankish
*wala hlaupan, 'to run well'. The first element is
rel. to OHG. wala, vela, wola, OE. wel, 'well';
see well, adv. The second element is rel. to
OHG. hlauffan, loufan, 'to run'; see leap. Cp.
galop, wallop.
Derivatives: gallop, п., gallop-er, п., gallop-ing-
ly, adv.

## gallopade
gallopade, n. — F., fr. galoper, 'to gallop'. See
prec. word and -ade.

## Gallophile
Gallophile, Gallophil, п., a friend of France or
the French. — Compounded of Gallo- and Gk.
φίλος, 'friend'. See -phile, -phfi.

## Gallophobe
Gallophobe, п., one who fears or hates France or
the French. — Compounded of Gallo- and Gk.
-φόβος, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobe.

## Gallophobia
Gallophobia, п., fear or hatred of France or the
French. — Compounded of Gallo- and -φοβίϊ,
'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## Galloway
Galloway, п., a small horse. — Orig. meaning
'horse bred in Galloway, Scotland'.

## gallows
gallows, n. — ME. galowes, galwes (pi.), fr. OE.
gealga, rel. to OS., OHG. galgo, ON. galgi,
OFris. galga, MHG. galge, 'gallows; cross', G.
Galgen, 'gallows', Goth, galga, 'cross', and to
ON. gelgja, 'pole, perch', and cogn. with Arm.
jalk, 'twig', Lith. zalga, Lett, zalga, 'pole, perch'.

## Callus
Callus, п., a genus of birds, the common domestic
fowl and the jungle fowl. — L. gallus, 'cock'.
See gallinaceous.

## galop
galop, п., a quick dance. — F. galop, fr. galoper.
See gallop.
Derivative: galop, intr. v.

## galore
galore, adv., in abundance. —Tr. go leor, 'to
sufficiency, enough'.

## galosh
galosh, п., an overshoe. — OF. (= F.) galoche,
fr. VL. gallicula, dimin. formed fr. L. solea
Gallica, 'Gaulish sandal'. Gallica is fern, of Gal-
licus, 'Gaulish' (see Gallic). VL. gallicula was
influenced in form by L. caligula, *a small
military boot'.

## galumph
galumph, intr. v., to prance about in a
self-satisfied manner. — Coined by Lewis Carrol (pen-
name for Charles Lutwidge Dodgson), as the
blend of gallop and triumph.

## galuth
galuth, п., the Diaspora (Jewish history). — Heb.
galuth, 'exile', fr. gala", 'he uncovered, removed;
he departed; he went into exile, was deported',
whence also Heb. golah, 'exile, exiles', gillayon,
'tablet'. Cp. Aram, g'la, 'he revealed,
uncovered; he departed, went into exile', Arab, jata,
'he made clear, revealed, disclosed; he ousted,
removed; he went away, departed, left', ajla,
'emigrated', Ethiop. taglegala, 'he was led into
exile', which are related to Heb. gala''. Cp. also
golah.

## galvanic
galvanic, adj., caused by, or producing, an electric
current. — See next word and -ic.
Derivative: galvanic-al-ly, adv.

## galvanism
galvanism, п., i)current electricity; 2) that branch
of physics which deals with electric currents;
3) treatment of disease by electricity. — F. gal-
vanisme, from the name of the Italian physicist
Luigi Gahani (1737-98), who discovered and
first described it. For the ending see surf.
-ism.

## galvanist
galvanist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.

## galvanize
galvanize, tr. v. — See galvanism and -rae.
Derivative: galvaniz-ation, n.

## galvano-
galvano-, combining form used for galvanic or
galvanism.

## Galwegian
Galwegian, adj., pertaining to Galloway; п., а
native of Galloway. — Formed fr. Galloway on
analogy of Norwegian (fr. Norway). For the
ending see suff. -ian.

## gam-
gam-, form of gamo- before a vowel.

## Gamaliel
Gamaliel, masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Γαμαλιήλ, fr.
Heb. GamlVil, lit. 'reward of God',
compounded of gamdl, 'he dealt out to; he rewarded', lit.
'he dealt fully with', and El, 'God'. From the
base of gSmal derive g'miil, 'recompense,
taghmul, 'benefit'. Cp. Aram, g'mdl, 'he dealt
out to, rewarded', Arab, jamah, 'he collected',
jamula, 'he was beautiful', kamula, 'he was
complete, perfect', Akkad. gitmalu, 'perfect', which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:330 COLUMN:2 -->
are rel. to Heb. gamut. For the second element
in the name Gamaliel see El.

## gainashes
gainashes, n. pi., a kind of legging (archaic). —
F. gamaches, fr. ModProvenc. gamacho, fr.
ΟΡΓονεης. galamacha, fr. Sp. guadamaci, fr.
Arab, ghadamast, lit. '(leather) from Ghadames
(a town in Tripolis)'.

## garnb
garnb, gambe, п., an animal's leg or shank; used
esp. in heraldry. — Dial. F. gambe,
corresponding to F. jambe, fr. ML. gamba, 'leg', fr. Late
L. camba, gamba, 'fetlock; hoof; leg', borrowed
fr. Gk. καμπή, 'a turn, bend, joint', which is
cogn. with L. campus, 'field'. See camp and cp.
gamba, gambol, gammon, 'ham', iamb.

## gamba
gamba, п., an organ stop (mus.) — Orig. an
abbreviation of viola da gamba (q.v.); fr. It. gamba,
'leg', fr. ML. gamba. See prec. word.

## gambade
gambade, п., gambado. — F. See next word.

## gambado
gambado, п., gambol, caper. — Sp. gambada, fr.
It. gambata, 'gambol'. See gambol.

## gambado
gambado, п., a long legging or gaiter. — It.
gamba, 'leg'. See gamb and cp. prec. word.

## gambe
gambe, n. — See gamb.

## gambeson
gambeson, п., a medieval military garment of
defense. — OF. gambaison, gambeson, fr. gam-
bais, wambais, fr. Frankish *wamba, 'stomach,
belly'. Cp. OHG., Goth, wamba and see womb.

## gambier
gambier, п., the extract of the shrub Uncaria
gambir. — Malay gambir.

## gambit
gambit, п., opening move in chess in which the
first player risks a pawn to gain an advantage
later. — F., fr. Sp. gambito, fr. Arab, janbt,
'lateral', fr. janb, 'side' (whence janaba, 'he put
aside'), which is rel. to Aram.-Syr. gabh, gabbd,
'side', Heb. ganabh, Aram.-Syr. g'ndbh, 'he
stole', lit. 'he put aside', Heb. gannabh, 'thief.
Cp. gonnof.

## gamble
gamble, intr. and tr. v. — Dial. ME. gammlen,
gamblen, fr. ME. gamenen, fr. OE. gamenian,
'to play', fr. gamen, 'sport, game, amusement'.
See game, n.
Derivatives: gamble, п., gambl-er, п., gamble-
some, adj., gambl-ing, n.

## gamboge
gamboge, п., a gum resin. — ModL. gambogium,
fr. Cambodia, a region (now a state) in
Indochina, fr. native Kambuja, which was named
after Kambu, the founder of the Khmer race.

## gambol
gambol, п., a skipping, a caper. — Earlier gam-
bold, gambalde, formed, with change of suff., fr.
F. gambade, fr. It. gambata, fr. gamba, 'leg',
fr. ML. gamba. See gamb.
Derivative: gambol, intr. v.

## gambroon
gambroon, п., a twilled cloth. — Fr. Gambroon,
Gombroon, now Bandar Abbas, name of a town
on the Persian Gulf. Cp. gombroon,

## game
game, п., sport, play. — ME. gamen, game, fr.
OE. gamen, 'sport, game, amusement', rel. to
OFris. game, OS., ΟΝ., OHG. gaman, Dan.
gamen, Swed. gamman, 'merriment'. Cp. gamble,
gammon, 'backgammon'.
Derivatives: game-some, adj., game-some-ly,
adv., game-some-ness, n.

## game
game, intr. and tr. v., to play. — ME. gamenen,
fr. OE. gamenian, 'to play, jest, joke', fr. gamen.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: gamester, n.

## game
game, adj., plucky, courageous. — Fr. gamecock.
Derivatives: game-ly, adv., game-ness, a.

## game
game, adj., lame, crippled. — Of uncertain origin,

## gamecock
gamecock, n. — Prop, 'cock (bred) for fighting'.

## Gamelion
Gamelion, п., name of the 7th month of the Attic
Greek calendar (corresponding to the second
half of January and first half of February). —
Gk. Γαμήλιων, lit. 'month of marriages', fr.
γαμήλιος, 'bridal, nuptial', fr. γαμεΐν, 'to
marry'. See gamo-.

## gamene
gamene, п., the common sort of Dutch madder. —
Inexact spelling of Du. gemean (18th century),
whence Du. gemeen, 'common', which is rel.
to OE. gemxne (whence ME. тепе, Е. mean),
Goth, gamains, OHG. gimeini (whence MHG.,
G. gemein); see Bense, Dictionary of the Low
Dutch Element in the English Vocabulary,
p. 117. The above words are formed fr. Teut.
pref. ge- (see y-), and I.-E. base *mei-, 'to
change'. See common, adj., and cp. words there
referred to.

## gamete
gamete, п., a germ cell (biol.) — ModL. gametes,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:330 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. Gk. γαμέτης, 'husband', or γαμετή, 'wife',
fr. γαμεΐν, 'to marry'. See gamo-. The name
gamete was introduced into science by the
Austrian biologist Gregor Johann Mendel
(1822-84).

## gamin
gamin, п., a street Arab. — F., of unknown origin.

## gamma
gamma, п., name of the 3rd letter of the Greek
alphabet. — ME., fr. L. gamma, fr. Gk. γάμμα,
for *γάμλα, fr. Heb.-Phoen. gimel, lit. 'camel';
see gimel and cp. gammadion, gamut. For the
form cp. Heb. gamal, Aram, gamld, 'camel'.

## gammacism
gammacism, п., difficulty in the pronunciation of
the guttural consonants. — ModL. gammacts-
mus, formed on analogy of Late L. lambdacismus,
etc., fr. Gk. γάμμα. See prec. word and -ism.

## gammadion
gammadion, п., a figure formed by four capital
gammas. — MGk. γαμμάδιον, dimin. of Gk.
γάμμα. See gamma.

## Gammarus
Gammarus, п., a genus of crustaceans. — ModL.,
fr. L. cammarus, gammarus, 'sea crab, lobster',
fr. Gk. κάμμαρος. See Cambarus and cp. Ho-
marus.

## gammer
gammer, п., an old woman. — Corrupted fr.
grandmother. Cp. gaffer.

## gammon
