gammon, п., backgammon. — ME.yemen.'game'.
See game, n.

## gammon
gammon, п., ham; the lower end of the side of
a bacon. — ONF. gambon (corresponding to
F. jambon), fr. ONF. gambe (corresponding to
F. jambe), 'leg'. See gamb.
Derivative: gammon, tr. v., to make bacon of.

## gammon tr. v.
gammon tr. v., to fasten (a bowsprit) to the stem
of a ship. — Of uncertain origin.

## gammon
gammon, п., nonsense, humbug. — ME. gamen,
'game', fr. OE. gamen. See game, 'sport, play'.
Derivative: gammon, tr. and intr. v., to hoax.

## gamo-
gamo-, combining form meaning 1) sexual union
(biol.); 2) union of parts (hot.) — Fr. Gk. γάμος,
'marriage', whence γαμεΐν, 'to marry, take to
wife'; fr. I.-E. base *gem-, 'to marry'. See bigamy
and cp. words there referred to.

## -ganious
-ganious, combining form meaning 'marrying',
as in monogamous, heterogamous. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. Gk. γάμος, 'marriage'. See
gamo-.

## gamp
gamp, п., a large umbrella. — From the umbrella
of Mrs. Sarah Gamp in Dickens's Martin
Chuzzlewit.

## gamut
gamut, п., range of musical sounds from gamma
(the lowest) to ut (the highest). — Coined by
Guido d'Arezzo fr. gamma, a name given by
him to the lowest note of the old (= medieval)
scale, and at, name of the highest tone of that
scale.

## gamy
gamy, also gamey, adj., having the flavor of
game. — Formed fr. game, п., with adj. suff. -y.

## -gamy
-gamy, combining form meaning 'marriage,
union', as in heterogamy, polygamy. — Gk.
-γαμίδ, fr. γάμος, 'marriage'. See gamo-.

## gunder
gunder, n. — ME. gandre, fr. OE. ganra, gandra,
rel. to Du. gander, MLG. ganre, Bavarian
gander, 'gander'. See goose and cp. gannet.

## ganef
ganef, n. — See gonnof.

## gang
gang, intr. v., to go, walk (dial.) — OE. gangan.
See next word.

## gang
gang, п., a group of people; a band. — ME. gang,
'going; passage', fr. OE. gang, 'going, passage,
channel', rel. to OS., OFris., Dan., Du., OHG.,
MHG., G. gang, ON. gangr, Swed. gang, Goth.
gagg, 'the act of going', verbal nouns to OE.
gangan, ON. ganga, Goth, gaggan, etc., 'to go'.
These words derive fr. I.-E. base *ghengh-,
'ghongh-, 'to step', whence also OI. jahgha,
'shank', Avestic zanga-, 'ankle', Lith. zengiu,
Ί stride, step'. The above words are not related
to E. go. Cp. gangue and the second element
in Doppelganger.
Derivative: gang-er, n.

## gange
gange, tr. v., to protect a fishing line by twisting
wire round it. — Of unknown origin.
Derivative: gang-ing, n.

## gangliated
gangliated, adj., having ganglia. — Formed with
the adj. suff. -ate and -ed, fr. γαγγλίον. See
ganglion.

## gangliform
gangliform, adj., having the form of a ganglion.
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. γαγγλίον (see
ganglion) and L. forma, 'form, shape' (see form, n.)

## ganglion
ganglion, п., swelling, excrescence; center of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:331 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GANGRENE | 304 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:331 COLUMN:1 -->
cavity; nerve center. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
γαγγλίον, 'encysted tumor on a tendon'.
According to Galen the proper sense of the word
is 'anything gathered into a ball' ('conglobatus').
The word γαγγλίον prob. stands for *γα-γλ-ιον
and is a loan word from Heb. galgdl, 'anything
round; a wheel', from the base of gdldl, 'he.
rolled', gilgil, of s.m.; see gelDah. For the
dissimilation of the first I in galgdl to л in Gk.
γαγγλίον ср. E.-F. gonfalon, gonfanon, 'flag'.
Perivatives: ganglion-ary, adj., ganglion-ate,
tr. v., ganglion-ic, adj.

## gangrene
gangrene, n„ mortification; decay. — L. gan-
graena, fr. Gk. γάγγραινα, lit. 'that which eats
away', formed through reduplication fr. γραν,
γραίειν, 'to gnaw, eat', whence also γράστις,
'green fodder'. See gastro-.
Derivatives; gangrene, tr. and intr. v.,
gangrenous, adj.

## gangster
gangster, п., member of a gang of roughs or
criminals. — Formed fr. gang with suff. -ster.

## gangue
gangue, п., the matrix in which valuable metals
or minerals occur. — F. gangue, fr. G. Gang,
'a going, walking, passage, vein (of ore)'. See
gang.

## gangway
gangway, n. — OE. gangweg, 'road', fr. gang,
'going, way, passage', and weg, 'way'. See gang
and way.

## ganister
ganister, п., a hard siliceous rock. — Dial. G.
Ganster, rel. to MHG. g(a)neist(e), fr. OHG.
gneisto, 'spark'. Cp. OPruss. knaistis, 'a
burning', and see gaeiss.

## ganja
ganja, gunja, п., the Indian hemp (Cannabissaliva,
formerly called Cannabis Indica). — Hirid. gSja,
fr. OI. ganja.

## gannet
gannet, п., the solan goose. — OE. ganot, 'sea
bird, gannet', rel. to Du. gent, OHG. gannajjo,
ganzo, 'gander'. See gander, goose.

## ganoid
ganoid, adj., i) smooth (said of fish scales); 2)
pertaining to the Ganoidei. — F. ganolde,
compounded of Gk. γάνος, 'brightness, brilliance,
splendor', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδας, 'form,
shape'. The first element stands for γά-νος and
is rel. to γάνυμαι (for γά-νυ-μαι), 'ί am glad,
I rejoice', γαίω (for *γά^ω), Ί rejoice'. See
gand, 'ornament', and cp. the first element in
Ganymede. For the second element see -oid.

## gantang
gantang, п., a weight in the Malay Archipelago,
— Malay gantang.

## gantlet
gantlet, also spelled gauntlet, п., a former
military punishment in which the offender was
compelled to run between twofilesof men who struck
him with switches, clubs, etc., as he passed. —
Formed under the influence of ganntiet, 'glove',
fr. earlier gantlope, fr. Swed. gatlopp, lit. 'a
running down a lane', a compound oigata, 'lane',
and lopp, 'a running, course', which is rel. to
Swed. lopa, 'to run'. The first element is rel. to
ON. gata, 'road'; see gate, 'passage'. For the
second element see leap.

## gantlet
gantlet, п., a glove. — See gauntlet.

## gantry
gantry, also gauntry, п., ι) a wooden frame for
barrels; 2) a spanning framework. — OF. gan-
tier, chantier (F. chantier), 'timber yard', fr. L.
cantherius, 'a gelding; trellis; rafter', fr. Gk.
κανΟήλιος, 'pack ass'. Cp. chantier, shanty.

## Ganymede
Ganymede, п., a beautiful boy, cupbearer to Zeus
(Greek mythol.) — L. Ganymedes, fr. Gk. Γανυ-
μήδης, lit. 'rejoicing in his virility', compounded
of γάνυμαι, Ί am glad, rejoice', and μήδεα
(pi.), 'counsels, plans, cunning'. For the first
element see ganoid. The second element is rel.
to μήδεσθαι, 'to devise, resolve, advise', μέδων,
μεδέων, 'guardian, ruler' (prop. pres. part of the
ancient verb μέδειν, 'to protect, rule over'), μέ-
δεσθαι, 'to be mindful of, give heed to, think
on', μέδιμνος, 'a measure', fr. I.-E. base "mid-,
'to measure, limit, consider', which is a -<i-en-
largement of base "me-, 'to measure'. See
meditate and cp. Andromeda and words there
referred to. Cp. also catamite.

## gaol
gaol, gaoler, gaoleress. See jail, jailer, jaileress.

## Gaon
Gaon, п., a title given to the heads of the two
Babylonian academies of Sura and Pumbedita
(Jewish hist.) — Heb. ga'on, prob. meant as an
abbreviation of g'on Ya'akobh, 'the pride of
Jacob' (Ps. 47:5). Heb. ga'on, 'exaltation, pride,
excellence', derives from the stem of ga'aK,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:331 COLUMN:2 -->
'rose', whence also ge, ge'e", 'pioud'.'gabwd'',
'pride, majesty', gl'uth, 'majesty'. Cp. Aram.
gla, ethga'e, Syr. ethga't, 'was proud'.
Derivative: Gaon-ic, adj.

## gap
gap, n. — ME. gap, fr. ON. gap, 'chasm, abyss',
rel. to ON. gapa, 'to gape'. See next word.
Derivative: gapp-y, adj.

## gape
gape, intr. v. — ME. gapen, fr. ON. gapa, whence
also Swed. gapa, Dan. gabe; rel. to Du. gapen,
MHG., G. gaffen, 'to gape, stare'. The ultimate
origin of these words is unknown. Cp. prec.
word. Cp. also gasp.
Derivatives: gape, п., gap-er, n.

## gar
gar, п., any of certain fishes having an elongate
body and spearlike jaws; called also garfish,
garpike. — ME., fr. OE. gar, 'spear', rel. to ON.
geirr, OS., OHG., MHG. ger, G. Ger, 'spear'.
See goad and cp. gore, 'a triangular piece of
land', and words there referred to. Cp. also the
first element in Gerald, Gerard, Gertrude, Ger-
vais, and the second element in Edgar, Oscar,
Roger.

## garage
garage, n.—F., orig. meaning 'a place for storing
something', fr. garer, 'to make safe, protect',
fr. Frankish *wardn, 'to guard', which is rel. to
OHG. biwaron, of s.m. See ware, 'alert', and -age.
Derivative: garage, tr. v.

## garb
garb, п., costume, style. — MF. garbe (F. galbe),
'graceful curb; graceful outline', fr. It. garbo,
'grace', which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG.
gar(a)wi, 'dress, equipment, preparation', and
see gear.
Derivative: garb, tr. v.

## garb
garb, п., representation of a sheaf of wheat (her.)
— ONF. garbe, corresponding to OF. jarbe,
F. gerbe, 'sheaf', fr. Frankish *garba, which is
rel. to OS.garVa,OHG.garba,MDu.garve,Da.
garf, MHG., G. garbe, 'sheaf, lit. 'that which is
gathered up or together', fr. I.-E. base *gher-
ebh-, 'ghrebh-, 'to seize'. OProvenc. and Sp.
garba, 'sheaf, are also Teut. loan words. See
grab, 'to seize', and cp. gerbe.

## garbage
garbage, n. — Perh. a blend of OF. garbe, 'sheaf
(see garb, 'sheaf'), and garble, 'to sift'.
Accordingly the original meaning of garbage would
have been 'things sifted'. For the ending see
suff. -age.
Derivative: garbage, intr. v.

## garble
garble, tr. v., to select improperly; to misquote.
— OF. garbeller, grabeller, 'to garble spices,
to sift', fr. Sp. garbillar, 'to garble, sift', fr.
Arab, gharbala, 'he sifted', fr. ghirbil, 'sieve',
ult. fr. Late L. cribellum, dimin. of L. cribrum,
'sieve', which is rel. to cernere, 'to distinguish,
separate, sift'. See cribriform.
Derivatives: garble, п., garbl-er, п., garbl-ing, n.

## garboard
garboard, п., in shipbuilding, the planks or plates
next to the keel. — Obsol. Du. gaarboord, fr.
garen, contraction of gaderen, 'to gather', and
boord, 'board'. See gather and board, 'plank'.

## garbure
garbure, п., a soup of bacon and cabbage. —
F., 'soup of bacon, cabbage, fat and ryebread',
rel. to Sp. gar bias, a kind of ragout; of unknown
origin.

## garce
garce, п., a measure of capacity in India. —
Telugu garisa (cp. Tamil karisai), fr. OI. gdriyas,
'very heavy', super), of guruh, 'heavy, weighty,
venerable', which is cogn. with Gk. βαρύς, L.
gravis, 'heavy'. See grave, 'weighty', and cp.
guru.

## garcon
garcon,n.— F., 'boy, waiter', orig. objective case
of OF. gars (this latter is still used as a
provincial word, pronounced go); prob. fr. Frankish
*wrakjo, which is rel. to the OHG. PN. Wrac-
chio and to OS. wrekkio, OHG. recko, 'a
banished person, exile', MHG., G. recke, 'renowned
warrior, hero', and to E. wretch (q.v.) Cp.
gossoon. Cp. also gasket.

## gardant
gardant, adj., having the head turned toward the
spectator (her.; said of animals). — F.,
'watching, looking at', pres. part, of garder, 'to keep,
watch, guard, protect, defend'. See guard, v.,
and -ant and cp. guardant.

## garden
garden, n. — ME. gardin, fr. ONF. gar din
(corresponding to OF. and F. jardin), derived fr.
ONF. gart (corresponding to OF. jari), fr.
Frankish *gardo, 'garden', which is rel. to OS.
gardo, OFris. garda, OHG. garto, MHG. garte,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:331 COLUMN:3 -->
G. Garten, 'garden', Goth, garda, 'fold', ON.
gardr, 'enclosure, court, yard', OE. geard,
'enclosure, piece of land, yard'. See yard,
'enclosure', and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
jardiniere and the second element in kindergarten.
Cp. also It. giardino, Sp. jardin, 'garden', which
are borrowed fr. F. jardin.
Derivatives: garden, intr. v., garden-ed, adj.,
garden-er, п., garden-ing, n.

## Gardenia
Gardenia, п., genus of trees and shrubs. —
ModL., named after the American botanist
Alexander Garden (1730-91). For the ending see
suff. -ia.

## garefowl
garefowl, п., the great auk. — ON. geirfugl, fr.
geirr, 'spear', and fugl, 'bird'. See gar and fowl.

## garfish
garfish, п., a pikelike fish. — ME. garfish, fr. OE.
gar, 'spear', and fisc, 'fish*. See gar and fish.

## Gargantuan
Gargantuan, adj., resembling, or reminding of,
Gargantua; very large. — From Gargantua,
name of the hero in Rabelais' satirical romance.
This name comes fr. Sp. garganta, 'gullet',
which is a derivative of the imitative base
*garg-; see next word. For the ending of
gargantuan see suff. -an.

## garget
garget, п., ι) inflammation of the throat in cattle
and swine; 2) inflammation of the udder in
cows, etc. — ME. gargate, 'throat', fr. OF. gar-
gate, from the imitative base *garg-, which
appears also in gargle, gargoyle (q.v.) Cp. prec.
word. Cp. also goglet.
Derivative: garget-y, adj.

## gargle
gargle, intr. and tr. v. — F. gargouiller, 'to gurgle,
dabble, paddle', fr. gargouille, 'throat', from the
imitative base 'garg-. See prec. word and cp.
next word and gurgle. Cp. also jargon, 'confused
speech'.
Derivative: gargle, п., a liquid used for gargling.

## gargoyle
gargoyle, n„ a grotesque waterspout representing
a human or animal figure. — OF. u
'throat, waterspout, gargoyle', compou*
the imitative base *garg- (see gurget) and g<
Western dial, form of gueule, 'mouth', fr.
guia. See gullet.

## garibaldi
garibaldi,, п., a kind of blouse worn by women. —
Named after the Italian patriot Giuseppe
Garibaldi (1807-1882); so called because it resembles
the red shirts worn by Garibaldi and his
followers.

## garish
garish, adj., showy; glaring.—Possibly rel. to ME.
gauren, 'to stare', which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: garish-ly, adv., garish-ness, n.

## garland
garland, п., a wreath of flowers, leaves, etc. —
ME., fr. OF. garlande, which is rel. to
OProvenc. and Catal. garlanda and to OProvenc.
guirlanda, It. ghirlanda (whence F. guirlande),
Sp. and Port, guirnalda; of uncertain, possibly
Teut., origin.
Derivative: garland, tr. v.

## garlic
garlic, n. — ME. garlek, fr. OE. garleac,
compounded of gar, 'spear', and leac, 'leak' (see
gar and leak); so called in allusion to the
spearlike leaves. -

## garment
garment, n. — ME. garnement, fr. OF. garniment,
garnement (F. garnement), fr. OF. garnir, 'to
fortify; to provide, furnish, adorn'. See garnish
and -ment.
Derivative: garment, tr. v.

## garner
garner, n. — ME. garner, gerner, fr. OF. gernier,
gerner, metathesized fr. OF. (= F.) grenier, fr.
L.· grandrium, 'granary', whence also Rum.
granar. It. granaio, ΟΡτονεης. granier, Catal.
graner, Sp. granero (whence Port, granel). See
granary, which is a doublet of garner. For tho
ending see suff. -er (in the sense 'receptacle for').
Derivative: garner, tr. v.

## garnet
garnet, п., ι) a hard silicate mineral of various
colors; 2) a deep red color. — ME. gernet,
metathesized fr. OF. (= F.) grenat, fr. ML.
рдтит granatum, 'pomegranate', lit. 'seeded
apple'; so called from its resemblance to the
seeds of a pomegranate; cp. G. Granat and
see grain. Cp. also grenade, pomegranate.

## garnierite
garnierite, п., a hydrous nickel magnesium
silicate (mineral.) — Named after the French
geologist Jules Garnier (died in 1904), the discoverer
of the New Caledonian nickel ores. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## garnish
garnish, tr. v., 1) to adorn; 2) to decorate (food).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:332 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 305 | GAUCHE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:332 COLUMN:1 -->
_ ME. garnisshen, fr. OF. (= F.) garniss-,
pres. part, stem of OF. garnir, 'to fortify; to
provide, furnish, adorn' (F. garnir, 'to provide,
furnish, adorn, trim, line, mount'), fr. Teut.
'warnjan, 'to provide, furnish', whence also
OProvenc. garnir, It. guarnire, Catal. gornir,
Sp. and Port, guarnecer. Cp. OHG. warndn, 'to
take head', and see warn and verbal suff. -Ish.
Derivatives: garnish, п., garnish-ee, п., adj. and
tr. v., garnisk-ing, п., garnish-ment, n.

## garniture
garniture, n. — F., fr. garnir. See prec. word
and -ure.

## garotte
garotte, n. — See garrote.

## gamut
gamut, n. — See garron.

## garret
garret, п., attic. — ME. garite, fr. OF. garite,
'watchtower, place of refuge' (whence F. guerite,
'sentry box, turret, watchtower'), fr. OProvenc.
garida, 'watchtower', fr. garir, 'to protect',
which is rel. to OF. garir, guerir, 'to protect,
defend' (whence F. guerir, 'to cure, heal'), and
to It. guarire, 'to cure, heal*. These words are
traceable to Teut. *warjan, 'to protect, defend'.
See weir and cp. next word.
Derivative: garrel-eer, n.

## garrison
garrison, n. — OF. gariton, warison, 'protection'
(whence F. guerison, 'cure, healing'), fr. garir,
'to protect'. See garret and cp. warison, which
is a doublet of garrison. F. garnison, 'garrison',
which has influenced the sense development of
E. garrison, derives fr. OF. garnison, 'provision;
munitions', fr. garnir, 'to provide, furnish'; see
garnish.
Derivative: garrison, tr. v.

## garron
garron, garran, п., a small breed of horse. —
Gael, gearran,

## garrot
garrot, п., the goldeneye (a kind of duck). — F„
of uncertain origin.

## garrote
garrote, garrotte, п., an instrument used for
execution in Spain and Portugal. — Sp.
garrote, 'club, bludgeon, stick, cudgel, garrote',
fr. F. garrot, 'racking stick', fr. OF. guaroc,
'shaft of the cross-bow' (with change of suff. -oc
to -ot, owing to the identical pronunciation of
these suffixes in later French). OF. guaroc is
back formation fr. garokier, 'to garrote,
strangle', fr. Frankish *wrokkan, 'to twist',
which is rel. to MDu. wroken, 'to twist'.
Derivatives: garrot(t)e, tr. v., garrot(t)-er, n.

## garrulity
garrulity, п., talkativeness. — F. garrulite, fr. L.
garrulitatem, ace. of garrulitas, 'chattering,
loquacity', fr. garrulus. See garrulous and -ity.

## garrulous
garrulous, adj., talkative. — L. garrulus,
'chattering, talkative', fr. garrire, 'to chatter, talk',
from the I.-E. imitative base *gar-, *ger-, 'to
cry'. See care and words there referred to, and
cp. esp. German and the first element in Gery-
goue. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivatives: garrulous-ly, adv. ,garrulous-ness,a.

## garry
garry, n. — A var. of gharri.

## garter
garter, n. — ONF. gartier (corresponding to
OF. jartier, whence F. jarretiere, of s.m.), fr.
ONF. garet, 'bend of the knee', from a Gaulish
base *garr-, meaning 'leg' (cp. W. garr, Bret.
gar, 'ham, shinbone'), whence also Sp., Port.
garra, 'claw'.
Derivative: garter, tr. v.

## garth
garth, п., enclosed space, garden (.archaic). —
ME., fr. ON. gardr, 'enclosure, court, yard'.
See yard, 'enclosure', and cp. garden.

## gas
gas, n. — First used in its usual sense by the
Belgian chemist Van Helmont (1577-1644). The
word is not his invention, although he says that
it suggested itself by Gk. χάος (see chaos). The
word gas was used for the first time by
Paracelsus (died in 1541), who named the air by it.
Derivatives: gas, tr. v., gaseity, gaseous, gasser,
gassy (qq.v.)

## Gascon
Gascon, п., ι) a native of Gascony (= F. Gas-
cogne); 2) (not capit.) a braggart. — F., fr. VL.
'Wasco, fr. L. Vascd, sing, of Vascdnis, name
of the ancient inhabitants of the Pyrenees. See
Basque and cp. next word.

## gasconade
gasconade, п., boastful talk; brag. — F. gascon-
nade, 'boastful talk, bravado', fr. Gascon,
'inhabitant of Gascony'; so called from the
proverbial boastfulness of the Gascons. — See
prec. word and -ade.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:332 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: gasconade, intr. v., gasconad-er, n.

## gaseity
gaseity, п., gaseousness. — Formed fr. gas with
suff. -ity.

## gaselier
gaselier, п., a chandelier for burning gas. —
Formed fr. gas on analogy of chande-lier. Cp.
electrolier.

## gaseous
gaseous, adj. — Formed fr. gas with suff. -eous.
Derivative: gaseous-ness, n.

## gash
gash, tr. v., to cui deeply. — Fr. earlier garsh,
fr. ME. garsen, fr. OF. garser, jarser, 'to incise'
(whence F. gercer, 'to chap, crack, cleave'), fr.
VL. *charissare, fr. earlier *charassare, fr. Gk.
χαράσσε'.ν, Ίο engrave, incise', whence χαρακ-
τήρ. 'graving tool, mark engraved, impress,
character'. See character.
Derivative: gash, n.

## gasification
gasification, n. — A hybrid coined fr. gas and
-fication.

## gasiform
gasiform, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. gas and L.
forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## gasify
gasify, tr. v. — A hybrid coined fr. gas and -fy.
Derivatives: gasifi-able, adj., gasifi-er, n.

## gasket
gasket, п., a piece of rope (naut.) — F. garcette,
dimin. of' garce, 'wench', femin. togar$on,'boy';
used only in a figurative sense. See garcon.

## gasoline
gasoline, gasolene, n. — A hybrid coined fr. gas,
-ol (fr. L. oleum, 'oil') and chem. suff. -ine,
resp. -ene.

## gasometer
gasometer, n. — A hybrid coined fr. gas and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## gasp
gasp, intr. and tr. v. — ME. gaispen, gaspen, 'to
yawn', fr. ON. geispa, 'to yawn', whence also
Swed, gdspa, Dan. gispe, 'to gasp'. ON. geispa
is prob. formed by metathesis fr. *geip-sa and
is rel. to ON. gapa, 'to gape'. Cp. LG. gapsen,
'to gasp', and see gape.
Derivatives: gasp, п., gasper (q.v.), gasp-ing,
adj., gasp-ing-ty, adv.

## Gaspar
Gaspar, masc. PN. — Of Persian origin; lit.
'treasure holder'. See Jasper,

## gasper
gasper, п., ι) one who gasps; 2) a cheap cigarette
(British Slang). — Formed fr. gasp with agential
suff. -er.

## gasser
gasser, п., one who or that which gasses. —
Formed fr. gas with agential suff. -er.

## gassy
gassy, adj., ]) full of, or containing, gas; 2) like
gas. — Formed fr. gas with adj. suff. -y.

## gastaldite
gastaldite, п., a variety of glaucophane (mineral.)
— Named after Professor Bartolomeo Gastaldi.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## gastero-
gastero-, before a vowel gaster-, combining form
meaning 'stomach' or 'belly1. — Gk. γαστερο-,
γαστερ-, identical in meaning with γαστρο-,
γαστρ-. See gastro-.

## gasteropod
gasteropod, п., any of the Gasteropoda. — See
next word.

## Gaste-opoda also Gastropoda
Gaste-opoda also Gastropoda, n. pi., a class of
mollusks including the snails, slugs, etc.
(zoology). — ModL., lit. 'having a foot in the ventral
surface'; compounded of Gk. γαστήρ, gen.
γαστρός, 'belly', and πους, gen. ττοδός, 'foot'.
See gastro- and -pod.

## gastrectomy
gastrectomy, п., the surgical removal of part of
the stomach. — Compounded of gastr- and
Gk. -εκτομίϊ, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a
cutting out'. See -ectomy.

## gastric
gastric, adj., pertaining to the stomach. —
Formed with suff. -ic, fr. Gk. γαστήρ, gen.
γαστρός, 'stomach'. See gastro- and cp.
digastric, epigastric, hypogastric, mesogastrlc.

## gastritis
gastritis, п., inflammation of the stomach (med.)
— Medical L., coined by the French pathologist
Francois-Boissier de la Croix de Sauvages
(1706-67) fr. Gk. γαστήρ, gen. γαστρός,
'stomach' (see gastro-), and suff. -itis.

## gastro-
gastro-, before a vowel gastr-, combining form
meaning 'stomach' or 'belly'. — Gk. γαστρο-,
γαστρ-, fr. γαστήρ, gen. γαστρός,*5ΐοηΊ3ΰ1ι, belly,
womb', which is dissimilated fr. "γραστήρ anp
lit. means 'eater, devourer', fr. γράν, 'to gnaw,
eat', whence also γράστις, 'green fodder', γάσ-
τρις (dissimilated fr. ·γράστρις), 'pot-bellied;
glutton'; prob. cogn. with OI. grdsali, 'eats,
devours'. See cress and cp. gangrene.

## gastrocnemius
gastrocnemius, п., the largest muscle of the calf
of the leg (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. γασ-
τροκνημίϊ, 'the calf of the leg', which is
compounded of γαστήρ, gen. γαστρός, 'belly', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:332 COLUMN:3 -->
κνήμη, 'part between knee and ankle, leg,
shank'. For the first element see gastro-, for
the second see cnemial.
Derivatives: gastrocnemi-al. gastrocnemi-an,
adjs.

## gastrology
gastrology, п., ι) the sciences of the structure,
functions and diseases of the stomach; 2)
gastronomy. — Gk. γαστρολογία, title of the
Greek Almanach des Gourmands, a poem
written by Archestratus, a contemporary of
Aristotle; compounded of γαστήρ, gen. γαστρός,
'stomach', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See gastro- and -logy.
Derivatives: gastrohg-er, п., gastrolog-ist, n.

## gastronome
gastronome, n. — F., back formation fr.
gastronomic See gastronomy.

## gastronomer
gastronomer, n. — See next word and agential
suff. -er.

## gastronomy
gastronomy, п., the act or science of caring for
the stomach, i.e. cookery. — F. gastronomie,
fr. Gk. γαστρονομία, another name for
γαστρολογία (see gastrology); formed fr. γαστήρ,
gen. γαστρός, 'stomach', on analogy of
αστρονομία, 'astronomy' (fr. αστήρ, 'star'). See gastro-
and -nomy.
Derivatives: gastronom-ic, gastr onom-ic-al, adjs.,
gastronom-ic-al-ly, adv., gastronom-ist, n.

## gastroscope
gastroscope, п., an instrument for examining the
interior of the stomach. — Compounded of
gastro- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, Ίο look
at, examine'. See -scope.

## gastroscopy
gastroscopy, п., examination of the interior of
the stomach. — Compounded of gastro- and
Gk. -σκοπιά, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'.
See -scopy.

## gastrotomy
gastrotomy, п., an incision into the stomach. —
Compounded of gastro- and Gk. -τομίά, 'a
cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.

## gastrula
gastrula, п., a form of embryo (embryol.) —
ModL., dimin. of I., gaster, 'belly; a big-bellied
vessel', fr. Gk. γάστρα, 'the lower part of a
vessel resembling a paunch; a vase with a
bulging belly', fr. γαστήρ, gen. γαστρός, 'belly';
see gastro- and -ule. The name gastrula was
coined by the German biologist Emil Helnrich
Haeckel (1834-1919).
Derivaiives: gastrul-ar, gastrul-ate, adjs., gas-
trul-ation, n.

## gate
gate, п., opening, entrance. — ME. gate, gat,
fr. OE. gaet, gat, geat, 'gate', rel. to ΟΝ., OS.,
OFris., Du. gat, 'an opening', and prob. also
to gate, 'passage' (q.v.) Cp. gait, gantlet.
Derivatives: gate, tr. v. (British), to confine to
the college grounds,gateage(q.v.),gat-ed,gate-
less, adjs., gating (q.v.)

## gate
gate, п., passage. — ME., fr. ON. gala, 'way,
path, road' (whence also Norw., Swed. gala,
Dan. gade), rel. to Goth, gatwo, OHG. ga^a,
MHG. ga33e, G. Gasse, 'street'. Finn, katu,
Lett, gatva, 'street', are Teut. loan words. Cp.
gate, 'opening'.

## gateage
gateage, п., the use of gates. — A hybrid coined
fr. gate, 'opening', and suff. -age.

## gather
gather, tr. and intr. v. — ME. gaderen, fr. OE.
gaderian, gxdrian, 'to gather, collect, store up',
rel. to OFris. gaderia, gadria, MLG. gadderen,
MDu.. Du. gaderen, of s.m., MHG. gatern, 'to
unite', OE. gxd, 'companionship', OE. gada,
ge-gada, MHG. gate, ge-gate, 'companion', Du.
gade, 'spouse', G. Gatte, 'husband', and to OE.
gxdeling, OS. gaduling, OHG. gatuling, Goth.
gadiliggs, 'companion', which are prop,
diminutives of Teut. *gad-, 'companion'. See good
and cp. gad, 'to rove about', together.
Derivatives: gather-er, п., gather-ing, n.

## gating
gating, п., confinement to college. — Formed fr.
gate, 'opening', with -ing, suff. forming verbal
nouns.
Catling gun. — Named after its inventor Richard
Jordan Galling (1818-1903).

## gauche
gauche, adj., left-handed; awkward, tactless. —
F., fr. gauchir, 'to turn aside, flinch', a blend of
OF. guenchir, 'to turn aside, slam, swerve', and
OF. gauchier, 'to full'. OF. guenchir derives fr.
Frankish 'wankjan, which is rel. to OHG. non-
kdn, ON. vakka, 'to stagger, toiter'; see wink
and cp. wince. OF. gauchier is a derivative of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:333 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GAUCHERIE | 306 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:333 COLUMN:1 -->
Frankish *walkan, 'to full'; see walk.
Derivatives: gauche-ly, adv., gauche-ness, n.

## gaucherie
gaucherie, п., awkwardness, tactlessness. — F.,*
fr. gauche. See prec. word and -ery.

## gaucho
gaucho, п., a cowboy. — Sp., prob. fr. Araucan-
ian cauchu, 'wanderer*.

## gaud
gaud, п., ornament. — ME. gaude, prob. fr. OF.

## gaudir
gaudir, 'to make merry, rejoice', fr. VL. *gau-
dire, corresponding to L. gaudere, 'to rejoice',
which stands for *gawidere and is cogn. with
Gk. γαίω (for *γ&τΊω), Ί rejoice, exult', γηθέω.
Dor. γίθέω (for *γί/ε*έω), Ί rejoice', γαύρος,
'exulting, superb', γαύρδξ, Ion. γαύρηξ,
'braggart', δγαυρος, 'proud', Mir. guaire, 'noble'. Cp.
joy, rejoice. Cp. also Gaura, the first element in
ganoid, Ganymede, and the seond element ir.
Origanum.
Derivative: gaud, tr. v.

## gaud
gaud, п., ornamental bead (hist.) — Prob. fr. L.
gaudium, 'joy', fr. gaudere, 'to rejoice'. See gaud,
'ornament'.
Derivatives: gaud-y, adj., gaud-i-ly, adv., gaud-
i-ness, n.

## gaudy
gaudy, п., feast, entertainment. — L. gaudium,
'joy, delight, occasion of joy', fr. gaudere, 'to
rejoice'. See gand, 'ornament*.
gauffer. — See goffer.

## gauge
gauge, gage, tr. v., i) to measure; 2) to estimate.
— ONF. gauger, corresponding to OF. and F.
jauger, fr. jauge, 'gauging rod', fr. Frankish
'galgo, prop, 'pole for measuring', and rel. to
ON. gelgja, 'pole, perch', OHG. galgo,
'gallows; cross'. See gallows.
Derivatives: gauge, n. (q.v.), the hybrid gauge-
able, adj., gaug-er, n.

## gauge
gauge, gage, n. — ONF. gauge, corresponding to
OF. and F. jauge. See gange, v.

## Gaul
Gaul, п., ι) name of an ancient country of W.
Europe; 2) one of the natives of Gaul; 3) (used
facetiously) a Frenchman. — F. Gaule, 'the
country of Gaul', fr. Gallia, fr. Gallus, 'a Gaul'.
See Gallic.
Derivatives: Gaul-ish, adj. and n.

## gault
gault, п., a heavy clay (dial. English). — Cp. ON.
gald, 'hard snow', Norw. gald, 'hard ground*.
Derivatives: gault, tr. and intr. v., gault-er, n.

## Gaultberia
Gaultberia, п., a genus of plants, the aromatic
wintergreen (hot.) — ModL., named after the
Canadian botanist Jean-Francois Gaulthier (also
spelled Gaultier, Gautier) (cca. 1708-56). For
the ending see sun", -in.

## gaunt
gaunt, adj., thin; lean. — ME., prob. of Scand.
origin. Cp. Norw. gand, 'a thin stick; a tall and
thin man'.
Derivatives: gaunt-ness, п., gaunt-y, adj.

## ganntiet
ganntiet, п., a glove. — ME. gantelet, fr. MF.
(= F.) gantelet, double dimin. of gant, 'glove',
fr., OF. want, guanl, gant, fr. Frankish wanth,
which is rel. to MDu. want, 'mitten', ON. vottr
(for *vantr), 'glove', Dan. vante, 'mitten'. These
words prob. stand in gradational relationship
to E. wind, 'to turn'. For sense development cp.
G. Gewand, 'garment', which is rel. to wenden,
'to turn', winden, 'to wind, twist, turn', and to
E. wind, 'to turn'. It. guanto, Sp. guante, 'glove',
are French loan words.
Derivative: gauntlet-ed, adj.

## gauntlet
gauntlet, n. — See gantlet,

## gauntry
gauntry, n. — See gantry.

## gaur
gaur, gour, п., the wild ox Bos gauros. — Hind.
gaur, fr. OI. gaurah, 'white, yellowish; the Bos
gaur us', fr. gauh, gen. goh, 'ox, bull, cow'. See
Gautama.

## Ganra
Ganra, п., a genus of American plants (hoi.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. γαύρος, 'exulting, superb'. See
gaud, 'ornament'.

## gauss
gauss, п., the C.G.S. unit of intensity of the
magnetic field. — Named after the German
mathematician Karl Friedrich Gauss (1777-1855).

## gaussage
gaussage, п., the intensity of a magnetic field
expressed in gausses. — Formed fr. gauss with
surf. -age.

## gausshergite
gausshergite, п., a kind of lava (petrogr.) — So
called from Gaussberg, a mountain in Kaiser
Wilhelm II Land, Antarctica, a name
compounded of Gauss, name of the ship used by the
German Antarctic Expedition, and of G. Berg,
'mountain'. See borough and subst. suff. -ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:333 COLUMN:2 -->

## Gautama
Gautama, п., the name of many sages, also
surname of Buddha. — OI. Gotamah, prop, a
patronymic meaning lit. 'descendant of the
greatest ox', and super!, of gauh, gen. goh,
'ox, bull, cow'. See cow and cp. gaur, the first
element in Gaekwar and in gopura and the
second element in nilgai.

## gauze
gauze, п., a very fine fabric of silk, cotton etc. —
F. gaze, fr. Gaza, a town in Palestine, famous
for the very fine transparent tissues fabricated
there.
Derivatives: gauz-y, adj., gauz-i-ly, adv., gauz-
i-ness, n^

## gavage
gavage, п., forced feeding (med.) — F. gavage,
fr. gayer, 'to gorge, to feed forcibly', a Picard
loan word, rel. to Provenc. gava, 'crop (of a
bird)', prob. of Gaulish origin. Cp. gavotte. For
the ending see surf. -age.

## gave
gave, past tense of give. — ME. gave, past tense
of given, 'to give'. See give.

## gavel
gavel, п., tribute (obsol.) — ME., fr. OE. gafol,
'tribute', rel. to MDu. gavel, MHG. gaffel,
'society, guild', and to OE. giefan, 'to give'. See
give and cp. gavelkind and gale, 'rent'.

## gavel
gavel, п., a small mallet. — Of uncertain origin.

## gavelkind
gavelkind, п., a kind of tenure (law). — ME.
gavelkynde. See gavel, 'tribute', and kind, n.

## gavial
gavial, п., crocodile of the Ganges. — F.,
corrupted fr. Hind, ghariyal.

## guvotte
guvotte, п., a lively dance. — F., fr. OProvenc.
gavoto, fr. gavot, 'inhabitant of the Alps' (hence
gavoto lit means 'dance of the inhabitants of
the Alps'). Cp. OProvenc. gavach, 'boor,
mountaineer' (whence F. gavache, 'coward, dastard*).
Both OProvenc. words derive fr. ΟΡτονεης.
gava, 'crop (of a bird)'. See gavage.

## gawk
gawk, п., an awkward person. — Of uncertain
origin; perh. fr. obsol. E. gaw, 'to stare', fr. ME.
gawen, fr. ON. go, 'to heed', which is of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: gawk-y, adj. and п., gawk-i-ness, n.

## gay
gay, adj. — F. gai, prob. fr. Frankish *gahi,
which is rel. to OHG. gahi, MHG. gach, 'rapid,
impetuous', G. jSh, 'rapid, sudden; steep,
precipitous'. OProvenc. gai and It. gaio are
French loan words. Cp. the second element in
nosegay.

## Gaylussacia
Gaylussacia, п., a genus of plants, the
huckleberry (hot.) — ModL., named after the French
chemist Joseph-Louis Gay-Lussac (1778-18^0).
For the ending see surf. -ia.

## gaze
gaze, intr. v. — ME. gasen, of Scand. origin.
Cp. dial. Swed. gasa, 'to stare, gaze'; of
uncertain origin.

## gazebo
gazebo, п., turret, balcony. — Facetious
formation fr. gaze after L. videbo, Ί shall see'.

## gazelle
gazelle, n. — F., fr. ghazil, N. African
pronunciation of Arab, ghazal.

## gazette
gazette, п., newspaper. — F., fr. It. gazzetia, of
s.m., fr. gazzetia, name of the smallest Venetian
coin, said to have been paid for the perusal of the
manuscript newspaper issued by the Venetian
Government once a month. It. gazzetta, 'coin',
is prob. a dimin. formed fr. L. gaza, 'treasure',
fr. Gk. γάζα, which is of Persian origin. See
genizah and cp. next word.
Derivatives: gazette, tr. v., gazetteer (q.v.)

## gazetteer
gazetteer, п., ι) a journalist; 2) a geographical
dictionary. — F. gazettier (now spelled gazetier),
lit. 'one who writes in a gazette', fr. gazette. See
prec. word and -eer.
Derivative: gazetteer, tr. v.

## gazogene
gazogene, п., an apparatus for fabricating aerated
water. — F. gazogene, a hybrid coined fr. gaz,
'gas', and combining form -gene. See gas and
-gen.

## ge-
ge-, combining form meaning 'earth'. — See geo-.

## gear
gear, п., equipment, harness, tackle. — ME. gere,
prob. fr. ON. gervi, 'apparel', which is rel. to
OE. gearwe, OS. garewi, OHG. garawi, garwi,
'clothing, dress', OE. gearwian, OS. garuwian,
gerwean, OHG. garawen, gariwen, 'to make
ready', MHG. gerwen, G. gerben, 'to tan', ON.
gorva, Dan. gjere, 'to make', OE. gearo, gearu,
OS. garo, ON. gorr, OHG. garo, garawer,
MHG., G. gar, 'ready, prepared*. See yare, and
cp. garb, 'style'.
Derivatives: gear, tr. and intr. v., gear-ing, п..

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:333 COLUMN:3 -->
gear-less, adj.

## gecko
gecko, п., a kind of house lizard. — Malay gikoq,
imitative of its cry.

## gedanlte
gedanlte, п., a variety of amber (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gedanum, the
Latin name of Danzig.

## gedrite
gedrite, n„ a variety of antophyllite (mineral.) —
F. gedrite, named after Gidre, in the French
Pyrenees. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## gee-gee
gee-gee, п., a horse (colloq.) — Reduplication of
gee, a child's word for 'horse', fr. gee a word
of command to a horse.

## geezer
geezer, п., an old fellow. — Dial, alteration of
guiser (q.v.)

## Gegenschein
Gegenschein, п., counterglow, a faint luminous
light seen opposite the sun's direction (astron.)
— G., formed fr. gegen, 'against, counter', and
Schein, 'shine, light, appearance'. See again
and shine.

## gebenna
gebenna, п., hell. — Eccles. L., fr. Gk. γέεννα,
fr. Heb. Ge Hinnom, 'the Valley of Hinnom',
shortened fr. Ge Ben-Hinnom, 'the Valley of the
Son of Hinnom', a valley S W. and S. of
Jerusalem, where children were sacrificed toMoloch.

## gehlenite
gehlenite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate,
CajAkSijOul (mineral) — Named by the
German chemist Johann Nepomuk Fuchs (1774-
1856) after his colleague A. F. Gehlen (1775-
1815). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## geikelite
geikelite, п., magnesium titanate (mineral.) —
Named after Sir Archibald Geikie, director of
the Geological Survey of Great Britain (1835-
1924). For the ending see combining form -lite.

## geikla
geikla, п., a toothless reptile from the New Red
Sandstone of Scotland (paleontol.) — ModL.,
named after Sir Archibald Geikie. See prec.
word.

## geikielite
geikielite, п., magnesium titanate, MgTi03
(mineral.) — Named after Sir Archibald Geikie.
See geikelite and subst. suff. -ite.

## geisha
geisha, п., a Japanese professional singing and
dancing girl. — Jap., composed of gei-sha, lit.
'artistic person'.

## gelada
gelada, п., an Abyssinian ape. — A native name.

## gelatin
gelatin, gelatine, п., animal jelly. — F. gelatine,
fr. It. gelatina, fr. gelata, 'jeliy', fr. L. gelata,
fern. pp. of gelare, 'to freeze, stiffen'. See gelid
and chem. suff. -in, -ine and cp. jelly.

## gelatiniform
gelatiniform, adj. — Formed fr. gelatin and L.
forma, 'form, shape*. See form, n.

## gelatinize
gelatinize, tr. v., to change into gelatin; intr. v.,
to be changed into gelatin. — A hybrid coined
fr. gelatin and -ize, a suff. of Greek origin.

## gelatinoid
gelatinoid, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. gelatin and
Gk. -οειδής,'Μβ', fr. είδος,'ίοπτι, shape'. See -oid.

## gelatinous
gelatinous, adj. — F'. gelatineux(fem. gelatineuse),
fr. gelatine. See gelatin and -ous.
Derivatives: gelatinous-ly, adv., gelatinous-
ness, a.

## gelation
gelation, п., freezing. — L. gelatio, gen. -onis,
'freezing', fr. gelatus, pp. of gelare, 'to freeze'.
See gelid and -ion.

## geid
geid, tr. v., to castrate; to spay. — ME. gelden,
fr. ON. gelda, 'to geld', fr. ON. geldr, 'barren',
which is rel. to OSwed. galder, Swed. gall, Dan.
gold,Norw.gjeld, MLG.gelde, OE.gielde, MHG.
gait, G. gait, gelt, 'barren', and prob. also to OE.,
OHG. galan, 'to sing', OE. giellan, 'to scream,
cry'. Accordingly, ON. geldr, etc., prob. meant
originally 'enchanted, bewitched'. See yell and
cp. gale, 'a strong wind', and the last element
in nightingale.

## geld
geld, п., payment, tax (English history). — OE.
geld, gield, gild, 'payment', rel. to OS. geld,
OHG., MHG. gelt, 'payment, contribution',
Du., G. geld, 'money', ON. gjald, 'payment';
Goth, gild, 'tribute, tax', and to E. yield (q.v.)
Cp. the second element in Danegeld.

## gelding
gelding, п., a castrated animal. — ON. geldingr,
fr. geldr, 'barren'. See geld, 'to castrate', and
subst. suff. -iag.

## Gelechla
Gelechla, п., a genus of moths, the pink boll-
worm (eniomol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-ia fr. Gk. γηλεχής, 'sleeping on the earth',
fr. γη, 'earth', and λέχος, 'bed'. For the first
element see geo-. The second element is cogn.
with OE. licgan, 'to lie'; see lie, 'to recline'. For
the ending see suff. -la.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:334 COLUMN:1 -->

## Gelecbffdae
Gelecbffdae, η. pi., a family of moths (entomol.)
— ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -idae.

## gelid
gelid, adj., freezing, frosty. — L. gelidus, 'icy,
frosty', formed—prob. on analogy of calidus,
'warm'—fr. gelu, 'frost'; which is rel. to gla-
ciis, 'ice', fr. I.-E. base *gel-, 'to freeze, be cold',
whence also Gk. γελανδρός, 'cold', OE. cald,
ceald, 'cold'. See cold and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see adj. suff. -id.
Derivatives: gelid-ily, п., gelid-ly, adv., gelid-
ness, n.

## geliguite
geliguite, п., a high explosive. — Formed from
the abbreviation of gelatin, L. ignis, 'fire' (see
igueous), and subst. suff. -ite.

## geliiah
geliiah, п., the wrapping up of the Scroll of the
Law (Jewish liturgy). — Heb. gllilah, 'a rolling
up', fr. galal, 'he rolled, unfolded', rel. to Aram.
g4al, gallil, of s.m., Heb. gilgil, Aram, galgel,
'he rolled away', Heb. gal, Aram, gal, galli,
'heap, wave, willow', Akkad. gillu, 'wave', Heb.
guild", 'basin, bowl', Akkad. gullatu, 'a vessel',
Heb. galal, Aram, galli, galIHe (pi.), g'lala,
Arab. jallah, 'dung', Heb. gattt, 'cylinder;
district', Haggalfl, 'Galilee', gillulim (pi.), 'idols',
galgal, 'wheel, whirlwind', Aram, galgal, gil-
g'la, 'wheel', Mishnaic Heb. galgal (ha'ayin),
Aram, galg'li (d*'eni), Akkad. gaggultu, 'apple
of the eye', Heb. gulgaleth, Aram, gulgulta,
gugalta, Akkad. gulgullu, Arab, jalaja", jiim-
juma*, 'skull'. Cp. Megllloth. Cp. also Galilee,
Golgotha and the second element in Abigail.
Cp. also ganglion.

## gelo-
gelo-, combining form meaning 'laughter'. — Fr.
Gk. γέλως, 'laughter'. See geloto-.

## geloscopy
geloscopy, п., divination by laughter. —
Compounded of gelo- and Gk. -σκοπίϊ, fr. σκοτιεΓν,
'to look at, examine'. See -scopy.

## geloto-
geloto-, combining form meaning 'laughter'. —
Gk. γελωτο-, fr. γέλως, gen. γέλωτος, 'laughter',
rel. to γελάν, 'to laugh', γαληνός, 'calm, serene',
γαλήνη, 'stilness of wind and wave', and cogn.
with Arm. calr, gen. calu, 'laughter, ci-caiim,
1 laugh'. Cp. gelo-, Aglaia, Aglaspis, glenoid.
Cp. also clean.

## Gelsemium
Gelsemium, п., a genus of plants, the yellow
jessamine (bot.) — ModL., fr. gelsomino, the
Italian name of the jessamine. See jasmine,
jessamine. For the ending see ist -ium.

## gem
gem, п., precious stone. — ME. gemme, fr. MF.
(= F.) gemme, 'precious stone', fr. L. gemma,
'precious stone; bud'. See gemma.
Derivative: gem, tr. v.

## Gemara
Gemara, п., commentary on the Mishnah
(together with which it forms the Talmud). —
Aram, g'mdrd, emphatic state of g'mdr,
'completion ; learning', fr. g'mdr, 'he finished,
completed; he learned completely; he learned',
which is rel. to Heb. gamar, 'he ended,
completed', and to Arab, jammara, 'he collected,
assembled'.

## gematria
gematria, п., explanation of the sense of a word
by substituting for it another word, so that the
numerical value of the letters constituting either
word is identical. — Mishnaic Heb. gimafriyya,
metathesis of Gk. *γραμματεία, 'play upon
letters', fr. γράμμα, gen. γράμματος, 'letter', lit.
'that which is written'. See -grain, -graph.

## gemel
gemel, п., one of a pair of bars (her.) — OF.
(whence F. gemeau, jumeau), 'twin', fr. L.
gemellus, dimin. of geminus. See Gemini and cp.
next word and gimbal.

## gemellus
gemellus, п., name of either of two small muscles
(anal.) — L„ 'twin'; in the modern, anatomical
sense, it is a loan translation of F. lesjumeaux,
'the twins', a name coined by the French
surgeon Ambroise Part (died in 1590). See
gemel.

## geminate
geminate, adj., found in pairs. — L. geminatus,
pp. oigeminare, 'to double, repeat', fr. geminus.
See Gemini and adj. suff. -ate.

## geminate
geminate, tr. v., to double. — See prec. word.

## gemination
gemination, n. — L. geminatio, gen. -onis, 'a
doubling', fr. geminatus, pp. of geminare. See
geminate, adj., and -ion.

## Gemini
Gemini, n. pi., 1) the constellation of Castor and
Pollux; 2) the third sign of the Zodiac. — L.,
'twins', specif, 'the constellation Castor and
Pollux'; prob. cogn. with OI. yamdh, Avestic

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:334 COLUMN:2 -->
y'md, 'twin', Mir. emon (masc.), emuin (fern.),
'pair of twins'. These words possibly derive fr.
I.-E. base "gem-, 'to press', whence also Gk.
γέμειν, 'to be pregnant, to be full of, Mir.
gemel, W. gefyn, 'fetter'. Gk. γαμεΐν, 'to marry',
is not cogn. with L. geminus. Cp. gemel, trl-
geminous.

## gemma
gemma, п., ι) a bud (bot.); 2) a budlike growth
(zool.) — L., 'bud; precious stone', possibly for
"gembh-ma, fr. I.-E. base 'gembh-, 'to cut to
pieces', whence also Lith. zemba, zembeti, 'to
sprout', zembiii, zembti, 'to cut to pieces',
OSlav. zebp, Ί tear to pieces', pro-zebati, 'to
sprout, shoot forth', OI. jambhate, jabhate,
"snaps at', jambhah, 'tooth', OE. camb, 'comb'.
See camb and cp. gem, gemmule.

## gemmate
gemmate, adj., having buds. — L. gemmatus,
'provided with buds', pp. of gemmare, 'to put
forth buds', fr. gemma, 'bud'. See gemma and
adj. suff. -ate.

## gemmate
gemmate, intr. v., to bud. — L. gemmatus,
'provided with buds'. See prec. word.
Derivative: gemmat-ion, n.

## gemmiferous
gemmiferous, adj., 1) yielding gems; 2) bearing
buds (bot. and zool.) — Compounded of gemma
and -ferous.

## gemmiparous
gemmiparous, adj., producing buds (biol.) —
Compounded of gemma and -parous,

## gemmule
gemmule, п., a small gemma or bud. — L. gem-
mula, 'a little bud', dimin. of gemma. See gemma
and -ule.

## gemmy
gemmy, adj., full of gems. — Formed fr. gem
with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: gemmi-ly, adv., gemmi-ness, n.

## Gemonies
Gemonies, n. pi. (Roman antiq.) — L. Gemoniae,
shortened fr. Gemoniae scalae, steps on the
Aventine Hill down which the bodies of
executed criminals were dragged to be thrown into
the Tiber. The name is prob. of Etruscan origin;
its connection with L. gemere, 'to sigh, groan',
is folk etymology.

## gemot
gemot, п., a meeting (English hist.) — OE. gemot,
'meeting'. See moot, 'meeting', and cp. hallmoot,
witeangemot.

## gemsbok
gemsbok, п., a South African antelope. — Du.,
rel. to G. Gemsbock, lit. 'the male of the
chamois', fr. Du. gems (resp. G. Gemse), 'chamois',
and bok (resp. G. Bock), 'buck'. The first
element is a loan word fr. L. camox, 'chamois',
which itself is a loan word from an
Indo-European language spoken by the ancient
inhabitants of the Alps. This word derives fr. I.-E.
base *kem-, 'hornless', whence also Gk. κεμάς,
'young deer, gazelle'. See hind, 'female of the
deer', and cp. chamois. For the second element
in gemsbok see buck.

## -gen
-gen, combining form used in the senses: 1)
something produced; 2) something that produces as
in oxygen, hydrogen. The second sense is
modern; it was introduced by the French chemist
Antoine-Laurent de Lavoisier (in his Traitede
Chimie, published in 1789). — F. -gene, fr. Gk.
-γενής, 'born of, produced by*, from the stem of
γενναν, 'to beget, bring forth, generate,
produce'. See genus and cp. words there referred to.

## gena
gena, п., the cheek (zool.) — L., 'cheek'. See
chin and cp. words there referred to.

## genappe
genappe, п., a smooth worsted yarn. — Fr. Ge-
nappe, a town in Belgium; so called because
first made at Genappe.

## gendarme
gendarme, п., an armed policeman. — F. gens

## d'armes
d'armes, 'men at arms', lit. 'men of arms'. F.

## gens
gens, 'men', is the plurai of gent, 'nation,
people', fr. L. gentem, ace. of gens, 'race,
nation, people'; F. de, 'from, of, comes fr. L. de,
'from, away from'; F. amies derives fr. L. arma,
'weapons'. See gens, de- a>d arm, n.

## gendarmerie
gendarmerie, п., gendarmes collectively. — F.
See prec. word and -ery.

## gender
gender, n. — ME. gendre, fr. OF. gendre (F.

## genre)
genre), fr. L. genus, gen. generis, 'sort, kind,
class; sex, gender'. See genus and cp. genre,
which is a doublet of gender.
Derivative: gender-less, adj.

## gender
gender, tr. v., to engender (Biblical and archaic). —
OF. gendrer, fr. L. generare, 'to engender', fr.

## genus
genus, gen. generis. See prec. word and cp.
engender.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:334 COLUMN:3 -->

## gene
gene, п., a hypothetical agent transmitted from
parent to offspring (biol.). — See -gen.

## -gene
-gene, combining form, identical in meaning and
origin, with -gen (q.v.)

## genealogical
genealogical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. Gk. γενεαλογικός, 'of genealogy', fr.
γενεαλογία. See next word and -ic.
Derivative: genealogical-ly, adv.

## genealogy
genealogy, n. — ME. genealogie, fr. OF. genea-
logie (F. genealogie), fr. Late L. genealogia, fr.
Gk. γενεαλογία, 'account of a family, making
of a pedigree, genealogy', fr. γενεαλόγος, 'maker
of a pedigree, genealogist', which is formed fr.
γενεά, 'descent', and -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See genus and -logy.
Derivatives: genealogical (q.v.), genealog-ist,
п., genealog-ize, v.

## gener
gener, п., son-in-law. — L., prob. fr. *gemeros
(the л being due to the influence of words like
gens, 'nation', genitor, 'parent, creator'), fr.
I.-E. base "gem-, 'to marry'; cogn. with Gk.
γαμβρός, 'son-in-law, brother-in-law, father-in-
law', and with Gk. γαμεΐν, 'to take to wife, to
marry'. See bigamy and cp. words there
referred to.

## generable
generable, adj., capable of being generated. —
L. generabilis, 'that which has the power of
generating', fr. generare. See generate and -able.

## general
general, adj. — OF. (F. general), fr. L. generalis,
'of a specific kind; relating to all, general', fr.
genus, gen. generis, 'sort, kind, class'. See genus
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: general, п., generality (q.v.),
general-ize, tr. and intr. v., general-ly, adv.

## general
general, n. — OF. (F. general), fr. general, adj.
See general, adj.

## generalissimo
generalissimo, п., supreme military commander.
— It. superl. of generate, 'general', fr. generate,
adj., 'general', fr. L. generalis. See general, adj.
and n.

## generality
generality, n. — F. gineraliti, fr. L. generalitatem,
ace. of generdlitas, 'generality', fr. generalis. See
general, adj., and -ity.

## generate
generate, tr. v. — L. generatus, pp. of generare,
'to beget, bring forth, produce, generate', fr.
genus, gen. generis, 'birth, descent, race'. See
genus and verbal suff. -ate and cp. gender, v.,
engender.
Derivatives: generation (q.v.), general-ive, adj.,
generative-ly, adv., generative-ness, п.,
generator (q.v.)

## generation
generation, n. — L. gen?ratio, gen. -onis, 'a
generating, generation', fr. L. generatus, pp. of
gemrare. See geuerate and -ion.

## generator
generator, п., ι) a person who or a thing that
generates; 2) an apparatus for producing steam
or gas; 3) an apparatus for changing mechanical
into electrical energy; a dynamo. — L.,
'engendered producer, generator', fr. generatus,
pp. of generare. See generate and agential suff.
-or.

## generatrix
generatrix, п., a point, line or surface that
generates a line, surface or solid (geom.) — L., 'she
that generates', fem. of generator. See prec.
word and -trix.

## generic
generic, adj., pertaining to a genus, kind or class.
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. genus, gen. generis,
'sort, kind, class'. See genus.
Derivatives: generic-al-ly, adv., generic-al-
ness, n.

## generosity
generosity, n. — F. generosite, fr. L. generdsi-
tatem, ace. of generositas, 'nobility, excellence,
magnanimity', fr. generosus. See n;xt word
and -ity.

## generous
generous, adj. — F. genereux (fem. genereuse),
fr. L. generosus, 'of noble birth, noble,
excellent, magnanimous', fr. genus, gen. generis,
birth, descent, origin'. See genns and -ous.
Derivatives: generous-ly, adv., generous-ness, n.

## genesis
genesis, п., ι) (cap.) the first book of the
Pentateuch; 2) origin, creation. — L., fr. Gk. γένεσις,
'birth, descent, origin', which is rel. to γένος,
'birth, descent, race', γενεά, γενεή, γενετή, of
s.m., γενετήρ, 'father', fr. I.-E. base *gei\-,
*geni-, 'to beget, produce'. S;e genus and cp.
words thsre referred to.

## -genesis
-genesis, combining form meaning 'origination,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:335 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GENET | 308 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:335 COLUMN:1 -->
generation, formation', as in biogenesis,
pathogenesis. — Fr. L. genesis, fr. Gk. γένεσις. See
pre:, word.

## genet
genet, п., a small civetcat; also its fur. — OF.
genets, gemtte (F. genette), fr. Sp. gineta, fr.
Arab, jarnait.

## genethliac
genethliac, adj., pertaining to the casting of
nativities; pertaining to a birthday. — L. geneth-
liacus, fr. Gk. γενεθλιακός, 'pertaining to birth,
pertaining to nativity', fr. γενέθλιος, 'of one's
birth', fr. γενέθλη, 'birth', which is rel. to
γένεσις, 'birth, descent, origin'. See genesis.

## genethliacon
genethliacon, п., a birthday ode. — Gk. γενεθλι-
ακόν, prop. neut. of the adjective γενεθλιακός,
'pertaining to a birthday', used as a noun. See
prec. word.

## genethlialogy
genethlialogy, п., the art of casting nativities;
astrology. — Gk. γενεθλιάλογίά, 'casting of
nativities, astrology', fr. γενεθλιάλόγος, 'caster
of nativities', which is compounded of
γενέθλιος, 'of one's birth', and -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See genethliac and -logy.

## genetic
genetic, adj., pertaining to genesis. — A modern
word formed fr. genesis on analogy of Greek
adjectives ending in -ετικός, which correspond
to nouns ending in -εσις. See sun*, -etic.
Derivatives: geneiic-al-ly, adv., genetics (q.v.)

## -genetic
-genetic, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
genesis or generation', as in biogenetic. — See
prec. word.

## genetics
genetics, п., that branch of biology which deals
with heredity. — Coined by the English
biologist and geneticist William Bateson (1861-1926)
fr. genetic and sun", -ics.

## genetrix
genetrix, п., a mother. — L. genetrix, genitrix,
'a mother', lit. 'she that bears', fem. of genitor,
'parent, father'. See genitor and -trix.

## geneva
geneva, п., gin {liquor). — Earlier Du. genever
(now Jenever), fr. ON. genevre (F. geniivre), fr.
L. juniperus, 'juniper'. See juniper and cp. gin,
'liquor'.

## Genevieve
Genevieve, fem. PN. — F. Genevieve, fr. Late L.
Genovefa, which is prob. of Celtic origin.

## genial
genial, adj., mild, kindly. — L. genialis,
'pertaining to birth or generation; nuptial, festival;
pleasant', fr. genius, 'tutelary spirit'. See genius
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: geniality (q.v.), genial-ize, tr. v.,
genial-Iy, adv., genial-ness, n.

## genial
genial, adj., pertaining to the chin. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. γένειον, 'chin', which
is related to γένυς, 'the lower jaw, cheek, chin',
and cogn. with L. gena, 'cheek', Goth, kinnus,
'cheek', OE. cinn, 'chin'. See chin and cp. words
there referred to.

## geniality
geniality, n. — Late L. genialitas, 'festivity,
pleasantness', fr. L. genialis. See genial, 'mild',
and -ity.

## genie
genie, adj., pertaining to a gene (biol.) — See
gene and -ic.

## -genie
-genie, combining form meaning 'producing', as
in endogenic, eugenic. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. nouns ending in -gen or -geny.

## geniculate
geniculate, geniculated, adj., having knots or
joints. — L. geniculatus, 'having knots or joints',
fr. geniculum, 'little knee; knot on the stalk of
a plant', dimin. of genu, 'knee'. See genu and
the suff. -cule, and -ate, resp. also -ed.
Derivatives: genicutat-ed, adj., geniculate-Iy,
adv., geniculation, n.

## geniculum
geniculum, п., a small kneelike structure (anat.)
— L., 'little knee'. See prec. word.

## genie
genie, п., a jinni. — F. genie, fr. L. genius, 'tutelary
spirit' (see genins); confused in sense with jinni.

## genio-
genio-, pertaining to the chin (anat.) — Gk.
γενειο-, fr. γένειον, 'chin'. See genial, 'pertaining
to the chin'.

## Genista
Genista, п., a genus of plants, the woad waxen
(bot.) — L. genista, 'broom', a foreign word, as
proved by its ending, -ista. The var. genistra
points to Etruscan origin. See fenestra and cp.
Herbig, Indogermanische Forschungen, 37,
171 n".

## genital
genital, adj., 1) pertaining to reproduction;
2) pertaining to the reproductive organs. — L.
genitalis, 'pertaining to generation or birth',
fr. genitus, pp. of gignere, 'to beget, bear, bring

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:335 COLUMN:2 -->
forth, produce'. See genus and adj. suff. -al and
cp. congenital. Cp. also genesis.

## genitalia
genitalia, n. pi., the genitals. — L. genitalia (scil.
membra), 'genitals', neut. pi. of genitalis. See
prec. word.

## genitals
genitals, n. pi., the reproductive organs. —
Formed from genital.

## genitive
genitive, adj. and n. — Fr. L. (casus) genitivus,
lit. 'the case expressing origin', fr. geniiivus,
'pertaining to birth or generation', fr. genitus,
pp. of gignere, 'to beget, bear, bring forth' (see
genus and -ive and cp. Gentoo). L. casus geni-
ttvus is prop, mistranslation of Gk. γενική
(7ττώσις),"41ΐ6 case expressing race or kind', fr.
γένος, 'race, kind' (see genus). For the Latin
mistranslation of another Greek case name see
accusative.
Derivatives: genitiv-al, adj., genitive-ly, adv.

## genito-
genito-, pertaining to the genitals. — Fr. L.
genitus, pp. of gignere. See genital.

## genins
genins, n. — L., 'tutelary spirit; inclination', orig.
'generative power', for *gen-yos, fr. I.-E. base
'gen-, 'to beget, produce'. See genus and cp. king.

## genius loci
genius loci, the tutelary of a place. — See prec.
word and locus.

## genizah
genizah, п., storeroom of a synagogue in which
Hebrew books are preserved. — Mishnaic Heb.
gtnizah, 'hiding place', fr. ganaz, 'he saved; he
hid', rel. to Biblical Heb.g'ndzim (pi.),'treasury'
(in the Biblethe word occurs only in the construct
state pi. ginzi); borrowed fr. Pers. garij,
'treasure', whence also Aram, g'naz, 'he saved',
ginzd, gazzd, 'treasure', Arab, janaza, 'he
covered up'. Cp. Arm. ganj, Gk. γάζα (whence L.
gaza), and Hung, kincs, 'treasure', which are
also Persian loan words. Cp. also gunge. Cp.
also gazette and the first element in Caspar,
Jasper.

## genocide
genocide, п., extermination of an ethnic group. —
Lit. 'killing a tribe'; a hybrid coined fr. Gk.
γένος, 'race, tribe', and L. -cidere, fr. caedere,
'to kill'; see genus and -cide, 'killing'. The
correct word would be genticide, in which both
elements are of Latin origin. The word genocide
was introduced by Raphael Lenikin in his Axis
Rule in Occupied Europe, 1944, p. 19. See
Encyclopedia Britannica, Book of the Year 1949, p. 386.

## -genous
-genous, suff. forming adjectives meaning
1)'generating, producing, yielding', as in erogenous;
г) 'produced by', as in autogenous. —
Compounded of the suffixes -gen and -ous.

## genre
genre, п., ι) kind, sort; 2) style. — F., fr. L. genus,
gen. generis, 'sort, kind, class'. See genus and cp.
gender, п., which is a doublet of genre.

## genro
genro, п., the elder statesmen of Japan. — Jap.,
lit. 'first elders\

## gens
gens, п., a tribe, clan (Roman hist.) — L. gens,
gen. gentis, 'race, clan, nation, people', rel. to
genus, gen. generis, 'birth, descent, origin, race,
sort, kind, class'. See genus and cp. genteel,
gentile, gentie, Gentoo, gentry, jaunty. Cp. also
the first element in gendarme.

## genteel
genteel, adj., well-bred. — Re-adopted in the
16th cent. fr. F. gentil, which appears first in
English under the form gentle (q.v.) See also
gens and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: genteel-ly, adv., genteel-ness, п.,
genteel-ism, a.

## gentian
gentian, п., any plant of the genus Gentiana.
— OF. (= F.) gentiane, fr. L. gentiana, a word
of prob. Illyrian origin (the suff. -an frequently
occurs in Illyrian words). The connection with
the Illyrian king Gentius, suggested by Pliny,
is folk etymology. See Walde-Hofmann, LEW.,
I, P. 592.

## Gentiana
Gentiana, п., a genus of plants (hot.) — ModL.
See prec. word.

## Gentianaceae
Gentianaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## gentinnaceous
gentinnaceous, adj., — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## gentile
gentile, adj., not Jewish; п., a non-Jew. — F.
gentil, fr. L. gentllis, 'belonging to the same gens
(stock); heathen, pagan, non-Jew', fr. gens, gen.
ge.itis, 'race, clan'. See gens and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: gentil-ic, adj. and п., gentil-ish,
adj., gentil-dom, п., gentil-ism, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:335 COLUMN:3 -->

## gentilicious
gentilicious, adj. (obsol.), pertaining to a gentile.
— See prec. word and -ous.

## gentilitial
gentilitial, adj., pertaining to a gens; peculiar to
a nation. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
gentiltcius, 'pertaining to a gens', fr. gentilis.
See gentile.

## gentility
gentility, п., ι) gentle birth; 2) politeness. — OF.
gentilite (F. gentilite), fr. L. gentilitatem, ace. of
gentilitas, 'relationship of those who belong to
a gens', fr. gentilis. See gentile and -ity.

## gentle
gentle, adj., 1) well-born; 2) honorable; 3)
respectable. — OF. gentil, 'of good family, noble*
(whence F. gentil, 'nice, graceful, pleasing, fine,
pretty'), fr. L. gentilis, 'belonging to the same
gens'. See gentile and cp. genteel.
Derivatives: gentle, п., gentle-ness, п., gently
(q.v.)

## gentleman
gentleman, n. — Compounded of gentle, in the
sense of 'well-born', and man.
Derivatives: gentleman-hood, п., gentleman-like,
adj., gentleman-ly, adj., gentleman-li-ness, п.,
gentleman-ship, a.

## gentlewoman
gentlewoman, n. — Compounded of gentle, in the
sense of 'well-born', and woman. Cp.
gentleman.
Derivatives: gentlewoman-hood, п.,
gentlewoman-like, adv., gentlewoman-ly, adj., gentle-
woman-li-ness, n.

## gentiy
gentiy, adv. — Formed fr. gentle with adv. suff.
-ly.

## Gentoo
Gentoo, п., a Hindu; a Telugu; the Telugu
language. — Corruption of Port, gentio, 'a
gentile', fr. L. genitivus, 'pertaining to generation',
fr. genitus, pp. of gignere, 'to beget'. See genus
and cp. genitive, gens, gentile.

## gentrice
gentrice, п., noble birth; gentry (archaic). —
ME., fr. OF. genterise, a var. of gentelise,
'nobility', fr. gentil. See gentie and cp. next word.

## gentry
gentry, n. —ME.,'nobility', prob. back formation
fr. prec. word, the ending of which was mistaken
fort he plural suff. -s. For similar backformations
cp. pea and words there referred to.

## genu
genu, п., the knee (anat.) — L. genu, cogn. with
OI. jinu, Gk. γόνυ, Goth, kniu, OE. сто,
'knee'. See knee, and cp. geniculate, genuflect,
-gon.
Derivative: genu-al, adj.

## gennflect
gennflect, intr. v., to bend the knee. — ML.
genuflectere, 'to bend the knee', fr. L. genu,
'knee', and flectere, 'to bend'. See prec. word
and flex.
Derivatives: genuflection (q.v.), genuflect-ory,
adj.

## genuflection
genuflection, genuflexion, n. — F. genuflexion,
fr. ML. genuflexidnem, ace. of genuflexig,
'bending of the knee', fr. genuflex-(um), pp.
stem of genuflectere. See prec. word and -ion
and cp. flection, flexion.

## genuine
genuine, adj. — L. genuinus, 'innate, native,
natural', back formation fr. ingenuus, 'native, free-
born, upright.' (the ending was influenced by
adulter-inus, 'born of adultery, bastard,
counterfeit'), fr. I.-E. base *gen-, 'to beget; to be born'.
See next word and cp. ingenuous.
Derivatives: genuine-ly, adv., genuine-ness, a.

## genus
genus, п., a class; a kind, sort. — L., 'birth,
descent, origin, race, sort, kind, class; sex,
gender', fr. I.-E. base *gen-, *gene-t *geno-,
*gn-, 'to beget, bear, bring forth; produce',
whence also L. gens, 'race, clan, nation, people',
gignere (for gi-gn-ere), 'to beget, bear, bring
forth, produce', nasci (for *gnasci), 'to be born',
natus, gnatus, 'bom', natio, 'birth, breed, race,
people, nation', natura, 'birth, nature', Gk.
γένος, 'race, descent, gender, kind', γίγνεσθκι,
(for γί-γνε-σθκι), 'to be born, become,
happen', γένεσις, 'origin, source, birth, race,
descent', γενεά, γενεή, γενετή, 'birth', γενετήρ,
γενέτωρ, γενετής, 'begetter, father, ancestor',
γονεύς, 'father, ancestor', γονή, 'that which is
begotten, offspring; that which generates, seed,
semen; genitals; the act of generation; race,
family', γόνος, 'that which is begotten, child,
offspring; procreation; race, birth, descent;
seed, semen; genitals', -γνητος (in compounds),
'born', γνωτός, 'kinsman, brother', OI. janati,
'begets, bears', janitar-, 'begetter, father', jam-
man-, fanman-, 'birth', jartah,'race',jatah, 'born',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:336 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 309 | GERENT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:336 COLUMN:1 -->
jatih, 'birth, family', jnatUf, 'kinsman', Avestic
zizan'nti, 'they bear', zaz'nti, 'they beget', zata-,
'born', Arm. cnanim (aor. cnay), Ί bear; I am
born', Lett, znuols, 'son-in-law, brother-in-law',
Lith. gentis, 'kinsman', Olr. ro-genar, Ί was
born', W. geni, 'to be born'. Cp. Antigone, ar-
chegonium, benigu, cognate, congener, connate,
degenerate, engine, epigone, Erigenia, eugenic,
-gen, gendarme, gender, gene, genealogy, gener,
geueral, generate, generation, generous, genesis,
genetic, genial, 'mild', genie, genital, genitive,
genius, genre, gens, genteel, gentile, gentility, gentie,
gentieman, Gentoo, gentry, geauine, -geny, ge-
nyo-, germ, german, germane, germen, germinal,
Gerygone, gingerly, gonad, gonidium, gonorrhea,
-gony, heterogeneous, homogeneous, indigene,
indigenous, ingenuous, innate, Iphigenia, Jataka,
jaunty, kin, kinchin, kind, п., kind, adj., kindred,
king, malign, mirza, miscegenation, nascent,
natal, nation, native, nature, nevus, oogoninm,
perigonium, Prajapati, primogeniture, progeny,
shahzada, Telegonus, ultimogeniture.

## -geny
-geny, suff. denoting 'genesis, origin, production',
as in biogeny, embryogeny. — F. -genie, fr. Gk.
-γένεια, fr. -γενής, 'born, produced'. See -gen
and -y (representing Gk. -ίδ, -em).

## genyo-
genyo-, combining form denoting the lower jaw.
— Fr. Gk. γένυς, 'the lower jaw', which is rel.
to γένειον, 'chin'. See genial, 'pertaining to the
chin', and cp. genio-.

## geo-
geo-, combining form meaning 'earth'. — Gk.
γεω-, fr. γη, 'the earth', rel. to Dor. Gk. γϊ,
Homeric γαία, Cyprian ζα, 'the earth'; of
unknown origin. Cp. Gaea, apogee, Epigaea, epi-
geous, George, georgic, hypogeum, perigee.

## geocentric
geocentric, adj., having the earth as center. —
Compounded of geo-, and centric. Cp.
heliocentric.
Derivatives: geocentric-at-ly, adv., geocentric-
ism, n.

## geocronite
geocronite, п., a lead antimony sulfide (mineral.)
— Compounded of geo-, Gk. Κρόνος, 'Cronus'—
here used in its alchemistic sense 'lead'—and
subst. suff. -ire. Cp. Saturn, which is the Roman
equivalent of Cronus and is used in alchemy in
the same sense, and see Cronus.

## geode
geode, п., a rounded stone having a hollow center
lined with crystals. — F. geode, fr. L. geodes,
fr. Gk. γεώδης, 'earthlike', fr. γη, 'earth', and
-ώδης, 'like'. See geo- and -ode, 'like', and cp.
geoid.

## geodesic
geodesic, adj., pertaining to geodesy. — See
geodesy and -ic.

## geodesist
geodesist, п., a student of geodesy. — See next
word and -ist.

## geodesy
geodesy, п., the science of determining the shape
and size of the earth. — Gk. γεωδαισία, 'division
of the earth',compounded of γεω-(see geo-) and
the stem of δαίεσ&αι, 'to divide'. See demon.

## geodetic
geodetic, geodetical, adj., geodesic. — See
geodesic.
Derivative: geodetical-ly, adv.

## geodic
geodic, adj., pertaining to a geode. — See geode
and -ic.

## Geoffrey
Geoffrey, masc. PN. — OF. (= F.) Geoffroi, fr.-
ML. Galfridus, Gaufridus, a compound
traceable to OHG. gewi, gouwes (MHG. gou, gou,
G. Gau), 'district', which is perh. cogn. with
Arm. gav-af, 'region', and to OHG. fiidu,
'peace', for which see free and cp. words there
referred to.

## geogaostic
geogaostic, adj., pertaining to geognosy. —
Formed fr. geo- and Gk. γνωστικός, 'pertaining
to knowing', fr. γνωστός, later form of γνωτός,
'known*, verbal adj. of γιγνώσκειν, 'to know'.
See guosis, and -ic and cp. next word.

## geognosy
geognosy, п., that part of geology which deals
with the structure of the earth. — F. geognosie,
lit. 'the knowledge of the earth', fr. Gk. γεω-
(see geo-) and γνώσις, 'knowledge'. See gaosis
and cp. prec. word.

## geogony
geogony, п., the science of the genesis of the
earth. — Compounded of geo- and -gony.

## geographic
geographic, adj., geographical. — See next word.

## geographical
geographical, adj. — L. geographicus, fr. Gk.
γεωγραφικός, 'pertaining to geography", fr.
γεωγραφία. See next word, -ic and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: geographical-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:336 COLUMN:2 -->

## geography
geography, n. — F. geographic, fr. L. gedgraphia,
fr. Gk. γεωγραφία, 'geography', lit. 'description
of the earth', fr. γεωγράφος, 'earth-describing',
which is compounded of γεω- (see geo-) and
-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy and
cp. antkropogeography, phytogeograph,
zoogeography.

## geoid
geoid, п., a geometrical solid nearly identical
with the figure of the earth. — G. Geoid, coined
by the German geodesist JohannBenedikt Listing
(1808-82) in 1872 fr. Gk. γεοειδής, 'earthlike',
which is compounded of γη, 'the earth', and
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See geo-
and -oid and cp. geode.

## geology
geology, n. — ModL. geologia, 'the study of the
earth' (to be distinguished fr. ML. geologia,
which was used in the sense of 'the study of
earthly things', esp. applied to law);
compounded of geo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: geolog-ic, geolog-ic-al, adjs., geo-
log-ic-al-Iy, adv., geolog-ist, п., geolog-ize, intr.
and tr. v.

## geomancy
geomancy, п., divination by means of figures;
orig. divination by means of figures formed by
handfuls of earth. — F. geomancie, fr. ML. ged-
mantia, which is compounded of geo- and Gk.
μαντεία, Oracle, divination'. See -mancy.

## geomantic
geomantic, adj., pertaining to geomancy. — See
prec. word and mantic

## geometer
geometer, n. — L. geometris, geometra, fr. Gk.
γεωμέτρης, 'land measurer, geometer', which is
compounded of γεω- (see geo-) and μετρεϊν, 'to
measure', fr. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## geometric
geometric, adj. — Gk. γεωμετρικός, 'of geometry,
geometrical', fr. γεωμετρία. See geometry and -ic.
Derivatives: geometric-al, adj., geometrical-ly,
adv.

## geometrician
geometrician, n. — Formed fr. geometry with
suff. -ician.

## Geometridae
Geometridae, n. pi., a family of moths (entomol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idae, fr. L.
geometris, geometra, 'measurer of the earth' (see
geometer); so called because the larvae owing
to their bending and twisting motion appear as
if they were measuring the ground.

## geometrize
geometrize, intr. v., to study geometry; tr. v., to
work out by geometrical methods. — Formed
from next word with suff. -ize.

## geometry
geometry, n. — F. geometrie, fr. L. geometria, fr.
Gk. γεωμετρία, 'geometry', lit. 'measurement of
the earth', fr. γεωμέτρης. See geometer and -y
(representing Gk. -is).

## Geonoma
Geonoma, п., a genus of American palms of the
family Arecaceae (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γεω-
νόμος, 'one who distributes land; one who
receives a portion of distributed lands, colonist',
which is compounded of γεω- (see geo-) and
-νόμος, fr. νέμειν, 'to deal out, distribute'. See
geo- and Nemesis and cp. gnome, 'a dwarfish
person'.

## geophagy
geophagy, п., the practice of eating earth. — Lit.
'eating of earth'; compounded of geo- and Gk.
-φαγία, 'eating of. See -phagy.
Derivative: geophag-ist, n.

## geophone
geophone, п., instrument for detecting sounds
passing underground. — Compounded of geo-
and Gk. φωνή, 'sound'. See -phone.

## geophysics
geophysics, п., the physics of the earth. —
Compounded of geo- and physics.
Derivative: geophysic-al, adj.

## geoponic
geoponic, adj., pertaining to agriculture. — Gk.
γεωπονικός, 'pertaining to a husbandman', fr.
γεωπόνος, 'husbandman', which is compounded
of γεω- (see geo-) and πόνος, 'toil, labor', whence
πονεΐν, 'to toil, work hard', πονηρός, 'painful,
distressed; bad, worthless*. Gk. πόνος stands in
gradational relationship to πένης, 'poor', πενία,
'poverty', πένεσ&αι, 'to work for one's living,
to toil, labor'. Cp. Ponera and the second
element in Melipona, leucopenia.

## geoponics
geoponics, п., agriculture. — See prec. word and
-ics.

## George
George, masc. PN. — F. George(s), fr. Late L.
Georgius, fr. Gk. γεωργός, 'husbandman*, which
is compounded of γη, 'earth', and the base of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:336 COLUMN:3 -->
έργον, 'work'. See geo- and ergon and cp.
georgic.
Derivatives: Georgi-an, adj. and n.

## georgette
georgette, п., a thin silk crepe. — F., namsd after
Mme. Georgette de la Plante, a French
dressmaker.

## Georgian
Georgian, adj., pertaining to any of the four
Georges, kings of England. — See George and
-ian.

## Georgian
Georgian, adj., pertaining to the country of
Georgia in the Caucasus. — Formed fr. Georgia
with suff. -an.

## Georgiana
Georgiana, Georgina, fern. PN. — Fern,
derivatives of George (q.v.)

## georgic
georgic, adj., relating to agriculture. — L. geor-
gicus, fr. Gk. γεωργικός, 'of husbandry,
agricultural', fr. γεωργός, 'husbandman'. See
George and -ic.

## geotropic
geotropic, adj., pertaining to geotropism. — See
next word and -tropic.

## geotropism
geotropism, п., tendency to grow toward the
center of the earth (biol.) — Coined by the
German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank (1839-
1900) in 1868 fr. geo-, Gk. τροπή, 'a turning',
and suff. -ism. See trope, tropism, and cp. helio-
tropism and words there referred to.

## gephyr-
gephyr-, form of gephyro- before a vowel.

## Gephyrea
Gephyrea, п., a class of marine worms (ζοσί.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. γέφυρα, 'bridge'. See gephyro-.

## gephyro-
gephyro-, before a vowel gephyr-, combining
form meaning 'bridge'. — Fr. Gk. γέφυρα,
'bridge', which is prob. cogn. with Arm.
kamurj, 'bridge'.

## ger
ger, п., a proselyte to Judaism. — Heb. ger, lit.
'sojourner', from the stem of gur, 'to sojourn',
rel. to Arab, jar, Ethiop. gor, 'neighbor', Aram.
giyyora, Syr. giyyure, 'proselyte'. Cp. the first
element in Gershom.

## gerah
gerah, п., i/2oth of a shekel (Hebrew antiq.) —
Heb. gird", 'bean; the i/2oth part of the shekel',
rel. to Akkad. giru, Ί/20 of a shekel', and to
Heb. gargar, Aram. gargera, 'berry', Arab, jar-
jar, 'bean', Akkad. gurgurru, gingirru, name of
a plant. Cp. Gigartina.

## Gerald
Gerald, masc. PN. — OF. Giralt, Giraut (cp. F.
Geralde, Geraud, Giraud), introduced into
England by the Normans; fr. OHG. Gerwald, lit.
'spear wielder', compounded of ger, 'spear', and
-wald, from the base of waltan, 'to ruie', which
is rel. to OE. wealdan, of s.m. For the first
element see gar and cp. Gerard, for the second
see wield.

## Geraldine
Geraldine, fern. PN. — Formed fr. prec. word
with suff. -ine.

## Geraniaceae
Geraniaceae, n. pi., the geranium family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Geraninm with suff. -aceae.

## geraniaceous
geraniaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Geranium
Geranium, п., a genus of plants, the cranesbill
(bot.) — L. geranion, geranium, 'cranesbill', fr.
Gk. γεράνιον, of s.m., fr. γερανός, 'crane', which
is cogn. with L. grus, OE. cran, 'crane'; so called
because the fruit resembles a cranesbill. See
crane and cp. words there referred to.

## Gerard
Gerard, masc. PN. — OF. Gerart (F. Gerard), of
Tent, origin; cp. OHG. Gerhard, lit. 'strong
with the spear', compounded of ger, 'spear',
and hart, 'hard'. For the first element see gar
and cp. Gerald; for the second see hard.

## Gerardia
Gerardia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the English botanist John Gerarde
(1545-1612). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## geratology
geratology, п., the study of decadence, esp. in
groups of animals approaching extinction. —
Lit. 'the study of old age', compounded of Gk.
γήρας, gen. γήρατος, 'old age', and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See ger-
onto- and -logy.

## gerbe
gerbe, gerb, п., a wheat sheaf.— F.gerbe. See garb.

## gerent
gerent, п., one who rules, governs. — L. gerlns,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of gerere, 'to bear, carry,
produce, show, manifest, manage, rule, govern,
accomplish, perform, do', of uncertain origin;
not connected with ON. kasta, 'to cast' (see
cast). Cp. gest, jest and the second element in
armigerent, belligerent, vicegerent, claviger,
Globigerina, Peltigera. Cp. also gerund,
gestation, gesticulate, gesture, agger, cougestion, di-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:337 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GERFALCON | 310 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:337 COLUMN:1 -->
gest, egest, exaggerate, ingest, progestion,
register, registration, registry, res gesta, suggest.

## gerfalcon
gerfalcon, gyrfalcon, п., a large falcon of the
northern regions. — ME. gerfaucon, fr. OF.
gerfalc, gerfauc, gerfaucon (F. gerfaut), of Teut
origin; cp. ON. geirfalki, MHG. girfalc,
gerfalc. The first element of these Teut. words is
prob. related to Du. gier, OHG., MHG. glr,
G. Geier, 'vulture'; see lanunergeier. For the
second element see falcon.

## gerhardtite
gerhardtite, п., a basic copper nitrate (mineral.)
— Named after the French chemist Charles-.
Frederic Gerhardt (1816-56). For the ending see
subst. surf. -ite.

## geriatrics
geriatrics, п., that part of medicine which deals
with the diseases of old age. — Coined by I.L.
Nascher (1863-1944) in 1914 fr. Gk. γέρων, 'an
old man', and Ιατρίϊ, 'a healing'. See geronto-
and -iatric. The correct form would have been
gerontiatrics.

## germ
germ, n. — F. germe, fr. L. germen, 'sprig,
offshoot, bud, germ', dissimulated from "gen-men
and cogn. with OI. janman-, 'birth, origin'; fr.
I.-E. base *gen-, 'to beget, bear' (see genus and
cp. german, germen, germinate). For a similar
dissimilation of the consonants nm to rm, cp.
L. carmen, 'song', which derives from the stem
of canere, 'to sing'.
Derivative: germ, intr. v.

## german
german, adj., having the same parents. — ME.,
fr. OF. germain, fr. L. germanus, 'having the
same parents' (said of brothers or sisters),
'genuine', lit. Of the same seed', fr. germen,
'bud, germ'. See germ and cp. hermandad.

## Germaa
Germaa, n. and adj. — L. Germanus, 'German',
prob. of Celtic origin and orig. meaning "noisy',
from the I.-E. imitative base "gar-, 'to shout,
cry', whence also W. garm, Olr. gairm, 'shout,
cry'. See care and cp. garrulous.
Derivatives: Germanic (q.v.), German-ism, п.,
German-ist, a.,German-ist-ic, ad).,German-ize,lr.
and intr. v., German-iz-ation, n.,German-iz-er,n.

## germander
germander, п., any plant of the genus Teucrium
(bot.) — ME. germaunder, fr. OF. germandree,
fr. ML. germandra, fr. earlier gamandria, fr.
MGk. χαμανδρυά, fr. Gk. χαμαίδρϋς,
'germander', lit. 'tree on the ground', fr. χαμαί, "on the
ground', and δρυς, 'oak tree, tree'. See chamae-
and dryad.

## germane
germane, adj., relevant, appropriate. — A var. of
german. Cp. human and humane, urban and
urbane.
Derivatives: germane-ly, adv., germane-ness, n.

## Germanic
Germanic, adj. — L. Germanicus, 'pertaining to
the Germans or Germany*, fr. Germanus. See
German and -ic.
Derivative: Germanic, n.

## germanite
germanite, n„ a copper iron germanium sulfide
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr.
germanium; so called because it contains
germanium.

## germanium
germanium, п., name of a rare metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., coined by its discoverer, the
German chemist Klemens Alexander Winkler
(1838-1904) in 1886 after Germania, the Latin
name of his country. See German and -ium.

## Germano-
Germano-, combining form meaning 'German'.
— See German.

## Germanopbile
Germanopbile, Germanophil, п., a friend of
Germany or the Germans; adj., friendly to Germany
or the Germans. — Compounded of Germano-
and Gk. φίλος, 'friend'. See -phile, -phll.

## Germanophobe
Germanophobe, п., one who'fears or hates
Germany or the Germans. — Compounded of
Germane- and Gk. -φόβος, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See
-phobe.

## Germanophobia
Germanophobia, п., fear or hatred of Germany or
the Germans. — Compounded of Germano- and
Gk. -φοβία, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## Germantown
Germantown, germantown, п., a small, four-
wheeled, covered wagon. — Orig. a wagon
made at Germantown in Pennsylvania.

## germen
germen, п., germ (now used only figuratively). —
L. germen, 'bud, germ'. See germ.

## germicide
germicide, adj., destroying germs; п., a substance
destroying germs. — Compounded of germ and
L. -cida, 'killer', fr. caedere, 'to kill". See -cide,
'killer'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:337 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: germicid-al, adj.

## germinal
germinal, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
a germ. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
germen, gen. germinis, 'bud, germ'. See germ
and cp. germen.
Derivative: germinal-ly, adv.

## Germinal
Germinal, п., name of the 7th month of the
French revolutionary calendar (lasting from
March 21st to April 19th). — F., lit. 'the seed
month'; coined by Fabre d'Eglantine in 1793,
fr. L. germen, gen. germinis. See prec. word.

## germiaant
germiaant, adj., germinating. — L. germinans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of germinare. See next
word and -ant.

## germinate
germinate, intr. and tr. v. — L. germinaius, pp.
of germinare, 'to sprout, bud', fr. germen, gen.
germinis, 'sprig, offshoot, bud, germ*. See germ
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: germination (q.v.), germinat-ive,
