adj., germinative-ly, adv., germinat-or, n.

## germination
germination, n. — L. germinatio, gen. -onis, 'a
sprouting forth, budding', fr. germinaius, pp. of
germinare. See prec. word and -ion.

## germon
germon, п., the albacore (Germo alalunga). —
F., of unknown origin.

## geront-
geront-, form of geronru- before a vowel.

## gerontic
gerontic, adj., pertaining to old age. — Gk.
γεροντικός, 'pertaining to an old man', fr. γέρων,
gen. γέροντος, 'old man'. See geronto- and -ic.

## geronto-
geronto-, before a vowel geront-, combining form
meaning 'old man'. — Gk. γεροντο-, γεροντ-,
fr. γέρων, gen. γέροντος, 'old man', rel. to
γεραιός, 'old', γήρας, 'old age', γηραλέος, 'old',
γέρας, 'gift of honor, gift, present', γραΰς, 'old
woman; wrinkled skin', fr. I.-E. base *ger(ey,
'to become ripe, grow old', whence also OI.
jara, jaras-, 'old age', jdrati, jlryati, 'makes old,
grows old', jarimdn-, 'old age', jarah, 'growing
old', jirndfi, 'old', Avestic zaurvan, 'old age',
ModPers. zar, 'old man', Arm. cer, 'old; old
man'. Formally Gk. γέρων represents a pres.
part, and is the exact equivalent of OI. jarant-,
Ossetic zarond, 'old man'. See cora, 'grain', and
cp. Ageratum, caloyer, gcratology, geriatrics,
gerusia, progeria. Cp. also Zoroaster. For the
participial suff. (OI. -ant, Gk. -ων (for *-οντ)
see -ant.

## gerontocracy
gerontocracy, п., rule of old men. —
Compounded of geronto- and Gk. -κρατίϊ, 'rule of, fr.
κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'. See -cracy.

## gerontology
gerontology, п., study of the phenomena of old
age. — Compounded of geronto- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See -logy.

## -gerous
-gerous, combining form meaning 'bearing,
carrying, producing', as in lanigerous. — Formed
on analogy of -ferous fr. Latin adj. suff. -ger,
from the stem of gerere, 'to bear, carry,
produce'. See gerent.

## gerrymander
gerrymander, tr. v., to divide (a county, etc.) into
electoral divisions so as to gain advantage for
one's own party. — Formed from the name of
Elbridge Gerry, governor of Massachusetts,
U.S.A., and the ending of salamander.
Derivative: gerrymander, n.

## gersdorffite
gersdorffite, п., a nickel sulfarsenide (mineral.) —
Named after von Gersdorff, proprietor of the
mine where it was found. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## Gershom
Gershom, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the
firstborn son of Moses. — Heb. Ger'shom, a
derivative of the base of garash (Qal), gerash (Pi'el),
'he drove out, cast out', hence lit. meaning
'exile'. The explanation of the name Ί have
been a sojourner in a foreign land' (Ex. 2:23;
18:3) indicates that Moses chose for his son.
such a current name (cp. Ger'shon, name of a
son of Levi), as might also be interpreted as a
compound of the words glr, 'a sojourner' (see
ger), and sham, 'there*, thus commemorating
the fact that at the time of his first son's birth
Moses was a sojourner in a foreign land (cp.
the Septuagint rendering of the name: Γηρσάμ,
which is the transliteration of ger sham, 'a
sojourner there'). Heb. garash, gerash is rel. to
Aram, g'rash (Pe'al), garish (Pa'el), 'he
divorced', and prob. also to Arab, jashara, 'he sent

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:337 COLUMN:3 -->
beasts to pasture [for sense development cp.
Heb. mighrash, 'pasture land', orig. 'place of
(cattle) driving', fr. garash, 'he drove out'].

## Gertrude
Gertrude, fern. PN. — F., fr. OHG. Geretrudis,
Geredrudis, compounded of ger, 'spear', and
trut, drut (whence MHG trut, G. traut), 'beloved,
dear'. For the first element see gar and cp.
Gerald, Gerard, Gervais. For the second element
see true and cp. the second element in Astrid,
Ermentrud.

## gerund
gerund, п., verbal noun used for all cases of the
infinitive but the nominative (Latin grammar).
— L. gerundium, fr. gerundum = gerendum,
'that which is to be done', fr. gerere, 'to bear,
carry, accomplish, do'. See gerent.
Derivatives: gerund-ial, adj., gerund-ial-ly, adv.

## gerundive
gerundive, adj., pertaining to the gerund; п.,
verbal adj., formed from the stem of the gerund
and expressing necessity, fitness, etc. (Latin
grammar). — L. gerundivus, fr. gerundium. See
prec. word and -ive.
Derivatives: gerundiv-al, adj.,gerundive-ly, adv.

## gerusia
gerusia, п., council of the elders; spec, the senate
of Sparta and other Dorian cities. — L. gerusia,
fr. Gk. γερουσία, Att. form of γερόντια,
'council of the elders', fr. γέρων, gen. γέροντος, 'old
man'. See geronto-.

## Gervais
Gervais, Gervas, Gervase, masc. PN. — F.
Gervais, fr. OHG. Gervas, lit. 'serving with one's
spear', fr. ger, 'spear', and the Celtic base *vas-,
meaning 'servant'. For the first element see gar
and cp. Gertrude and words there referred to.
For the second element see vassal.

## Gerygune
Gerygune, п., a genus of small Australian singing
birds (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γηρυγόνη,
fern. οίγηρυγόνος,'ΡΟΓη of sound', compounded
of γηρυς, 'voice, sound', and -γόνος, 'born of,
from the stem of γίγνεσθαι, 'to be bom'. See
garrulous and genus and cp. gono-.

## Gesneria
Gesneria, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Swiss naturalist Konrad von
Gesner (1516-65). For the ending see suff. -ia.

## gesso
gesso, п., plaster of Paris. — It., fr. L. gypsum,
'plaster, gypsum'. See gypsum.

## gest
gest, п., an exploit, a deed (archaic). — F. geste,
lit. 'something done', fr. L. gesta, 'deeds, acts',
neut. pi. of gestus, pp. of gerere, 'to bear, carry,
produce, do'. See gerent and cp. jest, which is a
doublet of gest. Cp. also res gestae.

## Gestalt
Gestalt, п., an organized whole in which all
elements affect one another, the whole being more
than the simple sum of its elements; a
configuration (psychology). — G., 'shape, form,
figure, configuration', fr. MHG. gestalt,
'appearance, quality', prop. pp. of MHG. stellen,
'to place; to fashion' (whence G. stellen, 'to
place'). See stalL The term Gestalt was
introduced into psychology by the German
philosopher Christian von Ehrenfels (1859-1932) in
1890.

## Gestalt psychology
Gestalt psychology, the psychology of a school
founded about 1912 by M. Wertheimer, K.
Koffka and W. Kohler and based on the
concept of Gestalt or Organized whole'; configur-
ationism. — See prec. word.

## Gestapo
Gestapo, п., the German secret state police under
the Nazis. — From the abbreviation of Geheime
Stoatspolizei, lit. 'secret state police'.

## gestate
gestate, tr. v., to carry in the womb during
pregnancy. — L. gestdtus, pp. of gesture, 'to carry,
carry about', intensive of gerere (pp. gestus),
'to carry'. See gerent and verbal suff. -ate.

## gestation
gestation, п., ι) the act of carrying in the uterus,
pregnancy; 2) the period of gestation. — L.
gestatio, gen. -onis, 'a carrying about', fr.ge-
status, pp. of gesture. See prec. word and -ion.

## gestatorial
gestatorial, adj., used for carrying about
(applied to the chair in which the Pope is carried
on certain occasions.) — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. gestatorius, 'that which serves for
carrying', fr. gestus, pp. of gerere, 'to carry'. See
gestate and adj. suff. -ory.

## gesticulate
gesticulate, intr. v., to make gestures; tr. v., to
indicate by gesticulating. — L. gesticulatus, pp.
of gesticularl, 'to make pantomimic gestures',
fr. gesticulus, 'gesticulation, gesture', dimin. of
gestus, 'gesture', lit. 'carriage, posture', fr.
gestus, pp. of gerere, 'to bear, carry'. See gerent

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:338 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 311 | GIGOT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:338 COLUMN:1 -->
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: gesticulation (q.v.), gesticulal-ive,
adj., gesticulat-ive-ly, adv., gesticulator (q.v.),
gesticulat-ory, adj.

## gesticulation
gesticulation, n. — L, gesticulatio, gen. -onis, 'a
pantomimic motion, gesticulation', fr. gesticu-
latus, pp. of gesticulari. See prec. word and -ion.

## gesticulator
gesticulator, n. — L., fr. gesticuldtus, pp. of
gesticulari. See gesticulate and agential surf. -or.

## gesture
gesture, n. — ML. gestura, 'behavior, conduct',
fr. L. gestus, pp. of gerere, 'to bear, carry'. See
gerent and -ure.
Derivatives: gesture, intr. and tr. v., gestur-er, n.

## get
get, tr. and intr. v. — ME. geten, fr. ON. geta,
'to reach, get', rel. to OE. -gilan, -gietan (only
in compounds, as be-gitan, be-gietan, 'to get,
beget', for-gietan, 'to forget'), fr. I.-E. base
*ghe(n)d-, 'to clasp, seize, reach, attain, hold',
whence also Gk. χανδάνειν, 'to hold, contain',
L. -hendere in prekendere, 'to grasp, seize, lay
hold of, hedera, 'ivy', lit. 'the clasping plant',
praeda (for *prai-heda), 'prey', Alb. gen, gen,
Gheg gej, Ί find', W. gannu, 'to hold, contain',
genni, 'to be held, contained', and perh. also
OSlav. gadati, 'to guess, suppose'. Cp. beget,
forget, guess. Cp. also apprehend, apprentice, apprise,
comprehend, comprise, depredate, emprise,
enterprise, entrepreneur, epris, Hedera, impregnable,
impresa, impresario, lierre, misprision,
predatory, pregnant, 'with child', prehensile, presa,
prey, prison, purpresture, pry, 'to raise',
reprehend, reprehensible, reprisal, reprise, surprise.
Derivatives: get, n. (lit. 'something got'), gett-er,
п., gett-ing, n.

## Geullah
Geullah, п., the benediction which follows the
Shema in the morning and evening service
{Jewish liturgy). — Heb. ge'ullak, 'redemption',
from the stem of ga'al, 'he has redeemed': so
called because it ends with the words "who has
redeemed Israel". Cp. goel.

## Geum
Geum, п., a genus of plants, the avens (bot.) —
L. 'geum, 'the herb bennet, avens'.

## gewgaw
gewgaw, п., a toy, a specious triHe. — Of
uncertain origin.

## geyser
geyser, n. — Icel. Geysir, name of a geyser in
Iceland, lit. meaning 'the gusher', fr. geysa, 'to
gush*, which is rel. to ON. gjosa, 'to gush', freq.
of gjdta, 'to pour'. See found, 'to cast', and cp.
gust, 'blast of wind'.
Derivatives: geyser-ic, adj., geyserite (q.v.)

## geyserite
geyserite, п., a variety of opal (mineral.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with subst. suff. -ite.

## gharry
gharry, gharri, garry, п., cart, carriage (Anglo-
Indian). — Hind. gari.

## ghastly
ghastly, adj., horrible. — ME. gastly, fr. OE.
gastlic, 'spiritual', fr. gust, 'spirit'. See ghost and
adj. suff. -ly and cp. aghast.
Derivatives: ghastli-ly, adv., ghastli-ness, n.

## ghat
ghat, ghaut, п., a mountain pass; a landing place
(India). — Hind, ghat, fr. OI. ghaftah, 'landing
place, bathing place', which is of uncertain
etymology.

## ghazi
ghazi, п., among Mohammedans, a warrior
fighting against infidels. — Arab, ghazt, prop,
panic, of ghaia (stem gh-z-w), 'he made war'.
Cp. razzia.

## Gheber
Gheber, Ghebre, п., a member of the Persian sect
of fireworshipers. — F. guebre, fr. Pers. gdbr,
'fireworshiper'; not borrowed fr. Arab, kdfir,
'unbeliever' (as most lexicographers would have
it), but a native Persian word. Cp. giaour.

## ghee
ghee, п., boiled butter (India). — Hind, ghi, fr.
OI. ghrtam, 'clarified butter, ghee', which is
cogn. with Mir. gert, 'milk', and prob. rel. to
OI. jlgharti, 'besprinkles'.

## gherkin
gherkin, п., a small cucumber. — Fr. Du. gurken
(pi. of gurk, but mistaken for a singular),
shortened form of a(u)gurk(je); rel. to EFris.
augurke, G. Gurke, Dan. agurk, Swed. gurka.
These words are traceable to a Slavic source (cp.
Pol. ogorek, Russ. ogurec, etc.). The Slavic words
themselves derive fr. Late Gk. άγγούριον,
'watermelon', which is a loan word fr. Pers.
angarah. Cp. anguria.

## ghetto
ghetto, п., the Jews' quarter in a city. — It.,
perhaps aphetic for borghetto, dimin. of borgo, *a
small market town, borough', which is of Teut.
origin. See borough.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:338 COLUMN:2 -->

## Ghibelline
Ghibelline, п., an adherent of the emperor in
medieval Italy (opposed to the Papal party; see
Guelph). — It. Ghibellino, fr. G. Waibiinger,
named after Waiblingen, a castle of the Hohen-
staufen family in the valley of the Rems River
in Wiirttemberg, Germany.
Derivative: Ghibelline, adj.

## ghost
ghost, n. — ME. gast, gost, fr. OE. gast, 'breath,
spirit, soul, life', rel. to OS. gist, OFris. jest,
gast, MDu. gheest, Du. geest, OHG., MHG.,
G. geist, 'spirit, ghost', OE. gxstan, 'to frighten,
alarm', fr. I.-E. base *gheizd-, 'to frighten; to
be angry', whence also OI., hidah, 'wrath',
hidati, 'excites, vexes', Avestic zoizdishta-, 'the
most abominable'. Base "gheizd is a
-(/-enlargement of base 'gheis-, whence Avestic zaesha-,
'horrible', zoishnu-, 'shuddering', Goth, us-
gais-jan, 'to frighten', ON. geiski, 'fright, terror',
geis-ka-futtr, 'terrible'. Cp. aghast, ghastiy. Cp.
also the second element in Zeitgeist,

## ghostly
ghostly, adj. — ME. gostly, fr. OE. gastlic,
'spiritual'. See ghastly.
Derivatives: ghost-li-ly, adv., ghost-li-ness, n.

## ghoul
ghoul, п., an evil demon who robs graves and
feeds on the dead. — Arab, ghul, fr. ghala, 'he
took suddenly'. Cp. Algol.
Derivatives: ghoul-ish, adj., ghoul-ish-ly, adv.

## ghurry
ghurry, п., clepsydra, clock, watch, space of time,
hour (India). — Hind, ghari, fr. OI. ghafika,
'water jar, pot' (serving as a water clock), fr.
gkafah, of s.m., which is of uncertain origin.

## ghyll
ghyll, п., a ravine. — A N. Engl, dialectal var.
of gill, 'ravine'; introduced into English by the
English poet William Wordsworth (1770-1850).

## giant
giant, n. — ME. geant, fr. OF. geant (F. geant),
fr. earlier jaiant, fr. VL. *gagantem, ace. of
"gagas, assimilated vr. L. gigas, 'a giant', fr.
Gk. γίγας, 'a giant', fr. Γίγας, 'any of the sons
of the Earth and Tartarus', which is prob. a
pre-Hellenic word. Cp. gigantic.
Derivatives: giant, adj., giant-ess, a., giantism
(q.v.), giant-like, adj.

## giantism
giantism, п., pathological condition characterized
by abnormal tallness (med.) — A hybrid formed
from prec. word with -ism, a suff. of Greek
origin. The correct form is gigantism (q.v.)

## giaour
giaour, п., a term applied by the Turks to all non-
Mohammedans. — Turk, giaur, 'infidel', fr.
Pers. gaur, a variant of gdbr, 'fireworshipper'.
See Gheber.

## gib
gib, п., a tomcat. — From Gib, pet form of the
name Gilbert.

## gib
gib, п., a hook. — Of uncertain origin.

## gibbar
gibbar, п., a finback whale (obsol.) — F., fr. Arab.
jabbar, 'giant, tyrant', which is rel. to Heb.gibbor,
'strong, mighty; mighty man, hero'. See Gabriel.

## gibber
gibber, intr. v., to speak unintelligibly. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. jabber,

## gibberish
gibberish, п., unintelligible talk. — Formed from
prec. word with adj. suff. -ish.

## gibbet
gibbet, п., gallows. — ME. gibet, fr. OF. (= F.)
gibet, 'gallows; a bent stick', dimin. of OF.
gibe, 'staff, stick', which is perh. of Teut. origin;
see Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p.281 s.v. gibet.
Cp. jib, 'the projecting arm of a crane'.
Derivative: gibbet, tr. v.

## gibbon
gibbon, п., a small, long-armed ape. — F., a name
of Indian origin brought to Europe by the
Marquis Joseph-Francois Dupleix (1697-1763),
governor-general of the French possessions in
India (1742-54).

## gibbose
gibbose, adj., gibbous. — See gibbous.

## gibbosity
gibbosity, n. — F. gibbosite. See next word and
-йу.

## gibbous
gibbous, adj. — L. gibbosus, 'humpbacked', fr.

## gibbus
gibbus, 'hump', which is of uncertain origin. It
is possibly a loan word fr. Heb. gibbin,
'humpbacked'; see Heinrich Lewy, Die semitischen
Fremdworter im Griechischen, p. 71. — heb.
gibbin is rel.· to Heb. gabhnin, 'peak,
summit', Talmudic Heb. gabhnun, 'humpbacked',
Mishnaic Heb. gabhtn, Aram.-Syr. g'bhina,
'eyebrow', Arab, jabtn, 'side of the forehead'.
Derivatives: gibbous-ly, adv., gibbous-ness, n.

## gibe
gibe, jibe, intr. v., to sneer. — Prob. rel. to Du.
gijbelen, 'to sneer', and possibly also to ON.
geip, 'idle talk', geipa, 'to talk nonsense'.
Derivatives: gibe, jibe, п., gib-ing-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:338 COLUMN:3 -->

## giblets
giblets, n. pi., edible internal parts of poultry. —
ME. gibelet, fr. OF. gibelet, 'game' (whence F.
gibelotte, 'ragout, stew'), formed fr. *giberet,
dimin. of OF. (= F.) gibier, 'game', a var. of
OF. gibiez, it. Frankish 'gabaiti, 'the act of
hunting with falcons', which is rel. to OHG.
beisan, 'to fly a falcon', lit. 'to cause to bite'
(whence MHG. gebeije = Frankish *gabaiti)
fr. Ыззап, 'to bite'. See bite.

## Gibraltar
Gibraltar, п., name of the Rock at the western
entrance to the Mediterranean. — Fr. Arab.
jabal (in vulgar pronunciation jebel) at Tariq,
'mount of Tariq', named after Tariq, the
Moslem invader of Spain who landed there in 711.
See javali and cp. Bible.

## gibraltar
gibraltar, п., American name of a hard ('rocky')
candy. — Named after the fortress Gibraltar.
See prec. word.

## gibus
gibus, п., an opera hat. — F., named after its
inventor, a Parisian hatmaker, who lived in the
1st half of the 19th century.

## gid
gid, п., a brain disease of sheep. — Back
formation fr. giddy.

## giddy
giddy, adj. — ME. gidy, 'mad', fr. OE. gydig,
'insane', orig. 'possessed by a god', fr. Teut. base
*gud-, 'god'; see god. For sense development cp.
Gk. ένθεος, 'full of the god, inspired by a god'
(see enthusiasm). Cp. gid.
Derivatives: giddy, tr. and intr. v.,giddi-ly, adv.,
giddi-ness, n.

## Gideon
Gideon, 1) masc. PN.; г) in the Bible, a hero and
judge of Israel. — Heb. Gidh'dn, lit. 'feller',
from the stem of gddha', 'he cut off, hewed,
felled', which is rel. to Aram, g'dha', Arab.
jada'a, of s.m.

## gidya
gidya, n.,'an Australian tree. — A native name.

## gieseckite
gieseckite, п., a variety of pinite (mineral.) —
Named after Sir Charles Giesecke, who brought
it from Greenland. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Gifola
Gifola, п., a genus of plants, the cotton rose (bot.)
— ModL., anagram of Filago, the name of a
related genus.

## gift
gift, n. — ME., fr. ON. gift, gipt, which is rel.
to OE. gift (whence ME. yift), OS., Du. gift
OFris. jefte, MLG. gifte, MDu. ghifte, Goth.
-gifts (in compounds), OHG., MHG. gift, 'gift;
poison', G. Gift (neut.), 'poison', Mil-gift (fern.),
'dowry'; prop, verbal nouns formed fr. ON.
gefa, OE. gifan, giefan .etc., 'to give'. See give.
Derivatives: gift, tr. v., gift-ed, adj.

## gig
gig, п., a light two-wheeled carriage. — Prob. of
Scand. origin and lit. meaning 'a whipping top'.
Cp. Dan. gig, 'top', ON. geiga, 'to turn aside,
waver', which are prob. of imitative origin. Cp.
fizgig, whirligig.

## gigantean
gigantean, adj., gigantic. — Formed with suff.
-an fr. L. giganteus, fr. gigas, gen. giganlis,
'giant'. See giant.

## gigantic
gigantic, adj. — Formed with suff. -ic, fr. L.
gigas; gen. gigantis, 'giant'. See giant.
Derivatives: gigantic-al-ly, adv., gigantic-ness, n.

## gigantism
gigantism, п., abnormal tallness, — See giant
and -ism and cp. giantism.

## giganto-
giganto-, combining form meaning 'giant'. — Gk.
γίγαντα-, fr. γίγας, gen. γίγαντος, 'giant'. See
giant.

## gigantomachy
gigantomachy, gigantomachia, п., the war
between the Olympian gods and the giants (Greek
mythol.) — Gk. γιγαντομαχία, 'battle of the
giants', compounded of γίγας, gen. γίγαντος,
'giant', and μάχη, 'battle'. See giant and -machy.

## Gigartina
Gigartina,n., a genus of red algae (bot.)—ModL.,
fr. Gk. γίγαρτον, 'grapestone', prob. fr. Aram.
gighartd, 'kernel, stone', which is rel. to Aram.
garg'rd, 'berry, grain'. See gerah.

## giggle
giggle, intr. v. and n. — Of imitative origin.

## gigliato
gigliato, п., name of a Neapolitan silver coin,
issued by Charles II of Anjou. — It., fr. giglio,
'lily', a word formed with dissimilation fr. L.
lilium, which, for its part, was assimilated fr.
Gk. λείριον, 'lily'. See lily.

## gigolo
gigolo, п., a paid male dancing partner. — F.,
fr'. gigoier, 'to move the shanks, to hop', fr.
gigue, 'shank, fiddle', which is of Teut. origin.
See gigue.

## gigot
gigot, п., leg of mutton. — F., 'leg of mutton',
fr. OF. gigue, whence also E. gigue (q.v.). Cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:339 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GIGUE | 312 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:339 COLUMN:1 -->
prec. word.

## gigue
gigue, п., ι) a stringed instrument; 2) a kind
of dance. — F., reborrowed fr. E. jig, 'a quick
dance' (q.v.), which itself was borrowed fr. OF.
giguer, 4o move the shanks, hop, dance', fr.
gigue, 'shank; fiddle'. Cp. the two prec. words.

## Gila monster
Gila monster, a kind of venomous lizard. — From
Gila, name of a river in Arizona.

## Gilbert
Gilbert, masc. PN. — A blend of OF. Guillebert
(whence F. Guilbert) and OF. Gilebert (whence
F. Gilbert). Both OF. names are of Teut. origin.
OF. Guillebert derives fr. OHG. Williberht, lit.
'a bright will', fr. willio, willo, 'will", and beraht,
'bright'; see will and bright. OF. Gilebert comes
fr. Gisilbert, lit. 'a bright pledge', fr. OHG. gisil,
'pledge', which is a Celtic loan word (cp. Olr.
giall, W. gwystl, 'pledge'), and fr. OHG. beraht,
'bright'.

## gilbert
gilbert, п., name of the C.G.S. unit of
magnetomotive force (electr.) — Named after the
English physician and physicist William Gilbert
(1544-1603).

## Gilbertian
Gilbertian, adj., resembling the style of the
English author Sir William Schwenck Gilbert (1836-
1911). For the ending see suff. -ian.

## Gilbertine
Gilbertine, п., a member of the religious order
founded by St. Gilbert in the 12th century. For
the ending see suff. -ine (representing L. -tnus).

## gilbertite
gilbertite, п., a variety of damourite (.mineral.) —
Named after Davies Gilbert (1767-1839). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
gild.'n. — See guild.

## gild
gild, tr. v. — ME. gilden, fr. OE. gyldan, fr. OE.
gold, 'gold'. Cp. ON. gylla, 'to gild', fr. ON.
gull, goll, 'gold', and see gold.
Derivatives: gild-ed, adj., gild-er, п., gild-ing, n.

## Giles
Giles, masc. PN; often used to denote a simple-
minded farmer. — OF. Gil(l)es (F. Gilles), fr.
L. Aegidius, fr. aegis. See aegis.

## gilet
gilet, п., a waistcoat. — F., fr. Sp. jileco, gileco
(the modern Sp. form is chaleco), fr. Algerian
Arab, jaleco, 'coat· of Christians in Moorish
captivity', ult. fr. Turk, yelek.

## Gilia
Gilia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named in 1794 after the Spanish botanist Felipe
Luis Gil.

## gill
gill, п., the organ of respiration in fishes. — ME.
gile, gille, from Scandinavian; cp. ON.giolnar
(pi.), 'jaws', Swed. gal, 'gill, jaw', Dan. guile,
'gill', which are cogn. with Gk. χείλος, 'lip',
χελυνη, 'lip, jaw'. Cp. chilo-.
Derivative: gill-ed, adj.

## gill
gill, п., a small measure. — ME. gille, gylle, fr.
OF. gille, gelle, fr. L. gillo, gelid, 'cooling vessel',
which is prob. of Sem. origin. Cp. Heb. gullah,
'oilcan', Arab. gul/ah, 'earthen pitcher".

## gill
gill, ghyll, п., a ravine (Scot, and dial. Engl.) —
ME. gille, gylle, fr. ON. gil, 'a narrow valley,
glen', which is rel. to MLG. gil, 'throat', OHG.
gil, 'hernia', OE. gilan (for *gailjan), 'to
hinder, impede'. Cp. goal.

## Gill
Gill, also Jill, 1) fem. PN.; 2) girl sweetheart. —
Abbreviation of Gillian, resp. Jillian, fr. L.
Juliana. See next word and cp. jilt.

## Gillian
Gillian, fem. PN. — Fr. F. Juliane, fr. L. Juliana,
fem. of Julianus, lit. 'of Julius'. See Julian,
Juliana.

## Gillenia
Gillenia, п., a genus of plants, the Indian physic
(bot.) — ModL., named after the German
botanist Arnold Gill (latinized into Gillenius),
who wrote on horticulture in 1627. For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## gillie
gillie, п., a male attendant on a Highland chief.
— Gael, gille, giolla, 'boy, servant'.

## gillyflower
gillyflower, n. — Altered fr. ME. gilofre, fr. OF.
gilofre, girofre (F. girofle), 'clove', fr. L. cary-
ophyllon, fr. Gk.xapuotpuXXov, 'clove tree', which
is compounded of κάρυον, 'nut', and φύλλον,
'leaf. See careen and phyllo- and cp. Caryo-
phyllaceae.

## gilt
gilt, п., gilding.—Prop. pp. of gild, used as a noun.

## gimbal
gimbal, п., a device consisting of a pair of rings.
— Fr. earlier gimrnal, fr. OF. gemel (whence F.
jumeau), 'a twin'. See gemel.

## gimcrack
gimcrack, п., a tawdry, useless thing. — Of
unknown origin.
Derivatives: gimcrack, adj., gimcrack-ery, n.

## gimel
gimel, п., name of the 3rd letter of the Hebrew

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:339 COLUMN:2 -->
alphabet. — Heb. gimel, rel. to gamdl, 'camel'
(whence Gk. κάμηλος, L. camelus, 'camel'); so
called in allusion to the ancient Hebrew form
of this letter representing the neck of a camel.
See camel and cp. gamma,

## gimlet
gimlet, gimblet, n„ a small tool for boring holes.
— ME. gymelot, fr. MF. guimbelet, gimbelet
(F. gibelet), fr. MDu. wimmelkijn, dimin. of
wimmel, 'auger, drill'; see wimble. The dimin.
suff. -et in OF. guimbelet, etc., is the exact
rendering of the Dutch dirr.in. suff. -kijn (see -kin).
Cp. wimble.
Derivatives: gimlet, tr. v., gimlet-y, adj.

## gimmal
gimmal, n. — See gimbal.

## gimmer
gimmer, п., she lamb. — ON. gymbr, 'ewe lamb
of one year'. See chimera.

## gimmick
gimmick, п., a secret device (slang). — Of
uncertain origin.

## gimp
gimp, п., ornamental material used for trimming
women's dresses, furniture, etc. — F. guimpe,
fr. OF. guimpte, wimple, fr. OHG. wimpal. See
wimple and cp. guipure.

## gin
gin, п., liquor. — Abbreviation of geneva (q.v.)

## gin
gin, п., machine. — ME., aphetic for engine (q.v.)

## gin
gin, tr. and intr. v., to begin (poetic). — ME.
ginnen, aphetic for beginnen; fr. OE. beginnan,
'to begin". See begin.

## gin
gin, п., an aboriginal Australian woman. — A
native name.

## ginete
ginete, п., a horseman. — Sp. ginete, jinete, fr.
Arab. Zanatah, in VArab. pronunciation Zeneta,
Zenite, name of a great Berber tribe, famous
for its horsemen, many of whom served the
sultans of Granada. For the change of Arab, ζ
to Sp. g cp. giraffe.

## gmgai
gmgai, n. — See jingal.

## gingeli
gingeli, n. — See giagili.

## ginger
ginger, n. — ME. gingevir, gingivere, fr. OE.
gingiber, fr. OF. gingibre, gingembre (F. gin-
gembre), fr. L. gingiber, zingiber, fr. Gk. ζιγ-
γίβερις, fr. Pali singivera-, fr. OI. sfngavera-,
'ginger', lit. 'hornlike', fr. sj-ngam, 'horn', and
vera, 'body'; so called in allusion to the
hornlike shape of the root. See horn and cp. Zingiber.
Derivatives: ginger, tr. v., ginger-y, adj.

## gingerly
gingerly, adj., wary; adv. warily. — Of uncertain
origin; possibly formed with suff. -ly fr. OF.
gencbr, gensor, 'prettier', compar. of gent, 'of
noble birth, noble, gentle, pretty', fr. L.genitus,
'born', pp. of gignere, 'to beget, bear, bring
forth'. See genus.

## giugham
giugham, п., a kind of striped cotton or linen. —
F. guingan, fr. Malay ginggang, 'striped', used
as a noun in the sense of 'striped cotton'.

## gingili
gingili, also gingeli, п., sesame seed (India). —
Hind, jinjali, fr. Arab, juljutan, 'sesame seed'.
For the corruption of this Arabic word in Hind,
cp. Sp. aljonjoli, ajonjoli, 'sesame seed', fr.
Arab, al-juljulan, 'the sesame seed'.

## gingiva
gingiva, п., gum (anal.) — L. gingiva, 'gum', of
uncertain origin; possibly meaning lit.
'something round', and cogn. with Gk. γογγύλος,
'round', γόγγρος, 'tubercular growth on trees;
sea eel, conger', lit. 'something round'; not
cogn. with E. chew. Cp. conger.

## gingival
gingival, adj., pertaining to the gums. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. gingiva, 'gum'. See
prec. word.

## gingivitis
gingivitis, п., inflammation of the gums (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. gingiva (see
giagiva) and -itls, a suff. of Greek origin.

## ginglymoid
ginglymoid, adj., resembling a hinge joint (anal.)
— Gk. γιγγλυμοειδής, 'having the shape of a
hinge joint', lit. 'like a hinge', fr. γίγγλυμος,
'hinge', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. ε18ος, 'form,
shape'. See next word and -oid.

## ginglymns
ginglymns, п., a hinge joint (anat.) — Medical
L„ lit. 'hingelike joint', fr. Gk. γίγγλυμος,
'hinge', which is of unknown origin. The name
γίγγλυμος was introduced into anatomy by
Hippocrates and denoted originally the roll-like
part of the bone of the upper arm. See Joseph
Hyrtl, Onomatologia anatomica, p. 238.

## ginkgo
ginkgo, п., an ornamental tree of Japan and
China. — Jap. gingko.

## ginseng
ginseng, п., a Chinese medical plant. — Chin.
jen-shen.

## Giottesque
Giottesque, adj., in the style of Giotto di Bon-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:339 COLUMN:3 -->
done, an Italian painter who lived about 1300.
For the ending see suff. -esque.

## gipsy
gipsy, n. — See gypsy.

## giraffe
giraffe, n. — F. girafe. It. giraffa, fr. Arab.
zardfa", which is prob. of African origin. The
circumstance that Arab, z has become g
(pronounced j) proves that the word came into the
European languages through the medium of the
Italians.

## girandole
girandole, п., 1) a kind of firework; 2) a water jet;
3) a kind of earring. — F., fr. It. girandola,
dimin. of giranda, 'a revolving jet', fr. L. gyran-
dus, gerundive of gyrare, 'to turn round in a
circle, revolve". See gyrate and cp. next word.
For other Latin gerundives or their derivatives
used in English cp. agenda and words there
referred to.

## girasol
girasol, girasole, п., ι) the sunflower; 2) the fire
opal. — It. girasole (whence also F. girasol), lit.
'turning toward the sun', fr. girare, 'to rotate,
turn' (fr. L. gyrare), and sole (fr. L. solem, ace.
of sol), 'sun'. See gyrate and Sol and cp.
Jerusalem, artichoke. For sense development cp.
heliotrope, and It. tornasole (see turnsole).

## gird
gird, tr. v., to encircle. — ME. girden, gerden,
etc., fr. OE. gyrdan, rel. to OS. gurdian, ON.
gyrda, OFris. gerda, OHG. gurtan, gurten,
MHG. gurten, gurten, G. gurten, Goth. Ы-
gairdan, uf-gairdan, 'to gird', ON. gjord, MHG.,
G. gurt, Goth, gairda, 'girdle', and to OE. geard,
ON. gardr, 'hedge, enclosure'. See yard,
'enclosure', and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also girdle, girt, girth.

## gird
gird, intr. v., to gibe, tanrr. — The original
meaning was 'to strike'; fr. ME. girden,gerden,
etc., 'to strike, cut through', which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. gride.
Derivative: gird, п., a taunt, gibe.

## girder
girder, п., a wooden or steel beam. — Formed
with agential suff. -er fr. gird, 'to encircle'.
Derivative: girder-age, n.

## girder
girder, п., one who gibes or taunts. — Formed
with agential suff. -er fr. gird, 'to gibe, taunt'.

## girdle
girdle, п., belt. — ME. girdil, gerdelle, gurdel, fr.
OE. gyrdel, rel. to ON. gyrdill, Swed. gordel,
OFris. gerdel, MLG. gordel, Du. gordel, OHG.
gurtil, gurtila, MHG., G. giirtel, 'belt', and to
OE. gyrdan, 'to gird'. See gird, 'to encircle', and
instrumental suff. -le. Derivative: girdle, tr. v.

## girdle
girdle, n. — A var. of griddle.

## girl
girl, n. — ME. gurle, gurl, gerle, gerl, 'boy, girl',
rel. to LG. gore, gor, 'a child'; of uncertain
origin. Derivatively, the -/ in girl is identical
with dimin. suff. -el.
Derivatives: girl-hood, п., girl-ish, adj., girl-ish-
ly, adv., girl-ish-ness, n.

## giron
giron, n. — See gyron.

## Girondist
Girondist, п., a member of the moderate
republican party in France (1791-93). — F. Giron-
diste, formed with suff. -iste (see -ist) fr. Gironde,
name of a department in Southwestern France;
so called because the.leaders of the party were
deputies of that department.

## girt
girt, past tense and pp. of gird.

## girt
girt, п., measure around something. — A var. of
girth.

## girth
girth, n. — ME. gerth, fr. ON. gjord, 'girdle'. See
gird, 'to encircle'.
Derivative: girth, tr. v., to gird.

## gisarme
gisarme, п., battle-ax with a long shaft carried
by foot soldiers in the Middle Ages. — ME.,
fr. OF., fr. OHG. getisarn, lit. 'weeding iron',
fr. getan, 'to weed', and isarn, 'iron' (see iron).
OF. gisarme was influenced in form by OF.
arme, 'weapon' (see arm, 'weapon').

## gismondite
gismondite, п., a hydrous calcium aluminum
silicate (mineral.) — Named after the Italian
mineralogist Carlo Giuseppe Gismondi (1762-1824),
who first analyzed it. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## gist
gist, п., essence, pit, main point of a matter. —
OF. giste (F. gite), 'lying place, resting place',
fem. pp. of OF. gesir (F. gesir), 'to lie', used as
a noun, fr. VL. jacita, fem. pp. of L. jaceo,
jacere, 'to lie'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and cp.
agist. Cp. also joist.

## gitano
gitano, п., a gypsy. — Sp., 'gypsy', fr. Egiptano,
'Egyptian', fr. Egipto, fr. L. Aegyptus, 'Egypt'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:340 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 313 | GLAUCUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:340 COLUMN:1 -->
See gypsy.

## gith
gith, η , ι) any plant of the genus Nigella; 2) the
corn cockle. — OE. gip-corn, fr. L. git (later
forms gitti, gitte), 'the plant Nigella sativa\
which is prob. a Punic loan word, and ult.
derives fr. Heb. gadh, 'coriander'. In an addition
to Dioscurides 3,63 it is mentioned that the
Africans call the coriander yoiS (pronounced
in Late Gk. gid). It is very probable that Latin
git was influenced in form by the pronunciation
mentioned.

## gittern
gittern, п., an obsolete musical instrument
resembling a guitar. — ME. giterne, fr. OF. gui-
terne, fr. L. cithara, fr. Gk. κιθάρα. See cither.
Derivative: gittern, intr. v. (obsol.)

## give
give, tr. and intr. v. — ME. given, of Scand.
origin ; cp. ON. gefa, Dan. give, Swed. gifva, giva,
which are rel. to OE. giefan, gifan, OS. geVan,
OFris. jeva, MDu. gheven, Du. geven, OHG.
geban, MHG., G. geben, Goth, giban, 'to give',
Goth, gabei, 'riches', gabeigs, gabigs, 'rich', fr.
I.-E. base *ghab(h)-, 'to take, hold, have; to
give', whence also Olr. gaibim, Ί take', gabal,
'the act of taking', Lith. gabenti, 'to remove',
L. habere, 'to have, possess' and prob. also OI.
gabhastih, 'hand'. See habit and cp. gavel,
'tribute', gift. Derivatives: giv-er, п., giv-ing, n.

## given
given, pp. of give.

## gizzard
gizzard, п., the muscular stomach of a bird. —
ME. giser, fr. OF. gezier, giser, gisier, gusier
(F. gesier), fr. L. gizeria, 'cooked entrails of
poultry', which is prob. a Punic-Phoen.-Heb.
loan word. Cp. Heb. g'zartm, construct state
gizri, 'pieces of sacrificed animals', pi. of gezer,
'anything cut, a piece', from the stem of gazar,
'he cut, divided', in Mishnaic Heb. 'he
circumcised; he decided, decreed', rel. to Aram.-Syr.
g'zar, 'he cut, split, circumcised; he decided,
decreed', Arab, jazara, Ethiop. gazara, 'he cut,
slaughtered'. In L. gigeria, a collateral form of
gizeria, ζ has been assimilated to the preceding
g. The final d in gizzard is due to a confusion of
this word with words ending in -ard; cp, the
final d in hazard, mallard, scabbard.

## glabella
glabella, п., the space between the eyebrows
(anat.) — Medical L., prop. fern, of the adj.
glabellus, 'without hair, smooth', used as a
noun. This latter word is the dimin. of glaber,
for which see next word.

## glabrous
glabrous, adj., bald; smooth. — Formed with
suff. -011s. fr. L. glaber, 'without hair, smooth,
bald', which stands for *gh!adh-ros, and is cogn.
with OE. ghed, 'bright, glad'. See glad and cp.
gabbro.

## glace
glace, adj., having a smooth surface. — F., pp.
of glacer, 'to freeze; to glaze', fr. glace, 'ice'.
See next word and cp. glacier.

## glacial
glacial, adj., pertaining to ice; icy. — F., fr. L.
glacialis, 'icy', fr, glacies, 'ice', prob. formed
on the analogy of acies, 'sharp edge, point', fr.
orig. "gla-gies, fr. I.-E. base *gel-, 'to freeze',
whence also L. geld, 'frost'. See gelid and adj.
suff. -a] and cp. glace, glacier, glacis.

## glacialist
glacialist, п., one who supports the glacial theory.
— See prec. word and -ist.

## glaciate
glaciate, tr. v., to freeze. — L. glaciatus, pp. of
glaciare, 'to turn to ice', fr. glacies. See giacinl
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: Glaciat-ion, п., the act or process
of freezing.

## glacier
glacier, п., mass of ice moving slowly down a
mountain slope or valley. — F., fr. glace, 'ice',
fr. VL. glacia (whence also OProvenc. glassa.
It. ghiaccia), corresponding to L. glacies, 'ice'.
See glacial and -ier and cp. glance, 'to glide on".

## glaciology
glaciology, п., the study of glaciers. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. glacies, 'ice', and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
glacial and -logy.
Derivatives: glaciolog-ical, adj., glaciolog-ist, n.

## glacis
glacis, п., a gentle slope; an external slope (fort.)
— F., fr. OF. glacier, 'to slip', fr. L. glaciare,
'to make or turn into ice', fr, glacies. See
glacial.

## glad
glad, adj. — ME., fr. OE. glxd, 'bright; glad,
cheerful', rel. to ON. gladr, 'smooth, bright,
glad', Dan., Swed. glad, 'glad, joyful', OS. glad-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:340 COLUMN:2 -->
mod, 'glad', OFris. gled, Du. glad, 'slippery',
OHG., MHG. glat, 'shining, smooth', G. glatt,
'smooth', fr. I.-E. "ghl'dho-, 'bright, smooth',
whence also L. glaber (for *ghladh-ros), 'smooth;
bald', OSlav. gladuku, Lith. glodits, glodnus,
'smooth', OPruss. glosto, 'whetstone'. Cp.
glade. Cp. also glabrous.

## glad
glad, tr. v., to gladden (archaic). — ME. gladien,
fr. OE. gladian, fr. glsed. See glad, adj.

## gladdeu
gladdeu, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. glad, adj.,
with verbal suff. -en.

## glade
glade, п., an open space in a forest. — Rel. to
glad, adj., in its orig. sense 'bright, clear', hence
glade means lit. 'a bright, clear place'. For sense
development cp. E. clearing; cp. also F. clairiire,
'glade', fr. clair, 'clear, bright', and G. Lichlung,
'clearing, glade', fr. Licht, 'light'.
Derivative: glad-y, adj.

## gladiate
gladiate, adj., sword-shaped (bot.) — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. gladius, 'sword'. See
next word.

## gladiator
gladiator, п., a Roman swordsman who fought
in the arena for the eniertainment of spectators.
— L. gladiator, 'swordsman, fighter', fr.
gladius, 'sword', of Celtic origin. Cp. Olr. claid-eb,
W. cleddyf, Co. clethe, Bret, kleze, 'sword'; fr.
I.-E. base "qelad-, 'to strike, beat', whence also
MIr. claidim, Ί dig', caill (for *caldet), 'forest',
Gk. κλάδος, 'young branch or shoot', lit.,
'branch lopped off', OE. holt, 'copse, wood;
timber'. See holt and cp. gladius, gladiolus,
glaive. Cp. also halt, 'lame'.
Derivatives: gladiatori-al, gladiatori-an, adjs.

## gladiolus
gladiolus, п., ι) (cap.) a genus of plants of the
iris family; 2) any plant of this genus. — L., 'a
small sword*, dimin. of gladius, 'sword' (see
prec. word and -ole); so called by Pliny from
the swordlike leaves.

## gladius
gladius, п., ι) the swordfish; 2) the pen of a
cuttlefish. — L., 'sword'. See gladiator.

## gladly
gladly, adv. — ME., fr. OE. glxdlice. See glad,
adj., and adv. suff. -ly.

## gladness
gladness, n. — ME. gladnesse, fr. OE. glxdnes.
See glad, adj., and -ness.

## gladsome
gladsome, adj. — ME. gladsum. See glad, adj.,
and -some.

## Gladstone bag
Gladstone bag, also gladstone. — Named after
the English statesman William Ewart Gladstone
(1809-98).

## Gladys
Gladys, fern. PN. —W. Gwladys, prob. Welshified
fr. L. Claudia. See Claudia.

## Glagolitic
Glagolitic, adj., pertaining to the ancient Western
Slavic alphabet. — A hybrid coined fr. OSlav,
glagolu, 'word', and-itic, a suff. of Greek origin.
OSlav. glagolu is cogn. with ON. kalla, 'to
shout, sing', OE. ceallian, 'to call'. See call.

## glair
glair, п., white of egg. — ME. gleyre, fr. OF.
(= F.) glaire, fr. VL. *claria (ovi), 'white part
(of an egg)!, fr. L. clarus, 'bright, clear'. See
clear, adj.
Derivatives: glair, tr. v., glair-eous, glair-y, adjs.,
glair-i-ness, a.

## glaive
glaive, п., sword; spear. — ME., fr. OF. (■= F.)
glaive, a blend of L. gladius, 'sword', and clava,
'knotty branch, cudgel, club', which is rel. to
clavus, 'nail'. See gladiator and close, adj.

## glamonr
glamonr, glamor, п., magic; alluring charm. —
Corruption of grammar, used in the sense of
gramarye; popularized by Sir Walter Scott
(1771-1832).
Derivatives: glamo(u)r, tr. v., glamo(u)r-ous,
adj., glamo(u)r-ous-ly, adv., glamo(u)r-y, adj.

## glance
glance, intr. and tr. v., to glide off obliquely; to
flash; to look quickly. — ME. glacen, fr. OF.
glacier, 'to slip, slide', fr. glace, 'ice'; see glacier.
The word glance was prob. influenced both in
form and meaning by ME. glenten, 'to shine*
(see glint). Cp. glissade. Cp. also next word.
Derivative: glance, п., a gliding off obliquely;
a flashing; a quick look.

## glance
glance, п., a lustrous metallic sulfide (mineral.) —
Du. glans, 'brightness, luster'. See next word.

## glance
glance, tr. V., to polish (metal). — Prob. fr. Du.
glanzen, 'to gleam, polish', fr. MDu. glansen,
'to gleam', fr. glans, 'brightness', fr. MHG. glanz
(whence G. Glanz),it. Late OHG. #/αηζ, of s.m.,
fr. OHG. glanz, adj., 'bright', which is rel. to
ME. glenten, 'to shine'. See glint

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:340 COLUMN:3 -->

## gland
gland, n. — F. g/ande, fr. L. glandem, ace. of
glans, 'acorn' (used in the sense of L. glandula,
'gland', dimin. of glans), which is cogn. with
Gk. βάλανος, Arm. kalin (gen. kalnoy), OSlav.
ielgdi, 'acorn', Lith. gile, Lett, (d)zile, OPruss.
gile, 'oak; gland'. Cp. next word and the second
element in Euglandina and in Juglans. Cp. also
the first element in balanlferous and the second
element in myrobalan. Cp. also valonia.
Derivatives: glandi-ferous, adj., glandi-form, adj.

## glanders
glanders, n. pi., a contagious disease of horses,
mules, etc., characterized by the swelling of the
glands beneath the lower jaw. — OF. glandres
(pi.), fr. L. glandulae (pi.), 'glands of the throat'.
See glandule.
Derivatives: glander-ed, glander-ous, adj.

## glundular
glundular, adj., consisting of, or pertaining to,
glands. — Fr. L. glandula. See next word and -ar.

## glandule
glandule, п., a small gland. — F., fr. L. glandula,
'gland of the throat', dimin. of glans, gen. glan-
dis, 'acorn'. See gland and -tile.
Derivatives: glandul-ar (q.v.), glanduli-ferous,
adj., glandul-ous, adj. (q.v.), glandul-os-iiy, n.

## glandulous
glandulous, adj., glandular. — F. glanduleux (fern.
glanduleuse), fr. L. glandulosus, 'full of glands,
glandulous', fr. glandula. See prec. word and
-ous.
Derivative: glandulous-ness, n.

## glare
glare, intr. v. — ME. glaren, 'to shine', rel. to
MDu. and MLG. glaren, 'to glow', and to
next word.
Derivatives: glare, п., glar-ing, п., glar-ing-ly,
adv.

## glass
glass, n. — ME. glas, gles, fr. OF. glxs, rel. to
OS. glas, gles, ON. gler, Dan. glar, MDu., Du.
glas, 'glass', OHG., MHG. glas, 'amber, glass',
G. Glas, 'glass', OE. glxr, 'amber', and cogn.
with L. glaesum, glesum, 'amber', Olr. glass,
'green, blue, gray', W. glas, 'blue', MIr. glaisin,
woad', fr. I.-E. base 'ghles-, 'ghl's-, 'to shine,
glitter', which is an enlargement of base *ghel-,
*ghel-, "ghle-, 'to gleam, glimmer; to be green
or yellow'. Cp. glare, glaze, glow. Cp. also gleam
and words there referred to. Cp. also yellow.
Derivatives: glass, tr. v., glass-ful, adj., glass-y,
adj., glass-i-ly, adv., glass-i-ness, n.

## Giassite
Giassite, п., an adherent of the teachings of John
Glas(s) (1695-1773), the founder of a Scottish
sect. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## glauberite
glauberite, п., a sodium calcium sulfate (mineral)
— Named after the German physician and
chemist Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604-68). Cp.
next word. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Glauber*s salt,, sodium sulfate. — Named after
J. R. Glauber. See prec. word,

## glaucescent
glaucescent, adj., somewhat glaucous. — See
glaucous and -escent.

## Glaucidium
Glaucidium, п., a genus of small owls (ornithol.)
— ModL., dimin. formed fr. Gk. γλαϋξ, gen.
γλαυκός, 'owl', which seems to be a hypocor-
istic abbreviation of γλαυκώτης, '(the bird) with
the gleaming eyes', fr. γλαυκός, 'gleaming,
bright', and ώψ, gen. ώττός, 'eye, face'. See
glaucous, -opia and -idinm.

## Glaucium
Glaucium, п., a genus of plants of the poppy
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γλαύκιον, 'juice
of the horned poppy', fr. γλαυκός (see
glaucous); so called from the color of its foliage.

## glaucoma
glaucoma, п., an eye disease (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. γλαύκωμα, fr. γλαυκός. See glaucous
and -oma.

## glaucomatous
glaucomatous, adj., pertaining to glaucoma. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. γλαύκωμα, gen.
γλαυκώματος. See prec. word.

## Glaucoma
Glaucoma, n„ a genus of snakes, the burrowing
snake (zool.) — ModL., fr. γλαυκός. See
glancous and cp. next word. For the ending see
suff. -ia.

## glauconite
glauconite, п., a dull-green silicate (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. γλαυκός
(see glaucous); so called from its color. Cp.
prec. word.

## glaucous
glaucous, adj., bluish green. — L. glaucus, fr. Gk.
γλαυκός, 'gleaming, bright; gray, bluish green',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. Glaucidium,
Glancium, glaucoma, Glauconia, Glaucns, Glaux.
Derivative: glaucous-ly, adv.

## Glaucus
Glaucus, п., a fisherman of Boeotia, changed into

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:341 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GLAUCUS | 314 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:341 COLUMN:1 -->
a sea god (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Γλαυκός,
fr. γλαυκός, 'bluish green', so called in allusion
to the glaucous color of the sea. See prec. word.

## Glaucus
Glaucus, п., a genus of mollusks (zool.)— ModL.,
fr. Gk. γλαυκός, 'bluish green' (see glaucous);
so called in allusion to their color.

## Glanx
Glanx, п., a genus of plants of the primrose family
(bot.)— L.glaux, name of a plant, fr. Gk. γλαΟξ,
'the milk vetch', which is prob. rel. to γλαυκός,
'gleaming, bright; bluish green'. See glaucons,
and cp. Glaucidium, Glaucium.

## glaze
glaze, tr. v., to furnish with glass; intr. v., to
become glassy. — ME. gtasen, fr. glas, 'glass',
fr. OE. ghes. See glass.
Derivatives: glaze, п., glaz-er, п., glazier (q.v.),
glaz-ing, п., glaz-y, adj., glar-i-ly, adv., glaz-
i-ness, a.

## glazier
glazier, n. — Formed ft. glaze with suff. -ler.
Derivative: glazier-y, n.

## gleam
gleam, п., a beam of light. — ME. glem, gleam,
fr. OE. glim, 'brightness, splendor', rel. to OS.
glimo, of s.m., MHG. glim, 'spark', OHG. glei-
mo, MHG. gleime, 'glowworm', lit. 'the gleam-
er', MHG., G. glimmen, 4o glimmer, glow', and
to ON. glJS, 'to shine, glitter', fr. I.-E. base
*ghlei-, 'to shine, glitter, glow; to be warm',
whence also Gk. χλίειν, 'to become warm',
χλιαρός, 'warm', χλιαίνειν, 'to warm', Olr. gle,
W. gloew, 'bright, clear'. Base 'ghlei- is an
enlargement of base *ghel-; 'ghel-, *ghle-, 'to
gleam, glimmer'. See glass and cp. glee,
glimmer, glimpse, glisten, glister, glitter.
Derivatives: gleam-y, adj., gleam-i-ly, adv.,
gleam-i-ness, n.

## gleam
gleam, intr. v. — ME. glemen, fr. glem. See
gleam, n.

## glean
glean, tr. v., to gather after the reapers; intr. v.,
to gather what is left after the reapers. — ME.
glenen, fr. OF. glener (F. glaner), fr. Late L.
glenare (whence also OProvenc. glenar), a word
occurring in the Salic Law; of Celtic origin;
cp. Olr. ao-glinn, 'he collects, gathers'.
Derivatives: glean, n. (q.v.), glean-er, п.,
gleaning, n.

## glean
glean, п., something gleaned. — OF. glene, fr.
Late L. glena, fr. glenare. See glean, v.

## glebe
glebe, п., soil; land; field. — L. gleba, fr. earlier
glaeba, 'clod, soil, land', in gradational
relationship to globus, 'ball, sphere', and cogn. with Lith.
glebys, 'armful; clue, ball', globiu, globti, 'to
embrace, support', Lett, glabt, glebt, 'to
protect', Polish ghbii, 'to press', Czech hlobiti, 'to
fasten with tags', OHG. klaftra, MHG. klafter,
G. Klafter, 'fathom', lit. 'the outstretched arms',
OE. clyppan, OFris. kleppa, 'to embrace, love',
fr. I.-E. base 'gelebh-, 'glebh-, 'to roll up into
a ball, compress', which is an enlargement of
base *gel-, of s.m. See clamp, 'a device for
fastening', and cp. globe. Cp. also gall, 'gallnut'.

## Glecoma
Glecoma, п., a genus of plants of the mint family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γλήχων, βλήχων,
'pennyroyal'; of unknown origin.

## glede
glede, п., the common kite. — ME., fr. OE. glida,
'kite', lit. 'the gliding (bird)', rel. to ON. gleda,
'kite', and to OE. glidan, 'to glide'. See glide.

## Gleditsia
Gleditsia, п., a genus of plants, the honey locust
(bot.) — ModL., named after the German
botanist Johann Gottlieb Gleditsch (1714-86). For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## glee
glee, п., joy; mirth. — ME. gle, gleo, fr. OE.
gliw, gleo, 'mirth, jest; music minstrelsy', fr.
ON. gly, of s.m., which is rel. to gljd, 'to shine'.
See gleam and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: glee-ful, adj., glee-ful-ly, adv.,
glee-ful-ness, n.

## gleed
gleed, п., a live coal (dial.) — ME. glede, fr. OE.
gild, 'live coal; flame, fire', rel. to ON. glad,
Du. gloed, OHG., MHG. gluot, G. Glut,
'glowing fire', and to OE. gldwan, 'to glow'. See glow
and cp. words there referred to.

## gleek
gleek, п., an old card game (obsol.) — OF. glic,
fr. earlier ghelicque, fr. MDu. ghelijc (whence
Du. gelijk), 'equal', which is rel. to OE. gelic,
'similar, equal'. See like, adj. The game is so
called because it is three cards of the same rank
that form a gleek.

## gleemaiden
gleemaiden, п., a female minstrel (archaic). —
OE. gleo-rmegden, 'female minstrel'. See glee

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:341 COLUMN:2 -->
and maiden.

## gleeman
gleeman, п., a minstrel (archaic). — OE. gleo-
man, 'minstrel, jester'. See glee and man.

## gleesome
gleesome, adj., gleeful, merry. — Compounded
of glee and 1st -some.
Derivatives: gleesome-ly, Sidv.,gleesome-ness, n.

## gleet
gleet, п., morbid discharge from the urethra
(med.) — ME. glet, glette, fr. OF.-MF. glete,
'slime, filth' (whence F. glette, 'litharge'), fr. L.
glltem, ace. of glls, 'sticky, glutinous ground',
which is a back formation fr. glittus, 'sticky',
suggested by the analogy of the related glus,
gen. glutis. See glne.

## gleg
gleg, adj., quick of perception (Scot.) — ME.,
fr. ON. gloggr, 'clear-sighted, clear, distinct',
rel. to OS., OHG. glau, 'clever', OE. gleaw,
'clever, wise', Goth, glaggwo, 'exactly', glagg-
waba,glaggwuba, 'carefully', ON.gluggi,gluggir,
'loophole, light', Swed., Norw. glugga, 'to look
at, lie in wait, lurk', OE. gldwan, 'to shine, glow'.
See glow.

## glen
glen, п., a narrow valley. — ME., fr. Gael, gleam,
'mountain valley, glen', which is rel. to Mir.
glenn, glend, W. glyn, of s.m. Cp. the next two
words.

## Glengarry cap or Glengarry bonnet
Glengarry cap or Glengarry bonnet, also
glengarry. — Named after a valley in Inverness-
shire (Scotland), lit. glen of the river Garry.

## Glenlivet
Glenlivet, Glenlivat. п., a kind of whisky. —
Named after Glenlivet (or Glenlivat) in
Scotland; so called from the place where it was first
manufactured. The name lit. means 'the glen of
the Livet ( a tributary of the Avon)'.

## glenoid
glenoid, adj., having the form of a shallow cavity
(anal.) — Gk. γληνοειδής, 'resembling the socket
of a joint', compounded of γλήνη, 'eyeball;
socket of a joint', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. The first element is prob. rel. to
γελεΐν (Hesychius), 'to shine, be bright', γελάν,
'to laugh', γελϊνής, 'smiling, joyful'. For the
first element see geloto-, for the second see -oid.

## glib
glib, adj., 1) smooth; 2) fluent. — The orig.
meaning of this word was 'slippery'. It is of
Dutch origin. Cp. Du. glibberen, 'to slide', glib-
berig, 'slippery', glibber, 'jelly'.
Derivatives: glib-ly, adv., glib-ness, n.

## glide
glide, intr. v. — ME. gliden, fr. OE. glidan, rel.
to OS. glidan, OFris. glida, MLG. gliden, Du.
glijden, OHG. glitan, MHG. gliten, G. gleiten,
'to glide'. Dan. glide, Swed. glida, are borrowed
fr. MLG gliden. Cp. glede, glissade.
Derivatives: glide, п., glid-er, п., glid-ing-ly, adv.

## gliff
gliff, intr. and tr. v., to glance, glimpse; п., а
glimpse. — Of uncertain origin.

## glim
glim, п., ι) a light, as a lamp; 2) an eye (slang). —
Rel. to gleam, glimmer.

## glimmer
glimmer, intr. v. — ME. glemeren, glimeren, 'to
shine', rel. to Du. glimmeren, MHG., G.
glimmen, G. glimmern, 'to shine dimly, glimmer',
G. Glimmer, 'a faint glow', and to OE. glim,
'brightness, splendor'. See gleam and cp.
glimpse.
Derivatives: glimmer, п., glimmer-ing, n. and
adj., glimmer-ing-ly, adv., glimmer-y, adj.

## glimpse
glimpse, tr. and intr. v. — Formerly glimse, fr.
ME. glimsen, fr. Teut. base 'glim-, whence also
gleam, glim, glimmer (qq.v.) For the excrescent
ρ ср. empty, sempstress.
Derivatives: glimpse, п., glimps-er, a.

## glint
glint, intr. v. — ME. glenten, 'to shine', rel. to
dial. Swed. glanta, glinta, 'to shine', OHG. glanz,
'bright', fr. I.-E. base •ghlendh-, 'to shine',
whence also OSiav. gledati, 'to see'. See glance,
'to polish'.
Derivative: glint, n.

## glioma
glioma, п., a tumor of the brain, spinal chord,
etc. (med) — Medical L., lit. 'glue tumor',
coined by the German pathologist Rudolf Vir-
chow (1821-1902), fr. Gk. γλίά, 'glue', and surf.
-ωμχ. See glue and -oma and cp. the second
element in neuroglia.

## gllomatosls
gllomatosls, п., disease characterized by glioma
(med.) — Medical L. See prec. word and -osls.

## gliomaruus
gliomaruus, adj., pertaining to gliomata (med.)
— See glioma and -ous.

## Glires
Glires, n. pi., a synonym of- Rodentia (zool.) —
L. gttres, pi. of glis, 'dormouse', cogn. with OI.
girih, 'mouse', Gk. γαλέη, Att. γαλ?), 'weasel,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:341 COLUMN:3 -->
polecat, marten'. See galea,

## gliriform
gliriform, adj., resembling the Rodentia (zool.)
— Compounded of L. glis (see prec. word) and
forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## glirine
glirine, adj., pertaining to the Rodentia (zool.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ine fr. L. glis, gen. gliris,
'dormouse'. See Glires.

## glissade
glissade, п., a sliding down a slope of snow. —
F., formed with suff. -ade fr. F. glisser, 'to slip,
glide, slide', which is a blend of OF. glier, 'to
glide', and OF. glacer, of s.m. OF. glier derives
fr. Frankish 'glidan, which is rel. to OHG.
glitan, OE. glidan, 'to glide'; see glide. OF. glacer
comes fr. glace, 'ice', fr.L. glacies; see glacial.
Derivatives: glissade, intr. v., glissad-er, n.

## glisten
glisten, intr. v., to glitter. — ME. glisnen, glist-
nen, fr. OE. glisnian, rel. to OE. glisian and to
OFris. gITsa, 'to shine', fr. I.-E. base 'ghleis-,
enlargement of base 'ghel-, *ghle-, 'to gleam,
glimmer'. See glass and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also next word.
Derivative: glisten, n.

## glister
glister, intr. v. — ME. glislren, glisteren, prob.
fr. LG. glisten, which derives fr. I.-E. base
'ghleis-, 'to gleam, glimmer*. See prec. word.
Derivatives: glister, п., glister-ing-Iy, adv.

## glitter
glitter, intr. v. — ME. gliteren, fr. ON. glitra;
rel. to OE. glitenian, OS. glitan, OHG. glidan,
MHG. glijen, G. gleifien, MHG., G. glitzern,
Goth, glitmunjan, 'to glitter, glisten', fr. I.-E.
'ghleid-, 'ghlid-, whence also Gk. χλιδών,
χλϊδος, 'ornament', χλιδή, 'luxury, delicacy'.
I.-E. 'ghleid- is a dental enlargement of base
'ghlei-, 'to shine, glitter, glow; to be warm'. See
gleam and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: glitter, п., glitler-ing, adj., glitter-
ing-ly, adv., glitter-y, adj.

## gloaming
gloaming, п., twilight. — ME., fr. OE. glomung,
'twilight', fr. gldm, of s.m., which is rel. to OE.
glowan, 'to glow'. See glow.

## gloat
gloat, intr. v., to gaze with malicious joy. — ON.
glotta, 'to smile scornfully', rel. to MHG., G.
glotzen, 'to stare, gloat'. Cp. glout.
Derivatives: gloat, п., gloat-er, п., gloat-ing, ad/.
gloat-ing-ly, adv.

## global
global, adj., spherical. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. globus. See globe.

## globate
globate, adj., spherical. — L. globulus, pp. of
globare, 'to make into a globe', fr. globus. See
next word and adj. suff. -ate.

## globe
globe, n. — F., fr. L. globus, 'a round body, ball,
sphere', in gradational relationship to L. glaeba,
gleba, 'clod, soil, land'. See glebe and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also globose, globule,
conglobate and the second element in hemoglobin.

## Globigerina
Globigerina, п., a genus of Foraminifera (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of L. globus, 'a round
body', and gerere, 'to bear, carry'. See globe
and gerent.

## globose
globose, adj., spherical. — L. globosus, 'round as
a ball, spherical', fr. globus. See globe and adj.
suff. -ose.
Derivatives: gtobose-ly, adv., globose-ness, п.,
glohos-ity, n.

## Globularia
Globularia, п., a genus of plants, the globe daisy
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. globulus, 'a little ball'.
See globule,

## globule
globule, п., a very small spherical body; a drop.
— F., fr. L. globulus, 'a little ball', dimin. of
globus. See globe and -ule.
Derivatives: globul-ar, adj., globulin (q.v.), glo-
bulous (q.v.)

## globulin
globulin, п., a protein substance (biochem.) —
Coined by the Swedish chemist Jons Jakob Ber-
zelius (1779-1848) from L. globulus (see prec.
word) and chem. suff. -in.

## globulite
globulite, п., a variety of crystallite (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. globulus. See
globule,

## globulous
globulous, adj., globular. — F. globuleux (fem.
globuleuse), fr. globule. See globule and -ous.
Derivative: globulous-ness, n.

## glochldiate
glochldiate, adj., barbed (bot.) — Formed with
adj. suff. -ate fr. Gk. γλωχίς. See next word.

## glochidium
glochidium, п., larva of fresh-water mussel (zool.)
— ModL., dimin. of Gk. γλωχίς, 'point of an
arrow; projecting point'. See gloss,
'interpretation', and -idium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:342 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 315 | GLUTTON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:342 COLUMN:1 -->

## glockenspiel
glockenspiel, п., a percussion instrument (mus.)
— G. Glockenspiel, lit. 'play of bells'; fr. Glocke,
'bell', and Spiel, 'a play'. See clock and spiel, and
cp. the second element in bonspiel, kriegspiel.

## glomerate
glomerate, tr. v., to roll up, accumulate. — L.
glomerulus, pp. of glomerare, 'to make into a
ball, gather into a round heap', fr. glomus, gen.
glomeris, 'a round heap, ball, clue', fr. I.-E.
*gle-m-, a collateral form of base *gleb(h)-,
'to make into a ball, press together', enlarged
fr. base "gel-, of s.m. See clamp, 'a device for
fastening', and verbal suff. -ate and cp. Glomer-
ella, glomerulus, agglomerate, conglomerate. Cp.
also glebe, globe.

## glomerate
glomerate, adj., rolled up, accumulated. — L.
glomerulus, pp. of glomerare. See prec. word.

## glomeration
glomeration, п., accumulation; ball. — L. glo-
meratio, gen. -onis, fr. glomerulus, pp. of
glomerare. See glomerate, v., and -ion.

## Glomerella
Glomerella, п., a genus of fungi (hot.) — ModL.,
a dimin. formed fr. glomus, gen. glomeris, 'ball'.
See glomerate, v., and -ella and cp. next word.

## glomerulus
glomerulus, п., a capillary tuft ((mat.) — Medical
L., coined by Schumlansky fr. L. glomus, gen.
glomeris, 'ball' (see glomerate), and dimin. suff.
-ule.

## gloom
gloom, intr. v., to look sullen. — ME. gloumen,
gloumben, 'to look sullen, be gloomy', rel. to
MLG. glum, 'turbid', glomen, 'to make turbid',
LG. gluren, Du. gluren, 'to leer'; not rel. to OE.
gldm, 'twilight'. Cp. glower, 'to lour', glum.
Derivatives: gloom, п., gloom-y, adj., gloo-mi-ly,
adv., gloom-i-ness, n.

## Gloria
Gloria, п., the great doxology in Christian liturgy.
— L.; so called from the first word of the text,
which begins "Gloria in excelsis Deo" ("Glory
be to God on high"). See glory.

## clarification
clarification, n. — Late L. glorificatio, gen. -onis,
fr. gldrificatus, pp. of glorificare. See next word
and -ation.

## glorify
glorify, tr. v. — ME. gloriften, fr. F. glorifier, fr.
Late L. gldrificare, 'to glorify', which is formed
fr. L. gloria, 'glory', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to
make, do'. See glory and -fy.
Derivative: glorifi-er, a.

## gloriole
gloriole, celestial crown, aureole. — F., fr. L.
gloriola, 'a small glory', dimin. of gloria. See
glory and -ole.

## glorious
glorious, adj. — OF. glorious (F. glorieux), fr. L.
gloriosus, 'glorious, famous', fr. gloria. See
glory and -ons.
Derivatives: glorious-ly, adv.,glorious-ness, a.

## glory
glory, n. — ME. glorie, fr. OF. glorie (F. gloire),
fr. L. gloria, 'glory, fame, renown, praise',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. gloriole.
Derivative: glory, intr. v.

## gloss
gloss, п., interpretation. — L. glossa, 'an
antiquated or foreign word that requires

## explanation'
explanation', hence also 'explanation, note', fr. Gk.
γλώσσα, Att. γλώττα, 'tongue, speech', which
stands for *γλωχ-ια, prop, 'that which is

## projected'
projected', and is rel. to γλωχίς, 'a projecting point',

## and perh. cogn. with OSlav. glogu
and perh. cogn. with OSlav. glogu, 'thorn'. Cp.

## glottis
glottis, epiglottis, and gloze, 'a note'. Cp. also

## the second element in monoglot
the second element in monoglot, diglot, triglot,

## polyglot
polyglot, and in bugloss, Cynoglossum, Doco-

## glossa
glossa, Hippoglossus, hypoglossus, Odontoglos-

## sum
sum, Ophioglossum, Pangloss, Salpiglossis,

## Tachyglossus
Tachyglossus, Triglochin.
Derivative: gloss, tr. v., to write glosses to.

## gloss
gloss, п., polish. — Rel. to obsol. Du. gloos, 'a

## glowing'
glowing', MHG. glosen, Norw. glosa, 'to glow',

## and prob. also to OE. glowan
and prob. also to OE. glowan, of s.m. See glow

## and cp. gloze
and cp. gloze, 'to shine'.
Derivative: gloss, tr. and intr. v., to polish.

## glossary
glossary, п., a collection of glosses; a partial
dictionary. — L. glossarium, 'vocabulary of

## antiquated or foreign words
antiquated or foreign words, glossary', formed

## with suff. -arium
with suff. -arium, fr. glossa. See gloss,
'interpretation', and subst. suff. -ary.
Derivative: glossari-al, adj.

## glossator
glossator, п., a writer of glosses. — ML., formed

## with suff. -ator fr. L. glossa. See gloss
with suff. -ator fr. L. glossa. See gloss,
'interpretation',

## glossic
glossic, п., a phonetic system invented by
Alexander John Ellis (1814-90). — Coined by A.J.
Ellis fr. Gk. γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss,
'interpretation', and -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:342 COLUMN:2 -->

## glossitis
glossitis, п., inflammation of the tongue (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -itls fr. Gk.
γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## glossa-
glossa-, combining form denoting the tongue. —
Gk. γλωσσο-, fr. γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss,
'interpretation'.

## glossograph
glossograph, п., an instrument for recording the
movements of the tongue in speaking. —
Compounded of glosso- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See -graph.

## glossographer
glossographer, п., a writer of glosses. — Formed
with suff. -er fr. Gk. γλωσσογράφος, 'a writer of
glosses', which is compounded of γλωσσο- (see
glosso-) and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write' (see
-grapher).

## glossology
glossology, п., the science of language (obsol.) —
Compounded of glosso- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy
and cp. glottology.
Derivatives: glossolog-ical, adj., glossolog-ist, n.

## glossotomy
glossotomy, п., the cutting out of the tongue
(surg.) — Compounded of glosso- and Gk.
-τομία, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See
-tomy.

## glottis
glottis, п., the opening between the vocal cords
of the larynx (anal.) — Att. Gk. γλωττίς, 'the
mouth of the windpipe', fr. γλώττα, 'tongue'.
See gloss, 'interpretation', and subst. suff. -id
and cp. epiglottis.

## glotto-
glotto-, combining form meaning 'language'. —
Att. Gk. γλωττο-, fr. γλώττα, 'tongue;
language'. See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## glottology
glottology, п., the science of language (obsol.) —
It. gloltologia, coined by the Italian comparative
philologist Graziadio Isaia Ascoli (1829-1907)
fr. glotto- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy and cp.
glossology.

## glout
glout, intr. v., to frown, scowl (archaic). — ME.
glouten, prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. gloiia,
'to smile scornfully', and see gloat.

## glove
glove, n. — ME. glofe, glove, fr. OE. glof, 'palm
of the hand', rel. to ON. glofi. Both these words
are a contraction of Teut. "ge-Wf, fr. pref. ge-
(see y-) and *lof-, 'palm of the hand', whence
also ON. Idfi, Goth, lofa and (with vowel
gradation) OHG. laffa, 'palm of the hand; oarblade'.
These words are cogn.. with Lith. lopa, 'claw',
lopeta, 'shovel, spade'; waterlily', Lett, lepa,
'paw', lapusta, lapsta, 'shovel, spade'. OPruss.
lopto, 'spade', Russ. lopa, 'paw', lopata, 'shovel'.
Cp. loof, aloof, luff, laveer.
Derivatives: glove, tr. v., glov-er, n.

## glow
glow, intr. v. — ME. glowen, fr. OE. glowan, rel.
to OS. gldian, ON. gloa, OHG. gluoen, MHG.

## gliien
gliien, gliiejen, G. gliihen, 'to glow', fr. I.-E.
*ghlou-, enlargement of base *ghel-, *ghel-, 'to
gleam, glimmer'. See glass and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also gleg, gloaming.
Derivatives: glow, п., glow-ing, adj., glow-ing-ly,
adv.

## glower
glower, intr. v., to lower; to scowl. — Cp. LG.

## gluren
gluren, Du. gluren, 'to leer', see gloom.
Derivatives: glower, п., glower-er, п.,

## glowering
glowering, adj., glower-ing-Iy, adv.

## Gloxinia
Gloxinia, п., a genus of tropical plants (bot.) —

## ModL.
ModL., named after Benjamin Peter Gloxin,
an iSth century German botanist and physician.
For the ending see suff. -ia.

## gloze
gloze, intr. v., to shine, blaze (Scot.) — See gloss,
'to polish'.
Derivative: gloze,,a blaze,

## gloze
gloze, п., ι) a note (obsol.); 2) flattering speech;
flattery (archaic). — OF. glose, fr. ML. glosa,

## a var. of L. glossa
a var. of L. glossa, 'a word that requires

## explanation'. See gloss
explanation'. See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## gloze
gloze, intr. v., 1) to make glosses (obsol.); 2) to
Ratter (archaic). — ME. glosen, fr. OF. gloser,

## fr. glose. See gloze
fr. glose. See gloze, n.

## glucase
glucase, п., maltase, i.e. an enzyme capable of
converting maltose into glucose (chem.) —
Formed fr. gluc(ose) with suff. -ase.

## gluchia
gluchia, п., another name for beryllia (chem.) —

## ModL.
ModL., coined by the French chemist Nicolas-
Louis Vauquelin (1763-1829) in 1798 fr. Gk.
γλυκύς, 'sweet' (see glyco-); so called by him

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:342 COLUMN:3 -->
in allusion to the sweet taste of some of its salts.

## glucinum
glucinum, also glucinium, п., another name for
beryllium (chem.) — ModL. See prec. word.

## glucose
glucose, п., a sugar, QHuOa (chem.) — F.
glucose, fr. misspelling of Gk. γλεύκος, 'must,
sweet wine', which is rel. to Gk. γλυκύς, 'sweet'.
See glyco- and subst. suff. -ose.

## glucoside
glucoside, also spelled glycoside, п., a group of
compounds yielding glucose (chem.) — Formed
from prec. word with suff. -lde.

## glue
glue, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) glu, 'birdlime',
fr. Late L. glulem, ace. of glus, it. L. gluten, of
s.m., which derives fr. I.-E. base 'gleit-, 'to
glue, paste', whence also Lith. glitus, 'sticky,
glutinous, smooth', glytus, 'smooth, even',
glltas,glilis, 'slime, mucus',OE. ctidan, 'to adhere
to', cttda, 'plaster', elide, 'bur'. I.-E. *gleit- is a
-(-enlargement of base *glei-, 'to glue, paste,
stick together'. Port, grude, 'paste', is of the
same origin as OF. glu. See clay and cp. gluten.
Cp. also gleet. Cp. also cloth.
Derivatives: glue, tr. v., glue-y, adj.

## glum
glum, adj., gloomy; sullen. — MT. gloumen,
gloumben, 'to look sullen, gloomy'. See gloom,
v., and cp. grnm. Derivatives: glum-ly, adv.,
glum-ness,a.,glumm-y, adj.

## glume
glume, п., a bract of grasses. — L. gluma, 'husk,
hull', for 'glubh-sma, from the stem of glubo,
glubere, 'to peel, shell', which stands for
*gleubho and is cogn. with Gk. γλύφειν, 'to
hollow out, engrave, carve', γλυφίς, 'notch', OE.
cleofan, 'to cleave'. See cleave, 'to split', and
cp. glyph,

## glumous
glumous, adj., bearing glumes. — Formed from
prec. word with suff. -ous.

## glut
glut, tr. v., to swallow. — OF. glotir, glutir, fr.
L. gluttire, 'to swallow, gulp down', fr. I.-E.
base "glu-, 'to swallow', whence also L. in-
glu-vies, 'crop, maw; gluttony, voraciousness',
Russ. giot, 'draft, gulp', glotat', 'to gulp,
swallow', OSlav. po-gluStati, 'to gulp, swallow
down'. Base "gl-u is a -«-enlargement of base
*gel-, 'to swallow', whence OHG. ceole, 'throat',
L. gula, 'throat'. See gullet, and cp. glutton,
deglutition, ingluvies.
Derivative: glut, п., a swallow, gulp.

## glut
glut, tr. v., to feed to satiety; intr. v., to eat to
satiety. — ME. glotten, fr. OF. glut, glout,
'gluttonous', back formation fr. glotir, glutir,
'to swallow, gulp down'. Cp. OF. glotoler, Ίο

## eat greedily'
eat greedily', freq. of glotir, and see glut, 'to
swallow'.
Derivatives: glut, п., the act of glutting; full

## supply
supply, glutt-ing, adj., glut-ing-ly, adv.

## gluteal
gluteal, adj., pertaining to the muscles of the
buttocks. — Formed from next word with adj.
suff. -al.

## gluteus
gluteus, п., any of the three large muscles of the
buttocks (anat.) — Medical L. glutaeus,

## gluteus
gluteus, fr. Gk. γλουτός, 'rump', in the pi.
'buttocks', which is cogn. with MHG. kloz, 'lump,

## ball'
ball', Du. kloot, 'ball, testicle', OE. cleat,
'wedge'. See cleat, and cp. words there
referred to.

## gluten
gluten, п., a viscid albuminous substance made
from wheat flour. — L. gluten, 'glue'. See glue,

## glutinous
glutinous, adj., of the nature of glue, sticky. —

## L. glutindsus
L. glutindsus, 'gluey, viscous, tenacious', fr.

## gluten
gluten, gen. glutinis, 'glue'. See glue and -ous
and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: glulinous-ly, adv., glutinous-ness, n.

## glutton
glutton, п., ι) a gormandizer; 2) a carnivorous
mammal (Gulo luscus); wolverine. — ME. glo-

## ton
ton, glutun, it. OF. gloton, gluton (F. glouton),

## fr. L. gluttdnem
fr. L. gluttdnem, ace. of gluttd, 'glutton,

## gormandizer'
gormandizer', fr. gluttire, 'to swallow, gulp down':

## see glut
see glut, 'to swallow'. In the sense of 'wolverine',

## glutton is the loan translation of G. Vielfrafi
glutton is the loan translation of G. Vielfrafi,
'gormandizer; wolverine', fr. vie/, 'much', and

## fressen
fressen, 'to devour'. The name Vielfrafi itself
arose from an erroneous translation of earlier

## Norw. fjeldfross
Norw. fjeldfross, 'wolverine', lit. 'mountain cat',

## fr. field
fr. field, 'mountain', and fross, 'tomcat; bear"
(cp, ON. fross, 'tomcat; bear'), but folk
etymology identified Norw. fjeldfross with MHG.

## villefras (G. Vielfrafi)
villefras (G. Vielfrafi), lit. 'much devourer'.
(ModNorw. fjeldfras, in its turn, shows the
influence ofG. Vielfrafi.)Deriva.tives:glutton-ize,
