<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:343 COLUMN:1 -->
intr. and tr. v., gluiion-ous, adj., gluttony (q.v.)

## gluttony
gluttony, n. — ME. glolonie, fr. OF. glotonie,
glutonie, fr. OF. gloton, gluton. See glutton and
-y (representing OF. -ie).

## Glyceria
Glyceria, п., a genus of grasses, the manna grass
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γλυκερός, 'sweet', fr.
γλυκύς, 'sweet' (see glyco-); so called in allusion
to the taste of its grain.

## glyceride
glyceride, п., a compound of glycerol and organic
acids (chem.) — Formed fr. glycer(la) with surf.
-ide.

## glycerin
glycerin, glycerine, n. (chem.) — F. glycerine,
coined by the French chemist Michel-Eugene
Chevreul (1786-1889) fr. Gk. γλυκερός, 'sweet',
fr. γλυκύς, 'sweet'. See glyco- and chem. suff.
-in, -Ine.

## glyco-
glyco-, combining form meaning 'sweet'. — Gk.
γλυκό-, fr. γλυκύς, 'sweet', assimilated to the
following κ from orig. *8λυκ-ύς, and cogn. with
L. dulcis (for *d]kwis), 'sweet'. See dulcet and
cp. glucinum, glncose, licorice.

## glycogen
glycogen, п., a carbonhydrate found in the liver
of animals (chem.) — Coined by the French
physiologist Claude Bernard (1813-78) in 1848
from Gk. γλυκύς, 'sweet' (see glyco-), and -gen.

## glycol
glycol, п., an alcoholic liquid, regarded as
intermediate between glycerin and ethyl alcohol,
C2H4(OH)2 (chem.) — Formed fr. glyc(erine)
and (alcoh)ol. Derivative: glycol-ic, adj.

## glyconic
glyconic, adj., pertaining to a monoacid, dH^O,
(chem.) — See glycose and -onic.

## Glyconic
Glyconic, also Glyconian, adj., denoting a form
of classical meter or verse. — Formed with suff.
-ic fr. Gk. Γλύκων, name of a Greek lyric poet.
For the ending see suff. -ic, resp. -ian.

## glycose
glycose, п., glucose. — F. See glucose.

## glycoside
glycoside, п., glucoside. — See glncoside.

## glycosuria
glycosuria, п., a form of diabetes in which glucose
is excreted in the urine (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of glucose and Gk. -ουρία,
'diseased condition of urine*. See -uria.

## Glycyrrhiza
Glycyrrhiza, п., a genus of plants, the licorice
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γλυκύρριζα, lit. 'sweet
root' (see licorice); so called in allusion to the
taste of its root.

## glyph
glyph, п., a vertical channel or groove. — F.
glyphe, fr. Gk. γλυφή, 'a carving' fr. γλύφειν,
'to hollow out, engrave, carve', which is cogn.
with L. glubere, 'to peel, shell', OE. cleofan, 'to
cleave'. See cleave, 'to split', and cp. glume. Cp.
also glyptic and the second element in anaglyph,
dactylioglyph, hieroglyph, petroglyph, triglyph.

## glyphic
glyphic, adj., pertaining to carving or sculpture.
— Gk. γλυφικός, 'pertaining to carving', fr.
γλυφή. See glyph and -ic.

## glyphograph
glyphograph, п., an etched plate made by glypho-
graphy. — See next word and -graph.

## glyphography
glyphography, п., process by which a raised plate
suitable for printing is made from an etching. —
Compounded of Gk. γλυφή, 'carving' and -γρα-
φίϊ, 'writing', fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See glyph
and -graphy. Derivative: gtyphograph-ic, adj.

## glyptic
glyptic, adj., pertaining to carving. — Gk.
γλυπτικός, 'pertaining to carving', fr. γλυπτός,
'engraved, carved; fit for carving', verbal adj. of
γλύφειν. See glyph and -ic.

## Glyptodon
Glyptodon, п., a genus of extinct gigantic
mammals (paleontol.) — Compounded of Gk.
γλυπτός, 'engraved', verbal adj. of γλύφειν, and 68ών,
gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See prec. word and odonto·.

## glyptograph
glyptograph, п., an engraved gem. —
Compounded of Gk. γλυπτός, 'engraved', verbal adj. of
γλύφειν, 'to engrave', and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See glyptic and -graph.

## glyptography
glyptography, п., the art or process of gem
engraving. — See prec. word and -graphy.

## Gnaphalium
Gnaphalium, п., a genus of plants, the cudweed
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. gnaphalium, 'cudweed*,
fr. Gk. γναφάλλιον, of s.m., fr. γνάφαλλον,
'flock of wool', fr. γνάπτειν, 'a collateral form
of κνάπτειν, 'to card', which is cogn. with W.
cnaif, Olr. спае, 'fleece', and prob. also with
Lith. knabett, 'to peel', ON. hneppa, 'to squeeze,
pinch, rob', OE. hnxppan, 'to strike', Dan.
nappe, Swed., Norw. nappa, 'to pinch'.

## guar
guar, guarr, intr. v., to snarl. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. MHG. gnarren, knarren, G. knarren,
'to creak, rattle', G. knurren, Du. knorren, Dan.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:343 COLUMN:2 -->
knurre, 'to snarl, growl', which all are of
imitative origin. Cp. knar.

## gnarl
gnarl, intr. v., to snarl. — Formed from prec.
word with frequent, suff. -/.

## gaarled
gaarled, adj., knotted. — A var. of knurled,
'knotted', fr. knurl (q.v.); first used by
Shakespeare.

## gnash
gnash, tr. v. — ME. gnasten, 'to gnash the teeth',
rel. to ON. gnastan, 'a gnashing', gnista, of
s.m.; of imitative origin. Cp. G. knistern, 'to
crackle'. Derivatives: gnash, п., gnash-ing, n.

## gnat
gnat, n. — ME., fr. OE. gnxtt, rel. to LG. gnatte,
in gradational relationship to MLG. gnitte,
'gnat', G. Gnijze, 'gnat' and prob. also to OE.
gnagan, 'to gnaw'. See gnaw.

## gnathic
gnathic, adj., pertaining to the jaw. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. γνάθος, 'jaw, cheek', which
is cogn. with Lith. zandas, 'jaw', and prob.
stands in gradational relationship to Gk. γένυς,
'the lower jaw, cheek, chin', γένειον, 'chin'. See
genial, 'pertaining to the chin', and cp. words
there referred to.

## gaathism
gaathism, п., relative projection of the lower jaw
(a term of craniometry). — See prec. word and
-ism.

## gaathltis
gaathltis, п., inflammation of the jaw or cheek
(med.) — Medical L. See gnathic and -Ms.

## -gnathous
-gnathous, combining form lit. meaning '-jawed',
as in orthognathous, prognathous (a term of
craniometry). — See gnathic and -011s.

## gnaw
gnaw, tr. and intr. v. — ME. gnawen, fr. OE.
gnagan, rel. to OS. gnagan, ΟΝ., Swed. gnaga,
Dan. gnave, MDu., Du. knagen, OHG.
gnagan, nagan, MHG. gnagen, nagen, G. nagen.
Outside Teut. cp. the second element in Avestic
aiwt-ynixta, 'gnawed, nibbled, eaten'. Cp. nag,
'to worry'. Cp. also gnat.
Derivatives: gnaw-er, п., gnaw-ing, n. and adj.,
gnaw-ing-ly, adv.

## gneiss
gneiss, п., a composite rock consisting of
feldspar, quartz, mica and hornblende. — G., rel.
to OHG. gneisto, MHG. g(a)neist(e), ON.
gneisti, OE. gnast, 'spark'. Cp. OPruss. knaistis,
'a burning', and see ganister.

## gnome
gnome, п., a fabulous dwarfish person. — F., fr.
ModL. gnomus, a word coined by the Swiss-
German physician and alchemist Paracelsus
(died in 1541) prob. fr. Gk. γνώμη, 'intelligence'
(see next word; gnomes were supposed to be
intelligent people) or perh. fr. Gk. "γηνόμος,
'inhabitant of the earth', formed on the analogy
of θαλασσονόμος, 'inhabitant of the sea'. See
Geonoma.
Derivative: gnom-ish, adj.

## gnome
gnome, п., a moral maxim. — Gk. γνώμη, 'a
means of knowing; mind, judgment,
intelligence; maxim, opinion', from the base of
γιγνώσκειν, 'to know, perceive, understand'. See
can, aux. v., and cp. gnomon, gnosis. Cp. also
prec. word.

## gnomic
gnomic, gnomical, adj., pertaining to gnomes,
sententious, aphoristic. — Gk. γνωμικός,
'suited to maxims', fr. γνώμη. See prec. word
and -ic, resp. also -a].

## guomon
guomon, п., index on a sundial. — L. gnomon,
fr. Gk. γνώμων, 'judge, indicator', lit. 'one that
kn»ws', rel. to γνώμη, 'mind, judgment, maxim,
opinion'. See gaome, 'maxim', and cp. the
second element in pathognomonic and in
physiognomy.

## gaomonic
gaomonic, adj., pertaining to a gnomon. — L.
gndmonicus, fr. Gk. γνωμονικός, fr. γνώμων. See
prec. word and -ic.

## gnosis
gnosis, п., knowledge, especially that claimed by
the Gnostics. — ModL. gnosis, fr. Gk. γνώσις,
'knowledge', from the base seen also in γνώμη,
'mind, judgment; maxim, opinion'. See gnome,
'maxim', and cp. diagnosis, prognosis.

## gnostic
gnostic, adj., pertaining to knowledge. — Gk.
γνωστικός, 'of knowing', fr. γνωστός, 'known,
perceived, understood', a later collateral form
of γνωτός, verbal adj. of γιγνώσκειν, 'to know*.
See gnosis and -ic and cp. next word. Cp. also
diagnostic, prognostic.

## Gnostic
Gnostic, п., a member of the sect of Gnostics;
adj., pertaining to Gnosticism. — Late L. Gnos-
ticus, fr. Gk. γνωστικός, 'Gnostic, member of
a religious sect of the 2nd cent.*, lit. 'knowing*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:343 COLUMN:3 -->
See prec. word and cp. Mandaean.
Derivative: Gnostic-ism, n.

## gnu
gnu, п., a large S. African antelope. — Fr. gnoo,
the word by which the German traveler Georg
Forster (1754-1794) rendered Kaffir ngu (in his
book Ά Voyage Around the World', I, p. 83).

## go
go, intr. v. — ME. gon, fr. OE. gan, rel. 'to OS.,
OFris., MLG. gan, Dan. gaa, Swed. gu, MDu.
gaen, Du. gaan, OHG., MHG. gan, gen, G.
gehen, Crimean Gotb. geen, 'to go', fr. I.-E.
base "ghi-, *ghei-. The same base appears
reduplicated in OI. jihtte (for *ghi-ghe-te), 'goes
away', jd-ha-ti (for *ghe-ghe-ti), 'leaves,
abandons', Gk. κιχάνω (for *ghi-ghe-nS), κίχημι
(for *ghi-ghe-mi), Ί reach, meet with', Avestic
lazami, Ί dismiss'. Base *ghe-, *ghei-, 'to go',
is identical with base *ghe-, *ghli-, 'to lack, be
in want of (prop, 'to go without'), whence Gk.
χήτος, 'want, need', χατεϊν, 'to want, be in
need of, long for, desire', χήρος, 'bereaved of,
L. hires, 'heir'; see heredity and cp. chorl-. Cp.
ago.
Derivatives: go, п., that which goes, go-er, п.,
go-ing, n.

## goad
goad, n. — ME. gode, fr. OE. gad, 'point, sting,
goad, arrow', rel. to Lombard gaida, 'spear',
and cogn. with OI. hltih, 'missile, projectile',
hayati, hindti, 'pushes on, hurls', Avestic zaena-,
'weapon', Gk. χαϊος, 'shepherd's staff', Gaul.-
L. gaesum, 'a long heavy javelin', Olr. gae,
'spear', OE. gar, 'spear', Du. gesel, OHG.
geisila, MHG. geisel, G. Geifiel, 'whip, lash'.
All these words are traceable to I.-E. base 'ghei-,
'to drive on, push on'. Cp. gore, 'a triangular
piece of land', and words there referred to.
Derivative: goad, tr. v.

## goaf
goaf, п., the open space from which the coal has
been extracted (dial. E.) — ME. golf, 'heap of
sheaves placed in a barn', fr. ON. golf 'floor,
apartment, division*.

## goal
goal, n. — ME. got, 'limit, boundary*, prob. fr.
OE. "gal, 'hindrance', whence gxlan, 'to
hinder'; see gill, 'ravine'. For sense development
cp. L. meta, 'end, boundary; goal'.

## goat
goat, n. — ME. goot, gote, fr. OE. gat, rel. to OS.
get, ON., Norw. gelt, Swed. get, Dan.gjed, MDu.
gheet, Du. geit, OHG., MHG. gei^, G. Geifi,
Goth, gaits, 'goat', fr. I.-E. base "ghaido-, 'kid,
goat', whence also L. haedus, 'kid, young goat*.
Derivatives: goatee (q.v.), goat-ish, adj., goat-
ish-ly, adv., goat-ish-ness, п., goat-ling, п.,
goat-ly, adj.

## goatee
goatee, п., a man's beard resembling a goat's
beard. — Formed from prec. word with suff. -ее.
Derivative: goate-ed, adj.

## gob
gob, п., a mouthful of saliva; a lump of slimy
subsiance. — OF. gobe, 'a mouthful, a lump'
[whence F. gobe, gobbe, 'fattening ball (for
poultry); poisoned ball (for a dog)'], of Celtic
origin; cp. Ir. gob, 'mouth', Gael, gob, 'beak'.
Cp. gobbet, gobble, 'to eat greedily', goblet.

## gob
gob, п., a sailor in the navy (slang). — Perh. lit.
'a lump', and orig. identical with prec. word.

## gobang
gobang, also goban, п., a Japanese game
resembling checker. — Japan, goban, corruption of
Chinese k'i-p'an, 'checkerboard'.

## gobbet
gobbet, п., a piece of flesh; a lump of food
(archaic or rare). — ME. gobet, fr. OF. gobet,
dimin. of gobe, 'a mouthful, a lump'. See gob, 'a
mouthful', and dimin. suff. -et and cp. goblet.

## gobble
gobble, tr. and intr. v., to eat greedily. — Formed
with freq. suff. -Ie fr. F. gober, 'to gulp down,
swallow', fr. OF. gobe, 'a mouthful, a lump'.
See gob, 'a mouthful'.

## gobble
gobble, intr. v., to make the characteristic noise
of a turkey cock. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
gabble.
Derivative: gobble, п., the noise made by a
turkey cock.

## gnbble
gnbble, п., a successful putt into the hole (a term
of golf)· — Prob. fr. gobble, 'to eat greedily*.

## gobbledegook
gobbledegook, gobbledygook, п., the overinvol-
ved, pompous talk of officialdom (slang). —
Coined by Maury Maverick (1895-1954), a U.S.
public official.

## gobbler
gobbler, п., one who eats greedily. — Formed fr.
gobble, 'to ent greedily', with agential suff. -er.

## gobbler
gobbler, п., a turkey cock. — Formed fr. gobble,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:344 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 317 | -GONIUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:344 COLUMN:1 -->
'to make the noise of the turkey cock', with
agential suff. -er.

## Gobelin
Gobelin, adj., pertaining to tapestry produced at
the Gobelin looms; resembling such tapestry.
— Named after the French dyers Gilles and
Jehan Gobelin, who established near Paris a
factory of tapestry (about the middle of the
fifteenth century).
Derivative: Gobelin, п., a Gobelin tapestry.

## gobi
gobi, п., lenticular mass of deposits (geol.) —

## Mongolian gobi
Mongolian gobi, 'desert'. Cp. the Gobi Desert,

## which is a pleonasm
which is a pleonasm, because gobi means the
same as English desert.

## gobiid
gobiid, adj., pertaining to the Gobiidae. — See
next word.

## Gobiidae
Gobiidae, n. pi., the family of fishes constituted
by the gobies (ichlhyol.) — ModL., formed with

## suff. -idae fr. L. gobius
suff. -idae fr. L. gobius, a kind of fish. See goby,

## goblet
goblet, n. — ME. gobelel, fr. OF. (= F.)gobelet,
'goblet, cup', fr. OF. gobel, of s.m., orig.

## identical with OF. gobel
identical with OF. gobel, 'mouthful', dimin. ofgobe.

## See gob
See gob, 'a mouthful', and -et.

## goblin
goblin, п., an evil spirit. — F. gobelin, formed fr.
ML. cobalus, fr. Gk. κόβϊλος, 'rogue, knave;

## an evil spirit'
an evil spirit', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
kobold, cobalt.
Derivative: goblin-ry, n.

## goby
goby, п., a small marine fish. — L. gobius, fr. Gk.
χωβιός, which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
Gobiidae, gudgeon, the fish.
God; god, n. — ME., fr. OE. god, rel. to OS.,
Du. god, OHG., MHG. got, G. Gott, ON. gud,
Dan., Swed. gud, Goth, gup, for Teut. "guda-,
which is prob. a participial formation (cp. cold,
loud, old) meaning 'the invoked being', and
corresponds to I.-E. ghu-to-m, fr. base *gku-,
'to invoke', whence OI. hu-ta-, 'invoked' (epithet
of Indra), pp. of havati, 'invokes', which is rel.
to Avestic zavaiti, of s.m., Gk. καυχάομαι, Ί
boast', OSlav. zovo, zuvati, 'to call'. Cp. bigot,
giddy, good-by, gossip.
Derivatives: goddess (q.v.), god-like, adj., god-ly,
adj., god-li-ness, n.

## goddess
goddess, n. — ME. godesse, goddesse, a hybrid
coined fr. god and -esse, a suff. of ult. Gk.
origin. See god and -ess.

## Godetia
Godetia, п., a genus of plants of the evening
primrose family (бог.) — ModL., named after the
Swiss botanist Charles-Η. Godet (1797-1879).
For the ending see suff. -ia,

## Godfrey
Godfrey, masc. PN. — OF. Godefrei (F. Gode-
froi), fr. OHG. Godafrid(G. Gottfried), lit. 'the
peace of God', fr. OHG. got, 'God', and fridu,
'peace'. See god and free and cp. the first
element in Frederic and the second element in
Geoffrey,

## godown
godown, п., a warehouse; a store (Anglo-Ind.) —
Anglicized fr. Malay godong, 'warehouse',
which prob. derives fr. Telugu gidangi, fr. Tamil
kidangu, prop, 'a place where things lie', fr. kidu,
'to lie'. For sense development cp. G. Lager,
'storehouse, warehouse, store', lit. 'a place
where things lie', fr. liegen, 'to lie'.

## godsend
godsend, п., that which comes unexpectedly, as
if sent by God.; a welcome event. — For God's
send, in which send derives fr. ME. sonde, sonde,
'that which is sent, message', fr. OE. sand, fr.
sendan, 'to send'. See send,

## goel
goel, п., next of kin; redeemer; avenger of blood
(Hebrew antiq.) — Heb. gu'il, 'redeemer', active
part, of ga'al, 'he has redeemed', whence g''ul-
lah, 'redemption'. See Geullah.

## golf
golf, п., a stupid fellow (now dial.) — ME. goffe,
prob. fr. F. goffe, 'awkward', fr. It. goffo, of
s.m., which is of uncertain origin. Cp. goof,

## goffer
goffer, tr. v., to plait, flute. — F. gaufrer, 'to
figure (cloth, leather or velvet)', fr. gaufre,
'honeycomb, waffle', fr. Frankish *wafel, which
is rel. to MDu. wafel, 'wafer'. See wafer and cp.
gopher, 'a rodent'.
Derivatives: goffer, п., goffer-er, п., goffer-ing, a.

## goggle
goggle, intr. v. — ME. gogelen, prob. formed with
freq. suff. -le fr. the imitative base *gog-, Cp.
jog, joggle.
Derivatives: goggle, n. and adj., goggl-ed, adj.,
goggl-y, adj.

## goggler
goggler, п., name of a fish (Trachurops crumen-
ophthalmus). — Formed from prec. word with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:344 COLUMN:2 -->
agential suff. -er.

## goglet
goglet, also guglet, п., a waterbottle. —
Corruption of Port, gorgoteta, 'a narrow-mouthed
vessel out of which the water guggles', which is
rel. to gorgolejar, 'to drink by draughts or
gulps', an alteration of gargarejar, '10 gargle',
fr. L. gargarizare, from the imitative base
*garg-. See garget.

## goi
goi, goy, п., a gentile, a non-Jew. — Heb. gay,
'people, nation' (in Mishnaic and Modern
Hebrew, also 'gentile'), pi. goyfm. Cp. goyim.

## Goidelic
Goidelic, adj., pertaining to the Gaelic language.
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. Olr. Goidel, 'Gael'.
See Gael.

## goiter
goiter, goitre, n. — F. goitre, fr. OF. goitron,
'throat', fr. VL. *gutturionem, ace. of *gutturiot
fr. L. guttur, 'throat'. See guttural.
Derivatives: goiter-ed, goitr-ed, adj., goitrous
(q-v.)

## goitrous
goitrous, adj. pertaining to, or affected with,
goiter. — F. goitreux (fern, goitreuse), fr. goitre.
See goiter and -ous.

## gola
gola, п., a storehouse for grain. — Hind, goto, prop,
'a round house', fr. got, 'round'; so called from
the usual form of such storehouses.

## golah
golah, п., Diaspora, galuth {Jewish hist.) — Heb.
g6lah, 'exile; exiles', fr. gala", 'he uncovered,
removed; he departed; he went into exile, was
deported'. See galuth.

## Golconda
Golconda, п., a mine of wealth. — From Gol-
conda, the old capital of the kingdom of The
Deccan in India, a famous center of the
diamond trade.

## gold
gold, n. —ME., fr. OE. gold, rel. to OS., OFris.,
OHG. gold, MHG. golt, G. Gold, MDu. gout,
Du. goud, ON. gull, goll, Swed. gull, Dan. guld,
Goth, gulp, 'gold', and cogn. with OSlav. zlato
(for *zol-to), Russ. zaloto, Lett, zelts, OI. hiran-
yam, Avestic zaranya-, 'gold'. All these words are
traceable to I.-E. base "ghel-, "ghel-, 'to shine;
yellow', and orig. meant 'the yellow metal'. See
yellow and cp. gild, guilder, gulden. Cp. also zloty.
Derivatives: gold, gold-en, adjs.

## golem
golem, п., an artificial man; an automaton. —
Heb. golem (in Ps. 139:16), 'embryo', fr. galam,
'he wrapped up, folded'.

## golf
golf, п., a game of Scottish origin. — Of uncertain
origin. It derives pern. fr. MDu. coif, colve (Du.
kolf), 'club for striking balls', which is rel. to
ON. kolfr, 'clapper of a bell; a kind of bolt',
OHG. kolbo, MHG. kolbe, G. Kolben, 'mace,
club'.
Derivatives: golf, intr. v., golf-er, n.

## Golgotha
Golgotha, п., calvary. — Greek transliteration
of Aram, gulgultn, 'skull' (= Heb. gulgaleth),
the name given to л hill near Jerusalem (so called
in reference to its shape); cp. Calvary. For the
etymology of Aram, gulgulta see gelilah.

## goliard
goliard, п., jester, buffoon, poet. — OF. goliard,
goliart, 'glutton; buffoon', fr. gole (whence F.
gueule), 'mouth', fr. L. gula. See gullet and -ard.

## Goliath
Goliath, п., a giant. — Late L. Goliath, fr. Heb.
Golyath, name of a Philistine giant killed by
David (see I Sam., chapter 17).

## golliwog
golliwog, п., ι) a grotesque doll; 2) a grotesque
person. — Coined by the portrait painter and
illustrator Florence K. Upton (died in 1922).
The word was prob. modeled on polliwog.

## golosh
golosh, n. — A var. of galosh.

## golnptlous
golnptlous, adj., luscious. — Facetiously formed
on the analogy of voluptuous.

## gomasta
gomasta, gomastah, gomashta, п., a native agent
or factor (India). — Pers. gumashtah,
'appointed'.

## gombeen
gombeen, п., usury (Irish-English) — Ir. gaimbin,
'interest', fr. Late L. cambium, 'exchange', fr.
cambiare, 'to exchange'. See cambinm and cp.
words there referred to.

## gombroon
gombroon, gomroon, п., a kind of white semi-
porcelain. — Fr. Gombroon (now Bandar
Abbas), name of a town on the Persian Gulf.
Cp. gambroon.

## gonter
gonter, п., a measure. — L. gomor, Gk. γόμορ,
fr. Heb. 'omer. See omer.

## gomer
gomer, a conical chamber. — Named after its
inventor.

## gunteral
gunteral, gomerel, п., a fool.—Of unknown origin.

## gomphosis
gomphosis, п., an immovable union of bony parts

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:344 COLUMN:3 -->
in the body (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. γόμ-
φωσ',ς, 'a bolting together', fr. γομφοϋν, 'to
fasten with bolts', fr. γόμφος, 'bolt', which is
cogn. with OE. comb, 'comb'. See comb and
-osis and cp. agomphious.

## Gomphrena
Gomphrena, п., a genus of plants of the family
Amaranthaceae (bot.) — Altered fr. L. grom-
phaena, name of a kind of amaranth.

## gomroon
gomroon, n. — See gombroon.

## gomuti
gomuti, n„ a palm growing in the Archipelago
(Arenga saccharifera). — Malay gumuti.

## gon-
gon-, form of gono- before a vowel.

## -gon
-gon, combining form meaning 'having (such and
such) a number of angles', as in trigon, pentagon.
— Gk. -γωνος, from the stem of γωνία, 'angle,
corner', which is rel. to γόνυ, 'knee', and cogn.
with OI. jdnu, Goth, kniu, OE. слёо\'кпее\ See
knee and cp. gonio-, gonion, gony-1 Cp. also
agonic, Coregonus, diagon, diagonal, Eriogonum,
isogenic, orthogonal.

## gonad
gonad, п., a reproductive gland (biol.) — Formed
with suff. -ad fr. Gk. γονή, 'that which is
begotten; offspring; that which generates, seed,
semen; genitals; the act of generation; race,
family'. See gono-.

## gondola
gondola, п., a narrow boat used in the canals of
Venice. — It., fr. Friaul. gondola, 'to waver,
vacillate', which is prob. of imitative origin. It
is not connected with L. gandeia, 'a kind of
African ship'.
Derivative: gondola, intr. v.

## gondolet
gondolet, п., a small gondola. — It. gondoletta,
dimin. of gondola. See prec. word and -et.

## gondolier
gondolier, п., one who rows a gondola. — F., fr.
It. gondoliere, fr. gondola. See gondola and -ier.

## gone
gone, adj., lost; prop. pp. of go. — ME. gon,
fr. OE. gan, pp. of OE. gan, 'to go'. See go.
Derivatives: gone-ness, п., goner (q.v.)

## goner
goner, п., one ruined, lost (slang). — Formed fr·
gone with suff. -er.

## gonfalon
gonfalon, п., an ensign. — OF. (— F.), formed
with dissimilation from gonfanon (q.v.)

## gonfalonier
gonfalonier, п., one who bears the gonfalon. —
F., fr. gonfalon. See prec. word and -ier.

## gonfanon
gonfanon, п., a gonfalon. — F., fr. OHG. gundfano
(cp. OE. gupfana, ON. gunnfani), lit. 'banner of
war', fr. gund, gunt, 'war', and fano, 'flag,
banner'. The first element is rel. to OE. gud, ON.
guar, gunnr, 'war', fr. I.-E. base *gwhen-, 'to
strike', whence also Gk. θείνειν, 'to strike^ L.
de-fendere, 'to ward off, keep away, defend,
guard, protect'; see defend and cp. the first
element in Gunther. The second element is rel. to
OE., Goth, /ела, 'cloth', and cogn. with L. pan-
nus, 'piece of cloth1; see pane, 'sheet of glass',
and cp. fanon. Cp. also gonfalon.

## gong
gong, n. — Malay gong, of imitative origin. Cp.
gum-gum.
Derivative: gong, intr. v.

## Gongorism
Gongorism, п., an artificial, affected style. —
Prop, 'a style resembling that of the Spanish
poet Luis de Gongora у Argote (1561-1627)'.
For the ending see suff. -ism.

## Goniarites
Goniarites, п., a genus of cephalopods (paleon-
tol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γωνία, 'angle' (see -gon);
so called from the angular sutures.

## gonidium
gonidium, п., an asexual reproductive spore(oo<.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idhim fr. Gk.
γόνος, 'that which is begotten, offspring'. See
gono-.

## gonio-
gonio-, combining form meaning 'angle, corner'.
— Gk. γωνιο-, fr. γωνία, 'angle, corner'. See
-gon.

## goniometer
goniometer, п., an instrument for measuring
angles. — F. goniometre, fr. Gk. γωνία, 'angle',
and μέτρον, 'measure'. See gonio- and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## goniometry
goniometry, п., the measurement of angles. —
F. goniometrie. See prec. word and -merry.
Derivatives: goniometr-ic, goniometr-ic-al, adjs.,
goniometr-ic-al-ly, adv.

## gonion
gonion, п., the point at the angle on either side
of the lower jaw (craniol.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
γωνίϊ, 'angle, corner'. See -gon.

## gonitis
gonitis, п., inflammation of the knee (med.) —
Medical L., formed fr. Gk. γόνυ, 'knee', with
suff. -itis. See -gon.

## -gonlnm
-gonlnm, combining form denoting a mother cell

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:345 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GONNARDITE | 318 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:345 COLUMN:1 -->
(biol.) — ModL. -gonium, fr. Gk. -γόνος, 'be-
getting, producing; born of, fr. γόνος, 'that
which is begotten, offspring'. See gono-.

## gonnardite
gonnardite, п., a zeolite (mineral.) — Named after
the French mineralogist Ferdinand Gonnard,
who first analyzed it. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## gonnof
gonnof, gonnoph, also ganef, п., a thief. — Yiddish
ganef, fr. Heb. gannabh (in Modern Heb.
pronunciation gannav), 'thief, fr. gartabh, 'he
stole'. See gambit

## gono-
gono-, before a vowel gon-, combining form
meaning 'sexual, reproductive'. — Gk. γόνο-,
γον-, fr. γόνος, 'that which is begotten, child,
offspring; procreation; race, birth, descent;
seed, semen; genitals', or fr. γονή, 'that which
is begotten, offspring; that which generates,
seed, semen; genitals; the act of generation;
race, family'. See genus and cp. gonad, gonldium,
-gonium, -gony.

## gonococcus
gonococcus, п., the micro-organism that causes
gonorrhea (bacteriol.) — Medical L., coined
by the German physician Albert Ludwig Sig-
mund Neisser (1855-1916) in 1882 fr. gono- and
Gk. κόκκος, 'kernel, berry'. See coccus.

## Gonolobus
Gonolobus, п., a genus of plants, the anglepod
(hot.) — ModL., compounded of the stem of
γωνία, 'angle' and λοβός, 'pod' (see gonio- and
lobe). The genus is so called from the shape of
the fruit.

## gonophore
gonophore, п., 1) elongation of the axis of a flower
above the perianth (bot.); 2) one of the
generative buds containing the reproductive elements
in Hydrozoa (zool.) — Compounded of gono-
and -phore.

## gonorrhea
gonorrhea, gonorrhoea, n. (med.) — Late L.
gonorrhoea, fr. Gk. γονόρροικ, which is
compounded of γόνος, 'seed, semen', and £οία,
'flux', fr. ρεΐν, 'to flow'. See gono- and -rrhea.
Derivative: gonorrhe-al, gonorrhoe-al, adj.

## gony-
gony-, combining form denoting the knee. — Fr.
Gk. γόνυ, 'knee', rel. to γωνίϊ, 'angle, corner'.
See -gon.

## -gony
-gony, combining form meaning 'generation,
genesis, origination', as in cosmogony, geogony.
— L. -gonia, fr. Gk. -γονίϊ, fr. γόνος, 'that
which is begotten, offspring'. See gono- and
cp. -geny,

## good
good, adj. — ME. good, fr. OE. god, rel. to OS.,
OFris. god, ON. godr, Dan., Swed. god, Du.
goed, OHG, MHG. guot, G. gut, Goth, gaps,
'good'. The original meaning of these words was
'fit, adequate, belonging together'. They stand
in gradational relationship to OE. gada, ge-
gada, 'companion', gaderian, gxdrian, 'to gather,
collect, store up'; see gather and cp. the first
element in gospel. Cognates outside Teutonic
are OSlav. godu, 'pleasing time', godtnu,
'pleasing', goditi, 'to be pleasing'.
Derivatives: good, п., good-ly, adj., good-li-ness,
goodness (q.v.), goody (q.v.)

## good-by
good-by, good-bye, interj. and n. — Contraction
of God be with ye.

## goodness
goodness, n. — ME. goodnesse, fr. OE. godnes,
fr. god, 'good'. See good and -ness.

## goody
goody, п., sweetmeat, bonbon. — Formed fr.
good with adj. suff. -y.

## goody
goody, п., civility applied to a woman of humble
station. — From goodwife.

## goody
goody, also goody-goody, adj., affectedly pious,
sanctimonious. — Formed fr. good with adj.
suff. -y.

## goof
goof, п., a stupid person (U.S. Slang). — Of
uncertain origin; possibly a var. of goff.
Derivatives: goof-y, adj., goof-i-ly, adv., goof-
i-ness, n.

## googly
googly, adj. (a term of cricket). — Of uncertain
origin.

## googul
googul, n. — A var. of gugal.

## goon
goon, п., a ruffian. — Fr. Alice the Goon, a
subhuman character in the comic strip Thimble
Theatre by the American cartoonist Elzie Crisler
Segar (1894-1938).

## gooroo
gooroo, n. — A var. of guru.

## goorul
goorul, n. — A var. of goral.

## goosander
goosander, п., the merganser. — Prob. formed fr.
goose on analogy of bergiinder (q.v.)

## goose
goose, n. — ME. gos, goos, fr. OE. gos, rel. to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:345 COLUMN:2 -->
OFris., MLG. gos, ON. gas, OHG., MHG., G.
gans, 'goose', and cogn. with OI. hamsdh (masc),
hamsi (fern.), 'goose, swan', Dor;, Boeot. Gk.
χάν, Gk. χήν, L. anser (for "hanser), Lith. zqsis,
OPruss. sansy, 'goose', Olr. ggiss, 'swan'.
OSlav. gust, 'goose', and Sp. ganso, 'gander,
goose', are Teut. loan words. Cp. gander, gan-
net, gosling and the first element in goosander,
goshawk, gossamer. Cp. also anserine, Chen.
Derivatives: goos-ish, goos-y, adjs.

## gooseberry
gooseberry, n. — Prob. fr. G. Krausbeere or
Krausetberre, which are rel. to MDu. croesel,
'gooseberry'. These words prop, mean 'curly
berry', and derive fr. G. kraus, resp. MDu.
croes, 'crispy, curly; cp. ME. crous, 'curly'. E.
gooseberry owes its form to an association with
goose (as if it were a compound of goose and
berry). Cp. F. groseille, It. grossularia and Sp.
grosella, 'gooseberry', which are Dutch loan
words. Cp. also Grossularia.

## gopher
gopher, п., a burrowing rodent. — F. gaufre,
'waffle, honeycomb' (see goffer); so called in
allusion to its burrows.

## gopherwood
gopherwood, n. — Heb. gopher, name of the wood
of which Noah's ark was made. See cypress.

## gopura
gopura, п., a pyramidal tower above the entrance-
gate of a Hindu temple. — OI., 'city gate', lit.
'cow city', fr. gauh, gen. goh, 'ox, bull, cow', and
puram, 'city'. Gopura prob. denoted orig. that
part of the city (usually the suburb), in which
cattle breeding was practiced. For the first
element see cow and cp. Gautama and words there
referred to, for the second element see policy,
'method of government'.

## goral
goral, goorul, п., the Himalayan goat antelope. —
Hind, gural, goral.

## Gordian
Gordian, adj., pertaining to Gordius, king of
Phrygia or to the knot tied by him. For the
ending see suff. -ir....

## Gordonia
Gordonia, п., a genus of plants of the tea family
(bot.) — ModL., named after James Gordon, a
London nurseryman (1728-91). For the ending
see suff. -ia.

## gore
gore, п., ι) dirt (obsol.); 2) clotted blood. — ME.,
fr. OE. gor, 'dung, dirt', rel. to ON. gor, 'cud',
Swed. gorr, 'dirt', OHG., MHG. gor, 'dung',
Du. goor, 'foul, dirty', OE. gyre, 'dung', Norw.
gyrja, 'mud, mire'.

## gore
gore, п., a triangular piece of land. — ME. gare,
gore, fr. OE. gara, 'a triangular piece of land',
lit. 'a spearshaped piece of land', fr. OE. gar,
'spear', which is rel. to ON. geirr, OS., OHG.,
MHG.^Fr, G Ger, of s.m. See goad and cp. gore,
'to pierce'. Cp. also gar, and words there referred
to. Cp. also auger, garlic, gyron, the first element
in gerfalcon, and the second element in eagre,
'a tidal wave'.

## gore
gore, to pierce. — Fr. OE. gJr, 'spear'. The orig.
meaning was 'to pierce with a spear'. See prec.
word.

## gorge
gorge, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. VL. gurga,
'whirlpool, abyss', fr. L. gurges, gen. gurgitis, of s.m.
See voracious and cp. gorgeous, gorget,
disgorge, regorge. Cp. also gurgitation.
Derivatives: gorge, intr. and tr. v., gorg-ed, adj.

## gorgeous
gorgeous, adj. — OF. gorgias, 'finely dressed,
luxurious', formed from the name of Gorgias,
a Greek sophist and rhetorician (about 483-
375), who took pleasure in showing off his
luxury.
Derivatives: gorgeous-ly, adv., gorgeous-ness, n.

## gorget
gorget, п., a piece of armor defending the throat.
— OF. gorgete, dimin. of gorge, 'throat'. See
gorge and -et.
Derivative: gorget-ed, adj.

## Gorgon
Gorgon, п., one of the three sisters in Greek
mythology who had the power to turn to stone
all who looked upon them. — L. Gorgo, fr. Gk.
Γόργω, fr. γοργός, 'terrible', which is of
uncertain etymology. It is perh. cogn. with Olr. garg,
'rough, fierce, wild', OSlav. groza, Russ. groza,
Pol. groza, Czech hruza, 'horror'. Cp. Demo-
gorgon.

## gorgoneion
gorgoneion, п., representation of the head of a
Gorgon, esp. that of Medusa. — ModL., fr.
Gk. Γοργόνειαν, fr. Γοργώ. See prec. word.

## Gorgonian
Gorgonian, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
Gorgon. — Formed fr. Gorgon with suff. -ian.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:345 COLUMN:3 -->

## Gorgonzola
Gorgonzola, п., a kind of Italian cheese. — Short
for Gorgonzola cheese; so called from a village
near Milan.

## goriila
goriila, n. — An African word quoted by the
Punic navigator Hanno in his Periplus (about
450 B.C.E.)

## gormandize
gormandize, п., indulgence in good eating and
drinking. — F. gourmandise, 'gluttony,
greediness', fr. gourmand, 'glutton'. See gourmand.
Derivatives: gormandize, intr. v., gormandiz-er,
n.

## gorse
gorse, п., furze. — ME. gorst, fr. OE. gorst, rel.
to OS., OHG. gersta, MDu. gherste, Du. gerst,
MHG., G. gerste, 'barley', and cogn. with L.
hordeum, 'barley'. See Hordeum.

## gory
gory, adj., 1) covered with blood; bloody; 2)
characterized by much bloodshed. — Formed fr.
gore, 'clotted blood', with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: gori-ly, adv., gori-ness, n.

## goshawk
goshawk, п., a kind of large hawk. — ME. gos-
hawke, fr. OE. goshafoc, compounded of gos
and ha foe, lit. 'goose hawk'. See goose and hawk,

## goshenite
goshenite, п., a variety of beryl (mineral.) —
Named after Goshen in Massachusetts. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## goslet
goslet, п., a very small goose. — Formed with
suff. -let fr. ME. gos, 'goose'. See goose.

## gosling
gosling, п., a young goose. — Formed fr. ME.
gos, 'goose', with dimin. suff. -ling.

## gospel
gospel, n. — ME. godspel, gospel, fr. OE. god-
spell, lit. 'the good message', fr. god, 'good', and
spelt, 'narrative, story, saying, message' (see
good and spell, 'charm'). Gospel is prop, a loan
translation of Eccles. L. evangelium (seeevangel).

## gospelize
gospelize, tr. v., to evangelize. — A hybrid
formed fr. gospel with -ize, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## gospeler
gospeler, gospeller, n. — OE. godspellere,
'evangelist', fr. godspel. See gospel and agential suff. -er.

## gospodar
gospodar, n. — See hospodar.

## gossamer
gossamer, п., a filmy cobweb. — ME. gossomer,
gosesomer, lit. goose summer; so called because
it appears early November, at the time when
geese are in season. See goose and summec.
Derivatives: gossamer-ed, gossamer-y, adjs.

## gossip
gossip, п., ι) godparent (obsol. or dial.); 2) one
given to idle talk; 3) idle talk. — ME. godsib,
gossib, fr. OE. godsibb, 'sponsor', fr. god, 'God',
and sibb, 'relationship'. See god and sib.
Derivatives: gossip, intr. v., gossip-y, adj.

## gossoon
gossoon, п., a boy. — Corruption of F. gargon,
'boy'. See garcon.

## Gossypinm
Gossypinm, п., a genus of plants of the mallow
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. gossypion, 'the
cotton tree', which is of uncertain origin.

## got
got, past tense and pp. of get. — ME. past tense
gat, pp. geten, goten, fr. geten, 'to get'. See get.

## Goth
Goth, п., member of an East Teutonic people. —
Late L. Gothi (pi.), fr. Gk. Γότθοι, Γό»οι, fr.
Gut-, the first element in Gothic Gut-piuda, 'the
Gothic people'. For the second element in Gut-
piuda see Teuton. Cp. Jocelin, Joyce.

## Gothamite
Gothamite, п., a simpleton. — Formed fr.
Gotham, name of a village in England, whose
inhabitants were proverbial for their stupidity.
For the ending see subst. suff. -Ite. Cp. Abderite.

## Gothic
Gothic, adj. — F. gothique, fr. Late L. Gothicus,
fr. Gothus, 'Goth'. See Goth and -ic.
Derivatives: Gothic, п., Gothic-al-ly, adv.,
Gothic-ism, п., Gothic-ist, п., Gothic-ize, tr. and
intr. v.

## gouache
gouache, п., a method of painting with water-
colors mixed with gum and honey. — F., fr. It.
guazzo, orig. meaning 'a place where there is
water', derived fr. L. aquatid, 'the act of
watering', fr. aquatus, pp. of aquart, 'to bring water
'for drinking, fr. aqua, 'water'. See aquatic.

## Gouda
Gouda, п., also Gouda cheese. — Named after
the town of Gouda in Holland.

## gouge
gouge, п., a tool for making grooves. — F., 'a
hollow chisel', fr. Late L. gubia (for *gulbia),
of s.m., which is of Celtic origin; cp. Olr. gulban,
'prick,prickle',MIr.gulba,y/.gylfin,OCo.geluin,
'beak'. These words are prob. cogn. with Gk.
γλάφειν, 'to hollow out, hew, carve', γλαφυρός,
'hollowed out, hollow', Bulg. glob, 'eyesocket',
Slovenic globati, 'to hollow out, to gnaw'.
OProvenc. goja and Sp. gubia, 'gouge', also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:346 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 319 | GRAHAM BREAD -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:346 COLUMN:1 -->
derive fr. L. gubia. Cp. gudgeon, 'a pivot'.
Derivatives: gouge, tr. v., goug-er, n.

## goulard
goulard, п., a solution of lead subacetate. — Short
for Goulard's extract or Goulard's cerate; named
after Thomas Goulard, a French surgeon of the
18th cent.

## goulash
goulash, п., a stew made of beef or veal, flavored
with paprika. — Fr. Hung, gulyas (hus), lit.
'(meat) of a herdsman', fr. gulya, 'herd'.

## gour
gour, n. — A var. of gaur.

## Goura
Goura, п., a genus of pigeons, the crowned pigeon
(ornithol.) — ModL., from native name in
New Guinea, fr. Javanesegora, lit. 'great noise';
so called in allusion to the moaning cries with
which the male calls the female; gora is rel. to
the verb gheroq, 'to low, moan, snore'.

## gourami
gourami, п., a large fish of the Malay
Archipelago. — Malay gurameh.

## gourd
gourd, п., the fruit of cucurbitaceous plants. —
F. gourde, fr. OF. cohourde, courde, fr. L. cucur-
bita, 'gourd; pumpkin'. See cucurbit.

## gourde
gourde, п., the monetary unit of Haiti. — F.
gourde, prop. fern, of the adjective gourd, 'numb,
stifT, heavy*, fr. L. gurdus, 'dull', which is of
Iberian origin. Accordingly gourde prop,
denotes 'a heavy or thick coin'. Cp. next word.

## gourdy
gourdy, adj., swollen in the legs (veter.) — OF.
gourdi, 'benumbed, swollen', pp. of gourdir,
fr. gourd, See prec. word and -y (representing
F. -i).

## gourmand
gourmand, п., one very fond of eating. — F„ of
uncertain origin; not connected with gourmet.
Cp. gormandize, n.
Derivatives: gourmand-er, п., gourmand-ery, n.

## gourmet
gourmet, п., a connoisseur in eating and
drinking. — F., 'gourmet, epicure', fr. OF. gromet,
groumet, gourmet, 'servant, page; wine
merchant's assistant, shopboy'; of uncertain origin.
F. gourmet was influenced in meaning by F.
gourmand. Cp. groom.

## gout
gout, n. — OF. goute (F. goutte), 'drop; gout',
fr. L. gutta, 'drop', which is prob. cogn. with
Arm. kat\ kat'n, 'drop', kit', kl'an, 'milk'(see
Ernout-Meillet, DELL., p.286 s.v. gutta). This
disease was ascribed to the influence of the
drops of certain fluids in the body (whence the
sense development of OF. goute). Cp. gutter.
Derivatives: gout-y, adj., gout-i-Iy, adv.,
goutiness, n.

## gout
gout, п., taste. — F., fr. L. gustus. See gust,'taste',
and cp. gnsto.

## govern
govern, tr. and intr. v. — OF. governer (F. gou-
verner), fr. L. gubernare, 'to steer or pilot a
ship; to govern', a loan word introduced through
the medium of the Etruscans fr. Gk. κυβερΜΪν,
which is often compared with, but prob. not
related to, OI. kubarah, 'pole, beam, tiller', Lith.
kumbryti, 'to govern', kumbras, 'tiller'. Cp.
gubernatorial. Cp. also cybernetics.
Derivatives: govern-able, adj.,governabil-iiy, п.,
governabte-ness, п., governabl-y, adv.,
governing, adj., governor (q.v.)

## governail
governail, п., ι) a rudder; 2) government. — OF.
governail (F. gouvernait), fr. L. gubernaculum,
'rudder*, fr. gubernare. See prec. word.

## governance
governance, n. — OF. gouvernance. See govern
and -ance.

## governess
governess, n. — Shortened fr. ME. governeress,
fr. OF. go{u)verneresse. See govern and -ess and
cp. governor.
Derivative: governess, tr. and intr. v.

## government
government, n. — OF. government (F. gouverne-
meni), fr. governer, 'to govern', fr. L. gubernare.
See govern and -ment.
Derivatives: government-al, adj.,
government-ally, adv., and the hybrid nouns
government-alum, government-al-ist.

## governor
governor, n. — OF. governeiir (= F. gouverneur),
fr. L. gubernatorem, ace. of gubernator,
'steersman, pilot, ruler, governor', fr. gubernatus, pp.
of gubernare. See govern and agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: governor-ate, п., governor-ship, n.

## gowan
gowan, п., the daisy (Scot.) — Fr. obsol. gowlan,
golan (whence dial. E. golland), 'a gold-colored
flower', which is rel. to gold (q.v.)
Derivative: gowan-y, adj.

## gowk
gowk, п., ι) cuckoo; 2) a fool. — ME. goke,
gowk, fr. ON. gaukr, 'cuckoo', rel. to OE. giac.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:346 COLUMN:2 -->
OS. gak, gok, MLG. gok, MDij. gooc, OHG.
gauh, MHG. gouch, G. Gauch, "cuckoo'; of
imitative origin. Cp. cuckoo.
Derivatives: gowk, intr. v., to stare foolishly,
gowk-ed, adj., foolish, gowk-ed-ly, adv., gowk-
ed-ness, n.

## gown
gown, п., a loose robe; a woman's dress. — ME.
goune, fr. OF. gone, goune, fr. Late L. gunna,
'fur', prob. a word adopted from a language of
the Apennine or the Balkan Peninsula. W. gwn,
'gown', is a loan word fr. ME. goune.
Derivative: gown, tr. and intr. v.
go«pen, п., the hollow of the hand; a handful or
double handful (Scot, and dial.) — ON. gaupn,
'the hollow of the hand', rel. to OHG. goufana,
of s.m., OE. geap, 'open, wide', geoptm, 'to
swallow', ON. gaupa, 'lynx', Norw. gop,
'ravine'.

## goyim
goyim, pi., gentiles; all non-Jewish nations. —
Heb. goyim, pi. of gdy, 'people, nation'. See goi.

## Graafian follicle
Graafian follicle, Graafian vesicle (anat.) —
Named after the Dutch anatomist Regnier
de Cree/(1641-73).

## grab
grab, tr. and intr. v., to seize suddenly. — MDu.
grabben, rel. to OS. garva, MDu. garve, OHG.
garba, 'sheaf, lit. 'that which is gathered up or
together', fr. I.-E. base *gherebh-, *ghrebh-, 'to
seize', whence also 0\.g[bhnati,grhnati, 'seizes',
OS lav. grabiti,'lo seize, rob', Lith. grebiu, grebti,
'to rake'. Cp. garb, 'sheaf, grabble.
Derivatives: grab, п., a sudden grasp,
grabber, n.

## grab
grab, п., a kind of vessel used in the Indian
ocean. — VArab. ghrab, fr. Arab, ghurab,
'raven; galley', of imitative origin. Cp. Heb..
'oribh, Aram, 'orbha, Syr. 'urbha, Akkad. aribu,
'raven', which all are imitative.

## grabble
grabble, intr. v., to grope; tr. v., to seize. — Du.
grabbelen, freq. of MDu. grabben. See grab,
'to seize', and freq. suff. -ie.
Derivatives: grabbl-er, п., grabbl-ing, n.

## grace
grace, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) grace, fr. OF.
grace, fr. L. gratia, 'favor shown to another,
kindness, loveliness, charm; thanks,
thankfulness, gratitude', fr. gratus, 'beloved, pleasing,
dear, agreeable; grateful', fr. I.-E. base *g"er-,
'to praise, welcome', whence also OI. grndti,
genili, 'sings, praises, announces', gfr, girdh,
'praise, song', gurtih, of s.m., gurtah, 'welcome',
Avestiv gar-, 'to praise', Lith. giriu, girti, 'to
praise, celebrate', Lett, dzirtiis, 'to boast',
OPruss. girtwei, 'to praise', girsnan, 'praise,
reputation'. Cp. gracious, grateful, gratify,
gratis, gratuitous, gratulate, agree, congrata-
late, disgrace, ingrate, ingratiate, mauger.
Derivatives: grace, v. (q.v.), grace-ful, adj.,
grace-ful-ly, adv., grace-ful-ness, п., grace-less,
adj., grace-less-ly, adv., grace-less-ness, n.

## grace
grace, tr. v. — OF. grader, fr. grace. See grace, n.

## Grace
Grace, fern. PN. — Lit. 'favor, grace', fr. L.
gratia. See grace, n.

## Gracllaria
Gracllaria, п., a genus of algae (hot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. gracilis, 'slender'. See gracile.

## gracile
gracile, adj., 1) slender; 2) gracefully slender. —
L. gracilis, 'slender, thin, slight, meager', dis-
similated fr. *cracilis, rel. to cracens, 'slender',
and prob. cogn. with OI. krsah, 'thin, weak',
Avestic k'r'sa-, 'lean, meager', Lith. karStu,
karsli, 'to be very old, to age*, Lett, karst, karst,
'to grow old, ripen'. Cp. Gracilaria. For the
ending of grac-ilis cp. habilis, 'handy, supple,
suitable', fr. habere, 'to have, hold' (see able).
Derivatives: gracile-ly, adv., gracile-ness, п.,
gracil-ity, n.

## gracious
gracious, adj. — OF. gracious (F. gracieux), fr.
L.gratiosus, 'enjoying favor, agreable, obliging',
fr. gratia. See grace, п., and suff. -011s.
Derivatives: gracious-ly, adv., gracious-ness, n.

## grackle
grackle, п., any of various birds of the starling
family. — L. graculus, 'the jackdaw', of
imitative origin; cp. croak, v., and words there
referred to.

## gradatim
gradatim, adv., gradually. — L., 'step by step',
formed fr. gradus, 'step, degree', with the suff.
-atim. This suff. was formed on analogy of L.
statim, 'immediately' (prop. ace. of the ancient
noun sta-ti-s, 'a standing'), and was used to
form adverbs. Cp. literatim, seriatim, verbatim.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:346 COLUMN:3 -->

## gradate
gradate, intr. and tr. v..— Back formation fr.
gradation.

## gradation
gradation, п., ι) a scale of degrees; 2) the act of
arranging in degrees; 3) (philology) ablaut. —
L. gradatid, gen. -onis, 'that which goes up or
down by degrees; staircase; gradation', fr.
gradus, 'step, degree'. See grade and -ation.
Derivatives: gradation, tr. v., gradation-al, adj.

## grade
grade, п., a degree. — F., fr. L. gradus, 'step,
degree; stage, position; that on which one
steps, a stair', rel. to gradi, 'to step, walk, go',
and cogn. with Lith. grldyu, gridyti, 'to go,
wander', OSisiV.gredp,gresti, 'to come', Olr. in-greinn,
do-greinn, 'he pursues', prob. also with Avestic
aiwi-g'r'dmahi, 'we begin'. Cp. -grade,
gradatim, gradation, gradieut, gradin, gradual,
graduate, gradus, aggress, congress, degrade,
degree, degression, digression, egress, grail, 'book
for the use of the choir', Grallatores, grec,
'superiority', gressorial, ingredient, ingress,
progress, regress, retrograde, retrogress,
transgress.
Derivatives: grade, tr. and intr. v., grad-ed, adj.,
grad-er, n.

## -grade
-grade, combining form denoting 'mode of
walking', as in digitigrade, plantigrade. — F. -grade,
fr. L. -gradus, 'stepping, walking, going', from
gradi, 'to step, walk, go'. See grade.

## Gradgrind
Gradgrind, п., a hard utilitarian. — Character in
Charles Dickens' Hard Times.
Derivatives: Gradgrind-ian, Gradgrind-ish, adjs.

## gradient
gradient, adj., walking, capable of walking. —
L. gradiins, gen. -ends, pres. part, of gradi, 'to
step, walk, go'. See grade and -ent.

## gradient
gradient, п., degree of inclination; grade. See
prec. word.

## Gradientia
Gradientia, n. pi., an order of Amphibia; also
called Caudata (zool.) — ModL., fr. L.
gradientia, neut. pi. of gradiins, 'walking, going',
pres. part, of gradi. See gradient, adj.

## gradin
gradin, gradiae, n„ a series of steps rising one
upon another. — F. gradin, fr. It. gradlno,
dimin. oi.grado, fr. L. gradus, 'step'. See
grade, n.

## gradometer
gradometer, n„ an instrument for measuring
grades. — A hybrid coined fr. L. gradus, 'step,
degree', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See grade
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## gradual
gradual, adj. — ML. gradualis, fr. L. gradus. See
grade and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: gradual, n. (q.v.), graduai-ity, п.,
gradual-ness, п., gradual-ly, adv.

## gradual
gradual, п., ι) an antiphon; 2) a book for the use
of the choir (eccles.) — ML. graduate, prop,
neut. of the adjective gradualis (see prec. word),
used as a noun; so called because the antiphon
was sung originally from the steps (L. gradus) of
the altar. Cp. grail,'book for the useof the choir'.

## graduate
graduate, n. — ML. graduatus, fr. L. gradus,
'step, degree'. See grade and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: graduate, tr. and intr. v.

## graduation
graduation, n. — ML. graduatio, 'raising to a
degree', fr. L. gradus, 'step, degree'. See grade
and -ation.

## gradus
gradus, п., a dictionary of prosody, used as an
aid for writing Greek or Latin verses. — L.,
short for 'gradus ad Parnassum', 'steps to
Parnassus'. See grade.

## Graecism
Graecism, Graecize, Graeco-. — See Grecism,
Grecize, Greco-,

## Graf
Graf, п., a German title of nobility equivalent to
F. comte (whence E. count) and to E. earl. —
See grave, 'a count'.

## graffitu
graffitu, п., ancient writing scratched on rocks,
walls, etc. — It., dimin. of graffio, 'a scratching',
fr. graffiare, 'to scratch', which prob. derives
fr. grafio, 'a writing style', fr. L. graphium, of
s.m., fr. Gk. γρκφίον. See next word.

## graft
graft, n. — ME. graffe, graff, fr. OF. grafe, a
collateral form of grefe, 'pencil; a shoot for
grafting' (whence F. greffe, 'a shoot for grafting'),
fr. L. graphium, 'a writing style', fr. Gk. γραφίον,
γραφεΐον; so called from the resemblance of
the shoot to a pointed pencil. See -graph and cp.
archaic E. graff (which is the original form of
graft). Cp. also graffito, greffler.
Derivatives: graft, v., graft-er, п., graft-ing, n.
graham bread. — Named after Sylvester Graham,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:347 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GRAHAMITE | 320 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:347 COLUMN:1 -->
an American advocate of temperance (1794-
1851).

## grahamite
grahamite, п., a bituminous mineral (mineral.) —
Named after J.A and J.L.Graham, in whose
mine it was discovered. For the ending see subst.
sufT. -ite.

## grail
grail, also grnal, п., according to medieval legend
the platter used by Jesus at the Last Supper. —
OF. graal, grael, fr. ML. gradalis, 'cup, platter',
fr. VL. "cratalis, fr. "crdtus, 'a mixing bowl',
fr. L. crater, fr. Gk. κράτήρ. See crater.

## grail
grail, п., book for use of the choir (eccles.) —
OF. grael, fr. ML. gradale, a collateral form of
graduate. See gradual, n.

## grain
grain, п., seed, corn. — F., fr. L. granum, 'grain,
seed, small kernel'. See cora, 'grain', and cp.
garner, garnet, gram, 'chick-pea', granadilla,
granary, grange, graniila, granite, granule,
grenade, grenadier, grenadine, engrain, fiilgrane,
pomegranate, grogram. Cp. also gravy.
Derivatives: grain, intr. and tr. v., grain-ed, adj.,
grain-er, п., grain-ing, п., grain-y, adj.

## grain
grain, п., branch, prong of a fork. — ON. grein,
'branch, fork', whence also Dan. and Swed.
gren, 'branch'.

## graith
graith, tr. v., to make ready (Scot, and dial. E.)
— ME. greithen, fr. ON. greida, 'to make ready',
fr. greidr, 'ready', which is rel. to OE. gerxde,
rxde, of s.m. See ready,

## graith
graith, adj., ready; direct, exact. — ON. greidr,
'ready'. See graith, v.

## graith
graith, п., ι) readiness (obsol); 2) apparatus,
equipment (Scot.); 3) material (Scot.) — ON.
greidi, fr. greidr, 'ready'. See graith, v.

## Grallatores
Grallatores, n. pl„ the wading birds (ornithol.) —
ModL., fr. L. grallatores, 'stilt-walkers', pi. of
grallator, fr. grallae, 'stilts', assimilated fr.
*grad-lae, from the stem of gradt. 'to walk, go'.
See grade,

## grallatorial
grallatorial, adj., pertaining to the Grallatores.
— See prec. word and -fad,

## gralloch
gralloch, n„ offal of a deer. — Gael, grealach,
'intestines'.

## gram
gram, п., the chick-pea; the horse gram. — Port.
grab, 'grain', fr. L. granum. See grain, 'seed, corn'.

## gram
gram, gramme, п., the metric unit of weight. —
F. gramme, fr. Late L. gramma, fr. Gk. γράμμα,
'that which is written; written character, letter;
a small weight'. See -gram.

## -gram
-gram, combining form denoting 'something
written', as in anagram, cardiogram, diagram. —
Gk. -γράμμα (rarely -γραμμον), fr. γράμμα, gen.
γράμματος, 'that which is written; a written
character, letter', from the stem of γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graph.

## grama (grass)
grama (grass), pasture grass belonging to the
genus Bouteloua. — Sp. grama, a kind of grass,
fr. L. gramen, 'grass'. See grammi-.

## grainarye
grainarye, gramary, п., magic (archaic). — ME.
gramarye, grammarie, 'grammar; magic', fr.
OF. gramaire, grammaire, 'grammar', esp.
'Latin grammar', whence arose the meanings 'an
obscure, unintelligible book; book of spells,
magic'. Cp. F. grammaire, 'grammar',
differentiated from grimoire, 'book of spells, black
book; unintelligible language', which both
derive from OF. gramaire. See grammar and cp.
glamour,

## gramercy
gramercy, interj., exclamation expressing 1)
thanks; 2) surprise. — F. grand-merci, 'great
thanks'. See grand and mercy.

## gramicidine
gramicidine, gramicidin, п., a crystalline
antibiotic obtained from a soil bacterium. — Coined
by the bacteriologist Rene Jules Dubos, of the
Rockefeller Institute (born in 1901), in 1940 fr.
gram- (in gram-positive), 1 st -cide and chem. suff.
-ine-, -ia.

## gramineous
gramineous, adj., resembling grass; pertaining to
the family of grasses. — L. gramineus, 'of grass,
grassy', fr. gramen, gen. graminis, 'grass'. See
gramini-. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## gramini-
gramini-, combining form meaning 'grass'. — Fr.
L. gramen, gen. graminis, 'grass', which prob.
stands for "ghras-men and is cogn. with OE.
grxs, 'grass*. See grass and cp. grama (grass).

## graminiferous
graminiferous, adj., bearing grass. —
Compounded of gramini- and -ferous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:347 COLUMN:2 -->

## graminivorous
graminivorous, adj., feeding on grass. —
Compounded of gramini- and -vorous.

## grammalogue
grammalogue, п., a word represented by a
logogram. — Compounded of Gk. γράμμα, 'letter',
and λόγος, 'word'. See -gram and -logue and cp.
logogram.

## grammar
grammar, n. — ME. gramere, grammere, fr. OF.
gramaire, grammaire (F. grammaire), fr. L.
grammatica, fr. Gk. γραμματική (scil. τέχνη),
'grammar', orig. 'the art of reading and writing
letters'. Γραμματική is prop. fern, of the adj.
γραμματικός, 'knowing one's letters; knowing
grammar', fr. γράμμα, gen. γράμματος, 'letter',
lit. 'that .which is written', from the stem of
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph and cp. gramarye,
grammatical.

## grammarian
grammarian, п., a student of, or an expert in,
grammar. — ME. gramarien, fr. OF. gramarien
(F. grammairien), fr. OF. gramaire (F.
grammaire), 'grammar'. See prec. word and -ian.

## grammatical
grammatical, adj. — L. grammaticalis, fr. gram-
maticus, 'pertaining to grammar', fr. Gk.
γραμματικός, 'knowing one's letters; knowing
grammar'. See grammar.
Derivatives: grammatical-ly, adv., grammatical-
ness, n.

## grammaticaster
grammaticaster, п., a petty grammarian. — ME.,
fr. L. grammaticus, 'grammarian', fr. gram-
maticus, 'pertaining to grammar'. See prec.
word and -aster.

## grammaticize
grammaticize, tr. v., to make grammatical; intr.
v., to discuss points of grammar. — See
grammatical and -ize.

## gramme
gramme, n. — See gram.

## Gramophone
Gramophone, п., trademark used for a type of
phonograph. — Coined by its inventor Emile
Berliner (1851-1929) fr. Gk. γράμμα, 'something
written*, and φωνή, 'sound, voice*. See -gram
and phone, 'speech sound', and cp. phonograph.

## gram-positive
gram-positive, adj., holding the purple dye when
stained by Gram's method; said esp. of bacteria.
— So called after the Danish physician Hans
Christian Joachim (1853-1938).

## grampus
grampus, п., a cetacean (Grampus griseus). — Fr.
earlier graundepose, altered—after grand—
fr. ME. graspeys, grapeys, fr. OF. craspeis,
graspeis, lit. 'fat fish', fr. L. crassumpiscem, ace.
of crassus piscis. See crass and Pisces.

## granadilla
granadilla, п., the fruit of certain kinds of passion
flower. — Sp., dimin. of granada,
'pomegranate'. See pomegranate.

## granary
granary, п., a storehouse for grain. — ~L.granari-
um, 'granary', fr. granum, 'grain, seed, small
kernel'. See grain, 'seed, corn', and subst. suff.
-ary and cp. garner, which is a doublet of
granary.

## grand
grand, adj., great. — ME. grant, fr. OF. grant,
grand (F. grand), fr. L. grandem, ace. of grandis,
'large, tall, fullgrown, great, lofty, powerful',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. grandee,
grandiose, aggrandize, and the first element in
gramercy.
Derivatives: grand, п., grand-ly, adv., grand-
ness, a.

## grandam
grandam, grandame, п., a grandmother; an old
woman. — AF. ground dame, 'grandmother',
corresponding to OF. grand dame. See grand
and dame.

## granddaughter
granddaughter, n. — Formed on analogy of
grandmother.

## grandee
grandee, п., nobleman of the highest rank in
Spain and Portugal. — Anglicized form of Sp.
grande, 'nobleman of the first rank', from the
adj. grande, 'great*, fr. L. grandem. See grand
and -ее.

## grandeur
grandeur, n. — F., 'greatness', fr. grand, 'great'.
See grand.

## grandfather
grandfather, n. — A hybrid coined fr. grand and
father on analogy of F. grand-pere.

## grandiloquence
grandiloquence, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce.

## grandiloqueat
grandiloqueat, adj. — Formed with suff. -ent fr.
L. grandiloquus, 'speaking loftily, bombastic',
fr. grandis, 'great, lofty', and loqut, 'to speak'.
See grand and loquacious.
Derivative: grandiloquent-ly, adv.

## grandiose
grandiose, adj., grand, imposing, impressive. —
F., fr. It. grandiose, fr. grande, 'great', fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:347 COLUMN:3 -->
grandem. See grand and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: grandiose-ly, adv., grandios-ity,-n.

## grandmother
grandmother, n. — A hybrid coined fr. grand and
mother on analogy of F. grand-mere.

## grandparent
grandparent, п., grandson etc. — Formed on
analogy of grandfather.

## grange
grange, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) grange, fr. VL.
*grdnica, fr. L. granum, 'grain'. See grain, 'seed,
corn*.

## granger
granger, п., a farm steward. — OF. grangier, fr.
grange. See grange and -er (representing OF.
-ier).

## grangerism
grangerism, п., the practice of grangerizing. —
See next word and -ism.

## grangerize
grangerize, tr. v., to illustrate a book by the
addition of prints, engravings, etc. — Lit. 'to
illustrate a book in the manner in which James
Granger's 'Biographical History of England'
(1769) was illustrated.
Derivatives: grangeriz-ation, п., grangeriz-er, п.,
grangerism (q.v.)

## graniferous
graniferous, adj., producing grain. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. L. granifer, 'grain-bearing', fr.

## graniila
graniila, п., the refuse of cochineal. — Sp.,
dimin. of grana, 'cochineal', rel. to grano, 'grain',

## granite
granite, n. — F., fr. It. granito, lit. 'grainy', pp.
of granire, 'to make grainy', fr. grano, 'grain',
fr. L. granum. See grain, 'seed, corn', and cp.
prec. word.
Derivative: granit-ic, adj.

## granitiform
granitiform, adj., shaped like granite. —
Compounded of granite and -form.

## granivorous
granivorous, adj., feeding on grain. — Corn-
pounded of L. granum, 'grain', and vorare, 'to
devour'. See grain, 'seed, coin', and -vorous.

## granny
granny, also grannie, п., a familiar form of
grandmother. — Formed from the first syllable of
grandam and dimin. suff. -y, resp. -ie.

## granophyre
granophyre, п., a porphyritic igneous rock (pe-

syllable of Granit and the second syllable of
Porphyr. See granite and porphyry.
Derivative: granophyr-ic, adj.

## grant
grant, tr. v. — ME. gramen, fr. OF. granter, a
collateral form of craanter, creanter, fr. VL. *cre-
de/rtare.'io promise', ΪΓ. L. credens,gen. credentis,
pres. part, αϊ credere, 'to believe'. See creed and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: grant, n. (q.v.), grant-able, bdj.,
grant-ee, п., grant-er, п., grant-or, n.

## grant
grant, n. — ME. grant, fr. gramen. See grant, v.

## granular
granular, adj. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. Late
L. granulum. See granule.

## granulate
granulate, tr. and imr. v. — Formed with verbal
suff. -ate fr. Late L. granulum. See granule.
Derivatives: granulat-ed, adj., granulat-ίοη, п.,
granulat-ive, adj., granulat-or, n.

## granule
granule, п., a small grain. — Late L. granulum,
'small grain', dimin. of L. granum, 'grain*. See

## granuliform
granuliform, adj. — See prec. word and -form.

## granulose
granulose, adj., granular. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ose fr. Late L. granulum. See granule.

## granulose
granulose, п., part of starch convertible into
sugar. — Formed with subst. suff. -ose, fr. Late
L. granulum. See granule.

## granulous
granulous, adj., granular. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. Late L. granulum. See granule and cp.

## grape
grape, n. — OF. grape, grappe, 'hook; a bunch

grapes'), fr. OF. craper, graper, 'to seize with a
hook; to gather grapes', which is of Teut.
origin. Cp. MDu. crappe, OHG. krapfo, 'a hook',
G. Krapfen, 'fritter', OHG. krampho, 'an iron
hook'. OF. grapin, 'hook' (whence F. grappin,
grapnel,hook'), derivesfr.OF.ira/w.Cp.OProv-
εης., Sp. grapa. It. grappa, 'hook', which are
also Teut. loan words. See cramp, 'a bent piece
of iron', and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also agraffe.
Derivative: grap-y, adj.

## graph
graph, n', a diagram. — Abbreviation of graphic
formula. See -graph.

## -graph
-graph, combining form meaning 1) 'something

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:348 COLUMN:1 -->
written', as in autograph: 2) 'something that
writes', as in telegraph. — F. -graphe, fr. Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to scratch, engrave, draw,
paint, write, inscribe', which is cogn. with OE.
ceorfan, 'to cut, engrave, tear'. See carve and
cp. graph, -graphia, graphite, grapho-, -graphy,

## grapheme
grapheme, η., ι) a letter of an alphabet; 2) the
sum of all letters representing one phoneme. —
Gk. γράφημα, 'letter', fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
-graph and cp. the second element in phoneme
and in words there referred to. Cp. also Gk.
γράμμα, 'letter', from the stem of γράφειν (see
-gram).
Derivatives: graphem-ic, adj., graphem-ic-al-ly,
adv.

## -grapher
-grapher, combining form; the English equivalent

See -graph and agential suff. -er and cp. -graphy.

## -graphia
-graphia, combining form identical in meaning

sphere of abnormal psychology.

## graphic
graphic, adj. — L. graphicus, fr. Gk. γραφικός,
'pertaining to writing or drawing', fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See -graph and -ic.
Derivatives: graphic-al, adj., graphic-al-ly, adv.,
graphics (q.v.)

## graphics
graphics, п., the art of drawing. — See graphic
and -ics.

## graphite
graphite, п., a form of carbon, black lead,
plumbago (mineral.) — G. Graphit, coined by the
German mineralogist Abraham Gottlob

used for making pencils. See -graph and subsi.
suff. -ite.
Derivatives: graphite, tr. v., graphit-ic, adj.

## grapho-
grapho-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to,
or used for, writing', as in graphology. — Gk.
γραφ.ο-, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## graphology
graphology, п., the study of handwriting. — F.
grapho/ogie, coined by Abbe Jean-Hippolyte
Michon (1806-81) in 1868 fr. Gk. γράφειν, 'to
write', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See grapho- and -logy.
Derivatives: graphoiog-ic, grapho/og-ic-al, adjs.,
grapholog-ist, n.

## graphomania
graphomania, п., a morbid desire for writing. —
Compounded of grapho- and Gk, μανία,
'madness, frenzy'. See mania.

## graphomaniac
graphomaniac, п., one suffering from

## graphometer
graphometer, п., surveyor's instrument for
measuring angles. — F. graphometre, coined by the
French engraver Philippe Danfrie (1535-1606)

'measure'. See grapho- and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## graphophone
graphophone, п., an instrument for sound
recording. — Lit. 'that which writes the sounds';
compounded of grapho- and Gk. φωνή, 'sound,
voice'. See phone, 'speech sound'.

## -graphy
-graphy, combining form denoting: 1) processes
of writing, drawing, representing, recording, as
in phonography; 2) names of descriptive
sciences, as in geography. — F. or G. -graphie, fr.
L. -graphia, fr. Gk. -γραφιά, 'description of,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph and -y
(representing Gk. -'5c), and cp. -graphia,

## grapnel
grapnel, п., a small hook. — ME. grapenel, di-
min. formed fr. OF. grapin, 'hook'. See grape.
Derivative: grapnel, tr. v.

## grapple
grapple, п., grappling iron, grapnel. — OF. *gra-
pelle, dimin. of grape, 'hook'. See grape and cp.
prec. word.
Derivatives: grapple, tr. and intr. v., grappl-er,
п., grappl-ing, n.

## grapsold
grapsold, adj., pertaining to the genus Grapsus
(zool.) — Lit. 'resembling a crab'. See
Grapsus and -oid.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:348 COLUMN:2 -->

## Grapsus
Grapsus, п., a genus of crabs (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. γραψκΐος, 'crab', which is of uncertain
origin; it is prob. not connected with It. gra-
vosta, ravosta, OHG. krebij, OE. crabba, 'crab*.

## graptolite
graptolite, п., a fossil zoolite bearing markings
resembling writing (paleontol.) — ModL. Grap-
tolithus, lit. 'a stone with engraving', fr. Gk.
γραπτός, 'engraved, written, painted' (verbal
adj. of γράφειν), and λίθος, 'stone'. See -graph

Derivative: graptolit-ic, adj.

## grasp
grasp, tr. and intr. v. — ME. graspen, metathe-
sized fr. grapsen, 'to grope', from the stem of
OE. grdpian, 'to touch, feel, grope'. Cp. LG.
grapsen, 'to grasp', MDu. grapen, Ίο seize,
grasp', and see grope. Cp. also grip, gripe.
Derivatives: grasp, п., grasp-er, п., grasp-ing,
adj., grasp-ing-ly, adv., grasp-ing-ness, n.

## grass
grass, n. — ME. gras, gres, gers, fr. OE. grxs,
gxrs, rel. to ΟΝ., OS., Du., OHG., MHG., G.,
Goih. gras, Dan. grxs, Swed. grits, 'grass', and
prob. cogn. with L. grdmen (for ghras-men),
'grass', fr. I.-E. base *ghros-, 'young shoot,
sprout'. This base is an -^-enlargement of base
*ghro-, 'to grow', whence OE. growan, ON.
grda, 'to grow'. Enlarged by suff. -л, base "ghrd-
appears in OE. grene, ON. gram, 'green'. See
grow and green and cp. grama (grass), gramini-,
graze (in both senses).
Derivatives: grass, tr. v., grass-less, adj.,
grasslike, adj., grass-y, adj.

## grass widow
grass widow, a woman separated from her
husband. — Orig. 'a discarded mistress'; cp. Du.

'grass widow' (in modern sense); prob. so called

## grass widower
grass widower, a man separated from his wife. —
Cp. Swed. grasdnk, grasanker, grasenkling,
'grass widower*, and see prec. word.

## grate
grate, tr. and intr. v., to scrape, rub. — ME.
graten, fr. OF. grater (F. gratter). Ίο scratch,
scrape', fr. Teut. *kratton (whence also It. grat-
tare, OProvenc. gratar). Cp. OHG. krazzdn,
'to scratch, scrape', and see scratch. Cp. also
regrate, regrater.
Derivatives: grat-er, п., grat-ing, n. and adj.,
grat-ing-ly, adv.

## grate
grate, п., a frame of metal bars. — ME. grate,
fr. ML. grata, 'lattice' (whence also It. grata,

hurdle'. See crate and cp. graticule, griddie,
hurdle.
Derivative: grate, tr. v., to furnish with a grate.

## grateful
grateful, adj. — Formed with suff. -ful from ob-
sol. grate, 'agreable, thankful', fr. L. grdtus,
'agreable, grateful', whence gratia, 'kindness,
loveliness'. See grace, п., and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: grateful-ly, adv.

## graticule
graticule, п., a design divided into squares. — F.,
fr. ML. grSticula, 'gridiron', dimin. of grata.
See grate, 'frame of metal bars', and -cule.

## gratification
gratification, n. — L. gratificatid, gen. -onis.
Obligingness, complaisance', fr. grdtifiedtus,
pp. of gratificari. See next word and -ation.

## gratify
gratify, tr. v., to please. — F. gralifier, fr. L. gra-
tificare, a collateral form of gratificari, Ίο do
favor to, to oblige, gratify', formed fr, gratus,
'agreeable, grateful', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to
make, do'. See grace, п., and -fy.
Derivatives: gratifi-ed, adj., gratifi-ed-ly, adv.,
gratifi-er, п., gratify-ing, adj., gratify-ing-ly, adv.

## gratin
gratin, п., light crust over a dish. — F., 'burnt

Ίο scrape'.

## gratmate
gratmate, tr. v., to cook until a crust is formed. —
Formed with verbal suff. -ate fr. F. gratiner,
'to prepare a dish with bread crumbs', fr. gratin.
See prec. word.

## Gratiola
Gratiola, п., a genus of plants, the hedge hyssop
(bot.) — ML., dimin. formed fr. L. gratia,
'kindness, loveliness' (see grace, n„ and -ole);
so called in allusion to its supposed medicinal
properties.

## gratis
gratis, adv., for nothing; freely. — L. gratis,
contraction of grdtiis, 'out of favor; without
reward, for nothing, gratuitously', abl. pi. of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:348 COLUMN:3 -->
gratia, 'favor, kindness'. See grace, n.
Derivative: gratis, adj.

## gratitude
gratitude, n. — F., fr. Late L. gratitude,
'thankfulness, gratitude', fr. gratus, 'beloved, pleasing,
dear, thankful'. See grace, п., and -tude.

## gratuitous
gratuitous, adj., given for nothing; free. — L.
gratuUus, 'that which is done without pay,
spontaneous, gratuitous', formed — on analogy of
fortuitus, 'casual' — fr. gratus, 'pleasing,

Derivatives: gratuitous-ly, adv., gratuitous-ness,
n.

## gratuity
gratuity, п., gift; tip. — F. gratuite, fr. ML. gra-
tuitatem, ace. of gratuitas, 'free gift', fr. L.
gratuUus. See prec. word and -ity.
(■ratulate, tr. v., to congratulate. — L. gratulatus,
pp. of gratulari, 'to manifest joy, congratulate',
contracted fr. "grati-tulari, 'to bring something
agreeable', compounded of gratus, 'pleasing,
agreeable', and tuld = fero, Ί bring'. See grace,

## gratulation
gratulation, п., congratulation. — L. gratulatio,
gen. -onis, 'manifestation of joy,

word and -ion.

## gratulatory
gratulatory, adj., congratulatory. — Late L. gra-
tulatorius, 'pertaining to congratulation', fr. L.

## gravamea
gravamea, п., a grievance. — Late L. gravamen,
'trouble, physical inconvenience', fr. gravdre,
'to burden, aggravate', fr. gravis, 'heavy'. See

## grave
grave, tr. and intr. v., to engrave. — ME. graven,
fr. OE. grafan, 'to dig, carve', rel. to ON. grafa,
Dan. grave, Swed. grava, OFris. greva, Du.
graven, OHG. graban, MHG-, G. graben, Goth.
graban, 'to dig, carve', fr. I.-E. base *ghrebh-,
"ghrobh-, Ίο scratch, scrape', whence also
OSIav. grebg, greti, Ίο dig', pogrebg, pogrett,

out'. Cp. grave, 'mound, tomb', graven,
engrave. Cp. also groove, grub, 'to dig'.
Derivative: grav-er, n.

## grave
grave, п., mound, tomb. — ME., fr. "OE. grxf,
rel. to OS. graf, OFris. gref OHG., MHG., G.
grab, 'grave, tomb', OE. grafu, ON. grof, 'cave;
grave', Goth, graba, 'ditch', OE. grafan, 'to
dig, carve', and cogn. with OSIav. grobu, 'grave,

## grave
grave, tr. v., to clean (the wooden hull of a ship)

## grave
grave, adj., weighty. — F., fr. L. gravis, 'heavy,

important, honorable', which is cogn. with OI.
guruh, 'heavy, weighty' (compar. gariyas-;
superl. garisihah), Avestic gouru- (only in
compounds), 'heavy, weighty', Gk. βάρος, 'weight',
βκρύς, 'heavy', βρίθειν, Ίο be laden with', βρϊθιΐς,
'heavy', βριαρός, 'strong', Goth, kaurus, 'heavy',
Lett, gruts, 'heavy'. Cp. gravedo, gravid, gravity,
grief, grieve, grievous, aggravate, aggrieve,
Ingravescent. Cp. also baro-, bary, Briareus, brute,
centrobaric, charivari, garce, guru, isobar.

## grave
grave, п., a count; used esp. of the counts of
Nassau. — MDu. grave (whence Du. graaf),
'count', rel. to OHG. gravo (whence MHG.
grave, G. Graf), MLG. grive (whence ON.
greifi, Dan., Swed. greve), 'count'. The orig.
meaning of these words seems to have been
'judge'; cp. Goth, ga-grefts, 'decision'. Cp. -grave
and words there referred to. Cp. also Graf.

## -grave
-grave, suff. meaning 'ruler'. — Fr. grave, 'count'.
Cp. bargrave, landgrave, margrave, palsgrave.

## gravedo
gravedo, п., cold in the head (med.) — L. gravede,
'heaviness of the limbs, cold in the head', lit.
'heaviness', fr. gravis, 'heavy'. See grave,
'weighty'.

## gravel
gravel, n. — ME. gravel, fr. OF. gravele, gravelle,
'gravel, sand, beach, strand' (whence F.
gravelle, 'gravel', a medical term), dimin. of OF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:349 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GRAVEN | 322 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:349 COLUMN:1 -->
grave (F. greve), 'strand of sand, sandbank',
which is of uncertain, possibly Celtic, origin.
Cp. W. gro, 'coarse gravel', Bret, grouan, Co.
grow, 'gravel'. Cp. also grave, 'to clean (the hull
of a ship)', grit, groats, gront.
Derivatives: gravel, tr. v., gravel-ly, adj., gravel-
li-ness, n.

## graven
graven, adj., carved (archaic). — ME. graven, fr.
OE. grafen, prop. pp. of grafan, 'to dig, carve'.
See grave, 'to dig, carve'.

## graveolent
graveolent, adj., having a rank smell. — L. grave-
olens, gen. -entis, 'strong-smelling', prop, grave
olens, fr. grave, neut. of gravis, 'heavy', and
pres. part, of olere, 'to smell'. See grave,
weighty', olfactory and -ent.

## graves
graves, n. pi. — A var. of greaves.

## Graves
Graves, п., wine from the Graves district of the
Gironde in the SW. of France. — The name
Graves lit. means 'gravelly place'. See grave,
'to clean (the hull of a ship)'.
Graves' disease. — Named after the Irish
physician Robert James Graves (1796-1853).

## graveward
graveward, adv. and adj., gravewards, adv.,
toward the grave. — Compounded of grave and
-ward, resp. -wards.

## gravid
gravid, adj., being with child; pregnant. — L.
gravidus, 'loaded; pregnant', fr. gravis, 'heavy'.
See grave, 'weighty'.
Derivatives: gravid-ly, adv., gravid-ness, n.

## gravidity
gravidity, n. — L. graviditas, 'pregnancy,' fr.
gravidus. See prec. word and -ity.

## gravimeter
gravimeter, п., an instrument for measuring
specific gravity. — F. gravimitre, a hybridcoined
fr. L. gravis, 'heavy', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See grave, 'weighty', and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## gravitate
gravitate, intr. v. — ModL. gravitatus, pp. of
gravitare, coined by Sir Isaac Newton (1642-
1727) fr. L. gravitas, 'weight'. See gravity and
verbal surf. -ate.
Derivatives: gravitation (q.v.), gravitat-ive, adj.

## gravitation
gravitation, n. — ModL. gravitatid, gen. -dnis,
coined by Newton. See prec. word and -Ion.
Derivatives: gravitation-al, adj.,
gravitation-ally, adv.

## gravity
gravity, n. — F. gravite, fr. L. gravitatem, ace. of
gravitas, 'weight, seriousness', fr. L. gravis,
'heavy'. See grave, 'weighty', and -ity.

## gravure
gravure, n. — Short for photogravure. Cp.
heliogravure, rotogravure.

## gravy
gravy, n. — ME. graue (pronounced grave), from
misreading of OF. grane, 'a dish powdered with
grains', lit. 'grained', fr. ML. granatus, pp. of
grandre, *to grain', fr. L. granum, 'grain'. See
grain, 'seed, corn'.

## gray
gray, grey, adj. — ME. gray, grey, fr. OE. grxg,
rel. to ON. grar, Dan. graa, Swed. gra,
OFris. gre, MDu. gra, Du. grauw, OHG. grao,
MHG. gra, G. grau, 'gray', and cogn. with L.
ravus, 'gray'. See roan, 'chestnut-colored', and
cp. grizzle, 'gray', and words there referred
to.
Derivaiives: gray, grey, n. and tr. and intr. v.,
gray-ish, adj., gray-ly, adv., gray-ness, n.

## graylag
graylag, greylag, п., the gray goose. — Short for
gray lag goose, i.e. 'the gray lagging goose' (see
lag, adj., and goose); so called because ii is late
in migrating.

## grayling
grayling, п., a freshwater fish. — Formed fr. gray
with suff. -ling.

## graze
graze, tr. and inir, v., to feed on grass. — ME.
grasen, fr. OE. gran'an, fr. grses, 'grass'. See
grass and cp. next word.
Derivative: graze, п., pasturage.

## graze
graze, и-, v., to touch slightly. — Formed from
prec. word and orig. used in the sense 'to touch
the (grassy) ground' (said of bullets that touched
the ground and rebounded). Cp. G.grasen, 'to
feed on grass' (fr. Gras, 'grass'), which is used
also in the above mentioned military sense.
Derivative: graze, п., a slight contact.

## grazier
grazier, п., one who grazes cattle. — Formed fr.
graze, 'to feed', with agential suff. -ier.

## grazioso
grazioso, adj., graceful {musical direction). — It.,
fr. L. giatiosus. See gracious.

## grease
grease, n. — ME. gresse, grese, fr. OF. gresse,
graisse (F. graisse), fr. VL. *crassia, 'thickness,
fatness', fr. L. crassus, 'ihick, fat'. Cp. Oil.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:349 COLUMN:2 -->
grascia, OProvenc. graissa, Catal. graxa. Port.
graixa, 'fat', It. grasce (pi.), 'victuals' [Sp. graso,
'fat', п., is formed fr. graso, 'fat', adj., a
collateral form of craso, fr. L. crassus], and see
crass. Cp. also degras.
Derivatives: grease, tr. v., greas-er, п., greas-y,
adj., greas-i-ly, adv., greas-i-ness, n.

## great
great, adj. — ME. great, gret, greet, grete, fr.
OE. great, rel. to OS. grot, OFris. grot, Du.
groot, OHG., MHG. groj, G. gross, 'great'. The
original meaning of these adjectives was prob.
'gross-grained, coarse'. Cp. ON.grautr, 'groats',
E. greot, 'grit, sand, dust, gravel', and see grit,
■coarse sand', and words ihere referred to.
Derivatives -.great, п., great-en, v.,great-ly, adv.,
great-en (tr. and intr. v.), great-ness, n.

## greave
greave, п., armor for the leg. — ME. greve, fr.
OF. greve, 'shin; greave', fr. Port, greba, fr.
Egypt. Arab, gaurab, corresponding to Arab.
jaurab, 'stocking, apparel for the leg'.
Derivative: greav-ed, adj.

## greave
greave, п., sediment of melted tallow. — LG.
greven (pi), rel. to OHG. griobo (MHG., G.
griebe); of uncertain origin.

## greve
greve, п., a diving bird. — F. gribe, of doubtful
origin.

## Grecian
Grecian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Graecia, 'Greece', fr. Graecus, 'Greek'. See
Greek.

## Grecism
Grecism, Graecism, n. — F. grecisme, fr. ML.
Graecismus, fr. L. Graecizare, 'to imitate the-
Greeks'. See next word and -ism.

## Grecize
Grecize, Graecize, tr. v., to make Greek; intr. v.,
to imitate the Greeks. — F. greciser, fr. L.
Graecizare, 'to imitate the Greeks', fr. Gk.
Τραικίζαν, fr. Γραικός, 'Greek'. See Greek
and -ize.

## Greco-
Greco-, Graeco-, combining form denoting the
Greeks. — Fr, L. Graecus, 'Greek'. See Greek.

## greed
greed, n. — Back formation fr. greedy.

## greedily
greedily, adv. — ME. grediliche, OE. grxdiglice,
fr. grxdig, 'greedy', and -lice, 'like'. See greedy
and adv. suff. -ly.

## greediness
greediness, n. — ME. gredinesse, fr. OE. grxdig-
nes, formed fr. grxdig, 'greedy', with suff. -nes.
See greedy and -ness.

## greedy
greedy, adj. — ME. gredy, fr. OE. grxdig, rel. to
OS. gradag, 'greedy', ON. graor, 'greed,
hunger', ON. gradugr, Dan. graadig, Du. gretig,
OHG. gratag, 'greedy', Goth, gredus, 'hunger',
gredags, 'hungry', and perh. cogn. with Ol.
gfdhyati, 'is greedy', gardhah, 'greed'. Cp.
greed.

## Greek
Greek, n. — OE. Grecas, Crecas, (pi), 'the
Greeks', fr. L. Graecus, 'Greek', fr. Γραικός,
'inhabitant of Γραία (Grata) in Boeotia', a name
orig. given by the Latins to Greek colonists,
coming from Grata and settling at Cumae in
southern Italy, but later applied to every Greek.
[The Greeks reborrowed Γραικός in this new
sense from the Latins: Aristotle was the first
Greek to use Γραικοί (the pi. of Γραικός) in the
sense of "Ελληνες (i.e. 'Hellenes, Greeks').] Cp.
Grecian, grego, Gringo, and the second element
in fenugreek and in galligaskins.

## Greek
Greek, adj. — ME. Grec, fr. F. grec, fr. L.
Graecus, 'Greek'. See Greek, n.

## green
green, adj. — ME. grene, fr. OE. grene, rel. to
OFris. grene, OS. groni, ON. grornn, Dan. gren,
Swed. gron, Du. groen, OHG. gruoni, MHG.
gruene, G. grim, 'green'. These adjectives are
-л-enlargements of I.-E. base *ghro-, 'to grow'.
See grow and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: green, п., green, v. (q.v.), green-ish,
adj., green-ish-ness, п., green-ly, adv.,
greenness, п., greenth (q.v.), green-y, adj.

## greengage
greengage, п., a variety of plum. — Compounded
of green and the surname of the English botanist
Sir William Gage (died in 1820), who was the
first to cultivate this fruit in England.

## greening
greening, п., a green variety of apple. — MDu.
groeninc. See green and -ing, 'related to'.

## greenling
greenling, п., a fish, called also rock trout. —
Formed fr. green with suff. -ling.

## greenockite
greenockite, п., cadmium sulfide (mineral.) —
Named in 1841 after the English soldier Charles
Murray Cathcart (1783-1859), styled Lord
Greenock (1807-43), wn0 discovered it. For the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:349 COLUMN:3 -->
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## greenovite
greenovite, п., manganese titanite (mineral.) —
Named by the French geologist Ours-Pierre-
Armand-Petit Dufrenoy (1792-1857) in 1840
after the English geologist George Bellas
Greenough (1778-1855). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## greet
greet, tr. v., to salute. — ME. greten, fr. OE.
gretan, 'to address, approach, visit, greet", rel.
to OS. grotian, OFris. greta, Du. groeten, OHG.
gruosen, MHG. griiejen, G. grufien, 'to salute,
greet', fr. Teut. base *grotjan, orig. 'to cause to
speak', whence also OE. gretan, grStan, 'to
weep, bewail'. See next word.
Derivatives: greet-er, п., greet-ing, п., greet-ing-
ly, adv.

## greet
greet, intr. v., to weep; tr. v., to bewail (archaic
or dial.) — ME. greten, graten, fr. OE. gretan,
grxtan, 'to weep, bewail', rel. to OS. gratan,
ON. grata, Dan. grxde, Goth, gretan, greitan,
'to weep', ON. grata, 'to cause to weep, cry'.
The orig. sense of all these verbs was 'to sound,
speak, shout'. They derive from I.-E. base
*ghrid-, 'to sound, clash, speak loudly', whence
