also OI. hradate, 'it sounds, rustles'. See greet,
'to salute', and cp. regret.
Derivatives: greet-er, п., greet-ing, n.

## greffler
greffler, п., registrar. — F., 'clerk of the court,
registrar', fr. ML. graphiarius, fr. L. graphium,
'a writing style'. See graft and -ier.

## gregarions
gregarions, adj., pertaining to a flock; living in
flocks. — L. gregarius, 'pertaining to a flock',
fr. grex, gen. gregis, 'flock', fr. I.-E. base *gre-g-,
partial reduplication of base *gere-, "ger-, 'to
gather together, assemble', whence Gk. άγεί-
ρειν, 'to assemble', αγορά, 'assembly; place of
assembly', αγυρις, 'assembly', αγύρτης,
'beggar', OSlav. grusti (for *g[-s-ti-), 'handful',
Lith. gurgulys, 'chaos, confusion', gurguole,
'crowd, mass', and Gk. τά γάργαρα (Hesychius),
'crowd, plenty' and possibly also OI. ganah
(for *grna-), 'herd, troop, company'. Cp.
aggregate, congregate, egregious, segregate. Cp. also
agora, allegory, category, panegyric, paregoric.
Cp. also cram.
Derivatives: gregarious-ly, adv., gregarious-
ness, n.

## grego
grego, п., a short cloak. — Port. Grego or Sp.
Griego, 'Greek', fr. L. Graecus. See Greek.

## Gregorian
Gregorian, adj. — Lit. 'pertaining to Gregory',
fr. Late L. Gregorianus, fr. Gregorius. See next
word and -an.

## Gregory
Gregory, masc. PN. — Late L. Gregorius, fr. Gk.
Γρηγόριος, fr. γρήγορος, 'watchful', which is
rel. to έγρήγορα, second perfect of έγείρειν, 'to
awaken', fr. I.-E. base *ger-, 'to be awake',
whence also OI. jOgarti, 'he is awake', Avestic
a-garayeiti, 'wakes up, arouses'.
Gregory powder. — Named after the Scottish
physician James Gregory (1753-1821).

## grelsen
grelsen, п., a crystalline rock consisting of quartz
and mica (petrogr.) — G., fr. greifien, 'to cleave,
split'.

## gremial
gremial, adj., pertaining to the lap or bosom. —
Late L. gremialis, fr. L. gremium, 'lap, bosom',
fr. I.-E. base *grem-, 'to press, squeeze', whence
also OE. crammian, 'to cram, stuff'. See cram,
v., and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: gremial, п., a bishop's apron.

## gremlin
gremlin, п., a mischievous imp. — A word coined
in the time of World War II.

## grenade
grenade, п., a small bomb. — F., fr. It. granata,
'pomegranate; grenade', fr. \L.(pomum) grana-
tum, 'pomegranate', lit. 'an apple having many
grains', fr. L. pomum, 'fruit' (in VL. 'apple'),
and granum, 'grain'. See grain, 'seed, corn', and
-adc and cp. garnet, pomegranate.

## grenadier
grenadier, п., a member of a special regiment or
corps. — F., orig. 'a soldier for throwing
grenades', formed fr. grenade. See grenade and -ier.

## grenadin
grenadin, grenadine, п., carnation. — F. grenadin,
fr. grenade, 'pomegranate'. See grenade and
-in, -ine.

## grenadine
grenadine, п., fine woolen fabric. — F., fr.
grenade, 'pomegranate'. See prec. word.

## Gresham's law
Gresham's law,' the tendency for inferior
currency to drive the superior one out of
circulation. — So called after the English financier Sir

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:350 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 323 | GRISLY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:350 COLUMN:1 -->
Thomas Gresham (about 1519-79), who
explained this theorem to Queen Elizabeth.

## gressorial
gressorial, adj., adapted for walking (zool.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. ModL.gressorius,
'pertaining to walking', fr. L. gressus, pp. of
grodi, 'to walk, go'. See grade.

## Grevillea
Grevillea, п., a genus of Australian trees (bo!.) —
ModL., named in 1809 after the Rt. Hon.
Charles Francis Greville (1749-1809).

## grew
grew, past tense of grow. — ME. greu, fr. OE.
greow, past tense of grdwan, 'to grow'. See grow.

## grey
grey, adj. — See gray.

## greyhound
greyhound, п., a tall and slender dog. — ME.
grihond, grehund, grehounde, fr. OE. grighund,
rel. to ON. greyhundr, fr. grey, 'dog', and hundre,
'hound' (see hound). The word is not related
to grey.

## gribble
gribble, п., a small marine crustacean. — Prob.
in gradational relationship to grub; formed with
dimin. suff. -le.

## grid
grid, п., a grating or gridiron. — Back formation
fr. gridiron, the ending of which was mistaken
for the noun iron.

## griddle
griddle, п., a shallow frying pan. — ME. gredil,
gridell, fr. AF. gridil, fr. OF. gredil, a var. of
grail, gralle, fr. Late L. *craticulum, fr. L. crati-
cula, 'fine hurdle work, small gridiron', dimin.
of oralis, 'hurdle'. See crate and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also grill, grille, gridiron.
Derivative: griddle, tr. v., griddl-er, n.

## gride
gride, tr. and intr. v., to cut, pierce; to grate. —
Metathesized fr. gird, 'to strike' (now 'to taunt,
gibe').
Derivative: gride, п., a grating noise.

## gridelin
gridelin, п., a grayish violet color. — F. gris-de-
lin, gridelin, lit. 'gray of flax', i.e. 'flax gray'. For
the etymology of gris see grizzle, adj.; de, 'from,
of', comes fr. L. de, 'away from, from' (see
de-); lin, 'flax, linen', derives fr. L. linum (see
linen).

## gridiron
gridiron, n. — ME. gredirne, gridirne, folk-
etymological variants of ME. gredire, gridire
(due to a confusion of the ending -ire with ME.
iren, 'iron'). ME. gredire, gridire are altered fr.
ME. gredil, gridell, 'griddle'. See griddle and
cp. andiron.

## grief
grief, n. — ME. grief, gref, greve, fr. OF. grief,
gref, fr. grever, 'to burden'. See grieve.
Derivative: grief-less, adj.

## grievance
grievance, n. — ME. grevance, fr. OF. grevance,
fr. grever, 'to burden'. See grieve and -ance.

## grieve
grieve, tr. and intr. v. — ME. greven, fr. OF.
grever, 'to burden, oppress; aggravate' (whence
F. grever, 'to burden, wrong, encumber'), fr.
L. gravare, 'to charge with a load, burden, weigh
down, oppress', fr. gravis, 'heavy'. Cp. It.
gravare, Sp. gravar, 'to load, burden', OProvenc.
grevar, 'to vex', which all derive fr. L. gravare.
See grave, 'weighty', and cp. grief.
Derivatives: griev-ed, adj., griev-ed-ly, adv.,
grier-er, п., griev-ing-ly, adv.

## grievous
grievous, adj. — ME. grevous, fr. OF. grevos,
grevous, 'heavy, hard, toilsome'. See grief and
-ous.
Derivatives: grievous-ly, adv., grievous-ness, n.

## griff
griff, п., a narrow glen (North. Engl.) — Of
uncertain origin.

## griff
griff, п., a claw. — F. griffe. See next word.

## grille
grille, п., an ornament resembling a claw. — F.
griffe, 'claw', fr. griffer, 'to seize', which is prob.
borrowed fr. OHG. grifan, 'to seize'. See
gripe and cp. griffonage.

## griffin
griffin, griffon, gryphon, п., a mythical animal. —
ME. griffon, fr. OF. grifoun (F. griffon), fr. Late
L. gryphus (whence also It., Sp. grifo, OHG.,
MHG. grif G. Greif, 'griffin'), fr. Gk. γρ4ψ,
gen. γρυπός, which was prob. borrowed from
the Semites through the medium of the Hittites.
Cp. Heb. k'rubh, 'a winged angel', Akkad.
kSribu, epithet of the bull-colossus, lit. 'one who
blesses', and see cherub. Cp. also the second
element in hippogriff. The connection of Gk. γρ<5ψ,
'griffin', with γρυπός, 'curved, hooked,
hooknosed', is folk etymology.

## griffin
griffin, п., in India, a new comer (Anglo-Ind.) —
Of uncertain origin.

## Griffith
Griffith, masc. PN. — Fr. W. Gruffydd, which
prob. derives fr. L. Rufus, fr. rufus, 'red'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:350 COLUMN:2 -->
rufous, Rufus.

## griffon
griffon, n. — A var. of griffin, 'mythical animal'.

## griffon
griffon, п., a sporting dog. — Prob. fr. prec.
word.

## griffonage
griffonage, п., scrawl, scribble. — F. griffonnage,
fr. griffonner, 'to scrawl, scribble', fr. griffer,
'to seize'. See griffe and -age.

## griffon vulture
griffon vulture, n„ a large species of vulture (Gyps
fulvus). — Fr. griffon, 'mythical animal'. Cp.
G. Greif, 'griffin; condor'.

## grig
grig, п., ι) a lively person; 2) (obsol. or dial.) a
small eel; 3) (obsol. or dial.) a cricket. — Prob.
of imitative origin. Cp. Du. kriek, 'cricket', and
E. cricket, the insect.

## grill
grill, п., a gridiron. — F. gril, a var. of grille, fr.
OF. grille, fr. earlier graille, grellle, fr. L. crati-
cula, 'fine hurdle work, gridiron'. See griddle
and cp. words there referred to.

## grill
grill, п., the act of grating. — From grille (q.v.)

## grill
grill, tr. and intr. v., to broil on a grill. — F. gril-
ler, fr. gril, whence E. grill, 'gridiron' (q.v.)
Derivative: grill, п., the act of grilling.

## grillage
grillage, п., a framework of crossbeams used to
form a foundation in marshy soil. — F., 'frame',
fr. grille, 'fine hurdle work'. See grille and -age.

## grille
grille, п., ornamental metal grating. — F., 'metal
grating; frame', fr. L. craticula, 'fine hurdle
work, gridiron'. See grill, 'gridiron'.

## grilse
grilse, п., salmon on its return to the river for the
first time. — Prob. metathesis of OF. grisle,
'grayish', fr. gris, 'gray'. See grizzle, 'gray'.

## grim
grim, adj. — ME., fr. OE. grimm, grim, 'cruel,
fierce, terrible, severe', rel. to OS., OFris., OHG.,
MHG., G. grimm, ON. grimmr, Swed. grym,
'fierce, furious', Dan. grim, 'ugly', OS. grim-
mag, Du., OHG., G. grimmig, MHG. grimmec,
'fierce, furious', MDu. grimmen, grimmelen, 'to
grumble', and in gradational relationship to OE.,
OS., OHG., MHG. gram, 'angry, fierce', ON.
gramr, Dan. gram, 'angry', G. gram, 'averse
to', Gram, 'grief, sorrow'. These words are
traceable to I.-E. base *ghrem-, 'to give a hollow
sound, to thunder', whence also Gk. χρεμίζειν,
'to neigh', χρόμαδος, 'a crashing sound', OSlav.
vuzgrimeti, 'to thunder', gromu, 'thunder', Russ
gremef, 'to thunder', Lith. gramit, grameti, 'to
fall into the deep with a rumbling sound',
grumu, grumlti, 'to thunder'. Cp. gram, gramble.
Cp. also pogrom.
Derivatives: grim-ly, adv., grim-ness, n.

## grimace
grimace, п., distortion of the face. — F., 'wrinkle,
wry face; sham, humbug, cant', fr. MF., prob.
fr. OSp. grimazo, lit. 'mask', formed with pejor.
suff. -azo (fr. L. -aceus), fr. Goth, 'grima, which
may be inferred fr. OE. grima, 'mask, helmet,
ghost, specter', ON. grima, MDu. grime, 'soot;
mask'. These latter words lit. mean 'blackened
face', and are rel. to MLG. grimel, 'striped
black', MLG. grime, 'dirt'. Cp. grime.
Derivatives: grimace, intr. v., grimac-er, п.,
grimac-ing-ly, adv.

## grimalkin
grimalkin, п., a cat, a she-cat. — Fr. earlier gray-
malkin (cp. Graymalkin in Shakespeare's
Macbeth), which is compounded of gray and malkin,
dimin. of ME. Malt, Mault, 'Maud'. See
malkin.

## grime
grime, п., dirt. — Flemish grijm, it. MDu. grime,
'soot; mask'. See grimace and cp. begrime.
Derivatives: grim-y, adj., grim-i-ly, adv., grim-
i-ness, a.

## grime
grime, tr. v., to soil. — ME. grimen, fr. Flem.
grijmen, fr. grijm. See grime, n.
Grimm's law. — Named after the German
philologist Jacob Grimm (1785-1863), who was the
first to describe this law in a comprehensive,
generalizing manner.

## grin
grin, intr. and tr. v., to smile broadly. — ME.
grennen, grinnen, fr. OE. grennian, 'to grin1, rel.
to ON. grenja, 'to howl', ON. grina, Dan. grine,
Swed. grina, 'to grin', Du. grienen, 'to sniffle,
blubber, whine', OHG. grinan, MHG. grinen,
'to grumble, growl, snarl', G. greinen, 'to cry,
whine', MHG. grinnen, 'to grate, creak', OHG.
grennan, 'to mutter', MHG. grennen, 'to snarl',
and to OHG. granon, 'to grunt', MHG. grannen,
'to grunt, wail', OB.granian, 'to groan, murmur'.
See groan. OF. grignier, grigner. It. digrignare,
'to gnash the teeth', and Provenc. grinar, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:350 COLUMN:3 -->
grunt', are Teut. loan, words.
Derivatives: grin, п., grinn-er, п., grinn-ing, adj.,
grinn-ing-ly, adv.

## grind
grind, tr. and intr. v. — ME. grinden, fr. OE.
grindan, cogn. with L. frendere, 'to gnash the
teeth', Gk. χόνδρος (dissimilated fr. *χρόνδρος),
'corn, grain', Alb. grunde, 'bran', Lith. grendu,
gr'esti, 'to scrape, scratch'; fr. I.-E. *ghren-d(h)-,
enlargement of base 'ghren-, 'to rub', whence
Gk. χραίνειν, 'to touch slightly'. Base "ghren-
itself has been enlarged fr. 1-Е. base *gher-,
'to rub', whence Gk. χέραδος, 'gravel'. Fr.
base "ghrii-, *ghri-, another enlargement of
base *gher-, derives Gk. χρίειν, 'to anoint with
oil, smear'. Cp. grist, 'corn for grinding', ground,
'bottom'. Cp. also chondro-, chrism, chrome,
furfur.
Derivatives: grind, п., grinder (q.v.), grind-ing,
n. and adj., grind-ing-ly, adv.

## grinder
grinder, n. — ME. grindere, fr. OE. grindere, fr.
grindan, 'to grind'. See grind and agential
suff. -er.

## Gringo
Gringo, п., Mexican contemptuous name for an
Englishman or an American of the U.S. — Sp.
gringo, corruption of griego, 'Greek', fr. L.
Graecus. See. Greek,

## griotte
griotte, п., morello (cherry). — F., fr. earlier
agriote, fr. Provenc. agriota, fr. agre, 'sour', fr.
L. acer. See acrid and cp. words there referred to.

## grip
grip, п., a grasp, clutch. — ME., fr. OE. gripe,
fr. gripan, 'to gripe', rel. to ON. gripr, OFris.
gripe, OHG., MHG. grif, G. Griff, 'grasp, hold;
claw; handle'. See gripe,

## grip
grip, tr. v., to grasp, clutch. — ME. grippen, fr.
OE. grippan, rel. to OHG. gripfen, griffen, 'to
rob', and to OE. gripan, 'to seize'. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: gripp-er, п., gripp-ing, adj., gripp-
ing-ly, adv., gripp-ing-ness, n.

## grip
grip, п., trench (dial. English) — OE. gripe, grype,
rel. to MLG. griippe, of s.m., MLG. gropen, 'to
hollow out', Swed. gropa, grypa, 'to cut out',
OE. gropa, 'pot'.

## gripe
gripe, tr. v., to grasp. — ME. gripen, fr. OE.
gripan, 'to seize', rel. to OS. gripan, ON. gripa,
Dan. gribe, Du. grijpen, Goth, greipan, OHG.
grifan, MHG. grifen, G. greifen, 'to seize', fr.
I.-E. base *ghrlb-, whence also Lith. griebiii,
griebti, 'to seize', Lett, griba, 'will', gribet, 'to
wish, will, want'. F. gripper, 'to seize', griffer,
'to seize', griffe, 'claw', are Teut. loan words.
Cp. griffe, griffonage, grip, 'a grasp', gripple,
grasp, grope.
Derivative: gripe, a.

## grippe
grippe, п., influenza. — F., prob. fr. Russ. chrip,
'hoarseness', which is of imitative origin.

## gripple
gripple, adj., griping (dial.) — ME. gripej, fr.
OE. gripul, fr. gripan, 'to seize'. See gripe,

## gripsack
gripsack, п., a handbag. — Compounded of grip,
v., and sack,

## grisaille
grisaille, п., a kind of painting in gray. — F., fr.
gris, 'gray*. See grizzle, 'gray'.

## Griselda
Griselda, fern. PN. — It., fr. G. Grishilda, Grisel-
de, fr. OHG. grisja hilda, 'gray battle maid'.
The first element derives fr. OHG. gris, 'gray';
see grizzle, 'gray'. The second element comes fr.
OHG. hildi, 'battle'; cp. the second element
in Clothilda, Kriemhild.

## grisette
grisette, п., a French working girl. — F., prop.
'a girl wearing a gray gown', fr. grisette, 'a gray
gown', fr. gris, 'gray', fr. Frankish 'gris, 'gray'.
See grizzle, 'gray'.

## griskin
griskin, п., the lean part of a pork loin (Engl.) —
Lit. 'a little pig', formed with suff. -kin fr. ME.
grys, grice (whence archaic E. grice, 'a little
pig'), fr. ON. griss, 'a young pig', lit. 'a gray
animal', rel. to Du. grijs, 'gray'. See grizzle,
'gray*, and cp. prec. word.

## grisly
grisly, adj., terrible. — ME. grislich, grisly, fr.
OE. grislic, 'terrible', formed with suff. -lie (see
adj. suff. -ly) from the stem of OE. a-grisan, 'to
shudder, fear', which is rel. to MLG. grisen,
gresen, Du. griezelen, OHG. gruson, MHG.
grusen, G. grausen, MHG. griuseln, 'to shudder,
fear', MLG. greselik, MDu. griselijk, Du.
griezelig, OHG. grisenlih, G. gruselig, 'terrible'.
Cp. gruesome.
Derivative: gristi-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:351 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GRISON | 324 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:351 COLUMN:1 -->

## grison
grison, η. a South-American mammal. — F.
grison, grayish, gray-haired*, fr.gris, 'gray'. See
grizzle, adj.

## grist
grist, η., ι) grain for grinding; 2) grain that has
been ground. — ME., fr. OE. grist, 'grinding;
corn to be ground', from the root of OE. grin-
dan, 'to grind'. See grind and cp. gristle.

## grist
grist, п., size of rope. — Of uncertain origin;
perh. rel. to gird, 'to encircle'.

## gristle
gristle, п., cartilage. — ME. gristit, fr. OE. gristle,
rel. to OFris., MLG. gristel, and to OE. grost,
MHG. gruschel, 'cartilage', and prob. also to
OE. grist, 'grinding'. See 1st grist.
Derivatives: gristl-y, adj., gristl-i-ness, n.

## grit
grit, п., coarse sand, gravel. — ME. grete, fr. OE.
griot, 'grit, sand, dust, gravel', rel. to OS. griot,
OFris. grit, ON. grjot, 'rock, stone', OHG.
gri03, MHG. gries, grii^, G. Griefi, 'grit, sand,
gravel', and cogn. with Lith. grudas, Lett.
grands, 'corn, kernel', Lith. graudus, 'brittle',
grudziu, griisti, 'to stamp', OSlav. gruda, 'clod',
fr. I.-E. 'ghreud-, a -rf-enlargement of base
*ghreu-, 'to grind, pulverize, crush'. Cp. W.
gro, 'coarse gravel', Bret, grouan, Co. grow,
'gravel', which derive from the unenlarged form
of the base. L. rudus, 'rubbish', is not cognate
with the above words. Cp. grit, 'coarsely ground
grain'. Cp. also gravel, groats, grant, 'coarse
meal', gruel, and the first element in gromwell.
Cp. also great.
Derivatives: grit, tr. v., to cover with grit; intr.
v., to make a grating sound, gritt-y, adj., gritt-i-
ly, adv., gritt-i-ness, n.

## grit
grit, п., coarsely ground grain. — OE. grytt,
rel. to MLG. griitte, gone, Du. gort, OHG.
gruzzi, MHG., G. griitze, 'peeled grain, groats'.
These words originally meant 'that which is
coarsely ground', and derive fr. I.-E. *ghreud-,
'to grind, crush'. See grit, 'coarse sand'.

## grivet
grivet, п., a monkey of N. East Africa. — F., of
unknown origin. Cp. vervet.

## grizzle
grizzle, adj., gray. — ME. grisel, fr. OF. grisel,
dimin. of gris, 'gray', fr. Frankish 'gris, 'gray',
which is rel. to OS., OFris., gris, MDu., Du.
grijs, OHG. gris, 'gray', MHG gris 'gray, gray-
haired', grise, 'old man' (whence G. Greis, 'old
man'), ON. griss, Dan., Swed.^rir, 'young pig'
(prop, 'the gray animal'). Sp., Port, gris, It.
griso, grigio, 'gray', are Teut. loan words. Cp.
grilse, grisaille, grisette, grlskin, grison, the first
element in Griselda and the second element in
ambergris. — The above Teut. words are prob.
rel. to OE. grig, 'gray', and its equivalents in
the other Teut. languages; see gray.
Derivatives: grizzle, tr. v., to make gray;
intr. v., to become gray; grizzle, п., the color
gray, grizzl-y, adj.

## grizzle
grizzle, intr. v., to grin (Engl.) — Of uncertain
origin.

## groan
groan, intr. and tr. v. — ME. gronen, fr. OE.
granian, 'to groan, murmur', rel. to ON. grenja,
'to howl', OE. grennian, 'to grin'. See grin.
Derivatives: groan, п., groan-er, п., groan-'mg,
n. and adj., groan-ing-ly, adv.

## groat
groat, п., a small coin. — ME. groot, fr. MDu.
(— Du.) groot, 'great, big', used as a noun in
the sense of 'a thick (coin)'. See great and cp.
words there referreed to. For sense
development cp. gross, name of coins, and groschen.

## groats
groats, n. pi., hulled oats. — ME. grotes, fr. OE.
grot, 'particle, atom', rel. to greot, 'grit'. See
grit, 'coarse sand', and cp. groat.

## grobian
grobian, п., a rude, boorish person. — G. Gro-
blan, fr. facetious L. grobianus, fr. G. grob,
'coarse, rough', which is cogn. with E. gruff (q.v.)

## grocer
grocer, n. — ME. grosser, fr. OF. grossier, fr.
ML. grossarius, 'one who sells wholesale',
which is formed fr. Late L. grossus, 'great, thick,
gross', with Latin sufT. -arius. See gross, adj., and
-ier and cp. F. vendre en gros, 'to sell wholesale'.

## grocery
grocery, n. — ME. grosserie, fr. OF. grosserie, fr.
grossier, 'grocer'. See grocer and -y(representing
OF. -ie).

## grog
grog, п., alcoholic drink diluted with water. —
Shortened fr. Grogram, nickname of Admiral
Edward Vernon (1684-1757), who used to wear
a grogram cloak (see grogram); the drink was
so called because he was the first to order

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:351 COLUMN:2 -->
dilution of sailor's rum.
Derivatives: grog, tr. v., grogg-ery, n. (U.S.),
grogg-y, adj., grogg-i-ness, n.

## grogram
grogram, п., a coarse kind of cloth made of silk
or of silk and mohair. — Corruption of F. gros
grain, 'coarse grain'. See gross, adj., and grain
and cp. grog. For a similar corruption cp.
fingering, 'a fine woolen yarn'. For the change
of final η to m cp. also pilgrim and venom.

## groin
groin, п., the fold between the abdomen and the
thigh. — Formed (prob. on analogy of loin) fr.
earlier grine, fr. ME. grynde, fr. OE. grynde,
'abyss' (which may have meant also 'depression,
hollow'), a wprd rel. to OE. grund, 'bottom'.
See ground, п., 'bottom'.
Derivatives: groin, tr. v., groin-ed, adj.,
groining, n.

## grommet
grommet, grummet, п., ring of a rope (naut.) —
OF. gromette (whence, with metathesis, F.
gourmette, 'curb of a bridle'); of uncertain
origin.

## gromwell
gromwell, п., any plant of the genus Lithosper-
mum. — OF. gromil(¥. gremil), compounded of
OF. gres (F. gris), 'sandstone', and mil, 'millet'.
The first element derives fr. Frankish "griot,
which is rel. to OHG. grioj, 'grit, gravel'; see
grit, 'coarse sand'. For the second element see
millet.

## groom
groom, n. — ME. grome, grom, orig. 'boy', fr.
OF. grome, gromet, groumet, gourmet, 'servant,
page'. See gourmet and cp. the second element
in bridegroom.
Derivatives: groom, tr. v., groom-er, a.,groom-y,
adj.

## groove
groove, п., a furrow. — ME. groof, grofe, fr.
MDu. groeve (Du. groef), 'trench, channel,
groove', which is to related Du. groeve, 'furrow,
pit', ON. grof, Norw. grov, 'brook, river bed',
OHG. gruoba, MHG. gruobe, G. Grube, 'pit,
ditch', Goth, groba, 'pit, cave', OE. grief, 'cave,
grave', grafan, 'to dig, carve'. See grave, 'to
engrave', grave, 'tomb'.
Derivatives: groove, tr. v., groov-ed, adj.,
groov-er, п., groov-ing, п., groov-y, adj., groov-
i-ness, n.

## grope
grope, intr. and tr. v. — ME. gropien, gropen, fr.
OE. grapian, 'to touch, feel', fr. grap, 'a grasp,
clutch', which stands in gradational relationship
to OE. gripan, 'to clutch'. See gripe-
Derivatives: grop-er, п., grop-ing-ly, adv.

## grosbeak
grosbeak, п., any of various finches. — F. gros-
bec, lit. 'large beak'. See gross, adj., and beak.

## groschen
groschen, п., a small silver coin, formerly current
in Germany. — G., fr. Czech groS, name of a
coin, fr. ML. (denarius) grossus, lit. 'a thick
coin', fr. L. grossus, 'thick'. See gross, adj., and
cp. gross, name of various coins.

## j gross
j gross, adj., big. — ME. groos, grose, fr. OF. gros,
'thick', fr. L. grossus, of s.m., which is cogn.
with Olr. bres, Mir. bras, 'big', Co. bras, 'thick'.
Cp. grocer, grogram, grosbeak, engross (in both
senses).
Derivatives: gross, n. (q.v.), gross, tr. v., gross-
en, tr. and intr. v., gross-er, п., gross-ly, adj.,
gross-ness, п., gross-i-fy, tr. and intr. v., gross-i-
ficaiion, 11.

## gross
gross, п., bulk, mass. — Fr. L. grossus, 'thick*.
See prec. word.

## gross
gross, п., twelve dozen. — Fr. F. la grosse (dou-
zaine), 'the great dozen', fr. gros, fern, grosse,
'big'. See gross, adj.

## gross
gross, п., name of various coins (obsol.) — Lit.
'something thick', partly fr. F. gros, 'thick',
partly fr. It. grosso, of s.m., which both derive
fr. L. grossus, 'thick'. See gross, adj., and cp.
groschen.
grossulaceous. — Contraction of grossulari-
aceous (q.v.)

## grossular
grossular, adj., belonging to the gooseberry. —
ModL. grossularius, fr. Grossularia (q.v.)

## Grossularia
Grossularia, п., a genus of plants of the
gooseberry family (hot.) — ModL., fr. F. groseille,
'gooseberry', fr. MDu. croesel, 'gooseberry'.
See gooseberry.

## Grossulariaceae
Grossulariaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the
gooseberry family (hot) — ModL., formed
from prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## grossulariaceous
grossulariaceous, adj., pertaining to the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:351 COLUMN:3 -->
gooseberry family. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## grot
grot, п., a grotto. — F. grotte, fr. It. grotta. See
grotto.

## grotesque
grotesque, adj., fantastic. — F. grotesque, fr. It.
(pittura) grottesca, 'grotesque painting', orig.
'painting (found) in a grotta', fr. grotta, 'crypt,
cave'. See grotto and -esque.
Derivative: grotesque-ly, adv., grotesque-ness, n.

## grotto
grotto, п., a cave. — It. grotta, fr. VL. crupta, fr.
L. crypta, fr. Gk. κρυπτή, short for κρυπτή
καμάρα, 'a hidden vault'. See crypt.

## grouch
grouch, intr. v., to be sulky. — Prob. fr. ME.
grouchen, 'to grumble'. See grudge.
Derivatives: grouch, п., grouch-y, adj., groitch-
i-ly, adv., grouch-i-ness, n.

## ground
ground, п., bottom. — ME. ground, fr. OE. grund,
rel. to OS., OFris., Dan., Swed. grund, Du.
grond, OHG., MHG. grunt, G. Grund, 'ground,
soil, bottom', ON. grunn, 'a shallow place',
grund, 'field, plain', grunnr, 'bottom', Goth.
grundu- in grundu-waddjus, 'foundation wall'.
These words prob. derive fr. I.-E. *gh[n-tu-,
'sandy soil*, fr. base *ghren-, 'to rub', whence
also Gk. χραίνειν, 'to touch slightly'. A
-d(h)-en\ argement of base 'ghren- appears i n OE.
grindan, 'to grind'. See grind and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also groin.
Derivatives: ground, intr. and tr. v., groundage
(q.v.), ground-ed, adj., grounder (q.v.),
grounding, n.

## ground
ground, adj., reduced to particles by grinding. —
Prop. pp. of grind.

## groundage
groundage, п., fee for letting a ship in a port. —
A hybrid formed fr. ground, п., with -age, a suff.
of ult. Latin origin.

## grounder
grounder, п., a ball moving along the ground
(baseball). — Formed fr. ground, п., with
agential suff. -er.

## groundless
groundless, adj. —· ME. groundeles, 'bottomless',
fr. OE. grundleas. See ground, п., and -less.
Derivatives: groundless-ly, adv.,
groundlessness, n.

## groundling
groundling,п., Oafish that lives near the bottom;
2) a spectator in the pit of a theater; hence 3) an
uncritical person. — The original meaning of
this word is 'that which lives on, or is near to,
the ground. It is formed fr. ground, п., with suff.
-ling, 'pertaining to*.

## groundsel
groundsel, п., any plant of the genus Senecio. —
ME. gwundeswele, fr. OE. grundeswelge, fr.
earlier gundeswelge, lit. 'pus swallower', fr. gund,
'pus', and swelgan, 'to swallow'; so called in
allusion to its use in making poultices. OE. gund
is rel. to OHG. gunt, 'pus', Goth, gund,
'cancer', dial. Norw. gund, 'scurf, scab', and
possibly cogn. with Gk. κανθύλη (dissimilated fr.
*χαν»ύλη), 'swelling, tumor'. For OE. swelgan
see swallow, v.

## groundsel
groundsel, п., threshold, sill. — Compounded of
ground and sill.

## group
group, n. — F. groupe, fr. It. gruppo, 'group',
orig. 'cluster, packet, knot', fr. OProven?.
grop, 'knot', which derives fr. Teut. "kruppa,
'a rounded lump or mass'. See crop.
Derivatives: group, tr. and intr. ν.,group-ed, adj.
group-ing, n.

## grouper
grouper, п., any of various fishes. — Port, garupa,
of uncertain, possibly Am. Indian, origin..

## grouse
grouse, п., a game bird. — Of unknown origin.

## grouse
grouse, intr. v., to grumble. — Prob. of imitative
origin; cp. Gk. γρϋ, 'a grunt', γρύζειν, 'to
grunt, grumble', L. grundire, grunmre, OE.
grunian, 'to grunt', which all are of imitative
origin. Cp. grunt. Cp. also grouch, grudge,grutch.
Derivative: grous-er, n.

## grout
grout, intr. and tr. v., to dig with the snout. —
Of uncertain origin. Cp. rout, 'to dig with the
snout'.

## grout
grout, п., coarse meal (archaic). — ME., fr. OE.
grut, 'coarse meal, grains of meal', rel. to
MLG. grut, 'dregs', and cogn. with Lith. grudas,
Lett, grduds, 'corn, kernel'. See grit, 'coarse
sand'.

## grout
grout, п., coarse mortar. — A special use of prec.
word.
Derivatives: grout, intr. and tr. v., to fill up
with cement, grout-ing, n.

## grove
grove, n. — ME., fr. OE. graf, 'grove, copse', rel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:352 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 325 | GUERRILLA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:352 COLUMN:1 -->
to OE. graefa, 'grove, thicket, brushwood',
Norw. greivla, 'to branch out'.

## grovel
grovel, intr. v., i) to lie flat on the ground; 2) to
behave abjectly. — Coined by Shakespeare
through back formation fr. obsol. E. grovelling,
fr. ME. grufelinge, 'on the face', which was
mistaken for a pres. part., whereas it is formed fr.
ME. (on) grufe (fr. ON. a grufu), 'on the face,
prone', with adv. suff. -ling. ON. grufa, 'prone-
ness', is rel. to ON. gryfa, 'to bend over'.
Derivatives: grovel(T)-er, п., grovel(T)-ing, adj.
and adv., grovel(l)-ing-ly, adv.

## grow
grow, intr. and tr. v. — ME. growen, fr. OE.
growan, rel. to ON. grda, OFris. grdia, Du.
groeien, OHG. gruoen, MHG. griiejen, 'to grow',
fr. I.-E. base *ghro-, 'to grow'. See grass, green,
and cp. gramlai-.
Derivatives: grow-er, п., grow-ing, n. and adj.,
grow-ing-ly, adv.

## growl
growl, intr. and tr. v. — Prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives: growl, п., growl-er, п., growl-ery, n.

## grown
grown, pp. of grow.

## growth
growth, n. — Formed with subst. suff. -th fr. grow,
on analogy of ON. grodi, 'growth* (fr. ON.
grda,.'to grow').

## groyne
groyne, n. — A var. of groin.

## grub
grub, tr. and intr. v., to dig up. — ME. grobben,
grubben, rel. to OHG. grubilon, MHG. grii-
bilen, 'to dig, search, investigate', G. grubeln,
'to rack one's brains, meditate, ponder', and to
OHG. graban, OE. grafan, 'to dig, carve'. See
grave, 'to engrave'.
Derivatives: grub, п., grubber (qq.v.), grubb-y,
adj., grubb-i-ness, n.

## grub
grub, п., the larva of an insect. — ME. grubbe,
lit. 'digger', fr. grubben, 'to dig'. See grub, n.

## grubber
grubber, п., one who or that which grubs. —
ME. grubbare. See grub, 'to dig', and agential
suff. -er.

## grudge
grudge, intr. and tr. v. — Fr. dial, grutch, fr. ME.
grochen, gruchen, 'to murmur, grudge', fr. OF.
groucier, grouchier, which is of Teut., ult.
imitative, origin. Cp. OHG. grunnizon, 'to grunt',
and see grant.
Derivatives: grudge, п., grudg-ing, adj., grudg-
ing-ly, adv.

## gruel
gruel, п., thin broth made by boiling oatmeal in
water. — OF. (F. gruau), 'oatmeal, grits, groats',
dimin. of OF. gru, fr. Frankish *grut, which is
rel. to Du. grut, OHG. gruzzi, 'groats'. See grit,
'coarsely ground grain'.

## gruesome
gruesome, adj., horrible. — Formed with tst suff.
-some fr. dial. E. grue, 'to shudder', which is
prob. of LG. origin. Cp. MLG. gruwen, 'to
shudder', grusam, 'gruesome', which are rel.
to MDu. gruwen, grouwen, Du. gruwen, OHG.
ingruen, MHG. gruwen, G. grauen, 'to shudder',
MDu. gruwel, MHG. griuwel, griul, G. Greuel,
'horror, terror', and to MLG. grlsen, gresen,
etc., 'to shudder'. Cp. Du. gruwzaam, MHG.
gruwesam, grusam, G. grausam, 'cruel', and see
grisly. Dan. grue, 'to dread', gruelig, 'dreadful,
terrible*, are LG. loan words.
Derivatives: gruesome-ly, adv.,gruesome-ness,n.

## gruff
gruff, adj., surly. — MLG. or MDu. (= Du.)grof,
rel. to OHG. gerob, grob, MHG. gerop,grop, G.
grob, 'coarse, rough', OHG. hriob, riob, OE.
hriof, ON. hrjufr, 'rough, scabby', and prob.
cogn. with Lith. kraupus, 'rough', Lett, k'raupa,
'scab, scurf, W. crawen, Co. crevan, 'crust'.
Derivatives: gruff-ish, adj., gruff-ly, adv.,gruff-
ness, п., gruff-y, adj., gruff-i-ly, adv., gruff-i-
ness, n.

## gruiform
gruiform, adj., cranelike. — See next word.

## Grulformes
Grulformes, n. pi., the order of the cranes (orni-
thol.) — Formed fr. L. grus, gen. gruis, 'crane',
and forma, 'form, shape'. See crane and form, n.

## gram
gram, adj., morose. — Prob. a blend of glum
and grim.

## grumble
grumble, intr. and tr. v. — F. grommeler, fr.
MDu. grommelen, freq. ofgrommen, 'to grumble'
(see freq. suff. -le). which stands in gradational
relationship to MDu. grimmen, grimmelen, 'to
grumble', and to OE. grimm, grim, 'cruel,
fierce, terrible, severe'. See grim and cp. words
there referred to. The b in grumble is intrusive.
Cp. ramble.
Derivatives: grumble, п., grumbl-er, п.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:352 COLUMN:2 -->
grumbling, adj., grumbl-ing-ly, adv.

## grume
grume, п., a clot of blood; a viscous fluid. —
Obsol. F. grume, 'clot' (whence F. grumeau, a
dimin.), fr. L. grumus, 'a little heap, hillock',
which is cogn. with OE. cruma, 'crumb'. See
crumb.

## grummet
grummet, n. — See grommet.

## grumose
grumose, adj., consisting of granules (bot.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ose fr. L. grumus, 'a
little heap'. See grume.

## grumous
grumous, adj., 1) containing grume; clotted;
2) grumose. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
grumus. See prec. word.
Derivative: grumous-ness, n.

## grumpy
grumpy, adj., irritable, peevish. — Formed with
adj. suff. -y fr. obsol. grump, 'ill humor', whicji
is rel. to gram, grumble, grim.
Derivatives: grumpi-ly, adv., grumpi-ness, n.

## Mrs. Grundy
Mrs. Grundy, a name denoting a prudish and
excessively conventional woman. — A character
of the comedy Speed the Plough (1798) by
Thomas Morton, often referred to in the phrase
' What will Mrs. Grundy say?'
Derivatives: Grundy-ism, п., Grundy-isl, n.

## grflnerlte
grflnerlte, п., a variety of amphibole (mineral.) —
Named after the German mineralogist E. L.
Griiner, who analyzed it. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## grunt
grunt, intr. and tr. v. — ME. grunten, fr. OE.
grunnettan, freq. of grunian, 'to grunt', rel. to
Dan. grynte, OHG. grunnizon, MHG., G. grun-
zen, 'to grunt'; of imitative origin. Cp. L. grun-
djre, grunnire, 'to grunt', which is also imitative.
Cp. also grouse, 'to grumble', and words there
referred to. Cp. also gurnard.
Derivatives: grunt, п., grunt-ing, adj., grunt-ing-
ly, adv.

## gruntle
gruntle, intr. v. — Freq. of grunt. Cp. disgruntle.

## grutch
grutch, intr. v., to grudge (dial. English). — ME.
gruchen, 'to murmur, grudge'. See grudge.
Derivative: grutch, n.

## Gruyere
Gruyere, n. — Short for Gruyere cheese, so called
fr. Gruyere, a town in Switzerland, where it was
originally made.

## Gryilidae
Gryilidae, n. pi., a family of insects, the crickets
(zool.) — ModL., formed fr. GryUus with suff.
-idae.

## GryUus
GryUus, п., the typical genus of the crickets. —
L. grillus, gryllus [whence also OHG. grille,
(MHG., G. grille), 'cricket'], fr. Gk. γρύλλος,
'an Egyptian dance; a performer in such a dance;
comic figure, caricature'.

## gryphon
gryphon, n. — See griffin, 'a mythical animal'.

## grysbok
grysbok, п., a small grayish S. African antelope.
— S. Afr. Du., fr. Du. grijsbok, lit. 'gray buck',
fr. grijs, 'gray', and bok, 'buck'. See grizzle,
'gray', and buck.

## gnacharo
gnacharo, п., a South-American night bird. —
Sp. guacharo, fr. guacho, 'orphan', fr. Quechua
wahcha, 'poor; orphan', dim. of wah, 'strange,
foreign'.

## guaco
guaco, п., a South American climbing plant. —
— Sp., borrowed from a native language spoken
in Central or South America.

## guaiacol
guaiacol, п., a colorless liquid. — Formed fr. next
word with suff. -ol.

## gnaiacum
gnaiacum, п., ι) any of tropical American trees
of the genus Guaiacum; 2) resin from any of
these trees. — ModL., fr. Sp. guayaco, from
a Haitian word.

## guan
guan, п., any of large gallinaceous birds of
Central and South America. — Sp. guan, from W.
Indian native name.

## gnana
gnana, n. — A var. of iguana.

## guanaco
guanaco, п., a kind of large wild llama. — Sp.,
fr. Quechua huanaco, huanacu.

## guano
guano, п., a manure consisting of the dung of sea
birds. — Sp., fr. Quechua huanu, 'dung1.
Derivative: guano, tr. v., to manure with guano.

## guarana
guarana, п., a paste made from the seeds of the
Brazilian climbing plant Paullinia cupana. —
Port, and Sp. guarana, fr. Tupi guarana.

## gnarantee
gnarantee, n. — Formed fr. guaranty, on analogy
of other legal terms ending in -ее.
Derivative: guarantee, tr. v.

## guarantor
guarantor, n.—See guaranty and agential suff. -or.

## guaranty
guaranty, n. — OF. guarantie, garantie,
corresponding to ONF. warantie. See warranty.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:352 COLUMN:3 -->
which is a doublet of guaranty.

## guard
guard, tr. and intr. v. — OF. guarder, garder (F.
garder), 'to keep, watch over, guard, protect,
defend', corresponding to ONF. warder. See
ward, v., which is a doublet of guard, v.
Derivatives: guard-ed, adj., guard-ed-ly, adv.
guard-ed-ness, п., guard-er, n.

## guard
guard, n. — OF. guarde, garde (F. garde),
'watching, keeping, custody'. See ward, 'the act of
guarding', which is a doublet of guard, n.

## guardant
guardant, adj., the same as gardant (her.) — F.
gardant, pres. part, of garder. See gardant.

## gnardian
gnardian, n. — ME. gardein, fr. AF. gardein,
corresponding to OF. (= F.) gardien, which
was formed with change of suff. fr. OF. gardenc,
fr. garder. See gnard, v., and -ian, and cp.
warden, which is a doublet of guardian.

## guarinite
guarinite, п., a calcium titanium silicate (mineral)
— Named after Professor G. Guarini of Naples.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## guarneri
guarneri, n. — Short for Guarneri violin, prop, a
violin made by members of the Guarneri family
at Cremona in Italy. Cp. amati and stradivarius.

## gnava
gnava, п., a tree of the genus Psidium. — Sp.
guayaba, 'fruit of the guava tree', guayabo, 'the
guava tree', fr. Tupi guajava.

## gubernatorial
gubernatorial, adj., pertaining to a governor. —
Formed with suff. -ial fr. L. gubernator,
'steersman, pilot, ruler, governor', fr. gubernatus, pp.
of gubernare, 'to steer, direct, conduct, govern'.
See govern, governor.

## gnddee
gnddee, guddy, n. — Variants of gaddi.

## gudgeon
gudgeon, п., a small freshwater fish of the carp
family. —■ ME. gojon, fr. F. goujon, fr. L. gdbio-
nem, ace. of gdbid, a collateral form of gobius,
fr. Gk. κωβιός 'gudgeon', which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. goby.

## gudgeon
gudgeon, п., a pivot. — ME. gojone, fr. OF.
gojon (F. goujon), 'dowel', dimin. of gouge, 'a
tool for making grooves, a hollow chisel'. See
gouge and -on.

## guelder rose
guelder rose, n. — Lit. 'rose of Gelderland', from
the name of a province in Holland. Cp. F. rose
de Gueldre, of s.m.

## Gnelph
Gnelph, Guelf, п., a member of the papal party
in Italy during the Middle Ages. — It. Guelfo,
fr. ML. Guelphus, fr. MHG. Welf, name of the
ancestor of a family of princes. The name derives
fr. OHG. Hwelp, orig. a nickname meaning
"whelp, cub'. See whelp.
Derivative: Guelph-ic, Guelf-ic, adj.

## Guendoien
Guendoien, fern. PN. — A var. of Gwendolin (q.v.)

## guenon
guenon, п., any of a genus of long-tailed African
monkeys. — F., 'she-monkey, monkey', of
uncertain origin.

## guepard
guepard, п., the cheetah. — F. guepard, fr. earlier
gapard, shortened fr. It. gattopardo, lit. 'cat-
leopard'. See cat and pard and cp. leopard. Cp.
also F. chat-pard, 'mountain cat', lit. 'cat-
leopard'.

## guerdon
guerdon, п., a reward. — ME., fr. OF. guerredon,
guerdon, fr. ML. widerdonum, which is a blend
of OHG. widarlon, 'recompense' and L. donum,
'gift'. OHG" widarlon lit. meant 'return gift',
fr. widar, 'against', and Ion, 'reward, gift'. The
first element is rel. to OE. wider, 'against', wid,
'against, opposite'; see withers, with. The second
element is rel. to OE. lean, 'reward', fr. I.-E.
base *lau-, 'to gain, enjoy', whence also L.
lucrum, 'gain, profit, advantage'; see lucre. For
the etymology of L. donum see donation,

## guerdon
guerdon, tr. v., to reward. — ME. guerdonen, fr,
OF. guerredonner, guerdonner, 'to recompense,
reward', fr. guerdon. See guerdon, n.

## guereza
guereza, п., an Abyssinian monkey. — From
native name.

## guerilla
guerilla, n. — See guerrilla.

## Guernsey
Guernsey, п., name of a breed of cattle. — So
called because orig. reared on the Island of
Guernsey.
Guernsey lily. — This flower was discovered in
Japan by Kaempfer, the Dutch botanist. Its
name is due to the circumstance that the ship
which brought the first specimens of this plant
to Europe was wrecked on the coast of
Guernsey, in whose soil some of the bulbs germinated.

## guerrilla
guerrilla, also guerilla, п., ι) irregular warfare;
2) a person who engages in irregular warfare. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:353 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GUESS | 326 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:353 COLUMN:1 -->
Sp. guerrilla, lit. 'little war', dimin. of guerra,
'war', fr. OHG. werra, 'war' (whence also Port.,
Proveng., It. guerra, F. guerre). See war.

## guess
guess, tr. and intr. v. — ME. gessen, 'to think,
believe', prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. Dan. gisse,
Swed., Norw. gissa, 'to guess', which are rel.
to MLC, MDu. and G. gissen, of s.m., and
ult. to ON. geta, 'to get; to guess'. See get.
Derivatives: guess, п., guess-er, n.

## guest
guest, n. — ME. gest, fr. ON. gestr, which is rel.
to OE. gxst, giesl, OFris. jest, OS., Du. gast,
OHG. gast, gesti, MHG. gast, geste, G. Gast,
Goth, gasts, 'guest', orig. 'stranger', and cogn.
with L. kostis, 'stranger; enemy', hospes (for
hosti-potis), 'host, guest', orig. 'lord of
strangers', OSIav. gosli, 'guest', and perh. also with
Gk. ξένος, Ion. ξεΐνος, Dor. ξέν/ος, 'stranger,
guest'. Cp. host, 'landlord, guest', host, 'army',
hospital, hostile, hotel, xino-.
Derivatives: guest, tr. and intr. v., guest-less,
adj.

## Gueux
Gueux, n. pi., the patriot nobles of the
Netherlands (hist.) — F., lit. 'beggars', fr. earlier *gueu
(to be inferred from the fem. gueue), prob. fr.
Du. guit, 'rogue, rascal'.

## guff
guff, п., foolish talk. — Orig. 'a breath, puff'; of
imitative origin. Cp. next word.

## guffaw
guffaw, intr. v., to laugh loudly; п., a loud
laughter. — Of imitative origin.

## gugal
gugal, googul, п., an aromatic gum resin;
bdellium. — Hind, gugal, guggul, fr. Ol. guggulu.

## guggle
guggle, intr. v., to gurgle. — Of imitative origin.
Cp. gurgle.

## gugJet
gugJet, n. — A var. of goglet.

## guhr
guhr, п., an earthy deposit. — Dial. G., 'earthy
deposit', lit. 'fermentation', from the stem of
G. garen, 'to ferment' (tr.), fr. MHG. jesen, 'to
ferment' (intr.), fr. OHG. jesan, of s.m. See
yeast and cp. the second element in kieseiguhr.

## guidage
guidage, п., ι) guidance; 2) fee for guidance (ob-
sol.) — A hybrid coined fr. guide and -age, a
suff. of Latin origin.

## guidance
guidance, n. — A hybrid coined fr. guide and
-ance, a suff. of Latin origin.

## guide
guide, tr. v. — ME. gulden, guyden, gyden, fr. F.
guider, 'to guide, lead, conduct', refashioned—
after the noun guide—fr. OF. guier (whence
ME. gyen), 'to guide, lead', which derives fr.
Frank ish *mtan, 'to show' (whence also OProv-
eng. guidar, guizar). Cp. OS. wisian, ON. visa,
Dan. vise, Swed., Norw. visa, OFris. wlsa,
MDu. wisen, Du. wijzen, OHG., MHG. wiseri,
G. weisen, 'to show, point out', OE. witan, 'to
see'. See wise, adj. and п., wit, v., and cp. guise.
Cp. also guidone, guy, 'rope', Guy.

## guide
guide, n. — F., fr. OProveng. or It. guida, 'guide,
leader', fr. OProven?. guidar, 'to lead'. See
guide, v.

## guidon
guidon, п., ι) a small flag or pennant; 2) an
officer carrying such a flag. — F., fr. It. guidone,
'standard', fr. guida, 'guide'. See guide, n. and v.

## guige
guige, п., a long leather strap serving to fasten the
shield to the neck. — OF. guiche, guige, fr.
Frankish *wipig, 'withe, wickerwork', which
is rel. to OHG. wida, 'willow', OE. wide, 'withe*,
widig, 'willow'. See withy.

## guild
guild, gild, п., an'association for mutual aid. —
ME. gilde, fr. ON. gildi, 'payment, contribution,
fraternity', which is rel. to ON. gjald, 'payment'.
See geld.
Derivative: guild-ry, n.

## guilder
guilder, п., a Dutch coin. — Altered fr. Du.
gulden, lit. 'golden'. See gold and cp. gulden.

## guile
guile, п., cunning. — ME. guile, gile, fr. OF.
guile, which is of Teut. origin. See wile and cp.
beguile.
Derivatives: guile-ful, adv., guile-ful-ly, adv.,
guile-ful-ness, п., guile-less, adj., guile-less-ly,
adv., guile-less-ness, n.

## guillemot
guillemot, п., a seabird of the auk family. — F.,
dimin. of PN. Guitlaume, 'William'. For sense
development cp. jay, martin, martlet, which all
are traceable to proper names.

## guilloche
guilloche, п., an ornament formed by two or
more bands. — F. guillochis, formed from
Guilloche, a PN. altered fr. Guillot, which is a pet
form of Guillaume, 'William'. See Wiiliam. For
sense development cp. F. guillaume, 'rabbet-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:353 COLUMN:2 -->
piane' (fr. Guillaume). Cp. also guillemot and
words there referred to.

## guilloche
guilloche, tr. v., to ornament with guilloche. —
F. guillocher, fr. guillochis. See guilloche, n.

## guillotine
guillotine, п., an instrument for beheading. —
F., named after the physician Joseph-lgnace
Guillotin (1738-1814), who recommended its
adoption by the National Convention in 1789.
His aim in inventing this machine was to make
the execution of those condemned as swift and
painless as possible.

## gnillotine
gnillotine, tr. v., to behead with a guillotine. —
F. guillotiner, fr. guillotine. See guillotine, n.

## guilt
guilt, п., the fact of having committed a wrong.
— ME. gult, gilt, fr. OE. gylt, 'guilt, crime, debt,
fine'; of unknown origin.
Derivatives: guili-less, adj., guilt-less-ly, adv.,
guilt-less-ness, п., guilt-y, adj., guilt-i-ly, adv.,
guilt~i-ness, n.

## guimpe
guimpe, n. — See gimp.

## guinea
guinea, п., ι) a former English gold coin; a sum
of 2f shillings. — From Guinea, a country in
W. Africa; so called because first coined in
1663 from gold brought from the Guinea coast.

## guinea pig
guinea pig, n. — The guinea pig comes from
Brazil and owes its name to the circumstance
that it was brought to England by Guinea men,
i.e. ships trading between England, Guinea and
South America.

## Guinevere
Guinevere, fem. PN. — W. Gwenhwyvar, lit.
'white cheeked'. See Gwendoline), gwyniad.

## guipure
guipure, п., any of various kinds of laces. — F.,
fr. OF. guiper, "to cover with silk', fr. Frankish
wJpan, 'to cover with silk', which is rel. to Du.
wippen, OHG. wifan, MHG. wifen, G. weifen,
'to wind, reel', and cogn. with L. vibrare, 'to
move rapidly to and fro, shake, brandish,
agitate'. See vibrate and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending see suff. -ure.

## guise
guise, п., ι) manner, fashion; 2) appearance;
3) disguise. — ME. guise, gise, fr. OF. (— F.)
guise, which is borrowed fr. Teut. *wisa,
'manner' (whence also OProvenc. guiza, It., Sp.,
Port, guisa). See wise, п., which is a doublet of
guise, and cp. disguise.

## guiser
guiser, п., a mummer (Engl, and Scot.) — Formed
fr. guise with agential suff. -er.

## guitar
guitar, п., a stringed musical instrument. — F.
guitare, fr. Sp. guitarra, fr. Arab. qitarah, fr.
Gk. κιθάρϊ, fr. Pers. sihtar. See cither and cp.
gittern, zither.
Derivative: guitar-ist, n.

## gula
gula, п., the upper throat (zool.) — L., 'throat'.
See gullet.
Derivative: gul-ar, adj.

## gulch
gulch, п., a deep ravine. — Prob. fr. dial. E.
gulch, 'to swallow greedily', fr. ME. gulchen,
which is of imitative origin.

## gulden
gulden, п., formerly, a German and Dutch silver
coin (orig. a gold coin). — Du. and G. gulden,
shortened fr. Du. gulden florijn, 'a gold coin'.
See gold and cp. guilder.

## gules
gules, п., the color red; adj., red. — ME. goules,
fr. OF. goules, gueules (F. gueules\ 'gules',
prop, 'neckpieces of (red) fur', pi. of gole,
gueule (F. gueule), 'throat', fr. L. gula, 'throat'.
See gullet.

## gulf
gulf, n. — ME. goulf, golf, fr. It. golfo, fr. Gk.
χόλπος, 'bosom, lap, bay, gulf, womb', for
"qolpos, dissimulated fr. *qwolpos, 'something
vaulted', fr. I.-E. base "qwelp-, 'to vault',
whence also ON. hvalf, OE. hwealf OHG. walbo,
MHG. walbe, MLG. welve, OHG. gi-welbi, G.
Gewolbe, 'vault, arch', ON. hvelfa, 'to vault',
OE. ά-hwielfan, 'to cover with a vault; to
overwhelm', OS. Ы-hwelbian, MDu., Du. welven,
OHG., MHG. welben, G._ wolben, 'to vault',
Goth, hilf-lrjom (dat. pi.), 'coffin'. See whelm
and cp. colpo-.
Derivatives: gulf, tr. v., gulf-y, adj.

## gulix
gulix, п., a kind of fine linen. — Fr. Guliche,
former name of the town Julich in Western
Prussia.

## gull
gull, п., an unfledged bird (now dial.) — ME.
goll, prob. rel. to ME. gull, 'yellow', fr. ON.
gulr, 'yellow'. See yellow.

## gull
gull, tr. v., to deceive. — Prob. fr. prec. word.
Derivatives: gull, п., a dupe, gull-ish, adj., gull-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:353 COLUMN:3 -->
ish-ly, adv., gull-ish-ness, n.

## gull
gull, п., a long-winged, web-footed aquatic bird.
— ME. gull, of Celtic origin. Cp. Co. gullan,
gwilan, W. gwylan, Bret, gwelan (whence F.
goiland), 'gull'.

## gullet
gullet, п., the throat. — ME. golet, fr. OF. golet,
goulet, dimin. of gole, goule, 'throat' (whence
F. gueule, 'mouth of some animals'), fr. L. gula,
'throat', which derives fr. I.-E. base *gel-,
*gwel- (this latter is prob. a blend of the bases
"gel- and *g"er-), 'to swallow, devour', whence
also L. glutlire, 'to swallow, gulp down, devour',
OE. ceole, OHG. kela, MHG. kel, G. Kehle,
ON. kjolr, 'throat', OSIav. glutu, 'gullet', Olr.
gelim, Ί eat up, devour', W. gel, 'leech', and
prob. also Gk. δέλεαρ (for "δέλείαρ), 'bait, lure'.
See glut, 'to swallow', and cp. glutton, gula,
gully, gulosity. Cp. also goliard. For the dei iv-
atives of base *g">er- see voracious and cp. gurgi-
lation and words there referred to.

## gullible
gullible, adj., easily deceived. — A hybrid coined
fr. gull, 'to deceive', and suff. -ible.
Derivative: gullibil-ity, n.

## gully
gully, п., a small ravine. — Altered fr. gullet.
Derivative: gully, tr. v.

## gulosity
gulosity, п., gluttony (rare). — Late L. gulositas,
fr. L. gulosus, 'gluttonous', fr. gula. See gullet,
adj. suff. -ose and suff. -ity.

## gulp
gulp, tr. and intr. v. — ME. gulpen, golpen, glub-
ben, of imitative origin. Cp. Du. gulpen, !to
gulp, guzzle', Swed., Norw. glupa, 'to swallow,
devour', which are also imitative. Cp. also OE.
gielpan, 'to boast*, OHG. gelph, 'outcry', MHG.
gelfen, 'to boast', and see yelp.
Derivatives: gulp, п., gulp-ing-ly, adv., gulp-y,
adj.

## gum
gum, п., flesh in which the teeth are set. — ME.
gome, fr. OE. gdma, 'palate' (pi. gdman, 'jaws'),
rel. to ON. gdmi, 'palate', gdmr, 'gum', Swed.
gom, 'palate', Dan. gumme, 'gum', OHG. gou-
mo, MHG. goume, G. Gaumen, 'palate', and
cogn. with Lith. gomurys, 'palate', Lett, ga-
murs, 'windpipe, trachea', fr. I.-E. base *ghdu-,
"gheu-, *gh'u-, 'to gape', whence also Gk.-χάος
(for "χάίος), 'gulf, chasm, abyss, the rude
unformed mass', χαΰνος, 'gaping', χάσμα, 'chasm,
gulf. The above base is rel. to base *ghei-, *ghi-,
'to gape, yawn'. See yawn and words there
referred to.

## gum
gum, п., a viscid substance. — ME. gomme, fr.
OF. (= F.) gomme, fr. VL. gumma, fr. L. cum-
mi, gummi, fr. Gk. κόμμι, ult. fr. Egypt, kmj-t.
Cp. gumma.
Derivatives: gumm-y, adj., gumm-i-ness, n.

## gum
gum, tr. and intr. v., to fasten with gum. — F.
gommer, fr. gomme. See prec. word.
Derivatives: gumm-ed, adj., gumm-er, п.,
gumming, n.

## gumbo
gumbo, gombo, п., the okra plant. — From native
name in Angola.

## gum-gum
gum-gum, п., a bowl of iron used as a musical
instrument in India and S. Africa. — Prob. pi.

## of Malay gong. See gong
of Malay gong. See gong,

## gumma
gumma, п., a soft tumor, characteristic of tertiary
syphilis. — Medical L., fr. L. gummi. See gum,
'a viscid substance'.

## gummatous
gummatous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
gumma. — Formed with suff. -011s fr. Medical

## L. gumma
L. gumma, gen. gummatis. See gamma,

## gummiferous
gummiferous, adj., producing gum. — See gum,
'a viscid substance', and -ferous.

## gum mogador
gum mogador, Morocco gum. — So called from

## Mogador
Mogador, a seaport in Morocco, whence it is
exported.

## gummous
gummous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, gum;
gummy. — L. gummdsus, 'gummy', fr. gummi.

## See gum
See gum, 'a viscid substance', and -ous.

## gumption
gumption, п., shrewdness, common sense (col-
loq.) — Orig. Scot.; οϊ uncertain origin.

## gun
gun, n. — ME. gunne, gonne, prob. from the fem.

## PN. Gunne
PN. Gunne, shortened from the name Gunhild,
which was applied to a war engine (in 1330-31).
For sense development cp. the gun names

## Mons Meg
Mons Meg, Big Bertha, etc.
Derivatives: gun^ intr. v., gunnage (q.v.),

## gunner
gunner, п., gunn-eryt п., gunn-ing, n.

## gunge
gunge, п., a storehouse; a market (India). —

## Hind
Hind, ganj, fr. OI. ganjah, 'treasury', which is

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:354 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 327 | GYMNOPHIONA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:354 COLUMN:1 -->
an Iranian loan word. Cp Pers. ganj, 'treasure',
and see genizah.

## gunja
gunja, n. — A var. of ganja.

## gunnage
gunnage, п., number of guns carried by a
warship. — A hybrid coined fr. gun and -age, a
stiff, of Latin origin.

## gunnel
gunnel, п., a kind of blenny. — Of uncertain
origin.

## gunnel
gunnel, n. — A var. of gunwale.

## Gunnera
Gunnera, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Norwegian botanist Johan
Ernst Gunnerus (1718-73).
gunter n. — Shortened fr. gunter ride, scale,
resp. rig; named after the English
mathematician Edmund Gunter (1581-1626).

## Gunther
Gunther, Gunter, masc. PN. — OHG. Gundhard,
lit. 'bold in war', fr. gund, 'war', and karli, hart,
'hard, strong, bold'. For the first element see
gonfanon, for the second see hard.

## gup
gup, п., gossip (India). — Hind, gap, fr. Pers. gap,
'prattle, gossip'.

## gurge
gurge, п., a whirlpool (rare). — L. gurges. See
next word.

## gurges
gurges, п., a spiral representing a whirlpool (her.)
— L. gurges, 'whirlpool'. See next word.

## gurgitation
gurgitation, п., a boiling liquid. — Formed with
suff. -ion fr. L. gurgitatus, pp. of gurgitare, 'to
surge, flood', fr. gurges, gen. gurgitis,
'whirlpool, gulf; fr. base *gurg-, which is formed
with defective reduplication fr. I.-E. base
*gwer-, 'to devour'. See voracious and -ation and
cp. ingurgitate, regurgitate. Cp. also next word
and garget, gargle, gargoyle, gorge, gurge,
gurges.

## gurgle
gurgle, intr. v., to flow with a bubbling sound. —
Prob. fr. OF. gorguler, fr. L. gurgutio, 'gullet'
[whence MLG., Du. gorgel, OHG. gurgula
(MHG., G. gurgel), 'throat'], which is
dissimulated fr. *gurgurio, is rel. to gurges, 'whirlpool',
and cogn. with OI. gargarah, 'whirlpool', OHG.
querchala, querka, 'throat, gullet', ON. kverk,
'crop, maw'. See prec. word.
Derivative: gurgle, п., a gurgling sound.

## gurnard
gurnard, п., a small marine fish of the family
Triglidae. — OF. gornard, gornart, formed with
metathesis fr. OF. gronir, grognir, fr. L. grun-
nire, 'to grunt'. See grunt and -ard. The fish is
so called because it emits a grunting sound
when drawn out of the water.

## gurnet
gurnet, n. — A var. of gurnard.

## gurry
gurry, п., a little fort (India). — Hind, garhi,
'a fort'.

## guru
guru, also gooroo, п., a teacher, a priest (India).
— Hind, guru, fr. OI. guruh, 'heavy, weighty,
venerable; teacher', which is cogn. with Gk.
βαρύς, L. gravis, 'heavy'. See grave, 'weighty',
and cp. garce.

## gush
gush, intr. v. — ME. guschen, prob. of imitative
origin.
Derivatives; gush, п., gush-er, п., gush-ing, adj.,
gush-ing-ly, adv., gush-ing-ness, п., gush-y, adj.

## gusset
gusset, п., a piece of chain mail at the armpit. —
F., 'armpit; fob pocket', dimin. of gousse, 'pod,
husk', which is of unknown origin. For the
ending see suff. -et.
Derivative: gusset, tr. v.

## gust
gust, п., a sudden blast of wind. — ON. gustr,
'gust, blast', formed with suff. -r from gus-,
weak grade of gjosa, 'to gush'. See geyser.
Derivatives: gustful (q.v.), gust-y, adj., gusti-ly,
adv., gust-i-ness, a.

## gust
gust, п., relish. — L. gustus, 'tasting, taste'. See
choose and cp. gout, gustation, gusto, degust,
disgust, ageustia, ragout.
Derivative: gustful (q.v.)

## gustatiou
gustatiou, п., the act of tasting. — L. gustatid,
gen. -dnis, 'a tasting', fr. gustatus, pp. of
gustare, 'to taste', fr. gustus. See prec. word and
-atlon.

## gustative
gustative, adj., pertaining to the sense of taste. —
Formed with suff. -ive fr. L. gustatus, pp. of
gustare. See gustation.
Derivative: gustative-ness, n.

## gustatory
gustatory, adj., gustative. — Formed with suff.
-ory fr. gustatus, pp. of gustare. See gustation.

## Gustavus
Gustavus, masc. PN. — Latinized form of Swed.
Gu-staf, a name compounded of two elements.
The first element is of uncertain origin, the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:354 COLUMN:2 -->
second means 'staff' (see staff").

## gustfal
gustfal, adj., windy. — Compounded of gust, 'a
blast of wind', and -ful.

## gustful
gustful, adj:, tasty. — Compounded of gust,
'relish', and -ful.
Derivatives: guslful-ly, adv., gustful-ness, n.

## gusto
gusto, п., taste; keen relish. — It., fr. L. gustus,
'tasting, taste'. See gust, 'taste'.

## gut
gut, п., the alimentary canal; the intestines. —
ME. gut, gutte, fr. OE. guttas (pi.), 'entrails',
rel. to MDu. g6te, Du. goot, G. Gosse, 'gutter,
drain', ME. gate, 'channel, stream', and in grad-
ational relationship to OE. geotan, 'to pour'.
See found, 'to cast', and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also guttie.
Derivative: gut, tr. v.

## gutta
gutta, п., in the Doric entablature, one of a series
of ornaments, attached to the lower side of the
mutules. — L., 'drop'. See gatter.

## gutta
gutta, п., the principal constituent of
guttapercha (chem.) — See gutta-percha.

## gutta-percha
gutta-percha, п., a rubberlike substance formed
from the juice of various Malaysian trees. —
Lit. 'gum of the gutta-percha tree', fr. Malay
getah, 'gum, balsam', and percha, name of the
tree yielding this gum; influenced in form by
L. gutta, 'a drop'.

## guttate
guttate, adj., 1) resembling drops; 2) spotted as
if with drops. — L. guttatus, pp. of guttare, 'to
drop', fr. gutta, 'drop'. See gutter and adj. suff.
-ate and cp. gutte, which is a doublet of guttate.

## gutte
gutte, guttee, gutty, adj., sprinkled with drops
(her.) — AF. gutte, corresponding to F. goutte,
'sprinkled with drops', fr. L. guttatus, pp. of
guttare. See prec. word.

## gutter
gutter, n. — ME. goter, gotere, fr. OF. gutiere,
goutiere (F. gouttiire), 'gutter, spout (of water),
channel; groove', fr. gute, goute (F. goutte),
'drop', fr. L. gutta, 'drop'. See gout, and cp.
gutta, 'ornament', gattate, gutte, guttula. OF.
subst. suff. -iere (F. -lire) is prop, the fern, form
of the adj. suff. -ier (fr. L. -arius). See -ier.
Derivatives: gutter, tr. and intr. v., gutter-ing, n.

## guttiferous
guttiferous, adj., producing drops. —
Compounded of L. gutta, 'drop', and the stem of ferre,
'to bear, carry'. See gutter and -ferous.

## guttiform
guttiform, adj., drop-shaped. — Compounded of
L. gutta, 'drop', and forma, 'form, shape'. See
gout and form, n.

## guttle
guttle, intr. and tr. v., to gormandize. — Formed
fr. gat wit freq. suff. -le.
Derivative: guttl-er, a.

## guttula
guttula, п., a small droplike spot (hot. and zool.)
— L., 'a small drop', dimin. of gutta. See gutter.
Derivatives: gullul-ar, guttul-ate, adjs.

## guttural
guttural, adj., pertaining to the throat. — F., fr.
ML.gutturalis, fr.L. guttur,'throat', which prob.
stands for *gutur and derives fr. I.-E. base
'gwet-, *geut-, "gut-, 'to vault', whence also OE.
cwid, 'belly, womb', Goth, qipus, 'stomach,
belly, womb', ON. kvidr, 'belly'. See bowel and
adj. suff. -al and cp. botulism. Cp. also goiter.
Derivatives: guttural-ity, п., guttural-ly, adv.,
guttural-ness, п., gutturalism, gutturalize (qq.v.)

## gutturalism
gutturalism, п., tendency to gutturalize.'— See
guttural and -ism.

## gutturalize
gutturalize, tr. v., to pronounce gutturally. —
See gartural and -ize.
Derivative: gutturaliz-ation, n.

## gutturo-
gutturo-, combining form meaning guttural. —
Fr. L. guttur, 'throat'. See guttural.

## gutty
gutty, adj. — See gatte.

## gutty
gutty, п., a gutta-percha ball. — Formed from
the abbreviation of gutta-percha and suff. -y.

## guy
guy, п., a rope. — OF. guie, 'a guide', fr. guier.
See next word.

## guy
guy, tr. v., to guide with a guy. — OF. guier, 'to
guide'. See guide.

## Guy
Guy, masc. PN. — F., rel. to It., Sp., Port. Guido,
lit. 'leader'; of Tout, origin. See guide, n. and v.,
and cp. guy, 'rope'.

## guy
guy, п., ι) a grotesque effigy of Guy Fawkes; 2) a
grotesquely dressed person. — From the name
of Guy Fawkes, the ill-famed conspirator. For
the etymology and meaning of this PN. see
Guy.
Derivative: guy, tr. v., to make fun of.

## guzzle
guzzle, intr. and tr. v., to drink greedily. — OF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:354 COLUMN:3 -->
gosillier, gosiller, 'to go down the gullet; to
vomit; to chatter', fr. gosillier, 'throat, gullet',
which prob. derives fr. OF. (= F.) gosier, of
s.m., which derives fr. Gaul.-L. geusiae, 'gullet';
influenced in form by F. gorge, 'throat'.
Derivatives: guzzle, п., guzzl-er, n.

## gweduc
gweduc, п., a large edible clam. — N. American
Ind.; lit. 'dig deep'.

## Gwen
Gwen, fern. PN. — Dimin. of Gwendoline.

## Gwendolin(e)
Gwendolin(e), also Gwendolen, Gwendolyn, fern.
PN. — A compound of Celtic origin; the first
element is Bret, gwenn, 'white'. See next word.

## gwyniad
gwyniad, п., a fish of the salmon family. — Lit.
'white (fish)', a hybrid formed with suff. -iad
fr. W. gwyn, 'white', which is rel. to Bret, gwenn,
Co. guyn, Olr. find, Gael., Ir. fionn, Gaul.
vindo-, 'white', fr. Celtic *vindo-, 'visible;
'shining; white', a nasalized form of *vid-, 'to
see', whence Olr. fiss, Gael., Ir. fios,
'knowledge', fr. I.-E. base *weid-, *woid-, *wid-, 'to
see; to know', whence also L. vidire, 'to see'.
See vision and cp. winter and words there
referred to. Cp. also Guinevere, Gwendolin(e).

## gybe
gybe, v. — A var. of jibe, 'to swing round'.

## Gygis
Gygis, п., a genus of terns (ornithol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. γύγης, name of a water bird, which is
prob. of imitative origin.

## gyle
gyle, п., ι) amount of beer produced at one
brewing; 2) fermenting wort; 3) fermenting vat. —
ME., fr. MDu. ghijl, ghijle (Du. gijl), 'ferment',
from the verb ghijlen, 'to ferment', whence F.
guiller, of s.m.

## gymkhana
gymkhana, п., display of athletic sports (orig.
Anglo-Indian). — A blend of Hind, gend-khana,
'ball house' (fr. gend, 'ball', and khana, 'house'),
and E. gymnastics (q.v.)

## gymn-
gymn-, form of gymno- before a vowel.
gymnasinl. — Formed fr. gymnasium with adj.
suff. -al.

## gymnasiarch
gymnasiarch, п., at ancient Athens, a
superintendent of athletic training. — L. gymnasiar-
chus, fr. Gk. γυμνασίαρχος, which is compounded
of γυμνάσιον, 'gymnasium', and άρχος, 'leader,
chief, ruler'. See next word and -arch.

## gymnasium
gymnasium, п., ι) a building equipped for
gymnastics; 2) in Germany and some other
countries, a secondary school for students. — L., fr.
Gk. γυμνάσίον, 'gymnastic school, school', fr.
γυμνάζειν, 'to practice gymnastic exercises', lit.
'to train naked', fr. γυμνός, 'naked'; so called
because the athletes trained naked. See gymno-.

## gymnast
gymnast, п., one who teaches gymnastics. — Gk.
γυμναστής, 'trainer of athletes', fr. γυμνάζειν.
See prec. word and -ast.

## gymnastic
gymnastic, also gymnastical, adj., pertaining to
physical exercises. — L. gymnaslicus, fr. Gk.
γυμναστικός, 'pertaining to, or fond of,
gymnastic exercises', fr. γυμνάζειν. See prec. word
and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivatives: gymnastics (q.v.), gymnaslic-al-ly,
adv.

## gymnastics
gymnastics, п., physical exercises. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## gymno-
gymno-, before a vowel gymn-, combining form
meaning 'naked'. — Gk. γυμνό-, γυμν-, fr.
γυμνός, 'naked', cogn. with OI. nagnah, L.
nudus, Goth, naqaps, OE. nacod, 'naked'. See
naked and cp. nude.

## Gymnocladus
Gymnocladus, п., a genus of plants, the Kentucky
coffee tree (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
gymno- and Gk. κλάδος, 'branch'. See clado-.

## Gymnoconia
Gymnoconia, п., a genus of rusts (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of gymno- and Gk. κόνις, 'dust',
which is cogn. with L. cinis, 'ashes'. See cinerary
and cp. conio-, conidi-. For the ending see suff.
-ia.

## Gymnodontes
Gymnodontes, n. pi., a group of fishes (ichthyol.)
— ModL., compounded of gymno- and Gk.
δδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-,

## Gymnonoti
Gymnonoti, n.pl., an order of fishes including the
electric eel and allied forms (ichthyol.) — ModL.
Gymnonoti, compounded of gymno- and Gk.
νώτος, 'the back', which is cogn. with L. nates,
'rump'; so called in allusion to the absence of
the dorsal fin. See noto- and cp. nates. Cp. also
the second element in Gymnotus.

## Gymnophiona
Gymnophiona, п., an order of Amphibia (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of gymno- and Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:355 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: GYMNORHINA | 328 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:355 COLUMN:1 -->
όφιόνεος, 'pertaining to, or like, a serpent', fr.
δφις, 'serpent1. See ophidian.

## Gymnorhina
Gymnorhina, п., a genus of birds, the piping crow
(ornilhol.) — ModL., prop, 'having naked
nostrils', compounded of gymno- and Gk. ρίς,
gen. ρινός, 'nose'. See rhino- and cp. next word.

## gymnorhinal
gymnorhinal, adj., having naked nostrils (said of
crows). — See prec. woid and rhinal.

## gymnosophist
gymnosophist, п., member of a sect of
philosophers in ancient India, who walked naked. —■
L, gymnosophistae (pi.), fr. Gk. γυμνοσοφισταί
(pi.), which is compounded of γυμνός, 'naked',
and the pi. of σοφιστής, 'philosopher'. See
gymno- and sophist.

## gymnosophy
gymnosophy, п., the doctrine ot the gymno-
sophists. — See prec. word and -soohv.

## gyuinosperm
gyuinosperm, п., a plant that has its seeds naked
(i.e. not enclosed in an ovary). — ModL. gym-
nospermus, fr. Gk. γυμνόσπερμος, 'having naked
seeds', compounded of γυμνός, 'naked', and
σπέρμα, 'seed'. See gymno- and sperm and cp.
angiosperm.

## gymnospermous
gymnospermous, adj., having the seeds not
enclosed in an ovary. — See prec. word and -ous.

## Gymnotus
Gymnotus, п., a genus of fishes, the electric eel
(ichthyol.) — ModL. Gymnotus, contraction of
Gymnonotus, which is compounded of Gk.
γυμνός, 'naked', and νώτος, 'the back'; so called
because of the absence of the dorsal fin. See
gymno- and noto-. The contraction of Gymno-notus
into Gymnotus is due to haplology. (Cp. Gym-
nonoti, which is formed without such
contraction).

## gyn-
gyn-, form of gyno- before a vowel.

## gynaeceum
gynaeceum, п., ι) apartment for women {Greek
antiq.); 2) the pistils of a flower collectively (hot.)
— L. gynaeceum, fr. Ok. γυναικεΐον, 'women's
apartment', prop. neut. of the adjective
γυναικείος, 'pertaining to a woman; womanly,
feminine,' used as a noun, fr. γυνή, gen. γυναικός,
'woman'. See gyneco-.
gynaeco-. — See gyneco-,

## gynandrous
gynandrous, adj., having the gynoecium and an-
droecium united in a column (as in orchids). —
Gk. γύνανδρος, 'of doubtful sex', fr. γυνή,
'woman', and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man*. See
gyneco- and andro- and cp. androgynous. For
E. ~ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## gynarchy
gynarchy, п., government by a woman or women.
— Compounded of gyn- and Gk. -αρχία, 'rule'.
See -archy.

## gynec-
gynec-, form of gyneco- before a vowel.

## gynecium
gynecium, n. — See gynoecium.

## gyneco-
gyneco-, before a vowel gynec-, combining form
meaning 'woman'. — Gk. γυναικο-, γυναικ-,
fr. γυνή, gen. γυναικός, 'woman', rel. to
Boeotian βανά, fr. I.-E. *g<»una, *gwena, 'woman',
whence also OI. gnu, gana, 'wife of a god,
goddess', janih, 'wife', Goth, qino, 'woman, wife',
qens, 'woman', OE. cwen, 'woman, wife, queen'.
See quean and cp. queen. Cp. also agynary,
androgynous, misogyny, monogynous.

## gynecocracy
gynecocracy, gynaecocracy, п., government by a
woman or women. — - Gk. γυναικοκρατίϊ,
compounded of γυνή, gen. γυναικός, 'woman', and
-κρατίδ, 'rule of, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power,
rule'. See gyneco- and -cracy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:355 COLUMN:2 -->

## gynecocrat
gynecocrat, gynaecocrat, п., an adherent of
gynecocracy. — See prec. word and -crat.
Derivatives: gynecocrat-ic,gynecocrat-ic-al, adjs.

## gynecology
gynecology, gynaecology, п., the study of diseases
peculiar to women. — Compounded of gyneco-
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: gynecolog-ic, gynecolog-ical, adjs.,
gyneco/og-ist, a.

## gyniatrics
gyniatrics, п., the treatment of diseases peculiar to
women. — Compounded of Gk. γυνή, 'woman',
and Ιατρικός, 'pertaining to healing'. See gyneco-
and -mtric.

## gyno-
gyno-, combining form, equivalent to gyneco-, —
Fr. Gk. γυνή, 'woman'. See gyneco-.

## gynobase
gynobase, п., the flat enlargement of the
receptacle of a flower bearing the gynoecium (йог.) —
Compounded of gyno- and base, n.

## gynocracy
gynocracy, п., gynecocracy. — Compounded of
gyno- and -cracy. Cp. gynecocracy.

## gynoecinm
gynoecinm, gynecium, п., the pistils of a flower
collectively (bot.) — ModL., usually explained
as compounded of Gk. γυνή, 'woman', and
οίκος, 'house' (see gyno- and economy), but in
reality a corruption of gynaeceum (taken in its
second meaning). This corruption was suggested
by the ending -oecium in androecium.

## -gynous
-gynous, combining form meaning i) 'female', as
in polygynous; 2) 'having female organs or
pistils', as in androgynous (bpt.) — Gk. -γυνος, fr.
γυνή, 'woman'. See gyneco- and -ous.

## gyp
gyp, п., a male college servant (at Cambridge
or Durham). — Of uncertain origin; possibly
short for gypsy.

## Gypaetus
Gypaetus, п., a genus of birds, the lammergeier
(ornilhol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. γυψ,
gen. γΰπός, 'vulture', and αετός, 'eagle'. See
Gyps and aeto-.

## Gyps
Gyps, п., a genus of birds, the griffon vulture
(ornilhol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. γυψ, gen. γϋπός,
'vulture', rel. to γύ7τη, 'cave, den, hole', fr. I.-E.
*geu-p-, a-p-enlargement of base *geu-, 'to bend,
curve, arch'. See cove, 'a small bay', and cp.
gyre.

## gypseous
gypseous, adj., i) containing gypsum; z)
resembling gypsum. — L. gypseus, 'of gypsum', fr.
gypsum. See gypsum and -ous.

## gypsiferous
gypsiferous, adj., producing gypsum. — See
gypsum and -ferous.

## Gypsophila
Gypsophila, п., a genus of plants of the pink
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
γύψος, 'chalk, gypsum', and φίλειν, 'to love'.
See gypsum and philo-.

## gypsous
gypsous, adj. — A var. of gypseous.

## gypsnm
gypsnm, n. — L., fr. Gk. γύψος, 'chalk', of Sem.
origin. Cp. Arab, jibs, Mishnaic Heb. gebhes,
gephes, 'plaster, mortar, gypsum', which prob.
derive fr. Akkad. gassu (whence also Aram.
gassd, whence Arab, jass, jiss, jugs, qass, qifs),
'gypsum'. — Cp. gesso.

## gypsy
gypsy, gipsy, n. — Fr. earlier gypcian, aphetized
fr. still earlier Egypcian, 'Egyptian, gypsy', fr.
OF. Egyptien (F. Egyptien), fr. L. Aegyptianus,
'Egyptian'. See Egyptian andep. gitano. Cp.
also gyp.
Derivatives: gypsy, intr. v., gypsy-ish, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:355 COLUMN:3 -->

## gyr-
gyr-, form of gyro- before a vowel.

## gyral
gyral, adj., moving in a gyre or circle. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. gyrus. See gyre.
Derivative: gyral-ly, adv.

## gyrate
gyrate, intr. v., to revolve. — L. gyratus,
'circular', pp. of gyrare, 'to turn round in a circle',
fr. gyrus. See next word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: gyrat-ion, п., gyrat-ion-al,
gyratory, adjs.

## gyre
gyre, п., a circular motion. — L. gyrus, fr. Gk.
γϋρος, 'circle, ring', which is rel. to γϋρός,
'rounded, curved', and cogn. with Arm. kor,
'crooked', kufn, 'the back', Lith. gufnas, hip,
ankle, bone', Norw. kaure, 'a curly lock of hair',
Swed. kura, Dan. kure, 'to squat', MLG. kiiren,
'to lie in wait', G. kauern, 'to squat, cower'. All
these words are derivatives of I.-E. *geu-r-, an
-r-enlargement of base *geu-, 'to bend, curve,
arch'. See cove, 'a small bay', and cp. cower. Cp.
also gyrus, the first element in girandole, virelai,
and the second element inautogiro,circumgyrate,
helicogyre. Cp. also Gyps.

## gyre
gyre, intr. v., to gyrate. — L. gyrare, 'to turn
round in a circle*, fr. gyrus. See gyre, n.

## gyrfalcon
gyrfalcon, n. — A var. of gerfalcon.

## gyro-
gyro-, combining form meaning 'circle, circular,
spiral'. — Gk. γϋρο-, fr. γϋρος, 'circle'. See
gyre, n.

## gyrocompass
gyrocompass, п., a compass with gyroscope. —
Compounded of gyro and -compass.

## gyrograph
gyrograph, п., an instrument for recording
revolutions of a wheel, etc. — Compounded of
gyro- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graph.

## gyromancy
gyromancy, п., divination by walking in a circle
till one falls from dizziness (the prognostic being
made from the place or direction of the fall). —
Compounded of gyro- and Gk. μαντεία, 'oracle,
divination'. See -mancy.

## gyron
gyron, also giron, п., an ordinary of triangular
form (her.) — F. giron, orig. 'piece of cloth of
triangular shape', fr. Frankish Va/ro-, of s.m.,
which is rel. to OHG. ger, OE. gar, 'spear'.
See gore, 'a triangular piece of land'.

## gyronny
gyronny, adj., divided into gyrons (her.) — F.
gironne, fr. giron. See prec. word and -y
(representing F. -e).

## gyroplane
gyroplane, п., a flying machine furnished with
rotating horizontal planes. — Compounded of
gyro- and plane, 'airplane*.

## gyroscope
gyroscope, п., a heavy rotating wheel, having its
axis free to turn in any direction. —
Compounded of gyro- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκο-εϊν, 'to
look at, examine'. See -scope.
Derivative: gyroscop-ic, adj.

## gyrostat
gyrostat, п., a modified form of a gyroscope. —
Compounded of gyro- and Gk. στατός, 'placed;
standing'. See static and cp. aerostat, and words
there referred to.
Derivatives: gyrostat-ic, adj., gyrostatics (q.v.)

## gyrostatics
gyrostatics, п., that branch of dynamics which
deals with rotating bodies. — Compounded of
gyro- and statics.

## gyrus
gyrus, п., a convolution between grooves (anat.)
— L. gyrus, 'circle'. See gyre, n.

## gyre
gyre, n. (usually pi.: gyves), shackle. — ME.
gives, gyves (pi.), of uncertain origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:356 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:356 COLUMN:1 -->

## hn
hn, interj. — This imitative word occurs in most
languages.

## Habakkuk
Habakkuk, η., ι) the eighth in the order of the
Twelve Prophets; 2) the Book of Habakkuk
(Bible). — Heb. Hubhaqquq, prob. from the
base of habhaq, 'he embraced'. Cp. Akkad. ham-
baququ, name of a garden plant, Arab, habaqlq,
name of a plant in Yemen ('the basil').

## habanera
habanera, п., a Cuban dance imported from
Africa. — Sp. (danza) habanera, 'Havanan
dance', fern, of habanero, 'Havanan', formed fr.
Habana, 'Havana', with suff. -его, fr. L. -arius;
see adj. suff. -ary.

## habdalah
habdalah, п., ceremony terminating formally
sabbaths and festivals. — Mishnaic Heb. habh-
dala", 'separation, distinction, division', verbal
noun ofhibhdi/, 'he divided, separated, set apart,
distinguished', rel. to Mishnaic Heb. badhat,
'he separated, divided', Aram, b'dhal, 'he was
separated, he abstained', Arab, badala, 'he
changed, substituted', Heb. b'dhil, 'tin; dross',
lit 'that which is separated' (scil. from the
precious metal).
abea^ corpus, п., a writ commanding the pro-
juctii.ii of the detained person before the judge
(чгл). — L. 'have thou the body'. L. habeas is
Ые second person sing, of the pres. subj. of
habere, 'to have'; see habit. For the etymology
of L. corpus, 'body', see corpus.

## Habenaria
Habenaria, п., a genus of plants, the rein orchis
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. habena, 'thong, rein',
which stands for habe-na, fr. habere, 'to hold,
to have'; habena prop, means 'that by which
something is held'; see habit. The genus is so
called in allusion to the shape of the spur.

## habendum
habendum, п., part of a deed that defines the
estate which the grantee is to have (law). — L.,
'to be had', neut. gerundive of habere, 'to have'
(see habit); so called because it begins in Latin
with the word habendum. For other Latin
gerundives used in English cp. agenda and words
there referred to.

## haberdasher
haberdasher, п., a seller of small wares. — ME.
haberdassher, formed with agential sufT. -er fr.
AF. haperias, name of a material, which is of
unknown origin.
Derivative: haberdasher-y, n.

## habergeon
habergeon, п., a short coat of mail. — ME. hau-
bergoun, fr. OF. haubergeon, dimin. of hauberc.
See hauberk and -on.

## habile
habile, adj., able; ready. — F. habile, fr. L. ha-
bilis, 'that which may be easily handled,
suitable, fit, proper'. See able, which is a doublet
of habile, and cp. next word.

## habiliment
habiliment, n„ an article of clothing; in the pi.,
dress. — F. habitlement, 'clothing', fr. habiller,
'to dress', fr. OF. abiller, 'to fit out, make
ready', fr. Gaulish-VL. *btlia, 'stump, trunk'
[whence also F. bille, 'billet (of timber')];
influenced both in form and meaning by the word
habit (see next word). See billet, 'stick, log', and
cp. dishabille. For the ending see suff. -ment.
Derivatives: habiliment-al, habiliment-ary, ha-
biliment-ed, adjs.

## habilitate
habilitate, tr. v., to clotne; to equip. — ML.
habilitatus, pp. of habiUtare, 'to make fit', fr.
habilitds, 'suitability, fitness', fr. habilis,
'suitable, fit, proper'. See habile and verbal suff. -ate
and cp. rehabilitate.

## Habiru
Habiru, also Habirl, п., a name used to denote
various groups of invaders of Palestine,
mentioned in the Tell el-Ainarna letters from the
19th and 18th centuries B.C.E. — Akkad.
Habiru, which is prob. a blend of the plur. panic,
of base h-b-r, 'to pass, wander' (corresponding
to Heb. 'abhor, Arab, 'abara, etc.), and of Heb.
'ibhri, 'Hebrew', which itself derives from the
stem of Heb. 'abhor; see Hebrew. Since there is
no 'ayin in the Akkadian, this letter is usually
rendered in Akkad. PN s of Hebrew origin by

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:356 COLUMN:2 -->
h. Cp. Akkad. Humr'i -= Heb. 'Omrt, Akkad.
haparu = Heb. 'aphar, dust', Akkad. hullu —
Heb. 'ol, 'yoke', Akkaa. zuruh — Heb. z'ro"',
'arm'.

## habit
habit, п., practice, custom; dress. — ME. habit,
abit, fr. OF. habit, abil (F. habit), fr. L. habitus,
'condition, state, habit, dress', fr. habere, 'to
have, hold, possess', se habere, 'to be
constituted, be in a condition', fir. 1-Е. base *ghab(h)-,
'to seize, take, hold, have', whence also
Olr. gaibim, Ί take, hold; I have', gabal, 'the
act of taking', W. gafael, 'the act of holding
fast', Lith. gabana, 'armful', gabenti, 'to remove',
gobti (with vowel gradation), 'to wrap up', Goth.
gabei, 'riches,' gabeigs, rich', Goth, giban, OE.
gifan, giefan, 'to give'. Goth, haban, OE. habban,
'to have', are not cogn. with L. habere. L. habitus
is prop, a loan translation of Gk. έξις,
'condition, habit', fr. έχειν, Ίο have'. Ср. gi»e. Ср.
also able, adhibit, binnacle, cohabit, debt, due,
duty, exhibit, Habenaria, habendum, habile, hn-
bilitate, habitat, habitual, havior, inhabit, inhibit,
malady, prebend, prohibit.

## habit
habit, tr. v., to dwell, inhabit. — ME. habiten,
'to inhabit', fr. F. habiter, fr. L. habitare, 'to
inhabit, dwell, reside', prop, 'to have frequently',
freq. of habere (pp. habitus), 'to have'. See habit,
п., and cp. inhabit. Cp. also binnacle.

## habitable
habitable, adj. — ME., fr. F. habitable. Гг. L. ha-
bitabilis, 'habitable', fr. habitare. See habit, v.,
and -able.
Derivatives: habitabil-Uy, п., habitable-ness, п.,
habitabl-y, adv.

## habitant
habitant, п., inhabitant. -— F., pres. part, of
habiter, 'to inhabit, dwell'. See habit, v., and suff.
-ant and cp. inhabitant.

## habitat
habitat, п., natural location of an animal or
plant. — L., 'it dwells', 3rd person sing. pres. of
habitare, 'to dwell'. See habit, v.

## habitation
habitation, п., ι) the act of inhabiting; 2) a
dwelling place. — ME. habitacioun, fr. F. habitation,
fr. L. habitationem, ace. of habitdtio, 'a dwelling,
inhabiting, habitation,' fr. habitants, pp. of
habitare. See habit, v., and -ation.
Derivatives: habitatiqn-al, adj.

## habitual
habitual, adj. — ML. habitualis (whence also F.
habituel), fr. L. habitus. See habit and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: habitual-ly, adv., habitual-ness, n.

## habituate
habituate, tr. v., to accustom. — Late L. habi-
tuatus, pp. of habitudre, 'to bring into a habit
or condition' (whence also F. habituer), fr.
habitus. See habit, п., and verbal surf, -ate and cp.
habitue.
Derivative: habituat-ion, n.

## habitude
habitude, п., custom, habit. — F., fr. L. habi-
tudinem, ace. of habitude, 'condition, habit', fr.
habitus. See habit, п., and -ude.

## habitue
habitue, п., one who habitually visits a place. —
F., pp. of habituer, 'to habituate'. See habituate.

## habro-
habro-, combining form meaning 'graceful'. —
Gk. άβρο-, fr. αβρός, 'graceful, delicate, pretty';
rel. to όίβρα, 'a favorite slave', which is
borrowed fr. Aram, habhra, 'companion; female
companion', from the stem of habb4r, 'he joined',
which is rel. to Heb. habhar, 'he joined, was
joined; he charmed', habher, 'companion',
hebher, hebhra, 'company', Ethiop. habara, 'he
bound', Akkad. ebru, 'companion', ubburu, 'to
bind, ban'. See H. Lewy, Die semitischen Fremd-
worter im Griechischen, p. 68, and Muss Ar-
nolt, Semitic Words in Greek and Latin, in
Transactions of the American Philological
Association, Vol. XXIII, p. 65.

## hachure
hachure, п., a short line used in shading. — F., fr.
hacher, 'to cut'. See hatch, 'to engrave', and -ure.
Derivative: hachure, tr. v.

## hacienda
hacienda, п., a large estate, ranch. — Sp., 'landed
