estate', fr. earlier facienda, fr. L. facienda,
'things to be done', neut. pi. gerundive of facere.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:356 COLUMN:3 -->
'to do'. See fact. For other words traceable to
Latin gerundives cp. agenda and words there
referred to.

## hack
hack, tr. and intr. v., to chop, cut. — ME. hacken,
fr. OE. -haccian (only in compounds), rel. to
OFris. hackia, Du. hakken, OHG. hacchon,
MHG., G. hacken, 'to chop, cut', and prob. also
to OE. haca, 'bolt'. See hook and cp. hnck,
'cutting tool', and the second element in nuthatch.
Derivative: hack, п., the act of hacking.

## hack
hack, п., a cutting tool. — Fr. hack, 'to cut'. Cp.
Dan. hakke, 'mattock', G. Hacke, 'pickax,
hatchet, mattock, hoe'.

## hnck
hnck, п., board on which a hawk's meat is placed.
— OE. hxc, 'grating; gate'. See hatch, 'door'.
Derivative: hack, tr. v., to put on a hack.

## hack
hack, п., a horse let out on hire. — Fr. hackney.
Derivative: hack, tr. v., to let out on hire; intr.
v., to ride on a hack.

## hackamore
hackamore, п., a halter, esp. for breaking horses.
— Folk-etymological alteration of Sp. jaquima,
'headstall of a halter', fr. Arab, shaklma", 'bit
of a bridle; curb, restraint'.

## hackberry
hackberry, n. — A var. of hagberry.

## hackbut
hackbut, п., a kind of harquebus. — OF. (= F.)
haquebute, fr. MDu., hakebusse. See harqnebns.
hackery· п., an Indian bullock cart (India). —
Corruption of Hind, chakra, 'cart', fr. OI.
cakrah, 'wheel'. See cycle andwords therereferred
to and cp. esp. chukker.

## hackle
hackle, п., ι) a comb for dressing flax; 2) one of
the long feathers on the neck of a cock. — ME.
hekete, 'an instrument for cleansing and carding
flax or hemp'. See hatchel, п., and cp. heckle.
Derivatives: hackle, v., hackl-er, n.

## hackney
hackney, п., a horse or carriage let out on hire.
— ME. hakene, hakenei, fr. Hackney, a town
in Middlesex, renowned for its horses. Cp. hack,
'a horse let out on hire'. F. haquenee, 'an
ambling nag', is an English loan word.
Derivative: hackney, tr. v.

## had
had, past tense and pp. of have. — ME. hadde,
had, fr. habben, 'to have'. See have.

## haddock
haddock, п., a small fish related to the cod. —
ME. haddok, hadok, of unknown origin. Gael.
adag and OF. hadot, F. haddock, are English
loan words.

## hade
hade, п., the inclination of a vein from the vertical
(geol.) — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: hade, intr. v., to incline from the
vertical.

## Hades
Hades, п., the lower world. — Gk. "Αιδης, also
Άίδης, 'the god of the lower world, Pluto', a
name of uncertain origin. It meant perh. ortg.
'invisible', fr. "iFiSeiv, 'to make invisible', fr.
&- (see priv. pref. a-) and Ιδεϊν, 'to see', which
is cogn. with L. vidire, 'to see'; cp. Gk. άίδηλος,
'making unseen', which is of the same origin.
See vision and cp. words there referred to.

## Hadith
Hadith, п., the whole of Mohammedan traditions
(Islam). — Arab, hadith, 'tradition', rel. to the
adjective hadith, 'new, young', hadatha, 'it
happened, occurred', hadutha, 'was new, was young',
hdddatha, 'he told, related', and to Heb. haddsh,
'new'. See Rosh Hodesh.

## hadj
hadj, п., pilgrimage to Mecca. — Arab, hajj,
'pilgrimage', fr. hajja, 'he went on a pilgrimage',
which is rel. to Heb. haghagh, 'he made a
pilgrimage, celebrated a feast', hagh, 'a festival
gathering, a feast'. See Haggai and cp. next
word.

## hadji
hadji, hajji, п., a Moslem who has made his
pilgrimage to Mecca. — Arab, hajjt, fr. hajj, part,
of hajja, 'he went on a pilgrimage'. See prec.
word.

## hadro-
hadro-, combining form meaning 'thick'. — Gk.
άδρο-, fr. αδρός (for *sadros), 'thick, stout; full-
grown, ripe', which stands for άδ-ρο-ς and is
rel. to άδίνός (for *sadinos); 'crowded', lit.
'thick', όίδην (for "saden), 'to one's fill, to sa-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:357 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HADROMERINA | 330 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:357 COLUMN:1 -->
tiety', and cogn. with L. satis, 'enough', OE.
sxd, "sated, satisfied'. See sad and cp. the first
element in Adephaga.

## Hadromerina
Hadromerina, п., a group of sponges (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of hadro-, Gk. μέρος,
'part1 (see ist mero-), and surf. -ina.

## hadrosaur
hadrosaur, п., any reptile of the genus Hadro-
smtrus. — See next word.

## Hadrosaurus
Hadrosaurus, п., a genus of extinct dinosaurian
reptiles (paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of
hadro- and Gk. σαΰρος, 'lizard'. See sauro-.

## haecceity
haecceity, п., thisness; individuality (scholastic
philos.) — ML. haecceitas, fr. L. haecce (res),
'this (thing)', with better spelling haece, fern,
of htce (hicce), intensive form of hie (fem. haec,
neut. hoc), 'this'. See hodiernal and cp. encore,
iangue d'oc. For the ending see surf. -ity.
haem-. — See hem-.

## Haemanthus
Haemanthus, п., a genus of plants of the ama-
ryllis family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
Gk. αίμα, 'blood', and άν&ος, 'flower'. See
hemal and -anthus.

## haemat-
haemat-, haemato-, haemo-. — See hemat-, he-
mato-, hemo-.

## haemarrnon
haemarrnon, п., a hard red glass. — L. haema-
timis, 'blood-colored, blood-red', fr. Gk.
αιμάτινος, fr. αίμα, gen. αίματος, 'blood'. See hemal
and adj. surf, -ine (representing L. -inus).

## Haemodoraceae
Haemodoraceae, n. pi., the bloodwort family
(bot.) — ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr.
haemo-, and Gk. δώρον, 'gift', fr. I.-E. base
mdo-, 'to give', whence also L. donum, 'gift'. See
donation.

## haemodoraceous
haemodoraceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## hafT
hafT, п., a lagoon separated from the open sea
by a sandy bar, as esp. along the Baltic coast
of Eastern Germany. — G., fr. LG. haf, fr.
MLG. haf, 'sea', which is rel. to ΟΝ., Swed.
haf, Dan. hav, OFris. kef, OE. laef, which all
mean 'sea'. The primitive sense of these words
was 'the rising one'. They are rel. to heave and
to have, haven (qq.v.)

## hafiz
hafiz, п., a Mohammedan who knows the Koran
by heart. — Pers., fr. Arab, hafiz, 'watch, guard;
one who knows the Koran by heart', prop. part,
of hdfiza, 'he watched, kept, protected, learned
by heart', rel. to Heb. haphitz, 'he delighted in,
desired', hephetz, 'delight, pleasure, desire;
business matter', in Mishnaic Hebrew 'thing,
object' (lit. 'that in which one takes delight'),
Aram, hephtzd, 'thing, object'. Cp. Hephzibah.

## hafnium
hafnium, п., name of a rare element (chem.) —
ModL., coined by the Dutch chemist Dirk
Cosier (1889- ) and the Hungarian chemist
George de Hevesy (1885- ) in 1923 fr. Haf-
nia, the Latin name of Copenhagen. For the
ending see sun*, -ium.

## haft
haft, п., handle. — ME., fr. OE. hseft, rel. to ON.
hepti, Du. heft, hecht, OHG. hefti, MHG. hefte,
G. Heft, 'handle', lit. 'that which holds', fr.
Teut. base *haf-, whence also E. have, heave,
heavy (qq.v.) Cp. heft, n.
Derivative: haft, tr. v., to supply with a haft.

## haftarah
haftarah, n. — See haphtarah.

## hag
hag, п., a witch; a repulsive old woman. — ME.
hagge, hegge, fr. OE. hxgtesse, 'witch', rel. to
MDu. haghetisse, Du. heks, OHG. hagzusa,
hagazussa, hagzissa, MHG. hecse, hdxe, G.
Hexe, 'witch'. The first element of OE.
hsegtesse, etc., is rel. to OE. haga, hxg, OHG. hag,
'hedge'; the second element is rel. to Norw.
tysja, 'fairy; crippled woman', Gaul, dusius,
'demon', Co. dus, diz, 'devil', Lith. dvasia,
'spirit', OE. dust, 'dust', fr. I.-E. base *dhewes-,
"dhiis-, 'to fly about like dust, to smoke, be
scattered, vanish'. Accordingly, OE. hxg-tesse,
etc. orig. meant 'woman of the hedge'. For the
first element of these words see hedge and cp.
hagberry, hagfish, haggard, for the second see
thio- and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: hagg-ish, adj., hagg-ish-ly, adv.,
hagg-ish-ness, n.

## hag
hag, п., a notch. — ON. hogg, 'a cutting, hewing',
from the stem of hoggva, 'to cut, hew'. See hag,
'to hew'.

## hag
hag, tr. v., to hew, cut. — ME. haggen, of Scand.
origin. Gp. ON. hoggva, 'to cut, hew', which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:357 COLUMN:2 -->
is rel. to OE. hlawan, 'to cut, strike, hew'. See
hew and cp. haggis, haggle.

## Haganah
Haganah, п., defense force of Jewish settlers in
Palestine during the British mandate. After the
proclamation of independence it was
incorporated into the Army of Israel. — Heb. ha-
ghannd", lit. 'defence', verbal noun of heghgn, 'he
covered, defended', Hiph'il (= causative) of
ganan, of s.m., whence maghin, 'shield' (lit. 'that
which covers'), gan, gonna*, 'garden' (lit.
'enclosure'; for sense development cp. L. hortus,
E. garden); rel. to Akkad. gananu, 'to cover',
ganunu, 'chamber' (whence Aram. glnand,
'bridal chamber'), Arab, janna, 'he covered',
Aram. mgghinnd, Arab, mijann, 'shield', Aram.
ginna, ginn'thd, Syr. gann'tha (whence Arab.
janna", Ethiop. ganat), 'garden'.

## Hagar
Hagar, п., Sarah's Egyptian handmaid (Bible). —
Heb. Haghdr, prob. rel. to Arab, hdjara, 'he
fled, emigrated', hyra", 'flight, emigration'. See
hegira.

## hagberry
hagberry, also hackberry, n. — Of Scand. origin.
Cp. Dan. hxggebxr, ON. heggr, Swed. hagg,
'the bird cherry tree'. Dan hxggebxr, lit.
means 'hedge berry'. See hedge and berry and
cp. hag, 'witch'.

## hngfish
hngfish, п., a marine cyclostome (Myxine gluti-
nosa). — Compounded of hag, 'witch', and fish.

## haggadah
haggadah, haggada, п., ι) rabbinical teaching of
an edifying character; popular lecture; the
opposite of halakah; 2) the narrative of the Exodus
read at the Seder on the first two nights of
Passover; 3) the book containing this narrative and
the ritual of the Seder. — Talm. Heb. haggadha",
'narration, exposition', verbal n. of Heb. higgfdh,
'he narrated, related, declared, expounded', from
higgtdh hakkatubh, maggtdh hakkatabh ('the
verse expounded', resp. 'the verse expounds'),
the usual term introducing haggadic
interpretations. Higgfdh is a Hiph'il (= causative) form
of the Semitic base n-g-d, 'to rise', whence 'to be
conspicuous'. From this base are derived Heb.
neghedh, 'in front of, before, in sight of', ndghtdh,
'leader' (lit. 'he who is in front'), Aram.-Syr.
n'ghadh, 'he led; he dragged', Aram, naghddhd,
Syr. naghudhd 'leader, ruler', Arab, najada, 'he
conquered; was conspicuous', najd, 'high land',
najuda, najida, 'was courageous', najid, 'noble-
minded'. For the sense development of these
words cp. Heb. nasi, 'prince, chief, lit. 'one
lifted up', fr. nusd, 'he lifted'.
Derivatives: haggad-ic, haggad-ic-a], adjs., hag
gad-ist, п., haggad-ist-ic, adj.

## Haggai
Haggai, п., ι) a prophet who lived about 500
B.C.E., the tenth in the order of the Twelve
Prophets; 2) the Book of Haggai (Bible). —
Heb. Haggay (whence Gk. Άγγαϊος, L. Aggae-
us), lit. 'festal, born on a feast day', fr. Heb.
ftagh, 'a festival gathering, a feast', from the stem
of haghagh, 'he made a pilgrimage, celebrated a
feast', which is rel. to Syr. haggt, 'he made a
pilgrimage, celebrated a feast', Aram.-Syr.
haggd, 'a feast', Arab, hdjja, 'he went on a
pilgrimage'. Cp. hadj, hadji.

## haggard
haggard, n„ an untamed hawk; adj., hard to tame
(said of a hawk). — MF. (= F.) hagard, 'a
haggard', which is of Teut. origin and orig. meant
'(a bird) of the hedge', i.e. 'a wild, untameable
(bird)'. Cp. ME. hagger, 'wild; an untamed
hawk, haggard', and see hedge and -ard. Cp.
also hng, 'witch'.

## haggard
haggard, adj., harassed. — From prec. word.
The orig. meaning was 'wild-looking'.
Derivatives: haggard-ly, adv., haggard-ness, n.

## haggis
haggis, п., a Scottish dish made of the lungs,
heart, liver, etc., of a sheep or calf. — ME.
hagese, hageys, hagas, 'a kind of pudding', prob.
fr. haggen, 'to hew'. See hag, 'to hew'.

## haggle
haggle, tr. v, to mangle; intr. v., to bargain in a
mean way. — Freq. of hag, 'to cut' (q.v.) For
the ending see freq. sufT. -le. Cp. higgle.
Derivatives: haggle, п., haggl-er, n.

## hagl-
hagl-, form of hagio- before a vowel.

## hagiarchy
hagiarchy, п., government by men in holy orders.
— Compounded of hagi- and Gk. -αρχίϊ, 'rule',
fr. άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See -archy.

## hngio-
hngio-, before a vowel hagi-, combining form
meaning "holy, sacred'. — Gk. άγιο-, άγι-, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:357 COLUMN:3 -->
άγιος, 'holy, sacred', which is rel. to άζεσθαι
(for *άγιεσθαι), 'to stand in awe of, to revere',
άγος, 'sacrifice, expiation', άγίζειν, 'to hallow',
αγνός, 'holy, chaste', and prob. cogn. with OI.
yajati, 'reveres (a god) with sacrifices, worships',
yajas-, 'worship', yajnah, 'worship, sacrifice',
OPers. a-yadana 'temple'. Cp. the second
element in Trlsagion. Cp. also Yajna.

## hagiocracy
hagiocracy, п., government by persons considered
holy. — Compounded of hagio- and Gk.
-κρατίά, 'rule of, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power,
rule'. See -cracy.

## Hagiographa
Hagiographa, n. pi., the third and last division
of the Hebrew Bible. — L., fr. Gk. άγιόγραφα
(βιβλία), lit. 'sacredly written (books)'; see
hagio- and -graph. Since all the 3 parts of the
Hebrew Bible are sacred books (— kithbhi
haqqodesh in Hebrew), the word Hagiographa
denoting the third division of the Bible can only
be meant as an abbreviation of τα άλλα βιβλία
άγιογραφα, i.e. 'the other sacred books'. Cp. the
rendering of Hebrew k'thubhim (name of the 3rd
division of the Bible, lit. 'writings') by the
grandson of Sirach with the words τά άλλα
πάτρια βιβλία ('the other books of the fathers')
and τά λοιπά των βιβλίων ('the remaining books').
Derivatives: hagiographer (q.v.), hagio-graph-
ic, hagio-graph-ic-al, adjs.

## hagiographer
hagiographer, п., ι) a writer of any of the
Hagiographa; 2) a writer of lives of the saints. —
Formed with agential suff. -er fr. ML. hagio-
graphus, 'a writer of holy things'. See prec.
word.

## hagiography
hagiography, п., the saints' lives. — Compounded
of hagio- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graphy.

## hagiolater
hagiolater, п., a worshipper of saints. —
Compounded of hagio- and -later.

## hagioiatry
hagioiatry, п., the worship of saints. —
Compounded of hagio- and Gk. λατρεία, 'service,
worship'. See -latry.

## hagiology
hagiology, п., the study of the lives of the saints.
— Compounded of hagio- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: hagiolog-ic, hagiotog-ic-at, adjs.,
hagio/og-ist, n.

## hagioscope
hagioscope, п., an opening in a church to enable
the worshippers in the side aisle to see the altar.
Compounded of hagio- and Gk, -σκόπιον, fr.
σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scope.

## hagride
hagride, tr. v., to ride as a hag does, to oppress. —
Compounded of hag, 'witch', and ride; esp.
used in the pp. hagridden.

## ha ha
ha ha, interj. imitative of laughter or surprise.

## ha-ha
ha-ha, п., a sunk fence, usually visible only when
one is close to it. — F., prob. from the
interjection ha ha, expressing the surprise of iiim
who faces suddenly such a fence.

## haiduk
haiduk, heiduck, п., a brigand or bandit among
the Balkan Slavs; a Hungarian lackey. — G.
Heiduck, fr. Hung, hajduk, pi. of hajdu, but
mistaken for a singular. Hung, hajdu is prob.
a loan word fr. Turk, haidud, 'brigand'.

## haik
haik, haick, п., a piece of cloth worn by Arabs. —
Arab, hayk, fr. hdka, 'he wove'.

## hail
hail, п., small pellets or masses of ice. — ME.
hagel, hawel, hail, fr. OE. hagol, hxgl, 'hail', rel.
to OS., OHG. hagal, ΟΝ., Dan. hagl, Du.,
MHG., G. hagel, 'hail'. These words prob.
derive fr. I.-E. base *kaghlo-, "pebble', whence
also Gk. κάχληξ, 'round pebble'.
Derivative: hail-y, adj.

## bail
bail, intr. v., to shower down (said of hail); tr. v.,
to pour down like hail. — ME. hagelen, hawelen,

## hailen
hailen, fr. OE. hagalian, fr. hagol, 'hail'. See
prec. word.

## hail
hail, interj. — Short for original "be thou hall'.",

## fr. obsol. adj. hail
fr. obsol. adj. hail, 'sound, healthy', fr. ME.

## hail
hail, heil, of s.m., fr. ON. heill, 'whole, healthy'.
See whole and cp. words there referred to.

## Cp. also hale
Cp. also hale, 'healthy', and the second element
in wassail.
Derivatives: hail, to greet (q.v.), hail, п.,
greeting

## hail
hail, tr. and intr. v., to greet. — ME. hailen, 'to

## greet'
greet', lit. 'to say "hail", fr. hail, heil, interj. See

## hail
hail, interj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:358 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 331 | HALLUX -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:358 COLUMN:1 -->

## hailstone
hailstone, η. — ME., fr. OE. hagolstan, rel. to
ON. haglsteinn, Du. hagelsteen, MHC, G.
Hagelstein. See hail, 'pellets of ice', and stone.

## hair
hair, n. — ME. her, heer, hare, fr. OE. Air, rel.
to OS., ΟΝ., OHG., MHG. Mr, Dan. hor,
Swtd. hdr, OFris. her, Du., G. haar, 'hair'.
These words are cogn. with Lith. serys, 'bristle',
and with the second element in OI. kapucchala-,
'hair on the hind part of the head'. E. hair was
influenced in form by a confusion with ME.
haire, 'haircloth', fr. OF. (= F.)haire, fr. Frankish
*harja, which is rel. to OE. hire, OHG. hurra,
'haircloth', and further to OE. hSr, 'hair'.
Derivatives: hair-ed, hair-less, hair-like, hair-y,
adjs., hair-i-ness, n.

## hake
hake, п., any of several marine fishes of the genus
Merluccius. — ME. hake, related to OE. haca,
'hook', hacod, hseced, 'pike (fish)', OS. had,
MLG. hekel, OHG. hachil, hechit, MHG. hechit,
hecht, G. Hecht, of s.m., and to OE. hok, 'hook'.
See hook.

## hakeem
hakeem, hakim, п., in Mohammedan countries,
a physician. — Arab, hakim, lit. 'wise', from the
stem of hakuma, 'he was wise', whence also
hakam, 'judge', hikma", 'wisdom, science', hdk-
kama, 'he was a physician', (iukm, 'judgment,
sentence', rel. to Heb. hakham, 'he was wise',
hakhdm, 'skillful, learned, wise', hokhmd",
'wisdom', Aram.-Syr. hakham, 'he was wise'.
See hokhmah and cp. next word.

## hakenkreuz
hakenkreuz, п., swastika; used as the emblem of
Nazism. — G. Hakenkreuz, lit. 'hook-cross'. See
hook and crass, n.

## hakim
hakim, п., in Mohammedan countries, a judge,
ruler. — Arab, hakim, prop. part, of hakuma,
'he was wise'. See hakeem.

## halakah
halakah, also halachah, п., oral law; rule
prescribed by oral law (Jewish religion). — Mish-
naic Hebrew hulakha*, 'rule, practice, tradition',
lit. 'something to go by', fr. Heb. halakh, 'he
went', which is rel. to Aram, halakh, hakh, hal-
llkh, 'he went', Akkad. alaku, 'to go', Arab.
hdlaka (used euphemistically), 'he perished',
Heb. hilekh, 'traveler', hallkhd1*, *a going', ma-
hutdkh, 'a going', tahulnkha", 'procession'.

## halalcor
halalcor, halalcore, п., a person of the lowest
class, a scavenger (India). — Hind., fr. Arab.-
Pers. halal-khor, 'one to whom all food is
lawful', a hybrid coined fr. Arab, haldl, 'that which
is allowed or lawful', and Pers. khor, 'eating'.
Arab, balal derives fr. holla, 'he unknotted,
untied, undid', which is rel. to Heb. hillel, 'he
profaned', hehil, 'he began', Aram.-Syr. ballet,
abet, 'he profaned', Heb. hoi, 'profaneness,
commonness', baltla", 'far be it'.

## halation
halation, п., a term of photography. — Lit. 'a
halolike appearance', irregularly formed fr. halo
with suff. -ation.

## halherd
halherd, halbert, п., a kind of battle-ax.' — ME.
halberd, fr. MF. (= F.) hallebarde, fr. MHG.
helmbarte (whence G. Hettebarde), lit. 'an ax
with a long handle', fr. helm, halm, 'handle', and
barte (fr. OHG. barta), 'ax'. It. alabarda, Sp.
and Port, alabardo, 'halberd', are also borrowed
fr. MHG. helmbarte. See helm, 'handle', and
beard.

## halberdier
halberdier, п., soldier armed with a halberd. —
MF. (= F.) hallebardier, fr. hallebarde. See
prec. word and -ier.

## halcyon
halcyon, п., kingfisher. — L. alcyon, also halcyon,
fr. Gk. άλκυών, incorrectly spelled άλκυών,
'kingfisher', which is of uncertain origin. The form
άλκυών (with the rough spirit) arose from a
confusion with Gk. άλς, 'salt; sea'. L. alcedd,
'kingfisher', isa loan wordfr. Gk. aXxuov(with change
of Gk. suff. -ών to L. suff. -edo). Cp. next word.
Cp. also Aleedinidae.

## Halcyone
Halcyone, п., daughter of Aeolus, who, when
widowed, threw herself into the sea and became
a kingfisher. — L. Halcyone, Alcyone, fr. Gk.
'Αλκυόνη, fr. άλκυών. See prec. word.

## hale
hale, adj., sound, healthy. — ME. hale, hal, fr.
OE. hal, 'whole, uninjured, healthy', rel. to ON.
heill, of s.m. See whole and cp. hail, interj.
Derivative: hale-ness, n.

## hale
hale, tr. v., to haul. — ME. halien, halm. See
haul.

## Halenia
Halenia, п., a genus of plants of the gentian

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:358 COLUMN:2 -->
family (bol.) — ModL., named after the
German botanist Johann Halen. For the ending see
suff. -ia.

## Halesia
Halesia, п., a genus of plants of the storax family
(hot.) — ModL., named after the English
physiologist Stephen Hales (1677-1761). For
the ending see suff. -ia.

## half
half, n. — ME., fr. OE. healf. See half, adj.

## hnlf
hnlf, adj. — ME. half, fr. OE. healf, 'side, half,
rel. to ON. halfr, OS., OFris., MDu., Du. half,
Dan., Swed., hah, OHG., G. halb, MHG. halp,
Goth, halbs, 'half, and to the nouns OS. halba,
ON. halfa, MDu. halve, OHG. halba, MHG.
halbe, Goth halba, 'side'. The original meaning of
these words was '(something) divided'. They are
cogn. with OI. kjptafr, 'arranged', kalpate, 'is
arranged', kalpayati, 'arranges, allots', L. scal-
pere, 'to cut, carve, scrape'. See shelf, 'slab of
wood', and cp. words there referred to. The
original meaning of OE. healf was 'side'. This
meaning is still alive in behalf (q.v.) Cp. halve,
helve.
Derivative: half, adv.

## half joe
half joe, name of a Portuguese gold coin. — Short
for half Johannes, fr. Johannes, name of a gold
coin struck in honor of King Johannes V of
Portugal. Cp. Johannes.

## hali-
hali-, combining form meaning 'salt' or 'the sea'.
— Gk. άλι-, fr. ίίλς, gen. αλός (masc.), 'salt';
(fern.) 'sea'. See halieutic.

## Haliaeetus
Haliaeetus, п., a genus of eagles (ornithol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. άλιαίετος, άλιάετος, 'sea eagle9,
prob. 'osprey', which is compounded of άλς,
gen. αλός (fern.), 'sea' and αΐετός, αετός, 'eagle'.
See halieutic and aeto-.

## halibut
halibut, holibut, п., the largest species of flatfish.
— ME. halybuile, compounded of haly, 'holy',
and but, butte, 'flatfish' (cp. LG. hilligbutt, hille-
butt, Du. heilbot, G. Heilbutt);socalled because
usually eaten on holy days. See holy and butt,
'flatfish', and cp. turbot.

## Halicore
Halicore, n„ a genus of aquatic mammals, the
dugong (zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
όίλς, gen. αλός (fern.), 'sea', and κόρη, 'maiden'.
See halientic and Cora.

## halidom
halidom, п., a holy thing (obsol. or archaic). —
ME., fr. OE. haligdom, 'holiness, relic,
sanctuary', formed fr. halig, 'holy', with suff. -dom.
See holy and -dom.

## halieutic
halieutic, halieutical, adj., pertaining to fishing.
— L. halieuticus, fr. Gk. αλιευτικός, 'pertaining
to fishing', fr. άλιεΰειν, 'to fish', fr. αλς, gen.
αλός (fern.), 'sea', which stands for *sal- (cp.
Gk. £ξ, L. sex, 'six'; Gk. επτά, L. septem,
'seven', etc.), whence also L. sal, gen. satis,
'salt; sea'. See salt and cp. hali-, halo-, the first
element in Haliaeetus, Halicore, alurgite, and
the second element in aphthitalite, Enaliosauria.

## halieutics
halieutics, д., the art of fishing. — See prec. word
and -ics.

## haiiography
haiiography, п., description of the sea. —
Compounded of hali-, 'sea', and Gk. -γραφίϊ, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.

## Haliotis
Haliotis, п., a genus of univalve shells (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'ear of the sea', fr. Gk. άλς, gen.
αλός (fern.), 'sea', and ους, gen. ώτός, 'ear'; so
called because of the resemblance to the ear.
See halieutic and oto-.

## balipiankton
balipiankton, п., oceanic plankton. — ModL., fr.
Gk. άλίπλαγκτον, neut. of άλίπλαγκτος, 'sea-
wandering', which is compounded of δλς, gen.
αλός (fem.), 'sea', and πλαγκτός, 'wandering',
verbal adj. of πλάζειν, 'to wander'. See halieutic
and plankton.

## halite
halite, п., rock salt (mineral!) — Formed with
subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. άλς, gen. αλός (masc.),
'salt'. See halieutic.

## halitosis
halitosis, п., offensive breath. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. halitus, 'breath' (see next word), and
-osis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## halitus
halitus, п., breath, exhalation. — L. halitus,
'breath', rel. to halare, 'to breathe'. See exhale.

## hall
hall, n. — ME. halle, hal, fr. OE. heall, hall, rel.
to OS., OHG. halla, MHG., G. halle, Du. hal,
ON. holl, 'hall', and to OE. hell, Goth, halja,'
'hell', fr. I.-E. base "icel-, 'to hide, conceal',
whence also OE., OS., OHG. helan, OFris. hela,
MDu. helen, Du. (ver)helen, MHG. heln, G.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:358 COLUMN:3 -->
hehlen, 'to conceal', OI. sola, 'hut, house, hall,
stable', salah, 'hedge, enclosure, wall', Gk. καλιά,
'hut, nest', καλύβη, 'hut, cabin', καλύπτειν, 'to
cover, hide, conceal', Olr.ci/i'fe,'cellar, magazine',
L. cella, 'store room, granary; cell', celare, 'to
hide, conceal', occulere, 'to cover, conceal'. See
cell and words there referred to and cp. esp.
hell, Valhalla.

## hallah
hallah, п., ι) a kind of cake used in offerings;
2) priest's share of the dough; 3) twisted bread
used at the Sabbath meals (Jewish religion). —
Heb. halldh, 'cake',prob. meaning lit. 'perforated
(cake)', fr. billet, Pi'el of halal, 'he pierced,
perforated', whence also hallon, 'window', hal/l,
'pipe', halal, 'pierced; slain'; rel. to Syr. halt!,
'hollow', haloid, 'a cave', Arab, khdlla, 'he
perforated', Ethiop. hallat, 'a (hollow) reed'.

## hallel
hallel, п., psalm of praise especially applied 1) to
the group of Psalms 113-118, called the Egyptian
Hallel; 2) to Psalm 136, called the Great Hallel.
— Heb. halUl, 'praise, song of praise', prop. inf.
used as a noun fr. hillil, 'he praised', whence the
nouns hill&l, mahuldl, t'hitld", 'praise'; rel. to
Aram.-Syr. hallil, 'he praised', Arab, halla, 'he
shouted', hallala, ahalla, 'he praised (in
worship)', Aram, hilluld, 'marriage song', Akkad.
alalu, 'to shout for joy'. All these words are of
imitative origin, with the primary sense 'to trill'.
Cp. next word. Cp. also Hillel, Tehillim.

## hallelujah
hallelujah, halleluia, interj. and n. — Heb. hall'lu-
ydh, 'praise ye the Lord', compounded ot
hall'la, pi. imper. of hillel, 'he praised', and the
shortened form of the Tetragrammaton. See
prec. word and Elijah and cp. alleluia.

## halliard
halliard, n. — See halyard.

## halimoot
halimoot, п., the court of the lord of a manor
(English hist.) — ME. halimot, lit. 'hall
meeting', fr. hal, 'hall', and -imot, fr. OE. gemot,
'meeting'. See hall and moot, 'meeting', and cp.
gemot, witenagemot.

## ballo
ballo, halloa, interj., n. and intr. and tr. v. —
Variants of hollo.

## hnlloo
hnlloo, tr. and intr. v., to incite dogs by shouting
'halloo'. — ME. halowen, fr. OF. halloer, which
is of imitative origin.
Derivatives: halloo, interj. and n.

## hallow
hallow, п., now only in All-hallows. — OE. halga,
'a holy person', fr. halig, 'holy'. See holy and
cp. Halloween.

## hallow
hallow, tr. v. — ME. halowen, fr. OE. hdlgian,
'to hallow', fr. halig, 'holy'. Cp. OS. helagdn
(fr. helag), OHG. heitagdn (fr. heilag), and see
holy.

## hnllow
hnllow, v. — A var. of halloo.

## Halloween
Halloween, n. — Shortened tr. all hallow e'en.
See hallow, n„ and even, 'evening'.

## Hallowmas
Hallowmas, п., the Church festival of All-
hallows. — Shortened fr. All hallow mass. See
hallow, п., and mass.

## Hallstatt
Hallstatt, adj., pertaining to the period of
prehistoric civilization in Euiope, during wiiich
iron was introduced. — From Hallstatt, a
village in Austria, where various implements
belonging to this period were found.

## hallucinate
hallucinate, tr. v., to affect with visions. — L.
hallucinatus, pp. of hallucinari, more correctly
a/ucindrt, 'to wander in mind, dream', borrowed
fr. Gk. άλ-υειν, Att. άλ-υειν, 'to wander in
mind', which is rel. to άλ-η, 'ceaseless roaming',
άλ-ϊσθαι, άλ-αίνειν, 'to wander about', αλ-
εός, ήλ-εός, 'distraught, foolish, roaming
about', άλ-ήτης, 'wanderer, vagabond'. AH these
words derive fr. I.-E. base *dl-, 'to wander
about', whence also Lett, al-uot, 'to wander
about'. Cp. Alastor, aleatory, Aleochara. Cp.
also amble. For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.
The ending -cinar'i in aiucinan is prob. due to
the influence of vati-cinari, 'to prophesy', used
also in the meaning 'to rave'.
Derivatives: hallucination (q.v.), hallucinat-ive,
hallucinat-ory, adjs.

## hallucination
hallucination, п., a vision without reality. — L.
halliicinatio, gen. -onis, 'a wandering of mind,
dreaminess', fr. hallucinatus, pp. of hallucinari.
See prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: hallucination-al, adj.

## hallux
hallux, the first digit on the hind leg of a mammal;
the great toe of man; the hind toe of birds (anal.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:359 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HALM | 332 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:359 COLUMN:1 -->
— Medical L., a blend of L. allux and hallus,
which both mean 'the great toe'. — These Latin
words prob. stand for original *hal(o)-doik-s,
and lit. mean 'the great digit'. The first element
of this compound is cogn. with OSlav. golemu,
'great, high', W. gallu, Co. gatlos, 'power'; the
second element is rel. to L. digitus, 'finger',
whence digit (q.v.) See J.S.Schmidt, Die Plural-
bildungen der indogermanischen Neutra,
Weimar, (889, p. 183.
Derivative: halluc-al, adj.

## halm
halm, n. — See haulm.

## haima
haima, п., a game played on a board of 256
squares, with pieces moved or jumped from one
corner to the opposite. — Gk. άλμα, 'a leap',
from the stem of άλλεσθαι, 'to leap', which is
cogn. with L.salire, to leap'. See salient and-ma.

## halo
halo, п., ι) a circle of light surrounding the sun
or the moon; 2) radiance surrounding a head
— F., fr. L. halo, ace. of holds, fr. Gk. άλως,
'threshing floor; disk of the sun or of the moon',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. halation,
Haloa.
Derivative: halo-ed, adj.

## halo-
halo-, combining form meaning 1) 'salt; 2) sea'.
— Gk. άλο-, fr. άλς, gen. αλός (masc), 'salt';
(fern.) 'sea'. See halieutic.

## Haloa
Haloa, п., ancient Greek festival of harvest in
honor 01 Demeter. — Gk. ΑΛωα or Άλωα,
prop, 'threshing festival', fr. άλως, 'threshing
floor'. See halo.

## talogen
talogen, п., any of the four chemical elements
chlorine, bromine, iodine, fluorine. — Lit. 'salt-
producer', coined by the Swedish chemist Baron
Jons Jakob flerzelius (1779-1848,1 fr. Gk. άλς,
gen. άλύς (masc), 'salt', and yevvav, 'to
produce*. *эее halo- and -gen.
Derivative: halogen-ous, adj.
~<aloid, adj., resembling salt. — Compounded of
haio- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -oid.
4a'oni;mc>, п., divination by means of salt. —
Compounded of haio- and Gk. μαντεία, Oracle,
divination'. See -mancy.

## lialometer
lialometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
planes and angles of salt crystals. — Compound
ed of halo- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## halophilous
halophilous, adj., growing in salt water (said of
plants and animals). — Lit. 'salt-loving';
compounded of halo- and Gk. -φίλος, fr. φίλος,
friend'. See -pliilous.

## halophyte
halophyte, п., a plant growing naturally in a soil
impregnated with salt. — Compounded of halo-
and Gk. φυτόν, 'plant'. See -phyte.

## Haloragidaceae
Haloragidaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (hoi.)
— Λ ModL. hybrid formed with suff. -aceae fr.
halo- and Gk. ριίξ, gen. ραγός, 'berry', which is
cogn. with L. racemus, 'cluster of grapes'. See
raceme.

## haloragidaceous
haloragidaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-acccms.

## halse
halse, tr. v. (obsol.), 1) to conjure; 2) to greet.
— ME. halsen, '10.adjure, conjure; to greet',
fr. OE. halsian, 'to adjure, observe omens,
exorcise', fr. hal, 'whole, healthy'. Cp. OHG.
heilison, 'to adjure, predict', ON. heilsa, 'to
greet', and see hail, 'to greet'.

## halt
halt, adj., lame. — ME. halt, fr. OE. healt, halt,
rel. to OS., OFris. halt, ON. haltr, OHG. hah,
Goth, halts, 'lame', and cogn. with Russ. kol-
dyka, 'lame', koldykat', 'to limp, go lame', fr.
I.-E. *qeld-d-, enlargement of base *qel(a)-, 'to
break', whence Gk. χόλος, "docked, curtailed',
κολοβός, of s.m., lit. 'broken'. See holt, 'small
wood', and cp. words there referred to.

## halt
halt, intr. v., to be lame. — ME. halten, fr. OE.
healtian, haltian, fr. healt, halt, 'lame'. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: halt, п., lameness, halt-ing, adj.,
halt-ing-ly, adv., halt-ing-ness, n.

## halt
halt, п., stoppage. — F. halle, fr. G. Halt, in halt-
machen, where halt is prop, the imper. of
halten, 'to stop, halt', a word rel. to E. hold (q.v.)

## halt
halt, intr. v., to stop; tr. v., to make (troops)
halt. — Shortened fr. make halt, the literal
rendering of G. haltmachen. See prec. word.

## halter
halter, п., a rope for leading a horse. — ME. helf-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:359 COLUMN:2 -->
ter, helter, halter, fr. OE. hxlfter, hxlftre, rel. to
MDu. halfter, halchter. Du. holster. OS. haliftra.
OHG. halftra, MHG., G. halfter, 'halter', and
to OE. he/та, 'rudder'. See helm, 'tiller*.

## halukkah
halukkah, п., support of the Jewish poor of the
Holy Land with funds collected abroad. —
Heb. haluqqah, 'division, distribution', from the
stem of haldq, 'he divided, apportioned,
assigned', whence also heleq, helqa", 'part,
portion', mahdloqeth, 'division, course' (in Mishnaic
Hebrew: 'difference of opinion, controversy'),
re], to Aram, hdlaq, 'he divided', hdldq, 'field',
helqa, hulqa, 'portion', Arab, hdlaqa, 'he
measured'.

## halutz
halutz, alsa chalutz, fern, halutzah, chalntzah, п.,
Jewish pioneer immigrant to Israel. — Heb.
halutz, passive partic. of halatz, 'he equipped
for war', rel. to Syr. hdlitza, 'energetic,
vigorous', Akkad. halsu, 'fortification'.

## halve
halve, tr. v. — ME. halven, fr. half. See half.

## halyard
halyard, halliard, haulyard, п., a rope for hoisting
sails. — ME. holier, hallyer, lit. 'that which
hales or hauls'. See haul. The ending in hat-yard
is due to a confusion with the noun yard; cp.
lanyard.

## ham
ham, п., the inner or hinder part of the knee; the
thigh of an animal (anat.) — ME. hamme, fr.
OE. Itamm, rel. to ON. horn, MLG., MDu.,
MHG., dial. G. hamme, Du. ham, OHG. hamma,
and cogn. with Gk. κνήμη, 'part between knee
and ankle', Olr. cnaim, 'bone'. Cp. the first
element in hamshackle. Cp. also cnemial.
Derivative: hamm-y, adj.

## ham
ham, п., a hamlet, village, town; used as a suff.
in place names (now dial. Engl.) — OE. ham,
'dwelling, home'. See home.

## hama-
hama-, combining form meaning together with;
at the same time with. — Gk. άμα,' together
with'. See same.

## hamadryad
hamadryad, п., a wood nymph in Greek
mythology. — L. Hamadryas, gen. -adis, fr. Gk.
Άμαδρυάς, chiefly in pi. Άμαδρυάδες,
'hamadryads', i.e. 'nymphs whose life depended on
that of particular trees', lit. 'those being
together with trees', fr. άμα, 'together with', and
δρυάς, gen. δρυάδος, 'nymph whose life
depended on that of her tree', fr. δρυς, gen. δρυός,
'oak, tree'. See hama- and dryad.

## hamal
hamal, also hammal, hummaul, п., a burden bearer
in Turkey. — Arab, hammal, 'porter', fr. hd-
mala, 'he carried'.

## Hamamelidaceae
Hamamelidaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (hot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Hamamelis with suff.
-accae.

## hamamelidaceous
hamamelidaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Hamamelis
Hamamelis, п., a genus of plants (bol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. άμαμηλίς, 'a kind of medlar', which is
compounded of άμα (see hama-) and μήλον,
'apple, fruit'. See Malus, 'the genus of apple
trees'.

## hamartiology
hamartiology, п., that part of theology which
deals with sin. — Compounded of Gk.
αμαρτία, 'sin', and -λογία. The first element derives
from the stem of άμαρτάνειν, 'to miss the mark,
fail of one's purpose, err, sin', which is of
uncertain origin (for sense development cp. Heb.
hdtd' 'he sinned', prop, 'he missed the mark');
cp. Nemertinea. The second element comes fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'; see -logy.

## hamburger
hamburger, п., ι) ground beef; 2) cooked patty
of ground beef; 3) sandwich made of such a
patty. — Short for Hamburger steak; named
after Hamburg in Germany.

## hame
hame, п., either of the two curved pieces lying
round the collar of a horse. — ME. hame, fr.
OE. hama, 'cover, skin', rel. to MDu. hamme,
Du. Imam, 'collar of a horse', ON. hamr, 'skin,
covering', OHG. hamo, of s.m., OHG. hemidi,
'shirt', and cogn. with OI. sdmulydh, 'woolen
shirt'; fr. I.-E. base *kam-, *kem-, 'to cover'.
See henven and cp. chemise.

## hamesucken
hamesucken, п., assaulting of a person in his own
dwelling house. — ME. hamsoken, fr. OE. ham-
socn, compounded of ham, 'home', and socn,
'attack', which is rel. to ON. sokn, of s.m., and
to OE. secan, 'to seek; to try to get, attack'. Cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:359 COLUMN:3 -->
OFris. hamsekenge, 'attack on a house', G.
Heimsuchung, 'visitation', and see home and
seek.

## hametz
hametz, also chametz, п., leavened food;
forbidden during Passover (Jewish religion). —
Heb. hametz, 'that which is leavened', from the
stem of the verb hametz, 'was sour, was
leavened', which is rel. to Aram, hama', of s.m.
(passive part. hamia', 'leavened'), Arab, hdmuda,
'was sour'.

## Hamite
Hamite, n. — Lit. a descendant of Ham', formed
with subst. suff. -ite from the name Ham, fr.
Heb. Ham, son of Noah.
Derivative: Hamit-ic, adj.

## Hamites
Hamites, п., a genus of extinct cephalopods
(paleontol.) — ModL., fr. L. hamus, 'hook'. See
hamulus and subst. suff. -ite.

## hamlet
hamlet, п., a small village. — ME. hamelet, fr.
MF. hamelet, dimin. of hamel (whence F. ha-
meau), itself a dimin. of OF. ham, fr. Frankish
*haim, 'home', which is rel.. to OHG. heim, OE.
ham, 'home'. See home and the dimin. suffixes.
-el and -et.

## hammal
hammal, n. — See hamal.

## hammam
hammam, п., a Turkish bath. — Arab, hammam,
'bath', fr. hamma, 'became hot, was warm',
which is rel. to Heb. ham, Aram.-Syr. ham,
hamdm, of s.m., Heb. horn, 'heat', ham, 'hot',
hamma", 'heat; sun' (poet.), hamman, 'sun
pillar', Akkad. emmu, 'hot', ummu, 'heat'.

## hammer
hammer, n. — ME. hamur, hamer, fr. OE. hamor,
hamer, rel. to OS., OHG. hamur, hamar, ON.
hamarr, Dan. hammer, Swed. hammare, MDu.,
Du., MHG. hamer, G. Hammer, 'hammer',
orig. 'stone hammer'; cogn. with OI. asman-,
'stone; rock; sky', Avestic asman-, of s.m., Gk.
άκμων, '(stone) anvil', Lith. akmuo, OSlav.
kamv. 'stone'. All these words are traceable to
I.-E. base *αί-, 'sharp, pointed'. See acrid and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: hammer, tr. and intr. v., hammer-ed,
adj., hammer-er, п., hammer-ing, n. and adj.

## hammock
hammock, п., a swinging bed or couch, usually
made of canvas. — Sp. hamaca (whence also
F. hamac), of Caribbean origin. Cp. Yukuna
hamaca, Taino amaca, 'net for sleeping*.

## hammock
hammock, n. — A var. of hummock.

## hamose
hamose, hamous, adj., hooked. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ose, resp. -ous, fr. L. hamus, 'hook'.
See hamulus.

## haraotzi
haraotzi, п., name of the * ".nediction over bread
(Jewish liturgy). — Heb. hammdtzt, 'he who
brings forth'; so called from the first of the
concluding words of the benediction. The word
hammdtzt is formed from the article ha-, 'the',
and mdtzi, 'bringing forth', part. Hiph'il of
ydtzd, 'he went out', for whose etymology see
Asia.

## hamper
hamper, tr. v., to impede — ME. hampren, of
uncertain origin.

## hamper
hamper, п., things that are important for a ship
but are in the way at certain times. — Fr.
hamper, 'to impede'.

## hnmper
hnmper, п., a large basket. — A var. of hanaper.
Derivative: hamper, tr. v., to put into a hamper.

## hamshackle
hamshackle, tr. v., to fasten (an animal) by
binding the head to a foreleg; hence, to bind, to
impede. — The orig. meaning prob. was 'to tie by
the hams or legs'. See ham, 'thigh', and shackle.

## hnmster
hnmster, п., a ratlike rodent. — G., fr. MHG., fr.
OHG. hamustro (cp. OS. hamustra), fr. OSlav.
chomistorH; for the first element cp. Russ.
chomtak, 'hamster', for the second cp. Lith.
staras, of s.m.

## hamstring
hamstring, n. — Compounded of ham, 'thigh',
and string, n.
Derivative: hamstring, tr. v.

## hamulus
hamulus, п., a process resembling a small hook
(anat.) — L. hamulus, 'a small hook', dimin. of
hdmus, 'hook', which is prob. cogn. with Gk.
χαμός (Hesychius), 'hooked, crooked'. Cp.
Hamites, hamose.

## hamza
hamza, hamzah, п., the sign of the glottal stop (')
in Arabic grammar. — Arab, hamza",
'compression' (viz. of the upper part of the
windpipe), fr. hdmaza, 'he compressed'.
hanap. п., a medieval goblet. — F. See next word.

## hanaper
hanaper, п., a case for holding documents (or-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:360 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 333 | HAPLDLDGY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:360 COLUMN:1 -->
chaic). — OF. hanapier, 'a basket for holding
a goblet', fr. hanap, 'gobH', fr. Frankish *hnap
(whence also ML. hanappus, OProvenc. enap,
It. nappo), which is rel. to OE. hnxpp, OS.
hnapp, ON. hnappr, MLG., MDu., Du. nap,
OHG. hnapf, MHG., G. napf, 'cup, bowl'. Cp.
prec. word and hamper, 'a large basket'. The
first a in OF. hanap is an auxiliary vowel, which
arose from the tendency of facilitating the
pronunciation of the consonants hn- at the
beginning of the word. Cp. harangue.

## hnnce
hnnce, п., the haunch of an arch. — Prob. fr.
AF. haunct>, corresponding to OF. hauce (F.
hausse), 'a raising, rise', fr. haucer (F. hausser),
'to raise'. See enhance.

## hancockite
hancockite, п., a complex silicate containing
aluminum, calcium, iron, lead and other metals
(mineral.) — Named after E. P. Hancock of
Burlington, New Jersey. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## hand
hand, n. — ME., fr. OE. hand, hond, rel. to OS.,
Swed., OFris., Du., G., hand, ON. hond, Dan.
haand, MDu., OHG., MHG. hant, Goth, han-
dus, 'hand'. These words prob. stand in gra-
dational relationship to OE. hentan, 'to try to
seize, attack, seize', ON. henda, 'to grasp', Goth.
-hinpan (used only in compounds), 'to seize',
and orig. meant 'the grasper'. Cp. hunt and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: hand, tr. v., hand-ed, adj., handle
(q.v.), handy (q.v.)

## handcuff
handcuff, n. — Compounded of hand and cuff, n.
Cp. OE. hondcops, 'a pair of handcuffs'.

## handful
handful, adj. — ME., fr. OE. handful/. See hand
and -ful.

## handgrip
handgrip, n. — ME., fr. OE. handgripe, 'a grasp
of the hand'. See hand and grip.

## handicap
handicap, n. — For hand in cap, orig. a kind of
lottery game, in which the forfeit money was
held in the hand in a cap.
Derivatives: handicap, tr. v., handicapp-er, n.

## handicraft
handicraft, n. — Altered (on analogy of
handiwork) fr. handcraft, fr. OE. handcrxft, 'skill of
the hand, handicraft'. See hand and craft.

## handiwork
handiwork, n. — ME. handiwerk, fr. OE. hand-
geweorc, compounded of hand and geweorc,
'work* (in a collective sense), fr. weorc, 'work'
(see hand and work); the ί in handiwork is the
regular English equivalent of OE. ge-\ see y-.

## handkerchief
handkerchief, n. — Compounded of band and
kerchief. Etymologically the word contains a
contradiction, since kerchief denotes a covering
for the head, fr. OF. couvrechef couvrechief, lit.
'cover-head'. Cp. neckerchief.

## handle
handle, tr. v. — ME. handlen, fr. OE. handlian,
'to touch with the hands; to handle; to treat',
rel. to ON. hondla, 'to seize, capture; to treat',
Dan. handle, 'to trade, deal; to act', Swed.
handla, 'to trade', OFris. handelia, hondelia, 'to
seize, handle', Du. handelen, 'to trade, deal;
to act', OHG. hantalon, 'to touch with the
hands', MHG., G. handeln, 'to bargain, trade,
deal; to act'. See hand and verbal suff. -le.

## handle
handle, n. — ME. handele, fr. OE. handle; lit.
'that which is held by the hand', fr. hand. See
hand and instrumental suff. -le.

## handless
handless, adj. — ME. handles. See hand and
-less.

## handling
handling, n. — ME. handlinge, fr. OE. handlung,
formed fr. handlian with suff. -ung. See handle,
v., and -ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## handsel
handsel, hansel, п., a gift made as a token of luck
(archaic). — ME. handsale, hansel, it. ON.
handsal, 'the1 closing of a bargain by joining
hands', lit. 'hand sale'. Cp. Dan. handsel, Swed.
handsel, and see hand and sale.

## handsome
handsome, adj. — ME. handsom, lit. 'easy to
handle, treatable', compounded of hand and
ist -some. Cp. MDu. handsaem (Du. handzaam),
'treatable', which is the exact etymological
equivalent of E. handsome.
Derivatives: handsome-ty, adv.,
handsomeness, n.

## handy
handy, adj. — The original meaning was 'done
by the hand'; formed fr. hand with suff. -y
(representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: handi-ly, adv., handi-ness, n.

## hang
hang, tr. and intr. v. — Prop, a blend of three

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:360 COLUMN:2 -->
related verbs: ι) ME. hon, fr. OE. Ηδη (for
*hohan), tr. v., to cause to hang; to execute by
hanging'; rel. to OS., OHG., Goth, hahan, tr.
verbs, MHG. hahen, tr. and intr. v.; 2) ME.
hangen, hongen, fr. OE. hangian, intr. and tr. v.;
rel. to OS. hangon, ON. hanga, OFris. hangia,
hongia, OHG. hangen, MHG. hangen, G.
hangen, hangen, intr. verbs, Dan. hxnge, Swed.
hanga, Du. hangen, intr. and tr. verbs; 3) ME.
hengen, hingen, fr. ON. hengja, 'to cause to
hang', causative of hanga; rel. to OHG., MHG.
hengen, G. hangen, tr. verbs. All these words
derive fr. Teut. *hanhan, corresponding to I.-E.
base *kenq-, *konq-, 'to waver, be in suspense',
whence Hitt. gang-, kank-, 'to hang', ΟΙ. ίάή-
kate~, 'wavers', L. cunctari, 'to delay'. Cp.jcunc-
tation. Cp. also hangar, hank, hanker, hinge.
Derivatives: hang, п., hang-er, п., hang-ing, n.
and adj.

## hangar
hangar, п., a shed for airplanes and airships. —
F., 'shed', prob. cogn. with ML. angarium, 'a
shed for shoeing horses', and ult. traceable to
OHG. hangian, 'to hang'; see hang.
Accordingly hangar orig. denoted a place where horses
were suspended for the sake of being shod. See
Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 301 s.v. hangar.

## hanguail
hanguail, n. — Altered fr. aguail. Folk etymology
explained this word as the compound of hang
and nail.

## hanif
hanif, п., a faithful Moslem. — Arab, hanlf fr.
Aram. hdnSph, 'hypocrite, heathen, heretic',
which is rel. to Heb. haneph (verb), 'he was
wicked', helfintph, 'he polluted' (in Mishnaic
Hebrew: 'he was hypocritical, he flattered'),
hdneph (adj.), 'wicked, profane, impious', hu-
nuppd", 'profaneness, wickedness, impiety', Ak-
kad. hanpu, 'ruthlessness', hanapu, 'to exercise
ruthlessness toward'.

## hank
hank, п., a coil or skein of yarn. — Prob. of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. honk, 'coil, hank',
hanki, 'hasp, clasp', Swed. hanka, 'to tie up',
Dan. hank, 'handle', which are rel. to MLG.
hank, 'handle', OHG., MHG. henken, 'to hang'
(tr.), whence G. Henkel, 'handle'. OHG., MHG.
henken is a collateral form of hengen. (G.
hangen and henken are differentiated in sense; the
former means 'to cause to hang, to hang', the
latter, 'to execute by hanging'). See hang.

## hank
hank, tr. v., to form into hanks. — ME. hanken,
fr. ON. hanka, 'to coil', fr. honk, 'coil'. See
hank, n.

## hanker
hanker, intr. v., to long for or after. — Flem.
hankeren, 'to long for', rel. to Du. honkeren,
hunkeren, intensive and freq. of hangen, 'to
hang'. See hang.
Derivatives: hanker, п., hanker-er, п.,
hankering, verbal п., hanker-ing-ly, adv.

## hanky-panky
hanky-panky, п., jugglery, hocus-pocus. —
Coined on analogy of hokey-pokey (q.v.)

## Hannah
Hannah, 1) fern. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the mother
of the prophet Samuel. — Heb. Ηαηηά", lit.
'graciousness', from the stem of hanan, 'he was
gracious, showed favor', whence also hen,
'favor, grace', hinnam, 'for nothing,
gratuitously', hannan, 'gracious', t'hinna", tahanan,
'supplication for favor'; rel. to Aram, hanan, Syr.
han, Arab, hdnna, 'was favorable, merciful',
Akkad. jihnanuni, 'he has mercy on me', jenni-
nunu, 'he has mercy on us'. Cp. the first
element in the Punic PN. Hannibha'al, 'Hannibal',
lit. 'my favor is with Baal'. Cp. also Ann, Jane,
Jenny, Joanna, John.

## Hansard
Hansard, п., official reports of the Parliament at
Westminster. — So called fr. Luke Hansard
(1752-1828) and his descendants, printers of
these reports.
Derivative: Hansard-ize, tr. v., to confront (a
member of Parliament) with his former
statements as recorded in Hansard.

## Hansa
Hansa, п., medieval guild of merchants. — MF.
hanse, fr. MLG. hanse, 'merchants' guild', fr.
OHG. hansa, 'troop of warriors', which is rel.
to Goth, hansa, 'troop, company, multitude',
OE. Ms, 'attendants, retinue'. Finn, kansa,
'people, society', Russ.-Karelian kania,
'synagogue' are Teut. loan words.

## Hanscatlc
Hanscatlc, adj., pertaining to the Hansa. — ML.
Hanseaticus. See prec. word and -atic. ,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:360 COLUMN:3 -->

## hansom
hansom, п., also hansom cab, a light, covered
hackney carriage. — Named after its inventor
Joseph Aloysius Hansom (1803-82), a famous
English architect.

## Hanukkah
Hanukkah, also Chanukkah, п., the Feast of
Dedication (Jewish religion). — Heb. hanukkah,
'dedication', consecration', fr. handkh, 'he
dedicated, consecrated, trained up', which is
denominated fr. hekh (for *hink), 'palate', and
orig. meant 'to rub the palate of a child with
chewed dates'. Cp. Arab, hanak, 'palate'
(whence hannaka, 'he rubbed the palate of a
child', kanaka, 'he taught, instructed'), which
is rel. to Heb. hekh (see above). Heb. hanlkh,
'trained, experienced', Mishnaic Heb. hinnekh,
'he dedicated, inaugurated; he accustomed' (in
ModHeb. 'he brought up, educated'), hin-
nakh, 'inauguration; accustoming' (in ModHeb.
'education'), are derivatives of handkh. Cp.
Enoch.

## hap
hap, п., chance. — ME. happe, hap, fr. ON. happ,
'good luck', which is rel. to OE. gehsep, 'fit,
convenient', Swed. hampa sig, 'to occur, happen',
and cogn. with OSlav. kobu, 'fate, foreboding,
omen', Olr. cob, 'victory'. Cp. happy, perhaps.

## hap
hap, intr. v., to happen. — ME. happen, fr. hap,
'chance'. See prec. word and cp. happen.

## hap
hap, tr. v., to snap, seize (obsol.) — F. happer, a
Teut. loan word of imitative origin. Cp. Du.
happen,1 to snap; to bite', G. Happen,'& mouthful'.

## hapax legomenon
hapax legomenon, a word occurring only once. —
Gk. άπαξ λεγόμενον, 'once said'. Gk. όί-παξ,
'once', is a compound word whose first element
corresponds to I.-E. *sm-, 'one'; the second is
rel. to Gk. ττηγνύνοα, 'to make firm or fast*, and
cogn. with L. pangere, Ίο join, make firm'; see
haplo- and pact. Gk. λεγόμενον is neut. pass
pres. part, of λέγειν, 'to say'; see lecture. For
the Greek pass. suff. -μένος see alumnus and cp.
words there referred to.

## haphazard
haphazard, n. — Compounded of hap, 'chance',
and hazard.
Derivatives: haphazard, adj., haphazard-ly, adv.,
haphazard-ness, n.

## haphtarah
haphtarah, also spelled haftarah, п., a portion o!
the Prophets read in the synagogue, immediately
after the reading of the Torah, on Sabbaths,
feasts and fasts. — Mishnaic Heb. haphtdrah,
lit. 'conclusion', short for haptharah benabht\
'conclusion with a prophet(ic portionV, verbal
noun of hiphtlr. 'he concluded', also 'discarded,
dismissed', Hiph'il of Bibi. Heb. paiar, 'he broke
through, split, separated, removed' (in Mishnaic
Hebrew: 'he discharged, acquitted; he
exempted'), rel. to Arab, fatara, 'he cleft, split; he
created', Ethiop. fatara, 'he created', Aram.-
Syr. petar, 'he departed', Akkad. patdru, 'to
break through', iptiru, 'ransom'.

## hapless
hapless, adj. — Formed with suff. -less fr. hap,
'chance' (taken in the now obsol. sense 'good
luck').
Derivatives: hapless-ly, adv., hapiess-ness, n.

## haplo-
haplo-, combining form meaning 'simple, single,
simply, once'. — Fr. Gk. άπλόος, άπλοϋς,
'simple, single', compounded of ά- (fr. I.-E.
*sm-), 'one, together', and -πλό-ας, '-fold',
which is cogn. with L. -plus, -plex, of s.m. For
the first element see same and cp. words there
referred to; for the second see ply, 'to bend',
and cp. -fold. Cp. aplome, Aplopappus, hapax
legomenon, hexapla, tetrapia.

## baplography
baplography, п., copyist's error consisting in
writing only once a letter or letters that should
have been written twice. — Compounded of
haplo- and Gk. -γραφίί, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graphy.

## haplology
haplology, п., contraction of a word through the
omission of one of two adjacent similar syllab
les. — Compounded of haplo- and Gk. -λογίϊ,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
-logy. The following words owe their form to
haplology : amphora, Anthrenus, Artamus, calamint,
calamitous, cardamom, England, Erysiphe, fardel,
'fourth part', fastidious, fibula, formic, formi-
cide, gratulate, Gymnotus, hirundine, homily,
-itous, Lentibulariaceae, limitrophe, megaron,
mineralogy, monomial, nuncio, onomancy, paci-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:361 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HAPLY | 334 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:361 COLUMN:1 -->
fism, pacifist, palmistry, procuress, pulmotor,
quercitron, stipend, surgery, symbofogy, Tagetes,
tragicomedy, viper, volumeter.

## haply
haply, adv., by chance (archaic). — Formed fr.
hap, 'chance', with adv. suff, -ly.

## happen
happen, intr. v. — ME. happenen, hapcnen, hap-
nen, fr. happen, 'to happen'. See hap, 'to
happen', and verbal suff. -en.
Derivative: happen-ing, n.

## happy
happy, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -y fr. hap,
'chance' (taken in the now obsol. sense 'good
luck').
Derivatives: happi-h, adv., happi-ness, n.

## Hapsburg
Hapsburg, п., also Habsburg. — G. Habsburg,
from the castle of Habsburg or Habichtsbutg on
the Aar in Switzerland, lit. 'hawk's castle'. See
hawk and burgh.

## hapteron
hapteron, п., a special organ by which certain
plants are fixed to rocks (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. όίπτειν, 'to touch, fasten'. See hapto-.

## haptic
haptic, pertaining to the sense of touch. — Gk.
άπτικός, 'able to seize or touch', fr. ά-τός,
'tangible', fr. ϊπτειν, 'to touch, fasten". See
hapto-.

## hapto-
hapto-, combining form denoting contact. — Fr.
Gk. άίπτειν, 'to touch, fasten; to kindle'. See
apsis and cp. words there referred to.

## hara-kiri
hara-kiri, п., suicide by disembowelment. —
Vulgar Jap., lit. 'belly cutting', fr. hara, 'belly',
and kiri, 'to cut'.

## harangue
harangue, п., a formal speech. — ME. araug,
fr. MF. arenge, harangue (F. harangue), prob.
fr. It. aringare, 'to harangue', fr. aringo, 'public
place for assemblies and horse races', fr. Goth.
'hriggs (pronounced *hrings), 'circle": sec
Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 301 s.v. harangue
Ср. ОЕ., OHG. hring, 'circle, ring', and see
ring, n. The first a in harangue is an auxiliary
vowel with the aim of facilitating the pronun
ciation of the consonants hn at the beginning of
the word. Cp. hanaper.

## harangue
harangue, tr. and intr. v. —F. haranguer, fr.
harangue. See harangue, n.
Derivative: harangu-er, a.

## haras
haras, п., a stud farm (archaic). — OF. haraz (F.
haras), 'stud', prob. fr. Arab, faras, 'horse', thu
change of/to h being prob. due to Gascon
influence. A rab./arai(whence/an'i, 'horseman') is rel.
to Heb. parash, Ethiop. paras, 'horse'. Heb.
parish, Aram, parash, Syr. parrasha,
'horseman'. Cp. harridan.

## harass
harass, tr. v., to trouble, worry. — F. harasser,
fr. OF. harer, 'to set dogs on', fr. hare, cry to
set dogs on, which is of imitative origin.
Derivatives: harass-er, п., harass-ment, n.

## harbinger
harbinger, п., a forerunner. — Formed—with in
sertion of л—fr. ME. herbergeour, fr. OF. her-
bergeor, 'provider of lodging', fr. herbergiei
(whence F. heberger), 'to provide lodgings for',
fr. herberge, 'lodging, shelter', fr. Frankish
*heriberga, 'lodging, inn', orig. 'army shelter',
which is rel. to OHG., OS. heriberga, OFris.,
MLG. herberge, 'lodging, inn'. Cp. OProvenc.
alberga(whence F. auberge) andlt.efter^o.'inn',
and see next word. The я in harbinger is intrusive.
Cp. messenger, passenger, porringer, scavenger.

## harbor
harbor, harbour, n. — ME. hereberge, herberwe,
prob. fr. ON. herbergi, it. MLG. herberge,
'lodging, inn*, orig. 'army shelter', fr. MLG. here,
'army', and the stem of bergen, 'to protect,
defend, shelter'. The first element is rel. to OE.
here, OHG. heri, 'army'; see harry and cp. prec.
word. For the second element see bury and cp.
borrow. Cp. the first element in arriere-ban and
the second element in Walter. For the change of
ME. e (in hereberge, herberwe) to E. a (in harbor)
cp. arbor, 'a shady retreat', carve.

## harbor
harbor, harbour, tr. and intr. v. — ME. here-
bergen, herberwen, fr. hereberge, herberwe. See
harbor, n.
Derivatives: harbo(u)r-er, n.

## hard
hard, adj. — ME. hard, fr. OE. heard, rel. to
hearde (adv.), 'extremely', OS., Du. hard, ON.
hardr (adj.), 'hard', ON. harda (adv.), 'very',
Dan. hoard, Swed. hard, 'hard', OHG. harto
(adv.), 'extremely, very', harti, herti (adj.),
'hard', MHG. harte (adv.), 'very', herte (adj.),
'hard', G. hart, Goth, hardus, 'hard', fr. I.-E.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:361 COLUMN:2 -->
base *qar-, 'hard'. Fr. I.-E. *qret-, 'qft-, a
-r-enlargement of base *qar-, derive Gk.
κράτος, Ion. χάρτας, Aeol. κρέτος, 'strength', Gk.
κρατύς, 'strong'. Cp. hardy, -ard, arditi, and the
second element in Bernard, Everard, Gerard,
Gunther, Leonard, Reynard. Cp. also acratia,
-cracy, the first element in Epicrates, pancratium.
Cp. I.-E. *quar-q-, whence OI. karkafah, 'crab',
karkarah, 'rough, hard', Gk. καρκίνος, 'crab',
L. cancer (dissimilated fr. *carcro-), 'crab, ulcer,
cancer'. See cancer and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: hard, adv. (q.v.), hard, п., harden
(q.v.), hardly (q.v.), hardship (q.v.), hardy (q.v.)

## hard
hard, adv. — ME. horde, fr. OE. hearde,
'extremely', rel. to ON. harda (adv.), 'very', OE.
heard, adj., 'hard'. See hard, adj.

## harden
harden, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hardnen, fr. hard.
See hard, adj., and verbal suff. -en.
Derivatives: harden-er, п., harden-ing, n.

## hardly
hardly, adv. — ME., fr. OE. heardlice. See hard,
adj., and adv. surT. -ly.

## hardness
hardness, n. — ME. hardnesse, fr. OE. heardnes.
See hard, adj., and -ness.

## hardock
hardock, п., burdock. — Compounded of OE.
har, 'gray, hoary' (see hoar), and dock, 'the
plant'.

## hards
hards, n. pi. — See nurds.

## hardship
hardship, n. — ME. hardscipe. See hard, adj.,
and -ship.

## hardy
hardy, adj. — ME. hardi, fr. OF. (= F.) hatdi,
'bold, daring, fearless', prop. pp. of hardir, 'to
make bold', fr. Frankish 'hardjan, 'to harden',
which is rel. to OHG. herten, OFris. hc-da,
O.N. herda, O.S. herdian, OE. hierdan, Goth.
ga-hardjan, 'to harden', OHG. harti, herti, OE.
heard, 'hard'. See hard, adj., and cp. foolhardy.
Derivative: hardy, tr. v., to make hardy; intr. v.,
to become hardy.

## hardy
hardy, п., blacksmith's short chisel. — Formed
fr. hard, adj., with suff. -y.

## hare
hare, n. — ME. hare, fr. OE. hara, rel. to ON.
heri, Dan., Swed. hare, OFris. hasa, MDu. hase,
Du. haas, OHG. haso, MHG., G. hase, 'hare'.
These words lit. denote the gray animal, and
are rel. to OE. hasu, OHG. hasan, 'gray', ON.
hoss (for *haswa-), 'grayish brown', and cogn.
with OI. sa&ah, Afghan soe, OPruss. sasins, W.
ceinach, 'hare', L. canus (for *cas-nos), 'gray,
hoary, white', cascus, 'old' (orig. 'gray*, whence
'gray with age'). For sense development cp.
Russ. sirjak, 'gray hare', fr. seryj, 'gray'. Cp.
harrier, hound used for hunting hares'. Cp. also
canescent.

## hare
hare, tr. v., to frighten (obsol.) — Rel. to harry.
Cp. the first element in harum-scarum.

## harem
harem, п., women's section in an Oriental house.
— Arab, hartm, 'sacred, forbidden', fr. harama,
'he forbade', haruma, 'was forbidden', rel. to
Ethiop. harama, 'he prohibited from common
use, he devoted to God', Heb. hehirtm, 'he
banned, devoted to destruction,
excommunicated', h&em, 'person or thing devoted to
destruction'. See herem and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also harmattan, ihram, Muharram.

## haricot
haricot, п., ragout, meat. — F., fr. OF. harigoter,
'to cut in pieces'; of unknown origin.

## haricot
haricot, п., kidney bean. — F., fr. Nahuatl aya-
cotli; influenced in form by F. haricot, 'ragout'.

## hark
hark, tr. and intr. v., to listen. — ME. herkien,
herken, intensive form of the v. hear (to which
it stands in the same relationship as talk to tell
and lurk to lower); rel. to OFris. harkia, herkia,
MLG., MDu. horken, OHG. hdrechen, MHG.
hdrchen, G. horchen, 'to hearken, listen'. Cp.
hearkeu.

## harken
harken, v. — A var. of hearken.

## harl
harl, harle, п., fiber of flax or hemp. — ME. herle,
'fiber', rel. to MLG. herle, harle; of uncertain
origin.

## harl
harl, tr. v., to drag; intr. v., to drag oneself along
(Scot.) — ME. harlen, of uncertain origin.

## Harlequin
Harlequin, п., ι) a leading character in
pantomime; 2) (not cap.) a clown, buffoon. — F.
harlequin (whence It. arlecchino), fr. OF. Helle-
quin, Hierlekin, 'leader of a demon troop called
maisnie Hellequin, maisnie Hierlekin. The name
is traceable to Herrequin, the count of Boulogne,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:361 COLUMN:3 -->
whose sudden death in 882 was regarded as a
fit punishment for his wickedness (he had
waged war against his uncle). See KIuge-Mitzka,
EWDS., p. 289, s.v. Harlekin. F. arlequin was
reborrowed fr. It. arlecchino.

## harlequinade
harlequinade, п., a piece in which the Harlequin
plays a leading part. — F. arlequinade, fr.
arlequin. See prec. word and -ade.

## harlot
harlot, n. — ME. harlot, herlot, 'vagabond', fr.
OF. harlot, herlot, arlot, 'lad, vagabond', which
is rel. to OProvenc. arlot, Sp. arlote, 'vagabond',
It. arlotto, 'hedge priest'; of uncertain origin.
Derivative: harlot-ry, n.

## harm
harm, n. — ME. hearm, herm, harm, fr. OE.
hearm, rel. to OS. harm, ON. harmr, OFris.
herm, OHG. haram, harm, MHG., G. harm,
'grief, sorrow, harm', and cogn. with Pers.
sharm, 'shame', OSlav. sramu (metathesized fr.
*sormu), of s.m.
Derivatives: harm, v. (q.v.), harm-ful,
adj.,harmfully, adv., harm-ful-ness, п., harm-less, adj.,
harm-less-ly, adv., harm-less-ness, n.

## harm
harm, tr. v. — ME. hermen, harmen, fr. OE.
hearmian, 'to injure, harm', fr. hearm. See
harm, n.

## harmal
harmal, harmala, harmel, п., the wild rue (Pega-
num harmala). — ModL., fr. Gk. άρμαλά, fr.
Arab, harmal, 'rue'.

## harmattan
harmattan, п., a dry wind, charged with dust,
blowing from the Sahara to the Atlantic coast.
— Sp. harmatan, fr. Fanti haramata, fr. Arab.
haram, 'a forbidden thing', used in the sense of
'an evil thing', from the stem of harama, 'he
forbade', haruma, 'was forbidden'. See harem.

## Hannonia
Hannonia, п., the wife of Cadmus in Greek
mythology. — L., fr. Gk. 'Αρμονία, lit. 'concord'.
See harmony.

## harmonic
harmonic, adj. — L. harmonicus, fr. Gk.
αρμονικός, 'fitting, harmonious; skilled in music', fr.
αρμονία. See harmony and -ic.
Derivatives: harmonic-al, adj., harmonic-al-ly,
adv., harmonics (q.v.)

## harmonica
harmonica, п., an instrument consisting of a
series of glasses (mus.) — Fr. L. harmonica, fern,
of harmonicus; see prec. word. The name
harmonica was given to this instrument by its
inventor Benjamin Franklin (he spelled it ar-
monica).

## harmonicon
harmonicon, п., a small mouth organ (mus.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. άρμονικόν, neut. of αρμονικός.
See harmonic.

## harmonics
harmonics, п., the science of musical harmony.
See harmonic and -ics.

## harmonious
harmonious, adj. — F. harmonieux (fern, har-
monieuse), fr. harmonic, fr. L. harmonia. See
harmony and -ous.
Derivatives: harmonious-ly, adv., harmonious-
ness, n.

## harmoniphon
harmoniphon, harmoniphone, п., an obsolete wind
instrument (mus.) — Compounded of Gk.
αρμονία, 'harmony', and -φωνος, 'sounding', fr.
φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See harmony and phone,
'speech sound'.

## harmonist
harmonist, n. — See harmonize and -ist.
Derivatives: harmonist-ic, adj., harmonist-ic-al-
ly, adv.

## harmonium
harmonium, п., a small reed organ (mus.) —
ModL., coined by the French organ maker
Alexandre-Francois Debain (1809-77) fr. L.
harmonia. See harmony.

## harmonize
harmonize, tr. and intr. v. — F. harmoniserfi.
harmonic See harmony and -ize.
Derivatives: harmoniz-ation, п., harmoniz-er, n.

## harnionomcter
harnionomcter, п., an instrument for measuring
the harmonic relations of musical sounds. —
F. harmonometre. See harmony and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## harmony
harmony, n. — ME. harmonie, fr. F. harmonic, fr.
L. harmonia, fr. Gk. αρμονία, 'a fitting together,
joining, proportion, concord, agreement,
musical harmony', which is rel. to άρμόζειν, 'to fit
together, adapt, accomodate', αρμός, 'a
joining', fr. I.-E. base *ar-, 'to join'. See arm, 'the
upper limb", and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also Harmonia, harmonica, harmonicon,
harmonium.

## harness
harness, n. — ME. harneis, herneis, fr. OF. har-
neis, herneis, harnes (F. harnais), fr. ON. *her-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:362 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 335 | HASKALAH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:362 COLUMN:1 -->
nest, 'provisions for the army'. The first
element is rel. to OE. here, OHG. heri, 'army'; see
harry and cp. words there referred to. The
second element is rel. to OE. nest, "provisions',
and to OE., OS., OHG. nerian, MHG. nerigen,
nern, G. nahren, Goth, nasjan, 'to nourish', lit. 'to
cause to recover', fr. OE. genesan, resp. OS.,
OHG., ginesan, MHG., G. genesen, Goth.
ganisan, 'to recover'; see nostalgia. MHG. har-
nsest, harnas (whence G. Harnisch), 'harness,
armor', is reborrowed fr. OF. harnais.

## harness
harness, tr. v. — ME. harneisen, fr. harneis. See
harness, n.
Derivatives: harness-ed, adj., harness-er, п.,
harness-ry, n.

## haro
haro, interj — A var. of harrow, interj.

## Harold
Harold, masc. PN. — OE. Harald, Harold, fr.
ON. Haraldr, fr. Teut. *Hariwald, lit. 'ruler of
the army', compounded of *harja (whence ON.
herr, OE. here, etc.), 'host, army', and 'waldan
(whence ON. valda, OE. weatdan, etc.), 'to rule'.
For the first element see harry and cp. harbor,
for the second element see wield. Cp. herald,
Walter.

## harp
harp, n. — ME. harpe, fr. OE. hearpe, rel. to
ON. harpa, Du. harp, OHG. harpfa, MHG.
harphe, harfe, G. Harfe. These words lit. mean
'an instrument plucked with the crooked
fingers', and are rel. to ON. herpask, 'to contract
(one's fingers)', and cogn. with Russ. korobit',
'to bend', Gk. κράμβος, 'shriveled'. It., OProv-
βης., Catal., Sp., Port, arpa are Teut. loan
words. See rumple, v., and cp. arpeggio and
the first element in harpsichord.

## harp
harp, intr. v. — ME. harpien, fr. OE. hearpian,
'to play the harp', fr. hearpe. See harp, n.

## harpagon
harpagon, п., a grappling hook. — L. harpago, fr.
harpaga, 'hook', fr. Gk. αρπάγη, 'hook; rake',
from the stem of άρπάζειν, 'to grasp, seize; to
plunder'. See harpy and cp. next word.

## Harpagon
Harpagon, п., the chief character in Moliere's
I'Avare, the typical miser. — F., fr. L. harpago,
'grappling hook', whence, figuratively, 'a
rapacious person'. See prec. word.

## Harpalus
Harpalus, п., a genus of beetles (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. άρπαλέος, 'attractive, pleasant;
devouring, greedy', formed with dissimilation
fr. άλπαλέος and rel. to ΜΧπιστος, άλπνιστος,
'sweetest, loveliest' (superl. of obsol. άλττος,
όίλπνος), fr. I.-E. *w/p-, zero degree of base
*welp-, whence Gk. έλττις, 'hope'. Base *wel-p-
is a -^-enlargement of base *wet-, 'to will, wish,
hope, choose', whence L. void, telle, 'to will,
wish'. See voluntary.

## harper
harper, n. — ME. harpere, fr. OE. hearpere, fr.
hearpe. See harp, п., and agential sun", -er.

## harpings
harpings, n. pi., the stout wales round the bow
of a vessel (naut.) — Rel. to harpoon.

## harpist
harpist, п., a harper. — A hybrid coined fr. harp
and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## harpoon
harpoon, п., a barbed spear used against whales,
etc. — Fr. earlier E. harpon, prob. fr. Du. har-
poen, fr. MDu. harpoen (whence also earlier G.
Harpon, G. Harpune), fr. OF. harpon, 'clamp,
grappling iron, harpoon' (whence F. harpon,
'harpoon'), fr. OF. (= F.) harpe, 'claw', fr. OF.
(~ MF.) harper, 'to seize, grapple', which is
prob. of Teut. origin. Cp. ON. herpask, 'to
contract (one's fingers)', and see harp. F. harpon
was influenced in meaning by an association
with Late L. harpe (fr. Gk. ίίρπη), 'sickle', with
which, however, it is not connected.
Derivatives: harpoon, tr. v., harpoon-er, n.

## harpsichord
harpsichord, п., a keyboard stringed instrument,
forerunner of the piano (mus.) — Earlier harp-
sechord, fr. obsol. F. harpechorde, ft. It. arpi-
cordo, which is compounded otarpa, 'harp', and
corda, 'string, chord'. See harp and chord.

## harpy
harpy, п., ι) any of several rapacious monsters in
Greek mythology; 2) a rapacious person.
— F. harpie, fr. L. harpyia, fr. Gk. ίρπυιω
(pi.), lit. 'snatchers', which is rel. to ίρπη,
'sickle', άρπάζειν, 'to snatch, seize', αρπάγη,
'hook; rake', όίρπαξ, 'rapacious', prob. fr. I.-E.
base "srep-, 'sip-, 'to seize, rob', whence also
OSlav. srupu, 'sickle', Russ. serp', Lith. sirpe,
of s.m. Base *srep-, *sfp- is prob. rel. to base
*rep-, whence Gk. έρέπτεσθαι, 'to pluck off',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:362 COLUMN:2 -->
L. rapere,' to seize and carry off'. See rapid and cp.
sarmentose.

## harquebus
harquebus, also arquebus, п., an early form of
firearm. — F. arquebuse, harquebuse, fr. MDu.
hakebusse (Du. haakbus), fr. hake, 'hook', and
busse, 'box, tube, gun', hence lit. meaning 'hook
gun'. Cp. G. Hakenbiichse and see hook and
box, 'case'. Cp. also hackbut. The alteration of
the Dutch word into F. arquebus, It. arcobugio
is due to a confusion of the first element of the
word with F. arc, resp. It. arco (see arc). The
second element in F. arque-buse owes its form
to the influence of F. buse, 'buzzard' (see
buzzard), taken in a figurative sense to denote a
weapon; the ending of It. arcobugio is due to a
confusion with It. bugt'o, 'hole'.
Derivative: arquebu's-ier, harquebus-ier, n.

## harridan
harridan, п., a disreputable old woman. — Prob.
formed with change of suffix fr. F. haridelle, 'a
worn-out horse, a jade; a tall gaunt woman',
which is prob. rel. to F. haras, 'stud'. See haras,

## harrier
harrier, п., a hound used for hunting hares. —
Formed fr. hare, п., with suff. -ier.

## harrier
harrier, п., any of the hawks of the genus Circus.
— Lit. 'that which harries'. See harry and -ier.

## Harriet
Harriet, also Harriot, fern. PN. — E. equivalent
of F. Henriette, fern, dimin. of Henri. See
Henrietta.

## Harrisbuck
Harrisbuck, п., also Harris buck, the sable
antelope. — Named after the engineer William
Cornwallis Harris (1807-48), who first
described it.

## Harrisia
Harrisia, п., a genus of cacti. — ModL., named
after William Harris (i860-1920), a Jamaican
botanist. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## harrisite
harrisite, п., a plutonic rock (petrogr.) — So
called from Harris, on the Isle of Rum in the
Hebrides. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## harrow
harrow, п., an agricultural implement. — ME.
haru, harwe, rel. to ON. harfr, herfi, 'harrow',
and to OE. hserfest, OHG. herbist, 'harvest'. See
harvest.
Derivatives: harrow, tr. v., harrow-er, п., har-
row-ing, n. and adj., harrow-ing-ly, adj., harrow-
ing-ness, n.

## harrow
harrow, tr. v., to harry (archaic). — OE. hergian.
See next word.

## harry
harry, tr. v., 1) to ravage; 2) to harass. — ME.
harien, herien, fr. OE. hergian, 'to ravage, lay
waste', rel. to ON. herja, 'to make a raid, to
plunder', OHG. herion, MHG. hern, 'to ravage,
plunder', OHG. firherion, MHG. verhern, 'to
destroy by war', G. verheeren, 'to destroy'.
These words lit. mean 'to afflict with, or destroy
by, an army', being denominated fr. OE. here,
resp. ON. herr (whence Dan. hxr, Swed. har),
OHG. hari, heri, MHG. her, G. Heer, 'host,
army', which are rel. to OS., OFris. heri, Du.
heir, Goth, harjis, of s.m. These latter weirds
orig. meant 'that which pertains to war', and
are cogn. with Lith. karas, 'war, quarrel', kare,
'war*, kdrias, 'host, army', OPruss. kar/is,
'army', OSlav. kara, 'strife', Mir. cuire, 'troop',
OPers. kara, 'host, army', Gk. κοίρανος, 'ruler,
leader, commander' (prop, 'leader of an army',
fr. *κοΐρα, for *κόρια, 'army'). Cp. prec. word.
Cp. also the first element in arriere-ban,
harbinger, harbor, harness, Harold, herald, Herbert,
heretoga, heriot, Herman, hership, and the
second element in Lothario, Oliver, Walter.

## Harry
Harry, masc. PN. — F. Henri. See Henry,

## harsh
harsh, adj. — ME. harsk, of Scand. origin. Cp.

## Dan.
Dan., Norw., harsk, Swed. harsk, 'rancid',

## which are rel. to MLG.
which are rel. to MLG., G. harsch, 'harsh,

## rough
rough, raw'; fr. I.-E. base *qars-, 'to scrape,

## scratch
scratch, rub', whence Lith. karSiu, kafsti, 'to

## comb'
comb', OSlav. krasta (for *korsta), Russ.

## korosta
korosta, 'itch', MLG. harst, 'rake', L. carrere,
'to card (wool)', carduus, 'thistle*, OI. kasati
(for *karsati), 'rubs, scratches', kasdyah, 'acid,

## sharp'
sharp', kusthah, 'leprosy'. Cp. card, 'machine for

## combing'
combing', and words there referred to.
Derivatives: harsh-ly, adv., harsh-ness, n.

## hart
hart, п., a male deer. — ME. hert, heort, fr. OE.

## heorot
heorot, heort, rel. to ON. hjortr, Dan., Swed.

## hjort
hjort, OS. hirot, OFris., Du. hert, OHG. hirus,

## hirj
hirj, MHG. A/rj, G. Hirsch, 'deer, stag, hart',

## ON. hriitr
ON. hriitr, 'ram', and cogn. with W. carw, Co.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:362 COLUMN:3 -->
carow, 1.. cervus, 'deer'. All these words derive
fr. I.-E. base *ker-, 'the uppermost part of the
body, head, horn, top, summit', and lit. mean
'the horned animal'. See horn and cp. cervine.
Cp, also hurt, rother.

## hartal
hartal, п., cessation of all work, esp. a sign of
protest. — Hind, hartal, for hattal, fr. OI. hatjah,
'market', and tdlah, 'lock, bolt'.

## hartebeest
hartebeest, hartbeest, п., a large S. African
antelope. — S. Afr. Du., compounded of Du. hart
(an earlier collateral form of hert), 'deer, stag',
and beest, 'beast', fr. MDu. beeste, beest, fr.
OF. beste. See hart and beast.

## hartshorn
hartshorn, п., ammonium carbonate. — Lit.
hart's horn: so called because orig. obtained
from antlers of hart.

## harum-scarum
harum-scarum, adj.. reckless (colloq.) —
Facetious formation from the verbs hare and scare.

## haruspex
haruspex, п., an ancient Roman soothsayer. —
L., for haru-spex, 'inspector of the entrails'. The
first element is rel. to L. hernia, 'rupture', and
cogn. with Gk. χορδή, 'gut', OE. gearn, 'yarn'.
See yarn and cp. hernia and chord. For the
second element see species.

## harvest
harvest, n. — ME. hervest, harveste, 'autumn', fr.
OE. hxrfest, of s.m., rel. to OS. hervist, OFris.
Du. herfst, OHG. herbist, MHG. herbest,herbst,
G. Herbst, 'autumn', ON. haust, Dan. host,
Swed. host, 'harvest', fr. I.-E. *qarpistos, prop,
superl. meaning "the most suitable (season) for
harvesting', formed with super], suff. -istos fr.
I.-E. base *(s)qerp-, 'to cut; to pluck', whence
also OI. kj-panah, 'sword', Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'
(lit. 'that which is plucked'), L. carpere, 'to
pluck, cull, gather'. See carpel and superl. suff.
-ist and cp. harrow, n.

## harvest
harvest, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hervesten, fr.
hervest. See prec. word.
Derivatives: harvest-er, п., harvest-ing, n.

## hash
hash, tr. v., to chop (meat, etc.) into small pieces.
— Earlier hache, fr. F. hacher, 'to hack, chop',
fr. hache, ax, hatchet'. See hatch, 'to engrave'.
Derivative: hash, п., dish of chopped cooked
meat.

## hashish
hashish, п., an intoxicating drink made from
hemp. — Arab, hashish, 'hemp', prop, 'dried
grass', rel, to Heb. hashash, 'dried grass'. Cp.
assassin.

## Hasideans
Hasideans, Hasidaeans, also Assideans, Chassi-
deans, n. pi., the party of the Hasidim (in sense
no. 1) — Formed with suff.-an fr. Gk. Άσιδαΐοι,
fr. Heb. hasidim, 'pious ones'. See next word.

## Hasidim
Hasidim, also Chassidim, n. pi., 1) adherents of
the religious party that arose in opposition to
Hellenism and flourished during the time of the
Maccabean wars; it urged steadfast faith and
the strict observance of the ritual laws; 2)
adherents of the religious movement called Hasid-
ism, founded by Rabbi Israel ben Eliezer Baal
Shem Tobh about 1750 (Jewish hist.) — Heb.
hastdhtm, lit. 'pious ones', pi. of hastdh. 'kind,
pious', from the stem h-s-d, 'to be kind', whence
also hithhassidh, 'he showed himself kind' (in
MedHeb.: 'he pretended to be pious'), hesedh,
'piety, kindness, lovingkindness, mercy', hast-
dha", 'stork', lit. 'the pious bird' (so called in
allusion to its love to its young); rel. to Aram.
hisdd, 'piety, kindness, mercy', hasldhutha,
'piety, kindness'. Cp. prec. word. Cp. also the
second element in Bethesda.

## Hasidism
Hasidism, also Chassidism, п., the movement of
the Hasidim (Jewish hist.) — See prec. word
and -ism.

## Haskalah
Haskalah, п., Jewish movement which arose in
Eastern Europe about the middle of the 18th
cent, with the aim of acquainting the Jews of
Eastern and Central Europe with the languages
and cultures of the nations of Western Europe.
— ModHeb. haskala", 'enlightenment', prop,
a new meaning of haskala", 'understanding,
consideration', occurring in the Midrash, prop,
a verbal noun of Biblical Heb. hisktt 'was
attentive, had understanding, considered; was
successful, prospered', Hiph'il (= causative
form) of Sakhal, 'was prudent', whence sikhel,
'insight, prudence, understanding', Mishnaic
Heb. histakkil, 'he looked at attentively,
observed closely, considered*, Aram, askel, Syr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:363 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HASLET | 336 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:363 COLUMN:1 -->
sakkil, 'he taught', Bibl. Aram, histakkal, Aram.
istakkal, 'he looked at attentively'. As a
technical term in the sense 'enlightenment', the
word haskala" was introduced by the Jewish
orientalist and writer Judah Jeiteles (1773-1838)
in 1832.

## haslet
haslet, harslet, п., edible viscera of an animal. —
ME. hastelet, hastlet, fr. OF. hastetet (F. hate-
lette). The original meaning was 'something
roasted on a spit', fr. haste, 'a spit', fr. L. hasta,
'a spear'. See hastate and -et. The r in harslet is
due to the influence of OHG. harst, 'gridiron'.

## hasp
hasp, п., a clasp. — ME. haspe, hespe, fr. OE.
hxsp, hsepse, rel. to ON. hespa, Dan. haspe,
Swed. haspe, hasp, Norw. hasp, MLG., MDu.,
MHG., G. haspe, OHG. haspa, 'hasp, hook',
and cogn. with L. capsa, 'chest, box'. See case,
'box'. E. hasp is not cognate with L. cuspis
(see cusp).

## hasp
hasp, tr. v. — ME. haspen, fr. OE. hsepsian, fr.
hsepse. See hasp, n.

## hassock
hassock, п., a small cushion used as a footstool.
— ME. hassok, *a large tuft of grass', fr. OE.
hassuc, hassoc, of uncertain origin.
Derivative: hassock-y, adj.

## hasta
hasta, п., ι) symbolic position of the hands in
dancing; 2) a cubit (measure). — OI. hdstah,
'hand; trunk of an elephant', rel. to Avestic
zasta-, OPers. dasta- (whence Pers. dast), 'hand',
and cogn. with Lith. paiastl, 'armpit'. Cp. hath
and the second element in abdest.

## hastate
hastate, adj., spearlike; resembling the head of a
spear (hot.) — L. hastatus, 'armed with a spear',
fr. hasta, 'shaft, spear', which is cogn. with
Goth, gazds, 'goad', OE. gierd, geard, 'rod,
stick, yard'. See yard, 'unit of length', and adj.
suff. -ate.
Derivative: hastate-ly, adv.

## haste
haste, n, — ME. hast, haste, fr. OF. haste (F.
hate), fr. Frankish "haijst, 'violence', which is
rel. to OE. hxst, 'violence, fury', OFris. hast,
'haste', OHG. heisti, OFris. haste, OE. hxste,
'violent', OHG. heiftig, of s.m., ON. heipt (for
*heift), heifst, 'war, hatred', Goth, haifsts,
'struggle, strife'. Du. haast (whence MLG. hast,
whence G., Dan., Swed. hast), 'haste, hurry', is
borrowed fr. OF. haste.
Derivatives: haste-ful, adj., haste-ful-ly, adv.

## haste
haste, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hasten, fr. OF.
haster (F. hater), fr. haste. See haste, n.

## hasten
hasten, intr. and tr. v. — Formed from prec.
word with verbal suff. -en.

## hasty
hasty, adj. — ME. hasti, fr. OF. hasti, a var. of
hastif, fr. haste (see haste, п.). The ending -i
was confused in English with suff. -y
(representing OE. -ig). For the loss of OF. final /cp. F.
jolt (fr. OF. jolif) and see jolly.
Derivatives: hasti-ly, adv., hastiness, n.

## hat
hat, n. — ME., fr. OE. hsett, hset, rel. to Fris.
hat, ON. hattr, hour, 'hat, hood', and to E.
hood (q.v.)
Derivatives:hat, tr. v., hat-ful, adj.,hat-less, adj.,
hatt-er, п., hatt-ery, п., hatt-ing, n.

## hatch
hatch, п., door, wicket. — ME. hacche, hecche,
fr. OE. hsec, 'hatch, grating; gate', rel. to
MLG., MHG. heck, Du. hek, 'fence; gate'. Cp.
hnck, 'board', heck, 'frame'.

## hatch
hatch, tr. and intr. v., to produce (young) from
eggs by incubation. — ME. hacchen, rel. to
MHG., G. hecken, to hatch, breed', OHG.
