hegidruosa, MHG. hegedruos, 'testicle', MHG.,
G. hagen, 'bull kept for breeding', and cogn.
with Lett, kakale, 'membrum'.
Derivatives: hatch, п., hatch-er, п., hatch-ing, n.

## hatch
hatch, tr. v., to engrave. — F. hacher, 'to hack,
cKop' fr. hache, 'ax, hatchet'. See hatchet,

## hatchel
hatchel, п., a comblike implement for cleaning
flax or hemp. — ME. hechele, a var. of hekele,
rel. to Du. hekel, MHG. hachel, hechel, G.
Hechel, 'hatchel, hackle', Swed. hackla, Dan.
hegle, 'to hackle', from a Teut. base meaning 'to
sting', whence also OHG., MHG. hecchen,
hecken, 'to sting'; in gradational relationship
to ON. haki, OE. haca, 'hook'. See hook and cp.
hackle and heckle, which are variants of hatchel.

## hatchel
hatchel, tr. v. — ME. hechelen, fr. ME. hechel;
rel. to Du. hekelen, G. hecheln. See hatchel, n.
Derivative: hatchel(l)-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:363 COLUMN:2 -->

## hatchet
hatchet, п., a small ax. — ME. hachet, fr. OF.
{= F.) hachette, dimin. of hache, 'ax, hatchet',
fr. Frankish "hapja, 'sickle', which is rel. to
OHG. happa, 'sickle'; prob. derived fr. I.-E.
base *(s)qap-, *(s)qdp-, *(s)qdp-, 'to cut', whence
also Gk. κοπίς, 'knife', Liih. kaplys, Lett, kap-
lis, 'hatchet', Lith. kaponi, Lett, kapans,
'chopping knife'. See capon and cp. hash, hatch, 'to
engrave'. Cp. also the second element in
quebracho.

## hatching
hatching, n. — Formed fr. hatch, 'to engrave',
with -ing, a surf, forming verbal nouns.

## hatchment
hatchment, п., an escutcheon. — From earlier
atcheament, alteration of achievement.

## hate
hate, n. — ME. hete, hate (the second form is due
to the influence of the verb hate, see next word),
fr. OE. hete, rel. to OS. heti, ON. hair, Swed.
hat, Dan. had, OFris. hat, MDu. hate, Du. haat,
OHG., MHG. ha3, G. Hafi, Goth, hatis, fr.
I.-E. base "kad-, 'ill-humor, hatred', whence
also Avestic sadra-, 'grief, sorrow, calamity',
Gk. κηδος, Dor. κάδος, 'care; trouble, sorrow',
Gk. κηδεύειν, 'to take charge, tend', Mir. caiss,
W. cas, Bret, kas, Co. cueth, 'pain, anger'. Cp.
hatred, heinous. Cp. also acedia, epicedium.
Derivatives: hate-ful, adj., hate-ful-ly, adv., hate-
fut-ness, n.

## hate
hate, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hatien, haten, fr. OE.
hatian, rel. to OE. hete, 'hate', and to OS. halon,
ΟΝ., Swed., Norw. hata, OFris. hatia, Du.
haten, OHG. ha^on, ha^en, MHG. hasien,
G, hassen, Goth, hatan, 'to hate'. See hate, n.
Derivative: hat-er, n.

## hath
hath, hauth, п., a cubit. — Hind, hath, 'a cubit',
lit. 'the hand', fr. OI. hdstah, 'hand'. See hasta.

## Hathor
Hathor, п., the goddess of love and joy in
Egyptian mythology. — Gk. Ά»ωρ, fr. Egypt. Het-
Hert, lit. 'the house above'.
Derivative: hathor-ic, adj.

## hatred
hatred, n. — ME. hatereden, hatered,
compounded of hate, п., and OE. rxden, 'rule, condition'
(fr. ridan, 'to advise, discuss, rule, guess, read'),
used as a subst. suff. See rend and cp. the second
element in kindred.

## hatter
hatter, n. — Formed fr. hat with agential suff. -er.

## hauberk
hauberk, hawberk, п., a medieval piece of armor.
— ME. hauberc, fr. OF. halberc, hauberc (F.
haubert), fr. Frankish 'halsberg, which is rel.
to OHG. halsberc, halsberge, lit. 'neck cover',
fr. hals, 'neck', and bergan, 'to cover, protect'.
Further Teut. equivalents are MDu. halsberch,
OE. healsbeorg, ON. halsbjorg. See hawse and
bury and cp. habergeon.

## hauchecornite
hauchecornite, п., nickel and bismuth sulfide
{mineral.) — Named after VJ.Hauchecorn.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hauerite
hauerite, п., manganese disulfide (mineral.) — G.
Hauerit, named after the Austrian geologist
Franz von Hauer (1822-1899). The ending -it
goes back to Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## haugh
haugh, п., flat ground in the valley of a river. —
ME. holch, hawk, rel. to OE. heath, 'corner',
and to OE. hoi, 'cave, hollow, opening', holh,
'cave'. See hole and cp. hollow.

## haughtonite
haughtonite, п., a variety of biotite (mineral.) —

## Named in 1878 after Samuel Houghton
Named in 1878 after Samuel Houghton, Fellow
«of Trinity College, Dublin. For the ending see
subst. surf. -Ke.

## haughty
haughty, adj., proud; arrogant. — Formed with
adj. suff. -y fr. OF. (= F.) haul, 'high' (whence
archaic E. haught) fr. L. alius, 'high'; influenced
in form by OHG. huh, 'high'. See alt and cp.
hauteur.
Derivatives: haughti-ly, adv., haughti-ness, n.

## haul
haul, tr. and intr. v. — ME. halien, halen, haulen,
fr. OF. (= F.) haler, 'to pull, draw, haul', fr.
ODu. (= Du.) halen, which is rel. to OS. halon,
ON. hata, OFris. halia, OHG. halon, holon,
MHG. haln, holn, holen, G. holen, 'to draw,
haul; to fetch', OE. geholian, 'to obtain'. These
Teut. words possibly derive from an I.-E. base
*kal-, 'to draw, pull', whence also Gk. κάλως,
'rope'. Cp. hale, 'to haul', the first element in
halyard, and the second element in keelhaul.
Derivatives: haul, п., haul-age, п., haul-er, n.

## haulm
haulm, halm, п., stalk. — ME. halm, fr. OE.
healm, 'straw, stem of grass', rel. to OS., Dan.,
Swsd., Du., OHG., MHG., G. halm, ON.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:363 COLUMN:3 -->
halmr, and cogn. with L. culmus, 'stalk, stem',
Gk. κάλαμος, 'reed'. See culm and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also the second element in
marram.

## haunch
haunch, п., hip. — Earlier hanch, fr. ME. hanche,
haunche, fr. OF. (= F.) hanche, fr. Teut.
*hanka; cp. MDu. hanke, 'haunch'.
Derivatives: haunch-ed, adj., haunch-ing, n.

## haunt
haunt, tr. v., to visit, frequent. — ME. haunten,
fr. OF. (= F.) hanter, which is of Teut. origin.
Cp. ON. heimta, 'to bring home, fetch', which
derives fr. heimr, 'homeland', and OE. hamettan,
'to shelter', which comes fr. ham, 'home', and
see home. Cp. hamlet.
Derivatives: haunt, п., haunt-ed, adj., haunt-er,
п., haunt-ing, n. and adj., haunt-ing-ly, adv.

## haurient
haurient, also hauriant, adj., with the head in
chief; said of a fish (her.) — L. hauriens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of haurire, 'to draw out
(water), to drain, breathe'. See exhaust and -ent
and cp. haustellnm, haustorinm.

## hausen
hausen, п., a large kind of sturgeon. — G.,
'sturgeon', fr. MHG. huse(n), fr. OHG. huso. See
huso.

## hausroannite
hausroannite, п., manganese oxide (mineral.) —
Named after the German mineralogist J.F.L.
Hausmann (1782-1859). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Hausmannize
Hausmannize, tr. and intr. v., to reconstruct a
city by straightening and widening its streets. —
Prop, 'to follow the example of Baron Georges-
Eugene Haussmann (1809-91), who was prefect
of Paris between 1853 and 1870 and during this
period much contributed to its beautification.
For the ending see suff. -ize.

## hausse-col
hausse-col, п., a piece of armor. — F., 'neck
piece', fr. MF. houscot, prob. fr. MDu. *hals-
kote, 'clothing of the neck', which is
compounded of hals, 'neck', and kote, 'coat,
clothing', which is rel. to OHG. chozza, 'a coarse
coat'. See collar and coat. Folk etymology
converted houscot into hausse-col, i.e. 'that which
raises the neck'.

## haustellum
haustellum, п., in certain insects, a proboscis
adapted for sucking blood or juices of plants.—
ModL., fr. L. haustus, pp. of haurire, 'to draw
(water), to drain'. See haurient.

## haustorium
haustorium, п., a small sucker of a parasitic pkrnt
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L, haustus, pp. of haurire.
See prec. word and -oriuin.

## hautboy
hautboy, п., an oboe. — F. hautbois, fr. haul,
'high' and bois, 'wood'. See haughty and bush,
'shrub', and cp. oboe, tallboy.

## hauteur
hauteur, n„ haughtiness. — F., 'height, altitude;
haughtiness, arrogance*, formed fr. haul, 'high',
with suff. -eur. See haughty and -or, -our.

## hautefeuilltte
hautefeuilltte, п., magnesium calcium phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after the French chemist
Paul-Gabriel Hautefeuille (1836-1902). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Havana
Havana, п., Havana cigar. — Named after
Havana, the capital of Cuba. Cp. habanera.

## havdalah
havdalah, n. — A var. of habdalah.

## have
have, tr. v. — ME. habben, haven, fr. OE. hab-
ban, 'to hold, possess, have', rel. to ON. hafa,
OS. hebbjan, OFris. habba, hebba, OHG. habin,
MHG., G. haben, Goth, haban, 'to have', and
to OE. hebban, etc., 'to lift, raise', fr. Teut. base
*haf-, 'to hold, have', corresponding to I.-E.
*qap-, "to seize, hold, contain', whence L. ca-
pere, 'to catch, seize, take hold of. (The above
Teut. words are not cogn. with L. habere, 'to
have'.) See captive and cp. haff, haft, haven,
havoc, hawk, the bird, heave, heavy, behavior,
behoof, hobnob.

## havelock
havelock, п., a light covering for cap and neck.
— Named after Sir Henry Have/oci (1795-1857).

## haven
haven, n. — ME, havene, fr. OE. hxfen, hxfene,
rel. to MLG. havene (whence G. Hafen), MHG.
habene, ON. hofn, Dan. havn, 'haven'. These
words lit. mean 'receptacle', and derive fr. I.-E.
base *qap-, 'to seize, hold, contain', whence also
have and heave (qq.v.) Cp. haff.

## haver
haver, п., one who has (rare). — Formed fr. have
with agential suff. -er.

## haver
haver, intr.' v., to talk foolishly. — Of unknown
origin.
Derivative: haver, п., foolish talk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:364 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 337 | HEAP -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:364 COLUMN:1 -->

## haver
haver, п., the oat; oats (dial. E.) — ME. haver,
of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. hafri, Dan. havre,
Swed. hafre, which are rel. to MDu. havere, Du.
haver, OS. habero, OHG. habaro, MHG. habere,
haber (G. Hafer is a LG. loan word). Cp.next
word.

## haversack
haversack, п., soldier's bag for provision. — F.,
havresac, 'knapsack, wallet', fr. G. Habersack,
lit. 'a sack for oats'. See haver, 'oats', and
sack, 'bag'.

## havildar
havildar, п., a noncommissioned native officer
corresponding to a sergeant. — Hind, havildar,
fr. Pers. hwaldar, hawatadar, lit. 'one holding
an office', a hybrid coined fr. Arab, hawala",
'charge, office', and the Persian sufT. -dur,
'holder, possessor'. See aumildar and cp. words
there referred to.

## havior
havior, haviour, п., behavior (archaic). — ME.
haviour, 'possession', fr. earlier havour, fr. OF.
aveir (F. avoir), 'possession', prop, infinitive
used as a noun, fr. L. habere, 'to have, possess',
see habit, n. The A is due to a confusion with
ME. haven, E. have, with which the word havior
has nothing in common. Cp. behavior.

## havoc
havoc, п., destruction, devastation. — OF. havot,
'seizure; plunder', [aire havot, 'to take hold of,
rel. to haver, 'to seize, grasp, grab', hef, 'a hook',
havee, 'a handful'; of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG.
haben, 'to hold, have', heffan, 'to raise, heave',
and see have, heave. For the change of final -t
(in OF. havot) to -c (in E. havoc) cp. apricot
(from orig. apricock), bat (fr. МЦ. bakke) and
milk (in the sense of 'milt of fishes').
Derivatives: havoc, tr. v., havock-er, n.

## haw
haw, п., enclosure. — ME. hawe, fr. OE. haga,
'hedge; hawthorn', rel. to ON. hagi, hage,
pasture', OS. hago, Du. haag, OHG., MHG. hac,
hages, G. Hag, 'hedge', and in gradational
relationship to OE. hecg, 'hedge'. See hedge and
cp. next word, and the first element in
hawthorn. Cp. also hag, 'witch', haggard, hay,
'hedge', and the first element in hagberry.

## haw
haw, п., berry of the hawthorn. — OE. haga,
perh. short for *haguberige, lit. 'hedge berry'.
See prec. word.

## haw
haw, п., the nictitating membrane of a horse,
dog, etc. — Of unknown origin.

## haw
haw, intr. v., to hesitate in speech. — Imitative;
lit. 'to make the sound haw'.
Derivative: haw, п., hesitation in speech.

## hawk
hawk, п., any bird of the falcon family. — ME.
havec, hauk, fr. OE. heafuc, heafoc, hafoc, rel.
to OS. ha'Suc, ON. haukr, Swed. hok, Dan. heg,
MLG. havec, MDu., Du. havik, OHG. habuh,
MHG. habech, G. Habicht, 'hawk', and cogn.
with Russ. kpbec, a kind of falcon. These words
lit. mean 'seizer'. They derive fr. I.-E. *gabh-, a
var. of base *qap-, 'to seize', whence have and
heave. Cp. the first element in Hapsburg and
the second element in goshawk. L. accipiter,
'hawk', is not cognate with the above words.
Derivatives: hawk, tr. v., to hunt animals by
means of trained hawks, hawker (q.v.),
hawking, n.

## hawk
hawk, п., a small square board for holding
mortar. — Of unknown origin.

## hawk
hawk, intr. v., to clear one's throat. — Of
imitative origin.

## hawk
hawk, tr. v., to offer for sale. — Back formation
fr. hawker, 'vendor'.

## hawker
hawker, п., a falconer. — Formed fr. hawk, the
bird, with agential suff. -er.

## hawker
hawker, п., an itinerant vendor. — LG. hoker
(whence also G. Hoker), rel. to Du. heuker,
'retailer' (see huckster); influenced in form by
prec. word.

## hawse
hawse, п., ι) part of a ship's bow containing the
hawseholes; z) the hawseholes. — ME. liaise,
fr. ON. hals, 'neck; part of a ship's bow', which
is rel. to OS., OFris., LG., Du., OHG., MHG.,
G., Goth, hals, OE. heals, 'neck', and cogn.
with L. coitus (for *colsus), 'neck'. See collar and
cp. the first element in hauberk and in hausse-col.

## hawser
hawser, п., a large rope used for mooring, towing,
etc. (naut.) — Fr. earlier halser, lit. 'hoister', fr.
ME. halsen, 'to raise, lift, hoist', fr. OF. holder,
haucier (F. hausser), fr. VL. *altiare, 'to raise,
lift', fr. L. alius, 'high'. See alt and agential suff

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:364 COLUMN:2 -->
-er and cp. hance, enhance.

## hawthorn
hawthorn, n. — ME. hawethorn, fr. OE. haguporn,
hxgporn, compounded of haga, 'enclosure,
hedge', and porn, 'thorn', hence lit. meaning
'hedge thorn', i.e. 'thorns used for making
hedges'; rel. to ON. hagporn, MHG. hagendorn,
hagedorn, G. Hagedorn, 'hawthorn'. See haw,
'enclosure', and thorn.

## hay
hay, п., grass mown. — ME. haye, hey, fr. OE.
hleg, hig, heg, rel. to OS. hoi, ON. hey, Dan. he,
Swed. ho, Norw. hey, OFris. ha, he, MDu. hoy,
hooy, Du. hooi, OHG. houwi, hewi, MHG.
houwe, hou, G. Ней, Goth, hawi, 'hay', lit. 'that
which is to be cut', or 'that which is cut'. Cp.
OE. heawan, 'to cut', and see hew.
Derivative: hay, tr. v., to supply with hay.

## bay
bay, п., a kind of country-dance. — OF. haye,
of uncertain origin.

## hay
hay, n„ a hedge (archaic). — ME. hai, hei, a
blend of OE. hege, 'hedge', and F. haie, of s.m.
F. haie is a loan word fr. Frankish "hagja, which
is rel. to OHG. hegga, OE. hege, 'hedge', OE.
hecg, of s.m. See hedge and cp. the first element
in haybote, hayward.

## haybote
haybote, п., the right of the tenant to take thorns
or wood for repairing his hedge or fence. —
Compounded of hay, 'hedge', and bote (qq.v.)

## haydenite
haydenite, п., a variety of chabazite (mineral.) —
Named after the American dentist Horace H.
Hayden (1769-1844), who discovered it. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hayward
hayward, п., an officer appointed for the
inspection of hedges and fences. — ME. heiward,
compounded of hei, 'hedge' and ward. See hay,
'hedge', and ward, 'one who guards'.

## hazard
hazard, п., ι) a game played with dice; 2) chance;
3) risk. — OF. (= F.) hasard, fr. Sp. azar,
'unfortunate throw at dice, unforeseen accident',
usually derived fr. Arab, al-zahr (pronounced
az-zahr), 'the die'. This derivation is rightly
doubted by most lexicographers (see e.g.Devic's
Supplement to Littre's Dictionnaire de la langue
francaise, s.v. hasard, and Skeat's Etymological
Dictionary, s.v. hazard), owing to the fact that
the word zahr does not occur in the dictionaries
of Classical Arabic. According to my opinion
Sp. azar derives fr. Arab, yasara, 'he played at
dice'; ζ is the regular Spanish equivalent of
Arabic s. — The d in OF. hasard (whence E.
hazard) is due to a confusion of the ending -ar
with suff. -ard (see -ard).
Derivatives: hazard, v. (q.v.), hazard-ous, adj.
(cp. F. hasardeux), hazard-ous-ly, adv., hazard-
ous~ness, п., hazard-ry, n.

## hazard
hazard, tr. v. — F. hasarder, fr. hasard. See prec.
word.

## haze
haze, п., fog, mist. — Prob. back formation
fr. hazy.
Derivative: haze, tr. v., to make hazy; intr. v.,
to become hazy.

## haze
haze, tr. v., to harass. — OF. haser, 'to vex,
irritate', of unknown origin.

## hazel
hazel, n. ■— ME. hasel, fr. OE. hxsel, hxsl, rel.
to ΟΝ., Norw. hasl, Dan., Swed. hassel, MLG.,
MDu. hasel, Du. hazelaar, OHG. hasal, MHG.,
G. hasel, 'hazel', and cogn. with L. corulus,
corylus (for *kozulus), 'hazel, filbert tree', Olr.,
OCo., W., Bret, coll (for *coslo-), 'hazel', perh.
also with OLith. kasulas, 'a hunting spear' (so
called because it was usually made of hazel
wood). Cp. Corylus.
Derivatives: hazel, hazel-ed, hazel-ly, adjs.

## hazing
hazing, п., the act of harassing. — Formed fr.
haze, 'to harass', with -ing, suff. forming verbal
nouns.

## hazy
hazy, adj., characterized by haze. — Of unknown
origin. Cp. haze, 'fog'.
Derivatives: hazi-Iy, adv., hazi-ness, n.

## hazzan
hazzan, chazzan, also spelled hazan, chazan, п.,
Jewish cantor. — Mishnaic Heb. and Aram.
hazzan, 'superintendent, officer', later 'cantor',
prob. borrowed fr. Akkad. hazanu, hazannu,
'chief magistrate of a town' (cp. Aram, hazzane
matha, 'superintendents of the town', Talmud
Babha Metzi'a, 93Л). It is very probable,
however, that Akkad. hazanu was borrowed from a
WSem. language and that the word orig. meant
'overseer', from a verb meaning 'to see'; cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:364 COLUMN:3 -->
Heb. hazu", Aram, hazu, 'he saw'. (In Akkadian,
the verb haza, 'to see', does not occur; if it had
existed, hazanu might be its derivative.) If
Akkad. hazanu is a WSem. loan word, then Heb.
and Aram, hazzan were reborrowed from
Akkadian. See Heinrich Zimmern, Akkadisohe
Fremdworter als Beweis fur babylonischen
KultureinfluB, Leipzig, 1917, p.6, Note 3.

## he
he, nom. sing, of the 3rd pers. masc. pron. —
ME. he, fr. OE. hi [fern, heo, hio, neut. hit; pi.
(for all genders) hi, hie], rel. to OS., OFris. he,
hi, MDu. he, hi, Du. hij, OHG. hi, 'he', Goth,
neut. hita (ace), 'it', masc. himma'(dat.) (in
himma daga, 'on this day'), masc. hina (ace.)
(in und hina daga, 'until that day'), and to the
first element in OE. heodxg, OS. hiudu, OFris.
hiude, MDu. huden, OHG. hiutu, MHG. hiute,
G. heute, 'today' (for the second element, which
appears in its full form only in OE. heo-dxg,
see day); fr. Teut. base *hi-, corresponding to
I.-E. base *ki-, 'this one', whence also Hitt. ki,
'this', Gk. έ-κεΐ, 'there', Ion. Gk. κεΐ-νος,
Aeol. κη-νος, Gk. έ-κεΐ-νος, 'that person or
thing', σή-μερον, 'today' (for *κιάμερον, lit.
'this day', fr. I.-E. *kyo-, 'this', and Gk. ήμέρϊ,
'day'), L. cis, citer, citra, 'on this side', ce- and
-ce, emphatic particles meaning 'here, there',
OSlav. si, Lith. sis, 'this*. Cp. him, her, it, hence,
here, hither. Cp. also cede, cis-, citra-, cy-pres,
et cetera, hodiernal, sic.

## he
he, п., name of the 5th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb. he, probably meaning 'lattice
window'.

## head
head, n. — ME. heved, hed, fr. OE. heafod, rel.
to OS. hdtid, ON. hofud, Dan. hoved, Swed.
huvud, OFris. haved, hafd, MDu. hovet, hooft,
Du. hoofd, OHG. houbit, houpit, MHG. houbet,
houbt, houpt, G. Haupt, Goth, haubip, 'head',
and cogn. with OI. kaput-, 'head' (in kapuccha-
lam, 'hair of the hind part of the head'), L.
caput, 'head'. See capital, adj.
Derivatives: head, v., head-ed, adj., head-er, п.,
head-ing, п., head-y, adj., head-i-ly, adv., head-
i-ness, n.

## -head
-head, a rare collateral form of suff. -hood.

## headless
headless, adj. — ME. hevedles, hedles, fr. OE.
heafodleas. See head and -less,

## headlong
headlong, adv. — ME. hedling, formed with adv.
suff. -ling fr. hed, 'head'; see head. The form
headtong(fot *headling) is due to folk-etymolog-
ical association with -long (cp. sidelong).

## headman
headman, n. — ME. hevedman, hedman, fr. OE.
heafodman, fr. heafod, 'head', and man, 'man'.
See head and man and cp. ON. hofudsmadr,
Swed. huvudman, OHG. houbitman, MHG.
houbetman, 'headman, leader, chief, G. Haupt-
mann, 'captain'. Cp. also hetman.

## heal
heal, tr. and intr. v. — ME. helen, fr. OE. hxlan,
rel. to OS. helian, ON. heila, OFris. hela, Du.
heelen, OHG., MHG., G. heilen, Goth, ga-hail-
jan, 'to heal'. These verbs lit. mean 'to make
whole', and are denominated fr. OE. hSI, 'whole',
resp. its equivalents in the other Teut.
languages. See whole and cp. hale, 'healthy'.
Derivatives: heal-er, п., heal-ing, n. and adj.,
heal-ing-Iy, adv.

## heald
heald, п., a heddle. — ME. helde, fr. OE. hefeld.
See heddle.

## health
health, n. — ME. helthe, fr. OE. held, lit.
'wholeness', formed fr. hal, 'whole', with suff. -д. See
heal and substantial suff. -th. For sense
development cp. Heb. shalom, 'completeness,
wholeness, health, peace', fr. shaUm, 'was
complete, was safe'.
Derivatives: health-ful, adj., health-ful-ly, adv.,
health-ful-ness, п., health-y, adj., health-i-ly, adv.,
health-i-ness, n.

## heap
heap, n. — ME. heap, heep, hepe, 'troop, heap',
fr. OE. heap, 'troop, band, multitude', rel. to
OS. hop, MLG. hupe, Du. hoop, OHG. hufo,
houf, MHG. hufe, houfe, G. Haufe, 'heap', fr.
I.-E. base *qeu-p-, 'to bend, arch, vault', whence
also OSlav. кирй, Lith. kaupas, 'heap', kupra,
'hump'. See cup and cp. hive and hope, 'troop'.
Cp. also howitzer, Skupshtina.

## heap
heap, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hepen, fr. OE. hea-
pian, 'to heap', fr. heap. See heap, n.
Derivative: heap-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:365 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HEAR | 338 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:365 COLUMN:1 -->

## hear
hear, tr. and intr. v. — ME. heren, it. OE. hieran,
hyran, heron, rel. to ON. heyra, Swed. hdra,
Dan. here, OS. hdrian, OFris. hira, hdra, Du.
horen, OHG. hdran, hdrren, MHG. haren, G.
horen, Goth, hausjan, it. I.-E. base *(s)qeu-,
*(s)qeu-, 'to look at, observe, perceive', whence
also OI. kavih, 'wise', Gk. κοεϊν, 'to mark,
perceive, hear', and prob. also άκούειν (with copul.
pref. ά-), 'to hear'. See show and cp. hark, bear-
ken. Cp. also acoustic.
Derivatives: hear-er, п., hear-ing, a.

## heard
heard, past tense and pp. of hear. — ME. herde,
fr. OE. herde, fr. heran, 'to hear'. See hear.

## hearken
hearken, intr. and tr. v. (the latter is archaic). —
ME. herknien, herknen, fr. OE. heorcnian,
hyrcnian, rel. to OFris. harkia, herkla and to
E. hark (q.v.)
Derivative: hearken-er, n.

## hearse
hearse, n. — ME. herce, herse, fr. MF. herce
(F. herse), 'harrow; portcullis; triangular frame
for holding candles',. fr. L. hirpicem, ace. of
hirpex, 'harrow*, fr. Samnite hirpus, 'wolf';
so called in allusion to the teeth of the harrow,
which resemble the teeth of a wolf. Samnite
hir-pus is rel. to L. hir-cus, 'he-goat'. Both these
words are prob. rel. to L. hir-sulus, 'shaggy,
prickly, bristly'. See hirsute and cp, rehearse.
Derivative: hearse, tr. v.

## heart
heart, n. — ME. herle, hert, fr. OE. heorte, rel.
to OS. herta, ON. hjarla, OFris. herte, hirte,
ODu. herta, Du. hart, OHG. herza, MHG.
herze, G. Herz, Goth, hairtd, 'heart', and cogn.
with Hitt. kardiash (gen.), 'of the heart', Arm.
sir! (for *klrdi-), Gk. καρδία, poet, κήρ, L. cor
(gen. cordis), OSlav. srudlce, Russ. serdce,
'heart', Lith. Sinus, 'heart', OPruss. seyr (for
*klrd), ace. siran, Olr. cride, Ir. croidhe, 'heart',
W. craidd, 'heart; center', Bret, kreiz, 'middle',
OSlav. srida, Russ. seredd, 'middle', Avestic
z'r'daya-, 'middle'. For sense development cp.
Heb. libh, 'heart', and lebh yam, 'the midst (lit.
the heart) of the sea', lebh hd'eld", 'the midst
of the terebinth', Akkad. libbu, 'heart; middle'.
Cp. cordate, cordial, core, accord, accordion,
codling, 'a variety of apple', courage, concord,
discord, misericord, record. Cp. also cardiac,
cardio-, carditis, endocardium, epicardiuin,
pericardium. L. credere, 'to believe', is not related
to L. cor, 'heart' (see creed).
Derivatives: heari, tr. and intr. v., heart-ed, adj.,
heart-ed-ly, adv., heart-en, tr. and intr. v., heart-
en-er, п., heart-y, adj., heart-i-Iy, adv., heart-i-
ness, п., heart-less, adj., heart-less-ly, adv., heart-
less-ness, a.

## henrth
henrth, n. — ME. herth, fr. OE. heord, rel. to OS.,
OFris. herth, MDu. hert, Du. hoard, OHG.
herd, MHG. hert, G. Herd, 'hearth', fr. Teut.
base *her-, corresponding to I.-E. base *ker-,
'to singe, burn, glow', whence also Goth, hauri,
'coal', ON. hyrr, 'fire', OI. kudayati, kulayati,
'singes', OSlav. kurjo, kuriti se, 'to smoke',
Lith. kuriii, kurti, Lett, kuru, kuft, 'to heat',
Lith. karstas, 'hot', kafstis, 'heat', Lett, kafsts,
'hot', kafst, 'to grow hot', and prob. also L..
carbd, 'coal, charcoal'; see carbon. Cp. cremate.

## heat
heat, n. — ME. hete, Fr. OE. hztu, hSto, rel. to
OS. hittia, ON. hiti, Dan. hede, Swed. hetta,
OFris. hete, Du. hitte, OHG. hizzea, hizza,
heizi, MHG., G. hitze, 'heat', OE. hxda, 'hot
weather', Goth, heito, 'fever', and to OE. hat,
etc., 'hot', see hot. It. izza, 'wrath, anger', is a
Teut. loan word.

## heat
heat, tr. and intr. v. — ME. heten, fr. OE. hxtan,
'to heat', fr. hstu, 'heat'. See heat, n.
Derivatives: heat-ed, adj., heat-ed-ly, adv.,
heater, п., heat-ing, n.

## heath
heath, n. — ME. heth, fr. OE. hid, "heath (land);
heath (the plant), heather', rel. to OS. hetha,
ON. heidr, Dan. hede, Swed. hed, 'heath', OHG.
heida, 'heather', MHG., G., Du. heide, 'heath;
heather', Goth, haipi, 'field', and cogn. with
Gaulish ceto- in Gaulish-Latin place names like
Cetobriga, etc., and with Olr. ciad, OW. coit,
W. coed, OCo. curl, Bret, coer (for *kaito-),
'wood, forest', but L. bucetum, 'cow pasture',
is not cognate. Cp. heathen, heather.
Derivative: heath-y, adj.

## henthen
henthen, n. — ME. hethen, fr. OE. hxden, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:365 COLUMN:2 -->
and п., rel. to OS. hethin, adj., ON. heidinn, adj.,
OFris. hethen, adj., MDu. heidijn, heiden, Du.
heiden, п., OHG. heidan, MHG. heiden, adj.,
OHG. heidano, MHG. heiden, G. Heide, п.,
'heathen', Goth, haipno, 'heathen woman'.
These words prob. meant orig. 'dwelling on the
heath'. See prec. word and cp. hoyden.
Derivatives: heathen, adj., heathenish (q.v.),
heathenism, heathenize, heathenry (qq.v.)

## heathendom
heathendom, n. — ME., fr. OE. hxoendom,
'paganism', fr. hxden. See prec. word and -dom.

## heathenesse
heathenesse, п., heathenism (archaic). — ME.
hethenesse, fr. OE. hxdennes, lit. 'heathenness'.
See heathen and -ness.

## heathenish
heathenish, adj. — OE. hsdenisc, rel. to OHG.
heidanisc, G. heidnisch, 'heathenish'. See heathen
and adj. suff. -ish.
Derivatives: heathenish-ly, adv., heathenish-
ness, n.

## heathenism
heathenism, n. — A hybrid coined fr. heathen and
-ism, a surf, of Greek origin.

## heathenize
heathenize, tr. v., to render heathen; intr. v., to
become heathen. — A hybrid coined fr. heathen
and -iie, a sun*, of Greek origin.

## heathenry
heathenry, n. — A hybrid coined fr. heathen and
-ry, a suff. of L.-F. origin.

## heather
heather, п., a plant of the heath family. — ME.
hather, hadder, possibly derived fr. heth, 'heath,
heather'. See heath.
Derivative: heather-y, adj.

## heaume
heaume, п., a kind of large helmet, — F., fr. OF.
helme, fr. Frankish 'helm, which is rel. to OHG.
helm. See helmet.

## heave
heave, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hebben, heren, fr.
OE. hebban, 'to lift, raise', rel. to OS. hebbian,
ON. he/ja, Du. heffen, OHG. heffan, MHG.
heben, hewn, G. heben, Goth, hafjan, 'to lift,
raise', and to OE. habban, etc., 'to hold,
possess, have'. See have and cp. henvy. Cp. also
heddle.
Derivatives: heave, п., heav-er, n.

## heaven
heaven, n. — ME. heovene, hevene, heven, fr. OE.
heofon, hefon, rel. to OS. heban, LG. heben,
heren, ON. himinn, Goth, himins, OS., OHG.
himil, OFris. himel, himul, MDu., Du. hemel,
MHG. himel, G. Himmel, 'heaven, sky'. These
words prob. derive fr. Teut. base *hama(n)-, fr.
I.-E. base *icem-, *kam-, 'to cover'. See chemise
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: heaven, tr. v., heaven-ish, adj.,
heaven-ish-ly, adv., heavenly (q.v.)

## heavenly
heavenly, adj. — ME. hevenly, fr. OE. heofonlic.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ly.
Derivative: heavenli-ness, n.

## heavenly
heavenly, adv. (archaic). — ME. hevenly, fr. OE.
heofonlice, fr. heofonlic. See henven and adv.
suff. -ly.

## heavily
heavily, adv. — ME. hevily, fr. OE. hefiglice. See
heavy and adv. suff. -ly.

## heaviness
heaviness, n. — ME. hevinesse, fr. OE. hefigness.
See heavy and -ness.

## Heavlside layer
Heavlside layer, п., a layer of ionized air from
about 60 to ioo miles above the earth. — Named
after the English physicist Oiiver Heaviside
(1850-1925).

## heavy
heavy, adj. — ME. hevy, fr. OE. hefig, rel. to OS.
heVig, OHG. hebig, hevig, LG. hevig, ON.
hofugr, hdfigr, 'heavy', and to OE. hefe, 'weight',
hebban, 'to lift, raise'. See heave and -y
(representing OE. -ig).

## heavy
heavy, adv., heavily. — ME. hevy, fr. OE. hefige,
fr. hefig. See heavy, adj.

## hebdomad
hebdomad, п., a group of seven things; a week.
— L. hebdomas, gen. -adis, fr. Gk. έβδομάς, gen.
-άδος, fr. έβδομος, 'seventh', which is formed
with suff. -μος, fr. έ7ττά, 'seven'. See hepta- and
-ad and cp. seventh. The Greek suff. -μος forms
ordinal numerals and is cogn. with OI. -mah,
Hitt. -ma, L. -mus, OLith. and OPruss. -mas,
Ir. -mad (cp. e.g. OI. saptamah, Hitt. shiptama,
L. septimus, OLith. sikmas, OPruss. seplmas,
Ir. sechtmad, 'seventh'.

## hebdomadal
hebdomadal, adj., occurring every seventh day,
weekly. — Late L. hebdomadalis, fr. L.
hebdomas, gen. -adis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.

## hebdomadary
hebdomadary, adj., hebdomadal. — ML. hebdo-
madarius, fr. L. hebdomas, gen. -adis. See
hebdomad and adj. suff. -ary.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:365 COLUMN:3 -->

## Hebe
Hebe, п., the goddess of youth in Greek
mythology. — L„ fr. Gk. "Ηβη, name of the goddess of
youth, fr. ήβη,'youth, strength of youth', which
prob. stands for I.-E. *yegwa-, whence also
Lett. j(ga, 'strength, understanding, intellect',
Lith. nuo-jega, 'power, ability'. Cp. ephebus.

## hebe-
hebe-, combining form denoting puberty or the
pubes. — Fr. Gk. ήβη, 'youth, pubescence,
puberty, the pubes'. See prec. word.

## hebephrenia
hebephrenia, п., adolescent insanity (med.) —
Medical L., coined by the German psychiatrist
Ewald Hecker in 1871 fr. Gk. ήβη, 'youth,
puberty', and φρήν, gen. φρενός, 'mind'. See
Hebe, phrenetic and -ia.
Derivative: hebephren-ic, adj.

## hebetate
hebetate, tr. v., to make blunt or dull. — L. hebe-
tatus, pp. of hebetare, 'to make blunt or dull',
fr. hebes, gen. hebetis, 'blunt', whence also
hebere, 'to be blunt or dull'; of uncertain origin.

## hebetude
hebetude, п., dullness. — F., fr. L. hebetudinem,
ace. of hebetude, 'dullness', fr. hebere. See prec.
word and -ode.

## Hebraic
Hebraic, adj. — Late L. Hebraicus, fr. Gk.
"Εβραϊκός, fr. 'Εβραίος, 'Hebrew'. See Hebrew
and -ic
Derivative: Hebraic-al-ly, adv.

## Hebraism
Hebraism, n. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk.
"Εβραίος. See prec. word.

## Hebraist
Hebraist, n. — Formed with suff. -ist fr. Gk.
'Εβραίος. See Hebraic.
Derivatives: Hebraist-ic, adj., Hebraistic-al-ly,
adv.

## Hebraize
Hebraize, tr. and intr. v. — Gk. έβραίζειν, 'to
speak Hebrew' (whence also F. hebratser), fr.
'Εβραίος. See next word and -ize.

## Hebrew
Hebrew, n. and adj. — ME. Ebreu, fr. OF. Ebreu,
Ebrieu (F. Hibreu), fr. L. Hebraeus, fr. Gk.
'Εβραίος, fr. Aram, 'ibhray, 'ebhrdy, fr. Heb.
'ibhrt, 'Hebrew', lit. 'he who came from across
(the River)', fr. 'ebher, 'region across, side',
from the stem of 'abhor, 'he passed across or
over', which is rel. to Aram.-Syr. 'abhar, Arab.
'abara, 'he passed across', Akkad. eberu, 'to
pass over', Heb. 'ebhrah, 'fury, anger' (lit.
'overflow'), Mishnaic Heb. 'dbheraK, 'transgression,
sin' (for sense development ср. Е. transgression),
Heb. ma'abhdr, mtfabhura", 'ford, pass'. Cp.
Habiru. Cp. also averah.

## Hecate
Hecate, also Hekate, п., an ancient Greek
goddess, daughter of the Titan Perseus and Asteria
(Greek mythol.) — L. Hecate, fr. Gk. 'Εκάτη,
shortened fr. έκατηβόλος, which was regarded
already by the ancients as an enlarged form of
έκηβόλρς and accordingly explained as 'far-
darting, far-shooting'. See Hecuba.

## hecatomb
hecatomb, п., a sacrifice of a hundred oxen
(Greek antiq.) — F. hicatombe, it. Gk.
εκατόμβη, which is compounded of Ικατόν, 'a
hundred', and the stem of βοϋς, Όχ'. Gk.
εκατόν is formed fr. έν, 'one', or fr. ά- (fr. I.-E.
*sm-, 'one'), and *κατόν (fr. I.-E. 'femtom,
'hundred'). Accordingly εκατόν lit. means 'one
hundred' (cp. OI. sa-hasram, 'one thousand').
See heno- and hundred. For the second element
in Gk. εκατόμβη see bovine.

## Hecatombaeon
Hecatombaeon, п., name of the 1st month of the
Attic Greek calendar (corresponding to July-
August). — Gk. Έκατομβαιών, lit. 'the month
in which έκατόμβαι (i.e. a hundred oxen) were
sacrificed at Athens'. See prec. word.

## hecaton-
hecaton-, combining form meaning 'a hundred'.
— Gk. See hecatomb.

## heck
heck, п., frame for holding the warp threads. —
Dial. var. of hatch, 'door' (q.v.) Cp. hnck,
'board'.

## heckelphone
heckelphone, п., baritone oboe (mus.) — G.
Heckelphon, a hybrid coined fr. Wilhelm
Heckel, name of the inventor, who introduced
it in 1905, and Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See
phone, 'speech sound'.

## heckle
heckle, tr. v., 1) to hackle; 2) to embarrass the
speaker with questions. — ME. hekelen, it.
hekele, 'an instrument for cleansing and carding
flax or hemp'. See hatchel and cp. hackle.
Derivatives: heck-ler, п., heckl-ing, n.

## hect-
hect-, form of hectoJ before a vowel.

## hectare
hectare, n„ a surface measure containing 100
ares. — F., lit. 'a hundred ares', a hybrid coined

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:366 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 339 | HEIR -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:366 COLUMN:1 -->
in 1795 by a decree of the French National
Convention fr. Gk. εκατόν, 'a hundred', and L.
area, 'a vacant piece of ground'. See hecto- and
are, 'a square unit'.

## hectic
hectic, adj., 1) consumptive; 2) feverish. — F.
heclique, fr. Late L. hecticus, fr. Gk. έκτικός,
'habitual; consumptive', formed with suff.
-ικός, fr. έκτος, 'that which one may have' (in
the neut. pi. τα έκτα, 'the qualities of
substances'), verbal adj. of £χειν, 'to have, hold,
possess' (whence also έξις, 'being in a certain
condition, state of mind'). See scheme and -ic
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also Hector,
apocha, cachexy, cleruch, daduchus, Echeneis,
entelechy, epoch, eunuch, Ophiochus, pleonexia,
Stylochus.
Derivatives: hectic, п., hectic-al, adj.,
hectic-ally, adv.

## hecto-
hecto-, before a vowel hect-, combining form
meaning 'a hundred'. — F. hecto-, hect-,
arbitrarily shortened fr. Gk. εκατόν, 'a hundred'
(see hecatomb); introduced by the French
National Convention.

## hectocotylize
hectocotylize, tr. v., to change into a hectoco-
tylus. — See next word and -ize.
Derivative: hectocotyliz-ation, n,

## hectocotylus
hectocotylus, п., one of the tentacles of the males
of certain cephalopods. — ModL. name coined
by the French naturalist, Baron Georges-Leo-
pold-Chretien-Frederic-Dagobert Cuvier (orig.
meant to denote a supposed parasite);
compounded of becto- and Gk. κοτύλη, 'anything
hollow, a cup'. See cotyledon.

## hectogram
hectogram, п., weight of 100 grammes. — F.
hectogramme, coined fr. hecto- and F. gramme,
'gram', fr. Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written'.
See gram.

## hectograph
hectograph, n„ a device for multiplying a writing.
— Compounded of hecto- and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: hectograph, tr. v., heclograph-ic,
adj., hectograph-y, n.

## hectoliter
hectoliter, hectolitre, п., measure of 1000 liters.
— F. hectolitre, coined fr. hecto- and F. litre.
See liter.

## hectometer
hectometer, hectometre, п., measure of 100
meters. — F. hectometre, coined fr. hecto- and
F. metre, 'meter'. See meter, 'measure of unit'.

## Hector
Hector, п., ι) in Homer's Iliad, the eldest son of
Priam and Hecuba, and the greatest Trojan
hero; 2) masc. PN. — L., fr. Gk. "Εκτωρ, fr.
έκτωρ, 'holder, stayer', agent noun formed fr.
εχειν, 'to have, hold, possess'. See hectic.

## hector
hector, п., blusterer, bully. — Fr. prec. word.
Derivative: hector, tr. and intr. v.

## Hecuba
Hecuba, п., principal wife of Priam and mother
of Hector. — L., fr. 'Εκάβη,prob. short for *έκα-
βόλος (whence through metrical lengthening
έκηβόλος), which is of uncertain origin and
meaning. It possibly means lit.—as
explained already by the ancients—'far-darting, far-
shooting', fr. έκάς, 'far, afar, far off', and
-βόλος, 'thrower. Gk. έκάς stands for *σίε-κάς,
'by or for himself, which contains the base of
the reflexive pronoun (see sui-) and the suff.
-κάς (appearing also in άνδρα-κάς, 'man by
man'), and is cogn. with OI. ёка-sah, 'single'.
Gk.- -βόλος, 'thrower', is rel. to βάλλειν, 'to
throw, cast'; see ballistic. — Cp. Hecate.

## heddle
heddle, п., (a term of weaving). — Formed with
metathesis fr. OE. hefeld, hefel, hebeld, hebel,
'thread for weaving', for orig. *haf-ild, from the
root of OE. hebban, 'to lift, raise'. Cp. MLG.
hevelt, ON. hafald, 'heddle' and see heave. Cp.
also heald.
Derivative: heddle, tr. v.

## hedenberglte
hedenberglte, п., a calcium iron pyroxene
(mineral.) — Named after the Swedish chemist
M. A. Ludwig Hedenberg. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## Hedeoma
Hedeoma, п., a genus of plants, the mock
pennyroyal (pot.) — ModL., altered fr. Gk. ήδύοσμον,
'the mint', prop. neut. of the adj. ήδύοσμας,
'sweet-smelfing, fragrant*, which is compounded
of ηδύς, 'sweet', and οσμή, 'scent, odor'; so
called in allusion to the fragrant blossoms. See
hedonic and osmium.

## heder
heder, cheder, п., Jewish school for little children.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:366 COLUMN:2 -->
— Yiddish kheyder, fr. Heb. heder, lit. 'room',
rel. to Punic h-d-r, 'sepulchral vault', h-d-r-t,
'chamber in the sanctuary', Arab, hidr,
'sanctuary', and prob. also to Ethiop. khadara, 'he
dwelled'.

## Hedera
Hedera, п., a genus of woody vines of the
ginseng family (bot.) — L. hedera, 'ivy', prob. lit.
'the clasping plant', which possibly derives fr.
I.-E. base *ghed-, 'to clasp, reach, attain, hold',
whence also L. praeda (for "prai-heda), 'prey',
prehendere, 'to grasp, seize, take hold of. See
prehensile and cp. lierre.

## hederaceous
hederaceous, adj., pertaining to ivy. — L. hede-
raceus, f r. hedera,4vy*. See prec. word and -aceous.
Derivative: hederaceous-ly, adv.

## hederal
hederal, adj., pertaining to ivy. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. hedera, 'ivy'. See Hedera.

## hederated
hederated, adj., crowned with ivy. — Formed
with suff. -ed fr. L. hederatus, fr. hedera, 'ivy'.
See Hedera.

## hederic
hederic, adj., pertaining to ivy. — Formed with
suff. -ic fr. L. hedera, 'ivy'. See Hedera.

## hedge
hedge, n. — ME. hegge, fr. OE. hecg, rel. to MDu.
hegge, Du. heg, OHG. hegga, MHG. hegge,
hecke, G. Песке, 'hedge', ON. heggr, 'the bird
cherry (tree)', prop, 'a tree used for making
hedges', and in gradational relationship to OE.
haga, OS. hago, 'hedge', fr. I.-E. base *qagh-,
'to encompass, enclose', whence also L. caulae
(prop, a dimin. of 'cava, fr. orig. *qagha), 'a
hole, sheepfold, enclosure', Gaul, caia, 'circum-
vallation', W. cae, 'fence, hedge', Co. кё, 'hedge'.
Cp. haw and words there referred to. Cp. also
inchoate, quay.

## hedge
hedge, tr. and intr. v. — ME. heggen, fr. hegge,
'hedge'. See hedge, n.
Derivatives: hedg-er, п., hedg-ing, п., hedg-y,
adj.

## hedonic
hedonic, hedonlcal, adj., pertaining to pleasure. —
Gk. ηδονικός, fr. ηδονή, 'pleasure', fr. ηδύς,
'sweet', which stands for "swddu, 'sweet', and
is cogn. with L. suavis (for "suadvis), 'sweet',
OE. swete, 'sweet, pleasant'. See sweet and -k
and cp. the first element in Hedychium and the
second element in Moneses.

## hedonism
hedonism, п., the doctrine that pleasure is the
chief good (philos.) — Formed with suff. -ism
fr. Gk. ηδονή, 'pleasure'. See hedonic.

## hedonist
hedonist, п., an adherent of hedonism. — See
prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: hedonist-ic, adj., hedonist-ic-al-ly,
adv.

## -hedral
-hedral, combining form used to form adjectives
from nouns ending in -hedron, as in hexahedral.
— See -hedron and adj. suff. -al.

## -hedron
-hedron, combining form used to form nouns
with the meaning 'having a certain number of
faces' (said of geometrical solid figures), as in
hexahedron, polyhedron. — Gk. -εδρον, fr. έδρ£
(for *sedra-), 'seat; base, side, face', from the
stem of έζεσθαι, 'to seat oneself, to sit down',
which stands for *sezesthai and is cogn. with
L. sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary and cp. Ephedra,
exedra, Sanhedrin, hoiohedral.

## Hedwig
Hedwig, fern. PN. — G., fr. OHG. Haduwig, a
compound of two words which both mean
'strife, struggle'.

## Hedychium
Hedychium, п., a genus of plants of the Zingi-
beraceae family (bot.) — ModL., compounded
of Gk. ηδύς, 'sweet', and χιών, 'snow'. See
hedonic and cbjono-.

## Hedysarum
Hedysarum, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ήδύσαρον, 'the
sainfoin', compounded of ηδύς, 'sweet', and σάρον,
'broom; sweepings', which is rel. to σαίρειν,
'to sweep, clean'. See hedonic and syrma.

## heed
heed, tr. and intr. v. — ME. heden, heeden, fr.
OE. hedan, rel. to OS. hodian, OFris. hdda,
OHG. huotan, MHG. hiieten, G. hiiten, 'to
guard, watch', which are denominated fr. OS.

## hod
hod, resp. OFris. 'hod, OHG. huota, MHG.
huote, G. Hut, 'protection, care', OE. hod,
'hood'. See hood.

## heed
heed, n. — ME. hede, fr. heden. See heed, v.
Derivatives: heed-ful, adj., heed-ful-ly, adv.,

## heed-ful-ness
heed-ful-ness, п., heed-less, adj., heed-less-ty,
adv., heed-less-ness, n.

## heehaw
heehaw, п., ι) the bray of a donkey; 2) a guffaw,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:366 COLUMN:3 -->
intr. v., i) to bray like a donkey; 2) to guffaw. —
Imitative.

## heel
heel, п., the hind part of the foot. — ME. hele,
heele, fr. OE. hxla, hela, contracted fr. OE.
"hdhila, dimin. of OE. hah, 'heel'; rel. to ON.
hell, OFris. hel, hela, Du. hiel. See hock, 'joint',
and dimin. suff. -le.
Derivatives: heel, tr. v., to furnish with heels;
intr. v., to move one's heel, heel-er, n.

## heel
heel, intr. v., to lean to one side (said of ships). —
ME. helden, heelden, hielden, fr. OE. heldan,
hieldan, 'to lean, incline, bend down', rel. to
MLG., MDu. helden, Du. hellen, of s.m., OE.
heald, ON. hallr, OHG. hold, 'inclined', helden,
'to bow', OHG. halda, MHG., G. halde, 'slope,
declivity', OE., OS., OFris., OHG., MHG., G.
hold, ON. hollr, Goth, hulps, 'gracious, friendly',
lit. 'inclined', OE. hyldu, hyld, ON. hylli (for
*hylpi), OS. huldl, OFris. helde, MLG., Du.
hulde, OHG. huldl, MHG. hulde, G. Huld, 'favor,
grace'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *kel-,
'to bend, incline', whence also Lith. sails, 'side,
region'. Cp. hilding. For derivatives of base
*klei-, an enlargement of base *kel-, see clinical.
Derivative: heel-ing, n.

## heft
heft, п., ι) the act of heaving (dial.); 2) weight;
importance (colloq.) — Formed from the stem
of heave (q.v.); heft stands to heave as weft
stands to weave. Cp. haft.
Derivatives: heft, tr. v., 1) to lift; 2) to try (the
weight of something) by lifting; 3) to weigh,
heft-y, adj., muscular.

## Hegelian
Hegelian, adj., pertaining to the German
philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-
1831). For the ending see suff. -ian.
Derivatives: Hegelian, п., an adherent of Hegel
or his philosophy, Hegelian-ism, n„ the
philosophy of Hegel.

## hegemonic
hegemonic, adj., pertaining to hegemony;
leading. — Gk. ηγεμονικός, 'related to a leader',
fr. ήγεμών, gen. ήγεμόνος. See next word and -ic.
Derivative: hegemonic-al, adj.

## hegemony
hegemony, n. — Gk. ηγεμονία, 'leadership', fr.
ήγεμών, gen.. ήγεμόνος, 'leader', fr. ήγεΐσθαι
(Dor. άγεΐσθαι), 'to lead', orig. prob. 'to track
down the way', fr. I.-E. base *sag-, *s*g-, 'to
track down, trace, seek', whence also L. sagtre,
'to perceive quickly or keenly', sagus,
'presaging, predicting, prophetic', sdgax,
'sagacious', Goth, sokjan, OE. secan, 'to seek'. See
seek and -y (representing Gk. -ίϊ) and cp.
hegumen. Cp. also exegesis and words there
referred to.

## hegira
hegira, п., the flight of Mohammed from Mecca
(in 622). — Arab. hijrah, 'flight', fr. hajara, 'he
fled, emigrated'. Cp. Hagar.

## hegumen
hegumen, п., the first official in a monastery of an
Orthodox Eastern Church. — ML. hegumenus,
fr. Gk. ηγούμενος, lit. 'leading', pres. part, of
ήγεϊσθαι, 'to lead'. See hegemony. For the suff.
-μένος see alumnus and cp. words there
referred to.

## heifer
heifer, n. — ME. hay fare, fr. OE. hlahfore, of
uncertain origin.

## heigh
heigh, interj. — Imitative.

## heigh-ho
heigh-ho, interj. — Imitative.

## height
height, n. — ME. heighthe, heighte, fr. OE. hiehdu,
heahdu, hlhdu, 'height', rel. to ON. hxd, Dan.
heide, Swed. hojd, Du. hoogte, OHG. hohida,
Goth, hauhipa, 'height', and to OE. heah, 'high'.
See high and· subst. suff. -t.
Derivative: height-en, tr. and intr. v.

## heinous
heinous, adj., hateful. — ME. heynous, fr. OF.
haineus (F. haineux), 'full of hatred', fr. halne
(F. haine), 'hatred', fr. OF. (= F.) hair, 'to hate',
fr. Frankish "hatjan, which is rel. to OHG.
ha$30n, hasten, OE. hatian, 'to hate'. See hate,
v. and n. For the ending see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: heinous-ly, adv., heinous-ness, n.'

## heintzite
heintzite, п., a hydrous magnesium potassium
borate (mineral.) — G. Heintzit, named after
the German chemist Wilhelm Heinrich Heintz
(1817-80). The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ίτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## heir
heir, n. — ME., fr. OF. heir, eir (F. hoir), fr.
VL. *herem (whence also OProven?. er, 'heir'),
for L. heredem, ace. of heres, 'heir', prob. a
compound meaning 'he who obtains that which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:367 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HEIRDOM | 340 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:367 COLUMN:1 -->
is left'. The first element of this compound
derives fr. I.-E. base *ghe~(i)-, 'to lack, be empty;
to yawn', whence also Ol.jahati, 'leaves,
abandons, gives up', jihlte, 'goes away', Gk. χήρος,
'bereaved of, χαίνειν, 'to gape, yawn', χήτος,
'lack, want'. See go and cp. chori-. The second
element is *ld-. It is prob. formed from the
preposition *e, 'beside; close by' (which stands
in gradational relationship to prep. *o, 'close,
by', appearing in OI., Avestic a-, 'toward'; see
agama, 'Indian scripture'), and base 'do-, 'to
give'. See date, 'point of time'. Cp. heredity,
heritage, exheridate, inherit.
Derivatives: heir, tr. v., heirdom (q.v.), heirloom
(q.v.)

## heirdom
heirdom, n. — A hybrid coined fr. heir and suff.
-dom (fr. OE. -dom).

## heirloom
heirloom, n. — A hybrid coined fr. heir and loom
(this latter is here used in the original, now
obsol., sense 'tool, implement, piece of
furniture').

## heirship
heirship, n. — A hybrid formed fr. heir with suff.
-ship (fr. OE. -scipe).

## hejira
hejira, n. — See hegira.

## helcosis
helcosis, п., ulceration (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. ελκωσις, fr. έλκος, 'festering wound, sore,
ulcer', which is cogn. with L. ulcus. See ulcer
and -osis.

## held
held, past tense and pp. of hold. — ME. held, fr.
OE. heold, fr. healdan, haldan. See hold.

## Helen
Helen, fern. PN. — L. Helena (prob. through the
medium of F. Helene), fr. Gk. 'Ελένη, which
prob. derives fr. έλένη (Hesychius), 'torch of
reeds', a collateral form of έλάνη, of s.m. These
words, which have also the meaning 'bundle of
reeds', prob. derive from the stem of είλεΐν,
Att. είλεΐν, 'to roll, turn, twist'. See volute and
cp. Helenus, Helle.

## Helenium
Helenium, п., a genus of plants, the sneezeweed
(йог.) — L. helenium, 'elecampane', fr. Gk.
έλένιον, which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly derives fr. ε'λος, 'marsh, marsh meadow',
and was so called because it grows in humid
places. Gk. έλος stands for *se/os and is cogn.
with OI. saras-, 'pond'. Cp. Helonias.

## Helen of Troy
Helen of Troy, the beautiful sister of the Dioscuri,
and wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta (Greek
mythol.) — See Helen.

## Helenus
Helenus, п., a soothsayer, son of Priam, king of
Troy (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. "Ελενος,
which is rel. to 'Ελένη. See Helen.

## heliacal
heliacal, adj., pertaining to the sun. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. ηλιακός, 'of the sun',
fr. ήλιος, 'sun', which stands for 'sawelios and
is cogn. with L. sol (prob. fr. *sawel-, through
'sawdl, *sw6t), 'sun'. See Sol and cp. helio-,
anthelion, aphelion, ephelis, Heliothis, parhelion,
perihelion.

## heli-
heli-, form of helio- before a vowel.

## Helianthemum
Helianthemum, п., a genus of plants, the rock-
rose (bot.) — ModL., compounded of heii- and
Gk. άνθος, 'flower'. See anther.

## Helianthus
Helianthus, п., a genus of plants, the sun flower
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'sun flower', coined by
Linnaeus fr. Gk. ήλιος, 'sun', and άνθος,
'flower'. See heliacal and -anthus.

## helic-
helic-, form of helico- before a vowel.

## helical
helical, adj., having the form of a spiral. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. helix, gen.
helicis, 'coil, spiral'. See helix.
Derivative: helical-ly, adv.

## helico-
helico-, before a vowel helic-, combining form
meaning 'spiral'. — Gk. έλικο-, έλικ-, fr. έλιξ,
gen. άλικος, 'spiral'. See helix,

## helicogyre
helicogyre, п., a kind of helicopter. — Com
pounded of helico- and Gk. γύρος, 'circle, ring'.
See gyre.

## helicoid
helicoid, adj., spiral. — Gk. ελικοειδής, 'of spiral
form', compounded of έλιξ, gen. ελικος, 'spiral',
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
helical and -oid.
Derivative: helicoid, п., a screwlike surface.

## Helicon
Helicon, п., a mountain in Boeotia sacred to the
Muses. — L., fr. Gk. 'Ελικών (Boeotian
/ελίκων), lit. 'the tortuous mountain', fr. έλιξ, gen.
ϋλικος, 'spiral'. See helix.

## helicopter
helicopter, n. — F. helicoptere, compounded of
Gk. έλιξ, gen. ίλικος, 'coil, spiral', and πτερόν,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:367 COLUMN:2 -->
'wing'. See helix and ptero-.

## helicotrema
helicotrema, п., the opening connecting the two
scalae in the cochlea (anal.) — Medical L., fr.
F. helicolrime, a word coined by the French
anatomist Gilbert Breschet (1784-1845) fr. Gk.
δλιξ, gen. δλικος, 'spiral', and τρήμα, 'that
which is bored through, hole'. Accordingly
helicotrema lit. means 'hole in the cochlea (of the
ear)'. For the etymology of the first element see
helix. The second element is rel. to τι-τραν, Чо
rub, grind, pierce*, τείρειν, 'to rub away, wear
away', fr. I.-E. base *ter-, 'to rub, turn, twist',
whence also L. terere, 'to rub', OE. prawan, 'to
throw'. See throw. For the ending see suff. -ma.

## helio-
helio-, before a vowel heli-, combining form
denoting the sun. — Gk. ήλιο-, ήλι-, fr. ήλιος,
'sun'. See heliacal.

## heliocentric
heliocentric, adj., pertaining to the sun as the
center. — Compounded of helio- and centric.
Cp. geocentric.
Derivative: heliocentric-ism, n.

## heliochrome
heliochrome, п., photograph in natural colors. —
Compounded of helio- and Gk. χρώμα, 'color'.
See chrome.
Derivatives: heIiochrom-ic,_ud\., heliochrom-y, n.

## heliofngal
heliofngal, adj., tending to fly from the sun
(astron.) — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. ήλιος, 'sun',
L. fugere, 'to fly from, flee', and L. suff. -alis
(see helio-, fugacious and adj. suff. -al). The
correct form would be solifugal, in which both
elements are of Latin origin.

## heliogram
heliogram, п., a message conveyed by
heliograph. — Compounded of helio- and Gk.
γράμμα, 'that which is written'. See -gram.

## heliograph
heliograph, п., ι) an instrument for taking
photographs of the sun; 2) an instrument for
measuring the intensity of sunlight. — Compounded
of helio- and Gk. -γράφος, ίΓ.γράφειν, 'to write'.
See-graph.
Derivatives: heliograph, tr. v., heliograph-ic, adj.,
heliograph-y, n.

## heliogravure
heliogravure, п., photoengraving. — F.
heliogravure, a hybrid coined fr. Gk. ήλιος, 'sun',
and gravure, 'engraving', a word of Teut. origin.
See Helios and gravure.

## heliology
heliology, п., the study of the sun. —
Compounded of helio- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## heliometer
heliometer, п., an instrument for determining the
angular distance between two stars (astron.) —
F. heliomeire, orig. 'instrument for measuring
the diameter of the sun'; compounded of helio-
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.
Derivative: heliometr-y, n.

## Hellopsls
Hellopsls, п., a genus of plants, the oxeye (bot.)
— ModL., compounded of heli- and Gk. βψις,
'sight, appearance'. See -opsis.

## Helios
Helios, п., the sun aod in Greek mythology. —
Gk. "Ηλιος, personification of ήλιος, 'sun'. See
helio-.

## helioscope
helioscope, n„ a device for observing the sun
without injury to the eyes (astron.) — F.
helioscope, compounded of helio- and Gk. -σκόπιον,
fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scope.
Derivatives: helioscop-ic, adj., helioscop-y, n.

## heliosis
heliosis, п., injury caused to the body by
exposure to the sun (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
ήλίωσις, 'exposure to the sun', fr. ήλιοϋσθαι, 'to
be exposed to the sun', fr. ήλιος. See heliacal
and -osis.

## hellostat
hellostat, п., an instrument for reflecting the rays
of the sun in one direction. — ModL. heliostata
or ¥'. hiliostat, compounded of Gk. ήλιος, 'sun',
and στητός, 'placed, standing'. See heliacal and
static and cp. aerostat and words there referred to.
Derivative: heliostat-ic, adj.

## heliotherapy
heliotherapy, n„ treatment of disease by
sunlight. — Compounded of helio- and -therapy.

## Heliothis
Heliothis, п., a genus of moths, the bollworm
(zool.) — ModL., irregularly formed fr. Gk.
ήλιώτις, 'the dawn', prop. fern, of the adjective
ήλιώτης, meaning 'of the sun', fr. ήλιος. See
heliacal.

## heliotrope
heliotrope, п., orig. a plant that turns to the sun;
now any plant of the borage family, with
fragrant purple or white flowers. — F. heliotrope,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:367 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. L. heliotropium, fr. Gk. ήλιοτρόπιον,
'heliotrope', lit. 'that which turns toward the sun',
fr. ήλιος, 'sun', and -τρόπος, 'turning', fr.
τρέπειν, 'to turn'. See helio- and trope,

## heliotropic
heliotropic, adj., characterized by heliotropism.
— See next word and -tropic.
Derivative: heliotropic-al-ly, adv.

## heliotropism
heliotropism, п., tendency of a plant to turn
toward the sun's rays. — Compounded of helio-,
Gk. τρόπος or τροπή, 'a turning', and suff. -ism.
See trope, tropism and cp. geotropism,
hydrotropism, hygrotropism, nyctitropism, orthotropism,
selenotropism.

## Heliotropium
Heliotropium, п., a genus of plants, the turnsole
(bot.) — ModL. See heliotrope.

## heliotype
heliotype, п., picture produced by heliotypy. —
Compounded of helio- and type.

## heliotypography
heliotypography, п., a process of photoengraving.
— Compounded of helio- and typography,

## heliotypy
heliotypy, п., process in which prints are made
from a gelatin film exposed under a negative. —
See heliotype and subst. suff. -y.

## Heliozoa
Heliozoa, n. pi., an order of protozoans (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'sun animals', fr. helio- and ζωι, pi.
of ζωον, 'animal'. See zoo-.
Derivatives: heliozo-an, adj. and n.

## helium
helium, п., name of a gaseous element (chem.) —
MridL., fr. Gk. ήλιος, 'the sun'; so called by
the English astronomer Sir Joseph Norman
Lockyer (1836-1920) and the English chemist
Sir Edward Frankland (1825-99), because it was
first observed by them in the spectrum of the
sun (in 1868, during an eclipse). See heliacal
and -ium.

## helix
helix, п., spiral line. — L., fr. Gk. ϋλιξ (for
*5έλιξ), 'spiral, coil', from the stem of έλίσσειν
(for *5ελίκιειν), 'to turn about, wind, roll',
fr. I.-E. base *wel-, 'to bend, turn, twist, roll'.
See volute and words there referred to and cp.
esp. Helicon, helminth.

## hell
hell, n. — ME. helle, it. OE. hell, rel. to OS. hellja,
ON. hel, OFris. helle, hille, Du. hel, OHG. hel-
lia, hella, MHG. helle, G. Mile, Goth, halja,
'hell', lit. 'that which hides', fr. I.-E. base *kel-,
'to hide, conceal', whence also OE. heatt, hall,
'hall'. See hall.
Derivatives: hell-ish, adj., hell-ish-ly, adv., hell-
ish-ness, n.

## hellbender
hellbender, п., a large aquatic salamander. —
Formed fr. hell, bend, v., and agential suff. -er.

## Helle
Helle, п., the daughter of Athamas and Nephele,
who was drowned in the strait which was called
the Hellespont (now = the Dardanelles) after
her. — L„ fr. Gk. "Ελλη, which is of uncertain
origin. It possibly means 'the bright one', and
is rel. to έλάνη, 'torch of reeds'. See Helen.

## hellebore
hellebore, n. — F., fr. L. helleborus, fr. Gk. έλλέ-
βορας, which prob. means lit. 'eaten By fawns',
and is compounded of έλλός (έλλός), 'fawn',
and stem βρω- (whence βιβρώσκειν), 'to eat'.
For the first element see elk, for the second see
voracious.

## helleborine
helleborine, п., name of an orchidaceous plant. —
L. helleborine, fr. Gk. έλλεβορίνη, lit. 'a plant
resembling hellebore', fr. έλλέβορος. See
hellebore and -ine (representing Gk. -ίνη).

## Helleborus
Helleborus, п., a genus of plants, the hellebore
(bot.) — ModL. See hellebore.

## Hellen
Hellen, п., son of Deucalion and eponymous
ancestor of the Greeks. — Gk. Έλλην, 'Hellen'
(whence the pi. "Ελληνες, 'descendants of
Hellen; Greeks'), of uncertain origin; possibly
standing for "Ελ-λην and lit. meaning 'seizer,
taker', and rel. to έλ-εΐν, 'to take', έλωρ,
έλώριον, 'prey, booty'. See sell and cp. Hel-
lenize. Cp. also counsel.

## Hellene
Hellene, п., Greek. — Gk. "Ελλην. See prec.
word.

## Hellenic
Hellenic, adj., Greek. — Gk. 'Ελληνικός, 'Greek',
fr. "Ελληνες, 'Greeks'. See Hellen and -ic.

## Hellenism
Hellenism, п., ι) a Greek phrase or idiom; 2)
Greek culture; 3) adoption of Greek culture.
— Gk. 'Ελληνισμός, imitation of the Greeks,
Hellenism', fr. Έλληνίζειν, 'to speak Greek,
make Greek' (see Hellenize); introduced in 1836
by the German historian Johann Gustav Droy-
sen (1808-84) as a term denoting the
development of Greek culture from Alexander the Great

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:368 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 341 | HEMO- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:368 COLUMN:1 -->
to the end of antiquity.

## Hellenist
Hellenist, η., ι) an admirer of Greek culture; 2)a
Greek Jew. — Gk. 'Ελληνισμός, 'one who uses
the Greek language', esp. 'Greek Jew', fr. Έλ-
ληνίζειν. See next word.
Derivative: Hellenist-ic, Hellenist-ic-al, adjs.,
Hellenist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Hellenize
Hellenize, tr. v., to make Greek in character;
intr. v., to adopt the Greek speech, customs,
etc. — Gk. Έλληνίζειν, 'to speak Greek, make
Greek, Hellenize', fr. "Ελληνες, 'Greeks'. See
Hellen and -ize.
Derivatives; Helleniz-ation, п., Helleniz-er, n.

## Hellene-
Hellene-, combining form meaning 'Greek-'. —
Έλληνο-, fr. "Ελληνες, 'Greeks'. See Hellen.

## heller
heller, п., name of a small coin formerly current
in Germany and Austria. — G. Heller, fr.
MHG. holier, heller, short for Haller pfenninc,
i.e. 'pfennig coined at Hall (in Swabia)'. For
sense development cp. dollar. For the ending
see agential suff. -er.

## hellhonnd
hellhonnd, п., ι) a dog of hell, such as Cerberus;
2) a demon. — ME. hellehund, fr. OE. helle
hund, lit. 'hound of hell'. See hell and hound.

## hello
hello, interj. — A var. of hallo.

## helm
helm, п., tiller; steering wheel of a vessel. — ME.
helme, fr. OE. helma, 'rudder', rel. to OHG.
helmo, 'tiller', MHG. halm(e), helm, G. Helm,
'handle of an ax, helve', and to E. helve and
halter (qq.v.)

## helm
helm, п., helmet (poet.) — ME., fr. OE. helm. See
helmet. Derivative: helm-ed, adj.

## helmet
helmet, n. — OF., dimin. of helme (F. heaume),
'helmet', fr. Frankish *helm, which is rel. to
OHG., MHG., G., OFris., OS., OE. helm, ON.
hjalmr, Goth, hilms. These words prob. meant
orig. 'cover, protection', and derive fr. 1-Е.
base *kel-, 'to cover, hide, conceal', whence also
OE. helan, etc., 'to conceal'. See hall and cp.
the second element in Anselm, Kenelm,
William. Cp. also It. elmo, OProvenc. elm, Sp.
yelmo, 'helmet', which also are Teut. loan words.
Derivative: helmet-ed, adj.

## helminth
helminth, п., a parasitic worm. — Gk. ίλμις
(later form ελμινς), gen. ελμιν&ος, for *fέλμινς,
lit. 'that which rolls or twists', rel. to έλίσσειν
(for *5ελίκιειν), 'to wind, roll', έλιξ (ίθΓ*ίέλιξ),
'spiral'. See helix and cp.' the second element
in nemathelminth. Derivative: helminth-lc, adj.

## helminth-
helminth-, form of helmintho- before a vowel.

## helminthiasis
helminthiasis, п., a disease caused by the
presence of parasitic worms in the body (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. έλμινθιαν, 'to suffer from
worms', fr. ίλμις, gen. ϋλμινθος. See helminth
and -iasis.

## helmintho-
helmintho-, before a vowel helminth-, combining
form meaning 'worm' (med.) — Gk. έλμινθο-,
έλμιν*-, fr. έλμις, gen. ελμινθος, 'worm'. See
heiminth.

## helininthology
helininthology, п., the study of worms (esp. of
parasitic worms). — Compounded of
helmintho- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## helmless
helmless, adj., having no helm (said of a vessel).
— See helm, 'tiller', and -less,

## helmless
helmless, adj., having no helmet. — See helmet
and -less.

## helo-
helo-, combining form meaning 'marsh'. — Gk.
έλο-, fr. έλος, 'marsh'. See Helenium.

## helo-
helo-, combining form meaning 'nail'. — Gk.
ήλο-, fr. ήλος(= Dor. 5λος),'η3ΐΓ, which is rel. to
Aeol. Γάλλοι (pi.), written γάλλοι (Hesychius),
'nails', and prob. cogn. with L. vallus, 'stake,
pale', vallis, 'valley', fr. I.-E.base*wal-, *wel-,'to
bend'. See vale, 'valley', and cp. words there
referred to.

## Heloderma
Heloderma, п., a genus of lizards (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of helo-, 'marsh', and
derma.

## Helonias
Helonias, п., a genus of plants of the family
Melanthaceae (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'a marsh
plant', fr. Gk. έλος, 'marsh'. See Helenium.

## Helot
Helot, п., i)oneofthe original inhabitants of La-
conia, made serfs by the Spartans (Greek hist.);
2) (not cap.) a serf. — L. Helotes, fr. Gk.
Είλωτες, which is of uncertain origin. It possibly
stands for "ήλωτες, fr. *έ-5ελ-ωτες, lit. 'captives

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:368 COLUMN:2 -->
(scil. of the Spartans)', and is rel. to Gk.
άλίσκεσ&αι (for *5αλίσκεσί>αι), 'to be taken
captive', fr. I.-E. base *wel-, 'to seize, take,
steal', whence also L. vellere (for *wetsere), 'to
pluck, pull, twitch', volnus, vulnus, 'wound'. See
vellicate and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: helot-age, п., helot-ism, п., helot-
ry, n.

## help
help, tr. and intr. v. — ME. helpen, fr. OE. hel-
pan, rel. to OS. helpan, ON. hjalpa, Dan. hjselpe,
Swed. hjalpa, OFris. helpa, MLG., MDu., Du.
helpen, OHG. helfan, MHG., G. helfen, Goth.
hilpan, 'to help', and cogn. with Lith. Hetpiit,
Selpti, 'to help, support', pa-Salpa, 'support'.
Derivatives: help, n. (q.v.), help-er, п.,
helping, n.

## help
help, n. — OE. help (fern, and masc), helpe (fern.),
fr. helpan, 'to help', rel. to ON. hjalp, Dan.
hjxlp, Swed. hjalp, OFris. helpe, Du. hulp,OHG.
helfa, hilfa, MHG. helfe, hilfe, G. Hilfe. See
help, v.
Derivatives: help-ful, adj., help-ful-ly, adv.,
help-ful-ness, п., help-less, adj., help-less-ly, adv.,
help-less-ness, n.

## helpmate
helpmate, п., a companion; esp. applied to a
wife. — Corruption of helpmeet.

## helpmeet
helpmeet, п., a helpmate. — From a
misunderstanding of the English rendering of Heb. 'ezer
keneghdo in Gen. 2:18 and 20 'an help meet for
him'. See help, n. and meet, 'suitable'.

## helter-skelter
helter-skelter, adv., in haste and confusion. —
Of imitative origin.
Derivatives: helter-skelter, adj. and n.

## helve
helve, п., handle of an ax. — ME. hilve, helve,
fr. OE. hielf, helfe, rel. to OS. helm, MDu. helf,
helve, OHG. halb, MHG. halp, 'handle of an
ax, helve', OHG. helmo, 'tiller', and cogn. with
Lith. kilpa, 'stirrup', kdlpa, 'traverse of a
sledge'. Cp. halter and helm, 'tiller'.
Derivative: helve, tr. v.

## Helvetia
Helvetia, п., a genus of sac fungi (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. helvella, 'a small potherb', dimin. formed
fr. helvus, 'light bay'. See yellow and -ella and
cp. next word.

## helvite
helvite, п., a yellow mineral. — Formed with
subst. suff. -ite fr. L. helvus, 'light bay'. See
yellow and cp. prec. word.

## hem
hem, п., edge, border. — ME. hemm, hem, fr. OE.
hemm, hem, rel. to ON. hemja, 'to bridle, curb',
Dan. hemme, Swed. hamma, 'to stop, restrain',
OFris. hemma, 'to hinder', MDu., MHG., G.
hemmen, 'to hem in, stop, hinder', and to OE.
hamm, 'enclosed pasture land'.

## hem
hem, tr. v. — ME. hemmen, fr. OE. hemman, fr.
hem, 'edge, border'. See hem, v.
Derivative: hemm-er, n.

## hem
hem, п., interjection and intr. v. — Imitative.

## hem-
hem-, form of hemo- before a vowel.

## hemal
hemal, haemal, adj., pertaining to blood. —
Formed with adj. suff. -a] fr. Gk. αίμα, 'blood',
which possibly stands for *sai-men and is cogn.
with OS. sem, ON. seimr, MDu. seem, Du.
zeem, OHG., MHG., G. seim, 'virgin honey'.
The original meaning of both Greek αίμα and
these Teut. words seems to have been 'a viscid
liquid'. Cp. -emia.

## hemat-
hemat-, form of bemato- before a vowel.

## hematic
hematic, haematic, adj., pertaining to blood, of
the color of blood. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. αίμα, gen. αίματος, 'blood'. See hemal.

## hematin
hematin, hematiue, haematin, haematine, п., the
coloring matter of hemoglobin (biochem.) —
Formed with chem. suff. -in, resp. -ine, fr. Gk.
αίμα, gen. αίματος, 'blood'; see hemal.

## hematite
hematite, haematite, п., an ore of iron (mineral.)
— L. haematites, fr. Gk. αιματίτης, 'bloodlike',
used in the sense of λίθος αιματίτης, 'a red
iron ore', fr. αίμα, gen. αίματος, 'blood'. See
hemal and subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: hematit-k, adj.

## hemato-
hemato-, haemato-, before a vowel hemat-, пае-
mat-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
blood'. — Gk. αίματο-, αίματ-, fr. αίμα, gen.
αίματος, 'blood'. See hemal.

## hematocele
hematocele, haematocele, п., a tumor containing
blood (med.) — Compounded of hemato- and
Gk. κήλη, 'tumor'. See -cele.

## hemato-crystallin
hemato-crystallin, haemato-crystaliin,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:368 COLUMN:3 -->
hemoglobin in a crystalline condition. — See hemato-
and crystalline.

## hematocyte
hematocyte, haematocyte, п., a blood cell. —
Compounded of hemato- and Gk. κύτος, 'a
hollow vessel'. See -cyte.

## hematoidin
hematoidin, haematoidin, п., an ironfree yellowish
pigment (biochem.) — Coined by the German
pathologist Rudolf Virchow (1821-1902) fr.
hemato-, -oid and chem. suff. -in.

## hematology
hematology, п., the science of the blood (med.)
— Compounded of hemato- and -logy.
Derivatives: hematolog-ic adj., hematolog-ist, n.

## hemer-
hemer-, form of hemero- before a vowel.

## hemeralopia
hemeralopia, п., ι) day blindness; 2) night
blindness. — Medical L., fr. Gk. ήμεράλωψ, 'blind
by day', compounded of ήμέρί, 'day', άλαός,
'blind', and ώψ (gen. ώπός), 'eye'. For the
etymology of Gk. ήμέρϊ see hemero-. Gk. άλαός
prob. means lit. 'not seeing', and is formed fr.
a-(seepriv. pref.a)and the stem of λάειν, 'to see',
which is cogn. with OI. lasati, 'shines, beams'.
For the etymology of Gk. ώψ see -opia. Cp.
nyctalopia. Derivative: hemeralop-ic, adj.

## hemero-
hemero-, before a vowel hemer-, combining form
meaning 'day'. — Gk. ήμερο-, ήμερ-, fr. ήμέρϊ,
'day', which is re], to ήμαρ of s.m., and cogn.
with Arm. aur (fr. *amur), 'day'. Cp. ephemeral,
hemeralopia, Mesembryanthenium.

## Hemerocallis
Hemerocallis, п., a genus of plants, the day lily
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ήμεροκαλλές, 'a kind
of lily', which is compounded of ήμερα, 'day'
and κάλλος, 'beauty' (see hemero- and calo-);
so called because its flowers blossom only one
single day.

## hemi-
hemi-, pref. in words of Greek origin, meaning
'half. — Gk. ήμι-, for *semi-, cogn. with OI.
sami, 'half, L. semi-, OE. sam-, OHG. sami-,
'half. See semi-,

## -hernia
-hernia, haemia. — Variants of -emia.

## hemialgia
hemialgia, п., pain involving only one side of
the body (med.) — Medical L., compounded of
hemi- and Gk. -αλγίά, fr. άλγος, 'pain'. See -algia.

## hemicrania
hemicrania, п., a periodical headache, usually on
one side of the head only. — Late L. hemicrania,
fr. Gk. ημικρανία, 'pain on one side of the
head', which is compounded of ήμι- (see hemi-)
and κράνίον, 'head, skull'; see cranium. Cp.
migraine, megrim.

## hemicycle
hemicycle, п., semicircle. — F. hemicycle, fr. L.
hemicyclus, fr. Gk. ήμικύκλιον, 'semicircle',
prop. neut. of the adjective ημικύκλιος,
'semicircular', fr. ήμι- (see hemi-) and κύκλος, 'circle'.
See cycle.

## hemielytron
hemielytron, hemielytrum, п., one of the fore
wings of certain insects (entomol.) — ModL.,
compounded of hemi- and elytron.

## hemin
hemin, haemin, п., the hydrochloride of hematin
(biochem.) — Formed with chem. suff. -in fr.
Gk. αίμα, 'blood'. See hemal.

## hemiplegia
hemiplegia, п., paralysis of one side of the body
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of hemi-
and Gk. -πληγίϊ, fr. πληγή, 'stroke'. See -plegia.
Derivative: hemipleg-ic, adj.

## Hemiptera
Hemiptera, n. pi., an order of insects, the bugs
(entomol.) — ModL., compounded of hemi-
and Gk. πτερόν, 'wing'. See ptero-,

## hemipterous
hemipterous, adj., pertaining to the Hemiptera.
— See prec. word and -ous.

## hemisphere
hemisphere, п., half of the surface of a sphere
a sphere; esp. half of the surface of the earth. —
F. hemisphere, fr. L. haemisphaerium, fr. Gk.
ήμισφαίριον, which is compounded of ήμι- (see
hemi-) and σφαίρα, 'ball, globe, sphere'. See
sphere.

## hemispherical
hemispherical, adj. — See hemi-, spheric and adj.
suff. -al.

## hemistich
hemistich, п., half of a poetic line. — L. hemi-
stichium, fr. Gk. ήμιστίχιον, 'half line, half
verse', compounded of ήμι- (see hemi-) and
στίχος, 'row, line, rank; verse', which is related
to στείχειν, 'to go, march in order'. See acrostic
and cp. words there referred to.

## hemlock
hemlock, n. — ME. humlok, hemlok, fr. OE.
hymttc, hymlicet hemlic, of uncertain origin.

## hemo-
hemo-, haemo-, before a vowel hem-, haeni-,
combining form meaning 'blood'. — Gk. αίμο-,
αίμ-, fr. αίμα, 'blood'. See hemal and cp.
hemato-.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:369 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HEMOGLOBIN | 342 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:369 COLUMN:1 -->

## hemoglobin
hemoglobin, haemoglobin, п., the coloring matter
of the red blood corpuscles (biochem.) —
Shortened by the German chemist Ernst Felix Im-
manuel Hoppe-Seyler (1825-95) fr. earlier hae-
matogiobulin, fr. haemato- (in the sense of
haematin) and globulin.

## hemophilia
hemophilia, haemophilia, п., tendency to bleeding
(med.) — Medical L., coined by the German
physician Johann Lucas Schonlein (1793-1864)
in 1828 fr. haemo- and Gk. φιλίϊ, 'friendship',
here used in the sense of "tendency to'. See
philo-.

## hemoptysis
hemoptysis, haemoptysis, п., spitting of blood
(med.) — ModL., compounded of hemo- and
Gk. πτύσις, 'spitting', fr. πτύειν, 'to spit'. See
ptyalin.

## hemorrhage
hemorrhage, haemorrhage, п., bursting of a
bloodvessel (med.) — Medical L. haemorrhagia, fr.
Gk. αίμορραγίϊ, 'haemorrhage', which is
compounded of αίμα- (see hemo-) -ρραγία, 'a
bursting forth', fr. ρηγνύναι, 'to break, burst'. See
-rrhagia.
Derivatives: hemorrhag-ic, hemorrhag-ic-al, adjs.

## hemorrhoidal
hemorrhoidal, haemorrhoidal, adj. — F.
hemorrhoidal. See next word and adj. surf. -al.

## hemorrhoids
hemorrhoids, haemorrhoids, n. pi., piles. — F.
hemorr(h)ofdes, fr. L. haemorrhoidae, fr. Gk.
αιμορροΐδες (φλέβες),. '(veins) liable to
discharge blood' (esp. used in the sense of
'hemorrhoids') pi. of αίμορροίς, fr. αίμόρροος, 'flowing
with blood', compounded of αίμο- (see hemo-)
and £έειν, 'to flow', which stands for *σρέΓειν.
See stream.

## hemostasis
hemostasis, haemostasis, hemostasia, haemostasia,
п., stoppage of bleeding (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. αίμόστασις, which is compounded of
αίμο- (see hemo-) and στάσις, 'standing,
standing still'. See stasis.

## hemostat
hemostat, haemostat, п., anything that stops
hemorrhage; specif., an instrument used to
compress a bleeding vessel. — Fr. hemostatic.

## hemostatic
hemostatic, haemostatic, adj., serving to stop
hemorrhage; styptic. — Compounded of hemo-
and Gk. στατικός, 'causing to stand'. See static.

## hemp
hemp, n. — ME., fr. OE. hxnep, henep, rel. to
OS. hanap, ON. hampr, Swed. hampa, Dan.
hamp, MDu., Du. hennep, OHG. hanaf, MHG.
hanef, hanf, G. Hanf(=* Teut. *hanap). Cp. Gk.
κάνναβις (whence L. cannabis), Arm. kanap",
Alb. *алер, Russ.-Church Slav, konoplja (whence
Lith. kanapes), 'hemp'. Al] these words are
loan words from a foreign, possibly Scythian,
language. Cp. canvas, canvass. Cp. also sunn.
Derivative: hemp-en, adj.

## hen
hen, n. — ME., fr. OE. hen, henn, rel. to
OFris. henn, MDu. henne, Du. hen, OHG. henna,
heninna, MHG., G. henne, 'hen', OE., OFris.,
Goth, hana, OS., OHG. hano, ON. hani, Dan.,
Swed., MLG., MDu. hane, Du. haan, MHG.
hane, han, G. Hahn, 'cock'. These words lit.
mean 'the singing bird', and are cogn. with L.
canere, 'to sing'. For sense development cp. the
cogn. Gk. ήϊ-κανός, (Hesychius) 'cock', lit.
'singer of the dawn'. See cant, 'slang of beggars',
and words there referred to and cp. esp.
chanticleer.
Derivative: henn-ery, a.

## henad
henad, п., a unit, monad (Platonicphilosophy). —
Gk. ένας, gen. ένάδος, formed fr. ev, neut. of
εΤς, 'one', with sun", -άς, gen. -άδος. See heno-
and -ad,

## henbane
henbane, n. — Compounded of hen and bane.

## hence
hence, adv. — ME. hennes (formed with adv. gen.
suff. -s fr. earlier henne), contracted later into
hens (written hence, in order to show that the s
has the voiceless sound), fr. OE. heonan, heonon;
rel. to OS. hinan, hinana, OHG. hinnan, hinnan,
hinana, MHG., G. hinnen, fr. Teut. pronominal
base *hi-. See he and cp. hinder, adj. For the
spelling with -ce cp. thence, whence.

## henchman
henchman, п., ι) a page or squire; 2) a follower. —
ME. hengestman, henxtman, henksman, henche-
man, 'groom, squire', formed fr. OE. hengest,
hengst, 'horse', and man, 'man', lit. 'a man
attending on a horse'. The first element is rel. to
OFris. hengst, hanxt, Du. hengst, OHG. hengist,
MHG. hengest, hengst, G. Hengst, 'stallion'.
These words prob. mean lit. 'leaper, jumper',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:369 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. I.-E. base *kdq-, whence also Gk. κηκίειν,
'to gush forth', Lith. Sokti, 'to jump, dance',
Sankiis, 'quick, swift', MW., OCo. cassec, Bret.
kazek, 'a mare', lit. 'that which belongs to a
stallion'. For the second element see man.

## hendeca-
hendeca-, combining form meaning 'eleven'. —
Gk. ένδεκα, compounded of fiv, neut. of είς,
'one', and δέκα, 'ten'. See heno- and deca-.

## hendecagon
hendecagon, п., a plane figure with eleven angles
and.eleven sides. — Gk. ένδεκάγωνος, 'having
eleven angles'. See heudeca- and -gon and cp.
undecagon.

## hendeeasyllabic
hendeeasyllabic, adj., having eleven syllables. —
L. hendecasyllabus, fr. Gk. ένδεκασύλλαβος,
'having eleven syllables'. See hendeca- and
syllabic.

## hendiadys
hendiadys, п., a figure of speech in which two
nouns joined by and are used instead of a noun
with an adjective. — ML. alteration of Gk. ev
δια δυοΐν, 'one (thing) by means of two'. See
heno-, dia- and dual.

## henequen
henequen, п., the fiber of the plant Agave rigida
sisalana. — Sp. henequen, jeniquen, fr. Taino
henequen.

## henna
henna, п., the shrub Lawsonia inermis and the
reddish dye made from its leaves. — Arab.
hinnd', 'henna', a name of Persian origin. Cp.
alkanet, Alkanna, orcanet.

## heno-
heno-, combining form meaning 'one'. — Gk.
ένο-, neut. of είς (for *έμ-ς), fr. έν (for *έμ-),
'one', fr. I.-E. base *sem-,*sm-, 'one, together'.
See same and words there referred to and cp. esp.
hendeca-, hendiadys, henotic.

## henotheism
henotheism, п., a kind of polytheism in which one
god of the pantheon is raised over the rest. —
Coined by Friedrich Max Muller (1823-1900),
professor of comparative philology at Oxford,
in his Lectures on the Origin and Growth of
Religion (1878), fr. heno- and 1st theism.

## henotheist
henotheist, п., an adherent of henotheism. —See
prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: henotheist-ic, adj.

## henotic
henotic, adj., unifying; harmonizing. — Gk.
ενωτικός, 'serving to unite', fr. ένοϋν, 'to make
one, unite', fr. έν, neut. of εις, 'one'. See heno-.

## Henrietta
Henrietta, fern. PN. — F. Henriette, fern, dimin.
of Henri. See next word and cp. Harriet. Cp.
also Etta.

## Henry
Henry, masc. PN. — F. Henri, fr. Late L. Hen-
ricus, fr. G. Heinrich, fr. OHG. Heimerich, lit.
'the ruler of the house', fr. heim, 'house, home',
and rihhi, 'ruler'. The first element is rel. to
OE. ham, 'home'; see home. For the second
element see rich. Cp. Harry.

## henry
henry, п., the unit of inductance (electr.) —
Named after the American physicist Joseph
Henry (1797-1878).

## hent
hent, tr. v., to seize (archaic). — ME. henten, fr.
OE. hentan, 'to try to seize, to attack, seize',
which stands in gradational relationship to OE.
huntian, 'to hunt'. See hunt and cp. hint.

## heortology
heortology, п., the study of feasts. —
Compounded of Gk. εορτή, 'feast, festival', and -λογίϊ, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'·. The first
element is of uncertain origin. It possibly stands
for *Γε-ίορ-τά and lit. means 'a kindly act (to
a deity)' and is rel. to έρανος (for *Γέρανος),
'a meal to which everyone contributed his
share', and to ήρα, ace. (for *Fipa), in ήρα
φέρειν, 'to do a favor', έπί-ηρα, 'pleasing gifts',
and cogn. with L. sevirus, 'serious, grave, strict,
austere'; see severe. For the second element see
-logy.
Derivative: heortolog-i-cal, adj.

## hepar
hepar, п., 1) the liver; 2) a liver-colored substance.
— ML., fr. Gk. ήπαρ, 'liver'. See hepatic.

## heparin
heparin, п., an anticoagulant obtained from the
livers of animals (pharm.) — Coined by the
American physiologist William Henry Howell
(1860-1945) and the American physician Luther
Emmett Holt Jr. (1895- )(seethearticle"Two
new factors in blood coagulation — Heparin
and Pro-antithrombin" in American Journal
of Physiology, 47, 328, 1918), fr. Gk. ήπαρ
(gen. ήπατος), 'liver' (see hepatic), and chem.
suff. -in. The correct form would have been
hepatin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:369 COLUMN:3 -->

## hepat-
hepat-, form of hepato- before a vowel.

## hepatic
hepatic, adj., pertaining to the liver. — Gk.
ηπατικός, 'of the liver', fr. ήπαρ, gen. ήπατος,
'liver', fr. I.-E. base *yiqw-r(t), gen. yeqw-nes,
whence also OI. ydkft, gen. yaknah, Avestic
yakar*, MPers. Jakar, ModPers. jigar, b.jecur,
OLith. jeknos, jekanas, Lith. jaknos (pi.), Lett.
aknas, aknis (pi.), 'liver'. Cp. hepar, heparin,
jecoral.

## Hepatica
Hepatica, п., a genus of plants, the liverleaf (hot.)
— ML. hepatica, 'liverwort', fr. L. hepatica,
fem. of hepaticus, 'of the liver', fr. Gk. ηπατικός,
'of the liver', of s.m„ fr. ήπαρ, gen. ήπατος,
'liver' (see prec. word); so called because the
leaves of the plant resemble the liver.

## Hepaticae
Hepaticae, n. pi., a class of plants, the liverworts.
— ModL., prop. pi. of prec. word.

## hepatization
hepatization, п., consolidation of the lung owing
to pneumonia (med.) — Lit. 'appearance of a
liver'; coined by the Italian physician Giovanni
Battista Morgagni (1682-1771), fr. Gk. ήπα-
τίζειν, 'to be like a liver', fr. ήπαρ, gen. ήπατος,
'liver'. See hepatic and -ize.

## hepato-
hepato-, before a vowel hepat-, combining form
denoting the liver. — Gk. ήπατο-, fr. ήπαρ, gen.
ήπατος, 'liver'. See hepatic,

## hephaestic
hephaestic, adj., pertaining to smiths; — hephaes-
tic cramp, cramp caused by the excessive use
of the hammer. — See next word and -ic.

## Hephaestus
Hephaestus, п., the god of fire and metal-working;
identified later with Vulcan (Greek mythoi.) —
L., fr. Gk. "Ηφαιστος, a pre-Hellenic word of
uncertain origin.

## Hephzihah
Hephzihah, fem. PN. (Bible). — Heb. Hephlzibdh,
lit. 'my delight is in her', compounded of
hephtzt, 'my delight', fr. fiephetz, 'delight,
pleasure, desire', which derives fr. haphe'tz, 'he
delighted in, desired', and of bah, 'in her', fr.
b1-, 'in', with the fem. suff. of the 3rd person.
See hafiz.

## Hepplewhite
Hepplewhite, adj., relating to the style introduced
in England by the cabinetmaker George
Hepplewhite (died in 1786).

## hept-
hept-, form of hepta- before a vowel.

## hepta-
hepta-, before a vowel hept-, combining "form
meaning 'seven'. — Gk. έπτα-, έπτ-, fr. επτά,
'seven', which stands for *septm and is cogn.

## with L. septem
with L. septem, Goth, sibun, OE. seofon, 'seven'.
See seven.

## heptachord
heptachord, п., ι) a seven-stringed instrument;
2) diatonic system of seven tones (mus.) — Gk.
έπτάχαρδος, 'seven-stringed'; compounded of
επτά (see hepta-) and χορδή, 'chord'. See chord
