and cp. words there referred to.

## heptad
heptad, п., a group of seven things. — Gk. έπτάς,
gen. έπτάδος, 'a group of seven', formed fr.
έτττά, 'seven', with suff. -άς, gen. -άδος. See
hepta- and -ad.

## heptagon
heptagon, п., a plane figure with seven angles and
seven sides (geom.) — Gk. έπτάγωνος, 'seven-

## cornered'
cornered', compounded of επτά (see hepta·) and
-γωνος, from the stem of γωνία, 'angle'. See
-gon.
Derivative: heptagon-al, adj.

## heptahedron
heptahedron, п., a solid figure with seven plane
faces (geom.) — Compounded of hepta- and
Gk. εδρϊ, 'seat; base, side, face'. See -hedron.

## heptamerous
heptamerous, adj., consisting of seven parts. —
Compounded of hepta- and Gk. μέρος, 'part'.
See -merous.

## heptarch
heptarch, п., one of the rulers in a heptarchy. —
Compounded of hept- and Gk. άρχος, 'leader,

## chief
chief, ruler'. See -arch.

## heptarchy
heptarchy, п., government by seven persons. —
Compounded of hept- and Gk. -αρχίϊ, 'rule'.
See -archy.

## Heptateuch
Heptateuch, п., the first seven books of the Bible.
— Late L. Heptateuchos, fr. Gk. έπτάτευχος
(scil. βίβλος), 'a book consisting of seven

## volumes'
volumes', which is compounded of επτά (see
hepta-) and τεΰχος, 'tool, implement', later,
'book'. See Pentateuch and cp. Hexateuch,
Octateuch.

## her
her, pers. pron. — ME. hire, here, hir, fr. OE.

## hiere
hiere, hire, hyre, dat. heo, hio, 'she', fem. of he,
'he'. See he and cp. hers.

## her
her, possessive pronominal adj. — ME. hire, here,

## hir
hir, OE. hiere, hire, hyre, gen. of heo, hio. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:370 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 343 | HERITABLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:370 COLUMN:1 -->
prec. word.

## Hera
Hera, п., sister and wife of Zeus, queen of the
gods (Greek mythol.); identified by the Romans
with Juno. — L., fr. Gk. Ήρα, which stands for
•"Hpfi, lit. means 'protectress', and is rel. to
ήρως, 'hero', orig. 'defender,protector'. See hero.

## Heracles
Heracles, Herakles, n. — See Hercules.

## Heracleuin
Heracleuin, п., a genus of plants, the cow
parsnip (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ηράκλεια, name
of a plant, prop. fern, of the adj. 'Ηράκλειος,
'pertaining to Hercules', fr. 'Ηρακλής (see
Hercules). Accordingly Gk. ηράκλεια lit. means
'the flower dedicated to Hercules'.

## Heraclidae
Heraclidae, n. pi., the descendants of Hercules.
— L., fr. Gk. Ήρακλεϊδαι, pi. of 'Ηρακλείδης,
'son or descendant of Hercules'. See Hercules
and patronymic sufT. -id.

## herald
herald, п., ι) forerunner; 2) proclaimed — ME.
herald, heraud, fr. OF. heralt, heraut (F. heraut),
fr. Frankish 'hariwald, a compound lit. meaning
Officer of the army'. The first element is rel.
to OHG. heri, MDu., OE. here, 'host, army';
see harry. The second element is rel. to OHG.
waltan, 'to rule'; see wield and cp. the suffix in
spring-al, spring-aid. Cp. the name Chariovolda,
the Batavian chief, mentioned by Tacitus, and
ON. Harald (see Haroid), which are of the same
etymology as OF. heralt. It. araldo, Sp. heraldo,
G. Herold, are French loan words.
Derivatives: herald, tr. v., herald-ic, adj., herald-
ic-al-ly, adv., herald-ry, n.

## herapathite
herapathite, п., quinine sulfato-periodide
(mineral.) — Named after the English ■ chemist
William B. Herapath (1795-1868). For the
ending see subst. sulf. -ite.

## herb
herb, n. — ME. herbe, erbe, fr. OF. erbe (F. her-
be), fr. L. herba, 'grass, herb', which is of
uncertain origin. The spelling with h is due to the
influence of L. herba. Cp. verba and the second
element in contrayerva.
Derivatives; herb-y, kerb-less, adjs.

## herbaceous
herbaceous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
herbs. — L. herbaceus, 'grassy', fr. herba. See
herb and -aceous.

## herbage
herbage, п., herbs collectively. — ME. erbage, fr.
F. herbage, fr. ML. herbdticum, fr. L. herba.
See herb and -age,

## herbal
herbal, adj., pertaining to herbs. — ML. her-
balis, fr. L. herba. See herb and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: herbal, n. (q.v.), he.

## herbal
herbal, п., a treatise on herbs. — ML. herbale,
prop. neut. of the adjective herbalis, used as
a noun. See herbal, adj.

## herbarium
herbarium, п., a collection of plants. — Late L.
herbarium, prop, subst. use of the neut. of the
adj. herbarius, 'pertaining to herbs', fr. L. herba.
See herb and -arium and cp. herbary. Cp. also
arbor.

## herbary
herbary, п., ι) herbarium; 2) a garden of herbs
or vegetables. — Late L. herbarium. See prec.
word and subst. suff. -ary.

## herb bennet
herb bennet, a European herb with an astringent
root, Geum urbanum. — ME. Aerie beneit, fr.
OF. herbe beneile, fr. L. herba benedicta, 'the
blessed herb' (see herb and bennet); so called for
its medicinal properties.

## Herbert
Herbert, masc. PN. — Not the direct derivative
of OE. Herebeorht, but of its OHG. equivalent
Hariberct, through the intermediate Latinized
form Herbertus, introduced into England by the
Normans. OHG. Hariberct is compounded of
hari, heri, 'host, army', and beraht, 'bright'. See
harry and bright and cp. the first element in
Herman.

## herbiferous
herbiferous, adj., bearing herbs. — L. herbifer,
compounded of L. herba, 'grass, herb', and
ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See herb and -ferous.

## Herbivora
Herbivora, n. pi., a group of mammals (700/.) —
ModL., lit. '(mammals) feeding on grass',
compounded of L. herba, 'grass, herb', and vorare,
'to devour'. See herb and voracious.

## herbivore
herbivore, п., a herbivorous animal. — See prec.
word.

## herbivorous
herbivorous, adj., feeding on grass. — See
Herbivora and -ous.

## herborist
herborist, п., t) a collector of plants; 2) a
herbalist. — F. herboriste, fr. earlier herboliste, fr.
herboliser. See herborize and -ist.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:370 COLUMN:2 -->

## herborization
herborization, n. —F. herborisation, fr. herboriser.
See next word and -ation.

## herborize
herborize, intr. v., to botanize (archaic). — F.
herboriser, fr. earlier herboliser, a hybrid coined
fr. L. herbuta, 'a little herb', dimin. of herba,
and -iser, a suff. of Greek origin. See herb
and -ize.

## herb Paris
herb Paris, a liliaceous herb (Paris quadrifolia).
— ML. herba pans, of uncertain origin. Some
scholars see in paris the gen. of L. par, 'equal;
a couple, pair', and translate herba paris
accordingly 'herb of a couple' (see pair). The herb
should have been so called in allusion to the
regular formation of the four leaves. Others
explain the name herba Paris as 'the herb of Paris',
and see in it a reference to Paris, son of Priam
of Troy. Cp. Paris.

## herb Robert
herb Robert, п., a kind of geranium with red
flowers (Geranium roberiianum). — ME. herbe
robert, fr. ML. herba Robert!, lit. 'Robert's
herb'. It was possibly to called after Robert
Duke of Normandy.

## Herculean
Herculean, adj., 1) pertaining to Herculus; 2)
(usually not cap.) having the strength of
Hercules ; 3) (usually not cap.) very difficult,
dangerous. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Hercules.
See next word.

## Hercules
Hercules, п., a hero, son of Zeus and Alcmene
(Greek mythoL) — L. Hercules, fr. earlier Яег-
cles, fr. Gk. Ήράκλέης, 'Ηρακλής, lit. 'glory of
Hera', fr. "Hpi, 'Hera', and κλέος, 'glory'. See
Hera and lond and cp. Clio, cledonism, the first
element in Clianthus and the second element in
Damocles, Eteocles, Euclea.

## Hercynian
Hercynian, adj., designating, or pertaining to, the
forest-covered mountains of ancient Germany.
— Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Hercynia(siha),
Hercynius(sattus), 'Hercynian forest', which,
together with Gk. Άρκύνια 6ρη, Όρκύνιος
δρυμός, derives fr. OCeltic *Perkunyd, fr. I.-E.
base *perq (o)-, 'oak; oak forest; wooded
mountain'. See fir and cp. Quercus.

## hercynite
hercynite, п., iron aluminate (mineral.) — So
called because found at Ronsberg, in the
Bohemian Forest. See Hercynian. For the ending
see subst suff. -ite.

## herd
herd, п., a number of animals. — ME. heorde,
herd, fr. OE. heord, 'herd, flock', rel. to ON.
hjord, Dan., Swed. hjord, OHG. herta, MHG.
herte, G. Herde, Goth, hairdo, 'herd', and cogn.
with OI. sardhah, 'herd, troop', OSlav. crida,
'herd', Gk. κόρθυς, 'heap', κορθύνειν, 'to lift,
raise', MW. cordd, 'troop, family', Lith. kefd-
iius, 'shepherd' (derived fr. 'kerda, 'flock').
These words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *kerdh-,
mkordh-, 'row, herd, troop'. Cp. herd,
'herdsman', herder.

## herd
herd, п., herdsman, now used chiefly in
compounds as cow-herd, shep-herd. — ME. heorde,
herde, fr. OE. hierde, hyrde, rel. to OS. hirdi,
ON. hirdir, Dan. hyrde, Swed. herde, MLG.,
MDu. herde, OHG. hirti, MHG. Airfe, hurt,
G. Hirt, Goth, halrdeis, 'herdsman, shepherd',
and to OE. heord, 'herd, flock'. See herd, 'a
number of animals'.

## herd
herd, tr. v., to put into a herd; intr. v., to flock
together. — ME. herdien, fr. herde, 'herd'. See
herd, 'a number of animals'.

## herder
herder, п., one who herds, a herdsman. — Not
derived fr. the E. verb herd, but borrowed fr.
MDu. (— Du.) herder, of s.m., fr. herde, 'herd'
(see herd, 'a number of animals'). See J.F.
Bense, A Dictionary of the Low-Dutch Element
in the English Vocabulary, p. 142.

## herderite
herderite, п., a beryllium and calcium fluophos-
phate (mineral.) — Named after Baron Sieg-
mund A. W. von Herder (1776-1838), director
of the Saxon mines. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## herdic
herdic, п., a kind of cab with two or four wheels.
— Named after its inventor, the American Peter
Herdic (died in 1888).

## here
here, adv. — ME. her, fr. OE. her, rel. to OS.
her, hir, ΟΝ., Goth, her, Dan. her, Swed. har,
MDu., Du. hier, OHG. hiar, MHG., G. hier,
hie, 'here', fr. Teut. pron. base *hi-,
corresponding to I.-E. *ki-, 'this; here'. See he and cp.
hitber.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:370 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: here, n.

## hereafter
hereafter, adv. and n. —: ME. here after, fr. OE.
hersefter. See here and after,

## hereditable
hereditable, adj., heritable. — ML. hereditabilis,
fr. hereditare, 'to inherit', fr. heres, gen. heredis.
See heredity and -able and cp. heritable.
Derivative: hereditabii-ity, n.

## hereditament
hereditament, п., any property that may be
inherited (law). — ML. hereditamentum, fr.
hereditare. See prec. word and -ment.

## hereditary
hereditary, adj., 1) derived from ancestors; 2)
passed down by heredity; 3) transmitted by
inheritance. — L. hereditarius, 'relating to an
inheritance, hereditary', fr, hereditas, gen. here-
ditatis. See next word and adj. suff. -ary and
cp. heritor.
Derivative: hereditari-ly, adv.

## heredity
heredity, п., the transmission of bodily and mental
characters of parent to offspring. — F. heridite,
fr. L. hereditatem, ace. of hereditas, 'heirship',
fr. heres, gen. heredis, 'heir'. See heir and -ity.

## Hereford
Hereford, п., name of a breed of red and white
beef cattle. — So called because first bred in
Herefordshire in England.

## herem
herem, п., Biblical ban, excommunication. —
Heb. herem, 'person or thing devoted to
destruction', rel. to heherim, 'he banned, devoted to
destruction, excommunicated', Aram, aharim,
'he banned; excommunicated', Arab, harama,
'he forebade', haruma, 'was forbidden', hartm,
'sacred, forbidden', Ethiop. harama, 'he
prohibited from common use; he devoted to', Ak-
kad. haramu, 'to dedicate', harimtu, 'a dedicated
woman, a female hierodule'. Cp. maranatha,
marrano. Cp. also harem and words there
referred to.

## heresiarch
heresiarch, п., a founder or leader of heresy. —
Eccles. L. haeresiarcha, fr. Late Gk. αίρεσιάρ-
χης. See heresy and -arch.

## heresiography
heresiography, п., a treatise on heresies. — See
heresy and -graphy.

## heresiologist
heresiologist, п., a student of heresies. — Formed
from next word with suff. -ist.

## heresiology
heresiology, п., the study of heresies. —
Compounded of heresy and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## heresy
heresy, п., unorthodox belief or doctrine. — ME.
eresie, heresie, fr. OF. eresie, heresie (F. heresie),
fr. Late L. haeresis, fr. Gk. αιρεσις, 'a taking,
choosing, choice; sect, heresy', fr. αίρεϊσθαι,
'to take for oneself, middle voice of αίρεΐν,
'to take, choose', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. aphaeresis, diaeresis, synaeresis.

## heretic
heretic, п., a person guilty of heresy. — ME.
heretike, fr. F. heretique, fr. Eccles. L. haereticus,
fr. Gk. αιρετικός, 'able to choose; heretical',
fr. αιρετός, 'to be chosen, that which may-be
chosen', verbal adj. of αίρεΐν. See prec. word
and -etic.
Derivatives: heretic-al, adj., heretic-al-Iy, adv.,
heretic-al-ness, n.

## hereticate
hereticate, tr. v., to declare to be heretical. —
Eccles. L. haereticatus, pp. of haereticare, 'to
declare to be heretical', fr. haereticus, 'heretical'.
See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## heretoga
heretoga, п., leader of an army (OldEnglish hist.)
— OE. heretoga, compounded of here, 'host,
army', and -toga, 'leader', from the stem of
togian, 'to draw, drag', rel. to OS. heritogo,
ON. hertogi, OFris. hertoga, OHG. herizoho,
herizogo, 'leader of an army', prop, loan
translations of Gk. στρατηλάτες, 'leader of an army'
(fr. στρατός, 'army', and έλαύνειν, 'to drive,
draw'). See harry and tow, 'to draw', and cp.
herzog.

## tteriot
tteriot, п., feudal due paid to the lord on the death
of a tenant (English law). — ME. heriet, heriot,
fr. OE. heregeatwa, heregeatwe, (pi.), 'military
equipments', which is compounded of here,
'host, army', and geatwa, geatwe (pi.), fr. earlier

## getawe (pi.)
getawe (pi.), 'apparatus, equipments, arms'. For
the first element see harry. The second element
is rel. to OE. tawian, 'to prepare'; see taw, 'to
prepare'.

## heritable
heritable, adj., inheritable. — F. heritable, fr. he-
riter, fr. L. hereditare. See hereditable and -able
and cp. inherit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:371 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HERITAGE | 344 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:371 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: heritabil-ity, п., heritabl-y, adv.

## heritage
heritage, n. — OF. eritage, heritage (F. heritage),
fr. eriter, heriter (F. heriter), 'to inherii', fr. ML.
hlrlditare, fr. L. hires, gen. heredis, "heir". See
heir and -age and cp. heredity.

## heritor
heritor, п., an inheritor; heir. — ME. heriter, fr.
OF. heritier (F. heritier), 'heir', fr. L. heredi-
tarius, 'relating to an inheritance' (whence also
OProveng. heretier,'eretier, Sp. heredero. Port.
herdeiro, 'heir'). See hereditary.

## herma
herma, п., pillar representing a head of the god
Hermes {Greek antiq.) — L. Herma, fr. Gk.
Έρμης, 'Hermes; statue of Hermes'. See Hermes.

## Herman
Herman, masc. PN. — G. Hermann, fr. OHG.
Hariman, lit. 'man of war, warrior', fr. hari, heri,
'host, army', and man, 'man'. See harry and
man and cp. the first element in Herbert.

## hermandad
hermandad,n.,name of a league originally formed
against the violence of the nobles, organized
later as national police. — Sp. lit.
'brotherhood', fr. hermano, 'brother', fr. L. germanus,
'having the same parents' (said of brothers or
sisters); see german, 'having the same parents'.
Sp. suff. -dad derives fr. L. -tat- (nom. -tas, gen.
-talis); see subst. suff. -ty.

## hermaphrodlsm
hermaphrodlsm, п., hermaphroditism. — F.
hermaphrodisme, fr. hermaphrodite, fr. L.
hermaphroditus. See next word and -ism.

## hermaphrodite
hermaphrodite, п., a person or animal having
both male and female sexual organs. — L.
hermaphroditus, fr. Gk. ερμαφρόδιτος, fr.
'Ερμαφρόδιτος, the son of Hermes (= the male
principle) and Aphrodite (= the female principle).
See Hermes and Aphrodite.
Derivatives', hermaphrodit-ic, adj.,
hermaphroditism, n.

## hermeneutic
hermeneutic, adj., interpretative. — Gk.
ερμηνευτικός, 'interpreting', fr. ερμηνευτής,
'interpreter', fr. έρμηνεύειν, 'to interpret', fr. έρμηνεύς,
'interpreter', which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: hermeneutic-al-Iy, adv., hermeneu-
tics (q.v.)

## hermeneutics
hermeneutics, n„ the science of interpretation. —
Gk. ερμηνευτική (scil. τέχνη), 'the art of
interpretation', fern, of ερμηνευτικός, 'pertaining to
interpretation'. See prec. word and -ics.

## Hermes
Hermes, п., the son of Zeus and Maia, the god
of commerce and messenger of the gods in
Greek mythology; identified by the Romans
with Mercury. — L. Hermes, fr. Gk. Έρμης, of
uncertain origin. Cp. next word and herma,
Hermia, Hermione.

## hermetic
hermetic, adj. — ML. hermeticus, 'pertaining to
Hermes (Trismegistus)', fr. Gk. Έρμης Τρισ-
μέγιστος, 'Hermes thrice greatest', the Greek
name for the Egyptian god Toth, who is said
to have invented the art of making a glass-tube
airtight. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: hermetic-al-Iy, adv.

## Hermia
Hermia, fern. PN. — Fern, name formed fr. L.
Hermes, fr. Gk. Έρμης. See Hermes and cp.
next word.

## Hermione
Hermione, fern. PN. — Gk. Ερμιόνη, fr. Έρμης,
'Hermes'. See Hermes.

## hermit
hermit, n. — ME. ermit, hermit, fr. OF. ermite,
hermite (F. ermite), fr. Eccles. L. eremita, fr. Gk.
ερημίτης, 'hermit', lit. 'he who lives in the
desert', fr. έρημία, 'desert', fr. έρημος, 'solitary,
isolated', which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base
*ere-, 'to separate, be rare', whence also L.
rams, 'thin, loose'. See rare, 'thin*, and cp.
eremite, which is a doublet of hermit.
Derivatives: hermit-age, п., hermit-ess, n.

## hernia
hernia, п., protrusion of an organ or its part
through the containing cavity; rupture. — L.,
rel. to the first element in haruspex, 'diviner
inspecting entrails', and to hira, 'emtpy gut'. See
yam and cp. haruspex. Derivatives: herni-al,
herni-ate, herni-ated, adjs., herni-ation, n.

## hernio-
hernio-, combining form denoting the hernia. —
See hernia.

## herniotomy
herniotomy, п., operation of cutting for
strangulated hernia (med.) — A hybrid coined fr. hern
loan d -τομίβ, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'.
See -tomy.

## hero
hero, n. — MF. heroe, fr. heroe (F. heros), fr. L.
heroem, ace. of herds, 'hero', fr. Gk. ήρως (for
*ήρωΓ-ος), orig. 'defender, protector', rel. to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:371 COLUMN:2 -->
"HpS (for *"HpfS), 'Hera' (lit. 'tutelary
goddess'), and cogn. with L. servare, 'to save, deliver,
preserve, protect'. See conserve and cp. Hera.

## Hero
Hero, п., priestess of Aphrodite in Sestos; loved
by Leander of Abydos (see Leander). — L.
Hero, fr. Gk. Ήρώ; of uncertain origin.

## heroic
heroic, adj. — F. herolque, fr. L. heroicus, fr. Gk.
ήρωϊκός, fr. ήρως, gen. ήρωος, 'hero'. See hero
and-ic. Derivatives: heroic, п., heroic-al, adj.,
heroic-al-ly, adv., heroic-al-ness, n.

## heroin
heroin, also heroine, п., a poisonous drug
obtained from morphium. — G. Heroin, coined
by H.Dreser, who prob. formed it fr. Gk. ήρως,
'hero', and chem. suff. -in, resp. -ine.

## heroine
heroine, п., a· female hero. — L. heroina, fr. Gk.
ήρωΐνη, 'a heroine', fr. ήρως, 'a hero'. See hero
and -ine (representing Gk. -ίνη).

## heroism
heroism, n. — F. herolsme. See hero and -ism.

## heron
heron, n. — ME. heiroun, heroun, fr. OF. hairon,
heron (F. heron), fr. Frankish *haigiro, which
is rel. to OHG. heigir, heiger, heigaro, 'heron',
and to OE. higera, higere, 'magpie, woodpecker',
ON. hegri, heri, 'heron', Swed. hager, OHG.
hehara, MHG. heher, G. Hdher, 'jay', OE. hra-
gra, Du. reiger, OHG. reigaro, MHG. reiger,
G. Reiher, 'heron', and cogn. with OSlav. kriku,
'cry, scream', kricati, 'to cry, scream', Lith.
kryksti, 'to shriek', W. cryg, 'hoarse', Gk.
κρίζειν, 'to creak, screech'. All these words are
of imitative origin. Cp. next word. Cp. also
aigrette, egret.

## heronsew
heronsew, п., heron. — ME. heronsewe, fr. OF.
heroncel, heronceau, 'a young heron', dimin.
of heron. See prec. word.

## herpes
herpes, п., an inflammatory disease of the skin
(med.) — Gk. έρπης, 'shingles', lit. 'that which
creeps', fr. έρπειν, 'to creep' (whence also έρπε-
τόν, 'creeping animal, reptile'); cogn. with L.
serpere, 'to creep'. See serpent and cp. reptile.

## herpetic
herpetic, adj., pertaining to herpes (med.) —
Formed fr. Gk. έρπης, gen. έρπητος, 'shingles',
with suff. -ic. See prec. word.

## herpetifonn
herpetifonn, adj., resembling herpes (med.) —
A hybrid coined fr. Gk. έρπης, gen. έρπητος,
'shingles', and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See
herpes and form, n.

## herpetiform
herpetiform, adj., like a reptile. — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. έρπετόν, 'creeping animal,
reptile', and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See prec. word.

## herpetology
herpetology, the study of reptiles. —
Compounded of Gk. έρπετόν, 'creeping animal, reptile',
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who speaks (in a
certain form); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See herpes and -logy.
Derivatives: herpetolog-tc, herpetolog-ic-al, adjs.,
herpetolog-ic-al-ly, adv., herpetolog-ist, n.

## Herr
Herr, п., lord, master; Mr. — G., fr. MHG. herre,
fr. OHG. hiriro, herro, which is derivatively
compar. of OHG. her, 'noble', hence orig.
meant 'nobler, superior'; cp. OS., ODu. herro,
OFris. hera, Du. heer. These words are prop,
loan translations of the ML. title senior (whence
It. stgnore, F. seigneur, monsieur, Sp. senor,
Port, senhor), fr. L. senior, 'older'. See hoar and
cp. the second element in mynheer and in younker.

## herring
herring, n. —_ ME. hering, fr. OE. hxring, hiring,
rel. to OS., MLG. hering, OFris. hereng, MDu.
herinc, Du. haring, OHG. harinc, MHG. hserinc,
G. Hering; prob. orig. meaning 'the gray fish',
and rel. to OE. har, 'gray'. See hoar and subst.
suff. -ing and cp. prec. word.

## hers
hers, pron. — Earlier spelled her's, fr. ME. hires,
for hire's, formed with gen. suff. -s from the
possessive pronoun hire. See her and cp. ours,
yours.

## herse
herse, п., portcullis. — F. See hearse.

## hership
hership, п., a raid, foray (obsol.) — ME. heir-
schip, fr. OE. here, 'army', and -scipe, '-ship'.
See harry and -ship.

## Hertzian
Hertzian, adj. (e.g. Hertzian waves), discovered
by, or pertaining to, the German physicist
Heinrich Hertz (1857-94). For the ending see
suff. -Ian.

## Herzog
Herzog, п., a German or Austrian duke. — G.,
'duke', fr. MHG. herzoge, fr. OHG. herizoho,
herizogo, 'leader of an army'. See heretoga.

## Heshvan
Heshvan, п., name of the eighth Jewish month. —
ModHeb. heshwan, erroneously shortened fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:371 COLUMN:3 -->
Mishnaic Heb. marheshwdn. This latter was
namely misdivided into mar-heshwan and the
first 'element' so obtained was dropped (prob.
owing to an association with Heb. mar, 'bitter').
See Marheshvan.

## hesitance
hesitance, hesitancy, n. — L. haesitantia,
'stammering', fr. haesitans, gen. -antis. See next word
and -ce, resp. -cy.

## hesitant
hesitant, adj. — L. haesitans, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of haesitare. See next word and -ant.
Derivative: hesitant-Iy, adv.

## hesitate
hesitate, intr. and tr. v. — Fr. L. haesitatus, pp.
of haesitare, 'to stick fast, to be uncertain,
hesitate', freq. of haered, haerere, 'to stick, cling',
which stands for *ghais-ey6 and is cogn. with
Lith. gaistu, gaisti, 'to delay, tarry'. Cp. adhere
and words there referred to. For the ending see
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: hesitat-er, hesitat-or, п., hesitation
(q.v.), hesitat-ing-ly, adv., hesitat-ive, adj.,
hesitat-ive-Iy, adv., hesitat-ory, adj.

## hesitation
hesitation, n. — F. hesitation, fr. L. haesitatidnem,
ace. of haesitatio, 'irresolution, uncertainty,
hesitation', fr. haesitatus, pp. of haesitare. See
hesitate and -ion.

## hesped
hesped, п., a funeral oration. — Mishnaic Heb.
hespedh, fr. hisptdh, 'he delivered a funeral
oration', Hiph'il (= causative form) of Biblical Heb.
sdphadh,'he wailed, lamented', whence mispedh,
'wailing'; rel. to Aram.-Syr. s'phadh, 'he wailed,
lamented', Akkad. sipdu, sipittu, 'mourning',
Ethiop. sadaphe (metathesis), 'dirge'.

## Hesper
Hesper, n. — See Hesperus.

## Hesperian
Hesperian, adj., Western. — Formed with suff.
-an fr. L. hesperius, fr. Gk. έσπέριος, 'western',
fr. έσπερος (for *5έσπερος), п., 'evening'; adj.,
of the evening, western', which is cogn. with
L. vesper, 'evening'. See vesper.

## Hesperides
Hesperides, n. pi., the three nymphs who guarded
the golden apples which Gaea had given as a
wedding present to Hera (Greek mythol.) — L.,
fr. Gk. 'Εσπερίδες, lit. 'daughters of the west',
pi. of the fem. adj. έσπερίς, 'western'; so called
because they dwelt at the western end of the
world. See Hesperis.
Derivative: Hesperid-ian, adj.

## hesperidin
hesperidin, a crystalline glycoside, C2aH34015"
(chem.) — Formed from next word with chem.
suff. -in.

## hesperidium
hesperidium, п., a many-celled fleshy fruit with
a leathery rind, as the orange, lemon, etc. (bot.)
— ModL., fr. L. Hesperides (see Hesperides); so
called in allusion to the golden apples of the
Hesperides. For the ending see suff. -ium.

## Hesperis
Hesperis, п., a genus of plants of the family Bras-
sicaceae (bot.) — L. hesperis, 'the damewort',
fr. Gk. έσπερίς, prop. fem. of the adjective
έσπέριος, 'of the evening; western', fr. έσπερος,
'evening'. See Hesperian and cp. Hesperides.

## Hesperornis
Hesperornis, п., a genus of very large swimming
birds from the Cretaceous of Kansas (pale-
ontol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. έσπερος,
'of the evening; western', and όρνις, 'bird'. See
Hesperian and ornitho-.

## Hesperus
Hesperus, also (poet.) Hesper, п., the evening
star, esp. Venus. — L. Hesperus, fr. Gk.
έσπερος, short for έσπερος αστήρ, 'evening star'.
See Hesperian.

## Hessian
Hessian, adj., pertaining to Hesse in Germany.
— Formed fr. Hesse — G. Hessen, a subdivision
(formerly a grand duchy) in Germany. For the
ending see suff. -ian.

## hessian
hessian, п., a coarse cloth of hemp or of hemp
and jute. — Short for Hessian cloth. See prec.
word.

## hessite
hessite, п., a silver telluride (mineral.) — Named
after the Swiss chemist Henry Hess (1802-50)
in Russia, who first analyzed it. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## best
best, п., bidding, behest. — ME. hest, formed
with excrescent t fr. hes, fr. OE. hxs, from
the stem of htttan, 'to bid'. See hight and cp.
behest.

## hesternal
hesternal, adj., of yesterday. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. heslernus, 'of yesterday', which
stands for *hestrinos and is cogn. with OI.
hyastanah, Gk. χθεσινός, 'of yesterday'. L.
heslernus derives fr. heri, 'yesterday', as OI.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:372 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 345 | HEXODE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:372 COLUMN:1 -->
hyastanah derives fr. OI. hyah, 'yesterday', Gk.
χθεσινός fr. χ*ές, of s.m. See yester-,

## Hestia
Hestia, п., the goddess of the hearth in Greek
mythology. — Gk. 'Εστία, fr. έστίά, 'hearth;
house, home, family', whence έστιαν, 'to
receive at one's hearth'. See Vesta.

## hetaera
hetaera, hetaira, п., mistress. — ModL. hetaera,
fr. Gk. εταίρα, 'female companion, courtesan',
fern, of εταίρος, 'companion', fr. earlier έταρος,
'companion', fr. a dental enlargement of l.-E.
*ip-, a collateral form of base *swe-, 'his, her,
its; one's'. See sui and cp. sodality.

## hetaerism
hetaerism, hetairism, п., concubinage. — Gk.
έταιρισμός,'harlotry', fr. έταιρίζειν,'to associate
with a courtesan, hetaera', fr. εταίρα. See
hetaera and -ism.

## hetero-
hetero-, before a vowel heter-, combining form
meaning 'other, different'. — Gk. έτερο-, έτερ-,
fr. έτερος, 'the other (of two); another,
different', altered—under the influence of εις, gen.
ενός, "one'—fr. earlier άτερος (ср. Gk. έ-κατόν,
'one hundred', fr. *ά-κατον, which was also
influenced in form by *εΐς, gen. ενός). Gk. ατερος
stands for I.-E. *sm-tero-. The first element of
this compound means 'one at one, together';
see same and cp. haplo-, hecatomb. The second
element is the comparative suffix; it is cogn.
with the suffixes in L. al-ter, Goth, an-par, OE.
ό-oer, 'other'. See -ther and cp. words there
referred to.

## heterabiastic
heterabiastic, adj.. developed from cells of
another kind (biol.) — Compounded of hetero-
and Gk. βλαστός, 'bud, sprout, shoot'. See
-blastic and cp. homoplastic.

## heterochromous
heterochromous, adj., of different colors. —
Compounded of hetero- and Gk. χρώμα,
'color'. See chrome and -ous and cp. homo-
chromous.

## heteroclite
heteroclite, adj., irregular in declension (gram.) —
F. heteroclite, fr. Late L. heteroclitus, which is
compounded of hetero- and Gk. κλιτός,
'inflected', verbal adj. of κλίνειν, 'to bend,
incline, inflect'. See clinical.
Derivatives: heteroclite, п., an irregular noun,
heteroclit-al, heteroclit-ic, heteroclit-ic-al, hetero-
clit-ons, adjs.

## heterodont
heterodont, adj., having teeth of different kinds
(as man and most mammals) (zooi.) —
Compounded' of heter- and Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος,
'tooth'. See odonto- and cp. homodont.

## heterodox
heterodox, adj., unorthodox. — Gk. έτερόδοξος,
'holding opinions other than the right',
compounded of έτερος, the other' (see hetero-), and
δόξα, 'opinion', fr. δακεΐν, 'to think*. See decent
add dogma and cp. doxastic and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: heterodox-ly, adv., heterodox-
ness, n.

## heterodoxy
heterodoxy, п., the quality of being heterodox. —
Gk. έτεροδοξίά, 'a taking one thing for
another', fr. έτερόδοξος. See heterodox and -y
(representing Gk. -ίά).

## heterodyne
heterodyne, adj. (radio). — Coined by the
Canadian physicist and radio technician Reginald
Aubrey Fessenden (1866-1932) in 1908 fr.
hetero- and -dyne.

## heterogamous
heterogamous, adj., bearing flowers of sexually
two kinds (hot.) — Compounded of hetero- and
Gk. γάμος, 'marriage'. See -gamous and cp.
homogamous.

## heterogamy
heterogamy, n. (bot.) — See prec. word and -gamy
and cp. homogamy.

## heterogeneal
heterogeneal, adj., heterogeneous. — See
heterogeneous and adj. surf, -al and cp. homogeneal.

## heterogeneity
heterogeneity, п., quality of being heterogeneous.
— F. heterogeneite, fr. ML. heterogeneitas, fr.
heterogeneus. See next word and -ity and cp.
homogeneity.

## heterogeneous
heterogeneous,п., not homogeneous, disparate. —
ML. heterogeneus, fr. Gk. ετερογενής, 'of
different kind', fr. έτερος, 'another, different', and
γένος, 'race, descent, gender, kind'. See hetero-,
genus and -ous and cp. homogeneous.
Derivatives: heterogeneous-ly, adv., hetero-
geneous-ness, n.

## heterogenesis
heterogenesis,п., ι) abiogenesis; 2)alternation of
generations (biol.) — Coined by the French
anatomist Gilbert Breschet (1784-1845) fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:372 COLUMN:2 -->
hetero- and genesis. Cp. homogenesis.

## heterogenetic
heterogenetic, adj., pertaining to heterogenesis. —
Compounded of hetero- and -genetic. Cp.
homogenetic,

## heterogeny
heterogeny, п., ι) heterogenesis; 2) a
heterogeneous collection. — Compounded of hetero-
and -gcny. Cp. homogeny.
Derivatives: heterogen-ic, adj., heterogen-ic-ity,
п., heterogen-ist, n.

## heterography
heterography, п., incorrect spelling. —
Compounded of hetero- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: heterograph-ic, heterograph-ic-al,
adjs.

## heterogynous
heterogynous, adj., having females of two kinds,
as the ants and bees. — Compounded of hetero-
and Gk. γυνή, 'woman'. See gyneco-.

## heterologous
heterologous, adj., containing different elements;
not corresponding. — Compounded of hetero-
and Gk. λόγος, 'word, speech, discourse;
proportion'. See logos and -ous and cp. homotogous.

## heteromorphic
heteromorphic, adj., differing in shape. — See
heteromorphous and -ic and cp. homomorphic.

## heteromorphism
heteromorphism, п., the quality of being
heteromorphic. — See heteromorphous and -ism and
cp. homomorphism.

## heteromorphous
heteromorphous, adj., 1) heteromorphic; 2) of
irregular shape. — Gk. έτερόμορφος, 'of different
form', fr. έτερος, 'another, different', and μορφή,
'form, shape'. See hetero- and -morphous and
cp. homomorphous.

## heteromorphy
heteromorphy, п., heteromorphism. — See prec.
word and -morpby.

## heteronomous
heteronomous, adj., under the rule of another;
subject to, or having, different laws. —
Compounded of hetero- and Gk. νόμος, 'law'. See
nomo- and -ous and cp. autonomous.
Derivative: heteronomous-ly, adv.

## hcteroriomy
hcteroriomy, п., subjection to the rule of another;
subjection to different laws. — See prec. word
and -nomy and cp. autonomy,

## heteroousian
heteroousian, heterousian, adj., of different
essence (Eccles. hist.) — Formed with suff. -an
fr. Gk. έτεροούσιος, έτερούσιος, 'of different
essence', fr. έτερος, 'another, different' (see
hetero-), and ούσίά, 'essence, substance', which
derives fr. οδσα, fern, of ών, 'being', pres. part,
of είναι, 'to be'. See esse and cp. essence. Cp.
also homoiousian, homoousian.
Derivative: Heteroousian, Heterousian, n.

## heterophyllous
heterophyllous, adj., having different kinds of
leaves on the same plant (bot.) — Compounded
of hetero- and Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf. See -phyllous.

## heterosexual
heterosexual, adj., having sexual desire for those
of the opposite sex. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk.
έτερος, 'the other, different', and L. sexus,
'sex'. See hetero- and sexual and cp. homosexual.
Derivative: heterosexual-ity, n.

## heterousian
heterousian, n. — The same as heteroousian.

## hetman
hetman, п.. a Cossack commander. — Pol., fr.
G. Hauptmann, 'captain', lit. 'headman', fr.
Haupt, 'head', and Mann, 'man'. See head and
man and cp. headman. Cp. also ataman.

## Heuchera
Heuchera, п., a genus of plants of the saxifrage
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
German botanist Johann Heinrich von Heucher
(1677-1747).

## heulandite
heulandite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after the English mineralogist
Henry Heuland. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## heuristic
heuristic, adj., serving to discover or find out. —
G. heuristisch, fr. ModL. heuristicus, which was
formed with suff. -isticus (see -istic) from the
stem of Gk. εΰρίσκειν, Aor. εύρον, 'to find,
discover', which stands for *IFρίσκειν and is
cogn. with Olr. fuar, Ί have found', frith, 'was
found'. Cp. eureka, arytenoid.
Derivative: heuristic-al-ly, adv.

## hew
hew, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hewen, fr. OE. hea-
wan, 'to cut, strike, hew', rel. to OS. hauwan,
ON. hoggva, Swed. hugga, Du. houwen, OHG.
houwan, MHG. houwen, G. hauen, 'to cut,

## strike
strike, hew', fr. I.-E. base *qau-, *q'u-, 'to

## strike
strike, beat', whence also Toch. В kaut-, A kol-,
'to cleave, cut', OSlav. kovg, kovati, Lith. kauju,

## kauti
kauti, 'to beat, forge', Lett, kauju, kaut, 'to

## beat'
beat', Lith. kova, 'battle', L. cudere (for *cau-

## dere)
dere), 'to strike, beat'. Cp. hag, 'to hew', haggle,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:372 COLUMN:3 -->
hoe. Cp. also candal, candex, cause, codex,
concuss, coward, lacus.
Derivative: hew-er, n.

## hewettite
hewettite, п., a hydrous calcium vanadate
(mineral.) — Named after the American geologist
D. Foster Hewell (born in 1881). For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## hewn
hewn, adj., prop. pp. of hew. — ME. hewen, fr.
OE. heaven, pp. of heawan, 'to hew'. See hew.

## hexa-
hexa-, before a vowel hex-, combining form
meaning 'six'. — Gk. έξα-, έξ-, fr. έξ, 'six',
which is cogn. with L. sex, Goth, saihs, OE.
six, seox; see six. The ж in έξα- is due to the
analogy of επτά, 'seven', εννέα, 'nine', δέκα,
'ten'; cp. penta-, octa-.

## hexachord
hexachord, п., a diatonic series of six tones (Greek
and Medieval music). — Compounded of hexa-
and Gk. χορδή, 'chord'. See chord and cp.
words there referred to.

## hexad
hexad, п., a group of six things. — Late L. hexas,
gen. hexadis, fr. Gk. εξάς, gen. έξάδος, .'a group
of six', fr. έξ. See hexa- and -ad.

## hexagon
hexagon, п., a plane figure with six angles and
six sides (geom.) — L. hexagonum, fr. Gk.
εξάγωνος, 'having six angles', which is
compounded of έξα- (see hexa-) and -γωνος, from
the stem of γωνία, 'angle'. See -gon.
Derivative: hexagon-at, adj.

## hexagram
hexagram, n.—Compounded of hexa- and -gram.

## hexahedral
hexahedral, adj., having the form of a
hexahedron. — See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## hexahedron
hexahedron, п., a solid figure with six plane faces.
— Compounded of hexa- and έδρα, 'seat; base,
side, face'. See -hedron.

## hexamerous
hexamerous, adj., consisting of six parts in each
whorl (bot.) — Compounded of hexa- and Gk.
μέρβς, 'part'. See -nierous.

## hexameter
hexameter, п., a verse of six metrical feet (pros.)
— L., fr. Gk. έξάμετρος (scil. στίχος), lit. '(a
verse) having six measures'; compounded of
έξα- (see hexa-) and μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm', and cp. tetrameter,
pentameter.
Derivatives: hexameter, adj., having six metrical
feet, hexametr-al, hexametr-ic, hexametr-ic-al,
adjs., hexameter.

## hexapla
hexapla, п., a book containing six versions in
parallel columns; specif., the Hexapla compiled
by Origen. — Eccles. L. hexapla, fr. Gk. έξαπλ'?.
neut. pi. of έξαπλόος, έξαπλοΰς, 'sixfoldf, fr.
έξα- (see hexa-) and suff. -πλόος, '-fold', which
occurs also in άπλόος, άπλοϋς, 'simple'. See
haplo- and cp. tetrapla.

## hexapod
hexapod, п., ι) any six-footed insect; 2) any insect
of the class Hexapoda. — Gk. έξάπους, gen.
έξάποδος, 'six-footed', compounded of έξα- (see
hexa-) and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See -pod.

## Hexapoda
Hexapoda, п., a class of six-footed insects (ento-
mol.) — ModL. See prec. word.

## hexastich
hexastich, п., a stanza or poem consisting of six
verses or lines (pros.) — Gk. έξάστιχος, 'of six
lines', compounded of έξα- (see hexa-) and
στίχος, 'row, line, rank; verse'. See stichic and
cp. acrostic and words there referred to.

## hexastyle
hexastyle, adj., having six columns in front. —
Gk. έξάστϋλος, 'having six columns',
compounded of έξα- (see hexa-) and στϋλος, 'pillar,
column'. See style, 'gnomon'.

## Hexatench
Hexatench, п., the first six books of the Bible, i.e.
the Pentateuch and the book of
Joshua.—Compounded of hexa- and Gk. τεϋχος, 'tool,
implement', later 'book'. See Pentateuch and cp.
Heptateuch, Octatench.
Derivative: Hexaleuch-al, adj.

## hexathlon
hexathlon, п., an athletic contest in which each
competitor takes part in six events. — Formed
on analogy of pentathlon fr. hexa- and Gk.
5»λον, 'prize of contest'. See athlete.

## hexavalent
hexavalent, adj., having a valence of six (chem.)
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. έξ, "six", and L.
valens, gen. valentis, pres. part, of valere, 'to
have power'; see hexa- and -valent. The correct
form is sexivalent, in which both elements are
of Latin origin.

## hexode
hexode, adj., pertaining to a system of telegraphy
in which six messages can be transmitted
simultaneously. — Compounded of Gk. έξ, 'six', and
οδός, 'way'. See hexa- and odograph.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:373 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HEXONE | 346 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:373 COLUMN:1 -->

## hexone
hexone, п., any of certain compounds containing
six atoms of carbon in the molecule (biochem.)
— Fr. Gk. έξ, 'six*. See hexa-,

## hey
hey, interj. — Imitative. Cp. Du. and G. hei,
and E. hi.

## heyday
heyday, interj. — Du. heida; the ending was
influenced by day.

## heyday
heyday, п., time of vigor. — Perh. lit. meaning
'high day', fr. ME. hey day. See high and day.

## Hezekiah
Hezekiah, i) masc. PN; 2) in the Bible, any of
several persons, esp. a king of Judah, son of
King Ahaz. — Heb. Hizqiyya", lit. 'the Lord
has strengthened', compounded of hdzaq, 'he
was strong, he strengthened', and the shortened
form of the Tetragrammaton. See Ezekiel and
Elijah.

## hi
hi, interj. — Imitative. Cp. hey.

## hiatus
hiatus, п., a gap, lacuna. — L., Opening,
aperture, gap', fr. hial-(um), pp. stem of Шаге, 'to
yawn'. See yawn and cp. dehisce.

## hibernaculum
hibernaculum, n„ that, which serves for protection
during winter (zool.) — L. hibernaculum, 'winter
residence', fr. hibernare, 'to spend the winter'.
See hibernate and -culum.

## hibernate
hibernate, intr. v., to pass the winter. — L. hiber-
nat-(um), pp. stem of hibernare, 'to pass the
winter, to winter', fr. hibernus, 'pertaining to
winter, wintry', which is rel. to hiems (gen. hie-
mis), 'winter', fr. I.-E. base *ghei-, *ghi-,
'winter; snow', whence also OI. heman, 'in
winter', hemantah, 'winter,' himah, 'winter',
Hitt. gimmanza, 'winter', Avestic zaya(n)-, zya
(gen. zimd), 'winter', Arm. jiun, 'snow', jmefn,
'winter', Gk. χεΐμα, 'winter, winter weather,
storm', χειμών, 'the season of winter',
χειμερινός 'wintry', χιών (for *χιώμ), 'snow', Alb.
Gheg dimen, Tosk dimere, 'winter', OSlav. zima,
Lith. zlema, Lett, zlema, OPruss. semo, 'winter',
Olr. gaim (for Celtic *giamo-), Mir. gem-red,
'winter', Gk. χίμαρος, 'he-goat', χιμάρα,
χίμαιρα, 'goat' (lit. 'a goat one winter old'), Toch.
A cemdl, 'goat' (Ht. 'a goat one winter old'), L.
blmus (contraction of *bi-himos), 'two years
old' Qit. 'two winters old'), lrimus (contraction
of *tri-himos), 'three years old' (lit. 'three
winters old'), ON. gymbr, 'a ewe one year (lit. one
winter) old'. Cp. chimera, chiono-, hlemal, the
first element in Chimaphila, Himalaya and the
second element in Hedychium, isocheime. Cp.
also gimmer, 'a she-lamb'.
Derivative: hibernat-ion, n.

## Hibernian
Hibernian, adj., Irish. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Hibernia (cp. Ptolemy's Ίουερνίϊ)
'Ireland', fr. Iverna, Juverna (cp. Gk. 'Ι/έρνη,
Ίέρνη), fr. OCelt. 'Iverin, whence also Olr.
Erin, Ir. Eire (see Erin); influenced in form by
L. hibernus, 'wintry' (see hibernate).
Derivatives: Hibernian, п., Hibernian-ism, a.,
Hibern-ic, Hibernic-al, adjs., Hibern-ic-al-ly,
adv., Hibern-ic-ism, п., Hibern-ic-ize, tr. v.

## Hiberno-
Hiberno-, combining form meaning 'Irish'. —
Formed fr. L. Hibernia, 'Ireland'; see prec.
word.

## Hibiscus
Hibiscus, п., a genus of plants, the rose mallow
(bot.) — L. hibiscum, ibiscum, later hibiscus,
ibiscus, 'marshmallow', prob. a Celtic loan
word. Gk. ίβίσκος, of s.m., is borrowed fr.
Latin.

## hiccup
hiccup, hiccough, n. and intr. and tr. v. — Fr.
earlier hickup; of imitative origin.

## hie jacet
hie jacet, epitaph. — L., 'here lies'; so called
from the first words of Latin epitaphs.

## hick
hick, п., a rustic (Amer. Slang). — Fr. Hick, a
pet form of Richard.

## hickory
hickory, n. — Aphetic for pokahickory from the
Virginian native name powcohiccora denoting
the product made from the pounded kernels.

## hid
hid, past tense of hide. — ME. hid, fr. OE. hydde,
past tense of hydan. See hide.

## hidage
hidage, п., formerly, a tax paid for every hide of
land. — A hybrid coined fr. OE. higid, hid (see
hide, 'measure of land'), and -age, a suff. of
Latin origin.

## hidalgo
hidalgo, п., a Spanish nobleman of secondary
rank. — Sp„ fr. OSp. ftdalgo, contraction oifljo
de algo, lit. 'son of something; son of fortune',
fr. ftjo, 'son' (fr. L. fllius), de, 'from, of (fr.
L. de, 'from, away from'), and algo, 'something,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:373 COLUMN:2 -->
property, fortune' (fr. L. aliquod, something');
see Meyer-Liibke, REW., No. 345 and No. 3303.
For the origin of the above Latin words see
filial, de- and aliquot.

## hidden
hidden, adj., prop. pp. of hide. — ME. hidden,
a new formation. Cp. OE. (ge)hydd, 'hidden',
and see hide, 'to conceal'.
Derivatives: hidden-Iy, adv., hidden-ness, n.

## hide
hide, tr. and intr. v., to conceal. — ME. huden,
hiden, fr. OE. hydan, cogn. with Gk. κεύθειν,
'to hide, conceal', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeudh-, 'to
cover, hide, conceal'. See custody and cp. next
word. Cp. also board, hose, house, huddle, hut.

## hide
hide, п., skin. — ME. hide, hude, fr. OE. hyd,
'skin', rel. to OS. hud, ON. hud, Dan., Swed.
hud, OFris. hid, MDu. hum, Du. huid, OHG.,
MHG. hut, G. Haul, 'skin', lit. 'that which
covers', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeut-, 'to cover',
whence also Gk. κύτος, 'skin, cover', σκδτος,
'leather', L. cutis, 'skin', Lith. kiautas, 'husk',
OPruss. keuto, 'skin', W. cwd, 'scrotum', OFris.
hothan, OHG. hodo, MHG., G. hode, 'scrotum'.
Base *(s)qeu-t- is a collateral form of.base
*(s)qeu-d-. See prec. word. See also cutis.
Derivative: hide, tr. v., to take the hide off;
to flog.

## hide
hide, п., a measure of land (Engl, history). —
ME. hid, fr. OE. hid, contraction of higid, orig.
'land (sufficient) to support a family', rel. to
hlgan, hiwan (pi.), 'members of a family', hiwen,
'family, household'. See home and cp. hind, 'farm
servant'. Cp. also hud, husk.

## hideous
hideous, adj., very ugly. — ME. hidous, fr. OF.
hisdous, hidous (F. hideux), fr. OF. hisde,
'hideous', which possibly derives fr. L. hispidus,
'shaggy; prickly, bristly'; 'rough' (in a fig.
sense); see hispid and -eons. See R. Grandsaignes
d'Hauterive, Dictionnaire d'ancien francais,
P. 353 s.v. hisde, adj.
Derivatives: hideous-Iy, adv., hideous-ness, n.

## hiding
hiding, п., flogging. — Formed fr. hide, 'to flog' (fr.
hide,'skin'), with -ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## hiding
hiding, п., concealment. — Formed fr. hide, 'to
conceal', with -Ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## hidrosis
hidrosis, п., excessive perspiration (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -osis fr. Gk.
ίδροϋν, 'to sweat', fr. ίδρώς [(for *sw1dros),
'sweat, perspiration', which is rel. to ίδος, (for
"swidos), 'violent heat', fr. I.-E. base "sweid-,
*swoid-, *swid-, 'to sweat', whence also L. su-
dare (for *swoiddre), OE. swxtan, 'to sweat*.
See sweat and cp. sudation.

## hidrotic
hidrotic, adj., causing perspiration; sudorific
(med.) — Gk. ϊδρωτικός, 'sudorific', fr. ίδρώς,
gen. ίδρώτος, 'sweat'. See prec. word and -ic.

## hie
hie, intr. and tr. v., to hasten. — ME. highen,
hien, fr. OE. higian, 'to strive, hasten', which
is prob. cogn. with OI. sXghrah 'quick, fast',
Russ. sigat', 'to leap'.

## hiemal
hiemal, adj., pertaining to winter; wintry. — L.
hiemalis, 'of winter', fr. hiems, gen. hiemis,
'winter'. See hibernate and adj. surf. -al.

## hier-
hier-, form of hiero- before a vowel.

## Hieracium
Hieracium, п., a genus of plants, the hawk weed
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. Ιερακιον, name of a
plant, fr. ίέρϊξ, gen. ϊέρακος, 'hawk', lit. 'the
swift (bird)', fr. ιερός, 'quick, swift'. See hiero-.

## hierarch
hierarch, n„ the chief of a religious group; high
priest. — ML. hierarchia, fr. Gk. ιεράρχης,
'leader of sacred rites, high priest', which is
compounded of ιερός, 'holy, sacred', and -άρχης,
'leader'. See hiero- and -arch.

## hierarchic
hierarchic, hierarchical, adj., pertaining to a
hierarchy. — ML. hierarchicus, fr. hierarchia.
See next word and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: hierarchical-ly, adv.

## hierarchy
hierarchy, п., ι) church government by priests;
2) graded system of officials, esp. of sacred
persons. — F. hiirarchie, fr. ML. hierarchia, fr.
Gk. ιεραρχία, 'office of a hierarch', fr. ιεράρχης.
See hierarch and -y (representing Gk. -IS).
Derivatives: hierarch-al, adj., hierarch-al-ly,
adv., hierarchic (q.v.)

## hieratic
hieratic, adj., pertaining to sacred things;
priestly. — L. hieraticus, fr. Gk. Ιερατικός,
'pertaining to a priest', fr. ιερός, 'holy, sacred'. See
hiero- and -ic.

## hiero-
hiero-, before a vowel hier-, combining form

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:373 COLUMN:3 -->
meaning 'holy, sacred'. — Gk. iepo-, lep-, fr.
ιερός, 'holy, sacred', orig. 'filled with (divine)
force', and prop, identical with ιερός, 'strong,
lively, active, quick, swift', fr. I.-E. base *eis-,
'to set in quick motion, drive on, incite'. See ire
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
Hieracium and the first element in Jerome.

## Hierochloe
Hierochloe, п., a genus of plants, the holy grass
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'holy grass', fr. hiero- and
Gk. χλόη, 'a young green shot'. See Chloe.

## hierocracy
hierocracy, п., rule of sacred persons, hierarchy.
— Compounded of hiero- and Gk. -κρατία,
'rule of, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'.
See -cracy.

## hierocratic
hierocratic, hierocratical, adj., pertaining to, or
characterized by, hierocracy. — See prec. word
and -ic, resp. also -al.

## hierodule
hierodule, п., a temple slave in ancient Greece. —
Late L. hierodulus, fr. Gk. ίερίδουλος, lit.
'temple slave', compounded of ιερός, 'holy,
sacred' (see hiero-), and δοϋλος, 'slave', which
stands for "δόελος and derives fr. Aegean doero,
'slave'. Cp. the first element in dulocracy. For
sense development cp. devadasi.

## hieroglyph
hieroglyph, п., picture writing used by the ancient
Egyptians. — F. hieroglyphe, Ъаск formation
fr. hieroglyphique, fr. L. hieroglyphicus. See
next word.

## hieroglyphic
hieroglyphic, adj..pertaining to hieroglyphs. — L.
hieroglyphicus, fr. Gk. ιερογλυφικός,
'hieroglyphic', lit. 'pertaining to sacred carvings'
compounded of ιερός, 'holy, sacred' (see hiero-),
and γλύφειν, 'to carve'. See glyph and -ic and
cp. anaglyph.
Derivatives: hieroglyphic, п.,
hieroglyphic-ally, adv.

## hierogram
hierogram, п., a sacred character or symbol. —
Compounded of hiero- and Gk. γράμμα, 'that
which is written; a written character'. See -gram.

## hlerograph
hlerograph, п., a hierogram. — Compounded of
hiero- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graph.

## hierographic
hierographic, adj., pertaining to sacred symbols.
— Gk. ίερογραφικός, 'pertaining to sacred
writing', compounded of Ιερός, 'holy, sacred'
(see hiero-), and γράφειν, 'to write'. See graphic.

## hierolatry
hierolatry, п., worship of saints. — Compounded
of hiero- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρία, fr. λατρεία,
'worship'. See -latry.

## hierology
hierology, п., the sacred literature of a people. —
Compounded of hiero- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## hierophant
hierophant, п., an interpreter of religious
mysteries. — Late L. hierophantes, fr. Gk. ίερο-
φάντης, 'one who initiates into mysteries,
hierophant', lit. 'one who shows sacred things', which
is compounded of ιερός, 'holy, sacred' (see
hiero-), and the stem of φαίνειν, 'to show'. See
phantasm.

## hierophantic
hierophantic, adj., pertaining to a hierophant or
his acts. — Gk. ίεροφαντικός 'pertaining to a
which the robber is supposed to bring his victim
to a sudden stop.

## hijra
hijra, n. — See hegira.

## hike
hike, intr. v. — Prob. a var. of hitch.

## hilarious
hilarious, adj., merry, gay. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. hilar us, hilaris, 'cheerful, gay', fr. Gk.
Ιλαρός, of s.m., which is rel. to "ϊλημι (for ·σ[-
σλη-μι), Ί am gracious' (only in the imper.:
Homeric ϊληθι, Dor. ΐλαθι, Aeol. έλλαθι, 'be
gracious!'), ϊλάσκομαι (for *σι-σλά-σκομαι), Ί
appease, propitiate, reconcile to myself , Les-
bic ϊλλαος, Homeric ΐλα(Γ)ος, Laconic ΐλη5ος,
Att. Ιλεως, 'propitious, gracious', and cogn.
with L. sotari, 'to comfort', salvus, 'whole, safe',
OE. sSIig, gesxlig, 'happy, fortunate'. See silly
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also Hilary,
exhilarate.
Derivatives: hitarious-ty, adv., hilarious-ness, n.

## hilarity
hilarity, п., merriment, gaiety. — F. hilarite, fr.
L. hilaritatem, ace. of hilaritas, 'cheerfulness,
gaiety', fr. hilaris. See prec. word and -ity.

## Hilary
Hilary, masc. PN. — Late L. Hilarius, lit.
'cheerful', fr. L. hilaris. See hilarious.

## Hilda
Hilda, fern. PN. — G., lit. 'battle maid', fr.
OHG. Midi, 'war, battle', which is rel. to OE.
hild, ON. hildr, of s.m., and prob; cogn. with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:374 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 347 | HIPPODAMIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:374 COLUMN:1 -->
Mir. cellach (for 'celdach), 'war'. Cp. the first
element in Hildebrand, Hildegard and the second
element in Clothilda, Matilda.

## Hildebrand
Hildebrand, masc. PN. — OHG. Hildibrand, lit.
'battle sword', fr, hildi, 'war, battle' and branda
'sword'. See Hilda and brand.

## Hildegard(e)
Hildegard(e), fern. PN. — OHG. Hildegard, lit.
'protecting battle maid', compounded of hildi,
'war, battle', and *gard, 'to enclose, protect'.
For the first element see Hilda, for the second
see yard, 'enclosure', and cp. garden.

## hilding
hilding, п., a base wretch; adj. base (archaic). —
Formed with suff. -ing fr. OE. hyldan, heldan,
'to lean, incline, bend down'. See heel, 'to lean'.

## hill
hill, n. — ME. hit, hul, hull, fr. OE. hyll, rel. to
MDu. hille, LG. hull, 'hill', ON. hallr, 'stone',
Goth, hallus, 'rock', ON. holmr, OE. holm,
'rising land, island', fr. I.-E. base *qel-, 'to rise,
be elevated', whence also OI. кЩат (for kul-
tam), 'top, skull' (orig. 'elevation'), Gk. κολωνός,
κολώνη, L. collis, 'hill', columen, 'top', columna,
'column'. See column and cp. holm. Cp. also
hillock.
Derivatives: hill, tr. v., hill-y, adj., hill-i-ness, n.

## hillebrandite
hillebrandite, п., a hydrous calcium orthosilicate
(mineral.) — Named after the American chemist
William Frances Hillebrand (1853-1925). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Hillel
Hillel, masc. PN. — Heb. НИШ, fr. hilWl, 'he
praised', whence hallel, 'to praise'. See hallel.

## hillock
hillock, n. — Formed fr. hili with dimin. suff.
-ock.

## hilsa
hilsa, hilsnh, п., a fish (Clupea ilisha). — Hind.
hilsa, fr. OI. ilisah.

## hilt
hilt, n. — ME., fr. OE. hill, hille, rel. to ON.
hjalt, OHG. helza, 'hilt', OS. hella, 'oar handle'
hierophant', fr. ίεροφάντης. See prec. word and
-ic.
Derivative: hierophantic-al-ly, adv.

## Hierosolymitan
Hierosolymitan, adj., of Jerusalem; п., a native
of Jerusalem. — L. Hierosolymitdnus, fr. Hiero-
solyma, fr. Gk. 'Ιεροσόλυμα, alteration of Heb.
Y'rushalayim owing to a mistaken association
with Gk. ιερής, 'holy', and Σόλυμοι, name of
a people in Lycia. See Jerusalem. For the ending
see subst. sufT. -ite and suff. -an.

## Hierosolymite
Hierosolymite, adj. and п., Hierosolymitan. —
■ See prec. word.

## higgle
higgle, intr. v., to haggle. — A weakened form of
haggle.
Derivative: higgl-ing, n.

## higgledy-piggledy
higgledy-piggledy, adv., in confusion; adj.,
confused; п., confusion. — Of uncertain origin.

## high
high, adj. — ME. heigh, hegh, heh, hey, fr. OE.
heah, heh, rel. to OS. huh, ON. har, Dan. hei,
Swed. hog, OFris. hack, MDu. hooch, Du. hoog,
OHG. hoh, MHG. hoch, G. hoch, Goth, hauhs,
'high', ON. haugr, 'mound', MHG. houc, hou-
ges, OSwed. hugli, G. Hiigel, 'hill', and cogn.
with Toch. А кос, В каис, 'high', Lith. kaukas,
'boil, tumor', kaukara, kaukaras, 'hill', Lett.
kukurs, 'hump', Olr. cuar, 'bent, crooked', OI.
kucati, kmcaie, 'bends, twists' (intr.). All these
words are derivatives of I.-E. *qeu-q-,
enlargement of base *qeu-, 'to bend', whence, with
reduplication, L. сасйтеп (prob. fr. orig. *kakud),
'tip, summit'. Cp. how, 'hillock', huckster, huge,
shock, 'group of sheaves', and the first word in
Hogen Mogen. Cp. also cacuminal, cubicle, cup.
Derivatives: high, n. and adv., highly (q.v.),
highness (q.v.)

## highboy
highboy, п., a high chest of drawers. — A hybrid
formed fr. E. high and F. bois, 'wood'. See bush
and cp. hautboy. Cp. also tallboy, lowboy.

## highfalutin
highfalutin, highfaluting, adj., bombastic; п.,
bombast. — Of uncertain origin.

## highly
highly, adv. — ME. heghly, heyly, fr. OE. healice,
formed fr. heah, 'high', with suff. -lice. See high
and adv. suff. -ly.

## highness
highness, n. — ME. heghnes, heynes, fr. OE.
hiahnes, formed fr. heah, 'high', with suff.
-nes. See high and -ness.

## hight
hight, v., called, named (archaic). — ME. highte,
a blend of OE. hatte, Ί am called, I was called',
passive pres. and past tense of hdtan, 'to call,
name, command', and OE. heht, 'called', active
past tense of the same verb; rel. to ON. heila,
MLG. heten, MDu., heeten, Du. helen, OHG.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:374 COLUMN:2 -->
heisjan, MHG. heijen, G. heifien, Goth, haitan,
'to call, be called; to command'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. *qeid-, *qoid-, a -^/-enlargement
of *ql-, 'to set or be in motion'. See cite and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also behight, hest,
behest,
high treason. — Loan translation of F. haute
trahison, whence also G. Hochverrat.

## hijacker
hijacker, п., robber who preys on bootleggers
(U.S. Slang). — Prob. fr. Hi Jack, words with
prob. also to OE. hoh, 'wood'. See holt, 'small
wood'. Derivative: hilt, tr. v.

## hilum
hilum, п., scar on a seed (bot.) — L. hilum, 'a
little thing, trifle'. The orig. meaning was
perhaps 'a little thread or fiber', in which case
hilum would be a var. of /Hum, 'thread'. See file,
'a collection of papers', and cp. nihil.

## him
him, pers. pron. — ME., fr. OE. him, dat. of he.
See he.

## Himalayas
Himalayas, n. pi. — OI. himalayah, lit. 'abode of
snow', fr. himah, 'snow', and alayah, 'abode'.
See hibernate.
Derivative: Himalay-an, adj.

## himation
himation, п., Greek garment worn over ihe chiton
(Greek antiq.) — Gk. ίμάτιον, for εΐμάτιον,
fr. εΤμα, 'a garment', which stands for *Γέσ-
μα, and is rel. to evvovca (for *Γεσ-νϋναα), 'to
clothe', and cogn. with L. vestis, 'garment,
clothes'. See vest and cp. Anemia, 'a genus of
plants'.

## himself
himself, pron. — ME., fr. OE. him se/fum, dat.
sing, of he self. See he and self,

## hin
hin, п., name of a liquid measure, the sixth part
of a bath (Bible). — Heb. hin, fr. Egypt, hm,
hsnw.

## hind
hind, п., female of the deer. — ME. hinde, fr.
OE. hind, rel. to ON. hind, Du. hinde, OHG.
hinta, MHG. hinde, G. Hinde, Hindin, 'hind',
fr. I.-E. base *kem-, 'hornless', whence also OI.
sdmah, 'hornless', Gk. κεμάς, 'young deer,
gazelle', Lith. smulas, of s.m. Cp, gemsbok.

## hind
hind, п., a farm servant. — ME. hine, fr. OE.
hina, gen. of hiwan (pi.), 'members of a family'.
See hide, 'measure of land'.

## hind
hind, adj., posterior. — ME., prob. back
formation fr. hinder, adj., influenced in form by OE.
hindan, 'from behind*. Cp. behind,

## hinder
hinder, adj., posterior. — ME. hindere, fr. OE.
hinder (adv.), 'behind', rel. to OHG. hintar,
MHG. hinter, hinder, G. hinter, Goth, hindar,
'behind' (prep.), ON. hindr- (in compounds, as
e.g. hindr-vitni, 'superstition'), orig.
comparatives to OE. hine, 'hence'. See hence and -ther
and cp. hinder, v. Cp. also the first element in
hinterland,

## hinder
hinder, tr. and intr. v., to prevent. — ME. hin-
deren, hindren, fr. OE. hindrian, rel. to ON.
hindra, Du. hinderen, OHG. hinraron, MHG., G.
hindern, lit. 'to keep back', fr. OE. hinder, etc.,
'behind'. See hinder, adj.
Derivative: hinder-er, n.

## Hindi
Hindi, п., the language of Northern India. —
Hind. Hindi, formed with suff. -i (expressing
relationship) fr. Hind, 'India'. See Hindu.

## Hindoo
Hindoo, Hindooism, Hindoostani. — See Hindu,
Hinduism, Hindustani,

## hindrance
hindrance, n. — A hybrid coined fr. hinder, v.,
and -ance, a sufT. of Latin origin.

## Hindu
Hindu, also Hindoo, п., one of the Hindu race. —
Pers. Hindu, fr. Hind, 'India', fr. OI. Sindhuh,
'the river Indus; the region of the river Indus'.
See India and cp. words there referred to.

## Hinduism
Hinduism, also Hindooism, п., the religion of the
Hindus. — Formed fr. Hindu with suff. -ism.

## Hindustani
Hindustani, also Hindoostani, п., the most
important dialect of Western Hindi; adj.,
pertaining to Hindustan or Hindustani. — Hind.

## Hindustani
Hindustani, formed with suff. -i (expressing

relationship) fr. Pers. Hindustan, lit. 'the country

of the Hindus', fr. Hindu, 'Hindu', and stan,

compounds), 'place', lit. 'a place where to

stand', from the stem of sta-, 'to stand', fr. I.-E.

Afghanistan, Baluchistan, lit. 'place (i.e. land) of the

Afghans, resp. Baluchis'. Cp. also the second

element in bezesteen and in bostangi.

## hing
hing, п., asafetida. — Hind, hing, fr. OI. hinguh.

## hinge
hinge, n. — ME. henge, lit. 'that on which the
door hangs', fr. hengen, 'to hang'. Cp. MLG.
henge, 'hinge', MDu. henge, 'hook, handle', Du.
hengsel, 'hinge', and see hang.
Derivatives: hinge, intr. and tr. v., hing-ed, adj.

## ninny
ninny, п., offspring of a stallion and a she-ass. —
L. hinnus, fr. Gk. ί'ννος = γίννος, which is of
uncertain origin.

## hinny
hinny, intr. v., to neigh. — ME., fr. L. hinnire,

## hint
hint, n. — ME. henten, 'to seize, take', fr. OE.
hentan, which stands in gradational relationship
to OE. huntian, to hunt'. See hunt and cp. hent.
Derivatives: hint, v., hint-ing-ly, adv.

## hinterland
hinterland, п., land lying behind a coast district.
— G., compounded of hinter, 'behind', and
land, 'land'. See hinder, adj., and land.

## hip
hip, п., the haunch. — ME. hipe, hippe, hupe, fr.
OE. hype, rel. to Du. heup, OHG., MHG. huf,
G. Hiifte, Goth, hups, 'hip', fr. I.-E. base
"qeu-b-, 'to bend', whence also Gk. κύβος,
'hollow above the hip of cattle'. See cubicle and
cp. hive.
Derivative: hip, tr. v., to sprain the hip of.

## hip
hip, п., seed vessel of the dog rose. — ME. hepe,
hipe, fr. OE. heope, rel. to OE. hiopa, 'briar',
OS. hiopo, dial. Norw. hjupa, OHG. hiafo, hiufa,
MHG., G. hiefe, Du. joop, 'bramble', Dan.
hyben, 'hip', and cogn. with OPruss. kaaubri,
'thorn'.

## hip
hip, п., melancholy. —For hyp, which is short for
hypochondria.

## hip
hip, interj. used in applauding (as in hip, hip,
hurrah). — Of imitative origin.

## hipe
hipe, also hype, п., a kind of throw in wrestling.
— Of uncertain origin; perhaps rel. to hip,
'haunch'. Derivative: hipe or hype, tr. and
intr. v., to throw by means of a hipe.

## hipp-
hipp-, form of hippo- before a vowel.

## hippalectryon
hippalectryon, п., an imaginary animal
combining the· forms of the horse and the cock
(Greek antiq.) — Gk. ίππαλεκτρυών,
compounded of 'ίππος, 'horse' and άλεκτρυών, 'cock'. See
hippo- and alecrryomachy.

## hipped
hipped, adj., having hips. — Formed with suff.
-ed fr. hip, 'haunch'.

## hipped
hipped, adj., depressed. — Formed with suff. -ed
fr. hip, 'melancholy'.

## hippish
hippish, adj., somewhat depressed (colloq.) —
Formed with suff. -ish fr. hip, 'melancholy'.

## hippo-
hippo-, before a vowel hipp-, combining form
meaning 'horse'. — Gk. ίππο-, ίππ-, fr. Ιππος,
'horse', rel. to dial. Gk. ΐκκος, for I.-E. *ekwos,
whence also OI. afrah, L. equus, 'horse'. See
equine and cp. the second element in Eohlppus,
ephippium, Philip, Xanthippe.

## hippo
hippo, n. — Short for hippopotamus.

## Hippoboscidae
Hippoboscidae, n. pi., a family of parasitic
bloodsucking flies (entomol.) — ModL., formed with
suff. -idae fr. hippo- and Gk. βόσκειν, 'to feed'.
See botany.

## hippocampus
hippocampus, п., sea horse. — L., fr. Gk.
ιππόκαμπος, compounded of ίππος, 'horse' (see
hippo-), and κάμπος, 'sea monster', which is
possibly rel. to κάμπη, 'caterpillar'. Cp. the
first element in Campephagidae, Campephilus,
Campodea.

## hippocras
hippocras, п., a highly spiced wine. — ME. ypo-
cras, fr. OF. ipocras, ypocras (F. hypocras),
prop. fr. Hippocrates, the celebrated Greek
physician; so called because the wine was
strained through a woolen bag named Hippocrates
sleeve. The French spelling hypocras is due to
a confusion with the numerous words beginning
with hypo-, fr. Gk. δπο, 'under, below'.

## Hippocratic
Hippocratic, adj., of, or pertaining to, the Greek
physician Hippocrates (460? — 357 B.C.E.) —
Late L. Hippocraticus, fr. L. Hippocrates, fr.
Gk. 'Ιπποκράτης. For the ending see suff. -ic

## Hippocrene
Hippocrene, п., a fountain on Mt. Helicon sacred
to the Muses. — L., fr. Gk. Ίπποκρήνη, lit.
'horse's fountain', which is compounded of
ίππος, 'horse', and κρήνη, 'fountain'. See hippo-
and crenic. Derivative: Hippocren-ian, adj.

## Hippodamin
Hippodamin, п., daughter of Oenomaus, king of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:375 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HIPPODROME' | 348 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:375 COLUMN:1 -->
Pisa, who offered her to the suitor who should
defeat him in a chariot race (Classical mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. 'Ιπποδάμεια, fr. ίππόδαμος, 'tamer
of horses', which is formed fr. ίππος, 'horse',
and the stem of δαμαν, 'to tame'. See hippo- and
tame and cp. adamant

## hippodrome
hippodrome, η., ι) in ancient Greece and Rome,
a course for horse races; 2) a circus for
equestrian performances. — F., fr. L. hippodromes,
fr. Gk. ιππόδρομος, 'race course', which is
compounded of Ιππος, 'horse', and δρόμος, 'course'.
See hippo- and dromedary. Derivatives:
hippodrome, intr. v., hippodrom-ic, adj.

## Hippoglossus
Hippoglossus, п., a genus of flatfishes, the halibut
(ichlhyot.) — ModL., compounded of hippo-
and Gk. γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss,
'interpretation'.

## hippogriff
hippogriff, also hippogryph, п., an imaginary
monster combining the forms of the horse and
the fabulous griffin. — F. hippogriffe, fr. It.
ippogrifo, a hybrid coined fr. Gk. Ιππος, 'horse'
(see hippo-), and grifo, 'griffin'. See griffin, 'a
mythical animal'.

## hippoid
hippoid, adj., resembling a horse (zool.) —
Compounded of hippo- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -old and cp. equoid.

## Hippolyte
Hippolyte, п., an Amazon, daughter of Ares;
taken prisoner by Theseus (Greek mythol.) —
L., fr. Gk. Ιππολύτη, fern, of the
name'Ιππόλυτος. See Hippolytus and cp. next word.

## Hippolyte
Hippolyte, п., a genus of prawns (zool.) — ModL.,
named after the Amazon Hippolyte. See prec.
word.

## Hippolytidae
Hippolytidae, п., pi., a family of prawns.—ModL.,
pi., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -idae.

## Hippolytus
Hippolytus, PN., a son of Theseus (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Ιππόλυτος, fr. Ιππόλυτος,
lit. 'letting horses loose', formed fr. Ιππος,
'horse', and the stem of λύειν, 'to loose, let
loose*. See hippo-, and -lysis.

## hippophagous
hippophagous, adj., eating horseflesh. —
Compounded of hippo- and Gk. -φάγας, 'eating',
from the stem of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See -phngous.

## hippophagy
hippophagy, п., the practice of eating horseflesh.
— Compounded of hippo- and -φαγίά, fr. -φάγος,
'eating'. See -phagy.

## hippopotainic
hippopotainic, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
a hippopotamus. — See next word and -ic.

## hippopotamus
hippopotamus, n. — L„ fr. Gk. Ιπποπόταμος, lit.
'horse of the river', fr. Ιππος, 'horse' and
ποταμός, 'river'. See hippo- and potamo-.

## Hipposelinum
Hipposelinum, п., a genus of plants, the lovage
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ίπποσέλΐνον, 'coarse
parsley', lit. 'horse parsley', fr. ίππος, 'horse',
and σέλΤνον, 'parsley'. See hippo- and parsley
and cp. the second element in Petroselmnm.

## hippuric
hippuric, adj., pertaining to the acid CjHpNOj
(chem.) — Compounded of Gk. Ιππος, 'horse',
and οΰρον," 'urine' (see hippo-, urine and adj.
suff. -ic). This acid was so called because it was
first found (by Rouelle) in the urine of horses.

## Hippuris
Hippuris, п., a genus of plants, the mare's tail
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'horse's tail', fr. hippo-
and Gk. ουρά, 'tail'. See uro-, 'tail-*.

## Hiram
Hiram, masc. PN. — Phoen.-Heb. Hiram, prob.
aphetic for Xhiram, lit. 'brother of the lofty',
fr. uht, construct state of ah, 'brother', and ram,
'high, lofty'. The first element is rel. to Aram.
ah, Ugar. 'h, Arab, ah, Ethiop. ahaw, Akkad.
ahu, 'brother', Heb. ahoth, Aram, яйагА, Syr.
hatha, Ugar. 'hi, Arab, uht, Ethiop. ahat,
Akkad. ahatu, 'sister'. For the second element in
Ahlram see Abram.

## Hiramite
Hiramite, n. (applied to Freemasons). — Lit.
'descendant of Hiram (king of Tyre)'. Formed
fr. Hiram with subst. suff. -ite.

## nircarra
nircarra, п., a messenger; a spy (India). — Pers.
harkara, 'messenger, spy', compounded of har,
'every, all' (fr. OPers. haruva-), and kar, 'work,
business', fr. OPers. kar-, 'to make'. See corpus
and cp. Sanskrit and words there referred to.

## hlrcine
hlrcine, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a he-
goat ; of a rank smell. — L. Mr anus, 'pertaining
to a he-goat', fr. hircus, 'he-goat', which is prob.
rel. to hirsulus, 'shaggy, prickly, bristly'. See
hirsute and adj. suff. -ine and cp. hearse.
Ыге, n. — ME., fr. OE. hyr, 'hire, wages, usury,
interest', rel. to OS. hura, huria, Dan. hyre,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:375 COLUMN:2 -->
Swed. hyra, 'hire, wages', OFris. here, MLG.,
MDu. hure, Du. huur, G. Heuer, 'hire, wages,
rent, lease'. The ulterior etymol. of these words
is unknown.

## hire
hire, tr. v. — ME. hiren, fr. OE. hyrian, rel. to
Dan. hyre, Swed. hyra, OFris. hera, MLG.,
MDu. huren, Du. huren, G. heuern, 'to hire,
rent'. These verbs are prob. denominated fr.
OE. hyr, resp. its equivalents in the other Teut.
languages. See hire, n.
Derivatives: hir-er, п., hire-ling, n.

## hirple
hirple, intr. v., to walk lamely; to hobble (chiefly
Scot.) — Of unknown origin.

## hirrient
hirrient, adj., snarjing; trilled. — L. hirriens, gen.
-entis, 'snarling,* pres. part, of hirrlre, 4o snarl',
of imitative origin. Cp. hirundine. For the ending
see suff. -ent.
Derivative: hirrient, п., a trilled sound.

## hirsute
hirsute, adj., shaggy, bristly. — L. hir-sutus,
'shaggy, prickly, bristly', rel. to hir-tus, 'rough,
shaggy, hairy', and in gradational relationship
to horrere, 'to stand on end, bristle, shake,
shudder, shiver, tremble'. See horror and cp.
hearse, hispid.
Derivatives: hirsute-ness, п., hirsut-ism, n.

## hirsuties
hirsuties, п., excessive growth of hair. — ModL.
hirsutils, lit. 'shagginess', fr. L. hirsulus. See
prec. word.

## Hirtella
Hirtella, п., a genus of plants of the peach family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. hirtus, 'rough, hairy,
shaggy'. See prec. word and -eila.

## Hirudo
Hirudo, п., a genus of leeches (zool.) — L. hirudd,
gen. hirudinis, 'leech', of uncertain origin.

## hirundine
hirundine, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
swallow. — Contraction of *hirundin-ine (see
haplology), which is formed with adj. suff. -ine
fr. L. hirundd, gen. -inis, 'swallow', fr. hirrlre,
'to snarl'. See hirrient.

## his
his, pron. — ME., fr. OE. his, 'of him, his', gen. of
masc. he, 'he', and of neut. hit, 'it'. See he and it.

## hisingerite
hisingerite, п., a hydrous ferric silicate (mineral.)
— G. Hisingerit, named after the Swedish
chemist Wilhelm Hisinger (1766-1852). The ending
-it goes back to Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## Hispania
Hispania, п., the Latin name of the country now
comprising Spain and Portugal. — L. Hispania,
'Spain', lit. 'the country of the Spaniards', fr.
Hispdnus, 'Spaniard', which is prob. of Iberian
origin. The i in (H)i-spania is prob. the Iberian
article. Cp. Spaniard, spaniel.

## Hispanic
Hispanic, adj., Spanish. — L. Hispanicus, fr.
Hispania. See prec. word and -ic.

## hispid
hispid, adj., bristly. — L. hispidus, 'shaggy, prickly,
bristly', prob. rel. to hirsutus, of s.m. See hirsute.
Derivative: hispid-ity, n.

## hiss
hiss, intr. v. and n. — ME. hissen, of imitative
origin. Derivatives: hiss-er, п., hiss-ing, п.,
hiss-ing-ly, adv.

## hist
hist, inter., hush. — Of imitative origin. Cp. hush,
whisht, whist, interj.

## hist-
hist-, form of histo- before a vowel.

## histamine
histamine, п., an amine, CSH,N3, occurring in ergot
and produced by the decomposition of histidine
(chem.) — Coined fr. histidine and amine.

## histidine
histidine, histidin, п., an amino acid QH^NjO,
(chem.) — Coined fr. Gk. ίστίον, dimin. of
Ιστές (see hlsto-), and suff. -idine.

## histo-
histo-, before a vowel hist-, combining form
meaning 'tissue'. — Gk. ίστο-, Ιατ-, fr. ιστός,
'ship's mast; loom; warp, web', which stands
for "σιστός and lit. means 'that which causes to
stand', fr. Ιστημι (for *σί-στη-μι), Ί make to
stand; I stand', fr. I.-E. base *sta-, 'to stand',
whence also Gk. στήμων, 'the warp in the
loom', L. stare, 'to stand', stamen, 'the warp
in the loom'. See state and cp. anhistous, Actin-
istia. Cp. also stamen.

## histogenesis
histogenesis, п., formation of organic tissue. —
Compounded of histo- and Gk. γένεσις, 'origin'.
See genesis.

## histogenetic
histogenetic, adj., pertaining to histogenesis. —
See prec. word and genetic

## histology
histology, п., the study of organic tissues. —
Compounded of histo- and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one
who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: histolog-ic, histolog-ic-al, adjs.,
histolog-ist, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:375 COLUMN:3 -->

## histolysis
histolysis, п., dissolution of organic tissue. —
Compounded of histo- and Gk. λύσις, 'a loosing',
fr. λύειν, 'to loose'. See -lysis.

## histolytic
histolytic, adj., pertaining to histolysis. — See
prec. word and -lytic.

## histone
histone, п., any of a group of basic proteins
(chem.) — Coined fr. Gk. ιστός (see histo-)-and
suff. -one.

## historian
historian, n. — F. historien, fr. L, historia. See
history and -an.

## historiated
historiated, adj., illustrated with figures of flowers
or animals, etc. — Formed with suff. -ed fr. ML.
historiatus, pp. of historiare, 'to narrate, depict;
to paint', fr. L. historia, 'history'. See history
and adj. suff. -ate and cp. storiated. For sense
development cp. story, 'horizontal section of a
building'.

## historic
historic, adj. — L. historicus, fr. Gk. Ιστορικός,
'historical', fr. ιστορία, 'historical narrative'.
See history and -ic. Derivatives: historic-al, adj.,
historic-al-ly, adv., historic-ity, n.

## historico-
historico-, combining form meaning 'historical'.
— Fr. Gk. ιστορικός. See historic.

## historied
historied, adj., having a history. — See history
and -ed.

## historiette
historiette, п., a short history, a short story. —
F., dimin. of histoire, 'history, story', fr. L.
historia. See history and -ette.

## historify
historify, tr. v., to treat in, or as in, history. —
Formed fr. history with suff. -fy.

## historiographer
historiographer, п., historian. — Formed with
suff. -er fr. earlier historiograph, fr. Late L. his-
toriogtaphtts, fr. Gk. Ιστοριογράφος, 'history
writer', which is compounded of ιστορία,
'history', and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See history and -graph.

## historiography
historiography, п., the wriiing of history. — See
prec. word and -graphy.
Derivatives: historiograph-ic, historiograph-ic-al,
adjs., historiograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## history
history, n. — L. historia, 'narrative, story,
narration, account', fr. Gk. ίστορίί, 'learning by
inquiry, knowledge obtained by inquiry;
account of one's inquiries; narration, historical
narrative; history', fr. ΐστωρ (Boeot. 5ίστωρ),
'knowing, learned', which stands for *.ρίδτωρ
and is re], to οΐδα (for *5οΐδχ), Ί know', εΐδον
(for *έ".Γιδον), Ί saw', Εδεΐν (for Τιδεΐν), 'to
see', ίδέά (prob. for *Γιδέσά), 'look, semblance;
kind, nature, class, species', and cogn. with L.
videre, 'to see'. See vision and cp. idea and words
there referred to. Cp. also story, polyhistor.

## histrionic
histrionic, adj., pertaining to an actor. — Late L.
histrionicus, 'pertaining to an actor', fr. histrio,
gen. -onis, 'actor', fr. hister, 'actor', which is of
Etruscan origin.
Derivative: hLtrionic-al-ty, adv.

## hit
hit, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hitten, fr. ON. A/Ho,
'to hit upon, meet with', whence also Dan. hitte,
Swed. An ία, 'to hit, find'.
Derivatives: hit, п., hitt-er, n.

## hitch
hitch, tr. and intr. v., 10 move by jerks. — ME.
hytchen, 'to move, remove', re], to dial. E. hike,
'to move with a jerk', Scot, hitch, 'a motion by
jerks'. Cp. hike.
Derivatives: hitch, п., hitch-er, п., hitch-y, adj.,
hitch-i-ly, adv., hitch-i-ness, n.

## hifhe
hifhe, п., landing place, port (archaic or in place
names). — ME. hyihe, fr. OE. Λ,ΡίΑ, 'landing
place', rel. to OS. huth, of s.m.

## hither
hither, adv. — ME. hider, hither, fr. OE. hider,
rel. to ON. hedra (for "hidra), 'here', Goth.
hidre, 'hither'; formed from the Teut.
demonstrative base "hi- (whence also he, here) with
the comparative suff. -ther. Cp. thither. Cp. also
cis-, citra-.
Derivative: hither, adj.

## hitherward
hitherward, also hitherwards, adv. — OE. hider-
vjeard. See hither and -ward, resp. -wards.

## Hittite
Hittite, n. — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr.
Heb. Hint, 'Hitiite' (pi. Hittim), fr. Hitt. Haiti.

## hive
hive,' n. — ME. hive, fr. OE. hyf, rel. to'oN.
hufr, 'hull of a ship', and cogn. with ΟΙ. kttpah,
'hollow, pit, cave', Gk. κύπη, 'a kind of ship',
κύπελλον, 'cup', L. сира, 'tub, cask, vat'. See
cup and cp. woTds ihere referred to.
Derivaiive: hive, tr. and intr. v.

## hives
hives, п., any of various eruptive skin diseases. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:376 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 349 | HOLD -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:376 COLUMN:1 -->
Of uncertain origin.

## Hivite
Hivite, п., one of an ancient tribe of Canaan
dispossessed by the Israelites. — Formed with
subst. stiff, -ite fr. Heb. Hiwwt, lit. 'villager', fr.
Iiawwah, 'tent-village, village', which prob.
derives fr. base h-w-h, 'to gather', and is rel. to
Arab, hawa, 'he collected, gathered', biwd',
'circle of tents'.

## ho
ho, interj. — Imitative. Cp. whoa.
hoactzin. n. — See hoatzin.

## hoar
hoar, adj. — ME. har, hor, fr. OE. har, 'gray,
gray-haired, old', rel. to ON. harr, of s.m., OS.,
OHG. her, 'distinguished, noble, glorious,
excellent', MHG. her, 'distinguished, noble,
proud, gay, holy', G. hehr, 'exalted, august,
noble, sublime', Herr, 'lord, master', herrlich,
'glorious, excellent', fr. Teut. base *haira,
corresponding to I.-E. *koiro-;cp. Mir. clar,'dark',
fr. base *keiro-, a vowel-gradation form of
*koiro-. Ср. Негг, herring, and the second
element in mynheer, younker. Cp. also hue.
Derivatives: hoar, п., and intr. and tr. v., hoar-y,
adj., hoar-i-ness, n.

## hoard
hoard, n. — ME. hord, fr. OE. hord, rel. to OS.
hord, ON. hodd, OHG., MHG., G. hor!, Goth.
huzd, 'treasure', lit. 'hidden treasure', fr. I.-E.
*quz-dho-. The first element in this base means
'hidden'; see hide, 'to conceal', and cp. words
there referred to. The second element in *quz-
dho- means 'placed', fr. base *dhe-, *dho-, 'to
place', whence also Gk. τι»ένοα, 'to place',
OE. don, 'to do'. See d,i and cp. theme. Cp. also
treasure.

## hoard
hoard, tr. and intr. v. — ME. horden, fr. OE.
hordian, fr. hord. See hoard, n.
Derivatives: hoard-er, п., hoarding (q.v.)

## hoarding
hoarding, п., the act of one who hoards. —
Formed fr. hoanS, >., with -Ing, suff. forming
verbal nouns.

## hoarding
hoarding, п., a temporary fence. — Formed with
subst. suff. -ing fr. obsol. E. hoard, fr. OF.
hourd, hourt, hort, 'scaffold', which is of Teut.
origin. Cp. OHG. hurd, 'hurdle', and see
hurdle.

## hoarhound
hoarhound, n. — See horehound.

## hoarse
hoarse, adj. — ME. hors, fr. earlier hos, fr. OE.
has, rel. to OS. hes, ON. hass, Dan. hies, Swed,
hes, Du. hees, OHG. heist, heis, MHG. heise,
heiser, earlier G. heisch, G. heiser, 'hoarse'.
These words prob. meant orig. 'dried out;
rough', and are rel. to OE. hat, etc., 'hot'; see
hot. The insertion of the r in ME. hors is prob.
due Ίο the influence of harsh.
Derivatives: hoarse-ly, adv., hoarse-ness, n.

## hoatzin
hoatzin, hoactzin, п., a bird of S. America. — Sp.,
fr. Nahuatl uatzin.

## hoax
hoax, n. and tr. v. — Fr. earlier hocus. See hocus-
pocus.
Derivative: hoax-er, n.

## hob
hob, п., ι) a rustic; a clownish lout; 2) a fairy. —
Fr. Hob, a pet form of Robin. Cp. hobgoblin.

## hob
hob, п., projection at the side of a fireplace; peg.
— Of uncertain origin. Cp. hub.

## hobble
hobble, intr. v., to go haltingly, to limp; tr. v.,
to cause to go haltingly. — ME. hobelen; rel.
to Du. hobbelen, 'to rock from side to side',
freq. of hobben, 'to toss, to rock'. Cp. hopple
and hobby, 'a small species of falcon'.
Derivatives: hobble, п., hobbler (q.v.), hobbl-
ing-ly, adv.

## hobbledehoy
hobbledehoy, also hobbadehoy, hobbedehoy, п.,
a clumsy youth. — Of uncertain origin.

## hobbler
hobbler, п., one who, or that which, hobbles. —
Formed from the verb hobble with agential
suff. -er.

## hobbler
hobbler, п., a retainer who maintained a horse
for military service (Engl, hist.) — ME. hobler,
hobeler, a blend of OF. hobin, hobi, 'a small
horse' (see hobby, 'a nag'), and OF. hobeler,
'to skirmish', fr. OF. hober, 'to bestir oneself;
shake, agitate', which is of Teut. origin. Cp.
Du. hobben, 'to toss', and see hobble.

## hobby
hobby, п., a small species of falcon. — ME. hobi,
hoby, fr. OF. hobet, dimin. of hobe, 'falcon'
(whence also F. hobereau, 'hobby; squireen'),
fr. OF. hober, 'to bestir oneself. See prec. word.

## hobby
hobby, п., ι) a nag; 2) hobby horse; 3) favorite
occupation. — ME. hobin, 'nag', fr. OF. hobin,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:376 COLUMN:2 -->
hobi, 'a small horse', orig. 'the ambling animal',
fr. OF. hober, 'to bestir oneself. See hobby,
*a species of falcon', and cp. aubin.

## hobgoblin
hobgoblin, п., ll (cap.) Robin Goodfellow; 2) an
elf, goblin; 3) a bogey. — Compounded of hob,
'a kind of fairy', and goblin.

## hobnail
hobnail, n. — Compounded of hob, 'fairy', and
nail.
Derivative: hobnail-ed, adj.

## hobnob
hobnob, intr. v., to be on intimate terms. — A
var. of early ModE. hab nab, fr. OE. habban,
'to have', and nabban, contraction of ne habban,
'not to have'. Hence hobnob orig. meant 'have
or have not'. See have.

## hobo
hobo, п., a tramp (American Slang). — Of
unknown origin.

## hobson-jobson
hobson-jobson, п., a festal excitement. —
Corruption of Arab, ya Hasan! ya Husayn! Ό
Hasan! О Husain!', cry of the Mohammedans
at the procession of the Moharram. See Yule
and Buraell, Hobson-Jobson, p. 419.
