## Hobson's choice
Hobson's choice, n. — So called after Thomas
Hobson (died in 1631), who had livery stables at
Cambridge and let out horses to customers on
the condition that they had to take the animal
standing in the stable nearest to the stable door.

## hock
hock, п., the joint in the hind leg of a horse. —
ME. hough, hoch, fr. OE. hdh, 'heel', rel. to the
first element in ON. ha-sin, OE. hoh-sinu, 'hock
sinew', OHG. hahsa, MHG. hahse, G. Hachse,
'hock', ON. hull, OE. hSIa, 'heel', and cogn.
with OI. kdksah, kaksa, Avestic kasha, 'armpit',
L. coxa, 'hip', Lith. kinka, kenkle, 'knee joint',
cinksla, 'knee sinew', Olr. coss, 'foot'. Cp. hough.
Cp. also heel. Cp. also coxa. For the second
element in ON. ha-sin, OE. hoh-sinu, see sinew.
Derivative: hock, tr. v., to hamstring.

## hock
hock, п., white Rhenish wine. — Orig. 'wine of
Hochheim', abbreviation of obsol. hockamore,
'wine of Hochheim', fr. G. Hochheimer, fr.
Hochheim, a village near Mainz in Germany.

## Hockday
Hockday, п., the second Tuesday after Easter. —
The first element in this compound is of
Unknown origin. It is not related to G. hoch, 'high'.

## hockey
hockey, n. — Prob. fr. OF. hoquet, 'bent club,
shepherd's crook', formed with suff. -et fr. OF.
hoc, 'a hook', which is of Teut. origin (cp. OE.
hoc and see hook); prob. so called because
played with clubs hooked slightly at the end.

## hocus
hocus, n. and tr. v. — Short for hocus-pocus.

## hocus-pocus
hocus-pocus, п., a conjurer's trick. — Sham L.
Cp. hoax, hokey-pokey.

## hod
hod, п., a portable trough for carrying mortar.
— MDu. hodde, 'basket', rel. to Frankish
*hotta (whence F. hotte, 'basket for the back')
and to dial. G. Hotte, 'basket for the back'.

## hodden
hodden, п., a coarse woolen cloth. — Perh. fr.
Northern E. dial, form of holden, pp. of held,
hence lit. .'cloth held (at home)'. See hold.

## Hodge
Hodge, п., the agricultural laborer. — A popular
form of the name Roger.

## hodgepodge
hodgepodge, n. — A var. of hotchpotch (q.v.)

## hodgkinsonite
hodgkinsonite, п., a hydrous zinc manganese
silicate (mineral.) — Named after H. H. Hodgkin-
son of Franklin Furnace, New Jersey. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hodiernal
hodiernal, adj., of this day. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. hodiernus, 'of this day', fr. hodie,
'today', which stands for hoc die, 'on this day',
fr. abl. of hie, 'this', and dies, 'day'. L. hie prob.
stands for hi-ce or he-ce, which is compounded
of the emphatic particle hi-, resp. he-, and the
demonstrative particle -ce. Particle hi-, he- is
cogn. with the emphatic particles: OI. ghc,
'just, indeed, certainly', ha, 'of course, surely',
OI. hi, Avestic zl, 'for, because; surely, indeed',
Gk. -χι (in ού-χί, μή-χι, 'not', votc-χι, 'yea,
verily'), OSlav. -go-, -ze (after a negation), Lith.
-gu, -gl· For the demonstrative particle -ce cp.
the second element in L. istic, 'this', illic, 'that'.
See he and cp. haecceity, encore and langue
d'oc. For the second element in L. hodie see
dies поп.

## hodograph
hodograph, hodometer. — See odograph,
odometer.

## hoe
hoe, n. — ME. howe, fr. MF. (= F.) houe, fr.
Frankish 'hauwa, which is rel. to OHG. houwa
(MHG. houwe, G. Haue), 'hoe, mattock, pickax',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:376 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. OHG. houwan, which is rel. to OE. heawan,
'to cut, hew'. See hew.

## hoe
hoe, tr. v. — ME. howwen, fr, howe. See hoe, n.
Derivative: ho-er, a.

## hoernesite
hoernesite, п., a hydrous magnesium arsenate
(mineral.) — G. Hoernesit, named after the
Austrian paleontologist Moritz Hoernes (1852-
1917). The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ίτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## hog
hog, n. — ME. hog, hogge, fr. OE. hogg, of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: hog, tr. and intr. v., hogg-ed, adj.,
hogg-ery, п., hogg-ish, adj., hogg-ish-ly, adv.,
hogg-ish-ness, n.

## Hogarthian
Hogarthian, adj., in the satirical manner of the
English painter and caricaturist William
Hogarth (1697-1764). —For the ending see suff. -ist.

## Hogen-Mogen
Hogen-Mogen, п., ι) 'Their High Mightinesses',
i.e. the States-General of the United Provinces
of the Netherlands (obsol); 2) the Dutch; a
Dutchman (used contemptuously). — Fr. Du.
Hoogmogendheden,'Higii Mightinesses' (fr. hoog,
'high', and mogend, 'mighty'), title of the States-
General in the Netherlands. See high, and may,
mighty.

## hoicks
hoicks, hoick, interj., a call to incite hounds. —
Of unknown origin. Cp. yoicks.

## hoiden
hoiden, n. — See hoyden.

## hoi polloi
hoi polloi, the common people, the rabble. —
Gk. οι πολλοί, 'the many', pi. of πολύς. See
poly-.

## hoise
hoise, tr. v., to hoist (obsol.) — Late ME. hoise,
alter, of earlier hyce, hysse, fr. MLG. hissen or
MDu. hischen (Du. hijsen), 'to hoist' (whence
also G. hissen, F. hisser, It. issare, Sp., Port.
izar); possibly of imitative origin. Cp. next word.

## hoist
hoist, tr. v., to raise, lift. — Alter, of hoise, prob.
due to a confusion with hoised, hoist, pp. of
hoise.
Derivatives: hoist, п., hoist-er, п., hoist-ing, n.
and adj.

## hoity-toity
hoity-toity, adj., 1) giddy, flighty; 2) haughty,
arrogant; 3) petulant. — From the obsol. v.
hoil, 'to indulge in riotous gaiety', which is of
uncertain origin.

## hokey-pokey
hokey-pokey, п., ι) hocus-pocus; 2) cheap
icecream sold in the streets. — Prob. altered fr.
hocus-pocus.

## bokhmah
bokhmah, п., wisdom; (cap.), wisdom literature,
a division of ancient Hebrew writings. — Heb.
hokhma4*, 'wisdom', from the stem of hakham,
'he was wise', whence also hakham, 'skillful,
learned, wise', rel. to Aram.-Syr. hakham, 'he
was wise', Arab, hakuma, 'he was wise', hakim,
'wise'. See hakeem.

## hoi-
hoi-, form of nolo- before a vowel.

## holcad
holcad, п., a ship of burden (Greek antiq.) —
Gk. όλκάς, gen. δλκάδος, 'ship of burden', lit.
'a ship that is towed', rel. to ϊλκείν, 'to draw'.
See Holcus and -ad and cp. hulk.

## holcodont
holcodont, adj., having the teeth set in a
continuous groove. — Compounded of Gk. ολκός,
'furrow', and the stem of οδών, gen. οδόντος,
'tooth'. See next word and ndonto-,

## Holcus
Holcus, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — L., a kind
of grass, fr. Gk. ολκός, adj., 'attractive', which is
rel. to ολκός, п., 'that which draws; a track made
by drawing, a furrow', and to Ιίλκειν, 'to draw,
attract', fr. I.-E. base *selq-, 'to draw', whence
also L. sulcus, 'furrow, trench'. See sulcate and
cp. holcad, holcodont, huik.

## hold
hold, tr. and intr. v. — ME. healden, halden,
holden, fr. OE haldan, healdan, rel. to OS. haldan,
ON. halda, Dan. holde, Swed. nulla, OFris.
halda, MLG. halden Du. houden, OHG. haltan,
MHG., G. halten, 'to hold', Goth, haldan, 'to
tend' (orig. prob. 'to drive on'), fr. Teut.
'haldan, which is prob. a dental enlargement of
I.-E. base *quel-, 'to drive'. The phases of the
sense development of the above words prob.
were 'to drive on' (cattle, etc.); 'to tend' (cattle;
as in Goth, haldan); 'to hold' (cattle, etc.)'. For
other derivatives of I.-E. base *qel-, see celerity
and words there referred to. Cp. behold, halt,
'stoppage', hodden, holt, 'lair of an animal'.
Derivatives: hold, п., hold-er, п., hold-ing, n.

## hold
hold, п., space in a ship below the lower deck,
in which cargo is stowed (naut.) — ME. holl,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:377 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HOLDEN | 350 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:377 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. MDu. hool, hoi, 'hole; hold'. See hole.

## holden
holden, archaic pp. of the verb hold.

## holdenile
holdenile, n„ a basic manganese zinc arsenate
(mineral.) — Named after the American mineral
collector Albert Fairchild Holden (1866-1913).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hole
hole, n. — ME., fr. OE. hoi, 'hollow place, hole'
(prop. neut. of the adj. hoi, 'hollow', used as a
noun), and OE. holh, 'hollow place, hole'; rel.
to OS., OFris., MDu., OHG., MHG. hoi, MDu.
hool, ON. holr, G. hohl, 'hollow', Goth, us-hulon,
'to hollow out', prob. fr. I.-E. base "qaul-, *qul-,
'hollow, a hollowed thing', whence also Gk.
καυλός, 'stem', L. caulis, colis, 'stem, stalk'; see
cole.
Derivatives: hole, tr. and intr. v., hole-ly, adj.

## Holi
Holi, Hoolee, Hooly, n„ spring festival in honor
of Krishna (Hindu religion). — Hind, holi, fr.
OI. holdka, which is prob. of imitative origin.

## holiday
holiday, n. — ME. holidei, fr. OE. haligdxg, lit.
'a holy day'. See hqly and day.

## holily
holily, adv. — ME., fr. OE. haliglice. See holy
and adv. suff. -ly.

## holiness
holiness, n. — ME. holynesse, fr. OE. halignes.
See holy and -ness.

## holism
holism, п., the theory that regards nature as
consisting of 'wholes' (philos.) — Coined with suff.
-ism fr. Gk. όλος, 'whole, entire'. See nolo-.

## Holland
Holland, п., the Netherlands. — Du. Holland, fr.
earlier Hohlant, lit. 'wood land' (in allusion to
the important district with the center
Dordrecht). MDu. holt, haul (Du. hout), 'wood', is
rel. to 1st E. holt (q.v.) For Du. land see land.
Cp. next word and Hollands.

## hollandaise
hollandaise, п., a seasoned sauce made of yolk of
eggs and butter. — Short for F. sauce
hollandaise, 'Dutch sauce'; hollandaise is the feminine
of hollandais, 'Dutch', fr. Hollande, 'Holland'.
See prec. word.

## hollandite
hollandite, п., manganate of barium, manganese
and iron (mineral.) — Named after the English
geologist Sir Thomas Henry Holland (1868-
1947), director of the geological survey of India.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Hollands
Hollands, п., gin made in Holland. — Du. Hol-
landsch genever (now spelled Hollands jenever),
'Holland gin'. See Hollund. The suff. -sch in
Hollandsch corresponds to E. -ish (q.v.)

## hollo
hollo, interj., n. and intr. and tr. v. — Imitative.

## hollow
hollow, adj. — ME. holh, holwe, fr. holh, 'hole',
fr. OE. holh, 'hollow, place, hole'. See hole.
Derivatives: hollow, adv., п., v., hollow-ly, adv.,
hollow-ness, a.

## holly
holly, n. — ME. holi, holin, fr. OE. holegn, holen,
rel. to OS., OHG. hulls, huts, ON, hulfr, MDu.,
MHG. huls, Du., G. hulst, 'holly', and cogn.
with Mir. cuilenn, W. celyn, Gael, cuilionn,
'holly'. These words lit. mean 'the pricking
tree'. They derive fr. I.-E. base "qel-, 'to prick',
whence also OSlav. koljq, klati, 'to prick',
OSlav. klasu, Russ. kolos, 'ear of corn', lit. 'that
which pricks'. See Solmsen in BeitrSge zur Gi-
schichte der Deutschen Sprache und Literatur,
27, 366. — F. houx, 'holly', is a loan word fr.
Frankish 'huts, 'which is rel. to OHG. huls,
'holly'. Cp. hoim oak, hulver.

## hollyhock
hollyhock, п., a plant of the mallow family. —
ME. holihoc, lit. 'holy mallow' compounded of
ME. holi, 'holy (see holy), and OE. hoc,
'mallow', which is of unknown origin.

## holm
holm, п., an island situated in a lake or river. —
OE., 'sea, island, hill', rel. to ON. holmr, 'island,
rising land', fr. I.-E. base "qel-, 'to rise, be
elevated'. See hill.

## holmia
holmia, п., holmium oxide (chem.) — ModL.,
named by its discoverer the Swedish chemist
Per Teodor Cleve (1840-1905) in 1879 after
Holmia, the Latin name of StockAo/m, his
native city. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## holmium
holmium, п., name of a metallic element (chem.)
— Coined by the French chemist Lecoq de Bois-
baudran (1838-1912) in 1886 fr. prec. word. For
the ending see suff. -ium.

## holm oak
holm oak, — ME. holm, fr. OE. holen, 'holly'. See
holly.

## nolo-
nolo-, before a vowel hoi-, combining form
meaning 'whole, entire, complete'. — Gk. όλο-, δλ-,
fr. δλος, 'whole, entire', which stands for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:377 COLUMN:2 -->
*8Xf ος, fr. I.-E. *sot-wos, whence also L. sollus
(for *solwos), 'whole, entire'. See safe and words
there referred to and cp. esp. the second element
in catholic.

## holocaust
holocaust, п., ι) a burnt offering; 2) complete
destruction by fire; 3) a great destruction. —
F. holocauste, fr. L. holocaustum, fr. Gk. 6λ6-
καυστον, lit. 'a thing wholly burnt', neut. of the
adj. όλόκαυστος, which is compounded of δλος,
'whole' (see holo-), and καυστός, verbal adj. of
καίειν (for *κά/ΐΕΐν), 'to burn'. See caustic.
Derivatives: holocaust-al, holocaust-ic, adjs.

## holograph
holograph, п., a document written entirely by the
person from whom it proceeds. — Late L.
holographs (whence also F. holographe), fr. Gk.
όλόγραφος, 'written in full, written entirely by
the same hand', which is compounded of δλος,
'whole' (see holo-), and -γρίφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: holograph-ic, holograph-ic-al, adjs.

## holohedral
holohedral, adj., having the full number of faces
required by complete symmetry (said of
crystals). — Compounded of holo- and Gk. έδρα,
'seat; base, side, face'. See -hedral,

## bolomorphic
bolomorphic, adj., of symmetrical form. —
Compounded of holo- and Gk. μορφή, 'form, shape'.
See -morphic

## holophote
holophote, adj., an optical apparatus by which
all the light of a lighthouse lamp is utilized. —
Compounded of holo- and Gk. φως, gen. φωτός,
'light'. See photo-,

## holophrasis
holophrasis, п., the expression of a whole phrase
in a single word (as in some agglutinative
languages). — Compounded of holo- and Gk.
φράσις, 'speech, expression, phrase'. See phrase,

## holopnrastic
holopnrastic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized
by, holophrasis. — Compounded of holo- and
Gk. φραστικός, 'expressive', fr. φράζειν, 'to
point out, show, tell', whence also φράσις. See
prec. word and -ic.

## holophyte
holophyte, п., a plant.capable of manufacturing
its own food. — Compounded of holo- and Gk.
φυτόν, 'plant'. See phyto-.

## Holosteum
Holosteum, п., a genus of plants, the jagged
chickweed (hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. δλόστεον,
used by Dioscorides for a plant. The word lit.
means 'wholly of bones', fr. δλος, 'whole', and
όστέον, δστοϋν, 'bone'. See holo- and osteo-,

## Holothuria
Holothuria, п., the genus of sea cucumbers (zool.)
— ModL., fr. L. holothuria (pi.), fr. Gk. όλο-
θούριον, 'a kind of marine zoophyte'.

## holpen
holpen, archaic pp. of help,

## noister
noister, п., leather case for a pistol. — Du., a

## collateral form of holfter
collateral form of holfter, rel. to OHG. huluft,

## MHG. hulft
MHG. hulft, 'cover, case, sheath', MHG. hulf-

## ter
ter, 'quiver', G. Holfter, 'holster', OE. heolstor,
'that which covers, hiding place, concealment,

## darkness'
darkness', ON. hulstr, 'case, sheath', Goth.

## hulistr
hulistr, 'covering, veil', and to OE. helan, 'to

## conceal'
conceal', fr. I.-E. base *kel-, 'to hide, conceal'.

## See cell and cp. housing
See cell and cp. housing, 'covering'. The suff.

## -tr
-tr, -str, in the above words is instrumental.
Derivatives: holster, tr. v., holster-ed, adj.

## holt
holt, п.,small wood.—OE.,rel. toOS.,ΟΝ.,Dan.,

## Norw.
Norw., OFris. holt, MDu. holt, hout, Du. hout,

## OHG.
OHG., MHG., G. holz, 'wood', and cogn. with
Gk. κλάδος, 'young branch or shoot', L. eludes,
'injury, mischief, disaster', Russ.-Church Slavic

## klada
klada, 'beam', kladivo, 'hammer', Mir. claidim,
Ί dig', caill (for "caldet), 'forest', W. clawdd,

## Co. claud
Co. claud, 'ditch', Olr. claid-eb, W. cleddyf
'sword' JL. gladius, 'sword', is a Celtic loan
word). All these words derive fr..I.-E. *qelad-,
'qolad-, *qlad-, *qjdo-, -^-enlargements of
base *qel(a)-, *qol(a)-, 'to strike, beat, break',
whence Gk. κλδν, 'to break', κλήρος, Dor.
κλαρος, prop, 'little piece of wood lopped off
(used for casting lots)', hence 'a casting of lots',

## L. calamitas
L. calamitas, 'damage, injury, loss, misfortune'
(with the primary meaning 'blow'), in-columis,
'unimpaired, uninjured', Lith. kalut, kalti, 'to

## strike
strike, forge', Lett. ka]u, kalt, 'to forge', OSlav.

## koljp
koljp, klati, 'to pierce, slaughter'. Cp. the second
element in clapholt and the first element in

## Holland. Cp. also halt
Holland. Cp. also halt, 'lame', hilt. Cp. also culamity,

## clastic
clastic, claymore, Clematis, clergy, cleric, cierk,

## colobium
colobium, coloboma, Colobus, coup, gladiator,

## glaive
glaive, Proceliaria. Cp. also the first element in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:377 COLUMN:3 -->
colure.

## holt
holt, п., retreat or lair of an animal. — A var. of
hold, n. See hold,

## holus-bolus
holus-bolus, adv., all at once. — Sham Latin
coined fr. whole and bolus,

## holy
holy, adj. — ME. halt, holi, fr. OE. halig, rel. to
OS. helag, ON. heilagr, Dan. hellig, Swed. helig,
OFris., MDu. hglich, Du. heilig, OHG. heilag,
MHG. heilec, G. heilig, Goth, hailags, 'holy',
and to OE. hal, 'whole, healthy'. See whole and
cp. hale, 'sound, healthy'. Cp. also halibut,
halidom, hallow, hollyhock. Cp. also Olga.

## horn-
horn-, form of homo- before a vowel.

## homage
homage, n. — ME., fr. OF. homage (F. hommage),
fr. ML. hominaticum, 'vassal's service', fr. L.
homo, gen. hominis, 'man', which is rel. to
humanus, 'human*. See human and -age and cp.
the second element in bonhomie.

## homalo-
homalo-, before a vowel homal-, combining form
meaning 'even'. — Gk. όμαλο-, όμαλ-, fr. ομαλός,
'even, level, of like degree', fr. όμός, 'one and
the same', which is cogn. with L. similis, 'like'.
See homo- and cp. anomalo-.

## Homarus
Homarus, п., a genus of crustaceans (zool.) —
ModL., fr. F. homard, fr. ON. humarr, which
is cogn. with Gk. κάμμαρος, 'lobster'. See
Cambarus.

## hombre
hombre, п., a man. — Sp., fr. L. hominem, ace.
of homo, 'man'. See homage.

## home
home, n. — ME. home, hoom, fr. OE. ham, rel. to
OS. hem, 'home', OFris. hem, ham, 'home,
village', ON. heimr, 'residence, world', heima,
'home', Swed. hem, Dan. h/em, MDu. heem,
heim, OHG., MHG., G. heim, 'home', Goth.
haims, 'village', and cogn. with Gk. κώμη,
'village', κοιμάν, 'to lull, put to sleep', Lith. kaimas,
OPruss. caymis, 'village', OSlav. semija, Lith.
seimyna, Lett, saime, OPruss. seimins, 'domestic
servants', Olr. coim, едет, 'dear, beloved', OW.
cum, ModW. си, of s.m., L. -haemum (a Teut.
loan word) in Boihaemum, 'Bohemia', lit. 'home
of the Boi'; formed—with -m-formative element
—fr. I.-E. base *kei-,'to lie, settle down', whence
also Goth, heiwa-frau/a, 'master of a house', OE.
hiwan (pi.), 'members of a family', hiwen, 'family,
household', OHG. Mwo, 'husband', hiwa, 'wife',
hiun (pi.), 'married couple', ON. hiun, 'married
couple, household', OE. higid, hid, 'hide of
land', lit. 'land (sufficient) to support a family',
OE. hiw-riden, hi-red, 'family, household',
OHG., MHG. Ы-rat, G. Hei-rat, 'marriage',
orig. 'care of the house' (the second element of
these latter words means 'advice, counsel'; see
rede, п.), and L. civis, 'citizen'. See civil and
cp. the first element in comedy. Cp. also ham,
'hamlet', hamesucken, hamlet, haunt, Henry,
hide, 'measure of land', hind, 'farm servant',
Bohemia. Cp. also eme, 00m.
Derivatives: home, adj., adv. and tr. and intr.
v., home-less, adj., home-less-ly, adv., home-less-
ness, п., home-ly, adj., home-li-ly, adv., home-
li-ness, n.

## homeo-
homeo-, homoeo-, combining form meaning
'similar to'. — Gk. όμοιο-, fr. όμοιος (also όμοιος),
'like, resembling', rel. to όμός, 'one and the
same'. See homo- and cp. the second element
in Ipomoea.

## homeomorphism
homeomorphism, homoeomorphism, п., similarity
in form. — See next word and -ism.

## homeomorphous
homeomorphous, homoeomorphous, adj., of
similar form. — Compounded of homeo- and
-morphous.

## homeopath
homeopath, homoeopath, п., homeopathist. —
Back formation fr. homeopathy.

## homeopathy
homeopathy, homoeopathy, п., a system of healing
based on the theory that a disease can be cured
by medicines which in a healthy person would
produce symptoms similar to those of the
disease treated. — G. Homoopathie, coined by the
German physician Samuel Hahnemann ('755-
1843), the founder of homeopathy, fr. Gk.
όμοιοπάθεια, 'likeness in feeling, likeness in
suffering', fr. όμοιος, 'like', and -πάθεια,
'feeling, suffering'. See homeo- and -pathy and cp.
allopathy.
Derivatives: homeopath-ic, adj., homeopath-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## homer
homer, п., a Hebrew measure of capacity. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:378 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 351 | HONE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:378 COLUMN:1 -->
Heb. bbrner, 'heap; measure', fr. fiamdr, 'he
heaped, piled up', rel. to Akkad. imeru, 'a
measure'.

## homer
homer, п., a homing pigeon. — Formed with
agential suff. -er from the verb home, 'to send
homeward', fr. home, n. See home.

## Homer
Homer, masc. PN. — L. Homerus, fr. Gk. "Ομη
ρος, 'Homer', name of the alleged author of the
Iliad and the Odyssey, fr. όμηρος, 'hostage
(prop, 'companion'); 'blind' (prop, 'going with
a companion') (whence όμηρεύειν, 'to
accompany, go together with'), which is prob. formed
fr. όμοΰ, 'together', and the stem of <£p-»pav,
'joint', άρ-αρ-ίσκειν, 'to join'. See homo- and
arm, 'upper limb*.

## Homeric
Homeric, adj., pertaining to Homer or his poems.
— L. Homericus, fr. Gk. 'Ομηρικός, 'pertaining
to Homer', fr. "Ομηρος. See Homer and -ic.

## homesick
homesick, adj. — Back formation fr. next word.
Derivative: homesick-ly, adv.

## homesickness
homesickness, n. — Loan translation of G. Heim-
weh, fr. Heim, 'home', and Weh, 'woe, pain'.

## homestead
homestead, n. — OE. hamstede, 'residence',
compounded of ham, 'home', and stede, 'place'. See
home and stead,

## homeward
homeward, adv. and adj. — ME. hamward, fr.
OE. hamweard. See home and -ward,

## homewards
homewards, adv. — OE. hamweardes, formed fr.
hamweard with adv. gen. suff. Cp. OHG. heim-
wartes, G. heimwarts, and see prec. word and
-wards.

## homey
homey, also homy, adj., homelike (colloq.) —
Formed fr. home with adj. suff. -y.

## homicidal
homicidal, adj., pertaining to homicide. — Late
L. homicidalis, 'pertaining to manslaughter', fr.
L. homicida. See next word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: homicidal-Iy, adv.

## homicide
homicide, п., manslayer. — F., fr. L. homicida,
'manslayer, murderer', which is compounded of
homi- (shortened for homini-, stem of homo, gen.
•inis, 'man') and -clda, 'killer', fr. caedere, 'to
kill'. See human and -cide, 'killer'.

## homicide
homicide, п., manslaughter. — F., fr. L. homi-
cidium, 'manslaughter', which is compounded
of homi- (shortened fr. homini·, stem of homo,
gen. -inis, 'man') and -cidium, 'killing', fr.
caedere, 'to kill'. See human and -cide, 'killing'.

## homiietic
homiietic, adj., pertaining to sermons or homi-
letics. — Gk. ομιλητικός, 'conversable', fr.
όμΐλητός, verbal adj. of όμϊλεϊν, 'to be together
with, converse with', fr. όμιλος, 'crowd,
assembly'. See homily.
Derivatives: homiietic, п., homiletic-al, adj.,
homiletical-ly, adv., homiletics (q.v.)

## homiletics
homiletics, п., the art of preaching. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## homiliary
homiliary, п., a book of homilies. — Eccles. L.
homlliarium, 'a book of homilies', fr. homilia.
See homily and -ary.

## homilist
homilist, п., one who composes or preaches
homilies. — See homily and -ist.

## hornlike
hornlike, п., an iron calcium borosilicate
(mineral.) — G. or Swed. homilit, formed fr. Gk.
όμϊλεΐν, 'to be together with, converse with'
with subst. suff. -it, which goes back to Gk.
-ίτης (see homily and subst. suff. -ite); so called
in·allusion to its association with erdmannite
and meliphanite.

## homily
homily, n„ sermon. — OF. omelie (F. homelie),
fr. Eccles. L. homilia, fr. Gk. όμϊλίϊ, 'converse,
meeting, assembly', fr. όμιλος, 'crowd, throng,
assembly', which is prob. a contraction of
*όμό-μϊλος, lit. 'a gathering together' (see
haplology). For the first element see homo-. The
second element is cogn. with OI. milati,
'meets', metah, 'assembly', L. miles, gen. -His,
'soldier', lit., 'one who marches in a troop';
see militia. Cp. homilite.
Derivatives: homil-ist, п., homil-ist-ic, adj.,
homil-ize, intr. v. (rare).

## homing
homing, adj., bound for home (esp. used in the
term homing pigeon). — Formed with adj. suff.
-ing from the verb home, 'to send homeward',
fr. home, n. See home.

## hominy
hominy, п., a meal made from maize. — Prob.
aphetic for Algonquian auhuminea, 'parched
corn'.

## homo
homo, п., man — L. homo. See human.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:378 COLUMN:2 -->

## homo-
homo-, before a vowel horn-, combining form
meaning 'one and the same, jointly'. — Gk.
όμο-, όμ-, fr. όμός (for *somos), 'one and the
same, belonging to two or more jointly', rel. to
όμοΰ, 'together', and cogn. with OI. samah,
'even, the same', L. similis, 'like', Goth, sama,
'the same', samana, 'together'. See same and
words there referred to and cp. esp. homeo-,
homalo-, hama-, the first element in Homer and
the second element in schorlomite.

## homoblastic
homoblastic, adj., developed from cells of the
same kind (biol.) — Compounded of homo- and
Gk. βλαστός, 'bud, sprout, shoot'. See -blastic
and cp. heteroblastic,

## homochromous
homochromous, adj., of the same color. —
Compounded of homo- and Gk. χρώμα, 'color'. See
chrome and -ous and cp. heterochromons.

## homodont
homodont, adj., having all the teeth of the same
form (zool.) — Compounded of horn- and the
stem of Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See
odonto- and cp. heterodont.

## homoeo-
homoeo-, a var. spelling of homeo-.

## homogamous
homogamous, adj., bearing flowers that do not
differ sexually (bot.) — Gk. όμόγαμος, 'married
together', compounded of όμο- (see homo-) and
γάμος, 'marriage'. See -gamous and cp. hetero-
gamous.

## homogamy
homogamy, n. (bot.) — See prec. word and -gamy
and cp. heterogamy,

## homogeneal
homogeneal, adj., homogeneous. — See
homogeneous and adj. suff. -al and cp. heterogeneal.

## homogeneity
homogeneity, п., the quality of being
homogeneous. — F. homogeneite, fr. ML. homogeneitdtem,
ace. of homogeneitds, fr. homogeneus. See next
word and -ity and cp. heterogeneity,

## homogeneous
homogeneous, adj., of the same kind, uniform. —
ML. homogeneus, fr. Gk. ομογενής, 'of the same
kind or race', which is compounded of όμο- (see
homo-) and γένος, 'race, descent, gender, kind'.
See genus and -ous and cp. heterogeneous.
Derivatives: homogeneous-ly, adv., homogene-
ous-ness, n.

## homogenesis
homogenesis, п., reproduction in which the
successive generations are alike. — Compounded
of homo- and genesis. Cp. heterogenesis.

## homogenetic
homogenetic, adj., pertaining to homogenesis. —
Compounded of homo- and -genetic. Cp. hetero-
genetic.

## homogenous
homogenous, adj., having a common descent. —
Compounded of homo- and Gk. γένος, 'race,
descent'. See genus and -ous.

## homogeny
homogeny, п., structural resemblance due to a
common ancestor. — Compounded of homo-
and -geny. Cp. heterogeny.

## homograph
homograph, п., a word of identical spelling with
another, but different from it in origin and
meaning. — Compounded of homo- and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: homograph-ic, adj., homograph-y,n.

## homoiousian
homoiousian, adj., of like essence. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. Gk. όμοιούσιος, 'of like essence',
fr. όμοιος, 'like' (see homeo-), and ουσία,
'essence', substance', which derives fr. οδσα, fem.
of ών, 'being', pres. part, of είναι, 'to be'. See
esse and cp. essence. Cp. also homoousian and
heteroousian.
Derivative: Homoiousian, n.

## homologate
homologate, tr. v., to approve (law). — ML.
homologdtus, pp. of homologare, fr. Gk. όμο-
λογεϊν, 'to agree, grant, concede', fr. ομόλογος,
'agreeing, of one mind'. See homologue.

## homologation
homologation, n,, approval (law). — See prec.
word and -ion.

## honiologize
honiologize, tr. v., to make homologous; intr. v.,
to be homologous. — See next word and -ize,

## homologous
homologous, adj., corresponding. — Gk.
ομόλογος, 'agreeing, of one mind', compounded of
όμο- (see homo-) and λόγος, 'word, speech,
discourse; proportion*. See logos. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous. Cp. heterologous,

## homologue
homologue, п., a homologuous thing. — F., fr.
Gk. όμόλογον, neut. of ομόλογος, 'agreeing, of
one mind'. See prec. word.

## homology
homology, п., I) quality of being homologous;
2) (biol.) correspondence in the structure of
animal organs. — F. homologie, fr. Gk.
ομολογία, 'agreement', fr. ομόλογος, 'agreeing'. See
prec. word and -y (representing Gk. -ίά). As a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:378 COLUMN:3 -->
biological term, F. homologie was prob. used
first by the French naturalist Etienne-Geoffroy
St. Hilaire (1772-1844).

## homomorphic
homomorphic, adj., of the same form. —
Compounded of homo-, Gk. μορφή, 'form, shape' (see
morpbo-), and suff. -ic. Cp. heteromorphic.

## homoniorphlsm
homoniorphlsm, п., resemblance of form. — See
prec. word and -ism and cp. heteromorphism.

## homoniorphous
homoniorphous, adj., homomorphic. — See
homomorphic and -ous and cp. heteromorphous.

## homomorphy
homomorphy, п., similarity of form. — See prec.
word and -morphy.

## homonym
homonym, п., a homonymous word. — F. horno-
nyme, fr. L. homonymum, fr. Gk. όμώνυμον, neut.
of ομώνυμος, 'having the same name'. See next
word.
Derivatives: homonym-ic, adj., homonymous
(q.v.)

## homonymous
homonymous, adj., like in sound, but different
in meaning. — F, homonyme, fr. L. hotnonymus,
fr. Gk. ομώνυμος, 'having the same name',
which is compounded of όμός, 'the same' (see
homo-), and όνυμα, dialectal form of βνομα,
'name'. See name and cp. onomato-.
Derivative: homonymous-ly, adv.

## homoousian
homoousian, homousian, adj., of the same essence
(Eccles. hist.) — Formed with suff. -ian fr. Gk.
ομοούσιος, όμούσιος, 'of the same essence',
which is compounded of όμο- (see homo-) and
ουσία, 'essence, substance'. See homoiousian and
cp. heteroousian.
Derivative: Homoousian, Homousian, o.

## homophone
homophone, п., like in sound, but differing in
origin and meaning. — F., fr. Gk. όμόφωνον,
neut. of ομόφωνος, 'having the same sound*,
which is compounded of όμο- (see homo-) and
φωνή, 'sound, tone, voice'. See phone, 'speech
sound'.
Derivatives: homophon-ic, homophon-ous, adjs.,
homophony (q.v.)

## homophony
homophony, п., quality of being homophonic. —
F. homophonie, fr. Gk. ομοφωνία, 'unison', fr.
ομόφωνος. See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -ία).

## homopiast
homopiast, п., a homoplastic
part.—Compounded of homo- and Gk. πλαστός, 'molded', verbal
adj. of πλάσσειν, 'to mold*. See plastic,

## homoplastic
homoplastic, adj., resembling in structure, but of
different origin. — Compounded of homo- and
Gk* πλαστικός, 'fit for molding', fr. πλαστός.
See prec. word.

## Homoptera
Homoptera, n. pi., an order of insects (entomol.)
— Compounded of homo- and Gk. πτερά, pi. of
πτερόν, 'wing'. See ptero-.
Derivatives: homopter-an, a., homopter-ous, adj.

## homorganic
homorganic, adj., lit., pertaining to the same
organs. — Compounded of horn- and organic,

## bomosexnal
bomosexnal, adj., having sexual desire for those
of the same sex. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk.
όμός, 'one and the same', and L. sexus, 'sex*.
See homo- and sexual and cp. heterosexual.
Derivative: homosexuat-ity, n.

## bomuncular
bomuncular, adj., pertaining to a homunculus. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. homunculus. See
next word.

## homunculus
homunculus, п., a little man; a mannikin. — L.,
dimin. of homo, gen. hominis, 'man'. See homo
and -cuius,

## homy
homy, adj., homelike (colloq.) — Formed fr.
home with adj. suff. -y.

## hone
hone, п., a whetstone. — ME. hoone, 'hone', fr.
OE. han, 'stone', rel. to ON. hein, 'hone', and
cogn. with OI. si-sd-ti, 'sharpens', Sanah,
'whetstone', satah, 'sharpened, sharp', Utah, of s.m.,
Avestic saeni-, 'pointed; point, top of a tree',
ModPers. sayad, 'rubs', Arm. sur (for *ko-ro-),
'sharp', sur (gen. sroy), 'sword, knife', srem,
Ί sharpen', Gk. κώνος, 'pine cone, fir cone',
L. cos, gen. cotis, 'whetstone', catus, 'sharp',
Mir. cath, 'wise, sage'. All these words derive
fr. Ι.-Ε. base *£ό(0-, ·£<?(<)-, *£'(0-, 'sharp,
whet; to sharpen, whet', whence also possibly
OI. sikhd, 'top, point; tuft of hair', sikharah,
'pointed; summit', sikharah, 'top, summit'. Cp.
cone and words there referred to. Cp. also sik-
hara. Base *ico(i)-, *fo(i>, *£'('>, prob.
developed fr. base *ak-, 'sharp'. See acrid.
Derivative: hone, tr. v., to sharpen.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:379 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HONEST | 352 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:379 COLUMN:1 -->

## honest
honest, adj. — ME., fr. OF. honeste (F. honnite),
fr. L. honestus, 'honorable, worthy', fr. honos,
honor. See houor.
Derivatives: honest-ly, adv., honest-ness, n.

## honesty
honesty, n. — ME. honeste, fr. OF. honeste (F.
honnetete), fr. L. honestatem, ace. of honestus,
'honor, honesty', fr. honestus. See prec. word
and -y (representing OF. -e, -ее).

## honey
honey, n. — ME. hunij, honi, fr. OE. hunig, rel.
to OS. huneg, honeg, ON. hunang, Dan. harming,
Swed. honung,OFris. hunig, MDu. honich, honinc,
Du. honig, honing, OHG. honang, honag, MHG.
honec, honic, G. Honig, 'honey', and prob.
cogn. with OI. kancanam, 'gold', Dor. Gk.
κνάκός, Gk. κνηκός, 'pale yellow', κνήκος,
'safflower', OPruss. cucan (= cuncari), 'brown',
W. canecon, 'gold'. Cp. Cnicus.
Derivative: honey-ed, honi-ed, adj.

## honeycomb
honeycomb, n. — ME. hunicomb, fr. OE. hunig·
camb. See honey and comb.
Derivative: honeycomb, tr. v.

## honeysnckle
honeysnckle, n. — ME. honisocle, hunisuccle,
formed with dimin. suff. -le fr. ME. honysouke,
fr. OE. hunig-suce, 'privet', lit. 'honey suck' (so
called because honey can be sucked from it).
See honey and suck.

## hong
hong, п., warehouse, factory. — Chin, hang,
'warehouse, factory', lit. 'a row (of houses)'.

## honk
honk, п., the cry of a wild goose; any sound
resembling the cry of the wild goose. —
Imitative.
Derivatives: honk, intr. and tr. v., honk-er, n.

## honor
honor, honour, n. — ME. honor, honour, fr. OF.
honor, honur (F. honneur), fr. L. honorem, ace.
of honos, honor, 'honor, dignity, office;
reputation', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
honesty, Honora.

## honor
honor, honour, tr. v. — ME. honouren, fr. OF.
honourer (F. honorer), fr. L. honorare, 'to
honor', fr. honos, honor. See honor, n.
Derivative: hono(u)r-er, n.

## Honora
Honora, Honoria, fern. PN. — L. Honoria, fern,
of Honorius, lit. 'a man of reputation', fr. honos,
honor. Cp. Nora.

## honorable
honorable, honourable, adj. — OF. honorable,
honurable (F. honorable), fr. L. honorabilis,
'honorable', lit. 'that which procures honor', fr.
honos, honor. See honor, п., and -able.
Derivative: hono(u)rabl-y, adv.

## honorarium
honorarium, п., an honorary payment; gratuity.
— L. honorarium, short for honorarium donum,
'a present made on being admitted to an honor';
prop. neut. of the adjective honorarius. See
next word.

## honorary
honorary, adj. — L. honorarius, 'pertaining to
honor, honorary', fr. honos, honor, 'honor'. See
honor, п., and adj. suff. -ary.

## honorific
honorific, adj. — L. honorificus, 'that which does
honor, honorable', compounded of honos, honor,
'honor', and -ficus, 'making, doing', from the
stem of L. -ficere, unstressed form oifacere. See
honor and -flc.
Derivative: honorific, n.

## hooch
hooch, п., an alcoholic liquor. — Shortened fr.
Hoochinoo.

## hoochinoo
hoochinoo, п., an alcoholic liquor made by the
Hoochinoo Indians of Alaska.

## hood
hood, n. — ME. hod, hood, fr. OE. hud, rel. to
OS., OFris. hod, MDu. hoet, Du. hoed, 'hat',
OHG., MHG. huot, 'helmet, hat', G. Hut (masc),
'hat', OE. hztt, 'hat*, ON. hattr, hottr, 'hat,
hood'. These words lit. mean 'protection of
the head', and are rel. to OFris. hade, 'guard,
protection', OHG. huota, MHG. huote, 'guard,
protection', G. Hut (fem.), of s.m.; fr. I.-E. base
*kadh-, 'to guard, watch; to cover', whence also
L. cassb (for *kadh-tis), 'helmet'. Cp. hat, heed,
hoodie. Cp. also Cassis.
Derivative: hood, tr. v.

## -hood
-hood, suff. denoting state or condition. — ME.
-had, -hod, fr. OE. -had, fr. had, 'person, rank,
state, condition, nature'; rel. to OS., OFris.
-hed, MDu., OHG., MHG., G. -heit, Du. -heid,
suffixes denoting state or condition, and to
OHG., MHG. heit, 'person, rank, state,
condition', OS. hid, 'position, dignity', ON. heidr,
'honor, dignity', Goth, haidus, 'manner', and to
ON. heid, 'clear sky', OE. hador, OHG. heitar.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:379 COLUMN:2 -->
MHG., G. heiter, 'clear, shining, cloudless', fr.
I.-E. base *(s)qail·, 'bright', whence also L.
caelum (for "caidslom, 'caislom), 'sky, heaven'.
See celestial and cp. -head and the second
element in Adelaide. Cp. also cheetah, chintz, chit,
chitty, 'a short letter'.

## hoodie
hoodie, hoody, п., the hooded crow. — Lit.
'provided with a hood'. See hood and adj. suff. -y.

## hoodlum
hoodlum, п., a young rowdy (colloq.) — Orig.
noodlum, coined by a newspaper reporter
through the inversion of Muldoon, name of the
leader of a gang of young ruffians in San
Francisco. Owing to an error, the letter η was changed
by the compositor to h, whence arose the word
hoodlum. See Crowther's Encyclopedia of
Phrases and Origins, p. 56.

## hoodoo
hoodoo, n. and tr. v. — A var. of voodoo.

## hoodwink
hoodwink, tr. v. — Compounded of hood, and
wink.
Derivatives: hoodwink, п., hoodwink-er, n.

## hoof
hoof, n. — ME. hoof, fr. OE. hof, rel. to OS.,
OFris. hof, ON. hofr, Dan. hov, Swed. hof, Du.
hoef OHG., MHG. huof G. Huf, 'hoof, and
cogn. with OI. saphah, 'hoof, Avestic safa-,
'hoof of the horse'.
Derivatives: hoof, tr. v., hoofed, adj.

## book
book, n. — ME. hok, fr. OE. hoc, rel. to OFris.,
MLG. hok, MDu. hoec, Du. hoek, 'angle,
corner, hook', in gradational relationship to OE.
haca, 'bolt', OS. haco, 'hook', ON. haka, Dan.
hage, 'chin', Swed. hake, Du. haak, 'hook',
OHG. hacko, hako, haggo, MHG. hake, hagge,
G. Haken, 'hook', and prob. cogn. with Russ.
kogot', 'claw'. Cp. hack, 'to chop', hake, hackle,
heckle, hatcheL hockey, hooker, 'fishing vessel',
and the first element in hackbut and in haken-
kreuz. Cp. also the first element in arquebus.
Derivatives: hook, tr. and intr. v., hook-ed, adj.,
hook-ed-ness, п., hooker (q.v.), hook-y, adj.

## hookah
hookah, hooka, п., Oriental tobacco pipe with a
long flexible stem. — Arab, huqqa", 'small
tobacco box'.

## hooker
hooker, one who or that which hooks. —Formed
fr. hook with agential suff. -er.

## hooker
hooker, п., a Dutch fishing vessel; an English or
Irish fishing boat. — Du. hoeker, fr. hoek,
'hook, fishhook'. See hook and agential suff.
-er.

## hooligan
hooligan, п., a young ruffian. — Prob. fr. Hooli-
han. Hooligan, name of an Irish family, whose
members were notorious hoodlums.
Derivative: hooligan-ism, n.

## hoolock
hoolock, п., the black gibbon (Hylobates hoo-
lock). — Fr. hulak, hulluk, native name in NE.
India, rel. to OI. ulukah, 'owl', from an imitative
base meaning 'to wail'. Both the gibbon and the
owl have the common feature that they are
'wailing animals'.

## hoon
hoon, п., a gold pagoda (coin). — Hind, hun,
prob. fr. Canarese honnu, 'gold'.

## hoondy
hoondy, n. — A variant of hundi.

## hoop
hoop, п., a circular band. — ME. hop, fr. OE.
hop, rel. to OFris. hop, MDu., Du. hoep, 'hoop',
ON. hop, 'a small bay', and cogn. with Lith.
kabl, 'hook'. Cp. hope, 'a small bay'.
Derivative: hoop, tr. v., to bind with a hoop.

## hoop
hoop, intr. v., to shout, whoop. — ME. houpen,
fr. OF. houper, fr. interj. houp, call to dogs or
horses. Cp. whoop, which is a later spelling
of hoop.

## hooped
hooped, adj., having hoops. — Formed with suff.
-ed fr. hoop, 'circular band'.

## hooper
hooper, п., one who makes hoops. — Formed
with agential suff. -er fr. hoop, 'circular band'.

## hooper
hooper, п., the common wide swan. — Lit. 'the
hooping bird'. See hoop, 'to shout', and agential
suff. -er.

## hoopoe
hoopoe, п., an Old World bird with a long curved
bill and a large crest. — Fr' early E. houpe, fr.
F. huppe, fr. L. upupa, a word of imitative
origin; cp. Gk. ётгоф, 'hoopoe'. Cp. also dupe.

## hoosegow
hoosegow, п., a jail (U.S. Slang). — Prob. fr. Sp.
juzgado, 'court of justice, tribunal', prop. pp.
oijuzgar, 'to judge', used as a noun, fr. L. judi-
care, 'to judge'. See judge, v.

## hoot
hoot, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
ME. hoten, houten and Swed., Norw. huta, lit.
'to utter the sound hut'. Cp. also F. huer, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:379 COLUMN:3 -->
shout, and see hue, 'an outcry'.
Derivatives: hoot, п., hoot-er, n.

## hop
hop, intr. and tr. v., to leap. — ME. hoppen, hup-
pen, fr. OE. hoppian, 'to hop, dance', rel. to ΟΝ.,
Swed. hoppa, Dan. hoppe, MLG., Du. huppen,
MHG., G. hiipfen, 'to hop', and perh. cogn. with
Gk. κυβιστάν, 'to tumble'. OI. kubhanyuh,
'dancing'. Cp. Cybister. Cp. also hope, 'expectation'.
Derivative: hop, п., the act of hopping.

## hop
hop, п., plant of the hemp family. — Late ME.
hoppe, fr. MDu. hoppe (Du. hop), rel. to Late
OHG. hopfo (MHG. hopfe, G. Hopfeh),
possibly also to dial. Norw. hupp, 'tassel'.
Derivative: hop, tr. v., to flavor with hops;
intr. v., to gather hops.
ope, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hopen, fr. OE. hopian,
'to hope', rel. to OFris. hopia, MLG., MDu.,
Du. hopen, MHG., G. haffen, 'to hope'. These
words are prob. related to OE. hoppian, ΟΝ.,
Swed. hoppa, etc., 'to hop', so that the orig.
meaning of OE. hopian, OFris. hopia, etc.,
would have been 'to leap with expectation'. See
hop, 'to leap'.

## hope
hope, п., expectation. — ME. hope, fr. OE. hopa,
'hope', fr. hopian, 'to hope'. Cp. OFris., MLG.,
MDu. hope, Du. hoop, MHG. hoffe, 'hope',
which derive from the respective verbs. See
hope, v.
Derivatives: hope-ful, adj. and п., hope-ful-ly,
adv., hope-fulness, п., hope-less, adj., hope-less-
ly, adv., hope-less-ness, n.

## hope
hope, п., a small bay. — ME. hope, fr. OE. hop
(in compounds, as fenhop, 'a piece of land in a
fen', mdrhop, 'piece of land in a marsh'), rel. to
ON. hop, 'a small bay*. See hoop, 'circular band'.

## hope
hope, п., troop. — Only in forlorn hope (q.v.)

## hopeite
hopeite, п., a mineral; prob. a hydrous zinc
phosphate (mineral.) — Named after Professor
Thomas С Hope (1766-1844) of Edinburgh.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hopl-
hopl-, form of hoplo- before a vowel.

## hoplite
hoplite, п., a heavy-armed foot-soldier (Greek
antiq.) — Gk. οπλίτης, 'heavy armed', fr. δπλον,
'tool, weapon', fr. επειν (for *σέπειν), 'to be
about, busy oneself, which is cogn; with OI.
sapati, 'applies himself to, caresses, fondles'.
The -λ- in δπ-λ-ον has instrumental force and
lit. means 'that with which one busies himself.
Cp. hoplo-, pauoply, sepulcher. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## hoplo-
hoplo-, before a vowel hopl-, combining form
meaning 'armed, heavy-armed' (used esp. in
zoology). — Gk. όπλο-, όπλ-, fr. όπλαν, 'weapon'.
See hoplite.

## hopper
hopper, п., one who, or that which, hops. —
ME. hoppere. See hop, v., and agential suff. -er.

## hopper
hopper, п., a hop picker. — Formed fr. hop, 'a
plant', with agential suff. -er.

## hopple
hopple, tr. v., to hobble; to fetter. — Formed fr.
hop, 'to leap', with freq. suff. -le. Cp. hobble.
Derivative: hopple, n.

## hopscotch
hopscotch, п., a children's game. —
Compounded of hop, 'to leap', and scotch, 'an incision,
line' (see scotch, 'to cut').

## Horace
Horace, masc. PN. — F., fr. L. Horatius, name
of a Roman gens. Cp. Horatio.

## Horae
Horae, n. pi., the goddesses of the seasons in
Greek mythology. — L., fr. Gk.Ώραι, fr. ώροκ,
pi. of ώρϊ, season; hour'. See hour.

## horal
horal, adj., pertaining to an hour or hours. —
L. horalis, fr. hora, 'hour'. See hour and adj.
suff. -al.

## horary
horary, adj., pertaining to an hour or hours. —
ML. hdrarius, fr. L. hora, 'hour'. See hour and
adj. suff. -ary.

## Horatian
Horatian, adj., pertaining to the Roman poet
Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65-8 B.C.E.) — L.
Horatianus, 'of, or pertaining to, Horatius', fr.
Horatius, 'Horace'. See Horace.

## Horatio
Horatio, masc. PN. — L. Horatius (see Horace);
influenced in form by It. Orazio, which is of
the same origin.

## horde
horde, п., ι) a wandering tribe; 2) a multitude.—
F., fr. Turk, ordu, 'camp, army', fr. Tatar urdu,
'camp' (lit. 'something pitched up'), fr. urmak,
'to strike'. Cp. Urdu.
Derivative: horde, intr. v.

## hordeaceous
hordeaceous, adj., pertaining to bailey. — L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:380 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 353 | HOSANNA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:380 COLUMN:1 -->
hordedceus, 'pertaining to barley', fr. hordeum,
'barley'. See Hordeum and -aceous.

## Hordeum
Hordeum, п., a genus of grasses, the barley (bot.)
— L. hordeum, 'barley', which prob. stands for
'horzdeyom (I.-E. *gh/-zdeyom) and is cogn.
with OS., OHG. gersta, MDu. gherste, Du.
gerst, MHG„ G. gerste (for pre-Teut. "gherz-
dd-), 'barley', Gk. κρϊ (for "κρΐθ), 'barley',
κριθή, pi. 'barley', sing, 'barleycorn' (prob. for
ghfzdd), Alb. dr№, dri&e (for ghfzd-), 'corn;
barley'. All these words prob. mean lit. 'the
bearded plant' and derive fr. I.-E. base 'ghers-,
'to bristle', whence also L. horrere, 'to stand
on end, bristle', horror, 'bristling, roughness'.
See horror and cp. crith, orgeat. Cp. also gorse.

## horehound
horehound, also hoarhound, п., name of a plant.
— ME. horehoune, fr. OE. hdrhune, which is
compounded of hdr, 'gray' (see hoar), and hune,
'horehound', a word of uncertain origin. The
din horehound is excrescent. Cp. bound, 'ready',
and words there referred to.

## horizon
horizon, n. — OF. orizon (F. horizon), fr. L.
horizon, fr. Gk. ορίζων (κύκλος), lit. 'bounding
(circle)', pres. part, of όρίζειν, 'to bound,
limit', fr. δρος, 'boundary, limit, border', which
prob. stands for *Fopf ος and lit. means 'furrow',
and is rel. to Att. όρεύς, Homeric ούρεύς,
'mule', lit. 'furrow drawer', and cogn. with L.
urvus, 'furrow, marking a boundary line', Oscan
uruvu, 'boundary', fr. I.-E. base *weru-, 'to
draw', whence also Gk. έρύειν (for *5ερύειν),
'to draw, drag'. Cp. aorist, aphorism, diorite,
Penthorum.
Derivative: horizon, tr. v.

## horizontal
horizontal, adj. — F. horizontal, fr. L. horizon,
gen. horizontis, 'horizon'. See horizon and adj.
sufT. -a].
Derivatives: horizontal, п., horizontal-ity, п.,
horizontal-ly, adv.

## hormone
hormone, п., endocrine gland secretion which
stimulates functional activity (physiol.) — Gk.
ορμών, 'that which urges or arouses', pres. part,
of όρμάν, 'to set in motion, urge, stimulate', fr.
ορμή, 'onset, impulse', fr. I.-E. base *ser-, 'to
run, flow', whence also Gk. ορός (for *σορός),
L. serum, 'watery fluid, whey'. See serum and
cp. words there referred to. The word hormone
was used by Hippocrates to denote a vital
principle. In its modern sense it was first applied
by the English physiologist Ernest Henry
Starling (1866-1927) in 1903.

## horn
horn, n. — ME., fr. OE. horn, rel. to ΟΝ., OFris.,
OHG., MHG., G. horn, Du. horen, hoorn, Goth.
haurn, 'horn' and cogn. with Gk. κέρας, Gala-
tian Gk. κάρνον, L. cornu, OI. ifngam, 'horn', fr.
I.-E. base ker-;'tae uppermost part of the body,
head, horn, top, summit', whence also L.
cerebrum (prob. for *icer's-rom),'brain'. See cerebrum
and cp. hornet. Cp. also hart, hurt and the
second element in krummhorn, waUhorn. Cp. also
cerato-, cervine, crio-, corn, 'hardened skin', the
first element in ginger and the second element
in Capricorn, unicorn.
Derivatives: horn, tr. v., horn-ed, adj., horn-er,
п., horn-ful, horn-less, horn-y, adjs., horn-i-
ness, n.

## hornblende
hornblende, n. (mineral.) — G. Hornblende. See
horn and blende.

## hornet
hornet, n. — ME. harnette, hernet, fr. OE. hyrnet,
rel. to OS. hornut, OHG. hornas, hornus, MHG.
hornus, hornij, G. Hornisse, MDu. huersel,
hursel, horsel, Du. horzel, 'hornet', and cogn.
with L. crabro (for *crdsrd), OSlav. sruseni,
'hornet', Lith. sirsuo, sirse, 'wasp', siriuonas,
'hornet', Lett, sirsis, 'wasp', OPruss. sirsilis,
'hornet', fr. I.-E. base *ker-, 'the uppermost
part of the body, horn*; see horn. E. hornet
was influenced in form by horn.

## horning
horning, п., the act of outlawing a person by
three blasts of horn (Scot. law). — Formed fr.
horn with subst. suff. -ing.

## hornito
hornito, п., an oven-shaped mound in volcanic
regions emitting smoke and vapors (geol.) —
Sp., dimin. of homo, 'oven', fr. L. furnus. See
furnace.

## horography
horography, п., the art of constructing
instruments for marking the hours. — F. horographie,
compounded of Gk. ώρϊ, 'hour', and -γραφιά,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:380 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See hour and -graphy.

## horologe
horologe, п., a sundial; a clock, watch. — ME.,
fr. OF. (= F.) horloge, fr. L. horologtum, fr.
Gk. ώραλόγιον, lit. 'that which tells the hour', fr.
ώρϊ, 'hour', and -λόγος, 'telling, saying'. See
hour and -logue.
Derivatives: horolog-er, п., horolog-ic, horolog-
ic-al, adjs., horolog-ist, п., horolog-y, n,

## horopter
horopter, п., the aggregate of points that are seen
single when both eyes are directed on the same
point (optics). — Compounded of Gk. 8ρος,
'boundary, limit', and ότττήρ, 'one who looks'.
For the first element see horizon. The second
element is rel. to όπτός, 'seen; visible', whence
οπτικός, 'pertaining to the eyes or sight'. See
optic, adj.

## horoscope
horoscope, п., a chart of the zodiacal signs used
by astrologers. — F., fr. L. horoscopus, fr. Gk.
ωροσκόπος, 'nativity', lit. 'watcher of the hour';
compounded of ώρδ, 'hour', and σκοπός,
'watcher'. See hour and scope-
Derivatives: horoscope, intr. and tr. v., horo-
scop-er, п., horoscop-ic, adj., horoscop-ist, п.,
horoscop-y, n.

## horrendous
horrendous, adj., dreadful. — L. horrendus, 'to
be regarded with horror', gerundive of horrere,
'to shudder, tremble'. See horror. For the
gerundive suff. cp. agenda and words there
referred to. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.

## horrent
horrent, adj., bristling. — L. horrens, gen. -entts,
pres. part, of horrere, 'to stand on end, bristle,
shake, shudder, tremble'. See horror and -ent.

## horrcscent
horrcscent, adj., expressing horror; shuddering.
— L. horrescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of hor-
rescere, 'to shudder', inchoative of horrere. See
horror and -escent.

## horribility
horribility, n. — ME. orriblete, horriblete, fr. OF.
horriblete, fr. horrible. See next word and -ity.

## horrible
horrible, adj. — ME., fr. OF. orrible, horrible
(F. horrible), fr. L. horribilis, fr. horrere, 'to
shudder, tremble'. See horror and -ible.
Derivatives: horrible-ness, п., horribl-y, adv.

## horrid
horrid, adj., repulsive, abominable. — L. horri-
dus, 'bristly, prickly, rough, horrid, frightful',
fr. horrere. See horror and cp. ordure.
Derivatives: horrid-ly, adv., horrid-ness, n.

## horrific
horrific, adj., horrifying. — Formed fr. L. horri-
ficus, 'terrible, dreadful' (either directly or
through the medium of F. horrifique), lit.
'making the hair to stand on end', fr. horrere,
'to stand on end', and -ficus, from the stem of
-ficere, unstressed form offacere, 'to make, do'.
See horror and -fie.

## bonification
bonification, n. — See next word and -ation.

## horrify
horrify, tr. v. — Formed fr. L. horrificare, lit. 'to
make the hair to stand on end' (on analogy of
E. verbs derived fr. L. verbs in -ficare through
the medium of F. verbs in -fler). See horrific
and -fy.

## borripilate
borripilate, tr. v., to cause (the hair) to bristle;
intr. v., to bristle. — L. horripildt (-um) pp. stem
of horripilare, 'to bristle with hair, be shaggy',
compounded of horrere, 'to stand on end,
bristle', and pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair', and
verbal suff. -ate.

## horripilation
horripilation, п., bristling of the hair. — L. horri-
pilatid, gen. -dnis, fr. horripildt(-um), pp. stem
of horripilare. See prec. word and -ion.

## horror
horror, n. — ME. horrour, fr. OF. orror, horror,
honour (F. horreur), fr. L. horrdrem, ace. of
horror, 'bristling, roughness, rudeness, shaking,
trembling', fr. horrere,''to stand on end, bristle,
shake, shudder, shiver, tremble', fr. I.-E. base
*ghers-, 'to bristle', whence also L. hirsutus,
'shaggy, prickly, bristly', OI. Mr sate, hfsyati,
'bristles', Avestic zarshayarraia-, 'ruffling one's
feathers'. Base "ghers- is an enlarged form of
base "gher-, which appears in Gk. χήρ, gen.
χηρός, L. er (for *hers), gen. iris, 'hedgehog',
lit. 'the prickly creature'. See urchin and cp.
Chersonese, -choerus, hideous, hircbte, hirsute,
hispid, Hordeum and the second element in
Hypocnaeris. Cp. also hearse.

## horror-stricken
horror-stricken, horror-struck,
adj.—Compounded of horror and the pp. of strike.

## hors de combat
hors de combat, out of the combat; disabled. —
F., lit. 'out of fight'. F. hors, 'outside', is a var.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:380 COLUMN:3 -->
of fors, which derives fr. L. forts, 'outside' (see
door); F. de, 'of, from', comes fr. L. de, 'from,
away from' (see de-); for F. combat, 'combat,
fight', see combat.

## hors d'oeuvre
hors d'oeuvre, an appetizer. — F. hors d'auvre,
'annexe, outwork, side-dish', lit. Outside of the'
work'. For hors see prec. word. F. d' in d'auvre
is the apostrophized form of de, 'of, from' (fr.
L. de, 'from, away from'); see de-. For the
etymology of F. auvre see oenvre.

## horse
horse, n. — ME. hors, fr. OE. hors, rel. to OS.
hros, ON. hross, OFris. hors, hars, MLG. ros,
ors. MDu. ors, Du. ros, OHG. hros, ros, MHG.
ros, ors, G. Rofi, wich possibly meant orig. 'the
jumping animal', fr. Teut. *hrossa-,
corresponding to pre-Teut. 'qru-td-s, participle of a
lost verb meaning 'to jump', from a dental
enlargement of I.-E. base '(s)qer-, 'to leap, jump,
bound', whence also OI. kurdati, 'leaps, hops'.
See Scarus and cp. cardinal, adj., and words
there referred to. Cp. also the second element
in walrus. F. rosse, OProvenc. rosa, It. rozza,
'mare', are Teut. loan words. Derivatives:
horse, v. (q.v.), horse, adj., horsy (q.v.)

## horse
horse, tr. and intr. v. — ME. horsen, 'to provide
with a horse or with horses', fr. OE. horsian,
fr. hors. See horse, n.

## horsfordite
horsfordite, п., a copper antimonide (mineral.) —
Named after the American chemist Eben
Norton Horsford (1818-93). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## horsy
horsy, adj., fond of horses. — Formed fr. horse
with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: hors-i-ly, adv., hors-i-ness, n.

## hortation
hortation, п., exhortation. — L. hortatid, gen.
-dnis, 'encouragement, exhortation', fr. hor-
tatus, pp. of hortdri, 'to urge, incite, instigate,
encourage, exhort', freq. of horior, gen. horiri,
'to urge, incite, encourage, exhort', fr. I.-E. base
*gher-, 'to desire', whence also OE. geornan,
giernan, 'to desire'. See yearn and -ation.

## hortative
hortative, adj., pertaining to exhortation;
exhortative. — L. hortdtlvus, fr. horldtus, pp. of
hortdri. See prec. word and -ive.

## hortatory
hortatory, adj., hortative. — L. hortdtdrius,
'encouraging', fr. hortatus, pp. of hortdri. See
hortation and adj. suff. -ory.
Derivative: hortatori-ly, adv.

## Hortense
Hortense, fern. PN. — F. See Hortensia.

## hortensia
hortensia, п., the plant Hydrangea L. — ModL.,
named by the French botanist Commerson after
Hortense, wife of the chronometer maker Le-
paute. Commerson, Lepaute and Hortense took
part in Bougainville's round-the-world voyage,
which lasted from 1766 to 1769, and it was in
the course of this voyage that Commerson found
this plant in China and gave it the above name.
For the etymology of the name Hortense see
next word.

## Horteosia
Horteosia, fern. PN. — L. Hortensia, fern, of
Hortinsius, the name of a Roman gens, rel. to
/tortus, 'garden'. See next word.

## horticulture
horticulture, п., the cultivation of gardens. — L.
hortl culture, 'cultivation of a garden'. Hortus
(gen. hortt), 'garden', lit. means 'an enclosed
place'. It derives fr. I.-E. *ghor-to-, whence also
Gk. χόρτος, 'enclosed place'. I.-E. *ghor-to- is
a dental enlargement of base *iherdh-, 'to
enclose'. See yard, 'enclosure', and cp. cohort,
court, cortege, curtain, Hortensin, ortolan. Cp.
also garden and the first element in orchard.
For the second element see culture.
Derivatives: horticultur-al, adj., horticultur-al-
ly, adv., horticultur-ist, n.

## hortus siccus
hortus siccus, a collection of dried plants; a
herbarium. — L. 'dry garden', fr. hortus, 'garden',
and siccus, 'dry'. See prec. word and siccative.

## Horns
Horns, п., name of the Egyptian hawk-headed
god. — L. Hants, fr. Egyptian Hdr, lit. 'the
highflying one'.

## Hosackia
Hosackia, п., a genus of plants of the family
Fabaceae (bot.) — ModL., named after
David Hosack (1769-1835), professor of botany
in Columbia College in New York City. For
the ending see suff. -in.

## hosanna
hosanna, interj., an exclamation of praise to
God. — Gk. Ωσαννά, fr. Heb. hdsha' na, 'save,
we pray'. Hdsha is the Hiph'il imper. of stem

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:381 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HOSE | 354 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:381 COLUMN:1 -->
y-sh-' (this form of the imper. occurs Jer.3i:i6
and Psalms 86:2); whence also the nouns
yesha', y'sha'a", t'shu'a", 'salvation,
deliverance, welfare'. This stem is rel. to Arab, wasi'a,
'was capacious'. Heb. na is a particle of
imitative origin, used esp. after the imper. to
emphasize a request. Cp. hSshf'dh nnd Psalms
118:25, which is the lengthened form of hoshd'
nd. In the Talmud, hosha'na (written as one
word) occurs as a noun denoting the willow
twigs used on the Feast of Tabernacles, whence
yam hosha'na = 'the day of hdsha'nd', i.e. the
seventh day of the Feast of Tabernacles. Cp.
also the first element in Isaiah, Hosea, and the
second element in Elisha.
Derivatives: hosarma, n. and tr. v.

## hose
hose, a., article of clothing for the legs;
stocking. — OE. hosa, rel. to OS., ΟΝ., OHG. hosa,
MHG. hose, 'covering for the leg', Dan. hose,
'stocking, hose', G. Hose, 'trousers', Du. hoos,
'waterspout'. These words lit. mean 'cover,
covering', and derive fr. I.-E. *qeus-, -i-enlarge-
ment of base *geu-, 'to cover, hide*. See hide,
v., and cp. house. OF. hose (whence F. houseau)
and It. uosa, 'gaiter', are Teut. loan words.
Derivatives, hose, tr. v., hosier (q.v.)

## Hosea
Hosea, 1) masc. PN; 2) in the Bible, the first in
the order of the Twelve Propnets; the Book of
Hosea. — Heb. Hoshfr', lit. 'salvation', fr.
stem y-sh-', 'to save'. See hosanna.

## hosier
hosier, n. — Formed fr. hose with suff. -ier.
Derivative: hosier-y, n.

## hospice
hospice, n. — F., fr. L. hospitium, 'inn,
hospitality', fr. hospes, gen. hospilis, 'host; guest'. See
host, 'landlord'.

## hospitable
hospitable, adj. — Obsol. F. hospitable, fr. L.
hospitare, 'to receive as a guest', fr. hospes, gen.
hospitis, 'host; guest'. See host, 'landlord', and
-able.
Derivatives: hospitable-ness, п., hospitabl-y, adv.

## hospital
hospital, a. — ME., fr. OF. hospital (F. hopital),
fr. Late L. hospitale, 'apartment for guests',
prop. neut. of the Latin adjective hospilalis,
'pertaining to a host or guest', fr. hospes, gen.
hospitis, 'host; guest'. See host, 'landlord' and
cp. hostel and hotel, which are doublets of
hospital.

## hospitaler
hospitaler, hospitaller, п., member of a religious
order formed for the care of the sick. — ME.
hospitaler, fr. OF. hospitalier, fr. ML. hospi-
talidrius, 'one who cares for guests', fr. L. hos-
pitdlis. See hospital and -er (representing L.
-drius), and cp. hostler, which is a doublet of
hospitaler.

## hospitality
hospitality, n. — F. hospitalite, fr. L. hospitali-
tatem, ace. of hospitdlitas, 'hospitality', fr.
hospilalis. See hospital and -ity.

## hospodar
hospodar, п., prince (hist.) — Rum., fr. OSlav.
gospodi, 'lord, master'. See host, 'landlord'.

## host
host, п., army. — ME. host, ost, fr. OF. host, ost,
'army', fr. L. hostis, 'stranger; enemy', in ML.
'army'; which is cogn. with Goth, gasts, OE.
giest, giest, 'guest', orig. 'stranger'. See guest
and cp. host, 'landlord', host, 'consecrated
bread', hostile.

## host
host, п., landlord. — ME. hoste, hoit, fr. OF.
hoste (F. hole), 'host; guest', fr. L. hospitem
(whence also It. ospite, Rum. oaspete, OProvenc.,
Catal. oste, Sp. huesped, Port, hospede), ace.
of hospes, 'host; guest', which stands for "hosti-
pol(i)s and orig. meant 'lord of strangers'. Cp.
OSlav. gospodi, 'lord, master', which also means
lit. 'lord of strangers' and is the exact equivalent
of L. hospes. The first element in L. hospes and
in OSlav. gospodi is cogn. with Goth, gasts,
OE. gsest, giest, 'guest'. See guest and cp.
hospodar, hospital, host, 'army', hostage, hostel. The
second element is cogn. with L. polls, 'able',
potins, 'powerful'. See potent and cp. despot.

## host
host, п., consecrated bread. — ME. oist, ost,
host, fr. F. oiste, hoiste (F. hostie), fr. L. hostia,
'sacrificial victim', which is prob. related to L.
hostis, 'stranger; enemy'. See host, 'army'.

## Hosta
Hosta, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(bot.) — ModL., named after the Austrian
physician and botanist Nicolaus Thomas Host
(1761-1834).

## hostage
hostage, n. — ME. ostage, hostage, fr. OF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:381 COLUMN:2 -->
outage, hostage (F. Stage), which is prob. a blend
of OF. ostage, hostage, 'lodging', fr. VL. *hos-
pitdticum (fr. L. hospes, gen. hospitis, 'host,
guest', see host, 'landlord') and OF. ostage,
'hostage', fr. VL. "obsiddticum, fr. Late L. ob-
siddtus, 'hostageship', which is formed with suff.
-dtus, fr. L. obses, gen. obsidis, 'hostage', fr. ob,
'at', and the stem of sedere, 'to sit'. See ob-,
sedentary and -age.

## hostel
hostel, п., an inn. — ME. hostel, ostel, fr. OF.
hostel, ostel (F. hotel), fr. Late L. hospitale. See
hospital and cp. hotel.

## hosteler
hosteler, n. — ME. See hostler,

## hostelry
hostelry, п., an inn. — ME. hostelrie, fr. OF.
hostelerie (F. hotellerie), fr. hostel. See hostel
and -ry.

## hostess
hostess, n. — OF. hostesse (F. hotesse), fr. hoste.
See host, 'landlord', and -ess.

## hostile
hostile, adj. — F., fr. L. hostilis, fr. hostis, 'enemy'.
See host, 'army', and -lie.
Derivatives: hostile-ly, adv., hostile-ness, n.

## hostility
hostility, n. — F. hostiliti, fr. L. hostilitutem, ace.
of hostilitds, 'enmity, hostility', fr. hostilis. See
prec. word and -ity.

## hostler
hostler, п., one who takes care of horses at an
inn. — ME. hosteler, 'innkeeper', fr. OF.
hosteller (F. hotelier), fr. hostel. See hostel and
agential suff. -er and cp. hosteler, ostler, which
are doublets of hostler.

## hot
hot, adj. — ME. hat, hoot, hot, fr. OE. hat, rel.
to OS., OFris. hit, ON. heitr, Dari. hed, Swed.
het, MDu., Du. heet, OHG., MHG. hei3, G.
heifi, 'hot', Goth, heito, 'heat of the fever', fr.
I.-E. base *qdi-, 'heat', whence also Lith. kaistit,
kaisti, 'to grow hot', kaitra, 'heat, glow', kai-
trus, 'hot'. Cp. heat. Cp. also hoarse.
Derivatives: hot, adv. (q.v.), hot-ly, adv., hot-
ness, a.

## hot
hot, adv. — ME. hoote, fr. OE. hate, 'hotly', fr.
hat, 'hot'. See hot, adj.
Hotchkiss gun. — Named after its inventor B.B.
Hotchkiss (1826-85).

## hotchpot
hotchpot, п., a blending of properties for equal
division (law). — ME., fr. F. hochepot, fr. F.
hocher, 'to shake', and pot, 'pot'. See pot. The
first element is of Teut. origin; cp. MHG. hol-
zen, Du. hotsen, 'to shake', LG. hotten, 'to
balance, rock'. For the second element see
pot.

## hotchpotch
hotchpotch, п., a stew of many ingredients. —
Formed fr. preceding word, with assimilation
of the second element of the word to the first.
Cp. hodgepodge.

## hotel
hotel, n. — F. hotel, fr. OF. hostel, ostel, fr. Late
L. hospitale. See hostel.

## Hottentot
Hottentot, n. and adj. — S. Afr. Du. hot en tot,
lit. 'hot and tot'; so called from the clicks and
jerks in the native speech of the Cape of Good
Hope.

## Hottonia
Hottonia, п., a genus of plants, the featherfoil
(hot.) — ModL., named after the Dutch
botanist Peter Hotton (1649-1709). For the ending
see suff. -ia.

## Houdan
Houdan, п., a French breed of domestic poultry.
— Named after Houdan, a town in the
department Seine-et-Oise in France.

## hough
hough, п., the hock (chiefly Scot.) — The orig.
spelling of hock, 'joint in the hind leg of the
horse'.

## houghite
houghite, п., a variety of hydrotalcite (mineral.)
— Named after Franklin B. Hough (1822-85)
of Somerville, New York. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## hound
hound, п., dog. — ME. hound, hund, 'dog', fr.
OE. hund, rel. to OS., Dan., Swed., OFris., G.
hund, ON. hundr, Du. hond, OHG., MHG. hunt,
Goth, hunds. These words derive from a dental
enlargement of I.-E. base 'kwori-, 'dog', whence
OI. svdn-, Vedic suvan-, Avestic spa (gen. siino),
Medean spdka (whence Russ. sobdka), Toch. A
ku, 'dog', Arm. shun (gen. shan), Gk. χύων, L.
canis, Lith. suo (gen. sunis), Olr. ей (gen. con),
W. ci, Bret., Co. ki, 'dog', and perh. also Russ.
suka, 'bitch'. Cp. Gk. σπάδακες (Hesychius),
'dogs', which seems to be metathesized fr.
•σπάκαδες, fr. Medean spdka. Cp. the second
element in dachshund, keeshond.Cp. also canaille,
Canidae, canine, Canis, chenilie, kennel, 'shelter

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:381 COLUMN:3 -->
for a dog', and the first element in cynanche,
Cynanchum, quinsy, squinancy, scybalum.
Derivatives: hound, tr. v., hound-er, п., hound-
ish, hound-y, adjs.

## hound
hound, п., projection at a masthead serving to
support trestletrees, etc. (naul.) — ME. Аил,
prob. fr. ON. hunn, 'knob, knob at the mast-
end; bear's cub', which is prob. cogn, with
OI. sunah, 'swollen', h.cavus, 'hollow, concave'.
See cave, n.

## hounds-tongae
hounds-tongae, п., name of a plant. — OE. hundes
tunge. See hound, 'dog', and tongue.

## hour
hour, n. — ME., fr. OF. ure, ore, hore (F. heure),
fr. L. hdra, 'hour', fr. Gk. ώρϊ, 'any limited
time, the time of day, hour, season spring, year',
which is cogn. with Avestic jar1, 'year', OSlav.
jaru, 'spring*, L. hornus (fr. 'ho-ydrinos), 'of this
year', Goth, jer, OE. gear, 'year'. See year and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also Horae,
horal, horary, the first element in horography,
horologe, horoscope, and the second element in
encore.
Derivatives: hour-ly, adj. and adv.

## houri
houri, п., a nymph of the Moslem Paradise; (fig.)
a seductive woman. — F., fr. Pers. Ай/ΐ, fr.
Arab, hur, pi. of dhwar, fern, haurd', 'having
beautiful black eyes', fr. hdwira, 'had black
eyes', which is rel. to Heb. hdwdr, Aram.-Syr.
huwdr, 'was white', Heb. hur, 'white stuff', hort,
'white bread'. The -Г in Pers. Auriis a formative
element serving to denote the singular.

## house
house, n. — ME. hus, hous, fr. OE. hus, rel. to
OS.,ON„ OFris., OHG. MHG, hits, Du. huis, G.
Haus, Goth. -A«s(in the compoundgudhus,'temp-
le', lit. 'the house of God'); orig. 'shelter', fr.
I.-E. *qeus-, -^-enlargement of base "qeu-, 'to
cover, hide'. See hide, v. and cp. hoard, hose,
hut. Cp. also husk, the first element in hushand,
husting and the second element in caboose.

## house
house, tr. and intr. v. — OE. husian, 'to take into
a house', fr. hus, 'house'. See house, n.

## housecarl
housecarl, п., member of the bodyguard of a
Danish or early English king or nobleman
(hist.) — OE. huscarl, fr. ON. huskarl, which is,
compounded of ON. hus, 'house', and karl,
'man'. See house and churl.

## housel
housel, п., the Eucharist (obsol.) — ME. husel,
fr. OE. husel, 'the Eucharist', rel. to ON. husl,
of s.m., Goth, hunsl, 'sacrifice', and prob. cogn.
with Lith. Sventas, OSlav. svetu, OPruss. swints,
'holy', Lett, svinet, 'to hallow, celebrate',
Avestic spenta-, 'holy'.

## housel
housel, tr. v., to administer the Eucharist to. —
ME. huslen, fr. OE. huslian, fr. husel, 'the
Eucharist'. Cp. ON. husla, 'to administer the
Eucharist', Goth, hunsljan, 'to sacrifice', which
also are denominatives, and see housel, n.

## housewife
housewife, n. — ME. houswif, fr. hous, 'house',
and wif, 'woman, wife'. See house and wife and
cp. hussy.
Derivatives: housewife-ly, adj., housewife-ry, n.

## housing
housing, п., the act of taking into a house. —
Formed fr. house, v., with -ing, suff. forming
verbal nouns.

## housing
housing, п., an ornamental covering for a horse.
— Formed with subst. suff. -ing fr. obsol. house,
'housing', fr. OF. houce (F. housse),
'horsecloth, housing', fr. Frankish 'hulftia (whence
also ML. hultia), which is related to OHG.
huluft, 'case, sheath'. See holster.

## Houstonia
Houstonia, п., a genus of plants of the madder
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the English
botanist William Houston (1695-1733). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## Houyhnhnm
Houyhnhnm, п., one of a race of noble horses (in
(Swift's Gulliver's Travels). — Coined by Swift
to 'suggest the whinnying sound made by
horses.

## hovel
hovel, п., a small hut. — ME. hovel, hovyl, of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: hovel, tr. v.

## hoveler
hoveler, traveller, п., coast boatman. — Of
uncertain origin.

## hover
hover, intr. v. — ME. hoveren, formed with freq.
suff. -er fr, hoven, 'to hover,' which is of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: hover, a., hover-er, п., hover-ing,
n. and adj., hover-ing-ty, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:382 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 355 | HUMANIST -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:382 COLUMN:1 -->

## how
how, adv. — ME. hou, hu, fr. OE. hu, 'how', rel.
to OS. hwo, hu, OFris., MDu. hu, Du. hoe,
'how', OHG. hwio, wio, MHG., G. wie, Goth.
haiwa, 'how', and cogn. with Lith. kai, 'how',
fr. I.-E. pronominal base *qwo-, *qwe-. See who
and cp. words there referred to.

## how
how, п., a mound; hillock. — ME., fr. ON.
haugr, 'mound', which is rel. to OE. heah,
'high'. See high.

## howardite
howardite, п., a meteorite (petrogr.) — Named
after the English meteorologist Luke Howard
(1772-1864). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## howbeit
howbeit, conj. — Compounded of how, be and it.

## howdah
howdah, п., a seat for riding on an elephant. —
Hind, haudah, fr. Arab, haudaj, 'Utter for riding
on a camel'.

## howitzer
howitzer, п., a kind of short cannon. — Du. hou-
wilser, fr. G. Haubilze, fr. MHG. haufeniz, hauf-
niz, borrowed fr. Czech houfnice, 'catapult', fr.
Czech houf 'heap, crowd', which is a loan
word fr. MHG. hufe, 'heap'. See heap.

## howl
howl, intr. and tr. v. — ME. houlen, fr. MDu.
hulen, huylen (Du. huilen), which is rel. to Dan.
hyle, Norw. hyla, MHG. hiuweln, hiulen, G.
heulen, 'to howl', and to OHG. hiwilon, 'to
rejoice' (prop, 'to shout with joy'), huwila, 'owl'
(lit. 'the screeching bird'); of imitative origin.
Derivatives: howl, п., howl-er, п., howl-ing, adj.
and п., howl-ing~ly, adv.

## howlet
howlet, п., owl; owlet. — A blend of F. hulotte,
'owlet', and E. owlet. F. hulotte itself is a blend
of Teut. ·«/- 'owl' (cp. OE. Hie, 'owl', and see
owl), and OF. huer, 'to hoot' (said of an owl),
which is of imitative origin.

## howlite
howlite, п., a calcium borosilicate (mineral.) —
Named after the Canadian mineralogist Henry
How(aiea in 1879). For the ending see combining
form -lite.

## hoy
hoy, interj., an exclamation to call attention. —
Imitative; cp. Du. and Dan. hui and E. ahoy.
Derivative: hoy, tr. and intr. v.

## hoy
hoy, п., a small vessel or barge (naut.) — ME.,
fr. MDu. hoey (obsol. Du. heu), 'hoy'. Cp.
Flem. hui, 'hoy',

## Hoya
Hoya, п., a genus of plants of the milkweed
family; the honey plant (hot.) — ModL., named
after the English horticulturist Thomas Hoy
(died in 1821).

## hoyden
hoyden, hoiden, п., a romping girl. — Prob. fr.
Du. heiden, 'a heathen; a rustic'. See heathen.
Derivative: hoyden-ish, hoiden-ish, adj.

## bsien
bsien,-n., subdivision of a department in China.
— Chin.

## hub
hub, п., the central part of a wheel. — Prob. a
var. of hob, 'projection'.

## hubba
hubba, п., a grain (used as a weight). — Arab.
habba", 'a grain', noun of unity fr. habb, 'grain'.
Cp. the first element in Abelmoschus.

## hobble-bubble
hobble-bubble, п., a hookah in its primitive form.
— Imitative; formed through reduplication on
bubble.

## hnbbub
hnbbub, п., uproar; turmoil. — Of Irish,
imitative, origin. Cp. Olr. abu, a war cry, Gael, ubub,
an exclamation of contempt.

## Hubert
Hubert, masc. PN. — F., fr. OHG. Hugubert, lit.
'bright-minded', fr. hugu, 'mind', and beraht,
'bright''. See hug and bright and cp. Hugh.

## hilbnerite
hilbnerite, п., a manganese tungstate (mineral.) —
Named in 1865 after the German mineralogist
Adolph Hubner, who analyzed it. For the
ending see subst. sufT. -ite.

## hubris
hubris, п., insolence, arrogance. — Irregular
(for hybris), fr. Gk. ΰβρις, 'wanton violence,
riotousness, insolence; outrage', which is prob.
a compound whose first element is identical
with ύ-, the equivalent of OI. ut, 'up, out',
Goth., OE. ut, 'out'; see out. The second
element of this compound is of uncertain origin.

## hubristlc
hubristlc, adj., insolent, arrogant. — Irregular
form (for hybristic), fr. Gk. υβριστικός, 'insolent,
wantonly', fr. ϋβρις. See prec. word and -istic.
Derivative: hubristic-al-ly, adv.

## huckaback
huckaback, п., a cotton fabric used esp. for
towels. — Of uncertain origin.

## hubshi
hubshi, hubshee, п., a Negro (India). — Pers.
Habshi, fr. Arab. Habasht, 'an Abyssinian',
formed with gentilic suff. -I fr. Habashah,
'Abyssinia', fr. Habash, 'Abyssinians'. Cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:382 COLUMN:2 -->
Abyssinia.

## huckleberry
huckleberry, n. — Prob. altered fr. hurtleberry,
a dial, form of whortleberry (q.v.)

## huckster
huckster, n. — ME. hokester, hukster, fr. MDu.
hokester, hoekster, fern, of hoeker (whence Du.
heuker), fr. hoken, hoeken, 'to bear on the back,
squat', which is rel. to ON. huka, 'to crouch,
squat', ON. hoka, hokra, MHG. huchen, G.
hoeken, of s.m. These words derive fr. I.-E.
"qou-g-, *qu-g-, enlargement of base *qeu-, 'to
bend'. For the ending see suff. -ster. Cp. hawker,
hunker, Cp. also I.-E. *qeu-q-, whence Goth.
hauhs, OE. heah, 'high' (see high).
Derivatives: huckster, intr. v., huckster-ess,
huckstr-ess, п., huckster-y, n.

## hud
hud, п., the husk of nuts, etc. — ME. hudde,
of uncertain origin.

## huddle
huddle, tr. and intr. v. — Prob. rel. to ME. huden,
hiden, 'to hide'. See hide, 'to conceal', and freq.
suff. -le.
Derivatives: huddle, п., huddl-er, n„ huddl-ing,
adv.

## Hudibrastic
Hudibrastic, adj., resembling the style of Samuel
Butler's "Hudibras"; mock-heroic. — Formed
fr. Hudibras on analogy of fantastic, etc.

## Hudsonia
Hudsonia, n„ a genus of plants of the rockrose
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the English
botanist William Hudson (1730-93). For the
ending see suff. -la.

## hue
hue, п., color. — ME. hew, hewe, fr. OE. hiw,
hiew, 'form, shape, appearance; color', rel. to
ON. hy, 'bird's down', Swed. hy, 'skin,
complexion', Goth, hiwi, 'form, appearance', OE.
hsewen, 'bluish gray, blue', prob. also to OE.
har, 'gray' (see hoar), and prob. cogn. with
OSlav. sivu, 'gray'. Lith. syvas, 'white', OPruss.
sywan, 'gray', OI. syavas, 'blackish brown'.
Derivatives: hue, tr. and intr. v., to color, hu-ed,
hue-less, adjs., hue-less-ness, n.

## hue
hue, п., an outcry. — ME., fr. OF. hu, fr. huer,
'to cry out, shout', which is of imitative origin.
Cp. boot. Cp. also howlet.
Derivatives: hue, intr. v., to cry out, hu-er, n.

## huff
huff, tr. v., 1) to hector, bully; 2) to anger; intr. v.,
1) to bluster; 2) to become angry. — The orig.
meaning was 'to puff, blow'; of imitative origin.
Derivatives: huff, п., huff-ish, adj., huff-ish-ly,
adv., huff-ish-ness, п., huff-y, adj., huff-i-ly, adv.,
huff-i-ness, n.

## hug
hug, tr. v., to embrace closely. — Of uncertain
origin; perh. fr. ON. hugga, 'to soothe,
comfort', which is rel. to ON. hyggja and huga, OE.
hyegan, OS. huggian, OFris. hugia, OHG. hug-
gen, hukken, Goth, hugjan, 'to think', and to
OE. hyge, ON. hugr, OS. hugi, OFris. hei, OHG.
hugu, Goth, hugs, 'mind, soul; thought'. Cp.
Hugh and the first element in Hubert.
Derivatives: hug, п., hugg-ing-ly, adv.

## huge
huge, adj. — ME. huge, hoge, shortened fr. OF.
ahoge, 'high', fr. a hoge, 'on high', fr. a, 'to, at,
on' (see a) and hoge, 'hill, high place', which
is of Teut. origin; cp. ON. haugr, 'mound',
OSwed. hugli, 'hill', and see high, Cp. also how,
'a mound'.
Derivatives: huge-ous, adj., huge-ous-ly, adv.,
huge-ous-ness, п., hug-y, adj.

## huggermugger
huggermugger, adv., secretly. — Fr. earlier hucker
mucker; of unknown origin.
Derivatives: huggermugger, п., adj. and v.

## Hugh
Hugh, masc. PN. — ONF. Hugues (ace. Hugon),
rel. to OF. Hue (ace. Huori), of Teut. origin;
cp. OHG. Hugi, which is rel. to OHG. hugu,
'mind, soul, thought'. See hng and cp. next
word.

## Hugo
Hugo, masc. PN. — ONF. Hugon, ace. of Hugues.
See prec. word.

## Huguenot
Huguenot, п., French protestant of the 16th and
17th centuries. — F., fr. earlier eiguenot, fr.
MHG. eitgend^e (G. Eidgenosse), 'confederate',
which is compounded of eit (G. Eid), 'oath', and
gend^e (G. Gehosse), 'comrade'. For the first
element see oath. The second element derives
fr. OHG. gind3o, 'comrade', which is rel. to
OS. gindt, OE. geneat, OFris. nat, ON. nautr,
'companion, comrade', Goth, niutan, 'to reach,
attain', OE. niotan, 'to enjoy', neat, 'ox, cow'.
See neat, 'an animal of the ox family'. F.
Huguenot was influenced in form by the name of Hugues

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:382 COLUMN:3 -->
Besancon, a Genevan party leader.

## Huldah
Huldah, 1) fem. PN.; 2) in the Bible, name of a
prophetess. — Heb. Huldah, lit. 'weasel', rel.
to Heb. holedh, Aram.-Syr. hitlda, Arab, khuld,
'mole', from a base meaning 'to dig, to hollow
out' (cp. Heb. Mladh, hehlidh, 'he dug,
undermined').

## hulk
hulk, п., a heavy ship. — ME. hulke, 'ship', fr.
OE. Ли/с, 'a light ship', fr. ML. holcas [whence
also OF. hulque, MLG. hoik, MDu. hulc (Du.
hulk), OHG. holcho (MHG. holche, hulk), G.
Hoik, Hulk)], fr. Gk. όλκάς, gen. όλκάδος, 'a
ship of burden', lit. 'a ship that is towed'. See
Holcus and cp. holcad.

## hulking
hulking, adj., unwieldy. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ing fr. dial. E. hulk, 'to be wieldy', fr. hulk,
'a heavy ship', taken in the sense of 'an
unwieldy person'.

## hull
hull, п., husk, pod, shell. — ME. hui, hule, hole,
fr. OE. hulu, fr. Teut. base "hui-, 'to cover',
weak grade of base *hel-, of s.m., whence OE.
helan, 'to conceal'. Cp. Du. huh, OHG. hulsa,
MHG., G. hulse, 'hull', OHG. hulla, MHG., G.
hiille, 'a covering', which also derive from Teut.
*hul-. See cell and cp. hall, hell.
Derivative: hull, tr. v., to remove the husk of.

## hull
hull, п., the body of a ship. — Figurative use of
prec. word. Cp. L. carina, 'keel of a ship', orig.
'shell of a nut', F. coque, 'shell (of walnuts,
other fruits, eggs, etc.); hull of a ship'. Cp. ahull.
Derivative: hull, tr. v., to strike or pierce the
hull of a ship.

## hullabaloo
hullabaloo, n„ uproar. — Of imitative origin.

## hulled
hulled, adj., deprived of the husk. — Formed
with suff. -ed fr. hull, 'husk'.

## hulled
hulled, adj., having a hull (said of a ship). —
Formed with suff. -ed fr. hull, 'the body of a ship'.

## huller
huller, n„ a machine for hulling grain. — Formed
with agential suff. -er fr. hull, 'to remove the
husk of. See hull, husk.

## hullo
hullo, interj. — Imitative.

## hnlsite
hnlsite, п., a hydrous iron magnesium tin borate
(mineral.) — Narned after Alfred Hulse Brooks
of the U.S. Geological Survey (1871-1924). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hum
hum, interj. — Imitative. Cp. hum, v.

## hum
hum, v., to utter an inarticulate sound. — ME.
hummen, of imitative origin. Cp. G. hummen,
of s.m. Cp. also hem, interj., bumblebee,
humdrum, hummingbird.
Derivatives: hum, п., humm-er, п., humm-ing,
adj. and п., humm-ing-ly, adv.

## hum
hum, п., a hoax; tr. v., to humbug (both colloq.)
— Short for humbug.

## human
human, adj. — ME. humayne, fr. OF. (= F.)
humain, fr. L. humanus, 'human', fr. homo, gen.
-ίηίι, 'man', which is rel. to humus, 'earth', hence
prop, means 'earthly being', and is cogn. with
ToCh. В saumo, OLith. zmud (ace. zmunO, Lith.
imogus (ace. zmdgif), OPruss. smoy, 'man, male
person', smuni, 'person', smonenawino, 'man',
Goth., OE. guma, 'man'; see bridegroom. All
these words lit. mean 'earthly being'. For sense
development cp. Heb. addm, 'man', which
derives fr. aaa"mah, 'ground' (see Adam). See
humus and cp. humane. Cp. also homage, hom-
bre, homo, homunculus, humble, omber, ombre,
and the first element in homicide. Cp. also the
first element in duniwassal.
Derivatives: human, п., humanist (q.v.),
humanitarian (q.v.), humanity (q.v.), human-ize, tr. and
intr. v., human-iz-ation, п., human-ly, adv.,
human-ness, n.

## humane
humane, adj. — Prop, identical with, and
representing an earlier spelling of, human (q.v.),
from which it was later differentiated in
meaning. For a similar differentiation in form and
meaning of orig. one and the same word cp.
german and germane, urban and urbane.
Derivatives: humane-ly, adv., humane-ness, n.

## humanism
humanism, n. — Formed after humanist fr.
human and suff. -Ism.

## humanist
humanist, n. — F. humaniste, fr. It. umanista,
which was coined by the Italian poet Lodovico
Ariosto (1474-1533) fr. umano (fr. L. humanus;
