see human) and suff. -isto (fr. Gk. -ιστής; see -ist).
Derivatives: humanist-ic, humanist-ic-al, adjs.,
humanist-ic-al-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:383 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HUMANITARIAN | 356 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:383 COLUMN:1 -->

## humanitarian
humanitarian, adj. and n. — Formed with sufT.
-arian fr. L. humanitas. See next word.
Derivative: humanitarian-ism, n.

## humanity
humanity, n. — F. humanite, fr. L. humanitatem,
ace. of humanitas, 'human nature, humanity',
fr. humanus, 'human'. L. humanitas is loan
translation of Gk. φιλανθρωπία, lit. 'love of
mankind'. See human and -ity.

## humanize
humanize, tr. and intr. v. — F. humanlser, fr. L,
humanus, 'human'. See human and -ize.
Derivative: humaniz-ation, n.

## humanoid
humanoid, adj., of human character (anthropoid)
— A hybrid coined fr. L. humanus, 'human', and
Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
human and -aid.
Derivative: humanoid, n.

## humble
humble, adj. — ME. humble, umble, fr. OF.( = F.)
humble, fr. L. humilem, ace. of humilis, 'low,
base, humble', lit. 'on the ground', fr. humus,
'earth, ground, soil'. See humus and words there
referred to and cp. esp. humiliate, humility.
Derivatives: humble, tr. v., humble-ness, п.,
humbl-er, п., humbl-ing, п., humbl-y, adv.

## bumblebee
bumblebee, п., a bumblebee. — ME. humbyl-bee,
a compound whose first element is rel. to Dan.
humle, humlebi, Swed., Norw. humla, MDu.
hummel, homel, hommel, Du. hommel, OHG.
humbal, MHG. hUmbel, hummel, G. Hummel,
'bumblebee', prop, 'the humming bee'. See hum,
'to utter an inarticulate sound', and freq. suff.
-le, and cp. Czech amel, Pol. czmiel, OPruss.
camus, Lith. kamane, 'bumblebee', which are
also of imitative origin. For the second element
in ME. humbyl-bee see bee.

## hnmble pie
hnmble pie, pie made of the umbles of a deer. —
For umble pie, 'pie made of umbles'. Cp. umble
pie, umbles and see nuinbles. The h in humble
pie is due to a confusion of umble with humble,
'low'.

## humbug
humbug, п., a hoax. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: humbug, tr. and intr. v., humbugg-
er, п., humbugg-er-y, n.

## humdrum
humdrum, adj. and n. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
hum, 'to utter an inarticulate sound'.

## humeral
humeral, adj., pertaining to the shoulder. — Late
L. humeralis, fr. L. humerus. See humerus and
adj. suff. -al.

## huinero-
huinero-, combining form meaning 'humeral;
humeral and' (anat.) — L. humero-, fr. humerus.
See humerus.

## humerus
humerus, п., the bone of the upper arm (anat.) —
L. (h)umerus, 'shoulder', fr. I.-E. *omesos; cogn.
with OI. dmsah, Toch. A es, В antse, Arm. us
(gen. usoys), Gk. ώμος (for *dmsos, less
probably for Omsos), 'shoulder', Umbr. uze,
onse, 'in the shoulder', ON. ass, Goth, ams,
amsa, 'shoulder'. Ср. ото-, 'shoulder-', and
words there referred to.

## humid
humid, adj. — F. humide, fr. L. (h)umidus, 'moist,
wet', fr. (h)umere, 'to be moist or wet'. See
humor.
Derivatives: humid-ly, adv., humid-ness, n.

## humidify
humidify, tr. v., to render humid. — See humid
and -fy.

## humidity
humidity, η. — F. humidile, fr. L. (h)umiditatem,
ace. of (h)umiditus, 'moisture, wetness', fr.
(h)umidus. See hnmid and -ity.

## humiliate
humiliate, tr. v. — Fr. L. humilidtus, pp. of humi-
liare, 'to humble', fr. humilis. See humble and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: humiliat-ing, adj., humiliat-ing-ly,
adv., humiliat-or, п., humiliat-ory, adj.

## humiliation
humiliation, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
humiliation, fr. L. humiliationem, ace. of humiliatio,
'humbling, humiliation', fr. humiliutus, pp. of
humiliare. See prec. word and -ion.

## humility
humility, n. — ME. humilite, fr. F. humilite, fr.
L. humilitatem, ace. of humilitas, 'lowness,
insignificance' (in Eccles. L. 'lowness, meekness'),
fr. humilis, 'low'. See humble and -ity.

## hummaul
hummaul, n. — A var. of hamal.

## hummingbird
hummingbird, n. — So called from iis humming
sound.

## hummock
hummock, п., '.) a knoll, hillock; z) pile of ice
in an icefield. — Dimin. of hump. See -ock and
cp. hillock, which is a dimin. of hill.
Derivative: hummock-y, adj.

## humor
humor, humour, n. — ME. humor, humour, итог,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:383 COLUMN:2 -->
umour, fr. OF. humor, итог (F. humeur), fr. L.
(h)itmorem, ace. oi(h)umor, 'fluid, moisture', rel.
to <h)umere. Ίο be moist, wet', {h)umidus, 'moist,
wet'. Humor stands for *ug"mor-, fr. I.-E. base
*ugw-, *wegw-, 'wet, moist, to sprinkle', whence
also Gk. υγρός, 'wet, moist', Arm. oyc, 'fresh',
ON. vo£r,'moist, damp', OI. uksati, 'sprinkles',
uksan-, 'ox', Goth, auhsa, OE. oxa, 'ox', and
prob. also Olr.fual (for *woguh-), 'urine'. The
correct spelling of the above Latin words is
итог, йтёге, Qmidus. The spelling with initial
h is due to folk etymology, which associated
ihese words with L. humus, 'earth'. Cp. humid,
hygro-, ox, udograph, udometer, Ulex, uliginose,
uxorious, wake, 'track left by a moving ship'.
Derivatives: humo(u)r, tr. v., humo(u)r-less,
humo(u)r-some, adjs., humoral, humoresque,
humorist, humorous (qq.v.)

## humoral
humoral, adj., pertaining to the humors of the
body (archaic). — See humor and adj. suff. -al.
humoralism; п., an obsolete doctrine which
attributes all diseases to the stale of the humors
of the body. — See prec. word and -ism.

## humoralist
humoralist, п., an adherent of humoralism. —
See humoral and -ist.

## humoresque
humoresque, п., a humorous or fanciful
composition. — G. Humoreske, 'humorous sketch'.
See humor and -esque.

## humorist
humorist, humourist, n. — F. humoriste, fr. It.
umorista, 'capricious', fr. ML. humorista, which
prop, denoted an adherent of 'humorism', i.e.
the doctrine that diseases are due to the change
of 'humors' in the body. See humor and -ist.
Derivative: humo(u)rist-ic, adj.

## humorous
humorous, adj. — L. (h)umorosus, 'moist', fr.
(h)umor. See humor and -ous.
Derivatives: humorous-ly, adv., humorous-
ness, n.

## hump
hump, п., a rounded protuberance. — Of LG.
origin. Cp. MLG. hump, 'bump, hunch', Du.
homp, 'lump, chunk', Norw. hump, 'knoll'.
These words derive fr. I.-E. base *qumb-, 'to
bend, curve', whence also OI. kumbhah, 'pot,
jar', Gk. κύμβη, 'the hollow of a vessel, cup,
boat'. See cymbal and cp. chime, 'set of bells'.
Derivatives: hump, tr.v., hump-ed, adj., hump-y,
adj., hump-i-ness, n.

## humpback
humpback, n. — Compounded of hump and back.
Derivative: humpback-ed, adj.

## humph
humph, interj. expressing doubt or contempt,
— Imitative.
Derivatives: humph, intr. v. and n.

## Humphrey
Humphrey, masc. PN. — OE. Hunfrid, prob.
formed fr. Teut. *hun, 'strength', and OE. fridu,
'peace' (see free); influenced in form by names
like Geoffrey, which, though also of Teut. origin,
came into English through the medium of
French.

## humpty-dumpty
humpty-dumpty, п., a short or dumpy figure. —
Fr. Humpty-Dumpty, hero of a nursery rhyme.
The name prob. arose through the reduplication
of Humpty, a pet form of Humphrey. Cp. Ernest
Weekley's Etymological Dictionary s.v.

## Humulus
Humulus, п., a genus of vines, the hop (bot.) —
ModL., fr. ML. humulus, 'hop', which, together
with ON. humli (OSwed. humbli, Dan., Swed.
Humle), OE. hymele, Frankish *humilo (whence
F. houblon), ModGk. χουμέλι, 'hop', is
traceable to OSIav. "chumeli(contracted into chmili),
which itself seems to be of Finnish-Tatar origin.
Cp. Finnish humala, Vogul qumlix, 'hop'.

## hnmus
hnmus, n. — L., 'earth, ground, soil' (cp. Oscan
huntrus, 'those below' (ace), Umbr. hutra,
hondra, 'below'), for "homos, fr. I.-E. *ghom-,
whence also Gk. χαμαί, 'on the ground', Lith.
zlme, Lett, zeme, OPruss. same, semme, OSIav.
zemlja, 'earth'. L. humilis, 'low', and homo,
'man', are rel. to humus. See chthonian and cp.
homage, human, humble," humiliate, exhume,
inhume.

## Hun
Hun, n. — Late L. Ηϋηϊ, Hunni, Chunni (pi.), re],
to Gk. Οδννοι (pi.), 'the Huns', OS., OHG.
HQni, Hun, MHG. Hiune, 'Hun'. Cp. MHG.
hiune (whence G. Hiine), 'giant', orig. 'a Hun'.
Derivative: Hunn-ish, adj.

## hunch
hunch, п., ι) hump; 2) a thick piece. — Prob.
altered fr. hump. For a similar alteration cp. lunch,
which prob. derives fr. lump. Cp. hunk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:383 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: hunch, tr. v.

## hundi
hundi, п., a bill of exchange (India). — Hind.
hundi, hundavi, fr. OI. hundikd, fr. hundate,
'collects'.

## hundred
hundred, n. — ME. hondred, honderd, fr. Late
OE. hundred, prob. fr. ON. hundrad (whence
also Dan. hundrede, Swed. hundrade, h'undra),
lit. 'the number of hundred', fr. Te\iK.*hunda-,
'hundred' (seen also in OE., OS., Goth, hund,
OHG. hunt), and *-rad, 'reckoning, number',
(seen in Goth, rapjo, 'a reckoning, account,
number', ga-rapjan, 'to count', see reason); cp.
OS. hunderod (whence MLG., MHG., G. hun-
dert, MDu. hondert, honderd (Du. honderd).
Teut. "hunda-, 'hundred', corresponds to I.-E.
*kipto-, which appears in OI. satam, Avestic
sat*m [OSIav. suto (Russ. sto), is prob. an
Iranian loan word], Toch. A kant, В kante,
kante, Gk. έ-κατόν, L. centum, Lith. Himtas,
Lett, simts, Olr. cet, W. cant, Bret, kant, Co.
kans, 'hundred-. I.-E. *kmto-, 'hundred', orig.
meant 'ten tens', fr. *kmt-, 'ten', which also
appears in the Latin ending -gintl, -ginta
(in viginti, 'twenty', triginta, 'thirty", quadra-
ginta, 'forty', etc.), in the Greek ending -κοντά
(in τριάκοντα, "thirty', τεσσαράκοντα, 'forty',
etc.), and in L. decern, 'ten', which stands for
*(d)kmtom)\ see decad, decimal, ten.
Accordingly hundred prop, means 'the great ten'. Cp.
cent, centenary, century, hecatomb, sotnia. Cp.
also the second element in thousand.
Derivatives: hundred, adj., hundreder (q.v.),
hundred-fold, adj., hundreth (q.v.)

## hundreder
hundreder, hundredor, п., the chief officer of a
hundred (hist.) — ML. hundredarius. See
hundred and -er (representing L. -arius).

## hundredth
hundredth, adj. and n. — Formed fr. hundred with
numeral suff. -th.
hung. — Past tense and pp. of hang.

## hunger
hunger, n. — ME., fr. OE. hunger, rel. to OS.,
OHG. hungar, ON. hungr, OFris., MHG., G.
hunger, Du. honger, Goth, huhrus (for "hunhruz),
'hunger', and cogn. with Gk. κάγκανος, 'dry',
lit. 'burning', κέγκειν, 'to starve, to hunger',
Lith. kanka, 'suffering', kehkti, 'to pain, ache';
fr. I.-E. base *kenk-, knk-, 'to burn, be dry,
pain'.

## hunger
hunger, intr. v. — ME. hungren, hingren, fr. ОЙ
hyngran; influenced in form by the noun. Cp.
OS. gi-hungrean, ON. hungra, OFris. hungeria,
OHG. hungerdn, hungiren, Goth, huggrjan, 'to
hunger', and see hunger, n.

## hungry
hungry, adj. — ME., fr. OE. hungrig, fr. hunger,
'hunger'. See hunger, п., and -y (representing
OE. -ig).
Derivatives: hungri-ly, adv., hungri-ness, n.

## hunk
hunk, п., a large lump (esp. of bread) — Cp.
Flem. hunke, which is prob. rel. to Du. homp,
'lump, chunk'. See hnmp and cp. hunk.

## hunker
hunker, intr. v., to squat, crouch (dial., esp.
Scot.) — Perh. of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. hoka,
hokra, "to crouch, squat', and see huckster.

## hunks
hunks, п., a niggard, miser. — Of uncertain
origin.

## hunt
hunt, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hunten, fr. OE. hun-
tian, in gradational relationship to OE. hentan,
'to try to seize, to attack, seize', Goth, -hinpan
(used only in compounds), 'to seize'. See haud
and cp. hent, hint.
Derivatives: hunt, п., hunt-er, п., hunt-ing, adj.
and п., huntress (q.v.)

## huntress
huntress, n. — Formed fr. hunter with suff. -ess.

## huppah
huppah, п., the bridal canopy (Jewish religion) —
Heb. huppa", 'canopy', orig. 'bridal chamber',
lit. 'that which encloses', from the stem of ha-
phdph, 'he enclosed, surrounded, covered', 'vhich
is rel. to Arab, haffa, 'he surrounded', hifaf
'side or border of something' (lit. 'that which
surrounds').

## hurdle
hurdle, n. — ME. hirdel, hurdel, fr. OE. hyrdel,
rel. to Du. horde, OHG. hurd, MHG. hurt,
hiirde, G. Hiirde, 'hurdle, fold pen', and to
ON. hurd, Goth, hatirds, 'door' (orig. 'door of
wickerwork'), and cogn. with L. cratis, 'hurdle,
wickerwork', Gk. κάρταλος, 'a kind of basket',
κύρτος, κύρτη, κυρτία, 'wickerwork', κροτώνη,
'excrescence on trees', OPruss. corto,
'enclosure', Mir. ceirtle, 'clew', OI. krnalti, 'spins',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:384 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 357 | HYDRA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:384 COLUMN:1 -->
tyati, 'binds'. All these words derive fr. I.-E.
base *qerat-, "qert-, 'to twist together, we?ve,
plait'. See crate and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also grate, 'frame', griddle, hoarding.
Derivatives: hurdle, tr. and intr. v., hurdl-er, n.

## hurds
hurds, also hards, n. pi., refuse of flax or hemp. —
ME. herdes, fr. OE. heordan (pi.), rel. to OE.
-heord (only in compounds), ON. haddr, 'hair
on a woman's head', Du., OFris., MLG., MDu.
hide, Du., G. hede, 'hurds', fr. I.-E. base *qes-,
'to scrape, scratch, comb', whence also Gk.
κέσκεον (for *κέσ-κεσ-ον), Russ. ieska, Czech
pa-fes, 'tow, oakum', OSlav. ieSg, iesati, 'to
comb'.

## hurdy-gurdy
hurdy-gurdy, п., an obsolete musical instrument.
— Of imitative origin.

## hurl
hurl, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hurlen, horlen, hour-
len, prob. an -/-enlargement of the Teut.
imitative base *hurr-. Cp. LG. hurreln, 'to toss',
and see hurry. Cp. also hurly-burly.
Derivatives: hurl, п., hurl-er, п., hurley (q.v.)

## hurley
hurley,п., ι) game of hurling; 2) stick used in the
game. — Formed fr. hurl with suff. -ey.

## hurly
hurly, п., uproar, tumult. — Back formation fr.
hurly-burly.

## hurly-burly
hurly-burly, п., turmoil; uproar. — From earlier
hurling and burling, which was formed through
reduplication fr. hurling, verbal noun of hurl,
used in the now obsol. sense 'commotion*.

## hurrah
hurrah, interj. — Imitative. Cp. Dan., Swed.,
Norw., G. hurra, Du. hoera. Cp. also huzza.
Derivative: hurrah, n. and v.

## hurricane
hurricane, n. — Sp. huracan,· fr. Taino hurakan,
fr. Maya hunraken, 'Charles's Wain', lit. 'ог.г-
legged (giant)'. Since the dangerous cyclonic
storms usually rose in the sign of Charles's
Wain, Maya hunraken became identical with
'evil spirit', and finally obtained the meaning
of hurricane. F. ouragan. It. uragano, Du. or-
kaan (whence G. Orkari), 'hurricane', are all
traceable to Taino hurakan. E. hurricane (fr. Sp.
huracan) was influenced in form by hurry.

## hurry
hurry, tr. and intr. v. — Formed from the Teut.
imitative base *hurr-, 'to move with haste',
whence also OSwed. hurra, 'to whirl round',
dial. Swed. hurr, 'haste, hurry', MHG. hurren,
'to move with haste'. Cp. hurl. Cp. also flurry.
Derivatives: hurry, п., hurri-ed, adj., hurri-ed-ly,
adv., hurri-ed-ness, n.

## hurry-scurry
hurry-scurry, hurry-skurry, п., intr., v., and adv.
— Compounded of hurry and scurry.

## hurst
hurst, п., wood, copse (used esp. in Place-
Names). — ME. hurst, fr. OE. hyrsl, 'wood,
copse', rel. to OS. hurst, 'thicket', MDu. horst,
hurst, 'underwood', Du. horst, 'thicket; eyrie',
OHG. hurst, 'thicket', MHG. hurst, hiirste,
'bushes, shrubbery', G. Horst, 'thicket,
shrubbery; eyrie', dial. Norw. rust, 'thicket'.

## hurt
hurt, tr. and intr. v. — ME. hurten, hirten, 'to
push, dash; to injure', fr. OF. hurter (F. heur-
ter), 'to strike against', OF. hurter, orig. meant
'to butt or toss like a ram'. It derives fr. Fran-
kish *hurt, 'ram', which is rel. to ON. hrutr,
'ram'; see hart. OProvenc. urtar, It. urtare, 'to
strike against', are French loan words.
Derivatives: hurt, п., hurter (q.v.), hurt-ful, adj.,
hurt-ful-ly, adv., hurt-ful-ness, n.

## hurter
hurter, п., one who, or that which, hurts. —
Formed from the verb hurt with the agential
suff. -er.

## hurter
hurter, п., shoulder on the axle of a wheel. —
OF. hurtoir, fr. hurter. See hurt and agential
suff. -er.

## hurtle
hurtle, intr. and tr. v. — ME. hurtlen, freq. of
hurten. See hurt and freq. suff. -le.
Derivative: hurtle, n.

## hurtleberry
hurtleberry, n. — See whortleberry.

## husband
husband, n. — ME. husbonde, 'master of a house,
husband', fr. OE. husbonda, 'master of a house',
fr. ON. husbondi, 'householder; husband',
which is shortened fr. husbuandi, a word lit.
meaning 'dwelling in the house', compounded
of ON. hus, 'house', and buandi, 'dwelling', prop,
pres. part, of bua, 'to dwell'. See house and
bond, 'serf.
Derivatives: husband, tr. v., husband-age, п.,
husband-er, п., husband-less, adj., husband-ly,
adj. and adv., husband-li-ness, п., husband-ry, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:384 COLUMN:2 -->

## hush
hush, tr. and intr. v. — Back formation from the
obsolete adj. husht (fr. ME. husht), a word of
imitative origin, which, however, was regarded
as the past participle of a verb (i.e. husht was
misdivided into hush-t and identified with
hushed, whence arose the verb hush). Cp. whisht,
whist, interj., and hist.
Derivatives: hush, n. and interj., hush-ing-ly, adv.

## hushaby
hushaby, intr. v., imper. — Prob. a blend of nosh
and lullaby.

## husk
husk, n. — Late ME. huske, it. MDu. huuskijn,
huusken, 'little house; husk of fruit', dimin. of
huus, 'house'. See house and -kin.
Derivatives: husk, tr. v., husk-ed, adj., husk-er,
п., husky (q.v.)

## husky
husky, adj., 1) abounding in, or resembling,
husks; 2) dry as husks; dry in the throat, hoarse.
— Formed fr. husk with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: husk-i-ly, adv., husk-i-ness, n.

## Husky
Husky, п., ι) an Eskimo; 2) an Eskimo dog;
3) the Eskimo language. — Prob. corruption
of Esky, a slang abbreviation of Eskimo.

## huso
huso, also huse, п., the great sturgeon. — ML.,
fr. OHG. huso (MHG. huse, husen, G. Hausen),
which is rel. to ON. hauss, 'skull, cranium'
(whence dial. Norw. huse, 'skull of fish'); fr.
I.-E. base *(s)qeu-, 'to covert hide'. See sky and
cp. hansen. Cp. also the first element in
isinglass.

## hussar
hussar, n. — G. Husar, fr. Hung, huszar, fr.
Serbo-Croatian gusar, husar, 'pirate, handit',
fr. It. corsaro, 'pirate', lit. 'runner', fr. ML. cur-
sarius, fr. L. cursus, 'a running, course, voyage'.
See corsair.

## hussif
hussif, n. — Contraction of ME. houswif. See
housewife.

## Hussite
Hussite, п., a follower of John Huss, the
Bohemian reformer (burnt in 1415). — For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hussy
hussy, n. — Contracted fr. housewife (q.v.)

## busting
busting, п., usually in the pi. hustings, a court
held in London; a platform. — OE. busting, fr.
ON. husping, lit. 'house assembly', fr. hus,
'house, and ping, 'thing; assembly'. See house
and thing, 'assembly'.

## hustie
hustie, tr. and intr. v. — Metathesized fr. Du.
hutselen, freq. of hutsen, 'to shake', which is
prob. of imitative origin. Cp. 2nd rustle, 'to act
energetically'.
Derivatives: hustle, п., hustle-ment, п.,
hustler, n.

## hut
hut, n. — F. hutte, fr. MHG. hutte or fr. OHG.
hutta [OS. hutta, Dan. hytte, Swed. hytta, Fris.,
MLG., MDu. hutte (Du. hut) and Sp. huta are
borrowed fr. HG.], which is rel. to OE. hydan,
'to hide'. See hide, 'to conceal', and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also cuddy, 'cabin'.
Derivative: hut, tr. and intr. v.

## hutch
hutch, п., ι) a chest or box for storage; 2) a coop
or case for small animals; 3) a hut, hovel; 4) a
mining trough; 5) a truck; 6) a measure. —
ME. huche, fr. OF. (= F.) huche, 'bin, kneading
trough', fr. ML. hutica, which is of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: hutch, tr. v.

## hntchinsunite
hntchinsunite, п., sulfarsenite of thallium, copper,
silver, etc. (mineral.) — Named after the
English mineralogist Arthur Hutchinson (1866-1937).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## hutment
hutment, п., ι) housing in huts; 2) a camp of
huts. — A hybrid coined fr. hut and -ment, a
suff. of French-Latin origin.

## huzoor
huzoor, п., a respectful title of address used by
natives (India). — Arab, hudar (pronounced in
India #«zffr), 'presence', prop, infin. of hadara,
'he was present'.

## huzza
huzza, interj. (archaic). — Of imitative origin.
Cp. G. hussa and E. hurrah.
Derivatives: huzza, intr. and tr, v. and n.

## hyacinth
hyacinth, п., ι) a fabulous flower supposed to
have sprung from the blood of Hyacinthus
(Greek mythol.); whence 2) among the ancients,
a precious stone of blue color; now, a red or
brownish variety of zircon. — F. hyacinthe, fr.
L. hyacinthus, a kind of flower, the jacinth', fr.
Gk. υάκινθος, 'wild hyacinth, bluebell', fr.
earlier νάκινθος, a pre-Hellenic word. Cp. Hya-
ciathus. Cp. also jacinth, Vacciaium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:384 COLUMN:3 -->

## hyacinthine
hyacinthine, adj., resembling the hyacinth in
color. — L. hyacinthinus, fr. Gk. ύακίνθινος,
fr. υάκινθος. See hyacinth and -ine (representing
Gk. -ϊνος).

## Hyacinthus
Hyacinthus, п., a beautiful youth, beloved and
slain by Apollo (Greek mythology). — L.
Hyacinthus, fr. Gk. 'Τάκινθος. See hyacinth.

## Hyacinthus
Hyacinthus, п., a genus of plants of the lily family,
the hyacinth (bot.) — ModL., fr. hyacinthus.
See hyaciath.

## Hyades
Hyades, n. pi., a group of stars near the Pleiades
(astron.) — L. Hyades, fr. Gk. 'Τάδες, lit. 'the
rain-bringers', fr. βειν, 'to rain' (see hyeto-); so
called because the wet weather begins when
they set.

## Hyaena
Hyaena, п., the typical genus of the hyena family.
— L. hyaena. See hyena.

## hyal-
hyal-, form of hyalo- before a vowel.

## byalin
byalin, n. — See hyaline, n.

## hyaline
hyaline, adj., glassy; transparent. — L. hyalinus,
fr. Gk. υάλινος, 'glassy', fr. ύαλος, 'alabaster,
crystal, amber', prop, 'a transparent stone', later
'glass', which prob. stands for-*sualo-, Cp. L.
sudli-ternicum, 'a kind of reddish amber', which,
according to Pliny 37, 33, is of Scythian, i.e.
North European, origin. See Boisacq, DELG.,
p. 996, s.v. ύαλος, and Walde-Hofmann, LEW,
II, 611, s.v. sualiternicum. For the ending see
suff. -ine (representing Gk. -ϊνος).

## hyaline
hyaline, п., ι) something glassy, as the smooth
sea or the clear sky; 2) (in this sense spelled also
hyalin) a substance forming the walls of hydatid
cysts. — See hyaline, adj.

## hyalite
hyalite, п., a colorless variety of opal (mineral.)
— G. Hyalit, coined by the German geologist
and mineralogist Abraham Gottlob Werner
(1750-1817) in 1794 fr. Gk. ϋαλος, 'glass', and
suff. -it (representing Gk. -f-της). See hyaline,
adj., and subst. suff. -ite.

## hyalitis
hyalitis, п., inflammation of the vitreous humor
of the eye (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. Gk.
δαλος (see hyaline, adj.), with suff. -itis.

## hyalo-
hyalo-, before a vowel hyal-, combining form
meaning 'glassy, transparent'. — Gk. ύαλο-,
ύαλ-, fr. ύαλος, 'glass'. See hyaline, adj.

## hyaloid
hyaloid, adj., glassy, transparent; п., the hyaloid
membrane (anat.) — Gk. υαλοειδής,
'resembling glass, glassy, transparent', compounded
of ύαλος, 'crystal, glass', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See hyaline, adj.,«and
-oid.

## Hybanthus
Hybanthus, п., a genus of plants, the green violet
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. όβός,
'humpbacked', which is of uncertain origin, and
άνθος, 'flower' (see anther); so called in allusion
to the dorsal gibbosity.

## hybrid
hybrid, п., ι) a mongrel; anything of mixed
origin; 2) in linguistics, a word compounded of
elements from different languages, as sociology.
— L. hybrida, hibrida, 'offspring of a tame sow
and a wild boar, mongrel', fr. Gk. *ύβρίς, gen.
"ύβρίδος, which is prob. of the same origin as
L. iber, 'mule' [cp. ίβηρ, rendered by Hesychius
as χερσαϊον τι θηρίον ('a land animal')], but
was assimilated in Greek to ύβρις, 'wanton
violence, insolence'. Cp. "ΐβρις as the name of
a dog (Xenophon, Cynegeticus 7,5). Gk. *ύβρίς
in the above sense is not identical with ύβρις,
a night bird of prey. See Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., I, 665-666 s.v. hybrida.
Derivatives: hybrid, adj., hybrid-ism, п.,
hybridist, п., hybridize (q.v.)

## hybridize
hybridize, tr. and intr. v., to cause to produce
hybrids. — Formed from prec. word with suff.
-ize.
Derivatives: hybridiz-able, adj., hybridiz-ation,
п., hybridiz-er, n.

## hydat-
hydat-, form of hydato- before a vowel.

## hydatid
hydatid, п., a cyst or sac in the body of man or

## animals
animals, containing a watery fluid (med. and
zool.) — Gk. ϋδατίς, gen. ΰδατίδος, 'a watery

## vesicle'
vesicle', fr. ύδωρ, gen. βδατος, 'water'. See
hydro- and -id.

## hydato-
hydato-, before a vowel hydat-, combining form
meaning 'water'. — Gk. ύδατο-, ΰδατ-, fr. ύδωρ,

-αινα, fr. 3ς, gen. ύός, 'swine'; see sow, 'female

## hyeto-
hyeto-, before a vowel hyet-, combining form

flow'. Cp. Hyades. Cp. also soma, 'a plant',
sura, 'fermented sap of plants', and the second
element in Dialister. For derivatives of bases
*seu-q-, *seu-g-, 'to suck; sap', enlargements of

## hygiene
hygiene, п., the science of health. — F. hygiene,
fr. Gk. ύγιεινόν, neut. of υγιεινός, 'pertaining
to health, healthful', but used by Aristotle also
as a noun in the' sense of 'health', fr. υγιής,
'healthy', which stands for *su-g"iyes and lit.
means 'living well', fr. I.-E. "su- (Gk. ύ-), 'well',
whence also OI. su-, OPers. hu, Olr. su-, so-,
'well' (cp. sundari), and *gwiye~s, 'living',
enlargement of *gai-, 'to live', whence also Gk. βίος,
'life'. See bio- and cp. words there referred to.
L. vegire, 'to be lively, vigorous, to thrive,
flourish', vegltus, 'lively, vigorous', are not
cognate with Gk. υγιής. As a formative element,
ύ- was replaced later by εΰ- (see ей-).
Derivatives: hygien-ic, adj., hygien-ic-al-ly, adv.,
hygien-ics, п., hygien-ist, n.

## Hyksos
Hyksos, n. pi., a dynasty of Egyptian Kings
called the Shepherd Kings.—Gk. 'ϊκσώς,
'shepherd kings', fr. Egypt. Hiq shasu, 'ruler of
nomads'.

## hyl-
hyl-, form of hylo- before a vowel.

## Hyia
Hyia, п., a genus of amphibians, the tree frog
or tree toad (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. 6λη,
'wood, forest'. See hyle.

## Hylas
Hylas, п., a beautiful youth, companion of
Hercules (Greek mythol.) — L. Hylas, fr. Gk. "Τλϊς,
prob. meaning 'of the woods', fr. Gk. δλγ]. See
hyle.

## hyle
hyle, п., matter, substance. — Gk. 6λη, 'wood,
forest, material, matter', of uncertain origin. Cp.
Hyla, Hylas, hylic, -yl, -ethyl, methylene, ylem.

## hylic
hylic, adj., material, corporeal (philos.) — ML.
hylicus, fr. Gk. υλικός, 'pertaining to matter,
material', fr. δλγ]. See prec. word and -ic.

## hylicism
hylicism, п., materialism. — See hylic and -ism.

## hylicist
hylicist, п., a materialist. — See hylic and -ist.

## hylo-
hylo-, before a vowel hyl-, combining form
meaning 1) wood, forest; 2) matter. — Gk. υλο-,
δλ-, fr. δλγ). See hyle.

## Hylobates
Hylobates, п., the genus of the gibbons (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. ΰλοβάτης, 'wood walker', which
is compounded of 6λη, 'wood' (see hylo-), and
βάτης, 'treading on', from the stem of βαίνειν,
'to go, walk'. See -bates.

## hylophagous
hylophagous, adj., eating wood (zool.) — Gk.
δλοιράγος, compounded of δλη, 'wood' (see
hylo-), and -φάγος, 'eater of, from the stem of
φαγεϊν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

## hylotheism
hylotheism, n„ the doctrine that the material
universe is God. — Compounded of hylo- and
theism, 'belief in a personal God'.

## hylozoic
hylozoic, adj.» pertaining to hylozoism. — See
next word and -ic.

## hylozoism
hylozoism, п., the doctrine that all life is derived
from matter. — Compounded of hylo-, Gk. ζωή,
'life' (see zoo-) and suff. -ism.

## hylozoist
hylozoist, п., a believer in hylozoism. — See prec,
word and -ist.
Derivatives: hylozoist-ic, adj., hylozoist-ic-al-ly.
adv.

## hymen
hymen, п., the virginal membrane. — Gk. ΰμήν,
'skin, membrane', prob. fr. I.-E. "syu-men, lit.
'tie', hence cogn. with OI. syaman-, 'tie, band',
syutah, 'sewed', L. sua, suere, 'to sew*, fr. I.-E.
•base *syu, *su-, "siw, 'to sow'; see sew and cp.
iuture, surra. The word hymen orig. denoted
any membrane. In its present specific meaning
it was first used by Vesalius in 1550. Cp. hymn.
Derivative: hymen-al, adj., pertaining to the
hymen.
Hymen; п., the god of marriage in Greek
mythology. — L. Hymen, fr. Gk. 'ϊμήν, fr. 'Τμήν ώ,
'ϊμέναι' ώ, etc., refrain of the song sung at the
marriages of the ancient Greeks. Cp. next word
and hymn.

## hymen-
hymen-, form of hymeno- before a vowel.

## hymeneal
hymeneal, adj., pertaining to marriage.—Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. hymenaeus, fr. Gk.
ϋμέναιος, 'wedding or bridal song', fr. 'Τμέ-
ναιος,βη enlarged form of 'ϊμήν, the god Hymen.
See prec. word.

## hymeno-
hymeno-, before a vowel hymen-, combining form
meaning 'membrane'. — Gk. ΰμενο-, ύμεν-, fr.
ΰμήν, gen. ΰμένος, 'membrane'. See hymen,
'membrane'.

## Hymenocallis
Hymenocallis, п., a genus of plants of the ama-
ryllis family (bol.) — ModL., compounded of
Gk. ΰμήν, gen. ΰμένος, 'membrane' and κάλλος,
'beauty'. See hymen, 'membrane', and calo- and
cp. the second element in Hemerocallis.

## Hymenophyllaceae
Hymenophyllaceae, n. pi., the filmy fern family
(bol.) — ModL., formed fr. Hymenophylluin
with suff. -aceae.

## hymenophyllaceoiis
hymenophyllaceoiis, adj. — See prec. word and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:387 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HYMENOPHYLLUM | 360 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:387 COLUMN:1 -->
-aceous.

## Hymenophyllum
Hymenophyllum, п., a genus of ferns (.hot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. ύμήν, gen. ύμένος,
'membrane' and φύλλον, 'leaf. See hymen,
'membrane', and phyllo-.

## Hymenoptera
Hymenoptera, п., the highest order of insects (en-
tomol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ύμενόπτερος,
'membrane-winged', which is compounded of ύμήν,
gen. ύμένος, 'membrane', and πτερόν, 'wing*.
See hymen, 'membrane', and ptero-.

## hymenopterons
hymenopterons, adj., pertaining to the
Hymenoptera. — Gk. ύμενόπτερος, 'membrane-
winged'. See prec. word. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## hymn
hymn, n. — ME. ymne, fr. OF. ymne (F. hymne),
fr. L. hymnus, fr. Gk. Αμνός, 'a song in praise
of gods or heroes', orig. 'a wedding song', and
prob. rel. to 'ϊμήν, 'the god of marriage'. See
Hymen and cp. Polyhymnia.
Derivatives: hymn, tr. and intr. v., hymn-al, adj.,
and п., hymn-ic, adj., hymn-ist, n.

## hymnary
hymnary, п., a hymnal. — ML. hymnarium, fr. L.
hymnus. See prec. word and subst. suff. -ary.

## hymnody
hymnody, п., ι) singing of hymns; 2) hymns
collectively. — Gk. ύμνωδίά, 'singing of hymns',
fr. υμνωδός, 'singing hymns', which is
compounded of ϋμνος, 'hymn', and ώδή, 'song'. See
hymn and ode.
Derivative: hymnod-ist, n.

## hymnographer
hymnographer, п., ι) a writer of hymns; 2) one
who writes about hymns. — Formed with
agential suff. -er fr. Gk. υμνογράφος, 'composer
of hymns', which is compounded of ΰμνος,
'hymn', and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
hymn and -graph.

## hymnography
hymnography, п., ι) composition of hymns;
writing about hymns. — See prec. word and
-graphy.

## hymnology
hymnology, п., ι) the study of hymns; 2) the
composition of hymns; 3) hymns collectively. —
Gk. υμνολογία, 'the singing of hymns',
compounded of Gk. ΰμνος, 'hymn' (see hymno-),
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in
a certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: hymnolog-ic, hymnotog-ic-al, adjs.,
hymnolog-ist, n.

## hyo-
hyo-, combining form denoting the hyoid bone
(anat.) — Fr. Gk. ύο-, short for ύοειδής. See
hyoid.

## hyoid
hyoid, adj., designating a bone at the base of the
tongue (anat. and zool.) — F. hyolde, fr. Gk.
ύοειδής, 'shaped like the Greek letter X', which
stands for ύ-οειδής and is compounded of the
letter ΐ and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'; see -oid. The letter was called later и
psilon (lit. 'mere or simple y'). See ypsilon.
Derivative: hyoid, п., the hyoid bone.

## hyoscine
hyoscine, hyoscin, п., a poisonous alkaloid (chem.)
— See Hyoscyamus and chem. suff. -in(e).

## Hyoscyamus
Hyoscyamus, п., a genus of plants, the henbane
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ύοσκύαμας, 'henbane',
compounded of ΰς, gen. ύός, 'hog, pig', which
is cogn. with L. sus (see sow, 'female pig'), and
of κύαμος, 'bean', a word of foreign origin. The
name prop.'means 'poisonous to swine'. Cp.
hyoscine.

## hyp-
hyp-, form of hypo- before a vowel.

## hypaethral
hypaethral, hypethrai, adj., open to the sky (ar-
chit.) — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. hypae-
thrus, fr. Gk. ύπαιθρος, 'under the open sky',
which is formed fr. ύπό (see hypo) and αίθήρ,
'sky, ether'. See ether,

## hvpallage
hvpallage, п., a figure of speech which consists
in the reversion of the syntactic relation between
two words (rhet.) — L., fr. Gk. ύπαλλαγή,
'interchange, exchange, substitute', from the stem of
ύπαλλάσσειν, 'to exchange', which is formed fr.
ύπό (see hypo-), and άλλος, 'other'. See else and
cp. alio-, alias. Cp. also diallage, allagite.

## hyper-
hyper-, pref. of Greek origin, generally equivalent
to super- and over-. It usually denotes excess;
abnormal excess (in terms of medicine);
abnormally great power' of sensation (in terms of
physiology and pathology); the highest in a
series of compounds (chem.) Hyper- is the
opposite of hypo-. — Gk. ύττερ-, fr. υπέρ, 'over,
above, beyond', cogn. with OI. updri, L. super,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:387 COLUMN:2 -->
'over, above, beyond', fr. I.-E. base *uper-,
"uperi-, 'over, above, beyond,' which is prop, a
comparative from base- *upo-, 'from below;
turning upward, upward; up, over, beyond',
whence also Gk. ύπό, 'under'. See over and cp.
Hyperion, hypo-. Cp. also super-.

## hyperacusis
hyperacusis, п., an abnormally acute sense of
hearing (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. hyper-
and Gk. άκουσις, 'a hearing', fr. ακούει (for
*άκούσιειν), 'to hear'. See acoustic and cp.
words there referred to.

## hyperalgesia
hyperalgesia, hyperalgesis, п., an abnormally
excessive sensitiveness to pain. — Medical L.,
formed fr. hyper- and Gk. όίλγησις, 'sense of
pain', fr. άλγεΐν, 'to feel pain'. See -algia.
Derivative: hyperalges-ic, adj.

## hyperbatic
hyperbatic, adj., pertaining to hyperbaton. — Gk.
υπερβατικός, fr. ύπέρβατον. See hyperbaton and
-ic.

## hyperbaton
hyperbaton, п., an inversion of the natural order
of words for.ihe sake of emphasis (rhet.) — L.,
fr. Gk. ύπέρβατον, neut. of ύπέρβατος,
'transposed', verbal adj. of ύπερβαίνειν, 'to go over',
which is formed fr. υπέρ (see hyper-) and
βαίνει, 'to go'. See base, n.

## hyperbola
hyperbola, п., one of the three conic sections
(geom.) — ModL., fr. Gk. υπερβολή, 'a
throwing beyond, overshooting; excess', fr. ύπερ-
βάλλειν, 'to throw over or beyond, overshoot;
to exceed', fr. υπέρ (see hyper-) and βαλλειν,
'to throw, shoot'; see ballistic. The
Pythagoreans used the word υπερβολή if the base of a
figure, that was to be constructed so that it
should be equal in area to a given figure of
different shape, 'exceeded' the base of the original
figure. Apollonius of Perga, 'the Great
Geometer', who lived in the 3rd cent. B.C.E.,
applied the term υπερβολή for the first time to
denote the hyperbola (in his Conica, 1, 12), in
reference to the circumstance that the square
on the ordinate is equal to a rectangle whose
height is equal to the abscissa, applied to the
parameter, but overlapping (lit. 'exceeding') it;
see parabola and cp. ellipse.

## hyperbole
hyperbole, п., exaggeration (rhet.) — L., fr. Gk.
υπερβολή, 'excess, exaggeration'. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: hyperbol-ism, п., hyperbol-ist, п.,
hyperbol-ize, tr. and intr. v.

## hyperbolic
hyperbolic, hyperbolical, adj. — L. hyperbolicus
fr. Gk. υπερβολικός, 'excessive', fr. υπερβολή.
See prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: hyperbolic-al-ly, adv.

## Hyperborean
Hyperborean, п., a fabulous people living beyond
the north'wind (Greek mythol.) — Late L. hyper-
boreanus, fr. L. hyperboreus, fr. Gk. ύπερβόρεος,
'pertaining to the region far north', fr. υπέρ,
'over, beyond' (see hyper-) and βορέας, 'north
wind'. See Boreas.

## hypercatalectic
hypercatalectic, adj., having an additional
syllable at the end of the verse (pros.) — Late L.
hypercatalicticus, fr. Gk. ύπερκατάληκτος, 'left
off beyond', which is formed fr. υπέρ (see
hyper-), and καταλήγειν, 'to leave off, stop'. See
catalectic.

## hypercritic
hypercritic, n. —· Compounded of hyper- and
critic.
Derivatives: hypercritical, adj., hypercritic-al-
ly, adv., hypercritic-ism, п., hypercritic-ize, tr.
and intr. v.

## hyperdimensional
hyperdimensional, adj., pertaining to a space of
more than three dimensions. — A hybrid coined
fr. Gk. υπέρ, 'over, beyond', L. dimensio,
'measuring' and L. suff. -alis; see hyper-, dimension
and adj. suff. -al. The correct form would be
superdimensional, in which both elements and
the suff. are of the same (i.e. Latin) origin.

## hyperemia
hyperemia, hyperaemia, п., increase of blood in
any part (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. hyper-
and Gk. αίμα, 'blood'. See hemal and -ia.

## Hypericaceae
Hypericaceae, n. pi., the St-John's-wort family
(hot.) — ModL., formed fr. Hypericus with suff.
-aceae.

## hypericaceous
hypericaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Hypericum
Hypericum, п., a genus of plants, the St.-John's-
wort (bot.) — L., fr. Gk. ύπέρεικον, ύπέρικον,
'St.-John's-wort', which is compounded of ύπό,
'under, among' and έρείκη, έρίκη, 'heath,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:387 COLUMN:3 -->
heather'. See hypo- and Erica.

## Hyperion
Hyperion, п., a Titan, the son of Uranus and
Gaea; identified later with Apollo (Greek
mythol.) — L. Hyperion, fr. Gk. 'Τπερίων, lit. 'he
who looks from above', fr. υπέρ, 'above'. See
hyper-.

## hyperkinesia
hyperkinesia, hyperkinesis, п., abnormally
excessive muscular movement (med.) — ModL.,
formed fr. hyper- and κίνησις, 'movement', fr.
κΐνεϊν, 'to move'. See kinesis.

## hypermeter
hypermeter, п., a hypercatalectic line (pros.) —
Gk. υπέρμετρος, 'going beyond the meter,
beyond measure', fr. υπέρ, 'over, beyond', and
μέτρον, 'measure'. See hyper- and meter,
'poetical rhythm', and cp. next word.
Derivatives: hypermetr-ic, hypermetr-ic-al, adjs.

## hypermetropia
hypermetropia, п., farsightedness, the opposite of
myopia. — Medical L., compounded of Gk.
υπέρμετρος, 'beyond measure', and ώψ, gen.
ώπός, 'eye*. See prec, word and -opia.
Derivative: hypermetrop-ic, adj.

## hyperopia
hyperopia, п., hypermetropia (med.) — Medical
L., formed fr. hyper- and Gk. ώψ, gen. ώπός,
'eye'. See -opia and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: hyperop-ic, adj.

## hyperosmia
hyperosmia, п., an abnormally acute sense of
smell (psychol.) — ModL., formed fr. hyper-,
Gk. οσμή, 'smell, odor' (see osmium), and suff.
-ia. Cp. hyposmia.
Derivative: hyperosm-ic, adj.

## hyperostosis
hyperostosis, п., outgrowth of bony tissue (med.)
— Medical L., formed fr. hyper-, Gk. όστέον,
όστοΰν, 'bone' (see osteo-), and suff. -osis. Cp.
ostosis and words there referred to.

## hypersensitive
hypersensitive, adj., excessively sensitive (med.)
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. υπέρ (see hyper) and
sensitive, a word of Latin origin. The correct
form would be supersensitive, in which both
elements are of Latin origin.
Derivative: hypersensitive-ness, n.

## hyperspace
hyperspace, п., a space of more than three
dimensions. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. υπέρ (see
hyper-) and space (fr. L. spatium). The correct
form would be superspace, in which both
elements are of Latin origin.

## hypertrophy
hypertrophy, п., excessive development of an
organ (med.) —■ Medical L. hypertrophia, formed
fr. hyper- and Gk. -τροφία, fr. τροφή, 'food,
nourishment'. See trophic and cp. atrophy,
dystrophy.
Derivatives: hypertrophy, intr. v., hypertroph-ic,
hypertrophi-ed, adjs.

## hypha
hypha, п., one of the threadlike elements in the
shallus of a fungus (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
ύφή, 'web', which is rel. to ΰφος, 'web', ύφαίνειν,
'to weave', fr. I.-E. base *webh-, 'to weave',
whence also OE. wefan, 'to weave'. See weave.

## hypheme
hypheme, п., a hyphened compound word. —
Coined fr. hyph(en) and (phon)eme.

## hyphen
hyphen, п., a short line (-) joining parts of a word.
— L., fr. Gk. ύφέν, 'together, in one, as a single
word', fr. ύφ* ev, which stands for ύπό εν, lit.,
'under one'. For the first element see hypo-;
for Sv which is the neut. of εΤς, 'one', see heno-.
Derivatives: hyphen, tr. v., hyphen-ate, tr. v.,
adj. and п., hyphen-at-ed, adj., hyphen-ic, adj.,
hyphen-ism, п., hyphen-ize, tr. v., hyphen-iz-
ation, n.

## hypn-
hypn-, form of hypno- before a vowel.

## hypnagogic adj.
hypnagogic adj., inducing sleep. — Compounded
of hypn-, Gk. αγωγός, 'leading' (see -agogue),
and suff. -ic.

## hypnic
hypnic, adj., inducing sleep. — Gk. ύπνικός,
'pertaining to sleep', fr. ύπνος. See hypno- and -ic.
Derivative: hypnic, п., a soporific.

## hypno-
hypno-, before a vowel hypn-, combining form
meaning 'sleep'. — Gk. ύπνο-, ύπν-, fr. ΰπνος,
'sleep', which stands for *sup-no-s and is cogn.
with OI. svapnah, 'sleep, dream', L. somnus (for
*swepnos or *swopnos), 'sleep'. See somnolent and
cp. Hypnos.
hypYjoid,adj.,resemblinghypnosis.—Compounded of hypn- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## hypnology
hypnology, п., the study of (hypnotic) sleep. —
Coined by James Braid (1795-1861) fr. hypno-
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:388 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 361 | HYPSI- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:388 COLUMN:1 -->
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: hypnolog-ic, hypnolog-ic-al, adjs.,
hypnolog-ist, n.

## hypnophobia
hypnophobia, п., a morbid fear of falling asleep.
— Compounded of hypno- and Gk. -φοβίϊ,
'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## Hypnos
Hypnos, Hypnus, n„ the god of sleep in Greek
mythology; identified with Somnus. — Gk.
"ϊπνος, personification of δπνος, 'sleep'. See
hypno-.

## hypnosis
hypnosis, n. — ModL., coined fr. Gk. ύπνοΰν,
'to put to sleep', and stiff, -osis. Gk. ύπνοΰν
derives fr. ύπνος, 'sleep'. See hypno- and cp.
hypnotism.

## hypnotic
hypnotic, adj. — L. hypndticus, fr. Gk. υπνωτικός,
'inclined to sleep', fr. ύπνοΰν, 'to put to sleep',
fr. ύπνος, 'sleep'. See hypno- and -otic.
Derivatives: hypnotic, п., hypnotic-al-ly, adv.

## hypnotism
hypnotism, n. — Coined by James Braid of
Manchester (1795-1861) fr. hypnotic and suff.
-ism. Cp. hypnosis.

## hypnotist
hypnotist, n. — Coined fr. hypnotic and suff. -ist.
Derivative: hypnotist-ic, adj.

## hypnotize
hypnotize, tr. v. — Coined fr. hypnotic and suff.
-ize.
Derivatives: hypnotiz-ation, п., hypnotiz-er, n.

## hypo
hypo, п., sodium hyposulfite. — Short for hypo-
sulfite.

## hypo-
hypo-, before a vowel hyp-, suff. of Greek origin
generally equivalent to sub- and under-. It
unites the following meanings: under, below,
in a lower position; in a lesser degree;, slightly,
gradually, somewhat; secretly. In terms of
medicine it is used to denote an abnormal decrease;
in psychology it expresses a deficient power of
sensation; in chemistry it indicates the lowest of
a series of compounds. — Gk. ϋπο-, ϋπ-, fr. ϋπό,
'under, below, from below', cogn. with ΟΙ. ύρα,
'near, under, up to, on', L. sub (for *sup-),
'under'. See sub- and cp. hyper-, Cp. also hyphen,
hypsi-, anthypophora.

## hypocaust
hypocaust, п., space in the floor of a building in
an ancient Roman house filled with hot air
from the furnace. — L. hypocaustum, fr. Gk.
ύπόκαυστον, lit. 'burnt below', which is formed
fr. ϋπό (see hypo-) and neut. of καυστός, 'burnt',
verbal adj. of καί,ειν (for "κάί-ιειν), 'to burn'.
See caustic.

## Hypochaeris
Hypochaeris, п., a genus of plants, the cat's ear
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ύποχοιρίς, 'swine's
succory', which is formed fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and
χοίρος, 'young pig'. See -choerus.

## hypochondria
hypochondria, п., morbid depression of spirits,
melancholy (med.) — L. hypochondria, gen.
-drum, 'the soft part of the body from the ribs
to the groin, the abdomen', fr. Gk. υποχόνδρια,
of s.m., prop. neut. pi. of the adjective
υποχόνδριος, 'that which is below the cartilage (of
the breastbone)', formed fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and
χόνδρος, 'granule, gristle, cartilage'. See' grind,
gristle. The abdomen was thought to be the
seat of hypochondria, whence the name of this
morbid condition.

## hypochondriac
hypochondriac, adj., and n. — F. hypochondria-
que, fr. ML. hypochondriacus, fr. Gk. ύποχον-
δριακός, 'pertaining to the abdomen', fr.
υποχόνδρια. See prec. word.
Derivative: hypochondriac-al, adj.

## hypocoristic
hypocoristic, adj., pertaining to pet names;
endearing. .— Gk. υποκοριστικός, 'pertaining to a
pet name, diminutive', fr. ύποκορίζεσθαι, 'to call
by a pet name', lit. 'to use childish language',
formed fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and κορίζεσθαι, 'to
caress', fr. κόρος (for *κόρΓος), 'a child', which
derives fr. I.-E. base *ker-, 'to grow'. See create
and cp. Cora, Corinna.

## hypocrisy
hypocrisy, n. — ME. ipocrisie, fr. OF. ypocrisie,
fr. Eccles. L. hypocrisis, fr. Gk. ύπόκρισις, 'an
acting on the stage; hypocrisy', from the stem
of ύποκρίνεσθαι, 'to answer, pretend, play a
part', fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and κρίνεσθαι, 'to
dispute', middle voice of κρΐνειν, 'to judge'. F.
hypocrisie and E. hypocrisy have been
refashioned after the Latin form of the word. See
critic and cp. words there referred to.

## hypocrite
hypocrite, n. — ME. ipocrite, ypocrite, fr. OF.
ipocrite, ypocrite (F. hypocrite), fr. Eccles. L.
hypocrita, fr. Gk. υποκριτής, 'an actor,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:388 COLUMN:2 -->
pretender, hypocrite', fr. ύποκρίνεσθαι. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: hypocritic-al, adj., hypocritic-al-ly,
adv.

## hypoderma
hypoderma, п., a tissue of cells beneath the
epidermis (hot.) — Medical L., formed fr. hypo-
and Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma.

## hypodermic
hypodermic, adj., pertaining to the parts under
the skin. — See prec. word and -ic
Derivatives: hypodermic, п., a hypodermic
injection, hypodermic-al-ly, adv.

## hypodermis
hypodermis, п., the layer of tissue that lies
beneath the cuticle of arthropods (zool.) —
Medical L. See hypoderma.

## hypogastric
hypogastric, adj., pertaining to the lower part of
the abdomen (final.) — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. ύπογάστριος, 'pertaining to the lower
belly', fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and γαστήρ, gen.
γαστρός, 'belly'. See gastric and cp. epigastric,
mesogastric.

## hypogastrium
hypogastrium, п., the lower part of the abdomen
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. ϋπογίστριον, 'the
lower belly (from the navel downward)', prop,
neut. of the adjective ύπογάστριος, 'pertaining
to the lower belly', used as a noun. See prec.
word and cp. epigastrium, mesogastrium.

## hypogeal
hypogeal, hypogenn, adj., subterranean. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al, resp. -an, fr. Gk. γη,
'earth'. See geo-,

## hypogene
hypogene, adj., formed beneath the earth's
surface. — Formed fr. hypo- and -gene, Cp. epigene.

## hypogeous
hypogeous, adj., subterranean. — L. hypogeus,
fr. Gk. υπόγειος, 'underground, subterranean',
which is formed fr. ύπο- (see hypo-) and Gk.
γαία, γη, 'earth'. Ср. next word. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to Gk. -ας, see suff. -ous.

## hypogeum
hypogeum, hypogaeum, п., the underground part
of a building (ancient archil.) — L., fr. Gk.
υπόγειος, όπόγαιος, 'underground,
subterranean'. See prec. word.

## hypoglossitis
hypoglossitis, п., inflammation of parts under the
tongue (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. next
word with suff. -itis.

## hypoglossus
hypoglossus, п., the hypoglossal nerve (anat.) —
Medical L., lit. 'that which is under the tongue',
incorrect formation fr. hypo- and Gk. γλώσσα,
'tongue'; see gloss, 'interpretation'. The correct
form would have been hypoglotticus, fr. Gk.
γλωττικός, 'pertaining to the tongue', fr. γλώτ-
τα, γλώσσα, 'tongue*.
Derivative: hypogloss-al, adj.

## hypophosphate
hypophosphate, п., a salt of hypophosphoric acid
(chem.) — Formed fr. hypo- and phosphate.

## hypophosphlte
hypophosphlte, п., a salt of hypophosphorous
acid (chem.) — Formed fr. hypo- and phosphite.

## hypophosphoric
hypophosphoric, adj., pertaining to the acid
Н4Р2Об (chem.) — Formed fr. hypo- and
phosphoric.

## hypophosphorous
hypophosphorous, adj., pertaining to the acid
HjPOj (chem.) — Formed fr. hypo- and
phosphorous.

## hypophyge
hypophyge, п., a hollow molding, esp. beneath
Doric capitals (archil.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ϋπο-
φυγή, lit. 'refuge*, from the stem of ύποφεύγειν,
'to withdraw', lit. 'to flee from under', fr. δπό
(see hypo-) and φεύγειν, 'to flee', which is cogn.
with L. fugere, 'to flee'. See fugitive.

## hypophysis
hypophysis, п., 1) the pituitary body (anat.); 2) a
part of the embryo (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
ύπόφυσις, Offshoot, outgrowth', fr. ύπό (see
hypo-) and φύσις, 'nature, natural growth'. See
physio- and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: hypophysi-al, adj.

## hypopituitarism
hypopituitarism, п., diminished activity of the
pituitary body (med.) — Formed fr. hypo-,
pituitary and suff. -ism.

## Hypopitys
Hypopitys, п., a genus of parasitic plants of the
Indian-pipe family (bot.) — ModL., lit.
'(growing) under pine trees', fr. hypo- and Gk. πίτυς,
'pine tree'. See pituitary.

## hyposcope
hyposcope, п., a form of altiscope, attached to a
rifle or the like. — Formed fr. hypo- and Gk.
-σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See
-scope.

## hyposmia
hyposmia, п., a weakening of the sense of smell
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. hypo- and Gk.
οσμή, 'smell, odor'. See osmium and cp. hyper-
osmia.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:388 COLUMN:3 -->
hypostasis, п., substance, reality (philos.) — L„
fr. Gk. ύπόστασις, 'substance, subsistence,
underlying nature, essence', from the stem of
ύφίστασθαι, 'to stand under, subsist', which is
formed fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and ϊστασθαι, 'middle
voice of ίστάναι, 'to cause to stand'. See state
and cp. snbstance, subsistence,
hypostatic, hypostatical, adj., pertaining to a
hypostasis. — Gk. υποστατικός, fr. ύπόστασις.
See prec. word and static.
Derivatives: hypostatical-ly, adv., hypostat-ize,
tr. v., hypostat-iz-ation, n.

## hypostyle
hypostyle, adj., having pillars to support the roof
(archil.) — Gk. ύπόστϋλος, 'resting on pillars',
formed fr. ύπό (see hypo-) and στΰλος, 'pillar'.
See style, 'gnomon*.

## hyposnlute
hyposnlute, п., ι) a thiosulfate; 2) a salt of hypo-
sulfurous acid (chem.) — Formed fr. hypo-
and sulfite.

## hyposulfurous
hyposulfurous, adj., pertaining to or designating
a dibasic acid, H^O» (chem.) — Formed fr.
hypo- and sulfurous.

## hypotaxis
hypotaxis, п., dependence (esp. of clauses) (gram.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. ύπόταξις, 'subjection',
lit. 'a placing under', from the stem of ύπο-
τάσσειν, 'to place under', which is formed fr. ύπό
(see hypo-) and τάσσειν, 'to arrange, array,
post, place, appoint'. See taxis and cp.
parataxis.

## hypotenuse
hypotenuse, п., the side of a right-angled triangle
opposite the right angle. — F. hypotenuse, fr.
L. hypoteniisa, fr. Gk. ύποτείνουσα [short for
ή τήν όρ&ήν γωνίαν ύποτείνουσα πλευρά, 'the
side subtending (lit. 'stretching under') the
right angle'], fern, of ύποτείνων, pres. part, of
ύποτείνειν, 'to stretch under, subtend', fr. ύπό
(see hypo-) and τείνειν, 'to stretch', which is
cogn. with L. lendere, 'to stretch'. See tend, 'to
move in a certain direction*, and cp. words
there referred to.

## hypothec
hypothec, п., security given to a creditor over a
debtor's property without transfer of possession
or title (law). — F. hypothique, fr. Late L.
hypotheca, fr. Gk. υποθήκη, 'a deposit, pledge,
mortgage', from the stem of ύποτιθέναι, 'to put
under, lay down, pledge', which is formed fr.
ύπό (see hypo-) and τιθέναι, 'to put, place'.
See thesis.

## hypothecary
hypothecary, adj., pertaining to a hypothec. —
Late L. hypoihecarius, 'pertaining to a
hypothec', fr. hypotheca. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -ary.

## hypothecate
hypothecate, tr. v., to pledge as security without
transferring possession or title; to mortgage. —
ML. hypothicutus, pp. of hypothecSre, 'to
pledge', fr. Late L. hypotheca. See hypothec and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: hypothecation (q.v.), hypothecat-
or, n.

## hypothecation
hypothecation, n. — ML. hypothecated, gen. -onis,
fr. hypothecatus, pp. of hypothecare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## hypothesis
hypothesis, п., a supposition. — ModL., fr. Gk.
ύπόθεσις, 'foundation, supposition", lit. 'a
placing under', from the stem of ύποτιθέναι,
'to put under, lay down', fr. ϋπό (see hypo-) and
τι&έναι, 'to put, place'. See thesis.

## hypothesize
hypothesize, intr. and tr. v. — Formed from prec.
word with suff. -ize.

## hypothetical
hypothetical, hypothetic, adj. — L. hypotheticus,
fr. Gk. υποθετικός, 'hypothetical', fr. ύπόθετος,
verbal adj. of ϋποτιθέναι. See hypothesis and
-ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: hypothetical-ly, adv.

## Hypoxis
Hypoxis, п., a genus of plants, the star grass
(bot.) — ModL., coined fr. hyp- and Gk. άξύς,
'sharp' (see oxy-); so called in allusion to the
base of the capsule.

## hypsi-
hypsi-, before a vowel hyps-, combining form
meaning 'on high'. — Gk. ύψι-, ύψ-, from ΰψι,
'alcft. on high', which stands for ΰπ-σι, is rel.
to ΰψος (for ΰπ-σος), 'height', and cogn. with
L, sus (for *sup-s) in the expression susque deque,
'both up and down', and with Olr. as, Has (for
*oup-su-), 'above, over', uasal (for *oup-selo-),
'high, noble', OSlav. vysoku (for *up-soko-),
'high'. All these words are ult. cogn. with Gk.
ύπό,' under', L. sub, of s.m. See hypo- and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:389 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: HYPSO- | 362 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:389 COLUMN:1 -->
hypso-. Ср. also the second element in
duniwassal.

## hypso-
hypso-, combining form denoting height. — Gk.
ύψο-, from βψος, 'height'. See hypsi-.

## hypsography
hypsography, п., a scientific description of the
form of the earth's surface. — Compounded of
hypso- and Gk. -γραφίϊ, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graphy.
Derivatives: hypsograph-ic, hypsograph-ic-al,
adjs.

## hypsometer
hypsometer, п., an instrument for measuring
altitudes. — Compounded of hypso- and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## hypsometry
hypsometry, п., the measuring of altitudes. —
See prec. word and -merry.
Derivatives: hypsometr-ic, hypsometr-ic-al, adjs.,
hypsometr-ic-al-ly, adv., hypsometr-ist, a.

## hypsophobia
hypsophobia, п., a morbid fear of high places. —
Compounded of hypso- and Gk. -φοβίϊ, 'fear
of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## hypsophyil
hypsophyil, п., a leaf below the sphorophylls
(hot.) — ModL. hypsophyllum, lit. 'high leaf,
formed fr. hypso- and Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf. See
phyllo- and cp. cataphyll, sporophyll. ModL.
hypsophyllum is prop, a loan translation of G.
Hochblatt, fr. hoch, 'high', and Blatt, 'leaf.
Derivative: hypsophyll-ary, adj.

## Hymcoidea
Hymcoidea, n. pi., an order of ungulates (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. υρκξ, 'shrew
mouse' and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See next word and -oid.

## hyrax
hyrax, п., any animal of the genus Procavia. —
Gk. δρκξ, 'shrewmouse', for "surak-s, cogn.
with L. sorex (for *sworak-s), of s.m. See Sorex.

## hyson
hyson, п., a kind of China tea. — Chin, hsi-chun,
lit. 'blooming spring'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:389 COLUMN:2 -->

## hyssop
hyssop, п., name of a plant. — ME. ysope, fr. OF.
(= F.) hysope, hyssope, fr. L. hysopus, hyssopus,
fr. Gk. δσσωπος, an aromatic plant, fr. Heb.
izobh, 'hyssop', which is rel. to Akkad. zupu,
Syr. zupha, Arab, zafa, Ethiop. azobh, of s.m.

## Hyssopus
Hyssopus, п., a genus of plants of the mint family
(bot.) — L. See hyssop.

## hyster-
hyster-, form of hystero- before a vowel.

## hysterectomy
hysterectomy, п., excision of the uterus (surg.) —
Compounded of hyster- and Gk. -έκτομίϊ, 'a
cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting out,
excision'. See -ectomy.

## hysteresis
hysteresis, п., the lagging in the magnetic force
behind the magnetizing force (magnetism). —
Gk. ύστέρησις, 'shortcoming, deficiency', fr.
ϋστερεϊν, 'to be behind, come late, lag', fr.
ύστερον, 'later'. See hysteron proteron.

## hysteria
hysteria, n. — Medical L., fr. Gk. ύστέρϊ, 'womb',
which is rel. to ϋστρος (Hesychius), 'belly,
womb', and cogn. with Maced. δδερος
(Hesychius), of s.m., OI. udaram, 'belly', L. uterus,
'womb'; see uterus and -ia. Hysteric
disturbances, which most frequently occur in women,
were ascribed erroneously to the influence of
the womb and were for this reason called
hysteria, 'disease of the womb'.

## hysteric
hysteric, more frequently hysterical, adj. — L.
hystericus, fr. Gk. υστερικός, 'pertaining to the
womb', fr. ύστέρϊ. See prec. word and -ic, resp.
also -ai.
Derivatives: hysteric, п., hysterics, n. pi., hys-
teric-al-ly, adv.

## hysteritis
hysteritis, п., inflammation of the womb (med.)
— Medical L., formed with suff. -Mis fr. Gk.
υστέρα, 'womb'. See hysteria.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:389 COLUMN:3 -->

## hystero-
hystero-, before a vowel hyster-, combining form
denoting ι) the womb; 2) hysteria. — See
hysteria.

## hysteron proteron
hysteron proteron, a figure in which the order of
words, phrases, or clauses is reversed (rhet.) —
Late L., fr. Gk. ΰστερον, ττρότερον, 'the latter
(is put) as the former'. Gk. ΰστερον is neut.
of ύστερος, for I.-E. *ud-tero-s (whence also OI.
uttarah, 'the higher, upper, latter, later'), which
is formed fr. base *ud-, 'up, out, away', with corn-
par, suff. *-ter. See out and -ther and cp. the first
element in Hystrix. For the etymology of
proteron see protero-.

## hysteropexy
hysteropexy, п., the operation of fixing the uterus
to the wall of the abdomen (surg.) — Medical
L. hysteropexia, compounded of hystero- and
Gk. πηξις, 'a making firm, fastening', which
derives from the stem of πηγνύναι, 'to join,
make firm'. See -pexy.

## hysterotomy
hysterotomy, n. (surg.), 1) the Caesarian section;
2) the operation of cutting into the uterus. —
Compounded of hystero- and Gk. -ταμία, 'a
cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.

## Hystrix
Hystrix, п., a genus of porcupines (zool.) — L.,
fr. Gk. ΰστριξ, 'porcupine', which is of
uncertain origin. It is perh. compounded of ύσ-,
'upward, up to', fr. I.-E. *ud-, 'up' (whence also
Gk. δσ-τερος, 'the latter', see hysteron proteron),
and *ρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair' (see tricho-).
Accordingly Gk. ΰστριξ would lit. mean 'having the
hair turned upward'.

## Hystrix
Hystrix, п., a genus of plants, the bottle brush
grass (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ΰστριξ,
'porcupine' (see prec. word); so called in allusion to
the bristly spikes.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:390 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:390 COLUMN:1 -->

## I
I, pers. pron. — ME. ich, /, fr. OE. fc, rel. to OS.,
OFris., Du. ik, ON. ek, Norw. eg, Dan. Jeg,
Swed. jag, OHG. /A, MHG., G. ich, Goth, ik,
T, and cogn. with OI. ahdm, Avestic azem,
OPers. adam, Hitt. йк. Arm. es, Gk. έγώ, dial.
Gk. έγών, L. ego, VL. eo (whence It. io, Rum.
eu, OF. jou, F. ;e, OProven?., Catal., Port, eu,
Sp. jo), OSlav. azu, ,/αζιί, Russ., Pol., Czech,
Slovak ja, OLith. ei, Lith. as, Lett, ej, OPruss. as,
Т. Ср. ego, egoism, egotism.
1-, pref. representing in-, 'not', before gn in
words of Latin origin, as in ignore.

## -ia
-ia, suff. used to form [) names of countries;
2) names of diseases; 3) names of alkaloids;
4) names of flowers from the name of the
discoverer or introducer. — L. -ia, or Gk. -is,
usually forming abstract nouns of feminine
gender. L. -ia and Gk. -is are compounded of
a thematic or connective i, resp. 1, and the fern,
suff. -a, resp. -a.

## -ia
-ia, pi. suff. used to form names of classes and
orders in botany and zoology. — 1) L. -ia, pi.
suff. of nouns ending in the sing, in -ium or -e;
2) Gk. -l«, pi. suflf. of nouns ending in the sing,
in -tov. L. -ia and Gk. -l« are compounded of a
thematic or connective i, resp. 1, and the neut.
pi. suff. -a, resp. -a.
-■■I, suff. forming English adjectives from Latin
adjectives in -is or ius. — L. -/a/15 (neut. -iale)
which consists of a thematic or connective /' and
suff. -alts (see adj. suff. -al). Cp. e.g. E. celestial
formed fr. L. caelestk, 'heavenly', and E.
senatorial, formed fr. L. senatorius, etc.

## iamb
iamb, п., a metrical foot consisting of a short
syllable followed by a long one (pros.) — F.
iambe, fr. L. iambus, fr. Gk. ίαμβος, which is a
loan word of pre-Hellenic origin. See Frisk,
GEW., I, p. 704 s.v. ίαμβος. Ср. the second
element in choliamb, choriamb, galliambic. For
the form and meaning of the word ίαμβος ср.
διθύραμβος and θρίαμβος (see dithyramb,
triumph).

## iambic
iambic, adj., pertaining to, or made up of, iambs;
п., ι) an iamb; 2) an iambic. — F. tambique, fr.
L. iambicus, fr. Gk. Ιαμβικός, fr. ίαμβος. See
prec. word and -ic.

## iambns
iambns, п., an iamb. — L. iambus. See iamb.

## -ian
-ian, suff.; used to form adjectives from PN.'s
and—to a lesser degree—from common nouns.
— L. -ianus (directly, or through the medium
of F. -ten); it consists of the vowel / (which
may be thematic or connective) and suff. -anus.
See -an.

## Iapetus
Iapetus, п., one of the Titans, son of Uranus and
Ge, and father of Atlas, Prometheus, Epi-
metheus and Menoetius (Greek mythol.) — L.,
fr. Gk. Ίάττετος, which is perh. of Sem. origin
and rel. to Heb. Yepheth, name of the youngest
of the three sons of Noah; see Japheth. See
D.S. Margoliouth in Hastings, Dictionary of
the Bible, II, p. 549.

## -iasis
-iasis, suff., used to indicate 1) a process (as in
odontiasis); 1) a morbid condition (as in
elephantiasis). — Medical L., fr. Gk. -Ίασις,
formed from the aorist of verbs ending in -ιάω,
which often express bodily or mental disease.
Cp. e.g. λαρυγγιάω, Ί have a sore throat',
όδοντιάω, Ί have toothache'.

## iatric
iatric, also iatrieal, adj., medical. — Gk. ιατρικός,
'healing', fr. ιατρός, 'physician', fr. ίϊσθαι, 'to
heal', which prob. stands for 'ίσάιεσθαι and
is rel. to ίαίνειν (for *ίσάν£ειν), 'to refresh,
invigorate', fr. I.-E. base *eis-, 'to set in quick
motion', whence also Gk. ιερός, 'holy, sacred',
orig. 'filled with (divine) force', and prop,
identical with ιερός, 'strong, lively, active, quick,
swift'. See hiero- and -ic and cp. ire. Cp. also
Jasione, Jason, 'leader of the Argonauts', the
first element in Jatropha and the second element
in pediatric.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:390 COLUMN:2 -->
I

## -iatrics
-iatrics, combining form denoting 'treatment of
disease', as in geriatrics, gyniatrics. — Gk.
ιατρική (scil. τέχνη), 'surgery, medicine'. See
prec. word and -ics.

## iatro-
iatro-, combining form meaning 1) physician;
2) medicine. — Gk. ίϊτρο-, fr. ιατρός,
'physician'. See iatric.

## iatrology
iatrology, п., the study of medicine. —
Compounded of iatro- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## -iatry
-iatry, combining form meaning 'medical
treatment'. — F. -iatrie, fr. Gk. ιατρεία, 'healing,
medical treatment', fr. ιατρός, 'physician',
(whence also ίϊτρεύειν, 'to treat medically').
See iatric.

## Iberia
Iberia, п., the ancient name of the Spanish
peninsula. — L. Hiberia, Iberia, 'Spain', prop,
'country of the Hiberes or Iberes', fr. Gk.
"Ιβηρες, 'the Spaniards', also name of an ancient
Asiatic people near the Caucasus. Cp. next
word.
Derivatives: Iberi-an, adj. and n.

## lberis
lberis, п., candytuft. — L. (quoted by Pliny), fr.
Gk. ίβηρίς, 'pepperwort', lit. 'the Iberian plant',
fr. "Ιβηρες. See prec. word.

## ibex
ibex, п., the wild goat of the Alps. — L. ibex,
'a kind of goat, chamois', loan word fr. an
I.-E. language spoken in the Alps.

## ibidem
ibidem, adv., in the same place. — L., formed fr.
ibi, 'there', and the particle of identity -dem.
The adv. ibi is rel. to TJmbr. ife, 'there, thither',
and cogn. withOI. /-Ad, Avestic «5a, 'here', Gk.
ιθαγενής, 'native, lawfully begotten, legitimate'
(lit. 'here born'). All these words derive fr.
I.-E. *i-dha, *i-dhe, from the pronominal base
* i-; see idem and cp. the second element i n alibi;
cp. also ubiety. The particle -dem in ibidem
derives fr. I.-E. *di; see de- and cp. tandem.

## -ibility
-ibility, subst. suff. expressing ability, capacity,
fitness. — L. -tbilitas, forming nouns from
adjectives ending in -Ibilis. See -ible and -ity and
cp. -ability.

## ibis
ibis, п., a large wading bird. — L. ibis, fr. Gk.
Ιβις, fr. Egypt, hlb.

## -ible
-ible, adj. suff. expressing ability, capacity,
fitness. — L. -ibilis or -ibilis (either directly or
through the medium of F. -ible), compounded
of Γ (stem vowel of the 4th conjugation), resp. I
(stem vowel of the 3rd conjugation) and -bilis.
See -ble and cp. -able.

## -ic
-ic, adj. suff. meaning 'pertaining to; of the
nature of. It is still in use to form adjectives
1) from PN.'s (as in Slavonic, Napoleonic, etc.);
2) from nouns ending in -ist (see -istic). In
chemistry, suff. -ic is used to denote a higher valence
of the element indicated in the adjective than is
expressed by suff. -ous. Cp. nitric acid (HNO3
with nitrousec/rffHNOj). — 1)Gk. -ικός:either
directly, or through the medium of L. -icus, or
through the medium of F. -ique and L. -icus. —
2) L. -icus, a native suff. (as in civicus, classicus):
either directly (as in civic) or through the
medium of F. -ique (as in classic). Cp. subst. suff.
-ic and suff. -atic.

## -ic
-ic, subst. suff. used to form names of arts and
sciences (as music, logic, rhetoric). — Gk. -ική
(short for -ική τέχνη, 'the art of), fem. of-ικός.
•Ср. e.g. Ε. music, fr. Gk. μουσική (scii. τέχνη),
lit. 'musical art'. See adj. sun", -ic. Another way
of forming names of arts and sciences in Greek
was to use -ικ'ά, the neut. pi. ending of
adjectives in -ικός; see -ics.

## -ical
-ical, adj. suff. compounded of the suffixes -ic
and -al.

## Icarian
Icarian, adj., pertaining to Icarus. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. Icarius, fr. Gk. Ίκάριος, 'of
Icarus', fr. "Ικαρος. See next word.

## Icarus
Icarus, п., the son of Daedalus (Greek mythol.) —
L. Icarus, fr. Gk. "Ικαρος, 'Icarus', a name of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:390 COLUMN:3 -->
uncertain origin.

## ice
ice, n. — ME. is, fr. OE. is, rel. to ON. iss, OS.,
OFris., MLG., OHG., MHG. Is, Dan., Swed.
is, Du. jte, G. Eis. Outside Teut. cp. Avestic
isav-, 'frosty', аёха-, 'ice', Afghanic asai, 'frost'.
Cp. iceberg, icicle, Isold.
Derivatives: ice, adj. and tr. v., ic-ing, п., icy
(q.v.)

## -ice
-ice, suff. forming concrete and abstract nouns.
— ME. -ice, -ise, fr. OF. (F.) -ice fr. L. -ilium (as
precipice, fr. OF. precipice, fr. L. praecipitium;
hospice, fr. OF. hospice, fr. L. hospitium). Cp.
the next two suffixes and subst. suff. -ise.

## -ice
-ice, suff. forming nouns denoting dependence,
attachedness. — OF., F. -ice, fr. L. -icius, -itius (as
novice, fr. OF. novice, fr. L. novicius, novitius).

## -ice
-ice, suff. forming abstract nouns denoting
quality, condition or function. — OF., F. -ice, fr. L.
-ilia (as avarice, fr. OF. avarice, fr. L. avaritia).

## iceberg
iceberg, п., a floating mass of ice. — Fr. Du. ys-
berg (lit. 'mountain of ice'), with substitution
of E. ice for Du. ijs (see ice); cp. Dan. isbjerg,
Swed., Norw. isberg, G. Eisberg. For the
etymology of the second element of these words
see borough and cp. barrow, 'mound'.

## icebone
icebone, п., the aitchbone. — Rel. to OS., MLG.
isben, Dan. isben, MDu. isebeen, Du. ijsbeen,
OHG. ispein (G. Eisbeiri). The first element
in these compound words is borrowed fr. L.
ischia (pi.), fr. Gk. τα ίοχία, pi. of το ίσχίον,
'the hip joint'. See sciatic. For the second
element in icebone see bone.

## Icerya
Icerya, п., a genus of scale insects (eniomol.)
— ModL., of unknown origin.

## ichneumon
ichneumon, п., ι) the mongoose; 2) the
ichneumon fly. — L., fr. Gk. [χνεύμων, lit. 'tracker',
fr. Ιχνεύειν, 'to track, trace, hunt', fr. ϊχνος,
'track, footprint' (see ichao-); so called because
it digs up the eggs of the crocodile.

## ichnite
ichnite, п., a fossil footprint (paleontol). —
Formed with subst. suff. -He fr. Gk. Ιχνος,
'track, footprint'. See ichao-.

## ichno-
ichno-, combining form meaning 'track, trace,
footprint'. — Gk. Ιχνο-, fr. ίχνος, 'trace,
footprint', of uncertain origin. It derives perh. fr.
I.-E. *ei-gh, 'to go', whence also Gk. οϊχομαι,
Ί go away", οίχνέω, Ί go, I come', Arm. ijanem
(aor. 3rd person sing, ej), Ί go down, descend',
Lith. eiga, 'going, course', Olr. oegi, 'guest'.
I.-E. *ei-gh- is an enlarged form of base *ei-,
'to go', whence Gk. είμι, L. eo (for *eio), Ί go'.
See itinerate.

## ichaography
ichaography, п., the art of making ground plans.
— F. ichnographie, fr. Late L. ichnographia, fr.
Gk. Ιχνογραφία, which is formed fr. ichno- and
-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: ichnograph-ic, ichnograph-ic-al,
adjs., ichnograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## ichnolite
ichnolite, п., a fossil footprint (paleontol!) —
Compounded of ichno- and Gk. λίθος, 'stone'.
See-lite,

## ichnology
ichnology, п., the study of fossil footprints. —
Compounded of ichno- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: ichnolog-ic-al, adj.

## ichor
ichor, п., an ethereal fluid supposed to flow in
the veins of the gods (Greek mythol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. ΐχώρ, 'ichor; watery fluid', of uncertain,
prob. foreign, origin.

## ichthus
ichthus, n. — See ichthys.

## fchthyo-
fchthyo-, before a vowel ichthy-, combining form
meaning 'fish'. — Gk. ίχθυο-, Ιχθυ-, fr. ίχθίς,
'fish', which is cogn. with Arm. jukn, 'fish',
Lith. zuvis, Lett, zuvs, OPruss. suckans (pi. ace.),
of s.m.

## Ichthyography
Ichthyography, п., a treatise on fishes. — Lit. 'a
description of fishes', formed fr. ichthyc- and
Gk. -γραφία, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivative: ichthyograph-ic, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:391 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ICHTHYOID | 364 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:391 COLUMN:1 -->

## ichthyoid
ichthyoid, adj., resembling a fish. — Gk. ίχθυ-
αειδής, compounded of ίχ-θΰς, 'fish' (see ichthy-)
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
-oid.

## ichthyolatry
ichthyolatry, п., the worship of fishes. —
Compounded of ichthyo- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρία
fr. λατρεία, 'worship'.. See -latry.

## ichthyolite
ichthyolite, п., a fossil hsh. — Compounded of
ichthyo- and Gk. λί&ος, 'stone'. See -lite.

## ichthyology
ichthyology, п., that branch of zoology which
deals with fishes. — Compounded of ichthyo-
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in
a certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ichthyolog-ic, ichthyolog-ic-al, adjs.,
ichthyolog-ic-at-ty, adv., ichthyolog-ist, n.

## ichthyophagous
ichthyophagous, adj., eating fish. — Gk.
Ιχθυοφάγος, compounded of ίχθός, 'fish' (see ichthy-),
and -φάγος, fr. ιραγεϊν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

## Ichthyomls
Ichthyomls, п., a genus of toothed birds (pa-
leontol.) — ModL., compounded of ichthy- and
Gk. όρνις, 'bird'. See ornitho-.

## Ichthyosaiiria
Ichthyosaiiria, n. pi., an order of Mesozoic
reptiles (paleontol.) — ModL., formed from next
word with suff. -in.

## Ichthyosaurus
Ichthyosaurus, п., the chief genus of Ichthyo-
sauria (paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of
ichthyo- and Gk. σαθρός, 'lizard'. See -sanrus.

## ichthyosis
ichthyosis, п., a scaly disease of the skin (med.) —
Medical L., lit. 'fish disease', coined by the
English physician Robert Willan (1757-1812) in 1801
fr. Gk. Ιχ*4ς, 'fish' and suff. -ωσις. See ichthyo-
and -osis.

## ichthys
ichthys, ichthus, п., early Christian symbol in the
form of a fish. — Gk. ιχθύς, 'fish'. See ichthyo-.

## -ician
-ician, sun", denoting a person skilled in a specified
art or science, as in musician. — F. -icien, a suff.
compounded of -ique (whence E. -ic or -ics)
and -ien (whence E. -ian). Cp. e.g. E. logician,
fr. F. logicien, which is formed from the noun
logique (whence E. logic) and suff. -ien (E. -ian).

## icicle
icicle, n. — ME. isikel, fr. OE. is, 'ice' (see ice)
and gicel, 'icicle', which is rel. to ON. jokull,
'icicle', jaki, 'broken ice', and cogn. with Olr.
aig, 'ice'. Cp. jokull.

## -icity
-icity, subst. suff. denoting quality. — F. -icite,
fr. L. -icitatem, ace. of -icitas, which is nothing
but suff. -las added to adjectives ending in -icus
or in -ex, gen. -ids. (Cp. e.g. simplicity, fr. L.
simplicitas, fr. simplex, gen. simpticis.) Cp.
-acity. In many cases -icity is merely suff. -ity
added to adjectives ending in -ic (cp. electric,
electr/ciiy).

## icon
icon, п., an image, esp. sacred portrait of a saint.
— L. icon, fr. Gk. είκών, gen. εικόνος, 'likeness,
image, portrait, picture, statue', rel. to έοικώς,
Att. είκώς, similar, like, reasonable*, έΌικε,
'is like, is fit', ϊκελος, 'like', and possibly cogn.
with Lith. i-vykti, 'to occur, come true', pa-
veikslas, 'example'. Cp. aecidiuin.
■conic, adj., 1) pertaining to an icon; 2)
conventional. — Late L. iconicus, fr. Gk. εικονικός,
'pertaining to an image', fr. είκών, gen. εικόνος,
'image'. See icon and adj. suff. -ic.

## icono-
icono-, combining form denoting an image, an
icon. — Gk. είκονο-, fr. είκών, gen. εικόνος.
'likeness, image'. See icon.

## iconoclasm
iconoclasm, п., the destruction of images. —
Compounded of icono- and Gk. κλάσμα, 'a
breaking', fr. κλαν, 'to break', fr. I.-E. base *qel(a)-,
*qol(S)-, 'to strike, beat'. See calamity and cp.
clastic and words there referred to.

## iconoclast
iconoclast, п., a destroyer of images. — ML.
iconoctastes, compounded of icono- and Gk.
-κλάστης, 'breaker', fr. κλαν. See prec. word.
Derivatives: iconoclast-ic, iconoclast-ic-al, adjs.,
iconoctast-ic-al-ly, adv., iconoclast-ic-ism, n.

## iconography
iconography, п., the study of portraits.—ML.fco-
nographia, fr. Gk. εικονογραφία, 'sketch,
description', which is compounded of είκών, gen.
εικόνος (see icono-) and -γραφία, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See -graphy.

## iconolatry
iconolatry, п., the worship of images. —
Compounded of icono- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρίδ,
fr. λατρεία, 'worship'. See -latry.

## iconology
iconology, п., the study of icons. — Compounded
of icono- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:391 COLUMN:2 -->
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## fcononiachy
fcononiachy, п., hostility to icons as objects of
devotion. — Gk. εικονομαχία, 'war against
images', compounded of είκών, gen. εικόνος,
'image' (see icono-), and μάχη, 'battle'. See
-machy.

## iconostasls
iconostasls,- п., in the Greek Church, a screen on
which the icons are placed, separating the
sanctuary from the rest of the church. — ModL., fr.
ModGk. είκονόστασις, which is compounded
of Gk. είκών, gen. εικόνος, 'image' (see icono-),
and στάσις, 'standing, position'. See state.

## icosahedron
icosahedron, п., a polyhedron with twenty planes
(geom.) — Gk. είκοσάεδρον, 'a body with twenty
surfaces', compounded of είκοσι, 'twenty', and
έδρα, 'seat; side, face, base'. See icosi- and
-hedron.

## icosi-
icosi-, before a vowel icos-, combining form
meaning 'twenty'. — Gk. είκοσι-, είκασ-, fr.
είκοσι, 'twenty', rel. to Dor. ίίκατι and cogn.
with OI. vimsatih, L. viginti, 'twenty'. See
vkenary-

## -ics
-ics, suff. used to form names of arts and
sciences. — Formally this suff. is nothing but the
plural of suff. -ic (= "ic-s"). It was formed in
imitation of Gk. -ικά (neut. pi. of the adj. suff.
-ικός), used to form names of arts and sciences
in Greek. Cp. e.g. Gk. τά μαθηματικά (neut. pi.
of μαθηματικός, 'mathematical'), which was
Anglicized into lmathematics* (meant as
mathematics, i.e. pi. of mathematic). Another way of
forming names of arts and sciences in Greek
was the subst. use of -ική (fern, of -ικός),
shortened fr. -ική τέχνη, 'the art of; the
corresponding English form is -ic. From the suffixes
-ic and -ics the former was used exclusively till
ihe end of the 15th cent. (Cp. arithmetic, logic,
magic, music, rhetoric, which all go back to ihe
time before 1500.) Since the second half of the
16th century, the suff. -ics has beengenerally used
to form new names of sciences in English. Orig.
a plural, the suff. -ics is now usually construed
as a singular.

## icteric
icteric, icterical, adj., affected with jaundice. —
L. ictericus, fr. Gk. ικτερικός, 'jaundiced', fr.
ίκτερος. See icterus and -ic, resp. also -al.

## Icteridae
Icteridae, n. pi., a family of American oscine
birds, the oriole (ornithol.) — ModL., formed
from next word with suff. -idae.

## icterus
icterus, п., jaundice (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
ίκτερος, 'jaundice; oriole' (lit. 'a yellowish
bird'), which is prob. rel. to Ικτίνος, 'kite', and
is cogn. with Arm. cin, 'kite', possibly also with
Ol. syenah, 'eagle, falcon'.

## icterus
icterus, п., a genus of American oscene birds,
the oriole (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ίκτερος,
'jaundice; oriole'. See prec. word.

## ictic
ictic, adj., 1) of the nature of a blow; 2) pertaining
to the ictus. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. ictus,
'blow'. See ictus.

## ictus
ictus, п., verse stress (pros.) — L. ictus, 'a blow,
stroke; metrical stress', fr. ictus, pp. of icere,
'to strike'; cogn. with Gk. αιχμή, 'point of a
spear, spear' (which stands for aiksma), Lith.
iesmas, Lett, iesms, 'roasting spit', OPruss. ays-
η/is (which prob. stand for aiksmos). Cp. the
first element in Aechmophorus.

## icy
icy, adj. — OE. isig, fr. is, 'ice'. See ice and -y
(representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: ici-ly, adv., ici-ness, n.

## id
id, п., inherited instinctive energies
(psychoanalysis). — L. id, 'it', neut. of is, 'he' (see idem);
used as the translation of G. es, 'it', in Freud's
Das- Ich una das Es.

## id
id, п., a hypothetical unit of germ plasm (biol.) —
Coined by the German biologist August Weis-
mann (1834-1914) from the first two letters of
Idioplasma. See idioplasm..

## -id
-id, adj. suff. denoting state or condition. — L.
-id(us), either directly or through 'he medium
of F. -ide.

## -id
-id, patronymic subst. suff. meaning 'daughter
of. — L. -is, gen. -idis, fr. Gk. -ίς, gen. -ίδος,
fern, patronymic suff. (cp. Nereid, fr. Gk.
Νηρν]'ίς, gen. -'ίδος, 'daughier of Nereus'; see
Nereid). This sun", is used also in astronomy,
where it is added to names of constellations and
serves to name meteors that appear to radiate

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:391 COLUMN:3 -->
in showers from the respective constellation. Cp.
e.g. Andromedid, i.e. the meteor which appears
10 radiate from the constellation Andromeda.
Cp. next suff.

## -id
-id, subst. and adj. suff. used in zoology to
indicate members of a family, as in Jelid. —
ModL. -idae, pi. of -ides, fr. Gk. -ιδης, masc.
patronymic suff. (lit. 'son or descendant of).
Cp. prec. suff. Cp. also -ida, -idae, Ido.

## -id
-id, suff. in nouns from Greek, as in chrysalid,
pyramid; in botany, denoting a member of a
family (as in orchid). — Gk. -ίς, gen. -ίδος,
either 1) directly or 2) through the medium of
L. -is, gen. -idis; 3) through the medium of F.
-ide, fr. L. -is, gen. -idis.

## -id
-id, sufT. used in chemistry. — A var. of -ide.

## Ida
Ida, fern. PN. — ML, fr. OHG. Ida, which is
prob. related to ON. id, 'labor'.

## -ida
-ida, pi. suff. used to form names of zoological
groups, classes, orders, as in Arachnida. —
ModL. neut. pi. sufT. See zool. suff. -id and
-idae.

## -idae
-idae, pi. subst. suff. used to form the names of
families in zoology. — L., pi. of -ides, fr. Gk.
-ίδης, masc. patronymic sufT. See zoo], suff. -id.

## Idalia
Idalia, п., a surname of Aphrodite (Greek my-
thol.) — L. Idalia, fern, of Idalius, 'of, or
pertaining to', Idaiium, fr. Idalium, name of an
ancient town in Cyprus, sacred to Aphrodite,
fr. Gk. -Ιδάλιον.

## -idan
-idan, suff. used to denote a member of the group
indicated by the suff. -ida (zool.) —
Compounded of the suffixes -ida and -an.

## idant
idant, п., a hypothetical unit of germ plasm (biol.)
— G., arbitrarily coined by August Weismann
fr. id, 'unit of germ pl.'sm', and suff. -ant. Id-ant
is supposed to mean 'an aggregation of ids'.

## ide
ide, п., a freshwater fish. — Swed. id.

## -ide
-ide, suff. used to form names of compounds of
two elements (chem.) — Back formation fr.
oxide, in which the ending -Ide was taken for a
suffix.

## idea
idea, n. — Late L. idea, fr. Gk. ιδέα, 'form,
kind, sort, nature, class, species, opinion, no-
lion, idea, ideal form'. The original, pre-
Platonic meaning is 'look, semblance'. 'Ιδέα
prob. stands for *Γιδέσά and derives fr. ίδεΐν
(for *ίιδεΐν), 'to see', which is rel. to οΐδα (for
♦FoTSa), Ί know', εΐδον (for έΐιδον), Ί saw',
είδος (for */εΓδος), 'form, shape', lit. 'that
which is seen', εϊδωλον, 'image, phantom',
ϊστωρ, Boeot. Πστωρ (for Τίδτωρ), 'knowing,
learned', Ιστορία, 'learning, knowledge', and
cogn. with L. videre, 'to see'. See vision and cp.
eido-, eidograph, eidolon, Hades, idol, idolatry,
idyll, iso-, kaleidophone, kaleidoscope, -oid.
Derivative: idea-ed, idae-'d, adj.

## -idea
-idea, suff. used to form names of groups, classes
and orders (zool.) — ModL. Cp. suff. -ida.

## ideal
ideal, adj. — F. ideal, fr. Late L. idealis, fr. idea.
See idea and adj. SufT. -ai.
Derivatives: ideal, п., ideal-ism, п., ideal-ist, п.,
ideal-ist-ic, adj., ideal-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., ideal-ity,
п., ideal-ize, tr. and intr. v., ideal-iz-ation, п.,
