idealiz-er, п., ideal-ly, adv., ideal-ness, n.

## ideate
ideate, tr. and intr. v., to form an idea. — Formed
fr. idea with verbal sufT. -ate.

## idem
idem, pron., the same. — L. idem (masc), eadem
(fern.), idem (neut.), 'the same'. This latter
stands for id-em, which is compounded of id,
'it' (neut. of is, 'he') and the emphatic particle
-em. The first element derives fr. I.-E.
pronominal base *i-, whence also L. i-ta, 'so', i-bi,
'there', i-terum, 'again', Umbr. itek, 'so', OI. i-ti,
'so, thus', ittha, 'here, there', itthdm, 'so, thus',
it, emphatic particle, ayam, 'he', iydm, 'she',
Goth, is, 'he', ita, 'it', OHG., MHG. er, 'he', ej,
'it', G. er, 'he', es, 'it'. Through a misdivision of
L. id-em into i-dem, the fern, eadem (fr. ea-dem)
and the masc. fife/7i(fr.iWeffi)havebeen formed.
For the emphatic particle -em in id-em cp. it-em
'just so, in like manner' (fr. ita, 'so'), aut-em,
'however', quid-em, 'indeed, certainly' (fr. quid,
what'). Cp. OI. iddm (neut.), 'this', which
corresponds' exactly to L. idem. See Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., I, 671 s.v. idem. Cp. id,
'instinctive energies', identic, identify, identity. Cp.
also item, iterate, the first element in ilk and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:392 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 365 | IGUANODON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:392 COLUMN:1 -->
the second element in cestui and in interim.

## identic
identic, adj. — ML. identicus, formed from the
stem of Late L. identi-tas, 'identity'. See identity
and -ic.
Derivatives: identic-ai, adj., identic-al-ly, adv.,
identic-al-ness, n.

## identification
identification, n. — See next word and -ation.

## identify
identify, tr. v. — Late L. identificare, formed
from the stem of idemitas, 'identity', and L.
-ficare, fr. -ficus, fr. -ficere, unstressed form of
facere, 'to make, do'. See identity and -fy.

## identity
identity, n. — F. identite, fr. Late L. identitatem,
ace. of identitds, 'identity', lit. 'sameness', fr. L.
idem, 'the same'; see idem and -ity. Late L.
identitds is prop, a loan translation of Gk. ταύ-
τότης, 'identity', which is formed with suff. -της
(= L. -las), fr. ταύτη, contraction of τ6 αυτό,
'the same' (= L. idem).

## ideo-
ideo-, combining form meaning 'idea'. — F.
ideo-, fr. Gk. Ιδέα, 'form, idea'. See idea.

## ideogram
ideogram, п., symbol used in writing. —
Compounded of ideo- and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which
is written, a written character, letter'. See -gram.

## ideograph
ideograph, п., an ideogram. — Compounded of
ideo- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graph.
Derivatives: ideograph-ic, ideograph-ic-al, adjs.,
ideographic-al-ly, adv., ideograph-y, n.

## ideology
ideology, n. — F. ideologic coined by the French
philosopher Destutt de Tracy (1754-1836) fr.
Gk. ιδέα, 'idea', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ideolog-ic-al, adj., ideolog-ic-al-ly,
adv., ideolog-ist, a.

## Ides
Ides, also ides, n. pi., the fifteenth day of March,
May, July, October; the thirteenth of the other
months (Roman calendar). — F., fr. L. idus,
which is prob. of Etruscan origin.

## -idine
-idine, -idin, suff. used in chemistry to denote a
compound which is related to another
compound. — Compounded of the chemical
suffixes -ide and -ine, resp. -in.

## idio-
idio-, combining form meaning 'one's own;
separate, distinct'. — Gk. ίδιο-, fr. ίδιος, 'one's
own, private, personal, separate, distinct',-for
*ίίδιας, fr. earlier *5Λέδιος (ср. Argive ·Λ>ε-
διέστας, corresponding to Gk. ιδιώτης, 'a
private person'), for I.-E. *swed-yos, fr. base
*swed-, 'separate, set apart', whence also L. sed,
'but', sed, se, 'without', ult. from I.-E. reflexive
base *swe-, *se-. See se- and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also idiom, idiot.

## idiobiast
idiobiast, п., a cell that differs from the
surrounding cells in form or contents (бог.) —
Coined by the German embryologist Oskar
Hertwig (1849-1922) fr. idio- and Gk. βλαστός,
'bud, sprout, shoot'. See -blast.

## idiocy
idiocy, n. — Formed with suff. -cy fr. idiot. The
original spelling of the word was idiolcy. Later
the t was dropped on analogy of words like
prophecy (from propket), etc.

## Idiom
Idiom, n. — F. idiome, fr. L. idioma, fr. Gk.
Ιδίωμα, 'peculiarity', esp. 'peculiarity in a
language', fr. ίδιοϋμαι, Ί make my own', fr. ίδιος,
'one's own'. See idio- and -ma.

## Idiomatic
Idiomatic, adj. — L. ididmaticus, it. Gk.
Ιδιωματικός, fr. Ιδίωμα, gen. Ιδιώματος. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: idiomatic-al-Iy, adv., idiomatic-al-
ness, a.

## idiomorphic
idiomorphic, adj., having its proper form. —
Compounded of idio- and Gk. μορφή, 'form,
shape'. See -morphic.

## idiomorphous
idiomorphous, adj., having its own form. — Gk.
Ιδιόμορφος, compounded of ίδιος, 'one's own',
and μορφή, 'form, shape'. See idio- and
-morphous.

## idiopathy
idiopathy, п., a primary disease i.e. a disease not
caused by another disease. — Gk. ίδιοπάθεια,
'a disease having its own origin, compounded
of ίδιος, 'one's own', and -πάθεια, fr. πάθος,
'suffering'. See idio- and -pathy.
Derivatives: idiopathic, adj., idiopathic-al-ly,
adv.

## idioplasm
idioplasm, п., that kind of protoplasm which is
supposed to be the physical basis of inheritance
(biol.) — G. Idioplasma coined by the botanist

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:392 COLUMN:2 -->
Karl Wilhelm von Nageli (1817-1901) in 1884
fr. idio- and Gk. πλάσμα, 'something molded'.
See plasma and cp. id, 'unit of germ, plasm',
idant.

## idiosyncrasy
idiosyncrasy, п., ι) temperament peculiar to an
individual; 2) mannerism. — Gk. ιδιοσυγκρασία,
'a peculiar temperament', lit. 'a proper blending
together', compounded of ίδιος, 'one's own,
proper', σύν, 'with', and κράσις, 'a blending'.
See idio-, syn- and crasis.

## idiosyncratic
idiosyncratic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized
by, idiosyncrasy. — See prec. word and adj.
suff. -ic.

## idiot
idiot, n. — F. idiot, fr. L. idiota, fr. Gk. Ιδιώτης,
'private person, one not holding office, layman,
an ignorant', fr. ίδιος. See idio- and cp. idiocy,
idiom.

## idiotic
idiotic, adj. — L. idioticus, 'uneducated,
ignorant', fr. Gk. Ιδιωτικός, fr. Ιδιώτης. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: idiotic-al-Iy, adv., idiotic-al-ness,
n.

## Miotism
Miotism, п., idiom (obsol.) — F. idiotisme, fr. L.
idiotismus, fr. Gk. Ιδιωτισμός, 'the way of a
private person', fr. Ιδιωτίζειν, 'to use common
language', fr. Ιδιώτης. See idiot and -ism.

## -idium
-idium, dimin. suff. — ModL., fr. Gk. -ίδιον.

## idle
idle, adj. — ME. idel, 'empty; idle', fr. OE. idel,
'empty, desolate, useless, vain, idle', rel. to OS.
idal, OFris. Idel, 'emtpy, worthless', ODu. idil,
Du. ijdel, 'idle, vain', OHG. ital, 'empty, useless',
MHG. Uel, G. eitel, 'vain, useless; mere, pure'.
The basic meaning of these words is 'empty';
they are not cogn. with Gk. αϊθειν, 'to burn', L.
aedes, 'a building, temple'.
Derivatives: idle, intr. and tr. v., idl-er, п., idle-
ship, п., idl-ing, п., idl-y, adv.

## Ido
Ido, п., an artificial language, prop, a simplified
and improved form of Esperanto devised in
1907 by a committee under the leadership of the
Frenchman Baudouin de Courtenay. — Fr.
Esperantic -ido, 'offspring', a suff. representing
L. -ida, fr. Gk. -ίδης (as in Πριαμίδης, 'son,
descendant, of Priam', etc.). Cp. -idae.

## idol
idol, n. — ME. idole, fr. OF. (= F.) idole, fr. L.
idolum, fr. Gk. εϊδωλον, 'image, phantom;
idol', which is rel. to είδος, 'form, shape'. See
idea and cp. idolum, eidolon.
Derivatives: idol-ize, tr. v., idoliz-alion, п.,
idoliz-er, n.

## idolater
idolater, п., a worshiper of idols. — F. idolatre,
it. Late L. tddlolatris, fr. Gk. είδωλολάτρης,
'idol-worshiper', compounded of εϊδωλον,
'idol', and -λάτρης, 'worshiper', which is rel. to
λατρεία, 'worship'; see idol and -later. For the
contraction of Late L. idololatres into F. idolatre
see haplology.

## idolatress
idolatress, п., a female idolater. — Formed fr.
prec. word with suff. -ess.

## idolatrous
idolatrous, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
idolatry. — Formed fr. idolater with suff. -ous.
Derivative: idolatrous-ly, adv.

## idolatry
idolatry, п., worship of idols. — OF. idolatrie
(F. idolatrie), fr. Late L. idololatria, fr. Gk.
είδωλολατρίά, 'worship of idols, idolatry',
which is compounded of εϊδωλον, 'idol', and
-λατρεία, -λατρία, fr. λατρεία, 'worship'. See
idol and -latry. For the contraction of Late L.
idololatria into OF. idolatrie see Idolater.

## idolum
idolum, п., ι) an idea; 2) a fallacy. — Late L.
idolum, fr. Gk. εϊδωλον, 'image, phantom, idea'.
See idol.

## idoneous
idoneous, adj., suitable, fit. — L. idoneus, 'fit,
becoming, suitable', of uncertain origin. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see suff. -ous.
Derivative: iddneous-ness, n.

## idrialin
idrialin, п., a crystalline compound (chem.) —
See next word and chem. suff. -in.

## Idrialite
Idrialite, п., a mineral whose main constituent
part is idrialin (mineral.) — Named after Idria,
a mining city in N. Italy. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## idyl
idyl, idyll, n. — L. idyllium, fr. Gk. είδύλλιον, 'a
little picture', whence 'a short descriptive poem',
dimin. of είδος, 'form, shape'. See idea and cp.
idol.
Derivatives: idyl(l)-er, п., idyl(I)-ist, п., ЫуКГу
ize, tr. v., idyl(l)-ic, adj., idyl(l)-ic-al-ly, adv.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:392 COLUMN:3 -->
idyl(l)-ic-ism, n.

## -le
-le, dimin. suff., as in birdie, dearie; frequently
spelled -y.

## -ier
-ier, suff. denoting occupation. — 1) OF. or F.
-ier, fr. L. -arius, as in cottier, financier, etc.;
2) added to English words as in glazier, graizier';
hosier, etc. See -ary and -eer and cp. -yer. Suff.
■ier is of the same origin and meaning as agential
suff. -er.

## if
if, conj. — ME. gif, if, fr. OE. gif, rel. to OS. ef,
ON. ef, if, OFris. gef ef, ief, 'if, OHG. ibu, uba,
oba, 'if, MHG. oba, ob, G. ob, Du. of, 'if,
whether', Goth, ibai (interrogative particle). All
these conjunctions are prob. traceable to the
dative of a noun meaning 'doubt', and orig.
meant 'on condition that'. (Cp. ON. if, 'doubt',
OHG. iba, 'doubt, condition'.)

## igloo
igloo, iglu, п., a snowhut. — Eskimo igdlu,
'snowhouse*.

## Ignatius
Ignatius, masc. PN. — L. Ignatius, a collateral
form of Egnatius. Gk. 'Ιγνάτιος is borrowed
from Latin. Cp. Inigo.

## igueous
igueous, adj., fiery. — L. igneus,'oi fire, fiery', fr.
ignis, 'Are', which is cogn. with OI. agnlb,
OSlav. ogni, Lith. ugnls, Lett, uguns, 'fire'. Cp.
Agni, gelignite. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L.
-us, see suff. -ous.

## ignescent
ignescent, adj., emitting sparks of fire. — L.
ignescens, gen. -entis, pees. part, of ignescere,
'to take fire', formed with inchoative suff. -escere
fr. L. ignis, 'fire'. See igneous and -escent.

## ignis fataus
ignis fataus, phosphorescent light seen hovering
over swamps, will-o'-the wisp; delusion. — L.,
lit. 'foolish fire'. See prec. word and fatuous.

## ignite
ignite, tr. v., to set on fire; intr. v., to take fire. —
L. ignitus, pp. of ignire, 'to set on fire', fr. ignis.
See igneous.
Derivatives: ignit-able, adj., ignit-er, п.,
ignition, n.

## ignivomous
ignivomous, adj., vomiting fire. — Late L. igni-
vomus, compounded of L. ignis, 'fire', and vo-
mere, 'to vomit'. See igneous and vomit.

## ignoble
ignoble, adj., 1) of low birth; 2) base; 3)
dishonorable. — F., fr. L. ignobilis, 'unknown,
undistinguished, obscure', fr. i- and OL. gndbilis
(L. ndbilis), 'known, famous, renowned, noble'.
See noble.
Derivatives: ignoble-ness, п., ignobl-y, adv.

## ignominious
ignominious, adj., disgraceful, dishonorable,
contemptible. — F. ignominieux (fern, ignominieuse),
fr. L. ignominiosus, 'disgraceful, shameful', fr.
ignominia. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: ignominious-ly, adv., ignominious-
ness, n.

## ignominy
ignominy, п., disgrace, dishonor. — F. ignominie,
fr. L. ignominia, 'disgrace, dishonor', lit.
'without a name', fr. i- and ndmen, gen. nominis,
'name'. See name and cp. nominal.
Derivative: ignominious (q.v.)

## ignoramus
ignoramus, п., an ignorant person. — L.
ignoramus, 'we do not know'. See iguore.

## ignorance
ignorance, n. — F„ fr. L. igndrantia, 'want of
knowledge', fr. ignorans, gen. -antis, pres. part,
of ignorare. See igaore and -ance.

## ignorant
ignorant, adj. — F., fr. L. igndrantem, асе. of
ignorans, pres. part, of ignorare. See ignore
and -ant
Derivatives: ignorant, п., ignorant-ly, adv.

## iguoration
iguoration, п., the act of ignoring. — L. igndratio,
gen. -onis, fr. ignoratus, pp. of ignorare. See
igaore and -ation.

## ignore
ignore, tr. v. — F. ignorer, fr. L. ignorare, 'not
to know, to have no knowledge of, to be
ignorant', fr. *in-gnd-rus, 'not knowing' (cp. the
gradational variant ignarus, of s.m.); formed
fr. i- and I.-E. suff. *gno-, 'to know', whence also
OL. gnoscere, L. noscere, 'to know', L. notus,
'known', Gk. γιγνώσκειν, 'to know', γνωτός,
'known'. See know and cp. noble, note. Cp. also
gnome, 'a maxim', gnosis, gnostic.

## ignana
ignana, п., a large tropical American lizard. —
Sp., fr. Caribbean iwana, ihuana, iuana. Cp.
gnana and legnan.

## Ignanidae
Ignanidae, n. pi., a family of lizards (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -idae.

## Iguanodon
Iguanodon, п., a genus of dinosaurs (paleontol.)
— A hybrid coined fr. iguana and Gk. οδών,
gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:393 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: IHLEITE | 366 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:393 COLUMN:1 -->

## ihleite
ihleite, п., a hydrous ferric sulfate (mineral.) —
Named in 1876 after Ihle, superintendent of
mines in Mugrau, Bohemia. For the ending see
subst. surf. -ite.

## ttiram
ttiram, п., the dress consisting of two white cloths
worn by Mohammedan pilgrims to Mecca. —
Arab, ihram, 'prohibition, interdiction', prop,
inf. of ahrama, 'he prohibited, interdicted', 4th
conjugation of Штата, 'he prohibited'. See
harem.

## il-
il-, assimilated form of in-, 'in', before /, as in
illumine.

## il-
il-, assimilated form of in-, 'not', before I, as
in ulegal.

## -il
-il, surf. — A var. of -ile.

## Uang-Uang
Uang-Uang, п., also ylang-yiang, a tree of the
Philippines, Malaysia, etc. (Canagiumodoratum).
— Tagala, lit. 'flower of flowers'.

## -ile
-ile, also -il, adj. suff. denoting ability or
capacity. — L. -Ям (either directly or through the
medium of OF. or F. -il, fem. -ile).

## ile-
ile-, combining form. — See ileo-.

## ileac
ileac, adj., pertaining to the ileus. — See iliac,
'pertaining to the ileus'.

## ileitis
ileitis, п., inflammation of the ileum (med.) —
Medical L., formed fr. ileum with suff. -itls.

## iieo-
iieo-, ile-, combining form denoting the ileum.
— See ileum.

## Ilesite
Ilesite, п., a hydrous manganese zinc iron sulfate
(mineral.) — Named after the metallurgist
M.W./fej of Denver (died in 1890), who
analyzed it. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Ileum
Ileum, п., the lower part of the small intestine
(anat.) — L. ileum, 'groin, flank'. See ilium.

## ileus
ileus, п., colic (med.) — L. ileos, ileus, 'a severe
kind of colic', fr. Gk. ειλεός, Ιλεός, of s.m.,
orig. 'a winding, twisting', fr. εΐλέω, Ί wind,
roll up tight', which stands for *5ελ-νέω, fr.
I.-E. base *wel-, 'to bend, turn, twist, roll'. See
volute and cp. words there referred to.

## ilex
ilex, п., ι) the holm oak; 2) (cap.) a genus of
plants, the holly (bot.) — L. ilex, prob. a pre-
Indo-European word.

## iliac
iliac, adj., pertaining to the ilium. — F. iliaque,
'pertaining to the ilium', fr. L. iliacus, fr. ilia,
pi. of ilium. See ilinm.

## llinc
llinc, also ileac, adj., pertaining to the ileus. —
F. iliaque, fr. L. Ileus, 'colic'; confused with
iliaque, 'pertaining to the ilium'. See ileus and
cp. prec. word.

## Iliad
Iliad, п., Greek epic poem attributed to Homer
telling of the siege of Troy. — L. Ilias, gen.
Iliadis, fr. Gk. Ίλιάς, gen. *Ιλιάδος, 'the Iliad',
short for Ίλιάς ποί-ησις, lit. 'poem treating of
Ilium', fr. "Ιλιος "Ιλιαν, 'Ilium, Troy', prop,
'city of Ilus', fr. "Ιλος, 'Ilus', founder of Ilium.
For the ending see suff. -ad.

## ilio-
ilio-, combining form meaning 1) 'of the ilium';
2) 'iliac and'. — Fr. L. ilium. See ilium.

## -ility
-ility, a suff. denoting ability. — F. -ilite, fr. L.
-ilitatem, ace. of -ilitas; formed from adjectives
ending in -ile, -il, -able, -ible, as in fragility,
civility, capability, sensibility.

## ilium
ilium, п., one of the broad upper bones of the
pelvis (anat.) — L. ilium (also ile and ileum),
usually pi. ilia, 'groin, flank', prob. cogn. with
Gk. ΐλια, explained by Hesychius as μόρια
γυναικεία (female genitals), possibly also with
Pol. jelito, 'gut, sausage'; pi. 'intestines'. Cp.
ileum, iliac, 'pertaining to the ilium', jade,
'nephrite'.

## ilk
ilk, adj., the same (obsol.); п., family, kind (col-
loq.) — ME. ilke, ilk, fr. OE. ilea, 'the same',
which prob. stands for *i-Iica, fr. 1-, 'the same'
(from the pronominal base *i-, whence also
Goth, is, 'he'), and OE. gelic, 'like'. See idem
and like, adj., and cp. each.

## ill
ill, adj. — ME. Hie, ill, fr. ON. illr, 'ill, bad', of
uncertain origin.

## illaqueate
illaqueate, tr. v., to ensnare. — L. illaqueatus,
pp. of illaqueare, 'to take in a snare, ensnare',
formed fr. in-, 'in', and laquedre, 'to ensnare',
fr. laqeus, 'noose, snare', which is rel. to lacere,
'to entice'. See lace and verbal suff. -ate and
cp. Illiclum.

## illation
illation, п., inference; that which is inferred. —
L. illatid, 'deduction', lit. 'a carrying or
bringing in', fr. Hiatus, 'brought in' (used as pp. of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:393 COLUMN:2 -->
inferre, 'to bring in'), fr. in-, 'in', and lotus,
'born, carried' (used as pp. of ferre, 'to bear,
carry'), which stands for "tlatos, fr. *</-, zero
degree of I.-E. base "tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry',
whence L. tollere, 'to lift up, raise', tolerare, 'to
bear, support'. See tolerate and cp. collate and
words there referred to. For the ending see
suff. -ion.

## illative
illative, adj., pertaining to an illation, inferential.
— Late L. illativus, fr. L. Hiatus, 'brought in'.
See prec. word and -ive.
Derivative: illative-ly, adv.

## illaudable
illaudable, adj., not laudable. — L. illaudabilis,
fr. in-, 'not' and laudabilis, 'praiseworthy,
laudable'. See laudable.
Derivatives: illaudabl-y, adv.

## ille
ille, pron., that one, he. — L., altered—prob.
under the influence of is, 'he', isle, 'this, that'—
fr. OL. ollus, olle, 'that one, he', which is rel.
to Oscan ulleis, 'his' (corresponding to L. illtus,
gen. of ille), and to L. ol-im, 'formerly', ul-tra,
'on the other side, beyond', prob. also to al-ius,
'another', and cogn. with OSlav. lani, Czech
loni, Pol loni (for *olnei), 'last year' (lit. 'in
that year'), Olr. oil, 'large, wide, ample', lit.
'beyond (measure)'. The personal pronouns:
It. egli, ella, 'he, she', Rum. el, ea, Provenc. el.
Ha, F. il, elle, Catal. ell, ella, Sp. el, ella, Port.
elle, ella, 'he, she', and the defin. articles: It.
il, lo, la, Rum. -le, Provenc. Ip, le, la, F. le, la,
Sp. el, lo, la, Port, o, a, 'the', all derive fr. L. ille,
'he', resp. ilia, 'she'. See else, ultra and cp. a la,
alarm, alfresco, Algernon, alligator, al segno,
dal seguo, del credere, El Dorado, laguiappe,
langue d'oil, lierre, lingot, louver, postil.

## illegal
illegal, adj. — F. illegal, fr. ML. illegalis,
'unlawful, illegal', which is formed fr. in-, 'not',
and L. Iggalis, 'pertaining to law, legal'. See
legal.
Derivatives illegal-ity, п., illegal-ly, adv., illegal-
ness, a.

## illegible
illegible, adj. — Formed fr. in-, 'not', and legible.
Derivatives: illegibil-ity, п., illegible-ness, п.,
illegibl-y, adv.

## illegitimacy
illegitimacy, n. — Formed fr. illegitimate with
suff. -cy. Cp. legitimacy.

## illegitimate
illegitimate, adj. — Formed fr. in-, 'not', and
legitimate.
Derivatives: illegitimate, n. and tr. v., illegi-
timat-ion, n.

## illiberal
illiberal, adj. — F. illiberal, fr. L. illiberalis,
'unworthy of a freeman, ungenerous', which is
formed fr. in-, 'not*, and Itberalis, 'pertaining
to a freeman, pertaining to freedom'. See
liberal.
Derivatives: illiberal-ity, п., illiberal-ly, adv.,
illiberal-ness, n.

## illicit
illicit, adj., not lawful. — F. illicite, fr. L. illi-
citus, 'not allowed, unlawful, illegal', which is
formed fr. in-, 'not', and licitus, 'allowed,
lawful'. See licit.
Derivatives: illicit-ly, adv., illicit-ness, n.

## Illicium
Illicium, п., a genus of trees of the magnolia
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. illicium,
'allurement', lit. 'that which entices or allures', fr. in-,
'in', and lacere, 'to entice'; see lace and cp.
illaqueate. For the change of Latin й (in lacere)
to i(in il-lfcere) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

## illinition
illinition, п., a smearing in or on. — Formed
with suff. -ition fr. L. illinire, a later var. of illi-
nere, 'to besmear', fr. in-, 'in', and linire, a later
var. of latere, 'to smear, daub'. See liniment
and -ion.

## illinium
illinium, п., an element of the rare-earth group,
now called promethium (chem.) — ModL.,
coined in 1926 by the American chemist B. Smith
Hopkins, of the University of Illinois, from the
name of the State of Illinois. For the ending see
suff. -ium.

## illiteracy
illiteracy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## illiterate
illiterate, adj. — L. illiteratus, 'unlearned,
ignorant', fr. in-, 'not', and literatus, 'learned'. See
literate.
Derivatives: illiterate, п., illiterate-ly, adv., il-
literate-ness, n.

## ill-starred
ill-starred, adj. — Coined fr. iil, star and -ed.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:393 COLUMN:3 -->
Cp. evil-starred.

## illth
illth, n. — Coined by the English author and art
critic John Ruskin (1819-1900) in i860 (see
Unto this Last, IV, 126) fr. ill and subst. suff. -th
on the analogy of wealth. Cp. coolth.

## illude
illude, tr. v., to mock (obsol.); to trick. — L. il-
ludere, 'to play with, sport with, mock at; to
deceive', fr. In-, 'in', and ludere, 'to play'. See
ludicrous and cp. allnde and words there
referred to.

## illume
illume, tr. v. — Shortened fr. illnmine.

## illuminant
illuminant, adj., illuminating. — L. illuminans,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of illuminSre. See next
word and -ant.

## illuminate
illuminate, tr. v. — L. illuminatus, pp. of
illuminare, 'to make light, illuminate', fr. in-, 'in',
and lumen, gen. luminis, 'light'. See luminous
and verbal suff. -ate and cp. allumette, limn.
Derivatives: illuminat-ed, adj., illuminat-ing,
adj., illuminat-ing-ly, adv., illumination (q.v.),
illuminat-ive, adj., illuminator (q.v.)

## illuminati
illuminati, n. pi., 1) persons professing to possess
superior enlightenment; 2) (cap.) name of
various sects. — L., lit. 'enlightened', pi. of
illuminatus, pp. of illuminare. See prec. word.

## illumination
illumination, n. — F., fr. L. illuminationem, ace.
of illuminutio, 'a lighting up; enlightening', fr.
illuminatus, pp. of illuminure. See illuminate and
-ion.

## illuminator
illuminator, n. — Eccles. L. illuminator, 'an en-
lightener' (in ML. also 'illuminator of books'),
fr. L. illuminatus, pp. of illuminSre. See illuminate
and agential suff. -or.

## illumine
illumine, tr. v., to illuminate. — F. illuminer, fr.
L. illuminare. See illuminate.

## IHumlnism
IHumlnism, п., the doctrines of the Illuminati. —
F. illuminisme, fr. L. illuminare. See Illuminati
and -ism.

## Illuminist
Illuminist, п., a believer in Illuminism. — Formed
with suff. -ist fr. L. illuminare. See Illuminati.

## illusion
illusion, n. — F., fr. L. illusionem, ace. of illusio,
'a mocking, jesting', in Eccles. L. 'deception,
illusion', fr. illusus, pp. of illudere, 'to play with,
sport with, mock at; to deceive'. See illude and
-ion and cp. allusion and words there referred to.
Derivatives: illusion-al, adj., illusion-ary, adj.,
illusion-ed, adj., illusion-ism, п., illusion-ist, n.

## illusive
illusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
illusus, pp. of illudere, 'to play with, sport with,
mock at; to deceive'. See illude, and cp. allusive
and words there referred to.
Derivatives: illusive-ly, adv., illusive-ness.

## illusory
illusory, adj. — Late L. illusorius, 'ironical', fr.
L. illusus, pp. of illudere. See illusion and adj.
suff. -ory and cp. elusory.
Derivatives: illusori-ly, adv., illusori-ness, n.

## illustrate
illustrate, tr. v. — L. illustratus, pp. of illustrare,
'to make light, light up, enlighten, illustrate,
render illustrious', fr. in-, 'in', and lustrdre, 'to
illuminate'. See luster, 'brilliance', and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: illustration (q.v.), itluslrat-ive, adj.,
illustrat-ive-ly, adv., illustrator (q.v.)

## illustration
illustration, n. — F., fr. L. illustrationem, ace. of
illustratio, 'an enl;shtening', fr. il'.us'.ratuj, pp.
of illustrare. See illustrate and -ion.
Derivative: illustration-al, adj.

## illustrator
illustrator, n. — L. illustrator, 'an enlightener',
fr. illustratus, pp. of illustrare. See illustrate and
agential suff. -or.

## illustrious
illustrious, adj. — L. illustris, 'light, bright,
brilliant; clear; famous', prob. back formation fr.
illustrare. See illustrate and -ous.
Derivatives: illustrious-ly, adv., illustrious-ness,a.

## Illyrian
Illyrian, adj., pertaining to Illyria, an ancient
country extending along the NE. shore of the
Adriatic. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Illyria,
fr. Gk. 'Ιλλυρία, which is short for ή χώρα ή
'Ιλλυρία, 'the Illyrian country', 'Ιλλυρία being
the fem. of 'Ιλλυριός, 'Illyrian'.
Derivative: Illyrian, п., ι) an inhabitant of
Illyria; 2) the language of the Illyrians.

## ilmenite
ilmenite, п., a mineral compounded of iron,
titanium and oxygen (mineral.) — Named after
the Ilmen Mountains in the Ural. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## ilvaite
ilvaite, п., an iron calcium silicate (mineral.) —
Named after L. Ilva, name of the island now

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:394 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 367 | IMMINENCE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:394 COLUMN:1 -->
called Elba, where it was found. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## Iiysanthes
Iiysanthes, л., a genus of plants, the false
pimpernel (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
ίλΰς, 'mud, mire', and όίνθος, 'flower'. The first
element is cogn. with OSlav. US, 'mud, mire'.
For the second element see anther.

## im-
im-, assimilated form of in-, 'in', before b, m,
p, as in imbibe. Immanent, imparl. In some
English words im- alternates with em- (q.v.)

## im-
im-, assimilated form of in-, 'not', before b, m,
p, as in imbecile, immature, impatient.

## image
image, n. — F., fr. OF. imagene, fr. L, imaginem,
ace. of imago, 'representation, likeness, picture,
image, appearance, idea', from the stem of
imitari, 'to copy, imitate'. See imitate.
Derivatives: image, tr. v., image-able, adj.,
imagery (q.v.)

## imagery
imagery, п., use of figurative language. — ME.
imagerie, fr. OF. imagerie, fr. imagier, 'painter'
(whence obso]. E. imager), fr. image. See prec.
word and -ery.

## imaginable
imaginable, adj. — Late L. imaginabilis, fr. L.
imaginary. See imagine and -able.
Derivatives: imaginable-ness, п., imaginabl-y,
adv.

## imaginal
imaginal, adj., pertaining to the imago of an
insect. — Formed with suff. -al fr. L. imago,
gen. imaginis. See image.

## imaginary
imaginary, adj. — L. imaginarius, 'that which
exists only in appearance, imaginary', fr. imago,
gen. imaginis. See image and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: imaginari-ly, adv., imaginari-ness, n.

## imagination
imagination, n. — ME., fr. L. imaginationem,
ace. of imaginatio, 'mental image, fancy', fr.
imaginatus, pp. of imaginari. See imagine and
-atfon.
Derivative: imagination-al, adj.

## imaginative
imaginative, adj. — OF. imaginatif (fern,
imaginative), fr. Late L. imaginativus, 'imaginative',
fr. L. imaginatus, pp. of imaginari. See next word
and -ive.
Derivatives: imagi/iaiive-ly, adv.,
imaginativeness, n.

## imagine
imagine, tr. and intr. v. — ME., fr. MF. (=F.)
imaginer, fr. L. imaginari, 'to picture to oneself,
imagine', fr. imago, gen. -into; see image. L.
imaginari is prop, a loan translation of Gk.
φαντάζεσθαι, 'to become visible, imagine'. See
image. Derivative: imagin-er, n.

## imago
imago, п., the final stage of an insect (entomol.) —
L. imago, 'picture'. See image.

## imam
imam, also iuianni, п., ι) the leading priest in a
Moslem mosque; z) religious leader of Islam. —
Arab, imam, 'leader', lit. 'one who precedes', fr.
amma, 'he preceded'.

## imamah
imamah, п., the office or dignity of an imam. —
Arab, imdma*, fr. imam. See prec. word.

## imaret
imaret, п., in Turkey, an inn. — Turk., fr. Arab.
'imarah, 'pious institution, hospice', fr. 'amara,
'he lived'.

## imbecile
imbecile, adj., mentally feeble; п., a mentally
feeble person. — F. imbecile, fr. L. imbecillus,
'weak, feeble', which prob. stands for *im-
baccillos and lit. means 'without a staff, without
support', fr. in-, 'not', and bacillum, *a small
staff', dimin. of baculum, 'staff'. See bacillus
and cp. debacle.
Derivative: imbecile-ly, adv.

## imbecility
imbecility, n. — F. imbecillite, fr. L. imbecilli-
tatem, ace. of imbecillitas, 'weakness,
feebleness', fr. imbecillus. See prec. word and -ity.

## imbed
imbed, tr. v. — Formed fr. im-, 'in', and bed; var.
of embed.

## imbibe
imbibe, tr. v., to drink in. — F. imbiber, fr. L. im-
bibere, 'to drink in', fr. in-, 'in', and bibere, 'to
drink', whence bibulus, 'drinking readily'. See
bibulous and cp. beverage. Cp. also imbrue.
Derivatives: imbib-er, п., imbibition (q.v.)

## imbibition
imbibition, n. — F., fr. L. imbibit-(um), pp. stem
of imbibere, 'to drink in'. See prec. word and
-Шоп.

## imbitter
imbitter, tr. v., obsol. var. of embitter.

## imbrex
imbrex, п., a roof tile (Roman antiq.) — L. See
next word.

## imbricate
imbricate, adj., overlapping like tiles (zool. and
bot.) — L. imbricatus, 'covered with tiles', pp.
of imbricare, 'to cover with tiles; to form like

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:394 COLUMN:2 -->
a tile', fr. imbrex, gen. imbricis, 'a hollow roof
tile to lead off the rain', fr. imber, gen. imbris,
'rain', which stands for "mbhros and is cogn.
with Gk. βμβρος, 'rain', OI. abhrdm, 'cloud,
atmosphere', Avesticflwr'm, 'cloud', OI. ambhah,
'water', Arm. amb, amp, 'cloud', ump, 'drink',
and also with L. nebula, 'mist'. See nebula and
cp. ombro-. Gk. αφρός, 'foam', is not cognate
with L. imber, but with Arm. p'rp'ur, 'foam'.

## imbricate tr. v.
imbricate tr. v., to lay so as to overlap; intr. v.,
to overlap. — L. imbricatus, pp. of imbricare.
See imbricate, adj.
Derivatives: imbricat-ed, adj., imbricat-ion, п.,
imbricat-ive, adj.

## imbroglio
imbroglio, п., a confused situation; perplexity. —
It., fr. imbrogliare, 'to entangle, confuse,
embroil', which prcb. derives fr. MF. (= F.) em-
brouiller. See embroil.

## imbrue
imbrue, tr. v., to stain, soil. — ME. embrowen,
embrewen, fr. OF. embevrer, embreuver, 'to give
to drink, to moisten', fr. VL. *imbiberare, 'to

L. bibere, 'to drink'. See bibulous and cp. imbibe.

## imbrute
imbrute, tr. v., to make like a brute; intr. v., to
sink to the level of a brute. — Formed fr. in-,
'in', and brute.

## imbue
imbue, tr. v., to saturate. — L. imbuere, 'to wet,
moisten, stain, taint; to accustom, inure,
initiate', of uncertain origin.

## imburse
imburse, tr. v., to put into one's purse or a purse.
(rare). — VL. imbursare (whence also F. em-
bourser), fr. in-, 'in', and Late L. bursa, 'leather

## imide
imide, Imid, п., a compound of the bivalent
radical NH united to a bivalent acid radical (chem.)
— Coined through alteration of amide, amid.

## imido-
imido-, combining form meaning 'containing the
bivalent radical NH united to a bivalent acid
radical' (chem.) — Fr. prec. word.

## imldogen
imldogen, п., the bivalent radical NH (chem.) —
Coined fr. imido- and -gen.

## inline
inline, imin, п., a compound containing the
bivalent radical NH united to a bivalent
hydrocarbon radical (chem.) — Coined through
alteration of amine, amin.

## imino-
imino-, combining form meaning 'containing the
bivalent radical NH united to nonacid radicals'
(chem.) — Fr. prec. word.

## imitable
imitable, adj. — F., fr. L. imitabilis, 'that which

Derivatives: imitabil-ity, п., imitable-ness, n.

## imitate
imitate, tr. v. — L. imitatus, pp. of imitari, 'to
represent, copy, imitate, counterfeit', rel. to
im-dgo, 'representation, likeness, picture, image,
appearance, idea', and in gradational
relationship to aemutus, 'striving to equal', aemularl,

-ate and cp. emulate. Cp. also even, adj.

## imitation
imitation, n. — F., fr. L. imitdtionem, ace. of imi-
tatio, 'imitation', fr. imitatus, pp. of imitari. See
prec. word and -ion.

## imitative
imitative, adj. — L. imitdtivus, fr. imitatus, pp.
of imitari. See imitate and -ive.
Derivatives: imitative-ly, adv., imitative-ness, n.

## immaculacy
immaculacy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## immaculate
immaculate, adj., spotless; pure. — L. imma-
culdtus, 'unstained', fr. in-, 'not', and maculatus,
'spotted, stained', pp. of maculdre, 'to make
spotted, to stain; to defile', fr. macula, 'spot,
mark'. See macula and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: immaculate-ly, adv., immaculate-
ness, n.

## immane
immane, adj. (archaic), i) monstrous, huge; 2)

euphemistic term. See manes.
Derivatives: immane-ly, adv., immane-ness, n.

## immanence
immanence, immanency, n. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## immanent
immanent, adj., indwelling; inherent. — Late L.
immanens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of immanere,
'to dwell in, remain in', fr. in-, 'in', and L. ma-
nere, 'to remain, stay*. See remain and -ent.
Derivatives: immanent-al, adj., immanent-ly,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:394 COLUMN:3 -->
adv.

## immanity
immanity, п., monstrosity, enormity. — L. im-
mdnitds, 'monstrous', fr. immanis. See immane
and -ity.

## Immanuel
Immanuel, masc. PN. — Heb. 'ImmanU'el, lit.
'God (is) with us'. This name is compounded
of Чттйпй, 'with us' (which is formed fr. 'im,
'with', with the pronominal suff. of the ist
person pi.), and Ё1, 'God'. Heb. 'im derives fr.
stem '-m-m, 'to join, be united', whence also
'am, 'people'. See Amhaarez. For the second
element in the name Immanuel see El. Cp.
Emmanuel, Mannel.

## immarcessible
immarcessible, adj., unfading, imperishable. —
Late L. immarcescibilis, 'unfading', fr. in-, 'not',
and marcescibilis, 'withering', fr. L. marcescere,
'to wither, pine away'. See marcescent and -ible.
Derivatives: immarcessible-ness, п., immarces-
sibi-y, adv.

## immaterial
immaterial, adj. — ML. immaterialis, fr. in-,
'not', and Late L. materidlis, 'of matter;

Derivatives: immaterial-ism, п., immaterial-ist,
п., immaterial-ity, п., immaterial-ize, tr. v.,
immaterially, adv., immaterial-ness, n.

## immature
immature, adj. — L. immaturus, 'unripe,

Derivatives: immatur-ity, п., immature-ly, adv.,
immature-ness, n.

## immeasurable
immeasurable, adj. — Formed fr. in-, 'not', and
measurable. Cp. immensurable.
Derivatives: immeasurabil-ity, п., immeasurable-
ness, п., immeasurabl-y, adv.

## immediacy
immediacy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## immediate
immediate, adj. — ML. immediatus, fr. in-, 'not',
and Late L. mediatus, pp. of mediare, 'to divide

Derivatives: immediate-ly, adv., immediate-
ness, a.

## immedicable
immedicable, adj., incurable. — L. immediedbilis,
'incurable', fr. in-, 'not', and mediedbilis,
'curable'. See medicable.

## immemorable
immemorable, adj., not memorable. — L. im-
memorabilis, fr. in-, 'not', and memorabilis,
'remarkable, memorable'. See memorable.

## immemorial
immemorial, adj., extending beyond memory. —
ML, immemoridlis, fr. in-, 'not', and L. memo-
rialis, 'of memory'. See memorial.
Derivative: immemorial-ly, adv.

## immense
immense, adj. — F., fr. L. immensus,
'immeasurable, boundless, vast, immense', fr. in-, 'not',
and mensus, 'measured', pp. of metior, metirT,
'to measure'. See measure, mete.
Derivatives: immense, п., immense-ly, adv., im-
mense-ness, п., immensity (q.v.)

## immensity
immensity, n. — F. immensite, fr. L. immensi-
tutem, ace. of immensitas, 'immeasurableness,
immensity', fr. immensus. See prec. word and
-ity.

## immensurable
immensurable, adj. — F., fr. Late L. immensura-
bilis, 'immeasurable', fr. in-, 'not', and men-
surubilis, 'measurable*. See mensurable.
Derivatives: immensurabil-ity, п., immensurable-
ness, n.

## imnterge
imnterge, tr. v., to immerse; intr. v., to plunge. —
L. immergere, 'to plunge into'. See next word.

## immerse
immerse, tr. v., to plunge into. — L. immersus,
pp. of immergere, 'to plunge into', fr. in-, 'in',
and mergere, 'to dip, immerse, plunge'. See
merge and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: immers-ed, immers-ible, adjs.,

## immersion
immersion, n. — Late L. immersio, gen. -onis, 'a
plunging into', fr. L. immersus, pp. οι immergere.
See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: immersion-ism, п., immersion-ist, n.

## immigrant
immigrant, adj. and n. — L. immigrdns, gen.
-anils, pres. part, of immigrdre. See next word and
-ant.

## immigrate
immigrate, intr. and tr. v. — L. immigrat-(um),

place to another)'. See migrate.
Derivatives: immigrat-ion, п., immigrat-ory, adj.

## imminence
imminence, inuninency, n. — Late L. imminentta.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:395 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: IMMINENT | 368 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:395 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. L. imminens, gen. -entis. See next word and
-ce, resp. -cy.

## imminent
imminent, adj. — L. imminens, gen. imminentis,
pres. part, of imminere, 'to hang over, project
over; to threaten, be imminent', fr. in-,'in', and
I.-E. base *men-, 'to stand out, project'. See

Derivatives: imminent-ly, adv., imminent-ness,a.

## immission
immission, п., injection. — L. immissio, gen.
-dnis, 'a sending in, introduction', fr. immissus,

## inunit
inunit, tr. v., to send in; to inject. — L. immittere,
'to send in, introduce', fr. iii-, 'in', and mittere,
'to send'. See mission.

## immitigable
immitigable, adj. — Late L. immUigabilis, 'not
mitigable', fr. in-, 'not', and L. mltigare, 'to
make soft, mitigate'. See mitigate and -able.

## immobile
immobile, adj. — F., fr. L. immobilis,
'immovable', fr. in-, 'not', and mobilis, 'movable'. See
mobile.

## immobility
immobility, n, — F. immobilite, fr. L. immobili-
tatem, ace. of immobilitas, 'immovableness', fr.
immobilis. See prec. word and -ity.

## immobilize
immobilize, tr. v. — F. immobiliser, fr. L. im-
mdbilis. See immobile and -ize.
Derivative: immobiliz-ation, n.

## immoderate
immoderate, adj. — L. immoderatus, 'without
measure; intemperate, unrestrained', fr. in-,
'not', and moderatus, pp. oimoderare, 'to
moderate'. See moderate, adj.
Derivatives: immoderate-ly, adv., immoderate-
ness, a.

## immoderation
immoderation, n. — L. immoderatio, gen. -dnis,
'want of moderation, excess', fr. immoderatus.
See prec. word and -ion.

## immodest
immodest, adj. — L. immodestus, 'unrestrained,
immoderate', fr. in-, 'not', and modestus,
'measured, moderate; modest'. See modest.
Derivative: immodest-ly, adv.

## immodesty
immodesty, n. — L. immodestia, 'immoderate
conduct', fr. immodestus, 'immoderate'. See
prec. word and -y (representing L. -ία).

## immolate
immolate, tr. v., to kill (a sacrificial victim), to
sacrifice. — L. immolatus, pp. of immolare, 'to
sacrifice', lit. 'to sprinkle (the sacrificial victim)
with meal', fr. in-, 'in', and mola, 'mealstone;

## immolation
immolation, n. — L. immolStio, gen. -dnis, 'a
sacrificing', fr. immolatus, pp. of immolare. See

## immoral
immoral, adj. — Formed fr. in-, 'not', and moral.
Derivatives: immoral-ity, п., immoral-ly, adv.

## immoralism
immoralism, п., moral indifference; immorality.
— G. Immoralismus, coined by the German
philosopher Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche (1S44-
1900) fr. F. (= E.) immoral (see prec. word) and
suff. -ismus, fr. L. -ismus. See -ism.

## immoraiist
immoraiist, п., an advocate of immoralism. —
See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: immoraiist, immoraiist-ic, adjs.

## immortal
immortal, adj. — L. immortalis, 'deathless,
undying, immortal, everlasting', fr. in-, 'not', and
mortalis, 'mortal'. See mortal and cp.
immortelle.
Derivatives: immortal, п., immortality (q.v.),
immortalize (q.v.)

## immortality
immortality, n. — F. immortalite, fr. L. immor-
talitatem, ace. of immortalitas, 'immortality', fr.
immortalis. See prec. word and -ity.

## immortalize
immortalize, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. L.
immortalis. See immortal.
Derivative: immortaliz-ation, n.

## immortelle
immortelle, п., any of various flowers which
preserve their shape and color even after being
dried. — F., fern, of immortel, 'immortal', used
as a noun. See immortal.

## immovable
immovable, adj. — Formed fr. in-, 'not', and
movable.
Derivatives: immovabil-ity, п., immovable-ness,
п., immovabl-y, adv.

## immune
immune, adj., 1) free from obligation, exempt;
2) protected from a certain disease. — L. im-
mfmis, 'exempt from public service, free from
taxes; exempt, free', formed fr. in-, 'not', and
■munis, from the stem of nulnia (pi.), 'duties,
services', which is rel. to L. сот-munis,
'common'. See common, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:395 COLUMN:2 -->

## immunity
immunity, n. — F. immunite, fr. L. immunitatem,
ace. of immunitas, 'exemption from public
service', fr. immiinis. See prec. word and -ity.

## immunize
immunize, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. L.
immunis. See imune.
Derivative: immuniz-ation, n.

## immuno-
immuno-, combining form meaning 'immune,
immunity'. —'Fr. L. immunis. See immune.

## immunology
immunology, п., that branch of science which
deals with immunity. — A hybrid coined fr.
immuno- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: i/nmunolog-ic, immunolog-ic-al,
adjs., immunolog-ist, a.

## immure
immure, tr. v., to shut up. — Lit. 'to shut up
within walls', fr. ML. immurare, fr. in-, 'in', and
L. murus, 'wall'. See mural.
Derivatives: immur-ation, п., immure-ment, n.

## immutability
immutability, n. — L. immutdbilitas, fr. immuta-
bilis. See next word and -ity.

## immutable
immutable, adj. — L. immutabilis, 'unchangeable*,
fr. in-, 'not', and miitabilis, 'changeable', fr.
mutare, 'to change'. See mntable.
Derivatives: immittable-ness, п., immutabl-y,
adv.

## imp
imp, п., a little devil. — ME. impe, fr. OE. impa,
'shoot, graft; young tree', fr. impian, 'to graft'.
See imp, v.
Derivatives: imp-ish, adj., imp-ish-ly, adv., imp-
ish-ness, n.

## imp
imp, tr. v., 1) to graft, engraft; 2) to repair (a
wing). — ME. impen, fr. OE. impian, 'to graft',
fr. VL. "imputare [whence also OHG. impfdn
(MHG., G. impferi), F. enter], fr. Late L.
impetus, 'graft', a word occurring in the Salic
Law, fr. Gk. έμφυτος, 'implanted', verbal adj.
of έμφύειν, 'to implant', which is formed fr. έν
(see 2nd en-) and φόειν, 'to bring forth,
produce'. See phyto-.

## impact
impact, tr. v., to press firmly. — L. impactus, pp.
of impingere, 'to strike against'. See impinge.

## impact
impact, п., a striking together; collision; the
force of a collision. — L. impactus, fr. impactus,
pp. of impingere. See impact, v.

## impaction
impaction, n. — L. impactio, gen. -dnis, 'a striking
against', fr. impactus, pp. of impingere. See
impact, v., and -ion.

## impair
impair, tr. v., to make worse; to damage. — ME.
empeiren, fr. OF. empeirier, earlier form of em-
pirier (F. empirer), fr. VL. *impejorare, 'to make
worse', fr. in-, 'in', and L. pejor, 'worse'. See
pejorative.

## Impale

-entis; see next word and -ее. L. indolenlia is
prop, a loan translation. It was formed by Cicero
to render the Greek philosophical term απάθεια,
lit. 'impassibility*, which was coined by Aristotle
from πάθος, 'suffering' (see apathy).

## indolent
indolent, adj. — Late L. indolens, gen. -enlis, fr.
priv. pref. in- and L. dolens, gen. -entis, pres. part,
of dolere 'to feel pain*. See dole, 'grief, and
-ent.
Derivatives: indolent, п., indolem-ly, adv.

## Indomitable
Indomitable, adj. — Late L. indomitdbilis,
'indomitable', fr. in-, 'not', domitdre, 'to tame', and
suff. -Obilis. See daunt, and -able.
Derivatives: indomitabil-ity, п., indomitable-
ness, п., indomitabl-y, adv.

## Indonesia
Indonesia, п., the East Indian Archipelago. —
Compounded of Indo- and Gk. νήσος, 'island',
which is prob. rel. to νή-χειν, 'to swim', fr.
I.-E. base *snd-, 'to flow', whence also OL sndti,
'bathes' (intr.), L. ndre, nature, 'to swim'. See
natation and cp. the second element in
Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia.
Derivatives: Indonesi-an, adj. and n.

## indorse
indorse, tr. v. — A var. of endorse (q.v.)
Derivatives: indors-ation, п., indors-ee, п., in-
dors-er, п., indorse-ment, a.

## indoxyl
indoxyl, п., a yellow crystalline compound,
CjHjNO (chem.) — Formed from the
abbreviation of ind(igo) and (hydr)oxyl.

## Indra
Indra, п., the god of the firmament in Hindu
mythology. — OI. Indrah, of uncertain origin.

## Indri
Indri, п., the short-tailed lemur (Indris brevicau-
datus). — Malagasy; prop, an interjection
meaning 'behold!', but mistaken for the name
of the animal.

## indubious
indubious, adj. — L. indubius, 'not doubtful,
certain', fr. in-, 'not', and dubius, 'doubtful,
dubious'. See dubious.

## indubitable
indubitable, adj. — L. indubitabilis, 'that cannot
be doubted', fr. in-, 'not', and dubitabilis. See
dubitable.
Derivatives: indubitable-ness, п., indubitabl-y,
adv.

## induce
induce, tr. v. — L. inducere, 'to lead in, bring in;
to introduce; to persuade', fr. in-, 'in', and du-
cere, 'to lead*. See duke and words there referred
to and cp. esp. andouDIe.
Derivatives: induc-ed, adj., induce-ment, п.,
induc-ible, adj.

## induct
induct, tr. v. — L. inductus, pp. of inducere. See

## inductance
inductance, п., the property of a circuit by virtue
of which induction occurs (elect.) — See prec.
word and -ance.

## inductile
inductile, adj., not ductile. — Formed fr. in-,
'not', and ductile.

## induction
induction, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. inductionem,
ace. of inductie, 'a leading in, introduction; a
mode of reasoning from the particular to the
general', fr. inductus, pp. of inducere. See induce
and -ion. As a term of logic, L. inductio is a loan
translation of Gk. επαγωγή, 'a bringing on or
in; induction', fr. έπάγειν, 'to bring on or in'.

## inductive
inductive, adj. — Late L. inductivus, fr. L.
inductus, pp. of inducere. See induce and -ive.
Derivatives: inductive-ly, adv., inductive-ness, n.

## inductor
inductor, n. — L., 'one who stirs up or rouses', fr.
inductus, pp. of inducere. See induce and agential
suff. -or.

## indue
indue, tr. v., to put on (a garment); to invest,
endow. — A var. of endne.

## indulge
indulge, tr. and intr. v. — L. indulggre, 'to be
kind, yield, indulge in', orig. 'to be
long-suffering, be bearing, be patient'; cogn. with OI.
dirghah, 'long', Gk. δόλιχος, 'long'! See dolicho-
and cp. indult.
Derivatives: indulg-er, п., indulg-ing, adj., in-
dulg-ing-ly, adv.

## indulgence
indulgence, n.—Either fr. F. indulgence, or directly
fr. L. indulgentia, 'indulgence, gentleness,
complaisance', fr. indulgens, gen. -entis. See next
word and -ence.
Derivatives: indulgence, tr. v., indulgenc-ed, adj.

## indulgent
indulgent, adj. — L. indulgens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of indulggre. See indulge and -ent.
Derivatives: indulgent-ly, adv., indulgent-ness,n.

## Induline
Induline, indulin, п., any of a group of blue black
and grayish aniline dyes (chem.) — Formed
from the abbreviation of ind(igo) and the
suffixes -ule and -ine.

## indult
indult, п., an extraordinary dispensation granted
by the Pope. — L. indultum, 'indulgence, grace,
favor', prop. neut. pp. of indulgere. See indulge.

## indurate
indurate, tr. and intr. v. — L. indurdtus, pp. of
indurdre, 'to make hard, harden', fr. in-, 'in',
and durure, 'to make hard, harden', fr. durus,
'hard'. See dure, adj., and verbal suff. -ate, and
cp. endure, obdurate.
Derivatives: indurat-ed, adj., induration (q.v.),
indur-at'ive, adj.

## Indurate
Indurate, adj. — L. indurdtus, pp. of indiirare. See

## induration
induration, n. — F., fr. ML. indurationem, ace. of

v., and -ion.

## indusium
indusium, п., ι) the covering of the sorus of a fern
(bat.); z) a cuplike collection of hairs (bot.);
3) a case enclosing an insect larva (entomol.) —
L. indusium, 'a tunic', fr. induere, 'to put on (a
garment)'. See induviae.
Derivatives: indusi-al, indusi-ate, indusi-at-ed,
adjs.

## industrial
industrial, adj. — ML. industrialis (partly through
the medium of F. Industrie!), fr. L. industria. See
industry and adj. stiff, -al.
Derivative: ihdustrial-ly, adv.

## industrialism
industrialism, n. — F. industrialisme, coined by
the comte de Saint-Simon (1760-1825) in his
work Catichisme des industriels, published in
1823 (pp. 163 ff.), fr. Industriel, 'industrial', fr.
Industrie, 'industry*. See industrial and -ism.

## industrialist
industrialist, n. — F. industrialiste, coined by the
comte de Saint-Simon in 1823 fr. industriel. See

## industrialize
industrialize, tr. v. — F. industrialiser, fr, ML.

Derivative: industrializ-ation, n.

## industrious
industrious, adj. — L. industriosus, 'diligent', fr.

Derivatives: industrious-ly, adv., industrious-
ness, n.

## industry
industry, n. — F. Industrie, fr. L. industria,
'diligence, industry', orig. fern, of industrius,
'diligent, industrious', used as a noun, fr. OL. in-
dostruus, lit. 'building into', fr. indu, 'in', and
struere, 'to build, erect'. See indigene and
structure.

## induviae
induviae, n. pi., leaves that remain attached to
the stem after withering (bot.) — L. induviae,
'clothes, garments', from the stem of induere,
'to put on (a garment)', which is formed fr.
ind(u)-, 'in', and -uere, for *-overe, earlier
*-evere, fr. l.-E. base *ew-, 'to put on'. For the
first element see indigene, for the second see
exuviae. Cp. indusium.

## -ine
-ine, adj. suff. meaning 'of, pertaining to; of the
nature of, like'. — L. Anus (masc), Ana (fem.),
-mum (neut.), either directly or through the
medium of OF., F. -in (masc), -ine (fem.) Cp.
e.g. canine (fr. L. caninus), saline (fr. L. satinus).
Cp. also adj. suff. -en.

## -ine
-ine, adj. suff. meaning 'of the nature of, like'. —
L. Anus (masc.), Ana (fem.), Anum (neut.), fr.
Gk. -ινος (masc), -ΐνη (fem.), -Ivov (neut.) —
Cp. e.g. adamantine, fr. L. adamantinus, fr. Gk.
αδαμάντινος.

## -ine
-ine, suff. forming abstract nouns as in doctrine,
discipline, medicine. — F. -ine, fr. L. Ana.

## -ine
-ine, suff. forming feminine common nouns. —■
L. Ana, fr. Gk. -(νη. Ср. e.g. heroine, fr. F.
heroine, fr. L. heroina, fr. Gk. ηρωίνη. Ср. 2nd
adj. suff. -ine.

## -me
-me, also -in, suff. used in chemistry to form
1) names of alkaloids and bases (as cocaine,
aniline, etc.); 2) names of elements (as bromine,
chlorine, etc.) — F. -ine, fr. Latin adj. suff. Ana,
fem. of Anus. See 1st adj. suff. -ine.

## -ine
-ine, also -in, dimin. suff. — Fr. It. dimin. suff.
■ino. Ana, either directly or through the medium
of F. -ine. Cp. e.g. mandolin(e), fr. F. mandoline,
fr. It. mandolino.

## -ineae
-ineae, pi. suff. used to form names of subfamilies
of plants (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. -ineae, fem. pi.
of -ineus (as in grdmineus, 'gramineous'). The
fem. form is due to L. plantae, 'plants', a fem.
noun in the pi., which is understood.

## inebriant
inebriant, adj., inebriating. — L. inebrians, gen.

and -ant.

## inebriate
inebriate, tr. v., to make drunk, intoxicate. —
L. inebriatus, pp. of inebriare, 'to make drunk,
inebriate', fr. in-, 'not', and ebridre, 'to make
drunk', fr. ebrius, 'drunk'. See ebrious and

## inebriate
inebriate, adj. — L. inebriatus, pp. of inebriare.
See inebriate, v.

inebriation, n. — Late L. inebriatid, gen. -Onis,
fr. L. inebriatus, pp. of inebriare. See inebriate,

v., and suff. -ion.

inebriety, n. — Prob. a blend of ebriety and

inelegance, inelegancy, n. — Formed from next

inelegant, adj. — F. inelegant, fr. L. inilegantem,

## ineluctable
ineluctable, adj., not to be avoided. — L. ineluc-
tabilis, 'unavoidable, inevitable', fr. ia-, 'not',
and eluctari, 'to struggle out of, to surmount',
fr. e- and luctdri, 'to struggle, wrestle', which is
cogn. with Gk. λύγος, 'any pliant twig', λυγίζειν
'to twist, bend', OE. locc, 'lock'. See lock, 'tuft',
and cp. reluctance.
Derivatives: ineluctahil-ity, п., ineluctabl-y, adv.

## inept
inept, adj., i) unfit; 2) foolish. — L. ineptus,
'unsuitable, improper, tactless', fr. in-, 'not', and
aptu.s, 'fitted, suited'. See apt and cp. inapt,

Derivatives: inept-ly, adv., inept-ness, n.

## ineptitude
ineptitude, n. — L. ineptitude, fr. ineplus. See

inequal, adj. — L. inaequalis, fr. in-, 'not', and

ineqnality, n. — Late L. inaequalitas, 'unevenness,

## inerm
inerm, adj., unarmed; destitute of thorns (bo!.) —
L. inermis, inermus. 'unarmed', formed fr. in-,
'not', and arma, 'arms'.' See arm, 'weapon'.
For the change of Latin a (in arma) to e (in
inermis, in-ermus) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.

## inerrable
inerrable, adj., not erring; infallible. — L. in-
errabilis, 'unerring', fr. iu-, 'not', and errare,
'to err'. See err and -able.
Derivatives: inerrabil-ity, п., inerrable-ness, п.,
inerrabl-y, adv.

## inerrancy
inerrancy, n. — Formed from next word with

## inerrant
inerrant, adj., not erring. — L. inerrans, gen.
-antis, 'not wandering', fr. in-, 'not', and errans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of errare, 'to err'. See
err and -ant
Derivative: inerrant-ly, adv.

## inert
inert, adj., I) without inherent power to move or
resist; 2) inactive. — L. iners, gen. -ertis,

a (in ars) to ё (in in-ers) see accent and cp. words

Derivatives: inert-Iy, adv., inert-ness, n.

## inertia
inertia, п., inertness; the tendency of matter to
remain at rest when at rest, and in motion when
moving. — L., 'unskillfulness; inactivity,
idleness', fr. iners, gen. -ertis. See prec. word. The
word inertia was introduced into physics by the
German astronomer and mathematician Johann
Kepler (1571-1630).

## inerndite
inerndite, adj. — L. ineruditus, 'unlearned,
illiterate, ignorant', fr. in-, 'not', and eruditus. See

Derivatives: inerudite-ly, adv., inerudit-ion, n.

## inestimable
inestimable, adj. — F., fr. L. inaestimabilis, 'that
cannot be estimated; inestimable, invaluable',
fr. in-, 'not', and aestimabilis. See estimable.
Derivatives: inestimabil-ity, п., inestimable-ness,
п., inestimabl-y, adv.

## inevitable
inevitable, adj. — L. inevitabilis, 'unavoidable',
fr. in-, 'not', and evitabilL·. See evitable.
Derivatives: inevitabil-ity, п., inevitable-ness, п.,
inevitabl-y, adv,

inexorable, adj. — L. inexdrabilis, 'that cannot

Derivatives: inexorabil-ity, п., inexorable-ness,
п., inexorabl-y, adv.

inexperience, n. — F. inexperience, fr. Late L.

See experience.
Derivative: inexperienc-ed, adj.

## inexpert
inexpert, adj. — OF., fr. L. inexpertus, 'unprac-
ticed, inexperienced', fr. in-, 'not', and expertus.
See expert.
Derivatives: inexpert-Iy, adv., inexpert-ness, n.

## inexpiable
inexpiable, adj. — L. inexpiabilis, 'that cannot
be atoned for, implacable', fr. in-, 'not', and
explore, 'to make amends or atonement for'.
See expiable.
Derivatives: inexpiable-ness, п., inexpiabl-y, adv.

## inexplicable
inexplicable, adj. — F., fr. L. inexplicabilis, fr.
in-, 'not', and explicabilis. See explicable.

Derivatives: inexplicit-ly, adv., inexplicit-ness,n.

## inexpugnable
inexpugnable, adj. — F„ fr. L. inexpugnabilis,
'not to be taken by assault', fr. in-, 'not', and

Derivatives: inexpugnabil-ity, п., inexpugnable-

## inextricable
inextricable, adj. — L. inextricabilis, 'that

cabilis. See extricable.
Derivatives: inextricabil-ity, п., inextricable-
ness, п., inextricabl-y, adv.

Inez, fern. PN. — Sp., equivalent to Agaes (q.v.)

## infallibjlism
infallibjlism, п., the doctrine of the infallibility of

infallibilist, п., a believer in the infallibility of the

infallibility, n. — ML. infallibilitas, fr. infallibilis.

infallible, adj. — ML. Infallibilis, fr. in-, 'not', and

Derivatives: infallible-ness, п., infallibl-y, adv.

## infamize
infamize, tr. v., to render infamous (archaic). —

## infamous
infamous, adj. — ML. infamosus, fr. L. infamis,
'ill spoken of, disreputable, notorious', fr. in-,
'not', and fama, 'talk, report, rumor'. See

Derivatives: infamous-Iy, adv., infamous-ness, n.

## infamy
infamy, n. — F. infamie, fr. L. xnfamia, 'bad

infancy, n. — L. Infantia, 'early childhood', lit.

## infangthief
infangthief, п., the right of a lord to try a thief

— OE. in/angenpeo/, fr. in (see in), fangen,
'taken' (pp. of fan, 'to take'), and peof 'thief.
See fang and thief and cp. outfangthief.

## infant
infant, n. — OF. (= F.) enfant, fr. L. infantem,
ace. of infans, 'a young child, a babe', lit. 'that
cannot speak, not yet able to speak', fr. in-,
'not', and fans, gen. fantis, pres. part, of /art,

Derivative: in/ant, adj.

## infanta
infanta, п., any daughter of a king of Spain or
Portugal. — Sp. and Port., fern, of in/ante. See
infante.

## infante
infante, п., any son of a king of Spain or
Portugal, except the heir to the throne. — Sp. and
Port., fr. L. ϊη/antem, ace. of In/ans, 'a young
child*. See infant

## infanticidal
infanticidal, adj., pertaining to infanticide (in
either sense). — Formed fr. infanticide with adj.

## infanticide
infanticide, п., one who kills an infant. — F., fr.
Late L. infanticida, compounded of L. in/ans,
gen. -fantis, and -cida, 'killer', fr. caedere, 'to kill'.
See prec. word and -cide, 'killer'.

## infanticide
infanticide, п., the killing of an infant; child
murder. — F., fr. Late L. in/anticldium,
compounded of L. infans, gen. -fantis, and -cidium,
'killing', fr. caedere, 'to kill'. See infant and
-cide, 'killing'.

## infantile
infantile, adj., childish. — L. infantilis, 'pertaining

## infantine

## infantry

## infarct
infarct, п., a region of necrosis of tissue (med.) —

ML. infarctus, corresponding to L. infartus,

Derivatives: infarct-ed, adj., infarct-ion, n.

## infatuate
infatuate, adj. — L. in/atuatus, pp. of in/atuare.

infatuation, n. — Late L. Infatuatio, gen. -dnis,

## infect
infect, tr. v., to taint; to corrupt. — L. infectus,

## infection

## infelicific
infelicific, adj., causing unhappiness. — Formed

## infelicitous
infelicitous, adj., unhappy. — See next word
and -ous.
Derivatives: infelicitous-ly, adv., in/elicitous-
ness, n.

## infelicity
infelicity, n. — L. in/llicitas, gen. -atis, 'ill luck,

unhappy', fr. in-, 'not', and fellx, gen. -icis,
'fortunate, happy'. See felicity.

## infer
infer, tr. v., to imply. — L. in/erre, 'to bring into,

'in', and ferre,'to bear.carry'. See bear,'to carry',
and cp. confer and words there referred to.

## inference
inference, n. — ML. inferentia, fr. L. in/erens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of tnferre. See infer and
suff. -ence.

## inferential
inferential, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
ML. inferentia. See prec. word.
Derivative: inferei tial-ly, adv.

## inferior
inferior, adj., lower. — L., 'lower in place, under,
nether', compar. of infer us. See infra and com-
par. suff. -tor.
Derivatives: inferior, п., inferior-ity, п., inferior-
ly, adv.

## infernal
infernal, adj., pertaining to hell; devilish. — F.,
fr. L. infernalis, 'pertaining to the lower regions',
fr. infernus, 'lying beneath, infernal', fr. inferus,
'lower'. See infra and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: infernal-ity, п., infernal-ly, adv.

## inferno
inferno, п., hell. — It., fr. L. infernus, 'lying
beneath, infernal'. See inferaal.

## infertile
infertile, adj. — Late L. infertilis, 'unfruitful', fr.
in-, 'not', and L. fertilis. See fertile.
Derivatives: infertile-ly, adv., infertile-ness, n.

## infertility
infertility, n. — F. infertilite, fr. Late L. inferti-
litatem, ace. of infertilitas, 'unfruitfulness', fr.
infertilis. See prec. word and -ity.

## infest
infest, tr. v., to harass. — F. infester, fr. L. in-
festare, 'to trouble, disturb, molest', fr. infestus,
'disturbed, molested, infested, unquiet, hostile',
lit. 'seized', rel. to manifeslus, 'evident', lit. 'that
which can be seized by the hand', and prob.
cogn. with OI. dharsati, 'dares', Gk. θάρσος,
θράσος, 'courage, audacity', OE. ic dearr, Ί
dare'. See dare and words there referred to and
cp. esp. manifest.

## infestation
infestation, n. — Late L. infestatid, gen. -dnis,
'a troubling, disturbing, molesting', fr. L. in-
festatus, pp. of infestare. See infest and -ation.

## infeudation
infeudation, п., enfeoffment (Engl. lav). — ML.
infeudatio, gen. -dnis, fr. Infeudatus, pp. of in-
feudare, 'to enfeoff'. See in-, 'in', feud, 'fief, and
-ation.

## infibulate
infibulate, tr. v., to fasten, buckle (esp. the sexual
organs). — L. infibulatus, pp. of infibulare, 'to
close with a clasp', fr. in-, 'in', лай fibula, 'clasp,
buckle, brooch'. See fibula and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: infibulat-ion, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:404 COLUMN:1 -->

## iafldel
iafldel, adj. — F. infidile, fr. L. infidelis, 'that
cannot be relied upon, faithless', fr. in-, 'not',
and fidilis, 'true, faithful'. See fidelity.
Derivative: infidel, n.

## infidelity
infidelity, n. — F. infidelite, fr. L. infidelitatem,
ace. of infidetitas, 'faithlessness', fr. Infidelis. See
prec. word and -ity.

## infinite
infinite, adj. — L. infinitus, 'boundless, unlimited,
endless', fr. in-, 'not', and finitus, pp. offinire.
See finite. Derivatives: infinite, п., infinite-ly,
adv., infinite-ness, n.

## infinitesimal
infinitesimal, adj., immeasurably small. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. ModL. infinitesi-
mus, which was coined by the German
philosopher and mathematician Baron Gottfried
Wilhelm von Leibniz (1646-1716) fr. L. infinitus
(see prec. word) on analogy of L. centesimus,
'the hundredth'.
Derivatives: infinitesimal, п., infinitesimal-ity,a.,
infinitesimal-ly, adv., infinitesimal-ness, n.

## infinitive
infinitive, adj. and n. — Late L. infinitivus, fr. L.
infinitus. See infinite and -ive.
Derivatives: infinitiv-al, adj., infinitiv-al-ly, in-
finitive-ly, advs.

## infinitude
infinitude, п., the state of being infinite. — Coined
by Milton fr. infinite and suff. -tide.

## infinity
infinity, n. — ME. infinite, fr. OF. infinite (F.
infinite), fr. L. infinitatem, ace. of infinitas,
'boundlessness, endlessness'. See infinite and
-ity. L. infinitas is prop, a loan translation of Gk.
άπειρίϊ, 'infinity', fr. ίίπειρος, 'endless, infinite'.

## infirm
infirm, adj. — ME. infirme, fr. L. infirmus, 'weak,
feeble, infirm, sick', fr. "in-, 'not', and firmus,
'strong, firm'. See firm, adj.
Derivatives: infirm-ly, adj., infirm-ness, n.

## infirmary
infirmary, n. — ML. infirmaria, 'hospital', lit. 'a
place for the infirm', fr. L. infirmus; cp. Sp. en-
fermo (fr. L. infirmus), 'sick', enfermedad (fr. L.
infirmitatem, ace. of infirmitas), 'sickness*. See
prec. word and subst. suff. -ary.
Derivative: infirmar-ian, n.

## infirmity
infirmity, n. — ME. infirmite, fr. MF. (— F.) in-
firmite, fr. L. infirmitatem, ace. of infirmitas,
'weakness', fr. infirmus. See infirm and -ity.

## infix
infix, tr. v. — L. infixus, pp. of infigere, 'to fix in',
fr. in-, 'in', and figere, 'to fix, fasten'. See fix.

## infix
infix, n. ~- L. infixus, pp. of infigere. See infix, v.

## inflame
inflame, tr. and intr. v. — ME. enfiamen, fr. OF.
enfiamer, enflammer (F. enfiammer), fr. L. m-
flammare, 'to set on fire, kindle', fr. in-, 'in',
and flammare, 'to flame', fr. flamma, 'flame'.
See flame. Derivatives: inflam-ed, adj., inflam-
■ed-ly, adv., inflam-ed-ness, п., inflam-ing, adj.,
inflam-ing-ly, adv.

## inflammable
inflammable, adj. — F., fr. L. infiammare. See
inflame and -able.
Derivatives:inflammable,п., inflammabil-ity, п.,
inflammable-ness, п., inflammabl-y, adv.

## inflammation
inflammation, n. — F., fr. L. infiammationem,
ace. of inflammatio, 'a setting on fire', fr. in-
flammalus, pp. of infiammare. See inflame and
-ation.

## inflammatory
inflammatory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory
fr. L. inflammatus, pp. of infiammare. See
inflame and cp. F. infiammatoire.
Derivative: inflammatori-ly, adv.

## inflate
inflate, tr. v. — L. infiatus, pp. of infiare, 'to blow
into, inflate; to pull up', fr. in-, 'in', and flare,
'to blow'. See flatus and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: inflat-ed, adj., infiat-ed-ly, adv.,
infiat-ed-ness, a., inflat-er, п., inflation (q.v.),
inflal-or, n.

## inflation
inflation, n. — L. inflatio, gen. -onis, 'a blowing
or puffing up, inflation', fr. infiatus, pp. of
Infiare. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: inflation-ary, adj., inflation-ism, п.,
infiation-ist, n. and adj.

## inflect
inflect, tr. v. — L. infiectere (pp. infiexus), 'to
bend, curve; to change, alter, modulate', fr.
in-, 'in', and flectere, 'to bend'. See flex and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: inflect-ed, adj., inflect-ed-ness, п.,
inflection (q.v.), inflect-ive, adj.

## inflection
inflection, inflexion, n. — L. inflexio, gen. -onis,
'a bending, inflection, modification', fr. in-
flectus, pp. of infiectere, 'to bend, curve'. See
inflect and -ion.
Derivatives: inflection-al, inflexion-al, adj., in-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:404 COLUMN:2 -->
flection-al-ly, inflexion-al-ly, adv., inflection-less,
inflexion-less, adj.

## inflexible
inflexible, adj. — L. inflexibilis, 'inflexible', fr.
infiexus, pp. of infiectere. See inflect and -ible.
Derivatives: inflexibil-ity, п., inflexible-ness, п.,
inflexibl-y, adv.

## inflict
inflict, tr. v. — L. inflictus, pp. of infligere, 'to
strike or dash against', fr. in-, 'in', and fligere
(PP· flictus), 'to strike'. See afflict and cp. words
there referred to. Derivatives: infiict-er, п.,
infliction (q.v.), inflict-ive, adj.

## infliction
infliction, n. — Late L. inflictid, gen. -onis, 'an
inflicting', fr. L. inflictus, pp. of infligere, 'to
strike or dash against'. See prec. word and -ion.

## inflorescence
inflorescence, п., ι) a flowering; 2) arrangement
of flowers on an axis (bot.) — ModL.· in-
fiorescentia, fr. Late L. inflorescens, gen. -entis.
pres. part, of inflorescere, 'to begin to blossom,
to put forth blossoms', fr. in-, 'in', and L. flore-
scere, 'to begin to blossom'. See florescence.

## inflorescent
inflorescent, adj., flowering. — Late L.
inflorescens, gen. -entis. See prec. word.

## inflow
inflow, n. — Formed fr. in-, 'in', and flow.
Derivatives: inflow-ing, adj. and n.

## influence
influence, n. — F-, fr. Late L. influentia, 'a flowing
in', fr. L. influins, gen. -entis. See influent and
-ce and cp. influenza. Derivative: influence, tr. v.

## influent
influent, adj., flowing in; п., a tributary stream,
— L. influins, gen. -entis, pres. part, of influere,
'to flow in', fr. in-, 'in', and fluere, 'to flow'.
See fluent.

## influential
influential, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
Late L. influentia. See influence.
Derivative: influential-ly, adv.

## influenza
influenza, п., an acute contagious disease. — It.,
lit. 'influence' (see iafluence). The disease was
so called because it was originally attributed to
the 'influence' of the stars.
Derivative: influenz-al, adj.

## influx
influx, п., a flowing in. — Late L. influxus, gen.
-us, 'a flowing in', fr. L. influxium), pp. stem of
influere, 'to flow in', fr. in-, 'in', and fluere, 'to
flow'. See fluent.

## iafluxion
iafluxion, n. — Late L. influxio, gen. -onis, 'a
flowing in', fr. L. influx-(um), pp. stem of
influere. See prec. word and -Ion.

## inform
inform, adj., without form, shapeless. — F. in-
forme, fr. L. informis, 'unformed, shapeless', fr.
in-, 'not', and forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## inform
inform, tr. and intr. v., to apprise, notify. —
ME. enformen, fr. OF. enformer (F. informer),
fr. L. informare, 'to give form to, to shape', fr.
in-, 'in', and formare, 'to form, shape'. See
form, v.
Derivatives: inform-al, adj., informant (q.v.),
information (q.v.), inform-ed, adj., inform-ed-ly,
adv., inform-er, n.

## informant
informant, n. — L. informans, gen. -antis, pres,
part, pf informare. See inform, v., and -ant.

## information
information, n. — ME. enformacion, fr. OF. en-
formacion (F. information), fr. L. informatidnem,
ace. of informStid, 'representation, outline,
sketch; idea, conception', fr. informatus, pp. of
informare. See inform, v., and -ation.
Derivatives: information-al, adj.

## informative
informative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
informatus, pp. of informare. See inform, v.
Derivative: informalive-ly, adv.

## informatury
informatury, adj. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ory fr. L. informatus, pp. of informare. See
inform, v.

## infra
infra, adv., under, below. — L. infra, 'below
(adv.); below (prep.), under', fr. I.-E. 'qdher-,
whence also OI. adhah, 'below\oi/Aai-aA, 'lower',
OE. under, 'under, among'. See under and cp.
inferior, infernal, inferno. Cp. also inter-,
interior, intra-. Cp. also fracas.

## infra-
infra-, pref. meaning 1) below; 2) within. — L.
infra-, fr. infra. See prec. word.

## infract
infract, tr. v., to break, infringe. — L. infractus,
pp. of infrlngere, 'to break'. See infringe.

## infraction
infraction, п., infringement. — L. infractid, gen.
-onis, 'a breaking', fr. infractus, pp. aiinfringere.
See infringe and -Ion.

## infra dig
infra dig, colloquial abbreviation of L. infra
dignitatem, 'beneath the dignity of.

## infraspinatus
infraspinatus, п., name of one of the muscles of
the shoulder (anat.) — Medical L. (musculus)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:404 COLUMN:3 -->
infraspinatus, a name coined by J.Riolan (in
Anthropographia, Book 5, chapter 24, quoted
by Joseph Hyrtl, Onomatologia Anatomica, pp.
501-503). The correct form of the name should
be musculus infra sptnam, lit. 'the muscle below
the backbone', fr. infra, 'below', and spina,
'spine, backbone'. See infra- and spine and cp.
supraspinatus.

## infrequency
infrequency, infrequence, n. — L, infrequentia,
'scantiness', fr. infrequins, gen. -entis. See next
word and -cy, resp. -ce.

## infrequent
infrequent, adj. — L. infrequins, gen. -entis,
'occurring seldom, unusual, uncommon, not
frequent', fr. in-, 'not', and frequens, gen. -entis.
See frequent.
Derivative: infrequent-ly, adv.

## infringe
infringe, tr. v. — L. infringere, 'to break off,
impair, destroy', fr. in-, 'in', and frangere, 'to
break'. See fraction and cp. words there referred
to. For the. change of Latin a (in frangere) to f
(in in-fringere) see contingent.
Derivative: infringe-ment, n.

## infructuous
infructuous, adj., fruitless. —- L. infructuosus,
'unfruitful, fruitless, useless', fr. in-, 'not', and
fructuosus, 'fruitful'. See fructuous.
Derivative: infructuous-ly, adv.

## infundibulnm
infundibulnm, п., name of several funnel-shaped
organs (anal.) — L. infundibulum, 'funnel', fr.
infundd, -ere, 'to pour in', fr. in, 'in', and fun-
dere, 'to pour' (see infuse). In the sense of 'the
funnel-shaped hollow in the brain', infundibulum
is a loan translation of Gk. χοάνη, 'funnel,
funnel-shaped hollow in the brain', fr. χεΐν, 'to
pour'.
Derivatives: infundibul-ar, infundibul-ate, adjs.

## infuriate
infuriate, adj., infuriated. — It. infuriate, fr. ML.
infuriatus, pp. of infuriare, 'to madden', fr. L.
in furia, 'in a fury', fr. in (see in-, 'in') and abl.
of furia (see fury). For the ending see adj. suff.
-ate.
Derivative: infuriate-ly, adv.

## infuriate
infuriate, tr. v. — ML. infuriatus, pp. of infuriare.
See infuriate, adj.
Derivative: infuriat-ion, n.

## infuscate
infuscate, adj., darkened with a brownish shade
(said of the wings of insects). — L. infuscatus,
'darkened', pp. of infuscare, 'to darken', fr. in-,
'in', and fuscare, 'to make dark, to make
swarthy', fr. fuscus. See fuscous and adj. suff. -ate.

## infuse
infuse, tr. v. — L. infusus, pp. of infundere, 'to
pour into; to wet, moisten', fr. in-, 'in', and
fundere, 'to pour'. See fuse, 'to melt' and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: infus-er, п., infus-ible, adj., infus-
ibil-ity, п., infusion (q.v.)

## infusion
infusion, n. — L. infusio, gen. -onis, 'a pouring
into', fr. infusus, pp. of infundere. See prec. word
and -ion.

## Infusoria
Infusoria, n. pi., a class of Protozoa (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'found in infusions', coined by
Ledermuller in 1763 fr. L. infusus, pp. of
infundere, 'to pour into'. See infuse and the
suffixes -ory and -ia.
Derivatives: infusori-al, adj., Infusori-an, adj.
and n.

## -ing
-ing, suff. forming nouns from verbs (i.e. 'verbal
nouns'). — ME. -ing, fr. OE. -ing, -ung, rel. to
ON. -ing, Du. -ing, OHG., MHG., G. -ung.

## -ing
-ing, suff. forming the present participle — ME.
-inge, -ing, altered fr. ME. -end, -and, -ind, fr.
OE. -ende, which is rel. to Du., G. -end, Goth.
-and, and cogn. with OI. -ant-, Gk. -ων (fern.
-ούσα, neut. -ov), L. -ans, -ens, -tens (from verbs
of the I, II and III, resp. IV conjugation). Cp.
the suffixes -ant, -ent.

## -ing
-ing, suff. meaning 'pertaining to, related to;
descended from; resembling'; used to form
patronymics (as in athelin^, king). — ME., fr.
OE. -ing, -ung, rel. to ON. -ingr, -ungr, OHG.
-ing, Goth. -iggs. Cp. adv. suff. -Ung.

## -ing
-ing, suff. occurring in place names. — Partly fr.
OE. ing, 'meadow' [rel. to ON. eng, engi,
'meadow' (whence Dan., Norw. eng, of s.m.)], as
in Reading, partly patronymic as in Buckingham
(see -ing, suff. meaning 'pertaining to*).

## Inga
Inga, п., a genus of plants of the mimosa family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Port, inga, fr. Tupi inga.

## ingeminate
ingeminate, tr. v., to repeat. — L. ingeminStus,

reiterate', fr. hi-, 'in", and geminare, 'to double', fr.
geminus, 'twin'. See Gemini,
ingenerate, adj., not generated. — Late L. in-
generatus, fr. in-, 'not', and L. generatus,
'engendered, produced, generated', pp. ofgenerate.
See generate,

## ingenerate
ingenerate, tr. v., to generate within, to engender.
— L. ingeneratus, pp. of ingenerare, 'to
engender, produce', fr. in-, 'in', and generare. See
generate and cp. engender,

## ingeuious
ingeuious, adj., clever. — F. ingenieux (fem. in-
genieuse), 'ingenious, clever', fr. L. ingeniosus,
'intellectual, clever', fr. ingenium, 'nature;
disposition', lit. 'that which is inborn', fr. in-, 'in',
and I.-E. base *gen-, 'to beget, bear, bring forth,
produce'. See genus and -ous and cp. engine.
Derivatives: ingenious-ly, adv., ingenious-ness, n.

## iagenue
iagenue, п., an artless, naive girl. — F., fem. of
inginu, 'ingenuous, artless, simple', fr. L. in-

## ingenuity
ingenuity, п., ingeniousness. — L. ingenuitas(gen.
-talis), 'frankness, nobility', fr. ingenuus: see
next word and -ity. The English meaning of the
word is due to a confusion with ingenious.

## ingenuous
ingenuous, adj. — L. ingenuus, 'native; freeborn,
noble; upright', fr. in-, 'in', and I.-E. base *gen-,
'to beget, bear, bring forth, produce'. See genus
and cp. ingenue. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
L. -us, see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: ingenuous-ly, adv.,
ingenuousness, n.

## ingest
ingest, tr. v., to take into the body. — L. in-
gestus, pp. of ingerere, 'to bring in, carry in',
fr. in-, 'in', and gerere, 'to carry'. See gerent and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: ingestion (q.v.), ingest-ive, adj.

## ingestion
ingestion, n. — L. ingestio, gen. -onis, 'a pouring
in', fr. ingestus, pp. of ingerere. See prec. word
and -ion.

## ingle
ingle, п., fire; fireplace. — Scot., fr. Gael, aingeal,
'fire', which is of uncertain origin.

## inglorious
inglorious, adj. — L. ingtoriosus, 'inglorious', fr.
in-, 'not', and gloridsus. See glorious.
Derivatives: inglorious-ly,&dv.,inglorious-ness,n.

## ingluvies
ingluvies, п., the crop (zool.) — L. ingluvies, 'crop,
maw', which stands for in-gluv-ies, fr. in-, 'in',
and I.-E. base *glu-, 'to swallow', whence also
L. glutttre, 'to swallow, gulp down'. See glut
and cp. words there referred to.

## ingot
ingot, п., a mass of unwrought metal. — ME.,
fr. OE. in (see in-, 'in') and goten, pp. of geotan,
'to pour'. See found, 'to cast', and cp. lingot.

## ingrain
ingrain, tr. v., ι) to dye in grain; 2) to work into
the texture. — See engrain.
Derivative: ingrain-ed, adj.

## ingrain
ingrain, adj., dyed in grain; п., ingrain yarn,
carpet, etc. — Fr. in grain. See in, prep., and
grain.

## Ingrain
Ingrain, masc. PN. — Prob. fr. Latinized OHG.
Angilramnus or Ingilramnus, lit. 'angel's raven',
fr. OHG. angil, 'angel', and Aram, a collateral
form of hraban, 'raven'. See angel and raven
and cp. the second element in Bertram.

## ingrate
ingrate, adj., ungrateful. — OF. ingrat, fr. L. in-
gratus, 'unpleasant; ungrateful', fr. in-, 'not',
and gratus, 'beloved, pleasing, dear, agreeable'.
See grace and cp. grateful.

## ingratiate
ingratiate, tr. v., to commend to favor. — It. in-

graziare, 'to bring into favor', fr. It. in grazia,

fr. L. in gratiam, 'into grace, into favor'. See

adv., ingratiat-ion, п., ingratiat-ory, adj.

## ingratitade
ingratitade, n. — F., fr. L. ingratitudinem, ace. of
ingratitude, 'ingratitude', fr. ingratus. See
ingrate and -ude.

## ingravescence
ingravescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## ingravescent
ingravescent, adj., gradually increasing in gravity.
— L. ingravescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of in-

## gravescere
gravescere, 'to grow worse', fr. in-, 'in', and

## gravescere
gravescere, 'to become burdened, grow worse',
an inchoative verb formed fr: gravis. See grave,

## adj.
adj., and -escent.

## ingredient
ingredient, п., that which enters into a mixture;
component. — L. ingrediens, gen. -entis, pres.

## part
part, of ingredi, 'to go into, to enter', fr. in-,
'in', and gradi, 'to step, walk, go', fr. gradus,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:405 COLUMN:2 -->
'step'. See grade and -ent.

## ingress
ingress, п., entrance. — L. ingressus, gen. -us,
'way in, entrance', fr. ingressus, pp. οι ingredi.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: ingression (q.v.), ingress-he, adj.,
ingress-ive-ness, n.

## ingression
ingression, п., the act of entering. — L. ingressio,
gen. -onis, 'a going into', fr. ingressus, pp. of
ingredi. See prec. word and -ion.

## inguen
inguen, п., the groin (anat.) — L., 'groin,
abdomen', fr. I.-E. "i}g"en, whence also Gk. άδήν,
'gland'; cogn. with ON. okkr, 'a swelling', ok-
kvinn, 'swollen'. Cp. adeno--

## inguinal
inguinal, adj. — Medical L. inguinalis, 'of the

## inguino-
inguino-, before a vowel inguin-, combining form

inguen.

## ingurgitate
ingurgitate, tr. v., to swallow greedily. — L. in-
gurgitatus, pp. of ingurgitare, 'to pour in like a
flood; to flood, fill', fr. in-, 'in', and gurges, gen.

## ingurgitation
ingurgitation, n. — L. ingurgitatio, gen. -onis,
'immoderate eating and drinking', fr. ingurgi-
tatus, pp. of ingurgitare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## inhabit
inhabit, tr. v. — ME. enhabiten, fr. OF. enhabiter,
fr. L. inhabitare, 'to dwell in', fr. in-, 'in', and
habitare, 'to dwell'. See habit, 'to dwell'.

## inhabitancy

## inhere

## inherence
inherence, inherency, n. — Formed from next

## inherent
inherent, adj., essential, innate. — L. inhaerlns,

## inherit

п., inherit-able-ness, п., inherit-abl-y, adv.,

## inheritance

## inhesion

## inhibit
inhibit, tr. v., to prohibit; to check. — ME. in·

For the change of Latin й (in habere) to ί (in

## inhibition
inhibition, n. — OF. inibicion, inhibicion (F.

prec. word and -ion.

## inhibitory
inhibitory, adj. — ML. inhibitorins, fr. I<.

## inhibitus
inhibitus, pp. of inhibere. See inhibit and adj.

inia], adj., pertaining to the inion. — See inion

Inigo, masc. PN. — Sp. Inigo, prob. altered fr. L.

## iniquity

## initiatory
initiatory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr.

ino-, before a vowel in-, combining form meaning

inodorous, adj., odorless. — L. inodorus,

inositol, п., a white crystalline compound,
Ο,ΗϋίΟΗ)^ (спет.) — Formed from prec. word
