## insurrection
insurrection, n. — ME. insurrecioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) insurrection, fr. Late L. insurrectionem,
ace. of insurrectio, 'a rising up, insurrection',
fr. L. insurrectus, pp. ofinsurgere. See insurgent
and -ion.
Derivatives: insurrection-al, adj., insurrection-
al-ly, adv., insurrection-ary, adj.,
insurrectionist, a.

## intact
intact, adj. — L. intactus, 'untouched, uninjured,
intact', fr. in-, 'not', and tactus, pp. of tangere,
'to touch'. See tact and cp. intangible.
Derivatives: intact-ly, adv., intact-ness, n.

## intagliated
intagliated, adj., carved in intaglio. — Formed
with suff. -ed fr. It. intagliato, pp. of intagliare.
See next word.

## intaglio
intaglio, п., incised carving. — It., back formation
fr. intagliare, 'to cut in, engrave', fr. in-, 'in',
and VL. *taliare, 'to cut', fr. L. talea, 'rod, stick,
bar'. See tailor and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: intaglio, tr. v.

## intangible
intangible, adj. — ML. intangibilis, fr. in-, 'not',
and L. tangibilis. See tangible.
Derivatives: intangibil-ity, п., intangible-ness,
п., intangibl-y, adv.

## intarsia
intarsia, п., mosaic woodwork. — It. imarsio, fr.
intarsiare, 'to inlay', fr. in-, 'in', and tarsiare,
'to inlay', fr. tarsia, 'inlaid work, tarsia', fr. Arab.
tarsi', 'inlaid work', inf. of rdssa'a, 'he laid in'.

## integer
integer, adj. — L., 'undiminished, unhurt,
unimpaired, whole, complete', lit. 'untouched', fr.
*entag-ros, fr. in-, 'not', and "tag-, the stem of
tangere, 'to touch'. See tangent and cp. intact,
intangible, integrity. Cp. also entire. For the
change of Latin й (in tu-n-gere) to ё (in in-teger)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: integr-able, adj., integr-abil-ity, n.

## integral
integral, adj., 1) pertaining to a whole; 2)
necessary to completeness; п., a whole. — ME.,
fr. Late L. integralts, fr. L. integer. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -al. The word integral was
introduced into mathematics by Jacques
Bernoulli! (1654-1705), professor of mathematics
at the University of Basel.
Derivatives: integral-ity, п., integral-ly, adv.

## integrant
integrant, adj., forming a whole. — L. integrans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of integrare, 'to make
whole, renew', fr. integer. See integer and -ant.

## integrate
integrate, adj., composite; complete, whole. —
L. integralus, pp. of integrare. See next word.

## integrate
integrate, tr. v., to form a whole. — L. integralus,
pp. of integrare, 'to make whole, renew', fr.
integer. See integer and verbal suff. -ate.

## integration
integration, n. — L. integratw, gen. -onis, 'a
renewing', fr. integralus, pp. of integrare. See
integrate, v., and -km.

## integrity
integrity, п., wholeness, completeness;
uprightness. — F. integrite, fr. L. integritatem, ace. of
integritas, 'completeness, soundness, blameless-
ness', fr. integer. See integer and -ity.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:409 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: INTEGUMENT | 382 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:409 COLUMN:1 -->

## integument
integument, п., a covering. — L. integumentum,
'a covering', fr. integere, 'to cover', fr. in-, 'in',
and legere, 'to cover'. See tegument.
Derivatives: integument, tr. v., integument-al,
integument-ary, adjs., integument-ation, n.

## intellect
intellect, n. — L. intellectus, gen. -us, 'perception,
discernment, understanding', fr. intellectus, pp.
of intellegere, intelligere, 'to understand,
comprehend'. See intelligent.

## intellection
intellection, n. — L. intellectid, gen. -onis, fr.
intellectus, pp. of intellegere, intelligere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## Intellective
Intellective, adj. — F. intellectif(fem. intellective),
fr. Late L. intellectivus, 'pertaining to
discernment', fr. L. intellectus, pp. of intellegere,
intelligere. See intellect and -ive.
Derivative: intellective-ly, adv.

## intellectual
intellectual, adj. — L. inletlecluatis. 'relating to
the understanding', fr. intellectus, pp. of
intellegere, intelligere. See intellect and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: intellectual, п., intellectualism(q.v.)
intellectual-ist, п., intellectuality (q.v.), intellec-
tual-ize, v., intellectualiz-ation, п.,
intellectually, adv.

## intellectualism
intellectualism, n. — G. Intellektualismus, coined
by the German philosopher Friedrich Wilhelm
Joseph von Schelling (1775-1854) in 1803 fr.
Late L. intellectualis, 'relating to understanding',
and suff. -ismus. See intellectual and -ism.

## intellectuality
intellectuality, n. — Late L. intellectualitas,
'understanding', fr. L. intellectualis. See intellectual
and -ity.

## intelligence
intelligence, n. — F., fr. L. intellegentia, intelli-
gentia, 'power of discerning, power of
understanding, intelligence', fr. intellegens, intelligens,
gen. -entis. See next word and -ce and cp.
intelligentsia.
Derivatives: intelligence, v., intelligenc-er, n.

## intelligent
intelligent, adj. — L. intellegens, intelligins, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of intellegere, intelligere, 'to
understand, comprehend', fr. inter- and legere,
'to gather, collect; to pick out, choose; to read'.
See lecture and cp. intellect.
Derivatives: intelligent, п., intelligenl-ly, adv.

## intelligential
intelligential, adj. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. intellegentia, intelligentia. See
intelligence.

## intelligentsia
intelligentsia, п., the intellectual classes taken
collectively. — Russ. intelligentsiya, fr. It. intel-
ligenzia, fr. L. intellegentia, intelligentia. See
intelligence.

## intelligible
intelligible, adj. — L. intellegibitis, wtelligibilis,
'that can be understood', fr. intellegere,
intelligere, 'to understand, comprehend'. See
intelligent and -ible.
Derivatives: intetligibil-ity, п., intelligible-ness,
п., intelligibl-y, adv.

## intemperance
intemperance, n. — F. intemperance, fr. L. in-
temperentia, 'intemperateness, immoderation,
excess', fr. in-, 'not', and temperantia. See
temperance.

## intemperate
intemperate, adj. — L. intemperatus,
'intemperate, immoderate', fr. in-, 'not', and temperatus.
See temperate.
Derivatives: intemperate-ly, adv.,
intemperateness, n.

## intend
intend, tr. v. — ME. entenden, fr. MF. (= F.)
entendre, 'to direct one's attention' (now, 'to
hear'), fr. L. intendere, 'to stretch out, extend;
to direct, turn, bend, aim; to direct one's
attention, to apply oneself to, endeavor, intend',
fr. in-, 'in', and tendere, 'to stretch out'. See
tend, 'to move in a certain direction', and cp.
entente, superintend. Derivatives: intendant
(q.v.), intend-ed, adj., intendment (q.v.)

## inteudance
inteudance, intendancy, n. — F. intendance, fr.
intendant. See next word and -cy.

## intendant
intendant, n. — F., back formation fr. surinten-
dant, fr. ML. superintendentem, ace. of
superintended. See superintendent.

## intendment
intendment, п., ι) intention (archaic); 2) meaning
(law). — ME. entendement, it. OF. (= F.) en-
tendement, 'understanding', fr. entendre. See
intend and -merit.

## latensc
latensc, adj. — F., fr. L. intensus, a collateral
form of intentus, 'stretched out, strained, bent,
tight', pp. of intendere, 'to stretch out, extend'.
See intend.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:409 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: intense-ly, adv., intense-ness, n.

## intensification
intensification, n. — See next word and -ation.

## intensify
intensify, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -fy fr. L.
intensus, 'stretched out' (see iatense); first used by
the English poet and philosopher Samuel Taylor
Coleridge (1772-1834).
Derivative: intensifi-er, n.

## intension
intension, n. — L. intensio, gen. -onis, 'a
stretching out, straining, effort', a collateral form of
intentio, gen. -onis, fr. intentus, pp. of intendere.
See intention.
Derivatives: intension-al, adj., intension-al-ly,
adv.

## intensity
intensity, n. — Coined by the English physicist
Robert Boyle (1627-91) fr. intense and suff. -ity.

## intensive
intensive, adj. — F. inlensif (fern, intensive), fr.
ML. intensivus, fr. L. intensus, a collateral form
of intentus, pp. of intendere. See intense and -ive.
Derivatives: intensive, п., intensive-ly, adv., in-
tensive-ness, n.

## intent
intent, п., an intending; intention; purpose. —
ME. entent, fr. OF. entent, fr. L. intentus, gen..
-us, 'a stretching out, extending', fr. intentus,
pp. of intendere. See intend.

## intent
intent, adj., firmly fixed. — L. intentus, 'stretched
out, extended', pp. of intendere. See intend.
Derivatives: intent-ly, adv., intent-ness, n.

## intention
intention, n. — OF. entention, intention (F.
intention), fr, L. intentionem, ace. of intentio, 'a
stretching out, straining, exertion, effort,
attention', fr. intentus, pp. of intendere. See intend
and cp. intension, which is a doublet of intention.

## intentional
intentional, adj. — ML. intentidnalis, fr. L.
intentio, gen. -onis. See prec. word and -al.
Derivatives: intentional-ity, п., intentional-ly,
adv.

## inter
inter, prep., among, between, occurring in Latin
phrases occasionally used in English, as inter
alia, 'among other things'. — L. inter, fr. I.-E.
'enter or *nter, 'between, among', whence also
Oscan anter, Umbr. anter, ander-, OI. antar,
Avestic antar', OPers. antar, 'among, between',
OI. dntarah, 'inner, interior', antrum, 'intestine',
Toch. В etsar, 'within', Arm. 'nder-k' (pi.),
'intestines', Gk. άντερα (pi.), 'intestines', Alb.
nder, 'between, in', OSlav. qtru, 'between',
qlroba, 'entrails', jetro, 'liver', Olr. eter, etar,
etir, OW. ithr, Co. ynter, Bret, entre, 'among,
between', Goth, undar, OHG. untar, OE. under,
in the sense of 'among', ON. idrar (pi.),
'intestines'. I.-E. *en-ter, *n-ter is compar. of *en, 'in'.
See in, prep., and -ther and cp. enteric and words
there referred to. Cp. also enter, enter-, entrails,
entr'acte, entre-, interior.

## inter
inter, tr. v., to bury. — ME. enterren, fr. MF.
(= F.) enterrer, fr. VL. *interrare, 'to place in
the earth', fr. in-, 'in, into', and terra, 'earth';
see terra; influenced in form by VL. *interrdre.
Derivative: inter-ment, n.

## inter-
inter-, pref. meaning 'among, between'. — L., fr.
inter. See inter, prep.

## interact
interact, п., interval between two acts. — Formed
fr. inter- and act, n. on analogy of F. entr'acte
(see entr'acte).

## interact
interact, intr. v., to act on each other. — Formed
fr. inter- and act, v.
Derivatives: interact-ion, п., interact-ive, adj.

## intercalary
intercalary, adj., inserted in the calendar. — L.
inlercalarius or intercalaris, it. intercalare. See
next word and adj. suff. -ary.

## intercalate
intercalate, tr. v., to insert (a day or a month)·
in the calendar. — L. intercalatus, pp. of
intercalare, 'to proclaim the insertion of an
intercalary day', etc., fr. inter- and calare, 'to call
out, proclaim'. See calendar and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: intercalation (q.v.), intercalat-ive,
intercalat-ory, adjs.

## intercalation
intercalation, n. — L. intercalated, gen. -onis,
'insertion of an intercalary day', fr. intercalatus,
pp. of intercalare. See prec. word and -ion.

## intercede
intercede, intr. v., to plead on behalf of. — L.
intercldere, 'to go between, intervene,
interpose, interfere', fr. inter- and cedere, 'to go,
depart'. See cede.

## intercept
intercept, tr. v. — L. interceptus, pp. of inter-
cipere, 'to seize while passing; to interrupt', fr.
inter- and capere (pp. captus), 'to catch, seize,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:409 COLUMN:3 -->
take hold of. See captive. For the change of
Latin й (in captus) to ё (in inter-ciptus) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: intercept-er, intercept-or, п.,
interception (q.v.), intercept-ive, adj.

## interception
interception, n. — L. intercepted, gen. -onis, 'a
seizing, taking away', fr. interceptus, pp. of in-
tercipere. See prec. word and -ion.

## intercession
intercession, n. — L. intercessio, gen. -onis, 'a
going between, intervention', fr. intercess-'um),
pp. stem of intercedere. See intercede and -km.
Derivative: intercession-al, adj.

## intercessor
intercessor, n. — L., 'one who intervenes', fr.
intercess-(um), pp. stem of intercedere. See
intercede and agential suff. -or.
Derivative: intercessor-ial, adj.

## intercessory
intercessory, adj, — ML. intercessorius, fr. L.
intercess-(um), pp. stem of intercedere. See
intercede and adj. suff. -ory.

## interchauge
interchauge, tr. and intr. v. — ME. entrechangen,
fr. OF. entechangier, fr. entre- (fr. L. inter-) and
ckangier, 'to change' (see inter- and change, v.),
remodeled after L. inter-.
Derivatives: interchange-able, adj., inlerchange-
abil-ity, п., interchange-able-ness,o., inlerchange-
abl-y, adv.

## iuterchange
iuterchange, n. — OF. entrechange, fr. entre-
changier. See interchange, v.

## intercolumniation
intercolumniation, п., the space between two
columns (archit.) — Formed with suff. -ation
fr. L. intercolumnium, 'the space between two
columns', fr. inter- and columna. See column.

## intercourse
intercourse, n. — ME. intercurse, fr. OF. entre-
cours, 'exchange, commerce', fr. Late L. inter-
cursus (gen. -us), 'a running between or amongst',
fr. L. intercursus, pp. of intercurrere, 'to run
between or amongst', fr. inter- and currere, 'to
run' (see current, adj.); remodeled after L.
intercursus.

## interdict
interdict, n. — ME. entredit, fr. OF. entredit, fr.
L. interdictum, 'prohibition, interdict', prop,
neut. pp. of interdicere, 'to forbid, prohibit,
interdict', fr. inter- and dicere, 'to say'; see
diction. F. interdit and E. interdict have been
remodeled after L. interdictum.

## interdict
interdict, tr. v. — ME. entrediten, fr. entredit,
'interdict'. See interdict, n.

## interdiction
interdiction, n. — L. interdictio, gen. -onis,
'prohibition, interdiction', fr. interdictus, pp. of
interdicere. See interdict, v. and п., and -ion.

## interdictory
interdictory, adj. — ML. interdictorius,
'pertaining to an interdict', fr. L. interdictum. See
interdict, п., and adj. suff. -ory.

## interdigitate
interdigitate, intr. v., to interlock like the fingers
of the two hands. — Formed fr. inter-, L.
digitus, 'finger' (see digit), and verbal suff. -ate.

## interest
interest, n. — ME., altered fr. earlier interess, fr.
AF. interesse, fr. ML. interesse, 'interest', prop,
subst. use of L. interesse, 'to be between, lie
between; to take part in; to import, be of
interest', fr. inter- and esse, 'to be'; see esse. The
alteration of earlier E. interess to interest is
prob. due to the influence of OF. interest
(whence F. interet), 'interest', a word derived fr.
L. interest, 'it imports, it is of interest', which
was, however, taken for a noun in the sense
of 'that which imports or is of interest'. Cp. G.
Interesse, 'interest', which also derives fr. ML.
interesse (see above).

## interest
interest, tr. v. — Fr. interess'd, pp. of earlier
English interess, 'interest'. See interest, n.
Derivatives: interest-ed, adj., interest-ed-ly, п.,
interest-ed-ness, п., interest-ing, adj.,
interestingly, adv., interest-ing-ness, n.

## interfere
interfere, intr. v. — OF. s'entreferir, 'to strike
each other', fr. entre, 'between', and ferir (F.
ferir), 'to strike', fr. L. ferire, 'to strike, smite',
which stands in gradational relationship to
forare, 'to bore, piece', and is cogn. with OE.
borian, 'to bore': see inter- and nore, v. E.
interfere was remodeled after L. inter-.
Derivatives: interfer-ence, п., interferent-ial,
adj., interfer-er, a., interfer-ing, adj., interfer-
ing-ly, adv., interfer-ing-ness, n.

## iaterferometer
iaterferometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the interference of light waves. — A hybrid
coined from interfere, a word of Latin origin,
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poet-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:410 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 383 | INTERREGNUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:410 COLUMN:1 -->
ical rhythm'.

## interfuse
interfuse, tr. and intr. v. — L. interfusus, pp. of
interfundere, 'to pour between, flow between',
fr. inter- and fundere, 'to pour'. See found, 'to
cast', and cp. words there referred to.

## interfusion
interfusion, n. — L. interfusio, gen. -onis, 'a
flowing between', fr. interfusus, pp. of interfundere.
See prec. word and -Ion.

## interglacial
interglacial, adj., pertaining to, or occurring in,
a period between two glacial epochs. — Coined
by the Swiss naturalist Oswald Heer (1809-83)
in 1865 fr. inter- and glacial.

## interim
interim, п., meantime. — L. interim, adv.,
'meanwhile', formed fr. inter, 'between' (see inter,
prep.), with adv. suff. -im, which derives from
the pronominal base *i- (whence also is, ea, id,
'he, she, it'). Cp. OL. im, em (= L. eum), 'him',
and see idem.
Derivative: interim, adj., temporary.

## interior
interior, adj. — L. interior, 'inner, within', corn-
par, of "interus, 'on the inside, inward' (cp.
intra,''within'), which itself is compar. of in,
'in'. See inter, prep., and -lor and cp. intra-,
intro-.
Derivatives: interior, п., interior-ly, adv.

## interjacent
interjacent, adj., lying between; intervening. —
L. interjacens, gen. -entis, 'lying between', pres.
part, of interjacere, 'to lie between', fr. inter-
and jacere, 'to lie', which orig. meant 'to cast
oneself down', fr, jacio, jacere, 'to throw, cast,
hurl'. See jet, 'to spirt forth', and -ent and cp.
adjacent and words there referred to. Cp. also
next word.

## interject
interject, tr. v. — L. interjectus, pp. of inxericere
(less correctly interjicere), 'to throw between,
insert; to intersect', fr. inter- and jacere (pp.
jactus), 'to throw'. See prec. word. For the
change of Latin α (in jactus) to ё (in inter-jectus)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: interjection (q.v.), interject-ory, adj.

## interjection
interjection, n. — F., fr. L. interjectionem, ace. of
interjectio, 'a throwing between, insertion;
interjection', fr. interjectus, pp. of intericere. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: interjection-al, adj.,
interjection-ally, adv., interjection-ary, adj.

## interlace
interlace, tr. and intr. v. — ME. entrelacen, fr. MF.
(= F.) entrelacer (see entre-, inter- and lace,
v.); remodeled after L. inter-.
Derivatives: interlace, п., interlac-ed, adj., inter-
lac-ed-ly, adv., interlace-ment, п., interlac-ery, ft.

## interlard
interlard, tr. v., to insert between, mix. — F.
entrelarder, 'to insert between' (see entre-, inter-
and lard); remodeled after L. inter-,

## iaterline
iaterline, tr. and intr. v. — ME. enterlinen, fr.
ML. interlineare, 'to interline', fr. inter- and L.
linea, 'line' (see line and cp. next word);
remodeled after L. inter-.

## interlinear
interlinear, adj. — ML. interlinedris, 'that which
is between the lines'. See inter- and linear.

## interlineation
interlineation, n. — Formed with suff. -ation fr.
ML. interlineatus, pp. of interlineare. See
interline.

## interlocution
interlocution, n. — L. interlocutio, gen. -onis, 'a
speaking between, interlocution', fr. interlocu-
tusr pp. of interloqui, 'to interrupt in speaking',
lit. 'to speak between', fr. inter- and loqui, 'to
speak'. See loquacious and cp. locution.
■uterlocutor, n. — Formed with agential suff. -or
fr. intertocutus, pp. of interloqui. See prec. word.

## Interlocutory
Interlocutory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory
fr. L. interlocutus, pp. of interloqui. See
interlocution.

## interlocutress
interlocutress, n. — See Interlocutor and -ess.

## interlocutrix
interlocutrix, п., an interlocutress. — See
interlocutor and -trix.

## interlope
interlope, intr. v. — Back formation fr.
interloper.

## interloper
interloper, п., an intruder. — Fr. earlier enter-
loper, which is prob. a hybrid coined fr. enter-
(fr. L. inter-) and Du. loper, 'runner', fr. lopen,
'to run'; see leap and cp. lope and words there
referred to. E. interloper was remodeled after
L. inter-.

## interlude
interlude, n. — ME. enterlude, fr. ML. interlu-
dium, 'interlude', fr. inter- and L. Indus, 'play'
(see ludicrous); remodeled after L. inter-.
Derivatives: interlude, v., interlud-ial, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:410 COLUMN:2 -->

## intermediary
intermediary, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ary
fr. L. intermedius. See next word.
Derivative: intermediary, n.

## intermediate
intermediate, adj1. — ML. intermediatus, 'lying
between, intermediate', fr. L. intermedius, 'that
which is between, intermediate', fr. inter- and
medius, 'middle'. See medium and adj. suff. -ate
and cp. mediate, immediate. Cp. also intermezzo.
Derivatives: intermediate, intr. v.,
intermediately, adv., inlermediat-ion, п., intermediat-or, n.

## intermedium
intermedium, п., an intermediate agent; medium.
— ModL., neut. of intermedius. See prec. word,

## intermezzo
intermezzo, п., a short dramatic performance
between the acts of a play or opera. — It., fr.
L. intermedius. See intermediate.

## interminable
interminable, adj. — Late L. interminabilis (prob.
through the medium of F. interminable). See
in-, 'not', and terminable.
Derivatives: inierminabil-ity, п., interminable-
ness, п., interminabl-y, adv.

## intermission
intermission, n. — L. intermissio, gen. -onis, 'a
breaking up, interruption', fr. intermissus, pp.
of intermittere. See next word and -ion.

## intermit
intermit, tr. and intr. v., to interrupt. — L.
intermittere, 'to leave off, break up, omit, neglect;
to cease, pause', fr. inter- and mittere, 'to send'.
See mission.
Derivatives: intermitt-ed, adj., intermitt-ed-ly,
adv., intermittent (q.v.), intermitt-ing, adj.,
intermitt-ing-ly, adv.

## intermlttence
intermlttence, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ее.

## intermittent
intermittent, adj. — L. intermittens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of intermittere. See intermit and -ent.
Derivative: intermittent-ly, adv.

## intermix
intermix, tr. and intr. v. — Back formation fr.
intermix!, which derives fr. L. intermixtus,
'intermixed', but was mistaken for the pp. of
an English verb (i.e. intermixt was supposed to
have been formed from the verb intermix and
the pp. suff. -()■ L. intermixtus is pp. of inter-
miscere, 'to intermix', lit. 'to mix among', fr.
iater-, and miscere, 'to mix'. See mixed and cp.
mix, admix, commix.
Derivative: intermix-ture, n.

## intern
intern, adj., internal (archaic). — F. interne,
'inward, internal, resident within', fr. L. inlernus,
'inward, internal', fr. *interus, 'on the inside,
inward'. See interior and cp. internal. Cp. also
extern.

## intern
intern, also interne, п., a resident physician in a
hospital. — F. interne, fr. interne, adj. See
latent, adj.

## intern

ν„international-iz-ation, п., international-ly, adv.

Internationale, п., ι) the same as International;

Derivative: interpretation-al, adj.

## interpretative
interpretative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr.
L. interpretatus. pp. of interpretari. See interpret.
Derivative: interprelative-ly, adv.

## interpreter
interpreter, n. — ME. interpretour, fr. OF.
interpreter, fr. Late L. interpretatorem, ace. of
interpretator, 'explainer, interpreter', fr. L.

interpretatus, pp. of interpretari, 'to explain,

interregnum, п., time between two reigns. — L.

interrogation, n. — L. rnterrogatid, gen. -onis,

interstice, п., an imei'vening space, interval. —

## invertase

into fruit sugar (biochem.) — Coined by the
German chemist Emil Fischer (1852-1919) from
the stem of L. invertere, 'to turn about' (see

('converting ferment'), a name given to this ferment by
the French physiologist Claude Bernard
(1813-78).

1832) in [805 (in Lecons d'anatomiecomparee).

involucre, involucrum, п., ι) a covering (esp. a

## iodine
iodine, п., name of a nonmetallic element
belonging to the halogen family (chem.) — Formed

(1778-1829) fr. F. iode, 'iodine' (to make the
name of this element equal in ending to chlorine
and fluorine), which was coined by its
discoverer, the French chemist Bernard Courtois
(1777-1838), in r8u fr. Gk. ίοειδής, 'like a
violet', fr. tov, 'violet', and -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'; so called by him from
the color of its vapor. See iolite and -oid. For
the ending see chem. suff. -ine.

## iodoform

A blend of iodine and chloroform.

## iolite
iolite, п., a blue mineral. — G. Iolit, coined by

Abraham Gottlob Werner (1750-1817) in 1810 fr.
Gk. tov, 'violet', and λί&ος, 'stone'. Gk. ϊον
is prob. a Mediterranean loan word. Cp. the
first element in Janthine and the second element
in Leucojum. Cp. also violet. For Gk. λίθος
see -lite, litho-,

## ion

compound is decomposed through electrolysis.
— Gk. ϊον, neut. of ϊων, 'going', pres. part, of
Uvea, 'to go', fr. I.-E. base *i-, 'to go', whence
also L. ire, 'to go', iter (gen. itineris), 'a journey';
see itinerate. The word ion was introduced into
electricity by the English physicist and chemist
Michael Faraday (1791-1867); cp. anion, cation.

-ion). Cp. -ation, -ition.

Akkad. lamanu, Iavanu, Egypt. Ylv"na, Y'-
vanna, 'Greek'. Cp. also OI. Yavanah, OPers.
Yauna, 'Greek', OI. yavanika, 'Greek woman';
'curtain (in the theater)', lit. 'Greek (partition)'.

iota, п., the 9th letter of the Greek alphabet. —

## ipecuc
ipecuc, n. — Shortened fr. ipecucnanha.

## ipecacuanha
ipecacuanha, п., the dried root of a S. American

## Iphigenia
Iphigenia, п., the daughter of Agamemnon and

Ις, 'sinew, tendon; muscle, fiber', and γένος,

## Ipomoea
Ipomoea, п., a genus of plants, the morning glory

Ιπάς, 'a kind of worm', which is possibly rel.
to Ιψκσθαι, 'to press hard, oppress', and δμοιος,
'like'. See homeo-.

## ipse dixit
ipse dixit, п., dictum. — L., 'he himself has said

used by the disciples of Pythagoras when
quoting their master. See next word and diction.

## ipseity
ipseity, п., selfhood. — Formed from L. ipse,
'himself, contraction of *is-pse, fr. is, 'he' (see
idem), and the emphatic panicle -pse (= Gk.
-ψέ). For the ending see suff. -ity. Cp. the second

## ir-
ir-, assimilated form of in-, 'in', before r.

## ir-
ir-, assimilated form of in-, 'not', before r.

## Ira
Ira, masc. PN. (Bible) — Heb. 'Ira, lit.

oneself", rel. to Aram.-Syr. 'ur, 'to be awake',
Aram, 'fr, 'awake', Bibl.-Aram. 'ir, 'angel',
Arab, 'dra (base Ό-y-r), 'was awake', ghara
(stem gh-y-r), 'he was jealous', Akkad. era, 'to
be awake, to watch'.

## irade
irade, n„ written decree of a Mohammedan ruler
formerly, a written decree of the Sultan of
Turkey. — Turkish, fr. Arab. irddah, 'will',
verbal noun of ardda, 'he wished, wanted to',

## Iran
Iran, п., Persia. — Pers. Iran, fr. OPers. ariya,

Derivatives: Iran-ian, adj. and n.

## irascible
irascible, adj. — ME., fr. F. irascible, fr. L.

Derivatives: irascibil-ity, п., irascible-ness, п.,
irascibl-y, adv.

## irate
irate, adj. — L. Trdtus, 'angry, enraged, violent,

## ire
ire, п., anger. — OF., fr. L. ira, 'anger', which
prob. stands for *eisa and is cogn. with Avestic

isnati, isyati, 'sets in motion', isanyali, 'stirs up,

ίαίνειν (for "ισάνιειν), 'to warm, heat, cheer,
refresh', ON. eisa, 'to hasten forward'. Cp. hiero-,

Derivatives: ire-ful, adj., ire-ful-ly, adv., ire-
ful-ness, n.

## Irene
Irene, fern. PN. — F. Irene, fr. L. Irene, fr. Gk.
Ειρήνη, lit. 'peace'. See next word.

## irenic
irenic, irenical, adj., promoting peace. — Gk.
εΙρηνικός, 'peaceful, peaceable', fr. ειρήνη,
'peace', a word of unknown etymology. Cp.
Irene.
Derivatives: irenical-ly, adv., irenic-ism, п.,
irenic-isl, n.

## irenicon
irenicon, n. — See eirenicon.

## Iresine
Iresine, п., a genus of plants of the amaranth

wreath of olive wound round with wool', fr.
είρος, 'wool', which is rel. to έριον, 'wool' (see

## Iridaceae
Iridaceae, n. pi., the iris family (bot.) — ModL.,

## iridaceous
iridaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Iridescence
Iridescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## iridescent
iridescent, adj., showing rainbowlike colors. —

Lit. 'rainbow colored', formed with suff. -escent
fr. L. Iris, gen. iridis (fr. Gk. Ιρις, gen. Ιριδος),
'rainbow' (see iris).
Derivative: iridescent-ly, adv.

## iridium
iridium, п., name of a silverwhite metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., coined by its discoverer, the
English chemist Smithson Tennant (1761-1Ϊ15),
fr. Gk. ΐρις, gen. {ριδος, 'rainbow' (see iris),

Derivatives: irid-ate, п., irid-ious, adj., irid-ite,

## irido-
irido-, before a vowel irid-, combining form

## iris
iris, п., ι) the rainbow; 2) the colored portion of
the eye. — L. iris, fr. Gk. Τρις, 'the rainbow',
orig. form "Ήρις, lit. 'something bent or curved',
fr. I.-E. base *wei-, 'to bend, twist', whence also
Gk. ϊτυς, Aeol. *Γίτυς, 'the edge or rim of
anything', ί/τέα, 'willow', L. viere, 'to bend, twist',
OE. widig, 'willow'. See withy and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also orris, 'the Florentine

## Ms
Ms, п., the goddess of the rainbow in Greek
mythology. — L. Iris, fr. Gk. *1ρις, personification

## Irish
Irish, adj. and n. — ME., fr. OE. *Irisc, fr. Iras,

## iritis
iritis, п., inflammation of the iris of the eye (med.)

## irk
irk, tr. v., to vex, annoy. — ME. irken, yrken,

Derivatives: irk-some, adj., irk-some-ness, n.

## lrma
lrma, fern. PN. — A var. of Erma, which is a

## iron
iron, n. — ME. iren, iron, fr. OE. ise(r)n, iren, rel.
to OS. isarn, ON. isarn, jam, OFris. lser(n),
MDu. iser, Du. ijzer, OHG. Isarn, isan, MHG.
Isern, iser, isen, G. Eisen, Goth, eisarn, isarn.
These words, as well as the Gaul. PN. Isarno- and
Olr. iarann, iarn, W. haiarn, OCo. hoern, 'iron',
are prob. Ulyrian loan words, and orig. denoted
the 'strong' metal (in contradistinction to the
softer bronze). Cp. OI. isirah, 'vigorous, strong',
Gk. Ιερός, 'strong', and see ire.
Derivatives: iron, adj. and v., iron-er, п.,
ironing, п., irony (q.v.)
Iron Curtain. — Coined by Winston Churchill in
1946 (in a speech at Fulton, Mo., U.S.A.)

## ironic
ironic, also ironical, adj. — Late L. irdnicus, fr.

Derivative: ironical-ly, adv.

## ironmold
ironmold, n. — Altered fr. iron mole by folk

See iron and mole, 'spot'.
Derivative: ironmold, tr. and intr. v.

## irony
irony, n. — L. irdriia, fr. Gk. είρωνείϊ, 'irony',

See word and cp. rhetor. Cp. also verb.

## irony
irony, adj. — Formed fr. iron with adj. suff. -y.

irradiance, irradiancy, n. — Formed from next

irradiant, adj. — L. irradians, gen. -amis, pres.

## irradiation
irradiation, n. — F., fr. Late L. irradiationem,

rational-ist, п., irrational-ist-ic, adj.,

irrationality, п., irrational-ize, tr. v., irrational-ly, adv.

irrefrangible, adj., 1) that cannot be broken;

irreverence, n. — L. irreverentia, 'want of

irreverent, adj. — L. irreverens, gen. -entis,

## irrevocable
irrevocable, adj. — L. irremeabilis, 'that cannot

vocabilis. See revocable. Derivatives:
irrevocability, п., irrevocabte-ness, п., irrevocabt-y, adv.

## irrigate
irrigate, tr. v., to water. — L. irrigatus, pp. of

irrigative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.

## irritable
irritable, adj. — L. irritubilis, 'easily excited', fr.

irritancy, п., the act of rendering null and void

and void', and -ant.

irritate, tr. v., to anger. — L. irritatus, pp. of

## irritate
irritate, tr. v., to make null and void (law). —
L. irritatus, pp. of irritare, 'to make void,
invalidate', fr. irrltus, 'invalid, void', formed fr.

suff. -ate. For the change of Latin й (in ratus)

## irritation
irritation, n. — L. irrttdtio, gen. -onis,

## irrupt
irrupt, intr. v. — Back formation fr. irruption.

irruption, n. — L. irruptio, gen. -onis, 'a breaking

## irruptive
irruptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.

## is
is, v., 3rd sing. pres. indie, of be. — Rel. to OHG.,
MHG., G., Goth. is-t, ON. es, er, 'is', fr. I.-E.
*es-ti, whence also OI. asti, Gk. εστί, L. est,
Oscan-Umbr. est, Lith. esti, OSlav. jestl, Olr.

and cp. am, art, are and the 2nd element in yes.

## is-
is-, form of iso- before a vowel.

Isaac, i) masc. PN; г) in the Bible, one of the

father of Jacob and Esau. — Late L., fr. Gk.
Ίσοίάκ, fr. Heb. Yitzlfaq, lit. 'he laughs', prop,
imperf. of tzahaq, 'he laughed', which is rel. to
Aram.-Syr. g*bekh, Arab, daliika, 'he laughed'.

## Isabel
Isabel, fern. PN. — Sp. See Isabella.

## isabelita

## Isabella
Isabella, fern. PN. — Sp. Isabel, altered fr.

## Isabella
Isabella, п., a brownish yellow color. — Fr. prec.

## isabelline
isabelline, adj., of the color Isabella. — Formed

## isagoge
isagoge, п., an introduction. — L. Isagoge, fr.
Gk. είσαγωγή, 'introduction', which is formed

fr. είς, 'into', and αγωγή, 'a leading, carrying',
fr. άγειν, 'to lead'. Gk. εις stands for 'ens and

## isagogic
isagogic, adj., introductory. — L. isagogicus, fr.

## isagogics
isagogics, п., introduction; esp., introduction

## Isaiah
Isaiah, i) masc. PN.; 2) name of the great

Heb. Y'sha'yah, shortened fr. Y'sha'yahu, lit.

## Isanthous
Isanthous, adj., having regular flowers. — Formed

## Isanthus
Isanthus, п., a genus of plants, the false

## isatin

## Isatis
Isatis, п., a genus of plants of the mustard family

isha, п., a hut. — Russian, fr. OSlav. istuba, a

## isch-

compounded of ϊσχειν, 'to keep back', and
αΤχμα, 'blood'. See ischo- and -emia.

## ischi-

## ischiadic
ischiadic, adj., ischial. — L. ischiadicus, fr. Gk.
ίσχιαδικός, 'pertaining to the hip', fr. ίσχίαν.
See ischium and cp. sciatic,

## ischial
ischial, adj., pertaining to the hip. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. ischium. See ischium,

ischialgia, п., sciatica. — ModL., lit. 'pains in

## ischiatic
ischiatic, adj., ischial. — ML. ischiaticus, altered

## ischio-
ischio-, before a vowel ischi-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining to the hip'. — Gk. Ισχίο-,

ischium, п., the seat bone (anat.) — L., fr. Gk.
Ισχίον, 'hipjoint', in pi. 'the hips', prob. formed
fr. ΐσχι (Hesychius), 'loin', which is of uncertain
origin. It is prob. not cogn. with OI. sakthi,
'thigh'; see Frisk, GEW., I, p. 741 s.v. Ισχίον.
Ср. ischiadic, sciatic, and the first element in
icebone.

## ischo-
ischo-, before a vowel isch-, combining form
meaning 'checking, suppression, deficiency'
(med.) — Gk. ίσχο-, ίσχ-, fr. ίσχειν, 'to keep
back, restrain, check, stop', reduplicated form
of έχειν, 'to have, hold, possess'. See hectic
and cp. words there referred to.

## -ise
-ise, suff. forming nouns denoting quality,
condition or function. — OF. and F. -ise, fr. L.

## -itia
-itia,-itia, -ilium, -icium. Suff. -ise is the regular
form for the ending of nouns formed in French
itself (e.g. in franchise, merchandise). French
and English nouns borrowed directly from
Latin are usually spelled -ice (as justice, service).
See the suffixes -ice and cp. 2nd -ess.

## -ise
-ise, verbal suff. — See -ize.

## -ish
-ish, adj. suff. — ME. -isch, -ish, -issh, fr. OE.

## -ise
-ise, rel. to OS., OFris., OHG. ise, ON. -iskr,

## Du.
Du., G. -isch, Goth. -Mi, and cogn. with Gk.
-ισκος. Ср. -esqne.

## -ten
-ten, verbal suff. — ME. -ischen, -ishen, -issen, fr.

## OF.
OF., F. -is, -iss-, occurring in the pres. part, and

## some other forms of certain French verbs in -ir
some other forms of certain French verbs in -ir,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:415 COLUMN:3 -->
and corresponding to the Latin inchoative suff.
-ise-. E.g. the E. verb finish derives fr. F. je finis,
Ί finish', fr. VL. *finisco, an inchoative verb
formed fr. L. finio, Ί finish'. Cp. the verbs
abolish, cherish, furnish, polish, punish, etc.

## Ishmael
Ishmael, п., son of Abraham and Hagar (Bible);
used in a figurative sense to denote an outcast
(see Gen. 16:12) — Heb. Yishma'il, lit. 'God
hears'. Heb. yishma', 'he will hear', is imperf.
of shama*, 'he heard'. See Shema and cp. Simeon,
Simon. For the second element in the name
Ishmael see El and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: Ishmael-ite, n.

## Ishtar
Ishtar, п., the chief goddess of the Assyrians and
Babylonians, the counterpart of the Phoenician
Astarte. — Akkad. Ishtar. See Ashtoreth.

## Ishvara
Ishvara, Isvara, п., a title given to Siva (Hindu
mythol.) — OI. isvarah, 'ruler, lord', fr. isah,
'owner, lord', fr. is-, 'to have, possess', which
is rel. to Avestic is-, 'riches, fortune', Isvan,
'well off, rich', fr. I.-E. base *aiic-, 'to own',
whence Goth, aigan, OE. agan, 'to have,
possess'. See owe and cp. Ixora.

## Isiac
Isiac, adj., pertaining to the Egyptian goddess
Isis or her cult. — L. Jsiacus, fr. Gk. *Ισιακός,
fr. Τοις. See Isis.

## Isidore
Isidore, masc. PN. — F., fr. L. Isidorus, fr. Gk.
ΧΙσίδωρος, lit. 'gift of Isis', compounded of
Τσις, 'Isis', and δώρον, 'gift'. See Isis and
donation.

## isinglass
isinglass, п., a gelatinous substance prepared
from the airbladders of certain fishes. —
Corruption of obsol. Du. huizenblas, fr. MDu. huus-
blase, fr. huus, 'sturgeon', which is rel. to OHG.
huso, of s.m., and blase (— Du. blaas),
'bladder', which is rel. to OHG. blasa, of s.m.,
bldsan, 'to blow'. For the first element see huso,
for the second see blast and cp. bladder.

## Isis
Isis, п., an Egyptian goddess, sister and wife of
Osiris. — L. his, fr. Gk. Τοις.

## Islam
Islam, n. — Arab, islam, 'submitting oneself to
God, surrender, obedience', infin. of aslama,
'he surrendered, submitted', IV (= causative)
conjugation of salima, 'he was safe'. See salaam
and cp. selamlik, Moslem, Mussulman. Cp. also
shalom. Derivatives: Islam-ic, adj., Islam-ism,
п., Islam-ite, n.

## islaud
islaud, n. — ME. Hand, fr. OE. egland, Igland,
iegland, 'island', which is compounded of eg, tg,
ieg, 'island', and land, 'land', and rel. to ON.
eyland, OFris. eiland, 'island'. The first element
of these words is rel. to OE. ёа, 'water, river',
ON. a, 'river', ey, 'island', Norw. ey, Swed. 6,
Dan. 0, 'island', MLG. age, 6ch, ouwe, ou, OHG.
aha, 'river', OHG. auwia, ouwa, MHG. ouwe,
'island, damp meadow', G. Aue. Au, 'meadow
watered by a brook, brook, a small island',
Goth, aha, 'water, river', and cogn. with L. aqua,
'water'. See aquatic and words there referred to
and cp. esp. eyot. For the second element in
island see land. The spelling of island was
influenced by a confusion with isle.
Derivatives: island, tr. v., island-er, n.

## isle
isle, п., an island. — OF. isle (F. He), fr. L.
insula, 'island', which is of uncertain origin.
Following the ancients, some modern philologists
derive L. insula fr. in salo, 'that which is in the
sea', fr. in, 'in', and abl. of solum, 'the open sea,
the high sea', which is cogn. with Mir. sal (gen.
saile), 'sea:; cp. Gk. έν-αλος, έν-άλιος, 'in the
sea', fr. έν, 'in', and αλς, gen. αλός (masc), 'salt';
(fern), 'sea'. Cp. islet and
insular,isolate,peninsula.

## islet
islet, п., a very small island. — MF. islette (F.
itette), dimin. of isle, 'island'. See prec. word
and -et.

## -ism
-ism, subst. suff. denoting 1) action; 2) state,
condition; 3) usage, characteristic; 4) doctrine.
— F. -isme, fr. L. -isma, fr. Gk. -ισμα, which is
formed from the stem of verbs in -ίζειν. See
-ize and -ma and cp. -ist.

## ism
ism, п., a doctrine or system (usually derisive). —
Back formation from words ending in -ism.
Derivative: ism-y, adj.

## iso-
iso-, before a vowel is-, combining form meaning
'equal'. — Gk. ίσο-, ίσ-, fr. 'ίσος, 'equal', which
possibly stands for *Κτσ-ίο-ς (ср. Cretan
FiaFoQ, 'equal'), and is rel. to Gk. είδος (for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:416 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 389 | ITALIC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:416 COLUMN:1 -->
*ΓεΐδΌς), 'form, shape', ιδέα (prob. for *f ι8έσϊ),
'form, kind, nature'. See idea and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also aniso-.

## isohar
isohar, п., a line connecting places on the earth's
surface having the same barometric pressure at
a given time or for a given period (meleorol.) —
Compounded of iso- and Gk. βάρος, 'weight'.
See baro-. Derivative: isobar-ic, adj.

## isobath
isobath, adj., having the same depth. — Gk.
Ισοβαρής, 'of equal depth', compounded of
ίσος, 'equal', and βάθος, 'depth'. See iso- and
bathos. Derivative: isobath-ic, adj.

## isocephalic
isocephalic, adj., having the heads of the
principal figures at about the same level (art). —
Gk. ίσοκέφαλος, 'like-headed', compounded of
ίσος, 'equal', κεφαλή, 'head', and suff. -ic. See
iso- and cephalic. .
Derivatives: isocephal-ism, п., isocephal-y, n.

## isocheimc
isocheimc, isochime, п., a line connecting places
on the earth's surface having the same mean
winter temperature (phys. geogr.) —
Compounded of iso- and Gk. χεΐμα, 'winter'. See
chimera and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: isoch(e)im-al, isoch(e)im-ic, adjs.

## isochromatic
isochromatic, adj., having the same color (optics).
— Compounded of iso- and Gk. χρωματικός,
'relating to color'. See chromatic.

## isochronal
isochronal, isochronous, adj., equal in time. —
Gk. ισόχρονος, 'equal in time, contemporary,
regular', compounded of ίσος, 'equal' (see iso-),
and χρόνος, 'time' (see chronic), and adj. suff.
-al, resp. -ous.

## isoclinal
isoclinal, isoclinic, adj., having the same
inclination (magnetism). — Compounded of iso-, Gk.
κλίνειν, 'to incline' (see clinic), and adj. suff.
-al, resp. -ic.

## isocracy
isocracy, п., equal power. — Gk. Ισοκρατία,
'equality of power', compounded of Εσος, 'equal',
and -κρατία, 'rule of, fr. κράτος, 'strength,
power, rule'. See iso- and -cracy and cp. words
there referred to,

## isocryme
isocryme, п., a line connecting points on the
earth's surface at which the temperature is the
same during a specified coldest period of the
year. — Compounded of iso- and Gk. κρϋμός
(for *κρυσ-μός), 'frost', which is rel. to κρύος
(for *κρύσος), 'frost', and cogn. with L. crusta,
'crust'. See crust and cp. cryo-.

## Isoetaceae
Isoetaceae, n. pi., the quillwort family (bot.) —
ModL., formed from next word with suff.
-aceae.

## Isoetes
Isoetes, п., a genus of plants, the quillwort (bot.)
— L,- isoetes, name of a plant mentioned by
Pliny, prob. denoting the houseleek, fr. Gk.
Ισοετές, name- of an evergreen plant, prop,
neuter of ίσοετής, 'that whose duration equals
a year', fr. ίσος, 'equal', and ίτος, 'year'. For
the first element see iso-, for the second see
veteran.

## isogenous
isogenous, adj., of the same origin (biol.) —
Compounded of iso- and Gk. γεν-, the stem of
γενναν, 'to beget, bring forth, generate,
produce'. See -genous.

## isogonic
isogonic, adj., having, or pertaining to, equal
angles. — Compounded of iso- and Gk. γωνία,
'angle, corner'. See -gon and -ic.
Derivative: isogonic, n.

## isolate
isolate, tr. v., to insulate. — Back formation frorn
the participial adjective isolated, fr. F. isole, fr.
It. isolato, pp. of isolare, 'to isolate', fr. isola,
'island', fr. L. insula. See isle and verbal suff.
-ate and cp. insulate, which is a doublet of
isolate.

## isolation
isolation, n. — F., fr. isoler, back formation fr.
isole, fr. It. isolato. See prec. word and -ion.

## Isold
Isold, fem. PN. — OF. Isolt, Iseut; of OHG.
origin and lit. meaning 'ice rule', fr. OHG. is,
'ice', and waltan, 'to rule'. For the first element
see ice, for the second see wield and cp. words
there referred to.

## Isoloma
Isoloma, п., a genus of plants of the gesneria
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of iso-
and Gk. λώμα, 'fringe, border'. See loma and
cp. words there referred to.

## isomer
isomer, п., a compound isomeric with one or
more compounds (chem.) — See isomeric.

## isomeric
isomeric, adj., compounded of the same elements
in the same proportion by weight, but differing

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:416 COLUMN:2 -->
in one or more properties (chem) — Formed
after G. isomerisch, a word coined by the
Swedish chemist Jons Jakob Berzelius (1779-1848)
fr. Gk. Ισομερής, 'composed of equal parts', fr.
ίσος, 'equal', and μέρος, 'part'. See iso-, mero-
and -ic.

## isometric
isometric, adj., of the same measure;
characterized by equality of measure. — Formed with
suff. -ic fr. Gk. ισόμετρος, 'of equal measure',
fr. ίσος, 'equal' and μέτρον, 'measure'. See iso-
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: isometric, п., isometric-al, adj.,
isometric-al-ly, adv.

## isomorph
isomorph, n. — See next word.

## isomorphic
isomorphic, isomorphous, adj., equal in formj
crystallizing in the same form. — Formed with
suff. -ic, resp. -ons, fr. iso-, Gk. μορφή, 'form,
shape' (see next word), and suff. -ic, resp. -ous.

## isomorphism
isomorphism, п., the property of being
isomorphic. — G. Isomorphismus, coined by its
discoverer, the German chemist Eilhardt Mitscher-
lich (1794-1863) in 1828 fr. iso-, Gk. μορφή,
'form, shape' (see morpho-), and suff. -ismus
(see -ism).

## -ison
-ison, subst. suff. of OF. origin, as in comparison,
orison, venison. This suff. represents 1) OF.
-aison (fr. L. ationem, fr. -atus, pp. suff. of verbs
in -are); 2) OF. -eison (fr. L. -itionem, fr. -elus,
pp. suff. of verbs in -ere); 3) OF. -ison (fr. L.
-itionem or -itionem), fr. -itus or -itus, pp. suff.
of verbs in -ire, resp. -ere, -ere). Cp. the suffixes
-ation (fr. L. -ationem), and -ition (fr. L. itionem
or -itionem), which are learned doublets of -ison.

## isopod
isopod, п., one of the Isopoda. — See next word.

## Isopoda
Isopoda, п., an order of crustaceans with seven
pairs of usually similar legs (zool.) — ModL.,
lit. 'equal-footed', fr. iso- and -pod.

## isopolity
isopolity, п., equality of rights of citizenship. —
Gk. Ισοπολιτεία, 'equality of civil rights', fr.
Ισοπολίτης, 'one having equal civil rights',
which is compounded of ίσος, 'equal' (see iso-),
and πολίτης, 'citizen', fr. πόλις, 'fortified city,
city'. See policy, 'method of governing'.

## isoprene
isoprene, п., a colorless volatile liquid compound,
CSH,, obtained by the dry distillation of raw
rubber (chem.) — Coined by the English chemist
Charles Hanson Greville (1829-191°) fr. pr(opyi)
and suff. -ene. Cp. the second element in chlo-
roprene and in neoprene.

## isosceles
isosceles, adj., having two equal sides (said of a
triangle). — L., fr. Gk. Ισοσκελής, 'equal-
legged', fr. ίσος, 'equal', and σκέλος, 'leg'. For
the first element see iso-, for the second see
scalene and cp. triskelion.

## isothere
isothere, isotheral, п., a line connecting places on
the earth's surface having the same mean
summer temperature (phys. geogr.) — Compounded
of iso- and Gk. θέρος, 'summer, harvest', which
is rel. to θερμός, 'warm', θέρμη, 'heat'. See
therm,

## isotherm
isotherm, п., a line connecting places on the
earth's surface having the same mean
temperature (phys. geogr.) — Compounded of iso- and
Gk. θέρμη, 'heat'. See therm and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: isotherm-al, adj., isoiherm-al-ly,
adv., isotherm-ic, adj.

## isotonic
isotonic, adj., pertaining to, or having, equal
tones. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. ίσότονος,
'of level pitch', fr. ίσος, 'equal' and τόνος,
'pitch of the voice, tone'. See iso- and tonic.

## isotope
isotope, п., one of two or more forms of an
element having the same properties and the same
atomic number but different atomic weights. —
Lit. 'having the same place', compounded of
iso- and Gk. τόπος, 'place' (see topic). The
term isotope was introduced into chemistry by
the English chemist Frederick Soddy (1877-1956)
in 1913 at the suggestion of Margaret Todd.
Derivatives: isotop-ic, adj., isotop-ism, п.. iso-
top-y, n.

## Israel
Israel, n. — L. Israel, fr. Gk. 'Ισραήλ, fr. Heb.
Yisra'il, lit. 'he contends with God', fr. sarah,
'he fought, contended', and Ё1, 'God'. The first
element is rel. to Arab, shard, 'he was angry',
in the III conj. 'he contended'. For the second
element see EL

## Israelite
Israelite, n. — L. Israelita, fr. Gk. 'Ισραηλίτης,
'Israelite', fr. 'Ισραήλ. See prec. word and subst.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:416 COLUMN:3 -->
suff. -ite.
Derivatives: Israelit-ic, adj., Israelit-ish, adj.,
Israelit-ism, n.

## Issachar
Issachar, п., son of Jacob by Leah; a tribe of
Israel (Bible). — Gk. Ίσσάχαρ, fr. Heb. Yissa-
khar, which prob. stands for ye~sh sakhar, 'there
is a reward'. See Gen. 30:18.

## issue
issue, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) issue, 'way out,
exit', fr. OF. eissue, issue, prop. fem. pp. of
eissir, issir (MF. issir), 'to go out', fr. L. exire,
of s.m. (whence also It. uscire, Rum. iesi,
OProvenc. eissir, Catal. exir), fr. 1st ex- and
ire, 'to go'. See itinerate.

## issue
issue, intr. and tr. v. — ME. issuen, fr. MF. issu,
pp. of issir. See issue, n.
Derivatives: issu-able, adj., issu-ance, п., issue-
less, adj., issu-er, n.

## -ist
-ist, suff. forming a) agent nouns from verbs in
-ize (e.g. apologist, dramatist); b) nouns
denoting the adherent of a certain doctrine,
principle or custom (e.g. socialist). — F. -iste, fr.
L. -ufa, fr. Gk. -ιστής, which stands for -ισ-τής
and is formed fr. -ισ- (ending of the stem of the
verbs in -ίζειν) and agential suff. -τής. Ср.
-ism, -ize. Cp. also -ast.

## -ister
-ister, suff. — OF. -istre, formed fr. original -iste,
on the false analogy of the word ministre (see
minister). Cp. e.g. chorister, fr. choriste, fr.
Eccles. L. chorista.

## isthmian
isthmian, adj., pertaining to an isthmus; esp.
(cap.) pertaining to the Isthmus of Corinth. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. isthmius, Isthmius,
fr. Gk. ϊσθμιος, Ίσθμιας, 'Isthmian', fr. 'Ισθμός.
See isthmus and -ian.

## isthmus
isthmus, п., a narrow neck of land connecting
two larger portions of land. — L., fr. Gk.
Ισθμός, 'neck of land, isthmus, any narrow
passage' (as a proper name, 'the Isthmus of
Corinth'), which is of uncertain origin. It is perh.
formed with suff. -θμο, fr. είμι, Ιέναι, 'to go'
(cp. είσ-ί-θμη, 'entrance', ί-θμα, 'a step,
movement'). Cp. ON. eid, 'isthmus', and see itinerate.

## -istic
-istic, adj. suff. — L. -isticus (often through the
medium of F. -istique), fr. Gk. -ιστικός, prop,
adj. suff. -ικός added to subst. suff. -ιστής. See
-ist and adj. suff. -ic.

## istie
istie, п., fiber obtained from various tropical
plants. — Mexican Sp. ixtle, Tr. Nahuatl ichtli.

## Isurus
Isurus, п., a genus of sharks (ichthyol.) — ModL.,
compounded of is- and Gk. ουρά, 'tail'. See
uro-, 'tail-'.

## it
it, pron. — ME. hit, it, fr. OE. hit, neut. of he,
'he'. Cp. OFris. hit, Du. het, Goth, hita, 'it', and
see he and words there referred to. Cp. also Its.
Derivative: it, n.

## itabirite
itabirite, п., a kind of quartz (mineral.) — Named
after Itabira in Minas Geraes, Brazil. For the
ending see subst. suff. -Ke.

## Itacism
Itacism, п., pronunciation of Gk. eta (i.e. the
letter η) as / (as in Modern Greek), in
contradistinction to etacism. — Formed with suff.
-ism fr. Gk. ήτα, name of the letter ё. See
etacism and cp. iotacism.

## itacolumite
itacolumite, п., a kind of quartzite (mineral.) —
Named after Itacolumi, a mountain in Brazil,
where it occurs. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## Italian
Italian, adj. and n. — It. italiano, fr. Italia, fr. L.
Italia, fr. Vitelia (cp. Oscan Vlteliu, 'Italy'),
which prob. meant orig. 'Land of cattle", and
is rel. to L. vitulus, 'calf. See veal and -an.
Derivatives: Italianate, Italianated (qq.v.),
Italian-ism, п., Itatian-ity, п., Italianize (q.v.)

## Italianate
Italianate, adj., rendered Italian. — It. italianato,
fr. italiano. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.

## Italianate
Italianate, tr. v., to render Italian. — Back
formation fr. Italianated.
Derivative: italianat-ion, n.

## Italianated
Italianated, pp. adj., rendered Italian. — Formed
fr. It. italianato (see Italianate, adj.) with pp.
suff. -ed.

## Italianize
Italianize, intr. v., to play the Italian; to become
Italian; tr. v., to render Italian. — F. italianiser,
fr. italien, 'Italian', fr. It. italiano. See Italian
and -ize.
Derivatives: Italianiz-ation, п., Italianiz-er, n.

## Italic
Italic, adj. — L. Italicus, from Italia. See Italian
and adj. suff. -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:417 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ITALIC | 390 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:417 COLUMN:1 -->

## italic
italic, п., Italic type of letters. — From prec.
word; so called because it was first used in an
Italian edition of Virgil, printed (in Venice)
by Aldus Manutius in 1501.

## Italiot
Italiot, Itaiiote, п., a Greek inhabitant of Italy.
— Gk. Ίταλιώτης, fr. 'Ιταλία, fr. L. Italia. See
Italian.

## Italo-
Italo-, combining form meaning 'Italian and". —
Fr. L. Itatus, 'Italian'. See Italian.

## itch
itch, intr. v. — ME. ylcchen, icchen, fr. OE.
giccan, rel. to MDu. /oken, Du. feuken, OHG.
jucchen, MHG., G.Jucken, 'to itch'.

## itch
itch, n. —■ ME. Jicche, icche, fr. OE. gicce, fr.
giccan, 'to itch*, See itch, v.
Derivatives: itch-y, adj., itch-i-ness, n.

## -ite
-ite, subst. suff. denoting 'origin' or 'relationship'
(as in Israelite, Canaanite, etc.). It is used also
to form names of minerals and fossils (as in
ammonite, dolomite, trilobile), chemical
compounds (as in phosphite), explosives (as in
dynamite, lyddite), commercial products (as in
vulcanite). — F. -ite, fr. L. -ha, -itis, fr. Gk.
-ίτης (fern, -ϊτις), 'pertaining to'. Cp. -itls.

## -ite
-ite, suff. forming adjectives, nouns and verbs
and representing Latin -Itus in past participles
of verbs ending in -ire and -ere. Cp. e.g. polite
(fr. L.poiitus, pp. oipolire); unite (fr. L. unilus,
pp. of unire); appetite (fr. L. appetitus, pp. of
appetere); composite (fr. L. compositus, pp. of
componere).

## Itea
Itea, п., a genus of shrubs. — ModL., fr. Gk.
ίτέϊ (prob. for *Feit£S), "willow', which is rel.
to ϊτυς, 'the edge or rim of anything round',
fr. I.-E. base *wei-, 'to bend, twist', whence also
OE. widig 'willow*. See withy and words there
referred to and cp. esp. the second element in
Stomoisia.

## item
item, adv., likewise. — L., 'just so, in like
manner, likewise, also', rel. to ita, 'so', itaque, 'and
so, accordingly, in like manner', itidem/so, just,
in like manner', idem (masc), idem (neut.), 'the
same'. See idem and words there referred to and
cp. esp. iterate.
Derivatives: item, n. (q.v.), item, tr. v.,
itemize, tr. v,

## item
item, п., detail; article. — L. item, 'likewise';
see prec. word. The sense of the English noun
arose from the circumstance that the word item
was generally used to introduce all the sections
of a bill, except the first.

## iterance
iterance, iterancy, п., the quality of being iterant.
— Formed from next word with suff. -ce, resp.
-cy.

## iterant
iterant, adj., iterating. — L. iterans, gen. -amis,
pres. part, of iterdre. See next word and -ant.

## iterate
iterate, tr. v., to do again, repeat. — L. iteratus,
pp. of iterare, 'to do over a second time, repeat,
say again', fr. iterum, 'again', which stands for
i-terum and prop, is the neuter of *i-teros,
comparative formed from the pronominal base */'-
whence also OI. i-tarah, 'the other'. For other
derivatives of the I.-E. pronominal base *i- see
idem, for the comparative suff. see -ther, for the
ending 'of iterate see verbal sufT. -ate.

## iteration
iteration, n. — L. iterdtio, gen. onis, 'repetition',
fr. iteratus, pp. of iterare, 'to repeat'. See iterate
and -ion.

## iterative
iterative, adj. — F. iteralif (fem. iterative), fr.
Late L. iterativus, fr. L. iteratus, pp. of iterare,
'to repeat'. See iterate and -ive.
Derivatives', iterative-ly, adv., iterative-ness, n.

## ithyphailic
ithyphailic, adj., pertaining to the phallus carried
in the Bacchic rites; obscene; pertaining to the
meter used in the Bacchic hymns. — L. ithy-
phallicus, fr. Gk. ίθυφαλλικός, 'ithyphailic', fr.
ίθύφαλλος, 'phallus carried erect in the Bacchic
rites', which is compounded of ίθύς, 'straight,
erect', and φαλλός, 'phallus'. The first element
stands for "sidhus and is cogn. with OI. sadhub,
'straight, direct, right', sidhyati, 'succeeds', Arm.
a] (for *sadhyo-), 'right, just'. For the second

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:417 COLUMN:2 -->
element see phallus. Cp. next word.
Derivative: ithyphailic, п., an ithyphailic.

## Ithyphallus
Ithyphallus, п., a genus of fungi of the family of
the true stinkhorns (bot.) — ModL. See prec.
word.

## -itic
-itic, suff. forming adjectives from nouns ending
in -ite or -itis. — L. -iticus, /г. Gk. -ιτίκός.
See the suffixes -ite, -itis and -ic.

## itinerancy
itinerancy, n. — Formed from next word with
sufT. -cy.

## itinerant
itinerant, adj. — L. itinerans, gen. -amis, pres.
part, of itinerurl, 'to travel'. See itinerate and
-ant.

## itinerary
itinerary, adj. — L. itinerarius, 'pertaining to a
journey', fr. iter, gen. itineris, 'journey'. See
itinerate and -ary.

## itinerary
itinerary, n. — L. itinerarium, 'account of a
journey', prop. neut. of the adjective itinerarius,
'pertaining to a journey', used as a noun. See
itinerary, adj.

## itinerate
itinerate, intr. v., to travel from place to place. —
L. itineratus, pp. of itinerdri, 'to travel', fr. iter,
gen. itineris, 'a journey', which is cogn. with
Toch. A ytdr, В ytarye, 'way', Hitt. itar, 'going',
way', fr. I.-E. base *ei-, 'to go', whence also
OI. imi, Gk. είμι, L. eo (for *eio), Lith. eimi,
elti, OSlav. ido, iti, 'to go', Olr. ethaim, Ί go'
(corresponding in form to L. ito, freq. of eo,
Ί go'), possibly also Gk. ϊ-*μα, 'a step,
movement', ε1σ-ί-*μη, 'entrance', possibly, also
ί-σ*μός, 'neck of land, isthmus, any narrow
passage'. Cp. Abeona, abiturient, adit, ambit,
ambition, anion, cation, circuit, cocno-, coetus,
coition, coitus, comitia, commence, count, 'title
of nobility', dysprosium, errant, exeat, exeunt,
exit, eyre, Ichno-, inevitable, initial, introit, ion,
issue, iathmns, jadoo, janitor, Jaun, limit, obit,
obituary, perish, praetor, preterit, Rathayatra,
sedition, seditious, sudden, trance, transient,
transire, transit. Cp. also oath and the second
element in wide.
Derivative: itinerat-ion, n.

## -ition
-ition, subst. suff. — F. -ition (or directly) fr. L.
-Itionem, ace. of -Itid, a suff. forming nouns of
action fr. -Itus, or -itus, pp. suff. of verbs of the
4th, resp. 3rd Latin conjugation. See adj. suff.
•ite and cp. suff. -ation.

## -itious
-itious, adj. suff. representing L. -icius, which is
added usually to past participles ending in -tus.
Cp. e.g. factitious, fr. L.facticius, 'made by art',
fr. /actus, 'made', pp. of facere, 'to make'. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## -itious
-itious, adj. suff. representing L. -Itiosus, which is
formed fr. -ftio, gen. -onis, fr. -itus, pp. suff.
Cp. e.g. ambitious, fr. L. ambitiosus, fr. ambitio,
which is formed fr. ambitus, pp. of ambire, 'to
go round'. See the suffixes -ition and -ous.

## -itis
-itis, subst. suff. denoting diseases characterized
by inflammation. — ModL., fr. Gk,- ϊτις, prop,
fem. of the adjectival suff. -ίτης, 'pertaining to'
(see subst. suff. -ite), used with the feminine
noun νόσος, 'disease', either expressed or
understood, as e.g. (νόσος) νεφρΐης, 'disease' of the
kidneys'. The generalization of suff. -itis is due
to Sauvages.
-itish, adj. suff, compounded of subst. suff. -ite
and adj. suff. -ish. Cp. e.g. Israelitish, which is
formed fr. Israelite, fr. Israel.

## -itoi
-itoi, a suff. used to form the names of certain
alcohols, as in inositol, mannitol (chem.) —
Compounded of subst. suff. -ite and suff. -ol
(for alcohol).

## -itous
-itous, adj. suff. — F. -iteux (fem. -iteuse), fr. L.
-itosus, contraction of *-itdtosus, from nouns
in -itas (gen. -itdtis); see -ity and -ous. Cp. e.g.
calamitous, fr. L. calamitosus, contraction of
*calamitdtdsus, fr. catamites, gen. -atis (see
calamitous). The contraction of L. "-itdtosus
to -itosus is due to haplology. In many cases
suff. -itous is formed directly from nouns
ending in suff. -ity.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:417 COLUMN:3 -->

## its
its, adj. — For earlier it's; formed from the
pronoun it with s, the ending of the possessive case.

## itself
itself, pron. — Compounded of it and self.

## -ity
-ity, suff. forming abstract nouns. — F. -ite, fr.
L. -itdtem, ace. of -itas, which prop, consists of
thematic -/ and suff. -Ids (see -ity). Cp. e.g.
sincerity, fr. F. sincerite, fr. L. sinceritdtem, ace.
of sinceritds, fr. sincerus, 'sincere'.

## -iuin
-iuin, suff. used to form ModL. scientific names.
— L. -turn, fr. Gk. -iov, frequently of
diminutive force. Cp. e.g. geranium.

## -ium
-ium, modern suff. used to form names of metallic
elements (chem.) — See prec. word and cp. e.g.
radium, sodium.

## Iva
Iva, п., a genus of plants', the marsh elder (bat.)
— ModL., fr. Gaulish ivos, whence also F. if,
'yew*. See yew and cp. uva.

## Ivan
Ivan, masc. PN. — Russ., fr. Gk Ιωάννης. See
John.

## -ive
-ive, suff. meaning 'tending to; of the quality of.
t— L. -ivus (mostly through the medium of F.
-if, fem. -ive).

## ivory
ivory, n. — ME. ivorie, fr. OF. ivurie (F. ivoire),
fr. L. eboreus, 'of ivory', fr. ebur, 'ivory',
borrowed fr.- Egyptian db, abu, 'elephant, ivory',
prob. through the medium of the Phoenicians.
The same word appears in the second element
of Heb. shen-habbtm, 'ivory' (lit. 'tooth of the
elephant'), whence Yebu (= Heb. Yebh),
original name of the island Elephantine; cp. also
OI. ibhah, 'elephant', and the second element
in Gk. έλ-έφϊς, 'elephant'. Cp. eburnine,
elephant.

## ivy
ivy, n. — ME. w, fr. OE. ifig, rel. to MLG. if-ldf,
iw-lof, Du. ei-loof, OHG. ebah, eba-hewi, ebe-
hewi, MHG. ebe-hou, ep-hbu, G. Efeu.
Derivative: ivi-ed, adj.

## Ixia
Ixia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. ίξός, 'mistletoe; birdlime', which stands
for "ίιξός and is cogn. with L. viscum, of s.m.
See viscum.

## Ixion
Ixion, п., king of the Lapithae in Thessaly, who
was tied to an ever-revolving wheel in Hades
for having sought the love of Hera (Greek ray-
thol.) — L. Ixion, fr. Gk. Ίξίων.

## Ixodidae
Ixodidae, n. pi., name of a family of acarids
(zool.) — ModL., formed fr. Ixodes, name of
the typical genus, fr. Gk. Ιξώδης, 'like
birdlime', which is compounded of ίξός, 'mistletoe;
birdlime', and -ώδης, 'like'. See Ixia, -ode, 'like',
and -idae.

## Ixora
Ixora, п., a genus of tropical plants of the
madder family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Isvara, a
title of Siva, fr. OI. isvardh, 'ruler, lord'. See
Ishvara.

## Iyar
Iyar, п., name of the second Jewish month. —
Heb. iyydr, a loan word fr. Akkad. aaru.

## tear
tear, п., ι) the outer garment of Mohammedan
women covering the whole figure; 2) loincloth
(part of the ihram). — Arab, izar, 'veil,
covering', from the stem of azara, dzzara, 'he girded,
encompassed', rel. to Heb. dzar, 'he girded',
ezor, 'waistcloth, girdle'.

## izard
izard, п., chamois inhabiting the Pyrenees. — F.
isard, of Basque origin; cp. Basque izar, 'star;
white spot on the forehead'; cp. also Berber
ichri, of s.m., which is a Basque loan word. The
spelling with d is prob. due to a confusion with
suff. -ard.

## -ization
-ization, a suff. forming nouns fr. verbs ending
in -ize. — L. -izdtio, gen. -onis, fr. -izdtus, pp.
suff. of verbs in -izdre. See -ize and -ation.

## -ize
-ize, -ise, suff. forming verbs in one of the
following senses; 1) 'to act in a certain way' (as in
Attic-ize, philosoph-ize); 2) 'to treat in a
certain way' (as in sympath-ize); 3) 'to make into*
(is in Christian-ize, civil-ize, Gallicize; 4) 'to
treat with' (as in chloral-ize). — F. -iser, fr.
Late L. izdre (whence also It. -izzare, Sp. -izar),
fr. Gk. -ίζειν, 'to act in a certain way'. Cp.
-ism, -ist.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:418 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:418 COLUMN:1 -->
jaal goat. — Heb. yd'il, 'wild goat', rel. to Aram.
yt'eta, Syr. ya'la, Arab, wa'al, wa'I, Ethiop.
we'la, 'wild goat*. Cp. Jael.

## jab
jab, tr. v., to strike. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
job, 'to stab'.
Derivative: jab, n.

## jabber
jabber, intr. and tr. v., to chatter. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. gibber.
Derivatives: jabber, n.,jabber-er, п., jabber-ing,
adj., jabber-ing-ly, adv.

## jabiru
jabiru, п., a large stork of South America. — Sp.
jabiru, fr. Tupi jabiru.

## jaborandi
jaborandi, п., the dried leaflets of S. American
shrubs of the genus Pilocarpus. — Port., fr. Tupi
yaborandi.

## jabot
jabot, п., frill of a shirt. — F., 'crop, maw; frill
of a shirt', prob. rel. to F. gaver, 'to cram,
gorge', OProvenc. gava, 'crop, maw'. See jaw.

## jacamar
jacamar, п., an insectivorous bird of tropical
America. — F., erroneously formed by the
French naturalist, Comte Georges-Louis Le-
clerc Buffon (1707-88) fr. Tupi jacama-ciri.

## jacana
jacana, п., a S. American wading bird resembling
the rail. — Port, jacana, fr. Tupi yasana.

## jacaranda
jacaranda, п., a tropical American tree. — Port.
jacaranda, fr. Tupi yacarandd.

## jacinth
jacinth, n. — ME. iacynlh, iacinth, fr. OF. ia-
cinthe (F. jacinthe), fr. L. hyacinthus, fr. Gk.
υάκινθος. See hyaciath.

## Jack
Jack, masc. PN. — Familiar form of John, but
derived fr. OF. Jaques (F. Jacques), fr. Late L.
Jacdbus, for earlier Jacobus, fr. Gk. fr. Heb.
Yadqobh, 'Jacob'. See Jacob and cp. next word.

## jack
jack, п., ι) fellow; 2) knave in playing-cards;
3) the male of certain animals; 4) a small flag;
5) the name of various machines, vessels and
devices. — Fr. prec. word. For the use of proper
names to form names of vessels cp. Jeroboam,
toby.

## jack
jack, п., ι) a sleeveless coat; 2) a vessel for liquor.
— OF. jaque, 'sleeveless coat', fr. Jacques,
'Jack', a nickname given to the French peasant
in the 14th century, for this kind of garment
was used especially by the peasants of that era.
See Jack and cp. Bloch-Wartburg, DELF.,
p. 333 s.v. jaquette. Cp. also jacket For sense
development cp. jacquerie,

## jack
jack, п., an East Indian tree (Artocarpus inte-
grifolia). — Port, jaca, fr. Malayalam chakka,
lit. 'something round', fr. OI. cakrdb, 'wheel,
circle', which is cogn. with Gk. κύκλος, 'ring,
circle'. See cycle and words there referred to
and cp. esp. chukker, hackery,

## jackal
jackal, n. — Turk, chagal, fr. Pers. shaghal, fr.
OI. srgaldb, lit. 'the howler'.

## jackanapes
jackanapes, п., ι) a monkey (archaic); 2) an
impertinent, conceited fellow, a coxcomb. — Fr.
Jacha Napes = Jack o'Napes, Jack of Napes, =
'a monkey from Naples (in Italy)'.

## jackaroo
jackaroo, п., a new apprentice on a sheep farm
in Australia (slang). — A blend of Jack and
(kang)aroo.

## jackass
jackass, n„ a male ass. — Compounded of jack,
'male of animals', and ass.
Derivative: jackass, intr. v., to ride a jackass.

## jackass copal
jackass copal, Zanzibar copal. — Corruption of
chakazi copal, fr. Zanzibar chakazi, chakazzi.

## jackdaw
jackdaw, n. — Compounded of jack, 'male of
animals', and daw.

## jacket
jacket, n. — OF. jaquet (F. jaquette), dimin. of

## jaque. See jack
jaque. See jack, 'a sleeveless coat', and -et.

## jack rabbit
jack rabbit, a long eared American hare. —
Short for jackass rabbit; so called in allusion
to its long ears. Cp. its earlier names mule-eared
rabbit, mule rabbit.

## Jacksonia
Jacksonia, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — Named after the English botanist
George Jackson. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## Jacob
Jacob, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, one of the
patriarchs, son of Isaac and Rebecca and father

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:418 COLUMN:2 -->
J
of the founders of the twelve tribes. — Late L.
Jacdbus, fr. Gk. 'Ιάκωβος, fr. Heb. Ya'aqobh,
lit. 'one that takes by the heel', a derivative of
'aqibh, 'heel', whence 'Sqdbh, 'he followed at
the heel, he overreached, circumvented', whid
is rel. to Aram, 'iqbd, Akkad. iqbu, 'heel; trace,
mark', Arab, 'dqib, 'heel', 'iqbab, 'mark, trace,
sign', 'dqaba, 'he followed (at the heel),
succeeded'. Cp. Jack, jack, 'sleeveless coat',
Jacobin, jacobus, jacquery, jakes, James.

## Jacobin
Jacobin, п., ι) a Dominican friar; 2) a member of
the political club of the Jacobins. — F., fr. ML.
Jacobinus, fr. L. Jacobus [see Jacob and -ine
(representing L. -inus)]. The Dominican friars
are so called because their first convent in Paris
was established in the rue St. Jacques (= St.
James Street). As a political term, the word
Jacobin refers to the fact that (after Oct. 6,1789)
the club of the Jacobins used to meet in the
monastery of the Jacobins in the rue St.
Honored
Derivatives: Jacobin, Jacobin-ic, Jacobin-ic-al,
adjs., Jacobin-ic-al-ly, adv., Jacobin-ism, п., Ja-
cobin-ize, tr. v., Jacobin-iz-ation, n.

## jacobin
jacobin, п., a kind of pigeon. — F.jacobine, fern,
form of jacobin, 'Jacobin, Dominican'; so called
because the neck-feathers resemble a monk's
cowl.

## Jacobite
Jacobite, п., an adherent of James II after his
abdication (English hist.) — Formed with subst.
suff. -ite fr. Late L. Jacobus, 'Jacob, James'. For
the etymology of the name see Jacob. Cp. next
word.
Derivatives: jacobit-ical, adj., Jacobit-ism, n.

## jacohns
jacohns, п., an English gold coin. — From Latin
Jacobus, 'James' (see Jacob); so called because
struck during the reign of James I.

## jaconet
jaconet, п., a kind of soft white cotton fabric. —
Corruption of Jagannath, name of a town in
Bengal, where it was first manufactured. For
the meaning of the name see Juggernaut.

## Jacquard
Jacquard, n. — Short for Jacquard apparatus,
Jacquard fabric, Jacquard loom, etc. Named
after the French inventor Joseph Jacquard
(1752-1834)-

## jacquerie
jacquerie, п., peasants' revolt, esp. revolt of the
French peasants in 1358. — F. jacquerie, prop,
'rising of peasants', fr. Jacques, a contemptuous
name given by the nobles to the French peasant.
See jack, 'sleeveless coat' and -ery.

## jactitation
jactitation, п., restlessness (med.); assertion of a
false claim (law). — ML. jactitatid, gen. -onis,
fr. jactitatus, pp. of jactitare, 'to toss about', fr.
L. jactus, pp. of jacire, 'to throw, cast, hurl'.
See jet, 'to spirt forth', and -ation.

## jade
jade, п., a kind of silicate. — F. le jade, fr. earlier
I'ejade, fr. Sp. (piedra de) i/ada, 'stone for curing
pains in the side', a derivative of L. ilia, 'the
flanks'. See iliac.

## jade
jade, п., a worn-out horse. — ME., fr. ON.jalda,
'mare', whence also dial. Swed. jalda, 'mare'.
Derivatives: jade, tr. v., to make a jade of (a
horse); to make weary; intr. v., to become
weary; jad-ed, adj., jad-ed-ly, adv., jad-ed-ness,
n.,jad-ish, adj., jad-ish-ly, adv., jad-ish-ness, n.

## jadeite
jadeite, п., a variety of jade (mineral.) — Formed
with subst. suff. -ite fr. Jade, 'a kind of silicate'.

## Jadoo
Jadoo, jadn, п., conjuring, magic. — Pers.-Hind.
jadH, fr. OI. yatub, 'magic, sorcery', prob.
meaning lit. 'a going against', from the stem oiyati,
yate, 'goes, moves, proceeds; advances, marches
against (the. enemy)', fr. I.-E. base 'yd-,
enlargement of base *ei-, 'to go'. See janitor and
cp. jaun and the second element in Rathayatra.

## jaeger
jaeger, п., a sharpshooter. — G. Jager, 'hunter',
fr. jagen, 'to hunt', fr. MHG. jagen, fr. OHG.

## jagon
jagon, which is rel. to OFris. jagia, Du. jagen, 'to
hunt'. ON. jaga, 'to drive; to move to and fro',
orig. 'to hunt', is a MLG. loan word. Cp. yager,
yacht, yaw.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:418 COLUMN:3 -->

## jaeger
jaeger, п., a flannel coat. — Named after Jager,
professor at Stuttgart, who emphasized the
hygienic value of flannel clothing.

## Jael
Jael, п., the wife of Heber the Kenite, who killed
Sisera with a tent nail (Judges 4:17-22). — He.b.
Ya'el, lit. 'wild goat'. See jaal goat

## jag
jag, п., a tooth; a notch. — Prob. of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: jag, tr. v.,jagg-ed, adj., jagg-ed-ly,
adv., jagg-ed-ness, a.,jagg-y, adj., jagg-er, a.

## Jagannath
Jagannath, n. — See Juggernaut.

## jagat
jagat, п., moving beings (Hinduism). — OI. jagat,
'moving', participial formation from the base
of OI. jigdti, 'goes', Aor. agat, 'went', which is
cogn. with Lett, gaju, Gk. έβην, Dor. ίβαν,
Ί went', Gk. βαίνειν, 'to go', fr. I.-E. base
*gmem-, 'to go, to come'. See come and cp. the
first element in Juggernaut.

## jaggery
jaggery, п., coarse dark brown sugar. —
Anglicized fr. Hind, jagri, fr. OI. iarkara, sarkarah,
'sugar'. Accordingly jaggery is prop, a doublet
of sugar (q.v.)

## jaghire
jaghire, jagheer, jagir, п., an assignment of land
as an annuity (India). — Pers. jagir, lit. 'place-
holding', compounded of ja, 'place', and gir,
'holding'.

## jaghiredar
jaghiredar, jagheerdar, jagirdar, п., the holder
of a jaghire (India) — Formed fr. prec. word
and the Persian suff. -dor, 'holder, possessor'.
See aumildar and cp. words there referred to.

## jaguar
jaguar, n. — Tupi yaguara, a name denoting any
larger beast of prey. In its modern zoological
sense (— Felis onca) the name jaguar was first
used by the French naturalist Comte Georges-
Louis LeclercBuffon (1707-88).

## Jah
Jah, п., the Lord. — Heb. Yah, shortened form
of the Tetragrammaton. Cp. the second
element in halleluyah. Cp. also the second element
in Elijnh and in words there referred to.

## jail
jail, gaol, n. — ME. jaile, gail, fr. OF. jaiole (F.
geole), fr. VL. caveola, dimin. of L. cavea, 'cage'.
See cage.
Derivatives: jail, gaol, tr. v„jail-er, gaol-er, n.

## Jain
Jain, п., an adherent of a non-Brahmanic sect
in India. — Hind. Jaina, fr. OI. Jainah, 'of a
Buddha', fr. jinab, 'hero, saint', which is rel. to
jdyati, 'conquers', jaydb, 'victory', jinati,
Overcomes, subdues',/yii,;«i, 'superior force',jydyan,
'mightier', jyesfbdh, jyesthah, 'mightiest', and
cogn. with Gk. βίϊ, 'force, might, violence'.
Ср..the second element in Zenobia.
Derivatives: Jain-ism, п., Jain-ist, n.

## jakes
jakes, п., a privy (archaic). — Fr. F. Jacques,
'Jack'. See Jack.

## jalop
jalop, п., root of a Mexican plant (Exogonium
jalapa), used as a purgative. — F., fr. Sp. jalapa,
fr. Jalapa for Xalapa, a town in Mexico.

## jalousie
jalousie, п., a window shutter made with slats. —
F., lit. 'jealousy'. See jealousy.
Derivative: jalousi-ed, adj.

## jalpaite
jalpaite, п., a cupriferous argentite (mineral.) —
Named after Jalpa in Mexico. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## jam
jam, also jamb, tr. and intr. v., to press tightly.
— Prob. a variant of champ.
Derivative: jam, п., congestion; crush.

## jam
jam, п., conserved fruit. — Prob. fr. Jam, 'to press
tightly', and orig. meaning 'fruit pressed
together'.
Jamaica. — Short for Jamaica rum.

## jamb
jamb, п., sidepost. — F. jambe, fr. Late L. gamba,
'leg'. See gamb and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also enjambment

## jamb
jamb, v. — See jam, v.

## jamboo
jamboo, jambool, jambul, п., the Java plum; the
rose apple. — Hind, jambu, 'the rose apple', fr.
OI. jambub, jambah, which is prob. of non-
Aryan origin.

## jamboree
jamboree, п., gathering (esp. of boyscouts). —
Of Hindu origin; introduced by Rudyard
