Roman Empire. — Late L. (whence Byzant. Gk.
λάβαρον), of uncertain etymology; possibly a
Gaulish word cogn. with OS. lappo, OHG.
lappa, 'rag, shred', OE. tseppa, 'tip, end, skirt,
district' ; see lap, 'flap of a garment', and cp. label.
See Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, 737.

## labdanum
labdanum, п., a fragrant, bitter resin. — ML.
labdanum,ΐτ. L. ladanum, ledanum, fr. Gk. λάδανον,
λήδανον, fr. ληδον, 'mastic', which is of Sem.
origin; cp. Akkad. tadunu, Arab. Iddan, Heb.
lot, 'labdanum'. Pers. ladan is an Arabic loan
word. Cp. laudanum, lotus.

## labefaction
labefaction, п., the process of shaking; downfall.
— Formed with suff. -Ion fr. L. tabefactus, pp.
of labefacere, 'to cause to totter, shake,
overthrow', which is compounded of labi, 'to slip,
slide, glide', and facere, 'to make, do'. See labor
and fact and cp. next word.

## label
label, n. — ME., fr. OF. label, lambel, 'a strip'
(whence F. lambeau, 'strip, rag, shred, tatter,
fragment, scrap'), prob. fr. Fianklsh *labba. Cp.
OHG. lappa, 'rag, shred', and see lap, 'Hap of a
garment'. Cp. also labarum.
Derivatives: label, tr. v., label(l)-er, n.

## labellum
labellum, п., one of the three parts forming the
corolla in orchidaceous plants (bot.) — L., 'a
little lip', dimin. of labrum. See lip and cp.
labium. Cp. also next word.

## labial
labial, adj., pertaining to, or formed by, the lips.
— ML. labialis, fr. L. labium, 'lip'. See lip and
adj. suff. -til and cp. labrum.
Derivatives: labial, п., a labial sound, labial-ly,
adv., labialism, labialize (qq.v.)

## labialism
labialism, п., 1) quality of being formed by the
lips; 2) tendency to labialize. — See labinl and
-ism.

## labialize
labialize, tr. v., to make labial. — See labial and
-ize.
Derivative: labializ-ation, n.

## labiate
labiate, adj., 1) having a labium; 2) having one or
several liplike parts (bot. and zool.) — ModL.
labidtus, lit. 'lipped', fr. L. labium, 'lip'. See Up
and adj. suff. -ate and cp. labial.
Derivative: labiate, п., a labiate plant.

## labile
labile, adj., unstable. — ME. labyl, fr. MF. ( = F.)
labile, it. L. labilts, 'slipping, gliding', lit. 'prone
to slip', fr. labi, 'to slip, slide, glide'. See labor
and -ile and cp. lapse. Cp. also the second
element in thermolabile.
Derivative: labil-ity, n.

## labio-
labio-, combining form denoting 1) the lips; 2)
labial and. — Fr. L. labium, 'lip'. See labial.

## labiodental
labiodental, adj., pertaining to, or formed with,
the lips and teeth. — Compounded of labio- and
dental.
Derivative: labiodental, п., a sound formed with
the lips and teeth.

## labium
labium, п., a lip or a liplike part (anal., zool., bot.
etc.) — L., 'lip'. See labial.

## labor
labor, labour, n. — ME. labour, fr. OF. labour (F.
labeur), fr. L. laborem, ace. of labor, 'labor, toil,
exertion, hardship, fatigue, distress, pain, work',
orig. prob. meaning 'a tottering under a burden',
and rel. to labare, 'to totter', labi, 'to slide, slip,
glide', fr. I.-E. base *lab-, *leb-, 'slack, loose; to
hang down', whence also OI. lambate, 'hangs
down', L. limbus (for *tembos), 'hem, border',
OS. lappo, OHG. lappa, 'rag, shred', OE. Iseppa,
'tip, end, lappet; district', and perh. also Olr.
lobur, 'weak' (see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I,
739-40 s. w. labo and labor). See lap, 'flap of a
garment'., and cp. laboratory, belabor,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:433 COLUMN:2 -->
L
collaborate, elaborate. Cp. also labefaction, lapse, lava.
Cp. also limb, 'border', limp, v. and adj. For
derivatives of I.-E. 'slab-, *slib-, -i-enlargement
of base *lab-, Heb-, see sleep, v.

## labor
labor, labour, intr. and tr. v. — ME. labouren, fr.
MF. (= F.) labourer, 'to labor, drudge, toil,
take pains', fr. OF. laborer, labourer, fr. L.
labdrure, 'to labor, take pains, suffer, be
afflicted, be in difficulty; to work out, elaborate,
work', fr. labor. See labor, n.
Derivatives: labo(u)r-ed, adj., labo(u)r-ed-ly,
adv., labo(u)r-ed-ness, п., labo(u)r-ing, adj.,
labo(u)r.-ing-ly, adv., Labo(u)r-ite, n.

## laboratory
laboratory, n. — ML. laboratorium, 'workshop',
fr. L. laboratus, pp. of laborare, 'to work'. See
labor, v., and subst. sufT. -ory.

## laborer
laborer, labourer, n. — ME. labourer, laborer, fr.
MF. (= F.) laboureur; fr. OF. laboreor, fr.
laborer, labourer, 'to labor'. See labor, v., and
agential suff. -er.

## laborious
laborious, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) laborigux,
fr. L. laboriosus, 'toilsome, wearisome,
troublesome; industrious', fr. labor. See labor, п., and
-ous.
Derivatives: laborious-ly, adv., laborious-ness, a.

## labradorite
labradorite, п., a brilliant variety of feldspar
(mineral.) — Named after the peninsula oh the
N.E. of North America. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: labradorit-ic, adj.

## labret
labret, п., an ornament of wood, shell or bone
worn in a hole pierced through the lip. —
Formed with dimin. suff. -et fr. L. labrum, 'lip'. See
next word.

## labrum
labrum, п., a lip; applied to liplike parts (zool.) —
L., 'a lip', rel. to labium, of s.m. See labial and
cp. prec. word.

## Laburnum
Laburnum, п., a genus of poisonous plants of the
pea family (bot.); (not cap.) any plant of this
genus. — L. laburnum, prob. an Etruscan loan
word. For the suff. cp. viburnum, 'thewayfaring
tree'.

## labyrinth
labyrinth, n. — L. labyrinthus, fr. Gk. λαβύρινθος,
'maze; large building with intricate passages',
re], to λάβρυς, 'double hatchet', a word of
Carian origin. Accordingly λαβύρινθος
originally denoted the 'palace of the double hatchet'.
In its anatomical sense ('the internal ear') the
word labyrinthus was first used by the Italian
anatomist Gabriello Fallopia (1523-62).
Derivatives: labyrinth, tr. v., tabyrinlh-al, adj.,
labyrinth-al-ly, adv., labyrinth-ian, adj., laby-
rinthic (q.v.), labyrinth-ine, adj.

## labyrinthic
labyrinthic, labyrinthical, adj. — L. labyrinthicus,
'pertaining to a labyrinth', fr. labyrinthus. See
prec. word and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: labyrinthical-ly, adv.

## labyrinthitis
labyrinthitis,' п., inflammation of the labyrinth
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. L. labyrinthus
(see labyrinth) with suff. -itis.

## lac
lac, lakh, п., 1) one hundred thousand; 2) a great
number. — Pers. lak, fr. Hind, lakh, ult. fr. OI.
laksa, 'one, hundred thousand', prop, 'sign,
mark', rel. to laksati, laksayati, 'marks,
characterizes, defines', and prob. also to raksa,
'protection, deliverance, preservation, observation',
raksati, 'protects, delivers, preserves, observes',
and cogn. with Gk. άλέξειν, άλέκειν, 'to ward
off'. See Alexander and cp. Lakshmi.

## iac
iac, п., a red resinous substance. — Pers. lak, fr.
Hind, lakh, fr. OI. Isksd, lit. 'one hundred
thousand' (see prec. word), a name given to the
insects Cocca ilicis, in allusion to their great
number. Their name is used also to denote the
resin of the Quercus coccifera, which flows from
this tree in consequence of the sting of these
insects. Cp. lacquer and the second element in
shellac. Cp. also the second element in
Phytolacca.

## lace
lace, n. — ME. las, lace, it. OF. laz, las (F. lacs),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:433 COLUMN:3 -->
'noose, snare', fr. L. laqueus, of s.m. (whence
also It. laccio, Sp. lazo), fr. Italic base *laq-, 'to
ensnare', whence also L. lacere, 'to entice', deli-
cere, 'to entice, allure, delight'. Cp. F. lacet,
'lace, noose, snare', dimin. of lacs. Cp. also
lasso! which is a doublet of lace. Cp. also lash,
'to bind', latchet, delectation, delicate, delicious,
delight, elicit, enlace, IUicium, interlace.
Derivatives: tac-y, adj., laci-ly, adv., laci-ness, n.

## lace
lace, tr. and intr. v. — ME. lacen, fr. OF. lacier
(F. lacer), fr. OF. laz, las. See lace, n.
Derivatives: lac-ed, adj., lac-ing, n.

## Lacedaemonian
Lacedaemonian, also Lacedemonian, adj., of, or
pertaining to, Lacedaemon or Sparta; п., а
Lacedaemonian or Spartan.—Formed with suff.
-ian fr. L. Lacedaemonius, fr. Gk.
Λακεδαιμόνιος, 'Lacedaemonian, Spartan', fr. Λακε-
δαίμων, 'Lacedaemon, Sparta'. Cp. Laconic.

## lacerable
lacerable, adj. — Late L. lacerabilis, 'that can be
easily lacerated', fr. L. lacer, 'torn'. See lacerate
and -able.
Derivative: lacerabil-ity, n.

## lacerate
lacerate, adj. — L. laceratus, 'torn', pp. of lace-
rare, 'to tear to pieces'. See lacerate, v.
Derivative: lacerate-ly, adv.

## lacerate
lacerate, tr. v., to tear. — L. laceratus, pp. οι lace-
rare, 'to tear to pieces, rend, lacerate', fr. lacer,
'torn', fr. I.-E. base *leq-, Veq-, 'to rend', whence
also Gk. λακίς, 'tatter, rag', λακίζε'ιν, 'to tear
to pieces, lacerate', Alb. I'akur, 'naked', I'ekure,
I'ikure, 'hide, leather, rind'. Cp. lacinia, lancina-
te. For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: lacerat-ed, adj., laceration (q.v.)

## laceration
laceration, n. — L. laceratid, gen. -onis, *a tearing,
rending, laceration', fr. laceratus, pp. of lacerare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## Lacerta
Lacerta, п., a genus of lizards (zool.) — L. lacerta,
'lizard'. See lizard.

## lacertian
lacertian, adj., pertaining to lizards. — Formed
with suff. -ian fr. L. lacertus, lacerta. See prec.
word.
Derivative: lacertian, n.

## Lacertilia
Lacertilia, n. pi., an order of reptiles comprising
the ordinary lizards, chameleons, etc. (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. lacertus, lacerta, 'lizard'. See
lizard and cp. Lacerta.

## lacertilian
lacertilian, adj., pertaining to the Lacertilia. —
Formed from prec. word with suff. -an.
Derivative: lacertilian, п., one of the Lacertilia.

## laches
laches, п., remissness in asserting a right. — ME.
lachesse, fr. OF. laschesse, fr. lasche (F. lache),
'loose, slack', fr. VL. *lascus(whence also OProv-
enc. lasc), which was formed—through the
metathesis of x· (= cs) into sc—fr. L. laxus,
'wide, loose, open'. See lax and cp. lash, 'soft
and watery'. The regular E. equivalent of the F.
suff. -esse is -ess (q.v.); laches (with a single -s)
forms an exception to this rule (cp. riches).

## Lachesis
Lachesis, п., one of the Fates in Greek
mythology. — L., fr. Gk. Λάχεσις, lit. 'the appor-
tioner,· disposer of lots', fr. λαχεΐν, aor. II inf. of
λαγχάνειν, 'to obtain by lot'; of uncertain
origin.

## Lachnanthes
Lachnanthes, п., a genus of plants, the redroot
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. λάχνη,
'woolly hair', and άνθος, 'flower'. The first ele-
■ment prob. stands for *Γλακ-σν-5, fr. I.-E.
*wolk-o-, whence also Avestic var sa-, ModPers.
gurs, OSlav. vlasu, Russ. volos, 'hair'; for the
second element see anther. The genus was so
called in allusion to the woolly flowers.

## lachrymal
lachrymal, also lacrimal, adj., 1) related to tears;
2) marked by tears. — ML. lacrimalis, fr. L.
lacrima, a var. of lacruma, fr. OL. dacruma,
'tear from the eye', which is a loan word fr. Gk.
δάκρϋμα, 'tear', fr. δακρύέιν, 'to shed tears', fr.
δάκρυ, 'tear', which is cogn. with Goth, tagr,
OE. tear', 'tear'. See tear from the eye and cp.
larmoyant. The change of Latin d- to I- (the so
called 'Sabine' /) is prob. due to dialectal influ-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:434 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 407 | LAERTES -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:434 COLUMN:1 -->
ence. Ср. L. lingua (fr. OL. dingua), 'tongue', L.
levir (for I.-E. *daiwir) 'husband's brother'. Cp.
also L. solium (for *sodium), 'chair of state,
throne', which is rel. to sedere, 'to sit', olere (for
*odere), 'to smell', which is rel. to odor, 'smell',
and malus (for *mazdos), 'mast of a ship', which
is cogn. with OHG. mast, OE. mxst, of s.m., and
Ulixes, L. equivalent of Gk. 'Οδυσσεύς,
'Odysseus'. Outside Indo-European cp. Malagasy,
'a native of Madagascar', which is rel. to
Madagascar. The spelling lachrymal, lachrymation,
etc. (with -у- instead of with -;-), is due to the
influence of the Greek cognates δάκρυ, δάκρυον,
δάκρϋμα, 'tear'.
Derivative: lachrymal, n.

## lachrymation
lachrymation, also lamination, п., weeping. — L.
lacrimatid, gen. -onis, fr. lacrimat-(um), pp. stem
of lacrimare, 'to shed tears, weep', fr. lacrima.
See prec. word and -ation

## lachrymatory
lachrymatory, also lacrimatory, adj., pertaining
to tears. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L.
lacrimdt-(um), pp. stem of lacrimare. See
lachrymal.
Derivative: lachrymatory, n.

## lachrymose
lachrymose, adj., tearful. — L. lacrimosus, fr.
lacrima, 'tear'. See lachrymal and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: lachrymose-ly, adv., lachrymose-
ness, п., lachrymos-ity, n.

## lachrymous
lachrymous, adj. — A rare var. of lachrymose. For
the ending see suff. -oils,

## lacinia
lacinia, n. (bot. and loot.) — L., 'lappet, flap, or
edge of a garment', rel, to lacer, 'torn'. See
lacerate,

## laciniate
laciniate, laciniated, adj. — Formed from prec.
word with adj. sufT. -ate, resp. also 1st -ed.
Derivative: laciniat-ion, n.

## lacinula
lacinula, п., a small lacinia (bot. and zool.) —
ModL., dimin. of lacinia. For the ending see
suff. -ule.
Derivatives: lacinul-ate, lacinul-ose, adjs.

## lack
lack, n. — ME. lac, prob. fr. MDu. lac,
'deficiency, fault', which is rel. to ON. lakr, 'lacking',
and to E. slack (q.v.)

## lack
lack, tr. and intr. v. — Either fr. lack, п., or fr.
MDu. taken, 'to be wanting; to blame', which is
rel. to MDu. lac.

## lackadaisical
lackadaisical, adj., listless. — Formed from the
interj. lackadaisy, fr. lackaday; coined by the
English novelist Laurence Sterne (1713-68).

## lackaday
lackaday, interj. — Aphetic form of alack-a-day.
See alack and day.

## lacker
lacker, n. — A var. of lacquer,

## lackey
lackey, also lacquey, n. — MF. (= F.) laquais, fr.
Sp. lacayo, fr. It. lacche, fr. ModGk. ούλάκης
(read ulakis), ult. fr. Turkish ulak, 'runner,
courier', from'stem ul-, 'to go'.
Derivatives: lackey, intr. v., lackey-ed, adj.

## Laconian
Laconian, adj., pertainining to Laconia; п., a La-
conian or Lacedaemonian. — See Laconic and
suff. -an.

## lacmus
lacmus, п., litmus. — Du. lakmoes, fr. MDu.

## leecmos
leecmos, fr. liken (Du. lekkeri), 'to drip, leak',
and mos (= Du. moes), 'green vegetables; pulp'.

## The first element is rel. to OE. leccan
The first element is rel. to OE. leccan, 'to

## moisten
moisten, water'; see leak. The second element is rel.

## to OE.
to OE., OS., OFris. mos, 'food', OE. mete,
'food'; see meat.

## Laconic
Laconic, adj., pertaining to Laconia; (not cap.)

## concise
concise, abrupt (lit. 'resembling the style of the
Lacedaemonians or Spartans'). — L. Laconicus,
fr. Gk. Λακωνικός, 'pertaining to, or

## characteristic of
characteristic of, the Lacedaemonians', fr. Λάκων,
'Laconian, Lacedaemonian, Spartan', which is
prob. a hypocoristic form of Λακεδαιμόνιος.
See Lacedaemonian.
Derivatives: laconic-al-ly, adv., laconic-al-ness, n.

## laconiclsm
laconiclsm, п., laconism. — Formed fr. laconic
with suff. -ism.

## laconism
laconism, п., 1) laconic (i.e. brief) way of
expression; 2) a laconic utterance. — MF (= F.) la-

## conisme
conisme, fr. Gk. Λακωνισμός, 'imitation of the

## Lacedaemonians
Lacedaemonians, laconism', from the stem of
Λακωνίζειν. See next word and -ism.

## laconize
laconize, tr. and intr. v., to imitate the
Lacedaemonians. — Gk. Λακωνίζειν, 'to imitate the

## Lacedaemonians (in dress
Lacedaemonians (in dress, manners etc.)', fr.
Λάκων, Laconian, Lacedaemonian, Spartan'.
See Laconic and -ize.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:434 COLUMN:2 -->

## lacquer
lacquer, lacker, п., a kind of varnish. — MF.
lacre, fr. Port, lacre, 'sealing wax', fr. laca, 'gum
lac', which derives fr. Hind, lakh, 'lac', fr. OI.
laksa. See lac, 'a resinous substance'.
Derivatives: lacquer, tr. v., lacquer-er, п., lac-
quer-ing, n.

## lacquey
lacquey, n. — A var. of lackey.

## lacrimal
lacrimal, adj. — See lachrymal.

## lacrimatory
lacrimatory, adj. — See lachrymatory.

## lacroixite
lacroixite, п., a complex basic fiuophosphate
(mineral.) — Named after the French
mineralogist Franiois-Antoine-Alfred Lacroix (1863-
1948). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## lacrosse
lacrosse, п., a game in which a ball is thrown by
means of a long-handled racket, the crosse,—F.
la crosse, 'the crozier, the racket used in certain
games', fr. fern. def. article la (fr. L. ilia, fem. of
Ule, 'that') and WTeut. *krukja, 'crutch'. See
ille and crutch and cp. crosse, crossette, crosier.

## lactarene
lactarene, also lactarine, п., material made from
casein of milk, used in calico printing. —
Formed with suff. -ene, resp. -me, fr. L. lac, gen. lac-
lis, 'milk'. See lacteal.

## Lactarius
Lactarius, п., a genus of agarics (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. lactarius, 'pertaining to, or containing,
milk; milky' (see next word); so called in
allusion to the milky juice it exudes when broken.

## lactary
lactary, adj., pertaining to milk. — L. lactarius,
'pertaining to, or containing, milk; milky', fr.
lac, gen. lactis, 'milk'. See lacteal, adj., and cp.
prec. word.

## lactase
lactase, п., an enzyme capable of decomposing
lactose (biochem.) — Formed with suff. -ase fr.
L. lac, gen. lactis, 'milk'. See lacteal, adj.

## lactate
lactate, intr. v., to secrete milk (rare). — L.
lactams, pp. of lactare, 'to contain milk; to suckle
young', fr. lac, gen. lactis, 'milk'. See lacteal,
adj., and verbal suff. -ate.

## lactate
lactate, п., a salt of lactic acid (chem.) — See
lactate, v.

## lactation
lactation, n. — Late L. lactatio, gen. -onis,
'a suckling' [prob. through the medium of MF.
(= F.) lactation], fr. L. lactdtits, pp. of lactare.
See lactate, v., and -ion.
Derivative: lactation-al, adj.

## lacteal
lacteal, adj., pertaining to milk. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. lacteus, 'milky, full of milk',
fr. lac, gen. lactis, 'milk', which is cogn. with
Gk. γάλα, gen. γάλακτος, 'milk'. The original
base was "glact- (cp. Gk. γλακτοφάγος, 'eating
milk', Homeric γλάγος, 'milk'). This base was
partly enlarged into Gk. γαλακτ-, partly dis-
similated into L. *lact-. Mir. lacht, W. Ilaeth,
'milk', are Latin loan words. See galactic, and
cp. lactate, v., lactation, lettuce.

## lacteal
lacteal, п., any one of the lymphatic vessels of the
small intestine that take up the chyle (anal.) —
Fr. prec. word.

## lactesce
lactesce, intr. v., to become milky. — L. lacti-
scere, 'to become milky', inchoative of lactere,
'to contain milk, be milky', fr. lac, gen. lactis.
See lacteal, adj., and -esce.

## lactescence
lactescence, п., the process of becoming milky. —
Formed from next word with suff. -ce.

## lactescent
lactescent, adj., becoming milky. — L. lactescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of lactescere, 'to become
milky'. See lactesce and -ent.

## lacti-
lacti-, combining form meaning 'milk, milky,
milklike'. — L. lacti-, fr. lac, gen. lactis, 'milk'.
See lacteal, adj.

## lactic
lactic, adj., pertaining to milk (used in chemistry).
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. lac, gen. lactis,
'milk'. See lacteal, adj., and -ic and cp. galactic.

## lactide
lactide, п., a compound formed from lactic acid
(chem.) — Formed with suff. -Ide fr. L. lac, gen.
lactis, 'milk'. See lacteal, adj.

## lactiferous
lactiferous, adj., yielding milk. — Compounded
of lacti- and b./erre, 'to bear.carry'. See-ferous.

## lacto-
lacto-, combining form meaning 'milk'. — Fr. L.
lac, gen. lactis, 'milk'. See lacteal, adj.

## lactometer
lactometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
purity of milk. — A hybrid coined fr. L. lac,
gen. lactis, 'milk', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See lacteal, adj., and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
The correct form is galactometer (q.v.), in
which both elements are of Greek origin.

## lactose
lactose, п., sugar of milk (chem.) — Coined by
the French chemist Marcelin-Pierre-Eugene

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:434 COLUMN:3 -->
Berthelot (1827-1907) fr. L. lac, gen. lactis,
'milk' (see lacteal, adj.), and subst. suff. -ose.

## lacuna
lacuna, п., a gap. — L. lacuna, 'ditch, pit, pool,
pond, hole, hollow, cavity', dimin. of lacus,
'basin, tank, tub, a large reservoir for water, lake'.
See lake, 'pool', and cp. lagoon.
Derivatives: lacun-al, lacun-ar, lacun-ary, adjs.

## lacunar
lacunar, п., 1) a caisson; 2) a ceiling consisting of
caissons. — L. lacunar, 'a wainscoted and gilded
ceiling', prop. neut. of the adj. "lacunaris,
'provided with cavities', fr. lacuna. See prec. word.

## lacunose
lacunose, adj., full of lacunae. — L. lacunosus,
'full of holes or pits', fr. lacuna. See lacuna and
adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: lacunos-ity, a.

## lacunule
lacunule, п., a small lacuna. — Formed fr. lacuna
with dimin. suff. -ule.
Derivative: lacunul-ose, adj.

## lacustrian
lacustrian, adj., lacustrine; п., a lake dweller. —
See next word and -ian.

## lacustrine
lacustrine, adj., pertaining to a lake. — Prob. fr.
F. lacustre, which was formed fr. L. lacus, 'lake,'
on analogy of paluster, 'marshy, swampy' (fr.
palus, 'marsh, swamp'). See lake, 'pool*, and
adj. suff. -ine.

## lad
lad, n. — ME. ladde, 'a youth, manservant'; of
unknown origin.

## ladanum
ladanum, n. — L. See labdanum.

## ladder
ladder, n. — ME. laddre, fr. OE. hinder, hlSdder,
rel. to OFris. hledere, MDu. ledere, leder (Du.
leer), Du. ladder, OHG. leitara, MHG. leitere,
letter, G. Letter, 'ladder', fr. I.-E. base *kli-, 'to
slope, incline', whence also Goth, hleipra, 'tent'.
See lean, v., and cp. climax, clinical.
Derivatives: ladder, intr. v., ladder-y, adj.

## laddie
laddie, п., a young lad (chiefly Scot.) — Dimin. of
lad.

## lade
lade, tr. v. — ME. laden, fr. OE. hladan, ladan, 'to
load, put as a load, pile; to draw (water)', rel.
to ON. hlada, Dan. lade, Swed. ladda, OFris.
hlada, MDu., Du. laden, OHG. hladan, ladan,
MHG., G. laden, Goth, -hlapan (in af-hlapan),
'to lade, load', fr. I.-E. base *qla-, 'to spread',
whence also Lith. kloju, ktoti, Lett, klaju, klat,
'to spread', OSlav. kladg, klasii (for *klad-ti),
'to lay, set, place', Lith. paklodi, 'sheet'. Cp.
ladle, last, 'measure of weight', lathe, 'machine
for turning', and the first element in larboard.
Derivative: lad-ing, n.

## laden
laden, pp. of lade. — OE. hladen, fr. hladan, 'to
lade'. See lade.

## ladida
ladida, п., an affected person, a fop; adj., affected,
foppish (slang). — Orig. 'affected imitator of
fine speech'; prob. of imitative origin.

## Ladin
Ladin, п., a Rhaeto-Romanic dialect (esp. the
chief dialect) spoken in Switzerland and Tyrol.—
Rhaeto-Romanic, fr. L. Latinus, 'Latin'. See
Latin and cp. next word.

## Ladino
Ladino, п., Spanish mixed with Hebrew, Arabic
and other elements, spoken by Sephardim in
Turkey, Greece and elsewhere. — Sp. ladino,
'sagacious, cunning, crafty', orig. 'Latin', fr. L.
Latinus. See Latin and cp. prec. word.

## ladle
ladle, n. — ME. ladel, fr. OE. hlxdel, fr. hladan,
'to draw (water)'. See lade and instrumental suff.
-le.
Derivatives: ladle, tr. v., ladl-ed, adj., ladl-er, п.,
ladle-ful, adj.

## lady
lady, n. — ME. lafdi, lavede, ladi, fr. OE. hlsef-
dige, 'mistress of the house', lit. 'loaf-maker',
compounded of hlaf, 'loaf, and dxge, 'maid'.
For the first element see loaf, n. The second
element is rel. to Goth, deigan, 'to knead'. See
dough and cp. lord.
Derivatives: lady, adj., lady-hood, п., lady-like,
adj., lady-ship, n.

## ladybird
ladybird, n. — In this compound—as in many
others—lady refers to Virgin Mary. For sense
development cp. G. Marienkafer, 'ladybird', lit.
'Mary's chafer'.

## laeotropic
laeotropic, laeotropous, adj., sinistral. —
Compounded of Gk. λαιός, 'left', and τρόπος, 'a
turn'. The first element stands for *λαι5ός and
is cogn. with L. laevus, 'left'; see levo-. For the
second element see -tropic.

## Laertes
Laertes, п., king of lthace and father of Odysseus
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Λαέρτης, lit.
'gatherer of the people', compounded of λαός,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:435 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LAEVO- | 408 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:435 COLUMN:1 -->
'people', and εϊρειν, 'to fasten together, string
together'. For the first element cp. liturgy, for
the second see series.

## laevo-
laevo-, combining form. — See levo-.

## laevulose
laevulose, n. — See levulose.

## lag
lag, п., stave of a cask. — Prob. of Scand. origin.
Cp. ON. logg, 'rim of a barrel', Swed. lagg,
'stave of a barrel'.
Derivatives: lag, tr. v., to cover with lags,
lagging, n.

## lag
lag, adj., last, hindmost. — Of uncertain origin,
perh. a childish distortion of last, adj.

## lag
lag, intr. v., to walk behind. — Of uncertain
origin; perh. fr. lag, adj. Cp. graylag.
Derivatives: lag, п., one who lags, laggard (q.v.),
lagg-er, n.

## lag
lag, п., retardation. — Fr. lag, 'last'.

## lag (slang)
lag (slang), tr. v., I) to transport as a convict; 2)
to arrest; п., 1) a convict; 2) a term of
transportation. — Of unknown origin.

## lag-
lag-, form of lago- before a vowel.

## lagan
lagan, п., cargo sunk in the sea. — OF. lagand,
lagan, of Teut. origin and lit. meaning 'that
which is lying'. See lay, 'to place', lie, 'to recline'.

## lagena
lagena, п., flask, bottle. — L., fr. Gk. λάγϋνος, a
loan word fr. Heb. logh, 'a liquid measure' (cp.
Copt, lok), to which the Syriac suff. -ena has
been added; see Noldeke, Syrische Grammatik,
§ 132. See log, 'a liquid measure'.

## lager (beer)
lager (beer), п., a kind of beer which is kept on
store for some months before being drunk. —
G. Lager, 'camp; storehouse', rel. to OE. leger.
See lair and cp. laager, leaguer, 'camp'.

## laggard
laggard, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -ard fr.
lag, 'to walk behind'.
Derivatives: laggard-ly, adv., laggard-ness, n.

## lagniappe
lagniappe, п., gift, gratuity. — Amer. F., fr. Amer.
Sp. la пара, 'the gift', fr. Sp. la, 'the', fem. of el,
fr. L. ille, 'that' (see Hie), and Amer. Sp. пара,
yapa, 'lagniappe', fr. Quechua yapa, 'something
added, gift'.

## lago-
lago-, before a vowel lag-, combining form
meaning 'hare'. — Gk. λαγό-, λαγ-, fr. λαγώς,
'hare', which stands for *λαγ(ο)-ω[υσ]-ός and
lit. means 'the animal with the flapping ears'.
The first element of this compound is rel. to Gk.
λαγαρός, 'slack, hollow', and cogn. with L. lan-
guere, 'to faint, weary'; see languid. The second
element is rel. to Gk. ους, gen. ώτός, 'ear'; see
oto-.

## lagomorph
lagomorph, п., an animal of the order Lago-
тотрпа. — From next word.

## Lagomorpha
Lagomorpha, n.pl., an order of rodent mammals
including the hares, rabbits and pikas (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of lago- and Gk. μορφή,
'form, shape'. See morpho-.

## lagoon
lagoon, п., a shallow pond connected with a lake
or sea. — F. lagune, fr. It. laguna, fr. L. lacuna,
'pool, pond'. See lacuna.

## lagophthalmos
lagophthalmos, lagophthalmus, п., a morbid
condition in which the eyes cannot be entirety closed
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. λαγόφθαλμος, lit.
'hare-eyed', fr. λαγώς, 'hare', and οφθαλμός,
'eye*'; so called from the belief that hares cannot
close their eyes entirely. See lago- and ophthal-
mo- and cp. exophthalmos.

## Lagopus
Lagopus, п., a genus of birds, the ptarmigan and
the red grouse (ornithol.) — ModL., lit. 'hare-
footed', compounded of Gk. λαγώς, 'hare', and
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See lago- and -pod.

## Lagurus
Lagurus, п., a genus of grasses, the hares-tail
grass (hot.) — ModL., lit. 'hare's tail',
compounded of Gk. λαγώς, 'hare', and ούρα, 'tail'.
See lago- and uro-, 'tail-'.

## laic
laic, adj. — F. latque, fr. Late L. Idicus, fr. Gk.
λαϊκός, 'of, or belonging to, the people', fr.
λαός, 'people'. See lay, 'pertaining to the laity'.
Derivatives: laic, п., laic-al, adj., taic-at-ity, п.,
laic-al-Iy, adv., laic-iz-ation, п., laic-ize, tr. v.

## laid
laid, past tense and pp. of lay, 'to place'.

## lain
lain, pp. of lie. — ME. lein, fr. OE. (ge)legen, pp.
of licgan. See lie, 'to recline'.

## lair
lair, п., resting place, den of wild beasts.—MB.Ieir,
fr. OE. leger, rel. to ON. legr, OFris. leger, OS.,
OHG. legar, MHG. leger, G. Lager, Goth, ligrs,
'place of lying, lair, couch, bed', fr. I.-E. base
*legh-, 'to lie'. See lie, 'to recline', and cp. laager,
lager, leaguer, 'camp', beleaguer.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:435 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: lair, intr. and tr. v.

## laird
laird, п., a landed proprietor. — Scot, form of
lord.

## laissez-faire
laissez-faire, п., noninterference. — F., lit. 'let do'
(i.e. 'let people do what they like').

## laity
laity, n. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. lay,
'pertaining to the laity'.

## lake
lake, п., a pool. — ME. lac, lake, fr. OF. (= F.)
lac, fr. L. lacus, 'basin, tank, pond, lake,
cistern', which is cogn. with Gk. λάκκος (for
*λάκ5ος), 'pond, cistern, pit', OSlav. loky,
'pool, puddle, cistern', ON. logr, OS., OE. lagu,
'sea, flood, water', Olr. lock, 'lake, pond'. Cp.
lacuna, lacustrine, lagoon, loch.
Derivative: lak-y, adj.

## lake
lake, п., pigment prepared from lac. — F. tuque,
fr. OProvenc. laca, fr. Pers. lak. See lac,
'resinous substance'.

## lakh
lakh, n. — See lac, 'one hundred thousand
(rupees)'.

## Lakshmi
Lakshmi, п., goddess of beauty (Hindu mylhol.)
— OI. Laksml, fr. laksmi, 'mark, fortune, riches,
beauty', rel. to laksati, laksayati, 'marks,
characterizes, defines'. See lac, 'one hundred
thousand rupees'.

## Lalage
Lalage, Roman fem. PN. — L., fr. Gk λαλαγή,
'babble, prattle' (whence λαλαγεΐν, *to babble,
prattle'), fr. λαλεϊν, 'to talk, chat, prattle', fr.
λάλος, 'talkative, loquacious', fr. I.-E.
imitative base *lal-, whence also OI. lalalla, imitation
of stammering, L. lallare, 'to sing to sleep, to
lull', G. lallen, 'to stammer', Lith. laluoti, 'to
stammer'. Cp. Eulalia, paralalia. Cp. also lull.

## lalique
lalique, п., a kind of decorative glassware. —
Short for Lalique glassware; named after its
inventor Reni Lalique (1860-1944).

## lam
lam, tr. v., to beat, thrash (slang). — The original
meaning was 'to make lame'; rel. to lame.

## lama
lama, п., priest. — Tibetan blama, lama, 'priest'.
Cp. Dalai Lama.

## Lamaism
Lamaism, п., the religious system of the lamas. —
Coined fr. lama with suff. -ism.

## Lamaist
Lamaist, п., an adherent of Lamaism. — Formed
fr. lama with suff. -ist.
Derivative: Lamaist-ic, adj.

## Lamarckian
Lamarckian, adj., pertaining to, or based on, the
teachings of the French naturalist Lamarck
(1744-1829); п., a follower of Lamarck. — For
the ending see suff. -Ian.

## Lamarckism
Lamarckism, п., the teachings of Lamarck. —
See prec. word and -ism.

## lamasery
lamasery, п., monastery of lamas. — F. lamaserie,
fr. lama. See lama.

## lamb
lamb, n. — ME. lamb, lomb, fr. OE. lamb, rel. to
OS., ΟΝ., OFris., OHG., Goth, lamb, MHG.
lamp, Dan., Du. lam, Swed. G. lamm, 'lamb',
for orig. *lon-bho-s; cogn. with Gk. ϊλαφος
(for *eln-bhos), 'hart', έλλός (for *elnos), 'fawn'.
All these words are traceable to I.-E. base *el-,
Tjrown'. See eland, elk, and cp. the first element
in lammergeier.
Derivatives: lamb, intr. v., lamb-ing, п.,
lamblike, adj.

## lambda
lambda, п., name of the 11th letter of the Greek
alphabet. — Gk. λάβδα, λάμβδα, fr. Heb.-
Phoen. lamedh; see lamed. The final α was added
because a Greek word cannot end with a δ; cp.
alpha and words there referred to.

## lambdacism
lambdacism, lambdacismus, п., 1) too frequent use
of the letter / in speaking or writing; 2)
confusion of / and r in pronunciation; 3) lallation. —
Late L. labdacismus, lambdacismus, fr. Gk. λαβ-
δακισμός, λαμβδακισμός, 'too frequent use of
the letter lambda', fr. λάβδα, resp. λάμβδα, the
letter /. See prec. word and -ism.

## lambdoid
lambdoid, adj., shaped like the Greek lambda
(Λ); in anatomy, designating the suture that
connects the two parietal bones with the
occipital. — Gk. λαβδοειδής, λαμβδοειδής, 'of
the shape of а Л', compounded of λάβδα, resp.
λάμβδα, and -οειδής, 'like', fr είδος, 'form,

## shape'. See prec. word and -oid
shape'. See prec. word and -oid, and cp. hyoid.
Derivative: lambdoid-al, adj.

## lambency
lambency, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## lambent
lambent, adj., moving about lightly; flickering. —

## The orig. meaning was 'licking'
The orig. meaning was 'licking', fr. L. lambens,

## gen. lambentis
gen. lambentis, pres. part, of lambere, 'to lick',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:435 COLUMN:3 -->
which is cogn. with Gk. λάπτειν, 'to sip, lick',
OE. lapian, 'to lick, lap up, sup'. See lap, 'to
lick up', and -ent.

## Lambert
Lambert, masc. PN. — F., fr. G. Lambert, fr.
OHG. Lambreht, Landberht, which is
compounded of lant, 'land', and berahi, 'bright',
hence lit. meaning 'illustrious with land'. See
land and bright and cp. Albert.

## lambkin
lambkin, n. — Formed fr. lamb with dimin. suff.
-kin.

## lambrequin
lambrequin, п., valance, hanging; mantling (her.)
— F., fr. MDu. *lamperkijn, dimin. of tamper,
'veil', lit. 'something hanging'. For the ending
see suff. -kin.

## lame
lame, adj. — ME. lame, fr. OE. lama, rel. to ON.
lami, OS. lamo, ON. lami, Dan., Swed., MDu.,
Du., OHG., MHG. lam, G. lahm, 'lame', lit.
'broken', fr. I.-E. base *lem-, 'to break', whence
also OSlav. lomiti, 'to break', lomitise, 'to grow
lame', Russ. lomit', to break', lorn, 'fragment',
lomota, 'gout', Lith. liiomas, 'lame', I'imt, 'to
break down', OPruss. limtwei, 'to break', Olr.
laime, 'ax', and prob. also Gk. νωλεμές,
'unceasingly', lit. 'unbroken' (fr. negative particle
*νε- and 8-λεμος, 'a breaking').
Derivatives: lame, tr. and intr. v., lame-ly, adv.,
tame-ness, n,

## lame
lame, п., a thin plate. — F., fr. L. lamina, 'a thin
'piece of metal'. See lamina and cp. lamella.

## lamed
lamed, lamedh, п., name of the 12th letter of the
Hebrew alphabet. — Heb. lamedh, lit. prob. 'the
rod of the teacher', from the stem of lamadh, 'he
exercised, learned', whence also malmadh, 'ox
goad', talmtdh, 'scholar, pupil'. See Talmud and
cp. lambda.

## lamella
lamella, п., a thin plate. — L. lamella, 'a small
thin plate', dimin. of lamina, 'a thin plate of
metal or wood'. See lamina and -ella and cp.
omelet.

## lamellar
lamellar, lamellary, lamellate, adjs., composed of
lamellae. — Formed fr. L. lamella (see prec.
word) with suff. -ar, resp. -ary, -ate.

## l.amellibranchia
l.amellibranchia, also Lamellibranchiata, n. pi., a
class of mollusks (zool.) — ModL., lit. 4hose
with lamellate gills'. See lamella and branchia,
resp. branchiate.

## lamellibranchiate
lamellibranchiate, adj., pertaining to the Lamelli-
branchla. — See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.

## lamelliform
lamelliform, adj., having the form of a lamella. —
See lamella and -form.

## lament
lament, intr. v. — MF. (= F.) lamenter, fr. L. la-
mentari, 'to wail, moan, weep, lament', fr. Ш-
mentum, 'a wailing, moaning, weeping,
lamentation', which stands for *Id-men-tom, from the
I.-E. imitative base */<?-, 'to shout, cry', whence
also L. latrare (for la-trure), 'to bark', Arm. lam,
Ί weep', Gk λαίειν, λαήμεναι (Hesychius), 'to
speak loud', Lith. loju, loli, Lett, tat, 'to bark',
OSlav. lajo, lajati, 'to bark; to abuse'. Cp. Larus.
For the ending of lament see suff. -ment.
Derivatives: tament-at-ory, adj., lament-ed, adj.,
tament-ed-ty, adv., lament-er, п., lament-ing, n.
and adj., lament-ing-ly, adv., lament-ive, adj.

## lament
lament, n. — L. /amentum. See lament, v.

## lamentable
lamentable, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
lamentabilis, 'full of sorrow, mournful,
lamentable', fr. lamentari. See lament, v., and -able.
Derivatives: lamentable-ness, п., lamentabl-y,
adv.

## lamentation
lamentation, n. — ME. lamentacioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) lamentation, fr. L. lamentdtionem, ace. of
lamentatio,' wailing, moaning,
weeping,lamenting', fr. lamentarus, pp. of lamentart. See
lament, v., and -ation.

## lamia
lamia, п., a devouring monster; vampire, witch.
— L., fr. Gk. Λάμια (fem.), 'monster, specter',
which is rel. to λαμυρός, 'voracious, gluttonous',
λάμια (neut. pi.), 'chasm', λαιμός, 'throat,
gullet', and cogn. with L. lemures, 'spirits of the
dead; ghosts, specters', and prob. also with Lett.
lamat, 'to scold', lamatas, 'mousetrap'. The idea
underlying all these words is 'jaws open wide'.
Cp. Lamium, Lamnidae. Cp. also lemur.

## Lamiaceae
Lamiaceae, n. pi., a family of plants; synonym of
Menthaceae (bot.) — ModL., formed fr.
Lamium with surf, -aceae.

## iamiaceous
iamiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceons.

## lamina
lamina, п., a thin piece of metal. — L. lamina, 'a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:436 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 409 | LANGUED'OC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:436 COLUMN:1 -->
thin piece of metal or wood, leaf, layer'; of
uncertain origin. Cp. lame, 'a thin plate', and
lamella.

## laminal
laminal, laminar, adj., arranged in laminae. —
Formed with suff. -al, resp. -ar, fr. L. lamina.
See prec. word.

## laminate
laminate, tr. v., to cause to form laminae; intr. v.,
to split into thin layers. — Formed with verbal
suff. -ate fr. L. lamina. See lamina.
Derivatives: /aminat-ed, adj., laminat-ion, n.

## laminiferous
laminiferous, adj., having laminae. —
Compounded of L. lamina, 'a thin piece', andferre,
'to bear, carry'. See lamina and -ferous.

## laminitis
laminitis, n-, inflammation in the laminae of the
horse's foot (veter.) — A ModL. hybrid coined
fr. L. lamina (see lamina) and -ids, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## Lamium
Lamium, п., a genus of plants, the dead nettle
(bol.) — L., 'dead nettle', fr. Gk. "λάμίον, which
is rel. to Λάμια, 'monster' (see lamia); so called
from the labiate flower.

## Lammas
Lammas, п., the first day of August'. — ME.
Lammasse, fr. OE. hlafmxsse, hldmmxsse, lit.
'loaf mass', a compound of hid/, 'loaf', and
mxsse, 'mess'. See loaf, п., and Mass.

## lammergeier
lammergeier, the largest European bird of prey.
— G. Lammergeier, compounded of hammer,
pi. of Lamm, 'lamb' (see lamb), and Geier,
'vulture', fr. 'MHG. glr, fr. OHG. gir, a noun
derived from the OHG. adjective giri (whence
MHG. gire), 'greedy', which is formed with -ro-
formative element fr. I.-E. base *ghl-, 'to open
the mouth wide'. Cp. Du. gier, 'vulture', and see
yearn. Cp. also the first element in gerfalcon.

## Lamnidae
Lamnidae, n. pi., a family of sharks (ichthyol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk. λάμνα,
'a-large fish of prey', which is rel. to Λάμια,
'monster'. See lamia and cp. words there
referred to.

## lamp
lamp, n. — ME. lampe, lamp, fr. OF. (= F.)
lampe, fr. Late L. lampada (nom.), fr. L. lam-
pada, ace. of lampas, fr. Gk. λαμπάς, ace.
λαμπάδα, 'torch', fr. λάμπειν, 'to shine, be
bright', whence also λαμπρός, 'bright, clear',
λαμπτήρ, 'light, torch, lantern', λαμπυρίς,
'glowworm', fr. I.-E. base 'lap-, *llp-, 'to shine',
whence also Lith. lope, 'light', Lett, lapa, 'torch',
OPruss. lopis, 'flame'; fr. *lap-s, an -i-enlarge-
ment of base 'lap-, derive Olr. lassar, 'flame',
lassaim, Ί flame', W. ttachar, 'shining, bright'.
Cp. lantern. Cp. also lampro-, Lampsilis, Lam-
pyridae, eclampsia.
Derivatives: lamp, tr. and intr. v., lamp-less,
adj., lamp-let, n.

## lampadedromy
lampadedromy, п., a torch race in honor of
Prometheus in which a lighting torch was handed
on from runner to runner (Greek antiq.) — Gk.
λαμπαδηδρομία, 'torch race', compounded of
λαμπάς, gen. λαμπάδος, 'torch', and δρόμος,
'course, race'. See lamp and dromedary and cp.
next word.

## lampadephore
lampadephore, п., a torchbearer (Greek antiq.) —
Gk. λαμπαδηφόρος, 'torchbearer',
compounded of λαμπάς, gen. λαμπάδος, 'torch', and
-φόρος, 'bearer'. See lamp and -phore.

## lampadephoria
lampadephoria, п., torch race (Greek antiq.) —
Gk. λαμπαδηφορία, 'torch bearing', fr.
λαμπαδηφόρος. See prec. word and -la.

## lampas
lampas, п., a disease in horses. — F., fr. tamper,
'to guzzle'. See lampoon.

## lampas
lampas, п., silk damask— F., of unknown origin.

## lampern
lampern, п., the river lamprey. — ME. lamproun,
lampurn, fr. OF. lamprion, lampreon, dimin, of
lampreie, 'lamprey'. See lamprey.

## lampoon
lampoon, п., a virulent satire. — F. lampon,
'drinking song', from the cry of students in
coffeehouses lampons, 'let us drink', fr. tamper,
'to guzzle', a nasalized form of taper, 'to lap',
which is of imitative origin. Cp. lampas, 'a
disease in horses'. Cp. also OE. lapian, 'to lap' (see
lap).
Derivatives: lampoon, tr. v., lampoon-er, п.,
lampoon-ery, п., lampoon-ist, n.

## lampr-
lampr-, form of lampro- before a vowel.

## lamprey
lamprey, п., any of a group of eellike aquatic
animals. — ME. lampreie, fr. OF. lampreie (F.
lamproie), fr. ML. lampreda, a blend of L. nau-

## preda
preda, 'mud-lamprey, limpet', which is of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:436 COLUMN:2 -->
Gaulish origin, and L. lambere, 'to lick'. See lambent
and cp. limpet.

## lampro-
lampro-, before a vowel lampr-, combining form
meaning 'bright'. — Gk. λαμπρό-, λαμπρ-, fr.
λαμπρός, 'bright', rel. to λάμπειν, 'to shine, be
bright', λαμπάς, gen. λαμπάδος, 'torch'. See
lamp.

## Lampsilis
Lampsilis, п., a genus of N. American mussels
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. λάμπειν,
'to shine, be bright', and ψιλός, 'naked, bare,
stripped of feathers, smooth'. See lamp and
psilo-.

## Lampyridae
Lampyridae, n. pi., a family of beetles including
many luminous insects (entomol.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. L. lampyris, fr. Gk.
λαμπυρίς, 'glowworm', which derives fr.
λάμπειν, 'to shine, be bright'. See lamp.

## lanarkite
lanarkite, п., a basic lead sulfate (mineral.) —
Named after Leadhills, Lanarkshire, in
Scotland. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## lanate
lanate, adj., woolly; covered with wool.—L. Id-
natus, 'woolly, downy', fr. tana, 'wool, soft hair,
down', fr. I.-E. *wefnd, "w'jnd, whence also
OE. wull, 'wool'. See wool and words there
referred to and cp. esp. delaine, flannei, laniferous,
lanigerous, lanolin, lanose, lanugo. For the
ending see adj. suff. -ate.

## lance
lance, n. — ME. launce, lance, fr. OF. (= F.)
lance, fr. L. lancea, 'a light spear, lance', which
is a Celtic loan word. Cp. It. lancia, OProveng.
/ansa, Catal. tlansa, Sp. lanza. Port, lanca, Du.,
Swed. tons, G. Lanze, etc., which all are
borrowed from Latin. Cp. elan, launch, fer-de-lance.

## lance
lance, tr. v. — ME. launcen, fr. MF. lander,
lancer (F. lancer), fr. Late L. lanceure, 'to wield a.
lance' (whence also It. lanciare, Sp. lanzar), fr. L.
lancea. See lance, n.

## lance-knight
lance-knight, п., a lansquenet (hist.) —
Folk-etymological alteration of G. Landsknechi, 'foot
soldier' (lit. 'land servant'; see lansquenet), due
to a confusion of the first element of the word
with lance.

## lancelet
lancelet, n. — Formed fr. lance, п., with dimin.
suff. -let.

## Lancelot
Lancelot, masc. PN.—F., formed withthedouble
dimin. suff. -el-ot fr. OHG. Lanzo, lit. 'landed'
fr. OHG. land, 'land'. See land, -el and -ot.

## lanceolate
lanceolate, adj., lance-shaped (zool. and йог.) —
L. lanceoldtus, 'shaped like a small lance", fr.
lanceola, dimin. of lancea, 'lance'. See lance, п.,
-ole and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: lanceolat-ed, adj.

## lancer
lancer, n. — F. lander, 'a soldier armed with a
lance', fr. lance. See lance, п., and agential suff.
-er.

## lancet
lancet, п., a small surgical instrument. — F. lan-
cette, lit. 'a small lance', dimin, of lance. See
lance, п., and the suffixes -et and -ette.

## lanciform
lanciform, adj., lance-shaped. — Compounded of
L. lancea, 'lance', and forma, 'form, shape'. See
lance, п., and form, n.

## lancinate
lancinate, tr. v., to tear. — L. lancinatus, pp, of
lancinare, 'to tear to pieces, rend, lacerate',
which is rel. to tacerare, of s.m. See lacerate.
Derivatives: lancinat-ing, adj., lancinat-ion, n.

## land
land, n. — ME. land, land, fr. OE. land, land, rel.
to OS., ON., Dan., Swed., OFris., Du., G.,
Goth, land, MDu., OHG., MHG. lant, fr. I.-E.
base *lendh-, 'land, heath', whence also Olr.
land, MW. llan, 'an open space', Ir. lann,
'enclosure', W. llan, 'enclosure, yard, churchyard',
Co. Ian, Bret, lann, 'heath' (F. lande, 'heath,
moor', is borrowed fr. Gaul. *landa), OPruss.
lindan (ace.), 'valley', OSlav. ledina, ledo, 'waste
land, heath', Russ. Ijada, 'land newly cleared',
Czech lada, 'fallow land'. Cp. inwn, 'stretch
of grass'. Cp. also Lancelot, the first element
in Lambert and the second element in Roland,
uitlander.
Derivatives: land, tr. and intr. v., land-ed, adj.,
land-er, п., land-ing, п., land-less, adj.

## landau
landau, п., a four-wheeled covered
horse-carriage. — Usually connected with Landau, name
of a town in Bavaria, Germany, but in reality
derived fr. Sp. lando, orig. 'a light four-wheeled
carriage drawn by mules', fr. Arab, at-andul,
misread as a-landul. Arab, andul is traceable to
OI. an-dolah, hin-dolah, 'swing, seesaw, litter';

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:436 COLUMN:3 -->
see Manfred Mayrhofej-, A Concise
Etymological Sanskrit Dictionary, I, 549 and Brockelmann
in ZDMG., vol. 51 (1897), p. 658; vol. 52, p.
282, "Nochmals Landauer". Cp. doolie,

## landaulet
landaulet, п., 1) a small landau; 2) a kind of
automobile. — Formed fr. prec. word with dimin.
suff. -let.

## landgrave
landgrave, n-, 1) formerly, a German count having
jurisdiction over a certain territory; 2) later, the
title of certain German princes. — G. Landgraf,
lit. 'landcount', compounded ofLand(ft. MHG.
lant, fr. OHG. lant), 'land', and Graf (ft. MHG.
grave, fr. OHG. gravo), 'count, earl'. See land
and grave, 'count', and cp. margrave.

## landgraviate
landgraviate, п., the office, jurisdiction or
territory of a landgrave. — ML. landgravidtus, a
hybrid coined fr. landgrave and L.- atus (see 3rd
suff. -ate).

## landgravine
landgravine, п., wife of a landgrave. — G. Land-
grdfin, lit. 'landcountess'. See prec. word.

## landloper
landloper, landlouper, п., a vagabond. — Du.
landloper, lit. 'landrunner', fr. land, 'land', and
lopen, 'to run'. See land, leap and cp. elope,
interloper.

## landmark
landmark, n. — OE. landmearc. See land and
mark, n.

## landscape
landscape, n. — Du. landschap, fr. MDu. land-
scap, 'region' (which is rel. to OE. landsctpe,
ON. landskapr, OHG. lantscaf, G. Landschaft,
'region'), fr. land, 'land', and -scap, '-ship'. See
land and -ship.
Derivative: landscape, tr. and intr. v.

## landstarm
landstarm, п., a general levy. — G., compounded
of Land, 'country', and Sturm, 'storm'. See land
and storm.

## landtag
landtag, п., the legislative assembly in German
states. — G., lit. 'day of the country'. See land
and day. For sense development cp. diet,
'parliamentary assembly'. Cp. also the second
element in Reichstag, Rigsdag, Riksdag.

## landwehr
landwehr, п., military reserve of trained armed
forces in Germany and other countries (mil.) —
G., fr. MHG. lantwer, fr. OHG. lantweri, 'army
for the protection of the country', which is
compounded of lant, 'land', and weri, 'protection'.
See land and weir.

## lane
lane, n. — ME. lane, fr. OE. lane, rel. to OFris.
lana, lona, MDu. lane, Du. laan, 'lane', ON. Ion,
'row of houses'. The ultimate etymol. of these
Teut. words is unknown. Cp. the second
element in slalom.

## langbanite
langbanite, п., a manganese silicate with ferrous
antimonate (mineral.) — Swed. Idngbanit, named
after Langban in Varmland, Sweden. The end-
ing-/i goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## langbeinite
langbeinite, п., double sulfate of potassium and
magnesium (mineral) — G. Langbeinit, named
after the chemist A. Langbein of Dessau,
Germany. The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## langley
langley, п., a unit of solar radiation,
corresponding to one gram calorie per square centimeter
per unit of time. — Named after the American
astronomer Samuel Pierpont Langley (1834-
1906).

## Langobard
Langobard, п., Lombard. — L. Langobardt (pi.),
name of a people of Northern Germany. See
Lombard.

## langrage
langrage, п., a kind of shot. — Formed on
analogy of cartridge fr. earlier langrel, a word of
unknown origin.
Derivative: langrag-ed, adj.

## lang syne
lang syne, adv., long since; п., the long ago,
ancient times — Scot, form of long since.

## language
language, n. — ME. langage, language, fr. OF.
(— F.) langage, fr. VL. *linguaticum, fr. L.
lingua, 'tongue; speech, language'. See tongue and
-age and cp. lingual. The spelling language
(with к) is due to the influence of F. langue,
'tongue; language'. Cp. next word and languet.

## langned
langned, adj., having the tongue of a tincture
different from the rest (her.) — Formed with 3rd
suff. -ed fr. L. langue, 'tongue'. See prec. word.

## langne d'oc
langne d'oc, the Romance language of Southern
France; the Provencal language. — OF. langue
d'oc, 'language of oc', lit. 'yes language' (i.e. the
language in which oc, fr. L. hoc, 'this thing', is
used for 'yes'). L. hoc is the neut. form of hie;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:437 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LANGUED'OIL | 410 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:437 COLUMN:1 -->
see hodiernal and cp. haeccclty. Cp. next word.

## langned'oil
langned'oil, the Romance language spoken in the
center and north of France; the French
language. — OF. langue d'oil, 'language of oil, lit.
'yes language', i.e. the language in which of/(now
out; derived fr. L. hoc ille, scil. fecit, 'he did it')
is used for 'yes'. See prec. word and ille.

## languet
languet, languette, п., a4ittle tongue; used of
various tongue-shaped parts of objects. — ME.
languet, languette, fr. MF. (— F.) languette, dimin.
of langue, 'tongue'. See tongue and -et, -ette,
and cp. language.

## languid
languid,adj., 1) drooping; weak; 2) duli. — ME.
languide, fr. L. tanguidus, 'faint, weak, dull,
sluggish, languid' (prob. through the medium of
F. languide), fr. languere, 'to faint, weary', rel.
to laxus, which stands for *(s)leg-sos, 'wide,
loose, open*, fr. I.-El base *(s)le"g-, "(s)llg-,
*(s)leng-, 'to be slack', whence also Gk. λήγειν,
'to leave off, stop', lit. 'to grow tired or weary',
λαγαρός, 'slack, hollow, sunken', λαγώς, 'hare'
[for *λαγ(ο)-ω(υσ)ός, lit. 'the animal with the
flapping ears'], Olr. lace, 'slack, loose', Gael.,
lr. lag, 'slack, weak', ON. slakr, OE. slxc, 'slow,
slack'. See slack and cp. lack, slake. Cp. also
languish, languor. Cp. also catalectic, delay,
laches, lago-, lash, adj., lax, laxative, leash, lush,
relay, release, relish, and the second element in
algolagnia.
Derivatives: languid-ly, adv., languid-ness, n.

## languish
languish, intr. v., I) to become languid; 2) to
become dull. — ME. tanguishen, fr. OF. (= F.)
languiss-, pres. part, stem of languir, fr. VL.
*languire, corresponding to L. languere, 'to faint,
weary'. See languid and verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: languish, п., languish-ing, adj., lan-
guish-ing-ly, adv., languish-men], n.

## languor
languor, п., 1) weakness; 2) dullness. — ME. lan-
gour, fr. OF. languor (F. langueur), fr. L. lan-
guorem, ace. of languor, 'faintness, feebleness,
weariness', fr. languere. See languid.
Derivatives: languor-ous, adj., languor-ous-ly,
adv.

## langur
langur, п., a long-tailed monkey of Asia (genus
Presbytis). — Hind, langur, fr. OI. langulin,
'having a (long) tail'.

## lani-
lani-, combining form meaning 'wool'. — L. ISni-,
fr. lana, 'wool'. See lanate.

## laniard
laniard, n. — A var. of lanyard.

## laniary
laniary, adj., canine (anat.) — L. laniarius,
'pertaining to a butcher', fr. lanius, 'butcher', which
is of Etruscan origin and rel. to lanista, 'trainer
of gladiators'. See lanista and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivative: laniary, п., a laniary tooth.

## laniferous
laniferous, adj., wool-bearing. — L. lanifer,
'wool-bearing', compounded of lana, 'wool',
and ferre. Ίο bear, carry'. See lanate and -ferous.

## lanigerous
lanigerous, adj., wool-bearing. — L. laniger,
'wool-bearing', compounded of lana, 'wool',
and gerere, 'to bear, carry'. See lanate and
gerent.

## Laniidae
Laniidae, n. pi., a family of birds, the true shrikes
(ornithol.) — ModL., formed fr. Lanius with
suff. -idae.

## lanista
lanista, п., a trainer of gladiators. — L., 'trainer
of gladiators, fencing master'; as shown by the
suff. -hie, a word of Etruscan origin; cp.
fenestra. Cp. laniary, Lanius, lanner, lanneret.

## Lanius
Lanius, п., a genus of birds, the shrike (ornithol.)
— L. lanius, 'butcher'. See laniary.

## lank
lank, adj., slender; lean. — ME. lank, fr. OE.
hlanc, 'lank, lean', rel. to OHG. (h)lanca, MHG.
lanke, 'hip, flank', and to OE. hlence, 'link of
a coat of mail, (pi.) armor', MHG., G. lenken,
'to bend, turn, lead', MHG. gelenke, 'bending',
G. Gelenk, 'joint', fr. I.-E. base "qleng-, 'to
bend', whence also L. dingo, clingere, 'to girdle'.
Cp. the var. base *qlenq-, whence OSlav. klelq,
-ati, 'to kneel', Russ. kljaeu, 'cudgel, crossbar',
Lith. lenkti, 'to bend'. See link, 'ring of chain',
and cp. dank.
Derivatives: lank-ly, adv., lank-ness, п., lank-y,
adj., lank-i-ly, adv.,lank-i-ness, n.

## lanner
lanner, п., a falcon. — ME. laner, fr. OF (= F.)
lanier, fr. L. laniarius, 'butcher'. See laniary.

## lanneret
lanneret, п., the male lanner (falconry). — F.
laneret, formed fr. lanier, 'lanner' (see prec.
word), with dimin. suff. -et (the male lanner is

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:437 COLUMN:2 -->
smaller than the female).

## lanolin
lanolin, lanoline, п., wool fat. — Coined by the
German physician Mathias Eugenius Oscar
Liebreich (1838-1908) in 1886 fr. L. lana, 'wool',
oleum, 'oil, fat', and chem. suff. -hi, -ine. See
lanate and -ole (fr. L. oleum).

## lanose
lanose, adj., woolly. — L. lanosus, 'woolly', fr.
lana, 'wool'. See lanate and adj. suff. -ose.

## lansfordite
lansfordite, п., a hydrous basic magnesium
carbonate (mineral.) — Named after Lansford in
Pennsylvania. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## lansquenet
lansquenet, п., 1) a German mercenary in the 16th
and 17th centuries; 2) a card game. — F., fr. G.
Landsknecht, «lit. 'servant of the country-', fr.
Lands, gen. of Land, 'land, country', and Knecht,
'slave, servant'. See land and knight and cp.
lance-knight.

## Lantana
Lantana, п., a genus of plants of the vervain
family (hot.) — ModL., 'viburnum', altered fr.
lentana (form used by Gesner), of s.m., lit. 'the
pliant plant', fr. L. lentus, 'flexible, pliant'. See
lithe and cp. lentiscus, lentitude.

## lantern
lantern, n. — ME. lanterne, fr. OF. (= F.) lan-
terne, fr. L. tanterna, fr. Gk. λαμπτήρ (see
lamp), to which the Etruscan diminutive suff.
-na has been added. The same suff. appears in
L. persona (see person).
Derivatives: lantern, tr. v., lantern-ist, n.

## lanthana
lanthana, п., lanthanum oxide. — ModL., coined
by its discoverer, the Swedish chemist Carl Gus-
taf Mosander (1797-1858) in 1839 fr. Gk. λαν»ά-
veiv, 'to escape notice, lie hid, be unseen', which
is cogn. with L. latere, 'to lie hid' (see latent); so
called by him, because it lay concealed in erbia.

## lanthanum
lanthanum, п., name of a metallic element of the
rare-earth group (chem.) — ModL., from prec.
word.

## lanthorn
lanthorn, п., lantern. — An old var. of lantern.

## lanuginous
lanuginous, adj., covered with soft hair, downy.
L. lanuginosus, fr. lanugo, gen. lanuginis. See
next word and -ous.
Derivative: lanuginous-ness, a.

## lanugo
lanugo, п., downy hair that covers the fetus (anat.)
— L. lanugo, gen. lanuginis, 'down', fr. Una,
'wool'. See lanate.

## lanyard
lanyard, laniard, п., a short, thick rope.— ME.
lanyer, fr. MF. (= F.) laniere, 'thong, lash', fr.
OF. lasniere, fr. lasne, 'strap, thong', a
metathesis form of nasle, 'lace', fr. Frankish *nastila,
which is related to OS., OHG. nestila, MHG.,
G. nestel, 'string, lace, strap'. These words
derive fr. I.-E. base *ned-, 'to knot'; see net. The
transposition of nasle to lasne was prob. made
under the influence of OF. laz, 'noose'. The
change of the French ending -iere (in laniere) to
-yard (in E. lanyard) is due to a confusion with
the noun yard; cp. halyard.

## Laocoon
Laocoon, п., a priest of Apollo (Greek mythol.) —
L. Laocoon, fr. Gk. Λαοκόων, compounded of
λαός, 'people', and κοέω (for *κο5έω), Ί
mark, perceive', which is cogn. with OI. kavih,
'wise, sage; seer, poet*, L. cavere (for *covere),
'to be on one's guard, take care, beware'. For
the first element see lay, 'pertaining to the laity',
for the second see show and cp. cave, interj.

## Laodicean
Laodicean, adj., 1) pertaining to Laodicea;
lukewarm in religion (in allusion to Revelations III,
14-16); 2) п., an inhabitant of Laodicea; one
lukewarm in religion. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Laodicea, fr. Gk. Λόίοδίκεια, name of a
city in Phrygiatin Asia Minor). Cp. latakia.

## lap
lap, п., flap of a garment. — ME. lappe, fr. Ixppa,
'tip, end, skirt, district', rel. to OS. lappo, 'tip,
lappet', MDu, lappe, Du. lap, 'tip, end', OHG.
lappa, MHG. lappe, G. Lappen, 'rag, shred',
ON. leppr, Norw. lap, 'patch, rag', Norw. lapa.'to
hang loosely', fr. I.-E. base *lab-, *leb-, 'loose;
to hang down', whence also L. labare, 'to totter',
labi, 'to slide, slip, glide down' and prob. also
labor, 'labor'. See labor and cp. lapel, lappet.
Cp. also labarum.
Derivative: lap, tr. and intr. v., to wrap, enfold.

## lap
lap, tr. v., to lick up; intr. v., to lick up a liquid.
— ME. lapen, lappen, fr. OE. lapian, 'to lick,
lap up, sup', rel. to Swed. lapa, 'to drink, lap',
OHG. laffan, 'to lick', OS. lepil, MLG., Du.
lepel, OHG. leffil, MHG. leffel, G. Loffel,
'spoon', OE. Ixpeldre, 'pot', and cogn. with Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:437 COLUMN:3 -->
λάπτειν, 'to sip, lick', λαφύσσειν, 'to swallow
greedily, gulp down', Arm. lap'el, L. lambere,
'to lick'. All these words derive from the I.-E.
imitative base *lab-, *lap(h)-. Cp. lambent.
Derivatives: lap, п., the act of lapping, Iapp-er,a.

## lapar-
lapar-, form of laparo- before a vowel.

## laparectomy
laparectomy, п., surgical removal of a part of the
abdominal wall. — Compounded of lapar- and
Gk. -εκτομίϊ, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a
cutting out'. See -ectomy.

## laparo-
laparo-, before a vowel lapar-, combining form
denoting the flank or, less exactly, the abdominal
wall(anat.) — Fr. Gk. λαπάρά, 'theflank, loins',
which is rel. to λαπαρός, 'soft, flaccid, hollow',
λαπάζείν, λαπάσσειν, 'to empty', and in gra-
dational relationship to λε7ττός, 'fine, thin,
small'. See lepto-.

## laparotomy
laparotomy, п., incision into the abdominal wall
(surgery). — Coined by the English surgeon Sir
Thomas Bryant (1828-1914) fr. laparo- and Gk.
—τομίϊ, 'cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting,
section'. See-tomy.

## lapel
lapel, п., part of a coat folded back. —
Diminutive of lap, 'flap of a garment'.
Derivatives: lapel-er, п., lapell-ed, adj.

## lapidary
lapidary, adj., 1) pertaining to stones; 2)
pertaining to, or suitable for, engraving on stone
monuments. — L. lapidarius, 'pertaining to
stone', fr. lapis, gen. lapidis, 'stone', which is
cogn. with Gk. λέπας, 'a bare rock, crag', and
prob. also with λέπείν, 'to strip off, peel'; see
ieper and cp. Lepas. For the relationship
between Gk. λέπας and λέπειν ср. L. saxum,
'stone', which is rel. to secure, 'to cut', and
rupes, 'rock', which is rel. to rumpere, 'to tear,
break, rend' (see saxatile and rupestrian).

## lapidary
lapidary, п., one who cuts or polishes precious
stones. — L. lapidarius, 'a worker in stone',
prop, the adjective lapidarius, 'pertaining to
stone', used as a noun. See prec. word.

## lapidate
lapidate, tr. v., to stone. — L. lapidatus, pp. of
lapidare, 'to pelt with stones, to stone', fr. lapis,
gen. lapidis. See lapidary, adj., and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: lapidat-ion, п., lapidat-or, n.

## lapidiflcation
lapidiflcation, п., the state of being converted into
stone. — See next word and -ation.

## lapidify
lapidify, tr. v., to convert into stone; intr. v., to be
converted into stone. — F. lapidifier, fr. ML.
lapidificare, 'to convert into stone', which is
compounded of L. lapis, gen. lapidis, 'stone',
and -ficare, fr. -ficere, unstressed form oifacere,
'to make, do*. See lapidary, adj., and -fy.

## lapilli. n. pi.
lapilli. n. pi., small stones; specif, small stones
erupted by volcanoes. — L., pi. of lapillus, 'a
little stone', dimin. of lapis, 'stone'. Seelapidary,
adj.

## lapis lazuli
lapis lazuli, an azure blue stone. — ML., fr. L.
lapis, 'stone', and gen. of ML. lazulum, 'lapis
lazuli', fr. Arab, lazaward. See lapidary, adj.,
and azure.

## Laportea
Laportea, п., a genus of plants, the wood nettle
(boi.) — ModL., named after Fran?ois L. de
Laporte, a 19th-century entomologist.

## lappet
lappet, п., a small flap. — Formed with dimin.
suff. -et fr. lap, 'flap of a garment'.
Derivatives: lappet, tr. v., lappet-ed, adj.

## Lappula
Lappula, п., a genus of plants, the stickseed (bot.)
— ModL.,, dimin. of L. lappa, 'a bur'; of
uncertain origin.

## Lapsana
Lapsana, п., a genus of plants, the nipplewort
(bot.) — L. lapsana, lampsana, 'charlock', fr.
Gk. λαψάνη, λαμψάνη, of s.m.

## lapse
lapse, п., 1) a slip; 2) an error. — L. lapsus, 'a
slipping, a fall', fr. lapsus, pp. of labi, 'to slide,
slip, glide down'. See labor, п., and cp. words
there referred to.

## lapse
lapse, intr. v., I) to slip; 2) to fail. — L. lapsare,
'to slide', fr. lapsus, pp. of labi. See lapse, п., and
cp. collapse, elapse, prolapse, relapse.
Derivatives: laps-able, adj., laps-ed, adj., laps-
er, п., laps-ing-ly, adv.

## lapsus calami
lapsus calami, a slip of the pen* — L. See lapse,
п., and calamary.

## lapsus linguae
lapsus linguae, a slip of the tongue. — L. See
lapse, п., and lingual,

## lapwing
lapwing, п., a bird of the plover family. — ME.
lappewinke, fr. OE. hleapewince, lit. 'leaper-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:438 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 411 | LAST -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:438 COLUMN:1 -->
waverer', fr. hleapan, 'to leap', and wincian, 'to
blink, wink' (the original meaning of this latter
was 'to move rapidly, to waver'); influenced in
form by a folk-etymological association with
wing. See leap and wink.

## larboard
larboard, п., left-hand side of a ship to a person
on board looking from the stern toward the
bow. — ME. ladeborde, lit. 'the loading side'.
The first -r- in E. larboard is due to the analogy
of starboard. See lade and board of a ship.
Derivatives: larboard, adj. and adv.

## larcener
larcener, п., one guilty of larceny. — See larceny
and agential suff. -er.

## larcenist
larcenist, п., a larcener. — See larceny and -ist.

## larcenous
larcenous, adj., of the nature of larceny. — See
next word and -ons.
Derivative: larcenous-ly, adv.

## larceny
larceny, п., theft. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) larcin,
fr. OF. larrecin, fr. L. latrdcinium, 'service of
mercenaries; freebooting, robbery', which is
compounded of latro, 'a mercenary soldier;
robber', and suff. -cinium. L. latro is prob.
borrowed fr. Gk. *λάτρων, 'a mercenary soldier',
which is rel. ίολάτρον, 'pay, hire', λάτρις,
'servant, worshiper', λατρεία; 'hired labor, service
paid to the gods, worship'. Several philologists
derive these Greek words fr. I.-E. base *la-,
*le~(i)-, 'to grant; possession'. See-latry and cp.
lathe, 'administrative district'. Suff. -cinium is
prob. cogn. with Gk. -κονος in διάκονος, 'a
servant'. See deacon and cp. tirocinium.

## larch
larch, п., a tree of the genus Larix. — Introduced
by the English botanist W. Turner in 1548
through adaptation of G. Larche, fr. MHG.
larche, lerche, fr*. OHG. *larihha, */erihha,
borrowed fr. L. larix, gen. laricis, 'larch', which is
prob. a Gaulish loan word from the Alpine
region, ult, derived fr. I.-E. base *derev(o)-, 'tree'
(see tree). See Walde-Hofmann LEW., 1. p. 765.
For the change of d- to /- cp. L. lacrima, fr. OL.
dacruma, 'tear' (see lachrymal). It is also
possible, however, that L. larix is a word of non-
Indo-European origin.

## lard
lard, n. — OF. (= F.), fr. L. laridum, lardum,
'bacon', which is cogn. with Gk. λάρΤ-νός, 'fat'.
Derivatives: lard, tr. v., lard-aceous, adj., larder
(q.v.), lard-y, adj.

## larder
larder, n. — ME., fr. AF. larder, corresponding
to OF. tardier, 'a place where bacon is kept',
fr. lard, 'bacon'. See lard and suff. -er, in the
sense 'receptacle for'.
Derivative: larder-er, n.

## lardite
lardite, п., agalmatolite (mineral.) — Formed
with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. lardum, 'lard'. See
lard.

## lardon
lardon, lardoon, п., a strip of bacon used in
larding. — See lard and -oon.

## lares
lares, n. pi., tutelary gods (Roman mythol.) —
L. lares, 'tutelary gods, household deities;
home', pi. of tar; prob. derived fr. I.-E. base
*las-, 'greedy', whence also L. lascivus, 'wan*-
ton'. See lascivious and cp. Lariidae, larva.

## large
large, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) large, 'broad,
wide', fr. L. largus, 'abundant, copious,
plentiful; liberal', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. largess, largo, enlarge.
Derivatives: targe, adv. and п., large-ly, adv.,
large-ness, п., targ-ish, adj.

## largess
largess, largesse, п., a gift generously given. —
ME. largesse, fr. OF. (= F.) largesse, 'bounty,
munificence', fr. VL. *largitia, 'abundance', fr.
L. largus, 'abundant', See large and -ess.

## larghetto
larghetto, adj. and adv., rather slow (musical
direction). — it., dimin. of largo, 'slow'. See next
word.

## largo
largo, adj. and adv., very slow (musical
direction). — It., 'broad, wide; slow', fr. L. largus,
'broad, wide'. See large.

## lariat
lariat, п., a lasso. — Sp. la reata, 'the rope', from
the fem. article la and reata, 'rope'. Sp. la
derives fr. L. ilia, fem. of Hie, 'that'; seeille. For Sp.
reata see reata.
Derivative: lariat, tr. v.

## Laridae
Laridae, n. pi., a family of birds including the
gulls and terns (ornithol.) — ModL., formed fr.
Larus with suff. -idae.

## Lariidae
Lariidae, n. pi., a family of beetles (entomol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Laria (name

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:438 COLUMN:2 -->
of the type genus), fr. L. Mr. See lares.

## Larinae
Larinae, n. pi., a subfamily of the Laridae; the
typical gulls (ornithol.) — ModL, formed fr.
Larus with suff. -inae.

## Larix
Larix, п., a genus of trees of the pine family (bot.)
— L. larix, 'larch'. See larch.

## lark
lark, n. — ME. larke, fr. OE. lawerce, Ixwerce,
rel. to OS. lewerka, ON. Ixvirki, Dan. lerke,
OSwed. Ixrikia, Swed. larka, Norw. lerka, LG.
lewerke, Du. leeuwerik, OHG. lerahha, MHG.
lewreche, lereche, G. Lerche, 'lark'; of uncertain
origin.

## lark
lark, intr. v., to make sport. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: lark-er, п., lark-ing, adj., lark-ing-
ly, adv., lark-ish, lark-some, lark-y, adjs.

## larkspur
larkspur, п., the delphinium. — Compounded of
lark, п., and spur; so called in allusion to the
shape of its leaves.

## larmoyant
larmoyant, adj., tearful. — F., pres. part, of lar-
moyer, 'to shed tears, whimper', fr. larme, 'tear',
fr. L. lacrima. See lachrymal and -ant.

## larnax
larnax, п., a chest; a coffin. — Gk. λάρναξ, 'chest,
coffer, box', dissimilated fr. νάρναξ (Hesychius),
of s.m., which is of uncertain origin.

## larrup
larrup, tr. v., to beat, thresh. — Of uncertain
origin; perh. borrowed fr. Du. larpen, 'to thresh'.

## Larus
Larus, п., a genus of birds, the gull, the tern and
the jaeger (ornithol) — Late L. larus, 'gull', fr.
Gk. λάρος, which is prob. rel. to λήρος, 'idle
talk', and lit. means 'the chattering bird', fr. the
l.-E. imitative base *ld-, *Ie-, 'to shout, cry',
whence also L. lamentare, 'to wail, moan, weep,
lament'. See lament.

## larva
larva, n. — L. larva, 'ghost, specter, mask', for
*lasowa~-, lit. 'having the shape of a lar,
resembling a lar', fr. lar, 'a tutelary god'. See lares.

## larval
larval, adj. — L. larvalis, 'pertaining to a ghost',
fr. larva. See larva and adj. suff. -al.

## larvi-
larvi-, combining form denoting a larva. — Fr. L.
larva. See larva.

## laryng-
laryng-, form of Iaryngo- before a vowel.

## laryngeal
laryngeal, adj., pertaining to the larynx. —
Formed with adj. suff.-al fr. Gk. λάρυγξ, gen.
λάρυγγος, 'throat'. See larynx.

## laryngitis
laryngitis, п., inflammation of the larynx (med.)
— Medical L., formed with suff. -itls fr. Gk.
λάρυγξ, gen. λάρυγγος, 'throat'. See larynx.
Derivative: laryngit-ic, adj.

## Iaryngo-
Iaryngo-, combining form denoting 1) the larynx;
2) laryngeal and. — Gk. λαρυγγο-, fr. λάρυγξ,
gen. λάρυγγος, 'throat'. See larynx.

## laryngology
laryngology, п., that branch of medicine which
deals with the diseases of the larynx. —
Compounded of Iaryngo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: laryngolog-ic, laryngolog-ic-al,
adjs., laryngotog-ist, ri.

## laryngoscope
laryngoscope, п., an instrument for examining the
larynx. — Compounded of Iaryngo- and Gk.
-σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine'.
See -scope.
Derivatives: laryngoscop-ic, laryngoscop-ic-al,
adjs., laryngoscop-ist, п., laryngoscop-y, n.

## larynx
larynx, п., the upper part of the windpipe (anat.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. λάρυγξ, gen. λάρυγγος,
'throat, upper part of the windpipe', which is
prob. a blend of φάρυγξ, 'throat' (see pharynx),
and λαιμός, 'throat, gullet'. See Frisk, GEW.,
II 87 s.v. λάρυγξ It is also possible, however,
that Gk. λάρυγξ derives from the l.-E imitative
base "(s)lcg- 'to sip', whence also MHG. slurc,
'gullet, gorge', slurken, 'to sip', Swed. slurca, 'to
sip in big quaffs', and possibly also L. lurco, lur-
care (also lurcor, lurcSri), 'to devour' (fr. "lurgi-
cos, 'devouring'); see Walde-Hofmann, LEW.,
I, 837 s.v. lured. If this latter etymology is
correct, the form of λάρυχξ is prob. due to the
influence of φάρυγξ, 'throat'.

## lascar
lascar, п., an East Indian sailor. — Pers. Ioshkar,
'army', fr. Arab, al'askar, 'the army', fr. al-,
'the', and 'askar, 'army', which prob. derives fr.
Late Gk. έξέρκητον, fr. L. exercitus, 'army', fr.
exercere, 'to train, drill'. See exercise and cp.
askari and the second element in seraskier. E.
lascar was influenced in meaning by Pers. lash-
kari, 'soldier', lit. 'of the army', fr. lashkar.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:438 COLUMN:3 -->

## lascivious
lascivious, adj., wanton, lustful. — Late L. lasci-
viosus, fr. L. lasavia, 'wantonness, playfulness,
lustfulness', fr. lascivus, 'wanton, playful,
lustful', fr. I.-E. base *lds-, 'greedy, desirous',
whence also OI. -lasati (dissimilated fr. *lalsati),
'yearns', lasati, 'plays, frolics' (also 'flashes,
glitters'), Hitt. ilaliya-, 'to desire, covet', Gk.
λι-λαίομαν (for *λι-λάσιομαι), Ί desire',
λάστη, 'harlot', λάσθη, 'mockery, insult', O-
Slav. laska, 'flattery', laskajq, laskati, 'to outwit,
flatter', laskanije, 'flattery', laskrudu, 'loving
dainties', Czech and Slovak laska, 'love', Pol.
-laska, 'favor', Olr. lainn (for *las-nis), 'greedy',
Goth, lustus, OE. lust, 'lust'. Cp. list, 'to please',
lust. Cp. also lares, larva.
Derivatives: lascivious-ly, adv., lascivious-ness,
n.

## laser
laser, n. — Coined from the initials of iight
amplification (by) Stimulated amission (of)
Radiation.

## lash
lash, tr. v., to bind. — ME. lasshen, 'to lace', fr.
MF. lachier, lacier, fr. OF. See lace, v.

## lash
lash, adj., soft and watery. — OF. lasche (F.
lache), 'loose', fr. L. laxus, of s.m. See lax and
cp. laches, lush.

## lash
lash, tr. and intr. v., to strike with, or as with, a
whip. — ME. lashen, 'to strike', prob. of
imitative origin.
Derivatives: lash, п., a stroke with a whip,
lasher, п., lash-ing, n.

## lashkar
lashkar, п., a body of soldiers (India). — Pers.
lashkar, 'army'. See lascar.

## lasio-
lasio-, before a vowel lasi-, combining form
meaning 'shaggy'. —■ Gk. λάσιο-, λασι-, fr.
λάσιος, 'shaggy', for *5λάτ-ιος, fr. I.-E. "wltios,
'hairy, woolly, shaggy', whence also Lith. valtis,
'panicle of oats', Little Russian voloti, 'panicle',
ON. foil, 'hair'. The above base is prob. a -(-
enlargement of base *wel-, 'to break, tear,
pluck', whence also Gk. λήνος, Dor. λανος (for
*5ληνος, resp. *5λανος), 'wool', L. vellere, 'to
pluck, twitch', vellus, 'wool shorn off, fleece'.
See vellicate and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also next word.

## Lasius
Lasius, п., a genus of ants (entomol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. λάσιος, 'hairy, woolly, shaggy'. See lasio-.

## laspring
laspring, п., a young salmon (dial. English). —
Perh. altered fr. laxpink, a compound of OE.
lax, 'salmon', and dial. E. pink, 'a young
salmon'. See lax, 'salmon'.

## lass
lass, п., a girl. — ME. lasse, of uncertain origin.

## lassie
lassie, п., a young girl. — Dimin. of iass.

## lassitude
lassitude, п., weariness, exhaustion. — MF. (=
F.), fr. L. lassitudinem, ace. of lassitudo, 'faint-
ness, weariness, languor, exhaustion', fr. lassus,
'faint, weary, languid, exhausted', which stands
for *lad-to-s, and is cogn. with OE. bet,
'sluggish, slow'. See late and -tude and cp. alas.

## lasso
lasso, п., a long rope with noose for catching
cattle and horses. — Sp. lazo, fr. L. laqueus,
'noose, snare'. See lace, п., which is a doublet of
lasso.
Derivatives: lassot tr. v., lasso-er, n.

## last
last, adj. — ME. last, dissimilated fr. latst,
contraction of latest, fr. OE. latost, superl. of Ixt,
adj., late, adv.; rel. to the superlatives OFris.
lest, MDu. latest, laest, lest, Du. laatst, OHG.
Ie33ist, Ia336st, MHG. lesiist, lest, G. letzt,
last', ON. latastr, 'slowest'. See late. For the
dissimilation of ME. latst to last cp. best.
Derivatives: last, n. and adv., last-ly, adv.

## last
last, п., a model of foot. — ME. lasle, fr. OE.
liiste, 'last', fr, OE. lust, 'sole of foot, footprint,
track', rel. to ON. leistr, 'the foot below the
ankle, sock', Dan. best, Du. leest, 'last', OHG.
leist, 'track, footprint, last', MHG. leist, G.
Leisten, 'last', Goth, laists, 'footprint, track',
laistjan, 'to follow', laisjan, 'to teach', lais, Ί
know', OE. Ixran (for *lar-jan), 'to teach'. See
learn and cp. last, 'to continue'.
Derivative: last, tr. v., to shape with a last.

## last
last, intr. v., to continue, endure. — ME. lasten,
fr. OE. Ixstan, 'to follow, carry out, perform; to
continue, last, endure'. The orig. meaning was
'to follow a track', fr. OE. last, 'sole of foot,
footprint, track'. Cp. Goth, laistjan, 'to follow',
OHG. leistan, MHG., G. leisten, 'to perform,
achieve, afford', and see last, 'model of foot'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:439 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LAST | 412 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:439 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: last, п., staying power, last-ing, adj.,
last-ing-ly, adv., last-ing-ness, n.

## last
last, п., 1) load (obsol.); 2) unit of weight. — ME.
last, 'load; unit of weight', fr. OE. hlsest,
'burden', rel. to OFris. hlest, MDu., Du. last, OHG.
hlast, last, MHG., G. last, 'load', and to OE.,
OHG. hladan, 'to load'. E. last prop, means
'that which is laden'. See lade and cp. the second
element in ballast. Cp. also alastrim.

## lat
lat, п., the unit of currency in Latvia. — Lett, tats
(pi. lati), formed from the first syllable of Lat-
vija, the Lett name of the country.

## latakia
latakia, п., a kind of Syrian tobacco. — Prop,
'tobacco grown in Latakia', a town in N. W.
Syria. The name Latakia is traceable to Gk. Λαο-
δίκεια, name of a city in Phrygia. See
Laodicean.

## latch
latch, tr. v., to fasten. —- ME. lacchen, 'to seize,
catch, take hold of, fr. OE. Ixccan, prob. cogn.
with Gk. λάζαμαι, Ί take, grasp', which stands
for *λάγ-ιομαι or *λάγγ-ιομοα and is rel. to
λαμβάνω, of s.m. See lemma.

## latch
latch, п., a fastening; a device for fastening. —
ME. lacche, 'catch, fastening', fr. lacchen. See
latch, v.

## latchet
latchet, n. — ME. lachet, fr. OF. lachet, a dial,
var. of lacet, 'a thong', dimin. of laz, 'noose'.
See lace, n.

## late
late, adj. — ME. lat, fr. OE. Ixt, 'sluggish, slow;
late', rel. to OFris. let, 'late', OS. lat, ON. latr,
Dan. lad, 'sluggish, lazy', MDu. lat, of s.m.
(whence Du. /ее/, 'late', laatst, 'last'), OE.
latost, OHG., MHG. las, G. Ιαβ, 'idle, weary',
Goth, lats, 'weary, sluggish, lazy', OHG.
legist, 'last', lit. 'slowest, tardiest', Goth, latjan, 'to
hinder', OHG. lezzen, MHG. letzen, 'to stop,
check' (whence MHG., G. ver-letzen, 'to hurt,
injure'), fr. Teut. base "lata-, corresponding to
I.-E. base *te(i)d-, *led-, 'to leave behind, leave,
yield', whence L. lassus (for *lad-to-s), 'faint,
weary, languid, exhausted', Gk. λη8εϊν (He-
sychius), 'to be weary'. See let, 'to leave', and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also latter, last,
adj.
Derivatives: late-ly, adv., lat-en, tr. and intr. v.,
late-ness, п., lat-ish, adj.

## lateen
lateen, adj., 1) designating a triangular sail
suspended from a short mast at an angle of 45°; 2)
having such a sail. — F. {voile) latine, lit. 'Latin
(sail)'; so called because used on Mediterranean
vessels. See Latin.
Derivative: lateen, п., a vessel having such a sail.

## latence
latence, latency, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## latent
latent, adj., hidden, concealed. — L. latins, -entis,
pres. part, of latere, 'to lie hid or concealed, to
lurk', which is cogn. with Gk. λήθη, 'forgetful-
ness, oblivion', ά-λη*ής, 'true', lit. 'not
concealing anything' (fr. priv. pref. i- and λήθη, 'for-
getfulness'), λανθάνειν, 'to escape notice, lie
hid, be unseen', and with OSlav. lajati, 'to lie in
wait for'. Cp. lanthanum, Lethe, lethargy, Ale-
thea, alethiology.

## -later
-later, combining form meaning 'worshiper', as
in bardolater, idolater. — Fr. Gk. -λάτρης,
'worshiper of, which is rel. to λατρεία,
'worship'. See -latry.

## lateral
lateral, adj., pertaining to the side; sideways. —
L. lateralis, 'pertaining to the side', fr. latus,
gen. lateris, 'side', which is prob. rel. to latus,
'broad'. See latitude and adj. SUIT, -al and cp.
collateral.
Derivatives: lateral, п., lateral-ly, adv., and the
hybrids lateral-ize, tr. v., lateral-iz-ation, n.

## Lateran
Lateran, п., 1) the church of St. John Lateran in
Rome; 2) the palace adjoining it; adj., pertaining
to this church or palace; specif., designating a
number of general councils held there. — L.
Lateranus, name of a Roman family whose
palace stood on the site of the present basilica.

## lateri-
lateri-, combining form meaning 'lateral'. See
latere-.

## laterite
laterite, п., a reddish soil formed by the
decomposition of rocks (geol.) — Formed with subst.
suff. -ite fr. L. later, gen. lateris, 'brick, tile',
which is of uncertain etymology.

## latero-
latero-, combining form meaning 'lateral'. — Fr.
L. latus, gen. lateris, 'side'. See lateral.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:439 COLUMN:2 -->

## latescence
latescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## latescent
latescent, adj., becoming latent. — L. latescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of latescere, 'to hide
oneself, inchoative of latere. See latent.

## latex
latex, п., a milky juice in plants (bot.) — L., 'a
liquid, fluid', prob. borrowed fr. Gk. λάταξ,
'drop of wine', which has been connected by
several philologists with Gaul. Are-late, lit. 'city
east of the swamp', Mir. laith (for *lati-), 'beer;
swamp', Co. lad, OW. Hat, 'liquor', W. /laid,
Mir. lathach, 'mud, mire', Lith. latukas, 'pool,
puddle', ON. lepja, 'filth', OHG. letto, G. Let-
ten, 'potter's clay, loam'; see Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., I, 770 s.v. 1. latex. Cp. the first element in
laticiferous.

## lath
lath, n. — ME. laththe, fr. OE. Ixtt, rel. to OS.,
ΟΝ., OHG. latta, MDu., MHG., G. latte,
Du. lat, 'lath', MHG. lade, 'plank', G. Laden,
'shop', and cogn. with Olr. (= Ir.) slat, W.
Hath, Bret, laz, 'rod, pole'. Cp. lattice.
Derivatives: lath, tr. v., lath-en, adj., lather, one
who puts up laths (q.v.), laih-ing, n.

## lathe
lathe, п., a machine for turning. — Prob. of
Scand. origin; cp. Dan. -Win dreje-lad,
'turning lathe', which is rel. to ON. hlada, 'to lade,
load'. See lade.
Derivatives: lathe, tr. v., lath-er, n.

## lathe
lathe, п., one of the five (orig. six) districts of the
county of Kent in England. — ME., fr. OE. Ixd,
'landed property, district', rel. to ON. lad, of
s.m., OE. un-lxd, un-lxde, 'poor, miserable',
Goth, un-leds, 'poor', orig. 'without property',
and prob. cogn. with Gk. λάτρον, 'pay, hire'.
See -latry.

## lathee
lathee, n. — See lathi.

## lather
lather, п., froth, foam. — ME., fr. OE. leabor, rel.
to ON.Iaudr,'washing soap.foam', and cogn.with
Gaul, lautron, Olr. Idathar, lothar, 'bathing tub',
Gk. λούειν, 'to bathe', λουτρόν, 'bath, water for
bathing', L. lavdre, 'to wash, bathe'. See lave and
cp. lye.
Derivatives: lather, intr. and tr. v., to cover with
lather, lather-er, п., lather-y, adj.

## lather
lather, п., one who puts up laths. — Formed fr.
lath with agential suff. -er.

## lathi
lathi, also lathee, п., a heavy wooden staff bound
with iron (India). — Hind, lathi, fr. Prakrit lat-
thi, 'staff, stick, rod, club', which is rel. to Ol.
yastih of s.m., Avestic yaxshti-, 'branch'.

## lathyrism
lathyrism, п., a morbid condition caused by the
use of meal from the seeds of certain species of
Lathyrus (med.) — Formed from next word with
suff. -Ism.

## Lathyrus
Lathyrus, п., a genus of plants, the vetchling (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. λάθυρος, 'a kind of pulse'.
See lentil.

## laticiferous
laticiferous, adj., containing latex. —
Compounded of L. latex, gen. laticis, 'a liquid, fluid',
and ferre, 'to bear, carry . See latex and -ferous.

## laticlave
