laticlave, п., one of two broad purple stripes on
the front of the tunic, worn by senators, etc., as
a badge of their rank (Roman antiq.) — L. Idri-
cldvus, 'a broad purple stripe (on the tunic)'. See
latitude and clavicle.

## latifundium
latifundium, п., a large landed estate. — L.,
compounded of latus, 'broad', and fundus, 'bottom,
foundation, estate'. See latitude and fund.

## Latin
Latin, adj. — ME., fr. L. Latlnus, 'Latin', prop,
'pertaining to Latium', fr. Latium, name of a
district of Italy in which Rome was situated.
According to P.P. Persson Latium stands for *stle-
t-iom and lit. means 'the flat or plain land' (in
contradistinction to the mountainous country
inhabited by the Sabines) fr. 1-Е. base "stela-,
'to spread, extend', whence also latus (for "stld-
tos), 'broad, wide'; see latitude. It is also
possible, however, that the name Latium is of non-
Indo-European origin. See Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., I, 770-71 s.v. Latium.
Derivatives: Latin, a. and tr. v., Latin-ate, adj.,
Latin-ic, adj., Latin-ism, п., Laiin-ist, п., Latin-
ist-ic, adj., Latinity (q.v.), Latinize (q.v.)

## Latine
Latine, adv., in Latin. — L. Latine, fr. Latinus,
'Latin'. See Latin.

## Latinity
Latinity, n. — L. latinitas, fr. Latinus. See Latin
and -ity.

## Latinize
Latinize, tr. and intr. v. — Late L. latinizare, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:439 COLUMN:3 -->
L. Latinus. See Latin and -ize.
Derivatives: Latiniz-atton, п., Latiniz-er, n.

## latitude
latitude, п., breadth. — ME., fr. L. latitude,
'breadth', Ιτ. latus, 'broad',which stands for "stlu-
tos and is rel. to stlatta, 'a kind of broad ship',
and prob. also to latus, gen. lateris, 'side', fr.
l.-E. base "stela-, 'to spread', whence also OSlav.
steljo, stilati, 'to spread out', po-stelja, 'bed',
Arm. lain, 'broad'. Cp. lateral, laticlave,
latifundium, Latin. For the ending see suff. -tude.
Derivatives: latitudin-al(q.v.), latitudin-ous, adj.

## latitadinal
latitadinal, adj., pertainingto latitude. — Formed
with adj. suff, -al fr. L. latitude, gen. latitudinis,
'breadth'. See prec. word.
Derivative: latitudinal-ly, adv.

## latitudinarian
latitudinarian, adj., characterized by latitude in
opinion or behavior. — Formed with suff. -arian
fr. L. latitude, gen. latitudinis, 'breadth'. See
latitude.
Derivatives: latitudinarian, п., latitudinarian-ism,
n.

## Latona
Latona, п., the mother of Apollo and Diana in
Roman mythology; equivalent to the Greek
Leto. — L. Latona, Latinized form of Gk.
Λητώ, Dor. Λατώ. See Leto and cp. Leda. For
the suff. -na in Latona cp. L. Bello-na, the
Roman goddess of war (fr. helium, 'war'), and L.
matro-na, 'matron' (fr. mater, 'mother'); see
Bellona, matron.

## latria
latria, п., the highest kind of worship, which may
be offered to God only. — Eccles L., fr. Gk.
λατρεία, 'service, worship'. See-latry.

## latrine
latrine, п., a privy. — F. latrines (pi.), fr. L. la-
trina, 'a privy', contraction of early lavdtrina,
'bath', fr. lavatus, pp. of lavdre, 'to wash'. See
lave. For sense development cp. lavatory.

## latrobite
latrobite, п., a variety of anorthite (mineral.) —
Named after its discoverer, the Reverend C. J.
Latrobe. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## latrocinium
latrocinium, п., robbery; brigandage (Roman law).
— L. See larceny.

## -latry
-latry, combining form meaning 'worship'. It
occurs not only in original Greek words, but also
in new coinages (cp. e.g. bibliolatry). — Gk.
-λατρεία, -λατρία, fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor,
service, service paid to the gods, worship', which
is rel. to λάτρον, 'pay, hire', λάτρις, 'servant,
worshiper', λατρεύειν, 'to serve, worship'.
Several philologists derive these words fr. I.-E. base
"la-, *le(i)-, 'to grant; possession', whence also
ON. lad, OE. ШО, 'landed property, district',
Goth, un-leds, 'poor', OE. un-lxd, un-lxde, 'poor,
miserable', orig. 'without property' (for I.-E.
*n-Ielo-s). Cp. -later, latria, larceny. Cp. also
lathe, 'administrative district'.

## latten
latten, n. I) an alloy of copper and zinc; 2) a thin
sheet of metal. — ME. latoun, lawn, fr. OF. la-
ton (F. laiton), fr. Arab, latan, 'copper' [whence
also Sp. latan, Port, latdo, OProvenc. laton, le-
ton, It. ottone (in which the / of the Arabic word
was mistaken for the It. article and consequently
dropped)]; ult. fr. dial. Turk, altan, 'gold'.

## latter
latter, adj. — ME. later, Ixt'er, 'later', fr. OE.
Intra, 'slower; later', compar. oilxt. Cp. the
comparatives ΟΝ. latari, MHG. /ajjer, 'slower',
OFris. letora, lettera, 'latter', Du. later, 'later',
and see late.
Derivative: latter-ly, adv.

## lattice
lattice, n. — ME. talis, fr. OF. lattis, fr. latte,
'lath', which is of Teut. origin. See lath.
Derivatives: lattice, tr. v., lattic-ed, adj.,
latticing, n.

## Latvia
Latvia, n. — Lit. 'the country of the Letts'. See
Lett and cp. lat.
Derivatives: Latvi-an, adj. and n.

## laubanite
laubanite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after Lauban in Silesia. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## laud
laud, п., praise. — ME, laudes (p\.), fr. MF. laudes
(pi.), fr. L. laudes, pi. of laus, 'praise', which is
prob. cogn. with OE. leod, 'song, poem', ON.
Ijod, 'strophe' (in the pi., 'song'), OHG. Hod,
MHG. liet, G. Lied, 'song', Goth, liupon, 'to
praise', awiliup, 'thanksgiving'. Cp. allow, 'to
permit'. Cp. also lied.

## laud
laud, tr. v. — L. laudare, 'to praise', fr. laus, gen.
laudis. See laud, n.
Derivative: laud-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:440 COLUMN:1 -->

## laudabUity
laudabUity, η. — Late L laudabilitas, fr. L. lauda-
bilis. See next word and -ity.

## laudable
laudable, adj. — ME., fr. L. laudabilis,
'praiseworthy, laudable', fr. laudare, 'to praise'. See
laud, v., and -able.
Derivatives: laudable-ness, п., laudabl-y, adv.

## laudaninc
laudaninc, п., a poisonous alkaloid (chem.) —
Formed from next word with subst. surf. -ine.

## laudanum
laudanum, п., a tincture of opium. — A ModL.
word used by the Swiss alchemist and physician
Paracelsus; prob. a var. of L. ladanum. See lada-
num, labdanum,

## laudation
laudation, п., praise. — L. laudatio, 'a praising,
commendation', fr. lauddtus, pp. οι laudare. See
laud, v., and -ation.

## laudative
laudative, adj., laudatory. —L. laudalivus,
'relating to praise, laudatory', fr. laudatus, pp. of
laudare. See laud, v., -ive.

## laudatory
laudatory, adj., expressing praise. — Late L. lau-
datorius, 'relating to praise, laudatory', fr. L.
laudatus, pp. of laudare. See laud, v., and adj.
suff. -ory.
Derivative: laudatori-ly, adv.

## Laudian
Laudian, adj., pertaining to Archbishop Laud
(J 573-1645) or his principles.

## laugh
laugh,intr. and tr. v.— ME. lahen, laughen, fr.OE.
hleahhan, hliehhan, rel. to ON. hlstja, Dan. lee,
Swed. /e,Du., MHG., G. lachen, OHG.(h)lahhen,
hlahhan, Goth, klahjan, 'to laugh'. Cp. Gk. κλαγ-
γή, 'a sharp, quick sound, twang', κλάζειν (for
*κλάγγ-ιειν), 't0 make a sharp, quick sound',
L. clangere, 'to resound, clang', Lith. klageti,
Lett, kladzet, 'to cackle', OSlav. klokotati, 'to
clack, cackle'. All these words derive from the
bases *qleg-, *qlog-; cp. clang.
Derivatives: laugh, п., laugh-er, п., laugh-ing, n.
and adj., laugh-ing-ly, adv., laughable (q.v.),
laughter (q.v.)

## laughable
laughable, adj. — A hybrid coined from the verb
laugh and suff. -able; first used by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: laughable-ness, п., laughabl-y,
adv.

## laughing jackass
laughing jackass, a bird of the kingfisher family in
Australia. — So named from its laughlike call
suggesting the braying of an ass.

## laughter
laughter, n. — ME. lahter, fr. OE. hleahtor, fr.
hleahhan, '.to laugh'. Cp. ON. hlatr, Dan. latter,
Norw. laatt, OHG. hlahtar, MHG. lahter, ge-
lehter, G. Gelachier, 'laughter', and see laugh.

## laumontite
laumontite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after the French mineralogist
Gillet Laumont (1747-1834), its discoverer. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## launch
launch, tr. and intr. v., to hurl, cast.— ME. lan-
chen, hunchen, fr. ONF. lanch'ier, which
corresponds to OF. lancier (F. lancer), 'to fling, hUTl,
throw, cast, launch', fr. Late L. lanceare, 'to
wield a lance', fr. L. lancea. See lance, n. and v.
Derivatives: launch, п., the sliding of a boat
from the land into the water, lauhch-er, n.

## launch
launch, п., a large boat carried by a warship. —
Sp. and Port, lancha, fr. Malay lancharan, 'a
kind of boat', fr. lanchar, 'swift, speedy'.

## launder
launder, п., a conduit or trough for conveying
water. — The orig. meaning was 'one who
washes', fr. ME. lander, launder, contraction· of
lavender, fr. OF. lavandter, 'washerman', fern, la-
vandiere (F. lavandiere), 'washerwoman', fr. Late
L. lavandaria (pi.), 'things to be washed', fr. L.
lavandus, 'to be washed', gerundive of lavare, 'to
wash'. See lave. For Latin gerundives or their
derivatives used in English see agenda and cp.
words there referred to.

## launder
launder, tr. v., to wash (clothes, etc.); intr. v., to
wash clothes, etc. — Obsol. launder, 'launderer,
laundress', fr. ME. launder. See launder, n.
Derivative: launder-er, n.

## laundress
laundress, n. — Formed fr. launder, п., with suff.
-ess.

## laundry
laundry, n. — ME. lavenderie, lavendrie, fr. OF.
lavanderie, fr. Late L. lavandaria (pi.), 'things to
be washed'. See launder and -y (representing OF.
-ie).

## Laura
Laura, fern. PN. — It., prob. pet form of L. La«-

## rentia
rentia, fern, of Laurentius, 'of Laurentum'. See
Laurence.

## Lauraceae
Lauraceae, n. pi., the laurel family (bot.) —
Formed fr. Laurus with suff. -aceae.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:440 COLUMN:2 -->

## laureate
laureate, adj. and n. — L. laureatus, 'crowned
with laurel, laureate', fr. laureus, 'laurel'. See
laurel and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: laureate-ship, n.

## laureate
laureate, tr. v., to crown with laurel. — L.
laureatus. See laureate, adj.
Derivative: laureat-ion, n.

## lanrel
lanrel, n. — ME. laurer, lorer, lorel, fr. OF. lau-
rier, lorier (F. laurier), 'laurel', fr. OF. lor, fr. L.
laurus, 'bay tree, laurel; laurel crown', which is
prob. borrowed from a Mediterranean language,
whence prob. also Gk. δάφνη, 'laurel* (cp.
the variants δ&ΰκον, Thessal., Cypr. δαύχνα,
δαυχμός, Pergamene λάφνη). Ср. Daphne. Ср.
also Laurus, Laura, Laurence.
Derivative: laurel, tr. v.

## Laurence
Laurence, Lawrence, masc. PN. — OF. Lorenz
(F. Laurent), fr. L. Laurentius, prop. Of Lauren-
turn', fr. Laurentum, name of a maritime town in
Latium, lit. 'town of bay trees', fr. laurus, 'bay
tree'. It. Lorenzo is of the same origin. See laurel
and cp. Laura.

## Laurentian
Laurentian, laurentian, п., a kind of granite and
granitic gneiss in Canada (geol.) — Named from
the Laurentian Mountains in Canada,
themselves called after the St.Lawrence River. For the
ending see suff. -ian.

## laurite
laurite, п., an osmium ruthenium sulfide
(mineral.) — Named by the German chemist Friedrich
Wohler (1800-82) in 1866 after Mrs. Laura Joy,
the wife of a friend. — For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Laurus
Laurus, п., a genus of plants of the laurel family
(bot.) — L. laurus, 'laurel'. See laurel,

## laurustine
laurustine, п., a shrub with evergreen leaves (bot.)
— ML. laurustfnus, compounded of L. laurus,
'laurel', and tinus, 'laurustine'. For the first
element see laurel. The second element is prob.
cogn.withGk.TlXo;, 'a purging', W. tail, 'dung',
OSlav, tina, timenije, 'mud, mire', OE. bittatt, 'to
become moist', pawian, 'to thaw' (see thaw); so
called in allusion to its purging qualities.

## laurustinus
laurustinus, п., the laurustine. — See prec. word.

## lautarite
lautarite, п., calcium iodate (mineral.) — G. Lau-
larii.named after theOficinai.a«it7roinChile.The
ending -it goes back to Gk. -ϊτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## lava
lava, n. — It., orig. 'torrent, stream', fr.
Neapolitan lave, fr. L. lubes, 'a fall, falling down', which
is rel. to labi, 'to slide, slip, glide' (see labor); not
connected with L. lavare, 'to wash'.

## lavabo
lavabo, n. (eccles.) — L. lavabo, Ί will wash', fut.
of lavare, 'to wash' (see lave); so called from the
first word of Ps. 26:6 in the yulgate text recited
by the priest in the Mass while washing his
hands,

## lavage
lavage, п., washing; specif., in med., the washing
out of an organ. — F., 'a washing', fr. laver, 'to
wash'. See lave and -age.

## lavalliere
lavalliere, п., an ornament. — F. lavalliere,
'necktie', named after La Valliere (1644-1710),
mistress of Louis XIV.

## Lavandula
Lavandula, п., a genus of plants of the mint
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. ML. lavandula, laven-
dula, 'lavender'. See lavender,

## lavation
lavation, п., washing. — L. lavatid, gen. -dnis, 'a
washing, bathing', fr. lavatus, pp. of lavare. See
lave and -ation.

## lavatory
lavatory, n. — ME. lavatorie, fr. Late L. lavatd-
rium, 'place for washing', prop. neut. of the adj.
lavutdrius, 'pertaining to washing', used as a
noun, fr. L. lavatus, pp. of lavare. See lave and
subst. suff. -ory and cp. laver, 'vessel for
washing'.

## lave
lave, tr. and intr. v., to wash, bathe. — ME. laven,
prob. a blend of OF. (= F.) laver, 'to wash' (fr.
L. lavare, 'to wash, bathe'), and OE. lafian, 'to
wash' (which is prob. also a derivative of L.

## lavare). L. lavare is prob. assimilated fr
lavare). L. lavare is prob. assimilated fr, 'lovare
and is rel. to L. luere, 'to wash', and cogn. with
Gk. λαύειν, Homeric λόειν (for *X6Fciv), 'to

## wash
wash, bathe', Arm. loganam, Ί bathe, take a

## bath'
bath', Olr. Idathar, lothar, 'basin', MBret. lo-

## vazr
vazr, Bret, laouer, 'trough', iBaith, W. Iludw,

## Bret
Bret, ludu, 'ashes', OE. leah, 'lye, ashes and

## water for washing'
water for washing', leabor, 'lather'. See lye, lather

## and cp. ablution
and cp. ablution, alluvion, alluvium, deluhrum,

## deluge
deluge, dilute, diluvium, latrine, launder, lavabo,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:440 COLUMN:3 -->
lavage, lavatory, lavender, lavish, loment, lotion,
and the second element in aurilave, pyrolusite.

## laveer
laveer, intr. v., to beat against the wind (naut.;
archaic). — Du. laveren, fr. MDu. loveren, laveren,
fr. MF. louvier (F. louvoyer), fr. MF. (= F.) lof,
'windward side of a ship', which is a loan word
fr. MDu. /iJ/(Du. loef), 'luff'. See luff.

## Javement
Javement, п., a washing. — F., fr. laver, 'to wash'.
See lave and -ment.

## lavender
lavender, п., a fragrant plant of the mint family.
— ME. lavendre, fr. AF. lavendre, fr. ML.
lavandula, fr. It. lavandula, dimin. of lavande (whence
F. lavande), fr. lavare, 'to wash', fr. L. lavare; so
called from the use of this plant to perfume the
water for bathing. See lave, 'to wash'.

## lavenite
lavenite, п., a complex zirconium mineral. —
Named after the Island of Laven, Langesund
Fiord, in Norway. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite,

## laver
laver, п., a vessel for washing. — ME. lavour, fr.
MF. (= F.) /avoir, fr. Late L. lavatorium, 'place
for washing'. See lavatory.

## laver
laver, п., a seaweed. — L. laver, -'a water plant',
of uncertain origin.

## laverock
laverock, п., an archaic var. of lark.

## lavish
lavish, adj., profuse, prodigal. — Fr. earlier lavish,
п., 'profusion', fr. ME. lavas, fr. OF. lavasse, la-
vache, 'deluge of rain', fr. laver, 'to wash'. See
lave, 'to wash'.
Derivatives: lavish, tr. v., lavish-er, п., lavish-ly,
adv., lavish-ness, n.

## lavrovite
lavrovite, also lavroffite, п., pyroxene colored
green by vanadium (mineral.) — Russ. lavrovit,
named after N. von Lavrov. The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## law
law, n. — ME. laghe, lawe, fr. OE. lagu, 'law', of
Scand. origin; cp. ON. log, 'law', prop. pi. of lag,
'something laid down, a layer', fr. Teut. base
*lag-, 'to lay'; see lay, 'to place', lie, 'to recline'
and cp. outlaw. Hence law lit. means 'something
laid down, something fixed'. For sense
development cp. statute, lit. 'something made to stand*
(fr. L. statuere), G. Gesetz, 'law', and Satzung,
'statute', lit. 'something set' (fr. setzen, 'to set').
Cp. also Gk. κείται νόμος, 'the law is laid
(down), fr. κεΐμαι, Ί lie'.
Derivatives: taw-fut, adj., law-ful-ly, adv., law-
ful-ness, п., law-less, adj., law-less-ly, adv., law-
less-ness, п., lawyer (q.v.).

## law
law, interj. — Imitative. Cp. the interjection la.

## law
law, п., a hill. — OE. hldw, hlsew. See low, 'a
hill'.

## lawn
lawn, п., a kind of fine linen. — Formerly called
laune lynen, 'linen from Laon', fr. Laon, a town
in France, where it was originally manufactured.
F. Laon comes from OF. Lan, fr. L. Laudunum,
a name of Celtic origin.

## lawn
lawn, п., a stretch of grass. — ME. launde, laund,
fr. OF. launde, lande (F. lande), 'heath, moor',
which is borrowed fr. Gaul. *landa. See land.
The omission of the d in lawn (for *lawn-d) is
prob. due to its having been confused with the
suff. -ed. For a similar omission of the final -dcp.
scan.
lawn tennis. Lit. 'tennis played in the lawn'.

## lawny
lawny, adj., made of, or resembling, lawn (cloth).
—Formed with adj. suff. -y fr. lawn, 'a kind of
fine linen'.

## lawny
lawny, adj , 1) like a lawn; containing lawns. —■
Formed with adj. suff. -y fr. lawn, 'a stretch of
grass'.

## Lawrence
Lawrence, masc. PN. — See Laurence.

## lawrencite
lawrencite, п., ferrous chloride (mineral.) — F.,
named after the American chemist and
mineralogist J. Lawrence Smith (died in 1883). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## lawsonite
lawsonite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate
(mineralogy). — Named after the American geologist
Andrew Cowper Lawson (1861-1952). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## lawyer
lawyer, n. — ME. lawyere. See law and -yer. Cp.
bowyer, sawyer.
Derivatives: lawyer-ess, п., lawyer-ly, adj.,
lawyer-y, n.

## lax
lax, adj., 1) loose; 2) slack. — ME., fr. L. laxus,
for *(s)^g-sos, 'wide, loose, open', rel. to lan-
guere, 'to faint, weary', whence languidus, 'faint,
weak, dull, sluggish, languid'. See languid and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:441 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LAX | 414 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:441 COLUMN:1 -->
words there referred to. Cp. also laxate,
taxation, laxative, laxity, relax.
Derivatives: lax, n. (q.v.), lax-ly, adv., lax-ness,
a.

## lax
lax, п., looseness of the intestines. — Fr. prec.
word.

## lax
lax, п., a salmon. — Norw. laks, fr. ON. lax, rel.
to OE. leax, OS., OHG., MHG. lahs, G. Lachs,
LG. las, 'salmon-, and cogn. with Lith. lasis,
Lett, lasis, OPruss. lasasso, Russ. losos, 'salmon',
and with Toch. В laks, 'fish'. Cp. the first element
in laspring.

## laxate
laxate, tr. v., to loosen. — L. laxatus, pp. of
laxare, 'to open, unloose, relax', fr. laxus. See lax,
adj., and verbal suff. -ate.

## laxation
laxation, n. — ME., fr. L. laxdtio, gen. -onis, 'a
widening, mitigation', fr. laxatus, pp. of laxare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## laxative
laxative, adj., loosening; mildly purgative. —
ME. laxatif, fr. ML. laxuttvus, fr. L. laxatus, pp.
of laxare, 'to open, relax', fr. laxus, 'wide'. See
lax, adj., and -alive.
Derivatives: laxative, п., a purgative medicine,
laxative-ly, adv., laxative-ness, n.

## laxity
laxity, п., the quality or state of being lax. — F.
laxite, fr. L. laxitatem, ace. of laxitas,
'spaciousness, roominess; languor, laxity', fr. laxus. See
lax, adj., and -ity.

## lay
lay, tr. and intr. v., to place. — ME. leggen, leyen,
leiert, fr. OE. lecgan, 'to lay, put, place', re], to
OS. teggian, ON. leggja, OFris. ledza, MDu.
legghan, leghan, Du. leggen, OHG., MHG. lec-
ken, legen, G. legen, Goth, lagjan, 'to lay, put,
place'. These verbs lit. mean 'to cause to lie', and
are causatives of OE. licgan, 'to lie', resp. its
equivalents in the other Teut. languages. See He,
'to recline', and words there referred to and cp.
esp. lagan, law, ledge, ledger and the second
element in fellow. Cp. also layer, allay, underlay.
Derivatives: lay, п., the way in which something
lies, layer (q.v.), lay-ing, n.

## lay
lay, past tense of lie.

## lay
lay, п., a short song. — ME. laye, lay, fr. OF. ( =
F.) lai, a word of Celtic origin; cp. Olr. laid, Ir.
laid, Gael, laoidh, 'poem, verse, play'. These
words are not connected with L. ludus, 'play'.
Cp. roundelay.

## lay
lay, adj., pertaining to the laity, secular. — ME.,
fr. OF. lai, fr. Late L. laicus, 'pertaining to the
people', fr. Gk. λαϊκός, of s.m., fr. λαός (Att.
λεώς), 'people', which is of unknown origin.
Cp. laic, laity, the first element in Laertes, Lao-
coon, liturgy and the second element in Mene-
laus, Nicholas. Cp. also lewd.

## layer
layer, n. — ME. legger, leyer, fr. leggen, leyen, 'to.
lay'. See lay, v., and subst. suff. -er. Accordingly
layer lit. means 'that which is laid'.
Derivatives: layer, tr. v., layer-ed, adj.

## layette
layette, п., baby's outfit. — F., 'baby's outfit',
dimin. of MF. laie, 'drawer, case', fr. MDu.
laeye, which is rel. to G. Lade, of s.m., and to E.
lade, load (qq. v.) For the ending see suff.
-ette.

## lay figure
lay figure, п., a jointed model of the human form.
—Fr. earlier layman, fr. Du. leeman, lit. 'jointed
man', fr. MDu. led, lit, ghelit (Du. lid, gelid),
'limb, joint', and man, 'man'. MDu. led, lit,
ghelit is rel. to OE. lip, OS., OFris. lith, ON. lidr,
Dan., Swed. led, OHG. gilid, MHG. gelit, gelid,
G. Glied, Goth, lipus, 'limb, joint', fr. Teut. base
*ll-, corresponding to I.-E. base *lei-, 'to bend,
be movable, be nimble'. See limb.

## lazar
lazar, п., a filthy beggar; esp. a leper. — ME., fr.
ML. lazar us, named after Lazarus mentioned
Luke 16:20. See Lazarus and cp. lazaretto, laz-
zarone.

## lazaret
lazaret, п., lazaretto. — F., fr. It. lazzaretto. See
next word.

## lazaretto
lazaretto, п., a hospital for lepers; place in a ship
used as storehouse. — Venetian lazareto (whence
It. lazzaretto), a blend of Lazaro (It. Lazzaro),
name of the Venetian hospital for lepers (so
called after Luke 16:20) and Nazaret, the name
of another hospital in Venice, which was so
called because it was established after the decay
of the former, in the neighborhood of the church
Santa Maria di Nazaret, See Lazarus and cp.
lazar.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:441 COLUMN:2 -->

## Lazarus
Lazarus, masc. PN. — L. Lazarus, fr. Gk.
Λάζαρος, aphetic for Έλεάζαρος, fr. Heb. El'dzar, lit.
'God has helped'. See Eleazar.

## laze
laze, intr. v. — Back formation fr. lazy.

## iazy
iazy, adj. — Fr. earlier laysy; of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: lazi-ly, adv., lazi-ness, n.

## lazzarone
lazzarone, п., one belonging to a very low class of
people in-Naples, living by odd jobs or by
begging. — It., augment, of lazzaro, fr. Lazzaro,
'Lazarus'. See lazar. For the suff. -one see -oon.

## -le
-le, suff. forming diminutive nouns. — 1) ME. -el,
-ele, -elle, fr. OE. -el, -ela, -ele; cp. e.g. knuckle;
2) ME. -el, -elle, fr. OF. -el, fr. L. -ellum; cp. e.g.
castle, fr. OF. chastel (F. chateau), fr. L. castel-
lum; 3) ME. -el, fr. OF. -eille, fr. L. -icula; cp.
e.g. bottle, fr. OF. botele (F. bouteille), fr. VL.
butticula.

## -le
-le, agential suff. — ME. -le, fr. Teut. -el (often
through the medium of French). Cp. e.g. beadel,
fr. ME. bedel, fr. OF. bedel (F. bedeau).

## -le
-le, suff. denoting an instrument. — ME. -el, fr,
OE. -el. Cp. e.g. ladle, fr. ME. ladel, fr. OE.
hlxde/, fr. hladan, 'to draw (water)'.

## -le
-le, suff. forming adjectives from verbs. This suff.
indicates tendency toward the action or process
expressed by the verb. — ME. -el, -il, -le, fr. OE.
-ol. Cp. e.g. brittle, fr. ME. britel, fr. OE. brio-
tan, 'to break'.

## -le
-le, suff. forming verbs with freq. or dimin.
meaning. — ME. -elen, -ten, fr. OE. -lian. Cp. e.g.
wrestle, fr. ME. wrestlen, fr. OE. mrxstlian, 'to
wrestle', freq. of wrxstan, 'to twist, wrest'.

## lea
lea, п., a tract of open country. — ME. lee, leye,
fr. OE. leak, 'open field, meadow', rel. to OHG.
loh, 'cluster of bushes' (whence the PN. Hohen-
lohe), Flem. loo, of s.m. (whence the place name
Water-loo), and cogn. with Ol. lokah, 'open
space', L. lucus, 'grove', Lith. laiikas, Lett, lauks,
'open field', Toch. A lok, В lauke, 'far away',
and with L. lucere, 'to shine'; see light,
'brightness'. For sense development ср. Е. clearingKir.
clear).

## lea
lea, п., a measure of yarn (varying in different
places). — ME. lee, prob. fr. F. tier, 'to bind',
fr. L. ligare. See ligament.

## leach
leach, tr. v., to moisten; intr. v., to melt. — A
blend of OE. leccan, 'to moisten', and ON. leka,
'to leak' (whence E. leak, q.v.)
Derivative: leach, n.

## lead
lead, п., a heavy, bluish grey metal. — ME. lede,
fr. OE. lead, rel. to OFris. lad, MDu. loot, hod,
Du. hod, MHG. lot, 'lead', G. Lot, 'weight,
plummet'; of Celt, origin. Cp. Olr. luaide (for
"loudia, fr. *phudia), fr. I.-E. base *plou(d);
*pleu(d)-, 'to flow', for which see fleet, 'to pass
swiftly'.
Derivatives: lead, adj. and tr. v., leaden (q.v.),
lead-y, adj., leading (q.v.)

## lead
lead, tr. and intr. v., to guide. — ME. leden, fr.
OE. liidan, 'to lead, guide', rel. to OS. ledian,
ON. leida, OFris. leda, Du. leiden, OHG. leittan,
leiten, MHG., G. leiten, fr. Teut. *laidian, 'to
lead', lit. 'to make go', causative formed fr. *ti-
pan, 'to go', which appears in OE. lidan, 'to go,
travel, sail', OS. lithan, ON. lida, 'to go', OHG.
ga-ltdan, 'to travel', Goth, ga-leipan, 'to go'. Cp.
Teut. *laidd-, 'way, guidance', appearing in OE.
lad, 'path, track, way, course', OS. ledn, ON.
leid, 'guidance'. Cp. also load, lode, and the first
element in leitmotiv.
Derivatives: lead, п., lead-er, п., lead-er-ship, п.,
leading (q.v.)

## leaden
leaden, adj., made of lead. — ME. leden, fr. OE.
leaden, fr. lead. See lead, 'a metal', and adj. suff.
-en.
Derivative: leaden-ness, n.

## leaderette
leaderette, п., a short editorial paragraph. — Lit.
'a short leading article', a hybrid formed fr.
leader and -ette, a suff. of French origin.

## leadtug
leadtug, п., leadwork. — Formed fr. lead, 'a
metal', with subst. suff. -ing.

## leading
leading, п., guidance. — Formed from the verb
lead with -ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## leading
leading, adj., directing, guiding. — Formed from
the verb lead with part. suff. -ing.

## leaf
leaf, n. — ME. lee/, lef, fr. OE. leaf, rel. to OS.
lof, ON. fan/; Dan. lev, Swed. lof, OFris. laf Du.
loof, OHG. hub, MHG. hup, hub, G. Laub,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:441 COLUMN:3 -->
'foliage', Goth, lauf, 'foliage', laufs, 'leaf, and
cogn. with Lith. lupu, lupti, 'to shell, peel', Lett,
/ирг, 'to peel; to rob,' Russ. lupljii, lupit', 'to
peel', OSlav. lubu, 'bark, rind', Lith. luba,
OPruss. lubbo, 'board',.Lith. liiobas, 'bark,rind'.
All these words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base
*leub(h)-, *leup-, 'to strip, to peel', whence prob.
also L. liber (fr. ЧйЬег), 'bast, book'; see library
and cp. ah pin. I.-E. base *leub(h)-, "leup- is rel.
to base *lep-, 'to peel', whence Gk. λέπειν, 'to
strip off the rind, peel, bark'; see leper and cp.
lodge.
Derivatives: leaf, intr. v., leaf-less, adj., leaf-less-
ness, п., leaf-y, adj., leaf-i-ness, n.

## leant
leant, п., leaflet (.archaic). — Coined by the
English poet John Keats (1795-1821) fr. leaf and
diminutive suff. -it ~ -et.

## leaflet
leaflet, n. — A hybrid coined fr. leaf and -let, a
dimin. suff. of French origin.

## league
league, п., alliance. — OF (= F.) ligue,
'confederacy, league', fr. Olt. liga, fr. L. ligare, 'to bind'.
See ligament (It. lega is a back formation fr. It.
legare, 'to bind', fr. L. ligare).
Derivative: leaguer (q.v.)

## league
league, tr. v., to form into a league; intr. v., to
form a league. — Fr. prec. word. Cp. F. se
liguer, 'to form a league'.

## league
league, п., an old measure of distance varying in
different times and countries. — OF. legue (F.
lieu), fr. Late L. leuga, leuca (whence also О
Proven?, lega, Sp. legud), which is of Gaulish origin.

## leaguer
leaguer, п., member of a league. — Formed with
agential suff. -er fr. league, 'alliance'.

## leaguer
leaguer, п., camp. — Du. leger, 'camp'. See lair
and cp. laager, lager.
Derivative: leaguer, intr. and tr. v.

## Leah
Leah, l)fem. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the elder
daughter of Laban and wife of Jacob. — Lit. 'wild-
cow'; cp. Arab, loan, 'wildcow'. See Friedrich
Delitzsch, Prolegomena eines neuen hebr.-aram.
Worterbuchs zum Alten Testament p. 80, G.
Buchanan, Studies in Hebrew Proper Names,
p. 96, and Martin Noth, Die israelitischen Per-
sonennamen im Rahmen der gemeinsemitischen
Namengebung, p. 10.

## leak
leak, intr. v. — ME. leken, fr. ON. leka, 'to leak,
drip', which is rel. to OE. leccan, 'to moisten,
water', MDu. lecken, Du. lekken, 'to leak',
OHG. lecchen, MHG. lechen, 'to become dry',
MHG. lechezen, lechzen, G. lechzen, 'to be
parched with thirst', ON. lekr, OE. hlec. MDu.
leek, Du. lek, G. leek, 'leaky'. Outside Teut. cp.
Olr. legaim, Ί melt, dissolve' (intr.), ModW.
llaith (for "lekto-), 'moist'. Cp. leach and the
first element in lacmus.

## leak
leak, n. — ON. leki, fr. leka, 'to leak, drip'. See
leak, v.
Derivatives: leak-y, adj., leak-i-ness, п., and the
hybrid noun leak-age.

## leal
leal, adj., loyal (dial, от poet.). — ME. leel, lei, fr.
OF. leial, leal, loial (F. loyal); a doublet of legal
and loyal,

## lean
lean, intr. and tr. v., to incline, bend. — ME.
lenen, fr. OE. hleonian, hlinian, 'to lean; to
recline, lie', rel. to OS. hlinon, OFris. lena, MDu.
linen, Du. leunen, OHG. hlinen, linen, MHG.
linen, lenen, G. lehnen, 'to lean'; fr. I.-E. base
*klei-, 'to incline, lean', whence also Gk. xXi-
veiv, 'to cause to slope, slant, incline'. See
clinical and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
lean, 'thin', ladder, lid, linch, linchet, links, 'sand
hills', low, 'hill'.
Derivatives: lean, п., a slope, lean-ing, n.

## lean
lean, adj., thin. — ME. /еле, fr. OE. hlzn, 'lean,
thin', which is of uncertain origin. It possibly
meant orig. 'bending, drooping', and is rel. to
OE. hleonian, 'to lean'. See lean, v.
Derivatives: lean, п., lean-ish, adj., lean-ly, adv.,
lean-ness, n.

## Leander
Leander, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in Greek mythology, a
young man of Abydos, lover of Hero. He swam
nightly across the Hellespont to visit Hero in
Sestos. — L. Leander, fr. Gk. Λείανδρος,
Λέανδρος, lit. 'lion man', compounded of λέων, 'lion',
and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man'. See lion and an-
dro-.

## leap
leap, intr. and tr. v. — ME. lepen, fr. OE. hleapan,
'to jump, dance; to run', rel. to OS. hhpan, ON.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:442 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 415 | LEECH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:442 COLUMN:1 -->
Maupa, Dan. lobe, Swed. lopa, OFris. hlapa,
MDu. lopen, Du. lopen, OHG. hlouffan, louffan,
MHG. loufen, G. laufen, 'to run', Goth, us-
hlaupan, 'to jump up'. The ult. etymol. of these
words is uncertain. Cp. elope, gallop, gantlet,
interloper, landloper, lapwing, lope, loup, orlop,
wallop.
Derivatives: leap, п., leap-er, п., leap-ing, n.
and adj.

## learn
learn, tr. and intr. v. — ME. lernen, fr. OE. leor-
nian, rel. to OS. Ιϊηδη (for *liznon), OFris. lernia,
lirnia, OHG. lernen, lirnen, MHG., G. lernen,
'to learn', Goth, lais, Ί know', laisjan, OE. Ixran
(whence ON. lira), OS. lerian, OFris. lira, MDu.
leeren, Du. leren, OHG. lerran, leren, MHG.
teren, G. tehren, 'to teach', lit. 'to make known'.
All these words orig. meant 'to follow or find the
track, to follow, go after', resp. 'to cause to find
the track, to cause to follow'. They are related to
OHG. leisa (in wagenleisa), 'track of carriage
wheels', MHG. leise, geleis, G. Geleise, Gleis,
'track', OE. Ixst, 'sole of foot, track, footprint,
last', OHG. leist, 'track, footprint, last', MHG.
leist, G. Leisten, 'last', ON. leislr, 'foot, sock',
Goth.tails, 'track', taistjan, 'to follow'. Cognates
outside Teut. are L. lira (for *leisa), 'the earth
thrown up between two fuTrows, furrow',
OSlav. lecha, 'ridge (in a field)', OPruss. lyso, of
s.m., Lith. lyse, 'garden bed'. Cp. last, 'model of
foot', last, 'to endure', lore. Cp. also delirium.
Derivatives: learn-ed, adj., learn-ed-ly, adv.,
learn-ed-ness, п., teaming (q.v.)

## learning
learning, n. — ME. lerning, fr. OE. leornung,
'learning, study', fr. leornian, 'to learn'. See learn
and subst. surf. -ing.

## lease
lease, tr. v. — AF. lesser, fr. OF. iaissier, lessier,
lesser (F. laisser), 'to let, leave', fr. L. laxare, 'to
open, make wide, slacken, relax, relieve', fr.
laxus, 'wide, loose, open'. See lax, adj., and cp.
lessee.

## lease
lease, n. — ME. les. fr. AF., fr. OF. lais, 'a
letting, leaving', verbal n. of Iaissier (see lease, v.).
The F. equivalent of OF. lais is legs, whose
spelling is due to the erroneous derivation of
this word fr. L. legamm, 'bequest, legacy' (see
legacy).

## leash
leash, п., a thong for holding a dog. — ME. lese,
lees, fr. OF. lesse, laisse (F. laisse), fr. L. laxa,
fern, of laxus, 'wide, loose, open'. See lax, adj.,
and cp. lease.
Derivative: leash, tr. v.

## leasing
leasing, п., a lie, falsehood (archaic). — ME. le-
sing, fr. OE. leasung, 'falsehood, deception', fr.
leas, 'devoid of, without; false, feigned', rel. to
leosan, 'to lose'. See lose and -ing, suff. forming
verbal nouns, and cp. -less.

## least
least, adj. — ME. teste, lest, fr. OE. ISst,
contraction of ISsast, Ixsest, 'smallest', superl. of Ixssa,
'less'. See less.
Derivatives: least, п., least-ways, adv. (colloq.),
least-wise, adv.

## leat
leat, п., an open water trench. — ME. /eel, fr.
OE. gelxt, gelxte, 'junction of roads, outlet',
from pref. ge- (see y-) and the stem of IStan, 'to
leave'. See let, 'to leave'.

## leather
leather, n. — ME. lether, fr. OE. /e<3er, rel. to OS.
lethar, ON. ledr, Dan. Ixder, Swed. lader, OFris.
lether, MDu. leder, Du. leder, leer, OHG. ledar,
MHG., G. leder, and cogn. with Olr. lethar, W.
Iledr, Bret, lezr, 'leather'.
Derivatives: leather, adj. and tr. v., leather-ing,
п., leathern (q.v.), leather-y, adj., leather-i-ness,
n.

## leatherette
leatherette, n. — A hybrid coined fr. leather and
-ette, a suff. of French origin.

## leathern
leathern, adj. — Formed fr. leather with suff. -en.

## leatheroid
leatheroid, п., material used instead of leather;
artificial leather. — A hybrid coined fr. leather
and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. εί8ος, 'form, shape'.
See -oid.

## leave
leave, tr. and intr. v. — ME. leven, fr. OE. Ixfan,
'not to take away, to leave, bequeath', rel. to
OE. laf, 'what remains, remnant', OE. belifan,
OS. biliban, OHG. biliban, MHG. beliben, G.
bleiben, Goth, bileiban, 'to remain', and prob.
also to OE. Iff, 'life', libban, tifian, 'to live', orig.
'to remain'; cogn. with Gk. λίπος, 'grease, fat',
λιπαρός, 'oily, fat, greasy', λιπαρής,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:442 COLUMN:2 -->
'persisting, persevering', lit. 'sticky', λιπαρεΐν, 'to
persist, persevere', lit. 'to stick', OI. /i-mpari,'smears',
liptah, 'sticking together', tepab, 'unguent', L.
lippus, 'blear-eyed', Lith. limpii, lipti, 'to stick,
adhere', OSlav. pri-linqti, of s.m., При,
'birdlime', Alb. Vaparos, Ί soil', gl'ep, geVepe, Sklepe,
'mucus secreted by the glands of the eyelid', and
possibly also Hitt. lippanzi, 'they smear, paint'
(but Gk. λείπω, L. linquo, Ί leave', are not
cognate). All these words derive fr. I.-E. base "leip-,
'to anoint; to stick, adhere; to remain,
persevere, continue, live'. Cp. life, live, liver and the
second element in Olaf. Cp. also adipose, t.ipa-
ris, lipase, lipo-, 'fat', lipoma, the first element
in liparoid and the second element in celibate.
Derivative: leav-ing, n.

## leave
leave, n. — ME. leve, fr. OE. leaf, rel. to OE. leof,
'dear', ON. leyfi, MHG. loube, 'permission', OS.
orlef, OFris. orlof, orlef, OHG., MHG. urloup,
G. Urlaub, 'leave of absence', OE. liefan, ON.
leyfa, 'to permit, allow', OE. aliefan, alyfan,
OHG. irlouben, MHG. erlouben, G. erlauben,
Goth, uslaubjan, of s.m., OE. geleafa, OS. gild-
bo, OHG. giloubo, MHG. geloube, gloube, G.
Glaube, Goth, galaubeins, 'belief, OE. geliefan,
gellfan, OS. gildbian, MHG. gelouben, glouben,
G. glauben, Goth, galaubjan, 'to believe', fr.l.-E.
base*/ew6A-, 'to love, approve, praise*. See lief
and love and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
the second element in furlough.

## leave
leave, intr. v., to put forth leaves, to leaf. — ME.
leven, fr. lef, 'leaf'. See leaf.

## leaved
leaved, adj., having leaves. — Formed fr. prec.
word with suff. -ed.

## leaven
leaven, n. — ME. levain, levain, fr. F. levain, fr.
VL. *levamen, 'something that raises' (classical
L. levumen, means 'alleviation, mitigation'), fr.
levare, 'to lift, raise; to lighten, alleviate,
mitigate', fr. levis, 'light'. See level and cp. relieve.
Derivatives: leaven, tr. v., leaven-ing, n.

## leban
leban, lebban, also leben, п., coagulated sour milk
(an Arab beverage). — VArab. laban, leben,
'sour milk', fr. Arab, laban, 'milk', which is rel.
to Heb. lubhan, 'white', lebhanah, poetic name
for the moon (lit. 'the white one'), llbh6nah,
Aram.-Syr. Pbhunta, Arab, luban, 'frankincense'
(Gk. λίβανος, λιβανωτός, 'frankincense', are
Sem. loan words), Heb. LibhanOn, Akkad. Lab-
nanu, Aram. Libhnan, Arab. Lubnan, 'Mount
Lebanon', lit. 'the white one'; so called from
the whiteness of its cliffs. Cp. olibanum and the
first element in benzoin.

## Lecanium
Lecanium, п., a genus of scale insects
(entomology). — ModL., fr. Gk. λεκάνιον, dimin. of
λεκάνη, 'dish, pan'. Seelekane and cp. Lecidea.

## lecanomancy
lecanomancy, п., divination by the inspection of
water in a basin. — Compounded of Gk.
λεκάνη, 'dish, pan', and μαντεία, 'oracle,
divination'. See lekane and -mancy.

## Lechea
Lechea, п., a genus of plants, the pinweed (bot.)
— ModL., named after the Swedish botanist
JohanLecAe (1704-64).

## lecher
lecher, п., lecherous, lewd. — ME. lechour. fr.
OF. lecheur (F. Ucheur), 'libertine', lit. 'licker',
fr. lechier (F. lecher), 'to lick', fr. Frankish "lik-
kon, which is rel. to OHG. teckon, 'to lick'. See
lick.

## lecherous
lecherous, adj., lustful. — ME., fr. MF. leche-
reus, fr. OF., fr. lecheur, 'libertine'. See prec.
word and -ous and cp. lickerish.
Derivatives: lecherous-ly, adv., lecherous-ness,n.

## lechery
lechery, п., lust, lewdness. — ME. lecherie, fr. OF.
lecherie, fr. lecheur, 'libertine'. See lecher and -y
(representing OF. -ie).

## Lecidea
Lecidea, п., a genus of crustacean lichens (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk, λεκίς, gen. λεκίδος, dimin. of
λέκος, 'dish'. See lekane and cp. Lecanium.

## lecithin
lecithin, п., a waxy substance found in tissues of
the brain and the nerves (bibchem.) — Coined by
Gobley fr. Gk. λέκιθος, 'the yolk of an egg',
which is of uncertain, prob. foreign, origin, and
chem. suff. -in.

## lecontite
lecontite, п., a hydrous sodium ammonium
potassium sulfate (mineral.) — Named after the
American scientist John L. Le Conte, its
discoverer. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## lectern
lectern, п., a reading desk in a church. — ME.
lectorne, refashioned (after ML. lectorlnum, lec-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:442 COLUMN:3 -->
trinum) fr. ME. lettorne, lettron, fr. OF. letrin,
fr. ML. lectorinum, lectrinum, fr. Late L. lectrum,
'reading desk, pulpit', fr. L. lectus, pp. of legere,
'to read'. See lecture.

## lection
lection, п., a reading, a lesson. — L. lectio, gen.
■onis, 'a reading', fr. lectus, pp. of legere, 'to
read'. See lecture and -ion and cp. lesson, which
is a doublet of lection.

## lectionary
lectionary, п., a list of lections. — Ecclesiastic L.
lectionarium, fr. L. lectio, gen.-onis, 'a reading'.
See prec. word and subst. suff. -ary.

## lector
lector, п., a reader, esp. in a church or in a
university. — Late L. lector, 'reader', fr. L. lectus,
pp. of legere. See lecture and agential suff. -or.

## lectorate
lectorate, п., the office of a lector. — ML. Iect6-
ratus, fr. Late L. lector. See prec. word and subst.
suff. -ate.

## lecture
lecture, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) lecture, fr.
ML. Igctura, it. L. lectus, pp. of legere, 'to
gather, collect; to pick out, choose; to read, recite'
(prop, 'to choose words'), fr. I.-E. base *Ieg-, 'to
pick together, gather, collect', whence also Gk.
λέγειν, 'to pick out, choose; to say, tell, speak,
declare' (prop, 'to choose words'), λέξις (for
*λέγ-σις), 'speech, diction', λόγος, 'word,
speech, discourse, account, thought, reason',
Alb. mb-Vtb, Ί gather, collect, harvest'. Cp.
alexia, Aloglans, analects, analogue, analogy,
apologetic, apologize, apologue, apology, coil,
colleague, collect, college, curiologic, Decalog,
dialect, dialogue, diligeut, duologue, dyslogy,
eclectic, eclogue, elect, election, elegant, eligible,
elite, epilogue, eulogy, florilegium, intellect,
intelligent, lectern, lection, legal, legation, legend,
legible, legion, legislation, legitimate, legume,
lesson, lexicon, ligueous, logic, logos, monologue,
neglect, negligee, paralogy, predilection,
prolegomena, prologue, recollect, religion, sacrilege,
select, sortilege, syllogism, tetralogy, trilogy. For
the ending of lecture see suff. -lire.
Derivatives: lecture, intr. and tr. v., lectur-er, п.,
lecture-ship, n.

## lecythus
lecythus, п., a tall, slender vase with a single
handle (Greek antiq.) — Late L., fr. Gk.
λήκυθος, 'oil flask', which is of unknown origin.

## led
led, past tense and pp. of lead. — ME. ledde; fr.
OE. Ixdde, fr. OE. Ixdan, 'to lead'. See lead, v.

## Leda
Leda, п., mother of Castor and Pollux, Helen,
and Clytemnestra (Greek mythol.) — L. Leda,
fr. Gk. Λήδα, which prob. derives fr. Lycian
Lada, and lit. means 'wife, woman'. She is
identical with Latona and Leto (qq.v.)

## lederlte
lederlte, п., a variety of sphene (mineral.) —
Named after Baron Louis von Lederer,
Austrian Consul at New York, in recognition of his
interest in mineralogy. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## ledge
ledge, п., a shelf projecting from a wall; a ridge of
rocks. — ME. legge, 'support, bar', prob.
related to ME. leggen, 'to lay'. See lay, 'to place',
and cp. next word.
Derivative: ledg-y, adj.

## ledger
ledger, п., an account book. — ME. legger, fr.
leggen, 'to lay'; cp. the ME. var. lidger, which
prob. derives fr. liggen, 'to lie'. ME. legger,
lidger orig. meant 'a book that lies permanently in
the same place'. See lay, 'to place', lie, 'to
recline', and cp. prec. word.

## ledger
ledger, adj., stationery — From the stem of ME.
leggen, 'to lay', fr. OE. lecgan. See ledger, n.

## Ledum
Ledum, п., a genus of plants, the Labrador tea
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. λήδον, the plant Cistus
Cyprius. See ladanum.

## tee
tee, п., 1) shelter; 2) the side of a ship turned
away from the wind. — ME. lee, 'shelter', fr.
OE. hlio (gen. hleowes), 'shelter, protection', rel.
to OS. hleo, ON. hie, Dan. Ix, Swed. la, Du. lij,
'lee', and to ON. hip, 'shelter, warmth', hlpr,
hlxr, 'warm, mild', MLG., Du. lauw, MDu. laeu,
OHG. lao (inflected lower), MHG. la, lawes, G.
lau, 'tepid'; prob. fr. I.-E. *kleu-, enlargement
of base 4cel-, 'warm', whence L. calere, 'to be
warm'. See caldron and cp. lew, luke, 'lukewarm'.
Derivative: lee, adj.

## leech
leech, п., 1) physician (archaic); 2) a blood
sucking worm. — ME. leche, fr. OE. ISce,
'physician; leech', rel. to ON. Ixknir, OS. Iski, OFris.
letza, OHG. lahhi, lachi, Goth, llkeis, 'physi-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:443 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LEECH | 416 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:443 COLUMN:1 -->
cian', prob. meaning orig. 'magician', and cogn.
with Olr. liaig, 'charmer, exorcist, physician'.

## leech
leech, п., either edge of a square sail (naut.) —
Rel. to MLG. Ilk, Du. lijk, G. Leik, ON. Ilk,
'boltrope, leechrope'; prob. fr. I.-E. base *leig-,
'to bind', whence also L. ligare, 'to bind, tie'.
See ligament and cp. words there referred to.

## leechcraft
leechcraft, п., medical science (archaic). — ME.
lechecraft, fr. OE. Ixcecrseft. See leech,
'physician', and craft,

## leechdom
leechdom, п., medicine, remedy (obsol.) — ME.
lechedom, fr. OE. Ixcedom, 'medicine, remedy'.
See leeeh, 'physician', and -dom,

## leek
leek, n. — ME. lek, lik, fr. OE. leac, lee, 'leek,
onion, garlic', rel. to OS. lok, 'leek', ON. laukr,
'leek, garlic', Dan. leg, Swed. lok, 'onion', Du.
look, 'leek, garlic', OHG. huh, louhh, MHG.
touch, G. Lauch, 'leek', fr. I.-E. base *leug-,
*lug-, 'to bend, twist', whence also OE. locc,
'lock of hair'. Finn, lauka, Lith. tukat, Lett, lu-
oks and OSlav. luku are Teut. loan words.
See lock, 'tuft of hair', and cp. Lygodium,
reluct.

## leer
leer, п., cheek, face (obsol.) — ME. ler, fr. OE.
hleor, 'cheek, face', rel. to ON. hlyr, OS. hleor,
hlior; of uncertain origin.

## leer
leer, intr. v., to look askance. — Prob. fr. prec.
word.
Derivatives: leer, п., a side glance, \eer~ing, adj.,
leer-ing-ly, adv., leer-y, adj.

## Leersia
Leersia, п., a genus of grasses, the cut grass (bot.)
— Modi.., named after the German botanist
Johann Daniel Leers (1727-74). For the ending
see 1st sufT. -ia.

## lees
lees, n. pi. — ME. lie, fr. OF. (= F.) lie, 'lees', fr.
Gallo-L. lia (for *liga), 'sediment' (cp. Olr.
lige, 'a lying'); fr. I.-E. base *legh-, 'to lie'. See
lie, 'to recline'.

## leet
leet, п., a courtleet; its jurisdiction. — Cp. AF.
lete, AL. tela; of uncertain origin.

## leeward
leeward, adv., adj. and n. — Compounded of lee,
'shelter', and -ward.
Derivative: leeward-ly, adv.

## leeway
leeway, n.—Compounded oflee.'shelter', and way.

## left
left, past tense and pp. of leave. — ME. lafte,
lefte, past tense and pp. of leven, 'to leave'. See
leave, v.

## left
left, adj., adv. and n. — ME. /и/I, lift, left, orig.
'weak, infirm', fr. OE. lyft, 'weak' (whence OE.
lyftadl, 'paralysis'), rel. to MLG. lucht, MDu.
luchi, luft, 'left', prob. not connected with Gk.
λεπρός, 'scaly', λέπρα, 'leprosy' (see leper). See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, 786 s.v. lepidus.

## leg
leg, n. — ME. legge, leg, fr. ON. leggr, 'leg'
(which is rel. to ON. armleggr, 'arm'), which is
prob. rel. to OE. lira (for *ligiza), 'fleshy part of
the body, flesh', ON. liir, Swed. tdr, 'thigh', and
prob. cogn. with OI. rksala, 'foot joint of a
hoofed animal', L. lacenus, 'upper arm, arm',
lacerta, 'lizard', locusta, 'grasshopper, locust',
lit. 'the jumper', Gk. λάξ, λάγδην, 'kicking
with the foot', λακτίζειν, 'to kick with the foot',
λάκτις, 'pestle', λικερ-τίζειν (Hesychius), 'to
spring, leap', Lith. lekiu, lekti, 'to fly', lakstyti,
'to hop', Lett, lezu, lekt, 'to jump'. All these
words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *leq-, "fq-, 'to
bend, twist'. See Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I,
743-44, s.v. lacertus. Cp. Lacerta, lacertian,
lizard, lobster, locust. Cp. also polatonche.
Derivatives: leg, intr. v., legg-ed, adj., legg-ing,
п., legg-y, adj., legg-i-ness, n.

## legacy
legacy, n. — ME. legacie, fr. OF. legacie, 'legate's
office', fr. ML. llgatia, fr. L. legatus,
'ambassador, envoy'. See legate and -cy.

## legal
legal, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) legal, fr. L.
legalis, 'pertaining to the law, legal', fr. lex, gen.
legis, 'law', which is prob. rel. to legere, in the
sense of'to gather', and orig. meant 'collection';
see lectore, collection and cp. the second element
in privilege. For the lengthening of the e in lex
cp. the noun rex, 'king', which is rel. to regere,
'to guide, direct'. Cp. ieal and loyal, which are
doublets of legal.
Derivatives: legal-ism, п., legal-isl, п.,
legalistic, adj., legal-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., legality (q.v.),
legal-ize, tr. v., legal-iz-ation, п., legal-ly, adv.

## legality
legality, n. — ME. legalise, fr. MF. (= F.) liga-
lite, fr. ML. legalitStem, ace. of legalitSs, fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:443 COLUMN:2 -->
legalis, 'pertaining to the law'. See prec. word
and -ity.

## legate
legate, п., envoy. — ME., fr. OE. legal, fr. OF.,
fr. L. legatus, 'ambassador, envoy', prop. pp. of
legare, 'to send with a commission, to send as
ambassador', rel. to lex, gen. legis. 'law'. See
legal and adj. surf. -ate.
Derivative: legate-ship, n.

## legate
legate, tr. v., to bequeath by will. — L. legatus, pp.
of legare, 'to send with a commission; to
appoint by a last will'. See legate, n.

## legatee
legatee, п., one to whom a legacy is bequeathed.
— L. legatus, pp. of legare. See prec. word and
-ее.

## legatine
legatine, adj., pertaining to a legate. — See prec.
word and -me (corresponding to L. -inus).

## legation
legation, n. — ME. legacioun, fr. OF. (= F.)
legation, fr. L. legationem, ace. ailegatio, 'embassy',
fr. legatus, pp. of legare, See legate, п., and -ion.

## legato
legato, adv., to be played smoothly, i.e. without
intervals (mus.) — It. legato, 'tied, bound', pp.
of legare, fr. L. ligare, 'to bind'. See ligament.

## legator
legator, п., one who bequeaths. — L. legator, fr.
legatus, pp. of legare, 'to appoint by a last will'.
See legate, 'to bequeath', and agential surf. -or.

## legend
legend, n. — ME. legende, fr. OF. legende (= F.
ligende), fr. ML. legenda, 'a thing to be read', fr.
L. legendus, 'to be read', gerundive of legere, 'to
read'. See lecture. For other Latin gerundives
used in English cp. agenda and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: legendary (q.v.), Iegend-ry, n.

## legendary
legendary, adj. — ME. legendarius, fr. legenda,
'legend'. See prec. word and adj. surf. -ary.

## legerdemain
legerdemain, п., conjuring tricks, jugglery. — F.
leger de main, 'light of hand'. F. leger, 'light',
derives fr. VL. *leviarius, fr. L. levis, 'light in
weight'; see lever and cp. legerity. F. de, 'from,
of, comes fr. L. de, 'from, away from'; see de-.
F. main, 'hand', derives fr. L. manum, ace. of
manus, of s.m; see manual.
Derivative: legerdemain-ist, n.

## legerity
legerity, п., lightness, nimbleness. — F. le'gerete,
fr. leger, fr. VL. *leviarius, fr. L. levis, 'light in
weight'. See legerdemain and -ity.

## Leghorn.
Leghorn., 1) Leghorn straw; 2) a hat made from
this straw; 3) a Leghorn breed of fowl. —
Named fr. Leghorn (Livorno) in Italy.

## legible
legible, adj. — Late L. legibilis, 'readable', fr. L.
legere, 'to read'. See lecture and -ible.
Derivatives: legibil-ity, п., legible-ness, п., legibl-
y, adv.

## legion
legion, n. — ME. legioun, fr. OF. legiun, legion
(F. legion), fr. L. legionem, ace. of legio, 'a
legion', fr. L. legere, 'to gather, collect; to read'.
See lecture and -ion.

## legionary
legionary, adj. and n. — L. legionarius,
'pertaining to a legion', fr. legio, gen. -onis, 'a legion'.
See prec. word and -ary.

## legislate
legislate, intr. v. — Back formation fr. legislation.

## legislation
legislation, п., the making of laws. — L. legislatio,
prop, two words:
/(?fij/o(iiJ,'proposing'(lit.'bearing) of a law', fr. legis, gen. of lex, 'law', and
latid, 'a bringing (forward)', fr. lotus, 'borne,
brought, carried' (used as pp. oiferre, 'to bear,
carry'), which stands for "tlatos, fr. *(/-, zero
degree of l.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry',
whence L. tollere, 'to lift up, raise', tolerare, 'to
bear, support'. See legal and tolerate.

## legislative
legislative, adj. and n. — See prec. word and -ive.

## legislator
legislator, n. — L. legis lator, 'proposer' (lit.
'bearer') of a law', fr. legis, gen. of lex, 'law', and
tutor, 'proposer', fr. lotus, 'borne, brought,
carried'. See legislation and agential suff. -or.

## legislature
legislature, п., a law-making body. — See
legislation and -ure.

## legist
legist, п., one versed in the law. — MF. (= F.)
legiste, fr. ML. Iegista,it. L. lex, gen. legis, 'law'.
See legal and -ist.

## legitimacy
legitimacy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## legitimate
legitimate, adj. — ML. legiiimatus, pp. of legiti-
mare, 'to legitimate', fr. L. legitimus, 'lawful', fr.
lex, gen. legis, 'law'. See legal.
Derivatives: legitimate-ly, adv., legitimate-ness,
a., legitimation (q.v.), legitimat-ize, tr. v.

## legitimate
legitimate, tr. v. — ML. legiiimatus, pp. of legiii-
mare. See legitimate, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:443 COLUMN:3 -->

## legitimation
legitimation, п., the action of making legitimate.
— ME. legitimacioun, fr. MF. (— F)
legitimation, fr. ML. legiximationem, ace. of ligimatio,
fr. legiiimatus, pp. of legiiimare. See legitimate,
adj., and -ion.

## legitimism
legitimism, п., the principles of a legitimist. — F.
legiiimisme, fr. L. legitimus, 'lawful'. See
legitimate, adj., and-ism.

## legitimist
legitimist, п., a supporter of legitimate authority.
— F. legitimiste, fr. L. legitimus, 'lawful'. See
legitimate, adj., and -ist.
Derivatives: legitimist, legitimist-ic, adjs.

## legitimize
legitimize, tr. v., to legitimate. — Formed with
suff. -ize fr. L. legitimus. See legitimate, adj.
Derivative: legitimiz-ation, n.

## leguan
leguan, п., a large lizard. — Formed by the
agglutination of the Sp. def. article la, fr. I'eguan,
Viguan, fr. Sp. Viguana, lit. 'the iguana'. See
iguana, guana. Sp. la derives fr. L. ilia, fern, of
Hie, 'that'; see ille. For the agglutination of the
article cp. lierre and words there referred to.

## legume
legume, п., 1) a plant of the group of the pulse
family; 2) pod. — F. legume, fr. L. legumen,
'pulse or other leguminous plants', lit. 'that
which is gathered', fr. legere, 'to gather, collect'.
See lecture.

## legumen
legumen, п., the same as legume.

## legumin
legumin, п., a proteid obtained from the seeds of
leguminous plants (biochem.) — Formed with
suff. -in fr. L. legumen, gen. legHminis, 'pulse'.
See legume.

## Leguminosae
Leguminosae, n. pi., the pulse family (bot.) —
ModL. See leguminous and adj. suff. -ose.

## leguminous
leguminous, adj., 1) pulselike; 2) pertaining to the
Leguminosae. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
legumen, 'pulse'. See legume.

## Leibnizian
Leibnizian, also Leibnitzian, adj., pertaining to
the German philosopher, Baron Gottfried Wil-
helm von Leibniz (less correctly spelled
Leibnitz) (1646-1716) or to his doctrines.

## Leibnizianism
Leibnizianism, п., the doctrines of Leibniz. — See
prec. word and -ism.

## Leicester
Leicester, п., a breed of sheep. — Named fr.
Leicester, a county in Leicestershire, England.

## Leila
Leila, Leilah, fem. PN. — Arab. Laylah, prop,
'dark as night', fr. laylJ1, 'night', which is rel. to
Heb. Idyil, laylah, Aram. Ula, lilya, Syr. lelya,
Ethiop. lelit, 'night', Akkad. lilatu, 'evening'.
Cp. Lilith.

## leio-
leio-, combining form meaning 'smooth'. — Gk.
λείο-, fr. λείος, 'smooth', which stands for *λεΐ-
Γος, and is cogn. with L. levis (for *lei-wis),
'smooth', fr. I.-E. base *(s)lei-, 'slime, slimy,
sticky, dauby, slippery'. See slime and cp. words
there referred to.

## leiomyoma
leiomyoma, п., a tumor of smooth muscles (med.)
— Medical L., coined fr. Gk. λείος, 'smooth',
μΰς, 'muscle', and suff. -ωμα. See leio-, myo-
and -oma.

## Leiophyllum
Leiophyllum, п., a genus of plants, the sand myrtle
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of leio- and φύλ-
λον, 'leaf. See phyllo-.

## leister
leister, п., a spear with prongs for striking fish. —
ON. Ijostr, 'spear with prongs', fr. Ijdsta, 'to
strike', which is of uncertain origin. It is
possibly cogn. with Russ. Iiista, 'cut, slice'.
Derivative: leister, tr. v.

## leisure
leisure, n. — ME. leyser, fr. OF. leisir (F. loisir),
'leisure, spare time', orig. an inf. meaning 'to be
permitted', fr. L. licere. See license. For the use
of the inf. as a noun and for the change of F.
suff. -ir to E. -ure cp. pleasure.
Derivatives: leisure, leisur-ed, leisure-less, leis-
ure-ly, adjs., leisure-li-ness, a.

## leitmotiv
leitmotiv, also leitmotif, п., a short musical phrase
recurring with a given personage or situation. —
G. Leitmotiv, [it. 'leading motive', fr. leiten, 'to
lead', and Motiv, 'motive'. See lead, 'to guide',
and motive, n.

## Leitnerla
Leitnerla, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the German naturalist Edward F.
Leitner. For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Leitneriaceae
Leitneriaceae, n. pi., the cork wood family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## leitneriaceous
leitneriaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## lekane
lekane, п., a large dish or bowl (Greek antiq.) —
Gk. λεκάνη, 'dish, pot, pan', fr. λέκος, of s.m.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:444 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 417 | LEPIDOPTERA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:444 COLUMN:1 -->
prob. meaning lit. 'something bent', and cogn.
with L. lanx, gen. lands, "plate, dish; scale of
weighing machine'. See balance and cp. words
there referred to.

## Lelia
Lelia, fem. PN. — L. Laelia, fem. of Laelius, name
of a Roman gens.

## leman
leman, п., sweetheart; usually in the senseof
paramour. — ME. leofman, le/man, lemman, fr.
OE. leof, 'dear', and man, 'man'. See lief and
man.

## lemma
lemma, п., an assumption taken for granted. —
L., fr. Gk. λήμμα, 'something received;
something taken for granted, assumption, premise',
rel. to εϊ-λημμαι, perf. pass, of λαμβάνω, Ί
take, grasp, seize; I receive', which derives partly
fr. I.-E. base *(s)lagw-, 'to take, seize', whence
also λάζομαι (for ·λάγ-^ομαι or *λάγγ-ιομαι),
Ί take, grasp, (see iatch), and partly fr. base
*labh-, 'to take, seize', whence Gk. λάφϋρον,
'spoil, prey', άμφί-λαφής, 'wide-spreading' (lit.
'taking in on both sides'), OI. labkate, lambhate,
rabhate, 'seizes', Lith. lobis, 'possession, riches',
labas, 'good'. Cp. analemma, dilemma, trilemma,
astrolabe, catalepsy, epilepsy, narcolepsy, nym-
pholepsy, orolepsis, syllable. For base "rabh-, as
a probable secondary form of base "labh-, see
rabid. For the ending of lemma see suff. -ma.

## lemming
lemming, п., a small, ratlike animal. — Norw., fr.
Lapp, luomek.

## Lemna
Lemna, п., a genus of plants, the duckweed (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. λέμνα, 'a kind of marsh
plant'.

## Lemnaceae
Lemnaceae, n. pi., the duckweed family (bot.) —
Formed fr. Lemna with suff. -aceae.

## lemnaceous
lemnaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## lemniscate
lemniscate, n. (geom.) — Late L. lemniscatus,
'adorned with ribbons', fr. lemniscus, 'ribbon',
fr. Gk. λημνίσκος, of s.m. See next word and
adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: lemniscat-ic, adj.

## lemniscus
lemniscus, п., 1) the form -=- used in annotations;
2) a band of fibers (anat.) — Late L. lemniscus,
fr. Gk. λημνίσκος, 'ribbon', which is prob. rel.
to Λήμνος, 'Lemnos' (name of an island in the
Aegean Sea), hence orig. meant 'of Lemnos'.
Cp. lemniscate.

## lemon
lemon, n. — ME. lymon, fr. MF. (= F.) limon, fr.
Turk, limon, fr. Pers. limun, 'limon, citron'. Cp.
lime, 'a fruit', limonene.
Derivatives: lemon, adj. and tr. v., lemonade
(q.v.), lemon-y, adj.

## lemonade
lemonade, n. — F. limona.de, fr. limon, 'lemon'.
See prec. word and -ade.

## lemur
lemur, п., any of a group of nocturnal mammals
related to the monkeys. — ModL., fr. L. lemu-
res, 'spirits of the dead, ghosts, specters', cogn.
withGk. λαμυρός, 'voracious, gluttonous',
Λάμια, 'spirits of the dead, ghosts, specters'. See
lamia and cp. words there referred to. The
animal was called lemur in allusion to its nocturnal
habits.

## lemures
lemures, n. pi., the spirits of the dead (.Roman
religion). — L. lemures. See prec. word,

## lemuroid
lemuroid, adj., resembling, or pertaining to, the
lemurs or the Lemuroidea. — A hybrid coined
fr. lemur and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## Lemuroidea
Lemuroidea, n. pi., a suborder of Primates, the
lemur (zool.) — ModL. See prec. word.

## Lena
Lena, fem. PN. — Shortened fr. Helena or Mag-
dalena.

## lend
lend, tr. and intr. v. — ME. lenen, fr. OE. Шпап,
'to lend, grant', fr. lien, 'loan', rel. to Du.
lenen, OHG. Ighanon, MHG. tehenen, G. lehnen,
'to lend'. See loan.
Derivative: lend-er, n.

## length
length, n. — ME. lengthe, fr. OE. lengdu, for
*langida, fr. OE. lang, 'long', rel. to ON. lengd,
Dan. Ixngde, Swed. langd, OFris. lengelhe,
MLG. lengede, Du. lengte, 'length'. See long
adj., and subst. suff. -th and cp. Lent.
Derivatives: length-en, tr. and intr. v., length-y,
adj., length-i-ly, adv., length-i-ness, n.

## leniency
leniency, lenience, n. — Formed from next word

## with suff. -cy
with suff. -cy, resp. -ce.

## lenient
lenient, adj., mild. — L. leniens, gen. -entis, pres.

## part
part, of lenlre, 'to soften, alleviate, mitigate,'
allay, soothe, calm', fr. Ignis, 'soft, smooth,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:444 COLUMN:2 -->
mild, gentle, calm', which prob. derives fr. I.-E.
base *ll(i)-, 'to leave behind, leave, yield',
whence also Lith. lenas, 'quiet, tranquil; tame;
slow'. Lett, lens, "slow, lazy', OSlav. /ели, 'lazy'.
Fr. base *lg(i)d-, a -(/-enlargement of base *le(i)-,
derive L. lassus (for *lad-to-s), 'faint, weary,
languid', OE. last, 'sluggish, slow', Isetan, 'to
leave behind'.See let, 'to leave', and cp. lassitude,
late. For the ending see suff. -ent.
Derivative: lenient-ly, adv.

## lenify
lenify, tr. v., to soften, mitigate. — Compounded
of L. Ignis (see lenient) and suff. -fy.

## lenitive
lenitive, adj., softening, mitigating. — ML. llni-
tivus, fr. L. Ignitus, pp. of Igntre, 'to soften'. See
lenient and -ive.
Derivatives: lenitive, п., lenitive-ly, adv., leni-
tive-ness, n.

## lenity
lenity, п., leniency. — OF. lenite, fr. L. Ignitatem,
ace. of lenitas, 'softness, smoothness, mildness',
fr. Ignis. See lenient and -ity.

## leno
leno, п., a soft cotton fabric. — Prob. fr. F. linon,
'lawn' (= a fine linen fabric), fr. tin, 'linen'. See
linen,

## lens
lens, п., 1) a piece of glass resembling a lentil; 2) a
lens-shaped transparent body in the eye (anat.)
— L. lens, gen. lentis, 'lentil'; see lentil.

## Lent
Lent, n. — Fr. earlier Lenten, fr. ME. lenten, lente,
fr. OE. lengten, lencten, 'spring, Lent', rel. to OS.
lentin, MLG., MDu. lenten, OHG. lengizin, len-
zin, fr. Teut. *langat-tin, lit. 'long days'. For the
first element of this compound see long, adj. The
second element appears also in Goth, -teins (in
the compound sin-teins, 'daily') and is cogn.
with OI. dlna-, OSlav. dint, Lith. diend, Lett.
diena, OPruss. deinam (ace), 'day', L. -dinae (in
пйп-dinae, 'the ninth day, the market day'); and
with L. digs, 'day', deu\, 'god'; see dies поп,
deity. Accordingly OE. lengten, etc., prop,
meant 'the season of long days'. Cp. MDu., Du.
lente, OHG. lenzo, MHG. lenze, G. Lenz,
'spring', which arose from short dialectal forms.

## lent
lent, past tense and pp. of lend.

## lentamente
lentamente, adv., slowly (musical direction). — It.,
'slowly', formed fr. lenta, fem. of lento, 'slow',
and adverbial suff. -mente, fr. L. mente, abl.
of mgns, 'mind'. See lento and mental, 'relating
to the mind', and cp. tardamente, tostamente.

## lentando
lentando, adv., getting slower (musical direction).
— It., gerund of lentare, 'to render slow,
slacken', fr. lento. See lento and cp. rallentando.

## Lenten
Lenten, adj. — Formed fr. Lent with suff. -en; not
to be confused with the noun Lenten, which
derives .fr. OE. lencten (see Lent).

## Lentibulariaceae
Lentibulariaceae, n. pi., the bladderwort family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Lentibularia, name of the
genus (synonymous with Utricularia), shortened
from L. *Lenti-tubularia (see haplology), which
is compounded of Igns, gen. lentis, 'lentil', and
tubulus, dimin. of tubus, 'tube'. See lentil, tubule
and the suffixes -ary and -aceae.

## lentibulariaceous
lentibulariaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## lenticel
lenticel, п., a lenticular spot in the bark of a tree
(bot.) — F. lenticelle, dimin. of L. lens, gen.

## lentis
lentis, 'lentil'. See lentil.

## lenticula
lenticula, п., 1) a freckle (med.); 2) a lenticel (bot.);
3) a small lens (optics). — L., 'a small lentil',

## dimin. of lens
dimin. of lens, gen. lentis. See ientil.
Derivatives: lenticul-ar, adj., lenticul-ate, adj.
and tr. v.

## lentiginous
lentiginous, adj., pertaining to lentigo; freckly. —

## L. lentiginosus
L. lentiginosus, fr. lentigo, gen. lentiginis, 'a
lentil-shaped spot'. See next word and -ous.

## lentigo
lentigo, п., freckles. — L. lentigo, lit. 'a lentil-

## shaped spot'
shaped spot', fr. lens, gen. lentis, 'lentil'. See

## lens
lens, lentil.

## lentil
lentil, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) lentille, fr. L.

## lenticula
lenticula, 'a small lentil', fr. Igns, gen. lentis,
'lentil'. Cp. Gk. λάθυρος, 'a kind of pulse, OSlav.

## lesta
lesta, 'lentil', OHG. linsi, MHG., G. linse, of

## s.m. Cp. lens
s.m. Cp. lens, Lentibularia, lenticel, lenticula,

## Lentigo
Lentigo, lentiginous. Cp. also Lathyrus.

## lentiscus
lentiscus, also lentisc, lentisk, п., the mastic tree;
mastic. — L. lentiscus, fr. lentus, 'flexible; slow'.
See next word.

## lentirude
lentirude, п., slowness (rare). — L. lentitudo, gen.

## -tadinis
-tadinis, 'slowness, sluggishness', fr. lentus,
'flexible, pliant; tenacious; slow,sluggish,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:444 COLUMN:3 -->
immovable', which is cogn. with OS. lilhi, OE. tide, 'soft,
mild, gentle'. See lithe and Lantana, lentamente,
lentando, lentiscus, Ieuto, relent. For the ending
see suff. -rude,

## lento
lento, adj., slow; adv., slowly (musicaldirection).
— It. lento, 'slow', fr. L. lentus. See lentitude.

## lentoid
lentoid, adj. lens-shaped. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. lens, gen. lentis, 'lentil', and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape". See lens and -oid.

## Leo
Leo, 1) masc. PN.; 2) name of a northern
constellation. — L. Leo, 'lion'. See lion and cp. Lean-
der, Leonard, Leonid, Leonine.

## Leonard
Leonard, masc. PN. — F. Lgonard, fr. OF.
Leonard, fr. G. Leonhard, fr. OHG. 'Lewenhart, lit.
'strong as a lion', compounded of lewo, lewo (fr.
L. leo), 'lion', and hart, 'hard'. See lion and hard
and cp. Leo.

## Leould
Leould, п., any of a shower of shooting stars. —
Formed fr. Leo with patronymic suff. -id; cp.
F. Lionides (pi.); so called because they appear
to radiate from the constellation Leo.

## Leonidas
Leonidas, masc. PN. — L. Lednidas, fr. Gk.
Λεωνίδας.

## leonine
leonine, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a lion.
— L. leoninus (whence also F. Uoniri), fr. leo,
gen. lednis, 'lion'. See lion and suff. -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## Leonine
Leonine, adj., pertaining to one called Leo; esp.
pertaining to one of the thirteen popes called
Leo. See Leo and prec. word.

## Leonora
Leonora, fem. PN. — It. Leonora, of the same
origin as Eleanor (q.v.)

## Leontodon
Leontodon, п., a genus of plants, the hawkbit
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'lion's tooth', fr. Gk. λέων,
gen. λέοντος, 'lion', and οδών, gen. οδόντος,
'tooth'. See lion and odonto- and cp. dandelion.

## Leonurus
Leonurus, п., a genus of plants, the motherwort
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'lion's tail', fr. Gk. λέων,
'lion', and ούρα, 'tail'. See Hon and uro-, 'tail-'.

## leopard
leopard, n. — ME. leopard, lepard, fr. OF. /eo-
pard(¥. leopard), fr. L. leopardus, lit. 'lion pard',
fr. leo, 'lion', and pardus, 'pard'. See lion and
pard.
Derivative: leopard-ess, n.

## leopardite
leopardite, п., a quartz porphyry spotted with
stains of manganese (mineral.) — Formed fr.
leopard with subst. suff. -ite; so called in allusion
to its spotted appearance.

## Leopold
Leopold, masc. PN. — F. Leopold, of Teut.
origin. Cp. OHG. Leutpald, Liutbalt, lit. 'bold in
the people', fr. leudi, 'people' and bald, 'bold'.
For the first element see liberal and cp. Lett,
liege, for the second see hard.

## Lepadidae
Lepadidae, n. pi., a family of birds, the goose
barnacles (ornithol.) — Formed with suff. -idae fr.
Gk. λεπάς, gen. λεπάδος. See Lepas.

## Lepas
Lepas, п., a genus of birds, the goose barnacle
(ornithol.) — L., lepas, 'limpet', fromGk. λεττάς,
gen. λεττάδος, of s.m., which is rel. to λέττας,
gen. λέπαδος, 'a bare rock, crag', and prob. also
to λέπειν, 'to peel'. See next word and lapidary,
adj.

## leper
leper, n. — The word orig. meant 'leprosy'; ME.,
fr. OF. lepre (F. lipre), fr. L. lepra, fr. Gk. λέττρ δ,
'leprosy', lit. 'that which scales off', fr. λεπρός,
'scaly', which is rel. to λεπίς, λέττος, "scale',
λέπειν, to strip off the rind or husks, peel, bark',
fr. I.-E. base *lep-, 'to peel, scale', whence
possibly also L. lepos (lepor), gen. -oris,
'pleasantness, charm', lepidus, 'pleasant, charming, neat',
and OE. liefer, 'rush, bulrush, thin plate of
metal',. OHG. leber, 'rush'; cp. Lepas, Lepi-
dium, lepido-, lepto-, lapidary, adj. Base *lep- is
rel. to base *leub(h)-, *leup-, 'to peel'; see leaf.
Cp. lobe. Gk λέπρα, 'leprosy', is prob. not cogn.
with OE. left, 'weak' (see left).
Derivative: leper-ed, adj.

## Lepidium
Lepidium, п., a genus of plants, the pepperwort
(bot.) — L., 'pepperwort', fr. Gk. λεττίδιον, fr.
λεττίς, 'scale', which is re], to λέπειν, 'to peel,
strip'. See leper and cp. lepido-. For the ending
see 1st suff. -ium.

## lepido-
lepido-, combining form meaning 'scale or flake'.
— Gk. λεπιδ(ο)-, stem of λεπίς, gen. λεπίδας,
'scale'. See leper and -id.

## Lepidoptera
Lepidoptera, n. pi., insects with four scaly wings.
— ModL., lit. 'scale-winged animals', coined by
the Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus (Karl

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:445 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LEPORID | 418 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:445 COLUMN:1 -->
von Linne) (1707-78) in 1735 1'r. Gk. λεπίς,
'scale', and πτερόν, 'wing'. See lepido- and
ptera-.
Derivatives: lepidopter-al, adj., tepidopter-an,
adj. and п., lepidoprer-ous, adj.

## leporid
leporid, п., one of the Leporidae; adj., pertaining
to the Leporidae. — See next word.

## Leporidae
Leporidae, n. pi., the family of the hares and
rabbits (zool.) — ModL., formed with surf, -idae fr.
L. lepus, gen. leporis, 'hare'. See next word.

## leporine
leporine, adj., pertaining to a hare. — Formed
with suff. -hie (representing L.-inus) fr. L. lepus,
gen. leporis, 'hare', which is of
non-Indo-European, prob. Iberian origin. Cp. leveret.

## lepra
lepra, п., leprosy. — L., fr. Gk. λέπρϊ, 'leprosy'.
See leper.

## leprechaun
leprechaun, п., a pygmy sprite {Irish folklore). —
Ir. lupracan, metathesized fr. Mir. luchrupan, lit.
'a very little body', fr. lu, 'little', and corpan,
dimin. of corp, 'body', fr. L. corpus. See corpus.

## leprology
leprology, п., the study of leprosy. — Coined fr.
Gk. λέπρα, 'leprosy', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See leper and -logy.

## leprosery
leprosery, п., leper hospital. — F, le'proserie, fr.
lipreux, 'leprous', fr. lepre. See leper and -ery.

## leprosy
leprosy, n. — Formed fr. leprous with suff. -y
(corresponding to L. -id).
Derivative: leprosi-ed, adj.

## leprous
leprous, adj. — ME. leprous, lepros, fr. Late L.
leprosus, fr. L. lepra. See leper and -ous.
Derivatives: leprosy (q.v.), leprotts-ly, adv., lep-
rous-ness, n.
-lepsia. — The same as -lepsy.

## -lepsy
-lepsy, combining form meaning 'a violent
attack' as in catalepsy, epilepsy (med.) — Medical
L. -lepsia, fr. Gk. -ληψίά, lit. 'a seizing', fr.
ληψ-, the future stem of λαμβάνειν, 'to take,
grasp, seize'. See lemma.

## lepto-
lepto-, before a vowel lept-, combining form
meaning'thin,small,fine, delicate'.—Gk. λεπτό-,
λεπτ-, fr. λεπτός, 'cleaned of the husks; thin,
fine, slender, delicate, slight, small; pleasant,
elegant', lit. 'peeled', verbal adj. of λέπειν, 'to
peel'. See leper.

## leptodactyl
leptodactyl, п., a bird or another animal having
slender toes. — Compounded of lepto- and Gk.
δάκτυλος, 'linger, toe'. See dactyl.

## leptomeninges
leptomeninges, n. pi., the pia mater and the
arachnoid (anat.) — Medical L., prop, 'the delicate
membranes', fr. lepto- and Gk. μήνιγγες, pi. of
μήνιγξ, 'membrane' (see meniiix). The term
μήνιγξ λεπτή was used orig. by Galen in its literal
sense to denote 'delicate membranes'.

## leptomeningitis
leptomeningitis, п., inflammation of the pia mater
and the arachnoid (med.) — Medical L., prop,
meaning 'inflammation of the delicate
membranes'. See prec. word and -Ms.

## lepton
lepton, п., 1) a small coin in ancient Greece; 2) the
smallest coin of modern Greece, equivalent to
1/100 of a drachma. — Gk. λεπτόν, neut. of
λεπτός, 'thin, small'. See lepto-.

## Leptothrix
Leptothrix, п., 1) a genus of filamentous
organisms first observed by Leeuwenhoek (bacteriol.)
— ModL., coined by the English physician Sir
William James Erasmus Wilson (1809-84) fr.
Gk. λεπτός, 'fine, delicate', and θρίξ, 'hair'.
See lepto- and -thrix.

## lerot
lerot, п., a kind of dormouse. — F. leroi, orig.
written leyrot, dimin. of loir, 'dormouse'. See loir.

## Lesbian
Lesbian, adj., 1) pertaining to Lesbos; 2) erotic;
п., 1) an inhabitant of Lesbos; 2) a homosexual
woman; so called from the homosexuality
attributed to Sappho, who lived in Lesbos. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Lesbius, fr. Gk.
Λεσβίος, fr. Λέσβος, name of the island now
called Mytilene.

## Lesbianism
Lesbianism, п., homosexuality between women.
— See prec. word and -ism.

## iese majesty
iese majesty, high treason. — F. lese-majeste, fr.
L. laesa majestas, lit. 'hurt majesty', fr. fern. pp.
of laedere, 'to hurt, injure', and majestas,
'majesty'. See lesion and maiesty.

## lesion
lesion, п., an injury. — ME. lesioun fr. MF. ( =
F.) lesion, fr. OF., fr. L. laesionem, ace. of laesio",
'injury, attack', fr. laesus, pp. of laedere, 'to
hurt, injure, damage, offend, insult, violate',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. collide,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:445 COLUMN:2 -->
collision, elide, elision.

## Lespedeza
Lespedeza, п., a genus of plants, the bush clover
(pot.) — ModL., named by the French botanist
and traveler Andre Michaux (1746-1802) after
Vincente Manuel de Cespedez (misspelled Les-
pedes), the Spanish governor of East Florida, a
contemporary of Michaux.

## Lesquerella
Lesquerella, п., a genus of plants, the bladderpod
(hot.) — ModL., named after the
Swiss-American bryologist and paleobotanist Leo Lesque·
reux (1085-89). For the ending see suff. -ella.

## less
less, adj. — ME. lesse, partly fr. OE. lis, 'less',
partly fr. OE. Ixssa, compar. of lzs; rel. to OS.,
OFris. les, 'less', and prob. cogn. with Lith.
liesas, 'thin'; used as compar. of little, but not
rel. to it. Cp. least, lest, uuless.
Derivatives: less, adv. and п., lessen, lesser
(qq. v.)

## -less
-less, suff. — ME. -less, -lesse, fr. OE. -leas, fr.
leas, 'devoid of; false, feigned; incorrect,
worthless', rel. to Du. -loos, G. -los, '-less', ON.
lauss, 'loose, free, vacant, dissolute' (whence E.
loose), MDu., Du. los, OS., OHG., MHG. Ids,
G. los, 'loose, free', Goth, laus, 'empty, vain'.
See lose,

## lessee
lessee, п., one to whom a lease is given.—ME., fr.
AF. lessee, 'one to whom a lease is given',
corresponding to OF. lesse, pp. of OF. laissier, les-
sier, lesser (F. laisser), 'to let, leave'. See lease
and -ее.

## lessen
lessen, intr. and tr. v. — Formed fr. less with
verbal suff. -en.

## lesser
lesser, adj. — A double compar.; formed fr. less
with compar. suff. -er.

## lesson
lesson, n. — ME. lessoun, fr. OF. (= F.) lecon, fr.
L. lictionem, ace. of lectio, 'a reading', fr. lictus,
pp. of legere, 'to read'. See lecture and cp.
lection, which is a doublet of lesson.
Derivative: lesson, tr. v.

## lessor
lessor, п., one who grants a lease. — See lessee
and agential suff. -or.

## lest
lest, conj. — ME. teste, fr. OE. pp lies pe, 'lest',
lit. 'by that the less that'; py is the instrumental
case of the def. article pe, 'the'; for/£j see less,
pe is the indeclinable relative (see the). After the
dropping of py, Ixs pe was contracted into lest
(in the sense of the rule, according to which p
after i becomes t).

## -testes
-testes, combining form meaning 'robber'; used
to form generic names (zool. and paleontol.)
— Fr. Ion., Att. Gk. ληστής, 'robber',
contraction of ληΐστής, of s.m., from the stem of ληίζε-
σθαι, 'to win, plunder', fr. ληίς, 'prey, booty',
which is rel. to Ion. ληΐη, Att. λεία, Dor. λαΐα,
of s.m., άπολαύειν, 'to enjoy', and prob. cogn.
with OI. lotam, lotram, 'booty', L. lucrum, 'gain'.
See lucre and cp. apolaustic.

## let
let, tr. v., to leave. — ME. Ixten, leten, fr. OE.
IStan, 'to leave behind, bequeath, leave', rel. to
OS. latan, ON. lata, Dan. lade, Swed. lata,
Norw. lata, OFris. leta, MLG., MDu., Du. la-
ten, OHG. Шззап, MHG. Шзеп, G. lassen, Goth.
titan, Ίο leave, let', fr. I.-E. base *le(i)d-, *led-,
'to leave behind, leave, yield', whence L. lassus
(for *lad-to-s), 'faint, weary, languid, exhausted',
Gk. ληδεΐν (Hesychius), 'to be weary', Alb. VcS,
Ί tire, weary', I'odem, Ί grow tired', Gheg l'q,
Tosk Γε, Ί let, leave', Lith. liidiiu, leisti, 'to let,
to let loose'. Cp. let, 'to hinder', late, leat, inlet,
outlet. Cp. also alas, lassitude. I.-E. *le(i)d- is a
-^-enlargement of base *li(i)-, whence L. /ели,
'smooth, soft, geritle'. See lenient.
Derivatives: let, п., a letting of a house etc.,
lett-er, n.

## let
let, tr. v., to hinder (archaic). — ME. letten, fr.
OE. tettan, 'to delay, hinder, procrastinate', rel.
to OS. lettian, 'to hinder', ON. letja, Ίο hold
back', OHG. lezzen, MHG. Jetzen, 'to stop,
check' (whence MHG., G. ver-letzen, 'to hurt,
injure'), Goth, latjan, 'to hinder, make late,
tarry', and to OE. Ш, 'sluggish, slow; late'. See
late and cp. let, 'to leave'.
Derivative: let, п., hindrance.

## -let
-let, dimin. suff. — Not a contraction of the two
dimin. suffixes -ef and -et (as most lexicographers
suggest), but the dimin. suff. -et, to which the
letter / was prefixed. The addition of the / is due
to a misdivision of words that had an organic /

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:445 COLUMN:3 -->
before the suff., as e.g. in circlet, islet, etc. (which
were misdivided into circ-let, is-let, etc.; in
reality they stand for circl-et, isl-et as diminutives
of circle, resp.'/i/e). From the generalization of
the ending -let in the above and similar words
with organic / arose the new dimin. suff/-/e<.

## lethal
lethal, adj., deadly, mortal. — L. litalis (less
correctly lethatis), 'deadly, fatal', fr. Шит (lethum),
'death', which is of uncertain etymology. The
spelling with -h- (in lethum, lethatis) is due to a
confusion with Gk. λήθη, 'forgetfulness,
oblivion'. For the ending see adj. suff. -al.

## lethargic
lethargic, lethargical, adj. — MF. (= F.) tithar-
gique, fr. Late L. lethargicus, fr. Gk. ληθαργικός,
'lethargic', fr. ληθαργία. See lethargy and -ic,
resp. also -al.

## lethargy
lethargy, п., morbid drowsiness; torpidity. — F.
Uthargie, fr. Late L. lithargia,ir. Gk.ληθαργία,
'forgetfulness', fr. λήθαργος, 'forgetful', which
is compounded of λήθη, 'forgetfulness', and
αργός, 'idle, lazy', contraction of *ά-ίεργός,
lit. 'not working'. See Lethe, argon and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## Lethe
Lethe, п., 1) a river of Hades, whose water when
drunk caused forgetfulness of the past; 2)
forgetfulness, oblivion. — L. Lithe, fr. Gk. λήθη,
'forgetfulness, oblivion', which is rel. to
λήθαργος, 'forgetful', λάθρη, 'secretly, by stealth',
λάθριος, 'stealthy', λανθάνειν, Ίο be hidden';
cogn. with L. latere, 'to lie hid'. See latent and
cp. lethargy, lanthanum, Alethea, alethiology.

## Lethean
Lethean, adj., pertaining to Lethe. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. LSthius, fr. Gk. Ληθαϊος,
'of Lethe' (fr. ληθαΐος, 'causing forgetfulness'),
fr. Λήθη, 'Lethe'. See prec. word.

## Letitia
Letitia, fem. PN. — Lit. 'gladness', fr. L. laetilia,
fr. laetus, 'glad', which is of uncertain
etymology. Cp. Lettlce.

## Leto
Leto, п., daughter of the Titan Coeus and mother
of Artemis and Apollo by Zeus (Greek mythol.)
— Gk, Λητώ, Dor. Λατώ, prob. fr. Lycian
Lada, a word lit. meaning 'wife, woman'. Cp.
Leda, Latona.

## Lett
Lett, п., an inhabitant of Latvia. — The word
orig. meant 'people'. It comes fr. OHG. liuti
(whence MHG. liute, G. Leute), 'people', which
is possibly cogn. with Gk. ελεύθερος, L. liber,
'free'. See liberal and cp. eleuthero-. Cp. also
Latvia. For sense development cp. Dutch.
Derivatives: Lett-ic, Lett-ish, adjs. and n.'s.

## letter
letter, п., graphic symbol, character. — ME.
lettre, fr. OF. (= F.) lettre, fr. L. littera, 'letter
of the alphabet' (in pi. 'epistle, document'),
which is of uncertain origin. Ernout and Meillet
(in DELL., p. 363) point out that since the Latin
alphabet was borrowed from the Greeks
(through the medium of the Etruscans), it is not
improbable that littera itself would be of Greek
origin. According to Breal (quoted by Ernout-
Meillet I.e.) littera would derive fr. Gk. διφθέρ α,
'tablet', a word glossed by Hesychius; for the
change of d- to /- see lachrymal. Cp. literal,
literary, literate, literature, alliteration, belles-lettres,
obliterate.
Derivatives: letter, tr. v., letter-ed, adj., letter-er,
п., tetter-ing, n.

## Lettlce
Lettlce, fem. PN. — A var. of Letitia (q.v.)

## Letto-
Letto-, combining form meaning 'Lettish and'.—
See Lett.

## lettuce
lettuce, n. — ME. letuse, fr. OF. laitues, pi. of
taitue, fr. L. lactuca, 'lettuce', fr. lac. gen. lactis,
'milk' (see lacteal, adj.); so called in allusion to
the milky juice of this plant. For the suff. -йса
cp. L. ir-йса, 'a kind of colewort', alb-ucus, 'the
plant asphodel'.

## leu
leu, also ley, п., monetary unit of Rumania. —
