Rum. leu (pi. lei), lit. 'lion', fr. L. led. See lion
and cp. iev.

## leuc-
leuc-, form of ieuco- before a vowel.

## leucaemia
leucaemia, leucemia, n. — See leukemia.

## leucaemic
leucaemic, leucemic, adj. — See leukemic.

## leucine
leucine, also leucin, п., a white amino acid (bio-
chem.) — Coined by the French chemist Henry
Braconnot (1781-1855) in 1820 fr. Gk. λευκός,
'white' (see Ieuco-), and chem. suff. -ine, -in; so
called by him because of its color.

## leucite
leucite, п., a crystalline mineral found in volcanic
lava (mineral.).— G. Leucit (now spelled Leuzit),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:446 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 419 | LEWISITE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:446 COLUMN:1 -->
coined by the German mineralogist Abraham
Gottlob Werner (1750-1817) in 1791 fr. Gk.
λευκός, 'white', and suff. -it, which goes back
to Gk. -ίτης (see leuco- and subst. suff. -ite); so
called by him in allusion to its glassy
appearance.

## leuco-
leuco-, before a vowel leuc-, combining form
meaning 'white'. —Gk. λευκό-, λευκ-, fr. λευκός,
'white', which is cogn. with Goth, liuhap, OE.
leoht, 'light'. See light, п., and cp. words there
referred to.

## ieucocyte
ieucocyte, п., a white blood corpuscle (anat.) —
Coined by Littre and Robin fr. Gk. λευκός,
'white', and κύτος, 'a hollow vessel'. See leuco-
and -cyte.
Derivative: leucocyt-ic, adj.

## leucocythemia
leucocythemia, leucocythaemia, п., leukemia. —
Compounded of leuco-, Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow
vessel', and αίμα, 'blood'. See -cyte and -emia
and cp. leukemia.

## leucocytosls
leucocytosls, п., an increase in the number of
white blood corpuscles (med.) — Medical L.,
coined by the German pathologist Rudolf Vir-
chow (1821-1902) about 1865 fr. leucocyte and
sufT. -osis.

## leucodenna
leucodenna, п., abnormal whiteness of the skin
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of ieuco-
and Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma.

## Leucojum
Leucojum, п., a genus of plants, the snowflake
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. λευκόϊον,'snowflake',
fr. λευκόν ϊον, lit. 'white violet'. See leuco- and
iolite.

## leucoma
leucoma, п., disease of the eye characterized by
white opacity of the cornea (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. λεύκωμα, 'whiteness, anything
whitened; a white spot in the eye; a white tablet for
notices', fr. λευκός. See leuco- and -oma.

## ieucomaine
ieucomaine, п., any basic substance normally
produced in the living animal body through
metabolism (biochem.) — Coined by the French
chemist Armand Gautier (1837-1920) fr. Gk.
λεύκωμα, 'anything whitened' (see prec. word),
on analogy of ptomaine. See William Bulloch,
The history of bacteriology, Oxford University
Press, 1938, p. 135.

## leucopenla
leucopenla, п., a diminution in the number of
while blood corpuscles (med.) — Compounded
οι leuco-, abbrev. of leucocyte, and Gk. πενία,
'poverty', fr. πένης, gen. πένητος, 'poor',
which stands in gradational relationship to
πόνος, 'toil, labor', πονεΐν, 'to toil, work hard',
πονηρός, 'painful, distressed; bad, worthless'.
Cp. Ponera and the second element in geoponic,
Melipona.

## leucoplakia
leucoplakia, п., a disease characterized by the
formation of white patches on a surface (med.) —
Medical L., coined fr. leuco-, Gk. πλάξ,
'anything flat' (see placenta), and suff. -ia;
introduced by Schwimmer as a term for white
patches seen on the tongue, lips or cheeks.

## leucoplast
leucoplast, п., one of the colorless bodies found
in the cytoplasm of plants (hot.) —
Compounded of leuco- and Gk. -πλαστός, fr. πλαστός,
'molded, formed', verbal adj. of πλάσσειν. See
-plast.

## leucorrhea
leucorrhea, leucorrhoea, п., white discharge from
the vagina (med.) — Medical L., compounded
of leuco- and Gk. -ρροίϊ, 'a flow, flowing',
from the stem of £etv, 'to flow'. See -rrhea.

## Leucothoe
Leucothoe, п., the daughter of Orchamus, king of
Babylon; said to have been changed by Apollo
into a shrub (Greek and Roman mythol.) — L.

## Leucothoe
Leucothoe, п., a genus of plants, the fetter bush
(bot.) — ModL., fr. prec. word.

## leukemia
leukemia, leukaemia, n. (med.) — Medical L., lit.
'whitebloodedness', fr. λευκός, 'white', and
αίμα, 'blood'. See leuco- and -emia.

## lev
lev, п., the monetary unit of Bulgaria. — Bulg.
ley, 'lion', fr. OSlav. /ivtf, which prob. derives
through the medium of Goth. *liwa- fr. Gk.
λέων. See lion and cp. leu.

## Levana
Levana, п., the goddess of childbirth in Roman
mythol. — L. Levana, fr. levare, 'to lift up, raise'
(see lever); so called because she was supposed
to raise newborn infants from the ground.

## Levant
Levant, п., the countries of the Mediterranean
East of Italy. — ME. levaunt, orig. 'the East', fr.
F. levant, lit. 'the rising (of the sun'), fr. (se)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:446 COLUMN:2 -->
levant, pres. part, of (se) lever, 'to rise', fr. lever,
'to raise', fr. L. levare, 'to lift up, raise'. See
lever and -ant. For sense development cp. Bac-
trian.

## levant
levant, intr. v., to run away without paying one's
gambling debts. — Fr. Sp. levantar el campo, 'to
break up camp', fr. L. levans, gen. levantis, pres.
part, of levSre, 'to lift up. raise'. See prec. word.

## levanter
levanter, п., one who levants. — Formed fr.
levant, 'to run away', with agential suff. -er.

## levanter
levanter, п., a strong eastern wind blowing in the
Mediterranean. — Formed fr. Levant with
agential suff. -er.

## Levantine
Levantine, adj., related to, or connected with, the
Levant. — Formed fr. Levant with adj. suff. -ine.
Derivative: Levantine, п., a native of the Levant.

## levator
levator, п., a muscle serving to raise a part of the
body (anat.) — Medical L. levator, lit. 'a lifter',
fr. L. levatus, pp. of levare. See lever and
agential suff. -or.

## levee
levee, п., a reception held by a sovereign or his
representative. — F. leve, for lever, 'a rising',
prop, the inf. lever, 'to raise', se lever, 'to rise',
used as a noun. See lever and cp. Levant. The
word levee was applied orig. to the morning
reception held by the French king immediately
after rising from bed.

## levee
levee, п., a natural or artificial embankment. —
F. levee, 'raising, lifting; embankment', prop,
fern. pp. of lever, 'to raise', used as a noun. See
lever and cp. prec. word.

## level
level, n. — ME. livel, level, fr. OF. live!, level
(whence, with dissimilation, F. niveau), fr. VL.
'llbellus, fr. L. h'bella, dimin. of libra, 'pound,
measure for liquids, balance, level'; cp. It. II-
vello, OProvenc. livel (whence Sp. nivel), 'level',
which all derive fr. VL. 'llbellus. See libra and
cp. deliberate.
Derivatives: level, adj., adv. and tr. v., level(l)-er,
п., Ievel([)-ing, п., level-ness, n.

## lever
lever, n. — ME. levere, levour, fr. OF. leveor (F.
leveur), lit. 'a lifter', fr. lever, 'to lift, raise', fr. L.
levare, of s.m., fr. levis, 'light in weight', which
stands for 'legwis or 'lexwis, fr. I.-E. base
*le(n)gwh-, 'light, easy, agile, nimble', whence
also Ol. laghtih, Vedic raghuh, 'quick; small',
Toch. B. lykacke, A. lykaly, 'fine, mince', Gk.
έλαχύς (prob. for */ ghus), 'small', ελαφρός
(prob. for *lngwhros), 'light', OSlav. liguku,
'light', Lith. lengvas, lengvus, Lett, liegs, 'light',
Olr. laigiu (compar.), 'smaller; worse', Goth.
leihts, OE. leoht, 'light', OE. lungun, 'the lungs',
lit. 'the light organs'. See light, adj., and cp.
lights, lung. Cp. also Levant, levator, levee (in
both senses), levitate, levity, levy, v., alevin,
alleviate, elevate, elevator, leaven, legerdemain,
Levana, relief, relieve, and the second element in
cantilever, champleve, pontlevis.
Derivatives: lever, tr. v., lever-age, n.

## leveret
leveret, п., a hare in its first year. — MF.
*levrete, *levrette (F. levrette), dimin. of levre
(F. lievre), 'hare', fr. OF., fr. L. leporem, ace. of
lepus, 'hare'. See leporine and -et.

## Levi
Levi, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, son of Jacob
by Leah. — Heb. Lewi, lit. 'joining', from the
stem of Heb. lawah, 'he joined', rel. to Aram.-
Syr. lewS, 'he accompanied', Mishnaic Heb.
lewtyyd1', ltwayah, 'accompaniment, escort,
caravan'. Cp. Levite, Leviticus.

## leviable
leviable, adj. — Formed with suff. -able fr. levy,
v. See levy, n.

## Leviathan
Leviathan, n. — Late L. Leviathan, fr. Heb. liwy-
athan, 'serpent, dragon, leviathan', prop,
'tortuous', which is rel. to liwya , 'wreath', fr. base
l-w-h, 'to wind, turn, twist', whence also Arab.
lawa, 'the wound, turned, twisted', Akkad. lamu,
'to surround, encircle'.

## levigate
levigate, tr. v., to grind to a fine powder. — L.
levigatus, pp. of levigdre, 'to make smooth; to
pulverize', compounded of levis, 'smooth', and
agere, 'to drive, lead, do, make'. The first
element is cogn. with Gk. λείος, 'smooth, flat'; see
leio-. For the second element see agent, adj.,
and cp. the second element in castigate and
in words there referred to.

## levigation
levigation, n. — L. levigatio, gen. -dnis, 'a
smoothing; a pulverizing', fr. levigatus, pp. of levigdre.
See prec. word and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:446 COLUMN:3 -->

## levin
levin, п., lightning. — ME. levene, leven, levin
(revived by Walter Scott), rel. to ON. lyvna, OE.
leoma (whence obsol. E. learn, 'flash'), OS. Homo,
'brightness, .light', Goth, lauhmuni, 'lightning',
and cogn. with L. lumen, 'light', fr. I.-E. base
*leuq-, 'to shine', whence also L. lucere, 'to be
light, to shine', OE. leoht, 'light'. See light,
'brightness'.

## levirate
levirate, п., the ancient Jewish law according to
which a man was obligated to marry his
brother's widow if his brother had died childless. —
Formed with subst. suff. -ate fr. L. levir,
'husband's brother, brother-in-law', which stands
for I.-E. *daiwe~r and is cogn. with OI. devar-,
Homeric Gk. δάήρ (for *δαι5ήρ), Arm. laigr,
Russ.-Church Slav, deveri, Lith. dieveris, OE.
tacor, OHG. zeihhur, 'brother-in-law'. For the
change of initial d- to /- see lachrymal.

## Levisticum
Levisticum, п., a genus of plants, the lovage (bot.)
— VL. levisticum, fr. L. ligusticum, lit.
'belonging to Liguria'. See lovage and cp. words there
referred to.

## levitate
levitate, intr. v., to tend to rise, to rise; tr. v., to
raise. — Formed on analogy of gravitate fr. L.
levitas. See levity and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: levitat-ion, n.

## Levite
Levite, п., any member of the tribe of Levi —
ME., fr. Late L. Levites, fr. Gk. Λευίτης, fr.
Heb. Lewi, 'Levi, a Levite'. See Levi and subst.
suff. -ite.
Derivatives: Levit-ic, Levit-ic-al (qq. v.).

## Levitical
Levitical, also Levitic, adj. — Late L. Leviticus,
fr. Gk. Λευιτικός, 'pertaining to a Levite or
Levites', fr. Λευΐτης. See prec. word and -ic,
resp. also -al.

## Leviticus
Leviticus, п., the third book of the Pentateuch. —
Late L. Leviticus (scil. liber), 'Book of the
Levites', fr. Gk. τό Λευϊτικόν βιβλίον, of s.m.,
prop, the part of the Pentateuch dealing with
the function of the priests who were of the tribe
of Levi. Accordingly the name τό Λευΐτικον
βιβλίον corresponds to the orig. Hebrew name
of the Book, i.e. Torath Kohanim lit. 'the Law
of the Priests'. Gk. Λευΐτικόν is neut. of Λευΐ-
τικός. See prec. word.

## levity
levity, п., lightness; frivolity. — OF. levite, fr. L.
levitatem, ace. of levitas, 'lightness; fickleness,
inconstancy', fr. levis, 'light in weight'. See
lever and -ity.

## levo-
levo-, laevo-, combining form meaning 'left, to
the left' — L. laevus, 'left', cognate with Gk.
λαιός (for *λαίίός), OSlav. leva, 'left'. Cp. le-
vulose.

## levorotatory
levorotatory, laevorotatory, adj., turning the
plane of polarization to the left. —
Compounded of levo- and rotatory.

## levulose
levulose, laevulose, п., fruit sugar (chem.) —
Coined by the French chemist Pierre-Eugene-
Marcelin Berthelot (1827-1907) fr. L. laevus,
'left' (see levo-), dimin. suff. -ule and subst. suff.
-ose; so called by him because it is levo-rotatory
(q.v.) Cp. dextrose.

## levy
levy, п., the act of raising or collecting. — F.
levee, 'a raising, lifting, levying', prop. fern. pp. of
lever, 'to raise', used as a noun. See lever and cp.
levee (in both senses).
Derivative: levy, tr. and intr. v.

## levynite
levynite, п., acalcium aluminum silicate (mineral)
— Named after the French mineralogist
Armand Levy (died in 1841).

## lew
lew, adj., lukewarm (dial. E.) — ME. lew, lewe,
fr. OE. hleow, 'warm', rel. to hleo, 'shelter'. See
lee.

## lewd
lewd, adj., 1) ignorant {obsol.); 2) indecent; 3)
base. — ME. lewed, 'lay, ignorant', fr. OE. lx-
wede, 'lay, layman', of uncertain origin; perhaps
borrowed fr. L. laicus, fr. Gk. λαϊκός. See lay,
'pertaining to the laity'.
Derivatives: lewd-ly, adv., lewd-ness, n.

## Lewis
Lewis, masc. PN. — Anglicized form of Louis
(q.v.)

## lewis
lewis, п., a dovetailed tenon. — Prob. from the
PN. Lewis.

## lewis
lewis, also Lewis gun. — Named after its inventor
Isaac Newton Lewis (1858-1931).

## lewisite
lewisite, п., a calcium titano-antimonate
(mineral.) — Named after the English mineralogist
William J. Lewis (1847-1926). For the ending

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:447 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LEWISITE | 420 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:447 COLUMN:1 -->
see subst. suff. -ite.

## lewisite
lewisite, п., a vesicant used in chemical warfare.
— Named after the American chemist Winford
Lee Lewis (1878-1943). For the ending see subst.
siitf. -ite.

## lex
lex, п., law. — L. lex, gen. legis. See legal.

## lexical
lexical, also iexic, adj. — See lexicon and adj.
suff. -al.

## lexico-
lexico-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
dictionaries, lexical'. — See lexicon.

## lexicographer
lexicographer, п., writer of a dictionary. —
Formed with agential suff. -er fr. Gk. λεξικογράφος,
'lexicographer', which is compounded of λεξικόν
(see lexico-) and -γράφος, 'writer', fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See -graph.

## lexicography
lexicography, п., the act or process of making a
dictionary. — Formed fr. Gk. λεξικογράφος,
'lexicographer' (see prec. word), with suff. -y
(representing Gk. -ίϊ).
Derivatives: lexicograph-ic, lexicograph-ic-al,
adjs., lexicograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## lexicology
lexicology, п., the study of words. —
Compounded of lexico- and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: lexicolog-ic, lexicolog-ic-al, adjs.,
lexicolog-ist, n.

## lexicon
lexicon, п., a dictionary. — Gk. λεξικόν (scil.
βιβλίονί, 'dictionary', lit. 'book of words',
neut. of λεξικός, 'pertaining to words', fr. λέξις,
'word, phrase, speech, diction', from the stem
of λέγειν, 'to speak', which is cogn. with L.
legere, 'to read'. See lecture and cp. alexia.

## lexigraphy
lexigraphy, п., mode of writing in which each
character represents a word. — Compounded of
Gk. λέξις, 'word', and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See lexicon and -graphy.

## ley
ley, n. —See leu.

## Leyden jar
Leyden jar, a jar used for accumulating and
storing static electricity. — Named after Leyden
(now spelled Leiden) in Holland, because it was
first described by the physicist Pieter van Mus-
schenbroek of Leyden (1692-1761) in 1746.

## li
li, п., a Chinese measure of distance
corresponding to about one third of a mile. — Chin.

## liable
liable, adj. — Fr. F. Her, 'to bind', fr. OF., fr. L.
ligare. See ligament and -able.
Derivatives: liabil-ily, п., НаЫе-ness, n.

## liaison
liaison, п., relation, link. — F„ fr. MF., fr. Late
L. Hgatidnem, ace. of ligatid, 'a binding', fr. L.
ligatus, pp. of ligare, 'to bind'. Cp. OProvenc.
liazon, which is of the same origin and meaning,
and see ligament.

## liana
liana, п., any climbing woody tropical plant. —
F. liane, fr. dial. F. Hone, Home, fr. F. viorne, fr.
L. viburna, pi. of viburnum, 'wayfaring-tree* (in
VL. the L. neut. pi. became fem. sing.); initial
//- for vi- is due to the influence of L. ligare, 'to
bind'. See Viburnum.

## liar
liar, n. — ME. Her, liar, fr. OE. leogere, fr. leogan,
'to lie'. See lie, 'to tell an untruth'.

## Lias
Lias, п., the oldest division of the European
Jurassic (geot.) — OF. Hois (F. liais), 'calcareous
limestone'; of uncertain origin. F. lias, 'lias',
has been reborrowed from English.

## Hassle
Hassle, adj., pertaining to Lias. — Formed fr.
Lias with suff. -ic.

## Liatris
Liatris, п., a genus of plants, the button snake-
root (bot.) — ModL., of uncertain origin.

## libation
libation, п., the pouring out of a wine in honor of
a deity. — L. libstio, gen. -onis, 'a drink offering',
fr. libatus, pp. of llbare, 'to pour out, make a
libation', cogn. with Gk. λείβειν, 'to pour, pour
forth, make a libation', λοιβή, 'drink offering',
λίψ, gen. λιβός (masc), 'tbe southwest wind',
*λίψ, gen. λιβός (fem.), 'drop, stream, libation',
fr. I.-E. *(j)/etf>-, 'to pour, drop', enlargement
of base *lei-, 'to pour, drop', whence Lith. lieju,
Ileli, 'to pour', Ijlja, lyti, 'to rain', lytus, 'rain'.
Cp. also with—(-formative element—Goth.
leipu, OE. lip, 'strong drink'. For the ending
of libation see -ation. Cp. next word. Cp. also
littoral, Lithuanian.

## Ubeccio
Ubeccio, п., the southwest wind. — It., fr. Gk.
λίψ, gen. λιβός {masc), 'the southwest wind'.
See prec. word.

## libel
libel, n. — ME., fr. OF. libel (F. libelle), it. L.
libellus, 'a little book, pamphlet, lampoon', di-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:447 COLUMN:2 -->
min. of liber, 'book'. See library.
Derivatives: libel(i)-anl, п., Hbel(T)-ee, п.,
libeller, п., libel(f)-ous, adj., libel(l)-ous-ly, adv.

## liberal
liberal, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) liberal, fr. L.
liberalis, 'pertainng to freedom, befitting a free
man, honorable, noble, gracious, generous', fr.
liber, 'free', fr. I.-E. base *leudhero-s, whence
also Gk. ελεύθερος, 'free'. This base prob.
meant orig. 'belonging to the people', hence 'of
legal descent', and derives fr. base "leudho-,
"leudhi-, 'people', whence also OSlav. ljudu,
'people, nation', ljudije, 'people', ORuss. ljudini,
'free men', Lith. liaudis, 'people, nation', Lett.
laudis, 'men', OPruss. ludis, 'man', ON. lydr,
Ijodr, 'people, nation', OE. leod, pi. liede, liode,
ME. lede, OS. Hud, OFris. liod(e), MDu. liede,
OHG. liuli, MHG. liute, G. Leute, WGoth.
leodes, 'people'. I.-E. base "-leudho-, "leudhi-,
'people', is a derivative of base "leudh-, 'to grow,
rise'. This latter appears in OI. rSdhali, 'grows,
rises, climbs', Avestic raoda-, 'growth,
authority', Toch. A lut-k, 'to cause to grow'. Cp.
liberate, liberty, liege, livery, 'allowance of food',
deliver, eleuthero-. Cp. also Lett. For the ending
see adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: liberal, п., liberal-ly, adv., the
hybrids liberal-ism, п., Hberal-ist, п., liberal-ist-ic,
adj., liberal-ize, tr. and intr. v., liberal-iz-aiion,
п., liberal-iz-er, п., and liberality, liberty,
libertine (qq. v.)

## liberality
liberality, n. — ME. liberalite, fr. OF. (= F.)
Hberalite,'fr. L. liberalitatem, ace. of liberdlitds,
'way of thinking or acting befitting a freeman',
fr. liberalis. See prec. word and -i(y.

## liberate
liberate, tr. v. — L. liberatus, pp. of liberare, 'to
set free', fr. liber, 'free'. See liberal and verbal
surf. -ate.

## liberation
liberation, n. — ME. liberacion, fr. L. liberutid-
nem, ace. of liberatio, 'a setting or becoming
free', fr. liberatus, pp. of liberare, fr. liber. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: liberation-ism, п., liberation-ist, n.

## liberator
liberator, n. — L. liberator, 'one who sets free, a
deliverer', fr. liberatus, pp. of liberare. See
liberate and agential suff. -or.

## libertarian
libertarian, adj., believing in the doctrine of the
freedom of the will. — Formed fr. liberty with
suff. -arian.
Derivatives: libertarian, a., libertarian-ism, n.

## liberticide
liberticide, п., a destroyer of liberty. — Formed
from L. libertas, 'liberty', and -cida, 'killer', fr.
caedere, 'to kill*. See liberty and -cide, 'killer'.
Derivative: liberticid-al, adj.

## liberticide
liberticide, п., destruction of liberty. — Formed
fr. L. libertas, 'liberty', and -cidium, 'killing', fr.
caedere, 'to kill'. See liberty and -cide, 'killing'.
Derivative: liberticid-al, adj.

## libertine
libertine, п., a licentious man. — Fr. L. libertlnus,
'a freedman', fr. libertus, 'a manumitted slave, a
freedman', fr. liber. See liberal and -ine
(representing L. -inus).
Derivatives: libertin-age, п., liber tin-ism, n.

## liberty
liberty, n. — ME. liberie, fr. MF. (= F.)
liberie, fr. L. libertatem, ace. of libertas, 'freedom,
condition of a free man', fr. liber. See liberal and
-ty.

## libidinous
libidinous, adj., lustful; lascivious. — ME. lyby-
dynous, fr. OF. libidineus (F. libidineux), fr. L.
libidinosus, 'full of desire, lustful', fr. libido, gen.
libidinis, 'pleasure, desire, sensual passion, lust',
fr. libet, earlier lubet, 'it pleases, it is agreeable',
which is cogn. with OI. lubhyati, 'desires', OE.
lufu, 'love'. See love, п., and -ous and cp. quod-
libet. Cp. also quillet.
Derivatives: Hbidinous-ly, adv., libidinous-ness, n.

## libido
libido, п., the sexual instinct. — L. libido. See
prec. word.

## libra
libra, п., a pound. — L. libra, 'balance; Roman
pound', fr. earlier "libra, whence also Gk. λίτρα
(Dor. λίτρα is a later form), of s.m. Cp. librate,
deliberate, equilibrium. Cp. also litra, litre, livre.
Derivative: libr-al, adj.

## library
library, n. — ME. librarie, fr. OF. librairie,
'library' (F. 'bookshop'), fr. livraire, since the 13th
cent. Hbraire, 'copyist' (F. 'bookseller'), fr. L.
librarius, 'copyist, bookseller', fr. liber, gen.
Hbri, 'book', orig. 'the inner bark of a tree',
whence 'the text written on this', 'collection of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:447 COLUMN:3 -->
leaves for writing', and finally 'book'. L. liber
prob. stands for "tuber and is a derivative of
I.-E. base *leu-b(h)-, "leu-p-, 'to strip, to peel'.
See leaf and subst. suff. -ary and cp. leper, lepi-
do-. Cp. also libel, libretto, ex-libris.
Derivatives: Hbrari-an, п., librari-an-ess, п.,
librari-an-ship, n.

## librate
librate, п., land worth a pound a year (English
hist.) — ML. librata (scil. terra), fr. L. libra. See
libra and adj. suff. -ate.

## librate
librate, intr. v., to be balanced or poised — L.
libratus, pp. of librare, 'to balance, level, make
even', fr. libra, 'balance; pound'. See libra and
verbal suff. -ate.

## libration
libration, п., a librating. — L. libratio, gen. -onis,
'a balancing, leveling', fr. libratus, pp. of librare.
See librate, v., and suff. -ion.

## librettist
librettist, п., the writer of the libretto of an opera.
— A hybrid coined fr. libretto, and -ist, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## libretto
libretto, п., the words of an opera. — It., 'a little
book', dimin. of libro, 'book', fr. L. liber. See
library,

## license
license, licence, n. — ME. licence, fr. OF. (= F.),
fr. L. licentia, 'freedom, liberty, license', fr. li-
cens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of licere, 'to be
lawful, be permitted', which is prob. cogn. with
Lett. ITkstu, likstu, Ί come to terms'. Cp. licit,
illicit, scilicet, videlicet, leisure.
Derivatives: license, licence, tr. v., licens-ed, H-
cenc-ed, adj., Hcens-ee, licenc-ee, п., Hcens-er,
licenc-er, n.

## licentiate
licentiate, п., a person licensed to exercise a
profession. — ML. Hcentiatus, pp. of licentiare, 'to
permit, license', fr. L. licentia. See prec. word
and -ous.

## licentious
licentious, adj., 1) lawless; 2) lewd. — L. НсеМщ-
sus, 'unrestrained, wanton, licentious', fr. licen-
tua. See license and -ous.
Derivatives: licentious-ly, adv., licentious-ness,
n.

## lich
lich, lych, п., body; corpse (obsol. and dial.
English). — ME. liche, lyche, fr. OE. lie, 'body'. See

## lichen
lichen, n. — L. lichen, fr. Gk. λειχήν, 'lichen',
fr. λείχειν, 'to lick', hence lit. meaning 'the
licker'. See lick.
Derivatives: lichen, tr. v., lichen-ed, Hchen-ic,
lichen-oid, lichen-ose, lichen-ous, adjs., licheni-

## fication
fication, n.

## lichenology
lichenology, adj., the study of lichens. —
Compounded of Gk. λειχήν (see prec. word) and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: lichenolog-ic, lichenolog-ic-al, adjs.,
lichenolog-ist, n.

## lich-gate
lich-gate, lych-gate, п., gate to a churchyard
under which a bier is placed to await the coming of
the clergyman. — Lit. 'body gate'. See lich.

## Uchi
Uchi, n. — A var. spelling of litchi.

## licit
licit, adj., permitted, lawful. — F. licite, fr. L.
licitus, 'permitted, allowed, lawful', pp. of
licere. See license and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: licit-ly, adv., licit-ness, n.

## lick
lick, tr. and intr. v. — ME. licken, fr. OE. liccian,
rel. to OS. likkon, Du. likken, OHG. lecchdn,
MHG., G. lecken, 'to lick', Goth. Ы-laigon, 'to

OI. ledhi, redhi, also (a later form) lihati, 'he

λείχειν, 'to lick',λειχήν, 'lichen'fjit. 'licker'), λιχνεύ-
ειν, ito lick at', λιχανός (scil. δάκτυλος},

Heiiu, lilzti, OSlav. lizo, lizati, 'to lick', Olr. H-
gim, Ί lick', MBret. leal, Ίο lick', W. Ilyfu, llyv,

Derivatives: lick, п., lick-ing, n.

## lickerish
lickerish,liquorish, adj., 1) eager; 2) lecherous. —
Formed, with change of suff. -ous to -ish, fr.
ME. likerous, 'lecherous', fr. AF. *likerous,

which corresponds to OF. licherous, lecherous.

Derivatives: lickerish-ly, adv., Hckerish-ness, n.

## licorice
licorice, liquorice, п., 1) a plant of the pea family;

## lictor

## lid

hilt, lit, MHG. lit, 'lid, cover*, MHG. ougelit,
G. Augenlid, 'eyelid*; prob. fr. I.-E. base "klei-,

## lie
lie, intr. v., to tell an untruth. — ME. ligen, leyen,

OFris. liaga, Du. liegen, OS., OHG. liogan,
MHG., G. tOgen, Goth, liugan, 'to lie',andcogn.
with OSlav. Ιϋϊρ, lugati, 'to lie', luia, 'a lie'. Cp.
next word and the second element in warlock,

## lie
lie, п., an untruth. — ME. lige, leye, lie, fr. OE.
lyge, fr. leogan, 'to lie', rel. to ON. lygi, Dan.
tegn, Swed. logn, OS., OHG. lugina, OFris.
leyne, Du. leugen, MHG. lugen(e), lugen(e), G.
Luge, Goth. Hugn, 'a lie'. See prec. word.

## lie
lie, intr. v., to recline. — ME. liggen, lien, fr. OE.

ligga, Dan. ligge, OFris. lidzia, lidza, MDu.
ligghen, Du. liggen, OHG., MHG. ligen, licken,

σθαι, 'to lie down', λέχος, 'couch, bed, marriage

'couch, bed', L. lectus, 'bed', OSlav. lego, lezti,

## liebigite
liebigite, п., a hydrous uranium calcium

## lied

## lief
lief, adj. (archaic), 1) dear, beloved; 2) glad. —
ME. lee/, lef, lif, fr. OE. liof, 'dear, beloved', rel.
to OS. liof, ON. ljufr, OFris. liaf, Du. lief, OHG.
Hob, MHG. Hep, G. lieb, Goth, liufs, 'dear,
beloved', and to OE. /и/и, 'love'. See love, п., and

believe. Cp. also the first element in leman, livelong.
Derivative: lief, adv. (rare).

## liege
liege, adj. land n. — ME. lege, lige, liege, fr. OF.
//ege,'liege; free', fr. LateL.
*liticus(corresponding to Late L. laeticus), 'belonging to a serf,
formed with suff. -icus (see -ic) fr. litus, letus,

OFris. lethar, 'freedmen'; prob. nbt related to

## G. ledig
G. ledig, 'free'.

## lien
lien, п., the right to hold the property of another
till a debt is paid. — F., fr. L. ligamen, 'band,

tie', fr. ligare, 'to bind, tie'. See ligament.

## lien
lien, obsol. pp. of lie, 'to recline'. — ME. lien,

## lienal
lienal, adj., pertaining to the spleen (anal.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. lien, 'the spleen'.

## lienculus
lienculus, п., an accessory spleen (anat.) —
ModL., dimin. of L. lien, 'spleen'. See prec.

## lienee
lienee, п., owner of a property that is subject to a

## lieultis
lieultis, п., inflammation of the spleen (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. lien, 'the

## lleno-
lleno-, combining form denoting the spleen (anat.)·
— Fr. L. Hen, 'spleen'. See spleen.

## lienor
lienor, п., the holder of a lien (law). — Formed
from the noun lien with agential suff. -or.

## llenteric
llenteric, adj., pertaining to lientery. — Either

of F. Henterique fr. Gk. λειεντερικος, fr. λειεντε
ρία. See next word and -ic.

## lientery
lientery, п., a form of diarrhea (med.) — Either
directly fr. ML. lienteria or through the medium
of F. Henterie, fr. Gk. λειεντερία, which is
compounded of λείος, 'smooth', and έντερον,

## Heme
Heme, п., a short connecting rib in Gothic

## lieu
lieu, п., place. — ME. Hue (in in Hue of), fr. OF.
(= F.) lieu, fr. L. locum, ace. of locus, 'place'.

## lieutenancy
lieutenancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## lieutenant
lieutenant, n. — Lit., 'holding the place of
somebody'. See Ueu and tenant. The British
pronunciation of the word a» 'leftenant' is due to a

represented originally by one and the same letter (v)].

lieve. — The same as lief.

## life
life, n. — ME. lif, fr. OE. lif, rel. to ON. lif, 'life,
body', Du. Hjf, 'body', OHG. /;*, 'life', MHG.
lip, lib, 'life, body', G. Leib, 'body', prop,

## lifer
lifer, п., one sentenced to imprisonment for
life. — Formed fr. life with agential suff.
-er.

## lift
lift, lr. and intr. v. — ME. liften, leften, fr. ON.

G. luft, Goth, luftus, 'air', and lit. mean 'to

## ligament
ligament, п., 1) a tie, band; 2) a band of tissue
(anat.) — L. ligamentum, 'band, bandage', fr.
ligare, 'to bind, tie*, prob. cogn. with Alb. f i#,
Ί bind', Vide Vide, 'band, fetter', MLG. Ilk,
'band', ON. Ilk, 'boltrope', MHG. geleich,

Derivatives: ligament-al, ligament-ary,

## llgate
llgate, tr. v., to bandage. — L. Hgatus, pp. of
ligare. See ligament and verbal suff. -ate and cp.

religate.

## ligation
ligation, п., 1) that act of binding; 2) bond,

tio, 'a binding', fr. L. Hgatus, pp. of ligare. See

## ligature
ligature, п., anything that serves for binding; a

link, 'torch', loka, low, 'blaze', luce, lucent, lucid,
Lucifer, Lucius, lucubrate, luculent, lucule, lucus
a non lucendo, lucern, Lucy, luminous, lunar,
lunation, lune, luster, 'gloss', lustrum, lux, Luzu-
la, Lychnis, lynx.

## light
light, tr. v., to illuminate; intr. v., to light up
(said of the face). — ME. lihten, lighten, fr. OE.
lihtan, 'to shine, give light', rel. to OS. liohtian,
OHG. liuhtan, MHG. liuhten, G. leuchten, Goth.
liuhtjan, 'to light', and to OE. leoht, 'light' (n.)
See light, 'brightness'.

## light
light, adj., not dark, bright. — ME. liht, light, fr.
OE. leoht, rel. to OS., OHG. Hoht, OFris. liacht,
MHG. lieht, G. licht, 'bright', and to OE. leoht,
'light' (п.). See light, 'brightness'.
Derivatives: light-ish, adj., Hght-ly, adv.,
lightness, n.

## light
light, adj., not heavy. — ME. liht, light, fr. OE.
leoht, liht, rel. to OS. liht-, ON. lettr, Dan. let,
Swed. latt. OFris., MLG., MDu., Du. licht,
OHG. lihti, liht, MHG. lihte.liht, G. leicht, Goth.
leihts, 'light', fr. I.-E. base *le(n)gwh-, 'light,
easy, agile, nimble', whence also L. levis, 'light'.
See lever and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also lighter, 'a flat-bottomed boat'.
Derivatives: light-ly, adv., light-ness, n.

## light
light, adv., lightly, easily. — ME. lihte, lighte, fr.
OE. leohte, lihte, fr. leoht, liht, 'light'. See
light, 'not heavy'.

## light
light, intr. v., to dismount, get off. — ME. lihten,
lighten, fr. OE. lihtan, 'to alight', lit. 'to make
light', fr. leoht, liht, 'light'; orig. used in the
sense 'to relieve a horse of the rider's burden'.
See light, 'not heavy', and cp. alight and lighten,
'to make less heavy*.

## lighten
lighten, tr. v., to illuminate; intr. v., to shine. —
ME. lihtenen, lightenen, fr. liht, 'light'. See light,
'bright'.
Derivative: lighien-er, n.

## lighten
lighten, tr. v., to make less heavy; intr. v., to
become less heavy. — ME. lihtenen, lightenen, fr.
liht, light, 'light'. See light, 'not heavy', and
verbal suff. -en.
Derivative: lighten-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:449 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LIGHTER | 422 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:449 COLUMN:1 -->

## lighter
lighter, п., one who lights. — Formed fr. light, 'to
illumine', with agential suff. -er.

## lighter
lighter, п., a flat-bottomed boat. — Du. lichter,
fr. lichten, 'to lighten, unload', fr. licht, 'light'.
See light, 'not heavy', and agential suff. -er. For
the sense development of Du. lichter zp. F. allege,
'lighter', fr. alleger, 'to lighten', fr. L. alleviare,
of s.m., fr. levis, 'light'.
Derivatives: lighter, tr. v., to convey in, or as in,
a lighter, lighter-age, n.

## lightning
lightning, n. — ME. lightening, lightning, fr. light-
enen, 'to lighten'. See lighten, Ίο illuminate',
and -ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## lights
lights, n. pi., the lungs, — Lit. 'the light organs';
cp. Flemish lichte, 'lights', and see light, 'not
heavy'. Cp. also lung.

## lightsome
lightsome, adj., bright.—Formed fr. light, 'bright',
with 1st. suff. -some.

## lightsome
lightsome, adj., agile, nimble. — Formed fr. light,
'not heavy', with 1st suff. -some.

## lignaloes
lignaloes, п., 1) aloes wood; 2) the drug aloes. —
OF-, fr. Late L. lignum aloes, 'the wood of
aloe'. See ligueous and aloe.

## ligueous
ligueous, adj., of the nature of wood; woody. —
L. tigneus, 'woody', formed with suff. -eous fr.
lignum, 'wood', which stands for 'leg-пот and
lit. means 'that which is collected', fr. legere, 'to
gather, collect; to read'. See lecture and cp.
lignaloes, lignum vitae, pyroligueous.

## ligni-
ligni-, combining form meaning 'wood'. — Fr. L.
lignum, 'wood'. See prec. word.

## lignincation
lignincation, n. — See next word and -ation.

## Ugnify
Ugnify, tr. v., to make into wood; intr. v., to
become wood. — Lit. 'to make into wood',
compounded of ligni- and -fy.

## lignite
lignite, п., an imperfectly formed coal {mineral.)
— F., formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. lignum,
'wood'; see ligueous. F. lignite seems to have
been derived prop, from Lithanthrax Lignius, a
name given to woody coal by Wallerius (in Sys-
tema Mineralogicum, vol. II. p. 98, 1775). See
Encyclopedia Britannica, 1947 edition, vol. 14,
p. 118a.

## lignivorous
lignivorous, adj., eating wood (the same as xylo-
phagous). — Compounded of ligni- and L.
-vorus, from the stem of vordre, 'to devour'. See
-vorous.

## lignum vltae
lignum vltae, a S. American tree (Guaiacum
officinale). — ModL., fr. L. lignum vitae, 'wood of
life'. See ligueous and vital.

## llgroine
llgroine,ligroui, п., a volatile, inflammable liquid.
— Of unknown origin.

## ligula
ligula, п., a ligule. — L. See next word.
Derivatives: ligul-ar, adj., Hgul-ate, adj.

## Hgale
Hgale, п., a thin appendage at the base of the
blade of a leaf (bot.) — ModL. ligula, fr. L.
ligula, 'spoon', fr. I.-E. base *leigh-, 'to lick',
whence also L. lingere, 'to lick', Mir. Hag, W.
llwy, 'spoon'. For sense development cp. OHG.
leffil, 'spoon', fr. laffan, 'to lick'. See lick and -ule
and cp. lingula.

## Ligurian
Ligurian, adj., pertaining to Liguria, an ancient
country in northwestern Italy and southeastern
France; п., one of the inhabitants of Liguria. —
Formed with suit, -an fr. L. Liguria, fr. Ligures,
'the Ligurians', pi. of Ligus, 'a Ligurian',
whence Ligusticus, 'Ligurian'. Cp. lovage and
words there referred to.

## ligustlcum
ligustlcum, п., a genus of plants, the lovage (bot.)
— L., 'lovage', lit. 'of Liguria'. See lovage and
cp. words there referred to.

## Ligustrum
Ligustrum, п., a genus of plants, the privet (bot.)
— L., lit. 'of Liguria'. See prec. word.

## like
like, adj. — ME. lik, ilik, fr. OE. ge-llc, 'similar,
equal, like', rel. to OS. gilik, ON. glikr, likr,
Dan. lig, Swed. lik, OFris. Ilk, MDu. ghelijc, Du.
gelijk, OHG. gilih, MHG. gellch, G. gleich,
Goth, galeiks, 'equal, like'. For the pref. ge- in
OE. ge-lic, etc., see y-; lie in OE. ge-lic is identi-
al with OE. lie, 'body, form'. Accordingly OE.
ge-llc and its equivalents in the other Teut.
languages lit. mean 'having the same body or form'.
OE. lie, 'body, form', is rel. to ΟΝ., OS., OFris.,
ON. lik, Dan. lig, Swed. lik, MDu. lijc, Du. lijk,
OHG. 1th, MHG. Itch, Goth, leik, 'body,
corpse', G. Leiche, 'corpse', and cogn. with Lith.
Ifgus. Lett, lidzigs, OPrass. pollgu, 'equal',
Lith. lygstu, Ifgti, 'to equal'. Cp. llch, lich-gate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:449 COLUMN:2 -->
Cp. also alike, -ly, gleek and the second element
in each, ilk, such, which and in barley.
Derivatives: like, adv. (q.v.), like, п., prep, and
conj.

## like
like, adv. — ME. lik, like, ilik, Hike, fr. lik, ilik,
adj. See like, adj.

## like
like, a) intr. v., to be pleasing (obsol.); b) tr. v., to
be pleased with, enjoy. — ME. liken, fr. OE.
lician, 'to please', rel. to OS. llkon, ON. lika,
OFris. likia, OHG. lihhen, Goth, leikan, 'to
please'. The orig. meaning of these verbs was 'to
be like, be suitable to, be pleasing to; they derive
fr. OE. -lie in gelic, resp. from its equivalents in
OS. gilik, ON. glikr, OHG. gilih, Goth, galeiks,
'equal, like'. See like, adj.
Derivatives: lik(e)-able, adj., lik(e)-abil-ity, п.,
lik(e)-able-ness, n.

## -like
-like, adj. and adv. suff. — See like, adj. and like,
adv.

## likely
likely, adj.— ME. likli, fr. ON. glikligr, likligr,
'likely', fr. likr, 'like'. Cp. OE. geliclic and see
like, adj., and adj. suff. -ly.
Derivatives: liketi-hood, п., likeli-ness, n.

## likeiy
likeiy, adv. — ME. likli, adv., fr. likli, adj. — See
likely, adj.

## liken
liken, tr. v. — ME. liknen, fr. lik, 'like'. See like,
adj. and verbal suff. -en.

## likeness
likeness, n. — ME. liknesse, fr. OE. licnes, short
for gelicnes, fr. gelic, 'like'. See like, adj., and
-ness.

## likewise
likewise, adj. — Compounded of like, adj., and
-wise.

## likin
likin, п., a Chinese tax imposed on articles in
transit. — Chin., lit. 'ready money'.

## liking
liking, n. — ME., fr. OE. licung, 'pleasure', fr.
lician, 'to please'. See like, 'to be pleased with',
and subst. suff. -tug.

## Lila
Lila, fern. PN. — See Leila.

## lilac
lilac, n. — MF., fr. Sp. lilac, fr. Arab, laylak, lilak,
fr. Pers. lilak, var. of nilak, 'bluish', fr. nil, 'blue,
indigo', fr. OI. ntlah, 'dark blue', which is of
uncertain etymology. It possibly derives fr. I.-E.
base *ni-, 'to shine'. See neat, adj., and cp. anil
and the first element in nilgai and in nainsook.
Derivative: lilac, adj.

## Liliaceae
Liliaceae, n. pi., the lily family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Lilium with suff. -aceae.

## liliaceous
liliaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Lilith
Lilith, п., a female evil spirit. — Heb. Lilith, fr.
Akkad. Lilitu (whence also Syr. Lelitha), not
related to, but folk-etymologically connected with,
Heb. laylah, 'night', and explained accordingly
as 'night demon'.

## Lilium
Lilium, п., a genus of plants, the lily (bot.) — L.
lilium. See lily.

## Lilliputian
Lilliputian, adj., diminutive, tiny. — Prop,
'pertaining to LillipuC, a fabulous island with
inhabitants 6 inches high. The name was coined by
Swift in Gulliver's Travels (1726). For the ending
see suff. -ian.
Derivative: Lilliputian, n.

## lilt
lilt, intr. and tr. v., to sing rhythmically. — ME.
tutten, of uncertain, perhaps imitative, origin.
Derivative: lilt, n.

## lily
lily, n. — ME. lilie, fr. OE. lilie, fr. L. lilium, 'lily',
which, together with Gk. λείριον, of s.m., is
prob. borrowed fr. Egypt, hrr-t (pronounced in
Coptic hriri, hleli). Cp. flenr-de-Us, glgliato and
the second element in Chamaelirium, Dasylirion.

## limaceous
limaceous, adj., limacine (zool.) — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. Umax, gen. -acts, 'snail, slug'.
See Umax.

## limacine
limacine, adj., pertaining to the slugs or to the
genus Limax (zool.) — Formed fr. L. Umax, gen.
-acis, 'snail, slug' (see next word), with suff. -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## Limax
Limax, п., the genus containing the slugs (zool.)
— L. limax, gen. -ads, 'slug, snail', fr. Gk. λεί-
μδξ, which is cogn. with Russ. slimak, 'snail', lit.
'the slimy animal', OPruss. slayx, Lith. sllekas,
Lett, slieka, 'earth worm', OE. sldw-wyrm, 'slow-
worm' (see slowwonn). All these words are
derivatives of I.-E. base *(s)lei-, 'slimy', whence
also OE. sliw, 'tench', slim, 'mud'. See slime
and cp. lime, 'birdlime'.

## limb
limb, п., member. — ME. lim. fr. OE. lim, rel. to
ON. limr, 'limb', lim, 'small branch of a tree',
Norw. lim, Dan., Swed. lem, 'member'; formed

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:449 COLUMN:3 -->
with -m-formative element fr. Teut. base *li-,
which corresponds to I.-E. base *lei-, 'to bend'
be movable, be nimble'. With -ιί-formative
element, the same base appears in Goth, lithus,
OE. lip, 'joint, limb', and possibly also in L. li-
tuus, 'the crooked staff borne by the augurs'.
From base *tei- prob. derive also L. limus,
'aslant, sidelong", limen, 'threshold', and the first
element in limes, 'boundary, limit'. See limit and
cp. lituus. Cp. also lay figure.
Derivatives: limb-ed, limb-y, limb-less, adjs.

## limb
limb, п., edge, border. — L. timbus, 'hem, border',
for "lembos, cogn. with OI. Umbate, 'hangs
down', lambah, 'hanging down, long, big',
MHG. limpfen, 'to limp', and to E. limp (q.v.)

## limbate
limbate, adj., edged, bordered. — Late L. limba-
tus, fr. L. timbus, 'hem, border'. See prec. word
and adj. suff. -ate.

## limbec
limbec, п., alembic (archaic). — Aphetic for
alembic.

## limber
limber, п., the detachable fore part of a gun
carriage. — Prob. rel. to F. limoniere, 'wagon with
two shafts', fr. limon, 'shaft', which is rel. to Sp.
limon, 'shaft', Sp. and Port, leme, 'helm', Sp.
leman, 'helmsman'; prob. of Celtic origin.
Derivative: limber, tr. and intr. v.

## limber
limber, adj., pliant, flexible. — According to
W. W. Skeat, related to limp, 'flaccid'.
Derivatives: limber, tr. v., limber-ly, adv., lim-
ber-ness, n.

## limbers
limbers, n. pi. (naut.) — F. lumiere, 'light;
limbers', fr. L. luminaria, which is the plural of
luminare, 'a light, lamp, torch', but was mistaken
in Vulgar Latin for a fern. sing. noun. L.
luminare is prop. neut. of the adjective luminaris,
'giving light', used as a noun. See luminary.

## limbo
limbo, п., a region between heaven and hell. —
Prop. abl. of L. limbus, 'border' (see limb,
'border'). The abl. form was taken from the phrase
in limbo patrum ('in the border of hell, reserved
for the fathers or saints'), a phrase used by the
church fathers,

## Limburger
Limburger, п., a kind of cheese. — Short for
Limburger cheese, prop, 'cheese made in the
province Limburg in Belgium'.

## lime
lime, п., 1) birdlime (rare); 2) calcium oxide. —
ME. lim, fr. OE. lim, 'birdlime; calcium oxide',
rel. to OS., ΟΝ., MLG., OHG., MHG. lim,
Dan. lim. Du. lijm, G. Leim, 'birdlime', and
cogn. with L. limus, 'slime, mud, mire', Ср.,
with other formative elements, ON. leir, 'clay,
loam', OPruss. layso, 'clay', laydis, 'loam', Alb.
l'e&, 'watery clay'. All these words derive fr.
I.-E. base "lei-, 'slime, slimy, sticky'. See slime
and ср. 1оащ. Cp. also limno-, and words there
referred to. Cp. also oblivion.
Derivative: lime, tr. v., 1) to smear with
birdlime; 2) to mix with lime.

## lime
lime, п., a fruit allied to lemon. — F., fr. Proven?.
limo, fr. Arab, //та* (whence also Sp. lima),
noun of unity, formed from the collective noun
lim, which derives fr. Pers. limun. See lemon and
cp. Iimonene.

## lime
lime, п., the linden tree. — Fr. earlier line, fr. lind;
see linden. The change of line to lime prob.
occurred first in compounds whose second element
began with a labial (as in line-bark, line-bast,
etc.)

## limehouse
limehouse, п., defamation of one's political
opponents. — Named after the borough Lime-
house, near London, where David Lloyd George
(1863rl944) delivered a speech July 30, 1909.

## limejuicer
limejuicer, n. (slang), 1) a British ship; 2) an
English sailor; 3) an Englishman. — Formed fr.
lime, the fruit, juice, and suff. -er; so called from
the limejuice served on British ships to prevent
scurvy.

## limen
limen, п., the threshold of consciousness
(psycho!.) — L. limen, gen. liminis, 'threshold', prob.
rel. to limes, gen. limitis, 'boundary, limit'. See
limit and -men and cp. lintel, eliminate,
preliminary, postliminy, sublime, subliminal.

## Limerick
Limerick, п., a nonsense verse of five lines,
usually rhyming a a b b a. — So called after the Irish
place name Limerick, which is mentioned in the
refrain of a similar verse. (The refrain runs:
" Will you come up to Limerick!")

## limes
limes, п., boundary. — L. limes. See limit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:450 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 423 | LINEN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:450 COLUMN:1 -->

## lime tree
lime tree, the linden tree. — See lime, 'the linden
tree'.

## limey
limey, n. (slang), 1) an English sailor; 2) an
Englishman. — Shortened fr. limejuicer. For the
ending see adj. suff. -y.

## Limlcolae
Limlcolae, n. pi., a group of wading birds (orni-
thol.) — ModL., lit. 'mud dwellers',
compounded of L. limits, 'slime, mud, mire', and colere, 'to
till (the ground), inhabit'. For the first element
see Iimno-, for the second see colony.

## limmal
limmal, adj., pertaining to, or situated at, the li-
men. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. limen,
gen. liminis. See limen.

## limit
limit, n. — ME. limite, fr. MF. (= F.) limite, fr.
L. limitem, ace. of limes, 'boundary, limit',
which prob. stands for *lim-ii, lit. 'crossway',
and is compounded of limits, 'aslant, sidelong',
and *;'(-, 'going', from the stem of eo, ire, 'to go'.
L. limits is prob. rel. to L. limen, 'threshold',
both these words being prob. derived fr. I.-E.
base *lei-, 'to bend, be movable', whence also
ON. limr, OE. lim, 'mefhber'. See limb,
'member', and cp. Limulus, Htuus, oblique. For the
second element in limit see itinerate. Cp. also
delimit, delimitate.

## limit
limit, tr. v. — ME. limilen, fr. MF. (= F.) limiter,
fr. L. limitare, 'to bound, limit, fix', fr. limes,
gen. limitis. See limit, n.
Derivatives: limit-able, adj., limit-ed, adj., limit-
ed-ly, adv., limit-ed-ness, a., limit-er, п., limit-
-ing, adj.

## limitary
limitary, adj., serving as a limit, limited. — L.
limitaris, fr. limes, gen. limitis. See limit, п., and
-ary.
Derivative: limitar-ian, п., one who limits.

## limitation
limitation, n. — ME. limitacioun, fr. L. limitutio,
gen. -onis, 'a fixing', fr. limitatus, pp. oi limitare.
See limit, v. and п., and -ation.

## limitative
limitative, adj. — F. limitatij'(fern, limitative), fr.
ML. timitativus, 'limiting', fr. L. limitatus, pp.
of limitare. See limit, v. and п., and -ive.

## limitless
limitless, adj. — Formed fr. limit, п., and suff.
-less; first used by the English poet, statesman
and soldier Sir Philip Sidney (1554-86) in 1581.
Derivatives: limitless-ly, adv., limitless-ness, n.

## limitrophe
limitrophe, adj., bordering, adjacent. — F.
limitrophe, fr. Late L. timitrophus, 'set apart for the
support of troups', a hybrid coined fr. L. limes,
gen. limitis, 'boundary, limit', and Gk. τροφός,
'feeder', fr. τρέφειν, 'to feed, nourish'. See limit,
п., and trophic.Late L. timitrophus is shortened
fr. "limiwtrophus (see haplology),

## llmma
llmma, п., a semitone (pros.) — Late L., fr. Gk.
λεΐμμα, 'a semitone', lit. 'a remainder', from
the stem of λείπω, Ί leave', which stands for
*leiqwo, and is cogn. with L. linquo (for *li-n-
qwo), Ί leave, abandon', both deriving fr. I.-E.
base *liqw-, 'to let, leave', whence also OE. Ian,
'loan', Ixnan, 'to lend'. See loan and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see suff. -ma.

## limn
limn, tr. v., to illuminate. — ME. limnen, fr. lu-
minen, which is aphetic for enluminen, fr. MF.
enluminer, 'to illuminate', fr. OF. enluminer, 'to
light up, make brilliant', fr. en, 'in' (see 1st en-),
and L. luminare, 'to illuminate*. See illuminate.
Derivatives: limn-er, п., limn-ery, n.

## limn-
limn-, form of limno- before a vowel.

## Limnanthaceae
Limnanthaceae, n. pi., the false-mermaid family
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'marsh flower family',
compounded of limno-, Gk. £ν*ας, 'flower' (see
anther), and suff. -aceae.

## limnanthaceous
limnanthaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## limnetic
limnetic, adj., pertaining to, or inhabiting, fresh
water. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. λιμνήτης,
'Living in marshes', fr. λίμνη. See limno- and cp.
next word.

## Limnetis
Limnetis, n. a genus of crustaceans (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. λίμνητις, fern, of λιμνήτης,
'living in marshes'. See prec. word.

## limno-
limno-, before a vowel limn-, combining form
meaning 'marsh, marshy lake'. — Gk. λιμνο-,
λιμν-, fr. λίμνη, 'marsh, poo], lake', which is
rel. to λιμήν, 'harbor, haven', λειμών, 'a moist,
grassy meadow', and prob. cogn. with L. timus,
'slime, mud, mire'. See slime and words there
referred to and cp. esp. lime, 'birdlime'. Cp. also
limnetic, limonite, Limonium, Lymnaea, and the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:450 COLUMN:2 -->
first element in Limicolae and in Limosella.

## Limnobium
Limnobium, п., a genus of plants, the American
frogbit (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. λινμόβιος,
'living in lakes', which is compounded of λίμνη,
'pool, lake', and βίος, 'life'. See limno- and bio-,

## limnology
limnology, п., the study of fresh waters, esp. of
ponds and lakes. — Compounded of limno- and
Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: limnolog-ic, limnolog-ic-al, adjs.,
limnolog-ic-al-ly, adv., limnolog-ist, n.

## limonene
limonene, п., a terpene of lemonlike odor (chem.)
— Formed with suff. -ene fr. ModL. limonum,
'lemon', fr. F. limon. See lemon and cp. lime, 'a
fruit'.

## limonite
limonite, п., hydrous ferric oxide (mineral.) — G.
Limonit, lit. 'meadow ore', coined by Hausmann
in 1813 fr. Gk. λειμών, 'meadow', and suff. -//.
Gk. λειμών is rel. to λιμήν, 'harbor', λίμνη,
'marsh, pool, lake'; suff. -it goes back to Gk.
-ϊτης. See limno- and subst. suff. -ite. For sense
development cp. its former German name Wie-
senerz, lit. 'meadow ore'.
Derivative: limonit-ic, adj.

## Limonium
Limonium, п., a genus of plants, the sea lavender
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. λειμώνιον, 'the sea
lavender', fr. λειμών, 'meadow'. See prec.
word and 1st -inm.

## Limosella
Limosella, п., a genus of plants, the mudwort
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of L. limus,
'slime, mud, mire', and sella, 'seat', which
stands for *sed-la, from the stem of sedere, 'to
sit'. For the first element see limno-, for the
second see sedentary and cp. subsellium.

## limousine
limousine, п., a large automobile, orig. with a
closed compartment. — F., prop. fern, of the
adjective limousin, 'of Limousin', used as a
noun, fr. Limousin, name of an old province in
Central France.

## limp
limp, adj., flaccid, drooping. — Related to MHG.
lampen, 'to hang down', and to limp, v. Cp.
blimp.
Derivatives: limp-ly, adv., limp-ness, n.

## limp
limp, intr. v., to walk lamely. — Related to OE.
lemp-healt, 'halting', MHG. limp/en, 'to limp',
lampen, 'to hang down', and cogn. with OI. lam-
bate, 'hangs down', lambah, 'hanging down', L.
limbus (for "lembos), 'hem, border', Du. lomp,
'piece, mass', fr. I.-E. base *(s)lab-, *(s)leb-,
'slack, loose; to hang down', whence also OE.
slxpan, 'to sleep'. See sleep and cp. limp, 'flaccid'.
Cp. also limb, 'edge, border', lumber, 'to move
clumsily', lump, 'mass'.
Derivatives: limpyn., limp-er, п., limp-ing, adj.,
limp-ing-ly, adv., limp-ing-ness, n.

## limpet
limpet, п., a marine gastropod mollusk. — ME.
lempet, fr. OE. lempedu, fr. ML. lampreda,
'limpet, lamprey'. See lamprey,

## limpid
limpid, adj., clear; transparent. — F. limpide, fr.
L. limpidus, 'clear', fr. limpa, lumpa, 'water
goddess ; water' (see lymph). L. limpidus orig. meant
'as clear as water'. It was influenced in form by
liquidus, 'flowing, fluid'.
Derivatives: limpid-ly, adv., limpid-ness, n.

## limpidity
limpidity, n. — F. limpiditi, fr. Late L. limpidita-
tem, ace. of limpiditds, 'clarity', fr. L. limpidus.
See prec. word and -ity.

## Limulus
Limulus, п., the genus of the king crab (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. limulus, 'somewhat askance', di-

## min. of limus
min. of limus, 'askance', which is prob. rel. to
limen, 'threshold', limes, 'boundary'. See limit,
n.

## limy
limy, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -y fr. lime,
'birdlime'.

## Ltuaceae
Ltuaceae, n. pi., the flax family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Linum with suff. -aceae.

## linaceous
linaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## linage
linage, lineage, п., number of printed lines on a
page. — Formed fr. line, 'string, cord', with
suff. -age.

## Linaria
Linaria, п., a genus of plants, the toadflax (bot.)
— ModL., fr. linum, 'flax' (see Linum); so called
from the resemblance of the foliage to flax. For
the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## linen
linen, ljnchet, п., a strip of unplowed land. — OE.

## Mine
Mine, 'slope, hill', rel. to hlinian, 'to lean'. See

## lean
lean, 'to incline', and -et and cp. links.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:450 COLUMN:3 -->

## linchpin
linchpin, п., a pin passing through the end of an
axletree. — Fr. earlier linspin, lit. 'axle pin'. The
first element of this compound derives fr. OE.
tynis, 'axletree', which is rel. to OS. lunisa, MLG.
lunse (whence G. Liinse), MDu. Iitnse, Ions
(whence Du. luns), 'axletree', and cogn. with
Ol. Snih (for *.olni), 'part of the leg above the
knee'; see ell. For the second element see pin.

## linctus
linctus,п., a sirupy medicine. — L. linctus, 'a
licking', fr. linctus, pp. of lingere, 'to lick'. See lick.

## lindackerite
lindackerite, п., a complex nickel copper arsenate
(mineral.) — G. Lindackerit, named after the
I9th-cent. Austrian chemist Joseph Lindacker,
who analyzed it. The ending -it goes back to
Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## linden
linden, п., the lime tree. — Prop, subst. use of the
obsol. adjective linden, 'of linden wood', fr. ob-
sol. lind, 'linden tree', fr. OE. lind, which is rel.
to OS. linda, lindia, ON. lind, OHG. linta,
MHG., G. linde, 'the lime tree'. These words
prob. mean lit. 'the tree with pliant bast', and
derive fr. I.-E. base *lem-, 'flexible', whence also
dial. Russ. lut, 'lindenbast', Russ lutijo, 'a forest
of lime trees', Pol. iet, 'switch, twig', Lith. lenta,
'board, plank', L. lentus, 'flexible', OE. lide,
'soft, mild, gentle'. See lentitude and cp. the
second element in Ethelinda. Cp. also lime,
'linden'.

## line
line, п., flax (obsol.) — ME., fr. OE. tin, 'flax'. See
linen.

## line
line, п., a string, cord. — ME.; partly fr. F. ligne,
fr. L. linea, 'a linen thread, string, cord, line',
prop. fem. of the adj. lineus, 'of linen', fr. linum,
'flax, linen'; partly fr. OE. line, 'cord, rope, line',
which prob. derives fr. OE. tin, 'flax'. See linen
and cp. line, 'flax'. Cp. also allineate, collimate,
curvilinear, interline, interlhteage, lineament,
linear, lingerie, rectilinear.
Derivatives: lined, liner (qq.v.)

## line
line, tr. v., to mark with lines; intr. v., to form a
line — ME. linen, fr. line. See prec. word.

## line
line, tr. v., to cover the inner side of. — Orig. 'to
cover with linen'. See line, 'flax'.
Derivatives: lined (q.v.), lin-er, п., lining (q.v.)

## lineage
lineage, п., lineal descent, pedigree. — ME. lig-
nage, linage, fr. OF. lignage, fr. VL. 'tinealicum,
fr. L. linea, 'line'. See line, 'string, cord', and
-age.

## lineage
lineage, n. — A var. spelling of linage.

## lineal
lineal, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. linealis, 'pertaining
to a line', fr. L. linea, 'line'. See line, 'string,
cord', and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: lineal, п., lineal-ity, п., lineal-ly,
adv.

## lineament
lineament, п.,feature; contour.—MB.liniament,(r.
L. lineamentum, 'stroke made with a pen; a
feature, lineament', h.linedre^to reduce to a straight
line', fr. linea. See line, 'string, cord', and -ment.

## linear
linear, adj. — L. linearis, 'pertaining to a line or
lines, consisting of a line or lines', fr. linea. See
line, 'string, cord', and -ar and cp. collinear.
Derivative: linear-ly, adv.

## lineate
lineate, adj., marked with lines. — L. lineatus, pp.
of lineare, 'to make into a straight line', fr. linea,
'line'. See line, 'string, cord', and adj. suff.
-ate.

## lineation
lineation, n. — ME. lineacion, fr. L. lineatio, gen.
-onis, 'the making into a straight line, the
drawing of lines', fr. lineatus, pp. of lineare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## lined
lined, adj., marked with lines. — Formed with
3rd suff. -ed fr. line, 'string, cord'.

## lined
lined, adj., provided with a lining. — Pp. of line,
'to cover'.

## linen
linen, n. and adj. — Orig. an adjective in the
sense of 'made of flax'; ME., fr. OE. linen, fr.
tin, 'flax', which is rel. to OS., ΟΝ., OHG. tin,
'flax, linen', MHG. linin, linen, 'linen' (adj.), G.
Leinen and Linnen, 'linen' (п.), Goth, lein,
'linen cloth'. These words are prob. borrowed fr.
L. linum, 'flax, linen', which, together witlt Gk.
λϊνον, of s.m., prob. derives from a non-Indo-
European source.Cp. Lith. //лаГ(р1.), 'flax, linen',
Russ. le'n (gen. Una), of s.m., which are prob.
borrowed fr. Gk. λίνον. Alb l'i-ri, Gheg l'i-ni,

## and possibly also Corn.
and possibly also Corn., Bret, tin, W. //in, 'flax'

## are Latin loan words. See line
are Latin loan words. See line, 'string, cord', and

## cp. words there referred to. Cp. also crinoline
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also crinoline,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:451 COLUMN:1 -->
gridelin, linon, linnet, linoleum, linseed, lint,
Linum.
Derivatives: linen-ette, п., linen-ize, tr. v., linen-
iz-er, n.

## liner
liner, п., a ship belonging to a line of steamships.
— Formed fr. line, 'string, cord', with agential
suff. -er.

## ling
ling, п., a seafish allied to the cod. — ME. lenge,
rel. to ON. langa, Du. leng, G. Lange, 'ling', lit.
'the long fish', and to OE. fang, 'long'. See long,
adj.

## ling
ling, п., the common heather. — ME. lyng, fr.
ON. lyng (whence Dan. lyng, Swed. Ijung),
'heather', rel. to ON.slyng va, 'to throw,sling',and
to OE. slingen, 'to creep'. See sling, 'to throw'.
Derivative: ling-y, adj.

## -ling
-ling, subst. suff. meaning belonging to or having
the quality of (as in earthling, darling), or having
diminutive of depreciatory force (as in duckling,
gosling, resp. in lordling, underling). — ME., fr.
OE. -ling, rel. to ON. -lingr, OHG., MHG.,
G. -ling, Goth, -liggs. Cp. -tag, 'pertaining to'.

## -ling
-ling, -lings, adv. suff. expressing direction as in
back-lings. — ME. -ling, -linges, fr. OE. -tinge,
-tinges (the -s in -tinges is the adv. genitive suff.);
prob. rel. to OE. long, 'long', hence derivatively
identical with suff. -long, by which it has now
been replaced.

## linga
linga, lingam, п., the phallic emblem under which
Siva is worshiped. — OI. linga, nom. lingam,
'mark, token, sign, emblem', lit. 'something
attaching to an object'; of uncertain origin.

## linger
linger, intr. v. — Northern ME. tengeren, freq. of
tengen, 'to tarry', fr. OE. lengan, 'to prolong,
delay', fr. long, 'long'. Cp. Du. lengen, 'to
lengthen', and see long, adj.
Derivatives: linger-er, п., linger-ing, adj., linger-
ing-ly, adv.

## lingerie
lingerie, п., linen goods. — F., fr. linge, 'linen', fr.
OF. linge, 'linen', fr. linge (adj.), 'of linen', fr. L.
lineus, of s.m., fr. linum, 'linen'. "See linen and
-ery.

## lingo
lingo, п., language; dialect, jargon. — Provencal
lingo, tengo, 'tongue, language', fr. L. lingua. See
Ungual.

## lingot
lingot, п., an ingot (archaic). — F., formed by the
agglutination of the definite article te, /', from
I'ingot, lit. 'the ingot'. F. le derives fr. L. ille,
'that'. See ille and ingot. For the agglutination
of the article cp. lierre and words there referred
to.

## lingua franca
lingua franca, a hybrid language consisting esp.
of Italian, Spanish, French and Greek elements.
— It., prop, 'the language of the Franks'. See
Ungual and Frank.

## lingnal
lingnal, adj. — ML. lingualis, 'pertaining to the
tongue*, fr. L. lingua, 'tongue, speech, language',
fr. OL. dingua, which is cogn. with OE. tunge,
Goth, luggo, 'tongue'. See tongue and cp.
language, langued, languet, langue d'oc, langue d'oU,
lingo, lingula, dentilingual, bilingual, trilingaal.
The change of d(in OL. dingua) to /(in L. lingua)
was prob. due to dialectal influence (the so-
called 'Sabine /'); see lachrymal. It was
facilitated by a folk-etymological association with
lingere, 'to lick', the tongue having been
conceived as 'the licking organ'.
Derivatives: lingual, п., a lingual sound, lingual-
ity, п., lingual-ly, adv.

## lingulform
lingulform, adj., tongue-shaped. — Compounded
of L. lingua, 'tongue', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See lingual and form, n.

## linguist
linguist, n. — A hybrid coined fr. L. lingua (see
Ungual) and -1st, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivatives: linguist-ic, adj., linguist-ic-at-ly,
adv., linguistics (q.v.)

## linguistics
linguistics, п., the science of language. — See
prec. word and -ics.

## lingula
lingula, п., a tonguelike part (anat. and zool.) —
L., 'a little tongue', dimin, of lingua, 'tongue'.
See lingual and -ule and cp. ligule.

## Ungulate
Ungulate, adj., tongue-shaped. — L. lingulstus,
'tongue-shaped, Ungulate', fr. lingula, 'little
tongue'. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate and
cp ligulate.

## linguo-
linguo-, combining form meaning lingual, lin-
gually. — Fr. L. lingua, 'tongue'. See Ungual.

## Uniment
Uniment, п., an oily liquid for applying to the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:451 COLUMN:2 -->
skin. — ME. lynyment, fr. Late L. Ilnimentum, fr.
L. linire, a secondary form of linere, 'to daub,
besmear, anoint', which stands for *li-n(re and
is cogn. with OI. linati, layate, liyate, Ityati,
'adheres to; slips into; disappears', Gk. άλί-
νειν, 'to anoint, besmear', Olr. as-leinamm,
Ί soil', leinam, Ί follow' (lit. Ί stick to'); fr.
I.-E. base *(s)lei-, 'slime, slimy, sticky', whence
also OE. slim, 'slime'. See slime and -ment and
cp. lime, 'birdlime'. Cp. also delete. The change
of L. linire (3rd conj.) to linire (4th conj.) is
prob. due to the influence of polire, 'to polish'.

## linin
linin, п., a bitter white substance obtained from
the purging flax (chem.) — Formed with chem.
suff. -ia fr. L. linum, 'flax, linen'. See Linum.

## lining
lining, n. — Formed fr. line, 'to cover', with -tag,
suff. forming verbal nouns.

## link
link, п., ring of a chain. — ME. linke, of Scand.
origin; cp. Swed. lank, 'ring', and ON. hlekkr,
'chain, link', which are rel. to OE. hlence, 'link,
(pi.) armor', MHG. linken, G. lenken, 'to bend,
turn, lead', fr. I.-E. base 'qleng-, 'to bend'. See
lank.
Derivatives: link, tr. v., to join together with or
as with a link; intr. v., to join, link-age, n.

## link
link, п., a torch. — Prob. fr. ML. linchinus,
secondary form of lichinus, 'wick', fr. Gk. λύχνος,
'portable light, lamp', which stands for *luqs-
nos and derives fr. I.-E. base *leuq-, 'to emit
light, shine'. See light, 'brightness', and cp. lune.

## links
links, n. pi., sand hills; a golf course. — OE.
hlinc, 'slope, hill', rel. to OE. hlinian, 'to lean'.
See lean, 'to incline', and cp. linch, ltachet.

## Unn
Unn, п., a waterfall. — Prob. a blend of OE.
hlynn, 'torrent', and W. llyn, 'pool, pond'.

## Linnaea
Linnaea, п., a genus of plants, the twinflower
(hot.) — ModL., named after Linnaeus. See next
word.

## Ltanaean
Ltanaean, Ltanean, adj., pertaining to the system
or method of Linnaeus. — Formed fr. Linnaeus,
Latinized form of Linne, name of the great
Swedish botanist (1707-78). For the ending see suff.
-ean.

## linnet
linnet, п., a small singing bird of the finch family.
— OF. (F. linot, linotte), fr. tin, 'flax', fr. L.
linum, of s.m. (see Linum, line, 'string, cord');
so called because it feeds on the seeds of flax.

## linoleum
linoleum, n. — Orig. 'solidified oil'; coined by the
English inventor Frederick Walton in 1863, fr.
L. linum, 'flax', and oleum, 'oil'. See Linum and
oleo-.

## linotype
linotype, n. — Contraction of line o* type. See
line, 'string, cord', and type.

## Linsang
Linsang, п., a genus of long-tailed catlike
mammals of S. Asia (zool) — ModL., fr. Javanese
native word.

## linseed
linseed, п., seeds of flax. — ME. linsed, fr. OE.
linsxd. See Itue, 'flax', and seed.

## Ilasey-woolsey
Ilasey-woolsey, п., a coarse cloth made of wool or
cotton. — The first element derives fr. Lindsey,
a village in Suffolk (England). The second
element is formed fr. wool, on analogy of linsey,
which was supposed to be formed fr. lin(en)
with the alleged suff. -sey.

## linstock
linstock, п., formerly, a staff used for firing
cannon. — Du. lontstok, compounded of lont,
'match', and stok, 'stick'. See limt and stock.

## lint
lint, п., soft linen used for dressing wounds.—
ME. lynt, linnet, fr. L. linteum, 'linen cloth',
prop. neut. of the adjective linteus, 'of linen', fr.
linum, 'flax'. See linen and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: lint-en, lint-y, adjs.

## lintel
lintel, n. — ME., fr. OF. lintel (F. linteau), var. of
lintier, fr. VL. *limitaris, which is a blend of L.
liminaris, 'pertaining to the threshold', and
limes, gen. limitis, 'boundary'. See Iimen, limit.

## ltatonite
ltatonite, п., a variety of thomsonite (mineral.) —
Named after the American scientist Miss Laura
A. Linton (died in 1915), who analyzed it. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Linum
Linum, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — L. linum,
'flax'. See linen and cp. line, 'string, cord', and
words there referred to.

## liny
liny, adj., marked with lines. — Formed fr. line,
'string, cord', with adj. suff. -y.

## Uo-
Uo-, a var. of leio-,

## Uon
Uon, n. — ME. lion, leon, fr. OF. (= F.) lion, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:451 COLUMN:3 -->
L. leonem, ace. of ieo, fr. Gk. λέων, 'lion', which
is of uncertain, possibly Semitic, origin; cp.
Heb. labhV, Akkad. labbu, 'lion'. Cp. also
Homeric λίς, 'lion', which is prob. a loan word fr.
Heb. Idyish, 'lion'. OE. Ieo, OHG. lewo, lewo
(whence MHG. leu, lewe, G. Lowe), Goth. *liwa
(whence OSlav. livH), Olr. leon (gen. pi.), Mir.
Ieo, OCo. leu, W. Hew, 'lion', are Latin loan
words. Cp. Lionel, chameleon, codling, Lyon, 'a
variant of apple', dandelion, Leander, Leonard,
Leontodon, Leonurus, leopard, leu, lev,
pantaloon.

## Uoncel
Uoncel, п., a young lion. — OF. lioncel (F. lion-
ceati), dimin. of lion. See Uon.

## Lionel
Lionel, mast. PN. — F., lit. 'young lion'. See Uon.

## Uonesque
Uonesque, adj., resembling a lion. — A hybrid
formed fr. lion with -esque, a suff. of Italian, ult.
Teut. origin.

## Uoness
Uoness, п., a female Uon. — Formed fr. lion with
suff. -ess.

## lionism
lionism, п., the practise of lionizing. — A hybrid
coined fr. Uon with -ism, a suff. of Greek origin.

## lionize
lionize, tr. v., to treat as a lion; intr. v., to visit
the sights (lit. 'the lions') of a place. — A hybrid
coined fr. Uon with -ize, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivative: lioniz-ation, n.

## Up
Up, n. — ME. lippe, fr. OE. lippa, rel. to OFris.
lippa, MDu. lippe (whence F. lippe, 'thick lower
lip'), Du. lip, OHG. lefs, MHG. lefs, lefse, dial.
G. Lefze (G. Lippe is borrowed fr. LG.), Swed.
lapp, Dan. Ixbe, 'lip', and prob. cogn. with L.
labium, labrum, 'lip', and prob. also with Toch. A
lym-, 'lip'. Cp. labial, labrum.
Derivatives: lip, v. (q.v.), lip-less, adj.

## lip
lip, tr. v., to touch with the lips, to kiss. — Fr.
Up, n.; first used by Shakespeare.
Derivative: lipp-ed, adj.

## lipar-
lipar-, form of liparo- before a vowel.

## Llparis
Llparis, п., a genus of plants, the twayblade (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. λιπαρός, 'oily, fat, greasy'.
See Uparo-,

## liparo-
liparo-, before a vowel Upar-, combining form
meaning 'oily'. — Gk. λιπαρό-, λιπαρ-, fr.
λιπαρός, 'oily, fat, greasy', fr. λίπος, 'fat,
grease'. See Про-, 'fat'.

## liparoid
liparoid, adj., fatty. — Compounded of lipar- and
Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
-oid.

## lipase
lipase, п., a class of enzymes (biochem.) —
Formed with suff. -ase fr. Gk. λίπος 'fat, grease'.
See lipo-, 'fat'.

## lipide
lipide, lipid, п., any of a group of organic
substances comprising the fats. — F. lipide, coined
fr. Gk. λίπος, 'fat' (see Upo-, 'fat'), and chem.
suff. -ide.

## lipo-
lipo-, combining form meaning 'fat', as in lipo-
lysis. — Gk. λιπο-, fr. λίπος, 'fat, grease',
which is cogn. with L. lippus, 'blear-eyed', OE,
be-lifan, 'to remain'. See leave, v., and cp.
Llparis, lipoma.

## lipo-
lipo-, combining form meaning 'lacking', as in
lipography. — From the stem of Gk. λείπεσθαι,
'to be lacking', passive of λείπειν, 'to leave'.

## See loan
See loan,

## lipography
lipography, п., omission of a letter or syllable in
writing. — Compounded of Upo-, 'lacking', and
Gk. -γραφία, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
-graphy.

## lipoid
lipoid, п., a fatlike substance. — Coined fr. Gk.
λίπος, 'fat', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. ε!8ος 'form,

## shape'. See Upo-
shape'. See Upo-, 'fat', and -oid.

## Ilpolysis
Ilpolysis, п., decomposition of fat. —

## Compounded of lipo-
Compounded of lipo-, 'fat', and Gk. λύσις, 'a loosing,

## loosening
loosening, setting free; dissolution'. See-lysiz.

## lipolytic
lipolytic, adj., pertaining to, or causing, lipolysis.
— Compounded of lipo-, 'fat', and -lytic,

## lipoma
lipoma, п., a fatty tumor (med.) — Medical L.,
coined by the French physician Alexis Littri
(1658-1726), fr. Gk. λίπος, 'fat, grease'. See

## lipo-
lipo-, 'fat', and -oma.

## ipothymia
ipothymia, п., a fainting (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. λιποθυμία, 'swoon', fr. λιποθϋμεΐν, 'to

## fall into a swoon
fall into a swoon, to faint', which is
compounded of the base of λείπεσθαι, 'to be lacking',
and θυμός 'spirit, mind, soul'. For the first

## element see lipo-
element see lipo-, 'lacking', for the second see
thio-.

## Upper
Upper, п., a slight ruffling of the sea. — Prob. rel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:452 COLUMN:1 -->
to ON. hjeypa, 'to cause to leap', and to E. leap
(q.v.)

## Lippia
Lippia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Italian naturalist Agostino
Lippi. For the ending see 1st suff. -la.

## liquate
liquate, tr. v., to separate the more fusible
substance from the less fusible. — Orig. 'to melt',
fr. L. liquatus, pp. of liqudre, 'to make liquid, to
melt', from the stem of Hquere, 'to be liquid'.
See liquid and verbal suff. -ate.

## liquation
liquation, п., the process of liquating. — Late L.
liqudtio, gen. -onis, fr. L. liquatus, pp. of liquare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## llquefacient
llquefacient, adj., making liquid. — L. liquefa-
ciens, gen. -entis, pTes. part, of liquefacere. See
liquefy and -facient.
Derivative: liquefacient, n.

## liquefaction
liquefaction, n. — Late L. liquefactio, gen. -onis,
fr. L. lique/actus, pp. of liquefacere. See next
word and -ation.

## liquefy
liquefy, tr. and intr. v., to change into a liquid. —
MF. (= F.) liquefier, fr. L. liquefacere, 'to make
liquid, to melt', which is compounded of Hquere,
'to be liquid', and facere, 'to make, do' (but
assimilated in form to the numerous French verbs
ending in -fier). See liquid and fact and cp. -fy.
Derivatives: Hquefi-able, adj., liquefi-er, n.

## liquescent
liquescent, adj., tending to become liquid. — L.
liquescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of liquescere,
'to become liquid, to melt', inchoativeof Hquere,
'to be liquid'. See liqnid and -escent and cp.
deliquesce, deliquescent.

## liqueur
liqueur, п., any of certain alcoholic liquors
sweetened and flavored. — F., fr. L. liqudrem, ace. of
liquor, 'a fluid, liquid'. See liquor.
Derivative: liqueur, tr. v.

## liquid
liquid, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) liquide, fr. L.
liquidus, 'flowing, fluid, liquid, clear', fr. Hquere,
'to be fluid, be liquid', which is rel. to lix, gen.
licis, 'ashes', lixa, 'water; lye',prolixus,
'extended', orig. 'flowing forward', and prob. cogn.
with Olt.fliuch, 'moist, wet', OW. gulip, ModW.
gwfyb, of s.m., W. glwith, 'dew', MBret. gloeb,
ModBret. gleb, 'moist, wet'. Cp. lixiviate, prolix.
Derivatives: liquid, п., liquidate (q.v.), liquid-ly,
adv., liquid-ness, n.

## Liquldambar
Liquldambar, п., a genus of trees, the sweet gum
tree (bot.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. L.
liquidus, 'fluid', and Arab, anbar, 'amber'. See
liquid and amber.

## liquidate
liquidate, tr. and intr. v. -— ML. liquidatus, pp. of
liquidare, 'to liquidate', fr. L, liquidus. See
liquid and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: liquidat-ion, п., liquidat-or, n.

## liquiditiy
liquiditiy, n. — L. liquiditds, fr. liquidus. See
liquid and -ity.

## liquor
liquor, п., 1) any liquid substance; 2) any
beverage; specif, an alcoholic beverage. — ME. li-
kour, Hear, fr. OF. licour, licur (F. liqueur), fr.
L. liqudrem, ace. of liquor, 'a fluid, liquid', which
is rel. to Hquere. See liqnid and -or and cp.
liqueur, which is a doublet of liquor.
Derivatives: liquor, tr. and intr. v., liquorish
(q.v.)

## liquorice
liquorice, n. — See licorice.

## liquorish
liquorish, adj., fond of liquor. — Formed fr.
liquor with suff. -ish.
Derivatives: liquorish-ly, adv., liquorish-ness, n.

## liquorish
liquorish, adj. — A var. of lickerish.

## lira
lira, п., an Italian silver coin and monetary unit.
— It., 'pound', fr. L. libra. See libra and cp.
words there referred to.

## lirella
lirella, п., in lichens, the narrow shield with a
furrow along the middle (bot.) — ModL., di-
min. of L. lira, 'the earth thrown up between two
furrows, furrow', whence delirare, 'to turn aside
from the furrow; to deviate, become deranged,
crazy, delirious'. See delirium and -ella.
Derivatives: lirell-ate, lirell-ous, adjs.

## Liriodendron
Liriodendron, п., a genus of trees, the tulip tree
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. λείριον,
'lily', and δένδραν, 'tree'. See lily and dendro-.

## liripipe
liripipe, liripoop, п., the tail at the back of a hood
(hist.) — ML. liripipium, of uncertain origin.

## llsbon
llsbon, п., a kind of sweet wine. — Prop, 'wine
shipped from Lisbon', the capital of Portugal.
lisle thread. — From Lisle, original spelling of
Lille, town in France, where it was first made.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:452 COLUMN:2 -->
The town derived its name fr. OF. I'isle (F.
I'ile), 'the island', in allusion to its geographical
situation.

## lisp
lisp, intr. and tr. v. — ME. lispen, fr. OE. -wlis-
pian, 'to stammer, lisp', fr. wlisp, 'lisping*, which
is of imitative origin. Cp. MDu., Du., OHG.,
MHG. lispen (whence the dimin. lispeln), Dan.
Ixspe, Swed. Idspa, dial. Norw. leispa, which
all are imitative.
Derivatives: lisp, n. (q.v.), lisp-er, п., lisp-ing, n.

## lisp
lisp, n. — OE. wlisp. See lisp, v.

## lissome
lissome, adj. — For lithesome.

## list
list, п., border of cloth, selvage. — ME. liste, fr.
OE. liste, rel. to ON. llsta, MLG. Ifste, Du. lijst,
OHG. ITsta, MHG. liste, G. Leiste, 'border,
selvage'; prob. cogn. with Alb. I'e&, 'raised
border".

## list
list, n. (usually in the pi.), enclosed ground;
ground for holding tournaments. — A blend of
list, 'border of cloth', and OF. lice, 'barrier,
lists', which itself is prob. borrowed fr. Teut.;
cp. OHG. lista, 'border, selvage', and see prec.
word.

## list
list, п., a catalog. — F. liste, 'list, roll, catalog',
orig. 'strip of paper', fr. It. lista, which is a
Teut. loan word. Cp. OHG. lista, 'border,
selvage', and see list, 'border of cloth'.
Derivatives: list, tr. v., to make a list of, list-er,
п., list-ing, n.

## list
list, п., inclination (rtaut.) — Of uncertain origin;
perh. fr. list, 'to be pleased', taken in the sense
'to incline to'.
Derivative: list, tr. and intr. v.

## list
list, intr. v., to be pleased; to desire (obsol.) —
ME. lusten, listen, 'to please, desire', fr. OE.
lystan, of s.m., fr. lust, 'pleasure, desire'. See
lust.

## list
list, intr. and tr. v., to listen (archaic). — ME.
listen, fr. OE. hlystan. See listen.

## listen
listen, intr. v. — ME. lislnen, a blend of ME. listen
(fr. OE. hlystan, 'to hear, listen', fr. hlyst, 'a
hearing'), and OE. hlysnan, 'to listen'.whichisrel.
to OE. hlosnian, 'to listen in suspense', OHG.
hlosen, 'to listen', 'hliisken (whence MHG.
luschen, G. lauschen), 'to listen' (cp. also ON.
Must, 'hearing; ear', hlusta, 'to listen', Swed.
lystra, Du. luisteren, OHG. luslren, 'to listen'),
and cogn. with OSlav. slySati, slusati, 'to hear',
Lith. klausau, klaus-yti, 'to hear", Olr. cluas,
'ear', OI. srosatl, 'hears, obeys', fr. l.-E.
*kleu-s-, an -j-enlargement of base *kleu-, 'to
hear', whence Gk. κλέος, 'rumor, fame', OE.
hlud, 'loud'. See loud and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: listen, п., listen-er, п., listen-ing,
adj. and n.

## Listera
Listera, п., a genus of plants, the twayblade (bot.)
— ModL., named after the English naturalist
Martin Lister (1638-1711).

## listerine
listerine, п., an antiseptic. — Named after the
English surgeon Lord Joseph Lister (1827-
1912). For the ending see chem. suff. -ine.

## listerize
listerize, tr. v., to use an antiseptic during
operations. — Named after Lord Lister. See prec.
word and -ize.

## listless
listless, adj., languidly indifferent. — Formed fr.
list, 'to be pleased', with suff. -less.
Derivatives: listless-ly, adv., listless-ness, a.

## lit
lit, past tense and pp. of the verb light.

## iitany
iitany, п., form of prayer, — ME. letanie, fr. ML.
litania, fr. Gk. λιτανεία, 'prayer, entreaty,
supplication', fr. λιτανεύειν, 'to pray, entreat,
supplicate', fr. λιτανός, 'praying, entreating,
suppliant', fr. λιτή, 'prayer, supplication', which is
of uncertain origin. L. litare, 'to sacrifice under
auspicious signs', is prob. a denominative verb
fr. *lita, fr. Gk. λιτή.

## litchi
litchi, п., the fruit of a Chinese tree (Litchi chinen-
sis). — Chinese.

## -lite
-lite, combining form meaning 'stone', used esp.

e.g. foralite, chrysolite, graptolite). — F. -lite, a

and cp. -lith.

## liter
liter, litre, п., a measure of capacity. — F. litre,
fr. earlier litron, *an old measure for grain', fr.
ML. litra, 'a liquid measure', fr. Gk. λίτρα, 'a
pound'. See litra.

## literacy
literacy, n. — Formed fr. literate with suff. -cy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:452 COLUMN:3 -->

## literal
literal, adj. — ME., fr. MF. literal (F.
lateral), fr. L. litterdlis (literalis), 'pertaining to a
letter', fr. littera (litera), 'letter'. See letter and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: literal-ism, п., literal-ist, n. and adj.,
lileral-ist-ic, adj., literal-ity, п., literal-ize, tr. v.,
literal-iz-ation, п., literal-ly, adv., literal-nets, n.

## literary
literary, adj. — L. litterSrius (literarius),
'pertaining to reading and writing', fr. littera, 'letter'.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: literari-ly, adv., literari-ness, n.

## literate
literate, adj., learned, educated; п., an educated

educated', lit. 'one who knows the letters', fr. littera
(litera), 'letter'. See letter and adj. suff. -ate and

## literati
literati, n. pi., men of letters. — L. UtterSti
(literati), pi. οι litteratus (literatus). See literatus.

## literatim
literatim, adv., letter by letter; literally. — L. lit-
teratim (literatim), formed fr. littera (litera),

-atim see gradatim and cp. words there referred

## literature
literature, n. — ME. litterature, fr. L. litteratura
(literatura), 'writing; grammar; learning,
scholarship', fr. littera (litera), 'letter'. See letter and
-ure.

## literatus
literatus, п., a learned person. — L. litteratus
(literatus), 'learned, educated'. See literate and cp.
literati.
11th, п., a limb, a joint. — ME., fr. OE. lid. See
