## lith-
lith-, form of lltho- before a vowel.

## -lith
-lith, combining form meaning 'stone', used esp.
in archaelogy, biology and medicine (as in eolith,
chololith); in geology, mineralogy, and
paleontology, -lite is the regular combining form. — F.
■lithe, fr. Gk. λίθος, 'stone'. Seelitho- and cp. -lite.

## litharge
litharge, п., lead monoxide. — ME. litarge, fr.
OF. litarge (F. litharge), fr. L. Hthargyrus, fr.
Gk. λιθάργυρος, 'vitrified lead, lead monoxide',
lit. 'stone silver', fr. λίθος, 'stone', and άργυρος,
'silver'. See litho- and argent.

## lithe
lithe, adj., flexible, supple. — ME. lithe, lith, fr.
OE. tide, 'soft, mild, gentle', rel. to OS. lithi,
OHG. lindi, MHG. linde, G. lind, ON. linr, fr.
I.-E. base 'lent-, 'flexible', whence also L. len-
tus, 'flexible, pliant; slow', and prob. also ΟΝ.,
OE. lind, 'linden tree', lit. 'the tree with pliant
bast'. See lentitude, and cp. linden.
Derivatives: lithe-ly, adv., Ilthe-ness, п.,
lithesome (q.v.)

## lither
lither, adj., bad, wicked (obsol.); lazy (dial.);
flexible, pliant (archaic). — ME., 'bad, wicked', fr.
OE. lydre, 'base, bad, wicked', rel. to MLG.
luder, 'a lewd fellow', G. liederlich, 'lewd', OE.
loddere, 'beggar". See loiter.
Derivatives: lither-ly, adv., lither-ness, n.

## lithesome
lithesome, adj. — Formed fr. lithe with suff.
-some. Cp. lissom.

## lithia
lithia, п., the oxide of lithium (chem.) — ModL.,
changed fr. lithion (an earlier name for lithia),
which was formed fr. Gk. λίθειον, neut. of
λί&ειος, 'stony', fr. λίθος, 'stone'; see litho-.
The name was suggested by the Swedish
chemist, Baron Jims Jakob Berzelius (1779-1848)
for the fixed alkali discovered by his pupil Johan
August Arfvedson (1792-1841) in 1817, owing
to the former's belief that this oxide occurred
only in minerals.

## lithlasls
lithlasls, п., the formation of calculi in the body
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. λιθίασις, lit.
'disease of the stone', formed fr. λίθος, 'stone'
(see litho-), and suff. -δσις (see -asls).

## lithic
lithic, adj., of, or pertaining to, stone. — Gk.
λιθικός, 'of, or pertaining to, stone', fr. λίθος,
'stone'. See litho- and -ic.

## lithium
lithium, п., name of a silver-white metallic
element (chem.) — ModL., fr. lithia.
Derivatives: lithi-ate, tr. v., lith-ic, adj.

## litho-
litho-, before a vowel lith-, combining form
meaning 'stone'. — Gk. λίθο-, λιθ-, fr. λίθος,
'stone', of unknown origin. Cp. -lite, -lith.

## Lithobius
Lithobius, п., a genus of myriapods (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of litho- and Gk. βίος,
'life'. See bio-.

## Lithodes
Lithodes, п., a genus of crabs (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. λιθώ8τ;ς, 'stonelike', which is com-

pounded of λίθος, 'stone', and -ώδης, 'like'.
See litho- and -ode, 'like'.

## lithodid
lithodid, п., any of the crabs of the family Litho-
didae. — See next word.

## Lithodidae
Lithodidae, п., a family of crabs {zool.) — ModL.
See Lithodes and -idae.

## lithograph
lithograph, п., a print made by lithography; intr.
v., to make prints by^ithography; tr. v., to
reproduce by lithography. — Back formation fr.
lithography. See -graph.
Derivative: lithograph-er, n.

## lithography
lithography, п., the art or process of printing
<rom a prepared stone or metal plate. — Lit.
'writing on stone', compounded of litho- and
Gk. -γραφία, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
-graphy.
Derivatives: lithograph-ic, adj., tithograph-ic-al-
ly, adv.

## lithoid
lithoid, adj., stonelike. — Gk. λιθοειδής, 'like a
stone', compounded of λίθος, 'stone', and
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See

## lithology
lithology, п., the study of the formation of rocks.
— Compounded of litho- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, One who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: tithotog-ic, litholog-ic-al, adjs.,
litholog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## lithomancy
lithomancy, п., divination by stones. —
Compounded of litho- and Gk. μαντεία, Oracle,
divination'. See -mancy.

## lithomarge
lithomarge, п., a variety of kaolin. — ModL.
lithomarga, a hybrid coined fr. Gk. λίθος,
'stone', and L. marga, 'marl'. See litho- and marl,

## lithontriptic
lithontriptic, adj., destroying the calculi in the
bladder (med.) — Medical L. lithontripticus, for
lithonthrypticus, fr. Gk. λίθων θρυπτικά,
'(drugs) crushing stones'. Gk. λίθων is gen. pi.
of λίθος, 'stone'; see litho-. Gk. θρυπτικά is
neut. pi. of θρυπτικός, 'able to crush', fr. θρυ-
πτός, 'crushed', verbal adj. of θρύπτειν, 'to
crush'; see drop, n. The spelling lithontriptic (for
lithonthryptic), arose from a confusion of Gk.
θρυπτός, 'crushed', with τριπτός, 'rubbed,
ground, pounded', verbal adj. of τρΐβειν (see
trite).

## Lithospermum
Lithospermum, п., a genus of plants, the grom-
well and the puccoon (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of litho- and Gk. σπέρμα, 'seed' (see
sperm); so called in allusion to the hard nutlets.

## lithosphere
lithosphere, п., the solid part of the earth. —
Compounded of litho- and Gk. σφαίρα, 'ball,
globe, sphere'. See sphere and cp. words there
referred to.

## lithotomy
lithotomy, п., the operation of cutting for stone
in the bladder (surg.) — Late L. lithotomia, fr.
Gk. λιθοτομία, 'cutting for the stone', which is
compounded of λίθος, 'stone' (see litho-), and
-τομία, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'.
See -toiny.
Derivatives: lithotom-ic, adj., lithotom-ist, n.

## llthotrite
llthotrite, п., an instrument for performing litho-
trity. — Back formation fr. lithotrity.

## llthotrity
llthotrity, п., operation of crushing a stone in the
bladder into very small pieces capable of being
voided naturally (surg.) — A hybrid coined fr.
Gk. λίθος, 'stone', and L. tritus. pp. of terere,
'to rub, bruise, crush'. See litho- and throw and
cp. trite.
Derivatives: lithotrit-ic, adj., lithotrit-y, n.

## Lithuania
Lithuania, n. — Lith. Lietuvd, 'Lithuania', of
uncertain origin; perh. rel. to Lith. *lei-, 'to pour,

drop', fr. I.-E. base 'let-, 'to flow', whence

possibly also L. Iltus, 'shore'; see littoral.

sense development cp. ML. Ripudrii, lit. 'people

## litigant
litigant, adj., engaged in a lawsuit; п., a party in a

## part
part, oilitigdre. See next word and -ant.

## litigate
litigate, intr. v., to go to law; tr. v., to contest in a

'to dispute, quarrel, strive', formed from the

## term litem agere
term litem agere, lit. 'to lead a dispute or strife'.

## Litem is the ace. of /ft
Litem is the ace. of /ft, 'dispute, quarrel, strife,

lawsuit',for earlier ii/is,which stands for*5i/-i-r-5,

lit. 'that which is placed', fr. I.-E. base *stel-.

## litra
litra, п., name of a Greek weight and coin. — Gk.

whence also. L. libra, 'Roman pound*. Cp. libra,

## litre
litre, n. — See liter.

## Litsea
Litsea, п., a genus of plants of the laurel family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. F. titse, fr. Chin, li tsai,

## litter
litter, п., a portable bed. — ME. litere, liter, fr.
AF. litere, fr. OF. litiere (F. litiere), fr. VL. *lec-
tdria, fr. L. teclus, 'bed'. See lie, 'to recline'.
Derivatives: litter, tr. and intr. v., litter-y, adj.

## little
little, adj. — ME. lutel, litel, fr. OE. lytel, which
is prob. orig. a dimin. of OE. lyt, 'little, few';
rel. to OS. luttil, Du. luttel, OHG. luzzil, MHG.

finger'. Cp. lout, 'to bow, stoop'.
Derivative: tittle-ness, n.

## littoral
littoral, adj., pertaining to the seashore. — F., fr.
L. littordlis, prop, lltordlis, fr. thus, gen. litoris,
'seashore', which is of uncertain origin. It meant
perh. orig.' a place where water flows', and.
derives fr. I.-E. base */«-, 'to pour, flow', whence
also L. libdre, 'to pour out, make a libation'
(see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., 1, 815 s.v. thus).
See libation and adj. surf, -al and cp. Lithuanian.
Cp. also next word.
Derivative: littoral, n.

## Littorella
Littorella, п., a genus of plants of the plantain
family (bot.) — ModL., prop, meaning 'growing
on the shore', fr. L. litus, gen. litoris. See prec.
word and -ella.

## liturgies
liturgies, п., the study of public worship. —
Formed fr. liturgy with suff. -ics.

## llturglology
llturglology, п., the study of liturgy. —
Compounded of liturgy and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## litigation
litigation, п., the act of litigating; a lawsuit. —
Late L. litigdtid, gen. -onis, 'a dispute, quarrel',
fr. L. l!tigdt-(um), pp. stem of litigare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## litigator
litigator, п., one who litigates. — L. litigator, 'a
disputant', fr. lltigdt-(jim), pp. stem of litigare.
See litigate and agential suff. -or.

## litigious
litigious, adj., quarrelsome. — ME., fr. MF (=F.)
litigieux (fem. litigieuse), fr. L. litigiosus, 'full of

tigium, 'dispute, litigation', fr. litigare. See

Derivatives: litigious-ly, adv., litigious-ness, a.

## litmus
litmus, п., a dyestuff obtained from lichens. —
ON. litmose, lit. 'lichen for dyeing', fr. litr,

OE. wlite, 'splendor, appearance, face, form',
OS. wliti, of s.m., OFris. wlite, 'exterior, form',
Goth, wlits, 'face, form', and to the second
element in OE. and-wlita, ON. and-lit, OFris. and-
lete, OHG. ant-lizzi, MHG. ant-litze, ant-lutze,
G. Ant-litz,'(ace, countenance'(the first element

gaze', ON. lita, 'to look', tela, 'to seek, search',
Goth, wlaltdn, 'to spy, look'. These words are
prob. rel. to Goth, wulpus, 'splendor', and cogn.
with L. voltus, vultus, 'expression of the face,
countenance, look', W. gweled, 'to see' and ult.
derive fr. I.-E. base * wet-, 'to see'.

## litotes
litotes, п., a figure of rhetoric in which an
affirmative is expressed by the negative of its opposite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:453 COLUMN:3 -->
Oerivatives:liturgiolog-icat,adi.,liuirgiolog-ist,n.

## liturgy
liturgy, п., public worship. — F. limrgie, fr.
LateL. titurgia, fr. Gk. ληϊτουργία, λειτουργία,
'public duty, public worship', fr. ληϊταυργός,
λειτουργός, 'public servant', which is
compounded of λήϊτος, λεϊτος, 'of the people', and
a contracted form of έργον, 'work'. The first
element derives fr. λαός, Att. λεώς, 'people'.
See lay, 'pertaining to the laity'. For the second
element see work and cp. ergon and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: liturg-ic, liturg-ic-al, adjs., titurg-
ic-at-ty, adv., liturg-ist, n.

## lltuus
lltuus, п., the crooked staff borne by the augurs. —
L., of uncertain etymology; possibly a deriv. of
I.-E. base *lii-, 'to bend; to be movable, be
nimble', whence also OE. lip, 'joint, limb', OE.
lim, 'member'. See limb,'member', andep. words
there referred to.

## live
live, intr. and tr. v. — ME. liven, livien, fr. OE.
libban, liftan, rel. to OS. tibbian, ON. Ufa, OFris.
libba, liva, OHG. leben. MHG., G. leben,
Goth. liban, 'to live', fr. I.-E. base *leip-, 'to
remain, persevere, continue, live', whence also
Gk. λϊπαρεΐν, 'to persist, persevere'. See leave,
v., and words there referred to and cp. esp. life,
liver and the second element in celibate.
Derivatives: liv-able, adj., live, adj., tiv-ing, adj.
and n.

## live
live, adv. — Aphetic for alive.

## livelihood
livelihood, n. — Altered fr. ME. livelode, lit.
'course of life', fr. OE. llf-tad, 'life way'. See life
and lode.

## livelong
livelong, adj. — ME. lef long; see lief and long,
adj. The first element was confused later with
live.

## lively
lively, adj. —Partly fr. ME., fr. OE. llflic, 'living,
life-giving', lit. 'lifelike', fr. llf, 'life', and -tic,
'-ly'; partly newly formed fr. life and adj. suff.
-ly.
Derivative: liveli-ness, a.

## liven
liven, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. life with suff.
-en, Cp. enliven.

## liver
liver, п., one who, or that which, lives. — Formed
from the verb live with agential suff. -er.

## liver
liver, п., secreting organ of the body. — ME., fr.
OE. lifer, rel. to ON. lifr, Dan., Swed. lever,
OFris. livere, MDu. levere, lever, Du. lever,
OHG. lebara, MHG. lebere, leber, G. Leber,
'liver', and cogn. with Arm. leard (fr. "lepard),
'liver', and possibly also with Gk. λιπαρός 'oily,
fat, greasy'. See leave, v., and cp. life, live.

## livery
livery, п., 1) allowance of food; 2) distinctive
uniform of servants. — ME. livere, fr. OF. tivree
(F. tivree), orig. 'clothes delivered by the master
to his servants', prop. fem. pp. of livrer, 'to
deliver, hand over', which is a doublet of liberer,
"to set free', fr. L. liberdre, 'to set free', fr. liber,
'free'. See liberal and words there referred to.
For sense development cp. delivery.
Derivative: liveri-ed, adj.

## livery
livery, adj., resembling liver. — Formed fr. liver,
'secreting organ of the body', with -y
(corresponding to OE. -ig).

## livid
livid, adj., of a bluish color. — F. livide, fr. L.
lividus (for *sllvidus), 'bluish, livid*, fr. livere,
for 'slive're, 'to be of a bluish color', which is
cogn. witn OSlav. stiva, 'plum' (prop, 'the fruit
of blue color'), Olr. II, W. Itiw, 'color, splendor',
OE. sta, sldh, 'sloe'. See sloe and -id
(representing L. -idus).
Derivatives: livid-ity, п., lirid-ly, adv., livid-ness,
n.

## livor
livor, п., bluish discoloration of the surface of the
body. — L. /Ivor, 'bluish color', fr. livere, 'to be
of a bluish color'. See livid and -or.

## Uvre
Uvre, п., ancient French money of account. — F.,
lit. 'a pound', fr. L. libra. See libra and cp. lira,
liter, litra.

## lixiviate
lixiviate, tr. v., to leach. — Formed with verbal
suff. -ate fr. L. lixivius, 'made into lye', fr. lix,
'ashes, lye', which is rel. to liquire, 'to be fluid,
be liquid'. See liquid and cp. prolix.
Derivative: lixiviat-ion, n.

## lizard
lizard, n. — ME. lesard, fr. OF. laisard, lesard,
fem. laisarde (F. Uzard, fem. lizarde), formed—
with change of suffix—fr. L. lacertus (masc),
resp. lacerta (fem.), 'lizard', which stand for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:454 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 427 | LOCUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:454 COLUMN:1 -->
"lacer-tos, *lacro-tos, resp. *lacer-ta, "lacro-ta,
and derive fr. I.-E. base "leq-, *leq-, 'to bend,
twist', whence prob. also L. locusta,
'grasshopper, locust', lit. 'thejumper', ON. leggr, 'leg'.
See leg and cp. Lacerta, lacertian, lobster, locnst.
Cp. also It. lucerta, OProvenc. lazert, tauzert,
Sp. lagarto, 'lizard', which all derive fr. L.
lacerta, resp. lacertus. Cp. also alligator.

## llama
llama, п., a S. American ruminant animal. — Sp.,
fr. Peruv. native name.

## llanero
llanero, п., a cowboy. — Sp., lit. 'plainsman', fr.
llano, 'plain'. See next word.

## llano
llano, п., one of the extensive plains of S.
America. — Sp., 'plain, even, level, smooth', fr. L.
planus. See plain, adj.

## Lloyd
Lloyd, masc. PN. — W. Llwyd, lit. 'gray'.

## Lloyd's
Lloyd's, п., an association of marine
underwriters. — So called from Lloyd's Coffee House in
Tower St., London, opened by Edward Lloyd in
1688.

## lo
lo, interj. — A blend of ME. lo, fr. OE. IS, with
ME. lo, prob. a short form of loke, imper. of
loken, 'to look'. See look and cp. the second
element in wellaway.

## loach
loach, п., a small edible fish. — ME., fr. F. loche,
which is of unknown origin.

## load
load, п., a burden. — ME. lode, 'way, course;
load', fr. OE. lad, 'way, journey, course;
carrying of goods; sustenance'; rel. to lead, 'to guide',
and to lode; influenced in meaning by the verb
lade, to which, however, it is not related.
Derivatives: load, tr. and intr. v., load-ed, adj.,
load-er, n.

## loadstar
loadstar, n. — See lodestar.

## loadstone
loadstone, lodestone, п., magnetite; magnet. —
Compounded of load, lode (fr. OE. lad), and
stone.

## loaf
loaf, n. — ME. la/, lof, fr. OE. A/a/, 'bread, loaf,
rel. to ON. hleifr. Swed. lev, Norw. leiv, OFris.
hlef, OHG. hleib, leib, MHG. leip, leib, G. Laib,
Goth, hlaifs, 'bread, loaf. OSlav. ehlebu, Lett.
klaips and Finn, leipa, 'bread, loaf, are very
probably Teut. loan words. L. tibum, 'cake', is
not cognate with the above Teut. words. Cp.
lady, lord, Lammas.

## loaf
loaf, intr. v., to loiter about. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: loaf-er, п., loaf-ing, adj., loaf-ing-ly,
adv.

## loam
loam, n. — ME. lam, tome, fr. OE. lam, rel. to OS.
lemo, Du. leem, OHG. lelmo, MHG. leime,
leim, G. Lehm, 'loam', and to OE. Urn, 'lime'.
See lime, 'birdlime', and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: loam, tr. v., loam-y, adj., loam-i-ly,
adv., loam-i-ness, n.

## loan
loan, n. — ME. Ian, Ion, fr. ON. Ian, which is rel.
to OE. lin, 'lending, thing lent, loan', ISnan, 'to
lend', OS., OHG. lehan, OFris. ten, 'thing lent,
loan', Du. leen, 'loan, fief, MHG. lehen, G.
Lehen, Lehn, 'fief, OE. lion, ON. Ija, OFris.
lia, 'to lend', OHG. lihan, 'to borrow', MHG.
Шеп, 'to borrow; lo lend', G. leihen, 'to lend',
rarely, 'to borrow', Goth, leihan, 'to lend'. The
orig. meaning of these verbs was 'to let have,
leave'. They derive fr. I.-E. base 4tqw-, 'to let,
leave', whence also OI. rindkti, 'leaves', riktah,
'empty', reknah, 'possession, property', atire-
kah, 'remainder', Arm. Ik'anem, 'i leave', e-lik',
'he left', Gk. λείπειν, 'to leave', λοιπής,
'remaining, surviving'. L. linquere (perf. liqui), 'to
leave', Lith. liekii, likli, 'to leave behind', liktas,
Lett, likts, 'left, left over', Lith. lekas, 'left
behind', palaikas, 'remainder', the second element
in OSlav. otu-leku, of s.m., OPruss. polinka, 'he
remains', Olr. leicim, Ί leave', and the second
element in Lilh. viemio-lika, 'eleven', dvy-lika,
'twelve'. Cp. lend and the second element in
eleven, twelve. Cp. also relinquish and delict,
delinquent, derelict, eclipse, ellipse, ellipsis, elliptic,
limma, Про-, 'lacking', paraleipsis.
Derivatives: loan, tr. and intr. v., loan-able, adj.,
loan-er, n.

## loan word
loan word, — Loan translation of G. Lehnwort,
which is compounded of lehnen, 'to borrow',
and Wort, 'word'. See loan and word.

## Loasa
Loasa, п., a genus of American plants (bot.)—
ModL., from a S. American Indian native word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:454 COLUMN:2 -->

## Loasaceae
Loasaceae, n. pi., the loasa family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with surf, -aceae.

## loasaceous
loasaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## loath
loath, loth, adj. — ME. lath, loth, fr. OE. lad,
'hateful, hostile', rel. to OS., OFris. leth, ON.
leidr, of s.m., Dan., Swed. led, 'odious', OHG.
leid, MHG. leit. Offensive, grievous', G. leid,
'painful', OHG. leid, MHG. leit, G. Leid,
'sorrow', Du. leed, 'sorrow', and prob. cogn. with
Toch. Aa-litk, 'to beaverse', Gk. άλιτεΐν, 'tosin',
άλείτης, άλοιτός, 'sinner', Ir. liuss (for "litu-s),
'horror, disgust'. F. laid, 'ugly', is borrowed fr.
Frankish *laid, which corresponds to OHG.
leid, 'offensive, grievous'.
Derivatives: toath-ful, adj., loath-ful-ly, adv.,
loath-ful-ness, п., loath-some, adj., loath-some-ly,
adv., loath-some-ness, n.

## loathe
loathe, tr. v. — ME. lothen, fr. OE. ladian, fr. lad,
'hateful, hostile'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: loath-ing, п., loath-ing-ly, adv.

## loathly
loathly, adj. — ME. lothly, fr. OE. Iddlic,
'hateful, horrible, unpleasant', fr. lad, 'hateful,
hostile'. See loath.
Derivative: loathli-ness, n.

## lob
lob, п., a clumsy person. — Orig. prob. imitative
and suggesting 'something clumsy; a thick mass
of flesh or fat'. Cp. lop, 'to hang down'. Cp. also
looby, lubber.
Derivative: lob, intr. v., to move clumsily.

## lobar
lobar, adj., pertaining to a lobe or lobes. — ModL.
lobdris, fr. Late L. lobus. See lobe and -ar.

## lobate
lobate, adj., having lobes. — ModL. lobatus, fr.
Late L. lobus. See lobe and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: lobat-ed, adj., lobate-ly, adv., lobal-
ion, n.

## lobby
lobby, п., a hall; a vestibule. — ML. laubia,
lobia, fr. OHG. 'laubja. See lodge, which is a
doublet of lobby.
Derivatives: lobby, tr. and intr. v., lobby-er, п.,
lobby-ism, п., lobby-ist, n.

## lobe
lobe, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. Late L. lobus, fr. Gk.
λοβός, 'lobe of the ear; lobe of the liver; lobe of
the lung; seed, pod', prob. rel. to Gk. λέβινθοι,
'peas', λεβηρίς, 'husk of fruits'; fr. I.-E. base
*leb-, which is rel. to base 'lep-, 'to peel',
whence Gk. λέπειν, 'to peel'. See leper and cp.
lobule and the second element in bilobate,
trilobate, autilobluin, Gonolobus.
Derivative: lob-ed, adj.

## Lobelia
Lobelia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Flemish botanist Matthias de
Lobel (1538-1616). For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## Lobeliaceae
Lobeliaceae, n. pi., the lobelia family (bot.) —
ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## lolx'liaceous
lolx'liaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## loblolly
loblolly, п., 1) a thick gruel; 2) a mudhole. — Of
uncertain origin; perh. compounded of dial. E.
lob, 'to bubble in boiling', and dial. E. lolly,
'broth'.

## lobscouse
lobscouse, п., stewed dish of meat, vegetables,
etc. — Of uncertain origin; cp. prec. word and
scouse.

## lobster
lobster, п., an edible marine shellfish. — ME., fr.
OE. lopustre, loppestre, prob. corruption of L.
locusta, 'lobster; locust'. See locust.

## Lobularia
Lobularia, п., a genus of plants, thesweet alyssum
(.bot.) — ModL., fr. Late L. lobulus, 'lobule', fr.
F. lobule. See next word and adj. suff. -ary.

## lobule
lobule, п., a small lobe. — F. lobule, dimin. of
lobe. See lobe and -ule.
Derivative: lobul-ar, adj.

## lobworm
lobworm, п., a lugworm — Compounded of lob
and worm,

## local
local, adj. — ME. localle, fr. MF. (= F). local, fr.
Late L. localis, 'pertaining to a place', fr. L.
locus, 'place". See locus and'adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: local, п., local-ism, п., locality-
(q.v.), local-ize, tr. v., local-iz-ation, п., local-ly,
adv., local-ness, n.

## locale
locale, п., a place or locality. — F. local, fr. Late
L. localis, 'pertaining to a place'. See prec. word.

## locality
locality, n. — F. localiti, fr. Late L. localitatem,
ace. of locaUtas, 'locality', fr. localis. See local
and -ity.

## locate
locate, tr. v., to find the place of. — L. locatus,

## pp. of locdre
pp. of locdre, *to place, put, set, dispose,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:454 COLUMN:3 -->
arrange', fr. locus, 'place'. See locus and verbal
suff. -ate and cp. allocate, collocate, dislocate,
couch, accouchement,

## location
location, n. — L. locatio, gen. -6nis, 'a placing,
location, disposition', fr. locatus, pp. of locare.
See prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: location-al, adj.

## locative
locative, adj., pertaining to a case indicating
place; п., the locative case. — Incorrectly
formed fr. L. locus, 'place', on analogy of L. vocdti-
vus, 'vocative' (fr. vocdtus, pp. of vocare, 'to call,
summon'). See locus and -ive.

## loch
loch, п., a lake. — Gael, loch, 'lake', rel. to Olr.
loch, OCo:, Bret, lagen, 'lake', and cogn. with
L. lacus, 'lake'. See lake, 'a pool', and cp. lough,

## lochia
lochia, п., the discharge from the uterus after
childbirth '(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. λόχια,
neut. pi. of λόχιος, 'pertaining to childbirth', fr.
λόχος, 'childbirth', which stands in gradational
relationship to λέχος, 'bed'. See lie, 'to recline',
and cp. the second element in Aristolochla,
Gelecbla.
Derivative: lochi-al, adj.

## lochio-
lochio-, pertaining to childbirth. — Fr. Gk.
λόχιος, 'pertaining to childbirth'. See prec. word.

## lock
lock, п., tuft of hair. — ME. lokk, lokke, fr. OE.
locc, rel. to ON. lokkr, OS., OFris., Du. lok,
OHG., MHG. loc, G. Locke, 'lock of hair', fr.
I.-E. base*leug-, *Iug-,'to bend,twist',whencealso
Gk. λυγίζειν, 'to bend, twist', λύγος, 'any
pliant twig, withe', OL. luctdre, L. luctdrt, 'to
wrestle, struggle, strive, contend', lit. 'to twist,
intertwine', Lith. litgnas, Lett, lugt, 'flexible',
OE, Нас, lee, 'leek, garlic'. Cp. leek, lnck. Cp.
also ineluctable, luxate, luxe, relnct, Lygodiuin.

## lock
lock, п., a contrivance for closing doors. — ME.
lok, fr. OE. loc, 'lock, bolt', rel. to OE. Mean,
OS. Шкап, ΟΝ., OFris. Шка, OHG. luhhan,
Goth, ga-lukan, 'to close, shut up', ON. lok
(neut.), luka (fern.), 'fastening, lock', Goth, us-
luks, 'opening', OHG. loh, MHG. loch,
'dungeon, cavern, hole', G. Lech, 'hole, opening',
Du. luik, 'shutter; trapdoor', G. Luke, 'dormer
window', and cogn. with OI. rujati, 'breaks',
Lith. Iiiitl, 'to break' (intr.), lauzyti, 'to break'
(tr.); see Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p. 443 s.v.
Loch. See lugabrious and cp. locket and the
second element in padlock. Cp. also lucaroe.
Derivatives: lock, tr. and intr. v., lock-ed, adj.,
lock-er, п., locket (q.v.), lock-ful, п., lock-ing,
adj. and verbal п., lock-less, adj., lock-let, n.

## locket
locket, п., a small hinged case worn on a
necklace. — OF. (= F.) loquet, 'latch of door',
dimin. of OF. loc, 'lock, latch', fr. ON. lok,
'lock'. See 2nd lock and -et.

## Lockian
Lockian, adj., pertaining to John Lock (1632-
i704) or to his philosophy.

## lockram
lockram, п., also lockeram, a cheap kind of linen
cloth. — ME. lokerham, fr. MF. (— F.) locre-
nan, locronan, fr. Locronan, name of a place in
Lower Brittany where it was first made. The
name Locronan lit. means 'Ronan's cell' (fr.
Bret, lok, 'cell' and the PN. Ronan). Cp. St. Re-
nan, the modern name of the same place.

## loco-
loco-, combining form meaning 'from place to
place', as in locomotive. — Fr. L. locus, 'place'.
See locus.

## locomote
locomote, intr. v. — Back formation fr.
locomotion. Cp. donate, orate.

## locomotion
locomotion, n. — Compounded of L. loco, abl. of
locus, 'place' and motio, gen. -onis, 'amoving'.
See locus and motion.

## locomotive
locomotive, adj. — Compounded of L. loco, abl.
of locus, 'place', and Late L. mdtivus, 'moving'.
See locus and motive.
Derivatives: locomotive, п., locomottv-ity, n.

## locomotor
locomotor, adj. and n. — Compounded of L. loco,
abl. of locus, 'place', and motor, 'mover*. See
locus and morur.

## locuiar
locuiar, adj., having loculi. — Formed fr. loculus
with suff. -ar.

## loculus
loculus, п., a cell (bot. and zool.) — L., 'a little
place', dimin. of locus, 'place'. See locus and -ule.

## locumtenens
locumtenens, п., a deputy. — L., 'holding the
place', fr. locum, ace. of locus, 'place', and te-
nens, pres. part, of tenere, 'to hold'. See tenant
and cp. lieutenant

## locus
locus, n. — L„ 'place', fr. OL. stlocus, lit. 'where

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:455 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LOCUST | 428 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:455 COLUMN:1 -->
something is placed', fr. I.-E. base *st(h)el-, 'to
cause to stand, to place'. See stall and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also lieu and the second
element in milieu.

## locust
locust, n. — ME., fr. L. locusta, 'grasshopper,
locust', prob. fr. *lokos-ta, lit. 'the jumper', and
rel. to tacertus (masc.), lacerta (fem.), 'lizard';
see lizard and cp. lobster. For the form of L.
locusta cp. robustus, 'strong', onusius, 'laded,
loaden'. For the sense development of locusta
cp. F. sauterelle, 'grasshoper, locust', fr. sauter,
'to leap, hop', G. Heuschrecke, 'grasshopper,
locust', lit. 'hay-jumper', fr. Ней, 'hay', and
schrecken, in the orig. meaning of this verb, 'to
jump'.

## locusta
locusta, п., I) a spikelet (bot.); 2) (cap.) a genus of
grasshoppers (zool.) — ModL., fr. L. locusta,
'locust'. See locust.

## locution
locution, п., style of speech. — L. locmid, gen.
-onis, 'a speaking, speech, discourse', fr. locutus,
pp. of loqui, 'to speak'. See loquacious and -ion
and cp. allocution, elocution.

## lode
lode, п., 1) way, course; 2) vein of ore. — ME.
lod, lode, fr. OE. lad, 'way, journey, course;
carrying of goods; sustenance', rel. to OE. /Мол,
'to go, travel', Ixdan, 'to lead, guide'. See lead
and cp. load and the second element in
livelihood.

## lodestar
lodestar, also loadstar, n. — Compounded of
lode and star; lit. 'a leading star'.

## lodestone
lodestone, n. — See loadstone.

## lodge
lodge, n. — ME. loge, logge, fr. OF. loge, 'arbor,
hut' (whence F. loge, 'hut, cabin, lodge, box at
a theater'), fr. OHG. "laubja, louba, 'porch,
gallery', whence MHG. loube, of s.m. (whence
G. Laube, 'bower, arbor', which was influenced
in meaning by Laub, 'foliage'; see leaf). OHG.
louba is rel. to ON. lopt, 'upper room'. See loft
and cp. lobby, loge, loggia. Cp. also logistics.

## lodge
lodge, intr. and tr. v. — ME. loggen, fr. OF. logier
(F. loger), 'to lodge', fr. loge, 'lodge'. See lodge,
n.
Derivatives: lodg-er, п., lodg-lng, п.,
lodgement (q.v.)

## lodgment
lodgment, lodgement, n. — MF. (= F.) logement,
fr. OF., fr. loger. See lodge, v., and -ment.

## loess
loess, п., an unslratified deposit of loam. — G.
Loss, coined by K.C. von Leonhard in 1823
through the alteration of Losch, 'soil
interspersed with snail-shells', fr. dial. Swiss losch,
'loose', the equivalent of G. los, of s.m. See
loose.

## loft
loft, n. — ME., fr. Late OE. loft, fr. ON. lopt, 'air,
sky, upper room', which is rel. to OE. lyft (dial.
E. lift), Du. lucht, OHG., MHG., G. luft, Goth.
luflus, 'air'. Cp. aloft,lift. Cp. also lodge, n.
Derivatives: loft, tr. v., loft-er, п., loft-i-ly, adv.,
loft-i-ness, п., loft-ing, a.

## log
log, п., a heavy piece of wood. — ME. logge, of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. lag (whence Dan. laag,
Norw. log), 'felled tree', orig. 'that which lies',
from the stem of ON. liggja, 'to lie'. See lie, 'to
recline', and cp. the first element in ioggerhead.
Derivatives: log, tr. v., to cut into logs; intr. v.,
to fell trees and transport the logs to a sawmill,
adj., logged (q.v.), logg-er, п., logg-ing, n.

## log
log, п., a liquid measure, the 12th part of a hin.
— Heb. Ugh, rel. to Syr. laggd, laggetha, *a
(dessert) dish', and prob. also to Arab. Idjja, 'was
deep', laij, 'depth, abyss', Akkad. lignu, 'vase,
vessel'. Cp. also Copt, lok, 'a liquid measure',
and see lagena.

## log
log, n. — Abbrev. of logarithm.

## log-
log-, form of logo- before a vowel.

## loganberry
loganberry, п., a kind of dewberry. — So called
after the American jurist James Harvey Logan
(1841-1928), who first cultivated it.

## Logania
Logania, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after James Logan (1614-1751), an Irish
botanist, secretary to William Penn. For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Loganiaceae
Loganiaceae, n. pi., the logania family (bot.) —
ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## loganiaceous
loganiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## logan stone
logan stone, rocking stone. — For logging stone,
lit. 'rocking stone', fr. dial. E. log, 'to rock'.

## logarithm
logarithm, n. — Lit. 'ratio-number', fr. L. loga-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:455 COLUMN:2 -->
rithmus, a word coined by the Scottish
mathematician John Napier (1550-1617) in 1614 fr. Gk.
λόγος, 'word, ratio', and αριθμός, 'number'.
See logos and arithmetic.
Derivatives: logarithm-ic, adj., logarithmic-al-ly,
adv.

## loge
loge, п., box in a theater. — F. See lodge, n.

## logged
logged, adj., made heavy. — Formed with suff.
-ed fr. log, 'to cut into logs'. See log, 'a piece of
wood'.

## loggerhead
loggerhead, п., a blockhead. — Fr. obsol. log
head, compounded of log, 'a pieceof wood', and
head. For sense development cp. blockhead.
Derivative: loggerhead-ed, adj.

## loggia
loggia, п., a roofed gallery used as an open-air
room. — It., fr. F. loge. See lodge, п., and cp.
lobby.

## logic
logic, n. — ME. logike, fr. OF. (— F.) logique,
fr. L. logica, fr. Gk. λογική, which is short for
λογική τέχνη, 'logic art', i.e. 'the art of speaking
and reasoning'; λογική is fem. of λογικός,
'pertaining to speaking or reasoning, logical', fr.
λόγος, 'word, speech; reason'. See logos and -ic.

## logical
logical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
logicus, fr. Gk. λογικός, 'logical'. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: logical-ly, adv., logical-ity, n.

## logician
logician, п., one skilled in logic. — F. logicien, fr.
logique, 'logic'. See logic and -ian.

## logie
logie, п., a piece of sham jewellery. — Named
after the English inventor David Logie, who
invented it about 1860.

## loglon
loglon, p]. logia, saying of Jesus not recorded in
the Gospels. — Gk. λόγιον, 'a saying', fr. λόγος,
'word, speech'. See logos.

## logistic
logistic, adj., skilled in logic. — ML. logisticus
(prob. through the medium of F. logistique), 'of
calculation; of reasoning', fr. Gk. λογιστικός,
'skilled in calculation, skilled in reasoning', fr.
λογίζεσθαι, 'to calculate, reason', fr. λόγος,
'word, speech, reason; calculation'. See logos
and -istic.

## logistic
logistic, п., the art of calculation, arithmetic. —
See prec. word.

## logistics
logistics, п., the art of transporting, quartering
and supplying troops. — F. logistique (short for
Part logistique), a hybrid coined fr. F. logis, 'a
lodging' (fr. loger, 'to lodge', loger des soldats,
'to quarter soldiers', fr. loge, 'hut, cabin, lodge'),
and the Greek suff.-ιστικός. See lodge and -istic.
For the ending of logistics see suff. -ics.

## logo-
logo-, before a vowel log-, combining form
meaning 'word, speech', as in logogram, logo-
griph.—Fr. Gk. λόγος, 'word, speech'. Seelogos.

## logodaedaly
logodaedaly, п., a playing with words. — Gk.
λογοδαιδαλία. See logo-, daedal and -y
(representing Gk. -ίϊ).

## logogram
logogram, п., a letter or sign representing a word.
— Compounded of logo- and Gk. γράμμα, gen.
γράμματος, 'letter', lit. 'that which is written'.
See -gram and cp. grammalogue.
Derivative: logogrammat-ic, adj.

## logograph
logograph, п., a logogram. — Compounded of
logo- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graph.
Derivative: logograph, tr. v.

## logographic
logographic, adj., pertaining to logography. —
Gk. λογογραφικός, 'of writing speeches', fr.
λογογραφίδ. See next word and -ic.
Derivative: logographic-al-ly, adv.

## logography
logography, п., a method of reporting speeches in
longhand, each of several reporters taking down
a few words in succession. — Gk. λογογραφίδ,
'a writing of speeches', fr-λογογράφος, 'a speech
writer', compounded of Gk. λόγος, 'word,
speech', and -γραφίϊ, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See logo-, -graph and -y (representing Gk. -is).

## logogriph
logogriph, п., word puzzle. — Compounded of
logo- and Gk. γρίφος, 'fishing net; something
intricate; a riddle', which prob. stands for *grl-
bhos and is cogn. witn MHG. krebe, 'basket',
ON. kiarf kerfi, 'bundle', OI. grapsah, 'bundle'.

## logomachy
logomachy, п., a fight in, or about, words. — Gk.
λογομαχία, 'war about words4, compounded of
λόγος, 'word, speech', and μάχη, 'battle'. See
logo- and -machy.

## logometric
logometric, adj., serving to represent graphically
chemical elements (chem.) — Compounded of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:455 COLUMN:3 -->
logo- and Gk. μέτρ"ον, 'measure'. See metric.

## logos
logos, п., the divine Word. — Gk. λόγος, 'word,
speech; word which expresses the inward
thought; the thought itself; tale, story; maxim,
proverb, narrative; prose; ratio, reason;
relation, proportion, analogy, calculation,
reckoning, account; discussion, deliberation,
dialogue', fr. λέγειν, 'to pick out, choose; to speak,
declare', and cogn. with L. legere, 'to gather,
collect; to pick out, choose; to read, recite'. See
lecture and cp. logic, logistic, adj., -logue, -logy,
Alogians, apologue, curiologic, Decalog, dialect.
Cp. also paralogism, syllogism.

## logothete
logothete, п., name of various officers of the
Byzantine empire. — ML. logotheia, orig. 'an
auditor of accounts', fr. Gk. λογοθέτης, which is
compounded of λόγος, 'word, speech; account',
and -θέτης, a derivative of θη-, the stem of
τιθέναι, 'to place, set, lay down'. See logo- and
theme.

## logotype
logotype, п., two or more letters cast in a single
type (print) — Compounded of logo- and type.
Derivative: logotyp-y, n.

## -logue
-logue, combining form denoting a kind of
discourse as in dialogue, epilogue. — F. -logue, fr.
Gk. -λόγος. See -logy.

## -logy
-logy, combining form denoting a 'speaking,
discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science', as in
biology, geology. — Gk. -λογία (either directly
or through the medium of OF. or F. -logie or
ML. -logia), fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)', fr. λέγειν, 'to pick up, choose; to speak,
declare', whence also λόγος, 'word, speech;
account'. In some cases—as e.g. in τριλογία,
'trilogy', τετραλογία, 'tetralogy'—-λογία derives
directly from λόγος. See logos and cp. -ology.

## lohoch
lohoch, lohock, п., Iinctus. — MF. (= F.)
looch, fr. Arab, la'uq, in vulgar pronunciation
la'Oq, lit. 'anything licked', fr. Ia4qa, 'he licked'.
Cp. L. Iinctus, fr. lingere, 'to lick'.

## toimic
toimic, adj., pertaining to plague. — Gk. λοιμι-
κός, 'pertaining to pestilence or plague', fr.
λοιμός, 'pestilence, plague', which is prob. rel. to
λιμός, 'hunger', λοιγός, 'ruin, destruction,
disease, death', and possibly to ολίγος, 'small, little,
few'. See oligo- and -ic and cp. the second
element in bulimia.

## loimo-
loimo-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
plague, pestilential'. — Gk. λοιμό-, fr. λοιμός,
'pestilence, plague'. See prec. word.

## loin
loin, n. — ME. loyne, fr. loigne, logne, var. of
OF. (F.) longe, 'loin', fr. ML. *lumbea, fem. of
*Iumbeus, adj. used as a noun, fr. L. lumbus,
'loin'. See lumbar and cp. the second element in
sirloin.

## loir
loir, п., a species of dormouse. — F., fr. VL. gli-
rem, corresponding to L. glirem, ace. of gits,
'dormouse', which is cogn. with OI. girih, girika,
'mouse', Gk. γαλέη, 'weasel, polecat, marten'.
See galea and cp. lerot.

## Loiseleuria
Loiseleuria, п., a genus of plants, the Alpine
azalea (bot.) — ModL., named after the French
botanist J. L. A. Loi'se/eiw-Delongchamps (1774-
1849). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## loiter
loiter, intr. and tr. v. — ME. loitren, fr. MDu.
loteren, 'to be loose' (whence Du. leuteren, 'to
delay, linger, loiter'), which is rel. to OE. lod-
dere, 'beggar', ME. loader, 'good-for-nothing',
OHG. lotar, 'empty, vain', MHG. loter, 'loose,
vain, frivolous', G. Lotterbube, 'vagabond,
rascal', OE. lydre, 'base, bad, wicked'. Seelither.
Derivative: loiter-er, n.

## loka
loka, п., open space, universe, world (Hinduism).
— OI. lokah, lit. 'a clear place, clearing', rel. to
lokayati, locdyati, 'regards, looks at', fr. I.-E.
base *leuq-, 'to see, behold', which is identical
with base "leuq-, 'to emit light, shine; bright'.
See light, 'brightness', and cp. the first element
in lokapala.

## lokapala
lokapala, п., a guardian of the world, prop, one
of the eight deities who guard the eight cardinal
points (Hindu mythol.) — OI. lokapaldh,
compounded of lokah, 'open space, universe, world',
and paldh, 'guardian'. For the first element see
ioka. The second element derives fr. I.-E. base
*po-, 'to keep, guard, protect', whence also OI.
pdti, 'he guards, protects!, go-pah, 'shepherd'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:456 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 429 | LOQUACIOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:456 COLUMN:1 -->
This base is rel., and equivalent in meaning, to
base *pd-, whence pa-scere, 'to feed, nourish1,
pastor, 'shepherd'. See food.

## Lola
Lola, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Sp. Dolores (q.v.)

## Loligo
Loligo, п., a genus of squids (zool.) — L. lolligo,
loligo, 'cuttlefish1, of uncertain origin.

## Lolium
Lolium, п., a genus of plants, the darnel (pot.) —
L. lolium, 'darnel', of uncertain etymology.
OHG. lolli (whence MHG. lullick, lulche, G.
Lolch), 'darnel', is a Latin loan word.

## loll
loll, intr. v., to lounge; tr. v., to let hang. — ME.
lollen, lullen 'to lounge', of imitative origin. See
lull and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: loll, п., loll-er, n.

## Lollard
Lollard, п., memberof a sect of reformers,
followers of John Wycliffe. — MDu. Lollaerd, lit.
'mutterer (scil. of psalms)', formed fr. lollen, 'to
hum, mumble'. See lull and -ard and cp. loll.
Derivatives: lollard-ism, п., Lollard-y, adj.

## lollipop
lollipop, п., a sweetmeat. — Of uncertain origin.

## lollop
lollop, intr. v., to loll. — Enlarged fr. loll.
Derivative: lollop, a.

## loll shraub
loll shraub, loll sliroh, claret (India). — Hind, lal
sharab, 'red, wine', fr. Pers. lal, 'red', and Arab.
sharab, 'drink, wine' (see sirup).

## loma
loma, п., a membranous fringe (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. λώμα, 'hem, fringe, border', which prob.
stands for *Ρλώμα and is cogn. with L. lorum
(for *wlorum), 'strap, thong'. See lore, 'space
between the eyes and beak of birds', and cp.
next word and the second element in Cycloloma,
Isoloma, Tricholoma.

## Lomatium
Lomatium, п., a genus of plants (hot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. λωμάτιον, 'small border', dimin. of
λώμα. See prec. word.

## Lombard
Lombard, п., 1) an inhabitant of Lombardy; 2) a
banker or moneylender. — F., fr. Late L. Lango-
bardus, Longobardus (= G. Langbart, lit., 'Long
Beard'), one of a Teut. tribe which invaded Italy
in S68. See long, adj., and beard and cp. Lango-
bard. The Lombards were generally known as
pawnbrokers, hence the sense development of
the word Lombard in English. Cp. also OF.
lombart, 'usurer', and see lumber, n.
Derivatives: Lombard, Lombard-esque, Lorn-
bard-ic, adjs.

## loment
loment, n:, a legume which breaks at maturity
into one-seeded indehiscent joints (bol.) — L.
lomentum, 'bean meal (used as a wash)',
contracted fr. lovimentum, which derives fr. lavare
(for "lovare), 'to wash'. See lave and -merit.

## lomentaceous
lomentaceous, adj., bearing loments (bol.) —
Formed with suff. -aceous fr. L. lomentum. See
prec. word.

## loncho-
loncho-, before a vowel lonch-, combining form
meaning 'lance'. — Fr. Gk. λόγχη, 'lance',
which is of uncertain, possibly Sem., origin; cp.
Heb. romah, Aram, rumhd, Arab, rumh, 'lance'.

## lone
lone, adj. — Aphetic form of alone (q.v.)
Derivatives: lone-ly, adj., lone-li-ness, п.,
lonesome, adj., lone-some-ly, adv., lone-some-ness, n.

## long
long, adj. — ME. long, lang, fr. OE. long, lang,
rel. to OS., Dan., Du., OHG., MHG., G.
lang, ON. langr, Swed. lang, MDu., MHG.
lane, Goth, laggs, 'long', and cogn. with L. lon-
gus, 'long', fr. I.-E. base *dlonghos, whence also
MPers. drang, Pers. dirang, 'long'. Base *dlongh-
os is prob. a nasalized derivative of base *de-
legh-, which appears in OI. dirghdh, 'long', Gk.
δόλιχος, 'long', έν-δελεχής, 'constant,
continual', L. in-dulgere, 'to be kind', lit. 'to be long-
suffering'. See dollcho- and cp. indulge. Cp. also
length, Lent, ling, 'a fish', linger, long, v.,
longeron, longitude, lunge, allonge, belong, oblong,
prolong.
Derivatives: long, adv., long-ish, adj.

## long
long, п., a long note (mus.); a long sound
(prosody). — Fr. long, adj.

## long
long, intr. v., to desire. — ME. longen, fr. OE.
langian, 'to grow long; to desire, crave, long
after' (impers.), rel. to OS. langon (impers.), ON.
langa (pers. and impers), MDu. langhen, ver-
langhen (impers. and pers.), OHG. langen
(impers.), bilangen, gilangen (impers. and pers.),
MHG. belangen, also (rarely) verlangen, G. ver-
langen, 'to desire', and to E. long, adj.
Derivative: long-ing, n.

## -long
-long, adverbial suff. expressing direction. — ON.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:456 COLUMN:2 -->
-langr fin endlangr, 'endlong'), from langr, 'long'
(see long, adj.} This suff. has now displaced adv.
suff. -ling.

## longan
longan, п., the tree Euphoria longan or its fruit. —
Chin. lung-yen, lit. 'dragon's eye'.

## longanimity
longanimity, п., patience. — LateL. longanimttas,
'long-suffering, patience, forbearance', fr. L.
tonganimis, 'long-suffering, patient', which is
соmpounded оf longus, 'Iong', and animus, 'soul,
spirit, mind'. See long, adj., animus and -ity.

## longeron
longeron, п., a longitudinal member of an
airplane fuselage. — F., fr. longer, 'to skirt, extend
along', shortened fr. allonger, 'to lengthen'. See
allonge.

## longevity
longevity, п., long duration of life. — Late L.
longaevitds, 'great age, long life', fr. L. longae-
vus, 'of great age', which is compounded of
longus, 'long', and aevum, 'age'. See long, adj.,
age and -ity and cp. aeon and the second element
in coeval, primeval.

## longi-
longi-, combining form meanjng 'long'. — L.
longi-, fr. longus, 'long'. See long, adj.

## longjcorn
longjcorn, adj., having long antennae (zool.) —
Compounded of longi- and L. cornu, 'horn'. See
horn and cp. corn, 'horny induration'.

## longmquity
longmquity, п., remoteness. — L. longuinquitds,
gen. -dtis, 'length, extent, long duration', fr.
longinquus, 'long, extensive, remote, distant',
which is formed fr. longus, 'long', with suff. -in-
quus. See long, adj. For the suff. -inquus cp. L.
propinquus, 'near' (set propinquity).

## longipennate
longipennate, adj., having long wings. —
Compounded of longi- and pennate.

## longirostral
longirostral, adj., having a long beak (ornithol.)
— Compounded of longi- and Late L. rostrdlis.
See rostra].

## longitude
longitude, п., length (geogr. and astron.) — L.
longitude, 'length', fr. longus, 'long'. See long,
adj., and -rude.

## longitudinal
longitudinal, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. longitude, gen. longitudinis, 'length'. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: longitudinal, п., longitudinal-ly, adv.

## longshoreman
longshoreman, n. — Aphetic for along-shore-man.

## long-suffering
long-suffering, n. — First used by Tyndale.

## Loulcera
Loulcera, п., a genus of plants, the honeysuckle
(bot.) — ModL.; so called after the German
botanist Adam Lonilzer (Latinized into Lonicerus)
(1526-86).

## loo
loo, п., a card game. — Short for earlier lanterloo,
fr. F. lanturelu, orig. the refrain of a song.
Derivative: loo, tr. v.

## looby
looby, п., a clumsy fellow. — ME. loby, possibly
derived fr. lob (q.v.), or from the French PN.
Lubin, which was an abusive name for the monk
in the Middle Ages. The former sense of looby
was 'loafer'.

## loof
loof, n. — A variant of luff.

## loofah
loofah, n. — Fr. Arab. lufah. See luffa.

## look
look, intr. v. — ME. token, fr. OE. locian, rel. to
OS. lokon, MDu. loeken, 'to look', OHG. lu-
ogin, MHG. luogen, G. lugen, 'to look out',
and perh. cogn. with Toch. A lak-, 'to see',
and with OCorn. lagat, Bret, lagad, 'eye'. Cp. lo.
Derivatives: look, п., look-er, п., look-ing, adj.

## loom
loom, п., a machine for weaving. — ME. lome,
'tool', fr. OE. getdma, 'tool, utensil', rel. to OE.
andldman (pi.), 'utensils'; of uncertain origin.
Cp. heirloom.
Derivative: loom, tr. v., to weave on a loom.

## loom
loom, intr. v., to appear, lo come into view. —
Of uncertain origin; perhaps orig. meaning 'to
come slowly toward', and rel. to EFris. lomen,
dial. Swed. loma, 'to move slowly'.
Derivatives: loom, п., loom-ing, adj.

## loom
loom, п., a puffin, loon. — Of Scand. origin. Cp.
ON. lomr, Dan., Swed., Norw. lorn. Cp. also
loon, 'a water bird'.

## loon
loon, п., a lout, rascal. — ME. lowen, loun. Cp.
MDu. loen, 'a stupid person'.

## loon
loon, п., a waterbird. — Corrupted fr. loom, 'loon'
(q-v.)

## loony
loony, adj., crazy; п., a crazy person (slang). —
For tuny, short for lunatic.
Derivative: looni-ness, n.

## loop
loop, п., a noose. — Of uncertain, possibly, Celtic,
origin. Cp. Gael, and Ir. lub, 'bend'.
Derivative: loop, tr. and intr. v., to form into a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:456 COLUMN:3 -->
loop.

## loop
loop, п., a small opening. — ME. loupe, perhaps
fr. MDu. Iitpen, 'to lie in wait'. Cp. loophole.

## looper
looper, п., 1) one who or that which loops; 2) a
measuring worm. — Formed fr. loop, 'noose',
with agential suff. -er.

## loophole
loophole, n. — Compounded of loop, 'opening',
and hole.

## loose
loose, adj. — ME, loos, lous, los, fr. ON. lauss,
'loose, free, vacant, dissolute', rel. to OE. leas,
'devoid of: false, feigned, incorrect, worthless',
Dan. hs, 'loose, untied', Swed. los, 'loose,
movable, detached', MDu., Du. los. OS., OHG.,
MHG, los, G. los, 'loose, free', Goth, laus,
'empty, vain', and to OE. for-leosan, 'to lose; to
destroy', losian, 'to perish, be lost'. See lose and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: loose, adv. and tr. v., п., loose-ly,
adv., loos-en, tr. and intr. v., loos-en-er, п.,
looseness, n.

## loosestrife
loosestrife, п., any plant of the genus Lysimachia
(bot) — Compounded of loose, v., and strife;
loan translation of the Greco-Latin name
Lysimachia.

## loot
loot, п., plunder, booty. — Hind. 1Щ, fr. ΟΙ. Ιδ-
tam, lotram, 'booty', which is rel. to luntati,
'robs, plunders', and prob. cogn. with L.
lucrum, 'gain, profit, advantage'. See Incre.
Derivatives: loot, tr. and intr. v., loot-er, n.

## lop
lop, tr. v., to hew, cut. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: lop, п., lopp-ing, n.

## lop
lop, intr. v., to hang down; tr. v., to cause to lop.
— Prob. of imitative origin. Cp. lob.
Derivative: lop, adj.

## lope
lope, intr. v., to move with a long stride; tr. v., to
cause to lope. — ME. lopen, a var. of loupen, fr.
ON. hlaupa, 'to leap'. See leap and cp. loup,
elope, interloper, landloper.
Derivatives: lope, п., lop-er, n.

## Lopezia
Lopezia, п., a genus of plants of the evening
primrose family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
Spanish botanist J. Lopez. For the ending see 1 st
suff. -ia.

## loph-
loph-, form of lopho- before a vowel.

## lophio-
lophio-, before a vowel lophi-, combining form
meaning a 'small crest' or 'small tuft'. — Gk.
λοφίο-, λοφι-, fr. λόφιον, 'a small crest, a small
tuft', dimin. of λόφος, 'crest, tuft'. See lopho-,

## Lophlola
Lophlola, п., a genus of plants of the amaryllis
family (bot.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk.
λόφιον, 'a small crest' (see lophio-), and the L.
suff. -ola (see -ole). The correct form would be
Laphidium, fr. Gk. λοφίοΊον, fr. λόφος, 'crest',
and dimin. surf, -ίδιον (see -idium).

## lopho-
lopho-, before a vowel loph-, combining form
meaning 'crest, tuft'. — Gk. λόφο-, λοφ-, fr.
λόφος, 'back of the neck; crest, tuft', which is
prob. cogn. with Toch. lap, 'summit, head'. Cp.
Zalophus.

## lophobranchiate
lophobranchiate, adj., pertaining to the Lopho-
branchii; п., any of the Lophobranchii. — See
next word and adj. surf. -ate.

## Lophobranchii
Lophobranchii, n. pi., a suborder of teleost fishes
(ichthyol.) — ModL., compounded of lopho- and
Gk. βράγχιον, 'gill' (see branchiate); so called in
allusion to the gills, which are arranged in tufts.

## lophodont
lophodont, adj., having transverse ridges on the
upper surface of the molar teeth (zool.) —
Compounded of loph- and the stem of Gk. οδών,
gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-,

## Lophornis
Lophornis, п., a genus of humming birds, the
coquette (ornithol.) — ModL., compounded of
loph- and Gk. δρυις, 'bird'. See orultho-.

## Lophura
Lophura, п., a genus of pheasants, the fireback
(ornithol.) — ModL., compounded of loph- and
Gk. ούρα, 'tail'. See uro-, 'tail-'.

## lopsided
lopsided, adj., inclining to one side. —
Compounded of lop, 'to hang down', and side.,

## loquacious
loquacious, adj., talkative. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. loquax, gen. -dels, 'talkative', fr. loqui,
'to speak', which is of uncertain etymology. It is
perh. cogn. with Olr. -tluchur in atluchur, Ί
think', duttluchur, Ί pray' (see Ernout-Meillet,
DELL., p. 366 s.v. loquor). Cp. locution,
loquitur, allocution, coliocution, colloquy, elocution,
eloquent, grandiloquent, magniloquent, obloquy,
soliloquy, ventriloquism.
Derivatives: loquacious-ly, adv., loquacious-ness.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:457 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LOQUACITY | 430 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:457 COLUMN:1 -->
η.

## loquacity
loquacity, п., talkativeness. — L. loquacitus,
'talkativeness', fr. loquax, gen. -dcis. See prec. word
and -ity.

## loquat
loquat, п., the Japanese medlar (Eriobotrya ja-
ponica). — Canton Chin, lu kwet,
corresponding to Pekin Chinese lu chit, lit. 'rush orange'.

## loquitur
loquitur, intr. v., he or she speaks (stage
direction). — L., 3rd person pres. indie, sing, ofloqui,
'to speak'. See loquacious.

## Lora
Lora, fem. PN. — A var. of Laura.

## Loran
Loran, п., long range navigation system. —
Invented word, formed fr. the initials of/ongrange
navigation.

## Loranthaceae
Loranthaceae, п., pi., the mistletoe family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Loranthus with suff.
-aceae.

## loranthaceous
loranthaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## Loranthus
Loranthus, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Late Gk. λώρον, 'strap, thong', which is a
loan word fr. L. Idrum, and Gk. ίίνθος, 'flower'.
See lore, 'space between eyes and beak', and
anther.

## lorate
lorate, adj., having the shape of a thong (said of
leaves). — L. ISratus, fr. Idrum, 'thong'. See
lore, 'space between eyes and beak', and adj.
-ate.

## lorcha
lorcha, п., a light Chinese sailing vessel. — Port.

## lord
lord, n. — ME. laverd, loverd, lord, fr. OE. kid-
ford; lit. 'loaf keeper', fr. Maf, 'loaf, and weard,
keeper'. See loaf and ward, 'one who guards',
and cp. laird and the first element in lady.
Derivatives: lord, intr. and tr. v., lord-less, adj.,
lord-ling, п., lordly, adj. (q.v.), lord-ly, adv.,
lordship (q.v.)

## lordly
lordly, adj. — ME., contraction of loverdlich, fr.
OE. hlafordlic, fr. hldford. See lord and adj. suff.
-iy.
Derivative: lord-li-ness, n.

## lordosis
lordosis, п., forward curvature of the spine (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. λόρδωσις, fr. λορδός,
'bent forward', which is prob. cogn. with Arm.
Iorc-к' (pi.), 'distention of the posteriors', Gael.
loirc, 'a deformed foot', MHG. lerz, lurz, 'left'
(lit. 'curved'). For the ending see suff. -osis.

## lordship
lordship, n. — ME., fr. OE. hlafordscipe. See lord
and -ship.

## lore
lore, п., learning, knowledge. — ME. lare, lore,
loor, fr. OE. lar, 'learning, teaching, doctrine,
science', rel. to OS., OHG. lira, OFris. lore, Du.
leer, MHG. le~re, G. Lehre, 'teaching, precept,
doctrine', and to OE. Ixran, 'to teach'. See learn
and cp. words there referred to.

## lore
lore, п., space between the eyes and beak of birds.
— L. Idrum, 'strap, thong', for *wlorum, cogn.
with Gk. εΰληρα (for *έ-5ληρα), Dor. αΰληρα
(for *ιϊ-5ληρα), 'reins', Arm. lar (for *wlar),
'cord, rope', Gk. λώμα (for *Γλώμα), 'hem,
fringe, border', fr. I.-E. base *wel-, 'to turn,
twist, roll', whence also L. volvere, 'to roll, turn
about'. See volute and cp. loma and words there
referred to. Cp. also lorica, loricate, lorimer.

## lorgnette
lorgnette, п., eyeglass, esp. one with a long
handle; an opera glass. — F., fr. lorgner, 'to leer at,
ogle', fr. lorgne, 'squinting'; of uncertain origin.

## lorguon
lorguon, п., an eyeglass; a pair of eyeglasses. —
F., fr. lorgner. See lorgnette.

## lorica
lorica, п., a cuirass; a hard protective covering
(zool.) — L. lorica, 'leather cuirass, corselet of
thong; a plastering', fr. Idrum, 'thong'. See lore,
'space between eyes and beak', and cp. words
there referred to.

## loricate
loricate, adj., covered with a lorica. — L. lorica-
tus, pp. of Idricare, 'to clothe in mail, to plaster',
fr. lorica. See lorica and adj. suff. -ate.

## lorikeet
lorikeet, п., a small parrot allied to the lory. — A
blend of lory and parakeet.

## lorimer
lorimer, loriner, п., a maker of bits for bridles and
saddles (archaic). — ME. lorimer, loriner, fr.
OF. loremier (F. lormier), fr. loraim, lorain,
'bridle strap', fr. VL. *loramen, fr. L. lorum,
'strap, thong, the rein of a bridle'. See lore,
'space between eyes and beak'.

## loriot
loriot, п., the golden oriole. — F., fr. MR,
formed with the agglutination of the def. article
(loriot for OF. I'oriot) and change of suff., fr.
OProvenc. auriol, fr. L. aureolus, 'gold colored',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:457 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. aurum, 'gold' (see ille and aurora and cp.
oriole and the first element in oriflamme); so
called in allusion to its yellow plumage.
According 10 гтгу opinion, the change of suff. -ol to
-ot is due to the dissimilation of the final -/.

## loris
loris, п., either of two small nocturnal lemurs
found in Ceylon and Malaya. — F., of
uncertain origin.

## lorn
lorn, adj., lost, ruined (archaic). — ME. loren,
lorn, fr. OE. -loren, pp. of obsol. leosan, 'to lose',
whence forleosan, 'to lose'. See lose, forlorn.

## lorry
lorry, п., a truck. — Perhaps fr. dial E. lurry, 'to
pull, drag'.
Derivative: lorry, tr. and intr. v.

## lory
lory, п., a small parrot of New Guinea and
Australia. — Malay IQri, 'a kind of parrot', var. of
nuri.

## lose
lose, intr. and tr. v. — ME. losien, 'to perish,
lose', fr. OE. losian, 'to perish, be lost', fr.
los, 'dissolution, destruction', rel. to ON. los,
'breaking up (of the army)', OE. teas, 'devoid of,
for-leosan (pp. for-loren), 'to lose; to destroy',
OS. far-liosan, OFris. ur-liasa, MDu. ver-liesen,
Du. ver-liezen, OHG. vir-liosan, MHG. ver-
liesen, G. ver-lieren, Goth, fra-liusan, 'to lose',
fr. I.-E. base */eus-, an -s-enlargement of base
*le~u-, *1ёи-, *IS-, 'to cut off, untie, separate',
whenceGoth. lun, usluneins, 'ransom', Ol. lunati,
lunoti/cuts, cuts off', lavih, lavitram, 'sickle', Hitt.
la-, 'to untie, undo, unfasten', G.X'ktv, 'to loose,
loosen, untie, slacken; to set free, ransom,
dissolve', λύσις, 'a loosing, setting free,
releasing', λύτρον, 'ransom', Alb. I'aj, Ί pay',perVaj,
Ί rob, deprive', L. luere. Ίο loose, release, atone
for, expiate*, lues, 'plague, pestilence', solvere
(for *se-Iuere), 'to loosen, untie, dissolve'. See
lysis and cp. leasing, -less, loose, losel, loss,
forlorn. Cp. also lues, solve.
Derivatives: los-able, adj., los-er, п., los-ing,
adj., los-ings, n. pi., los-ing-ly, adv.

## losel
losel, п., a worthless person. — ME. losel, fr.
losen (pp. of lesen, 'to lose'), a var. of loren, fr.
OE. loren, pp. of leosan, 'to lose', which is rel. to
OE. losian, 'to perish, be lost'. See lose.

## loss
loss, n. —Back formation fr. lost, pp. of lose (q.v.)

## lost
lost, past tense and pp. of lose.

## lot
lot, n. — ME. lotte, fr. OE. Mot, rel. to ON. hlutr,
'lot, share', OHG, hluj, /ид, 'share of land', OS.
hlot, ON. hlaut, Swed. /oil, Dan. lod, OHG.
A/03, I03, MHG. I03, G. Los, Goth, hlauts, of
s.m., OE. hleotan, OS. hliotan, ON. hljota,
OHG. hliotan, Иозап, MHG. Незеп, 'to cast
lots, to foretell', fr. Teut. base *hlut-, which
possibly meant orig. 'to hook to', and corresponds
to I.-E. base *(s)qleu-, *qlau-, 'a hook, forked
branch, key; to close, shut; to catch, be caught
on'. See close, adj., and cp. words there referred
to. F. lot, 'lot, portion, share', It. lotto, 'lot,
portion, share', lotteria, 'lottery', are Tent, loan
words. Cp. lottery, lotto, allot.
Derivative: lot, tr. v.

## Lot
Lot, п., son of Haran and nephew of Abraham
(Bible). — Heb. Lot, lit. 'envelope, wrap,
covering'.

## lota
lota, lotah, п., a round water vessel. — Hind.
Iota.

## loth
loth, adj. — A var. of loath.

## Lothario
Lothario, п., a rake. — Fr. Lothario, a character
in Rowe's play "The Fair Penitent". The name
Lothario, and its French equivalent Lothaire,
are of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. Hlothari, Hludher
(whence G. Luther), lit. 'famous warrior'. The
first element of this name is rel. to OHG. tut,
'famous, celebrated', the second, to OHG. heri,
'host, army'. See loud and harry.

## lotion
lotion, п., a medicinal wash. — L. lotto, gen. -onis,
'a washing', fr. lotus, pp. of lavdre, 'to wash'.
See lave and -ion.

## Lotophagi
Lotophagi, n. pi., a people mentioned in Homer's
Odyssey, IX; they were supposed to live in a
state of indolence caused by their subsisting on
the fruits of the lotus. — L., fr. Gk. Λωτοφάγοι,
lit. 'lotus eaters', fr. λωτός, 'lotus', and the stem
of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See lotus and -phagous.

## lottery
lottery, n. — It. lotteria, 'public lottery', fr. lotto,
'lot, portion, share' (but F. loterie derives fr. Du.
loterije, fr. Du. lot, 'lot'). See lot and cp. lotto.

## Lottie
Lottie, Lotta, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Charlotte.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:457 COLUMN:3 -->
lotto, п., a game of change. — It., lit. 'a lot'. See
lot and cp. lottery,
lotus, n. — L., fr. Gk. λωτός, name of various
plants, fr. Heb. lot, 'labdanum'. See labdanum
and cp. the first element in Lotophagi and the
second element in melilot.

## loud
loud, adj. — ME. loud, fr. OE. Mud, rel. to OS.,
OFris. Mud, MDu. but, luud, Du. luid, OHG.
hlut, tut, MHG. lut, G. laut, 'loud', fr. I.-E. pp.
base *klu-to-s, whence also 01. srutab, Gk.
κλυτός, 'heard of, celebrated', L. in-clutus, in-
clitus, 'celebrated, famous', Arm. lu, 'known',
Mir. cloth, 'glory', W. clod, 'praise'; fr. I.-E.
base *kleu-, 'to hear', whence also 01. srnoti,
'hears', srutih, 'the act of hearing', srdtram,
Avestic sracSra- 'ear', Avestic srao-tu, 'he shall
hear', Toch. A klosam (dual), 'ears', В klautso,
'ear', A kaklyu, 'celebrated, famous', Arm. Isem
(aor. luaj), Ί hear', OSlav. slovg, sluti, 'to be
called', slovo, 'word', slava, 'glory', Lith. Slave,
Slove, 'glory, splendor', OSlav. sluchu, 'hearing',
Ol. Sravas-, 'praise, glory', Avestic sravah-,
'word', Gk. κλέος (<ίΊΆ\.*χλέ?ος),ίτιΐΓηοτ, report,
fame', κλείει,ν, κλέειν, 'to celebrate', L. cluere,
'to hear oneself called, be spoken of, Ofr. ro-
clui-nethar, 'hears', с/и, 'glory', W. clywaf, Co.
clewaf, Ί hear', Toch. A klyw, B. kalywe, 'glory'.
From base *kleus-, an -ί-enlargement of base
*kleu-, derive Arm. lur (for *klusri-), 'silent',
Olr. cluas (for *klousta), 'ear', OSlav. slySg,
slysati, Lith. klausau, klausyti, 'to hear'. Cp.
ablaut, anlaut, inlaut, auslaut. Cp. also
auscultation, cledonism, Clianthus, Clio, Clothilda, Cly-
temnestra, Damocles, Eteocles, Euclea, Heracles,
Lewis, Lothario, Louis, Slav, slave, sloka, sruti,
Thecla. Cp. also listen. For the formation of
Teut. adjectives from past participles cp. cold,
dead, old, sad.
Derivatives: loud-en, tr. and intr. v., loud-ly,
adv., loud-ness, n.

## lough
lough, п., a lake. — Ir. and Gael. loch. See loch.

## Louis
Louis, masc. PN. — F., fr. OF. Loots, which
derives—prob. through the medium of ML. Ludo-
vicus—fr. OHG. Hluodowig (whence G. Lud-
wig), lit. 'famous in war', fr. Teut. "hluda-,
'heard of, famous' (whence also OHG. hlut,
'loud'; see loud), and *wiga, 'war'. Cp. next
word, Lewis and Aloysius. Cp. also louisine.

## Louisa
Louisa, Louise, fem. PN. — F. Louise, fem. of
Louis. See prec. word.

## louis d'or
louis d'or, a French gold coin. — F., lit. 'gold
louis'; so called because first struck by Louis
XIII of France (in 1640).

## louisine
louisine, п., a twilled silk used for making dresses.
— F., formed fr. the PN. Louise, or, less
probably, fr. the PN. Louis. See Louis, Louisa. For
sense development cp. georgette.

## Louis Quatorze
Louis Quatorze, pertaining to Louis XIV of
France(1643-1715). — F., lit.'Louis fourteenth'.

## Louis Quinze
Louis Quinze, pertaining to Louis XV of France
(1715-74). — F., lit. 'Louis fifteenth'.

## Louis Seize
Louis Seize, pertaining to Louis XVI of France
(1774-93). — F., lit. 'Louis sixteenth'.

## lonnge
lonnge, intr. v., to loll idly. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: lounge, п., loung-er, п., loung-ing-ly,
adv.

## loup
loup, intr. v., to leap. — ME. loupen, fr. ON.
hlaupa, 'to leap'. See lope.

## lour
lour, v., to frown. — A var. of lower.

## louse
louse, n. — ME. lous, fr. OE. IBs, rel. to ΟΝ.,
MLG., MDu., OHG., MHG. lus, G. Laus, and
cogn. with OCo. lowen, W. lleuen, 'louse'.
Derivatives: louse, tr. and intr. v., lous-y, adj.,
lous-i-ly, adv., lous-i-ness, n.

## lout
lout, intr. v., to bow, stoop. — ME. luten, louten,
fr. OE. lutan, rel. to ON. lata, 'to stoop, fall',
OE. lot, 'deceit', lytig, 'deceitful', Goth, luton,
'to deceive', /ii/f j.'deceitful', fr. Teut. base *leut-,
'to bow, bend, stoop', whence also OE. lytel,
'little'. See Iktle and cp. next word.

## lout
lout, п., a clown; a clumsy fellow. — Prob.
meaning orig. 'a fellow bent down', and derived
fr. ON. luir, 'stooping', fr. Wta, 'to stoop, fall'.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: lout-ish, adj., lout-ish-ly, adv., lout-
ish-ness, n.

## louver
louver, п., a lantern-shaped turret on the roof of
an ancient building (medieval archil.) — ME.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:458 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 431 | LUCRE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:458 COLUMN:1 -->
lover, fr. OF. lover, louvert, formed by the
agglutination of the def. article, fr. Vouvert, lit. 'the
open (place)', from le (fr. L. Hie, 'that') and pp.
of ouvrir, 'to open', fr. VL. *operire, which
corresponds to L. aperire, 'to open'. See ille and
aperient. For the agglutination of the article cp.
lierre and words there referred to.
Derivative: louver-ed, adj.

## lovage
lovage, п., a European herb of the carrot family.
— ME. loveache, fr. OF. luvesche, levesche (F.
liveche), fr. VL. levistica, fr. L. ligusticum,
'lovage', prop. neuter.of the adj. ligusticus, 'of Ligu-
ria', used as a noun, fr. Ligus, 'a Ligurian'. See
Ligurian and cp. Levisticum, Ligusticum, Ligus-
trum.

## love
love, n. — ME. luve, love, fr. OE. lufu, 'love,
affection, friendliness', rel. to OE. leof, OS. Ho/,
OFris. liaf, Du. lie/, OHG. /106, MHG. Hep, G.
lieb, ON. Ijufr, Goth. liufs, 'dear, beloved',
OHG. Hub!, 'joy', MHG. Hebe, 'joy; love', G.
Liebe, 'love', OE., ΟΝ., Swed., OFris., Du. loj,
Dan. lov, OHG. lob, MHG. lop, G. Lob, 'praise',
fr. l.-E. base *leubh-, 'to love, approve, praise',
whence also L. lubel, later libet, 'pleases', OI.
Iiibhyati, 'desires', OSlav. I'ubu, 'dear, beloved',
I'uby, 'love', 1'ubiti, 'to love', Liih. liaupse, 'song
of praise'. Cp. leave, п., lief, belief, believe, and
the second element in furlough. Cp. also
libidinous.
Derivatives: love-less, adj., love-less-ly, adv.,
love-less-ness, n.

## love
love, tr. and intr. v. — ME. luvien, loven, fr. OE.
lufian, 'to love', fr. lu/u, 'love'. See love, n.
Derivatives: lov-er, п., lov-er-ly, adj., lov-ing,
adj., lov-ing-ly, adv., lov-ing-ness, n.

## love apple
love apple, п., the tomato. — Loan translation of
F. pomme d'amour, fr. It. porno d'amore, lit.
'apple of love', which is a popular
transformation of the original name porno de' Mori, 'apple
of the Moors, Moorish apple'. See pome and
Moor.

## love-lorn
love-lorn, adj., pining from love. — Coined by
Milton from love, п., and lorn.

## lovely
lovely, adj. — ME., fr. OE. luflic, 'loving,
amiable', fr. lu/u, 'love'. See love, n. and adj. surf.
-iy.
Derivatives: loveli-ly, adv., loveli-ness, n.

## lovingkindness
lovingkindness, n. — Coined by Coverdale fr.
loving, pres. part, of the verb love, and kindness.

## low
low, intr. v., to make the sound of a cow. — ME.
lowen, fr. OE. hlowan, rel. to OS. hlowan, MDu.
loeyen, Du. loeien, OHG. hluojen, 'to low'; fr.
Teut. base *hlo-, corresponding to I.-E. base
*kla-, whence L. cla-mdre, 'to call, shout, cry
out'. See claim, v.
Derivatives: low, п., low-ing, n.

## low
low, adj., not high; humble. — ME. lah, louh,
low, lowe, fr. ON. lagr, which is rel. to Swed. lag,
Dan. lav, OFris. lech, MDu. lage, Du. laag,
MHG. laege, dial. G. lege, 'low'. The orig.
meaning of these words was 'that which is lying
flat'; they are related to ON. liggja, Swed. ligga,
Dan. ligge, OE. licgan etc., 'to lie'. See lie, 'to
recline*.
Derivatives: low, adv. and п., low-ly, adj. and
adv., low-ness, n.

## low
low, п., a hill. — ME-, fr. OE. hldw, hlxw, 'hill,
mound', re], to OS., OHG. hieo, 'hill, mound',
Goth, hlaiw, *a grave', and to OE. hleonian,
hlinian, 'to lean', and cogn. with L. clivus, 'hill'.
See lean, 'to incline', and cp. clinical and words
there referred to. Cp. also iaw, 'a hill'.

## low
low, п., blaze (now Scot, and dial. English). —
ME., fr. ON. logi, 'blaze, flame', rel. to ON.
Loki, 'god of flame', OS. logna, OFris. loga,
MDu. /aye, Du. laai, OHG. hug, MHG. lohe, 16,
G. Lohe, 'flame', fr. I.-E. base *leuq-, 'to emit
light, to shine; bright', whence also OE. leoht,
'light'. See light, 'brightness', and cp. words
there referred to.

## low
low, intr. v., to flame. — ME. lowen, fr. ON. loga,
fr. logi, 'blaze, flame'. See prec. word.

## lowboy
lowboy, п., chest of drawers supported on short
legs. — A hybrid coined fr. E. low, adj., and F.
hois, 'wood'. See bush and cp. highboy, tallboy.
Cp. also hautboy,

## lower
lower, adj. — Compar. of low, adj.
Derivative: lower, tr. v., to cause to descend;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:458 COLUMN:2 -->
intr. v., to descend.

## lower
lower, lour, intr. v., to frown. — ME. louren,
luren, 'to frown, lurk', rel. to MDu. (= Du.)
loeren, of s.m., 'to lurk, lie in wait', MLG.,
MHG. luren, G. lauern, of s.m. Cp. lurk.
Derivatives: lower, п., lower-ing, adj., lower-ing-
ly, adv., lower-y, adj.

## lox-
lox-, form of loxo- before a vowel.

## loxia
loxia, п., wryneck (med.) — Medical L., formed
with 1st suff. -ia fr. Gk. λοξός. See loxo-.

## Loxia
Loxia, п., a genus of birds, the crossbill (orniihol.)
— ModL. See prec. word.

## loxo-
loxo-, before a vowel lox-, combining form
meaning 'oblique'. — Gk-λοξο-, λοξ-, fr. λοξός,
'slanting, crosswise, oblique', rel. to λέχριος,
'slanting, crosswise', and prob. also to λέκος,
λεκάνη, 'dish, pot, pan'. See lekane.

## loxodrome
loxodrome, п., rhumb line. — Back formation fr.
loxodromic.

## loxodromic
loxodromic, adj., pertaining to oblique sailing. —
Compounded of loxo- and Gk. δρόμος, 'a
running, course'. See dromedary and adj. surf. -ic.
Derivatives: loxodromic-al-ly, adv., loxodromics
(q-v.)

## loxodromics
loxodromics, loxodromy, п., the art of oblique
sailing. — See prec. word and -ics, resp. -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## loyal
loyal, adj. — MF. (= F.), fr. OF. loial, leial,
fr. L. ligdlis, 'pertaining to the law, legal', fr.
lex, gen. legis, 'law'; see leal and legal, which are
doublets of loyal. F. loyal orig. meant legal. Cp.
for this sense its OProven?. equivalent leial,
which means 'legal'.
Derivatives: loyal, п., loyal-ism, п., loyal-ist, п.,
loyal-ly, adv., loyal-ness, п., loyalty (q.v.)

## loyalty
loyalty, n. — ME. loyaltee, fr. OF. loialte (F.
loyaute), fr. loyal, 'legal'. See prec. word and -ty.

## lozenge
lozenge, п., a figure having four equal sides and
two acute and two obtuse angles, a rhomb. —
ME. losenge, fr. OF. losenge, 'a flattering device'
(whence losengier, *to flatter, praise'), fr. los (fr.
L. laus), 'praise*; see laud. The device was
usually painted or engraved into a rhomb, whence
OF. losenge (F. losange), became synonymous
with rhomb. See Darmesteter, La vie des mots,
13th edition, pp. 50 and 79.

## lozengy
lozengy, adj., divided into lozenges. — OF. lo-
sengie, fr. losenge. See prec. word and -y
(representing OF. -e, F. -e).

## L.s.d.
L.s.d., money (colloq.) — Abbreviation of the
Latin words librae, solidi, denarii (pounds,
shillings and pence).

## lubber
lubber, п., 1) a clumsy fellow; 2) a clumsy seaman.
— ME. lobre, lobur, prob. of Scand. origin. Cp.
dial. Swed. lubber, 'a plump lazy fellow'. Cp.
also lob, looby.
Derivatives: lubber-ly, adj. and adv.,
lubber-lines s, n.

## lubra
lubra, п., an aboriginal girl or woman in
Australia. — Native Tasmanian name.

## lubricant
lubricant, adj., reducing friction. — L. lubricans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of lubricare, "to make
smooth*. See next word and -ant.
Derivative: lubricant, п., a substance for
reducing friction.

## lubricate
lubricate, tr. v., to make slippery or smooth; to
apply as a lubricant; intr. v., to serve as a
lubricant. — L. lubricatus, pp. of lubricare, 'to
make slippery or smooth*, fr. lubricus, 'slippery,
smooth', which prob. stands for *slubricus and
derives fr. I.-E. base *(s)leub-, 'to slip, slide',
whence also Goth, sliupan, OE. slupan, 'to slip,
glide*. See sleeve and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see verbal sufT. -ate.
Derivatives: lubricat-ion, п., lubricat-ion-al, adj.,
lubricat-ive, adj., lubricat-or, п., lubricat-ory, adj.

## lubricity
lubricity, п., 1) slipperiness; smoothness; 2)
instability; 3) lewdness. — F. lubricUe, fr. Late L.
lubricitatem, ace. of lubricitds, 'slipperiness', fr.
L. lubricus. See prec. word and -ity.

## lubricous
lubricous, adj., 1) slippery; smooth; 2) unstable;
3) lewd. — L. lubricus. See lubricate. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## lubritorium
lubritorium, also lubritory, п., a place for
lubricating automobiles. — Formed fr. lubricate on
analogy of words like auditorium, etc. See suff.
-orium, resp. subst. suff. -ory.
Derivative: lubritor-ian, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:458 COLUMN:3 -->

## lucarne
lucarne, п., a dormer window {archaic). — F., a
blend of OF. lucanne, 'lucarne', and luiserne,
'light'. OF. lucanne is borrowed fr. ΟΡΓονβης.
lucana, which is a Teut. loan word; cp. Du. luik,
'shutter; trapdoor', G. Luke, 'dormer window',
G. Loch, 'hole, opening', and see lock for closing
doors. OF. luiserne derives fr. L. /ucerna, 'lamp';
see lucerne.

## luce
luce, п., 1) pike; 2) figure of a pike (her.) — ME.,
fr. MF. lus, fr. L. lucius, 'pike' (fish), prob. orig.
meaning 'the shining fish' and derived fr.
lucere, 'to shine' (see lucent); assimilated in
form to the PN. Lucius. See Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., I, p. 825 s.v. lucius.

## lucence
lucence, lucency, n. — Formed fr. lucent with suff.
-ce, resp. -cy.

## lucent
lucent, adj., bright; transparent. — L. lucens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of lucere, 'to shine', fr. lux, gen.
lucis, 'light', fr. I.-E. base *leuq-, 'to emit light,
to shine; bright'. See light, 'brightness' and -ent
and cp. luce, lucerne, lucid, lucule, luculent,
Luzula, relucent, translucent, Noctiluca.

## lucerne
lucerne, п., a plant grown for forage, alfalfa. —
F. luzerne, fr. ModProvenc. luzerno, which is
prob. a figurative use of luzerno, 'glowworm'; so
named in allusion to the glittering grains of the
lucerne. ModProve^ luzerno, 'glowworm'
derives fr. L. lucerna, 'lamp', which is prob. formed
fr. lucere, 'to shine'; see lucent. The ending of L.
lucerna is due to the analogy of its synonym
lanterna (see lantern).

## Lucia
Lucia, fern. PN. — L. Lucia, fern, of Lucius. See
Lucius and cp. Lucy.

## Lucian
Lucian, masc. PN. — L. Lucidnus (whence also F.
Lucien), a derivative of Lucius. See Lucius and
-an.

## lucid
lucid, adj., bright. — L. lucidus, 'full of light,
bright', fr. lucere, 'to shine*. See lucent and -id
(representing L. -idus) and cp. elucidate, pellucid.
Derivatives: lucid-ity, п., lucid-ly, adv., lucid-
nesst n.

## Lucifer
Lucifer, п., the planet Venus appearing as the
morning star. — L., lit. 'light-bearing',
compounded of lux, gen. lucis, 'light', and ferre, *to
bear, carry'. See lucent and -fer.

## luciferase
luciferase, п., an enzyme present in fireflies (bio-
chem.) — See Lucifer and -ase.

## luciferous
luciferous, adj., emitting light. — See Lucifer and
-ous.

## lucifugous
lucifugous, adj., avoiding light. — L. lucifugus,
'avoiding light', compounded of lux, gen. lucis,
'light', and fugere, 'to flee'. See lucent and
fugitive.

## Lucile
Lucile, Lucille, fern. PN. — F. Lucille, dimin.
formed fr. L. Lucia, fern, of Lucius. See Lucius.

## lucimeter
lucimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
intensity of light. — A hybrid coined fr. L. luxt
gen. lucis, 'light' (see lucent), and Gk. μέτρον,
' measure' (see -meter). The correct form is
photometer, in which both elements are of Greek
origin.

## Lucina
Lucina, п., the Roman goddess of childbirth
(Roman mythol.) — L. Lucina, lit. 'she who brings
to the light', fern, of luctnus, fr. lux, gen. lucis,
Might'. See lucent.

## Lucius
Lucius, masc. PN. — L. Lucius, fr. lux, gen. lucis,
'light'. See lucent and cp. Lucin, Lucian, Lncile,
Lucy.

## luck
luck, n. — ME. lucke, fr. early MDu. luc (whence
MDu. ghelucke, Du. geluk\ rel. to MHG. g(e)-
lucke, G. Gluck, 'fortune, good luck', lit. 'that
which bends together', fr. I.-E. base *leug-, 'to
bend'. See lock, 'tuft of hair', and cp. leek (see
J. F. Bense, A Dictionary of the Low-Dutch
Element in the English Vocabulary, p. 199).
Derivatives: luck-ful, luck-less, adjs., luck-less-

## ly
ly, adv., luck-less-ness, п., luck-y, adj., luck-i-ly,
adv., luck-i-ness, n.

## luck
luck, intr. and tr. v. — ME. lukken, 'to happen',
fr. MDu. lucken. See prec. word.

## lucrative
lucrative, adj., profitable. — ME. fucrati/, fr. OF.
(= F.) lucratif, fr. L. lucrativus, 'gainful,

## profitable'
profitable', fr. lucrdtus, pp. of lucrdri, 'to gain,

## acquire'
acquire', fr. lucrum. See lucre and -ative.
Derivatives: lucrative-ly, adv., lucrative-ness, n.

## lucre
lucre, п., riches, money. — ME., fr. L. lucrum,
'gain, profit, advantage', for *lu-tlom, in grada-

## tional relationship to OI. lotam
tional relationship to OI. lotam, lotram, 'booty',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:459 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LUCRECE | 432 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:459 COLUMN:1 -->
luntati, 'jobs, plunders', Gk. λεία, Dor. λαΐα,
Ion. λη'ίη, Ion., Att. ληΐς, 'prey, booty', ληστής,
Dor. λαστάς, 'robber', άπο-λαύειν, Чо enjoy*,
OE. lean, ON. /аил, OS., MLG. Ion, ON. laun,
OFris, Ian, OHG, MHG. Ion, G. -Lo/ш, Goth.
laun, 'reward', Olr. log, tuag, luach, 'reward',
prob. also with OSlav. tovu, 'hunt', loviti, 'to
pursue, seize'. Cp. apolaustic, guerdon, -lestes,
loot.

## Lucrece
Lucrece, fem. PN. — F. Lucrice, fr. L. Lucretia.
See next word.

## Lucretia
Lucretia, fem. PN. — L. Lucretia, fem. of
Lucretius. See next word.

## Lucretius
Lucretius, masc. PN. — L. Lucretius, name of a
Roman gens.

## lucubrate
lucubrate, intr. v., to work at night; to work
laboriously. — L. lucubratus, pp. of tucubrare, 'to
work by lamplight, to work at night', from the
stem of lucere, 'to shine'. See lucent and verbal
suff. -ate.

## lucubration
lucubration, п., nocturnal work; laborious study.
— L. tucubratio, gen. -onis, 'nocturnal study;
nightwork', fr. lucubratus, pp. of tucubrare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## lucule
lucule, n-, a small luminous spot on the surface of
the sun (astron.) — F-, fr. ModL. tucula, dimin.
of L. lux, gen. lucis, 'light'. See lucent and -ule.

## luculent
luculent, adj., clear, lucid. — ME., fr. L. luculen-
tus, 'bright, brightly burning', formed from the
stem of lux, gen. lucis, 'light' (see lucent), with
suff. -u-lentus, meaning 'full of, abounding in,
rich in'. Cp. L. opulentus, 'rich, wealthy', lit.
'resourceful, powerful', fr. ops. gen. opis, 'strength,
might; riches' (see opulent).
Derivative: luculent-ly, adv.

## Lucullan
Lucullan, Lucullean, adj., pertaining to, or
resembling L. Licinius Lucullus (about 110-57), a
Roman general famous for the luxury of his
banquets.

## lucullite
lucullite, п., a marble colored black by carbon
(mineral.) — L. marmor Luculleum, 'marble of
Lucullus', named after L. Licinius Lucullus. See
prec. word and subst. sufT. -ite.

## lucumo
lucumo, п., an Etruscan noble who performed the
functions both of a priest and a prince. — L.
lucumo, lucmd, fr. Etruscan *laujme.

## iucus a non lucendo
iucus a non lucendo, an absurd etymology. — L.,
lit. 'a grove because it is not light'. Prop, an
etymology as absurd as that which derives L.
Iucus, 'grove', fr. lucere, 'to light', although
a grove is dark, as a rule. Actually, however,
L. Iucus is related to lucere. Lucus, 'grove',
denotes not 'a place with no light', but 'a place
into which light may come'. It stands for *loukos
and is cogn. with OI. lokah, ulokdfi, 'open place,
space', Lith. laukas, Lett, laiiks, 'field, open
country', fr. I.-E. base *leuq-, 'to be light, to
shine; bright'. See light, 'brightness', and cp.
lea, 'a track of open country'.

## Lucy
Lucy, fem. PN. — F. Lucie, fr. L. Lucia, fem. of
Lucius. See Lucins and cp. words there referred
to.

## Luddite
Luddite, п., any of a band organized to destroy
machinery. — Named after Ned Ludd, who
broke stocking frames (in 1779). For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## ludicrous
ludicrous, adj., laughable, ridiculous. — L. IHdi-
crus, a secondary form of ludicer, 'sportive,
playful', fr. ludus, fr. OL. loidos, 'play, game,
sport, pastime', which is rel. to ludere (for *loi-
dere), 'to play, sport, frolic'; and cogn. with Gk.
λίζειν (Hesychius), 'to play', λοίδορος,
'abusing, insulting', λοιδορεΐν, 'to abuse, insult' (for
sense development cp. MHG. schimpf, 'joke,
amusement', whence G. Schimpf, 'disgrace,
insult'. Cp. allude, allusion, collude, collusion,
delude, delusion, elude, elusion, illude, illusion,
interlude, ludo, prelude, prelusion, prolusion. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: ludicrous-ly, adv., tudicrous-ness, n.

## Iudlamite
Iudlamite,n., a hydrous iron phosphate {mineral.)
— Named by Maskelyne and Field after Mr.
Ludlam, a friend of theirs. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## ludo
ludo, п., a kind of simple play. — L. ludd, Ί play'.
See ludicrous.

## Lndovic
Lndovic, Ludowick, Ludwig, masc. PN. — See
Louis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:459 COLUMN:2 -->

## ludwigite
ludwigite, п., an iron magnesium borate
(mineral.) — G. Ludwigit, named after Ernst
Ludwig, professor of chemistry in Vienna (died
in 1915). The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## lues
lues, п., a) any plague or pestilence (obsol.);b)
syphilis. — L. lues, 'a plague, pestilence', prop,
'dissolution', fr. lucre, 'to loose, release', which
is cogn. with Gk. λύείν, 'to unfasten, loosen,
untie, slacken; to loose, release, set free, ransom'.
See lose and cp. -lysis.

## luff
