luff, п., windward side, weather side. — ME. luf,
looff, fr. OF. (= F.) lof, fr. MDu. Idf (whence
also Du. loef), 'luff', which is rel. to ON. lofi,
Goth, lofa, 'palm of the hand' (G. Luv, Dan.
luv, Swed. luf ate Dutch loan words), Dan. lab,
Swed., Norw. labb, 'paw', and cogn. with Lith.
lopa, 'claw', lopeta, 'shovel, water lily', Lett.
lepa, 'paw', lapst, 'shovel, spade', OPruss. lopto,
'spade', Russ. lopata, 'shovel', lapa, 'paw'. Cp.
loof, aloof, laveer. Cp. also glove.
Derivative: luff, intr. v.

## Luffa
Luffa, п., a genus of plants of the family Cucur-
bitaceae (bot.); (not cap.) any plant of this genus;
also its fruit. — ModL., fr. Arab. Iafah. Cp.
loofah.

## lug
lug, tr. and intr. v., to drag, pull, tug. — ME.
luggen, prob. of Scand. origin; cp. Swed. lugga,
Norw. lugge, 'to pull', which derive fr. Swed.,
resp. Norw. lugg, 'tuft of hair, forelock'. Cp.
next word and luggage.

## lug
lug, п., 1) the ear (Scot.); 2) anything that
projects like an ear. — ME. lugge, perh. fr. Swed.
lugg, 'forelock'. See prec. word.

## lug
lug, п., a lugworm. — Of uncertain origin. Cp.
lnrg.

## luge
luge, п., a kind of small toboggan used in
Switzerland. — F., a Savoyard word derived fr. ML.
sludia, which occurs in glosses of the 9th cent,
and is of Gaulish origin.
Derivatives: luge, intr. v., lug-er, n.

## luggage
luggage, n. — Formed fr. lug, 'to pull', with suff.
-age.

## lugger
lugger, п., one who or that which lugs. — Formed
fr. lug, 'to pull', with agential suff. -er.

## lugger
lugger, п., a small ship rigged with a lugsail or
lugsails (naut.) — Back formation fr. lugsail.

## lugsail
lugsail, n. — The circumstance that the French
for lugsail is voile de fortune (lit. 'sail of luck'),
makes it probable that lugsail stands for *luck-
sail. Cp. the English PN. Higson, which stands
for Hickson. See E. Weekley, The Romance of
Words, p. 101.

## lugubriosity
lugubriosity, n. — See lugubrious and -ity.

## lugubrious
lugubrious, adj., mournful. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. lugubris, 'pertaining to mourning,
mournful, painful', fr. lugere, 'to mourn, lament,
bewail'; which is cogn. with Ol. rujati, 'breaks,
torments', rugnah, 'broken', rogah, 'frailty,
disease', Avestic uruxti-, 'a breaking, tearing', Gk.
λευγαλέος, λυγρός, 'mournful, sad, dismal',
λυγμός (Hesychius), 'a loud cry', Lith. luzti, 'to
break' (intr.), taufyti, 'to break' (tr.), Lett, lauzit,
'to break the heart', Lith. lulls, lauiis, 'breach'.
All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *leug-
(Baltic), *leug-, 'to break; to cause pain': see lock,
'contrivance for closing doors'. For the sense
development of this base cp. OI. lumputi,
'breaks', Gk. λύπη, 'pain' (both fr. base */eup·).
Derivatives: tugubrious-ly, adv., lugubrious-ness,
n.

## lugworm
lugworm, n. — Compounded of lug, 'lugworm',
and worm.

## luke
luke, adj., lukewarm (now dial. English). — ME.
lewk, luke, rel. to LG. luk, Du. leuk, 'tepid', and
to OE. hleow, gehleow, 'warm, sheltered, sunny".
See lew, lee.
Derivatives: luke-ly, adv., luke-ness, n.

## Luke
Luke, masc. PN. — L. Lucas, contraction of L.
Lucdnus, lit. 'of LQcania (a district in Lower
Italy). For the contraction of Lucas, fr. Lucanus
cp. Silas, which is a pet form of Silvanus (see
Silas).

## lukewarm
lukewarm, adj. — Compounded of luke, adj., and
warm.
Derivatives: lukewarm-ly, adv., lukewarm-ness,
n.

## lulab
lulab, п., palm branch used for the festive wreath

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:459 COLUMN:3 -->
during the Feast of tabernacles (Jewish
Religion). — Mishnaic Heb. lulabh, 'branch', esp.
'palm branch', dissi'milated fr. *tubhlabh, from
the verb libhtebh, 'it bloomed, blossomed',
which is prob. a Pilpel denominative fr. Heb.
lebh, 'heart',

## lull
lull, tr. and intr. v. — ME. lullen, Ollen, of
imitative origin. Cp. Swed. lulla, MLG., MDu. lollen,
G. lullen, 'to rock', Ol. lolati, 'moves to and fro',
lulitah, 'swinging', lalati, 'skips, frisks'. All these
words are derivatives of the I.-E. imitative base
"lei-, *lul-, 'to move to and fro'. Cp. loll, Lollard,
lollop. Cp. also the imitative base "lal-, seen in
Gk. λαλεΐν, 'to talk, chat, prattle', λάλος,
'talkative, loquacious', L. lalldre, 'to sing to sleep, to
lull'; see Lalage and words there referred to.
Derivative: lull, n.

## lullaby
lullaby, n. — Formed fr. lull and -by. For the
second element cp. bye-bye, a child's word for
good-b#e.
Derivative: lullaby, tr. v.

## lumbago
lumbago, п., rheumatic pain in the loins (med.) —
Late L., fr. L. lumbus, 'loin'. See lumbar.

## lumbar
lumbar, adj., pertaining to, or situated near, the
loins. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. lumbus,
'loin', which stands for *londhwos and is cogn.
with OSlav. ledvije, (pi.), 'loins;soul', Russ. Ijad-
veja, 'loin', OE. lendenu (pi.), 'loins', ON. lend,
Dan. Ixnd, Swed. land, Du. lende, OHG. lenti,
MHG., G. lende, 'loin', OHG. lunda, 'tallow',
ON. /under, 'ham, buttock'. Cp. loin and the
second element in sirloin. Cp. also numbles, um-
bles.

## lumber
lumber, п., useless furniture; timber. — OF. Lom-
bart (F. Lombard), 'a Lombard'. The noun
lumber orig. denoted a pawnbroker's shop, in
allusion to the fact that the Lombards were famous
bankers and pawnbrokers. See Lombard and cp.
Langobard.
Derivatives: lumber, tr. and intr. v., lumber-er,
п., lumbering (q.v.)

## lumber
lumber, intr. v., to move clumsily. — ME. lome-
ren; prob. rel. to dial. Swed. loma, 'to walk
heavily', lomra, 'to resound', and to E. lame.

## lumbering
lumbering, п., the act of cutting timber. —
Formed with subst. suff. -ing fr. lumber, 'timber'.

## lumbering
lumbering, adj., moving clumsily. — Formed with
part. suff. -ing fr. lumber, Ίο move clumsily'.
Derivatives: lumbering-ly, adj., lumbering-ness,
n.

## lumbo-
lumbo-, combining form denoting I) the loin; 2)
lumbar and. — Fr. L. lumbus, 'loin'. See lumbar.

## lumbrical
lumbrical, adj., pertaining to the lumbricales; п.,
a lumbrical muscle. — Medical L. lumbricalis.
See next word.

## lumbricalis
lumbricalis, п., any of four small muscles in the
hand and in the sole of the foot (anal.) —
Medical L. lumbricalis (short for musculus
lumbricalis), fr. L. lumbricus, 'earthworm', which is
possibly cogn. with W. llyngyr (pi.), 'earthworms';
so called from the supposed resemblance of
these muscles to earthworms. For the ending see
adj. suff. -al.

## lumen
lumen, п., a unit of light. — L. lumen, 'light'. See
luminary.

## luminary
luminary, n. — ME. luminarye, fr. OF. luminarie
(F. Iuminaire),(r. Late L. IBminare, 'light, torch,
lamp; heavenly body', fr. L. lumen (gen. luminis),
'light',which standsjfor *leuqs-menoi *louqs-men
and is rel. to lucere, 'to shine'. See lucent and
-men and cp. limbers. Cp. also allumetie,
Illuminate.

## luminesce
luminesce, intr. v. — Back formation fr.
luminescent. Cp. reminisce.

## luminescence
luminescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## luminescent
luminescent, adj. — Formed with suff. -escent fr.
L. lumen, gen. luminis, 'light'. See luminary.

## luminiferous
luminiferous, adj., producing or conveying light.
— Compounded of L. lumen, gen. luminis,
'light', and the stem of ferre, 'to bear, carry'.
See luminary and -ferous.

## luminosity
luminosity, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ity.

## luminous
luminous, adj., shining; bright. — ME., fr. L.
luminosus, 'full of light', fr. lumen, gen. luminis.
See lumen and -ous.
Derivatives: luminously, adv., luminous-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:460 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 433 | LUTEOLIN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:460 COLUMN:1 -->
lump, п., a shapeless mass. — ME. lompe, lumpe,
rel. to Du. lomp, 'piece, mass' (whence G.
Lumpen, 'rag, lump'), Лч!^ is prob. cogn. with Ol.
lambate, 'hangs down\ lambah, 'hanging down,
long, big1, L. limbus, 'hem, border', and with E.
limp, adj. and v. (qq.v.) Cp. limb, 'edge'. Cp. also
lunch.
Derivatives: lump, tr. v., to make into a lump;
intr. v., to form into lumps, lump-er, п.,
lumping, adj., lump-ing-ly, adv., lump-ish, adj., lump-
ish-ly, adv., lump-ish-ness, п., lump-y, adj., lump-
i-ly, adv., lump-i-ness, n.

## lump
lump, intr. v., to look sullen; tr. v., to dislike. —
Of uncertain origin.

## Luna
Luna, п., the moon-goddess {Roman mythol.) —
L. Luna 'moon', See lune.

## lunacy
lunacy, n. — Formed fr. lunatic with suff. -cy.

## lunar
lunar, adj., pertaining to the moon. — L. lunaris,
'pertaining to the moon', fr. luna, 'moon'. See
lune and -ar and cp. next word.

## Lunaria
Lunaria, п., a genus of plants, the moonwort (hot.)
— ModL., fr. L. lunaris, 'pertaining to the
moon' (see lunar); so called in allusion to the
silvery septum of the fruit.

## lunarian
lunarian, adj., pertaining to the moon; п., 1)
inhabitant of the moon; 2) student of the moon.
— Formed with suff. -ian fr. L. lunaris. See prec.
word.

## lunate
lunate, adj., crescent-shaped. — L. lunatus,
'crescent-shaped', fr. tuna, 'moon'. See lune and adj.
suff. -ate.

## lunatic
lunatic, adj., moonstruck, mad. — Late L. luna-
ticus, 'affected by the moon; moonstruck,
lunatic', fr. L. luna, 'moon'; see lune and -atic. Late
L. lunaticusia this sense is prop, a loan
translation of Gk. σεληνόβλητος or σεληνόπληκτος,
'moonstruck'.
Derivative: lunatic, n.

## lunation
lunation, п., time between two successive new
moons. — ML. lunatio, fr. L. luna, 'moon'. See
lune and -ation and cp. lunate.

## lunch
lunch, n. — Prob. altered fr. lump, 'piece' (the
original meaning of lunch was 'piece, lump').
For a similar alteration cp. hunch, which prob.
derives fr. hump.

## luncheon
luncheon, n. — A blend of lunch and nuncheon.

## lundyfoot
lundyfoot, п., a kind of snuff. — Named after a
tobacconist called Lundy Foot, who lived in
Dublin in the 18th century.

## lune
lune, п., any crescentlike object. — F., fr. L. luna,
'moon*, which stands for *louqs-na or *leuqs-na
and is rel. to L, /ha;, gen. lucis, 'light', lucere, 'to
shine', and cogn. with OSlav. luna (for *louqs-
na), 'moon', OPruss. lauxnos (pi.), 'stars', Mir.
luan, Ion (for *louqsno-), 'light, moon', Avestic
raoxshna-, 'shining, bright', Arm. lusin, 'moon'.
All these words are derivatives of l.-E. base
4leuq-, *to emit light, to shine; bright'. See light,
'brightness', and cp. lucent. Cp. also iunette,
demilune. MHG. lune (whence G. Laune),
'humor, temper, mood, whim, fancy', is borrowed
fr. L. luna, 'moon' (MHG. lune lit. meant
'influence of the moon').

## lunel
lunel, п., a muscat wine. — So called from the
town Lunel in the Pyrenees (France), a center of
viticulture.

## lunette
lunette, п., any of various objects resembling a
half-moon or a crescent. — F., lit. 'little moon',
fr. L. luna, 'moon'. Sec lune and -ette.

## lung
lung, n. — ME. lunge, fr. OE. lungen, rel. to OS.,
ΟΝ., Swed., Norw. lunga, Dan. lunge, OFris.
lungen, MDu. longhe, Du. long, OHG. lungun,
MHG., G. lunge, *lung\ lit. 'the light organ', fr.
I.-E. base *lengwh-, *legwh-, 'light, easy, agile,
nimble', whence also Arm. lanjk, 'breast' (orig.
'lung'), Russ. le'gkij, Pol. lekki, 'light', Russ. leg-
koje, Pol. lekkie, 'lung'; see light, 'not heavy',
and cp. lights. For sense development cp. Port,
/eve, 'lung' (fr. L. levis, 'light'), Ir. seaman,
'lungs' (fr. seaman, 'light'), W. ysgyfaint (dual),
'the lungs' (fr. ysgafn, 'light').
lunge» п., a thrust. — Aphetic for obsol. allonge,

## fr. F. allonge
fr. F. allonge, fr. allonger, 'to lengthen, extend7.
See allonge.
Derivative: lunge, intr. v., to make a lunge.

## lunge
lunge, п., a long rope for guiding a horse. — F.

## longet 'halter
longet 'halter, lunge', fr. OF. longe, fern, of the

## adj. long
adj. long, 'long' (in ModF. the fern, is longue).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:460 COLUMN:2 -->
See long and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: lunge, tr. v., to train (a horse) by the
use of a lunge.

## lung fish
lung fish, n. — Lit. 'a fish that has lungs'.

## luni-
luni-, combining form meaning 'moon'. — Fr. L.
luna, 'moon'. See lune.

## lunkah
lunkah, п., a strong kind of cheroot. — Hind.
lanka, a name derived from the Lankah islands
in the delta of Godavary River, where tobacco
is grown,

## lunt
lunt, n. (Scot.), \) a slow-burning match; 2)
smoke. — Du. lont. 'match, fuse*, rel. to MLG.
lunte, 'match, wick' (whence G. Lunte, 'match,
fuse'). Cp. the first element in linstock.
Derivative: lunt, tr. v., to kindle; intr. v., to emit
smoke.

## Lupercalia
Lupercalia, n. pi., a festival held annually on the
15th of February in honor of Lupercus (Roman
mythol.) — L. Lupercalia, fr. Lupercal, name of a
grotto at the foot of the Palatine Hill, fr.
Lupercus, a god identified with the Lycean Pan. The
name Lupercus derives fr. lupus, 'wolf. See
lupine, adj.

## lupin
lupin, n. — A var. of lupine, n.

## lupine
lupine, adj., wolflike, — L. lupinus, 'pertaining to,
or connected with, a wolf', fr. lupus, 'wolf. See
wolf and adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus)
and cp. lupine, n. Cp. also Lupercalia, lupulus,
lupus, robalo.

## lupine
lupine,n.,l) any plant of the genus Lupinus; 2) the
seed of this plant. — ME. lupine, fr. L. lupxnum,
also lup'mus, 'lupine', fr. lupus, 'wolf. See prec.
word.

## Lupinus
Lupinus, п., a genus of plants, the lupine (bot.) —
ModL., fr. lupus, 'wolf (see lupus, lupine); so
called from the belief that the plants of these
genus were harmful to the soil.

## lupulin
lupulin, п., the fine powder on the strobiles of the
hop (bot.) — ModL. lupulus, dimin. of L. lupus,
'hop'. See lupulus.

## lupulone
lupulone, п., an antibiotic obtained from hops. —
Coined fr. lupulus.

## lupulus
lupulus, п., the hop. — ModL., 'the hop', dimin.
of L. lupus, 'hop', which is prob. re], to lupus,
'wolf. See lupine, adj., and cp. prec. word.

## lupus
lupus, п., tuberculous disease of the skin (med.)
— L. lupus, 'wolf (see lupine, adj.); so called
because it is characterized by ulcerations
resembling the bite of a wolf.

## lurch
lurch, п., embarrassment, helpless plight; obsol,
except in the phrase to leave one in the lurch. —
F. lourche, a former gaming term.

## lurch
lurch, п., a sudden movement. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: lurch, intr. v.

## iurch
iurch, intr. v., to lie in wait, lurk. —A var.of lurk.

## lurcher
lurcher, п., 1) one who or that which lurches; 2) a
dog of mongrel breed. — Formed fr. prec. word
with agential suff. -er.

## lurdan
lurdan, п., a lazy person; adj., lazy. — ME., fr.
MF. lourdin, fr. OF. (= F.) lourd, 'heavy, dull,

## thick-headed
thick-headed, stupid', fr. L. luridus, 'pale yellow,

## wan'
wan', whence also OF., OProvenc. lort, 'foolish',

## Sp.
Sp., Port, lerdo, 'slow, dull, obtuse'; see lurid.
The most important phases of sense

## development fr. L. luridus to F. lourd
development fr. L. luridus to F. lourd, ModProveng.

## lurd
lurd, 'heavy', seem to nave been 'pale, wan,

## fainting
fainting, dull, heavy-headed', whence 'slow, clumsy,

## heavy7
heavy7,

## lure
lure, п., a bait. — ME-, fr. MF. hire (F. leurre),
'lure, decoy, bait', fr. OF. loirre, fr. Frankish
*lopr, which is rel. to MLG. loder, OHG, MHG.

## luoder
luoder, G. Luder, 'lure, decoy, bait; carrion',

## and to OE. ladian
and to OE. ladian, OS. lathian, ON. lada, OFris.

## lathia
lathia, MDu. laden, OHG. ladon, MHG., G.

## laden
laden, Goth. lapon, 'to call, summon, invite'.

## lure
lure, tr. and intr. v., to allure; to entice. — F.

## leurrer
leurrer, fr. leurre. See lure, п., and cp. allure.

## lurg
lurg, lurgworm, п., a marine worm. — Of

## uncertain origin. Cp. lug
uncertain origin. Cp. lug, 'lugworm'.

## lurid
lurid, adj., wan; gloomy. — L. luridus, 'pale

## yellow
yellow, sallow, wan, ghastly', of uncertain
etymology. For the ending see suff. -id (representing L.
-idus). Cp. lurdan.
Derivatives: lurid-ly, adv. lurid-ity, n. (rare),

## lurid-ness
lurid-ness, n.

## lurk
lurk, intr. v., to lie in wait. — ME. lurken, formed

## fr. ME. luren
fr. ME. luren, 'to frown, lurk' (see lower, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:460 COLUMN:3 -->
frown'), with the intensive suff. -k. The same
suff. occurs in the verbs smirk, stalk, talk.
Derivatives: lurk, п., lurk-er, n.

## lurry
lurry, n. — A var. of lorry,

## luscious
luscious, adj., delicious. — ME. luciusi a var. of
licius, which is aphetic for delicious.
Derivatives: lustious-ly, adv., luscious-ness, n.

## lush
lush, adj. — A var. of lash,'soft and watery' (q.v.)
Derivatives: lush-ly, adv., lush-ness, n.

## lust
lust, n. — ME., fr. OE., 'pleasure, desire, lust',
rel. to OS., OFris., Swed., Du., OHG., MHG.,
G. lust, ON. lyst, losti^ Dan. lyst, Goth, lustus,
'pleasure, desire, lust', fr. I.-E. base *las-,
'greedy, desirous', whence also L. lascivus, 'wanton,
playful, lustful'. See lascivious and cp. list, 'to
please'.
Derivatives: lust, intr. v., lust-er, п., lust-ful, adj.,
lust-ful-ly, adv., lust-ful-ness, п., lust-less, adj.,
lust-ly, adv., lust-y, adj., lust-i-hood, п., /ust-i-ly,
adv., lust-i-ness, n.

## luster
luster, lustre, п., a lustrum. — L. lustrum. See
lustrum,

## luster
luster, lustre, п., gloss, radiance. — MF. ( —F.)
lustre, fr. It. lustro, fr. lustrare, "to light, illu
minate', fr. L. lustrare, 'to light, illuminate'. See
lustrum.
Derivative: luster, lustre, tr. v., to render lustrous.

## lustral
lustral, adj., pertaining to purification. — L. iCts-
tralis, 'pertaining to purification from guilt,
expiatory, propitiatory', fr. lustrum. See lustrum
and adj. suff. -al.

## lustratc
lustratc, tr. v., to purify from guilt. — L. lustra-
tus, pp. of lustrare, 'to purify from guilt', fr.
lustrum. See lustrum and verbal suff. -ate.

## lustration
lustration, п., purification from guilt. — L. lus-
tratio, gen. -onis, 'purification from guilt*, fr.
lusiratus, pp. of lustrare. See prec. word and -ion.

## lustring
lustring, п., a silk fabric with glossy finish. — F.
lustrine, fr. It. lustrino, fr. lustro, fr. lustrare, 4o
light, illuminate'. See luster, 'gloss, radiance',
and cp. lutestring,

## lustrous
lustrous, adj., brilliant. — Formed fr. luster,
'gloss, radiance', with suff. -ous.
Derivatives: lustrous-ly, adv., lustrous-ness, n.

## lustrum
lustrum, luster, п., 1) purification of the Roman
people after the census every five years; 2) a
period of five years. — L. lustrum, '"purificatory
sacrifice made once in five years; a period of
five years' (whence lustrare, 'to purify from
guilt'), for *leuqs-trom, *louqs-tromt prop,
'illumination', fr. l.-E. base *leuq-, 'to emit light, to
shine; bright'; see light, 'brightness', and cp.
illustrious. The various phases of the sense
development of lustrum may prob. be as follows:
'illumination, inspection, review, mustering,
expiatory offering, expiation*. Accordingly the verbs
lustrare, 'to light, illuminate', and lustrare, 'to
purify from guilt', are identical.

## lutanist
lutanist, п., a lute player. — ML. lutanista, a
hybrid coined fr. lutana, a word of Arabic origin,
and suff. -ista (fr. Gk. -ι.στής). See lute, 'an
instrument', and -ist. Cp. lutist.

## lute
lute, п., a cohesive substance. — ME.,.fr. MF.
(= F.) lut, fr. L. lutum, 'mud, clay', which stands
for *lutom and is rel. to -lucre in polluere (for
*por-luere), 'to pollute, contaminate', and to
lustrum (for *lu-strom), 'slough, bog, morass'. See
pollute and cp. lutetia, Lutetian.
Derivatives: lute, tr. v., lut-er, п., lut-ing, n.

## lute
lute, п., a stringed instrument. — ME., fr. OF.

## lut (F. luth)
lut (F. luth), fr. OProvenc. laut, fr. Arab, al-
lud (whence also Sp. laud, Port, alaude. It.

## Iiuto)
Iiuto),\it. 'the wood', fr. a/-,'the', and'«i/,'wood'.
Cp. lutanist.
Derivative: lute, tr. and intr. v.

## lutecia
lutecia, n. — A var. of lutetia.

## lutecium
lutecium, n. — A var. of lutetium.

## lutein
lutein, п., a yellow pigment (biochem.) — Coined

## by Thudichum from L. luteum (in corpus luteum
by Thudichum from L. luteum (in corpus luteum,
'egg yolk'), neut. of luteus, 'of the color of egg

## yolk
yolk, yellow' (see luteous) and chem. suff. -in.
The pigment was so called because it occurs in
egg yolk.

## luteo-
luteo-, combining form meaning 'golden yellow,
orange yellow'. — Fr. L. luteus. See luteous.

## tuteolin
tuteolin, п., a yellow coloring matter (chem.) —

## Formed with chem. suff. -in fr. L. luteolus
Formed with chem. suff. -in fr. L. luteolus,
'yellowish', fr. luteus. See luteous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:461 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: LUTEOUS | 434 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:461 COLUMN:1 -->

## luteous
luteous, adj., of orange yellow color. — L. luteust
'golden yellow, orange yellow', fr. lutum, 'plant
used in dying yellow', which is of uncertain
etymology.

## lutestring
lutestring, п., lustring. — Alteration of lustring
which was misconceived as the compound of
lute (the instrument) and string,

## lutetia
lutetia, also lutecia, п., lutetium oxide (chem.) —
ModL., lit. 'of Paris', coined by the French
chemist Georges Urbain (1872-1938) in 1907
after Gaulish-L. Lutetia, a fortfied town of the
Gaulish tribe of the Parisii (hence also called
Lutetia Parisiorum), the ancient name of Paris,
his native city. The name Lutetia literally means
'swamps'; cp. Olr. loth, 'dirt', W. lludedic,
'muddy, slimy', and see lute, 'a cohesive
substance'. Cp. next word.

## Lutetian
Lutetian, adj., Parisian. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Lutetia, short for Lutetia Parisiorum,
'Paris'. See prec. word.

## lutetium
lutetium, also lutecium, п., name of a metallic
element of the rare-earth group {chem. )— ModL.
See lutetia.

## Lutheran
Lutheran, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
from the name of the German reformer Martin
Luther (1483-1546).
Derivative: Lutheran-ism, n.

## lutist
lutist, п., 1) a lute player; 2) a maker of lutes. —
A hybrid coined fr. lute, 'an instrument', and
suff. -ist (fr. Gk. -ίστής). Ср. lutanist.

## Lutra
Lutra, п., a genus of mammals, the otter. — L.
lutra, 'otter', for *mra, fr. orig. *udra, influenced
in form by lutum, 'mud, mire'; formed fr. I.-E.
base *udr-, 'water', and lit. meaning 'an aquatic
animal', whence also ON. otr, OE. otor, oter,
'otter'. See otter and cp. words there referred to.

## lutrine
lutrine, adj., pertaining to the otter. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ine fr. L. lutra, 'otter'. See prec.
word.

## luxate
luxate, tr. v., to displace, dislocate. — L. luxatus,
pp. of luxare, 'to dislocate*, fr. luxus,
'dislocated', which prob. stands for *lug-sos, and is
cogn. with OL. luctare, L. luctari, 'to wrestle,
struggle' (whence lucta, 'a wrestling'), fr. l.-E.
base *lug-, 'to bend, twist1, whence also OE.
locc, 'lock of hair'. See lock, 4uft of hair', and cp
luxe, luxury,

## luxation
luxation, n. — L. luxatio, gen. -onis, 'dislocation',
fr. luxatus, pp. of luxare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## luxe
luxe, п., elegance. — F., 'luxury; splendor,
magnificence ; extravagance, excess', fr. L. luxus (gen.
luxus), 'excess, luxury, pomp, magnificence',
which is prob. rel. to the adj. luxus, 'dislocated',
and orig. meant 'dislocation (in the figurative
sense), excess7. See luxate and cp. luxury.

## luxuriance
luxuriance, luxuriancy, n. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## luxuriant
luxuriant, adj. — L. luxurians, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of luxuriare. See luxuriate and -ant.
Derivatives: luxuriant-ly, adv., luxuriant-ness, n.

## luxuriate
luxuriate, intr. v. — L. luxuriatus, pp. of luxuriari
(also luxuriare), 'to be rank, be luxuriant, have
in abundance, be too fruitful; to Tevel, be
wanton', fr. luxuria. See luxury and verbal suff. -ate.

## luxurious
luxurious, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) luxu-
rieux, fr. L. luxuriosus, 'rank, luxurious,
exuberant', fr. luxuria. See luxury and -ous.
Derivatives: luxurious-ly, adv., luxurious-ness, n.

## luxury
luxury, n. — ME., fr. OF. luxurie (F. luxure),
fr. L. luxuria, 'rankness, luxury, excess,
extravagance, redundancy', fr. luxus, 'luxury'. See luxe.

## Luzula
Luzula, п., a genus of plants, the wood rush (bot.)
ModL., fr. It. luzziola, lucciofa (scil. erba), lit.
'the shining plant', dimin. of luce, 'light', fr. L.
lucem, ace. of lux, 'light' (see lucent and cp.
words there referred'to); so called from its
shining appearance when covered with dew. Cp.
It. lucciola, "firefly; glowworm'.

## -ly
-ly, suff. forming adjectives. — ME. -lich, -ly, -It,
fr. OE. -lie, -tic, orig. identical with OE. lie,
'body'. Cp. OS., OFris. -lie, ON. -ligr, Dan.,
Swed., Norw. -lig, Du. -lijk, OHG. -lih, -lih,
MHG. -lich, -lich, G. -lich, Goth, -leiks, '-ly',
and see lich, like, adj.

## -ly
-ly, suff. forming adverbs. — ME. -liche, -ly, -It,
fr. OE. -lice, -lice, fr. OE. -lie, -lie, '-ly' (adj.
suff.) See prec. suff.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:461 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: Lycian, n.

## Lycium
Lycium, п., a genus of plants, the matrimony vine
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. λύκιον, 'the dyer's
buckthorrf, prop. 'Lycian plant', fr. Λύκιον,
neut. of Λύκιος, 'Lycian'.

## lyco-
lyco-, before a vowel lye-, combining form
meaning 'wolf. — Gk. λύκο-, λυκ-, fr. λύκος,
'wolf. Seelyceum.

## Lycopersicon
Lycopersicon, п., a genus of plants of the potato
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. λυκοττέρσιον, a
kind of plant of the nightshade family, which is
compounded of λύκος, 'wolf' (see lyco-), and
πέρθει,ν, 'to destroy', which is of uncertain origin.

## Lycopodiaceae
Lycopodiaceae, n. pi., the club-moss family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Lyco podium with suff.
-aceae.

## lycopodiaceous
lycopodiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.
Lye о podium, п., a genus of plants, the club moss
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'wolf's foot', compounded
of Gk. λύκος, 'wolf, and πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. See lyco- and podo-.

## Lycopsis
Lycopsis, п., a genus of plants, the bugloss (bot.)
— ModL., compounded of lyco- and Gk. δψις,
'sight, appearance'. See -opsis.

## Lycopus
Lycopus, п., a genus of plants, the bugleweed and
the water horehound (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'wolf's
foot', fr. lyco- and Gk. ττούς, gen. ποδός, 'foot'.
See -pod and cp. Lycopodlum.

## lyddite
lyddite, п., a high explosive. — Named after Lydd,
a town in Kent (England), whereit was first
tested (in 1888). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Cp. cheddite.

## Lydian
Lydian, adj., pertaining to Lydia, an ancient
country of Asia Minor. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Lydius, fr. Gk. Λύδιος, 'Lydian', fr. Λΰδός,
of s.m.
Derivative: Lydian, n.

## lye
lye, ile, n.—ME. lye, leye, fr. OE. leag, leah, rel. to
MDu. loghe, Du. loog, OHG. louga, MHG.
huge, G. Lauge, 'lye', ON. laug, 'hot bath, hot
spring', laugardagr, Dan. hrdag, Swed. lordag,
'Saturday' (lit. 'washing day'), OHG. luhhen, 'to
wash', and cogn. with Gk. λούειν, L. lavare, 'to
wash'. See lave and cp. words there referred to.

## Lygeuin
Lygeuin, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. λυγούν, 'to bend, tie fast', which is rel.
to λύγος, 'aoy flexible twig'. See next word.

## Lygodium
Lygodium, п., a genus of plants, the climbing fern
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'flexible, pliant', fr. Gk.
λυγώδης, which is compounded of λύγος, 'any
flexible twig, a willow twig; a withy', and-ώδης,

## lye-
lye-, form of lyco- before a vowel.

## lycanthropc
lycanthropc, п., 1) a werewolf; 2) one affected
with lycatithropy (med.) — Gk. λυκάνθρωπος,
'werewolf, lit. 'man-wolf, compounded of
λύκος, 'wolf, and άνθρωπος, 'man'. Seelyceum
and anthropo-.

## Jycanthropy
Jycanthropy, п., 1) assumption of the form of a
wolf in legends; 2) insanity in which the patient
imagines himself to be a wolf (med.) — Gk.
λυκανθρωπία, fr. λυκάνθρωπος. See prec.
word and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## Lycaon
Lycaon, п., an Arcadian king who set before
Zeus a dish of human flesh, in order to test his
divinity (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Λυκάων,
fr. λυκάων, 'werewolf, fr. λύκος, 'wolf. See
lyceum and cp. lycanthropc.

## lycee
lycee, п., a French secondary school. — F., fr. L.
lyceum. See lyceum.

## lyceum
lyceum, п., a lecture hall. — L. lyceum, fr. Gk.
λύκει,ον, a gymnasium in Athens in which
Aristotle taught; so called after the neighboring
temple of Apollo, one of whose epithets was
Λύκειος, lit. 'wolf-slayer', from λύκος, 'wolf,
which is cogn. with L. lupus, 'wolf. See lupine,
adj.

## lych
lych, lych-gate. — See lich, lich-gate.

## Lychnis
Lychnis, п., a genus of plants, the campion (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. λυχνίς, 'campion', prop, 'of
bright red color', rel. to λύχνος, 'lamp1, which
stands for *λύκ-σνος and is cogn. with OI. ruh-
sah, 'shining; bright', L. luna (for *louqs-na or
*leuqs-na), 'moon'. See June and cp. link, 'torch'.

## Lycian
Lycian, adj., pertaining to Lycia, an ancient
country of Asia Minor. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Lycius, fr. Gk. Λύκιος, 'Lycian'. Cp. next
word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:461 COLUMN:3 -->
'like'. The first element derives fr. I.-E. base
*leug-, *lug-, 'to bend, twist', whence also ON.
lokkr, OE. locc, 'lock of hair'; see lock, 'tuft of
hair'. For the second element see-ode,'like', for
the ending see 1st suff. -ium.

## Lymnaea
Lymnaea, п., a genus of air-breathing snails (zool.)
— ModL., erroneous spelling for Limnaea, fr.
Gk. λίμναίος, 'from the marsh, pertaining to a
marsh', fr. λίμνη, 'marsh, pool, lake'. See
limno-.

## lymph
lymph, п., a yellowish fluid. — L. lympha, lumpa,
limpa,' goddess of water, water', prob. dissimilat-
ed fr. Gk. νύμφη. See nymph and cp. limpid.
Cp. also the second element in endolymph,
perilymph.
Derivatives: lymphoid (q.v.), lymph-ous, lymph-
y, adjs.

## lymph-
lymph-, form of lympho- before a vowel.

## lymphatic
lymphatic, adj., I) pertaining to, containing or
conveying, lymph; 2) having a temperament
formerly attributed to excess of lymph; sluggish;
п., a lymphatic vessel. — L. lymphaticus,
'distracted, frantic', fr. lympha, 'water'. See lymph
and -atic. For sense development cp.
hydrophobia.

## lymphatism
lymphatism, п., lymphatic temperament (med.)
See lymphatic and -ism.

## lymph a tit is
lymph a tit is, п., inflammation of a part of the
lymphatic system (med.) — Medical L. See lymph
and -itis.

## lympho-
lympho-, before a vowel lymph-, combining form
meaning 'connected with, orcontaining, lymph'.
— Fr. L. lympha. See lymph.

## lymphocyte
lymphocyte, п., any of the cells found in the
lymph. — Compounded of lympho- and Gk.
κύτος, 'a hollow vessel'. See -cyte.
Derivative: lymphocyt-ic, adj.

## lymphoid
lymphoid, adj., resembling lymph. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. lympha, 'water', and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See lymph and
-old.

## lyncean
lyncean, adj., pertaining to a lynx. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. lynceus, fr. Gk. λύγκειος, fr.
λύγξ, gen. λυγκός, 'lynx'. See lynx.

## lynch
lynch, tr. v., to punish by lynch law, esp. to inflict
capital punishment without legal procedure. —
See lynch law.
Derivatives: lynch-er, п., lynch-ing, n.

## lynch
lynch, lynchet, n. — See linch, linchet.

## lynch law
lynch law, summary punishment inflicted by the
mob without legal formalities. — Fr. earlier
Lynch's law, usually traced to Charles Lynch
(1736-96), a magistrate in Virginia, said to have
started the above practice.

## lynx
lynx, n. — L., fr. Gk. λύγξ, cogn. with Arm. lus-
an-un-k' (pi.), Lith. lii$is> Lett. l(isa, OPruss.
luysis (whence PN. Luyseri), OSlav. rysi (with
secondary r for /, prob. under the influence of
the verb ruvati, 'to tear to pieces'), OSwed. /o,
OS. lohs, OE. lox, MDu., Du. /oj,OHG., MHG.
luhs, G. Luchs, and with OI. rusant-, 'bright,
white'; fr. I.-E. base *leuk-, which is rel. to base
*leuq-, 'to emit light, to shine; bright'; so called
in allusion to the shining eyes. See light,
'brightness', and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
ounce, 'lynx'.

## Lyon in Lord Lyon King of Arms
Lyon in Lord Lyon King of Arms, title of the chief
herald of Scotland. — Old spelling of lion (see
lion); so called from the lion represented on the
Royal Arms of Scotland.

## lyonnaise
lyonnaise, adj., made in the fashion of the city of
Lyons (said of food). — F., fern, of lyonnais, 'of
Lyons'; prop, shortened from the French term
a la lyonnaise, 'in the fashion of Lyons'. Lyons is
a town in France situated at the confluence of
the Rhone and the Saonc.

## Lyra
Lyra, п., a northern constellation (astron.) — L.
lyra (see lyre); so called from the lyre of Orpheus
it is supposed to represent.

## lyrate
lyrate, adj., shaped like a lyre. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ate fr. L. lyra, 'lyre'. See lyre.

## lyre
lyre, n. — ME. lire, fr. OF. lire, fr. L. lyra, fr. Gk.
λύρα, a foreign word of uncertain origin; not
connected with L. laus, 'praise', laudare, 'to
praise'.

## lyric
lyric, adj. — MF. lirique (F. lyrique), fr. L. lyricus,
fr. Gk. λυρικός, 'pertaining to, or singing to,
the lyre', fr. λύρα. See prec. word and -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:462 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 435 | -LYZE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:462 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: lyric, п., Iyric-al, adj., fyric-al-ly>
adv., lyric-al-ness, п., lyric-ism, n.

## lyrico-
lyrico-, combining form meaning 'lyrical and'. —
Fr. lyric.

## lyrism
lyrism, п., lyricism. — F. lyrisme, fr. Gk.
λυρισμός, fr. λύρα. See lyre and -ism.

## lyrist
lyrist, п.,a) one who plays the lyre; b) a lyrical
poet. — F. lyriste, fr. L. lyristes, fr. Gk. λυρισ-
τής, fr. λύρα. See lyre and -ist.

## Lysimachia
Lysimachia, п., a genus of plants, the loosestrife
{bot.) — L. lysimachia, name of a plant, fr. Gk.
λυσίμαχία, fr. Λυσίμαχος, Lysimachus, King
of Thrace, discoverer of this plant. This PN. lit.
means 'ending strife', fr. λύσίς, 'a loosing,
setting free; releasing', and μάχη, 'battle'. See
lysis and -machy.

## lysin
lysin, п., any substance causing the dissolution of
bacteria (biochem.) — Coined fr. Gk. λύσις (see
lysis) and chem. suff. -in.

## lysine
lysine, lysin, п., an amino acid, ΟβΗ14Ν,0,
(biochem.) — See prec. word.

## lysis
lysis, п., 1) gradual recession of a disease (med.);
2) cell destruction by lysins (biochem.) — Gk.
λύσ^ς, 'a loosing, setting free; releasing;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:462 COLUMN:2 -->
dissolution', fr. λύε(.ν, 'to unfasten, loose, loosen,
untie, slacken; to loose; to set free, release,
ransom; to dissolve', whence alsoXUTpov, 'ransom',
which is cogn. with OI. lundti, lunoti, 'cuts, cuts
off*, L. luere, 'to loose, release; to atone for,
expiate', ОЕ- for-leosan, 'to lose; to destroy',
losian, 'to perish, be lost'. See lose and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also -lysis, -lytic.

## -lysis
-lysis, combining form meaning 'loosing,
dissolving, dissolution', as in catalysis, hydrolysis. —
Fr. Gk. λύσις. See prec. word and cp. -lytic.

## lysol
lysol, п., a brown oily liquid, soluble in water. —
Coined fr. Gk. λΰσι,ς (see lysis) and suff. -ol
(representing L. oleum, 'oil').

## lyssa
lyssa, п., rabies. — Medical L., fr. Gk. λύσσα,
Att. λύττα, 'rage, fury, madness, frenzy, rabies',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. lytta, Alyssum.

## -lyte
-lyte, combining form meaning 'that can be
solved'; corresponding to nouns ending in -lysis.
— Gk. -λυτός, fr. λυτός, 'that may be loosed'
or 'that is loosed', verbal adj. of λύεί,ν, 'to
loose'. See-lysis.

## Lythraceae
Lythraceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:462 COLUMN:3 -->
loosestrife family [bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Lyth-
rum with suff. -aceae.

## lythraceous
lythraceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Ly thrum
Ly thrum, п., a genus of herbs, the loosestrife {bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. λύθρος, λύθρον, 'dirt, gore',
which is rel. to λΰμα (for *λυτ-μα), 'filth, dirt,
disgrace', and cogn. with L. lutum, 'mud, clay'.
See lute, 'a cohesive substance', pollute.

## lytic
lytic, adj., 1) pertaining to lysis; 2) pertaining to
lysin. — See -lytic.

## -lytic
-lytic, combining form forming adjectives
corresponding to nouns ending in -lysis, as mhydrolyt-
ic, — Gk. -λυτικός, fr. λυτικός, 'able to loose,
loosing', fr. λυτός, 'loosed', verbal adj. of λύειν,
'to loose*. See -lysis.

## lytta
lytta, п., a wormlike cartilage in the tongue of
many mammals (as e.g. the dog). — L. 'worm
under the tongue of a dog, said to cause
madness'. See lyssa.

## -lyze
-lyze, combining form forming verbs
corresponding to nouns ending in -lysis. — F. -lyser, back
formation fr. -lyse, fr. L. -lysis, fr. Gk. -λυσι,ς.
See -lysis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:463 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:463 COLUMN:1 -->

## ma
ma, n. — A childish or colloquial abbreviation of
mamma, 'mother'.

## -ma
-ma, subst. suff. representing Gk. -μα, forming
nouns that indicate the result of verbal action.
— See suff. -men. which is the exact Latin
equivalent of Gk. -μα, and cp. suff. -ment. Cp. also
suff. -ism, which is compounded of the suffixes
-ize and -ma.

## ma'am
ma'am, n. — Contraction of madam.

## maarib
maarib, п., the daily evening prayer (Jewish
liturgy).— Heb. ma'aribh, lit.'bringing evening',
Hiph'il (= causative) partic. of the verb iarabh,
'it became evening', denominated fr. *e'rebh,
'sunset, evening', which is re], to Arab, gharaba,
Ethiop. 'araba, '(the sun) has set', Arab, gharb,
'place of sunset, west', Akkad. erebu, 'to enter,
go in', ereb shamshi, 'sunset'. The name maarib
is taken from the text of the first benediction.
Cp. Maghrib. Cp. also Erebus, Europe.

## Maarib Arabim
Maarib Arabim, the first of the two benedictions
preceding the Shema in the evening prayer
(Jewish liturgy). — Heb. ma 'artbh 'ardbhtm,
'bringing evenings'. See prec. word; "arabhim,
'evenings', is the plural of 'erebh. The name of the
benediction was taken from the words mctaribh
""urabhim occurring in the text.

## Maat
Maat,n., the goddess of truth and justice in
Egyptian mythology. — Egypt. Μαά-t, lit. 'truth'.

## Mabel
Mabel, fern. PN. — Short for Amabel.

## Mac-
Mac-, pref. in family names of Gaelic, Irish and
Scottish origin. — Gael., Ir,, mac, 'son', fr. Olr.
mace, 'son', which is rel. to OW. map, Co. mob,
map. These words are prob. rel. to Olr. maug,
mug, 'slave', and cogn. with ОЕ- mago, 'son,
attendant, servant*, ON. mogr, 'son', Goth, magus,
'boy, servant', magapst 'virgin*, OE. mxged,
mxgd, 'maid'. See maiden.

## macabre
macabre, adj., pertaining to the dance of death.
— F., in danse macabre, 'dance of death',
altered— owing to afalsereading — fr. MF.danse
macabre', fr. earlier Macabre la danse, which is
usually explained as 'dance of the Maccabees'.
The derivation of the PN. Macabre' fr. L. Ma-
chabeus is based on Machabeorum chora, the
Medieval Latin name of the 'dance of death'
(see Du Cange, Glossarium mediae et infimae
Latinitatis, Paris 1883-87, s.v. Machabeorum
chora). It is not improbable that the story of the
seven brothers with their mother and that of
Eleazar (II. Mace, chapters 6 and 7), who
suffered martyrdom, conveyed the idea of 'the dance
of death'. For the etymology of the name Ma-
chabeus see Maccabees. Some lexicographers
derive macabre fr. Syr. (marqadhta dhi) m qabb re,
'(dance of the) grave-diggers', or fr. Arab, maq-
bara , 'cemetery'.

## Macaca
Macaca, п., a genus of monkeys, the macaque
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Port, macaca, 'female
monkey', fem. of macaco. See macaco.

## macaco
macaco, п., any of several species of lemurs. —
Port., fr. African (Congo) name. Cp. macaque.

## macadam
macadam, п., material for road making. —
Named after the Scot, engineer John London
Macadam (1756-1836), inventor of the process.
Derivatives: macadam-ize, tr. v., macadam-iz-
ation, n.

## macao
macao, п., a game, a variety of vingt-et-un. — So
called from Macao, a seaport in China, where
this game is still in fashion.

## macaque
macaque, п., any monkey of the genus Macaca.
— F., fr. Port, macaco. See Macaca.

## macaroni
macaroni, п., 1) tube-shaped food made of dried
wheaten paste; 2) dandy. — It. maccaroni, now
maccheroni, pi. of maccarone, resp. maccherone,
'paste with cheese', fr. Late Gk. μακαρία, 'food
composed of broth and barley groats', which
derives (with obscure sense development) fr. Gk.
μακαρίϊ, 'happiness, bliss', fr. μάκαρ, 'blessed,
happy', a word of uncertain origin. Cp.
macaroon.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:463 COLUMN:2 -->

## macaronic
macaronic, adj., written in burlesque style; п., а
burlesque composition. — Formed fr. prec.
word with suff. -ic.
Derivative: macaronic-al-ly, adv.

## macaroon
macaroon, п., small cake made of almonds. — F.
macaron, fr. dial. It. maccarone, fr. It. maccaroni.
See macaroni.

## macartney
macartney, п., the fire-backed pheasant. — Short
for Macartney pheasant; named after Lord
Macartney (1737-1806).

## Macassar oil
Macassar oil, a hair oil orig. made from materials
obtained from Macassar. — From Macassar
(native Mangkasara), name of a district of the
island of Celebes. Cp. antimacassar.

## macaw
macaw, п., any parrot of the genus Ara. — Port.
macau, prob. fr. macauba^ 'macaw palm' (see
next word), and so called because it feeds on the
fruit of this tree.

## macaw palm
macaw palm, — Port, macauba, fr. Tupi macauba,
'the macaw palm'.

## Maccabean
Maccabean, adj., pertaining to the Maccabees. —
See next word and -an.

## Maccabees
Maccabees, n. pi. — F. Machabes, fr. Late L. Ma-
chabael, fr. Machabaeus, surname given to
Judas, the third son of Mattathias the Hasmonean,
usually connected with Heb. maqqabh,
'hammer', but prob. derived from an inexact
transliteration of Heb. matzbV, 'general, commander
of an army', fr. tzabha, 'host, army'. See Saba-
oth.
maccaboy» п., also maccoboy, maccabaw, a kind
of scented snuff. — Named from Macouba, a
district in Martinique.

## mace
mace, п., a weapon (hist.); a staff. — ME.,
fr. OF. mace (F. masse), fr. VL. *mattea, back
formation fr. L. mateola, 'mallet', fr. *matea,
which is cogn. with OI. matyam, 'harrow, club',
OSlav. motyka, 'mattock', OHG. medela, 'plow'.
Cp. It. mazza, Sp. тага, 'mace', which also
derive fr. VL. *mattea. Cp. also mashie, masse,
mattock, stramazon.
Derivative: mace, tr. v., to strike with a mace.

## mace
mace, п., a spice consisting of the dried outer
covering of nutmeg. — ME. macis, fr. F. macis,
fr. Late L. macis, which is prob. a scribal error
for L. macir, 'red bark of an Indian root', fr. Gk.
μακίρ, a word of uncertain origin. The -s in F.
macis was mistaken for the plural suff. and
accordingly dropped in English.

## mace
mace, п., swindling; tr. and intr, v., to swindle
(slang). — Of uncertain origin.

## macedoine
macedoine, п., a dish of fruit or vegetables
embedded in jelly. — F., fr. Macedoine, fr. L.
Macedonia, fr. Macedones, 'the Macedonians', fr.
Gk. Μακεδόνες, of s.m.; so called facetiously in
allusion to the medley of nations of different
origin by which Macedonia was inhabited. See
next word.

## Macedonian
Macedonian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Macedonius, fr. Git. Μακεδόνιος,
'Macedonian', fr. Μακεδόνες, 'the Macedonians', lit.
'the Highlanders', or 'the Tall Ones', rel. to
μακεδνός, 'long, tall', and to μακρός, 'long,
large'. See macro-.

## macer
macer, п., one who bears a mace. — Formed fr.
mace, 'a weapon', with agential suff. -er.

## macer
macer, п., a swindler (slang). — Formed fr. mace,
4o swindle', with agential suff. -er.

## macerate
macerate, tr. v., to steep by soaking; to cause to
waste away; to torment; intr. v., to waste away.
— L. maceratus, pp. of macerare^ 'to make soft
or tender', fr. I.-E. base *mag-, *meg-, 'to
knead', whence also Gk. μαγίς. 'kneaded mass,
cake', μαγεύς, 'one who kneads, baker*, OSlav.
maio, mazati, 'to anoint, smear', maslo, 'butter,
oil*, masti, 'ointment', Bret, meza, 'to knead',
Mir. maistir, 'to churn*. From *mak-, a var. of
*mag-, possibly derives Gk. μάσσω (if standing
for *meq-yo)> Ί squeeze, press into a mold,
knead'. See make v., and verbal suff. -ate and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:463 COLUMN:3 -->
magma, mazo-, 'placenta'. Cp. also mass, 'size,
quantity'. — Cp. *menq-, 'to knead', a
collateral base, for the derivatives of which see mingle.
(Gk. μάσσω could also stand for *mnq-yo,
hence be a derivative of base *menq-.)
Derivatives: macerat-er, macerat-or, п.,
maceration, n.

## machete
machete, п., a large, heavy knife. — Sp., derived
fr. machot 'hammer', fr. L. marculus, which was
prob. dissimilated fr. *malclos, for *mal-ilost
and rel. to malleus, 'hammer'; see malleus and
cp. march, 'to walk'. L. marcus, 'hammer', is a
back formation fr. marculus, which was
mistaken for a diminutive.

## Machetes
Machetes, п., a genus of birds, the ruff; synonym
of Philomachus (ornithol.)—ModL., fr. Gk.
μαχητής, 'fighter', fr. μάχεσθαι, 'to fight'. See
-madly and cp. Philomachus.

## -machia
-machia, combining form. — See -machy.

## Machiavellian
Machiavellian, adj., 1) pertaining to the
Florentine statesman Niccolo Machiavelli (1469-1527),
author of Ί1 Principe', or to his political
doctrines; whence 2) crafty, subtle, — For the
ending see suff. -ian.
Derivative: Machiavellian, n.

## Machiavellism
Machiavellism, n. — See prec. word and -ism.

## machicolate
machicolate, tr. v., to provide with
machicolations. — ML. machicolatus, pp. of machicolare,
fr. MF. machicouler, 'to provide with
machicolations', fr. MF. machecolis (whence F. machi-
oulis, 'machicolation'), which is perh. an
alteration of *machis coulis, fr. *machis, a derivative
of the verb macher, 'to crush, bruise' (whence F.
machure, *a bruise'), and coulis, 'the act of
flowing', fr. couler, 'to flow'; see Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 361 s.v. machicoulis. See coulisse and
cp. portcullis. For the ending see verbal suff.
-ate.

## machicolation
machicolation, п., an opening in the floor made
between the corbels that support the parapet. —
See prec. word and -ion.

## machicoulis
machicoulis, п., machicolation. — F. machicoulis.
See machicolate.

## machina
machina, п., a machine. — L. machina, 'machine'.
See machine.

## machinate
machinate, intr. v., to plot, scheme. — L. machi-
natus, pp. of machinari, 'to invent, devise, plot',
fr. machina. See machine, and verbal suff. -ate.

## machination
machination, п., plot, intrigue. — L. mdchindtio,
gen. -onis, 'machination, device, trick', fr. ma-
chinatus, pp. of machinari. See prec. word and
-ion.

## machina tor
machina tor, п., plotter, schemer. — L. machina-
tor, fr. mdchinatus, pp. of machinari. See
machinate and agential suff. -or.

## machine
machine, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. machina,
'machine, engine, fabric, frame, device, trick', fr.
Dor. μαχανα, corresponding to Att. μηχανή,
'machine, contrivance, artificial means,
expedient*, fr. Dor. μαχος (Attic μήχος),
'contrivance, means, expedient, remedy', fr. I.-E. base
*mdgh-, *m gh~, 'to be able', whence also OSlav.
mogg, moSti, 'to be able', OE. mxg, Ί can'. See
may, auxil. v., and cp. main, 'might', might. Cp.
also mechanic.
Derivatives: machine, tr. v,, machin-ery, п.,
machinist (q.v.)

## machinist
machinist, n. — A hybrid coined (on analogy of
F. machiniste) fr. L. machina and -1st, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## Machpelah
Machpelah, п., name of the cave in Hebron, in
which the patriarchs and their wives were buried
(Bible). — Heb. Makhpelah, lit. 'double cave',
fr. kaphal, 'he doubled', whence kephel, 'the
double'; rel. to Aram, к phal, 'he doubled',
kiphla, kuphla, 'double', Arab, kifl, 'the double',
Ethiop. kafala, 'he divided', kefel, 'a part'.
•machy, -machia, combining form meaning
'battle, war, contest', as in alectryomachy, gigan-
tomachy. — Gk. -μαχία^Γ. μάχη, 'battle, fight',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:464 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 437 | MAGDALEN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:464 COLUMN:1 -->
rel. to μάχεσθαι, 'to fight'; of uncertain origin.
Cp. the second element in Andromache, Tele-
machus.
mackerel, п., an edible fish (Scomber scombrus).
— OF. makerel, maquerel (F. maquereau), of
uncertain origin; possibly identical with next
word.
mackerel, п., a pimp, pander (archaic). — ME.
makerel, fr. OF. makerel, maquerel (F. maque-
reau), 'pimp, pander*, fr. MDu. makelaer (Du.
makelaar), 'broker, agent', fr. makelen, 'to act as
a broker', fr. maken, 'to make'; see make, v. G.
makeln, 'to act as a broker', and Makler, also
Makler, 'broker', are Dutch loan words.
mackinaw, n. — Short for Mackinaw boat, resp.
Mackinaw coat, Mackinaw blanket, etc., fr. Can.
F. Mackinac, fr. Mackinac, a port in Michigan,
fr. Ojibway Indian mitchimakinaky 'great turtle'.

## mackintosh
mackintosh, п., a waterproof outer coat. —
Named after Charles Mackintosh (1766-1843),
who invented the waterproofing of materials.

## mackintoshite
mackintoshite, п., a silicate of uranium, thorium
and other metals (mineral.) — Named after the
American chemist James B. Mackintosh. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## mackle
mackle, п., macule; blur. — F. macule, fr. L.
macula. See macula and cp. mascle.
Derivative: mackl-ed, adj.

## made
made, п., a twinned crystal. —F., fr. L. macula.
See macula and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: macl-ed, adj.

## Madura
Madura, п., a genus of trees, the Osage orange
(bot.) — ModL., named after the American
geologist William Maclure (1763-1840).

## macon
macon, п., a red Burgundy wine. — Named after
Macon, a French city and center of
viticulture.

## niacr-
niacr-, form of macro- before a vowel.

## macrame
macrame, п., a kind of ornamental work
embroidered into knots. — Turk, maqrama,
'handkerchief, fr. Arab, miqramd1, 'embroidered veil'.

## macro-
macro-, before a vowel macr-, combining form
meaning 'long'. — Gk. μακρό-, μακρ-, fr.
μακρός, 'long, large', cogn. with L. macer, 'lean,
thin', ON. magr, OE. mxger, 'lean, thin', fr.
I.-E. *mekros, derivative of base *malc-, *meJc-,
'long, thin', whence also Gk. μήκος, 'length',
μακε-δν-ός, 'long, tall'. See meager and cp.
Macedonian, meco-.

## macrobiotic
macrobiotic, adj., long-lived; tending to prolong
life.—Formed with sufT.-icfr. Gk. μακροβίοτος,
'long-lived', fr. μακρόβιος, of s.m., which is
compounded of μακρός,'long', and βίος, 'life'.
See macro- and bio-,

## macrocephalic
macrocephalic, also macrocephalous, adj., large-
headed. — Formed with suff. -ic, resp. -ous, fr.
Gk. μακροκέφαλος, 'large-headed', which is
compounded of μακρός, 'long', and κεφαλή,
'head'. See macro- and cephalic,

## macrocephaly
macrocephaly, п., the condition of being macro-
cephalic. — See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk.-ίά).

## macrocosm
macrocosm, п., the great world, the universe. —

## F. macrocosme
F. macrocosme, compounded of macro- and Gk.
κόσμος, 'world'. See cosmos and cp. microcosm,

## macron
macron, п., a short horizontal line placed over a
vowel to indicate its length. — Gk. μακρόν,
neut. of μακρός, 'long'. See macro-,

## macroscopic
macroscopic, also macroscopical, adj., large
enough to be seen by the naked eye. —
Compounded of macro- and Gk. σκοττεΐν, 'to look

## at
at, examine' (see -scope), and suff. -ic, resp. also

## -al
-al, Cp. microscope.
Derivative: macroscopical-ly, adv.
■microspore, п., a megasphore. — Compounded
of macro- and Gk. σπορά, 'a sowing, seed'. See
spore.

## Macrura
Macrura, п., a division of crustaceans (zool.) —

## ModL.
ModL., lit. 'long-tailed', compounded of macr-
and Gk. ούρα, 'tail'. See uro-, 'tail-'.
Derivatives: macrur-al, macrur-ous, adjs., ma-

## crur-an
crur-an, n.

## macula
macula, п., a spot, stain; a spot on the surface of
the sun; a spot on the skin. — L. macula, 'spot,

## mark
mark, stain, blot, mesh', prob. for *(s)me-tla, fr.
I.-E. base *sme(i)-, 'to rub', whence also Gk.
σμώ, σμην, *to anoint, smear, rub, wipe,
cleanse*, σμήλη, σμημα, 'unguent', σμήχειν, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:464 COLUMN:2 -->
clear ofT, soap, purge'. Accordingly, the original
meaning of macula seems to have been, 'a soiled
spot, a spot to be cleaned'. See smite and words
there referred to and cp. esp. mackle, mail,
'armor'. Cp. also maquls.
Derivative: macul-ar, adj.

## maculate
maculate, tr. v. — L. maculdtus, pp. of maculare,
*to make spotted, to speckle', fr. macula. See
prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: maculat-ed, adj.

## maculate
maculate, adj. — L. maculatus, 'spotted', pp. of
maculare. See maculate, v.

## maculation
maculation, n. — ME. maculacion, fr. L. macula·
tio, gen. -onis, 'a spotting', fr. maculatus, pp.
of maculare. See maculate, v., and -ion.

## macule
macule, п., a spot. — F., fr. L. macula. See macula.

## macule
macule, tr. and intr. v., to mackle. — F. maculer,
fr. macule. See macule, n.

## mad
mad, adj. — ME. mad, madde, fr. OE. gemxdd,
gemxded, pp. of a lost verb, fr. gemad, 'mad',
which is rel. to OS. gi-med, OHG. gi-meit,
'foolish, crazy', Goth, ga-maidans (ace. pi.),
'crippled, wounded', ON. meida, 'to hurt, maim*,
MHG. meidenen, 'to castrate', and prob. cogn.
with Gk. μίτυλος, 'maimed, hornless, weak',
μιστύλλειν, 'to cut into pieces', OLith. apmai-
tinti, 'to wound'. Cp. maim.
Derivatives: mad, tr. and intr. v. (rare), madd-en,
п., madd-en-ing, adj., madd-en-ing-ly, adv.,
madly, adv., madness (q.v.)

## madam
madam, n. — F. madame, for ma dame, 'my lady',
fr. L. mea domina. L. mea is fern, of meus, 'my;
mine'; see me, mine, adj. For the etymology of
dame see dame.

## madame
madame, п., a French title of respect, orig. for a
woman of rank, now given to every married
woman. — F., fr. ma dame, 'my lady'. See prec.
word.

## madarosis
madarosis, n., loss of the eyelashes (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. μαδάρωσις,'baldness', fr. μαδα-
poGv,*tomake bald'.fr. μαδαρός, 'wet, watery;
bald', from the stem of μαδάν, Чо be wet, to
flow', which is prob. rel. to μαζός, μαστός (for
*μαδ-τ-ός), 'breast'. See mast, 'fruit of beech',
and -osis.

## madarotic
madarotic, adj., affected with the loss of eyelashes
(med.) — See prec. word and -otic.

## madder
madder, п., a plant (Rubia tinctorum). — ME.
mader, fr. OE. maedere, rel, to ON. тадга, Swed.
madra, MDu. mede, Du. mede, mee-krap, OHG.
matara, 'madder', and cogn. with Pol. modry,
Czech modry, 'blue'.

## made
made, pp. of make. — ME. maked, made, fr. OE.
macod, 'made', pp. of macian, 'to make'. See
make, v.

## Madeira
Madeira, п., name of an island in the Atlantic and
name of the wine produced in the island. —
Port., fr. madeira (= Sp. madera), 'timber,
wood', fr. L. materia (see matter, 'substance');
so called because it was formerly rich in timber;
cp. madrier. For sense development cp. Cyprus,
'the island of cypress trees' (see Cyprian), and
Pityuses, 'the islands covered with pines'.

## Madeline
Madeline, fern. PN. — Fr. Magdalene (q.v.)

## mademoiselle
mademoiselle, п., a title given to an unmarried
French woman, equivalent to E. miss. — F., for
ma demoiselle, fr. VL. mea *dominicella, lit. 'my
young mistress'. For the first word see madam;
for the second see damsel and cp. demoiselle.

## madness
madness, n. — ME. maddnesse, fr. madd, 'mad'.
See mad and -ness.

## Madoc
Madoc, masc. PN. — W. Madawg, fr. madawg,
'benefiting', fr. mad, 'fortunate'.

## Madonna
Madonna, n. — It. madonna, fr. Olt. ma donna
(= It. mia donna), 'my lady', for L. mea domina,
'my lady'. See madam and donna.

## madrague
madrague, п., a large fishpond. — F. madrague,
fr. Proveng. madraga, fr. Sp. almadraba, fr.
Arab, almazraba , 'the enclosure', which is
formed fr. al-, 'the', and mazrabd1, 'enclosure',
fr. zaraba, 'he made an enclosure'.

## madras
madras, п., a light cotton fabric. — So called
from Madras, in India.

## madrasah
madrasah, п., a Mohammedan college. — Arab.
madrasa , lit. 'a place of study', formed with
local pref. ma- from the stem of darasa, 'he read
repeatedly, he studied', a loan word fr. Aram.-
Syr. d rash, 'he inquired into, examined', which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:464 COLUMN:3 -->
is rel. to Heb. darash, of s.m. Seemidrash.
Madreporaria, п., an order of Anthozoa (zool.)
— ModL. See next word.

## madrepore
madrepore, п., any of various corals of the genus
Acropora. — F. madrepore, fr. It. madrepora
which is compounded of madre, 'mother', and
poro, 'pore'. It. madre derives fr. L. mdtrem, ace.
of mater, 'mother'; see mother and cp. mater. It.
poro comes fr. L. porus, fr. Gk. πόρος, 'pore';
see pore. The change of It. poro to -pora (in
madrepora) is due to the influence of the gender of
madre (which is nat. feminine).
Derivative: madrepor~ic, adj.

## madrier
madrier, п., a thick plank serving various
purposes, esp. to receive the mouth of a petard.—F.,
fr. OProvenc. madier, 'cover of a kneading
trough', fr. VL. *materium, fr. L. materia,
'wood, timber'. See matter and cp. Madeira.

## madrigal
madrigal, п., 1) a short love poem; 2) music for
such a poem. — It. madrigale, of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: madrigal-ian, п., madrigal-ist,
n.

## madrona
madrona, madrono, п., an evergreen tree, Arbutus
menziesii. — Sp. madrono, 'strawberry tree', re].
to maduro, 'ripe, mature', fr. L. maturus, of s.m.
See mature, adj.

## Madura foot
Madura foot, infection of the foot caused by a
species of fungus; called also mycetoma (med.)
— Named after Madura, a district in Madras,
India, where this disease especially occurs.

## Maecenas
Maecenas, п., a patron of literature or art. — L.
Gaius Cilnius Maecenas (died in the year 8
B.C.E.), the patron of Virgil and Horace.

## Maelstrom
Maelstrom, п., a famous whirlpool off the NW.
coast of Norway. ■— Du. maelstrom (now maal-
stroom), lit. 'grinding stream', fr. malen, 'to
grind', and strom, 'stream'. See meal, 'flour',
and stream.

## Maemacterion
Maemacterion, п., name of the 5th month of the
Attic Greek calendar year (corresponding to
November-December). — Gk. Μαι.μακτηρι.ών,
fr. Μαίμάκτης, 'the god of storms', epithet of
Zeus at Athens, lit. 'stormy, boisterous,
impetuous', from the stem of μαψ.άσσεΐΜ, a secondary
form of μαιμαν, 'to be very eager', formed with
reduplication from the stem of μαίεσθαι, 'to
endeavor, seek, strive', which is rel. to μώσθαι,
'to seek after, covet'.

## Maenad
Maenad, п., priestess of Bacchus (Greek mythol.)
— L. maenas, gen. -adis, fr. Gk. μαινάς, gen.
-άδος, 'a raving woman; a bacchante', from
the stem of μα£νεσθα(., 'to rave, rage'. See
mania.

## Maenidae
Maenidae, n. pi., a small family of sea fishes
(zool.) — ModL., fr. L. maena, a kind of small,
spratlike sea fish, fr. Gk. μαίνη, of s.m., which
is possibly cogn. with Lith. menke, Lett, menza,
'codfish'. For the ending see suff. -idae.

## maestoso
maestoso, adj., majestic (musical direction). — It.,
fr. maesta, 'majesty', fr. L. majestatem, ace. of
majestas. See majesty and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: maestoso, adv. and n.

## maestro
maestro, п., a master, esp. an eminent musical
composer. — It., 'master', fr. L. magistrum, ace.
of magister, 'master'. See master,

## maffick
maffick, intr. v., to celebrate in a boisterous
manner. — Back formation fr. a supposed pres. part.
mafficking, facetious alteration of Mafeking,
name of a town in S. Africa, whose relief (on
May 17, 1900) was celebrated in London in a
boisterous, uproarious way.

## maffla
maffla, mafia, п., organized lawless hostility in
Sicily. — It. maffia, mafia, of uncertain origin.

## Mag
Mag, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Margaret. Cp.
maggot, magpie,

## magazine
magazine, n. — MF. magazin (F. magasin), fr.

## OF. magazin
OF. magazin, fr. It. magazzino, fr. Arab, ma-

## khdzin
khdzin, pi. of makhzan, 'storehouse', fr. khazana,
*he stored up', for the etymology of which see

## Paul de La garde
Paul de La garde, Gesammelte Abhandlungen,

## Leipzig
Leipzig, 1866, p. 25. Cp. alhacena, almacen.
Derivatives: magazine, tr. v., magazin-er, n.

## magdalen
magdalen, also magdalene, п., a reformed
prostitute. — Named after Mary Magdalene,
mentioned in Luke 8:2 (often identified with the
penitent woman in Luke 7:37-50). See
Magdalene.

Magdalene, also Magdalen, fem. PN. — Eccles.
L. Magdalene, fr. Gk. Μαγδαληνή,
'Magdalene', lit. 'woman of Magdala', fr. Μάγδαλα, fr.
Aram. Maghd'la, place on the Sea of Galilee
(see Yerushalmi 'Erubhin, 5,1), lit. 'tower', fr.
gldhal, 'he became great'; rel. to Heb. gddhdl,
'he became great, was great', gddhdl, 'great'. Cp.
Madeline, magdalen, maudlin.
mage, п., a magician. — F., fr. L. magus,
'magician'. See magus and cp. magic, adj.
magenta, п., a purplish red dye. — So called
because it was discovered shortly after the battle
of Magenta in 1859.
maggot, n. — Prob. formed (under the influence
οι Maggot, dimin. of Mag) fr. ME. maddock, fr.

matho, MLG., MDu., Du. made, OHG. mado,
MHG., G. made, Goth, тара, 'maggot', and
possibly cogn. with Arm. mat'i/, 'louse'. Cp.
