Derivative: maggot-y, adj.

## Maghrib
Maghrib, п., Barbary. — Arab. Maghrib, 'the
West', fr. ghdraba, '(the sun) has set', whence
gharb, 'place of the sunset, west'. See maarib.

## Maghribi
Maghribi, п., a native of Barbary. — Arab. Magli-
ribi 'an inhabitant of the West', formed fr.
Maghrib (see prec. word) with -i, a suflf.
expressing relationship and corresponding to Heb.
suff. -i.

## Magi
Magi, n. pi., a priestly caste in Media and Persia.
— L. magi, pi. of magus. See Magus.

## Magian
Magian, adj., pertaining to the Magi; п., one of
the Magi. — See prec. word and -ian.

## magic
magic, n. — ME. magik, fr. MF. (— F.) ma-
gique, fr. Late L. magice, fr. Gk. μαγική (scil.
τέχνη), lit. 'magic art', fem. of the adjective
μαγικός, 'Magian, magical'. See magic, adj.

## magic
magic, adj. — ME. magik, fr. OF. (= F.) ma-
gique, fr. L. magicus, fr. μαγικός, 'Magian,
magical', fr. μάγος, 'Magus, magician'. See Magas
and -ic.
Derivatives: magic-al, adj., magic-al-ly, adv.

## magician
magician, n. — ME. magicien, fr. MF. (= F.) ma-
gicien, fr. OF. magique. See magic, п., and -ian.

## magUp
magUp, n. — A var. of megilp.

## magisterial
magisterial, adj., 1) pertaining to a master; 2)
pertaining to a magistrate; 3) authoritative. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Late L. magis-
terius, fr. L. magister, 'master'. See master.
Derivatives: magisteriat-ly, adv., magisterial-
ness, n.

## magistracy
magistracy, п., the office of a magistrate. —
Formed fr. magistrate with suff. -cy.

## magistral
magistral, adj., I) magisterial; 2) guiding; 3)
prepared for a particular case {pharm.) — L.
magistral, 'of a master', fr. magister, gen. magistrt,
'master'. See master and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: magistral-ly, adv.

## magistrate
magistrate, п., a public civil officer. — ME.
magistral, fr. L. magistrdtus, 'high civil official,
magistrate', fr. magister, gen. magistri, 'master'.
See master and subst. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: magistrat-ive, adj., magislral-ure,
n.

## magma
magma, п., a pasty mass. — L., fr. Gk. μάγμα,
'a thick unguent', fr. μάσσω (for *μάγ-ιω), Ί
squeeze, press into a mold, knead'. See macerate.

## Magua Charta
Magua Charta, also Magna Carta, the Great,
Charter obtained from King John on June 15th
1215. — ML., 'great charter'. See magnum and
chart.

## maguanimity
maguanimity, n. — ME. magnanimite, fr. MF.
(= F.) magnanimite, fr. L. magnanimitdtem, ace.
of magnanimitas, 'highmindedness', fr. magna-
nimus. See next word and -ity.

## magnanimous
magnanimous, adj., of a generous, noble
character. — L. magnanimus, 'highminded,
magnanimous', lit. 'great-souled', compounded of
magnus, 'great', and animus, 'soul'. See magaum and
animus. For E. -ous, as epuivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivatives: magnanimous-ly, adv., magnani-
mous-ness, n.

## maguate
maguate, п., a great man; a man of high position.
— Late L. magnds, gen. magnalis, 'magnate', fr.
L. magnus, 'great'. See maguum.

## magnesia
magnesia, п., magnesium oxide {chem.) — ML.,
fr. Gk. μαγνησία, shortened fr. ή Μαγνησία

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:465 COLUMN:2 -->
λίθος, 'the Magnesian stone', fr. Μαγνησία,
the name of a peninsula and a town in East
Thessaly. Cp. maguet, manganese.
Derivatives: magnesi-al, magnesi-an, adjs.

## magnesite
magnesite, п., magnesium carbonate {mineral.) —
F. magnesite, fr. Gk. μαγνησία. See maguesia
and subst. suff. -ite.

## magnesium
magnesium, п., name of a silvery-white metallic
element (chem.) — ModL. See magnesia and
chem. suff. -ium.
Derivatives: magnesi-al, magnesi-an, magnes-ic,
adjs.

## maguet
maguet, n. — ME. magnete, fr. OF. magnete,
fr. L. magnitem, ace. of magnes, 'loadstone', fr.
Gk. Μαγνήτις λίθος, 'stone from Magnesia,
lodestone', fr. Μαγνησία, a town in Lydia,
Asia Minor.
Derivatives: magnet, tr. v., magnetic (q.v.),
magnet-ism, п., magnet-ist, п., magnet-ize, tr. v.,
magnet-iz-abte, adj., magnet-iz-abil-ity, п., mag-
net-iz-ation, п., magnet-iz-er, п., magnet-iz-ing,
adj.

## magnetic
magnetic, adj. — F. magnetique, fr. Late L. mag-
neticus, fr. L. magnes, gen. magnetis, 'loadstone'.
See magnet and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: magnetic-al, adj., magnetic-al-ly,
adv., magnetic-at-ness, n.

## maguetlte
maguetlte, п., a native oxide of iron; lodestone
{mineral.) — G. Magnetit, fr. L. magnes, gen.
-etis. See maguet. The ending -it goes back to Gk.
-ΐτης; see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: magnetit-ic, adj.

## magneto-
magneto-, combining form meaning 'magnetic'.
— See maguet.

## magneto
magneto, п., a magneto-electric machine. — See
magueto-.

## magni-
magni-, combining form meaning 'great'; used
either in a laudatory or a depreciatory sense. —
L. magni-, fr. magnus, 'great'. See magnum.

## magnific
magnific, adj., magnificent. — OF. (= F.)
magnifique, fr. L. magnificus. See magnificent
and -fie.
Derivatives: magnific-at, adj., magnific-al-ly, adv.

## Magnificat
Magnificat, п., the canticle of the Virgin Mary,
Luke 1:46-55. — So called fr. magnificat,
'magnifies', the first word of the Latin version of the
canticle; L. magnificat is 3rd pers. sing. pres. of
magnificare, 'to magnify'. See magnify.

## maguification
maguification, n. — Late L. magnifiedtid, gen.
-onis, fr. L. magnificatus, pp. of magnificare. See
magnify and -ation.

## magnificence
magnificence, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F), fr. L.
magnificentia, 'splendor, munificence', fr.
magnificus. See next word and -ce.

## magnificent
magnificent, adj. — OF., back formation fr. L.
magnificentior, compar. of magnificus, 'splendid,
munificent', lit. 'doing great things', fr. magnus,
'great', and -ficus, from the stem of L. -ficere,
unstressed form of facere, 'to make, do'. See
magnum, -fie and -ent.
Derivatives: magnificent-ly, adv., magnificent-
ness, n.

## magnifico
magnifico, п., title of a Venetian nobleman. — It.,
lit. 'magnific', fr. L. magnificus, 'splendid,
munificent'. See magnific, magnificent.

## magnify
magnify, tr. v. — ME. magnifien, fr. OF. (= F.)
magnifier, fr. L. magnificare, 'to praise highly,
magnify', which is compounded of magnus,
'great', and -ficare, fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See
maguum and -fr and cp. magnificent.
Derivative: magnifi-er, n.

## maguiloqueuce
maguiloqueuce, n. — L. magniloquentia, 'elevated
language; pompous language', fr. magniloquus.
See next word and -ce.

## magniloquent
magniloquent, adj., speaking pompously;
bombastic. — Formed with suff. -ent fr. L.
magniloquus, 'pompous in talk, boastful', fr. magnus,
'great', and -loquus, 'speaking', fr. loqui, 'to
speak'. See loquacious.
Derivative: magniloquent-ly, adv.

## magnitude
magnitude, п., greatness. — ME., fr. L. magnitudo,
'greatness, size, bulk', fr. magnus, 'great*. See
magnum and -tude.

## Magnolia
Magnolia, п., a genus of plants {hot.) — ModL.,
named after Pierre Magnol, French professor of
botany (1638-1715). For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## Magnoliaceae
Magnoliaceae, n. pi., the magnolia family (bot.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:465 COLUMN:3 -->
— ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## magnoliaceous
magnoliaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## magnum
magnum, п., a bottle holding two quarts of wine
and spirits. — Lit. 'something large', fr. L.
magnum, neut. of magnus, 'great, large, much,
abundant', which stands for *nfg-nds and
derives fr. I.-E. base *meg(h)-, *meg-, 'great, large',
whence also OI. mah-, maha-, mahdt-, 'great',
Gk. μέγας, fem. μεγάλη, neut. μέγα, 'great,
large', Goth, mikils, OE. mice!, mycel, 'great,
big, many'. See mickle and cp. words there
referred to.

## magnum bonum
magnum bonum, 1) a large variety of yellow plum;
2) a large variety of potato. — L., 'large and
good', fr. magnum, neut. of magnus, 'great,
large', and bonum, neut. of bonus, 'good'. See
maguum and bonus.

## maguum opus
maguum opus, a great work, masterpiece; a
person's greatest work. — L., 'great work', fr.
magnum, neut. of magnus, 'great, large', and
opus, gen. operis, 'work'. See maguum and opus.

## magot
magot, п., the Barbary ape. — F., fr. the PN.
Magot, corruption of Magog, fr. Heb. Mdghogh,
name of a country and of a nation (see Ezek.
38:2 and 39:6), applied derisively to the
Barbary ape.

## magpie
magpie, n. — Compounded of Mag,
abbreviation of Margaret and pie, the bird. For sense
development cp. F. margot, 'magpie', fr. Mar-
got, 'Mag, Maggy', a pet form of Marguerite,
'Margaret'.

## maguey
maguey, п., any of various species of Agave. —
Sp., fr. Taino.

## Magus
Magus, п., one of the Magi; {not cap.) a magician.
— L., fr. Gk. μάγος, fr. OPers. magush,
'magician', whence also Talmudic Heb. mdgosh,
Aram, amgusha, 'magician'.

## Magyar
Magyar, п., Hungarian. — Hungarian.

## Mahabharata
Mahabharata, п., one of the two great Hindu
epics (the other is Ramayana). — OI. Mahdbhdra-
tah, lit. 'the great (story of the) Bharatas'. OI.
maha-, 'great', is cogn. with L. magnus, 'great'.
See magnum and cp. maharaja and words there
referred to.

## mahaleb
mahaleb, п., a kind of European cherry (Prunus
mahaleb). — Arab, mdhlab, in VArab.
pronunciation mdhleb.

## maharaja
maharaja, maharajah, п., the title of great Hindu
princes. — OI. maharajah, 'a great king',
compounded of maha-, 'great', and rajan, 'king'. See
maguum and rajah and cp. Maratna and the first
element in Mahabharata, maharanee, mahatma,
mahout,

## maharanee
maharanee, maharam, п., 1) a great Hindu
princess ; 2) the wife of a maharaja. — Hind, mahdrd-
ni, 'a great queen', compounded of maha-,
'great', and rani, 'queen'. See prec. word and
ranee,

## mahatma
mahatma, п., great-souled, magnanimous. — OI.
mahdtman, 'great-souled', compounded of
mahdt-, 'great', and dtmdn, 'soul'. The first element
is cogn. with L. magnus, 'great'; see magaum
and cp. maharajah and words there referred to.
For the second element see atman.

## Mahdl
Mahdl, п., a Mohammedan prophet expected to
appear in the latter days; title assumed by the
leaders of various Mohammedan sects. — Arab.
mahdi, 'one who is guided aright', pass. part, of
hddd, 'he lead in the right way'; rel. to Heb.
hdddh, 'he stretched out (the hand)', Aram, had-
dt, 'he lead, guided'.

## Mahdism
Mahdism, also Mahdiism, п., belief in the coming
of the Mahdi. — See prec. word and -ism.

## mah-jongg
mah-jongg, п., a Chinese game usually played by
four persons with 144 dominolike 'tiles'. —
Corruption of Chin, machiao, 'sparrow', lit.
'hemp-bird'; so called in allusion to the bird
represented on the first tiles.

## mahlstlck
mahlstlck, n. — See maulstick,

## mahogany
mahogany, n. — Of uncertain origin.
Mahometan. — The same as Mohammedan.

## Mahonia
Mahonia, п., a genus of plants of the barberry
family {bot.) — Named after the American
horticulturist Bernard McMahon (1775-1816). For
the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Mahound
Mahound, п., 1) Mohammed, the founder of
Islam {arch.); 2) the devil {Scot.) — OF. Mahom,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:466 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 439 | MALACO- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:466 COLUMN:1 -->
Mahon, corruption of Mahomet, * Mohammed*.
Cp. Mohammedan,

## mahout
mahout, п., the keeper and driver of an elephant
(East Indies). — Hind, mahaut, contraction of
mahavat, fr. OI. maha-matrah, lit. 'great in
measure', fr. mahu-J" great', and matra(fem.), ma-
tram (neut.), 'measure'. The first element is cogn.
with Gk. μέγας, L. magnus, 'great, large'; see
magaum and cp. the first element in maharaja
and in words there referred to. For the
etymology of the second element see matra.

## mabseer
mabseer, mahsir, п., a large fresh-water fish of
India, allied to the barbel. — Hind, mahasir, lit.
'big head', fr. maha, 'great, big', and sir, 'head'.
The first element derives fr. Ol. maha-, 'great',
which is cogn. with Gk. μέγας, L. magnus,
'great'; see magnum. The second element is rel.
to OI. siras, 'head, summit', Avestic sarah-,
Pers. sar, 'head', and cogn. with Gk. κάρη,
'head', κράνιον, 'skull', L. cerebrum, 'brain';
see cerebrum and cp. the first element in seer-
band.

## mahzor
mahzor, п., the Hebrew prayerbook used for the
festivals. — Mishnaic Heb. mahzor, lit. 'cycle',
fr. hdzar, 'he went around; he repeated', which
is rel. to Heb. hadar, 'he surrounded, enclosed'
(Ezek. 21:19).

## Maia
Maia, п., Roman goddess of fertility. — L., rel.
to the god Maius, whose name stands for *ma-
gyos, lit. 'he who brings increase", and is
connected with magnus, 'great*. See magnum and
cp. May.

## Maia nth emum
Maia nth emum, п., a genus of plants of the family
Convallariaceae(ftor.)— ModL., lit.
'Mayflower', fr. Gk. Μάιος (fr. L. Maius)t 'May', and
ανθεμον, 'flower', fr. άνθος, 'flower*. See May
and anther,

## maid
maid, n. — Shortened fr. maiden.
Derivative: maid-ish, adj.

## maidan
maidan, п., an open space in towns of India. —
Hind, and Pers. maydan, fr. Arab, maydan.

## maiden
maiden, n. — ME. meiden, fr. OE. nmgden, di-
min. of mxgeS, maegd, 'maid', which is re], to
OS. magath, OFris. maged, megith, OHG. ma-
gad, MHG. maget, 'virgin, maid', G. Magd,
'maid, maidservant', Madchen, 'girl, maiden,
maid' (prop, contraction of Magdchen, 'a little
maid or maidservant'), OE. mago, 'son, man,
attendant, servant*, ON. mogr, 'son', Goth.
magus, 'boy, servant', magabs, "virgin", and
cogn. with Avestic mayava-, 'unmarried', Olr.
maug, mug, 'slave', and prob. also with Olr.
mace, W. mab, 'son'. Cp. may, 'maiden'. Cp.
also Mac-.
Derivatives '.maiden, adj., maiden-hood, п.,
maiden-head, п., maiden-ly, adj. and adv., maiden-
li-ness, n.

## maieutic
maieutic, adj., serving to elicit ideas (said of the
Socratic method of teaching).—Gk. μαιευτικός,
'pertaining to midwifery, obstetric', fr. μαιεύε-
σθαί, Чо act as midwife', fr. μαία, 'mother,
nurse, midwife', fr. μά (voc), 'mother', from
infants' babbling *ma-, whence also Dor. Gk.
μάτηρ, Gk. μήτηρ, 'mother', and—with
reduplication—μάμμη, 'mother'. See mother,
'female parent', and cp. mamma, 'mother'.

## malgre
malgre, adj., containing neither flesh nor its juices
(said of articles of diet), — F., 'meager'. See
meager,

## maigre
maigre, п., a large food fish. — F., lit. 'meager'.
See prec. word.

## mail
mail, п., armour. — ME. maille, maile, fr. OF.
maille (= F.), fr. L. macula, 'spot, mark; mesh'.
See macula and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also camall.
Derivatives: mail, tr. v., mail-ed, adj.

## mail
mail, п., bag; bag for letters; post. — ME. male,

## fr. OF. male (whence F. malle)
fr. OF. male (whence F. malle), 'bag', fr. Frank-
ish *malha, which is rel. to OHG. malaha,

## malha
malha, 'saddle bag; wallet', MDu, male, 'bag',

## Du. maal
Du. maal, 'postbag, mail'.
Derivatives; mail, tr. v., to send by post,

## mailable
mailable, adj., mail-er, n.

## mail
mail, п., rent, tax, payment (obsol. or Scot.). —

## ME. male
ME. male, 'tax, tribute*, fr. OE. mal,
'bargaining, agreement, pay', fr. ON. mal, 'speech,

## agreement'
agreement', which is rel. to OE. msedel, 'meeting,

## council'
council', mxl, 'speech', Goth, mapl, 'meeting

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:466 COLUMN:2 -->
place'. Cp. blackmail. Cp. also mallus.

## maim
maim, tr. v., to hurt, injure, mutilate. — ME.
may men, mahaymen, fr. OF. mehagnier, mahai-
gnier, mayner, which is of Teut. origin. Cp. ON.
meida, 'to hurt, maim', Goth, ga-maidans (ace.
pi.), 'crippled, wounded', OE. gemad, *mad'.
See mad and cp. mayhem. Cp. also mangle, v.
Derivatives: maim, n. (cp. mayhem), maim-ed,
adj., maim-ed-ness, п., maim-er, n.

## maimon
maimon, п., the mandrill. — It. maimone, fr. Pers.
таутйп, 'ape', fr. Arab, таутйп, "auspicious'.
See monkey.

## main
main, п., strength, power. — ME., fr. OE. maegen,
rel. to OS., OHG. magan, megin, ON. magn,
megin, 'strength, power', and to the E. auxiliary
verb may (q.v.)

## main
main, adj., most important, principal. — Partly
from prec. word, partly fr. ON. meginn, megn,
'strong', which is rel. to ON. magn, megin,
'strength, power'.
Derivative: main-ly, adv.

## main
main, п., 1) in games of hazard", any number
between five and nine; 2) a match in cockfighting.
— Of uncertain origin; possibly from prec.
word.

## mainour
mainour, manner, п., something stolen found on
the thief's person (Old English law). — ME.
manor, fr. AF. mainoure, corresponding to OF.
manuevre, maneuvre, lit. 'hand work'. See
maneuver, n.

## mainpernor
mainpernor, п., one who gives ma in prize for
another's appearance (hist.) — ME. mainpernour,
fr. AF. mainpernour, metathesized fr. OF.*main·
prenour, fr. OF. mainprendre, lit. 'to take into
the hand', fr. main, 'hand', and prendre, 'to
take'. See next word.

## ma in prize
ma in prize, п., an undertaking to be responsible
for the appearance of a released prisoner in
court on a certain day (hist.) — ME., fr. AF.
meinprise, mainprise, lit. *a taking into the hand',
fr. main, 'hand', and prise, 'a taking, seizing',
prop. fern. pp. of prendre, 'to take', used as a
noun. F. main derives fr. L. manus, 'hand'; see
manual. For the etymology of F. prise see prize,
n. Cp. prec. word.

## maintain
maintain, tr. v. — ME. maintenen, mainteinen, fr.
OF. (== F.) maintenen, mainteinen, fr. OF. (=
F.) maintenir, fr. L. тапй tenere, Чо hold in the
hand', fr. тапй, abl. of manus, 'hand', and
tenere, 'to'hold'. See manual and tenable.
Derivatives: maintain-able, adj., maintain-abil-
ity, п., maintain-er, n.

## maintenance
maintenance, n. — F., fr. maintenir. See maintain
and -ance.

## maiolica
maiolica, n. — See majolica.

## mair
mair, adj. — Scot. var. of more.

## maist
maist, adj. — Scot. var. of most.

## maitre
maitre, п., a master. — F., fr. OF. maistre, fr. L.
magistrum, ace. of magister, 'master'. See
master.

## maize
maize, п., Indian corn. — Sp. malz, fr. Taino ma-
hiz, mahis.

## majestic
majestic, adj. — Formed from next word with
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: majestic-al-ly, adv.

## majesty
majesty, n. — ME. magestee, fr. OF. majeste (F.
majeste), fr. L. majestatem, ace. of majestas,
'dignity, honor, excellence', from the base occurring
in major (neut. mujus), 'greater', compar. of
magnus. See major, adj., and cp. maestoso, lese
majesty. For the ending see subst. suff. -ty.

## Majlis
Majlis, also Mejbs, п., the Persian national
assembly.— Arab, majlis, 'assembly', lit. 'session',
fr.jdlasa, 'he sat down'.

## majolica
majolica, maiolica, п., Italian glazed pottery. —
It. maiolica, fr. Majolica, early form of Majorca;
so called because such pottery was first made on
the island of Majorca.

## majoon
majoon, п., a confection made of hemp leaves,
poppy seeds, etc. — Hind, majun, fr. Arab.
ma'jun, lit. 'kneaded', passive part, of'ajana, 'he
kneaded'.

## major
major, adj. — ME. majour, fr. L. major, 'greater',
fr. earlier *majjor, for *mag-yos (neut. mujus,
fr. earlier *majjus, for *mag-yos), comparative
of, and from the same base, as, magnus, 'great*,
rel. to magis, 'more, rather'. See magnum and
cp. mayor and the second word in force majeure.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:466 COLUMN:3 -->
Cp. also maximum.
Derivative: major, intr. v.

## major
major, п., an officer ranking between captain and
lieutenant-colonel. — F. major, fr. Sp. mayor,
fr. L, major, 'greater'. See major, adj.

## major
major, п., a person of full legal age. — Fr. L.
major, 'greater*. See major, adj.

## major-domo
major-domo, п., a man in charge of a royal or
princely household. — Sp. mayordomo, fr. ML.
major domus, 'chief of the house', fr. L. major,
'greater', and gen. of domus, 'house'. See major,
adj., and dome,' building'.

## majority
majority, n. — MF. (= F.) majorite, fr. ML.
majdritatem, ace. of majoritas, 'majority', fr. L.
major, 'greater'. See major, adj., and -ity.

## majuscule
majuscule, п., a large letter. — L. mdjuscula (scil.
litterd), 'a somewhat greater letter', fern, of
majusculus, 'somewhat greater', dimin. of major,
'greater*. See major, adj., and -cule.
Derivatives: majuscule, majuscul-ar, adjs.

## make
make, tr. and intr. v. — ME. maken, fr. OE. ma·
cian, rel. to OS. makon, OFris. makia, 'to build,
make', MDu., Du. maken, 'to make', OHG.
mahhon, 'to construct, make*, MHG., G. ma-
chen, 'to make', fr. I.-E. base *mag-, 'to knead,
mix; to make'. The sense development of the
base *mag-, from the original meaning 'to
knead'into that of'to make',may find itsexplana-
tion in the fact that the first human buildings
were houses of mud. 'To knead a mud house'
meant almost the same as 'to make a mud
house'. See macerate and cp. make, 'match',
mackerel, 'a pimp', mason, match, 'an equal'.
Cp. also mingle, among.
Derivatives: make, п., way of being made,
maker, п., mak-er-ess, п., mak-ing, part. adj. and n.

## make
make, п., match, mate, companion (now dial.
Eng.) — ME. make, так, fr. OE. gemaca, re],
to gemsecca, One of a pair, mate, consort*, ge-
тзесс, 'well-matched, suitable', and to OE. ma-
cian, 'to make'. See make, v., and cp. match, 'an
equal'.

## mal-
mal-, combining form meaning 'bad, badly, ill'.
— F., fr. mal, 'evil, ill, wrong; wrongly', fr. L.
male (adv.), 'badly, ill', fr. malus (masc.), mala
(fern.), malum (neut.), 'bad, evil', which is of
uncertain etymology. It meant perh. orig.
'insignificant, of inferior value', and is cogn. with OE.
smxl, 'narrow, slender, small'; see Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW., II, 19-20 s.v. 3. malus. See small
and cp. male-, malady, malice, malignant,
dismal, manilla, 'second highest trump', mauvais.

## mala
mala, п., the cheek or the cheekbone (anat. and
zool.) — L. mala, 'cheekbone, jawbone; cheek',
of uncertain etymology. Cp. maxilla,

## malabathrum
malabathrum, п., the Malabar leaf and the
ointment made from it. — L., fr. Gk. μαλάβαθρον,
prob. aphetic for OI. tamala-pattram, 'leaf of
the tamala tree', fr. tamalah, name of a tree,
which is perh. rel. to tamas-, 'darkness', and
patra-m, 'leaf, fr. I.-E. *petra-, zero degree
*ptera-, 'wing, feather; leaf. For the first
element see temerity, for the second see feather and
cp. ptero-. The omission of the first syllable of
the OI. word in Greek is prob. due to a mis-
division of tamala-pat(t)ra- into τα μαλάβαθρα;
see Frisk, GEW., II, 165 s.v. μαλάβαθρον.

## malac-
malac-, form of malaco- before a vowel.
mal асе а, п., a walking stick. — Short for Malac-
ca cane, prop, cane from Malacca, a district in
Malaya.

## Malaceae
Malaceae, n. pi., the apple family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -aceae fr. L. malus, 'apple
tree'. See Malus.

## malaceous
malaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Malachi
Malachi, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the last
in the order of the Twelve Prophets. — Heb.
MaVakhi, lit. 'my messenger', fr. mal'akh,
'messenger', fr. base l-'-k, 'to send', which is rel.
to Arab, la'aka, aVaka, 'he sent'.

## malachite
malachite, n. — F., formed with subst. suff. -ite
fr. Gk. μαλάχη, 'mallow'. See mallow,

## malacia
malacia, п., pathological softening of a tissue
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. μαλακία,
'softness', fr. μαλακός, 'soft'. See malaco- and 1st -ia.

## -malacia
-malacia, combining form denoting pathological
softening (med.) — See prec. word,

## malaco-
malaco-, before a vowel malac-, combining form

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:467 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MALACOLOGY | 440 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:467 COLUMN:1 -->
meaning'soft'.—Gk.μαλακό-, μαλακ-, fr.
μαλακός, 'soft', which stands for *meli-gos, and is rel.
to Gk. βλαξ, gen. βλακός, 'lazy, inactive,
sluggish', fr. I.-E. base *melaq-, 'to soften', whence
also Ir. malcaim, Ί rot', Mir. blin, 'the groins'.
Base 'melaq- is enlarged fr. base 4(s)mel-, 'to
rub, grind', whence Gk. μύλη, later μύλος,
'mill', L. molere, 'to grind', mollna, 'mill'. See
meal, 'edible grain', and cp. words there referred
to.

## malacology
malacology, п., the study of mollusks. —
Compounded of malaco- and Gk. -λογία, fr .-λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: malacolog-ic-al, adj., matacotog-ist,
n.

## malacon
malacon, п., a brown variety of zircon. — Gk.
μαλακόν, neut. of μαλακός, 'soft'. See malaco-,

## Malacostraca
Malacostraca, n. pi., a subclass of Crustacea
(zool.)— ModL.,fr. Gk. μαλακόστρακος, 'soft-
shelled', compounded of μαλακ- (see nialac-l and
δστρακον, 'shell'. See ostracon.
Derivative: malacostrac-an, adj.

## maladroit
maladroit, adj., awkward, clumsy. — F. See nial-
and adroit.
Derivatives: maladroit-\y, adv., maladroit-ness,
n.

## malady
malady, п., sickness, disease. — ME. maladie,
fr. OF. (= F.) maladie, fr. malade, 'sick', fr.
Late L. male habitus, 'ill', lit. 'ill-kept', fr. male,
'badly, ill', and habitus, pp. of habere, 'to hold,
keep, have'. See mal-, habit, n. and -y
(representing F. -ie), and cp. malinger.

## mala fide
mala fide, in bad faith. — L. mala fide, abl. of
mala fides, 'bad faith'. See mal- and fidelity and
cp. bona fide.

## Malaga
Malaga, п., white wine exported from Malaga,
port in Spain. — The name ρϊ Malaga, orig. a
Phoenician colony, comes fr. Phoen. malfta,
'salt', which is rel. to Heb. melah. See mallow.

## Malagasy
Malagasy, adj., pertaining to Madagascar, its
people or its language; п., 1) a native of
Madagascar; 2) the language of the Malagasy. —
Related to Madagas- in Madagas-car. For the
interchangeability of -/- and -d- cp. L. lingua,
'tongue', fr. OL. dingua (see lingual and cp.
words there referred to).

## malaise
malaise, п., a slight bodily discomfort. — F., lit.
'ill ease', fr. mal-, 'ill', and aise, 'ease'. See mal-
and ease.

## malapert
malapert, adj., impudent. — OF. mal apert, lit.
'ill-skilled', fr. mal-, 'badly, ill', and apert,
'skillful', which was formed—with change of
prefix—fr. OF. espert, 'experienced, skillful,
clever', fr. L. expertus. See expert.
Derivatives: malapert, п., malapert-ly, adv.,
malapert-ness, n.

## malapropian
malapropian, adj., of the nature of malapropisms.
— See next word and -ian.

## malapropism
malapropism, п., misuse of a word. — Fr. Mrs.
Malaprop, name of a character in Sheridan's
Rivals, coined fr. F. malάpropos, 'inopportune,
inappropriate'. See next word and -ism.

## malapropos
malapropos, adv., inopportunely, inappropriately.
— F. mal a propos, 'inopportunely,
inappropriately', fr. mal-, 'ill, badly' and a propos, 'to the
purpose'. See mal- and apropos.
Derivative: malapropos, adj.

## malar
malar, adj., pertaining to the cheek or the
cheekbone (anat. and zooi) — ModL. maldris, fr. L.
mala, 'cheekbone, jawbone, cheek'. See mala
and -ar and cp. maxilla.
Derivative: malar, п., cheekbone.

## malaria
malaria, n. — Lit. 'bad air', fr. It. malaria,
contraction οι mala aria, 'bad air', fr. mala, fern, of
malo (fr. L. malus), 'bad', and aria, 'air'. See
mal- and air, 'atmosphere'. The, term malaria
was prob. used first by the Italian physician
Francisco Torti (1658-1741).
Derivatives: malari-al, malari-an, malari-ous,
adjs.

## malario-
malario-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
malaria'. See prec. word.

## malax
malax, tr. v., to soften. — L. malaxare, 'to soften,
mollify', fr. Gk. μαλάσσειν (aor. μαλάξαι), of
s.m., fr. μαλχκός, 'soft'. See malaco- and cp.
Malaxis.
Derivatives: malax-able, adj., malaxage (q.v,),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:467 COLUMN:2 -->
malax-ate, tr. v., malaxation (q.v.)

## malaxage
malaxage, п., softening. — F., fr. malaxer, 'to
soften, mollify', fr. L. malaxare. See prec. word
and -age.

## malaxation
malaxation, п., softening. — Late L. malaxatio,
'a softening", fr. L. malaxatus, pp. of malaxare.
See malax and -ation.

## Malaxis
Malaxis, п., a genus of plants of the orchid family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μάλαξις, 'a softening',
ΓΓθΐη11ιβ5ΐβιηοΓμϊλάσσειν,4ο soften'.See malax.

## Malay
Malay, adj., pertaining to Malaya or the race
inhabiting it; п., a member of the race inhabiting
Malaya. — Native Maiayu.
Derivative: Malay-an, adj.

## Malayalam
Malayalam, п., the Dravidian language of
Malabar.

## malcontent
malcontent, adj., discontented, dissatisfied. — F.,
fr. mal-, 'ill, badly', and content, 'content'. See
mal- and content.
Derivatives: malcontent-ed, adj., malcontent-ed-
ly, adv., malcontent-ed-ness, п., malcontent-
ment, n.

## maldonite
maldonite, п., bismuthic gold (mineral) — Named
after Maldon in Victoria, Australia. For the
ending see subst. sufT. -ite.

## male
male, adj. and n. — ME. masle, fr. OF. mascle,
masle, male (F. male), fr. L. masculus, 'male,
masculine', dimin. οι mas, 'male'. See masculine.

## male-
male-, combining form meaning 'bad, badly, ill'.
— Fr. L. male (adv.), 'badly, ill'. See mal-.

## malediction
malediction, п., curse. — ME. malediccioun, fr. L.
maledictio, gen. -onis, 'a reviling, abuse', lit. 'an
evil-speaking', fr. maledictus, pp. of maledicere,
'to revile, abuse', lit, 'to speak ill', fr. male,
'badly, ill", and dicere, 'to say'. See male- and
diction and cp. malison, which is a doublet of
malediction.

## maledictory
maledictory, adj., of the nature of a malediction.
— Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. maledictus,
pp. of maledicere. See prec. word.

## malefaction
malefaction, п., evil deed, crime. — Formed with
suff. -ion fr. L. malefactus, pp. of malefacere.
See next word.

## malefactor
malefactor, п., an evildoer. — ME. malefactour,
fr. L. malefactor, fr. malefactus, pp. of
malefacere, 'to do evil, to injure', fr. male, 'badly, ill',
ani/dcere, 'to make, do'. See male- and fact and
cp. next word.

## malefic
malefic, adj., baleful — L. maleficus, 'evildoing,
wicked, criminal', compounded of male, 'badly,
ill', and -ficus, from the stem of -ficere,
unstressed form oifacere, 'to make, do'. See male-
and -fie.

## maleficence
maleficence, п., harmfulness, mischief. — L. male-
ficentia, 'evildoing, mischievousness, injury', fr.
maleficus. See next word and -ce and cp.
malfeasance.

## maleficent
maleficent, adj., harmful, mischievous. — Back
formation fr. L. maleficentior, compar. of
maleficus. See malefic and -ent.

## maleic
maleic, adj., designating a white crystalline acid
(chem.) — F. maleique, altered arbitrarily fr.
malique. See malic.

## malevolence
malevolence, п., ill-will, malice. — L. malevolen-
tia, 'ill will, ill disposition', fr. malevolens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -ce and cp.
benevolence.

## malevolent
malevolent, adj., ill-disposed, malicious. — L.
malevolens, gen. -entis, 'ill-disposed, envious',
fr. male, 'badly, ill', and volens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of velle, 'to wish, will'. See volition and cp.
benevolent.
Derivative: malevolent-ly, adv.

## malfeasance
malfeasance, п., misconduct (law). — F. malfai-
sance, 'evildoing, mischievousness', fr. malfai-
sant. See next word and cp. feasance,
misfeasance.

## malfeasant
malfeasant, adj., doing evil; п., evildoer. — F.
malfaisant, pres. part, of malfaire, 4o do evil',
compounded of mal-, 'ill, badJy' and faire, 'to
make, do', fr. L. facere. See mal-, fact and -aut
and cp. prec. word. Cp. also feasible.

## malgre
malgre, prep., in spite of. — See maugre.

## malic
malic, adj., pertaining to a crystallizable acid
occurring in apples (chem.) — F. malique, fr. L.
malum, 'apple'. See Malus, 'the apple tree',
and -ic.

## malice
malice, п., ill will. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:467 COLUMN:3 -->
malice, fr. L. malitia, 'wickedness, malice', fr.
malus, 'bad'. See mal- and 3rd suff. -ice.

## malicious
malicious, adj. — ME., fr. OF. malicius, fr. L.
malitiosus, 'wicked, malicious', fr. malitia. See
prec. word and -ious.
Derivatives: malicious-ly, adv., malicious-ness,
n.

## malign
malign, adj., 1) malevolent; 2) evil. — ME. ma-
ligne, fr. OF. maligne, fr. L. malignus,
'ill-disposed, malicious', orig. 'of a bad nature',
compounded οι male, 'badly, ill', and *gno-s, 'born,
of a certain nature', fr. I.-E. base *gn-, 'to beget,
bear, bring forth', whence also L. gignere, 'to
beget, bear, bring forth', W. gem, to be born'.
See mal- and genus and cp. benign.
Derivative: malign-ly, adv.

## malign
malign, tr. v., to speak ill of, to slander. — ME.
malignen, fr. OF. malignier, fr. L. maligndre,
malignari, 'to do maliciously', fr. malignus. See
malign, adj.

## malignancy
malignancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## malignant
malignant, adj., I)malign;2) wishing evil; 3)
tending to cause death. — L. malignans, gen. -antis,
pres. part, of malignare, malignari, 'to do
maliciously'. See maligu, v., and -ant and cp.
benignant.
Derivatives: malignant, п., malignant-ly, adv.

## malignity
malignity, п., state or quality of being malignant.
— ME. malignitee, fr. MF. (= F.) mali-
gnite, fr. L. malignilatem, ace. of malignitas,
'malice', fr. malignus. See malign, adj., and -ity.

## malik
malik, п., an owner (India). — Hind, malik, fr.
Arab, malik, 'owner', active part, of malaka,
'he owned'. See Mameluke and cp. words there
referred to.

## malines
malines, п., mechlin lace. — F., fr. Malines, name
of a town in Belgium. Cp. Mechlin.

## malinger
malinger, intr. v., to feign sickness. — Fr. F. ma-
lingre, 'sickly, weakly, ailing', which is prob. a
blend of OF. mingre, 'wretched', and malade,
'sick' (see malady). OF. mingre itself seems to be
a blend of OF. maigre, 'lean, meager' (see
meager), and OF. haingre, 'lean', which is of.
uncertain origin. See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p.
367 s.v. malingre.
Derivatives: malinger-er, п., malinger-y, adj.

## maKsm
maKsm, п., the doctrine that evil predominates
in this world. — A hybrid coined fr. L. malus,
'evil' (see male-), and -ism, a suff. of Greek
origin. The correct form would be cacism, fr. Gk.
κακός, 'bad, evil' (cp. Gk. κακισμός, 'blame,
reproach'.)

## malison
malison, п., curse. — ME. malisoun, fr. OF. ma-
leicon, maleisson, 'curse', fr. L. maledictionem,
ace. of maledictio. See malediction, which is a
doublet of malison, and cp. benison.

## malkin
malkin, mawkin, п., a slattern; a scarecrow (dial.
Eng.) — Orig. a fern. PN., formed fr. ME. Mal-
kyn, dimin. of Malt, Mault, 'Maud', fr. OF.
Mahoulte, Malde. See Mathilda, Maud, and cp.
the second element in grimalkin.

## mall
mall, п., the game of pall-mall. — Orig. 'the
mallet used in the game of pall-mall', fr. ME.
matte, fr. F. mail, 'mallet'. See maul.

## mall
mall, n. — A var. of maul.

## malladrite
malladrite, п., a sodium fluosilicate (mineral.) —
Named after Professor Alessandro Maltadra of
the Royal Observatory of Vesuvius (1868-1945).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## mallard
mallard, п., the wild duck. — ME., fr. OF. mat-
lart (F. matard, malari), 'wild drake', fr. Flemish
maskelaar, but influenced in form by OF. masle
(F. male), 'male'. The -I in OF. maltart is
excrescent and due to a confusion with suff. -art.

## malleable
malleable, adj., that can be hammered. —
" ME. malliable, fr. MF. (= F.) malleable, fr. ML.
malleabilis, fr. obsol. L. malleare, 'to beat with
a hammer, to hammer', fr. L. malleus. See
malleus and -able.
Derivatives: malleabil-ity, п., malleable-ness, n.

## mallee
mallee, п., a dwarfish Australian eucalypt. —
Native Australian.

## mallemuck
mallemuck, mallemock, mallemoke, п., fulmar,
petrel. — Du. mallemok, compounded of mal,
'foolish', and ток, 'gull, seamew'; so called
because it is easily caught.

## malleolus
malleolus, п., one of the two rounded projecting

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:468 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 441 | MAN | L. Melita, Meliti, fr. Gk, Μελίτη, fr. Phoen. | muimme, 'foster-mother'. In its unreduplicated | adv., mann-ish-ness, n. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:468 COLUMN:1 -->
bones on each side of the ankle (anai.) — L., 'a
small hammer', dimin. of malleus, 'hammer';
first used in anatomy byAndreas Vesalius (1514-
64), it orig. denoted simply a bony eminence.
See malleus and dimin. suflf. -ole.
Derivative: mafleol-ar, adj:

## mallet
mallet, п., a hammer with a heavy wooden head.
— ME. maillet, fr. MF. (= F.) maillet, fr. OF.,
lit. 'a small hammer', dimin. of mail, fr. L.
malleus, 'hammer'. See next word and -et.
Derivative: mallet, tr. v.
malleus» п., the outermost of the three small bones
of the middle ear (anat.) — L. malleus,
'hammer1; so called in allusion to its shape. L.
malleus is cogn. with OSlav. mlaru, Russ. molotu,
'hammer'. Cp. mall, malleable, malleolus,
mallet, maul, 'hammer', and the second element in
pall-mall. Cp. also machete, marc, march, to
walk'.
Derivative: malle-al, adj.

## mallow
mallow, п., name of a plant. — ME. malwe, fr.
OE. mealwe, fr. L. malva, which, together with
Gk. μαλάχη, of s.m., is borrowed fr. Heb. mal-
lQah, 'mallow' (Job 30:4), a derivative of melah,
'salt'; cp. Aram, milhd, Syr. melha, Arab, milh,
Akkad. milu, 'salt'. (See H. Lewy, Die semiti-
schen Fremdworter im Griechischen, 31 f., and
Immanuel Low, Flora der Juden, i 227 ff. and
242 ff.) Cp. malachite, malvacious, mauve. Cp.
also Malaga.

## malius
malius, п., the hundred court among the Salian
Franks. — L.„ a Teut. loan word; cp. ON. ma/,
'speech, agreement', OHG. mahal, court,
assembly', OE, mxpel, of s.m. See mail, 'tax,
payment', and cp. the second element in
blackmail.

## malm
malm, п., a soft friable limestone. — ME. malme,
fr. OE. mealm, rel. to ON. malmr, Swed. malm,
'ore', Goth, malma, 'sand', G. zer-malmen, 'to
bruise, crush', and to OS., MLG., OHG.,
MHG. melm, Du. molm, G. Mu/m, 'dust', and
cogn. with Lith. melmud, 'stone in the kidneys'.
All these words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*mel-, 'to grind'. See meal, 'edible grain', and
cp. malt.

## malmaison
malmaison, п., 1) a kind of carnation; 2) a kind of
rose. — From Malmaison, name of the palace
of the Empress Josephine, near Versailles.

## malmsey
malmsey, п., a sweet white wine; orig., the sweet
white wine made near Monemvasia. — ML.
malmasia, corruption of Gk. Μονεμβασιά,
'Monemvasia' (also called Napoli di Malvasia)
in the Morea. Gk. Μονεμβασία lit. means 'only
one entrance'. It stands for μον-εμβασία and
is compounded of μόνος, 'alone, only', and
έμβασες, 'entering into' (fr. έμ-, έν-, *in, into',
and βάσις, 'a going, stepping, a base'); the
town was so called because it is connected with
the continent only by a narrow dam (see mono-,
1st en- and base, n.) Cp. malvoisle.

## Malpighia
Malpighia, п., a genus of tropical shrubs and
trees (hot.) — Named after the Italian
anatomist Marcello Malpighi (1628-94). For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.
Derivative: Malpighi-an, adj., pertaining to, or
discovered by, Malpighi.

## Malpighiaceae
Malpighiaceae, n. pi., a family of tropical shrubs
and trees. — ModL., formed from prec. word
with sufT. -aceae.

## malpighiaceous
malpighiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## malpractice
malpractice, n. — A hybrid coined fr. L. malet
'badly, ill' (see male-), and practice.

## malt
malt, n. — ME., fr. OE. meall, malt, rel. to OS.,
ON. malt, Du. mout, OHG., MHG., G. mail,
'malt', and cogn. with OI. mrdufy, 'soft, mild',
Gk. βλαδαρός (for *μλαδαρός), βλαδύς (for
•μλαδύς), 'loose, spongy', μέλδειν, 'to melt,
make liquid', άμαλδύνειν, 'to grind, destroy', L*
mollis (for *moldY'is), 'soft'. All these words are
traceable to I.-E. *mel-d-, a -^-enlargement of
base *mel-, 'to grind', whence Gk. μύλη, 'mill',
L. molere, 'to grind', mollna, 'mill'. See mill,
'machine for grinding', and cp. meal, 'edible
grain', and words there referred to.
Derivatives: malt, tr. v., malt-ing, п., malt-y, adj.

## Malta
Malta, п., an island in the Mediterranean. — Fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:468 COLUMN:2 -->
melitd, lit. 'place of refuge', fr. Phoen.-Heb.
та/at, 'he escaped'.
Derivatives: Malt-ese, adj. and n.

## maltase
maltase, п., an enzyme that changes maltose into
dextrose (biochem.) — Coined fr. malt and -ase.

## maltha
maltha, п., mixture used as cement. — L., fr. Gk.
μάλθα, μάλθη, 'mixture of wax and pitch'
(according to F. Solmsen, Beitrage zur
griechischen Wortforschung, I, 55, prop. fem. of the
adjeciive *μάλθος, 'soft'), rel. to μαλθακός,
'sofi\ μαλθάσσειν, μαλθαίνει,ν, Ίο soften',
μάλθων, 'weakling', and cogn. with Goth.
mildeis, OE. milde, 'mild'. See mild and cp. milt.
Cp. also mollify.

## Malthusian
Malthusian, adj., pertaining to the English
economist Thomas Robert Malthus (1766-1834), who
maintained ihat the increase of population must
be checked in order to make it proportionate to
the means of subsistence; п., a follower of T.R.
Malthus. — For the ending see suff. -ian.

## Malthusianism
Malthusianism, п., the doctrine of T.R. Malthus.
— See prec. word and -ism.

## maltose
maltose, п., sugar formed by the action of
diastase of malt on starch. — Coined fr. malt and
subst. suff. -ose.

## maltreat
maltreat, tr. v. — F. maltraiter, 'to ill-treat',
compounded of mat-, 'ill, badly', and trailer, 'to
treat". See mal- and treat.
Derivatives: maltreat-ment, п., ma/treat-or, n.

## maltster
maltster, п., a maker of malt. —■ Formed fr. malt
with suff. -ster.

## Malus
Malus, п., the genus of apple trees {bot.) — L.
mdlus, 'apple tree', malum, 'apple', fr. Dor. Gk.
μαλον, 'apple', corresponding to Ion. μήλον;
prob. of Mediterranean origin. Cp. melinite,
melon, and the second element in marmalade,
camomile, Hamamelis.

## Malus
Malus, п., name of a southern constellation (as-
Iron.) — Lit. 'mast', fr. L. malus, fr. *mddos,
*mazdos; cogn. with OE. maest, 'mast'. See
mast, 'pole'. For the change of I.-E. d to / in
Latin cp. lachrymal and words there referred to.

## Malva
Malva, п., a genus of plants, the mallow {bot.) —
L., 'mallow'. See mallow and cp. malachite,
mauve.

## Malvaceae
Malvaceae, n. pi., the mallow family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suflf. -aceae.

## maivaceous
maivaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Malvastrum
Malvastrum, п., a genus of the false mallow plants
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. L. malva, 'mallow',
with -astrum, neut. of the pejorative sufT. -aster.
See Malva and -aster.

## malversation
malversation, п., maladministration. — MF.
(~ F.), fr. malverser, compounded of mal-, 'ill,
badly', and L. versuri, 'to move about, occupy
oneself, passive of versdre, 'to turn about', freq.
of vertere, 'to turn'. See mal-, version and -ation.

## malvotsie
malvotsie, malvoisier, п., malmsey. — F., fr.
Mal(e)vesie, fr. It. (Napoli di) Malvasia, fr. Gk.
Μονεμβασία, 'Monemvasia', name of a town
in the Morea. See malmsey.

## mamba
mamba, п., a S. African serpent (Dendraspis an-
gustoceps). — Zulu im-amba.

## Mameluke
Mameluke,n.,l) member of a military force,
originally of slaves, who held the throne of Egypt
between 1250 and 1517 and remained powerful
till their massacre in 1811; 2) a slave. — F.
mamel(o)uk, fr. Arab, mamluk, 'purchased
slave', lit. 'possessed', pass. part, of malaka, 'he
owned, possessed', which is rel. to Ethiop.
malaka, 'he possessed', Arab, malik, Heb. melekh,
Aram, melekh, malka, Akkad. maliku, tnalku,
'king'. Cp. malik, the first element in Melchior,
Melchizedek, and the second element in Alche-
milla.

## mamiila
mamiila, n. — See mammilla.

## mamma
mamma, also mama, п., mother. — Formed with
reduplication from infants' babbling *ma-,
whence also Gk. μάμμα (voc), μαμμη,
'mother, grandmother; mother's breast*, μαμμία,
'mother', L. mamma, 'mother, midwife,
grandmother; mother's breast, nipple', ModPers.
mam, mama, 'mother*, Alb. тете, Gheg mame,
"mother*, Russ. mama, Lith. mama, momd, Lett.
mama, 'mother', OHG. muoma, MHG. muome,
G. Muhme, 'mother's sister', F. ma man, Sp,
mama, Ir., W., Co., Bret, mam, 'mother', Olr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:468 COLUMN:3 -->
form, infants' babbling *ma- (whence Ol. ma,
'mother', Dor. Gk. μα (voc), 'mother') serves
as a basis to Ol. matar, Dor. ματηρ, Gk. μήτηρ,
L. mdter, etc. 'mother'. See mother and cp.
words there referred to.
mamma, п., mammary gland, milk-secreting
organ of mammals (normally only in females). —
L. mamma, 'breast', identical with mamma,
'mother1. See prec. word.

## mammal
mammal, n. — See Mammalia.

## Mammalia
Mammalia, n. pi. — ModL., coined by Linnaeus
in 1758 fr. Late L. mammalia, neut. pi. of mam-
malis, 'pertaining to the breast', fr. L. mamma,
'breast'. See mamma, 'mammary gland', and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: mammal-ian, adj. and п., mammal-
ity, n.

## mammaliferous
mammaliferous, adj., containing mammalian
remains (geol.) — Compounded of mammal and
-ferous.

## mammalogy
mammalogy, п., the study of mammals. —
Compounded of ModL. Mammalia and Gk. -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner), one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
Mammalia and -logy.
Derivatives: mammalog-ic-al, adj., mammalog-
ist, n.

## mammary
mammary, adj., pertaining to the mammae or
breasts.—Formed with adj. suflf. -ary fr. mamma,
'mammary gland'.

## mammee
mammee, п., a tropical American tree or its fruit.
— Sp. mamey, fr. Taino.

## mammiferous
mammiferous, adj., having mammae. —
Compounded of mamma, 'mammary gland', and
-ferous.

## mammiform
mammiform, adj., having the shape of a mamma.
— Compounded of mamma, 'mammary gland',
and -form.

## mammilla
mammilla, п., also mamiila, nipple (anat.) —
Inexact spelling of L. mamiila, dimin. of
mamma, 'breast' (see mamma, 'breast'). The
shortening of mm (in L. mamma) to m (in L. mamiila)
is due to the shifting of the accent. From the
above example this law has been called 'mamiila
law'. For other examples of this law see canal
and curule.
Derivatives: mammill-ary, mammill-ate, mam-
mill-ated, adjs., mammill-at-ion, n.

## Mammillaria
Mammillaria, п., a genus of plants, the cactus
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. mamiila, 'nipple' (see
mammilla); so called in allusion to the tubercles.

## mammilliform
mammilliform, adj., having the shape of a nipple.
— Compounded of mammilla and -form,

## mammon
mammon, п., personification of wealth. — L.
mammona, fr. Gk. μαμωνας, fr. Aram, тйтб-
nd, emphatic state of mdmon, 'money', which
prob. stands for ma'mon, fr. base "-m-n, 'to
trust', and lit. means 'trust, deposit'. See amen.
Derivatives: mammon-ism, п., mammon-ist, п.,
mammon-ist-ic, adj.

## mammoth
mammoth, n. — Russ. mammot, a dial. (Ostiak)
var. of mammant, fr. Yakut mamma, 'earth' (the
mammoth was believed to root up the earth like
a mole, whence its name.)

## mammy
mammy, п., I) child's word for mother; 2) a
Negro nurse. — See mamma, 'mother'.

## man
man, n. — ME. man, fr. OE. man, *human being,
man', rel. to OS., Swed., Du., OHG., MHG.
man, G. Mann, ON. madr (for "niannr), Dan.
mand, Goth, manna, 'man' (cp. Mannus, a tribal
deity, in Tacitus' Germania, chapt. 2(, OS. men-
nisco, OFris. manniska, MDu. men.sche, Du.
mens, OHG. mannisco, mennisco, MHG. men-
sche, mensch, Gi Mensch, 'man' (orig. adj.
meaning 'human'), and cogn. with OI. manuh,
'man; progenitor of mankind', Avestic martu-,
'man', OSlav. mgii, 'man'. All these words prob.
meant orig. 'one who thinks", fr. I.-E. base
*men-, 'to think', whence also OI. matif?, matih,
'thought', L. mens, gen. mentis, 'mind', Goth.
muns, 'thought', munan, 'to think", ON. minnit
'mind', OE. gemynd, 'memory'. See mind and
cp. Manu, muzhik, and the second element in
Marcomauni. Cp. also minx.
Derivatives: man, tr. v!, man-fui, adj.,
man-fully, adv., man-jul-ness, п., man-hood, п., man-ly,
adj., man-fi-ness, п., mann-ish, adj., mann-ish-ly,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:469 COLUMN:1 -->

## man
man, п., a unit of weight. — See maund.

## manacle
manacle, п., handcuff. — ME. manicle, fr. OF.
manicle, lit. 'a little hand', fr. L. manicula, dimin.
of manus, 'hand'. See manual, adj.. and -cle.
Derivative: manacle, tr. v.

## Manacus
Manacus, п., a genus of manakins {urnithoi.) —
ModL., fr. Du. manneken, 'liitle man*. See
manikin and cp. manakin.

## manada
manada, п., herd, flock, drove. — Sp., fr. VL,
*mindta, fr. Late L. minare, 'to drive (animals)
by threatening shouts', fr. L. ntindri. Ίο
threaten'. See minatory and cp. promenade and
words there referred to.

## manage
manage, tr. and intr. v. — It. maneggiare, 'to
control ahorse* (whence also F. manege,
'horsemanship, riding'), lit. 'to handle', fr. tnano,
'hand', fr. L. manus. See manual and -age and
cp. manege.
Derivatives: manage-able, п., manage-abil-ity,
п., manage-ab-ly, adv., manage-able-ness, п.,
manage-ment, п., manag-er, п., manag-er-ess, п.,
manag-er-ial, adj., manag-ing, adj.

## manage
manage, п., 1) manege; 2) management. — It.
maneggio, fr. maneggiare (see manage, v.);
influenced by F. menage (see menage).

## manakin
manakin, п., any of a group of birds, the Pipridae.
— Du. manneken, 'little man'. See manikin and
cp. Manacus.

## mariana
mariana, adv., tomorrow; in the near future. —
Sp., 'morning, morrow', fr. L. mane, 'in the
morning', which orig. meant 'in a good time',
and is rel. to L. mdnis, a collateral form of
manus, 'good'. See manes.

## manas
manas, п., mind (Hinduism). — ΟΪ. manas,
'heart, mind, spirit',rel. to motivate, 'thinks1, ma-
nati, 'mentions', Avestic manah-, 'mind', mainy-
eite, 'thinks', fr. I.-E. base *mett-, "to think',
whence also L. mens, gen. mentis, 'mind', Goth.
munsr 'thought', OE. gemynd, "memory'. See
mind and cp. man.
Μanasseh, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the elder
son of Joseph. — Heb. Μ nashshi , lit. 'one
who causes to forget', Pi'el part, of ndshaH, 'he
forgot' (see Gen. 41:51), rel. to Aram. neshd,

## manatee
manatee, п., any of aquatic herbivorous mammals

manavelins, n. p]., odds and ends {slang). — Of

## manchineel

## Manchu
Manchu, also Manchoo, n. and adj. — Manchu.

mancipable, adj., capable of mancipation (Roman

mancipate, tr. v., to transfer property (Roman

manceps (gen. mancipis), 'purchaser, contractor,

## owner'
owner', which stands for * man-caps, lit. 'he

## who takes by hand'
who takes by hand', fr. manus, 'hand', and

## mancipation

gen. -onis, 'a making over, transfer', fr.

mancipium, n. (Roman law). — L., 'the legal

purchase of a thing', lit. 'a taking by hand', fr.

## manciple

## Mancunian

## mancus
mancus, п., name of an Old English coin. — OE.,

η qash, 'he knocked, struck', which is rel. to

kel, Die aramaischen Fremdworter im Arabi-

## -mancy
-mancy, combining form meaning 'divination by

σθαι (for *μάνι[εσθαι}, 'to be mad', and cogn.

## Mandaean
Mandaean, п., member of a Gnostic

dayya\ lit. 'related to knowledge', fr. manda\

Mandaean Aram, manda" 'knowledge',
corresponds to Aram. manda\ a derivative of Aram.
yedha\ 'he knew', which is rel. to Heb. yddha",
'he knew', madda\ 'knowledge', Akkad. idu,
'to know'.

## Mandaic
Mandaic, adj. and n. — See prec. word and -ic.

## mandamus

## influenced in form by Port

## order'. See mind and cp. mantra

mandate, n. — MF. (= F.) mandat, fr. L. mandd-

tum, 'commission, order', prop. neut. pp. of

Mdhne, 'mane', OE. mene, OHG. menni,

## mangle

νεσθαι (for *μάν^εσθ-αι), 'to be mad', μαντεία,

-mania, combining form denoting \) a specific

maniable, adj. — MF. (= F.), fr. OF. maniable,

Manichaean, Μanichean, 1) п., a Manichee; 2)

Manihot, п., a genus of plants of the spurge

## Manila
Manila, п., cigar; elemi; hemp; nut; paper. —
From the name of the capital of the Philippine
Islands,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:470 COLUMN:3 -->

manoeuvre. — See maneuver.

## manometer
manometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
pressure of gases and vapors. — F. manometre,
lit. 'instrument for measuring that which is thin',
coined by Varignon (1654-1722), fr. Gk. μανός,
Att. μανός (Κ>Γ*μανΓός), 'thin, rare', and μέ-
τρον, 'measure'. The first element stands in
gradational relationship to Gk. μόνος (for *μόν-
f ος), 'single, alone', and is cogn. with Arm. manr
(gen. manu), 'thin, slender, small', and pern.
with OL mandk, 'a little', Toch. B. menki, 'less,
smaller', Lith. menkas, 'mediocre', Olr. menb,
'small'; cp. mono-. For the second element in
manometer see -meter.
Derivatives: manometr-ic, manometr-ic-al, adjs,,
manometr-y, n.

## manor
manor, п., residence of a nobleman. — ME.
maner, fr. OF. (= F.) manoir, 'manor*, prop.
subst. use of the infinitive manoir, 'to dwell', fr.
L. manere, 'to remain'. See mansion and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivative: manor-ial, adj.

## mansard
mansard, п., a garret. — F. mansarde, shortened
fr. toit a la mansarde; named after the French
architect Frangois Mansard (1598-1666).

## manse
manse, п., residence of a Scottish presbyterian
minister. — ML. mansus (also mansa and man-
sum), 'a dwelling', prop, masc, resp. fern, or
neut. pp. of L. manere, 'to remain', used as a
noun. See mansion and cp. manor.

## mansion
mansion, п., a stately residence. — ME. mansi-
oun, fr. OF. (~ F.) mansion, fr. L. mansionem,
ace. of mansio, 'a staying, remaining; night
quarters, station' (whence also OF., F. maison,
'house'), fr. mansus, pp. of manere, 'to stay,
remain' (in VL., 'to dwell'), which is cogn. with
Gk. μένειν, 'to remain', μονή, 'a staying', Aves-
tic man-, Pers. mandan, 'to remain', Arm, mnam,
Ί remain, wait for', possibly also with Toch.
AB mask- 'to be', fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to
remain, wait for'. Cp. manor, manse, immanent,
meinie, menage, menial, meno-, 'remaining',
permanent, remain, remnant.

## mansuete
mansuete, adj., lame, gentle, mild. — ME., fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:471 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MANSUETUDE | 444 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:471 COLUMN:1 -->
mansuetus, 'lamed', pp. of mansuescere, 'to
tame\ lit. 'to accustom to the hand', fr. manus,
'hand', and suescere, 'to accustom, habituate1.
See manual, adj., and custom and cp. mastiff.
Cp. also desuetude,

## mansuetude
mansuetude, п., tameness, gentleness, mildness'.
— ME., fr. L. mdnsuetudo, 'tameness', fr.
mansuetus, pp. of mansuescere. See mansuete and
-ude.

## manta
manta, п., a kind of cloak. — Sp., fr. VL. *manta,
fr. Late L. mantum, 'cloak', back formation fr.
L. mantellum, 'cloak'. See mantle,

## manteau
manteau, п., cloak, mantle. — F., fr. OF. mantel,
fr. L. mantellum, 'cloak*. See mantle and cp.
prec. word.

## mantel
mantel, n. — A var. of mantle,

## mantelet
mantelet, also mantlet, п., 1) a small cloak; 2) a
temporary shelter. — OF., dimin. of mantel.
See mantle and -et.

## mantic
mantic, adj., pertaining to divination, prophetic.
— Gk. μαντικός, 'prophetic, oracular', fr. μάν-
τις. See mantis and adj. suff. -ic.

## -mantic
-mantic, a combining form meaning 'divining,
foretelling', used to form adjectives
corresponding to nouns ending in -money, as in
chiromantic, oneiromantic. — Fr. Gk. μαντικός.
See prec. word and -mancy.

## mantilla
mantilla, п.. a short mantle. — Sp., dimin. of
manta, 'cloak", fr. VL. *manta. See manta.

## mantis
mantis, п., any of various insects holding up their
forelegs as if in prayer. — ModL., fr. Gk. μάν-
τις, 'seer, prophet, soothsayer', which is rel. to
μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'. See -mancy.

## mantissa
mantissa, п., the decimal part of a logarithm. —
L. mantisa, less correctly mantissa, 'a worthless
addition, makeweight', prob. a Celtic (Gaulish)
word introduced into Latin through the medium
of the Etruscans (cp. Olr. metf, ModW. maint,
'size'); so called because it is qdded to the
integral part called characteristic.

## mantle
mantle, n. — ME. mantel, fr. OF. mantel (= F.
manteau), and ME. mentel, fr. OE. mentel. Both
OF. mantel and OE. mentel derive fr- L.
mantellum, 'cloak, veil' (whence, with back
formation, Late L. mantum, 'cloak', mantus, 'a short
cloak'), which is prob. of Celtic origin. It. man-
tello, OHG. mantal, mandal (whence MHG.
mantel, mandel, G. Mantel), ON. mbttull, also
derive fr. L. mantellum. Cp. manta, manteau,
mantelet, dismantle, portmanteau.
Derivative: manr/e, tr. and intr. v.

## mantra
mantra, п., that part of the Vedas which contains
hymns (Hinduism) — OI. mantrah, lit. 'speech,
sacred text, counsel', rel. to Avestic тфга-, of
s.m. See mandarin.

## mantua
mantua, п., a mantle formerly worn by women.
— F. manteau, 'cloak, mantle' (see mantle);
influenced in form by Mantua, town in Italy (as if
the word meant 'a mantle manufactured in
Mantua*).

## Manu
Manu, п., any of the fourteen mythological
progenitors of mankind (Hindu mythol.) — OI.
manuh, 'man; progenitor of mankind', rel. to
Avestic manu-, and cogn. with OSlav. mqil,
Goth, manna, OE. mann, 'man'. See man.

## manual
manual, adj., pertaining to, or done by, the hand.
— ME. manuel, fr. MF. (= F.) manuel, fr. L.
manuaiis, 'relating to the hand', fr. manus,
'hand', which is rel. to Umbr. manim (ace),
mani, mani (abl.), 'hand', and cogn. with OE.
mund, 'hand; protection, guardianship;
protector, guardian', ON. mund, 'hand', mundr,
'the sum which the bridegroom had to pay for
his bride', OHG., MHG. murtt, 'hand,
protection', OHG. foramundo, MHG. vormunde,
'protector, guardian', G. Vormund, 'guardian',
OFris. mund, 'guardianship; guardian', Co.
manal, 'sheaf, MBret. malazn (metathesized
fr. *manazl), ModBret. malan (fr. *manatlo), of
s.m., and prob. also with Gk. μάρη, 'hand', Alb.
mat (for *mar-no), Ί take, receive'. All these
words prob. derive from the heteroclitic I.-E.
base *man[mar, 'hand; to take into one's hand'.
Cp. manus, mainpernor, mainprize, maintain,
manacle, manage, mancinism, manciple,
mandate and words there referred to, maneuver,
manicure, manifest, maniple, manipulate, manner,
mansuete, manubrium, manufacture,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:471 COLUMN:2 -->
manumission, manumit, manure, mastiff, amanuensis,
bimanual, emancipate, legerdemain, mortmain. Cp.
also mound, 'heap of earth", mund, Edmund,
Osmond, Raymond, Sigismund.
Derivatives: manual, n. (q.v.), manual-ly, adv.

## manual
manual, п., I) a handbook; 2) keyboard of an
organ. — ME. manuel, fr. ML. manuale,
'handbook' (whence also F. manuel, of s.m.), prop.
neut. of the Latin- adjective manuaiis, 'relating
to the hand', used as a noun. See manual, adj.

## mannbriated
mannbriated, adj., having a manubrium. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ed fr. L. manubriatus,
'furnished with a handle', fr. manubrium. See
next word.

## manubrium
manubrium, п., a handlelike process (anat. and
zool.) — L. manubrium, 'handle, hilt', prop,
'that which is held in hand', fr. L. manus, 'hand'.
See manual, adj.
Derivative: manubri-al, adj.

## manucode
manucode, п., a bird allied to the bird of
paradise. — F., fr. ModL. manucodiata, fr. Malay
mdnuq dewata, 'bird of the gods'.

## Manuel
Manuel, masc. PN. — Shortened fr. Emmanuel.

## manufactory
manufactory, п., a factory- — Lit. 'a place where
something is made with the hands', fr. L.
manus, 'hand', and a derivative of facere, 'to
make'; cp. factorium, 'oil press'. See next word
and subst. suff. -ory and cp. factory.

## manufacture
manufacture, n. — MF. (= F.), lit. 'something
made with the hands', fr. ML. manufactura, fr.
L. manu, abl. of manus, 'hand', and factura, 'a
making*, fr. /actus, pp. of facere, 'to make, do'.
See manual, fact and -urc.
Derivatives: manufacture, tr. v., manufactur-er,
п., manufactur-ing, verbal n. and adj.

## manuka
manuka, п., the New Zealand tea tree. — Maori.

## manul
manul, п., a small wild cat of Tibet, Mongolia
and Siberia. — Mongolian name.

## manumission
manumission, п., liberation. — ME., fr. MF.
(= F.), fr. L. manumissionem, ace. of manumis-
sio, 'the freeing of a slave', fr. manumissus, pp.
of manumittere. See next word and -ion.

## manumit
manumit, tr. v., to release, — ME. manumitten,
fr. MF. manumitter, fr, L. manumittere, 'to
release, set at liberty, emancipate', lit. 'to let out
of one's hand', fr. manu, abl. of manus, 'hand',
and mittere, 'to let go, send'. See manual, adj.,
and mission.

## manure
manure, tr. v., to fertilize. — ME. manouren,
orig. 'to till (the land)', contracted fr. OF. ma~
nouvrer (F. manauvrer), 'to work with the hand'.
See maneuver and cp. inure.
Derivatives: manure, п., manur-ial, adj.

## manus
manus, п., the end of the forelimb of a vertebrate
(anat. and zool.) — L., 'hand'. See manual, adj.

## manuscript
manuscript, adj. — Fr. L. manu scriptus, 'written
with the hand', fr. manu, abl. of manus, 'hand',
and pp. of scrtbere, 'to write'.
See manual, adj., and script.

## manuscript
manuscript, n. — ML. manuscrlptum, fr. L. manu
scriptum, 'something written with the hand',
neut. of manu scriptus. See prec. word.

## Manx
Manx, adj. — Earlier Monks, metathesized fr,
Manisk, 'of the Isle of Man', which was formed
with suff. -isk (see adj. suff. -ish) fr. Man- (fr.
Olr. Manu), 'the Isle of Man'.
Derivative: Manx, п., the language of the Isle
of Man.

## manx
manx, n. — Short for Manx cat.

## many
many, adj. and n. — ME. mani, moni, meni, fr.
OE. manig, monig, mxnig, rel. to OS. manag.
Late ON. mangr, Dan. mangen, Swed. mangen,
OFris. manich, menich, MDu. menich, Du.
menig, OHG. manag, MHG. manec, G. manch,
Goth, manags, 'many a, many', and cogn. with
OSlav. munogu, 'much, many', Olr- wmcc, W.
mynych, Co. menouch, 'frequent', possibly also
with OI. magham, 'gift', maghavant-, 'liberal,
generous'.

## manzamlla
manzamlla, name of various plants. — Sp., dimin.
of manzana, 'apple', fr. Mat(t)iana (mala),
'apples of Mat(t)ius'. See manchineel.

## manzanlllo
manzanlllo, п., manchineel. — See prec. word.

## manzanita
manzanita, п., the bearberry. — Sp., dimin. of
manzana, 'apple'. See manzanllla.

## Maori
Maori, п., 1) a member of the native of New
Zealand ; 2) the language spoken by them. — New
Zealand native word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:471 COLUMN:3 -->

## map
map, n. — MF. mappe in mappemonde, 'map of
the world', fr. OF., fr. ML. mappa mundi, of
s.m., fr. L, mappa, 'napkin, tablecloth; signal
cloth', fr. Heb.-Punic mappah, 'napkin, cloth,
flag', which stands for *manpa , contraction of
Mishnaic Heb. mendpha (see Mishnah Kelim,
16:7), 'streaming cloth, banner', lit. 'that which
is moved to and fro*, from stem n-w-p, 'to move
to and fro; to swing', whence also Biblical Heb.
nopheph, 'he brandished', heniph, *he wielded,
waved', naphah, 'sieve', t&nuphah, 'a swinging,
waviog, wave offering, offering'. Cp. nappe,
napkin, apron. G'p. also mop.
Derivative: map, tr. v.

## maple
maple, n. — ME. mapil, fr. OE. mapulder, mapel
(treow), 'maple tree', rel. to ON. mopurr, of s.m.

## maqui
maqui, п., a shrub of Chile (Aristotelia maqui). —
Sp., fr. Araucan maqui.

## maquis
maquis, n, 1) a zone of shrubby plants in the
Mediterranean region serving as cover for fugitives,
guerrilla fighters, etc.; 2) (often cap.) a member
of the French underground movement in World
War II, fighting against the Nazis. — F., 'scrub,
bush (in Corsica)', fr. It. macchia, 'thicket', fr.
L. macula, 'spot'. See macula.

## mar
mar, tr. v., to injure. — ME. merren, marren, fr.
OE. merran, mierran, 'to hinder, obstruct,
squander, waste', rel. to OFris. meria, OHG.
marren, merren, 'to hinder, obstruct', Goth.
marzjan, *to hinder, offend', OFris. mere, 'tie,
fetter', and prob. to ON. merja, 'to crush,
bruise', and cogn. with OI. mrnati, 'he crushes,
bruises', Gk. μαραίνειν, 'to put out, quench,
extinguish', fr. I.-E. base *mer-, 'to rub,
consume, wear away'. See smart, v., and cp. words
there referred to. OF. marrir, 'to afflict' (whence
F. marri, orig. pp., 'sorry, grieved'), OProven?.
marrir, It. smarrire, 'to lead astray", are Teut.
loan words.

## marabou
marabou, also marabout, п., a large stork of West
Africa. — F. marabou(t\ fr. Port, marabuto, fr.
Arab, murabit, 'hermit*; so called because of its
solitary habits. See next word.

## Marabont
Marabont, п., 1) a Mohammedan saint; 2),his
tomb or shrine. — F., fr. Port, marabuto, fr.
Arab, murabit, 'hermit', partic. of rdbata, 'he
applied himself continually, he was on duty',
3rd conjugation of rdbata, 'he bound'. Cp.
Almoravides, marabou, maravedi.

## Marah
Marah, п., the first oasis reached by the Israelites
after passing through the Red Sea. The waters
were bitter, but Moses sweetened them. See Ex.
15: 23-25; Nu. 33, 8:9. — Heb. Mardh, prop.
fern, of mar, 'bitter', used as a noun, from the
root of mar (contraction of mardr), 'was
bitter', whence also mor, 'myrrh', merorah, 'gall,
gallbladder', тёгёган, 'galP, m&rortm, 'bitter
herbs', meriri, 'bitter', memer, meriruth,
'bitterness', Mishnaic Heb. mardh, 'gall' (lit. 'the
bitter organ'). See myrrh.

## maranatha
maranatha, п., a curse. — Gk. μαραναθά, usually
explained as transliteration of Aram, mdran
atha, 'the Lord has come', or Ό Lord, come'.
But the association of μαραναθά, with ανάθεμα
in ήτω ανάθεμα, μαραναθά, 'let him be
anathema, maranatha' (1st Corinth. i6:22), makes
it probable that the words ανάθεμα, μαραναθά
express a double or intensified curse. It is very
probable that μαραναθά is the transliteration
of Heb. тоЬбгат attdh, 'thou art put under the
ban', the short Qamatz in the first syllable of the
word mohdram having been mistaken for the
long one (= a) and the letter Π (= A), which
has no exact equivalent in the Greek alphabet,
having been dropped in the transliteration. The
omission of the letter Π is the rule in the
transliteration of PN.'s in the LXX. Cp. e.g. Ένώχ,
translit. of -рЗП (ЩпоШг), Νώε, translit. of Π3
(Nosh), 'Ισαάκ, translit. of ргГГ (Yitzhak), Za-
ρά, translit. of ΓΠΪ (Zerah, Zarah), Όφέρ,
translit. of Ί2Π (Jiepher), Σαλτταάδ, translit. of
lnaSi' (Tzhophhad), Άγγί, translit. of МП
(ffaggi), ΆγγαΤος, rendering of МП fflaggdy).
The Hebrew word mohdram is the Hoph'al (=
passive of the causative) part, of bdram, 'he
devoted, banished', which is rel. to Arab, bdru-
ma, 'was forbidden, unlawful'; see hercm and
cp. harem. For the change of m to η ср. marrano.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:472 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 445 | MARGINALIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:472 COLUMN:1 -->
The identification of μαραναθά with Heb. mo-
hdram attah is supported by the fact that the LXX
usually renders the Heb. noun herem (e.g. in
Lev. 27: 28, 29) by άνά&εμα (see anathema) and
the verb hehirtm (e.g. in Nu. 21: 2,3) by άνα&ε-
ματίζειν (see anathematize).

## Maranta
Maranta, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Italian physician and botanist
Bartolomeo Maranta (1500-1571).

## Marantaceae
Marantaceae, n. pi., the arrowroot family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## marantaceous
marantaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## maraschino
maraschino, п., liqueur made from the fermented
juice of the marasca cherry. — It., fr. amarasca,
marasca, 'a kind of small, sour, cherry', fr.
amaro, 'bitter', fr. L. amarus. See amarine and
cp. margosa.

## marasmic
marasmic, adj., pertaining to or having marasmus
— See next word and -ic.

## marasmus
marasmus, п., wasting away of the body. —
ModL., fr. Gk, μαρασμός, 'consumption', fr.
μαραίνειν, 'to consume', fr. I.-E. base *mer-, 'to
rub, consume, wear away'. See mar and cp.
amaranth.

## Maratha
Maratha, п., member of a people in South India.
— Marathi Maratha, corresponding to Hind.
Marhaia, fr. 01. Maharastrah, lit. 'great
country', fr. maha-, 'great', and rastrah, 'kingdom,
country', which is rel. to rajan, 'king'. See
mall araja.

## Marathon race
Marathon race, a running race, 26 miles 385 yards
long. — From Marathon, 26 miles north of
Athens, scene of the victory of the Athenians
over the Persians, 490 B.C.E.; so called in
allusion to the Greek who ran from Marathon to
Athens to bring the news of victory to his
countrymen and fell dead on arrival.

## maraud
maraud, intr. v., to raid. — F. marauder, fr.
maraud, 'scoundrel, rascal', fr. dial. F. maraud,
'tomcat', a word of imitative origin. Dial. F.
maraud was prob. used also figuratively in the
sense 'vagabond', which accounts for the
development of meaning.
Derivative: maraud-er, n.

## maravedi
maravedi, п., an old Spanish gold coin. — Sp.
tnaravedi, fr. Arab, murabitt, adj. formed fr.
Murabitin (pi.), name of a Moorish dynasty
(= Almoravides). Hence maravedi prop, meant
'money of the Almoravides'. See Marabout,

## marble
marble, n. — ME. marbre, later changed to
inarbel, marble, fr. OF. (= F.) marbre, fr. VL.
marmorem, ace. of L. marmor (a neut. noun,
taken in VL. for masc), fr. Gk. μάρμαρος,
'white, glistening stone', fr. orig. 'stone, rock',
rel. to μάρναμαι, 'i fight, battle', lit. Ί strike
myself', μαραίνω, Ί put out, quench,
extinguish', and cogn. with OI. mrndti, 'crushes,
bruises', fr. I.-E. base *mer-, 'to rub, consume,
wear away'. See smart, v., and cp. marmoreal.
Cp. also marasmus, amaranth. The sense
development of Gk. μάρμαρος was influenced by
μαρμαίρειν, 'to shine', to which, however, it is
not related. OHG. marmul, murmul, G. Marmel,
Murmel, 'marble', are Latin loan words. G.
Marmor, 'marble', has been refashioned after L.
marmor.
Derivatives: marbl-ed, marbl-y, adjs.

## marc
marc, п., refuse of fruit, esp. of grapes. — F., lit.
'something trodden or beaten', fr. marcher, 'to
walk', in the original sense of this verb: 'to
tread'. See march, 'to walk'.

## marcasite
marcasite, п., a native iron disulfide FeSs
(mineral.) — F. marcassire, fr. ML. marchaslta, fr.
Sp. marcaxita (ModSp. marcasita), fr, Arab.
marqashttha, fr. Pers. marqashisha.

## marcella
marcella, п., a cotton quilting. — Lit. 'of
Marseilles', fr. F. Marseille, fr. L. Massilia. Cp.
Marseillaise, Marseilles.

## Marcellus
Marcellus, masc. PN. — L. Marcellus, dimin. of
Marcus (q.v.)
marcel wave. — Named after the French
hairdresser Marcel Grateau (died in 1936).

## marcescence
marcescence, n.—Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## marcescent
marcescent, adj., withering. — L. marclscens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, oi mar сё seer e, 'to wither,
droop, decay, pine away', inchoative of marcere.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:472 COLUMN:2 -->
'to wither, droop, be faint', fr. I.-E. base "mereq-,
'merq-, 'to decay, rot', whence also Lith. merkiu,
mefkti, 'to soak, steep', mirkstu, mifkti, 'to be
soaked, be steeped', and perh. Gaul, bracis, 'a
kind of corn used for making malt', Mir.
mraich, braich, W. brach, 'malt", Mir. bren, W.
braen (for *mrakno-), 'foul, rotten'. Cp. im-
marcessible. I.-E. base *mereq-, *merq-, 'to
decay, rot', is orig. identical with base *merq-,
'to rub', enlargement of base *mer-, whence OI.
mrnati, 'crushes, bruises', Gk. μαραίνει, 'to
put out, quench, extinguish'. See smart, v. and
cp. marasmus, amaranth, marble. Cp. also mar.
For the ending of marcescent see suff. -ent.

## march
march, п., boundary. — ME. marche, fr. OF.
(= F.) marche, 'boundary, frontier', fr. Frank-
ish *marka, which is rel. to OHG. marca,
marcha, MHG. marke, G. Mark, 'boundary,
frontier'. It., OProveng., Sp. marca, of s.m., are
also Teut. loan words. See mark, 'boundary;
sign', and cp. marchioness, marquis.
Derivative: march, intr. v., to border.

## march
march, intr. v., to walk. — MF. (= F.) marcher,
'to walk', fr. OF. marcher, 'to tread, trample; to
walk', which ртоЬ. derives fr. VL. 'marcare, 'to
hammer', fr. L. marcus, 'to beat the time; to
march in time; to march', fr. L. marcus,
'hammer', back formation fr. marculus, which was
mistaken for a diminutive. L. marculus has been
dissimilated fr. "malclos, for 'mahlos, which is
cogn. with L. malleus, 'hammer'; see malleus
and cp. machete, marc, mush, 'a march on foot'.
Several philologists derive OF. marcher fr.
Frankish "markBn, 'to mark, to imprint (one's
steps)'; see mark, 'boundary; sign'. It. marciare
and Sp. marchar, 'to march', are borrowed fr.
F. marcher.

## march
march, п., a walking. — MF. (= F.) marche, fr.
marcher. See prec. word and cp. demarche.

## March
March, n. — ME., fr. OF. march, also marz (F.
mars), fr. L. Martius (mensis), '(the month of)
Mars', fr. Mars, gen. Mortis, 'March'. Cp. It.,
Sp. marzo, 'March', and see Mars.

## Marchantia
Marchantia, п., a genus of plants, the liverwort
(bot.) — ModL., named after the French
botanist Nicolas Marchant (died in 1678). For the
ending see 1st suff. -in.

## Marchantiaceae
Marchantiaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the
liverwort family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr.
Marchantia with suff. -aceae.

## marctiantiaceous
marctiantiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## marcher
marcher, п., one who marches. — Formed tir.
march, 'to walk', with agential suff. -er.

## marcher
marcher, п., inhabitant of a march. — Formed fr.

## march
march, 'boundary', with agential suff. -er.

## marchesa
marchesa, п., an Italian marchioness. — It., fern,
of marchese. See next word.

## marchese
marchese, п., an Italian marquis. — It. See
marquis.

## Marcheshvan
Marcheshvan, n. — See Marheshvan.

## marchioness
marchioness, n. 1) wife or widow of a marquis;
2) a lady having in her own right the rank of a
marquis. — ML. marchionissa, fern, of marchio
(gen. -onis), 'marquis', prop, 'ruler of a march'.

## See march
See march, 'boundary', and marquis,

## marchpane
marchpane, n. —■ It. marzapane (whence also Sp.

marzapan, mazapon, ΟΡΓΟνεης. massapan, MF.

marcepain, F. massepairi), fr. Venetian matapan,

fr. ML, matapanus, name of a Venetian coin,

used also in the sense of 'weight' and 'box', ult.

fr. Arab, mauthabdn, 'a sitting king', name of a

## coin circulating in the East during the crusades
coin circulating in the East during the crusades,

fr. S. Arab, wdthaba, 'he sat; he dwelled' (in

Mark'. S. Arab, and Arab, wdthaba are rel. to

Heb. yashabh, 'he sat; he dwelled'. See Yeshibah.

## Marcia
Marcia, fern. PN. — L. Marcia, fern, of Mdrcius,
rel. to Marcus. See Marcus.

## Marcomanni
Marcomanni, n. pi., name of a Teutonic tribe. —

## L. Marcomanni
L. Marcomanni, a Teut. loan word lit. meaning
'men of the border'. The first element is rel. to

## OHG. mark
OHG. mark, OE. mearc, 'border, mark,
district'; see mark, 'boundary', and cp. march,
'boundary'. The second element is rel. to OHG.

## mart
mart, OE. mann, 'man'; see man.
