## marconigram
marconigram, п., a message sent by wireless
telegram; radiogram. — Formed from the name of
the Italian physicist Guglielmo Marconi (1874-
1937) and-gram.

## Marcus
Marcus, masc. PN. — L. Marcus, for * Mart-cos,
rel. to Mars, name of the Roman god of war.
See Mars and cp. Marcia, Mark,

## mare
mare, п., a female horse. — ME. mere, mare, fr.
OE. mere, fern, to OE. mearh, 'horse'; rel. to
OS. meriha, ON. merr, OFris. merrie, MDu.
merie, Du. merrie, OHG. meriha, merha, MHG.
merhe, G. Mahre, 'mare', ON. marr, OFris.
mar, OHG. marah, marh, 'horse', from pre-
Teut. marka, a form mentioned in Pausanias
Periplous and referred to as of Gaulish origin.
Cp. Ir. and Gael, marc, W. march, Co. margh,
march, Bret, marh, 'horse'. Cp. also the first
element in marshal,

## mare
mare, п., the sea. — L. mare, 'sea'. See mere,
'lake',

## mare
mare, п., incubus. — ME., fr. OE.,re]. to ON. and
OHG. тага, MDu. mare, Du. -merrie, MHG.
mar, G. Mahr, 'incubus', and cogn. with the first
element in Olr. Mor-rigain, demoness of corpses
(lit. 'queen of the nightmare'), Bulg., Serb., Pol.
mora, Czech mura, 'incubus'. Cp. the second
element in nightmare. Cp. also the second
element in cauchemar.

## maremma
maremma, п., marshy land near the seashore. —
It., fr. L. maritima, neut. p]. of maritimus,
'pertaining to the sea, near the sea', fr. mare, 'sea'.
Cp. OF. maresme, Catal. maresma, 'marsh',
which are of the same origin, and see maritime.

## Margaret
Margaret, fern. PN. — OF. Margaret (F.
Marguerite), fr. L. margarita, 'pearl'. See margarite
and cp. Margery,

## margaric
margaric, adj., pertaining to a white fatty acid
C16HJ3C02H (chem.) — F. margarique, fr. Gk.
μαργαρον, 'pearl'. See margarite and -ic.

## margarin
margarin, п., a fatty substance found in animal
fats and vegetable oils (chem.) — F. margarine,
fr. margarique, lit. 'of a pearl-like color' (see
margaric and chem. suff. -in); coined by the
French chemist Marie-Eugene Chevreul (1786-
1889).

## margarine
margarine, п., artificial butter. — F.; see prec.
word. The name arose from the erroneous
notion that all oils and fats contain margaric acid.

## margarite
margarite, п., 1) a pearl (archaic): 2) a basic
aluminum calcium silicate (mineral.) — ME., fr.
OF. margarite (F. marguerite), fr. L. margarita,
fr. Gk. μαργαρίτης (scil. λίθος}, 'pearl', which
is of uncertain origin. It possibly derives fr. OI.
maiijaram, manjari, 'bud, pear]'. Gk. αάργαρον
is prob. a back formation fr. μαργαρίτης. Ср.
Margaret, margaric, margarin, marguerite. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## inargaritiferous
inargaritiferous, adj., producing pearls. —
Compounded of L. margarita, 'pearl', and the stem
of J'erre, 'to bear, carry'. See prec. word and
-ferous.

## margar
margar, п., a spotted wildcat of South America.
— F., altered fr. earlier margaia, fr. Tupi mbara-
caia.

## marge
marge, п., edge, border. — F., fr. L. margo, gen.
marginis. See margin,

## margent
margent, п., margin. — An archaic var. of
margin.

## Margery
Margery, fern. PN. — OF. Margerie, rel. to L.

## margarita
margarita, 'pearl'. See Margaret,

## margin
margin, n. — ME. margine, fr. L. margo, gen.

## marginis
marginis, 'edge, brink, border', which is cogn.

## with Goth
with Goth, marka, 'boundary, frontier', OE.

## mearc
mearc, 'boundary, boundary sign, sign, mark'.

## See mark
See mark, 'boundary; sign', and cp. marge,
margent.
Derivatives: margin, tr. v., marginal (q.v.),
marginate (q.v.)

## marginal
marginal, adj. — ModL. marginalis, fr. L. margo,
gen. marginis. See margin and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: marginal, п., marginal-ly, adv.

## marginate
marginate, marginated, adj., having a margin. —

## L. marginatus
L. marginatus, pp. of marginare, 'to provide

## with a border
with a border, to border', fr. margo, gen.

## marginis. See margin and adj. suff. -ate
marginis. See margin and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also
-ed.

## marginalia
marginalia, n. pi., marginal notes. — ModL.,
prop. neut. pi. of the adjective marginalis. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:473 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MARGINELLA | 446 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:473 COLUMN:1 -->
marginal.

## Marginella
Marginella, п., a genus of marine snails (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. margo, gen. marginis. See margin
and -ella.

## margosa
margosa, п., an East Indian tree with bitter bark.
— Fr. Port, amargoso, 'bitter', fr. VL. *amari-
cosus, 'bitterish', fr. L. amarus, 'bitter'. See
amarine and cp. maraschino..

## margrave
margrave, п., I) orig. a governor of a border
region in Germany; 2) the hereditary title of
certain princes of the Holy Roman Empire. —
MDu. markgrave (Du. markgraaf), lit. 'count of
the border', fr. mark, 'border' and grave, 'count,
earl'. Cp. MLG. markgreve, OHG. markgravo,
'governor of a border region', G. Markgraf,
'margrave', and see march, 'boundary', and
grave, 'count'. Cp. also landgrave.

## margravine
margravine, п., wife of margrave. — Du. mark-
gravin, fern, of markgraaf. See margrave and
subst. suff. -ine.

## marguerite
marguerite, п., oxeye daisy. — F., 'pearl;
daisy', fr. OF. margarite, 'pearl', resp. OF.
margerite, 'daisy', fr. L. margarita, 'реат!', fr.
Gk. μαργαρίτης. See margarite.

## Marheshvan
Marheshvan, also Marheshwan, п., the eighth
month of the Jewish year. — Mishnaic Heb.
marheshwan, fr. Akkad. warhu samnu, lit.
'eighth month'. The first word is re], to Heb.
yerah, 'month', yareah, 'moon', Aram, yarha,
*month'. The second word is rel. to Akkad.
samane (masc), samanti(fem.), 'eight'. Cp. Heb.
sh топе (masc), sh топа (fem.), Ugar. Smn
(masc), Smnt (fem.), Aram. temane (masc),
remanyd (fem.), Arab, thamanin (masc), tha-
maniya (fem.), Ethiop. samani (masc), sama-
nitu (fem.), 'eight'. (The masc. forms are used
with fem. nouns, the fem. ones with masc.
nouns.) For the interchangeability of w and m
in Akkadian cp, Kislev. Cp. Heshvan.

## Maria
Maria, fem. PN. — Late L. See Mary.

## Marian
Marian, adj., 1) pertaining to the Virgin Mary;
2) pertaining to Mary, Queen of England; 3)
pertaining to Mary, Queen of Scots. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. Maria. See Mary.

## Marian
Marian, п., a follower of Mary, Queen of Scots.
See prec. word.

## Marian
Marian, Marianne, fem. PN. — Marian is a
collateral form of Marion, dimin. of F. Marie
(see Mary), but was mistaken later for the
compound of the two names Mary and Ann(e)
(whence the spelling Marianne).

## marigold
marigold, п., a yellow-flowered plant. — A
hybrid coined fr. Mary (prob. the Virgin) and
gold.

## marihuana
marihuana,marijuana, п., I) the hemp plant; 2) a
narcotic obtained from its dried leaves and
flowers. — Мех. Sp., prob. a contraction of
Maria Juana (= 'Mary Jane*), so called from
the alleged sexual appeal of the drug.

## Marilyn
Marilyn, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Mary.

## marimba
marimba, п., a kind of musical instrument. —
Bantu malimba, marimba, pi. of limba, name of
a musical instrument.

## marinade
marinade, п., a pickle seasoned with herbs and
spices. — F., fr. mariner, 'to pickle', fr. marin,
Of the sea', fr. L. marinus, of s.m. See marine
adj., and -ade.
Derivative: marinade, tr. v.

## marinate
marinate, tr. v., to steep in pickle. — See prec
word and verbal suff. -ate.

## marine
marine, adj. — ME. maryn(e), fr. OF. (— F.)
marin, fem. marine, fr. L. marinus, fem. marina,
'of the sea', fr. mare, 'sea'. See mere, 'the sea',
and adj. suff. -ine and cp. submarine,
transmarine.

## marine
marine, n. — F., 'seamanship, navy, seascape', fr.
marin, 'mariner1, from the adj. marin. See
marine, adj.

## mariner
mariner, n. — ME., fr. OF. marinier, fr. ML.
mannarius, 'sailor', fr. L. marinus, 'of the sea'.
See prec. word and agential suff. -er.

## Marin ism
Marin ism, п., extravagant style of writing. — Lit.
'style resembling that of the Italian poet
Giovanni Battista MarinV (1569-1625). For the
ending see suff. -ism.

## Marinist
Marinist, п., writer imitating the style of Marini.
— See prec. word and -ist.

## Mariolatry
Mariolatry, n. — Lit. 'worship of Mary',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:473 COLUMN:2 -->
compounded of Gk. Μαρία, 'Mary\ and -λατρεία,
-λατρία, fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor, service,
worship'. See Mary and -latry.

## Marion
Marion, fem. PN. — F., dimin. of Marie. See
Mary and cp. Marianne. Cp. also next word.

## marionette
marionette, п., puppet worked by strings. — F.
marionnette, double diminutive of Marie. See
prec. word and -ette.

## Mariposa lily
Mariposa lily, Mariposa tulip, any plant of ihe
genus Calochortus. — Fr. Sp. mariposa,
'butterfly', which is of uncertain origin; so called in
allusion to the appearance of the colorful
blossoms.

## mariposite
mariposite, п., a chromium-bearing mica
(mineral.) — Named after Mariposa County in
California. For the ending see subst, suff. -ite.

## marish
marish, п., a marsh. — ME. mares, mareis, fr.
OF. maarais, mareis, maresc (F. marais),
'marsh'. See marsh.
Derivatives: marish, marish-y, adjs., marish-
ness, n.

## marischal
marischal, п., Scot, form of marshal. — F. mari-
chal. See marshal.

## Marist
Marist, п., member of a Roman Catholic order.
— F. Mariste, fr. Marie. See Mary and -ist.

## marital
marital, adj., 1) pertaining ,to a husband; 2)
pertaining to marriage. — L. maritalis, 'of
marriage', fr. maritus, 'a married man, husband',
which is of uncertain etymology. It possibly
stands for *mari-tos and lit. means 'provided
with a young wife', and is cogn. with OI.
maryab, 'young man, lover, wooer', Gk. μεΐραξ,
'boy, girl', Lith. таги, 'bride', Opruss. martin
(ace), 'bride', Lith. merga, OPruss. mergo, 'girl,
maid, servant', W. merch, Co. myrgh, 'daughter;
wife', W, morwyn, 'virgin, girl'. Cp marry.
Derivatives: marital-ily, п., marital-ly, adv.

## maritime
maritime, adj., of, or pertaining to, the sea. — F.,
fr. L. maritimus, 'of the sea, near the sea', fr.
mare, 'sea'. See mare, 'sea'. Suff. -timus in
maritimus (also -tumus) is prop, a superl. suff., and
occurs also in L. in-timus, 'inmost', ul-timus,
'last', pos-tumus, 'last' (see intimate, ultimate,
posthumous).

## Marius
Marius, masc. PN. — L., fr. Marius, name of a
Roman gens.

## marjoram
marjoram, п., name of a plant. — ME. majoran,
fr. OF. majorane (F. marjolaine), fr. ML. majo-
rdna, fr. L. amaracus, fr. Gk. άμάρακος,
'marjoram', which, together with Macedonian Gk.
άβαρΰ, 'marjoram', prob. derives from a
language of India. Cp. OI. maruvahi, maruvakah,
'marjoram'. ML. majordna (fr. L. amaracus) owes
its form to a confusion with L. major, compar.
of magnus, 'great, large' (see major, adj.)

## Marjorie
Marjorie, Marjory, fem. PN. — Collateral forms
of Margery (q.v.)

## mark
mark, п., 1) boundary (archaic); 2) sign. — ME.
merke, marke, fr. OE. mearc,
'boundary,boundary sign, sign, mark', rel. to ON, merki, mark,
'boundary sign', mork, 'forest' (forests often
served as frontiers), OFris. merke, OS., Goth.
marka, 'boundary, frontier', Du. merk, 'mark,
brand', mark, 'borderland; mark, sign', OHG.
marcha, MHG. marke, G. Mark, 'boundary,
boundary land', G. Marke, 'sign, token; stamp',
and cogn. with Avestic mar za, 'border', L.
margo, gen. marginis, 'edge, brink, border', Olr.
mruig, lr. bruig, 'boundary; district', W., Co.,
Bret. bro, 'district'. Cp. mark, 'to put a mark
on', mark, a weight. Cp. also march,
'boundary', Marcomanni, margrave, marque, marquetry,
marquis, marquise, countermark, demarcation,
remark. Cp. also margin. Cp. also Cymric.

## mark
mark, tr. v., to put a mark on. — ME. merken,
marken, fr. OE. mearcian, 'to make a mark, to
mark', fr. OE. mearc, 'boundary, sign, mark*,
rel. to ON. merkja, Dan. merke, Swed. marka,
OFris. merkia, MDu., Du. merken, OHG.
merken, merchen, MHG., G. merken, 'to mark,
note', and to OS. markon, ON. marka, OHG.
marchon, markon, of s.m. See prec. word. OF.
merchier, 'to mark, note*, is a Teut. loan word.
Derivatives: mark-ed, adj., mark-ed-ly, adv.,
mark-ed-ness, п., mark-er. П., mark-ing, n.

## mark
mark, п., 1) a weight; 2) any of various coins; 3)
the monetary unit of Germany. — ME. marke,
fr. OE. marc, prob. fr. ON. mork, which is rel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:473 COLUMN:3 -->
to MHG. mark, marke, G. Mark, 'mark'. These
words are very prob. rel. to OE. mearc, ON.
mark, 'boundary sign', OHG. marcha,
'boundary, boundary land". See mark, 'boundary;
sign'.

## Mark
Mark, masc. PN. — L. Marcus. See Marcus.

## Markab
Markab, п., a star of the constellation of Pegasus.
Arab, markab, 'saddle; ship, vessel', fr. rakiba,
'he mounted a horse, he rode' (whence also
markaba , 'vehicle, carriage'), which is rel. to
Heb. rakhdbh, 'he mounted a horse, he rode',
rekhebh, 'chariot', merkabh, 'chariot, saddle',
merkabhd , 'chariot', Aram.-Syr. r khebh, 'he
mounted a horse, he rode', Syr. markfbha,
'ship', Ugar. rkb, 'to mount a horse, to ride',
Akkad. rakabu, of s.m., markabtu, 'chariot',
Ethiop. rakaba, 'he attained'.

## market
market, n. — ME., fr. ONF. market,
corresponding to OF. marchiet, marchie (whenceF. marche),
fr. L. mercatus, 'trade, business, marketplace'
[whence also It. mercato, OProveng. and Catal.
mercat, Sp. and Port, mercado, OS. markat,
MDu. market (Du, markt, dial. Du. mart),
OHG. markat (MHG. market, G. Markt)], fr.
mercatus, pp. of mercarx, 'to trade', fr. merx,
gen. mercis, 'ware, merchandise'. See merchant
and cp. mart, which is a doublet of market.
Derivatives: market, intr. and tr. v., market-able,
adj., market-abil-ity, п., market-abl-y, adv.,
market-ing, n.

## markhor
markhor, п., wild goat of the Himalayas. —
Pers. тйг-khor, 'snake eater'.

## marl
marl, п., clayey soil. — ME., fr. MF. marie
(whence F. marne), fr. ML. margila, dimin. of
L. marga, 'marl', which is a Gaulish word
according to Pliny. It. and Sp. marga, 'marl',
derive fr. L. marga, Late OHG. mergil, MDu.
merghel, Du., MLG., MHG., G., Dan. mergel,
Swed. mdrgel, W. marl, are loan words fr. ML.
margila.
Derivatives: marl, tr. v., marl-y, adj.

## marl
marl, tr. v., to fasten, — Du. marlen, freq. of
MDu. maren, meren, 'to tie, fasten'. See moor,
'to fasten', and cp. next word.

## marline
marline, п., a small cord of two strands used for
seizing (naut.) — Du. marlijn, formed (under
the influence of lijn, 'line'), fr. marling, fr. mar-
ren, fr. MDu. maren, 'to tie'. See marl, 'to
fasten', and dimin. suff. -ling.

## marlite
marlite, п., a variety of marl which resists the
action of the air. — Formed from marl with
subst. suff. -ite.

## marmalade
marmalade, n. — F. marmelade, fr. Port, marme-
lada, 'quince jelly, marmalade', fr. marmelo,
'quince', fr. L. melimelum, 'honey apple', fr. Gk.
μελίμηλον, 'sweet apple', which is
compounded of μέλι, 'honey', and μήλον, apple'. The
first element is cogn. with L. mel, gen. mellis,
'honey'; see melli-. For the second element see
Mai us, 'the apple tree'.

## marmolite
marmolite, п., pale green serpentine (mineral.) —
Compounded of Gk. μαρμ(α£ρει,ν}, to shine',
and λίθος, 'stone'. The first element is cogn.
with OI. mdricih, marici, 'beam of light, ray*,
and prob. also with L. merus, 'pure, unmixed'.
See mere, adj. For the second element see -lite.

## marmoreal
marmoreal, adj., pertaining to, or like, marble.
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. marmoreus,
'made of marble, resembling marble', fr. mar-
mor, 'marble'. See marble.
Derivative: marmoreal-ly, adv.

## marmoset
marmoset, n.( a small monkey of South and
Central America. — ME. marmusetxe, fr. MF.
marmouset, 'grotesque carved figure' [cp. Rue
des Marmousets, a street in Paris, in which there
were grotesque figures of stone. Referring to
this street, a Latin text from 1280 speaks of duo
marmoseti lapidel ['two stone marmosets' =
two grotesque figures of stone']; rel. to F.
marmot, 'little monkey; puppet, grotesque
figure', marmotter, 'to mutter, mumble'. All these
words are prob. of imitative origin. Cp. marmot.

## marmot
marmot, п., a burrowing rodent. — F. marmotte,
prop, 'the mumbling (animal)', fr. marmotter,
'to mutter, mumble'; see prec. word. It. mar-
motta and Sp. marmota are French loan words.
The F. forms marmotaine, marmontaine are a
blend of F. marmot with L. mus montanus, lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:474 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 447 | MARTYRIZE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:474 COLUMN:1 -->
'mountain-mouse'.
тагоса in, п., a dress material made of silk. —
F., lit. Of Morocco', fr. Maroc, 'Morocco'; so
called because this material was orig.
manufactured in Morocco. Cp. morocco.

## Maronite
Maronite, п., member of a Christian sect living
in the Lebanon district in Syria. — Named after
its founder Maro, a monk, who lived in the 5th
cent. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## maroon
maroon, п., one of a class of Negroes; orig. a
fugitive Negro slave. — F. marron, fr. Sp. ci-
marron, 'wild, untamed', derivative of cima, fr.
L. cyma, 'mountain top, summit', fr. Gk. κϋμα,
'anything swollen, wave'. See cyma.
Derivative: maroon, tr. and intr. v.

## maroon
maroon, п., and adj., brownish red. — F. marron,
'chestnut', fr. It. marrone, 'chestnut', which is
of unknown origin. Cp. marron.

## marplot
marplot, n. — Compounded of mar and plot.

## marque
marque, п., seizure by way of reprisal, — F., fr.
ΟΡΓΟνεης. marca, 'seizure, reprisal', fr. marcar,
'to seize in reprisal', prop, 'to mark by seizing
in reprisal', which is of Teut. origin. See mark,
'boundary; sign'.

## marquee
marquee, п., a large tent. — Back formation fr.
marquise, which was mistaken for a plural;
marquee orig. denoted 'a place suitable for a
marquise'.

## marquetry
marquetry, marqueterie, п., inlaid work of wood
or other material used in decorating furniture.
— F. marqueterie, 'inlaid work, marquetry', fr.
marqueter, 'to speckle, spot, inlay*, fr. marque,
'a mark'. See mark, 'boundary; sign', and cp.
marque.

## marquis
marquis, п., a title of nobility. — ME. markis,
marquis, alteration (due to the analogy of It,
marchese) of OF. marchis, fr. marche, 'border,
borderland', fr. Teut. *marka, 'boundary,
frontier'. Cp. OHG. marcha, 'boundary,
frontier', and see march, 'boundary'.

## marquisate
marquisate, п., the office or dignity of a marquis.
— Formed on analogy of F. marquisat, which
is derived fr. It. marchesato, but was assimilated
in form to marquis. See marquis and subst. suff.
-ate.

## marquise
marquise, п., 1) wife or widow of a marquis; 2) a
lady holding in her own right the rank equal
to that of a marquis; z) awning, marquee. — F.,
'marchioness; marquee (tent)', fern, of marquis.
See prec. word and cp. marquee.

## marquisette
marquisette, п., a thin cotton fabric. — Dimin.
of F. marquise, 'awning, marquee'. See prec.
word and -ette.

## marquois scale
marquois scale, a scale for drawing equidistant
parallel lines. — Named after its inventor
Marquois, who lived in London in the 18th
cent.

## marram grass
marram grass, bent grass. — ON. maralmr, lit.
'sea grass', fr. marr, 'sea', and halmr, 'straw'.
See mere, 'sea', and haulm.

## marrano
marrano, п., Jew or Moor converted to
Christianity. — Sp., 'pig, hog', fr. Arab, haruma, 'was
forbidden*. The pig was called the forbidden
animal', from the fact that the eating of pork is
forbidden by Jewish and Moslem religious law.
Cp. (Andalusian) Sp. maharrana, 'fresh bacon,
salt pork', which derives fr. Arab. muharramah,
fern, of muharram, 'anything forbidden', pass.
part, of hdrrama. See harem and herem. For the
change of m to η ср. maranatba.

## marriage
marriage, n. — ME. mariage, fr. OF. ( = F.)
manage, fr. VL. maritaticum (occurring in a
text from the year 1062), fr. L. maritatus, pp. of
maritare, 'to wed, marry, give in marriage*. It.
maritaggio, Sp. maridaje, 'marriage', also derive
fr. VL. maritaticum. See marry and -age.

## marron
marron, п., the European chestnut. — F. See
maroon, 'brownish red'.

## marrow
marrow, n. — ME. maro, merowe, fr. OE. mearg,
mearh, rel. to OS. marg, ON. mergr, OFris., Du.
merg, OHG. marag, marg, MHG. marc, G.
Mark, 'marrow', fr. I.-E. base *mozgho-,
whence also OI. majjan-, Avestic mazga-,
'marrow*, Toch. A massunt, 'marrow', OSlav.
mozgu, OPruss. muzgeno, Lith. smdgenes
(metathesized fr. *mdzgenes), 'brain*.
Derivatives: marrow, tr. v., marrow-ish,
marrow-less, marrow-y, adjs.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:474 COLUMN:2 -->

## marry
marry, tr. and intr. v. — ME. marien, fr. OF.
( = F-) marier, fr. L. maritare, 'to wed, marry,
give in marriage' (whence also It. maritare,
Rum. mdrita, OProvenc., Catal. Sp. and Port.
mar'tdar, 'to marry'), fr. maritus, 'married,
husband'. See marital and marriage.
Derivatives: marri-ed, adj., marri-er, n.

## Mars
Mars, п., the Roman god of war. — L. Mars, of
unknown etymology. Cp. March, Marcia,
Marcus, Mark, Martin, martin, martite. Gk.,
μάρναμαι, Ί fight', is not cognate with L.
Mars (see marasmus).

## Marsala
Marsala, п., a kind of wine produced in Sicily. —
So called from Marsala, a seaport in Sicily, fr.
Arab. Mirsd-llahi, lit. 'the Port of God'.

## Marseillaise
Marseillaise, п., name of the French national
Republican song, composed by Rouget de Lisle
in 1792. — F., fern, of the adj. MarseiUais, 'of
Marseilles'. Rouget de Lisle composed this
song for the Strassburg volunteers, yet it was
named Marseillaise because it was the
volunteers from Marseilles who sang it in Paris for
the first time.

## Marseilles
Marseilles, marseilles, п., a kind of cotton
material. — Prop, 'made at Marseilles'. Cp. mar-
cella, Marseillaise.

## marsh
marsh, n. — ME. mersh, fr. OE. mersc, merisc,
rel. to OS., OFris. mersk, MDu., MLG. mersch,
marsch (whence Du. mars, G. Marsch). All
these words are derivatives of Teut. *mari-, 'sea'.
See mere, 'lake', and cp. mare, 'sea', marish,
morass.
Derivatives: marsh, adj., marsh-y, adj., marsh-i-
ness, n.
-^marshal, n. — ME. mareschal, marshal, fr. OF.
mareschal (F. marechal), fr. Late L. mariscalcus,
a word occurring in the Salic Law, and derived
fr. Frankish *marhskalk, which is rel. to OHG.
marahscalc, lit. 'horse servant' (whence MHG.
marschalc, G. Marschall, 'marshal'), fr. marah,
'horse', and scale, 'servant*. For the etymology
of OHG. marah see mare, 'female horse'. OHG.
scale (= MHG. schalk, whence G. Schalk,
'rogue; wag*) is rel. to OE. scea/c, OS., OFris.
scale, Late ON. skalkr, servant', Dan., Swed.
skalk, Du. schalk, 'rogue; wag', Goth, skalks,
'servant', skalkinon, 'to serve'. Cp. It. scalco,
'steward; carver', marescial/o, Sp. mariscal,
'marshal', which are also Teut. loan words. Cp.
also marischal and the second element in
seneschal.
Derivatives: marshal, tr. v., marshal-су, п.,
marshal{l)-er, п., marshal-ship, n.

## Marshalsea
Marshalsea, п., a court formerly held in London
by the knight marshal. — ME. marschalcie, fr.
marschal, 'marshal'. See marshal and -cy.

## Marsilea
Marsilea, п., a genus of plants, the clover fern
(hot.) — ModL., named after the Italian
naturalist Luigi Ferdinando Marsili (1658-1730).

## Marsileaceae
Marsileaceae, n. pi., a family of plants {bot.) —
ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## marsileaceous
marsileaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## marsupial
marsupial, adj., pertaining to, or like, a pouch;
pertaining to the marsupials. — ModL. marsu-
pialis, 'having a pouch*, fr. L. marsupium. See
marsupium and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: marsupial, п., a marsupial animal.

## Marsupialia
Marsupialia, n. pi., an order of mammals, the
kangaroos, wombats, etc. {zool.) — ModL., fr.
ModL. marsupialis, 'having a pouch', fr. L.
marsupium. See marsupium.

## marsupium
marsupium, п., a pouch {anat. and zool.) — L., fr.
Gk. μαρσύπίον, dimin. of μάρσυπος,
μάρσιπος, 'bag, purse'; of foreign, prob. oriental
origin.

## mart
mart, п., market. — Dial. Du. mart, fr. Du.
markt, which is rel. to E. market (q.v.)
Derivative: mart, tr. and intr. v.

## martello tower
martello tower, also martello, п., a small fort. —
It. martello, 'hammer', altered fr. mortella, fr.
Cape Mortella in Corsica, name of a tower
captured by the English in 1794. Mortella comes fr.
VL. *myrte!la, *murtella, and means 'myrtle'.
See myrtle.

## marten
marten, п., a kind of weasel. — ME. martryn, fr.
MF. martrine, 'marten fur', fr. OF., fern, of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:474 COLUMN:3 -->
martrin, 'pertaining to the marten', fr. martre,
'marten'; influenced in form by MLG. marten
(see J. F. Bense, Dictionary of the Low-Dutch
Element in the English Vocabulary, p. 211). —
F. martre is a Teut. loan word; cp. OHG. mar-
dar (whence MHG., G. marder), OFris. merth,
OE. mearp, ON. mordr. According to Schrader
in Bezzenberger's Beitrage zur Kunde der indo-
germanischen Sprachen, 15, 129f., these Teut.
words are cogn. with Lith. таги, 'bride'. For
sense development cp. It donnola, 'young lady',
ModGk. νυμφίτσα, νυφίτσα, 'sister-in-law',
OSlav. nevesia, 'bride', all used in the sense of
'weasel'. Cp. also Hung, holgymenyet, 'ermine',
lit., 'lady-ermine'. — Lith mart] is possibly cogn.
with L. martius, 'husband', for the etymology
of which see marital. Cp. the second element in
foumart.

## martensite
martensite, п., a solid solution formed from iron
with 2 percent or less of carbon {mineral.) —
Named after the German metallurgist Adolf
Martens (1850-1914). For the ending see subst.
sufT. -ite.

## Martha
Martha, fern. PN. — Aram. Mdrethd, lit. 'lady,
mistress', fern, of mar, тага, 'lord, master'.

## martial
martial, adj., warlike. — ME., fr. L. Martialis, 'of
Mars', fr. Mars, gen. Martis. See Mars and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: martial-ity, п., martial-ly, adv.,
martial-ness, n.

## Martiaiist
Martiaiist, п., one born under Mars (astrol.) —
Formed with suff. -ist fr. L. Martialis, 'of Mars'.
See prec. word.

## Martian
Martian, п., an inhabitant of the planet Mars. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Martius, 'of Mars',
fr. Mars, gen. Martis. See Mars.

## Martin
Martin, masc. PN. — L. Martxnus, a derivative
of Mars, gen. Martis. See Mars and cp. martial.

## martin
martin, п., a kind of swallow. — MF. { = F.)
martin, fr. PN. Martin. See prec. word and cp.
martlet.

## martinet
martinet, п., a rigid disciplinarian. — Named
after Jean Martinet, an army officer under
Louis XIV of France.
Derivatives: martinet-ish, adj., martinei-ism, n.

## martingale
martingale, п., part of a horse's harness. — MF.
(= F.), fr. Sp. almartaga, 'litharge; a sort of
halter, rein', fr, Arab, almartak; influenced in
form by a confusion with OProveng. martegalo,
fern, of martegal, 'inhabitant of Martigue', used
in the sense 'worn in the manner of the
inhabitants of Martigue'.

## martini
martini, also martini cocktail, n. — Named after
Martini, an otherwise unknown person of
Italian origin.

## Martinmas
Martinmas, п., St. Martin's day, November 11th.
— Prop. Mass of St. Martin, Bishop of Tours
(died in 397).

## martite
martite, п., ferric oxide {mineral.) — Formed
with subst. suflf. -ite. fr. L- Marsy gen. Martis,
the Roman god of war, whose name was used in
alchemy as the symbol of iron. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## martlet
martlet, п., the bird martin. — MF. martelet,
derived, with change of suff., fr. martinet,
'martin'. See martin, 'swallow'.

## Martynia
Martynia, п., a genus of plants, the unicorn
plant {bot.) — ModL., named after John Mar-
tyn (1699-1768), professor of botany at
Cambridge. For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Martyniaceae
Martyniaceae, n. pi., the martynia family {bot.)
— ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## martyniaceous
martyniaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## martyr
martyr, n. — ME. martir, fr, OE. martyr, fr.
Eccles. L. martyr, fr. Gk. μάρτυς, Aeol. and
Dor. μάρτυρ, 'witness; martyr', which prob.
stands for I.-E. *mrtu- and is rel. to Gk.
μέριμνα, 'care, solicitude, thought', μέρμηρα
(poetic), 'care, trouble', μέρμερος, 'causing anxiety,
baneful', and cogn. with OI. smarati,
'remembers', L. memor, 'mindful'. See memory and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: martyr, tr. v., the hybrid поид
martyr-dom, martyrize (q.v.), martyry (q.v.)

## martyrize
martyrize, tr. v. — ME. martirizen, fr. Eccles. L.
martyrizare, fr. martyr. See martyr and -ize.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:475 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MARTYROLOGY | 448 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:475 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: martyriz-ation, n.

## martyrology
martyrology, п., a study of martyrs; a history of
martyrs. — Eccles L. martyrologium, fr. Eccles.
Gk. μαρτυρολόγιον, which is compounded of
Gk. μάρτυς (see martyr), and λόγος, 'word,
speech, discourse, account'. See logos.
See martyr and -logy.

## martyry
martyry, n. — Eccles. L. martyrium, fr. Gk. μαρ-
τύριον, 'testimony, proof; martyr's shrine', fr.
μάρτυς. See martyr and -y (representing L.
■ram).

## marvel
marvel, n. — ME. merveille, fr. OF. (= F.)
merveille, 'wonder', fr. L. mirabilia, 'wonderful
things', neut. pi. (but in VL. taken as fern, sing.)
of mirabilis, 'wonderful', fr. mirari, 'to wonder
at1. See miracle, admire.

## marvel
marvel, intr. v. — ME. merveillen, fr. MF. mer-
veillier, 'to wonder at', fr. merveille. See marvel,
n.

## marvelous
marvelous, marvellous, adj. — ME. merveihus, fr.
OF. merveillos (F. merveilleux), fr. merveille.
See marvel, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: marvel{l)ous-ly, adv., marvel(l)ous-
ness, n.

## Marxian
Marxian, adj., pertaining to Karl Marx (1818-83)
or his doctrine. — For the ending see suff. -ian.
Derivatives: Marxian, п., Marxian-ism, n.

## Marxism
Marxism, п., the doctrine of Karl Marx. — See
prec. word and -ism.

## Marxist
Marxist, п., an adherent of Marxism; adj.,
Marxian. — See prec. word and -ist.

## Mary
Mary, fem. PN. — ME. Marie, fr. OE. Maria,
Marie, fr. L. Maria, fr. Gk- Μαριάμ, Μαρία,
fr. Aram. (Targum) Maryam, fr. Heb. \firyamt
which is of uncertain origin. See Miriam, and
cp. Mariaune, Marion, marionette.

## marzipan
marzipan, n. — See marchpane.

## -mas
-mas, combining form for Mass, as in Christmas*
Lammas, Michaelmas.

## mascagulte
mascagulte, п., ammonium sulfate {mineral.) —
Named after its discoverer, the Italian
anatomist and physiologist Paolo Mascagni (1752-
1815). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## mascara
mascara, п., a cosmetic preparation for coloring
the eyelashes. — Sp. mascara, 'a mask', fr.
Arab. mdskharah, 'mockery; buffoon'. See mask.

## mascle
mascle, п., I) a steel plate; 2) a lozenge voided
{her.) — OF. mascle (F. made), fr. L. macula,
'spot'. See maekle, made.

## mascot
mascot, п., talismao, charm. —■ F. mascotte,
popularized by Audran's operette La Mascotte
(1880). F. mascotte is a loan word fr. Proveng.
mascoto, 'sorcery, charm', fr. masco, 'sorceress,.
witch', which is of uncertain origin.

## masculine
masculine, adj. — ME. mascalin, fr. OF. (= F.)
masculin (fem. masculine), 'of the male sex', fr.
masculus, 'male', fr. mas, 'male', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. emasculate.
Derivatives: masculine, п., masculine-ness, п.,
masculin-ity, n.

## maser
maser,n.—Coined from the initials of Microwave
amplification (by) Stimulated amission (of)
Radiation.

## mash
mash, п., crushed malt soaked in warm water to
form wort. — OE. mdsc-, max-, 'mash', in
mascwyrt, maxwyrt, 'mashwort, infused malt',
rel. to ME. maskefat, 'mashvaf, Swed. mask,
MHG. metschy G. Maisch, Maische, 'crushed
grapes', OE- meox, OS. mehsy mist, OHG.,
MHG., G. mist, Goth, maihstus, 'dung, filth*,
fr. I.-E. base *meigh-, 'to sprinkle', whence also
OI. mihati, 'urinates*, Gk. όμείχειν, later form
όμΐχεΐν, L. meiere, mingere, 'to urinate', Russ.
mezga, Pol. miazga, 'sap'. See micturition and
cp. mistletoe, mixen. Cp. also mush, 'a thick,
soft mass'.
Derivative: mash, tr, v., 1) to convert into a
mash; 2) to change into a soft mass.

## mash
mash, tr. v., to make love to; intr. v., to flirt. —
Fr. mash, 'to convert into a mash', etc. See prec.
word.
Derivative: mash-er, n.

## mashie
mashie, mashy, п., an iron golf club. — Prob. fr.
F. massue, 'club', fr. VL. *mattiuca, fr. *mat-
tia, which is rel. to L. mateola, 'a tool for
digging'. See mace, 'a staff', and cp. masse, mattock.

## masjid
masjid, п., a mosque. — Arab. See mosque.

## mask
mask, n. — MF. (~ F) masque, fr. ML. masca.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:475 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. It. maschera, fr. Arab, maskhara , 'mockery;
buffoon', fr. sakhira, 'he mocked, ridiculed'.
Cp. masque, masquerade.
Derivatives: mask, tr. and intr. v., mask-ed, adj.,
mask-er, п., mask-ette, n.

## maskery
maskery, masquery, n. — F. masquerie, fr.
masquer, 'to mask', fr. masque. See mask and -ery.

## maskelynite
maskelynite, п., a feldspar mineral {mineral.) —
Named after the English mineralogist Nevil
StOTy-Maskelyne (1823-1911). For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## maskinonge
maskinonge, n. — See miiskellunge.

## maslin
maslin, п., a kind of brass {obsol.) — ME., fr.
OE. mxstling, maesling, mxslin, rel. to MDu.,
MHG. messinc, missinc, Du. messing, G.
Messing, 'brass'. These Teut. words, as well as
Czech mosaz, Slovak mosadz, Pol. mosiqdz,
'brass', ult. derive fr. Gk. Μοσσύνοικος χαλκός,
'brass made by the Mossynoikoi', a people
living south of the Euxine, lit. 'those dwelling in
μόσσυνες (i.e. wooden houses)'. Brass is said
to have been first manufactured by the
Mossynoikoi, whence the name Μοσσύνοικος χαλκός.

## maslin
maslin, п., a mixture of different kinds of grain.
— ME. mastlyoun, mestlyon, fr. OF. mesteillon,
mestillon, fr. mestueil, mesteil (F. meteil), fr.
VL. *mistilium, which was formed from the
adjective *mistilis, fr. *mistus, a collateral form
of L. mixtus, pp. of miscere, 'to mix'. See mix.

## masochism
masochism, п., a form of sexual perversion in
which one finds pleasure in being hurt {med.)\
the opposite of sadism. — Named after the
Austrian novelist Leopold Sacher Masoch
(1836-95), who describes it in one of his works.
For the ending see suff. -ism.

## masochist
masochist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: masochist-ic, adj.

## mason
mason, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) maQon, fr.
Frankish *makjo, Latinized into machio, from
the verb *makon, *to make'. See make and cp.
freemason.
Derivatives: mason, tr. v., mason-ic, adj.,
masonry, n.

## masonite
masonite, п., a variety of chloritoid {mineral.) —
Named after Owen Mason of Providence,
Rhode Island. For the ending see subst. suff.
-Ite.

## Masornh
Masornh, also Masora, п., the system of notes
on the external form of the text of the Hebrew
Bible.( — Mishnaic Heb. masorah, a collateral
form of masoreth in masoreth habberfth, 'the
bond of the covenant' (Ezek. 20:37). The word
masoreth is prob. contracted fr. *ma,asoreth
and is formed with instr. pref. ma- fr. asar, 'he
bound*. Later, however, the word masora1* was
explained as the summary of traditions
concerning the correct writing and reading of the
Bible, and, accordingly, was regarded as a
derivative of the verb masar, 'he handed down,
handed over*.
Derivatives: Masor-ete, п., Masor-etic, Masor·
etic-al, adjs.

## masque
masque, п., 1) a masquerade; 2) a kind of
dramatic performance. — F. masque. See mask.

## masquerade
masquerade, п., an assembly of persons wearing
masks. — F. mascarade, fr. Sp. mascarada,
prop, 'a ball at which masks are worn', fr.
mascara, 'mask'. See mask and -ade, and cp.
mascara.
Derivatives: masquerade, intr. v., masquerad-er,
n.

## Mass
Mass, п., celebration of the Eucharist {Latin
Church).— ME. messe, masse, fr. OE. mxsse, fr.
VL. *messa, for Eccles. L. missa, prop. fem.
pp. of mittere, 'to send'; so called from the
words of dismissal at the endof the service: Ite,
missa est (scil. ecclesia), 'Go, (the congregation)
is dismissed'. See mission and cp. mess, missal
and the second element in kermess, Christmas,
Lammas, Michaelmas.

## mass
mass, п., quantity, size. — ME. masse, fr. OF.
(= F.) masse, fr. L. massa, 'that which adheres
together like dough, lump, mass', fr. Gk. μάζα,
μάζα, 'barley cake, lump, mass, ball', which is
rel. to μάσσειν, 'to knead'. See macerate and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: mass, v. (q.v.), mass-y, adj,, mass-i-
ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:475 COLUMN:3 -->

## mass
mass, tr. and intr. v. — F. masser, fr. masse. See
mass, n.

## massacre
massacre, п., indiscriminate killing. — F., fr.
earlier macacre, re], to OF. macecley macecre,
'shambles, butchery'; of uncertain origin.

## massage
massage, n. — F. massage, fr. masser, 'to
massage', fr. Arab, massa, 'he felt, touched', which
is rel. to Heb. mdshash, 'he felt, touched',
mishshesh, 'he felt through, groped*, Aram.
mashshesh, 'he felt through, groped', Ethiop.
marsasay 'he felt, touched', Akkad. mashashu,
'to smear over, spread over*. The practice of
massage has come to Europe from the East and
consisted originally in the simple touching of
the superficial parts of the body. This word has
nothing to do with Gk. μάσσειυ, 'to knead',
with which it is connected by most
lexicographers. For the ending see suff. -age.
Derivatives: massage, tr. v., massag-er, п.,
massag-isi, n.

## massasauga
massasauga, п., a small kind of rattlesnake. —
Fr. Missisauga, name of a river and Indian tribe
in Ontario.

## masse
masse, п., stroke in billiards made with the cue
held perpendicularly. — F. masse, pp. of
masser, 'to strike with the cue held perpendicularly',
fr. mace, 'club'. See mace, 'a staff', and cp.
mashie.

## massebah
massebah, п., stone pillar. — Heb. matztzebhah,
'pillar', from stem n-tz-bh, 'to stand, set, place',
whence also nitztzabh, 'he stationed himself,
took his stand, stood', hitztztbh, 'he stationed,
placed, set up, erected', nitztzabh, 'handle (of a
knife or sword); prefect, deputy', netztbh,
'pillar; prefect', matztzdbh, 'station, position;
garrison, post, outpost' (lit. 'place where one
stands'), rel. to Aram. netzabh, 'he set up,
erected, planted', Arab, nasaba, 'he set up, erected',
nasb, 'something set up; sign, mark, waymark',
nisdb, 'handle (of a knife)', nusub, 'statue
graven image, idol', mdnsab, 'place where
something is set up, origin, rank, dignity',
Akkad. nasabati, 'pillars'.

## masseter
masseter, п., either of a pair of muscles used in
mastication {anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
μασητήρ, incorrectly spelled also μασσητήρ,
'chewer', fr. μασάομαι (for *μαθιάομαί), Ί
chew, bite', which is rel, to μάθυί,αι, 'jaw',
μαστάζει,ν, 'to chew', μαστιχαν, 'to gnash the
teeth', μαστίχη, 'mastic', lit, 'chewing gum'.
See masticate and cp. mastic. In its anatomical
sense as name of a muscle of the lower jaw, lit.
'the chewing muscle', the word was first used by
Hippocrates. See Joseph Hyrtl, Onomatologia
Anatomica, p. 314.

## masseur
masseur, п., a man who practices massage. — F.,
formed fr. masser, 'to massage', with suff. -eur,
representing L. -or. See massage, and agential
suff. -or.

## masseuse
masseuse, п., a woman who practices massage. —
F., fem. of masseur. See prec. word.

## massicot
massicot, п., yellow oxide of lead. — ME. mas-
ticote, fr. MF. (= F.) massicot, fr. It. marza-
catto, 'potter's varnish', fr. Sp. mazacote, 'kali,
mortar; dry, tough mass', which is of uncertain
origin. It is perh. an alteration of Arab, shabb
qubtt, 'Coptic alum' (see Lokotsch, EW. No.
1735); influenced in form by Sp. masa, 'dough;
mass'.

## massif
massif, п., a compact group of mountains
forming a unit {physical geogr.) — F., prop, subst.
use of the adjective massif. See next word.

## massive
massive, adj.—- ME. massiffe, fr. MF. (= F.)
massif (fem. massive), 'massive, massy, bulky,
solid', fr. masse. See mass, 'quantity, size', and
-ive and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: massive-ly, adv., massive-ness, n.

## mast
mast, п., a long pole. — ME., fr. OE. mxst, rel.
to ON. mastr, MDu. maste, Du., OHG., MHG.,
G. mast, and cogn. with L. mdlus (which stands
for *mados, *mazdos), 'mast', Olr. matan, 'club',
Ir. maide, 'a stick', OSlav. mostu, 'bridge'. Cp.
Malus, 'name of a constellation'.
Derivatives: mast, tr. v., mast-ing, n.

## mast
mast, п., fruit of the beech, etc. — ME. maste,
mast, fr. OE. maest, rel. to Du., OHG., MHG.,
G. mast, 'mast', OE. msestan, Du.( OHG.,
MHG., mesten, 'to fatten, feed', and cogn. with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:476 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 449 | MATHEMATICAL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:476 COLUMN:1 -->
ΟΙ. midah, 'fat, marrow', madati, madate, 'is
drunk', fr. I.-E. base *mdd-, 'wet, moist,
dripping; to drip (esp. with fat)'. See meat and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the second
element in durmast.

## mast-
mast-, form of masto- before a vowel.

## mastaba
mastaba, mastabah, п., an ancient Egyptian tomb,
— Arab. mastabah.

## mastectomy
mastectomy, п., surgical removal of a breast. —
Compounded of mast- and Gk. -εκτομία, 'a
cutting out of*, fr, έκτομή, 'a cutting out'. See
-ectomy.

## master
master, n. — ME. maistre, fr. OE. maegester and
OF. maistre (F. maitre). Both OE. msegester and
OF. maistre derive fr. L. magister, 'master,
chief, head, leader', whence also It. maestro,
Ruman. maestru, OProveng., Catal. maestre,
Sp. maestro, Port, mestre. L. magister stands for
*mag-is-teros, which is formed with double
comparative surf, from the stem of L. magnus,
'great'. For the compar. suflf. -is cp, L. magis,
'more', which is rel. to magnus, 'great'; for the
compar. suff. *-teros see -ther; for the use of the
double compar. suff. in L. magister cp. minister.
OHG. meistar (whence MHG., G. meister), OS.
mistar, OCo. maister, W. meistr, etc. are Latin
loan words. See mickle and cp. maguum,
megalo-. Cp. also magisterial, magistrate,
maestro, mister» mistral.
Derivatives: master, tr. v., master-ful, adj.,
master-ful-ly, adv., master-ful-ness, п., master-
hood, п., master-ly, adj. and adv., master-li-ness,
n.

## masterpiece
masterpiece, n. — Loan translation of G. Meis-
terstuck, which is compounded of Meister,
'master', and Stuck, 'piece'. See master and
piece.

## mastery
mastery, n. — ME. maistrie, fr. OF. maistrie, fr.
maistre, 'master'. See master a°d -y
(representing OF. -ie) and cp. the second element in
palmistry.

## mastic
mastic, п., resin obtained from certain trees. —
ME. mastik, fr. OF. mastic, fr. VL. mastichum,
fr. Gk. μαστίχη, 'mastic'. See masticate and cp.
almaciga.
Derivative: mastfc-tc, adj.

## masticable
masticable, adj. — Formed with suff. -able fr.
Late L. masticare. See next word.
Derivative: masticabil-ity, n.

## masticate
masticate, tr. v., to chew. — Late L. masticatus,
pp. of masticare, 'to chew' (whence also OF.
maschier, F. macher), fr. Gk. μαστιχαν, 'to
gnash the teeth', which is re], to μαστίχη,
'mastic', lit. 'chewing gum', and to μαστάζείν, 'to
chew", μάστας, 'jaws, mouth' (lit. 'that with
which one chews'); a morsel' (lit. 'that which is
chewed*), μασάομαι (for *μαθιάομα!.), 'i
chew, bite', and prob. cogn. with L. mandere,
'to chew", Goth, munps, OE. mud, 'mouth'. See
mouth and verba] suff. -ate and cp. mastic. Cp.
also mandible.
Derivatives: masticat-or, п., masticat-ory, adj.
and n.

## mastication
mastication, n. — Late L. masticdtio, gen. -onis,
'chewing, mastication', fr. masticatus, pp. of
masticare. See masticate and -ion.

## mastiff
mastiff, n. — ME. mastif, fr. OF. mastin (whence
F. matin), fr. VL. *md(n)suetinus, 'tamed', fr.
L. mdnsueius, of s.m., pp. of mansuescere, 'to
lame'; see mansnete. The ending of E. mastiff'is
due to a confusion with OF. mestif, 'mongrel'.

## mastitis
mastitis, п., inflammation of a breast (med.) —
Medical L., coined by Konig fr. Gk. μαστός,
'breast'» and suff. -ΐτις. See masto- and -itis.

## masto-
masto-, before a vowel mast-, combining form
meaning "breast'. — Gk. μαστό-, μαστ-, fr.
μαστός, 'breast', which prob. stands for *μαδ-
τός and derives from the stem of μαδαν, 'to be
wet, to flow', fr. I.-E. base *mdd-, 'wet, moist,
dripping'. See mast, 'fruit of the beech', and cp.
prec. word, mastoid, ma го-, 'breast', amastia,
bimastism.

## mastodon
mastodon, п., an extinct elephantlike mammal. —
ModL., compounded of mast· and Gk οδών,
gen. οδόντος, 'tooth' (see odonto-); so called
from the nipple-shaped projections on the
molar teeth.

## mastodontic
mastodontic, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:476 COLUMN:2 -->
mastodon. — See prec. word and -ic.

## mastoid
mastoid, adj., resembling a breast or nipple. —
Gk. μαστοειδής, compounded of μαστός,
'breast*, and -οε^δής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See masto- and -oid.
Derivative: mastoid, п., the mastoid process or
bone.

## masturbate
masturbate, intr. v., to practice onanism. — L.
masturbdtus, pp. of mdsturbari, 'to masturbate',
prob. from *man-stuprare, for тапй stuprare,
'to defile oneself with the hand', fr. тапй, abl.
of /nanus, 'hand', and stuprare, 'to defile
oneself, fr. stuprum, 'defilement, dishonor,
disgrace4. See manual, stuprum, and verba] suff.
-ate. The ending of L. mdsturbari is due to a
popular connection of the word with L. rurbdre,
'to disturb, agitate, confuse'. See Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW-, II, 48 s.v. masturbor.
Derivatives: masturbat-ic, adj., masturbat-ion,
п., masturbat-ion-al, adj., masturbat-or, п.,
masturbat-ory, adj.

## masurium
masurium, п., name of a chemical element; now
called technetium (chem.) — ModL., named by
its discoverers, the German chemists Walter
Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg, after Masu-
ria, a district in East Prussia; so called by them,
because the platinum ore, from which it was
first extracted, occurs frequently in this district.

## mat
mat, п., a coarse fabric made of straw, hemp,
rushes, etc. — ME. matte, fr. OE. matt, fr. Late
L. matta, 'mat made of rushes' (whence also
OHG. matta, MHG., G. matte), fr. Phoen.-
Punic mafta, corresponding to Heb. mittah,
'bed', which is formed from the stem of natd ,
'he bent' (for sense development cp. Gk. κλίνη,
'bed', fr. κλίνειν, 'to bend'). From Late L.
nana, a secondary form of Late L. matta, which
occurs in the writings of Gregoire de Tours,
derives F. natte, 'mat, matting'. For the change
of Heb.-Punic initial m to я ср. F. nappe,
'tablecloth*, fr. L. riappa, which derives fr. Heb.-
Punic mappd (see napery, napkin).
Derivatives: mat, tr. v., to cover with a mat or
mats, matt-ed, adj., matt-ed-ly, adv., matt-ed-
ness, п., matting (q.v.)

## mat
mat, adj., dull (said of color or a surface). — F.,
'dull, lusterless, unpolished', fr. OF. mat,
'defeated, afflicted, depressed, dejected; dull', fr.
Arab, mat in the sentence mat ash-shah, 'the
king has died'. The word mat, orig. used only
as a term of chess, gradually developed also the
meanings 'faint, feeble, dull-colored'. See
checkmate and cp. matador, mate, adj.

## matador
matador, п., 1) the man who kills the bull in the
bullfight; 2) one of the three chief cards in the
game of ombre and quadrille. — Sp., 'killer,
murderer', fr. matar, 'to kill, murder', fr. Arab.
mata, 'he died'. Cp. checkmate. Cp. also mat,
'dull'.

## matamata
matamata, п., a freshwater turtle, Chelys fim-
briata. — Port, matamata, fr. Tupi. matamatd.

## match
match, п., an equal.—ME. macche, fr, OE. тзесс.а,
ge-mxcca, 'one suited to another, one of a pair,
mate', fr. mac-ian, 'to make'. Cp. OHG. gi-
mah (п.), 'comfort, advantage', MHG. ge-
mach, 'comfort, ease', OHG. gi-mah (adj.),
'suitable, comfortable', MHG. ge-mach,
'comfortable, quiet', G. ge-mach, 'easy, leisurely',
and see make, v. For formation cp. batch, fr.
bake.
Derivatives: match, tr. and intr. v., match-less,

## adj
adj,, match-less-ly, adv., match-less-ness, n.

## match
match, п., 1) wick or cord for firing a gun; 2) a
slender piece of wood tipped with a substance
that catches fire by friction. — ME. macche, fr.

## OF. mesche (F.meche)
OF. mesche (F.meche), 'wick' (of acandle, lamp,

## etc.)
etc.), match, fuse', fr. VL. *micca, which is a
blend of L. myxa (fr. Gk. .μύξα), 'wick of a

## lamp'
lamp', and L. mucus, 'slime from the nose'.
See my со-, mucus.
Derivative: match, tr. v,

## matchet
matchet, n. — A var. of machete,

## mate
mate, tr. v., to checkmate; to overcome. — ME.

## maten
maten, fr. OF. mater, 'to checkmate; to defeat,

## overcome'
overcome', fr. mat, 'checkmated; defeated,

## overcome'. See cp. mat
overcome'. See cp. mat, 'dull'.

## mate
mate, n„ checkmate. —ME. mat, fr. MF., fr. OF.
See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:476 COLUMN:3 -->

## mate
mate, п., a companion. — ME., fr. MLG. mate,
mat, 'companion', orig. 'a messmate', whence
also Du. moat; cp. Dan., Swed. mat, OHG.
gimazzo, MHG. gema$se, 'messmate', G. Maat,
'mate'; fr. Teut. base *mati-, 'food', whence
also E. meat (q.v.) See also matelote.
Derivatives: mate, tr. and intr. v., mate-less, adj.

## mate
mate, п., \) paraguay tea; 2) the plant from which
it is made. — Sp. mate, fr. Quichua mati, prop.
'calabash, a vessel made of calabash', hence
also 'a vessel in which mate" is made'.

## matelasse
matelasse, adj., woven in a manner suggestive of
quilting. — F., pp. of matelasser, 'to stuff, pad,
cushion', fr. matelas, "mattress, pad, cushion'.
See mattress.

## matelasse
matelasse, п., a matelasse fabric. — Fr. prec.
word.

## matelote
matelote, п., a dish of fish. — F., fr. matelot.
'sailor', fr. MF. matenot, a loan word fr. MDu,
mattenoot, which is rel. to ON. motunautr,
MHG. masgenose, lit. 'messmate'. For the first
element in these words see mate, 'companion'.
The second element is rel. to ON. nautr, OE.
geneat, OS. ginot, OFris. ndt, OHG. ginJj,
gino^o, MHG. genos, G. Genosse, 'mate,
companion'. These words orig. meant 'one who
shares cattle with others'. They are rel. to ON.
naut, OE. neat, 'ox, cattle'; see neat, n. Cp.
matross.

## mater
mater, n. 1) mother (colloq.); 2) either of the two
membranes of the brain (pia mater and dura
mater). — L. mater, 'mother'. See mother,

## materfamilias
materfamilias, п., the mother of a family. — L.
mater familids, compounded of mater, 'mother',
and familids, ancient gen. of familia, 'family'.
See mater and family and cp. paterfamilias.

## material
material, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. mdteridlis, 'of
matter', fr. L. materia, 'wood, timber, stuff,
matter'. See matter and cp. materiel.
Derivatives: material, п., material-ism, п.,
materialist, п., material-ist-ic, adj., material-ist-ic-
al-ly, adv., material-ity, п., material-ize, tr. and
intr. v., material-iz-ation, п., material-ly, adv.,
material-ness, n.

## materia medica
materia medica, 1) substances used in medicine;
2) that branch of medicine which deals with the
properties of drugs and with their application
in the cure of diseases. — Med. L., lit. 'medical
matter'. See matter and medical,

## materiel
materiel, п., material equipment. — F., from the
adj. materiel, 'material, physical', fr. Late L.
materidlis. See material.

## maternal
maternal, adj. — ME., fr. MF- (= F.) materne/,
fr. L. maternus, 'of a mother*, fr. mater. See
mother and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: maternal-ity, п., maternal-ly, adv.,
maternal-ness, n.

## maternity
maternity, п., motherhood. — F. mater nite, fr.
MF., fr. L. mdternitatem, ace. of mdternitds,
'motherhood1, fr. maternus. See prec. word and
-ity.

## matey
matey, adj., friendly (British colloq.) — Formed
with suff. -y fr. mate, 'companion*,

## math
math, п., a mowing. — ME. *math, fr. OE. mxp,
'harvest, crop', rel. to OFris. meth, OHG. mad,
MHG. mat, G. Mahd, 'a mowing', fr. Teut.
*mdpa-, lit. 'that which is wown', pp. form of
I.-E. base *me-, *тё-, 'to mow'. See mow, 'to
cut (grass)', and cp. aftermath. Cp. also meadow.

## mathematic
mathematic, adj., mathematical (now rare). —
See next word.

## mathematical
mathematical, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. F.mathematique, fr. Gk. μάθηματί,κός,
'scientific, mathematical', fr. μάθημα, 'that which is
learned, learning, science', from the aorist
μαθεΐν (whence the pres. μαυθάνεω), *to learn',
fr. *mndh-, reduced form of I.-E. base *men-dh-,
'to have one's mind aroused, apply oneself
to'. From the same base (resp. its reduced form)
prob. derive Gk. μενθήρη, 'care', Lith. man-

## dras
dras, mandrus, 'wide-awake', OSlav. mqdru,
'wise, sage', Goth, mundon sis, 'to look at*, ON,

## munda
munda, 'to aim', OHG. mendan, 'to rejoice',

## OHG. muntar
OHG. muntar, MHG. munter, munder, 'eager,

## agile
agile, nimble', G. munter, 'awake, lively, gay,

## merry
merry, vigorous', W. mynnu, 'to want, wish',

## Alb. mund
Alb. mund, Ί can, I am, victorious', and

## possibly also OI. medha
possibly also OI. medha, 'wisdom, intelligence', Gk.

Μοϋσα (if fr. *M6v»loc ), 'Muse'. Base
"men-Mis an enlargement of base *men-, 'to think'.
See mind and cp. Muse, Epimetheus,
Prometheus. Cp. also the second element in chresto-
mathy, opsimath, polymath. Cp. also the second
element in Ormazd.
Derivative: mathematical-ly, adv.

## mathematician
mathematician, n. — F. mathematicien, fr. mathe-
matique. See prec. word and -ian.

## mathematico-
mathematico-, combining form meaning
'mathematical and'. — See next word.

## mathematics
mathematics, n. — F. mathematique, fr. L. mathi-
matica, fr. Gk. μαθηματική (scil. τέχνη"),
'mathematical art', fern, of μαθηματικός,
'scientific, mathematical'. See mathematical and
-ics.

## mathematize
mathematize, tr. and intr. v. — See prec. word
and -ize.

## Mathilda
Mathilda, fern. PN. — See Matilda.

## matico
matico, п., 1) a Peruvian shrub; 2) a styptic made
from its leaves. — Sp., fr. Matico, dimin. of
Mateo, 'Matthew'. See Matthew.

## Matilda
Matilda, Mathilda, fern. PN. — F. Matkilde, of
Teut. origin and lit. meaning 'mighty in battle'.
Cp. OHG. Mahthitda, compounded of mahti,
'might, power', and kildi, 'battle'. For the first
element see might, for the second cp. Hilda and
words there referred to. Cp. Maud.

## matildite
matildite, п., a silver bismuth sulfide (mineral.) —
Named after Matilda mine, near Morococha,
Peru. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## matin
matin, п., 1) morning song esp. of birds; 2) (pi.)
the first of the seven canonical hours; 3) (pi.)
morning service of the Church of England. —
F., 'morning', fr. L. mdtutinum (short for ma·
tutinum tempus, 'morning time'), neut. of mdtu-
tinus, 'of the morning' See matutinal and cp.
matinee.
Derivatives: matin, adj., matin-al, adj.

## matinee
matinee, п., afternoon performance. —■ F.
matinee, fr. matin. See matin.

## matlockite
matlockite, п., lead oxychloride {mineral.) —
Named after Matlock in Derbyshire, England.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## matra
matra, п., an Indian unit of measure. — OI.
mdtram (neut.), matra (fern.), 'measure', fr.
mati (fr. I.-E. *me-li), 'measures', fr. I.-E. base
'me-, 'to measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm',
and cp. words there referred to.

## matranee
matranee, п., a female sweeper; a female servant
(India). — Hind, mehtarana, mehtrdni, fr. Pers.
mihtardni, 'female sweeper', fern, of mihtar,
'sweeper'. See mehtar.

## matrass
matrass, п., a glass vessel with a long neck. — F.
matras, prob. fr. Arab, matara , 'leathern bottle,
skin, vase'.

## matri-
matri-, combining form meaning 'mother'. — L.
matri-, from the stem of mater, gen. matris,
'mother'. See mater.

## matriarch
matriarch, п., a mother who rules her family or
tribe. — Formed fr. matri- on analogy of
patriarch (q.v.)
Derivatives: matriarch-al, adj., matriarch-ate,
п., matriarch-ic, adj., matriarch-y, n.

## Matricaria
Matricaria, п., a genus of plants, the wild
camomile (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. matrix, 'womb' (see
matrix); so called for the reputed medicinal
value. For the ending see suff. -ia.

## matricidal
matricidal, adj. — See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## matricide
matricide, п., one who kills his mother. — L. ma~-
tricida, compounded of matri- and -clda, 'killer',
fr. caedere, 'to kill'. See -olde, 'killer'.

## matricide
matricide, п., the act of killing one's own mother.
— L. mdtricldium, compounded of matri- and
-cidium, 'killing', fr. caedere, 'to kill'. See -cide,
'killing'.

## matricular
matricular, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr.
Late L. matricula. See matriculate.

## matriculate
matriculate, tr. and intr. v. — i-ate L. mdtriculd-
tus, pp. of mdtricu'.dre, 'to register', fr. L.
matricula, 'register', dimin. of L. matrix, gen.
mdtricis. See matrix, and -ule and verbal suff,-ate.
Derivatives: matriculat-ion, п., matriculat-or, п.,
matriculat-ory, adj.
matrilinea], adj., pertaining to, or descended
from, the maternal line. — Compounded of L.
mater, gen. matris, 'mother', and linea, 'line'.
See mother, line and adj. suff. -al.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:477 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: matrilineal-ly, adv.

## matrimonial
matrimonial, adj. — MF. (== F.), fr. Late L. ma-
trimonidlis, fr. L. mdtrimonium. See next word
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: matrimoniat-ty, adv.

## matrimony
matrimony, п., I) wedlock; 2) a card game. —
ME. matrimoine, matrimony, fr. OF. matre-
moine, matrimoine, fr. L. mdtrimonium,
'marriage, matrimony', formed fr. mater, gen. matris,
'mother', with suff. -monium. See mother and
-mony.

## matrix
matrix, п., womb. — L. matrix, 'womb, matrix,
source, origin', formed fr. mater, gen. matris,
'mother', on analogy of tiutrix, 'wet-nurse,
nurse'. See mother. For the sense development
of L. matrix (fr. mater, 'mother') cp. Gk. μήτρ ά,
'uterus, womb', which derives fr. μήτηρ,
mother', and OHG. muodar, 'belly' (whence G.
Mieder, 'bodice'), which is rel. to OHG. muoter,
'mother' (cp. metralgia).

## matron
matron, п., a married woman. — ME. matrone,
fr. MF. (= F.) matrone, fr. L. mdtrona,
'a married woman, wife, matron', fr. mater,
'mother'; see mother. For the formation of the
word cp. L. patronus, 'protector, patron', fr.
pater, 'father' (see patron) and Bellona, 'the
goddess of war', fr. beltum, 'war' (see Bellona).
Derivatives: matron-age, п., matronal (q.v.),
matron-hood, п., matron-ize, tr. v., matron-like,
adj. matron-ly, adj., matron-li-ness, n.

## matronal
matronal, adj. — L. matronal is, 'of, or belonging
to, a married woman', fr. matrona. See matron
and adj. suff. -al.

## matross
matross, п., soldier in a train of artillery (hist.)
Du. matroos, corruption of F. matelots, pi. of
matelot, fr. MF. matenot, which itself is
borrowed fr. MDu. mattenoot, lit., 'messmate'. See
matelote.

## mattamore
mattamore, п., a subterranean dwelling or
storehouse. — F. matamore, fr. Arab, matmura',
'something hidden', prop. fern. pass. part, of
tamara, 'he hid, concealed', fr. Aram. / mar, of
s.m. See Siegmund Fraenkel, Die aramaischen
Fremdworter im Arabischen, p. 137. Aram.
fmar is rel. to Heb. tamdn, 'he hid, concealed'
(whence matmSn, 'treasure', lit. 'something
hidden'), Akkad. tamaru, 'to cover with earth'.

## matter
matter, n. — ME. matere, fr. OF. matere (F. ma-
tiere), fr. L. materia, 'wood, timber, stuff,
matter', formed fr. L. mater, 'mother', as
translation of Gk. ϋλη, 'wood, forest, timber, stuff,
matter'. See mother and cp. Madeira, madrier.
L. materia is not cogn. with Arm. mair, 'pine,
cedar', mairi, 'forest*.
Derivative: matter, intr. v.
matter of fact. — Loan translation of L. resfacti.
Cp. G. Tatsache, which is the loan translation
of E. matter of fact.
Derivative: matter-of-fact, adj.

## Matthew
Matthew, masc. PN. — F. Mathieu, fr. Late L.
Matthaeus, fr. Gk. Ματθαίος, fr. Ματθίας,
contraction of Ματταθίϊς, fr. Heb. Mattiyydh,
shortened form of Mattithyah, Mattithyahu, lit.
'gift of the Lord'. For the first element cp. Heb.
mallath, 'gift', and see Nathan, for the second
see Elijah and cp. words there referred to. The
form Ματθαίος is due to change of suff. Cp.
Matthias. Cp. also matico.

## Matthias
Matthias, n. — Late L., fr. Gk. Ματθίας, fr.
Heb. Mattiyydh. See Matthew.

## mattock
mattock, n. — ME. mattok, fr. OE. mattuc, fr.
VL. *matteuca, which is rel. to L. mateola,
'mallet'. See mace, 'a staff', and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivative: mattock, tr. v.

## mattoid
mattoid, п., a person of abnormal mind verging
on insanity. — It. mattoide, a hybrid coined fr.
It. matto, 'mad', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'shape, form'. The first element derives

## fr. L. mattus
fr. L. mattus, intoxicated', fr. mad(i)dus, 'moist,
wet; drunk, intoxicated', fr. madere, 'to be wet;

## to be drunk or intoxicated'
to be drunk or intoxicated', fT. I.-E. base mad-,
'wet, moist, dripping; to drip'. See meat and cp.

## mast
mast, 'fruit of beech'. For the second element in
mattoid see -oid.

## mattress
mattress, n. — ME. materas, fr. OF. materas (F.

## matelas)
matelas), fr. It. materasso, borrowed in Sicily fr.

## Arab
Arab, mdtrah, 'place where something is thrown

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:477 COLUMN:3 -->
or laid', used also in the sense of 'mattress' (see
Dozy-Engelmann, Glossaire des mots espagnols
et portugais derives de I'arabe, p. 151); fr.
laraha, 'he threw'. Cp. Sp. almadraque,
'mattress', which is formed fr. Arab, al-, 'the' and
mdtrah, 'mattress' (see above). Cp. also mate-
lasse. Cp. also E. tare, 'allowance in weight'.

## maturate
maturate, tr. v., to make mature or ripe; to cause
to suppurate; intr. v., to ripen; to suppurate. —
L. mdturdtus, pp. of mdturdre, 'to ripen', fr. md-
turus. See mature, adj., and verbal suff. -ate.

## maturation
maturation, n. — F., fr. L. mdtiirdtionem, ace. of
maturdtio, 'a ripening', fr. mdturatus, pp. of
mdturdre. See prec. word and -ion.

## maturative
maturative, adj., promoting ripeness; promoting
suppuration. — F. maturatif (fern, maturative),
fr. L. mdturdtivus, 'tending to ripen', fr.
mdturatus, pp. of mdturdre. See maturate.

## mature
mature, adj., ripe. — L. mdturus, 'ripe', which is
rel. to mdnus, 'good' (whence immanis,
'monstrous'), manes, 'ghosts, the gods of the Lower
World', lit. 'the good gods', mane, 'early in the
morning', Mdluta, 'the goddess of dawn',
mdtutinus, 'of, or pertaining to, the morning'. All
these Words derive from base *md-, 'sood;
early*, whence possibly also Olr. maith, 'good',
W. mad, Co. mas, of s.m. See manes and cp.
demure, immanity, тайапа, matinee, Matuta,
matutinal.
Derivatives: maturate (q.v.), maturation (q.v.),
maturative (q.v.), mature-ly, adv., mature-ness,
п., mature, v. (q.v.), matur-er, п., maturescent
(q.v.), matur-ing, п., maturity (q.v.)

## mature
mature, tr. v., to cause to ripen; intr. v., to ripen.
— OF. maturer, fr. L. mdturdre, 'to ripen', fr.
mdturus. See mature, adj.

## maturescence
maturescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## maturescent
maturescent, adj., becoming ripe. — L. mdture-
scens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of mdturescere, 'to
become ripe, to ripen', formed with inchoative
suff. -escere, fr. mdturus, 'ripe'. See mature, adj.,
and -escent.

## maturity
maturity, п., ripeness. — ME. maturite, fr. L.
maturitds, 'ripeness, maturity' [prob. through
the medium of Late MF. (= F.) maturite], fr.
mdturus. See mature, adj., and -ity.

## Matuta
Matuta, п., name of the goddess of dawn in
Roman Religion. — L. Matuta (whence mdtutinus,
'of, or pertainig to, the morning'), rel. to
mdturus. See mature, adj., and cp. next word.

## matutinal
matutinal, adj., pertaining to, or happening, in
the morning. — L. mdtiitindlis, fr. mdtutinus, 'of,
or pertaining to, the morning'. See prec. word,
adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus) and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivative: matutinal-ly, adv.

## matutine
matutine, adj., matutinal. — L. mdtutinus. See
prec. word.
Derivative: matutine-ly, adv.

## matzah
matzah, also matza, matzoh, matzo, n. (pi. mat-
zoth, also matzos), a flat piece of unleavened
bread eaten by Jews during the Passover. —
Heb. matztzd1' (pi. matztzith), 'unleavened
bread', lit. 'that which is sucked out', hence
'sapless, juiceless', from the stem of mdtzatz, 'he
sucked out, drained out', which is rel. to Aram.-
Syr. metzatz, matz, 'he sucked out', Arab, mdssa,
'he sucked out', and to Heb. matza11, 'he drained
out'.

## maucherite
maucherite, п., a nickel arsenide (mineral.) —
Named after the German mineral dealer Wil-
helm Maucher (1879-1930). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## Maud
Maud, fern. PN. —OF. Mahaut, of Teut. origin.
Cp. OHG. Mahthilda and see Matilda.

## maud
maud, п., a woolen plaid worn by shepherds in
Scotland. — Prob. from the PN. Maud.

## maudlin
maudlin, adj., tearfully sentimental. — ME.
Maudlin, 'Mary Magdalene' (see Luke 8:2), fr.
OF. (= F.) Madelaine, fr. L. Magdalena, in
allusion to the fact that painters used to
represent Mary Magdalene weeping; maudlin
orig. meant 'shedding tears of penitence like
Magdalene'. See Magdalene.

## mauger
mauger, maugre, prep., in spite of (archaic). —
ME. maugrie, fr. OF. malgre, maugre (F. mat-
gre), lit. 'ill will', fr. mat, 'ill, badly', and gre

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:478 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 451 | ME -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:478 COLUMN:1 -->
(F. gre), 'will, pleasure'. For the first element
see mal-. The second element comes fr. L. gra-
tum, neut. of grams, *acceptable, pleasing,
agreeable, grateful', used as a noun. See gracet
п., and cp. malgre.

## maul
maul, mall, п., a heavy hammer. — ME. malle,
fr. OF. (= F.) mail, 'hammer', fr. L. malleus.
See malleus and cp. the second element in pall·
mall.
Derivatives: maul, mall, tr. v., maul-er, n.

## maulstick
maulstick, also mahlstick, п., a long rod used by
painters. — Du. maalstok, lit. 'painting stick*,
compounded of malen, 'to paint', and stok,
'stick'. The first element is rel. to ON. mxla,
OHG. malon, malen, MHG. malen, G. malen,
'to paint', OE. mal, 'mark, stain'; see mole,
'spot1. For the second element see stock, stick.

## maund
maund, also man, п., a unit of weight used in India,
Persia and Turkey. — Hind, and Pers. man,
'mina', fr. OI. mana, which is of Sem. origin.
See mina, 'unit of weight'.

## maund
maund, п., a hand basket. — ME. maund fr. MF.
mancfe, fr. MDu. mande (Du. mand), 'basket'.
Cp. F. manne, 'hand basket', which derives fr.
MDu. manne, a var. of mande.

## maund
maund, tr. and intr. v., to beg (slang). — Prob. fr.
F. mendier, 'to beg', fr. L. mendicare (whence
also It. mendicare, Sp., Port, mendigar). See
mendicant.

## maunder
maunder, intr. v., 1) to wander about aimlessly;
2) to mutter, mumble. — Prob. freq. of maund,
'to beg'.
Derivative: maunder-er, n.

## maundy
maundy, п., 1) ceremonial washing of the feet of
poor people; 2) distribution of alms. — ME.
maunde, fr. OF. mande, fr. L. mandatum,
'command', prop. neut. pp. of mandare, 'to commit
to one's charge' (see mandate); influenced in
form by mannd, 'basket'.

## Manndy Thursday
Manndy Thursday, п., Thursday preceding
Easter. — From prec. word.

## Maurice
Maurice, masc. PN. — F., fr. Late L. Mauritius,
Mauricius, fr. L. Maurus, 'inhabitant of Maure-
tania, Moor', fr. Gk. Μαύρος. See Moor.

## Mauser
Mauser, п., a kind of rifle. — Named after the
brothers Mauser who invented it (in the second
half of the 19th cent.)

## mausoleum'
mausoleum', п., a magnificent tomb. — L.
mausoleum, fr. Gk. Μαυσωλεΐον, 'tomb of Mausolus
(king of Caria)', fr. Μαύσωλος, 'Mausolus',
erected by his widow queen Artemisia; used
apellatively, the word denotes any magnificent
sepulchral monument.
Derivative: mausole-oiu adj.

## mauvais
mauvais, adj., false, worthless; used in French
terms (as in mauvais sujet, 'worthless fellow',
mauvaise honte, 'bashfulness', lit. 'bad shame').
— F. mauvais (fern, mauvaise), 'bad', fr. VL.
malifatius, 'who has a bad lot', which is
compounded of L. malus, 'bad', and fatum, 'fate';
see male- and fate. For the formation of the
word cp. the PN. Bonifatius, lit. 'of good luck'
(see Boniface).

## mauve
mauve, n. and adj., purple dye. — F., fr. L. mal-
va, 'mallow'. See mallow.

## maverick
maverick, п., unbranded cattle. — Named after
Samuel A. Maverick (died in 1870), a civil
engineer in Texas, in allusion to his unbranded
cattle.

## mavis
mavis, п., the song thrush. — ME. mavys, fr-
MF. (~ F.) mauvis, rel. to Sp. malvis, malviz;
of unknown origin. MBret. milhuit (whence
ModBret. milc'huid, milfid), is a French loan
word.

## mavrodaphne
mavrodaphne, п., name of a modern Greek wine.
— ModGk., lit. 'black laurel', fr. Late Gk.
μαύρος, 'black, dark', and. Gk. δάφνη, 'laurel*.
See Moor and Daphne.

## maw
maw, п., I) the stomach of an animal, specif, the
fourth stomach of a ruminant; 2) the craw or
crop of a bird; 3) the air bladder of a fish. —
ME. mawe, maugh, fr. OE, maga, rel. to OFris.
maga, ON. magi, Swed, mage, Dan. mave,
MDu. maghe, Du. maag, OHG. mago, MHG.
mage, G. Magen, 'stomach', and cogn. with W.
megin, 'bellows', and prob. also with Lith.
makas, Lett, males, OSlav. moSirta, 'bag, pouch'.
Rhaeto-Romanic magun, 'stomach', and It.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:478 COLUMN:2 -->
magone, 'crop of a bird', are Teut. loan words.

## mawkish
mawkish, adj., sickly, nauseating. — Lit.
'maggoty' ; formed with adj. suff. -ish fr. ME. mathek,
mawke (whence obsol. E. mawk), 'maggot",
alteration of ON. madkr. See maggot-
Derivatives: mawkish-ly, adv., mawkish-ness, n.

## mawworm
mawworm, п., worm infesting the stomach. —
Compounded of maw and worm.

## maxilla
maxilla, п., jaw or jawbone. — L., 'jawbone,
jaw', dimin. of mala, 'cheekbone, jawbone;
cheek'; see mala. Maxilla stands to mala as
axil/a, 'armpit', stands to ala, 'wing'.

## maxillary
maxillary, adj., pertaining to the jaw or jawbone,
— L. maxillaris, fr. maxilla. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ary.

## maxilliform
maxilliform, adj., having the form of a maxilla.
— See maxilla and -form.

## maxim
maxim, п., precept, principle. — Μ Ε.· maxime, fr.
MF. (— F.) maxime, fr. ML. maxima (short for
L. maxima sententia, 'the greatest sentence'),
fern, of maximus, 'greatest'. See maximum.

## maximal
maximal, adj., highest, greatest.«— Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. maximus. See maximum.
Derivatives: maximal-ly, adv., Maximalist(q.v.)

## Maximalist
Maximalist, п., formerly, a member of the
extreme radical group of the Russian Social
Revolutionary party. — Lit. 'one who insists on
all his demands', formed fr. L. maximus (see
maximum) and suff". -ist. Cp. Minimalist.

## Maximilian
Maximilian, masc. PN. — Compounded of the
L. names Maximus and Aemilianus. According
to Camden, Frederick III gave this name coined
by him to his son, hoping that the latter 'would
imitate the virtues' of Fabius Maximus and
Scipio Aemilianus.

## maximite
maximite, п., a synonym of cordite. — Named
after Hudson Maxim (1853-1927), its inventor.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## maximize
maximize, tr.v., to raise to the highest possible
degree. — Coined by the English philosopher
Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832) fr. L. maximus,
'greatest' (see maximum), and suff. -ize.
Derivative: maximiz-ation, n.

## maximum
maximum, n. — L., neut. of maximus, 'greatest',
for *mag-semos, superlative of, and from the
same base as magnus, 'great'. See maguum and
cp. major.

## maxwell
maxwell, п., an international magnetic unit. —
Named after the Scottish physicist James Clerk
Maxwell (1831-79).

## may
may, auxil. v. — ME. max, mei, fr. OE. mseg, Ί
am able' (inf. magan, 'to be able'), rel. to OS.
mugan, OFris. muga, ON. mega, Norw. moga,
Dan. maatte, Swed. md, MDu. moghen, Du.
tnogen, OHG. magan, mugan, MHG. mugen,
mugen, G. mogen, Goth, magan, 'to be able*, fr.
Ι.Έ. base *magh-, *megh-, 'to be able', whence
also Gk. μηχος, Dor. μαχος, 'means,
instrument', μηχανή, 'means, invention, machine',
OSlav. mogo, moSti, 'to be able', moSti, 'power;
force'. OPruss. massi, *I can', is a Teut. loan
word. See mechanic and cp. main, might,
dismay, Hogen Mogen and the first element in
Matilda.

## may
may, п., a maiden (archaic). — ME. may, mey,
fr. OE. mseg, 'woman, virgin', rel. to OE. mseged,
msegd, 'maid'. See maiden and cp. mayweed.

## May
May, п., the fifth month of the year. — ME. mai,
fr. OF. (= F.) mai, fr. L. Maius (mensis), '(the
month of) May', named after the god Maius,
whose name stands for *magjos, lit. 'he who
brings increase', and is rel. to magnus, great'.
See major, adj., and cp. Maia, Maianthemum.

## maya
maya, п., art, magic (Hinduism). — OI. maya,
'supernatural power; magic, deception, illusion',
of uncertain origin.

## Mayaca
Mayaca, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL., of
S. Amer. Indian origin.

## Mayaceae
Mayaceae, n. pi., the mayaca family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## mayaceous
mayaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## maybe
maybe, adv. — Compounded of may, auxil. v.,
and be.

## mayday
mayday, an international radiotelephone
distress signal. — F. m'aidez, 'help me', fr.
apostrophized form of me, 'me' (fr. L. me) and im-
per. of aider, to help' (fr. L. adjutare). See me
and aid, v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:478 COLUMN:3 -->

## mayhem
mayhem, п., the maiming of a person (law). —
ME. maym, fr. AF. mayhem, mahaim, 'injury',
corresponding to OF. mehaigne, makaigne, me-
haing, of s.m., fr. OF. mahaignier, 'to 'injure'.
See maim.

## mayonnaise
mayonnaise, п., a creamy sauce made of egg
yolks, oil and vinegar. — F., short for sauce
mayonnaise, for sauce mahonnaise, 'sauce of
Mahon'; so called fr. Mahon, a town on the
island of Minorca, in commemoration of the
capture of that town by the French in 1756.

## mayor
mayor, n. — ME. maire, mair, mer, fr. OF. ( = F.)
moire, fr. L. major, 'greater', compar. of magnus,
'great'. See major, adj.
Derivatives: mayor-α/, adj., mayoralty (q.v.),
mayor-ess, n.

## mayoralty
mayoralty, n. — ME. mairaltee, fr. MF. mairalte,
fr. maire, 'mayor'. See mayor, adj. suff. -al and
suff. -ty.

## mayweed
mayweed, п., the stinking camomile. — For
*maythe-weed, fr. OE. magede, magode, тзе-
gede, 'the stinking camomile', which is prob.
rel. to OE. mxged, mxgd, 'maid'; see maiden
and cp. may, 'a maiden'. For the second
element in mayweed see weed.

## mazapilite
mazapilite, п., a calcium iron arsenate (mineral.)
— Named after Mazapil, in Zacatecas, Mexico.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## mazard
mazard, п., 1) a mazer (obsol.); 2) the head or
skull (obsol.) — Altered fr. mazer.

## Mazdaism
Mazdaism, also Mazdeism, п., Zoroastrianism.
— See Ormazd and -ism.

## maze
maze, tr. v., to bewilder; to confuse. — ME.
masen, mazen, 'to confuse, puzzle', fr. OE.
masian in amasian, 'to confuse, confound',
which is rel. to OE. amasod, 'confused,
confounded', and prob. also to Norw. masast, 'to
doze off', Swed. masa, 'to be slow, be sluggish'.
Cp. amaze, mizmaze.

## maze
maze, п., a labyrinth. — ME. mase, maze, fr.
masen, mazen. See maze, v.
Derivatives: maz-y, adj., maz-i-ly, adv., maz-i-
ness,_n.

## mazer
mazer, п., a large drinking bowl. — ME. maser,
'maple wood; bowl made of maple wood', fr.
OF. masere, 'maple wood', which is of Teut.
origin. Cp. ON. mosurr, 'maple wood', mosurr
bolli, 'bowl made of maple wood', OS. masur,
'knot', MDu. maeser, 'maple wood', OHG.
masar, 'knot in maple wood' (whence MHG.,
G. maser, 'knot, excrescence in trees'). Cp.
mazard. Cp. also measles.

## mazo-
mazo-, combining form denoting the breast. —
Gk. μαζο-, fr. μαζός, 'breast'. See masto- and
cp. words there referred to.

## mazo-
mazo-, combining form used in the sense
of'placenta'. — ModL. mazo-, fr. ModL. тага,
'placenta', fr. Gk. μάζα, μάζα, 'flat barley cake',
which stands ίθΓ*μάγ-ι[α, fr. μάσσω (for *μά-
γιω), Ί squeeze, press into a mold, knead',
whence also μαγίς 'kneaded mass, cake', μα-
γεύς, 'one who kneads, baker'. See macerate and
cp. magma.

## mazuma
mazuma, п., money (U.S. Slang). — Yiddish, fr.
Mishnaic Heb. m zumman, 'designated, fixed,
appointed', used (in the pi. m zummdnfm) in
Medieval Heb. Responses in the sense of'cash'.
Mishnaic Heb. m zumman is passive part of
zimmen, 'he invited, designated, appointed,
fixed', a verb denominated fr. Heb. zeman,
'appointed time, time', which is rel. to Aram.
ζ man, Syr. ζ bhan, zabhna, Arab. zaman, za-
man, Ethiop. zaman, 'time'. All these words
derive directly or indirectly fr. Akkad. simanu,
'appointed time'.

## mazurka
mazurka, mazourkn, п., 1) a lively Polish dance;
2) music for this. — Pol. mazurka, 'a woman of
the province Mazovia (in Poland)'.

## mazzard
mazzard, п., wild sweet cherry (Prunus avium). —
Fr. earlier mazer (see mazer); so called in
allusion to the knotty appearance of the wood.

## me
me, pers. pron. — ME. me, fr. OE. me, rel. to
ΟΝ., Goth, mik, OHG. mih, G. mich, 'me' '(ace),
ON. mer, OHG., MHG., G. mir, Goth, mis,
'me' (dat.), and cogn. with OI., Avestic ma, OI.
mam, Avestic mam, OPers. mam, 'me' (ace),
OI. mahyam, 'me' (dat.), Gk. έμέ, με, L. me
(ace), Gk. έμοί, μοι,, L. mihi, Umhr. mehe, 'me*

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:479 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MEAD | 452 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:479 COLUMN:1 -->
(dat.), OSIav. me, Olr. me, Hitt. ammuk, am-
mugga, 'me' (ace.) Cp. mine, pron., my. Cp. also
meum and the first element in mayday.

## mead
mead, п., drink made of fermented honey and
water. — ME. mede, fr. OE. meodu, re], to ON.
mjodr, Dan. mjed, Swed. mjod, OFris., MLG.,
MDu. mede, Du. mee,OHG. metu, MHG. mete,
met, G.A/ef,'mead',fr.I.-E. base*meo7m-,'honey,
sweet drink', whence also Oi .mda7m,'sweet, sweet
drink, wine, honey', Toch. В mit, 'honey', Gk.
μέθυ, 'wine', μεθύειν, 'to be drunken', μέ&υσις,
'drunkenness', OSIav. medu, Lith. mediis,
'honey', Olr. mid (gen. medo), W. medd, Bret.
mez, 'mead'. Cp. methylene, amethyst.

## mead
mead, п., meadow (poetic). — ME. mede, fr. OE.
mxd, med. See meadow.

## meadow
meadow, n. — ME. medwe, medewe, fr. OE. mxd-
we, gen. of mSd (see prec. word); rel. to Du.
made, G. Matte, 'meadow', and to OE. mxp,
'harvest, crop', OHG. mad, 'a mowing', fr.
WTeut. 'тара-, lit. 'that which is mown', pp.
form of I.-E. base *me~-, *m -, 'to mow'. See
mow, 'to cut (grass)', and cp. math.
Derivative: meadow-y, adj.

## meager
meager, meagre, adj. — ME. megre, fr. OF.
maigre, magre, megre (F. maigre), fr. L. macer,
'lean, thin', which is cogn. with Gk. μακρός,
'long', OE. mxger, ON. magr, MDu. magher,
Du. mager, OHG. magar, MHG., G. mager,
'lean, thin', fr. I.-E. base *mekros, a derivative
of base *mdk-, *тёк-, 'long, thin', whence also
Avestic mas-, 'long', masah-, 'length, size'. Cp.
also—with /-surf.—Hitt. maklanza, 'thin,
meager'. Cp. emaciate, Macedonian, macro-, maigre,
mallager, meco-.
Derivatives: meager-ly, meagre-ly, adv., meager-
ness, meagre-ness, n.

## meal
meal, п., edible grain. — ME. rfele, fr. OE. melu,
rel. to OS. melo, ΟΝ., Swed., Norw. mjol, Dan.
met, OFris. mele, MDu. mele, Du. meet, OHG.
melo, MHG. met, G. Mehl, 'meal', orig. 'that
which is ground', and rel. to OS., OHG., Goth.
malan, ΟΝ., Swed. mala, Dan. male, MDu., Du.
malen, MHG. main, G. malen, 'to grind', fr.
I.-E. base *(s)mel-, 'to rub, grind', whence also
Toch. A malyw, B. mely, 'to press, tread under
foot', Hitt. mallanzi, 'they grind', miyalli, 'mill',
Arm. malem, Ί crush, bruise', Gk. μαλακός,
'soft', μύλη, later μύλος, 'mill', Alb. miel, 'meal,
flour', L. molere, 'to grind', mo/α,'millstone,
mil]', OSIav. meljp, mleti, Lith. malit, mdlti,
Lett. ma\u, malt, 'to grind', Lith. miltai, OPruss.
meltan, Lett, milti, 'meal', OSIav. moll, Goth.
mato, ON. molr, Norw. mot, Dan. mot, Swed.
mat, 'moth', OE. mselsceafa, 'malshave'
(caterpillar), OHG. miliwa, milwa, MHG. milwe, G.
Mitbe, 'mite', lit. 'a grinding, powder-making
animal', OHG. gimulli, G. Gemull, 'moldering
dust', Olr. melim, Ί grind', W. matu, Bret.

## meal
meal, п., food taken at one time. — ME. mele, fr.
OE. mxl, 'mark, sign; measure; fixed time; time
for taking food, meal', rel. to ON. mat,
'measure, time, meal', OFris. mel(tid), '(time of)
meal', Du. maal, 'time; meal', OHG., MHG.
mat, 'time; meal', G. Mai, 'time', Mahl, 'meal',
Goth, mil, 'time; hour', fr. I.-E. base *mi-, 'to
measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivative: meal, tr. v., to have a meal,
•meal, sufT. denoting quantity taken at one time;
now used only in piecemeal. — ME. -mele, fr.
OE. -mxlum, dat. pi. of OE. mxl, 'measure'.
See meal, 'food'.

## mealie
mealie, п., maize. — S. Afr. Du. milje, fr. Port.
milho, 'millet', fr. L. milium, 'millet'. See millet,

## mean
mean, tr. v., to have in mind. — ME. menen, fr.
OE. mxnan, 'to mean, signify, intend; to speak
of; to complain, mourn, moan', rel. to OS.
menian, 'to have in mind, intend, signify',
OFris, тёпа, MDu. menen, Du. menen, OHG.
meinan, meinen, MHG., G. meinen, 'to think,

mian, 'wish, desire', Ir. mian, 'intention', W.

Derivatives: mean-ing, n. and adj., meaning-ful,

## mean
mean, adj., intermediate. — ME. mene, fr. OF.

medius, 'middle'. See media, 'voiced stop
consonant', and cp. median, mesne, monial.
Derivative: mean, п., something intermediate.

## mean
mean, adj., of low rank, inferior, base. — ME.

meni, MLG. gemeine, gemene (whence Dan. and

mains, 'common', OE. man, ΟΝ., OHG. mein,
