ΟΝ., meineidr, Dan., Swed. mened, OS.,
OFris. · meneth, MDu. meineet, Du. meineed,
OHG. mei'neid, MHG. meineit, G. Meineid,
'perjury', lit. 'false oath', and cogn. with
L. munus (OL. moinos, moenus), 'service,
office, function', munia (OL. moenia), 'official,
duties, functions', communis (OL. ace. comoi-
nem), 'common', OSIav. тёпа, 'change', iz-
meniti, 'to change, exchange', Lith. maTnas,

ments of base *mei-, *moi-, 'to change,

*moi-t-, -(-enlargements of base *mei-, *moi-,

originally identical with base "met-, 'to change

## meander
meander, п., winding, as of a river. — L. Maean-
der, fr. Gk. Μαίανδρος, a river in Caria, noted
for its windings.
Derivatives: meander, intr. v., meander-ing, n.
and adj., meander-ing-ly, adv.

## measles
measles, n. pi. — ME. maseles, pi. of masel, lit.
'spot, excrescence', rel. to MDu. masel, Du.
mazelen, G. Masern, 'measles', and to E. mazer
(q.v.) E. measles was influenced both in form
and pronunciation by a confusion with ME.
mesel, 'leper', which derives fr. OF. mesel, fr. L.
misellus, dimin. of miser, 'wretched,
unfortunate, miserable'.
Derivative: measl-y, adj.

## measurable
measurable, adj. — ME. mesurable, fr. OF. (= F.)
mesurable, fr. Late L. mensurabilis, fr. mensu-
rare, fr. L. mensura. See measure and -able and
cp. mensurable.
Derivatives: measurabil-ity, п., measurable-ness,
п., measurabl-y, adv.

## measure
measure, n. — ME. mesure, fr. OF. (= F.)
тенге, fr. L. mensura, 'measure', fr. mensus, pp.
of metiri, 'to measure'. See mete, 'to measure'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:479 COLUMN:3 -->
and -ure and cp. meter, 'poetical rhythm'. Cp.
also admeasure, immeasurable, mensure,
mensurable, mensiirate, commensurable, dimension,
immense. Cp. also 1st mensal.
Derivatives: measure, tr. and intr. v., measur-ed,
adj., measur-ed-ly, aav.,measur-ed-ness, n.,meas-
ure-less, adj., measure-less-ly, adv., measure-
less-ness, п., measure-ment, п., measur-er, n.

## meat
meat, п., — ME. mete, it. OE. mete, rel. to OS.
meti, OFris. mete, ON. matr, OHG. таз, Goth.
mats, 'food', MLG., MDu., Du. metworst, G.
Mettwurst, 'German sausage', fr. Teut. *mati-,
'food', fr. I.-E. base *mad-, 'wet, moist,
dripping; to drip', whence OI. mddati, 'boils,
bubbles, gets drunk', medas-, 'fat' (п.), Alb. man, Ί
fatten, feed', Gk. μαδαν, 'to be wet, to flow',
μαδαρός, 'wet, watery', μαδάρωσις, 'baldness',
L. madere, 'to be wet; to be drunk, to be
intoxicated', madidus,'moist, wet,drunk;intoxicated',
mattus, 'intoxicated', OE. ma?.r/, 'mast (of
beech)', mxstan, 'to fatten', Olr. mat, 'pig,
swine* (prop, 'a fattened animal'), Oir. maisse
(for *mad-tja),'fooa'. Cp. the second element in

development of OE. mete, etc., 'food', into E. meat, etc.,

Derivatives: meat-less, meat-y, adjs.

## meatus
meatus, п., a duct or passage in the body (anat.)
— L. meatus, 'a going, passing; way, path,
passage', fr. meat-(um), pp. stem of meare, 'to go,
pass', which is cogn. with Czech mljim, mijeti,
'to go by, pass by, pass, cease', Pol. mijam,
mijac, 'to go by, avoid', and with the nasalized
forms OSIav. mino, minpti, 'to go by, pass by,
pass', MW. minet, 'to go'; fr. I.-E. base *mei-,
*moi-, 'to change; to change one's place; to go'.
See mean, 'of low rank', and cp. irremeable,
permeate. Cp. also conge.

## Mecca
Mecca, п., city in Arabia, birthplace of
Mohammed and place of pilgrimage for Mohammedans
hence 'the goal of one's highest aspirations'.. —
Arab. Makkcl·, in VArab. pronunciation:
Мёкка*, 'Mecca'.

## mechanic
mechanic, adj. — L. mechanicus, fr. Gk.
μηχανικός, 'resourceful, inventive; mechanical', fr.
μηχανή, 'means, invention, machine'. See
machine and -ic.
Derivatives: mechanic, п., mechanic-al, adj.,
mechanic-al-ly, adv., mechanic-al-ness, п., те-
chanic-ian, п., mechan-ics, n.

## mechanism
mechanism, n. — ModL. mechanismus, fr. Gk.
μηχανή, 'machine'. See prec. word and -ism.

## mechanist
mechanist, n. — Formed with suff. -1st fr. Gk.
μηχανή, 'machine'. See mechanic.
Derivatives: mechanist-ic, adj., mechanist-ic-al-
ly, adv.

## mechanize
mechanize, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. Gk.
μηχανή, 'machine'. See mechanic.
Derivatives: mechaniz-ation, п., mechaniz-er, n.

## mechano-
mechano-, combining form denoting mechanics
or mechanism. — Gk. μηχανο-, fr. μηχανή,
'machine'. See mechanic.

## Mechilta
Mechilta, also Mekhilta, п., a halakic
commentary on Exodus from the school of Rabbi Ish-
mael (2nd cent.) — Fr. Aram. mekhilta, 'rule',
lit. 'measure of capacity', fr. ksl, 'to
comprehend, measure', which is rel. to Heb. kal, 'he
comprehended, measured', hakhil, 'to hold,
contain', Ugar. kl, 'to contain, measure', Arab.
kala, 'he measured (grain)'.

## Mechlin
Mechlin, n. —; Short for Mechlin lace, i.e. lace
made at Mechlin, a town in Belgium. Cp.
malines.

## meco-
meco-, combining form meaning 'length' or
'long'. — Gk. μηκο-, fr. μήκος, 'length',
corresponding to Dor. Gk. μακος, of s.m., and rel. to
μακρός, 'long'. See macro- and cp. mekometer.

## meconic
meconic, adj., pertaining to an acid found in
opium. — Gk. μηκωνικός, 'of, or pertaining to, the
poppy', fr. μήκων. See next word and -ic.

## meconium
meconium, п., the fecal discharge of the newborn
infant (med.) — L. meconium, 'poppy-juice; the
first excrements of the newborn child', fr. Gk.
μηκώνιον, dimin. of μήκων, 'poppy', which
corresponds to Dor. μακων, of s.m., and is

## medal
medal, n. — MF. (= F.) medaille, fr. It. medaglia,

Derivatives: medal, tr. v., medat(l)-ed, adj.,

## medallion
medallion, n. — F. medallion, fr. It. medaglione,

## meddle

se meter, 'to meddle'), fr. ML misculare, fr. L.

Derivatives: meddl-er, п., meddle-some, adj.,
meddle-some-ness, a.

## Mede
Mede, п., inhabitant of Media. — L. Medus, fr.
Gk. Μήδος, 'Mede'.

## Medea
Medea, п., sorceress, daughter of Aeetes, king of
Colchis (Greek mythol.) — L. Medea, fr. Gk.
Μήδεια, lit. 'cunning', rel. to μηδος, 'counsel,
plan, device, cunning', μήδεσθαι, 'to devise,
resolve, advise', μέδων, μεδέων, 'guardian, ruler'
(prop. pres. part, of the ancient verb μέδειν, 'to
protect, rule over'), μέδεσθαι, 'to be mindful of,
give heed to, think on', μέδιμνας, 'a measure',
fr. I.-E. base "med-, 'tomeasure,limit,consider',
which is a -(/-enlargement of base "me-, 'to
measure'. See meditate and cp. Andromeda and
words there referred to. Cp. also Medeola.

## Medeola
Medeola, п., a genus of plants, the Indian
cucumber-root (bot.) — ModL., dimin. formed
from the name of Medea, the sorceress; so
called for its reputed medicinal value.

## medi-
medi-, combining form. — See medio-,

## media
media, п., formerly, a voiced stop consonant (b,

mi}, 'the middle', Alb. mjel, 'means', mes, mjes,

meta-, metayer, mezzanine, mezzotint, Midi,

## media
media, п., middle membrane of an artery (anat.)

media, n. pi. — PI. of medium,

mediant, п., the third note of the diatonic scale

## mediastinals
mediastinals, п., inflammation of the tissue of the

## mediastino-
mediastino-, combining form denoting 'of the

## mediastinum
mediastinum, п., 1) a membranous partition
separating two cavities of the body; 2) space in
the middle of the chest between the two pleurae
(anat.) — Medical L., neut. of mediastinus,

## mediate
mediate, intr. v., to intervene; tr. v., to bring

## mediation
mediation, n. — ME. mediacioun, fr. OF. media-
cion (F. mediation), fr. Late L. medidtionem,
ace. of mediatio, lit. 'a division in the middle',
fr. mediatus, pp. of mediare. See mediate, adj.,

mediatize, tr. v., formerly in Germany, under the

pendance or vassalage. — F. mediatiser, fr.

## mediator
mediator, n. — ME. mediatour, fr. OF. media-
tour (F. mediateur), fr. Late L. mediatorem, ace.

mediate, adj., and agential suff. -or.

## mediatory
mediatory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr.

adj.

## Medic
Medic, adj., Median; п., the language of ancient
Media. — Gk. Μηδικός, 'Median', fr. Μηδος.
See Mede and cp. Median. Cp. also next word.

## medic
medic, п., any plant of the genus Medicago (bot.)
— L. medica, fr. Gk. Μηδική (scil. πόα},
'(grass) from Media', fem. of Μηδικός, 'Median'
(see Medic); so called because it came to the
Greeks from Media.
medicable. — L. medicabilis, 'that which can be
healed, curable', fr. medicari, 'to heal, cure', fr.
medicus. See medical Aid -able.

## Medicago
Medicago, п., a genus of plants, the medic (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. Μηδική, name of the alfalfa,
lit. 'the Median (plant)'. See medic.

## medical
medical, adj. — F. medical, is. Late L. medicalis,
'of a physician', fr. L. medicus, 'physician',
which is rel to mederi, 'to heal', and cogn. with
Avestic vt-mad, 'physician', fr. I.-E. base *med-,
'to measure, limit, consider, advise', whence also
Gk. μηδος, 'counsel, plan, device, cunning', the
PN's Μήδος, Μήδη, etc., which originally
denoted healing deities, μήδεσθαι, 'to devise,
resolve, advise', μέδεσθαι, 'to he mindful of, give
heed to, think on'. See meditate and Medea and
cp. remedy. Cp. also metheglin. The word
medical was introduced into English by Thomas
Browne (1605-82).
Derivatives: medical, п., medical-Iy, adv.

## medicament
medicament, n. — F. medicament, fr. L. medicd-
mentum, 'drug, remedy, medicament', lit.
'means or instrument of healing', formed from
the verb medicari, 'to heal, cure', with -mentum,
a suffix denoting instrument. See medicate and
-ment.
Derivatives: medicament, tr. v., medicament-ary,
adj., medicament-ation, п., medicament-ous, adj.

## medicaster
medicaster, п., a quack. — Formed fr. L. medicus,
'physician', with the pejorative suff. -aster. Cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:480 COLUMN:3 -->
poetaster.

## medicate
medicate, tr. v. — L. medicatus, pp. of medicare,
medicari, 'to heal, cure', fr. medicus. See medical
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: medication (q.v.), medicat-ive, adj.,
medicator (q.v.), medicat-ory, adj.

## medication
medication, n. — L. medicatio, gen. -onis,
'healing, cure', fr. medicatus, pp. of medicare,
medicari. See prec. word and -ion.

## medicator
medicator, n. — Late L. medicator, 'physician',
fr. L. medicatus, pp. of medicare, medicari. See
medicate and agential suff. -or.

## medicine
medicine, n. — ME., fr. OF. medicine, medecine
(F. medecine), fr. L. mediana, 'healing art, the
shop of a physician, remedy, relief, prop. fem.
of the adjective medicinus, 'of a physician', used
as a noun, fr. medicus. See medical and subst.
suff. -ine.
Derivatives: medicine, tr. v., medicin-al, adj.
and п., medicin-al-ly, adv.

## medico
medico, п., physician (colloq.) — It. medico, fr.
L. medicus. See medical,

## medico-
medico-, combining form meaning 1) 'medical,
medicinal'; 2) 'medical and'. — Fr. L. medicus.
See medical,

## medieval
medieval, mediaeval, adj., pertaining to, or
suggestive of, the Middle Ages. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. medius, 'middle', and aevum,
'age'. See media, 'voiced stop consonant', and
age.
Derivative: medi(a)eval-ly, adv.

## medievalism
medievalism, mediaevalism, п., 1) the spirit of the
Middle Ages; 2) devotion to medieval
practices. — See prec. word and -ism.

## medievalist
medievalist, mediaevalist, п., 1) a student of
medieval history, etc.; 2) one devoted to the
spirit and practices of the Middle Ages. — See
medieval and -ist.

## medievalize
medievalize, mediaevalize, tr. v., I) to render
medieval; 2) to adopt medieval customs, etc. —
See medieval and -ize.

## medio-
medio-, medi-, combining form meaning 'middle'.
— Fr. L. medius, 'middle'. See media, 'voiced
stop consonant'.

## mediocre
mediocre, adj., of middle quality; average. —
MF. (= F.) mediocre, fr. L. mediocris,
'middling, moderate, indifferent, tolerable', orig.
'being half-way up the height of a mountain',
compounded of medius, 'middle', and ocris, 'a
rugged, stony mountain'. For the first element
see media, 'voiced stop consonant'. The second
element is rel. to Umbr. ukar, ocar, 'fortress,
citadel, mountain', and cogn. with Gk. δκρις,
'peak, point', Homeric όκριαν, 'to make rough
or rugged', όκριασθαι, 'to be exasperated', Mir.
ochar, W. ochr, 'corner, border', and in grada-
tional relationship to L. deer, acris, acre, 'sharp'.
See acrid and cp. Oxalls.

## mediocrity

mediocrite, fr. L. mediocritatem, ace. of medio-
critas, 'moderateness, moderation, indifference,
inferiority', fr. mediocris. See prec. word and
-ity.

cunning', μήδεσθαι, 'to devise, resolve, advise',

## meditation
meditation, n. — ME. meditacioun, fr. OF.
meditation (F. meditation), fr. L. meditationem, ace.
of meditutw, 'a thinking over, meditation', fr.
meditatus, pp. of meditare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## meditative
meditative, adj. — Late L. meditattvus, fr. L.
meditatus, pp. of meditare. See meditate and
-ive.
Derivatives: meditative-ly, adv., meditative-ness,
n.

## mediterranean
mediterranean, adj., enclosed, or nearly enclosed,
by sea; n.) a mediterranean sea; (cap.) the
Mediterranean sea. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L.
mediterraneus, 'inland', lit. 'in the middle of
land', fr. medius, 'middle', and terra, 'land'. See
media, 'voiced stop consonant', and terra.

## meditullium
meditullium, п., I) the diploe (anal.); 2) the
mesophyll (bot.)—L., 'themiddle',compounded
of medius, 'middle', and *tullium, *tollium,
'earth', which stands in gradational relationship
to tellus, 'earth'. See media, 'voiced stop
consonant', and tellurian.

## medium
medium, n. — L., 'the middle', neut. of the
adjective medius, 'middle', used as a noun. See
media, 'voiced stop consonant'.
Derivatives: medium, adj., medium-istic, adj.,
medium-ize, tr. v.

## medlar
medlar, п., 1) a small tree of the rose family; 2)
its fruit. — ME. medler, fr. OF. medler, mesler,
'medlar tree', fr. OF. mesple, mesle (F. nefle),
'medlar (the fruit)', fr. L. mespita (also mes-
pilus, mespilum), of s.m., fr. Gk. μέσπιλον,
'medlar (the fruit)', which is a foreign word of
unknown origin. Cp. naseberry.

## medley
medley, п., mixture. — ME. medle, fr. OF. mesd-
lee, medlee, meslee (F. melee), prop. fem. pp. of
medler, mesler (F. miler), 'to mix, mingle', fr.
ML. misculare, fr. L. miscere, 'to mix, mingle'.
See mix and cp. chance-medley. Cp. also meddle,
melee, mell, pell-mell, melange.
Derivative: medley, adj. and tr. v.

## Medoc
Medoc, п., a kind of claret. — So called from
Medoc, name of the plain between the Gironde
and the Atlantic, where it is produced.

## medulla
medulla, п., the marrow of bones (anat.) — L.,
'marrow; pith of plants', of uncertain
etymology; perh. fr. orig. *(s)merullu (with -d- for -r-,
under the influence of medius, 'middle'), fr.
I.-E. base 'smeru, 'fat', whence also OE. smeoru,
'fat, grease', Olr. smiur, 'marrow', W. mer, of
s.m. See smear, п., and words there referred to.
Derivatives: medull-ar, adj., medullary (q.v.),
medullat-ed, adj., medullation (q.v.), medull-iz·
ation, п., medullose (q.v.)

## medullary
medullary, adj., pertaining to, or consisting of,
the medulla. — L. medullaris, 'situated in the
marrow', fr. medulla. See prec word and adj.
suff. -ary.

## medullation
medullation, п., the development of marrow. —
Formed fr. Late L. medultatus, 'possessed of
marrow, marrowy', pp. of medutlare, 'to fill
with marrow', fr. L. medulla. See medulla and
-ation.

## meduliitis
meduliitis, п., inflammation of marrow (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. medulla and
Gk. suff. -ΐτις. See medulla and -itis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:481 COLUMN:2 -->

## medullose
medullose, adj., pithlike. — L. medullosus, 'full of
marrow', fr. medulla. See medulla and adj. suff.
-ose.

## Medusa
Medusa, п., one of the three Gorgons, whose
gaze turned to stone everyone that looked at her
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Μέδουσα, lit.
'guardian', prop, fem pres. part, of the ancient
verb μέδειν, 'to protect, rule over'. See Medea
and Cp. words there referred to.

## medusa
medusa, п., a jellyfish (zool.) — Fr. prec. word.
Derivatives: medus-al, medus-an, adjs.

## medusoid
medusoid, 1) adj., like a medusa; 2) a medusalike
gonophore of a hydrozoan (zool.) —
Compounded of medusa and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'shape, form'. See -oid.

## meed
meed, п., reward (poet.) — ME. mede, fr. OE.
med, meord, 'reward, requital', rel. to OS. meda,
OHG. mita, miata, mieta, MHG., G. miete,
Goth, mizdo, 'reward', and cogn. with OI. mi-
dham (for *mizdha-), 'prize, reward, contest,
booty', midhvah, 'giving in abundance', Avestic
miida, 'reward', Gk. μισθός (for "mizdhos),
'wages, pay', OSlav. mizda, 'salary'.

## meek
meek, adj. — ME. тек, fr. earlier meoc, fr.
ON. mjukr, 'mild, soft, gentle', which is rel. to
Goth, тйка-mqdei, 'humility', and prob. cogn.
with Olr. mochl (for 'rnukto-), 'mild, gentle",
L. mucus, 'mucus, of the nose'. See mucus and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: meek-ly, adv., meek-ness, п.,

## meerkat
meerkat, п., 1) a monkey (obsol.); 2) the suricate.
— Du., 'monkey', fr. MDu. meercatte, lit. 'sea
cat'; cp. MLG. merkatte, Dan. marekat, Swed.
markatta, OHG. merikazza, MHG. merkatze,
G. Meerkatze. See mere, 'sea', and cat. These
words are not connected with OI. markalah,
'ape, monkey'.

## meerschaum
meerschaum, п., a porous, claylike mineral
composed of silicate of magnesia. — G., lit. 'sea

which itself is a loan translation of Gk. αλός
άχνη; orig. name of the Alcyonium, popularly
named 'mermaid's glove'; so called from its

See mere, 'sea', and scum,

## meet

mata, OS. motion, 'to meet', and to OS., OE.
mot, 'a meeting'. See moot, 'meeting', and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: meet, п., meet-er, п., meet-ing,r\.

## meet
meet, adj., suitable. — ME. mete, fr. OE. gemxte,

MHG. gemxte, G. gema\/3, 'suitable', OE.
metan, etc., 'to measure'; fr. I.-E. base *med-,
^-enlargement of *me-, 'to measure'. See mete,

Derivatives: meet-ly, adv., meet-ness, n.

Meg, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Margaret,

megalocardia, п., abnormal enlargement of the

## meinie
meinie, meiny, п., household; retinue. — OF.

meiosis, п., 1) litotes (rhet.); 2) the process by

μείων, 'lesser, less', fr. I.-E. base "met-, 'to

meistersinger, n. — G. Meistersinger, lit. 'master

singer', fr. Meister, 'master', and Singer, 'sing-

Mekhilta, n. — See Mechilta.

## mekometer
mekometer, п., a range finder. — Compounded

## mel
mel, п., honey (pharm.) — L., cogn. with Hitt.

meir, gen. meiu, 'honey', Gk. μέλι, 'honey',

## melammed
melammed, melamed, п., a Jewish teacher, esp.

## Melampyrum
Melampyrum, п., a genus of plants, the cow-

melan-, form' of melano- before a vowel.

melancholia, n. — Late L. See melancholy.

(= F.) melancolique, fr. Late L. meiancholicus,

melancholy, n. — ME. melancolie, fr. OF. melan·

## Melanesia

Derivatives: Melanesi-an, adj. and n.

## melange

## melanism

melanite п., a black variety of garnet {mineral.)
— G. Melanit, coined by the German geologist

## melano-
melano-, before a vowel melan-, combining form

Alb. mei-enE, 'elm*, Gk. μύλλος (whence L.

## Melanochroi
Melanochroi, n. pi., members of the Caucasian

## melanochroid
melanochroid, adj., melanochroic. —

melanoma, п., a tumor containing melanin (med.)

## Melanthium
Melanthium, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,

Melchior, masc. PN. — Lit. 'king of light',

meldometer, п., an instrument for measuring

## Meleagris
Meleagris, п., the genus of turkeys (ornithol.) —
ModL., fr. L. meleagris, 'guinea hen', fr. Gk.
μελεαγρίς, which is of uncertain origin. It is
perh. cogn. with Avestic nfrlga, 'bird', Afghan
marya, of s.m. The Greek word was prob.
influenced in form by the name of the Greek hero
Μελέαγρος, Meleagrus, son of Oeneus, king of
Calydon.

## melee
melee, melee, п., conflict, fray, skirmish. — F.
melee, prop. fern. pp. of meter, 'to mix, mingle'.
See medley and cp. melange.

## mell-
mell-, combining form meaning 'honey'. — Gk.
μέλι-, fr. μέλι, gen. μέλιτος, 'honey', which
is cogn. with L. mel, gen. mellis, 'honey'. See
me].

## Melia
Melia, п., a genus of trees (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. μελιά, 'ash tree', which is of unknown
origin.

## Melianthaceae
Melianthaceae, n. pi., a family of S. African
plants (bot.) — ModL., formed from next word
with suff. -aceae.

## Melianthus
Melianthus, п., a genus of S. African plants (bot.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. μέλι, 'honey',
and άνθος, 'flower'. See mell- and anther.

## mellc
mellc, adj., pertaining to song. — Gk. μελικός,
'of'a song', fr. μέλος, 'limb, joint; part of
musical phrase; song, tune', which is perh. cogn.
with Bret, mell, Co. mat, 'knuckle, joint', W.
cym-mal, 'joint', and with Toch. A malk-, 'to
join, unite'. Cp. the first element in melisma,
melodrama, melody, and the second element in
Philomel, dulcimer. For the ending see adj. suff.
-ic. For the sense development of Gk. μέλος
ср. Ir. alt, 'limb; poem'.

## Melica
Melica, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) — ModL., fr.
It. melica, meliga, melga, 'sorghum', which
prob. comes fr. ML. milica, a derivative of L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:482 COLUMN:3 -->
milium, 'millet'. See millet.

## Melicent
Melicent, fem. PN. — See Milicent.

## meliceris
meliceris, also melicera, п., a kind of tumor (med.)
— L. meliceris, fr. Gk. μελικηρίς, 'a tumor
looking like honeycomb', compounded of μέλι,
'honey', and κηρός, 'beeswax'. See mell- and
cere.

## melilot
melilot, п., a kind of clover. — ME. mellilot, fr.
MF. (= F.) melilot, fr. L. melilotos, 'a kind of
clover', fr. Gk. μελίλωτος, μελίλωτον, which
is compounded of μέλι, 'honey', and λωτός,
'lotus'. See meli- and lotus.

## Melilotus
Melilotus, п., a genus of plants, the sweet clover
(bot.) — L. melilotos. See melilot.

## melinite
melinite, п., a high explosive containing chiefly
picric acid. — F. melinite, formed with subst.
suff. -ite. fr. Gk. μήλινος, 'pertaining to an
apple', fr. μήλον, 'apple'. See Malus, 'the genus
of apple trees', and cp. the second element in
marmalade and in camomile.

## meliorabillty
meliorabillty, п., the capability of being
improved.— Coined by the English philosopher Jeremy
Bentham (1748-1832) fr. L*. melior, 'better'.
See meliorate and the suffixes -able and -ity.

## meliorate
meliorate, tr. and intr. v. — Late L. melioratus,
pp. of meliorate, 'to make better, improve', fr.
melior, 'better', prob. with the original meaning
'stronger', fr. I.-E. base *mel-, 'strong, great,
numerous', whence also Gk. μάλα, 'very, very
much, quite', μάλλον, 'more, rather' (changed
from original *μέλλον, under the influence of
θαττον, θασσον, 'quicker, sooner, rather'),
μάλιστα, 'most, most strongly', L. multus (for
*mltos), 'much', Lett, milns, 'very much'. See
multi- and verbal suff. -ate and cp. ameliorate.
Derivatives: meliorat-ion, п., meliorat-ive, adj.,
meliorat-or, n.

## meliorism
meliorism, п., the belief that the world tends to
become better. — Prob. coined by the English
novelist George Eliot (1819-80) fr. L. melior,
'better' (see prec. word), and suff. -ism.

## meliorist
meliorist, п., one who believes in meliorism. —
Formed with suff. -1st fr. L. melior, 'better'. See
meliorate.
Derivative: meliorist-ic, adj.

## Mellpona
Mellpona, п., a genus of honeybees of South
America (zool.) — ModL., compounded of
mell- and Gk. πονεϊν, 'to toil, work hard'. For
the first element see meli-. The second element
derives fr. πόνος, 'toil, labor', which stands in
gradational relationship to πένης, 'poor',
πενία, 'poverty', πένεσθαι, 'to work for one's
living, to toil, labor'. Cp. Ponera and the second
element in geoponic, leucopenia.

## melisma
melisma, п., melody, tune, vocal ornamentation
(mus.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μέλισμα, gen. μελί-
σματος, 'song', fr. μέλος, 'song, tune'. See melic.
For the ending see suff. -ma.
Derivative: melism-atic, adj.

## Melissa
Melissa, п., name of a genus of mints (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. μέλισσα, Att. μέλιττα (for *μέ-
λιτια), 'bee', prop, 'honey fly', fr. μέλι, gen.
μέλιτος, 'honey', which is cogn. with L. mel, gen.
mellis, 'honey' (see mel); so called in allusion to
the abundant honey yielded by the flowers.

## Melissa
Melissa, fem. PN. — L., lit. 'bee', fr. Gk.
μέλισσα. See prec word.

## Melkarth
Melkarth, Melcarth, п., name of the chief divinity
of Tyre. — Contraction of Phoen. melekh qart,
'king of the city'. Phoen. melekh, 'king', is rel.
to Heb. melekh, 'king'; see Mameluke and cp.
the first element in Melchior, Melchizedek.
Phoen. qart, 'town, city', is rel. to Heb. qiryah,
qireth, of s.m., Aram. qiryah, qirya, 'town,
village', Arab, qarycl·, 'village, town', of s.m.
Heb. qlryah, etc., prob. meant orig. 'meeting
place', and derive fr. Heb. qara*, 'he met,
encountered', resp. from its corresponding
equivalents. Cp. Phoen. Qarthadasht (whence Gk.
Καρχηδών, L. Karthago, Carthago), 'Carthage',
lit. 'Newtown'.

## mell
mell, tr. and intr. v., to mix; to meddle (obsol.
and dial.) — ME. mellen, fr. OF. meller, mesler,
'to mix, mingle'. See meddle,

## melli-
melli-, combining form meaning 'honey'. — L.
melli-, from the stem of mel, gen. mellis, 'honey".
See mel.

## melliferous
melliferous, adj., producing honey. — Com-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:483 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MELLIFLUENCE | 456 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:483 COLUMN:1 -->
pounded of L. mel, gen. mellis, 'honey', and the
stem of ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See melli- and
-ferous.

## mellifluence
mellifluence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## mellifluent
mellifluent, adj., mellifluous. — Lit. 'flowing
with, or as with, honey', fr. L. mel, gen. mellis,
'honey', and fiuins, gen. -entis, pres. part of
ftuere, 'to flow'. See met and fluent.
Derivatives: mellifiuent-ly, adv.

## mellifluous
mellifluous, adj., flowing with honey; sweet-
sounding. — Late L. mellifluus, 'flowing with,
or as with, honey', compounded of L. met, gen.
mellis, 'honey', and fluere, 'to flow'. See prec.
word. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivatives: mellifluous-ly, adv., mel/ifluous-
ness, n.

## mellow
mellow, adj., soft and ripe. — ME. melwe, mel-
owe, 'ripe, mature', prob. fr. OE. melu, 'meal,
flour'. See meal, 'edible grain'.
Derivatives: mellow, tr. and intr. v., mellow-ly,
adv., mellow-ness, п., mellow-y, adj.

## melodeon
melodeon, п., 1) a kind of Teed organ; 2) a kind of
accordion (mus.) — Coined fr. Late L. melodia.
See melody.

## melodic
melodic, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
melody. — Late L. melddicus, fr. Gk.
μελωδικός, fr. μελωδία. See melody and -ic.

## melodious
melodious, adj., 1) full of melody; 2) pleasant to
theear. — ME.,fr. MF. melodieus(¥. melodieux),
fr. melodie (F. melodie). — See melody and -ous.
Derivatives: melodious-ly, adv., melodious-ness,
a.

## melodist
melodist, п., a composer or singer of melodies. —
Formed fr. melody with suff. -ist.

## melodize
melodize, tr. v., to render melodious; intr. v., to
compose melodies. — Fotjmed fr. melody with
suff. -ize.

## melodrama
melodrama, п., 1) orig. a play with interspersed
songs; 2) now, a romantic and sensational
drama. — F. milodrame, fr. Gk. μέλος, 'song',
and δράμα, gen. δράματος, 'drama'. See mellc
and drama.
Derivatives: melodramat-ic, adj., melodramat-ic-
al-ly, adv., melodramat-ist, п., melodramat-ize,
tr. v.

## melody
melody, n. — ME. melodie, fr. OF. melodie (F.
melodie), fr. Late L. melodia, fr. Gk. μελωδία,
'chant, choral song', which is compounded of
μέλος, 'song', and ωδή, 'song'. See mellc and
ode.
Derivative: melody, v.

## Melolonthinae
Melolonthinae, n. pi., a subfamily of beetles
including the cockchafers (entomol.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -mae fr. Gk. μηλολόν*η,
'cockchafer', which is of uncertain origin.

## melon
melon, n.—Late ME. meloun, fr. MF. (= F.) melon,
fr. L. meWnem, ace. of meld, fr. Gk. μηλοπέπων,
'melon', lit. 'apple-shaped ripe fruit', fr. μήλον,
'apple', and πέπων, 'ripe'. Cp. It. mellone, Sp.
melon, 'melon', which are of the same origin.
See Mains, 'the genus of apple trees', and pepsin.

## Melothria
Melothria, п., a genus of vines (йог.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. μήλωθρον, a kind of white vine.

## Melpomene
Melpomene, п., the Muse of tragedy (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Μελπομένη, lit.
'songstress', fr. μέλπειν, μέλπεσθαι, 'to sing', which
is of uncertain origin.

## melt
melt, intr. v., to become liquid; dissolve; tr. v., to
cause to melt. — ME. melten, fr. OE. meltan
(intr. v.), mieltan (tr. v.), rel. to ON. mella, 'to
digest', fr. I.-E. base 'meld-, whence also Gk.
μέλδειν, 'to melt', L. mollis (for *moldwis), 'soft,
mild'. See mollify.
Derivatives: mell-er, п., melt-ing, п., melt-ing-ly,
adv., melt-ing-ness, n.

## melt
melt, п., molten metal. — Fr. melt, v.

## melton
melton, п., smooth woolen cloth. — From
Melton Mowbray, in Leicestershire (England), a
famous hunting center.
Derivative: melton, adj.

## mem
mem, п., name of the 13th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb mem, contraction of mdyim,
'water', which is rel. to Aram, mayya, mayyin,
Arab, ma', Akkad. тй, 'water'; so called in
allusion to the ancient form of this letter Cp. mlm-
mation.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:483 COLUMN:2 -->

## member
member, n. — ME. membre, fr. OF. (= F.) mem-
bre, fr. L. membrum, 'limb, member, part',
which stands for *mems-rom and is cogn. with
Ol. mdmsdm, 'flesh', Toch. B. misa (pi.), Arm.
mis (gen. msoy), 'flesh', Gk. μηρός (for *mems-
ro- or *mes-ro-), 'thigh' (lit. 'fleshy part'), Alb.
mis', 'flesh', Goth, mims, OSlav. meso, OPruss.
mensd, Lett, miesa, 'flesh', Olr. mir (for mems-
ro-, "mes-ro-), 'piece, bit', and prob. also with
Gk. μήνιγξ (for 'memsninx, *mesninx),
'membrane'. Cp. membrane, dismember, meninx.
Derivatives: member-ed, adj., member-less, adj.,
member-ship, n.

## membranaceous
membranaceous, adj., membranous. — Late L.
membrdndceus, fr. L. membrana. See next word
and -aceous.

## membrane
membrane, n. — L. membrana, 'fine skin,
membrane, parchment', fr. membrum-, see member.
The orig. meaning of L. membrana was 'that
which covers the members (or a member) of the
body'.

## membranous
membranous, adj. — F. membraneux (fern, mem-
braneuse), fr. membrane, fr. L. membrana. See
prec. word and -ous.

## membranula
membranula, membranule, п., a little membrane.
— L. membranula, dimin. of membrana. See
membrane and -ule.

## memento
memento, п., something serving as a reminder. —
L. memento, 'remember', imper. of meminisse,
'to remember', which is cogn. with Gk. μέμονα,
Ί am very eager, I purpose, intend', fr. I.-E.
base 'men-, 'to think, to have one's mind
aroused', whence also L. mens, 'mind,
understanding, reason', Goth, muns, 'thought, mind', OE.
gemynd, 'memory'. See mind and cp. words
there referred to.

## Memnon
Memnon, п., an Ethiopian king slain by Achilles
in the Trojan war (Greek mythol.) — L.
Memnon, fr. Gk. Μέμνων, a word of uncertain
etymology. It possibly stands for 'Μέδμων and lit.
means 'ruler", fr. μέδων, which is prop, the
pres. part, of the ancient verb μέδειν, 'to
protect, rule over', hence is of the same origin as the
second element in the name 'Αγαμέμνων. See
Agamemnon.

## memo
memo, n. — Short for memorandum.
Derivative: memo, tr. v., to make a
memorandum of.

## memoir
memoir, п., biography, biographical notice. — F.
mimoire, orig. 'something written to be kept in
mind', mast., derived fr. memoire, fern.,
'memory', fr. L. memoria. See memory,

## memorabilia
memorabilia, n. pi., things worth remembering.
— L. memorabilia, neut. pi. of memorabilis. See
next word.

## memorable
memorable, adj. — ME., fr. L. memorabilis,
'memorable, remarkable, worthy to be
remembered', fr. memordre, 'to call to mind', fr. memor.
See memory and -able.
Derivatives: memorable-ness, п., memorabl-y,
adv.

## memorandum
memorandum, n. — L., 'something to be
remembered', gerundive of memordre. See prec. word.
For other Latin gerundives used in English cp.
agenda and words there referred to.

## memorial
memorial, adj. — ME., fr. OF. memorial (F.
memorial), fr. L. memoridlis, 'of memory', fr.
memoria. See memory and adj. suff. -al.

## memorial
memorial, n. — Subst. use of prec. word. Cp. L.
memoridle, 'a memorial', prop. neut. of the adj.
memoridlis.
Derivatives: memorial-ist, п., memorial-ize, tr. v.

## memorize
memorize, tr. v., to commit to memory. —
Formed fr. memory with suff. -ize.
Derivative: memoriz-ation, n.

## memory
memory, n. — ME. memorie, fr. OF. memorie (F.
mimoire), fr. L. memoria, 'memory', fr. memor,
'mindful', which stands for *me-mor and
derives fr. I.-E. 'mer-(s)mer-, reduplication of
base *(s)mer-, 'to care for, be anxious about,
think, consider, remember'. From the
reduplicated base derive also Avestic mimara-,
'mindful', OE. gemimor, 'known', mdmrian, 'to plot,
design', Du. mijmeren, 'to ponder'. Cp.—with
full reduplication of base *mer—Gk. μέρμερος,
'causing anxiety, mischievous, baneful', μέρ-
μηρα (poet.), 'care, trouble', μερμαίρειν, μερ-
μηρίζειν, 'to be anxious, to ponder', Arm. mor-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:483 COLUMN:3 -->
ток1 (for 'mermero- or 'mormoro-), 'regret,
grief. The simple base *(s)mer- appears in OI.
smarati, Avestic maraiti, 'remembers', Gk.
μέριμνα, 'care, thought', μεριμνϊν, 'to care for, be
anxious', Serbo-Croat mdriti, 'to care for',
Goth, maurnan, OE. murnan, 'to be anxious
for', W. marth, 'sadness, anxiety', and possibly
also in L. mora, 'hesitation, delay', Olr. maraim,
Ί remain'. Cp. memoir, commemorate,
remember. Cp. also martyr, mourn, smriti. Cp. also
moratory.

## mem-sahib
mem-sahib, п., a word by which Indian speakers
address a European woman. — Hind, mem-
sahib, fr. mem, 'woman, lady' (fr. E. ma'am),
and Arab, sahib, 'master'. See ma'am and sahib.

## men
men, n. — PI. of man.

## -men
-men, L. suff. used to form neuter nouns. — Fr.
I.-E. '-mn, whence also the Greek suff. -μα.
See -m, -ma, -ment.

## menace
menace, n. — ME. manace, fr. OF. manace,
menace (F. menace), fr. VL. minacia (occurring
already in Plautus), 'threat, menace', fr. L.
mindx, gen. mindcis, 'projecting; threatening',
fr. mindri, 'to threaten'. Cp. It. minaccia, Sp.
amenaza, 'threat', which, also derive fr.VL.
minacia. See minatory and cp. amenable, demeanor,
imminent, manada, promenade.

## menace
menace, tr. and intr. v. — ME. menacen, fr. OF.
manacer, menacer (F, menacer), fr. VL. 'rnind-
cidre, 'to threaten', fr. minacia. See menace, n.
Derivatives: menac-er, п., menac-ing, adj.,
menac-ing-ly, adv.

## manage
manage, menage, п., 1) household; 2)
management of a household. — F. menage, fr. OF. mais-
nage, mesnage, fr. VL. mansiondticum, lit. 'that
which pertains to the house', fr. L. mdnsio,
gen. mdnsionis, 'a staying, remaining, night
quarters, station, place of abode, halting place',
fr. manlre, 'to stay, remain' (in VL., 'to dwell').
See remain and -age and cp. manor, manse,
mansion, messuage,

## menagerie
menagerie, п., collection of wild animals kept in
captivity. — F. menagerie, formed fr. menage
with suff. -erie. See prec. word and -ery.
Derivative: menager-ist, n.

## Menaspis
Menaspis, п., an extinct genus of sharks (paleon-
tol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. μήνη,
'moon', and ασπίς, 'shield'; so called in
allusion to the crescentlike shape. See meno-,
'month1, and aspidium.

## mend
mend, tr. and intr. v. — Aphetic for amend (q.v.)
Derivatives: mend, п., mend-er, п., mend-ing, п.,
mend-able,ua\.

## mendacious
mendacious, adj., lying, untruthful. — Fr. L.
menddx, gen. -dcis, 'lying, false, mendacious',
orig. meaning 'faulty', which is rel. to mendum,
menda, 'defect, blemish, fault'; see amend and
-aclous and cp. mendicant. The sense
development of L. menddx was influenced by menttor,
mentiri, 'to speak falsely, lie, deceive", with
which it has nothing in common.
Derivatives: mendacious-ly, adv., mendacious-
ness, n.

## mendacity
mendacity, n. — Late L. menddciUts, 'falsehood,
mendacity', fr. L. menddx, gen. -dcis. See
mendacious and -ity.

## mendelevium
mendelevium, п., a radioactive element, produced
esp. by bombardment of einsteinium (chem.) —
ModL., named after the Russian chemist
Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev (1834-1907). For the
ending see chem. suff. -iuin.

## Mendelian
Mendelian, adj., pertaining to the Austrian
biologist Gregor Johann Mendel (1822-84) or his
laws of heredity.

## Mendelianism
Mendelianism, Mendelism, п., the laws of
heredity enunciated by Gregor Johann Mendel. —
See prec. word and -ism.

## mendicancy
mendicancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## mendicant
mendicant, п., a beggar. — L. mendicdns, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of mendicdre, 'to beg', fr.
mendicus, 'beggar', prop, 'an infirm, wretched,
miserable person', fr. mendum, 'blemish, fault'.
See mendacious and -ant and cp. mauud, 'to
beg'.

## mendicity
mendicity, п., state of being a beggar. — ME.
mendicite, fr. OF. (= F ) mendicite', fr. L. men-
dtcitdtem, ace. of mendicitds, 'beggary, mendic-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:484 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 457 | MEPHISTOPHELES -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:484 COLUMN:1 -->
ity', fr. mendicus. See prec. word and -ity.

## meneghinite
meneghinite, п., a lead antimony sulfide
{mineral.) — Named after the Italian mineralogist
Giuseppe Meneghini (1811-89). For the ending
see subst. sulT. -Ite.

## Menelaus
Menelaus, п., a king of Sparta, brother of
Agamemnon and husband of Helen (Greek mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. Μενέλαος, lit. 'resisting the
people', fr. μένειν, 'to stay, abide, remain', and
λαός, 'people'. See meno-, 'remaining', and lay,
'pertaining to the laity'.

## menhaden
menhaden, п., a kind of large herring used as
fertilizer. — Corruption of Narragansett Indian
munnawhatteaug, 'menhaden', fr. munnawhat,
'fertilizer'.

## menhir
menhir, п., an upright monumental stone (archae-
ol.) — F., lit. 'a long stone', fr. Bret, maen, men,
'stone*, and hir, 'long'. Bret, maen, men is rel. to
W. maen, Co. mln, 'stone'; cp. the second
element in dolmen. Bret, hir is rel. to Olr. sir, 'long,
everlasting', and cogn. with L. serus, late'; see
serotine and cp. siuce.

## menial
menial, adj., fit for servants; domestic; servile; п.,
a domestic servant. — Orig. 'pertaining to the
household', fr. ME. meynal, fr. AF. menial,
meignal, fr. meinie, 'household', which
corresponds to OF. mesnie, fr. VL. *mansionata, fr.
L. mansionem. See mansion and cp. meinie,
menage.
Derivative: menial-ly, adv.

## mening-
mening-, form of meningo- before a vowel.

## meninges
meninges, n. pi., the three membranes
enveloping the brain and spinal cord (anal.) —
Medical L., pi. of meninx, fr. Gk. μήνιγξ,
'membrane'. See meninx.

## meningitis
meningitis, п., inflammation of the meninges
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -Ms fr.
Gk. μήνιγξ, gen. μήνιγγος, 'membrane'. See
meninx.
Derivative: meningit-ic, adj.

## meningo-
meningo-, before a vowel mening-, combining
form meaning 'pertaining to the meninges,
meningeal'. — Gk. μηνιγγο-, μηνιγγ-, fr.
μήνιγξ, gen. μήνιγγος, 'membrane'. See meninx.

## meningocele
meningocele, п., tumor on the brain (med.) —
Compounded of meningo- and Gk. κήλη,
'tumor, swelling'. See -cele.
meninx. п., one of the three membranes
enveloping the brain and spinal cord (anal.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. μήνιγξ, 'membrane', which
prob. stands for *me~msninx, *mesninx, and is
rel. to Gk. μηρός (for *mems-ro- or *mes-ro-),
'thigh', and cogn. with L. membrum (for *mems-
rom), 'member'. See member and cp. myringa.
Derivatives: meninge-al, adj., mening-ism. п.,
meningitis (q.v.)

## meniscus
meniscus, п., a crescent. — ModL., fr. Gk. μηνί-
σκος, 'lunar crescent', dimin. of μήνη, 'moon',
which is rel. to μην, 'month'. See meno-,
'month'.
Derivatives: menisc-at, menisc-ate, adjs.

## menispermaceae
menispermaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the
moonseed family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr.
Menispermum with suff. -aceae.

## menispermaceous
menispermaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Menispermum
Menispermum, п., a genus of plants, the moon-
seed (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'moonseed', fr. Gk.
μήνη, 'moon', which is rel. to μήν, 'month', and
σπέρμα, 'seed'. See meno-, 'month', and sperm.

## meno-
meno-, combining form meaning 'month'. — Gk.
μηνο-, fr. μήν, gen. μηνός, 'month', which is
rel. to μήνη, 'moon'. See moon and cp.
meniscus, catameiria, emmenic, neomenia.

## meno-
meno-, combining form meaning 'remaining',
as in Menobranchus (zool.) — Fr. Gk. μένειν, 'to
remain', which is cogn. with L. manere, 'to
remain'. See mansion and cp. the first element in
Menelaus.

## Menobranchus
Menobranchus, п., a genus of amphibians having
a broad tail and large external gills; called also
Necturus (zool.) — ModL., compounded of
meno-, 'remaining', and βράγχια (pi.) 'gills'.
See branchia.

## menology
menology, п., a calendar of the months. — ModL.
minologium, fr. Late Gk. μηνολόγιον, which is
compounded of Gk. μήν, gen. μηνός, 'month',
and λόγος, 'word, speech, discourse, account'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:484 COLUMN:2 -->
See meno-, 'month', and -logy.

## menopause
menopause, п., period of life during which
menstruation ceases.. — Compounded of meno-,
'month','and Gk. παϋσις, 'a stopping, ceasing',
fr. παύειν, 'to cause to cease'. See pause.
Derivative: menopaus-at, adj.

## Menorah
Menorah, п., the seven-branched candelabrum in
the Tabernacle and in the Temple of Jerusalem.
— Heb. mln6rah, 'candlestick', from stem n-w-r,
'to give light, shine', whence also ner, 'lamp'; rel.
to Aram.-Syr. niir, 'fire', Arab, mra, 'shone',
лиг, 'light', nar, 'fire', Aram, m narta,
'candlestick', Arab, mandra1', 'candlestick; lighthouse;
tower of a mosque', Akkad. nuru, 'light', nawa-
ru, namaru, 'to give light, shine'. Cp. the second
element in Abner. Cp. also minaret and the last
element in Koh-i-noor.

## menorrhagia
menorrhagia, п., excessive menstruation (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of meno-, 'month',
and Gk. -ρραγίϊ, 'a bursting forth', from the
stem of ρηγνύναι, 'to burst forth'. See -rrhagla.

## mensai
mensai, adj., pertaining to, от used at, the table.
— Late L. mensalis, fr. L. mensa, 'table', which
is prob. identical with mensa, fern. pp. of metiri,
'to measure', and short for tabula mensa, 'a
measured board'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm',
and adj. suff. -al and cp. commensal. Cp. also
mesa.
mensa], adj., monthly. — Fr. L. mensis, 'month'.
See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## menses
menses, п., the monthly discharge of blood from
the uterus. — L. menses, 'months', pi. of mensis.
See moon and cp. words there referred to.

## Menshevik
Menshevik, menshevik, п., 1) orig. (from 1903) a
member of the less radical faction of the Russian
Social Democratic Party; 2) later (since the
revolution of Nov. 7, 1917), a member of a group
forming one of the parties opposing the policy
of the Soviet government. — Russ., lit. 'one of
the minority' (i.e. mensheviki), fr. menshe,
'smaller, less'; so called with reference to the
party that fought the more radical faction of the
Bolsheviki, i.e. the 'majority' party (see
Bolshevik). Russ. menshe derives fr. I.-E. base *men-,
'to lessen, diminish'. See minimum.
Derivative: Menshevik, menshevik, adj.

## menstroal
menstroal, adj., 1) pertaining to the menses; 2)
monthly (astron.) — ME. menslruall, fr. L.
menstrudlis, 'monthly', fr. menstruus, 'pertaining
to a month, monthly', fr. mensis. See menses.

## menstraate
menstraate, intr. v., to discharge the menses. —
L. menstruatus, pp. of menstrudre, 'to
menstruate', fr. menstruus. See menstroal and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: menstruat-ion, n.

## menstruous
menstruous, adj., pertaining to, or having, the
menses. —-L. menstruus; see menstrual. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## menstruum
menstruum, п., a liquid dissolving a solid body
(originally a term of alchemy). — ML., prop,
neut. of L. menstruus, 'monthly'. See menstraal.

## mensurable
mensurable, adj. — Late L. mensurabilis, 'that
which can be measured', fr. mensurdre, 'to
measure', fr. L. mensura. See measure and -able and
cp. measurable.
Derivatives: mensurabil-ity, п., mensurable-ness,
п., mensurabl-y, adv.

## mensural
mensural, adj., 1) pertaining to measure; 2)
measurable (mus.) — ML. mensurdlis, 'pertaining to
measure', fr. L. mensura. See measure and adj.
suff. -ai.

## mensuration
mensuration, п., the act of measuring. — Late L.
mensuratid, gen. -dnis, 'a measuring', fr. mensu-
ratus, pp. of mensurdre, 'to measure', fr. L.
mensura. See measure and -ation.

## -ment
-ment, suff. expressing 1) verbal action or its
result; 2) place of action. — L. -mentum, a
secondary form of suff. -men. See -men.

## mental
mental, adj., pertaining to the mind. — ME., fr.
MF. (= F.), fr. Late L. mentdlis, 'mental', fr. L.
mens, gen. mentis, 'mind, understanding,
reason', which is cogn. with OI. matih, matih,
'thought, mind', Goth, gamunds, OE. gemynd,
'memory, remembrance'. See mind and cp. words
there referred to. For the endingsee adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives; mental-ity, п., memal-ly, adv.

## mental
mental, adj., pertaining to the chin (anat. and
zool.) — F. mental, formed with adj. suff. -al fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:484 COLUMN:3 -->
L. mentum, 'chin', for I.-E. *mntom, fr. *mnto-,
whence also W. там, 'jawbone, mouth' (Mir.
mant, 'gums', is a Welsh loan word); lit.
'something projecting', fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to
project', seen in minor!, 'to jut out, project', ё-
minere, 'to stand out, project', mons, gen.
mentis, 'mountain'. See mount, 'mountain', and
cp. mento-, mentonniere.

## mentation
mentation, п., mental function. — Formed with
suff. -ation fr. L. mens, gen. mentis. See mental,
'pertaining to the mind'.

## Mentha
Mentha, п., a genus of plants, the mint (bot.) —
L. mentha. See mint, 'an aromatic plant'.

## Menthaceae
Menthaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the mint
family; synonym of Lamiaceae (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Mentha with suff. -aceae.

## menthaceous
menthaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## menthene
menthene, п., a hydrocarbon, C10H1B, obtained
fr. menthol (chem). — Formed fr. menth(ol)
with suff. -ene.

## menthol
menthol, п., a white crystalline substance,
C10H„OH, obtained from oil of peppermint
(chem.) — Coined by Oppenheim in 1861 (see
Annalen der Chemie und Pharmacie, CXX,
352) fr. L. mentha (see Mentha) and suff. -ol (fr.
L. oleum, 'oil').

## menti-
menti-, combining form denoting the mind. — Fr.
L. mens, gen. mentis. See mental, 'pertaining to
the mind'.

## mention
mention, n. — ME. mencioun, fr. OF (= F.)
mention, fr. L. mentidnem, ace. of mentid, 'a
speaking of, a calling to mind', fr. mens, gen.
mentis. See mental, 'pertaining to the mind', and
-ion.

## mention
mention, tr. v. — F. mentionner, fr. mention. See
mention, n.
Derivatives: mention-able, adj., mention-er, n.

## mento-
mento-, combining form denoting the chin (anat.)
— Fr. L. mentum, 'chin'. See mental, 'pertaining
to the chin'.

## mentonniere
mentonniere, п., a piece of armor for the
protection of the chin. — F., fr. menton, 'chin', fr. VL.
*mentdnem, ace. of *mentd, fr. L. mentum
(whence It. mento, 'chin'). See mental,
'pertaining to the chin'.

## Mentor
Mentor, п., friend and adviserof Odysseus (Gree/t
mythol.); hence mentor, a wise adviser. — L.
Mentor, fr. Gk. Μέντωρ, lit. 'one who thinks',
cogn. with OI. man-tar-, 'one who thinks', L.
mon-i-tor, 'one who admonishes' (fr. monitus,
pp. of monere, 'to advise, warn, admonish'), fr.
I.-E. base *men-, 'to think'. See mind and -tor
and cp. monitor.

## mentum
mentum, п., the chin (anat.) — L. See mental,
'pertaining to the chin'.

## Mentzelia
Mentzelia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the German botanist Christian
Mentzel (\622-i70i). Forthe endingsee 1st suff.
-ia.

## menu
menu, п., I) a detailed list of food; 2) bill of fare;
3) the food served. — F., fr. the adj. menu,
'small, detailed', fr. L. minutus, 'small', lit. 'made
smaller', pp. of minuere, 'to make smaller,
diminish, lessen*. See minute, adj., and cp. minuet
and the first element in miniver.

## Menyanthaceae
Menyanthaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Menyanthes with suff. -aceae.

## menyanthaceous
menyanthaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Menyanthes
Menyanthes, п., a genus of plants, the buckbean
(bot.) — ModL., irregularly formed fr. Gk. μήν,
'month' and £ν*ος, 'flower'. See meno-, 'month',
and anther.

## Menziesia
Menziesia, п., a genus of plants of the heath
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
botanist Archibald Menzies (1754-1842), who
brought the species from the North West Coast
of America. For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Mephistopheles
Mephistopheles, п., the name of the evil spirit in
the Faust legend. — G., according to Schruer
(see Faust, ed. 1886,1, 25), compounded of Heb.
mephitz, 'destroyer*, and tdphel, 'liar' (which is
short for tdphel sheqer, lit. 'falsehood plasterer',
see Job 13:4). This etymology is supported by
the fact that the names of devils are in most
cases derived from Hebrew.
Derivatives: Mephistophele-an, Mephistopheli-

## an
an, Mephistophel-ic, Mephistophel-ist-ic, adjs.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:485 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MEPHITIC | 458 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:485 COLUMN:1 -->

## mephitic
mephitic, adj., exhaling poison from the earth; of
poisonous smell. — Late L. mephiticus, fr. L.
mephitis. See mephitis and adj. sufT. -ic.

## mephitis
mephitis, п., poisonous exhalation from the earth;
a poisonous smell. — L. mefitis (less correctly
spelled mephitis); of Oscan origin.

## mercantile
mercantile, adj., commercial. — F., fr. It.
mercantile, fr. L. mercans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of
mercdri, 'to trade, traffic, buy, purchase', fr.
merx, gen. mercis, 'merchandise, wares', which
is of uncertain origin. Cp. market, mart,
Mercedes, mercenary, merchandise, merchant, mercy,
amerce, commerce.

## mercantilism
mercantilism, п., the mercantile system. — F.
mercantilisme, fr. mercantile. See mercantile and
-ism.

## mercantilist
mercantilist, п., a believer in mercantilism. —
See mercantile and -izt.

## mercaptan
mercaptan, п., any of a class of compounds
analogous to the alcohols and combining readily
with mercury (chem.) — G. Mercaptan, Mer-
kaptan, coined by Zeise in 1834 fr. ML. (corpus)
mer(curium) captdns, 'striving to seize mercury'.
For the first element see mercury. L. captans is
pres. part, of capture, 'to seize; to strive after',
which is freq. of capere (pp. captus), 'to seize'.
See captive and cp. captatiou.

## Mercator Gerhardus
Mercator Gerhardus, Flemish geographer (1512-
94). — Latinized from his original name
Gerhard Kremer (kremer means 'tradesman, dealer',
and was rendered lit. by L. mercator). — Hence
Mercator's projection, a method of making
maps.

## Mercedes
Mercedes, fern. PN. — Sp. (abbreviation of Maria
de las Mercedes, 'Mary of mercies'), pi. of mer-
ced, 'mercy, grace', fr. L. mercedem, ace. of
merces, 'hire, pay, reward'. See next word.

## mercenary
mercenary, adj. — ME. mercenarie, fr. L. тегсё-
ndrius, 'hired, paid', which prob. derives fr.
*mercennos, for *mercednos, 'of pay, for hire',
fr. merces, gen. -edis, 'hire, pay, reward', fr.
merx, gen. mercis. See mercantile and adj. suff.
-ary and cp. mercy.
Derivatives: mercenary, п., mercenari-ly, adv.,
mercenari-ness, n.

## mercer
mercer, п., a dealer in textile. — F. mercier,
'trader', fr. VL. *mercidrius, fr. L. merx. gen.
mercis. See mercenary.

## mercerize
mercerize, tr. v., to treat (cotton) with a caustic
alkali. — Formed with suff. -ize from the name
of the inventor John Mercer (1791-1866).
Derivative: merceriz-ation, n.

## mercery
mercery, п., 1) mercers' goods; 2) a mercer's
trade or shop — ME. mercerie, fr. OF. (= F.)
mercerie, fr. mercier. See mercer and -y
(representing F. -ie).

## merchandise
merchandise, n. — ME. marchaundise, fr. OF.
marcheandise (F. marchandise), fr. OF. mar-
cheant, 'merchant'. See next word and subst.
suff. -ise.
Derivative: merchandise, intr. and tr. v.

## merchant
merchant, n. — ME., fr. OF. marcheant (later
marchant, marchand, F. marchand), fr. VL.
*mercatantem, ace. of *mercdtdns, pres. part, of
*mercatare (whence OProvenc. mercadar, 'to
trade'), fr. L. mercatus, 'trade, place for trade,
market place', fr. mercdri. See mercantile and
-ant. It. mercatante, Sp. mercadante, 'merchant',
also derive fr. VL. *mercatantem.
Derivative: merchant-ry, n.

## merchant
merchant, intr. and tr. v. — ME. marchaunden, fr.
OF. marcheander (F. marchander), fr.
marcheant. See merchant, n.
Derivative: merchant-able, adj.

## Mercurialis
Mercurialis, п., a genus of plants, the mercury
(pot.) — L., short for herba Mercurialis, name
.of a plant mentioned by Pliny, lit. meaning
'belonging to the god Mercury'. See Mercury.

## Mercury
Mercury, п., 1) the god of traders and thieves and
the messenger of the gods in Roman mythology;
identified later with the Greek Hermes; 2)
name of the smallest planet in the solar system.
— L. Mercurius, fr. Etruscan *Mercura, a
divinity introduced from Etruria into Rome
about the end of the sixth century B.C.E. (see
Ribezzo in Rivista indo-greco-italica, 15,99);

## prob. not related to L. merx
prob. not related to L. merx, gen. mercis,
'merchandise'. Cp. mercury, the element.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:485 COLUMN:2 -->

## mercury
mercury, п., name of a silvery-white, fluid
metallic element (chem.) — Named after Mercury,
the messenger of the gods in Greek mythology;
prob. so called because of the great mobility of
this element.
Derivatives: mercuri-al, adj., mercuri-al-ly, adv.,
mercuri-al-ness,a.,mercur-ic,Sidj.,mercur-ous,ud}.

## mercy
mercy, n. — ME. merci, fr. OF. mercit, merci (F.
merci), fr. L. mercedem, ace. of merces, 'hire,
pay, reward' (in VL. also 'favor, pity'), fr. merx,
gen. mercis, 'merchandise, wares'. It. merce, Sp.
merced, 'favor, grace, mercy', also derive fr. L.
mercedem. See mercantile and cp. gramercy.
Derivatives: merci-ful, adj., merci-ful-ly, adv.,
merci-ful-ness, a., merci-less, adj., merci-less-ly,
adv., merci-less-ness, n.
mercy seat. — Coined by Tyndale; prop, a loan
translation of Luther's gnadenstuhl, an inexact
rendering of Heb. kapporeth, which lit. means
'propitiatory', fr. kipper, 'he propitiated,
expiated'.

## merd
merd, п., dung (obsol.) — F. merde, fr. L. merda,
'dung', which is of uncertain origin.

## mere
mere, п., 1) the sea; 2) a lake (archaic or dial.) —
ME. mere, fr. OE. mere, 'sea, lake', rel. to ON.
marr, OS. meri, 'sea', Du. meer, 'lake', OHG.
mari, meri, MHG. mer, G. Meer, 'sea', Goth.
marei, 'sea', mari-saiws 'lake', and cogn. with
L. mare, 'sea', OSlav. morje, 'sea', Lith. mures,
'sea, Baltic Sea', Olr. muir (fr. OCeltic *mori),
Co., W. mor, 'sea', Gaul. Are-moricl, 'people
living near the sea'. Cp. mare, 'sea', maremma,
marine, marram grass, marsh, moor, 'waste
ground', morass, the first element in meerkat,
meerschaum, Merlin, mermaid, merman, Muriel,
the second element in cormorant, Pomeranian,
rosemary, and the last element in bechc-de-mer.

## mere
mere, п., a boundary; a landmark. — ME., fr.
OE. mxre, gemzre, 'boundary', rel. to ON.
mxri, lanaa-mxri, 'boundary, border land*,
MDu. mere, 'boundary mark, stake', and prob.
cogn. with L. murus, 'wall'. See mural.

## mere
mere, adj., pure. — ME., fr. L. merus, 'pure,
unmixed', orig. prob. 'bright, clear', cogn. with
OE. d-merian, 'to purify', Olr. i-mer, 'not clear',
and prob. also with OI. maricih marici, 'ray,
beam', Gk. μαρμαΕρειν, 'to gleam, glimmer', fr.
I.-E. base "mer-, 'to gleam, glimmer, sparkle'.
See morn and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: merely, adv.

## merel
merel, п., the morris game. — ME. merel,
'counter', fr. OF. merel, marel, 'counter quoit' (whence
F. marelle, 'hopscotch'); of uncertain origin.
Cp. morris, 'an old game'.

## meretricious
meretricious, adj., pertaining to a prostitute. —
L. meretricius, 'pertaining to harlots', fr. mere-
trix, gen. -ids, 'harlot', lit. 'one who earns
money (scil. by prostitution)', fr. merer! (pp. meri-
tus), 'to earn'. See merit and -ous.
Derivatives: meretricious-ly, adv., meretricious-
ness, n.

## merganser
merganser, п., any of several ducks constituting
the subfamily Merginae (ornithol.) — ModL.,
compounded of L. mergus, a kind of diving bird,
fr. mergere, 'to dip, immerse, plunge', and anser,
'goose'. See merge and Anser.

## merge
merge, tr. and intr. v., to combine. — L. mergo,
mergere, 'to dip, immerse, plunge', which stands
for *mezgd (see rhotacism) and h cogn. with OI.
mdjjati, 'dives under', majjayati, 'causes to dive
under', Lith. mazgoju, mazgoti, Lett, mazgaju,
mazgat, 'to wash'. Cp. Mergus. Cp. also
demersal, emerge, emergency, emersion, immerge,
immerse, immersion, Mergus, submerge,
submersion.
Derivatives: merge, п., merg-ence, п., merg-er, n.

## merger
merger, п., the absorption of an estate, contract,
etc., in another (law). — Formed on analogy of
OF. infinitives used as nouns. See prec. word
and cp. user.

## Merginae
Merginae, п., subfamily of the mergansers
(ornithol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -inae fr. L.
mergus. See next word.

## Mergus
Mergus, п., the typical genus of the mergansers
(ornithol.) — L. mergus, 'diver*, fr. mergere. See
merge.

## mericarp
mericarp, п., one of the two carpels forming a
cremocarp (hot.) — F. mericarpe, compounded

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:485 COLUMN:3 -->
of Gk. μέρος, 'part', and καρπός, 'fruit*. See
mero-, 'part', and carpel and cp. cremocarp,
carpophore.

## meridian
meridian, adj., pertaining to noon; on, or
pertaining to, a meridian; п., the highest point
attained by a heavenly body; (geogr.) an
imaginary circle passing through the poles and any
given point on the earth's surface. — ME. meri-
dien, fr. OF. meridien (F. meridien), fr. L. meri-
dianus, 'of midday, of noon, of the south', fr.
meridies, 'midday, noon, south', which was
formed—prob. under the influence of merus,
'pure',—fr. *medei-die, dissimilation of *mediei-
die, fr. medius, 'middle', and dies, 'day'. See
media, 'voiced stop consonant', and dies поп.
For the ending see suff. -an.

## meridional
meridional, adj., pertaining to a meridian;
southern. — Late ME., fr. OF. meridional (F.
meridional), fr. Late L. meridionalis, 'of midday, of
the south', enlarged fr. meridialis, of s.m., fr.
meridies, 'midday, noon, south' (see meridian),
on analogy of its antonym septentridnalis, 'of
the north', fr. septentrio, gen. -onis, 'north' (see
septentrional. Cp. Arab, shamlf, 'northern', and
janbt, 'southern', shortened fr. shamdlf, resp.
janubi, on analogy of sharqt 'eastern'," and
gharbi, 'western'.
Derivatives: meridionat-ty, adv., meridional-ity,
n.

## meringue
meringue, п., whites of eggs mixed with sugar,
baked and browned. — F. meringue, of
unknown origin.
Derivative: meringu-ed, adj.

## merino
merino, п., a fine-wooled breed of sheep
originating in NW. Africa.— Sp. merino, named after
Bern Merin, a Berber tribe of NW. Africa.

## merism
merism, п., synecdoche in which a totality is
expressed by two contrasting parts, as high and
low, rich and poor (rhet.) — ModL. merismus, fr.
Gk. μερισμός, 'dividing, partition', fr. μερίζειν,
'to divide', fr. μέρος, 'part'. See mero-, 'part',
and -ism and cp. next word. Cp. also allome-
rism, tantomerism.

## merlsmatic
merlsmatic, adj., capable of active division (of
cells). — Formed with 1st suff. -atic fr. ModL.
merisma, fr. Gk. μέρισμα, 'division', fr. με-
ρίζειν, 'to divide', fr. μέρος, 'part'. See mero-,
'part'.

## meristem
meristem, п., cell-tissue growing and capable of
division (bot.) — Fr. Gk. μεριστός, 'divided',
verbal adj. of μερίζειν, 'to divide', fr. μέρος,
'part'. See mero-, 'part'.
Derivative: meristem-atic, adj.

## merit
merit, n. — ME., merite, merit, fr. OF. merite (F.
merite), fr. L. meritum, 'desert, reward, merit',
prop. neut. pp. of merere, mereri, 'to earn,
obtain, deserve, merit', fr. I.-E. base *(s)mer-, 'to
allot, assign', whence also Gk. μέρος, 'part,
lot', μείρομαι (for "μέρι,ομαι), Ί receive my
share', μοίρα (for *μόρια), 'share, fate', μόρος,
'fate, destiny, doom', Hitt. mar-k, 'to divide (a
sacrifice)'. Cp. mero-, 'part', and words there
referred to. Cp. also demerit, emeritas,
meretricious.

## merit
merit, tr. v. — MF. (= F.) miriter, fr. merite. See
merit, n.
Derivatives: merit-ed, adj., merit-ed-ly, adv.,
merit-er, n.

## meritorious
meritorious, adj. — ME., fr. L. meritorius, 'that
for which money is paid, that by which money
is earned', fr. meritus, pp. of merere, mereri. See
merit, п., and -orious and cp. demeritorious.
Derivatives: meritorious-ly, adv., meritorious-
ness, n.

## merle'
merle', also meri, п., the blackbird. — F. merle, fr.
L. merula, 'blackbird', which stands for *mesola
(see rhotacism), and is cogn. with OE. osle (for
*amsle), 'ouzel'. See amsel, ouzel and cp. Meru-
lius.

## merlin
merlin, п., a small, strong European falcon (Fal-
co aesalon). — ME. meriloun, fr. AF. merilun, fr.
OF. esmerillon (F. emerillon), fr. OF. esmeril, fr.
Frankish 'smiril, which is rel. to OHG. smerlo,
smiril, MHG. smirel, smirlin, G. Schmerl,
'merlin', MHG. smerle, smerlinc, G. Schmerle,
'loach' (name of a fish). It. smeriglio, smeriglione,
ΟΡΓονεης. esmirle and Sp. esmerejon, 'merlin',
are also Teut. loan words.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:486 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 459 | MESOPOTAMIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:486 COLUMN:1 -->

## Merlin
Merlin, п., in medieval legend, a Welsh magician
and seer who lived at King Arthur's court. —
ML. Merlinus, fr. W. Merddin, Myrddin, fr.
OCeltic *Mori-dunon, a name lit. meaning 'of
the seahill', fr. *mori, 'sea', and "dunom, 'hill'.
See mere, 'sea', and dun, 'hill'.

## merlon
merlon, п., the solid part of a battlement. — F.
merlon, fr. It. merhne, augment, oimerlo, merla,
'battlement', prob. contraction of mergola, di-
min. formed fr. L. mergae, 'a two-pronged
pitchfork', lit. 'that which is used for plucking off',
rel. to merges, 'sheaf, and possibly cogn. with
Gk. άμέργειν, 'to gather (fruit, etc.)', όμορ-
γνύναι, 'to wipe', and Ol. mrjdti, 'wipes'.

## mermaid
mermaid, n. — Lit. 'maid of the sea', fr. ME.
meremaid. See mere, 'the sea', and maid.

## merman
merman, n. — Lit. 'man of the sea', fr. ME. mere-
man. See mere, 'sea', and man and cp. prec.
word.

## Mermis
Mermis, п., name of a genus of worms (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. μέρμϊς, 'cord', which is
possibly rel. to (σ)μήρινθος, 'thread'.

## mero-
mero-, before a vowel mer-, combining form
meaning 'part; partial'. — Gk. μερο-, μερ-, fr.
μέρος, 'part, lot', which is cogn. with L. merere,
mereri, 'to earn, obtain, deserve, merit'. See
merit and cp. merism, meristem, isomeric,
polymer. Cp. also Moira, morioplasty.

## mero-
mero-, before a vowel mer-, combining form
meaning 'thigh' (anat.) — Gk. μηρό-, μηρ,- fr.
μηρός, 'thigh', which stands for "mems-ro- or
*mes-ro- and is cogn. with L. membrum (for
*mems-rom), 'limb, member, part'. See member.

## meroblastic
meroblastic, adj., undergoing partial
segmentation (embryo!.) — Compounded of mero-,
'partial', and Gk. βλαστός, 'bud, 'sprout, shoot'.
See -blastic.

## meroplankton
meroplankton, п., plankton found only at
certain times of the year. — Compounded of mero-,
'part', and plankton.

## Merops
Merops, п., the typical genus of bee-eaters (orni-
thol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μέροψ, 'bee-eater',
which is of uncertain origin.

## -merous
-merous, adj., having a specified number of parts,
as in trimerous, decamerous. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. Gk. μέρος, 'part'. See mero-,
'part'.

## Merovingian
Merovingian, adj., pertaining to the first Fran-
kish dynasty in Gaul, founded by Clovis. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. Late L. Merovingl,
'descendants of Merovaeus', Latinized name of
a mythical early king of the Franks.
Derivative: Merovingian, n.

## merry
merry, adj., gay. — ME. merie, m.i 'e, fr. OE.
myrge, myrige, myrig, mirig, 'pleasing,
delightful, merry', orig. 'that which makes the time
short'; rel. to OHG. murg, murgi, 'short', Goth.
*maurgus, 'short' (only in the compound ga-
maurgjan, 'to shorten'), and cogn. with Gk.
βραχύς, L. brevis, 'short'. See brief,' adj., and cp.
brachy-. Cp. also mirth. For the sense
development of E. merry (from a base meaning 'short')
cp. G. Kurzweil, 'pastime', lit. 'a short lime'.
Derivatives; merri-ly, adv., merri-ment, п.,
merri-ness, n.

## merry
merry, п., the wild black cherry. — F. merise, for
*amerise, a blend of amer, 'bitter' (fr. L. ama-
rus), and cerise, 'cherry' (fr. VL. *ceresia)', see
amarine and cherry. The a in *amerisc was
mistaken for part of the article (I'amerise was mis-
divided into fa merise) and was dropped
accordingly. The s of F. merise was mistaken for the
plural suffix and so F. merise became merry in
English. Ср. Е. cherry (fr. F. cerise).

## Mertcnsia
Mertcnsia, п., a genus of plants of the borage
family (boi.) — ModL., named after the
German botanist Franz Karl Mertens (1764-1831).
For the ending see I st suff. -ia.

## Merulius
Merulius, п., name of a genus of fungi (bot.) —
ModL., lit. 'of the color of the blackbird', fr. L.
merula. See merle.

## merwinite
merwinite, п., a calcium magnesium orthosilicate
(mineral.) — Named after the American geo-
physicist Dr. Herbert E. Merwin (born in 1878).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## mes-
mes-, form of meso- before a vowel.

## mesa
mesa, п., table land, plateau. — Sp., 'table; table

## land
land, plateau', fr. VL. mesa, 'table' (whence also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:486 COLUMN:2 -->
Rum. masa, OF. moise, OProvenc., Port, mesa,
'table'), fr. L. mensa. See mensal, 'pertaining to
the table'.

## mesalliance
mesalliance, п., marriage with a person of lower
social position. — F., formed fr. pejorative pref.
mes- (fr. L. mis-) and alliance. See mis- and
alliance and cp. misalliance.

## mesati-
mesati-, combining form meaning 'midmost'. —
Fr. Gk. μεσάτος, 'midmost', superl. of μέσος,
'middle'. See meso-.

## mescal
mescal, п., an intoxicating spirit made from
pulque, which is prepared from the fermented juice
of the agave. — Sp. mezcal, fr. Nahuatl mexcatli.

## mescaline
mescaline, п., a crystalline alkali, id (CnH1703N)
(chem.) — Formed fr. mescal with chem. suff.
-ine; so called because it is found in mescal
buttons.

## mesdames
mesdames, п., pi. of madame, madam,

## mesdemoiselles
mesdemoiselles, п., pi. of mademoiselle,

## mesel
mesel, adj., leprous; п., a leper (obsol.)—ME., fr.
OF., 'leprous', fr. L. misellus, 'unfortunate' (in
ML. used also in the sense 'leper'), dimin. of L.
miser; see miser. Cp. Olt. misello, 'sick, leprous',
Rum. misel, 'miserable, base, mean', OProvenc.
mesel, 'leprous', Catal. meseil, 'sick', which all
derive fr. L. misellus.

## Mesembryanrhemum
Mesembryanrhemum, п., a genus of plants, the
fig marigold (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'noon flower',
compounded of Gk. μεσημβρία, 'noon', and
όίνθεμαν, 'flower'. The first element is
compounded of μέσος, 'middle', and ημέρα, 'day';
see meso- and hemero-. The second element
derives fr. £ν*ας, 'flower'; see anther. The correct
spelling of the word is Mesembrianthemum. The
у (corresponding to Gk. v) is a misspelling for i
(Gk. i) in μεσημβρία (see above), and prob.
due to a confusion with Gk. έμβρυον, 'embryo'.

## mesencephalon
mesencephalon, п., the middle part of the brain
(anat.) — Medical L., compounded of mes- and
encephalon.
Derivative': mesencephal-ic, adj.

## mesenchyme
mesenchyme, mesenchyme, п., that portion of the
mesoderm which produces all the connective
tissues of the body (embryol.) — Medical L.,
formed on analogy of parenchyma fr. Gk. μέσος,
'middle' and εγχυμα, 'filling (of a vessel),
instillation'. See meso- and enchymatous. The
term mesenchyme was introduced into
embryology by the German embryologists Oskar Hert-
wig (1849-1922) and his brother Richard (1850-
1937) in 1881.
Derivatives: mesenchym-al, mesenchym-at-ous,
adjs.

## mesenteric
mesenteric, п., inflammation of the mesentery
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -iris fr.
Gk. μεσεντέριον. See next word.
Derivative: mesenterit-ic, adj.

## mesentery
mesentery, п., a fold of the peritoneum attached
to the posterior abdominal wall (anal.) —
Medical L. mesenterium, lit. 'middle of the
intestine', fr. Gk. μεσεντέριον, shortened fr. δέρμα
μεσεντέριον, 'membrane to which the
intestines are attached', fr. μέσος, 'middle', and
έντερα (pi.), 'intestines'. See meso- and enteric.
Derivatives: mesenleri-al, mesenter-ic, mesenter-
ic-al, adjs., mesenter-ic-al-ly, adv.

## mesh
mesh, п., any of the open spaces of a net. —
Earlier meash, mash, meish, fr. obsol. Du.
maesche (whence Du. maas), fr. MDu. maessce,
rel. to OE. max (for *mxsc), OS. masca, ON.
moskvi, Dan. maske, Swed. maska, OHG.
masca, MHG., G. masche, 'mesh'; fr. I.-E. base
*mezg-, 'to knit, plait, twist', whence also
Lith. mezgit, megsti, 'to knit', mdzgas, 'knot',
Lett, mazgs, 'knot'.
Derivatives: mesh, tr. and intr. v., mesh-ed, adj.

## mesial
mesial, adj., middle, median. — Formed with
suff. -ial fr. Gk. μέσος, 'middle'. See meso-.
Derivative: mesiat-ly, adv.

## mesityl
mesityl, п., a hypothetical radical, C3Hs(chem.)
— Coined fr. Gk. μεσίτης, 'mediator' (fr.
μέσος, 'middle'), and suff. -yl. See meso-.

## mesitylene
mesitylene, п., a hydrocarbon С,Н,(СН3),, (chem.)
— Formed fr. mesityl with suff. -ene.

## mesmeric
mesmeric, adj., pertaining to mesmerism. — See
mesmerism and -ic.
Derivative: mesmeric-al-ly, adv.

## mesmerism
mesmerism, п., hypnotism. — Named after the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:486 COLUMN:3 -->
Austrian physician Friedrich Anton Mesmer
(1734-1815). For the ending see suff. -ism.

## mesmerist
mesmerist, п., a hypnotist. — See prec. word and
-ist.

## mesmerize
mesmerize, tr. v., to hypnotize. — See mesmerism
and -ize.
Derivative: mesmeriz-ation, n.

## mesnalty
mesnalty, п., the estate or the condition of a
mesne lord. — AF. mesnalte, menalte, fr. mesne,
mene, 'mesne'. See next word and -ty.

## mesne
mesne, adj., intermediate, middle; mesne lord,
one who is both a tenant of a superior lord and
a lord of a subordinate tenant. — AF. mesne, a
var. of AF. meen, which corresponds to OF.
meien, 'middle', fr. L. medianus, 'middle'. See
mean, 'intermediate', and cp. words there
referred to.

## meso-
meso-, before a vowel mes-, combining form
meaning 'middle, intermediate'. — Gk. μέσο-,
μεσ-, fr. μέσος, 'middle', which stands for
"medhyos, and is cogn. with OI. madhyah, L.
medius, 'middle'. See media, 'voiced stop
consonant', and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also mesati-, mesial·.

## mesohlast
mesohlast, п., the mesoderm. — Compounded of
meso- and Gk. βλαστός, 'bud, sprout, shoot'.
See -blast.
Derivative: mesobtast-ic, adj.

## mesocarp
mesocarp, п., the middle layer of a pericarp (bot.)
— Compounded of meso- and Gk. καρπός,
'fruit'. See carpel and cp. words there referred
to.

## mesocephalic
mesocephalic, adj., having a medium cranial
capacity (anat.) — Compounded of meso- and Gk.
κεφαλικός, 'pertaining to the head', fr. κεφαλή,
'head'. See cephalic.

## mesoderm
mesoderm, п., the middle germ layer of an embryo
(embryol.) — Lit. 'middle skin', coined by the
German physician Robert Remak (1815-65) fr.
meso- and Gk. δέρμα, 'skin'. See derma.
Derivative: mesoderm-ic, adj.

## mesollte
mesollte, п., a zeolitic mineral. — G. Mesolith, fr.
Gk. μέσος, 'middle', and λίθος, 'stone' (see
meso- and -lite); so called because it is
intermediate between natrolite and scolecite.

## nasogastric
nasogastric, adj., pertaining to the umbilical
region (anat.) — Formed from next word with
suff. -Ic. Cp. epigastric, hypogastric.

## mesogastrium
mesogastrium, п., the umbilical region. —
Medical L., compounded of meso- and Gk. γαστήρ,
'belly'. See gastric and cp. epigastrium, hypo-
gastrium.

## mesognathic
mesognathic, adj., mesognathous. — See
mesognathous and adj. suff. -ic.

## mesognathous
mesognathous, adj., having medium-sized and
slightly projecting jaws (anthropom.) —
Compounded of meso- and Gk. γνάθος, 'jaw, cheek'.
See guathic and -ous.

## meson
meson, п., the median or mesial plane. — ModL.,
fr. Gk. μέσον, neut. of μέσος, 'middle'. See
meso-.

## meson
meson, п., a musical tetrachord. — Gk. μέσων,
genit. pi. of μέση (short for μέση χορδή),
'middle note', fern, of μέσος, 'middle'. See meso-.

## meson
meson, п., a mesotron (phys.) — Short for
mesotron.

## mesonephros
mesonephros, п., the middle kidney of a vertebrate
embryo (embryol.) — Medical L.,
compounded of meso- and Gk. νεφρός, 'kidney'. See
nephro-. The term mesonephros was introduced
into embryology by the English zoologist Sir
Edwin Ray Lankester (1847-1930). Cp. meta-
nephros, pronephros.
Derivative: mesonephr-ic, adj.

## mesophyll
mesophyll, п., the green parenchyma inside a leaf
(bot.) — Compounded of meso- and Gk. φύλ-
λον, 'a leaf. See phyllo-.

## mesophyte
mesophyte, п., a plant that grows under
conditions of medium moisture (bot.)—Compounded
of meso- and Gk. φυτόν, 'plant'. See -phyte.
Derivative: mesophyt-ic, adj.

## mesoplast
mesoplast, п., the nucleus of a cell (Wo/.) —
Compounded of meso- and Gk. -πλαστός, fr.
πλαστός, 'molded, formed'. See -plast.
Derivative: mesoplast-ic, adj.

## Mesopotamia
Mesopotamia, п., name of the ancient country
between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers. — Gk.
Μεσοποταμία (scil. χώρα}, 'the country be-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:487 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MESOTHELIAL | 460 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:487 COLUMN:1 -->
tween two rivers', fem. of μεσοποτάμιος,
'situated between two rivers', which is
compounded of μέσος, 'middle', and ποταμός,
'river'. See mesa- and potamo-.
Derivatives: Mesopotami-an, adj. and n.

## mesotheUal
mesotheUal, adj. — Formed from next word with
adj. suff. -al,

## mesothellum
mesothellum, п., epithelium of mesodermic
origin (embryol.) — Medical L., an blend of meso-
and epithelium,

## mesothorax
mesothorax, п., the middle of the three segments
of an insect's thorax (entomol.) — ModL.,
compounded of meso- and thorax.
Derivative: mesothorac-ic, adj.

## mesothorium
mesothorium, п., either of two radioactive
disintegration products, intermediate between
radium and radiothorium (chem.) — ModL.,
compounded of mesa- and thorium; so called
because it is intermediate between radium and
radiothorium.

## mesotron
mesotron, п., an unstable particle, about 200
times the mass of the electron (phys.) —
Formed fr. meso- and (elec)tron.

## Mesozoic
Mesozoic, adj., designating the era between the
Paleozoic and the Cenozoic (geol.) —
Compounded of meso-, Gk. ζωή, 'life' (see zoo-),
and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: Mesozoic, n.

## mesquin
mesquin, adj., mean, sordid. — F., fr. It. meschi-
no, fr. Arab, misktn (in VArab. pronunciation
meskin), 'poor, wretched, miserable', which is
borrowed fr. Heb. or Aram, misken or Syr.
mesken, 'poor', which are perh. loan words fr.
Akkad. mushkenu, 'beggar, needy'.

## mesqnite
mesqnite, п., a mosque (obsol.) — Sp. mesquita
(ModSp. mezquita), 'mosque'. See mosque,

## mesquite
mesquite, also mesquit, п., cither of two shrubs of
the pea family. — Sp. mezquite, fr. Nahuatl miz-
quitl.

## mess
mess, п., food for one meal; pottage. — ME. mes,
fr. OF. mes (now spelled mets), 'food, dish (of
food)', fr. VL. missum, lit. 'that which is placed
(on the table)', neut. pp. of L. mittere, 'to send*
(in VL. also 'to put, place'). See mission and cp.
entremets.
Derivatives: mess, tr. and intr. v., mess-y, adj.,
mess-i-ly, adv., mess-i-ness, n.

## message
message, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. VL. *mis-
saticum, 'message', fr. L. missus, pp. of mittere,
'to send*. See mission and -age and cp.
messenger.
Derivative: message, tr. v.

## Messapian
Messapian, adj., pertaining to the Messapii; п., а
native of Messapia. — Formed with suff. -au fr.
L. Messapii, fr. Gk. Μεσσάπιοι, 'Messapians',
lit. 'they who live between two waters',
compounded of μέσσος, μέσος, 'middle', and base
*άπ-, 'water'. For the first element see meso-,
for the second see amine and cp. the second
element in doab.

## messelite
messelite, п., a calcium iron phosphate (mineral.)
— Named after Messel in Hesse, Germany. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## messenger
messenger, n. — ME. messager, messangere, mes-

## sengere
sengere, fr. OF. messagier (F. messager), fr.
message. See message and agential suff. -er. The
л in messenger is intrusive; cp. harbinger,

## passenger
passenger, porringer, scavenger, wharfinger.

## Messiah
Messiah, n. — Aram, m shiha, 'the anointed', fr.

## Heb. mashfuh
Heb. mashfuh, 'anointed', fr. mashdh, 'he

## anointed'
anointed', whence mishhah, 'ointment; consecrated
portion'; rel. to Aram.-Syr. nfshah, 'he

## anointed'
anointed', meshah, mishhah, Syr. meshha, Oil', Ethiop.

## masaha
masaha, 'he anointed; he feasted', Akkad.

## mashu'u
mashu'u, 'to spread (oil) over', Arab, masaha,
'he stroke or wiped with the hand*. Cp. Messias.
Derivatives: Messiah-ship, п., Messi-an-ic, adj.

## Messias
Messias, п., the Messiah. — Late L., fr. Gk. Μεσ-
σίας, fr. Aram, rrfshiha, 'the anointed'. See
Messiah.

## Messidor
Messidor, п., name of the 10th month of the
French revolutionary calendar (lasting fr. June
19th to July 18th). — F., a hybrid coined by

## Fabre d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. L. messis
Fabre d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. L. messis,
'harvest' [fr. mess-(um), pp. stem of metere, 'to reap,

## mow
mow, crop'], and Gk. δώρον, 'gift'. For the first

## element see mow
element see mow, 'to cut (grass)', for the second
see donation and cp. the second element in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:487 COLUMN:2 -->
with Gk. μέσος, L. medius, 'middle', OE. midd,
etc., 'mid'. See meso-, media, 'voiced stop
consonant', and cp. mid, middle and the first
element in midwife.

## metabasis
metabasis, п., transition (esp. in rhet., from one
subject to another); change (med.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. μετάβασις, 'a passing over, changing', fr-
μεταβαίνειν, 'to pass over', which is formed fr.
μετά- (see meta-) and βαίνειν, 'to go'. See base,
n.

## Metahola
Metahola, п., a division of insects that undergo
complete metamorphosis (zool.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. μεταβολή, 'change', fr. μεταβάλλειν, 'to
turn quickly, turn about, change', fr. μετα-
(see meta-) and βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See
ballistic and cp. words there referred to.

## metabolic
metabolic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized
by, metabolism (biol. and chem.) — G. meta-
bolisch, fr. Gk. μεταβολικός, 'changeable', fr.
μεταβολή. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ish,
resp. -ic.

## metabolism
metabolism, п., process of building up assimilated
food into protoplasm (anabolism) and breaking
down protoplasm into simpler substances
(catabolism) (physiol.) — Formed with suff.
-ism fr. Gk. μεταβολή. See Metaboin.

## metabolite
metabolite, п., a product of metabolism (physiol.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk.
μεταβολή. See Metahola.

## metabolize
metabolize, tr. v., to change by metabolism
(physiol.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ize fr. Gk.
μεταβολή. See Metahola.

## metacarpus
metacarpus, п., bones of the palm of the hand
(anat.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μετακάρπιον, fr.
μετά- (see meta-) and καρπός, 'wrist'. See carpus.
Derivative: metacarp-al, adj.

## metacenter
metacenter, metacentre, n. (hydrostatics and
shipbuilding). — Formed fr. meta- and center
(centre).
Derivatives: metacentr-al, metacentr-ic, adjs.,
metacentr-ic-ity, n.

## metachemistry
metachemistry, п., higher chemistry. — Formed
fr. meta- and chemistry.

## metachromatjsm
metachromatjsm, п., change of color (esp. due to
a change in temperature). — Formed fr. meta-
and Gk. χρώμα, 'color'. See chrome and -izm.

## metachronism
metachronism, п., an error in chronology
consisting in placing an event after its real date. — ML.
metachronismus, irregularly formed fr. Gk.
μετάχρονος, μεταχρόνιος, 'after the time, done
afterward', fr. μετά- (see meta-) and χρόνος,
Fructidor, Thermidor.

## messienrs
messienrs, п., pi. of monsieur.

## messire
messire, п., a French title of honor and form of
address. — OF., nom., lit. 'my lord'. See
monsieur, seigueur, sire.

## messmate
messmate, n. — Lit. 'companion in a mess';
compounded of mess and mate, 'companion'.

## messrs
messrs, n. pi. — Abbreviation of messieurs.

## messuage
messuage, п., dwelling (law). — ME., fr. AF.
messuage, mesuage, prob. orig. a clerical error
for mesnage. See menage.

## mestee
mestee, п., a mustee. — See mustee.

## mestizo
mestizo, п., a person of mixed parentage, esp. one
of Spanish and American Indian blood. — Sp.,
fr. Late L. mixticius, misticius, 'of mixed race',
fr. L. mixtus, 'mixed', pp. of misclre, 'to mix,
mingle'. See mix and cp. metis.

## met
met, past tense and pp. of meet.

## meta- (before consonants)
meta- (before consonants), met- (before vowels),
meth- (before aspirated vowels), pref. meaning
1) after, behind (as in metaphysics); 2) changed
inform, altered (as in metamorphosis); 3) higher
(used to designate a higher degree of a branch
of science (as in metachemistry — higher
chemistry). This usage is due to the analogy of the
word metaphysics, which was misinterpreted as
