'the science of that which is beyond the
physical'. In chemistry, meta- is used to denote 1) a
polymeric compound (as in metaldehyde = a
polymeric compound of aldehyde); 2) a
derivative of the compound given (as in metaprotein
= a derivative of protein). — Gk. μετά-, resp.
μετ-, μεθ-, fr. μετά, 'in the midst of, among,
between, with', cogn. with Goth, mip, OHG.
mil, mitt, MHG. mil. mite, G. mil. OFris. mith,
mithi, OS. mid, midi, ON. med, OE. mid, mid,
'with, together with, among', and prob. also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:487 COLUMN:3 -->
'time'. See chronic and -ism and cp.
anachronism, parachronism.

## metachrosis
metachrosis, п., change of color (esp. in certain
reptiles and fishes (zool.) — ModL., formed fr.
meta- and Gk. χρώσις, 'color, coloring', fr.
χρώζειν, 'to tinge, color', fr. χρως, gen.
χρωτός, 'color'. See chrome and cp. metachroma-
tism.

## metage
metage, п., official measuring of
weight.—Formed with suff. -age from the verb mete.

## Metageitnion
Metageitnion, п., name of the 2nd month of the
Attic Greek calendar (corresponding to August-
September). — Gk. Μεταγειτνιών, fr. μετα-
(see meta-) and γείτων, 'neighbor"; so called
because in this month people flitted and
consequently changed their neighbors. The
etymology of γείτων is unknown.

## metagenesis
metagenesis, п., alternation of generation. —
Formed fr. meta- and Gk. γένεσις, 'origin,
source, birth, race, descent'. See genesis.

## metagenetic
metagenetic, adj., pertaining to metagenesis. —
Formed fr. meta- and genetic. Cp. prec. word.

## metal
metal, n. — ME., fr. OF. metal, metail (F. metal),
fr. L. metallum, 'mine, quarry, mineral, metal',
fr. Gk. μέταλλον, 'mine, quarry", which is of
uncertain origin. It is perh. a loan word fr. Heb.
mitzolah, mitzulah, 'depth'; see H. Lewy, Die
semitischen Fremdworter im Griechischen, p.
132, and Gesenius-Buhl, Η WAT., 16th edition,
p. 452 s.v. *η/(ζσ/ά\ Heb. m6tz6lah is rel. to
tzUlah, 'ocean-deep', and to Heb. tzalal, 'he
sank', Ethiop. salala, 'he floated', Akkad. salalu,
'to sink down'. For the sense development of
Gk. μέταλλον fr. Heb. nftzOla', 'depth', cp.
Gk. μεταλλαν, 'to search after, inquire about',
which is connected with μέταλλον and prob.
meant originally 'to search in the depth'. Cp.
medal, mettle and the second element in
monometallism, bimetallism.
Derivatives: metall-ic, metall-ine, adjs., metail-
ist, п., metall-ize, tr. v., metall-iz-ation, n.

## metalliferous
metalliferous, adj., bearing metals. —
Compounded of L. metallum, 'metal', and the stem
of/его, ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See -ferous.

## metallography
metallography, п., the study of metals. — Lit.
'description of metals', fr. Gk.
μέταλλον,'metal', and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
metal and -graphy.
Derivatives: metallograph-ic, metallograph-ic-al,
adjs., metallograph-ic-cal-ty, adv.

## metalloid
metalloid, adj., resembling metals. —
Compounded of Gk. μέταλλον, 'metal', and -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: metalloid, п., 1) a nonmetal; 2) an
element resembling metals in some—but not in
all—respects.

## metallurgy
metallurgy, n. — ModL. metallurgia, fr. Gk.
μεταλλουργός, 'worker in metal', which ■ is
compounded of μέταλλον, 'metal', and έργον,
'work'. See metal and ergon.
Derivatives: metallurg-ic, metatlurg-ic-at, adjs.,
metallurg-ic-al-ly, adv., metallurg-ist, n.

## metamere
metamere, п., one of a series of similar
longitudinal segments of the body of the earthworm and
other animals (zool.) — Compounded of meta-
and Gk. μέρος, 'part'. See mero-, 'part'.

## metameric
metameric, adj. (zool.), 1) pertaining to meta-
meres; 2) characterized by metamerism. —
Formed fr. prec. word with adj. suff. -ic.

## metamerism
metamerism, п., the state of being composed of
metameres (zool.) — Formed fr. metamere with
suff. -Ism.

## metamorphic
metamorphic, adj., pertaining to, or
characterized by, change. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr.
meta-, a prefix denoting change, and Gk. μορφή,
'form, shape'. See niorpho-.

## metamorphism
metamorphism, п., change of form; specif.,
change in the structure of a rock. — Formed
with suff. -ism fr. meta-, a prefix denoting
change, and Gk. μορφή, 'form, shape'. See
morpho-.

## metamorphose
metamorphose, tr. and intr. v., to change in form.
— MF. (= F.) metamorphoser, fr.
metamorphose, fr. L. metamorphosis. See next
word.

## metamorphosis
metamorphosis, п., change of form,
transformation. — L., fr. Gk. μεταμόρφωσις,
'transformation', fr. μεταμορφοΰν, 'to transform',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:488 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 461 | -METER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:488 COLUMN:1 -->
which is formed fr. μετά (see nieta-), and μορ-
φοϋν, 'to give form to', fr. μορφή, 'form,
shape'. See morpho- and -osis.

## metanalysis
metanalysis, п., the analysis of words or groups
of words into elements contrary to their
structure» as an adder for a nadder. — Coined by the
Danish philologist Otto Jespersen (1860-1943)
fr. met- and analysis,

## metanephros
metanephros, п., the third kidney of a vertebrate
embryo (embryol.) — Medical L., compounded
of meta- and Gk. νεφρός, 'kidney'; see nephron
The term metanephros was introduced into
embryology by the English zoologist Sir Edwin
Ray Lankester (1847-1930). Cp. mesonephros,
pronephros.

## metaphor
metaphor, п., a figure of speech in which a thing
is likened to another, to which it is not literally
applicable (rhet.) — MF. (= F.) metaphore, fr.
L. metaphora, fr. Gk. μεταφορά, 'transference,
metaphor', lit. *a carrying over', from the stem
of μεταφέρειν, 'to carry over', which is formed
fr. μετά (see meta-) and φέρειν, 'to bear,
carry'. See bear, 'to carry', and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: metaphor-ic-al, adj., metaphor-ic-
al-ly, adv., melaphor-ist, n.

## metaphrase
metaphrase, п., a translation; esp., a literal
translation. — Gk. μετάφρασις, 'paraphrase', fr.
μεταφράζει, 'to paraphrase, translate', which
is formed fr. μετά- (see meta-) and φράζειν, 'to
show, tell'. See phrase and cp. paraphrase, peri-
phrase.
Derivative: metaphrase, tr. v.

## metaphrast
metaphrast, п., one who metaphrases; esp. one
who writes prose into poetry or poetry into
prose, or changes the meter of verse. — Gk
μεταφραστής, 'translator', fr. μεταφράζειν. See
prec. word and -ast.

## metapbrastic
metapbrastic, adj., literal in translation. — Gk.
μεταφραστικός, 'paraphrastic', fr. μετάφρασις.
See metaphrase and -Ic.

## metaphysical
metaphysical, adj. — See metaphysics and adj.
sufT. -al.
Derivative: metaphysical-ly, adv.

## metaphysician
metaphysician, п., one versed in metaphysics. —
F. metaphysicien, fr. ML. metaphysica. See
metaphysics and -ian.

## metaphysicize
metaphysicize, intr. v., to study metaphysics. —
See next word and -ize.

## metaphysics
metaphysics, п., that branch of philosophy which
deals with the first principles of being and of
knowledge. — Fr. earlier metaphysic, п., fr. ML.
metaphysica (neut. pi.), fr. Gk. τα μετά τα
φυσικά, 'the (works coming) after the physics'
(see meta- and physic), The name τά μετά τά
φυσικά was originally given by Andronicus of
Rhodes about 70 B.C.E. to a collection of
writings of Aristoteles, in reference to the (quite
accidental) circumstance that the treatises
dealing with metaphysics/o//oHWthe treatises on
physics. The interpretation of metaphysics as
'the science of that which is beyond the physical'
is, accordingly, erroneous (see meta-).

## metaphysiz
metaphysiz, п., the region of growth between the
diaphysis and epiphysis of a bone (med.) —
Medical L., formed fr. meta- and -physis as in
diaphysis, epiphysis (qq. v.)

## metaplasm
metaplasm, п., non-living matter in the
protoplasm of a cell (biol.) — L. metaplasmus, fr. Gk.
μεταπλασμός, fr. μετά- (see meta-) and πλασ-
μός, 'something molded1. See plasm.
Derivative: metaplasm-ic, adj.

## metapolitics
metapolitics, п., abstract political science. —
Formed fr. meta- and politics.
Derivatives: metapolitic-al, adj., metapolitic-iant
n.

## metastasis
metastasis, п., 1) metabolism (biol.); 2)
transference of disease from one part of the body to
another (med.); 3) a sudden transition from one
subject to another (rhet.) — Late L., fr. Gk.
μετάστασις, 'removal, change', fr. the stem of
μεθιστάναι, 'to place in another way, remove,
change', which is formed fr. μετά- (see meta-)
and ίστάναι, 'to cause to stand', which is cogn.
with L. stare, 'to stand'. See state and cp. stasis,

## metastatic
metastatic, adj., pertaining to metastasis. — Gk.
μεταστατικός, fr. μετάστατος, 'removed',
verbal adj. of μεθιστάναι. See metastasis and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:488 COLUMN:2 -->
static,

## metatarsal
metatarsal, 1) pertaining to the metatarsus; п.,
matatarsal bone. — See next word and adj. sufT.
-al.

## metatarsns
metatarsns, п., part of the foot between the tarsus
and the toes (anal, and zool.) — ModL., formed
fr. meta- and tarsus.

## metate
metate, п., a stone with a flat or concave surface.
— Sp., fr. Nahuatl metlatl.

## metathesis
metathesis, п., transposition, specifically 1) in
grammar, transposition of letters or syllables in
a word; 2) in chemistry, a double
decomposition. — Late L., fr. Gk. μετάθεσις, 'change of
position, transposition', from the stem of μετα-
τιθέναι, 'to transpose', which is formed fr.
μετά- (see meta-) and τιθέναι, 'to place, set'.
See theme and cp. thesis and words there
referred to.

## metathetic
metathetic, adj., of metathesis. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ic fr. μεταθετός, 'changed,
transposed', verbal adj. of μετατιθέναι. See prec. word.
Derivatives: metathetic-al, adj., metathetic-al-
ly, adv.

## metathorax
metathorax, п., the posterior segment of an
insect's thorax (entomol.) — ModL., formed fr.
meta- and thorax.
Derivative: metathorac-ic, adj.

## Metatron
Metatron, п., name of the highest angel in hag-
gadic and cabalistic literature (Judaism). —
Talmudic Heb. Metatron, prob. fr. Late Gk.
μητάτωρ, fr. L. metator, 'marker of
boundaries', fr. mltatus, pp. of metari, 'to measure off,
mark off', fr. meta, 'mark, boundary'. See mete,
'boundary'.

## metayage
metayage, п., the metayer system of agriculture.
— F. See next word and -age.

## metayer
metayer, п., one who cultivates the land for a
share (usually a half) of the yield. — F., fr.
MF., fr. OF. meteer, fr. ML. medietarius, fr. L.
medietas, 'middle, place in the middle, half, fr.
meatus, 'middle'. See media, 'voiced stop
consonant', and cp. moiety.

## Metazoa
Metazoa, n. pi., a large zoological division
comprising all animals except the Protozoa. —
ModL., coined by the German biologist Ernst
Heinrich Haeckel (1834-1919) fr. meta- and Gk.
ζωα, pi. of ζωαν, 'animal'. See zoo-.

## mete
mete, п., boundary mark, boundary. — OF., fr.
L. meta, 'column, pillar; a conical or pyramidal
figure; goal, mark, boundary' (whence metor,
metari, 'to measure off, mark off'), which is
cogn. with OI. methih, metht, 'post, pillar', Ir.
methos, 'boundary mark', ON. meidr, 'tree,
beam, pole'. Cp. Metatron.

## mete
mete, tr. v., 1) to allot; 2) (archaic and poet.) to
measure. — ME. meten, fr. OB.metan, 'to
measure', rel. to OS. metan, OFris., ΟΝ., Norw.
meta, Swed. mala, MDu., Du. meten, OHG.
теззап, MHG. теззеп, G. messen, Goth, mi-
tan, 'to measure', and to OE. metod, meotod, OS.
metod, ON. mjotudr, 'fate; God', Goth, mitaps,
'measure', ON. matt, Du. maat, OHG. таза,
'manner', MHG. таз, G. Μαβ, 'measure', OE.
(ge)mzle, ON. mxtr. OHG. (gi)ma3i, MHG.
{ge)mx3e, G. gemafi, 'suitable', Goth, mota,
'toll, tax' (whence G. Maut. OE. mot, 'toll tax'),
OS. motan, 'to find room, be obliged to', OHG.
тиозап, Чо be free to do, be allowed; to have
to', Goth, gamotan, 'to find room, be able'. All
these words derive fr. I.-E. base 'med-, 'to
measure, limit, consider, advise', whence also L.
meditarl, 'to think over, consider'. See meditate
and cp. words there referred to.

## metel
metel, п., a thorn apple. — ModL. (пал)
methel, lit. 'metel (nut)', fr. Arab. (Jauz)
mat hit.

## metempiric
metempiric, п., 1) metempirics; 2) an adherent of
the metempirical philosophy. — Compounded
of met- and empiric.

## metempirical
metempirical, adj., outside the field of experience.
— See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: metempirical-ly, adv.

## metempirics
metempirics, п., philosophy dealing with things
outside and yet related to human experience. —
See metempiric and -ics.

## metempsychosis
metempsychosis, п., passing of the soul at death
into another body. — Late L., fr. Gk. μετεμ-
ψϋχωσις, fr. μετεμψΰχαϋσθαι, 'to pass from one

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:488 COLUMN:3 -->
body into another' (said of the soul), formed fr.
μετά- (see meta-) and 'έμψϋχοϋν, 'to put a soul
into', fr. έν, 'in', and ψυχή, 'soul'. See 2nd en-,
psyche and -osis.

## metencephalon
metencephalon, п., 1) the posterior part of the
brain; 2) that part of the brain which consists of
the cerebellum and the pons Varolii (anat. and
embryol.) — Medical L., formed fr. met- and
Gk. εγκέφαλος, 'brain'; see encephalon. The
term metencephalon was introduced by the
English naturalist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825-
95). Cp. myelencephalon.

## meteor
meteor, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) meteore, fr.
ML. meteorum, fr. Gk. μετέωρον (pi. μετέωρα,
'things in the air'), prop. neut. of the adjective
μετέωρος, 'anything raised from the ground,
high, lofty', fr. μετά- (see meta-) and έώρα,
αιώρα, 'swing, oscillation, hovering in the air',
which is rel. to άείρειν, αίρειν, 'to lift, raise up,
bear', αορτή, 'the great artery'. See aorta and
cp. artery.
Derivatives: meteor-ic, meteor-ic-at, adjs., me-
teor-ic-al-ly, adv., meteorite (q.v.), meteorize
(qv.)

## meteorite
meteorite, п., mass of stone or metal that has
fallen on earth from outer space; fallen meteor.
— F. meteorite. See prec. word and subst. suff.
-ite.
Derivatives: meteorit-al, meteor-it-ic, adjs.,
meteor-it-ics, n.

## meteorize
meteorize, tr. v., to vaporize; intr. v., to resemble
a meteor. — Gk. μετεωρίζειν, 'to raise to a
height', fr. μετέωρος. See meteor and -ize.
Derivative: meteoriz-ation, n.

## meteoro-
meteoro-, combining form meaning 'meteor". —
See meteor.

## meteorograph
meteorograph, n. — F. meteorographe. See meteor
and -graph.
Derivatives: meteorograph-y, п., meteorograph-
ic, adj.

## meteoroid
meteoroid, п., one of the many small bodies in the
solar system which become meteors on entering
the earth's atmosphere. — Compounded of
meteor and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: meteoroid-al, adj.

## meteorolite
meteorolite, n. — F. meteorolithe, 'meteorite'.
See meteor and -lite.
Derivative: meteorolit-ic, adj.

## meteorologlc
meteorologlc, meteorological, adj. — MF. (= F.)
meteorologique, fr. Gk. μετεωρολογικός,
'skilled in meteorology", fr. μετεωρολογία. See next
word.
Derivative: meteorologic-al-ly, adv.

## meteorology
meteorology, n. — Gk. μετεωρολογία,
'meteorology', compounded of μετέωρον (see meteor)
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: meteorolog-ist, n.

## meteorometer
meteorometer, n. — Compounded of meteor and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## meter
meter, п., 1) one who measures; 2) an instrument
for measuring. — Formed fr. mete, 'to measure',
with agential suff. -er.

## meter
meter, metre, п., poetical rhythm. — ME. metre,
fr. OF. metre (F. metre), fr. L. metrum, fr. Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure, meter', which is rel. to μήτρα
(Hesychius), 'lot, portion', fr. I.-E. base 'me·,
'to measure', whence also Ol. matt (fr. I.-E.
*mi-ti), mimuti, 'measures', mdtram (neut.),
matra (fern.), 'measure', Avestic, OPers. ma-, L.
mettri, 'to measure'. Cp. matra, Metis, mensal,
'pertaining to the table', and the second element
in castrametation, firman, mahout, vimana. For
derivatives of base 'mid-, a -(/-enlargement of
base *тё-, see meditate.
Derivative: meter, metre, tr. and intr. v., to
compose in meter.

## meter
meter, metre, п., the unit of length in the metric
system. — F. metre (see prec. word); introduced
in France as a name of measure in 1791.

## -meter
-meter, combining form denoting measuring
instruments. It is formed: (1) from Greek nouns
(as in actinometer, barometer, cyclometer); 2)
from Latin nouns (as in altimeter, calorimeter,
colorimeter); 3) from modern nouns (as in gaso-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:489 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: -METER | 462 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:489 COLUMN:1 -->
meter, speedometer). — Fr. L. metrum,
'measure', fr. Gk. μέτρον. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm', and cp. -merry.

## -meter
-meter, -metre, combining form denoting a
specified multiple or fraction of a meter (e.g.
kilometer, lit. 'a thousand meters', millimeter, lit.
'the thousandth part of a meter'. — F. -mitre,
fr. mitre. See meter,.'unit of length'.

## meth-
meth-, form of metho- before a vowel.

## methane
methane, п., a highly inflammable hydrocarbon,
CH4 (chem.) — See methyl and -ane.

## methanol
methanol, п., an inflammable poisonous liquid,
CH3OH (chem.) — Coined fr. methane and -ol,
a surf, denoting an alcohol.

## metheglm
metheglm, п., a drink made of fermented honey.
— W. meddyglyn, compounded of meddyg,
'physician' (fr. L. medicus, see medical), and
llyn, 'juice'.

## methinks
methinks, impers. v., it seems to me. — ME. me
thinketh, fr. OE. me pync(e)p, fr. me, dat. of ic,
T, and pync(e)p, third person sing, of pyncan,
'to seem'. See me and 1st think.

## metho-
metho-, before a vowel meth-, combining form
meaning 'methyl' (chem.) — See methyl.

## method
method, n. — MF. (= F.) methode, fr. L. metho-
dus, fr. Gk. μέθοδος, 'pursuit, scientific inquiry,
method of inquiry, method', lit.' a going after',
fr. μετά- (see meta-) and οδός, 'way, path,
manner'. See odograph.

## methodic
methodic, methodical, adj. — MF. (= F.) metho-
dique, fr. Late L. methodicus, fr. Gk. μεθοδικός,
fr. μέθοδος. See method and lst-ic, resp. also-al·
Derivatives: methodic-al-ly, adv., methodic-al-
ness, n.

## methodics
methodics, п., methodology. — Formed fr.
method with suff. -Ics.

## Methodism
Methodism, п., the doctrines and worship of the
Methodists. — See next word and -ism.

## Methodist
Methodist, п., a member of a Christian
denomination that originated in the religious
association founded in 1729 by John and Charles
Wesley at Oxford University. — ModL. methodista;
see method and -ist. The name was orig. applied
to the followers of John and Charles Wesley to
ridicule their methodical practise.
Derivatives: Methodist-ic, adj., Methodist-ic-al-
ly, adv.

## methodize
methodize, tr. v., to make methodical. — See
method and -ize.
Derivative: methodiz-ation, n.

## methodology
methodology, п., the study of method. —
Compounded of Gk. μέθοδος, 'method', and -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
method and -logy.

## methought
methought, impers. v., past tense of methinks. —
ОЕ- mipuhte, 'it seemed to me'. See methinks.

## Methusela
Methusela, п., son of Enoch; he lived 969 years
(Bible). — Heb. Methushelah, prob. meaning
lit. 'man of the dart', and compounded of *methu
(occurring only as the first element in compound
PN's.), sing, of nfthim, 'men', and shelah, 'dart'.

## methyl
methyl, п., the univalent hydrocarbon radical,
CHS (chem.) — F. mithyle, back formation fr.
methylene. See next word. The term methyl was
introduced into chemistry by the Swedish
chemist J6ns Jakob BerzeUus (1779-1848).
Derivatives: methyl-ate, tr. v., methyl-ic, adj.

## methylene
methylene, п., the bivalent hydrocarbon radical,
CH (chem.) — F. methylene, coined by Jean-
Baptiste-Andre Dumas (1800-84) and Eugene-
Melchior Peligot (181 l-90)in 1835, fr.Gk^»u,
'wine1, and υλη, 'wood'. For the first element
see mead, 'a drink', and cp. amethyst. For the
second element see hyle.

## meticulosity
meticulosity, n. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. L.
meticulosus. See next word.

## meticulous
meticulous, adj., extremely careful. — F. miticu-
leux (fern, miticuleuse), fr. L. meticulosus, 'full
of fear', fr. metus, 'fear', which is of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: meticulous-ly, adv., meticutous-ness,
n.

## metier
metier, п., trade, occupation, one's line. — F.,
'trade, business, occupation', fr. OF. mistier,
mestier, mistier, earlier menestier, fr. L. minis-
terium, 'service, office, ministry'. See ministry
and cp. mystery, 'trade'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:489 COLUMN:2 -->

## metis
metis, п., a person of mixed parentage, esp. the
offspring of a French and American Indian. —
F. metis, fr. Late L. mixticius, 'of mixed race',
fr. L. mixtus, 'mixed', pp. of miscere, 'to mix'.
See mix and cp. mestizo.

## Metis
Metis, п., the first wife of Zeus (Greek mythol.) —
Gk. Μητις, fr. μήτις, 'wisdom, skill, craft', fr.
I.-E. base *me-, 'to measure', whence also Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm',
and cp. words there referred to.

## Metonic
Metonic, adj., pertaining to Melon, an Athenian
astronomer of the 5th cent. B.C.E., who
discovered the cycle of nineteen years, at the close
of which the new and full moons recur on the
same days. — Formed with suff. -ic fr. L. Melon,
fr. Gk. Μέτων.

## metonymical
metonymical, adj. — Gk. μετωνυμικός, *of
metonymy', fr. μετωνυμίϊ. See next word and
-ical.
Derivative: metonymical-ly, adv.

## metonymy
metonymy, п., the use of the name of one thing
for that of another closely associated with it. —
L. metonymia, fr. Gk. μετωνυμία, 'change of
name, the use of one word for another', lit.
'that which is beyond the name', fr. μετά- (see
meta-) and δνυμα, dialectal form of 6νομα,
'name*, which is cogn. with L. пбтеп, 'name'.
See name and cp. onomato-.
Derivatives: metonym-ous, adj., metonymous-ly,
adv.

## metope
metope, п., a marble slab filling the space
between two triglyphs in a Doric frieze (class,
arch.) — L. metopa, fr. Gk. μετόπη, 'the space
between two holes; the space between two
triglyphs', formed fr. μετά- (see meta-), and
όπή, Opening, hole', which derives fr. I.-E. base
*okw-, 'eye, to see', whence also 6ψομοα, Ί shall
see', βψις, 'sight'. See -opsy.

## metope
metope, п., the face of the crab (zool.) — Gk.
μέτωπον, 'forehead', prop, 'the space between
the eyes', fr. μετά- (see meta-) and ώψ, gen.
ώπός, 'eye, face, countenance', fr. I.-E. base
*oqw-, which is rel. to base *oqw-, 'eye', whence
όπή, 'opening'. See prec. word. As a term of
zoology, metope was introduced by Huxley.

## Metopias
Metopias, п., a genus of labyrinthodonts (paleon-
tol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μετωπίας, 'having a
broad forehead', fr. μέτωπον, 'forehead'. See
prec. word.

## metopic
metopic, adj., pertaining to the forehead (anat.)
— Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. μέτωπον,
'forehead'. See metope, 'face of the crab'.

## metopomancy
metopomancy, п., divination by means of the
forehead. — Compounded of Gk. μέτωπον,
'forehead', and μαντεία, 'divination'. See metope,
'face of the crab', and -mancy.

## metosteon
metosteon, п., ossification of the posterior lateral
processes of the sternum (ornithol.) — ModL-,
formed fr. Gk. μετά-, 'behind', and όστέον,
'bone'. See meta- and osteo-.

## metralgia
metralgia, п., pain in the uterus (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of Gk. μήτρα, 'uterus,
womb', and άλγος, 'pain'. See metro-, 'uterine',
and -algia.

## metre
metre, n. — Var. of meter, 'poetical rhythm', and
meter, 'unit of length'.

## metric
metric, adj., pertaining to the meter. — F. mitri-
que, fr. mitre, 'meter'. See meter, 'unit of length',
and -ic.

## metrical
metrical, also metric, adj., 1) pertaining to
measurement ; 2) pertaining to meter (in poetry). —
L. metricus, fr. Gk. μετρικός, fr. μέτρον,
'meter'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm', and adj. suff.
-ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: metrical-ly, adv.

## metrician
metrician, п., one who writes in meter; metrist.
— Formed with suff. -ician fr. meter, 'poetical
rhythm'. Cp. F. melricien.

## metrics
metrics, п., the study of meter. — Formed with
suff. -ics fr. meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## metrist
metrist, п., one skilled in the use of poetical
meters. — ML. metrista, fr. L. metrum, 'meter'.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm', and -ist.

## metritis
metritis, п., inflammation of the uterus (med.) —
MedicalL., formed with suff. -iris fr. Gk. μήτρα,
'womb'. See metro-, 'uterine',

## metro-
metro-, combining form meaning 'measure', as
in metrology. — Gk. μέτρο-, fr. μέτρον,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:489 COLUMN:3 -->
'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## metro-
metro-, combining form meaning 'mother, as in
metropolis. — Gk. μητρο-, fr. μήτηρ, gen.
μητρός, 'mother'. See mother and cp. mater.

## metro-
metro-, combining form meaning 'uterine', as in
metrorrhagia. — Gk. μητρο-, fr. μήτρα, 'uterus,
womb', which is rel. to μήτηρ, 'mother'; see
mother and cp. metritis, parametrium. For sense
development cp. L. matrix, 'breeding animal;
womb, matrix', fr. mater, 'mother' (see matrix)

## metrology
metrology, п., the study of weights and measures.
— Compounded of metro-, 'measure', and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: metrolog-ic-al, adj., metrolog-ist, n.

## metronome
metronome, п., a ticking pendulum for marking
exact time in music. — Compounded of metro-,
'measure', and Gk. νόμος, 'law'. See nomo-.
Derivative: metronom-ic, adj.

## metronymic
metronymic, adj., derived from the name of a
mother or of another female ancestor. — Late
Gk. μητρωνυμικός, 'named after one's
mother', compounded of Gk. μήτηρ, gen. μητρός,
'mother', 6νυμα, dial, form of όνομα, and suff.
-ικός. See mother, onomato- and adj. suff. -ic
and cp. patronymic.
Derivatives: metronymic, п., metronym-y, n.

## metropolis
metropolis, п., capital city. — Late L. metropolis,
fr. Gk, μητρόπολις, 'a mother city (i.e., a city
from which other cities have been colonized)',
compounded of μήτηρ, gen. μητρός, 'mother',
and πόλις, 'city'. See mother and police, 'method
of governing'.

## metropolitan
metropolitan, adj., belonging to a metropolis. —
Late L. metropolitanus, fr. Gk. μητροπολίτης,
'metropolitan', fr. μητρόπολις. See prec. word
and -an.

## metropolitan
metropolitan, п., a metropolitan bishop. — Orig.
'bishop of a metropolis'. See metropolitan, adj.

## metropolitanate
metropolitanate, п., the office of a metropolitan
bishop. — Formed fr. prec. word with subst.
suff. -ate.

## metrorrhagia
metrorrhagia, п., uterine hemorrhage (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of Gk. μήτρα, 'uterus,
womb', and -ρραγία, 'a bursting forth', from
the stem of ^ηγνύναι 'to burst forth'. See
metro-, 'uterine', and -rrhagia.
Derivative: meirorrhag-ic, adj.

## Metrosideros
Metrosideros, п., a genus of trees and shrubs of
the myrtle family (hot.) — ModL., compounded
of Gk. μήτρα, 'uterus, womb; heart or pith of a
tree', and σίδηρος, 'iron'. See metro-, 'uterine',
and siderite.

## Metroxylon
Metroxylon, п., a genus of palms of the family
Arecaceae (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
μήτρα, 'uterus, womb; heart or pith of a tree',
and ξύλον, 'wood'. See metro-, 'uterine', and
xylo-.

## -metry
-metry, combining form denoting the process of
measuring (as specified by the first element of
the compound ending in -metry). — ME.
-metric, fr. MF. (= F.) -metrie, fr. L. -metria, Gk.
-μετρία, 'a measuring of, fr.-μέτρης, 'measurer
of, fr. μέτρον 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm', and cp. -meter, 'measuri ng instrument*.

## mettle
mettle, п., disposition, spirit. — A var. of metal.
Derivatives: mettl-ed, adj., mettle-some, adj.,
mettle-some-ly, adv., mettle-some-ness, n.

## meturgeman
meturgeman, п., an official of the early Jewish
synagogue who translated into Aramaic the
verses read from the Scriptures in Hebrew. —
Aram. milhurgeman, inexact spelling of nfthdr-
geman, 'interpreter', which is a blend of targ1-
man and Heb. mithargem; see Targum. See
Bacher, Exegetische Terminologie, vol. l,p. 206,
note 2.

## meuin
meuin, п., mine used in meum and tuum, 'mine and
thine'; denoting right in property. — L., neut.
of meus, 'my, mine', which stands for *mey-os,
and is rel. to me, 'me', mihi (for *me-hi), 'to me',
and cogn. with OSlav. moji, OPruss. mats (for
"moyos), Hitt. -mesh, 'my', Goth, meins, OE.
min, 'my, of me'. See me, and cp. mine, pron.,
my. Cp. also the first element in monseigueur,
monsieur, monsigaor.

## Meum
Meum, п., a genus of plants of the carrot family
(bot.) — L. meum, 'baldmoney, spicknel', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:490 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 463 | MICROSCOPE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:490 COLUMN:1 -->
Gk. μηον, which is of unknown origin.

## mew
mew, п., the common gull. — ME. mewe, fr. OE.
maew, rel. to OS. mew, Fris. meau, mieu, MLG.
mewe, MDu., Du. meeuw (G. Mowe is a LG.
loan word), ON. mar, Dan. maage, Norw.
maase, Swed. mas, muse, 'gull'; of imitative
origin. OF. moue (whence F. mouette) and Lith.
mevas are Teut. loan words. Cp. the second
element in fulmar. Cp. also mew, 'to cry as a cat'.

## mew
mew, п., a cage for hawks. — ME. mue, mewe,
'cage for hawks while they are molting', fr.
MF. (= F.) mue, fr. muer, 'to molt'. See mew,
'to shed, moll'.
Derivative: mew, tr. v., to shut up in a cage.

## mew
mew, tr. v., to shed, molt. — ME. muwen, fr. MF.
(= F.) muer, 'to shed, molt', fr. L. mutare, 'to
change'. See mutation,

## mew
mew, interj. and п., the cry of a cat; intr. v., to
cry as a cat. — Of imitative origin. Cp. G.
miauen, F. miauler and see miaow, miaul,

## mewl
mewl, intr. v., i) to cry as a cat; 2) to whimper.
— Cp. mew, 'to cry as a cat', and miaul,

## mews
mews, п., a set of royal stables built on place
where mews for hawks were kept. — See mew,
'cage for hawks'.

## mezuzah
mezuzah, mezuza, п., a small roll of parchment
containing Deut. 6:4-9 (the Shema), and Deut.
11:13-21, affixed to the doorpost of every room,
on the right side of the entrance (Jewish religion),
— Heb. m ziiza , lit. 'doorpost', orig. prob.
meaning 'something standing', and rel. to
Akkad. nazdzu, 'to stand', manzdzu, 'doorpost'.
The mezuzah was so called from the doorposts
(Heb. m zuzSth), to which it is to be affixed (see
Deut. 6:9 and 11:20).

## mezzanine
mezzanine, п., a low story between two higher
ones. — F., fr. It. mezzanine, dimin. of mezzano,
'middle', fr. L. medidnus, 'middle', fr. medius.
See media, 'voiced stop consonant', and cp.
median. Cp. also mezzo.

## mezzo
mezzo, adj., half, moderate (mus.) — It., 'middle',
fr. L. medius. See media,'voiced stop consonant'.

## mezzo-relievo
mezzo-relievo, mezzo-rUievo, п., middle relief. —
It. mezzorilievo. See prec. word and relief and
cp. alto-relievo.

## mezzo-soprano
mezzo-soprano, п., a voice intermediate between
soprano' and alto (mus.) — Compounded of
mezzo and soprano.

## mezzotint
mezzotint, п., a form of engraving on copper or
steel. — It. mezzotinto, 'half-tint'. See mezzo-
tin to.
Derivatives: mezzotint, tr. v., mezzotint-er, n.

## mezzotinto
mezzotinto, п., mezzotint. —It., compounded of
mezzo, 'middle', and tinto, 'dyed', pp. oftingere,
'to dye, color". See mezzo and tint.
Derivative: mezzotinto, adj.

## mho
mho, п., the unit of conductance (i.e. the
reciprocal of the unit of resistance, the ohm) (electr.)
— The anagram of ohm (q.v.)

## mi
mi, п., a syllable used in solmization to denote
the third tone of the diatonic scale (mus.)

## miaow
miaow, interj. and п., the cry of a cat; intr. v., to
cry as a cat, to mew. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
mew, 'to cry as a cat', miaul.

## miargyrite
miargyrite, п., silver sulfantimonite (mineral.) —
G. Miargyrit, lit. '(having) less silver', fr. Gk.
μείων, 'less', and άργυρος, 'silver' (see mio-
and argyro-); so called because it contains less
silver than pyrargyrite. The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -Γτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## miasma
miasma, п., infectious exhalation from
putrescent matter. — ModL., fr. Gk. μίασμα, gen.
μιάσματος, 'stain, defilement', from the stem of
μιαίνειν, 'to stain, defile' (whence αμίαντος,
'undefiled'), rel. to μιαρός, later form μιερός,
'defiled with blood', fr. I.-E. base *mei~, *mai-,
'to stain, defile', whence perh. also Goth, mail,
OE. mdl, 'stain, mark'. See mole, 'spot on the
skin', and -ma and cp. Miastor, amianthus.
Derivatives: miasm-al, miasmat-ic, tniasmat-ous,
miasm-ic, adjs.

## miasmatology
miasmatology, п., the study of miasmata (med.)
— Compounded of Gk. μίασμα, gen.
μιάσματος, 'stain, defilement', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See prec. word and
-logy.

## Miastor
Miastor, п., a genus of flies of the family Itonidae

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:490 COLUMN:2 -->
(entomol.) — Gk. μιάστωρ, 'wretch who
pollutes others', lit. 'one stained or defiled',from the
stem of μιαίνειν, 'to stain, defile'. See miasma.

## miaul
miaul, intr. v., to cry as a cat. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. F. miauler, It. miagolare, Sp. mau-
llar, 'to cry as a cat, to mew', and E. mew, 'to
cry as a cat', mewl, miaow.

## mica
mica, п., any of a group of minerals (mostly
aluminum silicates) crystallizing in thin, often
transparent, layers. — L. mica, 'crumb', fr
"smik-S, соgn. with Homeric Gk. σμικρός, Ion.,
Att. μικρός, 'small', ON. smar, OHG. smahi,
'small, petty', OHG. smahi, 'littleness, small-
ness' (whence G. Schmach, 'disgrace'); fr. I.-E.
base *sme(i)k-, *smik-, 'ground grain; ground
down, pulverized', enlargement of *sme-, 'to
smear, to rub'; see micro-. The sense
development of English mica was influenced by a
confusion with L. micdre, 'to glisten'. Cp. micelle.

## micaceous
micaceous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
mica. — Formed fr. mica with suff. -aceous.

## Micah
Micah, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the sixth in
the order of the Twelve Prophets, who lived in
the 8th cent. B.C.E. — Heb. Mikhah, shortened
fr. Mikhayah, lit. 'Who is like the Lord?' Cp.
Michael.

## micelle
micelle, also micella, micell, п., a hypothetical
structural particle (biol. and chem.) — ModL.
micella, 'a little crumb', dimin. of mica. See
mica and -ella.

## Michael
Michael, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, an
archangel. — Late L., fr. Gk. Μιχαήλ, fr. Heb.
MikhS'el, lit. 'Who is like God?' See El and cp.
Micah.

## Michaelmas
Michaelmas, п., festival of the archangel Michael,
celebrated by the Christian church on
September 29th. — Compounded of Michael and -mas,
'mass'. See Mass.

## mick
mick, п., an Irishman (slang). — Corruption of
thePN.Michaei.

## lllickle
lllickle, adj., great, much (archaic or dial.) — ME.
mikel, muchel, fr. OE. micel, mycel, 'great, big,
many', rel. to OS. mikil, ON. mikill, OHG.
mihhil, Goth, mikils, fr. I.-E. base *meg(h)-,
*m g-> 'great, large', whence also OI. mah-,
mahd-, mahat-, 'great', mahas-, 'greatness',
Avestic maz-, mazant-, 'great', mazah-,
'greatness', Toch. А так, В. maka-, 'great, much',
Hitt. mekkish, 'great, large', Arm. mec
(instrumental case mecaw), 'large', Gk. μέγας, fern,
μεγάλη, neut. μέγα, 'great, large', Ion. μέζων
(for "μέγιων), 'greater, larger', Att. μείζων (of
s.m., formed on analogy of κρείττων,
'stronger', άμείνων, 'better, stronger'}, Gk. μέγιστος,
'greatest, largest', L. magnus, 'great, large,
much, abundant', major (for *mag-yos),
'greater', maximus (for 'mag-^mos), 'greatest', Alb.
mab (determined form maSi), 'great, large', Mir.
mag, maignech, 'great, large', mass (for *mak-
sos), 'stately', MW. maon (for *mag-ones), 'the
great ones', maith, meith (for *mag-tio-), 'long,
great', Olr. do-for-maig, 'increases'. Cp. much,
more. Cp. also almagest, maestro, magisterial,
magistrate, Magna Charta, magnanimous,
magnate, magnificent, magniloquent, magnitude,
maguum, maguuin bonum, magnum opus, mahat-
ma, Maia, majesty, major, majuscule, master,
maximum, May, mayor, mega-, mehtar, mister,
mistral, mistress, the first element in Mahabha-
rata, maharaja, maharanee, mahout, and the
second element in palmistry.
Derivative: mickle-ness, n.

## micr-
micr-, combining form. — See micro-.

## micrify
micrify, tr. v., to make small. — A hybrid coined
fr. Gk. μικρός, 'small' (see micro-), and E.
-fy (fr. L. -ficdre).

## micro-
micro-, micr-, combining form meaning 1) small;
2) microscopic; 3) one millionth part of a given
unit (as e.g. microgram denotes the millionth
part of a gram). — Gk. μϊκρο-, μϊκρ-, fr.
μικρός, 'small', which is cogn. with L. mica,
'crumb'. See mica.

## microanalysis
microanalysis, п., the chemical analysis of very
small quantities. — ModL., compounded of
micro- and analysis.

## microbarograph
microbarograph, п., a barograph for recording
very small changes. — Compounded of mlcro-
and barograph.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:490 COLUMN:3 -->

## microbe
microbe, п., a minute organism; popular name
for a bacterium. — Coined by the French
surgeon Sedillot in 1878 fr. Gk. μικρός, 'small',
and βίος, "'life'. See micro- and bio-.
Derivatives: microb-al, microb-ial, microb-ian,
microb-ic, adjs.

## microbiology
microbiology, п., that branch of biology which
deals with microorganisms. — Compounded of
micro- and biology.
Derivatives: microbiolog-ical, adj., microbiolog·
ist, n.

## microcephalic
microcephalic, adj., microcephalous. — See next
word and -ic.

## microcephalous
microcephalous, adj., small-headed. — ModL.
microcephalus, fr. Gk. μϊκροκέφαλος, 'small-
headed', which is compounded of μικρός,
'small', and κεφαλή, 'head'. See micro- and -ce-
phalons.

## microcephaly
microcephaly, п., the condition of being
microcephalic. — See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -15).

## microchemistry
microchemistry, п., that branch of chemistry
which deals with microscopic-objects or
quantities. — Compounded of micro- and chemistry.

## microcline
microcline, п., a kind of feldspar belonging to the
triclinic system (mineral.) — Compounded of
micro- and Gk. κλινειν, 'to incline'. See clinical.

## microcosm
microcosm, п., a miniature world. — F. micro-
cosme, fr. Late L. microcosmus, fr. Gk. μικρός
κόσμος, 'little world'. See micro- and cosmos and
cp. macrocosm.
Derivatives: microcosm-ic, microcosm-ic-al, adjs.

## mlcrocyte
mlcrocyte, п., a small red blood cell (anat.) —
Lit. 'a small cell', coined by the Canadian
physician Sir William Osier (1849-1919) fr. micro-
and Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow vessel'. See -cyte.
Derivative: microcyt-ic, adj.

## microfarad
microfarad, п., one-millionth part of a farad
(electr.) — Compounded of micro- and farad.

## microgram
microgram, ri., one-millionth part of a gram. —
Compounded of micro- and gram.

## micrograph
micrograph, п., an instrument for executing
minute writing, drawing or engraving. —
Compounded of micro- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γρά-
φειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## micrography
micrography, п., 1) the art of writing in very small
characters; 2) description of microscopic
objects. — Compounded of micro- and -γραφία,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.

## micrology
micrology, п., exaggerated attention to petty
things. — Gk. μϊκρολογία, 'pettiness, care for
trifles', fr. μΐκρολόγος, 'petty, careful about
trifles', which is compounded of μικρός,
'small; petty', and -λογία, fr. λόγος, 'word,
speech, discourse'. See micro- and -logy.

## micrometer
micrometer, п., an instrument for making exact
measurements. — Compounded of micro- and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.
Derivatives: micrometr-ic, adj., micrometr-y, n.

## micron
micron, п., one-millionth part of a meter. —
ModL., fr. Gk. μικρόν, neut. of μικρός, 'small'.
See micro-.

## Micronesia
Micronesia, п., groups of small islands in the
western Pacific, north of the equator and east of
the Philippines. — Compounded of micro- and
Gk. νήσος, 'island', which is prob. rel. to νή-
χειν, 'to swim'. See Indonesia and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: Micronesi-an, adj. and n.

## microorganism
microorganism, п., a microscopic organism. —
Compounded of micro- and organism.

## microphone
microphone, п., an instrument for intensifying
small sounds. — Compounded of micro- and
Gk. φωνή, 'voice, sound'. See phone, 'speech
sound'.

## microphotograph
microphotograph, п., a very small photograph. —
Compounded of micro- and photograph.

## microphyte
microphyte, п., a microscopic plant, esp. a
bacterium. — Compounded of micro- and Gk.
φυτόν, 'a plant'. See -phyte.
Derivative: microphyt-ic, adj.

## microscope
microscope, n. — ModL. microscopium, lit. 'an
instrument for examining small objects';
compounded of micro- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκο-
πεϊν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scope.
Derivatives: microscop-ic, microscop-ic-al, adjs.,

## microscop-ic-al-ly
microscop-ic-al-ly, adv., microscop-ist, п., mi-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:491 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MICROSOME | 464 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:491 COLUMN:1 -->
croscop-y, η.

## microsome
microsome, п., one of the minute granules in the
protoplasm (biol.) — Compounded of micro-
and Gk. σώμα, 'body'. See soma, 'body'.

## microspore
microspore, п., a minute spore (bot. and zool.) —
Compounded of micro- and Gk. σπορί, 'a
sowing, seed'. See spore.
Derivatives: microspor-ic, microspor-ous, adjs.

## microstomatous
microstomatous, adj., having a small mouth. —
Compounded of micro- and Gk. στόμα, gen.
στόματος, 'mouth'. See stoma and -ous.

## microstomous
microstomous, adj., microstomatous. — See prec.
word.

## microtia
microtia, п., abnormal smallness of the ear (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of micr- and Gk.
οΰς, gen. ώτός, 'ear'. See oto- and 1st -ia and
cp. Microtus.

## Microtinae
Microtinae, п., pi., a subfamily of rodents, the
field voles and the lemming mice (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -inae fr. Microtus
(q.v.)

## microtome
microtome, п., an instrument for cutting thin
sections for examination under the microscope. —
Compounded of micro- and Gk. -ταμον, fr.
τόμος, 'a cutting, a piece cut off'. See -tome.
Derivatives: microtom~ic, adj., microtom-y, n.

## Microtus
Microtus, п., the typical genus of the Microtinae
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of micr- and Gk.
ους, gen ώτός, 'ear'. See oto- and cp. microtia.

## microzyme
microzyme, also microzyma, п., a zymotic microbe
(biol.) — F. microzyme, coined by the French
physician and chemist Pierre-Jacques Bechamp
(1816-1908) fr. Gk. μικρός, 'small', and ζυμγ],
'leaven'. See micro- and zyme.

## micturate
micturate, intr. v., to urinate. — Formed
irregularly fr. L. micturire. See next word and
verbal suff. -ate.

## micturition
micturition, п., i) a morbid desire to urinate; 2)
excessive urination; Ъ) the act of urinating. —
Formed with suff. -ion fr. L. micturit-(um), pp.
stem of micturire 'to desire to urinate', desider-
ativeof mingere, pp. stem mict-(um), 'to urinate',
which is rel. to meiere (for *meigh[ere), of s.m.,
and cogn. with OI. mehati, 'urinates', pp. midhah,
Avestic maezaiti, 'urinates, manures, dungs',
Gk. όμείχειν, όμΐχεΐν, 'to urinate', μοιχός,-'adul-
terer', Arm. mez, 'urine', mizem, Ί urinate',
(prob. denominated fr. mez), Toch. В miso,
'urine', earlier Lith. miniu, Lith. meiit, Lett.
mizu, Ί urinate', OE. migan, ON. miga, MLG.
migen, 'to urinate', OE. micga, migoda, 'urine',
Goth, maihstus, OE. meox, 'dung, filth'. See
mash, п., and cp. mistletoe, mixen. For the desid-
erative suff. -ilrire in L. micturire cp. Abiturient
and words there referred to.

## mid
mid, adj. — ME., fr. OE. midd, rel. to ON. midr,
OS. middi, OFris. midde, OHG. mini, Goth.
midjis, 'mid', and cogn. with Ol. madhyah, Gk.
μέσος, L. medius, 'middle'. See media, 'voiced
stop consonant', and words there referred to
and cp. esp. middle.

## mid
mid, prep., amid. — Aphetic for amid.

## Midas
Midas, п., a king of Phrygia, to whom Dionysus
granted the favor of turning everything he
touched into gold (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Μίδϊς; of Phrygian origin.

## midday
midday, п., the middle of the day, noon. — ME.,
fr. OE. nudddxg. See mid, adj., and day.

## midden
midden, п., 1) a dunghill; 2) a prehistoric refuse.
— ME. midding, fr. Dan. medding, fr. earlier
megdynge, 'dunghill', which is compounded of
meg, 'muck, dung', and dynge, 'heap of dung'.
See muck and dung.

## middle
middle, adj. — ME. middel, fr. OE, middel, rel. to
OS. middil, MLG., Du. middel, OHG. mittil,
MHG., G. mittel, 'middle' and to OE. midd,
'mid'. See mid, adj.

## middle
middle, n. — Subst. use of middle, adj. Cp. G.
Mittel, п., fr. mittel, adj.
Derivative: middle, tr. v.

## middling
middling, adj. and n. — Formed fr. middle with
suff. -ing.

## middy
middy, п., midshipman (colloq.) — Shortened fr.
midshipman.

## midge
midge, n. — ME. migge, fr. OE. mycge, mycg, rel.
to OS. muggia, ON. my, Dan. myg, Swed. myg-
ga, mygg, MDu. mugghe, Du. mug, OHG. mucka,
MHG. mucke, тйске, G. Мйске, 'midge, gnat',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:491 COLUMN:2 -->
from the 1-Е. imitative base *mu-, 'to buzz',
whence also Arm. тип (for *mu-no), 'gnat',Alb.
mi-ζε, 'gnat' (formed with dimin. suff. -ze). Cp.
the imitative base *mus-, whence Gk. μυΐα (for
*μύσια), L. musca, OSlav. muc/ta (for *mousd),
Lith. muse, Lett, musa, OPruss. muso, 'fly', dial.
Swed. mausa, 'fly', OSlav. muSica, 'gnat'. Cp.
mosqmto, Musca, muscarine, musket, Myiar-
chus, Stegomyla. Cp. also mugwort.
Derivatives: midget (q.v.), midg-y, adj.

## midget
midget, п., a very small person; adj., very small.
— Formed fr. midge with dimin. suff. -et.
Derivative: midget-y, adj.

## Midi
Midi, п., southern France. — F., fr. midi, 'south',
lit. 'midday', compounded of mi, 'middle' (fr.
L. medius), and -di, 'day' (fr. L. dies). See media,
'voiced stop consonant', and dies поп and cp.
midlnette.

## Midianite
Midianite, п., one of a nomadic tribe of northern
Arabia (Bible). — Lit. 'descendant of Midian';
formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Heb. Midyan,
son of Abraham and Keturah. See Gen. 25:2.

## midinette
midinette, п., a Parisian work-girl who comes out
of the shop at noon time. — F., contraction of
midi-dinette (see haplology), lit. '(one who) dines
at noon', fr. midi, 'midday', and dinette, 'child's
dinner', dimin. of diner, 'dinner'. For the
etymology of F. midi and diner see Midi and
dinner.

## midmost
midmost, adj. — ME. midmest, fr. OE. midmest,
which is double super], of midd, 'mid'. See mid,
adj. The change of e (in OE., ME. midmest) to
о (in E. midmost) is due to an erroneous
association with most. See -most and cp. words there
referred to.

## midnight
midnight, n. — ME., fr. OE. midniht. See mid,
adj., and night.

## midrash
midrash, п., exposition of the Holy Scriptures
(Hebrew literature). — Heb. midhrash, 'study,
exposition', in Mishnaic Hebrew, 'homiletical
interpretation',*fr. Heb. darash, 'he sought,
inquired, investigated', in Mishnaic Heb. also 'he
expounded, interpreted'; hence Aram. dirash,
'he searched out, investigated, interpreted', and
—through the medium of this latter—Arab.
darasa, 'he read repeatedly, he studied', Ethiop.
darasa, 'he expounded'. Cp. madrasah.

## midriff
midriff, п., the diaphragm. — ME. mydrif, fr. OE.
midhrif, a compound of OE. midd (see mid, adj.)
and hrif, 'belly , which is rel. to OHG. href.
OFris. hrif, href, 'belly', OHG. href, 'body', and
cogn. with L. corpus, 'body'. See corpus and cp.
words there referred to.

## midst
midst, n. — ME. middest, midest, formed with
intensive suff. -t fr. middes, mides, adverbial gen.
of mid. See mid, adj., and cp. amid, amidst.
Cp. also against and words there referred
to.
Derivative: midst, prep.

## midsummer
midsummer, n. — ME. midsumer, midsomer, fr.
OE. midsumor. See mid, adj., and summer.

## midwife
midwife, n. — ME. midwif fr. OE. mid, 'with',
and wif, 'wife, woman'. The first element is rel.
to Goth, mip, ON. med, 'with', and cogn. with
Gk. μετά, 'between, among, with, after'; see
meta-. For the second element see wife.
Derivatives: midwife, tr. v., midwifery (q.v.)

## midwifery
midwifery, n. — A hybrid formed fr. midwife
and -ery, a suff. of Romance origin.

## mien
mien, п., manner, demeanor, appearance. — F.
mine, 'look, appearance, mien', borrowed fr.
Bret, min, 'beak, muzzle, nose'; prob.
influenced in meaning by the verb de-mean.

## miff
miff, п., a trifling quarrel; tr. v., to put or be out
of humor. — Orig. exclamation of disgnst. Cp.
G. muffen, 'to sulk'.

## might
might, v., past tense of may. — ME. mighte, fr.
OE. meahte, mihte, past tense of magan, 'to be
able'. See may, aux. v.

## might
might, п., power. — ME. mighte, fr. OE. miht, rel.
to ON. mdttr, OFris., MDu., Du. macht, OS.,
OHG., MHG. maht, G. Macht, Goth, mahts,
fr. Teut. *mahti-, 'might', fr. I.-E. base 'mdgh-,
*megh-, 'to be able'. See may, aux. v., and cp.
main, the first clement in Matilda, and the second
element in wehrmacht.

## mighty
mighty, adj. — ME., fr. OE. mihtig, fr. miht,
'might'. See might, п., and -y (representing OE.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:491 COLUMN:3 -->
■ig)-
Derivatives: mighti-ly, adv., mighti-ness, n.

## mignon
mignon, adj., dainty, delicate. — F., 'delicate,
charming, pretty', fr. OF. mignot, of s.m., orig.
'caressing, fondling, flattering', from the base
of minet, 'pussy, kitten; pet, darling', which is of
imitative origin. Cp. minion, which is a doublet
of mignon.

## mignonette
mignonette, п., French name of the plant Reseda
odorata. — Fem. dimin. of F. mignon, 'pretty,
delicate'. See prec. word and -ette.

## migraine
migraine, п., a periodical headache, usually on
one side of the head only. — F., fr. Late L.
hemicrania, fr. Gk. ημικρανία, 'a pain on one
side of the head', which is compounded of ήμι-,
'half, and κράνίον, 'head, skull'. See hemi-and
cranium and cp. hemicrania, megrim.

## migrant
migrant, adj., migrating; п., one who migrates;
a migratory bird. — L. migrans, gen. -antis,
pres. part, of migrare. See next word and -ant
and cp. emigrant, immigrant, transmigrant.

## migrate
migrate, intr. v. — L. migrat-{um), pp. stem of
migro, migrare, 'to move from one place to
another, change', which prob. stands for
*migwrav6 and is denominated fr. *migwros,
'moving from one place to another', fr. l.-E.
base *meigw-, *migw-, whence also Gk.
αμείβει, *to change', αμοιβή, 'change'; cp.
amoeba. Base *meigw-, *migw- is an enlargement of
base *mei-, *moi- 'to change; to change one's
place, to go', whence also OI. mayate, 'changes',
L. meare, 'to go, pass'. See mean, 'of low rank',
aod cp. meatus, emigrate, immigrate,
transmigrate. For the ending of migratesee verbal suflf.
-ate.

## migration
migration, n. — L. migratio, gen. -onis, 'removal,
change', fr. migrat-(um), pp. stem of migrare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## migrator
migrator, п., one who migrates; specif., a
migratory bird. — L., fr. migrat-(um), pp. stem of
migrare. See migrate and agential suflf. -or.

## migratory
migratory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory
fr. L. migrat-(um), pp. stem of migrare. See
migrate.

## mihrab
mihrab, п., in a mosque, the niche indicating the
direction of Mecca. — Arab, mihrab.

## mikado
mikado, п., the emperor of Japan (a title used by
поп-Japanese). — Jap., compounded of mi,
'august', and kado, 'gate'. Cp. Pharaoh, the title of
the Egyptian kings, which lit. means 'great
house', and the Sublime Porte, as the official
name of the Turkish Government.

## Mikania
Mikania, п., a genus of plants, the climbing
hempweed (bot.) — ModL., named after Joseph
Gottfried Mikan (1743-1814), professor of
botany at the University of Prague. For the ending
see 1st suff. -ia.

## mikra
mikra, п., 1) the Hebrew text of the Bible; 2) the
Bible. — Heb. miqrd\ lit. 'reading', fr. qara', 'he
called, proclaimed, read, recited', which is rel.
to Aram. q&ru\ of s.m. (Arab. qaraa\ 'he read,
proclaimed aloud, recited', is prob. an Aram,
loan word). Cp. Karaism, Koran.

## mil
mil, п., a unit of length equal to one-thousandth
part of an inch. — L. mille, *a thousand'. See
mile.

## milarite
milarite, п., a silicate of potassium, calcium and
aluminum (mineral.) — Named after Val Milar.
The name is due to the erroneous belief that
this mineral is found in Val Milar in
Switzerland. In reality, it occurs in Val Giuf in the same
country. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## milch
milch, adj., giving milk. — ME. milche, fr. OE.
-milce (in pri-milce, 'May' (i.e. the month in
which cows can be milked three times daily),
rel. to ON. mjolkr, milkr, Du. melk, OHG.,
MHG. melch, G. melk, 'giving milk', and to OE.
melcan, 'to milk', meolc, 'milk'. See milk.
Derivative: milch-er, n.

## mild
mild, adj. — ME. milde, mild, fr. OE. milde, rel.
to OS. mildi, ON. mildr, OFris. milde, Du. mild,
OHG. milti, MHG. milte, milde, G. milde,
Goth, mildeis, 'mild', and cogn. with Gk. μάλ^η,

## mixture of wax and pitch
mixture of wax and pitch, μάλθων, 'weakling',
μαλθακός, 'soft*, μαλθάσσειν, μαλθ-αίνειν 'to

## soften'
soften', and prob. also with OI. mardhati, 'leaves

## behind
behind, neglects', fr, I.-E. *mel-dh-, enlargement
of base *mel~, 4o rub, grind'. See meal, 'edible

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:492 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 465 | MILVINAE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:492 COLUMN:1 -->
grain', and cp. maltha, and the first element in
Mildred. Derivatives: mild-ly, adv., mild-neSs, n.

## mildew
mildew, n. — ME., fr. OE. meledeaw, rnildeaw,
'honeydew, nectar', rel. to OS. milidou, Swed.
mjoldagg, Du. meeldauw, OHG. milituo, MHG.
miltou, G. Mellau, 'mildew'. The first element of
these words prob. derives from a blend of I.-E.
*melit-, 'honey', and I.-E. *mel, 'to grind'; see
mel, resp. meal, 'edible grain'. For the second
element see dew.
Derivatives: mildew, tr. and intr. v., mildew-er,
п., mildew-y, adj.

## Mildred
Mildred, fern. PN. — Fr. OE. Milddryd,
compounded of milde, 'mild', and dryd, 'power,
strength'. For the first element see mild. The
second element is rel. to ON. prudr, OS. prup-,
'power, strength', ON. pro-ask, 'to ripen, thrive',
proskr, 'strong', OHG. triuwen, 'to bloom,
blossom', trouwen, 'to grow', MHG. druo,
'fruit'.

## mile
mile, n. — ME., fr. OE. mil, pi. mila, mile, fr. L.
milia, pi. of mille, 'a thousand' (in . . . miliapas-
suum,'. .. thousand paces', i.e. '. .. miles'). L.
mille is of uncertain origin. It is perh. cogn.
with Gk. χίλιοι, ΟΙ. sa-kasram, 'a thousand';
see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, 88 s.v. mille.
Cp. mil, millennium, millesimal, million. Cp.
also kilo-.

## mileage
mileage, п., distance in miles. — Formed fr. mile
with surf. -age.

## Milesian
Milesian, adj., pertaining to Miletus, an ancient
city of Asia Minor; п., a native of Miletus. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Mitesius, fr. Gk.
Μιλήσιος, fr. Μίλητος, 'Miletus'.

## Milesian
Milesian, adj., Irish; п., an Irishman. — Formed
with surf, -an fr. Mitesius, Latinized form of
Miledh, name of a legendary Spanish king,
whose sons are said to have conquered Ireland.
This name derives fr. Гг. mileadh, 'champion',
fr. Olr. mil, gen. miled, 'soldier', which is a loan
word fr. L. miles, gen. miliiis. See militia.

## milfoil
milfoil, п., the yarrow. — ME., fr. OF. milfoil
(F. mittefeuitte), fr. L. millefolium, 'milfoil',
which is compounded of mille, 'a thousand',
and folium, 'leaf. See mile and folio.

## miliaria
miliaria, п., skin disease caused by the
inflammation of the sweat glands (med.) — ModL., fr. L.
mitiarius, 'resembling millet'. See next word.

## miliary
miliary, adj., 1) resembling the seeds of millet,
2) in medicine, characterized by papules
resembling the seeds of millet. — L. milidrius,
'resembling millet', fr. milium. See millet and adj.
suff. -ary.

## Miliceut
Miliceut, also Mllllcent, Melicent, fern. PN. —
Fr. earlier Malasintha, fr. OHG. Amalswind,
lit. 'strong in work', fr. amal, 'work', and
*swind, 'strong'. For the first element cp. the
first element in Emery. The second element is
rel. to OS., OE. swid, Goth, swinps, 'strong',
OE. gesund, OHG. gisunt, 'healthy*. See sound,
'healthy'.

## milieu
milieu, п., surroundings. — F., 'middle, medium,
mean', lit. 'middle place', fr. mi, 'middle' (fr. L.
medius), and lieu, 'place' (fr. L. locus). See media,
'voiced stop consonant', and local and cp.
juste-milieu.

## Miliola
Miliola, п., a genus of Foraminifera (paleontol.)
— ModL., a diminutive formed fr. L. milium,
'millet' (see millet); so called from its
resemblance to the seeds of millet.

## miliollte
miliollte, п., a fossil foraminifer of the genus
Miliola (paleontol.) — Formed from prec. word
with subst. suff. -ite.

## militancy
militancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## militant
militant, adj., fighting. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.)
militant, fr. L. militantem, ace. of militans, pres.
part otmilitSre, 'to serve as a soldier', fr. miles,
gen. militis. See militia and -ant.
Derivatives: militant, п., militant-ly, adv.

## militarism
militarism, n. — F. militarisms, fr. militaire,
'military'. See military and -ism.

## militarist
militarist, п., 1) an expert in the art of war; 2) an
advocate of militarism. — Formed fr. military
with suff. -1st.
Derivatives: militarist, adj., militarist-ic adj.,
militarist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## military
military, adj. — MF. (= F.) militaire, fr. L. mili-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:492 COLUMN:2 -->
tdris, 'of, or belonging to, a soldier', dissimi-
lated ir.*milit-dlis, fr. miles, gen. militis, 'soldier';
see militia and 4th -ary. Cp. aldris, 'of the wing',
exemplaris, 'serving as a copy', and see adj. suff.
-ar.
Derivatives: military, п., militari-ly, adv., mili-
tari-ness, п., militarism (q.v.), militarist (q.v.),
militar-ize, tr. v., militar-iz-ation, n.

## militate
militate, intr. v., 1) to work as a soldier (now
rare); 2) to work against or for). — L. militat-
(um), pp. stem of militare, 'to serve as a soldier',
fr. miles, gen. militis. See prec. word and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: militat-ion, n.

## militia
militia, n. — L. militia, 'military service, warfare',
fr. miles, gen. militis, 'soldier', which is of
uncertain origin. It meant perh. orig. 'one who
marches in a troop*, and is cogn. with OI.
melah, melaka-, 'assembly', Gk. δμΐλος, 'an
assembled crowd, a throng'. See homily and cp.
militant, military, Milesian, 'Irish'.

## milk
milk, n. — ME. melk, milke, fr. OE. meoluc,
meolc, mile, rel. to OS. miluk, ON. mjolk, Swed.
and Norw. mjolk, OFris. melok, Dan., Du. melk,
OHG. miluh, MHG., G. milch, Goth, miluks,
'milk', OE. melcan, ON. molka, mjolka, OFris.
melka, Du. melken, OHG. mekhan, MHG., G.
melken, 'to milk', fr. I.-E. base *melg-, 'to press
out, to wipe off milk', whence also Gk. άμέλ-
γειν, 'to milk', Alb. mjet', miel', "1 milk', L. mul-
glre, 'to milk', OSlav. mluzo, mlisti, Lith. meliu,
militi, 'to milk', Mir. btigim, Ί milk', Olr. melg,
mlicht, blicht, 'milk', Toch. A malkant, 'they
gave milk', A malke, В malkwer, 'milk', Ol.
marsti, marjati, mrjati, 'wipes off'. Cp. milch.
Cp. also emulgent, emulsify, emulsion, milch,
and the second element in Caprimulgus.
Derivative: milk-y, adj., milk-i-ness, n.

## milk
milk, tr. and intr. v. — ME. melken, milken, fr.
OE. meolcian, milcian, fr. meolc, mile, 'milk'.
See milk, n.

## mill
mill, п., a building fitted with machinery for
grinding grain. — ME. milne, melle, mille, fr.
mylen, myln, fr. Late L. molina, 'mill', whence
also OS. mulin, ON-, Norw. mylna, Dan. melle,
Du. molen, OHG. muli, mulin (whence MHG.
mul, mule, G. Muhle), 'mill'. (Fr. Late L. moli-
num, 'mill', are borrowed It. mulino, F. moulin,
Sp. molino, Port, moinho, OSlav. тйИпй). Late
L. molina and molinum derive fr. L. mola, 'mill,
millstone' (whence It. mola, F. meule, Sp. muela.
Port, mo, 'millstone', Rum. moard, 'mill'), fr.
molere, 'to grind', fr. I.-E. base "mel-, 'to rub, to
grind', whence also Gk. μύλη, later μύλος, 'mill'.
See meal, 'edible grain', and words there
referred to an% cp. esp. molar, 'grinding', mole,
'false conception', molmary, moulin, mylo-. Cp.
also mall, 'to powder', mullet, 'star'.
Derivatives: mill, tr. v., to treat in a mill; intr.
v., to move confusedly in a circle; miller (q.v.),
mill-ing, n.

## mill
mill, п., the thousandth part of a dollar (used only
as a money of account). — Abbreviation of L.
mitlesimus, 'one thousandth'; formed on
analogy of cent, 'the hundredth part of a dollar'
(which is short for L. centesimus, 'one
hundredth'). See mile,

## mille
mille, п., a thousand. — L. mille. See mile.

## millefiori
millefiori, п., ornamental glasswork. — It., lit. 'a
thousand flowers', fr. mille, 'a thousand', and
fiori, pi. of fiore, 'flower'. It. mille derives fr.L.
mille; see prec. word. If. fiore comes fr. L. fio-
rem, ace. offlos, 'flower'; see floral.

## millenarian
millenarian, adj., pertaining to a thousand years;
pertaining to a millennium; п., one who believes
in the coming of the millennium. — Late L. mil-
Unarius, 'containing a thousand'. See millenary
and -an.

## millenarianism
millenarianism, п., belief in the millennium. —
Formed from prec. word with suff. -ism.

## millenary
millenary, adj., consisting of a thousand, esp. of
a thousand years. — L. millenarius, 'containing
a thousand', fr. milleni, 'a thousand each', fr.
mille. See mile and adj. suff. -ary.

## millenary
millenary, п., 1) peiiodof a thousand years; 2) a
thousandth anniversary. —. Fr. prec. word.

## millennium
millennium, п., period of a thousand years. —
ModL., formed on analogy of L. biennium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:492 COLUMN:3 -->
'period of two years*, etc., fr. L. mille, 'a
thousand', and annus, 'years'; see mile and annual
and cp. biennial.
Derivatives: millenni-al, adj., millennial-ly, adv.

## millepede
millepede, also millipede, millipede п., a myriapod
of the group Diplopoda, with two pairs of legs
for almost each segment. — L. mtttepeda, 'thou-
sandfeet', compounded of mille, 'a thousand',
and pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See mille and pedal.

## Millepora
Millepora, п., the genus of the millepores (zool.)
—ModL. See next word.

## millepore
millepore, п., any of a group of coralline hydro-
zoans, with numerous pores on the surface. —
ModL. millepora, lit. 'that which has a thousand
passages', fr. L. mille, 'a thousand', and porus,
'passage'. See mile and pore.

## miller
miller, n. — ME. millere, fr. mille, fr. myln, 'mill',
fr. OE. mylen. See mill and agential suff. -er.

## millerite
millerite, п., native nickel sulfide {mineral.) —
Named after the English mineralogist William
Hallowes Miller (1801-80). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## millesimal
millesimal, adj., thousandth; п., a thousandth
part. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
mitlesimus, 'thousandth*, fr. mille, 'a thousand'. See
mille.

## millet
millet, п., a cereal grass. —■ ME. milet, fr. MF.
(= F.) millet, dimin. of mil, fr. L. milium,
'millet', which stands for *meliyom and is cogn. with
Gk. μελίνη, 'millet', Lith. mdlnos (pi.), 'millet*.
Cp. mealie, Melica, Miliola and the second
element in gromwell. For the ending see suff. -et.

## milli-
milli-, combining form denoting one thousandth
part of a measure or weight. — Fr. L. mille, 'a
thousand'. See mile.

## milliard
milliard, п., one thousand millions. — F„ formed
fr. million with change of suffix. See million and
-ard.

## Mlilicent
Mlilicent, masc. PN. — See Milicent.

## milligram
milligram, milligramme, п., the thousandth part
of a gram. — F. milligramme, lit. 'a thousandth
part of a gramme', formed fr. milli- and gramme.
See gram, gramme.

## milliliter
milliliter, millilltre, п., lit. 'a thousandth part of a
liter'. — F. millilitre, formed fr. milli- and litre.
See liter, litre.

## millimeter
millimeter, millimetre, n. — F. millimetre, lit. 'a
thousandth part of a meter', formed fr. milli-
and mitre. See meter, 'unit of length'.

## milliner
milliner, n. — Earlier millaner, orig. 'inhabitant
of Milan', town in Italy, later used in the sense
of'dealer in hats, ribbons and other fancy goods
imported from Milan', whence arose the mean-
ning: 'a woman who makes up or trims women's
hats and other apparel'.
Derivatives: milliner, tr. v., milliner-ing, п., mil-
liner-y, п., milliner-ial, adj.

## million
million, n. — Late ME., fr. F. million, fr. It. mil-
Hone (now spelled milione), lit. 'a great
thousand', which is formed with the augmentative
suff. -one fr. L. mille, 'a thousand'. See mille and
cp. -oon.
Derivatives: million-th, adj. and n.

## millionaire
millionaire, n. — F. millionnaire, formed fr.
million with suff. -aire. See million and -ary.

## millipede
millipede, n. — See millepede.

## milord
milord, n. — F., fr. E. my lord.

## milrels
milrels, п., 1) name of a former Brazilian
monetary unit; 2) name of a former Portuguese
monetary unit. — Port., for mil reis, lit. 'a thousand
reis'. See mille and reis.

## milt
milt, п., the spleen. — ME. mille, fr. OE. miltre,
rel. to ON. milte, milti, Dan. milt, OSwed.
mjdlte, mjdlter, milter, Swed. mjelte, 'spleen',
Norw. mjelte, 'spleen; milt offish', OFris. milte,
'spleen', MDu. milte, Du. milt, 'spleen; milt of
fish', OHG. milzi, MHG. milze, milz, G. MHz,
'spleen'. These words prob. mean lit. 'the
softening or melting (gland)' and derive fr. I.-E.
*mel-d-, a -ιί-enlargement of base *mel-, 'to
rub, grind'. See meal, 'edible grain', and cp.
melt, mild.

## milt
milt, п., the male roe offish. — ME. milte, fr. OE.
milte; orig. identical with prec. word.

## milter
milter, п., a male fish, esp. in the breeding season.
— Formed from prec. word with agential suff.
-er.

## Mllvinae
Mllvinae, п., pi., a subfamily of the Falconidae,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:493 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MILVUS | 466 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:493 COLUMN:1 -->
the kites (ornithol.) — ModL., formed fr. Mil-
vus with suff. -inae.

## Mihus
Mihus, п., a genus of birds (ornithol.) — L. mil-
vus, 'kite', of uncertain origin.

## mim
mim, adj., prim, demure (dial.) — Of imitative
origin.

## miinbar
miinbar, п., the pulpit in a mosque. — Arab.
minbar, 'pulpit', which orig. denoted 'an
(elevated) seat', and is a loan word fr. Ethiop.
minbar, 'seat', fr. nabara, 'he was sitting'. Ethiop.
nabara is rel. to Arab, nabara^ 'he raised,
elevated'. For sense development cp. Arab, jdlasa,
'he sat down, was sitting', julus, 'sitting, sitting
down; accession to the throne*. See Theodor
Noldeke, Lehnworter in und aus dem Athiopi-
schen, in his Neue Beitrage zur semitischen
Sprachwissenschaft, Strassburg, 1910, p. 49. Cp.
almemar.

## mim-
mim-, form of mi mo- before a vowel.

## mime
mime, n. — L. mimus, fr. Gk, μίμος, 'imitator,
actor, mime' (whence μΐμεΐσθαι, 'to imitate'),
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. Mimosa and
the second element in pantomime.
Derivatives: mime, tr. and intr. v., mim-er, n.

## mimeograph
mimeograph, п., a machine for making copies by
means of a stencil. — Coined from the stem of
Gk. μΐμεΐσθαι, 'to imitate*, and -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See mime and -graph.
Derivative: mimeograph, tr- v.

## mimesis
mimesis,п., imitation, mimicry (biol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. μΤμησις, 'imitation', fr. μΐμεϊσθαι. See
mime.

## mimetic
mimetic, adj., imitative. — Gk. μιμητικός,
'imitative', fr. μιμητός, verbal adj. of μΐμεΐσθαι,
*to imitate'. See mime and -ic.
Derivative: mimetic-al-ly, adv.

## mimic
mimic, adj., apt to imitate, imitative. — L. mimi-
cus, fr. Gk. μΐμικός, 'pertaining to mimes,
farcical, mimic', fr. μίμος. See mime and adj.
suff. -ic.
Derivatives: mimic, n. and tr. v., mimick-er, п.,
mimic-ry, n.

## mimmation
mimmation, п., the addition of a final m in the
declension of nouns (as in Akkadian). — ModL.
mimmdtid, gen. -onis, fr. mim, name of the letter
m in Arabic, which is related to mem, name of
the letter m in Hebrew. See mem and -ation.

## mimo-
mimo-, before a vowel, mim-, combining form
meaning 'mime' or 'mimic'. — Gk. μίμο-,
μΐμ-, fr. μίμος, 'imitator'. See mime.

## Mimosa
Mimosa, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. mimus, 'mime'. See mime.

## Mimosaceae
Mimosaceae, п., pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Mimosa with suff. -aceae.

## mfmosaceous
mfmosaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Mimulus
Mimulus, п., a genus of plants, the monkey
flower (bot.) — Late L. mimulus, dimin. of L.
mimus (see mime and -ule); so called in allusion
to the masklike corolla.

## Mimus
Mimus, п., a genus of birds, the mockingbird
(ornithol.) — L. mimus, 'mime'. See mime.

## Mimusops
Mimusops, п., a genus of tropical trees of the
sapodilla family (bot.) — ModL., compounded
of Gk. μΐμώ, gen. μίμους, 'ape' (fr. μίμος,
'imitator'), and ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'face'. See mime
and -ops.

## mina
mina, п., an ancient unit of weight and money. —
L., fr. Gk. μνα, which is of Sem. origin. Cp.
Akkad. manu (fr. Sumer. mana) and Heb.
mdneh,Bi >lical Aram. mene(Oan. 5 : 25), Aram.-
Syr. manya (whence Arab, manan), Ugar. mn,
which are borrowed fr. Akkad. manu. Cp. mine,
'unit of weight'. Cp. also maund, 'unit of weight'.

## mina
mina, п., a myna. — See niyna.

## Mina
Mina, fem PN. — Shortened fr. Wilhelmina.

## minacious
minacious, δ dj., threatening. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. minax, gen. -acis, 'threatening', fr.
minari, 'to threaten'. See minatory.

## Minaean
Minaean, adj. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L.
Minaei (pi.), a people in South Arabia, fr. Gk.
Μιναΐοι, fr. Arab. Ma'an; they are mentioned
in the Bible under the names of MeiHntm (I Chr.
4: 41, II Chr. 26: 7) and Ma*on (Judg. 10 : 12).

## mtuaret
mtuaret, п., a slender tower attached to a
mosque. — Sp. minarete, fr. Turk, menaret, fr.
Arab, manarcl·, 'candlestick; tower of a mosque,
lighthouse', fr. nara, 'it lighted', rel. to Heb.
ner, 'lamp', m пбга \ Aram, m narta,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:493 COLUMN:2 -->
'candlestick'. See Menorah.
Derivative: minarett-ed, adj.

## minatory
minatory, adj., threatening. — Late L. minatoriusy
fr. L. minatus, pp. of mindri, 'to jut out, project
out, tower up; to threaten', fr. minae,
'projecting points, pinnacles; threats', fr. I.-E. base
"men-, 'to project, stand out', whence also mons,
gen. montis, 'mountain'. See mount, 'hill,
mountain', and adj. suff. -ory and cp. manada, menace,
commutation, demeanor, imminent, prominent.
Cp. also mane,

## mince
mince, tr. v. — ME. mincen, fr. MF. minder*
mincer (F. mincer), fr. VL. *minutiare, *ю make
small', fr. L. minutus, pp. of minuere, 'to make
less*. See minish, and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: mince, n,, minc-er, п., minc-ing,
adj., minc-ing-ly, adv.

## mind
mind, n. — ME. mind, mynd, minde, munde, fr.
ОЕ- gemynd, 'memory, remembrance', rel. to
OHG. gimunt, Goth, gamunds, of s.m., OS.
minnea, OHG. minna, OFris., MDu., MHG.,
G. minne (orig. 'memory; loving memory'),
ON. minni, 'mind', Dan. minde, 'memory,
mind', Goth, muns, 'thought', munan, 'to
remember', fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to think,
remember, have one's mind aroused, apply
oneself to', whence also OI. matih, matih (for
*mntis), 'thought, opinion', manas, 'spirit,
passion', manyate, 'thinks', munih, 'inspired',
Toch. Amnu, 'thought', Arm.
i-manam/lunderstand', Gk. μένος, 'desire, ardor, spirit,
passion', μέμονα, 4 remember, wish, long, yearn,
strive', μέντωρ, 'adviser', μνασθαι, Ίο
remember*, μιμνήσκει,ν, 'to remind, cali to mind',
μνησις, 'remembrance, memory', μηήσιος,
'pertaining to memory', αμνησία, 'forgetful-
ness', μνήμη, 'remembrance, memory*, μνήμων,
'mindful, remembering', μνημονικός, 'of
memory, having a good memory', μαίνεσθ=α, 'to be
mad', μανία, 'madness, frenzy', μάντις, 'seer*,
μαντεία, *oracle, divination', -ματος in
αυτόματος, 'acting of one's own will' (compounded
of αυτός, 'self, and *mntos, 'thinking'), L.
mens, gen. mentis (for I.-E. *mntis), 'mind,
understanding, reason, memini, meminisse, 'to
remember', monere, *to remind, warn, advise,
instruct', monstrum, 'an evil omen, portent,
monster' [for *mone-strom, lit. 'that which serves as
a warning' (fr. monere)], monstrdre, 'to show,
point out, indicate', Lith. minus, 'thought, idea',
atmintis, 'remembrance', OSlav. mineti, 'to
believe, think', pameti, 'remembrance', Russ.
pamjaV, 'memory', Olr. domoiniur, Ί believe,
think'. Cp. minnesinger, minikin. Cp. also
admonish, admonition, amentia, amnesia, amnesty,
anamnesis, automatic, Clytemnestra, comment,
dement, dementia, demonstrate, Epimetheus, Eu-
menides, lentamente, Maenad, man, manas,
-mancy, mandarin, mania, mantic, mantis,
mantra, mathematic, memento, mental, 'pertaining
to the mind', mention, Mentor, mnemonic, mne-
sic, mnestlc, monition, monitor, monstrance,
monster, monument. Muse, muster, necromancy,
premonition, Prometheus, reminiscence,
reminiscent, remonstrance, remonstrate, summon,
summons, tardamente, Trichomanes, Zamenis.
Derivatives: mind, tr. and intr. v., mind-ed, adj.,
mind-er, п., mind-ful, adj., mind-ful-ly, adv.,
mind-ful-ness, п., mind-less, adj., mind-less-ly,
adv., mind-less-ness, n.

## mine
mine, possessive pron. — ME. min, fr. OE. min,
'my, of me', rel. to OS., OFris., OHG., MHG.
min, ON. minn, Dan., Swed. min, MDu., Du.
mijn,G.mein, 'my, mine, of me',Goth. meins, 'my,
mine', meina, 'of me'. All these words stand for
I.-E. *mei-no-s and are cogn. with L. meus (for
*mei-os), 'my, mine'; see me, meum and cp. the
first element in mynheer.'In ME. the final -n was
dropped before a word beginning with a
consonant and so arose the form my (q.v.)

## mine
mine, п., excavation. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
mine, which is prob. of Celtic origin. Cp. Gael.,
MIr. mein, W. mwyn, Ore'. Cp. also mineral,

## mine
mine, tr. and intr. v., to dig a mine. — ME. minen,
fr. OF. (= F.), miner, fr. mine. See prec. word.

## miner
miner, n. — ME. minour, fr. OF. mineor, minour
(F. mineur), fr. OF. (= F.) mine. See mine,
'excavation', and agential suff. -er.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:493 COLUMN:3 -->

## mine
mine, п., unit of weight. — F., fr. L. mina. See
mina.

## mineral
mineral, n. — ME-, fr. OF. mineral (F. mineral),
fr. ML. minerdle, prop. neut. of the adjective
mineralis, 'pertaining to mines', fr. minera,
'mine', fr. OF. miniere, minere, of s.m., fr. mine.
See mine, 'excavation', and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: mineral, adj., mineralize (q.v.)

## mineralize
mineralize, tr. v., to convert into a mineral. —
Formed from prec. word with suff. -ize.
Derivatives: mineraliz-ation, п., mineraliz-er, n.

## mineralogy
mineralogy, п., the science of minerals. —
Contraction of *mineretiology, a hybrid coined fr.
ML. minerdle (see mineral) and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
For the contraction of *mineralology into
mineralogy see haplology. Cp. F. mineralogie.
Derivatives: mineralog-ic, mineralog-ic-al, adjs.,
mineralog-ic-al-ly, adv., mineralog-ist, n.

## Minerva
Minerva, п., the ancient Roman goddess of
wisdom; identified later with the Greek goddess
Athena. — L., fr. OL. Menerva, usually
connected with Gk. μένος, 'might, force, spirit,
passion', L. mens, 'mind, understanding, reason',
but prob. a word of Etruscan origin; cp. the
Etruscan names of the goddess Menrva,
Menerva. The change of the first e to ι is due to a
dissimilation suggested by a popular connection of
the name with L. minari, 'to threaten' (as if
Minerva meant 'the threatening goddess').

## minestrone
minestrone, п., a rich Italian vegetable soup
containing vermicelli, herbs, etc. — It., formed with
augment, suff. -one fr. minestra, 'soup', lit. 'that
which is served', fr. minestrare, 'to serve', which
derives fr. L. ministrare. See minister, v. and n.

## minever
minever, n. — See miniver.

## mingle
mingle, tr. and intr. v. — ME. mengelen, freq. of
mengen, fr. OE. mengan, rel. to OS. mengian, ON.
menga, OFris. mendza, MDu. menghen, Du. and
G. mengen, fr. Teut. base *mang-, 'to mix', orig.
'to knead together', which corresponds to I.-E.
base *menq-, 'to knead, mix', whence Ol. ma~
cati, mancate, 'crushes', OSlav. meknqti, 'to
become soft', текйкй, 'soft', тдка, 'meal, flour*,
Lith. minkau, minkyti, 'to knead', minkle,
'dough', minkStas, 'soft*, and possibly also Gk.
μάσσω (if standing for *mnq-yo), Ί squeeze,
press into a mold, knead'. Cp. among, mongrel.
— Cp. *mag-, 'to knead', a collateral base, for
the derivatives of which see macerate, make, v.
Derivative: mingl-er, n.

## minhag
minhag, п., custom, esp. local custom (Jewish
religion). — Mishnaic Heb. minhagh, 'usage,
custom', fr. Bibl. Heb. minhagh, 'driving', fr.
ndhdgh, 'he drove, conducted', which is rel. to
Aram. nehagh, 'he led', Arab, nahaja, 'he went
along the road'. For the sense development of
Heb. minhagh, ср. Е. condua, which derives fr.
L. conductus, pp. of conducere, 'to lead together*.

## minhah
minhah, п., the daily afternoon prayer (Jewish
liturgy). — Mishnaic Heb. minhah, fr. Bibl. Heb.
minhah, 'gift, present; tribute, offering', esp.
'meal offering' (whence Bibl. Aram. minhah, of
s.m.) The sense 'afternoon prayer', prob.
derives from Elijah's prayer 'at the time of the
offering of the evening minhah — sacrifice' (I
Kings, 18: 36). Bibl. Heb. minhahis rel. to Arab.
manaha, 'he gave a gift'.

## miniate
miniate, tr. v., to paint with vermilion. — L.
miniums, pp. of miniare. See next word and verbal
suff. -ate.

## miniature
miniature, п., 1) a small painting; 2) a small copy.
-^- F., fr. It. miniatura, fr. ML. miniatttra, fr. L.
miniatus, pp. of miniare, 'to paint with red lead
or vermilion', fr. minium, 'cinnabar, vermilion'.
See minium and -ure.
Derivatives: miniature, adj., miniatur-ist, n.

## Minie ball
Minie ball, a kind of rifle bullet. — Named after
its inventor Claude-Etienne Minie, a French
army officer (1814-79).

## minify
minify, tr. v., to make small, to lessen. — Formed
on analogy of magnify fr. L. mini- (in minimus,
'smallest') and -ficdre, ΐτ./acere, 'to make, do'.
See minimum and -fy.

## minikin
minikin, п., something very small; adj., delicate,
dainty. — MDu. minnekijn, 'darling', dimin. of
minne, 'love'. See mind and -kin and cp. minne-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:494 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 467 | MIRACLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:494 COLUMN:1 -->
singer.

## minim
minim, п., 1) the half note, i.e. half the time of the
semibreve or whole note (mus.); 2) a very small
object. — L. minimus, 'smallest, least'. See mlni-
mnm.

## minimal
minimal, adj., smallest, least. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. minimus. See minimum.

## Minimalist
Minimalist, п., formerly, a member of the right
(i.e. less radical) wing of the Russian Social
Revolutionary party. — Lit. 'one who insists
only on the minimum of his demands', formed
with suff. -ist fr. L. minimus. See minimum.

## minimize
minimize, tr. v. — Coined by Jeremy Bentham
(1748-1833) fr. L. minimus. See next word and
-ize.
Derivatives: minimiz-ation, п., minimiz-er, n.

## minimum
minimum, n. — L., neut. of minimus, 'smallest,
least', superl. corresponding to the compar.
minor, 'smaller, less', rel. to minuere, 'to make
smaller, lessen, reduce', which derives fr. l.-E.
*mi-nu-, 'small, less; to lessen, diminish',
whence also Gk. μινύθειν, 'to lessen', the first
element in μινύ-ωρος, μινυ-ώριος,
'shortlived', OSlav. miniji, 'smaller'. Base mi-пи- is
prob. an enlargement of base *mei-, 'to lessen,
diminish', whence OI. miyate, 'diminishes,
decays, declines', Gk. μείων, 'less'. Base *mei-,
'to lessen, diminish', was perh. orig. identical
with base *mei-, 'to change' (see mean, 'of low
rank'). — Cp. base *men-, *menu-, 'small',
appearing in Ol. manak, 'a little', Toch. В menki,
'less', Hitt. maninka-, 'short', Arm. manr (gen.
manu), 'small, thin', manuk, 'child, boy, servant',
Gk. μανός (for *μανΓός), 'thin, rare', μόνος
(for *μόνΓας), 'single, alone', Lith. menkas,
'mediocre', Olr. menb, 'small', Co. minow, 'to
lessen', Goth, minniza, OHG., OS. minniro,
MHG. minre, minner, G., Du. minder, OFris.
minnera, minra, ON. minni, 'less', Goth, min-
nists, OHG., OS. minnist, MHG. minnest, G.
mindest, OFris. minnusta, Du. minst, ON.
minnstr, 'least', OE. minsian, 'to diminish'. (Co.
minow, 'to lessen', and the Teut. words cited
above could also be derived from base *minu-.)
Cp. mince, mulish, minister, minor, minuet,
minus, minute, mister, ulmiety. Cp. also meionite,
meiosis, Ameiurus, Mensherik. Cp. also
manometer, mono-. Cp. also mangie, 'to mutilate'.

## minimus
minimus, adj., the youngest of several boys of the
same surname. — L., 'smallest'. See minimum.

## minion
minion, п., a favorite, darling. — MF. (= F.)
mignon, 'delicate, charming, pretty'. See mlgnon.

## minish
minish, tr. v. (archaic) — ME. menusen, fr. OF.
menuisier, menuiser, 'to make small, cut small'
(whence F. menuiser, 'to cut down'), fr. VL.
'minutiare, 'to make small' (whence also It.
minuzzare, Sp. menuzar), fr. L. minutus, pp. of
minuere, 'to reduce, lessen'. See minimuin and
cp. mince, diminish, diminution. Cp. also
minute.

## minister
minister, n. — ME. menistre, minisIre, fr. OF.
menislre (F. ministre), fr. L. minister, 'a servant',
