for *minis-teros, fr. earlier *minus-teros, formed
with comparative suff. from minor, minus,
'smaller, less'; see minimum; / for и in the second
syllable of the L. word minister is due to the
influence of its antonyme magister, 'master'. Cp.
minstrel. For the compar. suff. see -ther.

## minister
minister, intr. and tr. v. — ME. ministren, fr. OF.
ministrer, fr. L. ministrare, 'to serve'. See
minister, п., and cp. minestrone.
Derivatives: ministr-er, п., ministr-ess, n.

## ministerial
ministerial, adj. — F. ministeriel, fr. Late L. mi-
nisterialis, 'pertaining to service', fr. L. minis-
terium. See ministry.
Derivatives: ministerial-ist, п., ministerial-ity,
п., ministerial-ly, adv., ministerial-ness, a.

## ministerium
ministerium, n. — L. See ministry.

## ininistrant
ininistrant, adj. and n. — L. ministruns, gen. -an-
tis, pres. part of ministrare. See minister, v., and
suff. -ant.

## ministration
ministration, n. — ME. ministracioun, fr. L. mi-
nistratio, gen. -onis, 'service, assistance', fr. mi-
nistratus, pp. of ministrare. See minister, v., and
-ation.

## ministrative
ministrative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
ministratus, pp. of ministrare. See minister, v.

## ministrator
ministrator, n. — L. ministrdtor, 'an attendant,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:494 COLUMN:2 -->
servant', fr. ministratus, pp. of ministrare. See
minister, v., and agential suff. -or.

## ministry
ministry, n. — ME. mynysterie, fr. L. ministerium,
'service, attendance, ministry', fr. minister. See
minizter, п., and -y (representing L. -ium) and
cp. metier and mystery, 'trade', which are
doublets of ministry.

## miulum
miulum, п., red lead, vermilion. — L., 'cinnabar,
vermilion', of Iberian origin. Cp. miniature and
the second element in carmine.

## miniver
miniver, also minever, п., a white fur, formerly
used for trimming garments. — OF. menu vair,
'miniver', lit. 'small (and) variegated'. See menu
and vair.

## mink
mink, n. — Late ME. minke. Cp. Swed. menk,
'mink'.

## minnesinger
minnesinger, п., one of a circle of German lyric
poets of the 12th, 13th and 14th centuries. — G.,
fr. MHG. minnesinger, lit. 'singer of love', fr.
minne, 'love', and singer, 'singer'. The first
element orig. meant 'memory, loving memory',
and derives fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to think'; see
mind and cp. minikin. MHG. singer derives fr.
MHG. singen, 'to sing'. See sing and agential
suff, -er and cp. meistersinger.

## minnow
minnow, п., a small fresh-water fish of the carp
family. — ME. menow, 'a small fish', fr. OE.
myne, rel. to MLG. топе, Du. meun, OHG.
mun(i)wa (MHG. miinwe, G. Miinne), of
uncertain origin; perh. cogn. with Gk. μαίνη, μαινί-
διον, 'a small seafish', Russ. men', 'eelpout',
Lith. тёпкё, Lett, menza, 'cod'.

## mlno
mlno, п., a kind of cloak made from grass, rushes
or straw, or the like, worn by Japanese peasants.
— Jap.

## Minoan
Minoan, adj., pertaining to the prehistoric
culture and art of Crete. — Lit. 'pertaining to
Minos', formed with suff. -an fr. L. Minos, fr.
Gk. ΜΓνως, 'Minos', name of the legendary
king of Crete. Cp. Minotaur.

## minor
minor, adj. — ME., fr. L., 'smaller, less', compar.
corresponding to the superl. minimus. See
minimum.
Derivative: minor, n.

## Minorca
Minorca, п., a breed of domestic fowls. — Named
fr. Minorca, one of the Balearic Islands. The
name Minorca derives from Sp. Menorca, which
comes fr. L. Balearis Minor, 'the smaller
Balearic (Island)'.

## Minorite
Minorite, п., a Franciscan friar. — Formed with
subst. suff. -ite fr. L. minor, 'smaller, less' (see
minor); so called because the Franciscan friar
regarded himself as of humbler rank than
members of other orders.

## minority
minority, n. — ML. mindritas, fr. L. minor,
'smaller'. See minor and -ity.

## Minotaur
Minotaur, п., the monster, half man, half bull,
who was confined in the famous Labyrinth in
Crete. — ME. Minotaure, fr. L. Minotaurus, fr.
Gk. Μινώταυρος, lit. 'bull of Minos', which is
compounded of Μΐνως, 'Minos' and ταϋρος,
'bull'. See Mlaoan and Taurus.

## minster
minster, п., the church of a monastery. — ME.,
fr. OE. mynster, fr. VL. * monisterium (whence
also OF. moustier, F. moutier, Olr. manister), fr.
Eccles. L. monasterium. See monastery.

## minstrel
minstrel, п., 1) a medieval professional musical
entertainer; 2) a poet, singer (poetic). — ME.
menestrel, fr. OF. ministrel, menestrel, 'servant,
minstrel' (F. menestrel; cp. F. menetrier,
'strolling fiddler'), fr. Late L. ministrdlem,
ministerialem, ace. of ministralis, ministerialis,
'servant, retainer, jester'. See minister and -el
(representing L. -alls).

## minstrelsy
minstrelsy, п., 1) the art or occupation of a
minstrel; 2) a company of minstrels; 3) a
collection of songs. — ME. minstralcie, fr. OF.
menestratsie, fr. ministrel, menestrel. See prec.
word.

## mint
mint, п., an aromatic herb. — ME. minte, fr. OE.
minte, fr. L. menta, mentha, fr. Gk. μίνθη,
'mint', which is prob. a loan word from a South-
European language. See Meillet in Memoires de
la Societe de Linguistique de Paris, XV., 162.
Cp. Mentha and the second element in calamint.
Derivative: mint-y, adj.

## mint
mint, п., a place for coining money. — ME. minte,
mynt, fr. OE. mynet, 'coin', fr. L. moneta, 'mint,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:494 COLUMN:3 -->
coin, money', fr. Moneta. a surname of Juno, in
whose temple at Rome money was coined. The
name Moneta is of uncertain, possibly
Phoenician or Etruscan, origin. The usual derivation of
Moneta fr. monere, 'to admonish', suggested
already by the ancients, is prob. folk etymology.
Cp. Moneta. Cp. also money and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: mint, tr. v., mint-age, п., mint-er, n.

## minuend
minuend, п., the number from which another
number (the subtrahend) is to be subtracted. —
L. minuendus, 'to be diminished', gerundive of
minuere. See minimum. For other Latin
gerundives or their derivatives used in English cp.
agenda and words there referred to.

## minuet
minuet, п., a slow dance of French origin. — F.
menuet, fr. menu, 'small', fr. L. minutus, pp. of
minuere, 'to make smaller'. See minute, n.

## minus
minus, prep. —■ L., neut. of minor, 'smaller, less'.
See minor and cp. the first element in muscovado.

## minuscule
minuscule, п., a small letter. — L. minuscula (scil.
littera), 'a somewhat smaller letter", fern, of
minusculus, 'somewhat smaller', dimin. of
minor, neut. minus, 'smaller, less'. See minus and
-cule.
Derivatives: minuscule, minuscul-ar, adjs.

## minute
minute, п., the sixtieth part of an hour. — Late
ME. minute, fr. F. minute, fr. ML. minuta, short
for L. pars minuta prima, lit.'the first small part',
used by the mathematician Ptolemy (Claudius
Ptolemaeus) to denote the sixtieth part of a
degree. See minute, adj. For sense development
cp. second, n.
Derivative: minute, tr. v., to time to the minute,
to time exactly.

## minute
minute, п., a short draft or memorandum. — L.
minutum, neut. of minutus, 'small, minute', pp.
of minuere, 'to make small'. See minute, adj.

## minute
minute, adj., very small. — L. minutus, 'small,
minute', pp. of minuere, 'to make small'. See
minimum and cp. minute, п., menu, and minuet.
Cp. also comminute.
Derivatives: minute-ly (q.v.), minute-ness, n.

## minutely
minutely, adv., occurring every minute. —
Formed fr. minute, п., with adv. suff. -ly.

## minutely
minutely, adv., in a minute manner. — Formed
fr. minute, adj., with adv. suff. -ly.

## minutiae
minutiae, n. p]., small, trifling details. — L.,
'unimportant matters, trifles', pi. aiminutia, 'small-
ness', fr. minutus, 'small', pp. of minuere, 'to
make small'. See minute, adj.

## minx
minx, п., a saucy girl or woman. — Prob. fr. LG.
minsk, 'a man; an impudent woman', which is
rel. to MDu. mensche, OS. mennisco, 'man',
OHG. mannisco, mennisco, 'man', MHG.
mensche, 'man', whence G. Mensch (masc),
'man', Mensch (neut.), 'wench, hussy;
maidservant', and to OE. man, 'man'. See man.

## minyan
minyan, п., the quorum necessary for public
worship, consisting of at least ten males over
the age of thirteen years (Jewish religirmt). —
Mishnaic Heb. minyan, lit. 'number, count', fr.
Heb. mdna , 'he counted, numbered, reckoned,
assigned' (whence типа , 'portion'), which is rel.
to Aram.-Syr. mend, 'he counted, numbered',
Arab, mdna, 'he counted, numbered; he
assigned, apportioned', Akkad. manu, 'to count,
number, apportion".

## mio-
mio-, combining form meaning 'smaller, less'. —
Gk. μειο-, fr. μείων,'lesser, less', fr. I.-E. base
"met-, 'to lessen, diminish'. See minimum and
cp. meionite, meiosis, Ameiurus.

## Miocene
Miocene, adj., pertaining to the Middle
Tertiary Period, i.e., the period between the Oli-
gocene and Pliocene (geol.) — Coined fr. mio-
and Gk. καινός, 'new, recent'. See kainite.

## miquelet
miquelet, п., formerly, one of a body of bandits
in the Pyrenees. — F., fr. Sp. miquelete,
'mountain soldier, bandit', named after Miquelos de
Prats, chief of a troop of bandits.

## mir
mir, п., formerly, a Russian village community.
— Russ., 'peace; world; community'. See
mitigate and cp. the second element in Casimir.

## Mirabel
Mirabel, fern. PN. — Lit. 'wonderful, marvelous',
fr. L. mirabilis. See next word and cp. Miranda.

## miracle
miracle, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F), fr. L. miracu-
lum, 'wonderful thing, marvel', fr. mirari, 'to
wonder at', fr. minis, 'wonderful', which stands

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:495 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MIRACULDUS | 468 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:495 COLUMN:1 -->
for *smeiros, and is cogn. with OI. smerah,
'smiling', smayate, smayati, 'smiles', smitafa,
'smiling', Gk. μει,δαν, μειδιαν, 'to smile',
OSlav. smejo, smijati se, Lett, smeju, smiet, 'to
laugh', OSlav. smechu, 'laugh, laughter', Toch. A
smimam, В smimane v(pres. part.), 'smiling',
MHG. smielen, smieren, ME. smilen, 'to smile'.
All these words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*(s)mei-, *(s)mi-, 'to smile, be astonished'.
Cp. smile. Cp. also admire, marvel, Mirabel,
mirador, mirage, Miranda, mirific, mirror. For
the ending of miracle see suff. -cle.

## miraculous
miraculous, adj. — MF. (= F.) miraculeux (fern.
miraculeuse), fr. miracle. See miracle and -ous.
Derivatives: miraculous-ly, adv., miraculous-
ness, n.

## mirador
mirador, п., a watchtower. — Sp., fr. mirar, 'to
look, look at, behold', fr. VL. mirare, 'to look
attentively', fr. L. mirari, 'to wonder at'. See
miracle and cp. mirror.

## mirage
mirage, п., an optical illusion in which objects
are usually shown inverted in the air. — F., fr.
mirer, 'to look at', se mirer, 'to look at oneself
in a mirror', fr. VL. mirare, 'to look attentively',
fr. L. mirari, 'to wonder at'. See miracle and
-age.
Derivatives: mirage, tr. v., mirag-y, adj.

## Miranda
Miranda, fern. PN. — Lit. fern, of L. mlrandus,
'worthy to be admired', gerundive of mirari, 'to
admire'. See miracle and cp. Mirabel. For the
use of Latin gerundives or their derivatives in
English cp. agenda and words there referred to.

## mire
mire, n. — ME. myre, mire, fr. ON. myrr, 'bog,
swamp', which is rel. to OE. mos, 'marsh, moor',
meos, 'moss', fr. I.-E. base *meu-s, 'march,
moss'. See moss.
Derivatives: mire, tr. and intr.,v., mir-y, adj.,
mir-i-ness, n.

## Miriam
Miriam, 1) fern. PN., 2) in the Bible, the sister of
Moses and Aaron (see Ex. 15:20). — Heb.
Mirydm. Cp. Mary and words there referred to.

## mirific
mirific, adj., working wonders; marvelous. — F.
mirifique, fr. L. mirificus, 'causing wonder,
wonderful', which is compounded of mirus,
'wonderful', and -ficus, fr. -ficere, unstressed
form of facere, 'to make, do'. See miracle and
-He.

## mirk
mirk, n. — See murk.

## mirror
mirror, n. — ME. mirour, fr. OF. mireor, mire-
our, mirour (F. miroir), fr. VL. mirare, 'to look
at', fr. L. mirari, 'to wonder at'. See miracle.
Derivatives: mirror, tr. v., mirror-y, adj.

## mirth
mirth, n. —■ ME. myrthe, fr. OE. myrigd, mirigd,
mirgd, 'pleasure, joy', formed with suff, -d fr.
myrige, myrig, mirig, 'pleasing, delightful,
merry'. See merry and subst. suff. -th.
Derivatives: mirth-ful, adj., mirth-ful-ly, adv.,
mirth-ful-ness, п., mirth-less, adj., mirth-less-ly,
adv., mirth-less-ness, n.

## mirza
mirza, п., a Persian title placed: 1) after the name
(to denote a prince); 2) before the name (to
denote an officer or a scholar). — Pers. mir-za,
shortened fr. mir-zadah, lit. 'son of a prince', a
hybrid coined fr. Arab, amir, 'prince*, and Pers.
zadah, 'son of, fr. zadan, 'to be born', fr.
MPers. zatan, of s.m., which is re], to Avestic
zata-, 'born', and cogn. with L. gignere (for gi-
gn-ere), 'to beget, bear, bring forth, produce'.
For the first element see emir, for the second see
genus and cp. the second еДетеп! in shahzada.

## mis-
mis-, a pref. of two various origins used in the
senses amiss, wrong, wrongly, badly, ill. 1) In
words of Teut. origin it derives fr. OE. mis-,
which is rel. to ON. and Dan. mis-, Swed. miss·,
OHG. missa-, MHG. misse-, G. mifi-, Goth.
missa-. The orig. meaning of these prefixes was
'mutual', whence 'inverted; wrong'. They are
rel. to Goth, misso, 'mutually', missa-leiks, 'of
a different kind', ON. ymiss, 'mutual', and
derive fr. OTeut. * missa-, which stands for pre-
Teut. *mit-to-, lit. 'changed, exchanged', formed
with pp. suff. *-to fr. I.-E. base *mit(h)-,
*meit(h)-, 'to change'. To OTeut. *missa- are
also traceable OE. missan, OFris. missa, etc., 'to
miss (the mark)'; see miss, v. Goth, maidjan, 'to
change', OE. midan, OS. mithan, OFris. mitha, 'to
conceal*, Du. mijden, 'to shun', OHG. midan,
MHG. mlden, 'to conceal', G. meiden, 'to shun',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:495 COLUMN:2 -->
also derive fr. I.-E. base *meit(h)-. For other
derivatives of this base see mutable. 2) In words
of French origin pref. mis- represents OF. mes-
(whence F. mes-, me-), a pejorative pref.
derived fr. L. minus, 'less' (whence also Olt.
menes-, Sp., Port, menos·). See minimum.

## mis-
mis-, form of miso- before a vowel.

## misadventure
misadventure, n. — ME. mesaventure, fr. OF.
mesaventure (F. mesaventure). — See mis- and
adventure.

## misalliance
misalliance, n. — Formed on analogy of F.
mesalliance fr. mis- and alliance.

## misanthrope
misanthrope, п., one who hates mankind. — Gk.
μϊσάνθρωπος, 'hating mankind', compounded
of the stem of μΐσεΐν, 'to hate', and άνθρωπος,
'man'. See miso- and anthropo-.
Derivatives: misanthrop-ic, misanthrop-ic-al,
adjs., misanthrop-ic-al-ly, adv., misanthrop-ism,
п., misanthrop-ist, п., misanthrop-y, n.

## miscegenation
miscegenation, п., interbreeding of different
races. — Coined from the stem of L. miscere, 'to
mix, mingle', genus, 'kind, race', and suff.
-ation. See mix and genus.
misce]lanea,n., pi., a miscellany.—L. miscellanea,
'a writing on miscellaneous subjects', neut. pi.
of miscellaneus. See next word.

## miscellaneous
miscellaneous, adj., mixed, consisting of various
kinds. — L. miscellaneus, 'mixed,
miscellaneous', fr. miscellus, 'mixed', fr. miscere, 'to mix'.
See mix. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.
Derivatives: miscellaneous-ly, adv., misceliane-
ous-ness, n.

## miscellany
miscellany, п., \) a medley; 2) a collection of
writings on various subjects. — F. miscellanies
(pi.), fr. L. miscellanea, 'a writing on
miscellaneous subjects', neut. pi. of miscellaneus. See
miscellaneous.

## mischance
mischance, n. — ME. mescheance, fr. OF. mes-
cheance, meschance. See mis- and chance.

## mischief
mischief, n. — ME. meschef. fr. OF. meschef,
meschief, back formation fr. meschever, 'to fail,
be unfortunate', which is formed fr. pref. mes-
(see mis-) and OF. chever, 4o come to an end',
fr. chief, 'head, end'. See chief and cp. achieve.

## mischievous
mischievous, adj. — ME. meschevous, fr. AF.
meschevous, fr. OF. meschever. See prec. word
and -ous.
Derivatives: mischievous-ly, adv., mischievous-
ness, n.

## miscible
miscible, adj., capable of being mixed. — Formed
with suff. -ible fr. L. miscere, 'to mix'. See mix.

## miscreant
miscreant, adj., 1) unbelieving (obsol.); 2)
villainous; п., 1) unbeliever {obsol.); 2) villain. —
ME., fr. OF. mescreant (F. mecreant),
'disbelieving, unbeliever', formed fr. pejorative pref.
mes- and creant, pres. part, of croire, fr. L.
credere, 'to believe'. See mis- and creed and cp.
recreant.

## misdeed
misdeed, n. — ME. misdede, fr. OE. misdxd, rel.
to OHG. missitat, MHG. missetGt, G. Missetat,
Goth, missadeps, 'misdeed'. See mis- and deed.

## mise
mise, п., 1) pact, agreement; 2) the issue in a
writ of right (law). — AF., fr. OF. (= F.) mise,
lit. 'a putting, placing', prop. fern. pp. of mettre,
'to put, place', fr. L. mittere, 'to send'. See
mission.

## mise-en-scene
mise-en-scene, п., 1) setting on the stage; 2)
general surroundings. — F., 'setting on the
stage*. See prec. word, 1st en- and in-, 'in', and
scene.

## misenite
misenite, п., a potassium sulfate (mineral.) —
Named after Cape Miseno near- Naples in Italy.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## miser
miser, п., 1) orig. a wretched person (now obsol.);
2) a stingy person. — L. miser, 'wretched,
miserable, pitiable; for sense development cp. It. and
Sp. misero, 'miserable, -wretched, avaricious'.
See miserable.
Derivatives: miser-ly, adv., miser-li-ness, n.

## miserable
miserable, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) miserable,
fr. L. miserabilis, 'pitiable, deplorable,
lamentable', fr. miserari, 'to have compassion, to pity,
deplore', fr. miser, 'wretched, miserable,
pitiable', which is of uncertain etymology. Cp.
Miserere.
Derivatives: miserabil-ity, п., miserable-ness, п.,
miserabl-y, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:495 COLUMN:3 -->

## Miserere
Miserere, п., name of the 51st Psalm. — L.
miserere, 'have mercy', imper. of misereri, 'to
have mercy', fr. miser (see miserable); so called
from the word Miserere in the translation of the
Vulgate, rendering Heb. honneni ('Have mercy
upon me'), the first word of verse 3 in Psalm 5 \.

## misericord
misericord, n. — ME. misericorde, fr. MF. (= F.)
misericorde, fr. L. misericordia, 'mercy,
compassion*, which is compounded of misereri, 'to
have mercy', and cor, gen. cordis, 'heart'. See
miserable and cordate.

## misery
misery, n. — ME. miserie, fr. OF. miserie, fr. L.
miseria, 'wretchedness, misery', fr. miser. See
miserable and -y (representing OF. -ie).

## misfeasance
misfeasance, п., the doing of a lawful act in a
wrongful way (law). — MF. mesfaisance, fr.
mesfaisant, pres. part, of mesfaire, 'to do wrong',
fr. OF., formed fr. pejorative pref. mes- (see
mis-) and /aire, 'to make, do', fr. L. facere. See
fact and cp. feasance, malfeasance.

## mishap
mishap, n. — Formed fr. mis- and hap, prob. on
analogy of OF. meschance (see mischance).

## mishmash
mishmash, п., hodgepodge; a jumble. — Anti-
phonic reduplication of mash.

## Mishnah
Mishnah, Mishna, п., collection of the oral law,
specif, the collection of laws edited by Rabbi
Judah Hannasi (the Patriarch) (135-219). —
Mishnaic Heb. mishnah, 'repetition, oral study,
oral law', fr. Heb. shanah,'herepeated* (in
Mishnaic Heb. also 'he learned, studied; he taught'),
which is rel. to sh nayim, 'two*, mishne ,
'double, two', and to Aram.-Syr. ter€n, 'two*
(dissimilated fr. *tenen), Aram, tinydna, Syr. ten-
yana, 'second', Aram. tena, 'he repeated, learned',
tanna, 'teacher', Arab, ithnani, 'two*, thana, 'he
bent, folded, doubled', Akkad. shina, 'two',
shanu, 'to repeat'. Cp. tannaim.
Derivatives: Mishna-ic, Mishn-ic, adjs.

## miskal
miskal, п., a Mohammedan unit of weight
(equivalent to 71 grains in Persia and to 74 grains in
Smyrna). — Arab, mithqal (in VArab.
pronunciation misqal), lit. 'weight', fr. thakula, *was
heavy' (whence also thiql, 'heaviness, weight',
thaqal, 'load'), which is rel. to Heb. shaqal, 'he
weighed', sheqel, 'a weight; shekel', ruishqal,
'weight*. See shekel.

## misnomer
misnomer, п., an error in naming a person or
place. — ME. misnoumer, orig. an infinitive
derived fr. OF. mesnommer, 'to misname*, which
was formed fr. pejorative pref. mes- (see mis-)
and nommer, 'to name', fr. L. nominare, fr.
nomen, gen. nominis, 'name'. See name and cp.
nominal. For the subst. use of infinitives of OF.
origin cp. attainder and words there referred to.

## miso-
miso-, before a vowel mis-, combining form
meaning 'hater' or 'hatred'. — Gk. μΐσο-, fr. μΐσος,
'hatred, resp. μΐσεΐυ, 'to hate*; of unknown
origin.

## misogamy
misogamy, п., hatred of marriage. —
Compounded of Gk. μίσος, 'hatred', and γάμος,
'marriage'. See miso- and -gamy.
Derivatives: misogam-ic, adj., misogam-ist, n.

## misogynist
misogynist, п., a hater of women. — Formed with
suff. -1st fr. Gk. μισογύνης, 'a woman hater',
which is compounded of the stem of μΐσεΤν, *to
hate', and γυνή, 'woman'. See miso- and
gyneco-.
Derivatives: misogynist-ic, misogynist-ic-al,adjs.

## misogyny
misogyny, п., hatred of women. — Gk. μΐσο-
γυνία,ιτ. μισογύνης. See prec. word and-у
(representing Gk. -ία).

## misoneism
misoneism, п., hatred of anything new. — Coined
fr. miso-, Gk. νέος, 'new' (see neo-), and suff.
-ism.

## misoneist
misoneist, п., a hater of anything new. — Coined
fr. miso-, Gk. νέος, 'new' (see neo-), and suff.
-ist.
Derivative: misoneist-ic, adj.

## misprision
misprision, п., misdemeanor. — ME., fr. OF.
mesprision, mesprison, 'mistake, wrongdoing',
fr. mespris, pp. of mesprendre (F. se meprendre),
'to take amiss, do wrong', fr. pejorative pref.
mes- (see mis-) and prendre, 'to take*, fr. L. pre-
hendere,prendere. Cp. F. meprise, 'mistake', and
see prehensile. Cp. also prison.

## misprision
misprision, п., contempt (archaic). — Formed
with suff. -ion fr. OF. mesprisier, 'to despise'.
See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:496 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 469 | MIXEN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:496 COLUMN:1 -->

## misprize
misprize, misprise, tr. v., to despise. — ME. mes-
pris, fr. OF. mesprisier (whence F. mepriser), 'to
despise', formed fr. pejorative pref. mes- (see
mis-) and prisier (F. priser), 'to prize, value', fr.
L. pretidre, of s.m., fr. pretium, 'price, reward'.
See prize, 'to estimate',

## miss
miss, n. — Contraction of mistress,

## miss
miss, v., to fail to hit. — ME. missen, fr. OE.
missan, 'to miss (the mark); to escape (notice)',
rel. to ΟΝ., OFris. missa. Du., OHG., MHG.,
G. missen, 'to miss, fail', Dan miste, Swed.
mista, 'to lose, be deprived of, forfeit'. See mis-
and cp. amiss.
Derivative: miss, п., failure to hit or obtain.

## mimal
mimal, п., a book containing all the prayers said
at Mass throughout the year (R. C. Ch.) — ME.
missale, messel, fr. Eccles. L. missale, neut. of
the adj. missalis, 'pertaining to Mass', used as a
noun fr. missa, 'Mass'. See Mass and -al.

## missal
missal, adj., pertaining to the Mass. — Eccles L.
missalis. See prec. word.
missel thrush. — Missel stands for mistle; so
called because it feeds on mistletoe berries.

## missile
missile, adj. — L. missilis, 'capable of being
thrown', fr. missus, pp. of mittere. See mission,

## missile
missile, n. — L. missile, 'missile', lit. 'that which
is capable of being thrown', prop. neut. of the
adjective missilis, used as a noun. See missile,
adj.

## mission
mission, n. — L. missio, gen. -onis, 'a sending
mission', fr. missus, pp. of mitto, mittere, 'to
cause to go, to send, throw, hurl, cast', which is
prob. cogn. with Avestic maeft, 'to send',
possibly also with Goth, bi-smeitan, ga-smeitan, 'to
spread, smear', OHG. smizan, 'to rub. strike',
«tc. (see Walde-Hofmann. LEW., II, 98). See
smite and -ion and cp. admission, admit,
commissariat, commission, commit, committee,
compromise, demise, demit, dismiss, emission, emit,
immission, immit, intermission, intermit,
intromission, intromit, manumission, manumit, Mass,
mess, message, mise, missa], missile, missive,
mittimus, omission, omit, permission, permit,

## premise
premise, pretermission, pretermit, promise,

## remiss
remiss, remission, remit, submission, submit,

## surmise
surmise, transmission, transmit.
Derivatives: mission, v., mission-al, adj.,

## missionary
missionary, adj. and п., mission-er, п., missive (q.v.)

missis, also spelled missus. — Colloquial

alternation of mistress,

## missive
missive, adj., sent (archaic). — ME., fr. MF.

## mittere
mittere, 'to send'. See mission and -ive.

## missive
missive, п., an official letter. — F., shortened fr.

## lettre missive
lettre missive, lit. 'a letter sent'. See missive, adj.

## missy
missy, п., a ybung girl (colloq.) — Formed from
the noun miss with suff. -y.

## mist
mist, n. — ME., fr. OE. mist, 'darkness, gloom',

## rel. to ON. mistr
rel. to ON. mistr, Swed., MDu., Du. mist, 'mist',

fr. I.-E. base 'meigh-, whence also OI. meghah,
'cloud', mih-, 'mist, vapor', Avestic maeya-,
'cloud'. Arm. meg, 'mist', Gk. ομίχλη, 'cloud,

## mist'
mist', Alb. mjeguie, OSlav. migla, Lith. migld,

## Lett
Lett, migla, 'mist'. Cp. mizzle, 'to drizzle'.
Derivatives: mist, intr. and tr. v., misty (q.v.)

## mistake
mistake, tr. and intr. v. — ME. mistaken, fr. ON.

## mistaka
mistaka, lit. 'take in error', formed fr. mis- and

## taka
taka, 'to take'. See take.
Derivative: mistake, n.

## mister
mister, n. — Weakened form of master,

## mistery
mistery, n. — A var. of mystery, 'trade'.

## mistle
mistle, п., a kind of small coasting vessel. — Sp.

## mistico
mistico, prob. fr. Arab, musattah, 'an armed

## ship'
ship', lit. 'something spread out, something
even or level; surface', prop, passive part, of the
2nd conjugation of safaha, 'he spread abroad,

## spread out'
spread out', which is rel. to Heb. shatdh, Aram.

## sh tab
sh tab, Aethiop. satdha, of s.m.

## mistletoe
mistletoe, n. — OE. misteltan, compounded of

## mistel
mistel, 'mistletoe', and tan, 'twig, branch'. The

## first element is rel. to Du.
first element is rel. to Du., MHG., G., Dan.,

## Swed. mistel
Swed. mistel, OS., OHG. mistil, ON. mistilteinn,
'mistletoe', and prob. also to OHG. mist, 'dung'
(the plant being propagated by bird dung). See
mash and cp. mixen. Cp. also missel thrush. OE.

## tan
tan, 'twig', is rel. to OS., OFris. ten, ON. teinn,

## Du. teen
Du. teen, OHG. zein, Goth, tains, 'twig', OE.

## ISnel (whence obsol. E. leanal)
ISnel (whence obsol. E. leanal), OS. tinil,

'basket', Dan. telne (metathesized fr. 'tenia), 'weir
basket', OE. ISnen, 'of twigs', Norw. teinen,
'slender' (orig. 'twiglike'),

## mistral
mistral, п., a cold dry northerly wind on the
Mediterranean coast of France. — F., fr. Proven?.
mistral, fr. OProvenc. maistral, maestral, lit.
'predominating wind', fr. maestre, maistre,
'master', fr. L. magister. See master and adj. suff. -al.

## mistress
mistress, n. — ME. matstresse, fr. OF. maistresse
(F. mattresse), fern, of maistre (F. maitre). See
master and 1st -ess.

## misty
misty, adj. — ME., fr. <}E. mistig, fr. mist. See
mist and -y (representing OE. -ig).
Derivative: misti-ly, adv.

## Mitchella
Mitchella, п., a genus of plants, the partridge
berry (bot.) — ModL., named after the
American botanist Dr. John Mitchell (1680-1768).
mite, п., a small arachnid. — ME., fr. OE. mite,
rel. to MDu. mite, Du. mijt, OHG. mija, Dan.
mide, Norw. mil, 'mite', and prob. also to ON.
meita, etc., 'to cut'. See ant.

## mite
mite, п., a very small coin. — ME. mite, fr. MDu.
mite, 'a small coin', which is identical with
MDu. mite, 'a small arachnid'. See prec. word.
Cp. F. mite, 'mite' (in both senses of this word),
which is a MDu. loan word. Cp. also mitraille.

## Mitella
Mitella, п., a genus of plants, the miterwort (bot.)
— L. mitella, 'headband, turban', dimin. of
mitra (see next word and -ella); so called in
allusion to the shape of the young pod.

## miter
miter, mitre, п., head dress, turban. — F. mitre,
fr. L. mitra, 'cap, turban', fr. Gk. μίτρϊ, 'belt,
headband, turban', which is prob. a loan word
connected with Avestic Mipra-; see Mithras.
Derivatives: mitr-al, adj., mitrate (q.v.).

## Mithraism
Mithraism, п., the worship of Mithras. — See
next word and -ism.

## Mithras
Mithras, п., the Persian god of light. — L., fr.
Gk. Μίθρϊς, fr. Avestic Mipra-, which is rel.
to Ol. Mitrah. See Mitra and cp. next word.

## mithridate
mithridate, п., an antidote against poison. —
ML. mithridatum, fr. Late L. mithridatium,
prop. neut. of Mithridatius, 'pertaining to Mith-
ridates', fr. L. Mithridates.it. Gk. Μιθριδάτης;
so called in allusion to Mithridates, King of
Pontus, who made himself poison-proof.
Derivatives: mithridat-ism, n., mithridat-ize, tr. v.

## mitigate
mitigate, tr. v., to alleviate. — ME. mitigaten, fr.
L. mttigatus, pp. of mitigare, 'to make soft or
tender, to soothe, mitigate', compounded of
mitis, 'soft, mild, gentle', and agere, 'to set in
motion, drive, lead; to do, act'. The first
element prob. stands for *mi-tis and derives fr.
l.-E. base *mii-, *mi-, 'soft, mild, tender, gentle;
peaceful, lovely', whence also Olr. moith, Mir.
moeth, Ir. maoth, 'soft'. Cp. also—with
-/-formative element—OSlav. miltt, 'charitable', Russ.
milyj, Pol. miiy, Czech and Slovak mily, Lith.
mlelas, mylas, 'beloved, dear', Lith. myliu,
myleti, 'to love', Lett, mil'!, OPruss. mijls,
'beloved, dear', Russ. milovaC, 'to show mercy',
Pol. milovac, Czech milovati, Slovak milovat',
etc., 'to love', Russ. mllosf, 'mercy', Czech
milost, Slovak milost\ 'love, mercy'. Cp.—
with -r-formative element—Alb. mire, 'good',
OSlav. miru, Pol. mir, Czech mir, Slovak mier,
'peace', Russ. mir, 'peace, world, community';
with -л-formative element: Ir. min, 'soft, smooth,
fine', W. main, 'slender, slim', mwyn, 'soft,
kind', OCo. muin, moin, 'soft, tender'. Ol.
mayah, 'enjoyment, pleasure', and Toch. В
maiwe, 'little, subtle', prob. also derive fr. I.-E.
base *mei-, *mi-, Cp. mir arid the second
element in Casimir. For the second element in L.
mitigare see agent, adj., and cp. words there
referred to.

## mitigation
mitigation, n. — ME. mitigacioun, fr. L. mitigatid,
gen. -onis, 'a soothing, mitigating', fr. mttigatus,
pp. of mitigare. See prec. word and -ion.

## mitigatory
mitigatory, adj.—L. mitigdtorius, 'soothing, miti-

## gative'
gative', fr. mttigatus, pp. of mitigare. See
mitigate and adj. suff. -ory.

## mitochondria
mitochondria, n. pi., small granules in the
cytoplasm of cells (biol.) — Coined by the German
physician Carl Benda (1857-1933) in 'Die
Mitochondria' in 1897 fr. Gk. μίτος, 'thread', and
χονδρίον, 'small grain, granule', dimin. of
χόνδρος, 'corn, grain, groat'. See mitosis and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:496 COLUMN:3 -->
chondri-.

## mitosis
mitosis, п., the indirect method of cell division,
i.e. the division of the nucleus of a cell into tiny
threads (biol.) — ModL.,fr. Gk. μίτος, 'thread',
which is cogn. with Hitt. mitish, 'string, cord'.
Cp. dimity and samite. For the ending see surf.
-osis. The term mitosis was introduced by the
German anatomist Walther Fleming (1843-
1905) in 1882 for the early term miioschisis (fr.
Gk. μίτος, 'thread', and σχίσις, 'cleavage').

## mitotic
mitotic, adj., pertaining to mitosis. — See prec.
word and -otic.

## mitra
mitra, п., a miter. — See miter.

## Mitra
Mitra, п., a genus of snails (zool.) — ModL., fr.
L. mitra, 'cap, turban'. See miter.

## Mitra
Mitra, п., aVedic deity associated with Varuna,
corresponding to the Persian Mithras. — OI.
Mitrah, prob. personification of mitram,
'contract, agreement', hence lit. meaning 'partner to
a contract'; rel. to Avestic and OPers. Mipra-,
'Mithra', mipra-, 'contract, agreement'. These
words are prob. rel. to OI. minoti, 'fastens,
erects, builds'. For the connection of meaning
between 'to fasten', and 'to make a contract',
cp. L. pangere, 'to make firm', which is re], to
pacisci, 'to make a treaty', pax, 'peace' (see
pact); see Mayrhofer, A Concise Etymological
Sanskrit Dictionary, II, pp. 33-34 s.v. Mitrah.
Cp. Mithras,

## mitrailleuse
mitrailleuse, п., a kind of machine gun. — F. The
orig. meaning was 'small coins', hence 'old iron,
scrap iron', finally 'grapeshot'. (For sense
development it should be borne in mind that orig.
guns used to be loaded with scrap iron.) The
word mitraille is a secondary form of OF. mi-
wille, which is a dimin. of OF. mite, *a small
coin'. See mite, 'a small coin'.

## mitrate
mitrate, adj., resembling a miter. — L. mitrdtus,
'wearing a turban', fr. mitra. See miter and adj.
suff. -ate.

## mitt
mitt, п., a mitten. — OF. mite, back formation
fr. mitaine. See mitten,

## mitten
mitten, п., a kind of glove. — The word lit. means
'divided in the middle', fr. ME. meteyn, fr. OF.
mitaine, fr. VL. *medietdna, 'divided in the
middle; half-glove', fr. L. medius, 'middle'. See
media, 'voiced stop consonant', and cp. prec.
word.

## mittimus
mittimus, п., a warrant for putting a person into
prison (law). — L., 'we send', 1st pers. pi. pres.
indie, of mittere, 'to send'. See mission,

## mitzvah
mitzvah, п., a Biblical or rabbinical
commandment (Jewish religion). — Heb. mitzwa ,
'commandment, precept', from the base of tziwwah,
'he commanded, ordered, charged', which is rel.
to Arab, wdsd, 'he bound, united', wassa, 'he
enjoined, bequeathed', ausa, 'he charged', wa-
stya , 'injunction, testament'. For the
differentiation of the Hebrew and the Arabic base by
metathesis, cp. Heb. hiwwd , 'he showed,
declared*; with Arab, wabd, 'he inspired, revealed'.
Cp. bar mitzvah.

## mix
mix, intr. and tr. v. — Back formation fr. mix!
(earlier form of mixed), fr. F. mixte, fr. L. mix-
tus, pp. of misced, (fr. enlargement of orig.
*mik-sko), Ί mix', fr. l.-E. base *meik- (var.
"meig-), 'to mix', whence also OI. misrdh,
'mixed', meksdyati, 'stirs up', Gk. μειγνύναι,
μιγνύναί, μίσγειν (dissimilated fr. *μίγ-σκείν),
'to mix, mingle', OSlav. misg, misiti, 'to mix',
Lith. maisau, maisyti, Lett, maisu, maisit, 'to
mix, mingle', Olr. mescaim, Ί mix'. MLG.
mischen, OHG. miskan (whence MHG., G.
mischen) and OE. miscian, 'to mix', are
borrowed from (rather than cognate with) L. miscere.
It. mescere, OProvenc. meysse, 'to pour in, mix',
derive fr. L. miscere, OF. mesler (whence F.
meler)comesfr. VL. *misculdre, 'to mix,mingle',
a freq. verb formed fr. L. miscere. Cp. admix,
commix, intermix, maslin, 'mixture', meddle,

## medley
medley, mestizo, metis, miscegenation,

## miscellaneous
miscellaneous, mixo-, panmixia, pell-mell, promiscuous,
mnstang.
Derivatives: mix-er, п., mixture (q.v.)

## mixed
mixed, adj. — For mixt, fr. F. mixte. See mix.

## mixen
mixen, п., dunghill (archaic or dial.) — ME.,

## fr. OE.
fr. OE., 'dung, dunghill', rel to OE. meox,
'dung, filth', OS. mehs, mist, OHG., MHG., G.

iq-v.)
mist, Goth, mathstus, 'dung, filth', OE. migan,
ON. miga, MLG. migen, 'to urinate', OE. micga,
migoda, 'urine', and cogn. with Gk. όμείχειν,
L. meiere, mingere, 'to urinate'. See micturition
and cp. mash, mistletoe,

## mixo-
mixo-, combining form meaning 'mixed'. — Gk.
μιξο-, fr. μίξις, *Ъ. mixing, mingling,
intercourse', from the stem of μίγνύναι, μίσγειν,
Чо mix'. See mix.

## Mixodectes
Mixodectes, п., an extinct genus of insectivores
(paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of mixo-
and Gk. δήκτης, 'biter', which is rel. to δάκνειν,
Чо bite', fr. I.-E. base *denh-, 'to bite*, whence
also OI. dasati (for *dnketi), 'bites', OE. tang,
tange, 4ongs\ See tongs and cp. words there
referred to.

## Mixosaurus
Mixosaurus, п., a genus of extinct reptiles
(paleontol.) — ModL., compounded of mixo- and
Gk. σαϋρος, 'lizard'. See sauro-.

## mixture
mixture, n. — ME., fr, OF. misture (F. mixture),
fr. L. mixtura, *a mixing', fr. mixtus, pp. of
miscere, Чо mix'. See mix and -lure.

## Mizar
Mizar, п., the star Zeta (ζ) Ursae Majoris, a
double star at the middle of the handle of the
Great Dipper (astron.) — Arab, mi'zar, 'veil,
cloak', rel. to izar, 'loincloth', and to Heb. ezor,
'girdle, belt'.

## mizen
mizen, n. — See mizzen.

## mizmaze
mizmaze, п., mystification. — Antiphonic
reduplication of maze.

## Mizpah
Mizpah, п., a word usually inscribed on a ring
given to a friend in token of remembrance, in
allusion to the heap of stones raised to
commemorate the covenant between Jacob and Laban
(Bible). — Heb. mitzpah, lit. 'watchtower', fr.
tzaphah, 'he looked out, kept watch' (see Gen.
31:49), which is rel. to Ethiop. iasafawa, 'he
hoped', and prob. also to Akkad. §ubbu, 'to
look at'.

## mizzen
mizzen, also spelled mizen, п., the fore-and-aft
sail set on the mizzenmast. — Late ME. mesein,
fr. F. misaine, 'foresail', fr. It. mezzana, fr.
Egyptian Arab, mazzan, denoting the mast, the
sails of which keep the ship in equilibrium, and
rel. to Arab, mizan, 'balance', from the base
of wazana, 'he weighed', which is rel. to
тог ndyim, Bibl.-Aram. moz nayya, 'scales,
balance'. It mezzana in this sense is not related
to mezzano, fern, mezzana, "middle' (see
mezzanine).

## mizzle
mizzle, tr, and intr. v., to drizzle (pbsol. or dial.)
— Late ME. misellen, prob. fr. Late MDu.
mieselen. Cp. Du. miezelen, LG. miseln. These
words are rel. to MDu., Du. mist, 'mist'. See
mist and freq. surf. -le.
Derivative: mizzl-y, adj.

## mizzle
mizzle, intr. v., to sneak off (slang). — Of
uncertain origin.

## memonic
memonic, adj., helping the memory. — Gk.
μνημονικός, 'of memory; having a good
memory', fr. μνήμων, 'mindful, remembering1, fr.
μνήμη, 'memory', which is formed from the
stem of μνασθαι, 'to remember', fr. I.-E. base
*men-, 'to think'. See mind and words there
referred to and cp. esp. mnesic, mnestic. For the
ending see adj. surf. -ic.

## mnemonics
mnemonics, п., the art of improving the memory.
— See prec. word and -ics.

## Mnemosyne
Mnemosyne, п., a Titaness, mother of the Muses,
the goddess of memory (Greek mythol.) — L.
Mnemosyne, fr. Gk. Μνημοσύνη, lit. 'memory,
remembrance', fr, μνήμη, 'memory'. See
mnemonic.

## mnemotechny
mnemotechny, п., mnemonics. — Compounded
of Gk. μνήμη, 'memory'» and τέχνη, 'art'. See
mnemonic and technic.
Derivatives: mnemotechn-ic, mnemotechn-ic-al,
adjs., mnemotechn-ist, n.

## mnesic
mnesic, adj., pertaining to memory. — Gk. μνη-
σικός, 'of memory', fr. μνησις, 'memory,
remembrance', from the stem of μνασθαι, 'to
remember'. See mnemonic and cp. amnesia, anamnesis,
paramnesia.

## mnestic
mnestic, adj., pertaining to memory. — Formed
with adj. surf.-ύ:Λ\0^μνήστις, 'remembrance',
which is related to μνήσις, 'memory'. See mnesic.

## Mniaceae
Mniaceae, n. pi., a family of mosses (bot.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:497 COLUMN:2 -->
ModL., formed with surf, -aceae fr. Mnium

## Mnium
Mnium, п., a genus of mosses (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. μνίον, 'moss', which is prob. cogn. with
Lith. miniava, 'close-mown turf.

## -mo
-mo, suff. indicating the number of leaves into
which a sheet of paper is folded. — L. -mo, abl.
of -mus, the most frequent ending of ordinals.
Cp. e.g. 16mo (sextodeci-mo), 'a sheet folded
into sixteen leaves'.

## moa
moa, п., an extinct flightless bird of New Zealand.
— Native ( = Maori) name.

## Moa bite
Moa bite, n, — Late L. Moabites, fr. Gk. Μωα-
βΐτης, 'inhabitant of Moab', fr. Μωάβ, 'Moab,
land of Moab', fr. Heb. Mo'dbh, which is perh.
a derivative of Heb. abh, 'father'; see Gen.
I9: 37. See abbot and subst. sufT. -ite.
Derivatives: Moabite, adj., Moabit-ish, adj.

## moan
moan, n. — ME. топе, mane, from the stem of
OE. тгёпап, 'to complain, mourn, moan'. See
mean, 'to have in mind'.
Derivatives: moan, tr. and intr. v., moan-ful,
adj., moan-ful-ly, adv.

## moat
moat, п., dike, ditch. — ME. mote, fr. OF. mote,
'rampart, dike' (whence F. motte, 'mound,
clod, lump'); prob. of pre-Latin origin.

## mob
mob, п., the rabble. — Shortened fr. L. mobile
vulgus, 'the fickle crowd'; mobile is the neuter of
mobilis, 'movable, fickle', fr. movere, Чо move'.
See move.
Derivatives: mob, tr. v., mobb-ish, adj.

## mob
mob, п., a woman's headdress. — Short for mob-
cap.

## mobcap
mobcap, п., a woman's headdress. — Prob. fr.
mab-cap, lit. 'woman's cap', fr. PN. Mab, used
in the sense of 'woman', fr. Mabel (q.v.)

## mobile
mobile, adj. — MF. (=F.), fr. L. mobilis,
'movable; pliable, flexible; changeable, fickle', con
traction of *movibilis, fr. movere, 'to move'. See
move and cp. the second element in automobile,
locomobile.
Derivative: mobile, n.

## mobility
mobility, n, — F. mobilite, fr. L. mobilitatem,
ace. of mobi/itds, 'mobility', fr. mobilis. See prec.
word and -ity.

## mobilization
mobilization, n. — F. mobilisation, fr. mobiliser.
See next word and -ation.

## mobilize
mobilize, tr. v. — F. mobiliser, coined fr. L.
mobilis and surf. -iser. See mobile and -ize.

## monocracy
monocracy, п., rule by the mob. — A hybrid
coined fr. mob, the abbreviation of L. mobile
vulgus and Gk. -κρατία, 'rule of, fr. κράτος,
'strength, power, rule'. See -cracy.

## moccasin
moccasin, п., soft shoe worn by North American
Indians. — Of Alonquian origin; cp. Powhatan
mockasin.

## Mocha
Mocha, п., a fine variety of coffee. — Fr. Mocha,
name of a port on the Red Sea (in Arabia).

## mock
mock, tr. and intr. v. — ME. mokken, fr. MF.
(= F.) moquer, fr. OF., 'to mock', which is
prob. of imitative origin. Cp. OProveng. mocar,
Чо mock', Sp. mueca, *grimace, grin*.
Derivatives: mock, n. and adj., mock-er, п.,
mockery (q.v.), mock-ing-ly, adv.

## mockery
mockery, n. — ME. moquerie, fr. MF. (— F.)
moquerie, fr. moquer. See mock and -ery.

## modal
modal, adj. — ML. modalis, 'pertaining to a
mode', fr. L. modus. See mode and adj. surf. -al.
Derivatives: modality (q.v.), modal-ly, adv.

## modality
modality, n. — ML. modalitas, fr. modalis. See
prec. word and -ity.

## mode
mode, n. — F., 'manner, fashion, style', fr. L.
modus,* measure, limit,boundary, manner, mode,
mood' (whence modius, 'a corn measure*, mode-
ran, moderare,*to set limits to, moderate', modes-
tus, 'keeping measure, moderate, virtuous, sober,
discreet, modest', Late L. modernus, 'modern'),
fr. I.-E. base *med-, Чо measure, limit, consider,
advise', whence also L. meditari, 'to think over,
consider*. See meditate and cp. model, modern,
module, modus, mold, 'pattern', and the second
element in turmoil.
Derivatives: mod-ish, adj., mod-ish-ly, adv.,
mod-ish-ness, n.

## model
model, n. — MF. modelle (F. modele), fr. It. mo-
dello, fr. VL. *modellus, fr. L. modulus, * small
measure; rhythmical measure, rhythm, time,
melody, mode', dimin. of modus. See mode and
cp. mold, 'model*.

Derivatives: model, v., model(l)-er, п.,
modelling, n.

## modena
modena, п., deep purple. — Prop. 'Modena
color', named from the city of Modena in Italy.

## moderantism
moderantism, п., moderateness. — F. moderan-
tisme, a hybrid coined fr. moderant, pres. part,
of moderer (fr. L. moderari) and -isme, a sufT of
Greek origin (see -ism); introduced into English
by Burke. See next word.

## moderate
moderate, adj. — ME., fr. L. moderatus, pp. of
moderari, 'to set limits to, moderate', fr. modus.
See mode and adj. sufT. -ate.
Derivatives: moderate, п., moderate-ly, adv.,
moderate-ness, n.

## moderate
moderate, tr. v. — ME. moderaten, fr. L.
moderatus, pp. of moderari. See moderate, adj.

## moderation
moderation, n. — ME. moderacion, fr. MF. (= F.)
moderation, fr. L. moderationem, ace. of mode-
ratio, 'moderating', fr. moderatus, pp. of
moderari. See moderate, v., and -ion.

## moderator
moderator, n. — ME. moderatour, fr. L.
moderator, gen. -oris, 'manager, ruler, director', lit.
'he who moderates', fr. moderatus, pp. of
moderari. See moderate and agential sufT. -or.

## modern
modern, adj. — F, moderne, fr. Late L. modernus,
'modern', formed with surf, -e-rnus fr. L. modo,
*just now', which is prop. abl. of modus,
Measure', and lit. means'by measure'; see mode. For
the formation of Late L. modernus fr. L. modo
cp. L. hesternus, 'of yesterday', fr. fieri,
'yesterday*, hodiernus, 'of today'j fr. hodie, 'today'.
Cp. hesternal, hodiernal·, cp. also diurnal,
nocturnal.
Derivatives: modern, п., modern-ism, п.,
modernist, п., and adj., modern-ist-ic, adj., modern-ity,
п., modernize (q.v.), modern-ly, adv., modern-
ness, n.

## modernize
modernize, tr. and intr. v. — F. moderniser, fr.
Late L. modernus. See modern and -ize.
Derivatives: moderniz-ation, п., moderniz-er,
n.

## modest
modest, adj. — F. modeste, fr. L. modestus,
'keeping measure, measured, moderate, virtuous,
sober, discreet, modest', fr. modus. See mode.
^Derivatives: modest-ly, adv., modest-ness, n.

## modesty
modesty, n. — F. modestie, fr. L. modestia,
'moderateness, moderation, modesty', fr. modestus.
See modest and -y (representing F. -ie).

## modicum
modicum, п., a small quantity. — L., 'a little',
prop. neut. of modicus, 'having a proper
measure, moderate', used as a noun, fr. modus. See
mode.

## modification
modification, n. — MF. (= F.) modification, fr.
L. modificationem, ace. of modificatio, 'a
measuring', fr. modificatus, pp. of modificare. See
modify and -ation.

## modificatory
modificatory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory
fr. L. modificatus, pp. of modificare. See next
word.

## modify
modify, tr. v. — ME. modifien, fr. MF. (= F.)
modifier, fr. L. modificare, Чо measure, make
moderate', which is compounded of modus,
'measure', and -ficare, fr.facere, 'to make, do*.
See mode and -fy.
Derivatives: modlfi-able, adj., modifi-abil-ity,
п., modifi-er, n.

## modUlion
modUlion, п., a bracket found beneath the corona
of the cornice of the Corinthian entablature
(arch.) — F., fr. It. modiglione, fr. VL. *mutulio-
nem, ace. of *mutulio, fr. L. mutulus, 'mutule,
modillion'. See mutule.

## modiolus
modiolus, п., the central column in the cochlea
of the ear (anat.) — L., 'a small measure',
dimin. of modius, 'a corn measure', a derivative
of modus. See mode.

## modiste
modiste, п., a dressmaker, milliner. — F., fr.
mode, 'fashion*. See mode and -ist.
Derivative: modist-ry, n.

## modulate
modulate, tr. and intr. v. — L. modulatus, pp. of
modular!, Чо measure off properly, measure
rhythmically, modulate', fr. modulus, 'a small
measure, meter, melody', dimin. of modus. See
mode and v. sufT. -ate and cp. module, modulus.

## modulation
modulation, n. — ME. modulacion, fr. MF. (= F.)
modulation, fr. L. modulationem, ace. of modu-
latid, 'regular measure, rhythmical measure,
modulation', fr. modulatus, pp. of modulari. See
prec. word and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:498 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 471 | MOLLIFY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:498 COLUMN:1 -->

## modulator
modulator, η. — L. modulator, 'one who
modulates', fr. modulatus, pp.of modular!. See modulate
and agential suff. -or.

## module
module, п., a unit of measurement. — F., fr. L.
modulus, 'a small measure', djmin. of modus.
See mode] and -ule, and cp. mold, 'pattern',
which is a doublet of module. Cp. also moulage.
Derivative: modul-ar, adj.

## modulus
modulus, п., a constant quantity, a coefficient. —
L., 'a small measure'. See prec. word.
Derivative: modul-ar, adj.

## modus
modus, п., method, manner, mode. — L. See
mode.

## Moed
Moed, п., the second of the six orders of the
Mishnah, dealing with the Sabbaih, feasts and
fasts. — Heb. mo^ed, 'appointed time,
appointed season, feast', also "appointed meeting',
from ya'ad, 'he appointed, assigned, designated'
(whence also 'ё£/аА, 'congregation' lit. 'people
assembled by appointment'), which is rel. to
Aram, ya'ed, 'he designated', Syr. wa'da,
'appointment, agreement', wa'ed, 'he invited',
Arab, wa'ada, 'he promised', wa'ada, 'he
appointed (a time or place)'.

## mofette
mofette, п., noxious exhalation from the earth.
— F., fr. It. mofeta, related to muffo, 'moldiness,
mustiness', whence also G. Muff, 'a moldy smell'.

## mofussil
mofussil, п., in India, rural district; the country
— Hind, mufassil, mufassal, fr. Arab. mufassal,
'divided, separated', pass. part, of fassala, II
(= intensive) conjugation oifdsala, 'he divided,
separated'; rel. to Bibl. Heb. pitztzel, 'he
peeled'; in Mishnaic Heb., 'he split, divided; he
peeled', Aram.-Syr. petzal, 'he split, divided',
Arab, basala, 'he peeled'.

## mog
mog, intr. and tr. v., to move on {dial.) — Of
unknown origin.

## mogi-
mogi-, combining form meaning 'with toil and
pain', as in mogilalia, 'painful speech'. — Gk.
μόγις, 'with toil and pain', rel. to μόγος, 'toil,
trouble', whence μογεΐν, 'to toil, labor', μογε-
ρός, 'laboring, toilsome, painful', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)mog-, whence also Lith. smagus, 'heavy',
Lett, smags, smagrs, of s.m.

## mogilalia
mogilalia,п.,painful speech (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of mogi- and Gk. λαλίϊ, 'talk,
chat, speech', fr. λκλός, 'talkative, loquacious'.
See Lalage and 1st -la.

## Mogul
Mogul, п., a Mongol; specif, one of the
Mongolian invaders of India or their descendants. —
Pers. Mughul, 'Mongol; the Great Mogul'. See
Mongol.

## mohair
mohair, п., 1) the fine hair of the Angora goat; 2)
the fabric made from it; 3) an imitation of true
mohair. — Fr. earlier mocayere, fr. It. moccaia-
ro, fr. Arab, mukhayya·- 'fine cloth of goat's
hair', lit. 'choice', pass. part, of khdyyara, 'he
chose, selected', the II conjugation of khara, 'he
chose; he preferred', whence khayr 'good,
better, best'. Cp. moire, muktar.

## Mohammedan
Mohammedan, adj., pertaining to Mohammed,
founder of Islam (570-632). — Formed with
suff. -an fr. Arab. Muhammad, lit.
'praiseworthy', pass. part, of fidmmada, 'he praised'.

## Mohammedan
Mohammedan, п., a Moslem.—Lit. 'a follower of
Mohammed'. See prec. word.

## Mohammedanism
Mohammedanism, п., system of the religion
founded by Mohammed. — Formed fr.
Mohammedan, п., with sufT. -ism.

## Mohammedanize
Mohammedanize, tr. v., to make Mohammedan.
— Formed fr. Mohammedan, п., with suff. -ize.
Moharram. — See Mnharram.

## mohatra
mohatra, п., nominal sale (Medieval law). — Sp.,
fr. Arab. mukhatarah, 'risk', rel. to khatar,
'danger, risk'.

## Mohawk
Mohawk, п., a member of a North American
Indian tribe. — Algonquian native name meaning
'they eat living things' (i.e., 'they are
cannibals'). The name was given them by their
enemies. Cp. Mohock.
Derivatives: Mohawk-ian, adj. and n.

## mono
mono, п., the Hawaian honey eater. — ModL.,
fr. Hawaian native word.

## Mohock
Mohock, п., a member of a gang of aristocratic
ruffians. — A var. of Mohawk.

## mohur
mohur, п., formerly, a gold coin of India. — Hind.
muhur, muhr, fr. Pers. muhr, 'seal, coin', fr. OI.
mudrd, 'seal, coin*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:498 COLUMN:2 -->

## moidore
moidore, п., a Portuguese gold coin. —
Corruption of Port, moeda de ouro, lit. 'money of gold',
fr. moeda, 'money' (fr. L. moneta, 'mint,
money'), the prep, de, 'from, of (fr. L. de, 'from,
away from') and ouro, 'gold' (fr. L. aurum). See
mint, 'place for coining money', de- and aureate.

## moiety
moiety, п., a half. — ME. moite, fr. MF. moite
(F. moitie), fr. OF. meitiet, fr. L. medietatem,
ace. of medietas, 'the middle, a half, fr. medius,
'middle'. See media, 'voiced stop consonant',
and subst. suff. -ty.

## moil
moil, tr. v., to wet, to daub with dirt, to soil
{archaic and dial.); intr. v., to work in wet or
miTe; to toil, drudge. — ME. moillen, 'to wet*,
fr. OF. moillier, moiller (F. mouiller), 'to wet,
moisten', fr. VL. 'mollidre, 'to soften; to
moisten', fr. L. mollis, 'soft'. See mollify.

## Moira
Moira, п., one of the Fates (Greek mythol.) —
Gk. Motpoc (for *Μόρια), lit. 'share, fate', rel.
to μόρος, 'fate, destiny, doom', and in grada-
tional relationship to μέρος, 'part, lot', μείρε-
σθαι, 'to receive one's share'. See 1st mero- and
cp. words there referred to.

## Moira
Moira, fern. PN. — Prob. a var. of Ir. Maire,
which corresponds to E. Mary.

## moire
moire, п., watered silk. — F., fr. mohair (q.v.) Cp.
moreen.

## moire
moire, adj., watered (said of silk, metals, etc.) —
F., pp. of moirer, *to water (silk, etc.)', fr. moire.
See moire.

## moist
moist, adj. — ME. moisle, 'fresh (of fruit, wine,
etc.)', fr. MF. moisle (F. moite), 'moist', fr. VL.
*muscidus, which is a blend of L. mucidus, 'mo-
dy, musty', and musteus, 'of new wine, fresh,
juicy'. L. mucidus is a derivative of mucus; see
mucus and cp. must, 'mold'. L. musteus derives
fr. mustum, 'must, new wine'; see must, 'new
wine'.
Derivatives: moist-en, tr. and intr. v., moist-en-
er, п., moist-i/y, tr. v., moist-less, adj., moist-y,
adj.

## moisture
moisture, n. — ME., fr. MF. moislour, moisteur
(F. moiteur), fr. moiste. See moist and -ure.
Derivative: moisture-less, adj.

## moke
moke, п., a donkey (slang). — Prob. from a PN.
applied to the donkey.

## mol
mol, п., molecular weight in grams, gram
molecule (chem.) — G. Mol, short for Molekul,
'molecule'. See mole, 'gram, molecule'.

## molal
molal, adj., pertaining to the mol. — Formed fr.
mol with adj. suff. -al.

## molar
molar, adj., pertaining to mass. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ar fr. L. moles, 'a heavy mass, load,
burden'. See mole, 'structure'.

## molar
molar, adj., grinding. — L. molaris, 'pertaining
to a mill; grinding', fr. mola, 'mill, millstone',
fr. I.-E. base *mel-, 'to rub, grind'. See 1st mill
and cp. mole, 'false conception', moltuary.
Derivative: molar, п., a molar tooth.

## molasses
molasses, n. pi., thick, dark-colored sirup. —
Port, melaco, fr. Late L. mellaceum, 'must',
prop. neut. of mellaceus, 'resembling honey', fr.
L. mel. gen. mellis, 'honey'. See utel and -aceous.

## mold
mold, mould, п., a pattern, form. — ME. mold,
metathesized fr. OF modle, earlier form of mole,
molle (F. moule), 'mold', fr. L. modulus. See
module.
Derivative: mold, mould, tr. v., to form, model.

## mold
mold, mould, п., crumbling soil, humus. — ME.
molde, fr. OE. molde, 'earth, soil, dust', rel. to
OFris. molde, ON. mold, 'earth', OHG. molta,
'dust, earth', Goth, mulda, 'dust'. These words
prop, are pp.s lit. meaning 'that which is ground'
fr. I.-E. base *mel-, 'to rub, grind'. See meal,
'edible grain', and words there referred to and
cp. esp. mull, 'to powder'. Cp. also next word,
molder and mole, 'the burrowing animal'.

## mold
mold, mould, п., a furry fungoid growth. — ME.
mowlde, prob. fr. ME. mouled, mowled, pp. of
moulen, mowlen, 'to grow moldy', which is rel.
to ON. mygla, Swed. mogla, Norw. mugla, 'to
grow moldy', and to OE. molde, 'earth, soil,
dust'. See prec. word.

## mold
mold, mould, intr. v., to grow moldy, tr. v., to
make moldy. — Prob. fr. ME. mouled, mowled,
pp. of moulen, 'to grow moldy'. See prec. word.

## molder
molder, moulder, п., one who molds or forms. —
Formed with agential suff. -er fr. mold, 'to form'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:498 COLUMN:3 -->

## molder
molder, moulder, intr. v., to crumble away; tr. v.,
to cause to crumble away. — Formed with suff.
-er fr. mold, 'crumbling soil'.

## molding
molding, moulding, п., the act of forming. —
Formed fr. mold, 'to form', with -ing, suff.
forming verbal nouns.

## moldy
moldy, mouldy, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -y
fr. ME. mouled, pp. οι moulen, 'to grow moldy'.
See mold, 'fungoid growth'.
Derivative: moldi-ness, п., mouldi-ness, n.

## mole
mole, п., spot in the skin. — ME. mat, fr. OE.
mal, 'stain mark', rel. to OHG., MHG. meil,
G. Mal, Goth, mail, 'wrinkle', fr. I.-E. base
*mei-, *mai-, 'to stain, defile', whence also Gk.
μιαίνειν, 'to stain, defile'. See miasma and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the first
element in maulstick.

## mole
mole, п., a massive structure of stone built in the
sea as a breakwater. — F. mole, fr. It. molo, fr.
Late Gk. μώλος, fr. L. moles, 'a heavy mass,
load, burden' (whence mdlestus, 'troublesome,
irksome, grievous'), which prob. derives fr. I.-E.
*mo-li-, whence also Gk. μωλος, 'effort', μόλις,
'hardly, scarcely'. I.-E. *md-li- is an
enlargement of base *mo-, 'to tire, fatigue', whence
Goth. (af)mauit>s, 'weary, tired', OHG. muoen,
MHG. тйееп, mtiejen, G. miihen, MDu. moey-
en, moyen, Du. moeien, 'to tire', OHG. muodi,
MHG. muede, G. made, 'weary tired', MDu.
moede, Du. moede, moe, ON. modr, OS. modi,
ON. modr, OE. тебе, 'weary, tired', Russ.
majaV, 'to fatigue, exhaust', majd, majata, 'hard
work, scourge, plague'. Cp. molar, 'pertaining
to mass', molecule, molest, demolish, demolition.

## mole
mole, п., a small burrowing animal (Talpa euro-
pea). — ME. molle, rel. to OFris. moll, MLG.
mul, mol, MDu., Du. mol. These words are rel.
to OE. molde, 'earth, soil'. Cp. ME. moldewerp,
dial. E. moldiwarp, OS. moldwerp, OHG. mult-
wurf, MHG. moltwer/e (whence, influenced by
Maul, 'mouth', G. Maulwurf), 'mole', lit. 'soil-
thrower', and see mole, 'soil'.
Derivative: mole, tr. v., to free of moles; to
excavate.

## mole
mole, п., false conception. — F. mole, fr. L. mola,
'millstone; grits; false conception, mole'. See
1st mill and cp. molar, 'grinding'.

## mole
mole, п., a gram molecule (chem.) — G. Mol,
shortened by the German physical chemist Wil-
helm Ostwald (1853-1932), fr. G. Molekul,
'molecule'. See molecule.

## molecular
molecular, adj. — ModL. molecularis. See next
word and -ar.
Derivatives: molecular-ity, п., molecular-ly, adv.

## molecule
molecule, n. — F. molecule, fr. ModL. mdlecula,
dimin. of L. moles, 'mass'. See mole, 'mass',
and -cule. ModL. molecula was first used in the
modern sense of this term by Amedeo Avoga-
droiin 1811).

## molest
molest, tr. v., to trouble. — ME. molesten, fr.
MF. (= F.) molester, fr. L. mdlestdre, 'to annoy,
trouble', fr. mdlestus, 'troublesome, irksome,
grievous, annoying', lit. 'burdening', fr. moles,
'heavy mass, load, burden'. See mole,
'structure'.

## molestation
molestation, n. — ME. molestacioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) molestation, fr. molester. See molest and
-ation.

## molinary
molinary, adj., pertaining to a mill. — Late L.
molinarius, fr. molina, 'mill'. See 1st mill and
adj. suff. -ary and cp. molar, 'grinding*.

## Moliirism
Moliirism, п., 1) religious teachings of the
Spanish Jesuit Luis de Molina (1535-1600); 2)
religious teachings of the Spanish priest Miguel de
Molinos (1640-97) — For the ending see suff.
-ism.

## Molinfst
Molinfst, п., 1) an adherent of Luis de Mulina;2)
an adherent of Miguel de Molinos. — See prec.
word and -izt.

## Moll
Moll, fem. PN. — A dimin. of Mary.

## moll
moll, п., 1) female companion of a gangster; 2) a
prostitute (slang). — Fr. prec. word.

## mollification
mollification, n. — ME. mollificacioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) mollification, fr. ML. mollificaiionem,
ace. of mollificutio, 'a softening', fr. L. mollificd-
tus, pp. of mollificare. See next word and -ion.

## mollify
mollify, tr. v., to pacify, appease. — ME. molli-

## fien
fien, fr. MF. (= F.) mollifier, fr. L. mollificare,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:499 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MDLLUGO | 472 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:499 COLUMN:1 -->
'to make soft, soften', which is compounded of
mollis, 'soft, mild', and -ficare, fr. jacere, 'to
make, do'. For the first element see meal, 'edible
grain", and words there referred to and cp. esp.
emollient, moil, Mollugo, mollusk, mouitle,
mullein. For the second element see -fy.

## Mollugo
Mollugo, п., a genus of plants, the Indian chick-
weed (bot.). — L. mollugo, name of a burlike
plant, fr. mollis, 'soft'. See prec. word.

## mollusc
mollusc, n. — See mollusk.

## Mollusca
Mollusca, п., a large phylum of invertebrates
characterized by a soft and unsegmented body
(zool.) —■ ModL., neut. p]. of L. molluscus,
'soft'. See mollusk.
Derivatives: moliusc-ant adj. and n.

## molluscotd
molluscotd, adj., like a mollusk. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. molluscus, 'soft', and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See mollusk
and -oid.

## molluscous
molluscous, adj., molluscan. — See mollusk and
-ous.

## mollusk
mollusk, mollusc, п., any of the Mollusca. — F.
mollusque, coined by the French naturalist,
Baron Geo rges-Leopold-Chretien-Fred eric-
Dagobert Cuvier (1769-1832) fr. L. molluscus,
'soft' (in mollusca nox, *a soft kind of nut with a
thin shell'), fr. mollis, 'soft'. See mollify.

## molly
molly, п., a milksop, an effeminate person. — Fr.
Molly, a pet form of Mary, Cp. Moll, moll, and
next word.

## mollycoddle
mollycoddle, п., a person who coddles himself. —
Prop, 'a molly that coddles himself. — See prec.
word and coddle.
Derivative: mollycoddle, tr. v.

## Moloch
Moloch, п., 1) a Semitic god propitiated by the
sacrifice of children; hence 2) anything requiring
a dreadful sacrifice; 3) name of a spiny
Australian lizard (Moloch horridus). — L. (Vulgate),
fr. Gk. Μολόχ (Septuagint), fr. Heb. mo/ekh, a
word formed fr. Heb. melekh, 'king', by giving
it the vowels of bosheth, 'shame' (to show
Israel's horror of this hideous practice of the
heathen Semites). See Mameluke.

## molt
molt, moult, intr. and tr. v. — ME. mouten, fr.
OE. *mutian, 'to change' (cp. OE. bi-mutian,
'to exchange'), fr. L. mutare, 'to change'. See
mntable.
Derivatives: molt, moult, п., the process of
molting, molt-er, moult-er, n.

## molten
molten, pp. of melt. — ME., fr. OE. mo/ten, pp.
of meltan, 'to melt'. See melt.

## moly
moly, п., a fabulous plant with magic powers. —
L., fr. Gk. μωλυ, which is of uncertain
etymology. It is prob. not cogn. with OI. mula-m,
'root'.

## molybdenum
molybdenum, п., name of a metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., coined fr. Gk. μόλυβδος,
'lead', which together with L. plumbum, 'lead',
was prob. borrowed from a Mediterranean,
possibly the Iberian, language. See plumb.
Derivatives: molybden-ic,&d}., molybden-ite, n.
(mineral.), mo/ybden-ous, adj.

## molybdic
molybdic, adj., of, or containing, molybdenum
(in its higher valency). — Formed with adj. surf.
-ic fr. Gk. μόλυβδος, 'lead'. See prec. word.

## molybdous
molybdous, adj., of, or containing, molybdenum
(in its lower valency). — See prec. word and
-ous.

## moment
moment, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L.
momentum, 'movement, motioo; short time,
moment', which stands for *movimentum, fr.
movere, 'to move'. See move and -ment and cp.
movement. For sense development cp. Heb.
regha1, 'moment', which prob. derives fr. ragha',
'he disturbed', prop, 'he moved'. Cp. also
Czech okamiik (Slovak okamih), fit. 'twinkling
of the eye', fr. око, 'eye*, and mzik, 'moment',
which is re], to mzikaxi, 'to blink, wink', and
Hung, pillanat, 'moment', which is short for
szempillanat, now replaced by szempillantas, of
s.m., lit. 'a twinkling of the eye'.

## momentaneous
momentaneous, adj. — Late L. momentaneus,
'short, momentary', fr. L. momentum. See
moment and -aneous.
Derivatives: momentaneous-ly, adv., moment-
aneous-ness, n.

## momentary
momentary, adj. — L. momentdrius, 'of brief
duration, momentary', fr. momentum. See moment

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:499 COLUMN:2 -->
and adj. sun", -ary.
Derivatives: momentari-ly, adv., momentari-
ness, n.

## momentum
momentum, п., 1) the product of the mass of a
moving body and its velocity (mech.); 2)
impetus. — L. momentum. See moment.

## Momus
Momus, п., 1) the god of censure and sarcasm
(Greek mythol.); hence 2) a carping critic. — L.(
fr. Gk. Μώμος, fr. μώμος, 'blame, ridicule',
which is prob. rel. to ά-μυμων,
'irreproachable'; of uncertain origin.

## mon-
mon-, form of mono- before a vowel.

## Mona
Mona, fern. PN. — Ir. Muadhnait, prop, dimin.
of muadh, 'noble'.

## mona
mona, п., a small African monkey (Cercopithecus
mona). — Sp. and Port, mona, 'female monkey',
fern, of mono, 'monkey'. See monkey,

## monachal
monachal, adj., pertaining to a monk; monastic.
— Eccles. L. monachulis, 'pertaining to a monk',
fr. Late L. monachus, 'monk'. See monk and adj.
suff. -al.

## monachism
monachism, п., monasticism. — Formed with
suff. -ism fr. Late L. monachus, 'monk'. See
monk,

## monacid
monacid, n. — The same as monoacid.

## monad
monad, п., 1) a unit; 2) a single-celled organism
(biol.) ; 3) a univalent element, atom or radical
(chem.); 4) an ultimate unit of being {philos. of
Leibniz). — Late L. monas, gen. monadis, fr.
Gk. μονάς, gen. μονάδος, 'a unit', fr. μόνος,
'alone, single'. See mono-,

## monadelphous
monadelphous, adj., having the filamenis united
(bot.) — Compounded of mon- and Gk.
αδελφός, 'brother'. See adelpho- and -ous.

## monadism
monadism, п., the theory (of Leibniz) that the
universe is composed of monads. — See monad
and -ism.
mona], also monaul, п., a large pheasant of the
genus Lophophorus. — Hind, mortal, типа/.

## monandrous
monandrous, adj., \) baving but one husband at a
time; 2) (bot.) having a single stamen. — Gk.
μόνανδρος, 'having but one husband',
compounded of μόνος, 'alone', and άνήρ, gen.
ανδρός, 'man'. See mono- and -androus. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## monandry
monandry, n. \) the state of having but one
husband at a time; 2) (bot.) the condition of having
a single stamen. — Formed as if fr. Gk. *μουαν-
δρία, fr. μόνανδρος, 'having but one husband'.
See monandrous and -y (representing Gk.-ία).

## monarch
monarch, n.—Late L. monarcha, fr. Gk. μονάρχης
or μόναρχος, One who rules alone', which are
compounded of μόνος, 'alone', and -άρχης, resp.
άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See mon- and -arch.
Derivatives: monarch-al, adj., mortarch-al-ly,
adv., monarchic (q.v.), monorchism (q.v.), mon-
arch-ist, n. and adj., monarch-ist-ic, adj., mon-
arch-ize, intr. and tr. v., monarchy (q.v.)

## monarchic
monarchic, adj. — MF. (= F.) monarchique, fr.
Gk. μοναρχικός, fr. μονάρχης or, μόναρχος.
See prec word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: monarchic-al, adj., monarchic-al-ly,
adv.

## monarchism
monarchism, n. — F, monarchisme, fr. monarchic.
See next word and -ism.

## monarchy
monarchy, n. — ME. monarchic, fr. OF. (— F.)
monarchic, fr. Late L. monorchia, fr. Gk.
μοναρχία, 'nile of one', fr. μονάρχης or μόναρχος.
See monarch and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## Monarda
Monarda, п., a genus of plants, the horsemint
(bot.) — ModL., named after the Spanish
botanist Nicolas Monardes (1493-1588).

## Monardella
Monardella, п., a genus of plants' of the mint
family (bot.) — A ModL. diminutive formed
from the name of the botanist Nicolas
Monardes. See prec. word and -ella.

## monastery
monastery, n. — ME. monasterie, fr. Eccles. L.
monasterium, fr. Eccles.Gk. μοναστήριον,
formed with -ήριον, a suff. denoting place, fr. μονα-
στής, 'monk', which lit. means 'living alone', fr.
μονάζειν, 'to live alone", fr. μόνος, 'alone'. Cp.
minster, which is a doublet of monastery, and
see mono-. Cp. also monk.

## monastic
monastic, adj., 1) pertaining to monasteries; 2)
pertaining to monks or nuns; п., a monk. —
ML. monasticus, fr. Eccles. Gk. μοναστικός,
'living alone', fr. μονάζων, 'to live alone'. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:499 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: monastic-al-ly, adv.,
monasticism n.

## monazite
monazite, п., a-phosphate of the rare earth metals
(mineral.) — G. Monazit, fr. Gk. μονάζειν, 'to
be alone, live alone', fr. μόνοε. 'alone'; see
mono-. The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## Monday
Monday, n. — ME, monenday, moneday, fr. OE,
monandxg, lit. 'day of the moon', fr. mona,
'moon', and dxg, 'day'; cp. ON. manadagr, Dan.
mandag, Swed. mdndag, Norw. maandag, OFris.
monendei, Du. maandag, OHG. mdnetag, MHG.
montac, maniac, G. Montag. These words are
prop, loan translations of L. Lunae dies, 'the
day of the moon' (whence It. lunedi, OF. lunsdi,
F. lundi, Proven?, (di)luns, Catal. dilluns, Sp.
lunes), itself a loan translation of Gk. Σελήνης
ημέρα, 'the day of the moon'. For the first
element see moon, for the second see day.

## Mondayish
Mondayish, adj. — Prop, 'feeling as some people
do on Monday*, when the work of the week
begins. — See prec. word and adj. suff. -ish.
Derivative: Mondayish-ness, n.

## monde
monde, п., the world of fashion; society. — F.,
fr. L. mundus, 'world'. See mundane and cp.
mound, 'globe of a sovereign'.

## Monel metal
Monel metal, an alloy of nickel, copper, iron,
manganese, silicon and carbon. — Named after
Ambrose Monell, of New York City (died in
1921).

## Moneses
Moneses, п., a genus of plants, the one-flowered
pyrola (bot.). — ModL., compounded of mono-
arid Gk. ήσις, 'delight', which is rel. to ήδε-
σθαι, 'torejoice',ηδονή, 'pleasure',ηδύς,'sweet'.
See hedonic.

## Moneta
Moneta, п., a surname of Juno. — L. Moneta.
See mint, ''place for coining money*.

## monetary
monetary, adj. — Late L. monetarius, 'belonging
to a mint', fr. L. moneta, 'mint, money'. See
money and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivative: monetari-ly, adv.

## monetize
monetize, tr. v., \) to coin into money; 2) to
legalize as money. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. L.
moneta, 'mint, money'. See money.
Derivative: monetiz-ation, n.

## money
money, n. — ME. moneie, fr. OF. moneie (F.
monnaie), fr. L. moneta, 'mint, money'. See mint,
'place for coining money', and cp. Moneta,
monetary, the first element in moidore and the
second element in porte-monnaie.
Derivative: money-ed, also moni-ed, adj.

## moneyage
moneyage, п., payment for the privilege of
coining (hist.). — OF. moneage, monoyage (F. mon-
nayage), fr. monayer, monnayer (F, monnayer),
'to coin' (whence the obsol. E. verb, to money).
Sec money and -age.

## moneyer
moneyer, п., one who coins money. — ME. mon-
eyer, fr. OF. monoter (F. monnayeur), fr. Late L.
monetarius, 'master of the mint, minter, coiner'.
See money and agential suff. -er.

## monger
monger, n. — ME. mangere, mongere, fr. OE.
mangere, 'merchant, trader*, fr. mangian, 'to
traffic, trade', fr. L. mango, 'a dealer who
polishes his wares, trader, trafficker, a slave trader',
which is prob. borrowed fr. Gk. *μάγγων, a
word rel to μάγγανον, 'any means for tricking
or bewitching, philter, drug', fr. I.-E. base
*mang-, 'to embellish, dress, trim'; see Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., II, p. 28 s.v. mango. See
mangle, 'machine for smoothing linen', and cp.
mangonel.

## Mongol
Mongol, n. and adj. — Mongolian. Cp. Mogul.
Derivatives: Mongol-ian, adj. and п., Mongol-
ic, adj. and п., Mongol-ism, п., Mongol-ize, tr.
v., Mongol-iz-ation, п., Mongoloid (q.v.).

## Mongoloid
Mongoloid, adj., resembling the Mongols. —
Compounded of Mongol and Gk.-oti&r)c,'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: Mongoloid, n.

## mongoose
mongoose, n. — Folk-etymological alteration of
Tamil mangus.

## mongrel
mongrel, п., an animal of mixed breed. —
Formed fr. obsol. mong, 'to mix', with dimin. suff.
-rel (cp. cockerel, fr. cock). See among, mingle.
Derivatives: mongrel, adj., mongrel-dom, п.,
mongrel-ish, adj., mongrel-ism, п., mongrel-ity,
п., mongrel-ize, tr. v., mongrel-iz-ation, п.,
mongrel-ly, adj., mongrel-ness, п.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:500 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 473 | MONOLOGUE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:500 COLUMN:1 -->

## monial
monial, п., a mullion. — ME. maynel, moniel, fr.
MF. mayneau (F. meneau), 'mullion', probably
contraction of *meienel-, which is formed with
sufF. -el (corresponding to L. -alis), fr. L. media-
nus, 'that which is in the middle*. See media,
'voiced stop consonant', and adj. suff. -a], and
cp. mullion. Cp. also median» mean»
'intermediate', mesne,

## monilfform
monilfform, adj., shaped like a string of beads,
jointed (bot. and zool.). — Compounded of L.
monile, 'necklace', and forma, 'form, shape'.
The first element is cogn. with Ol. manya, 'nape
of the neck', Gaul.-Gk. μάννος, μανιακής,
'Celtic necklace', OE. manu, 'mane', mene,
'necklace'; see mane. For the second element see
form, n.

## monism
monism, п., the doctrine that there is only one
principle (philos.) — ModL. monismus, fr. Gk.
μόνος, 'alone'; first used by the German
philosopher Baron Christian von Wolff (1679-1754).
See mono- and -ism.

## monist
monist, п., a believer in monism. — See prec.
word and -ist; first used by Christian von Wolff.
Derivative: monist-ic, adj.

## monition
monition, n.— ME. monicioun, fr. OF. (= F.)
monition, fr. L. monitionem, ace. of monitio, 'a
reminding, advice, warning', fr. monitus, pp. of
топед, monere, 'to call to mind, remind, advise,
warn', which stands for *moneyo and is a
causative form of memini, meminisse, 'to remember';
cogn. with OI. manayati, 'he considers, honors',
Gk. μέμονα, Ί am very eager, I intend', Lith is-
тапай, is-manyti, 'to understand, think', OE.
man'tan, OS. manon, OHG. manon, marten,
MHG. manen, G. mahnen, 4o admonish'. All
these words derive fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to think*.
See mind and words there referred to andep. esp.
monitor, monster, monstrance, monstrous,
monument, admonish, admonition, premonition,
summon, summons,

## monitor
monitor, п., one who reminds. — L., fr. monitus,
pp. of monere. See prec. word and agential suff.
-or and cp. mentor. — In the sense of a heavily
armed slow-moving vessel the word monitor
derives fr. Monitor, name of the first vessel of this
kind, designed by Captain Ericsson in the
American Civil War (in 1862).
Derivatives: monitor, intr. and tr. v., monitor-ial,
adj.
monitory* adj., warning. — L. monitdrius, fr.
monitus, pp. of monere. See monition and adj. suff.
-ory.
Derivatives: monitory, п., a letter containing an
admonition, monitori-al, adj.

## monk
monk, n. —ME. munec, fr. OE. munuc (whence
also ON. munkr), fr. VL. *monicust
corresponding to Late L. monachus, fr. Eccles. Gk.
μοναχός, 'monk', fr. Gk. μοναχός, 'living alone,
solitary', fr. μόνος, 'alone, single'. See mono- and
cp. monachal, monastery, monastic. Cp. OS.
munik, OFris. munek, monink, MLG. mom'k,
monk (whence Dan., Swed. munk), MDu. mon'xc,
monc (whence Du. monnik), OHG. munih
(whence MHG. munich, miinech, munich, G.
Monch, 'monk',) which all derive fr. VL. *moni-
cus. Cp. also OSlav. munichu, Lett, muks and
Finn, munkki, of s.m., which are Teut. loan
words.
Derivatives: monk-ery, п., monk-hood, п.,

## monkish
monkish, adj., monk-ish-ly, adv., monk-ish-ness, n.

## monkey
monkey, n. — MLG. Monekc(ri), name of an ape,

## prob. fr. MIt. monnicchio
prob. fr. MIt. monnicchio, fr. Olt. monna (cp.
Sp. and Port, mono, топа), *ape, monkey',
aphetically formed fr. Turk, таутйп, of s.m., fr.

## Arab
Arab, таутйп, 'auspicious', used

## euphemistically to denote the ape or monkey
euphemistically to denote the ape or monkey, whose sight
is supposed to bring misfortune. See Theodor

## NOldeke
NOldeke, WOrter mit Gegensinn, in his Neue

## Beitrage zur semitischen Sprachwissenschaft
Beitrage zur semitischen Sprachwissenschaft,

## Strassburg
Strassburg, 1910, p. 89. Arab, таутйп is pass,

## part
part, of ydmana, *he was happy, he was
fortunate; it was auspicious', fr. yaman, 'right side,

## south'
south', yamfn, 'right hand', See Benjamin and
cp. maim on and mona/a small African monkey'.
— Olt. monna, 'ape, monkey', has been

## influenced in form by monna
influenced in form by monna, 'woman', contraction

## of ma donna
of ma donna, 'my lady'.
Derivatives: monkey, intr. and tr. v.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:500 COLUMN:2 -->
monkeyish, adj., mokey-ish-ly, adv., monkey-ish-ness, n.

## mono- (before a vowel mon-l
mono- (before a vowel mon-l, combining form
meaning 1) one, alone, single; 2) (chem.)
containing one single atom. — Gk. μονό-, μον-,
fr. μόνος, 'alone, single', which stands for
*μόνΓος, and is in gradational relationship to
μανός (for *μαν5ός), 'thin, rare'. See mano- and
cp. monad, monism. Cp. also monk and words
there referred to. Cp. also the first element in
malmsey.

## monoacid
monoacid, also monacid, adj.; п., an acid that has
only one replaceable hydrogen atom for the
molecule (chem.) — A hybrid coined fr. Gk.
μόνος, 'alone, single*, and L. acidus, 'sour'. See
mono- and acid.
Derivative: monoacid-ic, adj.

## monobasic
monobasic, adj., having only one hydrogen atom
replaceable by a basic atom {chem.) —
Compounded of mono- and basic.

## monocarp
monocarp, п., a monocarpic plant. — See next
word.

## monocarpic
monocarpic, adj., bearing fruit only once, and
then dying (bot.) — Compounded of mono- and
Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel and adj. suff.
-ic.

## monocarpous
monocarpous, adj., having a gynoecium which
forms a single ovary (bot.) — See prec. word
and -оич.

## monochord
monochord, п., an instrument having only one
string or chord. — ME. monocorde, fr. MF.
(= F.) monocorde, fr. Late L. monochordon, fr.
Gk. μονόχορδον, prop. neut. of the adjective
μονόχορδος, 'having but one string', used as a
noun; compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single',
and χορδή, 'string'. See mono- and chord.

## monochroic
monochroic, adj., of one color. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. μονόχροος, 'of one color', fr.
μόνος, 'alone, single', and χροιά, 'color',
which is rel. to χρώμα, 'color'. See mono- and
chrome and cp. next word.

## monochromatic
monochromatic, adj., having only one color. —
See next word and chromatic.

## monochrome
monochrome, п., a painting or drawing of a single
color. — Introduced into English by the diarist
John Evelyn (1620-1706) fr. Gk. μονόχρωμος,
'of one color', fr. μόνος, 'alone, single', and
χρώμα, 'color'. See mono- and chrome and cp.
monochroic.
Derivatives: monochrom-ic, monochrom-ic-al,
adjs., monochrom-ic-al-iy, adv., monochrom-i.st,
п., monochrom-ous, adj., monochrom-y, n.

## monocle
monocle, n. — F., 'single eyeglass', fr. Late L.
monoculus, 'one-eyed'. See monocular.

## monoctinal
monoctinal, adj., having a single dip (said of
geological strata). — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. mono- and Gk. κλΐνειν, 'to bend, incline*.
See clinical and cp. words there referred to.

## monoclfnic
monoclfnic, adj., pertaining to crystallization in
which the crystals have three unequal axes,
with one oblique intersection (crystallogr.) —
Lit. 'with one oblique intersection'. See prec.
word.

## monocotyledon
monocotyledon, п., a plant with only one
cotyledon (bot.) — Compounded of mono- and
cotyledon.
Derivative: monocotyledon-ous, adj.

## monocracy
monocracy, п., government by one person. —
Compounded of mono- and Gk. -κρατία, 'rule
of, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'. See
-cracy.

## monocular
monocular, adj., 1) having only one eye; 2) fitted
for the use of only one eye. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ar fr. Late h.monoculus,'one-eyed', a hybrid
coined fr. Gk. μόνος, *alone, single', and L.
oculus, 'eye'. See mono- and ocular and cp.
monocle. Cp. also binocular.

## monocycle
monocycle, п., a velocipede having only one
wheel. — Compounded of mono- and Gk.
κύκλος, 'wheel'. See cycle.

## monocyclic
monocyclic, adj., having only one cycle. — See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## monodactylous
monodactylous, adj., having only one finger or
one toe. — Gk. μονοδάκτυλος, compounded
of μόνος,'alone, single', and δάκτυλος, 'finger,
toe'. See mono- and dactyl. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## monodic
monodic, adj., pertaining to monody. — Gk.
μονωδικός, fr.μονωδία. See monody and adj. suff.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:500 COLUMN:3 -->
-ic.

## monodist
monodist, п., a writer of monodies. — See
monody and -ist.

## monodrama
monodrama, п., a drama performed, or to be
performed, by only one person. —
Compounded of mono- and drama.

## monody
monody, п., 1) an ode sung by a single person
(Ancient Greek lit.); a poem in which the author
mourns the death of a friend; 3) a composition
in which a single melody predominates (mus.)
— Gk. μονωδία, 'monody', lit. 'a song sung
alone', fr. μονωδός, 'singing alone', which is
compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single*, and ωδή,
'song'. See mono- and ode.

## monoecious
monoecious, adj., having both male and female
organs in the same individual (bot. and zool.) —
Compounded of mon- and Gk. οίκος, 'house'.
See economy and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see suff. -ious.
Derivatives: monoecious-ly, adv., monoecious-
ness, n.

## monogamous
monogamous, adj., having but one wife or
husband at a time. — Late L. monogamus, fr. Gk.
μονόγαμος. See next word and -ous.

## monogamy
monogamy, п., state of having but one wife or
husband at a time. — F. monogamie, fr. Late L.
monogamia, fr. Gk. μονογαμία, fr. μονόγαμος,
'marrying one wife', which is compounded of
μόνος, 'alone, single', and γαμεΐν, 'to marry'.
See mono- and gamo- and cp. bigamy.
Derivatives: monogam-ic, adj., monogam-ist, n.

## monogenesis
monogenesis, п., the theoretical development of
all living organisms from a single cell (biol.) —
ModL., lit. Oneness of origin', compounded
of mono- and genesis.

## monogenetic
monogenetic, adj., pertaining to mongenesis. —
Compounded of mono- and genetic.

## monogenism
monogenism, п., the doctrine that the whole
human race has descended from a single pair. —
Compounded of mono-, Gk. -γενής, 'born of'
(see -gen), and suff. -ism.

## monogeny
monogeny, п., the descent of the human race
from a single pair. — See prec. word and -geny.

## monoglot
monoglot, adj., knowing one language only. —
Gk. μονόγλωττος, compounded of μόνος,
'alone, single', and γλώττα, 'tongue, language'.
See mono- and gloss, 'explanation'.
Derivative: monoglot, n.

## monogram
monogram, п., two or more letters intertwined.
— Late L. monogramma, fr. Late Gk. μονόγραμ-
