μον, neut. of μονόγραμμος, 'drawn with single
lines', which is compounded of Gk. μόνος,
'alone, single', and γραμμή 'line', lit. 'that
which is written'. See mono- and gram.

## mo no gram ma tic
mo no gram ma tic, adj., like a monogram. — See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## monograph
monograph, п., a treatise on a single subject. —
Compounded of mono- and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: monograph, tr. v., monograph-er,
п., monograph-ic, monograph-ic-al, adjs., mono-
graph-ic-al-ly, adv., monograph-ist, n.

## monogynous
monogynous, adj., 1) having but one wife at a
time; 2) (bot.) having a singie pistil. —
Compounded of mono- and Gk. γυνή, 'woman, wife'.
See -gynous.

## monogyny
monogyny, п., the state of being married to one
woman only at a time. — See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## monolatry
monolatry, п., the worship of one god, where
several are recognized as existing. —
Compounded of mono- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρία,
fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor, service, worship'. See
-latry.
Derivatives: monolatr-ist, п., monolatr-ous, adj.

## monolith
monolith, п., a column consisting of a single large
block of stone. — F. monolithe, fr. L. monoli-
tftus, fr. Gk. μονόλιθος, 'made of one stone',
which is compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single',
and λίθος, 'stone'. See mono- and titho-.
Derivative: monolith-ic, adj.

## monologist
monologist, п., 1) one who recites monologues;
2) one who monopolizes the conversation. —
Formed with suff. -ist fr. Gk. μονόλογος,
'speaking alone*. See monologue.

## monologae
monologae, п., a long speech by a single person.
— F., fr. MGk. μονόλογος, 'speaking alone',
which is compounded of Gk. μόνος, 'alone,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:501 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MONOLOGUIST | 474 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:501 COLUMN:1 -->
single', and the stem of λέγειν, 'to speak*. See
logos and cp. dialogue.
Derivatives: monolog-ize, intr. v., monolog-iz-er,
п., monoiogist (q.v.)

## monologulst
monologulst, n. — The same as monoiogist

## monomachy
monomachy, п., a single combat. — F. mono·
machie, fr. Late L. monomachia, fr. Gk.
μονομαχία, 'a single combat', fr. μονομάχος, 'fighting
in single combat', which is compounded of
μόνος, 'alone, single,' and μάχη, 'battle, fight'. See
-machy.

## monomania
monomania, п., a mental disorder characterized
by irrationality on a single subject. — Medical
L., compounded of mono- and mania.
Derivatives: monomani-ac, adj. and п., mono-
mani-ac-al, adj.

## monomerous
monomerous, adj., having one flower in each
whorl (bot.) — Formed with surf, -ous fr. Gk.
μονομερής, 'single', which is compounded of
μόνος, 'alone, single', and μέρος, 'part*. See
mono- and mero- 'part\

## monometallic
monometallic, adj., using one metal; pertaining to
monometallism. — Compounded of mono-,
metal and adj. surf, -ic.

## monometallism
monometallism, п., the use of only one metal as
the monetary standard. — Compounded of
mono-, metal and sufT. -ism.
monometallism п., one who advocates
monometallism. — Compounded of mono-, metal and
suff. -1st.

## monometric
monometric, adj., isometric (crystallogr.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. mono- and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See metrical.

## monomial
monomial, adj., consisting of a single term —
Formed with sufT. -ial fr. *monome contraction
of *mono-nome, lit. 'one single name', a hybrid
coined fr. Gk. μόνος, 'alone, single*, and L.
nomen, 'name'; see mono- and nominal and cp.
binomial, trinomial, multinomial. The
contraction of *mononome into *mo-nome is due to
haplology. For similar contractions see
haplology.

## monomorphic
monomorphic, monomorphous, adj., having one
form only (biol.) — Compounded of mono- and
Gk. μορφή, 'form, shape'. See morpho- and adj.
sufT. -ic, resp. -ous.

## monopetalous
monopetalous, adj., having one petal only (bot.)
— Compounded of mono- and Gk. πέταλον, 'a
thin plate of metal, leaf*. See petalon and -ous.

## monophobia
monophobia, п., a morbid fear of being alone
(med.) — Compounded of mono- and Gk.
-φοβία, 'feat of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## monophthong
monophthong, п., a single vowel sound — Gk.
μονόφθογγος, 'having one sound',
compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single' (see mono-),
and φθόγγος, 'sound, voice, vowel', which is
rel. to φθέγμα, 'sound, voice, speech*, φθέγγε-
σθαι, 'to speak loud; to praise, sing'. Cp.
diphthong, triphthong.
Derivatives: monophthong-al, adj., mono-
phthong-ize, tr. v., monophthong-iz-ation, n.

## monophyletic
monophyletic, adj., 1) pertaining to a single tribe;
2) developed from a single ancestral type. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. μονόφϋλος, 'of
one tribe', which is compounded of μόνος,
'alone, single', and φυλή, 'tribe'. See mouo-
and phyle and cp. phyletic.

## monophyllous
monophyllous, adj., having one leaf only (bot.) —
Gk. μονόφυλλος, *one-leaved\ compounded of
μόνος, 'alone, single', and φύλλον, 'leaf. See
mono- and phyilo-,

## Monophysite
Monophysite, п., one who maintains that Jesus
had one nature. — Late Gk. μονοφυσίτης,
compounded of Gk. μόνος, 'alone, single', and
φύσις, 'nature'. See mono-, physio- and subst.
suff. -fte.
Derivatives: Monophysit-ic, adj., Monophysit-
ism, n.

## monoplane
monoplane, п., an airplane with only one plane.
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. μόνος, 'alone,
single', and Late L. plana. See mono- and plane,
'a flat surface'.

## monoplegia
monoplegia, п., paralysis of a single limb (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of mono- and Gk
πληγή, 'stroke', which is cogn. with L. pldga,
'stroke, injury, plague'. See mono- and plague
and cp. diplegia.

## monopode
monopode, adj., having only one foot. — Late L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:501 COLUMN:2 -->
monopodius, fr. Gk. μονόπους, gen. μονόποδος,
One-footed', which is compounded of μόνος,
'alone, single', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'.
See mono- and podo-.
Derivative: monopode, n.

## mono podium
mono podium, п., a single main axis which extends
at the apex, producing lateral branches beneath
it (bot.) — Mod L., compounded of mono- and
Gk. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See podo- and cp.
prec. word. Cp. also L. monopodium, fr. Gk.
*μονοπόδιον, 'a table with one foot*.

## monopoly
monopoly, п.,exclusive control of a commodity.
L. monopolium, fr. Gk. μονοπώλιον, 'right of
exclusive sale', μονοπωλία, 'exclusive sale',
compounded of μόνος, 'alone' (see mono-), and
πωλειν, 'to sell', which derives fr. l.-E. basc*pe/-,
'to sell, purchase, barter, gain', whence also OI.
panate (for *prnate, fr. plnate), 'barters,
purchases', panab (for prnah, fr./j/wdA), 'bet, wager',
Lith. pelnas, 'gain*, pelnau, pelnyti, 'to gain',
Lett, pelnit, 'to gain', pe'lns, реЧпа, 'gain',
OSlav. plenii, Russ. polon, 'prey, booty', ON.
fair, Swed.M Du. veil, OUG. fdlijeili, MHG.
veile, veil, G. feil, 'for sale, venal'. Cp. the
second element in bibliopole. Cp. also fanam.
Derivatives: monopol-ist,a., monopol-ist-ic, adj.,
monopol-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., monopol-ize, tr. v.,
monopol-iz-ation, п., monopol-iz-er, n.

## monopteral
monopteral, adj., having one row of pillars only
(arch.) — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk.
μονόπτερος, fr. μόνος, 'alone, single', and πτε-
ρόν, 'feather, wing; row of pillars'. See mono-
and ptero-.

## monoptote
monoptote, п., a noun having only one case
(gram.)— LateL. monoptota(pl.), fr. Gk. μονό-
πτωτα, pi. of μονόπτωτον, prop. neut. of the adj.
μονόπτωτος, 'having only one case', fr. μόνος,
'alone, single' (see mono-), and πτωτός, 'fallen',
verbal adj. of πίπτειν, 'to fall', which stands for
πΐ-πτειν, fr. *pt-, zero degree of I.-E. base *pet-,
'to fly, to fall'. See feather and cp. symptom and
words there referred to.

## monorail
monorail, п., 1) a single rail serving as a track; 2)
a railway on which the cars run on such a track.
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. μόνος, 'alone, single'
(see mono-), and E. rail, 'bar' (q.v.)

## mono rhyme
mono rhyme, п., a verse in which every line has the
same rhyme. — Compounded of mono- and
rhyme.

## monosperinous
monosperinous, adj., one-seeded (bot.) —
Compounded of mono- and Gk. σπέρμα, 'seed'. See
sperm and -ous.

## monostich
monostich, п., a poem consisting of one line —
Late L. monostichum, fr. Gk. μονόστιχον, neut.
of μονόστίχος, 'consisting of one row', fr.
μόνος, 'alone, single', and στίχος, 'order, row,
line, rank; verse'. For the first element see
mono-, for the second see acrostic and cp. words
there referred to.

## monostichous
monostichous, adj., arranged in a single row on
one side of the axis (bot.) — Gk. μονόστιχος,
'consisting of one row'. See prec. word. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## monostrophe
monostrophe, п., a poem in which all the strophes
have the. same metrical form. — Gk. μονόστρο-
φος, compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single',
and στροφή, 'a strophe'. See mono- and strophe.

## monosyllabic
monosyllabic, adj., consisting of one syllable. —
See monosyllable and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: monosyllabic-al, adj., monosyllabic-
al-ly, adv.

## monosyllable
monosyllable, n. — L. monosyllabus, 'of one
syllable', fr. Gk. μονοσύλλαβος, which is
compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single', and συλλαβή,
'syllable'. See mono- and syllable.

## monotheism
monotheism, п., the belief that there is but one
God. — Compounded of mono- and Gk. θεός,
'god'. See 1st theism.

## monotheist
monotheist, п., an adherent of monotheism. —
See prec. word and theist.
Derivatives: monotheist-ic, adj., monotheist-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## monotint
monotint, п., a single color; monochrome. — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. μόνος, 'alone, single'
(see mono-), and E. tint (fr. L. tinctum). The
correct form is monochrome, in which both
elements are of Greek origin.

## monotone
monotone, п., 1) an unvarying tone (mus.); 2) the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:501 COLUMN:3 -->
sameness of color. — See next word.
Derivatives: monotone, tr. v., monoton-ic, adj.

## monotonous
monotonous, adj., continuing in the same tone.
— Gk. μονότογος, 'of one tone, monotonous',
compounded of μόνος, 'alone, single*, and
τόνος, 'tone'. See mono- and tone. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.
Derivatives: monotonous-ly, adv., monotonous·
ness, n.

## monotony
monotony, n. — Gk, μονοτονία, 'sameness of
tone, monotony', fr. μονότονος. See prec. word
and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## Monotremata
Monotremata, n. pi., the lowest order of
mammals (zool.) — ModL., compounded of mono-
arid Gk. τρήμα, gen. τρήματος, 'hole* (see
Trema); so called because the animals belonging
to this order have only one opening for the
digestive, urinary and genital organs.

## Monotropa
Monotropa, п., a genus of plants, the Indian pipe
(bot.). — ModL., compounded of mono- and
τρόπος, 'a turn' (see trope); so called because the
stem is turned to one side.

## Monotropaceae
Monotropaceae, п., pi., the Indian pipe family
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. prec. word with
suff. -aceae.

## monotropaceous
monotropaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Monotropsis
Monotropsis, п., a genus of plants, the sweet
pinesap (bot.). — ModL., contraction of
Monotropa and Gk. 6ψις, 'appearance'. See -opsis.

## monotype
monotype, п., the only type of its group, as a
single species of a genus (biol.) — Compounded
of mono- and type.
Derivative: monotyp-ic, adj.

## monovalent
monovalent, adj., univalent (chem.) — A hybrid
coined fr. Gk. μόνος, 'alone, single', and L.
valens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of valere, 'to have
power'; see mono- and -valent. The correct form
is univalent, in which both elements are of Latin
origin.

## monoxide
monoxide, п., an oxide with one oxygen atom in
each molecule (chem.) — Compounded of mon-
and oxide.

## Monroe doctrine
Monroe doctrine, the doctrine laid down by
President Monroe of the United States in his
message to Congress, Dec. 2, 1823.

## monseigneur
monseigneur, п., a French title of honor. — F.,
lit. 'my lord', fr. топ, 'my', and seigneur, 'lord',
F. топ derives fr. L. meum, ace. of meus, 'my,
mine', which is rel. to me, 'me', mihi. Ίο me'; see
meum, me. F. seigneur comes fr. L. senidrem, ace.
of senior, 'older'; see seigneur and cp. next
word. Cp. also monsignor.

## monsieur
monsieur, п., the French equivalent of English
Mr. — F., lit. 'my lord', compounded of топ,
'my', and sieur, 'lord', a shortened form of
seigneur. See prec. word and cp. messire.

## monslguor
monslguor, п., a title conferred on some prelates.
— It. monsignore, lit. 'my lord', compounded
of топ, 'my', fr. L. meum, ace. of meus, 'my,
mine', and signore, 'lord', fr. L. senidrem, ace.
of senior, 'older'. See monseigueur, siguore.

## monsoon
monsoon, п., the trade wind of the Indian Ocean.
— MDu. monssoen, fr. Port, mongao, fr. Arab.
mausim (written mousim), 'time of the year,
season', fr. wasama, 'he marked with a brand,
he marked'. The final letters -im (in Arab.
mausim) were misread as -un (whence Du, -oen,
E. -oon). Cp. the word zenith, which owes its
form to a similar misreading.

## monster
monster, n. — ME. monsire, fr. OF. (= F.)
monstre, fr. L. monstrum, 'an evil omen,
portent, monster', for *mone-stromt lit. 'that which
serves as a warning', fr. monere, 'to remind,
warn, advise, instruct'. L. monstrdre, 'to show,
point out, indicate', is a derivative of monstrum.
See monition and cp. monstrance, monstrous,
demonstrate, premonstrate, remonstrate. Cp. also
muster.

## monstrance
monstrance, п., a receptacle in which the
consecrated host is shown (R. C. Ch.) — MF., fr.
Eccles. L. monstrantia, fr. L. mdnstrans, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of monstrare. See monster and
-ance; and cp. remonstrance.

## monstrosity
monstrosity, п., the quality of being monstrous.
— Late L. monstrositds, 'strangeness, unnatural-
ness\ fr. L. mdnstrosus, a collateral form of
monstruosus (whence F. monstruosite). See next

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:502 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 475 | MORDACIOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:502 COLUMN:1 -->
word and -ity.

## monstrous
monstrous, adj., enormous; horrible. — MF. (=
F.) monstrueux (fem. mons true use), fr. L. mon-
struosus, 'strange, unnatural, monstrous', fr.
monstrum. See monster and -ous.
Derivatives: monsirous-ly, adv., monstrous-ness,
n.
montage* п., the process of making a composite
picture. — F., lit. 'a mounting, putting
together', fr. monter, 'to go up, ascend; to mount, put
together'. See mount, v., and -age.

## montane
montane, adj., 1) mountainous; 2) living in
mountains. — L. montanus, 'pertaining to a
mountain; mountainous; living in the
mountains', fr. mons, gen. montis, 'mountain'. See
mount, 'hill, mountain', and -ane and cp. cis-
moutane, tramontane, ultramontane, verumon-
taniun.

## montbretia
montbretia, п., a plant of the genus Tritonia
(bot.) — ModL., named after Antoine-Fran-
cois-Ernest Coquebert de Montbret(1781-1801),
official botanist of Napoleon's expedition to
Egypt. For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## mont-de-piete
mont-de-piete, п., a public pawnshop in France.
— F., fr. It. monte di pieta, lit. 'credit of pity' (in
Olt., monte had also the meaning of 'money
due'). It. monte derives fr. L. montem, ace. of
mons, 'mountain'; see mount 'hill, mountain'.
It. di comes fr. L. de, 'from, away from'; see de-.
It. pieta derives fr, L. pietatem, ace. of pietas,
'dutiful conduct'; see piety and cp. pity.

## monte
monte, п., a gambling game of cards. — Sp.
monte, 'mountain; a pile of cards left after the
first deal; a game of cards', fr. L. montem, ace.
of mons, 'mountain'. See mount, 'hill,
mountain', and cp. prec. word.

## monteith
monteith, п., a large bowl for punch, usually of
silver. — Named after Monteith or Monteigh, a
Scot, who lived in the 17th cent.
Μontessori system, a system of education devised
in 1907 by the Italian educationist Dr.Maria
Montessori (1870-1952).

## month
month, n. — ME. moneth, month, fr. OE. monad,
rel. to OS. manuth, ON. manadr, Dan. moaned,
Swed. monad, Norw. maanad, OFris. monath,
MDu. manet, Du. maand, OHG. manod, MHG.
tndnot, G. Monat, Goth, menops, 'month', and
to OG. mdna, etc., 'moon'. See moon and subst.
suff. -th.
Derivatives: montk-ly, adj., п., and adv.

## Montia
Montia, п., a genus of plants of the purslane
family (bot.) — ModL., named after Giuseppe
Monti, professor of botany in Bologna.

## monticellite
monticellite, п., a calcium magnesium silicate
(mineral.) — Named after the Italian
mineralogist Teodoro Monticelii (1758-1856). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## monticule
monticule, п., a hillock. — F., fr. Late L. monti-
culus, 'a little hill, hillock', dimin. of L. mons,
gen. montis, 'mountain'. See mount, 'hill,
mountain', and -cule.

## monument
monument, n. — ME. moniment, fr. L. monumen-
tum, monimentum, 'monument', lit. 'that which
reminds', fr. monere, 'to call to mind, remind,
advise, warn'. See monition and -ment.

## monumental
monumental, adj. — L. monumentalis, 'pertaining
to a monument', fr. monumentum; first used by
Shakespeare. See monnment and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: monumental-ize, tr. v., monumen-
tal-iz-ation, п., monumental-ly, adv.

## -mony
-mony, nominal suff. denoting action, result of an
action or condition, as in patrimony,
sanctimony, testimony. — L. -mania, -monium (often
through the medium of F. -monie, -moine);
cogn. with the Greek suff. -μων in μνήμων
'mindful', τλήμων 'enduring, patient', etc.

## monzonite
monzonite, п., a complex silicate (mineral.) —
Named after Mt. Monzoni in Tirol. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## moo
moo, intr. v., to make the characteristic sound of
a cow, to low; п., the sound made by a cow. —
Imitative.

## mooch
mooch, also mouch, intr. v., to skulk, sneak. —
ME. mouchen, prob. fr. OF. muchier, a
collateral form* of mucier, 'to hide, skulk', fr. VL.
*mucidre, a word of Gaulish origin.

## mood
mood, п., grammatical form indicating the
function of a verb. — A doublet of mode (q.v.),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:502 COLUMN:2 -->
influenced in form by an association with mood,
'state of mind'.

## mood
mood, п., state of mind, temper. — ME. mode,
mood, fr. ОЕ- mod, 'mind, intellect, heart,
courage', rel. to OS., OFris. mod, 'mind, intellect,
courage', ON. тбдг, 'wrath, anger', Dan,,
Swed., Norw. mod, 'courage', MDu. moet,
Du. moed, OHG., MHG. muot, G. Mut,
'courage', Goth, mops, 'courage, anger'. The ultimate
origin of these Teut. words is uncertain.
Derivatives: mood-y, adj., mood-i-ly, adv.,
mood-i-ness, n.

## moon
moon, n. — ME. топе, moone, fr. OE. топа, rel.
to OFris. топа, OS., OHG. mdno, ON. mani
(whence Dan. and Norw. maane, Swed. mane,
MDu. mane, Du. maan, MHG. mane, G. Mond,
Goth, тёпа, 'moon', and cogn, with OI. mas-,
musah, 'moon, month', Avestic ma, ModPers.
mah, of s.m., Toch. А тай, 'moon, month', В
тепе, 'month', mem, 'moon', Arm, amis, gen.
amsoy, 'month', Gk. μήνη, 'moon', μήν, gen.
μηνός, 'month', Alb. muai, 'month', L. mensis,
'month', OSlav. mes^ci, 'moon, month', Lith.
menesis, menuo, of s.m., Lett, meness, 'moon',
menesis, 'month', OPruss. menig, 'month', Olr.
mi, gen. mis, W. and OCo. mis, Bret, miz,
'month'. All these words derive fr. l.-E.
*me(n)s-, 'moon; month', which is traceable to
I.-E. base me-, 'to measure', the moon being
referred to as 'the measurer (of time)'. See mete,
'to measure', and cp. month. Cp. also meniscus,
meno-, 'month', menses, menstrual, menstruum,
bimestrial, trimester, semester.
Derivatives: moon, v., moon-less, moon-y, adjs.

## moonlit
moonlit, adj., lit by the moon. — Coined by
Alfred Tennyson fr. moon and lit, pp. of light.

## moonstruck
moonstruck, adj. — Coined by Milton fr. moon
and pp. of strike.

## moor
moor, п., waste ground. — ME. mor, fr. OE. mor,
rel. to OS., MDu., Du. moer, 'swamp', OHG.
muor, 'swamp*, also 'sea', OHG. muorra, ON.
morr, 'moorland', marr, 'sea'. See mere, 'the
sea', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: moor-ish, moor-y, adjs.

## moor
moor, tr. v., to fasten (a vessel) by a cable; intr.
v., to be fastened by cables. — Late ME. more,
re], to OE. mxrels-rap 'mooring rope', and to
MDu. maren, meren, Du. meren, 'to moor a
ship', whence F. amarrer, of s.m. Cp. marl, 'to
fasten', marline.
Derivatives: moor-age, п., moor-ings, n. pi.

## Moor
Moor, п., 1) a native of Morocco; 2) one of the
Moslem iovaders of Spain or their descendants.
— F. More, Maure, fr. L. Maurus, 'an
inhabitant of Mauretania (N. W. Africa)', fr. Gk.
Μαϋρος,ίΓ. μαΰρος, μαυρός^ΐιϊοΐι is prob. aback
formation fr. μαυροΰν, 'to darken, blind*, a
form used (for metrical reasons) inst. of άμαυ-
ροΰν, fr. άμαυρός 'dark, dim, dull, faint', a
word of uncertain origin. Cp. amaurosis and the
first element in mavrodaphne. Cp. also Maurice,
morel, 'nightshade', morello, Moresque, Moris-
co, morris dance, morris pike.

## moose
moose, п., the North American elk. — Of Algon-
quian origin.

## moot
moot, п., 1) an assembly of freemen (Engl, hist.);
2) discussion, argument (obsol.) — ME. mot,
mote, fr. OE. mot, gemot, 'a meeting, assembly,
discussion', rel. to OS., ON. mot, MHG. muoz,
'meeting', OE. metan, 'to meet'. See meet, 'to
encounter', and cp. the second element in foik-
mote, ha 11 moot, witenagemot. Cp. also empty.

## moot
moot, tr. v., to debate. — ME. moten, motien, fr.
OE. motion, 'to meet, talk, discuss', fr. mot,
gemot. See moot, n.

## moot
moot, adj., debatable. — Fr. moot, n.

## mop
mop, п., an implement used for cleaning. — ME.
mappe, prob. fr. F. mappe, fr. L. mappa,
'napkin, tablecloth'. See map and cp. moppet.
Derivative: mop, tr. v., to wipe, clean.

## mop
mop, intr. v., to grimace (in to mop and mow); п.,
grimace (in mops and mows) — Prob. of
imitative origin.

## mope
mope, intr. v., to be depressed. — Of uncertain
origin. Cp. Du. moppen, 'to pout', dial. Swed.
тора, 'to sulk'.
Derivatives: mope, п., mop-ish, adj., mop-ish-ly,
adv., mop-ish-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:502 COLUMN:3 -->

## moplah
moplah, п., one of a class of Moslems inhabiting
chiefly Malabar. — Malayalam mappila.

## mopoke
mopoke, n. — See morepork.

## moppet
moppet, п., 1) a little girl (archaic); 2) a pet dog.
— Formed with dimin. suff. -et fr. ME. moppe,
'rag doll', which prob. derives fr. L. mappa,
'napkin, tablecloth'. See mop, 'implement for
cleaning'.

## moquette
moquette, п., a velvet pile. — F., alter, of earlier
moucade, which is of unknown origin.

## Moraceae
Moraceae, n. pi., the mulberry family of plants
(bot.) — ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr.
Morus (q.v.)

## moraceous
moraceous, adj., — See prec. word and -aceous.
Могаеа, п., a genus of plants of the iris family
(bot.) — ModL., named by Linnaeus in honor
of his father-in-law, Dr. Johannes Moraeus.

## moraine
moraine, п., the rock material deposited by a
gacier (geol.) — F., fr. Savoyard morena, fr.
pre-Latin *murrum-, 'hillock, mound', which is
of uncertain, possibly imitative, origin.
Derivatives: morain-al, morain-ic, adjs.

## moral
moral, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. mdralis,
'pertaining to manners', fr. mos, gen. maris,
'manner, habit, custom', which is of uncertain
origin. For the ending see adj. suff. -al. L. mo-
ralis is prop, a loan translation of Gk. ήίΗκός,
'pertaining to moral1, fr. ήθος 'habit, custom,
moral' (see ethical).
Derivatives: moral, п., morals, n. pi., moral-ism,
п., moral-ist, п., moral-ist-ic, adj., moral-ist-ic-
al-ly, adv., moral-ize, tr. and intr. v., moral-iz-
ation, п., moral-iz-er, п., moral-ly, adv.

## morale
morale, п., moral condition with respect to
courage, confidence, etc. — F., prop. fem. of the adj.
moral, 'moral', used as a noun. See prec. word.

## morality
morality, n. — ME. moralitee, fr. MF. (= F.)
moralite, fr. L. mdrulitatem, ace. of moralitas,
'marmer.character', fr.moralis. See moral and-ity.

## morass
morass, п., a bog, marsh. — Du. moeras, a blend
of MDu. maerasch (fr. OF. maresche, 'marsh1,
whence also F. marais) and Du. moer, 'moor'.
See moor, 'waste land'.
Derivatives: morass-ic, morass-ish, adjs.

## moratorium
moratorium, п., legal authorization to delay the
payment of a debt. — ModL., formed fr. neut.
of Late L. morawrius. See next word.

## moratory
moratory, adj., delaying, deferring. — Late L.
moratorius, 'delaying, dilatory', fr. L. moratus,
pp. of morari, 'to defer, delay', fr. mora,
'hesitation, delay', which is cogn. with Olr. maraim, Ί
remain*. L. mora and Olr. maraim possibly
derive fr. I.-E. base *mer-, 'to care for, be anxious
about, think, consider, remember'. See memory
and cp. demur, remora.

## Moravian
Moravian, n. and adj. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. Moravia, from Morava, name of a river ( =
L. Mar us).

## moray
moray, n., a fish of the family Muraenidae. — Port.
moreia, fr. L. muraena, murena, ''sea eel,
lamprey', fr. Gk. σμύραινα, μύραινα, of s.m., fr.
σμΰρος, μΰρος, 'sea eel', which is rel. to σμύρις,
'emery powder'. See emery and cp. Muraena.

## morbid
morbid, adj. — L. morbidus, 'sickly', fr. morbus,
'sickness, disease', which prob. stands for *mor-
bhos, or *m{-bhos, lit. 'that which consumes', fr.
I.-E. base *mer-, 'to rub, pound, wear away,
consume, exhaust, worry; to be consumed',
whence also Gk. μαραίνει, 'to consume-,
exhaust', μαρασμός, 'consumption'; see Walde-
Hofmann, II, pp. 110-111 s.v. morbus. See
smart, v., and cp. marasmus, marble, amaranth.
Cp. also mordant, mortal.
Derivatives: morbid-ity, п., morbid-ly, adv.,
morbid-ness, n.

## morbidezza
morbidezza, п., sensitiveness, delicacy. — It., fr.
morbido, 'morbid'. See prec. word.

## morbific
morbific, adj., causing disease (med.). — Formed
fr. L. morbus, 'disease', and suff. -ficus, fr. -fi-
cere, unstressed form of facere, 'to make, do'.
See morbid and -fie.

## morceau
morceau, п., 1) a piece, bit; 2) a short musical or
literary composition. — F., 'piece, bit, morsel'.
See morsel.

## Morchella
Morchella, п., a genus of edible fungi (bot.) —
ModL., fr. G. Morckel, 'morel'. See morel, 'an
edible fungus'.

## mordacious
mordacious, adj., biting; caustic (said of Ian-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:503 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MORDANT | 476 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:503 COLUMN:1 -->
guage). — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. mordax,
gen. morddcis, 'biting4, fr. mordere, *to bite'.
See next word and -acious.
Derivative: mordacious-ly, adv.

## mordant
mordant, adj., biting. — OF. (= F.), 'biting',
pres. part, of mordre, 'to bite', fr. VL. *mordere
(whence also It. mordere, OProveng., Sp.,
Port, mordre), fr. L. mordeo, mordere, 'to bite*,
which stands for *(s)mordeyo and is cogn. with
OI. mardayati, mardati, 'rubs, crushes', midnatt,
'presses, rubs', Gk. σμερδνός, σμερδαλέος,
'terrible, fearful', lit. 'rubbing, crushing', OE.
smeortan, OHG. smerzan, 'to pain', orig. 'to
bite'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*(s)merd-> a -(/-enlargement of base *mer-, 'to
rub, pound, consume, wear away, exhaust,
worry; to be consumed'. See smart, v. and cp.
morbid, morceau, mordacious, mordent, morse,
'a brooch', morsel, premorse, remorse. For the
ending see suff. -ant.
Derivatives: mordant, п., mordant-ly, adv.

## Mordecai
Mordecai, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the cousin of
Esther, who saved the Jews from the
extermination planned by Haman. — Heb. Morarkhay,
spelled also Mordokhay, fr. Akkad. Marduk
(whence Heb. Merodhakh, name of the chief
god of the city of Babylon, whence also the
Babylonian PN's Mardukea, Marduka.

## mordenite
mordenite, п., a zeolite (mineral.) — Named after
Morden in Nova Scotia. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## mordent
mordent, п., an ornament of three tones, a trill
(mus.) — G., fr. It. mordente* lit. 'biting', pres.
part, of mordere, fr. VL. *mordere,
corresponding to Classical L. mordere, 'to bite'. See
mordant and -ent.

## more
more, adj. — ME, more, fr. OE. nigra, 'larger,
greater, more' (used as compar. of micel, Marge,
great, much'); rel. to OE. ma, 'more' (neut. and
adv.), OS. mera> adj., mer, adv., ON. meiri, adj.,
meirr, meir, adv., OFris. тага, тёга, adj., та,
me (also mar, mer), adv., MDu. mere, merre,
adj. and adv., mee, adv., Du. meer, adv., OHG.
mero, adj., mer, adv., MHG. mere, adj., mer,
adv., G. mehr, adj. and adv. (cp. the adjectives
with double compar. suflf. Du. meerder, 'more,
greater', OHG. miroro, meriro, 'greater', MHG.
merer, merre, G. mehrere, 'several'), Goth.
maiza, adj., mais, adv., OE. mxre, OHG. man,
'great, glorious, famous', and cogn. with Aves-
tic mazjd, 'greater', Olr. mar, mar, 'great', таи,
то, 'more', Homeric Gk. έγχεσί-μωρος, 'great
with the £γχος', i.e. 'great with the spear', Os-
can mais, 'more'. Cp. most.
Derivatives: more, n. and adv.

## moreen
moreen, η., a coarse fabric of wool or of wool and
cotton. — Prob. formed fr. moire with suff.
-een.

## morel
morel, п., an edible fungus. — F. moril/e, of Teut.
origin. Cp. OHG. morhi/a, morhala (MHG.
morhef, morchel, G. Morchel), 'тогеГ, dimin. of
moraha, morha (MHG., morhe, morhe, G.
Mohre), 'carrot', which is rel. to OS. morha,
MLG. more, OE. moru, more, 'carrot', obsol.
E. more, 'root', and possibly cogn. with Gk.
(τά) βράκανα, 'wild herbs', OSlav. mrkvy,
'carrots', Russ. morkov', Serb, mrkva, etc.,
'carrot', Cp, Morchel la.

## morel
morel, п., the black nightshade. — F. morelle, fr.
VL. *maurella, fern, of *maurellus 'dark-
colored', diminutive formed
fr.L.MowrHi,'inhabitant of Mauretania\ See Moor and cp. next
word. Cp. also OF., OProvenQ. morel, F.
moreau, 'jet-black horse'.

## morello
morello, п., a bitter variety of cherry. — It., fr.
VL. *maurellus, dimin. of L. Maurus,
'inhabitant of Mauretania. The plant was so called
after its color. See Moor and cp. prec. word.

## morencite
morencite, п., a hydrated ferric silicate {mineral.)
— Named after Morenci in Arizona. For the
ending see subst. suflf. -ite.

## morenoslte
morenoslte, п., a hydrous nickel sulfate {mineral.)
— Sp. morenosita, named after Moreno, a
Spaniard who lived in the 19th century. For the
ending -ita, which goes back to Gk. -ΐτης, see
subst, suff. -ite.

## moreover
moreover, adv. — Compounded of more and
over.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:503 COLUMN:2 -->

## morepork
morepork, also mopoke, п., name of various
Australian birds. — Of imitative origin.

## mores
mores, n. pi., customs. — L. mores, pi. of mos,
'manner, habit, custom'. See moral.

## Moresque
Moresque, adj., Moorish (said of style in
architecture, etc.) — F. moresque, fr. It. moresco,
'Moorish', fr. Moro, 'Moor'- See Moor and
-esque.

## morganatic
morganatic, adj., pertaining to, or designating, a
form of marriage with a woman of inferior rank,
in which neither the wife nor the issue may lay
claim to the husband's resp. the father's rank or
property (excepting his private property). — F,
morganatique, fr. ML. morgandticum in matri-
monium ad morgandticum, 'morganatic
marriage', lit. 'a marriage based only on the morning
gift', formed with L. suff. -aticum (see 1st -atic),
fr. OHG. morgan, 'morning', in morgangeba
(whence MHG. morgengabe, G. Morgengabe),
'morning gift', i.e. 'gift of the husband to the
wife on the morning after the marriage'. See
morn and cp. morgen. The second element in
OHG. morgan-geba derives fr. OHG. geban,
'to give'; see give.
Derivative: morganatic-аЫу, adv.

## morganite
morganite, п., a rose-colored beryl {mineral.) —
Named after the American financier John Pier-
pont Morgan (1837-1913). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## morgen
morgen, п., an old land measure. — G., lit.,
'morning'; prop., 'amount that can be plowed
by a team in one morning'. See morn.

## morgue
morgue, п., haughtiness. — F., 'haughty look,
haughtiness', of unknown origin.

## morgue
morgue, п., mortuary. — F., orig. identical with
morgue in the sense of 'haughtiness'. The
original meaning of this French word seems to have
been 'look, face', whence developed the
meaning 'a place where prisoners were inspected at
their entering the prison', and 'a place where
dead persons are examined for the sake of
identification'. See prec. word.

## moribund
moribund, adj., dying. — L. moribundus, 'dying',
fr. mori, "to die'. See mortal.
Derivatives: moribund, п., moribund-ity, п.,
moribund-ly, adv.

## morin
morin, η., ayellow coloring matter found in the
fustic tree (chem).—Έ .mor ine, coined by the French
chemist Michel-Eugene Chevreul (1786-1889)
in 1837 fr. ModL. Morus (see Moras) and suff.
-ine (see chem. suff. -ine); so called by him
because the genus Morus formerly included the
fustic tree.

## morion
morion, п., a hatlike helmet worn in the 16th and
17th centuries. — F., fr. Sp. morridn, a
derivative of morro, 'anything round like the upper
part of the head'. See morro.

## morion
morion, п., a dark variety of quartz {mineral.) —
. G. Morion, shortened fr. L. mormorion, a kind
of dark brown crystal.

## Morisco
Morisco, п., a Moor, esp. one of the descendants
of the Moors in Spain (hist.) — Sp., 'Moorish',
fr. Moro, 'Moor*. See Moor and cp. Moro.
тогто, п., a bugbear. — Gk. μορμώ, 'bugbear,
hob, goblin', which is rel. to μόρμορος (Hesy-
chiusL 'dread, terror', μύρμος (Hesychius), of
s.m., Μυρμιδόνες, 'a warlike people of Thes-
saly', lit. 'the people of bugbears', and prob.
cogn. with L. formido, 'terror'. See formidable
and cp. Myrmidon. Cp. also the first clement in
Mormoops.

## Mormon
Mormon, n.f a member of the church founded
by Joseph Smith (1805-1844), April 6, 1830, in
Seneca County, New York. The name Mormon
was coined by Joseph Smith and explained by
him as more топ, 'more good'.

## Mormonism
Mormonism, п., the religious system of the
Mormons. — Formed fr. Mormon with suff. -ism.

## Mormoops
Mormoops, п., a genus of bats of tropical
America. — ModL., compounded of Gk. μορμώ,
'bugbear', and ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'face'. See
mormo and -ops.

## morn
morn, п., morning {poet.) — ME. morwen, morn,
morgen, fr. OE. morgen, 'morning, morrow',
rel. to OS., OHG. morgan, ON. morgunn, mor~
ginn, OFris. morgen, mergen, Swed. morgan,
Dan., Du., MHG., G. morgen, Goth, maurgins,
'morning', fr. l.-E. base *merq-, *mereq-, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:503 COLUMN:3 -->
blink, twinkle', whence also Lith. mirgeti, 'to
blink, twinkle', OSlav. mraku, Markness',
nmiknoti, 'to grow dark'. Cp. morning. Cp. also
morganatic, morgen, morrow, murk. I.-E. base
*merq-, mereq-, is an enlargement of base *mer-t
'to gleam, glimmer, sparkle'; see mere, 'pure'.

## morning
morning, n. — ME. morwening, morning, formed
fr. morwen, morn, with subst. suff. -ing (on
analogy of evening). See morn.

## Moro
Moro, п., a member of a group of Moslems in the
southern Philippine Islands. — Sp., 'Moor'.
See Moor and cp. Morisco.

## morocco
morocco, п., a kind of fine flexible leather. —
Named fr. Morocco, a city of NW. Africa,
where this kind of leather was originally made.

## moron
moron, п., a feeble-minded person. — Gk. μωρόν,
neut. of μωρός, 'foolish', prob. cogn. with OI.
mural}, 'idiotic'. L. morus, 'foolish', is a loan
word fr. Gk. μωρός. Ср. the second element in
oxymoron.
Derivatives: moron-су, п., moron-ic, adj.,
moron-ism, п., moron-ity, n.

## morose
morose, adj., gloomy, sullen. — L. morosus,
'capricious, peevish', lit. Of (bad) manners', fr.
mos, gen. mdris, 'custom, habit, manner'. See
moral and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: morose-ly, adv., morose-ness, n.

## morosity
morosity, n. — F. morosite, fr. L. morositatemy
ace. of morositas, 'capriciousness', fr. mdrdsus.
See prec, word and -ity.

## morosis
morosis, п., idiocy (now identical with moronity).
— MedL., fr. Gk. μώρωσις, 'dullness,
sluggishness*, fr. μωρός (see moron and -osis);
introduced into medicine by the Swedish botanist
Carolus Linnaeus (Karl von Linne) (1707-78).

## morph-
morph-, form of morpho- before a vowel.

## -morph
-morph, combining form used to form nouns
meaning 'characterized by a (certain) form', as
in isomorph; corresponding to adjectives ending
in -morphic or -morphous. See morpho-.

## morpheme
morpheme, п., that part of a word which contains
the affixes. — F. morpheme, coined fr. Gk.
μορφή, 'form, shape' (see morpho-), on analogy of
phoneme (see phoneme).

## Morpheus
Morpheus, п., the god of sleep and dreams in
Greek mythology. -— L., fr. Gk. Μορφεύς, 'the
god of sleep", lit, 'the maker of shapes', so
named because of his calling up different shapes
before the dreamer, fr. μορφή, 'form, shape';
see morpho-. Cp. Ovid, Metamorphoses, XI,
635.

## morphia
morphia, п., morphine. — ModL. See morphine.
Derivative: morphi-ate, tr. v.

## -morphic
-morphic, combining form used to form
adjectives meaning 'having a (specified) form', as in
anthropomorphic; corresponding to nouns
ending in -morphism or -morphy. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. μορφή, 'form, shape'. See
morpho-.

## morphine
morphine, п., a white crystalline alkaloid,
C17HieN03 (chem.) — F., formed with chem.
suff. -ine fr. Gk. Μορφεύς, name of the god of
sleep (see Morpheus); so called because of its
somniferous quality. Cp. morphia.

## morphinism
morphinism, п., the habitual use of morphia;
condition caused by this habit {med.) — See
prec. word and -ism.

## morphinomania
morphinomania, п., a morbid craving for
morphine (med.) — Compounded of morphine and
mania.
Derivative: morphinomani-ac, adj.

## Morpho
Morpho, п., an epithet of Aphrodite (Venus) —
Gk. Μορφώ, lit. 'the shapely', personification
of μορφώ, 'form, shape', which is related to
μορφή, 'form, shape'. See morpho-.

## Morpho
Morpho, п., a genus of tropical American
butterflies of the family Nymphalidae (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. Μορφώ. See prec. word.

## morpho-
morpho-, before a vowel morph-, combining form
meaning 'form, shape'. — Gk. μορφο-, μορφ-,
fr. μορφή, 'form, shape', of uncertain origin.
Cp. Morpheus, Morpho, paramorphism. Cp. also
form, n.

## morphology
morphology, n,, the study of the form and
structure of animals and plants. — G. Morphologic,
coined by Goethe (Zur Naturwissenschaft Uber-
haupt und besonders zur Morphologic, 1817) fr.
Gk. μορφή, 'form, shape1, and -λογία, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:504 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 477 | MOSS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:504 COLUMN:1 -->
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)*. See -logy.
Derivatives: morpholog-ic, morpholog-ic-al,
adjs., morpholog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## morpbosls
morpbosls, п., the mode of formation of an
organism (biol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μόροωσις,
'a forming, shaping', fr. μορφοϋν, 'to form', fr.
μορφή, 'form, shape'. Sec morpho- and -osls.

## -morphosis
-morphosis, combining form denoting change of
form, as in anamorphosis. — Fr. Gk. μόρφω-
σίς, 'a forming, shaping'. Sec prec. word.

## -morpbous
-morpbous, combining form equivalent in
meaning to -morphic, as in amorphous, dimorphous. —
Formed with suff. -011s fr. Gk. μορφή, 'form,
shape*. See morpho-,

## -morphy
-morphy, combining form used to form nouns
corresponding to adjectives ending in -morphic
or -morphouS) as in heteromorphy. — See
morpbo- and -y (representing Gk. -ία}.

## morris
morris, п., an old game played with stones, disks,
etc. — Fr. earlier merels, pi. See merel.

## morris
morris, morris dance. — Fr. earlier morys, the
same as Moorish.
Various—unsuccessful—attempts have been made to explain why this
Englishdance was called Moorish. Cp. next word.
morris pike» п., a kind of pike (hist.) — Prop.
' Moorish pike', fr. morris, a var. of Moorish. Cp.
morris dance.

## morro
morro, п., a round hill. — Sp. mono, 'round', rel.
to OF. mor (masc), more (fcm.), 'something
round, the head'; of unknown origin. Cp.
morion, *a hallike helmet'.

## morrow
morrow, n. — MF. morwe, a collateral form of
morwen, 'morning*. See morn. Cp. tomorrow.

## morse
morse, п., a large round brooch. — ME. mors, fr.
OF. mors, fr. L. morsus, 'a biting, a catching
hold, that which catches hold', fr. morsus, pp.
of mordere, *to biie'. See mordant.

## morse
morse, п., walrus — Lapp, morsha, 'walrus'.

## Morse
Morse, adj., pertaining to the system of recording
telegraph invented by Samuel Finley Breese
Morse (1791-1872).

## morsel
morsel, n. — ME., fr. OF. morcel (F. morceau\
dimin. of mors, 'bite', fr. L. morsus* of s.m., fr.
morsus* pp. of mordere, 'to bite*. See mordant
and dimin. surT. -<i and cp. morse, ^brooch'. Cp.
also morceau, which is a doublet of morsel.

## mort
mort, п., a note sounded on ihe hunting horn to
announce ihe death of the hunted beast. - - F.,
'death', fr. L. mortem, ace. of mors, 'death*; or
F. mort, 'dead', fr. VL. *mortus,
corresponding to L. mortuus, 'dead', pp. of morior, топ,
'to die'. See next word.

## mortal
mortal, adj.»— ME., fr. MF. mortal, mortel (F.
mortef), fr. L. mortaiis, 'mortal', fr. mors, gen.
mori/ί,'deaih', from the stem of morior, mori, *to
die'; which is cogn. with OI. mrtih, 'death',
mriyate, marati, mdrate, Avestic miryeite, 'dies',
Ol. martah, 'mortal, man', Avestic m6r*ti-,
Lith. mirtis, OSIav. sumrltl, of s.m.; Ol. mrtah,
Avestic mereta-t 'dead'. Arm. mard, 'man' (lit.
'mortal'), Gk. βροτός (for 'μβροτός j, 'mortal'
(for the original form cp. Gk. ίίμβροτος,
'immortal'), OSJav. mrurvu, 'dead', OSIav. miro,
mreti, *to die', umrutije, 'death', Lith. miritu,
miftiy 4o die', mdras, Lett, miris, 'pestilence',
Olr. marb, W., Co. marw, 'died' (pp.), OE.
morp, 'murder*. All these words derive fr. I.-E.
base *mer-* 'to die', which is orig. identical with
base *mer-, 'to consume, be consumed*. See
morbid, mordant and cp. mort, mortgage,
mortician, mortify, mortuary, amortize, immortal,
immortelle, ambrosia, amrlta, smorzando. Cp.
also murder, murrain.
Derivatives: mortal, п., mortal-ism, п., nwrtal-
ist, n.( mortdl-ize, tr. v., mortal-ly, adv.

## mortality
mortality, n. — ME. mortalitee, fr. MF. (= F.)
mortelite, fr. OF. mortalite, fr. L. mortalitutem,
ace. of mortalitus, fr. mortaiis. See mortal and
-ity.

## mortar
mortar, п., a vessel for pounding. — Partly fr.
ME. morter, fr. OE. mortert, partly fr. OF. ( —
F.) mortier. Both OE. mortere and OF. mortier
derive fr. L. mortarium, 'mortar' (i.e. 'vessel in
which material is pounded'), whence also MLG.
morter, OHG. morturi, morsuri, MHG. mor-
ssrre, G. Morser. L. mortarium derives fr. I.-E.
*mrtos, 'rubbed, pounded*, pp. form fr. I.E.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:504 COLUMN:2 -->
base *(s)mer-, 'to rub, pound, consume, wear
away, exhaust, worry". The same base appears
in L. moretum/a. salad', lit. 'a pounded mixture',
Gk. μαραίνειν, 'to waste, consume*, L. morbus
(for *mor-bkos), lit. 'that which consumes'. See
smart, v., and cp. morbid. Cp. also ihe two next
words.

## mortar
mortar, п., a kind of cannon. — MF. (=^ F.)
mortier, orig. 'a monarlike cannon', fr. L.
mortarium, 'vessel in which material is pounded';
whence also MDu. ( — Du.) mortier, G. Morser.
Dan. merser, Swed. morsart, 'a kind of cannon'.
See mortar, 'vessel for pounding'.

## mortar
mortar, п., cement. — ME. mortier, morter, fr.
OF. (= F.) mortier, 'moriar, cement*, fr. L.
mortarium, 'vessel in which materiahspounded;
pounded material', whence MHG. morter and
—with dissimilation of г - r to r - I—mortel, G.
Mortel, Du. mortel, 'mortar, cement*. See
mortar, 'vessel for pounding'.
Derivatives: mortar t ir. v., to bind together
wiih moriar, mortar-y, adj.

## mortgage
mortgage, n. — ME. morgage, fr. OF. morgage,
mongage, lit. 'dead pledge' (replaced in Modern
French by hypotheque). See mortal and gage,
'pledge*.
Derivatives: mortgage, ir. v., mortgage-able,
adj., mortgag-ee, п., mortgag-er, п., mortgag-or,
n.

## mortician
mortician, п., a funeral undertaker. - Coined on
analogy of physician fr. L. mors, gen. mortis.
See mortal.

## mortification
mortification, n. — MF. mortificacion, fr. MF.
(— F.) mortification, fr. Laie L. mortificationem,
ace. of mortificatio, 'a killing, putting to death',
fr. mortificatust pp. of mortificare. See next
word and -ion.

## mortify
mortify, tr. v., to subdue (ihe body) by abstinence
and discipline; intr. v., to practise mortification.
— Late ME. mortifien, fr. MF. (= F.)mortifier,
fr. Laie L. mortificare, *to kill, put to death", lit.
*io make dead*, compounded of L. mors, gen.
mortis, 'death*, and -ficdre, ΐτ./acere, 'to make,
do*. See mortal and -fy.
Derivatives: nwrtifi-ed, adj., mortifi-ed-ly, adv.,
mortifi-ed-ness, n.

## Mortimer
Mortimer, masc. PN. — Fr. Mortemer, name of
a place in Normandy.

## mortise
mortise, mortice, п., a cavity to receive a lenon.
— ME. mortays, fr. MF. (■-= F.) mortaise, fr.
OF. mortoise, prob. fr. Arab, murtazz (in vulgar
pronunciation mortazz), 'fixed in', pp. of the
Vlll form of razza, 'he fastend, fixed*.
mor ι main, п., inalienable ownership (law). —
Mb. morte mayne, fr. OF. mortemain [whence
OF. ( — F.) mainmorte], translation of ML.
mortua manus, lii. 'dead hand'. See monal and
manual.

## mortuary
mortuary, adj., I) pertaining ю death; 2)
pertaining ίο a burial. — Late L. mortuahus, 'of
the dead*, fr. L. mortuus, 'dead', fr. mors, gen.
mortis, 'deaih'. See mortal and adj. suff. -ary.

## mortuary
mortuary, п., I) formerly a gift claimed by a
parish minister from the estate of a deceased
parishioner; 2) a deadhouse, morgue. — ME.
mortuarie, fr. ML. moriudriumt prop. neut. of
ihe Laie L. adjeciive mortuurius, 'of the dead',
used as a noun. Sec prec. word.

## morula
morula, п., a mass of cells, resembling a mulberry
in shape, formed by an ovum in its early
development (embryol.) — ModL. morula, a
dimin. coined by the German biologist Ernst
Heinrich Haeckel (1834-1919) fr. L. morum,
'mulberry". See Morus and -ule.
Derivaiives: morul-ar, adj., morul-aiion, n.

## Morus
Morus, п., a genus of trees, the mulberry tree
{bot.) —■ L. morus, 'mulberry tree' (тбгит,
'mulberry'). See mulberry and cp. morula.

## Mosaic
Mosaic, adj., pertaining io Moses. - 1,. Mosai-
cus, fr. Moses, 'Moses'. See Moses and adj. sufT.
-k.
Derivative: Mosaic-ity, n.

## mosaic
mosaic, п., a form of decoration. — F. mosatque,
fr. It. mosaico, fr. ML. musaicum, formed, with
change of suff., fr. L. musivum, 'mosaic' (shon
for musivum opus, 'work of mosaic'), neut. of
musivus, a collateral form of museus, 'pertaining
to the Muses', fr. Musa, 'Muse'. Gk. μυυσεΐον

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:504 COLUMN:3 -->
in ihe sense of 'mosaic', is borrowed Гг. Latin.
See Muse and cp. museum. For the ending of
mosaic see suff. -lc.
Derivaiives: mosuii. adj. and tr. v., mosaic-al,
adj., mosaic-ist, n.

## mosandrite
mosandrite, п., a silicate of sodium, calcium and
the cerium meials (mineral.) — Swed. mosundrit,
named after the Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf
Mosander (1797-1858). For the ending, which
goes back io Gk. -ϊτης, see subst. suff. -ite.

## mosasaurus
mosasaurus, п., a large exiinct marine lizard. -
ModL., compounded of L. Mosa, 'the River
Meuse or Maas*, and Gk. σαθρός, 'lizard'. Sec
sauro-.

## moschatel
moschatel, п., a small plant having greenish
flowers with a musky smell. — F. moscatelle, fr.
li. moschatella, a dimin. formed fr. moscato,
'flavored with musk', fr. ML. muscatus, of s.m.,
fr. L. museus, 'musk'. See musk and cp. muscatel.

## moselte
moselte, n. — Wine from ihe valley of the River
Moselle.

## Moses
Moses, masc. PN.; specif, the grcai Hebrew
prophet, leader and lawgiver (Bible). — L.
Moses, Moyses, fr. Gk. Μουσής, Μωσής, fr.
Heb. Mosheh, which is of uncertain origin. Most
scholars see in it the Hebraization of Egyptian
mes,mesu, 'child, son', which is often used in
theophorous names. According io this
derivation the words of Pharaoh's daughter in Ex. 2.
10, 'for out of the water 1 drew him' are not the
explanation of the Hebrew name Mosheh, but
express the idea ihat the F.gyptian name given
by Pharaoh's daughter resembles in sound, and
therefore, reminds us of, the Hebrew verb
mashah, "he drew out', which is suggestive of the
words spoken by Pharaoh's daughter. — As a
Hebrew word, Moshe1' is ihe active pari, of
mashdh, 'he drew out", and accordingly means
'he who draws out", whence 'deliverer, savior'.

## mosesite
mosesite, п., a mercury ammonium compound
containing chlorine and sulfate (mineral.) —
Named after Alfred J. Moses (1859-1920),
Professor at Columbia University, New York. For
the ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## moshav
moshav, п., a cooperaiive small holders'
settlement in Israel. — ModHeb. moshabh, fr. Heb.
moshabh, 'sitting; seat, dwelling', fr. ydshabh,
'he sat down, was siiflng, remained, dwelled'.
See Yeshlbah and cp. next word.

## moshava
moshava, п., a settlement of independent farmers
in Israel. — ModHeb. moshabhah, a fem. noun
formed from the masc. noun moshabh. See prec.
word.

## Moslem
Moslem, п., a Mohammedan. — Arab, muslim,
la believer in Islam', lit. 'one who has submitted
himself to God", part, of aslama, 'he
surrendered, submitted', iV(= causative)formoi'salama,
'he was safe'. See salaam and cp. Islam.

## mosque
mosque, п., a Mohammedan place of worship. —
F. mosquee, fr. It. moschea, fr. earlier moscheta,
fr. Sp. mesquita (whence ModSp. mezquitu), fr.
Arab, masjid/piace of worship, mosque', which
is either borrowed fr. Nabatean masg dha,
'place of worship*, or formed independently,
with ma-, a pref. denoting place, fr. sajadu. 'he
was submissive, prostrated himself in prayer',
which is rel. to, or—more prob.—borrowed
from Aram. seghedh, of s.m. Cp. masjId, mes-
quite.

## mosquito
mosquito, п., gnat. — Sp., dimin. of mosca, 'fly',
fr. L. musca, 'fly', which derives from the l.-E.
imitative base*mw-, 'to buz/.'. See midge and cp.
words there referred to.

## moss
moss, n. — ME. mos, fr. OE. mos, 'marsh, moor',
rel. to OE. meos, 'moss', ON. mosi, Dan. mos,
'moss', Swed. mossa, 'moss*, masse, 'moor\
MDu. mosse, Du. mos, 'moss*, OHG., MHG.
mos, 'moss, swamp, moor', OHG. mios, MUG.
mies, 'moss*, G. Moos, 'moss', ON. myrr, 'bog,
swamp', fr. l.-E.*meu-s-, whence also L. museus,
'moss', Lith. musaly 'mold, mildew', OSIav.
muchu, 'moss' and perh. L. mustus, 'fresh, new'
(if fr. *mus-tos, 'wet, moist'), whence mustum
(short for mustum vlnum), 'new wine'. F. mousse,
'moss', is a Teut. loan word. I.-E. *meu-s- is an
-s-enlargement of base *meu-, 'moist; marsh;
moss'. Cp. mire, muscotd, muscology, mushroom,
must, 'new wine', mustard. For derivatives of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:505 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MOSSBUNKER | 478 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:505 COLUMN:1 -->
base *meu-d-, a -(/-enlargement of base *meu-,
see mother, 'dregs', and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: moss, tr. and intr. v., moss-ed, adj.,
moss-er, п., moss-y, adj., moss-i-ness, n.

## mossbunker
mossbunker, п., also mossbanker, the menhaden,
a large kind of herring.. — Corruption of Du.
marsbunker.

## most
most, adj. — ME. mest, mast, most, fr. OE. mxst,
mast (used as superl. of micel, 'large, great,
much'), formed fr. OE. ma, 'more', and superl.
suff. -est; rel. to OS. mest, ON. mestr, Du. meest,
OHG., MHG., G. meist, Goth, maists, 'most',
and to E. more (which has influenced the vowel
of ME., E. most). See mickle and superl. suff.
-est and cp. almost.
Derivatives: most, adv. and п., most-ly, adv.

## -most
-most, suff. forming superlatives of adjectives and
adverbs as in foremost, midmost. — ME. -most,
for ME. -mest, fr. OE. -mest, compounded of
two OE. superlative suffixes: suff. -ma (e.g. in
for-ma, 'first', medu-ma, 'midmost') and suff.
-est. Suff. -ma is cogn. with OI. -ma, Avestic -mo,
L. -mus. For the second superl. suff. see -est. The
vowel of ME. and E. -most (fr. OE. -mest) is due
to an erroneous association with most. See
aftermost.

## mot
mot, п., a witty saying. — F., 'word', fr. OF., fr.
Late L. muttum. See motto.

## Motacilla
Motacilla, п., a genus of oscine birds (ornithol.).
— L. motacilla, 'wagtail', formed with the dimin.
suff. -ilia fr. mature, 'to keep moving', freq. of
movere (pp. motus), 'to move'; so called because
they move their tail feathers continually. See
move and cp. motatorious. For sense
development cp, wagtail.

## Motacillidae
Motacillidae, n. pi., a family of oscine birds
(ornithol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr.
L. motacilla. See prec. word.

## motatorious
motatorious, adj., keeping in motion. — Formed
with suff. -orious fr. L. motare, 'to keep moving',
freq. of movere (pp. motus), 'to move'. See move
and cp. Motacilla.

## Motazilite
Motazilite, n. — See Mutazilitc.

## mote
mote, п., a small particle. — ME. mote, mot, fr.
OE. mot, 'atom, mote', rel. to Du. mot, 'dust,
sawdust', Swed. smutt, Norw. mutt, 'speck,
mote, splinter, chip, bit'; of uncertain origin.

## mote
mote, may, v., only used in the phrase so mote it
be, 'so may it be' (arch.) — OE. mot, 'may, can,
must'. See must, v.

## mote
mote, n. — A var. of moot.

## motel
motel, п., a hotel for automobile tourists. — A
blend of motor and hotel.

## motet
motet, п., a choral composition on a sacred text,
usually for unaccompanied voices (mus.) — F.,
dimin. of mot, 'word'. See motto and -et and cp.
It. mottetto.

## moth
moth, n. — ME. motthe, fr. OE. тодде, rel. to
ON. motti, MLG., MDu. motte, mutte, Du. mot.
Late MHG. motte, matte, G. Motte, 'moth', and
perh. also to OE. mada, 'maggot'. See maggot
and cp. mawkish.

## mother
mother, п., a female parent. — ME. moder, fr.
OE. modor, rel. to OS. mddar, ON. modir, Dan.,
Swed. moder, OFris. moder, 'mother', Du. moe-
der, OHG., MHG. muoter, G. Mutter, and
cogn. with OI. matar-, Toch. A macar, В macer.
Arm. mair (gen. maur), Gk. μήτηρ, Dor. μ£-
τηρ, 'mother', Alb. motre, 'sister', orig. 'the
elder sister', i.e. 'the sister replacing the mother',
L. mater, Olr. mathir, OSlav. mati, Lett, mate,
'mother', Lith. mote, OPruss. muti, 'wife'. All
these.words derive fr. I.-E. 'mater-, which is
traceable to child's lip word ma-. Cp. mater,
maternal, maternity, matrimony, matrix,
matron, matter, metropolis, Demeter, metronymic,
maieutic, cummer.
Derivatives: mother, to care for as a mother,
mother-hood, п., mother-less, mother-like, moth-
er-ly, adjs., mother-li-ness, n.

## mother
mother, п., dregs. — MDu. (— Du.) modder,
'filth, dregs' (whence also G. Moder, 'mold), rel.
to MLG. mudde, 'mud', muddig, 'muddy', Swed.
smuts, 'dirt', ME. bi-smoteren, bi-smudden, 'to
make dirty', and cogn. with OI. mudirdh, 'cloud',
mutram, 'urine', Avestic mutfra, 'filth', fr. I.-E.
*meu-d-, whence also Gk. μύδος, 'damp,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:505 COLUMN:2 -->
moisture', μύζω (for *μύδιω), Ί suck', OSlav.
myjo, myti, 'to wash', Lith. mdudvti, 'to bathe',
Lett, maut, 'to swim', Olr. muad, 'cloud', and
prob. also L. mundus (for *mu-ndo-s), 'clean'
(orig. 'washed'). I.-E. *meu-d- is a
-(/-enlargement of base *meu-, 'moist; marsh; moss'. Cp.
smut. Cp. also mud, mundify, Mydaus, Myzosto-
ma. For derivatives of I.-E. *meu-s-, an -s-
enlargement of base *meu-, see moss and cp.
words there referred to. E. mother, 'dregs', was
influenced in form by a folk-etymological
association with mother, 'female parent'.
Derivative: mother-y, adj.

## mother-of-pearl
mother-of-pearl, n. — Loan translation of ML.
mater perldrum, lit. 'mother of pearls'. Cp. It.
madreperla, F. тёге-perle, Du. parelmoer, G.
Pertmutter, Dan. perlemor.

## motif
motif, п., theme, predominant feature. — F. See
motive, n.

## motile
motile, adj., capable of movement (physiol.) —
Formed with suff. -ile fr. L. motus, pp. of
movere, 'to move'. See move and cp. motion.

## motility
motility, п., capacity of movement. — Formed fr.
prec. word with suff. -ity.

## motion
motion, n. — Late ME., fr. OF. (= F.) motion, fr.
L. motionem, ace. of motio, 'a moving, motion*,
fr. motus, pp. of movere, 'to move'. See move
and -ion and cp. commotion, emotion,
locomotion, promotion. Cp. also motive.
Derivatives: motion, tr. and intr. v., motion-able,
adj., motion-al, motion-less, adjs.

## motivate
motivate, tr. v. — Formed fr. motive, п., with
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: motivat-ion, n.

## motive
motive, n. — ME. motif, fr. MF. (= F.) motif, п.,
fr. motif, adj., fr. ML. motlvus, 'moving', fr. L.
motus, pp. of movere, 'to move'. See move and
-ire and cp. the second element in automotive,
leitmotive, locomotive.
Derivatives: motive, tr. v., motive-less, adj.

## motive
motive, adj. — ML. motlvus, 'moving'. See
motive, n.

## motivity
motivity, п., capacity of producing motion. —
Formed with suff. -ity fr. ML. motlvus, 'moving'.
See motive, adj. and n.

## motley
motley, adj., parti-colored. — ME. motteley,
motley, of Gaulish origin. The word was brought
over to England by the Normans.
Derivatives: motley, n. and tr. v.

## motmot
motmot, п., a tropical S. American bird. —
Imitative of its cry.

## moto-
moto-, combining form meaning 'motion' or
'motor'. — Fr. L. motus, pp. of movere, 'to
move'. See move.

## motograph
motograph, п., an instrument used in making a
loud-speaking telephone (electr.) — A hybrid
coined fr. L. motus, pp. of movere, 'to move',
and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν 'to write'. See
move and -graph.

## motometer
motometer, п., a device indicating the number of
revolutions made (mach.) — A hybrid coined
fr. L. motus, pp. of movere, 'to move', and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See move and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## motor
motor, n. — Lit. 'mover', fr. L. motor, fr. motus,
pp. of movere, 'to move'. See move and agential
suff. -or.
Derivatives: motor, adj. and intr. v., motor-ed,
adj., motor-ing, n.

## motorcade
motorcade, п., a procession of automobiles. — A
modern word formed fr. motor on analogy of
cavalcade (q.v.) See aho -cade and cp. the
synonym antocade.

## motorcycle
motorcycle, n. — A hybrid coined fr. motor and
cycle.
Derivatives: motorcycle, intr. v., motorcycl-ist,
n.

## motorist
motorist, n. — Formed fr. motor with suff. -ist.

## motorize
motorize, tr. v., to furnish with a motor or
motors. — Formed fr. motor with suff. -ize.
Derivative: motoriz-ation, n.

## mottle
mottle, tr. v., to mark with blotches. — Back
formation fr. mottled.

## mottle
mottle, п., a blotch. — Formed like mottle, v.

## mottled
mottled, adj. — Formed fr. motiey with 3rd suff.
-ed.

## motto
motto, п., a short saying, maxim. — It., 'a
saying', fr. Late L. muttum, 'grunt, muttering',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:505 COLUMN:3 -->
which is rel. to L. muttire, mutlre, mutire, 'to
grunt, mutter'. See mutter and cp. mot, motet,
moucharaby, п., a projecting latticed oriel
window (arch.) — F., fr. Arab. maskrabtyah, 'bay
window'.
mouchoir, п., a handkerchief. — F., fr. OF, mou-
cheur, fr. moucher, 'to wipe the nose', prop, 'to
remove the mucus of the nose', fr. VL. *muc-
care, fr. L. mucus, 'slime from the nose'. See
mucus.

## moue
moue, п., a pout. — F. See mow, 'grimace'.

## moufflon
moufflon, mouflon, п., a wild mountain sheep of
Sardinia and Corsica (Ovis musimon). — F.
mouflon, fr. It. mufflone, fr. Corsican muffolo, fr.
Late L. mufro, 'wild sheep', which is rel. to L.
musimo, musmo, of s.m. Cp. musimon.

## mouille
mouille, adj., softened, palatalized (said of a
consonant; as e.g. // in F.fille, Я in Sp. сайо.) — F.,
lit. 'wet, moistened', pp. of mouiller, 'to wet,
moisten', fr. VL. *molliare, 'to soften', fr. L.
mollis, 'soft'. See mollify.

## moujik
moujik, n. — A var. spelling of muzhik.

## moulage
moulage, п., molding. — F., fr. mouler, 'to mold,
cast', fr. moule, 'mold, pattern, form', fr. L.
modulus, 'a small measure'. See module and'-age.

## mould
mould, n. — See mold, 'pattern'.

## mould
mould, n. — See mold, 'crumbling earth'.

## mould
mould, n. — See mold, 'a fungoid growth'.

## mould
mould, v. — See mold, 'to grow moldy'.

## moulder
moulder, n. — See molder, n.

## moulder
moulder, v. — See molder, v.

## moulding
moulding, n. — See molding, n.

## mouldy
mouldy, adj. — See moldy.

## nioulin
nioulin, п., a nearly vertical shaft in a glacier
formed by surface water falling through a crack
in the ice (geol.) — F., lit. 'a mill', fr. Late L.
mollnum, 'mill', fr. L. mola, 'mill, millstone'.
See miil.

## mouit
mouit, v. and n. — See molt, v. and n.

## mound
mound, п., a heap of earth. — Prob. fr. MDu.
mond, 'protection', which is rel. to OE. mund,
'hand; protection, guardianship', ON. mund,
'hand', OHG., MHG. munt, 'hand; protection',
and cogn. with L. manus, 'hand'. See manual
and cp. the second element in Edmond,
Osmond, Raymond, Sigismund. E. mound was
influenced in form by mount, 'hill, mountain'.

## mound
mound, п., globe of a sovereign, orb. — F. monde,
'the world', fr. L. mundus. See mundane and cp.
monde.

## mount
mount, п., hill, mountain. — ME. том, mount,
partly fr. OE. munt (fr. L. montem), partly fr.
OF. (= F.) mont, 'hill, mountain', fr. L.
montem, ace. of mans, 'mount, mountain', which is
rel. to mentum, 'chin', monile, 'necklace', minae,
'projecting points or pinnacles' (of walls);
threats', i-minere, 'to stand out, project; to be
eminent', im-minere, 'to hang over, project over;
to threaten', pro-minere, 'to jut out, project', fr.
I.-E. base *men-, 'to stand out, project', whence
also W. mynydd, Co. meneth, ModBret. menez,
'mountain', ON. mrena, 'to tower above', manir,
'ridge of a roof, and possibly also Avestic
mart- (for *mnti-), 'promontory', fra-manyente,
'they get a head start'. Cp. mount, v., mountain.
Cp. also adminicle, amenable, amount, commma-
tion, demeanor, eminent, imminent, manada,
mane, marmot, menace, mental, 'pertaining to
the chin', minatory, moniliforin, moute, mont-de-
ρΐέτέ, muromontite, paramount, prominent,
promontory, rodomontade.

## mount
mount, intr. v., to go up, to climb; tr. v., to
ascend. — ME. monten, mounten, fr. OF. (=
F.) monter, 'to go up, ascend, climb, mount', lit.
to go up hill', fr. VL. 'montare, fr. L. mans, gen.
montis. See mount, 'hill', and cp. remount,
surmount, montage and the first element in
mountebank.
Derivatives: mount-ed, adj., mount-ing, n.

## mountain
mountain, n. — ME. montaine, fr. OF. montaigne
(F. montagne), fr. VL. 'montanea, 'mountain',
prop. fern, of montaneus, 'pertaining to, a
mountain, mountainous', which corresponds to L.
montanus, of s.m., fr. mons, gen. month. See
mount, 'hill'. Cp. montane and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: mountain-eer, п., mountain-eer-ing,
п., mountainous (q.v.), mountaln-y, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:506 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 479 | MUFFINEER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:506 COLUMN:1 -->

## mountainous
mountainous, adj. — F. montagneux (fem. mon-
tagneuse), fr. VL. *montaneosus, fr. L. montanus.
See mountain and -ous.
Derivatives: mountain-ous-ly, adv., mountain-
ous-ness, n.

## mountebank
mountebank, п., a quack, charlatan. — It. mon-
tambanco, contraction of monta-in-banco, lit.
'mount on bench*, with reference to the bench
from which quacks and buffoons used to address
the crowd gathered around them. It. monta is
the imper. of montare, 'to mount', fr. VL. *mon-
tare; see mount, v. For the etymology of It.
banco, 'bench*, see banco. For sense
development cp. saltlmbanco.

## mourn
mourn, intr. and tr. v. — ME. mournen, mornen,
fr. OE. murnan, 'to care for, be anxious about;
to lament over*, rel. to OS. mornian, OHG.
mornen, Goth, maurnan, 'to mourn*, ON. morna
'to pine away*, fr. I.-E. base *(s)mer-, 'to care
for, be anxious about, think, consider,
remember', whence—with reduplication of the base
—L. memor, 'mindful*, memoria, 'memory*. See
memory and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: moum-er, п., mourn-ful, adj.,
mourn-ful-ly, adv., mourn-ful-ness, п.,
mourning, n.

## mouse
mouse, n. — ME. mous, fr. OE. mus, rel. to OS.,
ΟΝ., OFris., MLG., MDu., Dan., Swed. mus,
Du. muis, 'mouse*, OHG., MHG. mus, G.
Maus, 'mouse; muscle*, and cogn. with OI.
mas-, 'mouse, rat', muskah, 'scrotum, testicle',
lit. 'a little mouse', OPers. mush, 'mouse', Arm.
mukn (gen. mkan), Gk. μΰς (gen. μυός),
'mouse; muscle', L. mus (gen. muris), Alb. mi,
Lith. muse, OPrus. muso, 'mouse', OSlav. mysi,
'mouse', mysica, 'arm*. Cp. dormouse, flitter-
mouse. Cp. also murex, Muridae, murine, Mus,
muscatel, muscle, muscular, musk, musteline,
marmot. Cp. also Mya, myelo-, myo-, amyous,
perimysium.
Derivatives: mouse, intr. and tr. v., mous-er, п.,
mouse-let, п., mouse-ling, n.,mous-ing, n. and adj.

## mousqnetoire
mousqnetoire, п., musketeer. — See musketeer.

## mousse
mousse, п., a dish made from whipped cream,
white of egg, etc. — F., 'foam', fr. Late L. mulsa,
'hydromeF. See mulse.

## mousseline
mousseline, п., muslin. — See muslin.

## moustache
moustache, n. — A var. spelling of mustache.

## Mousterian
Mousterian, adj., designating, or pertaining to,
the late paleolithic culture (geol.) — So called
from Le Moustier in southern France, where
remains of this type were found.

## mouth
mouth, n. — ME. mouth, mouthe, fr. OE. mud,
rel. to OS., OFris. muth, ON. munnr, mudr, Dan.
mund, Swed. тип, MDu. mont, mond, Du. mond,
OHG. mund, MHG. munt, G. Mund, Goth.
munps, 'mouth', OE. mlbl, ON. mil, OHG.
mindil, 'horse's bit', ON. minnask, 'to kiss'; fr.
I.-E. base *menth~, 'to chew', whence prob. also
Gk. μάθυιαι (Hesychius), 'jaw', μασάομαί, (for
*μαθιάομαι), Ί chew, bite', μαστάζω, Ί chew*,
μάσταξ, 'mouth, jaws' (lit. 'that with which one
chews'), L. mandere, 'to chew', Ir. meadal,
'orifice of the stomach'. Cp. malar, mandible,
manducate, mange, manger, masseter, mastic,
masticate, maxilla, mustache.
Derivatives: mouth, tr. and intr. v., mouth-ed,
adj., mouth-er, п., mouth-ful, adj., mouth-y, adj.,
mouth-i-ly, adv., mouth-i-ness, n.

## moutonnee
moutonnee, adj., 'shaped like the back of a sheep',
said of a rock {geology). — F., (in roche
moutonnee), fem. pp. of moutonner, 'to make similar
to a sheep; to make woolly or fleecy', fr. mou-
ton, 'sheep'. See mutton.

## movable
movable, adj. — ME., fr. OF-, fr. moveir, movoir,
'to move*. See move and -able.
Derivatives: movabil-ity, п., movable, п., mov-
ab/e-ness, п., movabl-y, adv.

## move
move, tr. and intr. v. — ME. moven, fr. AF.
mover, corresponding to OF. moveir, movoir (F.
mouvoir), fr. L. movere (pp. motus), 'to move,
set in motion', which is prob. cogn. OI. mivati,
'pushes, moves*, kdma-mutah, 'moved by love',
Toch. AB mus-, 'to move', Gk. άμεύσασθαι,
Чо surpass, outstrip*, άμυνειν, Чо keep off,
ward off, defend', Lith. mauju, mauti, 'to strip
off'. Cp. commove, remove. Cp. also emeute,
mob, 'rabble', mobile, moment, Motacillldae,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:506 COLUMN:2 -->
motatorious, motion, motive, motor, mutiny,
promote, remote.
Derivatives: move, п., mov-er, п., mov-ing, adj.,
mov-ing-ly, adv.

## movement
movement, n. — Late ME., fr. OF. movement (F.
mouvement), fr. ML. movimentum, fr. L. movere.
See move and -ment and cp. moment.

## movies
movies, n. pi., moving pictures (colloq.) —
Contraction of moving pictures.

## mow
mow, tr. v., to cut (grass) — ME. mowen, fr. OE.
mawan, rel. to MLG. maeyen (whence Ou.maai-
en), OHG. maen, MHG. mxjen, G. muhen, 'to
mow', OE. mxd, 'meadow', OHG. mad, *a
mowing, math', fr. I.-E. base *тё-, *тё-, Чо
mow', whence also Gk. ά-μαν, 'to mow', #-
μητος, 'crop gathered in', and prob. also L.
metere, Чо reap*, Mir. meithel, OW. medel, *a
group of reapers', ModBret. medi, 'to reap*. Cp.
math, meadow. Cp. also Messidor.
Derivative: tnow-er, n.

## mow
mow, п., a stack of hay. — ME. mowe, mow, fr.
OE. muga, muha, 'a heap, pile', rel. to ON.
mugi, mugr, of s.m., ON. mostr (for *mukstr)t
'crowd', Swed. moa, 'to crowd together', and
prob. cogn. with Gk. μύκων (Hesychius), 'heap'.
Derivative: mow, tr. v., to stack in, or as in, a
mow.

## mow
mow, п., a grimace. — ME. mouwe, mowe, fr. OF.
moe, moue (F. moue) 'pout, grimace', fr. Frankish
*mauwa, restored after the Dutch phrase mouwe
такеп, Чо pout, make a wry face'; prob. of
imitative origin.
Derivative: mow, intr. v., to make grimaces.

## moxa
moxa, п., a soft material prepared from the
leaves of a wormwood (Artemisia moxa) and
used as a counterirritant. — Jap. mogusa.

## moyen age
moyen age, the Middle Ages. — F., lit. 'middle
age'. The first word derives fr. L. medianus, 'that
which is in the middle'; see median. For the
second wopd see age.

## Mozarab
Mozarab, п., a Christian of Spain who assimilated
himself to the Moors' and adopted Arabic
speech. — Sp. mozarabe, fr. Arab. mustalrib,
'would be Arab', act. part, of the X conjugation
of iorubd' 'was Arabic (of speech)', fr. 'Arab
(coll.), 'Arabs'. See Arab.
Derivative: Mozarab-ic, adj.

## mozzetta
mozzetta, mozetta, п., a short cape with a small
hood worn by the Pope and other high
dignitaries of the Roman Catholic Church. — It.
mozzetta, prob. fr. ML. almucia. See amice,
'hood, headdress', and cp. almuce, mutch.

## much
much, adj. — ME. miche, muche, fr. earlier
michel, muchel, 'large much', fr. OE. micel, my-
cel. See mickle and cp. magnum.
Derivatives: much, n. and adv., much-ness, n.

## mucic
mucic, adj. designating, or pertaining to, a dibasic
acid (CHOH)4—(COEH)a (chem.) — F. muci-
que, fr. L. mucus. See mucus and adj. suff. -ic.

## mucid
mucid,adj., moldy, musty. — L. mucidus, 'moldy,
musty', fr. mucus. See mucus and -id
(representing L. -idus).

## mucilage
mucilage, п., a gelatinous substance found in
plants (bot.) — F., fr. Late L. mucilugo, 'a moldy,
musty juice', fr. L. mucus. See mucus.

## mucilaginous
mucilaginous, adj., viscous, sticky. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. Late L. mucilugo, gen. -aginis.
See prec. word.

## mucin
mucin, п., substance secreted by the mucous
membranes (biochem.) — F. mucine, coined by
Mozin in 1842 fr. L. mucus. See mucus and chem.
suff. -ine, -in.

## muck
muck, п., dung, manure. — ME. тис, тик, of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. mykr, myki. Dan. meg,
'dung, manure', which are prob. cogn. with L.
mucus. See mucus and cp. meek. Cp. also
midden.
Derivatives: muck, tr. v., muck-y, adj.

## mucker
mucker, п., a heavy fall (U.S. Slang) — Formed
from prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## muckle
muckle, adj. — A var. of mickle.

## muckna
muckna, п., a male elephant without tusks or
with only rudimentary tusks. — Hind, makhna,
fr. OI. matkunah, 'a bug, a flea; a beardless man;
an elephant without tusks'.

## muco-
muco-, combining form meaning 'mucous'. — L.
тйсо-, fr. mucus. See mucus.

## mucoid
mucoid, adj., resembling mucus. — A hybrid

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:506 COLUMN:3 -->
coined fr. L. mucus and Gk.-οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See mucus and -oid.

## mucoid
mucoid, п., any of a group of substances
resembling mucin Xbiochem.) — Coined fr. mucin and
-oid. See prec. word.

## Mucor
Mucor,n.( a genus of molds (bot.) — ModL., fr. L.
mucor, 'mold, moldiness*, rel. to тйсёге, Чо be
moldy or musty*, mucus, 'mucus of the nose'.
See mucus,

## mucosity
mucosity, n. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. L.
muedsus, 'slimy, mucous', fr. mucus. See prec.
word.

## mucoso-
mucoso-, combining form meaning 'mucous'. —
L. mucoso-, fr. mucosus. See next word,

## mucous
mucous, adj. — L. mucosus, 'tlimy, mucous', fr.
mucus. See mucus and -ous.

## mucro
mucro, п., a sharp point or tip (bot. and zool.) —
L. mucro, 'point of a sword', standing for *mu·
kros, 'pointed', and possibly cogn. with Gk. άμυ-
καλαί (Hesychius) 'arrowheads', άμύσσω,
Att. άμύττω (for *άμύκιω), Ί scratch, tear',
and with Lith. muSit, mitsti, 'to strike'.
Derivatives: mucron-ate(d), adj.; mucron-ate-ly,
adv., mucron-ation, n.

## mucus
mucus, п., a viscid secretion of the mucous
membranes. — L. mucus, 'mucus of the nose', rel. to
mucor, 'mold, moldiness*, mungere, imungere,
Чо blow the nose', fr. I.-E. base *(s)meuq-,
*(s)meug-, 'to slip; slippery, slime', whence also
OI. muncati, mucati, 'he releases', Gk. μύξα,
'mucus of the nose, slime', μύξος, 'mullet',
μύκης, gen. μύκητος, 'fungus', μυκτήρ, 'nose'
(lit. 4he mucous organ'), OSlav. smycati, 'to
draw or drag along', Lith. smunku, smukti, 'to
slip', ON. mykr, myki, 'dung, manure', mygla,
'mold', W. mign, 'mold, dirt', Ir. mocht, 'soft,
mild', W. tnwytho, 'to soften'. Cp. emunctory,
moist, mucid, mucilage, Mucor, Mugiladae,
myco-, mycosis, Mycteria, mycteric. Cp. also
match, 'wick of a lamp', mouchoir. Cp. also
meek, muck, muggy,

## mud
mud, п., wet earth. — ME. mode, mudde, of LG.
origin. Cp, OLG., MLG. mudde, 'mud', muddig,
'muddy', which derive fr. I.-E. base *meu-, 'wet,
moist', whence also MDu., Du. modder, 'filth,
dregs*. See mother, 'dregs', and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: mud, v., mudd-y, adj., mudd-i-ly,
adv., mudd-i-ness, n.

## mudar
mudar, п., the name of two East Indian trees,
Ca/otropis gigantea and Calotropis procera. —
Hind, madar.

## muddle
muddle, tr. and intr. v., to confuse. — Formed fr.
mud with suff. -le. (The original meaning was Чо
dabble in mud'.)
Derivatives: muddle, п., muddl-er, n.

## mudir
mudir, п., the governor of a province in Egypt or
Sudan. — Arab, mudir, 'governor', prop, active
part, of adara, 'he administered, governed', IV
(= causative) conjugation afdara, 'he moved in
a circle'. See dai'ra.

## mudiria
mudiria, п., a province in Egypt or Sudan. —
Arab. mudiriyah, fr. mudir, 'governor'. See prec.
word.

## Muehlenbeckla
Muehlenbeckla, п., a genus of plants of the
buckwheat family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
Alsatian physician H. G. Muehlenbeck (1798-
1845). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## muezzin
muezzin, п., in Mohammedan countries, an

## official who
official who, from the minaret of the mosque, calls
the people to prayer. — Arab. mu,adhdhin,prop.

## active part
active part, of adhdhana, II (= frequentative or

## intensive) conjugation of adhana
intensive) conjugation of adhana, 'he

## proclaimed'
proclaimed', fr. udhn, 'ear', which is rel. to Ethiop. ezn,

## Heb. ozen
Heb. ozen, Aram, udhna, Syr. edhna, Akkad.

## uznu
uznu, 'ear', Heb. he'ezin, 'he gave ear, heard,

## listened
listened, hearkened',

## muff
muff, п., a warm covering for the hands. — Du.

## mo/
mo/, shortened fr. moffel, fr. MDu. moffel, muf-

## fel
fel, 'mitten, muff', fr. MF. moufle. See muffie,
adj. and n.

## muff
muff, п., a clumsy person. — Of uncertain origin.

## muffetee
muffetee, п., a muffler. — Fr. muff, *a warm
covering'.

## muffin
muffin, п., alight cake made with eggs. — Cp. OF.

## pain mouffiet
pain mouffiet, 'soft bread*.

## muffineer
muffineer, п., a dish for keeping muffins hot. —
Formed fr. muffin with suff. -eer.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:507 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MUFFLE | 480 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:507 COLUMN:1 -->

## muffle
muffle, tr. v., to wrap up. — ME. muflen, fr. OF.
enmoufler, fr. moufte. See muffle, n.

## muffle
muffle, п., a mitten (obsol.); 2) a muff; a muffler.
— MF. ( = F.) moufle, 'mitten, muffle', fr. OF.,
fr. ML. mujfula, 'furred glove', which is of
uncertain origin.

## muffler
muffler, п., a wrap for the throat. — Formed fr.
prec. word with agential surf. -er.

## mufti
mufti, п., 1) an expounder of Mohammedan law;
2) civilian clothes esp. when worn by a naval or
military officer. — Arab, mufti, active part, of
afta, 'he expounded the law', IV (= causative)
conjugation of fata, 'he decided, declared'. See
futwa.

## mug
mug, п., a drinking cup. — Earlier mugg, rel. to
Sweti. mug, Norw. mugge, LG. mokke, mukke,
Du. ток, G. Muck, Mock; of uncertain origin.
Derivative: mug-ful, adj.

## mug
mug, п., face (slang). — Perhaps from prec. word.
Derivatives: mug, tr. v., to photograph, esp. to
photograph a criminal; intr. v., to make faces,
mugg-er, n.

## mug
mug, п., a fool, dupe (English Slang) — Of
uncertain origin.

## mugger
mugger, muggur, п., the common crocodile of
India (Crocodilus palustris). — Hind, magar, fr.
OI. makarah, 'sea monster, crocodile', which is
rel. to OI. nakral), 'crocodile', nakrah, 'a kind of
aquatic animal'; prob. of Dravidian origin.
■nugget, п., 1) the lily of the valley; 2) the
woodruff. — F. muguet, 'lily of the valley; woodruff',
fr. (noix) muguette, alteration of (noix) muscade,
'nutmeg' (cp. the transitory forms muguade,
mugate), fr. muse, 'musk'. See musk and cp.
muscardinc, mnscat.

## mnggins
mnggins, п., a simpleton. — From,the surname
Muggins. Cp. juggins.

## Muggletonian
Muggletonian, п., a member of a sect founded by
the English tailor LodowickeM«g^/eIon (1609-
98). For the ending see suff. -ian.

## muggy
muggy, adj., damp. — From dial, mug, 'a drizzle',
which is of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. mugga,
'drizzling mist', and Norw. mugg, 'mist, mold',
which are rel. to ON. mygla, 'mold', and cogn.
with L. mucus, 'slime from the nose'. See mucus
and cp. next word.
Derivative: muggi-ness, n.

## Mugilidae
Mugilidae, n. pi., a family of fishes, the gray
mullet (ichthyol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-Idae fr. L. mugil, 'the mullet', which is cogn.
with Gk. μύξος, 'mullet', μύξα, 'mucus of the
nose, slime', L. mucus, 'mucus of the nose'. See
mucus and cp. prec. word.

## mugwort
mugwort,n., the plant Artemisia vulgaris. — ME.,
fr. OE. mucgwyrt, lit. 'midge wort'. See midge
and wort,

## mugwump
mugwump, п., an independent man in politics. —
Algonquian mugquomp, 'great chief.

## Mnharram
Mnharram, also Moharram, п., the first month of
the Mohammedan year. — Arab, muharram, lit.
'sacred, forbidden', pass. part, of harrama, 'he
forbade', II (= intensive) conjugation of ha-
rama, 'he forbade', haruma, 'was forbidden'. See
harem, berem.

## Muhlenbergia
Muhlenbergia, п., a large genus of grasses (hot.)
— ModL., named after the American botanist
Gotthilf Henry Ernest Muhlenberg (1753-1815).
For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## muktar
muktar, п., an agent or attorney (India). — Hind.
mukhtar, fr. Arab, mukhtar, lit. 'chosen', pass,
part, of ikhlira, 'he chose', the VIII conjugation
aikhara, 'he chose', whence khayr, 'good, well-
being'. Cp. mohair,

## mulatto
mulatto, п., the offspring of a negro and a white
man. — Sp. and Port, mulato, 'of mixed breed',
fr. Arab, muwallad, 'one born of an Arab father
and a foreign mother', prop. pass. part, of the
II conjugation of walada, 'he begot', waladat,
'she bore (a child'), rel. to Ethiop. walada, Heb.
ydlddh, Ugar. yld, Aram. yel!dh,y ledh, Syr. iledh,
'he begot' (fern, 'she bore'), Akkad. waladu,
later form aladu, 'to beget, to bear (a child)'. The
word was influenced in form by a
folk-etymological association with Sp. mulo, 'mule', fr. L.
mulus.
mulberry» n. — ME. mulberie, dissimilated fr.
earlier ME. murberie, fr. OE. morberie, a hybrid
coined fr. L. morum, 'blackberry, mulberry', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:507 COLUMN:2 -->
OE. berie, 'berry' [cp. MDu. moerbeye, moerbesie
(Du. moerbezie, moerbei), OHG. murberi, MHG
mffrber and the dissimilated forms: MHG. mul-
ber, G. Maulbeere, which are also compounded
of L. тбгит and the respective equivalent of
OE. berie (see berry)]. L. morum is borrowed fr.
Gk. μόρον, μώρον, 'mulberry, blackberry',
which is prob. cogn. with Arm. mor, mori,
'blackberry', Mir. merenn, W. merwydden,
'mulberry'. It. mora, Rum. mura, OF. moure (F.
mure), OProven?., Cat-, Sp. and Port, mora,
'mulberry', derive fr. L. mora, pi. of morum,
'mulberry' (the neut. pi. ending a having been
mistaken for a fem. sing.) Cp. also Morus,
murrey, and the second element in sycamore.

## mulch
mulch, п., moist straw, leaves, etc., spread around
plants to prevent the evaporation of the
moisture. — ME. molsh, 'soft', rel. to OE. melsc,
'mellow', Du. mats, dial. G. molsch, mulsch,
'soft, ripe', OHG. molawen, 'to become soft',
MHG. molwic, G. mollig, 'soft', fr. I.-E. base
*mel-, 'to rub, grind'. See meal, 'edible grain',
and words there referred to, and cp. esp. moil,
mellow, mollify.
Derivatives: mulch, tr. v., mulch-er, n.

## Mulciber
Mulciber, п., a surname of Vulcan (Roman my-
thol.) — L. Mulciber, for *Mulce-dhros, lit. 'the
appeaser', fr. mulcere, 'to stroke, soften,
appease'. See demulcent and cp. words there
referred to.

## mulct
mulct, п., fine. — L. mulcta, more correctly multa,
'penalty, fine', which is either an Oscan or a
Samnite word.

## mulct
mulct, tr. v., to fine. — L. mulctare, more
correctly multdre, 'to punish, fine', fr. mulcta, multa.
See mulct, n.
Derivatives: mulct-able, adj., mukt-ary, adj.,
mulct-ation, п., mulct-ative, adj., mulctu-ary,
adj.

## mule
mule, п., a hybrid between the horse and the ass.
ME., fr. OF. mul, fr. L. mula, fem. of mulus,
'mule' (whence OF. mul, replaced in F. by its
diminutive mulet). L. mulus stands for *mugh-
slos (cp. the diminutive muscellus, fr. *muxellus)
and is cogn. with Gk. μυχλος (for "rnukslos),
'he-ass', Alb. musk, 'mule'. Cp. muleta.
Derivatives: mul-ish, adj., mul-ish-ly, adv., mul-
ish-ness, n.

## mule
mule, п., a kind of slipper. — MF. (= F.), fr. L.
mulleus, 'a reddish shoe', which is rel. to mullus,
'the red mullet'. See mullet, 'seafish'.

## muleta
muleta, п., a rod with a red flag used in bullfights.
— Sp., lit. 'a young she-mule', dimin. of mula,
'she-mule'. See 1st mule.

## muleteer
muleteer, п., a mule driver. — MF. (= F.) mule-
tier, fr. mulet, 'mule', dimin. of OF. mul, 'mule',
fr. L. mulus. See mule and -eer.

## muley
muley, adj. and n. — See mulley.

## muliebrity
muliebrity, п., womanliness, effeminacy. — L.
muliebritas, 'womanliness', fr. muliebris,
