'womanly, female', fr. mulier, 'woman, wife', fr.
earlier 'mulies; of uncertain origin. For the change
of s to b cp. funebris, 'pertaining to a funeral',
which stands for *funesris, fr. funus, 'funeral,
burial'. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## mull
mull, tr. v., 1) to powder (dial. English); to muddle
(dial. English). — ME. mullen, 'to grind', fr. ME.
mul, mol, 'dust', fr. OE. myl, 'dust', which is rel.
to Swed. mull, MLG., MDu., Du. mul, 'loose
earth', G. Mull, 'garbage'; fr. l.-E. base *mel-,
'to rub, grind'. See meal, 'edible grain', and
words there referred to and cp. esp. mulier, n.

## mull
mull, п., 1) dust, rubbish (dial. English); 2) mess,
muddle(colloq.English).— ME. mul, mol, 'dust'.
See prec. word and cp. mullock.

## mull
mull, п., a thin soft muslin. — Shortened fr.
mubnul (q.v.)

## mull
mull, п., a promontory; used in Scottish place
names. — Cp. ON. muli, 'a snout, muzzle; a
jutting crag', which is rel. to OFris. mula, MDu.
mule, muul, Du. muil, OHG. mula, MHG. mule,
miil, G. Maul, 'muzzle, mouth', Goth, faur-mul-
jan, 'to muzzle', and cogn. with Gk. μύλλον,
μύλλος, 'lip; lip of the vulva', μύλλειν, 'to close
the lips', μυλλαίνειν, 'to make grimaces'. All
these words are prob. formed from the I.-E.
imitative base *mu-.

## mull
mull, п., a snuff box. — Scot, form of mill for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:507 COLUMN:3 -->
grinding.

## mull
mull, tr. v., to heat wine or beer. — Of uncertain
origin.

## mullah
mullah, п., a Mohammedan teacher; an
expounder of the Koran.—-Pers. and Hind, mulla
(Turk, molla), fr. Arab, maula, 'master, sir,
judge, magistrate', fr. wdliya, 'he reigned,
governed'. Cp. vilayet and words there referred to.

## mullein
mullein, also mullen, п., a tall plant of the figwort
family. — ME. moleyn, fr. AF. moleine
(corresponding to F. molene), lit. 'the soft-leaved
plant', fr. OF. (= F.) mol, 'soft', fr. L. mollis.
See mollify and cp. words there referred to.

## mulier
mulier, п., a stone for grinding. — ME. mullen, 'to
powder, grind', fr. ME. mul, mol, 'dust'. See
mull, 'to powder'.

## mullet
mullet, п., two kinds of edible seafish: the red
mullet and the gray mullet. — ME. motet, fr.
MF. mulet, dimin. formed fr. Late L. mulus,
corresponding to L. mullus, 'the red mullet', fr.
Gk. μύλλος, 'name of a fish', which is rel.
to Gk. μέλας, 'black', and cogn. with L.
mulleus, 'reddish', OI. malinah, 'dirty, stained,
black', mlanalf, 'black'. See melano- andep. also
surmullet. Cp. also mule, 'a kind of slipper'.

## mullet
mullet, also molet, п., a star, usually five-pointed
(her.) — ME. molet, fr. MF. molette, 'mullet,
rowel' (F. molette, 'rowel'), dimin. formed fr. L.
mola, 'millstone, mill'. See mill for grinding and
cp. mull, 'a snuff box'.

## mulley
mulley, adj., hornless; n. 1) a hornless cow; 2)
any cow (dial. British). — Scot, motley, prob. of
Celtic origin and lit. meaning 'bald'. Cp. Ir.
maol, 'bald'.

## mulligatawny
mulligatawny, п., an East Indian soup flavored
with curry powder. — Tamil milagu-tannir,
compounded of milagu, 'pepper', and tannlr, 'cool
water', fr. tan, 'cool', and nir, 'water'.

## mulligrubs
mulligrubs, п., 1) colic; 2) low spirits (colloq.) —
Invented word.
■million, п., a vertical column between the lights
of a window. — Prob. dissimilated fr. earlier
munnion, fr. OF. monial, 'mullion'. See moulal
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: mullion-ed, adj.

## mullock
mullock, п., dirt, refuse. — Formed with suff.
-ock fr. muli, 'dust, rubbish'.

## mulmul
mulmul, п., muslin. — Pers. malmal, fr. Hind.
malmal. Cp. mull, 'muslin'.

## mulse
mulse, п., wine mixed with honey. — L. mulsum
(scil. vinum), neut. oimulsus, 'mixed with honey',
which stands for *mel-sos and is cogn. with L.
mel, gen. mellis, 'honey.' See mel.

## mult-
mult-, form of multi- before a vowel.

## multeity
multeity, п., the quality of being many. —
Formed with suff. -ity fr. L. multus, 'much, many'.
See multi-.

## multi-
multi-, combining form meaning 'much, many'.
— L. multi-, fr. multus, 'much, many', which
stands for *mltos, fr. I.-E. base 'me/·, 'strong,
great, numerous', whence also L. melior,
'better' (orig. prob. 'stronger'), Gk. μάλα, 'very,
very much, exceedingly', μάλλον, 'more, rather',
μάλιστα, 'most, mostly'. See meliorate and cp.
mulct.

## multicycle
multicycle, п., a cycle with manny wheels. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. multus, 'much, many', and
Gk. κύκλος, 'ring, circle'. See multi- and cycle.

## multifarious
multifarious, adj., manifold, various. — L. multi-

## farius
farius, 'manifold, various' (fr. multifariam, 'in
many places'), prob. orig. meaning 'that which
can be expressed in many ways'; compounded
of multus, 'much, many', and fas, in the sense of
'utterance, expression, manifestation', which is
rel. to furl, 'to speak'. See multi- and -furious and
• cp. bifarious.
Derivatives: multifarious-ly, adv.,
multifariousness, n.

## multifid
multifid, adj., cleft into many parts. — L. mulii-

## fidus
fidus, 'cleft into many parts', compounded of
multus, 'much, many' and fid-, past stem of fin-
dere, 'to split, cleave'. See multi- and fissile and
cp. bifid, triiid, quadrifid.
Derivative: multifid-ly, adv.

## multiform
multiform, adj., having many forms. — L.

## multiformis
multiformis, compounded of multus, 'much, many',
and forma, 'form, shape'. See multi- and form,
n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:508 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 481 | MUNTZ -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:508 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: multiform-ed, adj., multiform-ity,
n.

## Multigraph
Multigraph, п., trademark for a printing machine
used for reproducing typewritten letters. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. multus, 'much, many', and
Gk. -γφαρος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See rnulti-
and -graph.
Derivatives: multigraph, tr. v., multigraph-er, n.

## multilateral
multilateral, adj., many-sided. — Compounded
of multi- and L. latus, gen. laterls, 'side'. See
lateral.
Derivative: multilateral-ly, adv.

## multinomial
multinomial, adj., consisting of many terms,
polynomial (alg.) — Formed fr. L. multus, 'much,
many' (see multi-), on analogy of binomial (q.v.)

## multipara
multipara, п., a woman who has borne two or
more children. — ModL. See next word.

## multiparous
multiparous, adj., bearing more than one
offspring at a birth (zool.) — ModL. multiparus,
compounded of multus, 'much, many', and L.
parere, 'to bring forth, produce'. See multi-and
parent and cp. -parous,

## multipartite
multipartite, adj., divided into many parts. — L.
multipartita, 'divided into many parts', lit.
'much divided', compounded of multus, 'much,
many', and partitus, 'divided', pp. oipartirl, 'to
divide'. See multi- and partite,

## multiped
multiped, multipede, adj., having many feet. — L.
multipes, gen. multipedis, 'many-footed',
compounded of multus, 'much many', and pes, gen.
pedis, 'foot'. See multi- and pedal.
Derivative: multiped, multipede, п., a multiped
animal.

## multiple
multiple, adj., manifold, having many parts. —
F., fr. L. multiplex. See multiplex and cp.
equimultiple.
Derivative: multiple, n.

## multiplex
multiplex, adj., manifold. — L. multiplex, gen.
multipliers, 'that which has many folds,
manifold, numerous', compounded of multus, 'much,
many', and the base of plica, plrcare, 'to fold,
twist'. See multi- and plicate and cp. malti-
pUcity.

## multiplicable
multiplicable, adj., multipliable. — L. multiplica-
bilis, fr. multiplicare. See multiply and -able.
Derivative: multiplicabil-ity, n.

## multiplicand
multiplicand, п., the number that is to be
multiplied by another. — L. multiplicands, 'to be
multiplied', gerundive of multiplicare. See
multiply. For other Latin gerundives or their
derivatives used in English cp. agenda and words
there referred to.

## multiplicate
multiplicate, adj., multiple. — L., multiplicutus,
pp. of multiplicare. See multiply and adj. suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: multiplicate, п., multiplicat-ive, adj.,
multiplicat-ive-ly, adv.

## multiplication
multiplication, n. — ME. multiplicacioun, fr. OF.
(= F.) multiplication, fr. L. multrplicatidnem,
ace. of multiplicatio, pp. of multiplicare. See
multiply and -ion.

## multiplicity
multiplicity, п., the quality of being manifold. —
Late L. multiplicrtas, 'manifoldness, multiplicity',
fr. multiplex, gen. multipliers. See multiplex and
-ity.

## multiply
multiply, tr. and intr. v. — ME. multiplien, fr. OF.
(= F.) multiplier, fr. L. multiplicare, 'to
multiply*, fr. multiplex, gen. multipliers. See multiplex.
Derivatives: multipli-able, adj., multipli-er, п.,
multiply-ing, adj.

## multitude
multitude, п., a great number; numerousness; a
throng. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.); fr. L. multita-

## dinem
dinem, ace. of multitude, *a great number,

## multitude'
multitude', which is formed fr. multus, 'much, many',
with suff. -u'idd. See multiply and -rude.
Derivatives: multitudin-al, multitudin-ary, adjs.,

## multitudin-ism
multitudin-ism, п., multitudin-ist, п., multitudin-

## ist-ic
ist-ic, adj., multitudinous (q.v.)

## multitudinous
multitudinous, adj., consisting of a multitude. —

## Coined by Shakespeare fr. L. multitude
Coined by Shakespeare fr. L. multitude, gen.
-udinis. See multitude and -ous.
Derivatives: multitudinous-ly, adv., multitu-

## dinous-ness
dinous-ness, n.

## multure
multure, п., a toll or fee paid for the grinding of
grain (Scot. law). — ME. moulture, fr. OF.

## moulture (F. mouture)
moulture (F. mouture), fr. VL. molilura,
'grinding of grain' (whence also OProveng. moldura,

## Sp. moledura
Sp. moledura, 'grinding'), fr. L. molere, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:508 COLUMN:2 -->
grind'. See meal, 'edible grain', and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see suff. -tire.

## mum
mum, interj.-, be silent! silence! — Of imitative
origin. Cp. mumble, mump, mumps.
Derivatives: mum, adj., silent, mum, intr. v., to
be silent.

## mum
mum, п., a kind of strong beer, orig. made in
Brunswick, Germany. — LG. mumme (whence
G. Mumme, Du. mom); allegedly named after
the brewer Christian Mumme, who first brewed
this kind of beer in 1489.

## mum
mum, intr. v., to act in dumb show. — ME.
mommen, fr. OF. momer, mommer, 'to mask
oneself (whence OF. momon, 'mask', F. mo-
merie, 'mummery'), which prob. derives fr. the
child's word momo, expressing astonishment.
Cp. G. Mumme (now obsol.), 'mask' whence
mummen (now einmummen, vermummen), 'to
muffle'. Cp. also Sp. and Port, momo, 'grimace*.
Cp. also mummery.

## mum
mum, n. — Vulgar corruption of madam.

## mum
mum, п., chrysanthemum. — Formed from the
ending of chrysanthemum.

## mumble
mumble, intr. and tr. v., to speak indistinctly. —
ME. momelen, 'to speak indistinctly', derived fr.
ME. mom, 'a slight sound', which is of imitative
origin. Cp. Du. mommelen. The -b- in mumble is
excrescent. Cp. mum, 'to be silent'. Cp. also
mump. For the ending see freq. suff. -le.
Derivatives: mumble, п., mumbl-er, п., mumbl-
ing-ly, adv.

## Mumho Jumbo
Mumho Jumbo, 1) name of an African idol; 2)
(not cap.) an object of superstitious fear. —
Corruption of Mama Dyumbo, from Mandingo,
a West African Negro dialect.

## mummer
mummer, п., an actor in a dumb show. — MF.
momeur, mommeur, fr. momer, mommer, 'to
mask oneself. See mum, 'to act in dumb show'.

## mummery
mummery, п., a dumb show. — MF. (= F.)
momerie, fr. OF. momeur. See prec. word and -y
(representing OF. -ie).

## mummiflcation
mummiflcation, n. — See mummify and -ation.

## mummiform
mummiform, adj., shaped like a mummy. —
Compounded of mummy and -form.

## mummify
mummify, tr. v., to make into a mummy; intr. v.,
to become like a mummy, to dry up, shrivel. —
F. momifier, compounded of momie, 'mummy',
and -fier, 'to make into', fr. L. - ficare, fr.
facere, 'to make, do'. See mummy and -fy.

## mummy
mummy, п., an embalmed body. — ME. mummie,
fr. OF. (= F.) momie, fr. ML. mumia, fr. Arab.
mumiya1', 'mummy', fr. Pers. mum, 'wax*.
Derivative: mummy, tr. v.. to mummify.

## mump
mump, intr. v., to mumble; to whine like a
beggar. — Obsol. Du. mompen, 'to cheat, deceive',
orig. prob. 'to mumble, whine' (cp. Du.
mommelen, mompelen, 'to mutter, mumble'); of
imitative origin Cp. mumble.

## mump
mump, п., a grimace (obsol.) — Fr. prec. word.

## mump
mump, п., mumps. — See mumps.

## mumper
mumper, п., a deceitful beggar. — Formed fr.
mump, v., with agential suff. -er.

## mumps
mumps, п., an infectious disease, characterized
by the swelling of the salivary glands; parotitis.
— Fr. mump, 'grimace', so called in allusion to
the patient's appearance.

## munch
munch, infr. and tr. v., to chew. — ME. monchen,
prob. imitative; not connected with F. manger,
'to eat'. Cp crunch.
Derivatives: munch, п., munch-er, n.

## Munchausen
Munchausen, п., inexact for Munchhausen in the
name of Baron Karl Friedrich Hieronymus von
Munchhausen (1720-97), a German adventurer,
who served in the Russian army against the
Turks; pretended author of a book of wildly
exaggerated exploits really written by Rudolph
Erich Raspe (1734-94), and entitled Baron
Munchausen, Narrative of his Marvellous
Travels (published in 1785).
Derivatives: .Munchausen-ism, п., Munchausen-
ize, intr. v.

## mundane
mundane, adj., pertaining to the world; worldly.
— ME., fr. OF. (= F.) mondain, fr. Late L.
mundanus, 'of, or pertaining to, the world', fr.
L. mundus, 'world, universe, the heavens, the
heavenly bodies, the earth, the inhabitants of
the earth', of uncertain origin; not related to the
Latin adjective mundus, 'clean, cleanly, neat',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:508 COLUMN:3 -->
nor to L. movere, 'to move'. Cp. extramundane,
ultramondane, monde, demimonde, mound,
'globe'.
Derivatives: mundane-ly, adj., mundane-ness,
п., mundanity (q.v.)

## mundanity
mundanity, п., worldliness. — MF. (— F.) mon-
danite, fr. ML. mundanitatem, ace. of mundani-
tas, fr. Late L. mundanus. See prec. word and
-ity.

## mundungus
mundungus, п., tobacco with an offensive smell
(obsol.) — Sp. mondongo, 'paunch, tripe,
intestines', rel. to mondejo, 'paunch, belly (of a pig)\

## mungo
mungo, п., a kind of fine shoddy. — Of uncertain
origin.

## mungoos
mungoos, mungoose, n. — See mongoose.

## Munichion
Munichion, also Munychion, п., name of the 10th
month of the Attic Greek calendar
(corresponding to the second half of April and first half of
May). — Gk. Μουνιχιών, less exactly spelled
Μουνυχι,ών
municipal» adj., pertaining to the government of
a city or town. — L. municipals, fr. municipium,
'a town that possessed the right of Roman
citizenship, but was governed by its own laws, a
free town', fr. municeps, gen. municipis,
'inhabitant of a municipium or free town, citizen*,
lit. 'a receiver of duties', compounded of munia,
'official duties', and the stem of capere, 'to
catch, seize, take, hold'. The first element is rel.
to miinus, 'service, office, function', communis,
"common, universal, public'. See mean, 'of low
rank', and cp. common; cp. also
munificence,remunerate. For the second element see captive;
for the ending see adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: municipal, п., municipal-ism, п.,
municipal-ist, п., municipality (q.v.),
municipalize, tr. v., municipal-iz-ation, п., municipal-ly,
adv.

## municipality
municipality, n. — F. municipalite, fr. municipal,
fr. L. municipalis (see municipal); introduced
into English by the statesman Edmund Burke
(1729-97). For the ending see suff. -ity.

## munificence
munificence, п., great liberality. — F., fr. L.
munificentia, 'bountifulness, liberality,
generosity', fr. munificus. See next word and -ce.

## munificent
munificent, adj., very liberal. — Back formation
fr. munificentior, c*mpar. of munificus,
'bountiful, liberal, generous', lit. 'present-making', fr.
munusy 'service, office, function; gift', and -ficus,
'making', fr, -ficere, unstressed form of facere;
'to make, do*. See municipal and -fie.
Derivatives: munificent-ly, adv., munificem-ness
n.

## maniment
maniment, п., 1) protection; 2) pi. a document,
esp. a title deed (law). — ME. munimente, fr.
MF. muniment, fr. L. munimentum, 'defense,
fortification, protection' (in ML. 'title deed'),
fr. munire, *to surround with a wall, defend,
fortify, protect*, fr. moenia, 'walls, bulwarks',
which developed fr. *moi-ni- and is rel. to L.
murus (fr. *moi-ros), 'wall'. Cp. next word. Cp.
also mural and words there referred to. For the
ending see suff. -ment.

## munition
munition, п., I) pi., military stores, provisions; 2)
military material stored. — MF. (= F.)
munition, fr. L. тйпШдпет, асе. of mttnftio,
'fortification, defense', fr. munitus, pp. of munire. See
muniment and -ion and cp. premunition.
Derivatives: munition, tr. v., munition-eer, п.,
munition-er, n.

## munjeet
munjeet, п., Indian madder. — Hind, manjit, fr.
Ol. manjistha, which is perh. fem. of manjistha,
super], of manjufa, "beautiful, lovely, charming',
a word of uncertain etymology. For ihe ending
see superl. suff. -est.

## munnion
munnion, n. — See mulHon.

## munshi
munshi, also moonshee, п., a native interpreter; a
native teacher of Indian languages (Anglo-
India) — Hind, munshi, fr. Arab. munshi\ part,
of ansha'a, 'he caused to rise', IV (— causative)
conjugation of nashaO, 'he rose, was high; he
grew up', which is rel. to Heb. nasa, 'he lifted'.
See nasi.

## muntjac
muntjac, muntjak, п., a small deer ot eastern and
southern Asia. — Native Malay, fr. Javanese.

## Vluntz
Vluntz, Muntz's metal. — Named after its
inventor George F. Muntz of Birmingham, England
(died in 1857).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:509 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MURAENA | 482 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:509 COLUMN:1 -->

## Muraena
Muraena, Murena, the genus of morays. — L.
muraena, murena, 'sea eel, lamprey' (whence F.
morene), fr, Gk. σμύροανα, μύροανχ, of s.m.,
fr. σμΰρος, μϋρος, 'sea eel'. See moray.

## Muraenidae
Muraenidae, Murenidae. п., pi., the family of the
morays (zoo!.) — ModL., formed fr. prec.
word with surf, -idae (q.v.).

## muraenoid
muraenoid, murenoid, adj., resembling the moray.
— Compounded of muraena and Gk. -οε^δής,
'like', fr. εΐδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## murage
murage, п., formerly a tax paid for the building
and repairing ot" city walls. — ME., fr. OF., fr.
ML. muragium, fr. L. murus. See mural and -age.

## mural
mural, adj., pertaining to a wall. — F. mural, fr.
L. mwra//sv-'of, or pertaining to, a wall', fr.
murus (OL. moiros, moerus), 'wall', which
stands for *moi-ros and is rel. to moe/iia (fr.
*moi-ni-), 'walls, bulwarks'. See muniment and
cp. murage, mure, muromontite, extramural,
intramural, immure. Cp. also mere, 'boundary'.

## murder
murder, n. — ME. mordre, morder, morthre, fr.
OE. mordor, mordur, rel. to Goth. maurpr,
'murder', OE. mordt OS., OFris. morth, ON. mord,
Dan., Swed. mora, MDu. moort, mort, Du.
moord, OHG. mord, MHG. mort, G. Mord,
'murder', and cogn. with L. mors, gen. mortis,
'death', mori, 'to die'. See mortal.
Derivatives: murder, v. (q.v.), murder-ous (q.v.)

## murder
murder, tr. v, — ME. mortheren, murtkeren, fr.
OE. myrddrian, 'to murder', fr. OE. mordor,
'murder'; rel. to OF. morthia, OHG. murthiren,
Goth, maurprjan, 'to murder'. See murder, n.
Derivatives: murder-er, п., murder-ess, n.

## murderous
murderous, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. murder, a
word of Teut. origin, and -ous, a suff. traceable
to L. -osus.
Derivatives: murderous-ly, adv., murderous-ness,
n.

## mure
mure, tr. v., to enclose within walls, immure. —
ME. muren, fr. OF. (~ F.) murer, fr. L. murare,
'to enclose within walls', fr. murus. See mural.

## Murex
Murex, п., a genus of marine gastropods (zool.)
— L. murex, 'purple fish, purple dye', of
uncertain, possibly Mediterranean, origin.

## muriate
muriate, п., a salt of hydrochloric acid (chem.)
— See next word.

## muriatic
muriatic, adj., hydrochloric (scil. acid). — Coined
by the German chemist Johann Rudolf
Glauber (1604-70) fr. L. muriaticus, 'pickled in
brine', fr. muria, muries, 'brine', which is of
uncertain etymology.

## Muridae
Muridae, n. pi., a family of rodents, the rats and
mice (zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae
fr. L. mus, gen. muris, 'mouse'. See murine.

## Muriel
Muriel, fern. PN. — Prob. of Celtic origin and lit.
meaning 'sea-bright'. Cp. their. PN. Muirgheal,
which is compounded of muir, 'sea', and geal,
'bright". Olr. muir is rel. to Co., W. mor, 'sea',
and cogn. with L. mare, 'sea'. See mare, 'sea',
mere, 'sea', and cp. the first element in Merlin.

## murk
murk, adj., dark, gloomy (archaic and poet.) —
ME. mirke, prob. fr. ON. myrkr, Dan. merk,
Swed. mdrk, which is rel. to OE. mirce, OS.
mirki, 'dark'.
Derivatives: murk, п., murk-y, adj., murk-i-ly,
adv., murk-i-ness, n.

## murk
murk, n. — ME. mirke, prob. fr. ON. myrkr, п.,
fr. myrkr, adj. Cp. Dan. merk, Swed. mork,
'darkness', and see murk, adj.

## murmur
murmur, n. — ME. murmure, fr. OF. (= F.)
murmure, fr. murmurer, 'to murmur*. See
murmur, v.

## murmur
murmur, intr. and tr. v. — ME. murmuren, fr.
OF. (— F.) murmurer, fr, L. murmurare, fr.
murmur, 'a murmur, murmuring', which is of
imitative origin. Cp. OI. jnurmurah, 'crackling
fire', marmarah, 'rustling', Gk. μορμόρειν, Ίο
roar, boil*, Lith. murmlenti, murmenti, "to
murmur', murmeti, 'to grumble', OHG. murmuron,
murmuldn, MHG., G. murmeln, 'to murmur',
Du. murmelen, Arm. mrmram, mrmrim (for
mufmufam, resp. murmurim), *I murmur,
grumble, roar'. All these words are traceable to
the I.-E. reduplicated imitative base *mor-mor-,
*mur-mur-, 'to murmur, rustle, grumble'. The
simple base *mor-, *mur-, appears in Olr. muirn
(fr. *murni-), 'noise, rustle', ON. murra, MDu.,
Du. morren, MHG., G. murren, 'to murmer,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:509 COLUMN:2 -->
growl, grumble', OE. murnian, murcnian, 'to
murmur, complain, grieve'.
Derivatives: ^murmur-er, п., murmur-ing, adj.,
murmur-ing-iy, adv., murmur-ous, adj., murmur-
ous-ly, adv.

## muromontite
muromontite, п., a complex silicate containing
yttrium metals (mineral.) — So called because
fpund in Saxony at Maurersberg (in Latin
Muromontia), lit. 'wall mountain'. See mural,
mount and subst. suff. -ite.

## murphy
murphy, п., a potato (colloq.) — From the PN.
Murphy.

## murra
murra, murrha, п., a stone of which precious
vessels were made (Roman archaeol.) — L. See
murrhine.

## murrain
murrain, п., cattle plague. — ME. moreine, fr.
MF. morine, fr. VL. *morire, corresponding to
L. mori, 'to die'; see mortal. Cp. Sp. morriHa,
Port, morrinha, 'murrain', which also derive fr.
VL. *morire. Cp. murrina.

## murre
murre, п., 1) guillemot of the genus Uria; 2) the
razorbill — Related to dial. E. marrot, morrot,
'guillemot'; of uncertain origin. Cp, next word.

## murrelet
murrelet, п., any of various birds of the auk
family. — Formed fr. murre with dimin. sufT.
-let.

## murrey
murrey, adj., mulberry red; dark purplish red; п.,
murrey color. — ME., fr. MF. moree, fr. ML.
moratus, 'mulberry colored', fr. L. morum,
'mulberry*. See mulberry.

## murrhine
murrhine, adj., made of, or resembling, murra; п.,
a murrhine vase (Roman antiq.). — L. murr(h)t-
nus, 'of, or made of, murra', fr. murra, less
correctly, murrha, 'fluorspar; agate; a glass
imitation', which is of Iranian origin. Cp. Pers. mori,
muri, 'globule of glass'. Cp. also Gk. μόρρκχ,
μούρρινα {pi), which are of the same origin and
meaning as L. murra.

## murrina
murrina, п., a disease of horses (veter.) — Sp.
morrina, 'murrain'. See murrain.

## Mus
Mus, п., a genus of rodents, the mouse (zool.) —
L. mus, gen. muris, 'mouse'. See mouse.

## Musa
Musa, п., a genus of trees, the banana (hot.) —
ModL., fr. Arab. mauzah, 'banana', fr. mauz,
'banana tree'.

## Musaph
Musaph, also spelled Musaf, п., additional prayer
on the Sabbath and on festivals, immediately
following the morning prayer (= Shaharith). —
Mishnaic Heb. musaph, 'additional offering,
additional prayer', prop, subst. use of the Hoph'al
part, of yasaph, 'he added, increased', which is
rel. to Aram, osiph, Syr. auseph, 'he added', and
prob. also to Akkad. ussupu, 4o add', siptu,
'interest'.

## Mnsca
Mnsca, п., a genus of flies, the common housefly
(entomol.) — L. musca, 'fly'. See midge and cp.
words there referred to.

## muscadel
muscadel, n. — A var. of muscatel.

## muscadine
muscadine, п., a grape grown in the southern
U.S. — Formed with suff. -ine fr. OProveng.
muscada, fern, of muscat, 'flavored with musk'.
See muscat.

## muscardine
muscardine, п., dormouse (obsol. and rare). — F.,
fr. earlier F. muscardin, muscadin, 'lozenge
flavored with musk', fr. It. moscardino, of s.m., fr.
moscado, 'having the smell of musk', fr. VL.
muscatus, of s.m., fr. L. muscus; see musk and
cp. muscat. The animal was called muscardine
by the French naturalist, Comte Georges Louis
Leclerc de Buffon (1707-88) in allusion to its
musky smell.

## muscardine
muscardine, п., a disease of silk worms. — F., fr.
earlier muscardin. See prec. word.

## muscarine
muscarine, muscarin, п., an alkaloid found in the
fungus Agaricus muscarius (ckem.) — Formed
with chem. sufT. -ine resp. -in, fr. ModL.
Agaricus muscarius, 'fly agaric', from the L. adj.
muscarius, 'pertaining to flies', fr. musca, 'fly';
see midge. The fungus was so called from its
!iairy character.

## muscat
muscat, п., 1) a light musky grape; 2) a muscatel
wine. — F., fr. OProvenc. muscat, lit. 'having
the smell of musk', fr. VL. muscatus, of s.m.,
fr. L. muscus. See musk and cp. next word.

## muscatel
muscatel, п., I) a variety of white grape with a
musky flavor; 2) a sweet wine made from
muscatel grapes. — ME. muskadelle, fr. MF.
muscatel, muscadel, fr. OProveng. *muscadel, dimin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:509 COLUMN:3 -->
of muscat. See muscat and dimin. suff. -el and
cp. moschatel.

## muscle
muscle, n. — MF. (— F.), fr. L. musculus, *a little
mouse; muscle', dimin. of mus, 'mouse*; see
mouse and -cle and cp. mussel. The formof some
muscles resembles that of a mouse, whence the
sense development of L. musculus; cp. Arm.
mukn, Gk. μυς, 'mouse; muscle', OSlav. mySl,
'mouse', mysica, 'arm', OE., OHG-, MHG. mus,
G. Maus, 'mouse; muscle'; cp. also Arab.
tadalah, 'muscle', fr. 'adal, 'field mouse*. It.
muscolo, Rum. muschiu, OProvenc. muscle,
moscle, Sp., Port, musculo, 'muscle', Sp. muslo,
'thigh', and G. Muskel, 'muscle', all derive fr.
L. musculus.

## muscoid
muscoid, adj., mosslike. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
muscus, 'moss', and Gk.-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See moss and -oid and cp. next
word.

## muscology
muscology, п., the science of mosses. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. muscus, 'moss', and Gk. -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
moss and -logy and cp. prec. word.

## muscovado
muscovado, п., raw sugar obtained from the juice
of the sugar-cane after draining off the molasses.
— Sp. (azucar) mascabado or Port, (agurar)
mascavado, '(sugar) of inferior quality', fr.
mascabado, 'raw, unrefined', shortened fr. menosca-
bado, pp. of menoscabar, 'to impair, lessen,
deteriorate', which is compounded of menos, 'less'
(fr. L. minus) and cabo, 'head' (fr. L. caput). See
minus and capital, adj., and cp. mischief.

## Muscovite
Muscovite, п., an inhabitant of Muscovy, a
Russian. — Formed fr. Muscovy (F. Moscovie),
ancient name of Russia, with subst. suff. -ite.

## Muscovy duck
Muscovy duck, the musk duck (Cairina moschata)
— Corruption of musk duck.

## muscular
muscular, adj., pertaining to, or performed by, a
muscle or muscles. — Formed with adj. suff. -ar
fr. L. musculus. See muscle.
Derivatives: muscular-ity, п., muscular-ize, tr.
v., muscular-iz-ation, n.

## musculature
musculature, п., system of muscles. — F., fr. L.
musculus. See muscle and -ure.

## musculo-
musculo-, combining form meaning 'muscle' or
'muscular' (anat.) — L. musculo·, fr. musculus.
See muscle.

## mnsculus
mnsculus, п., a muscle (anat.) — L. musculus. See
muscle.

## muse
muse, intr. v., to reflect. — ME. musen, fr. OF.
(~ F.) muser, 'to loiter, dream, ponder deeply',
prop, 'to snuff about' (said of a dog), fr. ML.
musum, 'muzzle', whence also It. muso, OProv-
βης. mus, and the OF. dimin. musel(¥. museau),
whence E. muzzle (q.v.) Cp. amuse and musette.
Derivatives: muse, п., meditation, muse-ful, adj.,
muse-ful-ly, adv., muse-less, adj., muse-less-ly,
adv., mus-ing, n. and adj., mus-ing-ly, adv.

## Muse
Muse, п., one of the nine goddessess, daughters
of Zeus and Mnemosyne, protectors of the arts
(Greek mythol.) — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L.
Musa, fr. Gk. Μοϋσα, μοϋσα, 'Muse; music,
song', which stands perh. for *Μόνθι;α and is
rel. to μανθάνειν, 'to learn'. See mathematical
and cp. amusia, mosaic, museum, mnsic.

## musette
musette, п., 1) a small bagpipe; 2) a composition
for this instrument. — F., fr. MF., fr. OF., fr.
muser, 'to play the bagpipe', fr. OF. mus, 'mouth,
muzzle*, fr. ML. musum, of s.m. See muzzle and
-ette and cp. muse. Cp. also cornmuse.

## museum
museum, n. — L. museum, 'library, academy,
study, museum', fr. Gk. μουσεΐον, lit. 'seat of
the Muses', fr. Μαΰσα, 'Muse'. See Muse.

## mush
mush, п., 1) a thick soft mass; 2) a porridge (U.S.)
— A var. of mash.
Derivative: mush-y, adj.

## mush
mush, п., a march on foot with dogs
(Northwestern America). — Prob. corruption of F. mar-
che\ *go!' (imper. of marcher, 'to walk, march,
go'), a shout of command to the dogs. See
march, 'to walk'.
Derivatives: mush, intr. v., to travel on foot
with dogs; tr. v., to cause to travel, mush-er, n.

## mushroom
mushroom, n. — ME. muscheron, fr. OF. meis-
seron, moisseron (F. mousseron), fr. ML. mussi-
ridnem, ace. of mussirio, a word of pre-Latin
origin, used in the North of France; F. mous-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:510 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 483 | MUTTON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:510 COLUMN:1 -->
seron was influenced in form by F. mousse,
'moss', with which it has nothing in common.
Derivatives: mushroom, intr. v., mushroom-y,
adj.

## music
music, n. — ME. musik, fr. OF. (= F.) musique,
fr. L. musica, fr. Gk. μουσική (scil. τέχνη),
'musical art', orig. 'any art in which the Muses
presided', fem. of μουσικός, 'pertaining to the
Muses', fr. Μοΰσα, 'Muse'. See muse and -ic.

## musical
musical, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. ML.
miisicalis, 'pertaining to music', fr. L. musica.
See music and adj. surf. -al.
Derivatives: musical-ly, adv., musical-ness, n.

## musician
musician, n. — ME. musicien, fr. MF. ( — F.), fr.
musique. See music and -ian.
Derivative: musician-ly, adv.

## musimon
musimon, п., the moufflon. — L. musimo, musmo.
See moufflon.

## musk
musk, п., substance secreted by a gland near the
testicles of the musk deer. — ME. muske, fr.
OF. (= F.) muse, fr. L. muscus, fr. Gk. μόσχος,
fr. Pers. mushk, 'musk', fr. Ol. mufkdh,
'scrotum, testicle', lit. 'a little mouse', fr. ma}-,
'mouse'. See mouse and cp. muscle. Cp. also
muscadine, muscardine, muscat, muscatel. Cp.
also mugget and the second element in nutmeg.
Derivatives: musk-ish, musk-y, adjs.

## muskellunge
muskellunge, п., a large pike of North America.
— Algonquian maskinonge, lit. 'large pike'.

## musket
musket, п., hand gun, formerly used by infantry;
replaced by the rifle. — MF. (= F.) mousquet,
fr. It. moschetto, 'arrow for a crossbow' (now
meaning 'musket'), lit. 'a little fly', fr. mosca,
'fly', fr. L. musca. See midge and -et and cp.
mosquito. For sense development cp. zum-
booruk, 'a small gun', which is traceable to
Arab, zambur, 'a hornet'.

## Musketeer
Musketeer, п., a soldier armed with a musket. —
F. mousquetaire, fr. mousquet, 'musket'. See
musket and -eer and cp. mousquetaire.

## musketoon
musketoon, п., a short musket with large bore. —
F. mousqueton, formed fr. mousquet, 'musket',
on analogy of It. moschettone. See musket and
-ООП.

## musketry
musketry, п., muskets collectively. — F. mous-
queterie, formed fr. mousquet, 'musket', on the
analogy of It. moschetteria. See musket and -ry.
muskus grass. — Fr. Du. muskus, 'musk', fr. L.
muscus. See musk.

## Muslim
Muslim, n. — See Moslem.

## muslin
muslin, п., a fine soft cotton fabric. — F. mous-
seline, fr. It. mussolina, dimin. formed from
Mussolo, Italian name of Mosul, town in
Mesopotamia (now Iraq), where this material was
originally made. Cp. mousseline.

## muslinet
muslinet, n. — Dimin. of prec. word. For the
ending see suff. -"et.

## musnud
musnud, п., a large cushion used by princes in
India, Persia, etc. — Hind, masnad, fr. Arab.
masnad, lit. 'something to lean upon', fr. sanada,
'he leaned upon'. Cp. sunnud.

## musquash
musquash, п., 1) a muskrat; 2) its fur. — Prop,
'the red animal', from an Algonquian native
word meaning 'red'.

## muss
muss, п., mess, confusion, disorder. — Prob. a
var. of mess.
Derivative: muss, tr. v., to disarrange, confuse.

## mussel
mussel, п., any of several bivalve mollusks. —
ME. muscle, fr. OE. muscelle, muscle, fr. VL.
'musculo [whence also OF. musle (F. moule),
OS., OHG. musculo (MHG., G. muschel),
'mussel'], corresponding to L. musculus, 'little
mouse, muscle; sea mussel'. See muscle.
Derivatives: mussel-ed, adj., mussel-er, n.

## mussuck
mussuck, mussnk, п., a leathern skin for water
(India) — Hind, тайак, fr. OI. maiakah.

## Mussulman
Mussulman, п., a Moslem. — Turk, musulman,
fr. Pers. musulman, which is formed with the
adj. suff. -an fr. Arab, miislim, 'Moslem'. See
Moslem.

## must
must, aux. v., am (or is, are) obliged to. — ME.
moste, fr. OE. moste, pret. of motan, 'to be
allowed to, be able to, have opportunity to,
have to', rel. to OS. motan, 'to be obliged to,
have to', OHris. mota, MLG. mOten, MDu., Du.
moeten, 'to be obliged to', OHG. тиозап, MHG.
тйезеп, 'to be allowed to, have to', G. mussen,
'to be obliged to', Goth, gamotan, 'to have

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:510 COLUMN:2 -->
room to, be able to', fr. Teut. base 'motan, 'to
fix, allot, appoint, something; to have room;
to be able; to be obliged', σ-degree of l.-E. base
med-, 'to measure, limit', whence OE. metan, 'to
measure'. See mete, 'to measure', and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also mote, 'may'.
Derivative: must, n.

## must
must, п., mold, mustiness. — Prob. back
formation fr. musty.

## must
must, adj., frenzied, mad (said of male elephants).
— Hind, mast, fr. Pers. mast, rel. to OI. matta-,
'drunk, intoxicated', pp. of madati, 'boils,
bubbles, gets drunk', fr. I.-E. base *mad-, 'wet, to
drip'. See meat and cp. words there referred to.

## must
must, п., new wine. — ME., fr. OE. must, fr. L.
mustum, 'new wine', shortened fr. mustum vi-
num, fr. mustus, 'fresh, new', which possibly
stands for 'mus-tos, 'wet, moist', fr. I.-E. *meu-s-.
See moss and words there referred to and cp.
esp. mustard. F. mout, It. mosto. OSlav. mustu,
'new wine', also derive fr. L. mustum.

## mustache
mustache, moustache, n. — MF. (= F.)
moustache, fr. It. mostaccio, a collateral form of mo-
stacchio, fr. MGk. μουστάκι, fr. Gk. μύσταξ,
'upper lip, mustache', which is rel. to μάσταξ,
'mouth, jaws', lit. 'that with which one chews',
μαστιχάω, Ί gnash the teeth', μασάομαι (for
*μα»ιάομοα), Ί chew, bite', fr. I.-E. base
*menth, 'to chew'. See mouth and cp. mastic,
masticate.
Derivatives: mustach-ed, moustach-ed, adj.,
mustach-ial, moustach-iat, adj.

## mustachio
mustachio, mustache, n. — A blend of Sp. mos-
tacho and It. mostaccio. See mustache.
Derivative: mustachio-ed, adj.

## mustang
mustang, п., the small, half-wild horse of the
American prairies. — Mexican Sp. mesteno,
mestengo, 'ownerless animal, stray', fr. Sp.
mesteno, mestengo, 'belonging to graziers', fr.
mesta, 'company of graziers', fr. L. mixta, fem.
pp. of miscere, 'to mix' (see mix); influenced in
form by Sp. mostrenco, 'straying, wild', fr.
mostrar, fr. L. monstrare, 'to show'.

## mustard
mustard, n. — ME., fr. OF. moustarde (F. mou-
tarde), fr. moust (F. mout), 'new wine, must', fr.
L. mustum. Accordingly mustard lit. means
'seasoned with must'. See must, 'new wine', and
cp. -ard.

## mustee
mustee, п., an octoroon; a half-caste. —
Corruption of Sp. mestizo. See mestizo and cp. mestee.

## Mustelidae
Mustelidae, п., pi., a family of carnivorous
animals as weasels, badgers, skunks. — ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. L. mustela, 'weasel'.
See musteline.

## musteline
musteline, adj., of, or pertaining to, the family of
weasels. — Formed with suff. -ine fr. L. mustela,
'weasel', which is of uncertain origin; possibly
connected with mus, 'mouse' (the weasel is
referred to in classical antiquity as 'the catcher of
mice'; see mouse).

## muster
muster, tr. v., 1) to collect, gather together; 2)
intr. v., to come together. — ME. mustren, fr.
OF. moster, mustrer, monstrer (F. montrer), 'to
show', fr. L. monstrare. See monster and cp.
next word.

## muster
muster, п., an assembling of soldiers; an
assembly for inspection. — ME. moustre, fr. OF. mos-
tre, moustre (F. montre), lit. 'that which is
shown', fr. mostrer, mustrer, 'to show'. See
muster, v.

## musty
musty, adj., moldy. — Prob. for earlier moisty, fr.
moist (q.v.) Cp. must, 'mold'.
Derivatives: musti-Iy, adv., musti-ness, n.

## mutable
mutable, adj., liable to change, changeable. — L.
mutabilis, 'changeable', fr. mutare, 'to change',
which is rel. to mutuus, 'borrowed, lent,
reciprocal, mutual', and cogn. with OI. methati,
mithati, 'changes, alternates, joins, meets,
quarrels', mithdh, 'alternately, mutually', mithu,
'perverted', Avestic mi&o, 'perverted, false',
OSlav. mite, 'alternately', mlsti, 'vengeance',
Lett, miitus, 'change', mitudt, mietuot, 'to
exchange, barter', mitit, 'to change', Goth. maid-

## Jan
Jan, 'to change', Hitt. mutdi-, 'to be changed
into'. All these words are derivatives of I.-E.
base *meit(h)-, enlargement of base *mei-, 'to
change, exchange'. See mean, 'of low rank'. See
also mis-, miss, v., and cp. mew, 'to shed, molt',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:510 COLUMN:3 -->
molt, mutual, commute, permute, transmute,
remuda.
Derivatives: mutabil-ity, п., mutable-ness, п.,
mutabl-y, adv.

## mutate
mutate, tr. arid intr. v., to change. — L. mutatus,
pp. of mutare. See mutable and verbal suff. -ate.

## mutation
mutation, п., change. — ME. mustacioun, fr. OF.
(= F.) mutation, fr. L. mutdtionem, ace. of
mulatto, 'change', fr. mutatus, pp. of mutare. See
mutable and -ation.

## mutative
mutative, adj., liable to change (biol.) — Formed
with suff. -ive fr. L. mutatus, pp. of mutare. See
mutate.

## Mutazilite
Mutazilite, п., name of a Shiite sect in Islam,
founded by Wasil ibn Ata in the 8th cent. —
Formed with subst. suff. -fte fr. Arab, mu'td-
zilah, 'a body of seceders', fr. mu'tazil, 'seceder',
active part, ofi'taza/a, 'he seceded', VIII
conjugation of 'dzala, 'he went'.

## mutch
mutch, п., a close-fitting cap worn by women and
little children. — MDu. mutse, 'cap', fr. earlier
almutse. See amice, 'hood, headdress', and cp.
almuce, mozzetta.

## mutchkin
mutchkin, п., an old liquid measure. — MDu.
mutseken, orig. 'a little cap', formed with dim.
suff. -ken fr. mutse, 'cap'. See mutch and -kin.

## mute
mute, adj., dumb. — L. miitus, 'dumb', prob. fr.
I.-E. imitative base *mu-, whence also L. тй in
mufacere, 'to mutter', Ol. тй-kah, 'dumb', Gk.
μΰειν, 'to be shut or closed' (said esp. of the
lips and eyes); see 1st mystery. Cp. the imitative
base *mut-, whence L. muttire, mutire, 'to
grunt, mutter', and see mutter. Cp. also ob-
mutescence.
Derivatives: mute, a. and tr. v., mute-ly, adv.,
mute-ness, n.

## mutilate
mutilate, tr. v., 1) to maim; 2) to destroy. — L.
mutilatus, pp. mutilare, 'to mutilate', fr. mutilus,
'maimed, mutilated', orig. meaning 'short', and
cogn. with Olr. mut, 'short', Gael, mutach,
'short and thick'. For the ending see verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: mutilation (q.v.), mutilat-ive, adj.,
mutilat-or, п., mutitat-ory, adj.

## mutilation
mutilation, n. — Late L. mutilatio, gen. -onis, fr.
L. mutilatus, pp. of mutilare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## mutineer
mutineer, п., 1) one guilty of mutiny; 2) intr. v.,
to mutiny. — F. mutinier (a word used in the
16th cent.), fr. mutin, 'mutinous'. See mutiny
and -eer.

## mutinous
mutinous, adj., disposed to mutiny, rebellious. —
See mutiny and -ous.
Derivatives: mutinous-ly, adv., mutinous-ness, n.

## mutiny
mutiny, п., rebellion. — Formed with subst. suff.
-y fr. obsol. mutine, 'a mutiny', fr. F. mutiner, 'to
rebel, mutiny', fr. mutin, 'mutinous, riotous,
unruly', fr. OF. muete, meute, 'riot, revolte'
(whence F. meute, 'pack of hounds; crowd,
mob, band'), fr. VL. movita, subst. use of mdvita,
fem. of mdvitus, corresponding to classical L.
motus, pp. of movere, 'to move'. Cp. F. emeute
(fr. VL. *exmdvita), 'riot, tumult' (orig.
'movement, motion'), and see move.
Derivative: mutiny, intr. v.

## mutism
mutism, n-, dumbness. — F. mutisme, a hybrid
coined fr. L. mutus, 'dumb', and -isme, a suff. of
Greek origin. See mute and -ism.

## mutoscope
mutoscope, п., a device conveying the impression
of a moving picture. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
mutare, 'to change', and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκο-
πεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See mutable and
-scope.

## mutt
mutt, n. (slang), 1) a fool; 2) a mongrel dog. —
Prob. short fOT muttonhead.

## mutter
mutter, v., to utter indistinctly. — ME. moteren,
mutteren, from the l.-E. imitative base *mut-,
'to grunt, mutter', whence also L. muttire,
mutire, 'to grunt, mutter', Lith. mute, Lett.
mute, 'mouth', ON. mudla, 'to murmur', OHG.
mutilon, 'to murmur, mutter; to drizzle'. Cp.
mot, motet, motto. Cp. also the imitative base
*mS-, whence Gk. μυειν, 'to be shut or closed'
(said esp. of the lips and eyes). See 1st mystery
and cp. mute.
Derivatives: mutter, a.,'mutter-er, п., mutter-
ing-ly, adv.

## mutton
mutton, п., the flesh of sheep. — ME. motoun, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:511 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: MUTUAL | 484 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:511 COLUMN:1 -->
OF. moton, motion, 'a ram' (whence F. mouton,
'sheep'), fr. Gaul. L. 'multonem, ace. of 'multo,
'sheep' (whence also OProven?. molto, 'wether',
It. montone, 'a sheep'), which is of Celtic origin.
Cp. Gael, mult, Mir. molt, W. mollt, MBret.
том, Bret, maul, 'wether'. Cp. also moutonne.
Derivative: mutton-y, adj.

## mutual
mutual, adj., joint, reciprocal, done in common.
— ME. mutuall, fr. MF. (= F.) mutuel, fr. L.
mutuus, 'borrowed, lent; reciprocal, mutual',
which stands for *moitvos and is rel. to L.
mature, 'to change'. See mutable and adj. SUIT. -al.
Derivatives: mutual-ism, п., mutual-ity, п., ти-
tual-ize, v., mutual-iz-ation, п., mutual-ly, adv.

## mutule
mutule, п., an ornamental block projecting under
the corona of the cornice of the Doric order
(archil.) — F., fr. L. mutulus, 'mutule, modil-
lion', which is prob. of Etruscan origin and lit.
means 'something projecting', from the
Etruscan base *mut-, 'to project', which appears in
many geographical names (e.g. in the name of
the town Mutena (now Modena). Cp. modillion.

## muzhik
muzhik, also moujik, п., a Russian peasant. —
Russ. muzhik, lit. 'a little man', dimin. of muzh,
'man, husband', fr. ORuss. muit, fr. OSlav.
moil, 'man', which is cogn. with OI. manuh,
Goth, manna, OE. man, 'man': see man.
Peasants were called 'little men', because according
to the ancient Russian law, peasants were
regarded as minors.

## muzzle
muzzle, п., the projecting part of the head of an
animal; snout. — ME. musell, fr. OF. musel (F.
museau), fr. ML. musellum, dimin. of musum,
'muzzle, snout', whence It. muso, OProvenc.
mus, of s.m.; of unknown origin. Cp. muse.
Derivatives: muzzle, tr. v., muzzl-er, n.

## muzzy
muzzy, adj., confused; dazed. — Of unknown
origin.
Derivatives: muzzi-ly, adv., muzzi-ness, n.

## my
my, possessive pron. of the 1st person sing., of
me, mine. — Early ME. mi, short for min, fr.
OE. min, 'my, of me'. The final л was dropped
in ME. before words beginning with consonants.
See mine, pron. For the loss of the η before
consonants cp. thy and a, form of the indef. art.
an before consonants.

## my-
my-, form of myo- before a vowel.

## myalgia
myalgia, п., muscular pain (med.) — Coined on
the analogy of neuralgia fr. Gk. μϋς, 'muscle',
and £λγος, 'pain'. See myo- and -algia.
Derivative: mvalg-ic, adj.

## Mya
Mya, п., a genus of bivalves, the common long
clam (zool.) — L. mya, 'a kind of mussel', fr.
Gk. μύα, which is rel. to μϋς, gen. μυός,
'muscle'. See mussel and cp. muscle.

## niyalism
niyalism, п., a kind of Negro witchcraft in West
India. — Prob. formed from a native word
with surf. -ism.

## myall
myall, п., any of several Australian acacias. —
From native name.

## myall
myall, п., a wild Australian native. — From
Australian native maial, 'wild'.
Derivative: myall, adj.

## Myaria
Myaria, п., a group of bivalves (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Mya (q.v.)

## myasthenia
myasthenia, п., muscular weakness (med.) —
Medical L., coined fr. my- and Gk. ασθένεια,
'weakness'. See asthenia.

## myc-
myc-, form of myco- before a vowel.

## mycelium
mycelium, п., the thallus of a fungus (bot.) —
ModL., formed on the analogy of epithelium fr.
Gk. μύκης, 'fungus'. See myco-.
Derivatives: myceli-al, myceli-an, adj.

## Mycenaean
Mycenaean, adj., pertaining to Mycenae, an
ancient city of Greece, or to the civilization that
flourished there and in Greece, Crete and Asia
Minor between 1500 and 1100 B.C.E. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Mycenaeus, fr. Gk.
Μυκηναίος, 'of Mycenae', fr. Μυκηναι, Μυ-
κήνη, 'Mycenae'.

## mycet-
mycet-, form of myceto- before a vowel.

## -mycete
-mycete, combining form denoting one of a
(specified) group of fungi. — Fr. -mycetes.

## -mycetes
-mycetes, combining form denoting large groups
of fungi (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μύκητες, pi. of
μύκης, 'fungus'. See myco-.

## myceto-
myceto-, before a vowel mycet-, combining form
meaning 'fungus' (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:511 COLUMN:2 -->
μύκης, gen. μύκητος, 'fungus'. See myco-,

## mycetoma
mycetoma, п., a disease of the skin and
underlying tissue, esp. of the foot, caused by fungoid
bacteria (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. mycet-
and suff. -oma.

## myco-
myco-, before a vowel myc-, combining form
meaning 'fungus', as in mycology. — Fr. Gk.
μύκης, gen. μύκητος, 'fungus', fr. I.-E.
*(s)meuq-, 'to slip, slippery, slimy', whence also
Gk. μύξα, 'mucus of the nose, slime', L. mucus,
'mucus of the nose'. See mucus and cp. mycelium,
Mycteria, mycteric, myxo-, and the second
element in Actinomyces, phycomyces.

## mycology
mycology, п., that branch of botany which deals
with fungi. — Compounded of myco- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.

## mycorhlza
mycorhlza, mycorrhiza, п., mycelium found on
the roots of various trees (bot) — ModL.,
compounded of myco- and Gk. £ίζα, 'root'. See
rhizo-.

## mycosis
mycosis, п., 1) the growth of parasitic fungi in the
body; 2) disease caused by parasitic fungi (med.)
— Medical L., formed fr. myc- and suff. -osis.

## mycotic
mycotic, adj., pertaining to, or caused by,
mycosis. — See prec. word and -otic.

## Mycteria
Mycteria, п., a genus of birds, the American
wood ibis (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μυκτήρ,
'nose', lit. 'the mucous organ', re], to μύξα,
'mucus of the nose, slime', and cogn. with L.
mucus, 'nasal mucus'. See mucus and cp. myco-
and next word.

## mycteric
mycteric, adj., pertaining to the nasal cavities.
(anat.) — Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk.
μυκτήρ, 'nose'. See prec. word.

## Mydaus
Mydaus, п., the genus consisting of the teledu
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μυδαν, 'to be damp or
clammy', fr. μύδος, 'damp, moisture,
clamminess', fr. l.-E. base **meu-, 'whet, moist'* See
mother, 'dregs', and words there referred to and
cp. esp. Myzostoma.

## mydriasis
mydriasis, п., dilation of the pupil of the eye
(med.) — L., fr. Gk. μυδρίασις, which is of
uncertain origin. For the ending see suff. -iasis.

## mydriatic
mydriatic, adj., causing dilation of the pupil of
the eye (med.) — See prec. word and 1st -atic.

## myel-
myel-, form of myelo- before a vowel.

## myelencephalon
myelencephalon, п., the posterior part of the
rhombencephalon; the afterbrain (anat. and
embryo!.)—Compounded of myel- and encephalon.
The term myelencephalon was introduced by the
English naturalist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825-
95). Cp. metencephalon and rhombencephalon.

## myelic
myelic, adj., pertaining to the spinal cord (anat.)
— Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. μυελός,
'marrow'. See myelo-.

## myelin
myelin, myeline, п., a soft material found in nerve
tissue (anat. and biochem.) — G. Myelin, coined
by its discoverer, the German pathologist
Rudolf Ludwig Karl Virchow (1821-1902) in 1854
fr. Gk. μυελός, 'marrow' (see myelo-), and suff.
-in.

## myelitis
myelitis, п., inflammation of the spinal cord
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. myel- with suff.
-itis. Cp. osteomyelitis.

## myelo-
myelo-, before a vowel myel-, combining form
meaning 'marrow; the spinal cord' (med.) —
Gk. μυελό-, μυελ-, fr. μυελός, 'marrow'; of
uncertain origin.

## myeloid
myeloid, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, the
spinal cord (anat.) — Compounded of myel- and
Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
-oid.

## myeloma
myeloma, п., tumor of the bone marrow (med.) —
Coined fr. myel- and -oma.

## myelon
myelon, п., the spinal cord (anat.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. μυελός, 'marrow'. See myelo-.
Derivatives: myelon-al, myelon-ic, adjs.

## Myiarchus
Myiarchus, п., a genus of tyrant flycatchers (en-
tomol.) — ModL., lit. 'chief of the flies', fr. Gk.
μυϊα, "fly', and άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. For
the first element see midge and cp. words there
referred to, for the second element see -arch.

## myiasis
myiasis, п., disease caused by the larvae of flies
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -iasis fr.
Gk. μυΐα, 'fly'. See prec. word.

## mylo-
mylo-, before a vowel myl-, combining form

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:511 COLUMN:3 -->
meaning 'molar', as in Mylodon. — Gk. μύλο-,
μυλ-, fr. μύλη, 'mill', in the pi. also 'molar
teeth'. See mill for grinding and cp. words there
referred to.

## Mylodon
Mylodon, п., an extinct genus of giant sloths (pa-
leontol.) — Compounded of myl- and Gk.
οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-.

## myna
myna, mynah, п., a South-Indian bird of the
starling family (Acridotheres tristis) — Hind.
maina.

## Mynheer
Mynheer, п., 1) Sir; 2) (not cap.) a Dutchman. —
Du. mijnheer, 'sir', compounded of mijn, 'my,
mine', and heer, 'master, lord, sir'. For the first
element see mine, pron. The second element is
rel. to G. Herr, 'master, lord'; see Herr.

## myo-
myo-, before a vowel my-, combining form
meaning 'muscle' (anat.) — Gk. μυο-, μυ-, fr. μϋς,
'mouse; muscle'. See muscle and cp. Mya,
amyous, perimysium.

## myocarditis
myocarditis, п., inflammation of the myocardium
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. myocardium
with surf. -itis.

## myocardium
myocardium, п., the muscle of the heart (anat.) —
Medical L., compounded of myo- and Gk.
καρδία, 'heart'. See cardiac.

## myogenic
myogenic, adj., of muscular origin. —
Compounded of myo- and -genie.

## myograph
myograph, п., an instrument for recording
muscular contraction {physiol.) — From myograph-
ion, a name coined by the German physiologist
Emil Du Bois-Reymond (1818-96), the inventor
of this instrument, fr. myo- and Gk. -γράφος,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## myology
myology, п., that part of anatomy which deals
with the muscles. — Compounded of myo- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: myolog-ic, myolog-ic-al, adjs.,
myolog-ist, n.

## myoma
myoma, п., a tumor composed of muscular tissue
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. my- and suff.
-oma. Cp. leiomyoma.
Derivative: myomat-ous, adj.

## myopathy
myopathy, п., any disease of the muscles (med.)
— Compounded of myo- and Gk. -πάθεια,
fr. πάθος, 'suffering'. See -pathy.

## myope
myope, п., a shortsighted person. — F., fr. Late
L. myops, gen. myopis, fr. Gk. μύωψ, gen.
μύωπος, 'shortsighted', lit. 'closing the eyes',
compounded of μυειν, 'to be shut or closed' (said
esp. of the lips and eyes); 'to shut or close the
lips or eyes', and ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'the eye'. See
1st mystery, -ops, and -ous.
Derivatives: myop-ic, myop-ic-al, adjs., myop-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## myopia
myopia, п., shortsightedness. — Medical L., fr.
Late L. myops, gen. myopis. See prec. word.

## myosin
myosin, п., a protein occurring in muscle
(biochem.) — Coined fr. Gk. μϋς, gen. μυός,
'muscle' (see myo-), and chem. suff. -hi.

## myosis
myosis, п., excessive contraction of the pupil of
the eye (med.) — Medical L., formed with suff.
-osis fr. Gk. μΰειν. See myope.

## Myosotis
Myosotis, п., a genus of plants, the forget-me-not
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. fnyojof/i,''mouse-ear\ fr.
Gk, μυοσωτίς, lit. 'mouse's ear', fr. μΰς, gen.
μυός, 'mouse', and ούς. gen. ώτός, 'ear' (see
myo- and oto-); so called in allusion to the shape
of the short leaves.

## Myosurus
Myosurus, п., a genus of plants, the mousetail
(bot.) — ModL., [it. 'mouse's tail', fr. Gk. μΰς,
gen. μυός, 'mouse', and ουρά, 'tail'. See myo-
and uro-, 'tail-'.

## myotic
myotic, adj., pertaining to, or causing, myosis. —
See myosis and -otic.

## myria-
myria-, before a vowel myri-, combining form
meaning 1) 'ten thousand' (in the names of
weights and measures), as in myriameter = 'ten
thousand meters'; 2) 'very numerous', as in
myriapod, lit. 'that which has very many legs'.
— Fr. Gk. μΰριάς, 'a myriad'. See next word.

## myriad
myriad, п., 1) the number ten thousand; 2) a very
great number; adj., very numerous. — Gk.
μϋριάς, gen. μΰριάδος, 'the number ten

## thousand'
thousand', fr. μύριοι, 'ten thousand', fr. μϋρίος,
'numberless, countless', which is of uncertain
origin. For the ending see suff. -ad.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:512 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 485 | MYZOSTDMA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:512 COLUMN:1 -->

## myriapod
myriapod, adj., pertaining to the Myriapoda. —
See next word.

## Myriapoda
Myriapoda, п., pi., a group of arthropods (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'having very many legs',
compounded of myria- and Gk. πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. See podo-.
Derivatives: myriapod-an, myriapod-ous, adjs.

## Myriea
Myriea, п., a genus of plants (boi.) — L. myriea,
'tamarisk', fr. Gk. μυρίκη, which is perh. a
Sem. loan word of the same origin as Gk. μύρ-
ρά, 'myrrh'. See myrrh.

## Myricaceae
Myricaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## my ric aceous
my ric aceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## myriag-
myriag-, form of myringo- before a vowel.

## myringa
myringa, п., the tympanic membrane (anat.) —
ModL., fr. ML. miringa, dissimilated fr. Late L.
meninga, mininga, fr. Gk. μήνιγξ, gen. μή-
νιγγοι:, 'membrane'. See meninx.

## myringitis
myringitis, п., inflammation of the tympanic
membrane (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid
coined fr. myringa and -itis, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## myringo-
myringo-, before a vowel myring-, combining
form denoting the tympanic membrane. — See
myringa.

## Myriophyllum
Myriophyllum, п., a genus of plants, the water
milfoil (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μΰριόφυλλον,
'the water milfoil', which is compounded of
μΰρίος, 'numberless', and φύλλον, 'leaf* (see
myriad and phyllo-); so called in allusion to the
countless divisions of the leaves.

## myriorama
myriorama, п., a large picture made up of a
number of small pictures. — Compounded of myri-
and Gk. δράμα, 'that which is seen, view, sight*,
fr. όραν, 'to see1. See cosmorama and cp. words
there referred to.

## myristic
myristic, adj., pertaining to a crystalline acid
(chem.) — See next word.

## Myristica
Myristica, п., a genus of tropical trees (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. μυριστικός, 'fragrant', fr. μυρί-
ζειν, 'to anoint', fr. μύρον, 'sweet oil, unguent'.
See smear and cp. the first element in myro-
balan.

## Myristicaceae
Myristicaceae, п., pi., the nutmeg family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Myristica with suff. -aceae.

## myristicaceous
myristicaceous, adj. — See prec. word and-aceous.

## myrmeco-
myrmeco-, combining form meaning'ant'. — Gk.
μυρμηκο-, fr. μύρμηξ, gen. μύρμηκος, 'ant',
which is cogn. withOl. vamrah, L. formica, 'ant'.
See formic,

## myrmecology
myrmecology, п., that branch of entomology
which deals with ants. — Compounded of
myrmeco- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: myrmecolog-ic-a/y adj., myrme-
colog-ist, n.

## Myrmecophaga
Myrmecophaga, п., a genus of animals, the ant
bear (zool.) — ModL., compounded of
myrmeco- and the stem of Gk. φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See
-phagous.

## Myrmecophagidae
Myrmecophagidae, п., pi., the ant eater family
(zool.) — ModL., formed from prec. word with
sufT. -idae.

## myrmecophagous
myrmecophagous, adj., feeding on ants. —
Compounded of myrmeco- and Gk. -φάγος, 'eater
of, from the stem of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See
-phagous.

## Myrmidon
Myrmidon, п., 1) one of a warlike people of

## Thessaly
Thessaly, subjects of Achilles; 2) (not cap.), an
inferior who executes orders without pity. —
Gk. Μυρμιδόνες, 'the Myrmidons', a warlike

## people of Thessaly
people of Thessaly, lit., 'the people of bugbears',
fr. μύρμος (Hesychius), 'dread, terror'. See
mormo.

## myrobalan
myrobalan, п., the dried astringent fruit of
various tropical trees. — F., fr. L. myrobalanum, fr.
Gk. μυροβάλανον, 'balsam made from a palm
nut\ which is compounded of μύρον, 'sweet

## juice
juice, sweet oil, unguent, balsam', and βάλανος,
'acorn, nut'. For the first element see smear and

## cp. Myristica and the first element in next word
cp. Myristica and the first element in next word,
for the second element see b a la no-.

## Myroxylon
Myroxylon, п., a genus of tropical American
trees (box.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
μύρον, 'sweet juice, sweet oil*, and ξύλον,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:512 COLUMN:2 -->
'wood'. See smear and xylo- and* cp. Myristica
and the first element in prec. word.

## myrrh
myrrh, an aromatic resinous gum. — ME. myrre^
fr.OE- myrro.fr.L.myrr/ia, fr.Gk-μύρρα, 'myrrh,
the juice of the Arabian myrtle', a word of Sem.
origin. Cp. Heb. mort Aram, mora, Syr. тйга,
Arab, murr, Akkad. ти/ти, 'myrrh', lit. 'the gum
with the bitter taste', rel. to Heb. mar (contraction
of marar), Aram.-Syr. mar (contraction of m rar),
Arab., Ethiop. marra 'was bitter', Akkad. ma-
raru, 'to be bitter', Heb. mar, Arab, murr,
Akkad. marru, 'bitter'. Sfee Marah and cp.
Myrica and myrtle.
Derivatives: myrrh-ic, adj., myrrh-y, adj.

## Myrsinaceae
Myrsinaceae, n. pi., a family of tropical trees and
shrubs (bot.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-aceae fr. Gk. μυρσίνη, 'myrtle' (prop. fern, of
the adjective μύρσίνος, 'of the myrtle'), fr.
μύρτος, 'myrtle'. See myrtle.

## myrsinaceous
myrsinaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Myrtaceae
Myrtaceae, n. pi., the myrtle family. — Formed
with suff. -aceae fr. L. myrtus. See Myrtus.

## Myrtilus
Myrtilus, п., the charioteer of Oenomaus (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Μυρτίλος, fr. μυρτίλος,
'of the myrtle', fr. μύρτος. See next word.

## myrtle
myrtle, п., any shrub of the genus Myrtus. — OF.
myrti/le, fr. ML. myrtillus, dimin. formed fr. L.
murtus, myrtus, fr. Gk. μύρτος, 'myrtle', which
is a Sem. loan word of the same origin as Gk.
μύρρα, Lmyrrh'; see Heinrich Lewy, Die semi-
tischen Fremdworter im Griechischen, Berlin,
1895, p. 43. See myrrh and cp. Myrsinaceae,
Myrtus, Myrtilus. Cp. also martello tower.

## Myrtus
Myrtus, п., a genus of plants, the myrtle (bot.) —
L. myrtus, 'myrtle'. See myrtle.

## myself
myself, emphatic pron. of the 1st person sing. —
ME. meself compounded of me, acc.-dat. of
ich, (', T, and self. See me and self.

## Mysidacea
Mysidacea, п., an order of crustaceans (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. Mysidae with suff. -acea.

## Mysidae
Mysidae, n. pi., a family of crustaceans (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk. μύσις,
'a closing (of the lips or eyes'), fr. μυειν. See
1st mystery.

## mystagogic
mystagogic, adj., pertaining to a mystagogue or
mystagogy. — See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## mystagogue
mystagogue, п., a person who initiates into
mysteries. — L. mystagdgus, fr. Gk. μυσταγωγός,
'initiator into mysteries', which is compounded
of μύστης, 'one initiated into the mysteries*,
and αγωγός, 'leading; a leader'. See 1st mystery
and -agogue.

## mystagogy
mystagogy, п., the teachings of a mystagogue. —
See prec. word and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## mysterious
mysterious, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
mysterium. See 1st mystery.
Derivatives: mysterious-ly, adv., mysterious-
ness, n.

## mystery
mystery, п., a secret. — ME. mysterie, fr. L.
mysterium, fr. Gk. μυστήριον, 'secret rite,
mystery', usually in the pi. μυστήρια, 'the mysteries,
secret rites', fr. μύστης, 'one initiated into the
mysteries', prob. meaning lit. 'one whose eyes
are closed', fr. μυειν (for *μύσιειν), 'to be shut
or closed' (said esp. of the lips and eyes); 'to
shut or close the lips or eyes; to shut, close',
which derives fr. μΰ, 'a muttering sound made
with the lips, a groan', from the l.-E. imitative
base *mu-> 'to mutter'. Cp. Lett, mu-s-inat, 'to
murmur, whisper', L. тй (in тй facere, 'to
mutter'), mu-tusy 'dumb', which also derive from
the I.-E. base *mu-, and see mute. Cp. also the
first element in myope, Mysidae, mystagogue,
mystic.

## mystery
mystery, п., a trade, handicraft, guild (arch.) —
ME. mistere, later mistery, fr. ML. misterium,
fr. L. ministerium, 'service', fr. minister, 'servant'.
See minister and cp. ministry and metier, which
are doublets of mystery. ML. misterium was
influenced in form by L. mysterium. See 1st
mystery.

## mystic
mystic, adj., occult, mysterious. — ME. mistik,
fr. L. mysticus, fr. Gk. μυστικός, 'pertaining to
secret rites', prop, 'pertaining to an initiated',
fr. μύστης, 'an initiated'. See 1st mystery and
adj. suff. -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:512 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: mystic, п., mysttc-al, adj., mystic-
al-ly, adv., mystic-ism, n.

## mystification
mystification, n. — See next word and -ation.
"mystify, tr. v., to puzzle; bewilder. — F. mystifier.
See mystic and -fy.

## myth
myth, п., 1) story, legend; 2) a fictitious person.
— Late L. mythos, fr. Gk. μΰθος, *a word,
speech, tale, legend', which is of uncertain
origin.

## mythic
mythic, also mythical, adj. — Late L. mythicus,
fr. Gk. μυθικός, 'mythic, legendary', fr. μΰθος.
See myth and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: mythic-al, adj., mythic-al-ly, adv.

## mythicize
mythicize, tr. v., to make into a myth, treat as a
myth. — See mythic and -ize.

## mythico-
mythico-, combining form meaning 'mythical
and'. — Fr. Gk. μυθικός, 'mythic'. See mythic.

## niytho-
niytho-, combining form meaning 'myth', as in
mythology. — Gk. μύθο-, fr. μΰθος, 'myth'.
See myth.

## mythography
mythography, п., the graphic representation of
myth. — Compounded of mytho- and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write*. See -graphy.

## mythological
mythological, also mythologic, adj., pertaining to
mythology. — Late L. mythologicus, fr. Gk.
μυθολογικός, fr. μυθολογία. See mythology and
-ic, -ical.
Derivative: mythological-ly, adv.

## mythology
mythology, п., 1) the science of myths; 2) a
collection of myths. — Fr. Late L. mythologia
(prob. through ihe medium of F. mythologie), fr.
Gk. μυθολογία, which is compounded of
μΰθος, 'word, speech, tale, legend', and -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
-logy.
Derivatives: mytholog-isU п., mytholog-ize, intr.
v., mytholog-\z-er, n.

## mythomania
mythomania, п., a morbid tendency to lie and
exaggerate (med,) — Medical L., compounded
of mytho- and Gk. μανία, 'madness, frenzy'.
See mania.
Derivative: mythomani-ac, n. and adj.

## mythopoeic
mythopoeic, mythopeic, adj., making myths. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. μΰθοποιός,
'mythmaking', which is compounded of μύθος,
'word speech, tale, legend', and the stem of
7toLEiv, 'to make'. See p*oet.

## mythopoetic
mythopoetic, adj., mythopoeic. — Compounded
of mytho- and Gk. ποιητικός, 'capable of
making; pertaining to poetry, poetical'. See
poetic.

## Mytilus
Mytilus, п., a genus of marine mussels (zool.) —
L. mytiluSy fr. Gk. μϋτίλος, 'sea mussel', which
prob. derives fr. μΰς, 'mouse; mussel'. See
mouse and cp. niche.
тух-, form of myxo- before a vowel.

## myxedema
myxedema, myxoedema, п., a morbid condition
of the skin caused by a mucoid substance (med.)
— Medical L., coined by William Miller Ord
(1834-i902)inl877 fr.Gk.μύξα,'mucus of the
nose, slime', and οϊδημα, *a swelling*. See
myxo- and edema.

## Myxine
Myxine, п., a genus of fishes, the typical hagfish
(ichthyol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. μυξΐνος, 'slime
fish*, fr. μύξα, 'slime'. See myxo-.

## myxo-
myxo-, before a vowel тух-, combining form

## meaning 'slime
meaning 'slime, mucus', as in Myxomycetes
(med.) — Gk. μυξο-, μυξ-, fr. μύξα, 'mucus

## of the nose
of the nose, slime'. See myco- and ср. Муха,

## myxoma
myxoma, п., a tumor made up of mucous tissue
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. тух- and suff.
-oma.
Derivative: myxomat-oust adj.

## myxomatosis
myxomatosis, п., the presence of myxomas in the
body (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. myxoma
with suff. -osis.

## Myxomycetes
Myxomycetes, п., pi., the slime molds (bot.) —

## ModL.
ModL., compounded of myxo- and -mycetes.

## Myzostoma
Myzostoma, п., a genus of parasitic animals
(zool.)— ModL., compounded of Gk. μύζειν, 'to

## suck'
suck', and στόμα, 'mouth*. The first element
stands for *μύδιειν, and is rel. to μύδος, 'damp,

## clamminess'. See mother
clamminess'. See mother, 'dregs', and words
there referred to and cp. esp. Mydaus. For the
second element see stoma.

## Naaman
Naaman, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, an Ara-
mean general cured of leprosy by Elisha. — Heb.
Na'amdn, lit. 'pleasantness', from the stem of
nd'em 'was pleasant or lovely', whence also
nd'im, 'pleasant, lovely', nolam, 'pleasantness,
loveliness', and the PN's Na'dmah, Nogdmt; rel.
to Arab, na'ima, 'was easy or pleasant', driama,
'he granted a favor, favored'. Cp. enam, Naomi.
Cp. also anemone.

## Naassenes
Naassenes, п., pi., a sect of Gnostics who regarded
the serpent as the symbol of wisdom. They were
called also Ophites. — Fr. Heb. ndhdsh,
'serpent', which is rel. to Arab. hdnash, 'serpent,
viper'.

## nab
nab, tr. v., to seize, catch. — Prob. a var. of dial.
E. nap, 'to seize', which is of Scand. origin; cp.
Dan. nappe, 'to pinch', Swed. and Norw. nappa,
'to snatch'. Cp. also the second element in
kidnap. Cp. also nobble.
Derivative: nabb-er, n.

## Nabataean
Nabataean, Nabatean, п., 1) a member of an
ancient people of Arabia; 2) the Aramaic dialect
spoken by this people. —■ Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. Nabataeus, fr. Gk. Ναβαταΐος, fr. Arab.
Ndbatu, which is usually connected with Ne-
baioth, the first-born son of Ishmael (see Gen.
25 : 13). See Gesenius-Buhl, HWAT., p. 480.
Derivative: Nabat(d)ean, adj.

## nabk
nabk, n„ Christ's-thorn. — Arab. ndbiqa1'.

## nabla
nabla, п., an ancient musical instrument. — Gk.
νάβλα, fr. Aram, nabhla, fr. Heb. nebhel, name
of a stringed instrument, fr. nebhel, 'a large jar';
so called after its original shape.

## nabob
nabob, п., 1) a native deputy in India; 2) a
European who has come home from India with a
great fortune; 3) a very rich man. — Hind.
nawwdb, nabob, fr. Arab, nuwwab, pi. of na'ib,
'deputy, proxy, lieutenant governor', prop. act.
part, of naba (fr. base n-w-b), 'he took a person's
place'. The pi. nuwwab is used as a plural of
dignity and has, accordingly, singular meaning.
Cp. nawab.

## nacarat
nacarat, п., 1) the color geranium lake; 2) fine
crepe or linen of this color. — Sp. nacarado, fr.
nacar, 'mother-of-реагГ. See 1st nacre.

## nacelle
nacelle, п., 1) the basket attached to a balloon;
2) part of an airship containing the engines, crew,
cargo, etc. — F., fr. VL. naucella, fr. Late L.
navicella(whence also It. navicella),'a little ship',
dimin. of L. ndvis, 'ship'. See naval and -ella.

## nacre
nacre, п., mother-of-pearl. — F., fr. It. пассат
(now nacchera), fr. Arab, naqqara11, 'a drum', fr.
ndqra , 'hollow, cavity', fr. naqara, 'he hollowed
out, bored out', which is rel. to Heb. naqar,
Aram.-Syr. neqar, 'he bored, bored out, dug',
Heb. niqrd or neqdra , 'hole, crevice', Ethiop.
naqvdra, 'he was one-eyed', Akkad. naqdru, 'to
pull down, destroy'. Cp. naker.
Derivatives: nacr-ed, nacre-ous, adjs.

## nacre
nacre, adj., iridescent like nacre. — F. nacre, pp.
of nacrer, 'to give a pearly luster to', fr. nacre.
See nacre, n.

## nadir
nadir, п., the point opposite the zenith; the point
directly under one's feet; the lowest point. —
ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. Arab, nazir in the term
nazir assamt, lit. '(the point) opposite to the
zenith', fr. ndzara, 'he looked at; he considered,
examined', which is rel. to Heb. ndlzdr, 'he watch-
,ed over, guarded', Aram.-Syr. nl{ar, of s.m.,
Ethiop. nasdra, 'he looked at, observed', Akkad.
nasdru, 'to watch over, protect'. Cp. nazir.

## nadorite
nadorite, п., a lead chloride and stibnite {mineral.)
— Named after Jebel Nador in the department
of Constantine in Algeria. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## naevus
naevus, n. — See nevus.

## nag
nag, п., a small riding horse, pony. — ME. nagge,
rel. to Du. negge, neg.

## nag
nag, v., to worry persistently. — Of Scand. origin.
Cp. ON. gnaga, dial. Swed. and Norw. nagga.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:513 COLUMN:2 -->
'to gnaw', which are rel. to OE. gnagan, 'to
gnaw'. See gnaw.
Derivatives: nag, п., nagg-er, п., nagg-ing, n. and
adj., nagg-ing-ly, adv., nagg-ing-ness, n.

## Naga
Naga, п., a mythical being with a human face and
the tail of a serpent (Hindu mythol.) — OI.
ndgdh, 'serpent', of uncertain origin.

## nagana
nagana, п., an infectious cattle disease caused by
the tsetse fly. — From Zulu name.

## Nagari
Nagari, п., Devanagari. — OI. ndgari '(the script
of) the city', prob. of Dravidian origin; cp.
Tamil nakar, 'house, palace, temple, dwelling,
town, city', Telugu nagaru, 'palace'. Cp. the
second element in Devanagari.

## nagor
nagor, п., a West African antelope. — F., coined
by the French naturalist Comte Georges-Louis
Leclerc de Buffon (1707-88).

## nagyagite
nagyagite, п., a sulild of lead, gold, tellurium and
antimony (mineral.) — G. Nagyagit, named in
1845 by the Austrian mineralogist Wilhelm Karl
von Haidinger (1795-1871) after Nagydg in
Hungary (now Sdcardmbu in Romania). The
ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Nahuatl
Nahuatl, п., the language of the Aztecs. — Sp.,
fr. Nahuatl.
Derivatives: Nahuatt-an, adj. and n.

## Nahum
Nahum, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the seventh
in the order of the Twelve Prophets; he lived in
the 7th cent. B.C.E. and predicted the downfall
of Niniveh (which took place in 612). — Heb.
Nahum, lit. 'rich in comfort, comforter', from
the stem n-h-m, 'to be sorry, repent,
console oneself, whence nibdm, 'he comforted,
consoled', ndham, 'repentance', η hdmah,
'comfort, consolation', tanhum, 'consolation'; rel.
to Arab, ndhama, 'he breathed pantingly'.
Cp. Nehemiah.

## naiad
naiad, п., a water nymph (Greek mythol.) — L.
ndias, gen. naiadis, fr. Gk. ναΐάς, ναΐάδος,
'river nymph, water nymph'; rel. to νάω (for
NaFioi), Ί flow', fr. I.-E. "sndu-, whence also
OI. snduti, 'drips'. I.-E. "sndu- is an enlarged
form of base *snd-, seen in L. no, ndre, 'to swim*.
See natation and words there referred to and cp.
esp. Nama.

## Naiadaceae
Naiadaceae, п., pi., the pondweed family (hot.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. L. ndias,
gen. naiadis. See prec. word.

## naiadaceous
naiadaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## naiant
naiant, adj., swimming (said of a fish represented
horizontally) (her.) — OF. noiant (through the
medium of AF. "naiant), pres. part of noier,
noer, 'to swim', fr. VL. "nautdre, a blend of L.
nauta, 'sailor', and natdre, 'to swim'. See
natation and -ant.

## Nalas
Nalas, п., a genus of aquatic plants (bot.) — L.
ndias, 'a naiad'. See naiad.

## naif
naif, adj., naive. — See naive.

## naik
naik, naique, п., 1) a title of honor; 2) a native
non-commissioned officer in the British India
army. — Hind, ndyak, fr. OI. ndyakah, 'leader,
chief, general', fr. ndyati, 'leads', which is rel. to
Avestic nayeiti, 'leads', and cogn. with Hitt.
ndi-, ne-, 'to guide, lead', Mir. ne, nia, 'hero,
warrior'.

## nail
nail, п., 1) the horny substance on the ends of the
fingers and toes; 2) a small spike of metal or
wood. — ME. naite, neil, fr. OE. nxgt, nasgel,
'fingernail; metal nail, peg', jel. to OS., OHG.
nagal, OFris. neil, MDu. naghel, Du., MHG.,
G. nagel, 'fingernail; metal nail', ON. nagl,
'fingernail', nagli, 'metal nail', Goth, ganagljan, 'to
nail', fr. I.-E. base "nogho-. *ngho-, *ongho-,
'nail', whence also OI. anghrih, amhrih, 'foot',
Gk. ονυξ, L. unguis, 'nail, claw', OSlav. noga,
Russ. noga, Czech and Slovak noha, 'foot', Lith.
naga, 'hoof, ndgas, Lett, nags, 'nail', OPruss.
nage, 'foot', OSlav. nogitti, 'nail, claw', Lith.
nagutis, OPruss. nagutis, 'fingernail', Olr. ingen,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:513 COLUMN:3 -->
OW. eguin, W., Co., ewin, Bret, twin, 'nail, claw'.
Cp. OI. nakhdh, Pers. ndxun, 'nail, claw', where
qh- (for gh-) is prob. due to Caucasian influence.
— Cp. agnail. Cp. also onyx, ungual.
Derivatives: nail, v. (q.v.), nail-less, adj.

## nail
nail, tr. v., to fasten with a nail or nails. — ME.
nailen, fr. OE. meglian, fr. nseget, 'nail'; rel. to
OS. neglian, ON. negla, OHG. negilen, MHG.
negelen, nagelen, G. nageln, Goth, ganagljan, 'to
nail'. See nail, n.
Derivatives: nail-er, п., nail-ery, п., nail-ing, adj.

## nainsook
nainsook, п., a fine cotton fabric. — Hind, nain-
sukh, compounded of nain, 'eye', and sukh,
'pleasure'. The first element derives fr. OI.
nayanam, 'eye', which is prob. a derivative of
I.-E.base*ffi"-,'to shine', whencepossibly also OI.
nilah, 'blue, dark blue'; see lilac. The second
element comes fr. OI. sukhdh, 'ease, comfort,
pleasure, enjoyment'.

## naive
naive, naive, adj., natural, ingenuous, innocent,
artless. — F. naive, fern, of naif, fr. L. ndtivus,
'born, innate, natural, not artificial'. See native.
Derivatives: naive-ly, adv., nalve-ness, n.

## naivete
naivete, also naivete, п., ingenuousness, artless-
ness. — F. naivete, fr. naif, fern, naive. See prec.
word and cp. nativity.

## naivety
naivety, n. — Anglicized form of F. naivete. See
prec. word.

## naked
naked, adj., entirely unclothed; bare; nude. —
ME. naked, fr. OE. nacod, rel. to OFris. nakad,
MDu. naket, Du. naakt, OHG. nackot, nackut,
MHG. nacket, G. nackt, ON. nokkvidr, OSwed.
nakuper, Goth, naqaps, 'naked', fr. 1-Е. *nog*O-
dho-\ cogn. with L. nudus [fr. *now(e)dos, for
I.-E. *nogwedhos], Olr. nocht, W. noeth, Bret.
noaz (for *nogwtos), 'naked'. Cp.—with
-no-formative element—ON. nakinn, Swed., Norw.,
OFris. naken, Dan. negen, and OI. nagnah,
Avestic mayna- (prob. dissimilated fr. *ηαγηά-),
'naked'. Cp. also OSlav. nagu (for 'nog™-), Lith.
nuogas (for *ndgo-), and Gk. γυμνός, also
λυμνός (Hesychius), which prob. owe their
forms to dissimilation (see Boisacq, DELG., p.
158 s.v. γυμνός, Hofmann, EWG., p. 49 s.v.
γυμνός, and Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, p.
185 s.v. nudus). Hitt. nekumanza and Arm. merk
(for *megwro-; cp. Avestic mayna-) are cogn.
with the above words (see Frisk, GEW., I,
p. 333 s.v. γυμνός). Ср. gymno-, nnde.

## naker
naker, п., a kettledrum. — ME. nakere, fr. OF.
nacre, fr. It. nacchera, 'kettledrum', fr. Arab.
naqqara11, 'drum'. See I st nacre.

## Nakshatra
Nakshatra, п., lunar asterisms; daughters of
Daksha and wives of the moon in Hindu mythol.
— OI. ndksatra-, lit. 'rulers of the night', fr. ndk
(for *nakt), 'night', and ksatrdm, 'rule'. For the
first element see night. The second element is rel.
to OI. ksdyati, 'rules, possesses', and cogn. with
Gk. κτάομαι, Ί get, acquire'. See check, 'a
sudden stop', and cp. shah.

## Nama
Nama, п., a genus of plants also called Hydrolea
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. νϊμα, 'stream', lit.
'anything flowing', fr. νάω, Ί flow'. See naiad.

## namable
namable, nameable, adj., capable of being named.
— Formed fr. name, v., with suff. -able.
Derivative: nam-abil-ity, name-abil-ity, n.

## namda
namda, numda, п., a felt rug, a saddlecloth (India)
— Hind, namdd, fr. Pers. namad, 'felt'.

## namby-pamby
namby-pamby, adj., insipid, feebly sentimental.
— Formed from the name of Ambrose Philips
(16757-1749), in ridicule of his pastoral poems.
Derivatives: namby-pamby, п., namby-pamb-ic-
al, adj., namby-pamb-i-ness, п., namby-pamby·
ish, adj., namby-pamby-ism, n.

## name
name, n. — ME. name, fr. OE. nama, rel. to
OFris. nama, OS., OHG. namo, MDu., MHG.,
G. name, Du. naam, ON. nafn (for *namn), Dan.
navn. Swed. and Norw. namn, Goth, namo,
'name', fr. I.-E. base *enomen, *onomen, "no-

## men
men, whence also OI. noma, Avestic ndmaJOch.

Derivatives: name, v. (q.v.), name-less, adj.,

## name
name, tr. v. — ME. namen, fr. OE. namian, fr.
nama, 'name'. See name, n.
Derivatives: name-able, пат-able, adjs., name-
abil-ity, п., nam-abil-ity, п., nam-er, n.

## namesake
namesake, п., a person having the same name as
an other. — Contraction of name's sake.
Namesake lit. denotes 'a person named for the sake of
another's name4.

## nan-
nan-, form of nano-, before a vowel.

## Nancy
Nancy, fem. PN. — Prob. from a misdivision of
mine Ancy into my Nancy. Ancy is a dimin. form
of ME. Annis, 'Agnes'. See Agnes. For a similar
misdivision cp. Nanny.

## nanism
nanism, п., dwarflshness. — F. nanisme, formed
with suff. -isme fr. L. nanus, fr. Gk. νάνος, νάν-
νος, 'dwarf, which is of uncertain etymology.
It is perh. a child's lip word and rel. to νάννϊς,
νέννος, 'uncle', νάννα, 'aunt'. See nun and -ism.

## nankeen
nankeen, also nankin, п., a kind of cotton cloth.
— From Nankin, name of a town in China; so
called because orig. made at Nankin.

## nano-
nano-, before a vowel nan-, combining form
meaning 'dwarf, dwarfish'. — Gk. νάνο-, ναν-,
fr. νάνος, 'dwarf. See nanism.

## Nanny
Nanny, fem. PN. — Dimin. of Nan, which prob.
arose from a misdivision of mine Ann into my
Nan. See Ann. For a similar misdivision cp.
Nancy.

## nanny goat
nanny goat, a she-goat (colloq.) — Formed fr.
prec. word and goat,

## naology
naology, η., the study of temples and other sacred
places. — Compounded of Gk. ναός, 'temple',
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See naos and -logy.

## Naomi
Naomi, 1) fem. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the mother-
in-law of Ruth. — Heb. No'dmt, lit. 'my
delight', fr. no'am, 'pleasantness, delightfulness',
from the stem of nd'em, 'was pleasant'. See
Naaman and cp. enarn.

## naos
naos, п., 1) a temple; 2) the cella (Greek antiquity;
archit.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ναός (Ion. νηός,
Att. νεώς), 'temple; the inner part of a temple,
the shrine, the cella', which is of uncertain
origin. It stands perh. for *νασΓός and is rel. to
ναίω (for *νάσιω), Ί dwell', hence prop,
denotes 'the dwelling place of a god'. See nostalgia
and cp. pronaos.

## nap
nap, intr. v., to have a short sleep. — ME. nappen,
fr. OE. hnappian, hnseppian, rel. to OHG. hnaffe-
zan, MHG. napfen.
Derivative: пар, п., a short sleep.

## uap
uap, п., a downy surface of cloth. — ME. noppe,
MDu. noppe (Du. nop), rel. to OE. hnoppian, 'to
pluck, tear', й-hneopan, 'to pluck', OSwed. niu-

## pa
pa, 'to pinch', Goth, dis-hniupan, 'to tear'.
пар, п., a card game. — Shortened fr. napoleon.

## Napaea
Napaea, п., a genus of plants, the glade mallow
(bot.) — L. Napaea, 'a dell nymph', fr. Gk. va-
παϊος, 'belonging to a woodland vale', fr. νάπη,
'woodland vale', which is prob. of pre-Hellenic
origin.
паре, п., the back of the neck. — ME. naape,
nape, of uncertain origin,

## napery
napery, п., household linen, esp. table linen. —
ME., fr. OF. naperie, fr. nap(p)e (F. nappe), dis-
similated form of mappe, fr. L. mappa,
'tablecloth, napkin'. See map and cp. nappe, napkin,
apron. For the ending see suff. -ery.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:514 COLUMN:2 -->

## Naphtali
Naphtali, п., Bible, I) a son of Jacob; 2) the tribe
named after him. — Gk. Νεφθαλείμ, fr. Heb.
Naphtali, fr. naphtHlim, 'wrestlings', fr. niphtal,
'he wrestled', Niph'al (= passive) of the verb
pathal, 'he twisted'; see Gen. 30:8. Cp.Aram.-
Syr. pathal, 'he twisted, distorted', Ethiop. fa-
tdla, 'he turned, twisted', Akkad. patalu, 'to
wind, sling'.

## naphtha
naphtha, п., an inflammable liquid distilled from
petroleum. — L., fr. Gk. νάφ&α, fr. Aram.
naphtd, nephta (whence also Arab, naft, Pers.
neft), fr. Akkad. naptu, 'naphtha'. See Heinrich
Zimmern, Akkadische Fremdwdrter als Beweis
