fur babylonischen KultureinfluB, 2nd edition,
Leipzig, 1917, p. 60.

## naphthalene
naphthalene, п., a white crystalline hydrocarbon,
C10H8 (chem.) — Orig. naphthaline, coined by
John Kidd fr. naphtha and chem. suff. -ine. The
/ was inserted for the sake of euphony. For the
ending of naphthalene see suff. -ene. Cp. phtha-
lein(e), phthalin.

## naphthol
naphthol, п., either of two white crystalline
compounds used as antiseptics and in making dyes,
CJ0H7OH (chem.) — Coined by the English
chemist John Kidd (1775-1851) from prec.
word and 1st suff. -o].

## naphthyl
naphthyl, п., the univalent radical, C]0H. (chem.)
— Formed fr. naphtha with suff. -yl.

## napiform
napiform, adj., turnip-shaped (bot.) —
Compounded of L. napus, 'turnip', and forma, 'form,
shape'. For the first element see navew and cp.
parsnip, turnip. For the second element see form,
n.

## napkin
napkin, n. — ME. nappekin, napekin, formed with
dimin. suff. -kin fr. nappe, nape, fr. OF. nappe,
nape. See napery and -kin.
Derivative: napkin, tr. v.

## napoleon
napoleon, п., a former gold coin equivalent to 20
francs.—So called because struck by Napoleonl.

## napoleon
napoleon, п., a card game. — Named after
Napoleon i: Cp. nap, 'a card game'.

## Napoleonic
Napoleonic, adj., 1) pertaining to Napoleon I
(1769-1821) or his period; 2) resembling
Napoleon I.

## napoo
napoo, napooh, inter]., meaning 'no more, no
good, useless, all over'. —■ Corrupted fr. F. it
n'y a plus, 'there is no more'.

## nappe
nappe, п., a sheet. — F., 'tablecloth, cloth, cover,
sheet', dissimilated (under the influence of the
following p) from mappe. See napery.

## nappy
nappy, adj., downy. — Formed with adj. suff. -y
fr. nap, 'a downy surface' (q.v.)

## nappy
nappy, adj., 1) strong (said of ale); 2) tipsy; п.,
ale (Scot.) — Of uncertain origin; perhaps from
prec. word.
пари, п., any of various chevrotains of Java and
Sumatra. — Malay.

## Naraka
Naraka, п., hell (Hinduism) — OI. Narakah, fr.
I.-E. base *ner-, 'below; to the left', whence also
Gk. ё-νεροι, 'those below', ϊ-νερ*εν, 'from
beneath', νέρτερος, έ-νέρτερος, 'nether, infernal',
ON. nordr, OE. nord, 'north' (prop, left, when
facing east). See north.

## narceine
narceine, п., a bitter, white crystalline alkaloid,
C3iH3J08N (chem.) — F. narceine, coined by the
French pharmacist Pierre-Joseph Pelletier
(1788-1842) in 1832 fr. Gk. νάρκη, 'numbness'.
See narcotic and chem. suff. -ine.

## narcissism
narcissism, п., morbid self-love (psychoanalysis).
— G. Narzissismus, coined by the Jewish
physician Sigmund Freud (1856-1939), founder of
psychoanalysis, fr. Narcissus and suff. -izm.

## narcissist
narcissist, n. — See prec. word and -1st
Derivative: narcissist-ic, adj.

## Narcissus
Narcissus, п., a beautiful Greek youth who fell in
love with his own reflection. He pined away with
desire and was changed into the flower bearing
his name (Greek mythot.) — L., fr. Gk.
Νάρκισσος. See next word.

## Narcissus
Narcissus, п., a genus of bulbous plants (bot.);
(not cap.) any plant of this genus. — L. narcissus,
fr. Gk. νάρκισσος, 'narcissus', which is prob. of
Aegean origin but was assimilated to νάρκη,
'numbness' (in allusion to the sedative properties
of this plant). Cp. prec. word.

## narcolepsy
narcolepsy, п., recurring attacks of sleep (med.)
— F. narcolepsie, coined by the French
physician Jean-Baptiste-Edouard Gelineau (1859-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:514 COLUMN:3 -->
1928) in 1880 fr. Gk. νάρκη, 'numbness', and
ληψις, 'a taking, seizing, seizure'. See narcotic
and lemma and cp. words there referred to.

## narcoleptic
narcoleptic, adj., pertaining to, or affected with,
narcolepsy. — Formed fr. narcolepsy, to which
it stands as the adj. epileptic stands to the n.
epilepsy.

## narcomania
narcomania, п., an abnormal craving for a
narcotic drug. — Medical L., compounded of Gk.
νάρκη, 'numbness', and μανία, 'madness,
frenzy'. See narcotic and mania.
Derivatives: narcomani-ac, п., narcomani-ac-al,
adj.

## narcosis
narcosis, п., state of unconsciousness caused by
a narcotic (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. νάρ-
κωσις, 'a benumbing', fr. τίαρκοϋν, 'to benumb'.
See narcotic and -osis.

## narcotic
narcotic, adj., producing insensibility. — F. nar-
cotique, introduced into French in 1314 by Mon-
deville fr. ML. narcdticus, fr. Gk. ναρκωτικός,
'benumbing', fr. ναρκωτός, verbal adj. of ναρ-
κοΰν, 'to benumb', fr. νάρκη, 'numbness',
prop, 'a cramp', fr. I.-E. *(s)ner-q-, 'to turn,
twist', whence also Arm. nergev, 'fine, thin,
slender, slim', prop, 'shriveled up*; see Hof-
mann, EWG., pp. 211-12 s.v. νάρκη. I.-E.
*(s)ner-q- is a -^-enlargement of base *(s)ner-,
'to turn, twist, bind together', whence OE.
sneare, 'snare', nearu, 'narrow'. See snare and
cp. narrow. For the ending of narcotic see suff.
-otic.
Derivatives: narcotic, п., narcotic-al-ly, adv.,
narcotism (q.v.), narcotize (q.v.)

## narcotine
narcotine, also narcotin, п., an alkaloid found in
opium, C!2H23NO„ discovered by the French
chemist Charles Derosne (1780-1846) in 1803
(chem.) — See prec. word and chem. suff. -ine,
-in; so called because it was first supposed to be
the narcotic principle. Cp. cotarnine.

## narcotism
narcotism, п., 1) narcosis; 2) condition produced
by narcotic poisoning. — See narcotic and -ism.

## narcotize
narcotize, tr. v., to produce the condition of
narcosis ; to stupefy. — See narcotic and -ize.
Derivative: narcotiz-ation, n.

## nard
nard, п., spikenard. — ME. narde, fr. OF. narde
(¥. nard), fr. L. nardus, fr. Gk. νάρδος, fr. Heb.
nerdh, 'nard', which together with Aram, nirda
and Akkad. lardu of s.m., prob. derives fr. Indo-
Iranian "narda in OI. nadah, nalah, 'reed'. OI.
ndladam, 'nard', is possibly Sanskritization of
Gk. νάρδος; see Boisacq, DELG., p. 657 s.v.
νάρδος, and Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, 143
s.v. nardus. However, according to Manfred
Mayrhofer, A Concise Etymological Sanskrit
Dictionary, II, p. 140 s.v. ndladam, the above
Sem. words more prob. derive fr. OI. ndladam.
Cp. Nardius and the second element in
spikenard. Cp. also narthex.

## nares
nares, n. pi., the nostrils (anat.) — L. nares, pi. of
naris, 'nostril', which stands for "nasis (see rho-
tacism), fr. I.-E. base *nds-, whence also OE.
nosu, 'nose'. See nose and cp. nasal, nasion,
nasturtium, nasute.

## narghile
narghile, nargile, п., hookah, an Oriental pipe. —
Pers. nargil, 'coconut tree'; prob. fr. OI. narike-
rah, narikelafr, of s.m., which is of uncertain,
possibly Dravidian, origin; so called because
orig. narghiles were made of coconut shells.

## narial
narial, adj., pertaining to the nares. — Formed
fr. nares with suff. -ial.

## nark
nark, п., spy, informer, stool pigeon (British slang).
— From Gypsy nak, 'nose', fr. Hind, nak,
'nose', fr. OI. nakra, fr. Prakrit nakka-, nakka-,

## of s.m.
of s.m., which prob. stand for *nas-ka- and are

## rel. to OI. nasa (dual)
rel. to OI. nasa (dual), 'nose'. See nose,

## narrate
narrate, tr. v., to relate, recount. — L. narrdtus,

## pp. of narrare
pp. of narrare, 'to tell, relate, recount', prop, 'to
make acquainted with*, fr. *gndra~re, "narare,

## fr. gnarus
fr. gnarus, narus, 'acquainted with, knowing', fr.
I.-E. base *gno-, 'to know*, whence also OE.

## cndwan
cndwan, 'to know'. See know and words there
referred to and cp. esp. ignore. For the ending
see verbal suff. -ate. The doubling of the
consonant -r- in narrare is a compensation for the
shortening of the vowel δ in gnarus.

## narration
narration, n. — ME. narraciun, fr. MF. (= F.)

## narration
narration, 'a relating, recounting, narrating', fr.

## L. narrationem
L. narrationem, асе. of narratio, of s.m., fr. nar-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:515 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NARRATIVE | 488 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:515 COLUMN:1 -->
rdtus, pp. of narrare. See prec. word and -ion.

## narrative
narrative, adj., 1) that which narrates; 2)
pertaining to narration. — Late L. narrdtivus,
'suitable for narration' (prob. through the medium
of F. narratif), fr. L. narratus, pp. of narrare.
See narrate and -ive.
Derivative: narrative-ly, adv.

## narrative
narrative, п., a tale, story. — MF., from the adj.
narrative, fem. of narratif. See narrative, adj.

## narrator
narrator, п., relater, narrator. — L. narrator, fr.
narratus, pp. of narrare. See narrate and agential
suff. -or.

## narrow
narrow, adj., of small breadth. — ME. narewe,
narwe, nam, fr. OE. nearu, rel. to OS. naro,
MDu. nare; orig. prob. meaning 'twisted up,
shriveled up', fr. I.-E. base *(s)ner-, 'to turn,
twist, bind together', whence also OE. sneare,
'snare'. See snare and cp. narcotic.
Derivatives: narrow, n. and tr. and intr. v.,
narrow-er, п., narrow-ly, adv., narrowness, n.

## narthex
narthex, п., a porch at the west end of early
Christian churches for the use of penitents not
admitted to the body of the church (archil.) —
L., 'giant fennel, small casket for unguents', fr.
Gk. νάρθηξ, which is of uncertain origin. It
derives perh. fr. Ol. *narda-, 'reed', see nard.
The porch was called narthex from the alleged
resemblance to the reedlike stem of the giant
fennel.

## narwhal
narwhal, narwal, п., an arctic whale with a long
spiral horn. — Dan., Norw. narhral, or Swed.
narval, metathesized fr. ON. ndhvalr, lit. 'corpse-
whale', fr. ndr, 'corpse', and hvalr, 'whale'; prob.
so called in allusion to the whitish color of the
skin. ON. nar is rel. to OE. пё, пёо, Goth, naus,
'corpse', and cogn. with OCo. naun, OSlav. nan,
OPruss. nowis, 'corpse', Lett, ndwe,- 'death',
Lith. ndvyti, 'to torture, kill'. For the etymology
of ON. hvalr see whale.

## nary
nary, adj., never a (dial.) — Corruption of ne'er a,
'never a4.

## nasal
nasal, adj., 1) pertaining to the nose; 2) uttered
through the nose (said of sounds). — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. nasus, 'nose', which is
rel. to naris for *ndsis, 'nostril'. See nares and
cp. orinasal.
Derivatives: nasal, n.,nasal-ity, п., nasat-ly, adv.,
nasal-ize, tr. and intr. v., nasal-iz-arion, n.

## nascence
nascence, n. — See nascency,

## nascency
nascency, п., the process of being born; birth. —
L. ndscentia, fr. ndscens, gen. -entis. See next
word and -cy.

## nascent
nascent, adj., being born. — L. nascens, gen.
•entis, 'being born', pres. part, of ndscor, ndsct,
'to be born' (pp. ndtus). See nation and -ent.

## naseberry
naseberry, п., 1) the sapodilla tree; 2) its fruit. —
Corruption of Sp. nespera, 'medlar', fr. L. mespi-
lus, fr. Gk. μεσπίλη, 'medlar (the tree)'. See
medlar.

## Nashim
Nashim, п., pi., the third order of the Mishnah,
dealing with the laws concerning women, i.e.,
marriage and divorce. — Heb. nashim, 'women'
(used as the plural of ishshah); prob. assimilated
in form to the rel. dndshtm, 'men'; rel. to Aram.
neshayyd, Syr. neshshe, Arab, nisuna, 'women',
and to Heb. indsh, 'man, mankind', Aram.
enosh, Syr. (d)ndsha, Arab, ins, unas, 'men,
people' (all collective). Akkad. nishu, 'people',
tenisheti (pi.), 'human race, mankind', Arab.
nas, 'people' (collective).

## nasi
nasi, п., 1) prince of a tribe; 2) the president of
the Sanhedrin; 3) patriarch. — Heb. nasi, lit.
'one lifted up or exalted', fr. ndsa, 'he lifted,
took, carried', whence also nesiim, 'vapors,
clouds', massa, 'load, burden; utterance',
mas'eth, 'present, gift', si (for nlsi), 'loftiness',
s'e/A, 'rising; dignity'; rel. to Bibl.-Aram. nsid,
'he lifted, carried', Syr. massdthd, 'balance,
scales', Ugar. nsh\ 'to lift', Ethiop. nash'a, 'he
lifted; he transported', Arab, ndsha'a, 'he rose,
was high, he grew up', Akkad. nashu, 'to lift,
carry'. Cp. munshi.

## nasion
nasion, п., point in the skull where the frontal and
two nasal bones meet (craniometry). — ModL.,
fr. L. nasus, 'nose'. See nasal.

## nasitis
nasitis, п., inflammation of the nose (med.) — A
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. nasus, 'nose'
(see nasal), and -itis, a suff. of Greek origin. The

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:515 COLUMN:2 -->
correct form is rhinitis (q.v.)

## naso-
naso-, combining form meaning 'nose; nasal;
nasal and' (anat.) — Fr. L. nasus, 'nose'. See
nasal.

## nasofrontal
nasofrontal, adj., pertaining to the nose and the
frontal bone. — See naso- and frontal.

## nasology
nasology, п., the study of the nose. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. nasus, 'nose', and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See naso-
and -logy. The correct form is rhinology, in
which both elements are of Greek origin.
Derivatives: nasolog-ic-al, adj., nasolog-ist, n.

## nasonite
nasonite, п., a lead calcium silicate with chloride
(mineral) — Named after the American
geologist Frank L. Nason (died in 1928). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## nasturtium
nasturtium, п., 1) any plant of the genus Roripa;
2) any plant of the genus Tropaeolum. — L.
nasturtium, 'cress', for *nas-tortium, lit. 'nose-
twister', compounded of nasus, 'nose', and * tor-
tare, freq. of torquere (pp. tortus), 'to twist'; so
called from its pungent smell. See nasal and
torque.

## nasty
nasty, adj., dirty, foul, filthy, nauseous. — ME.
nasty, nasky, perh. derived from or rel. to Du.
nestig, 'foul, dirty', or of Scand. origin; cp. dial.
Swed. naskug, nasket, 'foul, dirty'.
Derivatives: nasti-ly, adv., nasti-ness, n.

## nasute
nasute, adj., having a large or long nose (zool.) —
L. nasutus, 'having a large nose', fr. nasus. See
nasal.
Derivatives: nasute, n. (q.v.), nasute-ness, n.

## nasute
nasute, п., one of a class of termites (zool.) —
ModL. nasutus, 'having a prolongation on the
front of the head' (said esp. of termites), fr. L.
nasutus, 'having a large nose'. See nasute, adj.

## nasutus
nasutus, п., nasute. — L. nusutus, 'having a large
nose'. See nasute, adj.

## natability
natability, п., capability pi floating. — Formed
with suff. -ity fr. Late L. natdbilis, 'capable 6f
floating', fr. L. nature, 'to swim, float'. See
natation.

## natal
natal, adj., pertaining to one's birth. — ME., fr.
L. natalis, 'pertaining to one's birth', fr. ndtus,
pp. of ndsci, 'to be born'. See nation and adj.
suff. -al and cp. Natalia, natality, Noel.

## Natalia
Natalia, Natalie, fem. PN. — F. Natalie, fr.
Eccles. L. Natalia, fr. L. (dies) natalis, 'birthday',
in Eccles. L. used also in the sense 'Christmas
Day'; orig. given to children born on Christmas.
See natal and cp. Noel.

## natality
natality, п., 1) birth (rare);!) birth rate. —
Formed with suff. -ity fr. L. natalis, 'pertaining to
birth'; see natal. In the sense 'birth rate' the
word was formed directly fr. F. natalite, which
derives from the adj. natal (fr. L. natalis).

## natant
natant, adj., floating. — Fr. L.,natdns, gen. -antis,
pres. part, of nature, 'to swim'. See next word
and -ant.
Derivative: natant-ly, adv.

## natation
natation, п., the act or art of swimming. — L.
natatio, gen. -onis, 'a swimming', fr. natdtus, pp.
of nato, nature, 'to swim', which stands for I.-E.
*sn -t-ό, enlargement of base *snd-, *sn -, 'to
flow'. Cp. Arm. nay (for *snet-), 'wet, liquid';
cp. also *snet-, *snot- in Gk. νότος, 'the south
wind, the south', prop, 'a rainy wind', νότιος,
νοτερός, 'damp, moist'. From the unenlarged
base *snd- derive L. no, ndre, 'to swim' (for
*snd-yo), Of. sndti, snayate, 'bathes' (intr.), the
second element in ghrta-sna-, 'dipped into
butter', Avestic snayeite, 'washes, cleans'·, Toch. В
ndskem, 'they bathe' (tr.), Gk. νή-χειν (for
*νά-χειν), 'to swim', Mir. snaim, Ί swim',
sndm, 'a swimming', MBret. neuff, 'to swim',
and prob. also Gk. νήσος, Dor. νϊσος, 'island'
(for *να-σος, lit. 'that which swims'). From Ι.-Ε.
*sndu-, *sneu-, an-и-enlargement of base *snd-,
derive 01. snauti (pp. snutdh), 'drips, gives
milk', Gk. νάω, Aeo]. ναίω, ναύω (for *vaf-
ιω), Ί flow'. Cp. natant, natatorial. Cp. also
naiad, naiant, Nama, necto-, Nereid, neso-,
nourish, the first element in Notogaea and the
second element in chersoneso- and in Indonesia,
Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia. Cp. also
snout. For the ending of natation see -ation.

## natatorial
natatorial, adj., natatory. — See next word and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:515 COLUMN:3 -->
adj. suff. -al.

## natatory
natatory, adj., swimming; characterized by
swimming. — Late L. natdtorius, 'pertaining to
swimming', fr. L. natatus, pp. of nature. See natation
and adj. suff. -ory.

## nates
nates, n. pi., the buttocks (anat.) — L. nates, pi.
of natis, 'rump', cogn. with Gk. νώτος, also
νώτον, 'the back'. Cp. noto-. Cp. also Natica
and the first element in aitchbone.

## Nathan
Nathan, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, a prophet
who lived during the reign of David and
Solomon. — Heb. Nathan, lit. 'He has given*, from
the verb ndthan, whence also mattan, mattdna1*,
mattath, 'gift'; η thinim, 'servants of the temple',
lit. 'those given (scil. to the sanctuary)'; rel. to
Phoen. imperf. y-t-n, Bibl.-Aram. imperf. yintin,
Syr. imperf. nettel, Ugar. imperf. ytn, 'he will
give', Akkad. naddnu, 'to give'. Cp. Nathaniel,
Jonathan, Nethuiim. Cp. also Matthew,
Matthias.

## Nathaniel
Nathaniel, Nathanael, masc. PN. — Late L. Na-
thanael, fr. Gk. Ναθαναήλ, fr. Heb. Nethan'el,
lit. 'God has given'. See Nathan and El.

## natheless
natheless, nathless, adv.,.nevertheless (archaic).
— ME. natheles, fr. OE. na pelxs, 'not the less'.
See no, adv., and nevertheless,

## Natica
Natica, п., a genus of marine snails (zool.) —
ModL., fr. ML. natica, 'buttock', dimin. of L.
natis. See nates.

## nation
nation, n. — ME. nacioun, fr. OF. (= F.) nation,
fr. L. nationem, ace. of ndtio, 'breed, race,
people, nation', lit. 'birth', fr. ndtus, pp. of ndsci, 'to
be born', which stands for *gndscl, fr. I.-E. *gn-,
zero degree of base *gen-, "genl-, 'to beget, bear,
bring forth', whence also L. genus, 'birth,
descent, origin, race, sort, kind, class'. See genus
and words there referred to and cp. esp. naive,
nascent, natal, native, nature, cognate, connate,
innate, nee, pregnant, 'with child', and the
second element in puisne and puny.

## national
national, adj. — MF. (= F.), fr. nation. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: national, п., national-ism, п., na-
tional-ist, n. and adj., national-ist-ic, adj., ha-
tional-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., national-ity, п., national*
ize, tr. v., national-iz-ation, п., national-iz-er, п.,
national-ly, adv., national-ness, n.

## native
native, adj. — ME. natif, fr. MF. (= F.) natif
(fem. native), fr. L. nativus, 'born, innate,
natural, primitive', fr. ndtus, pp. of ndsci, 'to be
born'. See nation and -ive and cp. naive, which
is a doublet of native.
Derivatives: native, п., nativ-ism, п., nativ-ist, п.,
nativ-ist-ic, adj.

## nativity
nativity, п., I) birth; 2) horoscope (astrol.) —
ME. nativite, fr. OF. (= F.) nativite, it. L. ndti-
vitdtem, ace. of ndtivitds, 'birth', fr. nativus. See
native and -ity. Cp. naivete, which is a doublet
of nativity.

## natrium
natrium, п., sodium (chem.) — ModL. See natron
and chem. suff. -ium.

## Natrix
Natrix, п., a genus of snakes, the grass snake
(zool.) — L. natrix, 'water snake'. See adder.

## natrolite
natrolite, п., a hydrous silicate of sodium and
aluminum (mineral.) — See natron and -lite.

## natron
natron, п., native sodium carbonate (chem. and
mineral.) — Fr. Sp. natron, fr. Arab, natrun, fr.
Gk. νίτρον. See niter.

## natterjack
natterjack, п., a toad having a yellowish stripe on
the back (Bufo calamita). — Of uncertain origin.

## natty
natty, adj., neatly smart. — Perhaps rel. to F. net,
'neat'; see neat, adj.
Derivatives: natti-ly, adv., natti-ness, n.

## natural
natural, adj., pertaining to, or in accordance with,
nature; inborn, real; not artificial. — ME., fr.
OF. natural, nature! (F. nature!), fr. L. ndturdlis,
'by^birth, belonging to nature, in accordance
with nature', fr. ndtura. See nature and adj. suff.
-al and cp. connatural.
Derivatives: natural, п., natural-ism, п.,
naturally, adv., natural-ness, n.

## naturalist
naturalist, п., 1) a student of nature; an adherent
of naturalism. — MF. (= F.) naturaliste, fr.
natural, nature! (F. nature!). See prec. word and
-ist.
Derivatives: naturatist-ic, adj., naturalist-ic-al-
ly, adv.

## natural Ity
natural Ity, n. — MF. (= F.) nattiralite, fr. Late

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:516 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 489 | NEAP -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:516 COLUMN:1 -->
L. natiirulitatem, ace. of ndturdlitas, fr. L. nutu-
rdlis. See natural.

## naturalization
naturalization, n. — MF. ( = F.) naturalisation,
fr. naturaliser. See next word and -ation.

## naturalize
naturalize, tr. v., I) to confer the rights of
citizenship on (an alien); 2) to acclimatize; intr. v., 1)
to become naturalized; 2) to study nature. —
MF. ( — F.) naturaliser, fr. natural, naturel. See
natural and -ize.
Derivatives: naturalization (q.v.), naturaliz-er, n.

## nature
nature, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) nature, fr. L.
natura, 'nature; natural character of a thing;
natural disposition; the course of things; the
universe', lit. 'birth', fr. natus, 'born', pp. of
ndsci, 'to be born'. See nation and cp. nascent,
natal, native.

## naturopath
naturopath, n.( naturopathist. — Back formation
fr. naturopathy.

## naturopathy
naturopathy, п., a system of therapy which rejects
the use of drugs and employs the healing power
of natural agencies, such as sunshine, air, water,
etc. — A hybrid coined fr. L. natura, 'nature',
and Gk. -πάθει»,, fr. πά#ας, 'suffering'. See
nature and -pathy. The correct form would be
physiopathy, in which both elements are of Greek
origin.
Derivative: naturopath-ist, n.
паи-, combining form meaning 'ship'. — Gk.
vocu-, fr. ναϋς, 'ship', cogn. with L. navis, 'ship'.
See naval.

## Naucratite
Naucratite, adj., pertaining to Naucratis, an
ancient Greek colony, established by colonists
from Miletus in the Nile Delta. — L. Naucratites,
fr. Gk. Ναυκρατίτης, fr. Ναύκρατις. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## naufragous
naufragous, adj., caused by shipwreck (archaic or
obsol.) — L. naufragus, 'shipwrecked; causing
shipwreck', for *ndvifragus, which is
compounded of navis, 'ship', and the stem of frangere, 'to
break'. See naval and fraction. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see suff. -ous.

## naught
naught, п., nothing. — ME. naught, nought, etc.,
fr. OE. nawiht, 'nothing', lit. 'no whit', fr. na,
'no'; and wiht, 'whit'. See no, adv., and wight
and cp. aught, nought, not, nix, 'nothing'.
Derivatives: naught, adj., naught-y, adj., naught-
i-ly, adv., naught-i-ness, n.

## naumacbia
naumacbia, nanmachy, п., 1) a mock sea fight; 2)
place where such a fight is presented (Roman
antiq.) — L., fr. Gk. ναυμαχία, 'naval battle',
compounded of ναϋς, 'ship', and -μαχία, fr.
μάχη, 'battle'. See паи- and -machy.

## naupllus
naupllus, п., a larval stage in the development of
many crustaceans (zool.) — L., 'a kind of
shellfish which sails in its shell as in a ship', fr. Gk.
ναύπλιος, lit. 'sailing (as) in a ship', fr. ναΰς,
'ship', and πλέειν, πλεΐν, 'to sail, navigate,
swim, float'. See naval and flow and cp. pluvial.

## nausea
nausea, п., 1) feeling of sickness at the stomach;
2) disgust, loathing. — L. nausea, nausia,
'seasickness', fr. Gk. ναυσίϊ, ναυτία, 'seasickness',
lit. 'ship sickness', fr. ναϋς, 'ship'. See naval and
cp. nautical. Cp. also noise, which is a doublet
of nausea.

## nanseate
nanseate, tr. v., to afreet with nausea, make sick;
intr. v., to become affected with nausea, feel
disgust (rare). — L. nausedt-(um), pp. stem of
nausedre, 'to feel seasick, to vomit', fr. nausea.
See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: nauseai-ing, adj., nauseat-ing-ly,
adv., nauseat-ion, n.

## nauseous
nauseous, adj., causing nausea, disgusting. —
Formed fr. nausea with stiff, -ous.
Derivatives: nauseous-ly, adv., nauseous-ness, n.

## Nausicaa
Nausicaa, п., in the Odyssey, daughter of Alci-
nous, king of the Phaeacians — L. Nausicaa, fr.
Gk. Ναυσικάα. The name prob. means 'burner
of ships', fr. ναΰς, 'ship', and καίειν, 'to burn'.
See nnval and caustic.

## nautch
nautch, п., performance of professional dancing
girls in India. — Lit. 'dancing', fr. Hind, пас, fr.
Prakrit nacca, fr. Oi. nrtya-, 'dancing', from
the stem of nrtyati, 'dances', which is of
uncertain etymology.

## nautical
nautical, adj., pertaining to ships, seamen or
navigation. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. now
rare nautic, fr. F. nautique, fr. L. nauticus, 'of,
or pertaining to, ships or sailors, seafaring,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:516 COLUMN:2 -->
naval, nautical', fr. Gk. ναυτικός, of s.m. See
naval and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
the second element in aeronaut, Argonaut,
astronaut.
Derivatives: nautical-ity, п., nautical-ly, adv.

## nautics
nautics, п., the science of navigation. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## nautilus
nautilus, п., 1) any of a group of mollusks; 2) the
paper nautilus (zool.) — L., fr. Gk. ναυτίλος,
'sailor, seaman; the paper nautilus' (so called
because it was supposed to be furnished with a
membrane which it used like a sail), fr. ναύτης,
'sailor, seaman'. See nantical.

## naval
naval, adj., pertaining to a navy, its ships or men.
— Orig. 'pertaining to ships', fr. L. ndvdlis, fr.
navis, 'ship', which is cogn. with OI. nduh, ace.
ndvam, 'ship, boat', Arm. nav, 'ship', Gk. ναϋς,
'ship' (whence ναύτης, 'sailor, seaman',
ναυτικός, 'of, or pertaining to, ships or sailors,
seafaring, naval, nautical, ναυτίλος, 'sailor,
seaman'), Olr. паи (gen. nde, dat. pi. ndib), 'ship',
W. noe, 'a flat vessel; a kneading trough', ON.
nor, 'ship'. Cp. nacelle, паи-, nausea, nautical,
nautilus, nave, 'the centra] part of a church',
navicular, navy, navvy, nef, noise, the first element
in naufragous, nauplius, navigate, and the second
element in Echeneis.
Derivatives: naval-ly, adv., and navalism, nava-
list (qq. v.)

## navalism
navalism, п., policy of building a strong navy;
sea power. — See naval and -ism.

## navalist
navalist, п., an advocate of navalism. — See
naval and -ist.
Derivatives: navalist, adj., navalist-ic, adj.,
navalist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## navarch
navarch, п., commander of a fleet (Ancient Greek
history). — L. ndvarchus, more correctly nauar-
chus, fr. Gk. ναύαρχος, 'the master of a vessel',
which is compounded of ναϋς, 'ship', and
άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See naval and -arch.

## nave
nave, п., the central part of a church. — L. navis,
'ship'. See naval and cp. nef.

## nave
nave, п., the hub of a wheel. — ME., fr. OE. nafit,
rel. to OS. naba, ON. nof, Dan. and Swed. nav,
MLG., MDu. nave, Du. naaf, OHG. naba,
MHG., G. nabe, 'nave', and to OE. nafela, etc.,
'navel', and cogn. with OI. ndbhyam, OPruss.
nabis, 'nave'. The nave of the wheel was
compared to the navel of the body. See next word
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also auger.
For sense development cp. OI. nabhih, OPruss.
nabis, 'nave, navel'.

## navel
navel, n. — ME., fr. OE. nafela, rel. to ON. nafli,
Dan., Swed. navie, OFris. navla, MDu. navel,
navele, Du. navel, OHG. nabalo, MHG., G.
nabet, fr. I.-E. base *ombh-, nobh-, *mbh-,
whence also OI. nabhyam, 'nave (hub)', nabhih,
'navel, nave, relationship', ndbhilam, 'umbilical
depression', Avestic nabd-nazdishta, 'next of
kin', Avestic nufa, ModPers. ndf, Gk. ομφαλός,
'navel; boss of a shield, knob', L. umbilicus,
'navel; umbilical cord', umbo, 'boss of a shield',
OPruss. nabis, 'nave, navel', Lett, naba, 'navel',
Olr. imbliu (gen. imblenn), Mir. imlecan,
'navel'. Cp. nave, 'hub of a wheel'. Cp. also om-
phalo-, omphalos, umbilicus, umbo, nombril.

## navew
navew, п., 1) the wild turnip; 2) the rape (rare) —
F. naveau, fr. OF. navel, fr. VL. *napellus, dim.
aindpus, 'a kind of turnip', fr. Gk. νϊπυ,
'mustard', which is prob. of Egyptian origin. (For
the sense development of L. ndpus from Gk.
ναπυ it should be borne in mind that the
mustard plant and the turnip resemble each other in
form.) Cp. neep and sinapism, the first element
in napiform and the second element in parsnip
and in turnip.

## navicert
navicert, п., a certificate issued to exempt a ship
from search for contraband. — Short for
navigation certificate.

## navicular
navicular, adj., boat-shaped (said of certain
bones in the fore and hind feet of animals) — L.
ndviculdrius, 'pertaining to a boat', fr. ndvicula,
'a boat', dim. at navis. See naval and the suffixes
-cule and -ar.
Derivative: navicular, п., a bone resembling a
boat (anat.)

## navigable
navigable, adj. — Fr. F. navigable, or directly fr.
L. ndvigabilis, fr. ndvigdre. See navigate and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:516 COLUMN:3 -->
-able.
Derivatives: navigabil-ity, п., navigable-ness, п.,
navigabt-y, adv.

## navigate
navigate, intr. v., to travel by ship; tr. v., to
travel through (on the water or in the air); to direct
(a ship or an aircraft). — L. ndvigdtus, pp. of
ndvigdre, 'to sail, set sail', lit. 'to drive a ship',
fr. *ndvigus, for *ndv-agos, 'driving a ship',
which is compounded of navis, 'ship', and
agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead, conduct'.
See naval and agent, adj., and verbal suff. -ate.
For the change of d (in agere) to ί (in *ndv-igus,
ndv-igdre) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also circumnavigate,

## navigation
navigation, п., the act and art of navigating. —
L. ndvigatid, gen. -onis, fr. ndvigdtus, pp. of
ndvigdre. See prec word and -ion.
Derivative: navigation-al, adj.

## navigator
navigator, п., 1) one who navigates; 2) a
navigating officer; 3) a navvy (British). — L. navigator,
'sailor', fr. ndvigdtus, pp. of ndvigdre. See
navigate and agential suff. -or and cp. next word.

## navvy
navvy, п., an unskilled laborer, esp. one
employed in making canals, roads, etc. —
Shortened fr. navigator (q.v.); for meaning cp.
navigation in the dialectal sense 'canal',

## navy
navy, n. — ME. navie, fr. OF. navie, 'fleet of
ships, ship', fr. Late L. navia, of s.m., fr. L.
navis. See naval,

## nawab
nawab, п., 1) a deputy ruler in India; 2) a
courtesy title, esp. for princes; 3) a nabob. — Hind.
nawwdb, nawab, fr. Arab, nuwwdb, pi. of na'ib,
'deputy, proxy, lieutenant-governor'. See nabob,

## nay
nay, neg. particle and n. — ME. nei, nay, fr.
ON. nei, 'no', compounded of ne, 'not', and
ei, 'ever'. The first element is cogn. with ΟΙ. ηά,
na, 'not', Avestic, OPers. na-, 'not, un-', Gk.
vr]-, 'not, un-', L. ne, 'that not', ne-, 'not, un-',
Olr. ni, ni, 'not'. See no, adv., and cp. the first
element in none, поп, null, nihil, nimiety; cp.
also the first element in necessary, nefarious,
Nemertinea, nepenthe, nescient, nolens-volens.
For the second element in nay see aye, 'ever'.

## Nazarene
Nazarene, п., 1) a native or resident of Nazareth;
esp. applied to Jesus; 2) a Christian. — ME.
Nazaren, fr. Late L. Nazarenus, fr. Gk. Ναζα-
ρηνός, fr. Ναζαρέτ,. 'Nazareth', fr. Heb. Ndtze-
rdth, a town in Lower Galilee in Palestine. Cp.
Talmudic Heb. notzri, 'Christian', lit. 'of
Nazareth'.
Derivative: Nazarene, adj., 1) of Nazareth; 2)
of the Nazarenes.

## Nazarite
Nazarite, Nazirite, п., a person who vowed to
abstain from wine, from cutting the hair, and
from touching the dead (Jewish religion). —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Late L. Naza-
raeus, fr. Gk. Ναζηραΐος, Ναζαραϊος, fr. Heb.
ndztr, 'consecrated, dedicated, devoted', lit.
'separated', from the stem n-z-r, 'to separate,
consecrate, dedicate', whence also imperf. yin-
ndzer, inf. hinndzer, 'to separate oneself, to
dedicate, devote oneself, nezer, 'consecration,
dedication, crown'; rel. to Aram. nezar, Syr. nezar,
ethnezdr, 'he abstained, he dedicated, devoted
himself, Arab, nadara, 'he consecrated,
dedicated, devoted', Akkad. nazdru, 'to curse', and to
Heb. nddhar, 'he vowed', nedher, nedher, 'a vow'.
Derivatives: Nazarit-ic, Nazarit-ish, adjs.

## naze
naze, п., a promontory. — Prob. fr. OE. nsess,
'promontory', which is rel. to OE. nosu, 'nose'.
See nose and cp. ness.

## Nazi
Nazi, п., a member of the National Socialist
German Workingmen's Party. — Formed from
two syllables in the name of the party (AOtional-
sozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei).

## nazim
nazim, п., a governor in India. — Arab, nazim,
lit. 'one who puts things in order', part, of
ndzama, 'he put in order, arranged'.

## nazir
nazir, п., title of various officials in Indian courts.
— Arab, nazir, 'overseer', prop. part, of ndzara,
'he looked at, considered, examined', whence
nazir, 'opposite'. See nadir.

## Nazirite
Nazirite, n. — See Nazarite.

## ne-
ne-, form of neo- before a vowel.

## Neanderthal
Neanderthal, adj., pertaining to the Neanderthal,
a valley in Germany, or to the skeletal remains
of an early type of man found there.

## neap
neap, adj., pertaining to the tide occurring at the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:517 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NEAPOLITAN | 490 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:517 COLUMN:1 -->
end of the first and third quarter of the lunar
month. — ME. neep, fr. OE. пёр in nepfldd,
'neap flood'; of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: neap, п., neap tide; neap, intr. v.,
to tend toward the neap.

## Neapolitan
Neapolitan, adj., of Naples. — L. Neapotitanus,
fr. Neapolis, 'Naples' (whence It. Napoli), fr.
Gk. Νεάπολη, lit. 'New Town', fr. νέα, fem.
of νέος, 'new', and πόλις, 'town'. See neo-,
policy, 'method of government', and -an.
Derivative: Neapolitan, an inhabitant of Naples.

## near
near, adv., at or to a short distance, close. — ME.
ner, nere, fr. OE. near, compar. of neah, 'ingh';
the change from the comparative to the
positive meaning was prob. aided by the analogy of
ON. nser, 'near', orig. compar. of na, 'nigh'.
See nigh.
Derivatives: near, adj. and v., near-ty, adv.,
near-ness, n.

## Nearctic
Nearctic, adj., pertaining to, or designating, the
arctic and temperate regions of North America;
used esp. in botanical and zoological
classification. — Compounded of ne- and arctic.

## neat
neat, п., an animal of the ox family; caule. —
ME. net, neet, fr. OE. neat, rel. to OS. not, ON.
naut, Swed. not, Dan. ned, OFris. not, OHG.
поз, 'ox, cattle', and to OE. neotan, 'to use,
enjoy', OS. niotan, ON. njota, OFris. nidta,
OHG. (gi)nio3an, MHG.genie^en, G.geniefien,
'to enjoy', Goth, niutan, 'to reach, attain', ga-
niutan, 'to catch', OE. nytt, ON. nyl, OHG.,
MHG. лиг, G. Nutzen, 'use, profit, advantage',
and cogn. with Lith. nauda, 'use, possession',
Lett, nauda, 'money'. All these words derive fr.
1-Е. *neud-, 'to possess, use, enjoy'.
Accordingly OE. neat, ON. naut, etc., lit. denote *a
useful animal'. Cp. the second element in Huguenot
and in matelote.

## neat
neat, adj., pure, undiluted; cleanly, tidy; elegant.
— MF. (= F.) net, 'clean, pure, neat', ft. OF.,
fr. L. nitidus, 'shining, bright, clear,
well-favored, elegant, smart, trim', fr. nitere, 'to shine', fr.
I.-E. base *nei-, *ni-, 'to shine', whence also
Mir. niam, 'gleam, splendor', niamda, 'shining',
Olr. noib, 'holy', niab, 'strength', W. nwyfiant,
'gleam, splendor', possibly also OI. ni-lah,
'swarthy, black, dark', OPers. naiba-, ModPers.
new, 'beautiful'. Cp. natty, net, adj., nitid, niton.
Cp. also lilac.
Derivatives: neat-ly, adv., neat-ness, n.
'neath, neath, prep., beneath. — Short for
beneath.

## neb
neb, n. 1) the beak or bill of a bird; 2) nose; 3)
point, tip. — ME. nebbe, fr. OE. nebb, 'beak,
nose, face', rel. to MLG., MDu, nebbe, 'beak',
ON. nef, 'beak, nose', Du. sneb, snavel, OHG.
snabul, MHG. snabel, G. Schnabel, 'beak*,
OFris, snavel, 'mouth'. Cp. nib, nipple, snaffle,
snap, snipe, snow, 'a kind of vessel'.
Derivative: nebb-ed, adj.

## Nebalta
Nebalta, п., a genus of marine crustaceans {loot.)
— ModL., of unknown origin.

## Nebiim
Nebiim, n. pi., the Books of the Prophets, the
second of the three parts into which the Hebrew
Bible is divided. — Heb. η bhVbn, pi. of nabhV,
'prophet', orig. 'the man who calls, proclaims',
fr. stem n-b-', whence nibba', 'he prophesied',
пеЬпй'а*, 'prophecy'; rel. to Akkad. nabu, 'to
call, announce, proclaim', Arab, naba'a, 'he
uttered with a low voice, announced', naba\
'announcement, information', ndb'ah, 'low sound';
cp. Ethiop. nababa, 'he spoke' (the original
meaning was 'he growled'). Cp. the second element in
Barnabas.

## Nebuchadnezzar
Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadrezzar, п., king of
Babylon (604-562 B.C.E.). — Heb. tfbhukhadh-
netztzar, a collateral form q{N bhukhadhretztzar,
fr. Bab. Nabu-kudurri-usur, which prob. means
lit. 'Nebo, protect the boundary'. Cp. Gk. Na-
βοκοδρόσορος in Strabo 15,1,6, and in Josephus
Flavius, Contra Apionem 1,146.

## nebula
nebula, п., a cloudlike patch in the sky (astron.)
— L., 'mist, fog, cloud', fr. I.-E. base *(e)nebh-,
'moist, vapor, mist, cloud', whence also OI.
nabhas-, 'vapor, cloud, fog, sky', Avestic nabah-,
'air, sky', Gk. νέφος, νεφέλη, 'cloud, mist', OS.
nebal, OFris. nevil, MDu., Du. nevel, OHG.
nebul, MHG., G. nebel, 'fog', ON. nifi- (in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:517 COLUMN:2 -->
Niflheimr, 'abode of darkness', i.e. 'the nether
world'), л/о', 'night', OE. nijol (adj.), 'dark',
MW. nyfel, 'cloud', W. niwl, Co. niul, 'cloud,
fog', Olr. пет, 'sky', OSlav. nebo (gen. nebese),
'sky', Lith. debesis (for *nebesis), 'cloud' (the
d- is prob. due to the influence of dangits,
'sky'), Hitt. nepish (gen. nepiskash), 'sky',
Avestic napta-, 'moist, humid'. Cp. nephelme, nepho-,
Neptune, Nibelungs, nimbns, imbricate.
Derivatives: nebul-ar, adj., nebul-iz-ation, п.,
nebut-ize, tr. v., nebul-iz-er, п., nebulous (q.v.)

## nebulosity
nebulosity, п., 1) condition of being nebulous; 2)
cloudiness; 3) a nebula. — F. nebulosite, fr.
Late L. nebulositatem, ace. of nebulositas, fr. L.
nebulosus. See nebulous and -ity.

## nebulous
nebulous, adj., 1) resembling a nebula; 2) clouded,
cloudy, misty; 3) vague — L. nebulosus, 'cloudy',
fr. nebula. See nebula and -ous.
Derivatives: nebutous-ly, adv., nebulous-ness, n.

## nebule
nebule, also nebuly, adj., composed of curves
supposed to represent clouds. — F. nebule, fr.
L. nebula. See nebnla.

## nebulium
nebulium, п., name of an unidentified chemical
element (astrophys.) — ModL., fr. L. nebula,
'mist, fog, cloud' (see nebula and chem. suff.
-turn); so called because supposed to occur in
nebulae.

## Necator
Necator, п., a genus of nematodes, the American
hookworm (zool.) — ModL., fr. Late L. necator,
'slayer', fr. necatus, pp. of necare, 'to kill, slay',
fr. nex, gen. necis, 'violent death, murder', which
derives fr. I.-E. base *nek-, 'to destroy; to
perish', whence also L. nocere, 'to harm, hurt',
noxius, 'harmful, injurious'. See noxious and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-tor.

## necessarian
necessarian, n. and adj. — See necessitarian.

## necessary
necessary, adj., certain to happen, inevitable,
requisite. — ME. necessarie, fr. L. necessarius,
'unavoidable, indispensable, necessary', fr. ne-
cesse, 'unavoidable, necessary', which stands
for *ne-cezd-tis, "ne-ced-tis, lit. '(there is) no
evasion, (it is) inevitable', fr. negative pref. ne-
and cedere, 'to go away, yield'. For the first
element see no, adj., and cp. nay, for the second
see cede, for the ending see adj. suff. -ary
Derivatives: necessary, п., necessari-ly, adv.,
necessari-ness, n.

## necessitarian
necessitarian, п., 1) an adherent of the doctrine
of necessity; 2) adj., pertaining to the doctrine
of necessity. — Formed fr. necessity with suff.
-arlan.
Derivative: necessitarian-ism, п., the doctrine of
necessity.

## necessitate
necessitate, tr. v., to render" necessary. — ML.
necessitatus, pp. of necessitare, 'to render
necessary', fr. L. necessitas. See necessity and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: necessitat-ion, п., necessitat-ive, ad>.

## necessitous
necessitous, adj., poor, needy. — See next word
and -ous and cp. F. necessiteux.
Derivatives: necessitous-ly, adv., necessitous-
ness, n.

## necessity
necessity, n. — ME. necessite, fr. OF. (= F.) ne-
cessite, fr. L. necessitatem, ace. of necessitas,
'unavoidableness, necessity, compulsion;
destiny', fr. necesse. See necessary and -ity.

## neck
neck, п., that part of the body which joins the
head to the trunk; the narrowest part of an
object. — ME. пекке, fr. OE. hnecca, 'nape of the
neck', rel. to OFris. hnekka, MDu. песке, Du.
nek, 'neck', ON. hnakkr, hnakki, Dan., Norw.
nakke, Swed. nacke, 'nape of the neck', OHG.
hnach, hnac, пас, MHG. пас, nacke, G. Nacken,
of s.m., and cogn. with Olr. cnocc, Ir. cnoc, W.
enweh, OBret. cnoch, 'hill', Toch. knuk, 'nape'.
Cp. nook. Cp. also knacker.
Derivatives: neck, tr. v:, to cut off the neck of
(a fowl); to fondle (U.S. Slang); intr. v., to
engage in necking (U.S. Slang); neck-ing, п., а
molding near the top of a column.

## neck
neck, п., the last sheaf cut at harvest. — Of
uncertain origin.

## neckerchief
neckerchief, п., a scarf for the neck. —
Compounded of neck and kerchief. Properly, the
word contains a contradiction, since kerchief
denotes a covering for the head, fr. OF. couvre-
chef, lit. 'cover-head'. Cp. handkerchief.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:517 COLUMN:3 -->

## necking
necking, п., 1) a molding around the top of"a
column below the capital (archit.); 2) the act
of fondling or caressing. — Formed fr. neck,
'part of the body', with -ing, suff. forming
verbal nouns.

## necklet
necklet, п., 1) an ornament worn abound the
neck; 2) a necklace. — Formed fr. neck, 'part
of the body', with dim. suff. -let.

## necro-
necro-, before a vowel necr-, combining form
meaning 'death, dead, corpse". — Gk. νεκρό-,
νεκρ-, fr. νεκρός, 'dead body, corpse', fr. I.-E.
base 'nek-, 'to destroy; to perish", whence also
L. nex, gen. necis, 'violent death, murder',
nocere, 'to harm, hurt', noxius, 'harmful,
injurious'. See noxious and cp. words there
referred to.

## necrobiosis
necrobiosis, п., physiologic death of body cells.
— Medical L., compounded of necro- and Gk.
βίωσις, 'manner oflife', fr. βίος, 'life'. See bio-
and -osis.

## necrolatry
necrolatry, п., worship of the dead. —
Compounded of necro- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρίί
fr. λατρεία, 'hired labor, service, worship'. See
-latry.

## necrology
necrology, п., a register of deaths, obituary. —
ML. necrologium, compounded of necro- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy and cp. eulogy.

## necromancer
necromancer, п., one who practices necromancy.
— Formed from next word with agential suff.
-er.

## necromancy
necromancy, п., divination by communication
with the dead; witchcraft, sorcery. — ME, nigro-
mancie, nigromaunce, fr. OF. nigromancie, ni-
gromance, fr. ML. nigromantia, fr. Late L.
necromania, fr. Gk. νεκρομαντεία, 'necromancy',
which is compounded of νεκρός, 'dead body,
corpse', and μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'; see
-mancy. The change of Late L. necromania to
ML. nigromantia is due to a confusion of Gk.
νεκρός, 'dead', with L. niger, 'black'
(necromancy was regarded as 'the black art'). F. ne-
cromancie and E. necromancy were influenced in
form by L. necromania.

## necromantic
necromantic, adj., pertaining to necromancy. —
See prec. word and adj. sufT. -ic.
Derivative: necromantic-at, adj.

## necrophagous
necrophagous, adj., feeding on dead bodies (said
of insects and bacteria). — Compounded of
necro- and Gk. -φάγος, 'eater of, from the
stem of φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

## necrophobia
necrophobia, п., an abnormal fear of death or
dead bodies. — Medical L., compounded of
necro- and Gk. -φοβία, 'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'.
See -phobia.

## necropolis
necropolis, п., a cemetery, esp. one belonging to
an ancient city. — Late L., 'city of the dead', fr.
Gk. νεκρόττολις, which is compounded of
νεκρός, 'dead body, corpse', and πόλις, 'city'.
See necro- and policy, 'government'.

## necropsy
necropsy, п., a post-mortem examination,
autopsy. — Compounded of necr- and Gk. ίψις,
'sight, appearance'. See -opsy.

## necroscopy
necroscopy, п., a necropsy. — Compounded of
necro- and Gk, -σκοπίά, fr. σκοττειν, 'to look
at, examine'. See -scopy.

## necrosis
necrosis, п., the death of bodily tissue. — Gk.
νέκρωσις, 'a becoming dead, state of death', fr.
νεκροϋν, 'to make dead, to mortify', fr. νεκρός,
'dead'. See necro- and -osis.

## necrotic
necrotic, adj. — See prec. word and -otic.

## nect-
nect-, form of necto- before a vowel.

## nectar
nectar, п., the drink of the gods (Greek mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. νέκταρ, 'drink of the gods', esp.
'wine', which prob. derives fr. Heb. (yayin) niq-
tar, 'smoked (wine), perfumed (wine)', Niph'al
( = passive form) of the Sem. base q-t-r, 'to
make sacrifices, smoke'; qi.tter and hiqtlr, 'he
made sacrifices, smoked', are Pi'el (= intensive
form), resp. Hiph'il (= causative form) of the
same base, whence also qetSreth, 'sweet smoke
of sacrifice, incense', Talmudic and Targumic
Aram, qitra, '(thick) smoke', Ethiop. qetare,
'incense'. From q-t-r, a collateral form of this

## base derive Arab
base derive Arab, qdtara, 'it exhaled odor' (said

## esp. of roast meat)
esp. of roast meat), 'it smoked' (said of fire),

## qutar
qutar, 'vapor, smoke, aroma', Akkad. qutrur

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:518 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 491 | NEKTON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:518 COLUMN:1 -->
'smoke', qutrinnu, 'incense offering'; cp. also
Syr. 'dtdr, 'he caused to smoke', 'etm,
'frankincense' (with change of q to'. Cp. Movers, Die
Phonizier, II, 3, 104, and W. Muss Arnolt in
Transactions and Proceedings of the American
Philological Association, volume ХХШ (1892),
p. 143. Cp. Keturah.
Derivatives: nectar-eal, nectar-ean, nectar-ed,
adjs., nectareous (q.v.), nectar-ian, nectar-ine,
adjs., nectarine, n. (q.v.), nectary (q.v.)

## nectareous
nectareous, adj., of the natureof nectar; delicious.
— L. nectareus, fr. Gk. νεκτάρεος,
'nectareous', fr. νέκταρ. See nectar. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives; nectareous-ly, adv., nectareous-nessr
n.

## nectariferous
nectariferous, adj., secreting nectar. —
Compounded of nectar and the stem of L. ferre, 'to
bear, carry'. See -ferous.

## nectarine
nectarine, п., a variety of peach with a thin,
smooth skin. — Formed fr. nectar with suff.
-ine; so called from its sweet, delicious taste.

## nectary
nectary, п., the organ that secretes nectar (bot.)
— ModL. nectarium, prop, subst. use of L. nec-
tarius, 'pertaining to nectar', fr. nectar. See
nectar and -y (representing L. -ium).

## necto-
necto-, before a vowel nect-, combining form
meaning'swimming'. — Fr. Gk. νηκτός,
'swimming', verbal adj. of νή-χειν, 'to swim', which
stands for *να-χειν, fr. I.-E. base *snd-, 'to
flow'. See natation and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also Nectria, nekton and the second
element in Eunectes, Pleuronectidae.

## Nectria
Nectria, п., a genus of sac fungi (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. νήκτης, 'swimmer', fr. νήχειν, 'to
swim'. See necto-.

## Necturus
Necturus, п., a genus of aquatic salamanders
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. νηκτός,
'swimming', and ούρα, 'tail'. See necto- and
uro-, 'tail-'.

## neddy
neddy, п., a donkey. — Fr. Neddy, a pet form of
Edward.

## nee
nee, nee, adj., born (introduces the maiden name
of a married woman). — F. nee, fr. L. ndta, fern,
of natus, pp. of nascl, 'to be born'. See nation.

## need
need, п., exigency, necessity; poverty. — ME.
ned, nede, fr. OE. nied, ned, neod, nyd, 'urgent
need, compulsion, requirement', rel. to OS.
nod, ON. naudr, Norw. naud, Dan. ned,
Swed. nod, OFris. ned. MDu. nood, noot, Du.
nood, OHG., MHG. not, G. Not, Goth, naups,
'need', and cogn. with OPruss. nautis, 'need';
formed with formative element -ti fr. I.-E. base
*naw-, *n w-, *пй-, 'to tire, fatigue', whence also

## OSlav. naviti
OSlav. naviti, 'to fatigue'. (Lith. novyti, of s.m.,
is an OSlav. loan word.) Cp. nudnik.
Derivatives: need-ful, adj., need-ful-ly, adv.,

## need-ful-ness
need-ful-ness, п., need-less, adj., need-less-Iy,
adv., need-less-ness, п., need-y, adj., need-i-ness,
n.

## need
need, tr. v., to want, be in need of; intr. v., to be
necessary. — ME. neden, needen, fr. OE. ne~o-
dian, 'to be necessary', fr. neod. See need, n.

## needle
needle, n. — ME. nedle, fr. OE. nzdl, rel. to OS.
nathla, ON. ndl, Swed. ndl, Dan. naal, OFris.
nedle, OHG. nadala, nadla, MHG. nddele, ηά-
del, G. Nadel, Goth, nepla, and, with
metathesis, OFris. nelde, MLG. nalde, MDu. naelde, Du.
naald, 'needle' (Finn, neula and nallo, 'needle',
are Teut. loan words), lit. 'a too] for sewing',
formed with I.-E. instrumental suff. *-tla fr.
I.-E. base *(s)ne-, 'to spin, to sew with a needle',
whence MLG. neien, MDu. naeyen, Du. naaien,
OHG. najan, MHG. nsejen, G. nahen, 'to sew',
OI. snayati, 'wraps up', snayuh, 'sinew', Gk.
νέω, νεΐν, 'to spin', νήμα, 'that which is spun,
thread', νητρον, 'distaff', L. neo, nere, 'to spin',
OSlav. niti, nista, 'thread', snujq, snovati, 'to
twist', Lett, sndte, 'a linen cover', Olr. snathe,
'thread', snuthat, 'needle', W. nyddu, Co. Heine,
'to sew', OW., OBret. notuid, W. nodwydd,
'needle'. Cp. -nema, nemato-, nerve. Cp. also
snood.
Derivatives: needle, tr. and intr. v., needle-ful,
adj.

## needs
needs, adv., of necessity; necessarily. — ME.
nedes, fr. OE. nedes, nydes, adverbial gen. of
ned, nyd, 'urgent need'. See need, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:518 COLUMN:2 -->

## neem
neem, п., the margosa. — Hind, nim, fr. Ol.
nimbab, which is of unknown origin.

## neep
neep, п., a turnip (Scot, and dial.) — ME. пере,
fr. OE. nsep, fr. L. napus, 'a kind of turnip'. See
navew.

## ne'er
ne'er, adv., never (poet.) — Contracted fr. never.

## nef
nef, п., a table ornament in the shape of a ship.
— F., 'ship', fr. L. navem, ace of navis. See
naval.

## nefarious
nefarious, adj., wicked, iniquitous. — L. nefarius,
'impious, abominable', fr. nefds, 'wrong, sin,
crime', formed from negative pref. ne- and fas,
'divine law, right', which is rel. to far!, 'to
speak', For the first element see no, adv., and
cp. nay. For the second element see -furious and
cp. bifarious.
Derivatives: nefarious-ly, adv., nefarious-ness, n.

## negate
negate, tr. v., to deny, nullify; to deny the
existence of. — L. negatus, pp. of negare, 'to say no,
deny, refuse', which derives fr. *neg(i), 'not, no',
a Strengthened form of *пё, 'not', and is cogn.
with Lith. negl, negu, 'not', OS. nee, 'and not'.
Cp. abnegate, renegade, renege, runagate and
deny. Cp. also the first element in neglect,
negotiate. For the ending of negate see verbal suff.
-ate. For the mode of formation of L. negare
(from *negi, *neg, 'not'), cp. G. verneinen, 'to
deny' (fr. nein, 'no').

## negation
negation, п., denial. — MF. ( — F.) negation, fr.
OF. negation, fr. L. negationem, ace. of negatio,
*a denying, denial', fr. negatus, pp. of negare.
See prec. word and -ion.

## negationist
negationist, п., one who contents himself with
mere negation. — See prec. word and -ist.

## negative
negative, adj., 1) expressing denial; 2) the
opposite of positive. — MF. (= F.) negatif (fern.
negative), fr. OF. negatif, fr. L. negdtivus, 'that
which denies', fr. negatus, pp. of negare. See
negate and -ive.
Derivatives: negative, n. and tr. v., negative-ly,
adv., negative-ness, п., negativ-ity, n.

## negator
negator, п., one who denies. — Late L. negator,
fr. L. negatus, pp. of negare. See negate and
agential suff. -or.

## negatory
negatory, adj., expressing negation. — MF. (=
F.) negatoire, fr. ML. negatorius, 'negative', fr.
L. negatus, pp. of negare. See negate and adj.
suff. -ory.

## negativism
negativism, п., the opposite of positivism. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. negdtivus (see negative) and
-ism, a suff. of Greek origin.

## negativist
negativist, п., an adherent of negativism. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. negdtivus (see negative) and
-ist, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivative: negativist-ic, adj.

## neglect
neglect, tr. v. — L. neglictus, pp. of neglegere,
negligere, 'to make light of, disregard, be
indifferent to, neglect', compounded of *neg(i),
'not', and legere, 'to pick up, gather; to read'.
See negate and lecture.

## neglect
neglect, n. — L. neglectus, 'a neglecting', fr.
neglectus, pp. of neglegere, negligere. See
neglect, v.
Derivatives: neglect-ful, adj., neglect-ful-ly, adv.,
negtect-fut-ness, n.

## negligee
negligee, negligee, also neglige, neglige, п., 1) a
woman's loose dressing gown; 2) any careless
attire. — F. neglige (fem. negligee), pp. of
negliger, 'to neglect', fr. L. neglegere, negligere.
See neglect, v.

## negligence
negligence, n. — ME. neglygence, fr. MF. (= F.)
negligence, fr. L. neglegentia, negligentia,
'negligence', fr. neglegens, negligens (gen. -ends). See
next word and -ce.

## negligent
negligent, adj. — ME. negligent, fr. MF. (= F.)
negligent, fr. L. neglegentem, negligentem, ace.
of neglegens, negligens, pres. part, οι neglegere,
negligere. See neglect, v., and -ent.
Derivative: negligent-ly, adv.

## negligible
negligible, adj. — Formed with suff. -Ible fr. L.
negligere. See neglect, v. Cp. F. negligeable.
Derivatives: negligibil-ity, п., negligible-ness,
п., negligibl-y, adv.

## negotiable
negotiable, adj. — See negotiate and -able.
Derivative: negotiabil-ity, n.

## negotiate
negotiate, tr. and intr. v. — L. negotiants, pp. of
negdtiSri, 'to carry on business, deal, trade,
traffic', fr. negotium, 'business, trade', lit. 'lack

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:518 COLUMN:3 -->
of leisure', from the sentence neg'otium est,
'there is no leisure'. The particle neg' derives fr.
*negi, 'not'; see negate. For the etymology of L.
otium, .'leisure', see otiose, for the ending of
negotiate see verbal suff. -ate.

## negotiation
negotiation, n. — L. negotiatio, gen. -onis,
'business, traffic', fr. negotiatus, pp. of negetidri,
'to carry on business'. See prec. word and -Ion.

## negotiator
negotiator, n. — L. negotiator, 'one who carries
on business by wholesale; a trader, tradesman',
fr. negotiatus, pp. of negotidri. See negotiate and
agential suff. -or.

## negress
negress, п., a female negro. — F. negresse, fem.
of negre, 'negro', fr. Sp. or Port, negro. See
Negro and -ess.

## Negrillo
Negrillo, п., a Pygmy or Bushman. — Sp., dim.
of negro, 'black'. See Negro.

## Negritlc
Negritlc, adj., 1) pertaining to Negroes; 2)
pertaining to the Negritoes. — See next word and
adj. suff. -ic.

## Negrito
Negrito, п., a member of a dwarfish race
inhabiting the Philippines, the East Indies, the Malay
Peninsula and South Africa. — Sp., dim. of
negro, 'black'. See Negro.

## Negro
Negro, п., a member of the black race of Africa.
— Sp. and Port, negro, 'black', fr. L. nigrum,
ace. of niger, 'black', which is of uncertain
origin. Cp nero-antico, niello, Nigella, nigger, nigri-
fy, ulgritude, denigrate. Cp. also the second
element in darnel.
Derivative: negro, adj.

## negroid
negroid, adj., resembling the Negro or Negroes.
— A hybrid coined fr. Negro and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: Negroid, п., a member of the Negro
race.

## negroism
negroism, п., 1) advocacy of the cause of the Ne-·
groes; 2) a negro idiom. — A hybrid coined fr.
Negro and -ism. a suff. of Greek origin.

## negrophile
negrophile,-negrophil, п., one who likes Negroes.
— A hybrid coined fr. Negro and Gk. φίλος,
'friend'. See -phile, -phil.

## negrophobe
negrophobe, п., one who fears or hates the
Negroes. — A hybrid coined fr. Negro and Gk.
φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobe.

## negrophobia
negrophobia, п., fear or hatred of the Negroes. —
A hybrid coined fr. Negro and Gk. -φοβία, 'fear
of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## Negus
Negus, п., title of the ruler of Abyssinia. —■ Am-
haric negush, 'king', from the stem of nagasha,
'he forced, ruled', which is rel. to Heb. ndgds,
'he pressed, drove, oppressed', Arab, najasa,
'he roused and started the game', Akkad. nagd-
shu, 'to throw down'.

## negus
negus, п., beverage made of wine, water and
sugar. — From its first maker, Colonel Francis
Negus (died in 1732).

## Nehemiah
Nehemiah, п., 1) masc. PN.; 2) a) a Jewish leader,
cupbearer of the Persian king Artaxerxes Lon-
gimanus and empowered by him to restore
Jerusalem and rebuild its walls; b) the Book of

## Nehemiah
Nehemiah, one of the books of the Bible. —
Heb. Nlhemyah, lit. 'the Lord comforts'. For

## the first element see Nahum
the first element see Nahum, for the second see
Elijah.

## neigh
neigh, intr. v. — ME. neien, fr. OE. hnxgan. Cp.

## ON. gneggja
ON. gneggja, Icel. hneggja, Swed. gndgga,
MHG. negen; of imitative origin.
Derivative: neigh, n.

## neighbor
neighbor, neighbour, n. — ME. neighebour,

## neighbour
neighbour, etc., fr. OE. neahgebur, lit., 'near-by

## farmer'
farmer', fr. neah, 'near' and gebur, bur,
'husbandman, peasant, farmer'; rel. to Du. (na)buur,

## OHG. ndhgibur(o)
OHG. ndhgibur(o), MHG. nachgebur, G. Nach-

## bar
bar, 'neighbor'. See ulgh and boor.
Derivatives: neighbo(u)r, adj.-, neighbo(u)r, tr.

## and intr. v.
and intr. v., neighbo(u)r-ed, adj.,

## neighbourhood
neighbourhood, п., neighbo(u)r-ing, adj., neighbo(u)r-less,

## adj.
adj., neighbo(u)r-ly, adj. and adv., neighbo(u)r-li-

## ness
ness, п., neighbourship, n.

## neither
neither, adj., pron., adv., and conj., not either. —

## ME. neither
ME. neither, neyther, nother, nouther, naither,

## fr. OE. nSwder
fr. OE. nSwder, contraction of ndhwxder, lit.
'neither of two', fr. ne, 'not', and ahwxder,
"either of two', which is compounded of a-,
'ever, always', and hwseder, 'which of two'. See
no and whether and cp. either. Cp. also nor.

## nekton
nekton, п., actively swimming organisms on the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:519 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NELEUS | 492 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:519 COLUMN:1 -->
surface of the sea (zool.) — ModL-, coined by
von Heusen fr. Gk. νηκτόν, neut. of νηκτός,
'swimming'. See necto-.

## Neleus
Neleus, п., the son of Poseidon and father of
Nestor {Greek mytkol.) — L. Neleus, fr. Gk.
Νηλεύς; of uncertain origin.

## Nelly
Nelly, also Nellie, Nell, fern. PN. — Pet forms of
Ellen, Hellen, Eleanor.

## nelly
nelly, п., the giant fulmar. — From prec. word.

## Nelumbo
Nelumbo, п., a genus of plants, the sacred bean
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Singhalese native name.

## -nema
-nema, combining form meaning 'thread*, used
to form generic names in botany and zoology.
— ModL., fr. Gk. νήμα, *thread\ See nemato-.

## nemat-
nemat-, form of nemato- before a vowel.
nemathelminth п., any of a group of round, un-
segmented worms (zool.) — Compounded of
nemat- and Gk. £λμις, gen. ελμίνθος, 'worm'.
See helminth.

## nemato-
nemato-, before a vowel nemat-, combining form
meaning 'thread' (bot. and zool.) — Fr. Gk.
νήμα, gen. νήματος, 'thread', from the stem
of νέειν, 4to spin', fr. I.-E. base *ne-, 'to spin,
sew with a needle', whence also OE. nxdl„
'needle', lit. 'a tool for sewing'. See needle and
cp. -nema.

## nematocyst
nematocyst, п., the stinging organ of coelentera-
tes (zool.) — Compounded of nemato- and Gk.
κύστις, 'bladder'. See cyst.
Derivative: nematocyst-ic, adj.

## Nematoda
Nematoda, п., pi., a class of worms (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of nemat- and Gk. -ώδης,
'like'. See -ode, 'like'.

## nematode
nematode, adj., pertaining to the Nematoda; п.,
a member of the Nematoda. — See prec. word.

## nematoid
nematoid, adj., pertaining to the Nematoidea; п.,
a member of the Nematoidea. — See next word.

## Nematoidea
Nematoidea, n. pi., 1) the same as Nematoda; 2)
the order containing the typical nematodes
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of nemat- and
Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
-oid.

## Nemean
Nemean, adj., pertaining to Nemea, a valley in
ancieni Argolis, in Greece. — Formed with
Suff. -an fr. L. Nemeus, Nemaeus, Nemeaeus, fr.
Gk. Νέμεος, Νέμειος, Νεμεαΐος, 'of Nemea',
fr. Νεμέα, Νεμέη, fr. νέμος, 'grove'. See
Nemophila.

## nemertean
nemertean, nemertian, adj., pertaining to the
Nemertinea; п., a member of the Nemertinea. —
See Nemertinea and -an.

## Nemertinea
Nemertinea, п., pi., a class of worms (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. Νημερτής, name of a sea
nymph, fr. νημερτής (Dor. ναμαρτής),
'unerring, infallible', formed fr. neg. pref. νη- (see
no, adv., and cp. nay) and άμαρτάνε^ν, 'to miss
the mark, fail of one's purpose, to err, sin'. See
hamartiology.

## nemertinean
nemertinean, adj. and п., nemertian. — Formed
from prec. word with suff. -an.

## Nemesis
Nemesis, п., J) the goddess of retributive justice
in Greek mythology; hence 2) punishment,
retributive justice. — Gk. Νέμεσις, fr. νέμεσις,
'just indignation, jealousy, vengeance (esp. of
the gods)', lit. "distribution', fr. νέμειν, 'to deal
out, distribute, allot', which is rel. to νομός,
*land allotted, pasture; district, province', νομάς
(gen. νομάδος), 'roaming about for pasture;
wandering from one place to another', νόμος,
'anything allotted or assigned; usage, custom;
law', fr. l.-E. base *nem-, 'to divide, distribute,
allot', whence also Goth., OE. niman, OHG.
neman, 'to take'. See nimble.

## Nemopanthus
Nemopanthus, п., a genus of plants, the
mountain holly (bot.) — ModL., contraction of Gk.
νήμα, 'thread', πους, 'foot', and άνθος, 'flower'.
See nemato-, podo- and anther.

## Nemophila
Nemophila, п., a genus of plants of the waterleaf
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of νέμος,
'grove', and φίλος, 'loving, friend'. The first
element is cogn. with L. nemus, 'grove', ΟΙ. nd-
mah, Obeisance, adoration', prop, 'a bending,
bowing' (cp. Ol. namati, 'bends, bows'), Olr.
nemed, 'chapel', MBret, neved, of s.m., Gk.
νεμητον, δρυνέμετον, 'holy place'; fr. 1.Е.-
base *nem-, 'to bend'; cp. next word. For the
second element see philo-.

## nemoral
nemoral, adj., pertaining to, or inhabiting, a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:519 COLUMN:2 -->
grove. — L. nemoraliSy fr. nemus, gen. nemoris,
*grove'; cogn. with Gk. νέμος, 'grove7. See
prec. word.

## nenuphar
nenuphar, п., the white or the yellow water lily.
— F., fr. ML., fr. Pers. ninujar, earlier niiufar,
nilupar, 'water lily', fr. OL mlotpala-, 'the blue
lotus', fr. ntlah, 'dark blue' (see lilac), and ut-
palam, 'blossom of the blue lotus', which is
prob. a loan word from anon-Indo-European
language. Cp. nuphar.

## neo-
neo-, combining form meaning 'new, recent'. —
Gk. νεο-, fr. νέος, 'new', for *νέΓος, fr. l.-E.
*newos, 'new', whence also Goth, niujis, OE.
neowe, 'new'. See new and cp. neon, neoteric,
Nerium, the first element in neossine and the
second element in misoneist.

## neodymium
neodymium, п., a rare metallic element (chem.) —
ModL., shortened fr. neodidymia, a name
coined by the discoverer of this element Carl Auer
von Welsbach (1858-1929) fr. Gk. νέος, 'new'
(see neo-), and ModL. didymium, the name
given by Mosander to a rare metal which he
thought to be a single chemical element; see
didymium. In 1885 von Welsbach succeeded in
splitting didymium into two elements which he
called neodidymia and praseodidymia (see
praseodymium).

## Neogaea
Neogaea, п., the Neotropical zoological realm.
— ModL., compounded of neo- and Gk. γη,
'earth'. See geo- and cp. the second element in
Arctogaea, Notogaea.
Derivative: Neogae-an, adj.

## neolith
neolith, п., a neolithic tool. — Back formation fr.
neolithic,

## neolithic
neolithic, adj., pertaining to the later Stone Age.
— Coined by John Lubbock, the later Baron
Avebury (1834-1913), fr. Gk. νέος, 'new', λίθος,
'stone', and adj. sun", -ic. See neo- and litho- and
cp. paleolithic.

## neologism
neologism, п., 1) a new word; 2) introduction or
use of new words or of new meanings of existing
words. — F. neologisme, fr. neologie. See
neology and -ism.

## neologlst
neologlst, п., a person who invents, introduces or
uses new words. — F. neologiste, fr. neologie.
See neology and -ist.
Derivatives: neologist-ic, neologist-ic-al, adjs.

## neologize
neologize, intr. v., to make a practice of using
new words or new meanings оГ existing words. —
F. neologiser, fr. neologie. See neology and -ize.

## neology
neology, п., neologism. — F. neologie,
compounded of neo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## neomenia
neomenia, п., the time of the new moon (Greek
and Jewish antiquities) — Late L., fr. Gk. veo-
μηνία, 'the new moon; the first of the month',
compounded of νέος, 'new' (see neo-), and
μήνη, 'moon', which is related to μην, gen. μηνός,
'month'. See moon and cp. meito- and words
there referred to.

## neomycin
neomycin, п., an antibiotic isolated by the
American microbiologist Selman Abraham Waks-
man (1888- ). — Coined fr. neo-, myco- and
sulf. -in.

## neon
neon, п., name of a gaseous element (chem.) —
ModL., lit. 'the new (element)', fr. Gk. νέον,
neut. of νέος, 'new' (see neo-); coined by the
discoverers of this element, the Scottish chemist
Sir William Ramsay (1852-1916) and the
English chemist Morris William Travers( 1872-1961)
in 1898. Cp. krypton, xenon.

## Neophron
Neophron, п., a genus of vultures (ornithol.) —
ModL., so called after Neophron, the name of a
man changed into a vulture, mentioned in the
Metamorphoses of Antoninus Liberalis. The
name is from Greek νεόφρων, which means
'childish in spirit', fr. νέος, 'young, youthful;
new', and φρήν, gen. φρενός, 'heart, mind,
spirit'. See neo- and phreno-.

## neophyte
neophyte, п., 1) a new convert, a proselyte; 2) a
novice. — Eccles. L. neophytus, fr. Gk.
νεόφυτος, lit. 'newly planted', whence 'newly
initiated, newly converted', fr. νέος, 'new', and
φυτός, 'grown', verbal adj. of φύειν, 'to cause
to grow'. See neo- and -phyte.

## neoplasm
neoplasm, п., a morbid growth of tissue, a tumor
(med.) — Lit. 'new formation'; coined by the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:519 COLUMN:3 -->
German physiologist Karl Friedrich Burdach
(1776-1847) fr. neo- and plasm.

## neoplastic
neoplastic, adj., pertaining to neoplasm. — See
prec. word and plastic.

## Neoplatonism
Neoplatonism, Neo-Platonism, п., a school of
philosophy founded in Alexandria in the 3rd
cent. C.E., that combined the teachings of
Plato and some other Greek philosophers with
the mystical doctrines of the East. —
Compounded of neo- and Platonism.

## Neoplatonist
Neoplatonist, Neo-Platonist, п., an adherent of
Neoplatonism. — See prec. word and -ist,

## neoprene
neoprene, п., a synthetic rubber formed by the
polymerization of chloroprene (chem.) —
Coined fr. neo- and (iso)prene.

## neossine
neossine, neossin, п., the chief substance of which
edible birds' nests are made (biochem.) —
Formed with chem. suff. -ine fr. Gk. νεοσσία, 'nest
of young birds', fr. νεοσσός, 'a young bird',
which stands for *ve(f )οκ!,ός, and lit. means
'new inhabitant (of the nest)', fr. νέος, 'new',
and the stem of κεΐσθαι,, 'to lie down, lie'. See
neo- and civil.

## neossology
neossology, п., the study of young birds. —
Compounded of Gk. νεοσσός, 'a young bird', and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See neossine and -logy.

## neoteric
neoteric, adj., recent, new. — Late L. neotericus,
fr. Gk. νεωτερικός, 'youthful, fresh, modern',
fr. νεώτερος, compar. of νέος, 'young, new'.
See neo-, -ther and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: neoteric, п., neoteric-al-ly, adv.

## neoterism
neoterism, п., 1) a new word or expression; 2) the
use of new words or expressions. — Gk.
νεωτερισμός, 'innovation', fr. νεωτερίζει, Чо make
innovations', fr. νεώτερος. See prec. word and
-ism.

## Neotoma
Neotoma, п., the genus consisting of the wood
rats (zool.) — ModL., compounded of neo- and
the stem of τέμνειν, 'to cut'. See tome.

## Neotragus
Neotragus, п., the genus consisting of the royal
antelope (zool.) — ModL., compounded of
neo- and Gk. τράγος, 'goat'. See tragic.

## Neotropical
Neotropical, adj., pertaining to a zoogeographi-
cal realm comprising Central and South
America and the West Indies. — Compounded of
neo- and tropica].

## Neozoic
Neozoic, adj., pertaining to, or designating, the
Mesozoic and Cenozoic periods (geol.) —
Compounded of neo- and -zoic.
Derivative: Neozoic, n.

## Nepa
Nepa, п., a genus of insects, the water scorpion
(zool.) — L. nepa, 'scorpion', of African origin.

## nepenthe
nepenthe, п., a drug that relieves grief and causes-
forget fulness,— Gk. νηπενθές, neut. οίνηπεν-
θής, 'fee from sorrow, soothing pain',
occurring in the Odyssey, IV, 221, as the attribute of
φάρμακον, 'drug*, formed fr. negative particle
νη- (see no, ad v., and cp. nay) and πέν&ος, 'pain,
grief, which is rel. to πάθος, 'a suffering'. See
pathos.

## nepenthes
nepenthes, п., 1) = nepenthe; 2) (cap.) a genus of
insectivorous plants — See prec. word.

## Nepeta
Nepeta, a genus of plants, the catnip (bot.) —
ModL., fr. L. nepeta, 'the Italian catnip', prob.
derived fr. Nepete, name of a city in Etruria.

## nephalism
nephalism, п., total abstinence from alcoholic
liquors. — Gk. νηφαλι,σμός, 'soberness', fr.
νηφάλιος, 'sober', fr. νήφω, Dor. ναφω, Ί am
sober'; prob. standing for. I.-E. *nagwho, Ί am
sober', whence also Arm. naut'i, 'sober*. For
the ending see sulf. -ism.

## nephel-
nephel-, form of nephelo- before a vowel.

## nepheline
nepheline, п., a silicate of aluminum, sodium and
potassium (KNa3Al4Si4018) (mineral.) — F.
nepheline, coined by the French mineralogist
Abbe Rene-Juste Hauy (1743-1822) in 1800 fr.
Gk. νεφέλη, 'cloud'; see nephelo- and chem.
suff. -Ine. Treated with acid, this mineral
becomes cloudy (whence its name).

## nephelinite
nephelinite, п., a dark volcanic rock containing
nephelite and pyroxene (petrogr.) — Formed
from prec. word with subst. suif. -ite.

## nephelite
nephelite, п., nepheline. — Formed—with
change of suffix—fr. nepheline. The name
nepheline was changed to nephel-ire, because
mineral names are generally formed with the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:520 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 493 | NEST -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:520 COLUMN:1 -->
subst. suff. -ite.
Nephclium, п., a genus of trees of the soapberry
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Late L. nephelion,
name of a plant, fr. Gk. νεφέλιον, prop. dim. of
νεφέλη, 'cloud'. See nepho-.
nephelo-, before a vowel nephel-, combining form
meaning 'cloud'. — Gk. νεφελο-, νεφελ-, fr.
νεφέλη, 'cloud'. See nepho-,
nephelometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the cloudiness of the sky. — Compounded of
nephelo- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: nephelometr-ic, nephelometr-ic-al,
adjs., nephehmetr-ic-al-ly, adv., nephelometr-y,
n.

## nephew
nephew, n. — ME. neve, neveu, fr. OF. neveu, ne-
vou (F. neveu), fr. L. nepotem, ace. of nepos,
'grandson', in post-Augustan L. 'nephew', in
general (poet.), 'descendant', which stands for
nepot-s and is cogn. with ΟΙ. nopal, Avestic na-
pat-, naptar-, OPers, napat-, 'grandson,
descendant', OLith. nepuotis, nepotis, 'grandson', Olr.
nia, gen. niath, 'son of a sister', W. net, nai, of
s.m., Co. noi, 'grandson', OE. nefa, OS. nebo,
ON. nefi, OFris. neva, Du. nee/, OHG. nevo,
MHG. neve, G. Neffe, 'nephew', Gk. ά-νεψίός
(for "sm-neptiyos), 'cousin, nephew'. Cp. Gk.
νέττοδες (Odyssey 4, 404; said of seals), which
prob. means 'children, descendants', and is the
plural of νέπως (equivalent to L. nepos), but
was refashioned according to the declension of
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. Cp. also niece, nepo-
tizm.

## nepho-
nepho-, combining form meaning 'cloud'. — Gk.
νεφο-, fr. νέφος, 'cloud' (whence νεφέλη,
'cloud'), which is cogn. with L. nebula, 'mist, fog,
cloud'. See nebula and cp. nepheUne, Nephelium,
nephelo-.

## nephology
nephology, п., that branch of meteorology which
deals with clouds. —■ Compounded of nepho-
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: nepholog-ic-al, adj. nepholog-ist, n.

## nephoscope
nephoscope, п., an instrumentfor determining the
altitude, velocity and direction of clouds. —
Compounded of nepho- and Gk. -σκόττιον, fr.
σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scope.
Derivative: nephosocop~ic, adj.

## nephr-
nephr-, form of nephro- before a vowel.

## nephralgia
nephralgia, п., pain in a kidney (med.) —
Compounded of nephr- and Gk. -αλγία, fr. άλγος,
'pain'. See -algia.

## nephrectomy
nephrectomy, п., excision of a kidney (med.) —
Compounded of nephr- and Gk. -εκτομία, 'a
cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting out'. See
-ectomy.

## nephria
nephria, п., Bright's disease (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. νεφρός, 'kidney'. See nephro- and 1st -ia.

## nephric
nephric, adj., pertaining to, or near, the kidneys.
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. νεφρός, 'kidney'.
See nephro-,

## nephridial
nephridial, adj., pertaining to a nephridium. —
See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## nephridium
nephridium, п., one of the excretory organs of
some invertebrates (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
νεφρίδιος, 'of the kidneys', fr. νεφρός, 'kidney'.
See nephro-.

## nephrite
nephrite, п., a variety of jade (mineral.) — G.

## Nephrit
Nephrit, coined by the German geologist and
mineralogist Abraham Gottlob Werner (1750-
1817) in 1794 fr. Gk. νεφρός, 'kidney' (see

## nephro-)
nephro-), and suff. -it, which goes back to Gk.
-ϊτης (see subst. suff. -ite); so called in allusion
to its supposed efficacy against diseases of the
kidneys.

## nephritic
nephritic, adj., pertaining to, or affecting, the
kidneys. — Late L. nephriticus, fr. Gk. νεφρΐτικός,
'pertaining to the kidneys', fr. νεφρός, 'kidney'.
See nephro-.

## nephritis
nephritis, п., inflammation of the kidney (med.)
— Late L. nephritis, fr. Gk. νεφρΐτις, fr.
νεφρός, 'kidney'. See nephro- and -iris,

## nephro-
nephro-, before a vowel nephr-, combining form

## meaning 'kidney'
meaning 'kidney', or 'nephric and'. — Fr. Gk.
νεφρός, 'kidney', which stands for I.-E. *neg"h-

## ros
ros, 'kidney; testicle', and is cogn. with L.
(Praenestine) nefrones (for *neg"hron-),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:520 COLUMN:2 -->
'kidneys; testicles', L. (Lanuvian) nebrundines,
'kidneys, testicles', ON. nyra, Dan. nyre, Swed.
njure, ONorw. nyra, Norw. ryggja-nyre,
'kidney', ME. nere, MDu. niere, Du. nier, 'kidney',
OHG. того, niero, 'kidney, testicle, loin', MHG
niere, nier, 'kidney, loin', G. Niere, 'kidney' (fr.
Teut. *neurian-, *neuran-, fr. I.-E. *neg"hron-).
Cp. pcrmephrium.

## nephrolith
nephrolith, п., a renal calculus (med.) —
Compounded of nephro- and Gk. λίθος, 'stone'.
See -llth.

## nephropexy
nephropexy, п., the frxing of a floating kidney
(med.) — Medical L. nephropexia, compounded
of nephro- and Gk. -πηξίδ, fr. πηξις, 'a making
firm, fastening', which derives from the stem of
ττηγνύναί, 'to join, make firm'. See -pexy.

## nephrosis
nephrosis, п., disease of the kidneys (med.) —
Medical L., coined by Miiller in 1905 fr. Gk.
νεφρός, 'kidney' (see nephro-), and suff. -osis.

## nephrotomy
nephrotomy, п., the operation of cutting into the
kidney (surg.) — Compounded of nephro- and
Gk. -τομίδ, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'.
See -tomy.

## nepotism
nepotism, п., favoritism shown to relatives esp. in
appointments to high offices. — Orig.
favoritism of Popes shown to their natural children,
euphemistically referred to as their 'nephews';
F. nepotisme, fr. It. nepotismo, a var. of nipotis-
mo, fr. nipote, 'nephew", fr. L. nepotem, ace. of
nepds. See nephew. For the ending see suff. -ism,

## nepotist
nepotist, п., one who practices nepotism. — See
prec. word and -ist.

## Neptune
Neptune, п., 1) the god of the sea in Roman
mythology; identified later with the Greek god
Poseidon; 2) name of a planet. — L. Neptunus,
'the sea god; the sea', prob. fr. I.-E. base
*(e)nebh-, 'moist', whence also Avestic napta-,
'moist, humid', L. nebula, 'mist, fog, cloud'. See
nebula.

## Neptunian
Neptunian, adj., 1) pertaining to Neptune; 2)
formed by water; 3) pertaining to the planet
Neptune. — See prec. word and -ian.

## Neptunist
Neptunist, п., an adherent of the now obsolete
view that the action of water had an important
part in the formation of rocks. — See Neptune
and -ist.

## neptunium
neptunium, п., a chemical element. — ModL.,
coined by Ε. Μ. McMillan of the University of
California fr. L. Neptunus (see Neptune and
chem. suff. -ium). He called this element, which
lies beyond uranium, after the planet Neptune,
because the orbit of this planet round the sun
lies beyond that of the planet Uranus.

## Nereid
Nereid, п., 1) a sea nymph; 2) (not cap.) any
member of the genus of worms called Nereis. — L.
Nereis, gen. Neriidos, fr. Gk. Νηρηίς, Νηρεΐς,
gen. Νηρηΐδος, Νηρε'ίδας, lit. 'a daughter of
Nereus', Γτ.Νηρεύς. See Nereus and 3rd -Id and
cp. aneroid.

## Nereis
Nereis, п., a genus of marine worms (zool.) — L.,
fr. Gk. Νηρηΐς, name of a sea nymph (see prec.
word); so called because they live in the sea.

## Nereus
Nereus, п., a sea god (Greek mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. Νηρεύς, which is rel. to νδρός, 'flowing,

## liquid'
liquid', νάω, Ί flow'. See naiad and cp. Nereid,
Nerine.

## Nerine
Nerine, п., a genus of South African plants of the
amaryllis family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. Nerine,
'Nereid', fr. Nereus. See Nereus.

## Nerita
Nerita, п., a genus of marine snails. — L. nerita,
'a kind of sea mussel', fr. Gk. νηρείτης, νη-
ρΐτης, prob. fr. Νηρεύς.(see Nereus); so called
because they live in the sea.

## Neritina
Neritina, п., a genus of snails (zool.) — ModL.,
from prec. word.

## Nerium
Nerium, п., a genus of plants of the dogbane
family (bot.) — L. nerion, nerium, 'oleander', fr. Gk.
νήριον, fr. νηρός, νεαρός, 'fresh', fr. νέος,
'young, fresh'. See neo-.

## nero-antico
nero-antico, п., a beautiful kind of black marble.
— It., fr. nero, 'black', and antico, 'antique,

## ancient'. The first element derives fr. L. nigrum
ancient'. The first element derives fr. L. nigrum,

## ace. of niger
ace. of niger, 'black'. See Negro. For the second
element see antic.

## nerol
nerol, п., a liquid alcohol contained in neroli oil.
— Back formation fr. neroli oil.

## neroli oil
neroli oil, oil obtained by the distillation of orange
flowers. — F. neroli, fr. It. neroli; so named after

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:520 COLUMN:3 -->
its discoverer Anna Maria de la Tremoille, wife
of the Italian prine'e of Nerole.

## Neronian
Neronian, adj., pertaining to, or resembling Nero,
emperor of Rome (54-68). — L. Neronianus, fr.
Nero, gen. Neronis, 'Nero'. For the ending see
suff. -ian.

## nervation
nervation, п., the arrangement in the veins of a
leaf or in an insect's wing (bot. and zool.) — See
nerve and -ation.

## nerve
nerve, n. — L. nervus, 'sinew, tendon; cord,
bowstring; nerve; vigor, force', cogn. with Gk. νεϋ-
pov (for *sneurom) of s.m., OI. snavan-, 'band,
sinew', Avestic snavar&, 'sinew', Toch. В snaura,
'sinews, nerves', Arm. neard, 'sinew', fr. I.-E.
base *(s)ne-, 'to spin, sew with a needle', whence
also Gk. νέειν, L. nere, 'to spin', MDu. naeyen,
OHG. najan, 'to sew'. See needie and cp. neuro-.
For the relationship between Gk. νεϋρον and
L. nervus, cp. Gk. παΰρος, 'little, small', and L.
parvus, of s.m., Gk. αυλός, 'flute, pipe, tube',
αυλών, 'a hollow way, canal, channel', and L.
alvus, 'stomach, womb'.
Derivatives: nerve, tr. v., nerve-less, adj., nerve-
less-ly, adv., nerve-less-ness, п., nerv-y, adj.

## nervine
nervine, adj., 1) pertaining to the nerves; 2)
affecting the nerves — ModL. nervinus, fr. L.
nervus. See nerve and adj. suff. -ine.
Derivative: nervine, п., a drug affecting or
soothing the nerves.

## nervous
nervous, adj., 1) pertaining to the nerves;
affecting the nerves; 2) agitated, excitable; 3) strong,
vigorous. — ME. neruous, fr. L. nervosus,
'sinewy, vigorous', fr. nervus. See nerve and
-ous.
Derivatives: nervous-ly, adv., nervous-ness, n.

## nervure
nervure, п., a rib or vein in a leaf or in an insect's
wing (bot. and zool.) — Formed fr. nerve with
suff. -иге.

## nescience
nescience, п., want of knowledge, ignorance. —

## Late L. nescientia
Late L. nescientia, 'ignorance', fr. L. nesciens,
gen. nescientis. See next word and -ce.

## nescient
nescient, adj., not knowing, ignorant. — L. ne-

## sciens
sciens, gen. nescientis, pres. part, oinescire, 'not

to know, to be ignorant', formed from the

negative particle ne- and scire, 'to know'. For the

first element see no, adv., and cp. nay, for the

second element see science, for the ending see

## Neslia
Neslia, п., a genus of plants, the ball mustard
(bot.) — ModL., named after the French
botanist J.-A.-N. de Nesle. For the ending see 1st
suff. -ia.

## neso-
neso-, combining form meaning 'island'. — Gk.
νήσο-, fr. νήσος (Dor. νδσος), 'island', which
prob. stands for *να-σος, lit. 'that which
