swims', and is rel. to νή-χειν (for *νά-χειν),
'to swim'. See natation and cp. the second

## element in chersonese
element in chersonese, Indonesia, Melanesia,

## Micronesia
Micronesia, Polynesia.

## Nesonetta
Nesonetta, п., a genus of ducks living in the
Auckland Islands. — ModL., lit. 'island duck',
compounded of Gk. νήσος, 'island', and νητ-
τα, Att. form of νήσσα, 'duck'. For the first
element see neso-. The second element is cogn.

## with L. anas
with L. anas, 'duck'; see Anas and cp. Nettapus,
Nettion.

## Nesotragus
Nesotragus, п., a small genus of antelopes (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of neso- and Gk.
τράγος, 'goat'. See tragic,

## ness
ness, п., headland, promontory. — ME. naisse,

## nasse
nasse, fr. OE. nxss, ness, rel. to ON. nes, Dan.

## nses
nses, Swed. nas, MLG. nes(s), MDu. nesse, nes,
'ness', and to OE. nosu, 'nose'. See nose and cp.

## naze
naze,

## -ness
-ness, suff. forming abstract nouns denoting

condition, state or quality. — ME. -nes, -ness, fr.

## OE. -nis
OE. -nis, -nys, -ness, -nes, rel. to OS. -nissi, -nus-

## si
si, MDu. -nisse, -nesse, Du. -nis, OHG. -nissa,

## -nassi
-nassi, -nussi, MHG. -nusse, -nisse, G. -nis,

## Goth
Goth, -inassus.

## Nessus
Nessus, п., a Centaur slain by Hercules for trying
to carry off Dejanira (Greek mythol.) — L.

## Nessus
Nessus, fr. Gk. Νεσσός; of uncertain origin.

## nest
nest, n. — ME., fr. OE., rel. to MLG., Du., OHG.,

## MHG.
MHG., G. nest, 'nest', fr. I.-E. 'nizdo-, whence

## also OI. nidah
also OI. nidah, 'resting place, nest', Arm. nist,
'seat', L. nidus (for "nizdos), 'nest', OSlav.

## gnizdo
gnizdo, Lith. t'izdas, Lett, ligzda, Olr. net, W.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:521 COLUMN:1 -->
nyth, Co. neid, Bret, nez, neiz, 'nest'. l.-E. *niz-
do~, stands for *ni-zd-o- and lit. means 'a place
to sit down in', fr. *ni-, 'down', and zero degree
of I.-E. base *sed-, 'to sit' [cp. OI. ni-satsuh,
'sitting', ni-sidati, 'sits down, settles', and Gk.
δ'ζος (metathesis for *oz-d-os), 'branch', Arm.
ost, Goth, asts, OHG., MHG., OS. oil, MDu.
aest, Du. rceif^'branch, bough', OE. ost, 'knot
in a tree', fr. I.-E. *ozdos, 'that which sits (close
to the trunk)', fr. zero degree of *sed-, 'to sit'].
See nether and sedentary and cp. eyas, nidus,
nidificate. Cp. also nestle.
Derivatives: nest, intr. and tr. v. nest-er, n.

## nestitherapy
nestitherapy, п., cure by reducing the quantity of
food (med.) — Compounded of Gk. νήστις, 'a
not eating, fasting', and θεραπεία 'a waiting
on, service, attendance'. The first element is
formed from the negative pref. νη- (see no, adv.,
and cp. nay) and the base of ϊδειν, 'to eat'; see
eat. For the second element see therapy.

## nestle
nestle, intr. v., to lie close and snug; tr. v., to
settle or shelter, as in a nest. — Prob. not the
equivalent of OE. nestlian, 'to build a nest', but
back formation fr. nestling (q.v.), which was
mistaken for a pres. part. Cp. darkle.

## nestling
nestling, п., a bird too young to leave the nest. —
Formed fr. nest with dimin. suff. -ling.

## Nestor
Nestor, п., 1) an old king, the son of Neleus and
Chloris, renowned for his wise counsel (Homer's
Iliad); hence used to denote 2) a wise old man.
— L., fr. Gk. Νέστωρ, lit. 'one who blesses'.
The word is related to Gk. νόστος, 'returning',
orig. 'blessing', νόστιμος, 'blessed'. See
nostalgia.

## Nestorian
Nestorian, adj., 1) pertaining to Nestorius,
patriarch of Constantinople (428-431 C.E.), who
was condemned for heresy; 2) pertaining to the
doctrine of Nestorius. — L. Nestorianus, fr.
Nestorius.
Derivatives: Nestorian, n. (q.v.), Nestorian-ism,
п., Nestorian-ize, intr. v.

## Nestorian
Nestorian, п., a believer in Nestorianism; a
member of the Nestorian Church. — See prec. word.

## net
net, n. — ME. net(t), fr. OE. net(t), rel. to OS.
net(ti), ΟΝ., Norw., Dan. Du. net, Swed. not,
MLG., MDu. net(te), OHG. nezzi, MHG. netze,
G. Netz, Goth, nati, 'net', fr. Teut. base 'natja,
lit. 'something knotted', and cogn. with Ol.
ndhyati, 'binds, ties', L. nassa (prob. for *nad-
sa), 'a basket for catching fish', nodus, 'knot',
Olr. nascim, Ί bind, oblige', for-naidm, 'a
binding'; cogn. also with L. nectere, 'to bind' (which
is a relatively new word, formed on analogy of
pectere, 'to comb'). All the above words derive
fr. I.-E. base *ned-, 'to twist, to knot', an
enlarged form of base *(s)ni-, whence L. neo, nere,
*to bind'. See needle and cp. nettie. Cp. also
nexus, annex, connect, node, noose, ouch.
Derivatives: net, tr. and intr. v., nett-ed, adj.,
nett-er, п., nett-ing, n.

## net
net, adj., free from all deductions. — ME., fr.
MF. (= F.), 'neat, clean'. See neat, 'pure'.
Derivative: net, tr. v., to gain as net profit.

## nether
nether, adj., lower. — ME. nethere, nithere, fr.
OE. neodera, nidera, 'lower', from the adverb
neodor, nider, 'downward'; rel. to the adverbs
OS. nithar, ON. nidr, OFris. nither, Du. neder,
neer, OHG. nidar, MHG. nider, G. nieder
(whence the adjectives OS. nithiri, ON. ned(ar)ri,
Dan., Swed. nedre, OFris. nithera, Du. neder,
OHG. nidari, nidaro, MHG. nider(e), G. nieder);
prop, comparatives formed fr. I.-E. *w-, 'down,
below', whence Ol. ni, 'down', nita/am, 'down-
wards', nica, 'below, down', nicah, 'low', Avestic
ni, 'down', Arm. ni, n-, 'low', Gk. νειόθεν, 'from
below', νειός (scil. γη), 'field', prop, 'lowland',
OSlav. ni-zu, 'low, down', ni-va, 'field'. Cp. I.-E.
*ni-zdo- (in L. nidus, OE. nest, etc.), 'nest', lit. 'a
place to sit down in*. Cp. nest, nidus, and the
second element in Upanishad. Cp. also beneath,
underneath.

## Nethinim
Nethinim, п., pi., servants who performed the
lowest service under the Levites in the Temple
(Bible) — Heb. пёМп\т, lit. 'those given (scil.
to the sanctuary)', pi. pass. part, of nathan, 'he
gave'. See Nathan.

## netsnke
netsnke, п., a small carved object of ivory, bone
or wood, pierced with holes. — Jap.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:521 COLUMN:2 -->

## Nettapus
Nettapus, п., a genus of very small geese, the
pygmy goose (ornithol.) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. νηττα, 'duck', and πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. See next word and podal and cp. the
second element in Nesonetta.

## Nettion
Nettion, п., a genus of ducks, the teal (ornithol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. νηττίον, dimin. of νηττα,
Att. form of νήσσα, 'duck', which is cogn. with
L. anas, 'duck'. See Anas and cp. prec. word.

## nettle
nettle, n. — ME. netle, netel, fr. OE. netle, netele,
netel, rel. to OS. netila, dial. Swed. natla, Norw.
netla, MDu. netele, netel, Du. netel, OHG.
netila, MHG. пеззе1, G. Nessel, fr. Teut. base
*natilon, dimin. of *naton, which appears in.
Ice], now (gras), Norw. brenne-nata, OHG.
пазза, 'nettle'. These words prob. meant orig.
'the textile plant', and are derivatives of I.-E.
base *ned-, 'to twist, tie, knot', whence also Olr.
ne-naid, 'nettles', and possibly also Gk. άδικη,
'nettle' (if derived fr. *nd-ika~). See net, n.

## neume
neume, also пеит, п., musical notation,
indicating the melody to be sung to a final syllable
(med. music). —■ F. neume, fr. ML. neuma, fr.
Gk. πνεϋμα, 'breath'. See pneuma.

## neur-
neur-, form of neuro-, before a vowel.

## neural
neural, adj., pertaining to a nerve or to the nerves.
— Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. νεΰρον,
'nerve'. See neuro-.

## neuralgia
neuralgia, п., pain along the course of a nerve
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of neur- and
Gk. -αλγίϊ, fr. άλγος, 'pain'. See -algia.

## neuralgic
neuralgic, adj., pertaining to neuralgia. —
Formed from prec. word with adj. suff. -ic.

## neurasthenia
neurasthenia, п., nervous exhaustion (med.) —
Medical L., lit. 'weakness of the nerves', fr.
neur- and Gk. ασθένεια, 'weakness'. See
asthenia.

## neurasthenic
neurasthenic, adj., suffering from neurasthenia.
— Formed from prec. word with adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: neurasthenic, n.

## neuration
neuration, п., nervation. — A hybrid coined fr.
Gk. νεΰρον, 'nerve' (see nerve), and -ation, a
suff. of Latin origin. The correct form is
nervation (q.v.)

## neurectomy
neurectomy, п., excision of a nerve (med.) —
Compounded of neur- and Gk. -εκτομίδ, 'a cut-*
ting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting out'. See
-ectomy.

## neurilemma
neurilemma, п., the sheath covering a nerve fiber
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. neurilema, a word
coined by the German anatomist John Christian
Reil (1759-1813) fr. Gk. νεΰρον, 'nerve', and
λημα, 'will, desire, purpose', which was
confused with λέμμα, 'rind, cover' (lit. 'that which
is peeled off'). The correct form should have
been neurolemma (cp. the numerous compounds
beginning with neuro-). See neuro- and iepto-.

## neurine
neurine, п., a poisonous ptomaine obtained

## through the putrefaction of flesh
through the putrefaction of flesh, C5H13ON
(chem.) — Formed fr. neur- with chem. suff.
-ine.

## ueuritic
ueuritic, adj., pertaining to, or having, neuritis.
— See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## neuritis
neuritis, п., inflammation of a nerve or nerves
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr.
Gk. νεΰρον, 'nerve'. See neuro-,

## neuro-
neuro-, before a vowel neur-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining to a nerve or nerves'. — Fr.
Gk. νεΰρον, 'sinew, tendon; cord, bowstring,
nerve; strength, vigor', which stands for *sneu-

## rom and is cogn. with L. nervus
rom and is cogn. with L. nervus, of s.m. See
nerve and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
perineurium.

## neuroglia
neuroglia, п., tissue which supports the essential
nervous tissue (anat.) — Medical L., coined by
the German pathologist Rudolph Ludwig Karl
Virchow (1821-1902) fr. neuro- and Gk. γλία,
'glue', which is cogn. with L. gluten, 'glue'. See

## glue
glue, п., and cp. glioma.

## neurology
neurology, п., the study of the nervous system. —
Prob. coined by the English physician Thomas
Willis (1621-75) fr. neuro- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner;
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: neurolog-ic-al, adj., neurolog-ist,
n.

## neurolysis
neurolysis, n., destruction of nerve tissue (physiol.)
— Medical L., compounded of neuro- and Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:521 COLUMN:3 -->
λύσις, 'a loosing, setting free', fr. λύειν„ 'to
loose'. See -lysis,

## neuroma
neuroma, п., a nerve tumor (med.) — Medical L.,
formed with suff. -oma fr. Gk. νεΰρον, 'nerve'.
See neuro-.

## neuron
neuron, also neurone, п., a complete nerve cell
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. νβΰρον, 'nerve'.
See neuro-.
Derivative: neuron-ic, adj.

## neuropath
neuropath, n. 1) one who suffers from nervous
disease; 2) a neuropathist. — Compounded of
neuro- and Gk. -παίτής, fr. πάθος, 'suffering'.
See -path,

## neuropathic
neuropathic, adj., suffering from neuropathy. —
See prec. word and -pathic.
Derivatives: neuropath-ic, п., neuropathic-al-ly,
adv.

## neuropathist
neuropathist, п., a specialist in nervous diseases.
— See neuropath and -1st.

## neuropathology
neuropathology, п., the study of the diseases of
the nervous system. — Compounded of neuro-
and pathology.
Derivative: neuropatholog-ist, n.

## neuropathy
neuropathy, п., nervous disease. — Compounded
of neuro- and Gk. -πάθεια, fr. πάθος,
'suffering'. See -pathy.

## neurophysiology
neurophysiology, п., the physiology of the
nervous system. — Compounded of neuro- and
physiology.

## neuropsychology
neuropsychology, п., the study of the connection
between the nervous system and psychological
processes. — Compounded of neuro- and
psychology.

## Neuroptera
Neuroptera, n. pi., an order of insects (entomol.)
— ModL., compounded of neuro- and Gk. πτε-
ρόν, 'wing'. See ptero-.
Derivatives: Neuropter-an, adj. and n.

## neuropteroid
neuropteroid, adj., resembling the Neuroptera. —
Compounded of prec. word and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: neuropteroid, n.

## neurosis
neurosis, п., functional disorder of the nerves
(med.) — Lit. 'nervous condition'; coined by the
Scottish physician William Cullen (1710-90) fr.
Gk. νεΰρον, 'nerve' (see neuro-), and suff. -osis.

## neurotic
neurotic, adj., pertaining to, or acting on, the
nerves. — Formed fr. Gk. νεΰρον, 'nerve' (see
neuro-), with suff. -otic. See prec. word.
Derivative; neurotic, n.

## neurotomy
neurotomy, п., the surgical cutting of a nerve. —
Compounded of neuro- and Gk. -τομία, 'a
cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.
Derivatives: neurotom-ic-al, adj., neurotom-ist,
n.

## Neustria
Neustria, п., the western kingdom of the Franks.
— Late L. Neustria, derived fr. Frankish niust,
'newest', and prop, denoting the 'newest
conquest' (of the Franks). Frankish niust is the
superl. of niu, 'new', which is rel. to OE. niwe,
neo we, 'new'. See new.
Derivative: Neustri-an, adj.

## neuter
neuter, adj., neither masculine nor feminine (said
of nouns); neithej active nor passive (said of
verbs). — L. neuter, 'neither the one nor the
other, neither of two', formed fr. neg. particle
ne- and uter, 'either of two'. For the first
element see no and cp. nay, for the second see
whether.
Derivative: neuter, п., the neuter gender; a
neuter word.

## neutral
neutral, adj., 1) not taking either side in a quarrel
or in a war; 2) belonging to neither of two classes
or categories; 3) (chem.) neither acid nor
alkaline; 4) (electr.) neither positive nor negative. —
MF. (= F.), fr. L. neutralis, fr. neuter. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: neutral-ly, adv., neutral-ness, n.

## neutrality
neutrality, n. — MF. (= F.) neutralite, fr. ML.

## neutralitatem
neutralitatem, ace. oineutralitas, fr. L. neutralis;
see prec. word and -ity. The word neutralite was
introduced into French by Jean Froissart (lived
about 1337-1410).

## neutralize
neutralize, tr. v., 1) to make neutral; 2) to render
ineffective. — F. neutraliser, fr. neutral, fr. L.
neutralis; see neutral and -ize. F. neutraliser
appears for the first time in Randle Cotgrave's
French-English Dictionary published in 1611.
Derivatives: neutraliz-ation, п., neutraliz-er.

## neutretto
neutretto, п., a neutral meson (phys. and chem.)
— Coined fr. neutron and It. dimin. suff. -etto
(corresponding to F. -el; see -et).

## neutrino
neutrino, п., a neutral particle smaller than
a neutron (phys. and chem.) — Coined by
the Italian physicist Enrico Fermi (1901-54)
fr. neutrone, 'neutron' (fr. E. neutron), and
dimin. suff. -ino (corresponding to F. -in). See
neutron and dimin. suff. -ine.

## neutrodyne
neutrodyne, п., a high frequency radio amplifier.
— A hybrid trade name coined fr. L. neuter,
'neither of two', and Gk. δύναμις, 'power'. See
nenter and dyne.

## neutron
neutron, п., an electrically neuter particle of the
atom discovered by the English physicist James
Chadwig (born in 1891) in 1932 (phys. and
chem.) — Coined fr. L. neuter, 'neither' (see
neuter), on analogy of electron.

## neutrophile
neutrophile, adj., that which stains with neutral
dyes (physiol.) — Lit. 'that which is fond of
neither' (i.e. 'the group of white corpuscles that
is neither oxyphile nor basophile'); a hybrid
coined by the Jewish bacteriologist and immu-
nologist Paul Ehrlich (1854-1915) fr. L. neuter,
'neither of two', and Gk. φίλος, 'lover, friend'.
See neuter and -phile.
ηένέ, п., a field of granular snow; firn. — F,, prob.
fr. Savoyard nevi, 'mass of snow', fr. [t. neve,
'snow', fr. L. nivem, ace. of nix, 'snow'. See snow
and cp. Nivose.

## never
never, adv., not ever; at no time. — ME. nevere,
never, fr. OE. nsefre, fr. ne, 'not', and sefre, 'ever'.
See no, adv., and ever.

## nevertheless
nevertheless, adv., none the less; yet. —
Compounded of never, the and less.

## nevus
nevus, naevus, п., mole, birttimark (med.) — L.
naevus, 'mole, wart', for *gnaevus, lit. 'born in,
birthmark', from the stem of gignere, 'to beget,
bear, bring forth, prdduce'. See genus and cp.
words there referred to.

## new
new, adj. — ME. newe, new, fr. OE. niwe, neowe,
rel. to OS. niuwi, niwi, OFris. nie, MDu. nieuwe,
nuwe, nie, Du. nieuw, OHG. niuwi, MHG. niuwe,
G. neu, ON. nyr, Dan., Swed., Norw. ny, Goth.
niujis, 'new', fr. Teut. base *neuja-,
corresponding to I.-E. base *newo-, *newio-, *nowio-,
whence Ol. navah, ndvyah, Avestic nava-, Mod-
Pers. паи, Toch. А пи, В n(u)we, Hitt. newash.
Arm. nor (gen. noroy), Gk. νέος (for *νέί"ος),
'new', νεαρός (for'vcf αρός), 'youthful', L. novus,
OSlav. novu, OPruss. neuwenen, Lith. naiijas,
Gaul, novio-, nevio-, Olr. пйе, W. newydd, Bret.
newez, 'new'. Cp. now, Neustria and the first
element in Newton. Cp. also neo-, nova, novel,

## novercal
novercal, novice, nuncio, innovate, renovate.
Derivatives: new-ish, adj., new-Iy, adv.,

## newness
newness, n.

## newberyite
newberyite, п., a hydrated magnesium phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after J. Cosmo Newbery of
Melbourne. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
newe], п., 1) a pillar from which the steps of a
winding stair radiate; 2) the post at the top or

noiel (F. noyau), 'kernel, stone', fr. Late L. nu-

## calis
calis, 'like a nut', fr. L. nux, gen. nucis, 'nut'.

See nucleus and cp. nux vomica. Cp. also nowel,

## noyau
noyau,

newfangle, adj., 1) new, novel; 2) tending toward
novelties. — ME. newefangel, compounded of

newe, 'new', and -fangel, from the base οΐ/angen,

## fongen
fongen, fon, fr. OE. fan, 'to catch, seize, take'.

## See fang
See fang,

## newfangled
newfangled, adj., newfangle. — ME. newe/angled,
fr. newefangel. See prec. word and 3rd -ed.

## Newmarket
Newmarket, п., 1) a close-fitting coat; 2) a card
game. — In both senses named after Newmarket,

## a town in Cambridgeshire
a town in Cambridgeshire, England,

## news
news, n. — Prop. pi. of the adjective new; formed

## on analogy of OF. noveles
on analogy of OF. noveles, F. nouvelles, Late L.

## nova (pi. neut.)
nova (pi. neut.), 'news', lit. 'new things',

## newsy
newsy, adj., full of news (colloq.) — Formed fr.
news with adj. suff. -y.
Derivative: newsi-ness, n.

## newt
newt, п., an amphibious batrachian, an eft. —

## ME. newte
ME. newte, fr. ewte, fr. earlier evet, fr. OE. efete.
ME. newte arose fr. ewte through a misdivision
of an ewte into a newte. See eft. For similar

## Newton
Newton, masc. PN. — Formed from the place
name Newton, fr. OE. neowa tun, 'new town'.
See new and town.

## Newtonian
Newtonian, adj., pertaining to Sir Isaac Newton
(1642-1727) or his teachings; п., a follower of
Newton.

## newtonite
newtonite, п., a hydrous aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Named after Newton county in
Arkansas. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## next
next, adj. — ME. nexte, next, fr. OE. nehst,
niehst, 'nearest', superl. of niah, nih, 'nigh';rel.
to ON. nxstr, Du. naast, 'next', OHG. nuhisto,
MHG. nxhest, 'neighbor' (lit. 'the one next'),
G. nachst, 'next'. See nigh and cp. near.
Derivatives: next, adv., prep., n.

## nexus
nexus, п., 1) link, tie, connection; 2) series. — L.,
lit. 'that which ties or binds together', fr. nexus,
pp. oinecto, neciere, 'to tie, bind, join'. See net,
п., and cp. annex, connect.

## Neziktn
Neziktn, п., pi., the fourth division of the Mish-
nah and Talmud, dealing with criminal and civil
law. — Mishnaic Heb. neziqtn, lit. 'torts,
injuries, damages', pi. of nezeq, fr. Bibl. Heb.
nezeq, 'injury, damage', which is an Aramaic
loan word. Cp. Bibl.-Aram, "n^zaq (whence
part, ndzlq, Dan. 6: 3), 'he suffered injury',
Aram, nizqd, 'injury, damage', which are related
to Akkad. nazaqu, 'to injure', and to Arab.
naqasa (a metathesized form), 'he impaired'.

## niacin
niacin, п., nicotinic acid (chem.) — Suggested by
the American Medical Association as the
abbreviation of nicotinic acid and suff. -in.

## nib
nib, п., 1) beak of a bird; 2) the sharpened point
of a quill pen; 3) the steel, gold, etc. point of a
pen, inserted in a holder. — A variant of nelr.
Derivatives: nib, tr. v., to furnish with a nib;
nibb-ed, adj., nibb-er, n.

## nib
nib, п., a gentleman. — Probably a gradational
var. of nob,,'a person of high position'.

## nibble
nibble, tr. v., to bite gently; intr. v.', to take bites
gently. — Prob. of LG. origin. Cp. MLG. nib-
beten, NLG. nibbeln, knibbeln, gnibbeln, MDu.
knibbelen, 'to gnaw', Du. knibbelen, 'to cavil,
squabble'.
Derivatives: nibble, п., nibble-er, n.

## Nibelungenlied
Nibelungenlied, п., name of a German epic poem
of the 13th century. — G., lit. 'song of the
Nibelungs'. See prec. word and lied.

## Nibelungs
Nibelungs, n. pi., 1) a race of dwarfs who lived in
Norway and owned a hoard of gold and a magic
ring; 2) the Burgundian kings of the
Nibelungenlied. — G.r lit. 'children of the mist', rel. to
OHG. nebul, OS. nebal, OE. nifol, 'mist,
darkness', and cogn. with L. nebula, 'mist, fog,
cloud'. Seenebula andep. words there referred to.

## niblick
niblick, п., a golf club with a heavy well-lofted
head. — Of uncertain origin.

## Nicaean
Nicaean, adj., Nicene. — See Nicene and -an.

## nice
nice, adj. — ME., 'not wise, foolish, wanton', fr.
OF. nice, 'ignorant, foolish5, fr. L. nescius, 'not
knowing, ignorant', fr. neg. part, ne- and the
stem of scire, 'to know', see nescient. The
original meaning of E. nice was 'not wise,
foolish'.
Derivatives: nice-Iy, adv., nice-ness, п., nicety
(q.v.)

## Nicene
Nicene, adj., pertaining to Nicaea (called also
Nice) or to the ecclesiastical council held there
in 325. — Late L. Nicaenus, fr. Nicaea, fr. Gk.
Νϊκϊίϊ, 'Nicaea, Nice', an ancient city of Asia
Minor (whence the modern Turkish name Isnik
i.e. εις Νϊκαίαν, orig. 'to Nicaea'.

## nicety
nicety, п., exactness, accuracy, carefulness,
delicacy ; (usually in pi.) minute points, small details
— ME. nicete, meaning also 'foolishness', fr.

## OF. nicete
OF. nicete, 'foolishness', fr. nice, 'ignorant,
foolish'. See nice and -ty.

## niche
niche, п., a small recess in a wall. — F., fr. It.

## nicchia
nicchia, 'nook, niche', fr. nicchio, 'shell', which

## prob. derives fr. L. mitulus
prob. derives fr. L. mitulus, mititus, mptilus,
'mussel'. See Mytilus.
Derivative: niche, tr. v., to place in a niche.

## Nicholas
Nicholas, Nicolas, masc. PN. — F. Nicolas, fr. L.

## Nichotaus
Nichotaus, Nicolaus, fr. Gk. ΝΤκόλαος, lit.
'prevailing among the people', fr. νίκη, 'victory',
and λαός, 'people'. See Nike and lay, 'pertaining

## to the laity'. Cp. Colin. Cp. also Nick
to the laity'. Cp. Colin. Cp. also Nick, nickel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:522 COLUMN:3 -->

## nick
nick, п., a small cut, a notch, a groove. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: nick, tr. v., to make a notch, nicker
(q-v.)

## Nick
Nick, п., the devil (used only in the phrase Old
Nick). — Dimin. of Nicholas,

## nickel
nickel, n. — Swed., shortened by the Swedish
mineralogist Baron Axel Fredric von Cronstedt
(1722-65) in 1754 fr. kopparnickel, which was
formed—through substitution of Swed. koppar
for G. Kupfer—fr. G. Kupfernickel, 'copper,
nickel, copper devil'. For the first element of
this compound see copper; its second element is
shortened fr. the PN. Nikolaus, 'Nicholas', fr.
Gk. Νικόλαος (see Nicholas). The name Nickel,
used in the sense of'devil' (cp. Nick, 'the devil')
was given to this ore in sign of contempt,
because, though being copper-colored, it yielded
no copper. For sense development cp. cobalt
and wolfram.

## nicker
nicker, п., a water sprite. — ME. niker, fr. OE.
nicor, 'a water monster', rel. to ON. nykr, ofs.m.
and to OHG. nihhus, 'water sprite', nihussa,
'female water sprite'. See nix, 'water sprite'.

## nicker
nicker, intr. v., to neigh. — Of imitative origin,

## nicker
nicker, п., one who nicks. — See nick, v., and
agential suff. -er.

## nickname
nickname, п., an additional name. — From earlier
пеке-name, which arose from a misdivision of
an ekename into a nekename, and lit. means 'an
additional name'. See eke and name. Cp. newt,
nonce, notch, which owe their form to a similar
misdivision.
Derivative: nickname, tr. v.

## Nicolas
Nicolas, masc. PN. — See Nicholas.

## Nicol prism
Nicol prism, — Named after its inventor, the
Scottish physicist William Nicol (17687-1851).

## ulcotian
ulcotian, п., tobacco smoker. — The original
meaning of this word was 'tobacco'. It derives
fr. F. nicotiane, 'tobacco', fr. ModL. (herba)
Nicotiana. See nicotine.

## Nicotiana
Nicotiana, п., a genus of the tobacco plants (bot.)
— ModL. (herba) Nicotiana, 'the herb of Nicot'.
See next word.

## nicotine
nicotine, п., a poisonous alkaloid '(C^HjjNj)
found in tobacco leaves (chem.) — F., formed
—with change of suff.—from earlier nicotiane,
fr. ModL. (herba) Nicotiana, 'herb of Nicot' (=
'tobacco'), from the name of Jean Nicot (1530 7-
1600), ambassador of France at Lisbon, who
introduced tobacco into France (in 1560). Cp.
nicotian, Nicotiana.
Derivatives: nicotin-ean, nicotin-ed, nicotin-ian,
nicotin-ic, adjs., nicotin-ism, п., nicotin-ize, tr. v.

## nictate
nictate, to nictitate. — L. nictatus, pp. of L.
nictare, 'to wink, blink'. See next word.

## nictitate
nictitate, intr. v., to wink. — ML. nictitatus, pp.
of nictitare, freq. of L. nictare, 'to wink, blink',
fr. nicere, 'to beckon', fr. I.-E. base *kneigwh-,
'to bend', whence also L. *nivere in conivere, 'to
close the eyes, blink, wink at, overlook (errors),
connive at'. See connive and verbal suff. -ate and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: nictitat-ion, n.

## nidal
nidal, adj., pertaining to a nidus. — See uldus aad
adj. suff. -al.

## nidamental
nidamental, adj., pertaining to a covering for an
egg or eggs (zool.) — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. nidamentum, 'materials for a nest, nest', fr.
nidus, 'nest'. See nidus.

## niddering
niddering, adj., base, cowardly; п., a coward. —
An erroneous form standing for ME. nithing,
'infamous person, coward'; used by the Scottish
novelist and poet Sir Walter Scott (1771-1832).
See nithing.

## nide
nide, п., a nest; specif., a brood of pheasants. —
L. nidus (whence also F. nid), 'nest'. See nidus.

## nidificate
nidificate, intr. v., to build a nest, to nidify. — L.
nidificdt(-um), pp. stem of nidificare, 'to build a
nest', compounded of nidus, 'nest', and -ftcdre,
fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See nidus, and -ficate.

## nidiheatinn
nidiheatinn, n. — ML. nidificatid, gen. -onis, fr.
L. nidificatus, pp. of nidificare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## nidify
nidify, intr. v., to make a nest, to nidificate. — F.
nidifier, fr. L. nidificare. See nidificate,

## nid-nod
nid-nod, intr. v., to nod repeatedly. — Anliphonic
reduplication of nod.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:523 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NIDOLOGY | 496 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:523 COLUMN:1 -->

## nidology
nidology, п., the study of birds' nests. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. nidus, 'nest', and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See nidus
and -logy. The correct form is caliology (q.v.), in
which both elements are of Greek origin.

## nidor
nidor, п., scent, savor. — L. nidor, 'smell of burnt
things, savor', for "cnidds, cogn. with Homeric
Gk. κνϊση (fr. *κνΙδ-σ-ϊ), Att. κνίσα, 'smell
of a burnt sacrifice, steam, savor', ON. hnissa,
'strong smell, vapor caused by cooking'. The
orig. meaning of these words was 'piercing
smell' (for sense development cp. Goth, stigqan,
'to thrust', which is rel. to OHG. stinkan, OE.
stincan, 'to emit an odor'). They are cogn. with
ON. hnlta, OE. hnltan, 'to strike, thrust, butt',
Gk. κνίζειν, 'to scratch, scrape', κνϊδη, 'nettle',
Lett, kniest, 'to itch', kniedet, 'to rivet', ON.
knita, 'to rivet', Mir. cned, 'wound'. All these
words derive fr. I.-E. *qneid-, *qnid-,
enlargement of base *qnei-, *qne-, 'to scrape, scratch,
peel', whence Gk. κναίειν, κνήν, 'to scrape,
scratch', Lith. knisu, knisti, 'to dig, burrow',
kntiti, 'to peel off (intr.), OHG. nuoen, 'to scrape
smooth'. Cp. cnida.

## nidorous
nidorous, adj., smelling like something burning
(rare). — Late L. nidorosus, 'steaming', fr. L.
nidor. See prec. word and -ous.

## nidulant
nidulant, adj., 1) nestling; 2) lying free in a
nestlike cavity [hot.) — L. nldulans, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of nidulari, 'to build a nest', fr. nldutus, 'a
little nest', dimin. of nidus. See next word, -ule
and -ant.

## nidus
nidus, п., a nest; a breeding place; a place where
germs of disease are developed. — L. nidus,
'nest', for "nizdos. See nest and cp. nidamental,
nide, nidulant.

## niece
niece, n. — ME. лесс, neyce, fr. OF. niece (F.
niece), fr. VL. neptia (whence also OProveng.
nepsa, 'niece'), a var. of VL. nepta (whence
ΟΡΓΟνβης. neta, 'niece', Sp. nieta, Catal., Portp
neta, 'granddaughter'), fr. L. neptis,
'granddaughter', in Late L., 'niece', which is rel. to
nepos, gen. nepotis, 'grandson', in
post-Augustan L., 'nephew', and cogn. with OI. naptih,
Avestic napli-, 'granddaughter', OLith. nepte, of
s.m., Czech net\ 'niece', Olr. necht, W., OBret.
nith, MBret. niz, Co. noith, 'niece', ON. nipt,
'sister's daughter, niece*, OE. nift, 'niece,
granddaughter, stepdaughter*, OHG. nift, of s.m.
(whence the dimin. OHG. niftila, MHG. niftel,
'niece, mother's sister, cousin'), MDu. nifte,
nichte (Du. nicht), MLG. nifte, nichte (whence
G. Nichte), 'niece'. See nephew,

## niello
niello, n:, metallic alloy of sulfur with silver,
copper, lead, etc. — It., fr. VL. *nigellum, 'a kind
of black enamel', subst. use of L. nige/ium, neut.
of nigellus, 'somewhat black', which is a dimin.
of niger, 'black'; so called in allusion to the
color of this alloy. See Negro and cp. Nigeila
and the second element in darnel.
Derivative: niello, tr. v., to decorate with niello.

## Niersteiner
Niersteiner, п., a white Rhine wine of fine quality.
—Piop. 'wine of Nierstein'', a village near Mainz,
Germany. For the ending see subst. suff. -er.

## Nietzschean
Nietzschean, adj., pertaining to the German
philosopher Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche (1844-
1900) or his doctrines; п., a follower of
Nietzsche.

## Nletzscheanism
Nletzscheanism, п., the philosophy of Nietzsche.
— Formed from prec. word with suff. -ism.

## nieve
nieve, п., a fist. — ME. neve, nefe, fr. ON. hnefi,
'fist' (whence Dan. nxve).

## nifle
nifle, п., a trifle (dial.) — Perh. a blend of L. nihil
(see nihil) and trifle. Cp. drail.

## nifty
nifty, adj., smart, stylish (American Slang). —
Of uncertain origin.

## Nigel
Nigel, Neal, Neil, Niall, masc. PN. — Fr. Niall,
lit. 'courageous'; rel. to lr. niadh, 'champion'.
The name was Latinized into Nigellus, whence
arose the form Nigel. Cp. the unrelated Roman
surname Nigellus; this latter prop, means
'somewhat black', and is the dimin. of niger, 'black'
(see next word).

## Nigeila
Nigeila, п., a genus of plants, the fennel flower
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. nigeila, fem. of nigellus,
dimin. of niger, 'black' (see Negro and -ella and
cp. niello); so called from the black color of the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:523 COLUMN:2 -->
seeds.

## niggard
niggard, п., a mean person, a miser; adj., mean,
miserly. — ME. niggard, nigard, fr.ME. nig, 'to
be stingy', which is prob. of Scand. origin; cp.
ON. hneggr, 'stingy'. Cp. niggle. For the ending
see suff. -ard.
Derivatives: niggard-ly, adj. and adv., niggard-
li-ness,4i.

## nigger
nigger, п., a Negro. — Earlier neger, fr. F. negre,
fr. Sp. negro. See Negro.
Derivatives: nigger-ish, adj., nigger-ling, n.

## niggle
niggle, intr. v., to busy over trifles — Related to
dial. Norw. nigla, 'to busy over trifles', and prob.
also to niggard.
Derivatives: niggl-ing, niggl-y, adjs.

## nigh
nigh, adv., near. — ME. neih, neigh, nigh, fr. OE.
neah, neh, 'near', adv. and adj., rel. to OS. nah,
adv. and adj., ON. na-, Dan., Swed. na- (in
compounds), OFris. net, ni, adv. and adj., MDu. na,
Du. na, adv., adj. and prep., 'nigh, after', OHG.
nah, MHG. nach, G. nah, adv. and adj.,
Goth, niha, adv., and prob. cogn. with MPers.
nox, 'the first' (see Chr. B. Bartholomae, Zum
altiranischen WOrterbuch, p. 48). Cp. near (fr.
OE. near, compar. of neah), and next (fr. OE.
nehst, nlehst, superl. of neah). Cp. also the first
element in neighbor.
Derivative: nigh, prep.

## nigh
nigh, adj., near. — ME. neigh, neih, neh, fr. OE.
neah, neh. See nigh, adv.

## night
night, n. — ME. niht, night, fr. OE. neaht, niht,
rel. to OS., OHG., MHG. naht, OFris., MDu.,
Du., G. nacht, ON. ndtt, nott, Dan. nat, Swed.
паи, dial. Norw. natt, nott, Goth, nahts, fr. Teut.
base *naht, corresponding to I.-E. *noqt-,
whenceOI. naktam(aav. ace), 'atnight', naktih
(ace. pi.), 'nights', Gk. νύξ (gen. νυκτός), L. nox
(gen. noctis), Alb. natt, OSlav. noSti, Lith. nak-
tis, 'night', Olr. in-nocht, 'tonight', W. he-noid,
'tonight', peu-noeth, 'every night', W., Co. nos,
Bret, noz, 'night', Toch. A n(o)ktim, 'toward
evening', Hitt. nekus (gen.),'evening'. Cp. nocti-,
nocturnal, nycti-, the first element in nightingale,
Nakshastra, and the second element in acron-
ychal, equinox.
Derivatives: night, adj., nightly (q.v.)

## nightingale
nightingale, п., a small singing bird, Daulias lu-
scinia. — ME. nihtegale, nightingale, fr. OE.
nihtegale, lit. 'the night-singer', fr. niht, 'night',
and galan, 'to sing'; cp. OS. nahtigala, Du.
nachtegaal, OHG. nahtagala, MHG. nachte-
gal(e), G. Nachtigall, and see night and yell. For
sense development cp. Gk. αηδών, 'nightingale',
fr. άείδειν, 'to sing', and L. luscinia 'nightingale·',
whose second element comes fr. canere, 'to sing'.

## nightjar
nightjar, п., the goatsucker. — Compounded of
night and jar, 'to creak'; so called from the
jarring sound made by the male goatsucker.

## nightiy
nightiy, adj., pertaining to, or happening, every
night. — ME. nihtlich, nightly, fr. OE. nihtlic, fr.
niht, 'night'. See night and adj. suff. -ly.

## nightly
nightly, adv., every night.— ME., fr. nihtlich, adj.
See alght and adv. suff. -ly.

## nightmare
nightmare, п., 1) an incubus; 2) a frightening
dream. — Compounded of night and mare,
'incubus'.
Derivatives: nightmare, tr. v., nightmar-ish, adj.,
nigh'tmar-ish-ly, adv., nightmar-y, adj.

## nightshade
nightshade, п., any of various poisonous plants of
the genus Solanum; the belladonna. — ME.
nighteschede, fr. OE. nihtscada, lit. 'shade of
night* (see night and shade); so called in allusion
to its narcotic or poisonous qualities. Cp. Du.
nachtschade, G. Nachtschatten, 'nightshade'.

## nighty
nighty, п., a nightgown or nightshirt (colloq.) —
Formed fr. night with dimin. suff. -y.

## nigrescence
nigrescence, п., 1) process of becoming black; 2)
blackness — Formed fr. nigrescent with suff. -ce.

## nigrescent
nigrescent, adj., 1) becoming black; 2) tending to
become black. — L. nigrescens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of nigrescere, 'to become black',
inchoative of nigrere, 'to be black', fr. niger, 'black'.
See Negro and -escent.

## nigrify
nigrify, tr. v., to blacken. — Late L. nigrificare,
lit. 'to make black', compounded of L. niger,
'black', and -ficare, (r.facere, 'to make, do'. See
Negro and -fy.

## nigritude
nigritude, п., blackness. — L. nigritude,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:523 COLUMN:3 -->
'blackness', fr. niger, 'black'. See Negro and -tude.

## nihil
nihil, п., nothing; a thing of no value. — L.,
'nothing', fr. nihilum, for *nehilum, lit. 'not even
a trifle', fr. negative pref. ne- and hiium, 'a little
thing, a trifle'. For the first element see no, adv.,
and cp. nay, for the second see hilum. Cp. nil,
nihilism, annihilate, vilipend,

## nihilism
nihilism, п., 1) the doctrine of negation; 2) (cap.)
the doctrines of the Russian revolutionary
anarchism (1860-1917). —G. Nihilismus, coined by
the German philosopher Friedrich Heinrich
Jacobi (1743-1819) fr. L. nihil, 'nothing', and
suff. -ismus. See nihil and -ism. In its political
sense, the word Nihilismus was first used by the
German journalist Joseph von Gorres (1776-
1848). Turgeniev also uses the words nihilism
and nihilist in their political meaning (in his
novel Fathers and Children, published 1862) and
claims to be the inventor of these words.

## nihilist
nihilist, п., 1) an adherent of nihilism; 2) (cap.) a
member of the Russian revolutionary party
(1860-1917). — Prob. fr. F. nihiliste, which is
formed fr. L. nihil, 'nothing', and suff. -iste. See
nihil and -ist and prec. word.
Derivatives: nihilist, nihilist-ic, adjs.

## nihility
nihility, п., nothingness. — ML. nihilitas, fr. L.
nihil, 'nothing'. See nihil and -ity.

## Nike
Nike, п., the goddess of victory in Greek
mythology ; identified by the Romans with the goddess
Victoria. — Gk. Νίκη, lit. 'victory', prob. rel.
to νεΐκος, 'quarrel, strife, feud', νεικεΐν, 'to
quarrel with, to chide, rail at', and cogn. with
Lith. ap-ninkit, apriikti, 'to assail, attack', Lett.
nikns, 'violent, angry', naiks, 'quick, violent'.
Cp. Nicholas, Berenice, Eunice, epinicion, Poly-
nices, varnish.

## nil
nil, п., nothing. — L., contraction of nihil. See
nihil.

## nilgai
nilgai, also nylghai, nylghau, п., a large Indian
antelope. — Pers. and Hind, nilgaw, lit. 'blue
cow', fr. Pers. nil, 'blue', and gaw, 'cow', which
is re], to Avestic gaush, of s.m. For the first
element see lilac, for the second see cow, and cp.
gaur and words there referred to.

## mil
mil, intr. and tr. v., not to will (now used only in
some archaic phrases as will he, nill he). — ME.
nillen, fr. OE. nyllan, contraction of ne wyllan,
'not to will'. Se*e will and cp. willy-nilly.

## Nllometer
Nllometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
rise of the Nile. — Gk. Νειλομέτριον,
compounded of Νείλος, 'Nile', and μέτρον,
'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## Nilotic
Nilotic, adj., pertaining to the Nile, the Nile
region or the Negroes who live in the valley of the
White Nile. — L. Niloticus, fr. Gk. Νειλωτικός,.
'of, or pertaining to, the Nile', fr. Νείλος,
'Nile'. For the ending see suff. -otic.

## nim
nim, tr. and intr. v., to take; to steal (archaic) —
OE. niman, 'to take', fr. I.-E. base *nem-, 'to
divide, distribute, allot'. See next word and cp.
words there referred to.

## nimble
nimble, adj., quick, agile, alert. — ME. nimel,
'quick, nimble', prob. with the original
meaning 'quick to take', and formed with adj. suff.
-le fr. nimen, 'to take', fr. OE. niman, which is
rel. to OS., ODu., Goth, niman, ON. пета,
OFris. пета, nima, OHG. neman, MHG. nemen,
G. nehmen, 'to take', fr. I.-E. base *nem-, 'to
divide, distribute, allot', whence also Avestic
nemah-, 'loan', Gk. νέμειν, 'to deal out,
distribute, allot*, νέμεσις, 'just indignation,
jealousy, vengeance (esp. of the gods)', νομός,
'land allotted, pasture; district, province',
νόμος, 'anything allotted or assigned; usage,
custom; law', L. numerus, 'number', Lith. ηύο-
ma, nudmas, Lett, пибта, 'rent, interest', Mir.
nos, MBret. naux, 'custom, usage'. See numb,
and cp. nim. Cp. also Nemesis, noma, nomad,
nome, Nomeus, Nornic, nomistic, nomo-, -noniy,
number, numeral, numeric, numismatic,
nummary, nummular, and the second element in
guome, 'a dwarfish person', and in withernam.
The b in nim-b-le is intrusive; cp. grumble,
ramble.
Derivatives: nimble-ness, п., nimbl-y, adv.

## nimbose
nimbose, adj., cloudy. — L. nimbosus, 'cloudy,
stormy', fr. nimbus. See nimbus and -ose.
Derivative: nimbos-ity, -n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:524 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 497 | NIX -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:524 COLUMN:1 -->
nimbus, п., 1) a cloudlike splendor round the
head of a divinity; a cloud surrounding a person
or thing; an aura, a halo (art); 2) a raincloud
(meteor.) — L., 'rainstorm, thundercloud', fr.
*nembhos; cogn. with Pahlavi namb, nam, *dew,
fog, mist', ModPers. пет, 'moist, moisture', fr.
I.-E. base 'nembh-, which isrel. to base *enebh-,
'moist, vapor, mist, cloud', whence OI. nabhas-,
'mist, cloud, sky', Gk. νέφος, νεφέλη, 'cloud,
mist', L. nebula, 'mist, fog, cloud'. See nebula
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: nimbus-ed, adj.

## nimiety
nimiety, п., excess, redundancy. — L. nimietas,
'excessiveness', fr. nimius, 'beyond measure,
excessive', fr. nimis 'too much, beyond measure,
excessively', which prob. stands for *nimis,
contraction of *ne-mi-is and lit. means 'not too
little', fr. negative pref. ne~ and I.-E. base *mei-,
'to lessen', whence also L. minor, minus, 'smaller,
less'. For the first element see no, adv., and cp.
nay, for the second see minimum,

## niminy-piminy
niminy-piminy, adj., mincing; affected; refined.—
Imitative of mincing, refined speech.

## Nimrod
Nimrod, п., 1) thesonofCush, referred to in Gen.
10:8-10 as 'a mighty hunter'; 2) hence the name
is used to denote an expert hunter. — Heb.
NimrSdh.

## Nina
Nina, fern. PN. — Russ., prob. formed with
aphaeresis of the first syllable from Annina,
dimin. of Gk. "Αννα, fr. Heb. Hannah, lit.
'grace'. See Ann, Hannah and cp. F. Ninon,
Ninette, which are diminutives of Anne, 'Ann'.

## nincompoop
nincompoop, п., a fool, simpleton. — Prob. an
invented word.
Derivatives: nincompoop-ery, п., nincompoop-
ist, adj.

## nine
nine, adj. — ME. nigen, nine, fr. OE. nigon, nigan,
rel. to OS. nigun, OFris. niugun, nigun, ON. rtiu,
Dan. ni, Swed. nio, dial. Norw. nio, nie, MLG.,
Du. negen, OHG., MHG. niun, G. neun, Goth.
niun, 'nine', and cogn. with OI. ndva, Avestic
nava, Toch. ли, Arm. inn (for "envan), Gk. εννέα
(for *έννέ5α), Alb. ncnde, L. novem (for *no-
ven; the change of -n to -m is due to the analogy
of L. septem, 'seven', decern, 'ten'), Lith. devyni,
Lett, dewini, OSlav. deveti (the change of the
initial n- to d- in the Balto-SIavonic languages
is due to dissimilation, n-n having become d-n),
Olr. noi n-, W., Co. naw, 'nine'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. *enewen, *enwn, *newn, 'nine',
and are prob. cogn. with OI. ndvaft, Gk. νέος
(for *νέ5ος), L. novus, etc. 'new', a supposition
corroborated by the fact that I.-E. *ohou, 'eight',
is a dual form, hence orig. meant 'two fours'
(tetradic system!) Accordingly nine seems to
have meant originally 'the new number (scil. of
the third tetrad i.e. the first of the numbers 9,
10, 11, 12). See new and cp. ennea-,
nonagenarian, nonagon, nonary, nones, noon, November.
Derivative: nine, n.

## nineteen
nineteen, adj. — ME. nigentene, nynetene, fr. OE.
nigontiene, nigontyne. See nine and -teen.
Derivative: nineteen, n.

## nineteenth
nineteenth, adj. — ME. nyntenthe, formed on
analogy of fourth by adding -th to nineteen. The
OE. form is nigon-teoda.
Derivative: nineteenth, n.

## ninetieth
ninetieth, adj. — ME. nyntithe, formed fr. ninety
with numeral suff. -th.

## ninety
ninety, adj. — ME. nigenty, nyneti, fr. OE. nigon-
tig. See nine and the numeral suff. -ty.
Derivative: ninety, n.

## ninny
ninny, п., a fool, a simpleton. — Fr. a ninny,
corrupted fr. an innocent and influenced in form
by It. ninno, 'baby, child'.

## ninth
ninth, adj. — Formed on analogy of fourth, etc.,
by adding -th to nine.
Derivatives: ninth, п., ninth-ly, adv.

## Niobe
Niobe, п., the daughter of Tantalus and wife of
Amphion whose seven sons and seven
daughters were slain by Apollo and Artemis (Greek
mythol.) — L. Nioba, Niobe, fr. Gk. Νιόβη,
prob. fr. Heb. neeyabhah, fern, of neeyabh, 'the
object of enmity (for the gods)', prop. Niph'al
(=passive) participle oidydbh, 'was hostile to',
whence also dyebh (prop, a participle), 'enemy',

## ebhah
ebhah, 'enmity', Akkad. ayabu, 'enemy', and the
Hebrew PN. Iyyobh. Cp. Job and niobium. For

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:524 COLUMN:2 -->
other Greek mythological names of Hebrew
origin see Cadmus, Danae, Danaiis.
Derivative: Niobe-an, adj.

## niobic
niobic, adj., columbic (chem.) — Formed fr.
niobium with adj. suff. -ic.

## niobite
niobite, п., columbite (mineral.) — Formed fr.
niobium with subst. suff. -ite.

## niobium
niobium, п., a metallic element now called colum-
bium (chem.) — ModL., coined by the German
chemist Heinrich Rose (1795-1864) in 1844
from the name of Niobe, the daughter of
Tantalus (see Niobe and chem. suff. -ium); so called
by him in allusion to its resemblance to
tantalum (q.v.)

## nip
nip, tr. and intr. v., to pinch sharply; to bite —
ME. nippen, prob. fr. MLG. nippen, 'to pinch'
(cp. Du. nijpen, 'to pinch').
Derivative: nip, a., a pinch, bite.

## nip
nip, п., a sip. — Cp. LG. and Du. nippen, 'to sip',
and E. nip, 'to pinch'.

## nipa
nipa, п., an East Indian palm. — Sp. and Port.,
fr. Malay nipah.

## nipper
nipper, п., 1) one who, or that which, nips or
pinches; 2) a small boy (British colloq.); 3) pi.,
small pincers. — Formed fr. nip, 'to pinch', with
agential suff. -er.

## nipping
nipping, adj., that which nips; sharp. -=- Formed
with part. suff. -ing fr. nip, 'to pinch'.
Derivative: nipping-ly, adv.

## nipple
nipple, п., mammilla, teat. — From earlier neble,
lit. 'a small projection', dimin. of neb. Cp. nib.
Derivative: nipple, tr. v.

## nippy
nippy, adj., 1) nipping, pinching; 2) sharp; 3)
quick, active (British colloq.) — Formed with
adj. suff. -y fr. nip, 'to pinch'.

## nirvana
nirvana, п., extinction of the individual soul by
absorption into the supreme spirit (Hinduism)
— OI. nirvana/], lit. 'a blowing out (of a light),
extinction, jdisappearance', which is formed fr.
nis-, nir-, 'out, forth, away' (which is rel. to
Avestic nish-, of s.m., and prob. cogn. with
OSlav. nisti, 'poor'), and vati, 'it blows', for
whose etymology see wind, n.
Derivative: nirvan-ic, adj.

## Nisan
Nisan, п., name of the first Jewish month — Heb.
Nisan, fr. Akkad. nisannu.

## nisi
nisi, corn., unless, if not (a term used in law, as
decree nisi, order nisi, etc.) — L., 'unless, if not',
assimilated fr. *ne-si, fr. neg. pref. ne-andj/, 'if.
For the first element see no, adv., and cp. nay.
The second element stands for set and is related
to Oscan svat, suae, Umbrian sve, sve. The
original meaning of L. if was 'so'; hence sic (for
si-c), 'so'. See sic and cp. the second element in
quasi.

## nisus
nisus, п., effort, endeavour. — L. nisus, 'a striving,
exertion, effort', fr. nisus, pp. of nltor, niti, 'to
strive, make an effort, exert oneself, which
stands for "nivitor (fr. *kneigKhetor) or "nhitor
(fr. *knigwheto~r) and is rel. to *nive~re in conive-
re, 'to close the eyes, blink, wink at, overlook
(errors), connive at'. See connive and cp.
nictitate, renitent.

## nit
nit, п., the egg of a louse. — ME. nite, fr. OE.
hnitu, rel. to Norw. nil. MDu. nete, Du. neet,
OHG. (h)ni3, MHG. ni3, тззе, G. Nifi, and
cogn. with Arm. anic, 'louse', Gk. κονίς, gen.
κονί8ος, 'egg of a louse' (prob. for *κνίς and
influenced in form by κόνις, 'dust'), Alb. bent (for
"knida), 'louse', Mir. sned (for *sknida), 'egg
of a louse'.
Derivatives: nit-t-er, п., nit-t-y, adj.

## niter
niter, nitre, п., nitrate of potassium (chem.) — F.
nitre, fr. L. nitrum, fr. Gk. νίτρον, 'native
sodium carbonate, natron', fr. Heb. nether,
'carbonate of soda, natron' (stem nithr-; cp. Aram.
nithra). Cp. nitrogen, natron.

## nithing
nithing, п., a cowardly person (archaic). — ME.,
fr. OE. niding, 'infamous man', fr. ON. nidingr,
fr. nid, 'envy, hatred' (whence also Dan. nid,
'envy, grudge, jealousy'), which is rel. to OE.
nid, 'quarrel, enmity, hatred, battle', OS., OFris.
nith, 'hatred, envy', Du. nijd, 'envy', OHG. nid,
nidh, nith, 'anger, envy, hatred', MHG. nil, nid,

## G. Neid
G. Neid, 'envy, grudge, jealousy', Goth, neip,
'ill-will, envy, jealousy', and cogn. with Olr.

## nith
nith, 'combat, fight'. Cp, ruddering,

## nitid
nitid, adj., bright. — L. nilidus, 'shining,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:524 COLUMN:3 -->
glittering, bright', fr. nitere, 'to shine'. See neat, adj.

## niton
niton, п., a chemical element — A Modi, hybrid
formed on analogy of argon fr. L. nitere, 'to
shine' (see neat, adj.); so called by the English
chemist Sir William Ramsay (1852-1916) in 1912,
because it glows in the dark.

## nitr-
nitr-, a form of nitro-, before a vowel.

## nitrate
nitrate, n. (chem.), 1) a salt of nitric acid; 2)
potassium nitrate or sodium nitrate. — Formed
fr. niter with chem. suff. -ate.
Derivative: nitrate, ir. v., to treat with nitric
acid.

## nitric
nitric, adj., 1) pertaining to niter; 2) pertaining
to nitrogen; 3) containing nitrogen. — F. nitri-
que, fr. nitre. See niter and adj suff. -ic.

## nitride
nitride, also nitrid, п., a compound of nitrogen
with a more electropositive element (chem.) —
Formed fr. niter with suff. -id(e).

## nitrification
nitrification, п., the act of nitrifying. — F., coined
by the French chemist Guyton de Morveau
(1737-1816) in 1787. See niter and -fication.

## nitrify
nitrify, tr. v. 1) to convert into niter; 2) to oxidize
(ammonium salts, etc.) into nitrites and
nitrates; 3) to impregnate with nitrates {chem. and
bacteriol.) — F. nitrifier (see niter and -fy); first
used by Thouvenel in 1797.

## nitrite
nitrite, п., a salt of nitrous acid (chem.) —
Formed fr. niter with suff. -ite.

## nitro-
nitro-, before a vowel nitr-, combining form used
in the senses: 1) containing nitrogen; 2)
containing nitric or nitrous acid. — Gk. νίτρο- (ср.
e.g. νιτρο-ποιός, 'producing niter'), fr. νίτρον,
'sodium, carbonate'. See niter.

## nitro
nitro, adj., containing nitrogen. — From nitro-.

## nitrogen
nitrogen, п., a colorless, tastless, odorless
gaseous chemical element. — F. nitrogene, coined
by the French chemist Jean-Antoine Chaptal
(1756-1832) in 1790 fr. nitro- and suff. -gene (fr.
Gk. -γενής, 'born of, produced by'). See -gen.
Derivative: nitrogen-ous, adj.

## nitroglycerine
nitroglycerine, п., an explosive oily liquid,
C3H5(NO,)3, obtained by treating glycerine
with nitric and sulfuric acids. — Compounded
of nitro- and glycerine.

## nitros-
nitros-, form of nitroso- before a vowel.

## nitrosify
nitrosify, v., to convert into nitrous acid (chem.)
— Formed fr. nitrous with suff. -fy. Cp. nitrify.

## nitroso
nitroso, adj., containing or designating the NO
radical (chem.) — See nitroso-.

## nitroso-
nitroso-, before a vowel nitros-, combining form
denoting the presence of the NO radical (chem.)
— Fr. L. nitrosus, 'full of natron'. See nitrous,

## nitrosyl
nitrosyl, п., the nitroso radical (NO). — See
nitroso and -yl.

## nitrous
nitrous, adj., 1) pertaining to, or containing, niter;
2) designating a compound, in which the
nitrogen has a lower valence than in the
corresponding nitric compound (chem.) — L. nitrosus,
'full of natron', fr. nitrum, 'natron'. See niter
and -ous.

## nitroxyl
nitroxyl, п., the radical NOz (chem.) —
Compounded of nitr-, ox(ygen) and -yl.

## nitryl
nitryl, п., the same as nitroxyl. — Compounded
of nitr- and -yl.

## nival
nival, adj., 1) pertaining to snow; 2) growing in
the snow (said of plants). — L. nivalis,
'pertaining to snow, snowy', fr. nix, gen. nivis,
'snow'. See snow and adj. suff. -al and cp. next
word.

## Nivdse
Nivdse, п., name of the 4th month of the French
Revolutionary calendar (lasting fr. Dec. 21st to
Jan. 19th). — F., lit. 'month of snow'; coined
by Fabre d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. L. nivdsus, 'full
of snow, snowy', fr. nix, gen. nivis, 'snow'. See
snow and adj. suff. -ose and cp. next word.

## nivosfty
nivosfty, п., snowiness — Formed with sufT. -ity
fr. L. nivosus. See prec. word.

## nix
nix, п., masc, nixie, fern., a water sprite. — G.
Nix, fern. Nixe, fr. rare MHG. nickes, fr. OHG.
nihhus, 'water monster, water sprite', nihussa,
'female water sprite', rel. to OE. nicor, 'a water
monster', ON. nykr, of s.m., and cogn. with OI.
nenekti, 'he washes', niktah, 'washed' (pp.), Gk.
νίζω (for *nigMyo), Ί wash', $-ν«ττος,
'unwashed', Olr. nigid, 'washes', Olr. necht, 'clean'
(lit. 'washed'). Cp. nicker, 'water sprite'.

## nix
nix, п., nothing (slang). — G. nichts, 'nothing',
fr. nicht, 'not', fr. MHG. niht, 'nothing', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:525 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NIXIE | 498 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:525 COLUMN:1 -->
OHG. niKiht, neowiht, which is rel. to OE.
nawiht, 'nothing'. See naught, and cp. not.

## nixie
nixie, п., a female water sprite. — G. Nixe, fem.
of Nix, 'water sprite'; introduced by the
.Scottish novelist and poet Sir Walter Scott (1771-
1832). See nix, 'a water sprite'.

## Nizam
Nizam, п., title of the ruler of Hyderabad, India.
— Hind, nizam 'arrangement, order, ruler', fr.
Arab, nizam, 'arrangement, order,
administration, reign', fr. nazama, 'he put in order,
arranged'. Cp. nazim.
. nizam, п., a soldier in the Turkish army. — Turk.,
fr. Arab, nizam. See prec. word.

## no
no, adv. — ME. na, no, fr. OE. no, no, adv., 'not',
lit. 'not ever', compounded of ne, 'not', and a,
δ, 'ever'. The first element is rel. to OS., ΟΝ.,
OFris., OHG. ne, Goth, ni, 'not', and cogn.
with ΟΙ. ηά, Avestic na, L. ne- in compounds,
OSlav. ne, Lith. ni, 'not'; fr. I.-E. *ni. Cp. I.-E.
*яе, whence Goth, ne, 'not', Gk. νη- (in
compounds), 'not, un-', L. ne, 'that not', ΟΙ. ηά, Olr.
ni, ni, MW. ni, Co. ny, 'not'. See an-, in-, 'not',
un-, 'not', and ср. поп, not. Cp. also nay and
words there referred to. For the second element
in OE. na (for ne a) see aye, 'ever'.

## no
no, adj. — ME., form of поп before a
consonant. ME. поп derives fr. OE. nan, lit. 'not one',
which is contracted fr. ne, 'not', and an, 'one'.
Accordingly the adj. no is derivatively identical
with the pron. none (q.v.) See also no, adv.

## Noachlan
Noachlan, also Noachic, adj., 1) pertaining to
Noah or his time; 2) ancient, antique — See
Noah and -ian, resp. adj. suff. -ic.

## Noah
Noah, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, son of La-
mech and father of Shem, Ham and Japheth. —
Heb. Nd'ft, lit. 'rest', fr. na°h, lit· 'rest', whence
also mano'h, 'resting-place', nfnuba , 'resting-
place, rest', hdndfta1', 'giving of rest' [formed
from the Hiph'il (= causative) conjugation of
nuah\, nahalh, 'quietness, rest', nihS"k, 'quieting';
rel. to Aram. пл°Ь, Akkad. ηάΙμι, 'to rest',
Arab, anaha, 'he made (a camel) lie down (on
its breast)', munah, 'resting place of a camel',
Ethiop. nalja, 'was extended'.

## nob
nob, n. 1) the head (slang); 2) the knave of the
suit of the card turned up (cribbage) — A later
spelling var. of knob.
Derivative: nob, tr. v., to hit on the head of.

## nob
nob, п., a person of high position (vulgar) —
Prob. fr. nob, 'the head'. Cp. nib, 'a gentleman'.

## nobble
nobble, tr. v., 1) to tamper with a race horse by
drugging or maiming it, etc.; 2) to win over (a
person) by bribery or other illicit means; 3) to
cheat. — Prob. a freq. verb formed fr. nab, 'to
seize' (q.v.) For the ending see verbal suff.
-le.
Derivative: nobbl-er, n.

## nobby
nobby, adj., smart, stylish (slang). — Lit. 'fit for a
nob'. See nob, 'a person of high position', and
adj. suff. -y.

## nobelium
nobelium, п., a radioactive element produced by
the bombardment of curium with ions of carbon
(ckem.) — ModL., named after the Swedish
chemist Alfred Bernhard Nobel (1833-96). For
the ending see chem. suff. -ium.

## nobiliary
nobiliary, adj., pertaining to nobility. — F. no-
biliaire, fr. L. nobilis. See noble and adj. suff.
-ary.

## nobility
nobility, n. — ME. nobilite, fr. OF. nobilite (F.
nobilite), fr. L. nobilitatem, ace. of ndbilitas,
'nobleness, nobility', fr. nobilis. See next word
and -ity.

## noble
noble, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) noble, fr. L.
nobilis, 'well-known, famous, celebrated,
renowned; of noble birth; excellent, superior',
which stands for *gndbilis, lit. 'knowable', fr.
*gno-, the stem of L. gnoscere, noscere, 'to
know'. See know and -ble and cp. ennoble,
ignoble. Cp. also gnosiz, gaome, 'maxim'.
Derivatives: noble, п., noble-ness,n.,nobl-y,adv.

## noblesse
noblesse, п., 1) noble birth, noble rank; 2) the
nobility. — ME., fr. OF. noblece (F. noblesse),
fr. VL. 'nobilitia, fr. L. nobilis. See prec. word
and 2nd -ess.

## nobody
nobody, n. — Formed fr. no, adj., and body.

## nocent
nocent, adj., causing harm, harmful (rare) — L.
nocens, gen. nocentis, pres. part, of nocere, 'to
hurt, injure, harm'. See noxious and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:525 COLUMN:2 -->
innocent, nocive.

## nocerite
nocerite, п., a calcium magnesium oxyfiuoride
(mineral.) — Named after Nocera near Naples.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## nocive
nocive, adj., injurious, harmful. — L. nocivus
[prob. through the medium of MF. (= F.) nocif
(fem. nocive)], from the stem of nocere, 'to
harm'. See noxious and cp. nocent.

## nock
nock, n, notch on a bow.— ME., prob. of Scand.
origin. Cp. Swed. nock, 'notch'. Cp. also LG.
nokk, Du. nok, 'tip of a sail'.
Derivative: nock, tr. v., to make a notch in.

## noct-
noct-, form of nocti- before a vowel.

## noctambulism
noctambulism, п., somnambulism. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. nox, gen. noctis, 'night', ambulare,
'to walk', and -ism, a suff. of Greek origin. See
nocti- and amble,

## noctambulist
noctambulist, п., a somnambulist. — See prec.
word and -ist.

## nocti-
nocti-, before a vowel noct-, combining form
meaning 'night'. — Fr. L. nox, gen. noctis,
'night', which is cogn. with OE. neahl, niht,
'night'. See night and cp. Nox, nocturnal and the
second element in equinox.

## Noctilio
Noctilio, п., a genus of bats (zool.) — ModL.,
formed fr. L. nox, gen. noctis, 'night' (see prec.
word), on the analogy of vesper-tilid, 'bat'.

## Noctiluca
Noctiluca, п., a genus of phosphorescent marine
flagellates (zool.) — ModL., fr. L. noctiluca,
'that which shines by night', compounded of
nox, gen. noctis, 'night', and lucere, 'to shine'.
See lucent.

## Noctuidae
Noctuidae, n. pi., a family of moths (entomol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. noctua,
'night owl', fr. nox, gen. noctis, 'night'. See
nocti-.

## noctule
noctule, п., a large brown bat (Nyctalus noctula).
— F., formed fr. L. nox, gen. noctis, 'night', on
the analogy of It. nottola, 'a bat', which derives
fr. nolle, 'night', fr. L. noctem, ace. of nox,
'night'. See nocti-,

## nocturn
nocturn, п., 1) evening service in church; 2 )=
nocturne. — ME. nocturne, fr. OF. (= F.)
nocturne, fr. ML. nocturna, prop, subst. use of L.
nocturna, fem. of nocturnus, 'pertaining to the
night'. See next word.

## nocturnal
nocturnal, adj., pertaining to the night; active by
night; done or occurring in the night; (of
flowers) opening by night. — Late L. nocturna-
lis, fr. L. nocturnus, 'pertaining to the night',
formed fr. nox, gen. noctis, 'night' (see nocti-),
with -urnus, a suff. forming adjectives of time.
The suffixes -u-rnus, -e-rnus, are traceable to
orig. *-ri-nos, an adaptation of the Gk. suff.
-ρι-νος. Ср. modern.

## nocturne
nocturne, п., a composition of a dreamy
character (mui.)—F., prop, 'a composition appropriate
to the night'. See nocturn.

## nocuous
nocuous, adj., harmful. — L. nocuus, 'harmful',
from the stem οι nocere, 'to hurt, injure, harm'.
See noxious. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## nod
nod, intr. v., to make a quick inclination of the
head; tr. v., to incline (the head). — ME.
nodden, of uncertain origin. Cp. nid-nod.
Derivatives: nod, п., nodd-er, п., nodd-ing, adj.,
nodd-ing-ly, adv.

## nodal
nodal, adj., pertaining to a node or nodes. — See
node and adj. suff. -al.

## noddle
noddle, п., head (cottoq.) — ME. nodle, of
uncertain origin. Cp. the second element in
jobbernowl.

## node
node, п., a knot, knob. — L. nodus, 'knot', rel. to
L. nassa (prob. for "nad-sa), 'a basket for
catching fish', and cogn. with ON. not, 'a large net',
ΟΝ., OE. net, 'net'. See net and cp. nodus, noose,
denouement, crunode, internode.

## nodical
nodical, adj., pertaining to the nodes (astron.) —
See node and -ical.

## nodose
nodose, adj., full of knots or nodes, knotty. —
L. nodosus, 'full of knots', fr. nodus. See node
and -ose.

## nodosity
nodosity, п., knottiness. — L. nodositas, *knot-
tiness', fr. nodosus, 'full of knots'. Cp. F. nodo-
site and see prec. word and -ity.

## nodular
nodular, adj., pertaining to nodules; having
nodules. — See nodule and -ar.

## nodulated
nodulated, adj., having nodules. — See next word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:525 COLUMN:3 -->
and the adj. suffixes -ate and -ed.

## nodule
nodule, п., a small knot; a small-lump. — F., fr.
L. nodulus, dimin. of nodus. See node and -ule.

## nodulose
nodulose, adj., having nodules. — See prec. word
and -ose.

## nodulous
nodulous, adj., nodulose. — See nodule and -ous.

## nodus
nodus, п., knot; difficulty, complication. —-L.
nodus, 'knot'. See node.

## noel
noel, n. 1) cry of 'noel' (in Christmas songs); 2)
Christmas carol; 3) (cap.) Christmas. — F. noel,
'Christmas carol', Noel, 'Christmas', fr. OF.
nouel, noel, fr. L. natalis (scil. dies), 'birth day',
used in Eccles. L. to denote 'Christmas', fr.
natalis, 'pertaining to birth', fr. natus, 'born'.
See natal and cp. next word.

## Noel
Noel, masc. PN. — OF., lit. 'of, or born on,
Christmas', fr. L. natalis (scil. dies)-, see prec.
word and cp. Natalia. The name was orig. given
to children of either sex born on Christmas.

## noetic
noetic, adj., pertaining to the intellect. — Gk.
νοητικός, 'pertaining to intelligence,
intellectual', fr. νοητός, 'perceptible by the mind,
mental', verbal adj. of νοέω, Ί perceive by the
mind', fr. νόος, νους, 'mind'. See nous and cp.
anoetlc.

## nog
nog, п., a wooden pin. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: nog, tr. v., to fasten with nogs.

## nog
nog, п., 1) a kind of strong ale; 2) eggnog. — Of
uncertain origin.

## noggin
noggin, п., I) a small cup or mug; 2) a measure of
liquor. — Prob. orig. 'a measure for nog (ale)'.
See prec. word.

## nohow
nohow, adv., in no wise; not at all. —
Compounded of no, adv., and how.

## noil
noil, п., refuse of wool, hair or silk. — Of
uncertain origin.

## noise
noise, п., a loud cry or shouting; clamor; din. —
ME., fr. OF. noise (in ModF. used only in the
phrase chercher noise, 'to pick a quarrel'), fr. L.
nausea, 'seasickness', which in Vulgar Latin
prob. had the meaning of 'unpleasant situation,
noise, quarrel'. For sense development cp.
OProvenc. nauza, noiza, 'noise, quarrel', which
also derive fr. L. nausea. See Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 412 s.v. noise. See nausea.
Derivatives: noise, tr. v., noise-ful, adj.,
noise-fully, adv., noise-less, adj., noise-less-ly, adv.,
noise-less-ness, п., nois-y, adj., nois-i-ly, adv.,
nois-i-ness, n.

## noisette
noisette, п., a small piece of meat cooked with
sauce. — F., lit. 'hazel nut', dimin. of noix, 'nut',
fr. L. nucem, ace. of nux. Cp. It. лосе, OProvenc.
notz, noze and Sp. nuez, 'walnut, nut', which
also derive fr. L. nucem, and see nucleus and
-ette.

## noisette
noisette, п., name of a kind of hybrid rose. — So
called after Philippe Noisette, who cultivated
this class of roses.

## noisome
noisome, adj., harmful, offensive. — For noy-
some; formed with suff. -some fr. obsol. /toy, 'to
annoy', an aphetic form of annoy (q.v.)
Derivatives: noisome-ly, adv., noisome-ness, n.

## nolens-volens
nolens-volens, adv., will-nilly.,— L. nolens vvlens,
'unwilling (or) willing', fr. nolens, pres. part, of
nolo, ηδ/le, 'to be unwilling', and volens, pres.
part, of vols, velle, 'to wish, will, be willing';
see voluntary. Nolo is a contraction of 'novoW,
assimilated fr. *ne-volo, Ί am unwilling'. For
the neg. pref. ne- in *ne-volo, see no, adv., and
cp. nay. Cp. noli-me-tangere, noUtion, nolle
prosequi.

## noll-me-tangere
noll-me-tangere, п., 1) any person or thing that
must not be touched or interfered with; 2) a
picture of Jesus as he appeared to Mary
Magdalene; 3) name of any plant of the genus Impa-
tiens, whose ripe seeds burst when it is touched;
4) any of several ulcerous skin diseases. — L.
noli me tangere, 'touch me not', fr. noli, imper.
of nolle, 'to be unwilling', me, 'me', and tangere,
'to touch'. See nolens-volens, me and tangent.

## nolltion
nolltion, п., 1) negative volition; 2) unwillingness.
— Formed on the analogy of volition (q.v.) fr.
L. nolo, nolle, 'not to will, to be unwilling'. See
nolens-volens.

## noil
noil, п., head (obsol.) — ME. no/, fr. OE. knoll,
'crown of the head', rel. to OHG. hnoll, hnetl,
MHG. nulle, 'back part of the head'. Cp. the
second element in jobbernowl.

## nolle prosequi
nolle prosequi, a formal notice that the plaintiff of
prosecutor will not continue a suit (law). — L.,
nolle prosequi, 'to be unwilling to pursue'. See
nolens-volens and prosecute,

## nom
nom, п., name. — F., fr. L. пбтеп. See nominal,

## noma
noma, п., gangrenous stomatitis (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. νομή, 'a feeding', lit. 'pasturage,
food from pasturage', which is rel. to νομός,
'land allotted, pasture'. See next word and pp.
no me.

## nomad
nomad, п., member of a wandering tribe; adj.
wandering. — L. nomas, gen. -adis, 'wanderer,
member of a pastoral tribe that wander about
with their flocks', fr. Gk. νομάς, gen. νομάδος,
'roaming about for pasture, wandering from one
place to another', fr. νομός, 'land allotted,
pasture; district, province', which is rel. to
νέμειν, 'to deal out, distribute, allot; to allot
pasture, to pasture, drive to pasture', fr. I.-E.
base "пет-, 'to divide, distribute, allot'. See
nimble and cp. Nemesis, noma, nome.
Derivatives: nomad-ic, nomad-ic-al, adjs.,
nomad-ism., n.

## nomarch
nomarch, п., ruler of a nome: a) in ancient Egypt;
b) in modern Greece. — Gk. νομάρχης, 'the
chief of an Egyptian province', compounded of
νομός, 'district, province', and -άρχης, fr. άρχος,
'leader, chief, ruler'. See nome and -arch.

## nomarchy
nomarchy, п., a province ruled by a nomarch. —
Gk. νομαρχία, 'district, province', fr. νομάρχης.
See prec. word and -y (representing Gk. -ίά I.

## nombril
nombril, п., the navel point on an escutcheon,
i.e. the point between the middle base point and
the fesse point (her.) — F., 'navel', dissimilated
fr. OF. lombril, lit. 'the navel', which is formed
from the apostrophized definite article /' (fr. L.
ille, 'that'), and ombril, fr. VL. 'umbiliculus,
dimin. of L. umbilicus, 'navel'. See ille and
umbilicus.

## nom de guerre
nom de guerre, pseudonym. — F., lit. 'war name'.
See nom, de- and guerrilla.

## nom de piume
nom de piume, a name assumed by a writer, a
pseudonym. — A phrase formed in English by
translating E. 'pen name' into French. See nom,
de- and plume.

## nome
nome, п., 1) a province in ancient Egypt; 2) a
province in modern Greece. — F., fr. Gk.
νομός, 'land allotted, pasture; district,
province'. See nomad and words there referred to.

## nomen
nomen, п., a name. — L. See nominal.

## nomenclator
nomenclator, п., 1) an announcer of names; 2) an
inventor of names, esp. of scientific names. —
L. nomenclator, 'callerof a name*. Compounded
of nomen, 'name', and calator, 'caller, слег', fr.
calare, 'to call, cry'. See nominal, claim and -tor.

## nomenclature
nomenclature, п., system of names; terminology.
— L. nomenclatura, 'calling of names'. See prec.
word and -ure.
Derivative: nomenclature, v.

## Nomeus
Nomeus, п., a genus of fishes, th&rnan-of-war
fish (ichthyol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ναμεύς,
'herdsman', which is rel. to νέμειν, 'to deal out,
distribute, allot; to allot pasture, to pasture,
drive to pasture'. See nomad and words there
referred to.

## nomic
nomic, adj., customary. — Gk. νομικός, 'legal,
customary', fr. νόμος, 'anything allotted or
assigned; usage, custom; law'. See nimble and
cp. Nemesis. For the ending see sufT. -ic.

## nominal
nominal, adj. — ME. nominalle, fr. L. nominalis,
'belonging to a name', fr. пбтеп, gen. nominis,
'name', which is cogn. with OE. noma, 'name'.
See name and cp. words there referred to.

## nominalism
nominalism, п., the doctrine that universal and
general abstract terms are mere names and have
no reality (philos.) — F. nominalisme, coined fr.
nominal, fr. L. nominalis. See nominal and -ism.
The word nominalisme occurs for the first time
in the famous Dictionnaire de Trevoux,
published in 1752.

## nominalist
nominalist, п., a believer in nominalism. — See
prec. word and -izt.
Derivative: nominalist-ic, adj.

## nominate
nominate, tr. v., to appoint to an office. — L. пв-
minatus, pp. of nominare, 'to name, nominate',
fr. пбтеп, gen. nominis. See nominal and verbal
sulT. -ate.

## nomination
nomination, п., the appointing of a person to an

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:526 COLUMN:2 -->
office. — ME. nominacioun, fr. MR (= F.)
nomination, fr. L. ndminationem, ace. of nomindtid,
fr. L. nominatus, pp. of nominare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## nominative
nominative, adj., 1) nominated; 2) indicating the
subject (gram.) — ME. nominatif, fr. MF. ( =
F.) nominatif (fern, nominative), fr. L. nominati-
vus, 'pertaining to naming, nominative', fr.
nomindtus, pp. of nominare. See nominate and
suff. -ive.

## nominative
nominative, п., the case indicating the subject,
the noun case. — L. nomindtivus (scil. casus),
'the nominative case'. See nominative, adj.

## nominator
nominator, п., one who nominates. — Late L.
nominator, fr. L. nomindtus, pp. of nominare. See
nominate and agential suff. -or.

## nominee
nominee, п., a person nominated for an office. —
See nominate and -ее.

## nomism
nomism, п., the basing of conduct on the
observance of religious or moral law. — Formed fr.
Gk. νόμος, 'law' (see nomo-), with suff. -Ism.

## nomistic
nomistic, adj., pertaining to, or based on,
nomism. — See prec. word and -istic.

## nomo-
nomo-, combining form meaning 'law, usage'. —
Gk. νομό-, fr. νόμος, 'law', lit. 'anything
allotted or assigned; usage, custom; law'. See nomic
and cp. anomo-.

## nomography
nomography, п., 1) the art of drafting laws; 2) a
treatise on laws. — Gk. νομογραφίϊ, 'drafting
of laws', compounded of νόμος 'law', and
-γραφίάΐ, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See nomo- and
-graphy.
Derivatives: nomograph-ic, nomograph-ic-al,
adjs., nomograph-ic-al-ty, adv.

## Homology
Homology, п., the science of law. — Compounded
of nomo- and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: nomolog-ical, adj., nomolog-ist, a.

## nomothetic
nomothetic, nomothetical, adj., 1) lawgiving,
legislative; 2) based on law. — Gk. νομοθετικός,
'relating to legislation, legislative', fr.
νομοθέτης, 'lawgiver', which is compounded of νόμος,
'law', and θετής, 'one who puts, places or
establishes', from the stem of τιθέναι, 'to put,
place'. See nomo- and theme and cp. thetic.

## -nomy
-nomy, combining form denoting systematic
knowledge in a certain field of learning, as in
agronomy. — Gk. -νομίϊ, fr. νόμος, 'law'; see
nomo- and -y (representing Gk. -ίϊ).
поп-, negative pref. — F., fr. L. ηδη, 'not', fr.
OL. noenum, for 'n'oinom, lit. 'not one', fr. neg.
pref. ne- and oinom (whence L. йпит), 'one'.
See no, adv., and one and cp. none.

## nonage
nonage, п., stale of not being of age. — ME., fr.
OF. See поп- and age.

## nonagenerian
nonagenerian, adj., ninety years old; between the
years 90 and 100; п., a person ninety years old
or between the years 90 and 100. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. nondggndrius, 'consisting of
ninety', fr. nondgenl, 'ninety each', which is rel.
to ndnaginta, 'ninety', fr. nanus, 'ninth'. See
nones, 'the ninth day before the ides', and cp.
words there.referred to.

## nonagon
nonagon, п., a plane figure having nine angles and
nine sides. — A hybrid coined fr. L. nanus,
'ninth', and Gk. γωνία, 'angle (see nones and
-gon). The correct form is enneagon (lit. 'nine-
angled'), in which both elements are of Greek
origin.

## nonary
nonary, adj., having nine as the base (math.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ary fr. L. n6nus, 'ninth';
cp. L. nonarius, 'of the ninth hour'. See nones,
'the ninth day before the ides', and cp. words
there referred to.

## nonce
nonce, п., in the phrase for the nonce, 'for a
special occasion'. — ME. nones, fr. nanes, which
arose from misdivision of then ones into the
nanes in phrases like to then ones, 'for the one
(purpose or occasion)', fr. to (see to), then, fr.
earlier than (corresponding to OE. pam, later
pan), dat. sing. neut. of the def. art. the (see 1st
the), and anes, 'one (purpose)', alter, (prob.
due to the influence of anes, 'once') of ane, dat.
sing. neut. of an, 'one', fr. OE. an. See one and
once. For similar misdivisions cp. newt,
nickname, notch.

## nonce word
nonce word, a word coined for a special occasion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:526 COLUMN:3 -->
— See prec. word.

## nonchalance
nonchalance, п., indifference, carelessness, lack of
enthusiasm. — F., fr. nonchalant. See next word
and -ce.

## nonchalant
nonchalant, adj., indifferent, careless, not
enthusiastic. — F., pres. part, of OF. nonchaloir,
'to be careless of, to neglect', fr. поп, 'not', and
chaloif, 'to be hot; to care', fr. L. callre, 'to be
warm'; F. chaland, 'customer, client', is of the
same origin. See поп-, caldron and -ant, and cp.
callant.
Derivatives: nonchalant-ly, adv., nonchalant-
ness, n.

## noncom
noncom, n. (colloq.) — Short for
noncommissioned officer.

## nondescript
nondescript, adj., not easy to describe; indefinite;
п., a nondescript person. — Formed fr. non-
and L. descriptus, pp. of describere. See describe.

## none
none, pron. — ME. none, поп, fr. OE. nan,
contraction of ne, 'not', and <?n,'one'. Cp. OS., Μ LG.
пел, ON. neinn, MDu., Du. neen, OHG., MHG.,
G. nein, 'no', which all are formed from the
Teut. neg. particle *ne, *ni, and the neut. of the
indef. article; see no, adv., and one and cp. no,
adj. Cp. the analogous formation of L. поп,
'not, no', fr. OL. noenum, lit. 'not one' (see
поп-).

## nonego
nonego, п., the external world; the objects as
opposed to the subject (philos.) — Formed fr.
поп- and ego.

## nonentity
nonentity, n. 1) state of not existing; 2)
something not existing; 3) a person of no importance.
— Formed fr. поп- and entity.

## nones
nones, n. pi., the ninth day before the ides
(Roman Calendar). — L. nonae (dies), 'ninth (days)',
fern. pi. of nonus, 'ninth', contraction of *noven-
os, fr. novem, 'nine'. See nine and cp. nonagon,
nonagenarian, nonary, nonuple. Cp. also next
word.

## nones
nones, n. pi., church office orig. said daily at the
ninth hour reckoned from sunrise, i.e. about 3
o'clock P.M.; now usually said somewhat
earlier. — PI. of none, 'ninth hour', fr. L. nana
(herd), 'ninth (hour)'. See prec. word and^cp.
noon.

## nonesuch
nonesuch,nonsuch,adj., unequalled; п., a person
or thing unequalled. — Compounded of none
and such.

## nonfeasance
nonfeasance, п., failure to do something that
should be done (law). — Formed fr. поп- and
feasance. Cp. malfeasance, misfeasance.

## norrillion
norrillion, п., 1) in the United States and France, a
million raised to the fifth power (i.e. 1 followed
by 30 zeros); 2) in Great Britain and Germany,
a million raised to the ninth power (i.e. 1
followed by 54 zeros). — F. nonillion, formed fr.
L. nanus, 'ninth' (see nones), on analogy of
million (q.v.) Cp. billion and words there
referred to.

## nonius
nonius, п., a contrivance formerly used for the
graduation of instruments. — Named after its
inventor, the Portuguese mathematician Pedro
Nunez (1492-1577), whose name was Latinized
into Petrus Nonius.

## nonjuror
nonjuror, п., one who refuses to take an oath;
specif, (cap.), any of the clergymen of the
English Established Church, who refused to take an
oath of allegiance to William III and Mary (at
their succession in 1689) — Formed fr. поп- and
juror.
поп obstante, notwithstanding. — L. поп obstante,
fr. поп, 'not', and abl. of obstans, pres. part, of
obstare, 'to stand in the way of, withstand'. See
obstacle.

## nonpareil
nonpareil, adj., unequalled. — F., 'unequalled',
fr. поп, 'not' (fr. L. ηδη), and pareil, 'equal' (fr.
VL. 'pariculus, dimin. of L. par, 'equal'). See
par, 'equality'.

## nonpareil
nonpareil, п., I) something unequalled; 2) a
printing-type (6 point size). — Fr. prec. word.

## nonplus
nonplus, п., perplexity. — Prop, 'state where
nothing more can be done', fr. L. ηδη plus, 'no
more, no farther'. See поп- and plus, plural.
Derivatives: nonplus, tr. v., nonplus(s)-ation, n.
поп possumus, statement of the impossibility of
doing something specified. — L. ηδη possumus,
'we cannot', fr. ηδη, 'not', and 1st person pi. of
the pres. indie, οι posse, 'to be able'. See поп-
