and potent,

## nonsense
nonsense, п., something that makes' no sense;'
senseless conduct; an absurd act. — Formed fr.
поп- and sense.
Derivatives: nonsens-ical, adj., nonsens-ical-ly,
adv.
поп sequitur, an inference which does not follow
from the premises. — L. поп sequitur, 4it does
not follow'. See поп- and sequel,

## nonsuch
nonsuch, adj. and n. — See nonesuch,

## nonsuit
nonsuit, п., dismissal of a plaintiff'ssuit for failure
to establish a valid case or for lack of evidence.
— ME. поп suyt, fr. AF. nounsute, fr. noun, 'not',
corresponding to OF. (= F.) поп, and sule, 'a
following, sequel', corresponding to OF. siute
(= F. suite). See поп- and suit, n.
Derivative: nonsuit, tr. v., to stop a plaintiff's
suit.

## nonuple
nonuple, adj., consisting of nine, ninefold. — F.,
formed on analogy of quadruple, quintuple, etc.,
fr. L. nanus, 'ninth'. See nones, 'the ninth day
before the ides', and cp. words there referred to.

## nonuser
nonuser, п., omission to use (law). — Formed fr.
поп- and user, 'right of use'.

## noodle
noodle, п., a fool, simpleton. — Of uncertain
origin.

## noodle
noodle, п., a strip or ball of dough served in soup.
— G. Nudel, of uncertain origin. WFlem.
noedel and F. nouille, of s.m., are German loan
words.

## noodledom
noodledom, п., fools collectively; foolishness. —
Coined by Sydney Smith fr. noodle and suff.
-dom.

## nook
nook, п., corner. — ME. noke, nok, rel. to Norw.
dial, nokke, nok, 'hook', and possibly also to
OE. knecca, 'neck'. See neck.
Derivatives: nook-ed, adj., nook-ery, п., nook-y,
adj.

## noon
noon, n. — ME., 'the ninth hour of the day
reckoned from sunrise, noon', fr. OE. поп, 'the
ninth hour of the day reckoned from sunrise', fr.
L. попа (hora), 'the ninth (houT)', fern, of nanus,
contraction of *noven-os, 'ninth', fr. novem,
'nine' (see nine), orig. used in the sense of nones,
'church office said daily at the ninth hour' (q.v.)
The prayers referred to were originally said at
the ninth hour from sunrise, i.e. at 3 o'clock
P.M.; later, however, their time was changed
from the end of the third three hour period to
its beginning, i.e. midday, whence noon came
to denote 'midday'. Cp. the first element in
nuncheon.

## noonday
noonday, n. — Compounded of noon and day;
first used by Miles Coverdale (1488-1568).

## noose
noose, п., a loop with a running knot. — Provenp.
nous, fr. L. nodus. See node.
Derivative: noose, tr. v.

## nopal
nopal, п., a Mexican cactus. — Sp., fr. Nahuatl
nopalli.

## nor
nor, conj. correlative to neither. — ME.,
contraction of nother, a var. of neither; see neither.
The negative conjunction nor was influenced in
form by the affirmative or.

## nor-
nor-, combining form denoting a parent
compound (regarded as the normal form) (chem.)
— Abbreviation of normal.

## Nora
Nora, fern. PN. — Irish; aphetic for Honora or
Leonora,

## norbergite
norbergite, п., a magnesium silicate with fluorine
and hydroxyl (mineral.) — Named after Nor-
berg in Sweden. For the ending see subst. suff.
-Ite.

## nordenskioldine
nordenskioldine, п., a calcium tin borate (mineral.)
— Named after the Swedish explorer and
mineralogist Nils Adolf Erik Nordenskiold (1832-
1901). For the ending see chem. suff. -ine.

## Nordic
Nordic, adj., pertaining to the Teutonic peoples
of Northern Europe. — F. nordique, 'of, or
pertaining to, the North', formed with suff. -ique
(see adj. suff. -ic) fr. nord, 'north', fr. OF. nord,
which is a loan word fr. OE. nord. See north.

## nordmarkite
nordmarkite, п., 1) a variety of staurolite
(mineral.) ; 2) a variety of syenite (petrogr.) — Named
chem. Nordmark in Sweden. For the ending see
after suff. -ite.

## noria
noria, п., a water wheel with buckets, Persian
wheel. — Sp., fr. Arab. na'arah (in vulgar
pronunciation, tia'Sra), fr. Syr. na'Sr, of s.m. (see

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:527 COLUMN:2 -->
Sigmund Fraenkel, Die aramaischen Fremd-
worter im Arabischen, p. 134), a derivative of
the verb η ar, 'he poured out', which is'rel. to
Heb. ηά'άτ, of s.m.; cp. Arab, nd'ara, 'it spurted,
gushed forth' (said of the blood of a wound),
na'ara1', 'earthen jug, pot'.

## norm
norm, п., standard, pattern, model. — L. norma,
'carpenter's square, rule, pattern', borrowed—
prob. through the medium of the Etruscans—
fr. Gk. γνώμονα, ace. of γνώμων, 'carpenter's
square', lit. 'one who, 0{ that which, knows,
judge, indicator', which is rel. to γνώμη, 'mind,
judgment, maxim, opinion'. See guome, 'maxim',
and cp. gnomon. Cp. also next word, Norma,
normal, enormous,

## norma
norma, п., 1) a norm; 2) (cap.) a southern
constellation (astron.) — L. norma, 'carpenter's square;
rule'. See prec. word.

## Norma
Norma, fem. PN. — Prob. fr. L. norma, 'rule,
pattern'. See norm,

## normal
normal, adj., 1) agreeing with the standard type;
2) regular, usual; 3) (geom.) perpendicular. —
L. normalis, 'made according to a carpenter's
square', fr. norma. See norm and adj. suff. -al
and cp. abnormal. Cp. also nor-.
Derivatives: normal, п., normalcy (q.v.),
normality, п., normal-ly, adv., normal- ness, п., and the
hybrids normal-ize, tr. v., normal-iz-er, п.,
normal-iz-ation, n.

## normalcy
normalcy, п., normality. — A hybrid coined by
Warren Gamaliel Harding (1865-1923),
president of the U.S.A. (1921-23), fr. normal with
suff. -cy. The correct form is normality.

## Norman
Norman, п., 1) one of the Northmen who
occupied Normandy in the 10th cent.; 2) one of the
Norman French who conquered England in
1066; 3) a native of Normandy. — OF. Nor-
mant, F. Normand, lit. 'Northman'. See
Northman.
Derivatives: Norman, adj., Norman-ize, intr.
and tr. v., Norman-iz-ation, n.

## Norn
Norn, п., one of the three goddesses of fate in
Scandinavian mythology. — ON. norn (pi.
nornir), rel. to Swed. dial, noma, nyrna, 'to
warn, to communicate secretly', ME. nyrnen, 'to
recite', MHG. narren, 'to growl, snarl'. All these
words are of imitative origin.

## Norse
Norse, adj., 1) Scandinavian; 2) Norwegian. —
Obsol. Du. Noorsch, 'Scandinavian, Norwegian'
(now Noors, 'Norwegian'), fr. Noordsch (now
Noords), 'Nordic', fr. Du. noord, 'North'. See
next word and cp. Northman.
Derivative: Norse, п., a) Scandinavians;
Norwegians; b) the Scandinavian languages; the
Norwegian language.

## north
north, adv., n. and adj. — ME., fr. OE. nord, adv.,
rel. to OS. north, adv., ON. nordr, OFris. north,
MDu. nort, noort, adv. and п., Dan. nord, Swed.
nord, norr, Du. noord, OHG., MHG., G. nord,
п., and cogn. with Ol. narakah, 'hell', Arm.
nerkUn, 'the lower one', Gk. ё-νεροι, 'those
below', έ-νερθεν, 'from beneath', νέρτερος,
έ-νέρτερος, 'nether, infernal', Oscan nertrak,
'left', Umbr. nertru (abl. sing.), 'left'. [OF. north
(F. nord) is borrowed fr. OE. nord, It. and Sp.
norte are French loan words.] All these words
are derivatives of I.-E. base *ner-, 'left; below'.
Cp. Nordic, Norse and the first element in
Norman, Norwegian. Cp. also Naraka. For sense
development it should be borne in mind that
most of the ancients used to take their, bearings
by turning toward the rising sun, so that they
had north to their left hand. Hence, the word
denoting north in manv languages lit. means
'left hand'. Cp. Heb. ssmot, Arab, shamal, 'left
hand; north'; Olr. tuath, 'left, northern', tiiaith,
'in the north', tuathun, 'on my left hand'; fochla,
'north, left hand seat in the war chariot'. For
sense development cp. south.
Derivatives: north, intr. and tr. v., norther (q.v.),

## norther-ly
norther-ly, adj., northern (q.v.), north-ing, n.

## norther
norther, п., a strong north wind in Texas and in
the Gulf of Mexico. — Formed fr. north with
agential suff. -er.

## northern
northern, adj., situated in, or pertaining to, the
north. — ME. northerne, fr. OE. nordern, fr.
nord. See north and -era.

## Norwegian
Norwegian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:527 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. ML. Norvegia, Norwegia, 'Norway', fr. ON.
Norvegr, lit. 'north way', fr. nordr, 'north', and
vegr, 'way'. See north and way.

## nose
nose, n. — ME., fr. OE. nosu, rel. to ON. nos,
Norw. nos, Dan. nsese, Swed. nasa, OFris. nose,
MDu. nose, nose, Du. neus, OHG. nasa, MHG.,
G. nase, and cogn. with OI. nasa (dual norn.),
'nose', prop, 'the two nostrils', OSlav. nosu,
Lith. ndsis, 'nose', Lett, nusis, OPruss. nozy, L.
ndsus, 'nose*, naris, for *nasis, 'nostril'. Cp.
naze, ness, nostril, nozzle, nuzzle and the first
element in nosegay. Cp. also nares, nark, nasal,
nasion, nasturtium.
Derivatives: nose, tr. and intr. v., nos-ed, adj.,
nose-y, nos-y, adj., nos-ing, n.

## nosegay
nosegay, п., a bunch of sweet-smelling flowers.
— Compounded of nose and the obsol. noun
gay, 'a gay or bright object' (from the adjective
gay).

## noslsui
noslsui, п., self-conceit on the part of a group;
use of "we" in speaking of oneself. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. nos, 'we' (see nostrum), and -ism,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## noso-
noso-, combining form meaning 'disease'. — Gk.
νόσο-, fr. νόσος, 'disease', which is of
unknown origin.

## nosography
nosography, п., classification of diseases. — Lit.
'description of diseases', compounded of noso-
and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφει, 'to write'. See
-graphy.
Derivatives: nosograph-ic, nosograph-ic-al, adjs.,
nosograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## nosology
nosology, п., 1) the science of diseases; 2) the
classification of diseases. — Compounded of
noso- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See-logy.
Derivatives: nosolog-ic-al, adj., nosolog-ic-al-ly,
adv., nosolog-ist, n.

## nost-
nost-, form of nosto- before a vowel.

## nostalgia
nostalgia, п., homesickness. — ModL., coined in
1668 by Johannes Hofer fr. Gk. νόστος, 'return
home', and -αλγία, fr. άλγος, 'pain'. The first
element is rel. to νέομαι (for *νέσομα&), Ί go,
come return', ναίω (for *νάσιω), Ί dwell', fr.
I.-E. base *nes-, *nos-, 'to return; to unite',
whence also OI. naspte, 'approaches, joins',
Nasatya, name of the physicians of the gods,
Toch. A nas, В nes, 'to be', A nasu, 'friendly',
Goth, ga-nisan, 'to heal', nasjan, 'to save', OE.
ge-nesan, 'to recover', nerian (for *nazjari) 'to
save', OS., OHG. gi-nesan, 'to survive, be
healed', MHG., G. genesen, 'to recover'. Cp.
Nestor and the second element in harness; cp.
also naos. For the second element in nostalgia
see -algia.
Derivative: nostalg-ic, adj.

## nosto-
nosto-, before a vowel nost-, combining form
meaning 'return home'. See prec. word.

## Nostoc
Nostoc, п., a genus of jellylike algae (bot.) —
ModL., coined by Paracelsus.

## Nostocaceae
Nostocaceae, n. pi., a family of algae (hot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Nostoc with suff. -aceae.

## nostology
nostology, п., the study of senility (biol.) —
Compounded of nosto- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one
who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## Nostradamus
Nostradamus, п., a prophet, seer. — Fr.
Nostradamus, Latinized name of Michel de Nostre-
dame, the famous physician and astrologer
(1503-66).

## nostril
nostril, n. — ME. nostrill, nosethirl, fr. OE. nos-
pyrl, lit. 'hole of the nose', fr. nosu, 'nose', and
pyrel, 'hole', fr. purh, 'through'. See nose and
thrill and cp. through.
Derivatives: nostril(l)-ed, adj., nostril-ity, n.

## nostrum
nostrum, п., a quack medicine. — Lit. 'our (scil.
medicine)', fr. L. nostrum, neut. of noster, Our',
fr. nos, 'we', fr. I.-E. *nos; see us and cp. our.
Cp. Gk. ημέτερος, Our', fr. ήμεϊς, 'we'. The
endings -ter (in L. nos-ter), -τερος (in Gk.
ημέτερος), are identical with the compar. suff. -lero;
see -ther.

## not
not, adv., negative particle. — ME. nat, not,
contraction of naught, nought. See naught, nought.

## not-
not-, form of noto- before a vowel.

## notabilia
notabilia, n. pi., notable things. — L. notabilia,
neut. pi. of notabilis. See notable.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:528 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 501 | NOVENNIAL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:528 COLUMN:1 -->

## notability
notability, η. — OF. notabilite (F. notabilite), fr.
ML. * notabilitatem, ace. of *notdbilitds, fr. L.
notabilis. See next word and -ity.

## notable
notable, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) notable, fr.
L. notabilis, 'worthy of note, notable', which
derives fr. notare, 'to note', fr. nota. See note, п.,
and surf. -able.
Derivatives: notable, п., notable-ness, п., notabl-
y, adv.

## notacanthous
notacanthous, adj., spiny-backed (zool.) —
Compounded of Gk. νώτος (also νώτον), 'the
back', and #κανθα, 'thorn'. See noto-, acantha
and -ous.

## notal
notal, adj., pertaining to the back. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. νώτος (also νώτον),
'the back'. See nolo-.

## notalgia
notalgia, п., pain in the back (med.) — Medical
L., compounded of Gk. νώτος (also νώτον),
'the back', and-κλγία,ίΓ.ϋλγος,'pain'. See-algia.

## notarial
notarial, adj., 1) pertaining to a notary; 2) drawn
up by a notary — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. notarius. See notary.
Derivative: notarially, adv.

## notarikon
notarikon, п., a system of shorthand consisting in
writing one letter (in most cases, the initial) of
each word. — MGk. νοταρικόν, fr. L. nota-
ricum, 'shorthand', fr. notarius. See next word.

## notary
notary, п., an official authorized to attest and
certify documents. — ME. notarye, fr. OF. (=F.)
notaire, fr. L. notarius, 'shorthand writer; clerk,
secretary', fr. notare. See note, v.

## notation
notation, п., a system of representing numbers
and quantities by signs or symbols. — L. notd-
tio, gen. -onis, 'a marking, designation;
etymology; the use of letters to denote words,
shorthand', fr. notatus, pp. of notare. See note, v., and
-ion.
Derivative: notation-al, adj.

## notch
notch, п., a V-shaped incision. — Prob. from
misdivision of an otch into a notch, fr. OF. osche
(F. hoche), 'notch', fr. OF. oschier, 'to cut,
make incisions', which is of unknown origin.
For similar misdivisions cp. newt, nickname,
nonce.
Derivative: notch, tr. v.

## note
note, п., a mark, sign. — L. nota, 'mark, sign,
note; character, letter, shorthand character',
which is pern. rel. to notus, pp. of noscere, OL.
gnoscere, 'to know'. See know and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also notable, notary,
notation, annotate, annotation, connotate,
connotation.

## note
note, tr. v., to make a note of— ME. noten, fr.
OF. (= F.) noter, fr. L. notare, 'to mark, make
a note, to note', fr. nota. See note, n.
Derivatives: not-ed,aaj., not-ed-ly, adv., not-ed-
tiess, п., note-less, adj., note-less-ly, adv., note'
less-ness, п., not-er, n.

## nothing
nothing, n. — Compounded of no, adj., and thing.
Derivative: nothing-ness, a.

## notho-
notho-, combining form meaning 'spurious'. —
Gk. νόθο-, fr. νόθος, 'bastard, spurious'; of
unknown origin.

## Nothofagus
Nothofagus, п., a genus of timber trees {bot.) —
A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk. νόθος,
'spurious' (see notho-), and L. fagus, 'beech' (see
beech). The correct form would be Nothophegus,
fr. Gk. νό&ος, 'spurious', and φηγός, 'oak'; see
Fagopyrum.

## Notholaena
Notholaena, п., a genus of plants, the cloak fern
(bot) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk. νόθος,
'spurious' (see notho·), and L. laena, 'woolen
cloak, mantle', fr. Gk. χλαίνα, which is rel. to
χλανίς, of s.m.

## nothous
nothous, adj., spurious; bastard. — L. notkus, fr.
Gk. νόθος; see notho-. For E, -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, L. -us, see -ous.

## notice
notice, n. — ME. notyce, fr. MF. (= F.) notice,
fr. L. ndtitia, 'a being known, knowledge, note,
information', fr. notus, 'known', pp. of noscere,
'to know'. See know and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see 3rd suff. -ice.
Derivatives: notice, tr. v., notice-able, adj.,
notice-abl-y, adv.

## notification
notification, n. — OF., fr. L. notificatus, pp. of
notificare. See next word and -ion.

## notify
notify, tr. v. — ME. notifien, fr. MF. (= F.)
notifter, fr. L. notificare, 'to make known,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:528 COLUMN:2 -->
notify', fr. notus, 'known', and -ficdre, tr.facere,
'to make, do'. See -fy.
Derivatives: notifi-able, adj., notifi-er, n.

## notion
notion, n. — L. notio, 'notice; idea, conception',
fr. notus, pp. of noscere, 'to know'; see notice
and -ion. L. notio was coined by Cicero as a loan
translation of Gk. Svvoia, 'act of thinking,
notion, conception', or πρόληψης, 'previous
notion, previous conception'.

## notional
notional, adj., pertaining to a notion. — Late L.
ndtionalis, fr. L. notio. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivative: notional-ly, adv.

## noto-
noto-, before a vowel not-, combining from
denoting 'the back', as in notochord. — Gk. νώτο-,
fr. νώτος (also νώτον), 'the back', cogn. with
L. natis, 'rump'. Cp. nates. Cp. also the second
element in Camponorus, Gymnonoti, Gymnotus.

## notochord
notochord, п., an elastic rod-shaped chord in the
back of embryos of animals {zool.) — Lit.
'chord of the back'; coined by the English
anatomist, Sir Richard Owen (1804-92) in 1848 fr.
νώτος (also νώτον), 'the back', and χορδή, *a
string'. See noto- and chord.

## notodontid
notodontid, adj., pertaining to the Notodontidae;
п., any moth of the family Notodontidae. —
See next word.

## Notodontidae
Notodontidae, n. pi., a family of moths (entomol.)
— Formed with suff. -ioae fr. not- and the stem
of Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-.

## Notogaea
Notogaea, п., a zoogeographical realm,
comprising the Australian, New Zealand and
Neotropical regions. — Gk., compounded of νότος,
'the south wind, the south', and γαία, 'earth'.
The first element prop, means 'the rainy wind',
and is rel. to νότιος, νοτερός, 'damp, moist',
νοτίς, 'moisture, damp*, νοτΕα, 'moisture,
rain'; see natation and cp. Notus. For the second
element in Notogaea see geo-.

## notonectid
notonectid, adj., pertaining to the Notonectidae;
п., one of the family Notonectidae. — See next
word.

## Notonectidae
Notonectidae, n. pi., a family of aquatic insects
{entomol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr.
noto- and Gk. νήκτης, 'swimmer'. See necto-
and cp. words there referred to.

## notoriety
notoriety, п., 1) the quality of being notorious;
2) a well-known person. — F. notoriite, fr. ML.
notorietatem, ace. of ndtorietas, fr. ndtorius,
'well-known'. See next word and -ity.

## notorious
notorious, adj., well-known, widely known
(usually in an unfavorable sense). — ML. ndtorius,
'well-known', fr. L. notus, 'known'. See know
and cp. words there referred to. For the ending
see suff. -orious.
Derivatives: notorious-ly, adv., notorious-ness,
n.

## Notornis
Notornis, п., a genus of flightless birds chiefly of
New Zealand (ornithol.) — ModL., lit. 'bird of
the south', compounded of not- and Gk. βρνις,
'bird'. See ornitho-.

## Notropis
Notropis, п., a genus of North American
minnows (ichthyol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
νώτος (also νώτον), 'the back', and τρόπις, 'a
ship's keel', lit. 'turner'. See noto- and trope.

## Notungulata
Notungulata, n. pi., an order of extinct mammals
(paleontol.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk.
νώτος (also νώτον), 'the back', and L. ungula,
'hoof, claw'. See noto- and Ungulata.

## notungulate
notungulate, adj., pertaining to the Notungulata;
п., one of the order Notungulata. — See prec.
word.

## Notus
Notus, п., the south wind. — L., fr. Gk. Νότος.
See Notogaea.

## notwithstanding
notwithstanding, prep., adv. and conj. —
Compounded of not and the pres. part, of the verb
withstand.

## nouch
nouch, n. — See ouch.

## nougat
nougat, п., sweetmeat of almonds and other nuts.
— F., fr. Provenc. nougat, fr. OProvenc. nogat,
'nutcake', fr. VL. *nucdtum, fr. L. nux, gen.
nucis, 'nut'. See nucleus and cp. words there
referred to.

## nought
nought, n. — ME. nought, nouht, etc., fr. OE.
nowiht, a var. of nawiht, 'nothing'. See naught.

## noumenal
noumenal, adj., pertaining to noumena or the
noumenon. — See next word and adj. suff.
-al.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:528 COLUMN:3 -->

## noumenon
noumenon, п., the object of intellectual intuition;
opposed to a phenomenon (philos.) — Gk.
νούμενον, 'that which is perceived', neut. pass,
pres. part, of νοέω, Ί perceive by the mind', fr.
νόος, νους, 'mind' (see nous); for the Greek
pass. suff. -μένος see alnmnus and cp. words
there referred to. The word noumenon was
introduced by Kant as the opposite of
phenomenon.

## noun
noun, n. — ME. nowne, fr. AF. noun, fr. OF. поп,
пот (F. пот), fr. L. nomen, 'name'. See name
and words there referred to and cp. esp.
nominal, nominate.
Derivatives: noun-al, adj., noun-al-ly, adv.

## nourish
nourish, tr. v. — ME. norischen, norisen, fr. OF.
noris(s)-, enlarged stem of norir', nurir (F. nour-
rir), fr. L. nutrire, 'to nourish', fr. *nu-tri, older
form of пй-trT-x, 'nurse', lit. 'she who gives
suck', fr. I.-E. base *sneu-, *snau-, whence also
OI. snauti, 'she drips, gives milk', Gk. νάω,
Ί flow'. See natation and cp. nurse, nurture,
nutrient, nutriment. For the ending of nourish see
verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: nourish-able, adj., nourish-er, п.,
nourishment (q.v.)

## nourishment
nourishment, n. — ME. norysshement, fr. OF.
norissement, fr. norir. See prec. word and -ment.

## nous
nous, п., I) intellect, mind; the reason; 2) common
sense (colloq.) — Gk. νους, Art. form of νόος,
'mind, intellect'; of uncertain origin. Cp. noetic,
paranoia.

## nouveau riche
nouveau riche, a person who has newly become
rich; a parvenu. — F., lit. 'new rich". See novel,
adj., and rich.

## nova
nova, п., a new star that appears suddenly and
then grows fainter gradually (astron.) — ModL.,
short for L. nova Stella, 'a new star*; fern, of
novus, 'new'. See new and cp. novel, adj.

## novaculite
novaculite, п., a hard slate used for whetstones
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. L.
novacula, 'a sharp knife, a razor", a noun formed
with instrumental suff. -cula, frorn the verb
*novdre,L 'to whet', which prob. derives fr.
*qsnewd-, from I.-E. *qsneu-, enlargement of
base *qseu-, whence also Oi. ksnotram,
'whetstone', ksnauti, 'grinds, whets' (pp. ksnutah),
ON. snoggr, 'short-haired', snaudr, 'bald, bare,
poor', Norw. snau, dial. Swed. stiauder, 'bald,
short', MDu. snode, Du. snood, 'base, heinous,
wicked', MHG. snoede, 'contemptible' (whence
G. schnode, 'base, disdainful'), orig. meaning
'shorn'. For derivatives of the primitive base
*qseu-, see xyster.

## novation
novation, п., the replacement of an old obligation
by a new one (law). — Late L. novatio, gen.
-onis, 'a making new, renewal", fr. L. novatus,
pp. of novare, 'to make new', fr. novus, 'new'.
See new, adj., and -ation and cp. next word.

## novel
novel, adj., new; strange; unusual. — ME., fr.
OF. novel, nouvel [F. nouveau (fem. nouvelle)],
fr. L. novellus, dimin. of novus, 'new'. See new
and cp. nova, novation, novice, innovate,
renovate.

## novel
novel, п., a fictitious prose narrative of
considerable length, representing human life. — MF. no-
velle (F. nouvelle), 'short story', fr. It. novella,
fr. L. novella, 'new things', neut. pi. of novellus,
'new', used as a fem. sing. noun. See novel, adj.

## novelette
novelette, п., a short novel. — Formed fr. novel;
п., with dimin. suff. -ette.

## novelist
novelist, п., a writer of novels. — A hybrid coined
fr. novei, n. (fr. L. novella), and -ist, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## novelty
novelty, п., 1) newness; 2) something new; 3) a
new article put on sale.—ME. novelte, fr. OF. no-
velte (F. nouveaute), fr. Late L. navellitatem,
ace. of novellitds, 'newness, novelty', fr. L.
novellus,1 new'. See novel, adj., and subst. suff.
-ty.

## November
November, n. — L. November (mensis), 'the ninth
month' (of the Roman year), fr. novem, 'nine';
see nine. (The Roman year began with March;
cp. September, October, December.)

## novennial
novennial, adj., recurring every nine years. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Late L. novennis,
'of nine years', which is compounded of novem,
'nine', and annus, 'year'. For the first element
see nine, for the second see annual. For the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:529 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NOVERCAL | 502 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:529 COLUMN:1 -->
change of Latin d (in annus) to i (in nov-innis)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.

## novercal
novercal, adj., like a stepmother. — L. novercdlis,
fr. noverca, 'stepmother', a derivative of novus,
'new'. See new.

## novice
novice, п., a beginner. — ME. novis, fr. MF.
(— F.) novice, fr. L. novicius, 'new; newly
arrived ; novice', fr. novus, 'new'. See new and 2nd
-ice.

## noviciate
noviciate, also novitiate, п., the state of being a
novice. — F. noviciat, fr. ML. novitiatus, fr.
Late L. novitius, inexact spelling of L. novicius.
See prec. word and subst. suff. -ate.

## novo-
novo-, combining form meaning 'new'. — Fr. L.
novus, 'new'. See new and cp. novel, adj.

## novocaine
novocaine, novocain, п., a local anesthetic
substitute for cocaine; a trade name (Novocain). —
Coined fr. novo- and (co)cain(e).

## now
now, adv. — ME. пои, пи, fr. OE. пй, rel. to ON.
пй, Dan., Swed., Du. nu, OS., OFris. пй, пи,
OHG., MHG. пй, пи, G. nun, Goth, nu, 'now',
and cogn. with Ol. пй, пи, nundm, Avestic пй,
OPers. nuram, Toch. nu, Hitt. nuwa, 'now', Gk.
νύ, νΰυ, L. nunc, OSlav. пупё, Lith. nu, 'now',
Olr. nu-, no- (presential pref.). The original
meaning of these words was 'newly, recently'.
They derive fr. I.-E. base *nu, which is rel. to
base *newo-, 'new'. See new.
Derivatives: now, conj. and n.

## nowadays
nowadays, adv., at the present time, in these
times. —Compounded of now, pref. a-, used in
the sense of 'on', and adv. gen. day's.

## nowel
nowel, п., 1) newel; 2) core of a mold for casting
large hollow objects. — A var. of newel.

## Nowel
Nowel, n. — A var. of Noel.

## nowhere
nowhere, adv., — ME. nowher, fr. OE. ndhwxr,
compounded of яд, 'по', and hwxr, 'where'. See
no, adv., and where.

## nowhither
nowhither, adv., to, or toward, no place, nowhere.
— ME. nowhider, fr. OE. nahwider,
compounded of пй, 'по', and wider, 'whither'. See no, adv.,
and whither.

## Nox
Nox, п., the goddess of night in Roman
mythology. — L., lit. 'night'. See nocti-, night.

## noxal
noxal, adj., injurious. — L. noxalis, 'harmful,
injurious', fr. noxa. See next word.

## noxious
noxious, adj., harmful, injurious. — L. noxius,
'harmful, injurious', fr. noxa, 'harm, injury',
rel. to noceo, nocere, 'to hurt, injure, harm', and
to nex, gen. necis, 'violent death, murder'. For
the change of e ■ о ср. memini, Ί remember',
and moneo, 'i remind, admonish' (see memento
and monition); decet, 'it is comely, it becomes',
and doceo, Ί teach' (see decent and docile); rego,
Ί guide, conduct, direct', and rogo, Ί ask', lit.
Ί reach after' (see regent and rogation). L. noceo
and nex derive fr. I.-E. base *nek-, 'to destroy;
to perish', whence also OI. ndsyati, 'disappears,
perishes, disappears', Avestic nasyeiti, of s.m.,
nasu-, 'dead body, corpse', Toch. B. nak-sentr,
'they blame', Gk. νέκϋς, νεκ-ρός, /dead body,
corpse', Olr. ёс, Bret. ankou,Co. ancow, 'death'.
Cp. obnoxious, nocent, innocent, nocuous, noxal,
nuisance. Cp. also internecine, Necator, necro-,
noyade, pernicious. Cp. also ninny. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: noxious-ly, adv., noxious-ness, n.

## noyade
noyade, п., the drowning of persons at Nantes
during the Reign of Terror in 1794. — F.,
'drowning', fr. noyer, 'to kill by drowning, to
drown', fr. L. necdre, 'to kill'. See noxious.
Derivative: noyade, tr. v.

## noyau
noyau, п., a liqueur flavored with peach kernels.
— F., 'stone of fruit; core of statues, casts, etc.;
newel (of staircase), noyau', fr. Late L. nucalem,
ace. of nucalis, 'pertaining to a nut', fr. L. nux,
gen. nucis, 'nut'. See nucleus and words there
referred to and cp. esp. newel.

## nozzle
nozzle, п., a spout. — Dimin. of nose (q.v.) Cp.
nuzzle.
Derivative: nozzle, tr. v.

## nu
nu, п., name of the 13th letter of the Greek
alphabet. — Gk. νΰ, shortened fr. Heb. nun, name of
the letter n. See nun, the letter.

## nuance
nuance, п., a slight difference. — F., 'shade, hue;
a slight difference', fr. MF., fr. nuer, 'to shade',
fr. nue, 'cloud', fr. L. nubes (see nubilous and
-ance); so called with reference to the different

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:529 COLUMN:2 -->
colors of the clouds.

## nub
nub, п., a knob, lump (rare) — Cp. LG. knubbe,
'knob, protuberance', and see knob, kriub.

## nubble
nubble, п., a small nub. — Formed fr. nub with
dimin. suff. -le.
Derivative: nubbl-y, adj.

## nubia
nubia, п., a woman's light scarf worn over the
head and neck. — Fr. L. nubes, 'cloud'. See
nubilous.

## Nubian
Nubian, adj., pertaining to Nubia, its people or
their language; п., a) an inhabitant of Nubia;
b) the Negro language spokeo by the Nubians.

## nubiform
nubiform, adj., resembling a cloud. —
Compounded of L. nubes, 'cloud', and forma, 'form,
shape'. See nubilous and form, n.

## nubile
nubile, adj., marriageable (said of a woman) — L.
nubilis, from the stem oinubere, 'to marry, wed'.
See nuptial and cp. connubial.
Derivative: nubil-ity, n.

## nubilous
nubilous, adj., cloudy, foggy, obscure. — Late L.
nubilosus, fr. L. nubes, 'cloud', which prob.
stands for 'snoudhis and is cogn. with Avestic
snaoba-, 'clouds', W. nudd, 'fog', Gk. νυθόν
(Hesychius), 'dark, dusky'. Cp. nuance, nubia,
nubiform. For the ending see suff. -ous.

## nuceUns
nuceUns, п., the central mass of the body of an
ovule (do/.) — ModL., fr. L. nucella, dimin. of
nux, gen. nucis, 'nut'. See nucleus and cp. words
there referred to.

## nucha
nucha, п., the spinal cord (anat.) — Medical L.,
fr. Arab. nukha\ 'spinal marrow'. See nuque.
Derivative: nuch-at, adj.

## nucha
nucha, п., паре of the neck (anat.) — Medical L.,
from a confusion of Arab, nukha', 'spinal
marrow', with ntiqrcr, 'nape of the neck' (see prec.
word); introduced by Constantine the African
about 1080.
Derivative: nuch-al, adj.

## nuchaL adj.
nuchaL adj., pertaining to the spina] cord. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. nucha, 'spinal
cord'.

## nuchal
nuchal, adj., pertaining to the nape of the neck.
— Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. nucha, 'the nape
of the neck'.

## nuchalgla
nuchalgla, п., pain in the nape of the neck (med.)
— A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. prec. word
and Gk. ίίλγος, 'pain'; see -algia,

## nuci-
nuci-, combining form meaning 'nut'. — L., from
the stem of nux, gen. nucis, 'nut'. See nucleus
and cp. words there referred to.

## nuciferous
nuciferous, adj., yielding nuts. — Compounded
of nuci- and the stem of L. ferre, 'to bear, carry'.
See -ferous.

## nuciform
nuciform, adj., nut-shaped. — Compounded of
nuci- and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form,
n.

## nucivorous
nucivorous, adj., nut-eating. — Compounded of
nuci- and L. -vorus, fr. vorare, 'to devour'. See
-vorous.

## nucleate
nucleate, nucleated, adj., having a nucleus. — L.
nucleolus, 'having a kernel', fr. nucleus. See
nuclens and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also -ed.

## nucleate
nucleate, tr. v., to form into a nucleus. — L. nu-
ctedt-(um), pp. stem of nucledre, 'to be kemelly',
fr. nucleus. See nucleus and verbal suff. -ate.

## nuclein
nuclein, п., any of a group of substances
occurring in cell nuclei (biochem.) — G. Nuklein,
coined by the Swiss biochemist Friedrich
Miescher in 1869 fr. L. nucleus (see nucleus) and
chem. suff. -in.

## nucleo-
nucleo-, combining form meaning 'connected
with, or related to, a nucleus'. — L. nucleo-, fr.
nucleus. See nucleus.

## nucleolus
nucleolus, п., a rounded body within the nucleus
of a cell. — L., 'a little nut', dimin. of nucleus,
'nut, kernel*, itself a dimin. of nux, 'nut'. See
next word and dimin. suff. -ole.
Derivatives: nucleol-ar, nucleol-ate, nucleol-ated,
adjs.

## nucleoside
nucleoside, п., a glycoside derived from nucleic
acid (chem.) — Coined from nucleo- and
(glycoside.

## nucleotide
nucleotide, п., phosphate of nucleoside (chem.) —
Coined fr. nucieo-, the letter -/- (which was
inserted for the sake of euphony or under the
influence of phosphatide) and suff. -ide (on the
analogy of nucleos-ide).

## nuclens
nuclens, п., a central core or kernel, about which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:529 COLUMN:3 -->
matter is gathered. — L. nuc(u)leus, 'kernel',
dimin. of nux, gen. nucis, 'nut', which stands for
*cnu-c-s and is formed with suff. -c fr. I.-E. base
*cnu-. Formed from the same base without any
suff. are Mir. cm, W. cneuen, MCo. knyfan,
MBret. knoen, 'nut'; formed from the same base
with suff. -d (i.e. fr. *cnu-d) are ON. hnot, OE.
hnutu, etc., 'nut'. All these words are traceable
to I.-E. *qnew-, 'formed into a ball,
compressed', fr. base *qen-, 'to form into a ball, to
compress'. Cp. nucleate, enucleate, newel, noisette,
'piece of meat', noyau, nucellus, nuci-, Nucula,
nux vomica. Cp. also nut.
Derivatives: nucle-ar, nucle-ary, adjs.

## Nucula
Nucula, п., a genus of marine bivalves (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. nucula, 'a little nut', dimin. of лих-,
gen. nucis, 'nut' (see nucleus and -tile); so called
from the nutlike shell.

## nude
nude, adj., naked bare, unclothed. — L. nudus,
'naked, bare', fr. *now(e)dos for I.-E. *nogwe-
dhos; cogn. with Goth, naqaps, OE. nacod,
'naked'. See naked.
Derivatives: nude, п., a nude figure, nude-ly,
adv., nude-ness, n.

## nudge
nudge, tr. v., to touch or push slightly with the
elbow. — Prob. rel. to dial Norw. nugga, nyggja,
'to push'.
Derivative: nudge, n.

## Nudlbranchiata
Nudlbranchiata, n. pi., a suborder of mollusks
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of L. nudus,
'naked', and bronchia, 'gill'. See nude and
branchia.

## nudibranchiate
nudibranchiate, adj., 1) pertaining to the
Nudlbranchiata ; 2) п., one o?the Nudlbranchiata. —
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.

## nudlcaul
nudlcaul, nudlcaulous, adj., having leafless stems
(bot.) — Compounded of L. nudus, 'naked,
bare', and caulis, 'stem, stalk'. See nude and
cole.

## nudism
nudism, п., the practice of going nude. — See
nude and -ism.

## nudist
nudist, п., one who practices nudism. — See nude
and -izt.

## nudity
nudity, п., 1) nakedness; 2) that which is nude. —
F. nudite, fr. L. nuditdtem, ace. of nuditus,
'nakedness', fr. nudus. See nude and -ity.

## nudnik
nudnik, п., a bore. — Yiddish nudnik, formed
with agential suff. -nik, fr. Russ. nudnyl,
'tiresome, tedious, boring', fr. nudd, 'need, want,
boredom', which is rel. to OSlav. nulda, Russ.
nuzdd, 'need', and cogn. with Goth, naups, OE.
nied, ned, 'need'; see need, n. The Yiddish suff.
-nik is of Slavic origin; cp. beatnik.

## nugacious
nugacious, adj., trifling (rare). — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. nugdx, gen. nugdeis, 'trifling', fr.
nugdrl. See nugatory.
Derivative: nugacious-ness, n.

## nugacity
nugacity, п., triviality (rare) — Late L. nugdeitds,
'a trifling, playfulness', fr. L. nugdx, gen.
nugdeis. See prec. word and -ity.

## nugatory
nugatory, adj., trifling, of no value. — L. nugdtd-
rius, 'trifling; worthless, useless', fr. nugdtor,
gen. -oris, 'jester, joker', fr. nugdtus, pp. of
nugdrl, 'to jest, trifle', fr. nugae, gen. -drum,
'jokes, jests, trifles'; which is of uncertain origin.
For the ending see adj. suff. -ory.

## nuggar
nuggar, п., a kind of boat used on the Nile. —
VArab. nuqqar.

## nugget
nugget, п., a lump of metal; esp. a lump of gold.
— For niggot (so spelled in North's Plutarch),
fr. a niggot, misdivision and corruption of an
ingot. See ingot.

## nuisance
nuisance, п., something causing annoyance or
inconvenience. — ME. nusaunce, fr. OF.
nuisance, fr. nuisant, pp. of nuire, 'to hurt, harm',
fr. VL. nocgre, corresponding to classical L.
nocere, 'to hurt, injure, harm'. See noxious and
cp. wotds there referred to. For the ending see
suff. -ance. F. nuisance has been reborrowed fr.
English.

## null
null, adj. — Fr. F. nul—or directly—fr. L.
nullus, 'not one, not any, none', contraction of
*ne(e) oin(o)los, 'not one', fr. neg. pref. ne- and
dimin. of OL. oinos (whence L. unus), One'. See
no, adv., and one and cp. nullify, nullity, annul.

## nullah
nullah, п., a ravine; a watercourse (Anglo-Ind.)
— Hind, nald, 'brook, watercourse, ravine',

## nullification
nullification, n. — Late L. nullificdtw, gen. -dnis,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:530 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 503 | NUT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:530 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. nullificatus, pp. of nullificare. See next word
and -ion.

## nullify
nullify, tr. v., to render invalid, make null and
void, annul. — Late L. nullificare, 'to esteem
lightly, despise', prop, 'to reduce to nothing*,
compounded of L. nullus, 'none', and -ficare,
ΐτ./acere, 'to make, do'. See null and -fy.

## nullipara
nullipara, п., a woman whojias never borne a
child (med.) — Medical L., coined on analogy
of L. vivipara (see viviparous) fr. L. nullus, 'none',
and -para, fern, of -parus, 'bringing forth', from
the stem of parere, 'to bring forth'. See null and
-parous.

## nulliparous
nulliparous, adj., having borne no children. —
See prec. word and -parous.

## nullipore
nullipore, п., any of various lime-secreting algae
(bot.) — Compounded of L. nullus, 'none', and
porus, 'passage, pore'. See null and pore.

## nullity
nullity, п., the quality or state of being null,
invalidity ; that which is null. — OF. (= F.) nullite,
fr. ML. nullitatem, ace. of nullitas, fr. L. nullus.
See null and -ity.

## numb
numb, adj. — ME. nume, lit. 'taken, seized', pp.
of nimen (fr. OE. niman), 'to take'. See nim and
nimble. The b in numb is excrescent. Cp. benumb.
Derivatives: numb,tr, and intr. \.,numb-ness, n.

## number
number, n. — ME. nombre, noumbre, fr. OF.
(= F.) nombre, fr. L. numerus (for *nomeros)
'number', fr. I.-E. base *nem-, 'to divide,
distribute, allot'. See nimble and cp. numeral,
numeric, numero, numerous.
Derivative: number-less, adj.

## number
number, tr. v. — ME. nombren, fr. OF. (= F.)
nombrer, fr. L. numerare, 'to count, reckon,
number', fr. numerus. See number, n.
Derivative: number-erx n.

## Numbers
Numbers, п., the fourth book of the Pentateuch.
— Translation of L. Numeri, itself translation
of Gk. 'Αριθμοί; it was so called because it
begins with the census of the people taken in the
second year of the Exodus.

## numbles
numbles, n. pi., certain inward parts of deer used
as food {archaic). — ME. noumbles, fr. OF.
numbles, nombles (pi.), 'loin of veal', dissimilated
fr. *lombles, pi. of *lomble, fr. L. lumbulus,
dimin. of lumbus, 'loin' (whence OF., F. lombe,
'loin'). See loin and -ule and cp. umbles and
humble pie.

## numda
numda, numdah, n. — See namda.

## numen
numen, п., a divine spirit; a presiding divinity. —
L. numen, 'divine will, divine command', prop.
'divine approval expressed by nodding the
head', fr. nuere, 'to nod', which is cogn. with Gk.
νεύειν, 'to nod'. See nut ant and -men and cp.
numinous.

## numerable
numerable, adj. — L. numerabilis, 'that can be
counted or numbered', fr. numerare. See
number, v. and п., and -able.
Derivatives: numberable-ness, п., numerabl-y,
adv.

## numeral
numeral, adj., pertaining to, or expressing, a
number or numbers. — MF. (= F.) numeral, fr.
Late L. numeralis, 'of numbers', fr. L. numerus.
See number, п., and adj. surf. -al.
Derivative: numeral, n.

## numerary
numerary, adj., pertaining to a number or
numbers. — ML. numerarius, fr. L. numerus. See
number п., and adj. surf. -ary.

## numerate
numerate, v., to count; to enumerate. — L. nu-
meratus, pp. of numerare. See number, v. and п.,
and verbal suff. -ate.

## numeration
numeration, n. — ME. numeracion, fr. L. nume-
ratio, gen. of -onis, *a counting', fr. numeratus,
pp. of numerare. See number, v. and п., and
-ation.

## numerator
numerator, п., that term of a fraction which shows
how many parts of a unit are taken. —VL.
numerator, lit. 'counter, numberer', fr. numeratus, pp.
of numerare. See number, v. and п., and -tor.

## numerical
numerical, adj. — Formed with suff. -icul fr. L.
numerus. Cp. F. numerique and see number, n.
Derivative: numerical-ly, adv.

## numerology
numerology, п., the study of the occult meaning
of numbers. — A hybrid coined fr. L. numerus,
'number', and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy. The correct
form would be arithmology, fr. Gk. αριθμός.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:530 COLUMN:2 -->
'number*, and -λογία.

## numerous
numerous, adj. — L. numerosus, 'numerous', fr.
numerus. See number, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: numerous-ly, adv., numerous-ness,
n.

## Numidia
Numidia, п., an ancient country in North Africa.
— L., fr. Numida, 'a Numidian', orig. *a nomad',
fr. Gk. νομάδα, ace. of νομάς, 'nomad'; see
nomad and 1st -ia. For the derivation of the
Latin word from a Greek accusative cp. onycha,
ore, speluncar, sportula.

## Numidian
Numidian, adj., pertaining to Numidia. — L. Nu-
midianus, fr. Numidia. See prec. word and -an.
Derivative: Numidian, п., one of the inhabitants
of Numidia.

## numinous
numinous, adj., divine, spiritual. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L- numen, gen. numinis, 'divine
will'. See numen.

## numismatic
numismatic, adj., pertaining to coins and medals.
— F. numismatique, fr. L. numisma, 'current
coin', fr. Gk. νόμισμα, 'usage, money, current
coin', lit. 'what has been sanctioned by custom
or usage', fr. νομίζειν, 'to adopt or practice a
custom or usage', fr. νόμος, 'law, custom,
usage', fr. I.-E. base *nem-, 'to divide, distribute,
allot'. See nimble and words there referred to
and cp. esp. nummary. For the ending see suff.
-atic.

## numismatics
numismatics, п., the study and collection of coins
and medals. — See prec. word and -ics.

## numismatist
numismatist, п., 1) a specialist in numismatics; 2)
a collector of coins or medals. — F. numisma-
tiste. See numismatic and -ist.

## numismatology
numismatology, п., numismatics. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. 'numisma, gen. -matis (see
numismatic) and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## numisinatologist
numisinatologist, п., a numismatist. — Formed
fr. prec. word with suff. -ist.

## nummary
nummary, adj., pertaining to coins or money. —
L. nummarius, 'of coins', fr. nummus, 'coin,
money', which is a loan word fr. Gk. νόμιμος,
'lawful, legal', fr. νόμος, 'law'. See numismatic
and adj. suff. -ary and cp. nummular, nummulite.

## nummiform
nummiform, adj., coin-shaped. — Compounded
of L. nummus, 'coin', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See nummary and form, n.

## nummular
nummular, adj., coin-shaped. — L. nummuldrius,
lit. 'of small coins', fr. nummulus, dimin. of
nummus, 'coin'. See nummary and the suffixes
-ule and -ar.

## nummulite
nummulite, п., a coin-shaped fossil shell —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. nummulus.
See prec. word.
Derivative: nummulit-ic, adj.

## numskull
numskull, п., a dolt, blockhead. — Compounded
of numb and skull.

## nun
nun, п., 1) a woman devoted to religious life, esp.
one living in a convent under vows of chastity,
poverty and obedience; 2) any of various birds.
— ME. nunne, nun, fr. OE. nunne, fr. Late L.
nonna, 'an old woman, a nun', fern, of nonnus,
'an old man, a monk', orig. a child's lip word.
Cp. OI. nana, ModPers. nana, 'mother', Gk.
νάννα, νέννα, 'aunt', Alb. папе, 'mother, nurse',
Bulg. neni, 'the older one', Serbo-Croatian nana,
nena, 'mother', W. nain, 'grandmother', which
all were orig. child's lip words. Olt. nonno,
'grandfather', nonna, 'grandmother', are loan
words fr. Late L. nonnus, resp. nonna. Cp.
nunnery. Cp. also nanism.

## nun
nun, п., the Nth letter of the Heb. alphabet. —
Heb. nun, lit. 'fish'; so called in allusion to the
ancient Hebrew form of this letter. Cp. nu.

## nuncheon
nuncheon, п., a light refreshment taken at noon
(obsol.) — ME. noneschench, lit. *a noon-drink',
fr. none, 'noon', and schenche, 'a pouring out, a
draft*. For the first element see пооЪ. The second
element derives fr. OE. scencan, 'to give to
drink', which is rel. to OS. skenkian, OFris.
sfcenka, OHG. skenken, 'to give to drink',
MHG., G., Du. schenken, 'to give'. The original
meaning of these verbs was 'to hold in a
slanting position'. They derive from the Teut.
adj. *skanka-, 'slanting, oblique', fr. I.-E. base
*sqeng-, of s.m. See shank and cp. skink, 'to
serve'. Cp. also luncheon.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:530 COLUMN:3 -->

## nunciature
nunciature, п., the office of a nuncio. — It. nun-
ciatura (now nunziatura), formed with suff. -ига
(fr. L. -ura), fr! nunciaw (now nunziato), pp. of
nunciare (now nunziare), 'to announce,
proclaim', fr. L. nuntiure, *to announce', fr. nuntius.
See next word and -ure.

## nuncio
nuncio, п., papal envoy. — Earlier it. nuncio (now
nunzio), fr. L. nuntius, 'messenger, envoy;
message', which prob. stands for *noventius, haplo-
logic contraction of *novi-ventius, lit. 'one new-
coming', fr. novus 'new', and vent-(um), pp.
stem of venire, 'to come'. See new and come, and
cp. announce, annunciate, denounce, denunciate,
enounce, enunciate, intemuncial, internuncio,
pronounce, pronunciamento, pronunciation,
renounce, renunciation.

## nuncle
nuncle, п., uncle (obsol.) — From misdivision of
an uncle (or mine uncle) into a nuncle (resp. my
nuncle).

## nuncupative
nuncupative, adj., declared orally, oral (said of
wills) — Late L. nuncupative, 'so-called,
nominal', fr. L. nuncupatus, pp. of nuncupare, 'to
call by name, to call, name', fr. *nomo-capos,
'taken by name', which is compounded of no-
men, 'name', and capere, 'to catch, seize, take,
hold'. See name and captive.

## nundinal
nundinal, adj., pertaining to a fair or market. — L.
nundinalis, 'pertaining to a market day', fr. пйп-
dinae, 'the market day', lit. 'the ninth day' (so
called because it was held every ninth day),
contraction of *noven-dinom, 'nine days', fr.
novem, 'nine', and *dinom, 'day'. For the first
element see nine. The second element is cogn.
with OI. -dtnam, OSlav. dim', 'day', Lith. diena,
OPruss. deinam (ace,), 'day', Olr. -denus (in
tre-denus), 'the space of three days', Goth.
-teins (in the compound sin-teins, 'daily', OHG.
-zin (in lengi-zin, 'Lent', lit. 'long days'),
OE. -ten (in lenc-ten), of s.m., and with L.
dies, 'day', deus, 'god'. See dies поп, deity, and
cp. the second element in Lent.

## nunnation
nunnation, п., the addition of a final л in the
Arabic declension of nouns. — ModL. nunna-
t'w, gen. -onis, fr. nun, the Arabic name of the
letter η, fr. Heb. nun. See nun, name of a Hebrew
letter, and -ation.

## nunnery
nunnery, п., 1) a community of nuns; 2) a
convent. — ME. nunnerie, fr. OF. nonnerie, fr.
nonne, 'nun', fr. L. nonna. See nun and -ery.

## nuphar
nuphar, п., the waterlily. — See nenuphar.

## nuptial
nuptial, adj., pertaining to a wedding. — L. nup-
tialis, 'of a marriage or wedding', fr. nuptiae,
'marriage, wedding', fr. nuptus, pp. of nubo,
nubere, 'to marry, wed', which prob. stands for
*sneubho and is cogn. with OSlav. snubiti, 'to
love, woo', Czech snoubiti, 'to seek in marriage,
woo', Czech za-snoubiti, Slovak zasnubit\ 'to
betroth', Gk. νύμφη, 'bride'. For the ending
see suff. -al. Cp. nubile, connubial, nymph.

## nuptials
nuptials, n. pi. — Fr. prec. word.

## nuque
nuque, п., the back of the neck, nape. — F.,
'back of the neck, nape'. The original meaning
of the word was 'spinal marrow'; it derives fr.
ML. nucha, which is borrowed fr. Arab, nukha",
of s.m.; see nucha. The meaning of F. nuque is
due to the influence of Arab, nuqra1, 'nape'. Cp.
OProveng. nuca, which unites both meanings:
'back of the neck' and 'marrow'.

## nuraghe
nuraghe, п., any of the prehistoric circular
buildings found in Sardinia. — Dial. It. (=
Sardinian) nuraghe.

## nurse
nurse, n. — ME. norice, nurice, fr. OF. nurice,
nourice (F. nourrice), fr. Late L. nutricia, 'nurse',
fern, of L. nutricius, adj., 'nourishing', fr.
nutrix, gen -icis, 'nurse'. See nourish and cp.
nurture.
Derivatives: nurse, tr. and intr. v., nurs-er, п.,
nurseling (q.v.), nurse-ry, п., nurs-ing, adj. and n.

## nurseling
nurseling, also nursling, п., 1) an infant; 2)
anything that is carefully fostered. — Formed fr.
nurse with dimin. suff. -ling.

## nurture
nurture, п., nourishment. — ME., fr. OF. nor(r)e-
ture (F. nourriture), fr. L. nutritura, 'a nursing,
suckling', fr. nutritus, pp. of nutrire, 'to
nourish'. See nourish and -ture.
Derivatives: nurture, v., nurtur-er, n.

## nut
nut, п., the dry fruit of various trees, containing
an edible kerne] inclosed in a hard shell. — ME.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:531 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: NUTANT | 504 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:531 COLUMN:1 -->
nute, fr. OE. hnutu, rel. to ON. hnot, Norw. not,
Swed. not, Dan. nod, Du. noot, OHG. hnu$,
пиз, MHG. пиз, G. Nufl, 'nut'; fr. I.-E. base
*cnu-d. Cp. L. nux, gen. nucis, 'nutT, fr. I.-E.
base *cnu-c, and see nucleus.
Derivatives: nut, intr. v., to gather nuts, nutt-y,
adj.

## nutant
nutant, adj., drooping, nodding (hot.) — L.
nutans, gen. -amis, pres. part, of nutare, freq. of
nuere, 'to nod'. See next word and -ant.

## nutation
nutation, п., 1) the act of nodding; 2) a slight
movement of the earth's axis (astron.) — L. пй-
tatio, gen. -onis, 'a nodding', fr. nutatus, pp. of
nutare, freq. of nuere, 'to nod', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)neu-, 'to move quickly, jerk, nod the head',
whence also Gk. νεύειν, 'to nod', perh. also Gk.
νύσσειν [fr. base *neu-q(h)-f!], 'to touch with a
sharp point, prick,stab', LG. nucken, 'to shake the
head threateningly', dial. G. einnucken, 'to fall
into a slumber', OSlav. nukati, njukati, 'to stir
up'. Cp. innuendo, numen. For the ending see
sulT. -ation.

## nuthatch
nuthatch, п., any of various small birds, feeding
esp. on nuts. — ME. notehach, nuttehache,
compounded of note, mate, 'nut' (see nut), and hach,
hache, which is rel. to hack, 'to chop', hatch, 'to
engrave". For the relation between hack and
hatch cp. bake and batch, wake and watch, dike
and ditch.

## nutmeg
nutmeg, п., the aromatic seed of an E. Indian tree.
— ME. notemuge, nutmuge, formed fr. OF. nois
muguete, 'nutmeg', through substitution of ME.
note, nut (see nut) forOF. nois, 'nut', and through
change of muguete into muge. OF. nois muguete
derives fr. OProvens. noz muscada, fr. noz, 'nut'
(fr. L. nucem, ace. ainux), and muscada, fern, of
muscat, 'musky'; see muscat. Cp. F. noix mus-
cade, It. noce moscada, Sp. nuez moscada, Du.
nootmuskaat, G. Muskatnufl, etc., 'nutmeg'.
Derivatives: nutmegg-ed, nutmegg-y, adjs.

## nutria
nutria, п., 1) the coypu (a S. American rodent);
2) its fur. — Sp., 'otter', fr. L. lutra. See otter.

## nutrient
nutrient, adj. — L. nutriens, -entis, pres. part, of
nutrire, 'to nourish'. See nourish and -ent and
cp. nurse, nurture.

## nutrify
nutrify, tr. and intr. v., to nourish (archaic). —
Compounded of L. nutrire, 'to nourish', and
-ficare, fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See prec. word
and -fy.

## nutriment
nutriment, п., food. — L. nutrimentum,
'nourishment', fr. nutrire, 'to nourish'. See nutrient and
-ment.
Derivative; nutriment-al, adj.

## nutrition
nutrition, п., the act or process of nourishing or
being nourished. — L. nutritw, 'nourishment',
fr. nutrire. See nutrient and -ion,
Derivatives: nutrition-al, adj., nutrition-al-ly,
adv., nutrition-ist, n.

## nutritious
nutritious, adj., nourishing. — L. nutricius, 'that
which nourishes, nurses', fr. nutrix, gen. nutricis,
'nurse'. See nourish and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending see suff. -itious.
Derivatives: nutritious-ly, adv., nutritious-ness,
n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:531 COLUMN:2 -->

## nutritive
nutritive, adj., nourishing, nutricious. — ME.
nutritif, fr. MF. (= F.) nutritif (fern, nutritive),
fr. Late L. nutritivus, 'nourishing', fr. L.
nutritus, pp. of nutrire. See nutrition and -ive.
Derivatives: nutritive-ly, adv., nutritive-ness, n.

## nux vomica
nux vomica, the seed of an E. Indian tree
containing strychnine; 2) medicine made from this
seed. — ML., lit. 'a nut to make (one) vomit',
fr. L. nux, 'nut', and vomere, 'to vomit'. For the
first word see nucleus, for the second see vomit.

## nuzzle
nuzzle, intr. v., to press the nose (against); tr. v.,
to touch with the nose. — ME. noselen, fr. nose.
See nose and freq. suff. -le and cp. nozzle.

## nyct-
nyct-, form of nycti- before a vowel.

## nyctalopia
nyctalopia, п., 1) night-blindness; 2)
day-blindness (med.) — Late L., fr. nyctatops, 'one who
suffers from night-blindness or from
day-blindness', fr. Gk. νυκτάλωψ, which is compounded
of νύξ, gen. νυκτός, 'night', άλαός, 'blind', and
ώψ, gen. ώττός, 'eye'. For the etymology of νύξ
see nycti-; άλαός prob. means lit. 'not seeing',
and is formed fr. a- (see priv. pref. a-) and the
stem of λάειν, 'to see', which is cogn. with OI.
lasati, 'shines, beams'; for the etymology of Gk.
ώψ see -opia. Cp. hemeralopia.
Derivative: nyctalop-ic, adj.

## Nyctanthes
Nyctanthes, п., a genus of East Indian plants
(hot.) — ModL., lit. 'night flower', compounded
of nyct- and Gk. £ν&ος, 'flower'. See anther.

## Nyctea
Nyctea, п., a genus of birds, the snowy owl (or-
nithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. νύξ, gen. νυκτός,
'night'. See nycti-.

## Nyctereutes
Nyctereutes, п., a genus of canine mammals, the
raccoon dog (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. νυκτε-
ρευτής, 'one who hunts by night', fr. νυκτε-
ρεύειν, 'to pass the night, hunt by night', fr.
νύκτερος, 'by night, nightly', fr. νύξ, gen.
νυκτός, 'night'. See nycti-.

## Nycteris
Nycteris, п., a genus of American bats (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. νυκτερΕς, 'bat', lit. 'the
nocturnal animal', fr. νύξ, gen. νυκτός, 'night'. See
nycti-.

## nycti-
nycti-, nycto-, before a vowel nyct-, combining
form meaning 'night'. — Gk. νυκτι-, νυκτο-,
νυκτ-, fr. νύξ, gen. νυκτός, 'night', which is
cogn. with L. nox, gen. noctis, 'night', Goth.
nahts, OE. neaht, niht, of s.m. See night and cp.
nocti-. Cp. also the second element in Calonyc-
tion.

## Nycticorax
Nycticorax, п., a genus of birds, the night heron
(ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. νυκτικόραξ, 'a
kind of owl', lit. 'night raven', fr. νυκτι- (see
nycti-) and κόρα.ξ, 'raven'. See coracoid.

## nyctitropism
nyctitropism, п., tendency of a plant to change its
position at night. — Compounded of nycti-, Gk.
-τρόπος, 'turning', fr. τρέπειν, 'to turn', and
suff. -Ism. See trope and troplsm and cp. helio-
tropism and words there referred to.

## nyctophobia
nyctophobia, п., morbid fear of night (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of nycto- and -φοβία,
'fear of, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.

## nylghau
nylghau, n. — See nilgai.

## nylon
nylon, п., an extremely elastic synthetic material
made from coal, air and water. — An invented

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:531 COLUMN:3 -->
word.
Derivative: nylon-ed, adj.

## nymph
nymph, п., 1) one of a class of inferior female
deities represented as inhabiting the sea, springs,
wells, woods, etc.; 2) a young woman (poet.); 3)
a) a young, not fully developed insect; b) pupa,
chrysalis. — ME. nimphe, fr. OF. nimphe (F.
nymphe), fr. L. nympha, fr. Gk. νύμφη, 'bride,
maiden, nymph', which is cogn. with L. niibere,
'to marry, wed'. See nuptial and cp. paranymph.
L. lumpa (also limpa, lympha), 'spring water', is
borrowed fr. Gk. νύμφη (see lymph).

## nympha
nympha, п., pi. nymphae, 1) a pupa; 2) (pi.) the
inner lips of the vulva (anat.) — L., fr. Gk.
νύμφη, 'bride, maiden, nymph'. See nymph.

## Nymphaea
Nymphaea, п., a genus of aquatic plants, the
yellow lily (hot.) — L., 'the water lily', prop, 'the
plant dedicated to the nymphs', fr. nympha. See
nymph.

## Nymphaeaceae
Nymphaeaceae, n. pi., the water lily family (bot.)
— Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## nymphaeaceous
nymphaeaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## nymphal
nymphal, adj., 1) pertaining to a nymph; 2)
pertaining to a young insect. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. nympha. See nymph.

## nymphean
nymphean, adj., nymphal. — Formed with suff.
-an, fr. Gk. νυμφαίος, 'of the nymphs;
nymphlike',· fr. νύμφη. See nymph.

## nymphitis
nymphitis, п., inflammation of the inner lips of
the vulva (med.) — Medical L., formed fr.
nymphae with suff. -iris.

## nympho-
nympho-, combining form meaning 1) a nymph;
2) one of the nymphae (anat.) — Gk. νυμφο-,
fr. νύμφη, 'nymph'. See nymph.

## nympholepsy
nympholepsy, п., ecstatic emotion. — Orig.
'frenzy supposed to take· hold of a man who looked
at a nymph'; formed on the analogy of epilepsy
fr. Gk. νυμφόληπτος, 'caught by the nymphs;
raptured, frenzied', which is compounded of
νύμφη, 'nymph', and ληπτός, 'that which can
be seized or apprehended', verbal adj. of
λαμβάνειν, Чо take, seize'. See iemma.

## nympholept
nympholept, п., a person seized with
nympholepsy. — Gk. νυμφόληπτος. See prec. word.
Derivative: nympholept-ic, adj.

## nymphomania
nymphomania, п., morbid sexual desire in women
(med.) — Medical L., compounded of nympho-
and Gk. μανίϊ, 'madness, frenzy'. See mania.
Derivative: nymphomani-ac, adj. and n.

## Nyssa
Nyssa, п., a genus of plants, the tupelo (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. νύσσα, 'turning post', which is
of uncertain etymology. It is possibly rel. to
νύσσειν 'to touch with a sharp point, prick,
stab'. See nutation.

## nystagmus
nystagmus, п., involuntary oscillation of the
eyeball (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. νυσταγμός,
'drowsiness', fr. νυστάζειν, 'to be sleepy, to be
drowsy, to doze', which is cogn. with Lith.
snaudziu, sndusti, 'to slumber'.
Derivative: nystagm-ic, adj.

## Nyx
Nyx, п., the goddess of night in Greek
mythology. — Gk. Νύξ, personification of the night.
See night.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:532 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:532 COLUMN:1 -->
О, interj., an exclamation expressing admiration
surprise, fear, etc. — Common to most lan-
gnages; (cp. e.g. Gk. ώ, L. δ, oh, OSlav., Lith.
o, Goth, o, Du., G. o, F. ο, ΟΙ. α, Olr. a, a);
of imitative origin. Cp. oh.

## o'
o', shortened form of, 1) of, as in o'clock, or 2)
{dial.) on.

## -o-
-o-, connective vowel, orig. used to join two
elements of Greek origin on the analogy of Greek
compounds in which the о usually belongs to
the stem of the first element (cp. e.g. λευκό-
φυλλος, 'white-leafed', χειρό-μαντις, 'diviner
by palmistry*), or represents another stem vowel
or is an addition to a stem ending in a
consonant. Later the use of this connective vowel was
applied to compounds whose elements are of
Latin origin, although in Latin itself, the
connective vowel is i (cp. e.g. art-i-fex, 'artist', the
stem of the first element being arti-). The use of
the connective о was extended later to form
compounds from elements of Late L., ML. and
even ModL. origin, first in ethnic names (as
Anglo-Saxon, Anglo-Indian) and later—esp. in
our time—to coin scientific terms (as
radioactive). As in Greek words (cp. e.g. άριστ-αρχία
in contradistinction to άρίστο-κρατία), the
connective о is usually dropped if the second
element begins with a vowel. Cp. the numerous
combining forms in -o throughout this
dictionary. Cp. also -oid, ology.

## oaf
oaf, п., \) orig. an elf's child; hence a child
allegedly substituted for another child; 2) an
idiotic child; 3) a clumsy fellow; a lout. —
Earlier auf, fr. ON. alfr, 'elf. See elf and cp.
ouphe. Cp. also Oberon.
Derivatives: oaf-isht adj., oaf-ish-ly, adv., oaf-
ish-ness, n.

## oak
oak, n. — ME. ook, ok, fr. OE. dc, rel. to ON.
eik, OS., OFris., MDu. ek, Du. eik, OHG. eih,
MHG. eich, G. Eiche, prob. cogn. with Gk.
αίγί-λωψ, 'a kind of oak', and pern, also with
L. aesculuslprob. standing for *aig-sclo- or *aig-
scolo-), 'the Italian oak'. Cp. Aesculus and the
second element in Crataegus.
Derivatives: oak-en, oak-y, adjs.

## oakum
oakum, п., loose fiber obtained from taking apart
old hemp ropes. — ME. okum, fr. OE. acumba,
'tow', lit. 'off combing', fr. a, 'off, away\ and the
stem of cemban, 'to comb'. See intensive pref. a-
and comb and cp. unkempt.

## oar
oar, n. — ME. oor, or, fr. OE. ar, rel. to ON. ar,
Dan. aare, Swed. ara, 'oar'; of uncertain origin.

## oarlock
oarlock, п., a device in the gunwale of a rowing
boat for keeping the oar in place, rowlock. —
Compounded of oar and lock, 'contrivance for
closing doors'. Cp. rowlock.

## oasis
oasis, п., a fertile place in a desert. — Late L.,
fr. Gk. δασ(.ς, which is of Egypt, origin; cp.
Coptic ouahe, 'oasis* (whence also Arab. wafaah,
of s.m.),prop/dwelling place', fr. ouah, 'to dwell'.

## oast
oast, п., a kiln for drying hops. — ME. ost, fr.
OE. dst, 'kiln', rel. to MDu. ast, Du. eest, fr.
Teut. *aist-, corresponding to I.-E. *aid-io, fr.
base *aidh-, 4o burn'; whence also Gk. αίθε^ν,
'to burn', L. aedes, *a building, temple', aestas,
'summer', aestus, 'heat'. See edify and cp. words
there referred to.

## oat
oat, n. — ME. ote, ate, fr. OE. ate (pi. dtan); of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: oat-en, adj.

## oath
oath, n. — ME. ooth, oth, ath, fr. OE. dp, rel. to
ON. eidr, Dan. eed, Swed. ed, OS., OFris. eth,
Du. eed, OHG. eid, MHG. eit, G. eid, Goth.
aips, 'oath'. These words are prob. of Celtic
origin. Cp. Olr. oeth, *oat\ which prob. stands
for I.-E. *oi-tb-s, lit. 'a going', fr. I.-E. base *ei-,
'to go', whence also Gk. εϊμι, L. ed (for *eio), Ί
go', Gk. οΐτος, 'a going; fate'. Hence Olr. oeth
prob. meant originally 'a going into some
obligation' ; see itinerate and cp. the second element

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:532 COLUMN:2 -->
о
in Huguenot. For sense development cp. Swed.
edgdng, 'taking an oath*, lit. 'a going to swear'.
For other terms of public law borrowed from
the Celts cp. ami, embassy, Reich, rich.
Derivative: oath-ed, adj.

## ob-
ob-, pref. meaning Ί) toward to; 2) against; 3)
across, over, upon; 4) down; 5) completely'. —
L. ob- (before c,/, g, p, assimilated into oc-, of-y
og~, op-', before m, ob- becomes o-), fr. ob,
'toward, against, in the way of; about; before; on
account of; instead of, which is re], to Oscan
op, up, Umbr. os (for *ops), and cogn. with Gk.
07U- in δπιθε(ν), Ion. and Att. 67ησθε(ν),
'behind, at the back, after', οπίσω, 'backward',
όψέ, Lesbian όψί, 'late in the day, at even', Hitt.
appizzis, 'younger, youngest', Lith. ap-, api-,
*about, near'; fr. I.-E. base *opi~, which siands
in gradational relationship to I.-E. *epi-, whence
Gk. έπ£, 'on, upon'. See epi- and cp.
operculum, opisometer, opistho-, opsimath, overt,
cover, covert, Oscines, ostensible.

## Obadiah
Obadiah, п., 1) masc. PN.;2) in the Bible, the
fourth in the order of the Twelve Prophets. —
Heb. 'Obhadydh, lit. 'servant of the Lord'. See
abodah and Elijah and ср. О bed.

## obbligato
obbligato, adj., obligatory, indispensable (said of
a necessary accompaniment by a single
instrument) (mus.) — It., lit. 'obliged', fr. L. obligatus,
pp. of obligdre, *to bind'. See oblige.
Derivative: obbligato, п., a necessary
accompaniment.

## obduracy
obduracy, п., the quality of being obdurate,
stubbornness. — Formed from next word with surT.
-cy.

## obdurate
obdurate, adj., hardened, stubborn. — ME. ob-
durat, fr. L. obdurdtus, 'hardened', pp. of ob-
durare, 'to harden, render hard', fr. ob- and
durare, 'to render hard', fr. durus, 'hard*. See
durable.
Derivatives: obdurate, tr. v., obdurate-ly, adv.,
obdurate-ness, п., obdurat-ion, n.
о be ah, also obi, n. 1) a form of witchcraft
practiced by Negroes in the West Indies; 2) a fetish
used in such witchcraft. — An African Negro
word.

## Obed
Obed, п., masc. PN. {Bible) — Heb. 'Obhedh, lit.
'servant, worshiper', prop. part, of 'dbhadh, 'he
served'. See abodah and cp. Obadiah.

## obedience
obedience, n. — ME., fr. OF., fr. L. oboedientia,
obedientia, 'obedience', fr. oboediens, obediens,
gen. -entis. See next word and -ce and cp.
obeisance, which is a doublet of obedience.

## obedient
obedient, adj. — ME., fr. OF., fr. L. oboedientem,
ace. of oboediens, pres. part, of oboedire, obedire,
'to obey'. See obey and -ent.
Derivatives: obedient-ly, obedientiary (q.v.)

## obedientiary
obedientiary, п., a minor official of the monastic
community dependent upon the abbot. — ML.
obedientiarius, fr. L. oboedientia, obedientia. See
obedience and -ary.

## obeisance
obeisance, п., bow of the head, curtsy. — ME.
obeisance, fr. OF. obeissance (F. obeissance),
'obedience', fr. obeissant, pres. part, of obeir, 'to
obey*. The orig. meaning of obeisance was
'obedience'. See obey and -ce and cp. obedience.

## obeisant
obeisant, adj., showing obeisance. — ME. obei-
saunt, fr. OF. obeissant (F. obeissant). See prec.
word and -ce.

## obelisk
obelisk, п., 1) a rectangular stone column,
tapering at the top into a pyramid; 2) an obelus. —
F. obelisque, fr. L. obeliscus, fr. Gk. οβελίσκος,
'a small spit, an obelisk', dimin. of όβελός, 'a
spit, needle, pointed pillar, obelisk'. See obelus.

## obelize
obelize, tr. v., to mark with an obelus. — Gk.
οβελίζεω, fr. όβελός, 'obelus'. See obelus and
-ize.

## obelus
obelus, п., a mark (— or -i-) used in manuscripts
to indicate a doubtful passage. — Late L., fr.
Gk. όβελός, 'a needle, spit', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. obelisk, obol, amphodelite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:532 COLUMN:3 -->

## Oberon
Oberon, п., the king of the fairies and husband of
Titania {medieval mythol.) — F. Oberon, fr. OF.
Auberon, which is prob. borrowed from a Teut.
source rel- to E. oaf, elf (qq. v.)

## obese
obese, adj., very fat, corpulent. — L. obesus, 'fat,
stout, plump', prop, 'that has eaten himself fat',
pp. of obedere, 'to devour', fr. ob- and edere, 'to
eat'. See edible.
Derivatives: obese-iy, adv., obese-ness, п.,
obesity (q.v.)

## obesity
obesity, n.( corpulence. — L. obesitas (gen. -atis),
'fatness, corpulence, obesity', fr. obesus. Cp. F.
obe'site and see prec. word and -ity.

## obex
obex, п., a band of white matter above the
calamus scriptorius (anat.) — L. ob{j)ex, gen. -ids,
'bolt, bar, barrier', rel. to obicere (less correctly
objicere), 4o throw against'. See object, v. and n.

## obey
obey, tr. and intr. v. — ME. obeyeti, fr. OF. obeir,
(F. obeir), fr. L. oboedire, obedire, for *ob-
d^izdire, 'to obey', fr. ob- and audire, 'to hear'.
See audible and cp. obedient, obeisance.

## obfuscate
obfuscate, tr. v., to darken, obscure. — L. ob-
fuscatus, pp. of obfuscare, 'to darken', fr. ob-
andfuscdre, 'to make dark, darken', fr. fuscits,
'dark'. See fuscous and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: obfuscat-ion, n.

## obi
obi, n. — See obeah.

## obi
obi, п., a broad sash worn by Japanese women
and children. — Jap.

## obiit
obiit, v., he died. — L. 3rd pers. sing. perf. of
obire, 'to die'. See obit.

## obtspo
obtspo, п., a four-horned sheep of S. America. —
Sp., lit. 'bishop', fr. Eccles. L. episcopus (see
bishop); so called because its head resembles a
bishop's mitre.

## obit
obit,п., death; an obituary. — ME. obite, fr. MF.
obit, fr. L. obitus, 'death', fr. obitus, pp. οι obire,
'to go toward, to go to meet: to die' (in this
latter sense short for obire mortem, lit. 'to go
toward death', or for obire diem supremum, lit.
'to go toward the last day'); formed fr. ob- and
ire, 'to go'. See itinerate and cp. obituary. Cp.
also post-obit.

## obiter
obiter, adv., by the way, incidentally. — L., not
compounded of L. ob, 'on, about', and iter,
'way'—as suggested by most lexicographers—
but formed fr. L. ob, with suff. -iter, on analogy
of circiter, 'about', which is formed from the
preposition circa, 'round, about, near'.

## obiter dictum
obiter dictum, 1) an incidental opinion of a j udge
(law); 2) any incidental remark. — L.,
'something said incidentally'. See prec. word and
dictum.

## obituary
obituary, adj., pertaining to, or concerning, death.
— ML. obitudrius, 'pertaining to death', fr. L.
obitus. See obit and adj. suff. -ary.

## obituary
obituary, п., a notice of a person's death, as in a
newspaper. — ML. obitudrius, 'a record of the
death of a person1, fr. obitudrius, 'pertaining to
death'. See obituary, adj.

## object
object, tr. and intr. v. — The original, archaic
meaning of this verb was *to put before'. It
derives fr. L. objectus, pp. of obicere (less
correctly, objicere), 'to throw or put before or
against', fr. ob- and jacere (pp. jactus), 'to
throw'; see jet, 'to spirt forth'. For the change
of Latin a (in jactus) to ё (in ab-jectus) see accent
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: object-or, n.

## object
object, n. — ME., fr. ML. objectum, lit.
'something thrown before', neut. of L. objectus, pp. of
obicere (see object, v.); prop, a loan translation
of Gk. πρόβλημα (see problem).
Derivatives: object-less, adj., object-less-ly, adv.,
object-less-ness, n.

## objectifies tion
objectifies tion, п., the act of objectifying; the state
of being objectified. — See next word and
-ation.

## objectify
objectify, tr. v., to make objective; to materialize.
— Compounded of object, п., and -fy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:533 COLUMN:1 -->

## objection
objection, η. — ME. objeccioun, fr. OF. (= F.)
objection, fr. Late L. objectionem, ace. of
objected, 'a throwing or putting before', fr. L. ob-
jectus, pp. of obicere. See object, v., and -ion.
Derivatives: objection-able, adj.,
objection-ability, п., objection-able-ness, п., objection-abl-y,
adv., objection-al, adj.

## objective
objective, adj. — ML» objectivus, fr. objectum,
'object'. See object, n. and v. and -ive.
Derivatives: objective-ly, adv., objective-ness, п.,
objectivism (q.v.), objectivity (q.v.)

## objective
objective, п., aim, purpose.—From objective, adj.

## objectivism
objectivism, п., the doctrine that knowledge is
based on objective reality (philos.) — See
objective, adj., and -ism.

## objectivity
objectivity, п., the quality or state of being
objective; objective reality. — Formed with suff.
-ity fr. ML. objectivus. See objective, adj.

## objurgate
objurgate, tr. v., to blame, reprove, chide. — L.
objurgaius, pp. of objiirgare, 'to blame, reprove',
fr. ob- and jurgdre, 'to quarrel, scold, chide',
contraction of earlier jurigare, formed horn jure
agere (a phrase occurring in Varro), lit. 'to deal
in a lawsuit'. L. jure is the abl. of jus, 'right, law,
suit'; see jury. For the etymology of L. agere,
'to set in motion, drive, lead; to do, act', see
agent, adj. For the formation of L. jurigare cp.
litigdre, 'to dispute, quarrel', which is formed
from the phase litem agere, 'to lead a dispute or
strife'; see litigate,

## objurgation
objurgation, п., blame, reproof. — L. objurgdtio,
gen. -ели, 'a chiding, reproving, reproof,
rebuke', fr. objurgaius, pp. of objiirgare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## objurgatory
objurgatory, adj., objurgating, reproachful. — L.
objurgdtorius, 'chiding, reproving,.reproachfuT,
fr. objurgaius, pp. of objiirgare. See objurgate
and adj. suff. -ory.
Derivative: objurgatori-ly, adv.

## oblanceolate
oblanceolate, adj., lance-shaped (bot.) — Formed
fr. ob- and lanceolate,

## oblate
oblate, adj., dedicated to monastic life. — L.
obldtus (used as pp. of offerre, 'to bring before,
to offer'), fr. ob- and latus, 'borne, carried' (used
as pp. of ferre, 'to bear, carry'), which stands
for *tldtos, fr. *//-, zero degree of I.-E. base
*tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence L. tollere, 'to
lift up, raise', tolerdre, 'to bear, support'. See
tolerate and cp. collate and words there referred
to.

## oblate
oblate, adj., flattened at the poles (geom.) —
MedL. obldtus, 'flattened', fr. ob- and L. -latus
in proldtus, 'lengthened'. See prec. word and
prolate.
Derivative: oblate, п., one dedicated to monastic
life.

## oblation
oblation, п., I) an offering, dedication; 2) a
donation — ME. oblacioun, fr. OF. (= F.) oblation,
fr. L. obldtidnem,-acc. of oblatio, 'an offering',
fr. obldtus. See oblate, adj., and suff. -ion.
Derivative: oblation-al, adj.

## oblatory
oblatory, adj., pertaining to an oblation. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. oblatus. See oblate,
adj.

## obligate
obligate, tr. v. — L. obligatus, pp. of obligare.
See oblige and verbal suff. -ate.

## obligation
obligation, n. — ME. obligacioun, fr. OF. (— F.)
obligation, fr. L. obligationem, ace. of obligdtio,
'a binding, obligation', fr. obligatus, pp. of
obligare. See oblige and -ation.

## obligate
obligate, adj. and n. — See obbligato.

## obligatory
obligatory, adj., compulsory. — Late L. obligato-
rius, 'binding', fr. L. obligatus, pp. of obligare.
See next word and adj. suff. -ory.
Derivatives: obligatori-ly, adv., obligatori-ness,
n.

## oblige
oblige, tr. v. — ME. obligen, fr. OF. obligier,
obliger (F. obliger), fr. L. obligare, 'to bind, put
under obligation, oblige', fr. ob- and ligdre, 'to
bind'. See ligament and cp. obbligato.
Derivatives: oblig-ed, adj., obligee (q.v.),
obliging, adj., oblig-ing-ly, adv., oblig-ing-ness, п.,
obligor (q.v.)

## obligee
obligee, п., a person to whom another is bound
by contract (law). — Formed fr. oblige with suff.
-ее.

## obligor
obligor, п., a person who binds himself to another
by contract (law). — Formed fr. oblige with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:533 COLUMN:2 -->
agential suff. -or.

## oblique
oblique, adj., 1) slanting, neither perpendicular
nor horizontal; 2) indirect. — ME. oblike,
fr. L. obliquus, 'slanting, sidelong, indirect'—
either directly or through the medium of F.
oblique. L. obliquus is formed fr. ob- and liquus,
'sloping,' which, together with liquis, 'sloping',
prob. derives fr. I.-E. *leiq-, a -^-enlargement of
base *lii-, 'to bend, be movable', whence prob.
limus, 'aslant, sidelong', limen, 'threshold' (orig.
'a crosspiece'). See limb and cp. limit, Limulus,
litous, lay figure. Cp. also the second element in
drill, 'twilled cotton', trellis, twill.
Derivatives: oblique, intr. v., oblique-ly, adv.,
oblique-ness, n.

## obliquity
obliquity, п., state or quality of being oblique. —
ME. obliquitee, fr. MF. (= F.) obliquite, fr. L.
obliquitdtem, ace. of obliquitds, 'slanting
direction, obliquity', fr. obliquus. See prec. word and
-ity.

## obliterate
obliterate, tr. v., to blot out; to wipe out, efface.
— L. oblitteratus (obliterans), pp. of oblitterdre
(obliterare), 'to blot out, erase', fr. ob- and littera
(litera), 'letter'. See letter and verbal suff. -ate
and cp. alliteration.

## obliteration
obliteration, п., — L. oblitterdtio (obliterdtid),
gen. -onis, fr. oblitteratus (obliterdtus), pp. of
oblitterare (obliterare). See prec. word and -ion.

## oblivial
oblivial, adj., pertaining to, or causing, oblivion.
— See next word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: oblivial-ity, n.

## oblivion
oblivion, п., the act of forgetting; the state of being
forgotten; the overfcoking of offenses; amnesty.
— ME., fr. MF., fr. L. оЫЫбпет, асе. of
oblivio, 'forgetfulness, oblivion', fr. oblivisci(pp.
oblttus), 'to forget', prob. meaning orig. 'to have
something (in one's memory) effaced', and rel.
to linere, 'to daub, besmear, rub out, erase',
oblinere, 'to rub out, efface', levis, 'smooth,
smoothed', and cogn. with Gk. aXtvecv (Hesy-
chius), 'to anoint, besmear'. See slime and cp.
lime, 'birdlime'.

## oblivious
oblivious, adj., forgetful, unmindful. — L. obll-
viosus, 'forgetful', fr. oblivio, 'forgetfulness'. See
prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: oblivious-ly, adv. oblivious-ness, n.

## obliviscence
obliviscence, п., forgetfulness. — Formed with
suff. -ce fr. L. obliviscens, gen. -entis, pres. part,
of oblivisci, 'to forget'. See oblivion.

## obliviscible
obliviscible, adj., that can be forgotten. —
Formed with suff. -ible fr. L. oblivisci, 'to forget'. See
oblivion.

## oblong
oblong, adj., more long than broad, elongated;
specif, rectangular with the adjacent sides
unequal.— ME. oblonge, fr. L. oblongus, 'longish,
rather long', later used also in the sense 'oblong',
fr. ob- and longus 'long'. See long, adj.
Derivative: oblong, п., an oblong figure.

## obloquy
obloquy, п., abuse, calumny; disgrace. — Late L.
obloquium, 'contradiction', fr. ob- and L. loqui,
'to speak'. See loquacious.

## obmutescence
obmutescence, п., a becoming silent (rare) —
Formed with suff. -ce fr. L. obmutescens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of obmute'scere, 'to become
dumb, be speechless', an inchoative verb formed
fr. ob- and tnutus, 'dumb, mute'. See mute and
-escence.

## obmutescent
obmutescent, adj., dumb, silent. — L. obmutescens,
gen. -entis. See prec. word and -ent.

## obnoxious
obnoxious, adj., 1) objectionable, offensive; 2)
(archaic) a) liable to injury; b) liable to censure;
3) (law) responsible. — L. obnoxiosus, 'hurtful,
injurious', fr. obnoxius, 'liable or exposed to
punishment, injury or danger', fr. ob- and noxa,
'harm, injury'. See noxious.
Derivatives: obnoxious-ly, adv., obnoxious-ness,
n.

## oboe
oboe, п., a musical double-reed woodwind
instrument. — It., fr. It. spelling of F. hautbois. See
hautboy.

## oboist
oboist, п., one who plays an oboe. — A hybrid
coined fr. oboe and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## obol
obol, п., a small ancient Greek coin and weight,
1/6 drachma. — L. obolus, fr. Gk. όβολός, orig.
identical with οβελός, 'a spit, needle'; ancient
Greek coins often had the form of metal nails
and needles. See obelus.

## Obolaria
Obolaria, п., a genus of plants, the pennyworth

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:533 COLUMN:3 -->
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. άβολος, 'a small Greek
coin' (see obol); so called in allusion to the
thick coin-shaped leaves.

## obolus
obolus, n. — See obol.

## obreption
obreption, п., the obtaining of something by fraud
(Canon and Scot. law). — ~L.obreptio, gen.-onis, 'a
creeping or stealing on, deceiving', fr. obreptus,
pp. of obripere, 'to creep or steal on, to deceive',
fr. ob- and rapere, 'to seize, snatch'. See rape, 'to
seize', and -ion and cp. subreption. For the
change of Latin a (in rdpere) to i (in ob-riptus)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.

## obreptitious
obreptitious, adj., characterized by obreption. —
Late L. obrepticius, fr. L.obreptus, pp. ofobripere.
See prec. word and -itious and cp. surreptitious.

## obscene
obscene, adj., 1) offensive; indecent; 2) disgusting.
— MF. obscene (F. obscene), fr. L. obscaenus,
obscenus, 'inauspicious, ill-boding; repulsive,
filthy, disgusting', of uncertain origin; pern.
formed fr. obs- — ob- (see ob-) and caenum, 'dirt,
filth, mud, mire', which is possibly rel. to cuntre,
'to defecate', in-quinare, 'to defile, pollute'. See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, 131-32 s.v. caenum.
Cp. cienaga, inquinate.
Derivatives: obscene-ly, adv., obscene-ness, n.

## obscenity
obscenity, n. — F. obscenite, fr. L. obscaenitatem,
ace. oiobscaenitds, 'inauspiciousness, filthiness',
fr. obscaenus. See prec. word and -ity.

## obscurant
obscurant, п., one who obscures; specif., one who
opposes enlightenment. — F., fr. L. obscuran-
tem, ace. of obscurdns, pres. part, of obscurdre.
See obscure, v., and -ant.

## ohscurant
ohscurant, adj., 1) obscuring; 2) pertaining to an
obscurant. — See obscurant, n.

## obscurantism
obscurantism, п., opposition to enlightenment. —
See obscurant, п., and -ism.

## obscurantist
obscurantist, п., an advocate of obscurantism,
an obscurant. — See obscurant, п., and -ist.

## obscuration
obscuration, n. — ME., fr. L. obscurdtio, gen.
-onis, 'a darkening, obscuring', fr. obscuratus,
pp. of obscurdre. See obscure, v., and -ation.

## obscure
obscure, adj., dark, gloomy; not clear, indistinct,
vague; difficult to understand. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) obscur, fr. L. obscurus, 'dark, dusky;
indistinct, uncertain, unintelligible', orig.
'covered', formed fr. ob- and I.-E. base *(s)qeu-,
*(s)qewd-, 'to cover', whence also L. scutum,
'shield', ON. sky, OE. sceo, OS. skio, 'cloud'. See
sky and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
the second element in chiaroscuro.
Derivatives: obscure, п., obscure, v. (q.v.), ob-
scure-ly, adv., obscure-ness, n.

## obscure
obscure, tr. v. — Fr. F. obscurer, fr. L. obscurdre,
'to make dark, to darken, obscure', fr. obscurus;
partly directly fr. obscure, adj. (q.v.)

## obscurity
obscurity, n. — OF. obscurite (= F. obscurite),
fr. L. obscuritdtem, ace. of obscuritds,
'darkness; indistinctness, uncertainty', fr. obscufus.
See obscure, adj., and -ity.

## obsecrate
obsecrate, tr. v., to entreat, implore (archaic) —
L. obsecrdtus, pp. of obsecrdre, 'to beseech,
entreat (on religious grounds)', fr. ob- and sacrdre,
'to make or declare sacred', fr. sacer, 'holy,
sacred'. See sacred and verbal suff. -ate. For the
change of Latin δ (in sacer) to ё (in ob-secrdre)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.

## obsecration
obsecration, п., supplication, entreaty. — L. ob-
secrdtio, gen. -dnis, 'supplication, entreaty', fr.
obsecrdtus, pp. οι obsecrdre. See prec. word and
-ion.

## obsequies
obsequies, n. pi., of obsol. obsequy, funeral rites.
— ME. obsequie, obseque, fr. OF. obseque, ob-
sequie, fr. ML. obsequiae, which was influenced
in meaning by a confusion of L. obsequium,
'compliance', with exsequiae, 'funeral rites'. See
obsequious.
Derivative: obsequi-al, adj.

## obsequious
obsequious, adj., excessively complying; cringing;
