fawning. — L. obsequiosus, 'complying,
complaisant', fr. obsequium, 'compliance,
complaisance', ir.obsequi, 'to accommodate oneself to the
will of another, to comply with, submit to'; fr.
ob- and sequi, 'to follow'. See sequel and cp. prec.
word.
Derivatives: obsequious-ly, adv.,
obsequiousness, n.

## observable
observable, adj. — L. observabilis, 'remarkable,
observable', fr. observare. See observe and -able.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:534 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 507 | DCCIDENT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:534 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: observable-ness, п., observabl-y,
adv.

## observance
observance, n. — ME. observaunce, fr. OF. (= F.)
observance, fr. L. observantia, 'attention, regard,
observance', fr. observdns, gen. -amis. See next
word and -ce.

## observant
observant, adj. — ME., fr. L. observantem, ace. of
observdns, pres. part, of observare, 4to watch,
heed, note, observe'. See observe and -ant.
Derivatives: observant-ly, adv., observant-ness,
n.

## Observant
Observant, п., a member of a Franciscan order
called the Friars Observant. — Fr. observant, adj.

## observation
observation, n. — Late ME. observacioun, fr. L.
observation gen. -dnis, 'a watching, observing;
remark, observation; precept, rule; regard,
respect', fr. observdtus, pp. of observare. See
observe and -ion.
Derivatives: observation-al, adj.,
observation-ally, adv.
observatory* п., a building for observing natural,
esp. astronomical, phenomena. — F. observa-
toire, fr. observer. See next word and subst.
suff. -ory.

## observe
observe, tr. and intr. v. — ME. observen, fr. OF.
(= F.) observer, fr. L. observare, 'to watch,
regard', fr. ob- and servdre, 'to save, deliver,
preserve, protect'. See cooserve.
Derivatives: observ-er, п., observ-ing, adj., ob-
serv-ing-ly, adv.

## obsess
obsess, tr. v., to hunt, trouble, harass. — L. ob-
sessus, pp. of obsidere, 'to sit at, hunt, besiege1,
and fr. ob- and sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: obsess-ive, adj., obsess-or, n.

## obsession
obsession, n. — L. obsessid, gen. -dnis, 'siege', fr.
obsessus, pp. of obsidere, 'to besiege'. See prec.
word and -ion.
Derivative: obsession-al, adj.

## obsidian
obsidian, п., a dark, very hard vitreous volcanic
rock (petrogr.) — L. Obsididnus lapis, 'the stone
of Obsidius', an erroneous reading in Pliny for
Obsius lapis, 'stone of Obsius\ so named after
Obsius, who discovered it in Ethiopia.

## obsolescence
obsolescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## obsolescent
obsolescent, adj. — L. obsolescens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of obsolescere, 'to wear out, grow
old, fall into disuse', rel. to exolescere, 'to grow
out, to grow out of use, become obsolete', and
prob. in gradational relationship to alere, 'to
nourish'; see aliment. L. obsolescere was
influenced both in form and sense by solere, 'to be
accustomed', to which it is not related. (The
confusion of exolescere and obsolescere with
solere was prob. suggested by a misdivision of
exolescere into *ec-solescere. See Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW., I, 427-428 sv. exolisco. For the
suff. in obsolescent see -escent.

## obsolete
obsolete, adj. — L. obsoletus, pp.. of obsolescere.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: obsolete-ly, adv., obsolete-ness, n.

## obstacle
obstacle, п., a hindrance, impediment. — ME.,
fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. obstdculum, 'a hindrance,
obstacle', standing for *obstd-t!om, which was
formed with instrumental suff. *~tlomfr.obstare,
'to hinder, thwart', lit. 'to stand in the way of '„
fr. ob- and stare, 'to stand'. See state and cp.
obstetric, obstinate.

## obstetric
obstetric, obstetrical, adj., pertaining to
midwifery. — ModL. obstetrJcus, for L. obstetricius,
'pertaining to a midwife', fr. obstetrix, gen.
obstetricis, 'midwife', lit. 'she who stands
before', fr. ob- and stare, 'to stand'. See state and
cp. prec. word.

## obstetrician
obstetrician, п., a physician specialized in
midwifery; accoucheur. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. obstetricia, 'midwifery', fr. obstetricus. See
prec. word.

## obstetrics
obstetrics, п., the science of midwifery. — See
obstetric and -ics.

## obstinacy
obstinacy,.n. — ML. obstinatia, fr. L. obstindtus.
See obstinate and -cy.

## obstinate
obstinate, adj. — ME. obstinat, fr. L. obstindtus,
'resolute, inflexible, stubborn', pp. of obstindret
4o set one's mind firmly on, to persist in', which
stands for *ob-stan-dre, fr. ob- and *sta-n, -n-
enlargement of I.-E. base *ste-, *std-, 'to stand*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:534 COLUMN:2 -->
See state and adj. suflf. -ate and cp. destine. For
the change of Latin a (in *standre) to Ϊ (in ob-
stindre) see abigeat and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: obstinate-ly, adv., obstinate-ness, n.

## obstipation
obstipation, п., severe constipation. — Late L.
obstipdtid, gen. -dnis, 'close pressure*, fr. ob- and
L. stipdre, 'to press together, stuff, cram'. See
stipate and -ion and cp. constipation.

## obstreperous
obstreperous, adj., noisy, clamorous, turbulent,
unruly. — L. obstreperus, 'clamorous', fr. ob-
strepere, 'to cry out against', fr. ob- and strepere,
'to make a noise, rattle, roar', which is of
imitative origin, Cp. L. stertdre, 'to snore', and
ON. prapt, 'chattering, garrulity', Icel. pre/a,
'to quarrel', OE. prxft, 'quarrel', which all are
imitative; see stertorous and cp. strepitous. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: obstreperous-ly, adv., obstreperous-
ness, n.

## obstruct
obstruct, tr. v., 1) to block, bar; 2) to hinder,
impede. — L. obstructust pp. of obstruere, 'to build
up, wall up; to bar, render impassable', lit. 'to
build against', fr. ob- and struere, *to build': See
structure and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: obstruct-er, п., obstruction (q.v.),
obstruct-ive, adj., obstruct-ive-ly, adv., obstruct-
ive-ness, n.

## obstruction
obstruction, n, — L. obslructio, gen. -dnis, 'a
building up', fr. obstructus, pp. of obstruere. See
prec. word and -ion.

## obstructionism
obstructionism, п., system of obstructing business,
as in Parliament. — Formed from prec. word
with suff. -ism.

## obstructionist
obstructionist, п., one who practices obstruction,
as in Parliamentary business. — Formed fr.
obstruction with suff. -ist.

## obstruent
obstruent, adj., obstructing, causing
obstruction; п., something that obstructs. — L. ob-
struens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of obstruere, 'to
build up'. See obstruct and -ent.

## obtain
obtain, tr. and intr. v. — Late ME. obteinen, fr.
MF. (= F.) obtenir, fr. VL. *obtenire, which
corresponds to L. obtinere, 'to take hold of,
hold, obtain', fr. ob- and tenure, 'to hold'. See
tenable and cp. abstain and words there referred
to.
Derivatives: obwin-able- adj., obtain-er, п., ob-
tain-mem, n.

## obtected
obtected, adj., covered with a hard outer shell
(said of the pupae of certain insects) — Formed
with 1st sufT. -ed fr. L. obtectus, pp. of obtegere,
Ίο cover up, cover over', fr. ob- and tegere, 'to
cover'. See tegument.

## obtest
obtest, v., 1) to call to witness (archaic); 2) to
beseech; to beg for. — L. obtestdrl, 'to call to
witness; to entreat, beseech, supplicate', fr. ob-
and tesrdri, 'to bear witness', fr. testis, 'witness'.
See testament and cp. words there referred to.

## obtestation
obtestation, п., supplication. — L. obtestdtio, gen.
-dnis, 'earnest entreaty, supplication', fr. ob-
testdtus, pp. of obtestdn. See prec. word and
-ation.

## obtrude
obtrude, ir. v., to thrust forward; to force upon;
intr. v., to intrude. — L. obtrudere, 'to thrust
against, push forward', fr. ob- and trudere, 'to
thrust, push, shove', fr. I.-E. base *treud-, 'to
press, push', whence also Goth, us-priutan, 'to
vex', OE. preotan, 'to press, afflict, threaten'.
See threat, and cp. thrust. Cp. also intrude and
words there referred to.

## obtruncate
obtruncate, tr. v., to cut the head or top from. —
L. obtrunedtus, pp. of obtruncdre, 'to cut off, lop
off', fr. ob- and truncdre, 'to cut off', fr. truncus,
'trunk'. See truncate, v.

## obtrusion
obtrusion, n. — Late L. obtrusio, gen. -onis, 'a
thrusting against', fr. L. obtrus-(um), pp. stem
of obtrudere. See obtrude and -ion and cp.
intrusion and words there referred to.

## obtrusive
obtrusive, adi. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
obtrusus, pp. of obtrudere. See obtrude and cp.
extrusive, intrusive, protrusive.
Derivatives: obtrusive-ly, adv., obtrusive-ness, n.

## obtund
obtund, tr. v., to blunt (obsol.) — ME. obtunden,

## fr. L. obtundere (pp. obtusus) 'to beat against'
fr. L. obtundere (pp. obtusus) 'to beat against',
fr. ob- and tundere, 'to beat'. See obtuse and cp.
retund.

## obturate
obturate, tr. v., 1) to close or stop (an opening);

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:534 COLUMN:3 -->
2) to close (the breech of a gun). — L. obturdtus,
pp. of obturare, 'to stop, close', fr. ob- and I.-E.
*iu-ros, 'made into a ball, compressed', fr. base
*teu-, *tu-, 'to swell, swollen', whence also tu-
me~re, 'to swell', tumidus, 'swollen'. See tumid
and verbal suff. -ate.

## obturation
obturation, n. — L. obturdtid, gen. -onis, 'a
stopping, closing', fr. obturdtus, pp. of obturare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## obturator
obturator, п., that which closes or stops an
opening; specif, a device for closing the breech of a
gun. — ModL. obturator, fr. L. obturdtus, pp. of
obturare. See obturate and agential suff. -or.

## obturator foramen
obturator foramen, a hole between the pubic and
ischial parts of the innominate bone, hipbone
(anat.) — Alteration of L·. foramen obturdtdrium,
a term coined by the anatomist Loder. The name
is erroneous. It lit. means 'the obstructing hole',
which is a contradiction in itself.The name should
be foramen obturatum, 'the obstructed hole'. See
Joseph Hynl, Onomatologia anatomica, p. 223.
For etymology see obturator and foramen.

## obtuse
obtuse, adj., 1) not pointed, blunt; 2) dull — L.
obtusus, 'blunted', pp. of obtundere, 'to beat
against, to blunt', fr. ob- and tundere, 'to beat,
strike, stump', which is re], to tudes, gen. -ditis,
'hammer', and cogn. with Ol. tudati, tundate,
'he thrusts', fr. I.-E. base *(s)tud-, 'to beat, strike
push, thrust'. See stint and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: obtuse-ly, adv., obtuse-ness, n.

## obverse
obverse, adj., turned toward the observer. — L.
obversus, pp. of obvertere, 'to turn toward', fr.
ob- and vertere, 'to turn'. See version and cp.
obvert.
Derivatives: obverse, п., obverse-ly, adv.

## obversion
obversion, п., the act of obverting. — Late L. ob-
versid, gen. -dnis, 'a turning toward', fr. L.
obversus, pp. of obvertere. See prec. word and -ion.

## obvert
obvert, tr. v. — L. obvertere. See obverse.

## obviate
obviate, tr. v., to prevent; to make unnecessary.
— L. obvidtus, pp. of obvidre, 'to meet; to
prevent, hinder', lit. 'to go toward', fr. ob- and via,
'way'. See via and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## obvious
obvious, adj., clear, manifest, evident. — L. ob-
vius, 'lying in the way', hence 'at hand, obvious*,
fr. ob- and via, 'way'. See via. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: obvious-ly, adv., obvious-ness, n.

## obvolute
obvolute, adj., overlapping; specif, used of leaves
with overlapping margins (bot.) — L. obvolutus,
pp. of obvolvere, 'to wrap round', fr. ob- and
vo/vere, 'to wrap'. See volute.

## oc-
oc-, assimilated form of ob- before с

## ocarina
ocarina, п., a small wind instrument with finger-
holes and a whistle mouthpiece. — It., dimin. of
oca, 'goose', fr. VL. *auca, 'goose', whence also
OProvenc. auca, OF. oue, oe, F. oie, 'goose'. VL.
*auca is a contraction of *avica, back formation
of L. avicula, dimin. of avis, 'bird'. See aviary
and cp. the second element in pettitoes. For the
sense development of VL. *auca, 'goose', fr. L.
avis, 'bird', cp. Gk. ΰρνις (masc. от Jem.), 'bird',
(masc.) 'cock'; (fern.) 'hen', ModGk. SpvL^ot,
'hen'. The instrument was called ocarina (lit. 'a
goose pipe') in allusion to its shape.

## occasion
occasion, n. — Late ME. occasioun, fr. OF. ( =
F.) occasion, fr. L. ocedsidnem, ace. of occasid,
'fit time, opportunity, occasion', fr. ocedsus, pp.
oioccidere, 'to fall down, fall', fr. ob- and cadere,
'to fall'. See cadence and -ion and cp. Occident.
Derivatives: occasion-al, adj., occasionalism
(q.v.), occasion-al-ity, п., occasional-ly, adv.

## occasion
occasion, tr. v. — F. occasionner, fr. occasion. See
occasion, n.

## occasionalism
occasionalism, п., the Cartesian doctrine of
occasional causes (phi/os.) — See occasion, п., and
-ism.

## Occident
Occident, п., the west; (cap.) the western countries.
— ME., fr. MF. (=. F), fr. L. occidentem, ace.
of occidens, 'quarter of the setting sun, the west',
prop, subst. use of pres. part, of oc-cidere, 'to
fall down, to set (said of the sun)', fr. ob- and
cadere, 'to fall'; see cadence and -ent and cp.
occasion, n. For the change of Latin d (in cadere)
to i (in oc-cidere) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:535 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OCCIDENTAL | 508 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:535 COLUMN:1 -->

## occidental
occidental, adj., 1) western; 2) (cap.) pertaining to
the western countries. — F. occidental, fr. L. oc-
cidentdlis, 'western', fr. occidens, 'west'. Seeprec.
word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: Occidental, п., a native of the
Occident, occidentat-ty, adv.

## Occidentalism
Occidentalism, п., occidental character. —
Formed from prec. word with suff. -ism.
Occidentalism п., an advocate of Occidentalism.
— See occidental and -1st.

## Occidentalize
Occidentalize, tr. v., to render Occidental. — See
occidental and -ize.

## occipit-
occipit-, form of occipitor before a vowel.

## occipital
occipital, adj., pertaining to the occiput or the
occipital bone. — ML. occipitalis, fr. L. occiput,
gen. occipitis. See occiput and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: occipital, п., the occipital bone.

## occipito-
occipito-, before a vowel occipit-, combining form
meaning: 1) occiput; 2) occipital and. — Fr. L.
occiput, gen. -itis. See next word.

## occiput
occiput, п., the back of the head (anal.) — L.
occiput (gen. occipitis), 'the back of the head', fr.
ob- and caput, 'head'. See capital, adj., and cp.
sinciput. For the change of Latin d (in caput) to
i(in oc-cipui) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

## occlnde
occlnde, tr. v., to shut in, to shut out. — L. oc-
cludere, (pp. occlusus), 'to shut up, close up', fr.
ob- and claudere, 'to shut, close'. See close, adj.
For the change of Latin au (in claudere) to й (in
oc-cludere) see accuse and cp. words there
referred to.

## occlusion
occlusion, п., the act of occluding; the state of
being occluded. — ML. occlusio, gen. -onis, fr.
L. occtusus, pp. of occludere. Seeprec. word and
-ion.

## occlusive
occlusive, adj., tending to occlude. — Formed
with suff. -ive fr. L. occlusus, pp. of occludere.
See occlude.

## occult
occult, adj., 1) hiddeo, concealed; 2) mysterious,
mystical. — L. occultus, 'hidden, concealed,
secret', pp. οι occulere, 'to cover up, hide, conceal',
fr. ob- and *celere, fr. I.-E. base *£e/-, 'to hide,
cover', whence also L. cgtdre, 'to hide'. See cell
and words there referred to and cp. esp. conceal.
Derivatives: occult, п., occultism (q.v.), occultist
(q.v.), occult-ly, adv., occult-ness, n.

## occult
occult, tr. v., to hide; specif, to hide by
occupation (astron.); intr. v., to be hidden. — L. oc-
cultare, freq. of occulere (pp. occultus), 'to hide'.
See occult, adj.

## occultation
occultation, п., hiding, concealment; specif, the
concealment or eclipse of one heavenly body
behind another (astron) — L. occultatio, gen.
-onis, 'a hiding, concealing, concealment', fr.
occultdtus, pp. of occultdre, freq. of occulere.
See occult, v., and -ation.

## occultism
occultism, п., 1) belief in occult forces; 2) the
study of occult arts. — See occult, adj., and -ism.

## occultist
occultist, п., one who believes in occultism. —
A hybrid coined fr. L. occultus, 'hidden,
concealed, secret' (see occult, adj.), and -ist, a suff.
of Greek origin.

## occupancy
occupancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## occupant
occupant, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. OF., fr. L. occu-
pantem, ace. aioccupans, pres. part, of occupare,
'to take possession of. See occupy and -ant,

## occupation
occupation, n. — F. occupation, fr. L. occupatio-
nem, ace. of occupatio, *a seizing, taking
possession of, fr. occupdtus, pp. of occupare. See
next word and -ion.
Derivative: occupation-al, adj.

## occupy
occupy, tr. v. — ME. occupien, fr. MF. (= F.)
occuper, fr. L. occupare, 'to seize, take
possession of, to possess', fr. ob- and capere, 'to catch,
seize, take hold'. See captive.
Derivative: occupi-er, n.

## occur
occur, intr. v. — MF. occurrer, fr. L. occurrere,
'to run toward, to meet; to present itself,
suggest itself, fr. ob- and currere, 'to run'. See
current, adj.

## occurrence
occurrence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## occurrent
occurrent, adj., occurring (rare) — F., fr. L. oc-
currentem, ace. of occurrens, pres. part, of
occurrere. See occur and -ent.
Derivative: occurrent, п., something that occurs.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:535 COLUMN:2 -->

## ocean
ocean, n. — F. ocean, fr. L. oceanus, fr. Gk.
ωκεανός, 'the great river encompassing the whole
earth'; hence 'the great Outward Sea' (opposed
to the Inward or Mediterranean), which is of
uncertain etymology. Derivative: ocean-ic, adj.

## Oceania
Oceania, п., collective name for the Central and
Western Pacific and its islands. — See prec.
word and 1st -la. Derivative: Oceani-an, adj.

## Oceanid
Oceanid, п., a daughter of Oceanus; an ocean
nymph (Greek mythol.) — Gk. Ώκεαυίς, gen.
Ώκεανίδος, fr. Ωκεανός 'Oceanus'. See
Oceanus.

## oceanography
oceanography, п., that branch of geography which
deals with the ocean. — Formed on analogy of
geography fr. Gk. ωκεανός, 'ocean', and
-γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See ocean and
-graphy.
Derivatives: oceanograph-er, п., oceanograph-ic,
oceanograph-ic-al, adjs.

## Oceanus
Oceanus, п., 1) son of Uranus and Gaia, god of
the sea before Poseidon; 2) the immense stream
supposed to encompass the whole earth (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. 'Ωκεανός,
personification of ωκεανός, 'the great river encompassing
the whole earth'. See ocean.

## ocellate
ocellate, ocellated, adj., having ocelli (zool.) — L.
ocellatus, 'having little eyes', fr. ocellus, 'little
eye'. See next word and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also
Ist -ed.

## ocellus
ocellus, п., 1) a little eye; 2) the rudimentary eye
of certain invertebrates; 3) an eyelike spot (as
on the feather of a peacock). — L., dimin. of
oculus, 'eye'. See ocular.

## ocelot
ocelot, п., a large wild cat of Central and South
America. — F., formed by the French naturalist
Comte Georges-Louis Leclerc de Buffon (1707-
1788) fr. Nahuatl ocelotl, 'jaguar'.

## ocher
ocher, ochre, п., an earthy iron oxid, of light
yellow or brownish color, used as a pigment. —
Late ME., fr. F. ocrf, fr. Late L. ochra, fr. Gk.
ώχρα, 'yellow ocher', fr. ωχρός, 'pale, pale
yellow, yellow', a word of uncertain origin. Cp.
the second element in Melanochroi and in
Xantochroi. Derivatives: ocher, ochre, tr. v.,
ocher-ish, ocher-ous, ocher-y, adjs.

## ochlocracy
ochlocracy, п., government by the mob; mob
rule. — F. ochlocratie, fr. Gk. δχλοκρατία,
'mob rule', which is compounded of δχλος,
'populace, mob' which is perh. rel. to όχεϊν
(for *ίοχεϊν), 'to carry', and cogn. with L.
vehere, 'to carry' (see vehicle), and -κρατίϋ,
'rule of, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'.
See -cracy.

## ochlocrat
ochlocrat, п., an advocate of ochlocracy. — See
prec. word and combining form -crat.

## ochlocratie
ochlocratie, adj., pertaining to ochlocracy. — See
ochlocracy and adj. suff. -ic.

## ochre
ochre, n. — See ocher.

## ochroid
ochroid, adj., resembling ocher; of a pale yellow
color. — Gk. ώχροειδής, 'like ocher, pale, pale
yellow', fr. ωχρός, 'pale, pale yellow, yellow',
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape*. See
ocher and -oid.

## ocimene
ocimene, п., an open-chain terpene
hydrocarbon, C10Hle, obtained from Ocimum basilicum
(chem.) — Formed fr. ModL. Ocimum (see next
word) and suff. -ene.

## Ocimum
Ocimum, п., a genus of mites (hot.) — ModL.
Ocimum, fr. L. ocimum, 'basil', fr. Gk. ώκιμον,
'basil', which is prob. rel. to άκινος, 'wildbasil',
fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp' (see acrid), and is so
called from the pungent smell.

## -ock
-ock, dimin. suff. — ME. -ok, fr. OE. -oc, -uc.
o'clock. — For of the clock. See o' and Clock.

## ocotillo
ocotillo, п., a Mexican pine. — Мех. Sp., dimin.
of ocote, 'Mexican pine', fr. Nahuatl ocoil.

## ocrea
ocrea, п., a tubelike sheath around a stem (bot.)
— L., 'a legging, greave', prob. meaning lit.
'something sharp-edged', and rel. to ocris, 'a
rugged, stony mountain', deer, 'sharp'. See acrid
and words there referred to and cp. esp. the
second element in mediocre.

## ocreate
ocreate, adj., having an ocrea. — Formed fr.
prec. word with adj. suff. -ate.

## octa-
octa-, before a vowel oct-, combining form
meaning 'eight'. — Gk. όκτα-, όκτ-, fr. οκτώ,
'eight', which is cogn. with L. octo, OI. astd,
astau, Goth, ahtau, OE. eahta, 'eight'; see eight.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:535 COLUMN:3 -->
The α in όκτα- is due to the analogy of επτά,
'seven', εννέα, 'nine', δέκα, 'ten'. Cp. penta-
and hexa-.

## octachord
octachord, п., 1) a musical instrument with eight
strings; 2) an octave. — Gk. οκτάχορδος,
'having eight strings', compounded of όκτα-
(see octa-) and χορδή, 'string'. See chord.
Derivative: octachord-al, adj.

## octad
octad, п., I) a series of eight numbers (math.);
2) an atom or radical with the valency of eight
(chem.) — Gk. οκτάς, gen. οκτάδος, 'the
number eight', fr. οκτώ. See octa- and -ad and
cp. ogdoad..

## octagon
octagon, п., л plain figure with eight angles and
eight sides (geom.) — L. octagonos, fr. Gk.
οκτάγωνος, 'eight-angled', which is compounded of
όκτα- (see octa-) and -γωνος, from the stem
of γωνία, 'angle'. See-gon.
Derivatives: octagon-al, adj., octagon-al-ly, adv.

## octahedral
octahedral, adj., having the form of an
octahedron. — See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## octahedron
octahedron, п., a solid figure with eight plane
faces (geom.) — Gk. όκτάεδρον, neut. of the
adjective όκτάεδρος, 'eight-sided', compounded
of όκτα- (see octa-) and εδρϊ, 'seat'. See -he-
dron.

## octamerous
octamerous, adj., consisting of eight parts in
each whorl (bot.) — Compounded of octa- and
Gk. μέρος, 'part'. See -merous.

## octameter
octameter, adj., having eight metrical feet (pros.)
— L., fr. Gk. όκτάμετρος, 'having eight
measures', which is compounded of όκτα- (see octa-)
and μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## octameter
octameter, п., a verse of eight metrical feet (pros.)
— See octameter, adj.

## octan
octan, adj., recurring every eighth day. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. octo, 'eight'. See octa-,

## octane
octane, п., a hydrocarbon of the methane series
CSH18 (chem.) — Coined fr. oct- and -ane.

## octangular
octangular, adj., having eight angles. — Formed
with suff. -ar fr. L. octangulus, 'eight-cornered',
fr. octo, 'eight', and angulus, 'corner'. See
octa- and angle and cp. angular.

## octant
octant, п., 1) the eighth part of a circle; an angle
or arc of 45° (geom.); 2) the position of one
heavenly body whenitis45° distant fromanother
(astron.); an instrument with an arc of 45 °, used
for measuring angles (opt.) — Late L. octdns,
gen. -amis, 'the eighth part', formed on analogy
of L. quadrdns (see quadrant) fr. odd, 'eight'.
See octa-.

## octarchy
octarchy, п., a government by eight rulers. —
Compounded of oct- and -αρχία, 'rule of, fr.
άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See -archy.

## octastich
octastich, п., a stanza or poem consisting of
eight verses. — Gk. όκτάστίχος, Of eight lines',
compounded of όκτα- (see octa-) and στίχος,
'row, line, rank; verse'; see stichic and cp.
acrostic and words there referred to.

## octastyle
octastyle, adj., having eight columns in front. —
L. octastylos, fr. Gk. όκτάστϋλος, 'having eight
columns', which is compounded of όκτα- (see
octa-) and στϋλος, 'pillar, column'. See style,
'gnomon'.

## Octateuch
Octateuch, п., the first eight books of the Bible —
Eccles. L. octateuchus, fr. Gk. όκτάτευχος (scil.
βίβλος), 'a book consisting of eight volumes',
compounded of όκτα- (see octa-) and τεύχος,
'tool, implement', later 'book', which is rel. to
τύχειν, 'to make, construct, fashion'. See
Pentateuch and cp. Hexateuch, Heptateuch.

## octavalent
octavalent, adj., having a valence of eight (chem.)
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. οκτώ, 'eight' (see
octa-), and L. valens, pres. part, of valere, 'to
have power'. See -valent.

## octave
octave, п., 1) the eight days beginning with a
feast day; 2) a stanza of eight lines; esp. the
first eight lines of a sonnet; 3) a) the interval
between the first and eighth degree of a diatonic
scale; b) the eighth full tone above or below
any note (mus.); 4) an organ stop — F., fr. L.
octava (scil.pars), 'an eighth (part)', fern, of oc-
tdvus, 'eight', fr. octo, 'eight'. See octa- and cp.
ottava rima, utas.
Derivative: octav-al, adj.

## Octavia
Octavia, fem. PN. — L., fern, of Octdvius. See
next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:536 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 509 | ODONTOLITH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:536 COLUMN:1 -->

## Octavlus
Octavlus, masc. PN. — L., lit. 'the eighth born",
fr. octavus, 'eighth', fr. octo, 'eight'. See octa-
and cp. octave.

## octavo
octavo, п., 1) a book in which each sheet is
folded into eight leaves or sixteen pages; 2) the
size of such a book. — Fr. L. in octavo, 'in the
eighth', fr. in, 'in*, and octavus, 'eighth'. See in,
prep., and octave.

## octennial
octennial, adj., happening every eight years. —
Formed with adj. suff. -a] fr. L. octennium, 'a
period of eight years', fr. octo, 'eight', and
annus, 'year'. See octa- and annual. For the change
of Latin d (in annus) to i (in oct-ennium) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.

## octet
octet, also octette, п., 1) a group of eight; esp. the
first eight lines of a sonnet; 2) (mus.) a
composition for eight instruments or eight voices. —
Formed on analogy of duet fr. L. octo, 'eight'.
See octa-.

## octillion
octillion, п., 1) in the United States and France,
athou sand raised to the ninth power (i.e. 1
followed by 27 zeros); 2) in Great Britain and
Germany, a million raised to the eighth power
(i.e. 1 followed by 48 zeros). — F. octillion,
formed fr. L. octo, 'eight' (see octa-), on analogy
of million (q.v.) Cp. billion and words there
referred to.

## octo-
octo-, combining form meaning 'eight'. — Gk.
όκτω-, fr. οκτώ, 'eight'. See octa-.

## October
October, n. — L. October (mensis), lit. 'the eighth
month (of the Roman year)', fr. octo, 'eight';
see octa-. (The Roman year began with March;
cp. September, November, December).

## octodecimo
octodecimo, п., 1) a book in which each sheet is
folded into eighteen leaves; 2) the size of such a
book. — Fr. L. in octodecimo, 'in the eighteenth',
fr. in, 'in', and octodecimus, 'eighteenth', fr. oc-
todecim, 'eighteen', which is compounded of
octo, 'eight', and decern, 'ten'. See octa- and
decimal and cp. octavo.

## octogenarian
octogenarian, adj., eighty years old; between the
years 80 and 90; п., a person eighty years old or
between the years 80 and 90. — Formed with
suff. -an fr. L. octogenarius, 'consisting of
eighty', fr. octogeni, 'eighty each', which is rel.
to octoginta, 'eighty', fr. octo, 'eight*. See octa-.

## octonal
octonal, adj., octonary. — See next word and adj.
suff. -al.

## octonary
octonary, adj., pertaining to the number eight;
consisting of eight; п., a group of eight; esp. a
stanza of eight lines {pros.) — L. octdnarius,
'consisting of eight', fr. octoni, 'eight each', fr.
octo, 'eight'. See octa-.

## octopod
octopod, п., any animal pertaining to the Octo-
poda. — See octopus.
Derivatives: octopod-an, octopod-ous, adjs.

## Octopoda
Octopoda, n. pi., a suborder of mollusks (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. όκτώπους, gen. όκτώποδος,
'having eight feet'. See next word.

## octopus
octopus, 1) (cap.) a genus of the eight-armed
Cephalopoda; 2) any member of this genus. —
ModL., fr. Gk. όκτώπους, 'eight-footed', fr.
οκτώ, 'eight', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See
octo- and -pod and cp. prec. word.

## octoroon
octoroon, п., the offspring of a white and a
quadroon. — Formed on analogy of quadroon fr.
L. octd, 'eight' (see octa-); so called in allusion
to his having one eighth negro blood.

## octosyllabic
octosyllabic, adj., having eight syllables. —
Compounded of octo- and syllable.

## octosyllable
octosyllable, п., a word or line of eight syllables.
— Compounded of octo- and syllable.

## octroi
octroi, п., 1) a tax levied on goods entering a
town; 2) the office where such taxes are
collected; 3) the officials collecting them. — F., prop,
'grant, concession', fr. octroyer, 'to grant,
concede', fr. VL. *auctdrizare, fr. Late L. auctorare,
'to grant', fr. L. auctor, 'he that brings about,
master; one who becomes security for
something'. See author and cp. authorize.

## octuple
octuple, adj., eightfold. — L. octuplus, 'eightfold',
formed fr. octo, 'eight', and suff. -plus '-fold',
which is rel. to plicare, 'to fold'. See octa- and
ply, v.
Derivative: octuple, tr. v., to multiply by
eight.

## ocular
ocular, adj., pertaining to the eye or sight. — L.
ocularis, 'pertaining to the eye', fr. oculus, 'eye',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:536 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. I.-E. base *oqw-, 'to see', whence also Goth.
augo, OE. cage, 'eye'. See eye and cp. optic. Cp.
also ocellus, inoculate, inveigle, oeil-de-boeuf,
oeillade, and the second element in monocle,
monocular, binocular, antler.
Derivatives: ocular, п., eyepiece of an optical
instrument, ocutar-ty, adv.

## oculist
oculist, п., a physician specializing in the
treatment of eye diseases; an ophthalmologist. — F.
ocutiste, formed fr. L. oculus, 'eye', with suff.
-iste. See ocular and -ist.

## oculomotor
oculomotor, adj., moving the eyeball (anat.) —
Compounded of L. oculus, 'eye', and motor,
'mover*. See ocular and motor,

## od
od, п., a hypothetical force supposed to manifest
itself in magnetism, mesmerism, etc. — G. Od,
an invented word; coined by Baron Karl von
Reichenbach (1788-1869) in 1850. Cp. odyl.

## odal
odal, п., among the early Teutonic peoples,
uninterrupted possession of land (law) — ON.
Odal (whence also Swed. odal, Dan. odel), rel.
to OE. sedele, 'noble'. See atbeling and cp.
words there referred to.

## odalisque
odalisque, п., a female slave in an Oriental
harem. — F., fr. Turk, odalique, 'maidservant',
lit. 'chambermaid', fr. odah, 'chamber', and -lik,
a suff. expressing function. This suff. was
confused with the Greek suff. -isk(os), 'of the nature
of, belonging to', thus odalique became
odalisque.

## odd
odd, adj. — ME. odde, 'odd, unique', fr. ON.
oddi, 'point of land, angle, triangle*, whence
the meaning 'third number; odd number', rel.
to ON. oddr, 'point (of a weapon)', Dan. od,
•point', Swed. udd, 'point', udda, 'odd', OE. ord,
'point of a weapon; spear; source, beginning,
origin; chief, OS. ord, 'point', OFris. ord, 'point,
place', Du. oord, 'place, region, (holiday)
resort', OHG. ort, 'point (esp. of a weapon or a
tool), angle, edge, beginning', MHG. ort, 'point'
(esp. of a weapon or a tool'), G. Ort, 'place', fr.
Teut. base "uzda-; cogn. with Alb. ust, 'ear of
grain', Lith. us-nis, 'thistle'.
Derivatives: odd-ly, adv., oddity (q.v.), oddment
(q.v.), odd-ness, п., odds (q.v.)

## oddity
oddity, n. — A hybrid coined fr. odd and -ity, a
suff. derived fr. L. -itds.

## oddment
oddment, п., an odd piece, a remnant. — A
hybrid coined fr. odd and -ment, a suff. derived fr.
L. -mentum.

## odds
odds, n. pi., difference in favor of one as against
another, balance of advantage; advantage. —
From the adjective odd.

## ode
ode, п., 1) orig. a poem intended to be sung; 2) in
modern use, a lyric poem of exalted style. —
MF. (= F.), fr. Late L. ode, 6da, fr. Gk. ωδή,
contraction of άοιδή, 'song', rel. to άείίω, Ί
sing', which prob. stands for *ά(υ)-εί-δω and
is rel. to άη8ών [for *ά (υ) -η-δών], 'nightingale',
αύδή (for ά-υδή), 'voice, tone, sound', αύδχω
(for ά-υδάω), Ί talk, speak', and cogn. with OI.
vadati, 'speaks, utters, sings', Lith. vadinu, vadin-
ti, 'to call, name', OSlav. vada, 'slander,
calumny', OHG far-wasan, 'to deny'. Cp. Odeum and
the second element in comedy, epode, hymnode,
melody, monody, palinode, parody, psalmody,
prosody, rhapsody, terpodion, threnody, tragedy,

## -ode
-ode, suff. meaning 'like, something like', as in
argyrode, geode. — Gk. -ώδης (masc. and fern.),
-ωδές (леи/.), 'like', formed fr. combining
vowel-o- and είδος, 'form, shape', hence lit.
meaning 'of the same form or shape'. See -oid and cp.
the second element in Aleyrodes, Campodes,
collodion, Lithodes, Lygodium, plasmodinm.

## -ode
-ode, suff. meaning 'way'. — Fr. Gk. δδός, 'way,
path'. See odograph and cp. the second element
in anode, cathode.

## Odeum
Odeum, п., 1) a hall for musical performances in
ancient Greece and Rome; 2) in modern use, a
concert hall. — L. ddeum, fr. Gk. ώδεΐον, 'a
public building at Athens designed for musical
performances', fr. ωδή, 'song. See ode.

## odic
odic, adj., pertaining to an ode. — See ode and
adj. suff. -ic and cp. Gk. ωδικός, 'fond of
singing, musical'.

## odic
odic, adj., pertaining to an od. — Formed fr. od
with adj. suff. -ic.

## Odin
Odin, п., the chief deity of Norse mythology. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:536 COLUMN:3 -->
Dan., fr. ON. Odinn, rel. to OS. Wodan, OE.
Woden, OHG. Wuotan. See Woden and cp.
words there referred to.

## odious
odious, adj., hateful; disgusting. — ME., fr. MF.
odieus (F. odieux), fr. L. odidsus, 'hateful,
offensive, unpleasant', fr. odium. See odium.
Derivatives: odious-ly, adv., odious-ness, n.

## odium
odium, п., hatred, opprobrium, disgust. — L.
odium, 'hatred, offense, annoyance, disgust', rel.
to odt, ddisse, 'to hate', cogn. with Arm. ateam,
Ί hate', ateli, 'hateful, odious', ON. atatt, OE.
atol, 'dire, horrid, loathsome', perh. also with
Gk. όδύσσασθαι, 'to be grieved at, be angry at';
fr. I.-E. base *od-, 'to hate', which is perh. orig.
identical with *od-, 'to smell'. See odor and cp.
Odysseus. Cp. also noisome, annoy.

## Odobenus
Odobenus, п., the genus consisting of the
walruses (zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. οδών,
'tooth', and βαίνειν, 'to walk' (see odonto- and
base, n.); so called in allusion to the use of the
tusks in walking.

## Odocoileos
Odocoileos, п., a genus including various species
of deer (zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
οδών, 'tooth', and κοίλος, 'hollow'. Seeodonro-
and coelo-.

## odegraph
odegraph, п., an instrument recording the
distance traveled. — Compounded of Gk. οδός,
'way', and -γράφος, fr. ypatpciv, 'to write*. The
first element derives fr. I.-E. base *sed-, 'to go',
whence also OSlav. chodii, 'a walking, going',
choditi,'ta walk, go'.OI. δ-sad-, 'to go,approach',
ut-sad, 'to step aside, disappear', L. cedere
(for "ce-zdere), 'to go, go away, yield'. Cp. -ode,
'way', and anode, cathode, Diodia, electrode,
episode, exodus, hexode, method, parodos, period,
stomodeum, synod. I.-E. base *sed-, 'to go', is
identical with *sed-, 'to sit', the original sense
of the base having been 'to place (either the
seat in order to sit down, or the foot on the
ground in order to go)'. See sedentary and cp.
cede. For the second element see -graph. The
spelling odograph is prob. due to the influence
of next word (q.v.)

## odometer
odometer, п., an instrument attached to the wheel
of a vehicle for measuring the distance traveled.
— Gk. όδόμετρον, 'instrument for measuring
distance', compounded of οδός, 'way', and μέ-
τρον, 'measure'. For the first element see prec.
word,for thesecond see meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
The spelling odometer is due to the influence of
F. odometre.

## odont-
odont-, form of odonto- before a vowel.

## -odont
-odont, combining form meaning 'tooth or teeth',
as in lophodont, conodont. — From the stem of
Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-.

## odontalgia
odontalgia, п., toothache (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of odont- and Gk. -αλγίδ, fr.
Άλγος, 'pain'. See -algia.
Derivative: odontalg-ic, adj.

## odontiasis
odontiasis, п., teething. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
όδοντίασις, 'teething', formed fr. όδοντιόίν, 'to
cut teeth', fr. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth*. See
odonto- and -iasis.

## odontic
odontic, adj., pertaining to the teeth. —Gk.
οδοντικός, fr. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See
odonto-,

## odonto-
odonto-, before a vowel odont-, combining form
meaning 'tooth' or 'teeth', as in odontoblast,
odontology. — Gk. όδοντο-, όδοντ-, fr. οδών,
gen. οδόντος, 'tooth', assimilated fr. *έδοντ-
(cp. Aeol. έδοντες, 'teeth'), prob. orig. a pres.
part, of I.-E. base *ed-, 'to eat', and lit. meaning
'that which eats'. See tooth and cp. words there
referred to.

## odontoblast
odontoblast, п., one of the layers of cells on the
outside of the pulp of a tooth which produce
the dentine (anat.) — Compounded of odonto-
andGk. βλαστός, 'bud,sprout,shoot'.See-blast.
Derivative: odontoblast-ic, adj.

## Odontoglossum
Odontoglossum, п., a genus of tropical American
orchids; (not cap.) any plant of this genus (bol.)
— ModL., compounded of odonto- and Gk.
γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## odontoid
odontoid, adj., toothlike. — Gk. όδοντοειδής,
compounded of οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth',
and -οειδής, '-like*, fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
odont- and -oid and cp. dentoid.

## odontolith
odontolith, п., dental tartar. — Compounded of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:537 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ODONTOLOGY | 510 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:537 COLUMN:1 -->
odonto- and Gk. λίθος, 'stone'. See -lith.

## odontology
odontology, п., the study of the teeth and their
diseases. — Compounded of odonto- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner; one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: odontolog-ic-al, adj., odontotog-ist,
n.

## odontoloxia
odontoloxia, n., irregularity of the teeth (dent.) —
Medical L., compounded of odonto- and Gk.
λοξός, 'slanting'. See loxo- and 1st -ia.

## odontoma
odontoma, п., a tumor originating from a tooth
(med.) — Medical L., coined by the German
pathologist Rudolf Ludwig Karl Virchow
(1821-1902) fr. odont- and -oma.

## odontophore
odontophore, п., a ribbonlike organ of certain
mollusks covered with minute teeth. — Gk.
όδοντοφόρος, 'bearing teeth', compounded of
οδών, gen. όδοντός, 'tooth', and -φόρος,
'bearer'. See odonto- and -phore.
Derivative: odontophor-ous, adj.

## odontosis
odontosis, п., dentition. — Medical L., formed
with suff. -osis fr. Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος,
'tooth'. See odonto-.

## odor
odor, odour, n. — ME. odour, fr. AF. odour, fr.
OF. odor (F. odeur), fr. L. odorem, ace. of odor,
'smell, scent, odor', which is cogn. with Gk.
δζειν, 'to smell', όσφραίνεσθαι (for *ότσ-φραί-
νεσθαι, -ts- having become -s-), 'to smell, scent,
track by scent', Arm. hot, 'smell, odor' (whence
hotim, Ί smell'), Lith. uodiiii, uosti, Lett, uoiu,
uost, 'to smell', OCzech. Jadati, 'to search,
inquire' (lit. 'to nose, smell out'), Alb. amt (for
*odma), 'unpleasant odor'. See olfactory and cp.
Olax, olid, redolent. Cp. also osmium and words
there referred to. Cp. also odium.

## odorant
odorant, adj., emitting an odor, fragrant. — ME.
odoraunt, fr. MF. ( — F.) odorant, fr. L. odoran-
tem, ace. of oddrans, pres. part, of odorare, 4o
scent, perfume', fr. odor. See odor and -ant.

## odorate
odorate, adj., scented (archaic). — L. odoratus,
'scented, fragrant', pp. of odorare. See prec.
word.

## odoriferous
odoriferous, adj., emitting an odor, fragrant. —
Formed with sufT. -ous fr. L. odorifer, 'fragrant',
lit. 'bearing odor', fr. odor, 'smell, scent, odor*,
and the stem of ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See odor
and -ferous.
Derivatives: odoriferous-ly, adv., odoriferous-
ness, n.

## odorimeter
odorimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
intensity of odor. — A hybrid coined fr. L. odor,
'smell, scent, odor', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure';
see odor and meter, 'poetical rhythm'. The
correct form is osmometer, fr. Gk. οσμή, 'smell',
and μέτρον, 'measure'.

## odorizc
odorizc, tr. v., to perfume. — Formed fr. L. odor
(see odor) with suff. -ize.

## odorous
odorous, adj., emitting an odor, scented,
fragrant.— L. oddrus, 'emitting an odor, fragrant',
fr. odor. See odor. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: odorous-ly, adv., odorous-ness, n.

## -odus
-odus, combining form meaning '-toothed'. —
ModL., fr. Gk. -οδούς, fr. οδούς, a secondary
form of οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See
odonto-.
ody], п., od. — A hybrid coined fr. od and Gk.
υλη, 'matter, material'. See -yl.

## Odynerus
Odynerus, п., a genus of wasps (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. οδυνηρός, 'painful', fr. οδύνη,
'pain'. See -odyiria.

## -odynia
-odynia, combining form denotingpoin (in aspeci-
fled part of the body or caused by specified
circumstances), as in acrodynia, crymodynia. —
Medical L., fr. Gk. -οδυνίϊ, fr. οδύνη, 'pain',
lit. 'that which eats or consumes', fr. I.-E. base
*ed-, 'to eat', whence also Gk. έδειν, L. edere,
'to eat'. See eat.

## Odysseus
Odysseus, п., king of Ithaca and one of the Greek
leaders of the Trojan war, hero of the Odyssey;
Ulysses. — Gk. 'Οδυσσεύς, 'Odysseus, Ulysses',
of uncertain origin; perh. rel. to όδύσσασθαι,
'to be grieved at, be angry at', and cogn. with L.
odi, odisse, 'to hate'. See odium and cp. next
word. Cp. also Ulysses.

## Odyssey
Odyssey, п., 1) the second of the Homeric epics,,
describing the wanderings and adventures of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:537 COLUMN:2 -->
Odysseus during the ten years after the fall of
Troy; 2) (sometimes not cap.) any long
wanderings. — L. Odyssea, fr. Gk. Όδυσσεία or
'Οδύσσεια, fr. 'Οδυσσεύς. See prec. word and
2nd -y.

## oecist
oecist, п., a colonist. — Gk. οικιστής, 'colonizer',
from the stem of οίκίζειν, 'to build a house, to
found a new settlement', fr. οίκος, 'house'. See
economy and -ist.
oeco- combining form. — See eco-.

## oecology
oecology, n. — See ecology.

## oecumenic
oecumenic, oecumenical, adjs. — See ecumenic,
ecumenical,

## oecus
oecus, п., a room or hall in a house. — L., fr. Gk.
οίκος, 'house'. See economy.

## oedema
oedema, n. — See edema.

## Oedipus
Oedipus, п., the son of Laius and Jocasta, king
and queen of Thebes, who unknowingly slew
his father and married his mother; he solved the
riddle of the Sphinx (Greek mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. ΟΙδίπους, lit. 'swell-foot', fr. οίδαν, 'to
swell', and πους (gen. ποδός), 'foot'. See edema
and -pod.

## oeil-de-boeuf
oeil-de-boeuf, п., a round or oval window (archit.)
— F. ail-de-bauf, lit. 'eye of an ox', fr. ail (fr.
L. oculus), 'eye', de, 'from, of (fr. L. de, 'from,
away from'), and breuf (fr. L. bovem, ace. of
bos), 'ox'. See ocular, de- and beef.

## oeillade
oeillade, п., an amorous glance. — F. aillade, fr.
ceil, 'eye', fr. L. oculus. See ocular and -ade.

## oen-
oen-, form of oeno- before a vowel.

## Oenanthe
Oenanthe, п., a genus of plants, the water drop-
wort (bot.) — L. oenanthe, 'vine shoot, the vine;
dropwort', fr. Gk. όίνάνθη, of s.m., which is
compounded of οΐνη, 'vine', and £ν*ος,
'flower'. See vine and anther.

## oenanthic
oenanthic, adj., having the odor of wine; hence
2) oenanthic acid (CuH2602), acid obtained
from oenanthic ether. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ic fr. L. oenanthe. See prec. word.

## Oeneus
Oeneus, п., king of Calydon in Aetolia, father of
Clymenus, Meleager, Dejanira and Gorgo
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Οίνεύς, fr. οίνος,
'wine'. See vine.

## oeno-
oeno-, before a vowel oen-, pertaining to wine.
— Gk. οίνο-, οίν-, fr. οίνος, 'wine'. See vine
and cp. wine.

## oenology
oenology, п., the study of wine. — Compounded
of oeno- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: oenolog-ical, adj., oenolog-ist, n.

## oenomel
oenomel, п., a beverage· made of wine and honey,
drunk by the ancient Greeks (Greek antiq.) —
Late L. oenomeli, fr. Gk. οίνόμελι, which is
compounded of οίνος, 'wine', and μέλι, 'honey'.
See vine and mel.

## oenometer
oenometer, п., an alcoholometer. — Compounded
of oeno- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm', and cp. vinometer.

## Oenone
Oenone, п., a nymph of Mount Ida, wife of
Paris (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Οίνώνη,
fr. οίνος, 'wine'. See vine.

## oenophilist
oenophilist, п., a lover of wine. — Formed with
suff. -ist fr. oeno- and Gk. φίλος, 'lover'. See
-phile.

## Oenothera
Oenothera, п., a genus of plants, the evening
primrose (bot.) — L., name of a plant fr. Gk.
οίνοθήρας, a plant, the root of which smells of
wine, compounded of οίνος, 'wine', and θηραν,
'to hunt after, seek'. For the first element see
vine. The second element is a derivative of θήρ 5,
'hunting, chase', fr. θήρ, 'wild beast'. See
therio- and cp. words there referred to.

## o'er
o'er, adv. and prep. — Poetic contraction of
over.

## oersted
oersted, п., the C.G.S. unit of magnetic
reluctance. — Named after the Danish physicist
Hans Christian Oersted (1777-1851).

## oesophageal
oesophageal, adj. — See esophageal.

## oesophagus
oesophagus, n. — See esophagus.

## Oestrelata
Oestrelata, п., a genus of petrels (ornithol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. οίστρήλατος, 'driven by a
gadfly', compounded of οίστρος, 'gadfly', and
verbal adj. of έλαύνειν, 'to drive'. See estrus
and elastic.

## oestrus
oestrus, n. — See estrus.

## oeuvre
oeuvre, п., a work; esp. a work of literature. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:537 COLUMN:3 -->
F. auvre, 'work', fr. L. opera. See operate, opus
and cp. chef-d'oeuvre, hors d'oeuvre.
of, prep. — ME. of, 'of, off', fr. OE. of,
unstressed form of xj, 'of, from, away from, off', rel.
to OS., ON. af OFris. af, of, of s.m., MLG. a/,
MDu. af, ave, Du. af, 'off, down', OHG. aba,
ab, MHG. abe, ab, G. ab, 'off, from, down',
Goth, af, 'away from', cogn. with ΟΙ. άρα,
Avestic ара, 'away from', Hitt. ара, 'behind',
Gk. άπό, 'away from, from', L. ab, 'away from,
from' (orig. *ap, cp. ap-erio, Ί open'), Alb.
prape (for *per-ape), 'back, again', Lith. apacia,
Lett, apaksa, 'the lower part'. Cp. off, ebb. Cp.
also ab-, apo-, post-,

## of-
of-, assimilated form of ob- before/.

## off
off, adv., prep, and adj. — The stressed form of
of. Cp. offal, offing, offish, and the second
element in doff.

## off
off, п., the offside (cricket) — Fr. off, adj.

## offal
offal, п., 1) waste parts; 2) refuse. — Lit. 'that
which falls off'; formed from off, adv., and fall,
n. Cp. Du. afval, G. Abfall.

## offcast
offcast, adj. and n. — Compounded of off, adv.,
and cast,

## offend
offend, intr. and tr. v. — ME. offenden, fr. MF.
offendre, fr. L. offendere, 'to strike against, hit
upon, hurt; to stumble, commit an offense; to
find fault with, be displeased with', formed fr.
ob- and -fendere (found only in compounds), 'to
thrust, strike', fr. I.-E. base *gwhen-, 'to strike'.
See defend and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: offend-ed, adj., offend-ed-ly, adv.,
offend-ed-ness, п., offend-er, n.

## offense
offense, offence, n. — ME. offense, offence, fr.
OF. (= F.) offense, fr. L. offensa, 'a striking
against; offense', prop, fem pp. of offendere.
See offend.

## offensive
offensive, adj. — ML. offensivus, fr. L. offlnsus,
pp. of offendere. See prec. word and -ive.
Derivatives: offensive, п., offensive-ly, adv.,
offensive-ness, n.

## offer
offer, tr. and intr. v. — ME. offren, fr. earlier
offrien, fr. OE. offrian, 'to bring offering, to
sacrifice', fr. L. offerre,' to bring before, present,
offer', fr. ob- and ferre, 'to bear, carry'; see
bear, 'to carry', and cp. words there referred to.
The sense development of the English word was
influenced by F. offrir, 'to offer'. See bear,
'to carry*, and cp. confer and words there
referred to.

## offer
offer, n. — ME. offre, fr. OF. (= F.) offre, verbal
n. fr. offrir, 'to offer', fr. VL. 'offerlre, which
corresponds to L. offerre. See offer, v.

## offering
offering, n. — ME. offring, offering, fr. OE. off-
rung, Offering', verbal n. fr. offrian, 'to offer*.
See offer, v., and subst. suff. -ing.

## offertory
offertory, п., that part of the mass at which
offerings are made; the offerings themselves. —
Eccles L. offertdrium, 'place to which offerings
were brought', fr. VL. offertus (corresponding
to L. oblatus), pp. of L. offerre. See offer and
subst. suff. -ory.
Derivative: offertori-al, adj.

## office
office, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. offtcium,
'service' (in Eccles. L„ 'church service'), which
stands for *opi-faciom, lit. 'work-doing', fr.
ops, gen. opis, 'power, might, abundance, means,
wealth, treasure', and the stem of facere, 'to
make, do'. (Cp. L. opi-fex, 'workman, artist',
lit. One who does a work', which is compounded
of the same two elements.) The first element is
rel. to L. opus, 'work, labor, exertion; see opus.
For the second element see fact. Cp. officinal,
usine. For the change of Latin й (in facere) to ί
(in of-ficium) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

## officer
officer, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) offtcier, fr. ML.
officiarius, fr. L. offtcium. See prec. word and
agential suff. -er.
Derivative: officer, tr. v.

## official
official, adj. — ME., fr. OF. official (F. offtciel),
fr. Late L. officialis, 'pertaining to an office or
service', fr. L. officium. See office and adj. suff.
-al.
Derivatives: official, п., official-ism, п., official-
ist, п., official-ize, tr. v., official-ly, adv.

## officiant
officiant, п., an officiating priest or minister. —
ML. officians, gen. -antis, pres. part, of officiare.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:538 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 511 | OLECRANON -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:538 COLUMN:1 -->
See officiate and -ant.

## officiary
officiary, adj., pertaining to, or connected with,
the holding of an office. — ML. officiarius, fr.
L. officium. See office and adj. suff. -ary.

## officiate
officiate, intr. v., to perform a duty; esp. to
perform the duties of a priest. — ML. officiat-(um),
pp. stem of officiare, 'to perform divine service',
fr. L. officium. See office and verbal suff. -ate.

## officinal
officinal, adj., kept in stock by a druggist. — ML.
officinalis, 'belonging to a workshop', fr. L.
officlna, 'workshop', which stands for 'opificina,
h.opifex, gen. opificis, 'workman'. See office, sy ff.
-iae (representing L. -inus) and adj. suff. -al.

## officious
officious, adj., 1) friendly, obliging (archaic); 2)
meddlesome, interfering; 3) unofficial, informal
(diplomacy). — L. officiosus, 'dutiful,
complaisant, obliging', fr. officium. See office and -ous.
Derivatives: officious-ly, adv., officious-ness, n.

## offing
offing, п., the distant part of the sea, as far as it
can be seen from the shore. — Formed fr. off,
adv., and subst. suff. -ing.

## offish
offish, adj., inclined to be aloof. — Formed fr.
off, adv., and adj. suff. -ish.
Derivatives: offish-ly, adv., offish-ness, a.

## offprint
offprint, п., a separate reprint of an article. —
Coined by Skeat fr. off and print, as loan
translation of G. Separatabdruck.
Derivative: offprint, tr. v., to reprint separately.

## offset
offset, п., that which sets off; an offshoot. —
Compounded of off, adv., and set, n.
Derivative: offset, tr. and intr. v.

## offshoot
offshoot, n.—Compounded of off, adj., and shoot,

## offspring
offspring, n. — ME. ofspring, fr. OE. ofspring, fr.
of, 'of, off', and springan, 'to spring'. See of and
spring, v.

## oft
oft, adv., often (archaic от poet.) — ME., fr. OE.
oft, rel. to OS. oft, ofto, OFris. ofta, Dan. ofte,
Swed. ofta, OHG. ofto, MHG. ofte, oft, G. oft,
ON. opt, Goth, ufta, 'often'; of uncertain origin,

## often
often, adv. — ME. ofte, often, extended fr. oft.
See oft.

## ogam
ogam, ogham, oguni, п., ancient Irish form of
writing. — Ir. ogham, fr. Olr. ogam, ogum,
generally derived fr. Ogma Mac Eladan, the
legendary inventor of this sytem of writing.
Derivative: ogam-ic, ogham-ic, ogum-ic, adj.

## ogdoad
ogdoad, п., 1) the number eight; 2) a group of
eight. — Late L. ogdoas, gen. -adis, fr. Gk.
όγδοάς, gen. -άδος, 'the number eight', fr.
δγδοος, eighth', fr. οκτώ, 'eight'. See octa- and
suff. -ad and cp. octad.

## ogee
ogee, п., 1) a molding having an S-shaped curve;
2) an S-shaped curve. — F. ogive. See ogive,

## ogival
ogival, adj., having the form of an ogive. — See
next word and adj. suff. -al.

## ogive
ogive, п., 1) the diagonal rib of a Gothic vault; 2)
a pointed or Gothic arch. — F. ogive, earlier
also spelled augive; of uncertain origin. Cp.
ogee,

## ogle
ogle, intr. v., 1) to keep looking amorously; 2) tr.
v., to look at amorously. — Of LG. origin. Cp.
LG. oegeln, freq. of oegen, 'to look at', rel. to
Du. ogen, 'to look at', fr. oog, 'eye'. See eye.
Derivatives: ogle, п., ogl-er, n.

## Ogpu
Ogpu, п., formerly, the secret service of Soviet
Russia. — Russ., formed from the initials of
Objedinionnoje Gosudarstvennoje Politicheskoje
Vpravlenie (United Government Political
Administration).

## ogre
ogre, п., 1) a man-eating giant; a hideous or
cruel man. — F., first used by Perrault in his

## fairy stories
fairy stories, 1697; in English it appears first
(spelled hogre) in a translation of a French
version of the Arabian Nights; fr. Byzantine
Ogur, 'Hungarian'. The sense development is
due to a confusion of the Hungarians with the

## Huns and the Tartars. See Wiener in Anglia
Huns and the Tartars. See Wiener in Anglia,

## XXIII
XXIII, 107, and Meyer-Liibke, Romanisches

## etymologisches Worterbuch
etymologisches Worterbuch, p. 446, No. 6048.
Cp. Ugrinn.
Derivatives: ogre-ish, adj., ogr-ess, n.

## Ogyglan
Ogyglan, adj., primeval, prehistoric. — Lit.
'pertaining to Ogygius', fr.L. Ogygius, fr. Gk.
Ώγύγιος, fr. Ωγύγης, name of a mythical king
of Attica. For the ending see suff. -ian.

## oh
oh, interj. — Of imitative origin. Ср. О.

## ohm
ohm, п., the unit of electrical resistance. — G.

## Ohm
Ohm, from the name of the German physicist

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:538 COLUMN:2 -->
Georg Simon Ohm (1787-1854).
Derivatives: ohmage (q.v.), ohm-ic, adj.
ohmage, n„ electrical resistance expressed in
ohms. — Formed fr. ohm with suff. -age.
ohmic, adj., 1) of an ohm; 2) measured in ohms.
— Formed fr. ohm with adj. suff. -ic.
ohm-meter, п., an instrument for measuring
electrical resistance. — Formed fr. ohm and -meter,
oho, interj. — Compounded of the interjections
О and ho.
-oic, a suff. used to form names of acid, as in
caproic (chem.) — From the ending of benzoic,
-oid, adj. suff. meaning 'like, resembling'. The
adjectives so formed are often used substantively
in the sense 'something resembling'. — Gk.
-οειδής, for -ο-ειδής, formed fr. -o-, stem
vowel belonging to the preceding element, and
-ειδής, 'like' (cp. e.g. δακτυλο-ειδής,
'fingerlike', and see dactyloid), lit. 'having the form of,
fr. είδος, 'form, shape', which stands for "fti-
δος, and lit. means'that which is seen', fr. I.-E.
base *weid-, *woid-, *wit-, 'to see; to know',
whence also Gk. ίδεΐν (for *Γΐδεϊν), 'to see',
οΐδα (for "^οΐδιχ), Ί know'. See -o- and idea
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also -ode,
'like'. Cp. also the second element in collidine,
iodine, Ixodidae.

## -oidal
-oidal, suff. forming adjectives from nouns
ending in -oid. — Compounded of the prec. suff.
and adj. suff. -al.

## Oidium
Oidium, п., a form genus of imperfect fungi (bot.)
— ModL., dimin. formed fr. Gk. ωον, 'egg*.
See oo-.

## oil
oil, n. — ME. olie, oile, fr. OF. oile (F. huile), fr.
L. oleum, fr. Gk. έλαιον (fr. *iXotifov), 'olive
tree', which, together with Arm. ewi, is prob.
of Aegean (most likely Cretan) origin. OE. (tie,
OS. oli, OFris. and Du. olie, OHG. dlei, oli
(whence MHG. die, ol, G. £>/), 'oil', are loan
words fr. h.*oleum. Cp. ole, oleagineous, olive
and elaio-. Cp. also the second element in anele,
carbolic, lanolin, linoleum, rhlgolene.
Derivatives: oil, tr. v., oil-er, п., oil-y, adj., oil-i-
ly, adv., oil-i-ness, n.

## ointment
ointment, n. — ME. oinement, oynement, fr. OF.
oignement, fr. VL. *unguimentum, for L. unguen-
tum. (The first t in E. ointment is due to an
association with the obsol. verb oint, 'to anoint').
See unguent.

## Oireachtas
Oireachtas, п., the legislature of the Irish Free
State. — Ir., 'assembly'.
O.K. or ОК., all right, correct. — Prob. fr.
Choctaw okeh, 'it is so'.
Derivative: O.K., tr. v., to approve.

## oka
oka, п., a weight used in Turkey. — Turk, dqah,
fr. Arab. ukiyah, fr. Gk. ούγγία, ουγκία, fr.
L. uncia. See ounce, a weight.

## okapi
okapi, п., a Central African animal related to the
giraffes, but with a short neck (zool.) — Native
African name.

## okenite
okenite, п., a hydrous calcium silicate (mineral.)
— Named after the German naturalist Lorenz
Oken (1779-1851). For the'ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## okra
okra, п., a tall plant, native in Africa, and
cultivated in the United States and the West Indies,
Abelmoschus esculentus. — Fr. W. African
nkruman.

## -ol
-ol, suff. denoting an alcohol or phenol (chem.) —
Fr. alcohol.

## -ol
-ol, a var. of the chem. mff. -ole.

## Olacaceae
Olacaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Olax with suff. -aceae.

## Olaf
Olaf, mas. PN. — ON. An-leifr, a compound lit.
meaning 'ancestor's relic'. The first element is
rel. to OHG. ano, 'ancestor'; see anile. The
second element is rel. to OE. ISfan,'to leave'; see
leave.

## Olam Habba
Olam Habba, also Olam Haba, the world to come
(Jewish Religion). — Heb. 'olam habba', 'the

## world to come
world to come, the future world'. Heb. Loldm
means 'long duration; antiquity, ancient time;

## uninterrupted future
uninterrupted future, eternity', in Mishnaic

## Hebrew also 'world'. It is rel. to Aram
Hebrew also 'world'. It is rel. to Aram, 'alam,
'at1 ma, 'eternity; world' (whence prob. Ethiop.
'я/ш, 'eternity; world'), Arab, 'ά/am, 'world'.

## According to Gesenius
According to Gesenius, Konig and others, these

## words lit. mean 'hidden
words lit. mean 'hidden, unknown time', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:538 COLUMN:3 -->
derive fr. Sem. base l-l-m, 'to hide'. Heb. habba\
'the coming or future one', is formed from the
def. article ha-, 'the', and bo", part, of bo" (stem
b-w-'), 'to come', which is rel. to Arab, ba'a, 'he
returned', Akkad. ba'u, 'to come'. Cp. Ahabath
Olam.

## Olax
Olax, п., a genus of evergreen plants (bot.) —
ModL. Olax, fr. Late L. olax, gen. olacis,
'smelling, odorous', fr. olfre, 'to smell'. See
odor and cp. olfactory.

## old
old, adj. — ME. aid, old, fr. OE. aid, eald, rel. to
OS. aid, OFris. aid, old, Du. oud, OHG., MHG.,
G. alt (for I.-E. "al-to-), Goth, alpeis (for l.-E.
*al-tyo-) 'old'; pp. formation orig. meaning
'nourished, grown up', from the Teut. verb
represented by Goth, alan, 'to grow up', ON. ala,
'to bring up, nourish', OE. alan, 'to nourish', fr.
I.-E. base *al-, 'to grow, nourish', whence also
Gk. iv-αλ-τος, 'not to be filled, insatiable', L.
alere, 'to nourish', alius, 'high' (prop. pp. of
alere, hence orig. meaning 'nourished, grown
up', and corresponding exactly to OE. aid, etc.),
almus, 'fostering', ad-oliscere, 'to grow up', Olr.
alim, Ί nourish', Toch. A alym, 'life, spirit'.
Enlarged with -d- or -dA-formative element, the
same base appears in Ol. ida, 'refreshment', Gk.
άλδη, 'growth', άλδαίνειν 'to cause to grow',
άλδήσκειν, 'to grow; to cause to grow' (base
*al-d-), Ol. rdhnoti, 'thrives, prospers', Gk.
άλθαίνειν, 'to heal' (base *al-dh-). Cp. auld,
alderman, eld, elder, 'older', the first element in
Eldred and the second element in world. Cp. also
abolish, adolescent, adult, aliment, alimony,
Alma Mater, alt, Althaea, altitude, alto, altissimo,
alto-relievo, alumnus, coalesce, enhance, exalt,
hautboy, hauteur, hawser, oboe, obsolete, proles,
proletary, rialto, soboles. For other Teut.
adjectives formed from past participles see cold,
dead, loud, sad.
Derivatives: old, п., olden (q.v.), old-ish, adj.,
oldster (q.v.)

## olden
olden, adj. — ME., fr. old. See old and adj. suff.
-en.

## olden
olden, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. old with
verbal suff. -en.

## oldhamite
oldhamite, п., a calcium sulfide. — Named after
the Irish geologist Thomas Oldham (1816-78).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## oldster
oldster, п., an old person (colloq.) — Formed fr.
old on analogy of youngster. See -ster.

## -ole
-ole, also -ol, a suff. used in chemistry to denote
1) a close-chained compound havine five
members as in pyrrole; 2) certain aldehydes and
ethers. — Fr. L. oleum, 'oil'. See oil.

## -oie
-oie, dimin. suff. — Fr. F. -ole, or directly fr. L.
■olus (masc), -ola (fern.), -olum (neut.), fr. orig.
*-e!o, which is cogn. with Ol. -ald-h (cp. Ol.
vrsalah, 'male'), Gk. -ύλος (ср. Gk. άρκτύλος,
'a bear whelp', fr. όίρκτος, 'bear'), OSIav. -ell
(cp. OSIav. pliveli, 'weed'), Lith. -ilis (cp. Lith.
parselis, 'a little pig'). L. suff. -olus, -a, -urn, is
used only after vowels (cp. e.g. L. petiolus, 'a
little foot'). After consonants the form of this
dimin. suff. is -ulus; see -ule.

## Olea
Olea, п., a genus of plants, the true olive. — L.
olea, 'olive tree, olive*. See olive.

## Oleaceae
Oleaceae, n. pi., the olive family (hot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Olea with suff. -aceae.

## oleaceous
oleaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## oleagiaous
oleagiaous, adj., oily, greasy. — F. oleagineux
(fern, oleagineuse), fr. L. oleaginus, 'belonging to
the olive', fr. olea, 'olive'. See oil and cp. Olea,
olive. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivative: oleaginous-ness, n.

## oleander
oleander, п., an evergreen Mediterranean shrub,
the rose bay. — ML. (whence also F. oleandre),
fr. Late L. lorandrum, which was formed fr. L.
rhododendron (through the intermediate forum
rodandrum). See rhododendron.

## oleaster
oleaster, п., a S. European shrub resembling the
wild olive, Elaeagnus angustifolia. — L., 'wild
olive', formed with the pejorative suff. -aster fr.
olea, 'olive tree'. See Olea.

## oleate
oleate, п., a salt of oleic acid (chem.) — Formed
with chem. suff. -ate fr. L. oleum, 'oil'. See oil.

## olecranon
olecranon, п., point of the elbow (anat.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. ώλέκρανου, shortened fr. ώλε-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:539 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OLEFIANT | 512 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:539 COLUMN:1 -->
νόκρανον, for ώλένης κρδνίον, 'head of the
elbow'. The first element is cogn. with L. ulna,
'elbow', Goth, aleina, OE. eln, 'ell'; see ell. For
the second element see cranium.

## oleflant
oleflant, adj., forming oil (chem.) — F. olefiant
(in gaz olefiant, lit. 'oil-making gas'), coined by
the Dutch chemists Deimann, Troostwyck,
Bondt and Lauwerenburgh in 1794 fr. ole- (fr.
L. oleum, 'oil') and -fiant (fr. L. -ficanlem, ace.
of -ficans, pres. part, of -ficare, fr. facere, 'to
make, do'). See oil and -fy.

## olefine
olefine, olefin, п., any of a series of hydrocarbons,
containing one double bond (chem.) — Formed
from prec. word with chem. suff. -ine, -in.

## oleic
oleic, adj., pertaining to, or contained in, oil. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. L. oleum, 'oil'. See
oil and cp. olive.

## olein
olein, п., a liquid glyceride of oleic acid (chem.) —
Coined by its discoverer, the French chemist
Michel-Eugene Chevreul (1786-1889), fr. L.
oleum, 'oil' (see oil), and suff. -in. Cp. acrolein,

## oleo-
oleo-, a combining form meaning oil, oleic or
olein. — Fr. L. oleum, 'oil'. See oil.

## oleograph
oleograph, п., a chromolithograph imitating an
oil painting. — A hybrid coined fr. L. oleum,
'oil', and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'
(see oil and -graph). The correct form is elaeo-
graph, fr. Gk. έλαιον, ΌίΓ, and -γράφος.
Derivatives: oleograph-ic, adj., oleograph-y, n.

## oleomargarine
oleomargarine, п., margarine. — Compounded of
oleo- and margarine,

## oleometer
oleometer, п., an instrument for.measuring the
specific gravity of oils. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
oleum, 'oil', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure' (see oil
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'). The correct form
is elaeometer, fr. Gk. eXottov, 'oil', and μέτρον,
'measure'.

## oleoresin
oleoresin, п., a solution of a resin in an essential
oil. — Compounded of oleo- and resla.

## oleraceous
oleraceous, adj., of the nature of potherbs. — L.
holeraceus, oleraceus, 'resembling vegetables',
fr. holus, olus, gen. holeris, oleris, 'kitchen herbs,
vegetables, cabbage, colewort', ft. OL. helus, of
s.m., which is rel. to L. helvus, 'light bay'. See
yellow and cp. olltory. For the ending see suff.
-aceous.

## Olethreutidae
Olethreutidae, n. pi., a family of small moths
(entomol.) — ModL., lit. 'destroyers', formed
with suff. -idae fr. Olethreutes, the type genus,
fr. Gk. όλεθρεύειν, 'to slay, destroy', fr.
όλεθρος, 'destruction, ruin', which is rel. to όλλύειν,
'to destroy'. Cp. Apollyon and the second
element in Azolla.

## olfaction
olfaction, п., 1) the act of smelling; 2) the sense of
smell. — Formed with suff. -ion fr. L. olfactus,
pp. of olfacere, 'to smell'. See next word and
-ion.

## olfactory
olfactory, adj., pertaining to the sense of smell. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. olfactus, pp. of
olfacere, 'to smell, scent; to cause to smell at',
which is compounded of ol-ire, 'to smell', and
facere, 'to make, do'. The first element stands
for *od-ere and is re], to odor, 'smell, scent,
odor'; see odor. For the second element see fact,
for the ending see adj. suff. -ory. The change of
■d- to -/- in olire is prob. due to the influence of
L. oleum, 'oil'. Cp. Olax, olid, redolent.

## Olga
Olga, fern. PN. — Russ., prob. fr. Norse helga,
'holy'. See holy,

## olibanum
olibanum, п., frankincense. — ML., fr. L. libanus
(Vulgate), fr. Gk. λίβανος, fr. Heb. fbhona1',
'frankincense', lit. 'the white one', fr. labkdn,
'white'. See leban.

## -olic
-olic, a suff. used to name certain acids, as tetrolic
(chem.) — Compounded of the suffixes -ol (for
alcohol) and adj. suff. -ic.

## olid
olid, adj., stinking. — L. olidus, 'smelling,
stinking, rank', fr. olere, 'to smell'. See olfactory and
-id (representing L. -idus).

## olig-
olig-, form of oligo- before a vowel.

## oligarch
oligarch, п., member of an oligarchy. — Gk.
όλιγάρχης, fr. ολίγος, 'small, little, few', and
-άρχης, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See oligo- and
-arch,

## oligarchic
oligarchic, oligarchical, adj., pertaining to an
oligarchy. — Gk. ολιγαρχικός, fr. όλιγάρχης.
See oligarchy and adj. suff. -ic.

## oligarchy
oligarchy, п., rule or government by a few

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:539 COLUMN:2 -->
persons. — Gk. ολιγαρχία, 'government by a few
persons', fr. όλιγάρχης. See oligarch and -y
(representing Gk. -iS).

## oligo-
oligo-, before a vowel olig-, combining form
meaning 'few'. — Gk. όλιγο-, όλιγ-, fr. ολίγος,
'small, little, few', of uncertain etymology; perh.
rel. to λοιγός, 'ruin, destruction, death', and
cogn. with Alb. /'ifc, 'evil, thin, lean', Lith. liga,
'illness'. Cp. loimic.

## OUgocene
OUgocene, adj., pertaining to the Tertiary period
between the Eocene and Miocene (geol.) —
Compounded of oligo- and Gk. καινός, 'new'.
See kamite.

## Ollgochaeta
Ollgochaeta,n.,pl., an order of chaetopod worms
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of oligo- and Gk.
χαίτη, 'long flowing hair, mane'. See chaeto-,

## oligochaetous
oligochaetous, adj. — See prec. word and -ous.

## oltgoclase
oltgoclase, п., a kind of feldspar (mineral.) —
Compounded of oligo- and Gk. κλάσις,
'fracture', fr. κλάν, 'to break'. See clastic and cp.
words there referred to.

## oligocythemia
oligocythemia, ollgcythaemia, п., a form of
anemia in which there is a deficiency of red
corpuscles in the blood (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of oligo-, Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow vessel',
and αίμα, 'blood'. See -cyte and -hernia.

## oliguria
oliguria, п., scantiness of urine secreted (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of olig- and Gk.
ούρον, 'urine'. See -uria.

## olio
olio, п., 1) an olla podrida; 2) a medley,
miscellany. — Sp olla, 'earthen pot', pronounced oPa,
fr. VL. olla, 'pot', fr. L. aulla, which stands for
"auxla (cp. the dimin. auxilla, 'small pot'), and
is cogn. with Goth, auhns (for *uqwnos), OE.
of en, 'oven', orig. 'firepot'. See oven and cp. olla
podrida.

## ollphant
ollphant, п., 1) an elephant (obsol.);2) a medieval
horn made of ivory (obsol.) — F. olifant, fr. OF.
See elephant.

## olitory
olitory, adj., 1) pertaining to a kitchen garden; 2)
producing potherbs. — L. olitorius, holitorius,
fr. olitor, holitor, 'kitchen gardener', from the
stem of olus, holus, gen. oleris, holeris, 'kitchen
herbs, vegetables, cabbage, colewort'. See
oleraceous and adj. suff. -ory.

## Oliva
Oliva, п., a genus of marine univalve mollusks
(zool.) — L. oliva, 'olive'. See olive.

## olivaceous
olivaceous, adj., resembling the olive; olive green.
— ModL. olivaceus, fr. L. oliva. See olive and
-aceous.

## olivary
olivary, adj., 1) shaped like an olive; 2) relating
to either of the two oval bodies protruding from
the medulla oblongata (anat.) — L. olivarius,
'pertaining to olives', fr. oliva. See next word
and adj. suff. -ary.

## olive
olive, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) olive, fr. L. oliva,
'olive, olive tree', fr. Gk. έλαια (for "έλαίία),
'olive tree'. See oil and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also olivet, Olivia, olivine.
Derivative; olive, adj.

## Oliver
Oliver, 1) masc. PN.; 2) one of Charlemagne's 12
peers and a friend of Roland. — F. Olivier, fr.
MLG. Alfihar, lit. 'elf-host', fr. alf, 'elf, and
Aari, 'host, army'. Cp. the OE. PN. jEljhere,
which is of the same meaning and origin, and
see elf and harry. F. Olivier was influenced in
form by OF. olivier, 'olive tree'.

## Oliver
Oliver, п., a small tilt hammer. — Prob. from the
PN. Oliver.

## olivet
olivet, п., olive yard. — L. olivltum, 'olive yard',
formed fr. oliva, 'olive tree', with -etum, a suff.
used to form names of gardens and woods. Cp.
L. arbor-etum, 'a place grown with trees',
querqu-etum, 'oak forest', palm-ёшт, 'palm
forest'. See olive.

## olivet
olivet, п., imitation pearl — F. olivette, dimin.
formed fr. olive. See olive and -et, -ette.

## Olivia
Olivia, also Olive, fern. PN. — It. Olivia, fr. L.
oliva, 'olive'. See olive.

## olivine
olivine, п., an olive green chrysolite (mineral.) —
G. Olivin, formed fr. L. oliva, 'olive', with suff.
-in, '-ine'. See olive and -ine (representing L.
-inus).

## olla podrida
olla podrida, 1) a dish consisting of various meats
and vegetables; 2) a medley, miscellany — Sp.,
lit. 'rotten pot'. See olio and putrid and cp.
potpourri.

## ology
ology, п., any branch of knowledge; science (col-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:539 COLUMN:3 -->
loq.) — Prop, s'ubst. use of -otogy, ft. Gk.
-ολογίά, a suff. formed fr. -o-, stem vowel
belonging to the preceding element, and -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
-o- and -logy.

## olpe
olpe, п., a leathern oil flask used in the palaestra
(Greek archaeol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. βλπη, 'a
leathern oil flask', which is rel. to ελπος, 'fat,
oil', fr. I.-E. *selp-, whence also OI. sarpis-,
'melted butter', OE. sealf, 'salve'. See salve,
'ointment for wounds'.

## Olympiad
Olympiad, п., a period of four years, reckoned
from one celebration of the Olympic games to
the next; used by the ancient Greeks in
computing time. — F. olympiade, fr. L. Olympiadem,
gen. Olympiadis, fr. Gk. 'Ολυμπιάς, gen.
'Ολυμπιάδος, fr. 'Ολυμπία (scil. χώρα), a
district in Elis in ancient Greece, where the Olympic
games were held, prop. fern, of the adj.
'Ολύμπιος, 'Olympian'. See next word and -ad.

## Olympian
Olympian, adj., 1) pertaining to Mount Olympus
in Macedonia; 2) heavenly; godlike; 3)
pertaining to Olympia in Elis in ancient Greece,
where the Olympian games were held; 4)
designating the Olympian games. — Late L. Olym-
pianus, Olympius, fr. Gk. 'Ολύμπιος,
'pertaining to Olympus or Olympia', fr. "Ολυμπος. See
Olympus and cp. Olympic.

## Olympian
Olympian, п., 1) an inhabitant of Olympus; esp.
any of the twelve great gods who were supposed
to live on Mount Olympus; 2) an inhabitant of
Olympia. — Fr. prec. word.

## Olympic
Olympic, adj., the same as Olympian. — Gk.
Όλυμπικός, fr. "Ολυμπάς, 'Olympus'. See next
word and -ic.

## Olympus
Olympus, п., a mountain in Macedonia, the
fabled dwelling place of the twelve great gods of
ancient Greece. — L., fr. Gk. "Ολυμπος, which
is of unknown etymology.

## om-
om-, form of ото- before a vowel.

## -oma
-oma, suff. meaning 'morii growth, tumor', as
in lymphoma, sarcoma (med.) — Gk. -ωμα, gen.
-ώματος, a suff. formed fr. -ω-, lengthened
stem vowel of verbs ending in -οϋν (passive
-οΰσ&αι) and -μα, termination of neut. nouns
of the third declension; see -ma.

## omadhaun
omadhaun, п., a fool, simpleton. — Ir. amaddn.

## omasitis
omasitis, п., inflammation of the omasum (med.)
— Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr. L.
omasum. See next word.

## omasum
omasum, п., the third stomach of a ruminant
animal (zool.) — L. omasum, 'bullock's tripe',
prob. of Gaulish origin. Cp. abomasum.

## omber
omber, ombre, п., a card game. — F. hombre, fr.
Sp. hombre, 'man', fr. L. hominem, ace. οι homo,
'man'. See human and cp. words there referred
to.

## ombro-
ombro-, combining form meaning 'rain'. — Gk.
όμβρο-, fr. ίμβρος, 'rain', cogn. with OI.
abhram, 'cloud, atmosphere'. See imbricate.

## ombrograph
ombrograph, п., a rain gauge. — Compounded of
ombro- and Gk.-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graph.

## ombrology
ombrology, п., that branch of meteorology which
deals with rain. — Compounded of ombro- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.

## ombrometer
ombrometer, п., a rain gauge. — Compounded of
ombro- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## omega
omega, п., the twenty-fourth and last letter of the
Greek alphabet. — Gk. ωμέγα, 'the great (i.e.
long) o\ Cp. omicron.

## omelet
omelet, omelette, п., eggs beaten up, seasoned and
fried. — F. omelette, fr. earlier omelette, meta-
thesized fr. *alemette, a secondary form for alu-
mette. This latter arose—through substitution
of suffix—fr. alumelle, a word derived fr. OF.
lemelle, fr. L. lamella, 'a small thin plate of
metal'; see lamella. Because of its flattened
shape, the omelet has been compared to a thin
plate.

## omen
omen, п., augury; foreboding. — L. omen, fr.
earlier osmen, of uncertain origin; perh.
standing for *ovis-men and cogn. with Gk. οιομαι,
Epic όίομαι (for "όίίσιομαι), Ί suppose,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:540 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 513 | ONER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:540 COLUMN:1 -->
think, believe'. Cp. ominous, abominable,
abominate.
Derivative: omen, tr. v.

## oment-
oment-, form of omento- before a vowel,

## omental
omental, adj., pertaining to the omentum. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. omentum. See
omentum.

## omento-
omento-, before a vowel oment-, combining form
denoting the omentum. See next word.

## omentum
omentum, п., a fold of the peritoneum enclosing
the intestines (anal.) — L. omentum, 'the fat-
skin, adipose, the membrane that encloses the
bowels', contraction of *owi-mentom, from the
same base as the second element in L. ind-uere,
'to put on, pull on', ex-uere, 'to pull off, strip
off'. See exuviae.
Derivative: oment-al, adj.

## omer
omer, п., a Hebrew measure, the tenth part of an
ephah (see Ex. 16:36). — Heb. 'omer. Cp.
gomer, *a measure'.

## omicron
omicron, omikron, п., the fifteenth letter of the
Greek alphabet. — Gk. δ μικρόν, 'small (i.e.
short) o\ Cp. omega.

## ominous
ominous, adj. — L. ominosus, 'full of foreboding,
portentous, ominous', fr, omen, gen. ominis. See
omen and -ous.
Derivatives: ominous-ly, adv., ominous-ness, n.

## omissible
omissible, adj. — Formed with suff. -ible fr. L.
omissus, pp. of omittere. See omit.
Derivative: omissibil-ity, n.

## omission
omission, n. — ME. omissioun, fr. Late L.
omissio, gen. -onis, 'an omitting', fr. L. omissus,
pp. of omittere. See omit and -ion.

## omlssive
omlssive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
omissus, pp. of omittere. See omit and -ive.

## omit
omit, tr. v. — ME. omitten, fr. L. omittere, 'to let
go, give up, dismiss, neglect', fr. o- (for ob, see
oh-) and mittere, 'to cause to go, to send'. See
mission.
Derivative: omitt-er, n.

## omttis
omttis, п., inflammation of the shoulder (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk. ώμος,
'shoulder'. See ото-, 'shoulder'.

## omlah
omlah, n. pi., the native officials of a civil court in
India. — Hind, amlah, fr. Arab. tumala\
'workers, agents, officials', pi. of 'amil, partic. of
*amila, 'he worked, labored, made'. See aumil.

## omnia-
omnia-, combining form meaning 'eye'; used esp.
in terms of entomology. — Fr. Gk. όμμα,
'eye', which is rel. to ο"ψ, gen. οπός, 'eye, face',
δψις, 'sight'. See optic and -ma.

## Ommastrephes
Ommastrephes, п., a genus of cephalopods (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'turning the eyes', compounded
of omma- and the stem of στρέφει,ν, 'to turn'.
See strophe.

## Ommiad
Ommiad, п., any of a dynasty of Mohammedan
caliphs who ruled in Damascus from 661 to 750
C.E. and in southern Spain from 756 to 1031
C.E. — Fr. Umayya (in vulgar pronunciation
Omayya), great-grandfather of the first caliph
in this dynasty. For the ending see suff. -ad.

## omni-
omni-, combining form meaning 'all'. — L.
omni-, fr. omnis, 'all, every'; of uncertain origin.

## omnibus
omnibus, п., a public vehicle. — F., short for voi-
ture omnibus (introduced by Laffitte in Paris in
1820), lit. 'a vehicle for all', fr. L. omnibus, 'for
all', dat. pi. fr. omnis. See prec. word and cp.
bus.

## omnifarious
omnifarious, adj., of all kinds, of all subjects. —
L. omnifarius, 'of all kinds', compounded of
omnis, 'all, every', and -fariusy*-fo\6\ For the first
element see omni-, for the second see bifarious.
Derivatives: omnifarious-ly, adv., omnifarious-
ness, n.

## omnifk
omnifk, adj., all-creating. — ML. omnificus,
compounded of L. omnis, 'all, every', and -ficus, from
the stem οΐ-ficere, unstressed form οΐ/acere, 'to
make, do'. See omni- and -fie.

## omnipotence
omnipotence, п., quality of being omnipotent. —
Late L. omnipotentia, 'almighty power', fr. L.
omnipotens, gen. -entis. See next word and
-ce.

## omnipotent
omnipotent, adj., almighty. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) omnipotent, fr. L. omnipotentem, ace. of
omnipotens, 'all-powerful, almighty', which is
compounded of omnis, 'all, every', and potens,
gen. potentis, 'able, powerful'. See omni- and
potent.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:540 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: omnipotent-ly, adv.

## omnipresence
omnipresence, adj., quality of being omnipresent.
— ML. omnipraesentia, fr. omnipraesens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -ce.

## omnipresent
omnipresent, adj., present everywhere at the same
time. — ML. omnipraesens, gen. -entis,
compounded of L. omnis, 'all, every', and praesens,
gen.praesentis, 'present'. See omni- and present.

## omniscience
omniscience, п., the quality of being omniscient.
— ML. omniscientia. See omni- and science.

## omniscient
omniscient, adj., all-knowing. — ModL. omni-
sciens, gen. -entis, back formation of ML.
omniscientia. See prec. word and -ent.
Derivative: omniscient-ly, adv.

## omnium gatherum
omnium gatherum, a miscellaneous collection of
persons or things. — A humorous coinage fr. L.
omnium, 'of all', gen. pi. of omnis, 'all, every'
(see omni-), and latinized form of E. gather.

## omnivorous
omnivorous, adj., \) eating everything; 2) taking
in everything; esp. reading everything. — L.
omnivorus, 'all-devouring', compounded of
omnis, 'all, every', and -vorus, 'devouring'. See
omni- and -vorous.
Derivatives: omnivorous-ly, adv., omnivorous-
ness, n.
ото-, before a vowel от-, combining form
meaning 'shoulder', as in omodynia. — Gk. ώμο-, fr.
ώμος, 'shoulder' (for *omsos, less probably
*omsos); cogn. with OI. amsab, L. umerus,
humerus (for *omesos). See humerus and cp. the
second element in acromion, exomis, Iniomi.
ото-, combining form meaning 'raw, unripe', as
in omophagia. — Gk. ώμο-, fr. ώμόςΤ cogn.
with OI. amah, 'raw, uncooked, unripe', Arm.
hum, Olr. от, W. of, of s.m., fr. I.-E. base *omo-.
Cp. amarine.

## omodynia
omodynia, п., pain in the shoulder (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of от- and Gk. -οδυνΐα,
fr. οδύνη, 'pain'. See -odynia.

## omophagin
omophagin, п., the eating of raw flesh. — ModL.,
