fr. Gk. ώμοφαγίϊ, 'eating of raw flesh', fr.
ώμοφάγος. See omophagous and 1st -ia.

## omophagic
omophagic, adj., omophagous. — See next word
and -ic.

## omophagous
omophagous, adj., eating raw flesh. — Gk.
ώμοφάγος, compounded of ώμάς, 'raw', and the
stem of φαγεΐν, Чо eat'. See ото-, 'raw', and
-phagous.

## omoplate
omoplate, п., the shoulderblade, scapula. —
MF. (— F.) omoplate, fr. Gk. ωμοπλάτη,
compounded of ώμος, 'shoulder*, and πλάτη,
'blade', which is rel. to πλατύς, 'flat, wide,
broad'. See ото-, 'shoulder', and plate, platy-.

## omphal-
omphal-, form of omphalo- before a vowel.

## omphalitis
omphalitis, п., inflammation of the navel (med.)
— Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk.
ομφαλός, 'navel'. See omphalo-,

## omphalo-
omphalo-, before a vowel omphal-, combining
form denoting the navel. — Fr. Gk. ομφαλός,
'navel', which is cogn. with L. umbilicus, ON.
nafti, OE. nafe/a, etc., 'navel'. See navel and cp.
umbilicus. Cp. also next word.

## omphalus
omphalus, п., 1) a round stone in the temple of
Apollo at Delphi, supposed to mark the center
of the earth; 2) the boss of a shield; 3) a center.
— Gk. ομφαλός, 'navel; boss on a shield; hub'.
See prec. word.

## omrah
omrah, п., a lord of a Mohammedan court in
India. — Prop, a plural: Arab, umara', pi. of
amir, 'commander'. See emir.

## on
on, prep. — ME., fr. OE. on, an, rel. to OS. an,
ON. a, Du. aan, OHG. ana, MHG. ane, G. an,
Goth, ana, 'on, upon', and cogn. with Avestic
ana, 'on', Gk, άνά, 'on, upon', L. an- in an·
helare, 'to pant, gasp', OSlav. na, OPruss. no,
rta, 'on, upon', Lith. nuo, 'down from', fr. I.-E.
base *ano, 'on'. Cp. a, prep., the first element in
anlaut and in uuless and the second element
in upon and in the verb don. Cp. also ana-, ano-.
Derivative: on, adj.

## on
on, п., the on or leg side of the field (cricket). —
Fr. on, adj. See prec. word.

## -on
-on, suff. used to denote some inactive gases, as in
argon, radon. — Gk. -ov, neut. ending of adjs. in
-ος

## -on
-on, suff. used to denote elementary atomic
particles, as in photon. — From the ending of ion,
anion, cation.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:540 COLUMN:3 -->

## onager
onager, п., \) the Asiatic wild ass; 2) a catapult
for throwing stones. — ME., 'wild ass', fr. L.
onager, onagrus, 'wild ass', fr. Gk. 6ναγρος,
which is compounded of βνος, 'ass', and άγριος,
'wild'. The first element is a loan word fr. Asia
Minor and rel. to L. asinus, 'ass'. The second
derives fr. Gk. αγρός, 'field'. See asinine and
acre.

## onanism
onanism, п., 1) incomplete coitus; 2) self-abuse,
masturbation. — Formed with suff. -ism from
Onan, name of a son of Judah. See Gen. 38 : 9.

## once
once, adv. — ME. ones, anes, gen. of on, an, 'one'.
See one and cp. nonce.
Derivatives: once, conj. and n.

## Onchidium
Onchidium, п., a genus of marine slugs (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idium fr. Gk. όγκος,
'barb of an arrow, hook'. See onco-, 'barb,
hook', and cp. next word.

## Oncidium
Oncidium, п., a genus of tropical American
orchids, the butterfly orchid, (boi.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -idium fr. Gk. δγκος, 'barb of
an arrow, hook'; so called in allusion to the
shape of the labellum. See onco-, 'barb, hook',
and cp. prec. word.

## onco-
onco-, combining form meaning 'barb' or 'hook'.
— Gk. όγκο-, fr. βγκος, 'barb of an arrow,
hook', which stands in gradational relationship
to Gk. όίγκος, 'a bend, hollow', άγκών, 'elbow',
ΐίγκϋρα, 'an anchor'. See angle, 'corner', and
cp. words there referred to.

## onco-
onco-, combining form meaning 'bulk, mass,
tumor'. — Gk. όγκο-, fr. δγκος, 'bulk, size, mass,
body', which stands in gradational relationship
to Gk. έν-εγκεΐν, 'to bear, carry', fr. I.-E. base
*enefc-, *neli-, 'to reach, attain, carry'. See
enough.

## ondograph
ondograph, п., an instrument for recording forms
of waves in alternating currents. — A hybrid
coined fr. F. onde, 'wave' (fr. L. undo), and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφει, 'to write'v See undate and
-graph.

## ondometer
ondometer, п., wavemeter (electr.) — A hybrid
coined fr. F. onde, 'wave' (fr. L. undo), and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See undate and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## ondoyant
ondoyant, adj., wavy. — F., 'waving', pres. part,
of ondoyer, 'to wave', fr. onde, 'wave', fr. L.
undo. See undate and -ant.

## one
one, adj. — ME. oon, on, an, fr, OE. an, 'one', rel.
to OS. en, ON. einn, Dan. een, Swed. en, OFris.
an, Du. een, OHG., MHG., G. ein, Goth, ains,
'one', fr. I.-E. *oi-nos, whence also Gk. οίνος
(masc), οίνή (fern.), 'the ace (on dice)', OL.
oinos, L. unus, 'one', OSlav. -inu (in jed-inu,
'one'), lit. prob. 'hardly one', and rel. to jedva,
'hardly'; cp. also ino-rogu, 'unicorn', Lith. vienas,
OPruss. ains, Olr. din, W., Co., Bret, un, 'one'.
The indef. article an is derivatively identical with
one. Cp. once, only, any, the first element in
Angus, the second element in alone, anon, atone,
nonce, none, eleven and the last element in zoll-
verein. Cp. also inch, ounce, uncia, uni-, uni,
Unio, Uniola, union, unique, unit, unity, the first
element in unanimous, unison, universe, and the
second element in triune. Cp. also eka.
Derivatives: one, n. and indef. pron., one-ness, n.

## -one
-one, a suff. indicating an organic compound of
the ketone group, as in acetone (chem.) — Gk.
-ώνη, a fern, partronymic, used in chemistry to
denote a weaker derivative.

## oneiro-
oneiro-, before a vowel oneir-, combining form
meaning 'dream'. — Gk. ovetpo-, ovstp-, fr.
ονειρος, 'dream', which is cogn. with Arm.
anurj, 'dream', Alb. Gheg qdefe, Tosk endete,
'dream'.

## oneirocritic
oneirocritic, п., an interpreter of dreams. — Gk.
όνει,ροκρι,τ!.κός, 'interpreting dreams', fr. όνει-
ροκρίτης, 'interpreter of dreams', which is
compounded of ΰνειρος, 'dream', and κριτής, 'dis-
cerner, judge'. See oneiro- and critic.
Derivative: oneirocritic-al, adj., pertaining to
the interpretation of dreams.

## oueiromancy
oueiromancy, adj., divination through dreams. —
Compounded of oneiro- and Gk. μαντεία,
Oracle, divination'. See -mancy.

## oneiromantic
oneiromantic, adj., pertaining to oneiromancy. —
Sae oneiro- and -mantic.

## oner
oner, п., a unique person or thing (slang). —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:541 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ONEROUS | 514 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:541 COLUMN:1 -->
Formed fr. one with agential suff. -er.

## onerous
onerous, adj., burdensome, troublesome,
oppressive. — ME., fr. MF. onereus (F. οηέ-
reux), 'onerous, burdensome', fr. L. onerosus, of
s.m., fr. onus, gen. oneris, 'burden, weight'. See
onus.
Derivatives: onerous-ly, adv., onerous-ness, n.

## oneself
oneself, pron. — Compounded of one and self.

## -onic
-onic, a suff. denoting-certain acids from an -ose
compound (sugar), as in glyconic (chem.)

## onion
onion, п., a bulbous plant, Allium сера — ME.
onion, fr. OF. (= F.) oignon, fr. L. unionem,
ace. of unio, 'onion', which is usually derived fr.
Qnus, 'one', whence unio (/em.), 'unity, union',
unio (masc), 'a kind of large pearl' (the sense of
'onion', would have developed through the
intermediary sense 'string of onions'; see one, union).
However, the diphthong oi in F. oignon, shows
that the и in L. unio, 'onion', is short and that,
accordingly, unio in this sense is not a derivative
of anus, unless it is assumed that the и was
shortened in Vulgar Latin; see Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., II, 820 s.v. 1. unio, and Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 421 s.v. oignon. Cp. OProveng.
onkon, 'onion', which also comes fr. L. unionem.
OE. уппё, 'onion', is a Romance loan word.

## only
only, adj., adv., and conj. — ME. anly, only, fr.
OE. antic, 'unique, single', formed fr. an, 'one',
with suff. -lie, 'like'. See one and -like, -ly.
Derivative; onli-ness, n.

## Onoclea
Onoclea, п., a genus of plants (bol.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. όνόκλεια, synonym of ίγχουσα, 'anchusa,
alkanet'.

## onomancy
onomancy, п., divination from names or from the
letters of a name. — Shortened fr. obsol. ono-
maiomancy, fr. ML. onomatomania, 'divination
from names', fr. Gk. όνομα, 'name', and
μαντεία, Oracle, divination'. Seeonomato- and -man-
cy. The shortening of onomatomancy to
onomancy is due to haptotogy.

## onomastic
onomastic, adj., pertaining to a name or names or
naming. — Gk. ονομαστικός, 'pertaining to
naming', fr. ονομαστός, 'named', verbal adj. of
ονομάζειν, 'to name', fr. δνομα, 'name'. See
onomato- and adj. suff. -ic.

## onomasticon
onomasticon, п., a vocabulary of names. — ML.,
fr. Gk. όνομαστικόν (scil. βιβλίον),
'vocabulary', lit. 'book of names', prop. neut. of the
adj. ονομαστικός. See prec. word.

## onomato-
onomato-, combining form meaning 'name', or
'word'. — Gk. όνοματο-, from the stem of
δνομα, gen. ονόματος, 'name'. See name, п.,
and cp. words there referred to.

## onomatopoeia
onomatopoeia, п., 1) the formation of words by
imitation of the natural sounds associated with
the object designated; 2) a word so formed; 3)
the use of such words in rhetoric, poetry, etc. —
Late L.p fr. Gk. ονοματοποιία, 'the formation
of a word in imitation of a sound', lit. 'name-
making', fr. 6νομα, gen. ονόματος, 'name', and
a derivative of ποιεΐν, 'to make'. See onomato-
and poet.

## onomatopoeic
onomatopoeic, onomatopoeical, adj., pertaining
to, or characterized by, onomatopoeia; echoic.
— Formed fr. prec. word with adj. suff. -ic,
resp. also -al.
Derivative; onomatopoeic-alAy, adv.

## onomatopoetic
onomatopoetic, adj., onomatopoeic. — See prec.
word.
Derivative: onomatopoetic-al-ly, adv.

## Onopordon
Onopordon, п., a genus of plants, the cotton
thistle (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. όνόπορδον,
'cotton thistle', lit. 'the breaking of wind of an
ass', fr. 8νος, 'ass' and πορδή, 'breaking of
wind', which is rel. to πέρδεσθαι, 'to break
wind'. See onager and petrel.·

## Onosmodium
Onosmodium, п., a genus of plants, the false
gromwell (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'ass-smell',
compounded of δνος, 'ass', οσμή, 'smell, odor', and
-ώδης, 'like'. See onager, osmium and the
suffixes -ode and 1st -ium.

## onslaught
onslaught, п., onset, assault. — Formed on the
analogy of Du. aanslag, 'an attempt' (see on and
slay and cp. G. Anschlag, 'stroke; plot, design');
influenced in form by slaughter.

## onto
onto, prep. — Formed on analogy of into fr. on
and to (qq.v.) Cp. unto.

## onto-
onto-, combining form meaning 'a being,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:541 COLUMN:2 -->
individual; being, existence'. — Gk. όντο-, from the
stem of δν, gen. δντος, 'being', neut. pres. part.
of είναι, 'to be'. See esse and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also the second element in
paleontography.

## ontogenesis
ontogenesis, п., ontogeny. — Formed fr. onto-
and Gk. γένεσις, 'origin, birth, descent, race'.
See genesis,

## ontogenetic
ontogenetic, adj., pertaining to ontogeny. —
Formed fr. onto- and -genetic.
Derivative: ontogenetic-al-ly, adv.

## ontogeny
ontogeny, п., development of an individual (med.)
— Formed fr. onto- and -geny.
Derivatives: ontogen-ic, adj., ontogen-ic-al-ly,
adv., ontogen-ist, n.

## ontologism
ontologism, п., the doctrine that we have an
immediate and certain knowledge of God (philos.)
— Formed with suff. -ism fr. ModL. ontologia.
See next word.

## ontology
ontology, п., that branch of metaphysics which
deals with the nature of being as such (philos.)
— ModL. ontologia, compounded of onto- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic'). See -logy.

## onus
onus, п., a burden; obligation, charge. — L. onus,
gen. oneris, 'load, burden, weight', cogn. with
OI. anah, 'cart, waggon', possibly also with Gk.
άνίϊ, 'grief, sorrow, distress, trouble', όίνιος,
ανιαρός, άνιηρός, 'grievous, distressing', άνιαν,
άνιάζειν, 'to grieve, distress'. Cp. onerous,
exonerate.

## onward
onward, adv. — Late ME. See on and -ward.
Derivatives', onward, adj.

## onwards
onwards, adv., onward. — Formed from prec.
word with adv. gen. suff. -s.

## onych-
onych-, form of onycho- before a vowel.

## onycha
onycha, п., one of the ingredients of the Mosaic
incense (Ex. 30: 34) — Late L., 'an aromatic
substance', fr. Gk. δνυχα, ace. of δνυξ,
'fingernail, claw; onyx'. See onyx. For the derivation
of the Latin word from a Greek accusative cp.
Numidia and words there referred to.

## onycho-
onycho-, before a vowel onych-, combining form
meaning 'nail' or 'claw'. — From the stem of
Gk. δνυξ, gen. βνυχος, 'nail'. See onyx.

## onychoid
onychoid, adj., resembling a fingernail. —
Compounded of onych- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'fora, shape'. See -oid.

## onyx
onyx, п., a variety of chalcedon. — L., fr. Gk.
βνυξ, gen. βνυχος, 'fingernail, claw; onyx'. See
nail and cp. onycha, paronychia. Cp. also
sardonyx.

## oo-
oo-, combining form meaning 'egg' or 'eggs'. —
Gk. ωο-, fr. φον, 'egg', which is cogn. with L.
ovum, ON. egg, OE. Sg, 'egg'. See egg, п., and
cp. oval, ovary, ovo-, ovum. Cp. also Dioon,
Oidlum.

## oocyte
oocyte, п., an egg before maturation (biol.) —
Compounded of oo- and Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow
vessel'. See -cyte.

## ooecium
ooecium, п., a sac containing the ova in certain
Polyzoa (zool.) — ModL. ooecium,
compounded of oo- and Gk. οίκος, 'house'. See
economy.

## oof
oof, n. (slang) — Short for ooftlsh.

## ooftish
ooftish, п., money (slang) — Yiddish of tish, for
G. auf (dem) Tische, 'on the table', used in the
sense 'money down'. See up and dish.

## oofy
oofy, adj., rich (slang) — Formed fr. oof with adj.
suff. -y.

## oogamous
oogamous, adj., having cells sexually
differentiated (biol.) — Compounded of oo- and Gk.
γάμος, 'marriage'. See -gamous.

## oogenesis
oogenesis, п., formation of the ovum (biol.) —
Compounded of oo- and Gk. γένεσις, 'origin,
birth, descent, race'. See genesis.

## oogonium
oogonium, п., 1) the female reproductive organ in
certain thallophytic plants (bot.); 2) any of the
cells from which the oocytes are derived (em-
bryol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. *φογόνος, 'egg-layer'
(cp. Gk. ώαγονεΐν, 'to lay eggs'), fr. φαν, 'egg',
and γονή, Offspring, race, family, generation'.
See oo- and genus and cp. archegonium.

## oold
oold, ooidal, adj., egg-shaped. — Gk. ωοειδής,
'egg-shaped', fr. ωον, 'egg', and -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See oo-, -oid, resp. also
-al, and cp. ovojd.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:541 COLUMN:3 -->

## oolite
oolite, п., 1) a rock consisting of small grains of
carbonate of lime, resembling the roe of fish
(petrogr.); 2) (cap.) the later division of the
Jurassic system (so called because it contains
oolitic rocks) (geol.) — Compounded of oo- and
Gk. λίθος, 'stone'. See -lite.
Derivative: oolit-ic, adj.

## oology
oology, п., that branch of ornithology which deals
with birds' eggs. — Compounded of oo- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: oolog-ic-al, adj., oolog-ist, n.

## oolong
oolong, п., a kind of China tea. — Chin, wu-lung,
lit. 'black dragon'.

## oom
oom, п., an uncle. — Du., rel. to MLG. ome,
OFris. em, OHG., MHG. oheim, G. Oheim,
Ohm, which stand for WTeut. 'awahaim, lit. 'he
who dwells with the grandfather'. The first
element is cogn. with L. avus, 'grandfather',
avunculus, 'mother's brother, maternal uncle'; see
uncle. For the second element see home. Cp.
erne.

## -oob
-oob, suff. — English spelling of French -on, It.
-one, Sp. -on, fr. L. -onem, ace. of -o (cp. L. naso,
gen. -onis, 'a big-nosed man'); usually of
augmentative force. As an English formative suff.
-oon is very rare. Cp. e.g. octoroon, spitton.

## oophor-
oophor-, form of oophoro- before a vowel.

## oophore
oophore, п., an oophyte. — Compounded of oo-
and Gk. -φόρος, 'carrying, bearing'. See oo- and
-phore.

## oophorectomy
oophorectomy, п., the surgical removal of an
ovary or both ovaries (med.) — Compounded
of oophor- and Gk. -εκτομίϊ, 'a cutting out of,
fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting out'. See -ectomy.

## oophoritis
oophoritis, п., inflammation of an ovary or both
ovaries (med.) — Medical L. oophoritis, formed
fr. oophoron with suff. -itls.

## oophoro-
oophoro-, before a vowel oophor-, combining
form denoting an ovary or the ovaries. —
Medical L. oophoron, 'ovary', which is compounded
of Gk. φον, 'egg', and -φόρον, neut. of-φόρος,
'carrying, bearing'. See oo- and -phore and cp.
next word.

## oophoron
oophoron, п., an ovary. — Medical L. oophoron.
See oophore.

## Oophyte
Oophyte, п., that stage in certain plants, as ferns
and mosses, in which the reproductive organs
are developed (bot.) — Compounded of oo- and
Gk. φυτόν, 'a plant'. See -phyte.

## oosperm
oosperm, n. 1) a fertilized egg (bot.); 2) a zygote
(zool.) — Compounded of oo- and Gk. σπέρμα,
'seed'. See sperm.

## oosphere
oosphere, п., an unfertilized egg (bot.) —
Compounded of oo- and Gk. σφαίρα, 'ball globe'.
See sphere.

## oospore
oospore, п., a fertilized spore (bot.) —
Compounded of oo- and Gk. σπορά, *a sowing,
seed'. See spore.

## ootheca
ootheca, п., a case containing eggs (zool.) —
ModL. ootheca, compounded of oo- and Gk.
θήκη, 'case'. See theca.

## ooze
ooze, п., 1) an oozing; 2) something that oozes;
3) liquor used in tanning leather. — ME. wose,
wos, fr. OE. was, 'sap, juice', rel. to, and
influenced by, OE. wase, 'soft mud, mire'; rel. also
to OS. waso, 'wet ground, mire', ON. veisa, 'pond
of stagnant water', and prob. cogn. with OI.
visum, 'poison', Gk. ΐός (for *5ισός), L. virus
(for *visos), 'poison'. See virus.
Derivative: ooze, intr. v., to flow slowly, drip,
exude, percolate; tr. v., to emit by oozing.

## ooze
ooze, п., soft mud, mire. — ME. wose, fr. OE.
wase, 'soft mud, mire', rel. to OE. wos, 'sap,
juice'. See prec. word.

## oozy
oozy, adj., gently flowing. — Formed with adj.
suff. -y fr. ooze, 'an oozing'.
Derivatives: oozi-ly, adv., oozi-ness, n.

## oozy
oozy, adj., muddy, slimy. — ME. wosie, fr. wose.
See ooze, 'soft mud, mire', and adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: oozi-ly, adv., oozi-ness, n.

## op-
op-, assimilated form of ob- before p.

## opacity
opacity, п., the state or quality of being opaque;
something opaque. — F. opacite, fr. L. opaci-
tatem, ace. of opacitds, 'shadiness', fr. opticus.
See opaque and -ity.

## opacous
opacous, adj., opaque (rare) — L. opacus, 'shady,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:542 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 515 | OPISTHOGNATHOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:542 COLUMN:1 -->
dark7. See opaque. For E. -ous, as equivalent to
L. -us, see -ous.

## opah
opah, п., a spotted, brilliantly colored fish of the
Atlantic (Lampris guttatus) — W. African uba.

## opal
opal, п., a gem stone of iridescent colors. — F.
opale, fr. L. opalus, fr. Gk. όπάλλι,ος, fr. OI.
upalah (masc), 'stone, gem' [upala (fem.), 'the
upper millstone'], prob./- form of uparah,'lower,
later', which is compar. of ύρα, 'near, under,
up to, on'. See sub-.

## opalescence
opalescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## opalescent
opalescent, adj., like opal in appearance;
iridescent. — Formed fr. opal with suff. -escent.

## opaline
opaline, adj., like opal, opalescent; п., a kind of
translucent glass. — Formed fr. opal with suff.
-ine.

## opalize
opalize, tr. v., to make opalescent. — Formed fr.
opal with suff. -ize.

## opaque
opaque, adj., not transparent; dark. — F., fr. L.
opacusy 'shady, dark', which is of uncertain
etymology.
Derivatives: opaque-ly, adv., opaque-ness, n.

## ope
ope, adj. and v., open (archaic) — Shortened form
of open.

## -ope
-ope, combining form denoting one having the
condition of sight or vision expressed by a
corresponding noun ending in -opia, as in myope.
— From the stem of Gk. ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye'.
See -opia.

## open
open, adj. — ME., fr. OE., rel. to OS. opan, ON.
opinn, opin, Swed. oppen, Dan. aaben, OFris.
epen, Du. open, OHG. offan, MHG., G. offen,
'open', and prob. also to E. up (q.v.) For sense
development cp. G. aufmachen, 'to open', lit. 'to
make up'.
Derivatives: open, п., the open space, the open
air, open-ly, adv., open-ness, n.

## open
open, tr. v., to make open; intr. v., to become
open; Jo begin. — ME. openen, fr. OE. openian,
fr. open, 'open'. Cp. OS. οραηόη, οροηδη, ON.
opna, MDu., Du. openen, OHG. offanon, MHG.
offenen, G. 6ffneny 'to open', and see open, adj.

## open-eyed
open-eyed, adj. — First used by Shakespeare.

## opera
opera, п., a drama sung. — It., "work, labor,
composition', fr. L. opera, 'service, pains, work,
labor' (whence also OF. uevre, oevre, F. auvre,
'work'), fr. opus, gen. operis (see opus and cp.
the second element in maneuver); introduced
into English by the diarist John Evelyn (1620-
1706).

## opera
opera, n. pi., works. — L., pi. oiopus\ 'work'. See
opus,

## operable
operable, adj., capable of treatment by operation.
— Late L. operabilis, 'working', fr. L. operari,
'to work'. See operate and -able.
Derivatives: operabil-ity, п., operabi-y, adv.

## operate
operate, intr. and tr. v. — L. operatus, pp. of
operari, 'to work, labor', fr. opus, gen. operis.
See opus and verba] suff. -ate.
Derivatives: operat-ing, adj., operation (q.v.),
operative (q.v.), operat-or, n.

## operatic
operatic, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
an opera. — Irregularly formed fr. opera, 'a
drama sung', on analogy of dramatic.
Derivative: operatic-al-ly, adv.

## operation
operation, n. — ME. operacion, fr. MF. (— F.)
operation, fr. L. operationem, ace. of operdtio, 'a
working, operation', fr. operatus, pp. of operari.
See operate and -ion.
Derivatives: operation-al, adj., operation-al-ly,
adv.

## operative
operative, adj. — MF. (= F.) operari/(fem.
operative), fr. Late L. operdttvus, 'formative,
creative', fr. L. operatus, pp. of operari. See operate
and -ive.
Derivatives: operative, п., I) worker in a factory,
artisan; 2) a detective, operative-ly, adj., oper-
ative-ness, n.

## operatize
operatize, tr. v., to make into an opera.—A hybrid
coined fr. opera 'a drama sung', and -ize, a suff.
of Gk. origin.

## opercular
opercular, adj., pertaining to an operculum. —
See operculum and adj. suff. -ar.

## operculate
operculate, operculated, adj., furnished with an
operculum. — See next word and the adj. suff.
-ate, resp. also -ed.

## operculum
operculum, п., 1) a lid or lidlike part; 2) in fishes»

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:542 COLUMN:2 -->
the gill cover; 3) in certain gastropod mollusks,
the lidlike process which closes the shell when
the animal is retracted {zoo/.); 4) the lid of the
seed capsules in certain plants (bot.) — L.
operculum, 'cover, lid', for *oper-tlom, formed with
instrumental suff. *-tlom fr. operire, 'to cover,
hide, conceal', which is formed fr. ob- and l.-E.
base *wer-, 'to enclose, cover'. See weir and cp.
aperient, cover.

## operetta
operetta, п., a light opera. — It., dimin. of opera.
See opera.

## operose
operose, adj., laborious. — L. operosus, 'taking
great pains, laborious', fr: opus, gen. operis,
'work'. See opus and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: operose-ly, adv., operose-ness,
n.

## Ophelia
Ophelia, fem. PN. — Fr. Gk. ωφέλεια, or ώφε-
λίϊ, 'help, aid', fr. ώφελεΐν, 'to help, aid, assist',
δφελος, 'advantage, help', which is of uncertain
origin. It is perh. cogn. with OI. phalam, 'fruit,
advantage', pha/ati, 'thickens, clots, curdles'.
о phi-, form of ophio- before a vowel.

## ophiasis
ophiasis, п., a kind of baldness (med.) — Gk,
όφίασις, 'bald place on the head, of serpentine
form', fr. *όφιάζειν, 'to have a serpentine form',
fr. όφις, 'serpent'. See ophidian and -iasis.

## ophfcleide
ophfcleide, п., a large brass wind instrument, —
F. ophicleide, lit. 'keyed serpent', fr. Gk. όφις,
'serpent', and κλείς, gen. κλείδας, 'key'. See
ophidian and cleido-.

## Ophidla
Ophidla, n. pi., the division of the snakes or
serpents (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. όφίδιο^, 'a little
snake', dimin. of βφις, 'snake'. See next word.

## ophidian
ophidian, adj., pertaining to. the Ophidia or
snakes; п., a snake. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
Gk. όφίδιον, 'a little snake', dimin. of βφις,
'snake', which is of uncertain etymology. It is
possibly borrowed fr. Heb. eph'eh or Aram.
арка, 'a viper', prop, 'the hissing animal', fr.
Heb. ρά'ά , resp. AraA. p&ia, 'it hissed'; see
Heinrich Lewy, Die semitischen Fremdworter
im Griechischen, Berlin, 1895, p. 13. Cp. ophio-,
ophiasis, ophite and the second element in
Gymnophiona, Carphophis.

## ophio-
ophio-, before a vowel ophi-, combining form
meaning 'snake, serpent'. — Gk. όφιο-, δφι-,
fr. ΰφις, 'snake, serpent*. See ophidian.

## Ophiogtossaceae
Ophiogtossaceae, n. pi., the adder's tongue
family (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Ophioglos-
sum with suff. -aceae.

## ophioglossaceous
ophioglossaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Ophioglossum
Ophioglossum, п., a genus of plants, the adder's
tongue. — ModL., compounded of Gk. δφις,
'serpent' and γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See ophidian
and gloss, 'interpretation'.

## ophiolatry
ophiolatry, п., serpent worship. — Compounded
of ophio- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρία, fr.
λατρεία, 'hired labor, service, worship'. See
-latry.

## ophiology
ophiology, п., that branch of zoology which deals
with snakes. — Compounded of ophio- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ophiolog-ic, ophiolog-ic-al, adjs.,
ophiolog-ist, n.

## ophiomancy
ophiomancy, п., divination by the observation of
the movements of serpents. — Compounded of
ophio- and Gk. μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'.
See -mancy.

## Ophir
Ophir, п., a land rich in gold, precious stones and
almug trees. — Heb. Ophir. See 1 Kings 9:28,
10:11,22:48; II Chron. 8:17 and 9:10.

## ophite
ophite, п., a green stone (mineral.) — L. ophites,
fr. Gk. οφίτης^α]. λίθος), 'a stone spotted like
a serpent', fr. 6φις, 'serpent'. See ophidian and
subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: ophit-ic, adj.

## Ophite
Ophite, п., one of a sect of Gnostics who
regarded the serpent as the symbol of wisdom.
They were called also Naassenes. — Formed
with suff. -ite fr. Gk. δφις, 'serpent'. See
ophidian and cp. prec. word.

## Ophiuchus
Ophiuchus, п., a northern constellation (astron.)
— L., fr. Gk. όφιοΰχος, lit. 'holding a serpent',
fr. όφις, 'serpent', and the stem of έχε^ν, 'to
hold, keep, have'. See ophidian and hectic and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:542 COLUMN:3 -->
cp. the second element in eunuch.

## ophthalm-
ophthalm-, form of ophthalmo- before a vowel.

## ophthalmia
ophthalmia, п., inflammation of the eyeball or the
conjunctiva. — Late L., fr. Gk. όφθαλμία, fr.
οφθαλμός, 'the eye*. See ophthalmo-.

## ophthalmic
ophthalmic, adj., pertaining to the eye. — L.
ophthalmicus, fr. Gk. οφθαλμικός, 'pertaining
to the eye', fr. οφθαλμός, 'the eye'. See
ophthalmo-.

## ophthalmitis
ophthalmitis, п., ophthalmia (med.) — Medical L
See ophthalm- and -itis.

## ophthalmo-
ophthalmo-, before a vowel ophthaim-, combining
form denoting the eye or the eyes. — Gk.
οφθαλμό-, όφθαλμ-, fr. οφθαλμός, 'the eye', which
prob. is of uncertain origin. It stands perh. for
*όπσ-θαλμός and lit. means 'eye socket', fr.
♦όττσ-, 'the eye', and *θάλμος, shortened form
of θάλαμος, 'inner room, chamber'. The first
element derives fr. I.-E. *oqw(e)s-, 'eye', whence
also 6σσε (for *6κιε}, 'both eyes'. See eye and
cp. optic. For the second element see thalamus.

## ophthalmology
ophthalmology, п., that branch of medicine which
deals with the eye, its functions and diseases. —
Compounded of ophthalmo- and Gk. -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)\ See
-logy.
Derivatives: ophthalmolog-ic-al, adj.,
ophthalmologist, n.

## ophthalmometer
ophthalmometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the eye. — Coined by the German physicist and
anatomist Hermann· Ludwig Ferdinand von
Helmholtz (1821-94) in 1852 fr. ophthalmo- and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## ophthalmoscope
ophthalmoscope, п., an instrument for the
examination of the interior of the eye.—Coined by
von Helmholtz (see prec. word) in 1852 fr.
ophthalmo- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to
look at, examine'. See -scope.
Derivatives: ophthalmo scop-ic,
ophthalmoscopic^/, adjs., ophthalmoscop-ist, п., ophthalmo-
scop-у, n.

## -opia
-opia, -ору, combining form denoting a
condition of sight or vision. — Gk. -ωπία, from the
stem of ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye', fr. I.-E. base
*okw-, a collateral form of base *okw-. See
optic and cp. -ope, -ops, -opsia, -opsis.

## opiate
opiate, adj., containing opium; narcotic; п., а
drug containing opium; anything soothing; tr.
v., to treat with an opiate; to narcotize. — ML.
opiatus, fr. L. opium. See opium and adj. suff.
-ate.

## opinable
opinable, adj., 1) that which is a matter of
opinion; 2) capable of being opined. — L. opinabilist
'that which rests on opinion; conjectured', fr.
opinari. See next word and -able.

## opine
opine, tr. and intr. v., to hold an opinion; to
think, suppose (now humorous). — MF. (= F.)
opiner, fr. L. opinari, 'to think, suppose', fr.
*opiot gen. -oniSy 'expectation', which is rel. to
optdre, "to choose, wish*, optio, 'choice', and
prob. cogn. with OSlav. za-Q)apu, 'conjecture',
ne-vuz-apinu, 'unexpected1. Cp. next word and
option.

## opinion
opinion, п., what one thinks, judgment, belief. —
ME., fi\ OF. (^ F.), fr. L. орХпхбпет, асе. of
opinio, 'opinion, conjecture', fr. opinari. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: opinion-at-ed, adj.,opinion-at-ed-ly,
adv., opinion-at-ed-ness, n.

## opisometer
opisometer, п., an instrument for measuring
curved lines. — Compounded of Gk. οπίσω,
'backward', and μέτρον, 'measure'. Seeopistho-
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## opisth-
opisth-, form of oplstho- before a vowel.

## opisthenar
opisthenar, п., the back of the hand (anat.) —
Medical L., compounded of Gk. οπίσω,
'backward' (see next word), and θέναρ, 'palm of the
hand', for which see thenar.

## opistho-
opistho-, before a vowel opizth-, combining form
meaning 'backward'. — Gk. όπι,σθο-, όπισθ-,
fr. δπισθεν, 'behind, at the back, after', rel. to
οπίσω, 'backward', and cogn. with L. obt
'toward, against'. See ob- and cp. the first element
in opizometer.

## opisthognathous
opisthognathous, adj., having retreating jaws. —
Compounded of opistho- and -gnathous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:543 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OPIUM | 516 | press, 'to squeeze'. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:543 COLUMN:1 -->

## opium
opium, п., the solidified juice of the opium poppy,
Papaver somniferum. — L., fr. Gk. δπιον,
'poppy juice', fr. οπός, 'vegetable juice', which is
prob. cogn. with OSlav. soku, 'juice of plants
and fruits', Lith. sakaT (pi.), OPruss. sackis,
Lett, svakas, 'resin*. Cp. opo-, opodeldoc.

## opiumism
opiumism, п., the habitual use of opium. —
Formed from prec. word with sun", -ism.

## opo-
opo-, combining form meaning 'juice'. — Gk.
όπο-, fr. οπός, 'juice'. See opium.

## opodeldoc
opodeldoc, п., a camphorated soap liniment
(med.) — Coined by Paracelsus, prob. fr. Gk.
οπός, 'juice'. See opium.

## opopanax
opopanax, п., a gum resin. — L., fr. Gk. όπό-
παναξ, 'gum resin', lit. 'juice of a herb that heals
all diseases', fr. οπός, 'juice', and πάναξ = παν-
ακές, name of a plant, which is prop neut. of
the adj. πανακής, 'all-healing', fr. παν, 'all', and
α*κος, 'remedy'. See opium and panacea.

## opossum
opossum, п., a small marsupial animal of
America. — Fr. Algonquian apasum, *a white animal'.

## oppidan
oppidan, adj., pertaining to a town; urban; п., 1)
a townsman; 2) at Eton College in England, a
member of the school who boards in town. —
L, oppidanus, 'pertaining to, or living in, a town',
fr. oppidum, 'town', which is of uncertain
etymology. It stands pern, for *op-pedom, fr. ob-
and *pedom = Gk. πέδον, 'ground, earth,
plain' (see foot), hence lit. meaning 'that which
is situated in the plain'.

## oppilate
oppilate, tr. v., to obstruct, esp. the bowels. — L.
oppilatus, pp. of oppilare, 'to block up', fr. ob-
ax\d pildre, 'to press, compress', fr. pila, 'pillar'.
See pillar and verbal suff. -ate and cp. compile.

## oppllation
oppllation, п., obstruction, esp. of the bowels. —
L. oppilutio, gen. -onis, 'a blocking up', fr.
oppilatus, pp. of oppilare. See oppilate and -ion.

## opponency
opponency, п., opposition, antagonism. —
Formed from next word with surT. -cy.

## opponent
opponent, adj., opposite; opposing; n. an
adversary. — L. opponens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
opponere, 'to oppose', fr. ob- and ponere, 'to
place'. See position and cp. opposite. For the
ending see surT. -ent.

## opportune
opportune, adj., 1) appropriate; 2) timely. — ME.,
fr. OF. (= F.) opportun (fem. opportune), fr. L.
opportunus, for ob-portunus, 'suitable,
convenient, seasonable, advantageous', lit. 'leading
to the port or harbor', fr. ob- and portus,
'harbor*. See port, 'harbor', and cp.
importunate.
Derivatives: opportune-Iy, adv., opportune-ness,
п., opportunism (q.v.), opportunist (q.v.),
opportunity (q.v.)

## opportunism
opportunism, п., the habit or policy of adapting
one's actions to circumstances. — F. opportu-
nisme. See next word and -ism.

## opportunist
opportunist, п., time-server. — F. opportuniste,
coined by the French politician and playwright
Henri Rochefort (1830-1913) in 1876 and
applied by him to Gambetta. See opportune and
-ist.

## opportnuity
opportnuity, n. — ME. oportunite, fr. OF. (= F.)
opportunite, fr. L. opportunitatem, ace. of oppor-
tunitas, 'fitness, convenience, suitableness', fr.
opportunus. See opportune and -ity.

## opposal
opposal, п., examination (obsol.) — Formed
from next word with adj. surT. -al. Cp. puzzle.

## oppose
oppose, tr. and intr. v. — F. opposer, fr. OF., fr.
L. opponere (pp. oppositus), 'to place against',
which was Gallicized after F. poser, 'to put,
place*. See opponent and cp. compose and words
there referred to. See also pose, *to place1.
Derivatives: oppos-ablet adj., oppos-abil-ity, п.,
opposite (q.v.), opposition (q.v.), opposit-ive,
adj., opposit-ive-lyt adv., opposit-ive-ness, n.

## opposite
opposite, adj. — ME., fr. OF. fr. L. oppositus, pp.
of opponere. See opponent.
Derivatives: opposite, п., opposite-ly, adv., op-
posite-ness, n.

## opposition
opposition, n. — ME. opposicioun, fr. L. oppositto,
gen. -onis, 'a placing against', fr. oppositus, pp.
of opponere. See prec. word and -ion.

## oppress
oppress, tr. v. — ME. oppresses fr. OF.
oppresses fr. Late L. oppressare, freq. of L. opprimere
(pp. oppressus), 'to press against or down, to
oppress', fr. ob- and premere, 'to press'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:543 COLUMN:2 -->

## oppression
oppression, n. — MR, fr. OF. oppression, fr. L.
oppressionem, ace. of oppressio, 'a pressing
down, violence, oppression', fr. oppressus, pp.
of opprimere. See prec. word and -ion.

## oppressive
oppressive, adj. — ML. oppressivus, fr. L.
oppressus, pp. of opprimere. See oppress and -ive.
Derivatives: oppressive-ly, adv.,
oppressiveness, n.

## oppressor
oppressor, n. — ME., fr. AF. oppressour,
corresponding to F. oppresseur, fr. L. oppressorem,
ace. of oppressor, fr. oppressus, pp, of opprimere.
See oppress and agential suff. -or.

## opprobrious
opprobrious, adj., disgraceful, infamous. — ME.,
fr. OF. opprobrieus, fr. Late L. opprobriosus, fr.
L. opprobrium. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: opprobrious-ly, adv., opprobrious-
ness, n.

## opprobrium
opprobrium, n. disgrace, infamy. — L.
opprobrium, 'reproach, taunt, disgrace', formed fr, ob-
andprobrum, 'reproach, disgraceful act, infamy',
which stands for *pro-bhr-om and is rel. to pro-
ferre, 'to carry forward'; opprobrium lit. means
'that which is brought forward against'. For
sense development cp. the cognate Gk.
προφέρει, 'to bring forward; to reproach'. See pro-
and bear, 'to carry', and cp. exprobrate.

## oppugn
oppugn, tr. v., to fight against, oppose; to
controvert. — L. oppugnare, 'to fight against,
attack, assail', fr. ob- and'pugnare, 'to fight'. See
pugnacious and cp. expugn, impugn.

## Ops
Ops, п., the wife of Saturn, mother of the gods,
and goddess of the harvest in Roman
mythology. — L. Ops, personification of ops, gen. opts,
'abundance, plenty, wealth, riches'. See opulent.

## -ops
-ops, combining form used in zool. and bot., in
the sense of '-eyed', as in Stylops. — Gk. -ωψ,
fr. ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye, face', fr. I.-E. base
*oqw-, 'eye'. See eye and cp. -opia.
•opsia, also -opsy, combining form denoting a
certain kind of vision, as in achromatopsia,
autopsy. — Gk. -οψία, fr. οψις, 'sight'. See -opsis.

## opsimath
opsimath, п., one who begins to learn late in life
(rare). — Gk. όψιμαθής, 'late to learn',
compounded of όψέ, 'late', and μαθ-, stem of μαν-
θ-άνειν, 'to learn'. The first element is rel. to
οπίσω, 'backward', δπισθεν, 'behind', and
cogn. with L. ob, 'toward, against*. See ob- and
cp. opistho- and the first element in opisometer.
For the second element see mathematic.

## opsimathy
opsimathy, п., learning acquired late (rare). —
Gk. όψιμαθίά, fr. αψιμαθής. See prec. word
and -y (representing Gk. -ία.).

## -opsis
-opsis, combining form meaning 'sight', as in
Ampelopsis, Galeops'ts (bot. and zool.) — Gk.
-οψις, fr. οψις, 'sight, appearance, view', fr.
I.-E. base *oqw-, 'to see; eye', whence also δψ,
gen. οπός, 'eye, face', οψομαι, Ί shall see'. See
optic.

## opsonic
opsonic, adj., pertaining to opsonin (bacteriol.)
— See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## opsonin
opsonin, п., a substance in the blood which
increases the power of the phagocytes to destroy
bacteria (bacteriol.) — Coined by the English
physician and pathologist Sir Almroth Edward
Wright (born in 1861) in 1903 fr. Gk. όψωνεΐν,
'to buy food', which is compounded of δψον,
'meat, fish', and ώνεΐσθαι, 'to buy'. Gk. #ψον
is of uncertain origin. It is perh. formed fr. pref.
o-, 'with, together with', and *ψον, 'food',
which is rel. to ψωμός, 'mouthful', ψην, 'to
rub, grind down, chew'; see psephism. Gk.
ώνεΐσθαι, 'to. buy', derives fr. ώνή, 'purchase',
which is cogn. with Ol. vasnah, 'purchase
money', vasnayati, 'he bargains for', L. vinus,
'sale', vendere, 'to sell'; see venal.
-opsy. — See -opsin.

## opt
opt, intr. v. — F. opter, fr. L. optdre, 'to choose,
wish'. See option, and cp. next word.

## optative
optative, adj., expressing wish or desire; п., the
optative mood. — MF. (= F.) optatif (fem.
optative), fr. Late L. optativus, fr. L. optatus, pp.
of optare, 'to choose, wish'. See option and -ive.

## optic
optic, adj., pertaining to the eye or sight. — MF.
(— F.) optique, fr. ML. opticus, fr. Gk. οπτικός,
'pertaining to the eyes or sight', fr. όπτός, 'seen;
visible', verbal adj. of δψομαι, Ί shall see', fr.
I.-E. base *oqw-, 'eye; to see', whence also δψ,
gen. οπός, 'eye, face', δψις, 'sight', δπωπα, Ί

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:543 COLUMN:3 -->
have seen', οπή, 'an opening, hole', δσσε (for
*okwye), 'the two eyes', βμμα, 'eye'. From
*oqw-, a collateral form of *oqw-, derives Gk.
ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye'. See eye and cp. omma,
ophthalmo-. Cp. also antelope, catoptric,Cecrops,
dtopstde, epopt, Ethiop, metope, myope,
orthoptic, Oxyopidae, panoptic, panopticon, scioptic,
stenopaic, synoptic, and the combining forms
-ope, -opia, -ops, -opsia, -opsis, -opto-.
Derivatives: optic, n. (q.v.), optic-al, adj.,
optically, adv., optician (q.v.), optics (q.v.)

## optic
optic, п., an eye (colloq.) — Fr. prec. word.

## opticinn
opticinn, п., one who makes or sells optical
instruments. — F. opticien, fr. ML. optica. See
next word and -ian.

## optics
optics, п., the science that deals with sight. — PI.
of the adjective optic, used as a noun, in
rendering ML. optica (pi.), fr. Gk. τά οπτικά,
'optics', neut. pi. of οπτικός, 'pertaining to the
eyes or sight'. See optic, adj., and -ics.

## optimates
optimates, n. pi., the aristrocracy of ancient
Rome. — L. optimates, 'aristocrats', lit.
'adherents of the best men', pi. of optimas, fr.
optimus, 'best'. See optimism.

## optime
optime, п., one of the second class {senior optime)
or third class (junior optime) in the
mathematical Tripos at Cambridge University
(differentiated from the wranglers, i.e. those belonging
to the first class). — L., 'best', adv. fr. optimus.
See optimism.

## optimism
optimism, п., \) in philosophy, a) the doctrine of
Leibnitz that this world is the best possible
world; b) the belief that good will ultimately
prevail over evil in the world; 2) the tendency
to take a hopeful view of things. — F. optimis-
me, fr. L. optimum, neut. of optimus, 'best'
(used as superl. of bonus, 'good'), which prob.
stands for *opitumos, fr. base *opi-t seen in ops,
'wealth'; accordingly optimus orig. meant 'the
richest1, but was used later in the senses 'the
most esteemed, the most distinguished, the
best'. See opulent and -ism. For the superl. suff.
*-tumos see aftermost and cp. words there
referred to. The term optimisme was coined by
the Jesuits. It first occurs in the Memoires de
Trevoux conducted by them (in the number for
February 1737, where it is introduced with the
words 'le systeme de XOptimum ou YOpti-
misme'*).

## optimist
optimist, п., a believer in optimism. — F. opti-
miste, fr. L. optimus, 'best'. See prec. wbrd and
-ist.
Derivatives: optimist-ic, optimist-ic-al, adjs.,
optimist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## optimum
optimum, п., the best condition, degree, etc. —
L., neut. of optimus, 'best'. See optimism.

## option
option, n. — F., fr. L. optionem, ace. of optio,
'choice', fr. *opio, opere, pp. *optus, 'to choose',
whence optivus, 'chosen', and the freq. verb op-
tare, 'ttrchoose, wish'. See opine and cp.
optative. Cp. also adopt, coopt.
Derivatives: option, tr. v., option-al, adj., op-
tion-al-ly, adv.

## opto-
opto-, combining form meaning vision, optic. —
Fr. Gk. απτός, 'seen, visible', verbal' adj. of
δψομαι, Ί shall see'. See optic.

## optometer
optometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
power and range of vision. — Compounded of
opto- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'; see meter,
'poetical rhythm'. The name optometer, which
orjg. denoted an instrument for measuring focal
distances, was coined by Porterfield in 1738.
Derivatives: optometr-ist, п., optometr-y, n.

## optophone
optophone, п., an instrument for converting light
energy into sound energy. — Compounded of
opto- and Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice*. See phone.

## opulence
opulence, also opulency, п., wealth; abundance.
— L. opulentia, fr. opulentus or opulens. See
next word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## opulent
opulent, adj., wealthy; abundant. — L. opulentus,
or opulens, gen. -entis, 'wealthy, rich', lit.
'resourceful, powerful', formed with suff. -u-lentus,
resp. -u-lens, 'full of, abounding in, rich in', fr.
ops, gen. opis, 'strength, power, might,
abundance, plenty, wealth, riches, treasure', which is
rel. to opus, gen. operis, 'work, labor, exertion',
and cogn. with άρ-n-as, 'produce, possession',
Avestic afnah-vant, 'rich in possession', Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:544 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 517 | ORCHIECTOMY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:544 COLUMN:1 -->
δμπνη, 'corn, food', ΐίμπνιος, 'of corn,
nourishing, "Ομπνια, 'mother of corn' (a name of
the goddess Demeter), Lith. apstus, 'copious*,
apstas, 'abundance'. Cp. also the Latin PN.
Opsct, Osci, lit. 'the worshipers of Ops'. See
opus and -ulent and cp. Ops, optimism, Oscan,
office. Cp. also copious, copy.

## Opuntia
Opuntia, п., a genus of plants, the prickly pear
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. Opuntia (herba), 'the
Opuntian plant', fern, of Opuntius, 'of Opus,
Opuntian', fr. Opus, fr. Gk. Όποΰς, name of a
town in Locris (in Greece), where this plant
grew in abundance.

## opus
opus, п., a work; a composition, esp. a musical
composition. — L. opus, gen. operis, 'work,
labor, exertion', whence opera, 'service, pains,
work, labor', operart, 'to work, labor'; re], to
ops, gen. opis, 'strength, power, might,
abundance, plenty, wealth, riches, treasure', and
cogn. with OI. apas-, 'work', dpas-t 'work,
religious act', OHG. uoben (fr. *objan), 'to start
work; to practice; to honor', MHG. ueben, G.
iiben, 'to exercise,-practice', OHG. uoba,
'celebration', uobo, 'farmer', MHG. uop,
'agriculture; usage, custom1, OS. obian, 'to celebrate*,
Du. oefenen, ON. a/a, Dan. eve, 'to exercise,
practice', ON. efna, 'to accomplish', OE. xjnan,
efnan, 'to perform'. All these words derive fr.
I.-E. base *op- (Teut. *ob-), 'to work', orig.
used of agriculture, in Old Indian, Latin and
Teutonic applied also to religious acts. See
opulent and cp. next word. Cp. also opera,
operate, operetta, operose, average, 'feudal service',
inure.

## opuscule
opuscule, п., a small work. — L. opusculum,
dimin. of opus, 'work'. See opus and -cule.

## oquassa
oquassa, п., a small lake trout. — Named after
Oquassa Lake in Maine.

## or
or, conj. indicating an alternative; often used in
correlation to either or whether. — ME. or, fr.
ME. other, outher, auther, 'either, or', fr. OE.
едба, одде rel. to OS. еддо, ON. еда, OHG.
odar, odo, eddo, MHG. oder, ode, G. oder, Goth.
aippau, OS. eftha, efthe, OFris. ieftha, MDu.
ofte, 'or'. The r in ME. other, OHG. odar, etc.,
is prob. due to the influence of either, resp.
OHG. wedar, 'neither'. Cp. nor.

## or
or, conj. and prep., ere, before (archaic) — ME.
ar, or,Sr. ON. or, 'early' (adv.) See ere.

## or
or, n. (her.), 1) gold; 2) the color yellow. — F.,
'gold', fr. L. aurum. See aureate and cp. oriole,
ormolu, oroide, orphrey, orpiment.
■or, suff. forming nouns of quality, state or
condition, as in error, terror. — ME. -our, fr. OF.
-our (F. -cur)t fr. L. -drem, ace. of -or, fr. earlier
-os, gen. -oris, a suff. added to verbal stems. In
Great Britain this suff. is usually spelled -our, in
correspondence with the OF. and ME. form.
The American spelling of this suff. is -or.

## -or
-or, suff. denoting an agent or an instrument. —
1) ME. -or, -our, fr. OE. -eor, -eur (F. -eur), fr.
L. -drem, ace. of -or, a suff. added to the pp.
stem of verbs (cp. e.g. actor, author); 2) ME.
-or, -our, fr. OF. -eor, -eur (F. -eur), fr. L. -ato-
rem, ace. of -ator (cp. e.g. donor, emperor); see
-tor, -ator. Cp. the agential suflf. -er. According
to the general rule, -or is added to words of
Latin, -er to those of English origin.

## orach
orach, orache, п., any plant of the genus Atriplex
— ME. arache, arage, fr. OF. arrache (F. arro-
che), fr. VL. *atrapica, *atripica, fr. L. atriplex
(whence also It. atrepice), ultimately fr. Gk.
άτράφαξυς, which is of unknown origin. Cp.
Atriplex.

## oracle
oracle, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) fr. L. oraculum
(for *6ra-tlom), 'divine announcement, oracle',
formed with instrumental suff. *-tlom fr. oro,
orare, 'to speak, pray, beseech'. See oration.

## oracular
oracular, adj, — L. drdculdrius, 'dealing in
oracles, prophetic', fr. oraculum. See oracle and -ar.
Derivatives: oracular-ly, adv., oracular-ity, n.

## oral
oral, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. os,
gen. oris, 'mouth, face; opening, entrance,
orifice*, fr. *ous-, whence the collective noun dra
(for *os-a), 'border, coast'; cogn. with OI. ah,
as-άη, 'mouth', dsyam, 'mouth; opening'', Aves-
tic ah-, 'mouth', Hitt. aish (gen. ishash), Mir a,
'mouth', ON. oss, 'mouth of a river', OE. or,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:544 COLUMN:2 -->
'beginning, origin, front', ora, 'bank, shore',
Alb. ane (for *ausna), 'side, border'. Cp. coram,
orifice, orle, orotund, oscitancy, ostiary, ostlole,
usher, Auriga, vera.
Derivative: oral-ly, adv.

## orange
orange, n. — ME. orenge, orange, fr. MF. orenge
(F. orange), in pomme d'Orenge, fr. It. arancia
(in Olt. melarancia, lit. Orange-apple'), fr.
Arab, ndranj (whence also Sp. naranja, Port.
laranja, MGk. υεράντζιον), fr. Pers. narang, fr.
OI. nurahgah, 'orange tree', which is of
uncertain origin. The change of nar-ange to or-ange is
prob. due to the influence of the name of the
town Orange, an important transit station for
the oranges bound for the north of France.
The usual explanation that the change
mentioned is due to a confusion with F. or, 'gold' (see
aurum), must be abandoned owing to the fact
that originally and for many centuries the fruit
was called in French pomme d4orange, which
makes it probable that orange was regarded as a
place name. See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p.
425 s.v. orange.
Derivative: orange, adj.

## oraugeade
oraugeade, п., a drink made of orange juice,
water and sugar. — F., formed fr. orange on the
analogy of lemonade. See prec. word and -ade.

## orangery
orangery, п., a place where orange trees are
cultivated. — F. orangerie, fr. orange. See orange
and -ery.

## orangutan
orangutan, n. — Malay, 'man of the woods, wild
man', fr. orang, 'man', and (h)utan, 'forest,
wild', used only of the savage tribes inhabiting
the Sunda Islands. The word was
misunderstood by the Europeans and applied to this
anthropoid ape.

## orate
orate, intr. v., to make a long oration. — Back
formation from oration.

## oration
oration, п., a formal speech. — L. ordtio, gen.
-onis, 'speaking, discourse, language, prayer', fr.
dratus, pp. of orare, 'to speak, pray, beseech',
which prob. derives from the I.-E. imitative base
*6r-, *er-, which appears also in OI. dryanti,
'they praise', Homeric Gk. αρή, Att. άρά (for
*apfa or *apaF5c), 'prayer, άράομαι, Ί pray,
supplicate', Arm. uranam, Ί deny', Hitt. ariya-,
'to ask the oracle', aruwa(i)-, 'to revere,
worship'. Cp. orison, which is a doublet of oration.
Cp. also oracle, orator, oratorio, oratory, adore,
inexorable, peroration. L. orare is not a
derivative of os, gen. 5hs, 'mouth' (see oral).

## orator
orator, n. — ME. oratour, fr. OF. oratour (F. ora-
tehr), fr. L. drdtorem, ace. of orator, 'speaker,
orator', fr. orare. See prec. word.
Derivatives: orator-ic, orator-ic-al, adjs., orator-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## oratorian
oratorian, adj., pertaining to an oratory. — See
oratory and -an.

## oratorio
oratorio, п., a long musical composition, usually
with a text based on Scriptures (mus.) — It., fr.
Eccl. L. oratdrium, 'place of prayer' (see oratory,
'a small chapel'); so called from the oratory of
St. Philip Neri in Rome, where such
compositions were first performed.

## oratory
oratory, п., the art of the orator, eloquence — L.
(ars) oratorio, "oratorical art', fern, of dratdrius,
'pertaining to an orator', fr. orator. See orator.

## oratory
oratory, п., a small chapel — ME. oratorie, fr.
Eccl. L. oratdrium, 'place of prayer' (whence
also F. oratoire), fr. L. dratorius, 'pertaining to
prayer; pertaining to an orator'. See prec. word.

## orb
orb, п., a sphere, globe; the emblem of
sovereignty. — MF. (= F.) orbe, fr. OF., fr. L. orbem,
ace. of orbis, 'circle, ring, round surface," disk',
whence orbita, 'rut or track made in the ground
by a wheel'; of uncertain etymology. Cp.
orbicular, orbit.
Derivatives: orb, tr. v., to form into a circle; to
encircle, orb-y, adj.

## orbicular
orbicular, adj., having the shape of an orb;
spherical. — ME. orbiculer, fr. Late L. orbicularis,
'circular, orbicular', fr. L. orbiculus, dimin. of
orbis. See orb and the Suffixes -cule and -ar.

## orbiculate
orbiculate, orbiculated, adj., orbicular. — See
prec. word and adj, suff. -ate, resp. also -ed.

## orbit
orbit, п., the eye socket (anat.) — L. orbiia, 'a
track or rut made in the ground by a wheel*, fr.
orbis; see orb. In its anatomical sense the word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:544 COLUMN:3 -->
orbita was first used by Gerard of Cremona, the
translator of Avicenna's Canon. Cp. periorbita.
Derivatives: orbit-al, orbit-ary, adjs.

## orbito-
orbito-, combining form denoting the orbit (anat.)
— See prec. word.

## ore
ore, п., the grampus. — L. orca, 'a kind of whale',
fr. Gk. ορυγα, ace. of δρυξ, 'a kind of whale'; с
for g in L. orca is due either to contamination
with L. orca in the sense of 'butt, tun' (see ur-
ceolate), or to Etruscan influence. For the
derivation of the Latin word from a Greek
accusative cp. Numidia and words there referred to.
Cp. next word and Orcinus.

## orca
orca, п., 1) a killer whale; 2) (tap.) the genus
consisting of the killer whale (zoo/.) — L., 'a
kind of whale'. See prec. word.

## Orcadian
Orcadian, adj., ]) pertaining to the Orkney
Islands; 2) a native of the Orkney Islands. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Orcades, 'the
Orkney Islands'.

## orchard
orchard, n. — ME., fr. OE. ortgeard, orceard, a
hybrid coined fr. VL. *orto (whence also It.
orto), 'garden', fr. L. hortus, of s.m., and OE.
geard, 'enclosure, yard'. Cp. the rel. Goth.
aurtigards, 'orchard', a hybrid coined fr. VL.
*orto and Goth, gards, 'house', and see
horticulture and yard, 'enclosure'.
Derivatives: orchard, tr. v., orchard-ing, п.,
orchard-ist, n.

## orchestic
orchestic, adj., pertaining to dancing. — Gk.
ορχηστικός, fr. δρχηστής, 'dancer'. See
orchestra and adj. suff. -ic.

## orchestics
orchestics, п., the art of dancing. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## orchestra
orchestra, п., 1) in the Greek theater, the place
where the chorus danced; 2) in the modern
theater, the space between the stage and
auditorium, reserved for the musicians. — L. orchestra,
fr. Gk. ορχήστρα, 'placein the theater in which
the chorus danced', lit. 'place for dancing',
formed with -τρα, a suff. denoting place, from
the stem of όρχεΐσθαι, 'to dance', which is
cogn. with OI. xghayati, 'trembles, rages, raves',
fr. I.-E. base *ergh-, which is prob. an
enlargement of base *er-, *or-, 'to set in motion',
whence opvuvoct 'to rouse, stir up', L. oriri, 'to
rise'. See orient, n. For the suff. -tra in orchestra
cp. palaestra.
Derivatives: orchestr-al, adj., orchestr-ate, tr. v.,
to write or arrange music for an orchestra, or-
chestr-αΰοη, п., the writing or arranging of
music for an orchestra.

## orchestrion
orchestrion, п., a large musical box resembling a
barrel organ. See orchestra.

## orchi-
orchi-, combining form denoting a testicle or the
testicles. — See orchio-.

## orchid
orchid, n. — Fr. ModL. Orchideae, later Orchida-
ceae (see Orchtdaceae), fr. L. orchis, fr. Gk.
ορχις, 'testicle', also 'orchis' (so called from the
resemblance of the roots to testicles), which is
cogn. witn Avestic er zi (dual), 'testicles', Arm.
orji-k\ 'testicles', orji, 'not castrated', Alb.
herde (for *erde), 'testicle', Lith. efiilas,
'stallion', Mir. uirgge, lr. uirge, 'testicle'.

## orchid-
orchid-, form of orchido- before a vowel.

## Orchidaceae
Orchidaceae, n. pi., the orchid family (bot.) —
ModL., incorrectly formed fr. L. orchis, whose
gen. was supposed to be orchidis (in reality, the
gen. is orchis) See orchid and -aceae.

## orchidaceous
orchidaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## orchido-
orchido-, before a vowel orchid-, combining form
meaning 1) testicle; 2) orchid. — In the first
sense orchido- is derived fr. ορχιδος,
erroneously formed gen. of 6ρχΐς, 'testicle' (the correct
forms of the gen. are ορχιος, όρχεως). In the
second sense orchido- stands for orchid. See
orchid.

## orchidology
orchidology, п., that branch of botany which
deals with orchids. — Compounded of orchido-
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)*. See -logy.
Derivative: orchidolog-ist, n.

## orchidotomy
orchidotomy, п., incision into a testicle (med.) —
Compounded of orchido- and Gk. -τομία, *a
cutting of, fr. τομή, *a cutting'. See -tomy.

## orchiectomy
orchiectomy, п., excision of a testicle (med.) —
Compounded of orchi- and Gk. -εκτομία, 'a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:545 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ORCHIL | 518 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:545 COLUMN:1 -->
cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting out'. See
-ectomy.

## orchil
orchil, n. — The same as archil.

## orchio-
orchio-, before a vowel orchi-, combining form
denoting a testicle or the testicles. — Fr. Gk.
δρχις, gen. δρχιος, 'testicle'. See orchid.

## orchiotomy
orchiotomy, п., orchidotomy. — See prec. word
and orchidotomy.

## Orchis
Orchis, п., a genus of plants of the orchid family
(bot.) — L. orchis, fr. Gk. όρχις, 'testicle;
orchid'. See orchid.

## orchitic
orchitic, adj., pertaining to, or affected with,
orchitis. — See next word and -itic.

## orchitis
orchitis, п., inflammation of the testicles (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. όρχις, 'testicle'. See
orchid and -itis.

## orchotomy
orchotomy, п., removal of one or both testicles;
castration (med.) — Gk. όρχοτομίδ,
compounded of δρχις, 'testicle', and -τομία 'a
cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See orcho-
and -tomy.

## orcin
orcin, п., orcinol. — See orcinol.

## orcinol
orcinol, also orcin, п., a colorless crystalline
compound, CeH, · CH3(OH)2 (chem.) — Fr. It. or-
cello, 'archil'. See archil and the chem. suffixes
-in and -ol.

## Orchitis
Orchitis, п., a genus of whales, the killer whale
(zool.) — ModL., fr. L. orca, 'a kind of whale'.
See ore, orca.

## Orcus
Orcus, п., 1) the lower world, Hades; 2) the god
of the lower world; Pluto (Roman mythol.) —
L., of uncertain origin.

## ordain
ordain, tr. v. — ME. ordeinen, fr. OF. ordener (F.
ordonner), 3 pers. ordeine, fr. L. ordinare, 'to set
in order, arrange, to order', fr. ordo, gen. ordi-
nis. See order and cp. ordinal. Cp. also ornament.
Derivatives: ordain-able, adj., ordain-er, п., or-
dain-ment, n.

## ordeal
ordeal, п., I) a primitive form of trial to test guilt
or innocence; 2) a trying experience. — ME.
ordal, fr. OE. ordal, ordel (rel. to OS. urdgli,
OFris. ordel, urdel, Du. oordeel, OHG., MHG.,
G. «rlei/, 'judgment'), lit. 'that which is dealt
out', fr. or-, 'out', and dxl, 'deal'. See intensive
pref. a- and deal, 'part, share', and cp. the first
element in ort.

## order
order, n. — ME. ordre, order, fr. MF. (= F.)
ordre, fr. OF. ordene, fr. L. ordinem, ace. atordo,
'a straight row, regular series, order, class, rank',
which is rel. to ordiri, 'to begin a web, lay the
warp, begin', and cogn. with Gk. όρδεΐν, Ίο
begin a web', όρδικόν (ace), 'a little tunic, a
short coat' (Hesych.); possibly derived fr. I.-E.
base *ar-, 'to join (see article); not related to
base *or-, 'to rouse, stir up'. Cp. ordain,
ordinance, ordinary, ordinate, ordination, coordinate,
exordium, inordinate, subordinate, primordial.
Derivatives: order rtr. v., order-ly, adj. and п.,
order-li-ness, n.

## ordinal
ordinal, adj. — Late L. drdinulis, 'denoting an
order of succession', fr. L. ordo, gen. ordinis.
See order and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: ordinal, п., an ordinal number.

## ordinal
ordinal, п., a book containing prescribed forms
to be used at ceremonies. — ME., fr. ML.
ordinate, prop. neut. of Late L. drdinulis,
'denoting an order of succession', used as a noun.
See prec. word.

## ordinance
ordinance, п., a decree. — ME. ordenaunce,
'ordinance', fr. MF. ordenance (F. ordonnance). See
ordain and -ance and cp. ordnance, ordonance.

## ordinand
ordinand, п., a candidate for ordination. — L.
ordinandus, gerundive of ordinare, 'to ordain'.
See ordain. For other Latin gerundives or their
derivatives used in English cp. agenda and words
there referred to.

## ordinary
ordinary, adj. — ME. ordinarie, fr. L. ordindrius,
'regular usual', fr. ordo, gen. -inis. See order
and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: ordinary, a. (q.v.), ordinari-ly, adv.,
ordinari-ness, n.

## ordinary
ordinary, п., 1) an officer holding jurisdiction in
his own right and not as a deputy; 2) a set meal
served at a fixed price. — Fr. prec. word.

## ordinate
ordinate, n. (math.) — L. (lined) ordinata,
'parallel (line)', fem. of ordinatus, 'well ordered', pp.
of ordinare. See ordain and adj. suff. -ate and cp.
co-ordinate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:545 COLUMN:2 -->

## ordination
ordination, п., the act of ordaining. — L. ordina-
tid, gen. -onis, 'a setting in order, arrangement',
fr. ordinatus, pp. of ordinare. See ordain and
-ation.

## ordinee
ordinee, п., one who is being ordained. — L.
ordinatus, 'set in order; ordered', pp. ofordindre.
See ordain and -ее.

## ordnance
ordnance, п., cannon, artillery. — Contraction of
ordinance (q.v.), which formerly meant also
'battle array; host in array'.

## ordonnance
ordonnance, п., 1) arrangement of parts; 2)
ordinance, decree. — F., fr. ordonner, 'to order'.
See ordinance.

## Ordovlcian
Ordovlcian, adj., pertaining to the period
following the Cambrian and preceding the Silurian
(geol.) — Coined by the English geologist
Charles Lapworth (1842-1920) from Ordovices^
the Latin name of an ancient British tribe
inhabiting Wales. For the ending see suff. -ian.

## ordure
ordure, п., dung, filth, manure. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) ordure, ft. OF. (= F.) ord, 'filthy', fr. L.
horridus, 'rough, rude, causing horror, terrible'.
See horrid and -иге.

## ore
ore, n. — ME. oor, or, fr. OE. ar, £r, 'brass', rel.
to ON. eir, 'brass, copper', OHG. й-, 'brass',
OHG., MHG. frin, G. ehern, 'brazen', Goth.
aiz, 'bronze', and cogn. with OI. ayah (gen.
dyasah), Avestic ayo (gen. ayahho), L. aes, gen.
aeris, 'brass', fr. I.-E. *ayos-, which is perh. a
derivative of Ayashya, later form of Alashya,
ancient name of Cyprus, hence I.-E. *aOs
would have meant orig. 'the Cyprian metal'.
Cp. aeneous, aes, aerarian, aerugineous, era,
esteem; see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, 19 s.v. aes.
For sense development cp. L. cuprum, 'copper',
fr. Κύπρος, ancient name of Cyprus (see
copper).

## ore
ore, п., a Dan. and Norw., resp. Swed. coin,
equal in value to 1/100 of a krone, resp. krona.
— Dan. and Norw. ere or Swed. ore, fr. L.
aureus, a gold coin, prop, subst. use of the adj.
aureus, 'of gold, golden', fr. aurum, 'gold'. See
aureate.

## oread
oread, п., a mountain nymph (Greek mythol.) —
L. Orgas, gen. -adis, fr. Gk. Όρειάς, gen. -άδος,
fr. όρος, 'mountain'. See ого-, 'mountain-', and
-ad.

## orectic
orectic, adj., pertaining to desire or appetite,
appetitive (phitos.) — Gk. ορεκτικός, 'appetitive',
fr. όρεκτός, 'stretched out', verbal adj. of όρέ-
γειν, 'to stretch out, reach after', which is cogn.
with L. regere, 'to keep straight, guide, lead,
conduct, direct, rule, reign'. See regent, adj.,
and -ic.

## oreide
oreide, n. — A var. of oroide.

## oregano
oregano, п., any of several plants of the mint
family. — Sp., 'wild marjoram', fr. L. origanus,
origanum, fr. Gk. όρείγανον, όρίγανον. See
Origanum.

## Orestes
Orestes, п., son of Agamemnon and Clytemnes-
tra and friend of Pylades (Greek mythol.) — L.,
fr. Gk. 'Ορέστης, lit. 'mountaineer', fr. Ορος,
'mountain'. See ого-, 'mountain-'.

## orfe
orfe, п., a variety of the ide. — G. Orf, fr. F.
orphe, fr. L. orfus, a kind of fish, fr. Gk. όρφών
or όρφώς, 'great sea perch', which is perh. rel.
to όρφνός, 'dark', όρφνη, 'darkness', and cogn.
with OHG. erpf, 'brown', OE. eorp, earp, 'dark,
dusky', ON.jarpr, 'dark brown'.

## organ
organ, n. — ME. organe, 'a musical instrument',
fr. L. organum, fr. Gk. όργανον, 'instrument;
bodily organ; musical instrument', which is rel.
to Οργια (for *f όργια), 'secret rites, orgies',
and in gradational relationship to έργον (for
•Γέργον), 'work'. See work and cp. orgy, ergon,
energy.

## organdie
organdie, organdy, п., a fine transparent muslin.
— F. organdi, of unknown-origin.

## organic
organic, adj. — L. organicus, fr. Gk. οργανικός,
'serving as an organ or instrument', fr. όργανον.
Sec organ and adj. suff. -ic and cp. homorganic.
Derivative: organic-al-ly, adv.

## organism
organism, n. — Formed fr. organ with suff.
-Ism.

## organist
organist, n. — MF. (= F.) organiste, fr. ML.
organism, 'one who plays on an organ', fr. L.
organum, in the sense of 'musical instrument'.
See organ and -ist.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:545 COLUMN:3 -->

## organization
organization, n. — ME. organizacion, fr. MF.
(= F.) organisation, fr. ML. organizdtionem.
ace. of organizatio, fr. organizatus, pp. of orga-
rtizare. See next word and -ation.

## organize
organize, tr. and intr. v. — ME. organysen, fr.
ML. organizare, prob. through the medium of
MF. (= F.) organiser, fr. L. organum, 'organ'.
See organ and -ize.
Derivatives: organiz-able, adj., organiz-er, n.

## organo-
organo-, combining form denoting relation to an
organ or organs. — Gk. όργανο-, fr. όργανον,
'organ'. See organ.

## organography
organography, п., description of the organs of
animals or plants. — Compounded of organo-
and Gk. -γραφίδ, fr. γραφειν, 'to write'. See
-graphy.
Derivatives: organograph-ic, organograph-ic-al,
adjs., organograph-ist, n.

## organology
organology, п., that branch of biology which
deals with the organs of animals and plants. —
Compounded of organo- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: organolog-ic,organolog-ic-al, adjs.,
organolog-ist, n.

## organon
organon, п., a system of philosophic
investigation — Gk. όργανον, 'instrument, organ' (often
used as the title of works on logic). See organ.

## organotherapy
organotherapy, п., treatment of diseases with
extracts from animal organs. — Compounded of
organo- and Gk. θεραπεία, 'a waiting on,
service, attendance'. See -therapy.

## organum
organum, п., an organon. — L., 'instrument,
organ', fr. Gk. όργανον. See organon.

## organzine
organzine, п., a fine kind of silk made of several
threads twisted together. — F. organsin, fr. It.
organzino, fr. Urgendj, a town in Russian
Turkestan.
Derivative: organzine, tr. and intr. v.

## orgasm
orgasm, п., violent excitement, paroxysm; specif,
the height of sexual excitement. — F. orgasme,
fr. Gk. οργασμός, 'swelling', fr. όργδίν, 'to
swell with moisture, teem, lust', fr. οργή,
'impulse, excitement, anger*, which is prob. cogn.
with OI. urja, 'nourishment, sap, vigor', Olr.
fere, /erg, 'anger'. Cp. orgiastic.

## orgeat
orgeat, п., a beverage made of barley water
flavored with almonds. — F., fr. OProvenc. orjat,
fr. F. orge, 'barley', fr. L. hordeum, 'barley'. See
Hordeum.

## orgiastic
orgiastic, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, an
orgy. — Gk. οργιαστικός, fr. όργιαστής, 'one
who celebrates orgies', fr. όργιάζειν, 'to
celebrate orgies', fr. βργια, 'secret rites, orgies'. See
orgy, -ast and adj. suff. -ic.

## orgy
orgy, п., 1) secret rites, esp. those connected with
the worship of Dionysus or Bacchus; 2) revelry.
— MF. (= F.) orgie, fr. L. orgia (pi.), fr. Gk.
όργια (pi.), 'secret rites, orgies', which prob.
stands for *5όργια and is rel. to όργανον (for
"Γάργανον), 'instrument, bodily organ, musical
instrument'. See organ.

## -orial
-orial, adj. suff., usually corresponding to nouns
ending in -ory (as in territorial), sometimes to
nouns ending in -or (as in cantorial). —
Compounded of subst. suffix -ory and adj. suff. -al,
resp. subst. suff. -or and adj. suff. -al.

## Oribatidae
Oribatidae, n. pi., a family of oval mites (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Oribates,
name of the type genus, fr. Gk. ορειβάτης,
'mountain-ranging', which is compounded of
ορός, 'mountain', and the stem of βαίυειν, 'to
go'. See ого-, 'mountain-' and base, n.

## oribi
oribi, п., any of several species of small African
antelopes. — S. African Du., from Hottentot
arab.

## orichalc
orichalc, п., a yellow metal highly prized by the
ancient Greeks. — L. orichalcum, fr. Gk.
ορείχαλκος, lit. 'mountain copper', fr. όρος,
'mountain', and χαλκός, 'copper'. See ого-,
'mountain', and chalco-, and cp. aurichalcite.

## oriel
oriel, п., a large recessed window (archil.) — ME.,
fr. MF. oriol, fr. ML. oriolum, 'porch, gallery',
fr.VL. *auraeolum,aisi\m.ft.aulaeolum,'2i small
chapel, shrine', dimin. of aulaeum, 'curtain', fr.
Gk. αυλαία, of s.m., fr. αυλή, 'the open court
before the house; the court; chamber'. See
aula.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:546 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 519 | ORONTIUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:546 COLUMN:1 -->

## orient
orient, п., 1) the east (poetic); 2) (cap.) the East;
adj. 1) oriental; 2) shining, bright, brilliant. —
ME., fr. MF. ( = F.) orient, fr. L. orientem, ace.

## of oriens
of oriens, 'the rising sun, east', prop. pres. part.
of orior, oriri, 'to rise, become visible, appear',
fr. I.-E. base *er-, *or-, 'to set in motion, stir up,
raise', whence also L. origo, gen. originis, 'a
beginning, source, origin', OI. rnoti, fnvati, 'rises,
moves', irta, 'he set out, moved' (intr.), Avestic
ar-, 'to move' (both tr. and intr.), OPers. rasaliy,
'he comes', Arm. y-arnem, Ί rise, get up', Gk.
όρνύναι, 'to rouse, start, chase', Ερνος, 'shoot,
twig, sprout', Goth, rinnan, OE. irnan, rinnan,
'to flow, run', Toch. A ar-, В er-, 'to call forth',
Hitt. arnuzzi, 'causes to go', ari, 'arrives'. Base
*er- appears enlarged into *erei- in Gk. έρις,
'discord', όρΐνειν, 'to stir up, rouse', L. ri-vus,
'brook, water course', ir-ri-tare, 'to excite,
stimulate'. Cp. origin, abort, abortion. Cp. also ar-
tha, congruent, erethism, Eris, Erinys, Evernia,
I st irritate, orchestra, ого-, Ortalis, russud. Cp.
also rival and words there referred to.

## orient
orient, tr. v. — F. orienter, 4to set toward the east',
fr. MF., fr. orient, 'east'. See orient, n.

## oriental
oriental, adj., I) eastern; 2) (cap.) pertaining to
the Orient or East, Eastern; п., (cap.) a native of
the Orient. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. orien-
tdlis, 'pertaining to the east, Eastern, Oriental',
fr. oriens, gen. orientis, 'the rising sun, east'. See
orient, n.

## Orientalism
Orientalism, п., oriental character, oriental
peculiarity; the study of the oriental languages. -^-
Formed with suff. -ism fr. L. orientatis. See
oriental.

## Orientalist
Orientalist, п., a student of the oriental languages.
— Formed with suff. -ist fr. L. orientalis. See
oriental.

## Orientalize
Orientalize, tr. v., to make Oriental; intr. v., to
become Oriental. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. L.
orientalis. See oriental.

## orientate
orientate, tr. v., to orient; intr. v., to face east. —
See orient, п., and verbal suff. -ate.

## orientation
orientation, n. — F. orientation, fr. orienter, 'to
set toward the east'. See orient, v., and -ation.

## orifice
orifice, п., an opening, aperture. — MF. ( = F.),
fr. L. orificium, 'an opening', lit. 'mouth-
making', fr. os, gen. oris, 'mouth', and -ficere,
unstressed form of facere, 'to make, do'. See
oral and fact.

## oriflamme
oriflamme, п., the ancient battle standard of the
kings of France, the banner of St. Denis; any
standard. — ME. oriflamble, fr. MF. oriflamble,
oriflambe, oriflamme, fr. OF., fr. ML. aurea
flamma, lit. 'golden flame', fr. L. aurum, 'gold',
and flamma, 'flame'. See aureate and flame.

## origan
origan, п., marjoram. — ME. origane, fr. OF
origane, origan (F. origan), fr. L. origanum. See
next word.

## Origanum
Origanum, п., a genus of plants, the wild
marjoram (bot.) — L. origanum, fr. Gk. όρείγανον,
όρϊγανον, 'wild marjoram, origan',
compounded of ορός, 'mountain' (see ого-, 'mountain'),
and γάνας, 'brightness, ornament', which is rel.
to γάνυμαι, 4 rejoice', γαίω (for *γάί-ιω), Ί
rejoice, exult', γηθέω, Dor. γαθέω (ίοΓ*γα5ε-
θέω), Ί rejoice', and cogn. with L. gaudere, 'to
rejoice'. See gaud, 'ornament', and cp. words
there referred to.

## Origenism
Origenism, п., the doctrines held by Origen of
Alexandria (cca. 185-253), who taught a
threefold (: i.e. literal, moral and mystical)
interpretation of Scriptures. — For the ending see suff.
-ism.

## origin
origin, n. — ME. origine, fr. MF. (= F.) origine,
fr. L. originem, ace. of origo, 'beginning, source,
origin', from the stem of oriri, 'to rise, become
visible, appear'. See orient, п., and cp. aboriginal,
aborigines.

## original
original, adj. —ME., fr. OF. ( = F.), fr. L. orlgi-
nalis, 'primitive, original', fr. origo, gen. originis.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: original (q.v.), original-ly, adv.

## original
original, n. — F., fr. original, adj. See prec. word.

## originality
originality, n. — F. originalite, fr. original. See
original, adj., and -ity.

## originate
originate, tr. v., to bring into existence; intr. v., to
come into existence. — Formed fr. origin with
verbal suff. -ate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:546 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: originat-ion, п., originat-ive, adj.,
originat-ive-ly, adv., originat-or, n.

## orillion
orillion, п., a projection at the shoulder of a
bastion. — F. oreillon, orillon, prop, 'a small ear',
dimin. of oreille, 'ear', fr. L. auricula, dimin. of
auris, 'ear'. See ear, 'organ of hearing', and cp.
auricle.

## orinasal
orinasal, adj., pertaining to the nose and mouth;
(of sounds) pronounced both through the mouth
and nose. — Compounded of L. os, gen. oris,
'mouth', and Late L. nasalis, 'pertaining to the
nose'. See oral and nasal.

## oriole
oriole, п., 1) any bird of the family Oriolidae; 2)
any of various American birds of the family
Icteridae. — F.oriol, fr. OF., fr. ML. oryolus,
fr. L. aureolus, 'golden', dimin. of aureus, fr.
aurum, 'gold'. See aureate and dimin. suff. -ole.

## Oriolidae
Oriolidae, n. pi., a family of birds (ornithol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. ModL. orio-
lus, fr. ML. oryolus. See prec. word.

## Orion
Orion, п., 1) a giant hunter slain by Artemis and
made into a constellation (Greek mythol.); 2) a
constellation near Tauris (astron.) — L. Orion,
fr. Gk. Ώριων, which is of uncertain origin.

## -orious
-orious, adj. suff. meaning 'pertaining to, serving
to', as in meritorious. — Compounded of L. ori-
in -dri-us (see adj. suff. -ory) and -ous.

## orison
orison, n. (usually in pi.), prayer. — ME. oreisun,
fr. OF. oreison, orison (F. oraison), fr. L. ordtio-
nem, ace. of oratio, 'speech, prayer'. See oration
and cp. words there referred to.

## -orium
-orium, subst. suff. denoting 'a place or a thing
used for something', as in auditor/Mm, 'a place
for hearing'. — L. -orium, prop. neut. of the adj.
suff. -orius. See adj. and subst. suff. -ory.

## Orlando
Orlando, masc. PN. — Italian form of Roland
(q-v.)

## orle
orle, п., a narrow border following the outline of
the shield (her.) — MF. (= F.) orle, fr. orler (F.
ourler), 'to border, edge, hem', fr. VL. *orulare
(whence also It. orlare, 'to border, edge, hem'),
fr. VL. *orulus (whence also It. orlo, 'border,
edge, hem'), dimin. formed fr. L. ora, 'margin,
border'; see oral. Sp. orla, 'border, fringe'
(whence orlar, 'to border, edge'), derives fr. VL.
*orula, dimin. of L. ora.

## Orleans
Orleans, п., 1) a kind of purple plum); 2) worsted-
and-cotton fabric. — In both senses named after
the city of Orleans, south of Paris.

## orlop
orlop, п., the lowest deck of a ship. — Du. over-
loop, 'deck of a ship', lit. 'that which runs over',
fr. overlopen, 'to run over'; (see over and leap);
so called because it covers the ship's hold.

## Ormazd
Ormazd, п., the principle of good in the Zoro-
astrian religion. — Pers., fr. OPers. Auramazda,
fr. Avestic Ahuramazda, lit. 'wise lord', a
compound of ahura-, 'a god, a good spirit' (see
ahura), and ma(n)dzdha^ 'wise', which is a
compound formed from the I.-E. bases *men-dh-, 'to
apply oneself to', and "dhe-, 'to put, place'.
From base *men-dh- derives also OI. medha,
'wisdom, intelligence'. For other derivatives of
this base see mathematical. For base *dhe- see
do and cp. theme, fact,

## ormer
ormer, п., a gastropod mollusk, Haliotis tuber-
culata; an ear shell. — Dial. F. (Channel
Islands), fr. F. ormier, fr. L. auris maris, 'sea ear'
(see ear, 'organ of hearing', and mere, 'sea'); so
called in allusion to-its shape.

## ormolu
ormolu, п., an alloy of copper, zinc and tin,
resembling gold. — F. or moulu, 'ground gold',
fr. or, 'gold', and moulu, pp. of moudre, 'to
grind, mill'. See aureate and meal, 'edible grain'.

## ornament
ornament, п., an adornment, decoration,
embellishment. — ME. ornement, ornament, fr. OF. "
ornement, fr. L. ornamentum, 'equipment,
decoration, ornament', fr. orndre, 'to fit out, equip,
decorate, adorn', which is contracted fr. *ord(i)-
nSre, 'to set in order, arrange'. See ordain and
-ment and cp. ornate, adorn, suborn.
Derivatives: ornament, tr. v., ornament-al, adj.,
ornament-at-ty, adv., ornament-al-ness, п., or-
nament-ation, п., orname/it-er, a.

## ornate
ornate, adj., richly adorned. — ME. ornat, fr. L.
drndtus, 'adorned', pp. of drnure. See prec. word
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: ornate-ly, adv., ornate-ness, n.

## ornery
ornery, adj. (dial, or vulgar). — Corruption of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:546 COLUMN:3 -->
ordinary.

## onus
onus, п., avifauna. — Gk. δρνις, 'bird'. See
ornitho-.

## ornith-
ornith-, form of ornitho- before a vowel.

## ornithic
ornithic, adj., pertaining to, or characteristic of,
birds. — Gk. όρνΐθικός, 'of birds', fr. δρνις,
gen. δρνΐθος, 'bird'. See ornitho- and adj. suff. -ic.

## ornithine
ornithine, also ornithin, п., an amino acid,
C5HlaOaN2, found in the urine and excrements
of birds (biochem.) — Formed fr. Gk. δρνις,
gen. όρνιθος, 'bird' (see ornitho-), with chem..
suff. -ine, resp. -in.

## ornitho-
ornitho-, before a vowel omith-, combining form
meaning 'bird'. — Gk. όρνΐθο-, όρνϊθ-, fr.
βρνις, gen. όρνιθος, 'bird', which is cogn. with
Goth, ara, OE. earn, 'eagle'. See erne and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also Ortalis.

## Omithogalum
Omithogalum, п., a genus of plants, the star of
Bethlehem (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. όρνΐθό-
γαλον, 'the star of Bethlehem', which is
compounded of βρνις, gen. δρνΐθος, 'bird', and
γάλα, 'milk'. See ornitho- and galactic.

## ornithology
ornithology, п., that branch of zoology which
deals with birds. — ModL. ornithologia, fr. Gk.
όρνΐθολόγος, 'one who speaks of birds', which
is compounded of δρνις, gen. δρνΐθος, 'bird'
(see oraltho-), and -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in
a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: ornitholog-ic, ornitholog-ic-al, adjs.,
ornitholog-ist, n.

## omithomancy
omithomancy, п., augury, divination by the
observation of the flight of birds. — Gk. όρνΐθο-
μαντεία, compounded of δρνις, gen. δρνΐθος,
'bird', and μαντεία, 'oracle, divination'. See
ornitho- and -mancy.

## ornithorhynchus
ornithorhynchus, п., a duckbill. — ModL.,
compounded of ornitho- and Gk. ρύγχος, 'snout,
beak', which is of imitative origin. See rhyncho-
and cp. words there referred to.

## ornithoscopy
ornithoscopy, п., augury. — Gk. όρνϊθοσκοπία\
lit. Observation of birds', fr. όρνΐθοσκόπος,
'augur', lit. 'observer of birds', fr. δρνις, gen.
βρνΐθος, 'bird', and σκοπός, 'watcher,
examiner'. See ornitho- and -scopy.
ого-, combining form meaning 'mountain', as in
orography. — Gk. όρο-, fr. βρος, 'mountain',
which is cogn. with OI. [fvdh, 'high', fr. I.-E.
base *er-, *or-, 'to set in motion, raise', whence
also L. orior, oriri, 'to rise'. See orient, adj., and
cp. oread, Orestes.
ого-, combining form meaning 'oral and'. — Fr.
L. os, gen. oris, 'mouth'. See oral.

## Orobanchaceae
Orobanchaceae, n. pi., the broomrape family
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Orobanche with suff.
-aceae.

## orobanchaceous
orobanchaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Orobanche
Orobanche, п., a genus of plants, the broomrape
(bot.) — L., 'broomrape', fr. Gk. όροβάγχη, lit.
'the plant that chokes the vetch', compounded
of δροβος, 'vetch', and £γχειν, 'to choke'. For
the first element see Errum. The second element
derives fr. I.-E. base "angh-, 'to press, choke',
whence also L. angere, 'to throttle, torment'. See
anger and cp. words there referred to.

## orography
orography, п., that branch of physical geography
which deals with mountains.— Compounded of
1st ого- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: orograph-ic, orograph-ic-al, adjs.

## oroide
oroide, п., an alloy of copper and zinc or tin,
resembling gold and used in making imitation
jewellery. — F. oreide, a hybrid coined fr. F. or,
'gold', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See or, 'gold', and -oid.

## orology
orology, п., the study of mountains, orography.
— Compounded of 1st ого- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## orometer
orometer, п., 'an instrument for measuring the
height of mountains. — Compounded of 1st
ого- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.
Derivative: orometr-ic, adj.

## Orontium
Orontium, п., a genus of plants, the golden club
(bot.) — ModL., prob. fr. Orontes, a river of
Syria. For the ending see 1st suff. -ium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:547 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OROTUND | 520 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:547 COLUMN:1 -->

## orotund
orotund, adj., 1) full, resonant (said of the voice);
2) pompous, bombastic (said of the style of
utterance). — L. (Horace, Ars Poetica, 323) ore
rotunds, 'with a round mouth', abl. of as ro-
tundum, fr. as, gen. oris, 'mouth', and neut. of
rotundus, 'round'. See oral and rotund.
Derivative: orotund-lty, n.

## orphan
orphan, n. — Late L. orphanus, fr. Gk. ορφανός,
'without father or mother, orphaned', which is
cogn. with L. orbus, 'bereft', OI. arbhah, 'weak,
