child', Arm. orb, Orphan', arbaneak, 'servant,
assistant', Olr. orbe, orpe, 'heir', OSlav. rabu,
'slave', rabota, 'servitude, slavery', Goth, arbja,
OHG. arpeo, erbo, MHG., G. erbe (m.),
OFris. erva, ON. arfi, OE. ierfa, 'heir', Goth.
arbi, OHG. arbi, erti, MHG., G. erbe (п.),
OFris. erve, OS. erbi, ΟΈ. ierfe, 'inheritance',
Goth, arbaips, 'hardship, toil, work', OHG.
arabeit, MHG. arebeit, arbeil, of s.m., G. Arbeit,
'work', OFris. orbed, OS. arabed(i); ON. erfidi,
OE. ear/од, 'hardship, suffering, trouble'. Cp.
robot.
Derivatives: orphan, adj., orphan-age, n.

## Orphean
Orphean, adj., pertaining to Orpheus. — Formed
with surf, -an fr. L. Orpheus, fr. Gk. Όρφεϊος,
'of Orpheus', fr. Όρφεύς, 'Orpheus'. See next
word.

## Orpheus
Orpheus, п., the famous singer of Thrace, son of
CEagrus and Calliope, and husband of Eurydice
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Όρφεύς, which
is of uncertain origin.

## Orphic
Orphic, adj., 1) pertaining to Orpheus or the rites
and mysteries connected with him; 2) mystic. —
L. Orphicus, fr. Gk. 'Ορφικός, fr. Όρφεύς. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -1c.

## Orphism
Orphism, п., the religious system of the Orphic
mysteries. — See Orpheus and -ism.

## orphrey
orphrey, п., gold embroidery; gold-embroidered
band. — ME., fr. MF. orfreis (F. orfrois), fr.
Late L. auriphrygium, 'gold embroidery', fr. L.
aurum, 'gold', and neut. olPhrygius, 'Phrygian'.
See aureate and Phrygian.

## orpiment
orpiment, п., arsenic trisulfjde, AssS3 — ME. or·
pemente, fr. MF. (= F.) orpiment, fr. L. auri-
pigmentum, 'ointment', which is compounded of
aurum, 'gold', and pigmentum, 'coloring
matter'. See aureate and pigment. For the sense
development of L. auripigmentum fr. aurum,
'gold', cp. Pers. zarniq, 'orpiment', fr. гаг, 'gold'
(see arsenic),

## orpine
orpine, orpin, п., stonecrop, Sedum telephium. —
F. orpin, 'stonecrop', lit. 'a plant with yellow
flowers', shortened fr. orpiment. See prec. word.

## Orpington
Orpington, п., a breed of domesticfowl. —Named
after Orpington, a village in Kent, England.

## orra
orra, adj., odd; extra; superfluous. — Dial. Scot.;
of uncertain origin.

## orrery
orrery, п., an apparatus showing the motions of
the planets. — Called by its inventor Rowley
after the name of his patron Charles Boyle, 4th
Earl of Orrery.

## orrho-
orrho-, combining form meaning 'serum'. — Gk.
δρρο-, fr. ορρός or ορός, 'watery fluid, whey',
which is cogn. with L. serum, of s.m. See serum.

## orris
orris, п., gold or silver lace or braid. —
Corruption of OF. orphreis. See orphrey.

## orris
orris, п., the Florentine iris. — Prob. fr. ML.
yreos, 'orris root', which is identical with Gk.
ΐρεως, gen. of Τρις, 'iris'. See iris.

## Orson
Orson, masc. PN. — Fr. F. ourson, dimin. of ours,
'bear', fr. L. ursus (see Ursus). The spelling
Orson was influenced by It. orso, 'bear'.

## ort
ort, п., remnants of food left from the meal. —
Prob. rel. to earlier Du. oor-aete, oor-ete,
'remains of food', which is formed fr. pref. oor-
and eten, 'to eat'. Du. pref. oor- is rel. to
E. pref. or- in ordeal. Du. eten is rel. to OE.
etan; see eat.

## Ortalidae
Ortalidae, n. pi., a family of Diptera (entomol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk. δρ-
ταλίς, 'young bird'. See next word.

## Orlalis
Orlalis, п., a genus of guans (ornithol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. δρταλίς, 'young bird', which is prob.
rel. to βρνις, 'bird'. See ornitho-.

## ortho-
ortho-, before a vowel orth-, combining form
meaning 'straight; rectangular; regular; true,
correct'. — Gk. όρ*ο-, fr. όρ&ός, ('straight;
right, true, exact; genuine; upright, righteous',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:547 COLUMN:2 -->
for *ίορ»ίός (ср. Dor. βορθό-); cognate with
OI. urdhvab, 'high', vardhate, 'causes to grow',
L. arduus, 'high, lofty, steep'. See arduous and
cp. vriddhi.

## Orthocarpns
Orthocarpns, п., a genus of plants of the flgwort
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of ortho-
and Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.

## orthocephalic
orthocephalic, also orthocephalous, adj., having
the bread th of the skull from about} to $ of the
length; intermediate between dolicho- and bra-
chycephalic. — Lit. 'right-headed*, compounded
of ortho- and Gk. κεφαλή, 'head'. See cephalic,
resp. cephalous.

## orthochromatic
orthochromatic, adj., producing true relations of
light and shade. — Compounded of ortho- and
Gk. χρωματικός, 'relating to color', fr. χρώμα,
gen. χρώματος, 'color'. See chromatic.

## orthoclase
orthoclase, п., potash feldspar (mineral.) — G.
Orthoclas, coined by A. Breithaupt in 1823 fr.
ortho- and Gk. κλάσις, 'a breaking', fr. κλάν,
'to break'; see clastic and cp. words there
referred to. The word orthoclase lit. means '(the
mineral) that has a cleavage at right angles'. Cp.
anorthoclase.

## orthoclastic
orthoclastic, adj., having the cleavage at right
angles (as the orthoclase). — See ortho- and
clastic.

## orthodontia
orthodontia, п., correction of the irregularities in
the teeth. — ModL., compounded of orth- and
Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'. See odonto-
and 1st -ia.
Derivatives: orthodont-ic, adj., orthodont-ics, п.,
orthodont-ist, n.

## orthodox
orthodox, adj., having the correct opinion (esp.
in religion). — Late L. orthodoxus, it. Gk.
ορθόδοξος, 'having the right opinion', fr.
ορθός, 'right' (see ortho-), and δόξα, 'opinion',
which stands for δόκ-σα and is rel. to δοκεϊν, 'to
seem good, to seem, think, believe'. See doxas-
tic and cp. dogma, doxology. Cp. also the second
element in heterodox, paradox.

## orthodoxy
orthodoxy, п., right opinion (esp. in religion). —
Late L. orthodoxia, fr. Gk. ορθοδοξία, 'right
opinion', fr. ορθόδοξος. See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -is).

## orthoepy.n.
orthoepy.n., correct pronunciation.—Gk.op4M-
πεια, 'correctness of diction', fr. ορθός, 'right,
correct', and -έπεια, fr. έπος, 'word'. See
ortho- and epic and cp. cacoepy.
Derivatives: orthoep-ic, adj., orthoep-ist, n.

## orthogenesis
orthogenesis, п., I) determinate evolution of
species (biol.); 2) the theory that the development
of society always proceeds in the same direction
(sociol.) — Coined by the Swiss naturalist
Gustav Heinrich Theodor Eimer (1843-98) in
his Die Entslehung der Arlen (1888) fr. ortho-
and genesis.

## orthognathism
orthognathism, also orthognathy, п., the quality
of being orthognathous. — See next word and
-ism, resp. -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## orthoguathous
orthoguathous, adj., straight-jawed. —
Compounded of ortho- and Gk. γνάθος, 'jaw'. See
guathic and -ous.

## orthogonal
orthogonal, adj., right-angled. — Formed with
adj. sufT.-al fr. L. orthogonius, 'right-angled', fr.
Gk. ορθογώνιος, which is compounded of
δρθός, 'right', and -γώνιος, fr. γωνία, 'angle,
corner'. See ortho- and -gon.

## orthographer
orthographer, п., one who spells correctly. — See
next word and agential sufT. -er.

## orthography
orthography, п., correct spelling. — ME. orto-
graphie, fr. MF. ortografie, ortographie (F. or-
thographie), fr. L. orthographia, fr. Gk.
ορθογραφία, 'correct writing', fr. ορθογράφος, 'one
who writes correctly', which is compounded of
ορθός, 'right, correct', and -γράφος, from the
stem of γράφειν, 'to write'. See ortho- and
-graphy.
Derivatives: orthograph-ic, orthograph-ic-al,
adjs., orthograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## orthopedic
orthopedic, orthopaedic, adj., pertaining to
orthopedics. — See next word.

## orthopedics
orthopedics, orthopaedics, п., correction of
deformities esp. in young children. — Formed
with suff. -ics fr. F. orthopedie, fr. Gk. ορθός,
'straight, right', and παιδεία, 'the training of
children', fr. παις, gen. παιδός, 'child'; see
pedo-. The word orthopedie was coined by the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:547 COLUMN:3 -->
French physician Nicholas Andry (1658-1742),
author of a work entitled Uorthopedie ou Vart
de prevenir et de corriger dans les enfants les dif-
formites du corps.
orthopedist,'orthopaedist, п., one who practices
orthopedics. — F. orthopediste, fr. orthopedie.
See next word and -ist.

## orthopedy
orthopedy, orthopaedy, п., orthopedics. — F.
orthopedic See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -iij.

## orthopnea
orthopnea, orthopnoea, п., a condition in which
.espiration is possible only in an upright
posture (med.) — Gk. όρθόπνοια, 'upright
breathing', coined by Hippocrates fr. ορθός, 'upright',
and πνοή, 'breathing'. See ortho- and pneuma.

## orthopneic
orthopneic, orthopnoeic, adj., pertaining to
orthopnea. — Formed from prec. word with adj.
suff. -ic.

## Orthoptera
Orthoptera, n. pi., an order of insects, including
the locusts, grasshoppers, cockroaches, etc.
(entomol.) — ModL., compounded of ortho-
and Gk. πτερόν, 'wing'. See ptero-.

## orthopteran
orthopteran, adj., orthopterous; п., one of the
Orthoptera. — See prec. word.

## orthopterous
orthopterous, adj., belonging to the order
Orthoptera. — See Orthoptera and -ous.

## orthoptic
orthoptic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized by,
normal binocular vision. — Compounded of
orth- and Gk. οπτικός, 'pertaining to the eyes
or sight'. See optic.
Derivative: orthopt-ics, n.

## orthoscopic
orthoscopic, adj., 1) pertaining to normal vision;
2) constructed to correct optical distortion. —
Compounded of ortho- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr.
σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scope and
adj. sufT. -ic.

## orthostichous
orthostichous, adj., arranged in orthostichies. —
See next word and -ous.

## orlhostichy
orlhostichy, п., vertical arrangement of leaves and
flowers on an axis or stem (bot.) —
Compounded of ortho- and Gk. ατίχος, 'order, row, rank;
verse'. See acrostic and -y (representing Gk.
-IS).

## ort ho tropic
ort ho tropic, adj., characterized by vertical growth.
— See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## orthotropism
orthotropism, п., tendency of a plant to grow
vertically. — Compounded of ortho-, Gk.
-τρόπος, 'turning' (fr. τρέπειν, 'to turn') and suff.
-ism. See trope, tropism, and cp. heliotropism
and words there referred to.

## ortolan
ortolan, п., 1) an Old World bunting, Emberiza
hortulana;!) the bobolink. — F., fr. It. ortolano.
'gardener; ortolan', fr. L. hortulanus,
'pertaining to a garden, gardener", fr. hortus, 'garden'
(see horticulture); so called from its frequenting
gardens.

## -ory
-ory, surT. forming adjectives with the meaning
'pertaining to, serving to, of the nature of, as in
preparatory, declamatory, hortatory,- — ME.
-oriey fr. AF. -ori (masc), -orie (fern.),
corresponding to OF. -oir (masc), -oire (fern.), F.
-oire (for both genders); fr. L. -drius (masc),
-oria (fern.), *6rium (neut.), which stand for
-or-ius, -or-ia, -or-iumt compound suff. formed
from subst. suff. -or (see agential suff. -or)
through the addition of the adj. suff. -ius, -iay
-ium. Cp. -orial.

## -ory
-ory, suff. forming nouns denoting 'place', as in
ambulatory, dormitory. — ME. -orie, fr. OF.
( = F.)- oire, fr. L. -orium, prop. neut. of the
adjectival suff. -orius, used as a subst. suff. See adj.
suff. -ory.

## orycto-
orycto-, combining form denoting/ow/Y, mineral,
as in oryctology. — Fr. Gk. ορυκτός, 'dug',
verbal adj. of ορύσσειν, 'to dig'. See oryx,

## oryctology
oryctology, п., 1) mineralogy; 2) paleontology. —
Lit. 'the science of things dug (from the earth)',
compounded of orycto- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: oryctolog-ic-al, adj., oryctolog-ist,
n.

## Oryx
Oryx, п., 1) a genus of African antelopes with
long, straight horns; 2) (not cap.) any antelope
of this genus. — Gk. δρυξ, 'a horned Egyptian
antelope', lit., 'the digging animal', fr. όρύσσω,
Ί dig', which prob. stands for *ό-ρύκίω and is
rel. to ρυκάνη, 'a plane', and cogn. with L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:548 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 521 | OSSIFIC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:548 COLUMN:1 -->
runcare, 'to root up*. See runcinate and cp.
orycto-.

## Oryza
Oryza, п., a genus of cereal grasses (bot.) — L.,
'rice', fr. Gk. δρυζα, See rice.

## Oryzomys
Oryzomys, п., a genus of rodents, the rice rat
(zool.) — ModL., lit- 'rice mouse', compounded
of Gk. δρυζα, 'rice', and μυς, 'mouse'. See rice
and mouse and cp. myo-,

## Oryzopsls
Oryzopsls, п., a genus of plants, the mountain
rice (bol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
όρυζα, 'rice' and δψις, 'sight, view'. See rice and
-opsis.

## os
os, п., a bone (anat.) — L. os, gen. <?jiij,''bone\
cogn. with OI. dsthi, Hitt. hashtdi-, Gk. δστέον
(Att. όστοΰν, Dor. όστίον, 'bone', όστρεον,
'oyster', δστρακον, Oyster shell, potsherd',
αστράγαλος (assimilated fr. "αστράγαλος),
'one of the vertebrae of the neck, anklebone,
molding', Alb. asht, ashte, 'bone', Avestic ascu-,
'shinbone', W. asgwrn, Co. ascorn, 'bone', and
possibly also with Arm. oskr, 'bone'. Cp.
osseous. Cp. also astragal, osphyo-, osteo-,
ostracize, oyster.

## os
os, п., a mouth (anat.).—■ L. os, gen. oris, 'mouth'.
See oral.

## Osage orange
Osage orange, an ornamental American tree,
Toxylon pomiferum; its fruit. — Named after
the Osage Indians.

## Oscan
Oscan, п., 1) a member of an ancient people who
lived in Southern Italy; 2) their language,
related to Latin. — Formed with surf, -an fr. L.
Opsci, Osci (pi.), 'the Oscans', lit. 'the
worshipers of Ops', the goddess of the harvest. See
Ops.

## Oscar
Oscar, masc. PN. — OE. Osgar, compounded of
os, 'a god', and gar, 'spear'. OE. os is rel. to OS.
as-, os-, ON. ass, OHG. arts- (in PN.s), 'god',
Goth, anses, ansis (ace. pi.), 'gods'. Cp. the first
element in Osmond, Oswald. For the etymology
of OE. gar see gar.

## oscheal
oscheal, adj., pertaining to the scrotum (anal.) —
Formed with adj. surf, -al fr. Gk. δσχεον,
'scrotum'. See oscheo-.

## oscheo-
oscheo-, before a vowel osche-, combining form
meaning the 'scrotum'. — Fr. Gk. δσχεον,
'scrotum', a collateral form of δσχη, of s.rn.,
prop, figurative use of δσχτ], 'vine with grapes',
which is of uncertain origin.

## oscillate
oscillate, intr. v., to swing to and fro; tr. v., to
cause to swing to and fro. — L. dscillat-(um), pp.
stem of oscillare, 'to swing, sway', fr. oscillum,
'a swing', which is of uncertain origin.

## oscillation
oscillation, n. — L. oscitlatio, gen. -onis, 'a
swinging', fr. oscilldt-(um), pp. of oscillare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## oscillator
oscillator, п., a person or thing that oscillates;
specif., a device producing oscillations. —
ModL., fr. L. oscilldt-(um), pp. stem of oscillare.
See oscillate and agential suff. -or.

## oscillatory
oscillatory, adj., tending to oscillate, oscillating.
—Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. 6scilldt-(um),
pp. stem of oscillare. See oscillate.

## oscillograph
oscillograph, п., an instrument for registering
oscillations. — A hybrid coined fr. L. oscillare,
'to swing', and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See oscillate and -graph.
Derivatives: oscillograph-ic, adj., oscillograph-
ic-al-ly, adv., oscillograph-y, n.

## oscilloscope
oscilloscope, п., an instrument for visually
recording an electrical wave. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. oscillare, 'to swing', and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr.
σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See oscillate and
-scope.
Derivative: oscilloscop-ic, adj.

## oscine
oscine, adj., belonging to the Oscines; п., one of
the Oscines — See next word.

## Oscines
Oscines, n. pi., a suborder of Passerine birds, the
true singing birds (orniihol.) — L., pi. of oscen,
gen. oscinis, 'singing bird' (esp. one used for
divining), which stands for *obs-cen, and is
formed fr. obs-, ob-, 'toward', and canere, 'to
sing'. See ob- and cant, 'slang of beggars'

## oscitance
oscitance, oscitancy, п., 1) yawning; 2) sleepiness,
drowsiness; 3) dullness. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## oscitant
oscitant, adj., 1) yawning; 2) sleepy, drowsy; 3)
dull. — L. oscitdns, gen. -antis, pres. part of
oscitare, 'to gape, yawn', for os citdre, 'to move

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:548 COLUMN:2 -->
the mouth', fr. os, gen. oris, 'mouth', and citare,
'to move', freq. of ciere. See oral and cite. For
the ending see suff. -ant.
Derivative: osciiant-ly, adv.

## oscitation
oscitation, п., 1) yawning; 2) sleepiness,
drowsiness; 3) inattention. — L. oscitatio, gen. -onis,
'yawning', fr. 6scitdt-(um), pp. stem of oscitare.
See prec. word and -ation.

## osculant
osculant, adj., kissing. — L. osculans (gen. -antis),
pres. part, ofosculdri, 'to kiss'. See osculate and
-ant.

## oscular
oscular, adj. — L. osculdris, fr. osculum, 'little
mouth; kiss'. See osculum and -ar.

## osculate
osculate, tr. and intr. v., 1) to kiss; 2) to touch
closely; 3) (math.) to touch at three or more
points (as of two curves). — Formed fr. oscula-
tus, pp. of osculart, 'to kiss', fr. osculum, 'little
mouth; kiss'. See osculum and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: osculat-ory, adj.

## osculation
osculation, п., 1) a kiss; 2) (math.) contact of two
osculating curves. — L. osculatio, gen. -onis,
'kiss', fr. osculatus, pp. of osculart. See prec.
word and -ion.

## oscule
oscule, n. — The same as osculum.

## osculum
osculum, п., \) one of the apertures of a sponge;
2) one of the suckers of the tapeworms. — L.
osculum, 'little mouth', dimin. of as, gen. -oris,
'mouth'. See oral and -cule.

## -ose
-ose, adj. suff. meaning 'full of, abounding in,
having the qualities of. — ME., fr. L. -osus,
which prob. stands for 'od-tos, fr. odor, gen.
odoris, 'smell', and must have meant originally
'smelling of; see odor. This meaning appears in
vinosus, 'smelling of wine', whence 'full of wine,
abounding in wine' (see vinous). The original
meaning 'smelling of was widened into 'full of,
abounding in'. Cp. -ous.

## -ose
-ose, a suff. used in chemistry, denoting 1)
carbohydrates (as in amylose, lactose); 2) a proteid
product (as in proteose). — Formed from the
ending -ose in F. glucose (see glucose).

## osier
osier, п., any of various willows. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) osier, 'willow' (in MF. and dial. F. also
osiere), fr. VL. *ausaria (cp. ML. auseria), which
is of Gaulish origin.

## Osiris
Osiris, п., one of the principal Egyptian gods,
judge of the dead. — L. Osiris, fr. Gk. "Οσϊρις,
fr. Egypt. As-ir. Cp. Isis.

## -osis
-osis, suff. expressing state or condition; in
medical terminology it is used to denote a state of
disease. — ME., fr. L. -osis, fr. Gk. -ωσις,
formed from the aorist of verbs ending in -όω,
-ώ (inf. -oetv, -οΰν). It corresponds to L. -alio
and stands to Gk. -ωτός, as h.-atid to -atus. Cp.
the suffixes -asis, -esis, -iasis. Cp. also -ation.

## -osity
-osity, suff. used to form nouns from adjectives in
■ose or -ous. — ME. -osite, fr. OF. -osite (F.
-osite), fr. L. -dsiidtem, ace. of -ositas, forming
nouns from adjectives in -osus. Accordingly
-osity is prop, compounded of the adj. suff. -ose
and suff. -i(y (qq.v.)
•osm-, form of osmo- before a vowel.

## Osmanli
Osmanli, п., an Ottoman Turk. —Turk. 'Osmdnli,
'of, or pertaining to, Osman', fr. 'Osmdn,
founder of the Ottoman empire (he reigned
1259-1326). 'Osmdn is prop, the Turk
pronunciation of the Arabic name ' Uthman. See
Ottoman.

## osmio-
osmio-, combining form meaning 'osmium'. —
See osmium.

## osmiridium
osmiridium, п., an alloy of osmium and iridium.
— Coined fr. osm(inm) and iridium.

## osmium
osmium, п., name of a metallic element of the
platinum group (chem.) — ModL., coined by
its discoverer, the English chemist Smithson
Tennant (1761-1815) in 1803 fr. Gk. οσμή,
'smell, odor', which stands for *όδσμή (ср. the
Dor. form όδμή) and is cogn. with L. odor,
'smell, odor'; so called because of the strong
odor of its oxide. See odor and 2nd -ium and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also osmo-, aosmlc,
Agathosma, anosmia, Barosma, Coprosma,
Diosma, euosmite, Hedeoma, hyperosmia, hy-
posmia, Onosmodium, osphresis, parosmia. Cp.
also ozo-, ozone.
Derivatives: osm-ic, osmi-ous, adjs.

## osmo-
osmo-, before a vowel osm-, combining form
meaning 'smell, odor', as in Osmorhiza. — Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:548 COLUMN:3 -->
όσμο-, fr. δσμή, 'odor'. See osmium.

## osmo-
osmo-, combining form for osmosis or osmotic, as
in osmology, osmometer. — See osmosis.

## Osmond
Osmond, masc. PN. — OE. Osmund, lit. 'divine
protection', compounded of os, 'a god', and
mund, 'protection'. For the first element see
Oscar and cp. Oswald. The second element is
rel. to ON. mund, OHG. muni, 'hand,
protection', and cogn. with L. manus, 'hand'. See
manual and cp. mound, 'heap of earth'. Cp. also
the second element in Edmond, Raymond, Si-
gismund.

## Osmorhiza
Osmorhiza, п., a genus of plants, the sweet cicely
(hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. οσμή,
'smell' (see osmium), and ρ4ζα, 'root' (see
rhizo-); so called in allusion to the aromatic root.

## osmose
osmose, tr. v., to subject to osmosis; intr. v., to
undergo osmosis. —■ Back formation fr. osmosis.

## osmosis
osmosis, п., intermixture of two fluids separated
by a porous membrane. — ModL., formed with
suff. -osis fr. Gk. ώσμός, 'a thrusting, impulse',
from the stem of ώθεΐν, 'to thrust, push', which
is rel. to εν-οσις, 'shaking, quake', fr. I.-E. base
*wedh-, 'to strike', whence also OI. vadhati,
'pushes, strikes, destroys', Avestic vddaya-, 'to
repulse'.

## osmotic
osmotic, adj., pertaining to osmosis. — See prec.
word and -otic.

## osmund
osmund, п., the royal fern. — ME. osmunde, fr.
OF. (= F.) osmonde, which is of uncertain
origin.

## Osmunds
Osmunds, п., a genus of plants, the flowering fern
(bot.) — ModL., fr. F. osmonde. See osmund.

## Osmundaceae
Osmundaceae, n. pi., the flowering fern family
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## osmundaceous
osmundaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Osnabarg
Osnabarg, п., a kind of coarse linen. — Orig.
'linen made at Osnaburg, more exactly Osna-
briick, a town in the province of Hanover in
Prussia.

## osphradium
osphradium, п., a sense organ of most aquatic
mollusks. —'ModL., fr. MGk. δσφράδιον,
'nosegay', fr. LGk. δσφρα, 'smell', which is rel.
to Gk. όσφραίνεσθαι, 'to smell'. See next word
and 1st -ium.

## osphresis
osphresis, п., I) the sense of smell; 2) the act of
smelling. — ModL., fr. Gk. βσφρησις, 'the
sense of smell', fr. όσφρασθαι, a collateral form
of όσφραίνεσθαι, 'to smell', a compound whose
first element is rel. to οζειν, 'to smell'; see odor.
The second element is of uncertain etymology.
It is perh. cogn. with OI. ji-ghr-ati, ghrd-ti,
'smells', ghrana-m, 'smell; nose', Toch. A krdm,
of s.m. Cp. prec. word.

## osphretic
osphretic, adj., pertaining to, or connected with,
smell. — Gk. οσφρητικός, fr. όσφρητός, 'that
which can be smelled', verbal adj. of όσφραί-
νεσθαι. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## osphyo-
osphyo-, before a vowel osphy-, combining form
denoting the loin. — Fr. Gk. δσφϋς, όσφΰς
(gen. όσφϋος), 'hip, hip bone', which possibly
stands for *όστ-φύς, a compound whose first
element is shortened fr. δστέον, 'bone'; see
osteo-. The second element is prob. related to
cpueLv, 'to bring forth, produce, make to grow';
see physio-.

## osprey
osprey, п., a large fishing-hawk, Pandion haliae-
tus. — Late ME. ospray, fr. MF. *osfraie, fr. L.
ossifraga. See ossifrage.

## ossein
ossein, п., the organic basis of bone (biochem.) —
Formed with suff. -in fr. L. osseus, 'bony'. See
next word.

## osseous
osseous, adj., bony. — L. osseus, 'bony', from the
stem of os, gen. ossis, 'bone'. See os, 'bone'. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## Ossianic
Ossianic, adj., 1) pertaining to Ossian, a
legendary bard and hero of the 3rd cent.; 2)
pertaining to, or resembling, the supposed
translations of Ossian by James Macpherson; 3)
bombastic. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Ossian, fr.
Gaelic Oisin, a name literally meaning 'a little
fawn', fr. os, 'a fawn'.

## ossicle
ossicle, п., a small bone (anat. and zool.) — L.
ossiculum, dim. of os, gen. ossis, 'bone'. See os,
'bone', and -cle.

## ossiric
ossiric, adj., forming bone. — Formed fr. L. os.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:549 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OSSIFICATION | 522 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:549 COLUMN:1 -->
gen. ossis, 'bone', and suff. -fie. See os, 'bone*,

## ossification
ossification, п., the act of ossifying; the state of
being ossified. — See ossify and -ation.

## ossifrage
ossifrage, п., 1) the lammergeier; 2) the osprey.
— L. ossifraga, 'sea eagle', fem. of ossifragus,
'bone-breaking', fr. os, gen. ossis, 'bone', and
frag-, stem offrangere, 'to break'. See os, 'bone*,
and fraction and cp. osprey, which is a doublet
of ossifrage.

## ossify
ossify, tr. and intr. v., to form or turn into bone.
— Formed fr. L. os, gen. ossis, 'bone*, and suff.
-fy. See os, 'bone*.
Derivatives: ossifi-ed, adj., ossift-er, n.

## ossuary
ossuary, п., an urn for the bones of the dead. —
Late L. ossuSrium, 'charnel house', formed fr.
L. os, gen. ossis, 'bone', on the analogy of mor-
tudrium, 'mortuary'. See os, 'bone', and 2nd
subst. sun", -ary.

## ost-
ost-, oste-, forms of osteo- before a vowel,

## osteal
osteal, adj., bony. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
Gk. όστέον, 'bone'. See osteo-.

## osteitis
osteitis, п., inflammation of a bone (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -iris fr. Gk.
όστέον, 'bone'. See osteo-.

## ostensible
ostensible, adj., shown, apparent; seeming. — F.,
fr. L. "ostensibilis, fr. ostensus, pp. of ostendere,
'to show, exhibit, display', which stands for obs-
tendere, lit. 'to stretch out before', fr.pbs-, ob-,
'before' (see ob-), and tendere, 'to stretch*. See
tend, 'to move in a certain direction', and -ible.
Derivatives: ostensibil-ity, п., ostensibl-y, adv.

## ostensive
ostensive, adj., ostensible. — ML. ostensivus^ fr.
L. ostensus, pp. of ostendere. See prec. word and
-ive.
Derivative: ostensive-ly, adv.

## ostentation
ostentation, п., vain display; showiness. — ME.
ostentacioun, fr. MF. (~ F.) ostentation, fr. L.
ostentationem, ace. of ostentatio, 'an idle show,
vain display', fr. ostentatus, pp. of ostentarey
freq. of ostendere. See ostensible and -ation.

## ostentatious
ostentatious, adj., pretentious, showy. — See prec.
word and -ous.
Derivatives: ostentatious-ly, adv., ostentatious-
ness, n.

## osteo-
osteo-, before a vowel oste-, ost-, combining form
meaning a 'bone' or 'bones'. — Gk. οστεο-,
άστε-, όστ-, fr. όστέον, 'bone', which is cogn.
with L. os, 'bone'. See os, 'bone' and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also periosteum,

## osteoblast
osteoblast, n,, a bone-forming cell. —
Compounded of osteo- and Gk. βλαστός, 'bud, sprout,
shoot*. See -blast,

## osteogenesis
osteogenesis, п., formation of bone; ossification
(physiol.) — Compounded of osteo- and Gk.
γένεσις, 'origin, source, birth, descent'. See
genesis,

## osteoid
osteoid, adj., like bone. — Compounded of osteo-
and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape*.
See -oid.

## osteology
osteology, п., the study of the bones. —
Compounded of osteo- and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## osteoma
osteoma, п., a bony tumor (med.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. oste- with suff. -oma.

## osteomalacia
osteomalacia, п., softening of the bones (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of osteo- and Gk.
μαλακία, 'softness', fr. μαλακός, 'soft'. See
malaco- and 1st -ia.

## osteomyelitis
osteomyelitis, п., inflammation of the bone mar-
rcrw (med.) — Medical L., compounded of
osteo- and myelitis.
Derivative: osteomyelit-ic, adj.

## osteopath
osteopath, п., one who practices osteopathy. —
Back formation fr. osteopathy. See -path,

## osteopathist
osteopathist, п., an osteopath, — Formed from
next word with surf. -1st.

## osteopathy
osteopathy, п., system of treating ailments by the
manipulation of bones (med.) — Compounded
of osteo- and Gk. -πάθε^α, fr. πάθος,
'suffering'. See -pathy.
Derivative: osteopath-ic, adj.

## osteophyte
osteophyte, п., a small bony outgrowth (med.) —
Compounded of osteo- and Gk. φυτόυ, 'a
growth'. See -phyte.
Derivative: osteophyt-ic, adj.

## osteoplastic
osteoplastic, adj., pertaining to the replacement
of a bone (surgery). — Compounded of osteo-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:549 COLUMN:2 -->
and Gk. πλαστικός, 'of molding', fr. πλαστός,
'molded'. See plastic.

## osteoplasty
osteoplasty, п., plastic operation on a bone
(surgery) — Compounded of osteo- and Gk. -πλα-
στ£α, fr. πλαστός, 'molded'. See -plasty.

## osteotome
osteotome, п., an instrument for cutting or
dividing of bone (surgery) — Compounded of
osteo- and Gk. -τόμος, 'cutting', from the stem
of τέμνειν, *to cut'. See -tome.

## osteotomy
osteotomy, п., the dividing of a bone or the cutting
out of part of it (surgery). — Compounded of
osteo- and -τομία, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a
cutting', from the stem of τέμνειν, 'to cut'. See
-tomy.

## ostiary
ostiary, п., doorkeeper, esp. of a church. — L.
ostiarius, 'doorkeeper', fr. ostium, 'door,
entrance', which is rel. to L. os, 'mouth*, and cogn.
with OSlav. usta, OPruss. austo, 'mouth', Lith.
uosias, uosia, 'mouth of a river, bay', Russ.
ustije, 'mouth of a river', OI. Osthah, Avestic
aoshtat aoshtra, 'lip', OSlav. ustina, 'lip*, ustitih
'to persuade'. See oral and adj. suff. -ary and cp.
ostiole, usher.

## ostiole
ostiole, п., a small opening, an orifice (bot.) — L.
ostiolum, 'a little door', dimin. of ostium. See
prec. word and -ole.

## ostler
ostler, п., a stableman. — A doublet of hostler
o(q.v.)
stosis, п., bone formation (physiol.) — Medical
L., formed fr. Gk. -όστωσις (e.g. in έξόστωσις,
*bone increase from without'), which is formed
fr. όστοΰν, 'bone', and suff. -ωσις. See osteo-and
-osis.

## Ostracion
Ostracion, п., a genus of trunkfishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. όστράκιον, 'a small shell',
dimin. of (ίστρακον. See ostracize.

## ostracism
ostracism, п., a method of banishment for ten
years, practiced in ancient Athens. — Gk. όστρα-
χιαμός, fr. όστρακίζειν. See next word and
-ism.

## ostracize
ostracize, tr. v., to banish by ostracism. — Gk.
όστρακίζε!.ν, 'to ostracize', lit. 'to banish by
voting with potsherds', fr. βστρακον, 'piece of
earthenware, tile, potsherd', which is rel. to
όστρέον, 'oyster', and to όστέον, όστοϋν,
'bone'. See os, 'bone', and cp. osteo-, oyster. Cp.
also MLG. astrak, esterik, OHG. astrih, estirih,
MHG. esterich, G. Estrich, 'pavement', which
derive fr. ML. astracus, astricus, 'pavement', ult.
fr. Gk. οστρακον. — For sense development cp.
petaiism.
Derivatives: ostraciz-ation, п., ostractz-er, n.

## ostracon
ostracon, п., \) a potsherd; 2) a potsherd used for
voting in ancient Athens. — Gk. οστρακον. See
ostracize.

## ostreger
ostreger, also ostringer.n., keeper of goshawks.—
ME., corrupted fr. OF. ostruchiery astrucier, fr.
ostor, ostur, ostoir (F. autour), 'goshawk*, fr.
Late L. auceptorem, ace. of auceptor, alteration
of acceptor, 'hawk' (under the influence of L.
auceps, 'birdcatcher, fowler'), which itself is an
alteration of L. accipiter, 'hawk'. See Accipiter
and cp. Astar. The η in ostringer is intrusive; cp.
messenger and words there referred to.

## ostrel-
ostrel-, combining form. — See ostreo-.

## ostreiculture
ostreiculture, п., the culture of oysters. —
Compounded of ostrei- and culture.
Derivatives: ostreocultur-al, adj., ostreocultur-
ist, n.

## ostreo-
ostreo-, ostrei-, combining form meaning Oyster'.
— Fr. Gk. όστρζον, 'oyster'. See oyster.

## ostreophagous
ostreophagous, adj., feeding on oysters. —
Compounded of ostreo- and Gk. -φάγος, fr. φαγειν,
'to eat'. See -phagous.

## ostrich
ostrich, n. — ME. ostrice, oystriche, fr. OF.
ostruce, fr. earlier OF. ostrusce (F. autruche), fr.
VL. avis struthid, lit., 'the bird ostrich', fr. L. avis,
'bird', and Gk. στρουθίων, 'ostrich'; see aviary
and Struthlo. A similar contraction of L. avis
occurs in E. bustard, which derives ult. fr. L. avis
turda.

## Ostrogoth
Ostrogoth, п., one of the East Goths. — Late L.
Ostrogothae (ρί.), fr. earlier Austrogoti (pi.), a
compound of Teut. origin lit. meaning 'the
shining (or splendid) Goths'. The first element
of this compound derives fr. Teut. *austr-, fr.
l.-E. *ausr-, 'shining', fr. I.-E. base *awes-, 'to
shine'; see aurora. For the second element see

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:549 COLUMN:3 -->
Goth and cp. Visigoth. Austrogoti was later ex.
plained as 'the Eastern Goths'; cp. OHG., OS.
ostar, 'to the east', fr. Teut. *austa-, 'east', ult-
fr. I.-E. *awes-, 'to shine'.

## Ostrya
Ostrya, п., a genus of trees, the hop hornbeam
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. όστρύα, 'the hop
hornbeam'.

## Oswald
Oswald, masc. PN. — OE. Oswea/d, compounded
of os, 'a god', and (ge)weald, 'power'. See Oscar
and wield.

## ot-
ot-, form of oto- before a vowel.

## otalgia
otalgia, п., earache (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of Gk. ούς, gen. ώτός, 'ear', and
-αλγία, fr. άλγος, 'pain'. See oto- and -algfa.

## Otariidae
Otariidae, n. pi., the family of pinnipeds, the
eared seals, sea lions, etc. — ModL., formed
with suff. -idae fr. ModL. Otaria, name of the
type genus, fr. F. otarie, 'eared seal', a name
coined by Peronfr. Gk. ώτάριου, dimin. of οδς,
gen. ώτός, 'ear'; so called by him in allusion to
the smallness of the ear. See oto-,

## -ote
-ote, a suff. meaning 'native of*. — F. -ote, fr. L.
-ota, fr. Gk. -ώτης (ср. e.g. 'Ηπειρώτης,
'native of Epirus, Epirote', fr. "Ηπειρος, 'Epirus').

## other
other, adj. — ME. other, adj., п., ргоп. and adv.,
fr. OE. dder, adj., n. and pron., 'the second,
following; the other', rel. to OS. athar, othar,
OFris. other, ON. annarr, Du. ander, OHG.
andar, MHG., G. ander, Goth, anpar, 'other',
and cogn. with Lith. antras, OPruss. antars, OI.
antarah, 'other'; formed with I.-E. compar. suff.
*tero- fr. base *eno~, *ono-, whence OI. anyah,
Avestic anya-, OPers. aniya-, 'other', Lith. anas,
ans, 'that one1, OSlav. опй, 'he', Gk. ε"νη, 'the
day after tomorrow', ^vtot, 'some', L. enirn,
'indeed', Umbr. enom, 'then', Goth, joins, OE.
geon, 'yon'. See yon and -ther.
Derivatives: other, pron. and adv., other-ness, n.

## otic
otic, adj., pertaining to the ear. — Gk. ώτικός,
fr. οδς, gen. ώτός, 'ear'. See oto- and adj. suff.
-ic and cp. entotic, epiotic.

## -otic
-otic, suff. meaning 'affected with, suffering from'.
It forms adjectives from nouns ending in -osis
(as neur-otic, fr. neur-osis). — Gk. -ωτικός,
formed from nouns in -ώτης or verbal adjectives
in -ωτός, through the addition of suff. -ικός.
See -osis and adj. suff. -ic.

## Otididae
Otididae, n. pi., a family of birds, the bustards
(ornithol.) — ModL., formed fr. Otis with suff.
-idae.

## Otiorhynchidae
Otiorhynchidae, n. pi., a family of weevils (ento-
mol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk.
ώτίον, dimin. of ους, gen. ώτός, 'ear', and
ρ'ύγχος, 'snout, beak'. See oto- and rhyncho- and
cp. words there referred to.

## otiose
otiose, adj., 1) at leisure \qrchaic)\ 2) useless,
futile. — L. otiosus, 'at leisure, at ease, idle', fr.
otium, 'leisure, idleness', which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. negotiate. For the ending see suff.
-ose.
Derivatives: otiose-ly, adv., otiose-ness, n.

## otiosity
otiosity, n. — MF. ociosite, fr. Late L. otio-
sitatem, ace. of otiositas, fr. L. otiosus. See
prec. word and -ity.

## Otis
Otis, п., a genus of bustards (ornithol.) — L. otis,
'a kind of bustard', fr. Gk. ώτίς, lit. 'long-
eared bird', fr. οδς, gen. ώτός, 'ear'. See oto-
and cp. the second element in Haliotis,
Myositis.

## otitis
otitis, п., inflammation of the ear (med.) —
Medical L. otitis^ formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk. οδς,
gen. ώτός, 'ear'. See oto-.

## oto-
oto-, before a vowel ot-, combining form denoting
the ear (med.) — Gk. ώτο-, ώτ-, fr. οδς, gen.
ώτός (Κ>Γ*οδσος, gen. *οΰσατος), 'ear', which
is cogn. with L. auris (for *ausis), 'ear', Goth.
auso, OE. eare, 'ear'. See ear, 'the organ of
hearing', and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also otic, Otis, Aotus, diota, lago-, microtin,
parotic, parotid, Plecotus.

## otocyst
otocyst, п., the auditory organ of Mollusca and
Vermes (zool.) — Lit. 'otic cavity'; coined by
the French naturalist Folix-Henri de Lacaze-
Duthiers (1821-1901) fr. Gk. οδς, gen. ώτός,
'ear', and κύστις, 'bladder, bag, pouch'. See
oto- and cyst.

## otolith
otolith, п., chalky matter in the internal ear of
animals (zool.) — Lit. 'ear stone'; coined by the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:550 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 523 | OVER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:550 COLUMN:1 -->
French anatomist and surgeon Gilbert Breschet
(1784-1843) in 1836 fr. Gk. οδς, gen. ώτος, 'ear',
and λίθος, 'stone'. See oto- and -lith.

## otology
otology, п., that branch of medicine which deals
with the ear and its diseases. — Compounded of
oto- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: otolog-ic-al, adj., otolog-ist, n.

## otoscope
otoscope, п., an instrument for examining the ear.
— Compounded of oto- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr.
σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See -scope.

## ottava rima
ottava rima, a stanza of eight lines, with the rhyme
scheme abababcc {pros.) — It., lit. 'octave
rhyme'. See octave and rhyme.

## otter
otter, п., an aquatic carnivorous mammal. —
ME. oter, fr. OE. olor, oter, re], to ON. otr,
Swed. utter, Dan. odder, MLG., MDu., Du.
otter, OHG. ottar, MHG. oter, otter, G. Otter,
and cogn. with OI. udrak, Avestic udra, 'otter',
Gk. ϋδρϊ, ϋδρος, 'waier-serpent', ελιυδρις, 'otter',
L. lutra (for 'utra, 'udra, influenced in form by
lutum, 'mud, mire'), OSlav. vydra, Lith. udra,
Lett, udris, OPruss. udro, 'otter', Olr. odar,
'dark-colored, brown', lit. 'otter-colored', odoir-
ne, 'otter', and prob. also with Gk. δλλος (for
*ϋδλος), 'water snake, ichneumon' (with change
of ρ to λ). AH these words derive fr. I.-E. "udr-,
'water', and lit. denote an aquatic animal. l.-E.
"udr- is an enlargement of base *ud-, 'water'. See
water and cp. hydra, Lutra, nutria.

## otto cycle
otto cycle, 1) a four-stroke cycle in internal-
combustion engines; 2) a kind of velocipede. —
Named after its inventor August Nikolaus Otto
(1839-91).

## Ottoman
Ottoman, adj., Turkish; п., a Turk. — F.
ottoman, fr. It. Oltomano, fr. ML. Ottomdnus, fr.
Arab. -'Utkmanf, 'pertaining to 'Uthman', fr.
'Uthman, 'Osman', name of the founder of the
Ottoman empire. Cp. Osmanli.

## ottoman
ottoman, п., a kind of sofa or divan. — F. otto-
mane, prop. fern, οι ottoman, 'Ottoman', hence
lit. 'Ottoman piece of furniture' (see prec. word);
so called because one can rest on it according to
the Oriental fashion.

## oubliette
oubliette, п., a secret dungeon, reached only
through a trapdoor from above. — F., fr. MF.,
fr. oublier, 'to forget', fr. OF. oblider, fr. VL.
"oblitare, fr. L. oblttus, pp. of obltvisci, 'to
forget'. See oblivion and -ette.

## ouch
ouch, also nouch, п., a brooch or clasp (archaic).
— ME. поиске, fr. OF. nosche, noche, поиске,
'jewel, necklace', fr. ML. nusca, fr. OHG. nusca,
a word of Celtic origin (cp. Olr. nasc, 'a tie,
chain', Bret, nask, 'a rope to tie animals'), fr.
I.-E. base *ned-, "to knot, twist'. See net and cp.
words there referred to. The loss of the initial
n- in ouck is due to a misdivision of о поиск into
an ouck. For similar misdivisions cp. adder and
words there referred to.

## ought
ought, aux. v., expressing duty or obligation. —
ME. aughten, oughten, fr. augkte, ougkte,
'owned, possessed', fr. OE. Okie, of s.m., past tense
of agan, 'to own, possess'; hence prop, past
tense of owe (q.v.)

## ought
ought, n. — An obsol. var. of aught.

## Ouija
Ouija, п., a trademark. — Coined fr. F. oui,.
'yes', and G. ja, 'yes'.

## ounce
ounce, п., a unit of weight, the twelfth part of a
pound in troy and apothecaries weight. — ME.
unce, ounce, fr. OF. unce (F. once), fr. L. uncia,
'the twelfth part (of anything); the twelfth part
of a pound, an ounce; the twelfth part of a foot,
an inch'. See uncia and cp. inch, which is a
doublet of ounce. Cp. also the second element in
quincunx.

## ounce
ounce, п., snow-leopard, lynx. — ME. u/ice, once*
fr. OF. (= F.) once, fr. lonce, misread as I'once,
the initial / having been taken for the definite
article and consequently dropped. Lonce goes
back to VL. *luncia, from L. lyncea, 'the
lynxlike animal', fern, of lynceus, 'lynx-like', used as
a noun, fr. lynx, gen. lyncis, 'lynx'. See lynx.

## ouphe
ouphe, п., an elf, sprite. — A var. of oaf.

## our
our, pron. — ME. ure, oure, fr. OE. ure, 'of us,
our', fr. earlier user, gen. of us; 'us'; re], to OS.
usa, user, OFris. use, user, OHG. unsar, unser,
MHG., G. unser, Goth, unsar, 'our'. See us and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:550 COLUMN:2 -->
cp. nostrum.

## ourali
ourali, n. — A var. of curare.

## ours
ours, pron. — ME. ures, formed fr. ure, 'our' (see
prec. word) with gen. suff. -s.

## -ous
-ous, suff. used to form adjectives meaning
'having, full of, abounding in'; in chemistry this
suff. means 'having a lower valence than is
expressed by suff. -ic. — ME., fr. OF. -ous-, -eus
(F. -eux), fr. L. -osus. See adj. suff. -ose. In many
cases E. -ous is equivalent to Gk. -ος or L. -us.
Cp. e.g. arduous, fr. L. arduus, E. pious, fr. L.
pius, etc.

## ousel
ousel, n. — See ouzel.

## oust
oust, tr. v., to drive out, expel, eject. — AF.
ouster, fr. OF. oster (F. oter), 'to take away', fr. L.
obstare, 'to stand against, oppose, obstruct', in
VL. used also in the sense 'to hinder', formed
fr. ob, 'against' (see ob-), and stare, 'to stand'.
See stand, v., and cp. obstacle.
Derivative; oust-er, n.

## ouster
ouster, п., ejection from property, dispossession
(law). — AF. inf. used as noun, fr. OF. oster, 'to
take away'. See prec. word. For the subst. use of
the infinitive cp. attainder and words there
referred to.

## out
out, adv. — ME. out, oute, fr. OE. ut, ute, rel. to
OS., ΟΝ., OFris., Goth, ut, Swed. ut, Dan. ud,
MDu. uut, Du. uit, OHG., MHG. из, G. aus, fr.
I.-E. *ud, 'up, out, away', whence also OI. ut,
'up, out', littarak, 'the higher, upper, latter,
later, northern', Avestic us-, uz- (for *ud-z), 'up,
out', Olr. pref. ud-, od-, 'out-', L. usque (for
*us-que), 'all the way to, from ... to, without
interruption', Gk. Αστέρος (for "ud-tero-s), 'the
latter'. Cp. abont, but, uitiander, utmost, utter,
adj. and v., and the second element in carouse.
Cp. also hysteron proteron. Cp. also hubris.
Derivatives: out, adj., п., tr. v., and inter).

## outcast
outcast, adj. and n. — ME., fr. pp. of out-
casten, fr. out, 'out', and casten, 'to cast'. See
out and cast.

## outcaste
outcaste, п., in India, a person expelled from his
caste. — Formed fr. out- and caste.

## outcome
outcome, п., result. — Scot., formed fr. out and
come; introduced into English by Carlyle.

## outlander
outlander, п., foreigner, used esp. in the sense of
'not of Boer birth'. — Formed in imitation of S.
African Du. uitiander, 'person from a foreign
land'; see out, land and agential suff. -er and cp.
uitiander.

## ontiandish
ontiandish, adj., 1) foreign; 2) strange. — ME.
utlandisch, fr. OE. Htlendisc, 'foreign'. See out,
land and adj. suff. -ish.

## outlaw
outlaw, n. — ME. ullage, fr. OE. utlaga, fr. ON.
tttlagi, 'an outlaw', lit. '(one placed) outside of
the law*. See out and law.
Derivatives: outlaw, tr. v., outlaw-ry, n.

## outline
outline, n. — Coined by the English diarist John
Evelyn (1620-1706) fr. out and line.
Derivatives: outline, tr. v., outlin-ed, adj.,
outlin-er, n.

## outrage
outrage, п., a violent injury; any serious violation
of the law. -^ ME., fr. OF. oltrage, oultrage,
outrage, fr. VL. "ultrdticum, fr. L. ultra,
'beyond'. See ulterior and -age and cp. outre.
Derivative: outrage, tr. v.

## outrageons
outrageons, adj., violent, excessive; very
offensive. — ME., fr. OF. oultrageus, outrageus (F.
outrageux), fr. oultrage, outrage. See prec. word
and -ous.
Derivatives: outrageous-ly, adv., outrageous-
ness, n.

## outrance
outrance, п., the utmost extremity. — MF.
outraunce, fr. OF. oultrance, outrance (F.
outrance), 'extreme, excess', lit. 'a going beyond',
fr. OF. oultrer, outrer (F. outrer), 'to go beyond'.
See ontre and -ance.

## outre
outre, adj., exaggerated; extravagant; eccentric.
— F., pp. of outrer, 'to carry to excess, overdo,
overstrain, exaggerate', fr. outre, 'beyond', fr. L.
ultra. See outrage.

## outrigger
outrigger, п., 1) a projecting spar for extending
sails; 2) a bracket at the side of a rowboat with
a rowlock for an oar. — Lit. 'something rigged
out'; formed fr. out, rig and agential suff. -er.

## outshine
outshine, tr. and intr. v. — Coined by Spenser
from out- and shine.

## outward
outward, adj. — ME., fr. OE. uteweard, Wtweard,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:550 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. Ut, 'out', and -weard, '-ward'. See out and
-ward.
Derivatives: outward, п., outward-ly, adv.

## outward
outward, adv. — ME., fr. OE. utweard. See
outward, adj.

## outwards
outwards, adv. — ME. outwardes, fr. OE. ut-
weardes, formed fr. utweard with adv. gen. suff.
•es. See prec. word and adv. suff. -s.

## ouzel also ousei
ouzel also ousei, п., 1) the European blackbird; 2)
any of certain other birds. — ME. osel, fr. OE.
osle, for *amsle, 'blackbird', rel. to OHG. am·
sala, amusla, MHG., G. amsel, and cogn. with
L. merula (for *mesola), 'blackbird', W.
mwyalck, 'blackbird, thrush', W. moelk, 'ouzel',
Bret, moualck, of s.m. Cp. amsel, merle, Merulius.

## oval
oval, adj., egg-shaped. — ML. ovalis (whence also
F. ovale), fr. L. ovum, 'egg'. See ovum and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: oval, п., ovat-ly, aav.,oval-ness, n.

## ovari-
ovari-, form of ovario- before a vowel.

## ovarian
ovarian, adj., pertaining to an ovary. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. Medical L. ovarium. See ovary.

## ovariectomy
ovariectomy, п., oophorectomy. — A hybrid
coined fr. Medical L. ovarium (see ovary) and
Gk. -εκτομίϊ, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή,
'a cutting out' (see -ectomy). The correct form is
oophorectomy, in which both elements are of
Greek origin.

## ovario-
ovario-, before a vowel ovarl-, combining form
denoting an ovary. — Fr. Medical L. ovarium.
See ovary.

## ovariotomy
ovariotomy, п., у an incision into an ovary; 2) in
its usual sense, the surgical removal of an ovary
or both ovaries (med.) — Lit. 'the cutting of an
ovary*; a hybrid coined fr. Medical L. ovarium
(see ovary) and Gk. -τομίϊ, 'a cutting of, fr.
τομή, 'a cutting' (see -tomy). In the first sense
ovariotomy should be replaced by oophorotomy,
in the second by oopkorectomy, in which both
elements are of Greek origin.

## ovaritis
ovaritis, п., inflammation of an ovary or both
ovaries (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr.
Medical L. ovarium and the Greek suff. -ΐτις
(see ovary and.-itis). The correct form is fiopko-
ritis (q.v.), in which both elements are of Greek
origin.

## ovary
ovary, n. (anat. and bot.) — Medical L. ovarium,
fr. L. ovum, 'egg'. See ovum and subst. suff. -ary.

## ovate
ovate, adj., shaped like an egg. — L. ovatus, fr.
ovum, 'an egg'. See ovum and adj. suff. -ate.

## ovation
ovation, п., 1) a lesser kind of triumph (Roman
antiq.); 2) an enthusiastic applause. — L. ovatio,
gen. -onis, fr. ovd, ovure, 'to exult, to triumph in
an ovation', for *ewayo, from the imitative base
е"а-, whence also Gk. εύάζειν, 'to utter cries of
joy', lit. 'to cry е\5а (in honor of Bacchus)'.

## oven
oven, n. — ME., fr. OE. ofen, rel. to OFris.,
MDu., Du. oven, OHG. ovan, MHG. oven, G.
Ofen, ON. ofn, Dan. ovn, OSwed. ogkn, Swed.
ugn, Goth, ailkns, and cogn. with OI. ukkdh,
ukka, 'pot, cooking pot', L. aulla for 'auxla,
'pot' (cp. the dimin. auxilla, 'small pot'), Gk.
Ιπνός (for *weqy"nos, 'oven'. Hence oven
originally meant 'a pot, a fire-pot' (cp. OE. ofnet, 'a
small vessel'). Cp. olio and olla podrida.

## over
over, adv. and prep. — ME., fr. OE. ofer, 'over,
above', rel. to OS', obar, ubar, OFris. over, ur,
ON. yfir (adv. and prep.), Dan. over (prep.),
Swed. over (prep, and adv.), Norw. yver (prep,
and adv.), OHG. ubar, ubir (adv. and prep.),
ubari, ubiri (adv.), MHG., G. iiber (prep, and
adv.), Goth, ufar, 'over, above*, and cogn. with
OI. upari, Avestic upairi, Over, above, beyond'
(adv. and prep.), Arm. ι ver, 'up, above', Gk.
υπέρ (adv. and prep.), L. super, 'over, above,
beyond' (adv. and prep.), Gaul, ver- in ver-tragus,
ver-tagus, 'greyhound', and in PN's (as in Ver-
cingetorix, etc.), Olr. for (for *upor), 'above,
beyond'. AH these words derive fr. I.-E. *uper,
*uperi, 'over, above, beyond', which is prop,
comparative of *upo, 'from below; turning
upward, upward; up, over, beyond'. See up, adv.,
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also hypo-,
hyper-; sub-, super-.
Derivatives: over, adj. (q.v.), over, tr. v., to get
over (rare); intr. v., to go over (rare); over, п.,
surplus, excess; also a term of cricket.

## over
over, adj. — ME., fr. uvere, 'upper, higher', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:551 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: OVERANXIOUS | 524 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:551 COLUMN:1 -->
OE. uferra, of s.m., compar. of ofer, adv.; see
over, adv. The change of ME. uvere to over is
due to the influence of over, adv. Cp. OHG.
obaro, MHG. obere, G. ober, 'upper, higher'.

## overanxious
overanxious, adj. — A hybrid coined by the
English novelist Samuel Richardson (1689-1761)
fr. over, adv., and anxions, which is of Latin
origin.
Derivative: overanxious-Iy, adv.

## overawe
overawe, tr. v. — Coined by Spenser fr. over, adv.,
and awe, v.

## overcome
overcome, tr. v. — ME. overcomen, fr. OE. ofer-
cuman, fr. ofer, 'over', and cuman, 'to come'. See
over, adv., and come.

## overplus
overplus, п., a surplus. — A hybrid coined fr.
over, adv., and plus.

## override
override, tr. v. — ME. overriden, fr. OE. oferridan,
fr. ofer, 'over', and ridan, 'to ride*. See over, adv.,
and ride.

## oversee
oversee, tr. v. — ME. overseen, fr. OE. oferseon,
fr. ofer, 'over', and seon, 'to see'. See over^ adv.,
and see, v.
Derivative: overse-er, n.

## overslaugh
overslaugh, tr. v., to pass over a turn of duty in
consideiation of another more important duty.
— Du. overslaan, 'to pass over, omit', lit. 'to
strike over', fr. over, 'over', and slaan, 'to strike'
(cp. G. uberschlagen, 'to skip, omit'). See over,
adv., and slay and cp. slag.

## overslaugh
overslaugh, п., 1) an overslaughing; 2) a bar in a
river obstructing navigation. — Du. overslag,
'omission', also 'obstruction', from the stem of
overslaan, 'to omit; to obstruct'. See prec. word.

## overt
overt, adj., open; public. — ME. overte, fr. OF.
overt (F. ouvert), pp. of ovrir (F. ouvrir), 'to-
open', fr. VL. *operlre, 'to open', fr. L. aperire,
'to open' (but influenced in form by L. cooperire>
'to cover'). See aperient and cp. cover. Cp. also
overture.
Derivatives: overt-ly, adv., overt-ness, n.

## overtone
overtone, п., an upper partial tone, a harmonic
(mus.) — Literal translation of G. Obertont
which was first used by the German physicist
Hermann Ludwig Ferdinand von Helmholtz
(1821-94) as a contraction of Oberpartiatton (i.e-
'upper partial tone'). See over, partial and tone, n.

## overture
overture, п., 1) an introductory proposal; 2) {mus.}
an instrumental prelude to an opera, oratorio,
etc. — ME., fr. OF. overture (F. ouverture),
'opening', fr. OF. overt, pp. of ovrir, 'to open'.
See overt and -ure.

## overwhelm
overwhelm, tr. v, — ME. overwhelmen, fr. over,
'over', and whelmen, 'to turn'. See over, adv.,
and whelm.
Derivatives: overwhelm-er, п., overwhelm-ing,
adj. and п., overwhelm-ing-ly, adv., overwhelm-
ing-ness, n.

## ovi-
ovi-, combining form meaning 'egg', as in oviduct,
oviparous. — L. ovi-, fr. ovum, 'egg'. See ovum.

## ovi-
ovi-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to-
sheep, ovine, as in ovibovine. — Fr. L. ovis, 'a
sheep'. See ovine.

## Ovibos
Ovibos, п., the genus consisting of the musk ox
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of ovi-, 'sheep',
and L. bos, gen. bovis, 'ox*. See bovine.

## Ovibovmae
Ovibovmae, n. pi., a subfamily of the Bovidae
(zool.) — ModL., fr. prec. word. For the ending
see sufT. -inae.

## ovibovine
ovibovine, adj., pertaining to the subfamily Ovi-
bovinae (zool.) — See prec. word.

## Ovidae
Ovidae, п., the family consisting of the sheep and
goals (zool.) — ModL., formed with surf, -idae
fr. L. ovis, 'a sheep'. See ovine.

## oviduct
oviduct, п., the duct through which the eggs pass
from the ovary (anat. and zool.) —
Compounded fr. ovi-, 'egg', and duct.

## oviform
oviform, adj., egg-shaped. — Compounded of
ovi-, 'egg', and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See
form, n.

## oviform
oviform, adj., resembling a sheep. —
Compounded of ovi-, 'sheep', and L. forma, 'form, shape'.
See form, n.

## ovine
ovine, adj., pertaining to, or having the nature of,
sheep. — L. ovinus, Of a sheep', fr. ovis, 'a
sheep', which is cogn. with OI. avih, Gk. й (F )ις
(Homeric δϊς, Att. οΐςΙ, OHG. ouwi, ou, OE.
eowu, 'sheep'. See ewe and adj. suff. -ine and cp.
Ovis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:551 COLUMN:2 -->

## oviparous
oviparous, adj., producing eggs that are hatched
outside the body of the female. — L. oviparus,
compounded of ovum, 'egg', and the stem of
parere, 'to bring forth'. See ovum and
-parous.

## oviposit
oviposit, intr. v., to deposit eggs (with the
ovipositor; said of insects). — Compounded of
ovi-, 'egg', and L. positus, pp. of pdnere, 'to
place'. See position.

## ovipositor
ovipositor, п., organ in insects to deposit eggs in a
suitable position. — See prec. word and agential
suflf. -or.

## Ovis
Ovis, п., the genus consisting of the domestic
sheep and most of the wild sheep (zool.) — L.
ovis, 'a sheep'. See ovine.

## ovo-
ovo-, combining form meaning 'egg'. — Fr. L.
ovum, 'egg'. See ovum.
«void, adj., egg-shaped. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
ovum, 'an egg', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See ovum and -oid. The correct
form is ooid (fr. Gk. φόν, 'egg', and -οειδής,
'like').

## ovolo
ovolo, п., a convex molding, usually forming a
quarter of a circle or ellipse (archit.) — It. ovolo
(now spelled uovolo), dimin. of ovo (resp. uovo),
'egg', fr. L. ovum. See ovum.

## ovoviviparons
ovoviviparons, adj., producing eggs that are
hatched out within the body of the female (zool.) —
Compounded of ovo- and viviparous.

## ovulate
ovulate, adj., having an ovule or ovules. —
Formed with adj. suflf. -ate fr. ModL. ovulum. See
ovule.

## ovulate
ovulate, intr. v., to produce ovules. — See prec.
word.
Derivative: ovulat-ion, n.

## ovular
ovular, adj., pertaining to an ovule. — ModL.
ovuldris, fr. ovulum. See next word and -ar.

## ovule
ovule, п., a small egg; specif., 1) an unfertilized
ovum (zool.); 2) that part of a plant which
develops into a seed (bot.) — F., fr. ModL. ovulum,
'a small egg', dimin. of L. ovum. See ovum and
-ule.

## ovum
ovum, п., an egg; the female germ cell (biol.) — L.
ovum, 'egg', cogn. with Gk. φόν, ON. egg, OE.
xg. See egg and cp. aviary. Cp. also oval, ovary,
ovate, ovolo, ovule.
«we, tr. and intr. v. — ME. owen, awen, fr. OE.
agan, 'to possess, have, own, owe', rel. to OFris.
aga, ON. eiga, Swed. dga, OHG. eigan, Goth.
aigan, 'to possess, have', fr. I.-E. base *aik-, 'to
own', whence also OI. ise, 'he owns', isah,
'owner, lord, ruler', Isvarah, 'owner, ruler, lord,
king', Avestic is-, 'riches, fortune', isvan-, 'well
off, rich'. Cp. ought, aux. v., own, adj. and v.,
fraught, freight. Cp. also Ishvara.
Derivative: owing (q.v.)

## owing
owing, adj. — Pres. part, of prec. word, used in a
passive sense (= owed).

## owl
owl, n. — ME. oule, owle, fr. OE. ule, rel. to Du.
uil, OHG. uwila, MHG. iuwel, iule, G. Eule, ON.
ugla (for 'uggvala), Dan. ugle, Swed. uggla; of
imitative origin. Cp. L. utulare,'la howl,screech,
cry out', и/и/о,'owl', prop, 'the screeching bird';
and see ululate. See also howl, howlet.
Derivatives: owl-er, п., owl-ery, п., owl-et, п.,
owl-ing, п., owl-lish, adj., owl-ish-ly, adv., owl-
ish-ness, n.

## own
own, adj. — ME. owen, awen, fr. OE. dgen,
'own', lit. 'possessed by', prop. pp. of agan, 'to
possess, have'; rel. to OS. egan, 'own', OFris.
igin, ON. eiginn, Dan., Swed. egen, Du. eigen,
OHG. eigan, MHG., G. eigen, 'own', of s.m.,
which all are orig. pp.s. and are rel. to Goth.
aigan, 'to possess, have', dih, Ί possess, have'.
See owe and cp. own, v.

## own
own, tr. and intr. v. — ME. ohnien, ahnien, fr. OE.
agnian, 'to possess, take possession of, fr. dgen,
'own' (adj.); rel. to ON. eigna, 'to own", Dan.
egne, OHG. eiginen, G. eignen, of s.m. See own,
adj.
Derivatives: own-er, п., owner-less, adj.,
ownership, п., own-ness, n.

## ox
ox, n. — ME., fr. OE. oxa, rel. to OS., OHG.
ohso, ON. oxi, uxi, OFris. oxa, MDu. osse, Du.
os, MHG. ohse, G. Ochse, Goth, auhsa, and
cogn. with W. ych, 'ox', Mir. oss, 'stag', OI,
uksa, Avestic uxshan-, 'ox, bull', Toch. В okso,
Jox', fr. 1-Е. base *uksen-, 'male animal', lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:551 COLUMN:3 -->
'besprinkler', fr. base^ * uks-, 'to sprinkle', whence
OI. uksdti, 'sprinkles'. This base is related to
base *ugw-, 'wet, moist, to sprinkle', whence Gk.
υγρός, 'wet, moist', L. итог (for *ug"m6r),
'fluid, moisture'. See humor and cp. nxorious.
Cp. also the second element in aurochs.

## oxalate
oxalate, п., a salt of oxalic acid (chem.) — F.,
coined by Guyton de Morveau (1737-1816) fr.
L. oxdlis, 'sorrel'. See Oxalis and chem. suff.
-ate.

## oxalic
oxalic, п., pertaining to the acid CjHjO, (chem.)
·— F. oxalique, fr. L. oxalis, 'sorrel'; so called by
the French chemist Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier
(1743-94) in 1787, because it occurs in the plant
sorrel. See Oxalis and adj. suff. -ic.

## Oxalidaceae
Oxalidaceae, n. pi., the wood sorrel family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Oxalis with suff. -aceae.

## oxalidaceous
oxalidaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Oxalis
Oxalis, п., a genus of plants, the wood sorrel
(bot.) — L. oxalis, 'a sort of sorrel', fr. Gk.
όξαλίς, 'sorrel', fr. οξύς, 'sharp', which is rel. to
βκρις, 'peak, point', Homeric όκριϊν, 'to make
rough or rugged', όκριΐσθοα, 'to be exasperated',
cogn. with L. ocris, 'a rugged, stony mountain',
medi-ocris, 'middling, moderate, indifferent,
tolerable', orig. 'being half-way up the height of a
mountain', Umb. ukar, ocar, 'fortress, citadel,
mountain', and in gradational relationship to L.
deer, 'sharp'. See acrid and cp. oxy-, oxytone,
paroxysm. Cp. also mediocre.

## oxidation
oxidation, п., the act of oxidizing or the state of
being oxidized. — F. (now spelled oxydation).
See oxide and -ation.

## oxide
oxide, also oxid, п., a compound of oxygen with
an element or radical (chem.) — F. oxide (now
spelled oxyde), coined by G. de Morveau fr. Gk.
οξύς, 'sharp', and aciife, 'acid'. The spelling
oxyde was influenced by Gk. δξύς, 'sharp, sour,
acid'.

## oxidize
oxidize, tr. v., to combine with oxygen; intr. v.,
to become oxidized (chem.) — Formed fr. prec.
word with suff. -ize.
Derivatives: oxidiz-able, adj., oxidiz-abil-ity, п.,
oxidiz-er, n.

## oxlip
oxlip, п., a kind of primrose. — OE. oxanslyppe,
fr. oxan, gen. of oxa, 'ox', and slyppe, 'slime'.
See ox and slip and cp. cowslip.

## Oxonian
Oxonian, adj., pertaining to Oxford or Oxford
University; п., a native or inhabitant of Oxford;
a member of Oxford University. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. ML. Oxonia, 'Oxford'.

## oxter
oxter, п., the armpit (Scot.) — OE. ohsta, oxta,
'shoulder', rel. to OE. oxn, 'armpit', and cogn.
with L. axilla, 'armpit'. See aisle.
oxy^, combining form meaning 1) 'sharp,
pointed', as in oxytone; 2) 'acid', as in oxygen. — Gk.
όξυ-, fr. οξύς, 'sharp'. See Oxalis.

## oxy-
oxy-, combining form meaning 1) 'containing
oxygen', as in oxycarbonate, oxyhydrogen; 2)
'containing the hydroxyl radical', as in oxy-
aldehyde, etc. (in this latter sense the form
hydroxy- is preferably used). — Short for
oxygen.

## oxyacetylene
oxyacetylene, adj., pertaining to a mixture of
oxygen and acetylene. — Compounded of oxy-,
'containing oxygen', and acetylene.

## oxyacid
oxyacid, п., an acid that contains oxygen (chem.)
— A hybrid coined fr. oxy-, 'containing oxygen',
and L. acidus, 'sour, acid'. See acid and cp.
hydracid.

## Oxydendrum
Oxydendrum, п., a genus of plants, the sorrel tree
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of oxy-, 'sharp,
sour', and Gk. δένδρον, 'tree'. See dendro- and
cp. the second element in rhododendron.

## oxygen
oxygen, п., a gaseous chemical element. — F.
oxygene, short forprincipe oxygene (earlierprin-
cipe oxygine), lit. 'the acidifying principle';
coined by the French chemist Antoine-Laurent
Lavoisier (1743-94) in 1777 fr. Gk. οξύς, 'sharp,
acid', and γείνομαι, Ί beget, bear, bring forth',
which stands for 'γένιομαι and is rel. to
γεννάω, Ί beget, bring forth, generate, produce'; see
oxy-, 'sharp; acid', and -gen. Hence oxygen lit.
means 'producing acids'; Lavoisier and the
other chemists of his time believed that oxygen
was an important compound of every acid.

## oxygenate
oxygenate, tr. v., to combine with oxygen (chem.)
— F. oxygener, fr. oxygene. See oxygen and

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 525 | OZONIZE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:552 COLUMN:1 -->
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: oxygenat-ion, n.

## oxygenize
oxygenize, tr. v., to oxygenate. — Formed fr.
oxygen with suff. -ize.

## oxyhemoglobin
oxyhemoglobin, oxyhaemoglobin, п., a substance
found in arterial blood, formed by the loose
union of hemoglobin with oxygen. —
Compounded of oxy-, 'containing oxygen', and
hemoglobin.

## oxyhydrogen
oxyhydrogen, adj., pertaining to, or using, a
mixture of oxygen and hydrogen; п.,
oxyhydrogen gas (chem.) — Compounded of oxy-,
'containing oxygen', and hydrogen..

## oxymoron
oxymoron, п., a figure of speech by which
contradictory terms are combined. — Gk. όξύμωρον,
neut. of οξύμωρος, 'pointedly foolish',
compounded of οξύς, 'sharp, pointed', and μωρός,
'foolish'. See oxy-, 'sharp', and moron.

## oxyntic
oxyntic, adj., secreting acid. — Formed with suff.
-ic fr. Gk. "όξυντός, verbal adj. of όξΰνειν, 'to
sharpen', fr. οξύς. See oxy-,1'sharp'.

## Oxyopidae
Oxyopidae, n. pi., a family of hunting spiders
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk.
όξυωπής, 'sharp-eyed', which is compounded of
οξύς, 'sharp', and ώφ, gen. ώπός, 'eye'. See
oxy-, 'sharp', and -opia.

## Oxyrrhyncha
Oxyrrhyncha, Oxyrhyncha, п., a division of crabs,
the spider crabs (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
άξύρρυγχος, 'sharp-snouted', which is
compounded of οξύς, 'sharp', and ρύγχος, 'snout'.
See oxy-, 'sharp', and rhyncho-.

## oxysalt
oxysalt, п., a salt of an oxyacid (chem.) —
Compounded of oxy-, 'containing oxygen', and salt.

## oxysulfide
oxysulfide, also spelled oxysuiphide, п., a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:552 COLUMN:2 -->
compound of oxygen and sulfur with an element or
positive radical (chem.) — Compounded of
oxy-, 'containing oxygen', and sulfide,

## oxytocia
oxytocia, п., rapid childbirth (med.) — Medical
L. See next word and 1 st -ia.

## oxytocic
oxytocic, adj., hastening childbirth (med.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. όξυτόκιον (scil.
φάρμακον), 'medicine for hastening childbirth',
fr. δξύς, 'sharp, quick', and τόκος, 'childbirth,
parturition'. See oxy- and toco-.
Derivative: oxytocic, п., a substance hastening
childbirth.

## oxytocin
oxytocin, п., a hormone of the posterior pituitary
gland, serving to stimulate the contractions of
the uterus in childbirth (med.) — See prec. word
and -in.

## oxytone
oxytone, adj., having an acute accent on the last
syllable; п., an oxytone word. — Gk. όξύτονος,
compounded of οξύς, 'sharp', and τόνος, 'tone'.
See oxy-, 'sharp', and tone.

## Oxytropis
Oxytropis, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(hot.) — ModL., compounded of oxy- and Gk.
τρόπις, 'keel', which is rel. to τρόπος, 'turn'.
See trope and cp. words there referred to,

## oyer
oyer, п., a hearing of causes; an assize. — ME.,
fr. AF., which corresponds to OF. oir, oyr (F.
outr), 'to hear', used as a noun, fr. L. audlre, 'to
hear'. See audible and cp. oyez. For the subst.
use of OF. infinitives cp. attainder and words
there referred to.

## oyer and terminer
oyer and terminer, in England, a court of judges
of assize; in the United States, a higher criminal
court. — AF., 'a hearing and determining', lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:552 COLUMN:3 -->
'to hear and determine'; infinitives used as
nouns. See prec. word and terminer.

## oyez
oyez, also oyes, interj. 'Hear! hear ye!', a cry
uttered usually thrice, to call attention. — ME.
oyes, fr. AF. oyes, which corresponds to OF.
oiez, oyez, 'hear ye!', imper. pi. of oir (F. ouir),
'to hear', fr. L. audidtis, 2nd pers. pi. of pres.
subj. fr. audire, 'to hear'. See audlbie and cp.
oyer.

## oyster
oyster, n. — ME., fr. OF. oistre, uistre (F. huitre),
fr. L. ostrea, oslreum, fr. Gk. βστρεον, 'oyster',
which is rel. to όστέον, όστοΰν, 'bone'; so
called from its hard shell. See osteo- and cp.
ostracize.

## ozo-
ozo-, combining form meaning 'smell' (generally
used in a bad sense. — Gk. όζο-, fr. οζειν, 'to
smell'. See odor and cp. ozone, osmium.

## ozocerite
ozocerite, п., a waxlike mineral. — G. Ozokerit,
coined by the German mineralogist Ernst Frie-
drich Glocker (1793-1858) in 1833 fr. ozo-, Gk.
κηρός, 'wax', and suff. -it, which goes back to
Gk. -ΐτης. See cere and subst. suff. -ite.

## ozone
ozone, п., an allotropic form of oxygen with a
pungent odor (chem.) — Coined by the German
chemist Christian Friedrich Schonbein (1799-
1868) in 1840 fr. Gk. δζειν, 'to smell'; so called
by him because of its strong smell. See ozo-.
Derivatives: ozon-ed, ozon-ic, adjs., ozonize
(q.v.), ozon~ous, adj.

## ozonize
ozonize, tr. v., to convert into ozone; to
impregnate with ozone (chem.) — Formed from prec.
word with suff. -ize.
Derivatives: ozoniz-ation, п., ozoniz-er, n.

## pa
pa, п., father (colloq.) — Abbreviation of papa.

## pabulum
pabulum, п., food, nourishment. — L. pabulum,
'food, fodder', for *pa-dhlo-m, formed with
instrumental suff. *-dhlo-m fr. I.-E. base *ρδ-, 'to
tend, keep, pasture, feed, guard, protect',
whence also L. pa-nis, 'bread', рй-scere, 'to
graze, pasture, feed', pastor, 'shepherd', lit.
'feeder'. See food and words there referred to,
and cp. esp. pastor.
раса, п., a rodent of Central and South America.
— Sp., fr. Tupi раса.

## pace
pace, п., a step. — ME. pas, fr. OF. (= F.) pas,
fr. b.passus, 'step, stride, pace', lit. 'a stretching
out (of the leg)*, fr. passus, pp. of pandere, 'to
stretch out'. See patent and cp. pas, passage,
compass, surpass, trespass, passport.
Derivatives: pace, intr. v., pac-er, n.

## pace
pace, п., with the leave of; a courteous form
expressing disagreement. — L. pace, abl. of pax,
'peace'. See pax, peace.

## pachisi
pachisi, п., name of a game played in India. —
Hind, pachisi, 'twenty-five', contraction of OI.
paRca, 'five', and vimsatib, 'twenty', so called
because the highest number thrown is 25. — OI.
panca is cogn. with Gk. πέντε, L. quinque,
Goth, fimf, OE. ///; see five. OI. viitisatlfi is
cogn. with Boeot. Gk. 'feixcm, *fixom,
Ion. and Att. είκοσι, L. viginti, 'twenty'; see
vicennial.

## pachnollte
pachnollte, п., a hydrous fluoride of aluminum,
calcium and sodium (mineral.) — G. Pachnolit,
compounded of Gk. πάχνη, 'frost', and λίθος,
'stone'. The first element stands for *παγ-σνα
and is rel. to πάγος, 'frost', fr. I.-E. base *pag-,
'to make firm, fix'; see pact and cp. words there
referred to. For the second element see -lite.

## pachouli
pachouli, n. — See patchouli.

## pachy-
pachy-, combining form meaning 'thick, dense'.
— Gk. παχύ-, fr. παχύς, 'thick, dense', for I.-E.
'bhnghiis, whence also OI. bahuh, 'much,
numerous'; cogn. with Avestic bazah-, 'height,
depth' (for *bhenghos), Hitt. pankush, 'large',
ON. bingr, 'heap', OHG. bungo, 'a bulb', Lith.
biess (for *bhenghus), 'thick'. Cp. the first
element in bahuvrihi.

## pachycephalia
pachycephalia, pachycephaly, п., thickness of the
skull (med.) — Medical L. pachycephalia, lit.
'thickness of the head', compounded of pachy-
and Gk. κεφαλή, 'head'. See cephalic. For the
ending see 1st -ia, resp. -y (representing Gk.
-IS).

## pachyderm
pachyderm, п., a thick-skinned animal, as the
elephant, rhinoceros and hippopotamus. — F.
pachyderme, fr. Gk. παχύδερμος,
'thick-skinned', which is compounded of παχύς,'thick', and
8έρμα, gen. δέρματος, 'skin'. See pachy- and
derma.

## pachydermatous
pachydermatous, adj., I) thick-skinned; 2)
insensitive. — See prec. word and -oils.

## pachydermia
pachydermia, п., abnormal thickness of the skin
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. παχυδερμίά,
'thickness of the skin', fr. παχύδερμος, 'thick-
skinned'. See pachyderm.
Derivative: pachydermi-al, adj.

## pachymeningitis
pachymeningitis, п., inflammation of the dura
mater (med.) — Medical L., formed from next
word with sufT. -itis.

## pachymeninx
pachymeninx, п., the dura mater (anal.) —
Medical L., compounded of pachy- and Gk. μηνιγξ,
'membrane'. See meninx.

## Pachysandra
Pachysandra, п., a genus of plants of the box
family (hot) — ModL., compounded of pachy- and
Gk. άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man', used in the
modern sense of stamen. See andro-,

## Pachystima
Pachystima, п., a genus of plants of the staff-tree
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of pachy-
and Gk. στίγμα, 'puncture, stigma'. See stigma.

## pacific
pacific, adj. — MF. (= F.) pacifique, fr. L.
pacificus, 'peace-making', fr. pax, gen. pads,
'peace', and -ficus, fr. -ficere, unstressed form of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:553 COLUMN:2 -->
Ρ
facere, 'to make, do". See pacify and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: pacific-al, adj., pacific-al-ly, adv.

## Pacific
Pacific, п., the Pacific Ocean. — From prec.
word; so called by its discoverer Vasco Nunez
De Balboa (cca. 1475-1517) in allusion to the
calmness of its waves.

## paciticate
paciticate, tr. v., to pacify. — L. pacificutus, pp.
of pacificare. See pacify and verbal suff. -ate.

## pacification
pacification, n.— MF. (= F.), fr. L. pacificatio-
nem, ace. of pdeifiedtid, 'making of peace', fr.
pacificatus, pp. of pacificare. See pacify and
-ation.

## pacificator
pacificator, n. — L. pacificator, 'maker of peace',
fr. pacificatus, pp. of pacificare. See pacify and
agential suff. -or.

## pacificatory
pacificatory, adj., tending to pacify. — L. pdcifi-
catorius, 'peace-making', fr. pacificatus, pp. of
pacificare. See pacify and adj. suff. -ory.

## pacifism
pacifism, n. — Contraction of pacificism, which is
formed fr. pacific with suff. -ism. For the
shortening of pacificism into pacifism see haplology.

## pacifist
pacifist, n. and adj. — Contraction οι pacificist.
See pacific and -1st and cp. prec. word. For the
shorteningofpac/^di( into pacifist see haplology.
Derivative: pacifist-ic, adj.

## pacify
pacify, tr. v. — ME. pacifien, £r. OF. (= F.)
pacifier, fr. L.pacificare, 'to make peace', ίτ.ράχ,
gen. pads, 'peace', and -ficere, unstressed form
of facere, 'to make, do'. See pax and -fy and cp.
pacificate.
Derivatives: pacifi-able, adj., pacifi-er, n.

## pack
pack, n. — ME. pakke, of LG. origin. Cp. MLG.
рак, packe, MDu., Du. рак, 'package, parcel,
bundle', orig. a term of wool trade in Flanders.
It. pacco is a Dutch loan word. Cp. next word.
Derivatives: pack, adj., pack-less, adj.

## pack
pack, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. pack, n. Cp. MLG.,
LG., MDu. and Du. pakken, 'to pack'.
Derivatives: pack-er, п., pack-ery, п., pack-ing,
n.

## package
package, n. — Prob. fr. Du. pakkage, 'baggage',
fr. рак, 'pack'. See pack, п., and -age.
Derivatives: package, tr. v., packag-ing, п.,
packag-er, n.

## packet
packet, n. — MF. pacquet (F. paquet), dimin. of
pacque, fr. MDu. (= Du.)pak. See pack, п., and
-et.
Derivative: packet, tr. v.

## pact
pact, n. — ME., fr. MF. pact (F. pacte), fr. L.
pactum, 'contract, covenant', prop. neut. pp. of
paclscor, paclsci, 'to covenant, make a treaty,
agree, stipulate', rel. to pax, gen. pacts, 'peace',

unite, make firm, fasten, fix', whence also L.
pangere, 'to join, make firm', pagus, 'district,
province, village', pagina, 'strips of papyrus
fastened together, page', palus (for *pak-slos),
'post, stake', ΟΙ.ραέ-,ράέα-, 'cord, rope', Avestic
pas-, 'to fetter', Gk. πηγνύναί, 'to fix, make
firm, fast or solid, to harden, freeze', πάγη,
'snare, noose', lit. 'anything that fixes', πάγος,
'something solid; mountain peak, rocky hill',
πάγιος, 'solid', παγετός, 'frost', πήγμα,
'something fastened together', πήξις, 'a making firm,
fastening', πάσσαλος (for *πάκ-ιαλος), 'peg',
Russ. pazit, 'joint', Slovenic pdi, 'partition (of
planks'), OE. fxc, 'space, period of time', OE.
fegan, 'to join', [δη, 'to catch, seize', OE. fxger,
OHG. [agar, 'beautiful'. Cp. appalto, appease,
Areopagus, compact, adj., п., and v., compages,
dispatch, fay, 'to join', парах legomenon,

pachnollte, pagan, page, 'side', pageant, Paguridae, pail,

'to requite', peace, pectin, pectolite, Peganum,
pegmatize, -pexy, pole, 'stake', propagate. Cp.
also fair, 'beautiful', fake, fang, fay, 'to join',
feague.

## Pactolian
Pactolian, adj., pertaining to the Pactolus:
golden. — Formed with suff. -ian fr. L. Pactolus, fr.

Gk. Πακτωλός, name of a river in Lydia,
famous for its gold-containing sand.

## pad
pad, п., road. — Du. pad, 'path', rel. to OE. ргер,
OHG. pfad. See path and cp. the second element
in footpad.

## pad
pad, п., a cushion; a stuffed saddle, etc. — Of
uncertain, possibly, LG. origin. Cp. MDu. pad,
'sole of the foot'.
Derivatives: pad, tr. v., to stuff, padd-ing, n.

## pad
pad, tr. and intr. v., to go along, trudge along. —
Of imitative origin; influenced in meaning by
pad, 'road'.

## pad
pad, п., a basket. — A var. of dial. ped. See
peddler.

## paddle
paddle, п., a short oar with a wide blade. — ME.
padell, 'a small spade', of uncertain origin.
Derivative: paddle, tr. v., to move (a boat, etc.)
by means of a paddle.

## paddle
paddle, intr. v., to dabble. — Of uncertain origin;
perh. freq. of pad, 'to go'. Cp. LG. paddeln, 'to
go with.short steps» to paddle'.
Derivative: paddle, n.

## paddock
paddock, п., an enclosure. — ME. parrock, fr. OE.
pearroc, 'fold, enclosure'. See parrock and cp.
park. For the change of -r- to -d- cp. pediment.
Derivative: paddock, tr. v.

## paddock
paddock, п., toad (archaic). — ME. paddok,
dimin. oi padde, 'toad', which is rel. to ON. padde,
Swed. padda, Dan. padde, Du. pad, padde, of
s.m. For the ending see suff. -ock.

## paddy
paddy, п., rice in the husk. — Malay pad!.

## Paddy
Paddy, п., an Irishman (colloq.) — Dimin. of
Padraig, the Irish form of Patrick (q.v.)

## paddymelon
paddymelon, п., a small kangaroo. — From
Australian native name.

## padishah
padishah, п., title of the Persian shah and the
Turkish sultan. — Turk, padishah, fr. Pers.
pddshah, which is compounded of pad, 'master',
and shah, 'king'. The first element is rel. to
OPers. pati, Avestic paiti-, OI.· patih, 'master,
husband', and cogn. with Gk. πόσις (for *πό-
τις), of s.m., L.potens, 'mighty'. See potent and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also the first
element in bezoar. For the second element see shah.
Cp. pashah.

## padlock
padlock, п., a removable lock. — Compounded
of pad, 'padlock', a word of uncertain origin,
and lock, 'a device foreclosing the door'.
Derivative: padlock, tr. v.

## padnag
padnag, п., an ambling nag. — Compounded of
pad, 'road', and nag.

## padre
padre, п., priest, chaplain. — It., Sp., Port, padre,
'father', fr. L.patrem, ace. of pater, 'father'. See
pater.

## padrone
padrone, п., patron; master. — It., fr. L. patro-
num, ace. of patronus, 'protector', fr. pater,
'father'. See patron.

## paduasoy
paduasoy, п., a corded silk fabric. — F. pou-de-
soie (see poult-de-soie); but influenced in form
by Padua, city in N. Italy (the word was
supposed to mean 'silk of Padua').

## paean
paean, pean, п., a song of joy and triumph. — L.,
fr. Gk. παιάν, 'a hymn, a song of triumph', fr.
Παιάν, Paean, name of the physician of the
gods, later Apollo, lit. 'one who touches',
whence used in the sense 'one who heals by a
touch', fr. παίω, παίειν, 'to touch, strike',
which prob. stands for *πά^ω and is cogn.
with L. pavio, pavtre, 'to strike, beat'. See pave
and cp. paeon, peony.
Derivative: paean, pean, tr. v., to praise in
paeans.

## paed-
paed-, form of paedo- before a vowel.

## paedagogic
paedagogic, adj. — See pedagogic.

## paedagogue
paedagogue, n. — See pedagogue.

## paedagogy
paedagogy, n. — See pedagogy.

## paederast
paederast, п., paederasty, n. — See pederast,
pederasty.

## paediatric
paediatric, adj. — See pediatric.

## paedo-
paedo-, before a vowel paed-. — See pedo-, ped-,

## paedobaptlsm
paedobaptlsm, n. — See pedobaptism.

## paedology
paedology, п., child study. — See 1st pedology.

## Paelignian
Paelignian, п., the language of the Paeligni, a
people of Central Italy. — Formed with suff.
-an fr. L. Paeligni, 'the Paeligni', a name prob.
rel. to paelex, 'concubine', and cogn. with Gk.
πάλλαξ, 'boy; girl', παλλακή, παλλακίς,
'concubine', παλλάς, 'virgin, maiden',- see Pallas.
Accordingly, Paeligni orig. must have meant
'the sons of unmarried girls'. See F. Altheim,
Geschichte der lateinischen Sprache und Litera-
tur,pp. 56-58.

## paenula
paenula, п., a long woolen sleeveless coat or
mantle worn esp. on journeys and in bad
weather {Roman antiq.) — L., fr. Gk. φαινόλη,
'mantle', lit. 'the shining one', fr. φαίνειν, 'to
show', φαΕνεσθαι, 'to appear, give light, shine
forth'. See phantasm,

## paeon
paeon, п., a metrical foot consisting of four
syllables, one long and three short {Greek and Lat.
pros.) — L. paeon, fr. Gk. παιών, 'a hymn; a
paeon', Att. form of παιάν. See paean.

## Paeonia
Paeonia, п., a genus of plants, the peony (bot.) —
See peony and 1st -ia.

## paeonic
paeonic, adj., pertaining to a paeon. — Late L.

## pagan
pagan, п., a heathen. — ME., fr. Late L. paganus,
'countryman, villager, civilian'. The early
Christians called the heathens 'civilians', in
contradistinction to the 'soldiers' of Christianity. Late
L. paganus derives fr. L. pdgus, 'district,
province, village', prop, 'something joined together,
something united', fr. I.-E. base *pag-, *pdk-,
'to join together', whence also L. pangere, 'to
join, make firm', pax, gen. pads, 'peace',pacisci,
'to make a.treaty'; see pact. Cp. F. paten,
'pagan', which also derives fr. Late L. paganus. Cp.
also paysage, peasant.
Derivatives: pagan, adj., pagan-dom, п.,
paganish, adj.

## paganism
paganism, п., the state of being a pagan;
heathenism. — Late ME., fr. Late L. pagdnismus,
'heathenism*, fr. paganus. Seeprec. word and-ism
and cp. paynim, which is a doublet of paganism.

## paganize
paganize, tr. v., to render heathenish, to
heathenize. — F. paganiser, fr. Late L. paganus. See
pagan and -ize.

## page
page, п., a boy attendant. — ME., fr. OF. ( = F.)

pedo-, 'boy, child'.

## page
page, п., one side of a leaf of a book. — OF. ( =

рак-, 'to join together', whence also L. pangere,
'to join, make firpi', pax, gen. pads, 'peace',
pacisci, 'to make a treaty'. See pact and cp.
pagan. Cp. also pail, peg.
Derivative: page, tr. v., to mark the pages of.

## pageant
pageant, п., exhibition, spectacle. Orig., a
movable scaffold on which a mystery play was
performed. — ME. pagin, pagen, pagent, fr.
Late L. pagina, 'movable scaffold, scene of a
play'.fr. L.pagina, 'leaf, slab'; seepage, 'side of
a book'. The t is excrescent; cp. the words
undent, peasant, pheasant, tyrant.
Derivatives -.pageant, adj. and tr. v.,pageant-ed,
adj., pageant-eer, п., pageant-ic, adj.,

## paginal
paginal, adj. — Late L. pagindlis, 'pertaining to a

## paginary
paginary, adj., paginal — Formed with adj. suff.

## paginate
paginate, tr. v., to mark the pages of, to page. —
Formed with verbal suff. -ate fr. L. pagina,

Derivative: paginat-ion, n.

## pagoda
pagoda, п., a temple in India or China. — Port.

fr. Bhdgah, 'a god of wealth'. See Bhaga.

## pagurian
pagurian, adj., pertaining to the Paguridae; п., а
member of the Paguridae.' — See next word and

## Paguridae
Paguridae, n. pi., the family of the typical hermit
crabs. — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L.
pagurus, fr. Gk. πάγουρος, *crab', lit. 'with stiff
tails', compounded of stem *παγ-, 'firmly fixed'
(whence also πάγος, 'something solid;
mountain peak, rocky hill', πάγιος, 'solid'), and
ούρα, 'tail'. The first element derives fr. I.-E.
base *pdg-, *pak-, 'to join together; see pact.
For the second element see uro-, 'tail'.

## pah
pah, interj., exclamation of disgust. — Imitative.

## Pahlavi
Pahlavi, п., an Iranian language spoken in Persia
from the 3rd to about the 10th century. — Pers.
Pahlavi, fr. OPers. Parthava, 'Parthia'.

## paideutics
paideutics, п., pedagogy. — Gk. παιδευτική (scil.
