paucitas, 'fewness, scarcity', fr. paucus, 'few,
little', which is rel. to L. paullus, later spelled
paulus, 'little', parvus, 'small, little', the first
element in pau-per, 'poor', and cogn. with Gk.
παϋρος, 'few, little', Goth, fawai, OE. feawe,
'few'. See few and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also poco. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## paughty
paughty, adj., haughty; pert (Scot.) — A blend of
proud and haughty.

## Paul
Paul, masc. PN.; name of the apostle of
Christianity to the Gentiles — L. Paulus, a Roman
surname of the Aemilian gens, prob. fr. paulus,
'little'. See paulo-post-future.

## pauldron
pauldron, п., a piece of armor to protect the
shoulder. — ME. polrond, fr. OF. espauleron, fr.
espaule (F. epaule), 'shoulder'. See epanlet.

## paulin
paulin, n. — Aphetic for tarpaulin.

## Paulina
Paulina, fem. PN. — Fem. of Pauliaus (q.v.)

## Pauline
Pauline, adj., pertaining to the apostle Paul. — L.
Paulinus, fr. Paulus. See Paul and -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## Paulinus
Paulinus, masc. PN. — L., lit. 'belonging to
Paulus'. See Paul and prec. word.

## paulo-post-future
paulo-post-future, future perfect tense in Greek
grammar. — Lit. 'the future a little later'. The
first element is abl. of L. paullus, later spelled
paulus, 'little' (whence the dimin. pauxillum,
'very little'), which is rel. to paucus, 'few, little';
see paucity. For the other two elements see post-,
resp. future.

## Paulowrua
Paulowrua, п., a genus of Chinese trees (bot.) —
ModL., named after the Russian princess Anna
Paulowna (1795-1865), daughter of Czar Paul 1.
For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## paunch
paunch, п., abdomen, belly. — ME. paunche, fr.
OF. panche, var. of pance (F. panse), fr. L. pan-
ticem, ace. of pantex, 'paunch', which is prob.
rel. topanus, 'swelling',paniculus, 'tuft, panicle'.
See panicle.
Derivatives: paunch, tr. v., paunch-ed, adj.,
paunch-ful, adj. ,paunch-y, adj. ,paunch-i-ly, adv.,
paunch-i-ness, n.

## pauper
pauper, п., a person who depends on charity; a
very poor person — L., 'poor', for *pauc(o)-pars,
lit. 'he who acquires little', fr. paucus, 'little,
few', and the stem of pario, parere, 'to bring
forth, produce; to acquire, gain'. For the first
element see few, for the second see parent. See
also poor, which is a doublet of pauper.
Derivatives: pauper, adj., pauper-dom, п.,
pauper-ed, adj.,pauper-ism, п.,pauper-ize, tr. v.,
pauper-iz-ation, a.

## pausation
pausation, п., the act of pausing. — Late L. pau-
satio, gen. -onis, fr. pausat-(um), pp. stem of
pausare. See pause, v., and -Ion.

## pause
pause, n. — MF. ( — F.), fr. L.pausa, 'stop,
cessation', fr. Gk. παϋσις, 'stopping, ceasing', fr.
παύειν, 'to cause to cease', which is prob. cogn.
with OPruss. pausto, 'wild', OSlav.puf tu, 'waste,
deserted',pustiti, 'to leave, to let'; see Sohnsen,
Indogermanische Forschungen XXXI, 483. The
ending -a in L. pausa (for -is fr. Gk. παϋσις) is
prob. due to the analogy of the synonym mora.
Cp. pose, 'to place'.
Derivatives:paus-at, adj.,pause-less, ad}.,pause-
less-ly, adv.

## pause
pause, intr. v. — Either fr. pause, п., or fr. Late L.

## pausare
pausare, 'to halt, cease, pause', or fr. F. pauser,
'to pause' (which itself derives fr. Late L.
pausare).

## pavage
pavage, п., 1) the act of paving; 2) tax to pay for
the paving of streets, etc. — F., fr. paver, 'to
pave'. See pave and -age.

## pavan
pavan, п., 1) a slow, stately dance; 2) the music

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:568 COLUMN:3 -->
for this dance — F. pavane, fr. Sp. pavana, fr.
pavo, 'peacock', fr. L. pavjis, a secondary form
of pavd, 'peacock' (see pavonine); so called from
the character of this dance.

## pave
pave, tr. v. — ME. paven, fr. OF. (= F.) paver, fr.
VL. *pavare (whence also OProvenc. pavar),
corresponding to L. pavlre, 'to beat, ram, tread
down', which is rel. to pavlre, 'to tremble', lit.
'to be struck down', prob. also to putare, 'to cut,
trim, prune, lop', and cogn. with Lith. piduju,
piduti, .'to cut', piuklas, 'saw'. See putative and
cp. pit, 'cavity', putamen.
Derivatives: paver, η.,ραν-ing, n.

## pave
pave, п., pavement — F., prop. pp. οι paver, 'to
pave', used as a noun. See prec. word.

## pavement
pavement, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. VL.
'pavamentum, fr. "pavare, 'to pave',
corresponding to L.pavimentum, *a beaten floor', it.pavire,
'to beat, ram'. See paye and -ment.
Derivatives: pavement-er, n.

## Pavia
Pavia, п., a genus of trees and shrubs, now
forming part of the genus Aesculus (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Dutch botanist Peter Paaw
(latinized into Pavinus) (1564-1617).

## pavilion
pavilion, n. — ME.paviton, fr. MF. (=
F.)pavilion, fr. L. papilionem, ace. aipapilio, 'butterfly',
used in the Middle Ages to denote a tent,
because it resembles a butterfly with outstretched
wings. See Papilio.
Derivative: pavilion, tr. v.

## pavior
pavior, paviour, п., paver. — ME. pavier, fr.
paven, 'to pave'. See pave and -ier.

## pavis
pavis, pavise, п., a large shield — ME. pavis,
pavise, fr. OF. paveis (F. pavois), 'shield', fr.
Olt. (= It.) pavese fr. Pavese, 'of Pavia'; so
called because originally made in Pavia, Italy.

## Pavo
Pavo, п., 1) the genus of the peacocks (zool.); 2)
name of a southern constellation. — L. pavo,
'peacock'. See peacock and cp. pavonine.

## pavonated
pavonated, adj., of the color of the peacock — Fr.
L. pavo, gen. pavdnis, 'peacock'. See prec. word
and the adj. suff. -ate and -ed.

## pavonazzo
pavonazzo, adj., of the color of a peacock. — It.,
lit. 'peacock-like', fr. pavone, 'peacock', fr. L.
pavonem, ace. of pavo, 'peacock'. See peacock
and cp. next word.

## pavonine
pavonine, adj., related to, or resembling, a
peacock. — L. pavoninus, 'of, or like, a peacock', fr.
ρδνδ, gen. pavonis, 'peacock'. See peacock and
-ine (representing L. -inus).

## paw
paw, n. — ME. pawe, powe, fr. MF. poue, from a
pre-Celtic form "pauta (whence also Proven?.
pauta and Catal. pote, MDu. poot, pott, Du.
poot, G. Pfote, 'paw'), which is prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. patois, patrol, pattee," patten, pud.
Derivatives: paw, tr. and intr. v., paw-er, п.,
paw-ing, n,

## pawk
pawk, п., trick (Scot.) — Of unknown origin.
Derivatives:paw/c-y, aa).,pawk-i-ly, SLdv.,pawk-
i-ness, n.

## pawl
pawl, п., a bar preventing a capstan from
recoiling — Prob. fr. F. epaule, 'shoulder'. See epaulet
and cp. pauldron.
Derivative: pawl, tr. v.

## pawl
pawl, п., a small tent with two poles and steep,
sloping sides (India). — Hind, pal, 'a shelter', fr.
OI. patalam, 'cover, roof, which is prob. rel. to
OI. patah, 'woven cloth'.

## pawn
pawn, п., piece of least value at chess. — ME.
poune,pown, fr. Οΐ.ραοη, avar. of peon, fr. ML.
pedonem, ace. oipedo, 'foot soldier' (whence
also It. pedone, Sp. peon, 'foot soldier, pawn'), fr.
L. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See foot and cp. peon,
pioneer.

## pawn
pawn, п., pledge — ME. paurt, fr. OF. pan, also
pand, 'piece of cloth', later used also in the sense
of 'pledge', fr. L. pannum, ace. oipannus, 'piece
of cloth', which is cogn. with Goth, fana, 'piece
of cloth', OS. fano, of s.m., Gk. πηνος, *web',
πήνη, 'web, bobbin'. OHG. pfant (whence
MHG. pfant, G. Pfand), OS., MDu. pand, pant
(whence Du. pand), OFris. pand, pond, 'pledge',
are loan words fr. OF. pan, panel. Cp. fanon,
gonfalon, vane. Cp. also pane, panel, panuelo,
Penelope, penology.
Derivatives: pawn, tr. v.,pawn-able, adj.,pawn-
age, п., pawn-ee, п., pawn-er, n.

## pawnee
pawnee, п., water (Anglo-Ind.) — Hind, pant.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:569 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PAX | 542 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:569 COLUMN:1 -->
'water', rel. to OI. pati, 'drinks',panam, 'drink',
pfbati, 'drinks', and cogn. with Gk. πίνειν, 'to
drink', L. pdtdre and bibere, 'to drink'. See
bibulous, and cp. poison, potable, potion.

## pax
pax, п., 1) peace; (cap.) the goddess of peace in
Roman mythology; 2) a tablet representing a
religious subject (R.C.Ch.) — L. pax, gen. pads,
'peace'. See peace.

## paxilla
paxilla, п., a pillarlike spine (zool.) — ModL., fr.
L. paxillus, 'a small stake, a peg', dimin. formed
fr. palus, 'strake, pale', which stands for *pacslos
and is rel. to paclscor, pacisci, 'to make a treaty',
pax, gen. pads, 'peace'. See pact and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: paxill-ar, paxill-ate, adjs.

## paxwax
paxwax, п., the nuchal ligament of mammals. —
ME., dissimilated fr. ME. faxwax, which is
prob. a compound of fax, 'hair' (fr. OE. feax),
and wax, 'growth' (fr. waxen, 'to grow'). The
first element is rel. to ON. fax, 'mane', OHG.
fahs, 'hair', and to ON./ет (for *faheza), 'sheep*,
fr. I.-E. base *pek-, 'to pluck (wool or hair)',
whence also Gk. ττέκος, 'fleece', b.pecus, 'cattle,
flock', pexus, 'woolly', pecten, 'comb'. See fee,
'cattle, money', and cp. words there referred to.
For the second element see wax, 'to grow'.

## pay
pay, tr. and intr. v., to requite, reward — ME.
paien, payen, fr. OF. pater, paer (F. payer), fr.
L. pacare, 'to pacify, appease', in VL. also 'to
pay', fr. pax, gen. pads, 'peace'. See pact and cp.
peace.
Derivatives: pay, n. (q.v.), pay-able, adj.,
payee, п., pay-er, п., pay-ing, п., payment (q.v.)

## pay
pay, n. — ME. paye, pay, fr. OF. paie (F. paye\
back formation fr. paler, paer. See prec. word.

## pay
pay, tr. v., to coat -with pitch (naut.) — Obsol. F.
peier, 'to coat with pitch', fr. OF. peier, fr. L.
picare, fr. pix, gen. picis, 'pitch', which is cogn.
with Gk. πίσσα, (for *к1ща.), 'pitch'. See pitch,
'a resinous substance'.

## payable
payable, adj. — ME. paiable, fr. OF. pal'able, fr.
paler, 'to pay'. See pay, 'to requite', and -able.
Derivatives: payabil-ity, п., payable-ness, п.,
payabl-y, adv.

## payetan
payetan, n. — Inexact var. of payyetan,

## payment
payment, n. — ME. payement, payment, fr. MF.
(= ¥.) paiement, fr. payer, 'to pay*. See pay, 'to
requite' and -ment.

## paynim
paynim, п., a pagan, heathen (archaic). — ME.
painim, fr. OF. patenime, fr. Late L. paganismus,
'heathenism', fr. paganus, 'heathen'. See
paganism.

## payola
payola, п., 1) an undercover payment or graft
given in return for a commercial favor; 2) the
practice of giving payolas. — Prob. formed fr.
pay with sufF. -ola. The same sufF. appears also
in pianola.

## paysage
paysage, п., landscape. — F., fr. pays, 'country',
fr. OF. pals, of s.m.,'fr. b.pagus, 'province,
district'. See pagan and -age and cp. peasant.

## payyetan
payyetan, also spelled payetan, п., an author of
religious poems forming part of the Jewish
liturgy on festivals and special Sabbaths. —
Talm. Heb. payyetan, 'poet*, in MedHeb.
'writer of liturgic poems', a hybrid coined fr. Gk.
ποιητής, 'poet' (see poet); and the Heb. sufF.
-an. Cp. piyyut.
pef п., name of the 17th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb. рё, peh, lit. 'mou^i', so called
in allusion to the ancient Hebrew form of this
letter.

## pea
pea, n. — Back formation fr. ME. pese, pees, *a
pea', the s having been mistaken for the plural
suff.; see pease. For similar back formations cp.
cherry, Chinee, gentry, marquee, pry, 'lever',
row, 'noise', sash, 'framework', shay, sherry,
shimmy, skate, trews.

## peace
peace, n. — ME. pais, pees, fr. OF. pais (F. paix),
fr. L. pacem, ace. οΐράχ, 'peace', which is rel. to
pacisci, 'to make a treaty'. See pact and words
there referred to and cp. esp. appease, pace,
'with the leave of, pacify, pax.
Derivatives: peaceable (q.v.), peace-ful, adj.,
peace-ful-ly, adv., peace-ful-ness, п., peace-less,
adj., peace-less-ly, adv., peace-less-ness, n.

## peaceable
peaceable, adj. — ME. peisible, fr. OF. (= F.)
paisible, fr. pais, 'peace'. See peace and -able.
Derivatives \ peaceaBi-y, adv., peaceable-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:569 COLUMN:2 -->

## peach
peach, п., the fruit of the tree Amygdalus Persica.
— ME. peche, fr. OF. pesche (F. peche), fr.
Late L. persica, taken for a fern. sing, noun, but
orig. pi. of L. Persicum (malum or pdmum),
'Persian apple', resp. 'Persian fruit', fr. Persia,
'Persia'; cp. It.pesca, Rum. pierseca, OProvenc.

## persega
persega, presega, Catal. presec, which all derive
fr. VL. persica. Cp. Parsee, Persian, perse.
Derivatives: peach-en, adj., peach-er, п., peach-
ery, п., peach-let, n. peach-y, adj., peach-i-ness,
n.

## peach
peach, intr. v., to inform against (slang) —Aphet-
ic for appeach (q.v.)

## peacock
peacock, n. — ME. ресок, fr. OE. pawa, pea,
'peacock', and coc, cocc, 'cock'. The first
element derives fr. L. ράνδ, gen. pavonis, 'peacock'
[whence also OHG. pfawo (MHG. pfdwe, pfa,
G. Pfau), MLG. pawe, Du. pauw and OSlav.
pavu], which, together with Gk. ταώς, prob.
comes ult. fr. Tamil tdkei, togei (whence also
Heb. tukkiyytm, 'peacocks'). The initial p- in L.
ράνδ is due to imitative influence; cp. L. pau-
pulo, 'the natural sound of the peacock'. Cp.
Pavo, pavonazzo, pavonine, ponceau, 'corn
poppy*. For the second element see cock.
Derivatives: peacock, intr. v., peacock-ery, п.,
peacock~ish, peacock-like, peacock-y, adjs.

## peag
peag, п., beads made of shells. — Aphetic for
Algonquian wampum peag, 'white strings'. See
wampum.

## pea jacket
pea jacket, n. — MDu. pie (Du. pij), 'pea jacket'.

## peak
peak, п., a pointed top. — A var. of pike, 'sharp
point'.
Derivatives: peak, tr. \.,peak-ed, adj., peak-ed-
ly, adv., peak-ed-ness, п., peak-er, п., реак-у,
adj.

## peak
peak, intr. v., to shrink, waste away. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: peak-ed, adj.

## peak
peak, tr. v., to raise vertically (naut.) -- Back
formation fr. apeak (q.v.)

## peal
peal, п., sound of bells — Aphetic for appeal.
Derivative: peal, intr. and tr. v.

## pean
pean, n. — See palan.

## pear
pear, n. — ME. pere, for OE. pere, fr. VL. pera,
(whence also OF. peire, F. poire), var. of pira,
fem. sing., for L. pira, pi. of pirum, 'pear',
which is a loan word from an unknown source,
whence also Gk. άπιον, 'pear', άπιος, 'pear tree'.
Cp.Perilla, perry, pyriform,Pyrus.Cp. alsoApios.

## pearceite
pearceite, п., a variety of geyserite (mineral.) —
Named after the English metallurgist Dr.
Richard Pearce of Denver. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## pearl
pearl, п., a concretion in the shell of various mol-
lusks, used as a gem. — ME. perle, fr. MF.
(= F.) perle, prob. borrowed fr. It. perla, fr.
VL. * perla (whence also OProvenc., Sp. perla.
Port, perola), which is a blend of L.perna, 'ham,
sea mussel, pearl', and sphaerula, 'a small ball',
dimin. of sphaera, 'ball'. L. perna stands for
*persna and is cogn. with OI. parsnip, 'heel*,
Avestic pushna- *heel', Gk. πτέρνη, Goth./oirz-
na, OHG. fersana, MHG. versene, verse, G.
Ferse, Du, verzenen (pi.), OS.fersna, OE.ftersn,
of s.m. For L. sphaera see sphere.
Derivatives: pearl, v., pearl-ed, adj., pearl-ish,
adj.,pearl-y, adj., pearl-i-ness, n.

## pearl
pearl, п., one of a series of loops forming an
edging on lace. — A var. of purl.

## pearlitc
pearlitc, п., a alloy of carbon and iron (metall.) —
F. periite, formed fr. perle, 'pearl', with surT.
-ite. See 1st pearl and subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: pearlit-ic, adj.

## pearlite
pearlite, п., perlite. — See perl ite.

## pearmain
pearmain, п., a kind of apple. — ME. parmayn,
fr. OF. permain, parmain, fr. VL. Parmanus, 'of
Parma', fr. L. Parma, a city, in Italy. Cp.
Parmesan.

## peart
peart, adj., 1) pert; brisk, lively, clever — A var.
of pert.
Derivatives: peart-ly, adv., pear-tness, n.

## peasant
peasant, n. — ME. paissaunt, fr. OF. palsant (F.
paysan), which was formed—with change of
suffix—fr. earlier pai'senc, fr. pais (F.pays), 'land,
country', fr. Late L. pdgensis, 'of a province or
district', fr. L. pagus, 'province, district'; see
pagan. OF. palsenc, palsant, orig, denoted man

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:569 COLUMN:3 -->
of a country. Cp. paysage.
Derivative.: peasant-ry, n.

## pease
pease, n. — ME. pese, fr. OE. pise, 'pea', fr. L.
pisum, fr. Gk. πίσος, 'pea*, a word of Thraco-
Phrygian origin. See Boisacq in Memoires de la
societe de linguistique, 17, 58. The vowel of ME.
pese shows the influence of OF. peis (whence F.
pois), 'pea'. Cp. pea, Pisum.

## peasecod
peasecod, п., pea pod (archaic). — ME. pescodde,
compounded of pese, 'pease', and codde, 'husk,
pod', fr. OE. codde, 'bag, shell, husk'. See pease
and cod, 'a small bag'.

## peat
peat, п., a piece of partly decomposed vegetable
matter. — ME. pete, fr. Anglo-L. peta, a word
of Celtic origin, which is prob. rel. to ML. pecia,
'piece'. See piece.
Derivatives: peat-ery, п., peat-y, adj.

## peat
peat, п., a pet (archaic) — Of uncertain origin;
not related to pet.

## peavey
peavey, п., a hook (lumbering). — Named after
its inventor Joseph Peavy.

## pebble
pebble, n. — ME. pobbel, pibbil, fr. OE. papol-
(stan), 'pebblestone', which is prob. of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: pebble, tr. v.,pebbl-ed, ad}.,pebbl-y,
adj.

## pebrine
pebrine, п., a silkworm disease. — F., fr.
Provens, pebrino, fr. pebre, 'pepper', fr. L. piper.
See pepper.

## pecan
pecan, п., 1) a kind of hickory; 2) its fruit (bot.)
— Earlier paccan, fr. F. pacane, which is of
Algonquian origin.

## peccable
peccable, adj., liable to sin. — ML. pecedbilis,
formed on analogy of L. impeccabilis,
'impeccable', fr. L. peccare, 'to sin'. See peccant and cp.
impeccable.
Derivative: peccabil-ity, n.

## peccadillo
peccadillo, п., a slight sin — Sp. pecadillo, dimin.
of pecado, 'sin', fr. L. peccatum, 'fault, error,
sin', prop. neut. pp. of peccare, 'to sin', used as
a noun. The spelling of peccadillo in English
shows the influence of Latin. See peccant.

## peccancy
peccancy, п., sinfulness; sin. — Late L. peccantia,
'sin', fr. L. peccans, gen. -amis. See next word
and -cy.

## peccant
peccant, adj., sinful; wrong. — L.peccans, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of peccare, 'to sin', which is of
uncertain origin. It. possibly stands for *peccos,
fr. *ped-cos, from the base of pes, gen. pedis,
'foot', hence prop, means 'to miss one's footing,
to stumble'. For form and sense development
cp. L. man~cus, 'maimed, crippled, lame', fr.
manus, 'hand'. See foot and -ant. (See Saussure
in Festskrift Thomsen, 2061, and Walde-Hof-
mann, LEW., II, 269.) Cp. peccable, peccadillo,
peccavi, impeccable.
Derivatives; peccant-ly, adv.,peccant-ness, n.

## peccary
peccary, п., piglike animal of South America. —
Sp. pecari, of Caribbean origin.

## peccavi
peccavi, intr. v., I have sinned; п., a confession
of guilt. — L. peccavi, Ί have sinned', pret. of
peccare, 'to sin'. See peccant.

## pech
pech, intr. v., to pant; п., a pant, panting— ME.
pechen, prob. of imitative origin,

## peck
peck, п., name of a dry measure. — OF. рек, rel.
to picot (whence F. picotin), 'peck', a word of
uncertain origin.

## peck
peck, tr. and intr. v., to strike, pick. — ME.
pecken, a var. afpikken, 'to pick'. See pick, 'to
pierce'.
Derivatives: peck, п., peck-er, п., peck-ish, adj.,
peck-ish-ly, adv., peck-ish-ness, п., peck-y,
adj.

## peckhamite
peckhamite, п., an iron magnesium silicate
(mineral.) — Named after the American chemist
Stephen F. Peckham (1839-1916). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Pecksniff
Pecksniff, п., an unctuous hypocrite — From
Seth Pecksniff, a character in Dickens's Martin
Chuzzlewit.
Derivatives: Pecksniff-ery, п., Pecksniff-ian,
adj., Pecksniff-ian-ism, n.

## Pecora
Pecora, n. pi., name of a division of ungulate
mammals (zool.) — L. pecora, 'cattle', pi. of
pecus. See pecuniary and cp. pekin, 'a civilian'.

## pectase
pectase, п., enzyme which turns pectin into pec-
tic acid (chem.) — Abbreviation of pect(m)-
(diast)ase.

## jpectate
jpectate, п., salt of pectic acid (chem.) — See
pectin and chem. sun", -ate.

## pecten
pecten, п., a comblike part, esp. one in the eyes
of birds and reptiles (zool.) — L. pecten, 'comb',
rel. to pectere, 'to comb', and cogn. with Gk.
πέκειν, Att. πεκτεϊν, 'to comb, shear', κτείς,
gen. κτενός (for *pkten-), 'comb', fr. I.-E. base
*pelc-, 'to pluck (wool or hair)'. See fee, 'cattle,
money', and words there referred to and cp. esp.
peignoir.

## pectic
pectic, adj., of, or pertaining to, pectin. — Gk.
πηκτικός, 'curdling', fr. πηκτός, 'solid, thick,
congealed, 'curdled', verbal adj. of πηγνύν'αι, 'to
make firm or solid'. See next word and -ic.

## pectin
pectin, п., a gelatinous substance obtained from
certain fruits, forming the basis of fruit jellies.
(chem.) — Coined by the French chemist Henri
Braconnot (1781-1855) fr. Gk. πηκτός, 'solid,
thick, congealed, curdled', verbal adj. of πηγ-
νύναι, 'to make firm or solid'; fr. I.-E. base
*pdg-, "рек-, 'to join together', whence also L.
pangere, 'to join, make firm', paciscl, 'to make a
treaty', pax, gen. pads, 'peace'. See pact and cp.
words there referred to.

## pectinate
pectinate, adj., shaped, or having teeth, like a
comb — L. pectinatus, pp. of pectinare, 'to
comb, card, hackle', fr. pecten, gen. peclinis,
'comb'. See pecten and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: pectinat-ed, adj.

## pectination
pectination, п., state of being pectinated —
Formed with suff. -Ion fr. L. pectinatus, pp.
of pectinare, 'to comb'. See prec. word and -ion.

## pectineus
pectineus, п., a muscle arising from the pubis and
inserted into the femur (anat.) — Short for
Medical L. musculus pectineus, lit. 'muscle of
the pubic region', a name coined by Riolan fr.
pecten, gen. -inis, 'comb', used also in the sense
of 'pubic bone'; see pecten. For sense
development cp. Gk. κτείς, 'comb; pubes; pudenda',
and see Joseph Hyrtl, Onamatologia anatomica,
pp. 387-88.

## pectini-
pectini-, combining form meaning 'comb', as in
pectiniform. — Fr. L. pecten, gen. peclinis,
'comb'. See pecten.

## pectiniform
pectiniform, adj., comblike. — Compounded of
pectini- and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## pectize
pectize, v., to coagulate. — See pectin and -ize.
Derivative: pectiz-ation, n.

## pectollte
pectollte, п., a sodium calcium silicate (mineral.)
— G. Pektolith, compounded of Gk. πηκτός,
'made firm, compacted' (verbal adj. of πηγνύναι,
'to make firm'), and λίθος, 'stone'; so called in
allusion to its appearance. See pact and -lite.

## pectoral
pectoral, adj., pertaining to the breast. — MF.
(= V.) pectoral, fr. L. pectoralis, 'of the breast',
fr. pectus, gen. pectoris, 'breast', which is cogn.
with Toch. A possum, В puscane (dual), 'the
breasts'. The L. and Toch. words possibly meant
orig 'the hairy part of the body', fr. base *pek-,
'hairy, woolly', whence also L. pecus, 'cattle',

## pectere
pectere, 'to comb'. See fee, 'cattle, money', and
cp. petronel, petto, poitrel and the second
element in parapet.

## pectoral
pectoral, п., something worn on the breast;
specif, the breast plate of the Jewish high priest.
— ME., fr. MF. (= F.) pectoral, fr. L.pectorale,
neut. of pectoralis, 'of the breast', used as a
noun. See pectoral, adj.

## pectose
pectose, п., a substance related to cellulose (chem.)
— See pectin and subst. suff. -ose.

## peculate
peculate, tr. and intr. v., to steal; to embezzle —
L. pecutatus, pp. of pecutari, 'to embezzle
public money', fr. peculium, 'private property', lit.
'property in cattle'. See peculiar and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: pecul-ation, п., peculator (q.v.)

## peculator
peculator, п., one who peculates. — L.peculator,
'embezzler of public money', fr. peculatus, pp.
of pecularX. See prec. word and agential suff. -or.

## peculiar
peculiar, adj., 1) one's own; 2) particular. — ME.

## peculier
peculier, fr. MF., or directly fr. L.peculidris, 'of,
or relating to, private property', fr. peculium,
'private property', lit. 'property in cattle', fr.

## pecu(s)
pecu(s), 'cattle', whence pecunia, 'money'. See
pecuniary.
Derivatives: peculiar-ism, п., peculiar-ity, п.,

## peculiar-ize
peculiar-ize, tr. v., peculiar-ly, adv.

## pecuniary
pecuniary, adj., pertaining to, or involving,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:570 COLUMN:2 -->
money — L. pecumarius, 'of, or pertaining to,
money', fr. pecunia, 'money', fr. pecu(s), 'cattle',
which is cogn. witn OI. pasu-, 'cattle', Goth.
faihu, 'money, fortune', OE. feoh, 'cattle,
money', fr. I.-E. base 'реки-, 'the woolly
animal', whence 'sheep, cattle, property, money'.
See fee and cp. Pecora. For the ending see adj.
suff. -ary.

## ped-
ped-, form of pedo- before a vowel.

## pedagogic
pedagogic, pedagogical, adj. — Gk.
παιδαγωγικός, 'suitable to a teacher', fr. παιδαγωγός,
'teacher'. See pedagogue and -Ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative:pedagogical-ly, adv.

## pedagogics
pedagogics, п., pedagogy. — See prec. word and
-ics.

## pedadogue
pedadogue, pedagog, п., teacher. — ME. peda-
goge, fr. MF. pedagogue (F. pedagogue), fr. L.
paedagggus, fr. Gk. παιδαγωγός, 'slave who
escorted a boy from home to school and back
again', tutor, teacher', for παιδος αγωγός,
'leader of a child', fr. παις, gen. παιδός, 'child',
and αγωγός, 'guide, leader', fr. δίγειν, 'to lead'.
See pedo- and agent and cp. -agogue.
Derivatives: pedagog(ue), tr. and intr. v.,
pedagogic (q.v.), pedagog-ist, n.,pedagogue-ish, adj.,
pedagogue-ry, n.

## pedagogy
pedagogy, n. — MF. (= F.)pe~dagogie, fr. L.pae-
dagogia, fr. Gk. παιδαγωγία, 'attendance on
children, education, culture', prop. Office of the
παιδαγωγός'. See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -is).

## pedal
pedal, adj., pertaining to the foot or feet. — L.
pedalis, of, or pertaining to, the foot', fr. pes,
gen. pedis, 'foot', which is cogn. with OI. pat,
ace. padam, 'foot', Dor. Gk. πώς, Att. πους
(gen. ποδός), Goth, fdtus, OE. fot, Toot'. See
foot and cp. words there referred to.

## pedal
pedal, п., lever worked by the foot. — F. pidale,
fr. It. pedale, fr. L. pedalis, 'of, or pertaining to,
the foot'. See pedal, adj.

## pedalier
pedalier, п., pedal keyboard. — Formed fr.
pedal, п., with suff. -ier.

## pedant
pedant, п., one who makes a display of his
learning. — F. pedant, fr. It. pedante, orig. meaning
'schoolmaster', fr. Late L. paedagdgantem, ace.
of paedagogans, fr. L. paedagogus. See
pedagogue and -ant.
Derivatives: pedant-ic, adj.,pedant-ic-al-ly, adv.,
pedant-ic-ism, п., pedant-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
pedantry (q.v.)

## pedantry
pedantry, n. — ¥.pedanterie, fr. It. pedanteria, fr.
pedante. See prec. word and -ry.

## pedate
pedate, adj., 1) having feet; 2) resembling a foot.
— L. pedatus, 'footed', pp. aipedare, 'to furnish
with feet, to foot', fr. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See
pedal, adj., and adj. suff. -ate.

## peddle
peddle, intr. and tr. v. — Back formation fr.
peddler (q.v.) For similar back formations cp.
cadge, swindle.

## peddler
peddler, pedlar, n. — Fr, earlier pedder, fr. dial.
ped, 'basket', fr. ME. pedde, which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. pad, 'basket'. For the ending
see agential suff. -er.
Derivative: peddler-y, pedlar-y, n.

## peddling
peddling, adj., trifling. — A collateral form of
piddling.
Derivative: peddling-ly, adv.

## -pede
-pede, combining form meaning 'footed, -foot'.
— Fr. L. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See pedal, adj.

## pederast
pederast, paederast, n. — L. paederasta, fr. Gk.
παιδεραστής. See next word.

## pederasty
pederasty, paederasty, п., sodomy with a boy. —
L. paederastia, fr. Gk. παιδεραστία, 'love of
boys', fr. παιδεραστής, 'lover of boys', fr. παις,
gen. παιδός, 'boy', and έρϊν, 'to love'. See pedo-,
erotic and -y (representing Gk. -ίδ).
Derivatives: p(a)ederast-ic, adj., p(a)ederast-ic-
al-ly, adv,

## pedesis
pedesis, п., Brownian movement — ModL., fr.
Gk. πήδησις, 'a leaping', fr. πηδαν, 'to bound,
leap', fr. I.-E. base *ped-, enlarged form of base
*ped-, 'foot', whence πέδη, 'fetter', πέδον,
'ground, earth', πους gen. ποδός, 'foot', L, pes,

## gen. pedis
gen. pedis, 'foot'. See foot and cp. diapedesis. Cp.
also Pedetes and the first element in

## pedology
pedology, 'the study of soils'. Cp. also pilot.

## pedestal
pedestal, n. — MF. (= F.) piedestal, fr. It. piedi-

## stallo
stallo, 'foot of a seat', which stands for pie

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:570 COLUMN:3 -->
(= piede) di stallo, lit. 'foot of a stall' (ср. Е.
footstall), and is compounded of piede, 'foot',
di, 'of, and stallo, 'stall, seat'. It. piede derives
fr. L. pedem, ace. of pes, 'foot'; see foot and cp.
pedal. It. di comes fr. L. de, 'from, away from';
see de-. It. stallo, is of Teut. origin; see stall,
'stable'. The change of F.piedestal to E.pedestal
is due to the learned influence of L. pes, pedis,
'foot'.

## pedestrian
pedestrian, adj., going on foot, walking; п.,
walker. — Formed fr. L. pedester, 'on foot,
pedestrian', fr.pes, gen.pedis, 'foot'; F'.pedestrien
is an English loan word. See foot and cp. pedal.
For the ending see suff. -ian.
Derivatives: pedestrian-ism., п., pedestrian-ize,
intr. v.

## Pedetes
Pedetes, п., a genus of rodents, the jumping hare
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πηδητής, 'leaper', fr.
πηδαν, 'to leap'. See pedesis and the second
element in Polypedates. Cp. also pilot.

## pedetic
pedetic, adj., pertaining to pedesis. — Gk. πηδη-
τικός, 'good at leaping', fr. πήδησις. See
pedesis and adj. suff. -ic.

## pedi-
pedi-, combining form meaning 'foot', as in
pedicure, pediform.— L. pedi-, from pes, gen. pedis,
'foot'. See foot and cp. pedal.

## pediatric
pediatric, paediatric, adj., pertaining to the
hygienic treatment of children — Compounded of
Gk. παις, gen. παιδός, 'child', and ιατρικός,
'pertaining to a physician', fr. Ιατρός,
'physician'. See pedo- and -iatric.
Derivatives: p(a)ediatr-ics, n.,p(a)ediatric-ian, n.

## pediatrist
pediatrist, paediatrist, n. — See prec. word and
-ist.

## pedicel
pedicel, п., stalk in a plant, footstalk (hoi. and
zool.) — ModL. pedicellus, fr. L. pediculus,
'little foot', dimin. of L. pes, gen. pedis. See
pedal, adj.
Derivatives: pedicell-ar, pedicell-ate, pedicell-at·
-ed, adjs., pedicell-ation, п., pedicell-ed, adj.

## pedicle
pedicle, п., pedicel. — L. pediculus, 'footstalk'.
See prec. word.

## pedicular
pedicular, adj., pertaining to lice; infested with
lice. — L. pedicularis, 'pertaining to lice', fr.
pediculus, 'louse', dimin. of pedis, 'louse',
which stands for 'pezdis, and is rel. to pedo,
pedere, 'to break wind', for *pezdo, from the
imit. base *pezd-. For sense development cp.
Little Russian bzd'ity, 'to break wind', and
bzdjuch, 'land bug', which are cogn. with L.
pedere. Cp. petard, petrel. For the related base
*perd- see partridge, for the ending see suff. -ar.

## pediculate
pediculate, adj., having a pedicel, pedicellate —
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. pediculus,
'footstalk'. See pedicel.
Derivative: pediculat-ed, adj.

## Pedicularis
Pedicularis, п., a genus of plants, the lousewort
(bot.) — L. herba pedicularis, 'lousewort'. See
pedicular.

## pediculosis
pediculosis, п., infestation with lice (med.) —
Medical L., formed with suff. -osis fr. L.
pediculus, 'louse'. See pedicular.

## pediculous
pediculous, adj., pedicular. — L. pediculosus,
'lousy', fr. pediculus, 'louse'. See pedicular and
-ous.

## pedicure
pedicure, n. — Lit. 'care of the feet', fr. pedi- and
L. cura, 'care'. See cure, n.
Derivatives: pedicure, tr. v., pedicur-ism, п.,
pedicur-ist, n.

## pediform
pediform, adj., having the shape of a foot. —
Compounded of pedi- and forma, 'form, shape*.
See form, n.

## pedigree
pedigree, п., 1) genealogical table; 2) genealogy.
— ME. pedegru, fr. MF. pie de grue, 'crane's
foot', so called from the shape of the
genealogical mark (-^) used to denote descent. MF. pie
(F. pied) derives fr. OF. pie, fr. L. pedem, ace.

## of pes
of pes, 'foot'; see foot and cp. pedal. F. de, 'of,

## from'
from', comes fr. L. de, 'from, away from'; see

## de-. F. grue comes fr. L. gruem
de-. F. grue comes fr. L. gruem, ace. of grus,
'crane', which is cogn. with Gk. γερανός, OE.
cran; see crane. The form of the English word
was influenced by an association with degree.
Derivative: pedigree, tr. v.

## pediment
pediment, п., a triangular ornament on the front
of buildings (archit.) — Altered from earlier

## perimenl
perimenl, which is prob. a corruption of
pyramid (q.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:571 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PEDIPALPIDA | 544 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:571 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: pediment-al, adj.,pediment-ed, adj.

## Pedipalpida
Pedipalpida, n. pi., an order of the Arachnida
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -ida fr.
ModL. pedipatpus. See next word.

## pedipalpus
pedipalpus, п., either of the second pair of palpi
attached to each side of the mouth of arachnids
(zool.) — ModL., lit. 'that which feels with the
feet', compounded of pedi- and L. palpus, 'a
feeler'. See palpus.
Derivative: pedipalp-ous, adj.

## pedlar
pedlar, n. — A var. spelling of peddler,

## pedo-
pedo-, paedo-, before a vowel ped-, paed-,
combining form meaning'boy, child'. — Gk. παιδο-,
παιδ-, fr. παις, gen. παιδος, 'child', fr. I.-E.
base *peu-, 'small, little, few, young'. See few
and words there referred to and cp. esp.
encyclopedia, orthopert, pedagogue,

## pedobaptlsm
pedobaptlsm, paedobaptism, п., infant baptism —
Compounded of pedo- and baptism,

## pedology
pedology, paedology, п., child study. —
Compounded of pedo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: p(a)edolog-ic-al, adj., p(a)edolog-
ist, п.,p(a)edolog-ist-ic-al, adj.

## pedology
pedology, п., the study of soils. — Compounded
of Gk. πέδον, 'ground, soil', and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. The first
element is rel. to πέδη, 'fetter', πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot', and cogn. with L. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot';
see foot and cp. pedesis, Pedetes. For the second
element see -logy.
Derivative: pedolog-isl, n.

## pedometer
pedometer, п., an instrument for measuring
distance covered by a walker. — F. pedometre, a
hybrid coined fr. L. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot', and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See foot, adj. and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## pedro
pedro, п., a card game. — Sp. Pedro, 'Peter', fr.
Late L. Petrus. See Peter,

## peduncle
peduncle, п., 1) a flower stalk [hot.); 2) a stalklike
part (zool.) — ModL. pedunculus, 'footstalk', fr.
L. pedicutus, 'a little foot; footstalk', dimin. of

## pes
pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'; see foot and cp. pedal. L.
pedicutus was prob. changed in Modern L. to
pedunculus because of the ambiguity of the
former word, which may be the diminutive of
either pes, 'foot', or pedis, 'louse'.
Derivative: pedunct-ed, adj.

## pedunculus
pedunculus, п., a peduncle. — ModL. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: peduncul-ar, peduncul-at-ed, adjs.,

## peduncul-ation
peduncul-ation, a.

## peek
peek, intr. v., to peep. — ME. piken, of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: peek, n.

## peel
peel, п., a small, square, tower. — ME.,
'palisade', fr. OF. pel (F. pieu), 'stake, post', fr. L.

## palum
palum, ace. oipalus, of s.m. See pale, 'stake',

## peel
peel, п., baker's shovel. — ME. pete, fr. OF. pele
(F. pelle), fr. L. pala, 'spade, shovel', which is

## of uncertain origin. It is perh. rel. to L. pains
of uncertain origin. It is perh. rel. to L. pains,
'stake'. See pale, 'stake', and cp. prec. word.

## peel
peel, tr. and intr. v., to strip off. — ME. pelen, fr.
OF. (= F.) peter, 'to peel', fr. L. pilare, 'to

## deprive of hair'
deprive of hair', fr. pilus, 'hair'. See pUL 'to peel',
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: peel, п., peel-ed, adj., peel-ed-ness,
п., peel-er, n.

## peeler
peeler, п., a policeman (cotloq.) — Orig. a
member of the Irish constabulary; so called from Sir
(at that time: Mr.) Robert Peel who founded
the Irish constabulary. See Peellte and cp. bobby.

## Peelism
Peelism, п., thedoctrine of the Peelites. — See
next word and -ism.

## Peelite
Peelite, п., an adherent of Peel in the repeal of the
Corn laws in 1846. — Formed from the name
of Sir Robert Peel (1788-1850) with subst. suff.
-ite.

## peen
peen, п., the sharp end of the head of a hammer.
— Of uncertain, possibly Scand., origin. Cp.

## dial. Norw. penn
dial. Norw. penn, 'peen'.
Derivative: peen, tr. v.

## peep
peep, intr. v., to chirp. — Of imitative origin.

## Cp. L. pipare
Cp. L. pipare, piplre, plpiare, F. pepier, piper,

## G. piepen. Cp. also pip
G. piepen. Cp. also pip, 'to chirp', pipe.
Derivatives: peep-er, п.,peep-ing, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:571 COLUMN:2 -->

## peep
peep, intr. v., to look through a small opening;
to peer furtively. — Prob. a var. of peek.
Derivatives: peep, a., peep-er, п., peep-ing, n.

## peepul
peepul, n. — A var. of pipal.

## peer
peer, intr. v., to look closely — Perhaps aphetic
for appear.

## peer
peer, п., 1) an equal; 2) a man of high rank, a
noble. — ME. per, fr. OF. per (F. pair), fr. L.
par, 'equal'. See pair and cp. par, 'equality',
compeer.
Derivatives: peer-age, п., peer-dom, п., peer-ess,
п., peer-less, adj., peer-less-ly, adv., peer-less-
ness, п., peer-ling, n.

## peer
peer, tr. v., 1) to equal; 2) to raise to the peerage.
— ME. peren, fr. OF. parer (3rd person sing.
pere), fr. L. parare, 'to make equal', fr. par,
'equal'. See prec. word.

## peeve
peeve, tr. v., to make peevish (cotloq.) — Back
formation fr. peevish.
Derivatives:peev-ed, adj.,peev-ed-ly,
adv.,peeved- ness, n.

## peevish
peevish, adj., fretful. — ME. pevish, of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: peevish-ly, adv.,peevish-ness, n.

## peewee
peewee, adj., tiny. — Of Algonquian origin.

## peewee
peewee, п., the flycatcher. — See pewee.

## peewit
peewit, n. — See pewit.

## peg
peg, n. — ME. pegge, fr. MDu. pegge, which is
rel. to LG. pegel, 'stake, pile', MLG., G. pegel,
'gauge rod, watermark', Du.peil, 'gauge,
watermark; standard', OE. pseget, 'a small measure,
wine vessel, gill', fr. ML. pagetla, 'a measure'.
See pail.
Derivatives: peg, v., pegg-ed, adj., pegg-er, п.,
pegg-ing., n.,pegg-y, adj.

## peganite
peganite, п., a basic aluminum phosphate
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk.
πήγανον, 'the herb rue' (see next word); so
called in allusion to its green color.

## Peganum
Peganum, п., a genus of herbs of the bean-caper
family (bol.) — ModL, fr. Gk. πήγανον, 'the
herb rue', which is prob. rel. to πηγνύναι, 'to
make firm', fr. I.-E. base *pag-, *pak-, 'to join
together'. See pact.

## Pegasus
Pegasus, п., name of a winged horse in Greek
mythology. — L., fr. Gk. Πήγασος. The suff.
-άσος shows that the name is of pre-Greek
origin; the connection with Gk. πηγή, 'fount,
spring', is folk etymology.

## pegmatite
pegmatite, п., a coarse granite rock (geol.) — F.,
coined by the French mineralogist Ren6-Just
Haiiy (1743-1822), fr. Gk. πήγμα, gen.
πήγματος, 'something fastened together', from the
stem of πηγνύναι, 'to make firm', fr. I.-E. base
"pug-, *pak-^ 'to join together'. See pact and
words there referred to and cp. esp. parapegm.
For the ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## pegomancy
pegomancy, п., divination by fountains. —
Compounded of Gk. πηγή, 'fountain, spring', which
is of uncertain origin, and μαντεία, μαντία,
'oracle, divination', for which see -mancy.

## peignoir
peignoir, п., lady's loose robe. — F., fr. peigner,
'to comb the hair', fr. peigne, 'comb', fr. L. pec-
tinem, ace. of pecten, 'comb'. See pecten.

## pejorate
pejorate, tr. v., to depreciate. — Late L.pejordtus,
pp. oipejdrare, 'to make worse'. See pejorative.
Derivative: pejorat-ion, n.

## pejoration
pejoration, п., depreciation. — Formed with suff.
-ation fr. L. pijor, 'worse'. See next word.
Derivative: pejoration-ist, a.

## pejorative
pejorative, adj., depreciative, disparaging. —
Formed with suff. -ive fr. L. pejoratus, pp. of
pejdrare, 'to make worse', fr. pejor, 'worse',
which stands for *ped-y6s and is rel. to L. pessi-
mus, 'worst' (for *ped-s mos; see pessimizm),
and to pessum, 'downward, to the ground', and
cogn. with OI. padyate, 'falls'; from the same
base as L. pis, gen. pedis, 'foot' (see Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., II, p. 275 s.v. peior, p. 296 s.v.
pessum, and p. 295 s.v. pes). See foot and cp.
impair. For the ending see suff. -ive.
Derivatives: pejorative, п., pejorative-ly, adv.

## pekan
pekan, п., a North American marten — Of
Algonquian origin.

## pekin
pekin, п., a kind of silk. — F. pekin, fr. Pekin,
'Peking', fr. Chin. Ре-king, which lit. means
'capital of the North', fr. pe, 'north', and king,
'capital'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:571 COLUMN:3 -->

## pekin
pekin, п., a civilian (slang) — F. pekin, fr. Pro-
venc. pequin, 'sickly', fr. pec, 'simple, foolish',
fr. b.pecus, 'cattle; beast, brute'. See fee, 'cattle,
money', and cp. Pecora.

## Pekingese
Pekingese, Pekinese, п., a small Chinese dog. —
Fr. Peking, capital of China. See pekin, п., 'а
kind of silk', and -ese.

## pekoe
pekoe, п., a superior kind of black tea. — Fr.
dial. Chin, pek-ho, 'white down'.
Derivative: pekoe, tr. v.

## pelage
pelage, п., coat of a mammal. — F., fr. OF. pel,
'hair', fr. L. pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair', and
-age.

## Pelagian
Pelagian, adj. and n. — ML. Pelagidnus, fr. Pela-
gius, Latinized name of a British monk who
lived in the 4th cent, and who denied the
doctrine of original sin. For the ending see suff.
-an.
Derivatives: Pelagian-ism, п., Pelagian-he, n.

## pelagian
pelagian, adj., pelagic. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L.pelagius, fr. Gk. πελάγιας, 'of the sea', fr.
πέλαγος. See next word.

## pelagic
pelagic, adj., pertaining to the sea. — L. pelagi-
cus, fr. Gk. πελαγικός, fr. πέλαγος, 'sea',
which is rel. to πλάγος, 'side', and cogn. with L.
plaga, 'hunting net, curtain, region', fr. base
*p(e)tag-, *p(e)/V. enlargement of base *p(e)ld-,
*p(e)l-, 'spread out, flat', whence L. planus,
'level, flat'. See plain, adj., and words there
referred to; and cp. esp. Pelasgic. For the ending
see adj. suff. -Ic.

## pelago-
pelago-, combining form denoting the sea. —
Gk. πέλαγο-, fr. πέλαγος, 'sea'. See prec. word.

## Pelargonium
Pelargonium, п., a genus of plants (hot.) —
— ModL., fr. Gk. πελαργός, 'stork', which
stands for *πελα-5αργός, lit. 'blackish white'.
The first element of this word is rel. to πελιός,
'livid', πελλός, 'dark-colored, dusky', πολιός,
'gray', and cogn. with L. pallere, 'to be pale',
pallor, 'paleness', OE. fealo, 'dull-colored,
yellow, yellowish red, brown'. See fallow,
'brownish yellow', and words there referred to and cp.
esp. Pellaea. For the second element see argent.

## Pelasgian
Pelasgian, adj., of the Pelasgi; п., one of the Pe-
lasgi. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. PelasgiuS,
fr. Gk. Πελάσγιος, 'of the Pelasgi', fr.
Πελασγοί, 'the Pelasgi', a prehistoric people of
Greece and Asia Minor. The name Πελασγοί
prob. stands for *Πελαγ-σκοί, fr. πέλαγος,
'sea', and orig. meant 'seamen'. See pelagic.

## Pelasgic
Pelasgic, adj., Pelasgian. — L. Pelasgicus, fr. Gk.
Πελασγικός, 'of the Pelasgi', ft. Πελασγοί.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## pelerine
pelerine, п., a woman's cape. — F.pelerine, 'cape,
mantle, tippet', prop. fern, of pilerin, 'pilgrim',
fr. Late L. pelegrmus, dissimilated form of L.
peregrinus, 'foreigner, stranger'. See pilgrim,

## Peleus
Peleus, п., a king of the Myrmidons and father of
Achilles by the sea nymph Thetis (Greek my-
thol.) — L.Peleus, fr. Gk. Πηλεύς, which is prob.
rel. to πάλλειν, 'to wield, brandish, swing', and
prop, means 'he who brandishes the spear'. See
polemic.

## pelf
pelf, п., money, wealth. — ME. pelfer, fr. MF.
pelfre. See pilfer.

## Pelias
Pelias, п., a son of Poseidon (Greek mythol.) —
L. Pelias, fr. Gk. Πελίϋς, which prob. means
lit. 'the gray one', and is rel. to πελιός, 'livid'.
See fallow, adj., and cp. words there referred to.

## pelican
pelican, n. — Late L. pelicanus, pelecanus, fr.
Gk. πελεκάν, 'pelican', fr. πέλεκυς, 'ax', which,
together with OI. parasuh, parsub, 'hatchet',
derives fr. Akkad. pilaqqu, *ax'.

## pelisse
pelisse, п., a long coat. — F., fr. VL. pellicia (scil.
vestis), '(garment) of skin', fern, of pellicius, 'of
skin', which derives fr. L. pellis, 'skin'. See fell,
'hide', and words there referred to and cp. esp.
surplice.

## petite
petite, п., rock of clay and quartz (pelrogr.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. πηλός,
'clay, mud'. See pelo-.
Derivative: pelit-ic, adj.

## pell
pell, п., skin. — ME. pel, fr. OF. pel (F. peau), fr.
L. pellem, ace. of pellis, 'skin'. See pellicle.

## Pellaea
Pellaea, п., a genus of plants, the cliff brake (bol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. πελλός, 'dark-colored,
dusky', which is rel. to πελιός, 'livid'. See
Pelargonium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:572 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 545 | PENDULUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:572 COLUMN:1 -->

## pellagra
pellagra, п., a chronic disease caused by a
deficiency of nicotine acid in the diet. — It., a
hybrid coined Гг. L. pellis, 'skin', and Gk. £γρ£,
'a catching, seizure'. See fell, 'hide', and chlragra.
Derivatives: pellagr-ic, pellagr-ous, adjs.

## pellet
pellet, п., a small ball. — ME. pelote, pelet, fr.
OF. (= F.) pelote, 'ball', fr. VL. *pilotta, dimin.
of L. pila, 'ball' (hence lit. meaning 'ball of hair'),
which is rel. to pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair', and
cp. pelota.
Derivatives: pellet, tr. v., pellet-ed, adj.

## pelletierine
pelletierine, п., a liquid alkaloid (chem.) —
Named after the French chemist Bertrand Pelle-
tier (1761-97).

## pellicle
pellicle, п., a thin skin, a membrane. — MF.
pellicle (F. pellicule), fr. L. pellicula, dimin. of
pellis, 'skin, hide', which stands for *pet-nis and
is cogn. with Gk. πέλλα (prob. for *πέλ-να),
'wooden bowl, milk pail' (the orig. meaning
prob. was 'a vessel made of skin'), ON. fjall,
'skin', OE. fell, 'hide, skin'. See fell, 'hide', and
-cle and cp. pelta. Cp. also paillasse.

## pellicular
pellicular, adj., pertaining to, or forming, a
pellicle. — Formed with adj. stiff, -ar fr. L. pellis,
'skin'. See prec. word.

## pellitory
pellitory, п., a small plant growing on walls (Pa-
rietaria officinalis). — Lit. 'the wall plant'; dis-
similated fr. ME. paritorie, fr. OF. paritaire
(F. parietaire), fr. L. parietaria, 'pellitory'. See
parietary.

## pellitory
pellitory, п., pyrethrum (hot.) — Fr. earlier pele-
tyr, fr. ME. peletre, which was dissimilated fr.
OF. peritre, piretre, fr. L. pyrethrum, fr. Gk.
πύρεθρον, 'feverfew', which is rel. to πϋρ, 'fire',
πυρετός, 'fever'. See Pyrethrum and cp, words
there referred to.

## pell-mell
pell-mell, adv., confusedly. — F. pile-mele, fr.
OF. pesle-mesle, a var. of mesle-mesle,
reduplication of the imper. of mesler (F. meter), 'to
mix', fr. VL. *misculdre, fr. L. miscere, of s.m.
See meddle, mix.

## pellucid
pellucid, adj., transparent, translucent. — L.
pellucidus, 'transparent', for *perlucidus, fr.
perlucere, 'to shine through', fr. per- and lucere,
'to shine'. See lucid and cp. translucent.
Derivatives: pellucid-ity, п., pellucid-ly, adv.,
pellucid-ness, n.

## pelmet
pelmet, п., valance over a door or window. — See
palmette.

## pelo-
pelo-, combining form meaning 'mud, clay'. —
Gk. πηλό-, fr. πηλός, which is prob. cogn.
with Arm. shalax, 'mud, mire', OSlav. kalu, of
s.m. Cp. pellte.

## pelpn
pelpn, adj., hairless (Sp. America) — Sp. pelon,
fr. pelo, 'hair', fr. L. pilus. See pile, 'hair'.

## Pelops
Pelops, п., the father of Tantalus (Greek mythol.)
— L. Pelops, fr. Gk. Πέλοψ, which is of
uncertain origin.

## peloria
peloria, п., abnormal regular development in
normally irregular flowers (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. πέλωρος, 'monstrous', fr. πέλωρ, 'portent,
prodigy, monster', an Aeolic var. of τέλωρ,
'great, long', which is dissimilated fr. *τέρωρ,
fr. τέρας, 'sign, wonder'. See terato-. For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## pelota
pelota, п., a Basque ball game. — Sp. pelota,
'ball', fr. VL. 'pilotta, fr. L. pila, 'ball'. See
pellet.

## pelt
pelt, п., skin. — Back formation fr. peltry (q.v.)

## pelt
pelt, tr. and intr. v., to strike. — ME. pelten, fr.
OF. peloter, 'to strike with a ball' (whence F.
peloter, 'to wind something into a ball; to treat
roughly'), fr. pelote, 'ball'. See pellet and cp.
pelota.
Derivatives: pelt, n.,pelt-er, tr. and intr. v., pelt-
er-er, n.

## pelta
pelta, п., a small, light shield (Greek antiq.) — L.,
fr. Gk. πέλ-τη, which is rel. to πέλ-μα, 'sole of
the foot', and cogn. with L. pellis (for *pel-nis),
'skin'. See pellicle and cp. the next four words.
Derivatives '.peltast (q.v.), peltate (q.v.), pelt-ate-
ly,adv.,pelt-ation, n.

## peltast
peltast, п., a soldier armed with a pelta (Greek
antiq.) — Gk. πελταστής, lit. 'one carrying a
pelta', fr. πέλτη. See prec. word and -ast.

## Peltandra
Peltandra, п., a genus of plants, the arrow arum
'(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. πέλτη
(see pelta) and ά\ιήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man', which

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:572 COLUMN:2 -->
is used in botany in the sense of 'stamen' (see
andro-); so called in allusion to the shape of the
stamen.

## peltate
peltate, adj., having the stalk attached to the
lower surface (said of a leaf) (bot.) — Lit.
'shield-shaped', fr. L. peltdtus, 'armed with a
pelta', fr. pelta. See pelta and adj. suff. -ate.

## Peltigera
Peltigera, п., a genus of lichens (bot.) — A ModL.
hybrid lit. meaning 'shield-bearer', formed fr.
Gk. πέλτη, 'shield' (see pelta), and L. gerere, 'to
bear, carry' (see gerent); so called in allusion to
its scutiform apothecia. The correct form would
be Peltophora (fr. Gk. πέλτη, 'shield', and
-φόρος, from the stem of οέρειν, 'to bear, carry').

## pelting
pelting, adj., paltry (archaic). — See paltry, adj.
Derivative: pelting-ly, adv.

## peltry
peltry, n. — ME., fr. AF. pelterie, corresponding
to OF. peletrie (F. pelletrie), 'fur skins, peltry',
fr. OF. peletier (F. pelletier), 'furrier', fr. pel (F.
peau), 'skin', fr. L. pellis. See pellicle and cp.
pelta. Cp. also pelt, 'skin', which is a back
formation fr. peltry. For the ending see suff. -ry.

## peM-
peM-, also pelvo-, combining form denoting the
pelvis. — Fr. L. pelvis. See pelvis,

## pelvic
pelvic, adj., pertaining to, or connected with, the
pelvis. — Irregularly formed fr. L. pelvis (see
next word) with adj. suff. -ic.

## pelvis
pelvis, п., the basinlike cavity in the lower part of
the trunk (anal, and zool.) — L. pelvis, 'basin,
laver', for *pelowis; cogn. with ΟΙ. ράΐανϊ,
'vessel', palah, 'spittoon', Gk. πήληξ, 'helmet',
πελίκη, πέλιξ, 'goblet, bowl', but OSlav. polu,
'bucket' and L. pellis, 'skin, hide', are not
cognate.

## pelvo-
pelvo-, combining form. — See pelvi-.

## Pembroke table
Pembroke table, also Pembroke. — So called after
Pembroke, the capital of Pembrokeshire in
Wales,

## pemmican
pemmican, п., dried lean meat pounded into a
paste with fat and pressed into cakes. — From
N. American Indian (Cree) pimecan, fr. pimiy,
'fat'.

## pemphigoid
pemphigoid, adj., resembling pemphigus. —
Compounded of pemphigus and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -old.

## pemphigus
pemphigus, п., skin disease characterized by
watery vesicles (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. πέμ-
φιξ, gen. πέμφιγος, 'blister, bubble', from the
imitative base *bamb-, "bhambh-, 'to swell',
whence also πομφός, 'blister', πομφόλυξ, 'water
bubble, bubble'. The name pemphigus was first
applied to this disease by Sauvages (1706-67).
Derivative: pemphig-ous, adj:

## pen
pen, п., enclosure for animals. — ME. penne, fr.
OE. penn, which is rel. to LG. penn, 'peg, pin',

## pennen
pennen, 'to bolt a gate', and to OE. pinn, 'pin'.

## See pin
See pin, 'peg', and cp. pin, 'to enclose in a pen'.
Derivative: pen, tr. v.

## pen
pen, п., a female swan. — Of unknown origin.

## pen
pen, п., 1) feather; 2) writing instrument. — ME,

## penne
penne, fr. MF. penne, fr. L. penna, 'feather',
which stands for *pet-nS and is cogn. with OI,

## patram
patram, 'wing, feather', Gk. πτερόν, 'wing',

## OSlav. pero
OSlav. pero, 'pen', ON.fjSdr, OE. feder,
'feather'. See feather and words there referred to and

## cp. esp. pennate
cp. esp. pennate, panache, panne. Cp. also pinna,
'leaf.
Derivative: pen, tr. v.

## penal
penal, adj., 1) pertaining to punishment; 2) liable
to punishment. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) penal,

## fr. L. poenalis
fr. L. poenalis, 'of punishment', fr. poena,
'punishment', fr. Gk. ποινή, 'bloodmoney, fine,

## penalty
penalty, punishment', which stands for *q*Oind-
and derives fr. I.-E. base *qwei-, *qwi-, 'to

## respect
respect, consider, honor, pay, expiate, punish',
whence also Gk. τίειν, 'to esteem, honor, value',
τιμή, 'price, worth, honor, esteem, respect',
τίνειν, 'to pay a price, punish, take vengeance',
τίσις, 'payment, punishment, vengeance', OI.

## cinoti
cinoti, cayati. Observes, notices, perceives', cay-

## ate
ate, 'revenges', Avestic kay-, 'to requite, be

## fined'
fined', каёпа, 'punishment, vengeance', OSlav.
сёпа, 'honor, price', ceniti, 'to estimate, value',

## kajati se
kajati se, 'to repent', Lith. kaina, 'value, price'.

## Cp. pain. Cp. also impunity
Cp. pain. Cp. also impunity, pine, v., Poinae,

## punish
punish, subpoenal, timocracy, Timothy, Tisi-

## phone
phone, xenothne. Cp. also Pinnotheres, synteresis.
Derivatives: penal-ist, п., penal-ize,li. v., penal-

iz-ation, п., penal-ly, adv., penalty (q.v.)

## penality
penality, п., the character of being penal. — F.
penalite. See penalty.

## penalty
penalty, n. — F. penalite, fr. ML. poenalitatem,
ace. of poenalitas, fr. L. poenalis, 'of
punishment', fr. poena, 'punishment'. See penal and -ty
and cp. penality, which is a doublet of penalty.

## penance
penance, п., repentance. — ME. penaunce, fr.
OF. peneance, penaance, fr. L. paenitentia,
'repentance'. See penitence, which is a scholarly
doublet of penance.

## penates
penates, n. pi., household gods (Roman mythol.)
— L. penates, lit. 'gods of the inside of the
house', rel. to penitus, 'within', penes, 'near',
penus, 'the innermost part of a temple of Vesta',
penetrare, 'to enter'. Cp. penetrate.

## pence
pence, n. — PI. of penny.

## penchant
penchant, п., inclination, taste. — F., prop. pres.
part, oipencher, 'to incline, bend, slope', fr. VL.
*pendicare, freq. formed fr. L. pendere, 'to hang'.
See pendant.

## pencil
pencil, n. — ME. pencel, fr. MF. pincel (F. pin·
ceau), 'a painter's brush', fr. OF. pincel, of s.m.,
fr. VL. *pinicellus, for L. penicillus, 'little tail',
dimin. of peniculus, 'brush, painter's brush or
pencil', itself dimin. of penis, 'tail, male organ of
generation'; see penis. For the sense
development οι pencil, it should be borne in mind that
formerly small brushes were used for writing.
Cp. penicil and penicillin.
Derivatives: pencil, tr. v., pencil([)-ed, adj.,
pencil(l)-ler, п., pencil(l)-ing, п., pencil-ry, n.

## pendant
pendant, n-, a hanging ornament. — ME. pen-
daunt, fr. MF. (= F.) pendant, prop. pres. part,
of pendre, fr. VL. pendere, for L. pendere, 'to
hang, hang down', which is rel. to L. pendere,
lit. 'to cause to hang down, hold in suspension',
whence 'to weigh, weigh out; to value, esteem',
and to pondus, gen. ponderis, 'weight'. The
origin of these Latin words is doubtful. Cp. pendent.
Cp. also append, appendant, appendix,
compendium, compensate, depend, dependence, dispense,
expend, expense, FUipcndula, impend,
independent, painter, 'rope', pansy, penchant, pendulous,
pendulum, pensile, pension, pensive, penthouse,
perpendicular, peseta, peso, poise, ponder and
words there referred to, pound, 'a weight',
prepense, propend, prepense, recompense, spend,
stipend, suspend, suspense, suspension, vilipend.
For the ending of pendant see suff. -ant.

## pendency
pendency, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## pendent
pendent, adj., hanging; п., a pendant. — Orig.
spelled pendant, fr. OF. pendaunt, pendant (F.
pendant), pres. part, of pendre, 'to hang'. See
pendant.

## pendentive
pendentive, n. (archil.) — F. pendentif, fr. L.
pendens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of pendere, 'to
hang'. See pendant and -ive.

## pending
pending,.adj. and prep. — Formed on analogy of
F. pendant, 'during', lit. 'hanging', fr. pendre, 'to
hang'. See pendant and adj. suff. -ing.

## pendragon
pendragon, п., chief leader. — Compounded of
W. penn, 'head', and E. dragon. Cp. pennill and
the first element in penguin.
Derivative: pendragon-ish, adj.

## pcndular
pcndular, adj., 1) pertaining to a pendulum; 2)
resembling the movement of a pendulum. — F.
pendulaire, fr. pendule, 'pendulum'. See
pendulum and adj. suff. -ar.

## pendulate
pendulate, intr. v., to swing like a pendulum; to
be undecided. — Formed with verbal suff. -ate
fr. L. pendulus, 'hanging down', fr. pendere, 'to
hang'. See pendant

## pendule
pendule, п., 1) something pendulous; 2) a
pendulum; a timepiece having a pendulum. — In
sense I, fr. L. pendulus; see pendulous; in sense
2, fr. F. pendule, which also derives fr. L.
pendulus.

## penduline
penduline, adj., pendulous. — F.penduline, fr. L.

## pendulus
pendulus, 'hanging down'. See next word and
-ine (representing L. -Inus).

## pendulous
pendulous, adj., hanging loosely, swinging. — L.

## pendulus
pendulus, 'hanging down', fr. pendere, 'to hang'.
See pendant. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## pendulum
pendulum, n. — ModL., prop, neuter of the L.
adjective pendulus, 'hanging'"introduced by the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:573 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PENELOPE | 546 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:573 COLUMN:1 -->
English physicist Robert Boyle (1627-91). See
pendant.

## Penelope
Penelope, п., name of the faithful wife of
Odysseus. — L., fr. Gk. Πηνελόπη, Πηνελόπεια,
which is rel. to πήνη, 'thread on the bobbin',
πήνος, Dor. πάνος, 'web', and cogn. with L.
pannus, 'cloth, garment'. See pawn, 'plegde', and
cp. pane.
Derivative: Penelope-an, adj.

## penetrability
penetrability, n. — F. penetrabilite, fr. penetrable.
See next word.and -ity.

## penetrable
penetrable, adj. — F. penetrable, fr. L. penetrabi-
lis, 'penetrable', fr. penetrare. See penetrate and
-able.
Derivatives: penetrable-ness, п., penetrabt-y,
adv.

## penetralia
penetralia, n. pi., the innermost parts of a place.
— L. penetralia, pi. of penetrate, 'inner part
(especially of a building)', fr. penetrare. See
penetrate.

## penetrant
penetrant, adj. and n. — F. penetrant, pres. part,
of penetrer, 'to penetrate', fr. L. penetrare. See
next word and -ant.

## penetrate
penetrate, tr. and intr. v. — L. penetratus, pp. of
penetrare, 'to go into, enter, pierce, penetrate',
h.penitus, 'within', which is rel. topenes, 'near',
penutes, 'household gods'. Cp. penates. For the
ending see verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: penetrat-ing, adj., penetrat-ing-ly,
adv., penetrat-ing-ness, n.

## penetration
penetration, n. — L. penetratio, gen. -onis, 'an
entering into, piercing, penetrating', fr.
penetratus, pp. of penetrare. See prec. word and -ion.

## penetrative
penetrative, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.)penetratif
(fem. penetrative), fr. ML. penetrativus, fr. L.
penetrare. See penetrate and -ive.
Derivatives: penetrative-ly, adv., penetrative-
ness, n.

## pengo
pengo, п., the former Hungarian currency unit.
— Hung., prop. pres. part, of pengeni, 'to ring,
sound', which is prob. of imitative origin.

## penguin
penguin, n. — Compounded of W. pen, 'head',
and gwyn, 'white'. The name orig. denoted the
garefowl (also called the great auk), in allusion
to the large white patch between the bill and the
eye of this bird, now extinct. For the first
element cp. pennill and the first element in pen-
dragon, for the second see gwyniad.

## penial
penial, adj., pertaining to the penis. — See penis
and -ial.

## penicil
penicil, п., a bundle of hair (hot. and zool.) — L.
penicillus, 'small brush', dimin. of peniculus,
'brush, painter's brush'. See pencil.
Derivatives: penicill-ate, adj.,penicitt-at-ed, adj.,
penicill-ate-ly, adv., penicill-ation, n.

## penkiilin
penkiilin, n. — Coined by the English
bacteriologist Sir Alexander Fleming (born in 1881) in
1929 fr. PenicilUinn and suff. -in.

## PeniciUium
PeniciUium, п., a genus of mold (hot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. penicillus or penicillum, 'painter's brush'
(see pencil); so called because the PeniciUium
develops organs resembling a brush.

## peninsula
peninsula, n. — L. paeninsula, lit. 'almost an
island', fr. paene, 'nearly, almost', and insula,
'island'. The first element is rel. to paenitere, 'to
cause to repent', paenitet me, 'it causes me to
repent', i.e. Ί repent'; see penitent. For the
second element see insular and cp. Isle.
Derivatives: peninsul-ar, adj. and п., peninsul-
ar-ity, п., peninsul-ate, tr. v.

## penis
penis, n.·, the male organ of generation. — L.
'penis, 'tail, penis', for *pes~nis; cogn. with OI.
pasas-, 'penis', Gk. πέος, πόσθη, of s.m., OE.
/ass/, 'progeny, offspring', ON. fosull, OHG.
fazel, of s.m., MHG. vasel, G. Fasel, 'young of
animals, brood'. Cp. pencil., penicil, penicillin.

## penitence
penitence, n. — ME., fr. OF. penitence, fr. L.
paenitentia, poenitentia, 'penitence', fr. paenitens
poenitens. See next word and -ce and cp.
penance, which is a doublet of penitence.

## penitent
penitent, adj. and n. — ME., fr. MF. (— F.)
penitent, fr. L. paenitentem, poenitentem, ace. of
paenitens, poenitens, pres. part, of paenitere,
poenitere, 'to cause to repent*, paenitet {poenitet)
me, 'it causes me to repent', i.e. Ί repant'. L.
paenitere is a derivative of paene, 'nearly,
almost'. (The spelling poenitet, etc., is due to the
influence of L. poena, 'punishment', to which,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:573 COLUMN:2 -->
however, paenitet is not related.) L. paene
derives fr. l.-E. base *pe-, *рё-, 'to damage, injure,
hurt', whence also L. patl, 'to suffer'. See patient
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: penitent-ly, adv.

## penitential
penitential, adj. — ML. paenitentialis,
'pertaining to penitence', fr. L. paenitentia. See prec.
word and -in].
Derivative: penitential-ly, adv.

## penitential
penitential, п., book of rules for penance. — ML.
paenitentidle, prop. neut. of the adj.
paenitentialis, used as a noun. See penitential, adj.

## penitentiary
penitentiary, adj. pertaining to penance. — ML.
poenitentiarius, fr. L. paenitentia, poenitentia,
'penitence'. See penitent and adj. suff. -ary.

## penitentiary
penitentiary, п., la) in the R.C.Ch., an officer
empowered to rule in cases of conscience; b) in
the R.C.Ch., the office or dignity of a
penitentiary ; 2) a prison in which convicts are held for
punishment and reformation. — In sense la) fr.
ML. poenitentiarius, п., fr. poenitentiarius, adj.
(see penitentiary, adj.); in senses lb) and 2) fr.
ML. poenitentiaria, prop. fem. of the adj.
poenitentiarius.

## penaa
penaa, п., feather (zool.) — L., 'feather'. See pen,
'feather'.

## pennant
pennant, п., a pennon. — Prob. a blend of peunon
and pendant. Cp. Sp. pendon, 'pennant'.

## pennate
pennate, peunated, adj., winged. — L. pennatus,
'winged', fr. penna. See pen, 'feather', and adj.
suff. -ate.

## penniferous
penniferous, adj., bearing feathers. —
Compounded of L. penna, 'feather', and ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See pen, 'feather', and -ferous.

## penniform
penniform, adj., having the form of a feather. —
Compounded of L. penna, 'feather' and forma,
'form, shape'. See pen, 'feather', and form, n.

## pennill
pennill, п., improvised verse. — W., fr. penn,
'head'. Cp. the first element in pendragon and in
penguin.

## pennon
pennon, п., a long, narrow triangular or swallow-
tailed flag. — ME., fr. MF. penon, fr. репе,
'feather', fr. L. penna. See pen, 'feather', and cp.
pennant.
Derivative: pennon-ed, adj.

## pennoncel
pennoncel, pennoncelle, n. — Dimin. of prec.
word.

## penny
penny, n. — ME. peni, fr. OE. penig, pening,
pending, rel. to OS. pending, ON. penningr, Swed.
panning, Dan. penge, OFris. panning, MDu.
Pennine, Du. penning, OHG. pfenning, pfenting,
MHG. pfenninc, pfennic, G. Pfennig. These
words have prob. been borrowed fr. L. pannus,
'piece of cloth', and arose in a time when pieces
of cloth were used instead of money; see B.
Schier in Beitrage zur Geschichte der deutschen
Sprache und Literatur, 72, 311 ff. For the
etymology of L. pannus see pawn, 'pledge', and cp.
words there referred to.

## pennyroyal
pennyroyal, п., a plant of the mint family. — Fr.
earlier pulyol ryal, fr. OF. puliol (F. pouliot),
'thyme', and royal, 'kingly, royal'. OF. puliol
derives fr. VL. *pulegiolum, dimin. of L. pule-
gium, puleium, 'pennyroyal', which is of
uncertain origin. The connection of L. pulegium with
pulex, 'flea' (ср. Е. fleabane) is folk etymology.

## pennywort
pennywort, n. — Compounded of penny and
wort.

## penology
penology, п., the study of the prevention and
punishment of crime. — Lit. 'study of
punishment'; compounded of Gk. ποινή,
'punishment', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See penal and -logy.
Derivatives: penolog-ic, penolog-ic-al, adjs.,
penolog-ist, n.

## penroseite
penroseite, п., a selenide of lead, copper and
nickel (mineral.) — Named after the American
geologist R. A. F. Penrose (Г863-1931). For the
ending see subst. suff. -Ite.

## pensile
pensile, adj., hanging down, suspended. — L.
pensilis, 'hanging down', fr. pensus, pp. of pen-
dere, 'to hang'. See pendant and -ile.
Derivatives: pensile-ness, п., pensil-ity, a.

## pension
pension, п., payment. — ME. pensioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) pension, fr. L. pensionem, ace. of pensio,
'weight, payment', fr. pensus, pp. of pendere, 'to
pay'. See pendant and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:573 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: pension, tr. v., pension-able, adj.,
pension-ary, adj., pension-less, adj.
pension, п., boardinghouse. — F. pension. See
prec. word.

## pensionary
pensionary, n. — ML. pensionarius, fr. L. pensio,
gen. -onis. See pension and adj. suff. -ary.

## pensioner
pensioner, n. — OF. (= F.) pensionnier, fr.
pension. See pension and agential suff. -er.

## pensive
pensive, adj., sadly thoughtful. — ME. pensif, fr.
OF. (= F.) pensif, fr. penser, 'to think', fr. L.
pensare, 'to weigh out carefully, ponder,
examine', freq. oipendire, 'to weigh'. See pendant and
-ive and cp. pansy.
Derivatives: pensive-ly, adv., pensive-ness, n.

## Penstemon
Penstemon, n. — Inexact var. of Pentstemon.

## penstock
penstock, п., sluice, gate, floodgate. —
Compounded of pen, 'enclosure', and stock.

## pent
pent, adj., kept in, confined. — A var. spelling of
penned, pp. of pen, 'to enclose'. See pen,
'enclosure'.

## penta-
penta-, before a vowel pent-, combining form
meaning 'five'. — Gk. πεντα-, πεντ-, fr. πέντε,
'five' (the α in πεντα- is due to the analogy of
έπτα-, 'seven-', έννεα-, 'nine-', δέκα-, 'ten-');
rel. to Aeol. πέμπε, 'five', whence πεμπάζειν,
'to count on the five fingers, to count by fives'.
See five and cp. words there referred to.

## pentacle
pentacle, п., a symbolic figure (usually a
pentagram) used in magic· — ML. pentaculum,
'symbolic figure, pentagram', a hybrid coined fr.
penta- and L. dimin. suff. -culum (see -cule).

## pentacular
pentacular, adj., pertaining to a pentacle. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. ML. pentaculum. See
prec. word.

## pentad
pentad, п., 1) the number five; 2) a group of five
things; 3) a period of five years. — Gk. πεντάς,
gen. πεντάδος, 'group of five', fr. πέντε, 'five'.
See penta- and -ad.

## pentadactyl
pentadactyl, pentadactyle, adj., having five fingers
or toes. — Gk. πενταδάκτυλος, 'with five ringers
or toes', compounded of πεντα- (see penta-) and
δάκτυλος, 'finger'. See dactyl.
Derivatives: pentadactyl-ate, pentadactyl-ous,
adjs.

## pentagon
pentagon, п., a plane figure with five angles and
five sides (geom.) — L. pentagonum, fr. Gk.
πεντάγωνον, neut. of the adj. πεντάγωνος, lit.,
'five-cornered', which is compounded of πεντα-
(see penta-) and -γωνος, from the stem of
γωνία, 'angle'. See -gon.
Derivatives: pentagon-al, adj., pentagon-al-ly,
adv.

## pentagram
pentagram, п., a five-pointed star. — Gk. πεν-
τάγραμμον, neuter of the adj. πεντάγραμμος,
'formed with five lines', fr. πεντα- (see penta-),
'five', and γραμμή, line', which is related to
γράμμα, 'that which is written, a written
character'. See -gram.

## pentahedral
pentahedral, adj.—See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## pentahedron
pentahedron, п., a solid figure having five faces
(geom.) — ModL., compounded of penta- and
Gk. εδρϊ, 'seat; base, side, face'. See -hedron.

## pentamerons
pentamerons, adj., consisting of five parts —
Compounded of penta- and Gk. μέρος, 'part'.
See -merous.

## pentameter
pentameter, п., a verse of five metrical feet (pros.)
— L. pentameter, fr. Gk. πεντάμετρος, *(a verse)
having five measures', fr. πεντα- (see penta-) and
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm',
and cp. hexameter.

## pentameter
pentameter, adj., having five metrical feet (pros.)
— See prec. word.

## pentane
pentane, п., any of three hydrocarbons (CSH12) of
the methane series (chem.) — Formed fr. pent-
with suff. -ane; so called because its molecule
contains five carbon atoms.

## pentarchy
pentarchy, п., a government by five rulers. —
Compounded of penta- and Gk. -αρχία, fr.
άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See -archy.
Derivative: pentarch-ic-al, adj.

## pentastlch
pentastlch, п., a stanza or poem consisting of five
verses. — Gk. πεντάστιχος, 'of five verses', fr.
πεντα- (see penta-) and στίχος, 'row, line'. See
acrostic and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: pentastich-ous, adj., pentastich-y, n.

## pentastyle
pentastyle, n. — Lit. 'having Ave columns';
compounded of penta- and Gk. στϋλος, 'column'.
See style, 'guomon'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:574 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 547 | PERCEPT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:574 COLUMN:1 -->

## Pentateuch
Pentateuch, η., the first five books of the Bible. —
L. pentateuchus, fr. Gk. πεντάτευχος (βίβλος),
'(collection of) five books', compounded of
πεντα- (see pcnta-) and τεϋχος, 'tool,
implement', later 'book', which is rei. to τεύχειν, 'to
make ready, construct, fashion', τύχη, 'fortune,
fate, providence', and cogn. with Goth, dugan,
OE. dugan, 'to avail, be of use, be strong'. See
donghty and cp. dow, 'to be able'. Cp. also
Tyche and the second element in Hexateuch,
Heptateuch, Octateuch.

## pentathlon
pentathlon, п., an athletic contest in which each
competitor takes part in five events. — Gk.
πένταθλον, fr. πεντα- (Ъее pcnta-) and αθλον,
'prize of contest', which is rel. to άθλος,
'contest'. See athlete.

## pentavalent
pentavalent, adj., quinquevalent (chem.) — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. πεντα- (see penta-) and L.
valens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of valire, 'to have
power' (see -valent). The correct form is
quinquevalent (fr. L. quinque, 'five', and valens, 'having
power').

## penteconta-
penteconta-, combining form meaning 'fifty'. —
Fr. Gk. πεντήκοντα, 'fifty'; cp. OI. paHcdiat,
Avestic pancasafm, Arm. yisun, L. quinquagin-
ta, Olr. coica, 'fifty'. Gk. πεντήκοντα is formed
fr. πέντε, 'five' (see penta-), and -κοντά, a suff.
denoting tens (cp. τρια-κοντα, 'thirty', τεσσα-
ρα-κοντα, 'forty', etc.) This suff. is cogn. with L.
-gintl (in vi-gintl, 'twenty'), -ginta (in tri-ginta,
'thirty', quadru-ginta, 'forty', etc.) Gk. suff.
-κοντά and L. suff. -gintl, -ginta, stand for I.-E.
*komt-, *kmt-), and are cogn. with Gk. δέκα,
L. decern, 'ten' (for I.-E. *dekm-), and with Gk.
εκατόν, L. centum, 'hundred' [for 1-Е. 'kmtom,
fr. *(d)krntom\. See ten, hundred and cp. trigin-
tal, quadragenarian, quinquagenary, sexagenary,
septuagenary, Septuagint. Cp, also next word.

## Pentecost
Pentecost, n. — Eccles. L. penticoste, fr. Gk.
πεντηκοστή (scil. ήμέρϊ), 'the fiftieth (day)',
fem. of πεντηκοστός, fr. πεντήκοντα, 'fifty',
fr. πέντε, 'five' (see penteconta-); so called
because Shabuoth (the Feast of Weeks) is
observed on the fiftieth day after the second day of the
Passover. See Lev. 23 : 16. Cp. Pinkster.
Derivative; Pentecost-al, adj.

## pentene
pentene, п., either of two hydrocarbons (C5H10)
of the ethylene series (chem.) — Formed fr.
pent- with suff. -ene; so called because its
molecule contains Ave carbon atoms.

## Penthorum
Penthorum, п., a genus of plants, the ditch stone-
crop (bot.) — ModL., compounded of penta-
and Gk. δρος, 'boundary, limit, mark' (see
horizon); so called in allusion to the quinary
order of the flower.

## penthouse
penthouse, n. — Folk-etymological alteration of
earlierpentice, fr. ME. pentis, fr. OF. apentis (F.
appentis), fr. VL. *appenditicium, fr. *appenditus,
fr. L. applnsus, pp. of appendire, 'to hang on
something', fr. ad- and pendere, 'to hang'. See
pendant and cp. appendix.

## pentose
pentose, п., a general name for a group of sugars
whose molecule contains five carbon atoms
(chem)— Formed fr. pent- with subst. suff. -ose.

## Pentothal Sodium
Pentothal Sodium, trade-mark name for an
anesthetic and hypnotic. — Coined fr. pento- for
penta- (in allusion to the methylbutyl
five-carbon group), the first two letters oithiobarbiturate
and adj. suff. -al.

## Pentstemon
Pentstemon, п., a genus of plants, the beard tongue
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'having five stamens', fr.
penta- and Gk. στήμων, 'warp', used in the sense
of stamen. See stamen,

## penult
penult, n. — Abbreviation of next wordv

## penulthna
penulthna, n. — L. paenultima (scil. syllaba), 'lasv
(syllable) but one', lit. 'almost last', fr. L·. paene,
'almost', and ultimus, 'last'. See penitence and
ultima.
Derivative: penullim-ate, adj.

## penumbra
penumbra, п., partial shadow outside the
complete shadow of a body, as in an eclipse. —
ModL., coined by the German astronomer
Johannes Kepler (1571-1630) fr. L. paene,
'almost', and umbra, 'shade'. See penitent and
umbra.
Derivatives: penumbr-al, penumbr-ous, adjs.

## penurions
penurions, adj., 1) needy; 2) parsimonious. —
ML. penuriosus, fr. L. penuria. See next word

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:574 COLUMN:2 -->
and -ous.
Derivatives: penurious-ly, adv., penurious-ness,
n.

## penury
penury, п., extreme poverty. — ME., fr. MF. (=
¥.)penurie, fr. L. penuria, paenuria, 'want, need',
which is rel. to paene, 'nearly, almost'. See
penitent.

## peon
peon, п., in Sp. America, an agricultural laborer;
in India, a footsoldier; a native policeman. —
Sp. peon, 'footsoldier', fr. L. pedunem, ace. of
pedo, of s.m. See 1st pawn.
Derivatives: peon-age, п., peon-ism, n.

## peony
peony, п., a plant with large pink or white
flowers ; formerly used in medicine. — ME. piony, fr.
OF. peonie (F. pivoine), fr. L. paeonia, fr. Gk.
παιωνίά, prop. fem. of παιώνιος, belonging to
Paeon, medicinal healing', fr. Παιών, the god bf
medicine in Gk. mythology. See paean and cp.
Paeonia.

## people
people, n. — ME. peple, poeple, fr. OF. pueble,
pueple (F. peuple), fr. L. populus, which is of
uncertain, possibly Etruscan, origin. Cp.
populace, popular, public, pueblo, depopulate,
dispeople.
Derivatives: peopl-et, п., peopl-ish, adj.

## people
people, tr. v. — MF. ( — F.) peupler, fr. peuple,
'people', fr. OF. pueble, pueple. See people, n.
Derivative: peopl-er, n.

## pep
pep, п., energy. — Shortened fr. pepper.
Derivatives:^/), tr. v.,pepp-y, adj.,pepp-i-ness,
n.

## peperino
peperino, п., a light, porous, volcanic rock (pet-
rogr.) — It., fr. pepere, 'pepper.', fr. L. piperem,
ace. of piper (see pepper); so called from the
resemblance of its small grains to peppercorns.

## peplos
peplos, peplus, п., a large garment worn by women
in ancient Greece. — L. peplus, fr. Gk. πέπλος,
'upper garment, mantle', which is of uncertain
etymology.

## peplum
peplum, п., a peplos; a short skirt attached to a
blouse or coat. — L., fr. Gk. πέπλος. See prec.
word.
реро, п., any fleshy fruit having a firm rind and
many seeds, as the gourd, melon, etc. — L. pepo,
'melon, pumpkin', fr. Gk. πέπων, 'a kind of
gourd or melon eaten only when ripe', subst. use
of the adjective πέπων, 'cooked by the sun, ripe,
soft, sweet', which is rel. to πέσσειν, πέπτειν,
'to soften, ripen, boil, cook', and cogn. with L.
coquere, 'to cook'. See cook and cp. pepsin,
peptic. Cp. also melon.

## pepper
pepper, n. — ME. peper, piper, fr. OE. pipor, fr.
L. piper, 'pepper', fr. Gk. πέπερι, ult., through
Persian mediation, fr. OI. pippalt, 'berry,
peppercorn', which is of imitative origin. OFris.
piper, Du. peper, OHG. pfeffar (whence MHG.,
G. pfeffer), It. pepe, OProvenc., Catal., Sp. pebre,
F. poivre, OSlav. pipru, Lith. pipiras, Olr. pio-
bhar, Vi/.pybyr,pubyr, 'pepper', are all borrowed
fr. L. piper. See papula and cp. paprika, pebrine,
pimpernel, Piperaceae, piperine, poivrade. Cp.
also pllpul, pipa).
Derivatives: pepper, tr. v.,pepper-er, a, pepper-
y, adj.

## peppermint
peppermint, n. — Compounded of pepper and
mint, 'aromatic plant'.

## pepsin
pepsin, п., an enzyme secreted by gastric juices
(biochem.) — G. Pepsin, coined by its
discoverer, the German naturalist Theodor Schwann
(1810-82) in 1835 fr. Gk. πέψις, 'cooking;
digestion', fr. πέπτειν, 'to ripen, cook'. See pepo
and -in and cp. apepsia, dyspepsia, eupepsia and
the second element in drupe.
Derivative: pepsin-ate, tr. v., to mix or treat
with pepsin.

## pepsinogen
pepsinogen, п., a zymogen present in the cells of
the gastric glands, from which pepsin is
produced (biochem.) — Lit. 'that which produces
pepsin'; compounded of prec. word and -gen.

## peptic
peptic, adj., promoting digestion (biochem.) —
Gk. πεπτικός, 'able to digest, promoting
digestion or concoction', fr. πεπτός, 'cooked', verbal
adj. of πέπτειν, 'to cook, digest'. See pepo and
-ic and cp. pepsin. Cp. also dyspeptic, eupeptic,

## peptone
peptone, п., a substance formed by the action of
pepsin. — Coined by C. G. Lehmann in 1849 fr.

## perdition
perdition, п., 1) ruin; 2) hell. — ME. perdicioun,
fr. OF. perdicion (F. perdition), fr. L. perditio·

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:574 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: pepton-ic, adj., pepton-ize, tr. v.,
pepton-iz-ation, п., pepton-iz-er, n.
per, prep., througn, by means of. — L. per,
'through, across, over; beyond, by means of,
cogn. with OI. pari, 'around, about, through',
Gk. περί, prep, and adv., 'around, about,
beyond', Oscanpert, 'through', OSlav.pre"-, Russ.
pere-, 'through', Litb.pef, OPruss. per, 'through',
Olr. air-, er-, ir-, W. ar-, er-, OBret., Co. er-,
pref. denoting intensity, Goth, fair-, OHG. fir-,
MHG., G. ver-, OE./er-, B.for-, pref. denoting
detriment or neglect, Goth.fairra, OB.feor, 'far'.
All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *per-,
'through, across, beyond'. This base is identical
with base per-, 'to lead across, drive across,
traverse, pierce', whence OI. pardyati, 'he carries
over', piparti, 'he brings over', Gk. πείρω (for
•πέριω), Ί pierce through', πόρος, 'passage',
L. porta, 'door', portus, 'port, harbor', portare,
'to carry'. See fore, adv., and words there
referred to and cp. esp. paradise, Perea, peri-,
peril, peroneal, poligar, port, 'harbor', port,
'gate', port, 'to carry', private and the first
element in palanquin. Cp. also 2nd par.

## per-
per-, pref. representing h.per, 'through'. See prec.
word,

## peracid
peracid, n. (chem.) — Formed fr. per- and acid,

## peracute
peracute, adj. — L. peracutus, 'very sharp'. See
per- and acute,

## peradventure
peradventure, adv. — ME. per aventure, fr. OF.
par aventure; refashioned after the Latin
etymons of the French words. See per- and
adventure and cp. perchance, perforce, perfume,
perjure, pertaia.
Derivative: peradventure, n.

## peral
peral, п., a S. American fresh water fish. — Fr.
Tupi piraya, 'scissors',

## perambulate
perambulate, tr. v., to walk through or over. —
L. perambutatus, pp. of perambutare, 'to ramble
through, go through', fr. per- and ambulure, 'to
walk, go'. See amble and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: perambulation (q.v.), perambulator
(q.v.), perambulat-ory, adj. and n.

## perambulation
perambulation, n. — ME. perambulacion, fr. ML.
perambulatio, gen. -onis, fr. L. perambutatus, pp.
of perambutare. See prec. word and -ion.

## perambulator
perambulator, п., 1) one who perambulates
(archaic); 2) an odometer; 3) a baby carriage. —
ML., 'one who perambulates', fr.
L.perambutatus, pp. of perambutare. See perambulate and
agential suff. -or.

## pericycle

Derivative: pericycl-ic, adj.

## peridental

## periderm

## peridium

## peridot

## peridotite

## perigee

geo-and cp. apogee.
Derivatives: perige-al, perige-an, adjs.

## perigonium
