## perigynous
perigynous, adj., growing around the pistil (bot.)
— ModL. perigynus, fr. peri- and Gk. γυνή,
'woman, female'. See -gynous.

## perihelion
perihelion, п., that point of the orbit of a celestial
body which is nearest to the sun. — Grecized fr.
ModL. perihilium, lit. 'about, near, the sun',
coined by Kepler fr. peri- and Gk. ήλιος, 'sun'.
See helio-.
Derivative: periheli-al, adj.

## peril
peril, п., danger. — ME., fr. OF. peril (F. peril),
fr. L. periculum, 'trial, experiment, risk, danger',
which is rel. to peritus, 'experienced', experlri,
'to try, prove, test', and cogn. with Gk. πείρα,
'trial, attempt, experience', έμπειρος,
'experienced', Arm. p'orj, 'trial, attempt', Olr. aire,
'vigilance', Mir. airim, Ί am awake, watch',
Goth, ferja, 'watcher', OE. fxr, 'danger, fear'.
Cp. empiric, experience, experiment, expert,
pirate. Cp. also fear. Ali these words derive fr.
Ι.-Ε. base 'per-, 'to lead across', which is ult.
identical with base "per-, 'through, across,
beyond'. See per and cp. words there referred to.

## Perilla
Perilla, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Sp. perilla, dimin. oipera, 'pear', fr. VL. pira, fern,
sing., for L.pira, pi. otpirum, 'pear'. See pear.

## perilous
perilous, adj., dangerous.—ME., fr. OF.perillous,
perilleus (F. peritleux), 'dangerous, hazardous',
fr. L. periculdsus, fr. periculum, 'danger'. See
peril and -ous.
Derivatives: perilous-ly, adv., perilous-ness, n.

## perilymph
perilymph, п., the fluid between the membranous
and the osseous labyrinth of the ear (anat.) —
Medical L. perilympha, a hybrid coined from
Gk. περί (see perl-) and L. lympha, 'pure spring
water'. See lymph.

## perimeter
perimeter, п., outline, circumference. — F. peri-
metre, fr. L. perimetros, fr. Gk. περίμετρος, fr
περί (see peri-) and μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: perimetr-ic, adj. and п., perimetr-
ic-al, adj., perimetr-ic-al-ly, adv., perimetr-y, n.

## perimysium
perimysium, п., the connective tissue that

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:576 COLUMN:3 -->
surrounds a muscle (anat.) — Medical L., lit. 'that
which surrounds a muscle*, formed fr. peri-, Gk.
μϋς, 'muscle' (see myo-), and 1st suff. -turn.
Derivative: perimysi-al, adj.

## perinephrium
perinephrium, п., the connective tissue
surrounding the kidney (anat.) — Medical L., formed
with 1st suff. -mm fr. Gk. περίνεφρος, 'fat
about the kidneys', fr. περί (see peri-) and
νεφρός, 'kidney'. See nephro-.

## perineum
perineum, n., region of the body between the anus
and the genital organs. — ModL., fr. Gk. περί-
ναιον, περΐνεος, 'space between the anus and
scrotum', fr. περί (see peri-) and -ΐναιον,-ΐνεος,
fr. ίνάω, ίνέω, ίνόω, Ί evacuate, purge',
which is of uncertain origin. It possibly derives
fr. *ϊνν-, *Εσν- and is cogn. with OI. isndti,
'sets in motion, pours out, discharges'.
See ire and cp. hiero-.
Derivative: perine-al, adj.

## perineuritis
perineuritis, п., inflammation of the perineurium
(med.) — Medical L., formed from next word
with suff. -itis.

## perineurium
perineurium, п., connective tissue investing a
bundle of nerve fibers (anat.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. peri-, Gk. veupov, 'nerve' (see nerve),
and 1st suff. -ium.

## period
period, n. — ME.pariode, fr. MF. (= F.)periode,
fr. L. periodus, fr. Gk. περίοδος, 'circuit,
compass, cycle, period of time', lit. 'way round', fr.
περί- (see peri-) and οδός, 'way'. See odograph.

## periodic
periodic, adj. — F. piriodique, fr. L. periodicus,
fr. periodus. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: periodic-al, adj. and п.,
periodic-ally, adv., periodic-al-ness, n.

## periodicity
periodicity, n. — F.periodicite, fr. periodique. See
prec. word and -ity.

## periodontal
periodontal, adj., around a tooth (anat.) —
Formed fr. peri-, Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'
(see odonto-), and adj. suff. -al.

## perioeci
perioeci, n. pi., citizens without political rights in
Sparta. — L., fr. Gk. περίοικοι, pi. of περίοικος,
'dwelling round, neighboring', fr. περί (see
peri-) and οίκος, 'dwelling, house'. See economy.

## periorbita
periorbita, also periorbit, п., the periosteum of the
orbit (anat.) — Medical L. periorbita, a hybrid,
coined fr. Gk. περί (see peri-) and L. orbita. See
orbit
Derivative: periorbit-al, adj.

## periosteo-
periosteo-, combining form denoting the
periosteum. — See next word.

## periosteum
periosteum, п., name of the membrane covering
the bones (anat.) — Medical L., fr. περιόστεον,
neut. of περιόστεος, 'round the bones', fr. περί
(see peri-) and δστέον, 'bone'. See osteo-.
Derivative: perioste-al, adj.

## periostitis
periostitis, п., inflammation of the periosteum
(med.) — Medical L., formed from prec. word
with suff. -itis.

## peripatetic
peripatetic, adj. — MF. (= F.) piripatetique, fr.
L. peripateticus, fr. Gk. περιπατητικός, 'given
to walking about (esp. while teaching)', fr. περι-
πατεϊν, 'to walk about', which is formed fr.
περί (see peri-) and πατεϊν, 'to tread, walk', fr.
πάτος, 'trodden way, path'; see find and -ic.
The Peripatetic philosophers were so called
from their practice of walking up and down
while teaching in the Lyceum.
Derivatives: peripatetic, п., peripatetic-al-ly,
adv., peripatetic-ism, a.

## Peripatus
Peripatus, п., a genus of land arthropods (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. περίπατος, 'a walking about',
fr. περί (see peri-) and πάτος, 'trodden way,
path'. See prec. word.

## peripeteia
peripeteia, peripetia, п., a sudden change in a
drama. — Gk. περιπέτεια, 'a turning about,
reversal', fr. περιπετής, 'falling round', fr. περί
(see peri-) and I.-E. base 'pet-, 'to fly, to fall
upon'; cp. εύπετής, 'falling well, favorable'.
See feather and cp. petition.

## periphery
periphery, п., circumference. — F. peripheric, fr.
Late L. peripheria, fr. Gk. περιφέρεια,
'circumference', lit. 'a carrying round', fr. περιφέρειν,
'to carry round', fr. περί (see peri-) and φέρειν,
'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to carry'.
Derivatives: peripher-al, peripher-ic, adjs.

## periphrase
periphrase, n. — MF. (= F.) periphrase, fr. L.
periphrasis. See periphrasis and cp. paraphrase,
metaphrase.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:577 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PERIPHRASE | 550 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:577 COLUMN:1 -->

## pertphrase
pertphrase, tr. and intr. v. — F. periphraser, fr.
periphrase. See periphrase, n.

## periphrasis
periphrasis, п., circumlocution. — L., fr. Gk. πε-
ρίφρασις, 'circumlocution', fr. περιφράζειν, 'to
express by circumlocution or by periphrasis', fr.
περί (see peri-) and φράζει/ν, 'to point out,
show, tell'. See phrase.

## periphrastic
periphrastic, adj., 1) circumlocutory; 2) formed
with a particle or auxiliary verbs. — Gk.
περιφραστικός, 'periphrastic', fr. περιφράζειν. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: periphrastical, adj., periphrastic-
al-ly, adv.

## peripteral
peripteral, adj., having a row of pillars on all
sides (archil.) — Formed with suff. -al fr. Gk.
περίπτερος, 'flying round about; having a
single row of pillars al] around', fr. περί (see
peri-) and πτερόν, 'wing'. See ptero-.

## perique
perique, п., a kind of strong tobacco. —
Louisiana F. perique, prob. fr. Perique, nickname of
Pierre Chenel, a pioneer tobacco grower. Cp.
Sp. Perico, dimin. of Pedro, 'Peter', the
equivalent of F. Pierre.

## periscope
periscope, n. — Formed fr. peri- and Gk. -σκό-
πιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See
-scope.
Derivatives: periscop-ic, periscop-ic-al, adjs.,
periscop-ism, n.

## perish
perish, intr. v. — ME. perissen, perischen, fr. OF.
periss- (F.periss-), pres. part, stem of perir (F.
perir), 'to perish', fr. L. perire, 'to be lost,
perish*, lit. 'to go through', fr. per- and ire, 'to go',
See itinerate. For the ending see verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: perish-able, adj. and п., perish-abil-
ity, п., perish-able-ness, п., perish-abl~y, adv.,
perish-er, п., perisk-ing, adj., perish-ing-ly, adv.

## perispomenon
perispomenon, п., having circumflex accent on the
last syllable (Greek grammar). — Gk. περισπώ-
μενον, neut. of περισπώμενος, pres. part. pass, of
περισπδν, 'to draw round, to circumflex.', fr.
περί (see peri-) and σπαν, 'to draw, drag, tear',
whence σπασμός, 'spasm, convulsion'. See
spasm. For the passive suff. σπασμός see alumnus
and cp. words there referred to.

## perissad
perissad, п., an element or atom of odd valence
(chem.) — Formed with suff. -ad fr. Gk.
περισσός (for *περι-κιό-ς), "beyond the regular
number, odd', lit. 'lying beyond', fr. περί, 'about,
over, beyond' (see peri-) and the stem of κεΐμαι,
Ί am lying'. See civil and ср. next word. Cp. also
the second element in neossin.

## per is so dactyl
per is so dactyl, adj., having an odd number of toes
on each foot (zool.) — Gk. περισσοδάκτυλος,
'beyond the usual number of fingers or toes', fr.
περισσός, 'odd' and δάκτυλος, 'finger'. See
prec. word and dactyl.
Derivative: perissodactyl-ism, n.

## Perissodactyla
Perissodactyla, n. p]., ala order of ungulate
mammals (zool.) — ModL. See prec. word.

## peristalith
peristalith, п., a ring of stones round a mound
(archaeol.) — Compounded of Gk. περίστατος,
'standing round', and λίθος, 'stone'. The first
element derives from the stem of περιΐστημί, Ί
stand round', fr. περί (see peri-) and Ι'στημι, Ί
stand'; see state. For the second element see
-lith.

## peristalsis
peristalsis, п., rhythmic movement of intestines
moving contents onward(physiol.) — ModL., fr.
peri- and Gk. στ^λσις. 'checking, constriction',
which is rel. to στέλλειν. See next word.

## peristaltic
peristaltic, adj., pertaining to, or of the nature of,
peristalsis. — Gk. περισταλτικός, 'clasping and
compressing', fr. περιστέλλειν, 'to dress, clothe,
wrap up, attend to', fr. περί (see peri-) and στέλ-
λειν, 'to put in order, equip, draw together',
which is rel. to στολή, 'equipment'. See stole,
'garment'.
Derivative: peristaltic-al-ly, adv.

## peristeronic
peristeronic, adj., pertaining to pigeons. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. περιστερών, 'dovecote',
fr. περιστερά, 'dove, pigeon', which prob.
stands for *πελιστερδ (with assimilation of the
λ to p) and is rel. to πέλεια, 'dove, pigeon',
πελλός, 'dark-colored, dusky', fr. I.-E. base
*pel-, 'dark-colored, gray'. Accordingly
περιστέρα prop, means 'the dark-colored bird'. See
fallow, 'brownish yellow'.

## peristome
peristome, п., 1) the fringe around the opening

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:577 COLUMN:2 -->
of the capsule in mosses (hot.); 2) a mouthlike
opening (zool.) — ModL. peristoma (altered on
analogy of pericarpium to peristomium), lit.
'that which is about the mouth', fr. peri- and
Gk. στόμα, 'mouth'. See stoma.
Derivatives: peristom-al, ptristomi-al, peris·
tomat-ic, adjs.

## peristyle
peristyle, п., a row of columns. — F. peristyle, fr.
L. peristylum, fr. Gk. περίστΰλον, 'colonnade
round a temple or inner court', fr. περί (see
peri-) and στϋλος, 'pillar, column'. See style,
'gnomon'.
Derivative: peristyl-ar, adj.

## perithecium
perithecium, п., a receptacle in certain fungi (bot.)
— ModL., formed on analogy of pericarpium fr.
peri- and Gk. θήκη, 'case', from the stem of
τιθέναι, 'to place', whence also θέμα, 'that
which is placed', θέσις, 'a setting, placing'. See
theme and cp. theca and words there referred to.

## peritoneo-
peritoneo-, perltonaeo-, combining form
denoting the peritoneum. — Gk. περιτόναιο-, fr.
περιτόναιον. See next word.

## peritoneum
peritoneum, peritonaeum, п., the serous
membrane lining the abdomen (anat.) — L.
peritonaeum, fr. Gk. περιτόναιον, 'peritoneum', prop,
meaning 'the membrane encompassing the
viscera', neut. of the adjective περιτόναιος,
'stretched over', fr. περίτονος, 'stretched over', fr. πε-
ριτείνειν, 'to stretch over', fr. περί (see peri-)
and τείνειν, 'to stretch', fr. I.-E. base *ten-,
*ton-, 'to stretch'. See tone and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: periton(a)e-a/, adj., periton(a)e-al-
ly, adv.

## peritonitis
peritonitis, п., inflammation of ihe peritoneum
(med.) — Medical L., coined by the French
pathologist Frangois-Boissier de la Croix de Sau-
vages (1706-67) about 1750 fr. Gk. περιτόναιον
(see prec. word) and suff. -itis. Cp. enteritis.
Derivative: peritonit-ic, adj.

## perityphlitis
perityphlitis, п., inflammation of the tissues
surrounding the caecum (med.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. peri-, Gk. τυφλός, 'blind, closed', and
suff. -ttls. See typhlitis.

## periwig
periwig, п., a peruke. — Earlier perwyke, pere-
wyke, fr. MR (= F.) perruque. See peruke and
cp. wig.
Derivative: periwigg-ed, adj.

## periwinkle
periwinkle, п., a creeping evergreen plant;
myrtle. — ME. pervinke, fr. OE. perwince, fr. L.
pervinca, 'periwinkle' (whence also F. per-
venche), fr. per- and vincire, 'to bind', which is
prob. rel. to vicia, 'vetch*. See vetch and cp.
Vlaca.
Derivatives: periwinkl-ed, adj., periwinkl-er, n.

## periwinkle
periwinkle, п., an edible marine mo Husk {zool.)
— ME. pinewinkle, fr. OE. pinewincle, in which
the first element is prob. borrowed fr. L. pina,
'mussel', fr. Gk. πίνη, πίνα, which is of Aegean
origin. The second element is rel. to OE. wincel,
MLG., MDu., Du. winkel, OHG. winkil,
MHG., G. winkel, 'corner', OE. wince, 'a pulley',
lit. 'that which turns*, and to E. wince, winch,
wink. Cp. winkle. This word ana periwinkle, the
plant, were mutually influenced in form by each
other.

## perjure
perjure, tr. and intr. v. — MF. (= V.)parjurer, fr.
L. perjurare, 'to swear falsely', fr. per- and
jurdre, 'to swear'; see jury, n. For the
substitution of L. per to OF. par cp. peradventure and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: perjur-ed, adj., perjur-ed-ly, adv.,
perjur-ed-ness, a.,perjur-er, п., perjurious (q.v.),
perjury (q.v.)

## perjurious
perjurious, adj. — L. perjuriosus, 'full of perjury',
fr. perjurium. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: perjuhous-ly, adv., perjurious-ness,
n.

## perjury
perjury, n. — ME. perjurie, fr. OF. parjurie, fr. L.
perjurium, 'perjury', fr. perjurare, 'to swear
falsely'. See perjure and -y (representing OF.
-«).

## perk
perk, intr. and tr. v., to lift up one's head. — ME.
perken (said of the popinjay), fr. ONF. perquer,
corresponding to F. percher, 'to perch, roost'.
See perch, 'to sit on a perch'.
Derivatives: perk, perk-ish, perk-y, adjs., perk-
i-ly, adv., perk-i-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:577 COLUMN:3 -->

## perks
perks, n. —■ Colloquial abbreviation of
perquisites.

## perlite
perlite, п., an igneous rock composed of
enamellike globules (petrogr.) — F., formed fr. perle,
'pearl', with suff. -He. See pearl and su'st. suff.
-ite.
Derivative: perlit-ic, adj.

## permanence
permanence, also permanency, n. — ME., fr. MF.
(— F.) permanence, fr. ML. permanentia, fr. L.
permanens, gen. -entis. See next word and -ce,
resp. -cy.

## permanent
permanent, adj. —■ ME., fr. MF. (— F.)
permanent, fr. L. permanentem, ace. of permanens,
pres. part, of permanere, 'to endure, continue,
remain', fr. per- and manere, 'to remain'. See
mansion and -ent and cp. remain.
Derivatives; permanent-ly, adv., permanent-
ness, n.

## permanganate
permanganate, n. (chem.) — Compounded of
per- and manganate.

## permanganic
permanganic, adj. (chem.) — Compounded of
per- and manganic.

## permeable
permeable, adj. — Late L. permeabilis,
'permeable', fr. permeare. See permeate and -able.
Derivatives, permeabil-ity, п., permeable-ness,
п., permeabl-yf adv.

## permeance
permeance, n. — See next word and -ce.

## permeant
permeant, adj. — L. permeans, gen. -amis, pres.
part, of permeare. See next word and suff. -ant.

## permeate
permeate, tr. v., to pass through the pores of; to
pervade; intr. v., to penetrate. — L. permeatus,
pp. οΐpermeare, 'to pass through, permeate', fr.
per- and meare, 'to go, pass'. See meatus.
Derivatives: permeat-ion, п., permeat-ivet adj.

## Permian
Permian, adj., pertaining to the uppermost strata
of the Paleozoic era (geol.) — Formed with suff.
-ian fr. Perm, name of a province in Eastern
Russia.
Derivative: Permian, n.

## permissible
permissible, adj. — ME., fr. OF. permissible^ fr.
ML. permissibilis, fr. L. permissus, pp. of
permitted. See permit and -lble.
Derivatives: permissibil-ity, п., permissible-ness,
n.,permissibl-y, adv.

## permission
permission, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)permission,
fr. L. permissionem, ace. of permissio, fr.
permissus, pp. of permittere. See perinit and -Ion.
Derivative: permission-ed, adj.

## permissive
permissive, adj. — OF. permissif (fern,
permissive), fr. L. permissus, pp. of permittere. See
permit and -ive.

## permissory
permissory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr.
L. permissus, pp. of permittere. See next word.

## permit
permit, tr. and intr. v. — L. permittere, 'to allow
to pass through, give- leave, allow, suffer', fr.
per- and mittere, 'to send'. See mission.
Derivatives -.permit, n.,permitt-ed, ad'].,
permittee, п., permitt-iv-ity, n.

## permutable
permutable, adj. — Late L. permutubilis, fr. L.
permuture. See permnte and -able.
Derivatives: permutabil-ity, п., permutable-ness,
п., permutabl-y, adv.

## permutate
permutate, tr. v., to change. — L. permutatus, pp.
οΐ permuture. See permnte and verbal suff. -ate.

## permutation
permutation, n. — ME. permutacioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) permutation, fr. L. permutationem, ace.
of permutatio, 'changing, alteration', fr.
permutatus, pp. of permuture. See permnte and -ation.
Derivative: permutation-al, adj.

## permute
permute, tr. v. — L. permuture, 'to change
completely', fr. per- and mutare, Чо change'. See
mutable.
Derivative: permut-ert n.

## pern
pern, п., the honey buzzard. — ModL. pernis, fr.
Gk. πέρνης, a wrong reading in Aristotle for
πτέρνις, 'a kind of hawk'.

## pernicious
pernicious, adj., hurtful; fatal. — MF.pernicieus
(F. pernicieux), fr. L. perniciosus, 'destructive,
ruinous', fr. pernicies, 'destruction, death, ruin',
fr. per- and nex, necis, 'violent death, murder',
which is rel. to nocere, 'to hurt, injure, harm',
noxa, 'harm, injury'. See noxious and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: pernicious-ly, adv., pernicious-ness,
n.

## pernickety
pernickety, adj., fussy; fastidious (colioq.) — Of
uncertain origin; perhaps corruption of
particular.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:578 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 551 | PERSONALITY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:578 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: pernicketi-ness, n.

## pernoctation
pernoctation, п., the act of passing the night. —
L. pemoctutio, gen. -onis, 'passing of the night',
fr. pernoctat-(um), pp. stem of pernoctare, 'to
pass the night', fr. per- and nox, gen, noctis,
'night'. See night and -ation and cp. nocturnal.

## peroneal
peroneal, adj., pertaining to the fibula (anat.) —
Formed with adj. sufT. -al fr. Gk. περόνη, 'pin,
brooch, buckle; the fibula', which is rel. to
πέραν, 'to drive across', πείρειν, 'to pierce
through, run through', fr. I.-E. base *per-, 'to
lead across, drive across, traverse, pierce*. .See
per and cp. words there refeerred to.

## Peronospora
Peronospora, п., a genus of downy mildews (bot.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. περόνη, 'pin,
brooch, buckle', and σπόρος, 'seed'. See
peroneal and spore.

## Peronosporaceae
Peronosporaceae, n. pi., a family of parasitic
fungi; the downy mildews (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. prec. word with sufF. -aceae.

## peronosporaceous
peronosporaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-асе о us.

## perorate
perorate, intr. v., 1) to speak at length; 2) to
conclude a speech. — L. perordtus, pp. of perorare,
'to speak from beginning to end', fr. per- and
drare, 'to speak'. See oration and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: peroration (q.v.), perorat-ive, adj.,
perorat-or, п., perorat-ory, adj. and n.

## peroration
peroration, n. — ME. peroracyon, fr. L. perordtio,
gen. -onis, fr. perordtus, pp. of perorare. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: peroration-al, adj.

## perovskite
perovskite, п., a calcium titanate (mineral.) —
Named after Count L. A. Perovski of Russia
(died in 1856). For the ending see subst. sufT.
-ite.

## peroxide
peroxide, peroxid, n. (chem.) — Formed fr. per-
and oxid(e).
Derivatives: peroxide, tr. v., peroxid-ic, adj.,
peroxid-ize, tr. and intr. v., peroxid-ize-ment, n.

## perpend
perpend, tr. and intr. v., to consider carefully. —
L. perpendere, 'to weigh carefully, examine,
consider', fr. per- and pendere, 'to weigh'. See
pendant.

(fern.), shortened from mappaqtd peshitta, 'the
simple version', fern, of рёshit, 'straight, plain,
simple'; prob. so called for its literal (not
periphrastic) rendering of the text. Aram.-Syr.
peshit is Pe'il part, of ρ shaf, 'he stretched out,
extended; he made plain, explained', and is rel.
to Heb. pashdt, 'he stripped off', in Mishnaic
Hebrew, 'he made plain, explained', Mishnaic
Heb. pdshut, 'straight, plain, simple' (prop.
pass. part, ofpdshat), Arab, bdsata, 'he stretched
out, extended', Akkad. pashdtu, 'to expunge,
obliterate'.

## peshwa
peshwa, п., title of the chief minister of the Ma-
ratha princes. — Pers. peshwa, 'chief, fr. pesh,
'before'.

## peso
peso, п., a former Spanish silver coin. — Sp., 'a
weight', fr. L.pensum, prop. pp. of pendere, 'to
cause to hang, to weigh'. See pendant and cp.
peseta.

## pessary
pessary, п., a device worn in the vagina as a
support of the uterus. — ME. pessarie, fr. ML.
pessdrium, fr. L. pessum, pessus, 'pessary', fr.
Gk. πεσσόν, ττεσσός, 'an oval stone', which is
prob. of Sem. origin; cp. Aram, pissd, pisa,
'clod, stone'. For the ending see suff. -ary.

## pessimism
pessimism, п., 1) in philosophy, a) the doctrine
that this world is the worst possible world; b)
the belief that the evil in life outweighs the
good; 2) the tendency to take the worst view of
things. — Fr. L.pessimus, 'worst', which stands
for *ped-semos, and is rel. to pijor (for *ped-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:580 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 553 | PETTITOES -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:580 COLUMN:1 -->
yos), 'worse'. See pejorative and cp. words there
referred to. Tile word pessimism was first used
by Coleridge.

## pessimist
pessimist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: pessimist-ic, pessimist-ic-al, adjs.,
pessimist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## pessulus
pessulus, п., a boltlike bone. — L., 'bolt', fr. Gk.
πάσσαλος, of s.m., fr. I.-E. base *pag-,pak-, 'to
fasten', whence also Gk. πηγνύναι, 'to make
firm', L. pangere, 'to fasten, fix'. See pact. The
change of Gk. πάσσαλος to pessulus in Latin
was influenced by folk etymology which
connected the word with L. pessum, 'latch bolt'.
See B. F. Friedmann, Die jonischen und atti-
schen W6rter im Altlatein, pp. 66 ff. For the
change of Greek ά (in πάσσαλος) to it (in L.
pessulus) see aplustre and cp. words there
referred to.

## pest
pest, n. — MF. (= F.) pesle, fr. L. pestis, 'pest,
pestilence, plague', which is of uncertain origin.

## pester
pester, tr. v. — Aphetic for MF. empestrer (F.
empetrer), 'to hobble; to entangle, intricate',
orig. 'to tether a grazing horse', fr. VL. "impas-
tdriare, fr. L. in, 'in' and VL. pastoria, 'tether
for a grazing horse', fr. L. pastura, 'pasture'.
See in and pastor and cp. pastern,
Derivatives: pester, п., pester-er, п., pester-ous,
adj.

## pestiferous
pestiferous, adj., pestilential. — ME., fr. L. pes-
tiferus, 'bringing pestilence, pestilential',
compounded ofpestis, 'plague, pestilence' aadferre,
'to bear, carry'. See pest and -ferous.
Derivatives: pestiferously, adv., pestiferous-
ness, n.

## pestilence
pestilence, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. pes-
tilentia, 'pestilentia, plague'. See next word and
-ce.

## pestilent
pestilent, adj. — ME., fr. L. pestilent, gen. -enlis,
fr. pestis. See pest and -ent.
Derivatives: pestilent, п., pestilent-ly, adv.

## pestilential
pestilential, adj. — ME. pestilencial, fr. ML. pes-
tilentialis, fr. L. pestilentia. See pestilence and -ial.
Derivatives: pestilential-ly, adv., pestilemial-
ness, n.

## pestle
pestle, n. — ME. pestel, fr. MF. pestel, pesteil,
pestail, fr. L. pistitlum, 'pounder, pestle', fr.
*pins-tto-, fr. pinsere, 'to beat, pound', whence
also/w/α, for *pins-la, 'mortar'. L.pinsere is cogn.
with OI pindsti, 'pounds, crushes', pistah,
'anything ground; meal', Gk. πτίσσειυ, 'to winnow',
OSlav.p/ίο andpichajo, pichati, 'to push, thrust,
strike, piseno, 'meal', pisenica, 'wheat', Russ.
pseno, 'millet'. Cp. pistil, which is a doublet of
pestle. Cp. also pile, 'a pointed stake', pise,
piston, ptisan.
Derivative: pestle, tr. and intr. v.

## pet
pet, п., fondled animal; darling. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: pet, tr. and intr. v., pett-ed, adj.,
pett-er, п., pett-ing, n.

## pet
pet, п., peevishness. — Of uncertain origin;
perhaps fr. pet, 'fondled animal'.
Derivatives: pett-ed, adj., pett-ed-ly, adv., pett-
ed-ness, n.,p'ett-ish, adj.

## petal
petal, п., one of the leaves of the corolla. —
ModL. petalum, fr. Gk. πέταλον, 'leaf. See pe-
talon.
Derivatives: petal(l)-ed, adj., petal-ine, adj., pe-
talite (q.v.), petal-ism, п., petat-oid, adj.

## petalism
petalism, п., a synonym of ostracism. — Gk.
πεταλισμός, method of temporary banishment
in Syracuse; so called because the names of
those to be banished were written on olive
leaves, fr. πέταλον, 'leaf. See petalon and -ism.

## petalite
petalite, п., a silicate of aluminum and lithium
(mineral.) — Formed fr. Gk. πέταλου, 'thin
plate of metal' (see petalon), with subst. suff.
-ite.

## petalody
petalody, п., the change of certain organs (as e.g.
stamens) into petals (bot.) — Formed with suff.
-y (fr. Gk. -ία J fr. Gk. πεταλώδης, 'leaflike', fr.
πέταλον, 'leaf' and -ώδης, 'like'. See petalon
and -/ode, 'like'.

## pctaloid
pctaloid, adj., resembling a petal. —
Compounded of petal and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## petalon
petalon, п., the gold plate on the Jewish high
priest's miter. — Gk. πέταλον, 'thin plate of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:580 COLUMN:2 -->
metal, leaf, neut. of the adj. πέταλος, 'spread
out', rel. to πεταννύναι, 'to spread out', fr. I.-E.
base *pet-, 'to spread out', whence also L. patere,
'to lie open', ON.fadmr, 'embrace, bosom', OE.
fsedm, 'embrace, bosom, fathom'. See fathom
and cp. petasus.

## Petalostemon
Petalostemon, п., the prairie clover (bot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. πέταλον, 'leaf,
and στήμων, 'warp'. See prec. word and stamen.

## -petalous
-petalous, combining form meaning 'having a
certain number or a certain shape of petals', as
in dipetalous, eleutheropetalous (bot.) — ModL.
-pelalus, fr. Gk. πέταλον, 'leaf. See petalon and
-ous.

## petard
petard, п., 1) a case filled with explosives; 2) a
kind of firecracker. — F. petard, fr. peter (earlier
peter), 'to break wind', fr. pet, 'a breaking of
wind', fr. L. peditum, prop. neut. pp. of pedere,
'to break wind', used as a noun. See pedicular.

## Petasites
Petasites, п., a genus of plants, the sweet
coltsfoot (bot.) — ModL., ft. Gk. πετασΐτης,
'coltsfoot', fr. πέτασος, 'a broad-brimmed hat' (see
next word); so called in allusion to its large
leaves. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## petasus
petasus, п., a low-crowned, broad-brimmed hat
worn by the ancient Greeks. — L., fr. Gk.
πέτασος, 'broad-brimmed felt hat', fr. I.-E. base
*pet-, 'to spread out'. See petalon and cp. prec.
word.

## Petaurista
Petaurista, п., a genus of marsupials (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. πεταυριστής, 'tumbler, торе-
dancer', fr. πέταυρον, πέτευρον, 'perch, roost',
which is prob. rel. to πέτεσθαι, 'to fly', fr. I.-E.
base 'pet-, 'to fly, fall upon'. See feather and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-izt.

## Pete
Pete, n. — Dimin. of Peter.

## petechia
petechia, п., one of a number of small crimson
or purplish spots on the skin (med.) — Medical
L-, fr. It. petecchia, 'speck', which prob. derives
fr. Gk. πιττάκιον, 'tablet for writing on, label,
ticket; plaster', dimin. formed fr. πίττα, πίσσα,
'pitch', which is cogn. with L. pix, gen. picis,
'pitch'. See pitch, 'a resinous substance'.
Derivatives: petechi-al, petechi-ate, adjs.

## Peter
Peter, mjasc. PN. — ME., fr. Late L. Petrus, fr.
Gk. Πέτρος, fr. πέτρος, 'stone, rock'; prop,
translation of Aram, kepha, 'rock'. See petro-
and cp. pedro, pierrot.

## peter
peter, intr. v., to be exhausted (colloq.) — Of
unknown origin.

## petersham
petersham, п., overcoat of knotted, woolen mite-
rial. — Named after Viscount Petersham, the
4th Earl of Harrington (1780-1851).

## petiole
petiole, п., a leafstalk (bot.) — Late L. petiolus,
more correctly peciolus, 'little foot, stalk of
fruit', contracted fr. *ped(i)ciolus, dimin. of L.
pediculus, of s.m., itself a dimin. of pes, gen.
pedis, 'foot'. See pedal, п., and -ole.
Derivatives: petiol-ar, petiol-ate, petiol-ated,
petiol-ed, adjs.

## petiolule
petiolule, n. — Formed fr. petiole with dimin.
suff. -ule.

## petit
petit, adj., small, little. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
petit, 'small, little'. See petty.

## petite
petite, adj., small, little (said of a woman or girl).
— F. fern, of petit, 'small, little'. See petty and
cp. prec. word. Cp. also the first element in
pettitoes.

## petition
petition, n. — ME. peticioun, fr. OF. petition (F.
petition), fr. L.petitionem, ace. of petitio, 'attack,
request, petition', fr. petitus, pp. of petere, 'to
fall upon, rush at, attack, assail; to seek, ask,
request', whence appetere, 'to strive after', com-
petere, 'to strive after something in company',
impetus, 'attack'; fr. I.-E. base "pet-, 'to fly, to
fall upon'. See feather and cp. appetence,
appetite, compete, competent, competition,
competitor, perpetual, petulant, propitious, repeat,
repetition.
Derivatives: petition, tr. and intr. v., petition-al,
adj., petition-ary, adj., petition-ee, п.,
petitioner, п., petition-ist, n.

## Petrea
Petrea, п., a genus of tropical American woody
plants (bot.) — ModL., named after Robert
James, Baron Petre (1713-43).

## petrel
petrel, п., a sea bird. — F. petrel, of uncertain
etymology. The connection with the name Peter

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:580 COLUMN:3 -->
is due to folk etymology,

## petrifaction
petrifaction, n. — See petrify and -ion.

## petrifactive
petrifactive, adj. — See-prec. word and -Ive.

## petrification
petrification, n. — F. petrification. See next word
and -ation.

## petrify
petrify, tr. and intr. v., to change into stone. —
MF. (= F.) petrifier, compounded of L. petra,
'rock, stone' (fr. Gk. πέτρα) and -ficare, fr.
facere, 'to make, do'. See 1st petro- and -fy.
Derivatives: petrifi-able, adj., petrifi-ed, adj.,
petrifi-er, n.

## petro-
petro-, combining form meaning 'stone, rock'. —
Gk. πετρο-, fr. πέτρος, 'stone', rel. to πέτρα,
'rock'; of uncertain origin. Cp. Empetrum,
parsley, pedro, perron, Peter, petroleum, pierrot,
saltpeter,

## petro-
petro-, combining form meaning 'containing
petroleum and'. — Shortened fr. petroleum,

## petroglyph
petroglyph, п., a carving in a rock. —
Compounded of 1st petro- and Gk. γλυφή, 'a carving'. See
giyph.
Derivatives:petroglyph-ic, adj.,petroglyph-y, n.

## petrograpber
petrograpber, n. — See next word and agential
suff. -er.

## petrography
petrography, п., scientific description of rocks. —
Lit. 'description of rocks', fr. Gk. πέτρα, 'rock',
and -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See 1st
petro- and -graphy.
Derivatives: petrograph-ic, petrograph-ic-al,
adjs., petrograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## petrol
petrol, п., 1) petroleum (rare); 2) gasoline. — F.
petrole, fr. ML. petroleum. See petroleum.
Derivative: petrol, intr. v.

## petrolatum
petrolatum, п., pure petroleum jelly. — ModL.,
formed fr. petroleum on analogy of chemical
terms ending in -atum, as acetatum, etc. (see
chem. suff. -ate),

## petroleum
petroleum, n. — ML-, fr. L.petra (fr. Gk. πέτρα),
'rock', and oleum, 'oil'. See petro- and oil.

## petrolic
petrolic, adj., pertaining to petroleum. — Chem.
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## petrology
petrology, п., the study of rocks. — Compounded
of 1st petro- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: petrolog-ic, petrolog-ic-al, adjs.,
petrolog-ic-al-ly, adv., petrolog-ist, n.

## petronel
petronel, п., an old firearm. — MF. (= F.) pi-
trinal, fr. OF. peitrine (F. poitrine), 'chest', fr.
VL. *pector\na, prop. fern, of the adj. *pectori-
nus, 'pertaining to the chest', used as a noun, fr.
L. pectus, gen. pectoris, 'chest' (see pectoral); so
called from its being rested against the chest in
firing. The English form of the word is due to a
confusion with L.petra, 'rock, stone', with which
it has nothing to do.

## petrosal
petrosal, adj., petrous. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. petrosus, 'rocky', fr. petra, 'rock'. See
petrous.
Derivative: petrosal, п., a petrosal bone.

## Petroselinum
Petroselinum, п., a genus of plants, the parsley
(bot.) — Late L., fr. Gk. πετροσέλϊνον, 'parsley'.
See parsley,

## petrous
petrous, adj., 1) stony; 2) pertaining to that part
of the temporal bone which protects the internal
ears. — MF. petreux, fr. L. petrosus, 'rocky', fr.
petra, 'rock', fr. Gk. πέτρα. See petro- and -ous.

## petticoat
petticoat, n. — ME. petycote, lit. 'a small coat'.
See petty and coat.
Derivatives: petticoat, adj. and tr. and intr. v.,

## petticoat-ed
petticoat-ed, adj., petticoat-ery, п.,petticoat-less,
adj.

## pettifog
pettifog, intr. and tr. v. — Back formation fr.
pettifogger (q.v.)
Derivative: pettifogg-ing, adj. and n.

## pettifogger
pettifogger, n. — The first element of this word is
petty. The second element is identical with obsol.
E.fogger, 'pettifogger', which is prob. traceable
to Fugger, the surname of a famous German
family of merchants and financiers in the 15th
and 16th cent.
Derivative: pettifogger-y, n.

## pettitoes
pettitoes, n. pi., pig's feet used for food. — The
original meaning was 'giblets (of any animal)'.
The word derives fr. OF. petite oe, 'goose
giblets', lit. 'little goose', fr. petite, fern, of petit,
'little', and oue, oe (F. oie), 'goose', fr. VL. *auca,
'goose', a contraction of *avica, fr. L. avis,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:581 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PETTY | 554 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:581 COLUMN:1 -->
'bird'. See petit and aviation and cp. ocarina,

## petty
petty, adj. — ME. pety, petit, ft. MF. (= F.)
petit, 'small, little', fr. OF., prob. from a base of
imitative origin, expressive of littleness in
infant's language. Cp. petit and the first element
in pettifogger. Cp. also It. piccolo, Sp. pequefto,
'small, little', and see piccolo.
Derivatives: petti-ly, adv., Qetti-ness, n.

## petulance
petulance, n. — F. petulance, fr. L. petulantia,
'sauciness, freakishness, impudence; petulance',
fr. petitions, gen. -amis. See next word and -ce.

## petulancy
petulancy, п., petulance. — L. petulentia. See prec.
word and -cy.

## petulant
petulant, adj., impatient; irritable; peevish. —
MF. (= F.) petulant, fr. L. petulantem, ace. of
petulans, 'saucy, freakish, impudent; petulant',
prop. pres. part, of *petulare, 'to attack in jest',
fr. petere, 'to attack'. See petition and -ant.
Derivative: petulant-ly, adv.

## Petunia
Petunia, п., a genus of plants of the potato
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. F. petun, 'tobacco plant',
fr. Port. petum(e), fr. Guarani pe/f (with
nasalized i). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## petuntse
petuntse, п., white clay used in China to make
porcelain. — Chin, pai-tun-tzu, fr. pai, 'white',
tun, 'stone', and formative element -tzu.

## petzite
petzite, п., a silver gold telluride (mineral.) —
Named after W. Pen, who analyzed it. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## peucites
peucites, п., fossil pine wood. — Fr. Gk. πεύκη,
'pine', which is cogn. with Lith. puSis, OPruss.
peuse, 'pine, spruce', OHG. fiuhta, MHG. viehte,
G. Fickle, Olr. ochtach, 'spruce'. For the ending
see subst. suff. -Ite.

## pew
pew, n. — ME. pewe, puwe, pywe, fr. MF.
puie, puiee, 'prop, stay, raised seat, balcony',
verbal noun formed ii.puier, 4o prop, support',
fr. VL. 'podidre, fr. L. podium, 'an elevated
place, parapet, balcony', fr. Gk. πόδιον, 'base,
pedestal, balcony', dimin. of πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. See foot and cp. -pod, podium, puy. Cp.
also appui, apoggiatura.
Derivatives: pew, tr. v., pew-age, n.

## pewee
pewee, also spelled peewec, п., 1) the flycatcher;
2) the lapwing. — Imitative of the bird's cry.

## pewit
pewit, peewit, п., the lapwing; the pewee. —
Imitative. See prec. word.

## pewter
pewter, п., any of various alloys having tin as
their chief constituent. — ME. pewtyr, pewtre,
fr. OF. peltre, peautre, fr. VL. peltrum (whence
also It. peltro, OProveng., Sp. peltre), which is
of uncertain origin. Cp. spelter.
Derivative: pewter-er, n.

## -pexy
-pexy, also -pexia, -pexis, combining form
meaning 'fixing (of a specified part)', as in cotopexy,
hysteropexy. — Medical L. -pexia, -pexis, fr. Gk.
πηξις, 'a fixing', from the stem of πηγνύναι, 'to
fix, make firm', fr. I.-E. base *pag-, *рдк-, Чо
join together'. See pact. ·

## peyote
peyote, п., a mescal cactus. — Mexican Sp., fr.
Nahuatl peyotl, 'caterpillar'; so called in
allusion to the downy center.

## Peziza
Peziza, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL., fr.
L. pezica orpezita, 'mushroom without a stalk',
fr. Gk. πέζεα, πέζις, of s.m., which is rel. to
πεζός (for 'πεδιός), 'on foot', and to πους, gen.
ποδός, 'foot'. See foot and cp. words there
referred to.

## pfennig
pfennig, п., a small bronze coin of Germany. —
G. See penny.

## Phacelia
Phacelia, п., a genus of plants of the waterleaf
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φάκελος,
'bundle, fascicle', which is of uncertain origin;
so called from the shape of its flowers. For the
ending see.lst sufT. -ia.

## phaeno-
phaeno-, before a vowel phaen-. — See pheno-,
pben-,

## Phaethon
Phaethon, п., the son of Helios, the sun god, who
once drove his father's sun chariot and almost
set the world on fire (Greek and Roman mythol.)
— L., fr. Gk. Φαέθων, lit. 'shining', fr. φάειν,
'to shine, gleam', fr. φάος, 'light'. See phantasm.

## phaeton
phaeton, п., a light four-wheeled carriage. — So
called from Phaethon, the unlucky driver of his
father's chariot. See prec. word.

## -phag
-phag, -phage, combining form meaning 'eater',
as in xylophage. — From the stem of Gk.
φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:581 COLUMN:2 -->

## phagedena
phagedena, phagedaena, п., gangrene (med.) — L.
phagedaena, fr. Gk. φαγέδαινα, 'cancerous sore,
cancer', lit. 'voracity', fr. φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See
-phagous.

## phagedenic
phagedenic, phagedaenic, adj. — Gk. φαγε-
δαινικός, 'of the nature of a cancer', fr. φαγέ-
δαινα. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: phaged(a)enic-al, adj.
-phagia. See -phagy.

## phago-
phago-, combining form meaning 'eating', as in
phagocyte. — Gk. φαγο-, fr. φαγεΐν, 'to eat'.
See -phagous.

## phagocyte
phagocyte, n. (biol. and med.) — Coined by the
Russian zoologist and bacteriologist Elie Metch-
nikoff (1845-1916) in 1884 from phago- and
Gk. κύτος, 'a hollow vessel'. See -cyte.
Derivatives: phagocyte, tr. v., phagocyt-ic, adj.,
phagocyt-ism, п., phagocyt-ize, tr. v.

## phagocytosis
phagocytosis, п., destruction of bacteria by
phagocytes. — ModL., coined by Metchnikoff from
prec. word and suff. -osis.

## -phagous
-phagous, combining form meaning 'eating,
feeding on', as in creophagous, xylophagous. — Gk.
-φάγος, 'eater of, from the stem of φαγεΐν, 'to
eat', which is cogn. with OI. bhdjati, 'assigns,
allots, apportions, enjoys, loves', bhagab, 'al-
lotter, distributor, master', bhdksati, 'eats,
drinks, enjoys', Avestic baya-, OPers. baga-,
'master, god', lit. 'distributor', OSlav. bogu,
'god', bogatu, 'rich', u-bogu, ne-bogu,
'unfortunate'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*bhag-, 'to distribute, share out'. Cp. the second
element in esophagus. Cp. also bahadur,
baksheesh, Bhaga, Bhagavad-Gita. For E. -ous (in
-phagous), as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ons.
•phagy, also -phagia, combining form meaning
'eating of (something specified)', as in anthro-
pohagy, geophagy. — ModL. -phagia, fr. Gk.
-φαγία, 'eating of, fr. -φάγος, 'eating'. See
-phagous and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## phalange
phalange, п., single bone of finger or toe (anat.
and zool·.) — F., fr. L. phalanx, gen. -angis. See
phalanx.
Derivative: phalange-al, adj.

## phalanger
phalanger, п., any of a number of Australian
arboreal marsupials with a long tail; (cap.) the
typical genus of phalangers (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. φάλαγξ, 'bone between two joints of the
fingers or toes' (see phalange); so called in
allusion to the characteristic formation of the toes.

## Phalaugerldae
Phalaugerldae, n. pi., a family of marsupials
.(zool.) — ModL., formed from prec. word with
suff. -idae.

## phalanstery
phalanstery, п., socialistic community proposed
by the French social scientist Fra^ois-Marie-
Charles Fourier (1772-1837). — F. phalanstire,
coined by Fourier fr. phalange, name of the
community in Fourier's system, prop, 'phalanx', and
the ending -ere, after monastere (= E.
monastery). See phalanx.
Derivatives: phalanster-ial, adj., phalanster-ian,
adj. and п.,phalanster-ian-ism, a.,phalanster-ic,
adj., phalanster-ism, п., phalanster-ist, n.

## phalanx
phalanx, п., heavy infantry in close order (Greek
antiquity); a single bone of finger or toe (anat.
and zool.) — L., fr. Gk. φάλαγξ, 'trunk, log,
line of battle, battle array; bone between two
joints of the fingers or toes', cogn. with OE.
balca, 'a ridge between furrows'. See balk, п.,
and cp. Falange. In anatomy, phalanx orig.
denoted the whole row of the finger joints, which
was so called because its arrangement is
suggestive of a battle array. See Joseph Hyrtl, Ono-
matologia anatomica, p. 104, and cp. phalange.
Derivative: phatanx-ed, adj.

## Phalarls
Phalarls, п., a genus of plants, the canary grass
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φαλϊρίς, 'coot; canary
grass'. See next word.

## phalarope
phalarope, п., any of small wading-birds that
resemble the sandpiper. — F., irregularly formed
fr. ModL. Phalaropus, name of the type genus,
fr. Gk. φαλϊρίς, 'coot' and πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. The first element prop, means 'white,
shining' (the coot is called φαλαρίς from the
white spot on its head), and derives fr. φαλός,
'white, shining' (whence also φαλαρός, 'having
a patch of white'), and is cogn. with L. fulica,
'coot', OHG. belihha, MHG., G. belche, 'coot'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:581 COLUMN:3 -->
All these words derive fr. I.-E. base "bhel-, 'to
shine', whence also OI. bhdtam, 'brightness;
forehead', OE. bxl, 'a blazing fire, a funeral
pyre', ME. balled, 'bald'. See hald and cp. words
there referred to. For the second element in
ModL. Phalaropus see -pod.

## phallic
phallic, adj., pertaining to the phallus or to phal-
licism. — Gk. φαλλικός, 'pertaining to the
phallus', fr. φαλλός. See next word and -ic.
Derivatives: phallic-ism, п., phallic-ist, n.

## phallus
phallus, п., an image of the male organ of
generation. — L. phallus, fr. Gk. φαλλός, 'phallus', for
I.-E. *bhl-no·; rel. to φάλλαινα, φάλλη, 'whale',
and cogn. with L.follis (prob. for *bhol-nis), 'a
pair of bellows' (orig. 'leather sack'), fr. I.-E.
base *bhel-, 'to swell', whence also ON. boli,
'bull', OE. bulluc, 'little bull'. See bull, 'male of
•the ox' and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: phallic (q.v.), phall-ism, п., phall-
ist, n.

## Phanar
Phanar, п., name of the Greek quarter in
Constantinople. — Turk. Fanar, fr. ModGk.
Φανάρι, 'lighthouse', fr. Gk. φϊνάριον, 'lantern',
dimin. of φανός, 'torch' (see phantasm); so
called from its lighthouse.

## Phanariot
Phanariot, Phanariote, п., a Greek residing in the
Phanar quarter of Constantinople. — ModGk.
Φαναριώτης, 'inhabitant of the quarter called
Φανάρι'. See prec. wor,d and -ote.

## -phane
-phane, combining form meaning 'having the
appearance of...', as in cellophane, cymophane. —
Gk. -φανής, from the stem of φαίνειν, 'to show',
φαίνεσθαι, 'to appear'. See phantasm and cp.
phanero-,

## phanero-
phanero-, before a vowel phaner-, combining
form meaning 'visible, manifest'. — Gk.
φανερό-, φανερ-, fr. φανερός, 'visible, manifest;
illustrious'. See phantasm and cp. words there
referred to.

## phanerogam
phanerogam, п., a plant bearing flowers (bot.) —
F. phanerogame, compounded of Gk. φανερός,
'visible' and γάμος, 'marriage'. See phanero- and
gamo-.
Derivatives: phanerogam-ic, phanerogam-ous,
adjs.

## phantasm
phantasm, п., illusion, phantom. — ME. fan-
tasme, fr. ΟΈ./antasme, fr. L. phantasma, fr. Gk.
φάντασμα, 'apparition', fr. φαντάζειν, 'to
make visible, display' (whence also φαντασία,
'appearance, imagination'), from the stem of
φαίνειν, 'to make appear, show; to shine',
whence also φανός, 'torch', φανερός, 'visible,
manifest; illustrious'; rel. to φάος, φως, 'light',
fr. I.-E. base "bha-, 'to shine", whence also OI.
bhati, 'shines, glitters', bhas-, 'light, glory', Arm.
banam, Ί open', prop. Ί make visible', Alb.
Gheg baj, Tosk ben, Ί make', lit. Ί make
appear' (both these words derive from the common
Albanian stem 'ban"δ), Olr. ban, 'white; light,
ray of light', but L. fenestra, 'window', is not
cognate. See fancy and cp. phantom, which is a
doublet of phantasm. Cp. also Aphanes, apha-
nite, aphotic, diaphanous, emphasis, hierophant,
paenula, Phaethon, phaeton, Phanar, -phane,
phanero-, -plumy, phenol, phenomenon,
phosphorus, photo-, sycophant.
Derivatives: phantasm-al, adj., phantasm-al-ity,
п., phantasm-al-ly, adv., phantasm-at-ic, phan-
tasm-at-ic-al, adjs., phantasm-at-ic-al-ly, adv.,
phantasm-ic, phantasm-ic-al, adjs.

## phantasmagoria
phantasmagoria, п., a series of optical illusions.
— ModL., fr. F. fantasmagorie, a word coined
by Mercier in 1801 fr. Gk. φάντασμα,
'apparition' and άγορεύειν, 'to speak'; assimilated in
form to F. allegoric See prec. word and agora
and cp. allegory.
Derivatives: phantasmagor-al, adj., phantasma-
gor-al-ly, adv., phantasmagor-ic, phantasmagor-
ic-al, adjs., phantasmagor-ist, п., phantasmagor-
y, n.

## phantasy
phantasy, n. — See fantasy.

## phantom
phantom, п., 1) specter; 2) illusion. — ME. fan-
tome, fantosme, fr. OF. fantosme (F. fantome),
fr. VL. *fantagma, *fantauma (whence also
Provenc. fantauma), fr. Gk. φάντασμα,
'apparition'. See phantasm.
Oerivauves :phantomat-ic,phantom-ic,phantom-
ic-al, adjs., phantom-ist, п., phantom-y, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:582 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 555 | PHILANTHROPE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:582 COLUMN:1 -->
-phany, combining form meaning 'appearance',
as in epiphany. — Gk. -φανία, -φάνεια,
'appearance', fr. φαν-, stem of φαίνειν, 'to make
appear, show'. See phantasm.
Pharaoh, n., title of the k^ngs of ancient Egypt. —
Late L. Pharao, fr. Gk. Φαραώ, fr. Heb. Par'dh,
fr. Egypt, рег-о(з), lit. 'great house'. Cp. faro.
Derivatives: Pharaon-ic, Pharaon-ic-al, adjs.

## Pharisaic
Pharisaic, adj. — Late L. Pharisaicus, fr. Gk.
Φαρισαικός, fr. Φαρισαϊος, 'Pharisee'. See
Pharisee and adj. sun*, -ic.
Derivatives: pharisaic-al, adj., pharisaic-al-ly,
adv., pharisaic-al-ness, a.

## Pharisaism
Pharisaism, n. — ModL. Pharisaismus, fr. Gk.
Φαρισαΐος, 'Pharisee'. See next word and -ism.

## Pharisee
Pharisee, п., a member of a Jewish religious sect
during the two centuries preceding and the
century following the beginning of the Common
Era (Jewish history). — ME. pharise, fr. OF.
pharise (F. pharisien), fr. Late L. Pharisaeus, fr.
Gk. Φαρισαΐος, fr. Aram. perlshayya, emphatic
pi. of ρrrish, 'separated', corresponding to Heb.
parush ; fr. Aram, ρ rash, resp. Heb. par ash, 'he
separated' (whence parSsha11, 'a section of the
Torah'). See parashnh and -ее.

## pharmaceutic
pharmaceutic, adj. — Late L. pharmaceutics, fr.
Gk. φαρμακευτικός, 'relating to drugs', fr. φαρ-
μακευτής, 'druggist', fr. φαρμακεύειν, 'to give
drugs', fr. φάρμακον, 'drug'. See pharmacy and
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: pharmaceut-ics, п.,
pharmaceutical, adj. and п., pharmaceutic-al-ly, adv.

## pharmaceutist
pharmaceutist, п., a pharmacist. — Formed from
prec. word with suff. -ist.

## pharniaco-
pharniaco-, combining form meaning 'drug,
medicine, poison'. — Gk. (ραρμακο-, fr. φάρμακον,
'charm, philter, drug, remedy'. See pharmacy,

## pharmacology
pharmacology, п., the science of drugs. — Lit.
'the study of drugs', fr. pharmaco- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See -logy.
Derivatives: pharmacolog-ic, pharmacolog-ic-al,
adjs., pharmacolog-ic-al-ly, adv.,
pharmacologist, n.

## pharmacopoeia
pharmacopoeia, also spelled pharmacopeia, п., an
official book containing a list of drugs and
directions for their preparation. — Medical L., fr.
Gk. φαρμακοποιία, 'preparation of drugs', fr.
φαρμακοποιός, 'preparing drugs', fr.
φάρμακον, 'drug', and ποιεϊν, 'to make'. See pharmacy
and poet. The name pharmacopoeia was first
used as title of a book by Anutius Foesius (1528-
95) of Basel.
Derivatives: pharmacopoei-al, pharmacopoei-an,
adjs., pharmacopoe-ist, n.

## pharmacy
pharmacy, п., the art of preparing and dispensing
drugs. — ME. farmacie, fr. MF. (= F.) phar-
made, fr. Late L. pharmacia, fr. Gk.
φαρμακεία, 'use of drugs', fr. φαρμακεύειν, 'to
administer drugs', fr. φάρμακον, 'medicine, drug,
remedy; poison; philter; charm, spell,
enchantment', which is perh. cogn. with Lith. buriu,

## bitrti
bitrti, 'to charm', Lett, bur'u, hurt, of s.m. Cp.
the second element in alexipharmic.
Derivative: pharmac-ist, n.

## pharos
pharos, п., lighthouse, beacon. — L„ fr. Gk.
φάρος. fr. Φάρος, name of an island off
Alexandria, on which King Ptolemy Philadelphus built
a lighthouse.

## pharyng-
pharyng-, form of pharyngo- before a vowel.

## pharyngal
pharyngal, adj., pharyngeal. — Formed with adj.

## suff. -al fr. ModL. pharynx. See pharynx
suff. -al fr. ModL. pharynx. See pharynx,

## pharyngeal
pharyngeal, adj., pertaining to the pharynx. —

## Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. ModL. pharyngeus
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. ModL. pharyngeus,
'pertaining to the pharynx', fr. pharynx. See
pharynx.

## pharyngitis
pharyngitis, п., inflammation of the pharynx
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. Gk. φάρυγξ
(see pharynx) with suff. -iris,

## pharyngo-
pharyngo-, before a vowel pharyng-, combining
form denoting the pharynx. — See pharynx,

## pharyngology
pharyngology, п., the study of the pharynx and its
diseases (med.) — Compounded of pharyngo-
and Gk. -λογίϊ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in
a certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: pharyngolog-ic-al, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:582 COLUMN:2 -->

## pharyngoscope
pharyngoscope, п., an instrument for examining
the pharynx. — Compounded of phnryngo- and
Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΤν, 'to look at, examine'.
See -scope.
Derivative: pharyngoscop-y, n.

## pharynx
pharynx, п., the part of the alimentary canal
between the palate and the esophagus — ModL.,
fr. Gk. φάρυγξ, gen. φάρυγγος, 'throat, chasm,
gulf, which is rel. to φάραγξ, 'cleft, chasm', and
cogn. with L. frumen (for *frug-smen or, less
prob., *frug-men), 'throat'. Arm. erbuc, 'breast;
thorax', ON. barki, 'neck, throat, windpipe', fr.
I.-E. base "bher-, 'to cut'. See bore, 'to pierce',
and cp. foramen. See also larynx,

## phase
phase, п., 1) each of the aspects of the moon or a
planet; 2) aspect; 3) stage of change. — Back
formation fr. phases, pi. of ModL. phasis, fr. Gk.
φάσις, 'appearance, (of a star), phase (of the
moon)', from the stem of φαίνειν, 'to make
appear, show',cpaivEO&atl'to appear'.See phantasm.

## Phaseolus
Phaseolus, п., a genus of plants, the kidney bean
(bot.) — L., 'kidney bean', fr. phaselus, of s.m.,
fr. Gk. φάσηλος, 'a kind of bean'. Cp. φακή,
φακός, 'bean'. Ср. also frijole.

## -phasia
-phasia, -phasy, combining form meaning
'speech'. — ModL. -phasia, fr. Gk. φάσις, 'a
saying, speech', from φα-, the stem of φημί,
φάναι, 'to speak'. See -phemia.

## phasianid
phasianid, п., a bird belonging to the family
Phasianidae. — See next word and -id.

## Phasianidae
Phasianidae, n. pi., a family of birds, the
pheasants (ornithol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-idae fr. L. phasianus, 'pheasant'. See pheasant.

## phasis
phasis, п., a phase. — ModL., fr. Gk. φάσις. See
phase.
Derivative: phas-ic, adj.

## pheasant
pheasant, n. — ME. fesant, fr. OF. (= F.)faisan,
fr. L. phasianus, fr. Gk. φασιανός (sell, 8ρνις),
lit. 'the Phasian bird', fr. Φϊσις, 'the Phasis', a
river in Colchis. The -(in pheasant is excrescent;
it is due to a confusion of the ending -an with
-ant, the suff. of the pres. part, of verbs
pertaining to the 1st Latin conjugation. Cp. peasant,
tyrant.
Derivative: pheasant-ry, n.

## Phegopteris
Phegopteris, n.\ a genus of plants, the beech fern
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. φηγός,
'oak' (taken in the sense of its L. cognate fagus,
'beech'), and πτέρις, 'fern'. For the first element
see beech and cp. Epiphegus, for the second see
Pteris.

## phello-
phello-, before a vowel phell-, combining form
meaning 'cork, bark', as in phellogen. — Gk.
φελλό-, φελλ-, fr. φελλός, 'cork tree, cork',
which is rel. to φλοιός, φλόος, 'the inner bark
of trees', φλέω, Ί teem, abound', φλύω, Ί boil
over, bubble, rise', φλύζω, Ί bubble', φλυκτίς,
φλύκταινα, 'blister', φλέψ, gen. φλεβός, 'vein'
and cogn. with L.fluere, 'to flow'. See fluent and
cp. phlebo-, Phleum, phloem, phlyctena, the first
element in phlobaphene and in phlorizin and the
second element in Conopholis. Cp. also blain,
bloat, blot, 'blackgammon', and the second
element in pantoffie.

## phelloderm
phelloderm, п., a layer of tissue developed on the
inner side of the cork (bot.) — Compounded of
phello- and Gk. Κέρμα, 'skin'. See derma.
Derivative: phelloderm-al, adj.

## phellogen
phellogen, п., the meristematic tissue out of which
cork is developed. — Lit. 'cork
producer';compounded of phello- and -gen.
Derivatives: phellogen-etic, phellogen-ic, adjs.

## -phemia
-phemia, combining form denoting 'speech' (med.)
— Gk. -φημίϊ, fr. φήμη, 'speech', from the
stem of φημί, Ί speak', which is cogn. with L.

## furl
furl, 'to speak', fama, 'report, reputation'. See
fame and cp. -phasia.

## phen-
phen-, form of pheno-, before a vowel.

## phenacetin
phenacetin, phenacetme, п., a crystalline
compound, used in medicine as an antipyretic. — See
phen-, acetic and chem. suff. -in, resp. -ine.

## phenacite
phenacite, п., a silicate of glucinum (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff.-ite fr. Gk. φένϊξ, gen.
φένακος, 'cheat, impostor', which is of
uncertain origin; so called because it was mistaken
for quartz.

## Phenician
Phenician, adj. and n. — A var. of Phoenician.

## Phenix
Phenix, n. — A var. of Phoenix.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:582 COLUMN:3 -->

## pheno-
pheno-, also spelled phaeno-, before a vowel phen-,
resp. phaen-, combining form meaning
'pertaining to, or derived from, benzene' (chem.) —
F. pheno-, phen-, fr. Gk. φαίνειν, 'to make
appear, show; to shine' (see phantasm); first used
by the French chemist Auguste Laurent (1807-
53) to indicate derivation from coal tar. Cp. next
word.

## phenol
phenol, п., a crystalline compound commonly
called carbolic acid (chem.) — A hybrid coined
fr. Gk. φαίνειν, 'to make appear, show; to
shine' (see pheno-), and -ol. The name phenol is
a modification of F. acide phenique, a name
given to this compound by the French chemist
Auguste Laurent (1807-53) in 1841.
Derivatives: phenol-ate, n. and tr. v.,phenol-ic,
adj., phenol-ize, tr, v., phenol-iz-aiion, n.

## phenological
phenological, adj., pertaining to the study of the
relation of the forms of organisms to their
environment. — G. phdnologisch, coined by C.
Fritsch in 1853 fr. Gk. φαινο- (fr. φαίνειν, 'to
make appear, to show'), -λογία (fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)', and suff. -isch. See
phantasy, -logy and -ical.
Derivative: phenological-ly, adv.

## phenology
phenology, n. — See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ίϊ).
Derivatives: phenolog-ic-al, adj., phenolog-ist, n.

## phenomenal
phenomenal, adj. — A hybrid coined by the
English poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772-
1834) fr. phenomenon and suff. -al (fr. L. -alis).
Derivatives: phenomenal-ism, п., phenomenal-
ist, п., phenomenal-ist-ic, adj., phenomenal-ist-ic-
al-ly, adv., phenomenal-ity, п., phenomenal-ize,
tr. v., phenomenal-iz-ation, п., phenomenal-ly,
adv.

## phenomenology
phenomenology, п., the scientific study of
phenomena. — G. Phanomenologie, first used as the title
of the fourth part of the Neues Organnn by the
German physicist Johann Heinrich Lambert
(1728-77) coined fr. Gk. φαινόμενον (see next
word) and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks
(in a certain mariner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: phenomenolog-ic-al, adj., phenom-
enolog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## phenomenon
phenomenon, п., 1) fact, circumstance or
experience; 2) a remarkable thing or person. — Late
L. phaenomenon, fr. Gk. φαινόμενον, neut. of
φαινόμενος, pres. part, of φαίνεσθαι, 'to
appear', passive of φαίνειν,'to make appear, show'.
See phantasm. For the Greek pass. suff. -μένος
see alumnus and cp. words there referred to.

## phenotype
phenotype, п., a type distinguished by visiblechar-
acters. — Compounded of pheno- and type, n.
Derivatives: phenotyp-ic, phenotyp-ic-al, adjs.,

## phenotyp-ic-al-ly
phenotyp-ic-al-ly, adv.

## phenyl
phenyl, п., the radical basis of phenol (chem.) —
Coined fr. phen- and -yl.
Derivatives: phenyl-ate, п., and tr. v., phenyl-
ation, п., phenyl-ene, n.

## pheon
pheon, п., arrowhead (her.)—Of unknown origin.

## phew
phew, inter/., exclamation of disgust. —
Imitative.

## phial
phial, п., a small glass bottle. — ME. fiole, fr. OF.

## fiole
fiole, phiole, fr. L. phiala, fr. Gk. φιάλη, 'broad,
flat bowl', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. vial,

## phialine
phialine, adj., resembling a phial. — See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ine.

## phil-
phil-, pref. — Form of philo- before a vowel.
-phi], suff. — The same as -phile.

## Philadelphus
Philadelphus, п., a genus of plants, the mock
orange or syringa (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φιλ-
άδελφον, 'mock orange', prop. neut. of the adj.
φιλάδελφος, 'loving one's brother; brotherly', fr.
φίλος, 'loving', and αδελφός, 'brother'. See
philo- and adelpho-.

## philander
philander, intr. v., to make love. — Fr. obsol. n.

## philander
philander, 'philanderer', fr. Gk. φίλανδρος,
'lover of men', which is compounded of Gk.
φίλος, 'beloved, loving', and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός,
'man'. See philo- and andro-.
Derivative: philander-er, n.

## philanthrope
philanthrope, п., a philanthropist. — F., fr. Gk.
φιλάνθρωπος, 'loving mankind, humane,

## benevolent
benevolent, kind-hearted', compounded of φίλος,
'loving' and άνθρωπος, 'man'. See philo- and
