<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PHILANTHROPIC | 556 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:583 COLUMN:1 -->
anthropo-.
Derivatives: philanthropic (q.v.), philanthrop-
ism, п., philanthrop-ist, п., pki/anthrop-ize, tr.
and intr. v., philanthropy (q.v.)

## philanthropic
philanthropic, also philanthropical, adj. — F. phi-
lanthropique, fr. Gk. φιλάνθρωπος. See prec.
word.
Derivative: philanthropical-ly, adv.

## philanthropy
philanthropy, n. — Late L. philanthropic., fr. Gk.
φιλανθρωπία, 'love to mankind, humanity,
benevolence,kind-heartedness',fr.9^av*p(imoi.
See philanthrope and -y (representing Gk. -is).

## philately
philately, п., collection of stamps. — F. philatelic,
fr. phil- and Gk. ατέλεια, 'exemption from
taxes', fr. ατελής, 'free from taxes', which is
formed fr. ά- (see priv. pref. -a) and τέλος, 'end,
completion, authority, tax, duty' (see tele-); so
called because the postage stamp exempted the
sender from paying taxes.
Derivatives: philatel-ic, philatel-ic-al, adjs.,
philatel-ic-al-ly, adv., philatel-ist, n.

## Philathea
Philathea, п., international organization of young
women's Bible classes. — Lit. 'lovers of the
truth', incorrectly formed fr. Gk. φιλεΐν, 'to
love', and αλήθεια, 'truth'. See philo- and
aletho-. The correct form would be Philalethea.

## -phile
-phile, before a vowel -phi], combining form
meaning 'loving', as in bibliophile). — F. -phile,
fr. ML. -philus, fr. Gk. -φίλος, fr. φίλος,
'beloved; loving'. See philo-.

## Philemon
Philemon, masc. PN-, a pious man, husband of
Baucis (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Φιλήμων,
lit. 'loving, affectionate', fr. φιλεΐν, 'to love'. See
philo-.

## philharmonic
philharmonic, adj., loving music. — F. philhar-
monique, fr. It. filarmonico, fr. fil-, 'phil-', and
armonico, fr. Gk. (τα) αρμονικά, 'theory of
music', neut. pi. of αρμονικός, 'harmonious'.
See phil- and harmonic.

## Philhellene
Philhellene, adj., loving the Greeks; п., one
loving the Greeks. — Gk. φιλέλλην, 'pne loving
the Greeks', compounded of φίλος, 'loving', and
Έλλην, 'Hellene'. See philo- and Hellenic.
Derivatives: Philhellen-ic, adj., Philhellen-ism,
п., Philhellen-ist, n.

## Philip
Philip, masc. PN. — L. Philippus, fr. Gk.
Φίλιππος, fr. φίλιππος, 'fond of horses',
compounded of φίλος, 'beloved; loving', and Ιππος,
'horse'. See philo- and hippo- and cp. philippic
and the second element in Xanthippe.

## Philippa
Philippa, fern. PN. — Modern formation fr.
Philip.

## philippic
philippic, п., invective speech. — Fr. L. Philippi-
cus, fr. Gk. Φιλιππικός, 'relating to Philip', fr.
Φίλιππος, 'Philip'; so called with allusion to the
orations of Demosthenes against Philip of Ma-
cedon. See Philip and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: philippic-ize, intr. v.

## Philippine
Philippine, also Philippine, п., the nameof a game.
— See philopena.

## Philippine
Philippine, adj., of the Philippine Islands. —
Formed fr. Sp. (Islas) Filipinos, lit. 'the islands
of Philip'; named after Philipp II, king of Spain.
For the ending see adj. suff. -ine.

## Philistia
Philistia, п., the land of the Philistines. — ML.,
fr. Gk. ΦιλιστΙα, Гг. Heb. PeUsheth. See
Philistine and 1st -ia.

## Philistine
Philistine, n. — F. Philistin, fr. Late L. Philistini
(pi.), fr. Gk. Φιλιστϊνοι (see Josephus,
Antiquities, I, 6, 2), fr. Heb. Pllishtfm, it. Pelesheth,
'Philistia, land of the Philistines'; cp. Akkad.
Palastu, Ptlistu. In the sense 'narrow-minded,
uncultured person' the word Philistine was
adapted by Thomas Carlyle (1795-1881) fr. G.
Philister.
Derivatives: Philistine, adj., Philistin-ism, n.

## philo-
philo-, before a vowel phil-, combining form
meaning 'loving, fond of, interested in', as in
philosopher. — Gk. φίλο-, φιλ-, fr. φίλος,
'loved, beloved, dear', as a noun, 'friend'; later,
in poetry, also used in an active sense, 'loving,
friendly', whence φιλεΐν, 'to love'; of uncertain
origin. Cp. philander, Philemon, philter, syphilis.

## Philoctetes
Philoctetes, п., a famous archer, who killed Paris
in the Trojan war with one of the poisoned
arrows given him by Hercules (Greek mythol) —
L. Philoctetes, fr. Gk. Φιλοκτήτης, lit. 'he who
loves to possess', fr. φίλο^, 'beloved; lover', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:583 COLUMN:2 -->
κτάομαι, Ί get, acquire'. See philo- and check,
'sudden, stop'.

## Philodendron
Philodendron, п., a genus of plants of the arum
family; (not cap.), any plant of the genus
Philodendron (bot.) — ModL., compounded of philo-
and Gk. δέν8ρον, 'tree'. See dendro-.

## philogynist
philogynist, п., a lover of women. — Formed with
suff. -ist fr. Gk. φιλαγύνης, 'fond of women',
which is compounded of φίλος, 'beloved;
loving', and γυνή, 'woman'. See philo- and
gyneco-.

## philogyny
philogyny, п., love of women. — Gk. φιλογυνία,
fr. φιλογύνης. See prec. word and -y (repre-^
senting Gk. -ία).

## philologue
philologue,п., a philologist. — MF. (= F), fr. L.
phitologus, Ίο ver of learning', fr. Gk. φιλόλογος.
See next word.

## philology
philology, n. — F. philologie, fr. L. philologia,
'love of learning, love of letters', fr. Gk.
φιλολογία, fr. φιλόλογος, 'fond of learning', which
is compounded of φίλος, 'beloved, loving',
and -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
philo- and -logy.
Derivatives: philolog-er, п., philolog-ian, п.,
philolog-ic, philolog-ic-al, adjs.,philolog-ic-al-ly,
Siav.,philolog-ist,a.,philolog-ist-ic,Siaj.,philolog-
ize, tr. and intr. v.

## Philnmachus
Philnmachus, п., a genus of birds, the ruff (orni-
thi'.); synonym of Machefes. — ModL.,
compounded of philo- and the stem of Gk. μά-
χειϊαι, 'to fight'. See -machy and cp. Machetes.

## philomath
philomath, п., a lover of learning (rare). — Gk.
φιλομαθής, 'fond of learning', compounded of
φίλος, 'loving', and μάθη, 'learning', from the
stem of μανθάνειν, 'to learn'. See philo- and
mathematical.

## philomathy
philomathy, п., love of learning. — Gk.
φιλομάθεια, φιλομαθία, 'love of learning',
^..φιλομαθής, 'fond of learning'. Seeprec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -εια, Λα.).
Derivatives: philomath-ic, philomath-ic-al, adjs.

## philomel
philomel, п., the nightingale (poet.) — F. philo- ·
mile. See next word.

## Philomela
Philomela, п., the nightingale (poet.) — L., ft.
Gk. Φιλομήλα, Φιλομήλη, the name of Pan-
dion's daughter in Greek mythology, who,
according to Ovid, was changed into a nightingale.
The name prob. means 'lover of song' and is
compounded of φίλος, 'loving' and the
lengthened form of μέλος, 'song'. See philo- and
melic.

## philopena
philopena, also phiHppina, Philippine, п., the name
of a game. — Corruption of philippina, fr. F.
Philippine, altered from Valentine. The meaning
of the noun phiiippina-philopena arose from the
custom, of sending sweethearts a nut with a
double kernel on Valentine's day (= February
14th). In German, Philippine was transformed
into Philippchen, 'little Philip' and this further
into Vielliebchen, lit. 'much loved'. See valentine.

## philosopher
philosopher, n. — ME. philosophre, filosofre, fr.
OF. (= F'.) philosophe, fr. L. philosophus, fr. Gk.
φιλόσοφος, 'lover of wisdom, philosopher', fr.
φίλος, 'loving', and σόφος, 'wise, learned'; see
philo-, sophism and -er. Pythagoras was the first
who called himself φιλόσοφος, instead of
σοφός, 'wise man', since this latter term was
suggestive of immodesty.

## philosophic
philosophic, philosophical, adj. — L. philosophical,
fr. Gk. φιλοσοφικός, fr. φιλοσοφία, 'philosophy'.
See philosophy and -ic, resp. also -al.

## pbilosophism
pbilosophism, п., sophistry. — F. philosophisme,
formed fr. philosophic with suff. -isme. See
philosophy and -ism and cp. sophism.
philosophise п., a sophist. — F. philosophiste,
formed fr. philosophic with suff. -iste. See
philosophy and -ist and cp. prec. word.

## philosophize
philosophize, intr. v. — See philosophy and -ize.
Derivative: philosophiz-ation, n.

## philosophy
philosophy, n. — ME. philosophic, fr. OF.
philosophic, filosofie(V. philosophic), fr. ~L.philosophia,
fr. Gk. φιλοσοφία, 'love of wisdom,
philosophy', fr. φιλόσοφος, 'lover of. wisdom,
philosopher'. See philosopher and -y (representing Gk.
-ία).
Derivatives: philosoph-ize, intr. v.,philosoph-iz-
ation, п., philosoph-iz-er, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:583 COLUMN:3 -->

## -philous
-philous, combining form meaning 'fond of, as in
ammophilous, entomophilous. — Gk. -φίλος, fr.
φίλος, 'beloved; loving'. See philo- and suff. -ous.

## philter
philter, philtre, п., love potion. — MF. (= F.)
philtre, fr. L. philtrum, fr. Gk. φίλτρον, 'love
charm', lit. 'a means to make oneself beloved',
formed fr. φιλεΐν, 'to love', with -τρον, a suff.
denoting instrument. See philo-.
Derivatives: philter, philtre, tr. v., philter-er, n.

## philtrum
philtrum, п., a dimple in the middle of the upper
lip (anal.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. φίλτρον,
'love charm; dimple in the upper lip'. See prec.
word.

## phit
phit, interj. — Imitative of the sound of a bullet.

## phiz
phiz, n. — Abbreviation of physiognomy,

## phleb-
phleb-, form of phlebo- before a vowel.

## phlebitis
phlebitis, п., inflammation of a vein (mea.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. φλέψ, gen. φλεβός, 'vein'.
See next word and -iris.
Derivative: phlebit-ic, adj.

## phlebo-
phlebo-, combining form meaning 'vein'. — Gk.
φλεβο-, fr. φλέψ, gen. φλεβός, 'vein', which is
rel. to φλέω, Ί teem, abound', φλύω, Ί boil over,
bubble, rise', φελλός, 'cork tree, cork'. See
phello-.

## phlebotomy
phlebotomy, п., bloodletting. — ME. flebotomye,
fr. OF. flebotomie (F. phlebotomie), ft. Medical
L. phlebotomia, fr. Gk. φλεβοτομία,
'bloodletting', fr. φλεβοτόμος, 'opening veins', which
is compounded of φλέψ, gen. φλεβός, 'vein', and
-τομίϊ, 'cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See
phlebo- and -tomy and cp. fleam.
Derivatives: phlebotom-ic,phlebotom-ic-al, adjs.,
phlebotom-ic-al-ly, adv., phlebotom-ist, п., phle-
botom-ize, tr. and intr. v., phlebotom-iz-ation, a.

## Phiegethon
Phiegethon, п., one of the rivers of Hades,
containing fire (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Φλε-
γέθων, lit. 'the blazing (river)', pres. part, of
φλεγέθειν, 'to burn, scorch, blaze up', poetic
collateral form of φλέγειν. See next word,

## phlegm
phlegm, п., 1) mucus; 2) apathy; 3) coolness,
calmness. — ME. fleume, fleme, fr. fteume (F.
flegtne), fr. Late L. phlegma, fr. Gk. φλέγμα,
'inflammation', fr. φλέγειν, 'to burn, scorch,
kindle', which is rel. to φλόξ, gen. φλογός,
'flame, blaze'; fr. I.-E. base "bhleg-, *bhelg-, 'to
burn, be hot', whence also OI. bhrajate, 'shines',
L. fulgere, 'to shine', fulgur, fulmen, 'lightning',
flagrare, 'to burn', OE. blsec, 'black'. See black
and words there referred to and cp. esp. Phle-
getlion, phlegmon, phlogiston, Phlox. For the
sufT. -m (fr. Gk. -μα) see -m and -ma.
Derivative: phlegm-y, adj.

## phlegmatic
phlegmatic, adj. — ME. fleumatike, fr. OF. fleu-
matique (F. flegmatique), fr. Late L.
phlegmonous, fr. Gk. φλεγματικός, 'abounding in
phlegm', fr. φλέγμα, gen. φλέγματος. See
phlegm and 1st -atit.
Derivatives: phlegmatical-ly, adv.,
phlegmatism, п., phlegmat-ist, п., phlegmat-ou's, adj.

## phlegmon
phlegmon, п., suppurative inflammation of the
connective tissue (med.) — L. phlegmon, phleg-
топё, 'inflammation beneath the skin', fr. Gk.
φλέγμων, resp. φλεγμονή, fr. φλέγειν, 'to burn'.
See phlegm.
Derivatives: phlegmon-ic, phlegmon-ous, adjs.

## Phleum
Phleum, п., a genus of grasses (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. φλέως, 'wool-tufted reed', which is rel.
to φλέω, Ί teem, abound'. See phloem,

## phlohaphene
phlohaphene, п., a reddish substance obtained
from tannin (chem.) — Compounded of Gk.
φλόος, 'bark', and βαφή, 'dipping, dyeing, dye'.
For the first element see phello- and cp. next
word. The second element-is rel. to βάπτειν, 'to
dip'; see baptism.
Derivative: phlobaphen-ic, adj.

## phloem
phloem, п., bast tissue in plants (bot) — G.

## Phloem
Phloem, coined by the botanist Karl Wilhelm
von Nageli (1817-91) fr. Gk. φλόος, 'bark',
which is rel. to φλέω, Ί teem, abound', φλύω,
Ί boil over, bubble, rise', φελλός, 'cork tree,
cork*. See phello-.

## phlogistic
phlogistic, adj., inflammatory (med.) — ModL.

## phlogisticus
phlogisticus, fr. phlogiston. See next word and
-ic and cp. dephlogisticate.
Derivatives: phlogistic-ate, tr. v., phlogistic-

## ation
ation, n.

## phlogiston
phlogiston, п., the inflammatory principle. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:584 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 557 | PHOSPHDRO- -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:584 COLUMN:1 -->
ModL., fr. Gk. φλαγιστόν, neut. of φλογιστός,
'burnt up; inflammable', fr. φλογίζειν, 'to set
on fire, burn', fr. φλόξ, gen φλογός, 'flame,
blaze'. See Phlox. The term phlogiston was first
used by Raphael Eglin (1559-1622).

## phlogopite
phlogopite, п., a brownish magnesium mica
(mineral.) — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr.
Gk. φλογωπός, 'fiery-looking', which is
compounded of φλόξ, gen. φλογός, 'flame, blaze',
and ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye'. See phlox and -opia.

## phlogosis
phlogosis, п., inflammation (med.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. Gk. φλόξ, gen. φλογός, 'flame, blaze'
(see Phlox), with suff. -osis.

## Phlomis
Phlomis, п., a genus of plants, the Jerusalem sage
(boi.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φλομίς, which is rel. to
φλόμος, 'mullein'.

## phloro-
phloro-, before a vowel phlor-, related to phlorizin.
— F., from next word.

## phlorizin
phlorizin, п., a bitter substance contained in the
bark of roots of the apple, pear, plum and
herrytree (chem.) — Compounded of Gk. φλόος,
'bark', and όίζα, 'root'. See phello-,rizo-and -in.
Derivative: phlorizin-ize, tr. v.

## Phlox
Phlox, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — L., name of
a flower, fr. Gk. φλόξ, gen. φλογός, 'flame;
•name of a plant', which is rel. to φλέγειν, 'to
burn', φλέγμα, 'inflammation'. See phlegm.

## phlyctena
phlyctena, phiyctaena, п., a pustule (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. φλύκταινα, 'blister (caused
by a burn) inflammation', which is rel. Ιοφλύειν,
'to boil over, bubble, ι^β',φλύζειν, 'to bubble',
φελλός, 'cork tree, cork'. See phello-.

## -phobe
-phobe, combining form meaning 'fearing', as in
Francophobe, Germanophobe. — F., fr. L. -pho-
bus, fr. Gk. -φόβος, fr. φόβος, 'panic flight;
panic fear; fear, terror', which stands in grada-
tional relationship to φέβεσθαι, 'to be put to
flight, to flee in terror; to fear', and is cogn.
with Lith. begu, bigli, 'to flee', OSlav. begu,
'flight', bizati, 'to flee, run'.

## -phobia
-phobia, combining form meaning 'irrational fear
of something', as in agoraphobia, claustrophobia
(psycho!, and med.) — Gk. -φοβία, 'panic fear
of, fear of, fr. φόβος. See -phobe and 1st -ia.

## phobia
phobia, п., an irrational fear. — Fr. prec.
combining form.

## phobiology
phobiology, п., the study of phobias. — Coined
fr. phobia and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## phoca
phoca, п., a seal; (cap.) a genus of seals, the
harbor seal. — L. phoca, fr. Gk. φώκη, 'a seal',
which is of uncertain origin.

## Phoebe
Phoebe, п., 1) Artemis, the goddess of the moon
(Greek mythol.); 2) fern. PN. — L., fr. Gk.
Φοίβη, prop. fern, of φοϊβος, 'pure, bright'. See
Phoebus.

## phoehe
phoehe, п., any of certain flycatchers. —
Imitative of its sound; influenced in form by prec.
word.

## Phoebus
Phoebus, п., Apollo (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Φοίβος, fr. φοϊβος, 'pure, bright', which is of
uncertain etymology.

## Phoenician
Phoenician, Phenician, adj. and. n. — ME.
phenicien, fr. MF. (= F.) phenicien, fr. L.
Phoenice (also Phoenicia), fr. Gk. Φανΐκη,
prob. meaning lit. 'land of purple', fr. φοίνιξ,
gen. φοίνικος. See next word and cp. Punic.
For the ending see suff. -an.

## phoenix
phoenix, phenix, n. — ME. fenix, fr. OF., fr. L.
phoenix, fr. Gk, φοίνιξ, 'purple, crimson; date-
palm, date; a fabulous bird, the phoenix', rel.
to φοινός, 'bloodred', φοίνιος, of s.m., φόνος
(for *gy"honos), 'murder', Φείνειν (for *g"hen-
yeiri), 'to strike' and cogn. with L. dl-fendere, 'to
ward off, defend, protect'. See defend,

## phonate
phonate, intr. v., to produce vocal sounds. — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. φωνή, 'voice, sound' (see
next word), and -ate, a suff. of Latin origin.
Derivatives: phonat-ion, п., phonat-ory, adj.

## phone
phone, п., speech sound. — Gk. φωνή, 'sound,
voice', in gradational relationship to φημί,φάναι,
'to speak', φήμη, 'voice, report, rumor', fr.
l.-E. base *bha-, 'to speak, tell, say', whence
also L. for, fari, 'to speak', fama, 'talk, report,
rumor, tradition, reputation', lit. 'a saying'. See
fame and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
phoneme, phonetic, euphony, symphony,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:584 COLUMN:2 -->
cacophony.
Derivative: phon-al, adj.

## phone
phone, n. (colloq.) — Abbreviation of telephone.

## -phone
-phone, combining form meaning 'voice', as in
megaphone, microphone, telephone. — Fr. Gk.
φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See phone, 'speech sound'.

## phoneme
phoneme, п., a distinctive sound or group of
sounds. — F. phoneme, fr. Gk. φώνημα, 'sound,
utterance', fr. φωνή. See phone, 'speech sound',
and cp. the second element in grapheme, hyph-
eme, semanteme, solideme, morpheme.
Derivative: phonem-ic, adj.

## phonendoscope
phonendoscope, п., an intensifying stethoscope.
— Compounded of Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice',
ένδον, 'within', and -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to
look at, examine'. See phone, 'speech sound',
endo- and -scope.

## phonetic
phonetic, adj. — ModL.phoneticus, fr. Gk.
φωνητικός, 'vocal', fr. φωνητός, 'utterable', verbal
adj. of φωνεϊν, 'to speak clearly, utter', fr. φωνή,
'sound, voice'. See phone, 'speech sound'.
Derivatives: phonetic, n.,phonet-ics, п.,phonet-
ic-at, adj., phone tic-al-ly, adv., phonetic-ian,
п., phonetic-ism., п., phonetic-ist, п.,
phoneticize, tr. v., phonetic-iz-ation, n.

## phonetism
phonetism, п., the use of a phonetic system of,
writing or spelling — See phonetic and -ism.

## phonetist
phonetist, п., an advocate of phonetic spelling. —
See phonetic and -ist.

## phoney
phoney, adj. — A var. of phony.

## phoniatrics
phoniatrics, п., the treatment of speech defects
(med.) — Lit. 'the healing of voice', fr. Gk.
φωνή, 'sound, voice', and Ιατρική (scil. τέχνη),
'surgery, medicine'. See phone, 'speech sound',
and -intrics.

## phonic
phonic, adj., pertaining to sound. — Formed
with adj. surf, -ic fr. Gk. φωνο-, 'sound, voice'.
See phone, 'speech sound'.
Derivatives: phonic, п., phonics, n.

## phono-
phono-, combining form meaning 'sound, voice'.
— Gk. φωνο-, fr. φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See
phone, 'speech sound'.

## phonodeik
phonodeik, п., an instrument for transforming
sound waves into light waves. — Lit. 'showing
sounds', fr. Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice*, and
δεικνύναι, 'to show', which is cogn. with L.
dicere, 'to show, tell'. See phone, 'speech sound',
and diction.

## phonogram
phonogram, n. — Compounded of phono- and
Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written'. See -gram.
Derivatives: phonogram(m)-ic, adj., phono-
gram(m)-ic-al-ly, adv.

## phonograph
phonograph, n. — Lit. 'writer of sounds',
compounded of phono- and Gk. -γράφος, from the
stem of γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph and cp.
gramophone.
Derivative: phonograph, tr. v.

## phonography
phonography, n. — Compounded of phono- and
Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: phonograph-ic, adj.,phonograph-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## phonollte
phonollte, п., a grayish volcanic rock (mineral.) —
Lit. 'sounding stone', compounded of phono-
and -lite.
Derivative: phonolit-ic, adj.

## phonology
phonology, n. — Lit. 'the study of sounds',
compounded of phono and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: phonolog-ic, phonolog-ic-al, adjs.,
phonolog-ic-al-ly, adv., phonolog-ist, n.

## phonophore
phonophore, п., a device for sending telephonic
messages simultaneously with telegrams. — Lit.
'carrying sounds', compounded of phono- and
Gk. -φόρος, 'bearer, carrier'. See -phore.
Derivative: phonophor-ic, adj.

## phonopore
phonopore, п., a phonophore. — Compounded of
phono- and Gk. πόρος, 'passage'. See pore.

## phonoscope
phonoscope, п., an instrument for observing the
properties of sounding bodies. — Compounded
of phono- and Gk. -σκόττιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to
look at, examine'. See -scope.

## phonotype
phonotype, n.—Prop.phonetic type, compounded
of phono- and -type.
Derivatives: phonotype, tr. v., phonotyp-er, п.,

## phonotyp-ic
phonotyp-ic, phonotyp-ic-al, adjs., phonotyp-ic-
al-Iy, adv., phonotyp-ist, n.

## phony
phony, phoney, adj., not genuine (coll.) — Of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:584 COLUMN:3 -->
uncertain origin.
Derivative: phony, n.

## -phony
-phony, also -phonia, combining form denoting a
specified kind of sound, as in acrophony. — Gk.
-φωνία, fr. φωνή, 'sound, voice, speech'. See
phone, 'speech sound'.

## phoongy
phoongy, n. — See poongee.

## Phoradendron
Phoradendron, п., a genus of plants, the false
mistletoe (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
φώρ, 'thief, and δένδρον, 'tree'; so called in
allusion to its parasitic habit. The first element is
cogn. with L. fur, 'thief; see furtive. For the
second element see dendro-,

## -phore
-phore, combining form meaning 'bearer', as in
chromatophore, thermophore. — ModL. -phorus
(masc), -phorum (neut.), ft. Gk. -φόρος, resp.
-φόρον, 'bearing, carrying', or 'bearer, carrier',
rel. to φέρειν, 'to bear, carry'. See bear, 'to
carry', and cp. -phorous.

## phoresis
phoresis, п., the movement of particles through a
membrane by the action of an electric current
(physical chem.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φόρησις, 'a
bearing, wearing', fr. φορεϊν, Ίο bear, wear',
which is rel. to φέρειν. See prec. word.

## phoresy
phoresy, п., transportation of an animal by its
attachment to another. — Gk. φόρηρις, 'a bearing,
a being borne'. See>prec. word.

## Phormium
Phormium, п., a genus of liliaceous plants (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. φορμίον, 'a woven or plaited
mat; name of a plant', dimin. of φορμός, 'mat',
which is prob. rel. to φέρειν, 'to bear.carry'. See
-phore.

## phorone
phorone, п., the name of an isomeric compound
(chem.) — Coined by the French chemist
Charles Frederic Gerhardt (1816-56) from the
contraction of (cam)phor (ket)one.

## -phorous
-phorous, combining form meaning 'bearing', as
in cryophorous, oophorous. — ModL. -phorus, fr.
Gk. -φόρος, 'bearing'. See -phore.

## phosgene
phosgene, п., a colorless gas, COClj (chem.) —
Coined by the English chemist Sir Humphrey
Davy (1778-1829) in 1812 fr. Gk. φως, 'light',
and -γενής, 'bom of, produced by'. See
phosphorus and -gen.

## phosgeulte
phosgeulte, n. (mineral.) — Formed from prec.
word with subst. suff. -ite.

## phosph-
phosph-, form of phospho- before a vowel.

## phosphate
phosphate, п., a salt of phosphoric acid (chem.) —
See phospho- and chem. surf. -ate.
Derivatives: phosphat-ed, phosphat-ic, adjs.,
phosphat-ize, tr. v., phosphat-iz-ation, n.

## phosphene
phosphene, п., a luminous image produced by
mechanical stimulation of the retina. — Lit.
'that which shows the light', compounded of
Gk. φως, 'light', and the stem of φαίνειν, 'to
show'. See phosphorus and phantasm.

## phosphide
phosphide, phosphid,n., compound of phosphorus
with another element (chem.) — See phospho-
and -ide, resp. -id.

## phosphine
phosphine, phosphin, п., hydrogen phosphide,
PH, (chem.) — See phospho- and chem. suff.
-ine.
Derivatives: phosphin-ate, п., phosphin-ic, adj.

## phosphite
phosphite, п., salt of phosphorous acid (chem.) —
See next word and subst. suff. -ite.

## phospho-
phospho-, before a vowel phosph-, combining
form used in the sense of phosphoric,
phosphorous. — Shortened fr. phosphorus.

## phosphoalum
phosphoalum, п., the univalent radical PH4 (chem.)
— ModL., coined fr. phosph- and the ending
■onium, on the analogy of amm-onium.

## phosphoprotein
phosphoprotein, п., any of a class of proteins in
which the protein molecule is combined with
some phosphorous substance other than lecithin
or nucleic acid (biochem.) — Compounded of
phospho- and protein.

## Phosphor
Phosphor, п., 1) the morning star (poetic); 2)
(not cap.) phosphorus. — L. Phosphorus,
'Phosphor'. See phosphorus.

## phosphor-
phosphor-, form of phosphoro- before a vowel.

## phosphoric
phosphoric, adj. — ¥.phosphorique, ir.phosphore.
See phosphorus and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: phosphoric-at, adj.

## phosphorize
phosphorize, tr. v. — F. phosphoriser, fr. phos-
phore. See phosphorus and -ize.

## phosphoro-
phosphoro-, before a vowel phosphor-,
combining form meaning phosphorus or
phosphorescence. — Fr. L. phosphorus. See next word.

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PHDSPHORUS | 558 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:585 COLUMN:1 -->

## phosphorus
phosphorus, η. — ModL. phosphorus,
'phosphorus', fr. L. Phosphorus, 'the morning star', fr.
Gk. φωσφόρος, 'light-bringer; the morning
star', which is compounded of φως, 'light',
contr. of φάος, and -φόρος, 'carrying'. The first
element derives fr. I.-E. base *bha-, 'to shine',
whence also OI. bhdti, 'shines, glitters', bhas-,
'light, glory'. See phantasm and words there
referred to and cp. esp. the second element in
Pasiphae'. For the second element see -phorous.
Derivatives: phosphor-ate, tr. v., phosphore-al,
phosphore-ous, adjs., phosphor-esce, intr. v.,
phosphor-esc-ence, п., phosphor-esc-ent, adj. and
п., phosphor-ism, n. (med.), phosphor-ite, n.
(mineral.), phosphor-it-ic, adj., phosphor-ous,
adj.

## phosphoryl
phosphoryl, п., the radical PO (chem.) — Coined
fr. phosphorus and suff. -yl.
Derivative: phosphorylation, n.

## phot
phot, п., the cgs unit of illumination (phys.) —
From the stem of Gk. φως, gen. φωτός, 'light'.
See phosphorus,

## photic
photic, adj., pertaining to light. — Formed with
■ adj. suff. -ic from Gk. φως, gen. φωτός, 'light'.
See phosphorus,

## photics
photics, п., the science of light. — See prec. word
and -ics.

## photism
photism, п., an illusory visual sensation (psychol.)
— G. Photismus, coined by the Swiss
psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (1857-1939) in 1881 fr. Gk.
φωτισμός, 'illumination', fr. φωτίζειν, 'to
illuminate' fr. φως, gen. φωτός, 'light'. See
phosphorus and -ism.

## photo-
photo-, combining form meaning 1) 'light', as in
photograph, photometer; 2) 'photographic', as
in photogravure. — Gk. φωτο-, from the stem
of φως, gen. φωτός, 'light'. See phosphorus,

## photo
photo, n. — Abbreviation of photograph,

## photogen
photogen, п., light oil distilled from bituminous
shale. — Lit. 'that which produces light';
compounded of photo- and -gen.

## photogenic
photogenic, adj., producing light; producing
phosphorescence; suitable for being
photographed. — Compounded of photo- and -genie.
Derivative: photogenic-al-Iy, adv.

## photogram
photogram, п., photograph. — Compounded of
photo- and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written'.
See -gram,

## photograph
photograph, n. — Compounded of photo- and
Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: photograph, tr. v., photograph-ee,
п., photograph-er, η., photograph-ic, photograph-
ic-al, adjs., photograph-ic-al-ly, adv.,
photographist, n.

## photography
photography, n. — Compounded of photo- and
Gk.-γραφίϊ, fr.γράφειν, 'to write'. See-graphy.

## photogravure
photogravure, n. — F., a hybrid coined fr. Gk.
φως, gen. φωτός, 'light', and F. gravure,
'engraving', fr. graver, 'to engrave', fr. Frankish
*graban, which is rel. to OHG. graban, 'to dig;
to carve'. See photo-, grave, 'to engrave' and
-ure.

## photoheliograph
photoheliograph, п., an instrument for
photographing the sun (astron.) — Compounded of
photo- and heliograph,

## photoheliography
photoheliography, п., photography of the sun
(astron.) — See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -(5).
Derivative: photoheliograph-ic, n.

## photokinesis
photokinesis, п., motion caused by light. —
ModL., compounded of photo- and kinesis,

## photokinetlc
photokinetlc, adj. — See prec. word and kinetic,

## photolysis
photolysis, п., decomposition due to the action of
light. — Compounded of photo- and -lysis,

## photolytic
photolytic, adj. — Compounded of photo- and
-lytic.

## photometer
photometer, an instrument for measuring the
intensity of light. — Lit. 'measurer of light', fr.
photo- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives \photometr-ic,photometr-ic-at, adjs.,
photometr-ic-al-ly, adv., photometric-ian, п.,
photometr-ist, a.

## photometry
photometry, п., study of the measurement of the
intensity of light. — Compounded of photo- and
Gk. -μετρία. See -metry.

## photomicrograph
photomicrograph, п., an enlarged photograph of
an object taken through a microscope. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:585 COLUMN:2 -->
Compounded of photo- and micrograph.
photomicrography, п., the art of making
photomicrographs. — Compounded of photo- and
micrography.
photon, п., a unit of the intensity of light (optics).
— Coined fr. phot and 2nd suff. -on.
photophobia, п., morbid sensitiveness to light
(med.) — ModL., lit. 'dread of light', fr. photo-
and Gk. -φοβίϊ, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See -phobia.
photophone, n. — Lit. 'sound through light', fr.
photo- and Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See phone,
'speech sound'.
photophore, п., a luminous organ. — Lit.
'carrying light', fr. photo- and Gk. -φόρος, 'bearer,
carrier'. See -phore.
photosphere, п., the luminous envelope surround-.
ing the sun (astron.) — Lit. 'ball of light',
compounded of photo- and Gk. σφαίρα, 'ball'.
See sphere.
Derivative: photospher-ic, adj.

## photostat
photostat, п., an automatic device for making
photographic copies of documents. —
Compounded of photo- and Gk. στατός, 'placed,
standing'. See static and cp. aerostat and words
there referred to.

## phototelescope
phototelescope, п., a telescope adapted fpr
photographing stars (astron.) — Compounded of
photo- and telescope.
Derivative: phototelescop-ic, adj.

## phototherapeutics
phototherapeutics, п., phototherapy. — See next
word and therapeutics.

## phototherapy
phototherapy, п., treatment of diseases by the
application of light (med.) — Lit. 'treatment
through light', fr. photo- and -therapy.
Derivatives: phototherap-ic, adj., phototherap-
ist, n.

## phragma
phragma, п., a septum. — ModL., fr. Gk.
φράγμα, 'hedge, fence, protection', from the stem
of φράσσειν, 'to fence in', which is possibly
cogn. with L.farcire, 'to stuff, cram'. See farce.
Phraginites. п., a genus of plants, the reed (hot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. φραγμϊτης, 'growing in
hedges', fr. φράγμα, 'hedge, fence, protection'.
See prec. word and subst. suff. -ite.

## phrase
phrase, n. — F., fr. Late L. phrasis, 'diction', fr.
Gk. φράσις, 'speech, expression, phrase', fr.
φράζειν, 'to point out, show, tell', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. the first element in
phraseology and the second element in holophrasis,
metuphrase, paraphrase, periphrasis.
Derivatives: phras-al, adj., phras-al-ly, adv.,
phrase, tr. and intr. v., phras-er, п., phras-ing, n.

## phraseogram
phraseogram, п., a symbol representing a phrase.
— Compounded of Gk. φράσις, gen. φράσεως,
'speech, expression, phrase', and γράμμα, 'that
which is written, a letter'. See phrase and -gram.

## phraseograph
phraseograph, п., a phrase represented by a
symbol. — Compounded of Gk. φράσις, gen.
φράσεως,'speech, expression, phrase', and-γραφος,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See phrase and -graph.
Derivative: phraseograph-er, n.

## phraseography
phraseography, п., representation of a phrase by
symbols. — See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -ία).

## phraseology
phraseology, п., diction, style. — Compounded
of Gk. φράσις, gen. φράσεως, 'speech,
expression, phrase', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See phrase and -logy.
Derivatives: phraseolog-tc, phraseolog-ic-al,
adjs., phraseotog-ic-al-ly, adv., phraseolog-ist, a.

## phratriac
phratriac, adj., pertaining to a phratry. — Gk.
φρατριακός, fr. φρατρίά. See next word and
-ac.

## phratry
phratry, п., 1) subdivision of a tribe in ancient-
Greece; 2) a clan among primitive races. — Gk.
φρατρίά, 'brotherhood; tribe, clan', fr. φρδ-
τηρ, 'brother', which is cogn. with L. /rater,
Goth, brdpar, OE. irodor.'brother'. See brother
and -y (representing Gk. -ία).
Derivatives: phratr-al, adj., phratriac (q.v.),
phratri-al, adj.

## phreatic
phreatic, adj., pertaining to underground waters.
— Lit. 'of, or pertaining to, a well', from Gk.
φρέϊρ (gen. φρέατος), 'a well', which stands for
•φρήΓαρ and is cogn. with Goth, brunna, OE.
burna, brunna, 'stream, brook*. See bourn,
'stream' and cp. words there referred to. For the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:585 COLUMN:3 -->
ending see 1st suff. -atic.

## phren-
phren-, form of phreno- before a vowel.
phrenetic, phrenetical, adj., delirious. — ME.
frenetik, fr. OF. frenetique, fr. L. phreneticus, fr.
Gk. φρενϊτικός, 'mad, delirious, frantic', fr.
φρενϊτις, 'delirium', fr. φρήν, gen. φρενός,
'diaphragm, heart, mind', which is of uncertain
origin. For the ending see suff. -ic. Cp. frantic,
which is a doublet of phrenetic. Cp. also the
second element in euphrasy, Euphrosyne,
Neophron, schizophrenia, Sophronia.
Derivatives: phrenetic, п., a madman.phrenetic-
al-ly, adv., phrenetic-neis, n.

## phrenic
phrenic, adj., pertaining to the diaphragm (anat.)
— Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. φρήν, gen.
φρενός, 'diaphragm, heart, mind'. See prec. word.

## phrenitis
phrenitis, п., inflammation of the brain, delirium
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. Gk. φρήν, gen.
φρενός, 'diaphragm, heart, mind' (see
phrenetic), with suff. -itis.
Derivative: phrenit-ic, adj.

## phreno-
phreno-, before a vowel phren-, combining form
meaning 'diaphragm, heart, mind'. — Gk.
φρένο-, fr. φρήν, gen. φρενός. See phrenetic.

## phrenology
phrenology, п., the study of the relation between
the shape of a person's skull and his mental
faculties. — Lit. 'the study of the mind',
compounded of Gk. φρήν, gen. φρενός, 'mind', and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, OneVho speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See phreno- and -logy.
Derivatives, phrenolog-ic, phrenotog-ic-at, adjs.,
phrenolog-ic-al-ly, adv., phrenolog-ist, n.,phren-
olog-ize, tr. v.

## Phronima
Phronima, п., a genus of amphipod crustaceans
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φρόνιμος, 'sane,
sensible, prudent', a derivative of φρονεϊν, 'to have
understanding, be wise', which is rel. to φρήν,
gen. φρενός, 'mind, heart', and to the second
element in σώ-φρων, Of sound mind'. See
phrenetic and cp. Sophronia.

## Phrygian
Phrygian, adj., of Phrygia. — L. Phrygianus, fr.
Phrygius, fr. Gk. Φρύγιος, 'Phrygian', fr. Φρύξ,
gen. Φρυγός, 'a Phrygian'. For the ending see
suff. -ian. Cp. the second element in orphrey.
Derivatives: Phrygian, п., Phrygian-ize, tr. v.

## Phrygian cap
Phrygian cap, a conical cap used by the
Phrygians. Identified in modern times with the cap of
liberty.

## Phryma
Phryma, п., a genus of plants, the lopseed (bot.)
— ModL., of unknown origin.

## Phrymaceae
Phrymaceae, n. pi., the lopseed family (bot.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## phthal-
phthal-, form of phthalo- before a vowel.

## phthalate
phthalate, п., a salt of phthalic acid (chem.) —
Formed fr. phthal- a'nd chem. suff. -ate.

## phthalein
phthalein, phthaleine, п., any of a group of
synthetic dyes (chem) — Abbreviation of (na)ph-
thalein, (na)phthateine. See naphtalene.

## phthalic
phthalic, adj., pertaining to any of three isomeric
acids (chem.) — Abbreviation of (na)phthalic.
See naphthalene and adj. suff. -ic.

## phthalht
phthalht, п., any of a series of compounds
obtained by the reduction of the phtaleins (chem.) —
Abbreviation of (na)phthalin. See naphthalene.

## phthalo-
phthalo-, before a vowel phthal-, related to
phthalic acid. — Back formation fr. phthalic (in
phthalic acid).

## phthiriasis
phthiriasis, п., pediculosis (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. φθειρίασις, fr. φθείρ, gen. φθειρός,
'louse', lit. 'the destroyer', fr. φθείρειν, 'to
destroy'. For sense development cp. κόρις, "bug',
which is prop, a verbal noun of κείρειν, 'to cut,
shear'. For the ending see suff. -asis.

## phthisic
phthisic, п., phtisis. — ME. tisike, fr. MF.'tisique,
fr. OF., earlier form of phtisique, orig. a fern,
adj. fr. L. phthisica, fern, of phthisicus, fr. Gk.
φθισικός, 'consumptive', fr. φθίσις. See phthisis
and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives:- phthisic, phthisic-al, phthisick-y,
adjs.

## phthisio-
phthisio-, combining form for phthisis. — See
phthisis.

## phthisis
phthisis, п., a wasting disease. — L., fr. Gk.
φθίβις, 'a wasting away, decay, consumption',
fr. φθίειν, 'to waste away', which is rel. ιοφθόη,
'consumption', and cogn. with OI. ksitib,
'destruction', ksinati, 'perishes', and possibly also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:586 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 559 | PHYTOGEOGRAPHY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:586 COLUMN:1 -->
with L. sltis, 'thirst'; cp. aphthitalite. For sense
development cp. E. starve, fr. OE. steorfan, 'to
die*.

## phugoid
phugoid, adj. (aeronaut.) — Lit. 'flightlike', fr.
Gk. φυγή, 'flight', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. The first element is rel. to φεύ-
γειν, 'to flee', and cogn. with L.fugere, of s.m.;
see fugitive. For the second element see -oid.

## -phyceae
-phyceae, combining form used to form names of
classes and orders of algae (boi.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. φΰκος, 'seaweed, sedge; red paint, dye', fr.
Heb. pukh. See Fucus.

## phyco-
phyco-, combining form meaning 'seaweed'. —
Gk. φυκο-, fr. φΰκός. See -phyceae.

## phycology
phycology, п., algology. — Lit. 'the study of
seaweeds', compounded of phyco- and Gk.
-λογία, fr.-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See -logy.

## Phycomyces
Phycomyces, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of phyco- and Gk. μύκης,
'mushroom, fungus'. See myco-.

## phylactery
phylactery, п., either of the tephillin (q.v.) —
Late ME. filakterie, fr. Late L. phylacterium, fr.
Gk. φυλακτήριον, 'guarded post, safeguard,
amulet', prop. neut. of the adj. φυλακτήριος,
'serving as a protection', fr. φυλακτήρ, 'watcher,
guard', fr. φύλαξ, gen. φύλακος, of s.m., from
the stem of φυλάσσειν, 'to watch, guard' which
is of uncertain origin. Cp. phylaxis.

## phylactic
phylactic, adj., pertaining to defense against
infection. — Gk. φυλακτικός, 'preservative', fr.
φυλακτός, 'capable of being preserved', from
the stem of φυλάσσειν. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -ic and cp. prophylactic.

## phylaxis
phylaxis, п., defense of the body against infection
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. φύλαξις, 'a
watching, guarding', from the stem of φυλάσσειν.
See phylactery and cp. anaphylaxis, prophylaxis,
calciphylaxis.

## phylarch
phylarch, п., chief of a tribe (Greek antiq.) — L.

## phylarchus
phylarchus, fr. Gk. φίλαρχος, 'chief of a phyle
or tribe', fr. φυλή, 'tribe', and άρχος, 'leader,
chief, ruler'. See next word and -arch.

## phyle
phyle, п., a political subdivision in ancient
Athens. — Gk. φυλή, 'tribe', rel. to φΰλον, 'tribe',
from the base of φύειν, 'to bring forth, produce,
make to grow', whence also φύσις, 'nature'. See
physio- and cp. phylo-, allophyllan, polyphylesis,

## phyletic
phyletic, adj., pertaining to a race; racial. — Gk.
φυλετικός, 'of one's tribe', fr. φΰλέτης, 'fellow
tribesman', fr. φυλή. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -ic and cp. monophyletic.
Derivative: phyletic-al-ly, adv.

## phyll-
phyll-, form of phyllo- before a vowel.

## Phyllanthus
Phyllanthus, п., a genus of plants of the spurge
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
φύλλον, 'leaf (see phyllo-), and £ν»ας, 'flower'
(see anther); so called from the shape of the
flowers.

## Phyllis
Phyllis, fern. PN. — L., fr. Gk. Φυλλίς, fr. φυλ-
λίς, 'leaf, foliage, bough', which is rel. to
φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo-.

## -phyll
-phyll, combining form meaning 'leaf, as in
chlorophyll, sporophyll. — Fr. Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf.
See phyllo-.

## phyllo-
phyllo-, before a vowel phyll-, combining form
meaning 'leaf. — Gk. φύλλο-, φυλλ-, fr.
φύλλον, 'leaf, which is cogn. with L. folium, 'leaf.
See folio- and cp. Phyllis, aphyllous, chervil,
gillyflower.

## Phyllodoce
Phyllodoce, п., a genus of plants of the heath
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. Phyllodoce, name
of a sea nymph.

## -phyilous
-phyilous, combining form meaning 'having a
certain number or a certain shape of leaves', as
in diphyllous, eleutherophyllous. — Gk. -φυλ-
λος, fr. φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo-. For E. -ous,
as corresponding to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## Phylloxera
Phylloxera, п., a genus of plant lice (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of phyllo- and Gk. ξηρός,
'dry'. See xero- and cp. Xerophyllum.

## phylo-
phylo-, before a vowel phyl-, combining form
meaning 'tribe'. — Gk. φύλο-, φΰλ-, fr. φΰλον,
'tribe', which is rel. to φυλή, of s.m. See phyle.

## phytogeny
phytogeny, also phylogenesis, п., evolution of a
race (biol.) — G. Phylogenie, coined by the
German biologist Ernst Heinrich Haeckel

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:586 COLUMN:2 -->
wind, bubble', from the imitative base *pu-,
*phu-, 'to blow, swell', whence also L. pustula,
'blister, pimple, pustule'. See pustule and -ia and
cp. the next two words. Cp. also emphysema.

## Physalis
Physalis, п., a genus of plants, the ground-cherry
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. φΰσαλ(λ)ίς, 'bladder;
a plant with a bladderlike calyx'. See prec.
word.

## Physeter
Physeter, п., cachalot, sperm whale (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. physeter, 'blowpipe; bellows;
sperm whale', Gk. φΰσητήρ, of s.m., fr. φΰσαν,
*to blow'. See Physalia.

## physeterid
physeterid, adj., pertaining to the family of the
Physeteridae; п., a whale of the family Physe-
teridae. — From next word.

## Physeteridae
Physeteridae, n. pi., a family of whales, the sperm
whales (zool.) — ModL., formed fr. physeter
with suff. -idae.

## physic
physic, n. — ME. fisike, fr. OF. fisique, phisi-
que(= F. physique), fr. L. physica, fr. Gk.
φυσική (scil.- επιστήμη), 'natural science', fern, of
φυσικός, 'pertaining to nature, natural', fr.
φύσις, 'nature'. See physio- and -ic and cp.
metaphysics.
Derivatives; physic, tr. v.,physic-al, adj., physic-
al-ly, adv.,physician (q.v.), physic-ism,
a.,physicist (q.v.), physick-y, adj.

## physician
physician, n. — ME.fisicien, fr. OT.fisicien,
'physician' (F. physicien means 'physicist'), fr. L.
physica, 'natural science, physics'. See physic
and -ian and cp. physicist.
Derivatives '.physician, tr. v., physician-ary, adj.,
physician-er, п., physician-Iy, adj.

## physicist
physicist, n. — Coined by the English
philosopher William Whewell (1794-1866) to denote a
'cultivator of physics', in contradistinction to a
physician, i.e. 'one who practices the medical
profession'. See physics and -ist.

## physico-
physico-, combining form meaning; 1) natural;
2) physical. — Fr. Gk. φυσικός, 'pertaining to
nature', fr. φύσις. See physic,

## physics
physics, n. — See physic and -ics.

## physio-
physio-, combining form meaning 'nature'. —
Gk. φυσιο-, fr. φύσις, 'nature', fr. φύειν, 'to
bring forth, produce, make to grow', whence
also φυτόν, 'growth, plant', φυλή, 'tribe, race',
φΰλον, 'tribe', φϋμα, 'a growth, tumor', fr.
I.-E. base *bheu-, *bhu-, 'to be, exist, grow',
whence also OE. beon, 'to be'. See be and words
there referred to and cp. esp. physic, -phyle,
phyma, -phyte. Cp. also apophysis, diaphysis,
diphy-, epiphysis, euphuism, hypophysis,
metaphysics, Monophysitic, paraphysls, symphysis,
Symphytum,

## physiocracy
physiocracy, n. — F. physiocratie, lit. 'the rule of
nature', a name coined in 1758 by Pierre-
Samuel DupontdeNemours(1739-1817),oneof
the members of the school of economists
founded by Francois Quesnay (1694-1774) fr. Gk.
φύσις, 'nature', and -κρατία, 'rule,
government', fr. κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'. See
physio- and -cracy.
(1834-1919). See phylo- and -geny, resp, genesis.
Derivatives: phylogen-etic, phylogen-etic-al,
adjs., phylogen-etic-al-ly, adv., phylogen-ic, adj.

## phylum
phylum, п., one of the divisions of the plant or
animal kingdom, (biol.) — ModL., coined by
the French naturalist, Baron Georges Leopold
Chretien Frederic Dagobert Cuvier (1769-1832)
fr. Gk, φΰλον, 'tribe, race'. See phyle.

## phyma
phyma, п., a swelling; skin tumor (med.) — Gk.
φϋμα, gen. φύματος, 'that which grows, a
growth, swelling, tumor', fr. φύειν, 'to bring
forth, produce, make to grow'. See physio- and
-ma.

## phys-
phys-, form of physo- before a vowel.

## Physalia
Physalia, п., a genus of hydrozoa (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. φϋσαλέος, 'full of wind', which
is rel. to φΰσαλ(λ)ίς, 'bladder', fr. φΰσαν, 'to
blow', fr. φΰσα, 'pair of bellows, breath, blast,

## physiocrat
physiocrat, n. — F. physiocrate, back formation
from prec. word; see -crat.
Derivative: physiocrat-ic, adj.

## physiogeny
physiogeny, п., the development of vital
functions (biol.) — G. Physiogenie, coined by the
German biologist Ernst Heinrich Haeckel
(1834-1919). See physio- and -geny.

## physiognomonic
physiognomonic, adj. — ML. physiognomonicus.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:586 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. Gk. φυσιογνωμονικός, 'pertaining to phy-
siognori.y', fr. φυσιογνωμονια. See next word
and adj. suff. -jc.

## physiognomy
physiognomy, п., 1) the art of determining
character from facial features; 2) face. — ME. fisno-
mye, phisonomie, fr. OF. fiznomie, phizonomie
(= F. physionomie), fr. ML. physionomia, fr.
Gk. φυσιογνωμονια, 'the science of judging a
man's nature by his features', fr. φυσιογνώμων,
'judging a man's nature by his features', which
is compounded of φύσις, 'nature' and γνωμών,
'judge, interpreter, indicator'; see physio- and
guomon. In the Έκλογαί of Joannes Stobaeus
φυσιογνωμία was miswritten φυσιογνωμονια,
whence arose its form in ML.
Derivatives: physiognom-ic, physiognom-ic-al,
adjs., physiognom-ic-al-ly, adv., physiognom-ist,
n.

## physiographer
physiographer, n. — See next word and agential
suff. -er.

## physiography
physiography, п., 1) a description of the
phenomena of nature; 2) physical geography. — Lit.
'description of nature', compounded of physio-
and -γραφίϊ, _ fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
-graphy.
Derivatives: physiograph-ic, physiograph-ic-al,
adjs., physiograph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## physiologic
physiologic, physiological, adj. — Late L. physio-
logicus, fr. Gk. φυσιολογικός, 'of inquiry into
nature', fr. φυσιολογία. See physiology and -ic,
resp. also -al.
Derivative: physiological-ly, adv.

## physiologico-
physiologico-, combining form used in the sense
of 'and physiological'. — See prec. word.

## physiologue
physiologue, п., a physiologist. — See next word
and -logue.

## physiology
physiology, п., that branch of biology which deals
with the functions of living organisms. — F.
physiologie, fr. L. physiologia, fr. Gk.
φυσιολογία, 'inquiry into nature', fr. φυσιολόγος, 'one
who inquires into nature', fr. φύσις, 'nature',
and -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner) ; one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
physio- and -logy.
Derivatives: physiolog-er, п., physiolog-ian, п.,
physiological (q.v.), physiolog-ist, п., physiolog-
ize, intr. and tr. v.

## physiotherapy
physiotherapy, п., medical treatment by physical
and mechanical means (as massage, heat,
electricity). — Compounded of physio- and
-therapy.
Derivative: physiotherap-ist, n.

## physique
physique, п., physical structure, constitution. —
F. physique, from the adj. physique, 'physical',
fr. L. physicus, 'natural, physical', fr. Gk.
φυσικός. See physic.

## physo-
physo-, before a vowel phys-, combining form
denoting the air bladder or the presence of air.
— Fr. Gk. φΰσα, 'a pair of bellows, breath,
blast, wind, bubble'. See Physalia.

## Physocarpus
Physocarpus, п., a genus of plants, the ninebark
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of physo- and
Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.

## phyt-
phyt-, form of phyto- before a vowel.

## -phyte
-phyte, combining form denoting a
characteristic of a plant, as in aerophyte, entophyte,
zoophyte. — Gk. -φυτον, fr. φυτόν, 'plant', fr.
φύειν, 'to bring forth, produce, make to grow'.
See physio- and cp. phyle, phylo-. Cp. also imp.

## phytm
phytm, п., a calcium-magnesium salt prepared
from the seeds and tubers of various plants (bio-
chem.) — Lit. 'derived from plants', fr. φυτόν,
'plant'. See phyto- and -in.

## phyto-
phyto-, before a vowel phyt-, combining form
meaning 'plant-'. — Gk. φυτό-, φυτ-, fr. φυτόν,
'plant'. See -phyte.

## phytogenesis
phytogenesis, п., the origin of plants. — ModL.,
compounded of phyto- and Gk. γένεσις, 'origin,
source, birth, descent, race'. See genesis,

## phytogenetic
phytogenetic, phytogenetical, adj. — See prec.
word and genetic.
Derivative: phytogenetic-al-ly, adv.

## phytogenic
phytogenic, adj. — See phytogenetic.

## phytogeny
phytogeny, п., phytogenesis. — See phytogenesis
and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## phytogeography
phytogeography, n. — Lit. 'geography of plants'.
See phyto- and geography.
Derivatives: phytogeograph-ic, phytogeograph-

ic-al, adjs., phytogeographic-al-ly, adv.

## phytography
phytography, n.( descriptive botany. — Lit.
'description of plants', compounded of phyto- and
Gk. -γραφίϊ, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
-graphy.
Derivatives: phytograph-ic, phytograph-ic-al,
adjs., phylograph-ist, n.

## phytol
phytol, п., an oily alcohol, C!0H3,OH, first
isolated from chlorophyll by the German chemist
Richard Willstatter (1872-1942) (chem.) —
Coined fr. phyt- and -o], a suff. denoting alcohol.

## phytology
phytology, n. — Another name for botany; lit.
'the study of plants', compounded of phyto- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: phylolog-ic, phytolog-ic-al, adjs.,
phytolog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Phytolacca
Phytolacca, п., a genus of plants, the pokeweed
(bot.) — A ModL. hybrid coined fr. Gk. φυτόν,
'plant' and ModL. lacca, fr. Hind. lakh. See
phyto- and lac, 'a resinous substance'.

## Phytolaccaceae
Phytolaccaceae, n. pi., the pokeweed family (bot.)
— Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## phytolaccaceous
phytolaccaceous, adj. — See prec. word, and
-aceous.

## phytophagic
phytophagic, adj., feeding on plants (zool.) —
See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## phytophagous
phytophagous, adj., feeding on plants (zool.) —
Compounded of Gk. φυτόν, 'plant', and φα-
γεΐν, 'to eat'. See phyto- and -phagous.

## phytosterol
phytosterol, п., a sterol of plant origin (biochem.)
— Formed fr. phyto- and sterol.

## phytyl
phytyl, п., the radical CI0H3„ derived from
phytol (chem.) — See phytol and -yl.
pit п., name of the 16th letter of the Greek
alphabet (=П, π). — Gk. πει, formed on analogy
of the letter-names ξεΐ (= xi), φεΐ (= phi), χα
(= chi), ψεΐ (= psi), fr. Heb. рё, lit. 'mouth'.
Seepe.

## pi
pi, the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its
diameter (math.) — So called by the Greeks fr.
π, the initial letter of the word περιφέρεια,
'circumference, periphery'.

## pi
pi, adj..pious,sanctimonious («■
W/s/an,cr)—Abbreviation of pious.
Derivative; pi, a.

## pi
pi, n. and tr. v. (printer's term). — See pie, 'mixed
type'.

## pi-
pi-, form of plo- before a vowel.

## piacular
piacular, adj., expiatory. — L. piacularis, fr. pia-
culum, 'propitiatory sacrifice', for *pia-tlom,
which is formed with instrumental suff. *-tlom,
fr. piare, 'to appease, propitiate', fr. pius,
'dutiful'. See pious and adj. suff. -ar.
Derivatives: piacular-ity, п., piacular~ly, adv.,
piacular'-ness, n.

## piaffe
piaffe, intr. v., a term of manege. — Fr. F. piaffer,
'to paw the ground' (said of a horse); of
imitative origin.

## piaffer
piaffer, п., the act of piaffing. — F., inf. See prec.
word.

## pia mater
pia mater, п., the inmost of the three membranes
surrounding the brain and spinal chord (anat.)
— ML., shortened fr. pia mater cerebri, which
is a loan translation of Arab, umm al-dimagh al-
raqtqa1', lit. 'thin mother of the brain'. Since
Arab, raqtq means also 'merciful, pious', the
'thin' membrane became pia mater, 'the pious
mother'. (In Arabic, the words 'father',
'mother' and 'son', are often used to denote
relationship between things.) See pious and mater,
mother, and cp. dura mater,

## pianette
pianette, п., a small, upright piano (music). —
Dimin. formed fr. piano with suff. -ette.

## planlsin
planlsin, п., the art of piano playing (music). —
See piano and'-ism.

## pianissimo
pianissimo, adv. and n. (music). — It., lit. 'very
softly', superl. of piano, 'soft'. See piano.

## pianist
pianist, n. — F. pianiste, fr. It. pianista, fr. piano.
See piano, n. and -ist.
Derivatives: pianist-ic, adj., pianist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## piano
piano, п., a musical instrument. — It.,
abbreviation of pianoforte or forteplano,

## piano
piano, adj., soft; adv., softly. — It., fr. L. planus,
'flat, smooth, even', later used also in the sense
of 'soft'. See pinia, adj.

## pianoforte
pianoforte, n. — Fr. earlier plan(o) e forte, 'soft

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:587 COLUMN:2 -->
and strong', so called by its inventor B. Chris-
tophori (1655-1731) to express its capability of
producing sounds of various grades. For the
etymology of It. piano see piano, adj. It. forte
derives fr. L.fortem, ace. oifortis, 'strong'; see
fort.

## pianola
pianola, п., player piano (music). — Invented
trade name for a player piano, apparently meant
as a diminutive of piano.

## piaster
piaster, piastre, п., 1) the Spanish dollar; 2) the
monetary unit and a coin of Turkey. — F.
piastre, fr. It. piastra, 'thin metal plate', shortened
fr. impiastro, 'plaster', fr. L. emplastrum, fr. Gk.
ε'μπλαστρον, 'plaster'. See 2nd en- and plaster,
п., and cp. pistole.

## piazza
piazza, п., a public square in an Italian town. —
It., fr. VL. plattea, fr. L. platia, 'broad street',
fr. Gk. πλατεία (scil. οδός), 'broad (street)',
fern, of πλατύς, 'broad'. See place and cp. plaza.

## pibal
pibal, п., observation of the atmosphere from a
pilot-balloon. — Abbreviation of pi(lot)
bal(loon).

## pibroch
pibroch, п., a kind of bagpipe music. — Gael.
piobaireachd, lit. 'piper's art', formed ir.piobair,
,'a piper' (fr. piob, 'pipe', a loan word fr. E.
pipe), with -achd, a suff. denoting function.

## pica
pica, п., a size of type (print.) — ML., 'collection
of rules, ordinal', prob. fr. L. pica, 'magpie'
(see pie, 'collection of rules'); so called because
this type was generally used to print ordinals.

## pica
pica, п., appetite for substances unfit for food
(med.) — Medical L., prop, 'an appetite like
that of the magpie', fr. L. pica, 'magpie'. See
pie, 'magpie', and cp. prec. word. For sense
development cp. Gk. κίσσα, κίττα, 'jay;
craving for strange food'.

## picador
picador, п., bullfighter. — Sp., lit. 'pricker', fr.
picar, 'to prick'. See pike, 'a sharp point', and
cp. words there referred to.

## picamar
picamar, п., bitter oil obtained from wood tar. —
G. Picamar, Pikamar^ lit. 'bitter pitch', coined
by the German natural philosopher and
industrialist, Baron Karl von Reichenbach (1788-
1869) in 1836 from the stem of L. pix, gen. picis,
'pitch', and that of amdrus, 'bitter'. See pitch, 'a
resinous substance', and amarine.

## picaninny
picaninny, n. — See pickaninny.

## picaresque
picaresque, adj., dealing with rogues and their
adventures. — Sp. picaresco, 'roguish, knavish',
fr. picaro, 'rogue', fr. picar, 'to prick'. See
picador and -esque.

## picaroon
picaroon, п., a rogue, adventurer. — Sp. picaron,
augment, of picaro, 'rogue'. See prec. word and
-ООП.
Derivative: picaroon, intr. v.

## picayune
picayune, п., name of a small coin. — F. picaillon,
fr. OProveric. picaioun, 'a small copper coin',
derived fr. picaio, 'money', fr. picar, 'to prick',
used in the sense 'to sound'; hence picaioun lit.
means 'a sounding coin'. See pike, 'a sharp
point', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: picayune, picayun-ish, adjs.

## piccalilli
piccalilli, п., pickle of chopped vegetables. —
Prob. altered from pickle.

## piccolo
piccolo, п., a small flute. — It., 'small; small
flute', prob. from an imitative base, expressive
of littleness in infant's language. Cp. F. petit,
Sp. pequeno, 'small, little' and see pickaninny.

## piccolo
piccolo, adj., small. — It. See piccolo, n.

## pice
pice, п., name of a copper coin in India. — Hind.
paisa.

## Picea
Picea, п., a genus of plants, the spruce (bot.) —
L. picea, 'the pitch pine', fr. pix, gen. picis,
'pitch'. See pitch, 'a resinous substance'.

## picene
picene, п., the hydrocarbon С2гН14 (chem.) —
Coined fr. L. pix, gen. picis, 'pitch' (see pitch,
п.), and surf. -ene.

## piceous
piceous, adj., resembling pitch. — L. piceus, fr.
pix, gen. picis, 'pitch'. See pitch, 'a resinous
substance', and -eous.

## picbiciago
picbiciago, п., a South American armadillo. —
Sp. pichiciego, prob. a hybrid coined fr. S.
American Indfan pichey, 'armadillo', and Sp. ciego,
'blind', fr. L. caecus. See caecum.

## pick
pick, п., a pointed instrument. — A var. of pike,
'a weapon'. Cp. the first element in pitchfork.

## pick
pick, tr. and intr. v., 1) to pierce; 2) to gather,
pluck; 3) to choose. '— ME. piken, a blend of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:587 COLUMN:3 -->
MF. (= F.)piquer, 'to prick, sting' (see pike, 'a
sharp point'), and the verb of OE. plcung, 'a
pricking', which is rel. to ON. pikka, 'to pierce',
Swed. picka, -Dan. pikke, MDu. picken, Du.
pikken, OHG. (ana) bickan, MHG. bicken, G.
picken, 'to pick, peck', fr. base *pik-, *pek-,
imitative of the sound made by the pecking of a
bird. Cp. peck, 'to strike'.
Derivatives: pick, п., the act of picking; a
portion picked; the best, pick-ed, adj., pick-ed-Iy,
adv., pick-ed-ness, п., pick-er, п., pick-ing, adj.
and п., pick-y, adj.

## pickaback
pickaback, adv., on the back. — Prob.
reduplication of pack, altered fr. earlier pickpack, under
the influence of back.

## pickaninny
pickaninny, also picaninny, п., a little child. —
Prob. fr. Port, pequenino, dimin. of pequeno,
'little, small' (= Sp. pequeno, of s.m.), which,
like It. piccolo, and F. petit, is of imitative
origin. See piccolo and cp. petty.

## pickax
pickax, pickaxe, n. — ME. pikeis, pikois, fr. OF.
picois, picot, fr. pic, 'pick, pickax'; the ending of
the word was influenced by ax. See pike, 'sharp
point'.
Derivative: pickax(e), tr. and intr. v.

## pickerel
pickerel, п., a young pike. — Dimin. of pike, the
fish. For the suff. cp. cockerel, dimin. of cock.

## Pickering
Pickering, n. — Corruption of pickerel.

## pickeringite
pickeringite, п., a hydrous magnesium aluminum
sulfate (mineral.) — Named after the American
scientist John Pickering (1777-1846). For the
ending see subst. surf. -ite.

## picket
picket, n. — F. piquet, 'pointed stake', fr. OE.,
dimin. of pic, 'pick, pickax'. See pike, 'sharp
point', and -et.
Derivatives: picket, tr. and intr. v., picket-eer,
п., picket~er, n.

## pickle
pickle, n. — ME. pekille, fr. MDu. pekel (whence
also G. Pokel), prob. named after the Dutch
fisher Willem Beukelz (died in 1397), who
developed the procedure of pickling. See Kluge-
Mitzka, EWDS, p. 557 s.v. Pokel.
Derivatives: pickle, tr. v., pickl-er, n.

## Pickwickian
Pickwickian, adj. — Relating to Mr. Pickwick, a
character invented by Charles Dickens (1812-
70) in his Pickwick Papers. For the ending see
suff. -ian.

## Pickwickian
Pickwickian, n. — Member of the Pickwick Club,
i.e. a club founded by Mr. Pickwick. See prec.
word.

## picnic
picnic, n. — F. piquenique, formed with
reduplication fr. piquer, 'to pick', used in a figurative
sense; see pike, 'a sharp point'. Cp. F. pile-
mele, 'pell-mell', formed with reduplication fr.
meter, 'to mix' (see pell-mell).
Derivatives: picnic, intr. v., picknick-er, п.,
picknick-ery, п., picnick-y, adj.

## picoline
picoline, п., any of three isomeric liquid
compounds, C„H,N, found in coal tar, ammonia
liquor, bone oil, etc. (chem.) — Coined fr. L.
pix, gen. picis, 'pitch' (see pitch, п.), suff. -ol (fr.
L. oleum ('oil') and chem suff. -ine.

## picot
picot, п., a small loop. — F., 'small point; picot',
dimin. of pic, 'peak, point'. See pike, 'a sharp
point' and cp. picket.
Derivative: picot, intr. and tr. v.

## picotee
picotee, п., a variety of carnation. — F. picote,
pp. of picoter, 'to mark with points', fr. picot,
'small point'. See prec. word and -ее.

## picquet
picquet, n. — The same as piquet.

## picrate
picrate, п., a salt or ester of picric acid (chem.) —
See next word and chem. suff. -ate.

## picric
picric, adj., bitter. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr.
Gk. πικρός, 'sharp, bitter', fr. I.-E. base *peik-.
Ίο adorn by coloring or carving', whence also
ποικίλος, 'variegated'. Cp. the related base
*peig-, whence L. pingere, 'to paint, embroider',
and see paint.

## Picris
Picris, п., a genus of plants of the chicory family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. picris, 'a kind of bitter
lettuce', fr. Gk. πικρίς, fr. πικρός, 'bitter'. See
prec. word.

## picrite
picrite, п., an igneous rock composed of augite
and olivine (petrogr.) — See picric and subst.
suff. -ite.

## Pict
Pict, п., one of an ancient people of Great
Britain. — Late L. Picti (pi.), usually explained as
'the painted or tattooed ones' (fr. L. pictS, pi. of

## pictus
pictus, 'painted', pp. of pingere), but prob.
alteration of the Celtic name Pehta, Peihta
(whence OE. Peohtas), lit. 'the Fighters'. This
alteration prob. suggested itself from the custom
of the members of this people to paint
themselves.
Derivative: Picl-ish, adj.

## pictograph
pictograph, п., a pictorial symbol representing
an idea. — A hybrid coined fr. L. pictus,
pp. of pingere, 'to paint, color', and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See paint and
-graph.
Derivatives: pictograph-ic, adj., pictograph-ic-
al-ly, adv.

## pictography
pictography, п., the art of writing with picto-
graphs. — See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -iS).

## pictorial
pictorial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
pictorius, 'of painters', fr. piclor, 'painter', fr.
pictus, pp. of pingere, 'to paint'. See paint.
Derivatives: pictorial, п., pictorial-ism, п.,
pictorial-ist, п., pictorial-ize, tr. v., pictorial-iz-
ation, п., pictorial-ly, adv., pictorial-ness, n.

## picture
picture, n. — ME., fr. L. pictura, 'painting', fr.
pictus, pp. of pingere, 'to paint; to embroider',
fr. I.-E. base *peig-, 'to adorn by coloring or
carving'. See paint and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending see suff. -ure. Cp. painture,
which is a doublet οι picture.
Derivatives: picture, tr. v., pictur-ed, adj.,
picture-ly, adj., picturesque (q.v.), pictur-ize, tr.
v., pictur-iz-ation, п., pictur-y, adj.

## picturesque
picturesque, adj., 1) like a picture; 2) colorful;
striking, vivid. — A blend of F. pittoresque and
E. picture. F. pittoresque is a loan word fr. It.
pittoresco, which derives fr. pittore, 'painter', fr.
L. pictorem, ace. of pictor. See pictorial and
-esque.
Derivatives: picturesque, n. and v.,
picturesquely, adv., picturesque-ness, a.

## picul
picul, п., a weight. — Malay and Javanese pikul,
'a man's load'.

## plcule
plcule, п., piculet. — See next word.

## piculet
piculet, п., a bird of the subfamily Picidae (orni-
thol.) — Dimin. formed fr. L. picus,
'woodpecker' (see pie, 'magpie'), with the suff. -ule
and -iet.

## piddle
piddle, intr. v., to trifle. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: piddl-er, п., piddl-ing, n.

## piddock
piddock, п., a bivalve mollusk of the genus Pho-
las. — Of uncertain origin.

## pidgin
pidgin, pigeon, п., a mixed language, especially
used in pidgin English, pigeon English. — A
Chinese corruption of E. business.

## pie
pie, п., magpie. — ME., fr. OF. pie, fr. L. pica,
'magpie', rel. to picus, 'woodpecker' and to
Umbr. peica (ace), 'the magpie' and cogn. with
OI. pikah, 'the Indian cuckoo', OPtuss. picle,
'fieldfare', ON. spStr, MDu., Du. specht, OHG.,
MHG. speht, G. Specht, 'woodpecker'. Cp. pica,
piculet. Cp. also speight.

## pie
pie, also pi, п., type mixed indiscriminately {print).
— Prob. fr. pie, 'magpie'. See next word.
Derivative: pie, also pi, tr. v., to mix up
indiscriminately.

## pie
pie, п., collection of rules. — Prob. fr. pie,
'magpie', fr. L. pica, whence ML. pica, 'collection of
rules, ordinal' (so called in allusion to the black
and white color of the printed page, suggestive
of a magpie). Cp. pica, 'a size of type'. Cp. also
prec. word.

## pie
pie, п., a dish covered with pastry. — ME., pern,
lit. 'mixture, mixed dish', and derived fr. pie,
'magpie'.

## pie
pie, п., name of a small copper coin of India. —
Hind, pa'i, fr. OI. pidika, 'quarter', fr. pat, ace.
padam, 'foot, quarter'. See foot.

## piebald
piebald, adj., of two different colors, esp. white
and black (like a magpie). — Compounded of
pie, 'magpie', and bald, in its old sense 'white'.
Cp. skewbald.
Derivatives .piebald, п., piebald-ly, adv. ,piebald-
ness, n.

## piece
piece, n. — ME. pece, piece, fr. OF. pece, fr. VL.
"pettia (whence also ML. pecia. It. pezza, Sp.
pieza), a word of Gaulish origin. Cp. W. peth,
Bret, pez, 'a little', and E. patch, 'a piece of
cloth'. Cp. also peat, bezetta.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:588 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: piece, tr. and intr. v., piec-er, п.,
piec-ing, n.

## piecemeal
piecemeal, adv. — ME. pecemele, fr. pece, 'piece',
and OE. mSlum, dat. pi. of mxl, 'measure'. See
piece and meal, 'repast'.

## pied
pied, adj., mottled, parti-colored. — Formed fr.
pie, 'magpie'; pied orig. meant 'colored as a
magpie i.e. 'black and white'. For the ending see
3rd suff. -ed.
pie jacket. — Prob. fr. Du. pij-jekker, fr. pi] (fr.
MDu. pie), 'cowl', and jekker, 'jacket'.

## piepoudre
piepoudre, piepowder, п., orig. a wayfarer itinerant
merchant; now used only in court of piepoudre
or piepowder, a court formerly attached to every
fair and market. — ME. pipoudre, fr. OF. pie
pouldre, 'traveler, peddler', lit. 'dustfooted', fr.
pie (F. pied), 'foot' and pouldre (F. poudre),
'dust'. See foot and powder.

## pier
pier, n. — ME. pere, per, fr. OE. per, fr. ML.
pera, which prob. derives fr. L. petra, 'rock,
stone', fr. Gk. πέτρϊ. See petro-.
Derivatives: pier, tr. v., pier-age, n.

## pierce
pierce, tr. and intr. v. — ME. percen, fr. OF.
percer, percier (F. percer), fr. VL. *pertusiare,
freq. of L. pertundere, pp. pertusus, 'to thrust
through', fr. per- and tundere, 'to beat, strike,
stump', which is rel. to OI. tudati, tundaie, 'he
thrusts', fr. I.-E. base *(s)tud-, 'to beat, strike,
push, thrust'. See stint and words there referred
to and cp. esp. perfuse.
Derivatives: pierc-ing, adj.,pierc-ing-ly, adv.

## Pierian
Pierian, adj., pertaining to Pieria; relating to
poetry. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Pierius,
fr. Pieria, fr. Gk. Πιερία, name of a mountain
in N. Thessaly, home of the Muses.

## pierrette
pierrette, п., a female pierrot. — Fem. of plerrot.

## pierrot
pierrot, п., a stock character in French
pantomime. — F., lit. 'little Peter', ft. Pierre, fr. L.
Petrus. See Peter.
Derivatives: pierrot, intr. v., pierrot-ic, adj.

## Pietism
Pietism, п., religious revival in the Lutheran
Church at the end of the 17th cent. — G. Pie-
tismus, formed after Pietist (q.v.) with suff.
-ismus (fr. L. -ismus); see -ism.

## pietism
pietism, п., 1) deep religious feeling; 2)
exaggeration of piety. — See prec. word.

## Pietist
Pietist, п., a name given to the adherents of the
German theologian PhilirD Jacob Spener (1635-
1705). — G. Pietist; so named fr. Spener's
Collegia pietatis. See piety and -ist.

## pietist
pietist, п., an adherent of pietism. — See prec.
word.
Derivatives: pietist-ic, pietist-ic-al, adjs., pietist-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## piety
piety, n. — MF. (= ¥.)piete, fr. L.pietatem, ace.
oipietds, 'duty, dutiful conduct, piety, devotion,
tenderness, kindness', fr. plus, 'dutiful, pious'.
See pious and -ty and cp. pity, which is a doublet
of piety. Cp. also piteous, pittance, mont-de-
piete.

## piezo-
piezo-, combining form denoting pressure, as in
piezometer. — Fr. Gk. τηέζειν, 'to press', which
is cogn. with OI. piddyati, 'presses, oppresses',
fr. I.-E. *pi-s(e)d-, 'to sit upon, to press', fr.
*pi-, short form of *epi, 'on' (see epi-), and *sed-,
'to sit', whence OI. sidati, 'sits', Gk. εζεσθαι,
L. sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary,

## piezometer
piezometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
pressure of liquids or gases. — Compounded of
piezo- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See meter,
'poetical rhythm', and cp. sympiezometer.
Derivatives: piezometr-ic, piezometr-ic-al, adjs.,

## piezometr-y
piezometr-y, n.

## piff
piff, interj. — Imitative.

## piffle
piffle, intr. v. — Of uncertain origin; possibly
formed fr. prec. word with suff. -le.
Derivative: piffl-er, n.

## pig
pig, n. — ME. pigge, rel. to LG. bigge, Du. big;
of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pig, intr. v., pigg-ery, п., pigg-ish,
adj., pigg-ish-ly, adv., pigg-ish-ness, п., pigg-y,
adj., pig-ling, п., pig-ly, adj.

## pigeon
pigeon, n. — ME. pijon, pigeon, fr. OF. pijon (F.

## pigeon)
pigeon), fr. Late L. pipionem, ace. of pipio,
'chirping bird', fr. L. pipire, 'to peep, chirp',
which like ptpare, of s.m., is of imitative origin.
See pipe and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: pigeon, tr. v., pigeon-ry, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:588 COLUMN:3 -->

## piggy
piggy, n. — A child's jvord for pig.

## piglet
piglet, п., a small hog. — Formed fr. pig with
dimin. suff. -let.

## pigment
pigment, п., paint, dye. — L. pigmentum,
'coloring matter, paint', from the stem of pingere, 'to
paint'. See paint and -ment and cp. pimento,
pimiento and the second element in orpiment.
Derivatives:pigment, tr. and intr. v.,pigmentary
(q.v.), pigment-ation, п., pigment-ize, tr. v.

## pigmentary
pigmentary, adj. — L. pigmentarius, 'pertaining
to paints', fr. pigmentum. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ary.

## pigmy
pigmy, n. — See pygmy.

## pignorate
pignorate, tr. v., to pledge. — L. pigneratus (pig-
nordtus), pp. of pignerare (pignordre), 'to give
as a pledge, to pledge', fr. pignus, gen. pignoris,
'pledge, gage, security', which is of uncertain
origin. For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## pike
pike, п., a sharp point. — ME. pic, pike, руке, fr.
OE. pic, 'point, pike', fr. OF. (= F.) pic, 'pick,
pickax; peak (of a mountain)', which is prob.
verbal n. oipiquer, 'to prick, sting' (see Dauzat,
DELF., p. 556 s.v. 2nd pic), fr. VL. *piccdre, 'to
prick, pierce' (whence also It. piccare, OPro-
venc., Sp. picar, 'to prick, sting"), fr. VL. *pic-
cus, fr. L. plcys, 'woodpecker', which is rel. to
pica, 'magpie'. See pie, 'magpie', and cp. peak,
'a sharp point'. Cp. also picador, picaresque,
picaroon, picayune, pickax, picket, picnic, picot,
picotee, pinch, pink, 'to pierce', pique, piquet,
pitch, 'to throw'. Cp. also pick, v.

## pike
pike, п., a weapon with a long shaft. — F. pique,
fr. piquer, 'to prick, pierce'. See pike, 'a sharp
point', and cp. pick, 'pointed instrument'.
Derivative: pike, tr. v., to pierce with or as with
a pike.

## pike
pike, п., a voracious fresh-water fish. — Short for
pikefish, lit. 'the fish with a pointed beak', fr.
pike, 'a sharp point'. Cp. pickerel. For sense
development cp. F. brochet, 'pike', fr. broche, 'a
spit'.

## pike
pike, п., top of a mountain. — Of Norse origin;
rel. to E. pike, 'a sharp point'.

## pike
pike, п., toll bar. — Abbreviation of turnpike.

## pikelet
pikelet, п., a crumpet {Local English). —
Shortened fr. obsolete bara-picklet, fr. W. bara-
pyglyd.

## pikul
pikul, n. — See picul.

## pilaf
pilaf, n. — See pilau.

## pilar
pilar, adj., hairy. — Formed with adj. suff. -ar
fr. L. pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair'.

## pilau
pilau, pilaf, pilaw, п., an Oriental dish of rice
boiled with meat, etc. — Turk, pilaw, fr. Pers.
paluv.

## pilaster
pilaster, п., a square column. — MF. (= F.) pi-
lastre, fr. It. pilastro, fr. ML. pilastrum, fr. L.
pila, 'pillar'. See pillar and -aster.
Derivatives: pilaster-ed, adj., pilaster-ing, n.

## Piinte
Piinte, п., a Roman surname, esp. surname of
Pontius, a governor of Judaea. — L. Ptlutus, lit.
'armed with javelins', fr. pilum, 'javelin' (see
pile, 'pointed stake').

## pilaw
pilaw, n. — See pilau.

## pilch
pilch, n, 1) orig. an outer garment made of skin;
2) a light saddle; 3) an infant's triangular
wrapper, worn over the diaper. —■- OE. pylece,
fr. ML. pellicea, 'furred garment', prop. fem. of
L. pelliceus, 'made of skins', fr. pellis, 'skin'. See
fell, 'hide', and cp. pelisse.

## pilchard
pilchard, п., name of a fish of the herring family.
— Fr. earlier pitcher, a word of uncertain origin.

## pile
pile, п., a heavy timber or beam driven into the
ground to serve as a support. — ME., 'dart,
stake', fr. OE.pil, 'pointed stake, prickle', fr. L.
pilum, 'javelin; pestle' (whence also ON. pila,
OHG., MHG. pfil (G. Pfeil), 'arrow'], which is
rel. to L. pila, 'mortar'. See pestle and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: pile, tr. v., to drive piles into,
piling, n.

## pile
pile, п., the reverse of a coin. — Prob. fr. pile, 'a
heap'.

## pile
pile, п., a large heap. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)pile,
fr. L. pila, 'pillar'. See pillar and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also the second element in
thermopile.
Derivative: pile, tr. v., to form a pile.

## pile
pile, п., soft, fine hair. — ME., fr. L. pilus, 'hair',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:589 -->

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:589 COLUMN:1 -->
rel. to pita, 'ball, playing ball', prob. also to
pilteus, 'a felt cap', and cogn. with Gk. πίλος,
'felt'. Cp. depilate, peel, 'to strip off', pelage,
pellet, pelon, peiota, pelt, 'to strike', Pilea, pileus,
pill, 'a little ball of medicine', pili, 'to rob; to
peel', pilule, platoon, plot, 'to press into cakes',
plot, 'conspiracy', pluck, plush, poilu, and the
second element in caryopilite, caterpillar, horri-
pilate.
Derivative: pit-ed, adj., covered with hair.

## Pllea
Pllea, п., a genus of plants, the richweed (bot.) —
ModL., fr. L. pileus, more exactly pilleus, 'felt
cap'. See pileus.

## piles
piles, n. pi., hemorrhoids. — Lit. 'balls', fr. L.
pila, 'ball'. See pile, 'hair'.

## pileus
pileus, the cap of a mushroom (bot.) — L. pileus,
more exactly pilteus, 'felt cap', which is prob.
rel. to pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair'.

## pilfer
pilfer, intr. v. — MF. pelfrer, fr. pelfre, 'booty'.
Cp. pelf.
Derivatives: pilfer-age, п., pilfer-er, п.,
pilfering, п., pilfer-ing-ly, adv.

## pilgarlic
pilgarlic, п., a bald-headed person. — Prop, 'one
' resembling a peeled garlic', fr. pill, 'to peel', and
garlic.

## pilgrim
pilgrim, n. — ME. pelegrim, fr. OF. peligrin,
peterin (F. pelerin), fr. Late L. pelegrinus, dis-
similated fr. L. peregrinus, 'foreigner, stranger'.
See peregrine and cp. pelerine. For the change
of final -л to -m cp. grogram and venom.
Derivatives: pilgrim, intr. v., pilgrimage (q.v.),
pilgrim-atic, pitgrim-atic-at, adjs., pilgrim-er, п.,
pilgrim-ess, п., pitgrim-ize, intr. and tr. v.

## pilgrimage
pilgrimage, n. — ME., fr. OF. peirimage, peleri-
nage, fr. peteriner, 'to go on a pilgrimage', fr.
pelerin. See prec. word and -age.
Derivative: pilgrimage, intr. v.

## pili-
pili-, combining form meaning 'hair'. — L. pili-,
fr. pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair'.

## piliferous
piliferous, adj., bearing hairs (bot.) —
Compounded of pili- and L. ferre, 'to bear, carry'.
See -ferous.

## pUifbrm
pUifbrm, adj., bairlike. — Compounded of pill-
and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## pill
pill, п., a little ball of medicine. — L. pilula, lit.
'a little ball', dimin. oipila, 'ball', which is rel.
to pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair'.
Derivative: pill, tr. v., to form into pills, dose
with pills.
рШ, tr. v., to rob, pillage (archaic); to peel (dial.
English) — ME. pillen, pilen, fr. OE. pilian, 'to
strip, plunder; "to peel' (whence also E. peel),
which prob. derives fr. MF. (= F.) piller, 'to
plunder', fr. VL. "pilleare, 'to plunder', fr. L.
pilteus, pilleum, 'cap of felt' (in Late L. pilteus
meant 'rag, scrap, bit*), which is rel. to pilus,
'hair'. See pile, 'hair', and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivative: pill-ed, adj.

## pillage
pillage, n. — ME-, fr. MF. (= F.) ft. filler, 'to
pillage, plunder', fr. VL. "pilleare. See prec.
word and -age.
Derivatives: pillage, tr. and intr. v.,pillag-er, n.

## pillar
pillar, n. — ME. piler, fr. OF. piler, fr. VL. pilare,
fr. L. pila, 'pillar', which stands for *peila, and
is rel. to Oscan eh-peilatasset, 'they are set up'.
Cp. pile, 'a large heap', pilaster, pillory. Cp. also
compile, oppilate.
Derivative: pillar, tr. v.

## pillaret
pillaret, n. — Dimin. formed fr. prec. word with
suff. -et.

## pillion
pillion, п., a kind of saddle. — Gael, pillean,
dimin. oipeall, 'skin', fr. L.pellis. See fell, 'hide'
and cp. pell, pellicle.

## pilliwinks
pilliwinks, п., an old Scottish instrument of
torture. — ME. pyrewinkes, of unknown origin.

## pillory
pillory, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) pilori, fr. ML.

## pilorium
pilorium, of s.m., a derivative of L. pila, 'pillar'.
See pillar and subst. suff. -ory.
Derivative: pillory, tr. v.

## pillow
pillow, n. — ME. pitwe, fr. OE. pyle, pylu, fr. L.

## pulnnus
pulnnus, 'cushion, pillow', whence also OS. puli,
MDu. polu (Du. peluw), OHG. pfuliwi, pfulwo
(MHG. pfulwe, G. Pfuhl), of s.m. See pulvinus.
Derivatives:pi//oM', tr. and intr. v.,pillow-y, adj.

## pilocarpine
pilocarpine, pilocarpi!!, п., an alkaloid CjjH^NjOj
(chem.) — See next word and chem. surf, -ine, -in.

## Pilocarpus
Pilocarpus, п., a genus of shrubs of the rue

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:589 COLUMN:2 -->
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. πίλος,
'felt', and καρπός, 'fruit'. See pile, 'hair', and
carpel,

## pilose
pilose, adj., covered with hair (bot.) — L. pilosus,
'hairy', fr. pilus, 'hair'. See pile, 'hair', and adj.
suff. -ose, and cp. pilous,
pllosity, п., the state of being pilose. — ML.
pilositas, fr. L. pilosus. See prec. word and -ity.

## pilot
pilot, n. — MF. (= F.) pilote, fr. It. pilota, fr.
OIL pedota, fr. Byzantine Gk. "πηδώτης,
'steersman', fr. Gk. πηδόν, 'the blade of an oar',
which is rel. to πηδάλιον, 'rudder', πηδαν, 'to
bound', πήδημα, 'a leaping, bounding', fr. l.-E.
base *ped-, enlarged form of base "ped-, 'foot',
whence Gk. πέδη, 'fetter', πέδαν, 'ground,
earth', πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot', L. pes, gen.
pedis, Goth, fetus, OE. fot, 'foot'. See foot and
words there referred to and cp. esp. pedesis.
Derivatives: pilot-less, adj., pilot-ry, n.

## pilot
pilot, tr. v. — F. piloter, fr. pilote. See pilot, n.
Derivatives: pilot-age, п., pilot-ing, п., pilot-ism,
n.

## pilous
pilous, adj., pilose. — L. pilosus, 'hairy', fr- pilus,
'hair'. See pilose and adj. suff. -ous.

## pilpul
pilpul, п., discussion, esp. discussion in the
Talmud. — Aram, and Heb. pilpul, 'discussion,
debate', rel. to Heb. pilpel, 'he spiced, he
seasoned' (whence arose the meaning 'he argued,
debated, he disputed violently'), denominated
fr. pilpel, 'pepper', fr. OI. pippali, 'berry,
pepper', whence also Gk. πέπερι, 'pepper'. Cp.
pepper.
Derivatives: pilpul-ist, п., pilpul-ist-ic, adj.

## pilule
pilule, п., a little pill. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. pilula,
lit. 'a little ball', dimin. of pila. See pill, 'a little
ball of medicine', and -ule.
Derivatives: pilul-ar, pilul-ous, adjs.

## pimelosis
pimelosis, п., obesity (med.) — Medical L.,
formed with suff. -osis fr. Gk. πϊμελής, 'fat' (adj.),
fr. πϊμελή, 'fat, lard', which is rel. to πϊαρ, 'any
fatty substance', πίων, 'fat'. See ptue, the tree,
and cp. words there referred to.

## pimento
pimento, n. 1) the Spanish paprika; 2) allspice. —
Sp. pimienta. Port, pimento, 'pepper' (whence
also F. piment), fr. Late L. pigmenta, pi. of
pigmentum, 'plant juice', fr. L. pigmentum,
'paint, coloring matter', in ML. 'aromatic spice',
from the stem of pingere, 'to paint'. See pigment,

## pimiento
pimiento, п., sweet pepper. — Sp., fr. pimienta.
See prec. word.

## pimp
pimp, п., procurer, pander. — Of uncertain
origin; possibly connected with V.pimper, 'to coax,
wheedle', OProvenc. pipar, pimpar, 'to dress
up', which are related to F. piper, 'to peep,
cheep, to lure birds'. See pipe.
Derivative: pimp, intr. v.

## pimpernel
pimpernel, п., a plant of the primrose family. —
ME. pympernele, fr. OF. (= F.) pimprenelle,
'burner, fr. ML. pimpernella, for *piperinella, a
derivative of L. piper, 'pepper' (see pepper); so
called because its fruit resembles peppercorns.

## Pimpinella
Pimpinella, п., a genus of plants of the carrot
family (bot') — ModL., fr. VL. 'bipinella,
dimin. of L. bipennis, 'two-winged'; so called in
allusion to the bipinnate leaves. The word
Pimpinella was prob. influenced in form by ML.
pimpernella. See prec. word.

## pimping
pimping, п., puny, petty; sickly. — Of uncertain
etymology; perh., like G. pimpeln, 'to whine,
complain, be sickly', pimpelig, 'sickly,
