effeminate', of imitative origin. For the ending see adj.
suff. -ing.

## pimple
pimple, n. — MB.pinple, prob. a nasalized
derivative of the imitative base *pap-, 'to swell',
occurring in L. papula, 'swelling, pimple', papilla,
'nipple'. See papula.
Derivatives: pimple, tr. and intr. v., pimpl-ed,

## pimpl-ous
pimpl-ous, pimpl-y, adjs., pimpl-i-ness, n.

## pin
pin, п., peg; short piece of wire.— ME. pinne, fr.
OE. pinn, 'peg, pin*, rel. to ON. pinni, 'peg, tack',
MDu. pin, pinne, 'pin, peg', OHG. pfinn, MHG.

## pfinne
pfinne, G. Pinne, 'pin, tack'; prob. fr. I.-E. base
*bend-, 'anything protruding', whence also Mir.
benn, 'horn, summit', W. балл, 'elevation'. Cp.
peen, pen, 'enclosure', pintle. E. pint, 'a measure',
is not related.
Derivatives: pin, tr. v., pinn-er, п., pinn-y, adj.

## pina
pina, п., pineapple. — Sp., fr. L. pinea,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:589 COLUMN:3 -->
'pineapple, pinecone', prop. fem. of pineus, 'of the
pine', used as a noun, fr. pinus, 'pine". See pine,
4he tree, and cp. pineal.

## Pinaceae
Pinaceae, n. pi., the pine family (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. pinus, 'pine'. See pine, the tree, and -aceae.

## pinafore
pinafore, п., a sleeveless apron worn by children.
— Lit. 'pinned in front', compounded of the
verb pin, 'to fasten with a pin' (see pin), and
afore.
Derivative: pinafor-ed, adj.

## pinaster
pinaster, п., a Mediterranean pine. — L.pinaster,
'wild pine', fr. pinus, 'pine'. See pine, the tree,
and -aster.

## pince-nez
pince-nez, п., folding eyeglasses. — F., lit. 'pinch-
nose', fr. pincer, 'to pinch' and nez, 'nose', fr. L.
nasus. See pinch and nasal.

## pincers
pincers, n. pi., a gripping tool with two parts prVr
oted together. — ME. pynceours, pinsours, fr.
MF. *pinceours, agent name formed fr. MF.pin-
cier, pincer (F. pincer), 'to pinch'. Ср. Е. pinchers
which is derived in a similar way from the verb
pinch (q.v.)

## pincette
pincette, п., small pincers. — F., a dimin. formed
fr. pincer, 'to pinch'. See prec. word and -ette.

## pinch
pinch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. pinchen, fr. ONF.
'pinchier, corresponding to OF. pincier (F.
pincer), fr. VL. *pinctidre (whence also It. pinzare,
Sp. pinchar, 'to prick, pierce'), which is prob. a
blend of VL. *punctiare, 'to prick, pierce' (fr. L.
punctum, 'point, puncture'), and VL. *plccare,
of s.m. See point, п., and pike, 'a sharp point',
and cp. pince-nez, pincers, pincette. ,
Derivatives: pinch, п., pinch-ed, adj., pinch-ed-
ly, adv., pinch-ed-ness, п., pinch-er, n.

## pinchbeck
pinchbeck, п., an alloy of zinc, tin and copper. —
Named after its inventor, C. Pinchbeck, a
London watchmaker, who died in 1732.
Derivative: pinchbeck, adj.

## Pindari
Pindari, п., one of a horde of marauders in India
in the 18th and early 19th centuries. — Hind.
pindara, Marathi pendhari, possibly from the
place-name Рапфаг.

## Pindaric
Pindaric, adj., pertaining to, or in the style of,
Pindar. — L. Pindaricus, fr. Gk. Πινδαρικός, fr.
Πίνδαρος, 'Pindar', a Greek lyric poet (about
522-443). For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: Pindaric, п., a Pindaric ode.

## pine
pine, intr. v. — ME. pinen, fr. OE. pinian, 'to
torture, torment, afflect', fr. *pin, 'pain', fr. L.
poena, 'punishment'. See penal and cp. pain. Cp.
also repine.

## pine
pine, п., a tree of the genus Pinus (bot.) — ME.,
fr. OE. pin, (in ME. fr. F. pin), fr. L.pinus, 'pine',
which is cogn. with OI. pituh, 'juice, sap, resin,
food', pltu-ddruh, 'a kind of pine', lit. 'resini-
ferous tree' (for Of. daru, 'tree', cp. Gk. δρυς,
'oak', and see dryad), Gk. πίτυς, 'pine'. These
words are traceable to I.-E. base pi-, 'sap, juice',
whence also Gk. πΐων, 'fat, wealthy', πϊμελή,
'fat, lard', πίσσα (for *пЫ\,л), 'pitch', L. pin-
guis, 'fat', pituita, 'slime, phlegm, viscous
moisture', opimus, 'fat, fertile, rich'. See fat and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also pina, pinaster,
pinea], pinetum, pinnace, piflon.
Derivatives: pin-er, п., pin-ery, п., pin-y, adj.
pinea], adj., pertaining to, or shaped like, a pine-
cone. — F. pineal, fr. L. pinea, 'pine cone', fem.
of pineus, 'of the pine', ft. pinus, 'pine'. See pine,
the tree, and adj. suff. -al, and cp. pina.

## piaetum
piaetum, п., a plantation of pine trees. — L.
pinetum, 'pine wood, pine grove', ft.pinus, 'pine'.
See pine, the tree. For the suff. cp. arboretum, 'a
place grown with trees', fr. arbor, 'tree' (see
arboretum).

## pinfold
pinfold, п., a pound for straying animals. — ME.
pynfold, fr. OE. pundfald, which is compounded
of *pund, 'pound', and fold, 'fold'. See pound,
'enclosure', and fold, 'pen'.

## ping
ping, п., the sound made by a bullet; intr. v., to
make a sound (said of a bullet). — Imitative.

## Ping-Pong
Ping-Pong, п., trade name for table tennis. —
Imitative.

## Pinguicula
Pinguicula, п., a genus of plants, the butterwort
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. pinguiculus, 'fattish',
dimin. of pinguis. See ptuguid and -cule.

## pinguid
pinguid, adj., fat, greasy. — L.pinguis, 'fat', cogn.
with opi-mus, 'rich', ρϊ-nus, 'pine', pi-tuita,
'slime', fr. I.-E. base "pi-, 'sap, juice'. See pine,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:590 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 563 | PIRN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:590 COLUMN:1 -->
the tree.
Derivative: pinguid-ity, n.

## pinion
pinion, п., distal or terminal segment of a bird's
wing. — ME. pynyon, fr. MF. pig/ton, a
secondary form of penon, pennon, fr. VL. 'pinnionem,
ace. of pinnio, fr. L. pinna, 'feather, wing'. See
pinna, 'leaf, and cp. next word.
Derivative: pinion, tr. v.

## pinion
pinion, п., a small cogged wheel which gears with
a larger one. — F. pignon, 'gable; pinion', fr.
VL. 'pinnionem, ace. of 'pinnio, 'battlement',
fr. L. pinna, 'battlement, pinnacle'. See pinna.

## pinite
pinite, п., a hydrous petassium-aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — G. Pinit, from the Pini mine in
Saxony. The suff. -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## pinite
pinite, п., a sweet crystalline substance (chem.) —
Formed fr. L. pinus, 'pine'. See pine, the tree,
and subst. suff. -ite.

## pink
pink, п., any plant of the genus Dianthus. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pink, adj., of the color pink,
pinkish, adj., pink-ness, п., pink-y, adj.

## pink
pink, п., a kind of sailing vessel. — MDu. pincke
(Du. pink).

## pink
pink, tr. v., to stab, pierce. — ME. pinken; prob.
a nasalized var. of the verb pick.
Derivatives: pink-er, п., pink-ing, n.

## pink
pink, п., a young salmon. — Cp. dial. G. Pinke.

## pinkie
pinkie, also pinky, п., a boat. — Formed fr. pink,
'vessel', with suff. -ie, resp. -y.

## Pinkster
Pinkster, also pingster, pinxter, п., Whitsuntide
(USA.) — MDu. pinxter, pinxieren, pinster
(Du. pinksier, pinksteren), fr. Gk. πεντηκοστή
(scil. ήμέρϊ), 'fiftieth (day)' (prob. through the
medium of Goth, paintekuste). See Pentecost.

## pinna
pinna, п., 1) a single leaf (bot.); 2) fin (zool.)\ 3)
the external ear (anal.) — L. pinna, 'feather,
wing; fin of a fish; battlement, pinnacle', which,
according to F. S. Sommer (in Kritische Erlau-
terungen zur lateinischen Laut- und Formen-
lehre, Heidelberg, 1914, pp. 15 f.), is a dial. var.
of penna. See pen, 'feather'. See also Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., 11, pp. 306-307 s.v. pinna.
Derivative: pinn-al, adj.

## Pinna
Pinna, п., a genus of marine bivalves (zool.) — L.
pinna, fr. Gk. πίννα, 'a kind of long-shaped
bivalve', which is of uncertain origin.

## pinnace
pinnace, п., a kind of light vessel. — MF. pinasse,
pinace (F. piniche), fr. OSp. (= Sp.) pinaza,
'pinnace', orig. 'a thing made of pinewood', fr.
pino, 'pine', fr. L. pinus. See pine, the tree.

## pinnacle
pinnacle, п., 1) a slender turret; 2) the highest
point. — Late L. pinnaculum, 'peak, pinnacle',
dimin. of L. pinna. See pinna and -ele.
Derivative: pinnacle, tr. v.

## pinnate
pinnate, adj., 1) shaped like a feather (zool); 2)
having leaflets arranged on either side of a
common axis (bot.) — L. pinnatus, .'feathered,
winged', fr. pinna, 'feather, wing'. See pinna, 'leaf,
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: pinnat-ed, adj., pinnate-ly, pinnat-
ed-ly, advs., pinnat-ion, n.

## pinnati-
pinnati-, combining form meaning 'pinnate'. —
Fr. L. pinnatus. See prec. word.

## pinnatifld
pinnatifld, adj., cleft in a pinnate manner (bot.) —
Compounded of pinnati- and L. -fidus, from the
stem of findere, perf. fidi, 'to cleave'. See -fid.

## pinnatiped
pinnatiped, adj., having lobes to the toes (orni-
thol.) — Compounded of pinnati- and the stem
of L. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See pedal.

## pinner
pinner, п., hairdress with long flaps; pinafore. —
Formed with agential suff. -er fr. pin, 'to fasten
with a pin'. See pin.

## pinni-
pinni-, combining form meaning^m от feather. —
Fr. L. pinna. See pinna, 'leaf'.

## Pinnigrada
Pinnigrada, n. pi., another name for Pinnipedia
(zool.) — ModL., lit. 'moving by means of
flippers', fr. L. pinna, 'fin', and the stem of gradior,
gradi, 'to walk', whence also gradus, 'step'. See
grade.

## pinnigrade
pinnigrade, adj. and n. — See prec. word.

## pinniped
pinniped, adj. and n. — See next word.

## Pinnipedia
Pinnipedia, n. pi., a suborder of aquatic
carnivorous mammals, the seals and walruses (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'having feet serving as fins', fr. L.

## pinna
pinna, 'fin', andpe's, gen.pedis, 'foot'. Seepinni-
and pedal.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:590 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: pinniped-ian, adj. and n.
pinnothere, pinnotere, n. — See next word.

## Pinnotheres
Pinnotheres, п., a genus of small crabs (zool.) —
L. pin(n)otheres, pin(n)otires, 'a small crab
(found in the shell of the mussel)', compounded
of Gk. πίννα, 'a kind of long-shaped bivalve'
(see Pinna), and τηρεΐν, 'to watch over, take
care of, guard', which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base
qwei-, *qw'-, 'to respect, consider'. See penal and
cp. synteresis.

## pinnula
pinnula, п., 1) pinnule (bot.); 2) barb of a feather
(zool.) — L. pinnula. See next word.

## pinnule
pinnule, п., 1) a small fin (zool.); 2) part of a
pinnate leaf (bot.) — L. pinnula, dimin. of pinna,
'feather*. See pinna, 'leaf, and -ule.

## pinochle
pinochle, pinocle, п., a card game resembling
bezique. — Of unknown origin.

## pinoie
pinoie, п., parched seeds of maize, etc.; an
aromatic powder used in making chocolate. — Sp.,
fr. Nahuatl pinolli.

## piflon
piflon, п., 1) any of various pine trees; 2) their
seed. — Sp. ρ'ιηόη, 'pine nut, kernel', fr. piha,
'pine nut', fr. L. pinea, 'pine nut', prop. fem. of
the adj. pineus, 'pertaining to a pine', fr. pinus,
'pine'. See pine, the tree.

## pint
pint, n. — ME. pinte, fr. OF. (= F.)pinte, fr. VL.
*pincta, the same as ~L.picta, fem. pp. o( pingere,
'to paint'; so called from the painted gauge sign.
ΟΡΓονεης., Sp. and It. pinta also derive fr.
VL. 'pincta. See paint and cp. next word. Cp.
also pintado.

## pinta
pinta, п., a tropical chronic skin disease (med.) —-
Amer. Sp., fr. Sp., 'spot, stain, mark', fr. VL.
'pincta. See prec. word.

## pintado
pintado, п., 1) a large fish of the mackerel
family; 2) the guinea fowl. — Port, pintado,
'painted', pp. of pintar, 'to paint', fr. VL. *pinctus,
corresponding to L. pictus, pp. of pingere, 'to
paint'. See paint and cp. prec. word. Cp. also
pint.

## pintle
pintle, п., a pin. — ME. pintel, 'penis, pintle', fr.
OE. pintel, 'penis', a diminutive form. Cp. LG.
pint, 'penis', and see dimin. suff. -Ie.

## Pinus
Pinus, п., a genus of trees, the pine (bot.) — L.
pinus. -See pine, the tree.

## pinxit
pinxit, v., he (or she) painted it. — L., 3rd sing,
perfect of pingere, 'to paint'. See paint.

## pio-
pio-, before a vowel pi-, combining form meaning
'fat', as in pioscope. — Fr. Gk. πΐων, 'fat',
which is cogn. with L. pinguis, 'fat'. See pinguid.

## piolet
piolet, п., ice ax. — F., fr. Piemont. piolet, dimin.
of piola, 'ax', aphetic form of "apiola, itself
dimin. of apia, 'ax', which is a Teut. loan word.
See hatchet.

## pioneer
pioneer, n. — F. pionnier, 'foot soldier; pioneer',
fr. pion, 'foot soldier', fr. OF. peon, fr. L. pedo-
nem, acc. of pedo, 'foot soldier', fr. pes, gen.
pedis, 'foot'. See foot and -eer and cp. pawn, 'a
piece at chess', and peon.
Derivative: pioneer, tr. and intr. v.

## pioscope
pioscope, п., a variety of lactoscope. —
Compounded of pio- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν,
'to look at, examine'. See -scope.

## pious
pious, adj. — L. pius, 'dutiful, pious, devout,
tender, kind' (whence piare, 'to appease,
propitiate, expiate'); rel. to Umbr. pihaz (— L. pia-
tus), 'appeased', and perh. also to L. pu-rus,
'pure, clean'. See pure and cp. piety, pity, expiate
impiety. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivatives: pious-ly, adv., pious-ness, n.

## pip
pip, п., a disease of fowls. — ME. pippe, fr. MDu.
pippe (Du. pip), fr. VL 'pittita, 'pipita, for L.
pituita, 'phlegm, the pip in fowls'. G. Pips and
F. pipie are of the same origin. See pituitary.

## pip
pip, п., seed of apple, pear, etc. — Abbreviation
of pippin.
Derivative: pipp-y, adj.

## pip
pip, п., a spot on cards, dice, etc. — Earlier peep,
of uncertain origin.

## pip
pip, intr. v., to chirp or peep, as a chick; tr. v. to
break through (the shell of the egg). — A var.

## of peep
of peep,

## pipal
pipal, peepal, п., the bo tree. — Hind, pipal, fr.

## OI. pippali
OI. pippali, 'berry of the pipal tree', later
'peppercorn', whence also L. piper, 'pepper'. See

## pepper
pepper,

## pipe
pipe, n. — ME., fr. OE. pipe, 'tube, pipe (musical

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:590 COLUMN:3 -->
instrument)', fr. VL. 'pipa, 'a tube-shaped
musical instrument', back formation fr. L. pipdre,
'to peep, pip, chirp', which is of imitative origin.
Cp. It. and Sp. pipa, F. pipe, OHG. pfifa
(whence MHG. pfife, G. Pfeife), Du. pijp, OS.,
ON.pipa, Swed.pipa, Osin.pibe, which all derive
from VL. 'pipa. Cp. fife, peep, Ίο chirp',
pibroch, pigeon, pimp, pip, 'to peep'.
Derivatives: pipe, v. (q.v.), pipe-fut, pipe-less,
pipe-like, adjs.

## pipe
pipe, intr. and tr. v. — ME. pipen, fr. OE. plpan,
'to play on a pipe', fr. pipe; partly fr. pipe, n.
Derivatives: pip-ed, adj., pip-er, п., pip-ing, adj.
and п., pip-ing-ly, adv., pip-ing-ness, n.

## Piper
Piper, п., a genus of plants, the true pepper (bot.)
— L. piper, 'pepper'. See pepper.

## Piperaeeae
Piperaeeae, n. pi., the pepper family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## piperaceous
piperaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## piperazine
piperazine, also piperazi, п., a crystalline
substance (chem.) — Formed fr. piper(idine), az(ote)
and chem. suff. -ine.

## piperidine
piperidine, also piperidin, п., a liquid alkaloid
(chem.) — Formed fr. piper(ine) and sufT. -idine
(prop, the compound of the suffixes -ide and
-ine, both frequently used in chemistry).

## piperine
piperine, also piperin, п., a crystalline alkaloid
(chem.) — Formed with chem. suff. -ine fr. L.
piper, 'pepper'. See pepper.

## piperylene
piperylene, п., an oily unsaturated hydrocarbon
'(chem.) — Coined ft. piper(idine) and -ylene.

## pipette
pipette, п., a small pipe or tube. — F., dimin. of
pipe. See pipe, п., and -ette.
Derivative: pipette tr.v.

## pipistrel
pipistrel, pipistrelle, п., a very small species of bat.
— F. pipistrelle, fr. It. pipistrello, corruption of
Olt. vispistrello, vipistrello, which was formed
through metathesis fr. L. vespertilio, 'bat'. See
Vespertillo.

## pipit
pipit, п., one of various small singing birds of the
genus Anihus (ornithol.) — Of imitative origin.

## pipkin
pipkin, п., a small earthenware jar. — Prob. a
dimin. formed fr. pipe, in the sense of'cask'. For
the ending see suff. -kin.

## pippin
pippin, п., any of numerous varieties of apple. —
ME. pipin, 'kernel, seed', fr. OF. pepin (F. pepiri),
'pip (of an apple)', which is of imitative origin.
Cp. It. pippolo, Sp. pepita, 'seed, kernel', which
are also imitative. Cp. also pip, 'seed'.

## piquancy
piquancy, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## piquant
piquant, adj. — F., pres. part, oipiquer, 'to prick'.
See pique, 'to nettle', and -ant.
Derivatives: piquant-ly, adv., piquant-ness, n.

## pique
pique, tr. and intr. v., to nettle — F. piquer, 'to
prick, sting'. See pike, 'a sharp point'.
Derivative: pique, n.

## pique
pique, п., in piquet, scoring of 30 points by one
player before the other player scores at all. —
F. pic, 'pick, pickaxe; pique'. See pike, 'a sharp
point', and cp. piqnet, repique.
Derivative: pique, tr. v., to score a pique against.

## pique
pique, п., cotton fabric. — F., prop. pp. oipiquer,
'to prick'. See pique, 'to nettle'.

## piquet
piquet, п., a card game. — F., dimin. οι pic, fr.
[aire pic, a term used in the game of piquet, fr.

## pic
pic, 'pick, pickaxe; pique'. See pike, 'a sharp
point', and -et.

## piracy
piracy, n. — ML. piratia, fr. Gk. πειρατεία,
'piracy', fr. πειρατής. See pirate and -cy.

## piragua
piragua, п., a canoe made from the hollowed
trunk of a tree. — Sp. See pirogue.

## piranha
piranha, п., a caribe (ichthyol.) — Port., fr. Tupi
piranha.

## pirate
pirate, n. — L. pirata, fr. Gk. πειρατής, 'pirate,
corsair', fr. πειρϊν, 'to attempt, attack', fr.
πείρα, 'trial, attempt, experience', which is cogn.
with L. peritus, 'experienced', periculum, 'trial,
experiment, risk, danger'. See peril and cp.
empiric, experience.
Derivatives: pirate, intr. and tr. v., piratical
(q.v.)

## piratical
piratical, adj., also piratic. — L. piraticus,
'pertaining to pirates', fr. Gk. πειρατικός, fr.
πειρατής. See prec. word and -ical.
Derivative: piratical-ly, adv.

## pirn
pirn, п., bobbin, spool, reed. — ME. pyrne, of
uncertain origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:591 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PIROGUE | 564 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:591 COLUMN:1 -->

## pirogue
pirogue, also piroque, п., a canoe made from the
hollowed trunk of a tree. — F., fr. Sp. piragua,
a word of Caribbean origin. Cp. piragua.

## pirouette
pirouette, п., a whirling about on tiptoe in
dancing. — F., *spinning top, pirouette', prob.
a blend of It. piruolo, 'peg top', and F. girouette,
'weathercock'.

## pirouette
pirouette, intr. v., to whirl about on tiptoe. — F.
pirouetter, fr. pirouette. See pirouette, n.
Derivatives: pirouett-er, п., pirouett-ist, n.

## pirssouite
pirssouite, п., a hydrous calcium sodium
carbonate (mineral.) — Named after the American
geologist Louis Valentine Pirsson (1860-1919).
For the ending see subst. surf. -ite.

## pis alter
pis alter, last resource. — F., lit. 'to go worse', fr.
pis, 'worse' (fr. L. pejus, neut. otpejor, 'worse'),
and alter, 'to go'. See pejorative and alley.

## pizanite
pizanite, п., a hydrous iron copper sulfate
(mineral.) — Named after the French chemist and
mineralogist Felix Pisani (1831-1920), who
analyzed it. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## piscary
piscary, п., the right of fishing (law). — ML.
piscaria, prop. neut. pi. of the L. adj. piscdrius,
'pertaining to fishing', fr. piscis, 'fish'. See
Pisces and adj. suflf. -ary.

## piscatology
piscatology, п., the science of fishing. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. piscatus, pp. of piscari, 'to fish', fr.
piscis, 'fish', and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See Pisces and -logy.

## piscator
piscator, п., a fisherman. — L. piscator, fr.
piscatus, pp. οι piscari, 'to fish'. See next word.

## piscatory
piscatory, adj., pertaining to'fishing. — L. piscd-
torius, 'of fishermen', fr. piscator, 'fisherman',
fr. piscatus, pp. of piscari, 'to fish', fr. piscis,
'fish'. See next word and adj. suff. -ory.
Derivatives: piscatory, п., piscatori-al, adj.

## Pisces
Pisces, n. pi., the twelfth sign of the zodiac. — L.,
pi. oipiscis, 'fish', cogn. with Goth, fisks, OHG.,
OE.fisc, 'fish'. See fish, 'an aquatic animal', and
cp. words there referred to.

## pisci-
pisci-, combining form meaning fish. — L. pisci-,
fr. piscis, 'fish'. See prec. word.

## pisciculture
pisciculture, п., fish culture. — Compounded of
pisci- and L. cultura, 'culture'. See culture.
Derivatives: piscicultur-al, adj., piscicultur-al-ly,
adv., piscicultur-ist! n.

## piscina
piscina, п., 1) fish pond; 2) stone basin in the wall
of a church. — L. piscina, 'fishpond, pond for
bathing, cistern, tank, reservoir', fr. piscis, 'fish'.
See Pisces and -ine (representing L. -ina).
Derivative: piscin-al, adj.

## piscine
piscine, п., bathing pool. — See prec. word.

## piscine
piscine, adj., pertaining to fish. — Formed with
sufT. -ine (representing L. -inus) fr. L.piscis, 'fish'.
See Pisces.

## pizcivorous
pizcivorous, adj., fish-eating. — Compounded of
pisci- and L. -torus, 'devouring'. See -vorous.

## pisi
pisi, п., puddled clay. — F., pp. of piser, 'to
pound', fr. L. pinsere, 'to beat, pound, crush',
whence pistillum, 'pestle'. See pestle.

## Pisgah
Pisgah, п., name of a mountain in Moab, from
which Moses saw the Promised Land. — Heb.
Pisgdh, lit. 'cleft'. Cp. the phrase Pisgah sight (in
allusion to Deut 3 : 27).

## pish
pish, interj., v. and n. — Imitative.

## pishogue
pishogue, п., witchcraft, sorcery. — Ir. piseog,
'sorcery'.

## pish-pash
pish-pash, п., rice soup containing small pieces of
meat (Anglo-Ind.)— Pers. pish-pash, 'broken to
pieces', fr. pashidan, 'to break to pieces'.

## Pisidium
Pisidium, п., a genus of freshwater bivalves (zool.)
— ModL., dimin. of L. pisum, 'pea'. See pease
and -idium.

## pisiform
pisiform, adj., shaped like a pea. — Compounded
of L. pisum, 'pea' and forma, 'form, shape'. See
pease and form, п., and cp. Pisum.

## pismire
pismire, п., ant. — ME. pissemire, pissemyre, lit.
'ejecting a urinelike fluid', fr. pisse, 'urine' (see
piss), and mire, myre, 'ant', which is rel. to ON.
maurr, Norw. maur, OSwed. tnyr, myra, Swed.
myra, Dan., Norw. myre, MDu. miere, Du.
mier, Crimean Goth, miera, 'ant', and cogn. with
Gk. μύρμηξ, L. formica, 'ant'. See formic and
cp. words there referred to.

## pisolite
pisolite, п., a limestone composed of globules
shaped like peas (petrogr.) — Lit. 'peastone', fr.
Gk. πίσας, 'pea' and λίθος, 'stone'. See pease

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:591 COLUMN:2 -->
and -lite.

## piss
piss, intr. and tr. v. — ME. pissen, fr. OF. pissier
(F. pisser), of imitative origin.

## pistachio
pistachio, n. — It. pistacchio (whence also F.
pistache, Sp. pistacho), fr. L. pistdcium, fr. Gk.
πιστάκιον, 'pistachio nut', fr. πιστάκη,
'pistachio tree', fr. Pers. pistalt, 'pistachio nut'. Cp.
fustic.

## pistareen
pistareen, п., an old Spanish coin. — Prob.
derived fr. Sp. peseta. See peseta.

## Pistia
Pistia, п., a genus of plants of the arum family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πιστός, 'liquid', rel. to
πίπίσκειν, 'to give to drink', which is formed
with reduplication fr. πϊνειν, 'to drink', fr. I.-E.
base "pi-, *po(i)-^ 'to drink', whence also L. po-
tdre, 'to drink', potio, 'a draft, drink'. See
potion.

## pistil
pistil, п., ovary of a seed plant (bot) — F., fr. L.
pistillum, 'pestle' (see pestle); so called in
allusion to its shape.
Derivatives: pistill-ar, pistill-ary, pistill-ate,
pistill-ine, adjs.

## pistilli-
pistilli-, combining form denoting the pistil. —
Fr. L. pistillum. See pistil.

## pistilliferous
pistilliferous, adj., containing a pistil. —
Compounded of pistilli- and -ferous.

## pistol
pistol, n. — MF. (= F.) pistole (whence the
dimin. piswlet), 'pistpl', fr. G. Pistole, fr. Czech
pistol, 'tube, pipe', formerly also 'fire-arm',
derived fr. pisk, whistle', which is of imitative
origin. For another weapon of Czech origin cp.
howitzer.
Derivative: pistol, tr. v.

## pistole
pistole, п., 1) a former Spanish gold coin; 2) any
of various former European gold coins. — F., fr.
It. piastola, dimin. of piastra, 'plate or leaf of
metal', fr. L. plastrum. See plaster, п., and cp.
piaster.

## pistoleer
pistoleer, pistolier, n. — F. pistolier, fr. pistole,
'pistol'. See pistol and -eer, resp. -ier.

## pistolet
pistolet, п., any of various former European gold
coins. — F., dimin. οι pistole. See pistole.

## pistolgram
pistolgram, п., an instantaneous photograph. —
Compounded of pistol and -gram.

## pistolgraph
pistolgraph, п., an apparatus for taking
instantaneous photographs. — A hybrid coined fr.
pistol and -graph.

## pistology
pistology, п., the study of faith. — Compounded
of Gk. πίστις, 'faith', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. Gk. πίστις stands
for *πίθ-τις, from the stem of πείθειν, 'to
persuade', fr. I.-E. base *bheidh-, *bhidh-, whence
also L.fidere, 'to trust, confide in'. See bid and
cp. fidelity. For the second element see -logy.

## piston
piston, п..— F., fr. MF., 'a large pestle', fr. OI.
(= It.) pistone, 'a piston', a var. of pestone, 'a
pestle', fr. pistare, a var. of pestare, 'to pound',
fr. Late L.pistdre, freq. ofL.pinsere (pp.pistus),
'to beat, pound'. See pestle and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -oon.

## pistrix
pistrix, п., a sea monster (Greek and Roman an-
tiq.) — L. pistrix, alteration of pristis, fr. Gk.
πρίστις, πρϊστις, 'a shark, whale, sea
monster', lit. 'sawyer', fr. πρΐειν 'to saw', whence
also πρίσμα, 'something sawn off'. See prism.
The change of pristis to pistrix (lit. 'a female
baker') is due to folk etymology.

## Pisum
Pisum, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — L. pisum, 'pea'. See pease and cp.
Pisidium.

## pit
pit, п., cavity. — ME. pyt, pit, put, fr. OE: pytt,
'pit, grave, pond', which—together with OS.
putti,Ofi.pyttr,T>a.put, OHG. p(f)uzza,p(f)uz-
zi (MHG., G. pfutze), 'pool, puddle', and It.
pozza, 'pool, puddle'—is borrowed fr. .L.
puteus, 'well, pit'. OF. puiz (whence F. putts),
'well, hole', derives fr. Frankish "putti, which
itself is a loan word fr. L. 'puteus. See puteal.
Derivatives: pit, tr. v., pitt-er, п., pitt-ing, n.

## pita
pita, п., the fiber of the century plant; agave. —
Sp., of Quechua origin.

## pit-a-pat
pit-a-pat, adv., palpitatingly; п., the sound of
something going pit-a-pat; intr. v., to go pit-a-
pat. — Of imitative origin.

## pitarrnh
pitarrnh, п., a basket or coffer used to carry the
clothes of a person traveling by palankin (India).
— Hind, pitdrd,petard, fr. OI. pitakah, 'basket',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:591 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. pitah, pitam, 'basket', which is rel. to Pali
pitaka-, petika-, pettdlah, 'basket', pela, pelikd,
'a large basket', Singhalesepelawa, pettiya,
'basket' ; prob. of non-Aryan origin.

## pitch
pitch, п., a resinous substance. — ME. pich, fr.
OE. pic, fr. L. pix, gen. picis, 'pitch', which is
cogn. with Gk. πίσσα (for *πίκι.α), Lith.pikis,
OSlav. pikla, 'pitch', fr. I.-E. base *pt-, 'sap,
juice', whence also L. pinus, 'pine', pituita,
'slime, phlegm, viscous moisture'. See fat, adj.,
and cp. pine, the tree, pituitary. Cp. also pay, 'to
coat with pitch', petechia, picamar, Picea, pitta-
cal, pizza.
Derivatives: pitch-y, ad).,pitch-i-ness, n.

## pitch
pitch, v., to set up; to throw. — ME. pichen,
picchen, prob. rel. to pick, 'to pierce', pike,'a
sharp point' (qq.v.)
Derivatives: pitch, n.,pitch-ed, adj.,pitch-er, п.,
pitch-ing, n.

## pitch
pitch, tr. v., to cover with pitch. — ME. pichen,
fr. OE. pician, fr. pic, 'pitch'. See pitch, n.
Derivative: pitch-er, n.

## pitchblende
pitchblende, n. (mineral) — Loan translation of
G. Pechblende. See pitch, 'resinous substance',
and blende.

## pitcher
pitcher, n. — ME. picher, fr. OF. pichier, fr. VL.
*piccdrium, a var. of bicdrium, fr. Gk. βίκος,
'earthen wine vessel'. See beaker.
Derivatives: pitcher-ed, pitcher-ful, adjs.

## pitchfork
pitchfork, n. — Fr. earlier pickfork, a compound
of pick, 'a pointed instrument', and fork;
influenced in form by an association with pitch, 'to
throw'.
Derivative: pitchfork, tr. v.

## pitchstone
pitchstone, n. — Loan translation of G. Pechstein.
See pitch, 'resinous substance', and stone.

## piteous
piteous, adj. — ME. pitous, fr. OF. pitos (F. pi-
teux), fr. VL. pietdsus, 'dutiful', fr. L. pietds. See
piety and -ous.
Derivatives: piteous-ly, adv., piteous-ness, n.

## pith
pith, n. — ME. pithe, pith, fr. OE. pipa, 'pith', rel.
to MDu. pitte, Du. pit.
Derivatives: pith, tr. v., to kill by piercing the
spinal cord, pith-less, adj., pith-y, adj., pith-i-ly,
adv., pith-i-ness, n.

## pithecanthrope
pithecanthrope, n. — See next word.

## Pithecanthropus
Pithecanthropus, п., a genus of extinct primates
(zool.) — ModL., lit. 'monkey man', coined by
Dr. Eugene Dubois (1858-1941), physician of
the Dutch army in Java, fr. Gk. πίθηκος, 'ape,
monkey', and ίίνθρωπος, 'man'. For the first
element see pitheco- and cp. the second element
in Cercopithecus. For the second element see
anthropo-.
Derivative: pithecanthrop-ic, adj.

## pitheco-
pitheco-, before a vowel pithec-, pertaining to an
ape or monkey. — Gk. πίθηκο-, πιθηκ-, fr.
πίθηκος, 'ape, monkey', which—like the
related πίθων, 'little ape'—is of uncertain
etymology.

## pithecoid
pithecoid, adj., resembling an ape. —
Compounded of Gk. πίθηκος, 'ape, monkey', and
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See prec.
word and -old.

## pithecology
pithecology, п., the study of apes. — Compounded
of pitheco- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic').
Derivative: pithecolog-ic-al, adj.

## pithos
pithos, п., a large earthen winejar (Greek archeol.)
— Gk. πίθος, which is dissimilated ίιι·*φίθος
and is cogn. with L. fidelia, 'clay vessel' (orig.
'anything tied up together'), fiscus, 'woven
basket, purse; treasury'. See fisc.

## pitiable
pitiable, adj. — ME. piteable, fr. OF. piteable (F.
pitoyable), fr. pile (F. pitie). See pity and -able.
Derivatives: pitiable-ness, п., pitiabl-y, adv.

## piton
piton, п., a peak. — F., 'peak of a mountain;
eyebolt'. Cp. Sp. piton, 'protuberance,
prominence'.

## pittucal
pittucal, п., eupittonic acid (chem.) — G. Pittacal,
Pittakal, coined by the German natural
philosopher and industrialist Baron Karl von Reichen-
bach (1788-1869) in 1835 fr. Gk. πίττα, πίσσα,
'pitch', and καλός, 'beautiful'. The first element
is cogn. with L. pix, gen. picis, 'pitch'; see pitch,
'resinous substance'. For the second element see
calo-, for the ending see adj. suff. -al.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:592 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 565 | PLAIN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:592 COLUMN:1 -->

## pittance
pittance, п., a dole. — ME. pitance, fr. OF. pi-
tance, 'pity' (whence F. pitance, 'allowance of
food, pious dole'), formed, with change of
suffix, fr. OF. pilie (F. pitie). See piety, pity, and
-ance.

## pittite
pittite, п., an auditor in the pit of a theater (col-
log.) — Formed fr. pit with subst. suff. -ite.

## pituitary
pituitary, adj., 1) pertaining to or secreting
mucus ; 2) of the pituitary gland. — L. pituitdrius,
'pertaining to phlegm', fr. pttuita, 'slime;
viscous moisture, phlegm', fr. I.-E. base *pt-, 'sap,
juice', whence also L. pinus, 'pine'. See pine, the
tree, and cp. Hypopltys. For the ending see
adj. suff. -ary.
Derivative: pituitary, n.

## pituitous
pituitous, adj., pituitary. — L. pituitdsus, 'full of
phlegm, pituitous', fr. pttuita. See prec. word
and -ous.
Derivative: pituitous-ness, n.

## pity
pity, n. — ME. pite, fr. OF. pile, pitet (F. pitie),
fr. L. pietdtem, ace. of pietds. See piety and cp.
piteous.
Derivatives: pity. tr. and intr. v., piti-ful, adj.,
piti-ful-ly, adv., piti-ful-ness, п., piti-less, adj.,
piti-less-Iy, adv., piti-less-ness, п., pity-ing, adj.,
pity-ing-iy, adv.

## pityriasis
pityriasis, п., a skin disease (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. Gk. πιτϋρίασις, 'scurf, dandruff', lit.
'branlike eruption of the skin', fr. πίτϋρον, 'bran',
which is cogn. with Mir. caith, 'dandruff'. For
the ending see surf, -iasis.

## piii
piii, adv., more (used in musical terms). — It., fr.
L. plus, 'more'. See plus.

## Pins
Pins, masc. PN. — L. pius, 'dutiful, pious'. See
pious.

## pivot
pivot, п., a point or pin, etc., on which something
turns. — F. pivot, of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pivot-at, adj., pivot-at-ly, adv.,
pivot-er, n.

## pivot
pivot, intr. v., to turn about on a pivot; tr. v., to
cause to pivot. — F. pivoter, fr. pivot. See pivot,
n.

## pixie
pixie, n. — A var. of pyxie.

## pixy
pixy, pixie, п., fairy, elf. — Fr. earlier pisky,
which is rel. to Swed. pysk, 'a little fairy'; of
uncertain origin.

## pixy
pixy, n. — A var. of pyxie.

## piyyut
piyyut,also spelledpiyut,п.,areligiouspoem added
to the liturgy of the Jewish festivals and
special Sabbaths. — Talmudic Heb. piyyut, 'poem,
hymn', in Medieval Heb. 'liturgic poem, liturgic
poetry', verbal nounoipiyyet, 'he wrote poetry',
in Medieval Heb. 'he wrote fiturgic poetry',
which is prob. a back formation fr. payyetan,
'poet'. See payyetan.

## pizza
pizza, also pizza pie, pie made of thinly rolled
bread dough. — It. pizza, prob. fr. VL. 'picea
(placenta), lit. 'pitchlike cake', which seems to
be a loan translation of MGk. πίττα, 'cake,
pie', fr. Gk. πίττα, 'pitch'. VL. "picea is prop,
fern, of the L. adj. piceus, 'of pitch', fr. pix, gen.
picis, 'pitch'. See pitch, 'resinous substance'.

## pizzicato
pizzicato, adv., adj. and п.,-direction to
performers on stringed instruments to pluck the
strings with the fingers instead of with the bow
(music). — It., 'plucked, twitched', pp. of pizzi-
care, 'to pluck, twitch', fr. pizzare, 'to sting,
prick', fr. pizzo, 'point, edge', which is prob. of
imitative origin.

## pizzle
pizzle, п., penis of an animal, esp. of a bull. —
Cp. Du. pees, 'sinew, string, pizzle'.

## placability
placability, n. — L. pldcdbilitds, 'placable
disposition', fr. placabilis. See next word and -ity,

## placable
placable, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) placable, fr.
L. placabilis, 'easily appeased, placable', fr.
pldcare, 'to appease'. See placate and -able.
Derivatives: placable-ness, п., placabt-y, adv.

## placard
placard, n. — ME. placquart, fr. OF. (= F.)
placard, fr. ptaquier (F. plaquer), 'to lay on,
plaster', fr. MDu.placken, 'to patch (a garment),
to plaster', which is related to MHG. placke, G.
Placken, 'spot, patch'. See plack and cp. plaque.
Derivatives: placard, tr. v., placard-er, n.

## placate
placate, tr. v., to appease. — L. placatus, pp. of
placdre, 'to appease', which is re], \ό placere, 'to
please', placidus, 'peaceful, quiet'. See please and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: placat-er, п., placat-ing-ly, adv.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:592 COLUMN:2 -->
placation (q.v.), placatory (q.v.)

## placation
placation, n. — L. pldcdtio, gen. -onis, 'an
appeasing', fr. ptdedtus, pp. of pldcare. See placate
and -ion.

## placatory
placatory, adj. — L. pldcdtorius, 'pertaining to
appeasing', fr. placatus, pp. οι pldcare. See
placate and adj. suff. -ory.

## place
place, n. — ME., fr. OF. (=- F.), fr. VL. *plattea
(whence also It. piazza, ΟΡΓΟνβης. plasa, Catal.
plassa, Sp. plaza, Port, ρταςα), fr. L. platea.
Open space, street', fr. Gk. πλατεία (οδός),
'street', lit. 'broad way', fern, of πλατύς, 'flat,
wide, broad', which is cogn. with OI. prathati,
'spreads out', prthiifi, 'broad, wide, spacious',
Avesticperepush, of s.m., Arm. lain, 'broad', L.
planta, 'sole of the foot', OSlav. plesno, of s.m.,
Lith. ptatus, '.broad', pletoti, 'to spread out',
plotyti, 'to fold', MDu. vlade, Du. via, vlade,
'cake', OHG. flado, Offering cake', MHG.
vlade, 'flat cake, honeycomb'. G. Fladen, 'flat
cake', Swed., Norw. flundra, MHG. vluoder,
G. Flunder, 'flounder', Olr. lethan, Co. ledan,
'broad'. All these words are derivatives of I.-E.
base *pldt-, *plet-, *plet-, *plot-, 'spread out,
broad, flat'. Cp. piazza and plaza, which are
doublets of place. Cp. also flat, 'level', flat,
'floor', flam), 'a kind of pie", Rounder, 'a fish',
placer, placeta, plaice, plantain, 'plant of the
genus Plantago', plane, the tree, plant, plantar,
plat, 'piece of ground', plat, 'course of meal',
plateasm, plateau, plate, platinum, Platon,
platter, platy-, plot, 'piece of ground', and the first
element in Plattdeutsch.
Derivatives: place, tr. v.,place-ment, n.,plac-er,
n.

## placebo
placebo, п., 1) the opening word of the antiphon
in verspers for the dead (R.C.Ch.); 2) a
medicine given merely to please a patient. — ME., fr.
L. placebo, Ί shall please', 1st pers. sing. fut. of
placere, 'to please' (see please); so called from
placebo, the initial word in the text of the
Vulgate, Ps. 114:9.

## placenta
placenta, п., a vascular organ on the wall of the
uterus with which the embryo is connected by
the umbilical cord (anat.) — L., 'cake', fr. Gk.
πλακόεντα, ace. of πλακόεις, 'fiat cake', which
is rel. to πλάξ, 'anything flat' (see plank); prob.
influenced in form by L. placere, 'to please'.
In its anatomical sense the word placenta was
first used by Realdo Colombo, Italian
anatomist of the 16th century. Cp. the second element
in leucoplakia.
Derivatives: placent-al, adj., placent-ary, adj.,
placent-ate, adj., placent-ation, n.

## Piacentaha
Piacentaha, n. pi., name of a division of
mammals (zool.) — ModL., neut. pi. of Late L. pla-
centdlis, fr. L. placenta. See prec. word.

## placentitis
placentitis, п., inflammation of the placenta
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. placenta with
suff. -iris.

## placer
placer, п., one who places. — Formed fr. place
with agential surf. -er.

## placer
placer, п., a glacial deposit containing valuable
minerals, as gold and platinum. — Am. Sp.
placer, fr. Sp. plaza, 'place', fr. L. platea, 'street,
open space', fr. Gk. πλατεία. See place.

## placet
placet, п., a vote expressed by the word 'placet1.
— L. placet, 'it pleases', 3rd sing. pres. indicat.
of placere, 'to please'. See please and cp. words
there referred to.

## placeta
placeta, п., a small garden by the side of a
building — Sp., 'small square', dimin. of plaza,
'square', fr. L. platea, 'street, open space'. See
place.

## placid
placid, adj. — L. placidus, 'peaceful, placid,
gentle, quiet', fr. placere, 'to please'. See please
and -id.
Derivatives: placid-ly, adv., placid-ness, n.

## placidity
placidity, n. — L. placiditds, 'mildness, placidity',
fr. placidus. See prec. word and -ity.

## plack
plack, п., a small coin formerly current in
Scotland. — Flemish placke, plecke, 'a small coin',
prop.'somethingflat'. Seeplaqueandcp. placard.

## placket
placket, п., pocket in a woman's skirt; a petticoat.
— Possibly a var. of placard.

## placoid
placoid, adj. and п., platelike. — Compounded
of Gk. πλάξ. gen. πλακός, 'level surface, plate'
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:592 COLUMN:3 -->
plank and -oid.

## plafond
plafond, n. — F., 'ceiling', fr. MF. platfond, lit.
'flat bottom'. F. plat derives fr. VL. *plattus,
fr. Gk. πλατύς, 'flat'; see platy-. F. fond comes
fr. L. fundus, 'bottom, basis'; see fund and cp.
fond, 'foundation'.

## plagal
plagal, adj., having its keynote in the middle of
its compass (music). — ML. plagalis, fr. plaga,
'plagal mode', back formation fr. plagius,
'plagal', fr. MGk. πλάγιος, 'plagal', fr. Gk.
πλάγιος, 'placed sideways, oblique, slanting', fr.
πλάγος, 'side', fr. I.-E. *p(e)ldg-, 'flat, spread
out', whence also Gk. πέλαγος, 'the open sea',
L. plaga, 'a hunting net'. I.-E. *p(e)ldg- is an
enlargement of base *р(е)Ш- whence L. planus,
'level, flat'. See plala, adj., and adj. suff. -al and
cp. pelagic, Pelasgic, plagiary, plagio-. Cp. also
flake, 'a thin flat piece', flake, 'rack for storing
goods', fleck, fluke, 'flatfish'.

## plagi-
plagi-, form of plagio- before a vowel.

## plagiary
plagiary, n. — L. plagidrius, 'plunderer,
oppressor, kidnapper; a literary thief, fr. plagium,
'kidnapping', fr.plaga, 'a hunting-net'. See prec.
word and -ary.
Derivatives: plagiar-ism, п., plagiar-ist, п.,
plagiar-ist-ic, adj., plagiar-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
plagiar~iz-ation, п., plagiar-iz-er, n.

## plagio-
plagio-, before a vowel plagi-, combining form
meaning Oblique, slanting'. — Gk. πλάγιο-,
πλάγι-, fr. πλάγιος, 'oblique, slanting'. See
plagal.

## plagioclase
plagioclase, п., triclinic feldspar (mineral) — G.
Plagioclas, coined by the German mineralogist
JohannAugustFriedrichBreithaupt(1791-1873)
in 1847 fr. Gk. πλάγιος, 'oblique, slanting' (see
plagal-), and κλάσις, 'a breaking', fr. κλαν, 'to
break'. See clastic and cp. words there referred
to.

## plagioclastic
plagioclastic, adj. — Compounded of plagio- and
Gk. κλαστος, verbal adj. of κλαν, 'to break'.
See clastic and cp. prec. word.

## plague
plague, n. — ME. plage, fr. MF. plague, fr. L.
pldga, 'stroke, blow, wound, pestilence', fr. I.-E.
base *pldq-, *pldg-, 'to strike', whence also Gk.
πλήσσειν, πληγνύναι, 'to strike',' πληγή, Dor.
πλϊγα, 'stroke, blow', L. plangere, 'to strike,
to beat the breast', 'to lament loudly' (orig. 'to
lament while beating the breast'), OE. fldcan, 'to
strike, beat', Goth., OS.ftokan, 'to bewail', OHG.
fluohhan, fluohhon, MHG. vluochen, G. fluchen,
OFris. floka, Du. vloeken, 'to curse' (orig. 'to
lament while beating the breast'). — According
to some philologists L. pldga is a -loan word fr.
Dor. πλϊγα. — It. piaga, F. plaie, 'wound,
sore, plague', Sp. plaga, 'plague, scourge,
calamity', llaga, 'wound, sore', Olr. plag (gen.
plaige), 'plague, pestilence', derive fr. L. pldga.
Cp. plain, 'to mourn', plaint, plangent, plankton,
plectrum, Plegadls, plessor, plexor, Aplectrum,
apoplexy, compinin, monoplegia, dyplegia,
paraplegia, Symplegades. Cp. also flaw, 'gust of
wind'.
Derivatives: plague, tr. v.,plagu-ed, adj., plagu-
er, п., plague-some, adj., plagu-y, adj.

## plaice
plaice, п., a European edible flatfish. — ME.
plais, plaice, fr. OF. plaise, plaie (F. plie), fr.
Late L. platessa, 'plaice, flatfish', which prob.
derives fr. Gk. πλατύς, 'flat'. See place.

## plaid
plaid, n. — Gael, plaid, 'blanket', prob.
contracted fr. peallaid, 'sheep skin', fr. peall, 'skin', fr.
L. pellis, 'skin, hide'. See fell, 'hide', and cp.
pillion.

## plain
plain, adj., flat; clear, distinct. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) plain, fr. L. planus, 'even, level, flat, clear,
distinct', fr. I.-E. base 'р(е)Ш-, 'broad, flat,
spread out', whence also Lith. plonas, 'thin',
Lett, plans, 'flat, thin', OPruss. plonis, 'threshing
floor', Gk. πέλανος, 'sacrificial cake'. Hitt.
palhi, 'broad'. Cp. plain, 'level country', plnne,
'even, level', plane, the tree, plane, 'tool for
smoothing', piano, llano, esplanade, explain,
explanation; cp. also Pole. Cp. I.-E. base "pld-ro
1= -r-enlargement of base *p(e)ld-], which
appears in Olr. Idr (gen. lair), 'ground, floor', OE.
ftdr, 'floor', MHG. vluor, G. Flur, 'meadow,
plain'; see floor. For a dental enlargement of
base *p(e)la- see field. Two other enlargements
of base *p(e)la- are *p(e)ldg- and *p(e)ldq-. The

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:593 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PLAIN | 566 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:593 COLUMN:1 -->
former appears in Gk. πλάγος, 'side', πλάγιος,
'placed sideways, oblique, slanting', πέλαγος,
'the open sea'; cp. flake» 'a thin flat piece', flake,
'rack for storing goods', flask, 'plate of the trail
of a gun carriage', flaw, 'crack', flay, fleck. For
derivatives of base *p(e)ldq- see please,

## plain
plain, п., level country. — ME. plein, playn, fr.
OF. plain, fr. L. planum, 'level ground, plain',
prop, neut. of the adj. planus, 'level, flat', used
as a noun. See plain, adj. F. plaine, 'level
country, plain', is formed fr. the fem. of the adj.
plain, 'even, level' (fr. L. planus).

## plain
plain, intr. v., to complain, lament. — ME.
pleinen, playnen, fr. OF. (= F.) plaindre, 'to
mourn', fr. L. plangere, 'to strike, to beat the
breast', 'to lament loudly* (orig. 'to lament while
beating the breast'). See plague and cp. esp.
plaint. Cp. also plangorous.

## plain chant
plain chant, plain song. — F. See plain song.

## plain song
plain song, ancient system of church music. —
Loan translation of F. plain chant, 'plain song",
compounded of plain, 'even', and chant, 'song'.
See plain, adj., and chant, п., and cp. plain
chant,

## plaint
plaint, n. — ME., fr. OF. plaint, fr. L. planctus,
'lamentation', fr. planctus, pp. of plangere, 'to
strike, to beat the breast; to lament loudly'.
See plain, 'to complain'.

## plaintiff
plaintiff, n. — ME. plaintif, fr. OF. (= F.) plain-
tif, п., fr. plaintif, adj., 'complaining'. See next
word.

## plaintive
plaintive, adj. — ME. plaintif, fr. OF.plaintif{fern.
plaintive), 'complaining', fr. plainte, 'complaint*,
fr. plaint, 'complaint, lamentation*. See plaint
and -ive.
Derivatives: plaintive-ly, adv., plaintive-ness, n.

## plait
plait, n. — ME. pleyt, playt, fr. OF. ploit, 'fold',
fr. earlier pleit, fr. VL. *plictum, fr. L. plicitum,
neut. pp. of plicare, 4o fold*. See ply, 'to bend',
and words there referred to and cp. esp. plat,
'braid*, and pleat and plight, 'condition', which
are doublets of plait.
Derivatives: plait, tr. v., plait-ed, adj., plait-er,
п., plait-ing, n.

## plan
plan, n. — F., 'sketch of a district; scheme,
project, design', which is prob. a blend of plan,
'plane' (fr. L. planum, 'level ground'), and
earlier F. plant, 'the act of planting', whence
'something planted', which is a back formation
fr. planter, 'to plant'. See plane, 'flat surface',
and plant, n.
Derivatives .plan, adj., tr. and intr. v., plan-less,
adj., plan-less-ly, adv., plan-less-ness, п.,
planned, adj., plann-er, п., plann-ing, n.

## planar
planar, adj., pertaining to a plane or flat. — Late
L. planaris, 'level, flat', fr. L. planus, 'even,
level, flat*. See plain, adj., and adj. suff. -ar.

## planarian
planarian, п., any of the flat, wormlike animals
of the class Turbellaria (zool.) — Late L. plana-
rius, 'level, flat*, fr. planahs, of s.m., fr. L.
planus, 'even, level, flat'. See plain, 'flat*, and -arian.

## planch
planch, also planche, п., a plank floor — {dial.
E.).— ME. pfaunche, fr. OF. (= F.) planche,
'plank', fr. L. planca, 'board, slab, plank'. See
plank,

## planchet
planchet, п., a metal disk out of which a coin is
made. — F. planchette. See next word.

## planchette
planchette, п., a small board. — F., dimin. of
planche. See planch and -ette.

## plancier
plancier, п., the underside of a cornice. — OF.
planchier, plancher, 'planking' - [whence F.
plancher, '(boarded) floor'], fr. planche, 'board,
plank*. See plank and cp. planch,

## plane
plane, п., plane tree. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.)
plane, fr. L. platanus, fr. Gk. πλάτανος, 'plane
tree*, prop, 'tree with large leaves', fr. πλατύς,
'wide, broad'. See place and cp. platan, Platanus.

## plane
plane, tr. v., to make smooth. — ME. planen, fr.
OF. (= F.), planen, 'to make smooth, make
even', fr. Late L. planare, 'to level, make flat', fr.
L. planus, 'even, level, flat'. See plain, adj.

## plane
plane, п., tool for smoothing. — ME., fr. MF.
(= F.) plane, refashioned after planer, 'to plane',
fr. OF. plaine, 'plane', fr. Late L. plana, of s.m.,
back formation fr. planare, 'to level, make flat',
See plane, 'to make smooth*.
Derivative: plane, tr. v., to make smooth with
or as with a plane; intr. v., to work with a plane;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:593 COLUMN:2 -->
plan-er, n.

## plane
plane, п., a flat surface. — L. planum, 'level
ground', prop. neut. of the adj. planus} 'even,
level, flat'. See plain, adj., and cp. plane,
'airplane'.

## plane
plane, adj., flat, level. — L. planus, 'even, level,
flat'. See plain, adj.

## plane
plane, п., airplane. — Short for airplane. Cp.
monoplane, biplane, triplane, emplane,
gyroplane, hydroplane.
Derivative: plane, intr. v.

## planet
planet, n. — ME. planete, fr. OF. p/anete (F.
planete), fr. Late L. planeta, fr. Gk. πλανήτης,
'wandering; wanderer*[in the pi. (αστέρες )πλα-
νηται, 'wandering stars'], a collateral form of
πλάνης, 'wanderer, roamer', fr. πλανασθαι, 'to
wander', pass, of πλαναν, 'to lead astray', fr.
πλάνη, 'wandering, roaming*, which is of
uncertain etymology.
Derivatives: planet-al, adj., planet-ed, adj.

## planetarium
planetarium, п., an orrery. — ModL.
planetarium, prop. neut. of Late L. planetarius,
'pertaining to planets*, used as a noun. See
next word and 1 st -ium.
Derivatives: planetar-ian, adj., planetary (q.v.)

## planetary
planetary, adj. and n. — Late L. planetarius,
'pertaining to planets', fr. planeta. See planet and
adj. suff. -ary and cp. prec. word.

## planetesimal
planetesimal, adj., pertaining to the small
planetary bodies of space. — Short for planet infini-
tesimal. See planet and infinitesimal.
Derivative: planetesimal, n.

## planetoid
planetoid, п., an asteroid. — Lit. 'resembling a
planet',.formed fr. planet and Gk. -οειδής, 'like*,
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -old.
Derivative: planetoid-al, adj.

## plaugency
plaugency, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## plangent
plangent, adj., beating with a loud sound (said
esp. of waves). — L. plangens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of plangere, 'to strike, beat'. See plain, 4o
complain', and -ent.
Derivative: plangent-ly, adv.

## plangorous
plangorous, adj., lamenting. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. plangor, 'lamentation', fr. plangere,
'to strike, to beat the breast; to lament loudly'.
See plain, 'to complain'.

## plani-
plani-, combining form meaning 'level, plane'. —
L. plani-, fr. planus, 'even, level, flat'. See plain,
adj., and cp. plain, n.

## planifonn
planifonn, adj., having the form nearly flat
(anat.) — Compounded of plani- and L. forma,
'form, shape'. See form, n.

## planimeter
planimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
area of a plane surface. — F. planimeire. See
plani- and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## planimetry
planimetry, п., the measurement of plane
surfaces. — ML. planimetria, fr. L. planus, 'even
level, flat*, and -metria, '-metry'. See plain, adj.,
and -metry.
Derivatives: planimetr-ic, planimetr-ic-al, adjs.

## planish
planish, tr. v., to polish. — Fr. obsol. F. planiss-,
pres. part, stem of planir (F. aplanir), 'to flatten,
smooth, planish', fr. plan, 'even, level, flat', fr.
L. planus. See plain, adj., and verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: planish-er, п., planish-ing, n.

## plank
plank, n. — ME. planke, fr. ONF. planque
[corresponding to OF. (= F.) planche], fr. L. planca,
'board, slab, plank', which is rel. to phalanga,
'pole to carry burdens', fr. Gk. φαλάγγη, of
s.m., which is rel. to φάλαγξ, gsn. φάλαγγος,
trunk, log*. See phalanx and cp. planch, planchet,
plancier.
Derivatives: plank, tr. v., plank-er, n., plank-ing,
n.

## plank-sheer
plank-sheer, п., also plane-sheer. — Folk
etymology for obsolete plancher, fr. F. plancher, 'floor'.
See plancier.

## plankton
plankton, п., collective name for plant and animal
organisms floating on the surface of seas. —
Coined by the German physiologist Viktor
Hensen (1835-1924) fr. Gk. πλαγκτόν, neut. of
πλαγκτός, 'wandering', verbal adj. of πλάζω,
*I go astray, wander', which stands for *πλάγ-
γιω, and is rel. to πληγή, 'stroke', πλήσσω, *\
strike*, and cogn. with L. plangere, 'to strike, to
beat the breast'. See plague and cp. words there
referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:593 COLUMN:3 -->

## piano-
piano-, combining form meaning 'level, flat,
plane'. — L.piano-, fr. planus, 'even, level, flat'.
See plane, adj.

## piano-
piano-, combining form meaning 'wandering,
roaming'. — Gk. πλάνο-, fr. πλανασθαι, 'to
wander'. See planet.

## planoblast
planoblast,n.,themedusaformofahydroid(z0o/.)
— Compounded of piano- and Gk. βλαστός,
'bud, sprout, shoot'. See -blast.
Derivative: planoblast-ic, adj.

## planoconcave
planoconcave, adj., plane on one side and
concave on the other. — Compounded of piano-,
'flat', and concave.

## planoconvex
planoconvex, adj., plane on one side and convex
on the other. — Compounded of piano-, 'plane',
and convex.

## planometer
planometer, п., a device for gauging a plane
surface. — A hybrid coined fr. piano-, 'plane', and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## plant
plant, n. — ME. plante, fr. OE. plante, fr. L.
planta, 'sprout, shoot, twig' (whence also It.
pianta, Sp. planta, F. plante, G. Pftanze, Ir.
eland, W. plant), which is prob. a back
formation fr. L. *plantare, 'to tread down with the
sole', whence 'to level the ground for sowing',
a denominative formed fr. planta, 'sole of the
foot'. See place and cp. plantar. Cp. also clan.
Derivatives: plant, v. (q:V.), plant-ling, n.

## plant
plant, tr. v. — ME. planten, fr. OE. plantian, fr.
L. plantare, 'to plant', fr. planta. See prec. word
and cp. implant, transplant.
Derivatives: plant-able, adj., plantation (q.v.),
plant-ing, n. and adj.

## Plantaginaceae
Plantaginaceae, n. pi., the plantain family (bot.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. L.
plantago, gen. -inis. See Planta go.

## plantaginacebus
plantaginacebus, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Plantago
Plantago, п., a genus of plants, the plantain (bot.)
— L. plantago, 'plantain'. See plantain, 'plant of
the genus Plantago'.

## plantain
plantain, п., any plant of the genus Plantago. —
ME. plantaine, fr. OF. plantaine, plantain, plan-
tein, fr. L. plantaginem, ace. of plantago,
'plantain', fr. planta, 'sole of the foot' (see place); so
called in allusion to its flat leaves.

## plantain
plantain, п., a species of banana. — Sp. platano,
plantano, a blend of Caribbean palatana,
'banana', and Sp. platano, 'plane tree' (see plane,
the tree). The English form of this word shows
the influence of prec. word.

## plantar
plantar, adj., pertaining to the sole of the foot. —
L. plantaris, fr. planta, 'sole of the foot', which
is cogn. with Gk. πλατύς, *flat, wide, broad'.
See place and adj. suff. -ar and cp. supplant.

## plantation
plantation, n. — L. plantatio, gen. -onis, fr. plan-
tatus, pp. of plantare, 'to plant'. See plant, v.,
and -ation.

## plantigrade
plantigrade, adj., walking on the whole sole; п., а
plantigrade animal. — F., compounded of L.
planta, 'sole of the foot', and the stem of gradi,
'to walk'. See plantar and grade.

## plantlet
plantlet, n-, a little plant. — Dimin. formed fr.
plant, п., with suff. -let.

## plantocracy
plantocracy, п., rule of planters in W. Indies
(hist.) — A hybrid coined fr. L. planta, 'plant',
and Gk. -κρατία, 'rule', fr. κράνος, 'strength,
power, rule'. See plant, п., and -cracy.

## planula
planula, п., the free-moving larva of coelenter-
ates (zool.) — ModL., dimin. formed fr. L.
planus, 'flat*. See plain, 'level', and -ule.
Derivatives: planuhar, planul-ate, adjs.

## plaque
plaque, п., an ornamental plate or tablet. — F.,
fr. MDu. placke, 'small coin', which is'related
to MHG. placke, G. Placken, 'spot, patch'. Cp.
placard, plack.

## plaquette
plaquette, п., a small plaque. — F., dimin. of
plaque. See prec. word and -ette.

## plash
plash, tr. v., to bend and interweave branches,
etc. — ME. plashen, fr. OF. plaissier, pleissier,
fr. VL. *plectiare, fr. L.plectere, 'to plaid, braid,
intertwine', which is cogn. with Gk. πλέκει, 'to
plait", πλοκή, 'network'. See ply, 'to bend*, and
words there referred to and cp. esp. pleach,
which is a doublet of plash.

## plash
plash, п., a shallow pool. — ME. plasche, fr. OE.
plxsc, rel. to MDu. plasch, Du. plas, 'pool.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:594 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 567 | PLAUSIBLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:594 COLUMN:1 -->
puddle'; prob. of imitative origin.
Derivative: plash-y, adj.

## plash
plash, tr. and intr. v., to splash. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. Du. plassen, G- platschen and E.
splash.
Derivatives: plash, n. and aav.,plash-y, adj.

## -plasia
-plasia, -plasis, -plasy, combining form meaning
'formation*. — ModL. -plasia, -plasis, fr. Gk.
πλάσης, 'molding, formation', fr. πλάσσειν, 'to
mold, form". See plasma.

## plasm
plasm, п., plasma. — See plasma.

## plasm-
plasm-, form of plasmo- before a vowel.

## -plasm
-plasm, combining forrri meaning 'something
molded", as in bioplasm, cytoplasm. — Gk.
-'πλάσμα, fr. πλάσμα, 'something molded'.
See Tiext word.

## plasma
plasma, also pJasm, п., ]) the liquid part of blood,-
2) the protoplasm. — Late L., fr. Gk. πλάσμα,
'something molded', fr. πλάσσειν, 'to mold,
form, model". Cp. πλάθανον, 'mold in which
bread or cakes are baked', and the second
element in κοροπλάθος, *modeller of small
figures'. Cp. also plasson, plaster, plastic, plastid,
plastron.
Derivatives: plasm-atic, plasm-ic, adjs.

## plasmo-
plasmo-, before a vowel plasm-, combining form
denoting 1) plasma; 2) the protoplasm; 3) the
cytoplasm. — Fr. Gk. πλάσμα, 'something
molded'. See prec. word.

## Plasmodium
Plasmodium, п., mass of protoplasm formed
through the fusion of a number of one-celled
organisms. — ModL., compounded of plasma
and Gk. -ώδης, 'like'. See -ode» 'like'.

## plasmolysis
plasmolysis, п., contraction of the protoplasm
owing to the withdrawal of water by exosmosis.
— ModL., compounded of plasmo- and Gk.
λύσι,ς, 'a loosing, setting free'. See -lysis.

## plasmolytic
plasmolytic, adj., pertaining·to plasmolysis. —
See prec. word and -lytic.

## plasmolyze
plasmolyze, tr. v., to subject to plasmolysis; intr.
v., to undergo plasmojysis. — Formed fr.
plasmolysis with surf. -ize.

## plasmosome
plasmosome, п., a nucleolus in the nucleus of a
cell (biol.) — Compounded of plasmo- and Gk.
σώμα, 'body*. See soma, 'body'.

## plasson
plasson, п., the protoplasm of primitive
organisms (biol.) — Coined by the German biologist
Ernst Heinrich Haeckel (1834-1919) fr. Gk.
πλάσσον, 'that which molds or forms', neut.
pres. part, of πλάσσειν. See plasma.

## -plast
-plast, combining form denoting 'something
made', as in bioplast, protoplast. — Gk.
-πλαστός, fr. πλαστός, 'molded, formed', verbal adj.
of πλάσσειν, See plasma.

## plastein
plastein, п., any of proteins formed under the
influence of pepsin during digestion (biochem.) —
Formed with suff. -in fr. Gk. πλαστός, 'molded,
formed', verbal adj. of πλάσσειν; see plasma.
For the suff. cp. casein.

## plaster
plaster, n. — ME., fr. OE., fr. L. emplastrum, fr.
Gk. έμπλαστρου, 'plaster, salve*, a word used
by Galen instead of the more usual έμπλαστον,
fr. έμπλαστός, -η, -ον, 'daubed on or over',
verbal adj. of έμπλάσσειν, 'to plaster up, stuff
in, form in', fr. έμ-, έν-, 'in' (see 2nd en-) and
πλάσσειν, 'to mold, form'. See plasma and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also It. empiastro,
F. emplatre, 'plaster', and see piaster.
Derivatives: plaster, v. (q-v.), plaster-y, adj.,
plaster-i-ness, n.

## plaster
plaster, tr. v. — ME. plasteren, partly fr. plaster,
partly fr. plastrir (F. platrer), 'to plaster', fr.
OF. piastre (F. pldtre), 'plaster'. See plaster, n.
Derivatives: plaster-er, plaster-ing, n.'s.
plaster of Paris. — So called because originally
obtained from large deposits in Montmartre, a
suburb of Paris,

## plastic
plastic, adj. — L. plasticus, fr. Gk. πλαστικός, 'of
molding, of forming', fr. πλαστός, 'molded,
formed", verbal adj. of πλάσσειν. See plasma
and adj. suff. -Ic.
Derivatives: plastic, п., plastic-al-ly, adv.,
plastic-ism, п., plastic-ity, п., plastic-ize, tr. v., plas-
tic-iz-ation, п., plastic-iz-er, n.

## plastid
plastid, п., a cell (biol.) — Coined by the German
biologist Ernst Heinrich Haeckel (1834-1919) fr.
Gk. πλαστός, 'molded, formed', verbal adj. of
πλάσσειν (see plasma), and suff. -id, fr. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:594 COLUMN:2 -->
dimin. suff. -ίδιον.

## plastometer
plastometer, п., an instrument for measuring
plasticity. — Compounded of Gk. πλαστός,
'molded, formed', verbal adj. of πλάσσειν, and
μέτρον, 'measure'. See plasma and meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## plastron
plastron, п., a breastplate. — MF. ( — ¥.),
'breastplate', fr. It. ρ iastrone, augment, oipiastra,
'breastplate', fr. impiastro, 'plaster' fr. L. em-
plastrum. See plaster and -oon.

## -plasty
-plasty, combining form denoting: 1) the act or
process of forming, as in dermatoplasty; 2)
plastic surgery applied to a specified part of the body,
as in labioplasty. — Gk. -πλαστία, fr. πλαστός,
'molded, formed', verbal adj. of πλάσσειν. See
plasma.

## plat
plat, п., piece of ground. — Fr. obsol. plat, 'a flat
surface', fr. ME. plat, platte, 'a flat thing, a flat
surface', fr. the adj. plat, 'flat', fr. OF. plat, of
s.m., which derives fr. VL. *plattus, fr. Gk.
πλατύς, 'flat, wide, broad'. See place and cp.
plot, 'piece of ground', which is a var. οι plat.

## plat
plat, п., one of several courses at a meal. — F.
plat, 'dish, course at a meal', prop, the adj. plat,
'flat', used as a noun. See prec. word.

## plat
plat, tr. v., to interweave. — A var. of plait.

## plat-
plat-, combining form. — See platy-.

## Platalefdae
Platalefdae, n. pi., the family of spoonbills
(ornithol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae
fr. L. platalea, 'spoonbill', fr. Gk. "πλαταλέα,
fr. πλατύς, 'broad' (see place); so called in
allusion to the shape of the bill.

## plataleine
plataleine, adj. — See prec. word and adj. suff.
-ine.

## platan
platan, platane, п., the plane tree. — L.platanus.
See plane, the tree.

## Platanaceae
Platanaceae, n. pi., the plane tree family (bot.) —
ModL., formed from next word with suff.
-aceae.

## Platanus
Platanus, п., a genus of trees, the plane tree (bot.)
— L. platanus, "the plane tree'. See plane, the
tree, and cp. platan.

## platband
platband, n. (archit.) — F. plate-bande, lit. 'a flat
band', fern, of plat, 'flat', and bande, 'a band'.
See plat, 'piece of ground', and band, 'a tie'.

## plate
plate, п., thin sheet of metal, etc. — ME. plate,
fr. OF. plate, 'sheet of metal', prop. fern, of plat,
'flat, even', used as a noun, fr. VL. *plattus, fr. Gk.
πλατύς, 'flat, wide, broad'. See place and cp.
plat, 'piece of ground', plat, 'course at a meal'.
Cp. also the second element in vamplate.
Derivatives: plate, tr. \.,plat-ed, plate-ful. adjs.,
plat-er, п., plat-ing, n.

## plateasm
plateasm, п., also plateiasm, broad, Doric
pronunciation. — Gk-πλατειασμός, fi-.πλατειάζειν,
'to pronounce broadly (like the Dorians)', fr.
πλατύς, fern, πλατεία, 'broad'. See pince and cp.
platy-.

## plateau
plateau, п., a tableland. — MF. (-= F.),
'tableland', fr. OF. plat, 'flat surface', fr. the adj. plat,
'flat'. See plat, 'piece of ground'.

## platelet
platelet, n.( a small platelike body. — Formed fr.
plate with dimin. suff. -let

## platen
platen, п., also platten, flat plate pressing paper
against the inked type {print). — MF. plateine>
fr. platine, 'a flat plate', fr. plat, 'flat'. See plat,
'piece of ground', and cp. plate.

## plateresque
plateresque, adj., in the decorative style of
Spanish Renaissance architecture. — Sp. plateresco,
lit. 'resembling the work of silversmiths', fr.
platero, 'silversmith', fr. plata, 'silver'. See
platinum and -esque.

## platform
platform, n. — MF. (= F.) plate-forme, lit. 'flat
form'. See plate, 'piece of ground', and form,
п., and cp. platband.
Derivatives: platform, tr. and intr. v., platform-
nl-ly, adv., platform-er, п., platform-ist, п.,
platform-ist-ic, adj.

## platin-
platin-, form of platino- before a vowel.

## platina
platina, п., crude native platinum (chem.)— Sp.
or ModL. See platinum.

## platmi-
platmi-, combining form meaning 'platinum;
platinic'. — Fr. ModL. platinum. See platinum.

## platiniferous
platiniferous, adj., containing platinum. —
Compounded of platini- and the stem of L.ferre, 'to
bear, carry'. See -ferous.

## platino-
platino-, before a vowel platin-, combining form
meaning 'platinum, platinous'. — See pintinum.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:594 COLUMN:3 -->

## platinoid
platinoid, adj., like platinum. — Formed fr.
platin- and Gk. -αειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -oid.

## platinum
platinum, n. — ModL., fr. earlier platina, fr. Sp.
platina in platina del Pinto, i.e. 'little silver of the
River Pinto'; so called because of its silver-
white color and because it was first found near
the River Pinto. Sp. plata comes either fr.
OProvenc. plata or fr. OF. plate, which mean
'sheet of metal·, and ult. derive fr. Gk. πλατύς,
'flat, wide, broad'. See plate and cp. platina. Cp.
also plateresque.
Derivatives: platinum, platin-ic, adjs., platinize,
tr. v., platin-iz-ation, п., platin-ous, adj.

## platitude
platitude, п., dullness, commonplaceness. — F.,
formed on analogy of latitude fr. plat, 'fiat'. See
plat, 'course of meal', and -tude.
Derivatives: platitudin-arian, п., platitudin-ari-
an-ism, п., platitudin-ism, п., plaiitudin-ist,
п., platitudin-ize, intr. v., platitudin-iz-ation, п.,
platitudin-iz-er, n.

## Platonic
Platonic, adj., pertaining to Plato or Platonism.
— L. Platonicus, fr. Gk. Πλατωνικός, 'of
Plato', fr. Πλάτων, 'Plato', the celebrated
Greek philosopher (427 7-347 B.C.E). His
original name was Aristocles. (Πλάτων prop, means
'broad-shouldered'. It derives fr. πλατύς,
'broad'; see" platy-.This name was given to him in
allusion to his broad shoulders.) For the ending
see adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: Platonic-al-ly, adv.

## Platonism
Platonism, n. — ModL. platonismus. See prec.
word and -ism.

## Platonist
Platonist, n. — ML. platonista. See Platonic and
-izt.

## Platonize
Platonize, intr. v., to follow the teachings of
Plato; tr. v., to render Platonic. — F. platoniser,
fr. Gk. Πλατωνίζειν, 'to imitate Plato', fr.
Πλάτων. See Plato and -ize.
Derivatives: Platoniz-ation, п., Platoniz-er, n.

## platoon
platoon, п., I) a small body of soldiers; 2) a
company of men. — F. peloton, 'ball, clew,
group of people, group of soldiers', dimin. of
pelote, 'ball.'clew*. See pellet and -oon.

## Plattdeutsch
Plattdeutsch, п., Low German spoken in North
Germany. — G., fr. Du. platduits, lit. 'fiat (or
low) German', fr. plat, 'flat, plain, clear' (fr.
OF. plat), and duits, 'German'. See plat, 'piece
of ground', and Dutch.

## platter
platter, п., a flat plate. — ME. plater, fr. AF.
plater, fr. OF. (= F.) plat, 'dish', fr. plat, 'flat'.
See plate.

## plattnerite
plattnerite, п., lead dioxide {mineral.)— G.Platt-
nerit, named after the German mineralogist
Karl Friedrich Plattner, who analyzed it. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## platy-
platy-, also plat-,combining form meaning'broad,
wide, flat'. — Gk. πλατύ-, fr. πλατύς. See
place and words there referred to and cp. esp.
plat, 'piece of ground', plat, 'course of meal',
plate, platinum, plane, the tree, plant,
plantar.

## Platyhelminthes
Platyhelminthes, n. pi., a genus of worms, the
fiatworm (zoo/.) — Lit. 'flat worms', fr. platy-
and Gk. έλμινς, gen. ελμίνθος, 'worm'. See
helminth.

## platypus
platypus, п., the duckbill. — Lit. 'flatfooted', fr.
platy- and Gk. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See
-pod.

## platyrrhme
platyrrhme, adj., having a broad nose. —
Compounded of platy- and Gk. (δις, gen. ρινός,
'nose'. See rhino-.

## ptatysma
ptatysma, п., a broad muscle on each side of the
neck (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. πλάτυσμα,
'a flat object; widening, dilation', fr. πλατύς,
'fiat, wide, broad'; see platy- and -ma. In its
anatomical sense the word platysma was
introduced by Oribasius, physician of Emperor
Julian.

## plaudit
plaudit, п., applause. — Fr. L.p/audite, imper. pi.
of plaudere, 'to clap, strike, beat, to clap the
hands', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
plausible, applaud, explode. Cp. also Apluda.

## plausible
plausible, adj.—l^plausibilis, 'worthy of applause,
praiseworthy', fr. plausus, pp. of plaudere.
See plaudit.
Derivatives: plausibil-ity, п., piausible-ness, п.,
plaustbl-y, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:595 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PLAUSIVE | 568 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:595 COLUMN:1 -->

## plausive
plausive, adj., applauding. — Formed with suflf.
-ive fr. L. plausus, pp. ofplaudere. See plaudit.

## Plautine
Plautine, adj., pertaining to, or in the style of, the
Roman comic poet Titus Maccius Plautus (254 ?-
184 B.C.E.) — L. Plautinus, fr. Plautus. For the
ending see suff, -ine (representing L. -Г/ни).

## Plautus
Plautus, п., a genus of birds, the great auk (or-
nithol.) — ModL., fr. L. plautus, 'flat, broad,
flat-footed', which is of uncertain origin.

## play
play, intr. v. — ME. pleien, fr. OE. plegian, ple-
gan, 'to exercise, busy oneself, play, applaud'
(whence prob. OE. plega, 'exercise, play,
applause'), prob. rel. to MDu. pleyen, playen, 'to
rejoice, be glad', and perh. also to OE. pleoh,
'danger, risk\ pleon (for *plehan), 'to expose to
danger, risk', and to MDu. pleghen, Du. plegen,
'to care for, be accustomed to', OHG. pflegan,
MHG., G. pftegen, of s.m. See plight and cp.
pledge.
Derivatives:play-able, adj.,play~ed, adj.,player
<q.v.), play-ing, adj., play-ing-ly, adv., play-
some, adj., play-some-ly, adv., play-some-ness,
n.

## play
play, n. — ME. plei, fr. OE. plega, 'exercise,
play, applause'. See play, v.
Derivatives: play-ful, adj., play-ful-ly, adv.,
phy-ful-ness, n.

## player
player, n. — ME, pleyer, fr. OE. plegere, fr. plegi-
an,plegan, 'to amuse oneself, play'. See play, v.,
and agential suff. -er.

## playlet
playlet, п., a short play. — Dimin. formed fr.
play, п., with suff. -let.

## plaza
plaza, п., a public square in a Spanish or
Spanish-American town. — Sp. plaza, fr. VL.
*plattea, fr. L. platea, 'broad street'. See place
and cp. piazza,

## plea
plea, n. — ME. plaid, plait, plai, fr. OF. plaid,
plait, fr. ML. placitum, 'lawsuit', fr. L.placitum,
'opinion, determination', lit. 'that which is
agreeable', prop. neut. pp. of placere, 'to
please', used as a noun. See please and cp. words
there referred to.

## pleach
pleach, tr. v., to bend and interweave (branches),
etc. — ME. plechen, fr. dial. OF. *plechier,
corresponding to OF. plessier, pleissier. See plash,
4o intertwine'.
Derivatives: pleach-ed, adj., pleach-er, n.

## plead
plead, intr. and tr. v. — ME. plaiden, fr. OF.
plaidier (F. plaider), fr. plaid, 'plea'. See plea.
Derivatives: pleader (q.v.), plead-ing, n. and
adj., plead-ing-ly, adv., plead-ing-ness, n.

## pleadable
pleadable, adj. — ME. pledable, fr. OF. plaidable,
fr. plaidier. See plead and -able.

## pleader
pleader, n. — ME. pleder, a var. of playdour, fr.
OF. plaideor (F. plaideur), fr. plaidier (F. plai·
der). See plead and agential suflf. -er.

## pleasance
pleasance, n. — OF. plaisance, fr. plaisant. See
next word and -ce.

## pleasant
pleasant, adj. — ME. plesaunt, fr. OF. plaisant,
pres. part, of plaisir, 'to please'. See please and
-ant.
Derivatives: pleasant-ly, adv., pleasant-ness, n.

## pleasantry
pleasantry, n. — F. plaisanterie, fr. plaisant. See
prec. word and -ry.

## please
please, intr. and tr. v. — ME- plaisen, plesen, fr.
OF. plaisir (F. plaire, 'to please', is due to the
analogy of /aire, 'to make, do'), fr. L. placere,
'to please', which is rel. to pldcare, 'to soothe,
pacify', orig. 'to be smooth', resp. 'to make
smooth', fr. l.-E. base *p(e)!aq-, 'to smooth,
make even', whence also Gk. πλάξ, gen.
πλακός, 'level, surface', πλακόεις, 'flat' (whence L.
placenta, 'cake'), Lett, plakt, 'to become flat',
plakans,'f\at' ,Tach.lAplaki, 'consent, agreement',
ON. flaga, 'layer of earth', Norw. flag, Open
sea', OB.floh, 'fragment, piece of stone', OHG.
fluoh, MHG. vluo, fluh, 'cliff'. See plain, adj.,
and cp. complacent, displacency, displease,
placate, placebo, placet, placid, plank, plea, plead,
supplicate.
Derivatives: pleas-ed, adj., pleas-ed-ly, adv.,
pleas-ed-ness, п., pleas-er, п., pleas-ing, n. and
adj., pleas-ing-ly, adv., pleas-ing-ness, n.

## pleasure
pleasure, n. — ME. plesir, plaisir, fr. OF. (~ F.)
plaisir, inf. used as a noun, fr. L. placere, 'to
please'. For the subst. use of the inf. and for the
change of the F. suff. -ir to E. -we, cp. leisure.
See please and -иге and cp. displeasure.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:595 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: pleasure, tr. and intr. v., pleasure-
ful, adj., pleasur-er, п., pleasur-ing, n.

## pleat
pleat, п., a fold. — A var. of plait. Cp. plight,
'condition'.
Derivatives: pleat, tr. v., pleat-er, n.

## pleb
pleb, п., 1) a plebeian; 2) a plebe. —
Abbreviation of plebeian.

## plebe
plebe, п., a member of the lowest class in the
military academies at West Point and
Annapolis. — F. plebe, 'the plebs, the common
people', fr. L. plebem, ace. of plebs. See plebeian.

## plebeian
plebeian, adj., of the common people. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. plebeius, 'belonging to the
common people', fr. plebes, plebs, gen. plebis,
'the common people', which prob. derives fr.
I.-E. base *ple~-, 'to be full', whence also Gk.
πλήθος, 'people, multitude, great number',
πλήρης, 'full', L. plenus, 'full', pled, plere, 'to fill'.
See full, adj., and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also next word.

## plebiscite
plebiscite, п., direct vote of the people. — F.
plebiscite, fr. L. plebiscftum, for plebis scitum, lit.
'the people's decree', fr. plebis, gen. of plebs,
'people' and scitum, 'decree', prop. neut. pp. of
sciscere, 'to seek to know, to decree', inchoative
afscio, scire, 'to know'. See plebeian and science.
Derivatives: plebiscit-ary, adj., plebiscit-ari-an,
adj., plebiscit-ar-ism,*n., plebiscit-ic, adj.

## plebs
plebs, п., the common people. — L. plebs. See
plebeian and cp. plebe.

## Plecoptera
Plecoptera, n. pi., an order of insects (entomol.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. πλέκειν, 'to
plait, twine, twist', and πτεράν, 'wing'. See
plecto- and ptero-.
Derivatives; plecopter~an, п., plecopter-id, adj.
and п., plecopter-ous, adj.

## Plecotus
Plecotus, п., a genus of mammals, the long-eared
bat (zool.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
πλέκει, 'to plait, twine, twist', and οδς, gen. ώτός,
'ear'. See plecto- and oto-.
Derivative: plecot-ine, adj.

## plecto-
plecto-, combining form meaning 'twisted*, as in
Plectognathi. — Fr. Gk. πλεκτός, 'twisted',
verbal adj. of πλέκειν, 'to plait, twine, twist',
related to πλοκή, 'network', πλόκος, 'tress', and
cogn. withL./j/ec/ere, 'to plait',plicare, 'to fold'.
See ply, 'to bend' and cp. words there referred
to.

## Plectognathi
Plectognathi, n. pi., an order of teleost fishes
(ichthyol.) — ModL., compounded of plecto-
and Gk. γνάθος, 'jaw'. See gnatho-.

## plectrum
plectrum, п., a small piece of metal, bone, etc.,
used for plucking the strings of a guitar,
mandolin, zither, etc. — L. plectrum, fr. Gk. πληκ-
τρον, *an instrument to strike with, instrument
for striking the lyre', a derivative of πλήσσείν,
'to strike'. See plague and cp. Aplectrum.

## pledge
pledge, n. — ME. plegge, fr. OF. plege, pleige,
plaige, etc. (F. pleige), 'hostage, security,
warrant, pledge', fr. ML. plebium, plevium, which is
prob. a blend of OS. plegan, 'to promise, pledge
oneself, and L. praebere, 'to give, grant,
furnish*. OS. plegan is re], to OHG. pflegan, 'to care
for, be accustomed to', OE. pleon (for *plehan),
'to risk, expose to danger'; see plight, 'pledge',
and cp, play, v. For the etymology of L.praebere
see prebend. Cp. replevin, replevy.

## pledge
pledge, tr. v. — ME. pleggen, fr. OF. plegier (F.
pleiger), fr. plege, 'pledge'. See pledge, n.
Derivatives: pledg-ee, п.,pledg-or, pledge-or, п.,
pledg-er, n.

## pledget
pledget, п., compress of lint (med.) — Of
uncertain origin.

## Plegadis
Plegadis, п., a genus oT birds including the ibises
(omithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πληγάς gen,
πληγάδος, 'sickle', from the stem of πλήσσείν,
*to strike'. See plague and cp. words there
referred to.

## -plegia
-plegia, -plegy, combining form denoting
paralysis, as in hemiplegia (med.) — Gk. -πληγία, fr.
πληγή, 'stroke, blow', from the stem of πλήσ-
σειν, 'to strike'. See plague and cp. words there
referred to.

## Pleiad
Pleiad, п., 1) one of the Pleiades; 2) a group of
seven 16th cent. French poets, the chief member
of which was Pierre de Ronsard. — L. Pleias,
pi. Pleiades, fr. Gk. Πλειάς, pi. Πλειάδες; in
sense 2) fr. F. Pleiade, fr. L. Pleias. See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:595 COLUMN:3 -->

## Pleiades
Pleiades, n. pi., 1) the seven daughters of Atlas
and Pleione, transformed by Zeus into a group
of stars (Greek mythol.)] 2) a group of several
hundred stars in the constellation Taurus,
commonly spoken of as seven, though only six are
visible to the average naked eye. — L. Pleiades
(pi.), fr. Gk. Πλειάδες (also Πληϊάδες) (pi.),
contracted fr. Πελειάδες and prob. lit. meaning
'constellation of the dove", fr. πελειάδες, pi. of
πελειάς, 'dove', a derivative of πέλεια, 'dove',
prop, 'the gray bird', fr. I.-E. base *pel-, 'dark-
colored, gray', whence also OE.fealo, 'brown'.
See fallow, 'brownish yellow', and cp. words
there referred to.

## pleio-
pleio-, pleo-, combining form meaning 'more'. —
Fr. Gk. πλείων (poet, πλέων), 'more, greater,
larger* (compar. of πολύς, 'much'), which is rel.
to πλέως, πλέος, 'full, filled', πλείστος, 'most,
largest' (superl. of πολύς), fr. I.-E. base *p/e-,
*pet-, 'to be full, to fill'. See full, adj., and cp.
poly-, plus. Cp. also next word and pleonasm.

## Pleistocene
Pleistocene, adj., pertaining to the period also
called Posttertiary or Glacial Period (geol.) —
Coined fr. Gk. πλείστος, 'most', and καινός,
'new'. See prec. word and -cene and cp. Pliocene.
Derivative: Pleistocene, adj.

## plenary
plenary, adj., full; absolute. — Late L. plenarius,
'fulF, fr. L. plenus, 'full'. See plenum, and adj.
suff. -ary.
Derivative: plenari-fy, adv.

## plenipotentiary
plenipotentiary, adj., having full power or
authority. — ML. plenipotentiarius (whence also F.
plenipotentiaire), fr. Late L. plenipotens, gen.
-entis, 'having full power', fr. L. plenus, 'full',
and potens, gen. -entis, 'powerful'. See plenum,
potent and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivative: plenipotentiary, n.

## plenish
plenish, tr. v., to fill up. — Fr. OF. pleniss-, pres.
part, stem of plenir, 'to fill', fr. L. plenus, 'full'.
See plenum and verbal suff. -ish and cp. replenish.
Derivatives: plenish-ing, п., plenish-ment, n.

## plenitude
plenitude, п., fullness. — ME., fr. L. plenitudo,
'fullness, plenitude', fr. plenus, 'full'. See plenum
and -tude.

## plenteous
plenteous, adj., plentiful. — ME. plentivous^len-
tevous, plenteus, fr. OF. plentivos, derived fr.
plentexf, 'plentiful', fr. plente, 'fullness'. See next
word and -ous.
Derivatives: plenteous-ly, adv., plenteous-ness,
n.

## plenty
plenty, n. — ME. plente, plentie, fr. OF. plente,
fr. L. plenitatem, ace. ofp/em'iai,''fullness,
plenty', fr. plenus, 'full'. See next word and -ty.
Derivatives: plenty, adv., plenti-ful, adj.,
plentifully, adv., pienti-ful-ness, n.

## plenum
plenum, п., 1) a space filled with matter; 2) a full
meeting. — L. plenum, 'a space occupied by
matter, a plenum', prop. neut. of the adj. plenus,
'full', fr. I.-E. base *ple-, 'to be full, to fill'. See
full, adj., and cp. words there referred to.

## pleo-
pleo-, combining form meaning 'more'. — A var.
of pleio-.

## pleomorphism
pleomorphism, п., the ability of crystallizing in
two or more distinct fundamental forms. —
Compounded of pleo- and Gk. μορφή, 'form,
shape'. See morpho-.

## pleonasm
pleonasm, п., the use of superfluous words,
redundancy (rhet.) — Late L. pleonasmus, fr. Gk.
πλεονασμός, fr. πλεονάζειν, 'to be more than
enough, abound, be superfluous', fr. πλέον,
neut. of πλέων, 'more'. See pleio-.

## pleonaste
pleonaste, п., ceylonite (mineral.) — F. pleonaste,
fr. Gk. πλεοναστός, 'abundant', verbal adj. of
πλεονάζειν, 'to be more than enough, abound'
(see pleonasm); so called by the French
mineralogist Rene-Just Hauy (1743-1822) in 1801 in
allusion to the number of faces.

## pleonastic
pleonastic, adj., superfluous, redundant. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. πλεοναστός. See
prec. word.

## pleopod
pleopod, п., an abdominal limb of a crustacean
(zool.) — Formed fr. pleo- and Gk. πους, gen.
ποδός, 'foot*. See -pod.

## plerome
plerome, п., the central part of the primary tissue
out of which the stele is said to rise (bot.) — Gk.
πλήρωμα, 'fullness', fr. πληρούν, 'to make full',
fr. πλήρης, 'full', fr. I.-E. base *ple-, 'to be full,
to fill'. See full, adj., and cp. words there re-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:596 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 569 | PL UM ATE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:596 COLUMN:1 -->
ferred to. For the ending of Gk. πλήρωμα see
suff. -ma.

## Plesiosaurus
Plesiosaurus, п., a genus of lizardlike marine
reptiles of the Mesozoic (paleontol.) — ModL.,
coined by William Daniel Conybeare (1787-
1857) fr. Gk. πλησίος, 'near', and σαϋρος,
'lizard'. The first element is rel. to πέλας, 'near',
πελάζειν, 'to approach', πλην, 'beyond', £μ-
πλην, 'quite near', and cogn. with L.pellere (pp.
pulsus), 'to push, strike, drive'. See pulse, 'throb'.
For the second element see saurian,

## plessor
plessor, п., a small hammer used in percussion
(med.) — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. πλήσσειν, 'to
strike', and the Latin agential sufF. -or. See
plague and cp. plexor. Cp. also plectrum.

## plethora
plethora, п., 1) excess, superabundance^) (med.)
superabundance of blood in the body. — ModL.
plethora, fr. Gk. πληθώρα, 'fullness', fr. πλή-
θειν, 'to be full', fr. i.-E. base *pti-, 'to be full'.
See full, adj., and words there referred to and
cp. esp. plerome, plethvsmograph.

## plethoric
