plethoric,adj., 1) overfull; 2) characterized by
plethora. — ModL. plethoricus, fr. plethora. See
prec. word and -ic.
Derivative: plethoric-al-ly, adv.

## plethysmograph
plethysmograph, п., an instrument for measuring
and recording variations in parts of the body,
esp. as caused by the changes in the circulation
of the blood. — Compounded of Gk.
πληθυσμός, 'enlargement',and-γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. The first element derives fr. πληθυς,
'multitude', which is rel. to πλήθος, of s.m.,
πλήθειν, 'to be full'; see plethora. For the
second element see -graph.

## pleur-
pleur-, form of pteuro- before a vowel.

## pleura
pleura, п., a thin membrane which lines the
thorax of mammals (anal.) — ML., fr. Gk.
πλευρί, 'side, rib', which is of doubtful origin.
Cp. pleurisy, pleuron.
Derivatives: pleur-al, adj. and n.

## pleuric
pleuric, adj., pleura]. — ML. pleuricus, fr. Gk.
πλευρικός, 'pertaining to the ribs', fr. πλευρά.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## pleurisy
pleurisy, п., inflammation of the pleural
membrane (med.) — OF. pliurisie (F. pleurisie), fr.
Late L. pleurisis, for Gk. πλευρϊτις, fr. πλευρά,
'side, rib'. See pleura and -itis.

## pleuritic
pleuritic, adj., i) pertaining to pleurisy; 2)
suffering from pleurisy. — L. pleuriticus, fr. Gk.
πλευριτικός, 'suffering from pleurisy', fr.
πλευρΐτις. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## pleuro-
pleuro-, before a vowel pleur-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining to the side', as in pleuro-
carpus; 'pertaining to the pleura', as in
pleuropneumonia. — Gk. πλευρό-, πλευρ-, fr.
πλευρά, 'side; rib'. See pleura.

## pleurocarpous
pleurocarpous, adj., bearing the fruit on the side
of the stem. — Compounded of pleuro- and Gk.
καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel and -ous.

## pleurodont
pleurodont, adj., having the teeth attached to the
side of the jawbone. — Compounded of pleuro-
and the stem of Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth'.
See odonto.

## pleuron
pleuron, п., the lateral part of a thoracic segment
in insects (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πλευρόν,
'rib', which is rel. to πλευρά, 'rib, side'. See
pleura.

## Pleuronectldae
Pleuronectldae, n. pi., a family of flatfishes (ich-
thyol.) — ModL., compounded of pleuro- and
Gk. νήκτης, 'swimmer', fr. νήχειν, 'to swim'.
See necto- and -idae.

## pleuropneumonia
pleuropneumonia, п., inflammation of the pleura
and the lungs. — See pleuro- and pneumonia.

## pleurotomy
pleurotomy, п., the surgical operation of the
pleura (med.) — Formed fr. pleuro- and Gk.
-τομίϊ, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See
-tomy.

## pleuston
pleuston, п., a kind of small vegetation floating
on the water. — Formed fr. Gk. πλεϋσις,
'sailing', fr. πλεΐν, 'to sail', fr. 1,-E. base "pleu-,
'to flow'. See flow.
Derivative: pleuston-ic, adj.

## plexal
plexal, adj., pertaining to a plexus. — Formed fr.
plexus with adj. suff. -al.

## plexiform
plexiform, adj., resembling a plexus. —
Compounded of plexus and L. forma, 'form, shape'.
See form, n.

## plexuneter
plexuneter, п., a thin plate placed over that part

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:596 COLUMN:2 -->
of the body which is to receive the blows in
percussion (med.) — Compounded of Gk. πλή-
ξις, 'stroke', from the stem of πλήσσειν, 'to
strike', and μέτρον, 'measure'. See plague and
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## plexor
plexor, п., a plessor. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk.
πλήξις, 'a striking' (from the stem of πλήσσειν,
'to strike'), and the Latin agential suff. -or. See
plague and cp. plessor.

## plexus
plexus, п., a network (anal.) — L., 'braid,
network', fr. plexus, pp. of plectere, 'to braid, plait,
twist'. See ply, 'to bend', and cp. words there
referred to.

## pliable
pliable, adj. — ME. pliabylle, fr. MF. (= F.)
pliable, fr. plier, 'to fold, bend', fr. L.plicare, 'to
fold, bend'. See ply, 'to bend', and -able.
Derivatives :pliabil-ity, n.,pliable-ness, n.,pliabl-
y, adj.

## pliancy
pliancy, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## piiant
piiant, adj.— ME. pliaunt, fr. MF. (= F.)pliant,
pres. part, of plier, 'to fold, bend', fr. L.plicare.
See prec. word and -ant.
Derivatives: pliant-ly, adv., plianl-ness, n.
.plica, п., fold, esp. fold in the skin; Polish plait
(med.) — ML., back formation fr. L. plicare, 'to
fold, bend'. See ply, 'to bend', and cp. next word.
Derivative: ptic-al, adj.

## plicate
plicate, adj., having folds; plaited. — L.plicStus,
pp. oiplicare, 'to fold, bend'. See ply, 'to bend',
and adj. suff. -ate and cp. duplicate, replicate.
Derivatives: plicat-ed, adj., plicate-ly, adv.,
plicate-ness, п., plicat-ion, n.

## plicatile
plicatile, adj., capable of being folded together. —
L. plicatilis, 'that which may be folded together,
flexible, pliable'. See prec. word and -lie.

## plier
plier, п., one who plies. — Formed fr. ply, 'to
bend', with agential suff. -er.

## pliers
pliers, n. pi., a small pair of pincers. — Prop. pi.
of prec. word.

## plight
plight, п., state, condition. — ME. plit,
'condition', fr. AF. plit, corresponding to OF. pleit,
ploit, fr. VL. 'plictum, fr. L. plicitum, neut. pp.
oiplicare, 'to fold, bend', hence prop, a var. of
plait (q.v.)The spelling oiplightv/ithgh is due to
a confusion with OE. pliht, 'danger, risk' (see
plight, 'pledge').

## plight
plight, п., pledge. — ME. pliht, pligt, 'danger;
engagement', fr. OE. pliht, 'risk, danger', rel. to
OFris., MDu., Du. plicht, 'care, carefulness',
OHG. pfliht, MHG., G. pflicht, Obligation,
duty', MDu. pleghen, Du. ptegen, 'to care for', be
accustomed to', OHG. pflegan, MHG., G. pfle-
gen, of s.m., MDu. plien, 'to answer for,
guarantee' OE. pleon (for *plehan), 'to risk, expose
to danger'. See play, v., and cp. plege.

## plight
plight, tr. v., to pledge. — ME. plighten, fr. OE.
plihtan, 'to pledge', fr. pliht, 'risk, danger'. Cp.
Du. ver-plichten, G. ver-pflichten, 'to bind,
oblige', and see plight, 'pledge'.
Derivatives: plight-ed, adj., plight-er, n.

## Plimsoll mark
Plimsoll mark, a mark on the hull of a British
vessel showing how deeply she may be loaded.
— Named after Samuel Plimsoll (1824-98), an
advocate of shipping reform.

## plinth
plinth, п., the square block below the base of a
column (archil.) — L. plinthus, fr. Gk. πλίνθος,
'brick', which is cogn. with OE. flint, 'flint'. See
flint and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: plinth-er, n.

## Pliocene
Pliocene, adj., pertaining to the latest epoch of
the Tertiary period (geol.) — Coined fr. Gk.
πλείων, 'more' and καινός, 'new'. See pleio- and
-cene and cp. Pleistocene.
Derivative: Pliocene, n.

## ploce
ploce, п., emphatic repetition of a word (rhet.) —
L-, fr. Gk. πλοκή, 'a plaiting, twining, twisting,
braiding', which is rel. to πλέκειν, 'to plait,
twine, twist, braid', and cogn. with L. plectere,
'to plait, braid', plicare, 'to fold'. See ply, 'to
bend', and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
next word.

## Ploceidae
Ploceidae, n. pi., the family of weaverbirds (orni-
thol.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Gk.
πλοκεύς, 'plaiter, braider', which is rel. to
πλοκή, 'a plaiting, braiding'. See prec. word.

## plod
plod, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative origin.
Derivatives: plod, п., plodd-er, п., plodd-ing.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:596 COLUMN:3 -->
adj., plodd-ing-ly, adv., plodd-ing-ness, a.

## -ploid
-ploid, combining form denoting a (specified)
multiple (biol.) — Contraction of Gk. -πλόος,
'-fold' (see haplo-), and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape' (see -oid).
Derivative: -ptoid-y (forms nouns from
adjectives in -ploid).

## plop
plop, interj., intr. v. and n. — Of imitative origin.

## plosion
plosion, п., implosion or explosion (phon.) — See
explosion.

## plosive
plosive, adj., and п., implosive or explosive (phon.)
— See explosive.

## plot
plot, п., a small piece of ground. — ME. plot,
plotte, 'piece of ground'; prop, a var. of plat,
'piece of ground' (q.v.)
Derivative: plot, tr. v.

## plot
plot, n., conspiracy. — Prob. a blend of F. peloter,
'to wind into a ball', and complot 'conspiracy',
itself a back formation fr. comp(e)loter, 'to roll
into a ball', fr. com- and pelote, 'a ball'. See
pellet and cp. complot.
Derivatives: plot, tr. and intr. v.,plott-ed, adj.,
plott-er, п., plott-ing, adj., plott-ing-ly, adv.

## plough
plough, n. — See plow.

## plover
plover, п., the name of several birds. — OF. plo-
vier, lit. 'the rain bird' fr. VL. *plovarius, fr.
*plovere, 'to rain', corresponding to L. pluere
(see pluvial). F. pluvier, 'plover', has been
refashioned after L. pluvia, 'rain'. The bird is so called
because its arrival usually coincides with the
season of rain.

## plow
plow, plough, n. — ME. plough, fr. Late OE. plog,
ploh, fr. ON. pldgr, which is rel. to OS. plog,
OFris. ploch, Du. ploeg, OHG., MHG. pfluoc,
G. Pflug. These words are traceable to L. ptovus
or plOvum, 'plow', a word of prob. Rhaetian
origin (see Pliny, Hist. Nat., 18, 172). — OSlav.
plugH, Lith. plugas, 'plow', are Teutonic loan
words.
Derivatives: plow,plough, tr. and intr. \.,plow-er,
plough-er, п., ptow-ing, plough-ing, n.

## ploy
ploy, intr. v., to diminish front (milit.) — Aphetic
for deploy.
Derivative: ploy-ment, n.

## Pluchea
Pluchea, п., a genus of plants, the marsh fleabane
(bot.) — ModL., named after the French Abbe
N.-A. Pluche (1688-1761).

## pluck
pluck, tr. and intr. v. — ME. plucken, fr. OE.
pluccian, ploccian, fr. VL. *piluccdre, 'to deprive
of hair' (whence also MHG., G. pflucken, MDu.
plucken, plocken, Du. plukken, ON. plukka,
plokka, Dan. plukka, Sv/ed.plocka), fr. L.pilSre,
'deprive of hair', h.pilus, 'hair'. It. piluccare, 'to
pluck grapes', Provenc. pelucar, 'to pluck out',
F. eplucher, 'to pick, clean, peel, pare', also
derive from VL. "piluccare. See pile, 'hair', and cp.
plush. Cp. also pill, 'a little ball of medicine', and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: pluck, п., pluck-ed, adj., pluck-ed-
ness,- п., pluck-er, п., pluck-y, adj., pluck-i-ly,
adv., pluck-i-ness, n.

## plug
plug, n. — MDu. plugge (Du. plug), rel. to Swed.,
Norw. plugg, Dan. pleg, MLG. pluck, MHG.
phloc, G. Pflock.
Derivatives: plug, tr. and intr. v.,·plugg-able,
adj., plugg-ed, adj., plugg-er, п., plugg-ing, a.,
and adj., plugg-ing-ly, adv.

## plum
plum, n. — ME. plumme, plum, fr. OE. plume, fr.
VL. pruna (fern. sing, for orig. L. neut. pi.), fr.
L. prunum, 'plum', fr. Gk. προϋμνον, of s.m.,
which is of uncertain, possibly Phrygian, origin.
The disappearance of the m in Latin is due to
dissimilation. Cp. MDu. prume (whence Du.
pruim), OHG. pfruma (whence MHG. pfrume,
G. Pflaume), which also are Latin loan words.
See prune, n.
Derivative: plumm-y, adj.

## plumage
plumage, п., the feathers of a bird. — ME., fr.
MF. (= F.) plume, fr. OF. plume, fr. L. plu-
ma, 'down, feather'. See plume, n. and -age.
Derivative: plumag-ed, adj.

## plumassier
plumassier, п., a dealer in ornamental feathers. —
F., derivative of MF. plumasse, 'plume of
feathers', fr. plume, 'feather'. See prec. word and
-ier.

## plumate
plumate, adj., having plumage (zool.) — L. plu-
matus, 'feathered', fr. pluma. See plume and adj.
suif. -ate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:597 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PLUMB | 570 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:597 COLUMN:1 -->

## plumb
plumb, п., a lead hung on a string to show the
vertical line; a plummet. — ME. plom, plum,
plumbe, fr. OF. (= F.) plomb, fr. L. plumbum,
'lead', which, together with Gk. μόλιβος,
μόλυβδος, 'lead', was prob. borrowed from a
Mediterranean, possibly the Iberian, language. Cp.
plumber, plummet, plunge, aplomb. Cp. also
molybdenum.
Derivatives -.plumb, tr. v., plumber (q.v.),
plumbing, n.

## plumb
plumb, intr. v., to work as a plumber (colloq.) —
Back formation fr. plumber.

## Plumbaguiaceae
Plumbaguiaceae, n. pi., the leadwort family (hot.)
— Formed fr. Plumbago with suff. -aceae.

## piumbaginaceous
piumbaginaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## plumbago
plumbago, n.} graphite. — L. plumbago, 'a species
of lead ore, black lead', fr. plumbum, 'lead*. See
plumb, n.

## Plumbago
Plumbago, п., a genus of plants, the leadwort
(bot.) — See prec. word.

## plumbeous
plumbeous, adj., lead-colored. — L. plumbeus,
'leaden', fr. plumbum. See plumb, п., and -eous.

## plumber
plumber, n. — ME. plummet, fr. MF. plommier,
plummier (F. plombier), fr. L. plumbarius,
'plumber', prop, the adj. plumbarius, 'pertaining to
lead', used as a noun. See plumb and agential
suff. -er.

## plumbery
plumbery, n. — ME. plomerye, fr. MF. plommerie
(F. plomberie), fr. plommier, 'plumber'. See prec.
word and -ery.

## plumbiferous
plumbiferous, adj., containing lead. —
Compounded of L. plumbum, 'lead' (see plumb), and
-ferous.

## pluinbism
pluinbism, п., lead poisoning. — Formed fr. L.
plumbum, 'lead', with suff. -ism. See plumb,

## plumbous
plumbous, adj., containing lead, especially in a
low valence. — L. plumbosus, 'full of lead'. See
plumb and -ous.

## plumbum
plumbum, п., lead (chem.) — L. See plumb,

## plume
plume, п., feather. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L.
pluma, 'feather, down', for "plus-ma, which is
cogn. with OE.fleos,flies, 'fleece'. See fleece and
cp. deplume, unplume, displume.
Derivatives -.plume, tr. v.,plume-less,plume-like,
adjs., plum-er, п., plum-ery, a.,plum-y, adj.

## plumelet
plumelet, п., 1) a plumule; 2) a little plume. —
Formed fr. plume with dimin. suff. -let.

## plumiped
plumiped, adj., having feet covered with feathers;
п., a plumiped bird. — Compounded of L.
pluma, 'feather', and pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See
plume and pedal,

## plummet
plummet, n. — ME. nlomet. fr. OF. plommet,
dimin. of plom, plon, 'lead', fr. L. plumbum,
'lead-. See plumb, п., and -et.
Derivatives: plummet, tr. v., plummet-ed, adj.,
plummet-less, adj.

## plumose
plumose, adj., covered with feathers; featherlike.
— L. plumosus, 'full .of feathers', fr. pluma. See
plume and adj. suff. -ose.

## plump
plump, adj., rounded, filled out. — MDu. plomp,
lit. 'falling suddenly'; of imitative origin. See
next word.
Derivatives: plump-en, tr. and intr. \.,plump-ly,
adv., plump-ness, п., plump-y, adj.

## plump
plump, tr. v., to cause to fall; intr. v., to fall
suddenly. — ME. p/umpen, fr. MDu. plompen,
which is of imitative origin.
Derivatives: plump-er, п., plump-ing, n.

## piump
piump, adv., with sudden fall. — Imitative. Cp.
plump, v.

## plumule
plumule, п., 1) a down feather (zoo/:); 2)
rudimentary bud of a young plant. — L. plumula,
dimin. of pluma. See plume and -ule.

## plunder
plunder, tr. v. — G.plundern, 'to plunder, pillage',
fr. MHG. plundern, 'to plunder', orig. 'to take
away household furniture', fr. MHG. blunder,
plunder, 'household furniture' (whence G.
Plunder, 'lumber, baggage'), fr. MDu. plunder,
plonder, 'household goods', which is rel. to Fris.,
Du. plunje (for "plundje), 'clothes'.
Derivatives: plunder, a.,plunder-age,
п.,plunderer, п., plunder-ess, п., plunder-ing, n. and adj.,

## plunder-ing-ly
plunder-ing-ly, adv., plunder-ous, adj.

## plunge
plunge, tr. and intr. v. — ME- plongen, plungen,
fr. OF. plongier (F. plonger), fr. VL. *plumbicd-
re, prop, 'to immerse fishing-nets provided with
lead', fr. L. plumbum, 'lead'. See plumb.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:597 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: plunge, п., plung-er, п., plung-ing,
adj., plung-ing-ly, adv.

## plunk
plunk, tr. v., 1) to pluck (a stringed instrument);
2) to throw heavily; intr. v., 1) to give forth a
twanging sound; 2) to fall heavily. — Of
imitative origin.
Derivatives: plunk, n. and interj.

## pluperfect
pluperfect, adj. and n. — Contraction of L. (tern-
pus) plus quam perfectum, 'more than perfect
(tense)', prop, a loan translation of Gk (χρόνος)
ύπερσυντελικός. Ср. F. plus-que-parfait and see
plus and perfect,

## plural
plural, adj. — ME. plurel, plural, fr. OF. plurel
(whence, with change of suff., F. pluriei), fr. L.
pluralis, 'belonging to more than one', fr. plus,
gen. pluris, 'more'. See plus and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: plural, п., plural-ism, п., plural-ist,
п., plural-ist-ic, adj., plural-ist-ic-al-ly, adv.,-
plurality (q.v.), plural-ize, tr. v., plurah-iz-ation,
п., plural-iz-er, п., plural-ly, adv.

## plurality
plurality, n. — ME. pluralite, fr. MF. (=
F.)plurality, fr. L. pluralitatem, ace. of pluralitas,
'plurality', fr. pluralis. See prec. word and
-ity.

## pluri-
pluri-, combining form meaning 'more'. — L.
pluri·, from the stem of plus, gen. pluris, 'more'.
See olus.

## pluriaxial
pluriaxial, adj., having more than one axis. —:
Compounded of pluri- and axial.

## plus
plus, prep, adj., and n. — L. plus, gen. pluris,
'more', whence ρ lurimus, 'most'; cogn. with OI.
purvi, purith, 'much', prayah, 'mostly', OPers.
paru, Gk. πολύς, 'much, many', πλείων,
πλέων, 'more', πλείστος, 'most', πολλάκις, 'often',
Olr. il, 'much', ilar, 'crowd', W. elu, 'much',
Lith. pilus, 'abundance", Goth, filu, OHG.filu,
MHG. vil, G. viel, ODu. vilo, OFris.felo,feI(e),
ON. fjol- (only in compounds), OS. filu, OE.
fela, feala, feola, 'much, many'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base 'pie-, 'to fill'. See full, adj.,
and cp. pleio-, poly-.

## plus fours
plus fours, n. pi., loose knickerbockers. — So
called because orig. they reached four inches
below the knees.

## plush
plush, п., a fabric with a long soft pile. — F.
pluche, fr. earlier peluche, back formation fr.
OF. peluchier, 'to pull, tug' (whence F. eplucher,
'to pick, clean, peel, pare'), fr. VL. "piluccare,
'to deprive of hair', fr. L. pilus, 'hair'. See pile,
'hair', and cp. pluck and words there referred
to.
Derivatives: plush, intr. v.,plush-ed, adj., plush-
ette, п., ptush-y, adj., plush-i-ly, adv., plush-i-
ness, n.

## plut-
plut-, form of pluto- before a vowel.

## piutarchy
piutarchy, п., plutocracy. — Compounded of Gk.
πλοϋτος, 'wealth', and -αρχίϊ, 'rule', fr. άρχος,
'leader, chief, ruler'. See pluto- and -archy and
cp. plutocracy.

## pluteus
pluteus, п., 1) a partition placed between columns;
a kind of penthouse to protect soldiers; a
bookshelf (Roman antiq.); 2) the larva of echinoids
and ophiuroids (zool.) — L. pluteus, *a shed,
penthouse, parapet, bookshelf, prob. in grada-
tional relationship to Lith. plautaT, 'the
crossbars of the dry kiln', plautas, 'path in the
beehive', Lett, plaukts, 'wallboard'.

## Pluto
Pluto, п., the god of the lower world in Greek
mythology. — L. Pluto, Pluton, fr. Gk.
Πλούτων = Πλουτοδότης, lit. 'giver of riches', fr.
πλούτος, 'riches', and δότης, 'giver', from the
stem of διδόναι, 'to give'; see plutocracy and
date, 'point of time'. See Otto Kern, Die
Religion der Griechen I (1926), p. 130, Note ?. Cp.
plutonium.

## Pluto
Pluto, name of the planet most remote from the
sun, discovered in 1930. — Named after Pluto,
the god of the lower world. See prec. word.

## pluto-
pluto-, before a vowel plut-, "combining form
meaning 'riches'. — Gk. πλούτο-, πλουτ-, fr.
πλοϋτος, 'riches'. See next word.

## plutocracy
plutocracy, п., government by the wealthy. — Gk.
πλουτοκρατία, 'plutocracy', compounded of
πλοϋτος, 'riches', and -κρατίά, 'rule,

## government'
government', fr. κράτος, 'strength, power, rule'. The
first element prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *pleu-,
'to flow', whence also L. pluere, 'to rain'; see
pluvial. For the second element in plutocracy see

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:597 COLUMN:3 -->
-cracy.

## plutocrat
plutocrat, п., a person who rules by his wealth. —
Back formation fr. Gk. πλουτοκρατία. See prec.
word.
Derivatives: plutocrat-ic, plutocrat-ic-al, adjs.,
plutocrat-ic-al-ly, adv.

## plutolatry
plutolatry, п., worship of wealth. — Compounded
of pluto- and -λατρεία, -λατρίϊ, fr. λατρεία,
'hired labor, service, worship'. See -latry.

## plutomania
plutomania, п., an excessive desire for wealth. —
Compounded of pluto- and -mania.

## Plutonic
Plutonic, adj., 1) of, or pertaining to, Pluto; 2)
subterranean; 3) crystallized (said of igneous
rocks). — Formed fr. 1st Pluto with suff. -ic. —
Plutonic theory, the theory which regards heat
as the main geological agency.

## Piutonism
Piutonism, п., Plutonic theory. — See prec. word
and -ism.

## Plutonist
Plutonist, п., an adherent of the Plutonic theory.
— See Plutonic and -1st.

## plutonium
plutonium, п., a transuranic element (chem.) —
ModL., a name suggested by Glenn Theodore
Seaborg (1912- ) and Arthur Charles Wahl
(1917- ) in 1942 after Pluto, the second
planet beyond Uranus, on the analogy of the
element пателер tunium, which was so named
by McMillan after Neptune, the first planet
beyond Uranus (see neptunium). For the ending
of plutonium see chem. suff. -ium.

## plutonomy
plutonomy, п., political economy. — Formed fr.
Gk. πλοϋτος, 'riches', and -νομίϊ, fr. νόμος,
'law'. See pluto- and -nomy.
Derivatives: plutonom-ic, adj., plutonom-ist, n.

## pluvial
pluvial, adj., rainy. — L. pluvialis, 'of rain', fr.
pluvia, 'rain', short for aquapluvia, 'rainy water,
rain', prop. fern, of the adjective pluvius, 'rainy,
bringing rain', fr. pluere, 'to rain', fr. I.-E. base
*pleu-, 'to flow, to swim', whence also OI.
pldvate, 'navigates, swims', Gk. πλΰνειν, 'to
wash', πλέειν, πλεΐν, 'to navigate', OE. flowan,
'to flow'. See flow and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also Pluvidse, plover. For the ending see
adj. suff. -al.

## pluvial
pluvial, n., an ecclesiastic's cope. — ML. pluviale,
'a raincloak', prop. neut. of the Latin adj.
pluvialis, 'pertaining to rain, rainy', used as a noun.
See pluvial, adj.

## pluviometer
pluviometer, п., rain gauge. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. pluvia, 'rain', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure', see
pluvial and meter, 'poetical rhythm'. The
correct form is hyetometer, fr. Gk. θετός, 'rain',
and μέτρον, 'measure'.
Derivatives :pluviometr-ic,pluviometr-ic-al,Sia'iS.,
pluviometr-ic-al-ly, adv., pluviometr-y, n.

## pluviose
pluviose, adj., pluvious. — L. pluviosus. See
piuvions.
Derivative: pluvios-ity, n.

## Pluviose
Pluviose, п., the fifth month of the French
revolutionary calendar (lasting fr. Jan. 20th to Feb.
18th). — Lit. 'therainy month', coined by Fabre
d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. L. pluviosus, 'rainy'. See
pluvious. For the form of the word cp. Nivose,
Ventdse.

## pluvious
pluvious, adj., pertaining to rain; rainy. — L.
pluviosus, 'rain' (whence also F.pluvieux), fr. pluvia,
'rain'. See pluvial and -ous.

## ply
ply, п., fold, layer. — OF. (= F.) pli, fr. plier. See
next word.

## ply
ply, tr. and intr. v., to bend. — ME. plien, fr. OF.
(= F.) plier, fr. earlierpleiet- (whence F. ployer),
'to fold, bend', fr. L. plicare, 'to fold, bend', fr.
earlier "plecare, refashioned on analogy of
compounds such as complicare, 'to fold together'
(see complicate), and expticare, 'to unfold' (see
explicate), implicdre, 'to infold' (see implicate);
rel. to L. plectere, 'to plaid, braid, intertwine',
and cogn. with OI. prasnah, 'wickerwork,
basket', Gk. πλέκειν, 'to plait', πλοκή, 'network',
OSlav. pletq, plesti, 'to braid, plait, twist', OS.,
OHG. flehtan, MHG. vlehten, G. flechten, Du.
vlechten, ON. fletta, Swed. fldta, OE. fleohtan,
of s.m. Goth, flahta, 'braid'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base "pletc-, 'to plait, twist', an
enlargement of base "pel-, 'to fall'. See fold and
cp. -fold. Cp. also accomplice, application,
applique, apply, complex, complicate, complice,
complicity, complin, decuple, deploy, display,
doblon, dobra, double, doubloon, duplex, dupli-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:598 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 571 | PDDOSTEMACEOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:598 COLUMN:1 -->
cate, duplicity, employ, explicate, explicit, exploit,
flask, 'bottle', flax, flex, haplo-, imply, multiplex
multiply, octuple, perplex, plait, plash, 'to
interweave', plat, 'to interweave', pleach, pleat, Ple-
cotus, plecto-, plexus, pliable, plica, plicate,
plight, 'condition', ploce, -ploid, quadruple,
quadruplex, replica, replicate, reply, sextuple,
simple, splay, symploce, Symplocos, triplex,
triplicate.
Derivatives: pliab/e (q.v.), pH-er, n.

## ply
ply, tr. v., to work at, pursue diligently; intr. v.,
to work (at something). —Shortened fr. apply.

## Plymouth Rock
Plymouth Rock, a breed of domestic fowls..— So
called after the famous rock in Plymouth, Mass.,
where the Mayflower landed in 1620.

## Plynteria
Plynteria, n. pi., name of the Greek festival, on
which the clothes of the statue of Athene were
washed. — Gk. Πλυντήρια (scil. ίερά), lit. 'the
feast of washing', neut. pi. of πλΰντήρ(.ος,
'pertaining to washing', fr. πλύνει, 'to wash', rel.
to πλέειν, πλεΐν, 'to navigate', and cogn. with
L. pluere, 'to rain'. See pluvial.

## plywood
plywood, n. — Compounded of ply, 'layer of
wood", and wood.

## -pnea
-pnea, -pnoea, combining form meaning
breathing'. — ModL., fr. Gk. -πνοι,α, fr. tcvolS,
πνοίή, πνοή, 'blowing, breathing', fr. πνεΐν,
'to breathe'. See pneuma.

## pneum-
pneum-, form of pneumo-, before a vowel.

## pnenma
pnenma, п., the vital spirit. — Gk. πνεϋμα,
'breath, wind, air', fr. πνεΐν, 'to blow', which is
of imitative origin. Cp. pneumatic, pneumonia.
Cp. also neume.

## pneumat-
pneumat-, form of pneuma to- before a vowel.

## pneumatic
pneumatic, adj., pertaining to, or acting by means
of, wind or air. — L. pneumaticus, fr. Gk.
πνευματικός, 'of wind or air', fr. πνεύμα, gen.
πνεύματος, 'breath, wind, air'. See prec. word
and 1st -atic.
Derivatives: pneumatic, adj., pneumatic-al-ly,
adv., pneumat-ics, n.

## pneuma to-
pneuma to-, before a vowel pueumat-, combining
form meaning 'wind, air; spirit; presence of air'.
— Gk. πνευματο-, πνευματ-, fr. πνεϋμα, gen.
πνεύματος. See pneuma.

## pneumatocyst
pneumatocyst, п., a sac containing air in the body
of some marine animals. — Cpmpounded of
pneumato- and Gk. κύστις, 'bladder, bag'. See
cyst.

## pneumatology
pneumatology, п., the doctrine concerning
spiritual beings. — ModL. pneumatologia,
compounded of pneumato- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: pneumatolog-ic, pneumatolog-ic-al,
adjs., pneumatohg-isty n.

## pneumatolysis
pneumatolysis, п., the process of forming minerals
by the pressure of heated air (mineral.) —
ModL., compounded of pneumato- and Gk.
λύσις, 'a loosing, setting free'. See -lysis.

## pneum atoly tic
pneum atoly tic, adj., formed by the pressure of
heated air (mineral.) — Compounded of
pneumato- and Gk. λυτικός, 'able to loose, loosing'.
See -lytic.

## pneumatometer
pneumatometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the force of respiration. — Compounded of
pneumato- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivative: pneumatometr-y, n.

## pneumatophore
pneumatophore, п., a respiratory organ on the
roots of some plants (bot.); an air cavity in the
body of certain marine animals, —
Compounded of pneumato- and Gk. -φόρος, 'bearing,
bearer'. See -phore.
Derivative: pneumatophor-ous, adj.

## pneumato therapy
pneumato therapy, п., the treatment of disease by
rarefied or condensed air. — Compounded of
pneumato- and -therapy.

## pneumectomy
pneumectomy, п., the surgical removal of lung
tissue. — Lit. 'removal of the lung'. See pueu-
mo- and -ectomy.

## pneumo-
pneumo-, before a vowel pneum-, combining form
denoting the lung. — Gk. πνευμο-, fr. πνεύμων,
gen. πνεύμονος, 'lung', assimilated fr. πλεύμων,
'lung', which is prob. cogn. with OI. kloman-,
'the right lung' (if dissimilated fr. *pliman-)t and
with L. pulmo, 'lung'; see pulmonary· The
assimilation of Gk. πλεύμων, to πνεύμων is due

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:598 COLUMN:2 -->
to folk etymology, which associated πλεύμων,
'lung', with πνεϋμα, 'breath' (see pneuma).

## pneumobacillus
pneumobacillus, п., a bacterium causing
pneumonia (bacteriol.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined
fr. pneumo- and Late L. bacillus, 'a little staff'.
See bacillus.

## pueumococcus
pueumococcus, п., any of the bacteria causing
pneumonia (bacteriol.) — Medical L.,
compounded of pneumo- and coccus.
Derivatives: pneumococc-al, pneumococc-ic,
pneumococc-ous, adjs.

## pneumoconiosis
pneumoconiosis, п., lung disease caused by the
inhalation of minute particles (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of pneumo-, Gk. κονία,
'dust' (fr. κόνις, 'dust', see conio-). and suff.
-osis.

## pneumodynamics
pneumodynamics, п., the dynamics of gases. —
Compounded of pneumo- and dynamics (see
dynamic).

## pneumo gastric
pneumo gastric, adj., pertaining to the lungs and
the stomach. — Compounded of pneumo- and
gastric.

## pneumon-
pneumon-, form of pneumono- before a vowel.

## pneumonia
pneumonia, п., inflammation of the substance of.
the lungs (med.) — Medical L.} fr. Gk.
πνευμονία, 'disease of the lungs', fr. πνεύμων, gen.
πνεύμονος, 'lung'. See pneumo- and -ia.

## pneumonic
pneumonic, adj., pertaining to the lungs;
pertaining to pneumonia. — Medical L. pneumoni-
cusy fr. Gk. πνευμονικός, fr. πνεύμων. See prec.
word and, adj. suff. -ic.

## pneumoniae
pneumoniae, adj. — See next word and adj. suff.
-ic.

## pneumonitis
pneumonitis, п., inflammation of the lungs (med.)
— Medical L., formed fr. Gk. πνεύμων, gen.
πνεύμονος, 'lung' (see pneumo-), with suff. -itis.

## pneumono-
pneumono-, before a vowel pneumon-, combining
form meaning 'lung'. — Gk. πνευμονο-, πνευ-
μον-, fr. πνεύμων, gen. πνεύμονος, 'lung'. See
pneumo-.

## pneumothorax
pneumothorax, п., air or gas in the pleural cavity
(med.) — Coined by Jean Itard (1775-1838), an
ear specialist of Paris, in 1803, fr. pneumo- and
thorax.

## -pnoea
-pnoea, combining form. — See -pnea.

## Poa
Poa, a genus, of plants, the meadow grass (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. πόα (Homeric and Ion.
ποίη, Dor. ποία;, 'grass, grassy place*, prob.
standing for *ποι5α and cogn. with Lith. peva,
'meadow'.

## Poaceae
Poaceae, n. pi., the grass family (bot.) — Formed
from prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## poaceous
poaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## poach
poach, tr. v., to steal (game or fish); intr. v., to
hunt or fish illegally. — MF. (= F.) pocher,
'to thrust one's fingers into', fr. LG. poken. See
poke, 'to push'.
Derivatives: poach-er, п., poach-ingt n.

## poach
poach, tr. v., to boil eggs without their shells. —
ME. pochen, fr. MF. (= F.) pocher, fr. OF.
pochier, 'to put into a pocket', hence 'to poach
an egg', i.e. 'to boil an egg so that the white
surrounds the yolk like a pocket*. See poke, 'bag',
and cp. pocket, pouch,

## pocan
pocan, п., the pokeweed. — See poke, 'the poke-
weed', and cp. puccoon.

## pochard
pochard, п., the male of the diving sea duck. —
Prob. derived fr, F. pocher, 4o thrust'. See poke,
'to push',

## pock
pock, п., pustule. — ME. pokke, fr. OE. росс,
'pustule', rel. to MDu. pocke, MLG. pocke, of
s.m., whence G. Pocke, 'pockmark', in the pi.:
'smallpox'), prop, 'baglike swelling', and to OE.
росса,pohha, 'bag', MLG. pukel, 'bag'; fr. I.-E.
imitative base *bhu-, *bu-, 'to blow', whence
also L. buccay 'mouth*. See buccal and cp. poach,
'to boil eggs', pocket, poke, 'a small bag', pouch,
pox, puck, 'disk', pucker.
Derivative: pock-y, adj.

## pocket
pocket, n. — ME. poket, fr. AF. pokete, dimin.
formed fr. O'NF.poque^poke, which corresponds
to OF. pouche, F. poche, 'pocket'. See poke, 'a
small bag', and cp. pock and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: pockety adj., pocket, v., pocket-ed,
adj., pocket-er, п., pocket-y, adj.

## poco
poco, adv., a little, slightly (musical direction). —

## It.
It., fr. L. paucus. See paucity.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:598 COLUMN:3 -->

## pococurante
pococurante, adj., caring little, indifferent. — It.,
'caring little', compounded of poco', 'little' (see
prec. word), and cuiante, pres. part, of curare,
'to care*. See cure, v. and n.
Derivatives: pococurante, п., pococurante-ism,
pococurant-ism, п., pococurante-lst, pococurant-
ist, n.

## pod
pod, п., seed of beans. — Of unknown origin.
Derivatives: podd-ed, adj., podd-er, n.

## pod
pod, п., a cluster of whales or seals. — Of
unknown origin.

## pod
pod, п., the socket of a brace. — A var. of pad,
'stuffing'.

## pod-
pod-, form of podo- before a vowel.

## -pod
-pod, combining form meaning 'having (a certain
number or a certain kind of) feet'. — Gk.
-ποδός, -ποδον, fr. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'.
See foot and cp. the second element in polyp.
Cp. also -poda, podo-, -podous.

## -poda
-poda, combining form denoting 'creatures
having (a certain number or a certain kind of)
feet'. — Gk. -πόδα, neut. pi. of-ποδός, fr. πους,
gen. ποδός, 'foot'; hence prop. pi. of-pod (q.v.)

## podagra
podagra, п., gout. — ME., fr. L., fr. Gk.
ποδάγρα, 'trap for the feet, gout in the feet',
compounded of πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot' and άγρα,
'a catching, seizure'. For the first element see
foot, for the second see chiragra.
Derivatives: podagr-ic, podagr-ous, adjs.

## podal
podal, adj., pertaining to a foot or feet. — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot',
and adj. suff. -al (fr. L. -alis). See foot. The
correct form is pedal (fr. L. pes, gen. pedis, 'foot',
and L. suff. -alis).
Derivative: podal-ic, adj.

## Podarge
Podarge, п., name of one of the Harpies in Gk.
mythology. — Gk. Ποδάργη, lit. 'swift-footed',
or 'white-footed', compounded of πους, gen.
ποδός, 'foot' (see foot), and αργός, 'shining,
glistening, white; swift', which is dissimilated fr.
*άργρός and cogn. with OI. rjrah, 'shining,
glowing, bright; swift', L. argentum, 'silver', lit.
'the white metal'. See argent.

## podesta
podesta, п., chief magistrate of an Italian town in
the Middle Ages. — It. podesta, potesm,
'governor*, lit. 'power', fr. L. potestatem, ace. of po-
settas, 'power, might', fr. potis, 'able, capable'.
See potent and cp. words there referred to.

## podge
podge, п., anything podgy. — A collateral form
of pudge.

## podgy
podgy, adj., short and thick; pudgy. — A
collateral form of pudgy.
Derivatives: padgi-ly, adv., podgi-uess, n.

## podiatry
podiatry, п., the treatment and cure of the feet
(med.)—Compounded of Gk. πους, gen.
ποδός, 'foot', and ιατρεία, 'healing'. See foot and
-in trie.

## podiatrist
podiatrist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.

## podium
podium, п., a small dais. — L., 'elevated place',
fr. Gk. πόδιον, dimin. formed fr. πους, gen.
ποδός, 'foot'. See foot and cp. pew, puy. Cp.
also sympodlum, appoggiatura.

## -podium
-podium, combining form denoting a footlike part,
as inpropodium. — ModL., lit. 'small foot'. See
prec. word.

## podo-
podo-, before a vowel pod-, combining form
meaning 'foot', 'hoof, or 'stalk' (as in Pod-
ophthalmia). — Gk. ποδο-, ποδ-, fr. πους,
gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See foot.

## Podocarpus
Podocarpus, п., a genus of trees of the yew family
(bot.) — ModL,, compounded of podo- and Gk.
καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.

## podocarpous
podocarpous, adj. — See prec. word and -ous.

## Podophthalmia
Podophthalmia, п., an order of Crustacea (zool.)
— ModL., lit. 'stalk-eyed', compounded of
podo-, Gk. οφθαλμός, 'eye' (see ophthalmo-),
and 1st suff. -ia.
Derivatives: podophthalmi-an, adj. and п.,
podophthalm-ic, adj.

## podophyllin
podophyllin, п., podophyllum resin. — Formed
from next word with suff. -in.

## Podophyllum
Podophyllum, п., a genus of plants of the barberry
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of podo-
and Gk. φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo-.

## Podostemaceae
Podostemaceae, n. pi., the riverweed family (bot.)
ModL., formed fr. Podostemon with suff. -aceae.

## podostemaceous
podostemaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:599 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PDDDSTEMDN | 572 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:599 COLUMN:1 -->

## Podostemon
Podostemon, п., a genus of plants, the riverweed
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of podo- and Gk.
στήμων, 'warp', used in the sense of stamen
(q.v.)

## -podous
-podous, combining form meaning '-footed'. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. nouns ending in -poda.

## pod sol
pod sol, n. — See podzol.

## Podura
Podura, п., a genus of insects (entomol.) — ModL.,
compounded of pod- and Gk. ούρα, 'tail'. See
uro-, 'tail'.
Derivatives: podur-an, adj. and п., podur-id, n.

## podzol
podzol, п., also podsol, ashlike soil. — Russ. pod-
zola, 'alkaline ashes', fr. pod, 'under', and zo/a,
'ashes'.
Derivative: podzol-ic, podsol-ic, adj.
рое, poebird, п., the parson bird. — Рое is a
Tahitian word meaning 'pearl bead'. Captain
Cook who thought the word meant 'earring',
named the bird рое in allusion to the tufts of
curled hair under its throat.

## poecilo-
poecilo-, before a vowel poecil-, combining form
meaning 'variegated, various'. — Gk. ποικίλο-,
ποικιλ-, fr. ποικίλος, 'many-colored,
variegated', fr. I.-E. base *peik-, 'to adorn by
coloring or carving'. See paint and cp. words there
referred to.

## poem
poem, n. — MF. роете (F. роете), fr. L. poema,
fr. Gk. ποίημα, 'something done; a composition
in verse, poem', from the stem of ποιειν, 'to
make'. See poet and -m.

## poesy
poesy, n. — ME. poesie, fr. MF. poesie (F. poesie),
fr. L .poesis, fr. Gk. ποίησις, 'a making; poetry',
fr. ποιεΐν, 'to make'. See poet and cp. poiesis,
posy.

## poet
poet, n. — ME. poete, fr. OF. poete (F. poete), fr.
L. poeta, fr. Gk. ποιητής, 'one who makes, an
artificer, a poet', fr. ποιεΐν, 'to make', fr. I.-E.
base *qwei-, 'to make7, whence also OI. cinSti,
cayati, 'gathers, heaps up, piles up', citih,
'heaping up, piling up, 'collecting, collection',
OSlav. cinu, 'act, deed, order', ciniti, 'to arrange,
put in order', Cp. poem, poesy, posy and the
second element in epopee, onomatopoeia,
pharmacopoeia. Cp. also payyetan, piyyut.
Derivatives: poetaster (q.v.), poet-ess, п., poetic
(q.v.), poetize (q.v.), poetry (q.v.)

## poetaster
poetaster, n. — ModL., formed fr. L. poeta (see
poet) with the pejorative suff. -aster.
Derivatives: poetaster-ing, п., poetaster-ism, п.,
poetastr-y, п., poetastr-ic, poetastr-ic-al, adjs.

## poetic
poetic, adj. — MF. (= F.) pbe'tique, fr. L. poiti-
cus, fr. Gk. ποιητικός, 'capable of making,
active, creative, productive; pertaining to poetry,
poetic*, fr. ποιητός, 'made', verbal adj. of
ποιεΐν, 'to make'. See poet and adj. suff. -ic
and cp. -poietic.
Derivatives: poet-ics, п., poetic-al, adj., poetic-
al-ly, adv., poetic-ize, tr, and intr. v.

## poetico-
poetico-, combining form meaning 'poetic and',
as in poetico-antiquarian.

## poetize
poetize, intr. and tr. v. — F. poetiser, fr. poete.
See poet and -ize.
Derivative: poetiz-ation, n.

## poetry
poetry, n. — ME. poetrie, fr. OF. poe'terie,
poetrie, fr. Late L. poetria, fr. L. poeta; not to be
confused with L. poetria, Gk. ποιήτρια,
'poetess'. See poet and -ry.

## Pogonia
Pogonia, п., a genus of orchids (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. πωγωνίας, 'bearded*, fr. πώγων,
'beard*; so called from the lip of several species
of ihis genus. Cp. the second element inAndro-
pogon, Cymbopogon, Tragopogon.

## pogrom
pogrom, п., organized massacre. — Russ. pogro-
тй, 'devastation, pillage', formed fr. po,
'behind, after', which is cogn. with L. post, 'behind,
after' (see post-), and gromu, 'thunder', which is
rel. to OSlav. gromu, 'thunder', vuzgrimeti, 'to
thunder', fr. I.-E. base *ghrem-, 'to give a
hollow sound, to thunder', whence also OE.
grimm, grim, 'cruel, fierce*. See grim and cp.
grum, grumble,

## poi
poi, п., food made of taro root. — Hawaiian.

## poiesis
poiesis, п., the action of doing or producing
something. — Gk. ποίησις, 'a making'. See poesy.

## -poiesis
-poiesis, combining form meaning 'production'
See prec. word.

## -poietic
-poietic, combining form meaning 'making,
producing'. — Gk. -ποιητικός, fr. ποιητικός,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:599 COLUMN:2 -->
'capable of making, active, creative, productive'.
See poetic.

## poignancy
poignancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## poigaant
poigaant, adj. — ME. poinaunt, fr. OF. (^ F.)
poignant, pres. part, of poindre, 'to prick, sting',
fr. L. pungere. See point, v., and cp. pungent.
Derivative: poignant-ly, adv.

## poikilo-
poikilo-, before a vowel poikil-. — A var. spelling
of poecilo-, poecil-,

## poilu
poilu, п., a French private soldier. — F., lit.
'hairy', fr. poil, 'hair', fr. L.pilus; see pile, 'hair'.
The word poilu was used in the sense 'strong,
brave, courageous' (so esp. by Balzac, in his
Medecin de campagne), whence, in French
military slang, the meaning 'private soldier'.

## Poinae
Poinae, n. pi., the goddesses of vengeance in
Greek mythology. — Gk. Ποιναί, pi. of ποινή,
'bloodmoney, fine, penalty, punishment', fr.
I.-E. base *qwoina-, whence also Avestic каёпй-,
'vengeance, punishment', OSlav. cena, 'price',
Lith. kaina, 'price'. L. poena, 'punishment', is
borrowed fr. Gk. ποινή. See penal.

## Poinciana
Poinciana, п., a genus of plants of the senna
. family (bot.) — ModL., named after M. de
Poincy, a governor of the French West Indies in
the 17th cent.

## poind
poind, tr. v., to distrain {Scot. law). — Scot, poynd,
corresponding to ME- pinden, fr. OE. pyndan,
'to shut up, enclose, impound'. See pound,
'enclosure'.
Derivatives: poind, п., poind-able, adj.,
poinding, n.

## Potusettia
Potusettia, п., a genus of plants of the spurge
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
American diplomat Joel Roberts Poinsett (1779-
1851). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## point
point, n. — ME. point and pointe, partly fr. OF.
(= F.) point, 'a pricking, piercing, dot, mark',
fr. L, punctum, 'that which is pricked, puncUire,
point', prop. neut. pp. of pungere, 'to prick,
pierce', and partly fr. OF. (= F.) pointe,
'anything pointed, a sharp point' (fr. Late L. puncta,
fern. pp. of L. pungere). See pungent and cp.
words there referred to. In its mathematical and
grammatical sense, L. punctum is a loan
translation of Gk, στιγμή, 'that which is pricked,
puncture, point', fr. στιζειυ, 'to prick'.
Derivatives: point, v. (q.v.), point-less, adj,,
point-less-ly, adv., point-less-ness, п., point-y,
adj.

## point
point, tr. and intr. v. — ME. pointen, partly, fr.
OF. pointer, fr. point or pointe, partly fr. point,
n. See point, n.
Derivatives: point-ed, adj., point-ed-ly, adv.,
point-ed-ness, п., point-er, п., point-ingy n.

## pointillism
pointillism, п., the French impressionist method
of painting based on the effect of dots. — F.
pointillisme, fr. pointiller, 'to dot', fr. point,
'point, dot'. See point, п., and -Ism.

## pointillist
pointillist, п., an artist who used pointillism. —
F. pointilliste, fr. pointiller. See prec. word and
-ist.

## point of view
point of view, — Loan translation of F. point de
vue, which itself is a loan translation of L.
punctum visus, whence also G. Gesichtspunkt.

## poise
poise, tr. v. — ME. peisen, poisen, fr. OF. (= F.)
peser, fr. VL. pesare, fr. L. pensure, 'to weigh
carefully', ireq. of pendere (pp. pensus), 'to
weigh'. See pendant and cp. pensile, pension,
pensive, peseta, peso, and the last element in
avoirdupois, counterpoise, v.

## poise
poise, n. — ME. poys, fr. OF. pois (F. poids), fr.
VL. pesum, fr. L. pensumt 'something weighed',
prop. neut. of pensus, pp. οι pendere. In F. poids,
the -d- is due to an erroneous association of this
word with h.pondus, 'weight'. See poise, v., and
cp. counterpoise, п., eqnipoise.

## poison
poison, n. — ME. poisoun, poison, fr. OF. poison,
puison (F. poison) fr. L. potionem, ace. of potto,
'a drinking, a draft; a magic potion, philter',
whence the meaning 'medicinal potion', and
later 'poisoned drink'. See potion, which is a
doublet of poison.
Derivatives :po/ion-oHj, dA).,poison-ous-ly, adv.,

## poison-ous-ness
poison-ous-ness, n.

## poison
poison, tr. v. — ME. poisonen, fr. poison. See
poison, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:599 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: poison-able, adj., poison-ed, adj.,
poison-er, п., poison-ing, n.
poitrel, poi trail, п., breastplate for a horse (arch.)
— MF. poitral, poitrel, fr. L. pectordle,
'breastplate', prop. neut. of the adj. pectoralis,
'belonging to the breast', fr. pectus, gen. -oris,
'breast'. See pectoral.

## poivrade
poivrade, п., pepper sauce. — F., fr. poivre,
'pepper', fr. L. piperem, ace. of piper, 'pepper'. See
pepper ane -ade.

## poke
poke, a small bag. — ME., fr. ONF. poque, poke,
corresponding to F. poche; of Teut. origin. Cp.
MDu. poke, ON. poki, OE. росса, pohha,
'pouch, bag'. See pock,

## poke
poke, tr. and intr. v., to push, thrust. — ME. po-
ken, rel. to MLG. boken, buken, puggen, MDu.
boken, boken, Du. beuken, MHG. bochen, pu-
chen, G. pochen, 'to knock, rap*; of imitative.
origin. Cp. poach, 'to thrust', pochard, poker,
'a card game'.
Derivatives: poke, п., pok-y, adj.

## poke
poke, п., the pokeweed. — Shortened fr. pocan,
fr. Virginian puccoon, lit. 'plant for staining', fr.
рак, 'blood'. Cp. pocan, puccoon.

## poker
poker, п., a card game. — Perh. fr. G. Poch,
Poche, Pochspiel, a card game resembling poker,
fr. pochen, 'to knock, rap; to brag, boast, defy*
(see poke, 'to thrust'). The game is so called in
allusion to the boastful words of the daring
player: 'Ich poche* (= Ί defy'). See Kluge-
Mitzka, DEW., p. 557 s.v. pochen.

## poker
poker, п., an instrument for poking a fire. —
Formed fr. poke,'to thrust',with agential suff. -er.

## poker
poker, п., a hobgoblin (rare) — Perhaps of Scand.
origin. Cp. Swed. pocker, Dan. pokker, 'the
devil', and E. puck, 'goblin'.
Derivative: poker-ish, adj.

## Polack
Polack, п., a Pole; adj. Polish. — Pol. Polak, 'a
Pole'. Cp. Pol. Poljane, 'Poles',Polsko, 'Poland*,
polski, 'Polish', and see Pole,

## polacre
polacre, polacca, п., a two- or three-masted
sailing vessel. — F. polacre; cp. It., Sp., Port.
polacra, Du. polaak, G. Polaker, of s.m. Origin
unknown.

## Poland
Poland, n. — Contraction of Pole and land (see
haplology).

## Polanisla
Polanisla, п., a genus of plants of the caper family
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of poly- and Gk.
άνισος, 'unequal' (see aniso-), and 1st suff. -ia.

## polar
polar, adj. — Mb.poldris (whence also F. polaire),
fr. L. polus, 'pivot, axis, pole*, fr. Gk. πόλος.
See pole, 'extremity', and adj. suff. -ar and cp.
circumpolar.
Derivatives: polar-ic, polar-ist-ic, adjs.,
polarity, п., polarize (q.v.), polar-ly, adv.

## polarimeter
polarimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
amount of polarization of light (opt.) —
Compounded of polar and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: polarimetr-ic, adj., polarimetr-y, n.

## Polaris
Polaris, п., the polestar. — ModL. Polaris, short
for"stella Polaris, lit. 'polar star'. See polar,

## polariscope
polariscope, п., an instrument for examining the
polarization of light (opt.) — Compounded of
polar and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look
at, examine*. See -scope.
Derivatives: polariscop-ic, adj., polariscop-ic-al-
ly, adv., polariscop-y, n.

## polarize
polarize, tr. v., to cause the vibration of light,
heat, etc., to be modified in a particular manner.
— F. polariser, fr. polaire. See polar and -ize.
Derivatives; polariz-able, adj., polartz-ation, п.,

## polariz-er
polariz-er, n.

## polatouche
polatouche, п., a small flying squirrel. — F., fr.
Russ. poletutcha, lit. 'the flying animal*, fr.

## poUtaV
poUtaV, 'to fly", fr. intensive pref. po-, fr. po,
'behind, after', and UtaC, freq. of letet\ 'to fly'.
Russ. po is rel. to OSlav. po, 'behind, after*; see
post-. Russ. letet't 'to fly", is rel. to Czech leteti.
Church Slav, leteti, Serbo-Croatian leteti, 'to

## fly'
fly', and prob. also to Lith. lekiu, lekti, 'to fly',
lakstiti, 'to fly about'; see leg.

## polder
polder, п., a tract of low land reclaimed from the
sea. — Du. polder, of uncertain origin.

## Pole
Pole, n.} a native of Poland. — G. Pole, sing, of

## Polen
Polen, fr. MHG. Polan, pi. Polane, fr. Pol.

## Poljane
Poljane, 'Poles', lit. 'field dwellers', fr. pole, 'field*,

## which is rel. to OSlav. polje
which is rel. to OSlav. polje, 'field', fr. I.-E. base

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:600 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 573 | POLLUTE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:600 COLUMN:1 -->
*р(ё)1й-, 'flat, plain', whence also L. planus,
'even, level, flat'. See plain, adj., and cp. field.
Cp. also Polack, polonaise, polonium, poulaine.
For the sense development of Pol. Poljane,
'Poles', fr. pole, 'field', cp. Dane.
Derivatives: Pol-ish, adj. and n.

## pole
pole, п., a long piece of wood, stake, mast. —
ME., fr. OE. pal, 'stake, pole', fr. L. palus, of
s.m. See pale, 'stake'.
Derivatives: pole, tr. v., pot-er, п., pol-ing,
n.

## pole
pole, п., either of the extremities of the axis of the
sphere. — ME., fr. OF. pole F. pole), fr. L.
potus, fr. Gk. πόλος, 'pivot, axis, pole', which
stands for 'q^olos, and is rel. to πέλειν, more
usually as deponent, πέλεσθαι, 'to be in
motion, to be', fr. I.-E. base *qKel-, 'to bend,
turn'. See wheel and cp. pulley.

## poleax
poleax, poleaxe, n. — Lit. 'head-axe', fr. ME.
pollax, (cp. LG. polkxe); compounded of poll,
'head', and axe. The spelling poleaxe is due to a
confusion with pole, 'a piece of wood'.
Derivatives: poleaxe, tr. v., poleaxer, n.

## polecat
polecat, п., a carnivorous animal of the weasel
family. — The first element derives fr. OF. pole
(F. poule), 'hen', fr. Late L. pulla, 'hen', fern, of
L.pullus, 'young animal'. See pullet. The second
element is cat. Hence polecat lit. means 'poultry
cat', i.e. 'cat preying on poultry'.

## polemarch
polemarch, п., commander of the army (Greek
hist.) — Gk. πολέμαρχος, compounded of
πόλεμος, 'war', and άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'.
See next word and -arch.

## polemic
polemic, adj. — F. polemique, fr. MF., fr. Gk.
πολεμικός, 'pertaining to war, warlike', fr.
πόλεμος, 'war', which is rel. to πελεμίζειν, 'to
shake, cause to tremble', and cogn. with Goth.
usfilma, 'frightened, terrified, amazed', usfilmei,
'fright, terror, amazement', fr. l.-E. *pelem-,
enlargement of base 'pel-, 'to shake, swing',
whence Gk. πάλλειν, 'to wield, brandish, swing;
to quiver', πολτός, 'wielded, brandished',
OSlav. plachu, 'wavering, cowardly', po-plachtt,
'terror'. Cp. catapult, pallesthesia, Papilio, Pe-
leus, Polemonium, Ptolemy, sympalmograph.
Cp. also pulse, 'throb', and words there
referred to. For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: polemic, n. (q.v.), polemic-al, adj.,
polemic-al-ly, adv., polemic-tan, п., polemic-ist,
п., polem-ics, n.

## polemic
polemic, n. — F. polemique, fr. MF., fr.
polemique, adj. See polemic, adj.
Derivative: polem-ics, n. (see -tcs).

## polemize
polemize, intr. v. — Gk. παλεμίζειν, 'to make
war', fr. πόλεμος, 'war'. See polemic and -ize.

## Polemoniaceae
Polemoniaceae, n. pi., the polemonium family
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Polemoalum with
suff. -aceae.

## polemoniaceous
polemoniaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## Polemonium
Polemonium, п., a genus of plants, the Greek
valerian (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. polemonia, fr.
Gk. πολεμώνιον, 'the Greek valerian',
derived fr. the PN. Πολέμων, fr. πόλεμος, 'war'. See
polemic, adj.

## polenta
polenta, п., porridge made of parched barley,
chestnut meal or cornmeal. — it., fr. L.pollenta,
polenta, 'peeled varley', which is rel. to pollen,
'fine flour'. See pollen.

## poll-
poll-, form of polio- before a vowel.

## polianite
polianite, п., manganese dioxide (mineral) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite from the stem of
Gk. πολιαίνεσθαι, 'to grow gray', fr. πολιός,
'gray' (see polio-); so called in allusion to its
gray color.

## police
police, n. — MF. (= F.)police, 'political
organization, administration'. (The modern meaning
'police', arose only about the end of the 17th
cent.) MF. police is a secondary form of policie.
See policy, 'method of governing'.
Derivatives: police, tr. v.,polic-ed, adj., polic-ize,
tr. v., polic-iz-er, n.

## Policbinelle
Policbinelle, п., grotesque hero of the French
comedy, corresponding to the English Punch.
— F., fr. Neapolitan Polecenella. See
Punchinello.

## policlinic
policlinic, n. — G. Poliklinik, orig. meaning
'clinic open to the patients of the town', fr. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:600 COLUMN:2 -->
πόλις, 'town' (see policy, 'method of
government'), and Klinik, 'clinic', fr. F. clinique (see
clinic).

## policy
policy, п., method of government. — ME. policie,
fr. MF. policie, 'political organization,
administration', fr. Late L. politia, 'administration of
the Commonwealth', fr. L. polltla, 'citizenship,
the state', fr. Gk. πολιτεία, 'citizenship, the
state; government, administration,
constitution', fr. πολίτης, 'citizen', fr. πόλις, 'fortified
city, state', which is cogn. with Ol. pur (fern.),
puram (neut.), purih (fern.), 'citadel, city, town',
Lith. pilis, Lett, pi'ls, 'citadel'. Cp. police, polity
and the second element in acropolis,
cosmopolitan, isopolity, metropolis, necropolis, propolis,
tetrapolis. Cp. also gopura.

## policy
policy, п., a document of insurance. — F. police,
'insurance policy', fr. It. polizza, corruption of
ML. apodixa, 'receipt', fr. MGk. άπόδειξις,
'receipt', fr. Gk. άπόδειξις, 'a showing forth,
demonstration, proof, from the stem of άποδει-
κνύναι, 'to show Gorth, demonstrate', fr. άπό,
'from, away from' (see apo-), and δεικνύναι, 'to
show', which is cogn. with L. dicere, 'to tell'.
See diction and cp. words there referred to.

## poligar
poligar, п., feudal chief in the former Madras
Presidency (India). — Marathi palegar, prob.
fr. OI. palayan, 'guarding', fr. palayate, 'guards,
protects', a secondary form of parayate, 'carries
over, guards, protects', which is prop, the
causative form of piparti, 'brings over', fr. I.-E. base
'per-, 'to lead across, drive across', which is
identical with base *per-, 'through, across,
beyond', whence L. per, 'through, across, over,
beyond'. See per and cp. words there referred to.

## polio
polio, n. — Short for poliomyelitis.

## polio-
polio-, before a vowel poll-, combining form
meaning'gray'. — Gk. πολιό-, πολι-, fr. πολιός,
'gray', fr. I.-E. base *pel-, 'dark-colored, gray',
whence also OE. fealo, 'dull-colored, yellow,
yellowish red'. See fallow, 'brownish yellow',
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
polianite.

## poliomyelitis
poliomyelitis, п., inflammation of the gray matter
of the spinal cord (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of polio- and myelitis.

## poliosis
poliosis, п., canities. — Medical L., lit. 'turning
gray (of the hair)', fr. Gk. πολιός, 'gray'. See
polio- and -osis.

## polish
polish, tr. and intr. v. — ME. polischen, fr. OF
(= F.) poliss-, pres. part, stem of polir, 'to
polish', fr. L. polire, 'to make smooth, polish',
which is of uncertain origin. It possibly stands
for *po-lire, 'to clean, polish', fr. pref. po- and
'lire, a verb rel. to linere, 'to smear'. For the
pref. po- cp; L. ρόηό, Ί place', which stands for
*po-s(i)n6 and lit. means Ί lay aside', fr. pref.
po- and sind, Ί set down, leave'; see position.
For the etymology of L. linere, 'to smear', see
slime; for the ending of polish see verbal suff.
-ish. Cp. polite, politesse, interpolate.
Derivatives: polish, п.,polish-ed, adj.,polish-ed-
ly, adv., polish-ed-ness, п., polish-er, п.,
polishing, n.

## polite
polite, adj. — ME. polyt, fr. L. politus, pp. of
polire, 'to make smooth, to polish'. See polish,
v., and adj. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: polite-ly, adv., polite-ness, n.

## politesse
politesse, п., politeness, civility. — F., fr. It. poli-
lezza, pulitezza, prop, the quality of bemgpolito,
pulito (= 'polite'). See prec. word and -esse.

## politic
politic, adj. — ME. politik, fr. MF. (= F.)
politique, fr. L. politicus, fr. Gk. πολιτικός,
'pertaining to a citizen, political', fr. πόλις, 'city,
state'. See 1st policy and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: politic, п., polit-ics, п., politic-al,
adj.,polltic-al-ly, Sidv.,politic-ian, п.,politic-ize,
intr. v., politic-iz-er, n.

## politico-
politico-, combining form meaning 'politics;
political and'. — See prec. word.

## polity
polity, п., the form or constitution of the
government of a state. — Late L. politia, fr. Gk.
πολιτεία, 'citizenship; policy'. See 1st policy.

## polka
polka, п., a lively dance. — F., fr. Slovak polka,
or Czech putka, 'half step.', dimin. of po/, resp.

## pul
pul, 'half.

## poll
poll, п., head. — ME. pol, polle, fr. MDu. polle,

## pol
pol, 'top of the head, head', which is prob. cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:600 COLUMN:3 -->
with L. bulla, 'bubble, knob' (with ρ for b). See
bull, 'edict', and cp. the first element in poleax
and polliwog and the second element in tadpole.

## poll
poll, tr. v., 1) to cut, trim; 2) to take the votes of;
intr. v., to vote. — Fr. prec. word. The orig.
meaning was 'to cut off the hair of the head'. Cp.
pollard.
Derivatives: poll-able, adj., poll-ing, adj. and
n.

## poll
poll, adj., cropped, shorn. — Short for pold,
polled, pp. of poll, 'to cut'.

## poll
poll, п., the poll, the undergraduates, the passmen
(Cambridge Univ. Slang). — Fr. Gk. οί πολλοί,
'the many', pi. of πολύς, 'much, many'. See
poly- and cp. hoi polloi.

## poll
poll, п., a parrot. — See Polly. For sense
development cp. cockatoo.

## pollack
pollack, pollock, п., an edible fish. — Prob. a
derivative of poll, 'head'.

## poilard
poilard, п., a tree polled of its top. — Formed fr.
poll, 'to cut, trim', with suff. -ard.

## pollen
pollen, п., the fertilizing male element of flowers.
— L., also pollis, 'fine flour, milldust', fr. I.-E.
base "pel-, 'dust, porridge made of meal',
whence also pollenta, polenta, 'peeled barley',
pulvis, 'dust', Gki πόλτος, 'pap, porridge'
(whence L. puis, gen. pultis, of s.m.), πάλη,
'sifted meal', OI. palalam, 'ground seeds',
OPruss. pelanne, 'ashes', Lith. pelenai, Lett.
pelni, OSlav. popelu, Russ. pepetu (formed
through the reduplication of the base), 'ashes'.
Cp. pollinate. Cp. also polenta, powder, pulse,
'seeds', poultice, pulverize, and the second
element in Paspalum.

## pollex
pollex, п., the thumb. — L., prob. cogn. with
OSlav.patici, 'thumb', Russ. pdlec, 'finger', dial.
Russ. pales, 'thumb'. L. palma, 'palm of the
hand', is not cognate.

## pollical
pollical, adj., pertaining to the pollex. —■ Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. pollex, gen. pollicis. See
prec. word.

## pollicitation
pollicitation, п., offer, promise (law) — L. pollici-
tdtio, gen. -onis, fr. pollicitaius, pp. of pollicitdri,
freq. of polliceri (pp. pollicitus), 'to promise',
which is formed ίτ.-prei. por-, 'forward, forth',
and licere, 'to be permitted'. Pref. por- is rel. to
pro, 'before, for'. See 1st pro- and cp. the pref.
in pollinctor, pollute, porrect, portend, post,
'pillar'. For the etymology of licere see license,

## pollinate
pollinate, tr. v., to fertilize with pollen (bot.) —
Formed with verbal suff. -ate fr. L. pollen, gen.
pollinis. See pollen,

## pollination
pollination, n. — Formed from prec. word with
suff. -ion.

## pollinctor
pollinctor, п., one who washes corpses and
prepares them for burning (Roman antiq.) — L.
pollinctor, pollictor, fr. pollingere, 'to wash a
corpse', which is rel. to lixa, 'lye'. Pref. pol-
prob. stands iotpor-; see pollicitation. For the
etymology of lixa see lixiviate. The л in L.
pollingere is due to the analogy of verbs like
fingere, 'to fashion' (pp. fictus), pingere, 'to
paint' (pp. pictus).

## pollinic
pollinic, adj., pertaining to pollen. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ic fr. L. pollen, gen. pollinis.
See pollen,

## polliniferous
polliniferous, adj., bearing pollen. —
Compounded of L. pollen, gen. pollinis, and the stem of

## ferre
ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See pollen and -ferous.

## pollinium
pollinium, п., a pollen mass. — ModL. See
pollen and 1 st -ium.

## polimosis
polimosis, п., hay fever (med.) — A Medical L.
hybrid lit. meaning 'disease caused by pollen',
coined fr. L. pollen, gen. pollinis (see pollen), and
the Gk. suff. -ωσις (see -osis).

## poiliwog
poiliwog, п., a tadpole. — -Earlier polwigge, fr.
ME. polwigle, which is prob. compounded of
pol, 'head', and wigelen, 'to move to and fro'.
See poll, 'head' and wiggie.

## pollock
pollock, n. — A var. of pollack,

## poilucite
poilucite, п., caesium aluminosilicate (mineral)
— Named after Pollux, the twin brother of
Castor in Greek mythology; cp. castorite. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## pollute
pollute, tr. v., to make foul, defile. — L. pottutus,
pp. oipolluere, 'to defile, pollute, contaminate',
for *por-luere. For the pref. por- see
pollicitation. L. -luere inpolluere is rel. to L. lutum, 'mud'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:601 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: POLLUTION | S74 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:601 COLUMN:1 -->
and cogn. with Gk. λΰμα, 'filth, dirt, disgrace',
λύμάξ, 'rubbish, refuse', λύθρος, λύθρον, 'dirt,
gore', Olr. loth, 'mud, dirt', W. lludedic,
'muddy', Lith. iutynas, 'pool, puddle'. Cp. lute, 'a
cohesive substance', and L у thrum.

## pollution
pollution, n. — Late L. pollutio, gen. -onis, fr. L.
pollutus, pp. of polluere. See prec. word and -ion.

## Pollux
Pollux, п., 1) the twin brother of Castor (Greek
mythology); 2) name of the second star of the
constellation Gemini. — L., fr. Gk.
Πολυδεύκης; see Polydeuces. The shortening of the
word and the shift of the accent to the first
syllable are due to Etruscan influence.

## Polly
Polly, Poll, fern. PN. — Polly is a rhyming
collateral form of Molly, which is a pet form of
Mary.

## polly
polly, п., a parrot. — Fr. prec. word.

## polo
polo, п., name of a game. — Lit. 'ball', fr. Balti
\nd. polo. Cp. Tibetanpulu, 'ball'.

## polonaise
polonaise, п., a Polish dance. — F., shortened fr.
dame polonaise, 'a Polish dance', fem. of polo-
nais, 'Polish', fr. Polonia, Latinized name of
Poland. See Pole.

## polonium
polonium, п., name of a radioactive element
(chem.) — ModL., fr. Polonia, Latinized name
of Poland (see Pole and cp. polonaise); so called
by its discoverers Pierre Curie (1859-1906) and
his wife, Maria Skiodowska (1867-1934), after
the latter's native land. Cp. prec. word.

## polony
polony, п., a kind of sausage. — Prob. from the
name of the Italian city Bologna.

## poltergeist
poltergeist, п., a noisy ghost. — G., lit. 'noisy
ghost', fr. poltern, 'to make a noise or row', and
Geist, 'ghost'. The first element derives fr.
earlier buldern, boldern, which is rel. to MDu.
balderen, from the I.-E. imitative base *bhel-,
'to sound, ring, roar', whence also OE. bellan,
'to bellow', belle, 'bell'. See bellow and cp. bell,
'to bellow', bell, 'metallic vessel'. For the second
element see ghost.

## poltroon
poltroon, п., a spiritless coward, dastard. — MF.
poultron (F. poltron), 'sluggard, coward1, fr. It.
poltrone, orig. meaning 'foal, colt', whence
'timid like a colt', augment, of poltro> 'foal', fr.
VL. *pulliter, a derivative of L. pullus, 'a young
animal'. See pullet and -oon and cp. poult,
poultry.
Derivatives; poltroon-ish, adj., poltroon-ish-ly,
adv., poltroon-ism, n.

## poltroonery
poltroonery, n. — F. poltronnerie, fr. poltron. See
prec. word and -ery.

## poly-
poly-, combining form meaning 'much, many'. —
Gk. πολύ-, fr. πολύς, neut. πολύ, *much, many',
which is cogn. with L. plus, 'more', plurimus,
'most'. See plus and cp. hoi polloi, poll,
'undergraduates'. Cp. also pleio-.

## polyandrist
polyandrist, n. — Formed fr. polyandry with suff.
-ist.

## polyandrous
polyandrous, adj., ]) practicing polyandry; 2)
(boi.) having 20or more stamens. —Gk. πολύαν-
δρος. See next word. ForE. -ous, as equivalent
to Gk. -ος, see suff. -ous.

## polyandry
polyandry, п., I) the condition of having more
than one husband at the same time; 2) (bot.)
the presence of 20 or more stamens in one
flower. — Gk. πολυανδρία, fr. πολύανδρος,
'having many husbands', introduced into
botany by Linnaeus in the sense of 'having many
stamens'; compounded of πολύς, 'much, many'
and άνήρ, gen. ανδρός, 'man, husband'. See
poly-, andro- and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## polyanthus
polyanthus, п., I) a cultivated variety of primrose;
2) any of the species Narcissus Tazetta. — ModL.,
fr. Gk. πολύανθος, 'abounding in flowers', fr.
πολύς, 'much, many', and άνθος, 'flower'. See
poly- and anther.

## polyarchic
polyarchic, polyarchical, adj. — See next word
and -ic, resp. also -al.

## polyarchy
polyarchy, п., government by several persons. —
Compounded of poly- and Gk. -αρχίά, 'rule',
fr. άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See -archy.

## poly basic
poly basic, adj., having more than one atom of
hydrogen replaceable by basic radicals (chem.)
— Compounded of poly- and basic. See base, n.
Derivative: polybasic-ity, n.

## polybasite
polybasite, п., an iron-black silver sulfantimonite
(mineral.) — See prec. word and subst. sufT. -ite.

## polycarpic
polycarpic, polycarpous, adj., having many

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:601 COLUMN:2 -->
carpels (bot.) — Formed fr. poly-, carpel and suff.
-ic, resp. -ous.

## polycarpy
polycarpy, n. — See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## Polychaeta
Polychaeta, n. pi., a class of annelids, comprising
most marine worms (zool.) — ModL.,
compounded of poly- and Gk. χαίτη, 'hair'. See
chaeto-.
Derivatives: polychaete, adj. and п., polychaet-
an, polychaet-ous, adjs.

## polychasium
polychasium, п., a form of cymose inflorescence
in which more than two branches are produced
from every main axis (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of poly- and Gk. χασίς, 'chasm,
separation, division', which is rel. to χάσμα, 'chasm'.
See chasm and 1st -iura.

## polychrestic
polychrestic, adj., having many uses. — Formed
with sufT. -ic fr. Gk. πολύχρηστος, 'useful for
many purposes', fr. πολύς, 'much, many' and
χρηστός, 'useful'. See poly- and chrestomathy.

## polychresty
polychresty, n. — See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## polychromate
polychromate, п., a substance which shows a
variety of colors. — See polychrome and adj. suff.
-ate.
Derivative: polychromat-ic, adj.

## polychrome
polychrome, adj., having many colors. —
Compounded of poly- and Gk. χρώμα, 'color'. See
chromatic.
Derivatives: polychrome, п., polychrom-ic,
polychrom-ous, adjs., polychrom-ia·, п., poly-
chrom-y, n.

## polyclinic
polyclinic, п., a clinic for the treatment of various
diseases. — Compounded of poly- and clinic.

## Polycodium
Polycodium, п., a genus of plants of the heath
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of poly-
and Gk. κώδων, 'bell' (see codon), and 1st suff.
-ium.

## polycyclic
polycyclic, adj., having many cycles. —
Compounded of poly- and cyclic.

## polycythemia
polycythemia, polycythaemia, п., a condition
characterized by too many red blood cells (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of poly-, Gk. κύτος,
'a hollow vessel' (see -cyte), αίμα, 'blood' (see
hemal), and 1st suff. -ia.

## polydactyl
polydactyl, adj., having more fingers or toes than
usual (zool.) — Lit. 'having many fingers';
compounded of poly- and Gk. δάκτυλος,
'finger'. See dactyl.
Derivatives: polydactyl, п., poly dactyl-ism, п.,
polydactyl-ous, adj.

## polydemic
polydemic, adj., living in many regions (said of
plants and animals). —■ Compounded of poly-
and demic, in the sense of endemic.

## Polydeuces
Polydeuces, Polydeukes, п., the twin brother of
Castor (Greek mythol.) — Gk. Πολυδεύκης, lit.
'very sweet', compounded of πολύς, 'much,
many', and δευκής = γλυκύς, 'sweet* (ср.
δεϋκος, 'sweetness', a var. οίγλεΰκος), for orig.
*δλυκύς. See glyco- and cp. Pollux.

## Polydorus
Polydorus, п., the youngest son of Priam (Greek
mythol.) — L. Polydorus, fr. Gk. Πολύδωρος,
from the adj. πολύδωρος, 'one who has received
many gifts; richly dowered', which is
compounded of πολύς, 'much, many', and δώρον,
'gift'. See poly- and donation.

## polyembryony
polyembryony, п., the existence of two or more
viable embryos in the same seed (bot.) —
Compounded of poly-, embryon, and suff. -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## Polygala
Polygala, п., a genus of plants, the milkwort
(bot.) — L., 'milkwort', fr. Gk. πολύγαλον,
which is compounded of πολύς, 'much, many',
and γάλα, 'milk'. See poly- and galacto-,

## Poiygalaceae
Poiygalaceae, n. pi., the milkwort family (bot.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## polygalaceous
polygalaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.
po!ygamist,n.—Formed fr.polygamy with suff. -ist.
Derivative: polygamist-ic, adj.

## polygamous
polygamous, adj. — See polygamy and -ous.
Derivative: polygamous-ly, adv.

## polygamy
polygamy, п., the condition of having more than
two wives at the same time. — MF. (= F.)
polygamic, fr. Late L. polygamia, fr. Gk.
πολυγαμία, fr. πολύγαμος, 'having many wives',
which is compounded of πολύς, 'much, many*,
and γάμος, 'marriage'. See poly- and gamo-.

## polygenesis
polygenesis, п., plurality of origin. — ModL.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:601 COLUMN:3 -->
compounded of poly- and genesis.
Derivative: polygenes-ist, n.

## polygenetic
polygenetic, adj. — See prec. word and -genetic.
Derivative: polygenetic-al-ly, adv.

## polygenic
polygenic, adj., forming two or more compounds
with hydrogen or other univalent elements
(chem.) — Compounded of poly- and -genie

## polygenous
polygenous, adj., consisting of many kinds. —
Compounded of poly- and -genous.

## polyglot
polyglot, adj., 1) speaking or writing many
languages; 2) containing many languages; п., one
who knows several languages. — Gk. πολύ-
γλωττος, 'many-tongued', compounded of
πολύς, 'much, many', and γλώττα, 'tongue,
language'. See poly- and gloss, 'explanation'.
Derivatives: polyglott-al, polyglott-ic, polyglott-
ous, adjs.
.polygon, п., a plane figure with more than four
angles and sides (geom.) — Late L. polygonum,
fr. Gk. πολύγωνον, prop. neut. of the adj.
πολύγωνος, 'polygonal', which is compounded of
πολύς, 'much, many', and -γωνος, '-angled',
from the stem of γωνία, 'angle'. See poly- and
-gon.
Derivatives :jjolygon-al, adj., polygon-α I- ly, adv.,
polygon-ic, adj., polygon-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Polygonatum
Polygonatum, п., a genus of plants, Solomon's
seal (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. polygonaton,
'Solomon's seal*, fr. Gk. πολυγόνατον, prop. neut.
of the adj. πολυγόνατος, 'having many joints',
which is compounded of πολύς, 'much, many*
(see poly-), and γόνυ, gen. γόνατος, 'knee'. See
poly- and -gon.

## Polygonella
Polygonella, п., a genus of plants of the
buckwheat family (bot.) — ModL-, formed fr.
Polygonum with dimin. suff. -ella.

## Polygonia
Polygonia, п., a genus of anglewing butterflies
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk- πολύγωνος,
'polygonal' (see polygon and 1st -ia); so called
because of their angular wings.

## Polygonum
Polygonum, п., a genus of plants, the knotweed
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. polygonos, polygonon,
'knotgrass', fr. Gk. πολύγονον, of s.m., which is
compounded of πολύς, 'much, many1, and γόνυ,
'knee' (see Polygonatum); so called in allusion
to the numerous joints.

## polygraph
polygraph, п., a device for multiplying copies of a
writing. — Gk. πολύγραφος, 'writing much', fr.
πολύς, *much, many', and -γράφος, fr. γρά-
cpetv, 'to write'. See poly- and -graph.
Derivative: polygraph-ic, adj.

## polygraphy
polygraphy, п., the art of multiplying copies of a
writing. — Gk. πολυγραφία, 'the act of writing
much', fr. πολύγραφος. See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ίαJ.

## polygynous
polygynous, adj., 1) having-several wives; 2) (bot.)
having many pistils. — See next word and -ous.

## polygyny
polygyny, п., the condition of having many wives,
polygamy. — Compounded of poly- and Gk.
γυνή, 'woman*. See gyno- and -y (representing
Gk. -ίά).

## polyhedral
polyhedral, adj., pertaining to a polyhedron. —
See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## polyhedron
polyhedron, n. (geom.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πολύε-
δρον, 'having many seats or sides', compounded
of poly- and έδρα, 'seat; base, side, face'. See
-hedron.

## polyhistor
polyhistor, п., a very learned man. — Gk. πολυ-
Έστωρ, 'very learned', compounded of πολύς,
'much, many', and ίστωρ, 'knowing, learned',
whence ίστορί ά, 'learning, knowledge*. See poly-
and history.
Derivatives: polyhistor-ic, adj., polyhistor-y, n.

## Polyhymnia
Polyhymnia, п., the Muse of lyric poetry (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Πολυμνία, contraction
of Πολυύμνια, lit. 'the Muse of the many
hymns', fr. πολύϋμνος, 'abounding in hymns',
which is compounded of πολύς, 'much, many',
and ύμνος, 'hymn'. See poly- and hymn and cp.
Polymnia.

## polymath
polymath, п., a very learned man, a polyhistor. —
Gk. πολυμαθής, 'having learned much;
knowing much', formed fr. πολύς, 'much, many',
and μαθ-, stem of μανθάνειν, 'to learn'. See
poly- and mathematical.
Derivatives: polymath-ic, adj., poly math- у, n.

## polymer
polymer, п., one of two or more polymeric
compounds (chem.) — See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 575 | POLYZOARY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: polymer-ism, п., polymer-iz-able,
adj., polymer-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
polymerization, п., polymer-iz-er, n.

## polymeric
polymeric, adj., consisting of the same chemical
elements in the same proportions by weight,
but differing in molecular weight (ckem.) — G.
polymerisch, coined by the Swedish chemist
Baron Jons Jakob Berzelius (1779-1848) in 1830
fr. poly- and Gk. μέρος, 'part*, which is cogn.
with L. mereri, 'to earn, obtain, deserve'. See
mero-, 'part', and cp. merit. For the ending see
adj. suff. -ic.

## Polynuu'a
Polynuu'a, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL", named after the Muse
Polyhymnia fr. Gk. Πολυμνία. See Polyhymnia.

## polymorph
polymorph, п., an organism of several forms. —
Gk. πολύμορφος, 'multiform, manifold', fr.
πολύς, 'much, many' (see poly-), and μορφή,
'form, shape'. See morpho-.

## polymorphism
polymorphism, n. — See prec. word and -ism.

## polymorphous
polymorphous, polymorphic, adj., having many
forms. — Gk. πολύμορφος. See polymorph and
-ous, resp. -Ic.

## Polynesia
Polynesia, n. — Compounded of poly- and Gk.
νήσος, 'island', which is prob. rel. to νή-χε'.ν,
'to swim', ft. I.-E. base *sna-, 'to flow'. See
Indonesia and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: Polynesi-an, adj. and n.

## polyneuritic
polyneuritic, adj. — See next word and -ic.

## polyneuritis
polyneuritis, п., inflammation of many nerves at
the same time (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of poly- and neuritis.

## Polynices
Polynices, п., the brother of Eteocles (Greek
mythol.) — L. Polynices, fr. Gk. Πολυνείκης,
from the adj. πολυνείκης, 'much wrangling',
which is compounded of πολύς, 'much', and
νεΤκος, 'quarrel, strife, feud', which is rel. to
νίκη, 'victory'. See poly- and Nike.

## polynomial
polynomial, adj., consisting of two or more terms
(alg.). — Formed on analogy of binomial (q.v.)
fr. Gk. πολύς, 'much, many'. See poly- and cp.
multinomial.

## polynuclear
polynuclear, polynucleate, adj. having many
nuclei. — Compounded of poly- and nuclear,
resp. nucleate.

## polyonymous
polyonymous, adj., having many names. — Gk.
πολυώνυμος, ft. πολύς, 'much, many', and
δνυμα, dial, form of δνομα, 'name'. See name
and cp. onomato-. For the ending see suff. -ous.

## polyonymy
polyonymy, n. — Gk. πολυωνυμία, 'a multitude
of names', fr. πολυώνυμος, 'having many
names'. See prec. word and -y (representing Gk.
-is).

## polyopia
polyopia, п., double or multiple vision (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of poly- and Gk.
-ωπία, from the stem of ώψ, gen. ώπός, 'eye'.
See -opia.

## polyp
polyp, п., 1) a many-tentacled coelenterate, as a
hydra or a coral; 2) = polypus. — MF. (= F.)
polype, fr. OF., fr. L. polypus, fr. Gk. πολύπους,
'octopus', lit. 'many-footed'; compounded of
πολύς, 'much, many', and πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. See poly- and foot, and cp. polypod,
polypus.
Derivatives: polyp-ean, adj. and п., polyp-ous,
adj.

## polypary
polypary, п., the hard structure of a colony of
polyps. — ModL., polyparium, fr. L. polypus.
See polyp and suff. -ary (representing L. -ariurri).
Derivative: polypar-ian, adj.

## Polypedates
Polypedates, п., the tree frog (zoo!.) — ModL.,
compounded of poly- and Gk. πηδδν, 'to jump,
spring'. See pedesis and cp. Pedetes.

## polypedatid
polypedatid, adj., pertaining to the Polypeda-
tidae; п., a tree frog of the family Polypedati-
dae. — From prec. word.

## Polypedatidae
Polypedatidae, n. pi., a family of tree frogs (zoo!.)
— Formed ft. Polypedates with suff. -idae.

## polypetalous
polypetalous, adj., having the petals separate
(bot.) — Formed fr. poly-, petal and -ons.

## polyphagia
polyphagia, п., an excessive desire for food (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. πολυφαγία, 'excess in
eating', fr. πολυφάγος, 'eating to excess', fr.
πολύς, 'much, many', and φαγεΐν, 'to eat'. See
poly-, -phagous and 1st -ia.

## polyphagic
polyphagic, polyphagous, adj., eating to excess. —
Fr. L. polyphagus, fr. Gk. πολυφάγος. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ic, resp. -ous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 COLUMN:2 -->

## polyphase
polyphase, п., having many phases. —
Compounded of poly- and phase.

## Polyphemus
Polyphemus, п., the one-eyed Cyclops who was
blinded by Odysseus (Greek mythol.) — L.
Polyphemus, fr. Gk. Πολύφημος, lit. 'much
spoken of, fr. πολύς, 'much, many', and φήμη,
'voice, report, reputation'. See poly- and -phe-
mia.

## Polyphemus
Polyphemus, п., a large American silkworm
moth (zool.) — ModL., fr. Polypehmus, the one-
eyed Cyclops (see prec. word); so called in
allusion to the eyespots on each of its hind wings.

## polyphone
polyphone, п., a graphic symbol representing
more than one sound. — Compounded of poly-
and -phone. See polyphonic.

## polyphonic
polyphonic, polyphonous, adj., consisting of more
than one sound. — Gk. πολύφωνος, 'having
many tones', compounded of πολύς, 'much,
many' and φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See poly- and
phone, 'a sound'. For the ending see suff. -ic,
resp. -ous.

## polyphonist
polyphonist, n. — Formed fr. polyphone with
suff. -1st.

## polyphony
polyphony, п., multiplicity of sounds. — Gk.
πολυφωνία, fr. πολύφωνος, 'having many
tones'. See polyphonic and -y (representing Gk.
-ii).

## polyphylesis
polyphylesis, п., descent from more than one
ancestor, polygenesis. — ModL., fr. Gk. πολύ-
φϋλος, Of many tribes', which is compounded
of πολύς, 'much, many', and φυλή, 'clan, tribe'.
See poly- and phyle.

## polyphyletic
polyphyletic, adj., descended from more than one
ancestor. — See prec. word and adj. suif. -ic.
Derivative: polyphyletic-al-ly, adv.

## polyphyllous
polyphyllous, adj., having many leaves {bot.) —
Gk. πολύφυλλος, 'many leaved', fr. πολύς,
'much, many*, and φύλλον, 'leaf. See poly-
and phyllo-. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk.
-ος, see -ous.

## polypidom
polypidom, п., a polypary. — Compounded of
Gk. πολύπους, 'polyp', and δόμος, 'house'. See
polyp and dome, 'a building'.

## polypite
polypite, п., an individual polyp (zoof.) — See
polyp and subst. sufT. -ite.

## polypod
polypod, adj., having many feet; п., an animal
having many feet. — F. polypode. See polyp and
cp. polypus.

## Polypodiaceae
Polypodiaceae, n. pi., the fern family {bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Polypodium with suff.
-aceae.

## polypodiaceous
polypodiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## Polypodium
Polypodium, п., a genus of ferns {bot.) — L., fr.
Gk. πολυπόδιον, 'a kind of fern, polypody'. See
polyp and -ium.

## polypody
polypody, п., any plant of the genus Polypodium
{bot.) — L. See prec. word.

## polypoid
polypoid, polypoidal, adj., resembling a polyp. —
Compounded of polyp and Gk. -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid and adj. suff.
-al.

## polyptych
polyptych, п., a door panel having more than
three folds. — Gk. πολύπτυχος, 'having many
folds', fr. πολύς, 'much, many' (see poly-), and
*πτύξ, gen. πτυχός, 'fold', which is related to
πτύσσειν, Чо fold'. Ср. diptych, triptych.

## polypus
polypus, п., 1) a polyp; 2) a soft tumor {med.) —
L., fr. Gk- πολύπους. See polyp.

## polystele
polystele, п., a cylinder with more than one stele
(bot.) — Compounded of poly- and stele.
Derivative: polystel-ic, adj.

## Polystichum
Polystichum, n.,a genus of ferns (бол)— ModL.,
compounded of poly- and Gk. στίχος, 'row,
line, rank, verse' (see stichic); so called in
allusion to the many rows of the sori.

## polys torn at ous
polys torn at ous, adj., having many mouths. —
Compounded of poly- and Gk. στόμα, gen.
στόματος, 'mouth'. See stomato- and -ous.

## Polystomella
Polystomella, п., a genus of Foraminifera {zool.)
— A ModL. hybrid coined fr. poly-, Gk. στόμα,
'mouth* (see stoma), and L. dimin. suff. -efla
(see -ella). The correct form would be Polysto-
matium, fr. poly- and Gk. στόματιον, 'a little
mouth', which is formed fr. στόμα, 'mouth',
with the dimin. suif. -ιον (see -ium).

## polystyle
polystyle, adj., having many columns {arch.) —
Gk. πολύστϋλος;, fr. πολύς, 'much, many', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 COLUMN:3 -->
στύλος, 'column, pillar*. See poly- and. style,
'gnomon'.
Derivative: polystyl-ous, adj.
pol> sulfide, polysulphide, п., a compound of more
than one atom of sulfur in a molecule {chem.) —
Compounded of poly- and sulfide,

## polysyllabic
polysyllabic, adj., having many (as a rule: more
than three) syllables. — ML. polysyllabus, fr.
Gk. πολυσύλλαβος, which is compounded of
πολύς, 'much, many', and συλλαβή, 'syllable'.
See poly- and syllabic.
