Derivatives: polysyllabic-al-ly, adv., polysyf-
tabic-ity, п., polysyllab-ism, n.

## polysyllable
polysyllable, п., a word of many (as a rule: more
than three) syllables. — Compounded of poly-
and syllable. Cp. prec. word.

## polysyndeton
polysyndeton, п., repetition of conjunctions (rhet.)
— ModL., prop. neut. of the Gk. adj. πολυσύν-
δετος, 'containing many conjunctions', which is
compounded of πολύς, 'much, many', and σύν-
δετος, 'bound together', fr. σύν, 'together', and
δεΐν, 'to bind'. See poly- and syndetic and cp.
asyndeton.

## polysyntbesis
polysyntbesis, п., a synthesis of several elements.
— Compounded of poly- and synthesis,

## polysynthetic
polysynthetic, adj., united by several elements. —
Compounded of poly- and synthetic.
Derivatives: polysynthetic-al-ly, adv., polysyn-
thetic-ism, n.

## polysynthetism
polysynthetism, п., union of several elements. —
See prec. word and -ism.

## polytechnic
polytechnic, adj., pertaining to the instruction in
many technical subjects; п., a polytechnic
school. — F. polytechnique, fr. Gk. πολύτεχνος,
'skilled in many arts', which is compounded of
πολύς, 'much, many', and τέχνη, 'art'. See poly-
and technic.
Derivatives: polytechn-ics, п., polytechnic-al,
adj., polytechn-ist, n.

## polytheism
polytheism, п., the belief in many gods. — F.
polytheisme, fr. Gk. πολυθεΐα, 'polytheism', fr.
πολύθεος, 'believing in many gods', which is
compounded of πολύς, 'much, many' and θεός,
'god'. See poly- and 1st theism.

## polytheist
polytheist, п., a believer in many gods. — See
prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: polytheist-ic, polytfieist-ic-al, adjs.,
polytheist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## polytomons
polytomons, adj., divided into more than two
subordinate parts {bot.) — Compounded of poly-
and Gk. τομή, 'a cutting', which is rel. to τέμ-
νειν, 'to cut'. See tome and -ous,

## polytopic
polytopic, adj., occurring at several places. —
Compounded of poly- and Gk. τόπος, 'place'.
See topic.

## polytrophic
polytrophic, adj., obtaining nourishment from
several substances. — Fr. Gk. πολύτροφος,
'nutritious', which is compounded of πολύς, 'much,
many' and τροφή, 'food, nourishment'. See
poly- and trophic.

## polytypic
polytypic, adj., having many types. —
Compounded of poly-, type and adj. suff. -ic.

## polynrine
polynrine, п., excessive urination {med.) —
Compounded of poly- and urine.

## polyvalence
polyvalence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## polyvalent
polyvalent, adj., multivalent. — A hybrid coined
fr. poIy: and L. valens, gen. valentis, pres. part,
of valere, 'to be worth*. See valent. The correct
form is multivalent, in which both elements are
of Latin origin.

## Polyxena
Polyxena, п., daughter of Priam and Hecuba and
bride of Achilles (Greek mytkol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Πολυξένη, prop, subst. use of the fem. of the
adj. πολύξενος, 'entertaining many guests, very
hospitable', which is compounded of πολύς,
'much, many', and ξένος, 'stranger, guest'. See
poly- and xeno-.

## Polyzoa
Polyzoa, n. pi., a class of aquatic animals, also
called Bryozoa {zool.) — ModL., compounded
of poly- and Gk. ζφα, pi. of ζφον, 'an animal'.
See zoo-.

## polyzoarium
polyzoarium, п., a bryozoan colony. — A ModL.
hybrid coined fr. ModL. Polyzoa, a word of
Greek origin (see prec. word) and the L. suff.
-arlum, on analogy of aquarium, vivarium.

## polyzoary
polyzoary, п., polyzoarium. — A hybrid coined
fr. ModL. Polyzoa (see prec. word) and suff.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: POMACE | 576 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 COLUMN:1 -->
-ary (representing L. -drium).

## pomace
pomace, п., the crushed pulp of apples. — OF.
pomaz, pi. of pomat, 'cider', fr. pome, 'apple'.
See pome.

## Pomaceae
Pomaceae, n. pi., synonym of Malaceae (hot.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. VL. poma,
'apple'. See pome.

## pomaceous
pomaceous, adj., 1) pertaining to, or resembling,
an apple; 2) pertaining to the Pomaceae. —
ModL. pomdceus, fr. VL. poma, 'apple'. See
pome and -aceous.

## pomade
pomade, п., a perfumed ointment for the hair. —
F. pommade, fr. It. pomata, fr. porno, 'apple', fr.
VL. pomum (see pome and -ade); so called
because orig. scented with the pulp of lady apples.
Cp. pomatum.

## Pomaderris
Pomaderris, п., a genus of shrubs of the
buckthorn family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πώμα,
'lid, cover', and δέρρις, 'skin, leather covering';
so called in allusion to the membranous
covering of the capsule. For the first element see
food, for the second see derma.

## pomander
pomander, п., a ball of perfumes. — ME., fr. MF.
pome d'ambre (F. pomme d'ambre), lit. 'apple of
amber', fr. pomme, 'apple', and ambre, 'amber1
(see pome and amber); so called from its shape.

## pomatum
pomatum, п., pomade. — ModL., fr. VL·.pomum,
'apple'. See pomade.

## pombe
pombe, п., an African beer made from grain. —
Swah ili.

## pome
pome, п., the characteristic fruit of the apple
family. — ME., fr. OF., 'apple' (F. pomme), fr.
VL. poma (fern. sing, for orig. L. neut. pi.),
'apple', fr. L. pomum, 'fruit', which is of
uncertain origin. It is possibly a contraction of *po-
emom, and lit. means 'something taken away,
something plucked', fr. pref. po- [occurring also
in ρδηδ, Ί place', which stands for *po-s(i)n3,
and lit. means 'Ilay aside'; see position] and
from a derivative of the verb emere, 'to take';
see exempt. For sense development cp. Gk.
καρπός, 'fruit', which is cogn. with L. carpere, 'to
pluck'. Cp. pommel, Pomona and the first
element in pomology.

## pomegranate
pomegranate, n. — ME. pomegarnet, pomgamet,
fr. OF. pome grenate (F. grenade), fr. Укротит
granatum, 'pomegranate', lit. 'an apple with
many grains or seeds'. See pome and grenade
and cp. grain, garnet, granadilla.

## pomelo
pomelo, п., 1) the shaddock; 2) the grapefruit. —
Altered fr. Du. pompelmoes. The change of Du.
pompelmoes to pomelo was prob. due to the
influence of pome. Cp. pompelmous. Cp. also
the second element in tangelo.

## Pomerama
Pomerama, η., a province of Prussia on the south
coast of the Baltic Sea. — Fr. Slav./w more, 'by
the Sea*. For the first word see post- and cp.
Prussia, for the second see mere, 'the sea'.
Derivatives: Pomerani-an, adj. and n.

## pomfret
pomfret, п., a marine fish. — Fr. earlier pamflet,
prob. fr. F. pample, fr. Port, pampo.
Pomfret cake (Engl.) — Lit. 'cake of Pontefract'
(pronounced Pomfret), from the name of a town
in Yorkshire, England. The name Pomfret is
said to derive from L. Ad Pontem Fractum
('Beside a Broken Bridge'), in allusion to a
broken bridge which was near the town.

## pomiculture
pomiculture, п., fruit culture. — Compounded
of L. pomum, 'fruit', and cultura, 'culture'. See
pome and culture.

## pomiferous
pomiferous, adj., fruit-bearing. — Compounded
of L. pomum, 'fruit' and L. ferre, 'tb bear, carry'.
See pome and -ferous.

## Pommard
Pommard, п., a kind of fine red Burgundy wine.
— Named from Pommar, south of Beaune, in
France.

## pommel
pommel, п., a rounded knob. — ME. pomel, fr.
OF. pomel (F. pommeau), dimin. of OF. pome
(F.pomme), 'apple'. See pome, and dimin. suff. -le.
Derivatives: pommel, tr. v., pommel(l)-er, п.,
pommel(l)-ing, n.

## pomologist
pomologist, п., one skilled in pomology. — See
next word and -ist.

## pomology
pomology, п., the art of fruit-growing. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. pomum, 'fruit', and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic)'.
See -logy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: pomolog-ic-al, adj., pomolog-ic-al-
ly, adv.

## Pomona
Pomona, п., the goddess of fruit in Roman
mythology.— L. Pomona, fr. pomum, 'fruit'. See
pome.
Derivatives: pomon-al, pomon-ic, adjs.

## pomp
pomp, n. — ME.,fr. OF. ( = F.)pompe, fr. L·.pom-
pa, fr. Gk. πομπή, 'a sending, solemn
procession', which stands in gradational relationship
to πέμπειν, 'to send1. Ср. pump, 'a kind of shoe',
and apopemptic.

## pompadour
pompadour, п., name of a kind of hairdress, a
dress, a color etc. — Prop, in the style of the
Marquise de Pompadour (1721-64).

## pompano
pompano, п., a kind of edible fish (Trachinotus).
-— Sp. pampana.

## Pompelan
Pompelan, adj., pertaining to Pompeii, a town in
the south of Campania, destroyed by an
eruption of Vesuvius in 79 C.E. — L. Pompeidnus,
fr. Pompeii. For the ending see suff. -an.

## pompelmous
pompelmous, pompelmoose, п., a shaddock. —
Du. pompelmoes (whence also F. pamplemousse),
lit. 'a thick lemon', fr. pompel, 'thick', and
limoes 'lemon* (see lemon). Cp. pomelo.

## pomphojyx
pomphojyx, п., 1) a vesicle; 2) a skin disease
characterized by an eruption of vesicles {med.)
— L., fr. Gk. πομφόλυξ, 'bubble', a compound
whose first element derives fr, πομφός, 'blister',
which, together with πέμφιξ, 'breath, blast,
pustule', is of imitative origin. The second
element in πομφόλυξ is possibly rel. to the second
element in οίνόφλυξ, 'given to drinking,
drunken', and to φλύειν, *to boil over, bubble', φλεΤν,
'to abound', and cogn. with ^fiuere, 'to flow'.
See fluent and cp. flimflam.

## pomphus
pomphus, п., blister (med.) — Gk. πομφός,
'blister*. See prec. word.

## pompier
pompier, pompier ladder, п., a fireman's scaling
ladder. — F. pompier, 'fireman', fr. pompe,
'pump'. See pump, 'device for raising water'.

## pom-pom
pom-pom, п., a kind of automatic gun. — Of
imitative origin.

## pompon
pompon, п., an ornament of feathers. — F.( prob.
of imitative origin.

## pomposity
pomposity, п., pompousness. — ML. pompositds,
fr. Late L. pompdsus. See next word and -ity.

## pompous
pompous, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (— F.) pompeux
(fem. pompeuse), fr. Late L. pompdsus,
'pompous, stately', fr. L. pompa. See pomp and -ous.
Derivatives \ pompous-ly, adv., pompous-ness, n.

## ponceau
ponceau, п., the corn poppy; the poppy color. —
F., fr. OF. poncel, a derivative of paon,
'peacock', fr. L. pavonem, ace. of pavo, 'peacock';
see peacock. The corn poppy was called in
French ponceau (lit. 'peacock flower*) from the
resemblance of its brilliant color to the bright-'
colored plumage of the peacock. For sense
development cp. F. paon, used in some NF.
dialects in the sense of'poppy'.

## ponceau
ponceau, п., a culvert. — F-, dimin. of pom,
'bridge', fr. L. pontem, ace. of pons. See pons.

## pond
pond, п., a small lake. — A var. of pound,
'enclosure' ; pond prop, means 'water enclosed'.
Derivatives: pond, tr. and intr. v., pond-age, n.

## poncho
poncho, п., a South-American cloak resembling a
blanket. — Amer. Sp. poncho, an Araucan loan
word.

## ponder
ponder, tr. and intr. v. — ME. ponderen, fr.
MF. ponderer, fr. L. ponderdre, 'to weigh; to
ponder, consider', fr. pondus, gen. ponderis,
'weight'. See pound, 'a weight' and cp.
ponderable, imponderable, ponderance, preponderate.
Derivatives: ponder-er, п., ponder-ing, adj.,
ponder-ing-ly, adv.

## ponderable
ponderable, adj. — Late L. ponderabifis, 'that
which can be weighed', fr. L. ponderdre, 'to
weigh'. See ponder and -able. Derivatives:
ponderability, п., ponderable-ness, п., ponderabl-y9
adv.

## ponderance
ponderance, п., weight (rare). — Formed with
suff. -ce fr. L. ponderdns, pres. part, of
ponderdre, 'to weigh'. See ponder.

## ponderate
ponderate, tr. v., to ponder. — L. ponderatus, pp.
οι ponderdre, 'to weigh*. See ponder and verbal
suff. -ate, and cp. equiponderate.

## ponderation
ponderation, n. — L. ponderatio, gen. -dnis, 'a
weighing', fr. ponderatus, pp. of ponderdre. See
prec. word and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 COLUMN:3 -->

## ponderosity
ponderosity, п., weightiness. — ML. ponderositdst
fr. Late L. ponderosus, 'weighty', fr. L. pondus,
gen. ponderis, 'weight'. See next word and -ity.

## ponderous
ponderous, adj., weighty. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.)
pondereux (fem. pondereuse), fr. Late L.
ponderosus, 'weighty', fr. L. pondus, gen. ponderis.
See ponder and -ous.
Derivatives:ponderous-ly, adv.,ponderous-ness,
n.

## pone
pone, п., maize flour cake. — Of Algonquian
origin.

## pone
pone, п., an obsolete writ for removing a case
from an inferior to a higher court (law). — L.
pone, imper. of ponere, 'to place". See position.

## Ponera
Ponera, n. pi., a genus of stinging ants (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. πονηρά, neut. pi. of πονηρός,
'painful, distressed; bad, worthless', fr. πόνος,
'toil, labor'. See geoponic.

## pongee
pongee, п., a fine, soft, unbleached kind of silk.
— Chin, pun-chi, 'own loom'.

## Pongo
Pongo, п., a genus of anthropoid apes. — Congo
mpongi.

## poniard
poniard, п., a dagger. — MF. (= F.) poignard,
formed, with change of suff., fr. OF. poignal,
'dagger', prop, 'anything grasped with the fist',
fr. poing, 'flst', fr. L. pugnus, 'fist'. See
pugnacious and -nrd. For sense development cp. L.
pugnus, 'fist', pugndre, 'to fight', pugio, 'dagger'.
Derivative: poniard, tr. v.

## pons
pons, п., a bridge (occurring in Latin phrases). —
L. pons, gen. pontis, 'bridge', cogn. with Ol.
panthdh, "path, way', Gk. πόντος, 'open sea',
πάτος (for *pntos), 'trodden way, path', πατέω,
Ί step', fr. Ϊ.-Ε. base *pent-, 'to go, pass; path,
bridge',whence also Goth, finpan, OE. findan, 'to
find', prop, 'to come upon'. See find and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also cisponrine,
transpontine.

## Pontederia
Pontederia, п., a genus of plants, the pickerel-
weed (bot.) ~ ModL., named after Guilio Pon-
tedera (1688-1757), professor of botany at
Padua. For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Pontederiaceae
Pontederiaceae, n. pi., the pickerelweed family
(bot.) — Formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## pontederiaceous
pontederiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## pontifex
pontifex, п., a member of the supreme college of
priests in ancient Rome. — L., 'Roman high
priest, pontiff', lit. 'bridgemaker', compounded
of p6ns\ pontis, 'bridge', and facere, 'to make'.
The orig. meaning was perhaps 'pathfinder,
waymaker". See pons and fact and cp. next word.

## pontiff
pontiff, п., 1) a pontifex; 2) a Jewish high priest;
3) a bishop; specif., the pope. — F. pontife, fr.
L. pontifex, 'high priest'. See prec. word.

## pontifical
pontifical, adj., pertaining to a pontiff. — L. pon-
tificdlis, 'of, or pertaining to, the high priest', fr.
pontifex, gen. -ficis, 'high priest*. See pontifex
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: pontifical-ity, п., pontifical-ly, adj.,
pontificate (q.v.)

## pontificate
pontificate, п., the dignity of a pontiff. — L. pon-
tifiedtus, 'the office or dignity of a pontifex', fr.
pontifex, gen. -ficis. See pontifex and subst. suff.
-ate.
Derivative: pontificate, intr. v.

## pontificate
pontificate, intr. v., to perform the functions of a
pontiff. — ML. pontifiedtus, pp. of pontificare,
'to perform the functions of a pontiff', fr. L.
pontifex, gen. pontificis. See pontifex and verbal
suff. -ate.

## pontlevis
pontlevis, п., a term of manege. — F., prop.
'drawbridge', fr. pont, 'bridge', and a derivative
of lever, 'to lift*, fr. L. levare. See pons and
lever:

## ponton
ponton, п., pontoon. — F. ponton. See pontoon.

## pontonier
pontonier,*n. — F. pontonnier. See pontoon and
-ier.

## pontoon
pontoon, п., a boat used to support a temporary
bridge. — F. ponton, fr. L. pontonem, ace. of
ponto, *punt; floating bridge', a derivative of
pons, gen. pontis, 'bridge'. See pons and -oon
and cp. punt.
Derivative: pontoon, tr- v., pontoon-ing, n.

## pontoon
pontoon, п., a gambling game, resembling vingt-
et-un. — Corruption of F. vingt-et-un, 'twenty-
one*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:604 -->

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:604 COLUMN:1 -->

## pony
pony, п., a small horse. — Scot, powney, fr. obsol.
F. poulenet, *little foal', dimin. of F. poulain,
'foal', fr. Late L. pullanus, fr. L. pullus, 'young
animal, foal'. See pullet and cp. words there
referred to.

## pood
pood, п., a Russian weight consisting of 40
Russian lb. -— Russ. pud, fr. hG.pund, which is
borrowed fr. L. pondo, 'by weight', whence also
Goth., OE. pund, OHG. pfunt. See pound, 'a
weight*.

## poodle
poodle, п., a breed of dog. — G. Pudel, shortened
fr. earlier Pudelkund, prop, 'a splashing dog', fr.
pudeln, 'to splash in water', which, like OE.
pudd, 'ditch, puddle*, is of imitative origin. Cp.
puddle.
poogye» п., a kind of Indian nose flute. — Hind.
Pugt.

## pooh
pooh, interj. expressing contempt. — Imitative.

## Pooh-Bah
Pooh-Bah, п., humorous name of a person that
holds many offices. — Fr. Pooh-Bah, a
character in Gilbert's and Sullivan's comic opera The
Mikado.

## pooh-pooh
pooh-pooh, interj. of contempt. — Reduplication
of the interjection pooh.
Derivatives: pooh-pooh, n. and tr. and intr.
.v.

## pool
pool, п., a small body of water. — ME., fr. OE.
pdh rel. to OFris., MLG. pot, Ou.poel, OHG.,
MHG. pfuol, G. Pfuhl. These words are prob.
cogn. with Alb. baVte, 'swamp, mud', OSIav.
blato (for *bolio), 'marsh, mud*, Lith. bala,
'swamp'.

## pool
pool, п., stakes in gambling. — Fr. f.poule, 'hen',
also used as a slang term in the sense of 'stakes
in gambling'. F. poule derives fr. L. pulla, fern,
of pullus, 'young animal'. See pullet and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: pool, tr. and intr. \.,pool-ert n.

## poon
poon, п., poon tree, a timber tree (Calophyllum
inophyllum). — Singhalese puna, fr. OI. punnd-
gah, which is of Dravidian origin; cp. Tamil
punnai, Kanarese/umni/ctf, 'poon tree'.

## poongee
poongee, phoongy, п., a Buddhist priest in Burma.
— Burmese phungyl, fr. phun, 'glory', and gyi,
'great'.

## poop
poop, п., the afterpart of a ship. — MF. (= F.)
poupe, fr. OProvenc. poppa, fr. h.puppis, 'stern,
poop', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. It.poppa,
Sp. and Port, popa, which also derive fr. L.
puppis.
Derivatives: poop, tr. v.,poop-ed, adj.

## poor
poor, adj. and n. — ME. poure, povre, fr. OF.
povre, poure (F. pauvre), fr. L. pauper, 'poor',
which stands for *pawo-pars and lit. means *he
who acquires little', fr. paucus, 'little', and the
stem of pario, parere, 'to bring forth, produce;
to acquire, gain'. See pauper and cp. poverty,
impoverish.
Derivatives: poorish, adj., poor-ling, п., poor-ly,
adv., poor-ness, n.

## pop
pop, intr. v., to make a short, quick sound; tr. v.,
to cause to pop; п., a short quick sound. —
Imitative. Cp. popple.
Derivatives: popp-able, adj., popp-ing, adj. and
п., ρορρ-ish, adj.

## pop
pop, п., father. — Short for poppa, a popular var.
of papa.

## pop concert
pop concert, also pop, n. — Short for popular
concert.

## pope
pope, n. — ME. pope, fr. OE. papa, fr. Eccles. L.

## papa
papa, 'bishop; pope*, fr. L. papa, 'father'. See
papa, 'pope', and cp. papal, poplin.
Derivatives: popedom (q.v.), pope-ling, п.,
popery, п., pop-ish, adj., pop-ish-ly, adv., pop-ish-
ness, n.

## popedom
popedom, n.— ME.,fr. OE.papdom, 'papacy', fr.

## papa
papa, 'pope'. See pope and -dom.

## popinjay
popinjay, п., ]) orig., a parrot; 2) a wooden
parrot hung on a pole as a target (hist.); 3) a fop. —
ME. papegay, papejay, papengay, fr. OF. papegai,

## papingai
papingai, fr. Sp. papagayo, fr. Ar. babagha, fr.
W. African pampakei, a word of lmit. origin.
The ending of popinjay was influenced by the
nouny'uy.

## poplar
poplar, n. — ME. popler, poplere, fr. OF. poplier
(F. peuplier), formed with suff. -ier (see -ier) fr.

## pople (also peuple)
pople (also peuple), 'poplar', fr. L. populus, of

## s.m.
s.m., which is prob. cogn. with Gk. πτελέα,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:604 COLUMN:2 -->
Epidauric πελέα, 'elm*. Cp. It. pioppo, Sp.
chopo, MHG. (— G.) pappel, OSIav. topoli
(dissimilated fr. *popoli), which all derive fr. L.
populus. Cp. also Populus.
Derivative: poplar-ed^ adj.

## poplin
poplin, п., a corded fabric. — Obsol. F. papeline,
fr. It. papalina, fem. of papalino, 'papal'; so
called because orig. made at Avignon while it
was a papal residence (i.e. between 1309 and
1408). F.popeline, 'poplin', is a loan word fr. E.
poplin. See pope.

## popliteal
popliteal, adj., pertaining to the ham (anat.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. poples, gen.
poplitis, 'ham', which is of uncertain origin.

## poppet
poppet, n. — Earlier form of puppet,

## popple
popple, intr. v., to bubble, ripple. — ME. poplen,
of imitative origin. Cp. pop, 'to make a short,
quick sound'.

## popple
popple, п., poplar (dial.) — ME. popul, fr. OE.
popul-, fr. L. populus. See poplar,

## poppy
poppy, n. — ME. popy, fr. OE. popig, fr. earlier
popseg, fr. VL. *papdvum (whence also OF.
pavo), alt. of L. papaver, *poppy*. See Papaver.
Derivative: popp-ied, adj.

## populace
populace, п., the common people. — MF. (= F.),
fr. It. popolaccio, formed with the pejorative
suff. -accio, fr. popolo, 'people', fr. L. populus,
of s.m. See next word.

## popular
popular, adj. — L. popularis, 'belonging to the
people' (whence also F. populaire), fr. populus,
'people'. See people and adj. suff. -ar.
Derivatives: popular-ism, п., popularity (q.v.),

iz-er, п., popular-ly, adv., popular-ness, n.

## popularity

Derivatives: populous-ly, adv., populous-ness, n.

## porbeagle
porbeagle, п., a kind of shark. — Of uncertain

## porcare

## pore
pore, п., a minute opening. — ME. poore, pore.

poriform, adj. — Compounded of L·. porus, 'pore'

porous, adj., full of holes. — VL. *porosus, fr. L.

porusy 'passage'. See pore, п., and -ous.

prophyrite, n. (petrogr.) — L. porphyrites, fr. Gk.

porphyrogenite, porphyrogenitus, п., born after his

prop, meant 'born in the porphyry-lined

porphyroid, п., a schistose, crystalline rock

## porraceous

## porrect
porrect, adj., stretched out, extended. — L.
porrectus, pp. of porrigere. See porrect, v.

η ср. harbinger, messenger, passenger, scavenger.

## port
port, п., harbor, haven. — ME., partly fr. OE.

s.m., fr. l.-E. base *per-, 4o lead across, drive

Cp. also ford.

## port

## port

traverse, pierce*, whence also Goth, faran, 'to
go', OE. ferian, 'to go; to carry'. See fare, v.,
and cp. port, 'gate', port, 'harbor', apport,
comport, deport, disport, export, import, portly,
purport, rapport, report, sport, support, transport,
and the first element in portmanteau.

## port
port, п., manner in which a person bears himself.
— OF., fr. porter, 'to bear, carry', fr. L. portare,
of s.m. See port, v.

## port

from stern to bow; larboard. — Either fr. port,

or fr. port, 'harbor'.

## portable

Late L. portabUis, 'portable', fr. L. portare, 'to
carry'. See port, 'to carry', and -able.

## portent

## porter

## Porthetria
Porthetria, п., a genus of moths, the tussock moth
(zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πορθήτωρ, 'destroyer,

## ravager'
ravager', fr. πορθεΐν, 'to destroy, ravage', freq.

porthole, n. — Compounded of port, 'gate;

## portico

## portion
portion, n. — ME. porcioun, fr. OF. porcion,

gen. partis, 'part'. See part and- ion. According

vol. XXXIX p. 93) L. portio arose through the
assimilation of the term pro *partione to pro por-
tioney 'for (his) part or share' (see proportion).
Moreover, the change of *partio to portio
might have also been furthered by the endeavor
to avoid a confusion with partio, 'a bearing,
bringing forth' (fr. parere). Cp. apportion.

## portion
portion, tr. v. — ME. portionen, fr. OF. porcion-

## portionist

Portland cement. — So called by its inventor, the

## portmanteau word

Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, 1832-98) to denote
the words coined by him through the
combination of two words.

portrait, n. — MF. (= F.),prop. pp. of portraire,

## portraitore
portraitore, п., the art of portraiting; a portrait;

## portray

## portreeve
portreeve, п., mayor, bailiff. — ME. portereve,

ons.

## posada
posada, п., an inn. — Sp., 'home, lodging', fr.
posar, 'to repose, rest; to lodge', fr. L. pausdre.

## posaune
posaune, п., 1) a trombone (mus.); 2) a reed stop

buisine, fr. L. bucina, for *bou-cana, 'an

sing1. See buccinator.

## pose

## pose
pose, п., attitude. — F., fr. poser, 'to place'. See

Derivative: pose-y, adj.

## pose
pose, tr. v., to embarrass, puzzle. — Shortened
fr. oppose.
Derivative : pos-er, п., a puzzling question.

## Poseideon
Poseideon, п., name of the 6th month of the Attic
Greek calendar (corresponding to December-
January). — Gk. Ποσειδεών, lit. 'month
dedicated to Poseidon',fr. Ποσειδών. See next word.

## Poseidon
Poseidon, п., the god of earthquakes and of the
sea in Greek mythology. — L. Poseidon, fr. Gk.
Ποσειδών (Dor. Ποτειδάν), which is of
uncertain origin. According to Wilamowitz the name
Ποσειδών is compounded of r.oaic, 'master',
and δα, a secondary form of γη, 'earth' (see
potent and Demeter), hence lit. means 'master of
the earth".

## poseur
poseur, п., one who poses. — F., fr. poser, 'to
pose'. See pose, 'to place'.

## posit
posit, tr. v., to assert. — L. positus, pp. of pond,
ponere, 'to place'. See next word.

## position
position, n. — MF, (= F.), fr. L. positionem, ace.
of positio, 'a placing, setting, situation,
position', fr. positus, pp. of pond, Ί put, place, lay',
which is a contraction of *pozno, from *po-
s(i)nd, lit. Ί lay aside', fr. pref. po- and sino, Ί
set down, leave'. See site and cp. component,
compose, composition, compost, compound,
contraposition, depone, deposit, dispose, disposition,
entrepot, exposition, expound, imponent, impose,
imposition, impost, 'task', impost, 'upper part of a
pillar', impostor, interposition, juxtaposition,
opponent, oppose, oviposit, pone, 'an obsolete writ*,
positive, post of a soldier, post for conveyinglet-
ters, posture, praepostor, pre po si tor, priest,
proponent, propose, proposition, propound, provost,
purpose, repository, superpose, suppose,
supposition, suppository, transpose. For po-, the prefix
of *po-s(i)no, cp. polish, pome.
Derivatives: position, tr. v., position-al, adj.

## positive
positive, adj. — ME. positif, fr. OF. (= F.)positif
(fern, positive), fr. L. positivus, 'settled by
agreement' (opposed to ndturalis, 'natural'), fr.
positus, pp. of ponere, 'to place'. See position and
-ive and cp. dispositive, expositive.
Derivatives; positive, п., positive-ly, adv., posi-
tive-ness, п., positivism (q.v.), positivist (q.v.),
positiv-ity, n.

## positivism
positivism, п., the philosophical system of Augus-
te Comte. — F. positivisme, coined by Auguste
Comte (1798-1857) fr. positif, fern, positive. See
prec. word and -ism.

## positivist
positivist, п., an adherent of positivism. — See
prec. word and -1st.
Derivatives: positivist~ic, adj., positivist-ic-al-ly,
adv.

## positron
positron, п., a positively charged electron (phys.
and chem.) — Coined from the abbreviation of
positive) (elec)tron.

## posologist
posologist, п., a compounder of doses. — See
next word and -ist.

## posology
posology, п., the science of doses (med.) — F.
posologie, compounded of Gk. πόσος, 'how
much', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)'. The first element derives fr. I.-E.
base *qwo-, whence also L. qui, quae, quod,
'which', quis ?, 'who ?', quid!, 'what ?', OI. kdti,
Hitt. kuwatta, L. quot, 'how many?'. See what,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:606 COLUMN:2 -->
who and cp. quod, quid. For the second element
see -logy.
Derivatives: posoiog-ic-ai, adj., posolog-ist, n.

## posse
posse, п., 1) possibility; 2) short for posse comila·
tus. — ML. posse, 'power', fr. L. posse, 'to be
able*, infin. of possum, Ί can, am able'. See pos*
sible.

## posse comitatus
posse comitatus, the power of the county (law). —
ML. posse comitdtus, fr. posse, 'power' (see prec.

## possess
possess, tr. v. — ME. possessen, fr. OF. possessier,

which stands for *pots-sidere, lit. 'to sit as a
master'. The first element is a contraction of
potis, 'able, mighty, powerful', whence potens,
gen. potentis, 'able, capable', possum (for potis
sum), Ί am able'; see potent and cp. words there
referred to. The second element is rel. to sedere,
'to sit', sidere, 'to sit down'. See sedentary.
Derivatives: possess-ed, adj., possession (q.v.),
possessive (q.v.), possessor (q.v.)

## possession
possession, n. — ME. possessioun, fr. OF. (= F.)

'a possessing, possessum', fr. possessus, pp. of
possidere. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: possession, intr. v., possession-al,
adj., possession-ary, adj., possession-ed, adj.

## possessive
possessive, adj. — MF. (= F.) possessi/ (fern.
possessive), fr. L, possessivus, 'relating to
possession, possessive', fr. possessus, pp. of
possidere; see possess and -ive. L. possessivus was
coined by the Roman rheto/ician Marcus Fa-
bius Quintilianus (cca 35-cca 95 C.E.) to

κτασθαί., Чо get for oneself, acquire').
Derivatives: possessive, п., possessiv-al, adj.,
possessive-ly, adv., possessive-ness, n.

## possessor
possessor, n. — ME. possessour, fr. MF. (= F.)
possesseur, fr. L. possessorem, ace. of possessor,
'possessor', fr. possessus, pp. of possidere. See

## possessory
possessory, adj. — Late L. possessorius, 'relating
to possession', fr. L. possessor. See prec. word
and adj. surf. -ory.
Derivative: possessor i-ness, n.

## posset
posset, п., a drink of hot milk curdled with ale or
wine. — ME. poshote, of uncertain origin.
Derivative: posset, tr. and intr. v.

## possibilist
possibilist, п., an adherent of a political party
which aims only at the realization of what is

posibilista, fr. posibie, 'possible', fr. L. possibilis.
See possible and -ist.

## possibility
possibility, n. — ME. possibilite, fr. OF. possi-
bitite (F. possibilite), fr. L. possibilitdtem, ace. of
possibilitds, fr. possibilis. See next word and
-ity.

## possible
possible, adj. — F., fr. L. possibilis, 'possible', fr.
possum, *1 am able'. See possess and -ible.
Derivatives: possible, п., possible-ness, п., pos-
sibi-y, adv.
'possum, n. — Aphetic for opossum.

## post
post, п., pillar. — ME., fr. OF., fr. L. postis,
'doorpost1, for *por-stis, lit. 'standing out',

πάστας, gen. παστάδος (fr. *παρσταδ-), a

## post
post, п., the place where a soldier is stationed. —
MF. (= F.) poste, fr. It. posto, fr. VL. postum,

## post
post, п., office for conveying letters. — MF.
(= F.) poste, fr. It.'posta, fr. VL. posta, whose
original meaning was 'a place where men are
stationed for the conveyance of messages or
letters', fr. L. (mdnsid) posita, 'a fixed halting place

See position and cp. prec. word. Cp. also

postilion, poste restante.

post-al, adj., pdttal-ly, adv.

## post

## post-
post-, pref. meaning 'behind, after'. — L., fr. post,

Toch. В postam, 'after', Arm. est, 'after',
Arcadian and Cypriote πός, Dor. ποτί, 'toward, to,

du, Mate" {adj.), poz-de, 'late' (adv.), hhh.pds, 'at,

## postdate
postdate, tr. v., to assign (to a document) a date
later than the real date. — Compounded of post-
and date, v. See date, 'point of time'.

## postdate
postdate, п., a date assigned (to a document) later
than the real date. — Compounded of post- and
date, 'point of time'.

## postdiluvial
postdiluvial, adj., later than the deluge. —
Compounded of post- and diluvial. Cp. next word.

## postdiluvian

— Compounded of post- and diluvian. Cp. prec.

## posteen
posteen, п., an Afghan leathern pelisse (Anglo-
Indian). — Pers. postin, Of leather', fr. post,

## poster
poster, п., bill, placard. — Formed fr. post,

## poste restante

— F., 'remaining post'. For the first word see

## posterior

Derivatives: posterior, п., posterior-ic, adj.,
posterior-ic-al-ly, adv., posterior-ist-ic, adj.,
posierior-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., posteriority (q.v.),

posterite, fr. L. posteritatem, ace. of posteritds,

## postern
postern, п., ]) formerly, a back door or gate; 2) a

posterne, fr. OF. posterne (F. poterne), fr. earlier
posterle, fr. Late h.posterula, 'a small door, back

## postero-

## postfrontal

(anat.) — Formed fr. post- and frontal.

## postglacial

{geol.) — Formed fr. post- and glacial.

## postgraduate
postgraduate, п., a student taking a course after
his graduation; adj., pertaining to studies
pursued after graduation. — Formed fr. post- and
the noun graduate.

## posthaste
posthaste, adv., п., and adj. — Compounded of
post, adv., and haste.

## posthumous
posthumous, adj. — L. posthumus, alteration of

postumus, 'the last; late born', prop, superl. of

postichet п., 1) adj., counterfeit; artificial; 2) п., а

post-mortem, adj., occurring after death. — L.

post-mortem, n. — Short for post-mortem

post-obit, adj., made after death, effective after

post-obit, n. — Short for post-obit bond.

Fr. L. post par turn, 'after birth', fr. post, 'after'

postpone, tr. v. — L. postponere, 'to put after,

place after, to postpone', fr. post- and ponere

postposition, п., the act of placing after. —

postulate, tr. v., to claim; to take for granted. —

postulation, n. — ME. postulacion, fr. MF.

latus, pp. οΐpostulare. See postulate, v., and -ion.

## postulatum
postulatum, п., a postulate. — L. See postulate, n.

## posture
posture, n. — F., fr. It. postura,

## posy
posy, п., 1) orig. a motto inside a ring; 2) a

## pot
pot, п., a round vessel. — ME., fr. OE. pott, fr.

## pot
pot, п., a deep hole {Scot, and dial. E.) — ME.

## potable
potable, adj., drinkable. — Late L. p5tabilis>

ness, n.

## potage
potage, п., a thick soup. — F., 'soup, broth',

## potam-
potam-, form of potamo- before a vowel.

## potamic
potamic, adj., pertaining to rivers. — Formed
with suff. -ic fr. Gk. ποταμός. See next word.

potamo-, before a vowel potam-, combining form

## potamology

Compounded of potamo- and Gk.-λογία, fr.-λόγος,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:607 COLUMN:3 -->
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who

## potash
potash, n. — Orig. pi. potashes, fr. Du. potaschen

potassamide, п., potassium amide, KNH2 (chem.)
— Short for potassium amide.

Latinized form of potash (q.v.) See also potass.
For the ending see 2nd suff. -ium.
Derivatives: potass-ic, adj., potassi-ferous, adj.

## potation

## potato

## potence

prec. word.

## potency
potency, n. — h.potentia, 'power', fr.potens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -cy and cp. potence (in
both senses).

## potent
potent, adj. — L. potens, gen. potentis, 'able,
mighty, powerful', pres. part, of posse (for potis
esse), 'to be able', fr. potis, 'able, capable,
powerful', which is cogn. with OJ. patih,
'master, husband', Toch. A pats, 'husband',
Gk. πόσις (for *πότις), 'husband', Lith. path,
pats, 'husband', Lith. pats, Lett, pats, Hitt. patt
'self, Alb. pata, Ί had' (imperf.) pase, 'had'
(pp.) and the second element in Goth, brup-
faps, 'bethrothed, fiance', and in L. hospes (for
*hosti'pots), 'visitor, guest', OSlav. gospodi
'lord, master'. Cp. potence, power, puissant, and
the first element in possess. Cp. also the first
element in padishah, Poseidon, and the second
element in despot, hospital, host, 'landlord', Fra-
japati.

## potentate
potentate, п., a powerful person; ruler, prince. —
L. potentatus, 'power, rule', Tr. potens, gen. -entis.
See potent, and subst. suff. -ate.
potentia], adj. — ME. potencial, fr. Late h.poten-
tialis, 'having power', fr. potentia. See potency,
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: potential, п., potent ial-ity, potential-
ize, potential-iz-ation, n.

## potentiate
potentiate, tr. v., to endow with power. —
Formed on the analogy of G. potenzieren fr. L.
potentia (see potency) with verbal suff. -ate.

## Fotentilla
Fotentilla, п., a genus of plants, the cinquefoil
(bot.) — ModL., a dimin. formed fr. L. potens,
gen. -entis, 'able, mighty, powerful' (see potent);
so called in allusion to the medicinal powers of
the Fotentilla anserina.

## potentiometer
potentiometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the electrical potential {electr.) — A hybrid
coined fr. L. potentia, 'power', and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See potency and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## Foterium
Foterium, п., a genus of plants of the rose
family (bot.) — L. poterium, *a drinking vessel;
name of a plant (prob. the astragalus)', fr. Gk.
ποτήριον, dimin. of ποτήρ, 'a drinking vessel',
fr. I.-E. base *po(i)-, 'to drink*. See potion and
cp. the second element in Hydropotes.

## potheen
potheen, n. — See poteen.

## pother
pother, п., disturbance, confusion. — Of
unknown origin.

## pothole
pothole, п., a deep hole. — Compounded of pot,

## Pothos
Pothos, п., personification of desire in Greek
mythology. — Gk. Πόθος, lit. 'a longing,
yearning4, fr. I.-E. base *gwedh, whence also
ON. ged, 'passion', OPers. Jadiyamiy, Ί ask,

## potiche
potiche, п., a kind of Chinese vase. — F., a

## potion
potion, п., a drink; a dose of liquid medicine or

lum (for *potlom), 'a drinking cup', posca, 'a

Ί drink', Gk. πίνειν, 'to drink*, πόσις, 'a drink',
ποτόν, 'that which one drinks, a drink', πότος,
'a drinking, a drinking bout*, πότης, 'drinker',
ποτήρ, ποτήριον, 'a drinking cup', Alb. pi, Ί
drink', OSlav. pijo, phi, 4o drink', pivo,

OPruss. pout, 'to drink', poieiti, 'drink!' (pi.),

Derivative: potion, tr. v.

## potomania
potomania, п., 1) dipsomania; 2) delirium tremens

μανία, 'madness, frenzy*. See prec. word and

## potometer
potometer, п., an instrument for measuring

## potpourri
potpourri, п., medley, miscellany. — F., lit. 'rotten

vessel'. F. pourri is the pp. of pourrir, 'to rot', fr.
VL. *putrire, which corresponds to L. putrere,
'to rot'. For change of conjugation cp. pave,
pervert. Cp. olla podrida.

## pottage
pottage, п., soup, broth. — OF. (= F.) potage.

## potter
potter, п., one who makes earthenware. — Prop.
'maker of pots', formed fr. pot, 'a round vessel',
with agential surT. -er.

## potto
potto, п., a small lemur in West Africa. — Native

potty, adj., insignificant, petty (slang). — Of

potwaller, п., a householder (hist.) — Lit. 'pot

pot-walloper, п., 1) a scullion; 2) potwaller. —

Alteration of potwaller after wallop, 'to boil

## pouch
pouch, n. — ME^pouche, fr. ONF. pouche,

See poke, 'bag', and cp. poach, 'to steal game',

## poulaine
poulaine, п., the long pointed toe of a shoe. — F.
(shortened fr. OF. souliers a la poulaine, 'shoes
according to the Polish fashion*), fem. of the
OF. adjectivepoulain, 'Polish'. See Pole,

## poulp
poulp, poulpe, п., an octopus. — F. poulpe, fr. L.

## ponlt
ponlt, п., a young chicken. — ME. pulte,
alteration of pulett. See pullet and cp. poultry,

## poult-de-soie
poult-de-soie, п., a kind of heavy corded silk. —
F. pou-de-soie, of unknown origin. Cp. padua-
soy.

## poulter
poulter, п., poulterer. — ME. pulter, fr. F. poufe-
tier, 'poulterer', fr. poulet, dimin. oipoule, 'hen'.
See pullet and cp. poult,

## poulterer
poulterer, n. — Formed fr. poulter with agential

cater-er, fruiter-er, sorcer-er, upholster-er.

## poultice
poultice, n. — Fr. earlier pultes, pi. of L.puls, gen.

Derivative: poultice, tr. v.

## poultry
poultry, n. — ME. pulterie, pultrie, fr. OF. poule-
terie. See poult and -ry.

## pounce
pounce, п., 1) claw of a hawk or of another bird
of prey; 2) (dial.) a punch; 3) (obsol.) a hole
made by punching — Prob. shortened fr. ME.
ponson, ponchon, 'pointed tool'. See puncheon,
'stamp'.

## pounce
pounce, intr. v., to swoop down. — From prec.

the pounces'.
Derivative: pounce, п., a sudden swoop,

## pounce
pounce, tr. v., 1) to emboss (metal) by punching

Prob. partly fr. F. poingonner, 'topunch, stamp',
fr. poincon, 'awl, bodkin, punch, stamp' (see
puncheon, 'stamp'), partly fr. pounce, 'claw of a
hawk; a punch*.
Derivatives: pounc-er, п., pounc-ing, n.

## pounce
pounce, п., a fine powder, dust. — F. ponce,
'pumice stone, pounce', fr. L. pumicem, ace. of
pumix. See pumice.

## pounce
pounce, tr. v., to smooth with pounce. — F.
poncer, fr. ponce. See prec. word.

## pounce box
pounce box, also pouncet box, a box for
sprinkling pounce. — MF. (= F.) poncette, 'box for
sprinkling pounce', fr. ponce. See pounce, 'a fine
powder'.

## pound
pound, п., a unit of weight. — ME., fr. OE. pund,

which is rel. to pondus, 'a weight, pound'
[whence also Goth, pund, OHG. pfunt (MHG.

## poussette
poussette, п., a dancing round of couples with

## pout
pout, intr. v., to thrust out the lips; to be sullen.

## poverty
poverty, n. — ME. poverte, fr. OF. poverte (F.

## powder
powder, n. — ME. poudre, fr. OF. (= F.) poudre,

powder, tr. and intr. v. — F. poudrer, fr. poudre.

power, n. — ME. poer, pouer, fr. OF. pooeir,

powwow, п., conference. — Fr. Algonquian
powaw, 'medicine man, wizard'.

## pox
pox, п., any disease characterized by the eruption

Derivative: pox, tr. v.

## pozzolann
pozzolann, puzzolana, п., volcanic ashes used foi

on the site of the Roman town Puteofi, lit.

see puteal); so called because first found in

Derivative: pozzolan-ic, puzzolan-ic, adj.

praam, n. — See pram, a kind of boat.

prabhu, п., lord, master, owner (India) — OI.

## practice
practice, also practise, tr. and intr. v., — ME.

ticore, fr. Late L. practicus, 'fit for action'. See

practice, also practise, n. — Earlier practyse,

practician, n. — Obsol. F.practicien (F. praticien)t

## Frado
Frado, п., name of promenade in Madrid. — Sp.,

## prae-
prae-, pref. — Fr. L. prae, 'before'. Prae- is a
yar. spelling of pre- (q.v.)

## praecipe
praecipe, п., a writ ordering a person to do
something. — L. imper. of praecipere, 'to
give orders'. See precept.

## praedial
praedial, predial, adj., pertaining to landed
property. — ML. praedidlis, *pertaining to an
estate', fr. L. praedium, 'estate, farm4, fr. praes
(fr. earlierpraevides), 'surety, security, bail', for
*prae-vasy lit. 'surety before somebody', it.prae,
'before', and vas (gen. vadis), 'bail, security',
which is cogn. with Goth, wadi, 'pledge, earnest
money', gawadjon, 'to pledge', OE. wedd,
'pledge, agreement'. See pre- and wed and cp.

the ending see adj. sufT. -al.

## praelect
praelect, preelection, praelector. — See prelect,
prelection, prelector.

## praemunire
praemunire, п., a form of writ (Med. Engl. Law).
— Fr. ML. praemunire, 'to forewarn', the first
word in the text of the writ, fr. L. praemonere,
'to warn', fr. prae, 'before', and monere, 'to
warn' (see pre- and monition). ML. praemunire
shows a confusion of L. monere, 'to warn',
with munire, 'to defend, protect' (see munition).

## praenomen
praenomen, п., the first name (Roman antiq.) —
L. praenomen, lit. '(the name) before the name',
fr. prae, 'before', and nomen, 'name'. See pre-
and name and cp. cognomen.

## praepostor
praepostor, prepostor, п., monitor at a public
school. — ML. praepositor, 'one who charges
another with the management of an office', fr.
L. praepositus, pp. of praeponere, 'to place
before, to appoint', fr. prae, 'before', and po-
nere'y 'to place*. See pre- and position and cp.
prepositor. Cp. also priest, provost.

## praetor
praetor, pretor, п., a magistrate in ancient Rome,
next in rank to the consuls. — L. praetor, prop,
'leader chief, for *prae-itor, lit. 'one who goes
before', fr. praeit-(um), pp. stem of praeire, 'to
go before', fr. prae, 'before', and ire, 'to go'.
See pre- and itinerate.

## praetorian
praetorian, pretorian, adj., pertaining to the
praetor; п., a person of praetorian rank. — L.
praetoridnus, 'belonging to the praetor', fr.
praetorius, of s.m., fr. praetor. See prec. word
and -ian.

## praetorian
praetorian, pretorian, adj., pertaining to the
bodyguard of the Roman emperor; n. (cap.), a
soldier of the Praetorian Guard. — L. praetor idnus,
'belonging to the bodyguard', fr. praetorium.
See next word.

## praetorium
praetorium, pretorium, п., 1) the commanding
general's tent in a Roman camp; 2) the
residence of the governor of a Roman province;
hence 3) a palace. — L., prop. neut. of the adj.
praetorius, 'belonging to the praetor', used as a
noun. See praetorian, 'pertaining to the praetor'.

## pragmatic
pragmatic, adj., active; practical. — L. prdgma-

ticus, 'skilled in the law', fr. Gk. πραγματικός,
prop, 'busy, skilled in business', fr. πράγμα,

from the stem of πράσσειν, πραττειν' 'to do,
effect, accomplish, practice'. See practical and
adj. sufT. -ic.
Derivatives: pragmatic-al, adj.,pragmat-ic-al-ly,

## pragmatism
pragmatism, п., 1) pedantry; 2) practical

Gk. πράγμα, gen. πράγματος. See prec. word.

## pragmatist
pragmatist, п., an adherent of pragmatism. —
See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: pragmatist, pragmatist-ic, adjs.

## pragmatize
pragmatize, tr. v. — See pragmatism and -ize.

## prairial
prairial, п., the ninth month of the French
revolutionary calendar (lasting fr. May 20th to
June 18th). — Lit. 'month of pasture', coined-
by Fabre d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. prairie,
'meadow, grassland'. See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## prairie
prairie, п., level grassland. — F., fr. OF. praerie,
fr. VL. *prataria, fr. L. prdtum, 'meadow'
(whence F. pre, of s.m.), which is prob. cogn.
with Mir. rath, rdith, 'earthbank', MW. bed-
rawt, W. beddrod, 'grave mound', fr. Ϊ.-Ε. base
*prd-, 'to bend', whence ahoprdvus, 'crooked'.
See pravity and cp. Prado, pratal, Prater,
pratincole.

## praise
praise, tr. v. — ME. preisen, fr. OF. priesier, fr.
L. pretidre, 'to prize, value', fr. pretium, 'price,
value'. See price and cp. prize, 'to value'.
Derivatives: praise, п., prais-able, adj., prais-er,
п., prais-ing, adj., prais-ing-ly, adv.
PrajapatL п., creator (Vedic mythol.) — OI. pra-
japatih, 'the lord of the creation', compounded
of praja, 'creature, descendants, people', and
patih, 'lord, possessor'. The first element is
formed ix.prd-, 'before, forward, forth' and the
stem of janati, 'begets', jdnah, 'race'. See 1st
pro- and genns and cp. the first element in pra-
bhu and in words there referred to. For the
second element see potent, adj.

## Prakrit
Prakrit, п., the popular dialects of India, in
contradistinction to Sanskrit. — OI. prakrta-,
'natural, original (opposite to samskrta-, 'prepared,
refined'); formed fr. pro-, 'before, forward,
forth', which is cogn. with Gk. πρό, 'before', L.
pro, 'before, for' (see 1st pro-) and krta-, 'done,
made, prepared', which is rel. to k{noti, karoti,
'does, makes, prepares', Avestic k&r&naoti,
'makes', fr. I.-E. base *qwer·, 'to make, form,
shape'. See Sanskrit and cp. next word.

## prakriti
prakriti, п., nature, natural condition, primary
matter (Hindu philos.) — OI. prakrtih, fr. prd-,
'before, forward, forth', and krtih, 'a doing,
making, creation'. See Prakrit.

## Pralaya
Pralaya, п., destruction, the end of the world
(Hinduphilos.) — OI., 'dissolution, destruction',
formed fr. prd-, 'before, forward, forth', and
Idyate, liyate, liyati, 'clings to; remains sticking;
slips into; vanishes'. The first element is cogn.
with Gk. πρό, 'before', L. pro, 'before, for'; see
1st pro-. The second element derives fr. I.-E.
base *(s)le(i)-, 'slime, slimy, sticky, dauby,
slippery', whence also Gk. λείος, 'smooth', L.
levis, 'smooth', limus, 'slime, mud, mire', linere,
'to daub, besmear, anoint', OE. slim, 'slime*;
see slime and cp. words there referred to.

## praline
praline, n. — F., so called after Marshal Duples-
sis Praslin (pronounce Pralin) (1598-1675),
whose cook invented this confection.

## pram
pram, praam, п., a fiat-bottomed boat used in the
Baltic. — Du. praam, of Slavonic origin; cp.
Pol. pram, 'boat*, Russ. poromu, 'ferryboat',
which are cogn. with Gk. πόρος, 'thoroughfare,
passage', L. porta, 'gate, door', portus, 'port,
harbor', fr. I.-E. base *per-, 'to lead across,
drive across, traverse, pierce'. See fare, v., and
cp. words there referred to.

## pram
pram, n. (colloq.) — Short for prambulator, a
syncopated form of perambulator.

## prana
prana, п., life principle (Hinduism). — OI. pranah,
'breath, breath of life', formed fr. pro-, 'before,
forward, forth', and the stem of dniti, 'breaihes".
The first element is cogn. with Gk. πρό, 'before',
L. pro, 'before, for'; see 1 st pro-. The second
element derives fr. I.-E. base *an-, 'to blow,
breathe', whence also Gk. άνεμος, 'wind', L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:609 COLUMN:3 -->
animus, 'soul, spirit, mind, courage'; see animus.

## prance
prance, intr. v. — ME. prauncen, of uncertain
origin. It derives perh. fr. OF. paravancier, fr.
par-, a particle denoting intensity, and avancier
(¥. avancer), 'to advance'. See par- (fr. L. per,
'through'), and advance.
Derivatives: prance, п., pranc-er, п., pranc-ing,
adj., pranc-ing-ly, adv.

## prandial
prandial, adj., pertaining to dinner (humor.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. prandium,
'luncheon', which stands for *pram-ed-yom, lit.
'that which is eaten early'. The first element is
cogn. with OI. pur-vah, 'the first, foremost',
Lith.pirmas, 'the first', OE. forma, 'the former';
see foremost. The second element derives fr.
I.-E. base *ed-, 'to eat'; see eat. Cp.
anteprandial, postprandial.

## prank
prank, п., a trick. — Prob. rel. to prank, 'to dress
up'.

## prank
prank, tr. and intr. v., to dress up, adorn. — ME.
pranken, rel. to Du. pronken, G. prunken, 'to
make a show, to strut', MLG., MHG., G.
prangen, of s.m. Cp. prink.
Derivatives: prank-ing, n. and adj., prank-ing-ly,
adv., pranlc-ish, adj., prank-ish-iy, adv., prank-
ish-ness, n.

## prase
prase, п., a green variety of quartz. — F., fr. L.
prasius, fr. Gk. πράσιος (scil. λίθ-ος), 'a precious
stone of a leek green color', fr. πράσον, Чеек',
fr. *prsom, whence also L. porrum, 'leek'. Cp.
porraceous and next word. Cp. also the second
element in chrysoprase.

## praseodymium
praseodymium, п., name of a rare metallic
element (chem.) — ModL., shortened fr. praseodi-
dymia, a name coined by the discoverer of this
element, Carl Auer von Welsbach (1858-1929)
fr. Gk. πράσιος, 'leek green' (see prase), and
ModL. didymium, the name given by Carl Gus-
tav Mosander to a rare metal which he thought
to be a single chemical element; see didymium.
In 1885 von Welsbach succeeded in splitting
didymium into two elements, which he called pra-
seodidymia and neodidymia (see neodymium).

## pratal
pratal, adj., pertaining to meadows. — Late L.
prdtalis, fr. L. pratum, 'meadow'. See prairie
and adj. suff. -al.

## prate
prate, intr. and tr. v. — ME. prate», fr. MDu.
praten, 'to chatter'. Cp. MLG. praten, protert
(whence MHG. braten, bradin), Swed., Norw.
prata, 'to talk, chatter'. All these words are
prob. of imitative origin. Cp. prattle.
Derivative: prate, n.

## Prater
Prater, п., name of the "Hyde Park" of Vienna.
— G., fr. L. prdtum, 'meadow'. See prairie and
cp. Prado.

## pratincole
pratincole, п., any bird of the genus Glareola
(ornithol.) — Lit. 'inhabiting the meadows', fr.
L. prdtum, 'meadow', and incofa, 'inhabitant',
which is rel. to colere, 'to till (the ground); to
inhabit", colonus, 'cultivator of the ground'. See
prairie a nd colony.

## pratinqolous
pratinqolous, adj., living in meadows. — See prec.
word and -ous and cp. the second element in
terricolous.

## pratique
pratique, п., permission to land. — F., prop,
'practice', fr. MF. practique, fr. Late L. practice,
fr. Gk. πρακτική (short for ή πρακτική τέχνη,
'the practical art'), fern, of πρακτικός, 'practi·
саГ. See practical.

## prattle
prattle, intr. and tr. v. — Formed fr. prate with
freq. sufT. -le. Cp. MLG. pratelen, 'to chatter'.
Derivatives: prattle, п., prattl-er, п., prattl-ing,
verbal n. and adj., prattl-ing-ly, adv., prattl-y,
adj.

## pravity
pravity, n. (rare), depravity. — L. pravitds,
'crookedness', fr. prams, 'crooked', fr. I.-E.
base *prd-, 'to bend', whence also L. prdtum,
'meadow'. See prairie and -ity and cp. deprave,
depravity.

## prawn
prawn, п., a marine crustacean — ME. prane, of
unknown origin.

## praxis
praxis, п., exercise; the opposite of theory. —
Gk. πραξις, from the stem of the verb πράσσειν,
πραττειν, 'to do'. See practical and cp. apraxia,
parapraxis.

## pray
pray, tr. and intr. v. — ME. preien, fr. OF. preier
(F. prier), fr. -VL. precdre = L. precdri, 'to ask,
beg, pray, request', fr. prex (most freq. in the pi.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 583 | PRECONIZATION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 COLUMN:1 -->
preces), 'prayer, request, entreaty', which is rel.
lo pro с us, 'wooer', fr. I.-E. base *perefc-, *perk-,
*P$-* 'to ask (questions), to request', whence
also 01. prasna-, Avestic frashna-, 'question',
OSlav. prosiri, Lith. praSyti, 'to ask, beg', OHG.
frahin, fragen, MHG., G. fragen, OS. fragoti,
OE. fricgatiy and, with present tense infix n-,
Goth, fraihnan, ΟΉ./regna, OE.fr'tgnan,frinan,
4o ask (questions)'. For further derivatives of
base *perek-, *perk-, *prk-, see postulate. Cp.
deprecate, imprecate, precarious, precatory, prie-
dieu, prithee, procacity.
Derivatives: prayer (q.v.), pray-'mg, n. and adj.,
pray-ing-ly, adv.

## prayer
prayer, n. — ME. preiere, fr. OF. preiere (F.
priere), fr. VL. *precaria, prop, subst. use of L.
precarla, fem. of the adj. precarius, 'obtained by
prayer*, fr. precari, 'to pray'. See prec. word and
subst. suff. -er.
Derivatives: prayer-ful, adj., prayer-ful-ly, adv.,
ртауег-jul-ness, п., prayer-less, adj.

## pre-
pre-, also spelled prae-, pref. meaning before
(both in time and place). — F. pre-, fr. L. prae,
'before', which is rel. to Oscan.prai, Umbrian
pre, and cogn. with OI. pare, 'thereupon', Gk.
■παραι, 'af, Gaul, are-, 'at, before', Lith. pre,
'at*, OSlav. pri, 'at', Goth, faura, OE. fore,
'before'. See fore, adv., and cp. preter-, prime, adj.,
and the first element in presby-.

## preach
preach, tr. and intr. v. — ME. prechen, OF. pree-
chier fr. (F. precher), fr. OF. prechier, fr. L.
praedicare, 'to cry in public, publish, proclaim,
announce, declare', in Eccies. L. 'to preach', fr.
prae- (see pre-) and dicere, 'to say'. See diction
and cp. predicate, which is a doublet of preach.
Derivatives: preacher (q.v.), preach-ify, intr. v.
(colloq.), preach-ing, п., preachment (q.v.),
preach-у> adj.

## preacher
preacher, n. — ME. prechour, fr. OF. preecheor
(F. precheur), fr. L. praedicatorem, ace. of prae-
dicator, 'proclaimer, publisher', in Eccies L.,
'preacher'. See preach and agential suff. -er.
Derivatives: preacher-ess, п., preacker-ize, intr.
v.

## preachment
preachment, n. — ME. prechement, fr. MF., fr.
precher, (F. precher), fr. OF. prechier, precher.
See preach and -ment.

## pre-Adamite
pre-Adamite, adj., existing before Adam. — See
pre-, Adam and subst- suff. -ite.

## preamble
preamble, п., introduction. — ME.,fr. MF. (= F.)
preambule, fr. ML. praeambulum, prop. neut.
adj. used as a noun fr. Late L. praeambulus,
'walking before', fr. praeambuldre, *to walk
before', fr. L. prae- (see pre-) and ambulare, 'to
walk'. See amble and cp. preambulate.

## preambulate
preambulate, intr. v., to make a preamble. —
Late L. praeambulai-(um), pp. stem of praeam-
bulare. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives \ preambulat-ion, п.,preambulat-ory,
adj.

## prebend
prebend, п., stipend granted to a canon out of the
estate of a cathedpal. — ME., fr. MF. prebende
(F. prebende), fr. Late L. praebenda, 'allowance,
pension', lit. 'things to be furnished', neut. pi.
adj. taken as a fem. sing, п., fr. L. praebendus,
gerundive of praebire, 'to supply, grant,
furnish', contraction ofprae-hibere, 'to hold forth',
fr. prae (see pre-) and habere, 'to have, hold'.
See habit and cp. provender. For other Latin
gerundives or their derivatives used in English cp.
agenda and words there referred to.
Derivative: prebend-al, adj.

## prebendary
prebendary, п., another name for an honorary
canon. — ML. prebendarius, 'holder of a
prebend', fr. Late L. praebenda. See prec. word and
1st subst. surf. -ary.

## Frecambrian
Frecambrian, adj., pertaining to the time
preceding the Cambrian (geol.) — See pre- and
Cambrian.
Derivative: Frecambrian, n.

## precarious
precarious, adj., 1) dependent onthe will of
another; 2) risky, dangerous. — L. precarius,
'obtained by begging or prayer; doubtful, risky',
fr. prex (most freq. in the pi. precis), 'prayer,
request, entreaty'; introduced by Sir Thomas
Browne (1605-82). See pray, prayer.
Derivatives: precarious-ly, adv., precarious-
ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 COLUMN:2 -->

## precarive
precarive, adj., precatory. — Late L. preedtivus,
'prayed for, obtained by entreaty', fr. L. preca-
tus, pp. οι precari, 'to ask, beg, entreat, pray'.
See pray and -ative.

## precatory
precatory, adi., of the nature of, or expressing, an
entreaty. — Late L. preedtorius, 'pertaining to
petitioning, precatory4, fr. L. preedtor, One who
prays or entreats', fr. preedtus, pp. οι precari.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ory.

## precaution
precaution, n. — F. precaution, fr. Late L. prae-
cautiOnem, ace. of praecautio, fr. L. praecautus,
pp. of praecavire, 4o guard against beforehand',
fr. prae (see pre-) and cavere, 'to be on one's
guard'. See caution.
Derivatives: precaution-al, precaution-ary, adjs.

## precautious
precautious, adj. — Formed fr. pre- and cautious.
Derivatives: precautious-ly, adv., precautious-
ness, n.

## precede
precede, tr. and intr. v. — ME. precede», fr. MF.
(= F.)preceder, fr. L. praecedere, 'to go before,
precede', fr. prae (see pre-) and cedere, 'to go'.
See cede.

## precedence
precedence, n. — Formed from the adj.
precedent with surf. -ce.

## precedency
precedency, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## precedent
precedent, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) precedent,
fr. L. praecedentem, ace. of praecedens, pres.
part, of praecedere. See precede and -ent.
Derivatives: precedent, п., precedent-ed, adj.,
precedent-ly, adv., precedent-ial, adj.

## precent
precent, v., to lead the choir in singing. — Back
formation from next word.

## precentor
precentor, п., the leader of the singing in a church
choir or congregation. — Late L. praecentor, a
leader in singing, precentor', fr. praecinere, 'to
sing before', fr. L. prae (see pre-) and canere, 'to
sing'. See cantor, chant. For the change of Latin
ά (in cantor) to ё (in prae-centor) see accent and
cp. accentor, succentor.
Derivatives: precentor-ial, adj., precentor-ship,
п., precent-ory, n.

## precept
precept, п., rule of conduct. — ME., fr. L. prae-
ceptum, 'rule, maxim', prop. neut. pp. used as a
noun fr. praecipere, 'to give rules, advise, teach',
lit. 'to take beforehand', fr. prae (see pre-) and
capere (pp. captus), 'to take*. See captive and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also praecipe. For
the change of L. a (in captus) to ё (in prae-cep-
tum) see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: precept-ist, п., precept-ive, adj.,
precept-ive-ly, adv., preceptor (q.v.)

## preceptor
preceptor, п., a teacher. — h.praeceptor, 'teacher,
instructor', fr. praecipere. See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: preceptor-ial, adj., precepior-ia\-ly,
adv., preceptory, (q.v.)

## preceptory
preceptory, п., a religious house of the Knights
Templars.— ML.praeceptoria, 'an estate
directed by a preceptor', fr. L. praeceptor. See prec.
word and -y (representing L. -id).

## precession
precession, n. — Late L. praecessio, gen. -onis, 'a
going forward', fr. L. praecessus, pp. of
praecedere. See precede and -ion.
Derivative: precession-af, adj.

## precieuse
precieuse, п., a pedantic woman. — F., fem. of
precieux, 'precious'. See precious and cp. the
title of Moliere's comedy Les Precieuses ridicules.

## precinct
precinct, п., boundary, limit. — ME. precincte,
fr. ML. praecinctum, 'a boundary', prop. neut.
pp. of L. praecingere, 'to gird about', used as a
noun, fr. prae (see pre-) and cingere, 'to gird'.
See cincture.

## preciosity
preciosity, n. — F. preciosite, fr. L. pretiOsitatem,
ace. ofpretiositds, 'preciousness, costliness'. See
next word and -ity.

## precious
precious, adj. — ME., fr. OF. precios, precieus
(F. precieux), fr. L. pretiosus, 'precious,
valuable*, fr. pretium, 'worth, price'. See price and
-ous and cp, precieuse.
Derivatives: precious-ly, adv., precious-ness, n.

## precipice
precipice, п., a steep cliff. — MF. (— F.)precipice,
fr. L. praecipitium, ia steep place', lit, 'a falling
down headlong', fr. praeceps, gen. praecipis,
'headforemost', which is formed fr. prae (see
pre-) and caput, gen. capitis, 'head*. See capital,
adj. For the change of Latin a (in caput) to ι (in
prae-cipitium) see abigeat and cp. words there

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 COLUMN:3 -->
referred to.

## precipitable
precipitable, adj., that which can be precipitated.
— See precipitate and -able,

## precipitance
precipitance, precipitancy, n. — Formed frpm next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## precipitant
precipitant, adj. — L. praecipitans, gen. -amis,
pres. part, ofpraecipitare, 'to throw down
headlong'. See precipitate, v., and -ant.
Derivatives: precipitant-ly, adv., precipitant-
ness, n.

## precipitate
precipitate, tr. v., to throw headlong; intr. v., to
fall headlong. — L. praecipitdtus, pp. of
praecipitare, 'to throw down headlong", fr. praeceps,
gen. praecipis. See precipice and verbal surf.
-ate.

## precipitate
precipitate, adj., rushing headlong. — L. praecipi-
tatus, pp. of praecipitare. See precipitate, v.
Derivatives: precipitate, п., precipitate-ly, adv.,
precipitate-ness, n.,precipitat-ive, adj.

## precipitation
precipitation, n. — MF. (= F.) precipitation, fr.
L. praecipitationem, ace. of praecipitatio, 'a
falling headlong', fr. praecipitdtus, pp. of
praecipitare. See precipitate, v., and -ion.

## precipitin
precipitin, п., an antibody developed through the
inoculation of foreign protein (immunof.) —
Coined by Kraus from the stem of L,
praecipitare. See precipitate and -in.

## precipitous
precipitous, adj., steep. — F. precipiteux (fem.
precipiteuse), fr. precipiter, 'to precipitate', fr.
L. praecipitare. See precipitate, v., and -ous.
Derivatives: precipitous-ly, adv., precipitous-
ness, n.

## precis
precis, п., 1) sing, and pi., a summary; 2) tr. v.,
to summarize. — F. See next word.

## precise
precise, adj. — MF. (= F.) precis (fem. precise),
fr. L. praecisus, pp. of praecidere, 'to cut off in
front*, fr. prae (see pre-) and caedere, 'to cut'.
See cement and cp. succise. For the change of
Latin ae (in caedere) to Г (in prae-cisus) see
acquire and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: precise-ly, adv.. precise-ness, п.,
precis-ian, п., precisian-ism, п., precisian-ist, п.,
precision (q.v.)

## precision
precision, n. —- F. precision, fr. L. praecisionem,
ace of praecisio, 'a cutting off', fr. praecisus, pp.
of praecidere. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: precision-ist, n.

## preclude
preclude, tr. v. — L. praecludere, 'to shut off,
close', fr. prae (see pre-) and claudere, 'to shut*.
See close, adj., and cp. words there referred to.

## preclusion
preclusion, n. — L. praeclusio, gen. -onis, 'a
shutting off', fr. praeclusus, pp. οι praecludere.
See prec. word and -ion.

## preclusive
preclusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.

## praeclusus
praeclusus, pp. of praecludere. See preclude.
Derivative: preclusive-ly, adv.

## precocial
precocial, adj., designating birds whose young
are covered with downy feathers and are able to
run about as soon as they are hatched.—
Formed with suff. -ial fr. L. praecox, gen. -ocis. See
next word.

## precocious
precocious, adj., developed before the usual
time. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. praecox,
gen. -ocis, 'ripe before its time, premature,
precocious', fr. praecoquere, 'to boil beforehand;
to ripen fully*, fr. prae (see pre-) and'coquere, 'to
boil, ripen'. See cook and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: precocious-ly, adv., precocious-
ness, n.

## precocity
precocity, п., the quality of being precocious. —
F. precocite, fr. precoce, 'precocious*, fr. L.

## praecocem
praecocem, ace. of praecox. See prec. word and
-ity.

## precognition
precognition, п., foreknowledge. — Late h.prae-
cognitio, gen. -onis, fr. L. precognitus, pp. of

## praecognoscere
praecognoscere, 'to foreknow', fr. prae (see
pre-) and cogndscere, 'to know'. See cognition,

## preconceive
preconceive, tr. v. — Formed fr. pre- and

## conceive
conceive,

## preconception
preconception, n. — Formed fr. pre- and

## conception
conception,

## preconcert
preconcert, tr. v., to arrange beforehand. —

## Formed fr. pre- and concert
Formed fr. pre- and concert, v.
Derivatives: preconcert-ed, adj., preconcert-ed-

## ly
ly, adv., preconcert-ed-nesst n.

## preconization
preconization, п., a public proclamation. — ML.

## praeconizatio
praeconizatio, gen. -onis, 'proclamation*, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:611 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PRECONIZE | S84 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:611 COLUMN:1 -->
praeconizatus, pp. of praeconizare. See next
word and -ation.

## preconize
preconize, tr. v., to proclaim in public. — ML.
praeconizare, 'to proclaim', fr. L. praecd, gen.
-dnis, 'crier, herald', contraction of *prai-dicd,
fr. prae (see pre-) and -died, fr. died, dicdre, 'to
proclaim, announce'- See predicate, v., and
-ize.

## precursive
precursive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
praecursus, pp. of praecurrere. See next word.

## precursor
precursor, n. — L. praecursor, 'forerunner', fr.
praecursus, pp. of praecurrere, 'to run before',
fr. prae (see pre-) and currere, 'to run'. See
current, adj., and agential suff. -or.

## precursory
precursory, adj. — L. praecursdrius, fr.
praecursus, pp. of praecurrere. See precursor and adj.
suff. -ory.

## predacious
predacious, also predaceous, adj., predatory. —
See predatory and -acinus, -aceous.
Derivative: predacious-ness, п., predaceous-ness,
n.

## predate
predate, tr. v., to antedate. — Formed fr. pre-
and date, v. See date, 'point of time'.

## predatory

## Pre-Raphaelite
Pre-Raphaelite, п., a member of the society of
painters called the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood;
adj., pertaining to Pre-Raphaelitism. — See next
word.

## Pre-Raphaelitism
Pre-Raphaelitism, п., the style of the Pre-Raphae-
lites. — Formed with suff. -Ism from the
forename of Raphael Sanzio (1483-1520) and the
suffixes -Ite and -ism. The members of the Pre-
Raphaelite Brotherhood, founded in England in
1847, called themselves Pre-Raphaelites, to
intimate that their style resembled that of the Italian

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:613 COLUMN:2 -->
painters before Raphael.

rogation and -ive.

## presby-
presby-, combining form meaning 'old', as in
presbyopia. — Gk. πρεσβυ-, fr. πρέσβυς, 'old,
venerable', which stands for *πρέσ-γυς (ср.
Cretan πρεΐγυς, Boeot. πρΐσγυς), and lit.
means 'he that goes first'. The first element of
this compound is rel. to Gk. πάρος, 'before,
aforetime, formerly', and cogn. with L. prae,
'before'; see pre-. The second element is a
derivative of l.-E. base *gwu-, 'to go', which is rel. to
base *gwem-, of s.m., whence Gk. βαίνει,ν, 'to
go', L. venire, 'to come', Goth, qiman, OE.
cuman, 'to come'; see come and cp. base,
'bottom*. Cp. priest.

ready' (whence also F. pret, 'ready'), fr. prae
(see pre-) and stare, 'to stand*. See state and cp.
appreteur, the first element in prestidigitator and
the second element in culprit.

## presume

adv., presum-ed-ly, adv., presum-ing, adj.,

presumptive (q.v.), presumptuous (q.v.)

sumption and words there referred to.

## presumptive
presumptive, adj. — F. presomptif(fern,

## presumptuous

pretense, pretence, п., a claim. — AF. pretensse

## pretension
pretension, п., a pretext; a claim. — ML. prae-

pretentious, adj., making claims. — F. preten-

Derivatives: pretentious-ly, adv.,

pretentiousness, n.
preter-, combining f»rm meaning 'beyond'. — L.

preterit, preterite, adj. — ME. preterit, fr. OF.

preternatural, adj., the same as supernatural. —

## pretone

## pretzel

## preux chevalier

proud, prude. For the second word se,e chevalier,

Derivatives :prevail-ing, adj., prevail-ing-ly, adv.,
prevail-ing-ness, n.

## prevalence
prevalence, n. — F. prevalence, fr. Late L. prae-

Derivatives: prevalent-ly, adv., prevalent-ness,

## prevaricate
prevaricate, intr. v., to speak evasively. — h.prae-
varicatus, pp. of praevdricdri, *to walk
crookedly, not to be upright, to collude', fr. varicus,
'with bent feet, with feet spread apart,

and verbal suff. -ate and cp. divaricate,

## prevarication
prevarication, n. — L. praevaricatio, gen. -onis,
fr. praevaricatus, pp. οΐ praevdricdri. See prec.

## prevaricator
prevaricator, n. — L. praevaricdtor, One who

crookedly', fr. praevdricdtus, pp. ofpraevdricdri.
See prevaricate and agential suff. -or.

## prevenance
prevenance, п., anticipation of the needs of others.
— F. prevenance, fr. privenant, pres. part, of

п., preveni-ative, adj. and п., prevent-er, п.,
prevent-ible, adj., prevent-ive, adj. and п.,

## prevention

Derivative: prevention-al, adj.

Derivatives: prevision-al, adj., prevision-al-lyy

## prey
prey, n. — ME. preye, fr. OF. preie (F. proie), fr.

cp. predatory, depredate,

## prey

ly, adv.

## Priacanthidae
Priacanthidae, n. pi., a family pf tropical fishes

thorn'. The first element is re], to πρΐειν,

Priam, п., king of Troy and husband of Hecuba

Pers. xaridan, 'to buy', Olr. crenaim, Ί buy',

'purchase',

priapism, п., persistent painful erection of the

αττι.σμος, fr. πριαπίζει,ν, 'to be lewd', fr. Πρί-
άπος, 'Priapus' (name of the god of fertility); the

price, n. — ME. pris, fr. OF. pris (F. prix), fr. L.

'against', Homeric Gk. προτί, Gk. προς,
'toward, to, upon, against; at hard by near*, Lett.

pret, Opposite', OSlav. protivu, protivo, 'in

opposition to, against', and with Gk. πέρνημι, Ί

self, prop. Ί give for equal value', L. par,

precious, appreciate, depreciate.

adj., price-less-ness, п., pric-er, n.

prick, n. — ME. prikke, prik, fr. OE. prica, 'a
point*; rel. to LG. prik, 'point', MDu. prick,

## prick

## prie-dieu
prie-dieu, п., a low desk for a person kneeling at

## priest
priest, n. — ME. prest," fr. OE. preost, fr. OF.
prevost (F. prevot), which prob. derives fr. VL.
*pre(p)ostus, *pre(v)ostus, fr. L. praepositus,
'chief, head, overseer', prop. pp. of praeponere,
'to place before'. See praepostor and provost.
The usual derivation- of OE. preost, fr. L
presbyter (see presbyter) is wrong. It is due to a
confusion of the origin of OE. preost, with that of
OS., OHG. prestar, 'priest', which actually
derive fr. L. presbyter [through the medium of OF.
prestre (whence F. pretre), 'priest'].
Derivatives: priest, v., priest-ess, п., priesthood
(q.v.), priest-like, adj. priest-ly, adj., priest-li·
ness, n.

priesthood, n. — ME. presthod, fr. OE. preosthdd.

## prig
prig, п., a fop, a pedant. — Of uncertain

ish-ly, adv., prigg-ish-ness, n.

## prig

Derivative: prig, п., a thief.

prim, adj., neat; formal, pedant. — ОF.prin, prim,

## primacy

## prima donna
prima donna, — It., lit. 'first lady', fr. prima, fern,

## primage
primage, п., percentage addition to the freight;

primal, adj., I) first in time; original; primitive;
2) first in importance; primary. — ML.primdlis,

## primate

cles. L., 'archbishop', fr. primus. See prime,

Derivatives: primatial (q.v.), primate-ship, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:615 COLUMN:3 -->

## prima rial
prima rial, adj., pertaining to a primate. — F., fr.

## Primates
Primates, n. pi., the order of mammals (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. primds, gen. primdtis, 'one of the
first, principal, chief, fr. primus. See prime, adj.,
and cp. primate.

## prime
prime, adj., first. — ME., fr. OF. prime, fern, of
prin, which derives fr. L. primus, 'first', whence
also It. primo, 'first', OProvenQ. prim, 'first,
excellent, fine, tender, delicate', Сг\,а\. prim, 'thin,
fine, cunning'. Sp. primo, adj., 'first, excellent',
п., 'cousin'. L. primus stands for *pris-mus,
superl. of *pris, an adverb meaning 'before',
and occurring also in pris-cus, 'old, ancient,
primitive*, pris-tinus, 'former, early, primitive'.
L. *pris is rel. to prae, 'before'. See pre- and cp.
prim, prima donna, prima facie, primage,
primary, primate, primer, primero, primeur,
primitive, primo, primrose, Primula, primum mobile,
primus. Cp. also prior, prince, Priscilla pristine,
Cp. also foremost. L. *prismus became primus
in the sense of the Latin phonetic law,
according to which s disappeared before d, I, m or n.
See comity and cp. words there referred to.

## prime
prime, п., the best period; the first canonical hour.
— ME., fr. OE. prime, 'the first canonical hour
(i.e. six o'clock)', fr. L. prima (hora), 'the first
hour', fern, of primus, 'first'. See prime, adj.

## prime
prime, tr. v., to make ready; intr. v., to supply a
firearm with priming. — Fr. prime, adj.
Derivatives: prim-er, cap or tube serving to
prime a firearm, prim-ing, n.

## primer
primer, п., 1) a prayer book; 2) an elementary
book; 3) a size of type. — ME., fr. ML.

## primero
primero, п., a card game. — Fr. Sp. primera, fern.
οι primero, 'first', fr. L. primdrius. See primary.

## primeur
primeur, п., early fruit; novelty. —■ F. primeur, fr.

## primeval

and aevum, 'age'. See prime, adj., and age.
Derivative: prim(a)eval-ly, adv.

## primi-

## primigenial

## priminc

## primipara

primipara, 'who has born for the first time',
compounded of primi- and the stem of pario, parere,

## primiparous
primiparous, adj., bearing young for the first time.
— See prec. word and -ous.

## primitive
primitive, adj. — ME. primitif, fr. MF. (= F.)

Derivatives: primitive, п., primitive-ly, adv.,
primitive-ness) n.,primitiv-ism, n.,primitiv-ist, п.,
primitiv-ist-ic, adj.

## primo
primo, п., the first or leading part (mus.) — It., fr.
L. primus, 'first'. See prime, adj.

## primo-
primo-, comb, form meaning 'first'. — L. primo-,
primo, adv., 'first', fr. primus, adj., 'first'. See

## primogenital
primogenital, adj., primogenitary. — Eccles. L.

'firstborn'. See primogeniture and adj. suff. -al.

## primogenitary
primogenitary, adj., pertaining to primogeniture.
— Formed with adj. suff. -ary fr. Late L.

## primogenitor
primogenitor, п., an ancestor. — ML·,
primogenitor, compounded of primo- and L. genitor,

progenitor.

## primogeniture
primogeniture, п., the state of being the first-born

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:616 COLUMN:1 -->
child of the same parents. — ML. primogeni-
tura (whence also F. primogeniture), fir. Late L.
primogenitus, 'first born', which is compounded
of L. primo (adv.), 'first', and genitus, pp. of
gignere, 'to bring forth, bear'. See primo-, genus
and -ure and cp. ultimogeniture,

## primordial
primordial, adj., original, primeval. — ME., fr.
Late L. primordialis, fr. L. primdrdium,
'beginning, origin*, fr. primus, 'first', and ordiri, 'to
begin a web, to begin', rel. to ordo, gen. ordinis,
'line, order'. See prime, adj., order, п., and -ial.
Derivatives: primordial-ism, п., primordial-ity,
п., primordial-ly, adv.

## primp
primp, intr. v., to dress up. — Prob. formed fr.

## primrose
primrose, n. — Late ME., fr. ME. primerole, fr.

## Primula
Primula, п., a genus of plants, the primrose (bot.)
— ModL., fr. ML.primula, 'primrose', lit.
