## Primulaceae
Primulaceae, n. pi., the primrose family {bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## primulnceous
primulnceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## primuline
primuline, п., a yellow dye. — Formed with suff.
-ine fr. ML. primula. See prec. word.

## primum mobile
primum mobile, the first source of motion. — L.,
'the first movable thing'. See prime, adj., and
mobile, adj. and n.

## primus
primus, adj. and п., the first. — L. primus. See
prime, adj.

## prince
prince, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. princeps,
'the first man, chief, leader', fr. *primo-capus,
'one occupying the first place', fr. primus, 'first'
(see prime, adj.), and the stem of capere, 'to
take, hold*. See captive and words there referred
to and cp. principal, principate, principle. For
the change of Latin ά (in capere) to ё (in
princeps) see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: prince-dom п., prince-hood, п.,
prince-kin, п., prince-ling, п., prince-ly, adj.

## princeps
princeps, adj., first. — L. See prec. word.

## princess
princess, n. — F. princesse, fr. prince. See prince
and 1st sufT. -ess.
Derivative: princess-ly, adj.

## principal
principal, adj. and n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr.
L. principalis, 'first, original; overseer, chief
magistrate', fr. princeps, gen. principis, 'first;
the first man'. See prince and adj. suff.. -al.
Derivative: principal-ly, adv.

## principality
principality, п., the dignity of a prince. — ME.
principalite, fr. OF. principalite (F, principalite),
fr. Late L. principalitdtem, ace. of principalitas,
fr. L. principalis. See prec. word and -ity.

## principate
principate, п., principality. — ME. principat, fr.
L. principatus, 'first place, pre-eminence', fr.
princeps, gen. principis. See prince and subst.
suff. -ate.

## princlpia
princlpia, n. pi., fundamental principles. — L.,
pi. ofprincipium, 'beginning, origin', fr. princeps,
gen. principis; see prince. L. principium is a loan
translation of Gk. αρχή.

## principle
principle, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) principe,
'principle', fr. L. principium. See prec. word.
For the intrusive / cp. participle, syllable.
Derivatives: principl-ed, un-principl-ed, adjs.

## prink
prink, tr. v., to dress up. adorn; intr. v., to dress
oneself up. — Prob. a var. of prank, 'to adorn'.
Derivative: prink-y, adj.

## print
print, n. — ME. prente, preinte, prime,
'impression mark', fr. OF. preinte, priente, prop. fern,
pp. used as a noun, fr. priembre, preindre (F.
preindre), 'to stamp, impress', fr. L. premere, 'to
press'. See press, 'to squeeze'.

## print
print, tr. and intr. v. — ME. prenten, preenten,
printen, fr. prente, preinte, prime. See print, n.
Derivatives:printable, &d'j.,print-ed,
adj.,printer, п., print-ing, n.

## prion
prion, п., name of several kinds of petrels, —
ModL., fr. Gk. πρΐων, 'a saw', which is rel. to
πρϊείν, πρίζείν, 'to saw'. See prism and cp. the
first element in Priacantiridae.

## prion-
prion-, form of priono- before a vowel.

## Prioninae
Prioninae, n. pi., a family of beetles. — ModL.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:616 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. Gk. πρΐων, 'a saw*. See prion and -inae.

## prionine
prionine, adj. and n. — See prec. word.

## priono-
priono-, before a vowel prion-, combining form
meaning 'a saw'. — Gk. πρΐονο-, fr. πρΐων,
gen. πρΐονος, *a saw'. See prion.

## prior
prior, adj., earlier. — L. prior, gen. prioris,
'former; first; superior', compar. of OL. pri-,
'before', which is rel. to L. prae, 'before*. See pre-
and prime, adj., and cp. prlus, a priori, pristine.

## prior
prior, п., the head of a priory. — ME. priour,
prior, fr. OE. prior, fr. OF. priour (F. prieur), fr.
Eccles. h.priurem, ace. of prior, from the L. adj.
prior. See prior, adj.
Derivative: prior-skip, n.

## priorate
priorate, п., the office of a prior. — Eccles. L.
prioratus, fr. L. prior. See prec. word and subst.
suff. -ate.

## prioress
prioress, n. — ME. prioresse, fr. OF. prioresse, fr.
Eccles. L. pridrissa, fr. prior. See prior, п., and
1st -ess.

## priority
priority, п., precedence. — ME. priorite, fr. OF.
priorite (F. prioriti), fr. ML. prioritatem, ace. of
prioritds, fr. L. prior. See prior, adj., and suff.
-ity.

## priory
priory, п., a monastery subordinate to an abbey.
— ME. priorie, fr. AF. priorie, fr. Eccles. L.
prioria, fr. prior. See prior, п., and -y
(representing OF., F. -ie),

## Priscilla
Priscilla, fern. PN. — L., fern, of Priscillus,
dimin. of Priscus, fr. priscus, 'old, ancient,
primitive'. See prime, adj., and cp. pristine.

## prise
prise, tr. v., to force. — A var. of prize.

## prism
prism, n. — Late h.prfsma, fr. Gk. πρΤσμα,
'something sawn off; prism', fr. πρίζειν, 'to saw', fr.
πρΐειν, of s.m., which is perh. cogn. with Alb.
priS, 'to break, destroy'. Cp. pistrix, Priacan-
thidae, prion, Pristis.

## prismatic
prismatic, adj. — F. prismatique, formed with
suff. -ique (see -ic) fr. Gk. πρίσμα, gen.
πρίσματος, 'prism'. See prec. word.
Derivative: prismatic-al-ly, adv.

## prismatoid
prismatoid, п., a solid resembling a prism. —
Compounded of Gk. πρίσμα, gen. πρίσματος,
'prism' (see prism), and -οειδής, 'like', fr. εϊδος,
'form, shape'. See -old.
Derivative: prismatoid-al, adj.

## prismoid
prismoid, п., a prismlike body with similar, but
not equal, bases. — Compounded of Gk.
πρΤσμα, 'prism', and -οε^δής, 'like'. See prec. word.
Derivative: prismoid-al, adj.

## prison
prison, n. — ME. prison, prisun, fr. OF. prison,,
prisun (F. prison), 'jail, prison', fr. VL. *pre-
sionem, fr. L. prensionem, ace. of prensio,
contracted form of prehensio, 'a seizing, arresting',
fr. prehensus, pp. of prehendere, 'to lay hold of,
seize, catch'. See prehensile and cp. misprision,
prize, 'the act of seizing'.

## prisoner
prisoner, n. — ME., fr. OF. prisonier (F. prison-
nier), prop, 'a jailer', fr. prison, 'jail, prison'. See
prison and agential suff. -er,

## prissy
prissy, adj., prim. — Prob. a blend of prim and
sissy.
Derivatives: prissi-ly, adv., prissi-ness, n.

## pristine
pristine, adj., belonging to the earliest time. — L.
pristinus, 'former, early, primitive'. See prime
adj., and cp. Priscilla. For the suff. -tinus cp. L.
diutinus, 'long lasting', crastinus, 'of tomorrow'.

## Pristis
Pristis, п., the genus of sawfishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., fr. L. pristis, 'shark, whale, sawfish,
sea monster*, πρίστΐς, πρΐστίς, of s.m., lit.
'sawyer', fr. πρΐειν, 'to saw*. See prism and cp.
words there referred to.

## pri'thee
pri'thee, interj. {archaic), — Fr. earlier prey the,
*(1) pray thee'.

## prius
prius, п., that which takes precedence. — L.,
neut. of prior, 'former, previous'. See prior.

## privacy
privacy, n. — ME. privacie, fr. privat. See private,
adj., and -cy.

## privatdocent
privatdocent, п., a university lecturer in Germany
and Austria, not paid by the university. — G.,
lit. 'private teacher*. See private, adj., and
docent.

## private
private, adj. — ME. privat, fr. L. privatus, 'apart
from the State, belonging to an individual', pp.
of privare, 'to bereave, deprive, rob', fr. privus,
'single', which stands for *prei-wos, and is rel.
to per, 'through', pro, 'for' (see per- and 1st
pro-); privus lit. means 'that which stands by

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:616 COLUMN:3 -->
itself. Cp. Umbr. preve, 'singularly,
particularly'. Cp. also deprive, privation, privy, privilege.
For the ending of private see adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: private, п., privat-eer, n. and intr.
v-, privat-eer-ing,private-ly, adv.,private-ness, n.

## privation
privation, n. — ME. privacion, fr. MF. (= F.)
privation* fr. L. privationem% ace. of privatio, fr.
privatus, pp. of privare. See prec. word and -ion.

## privative
privative, adj. — L. privdtivus, 'denoting
privation, negative', fr. privatus, pp. of privare. See
private and -ive.
Derivatives: privative, п., privative-ly, adv.,

## privet
privet, п., an evergreen shrub. — Of uncertain
etymology. The earlier forms primet, primeprint
suggest a connection with prime, n. Cp. ME.
primerole (see primrose.)

## privilege
privilege, a. — ME., fr. OF. privilege (F.
privilege), fr. L. privilegium, 'a bill of law in favor or
against an individual', compounded οι privus,
'single, private' (see private), and leg-, stem of
lex, gen. legis, 'law'. See legal and cp. words
there referred to.

## privilege
privilege, tr. v. — ME. privilegen, fr. privilege.
See privilege, n.
Derivatives: privileg-ed, adj., privileg-er, n.

## privity
privity, п., a special relationship between parties
(law). — ME. privite, fr. OF. privite, fr. prive (F.
prive), 'private'. See privy and -Ity.

## privy
privy, adj., private. — ME. prive, fr. OF. prive
(F. prive), fr. L. privatus. See private.
Derivatives: privy, n.,privi-ly, adv.,privity (q.v.)

## prize
prize, п., reward. — ME. pris, fr. OF. pris (F.
prix), 'price, prize*, fr. L. pretium, 'worth,
value, price'. Prize is the doublet of price (q.v.)
The spelling prize is due to the influence of
prize, 'act of seizing'. Cp. praise.

## prize
prize, tr. v., to estimate. — ME. prisen, fr. OF.
preisier, prisier (F. priser), fr. Late L. pretiare,
'to prize, value', fr. L, pretium. See prec. word
and cp. misprize.

## prize
prize, п., something taken by force. — ME. prise>
fr. OF. (= F.) prise, *a taking, seizing, holding',
prop. fern. pp. used as a noun, fr. prendre, 'to
take, seize', fr. L. prendere, contracted form of
prehendere. See prehensile and cp. prey, prison.
Cp. also mainprize.
Derivative: prize, tr. v., to force.

## prize
prize, п., a lever. — ME. prise, fr. OF. (= F.)
prise, *a taking, seizing'. See prec. word.
Derivative: prize, tr. v., to press, esp. with a
lever, to pry.

## pro-
pro-, pref. of Latin origin meaning 'before,
forward, forth, for, in favor of; in place of, on
behalf of; according to'. — L. pro-, fr. pro,
'before, in front of, for, on behalf of, instead of,
rel. to per, 'through', prae, 'before4, por- (for
*ρζ-), 'forward' and cogn. with Ol. para,
'beyond', pro-, 'before, forward, forth', Gk. πρό,
'before', πάρος, 'before'» παρά, 'from beside,
against, beyond', περί, 'around, about, toward',
Goth, fafira, 'before', OE. fore, 'before, for, on
account of. See fore, adv., and for and cp. 2nd
pro-, per, pre-. Cp. also proceres, prodigal,
prone, prose, province, proud, prow, 'valiant',
and the second element in reciprocal. Cp. alsa
the pref. in pollicitation and in words there
referred to. Cp. also the pref. in pourbolre,
pourparler, pourpoint.

## pro-
pro-, pref. of Greek origin meaning 'before,
forward'. — Gk. προ-, fr. πρό, 'before'. See 1st
pro- and cp. protero-, proto-, prow, 'fore part of
a ship*.

## proa
proa, п., a kind of outrigged sailing boat. —
Malay prahu, prau.

## pro and con
pro and con, adv., п., and v. — Short for pro and
contra, 'for and against', fr. L. pro, 'for' (see 1st
pro-), and contra, 'against' (see contra-).

## probabiliorism
probabiliorism, n. — F. probabiliorisme, lit. 'the
teaching of that which is more probable', fr. L.

## probabilior
probabilior, 'more probable', compar. of proba-
bilis. See next word and 1st -ior.

## probabilism
probabilism, п., the doctrine that real knowledge
is impossible (philos.) — F. probabilisme, lit.
'the doctrine of that which is probable'; formed
with suff. -isme fr. L. probdbifis. See probable
and -ism.

## probabilist
probabilist, п., a believer in probabilism. — F.
probabiliste. See prec. word and -ist.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:617 COLUMN:1 -->

## probabHity
probabHity, η. — MF. (= F.) probabilite, fr. L.
probdbilitdtem, ace. of probdbilitds, fr. proba·
bilis. See next word and -ity.

## probable
probable, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. pro·
bdbilis, 'that may be assumed or proved, likely,
probable', fr. probdre, 'to try, test, prove'. See
probate and -able.
Derivatives: probable, п., probable-ness, п.,
probabl-y, adv.

## pro bang
pro bang, п., a rod of whalebone provided with a
sponge used for the removal of obstructions
from the gullet. — Fr. earlier provang, which is
of uncertain origin; influenced in form by prove.

## probate
probate, п., 1) the proving of a will;2) the copy of
a will with a certificate that it has been proved.
— ME. probat, fr. L- probatum, neut. of
probatus, pp. of probdre, 'to try, test, prove', fr. pro-
bus, 'good, proper, serviceable, upright'. See
prove and adj. sufT. -ate and cp. probable,
probity.

## probate
probate, tr. v., 1) to prove the genuineness of (a
will); 2) to put (a convicted offender) on
probation. — L. probatus, pp. of probdre. See probate,
n.

## probation
probation, п., 1) the testing of a person's conduct,
character, etc.; 2) the releasing of a convicted
(usually) young offender dependent upon his
good behavior. — ME. probacioun, fr. MF.( =
F.) probation, fr. L. probdtionem, ace. of
probation 'a trying, proving, examination*, fr. pro-*
bdtus, pp. of probdre. See probate, п., and -ion.
Derivatives: probation-al, adj., probation-ary,
adj. and п., probation-er, п., probation-ism, п.,
probation-ist, n.

## probative
probative, adj., affording proof. — L. probdtivus,
'pertaining to proof, fr. probatus, pp. of pro-
bare. See probate, adj., and -ive.
Derivative: probative-ly, adv.

## probatory
probatory, adj., probative. — ML- probdtorius, fr.
L. probatus, pp. of probdre. See probate, п., and
adj. suff. -ory.

## probe
probe, n. — Late L. proba, 'proof, back
formation fr. L. probdre. See probate, adj.

## probe
probe, tr. and intr. v. — Partly fr. probe, п.,
partly directly fr. L. probdre.
Derivatives: probe-able, adj., prob-er, n.

## probity
probity, п., honesty, rectitude. — MF. (~ F.)
probite, fr. L. probitdtem, ace. of probitds,
'goodness, honesty, uprightness', fr. probus. See
probate, adj., and -ity.

## problem
problem, n. — Late ME. probleme, fr. F. pro-
Ыёте, fr. L. problema, fr. Gk. πρόβλημα,
'discussion, problem', lit. 'something thrown
forward', fr. προβάλλει, 'to throw forward', fr.
πρό (see 2nd pro-) and βάλλειν, 'to throw, cast*.
See ballistic and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: problematic (q.v.),problemat-ist, п.,
problemat-ize, tr. ν., problem-ist, п.,
problematic, adj., problem-ize·* intr. v.

## problematic
problematic, problematical, adj. — F. problema-
tique, fr. Late L. problematicus, fr. Gk.
προβληματικός, 'pertaining to a problem', fr.
πρόβλημα, gen. προβλήματος. See prec. word and
-ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: problematical-ly, adv.

## Proboscidea
Proboscidea, n. pi., an order of ungulate
mammals including the elephant and many extinct
genera, as the mammoth, mastodon, etc. —
ModL., fr. Gk. προβοσκίς, gen. προβοσκίδος,
'trunk'. See proboscis.

## proboscidian
proboscidian, adj. and n. — See prec. word and
-ian.

## proboscis
proboscis, п., the trunk of the elephant. — L., fr.
Gk. προβοσκίς, fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and βό-
σκειν, Чо feed', from stem βοτ-, whence also
βοτάνη, 'grass, fodder'. See botany.

## procacious
procacious, adj., pert. — Formed with suff. -ious
fr. L. procax, gen. -dcis. See next word.
Derivative: procacious-ly, adv.

## procacity
procacity, п., pertness. — F. procacite, fr. L. pro-
edeitdtem, ace. of proedcitas, 'boldness,
insolence', fr. procax, gen. -dcis, 'bold, insolent,
pert', fr. procdre, 'to ask, demand', which is rel.
to procus, 'wooer, suitor', precari, 4to ask, beg,
pray, request'. See pray and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## procaine
procaine, п., an alkaloid, C13H30O2Na (pkarm.) —
Contraction of pro- and (co)caine.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:617 COLUMN:2 -->

## procedendo
procedendo, п., a writ sent by a superior court to
an inferior, directing the latter to proceed to
judgment. — L. (de) procedendo (ad judicium),
'relating to a proceeding (to judgment)', abl. of
the gerund of procedere, 'to proceed'. See
proceed.

## procedure
procedure, n. — F. procedure, fr. proceder, 'to
proceed'. See next word and -иге.
Derivatives: procedur-al, adj., procedur-al-ly,
adv.
"proceed, intr. v. — ME. procedeny fr. OF.
proceder (F. proceder), fr. L. procedere (pp.
processus), 'to go forward, advance'. See 1st pro-
and cede.
Derivatives: proceeds, n. pi., proceed-er, п.,
proceed-ing, n.

## proceleusmatic
proceleusmatic, adj., animating; containing four
short syllables (pros.) — Late L. proceleusma-
ticus, fr. Gk. προκελευσματ^κός, fr. προκελεύ-
ειν, 'to give orders before', fr. πρό (see 2nd
pro-) and κελεύειν, 'to exhort, order', which is
rel. to κέλης, 'race horse', and cogn. with L.
celer, 'swift'. See celerity and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## Frocellaria
Frocellaria, п., a genus of birds including the
albatrosses, fulmars, etc. (ornithol.) — ModL.,
fr. L. procella, 'storm, tempest', which is rel. to
procellere, 'to throw down*, fr. 1st pro- and I.-E.
base *kwel-, 'to strike, cut', whence also Gk.
κλαν, 'to break in pieces', L. calamitds, 'defeat',
in-columis, 'uninjured'. See clastic and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see suff. -aria.
Derivatives: procellari-an, adj. and n.

## procephalic
procephalic, adj., pertaining to the front of the
head. —'Formed fr. 2nd pro- and Gk. κεφαλή,
'head'. See cephalic.

## proceres
proceres, n. pi., nobles, princes. — L. proceres,
prop, a collateral form of proci, pi. of procus.
Proci lit. means 'they who stand in front', fr.
I.-E. base *pro-qo-, which occurs also in L.
procul, 'at a distance, afar', in the second
element of reciprocus, 'alternating' and in Gk.
πρόκα, 'forthwith, straightway' (lit. 'turning
forward'). I.-E. *pro-co- is enlarged fr. *pro-,
'before, forward, forth', whence also Gk.
πρό, 'before', L. pro, 'before, for'. See 1st
and 2nd pro- and cp. the second element in
reciprocal. The alteration of L. proci into
proceres is due to the analogy of pauperis, 'the
poor', pi. of pauper.

## procerity
procerity, п., tallness. — L. proceritds, 'height,
tallness', fr. procerus, 'high, tall', which was
formed fr. 1st pro- and -cerus, from the stem
of crescere, 'to grow'; see crescent. For the
ending see suff. -ity.

## process
process, n. — ME. proces, fr. MF. ( — F.)prods,
fr. L. processus, 'a going forward, advance', fr.
processus, pp. of procedere. See proceed.
Derivatives: process, tr. v., to submit to a
process, process-al, adj., procession (q.v.)

## process
process, intr. v., to go in procession. — Back
formation fr. procession.

## procession
procession, n. — ME.processioun, fr. OF. (— F.)
procession, fr. L. processidnem, ace. oiprocessio,
'a going forward, advance', fr. processus, pp. of
procedere. See proceed and -ion.
Derivatives: procession, intr. and tr. v.,
processional (q.v.), processionary (q.v.),
processionist, n.

## processional
processional, adj. — ME., fr. ML. processiondlis,
'pertaining to a procession', fr. h.processio, gen.
-onis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: processional-ly, adv.

## processionary
processionary, adj., processional. — ML. pro-
cessionarius, fr. L. processid, gen. -onis. See
procession and adj. suff. -ary.

## proces-verbal
proces-verbal, an official report. — F., lit. 'a
verbal process'.

## prochein
prochein, prochain, adj., nearest, next (law). — F.
prochain, fr. VL. *propianus, formed fr. L. pro-
pe, 'near' (adv.), on analogy of VL. *antidnus,
'old, former', fr. L. ante, 'before'. L. prope
derives fr. I.-E. *pro-qwe. See propinquity and cp.
words there referred to.

## prochronism
prochronism, п., an ante-dating. — Formed with
suff. -ism fr. Gk. πρόχρονος, 'preceding in
time', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and χρόνος, 'time'.
See chronic and cp. anachronism, metachronism.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:617 COLUMN:3 -->

## procidentia
procidentia, n., the prolapse of an organ (med.) —
L. procidentia, 'a falling forward or down', fr.
procidens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of prdcidere,
'to fall forward, fall down', fr. 1st pro- and
cadere, 'to fall'. See cadence. For the change of
Latin a (in cadere) to i (in pro-cidere) see abigeat
and cp. words there referred to.

## proclaim
proclaim, tr. v. — ME. proclamen, fr. L. procld-
mdre, 'to call out, cry out', fr. 1st pro- and cld-
mdre, 'to call, cry'. See claim, v.
Derivative: proclaim-er, n.

## proclamation
proclamation, n. — ME. proclamacioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) proclamation, fr. L. procldmationem, ace.
of procldmdtio, 'a calling out, outcry', fr. pro-
cldrnutus, pp. of procldmare. See prec. word and
-ation.

## proclitic
proclitic, adj. — ModL. procliticus, formed on
analogy of encliticus fr. Gk. προκλινει,ν, 'to
lean forward', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and κλίνειν,
'to lean'. See enclitic.

## proclivity
proclivity, п., tendency, inclination. — F. procli-
vite, fr. L. prdclivitdtem, ace. of proclivitds,
'descent; tendency, inclination', fr. prdclivis,
'sloping downward; inclined', fr. 1st pro- and clJ-
vus, 'slope, hill*. See clivus and -ity.

## proconsul
proconsul, A. — ME., fr. L. proconsul, from the
phrase pro consule, 'for, instead of, the consul*,
fr. pro, 'for' (see 1st pro-), and abl. of consul.
See consul and cp. propraetor.
Derivative: proconsul-ship, n.

prohibitory, adj. — Late L. prohibitoris,
'restraining, prohibitory', fr. L. prohibitus, pp. of
prohibere. See prohibit and adj. surf. -ory.

## project
project, tr. and intr. v., to throw; to plan. — L.
project us, pp. of projicere, 'to throw forth or
before, to throw down', fr. 1st. pro- and jacere
(pp. jacts), 'to throw, cast'. See jet, *to spirt
forth', and cp. parget. For the change of Latin a
(in jactus) to ё (in pro-jectus) see accent and cp.
words there referred to.

## project
project, п., a plan. — L. projectum, 'something
thrown forth or before', neut. pp. of projicere.
Cp. F. projet and see project, v.
Derivatives; project-ile, adj. and п., project-ing,
adj., project-ing-ly, adv., project-ion, п.,
projective, adj., project-ive-ly, adv., project-iv-ity,
n·. project-or, n.

## prolamin
prolamin, prolamine, п., a kind of simple protein
(biochem.) — Contraction of proline, e/nmonia
and suff. -in(e).

## prolan
prolan, п., the gonadotropic principle found in
the urine of pregnant women (biockem.) —
Coined by Zondek from L. proles, 'offspring,
children' (see proles), and -an, a surf, frequently
used in chemistry and biochemistry.

## prolapse
prolapse, п., the falling or slipping out of place
of an internal organ. — L. prolapsus, 'a gliding
forward', fr. prolapsus, pp. of prolabi, 'to glide
forward', fr. 1st pro- and labi, 'to glide'. See
lapse.

## prolapse
prolapse, intr. v., to fall or slip out of place. — L.
prolapsus, pp. of prolabi. See prolapse, adj.

## prolate
prolate, adj., elongated. — L. prolatus (used as
pp. of proferre, 'to carry forward, bring forth,
extend'), formed fr.pro (see 1st p*ro-) and Idtus,
'borne, carried'(used as pp. ferre^Xo bear,carry')>
which stands for *tldtos, 'borne', fr. *//-, zero
degree of I.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry*,,
whence L. tollere, 'to lift up, raise*, tolerdre, 'to
bear, support'. See tolerate and cp. collate and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: prolate-ly, adv., prolate-ness, n.

## prolation
prolation, n. — h.proldtid, gen. -onis, 'a bringing
forward', fr. prolatus. See prec. word and -ion.

## prolative
prolative, adj. — Late L. prolativus, fr. L.
prolatus. See prolate and -ive.
Derivative: prolative-ly, adv.

## proleg
proleg, п., one of the abdominal legs of the larvae
of several insects. — A hybrid coined fr. L. pro,
'before, for' (see 1st pro-), and E. leg.

## prolegomenary
prolegomenary, adj., introductory. — See next
word and adj. suff. -ary.

## prolegomenon
prolegomenon, п., introduction. — Gk. προ-
λεγόμενον, neut. pass. pres. part of προλέγειν, 'to
say beforehand', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:619 COLUMN:3 -->
λέγειν, 'to say'; see lecture. For the Greek pass,
suff. -μένος see alumnus and cp. words there
referred to.

## prolegomenous
prolegomenous, adj., prolegomenary. — See prec.
word and -ous.

## prolepsis
prolepsis, п., anticipation. — L,, fr. Gk. πρό-
ληψις, 'a taking beforehand*, fr. προλαμβάνειν,
'to take beforehand', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and
λαμβάνειν, 'to take, grasp, seize'. See lemma
and cp. words there referred to.

## proleptic
proleptic, adj., anticipatory. — Gk. προληπτικός,
'anticipative', fr. *προληπτός, verbal adj. of
προλαμβάνειν. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: proleptic-al, adj., proleptic-al-ly,
adv.

## proles
proles, п., offspring, issue (law). — L. proles.
Offspring, children, descendants', contracted fr.
*pro-oles, fr. 1st pro- and base "a/-, 'to nourish',
whence also L. alere, 'to nourish'. See aliment
and cp. next word, prolan, prolific. Cp. a*lso
soboles.

## proletarian
proletarian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. proletdrius, 'belonging to that class of
citizens who owing to their poverty could serve,
the State only by having children (= L.proles)''.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: proletarian-ism, п., proletarian-ize,
tr. v., proletarian-iz-ation, n.

## proletariat
proletariat, proletariate, п., 1) the lowest class in
ancient Rome; 2) the lowest class in the
community. — F. proletariat, fr. L. proletdrius. See
prec. word and subst. suff. -ate.
Derivatives -.proletariate, adj., proletariat-ism, n.

## proletary
proletary, n. and adj., proletarian. —
^proletdrius. See proletarian.
Derivatives-.prole tar-ize, tr. v.,proletar-iz-ation,
n.

## prolicide
prolicide, п., the killing of one's child or children;
infanticide. — Compounded of L. proles,
'offspring, phild', and -cidium, 'killing', fr. caedere,
'to kill'. See proles and -cide, 'killing'.

## proliferate
proliferate, tr. v. and adj. — Back formation fr.
proliferation,

## proliferation
proliferation, п., rapid production. — F.
proliferation, fr. prolifere, 'proliferous'. See next word
and -ation.

## proliferous
proliferous, adj., reproducing offspring^freely. —
Formed fr. ML. prolifer (whence also F.
prolifere), 'bearing offspring', fr. L. proles, 'offspring*
and the stem offeroj'erre, 'to bear, carry*. See
proles and -ferous.

## prolific
prolific, adj., fertile, fruitful. — F. prolifique, fr.
ML. prolificus, which is compounded of L.
proles, 'offspring' and the stem of -ficere, unstressed
form of facere, 'to make, do'. See proles and -fie.
Derivatives: prolific-acy, п., prolific-al, adj.,
prolific-al-ly, adv., prolific-al-ness, п., prolific-
ity, п., prolific-ness, n.

## proligerous
proligerous, adj., producing offspring. — See
proles and -gerous.

## proline
proline, prolin, п., an amino acid, C5H„OaN
(biockem.) — Coined fr. pyrrole and suff. -in(e).

## prolix
prolix, adj., verbose. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
prolixe, fr. L.prolixus, 'stretched out, extended',
orig. meaning 'flowing forward', fr. 1st pro- and
the stem of liquere, 'to flow'. See liquid and cp.
lixiviate.
Derivatives: prolixity (q.v.), prolix-ly, adv.,
prolix-ness, n.

## prolixity
prolixity, п., verbosity. — ME. prolixite, fr. OF.
(— F.) prolixite, fr. Late L. prolixitdtem, ace. of
prolixitds, 'great extension*, fr. L. prolixus. See
prec. word and -ity.

## prolocutor
prolocutor, п., a speaker of the Lower House of
Convocation. — L. prolocutor, 'a pleader,
advocate', fr. prolocutus, pp. of proloquf, 'to speak
out, declare', fr. 1st pro- and loqul, 'to speak'.
See locution.
Derivative: prolocutor-skip, n.

## prolog
prolog, n. — See prologue,

## prologize
prologize, also prologuize, intr. v., to write or
deliver a prologue. — Gk. προλογίζει, fr.
πρόλογος. See next, word and -ize.
Derivative: prolog(u)iz-er, n.

## prologue
prologue, also prolog, n. — ME. prolog, fr. OF.
(= F.) prologue, fr. L. prologs, fr. Gk.
πρόλογος, 'a speech beforehand, a prologue', fr.
πρό (see 2nd pro-) and λόγος, 'speech'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 593 | PROPAROXYTONE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 COLUMN:1 -->
logos.
Derivatives: prologue, prolog, tr. v.,prologu-ist,
prolog-ist, n.

## prologuize
prologuize, v. — See prologize.

## prolong
prolong, tr. v. — ME. prolongen, fr. OF. prolon-
guer, prolonguier (F. prolonger), fr. Late L.
prolongare, 'to prolong', fr. 1st pro- and L. longus,
'long'. See long, adj., and cp. purloin, which is a
doublet of prolong.

## prolongate
prolongate, tr. v. — Late L. prolongatus, pp. of
prolongare. See prec. word and verbal sufT. -ate.

## prolongation
prolongation, n. — OF. {= F.), fr. Late L. prd-
longdtidnem, ace. of prdlongdtid, fr. prolongatus,
pp. οι prolongare. See prolong and -ation.

## prolusion
prolusion, п., a prelude. — L. prdlusid, gen. -onis,
*a preliminary exercise', fr. prolus-(um), pp. stem
of proludere, 'to play beforehand, prelude', fr.
1st pro- and ludete, 'to play'. See ludicrous and
-ion and cp. prelude, prelusion.

## prolusory
prolusory, adj., introductory. — Late L. prdlu-
sdrius, fr. L. prdlus-(um), pp. stem of pr oludere.
See prec. word and adj. sufT. -ory.

## promenade
promenade, n. — F., fr. promener, 'to take
(somebody) out for a walk', sepromener, 'to walk', fr.
Late L. promindre, 4o drive (cattle, etc.)
forward*, fr. 1st pro- and mindre, 'to drive', prop,
'to drive by threatening shouts*, fr. L. mindri, 'to
threaten', fr. minae (pi.), 'threats, menaces',
which is rel. to imminere, 'to project over; to
threaten'; fr. I.-E. base *men-, 'to stand out,
project', whence also L. mans, gen. montis,
'mount, mountain'. See mount, 'hill, mountain',
and cp. amenable, demean,'to conduct', eminent,
imminent, menace, minatory, prominent.
Derivative: promenade, intr. and tr. v.

## Promethean
Promethean, adj., pertaining to Prometheus. —
See next word and -ean.

## Prometheus
Prometheus, п., name of the Titan who stole fire
from heaven and was punished by being chained
to a rock {Greek mythology). — L. Prometheus,
fr. Gk. Προμη&εύς, lit. 'forethinker, foreseer',
fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and *μήθος,
corresponding to Dor. *μαΰ·ος, 'care', fr. I.-E. *md-dh-, a
var. of *men-dh-, enlargement of base *men-, 'to
think'; see Hofmann, EWG., p. 284 s.v. προ-
μηθής. See mathematical and cp. Epimetheus.
Cp. also next word.

## promethium
promethium, п., a metallic element of the rare-
earth group {chem.) — ModL., named after
Prometheus; so called by its discoverers, the
chemists G. A. Marinsky and L. E. Hendenin,
in 1948. For the ending see chem. suff. -ium.

## prominence
prominence, n. — Obsol. F. prominence, fr. L.
prominentia, *a jutting out, projection', fr. prd-
minens. See prominent and -ce.

## prominency
prominency, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## prominent
prominent, adj. — L·. prominens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of prominere, 'to jut out, project', fr. pro-
and I.-E. base *men-, 'to stand out, project'. See
mount, 'hill, mountain', and words there
referred to and cp. esp. promontory. For the
ending see suff. -ent.
Derivatives: prominent, п., prominent-ly, adv.,
prominent-ness, n.

## promiscuity
promiscuity, n. — F. promiscuite, formed fr. L.
prdmiscuus with suff. -ite. See next word and
-ity.

## promiscuous
promiscuous, adj., mixed. — L. prdmiscuus,
'mixed, indiscriminate', fr. 1st pro-, 'forward,-forth',
and the stem of miscere, 'to mix*. See mix. For
E. -o,us, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: prdmiscuous-ly, adv., promiscuous-
ness, n.

## promise
promise, n. — ME. promis, partly fr. L. promis·
sum, neut. pp. of L. promittere, 'to send forward,
foretell, promise', partly fr. F. promesse,
'promise', fr. L. prdmissa, neut. pi. of the pp. pro-
missus, taken as a fern. sing. noun. L. promittere
is formed fr. 1st pro- and mittere, 'to send'. See
mission.
Derivatives: promise, tr. and intr. v., promis-ee,
n.,promis-er, п., promis-ing, adj.,promis-ing-ly,
adv., promis-ing-ness, п., promis-or, n.

## promissory
promissory, adj., containing a promise. — ML.
prdmissdrius, fr. L. prdmissor, 'a promiser', fr.
prdmissus, pp. οι promittere. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ory.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 COLUMN:2 -->

## promontory
promontory, п., a headland. — ML. prdmontd-
rium, fr. L. promunturium, 'headland,
promontory', which is rel. to prominere, 'to jut forward,
jut out, project'; see prominent. ML. prdmontd-
rium was influenced in form by an association
with L. mdns, gen. montis, 'mount, mountain'.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ory.

## promote
promote, tr. v., 1) to further; 2) to advance. — L.
promotus, pp, of promovere, 'to move forward,
promote', fr. 1st pro- and movire, 'to move'. See
move and cp. words 'there referred to.
Derivatives: promot-er, п., promotion (q.v.),
promot-ive, adj., promot-ive-ness, n.

## promotion
promotion, n. — MEs, fr. MF. (= F.)promotion,
fr. L. promotidnem, ace. of prdmdtid, 'a moving
forward', fr. promotus, pp. of prdmovere. See
prec. word and -ion, and cp. motion.
Derivative: promotion-al, adj.

## prompt
prompt, adj. — L. prdmptus, lit. 'brought forth',
hence 'visible, apparent, evident, manifest', pp.
of pro mere, 'to take or bring out or forth*,
contraction of *pro-emere, fr. 1st pro- and emere,
'to take'. See exempt and words there referred
to and cp. esp. peremptory, premium, redeem.
Cp. also impromptu.
Derivatives: prompt, п., prompt-er, п.,
promptitude (q.v.), prompt-ly, adv., prompt-ness, n.

## prompt
prompt, tr. v. — ME. prompten, fr. ML. promp-
ture, fr. L. prdmptus. See prompt, adj.
Derivative: prompt-er, n.

## promptitude
promptitude, n. — ME., fr. MF. ( = F.), fr. ML.
prdmptitudinem, ace. of promptitudd, fr. L.
prdmptus. See prompt, adj., and -tude.

## promulgate
promulgate, tr. v., to proclaim officially. — L.
promulgdtus, pp. of promulgare, *to make
known, publish', of uncertain origin; not related
to vulgus, 'multitude', vulgdre, 'to publish'.

## promulgation
promulgation, n. — L. promulgated, gen. -onis, fr.
promulgdtus, pp. of promulgare. See prec. word
and -ion.

## promalgator
promalgator, n. — L. promulgator, One that
publishes', fr. promulgdtus, pp. of promulgare. See
promulgate and agential sufT. -or.

## pronaos
pronaos, п., the vestibule of a Greek temple
{arch.) — L., fr. Gk. πρόναος, fr. πρό (see 2nd
pro-) and ναός, 'temple'. See naos.

## pronate
pronate, tr. v., to bend or turn downwards. —
Late L. prondtus, pp. of prdnare, 'to bend
forward', fr. L. prdnus. See prone and verbal suff.
-ate.

## pronate
pronate, adj. — Late L. prondtus. See pronate, v.

## pronation
pronation, п., a bending or turning downwards.
— ML.prondtid, gen. -onis, fr. Late L. prondtus,
pp. of prdnare. See pronate, v., and -ion.

## pronator
pronator, п., name of the muscle pronating the
hand {anat.) — ML., fr. Late L. prondtus, pp.
of prendre. See prec. word and agential suff. -or.

## prone
prone, adj., 1) lying face downwards; 2) lying flat;
3) liable to. — ME., fr. L. pronus, 'leaning
forward, inclined, bent forward', for *prd-no-s, fr.
1st pro-. For the suff. -nus cp. L. inter-nus,
'inner', subter-nus, 'lying beneath'. Cp. pronate.
Derivatives: prone-ly, adv., prone-ness, n.

## pronephric
pronephric, adj., pertaining to a pronephros. —
See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## pronephros
pronephros, п., the first kidney of a vertebrate
embryo {embryol.) — Medical L., compounded
of 2nd pro- and Gk. νεφρός, 'kidney'; see
nephron The term pronephros was introduced into
embryology by the English zoologist Sir Edwin
Ray Lankester (1847-1930). Cp. mesonephros,
metanephros.

## prong
prong, п., a fork; a point. — ME.prange, prong,
rel. to MLG. prangen, 'to press, pinch', prange,
'stick', Goth, ana-praggan, 'to oppress, afflict',
MLG. prenger, 'pillory' (whence MHG., G.
pranger, of s.m.) Cp. pang.
Derivatives: prong, tr. v., prong-ed, adj., prong-
er, n.

## pronominnl
pronominnl, adj. — Late L. prdndmindlis,
'pertaining to a pronoun', fr. L.prdndmen, gen. -inis.
See pronoun and adj. suff. -ah
Derivatives: pronominal, п., pronominal-ize, tr.
v.
ргопопсё, adj., pronounced. — F., pp. of pro-
noncer, 'to pronounce'. See pronounce.

## pronoun
pronoun, n. — MF. (= F.) pronom, fr. L. prdno-
men, from the phrase pro nomine, 'instead of a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 COLUMN:3 -->
noun', fr. pro, 'for' (see 1st pro-), and abl. of
ndmen, 'name'; see conn. L.prdndmen is a loan
translation of Gk. αντωνυμία.

## pronounce
pronounce, tr. and intr. v. — ME. pronouncen, fr.
OF. pronuncier, prononcier (F. prononcer), fr. L.
pronuntidre, 'to make publicly known, tell,
announce, pronounce', fr. 1st pro- and nuntidre, 'to
announce*, fr. nuntius, 'messenger, envoy*. See
nuncio and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: pronounce-able, adj., pronounce-
able-ness, п., pronounc-ed, adj., pronounc-ed-ly,
adv., pronounc-er, n.

## pronouncement
pronouncement, n. — F. prononcement, fr.
prononcer. See prec. word and -ment.

## pronunciamento
pronunciamento, pronunciamiento, п.,
proclamation. — Sp. pronunciamiento, formed with suff.
-miento fr. pronunciar, fr. L. pronuntidre. See
pronounce and -ment, and cp. pronouncement.

## pronunciation
pronunciation, n. — ME. pronunciacion, fr. MF.
(= F.) prononciation, fr. L. prdnuntidtidnem,
ace. of pronuntidtio, 'a public declaration,
publication, proclamation', fr. pronuntidtus, pp. of
pronuntidre. See pronounce and -ation.

## pronunciator
pronunciator, n. — L. prdnuntidtor, 'a reciter', fr.
pronuntidtus, pp. of pronuntidre. See pronounce
and -ator.

## proof
proof, n. —* ME. profe, proeve, preove, preve, fr.
OF. prueve, proeve (F. preuve), fr. Late L. proba,
'proof, back formation fr. L. probdre, 'to prove'.
See prove and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: proof, adj., proof, tr. v., proof-ert
п., proof-ing, п., proof-less, adj., proof-less-ly,
adv., proof-ness, n.

## prop
prop, n. — ME. proppe, fr. MDu. proppe, 'stop-,
per' (whence Du.proppen, 'stop, cram'), which is
rel to OHG. pfropfo, pfroffo, 'a set, layer of a
plant' (whence MHG., G. pfropfen, 'to prop');
borrowed fr. L. propdgd, 'a set, layer of a plant*.
See propagate.

## prop
prop, tr. v. — ME. proppen, fr. proppe. See prop,
n.
Derivative: propp-er, n.

## propaedeutic
propaedeutic, propaedeutical, adj., pertaining to
preliminary education. — Formed fr. Gk. προ-
παιδεύειν, 'to teach beforehand', fr. πρό (see
2nd pro1) and παιδεύειν, 'to train, educate,
teach', fr. παϊς, gen. παιδός, 'child'. See pedo-.
For the ending see sufT. -ic, resp. also *al.

## propagable
propagable, adj. — See propagate and -able.
Derivatives: propagabil-ity, п., propagable-ness,
n.

## propaganda
propaganda, n. — From L. propaganda in
Congregated de~ propaganda fide (lit. 'congregation
for the propagation of faith'), name of the
committee of cardinals established in 1622 by Pope
Gregory XV. In this name propaganda is fern,
abl. sing, of prdpdgandus, gerundive ofprdpdgdre.
See propagate.
Derivatives: propaganda, tr. and intr. v.,
propagand-ic, bA\.,propagand-ism, п.,
propagandist, п., propagand-ist-ic, adj., propagand-ist-ic-
al-ly, adv., propagand-ize, tr. and intr. v.

## propagate
propagate, tr. and intr. v. — L. prdpdgdtus, pp. of
prdpdgdre, 'to fasten, peg down, to set slips; to
propagate', fr. prdpdges, 'a set, layer of a plant',
fr. 1st pro- and *pdg-, base ofpangere, 'to fasten,
fix*. See pact and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ate. Cp. prop,
prune, 'to trim (vines)'.
Derivatives: propagation (q.v.), propagat-ive,
adj., propagator (q.v.), propagat-ory, adj.

## propagation
propagation, n. — ME. propagacyon, fr. OF.
(= F.), fr. L. prdpdgdtidnem, ace. of propagdtid,
prdpdgdtus, pp. of prdpdgdre, 'to fasten'. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: propagation-al, adj.

## propagator
propagator, n. — L. propagator, fr. prdpdgdtus,
pp. of prdpdgdre. See propagate and agential
suff. -or.

## propane
propane, п., a hydrocarbon C3H8 {chem.) —
Shortened fr. propyl and methane.

## propargyl
propargyl, п., a hydrocarbon radical, C3H3
{chem.) — Formed fr. propinyl, Gk. άργυρος,
'silver' (see argent), and suff. -yl; so called
because one hydrogen atom is replaceable by
silver.

## proparoxytone
proparoxytone, adj., having an acute accent on
the antepenult. — Gk. προπαροξύτονος. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PROPEL | 594 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 COLUMN:1 -->
2nd pro- and paroxytone.
Derivatives: proparoxytone, n. and tr. v.

## propel
propel, tr. v. — ME. propellen, fr. L. propellere,
'to drive forward, propel', fr. 1st pro- and pel-
lere, 'to drive'. See pulse, 'throb', and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: propell-ant, п., propellent (q.v.),
propell-er, n.

## propellent
propellent, adj. and n. — L.prdpellens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of propellere. See prec. word and
-ent.

## propene
propene, n. (chem.) — A shortened form of
propylene.

## propend
propend, intr. v., to incline (obsol.) — L. propen-
dire (pp. propensus), 'to hang forward, be
inclined', fr. 1st pro- and pendere, 4o hang'. See
pendant.

## propense
propense, adj., prone {archaic). — L. propensus\
'inclined', lit. 'hanging forward', pp. of propen-
dire. See prec. word.
Derivatives: propense-ly, adv., propense-ness,
п., propens-iiy, n.

## proper
proper, adj. — ME. propre, 'one's own, proper',
fr. OF. ( — F.) propre, fr. L. proprius, 'one's
own, particular, special, proper', which is of
uncertain etymology. According to W- S. Schulze,
Zur Geschichte lateinischer Eigennamen,
Berlin, 1904, p. Ill, proprius stands for *pro-
p(a)trios, 'coming from one's forefathers', fr. 1st
pro- and pater, gen. patris, 'father'. See father
and cp. property, propriety, appropriate,
expropriate, improper.
Derivatives: proper, п., proper-ly, adv.

## properispomenon
properispomenon, adj., having a circumflex accent
on the penult. — Gk. προπερισττώμενον, neut.
pass. pres. part, of προπερισπάν, 'to circumflex
the penult'. See 2nd pro- and perispomenon.

## property
property, n. — ME. proprete, fr. OF. proprete
(whence F. proprete, 'propriety*, propriete,
'proprietorship'), fr. L. proprietatem, ace. of
proprietds, 'ownership, property, propriety', fr.
proprius, 'one's own*. See proper and 1st -ty,
and cp. propriety, which is a doublet of property.
L. proprietds is a loan translation of Gk. ίδίωμα,
fr. ίδιος, 'one's own'.
Derivative: properti-ed, adj.

## prophecy
prophecy, n. — ME. prophecie, fr. OF. profecie
(F. prophetic), fr. Late L. prophetla, fr. Gk.
προφητεία, fr. προφήτης. See prophet and -cy.

## prophesy
prophesy, prophecy, tr. and intr. v. — ME.prophe-
cien, prophesien, fr. OF. profecier, fr. profecie.
See prec word.
Derivatives: prophesi-able, adj., prophesi-er, n.

## prophet
prophet, n. — ME. prophete, fr. OF. prophete (F.
prophete), fr. L. propheta, fr. Gk. προφήτης,
'one who speaks for a god, interpreter,
expounder, prophet', lit. 'one who speaks for
another', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and φη-, stem of
φημί, Ί speak', which is cogn. with L. jdri, 'to
speak'. See fame and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: prophetess (q.v.), prophet-hood, п.,
prophetic (q.v.), prophet-ism, n.

## prophetess
prophetess, n. — ME. prophetesse, fr. OF. pro-
phetesse (F. prophetesse), fr. Late L. prophetissa,
fr. L. propheta. See prec. word and 1st -ess.

## prophetic
prophetic, adj. — MF. (— F.) prophetique, fr.
Late L. propheticus, fr. Gk. προφητικός,
'pertaining to a prophet', fr. προφήτης, See prophet
and adj. sufT. -ic.
Derivatives: prophetic-al, adj., prophetic-al~ity,
n·» prophetic-al-ly, adv.

## prophylactic
prophylactic, adj., preventive (med.)—Gk.
προφυλακτικός, fr. προφυλάσσει^, 'to guard
against, ward off, fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and
φυλάσσειν, 'to guard'. See phylactery.
Derivatives: prophylactic, п., prophylactic-al-ly,
adv.

## prophylaxis
prophylaxis, п., preventive treatment (med.) —
Medical L-, formed fr. Gk. πρό (see 2nd pro-)
and φύλαξις, 'a guarding', on analogy of
προφυλακτικός. See prec. word.

## propine
propine, tr. v., to ofTer, give to drink. — ME. pro-
pinen, fr. MF. propiner, fr. L. propinare, 'to
drink to one's health, to pledge', fr. Gk. προ-
πϊνειν, lit. 'to drink before', fr. πρό (see 2nd
pro-) and πΐνειν, 'to drink'. See potion and cp.
words there referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: propine, п., a gift.

## propinquity
propinquity, п., nearness. — ME. prop'mquite, fr.
OF. prop'mquite, fr. L. propinquitdtem, ace. of
propinquitds, 'nearness, neighborhood', fr. pro-
pinquus, 'near', which is formed fr. prope, 'near',
with sufT. -inquus. L. propre stands for I.-E. *pro-
qwe, enlarged fr. *pro-, 'before, forward, forth'.
See 1st pro- and cp. prochein, proximal. Cp.
also approach, rapprochement, reproach. For
the sufT. -inquus cp. L. longinquus, 'long,
extensive, remote, distant' (see longinquity).

## propiolic
propiolic,adj., pertaining to the acid CH:C.C02H
{chem.) — A blend of propionic and tetrolic.

## propionic
propionic, adj., pertaining to the fatty acid,
C2H5C02H (chem.) — Coined from the first
syllable of Gk. πρώτος, 'first' (see pro to-), πΐων,
'fat' (see pio-), and adj. sufT. -ic.

## propitiable
propitiable, adj. — L. propitiabilis, 'capable of
being propitiated', fr. propitidre. See propitiate
and -able.

## propitiate
propitiate, tr. v., to appease. — L. propitidtus, pp.
of propitiate, 'to render favorable'. See
propitious and verbal sufT. -ate.
Derivative: propitiat-ing-ly, adv.

## propitiation
propitiation, n. — ME, propiciacioun, fr. Late L.
propitidtio, gen. -onis, fr. L. propitidtus, pp. of
propitidre. See prec. word and -ion.

## propitiator
propitiator, n. — Late L. propitiator, 'one who
propitiates', fr. L. propitiatus, pp. of propitidre.
See propitiate and agential sufT. -or.

## propitiatory
propitiatory, adj. — ME. propiciatorie, fr. Late
L. propitidtorius, fr. L. propitidtus, pp. of
propitidre. See propitiate and adj. suff. -ory.

## propitious
propitious, adj., favorable. — ME. propicious, fr.
OF. propicieus, propicius (F. propice), fr. L. pro-
pit ius, 'favorable, kind', which stands for *pro-
pet-ios, prop, 'falling toward', fr. 1st pro- and
the stem of petere, 'to fall upon; to seek'. See
petition and cp. words there referred to. For E.
-ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: propitious-ly, adv., propitious-ness,
n.

## propolis
propolis, п., a resinous substance. — L., fr. Gk.
πρόπολις, 'suburb; bee glue', lit. 'before the
city', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and πόλις, 'city'. See
policy, 'method of government'.

## propone
propone, tr. v., to set forth. — ME. proponen, fr.
L. proponere. See propound.

## proponent
proponent, п., one who makes a proposal. — L.
ргбрбпёпз, gen. -entis, pres. part, of proponere,
'to set forth'. See propound and -ent.

## proportion
proportion, n. — ME. proporcioun, fr. MF.
(= F.) proportion, fr. OF., fr. L.proportio, gen.
-onis, formed from the phrase pro portione, 'for
(his) part or share', fr. pro, 'for' (see 1st pro-),
and abl. of portio, 'part, share'. See portion.

## proportion
proportion, tr. v. — ME. proporciounen, fr. MF.
proporcioner (F. proportionner), fr. Late L. pro-
portiondre, fr. L. proportio. See proportion, n.
Derivatives: proportion-ed, adj., proportion-er,
п., proportion-ment, n.

## proportionable
proportionable, adj. — ME. proporcionable, fr.
MF. proporcionable (F. proportionnable), fr.
Late L. proportidnabilis, fr. L. proportio. See
proportion, n. and -able.
Derivative: proportionabl-y, adv.

## proportional
proportional, adj. — L. proportiondlis, 'pertaining
to proportion, proportional', fr. proportio, gen.
-onis. See proportion, п., and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: proportional, п., proportionality
(q-v.), proportional-ly, adv.

## proportionality
proportionality, n. — Late L. proportiondlitds, fr.
L. proportiondlis. See prec. word and -ity.

## proportionate
proportionate, tr. v. — Late L. proportionatus, pp.
of proportiondre. See proportion, v., and verbal
suff. -ate.

## proportionate
proportionate, adj. — ME. proportionate, fr. Late
L. proportiondtus, pp. of proportionare. See
proportionate, v.
Derivatives: proportionate-1y, adv., proportion-
ate-ness, n.

## proposal
proposal, n. — See next word and subst. suff. -al,

## propose
propose, tr. and intr. v. — ME. proposen, fr. OF.
( — F.) proposer, fr. L. proponere (pp.
propositus), 'to set forth', which was Gallicized after F.

## poser
poser, 'to put, place'. See propound and cp.
purpose, v., which is a doublet οι propose. Cp. also
compose and words there referred to. See also

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 COLUMN:3 -->
pose, 'to place'.
Derivative: propos-er, n.
proposition, n. — ME. proposicioun, fr. OF. (= F)
proposition, fr. L». propositionem, ace. of
propositi, 'a setting forth, a proposition', fr.
propositus, pp. of proponere. See next word.
Derivative: proposition-al, adj.

## propound
propound, tr. v. — Fr. earlier propone, fr. L.
proponere, 'to set forth', fr. 1st pro- and ponere (pp.
positus), 'to put, place'. See position. For the

expound.
Derivative: propound-er, n.

## propraetor
propraetor, propretor, п., a magistrate under the
Roman Republic, who after his praetorship
governed a province, where there was no army
(Roman hist.) — L. propraetor, formed from the
phrase pro praetore, lit. 'for a praetor', fr. pro,

praetor and cp. proconsul.

## proprietary
proprietary, п., 1) proprietor; 2) proprietorship.
— Late L. proprietdrius, 'owner, proprietor*,
prop, subst. use of the adj. proprietdrius. See
proprietary, adj.

## proprietary
proprietary, adj., 1) owned as property; 2)
pertaining to property. — Late L. proprietdrius,
'pertaining to somebody as property', fr. L.
proprietds. See propriety.

## proprietor
proprietor, n. — Formed with change of suff. fr.
Late L. proprietdrius (whence F. proprietaire),
'proprietor'. See proprietary, п., and agential
suff. -or.
Derivatives: proprietor-ial, adj.,
proprietor-tally, adv., proprietor-ship, n.

## proprietress
proprietress, n. — Formed from prec. word with
1st suff. -ess.

## propriety
propriety, n,, peculiar nature; fitness,
appropriateness. — ME. propriete, fr. MF. (= F.)
propriete, fr. OF., fr. L. proprietatem, ace. of
proprietds, 'property'. See property, which is a
doublet of propriety.

## proprio-
proprio-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
oneself. — Fr. L. proprius. One's own*. See
proper,

## proprioception
proprioception, п., the reception of stimuli
produced within the organism (physiol.) — Formed
from next word on the analogy of receptive;
reception.

## proprioceptive
proprioceptive, adj., capable of receiving stimuli
which are produced within the organism
(physiol.) — Coined by the English physiologist Sir
Charles Scott Sherrington (1861-1952) fr.
proprio- and -ceptive, as in inceptive, perceptive,
receptive (qq.v.)

## proproctor
proproctor, п., a deputy proctor at an English
university. — See 1st pro- and proctor,

## props
props, n. pi. (slang). — Abbreviation of'properties,
pi. of property,

## proptosis
proptosis, п., a protrusion, esp. of the eye (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. πρόπτωσις, 'a falling
forward', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-) and πτώσις, *a

## propulsion
propulsion, n. — F., formed with suff. -ion fr. L.

## prdpulsus
prdpulsus, pp. of propellere, 'to drive forward'.
See propel,

## propulsive
propulsive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
prdpulsus, pp. of propellere. See prec. word,

## propyl
propyl, n. — The univalent radical C3H7 (chem.)
— Formed from the abbreviation of propionic
and suff. -yl,

## propylaeum
propylaeum, п., vestibule, entrance of an
important building. — L., fr. Gk. προπύλαιον,
'entrance', prop, subst. use of the neut. of the
adjective προπύλααος, 'before the gates', fr. πρό (see

pro pylon.

## propylene
propylene, п., the radical C3He (chem) — Coined
fr. propyl and suff. -ene.

## propylite
propylite, п., a form of andesite (petrogr.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. πρόπυλον,
'vestibule'. See next word.

## pro pylon
pro pylon, п., a gateway standing before the
principal entrance of a temple (egyptol.) — L., fr.
Gk. πρόπυλον, Vestibule', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-),
and πύλη, 'gate'. See pylon and cp. propylaeum.

## prorate
prorate, tr. and intr. v., to divide proportionally.
— Fr. L. pro rata (parte), 'according to the
reckoned part', fr. pro, 'for' (see I st pro-), and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:622 -->

fem. sing. pp. of riri, 'to believe, think, judge,
reckon'. See rnte, 'amount'.
Derivatives: prorat-able, adj., prorat-ion, n.

## pro re
pro re, п., the prow of a ship (poetic) — Obsol.
F., fr. L. prdra, 'prow'. See prow, n.

## prorogate
prorogate, tr. v., to prorogue. — ME. prorogates

## prorogation
prorogation, n. — ME. prorogation, fr. OF. ( =
F.) prorogation, fr. L. prdrogdtidnem, ace. of

## prorogue
prorogue, tr. v., to defer. — ME. prorogen, fr.
MF.(=F.)pre>re>gw,fr. L. prorogdre, 'to prolong,
protract, extend', fr. 1st pro- and rogdre, 'to

Derivative: prorogu-er, n.

## pros-
pros-, combining form meaning 'toward, nearby*.
— Gk. προσ-, fr. προς, 'toward, to, against; at,

and cogn. with OI. prdti, 'against', OSlav. pro-
tivu, protivg, 'in opposition to, against', L. pre-
tium, 'price*, par, 'equal'. See pair and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also proso-, Cp. also
dysprosium.

## prosaic
prosaic, adj. — ML. prdsaicus, fr. L. prosa. See
prose and adj. suff. -fc.
Derivatives: prosaic, п., prosaic-аПу, adv.,
prosaic-ism, п., prosaic-ness, n.

## prosaism
prosaism, n. — F. prosaisme, fr. prose. See prose
and -ism.

## prosaist
prosaist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.

## prosbul
prosbul, п., a declaration made in court, before
the execution of a loan, to the effect that thelaw
requiring the release of debts upon the entrance
of the Sabbatical year shall not apply to theloan
to be transacted (see Marcus Jastrow's
Dictionary, II, p. 1218). — Mishnaic Heb. perdzbol,
perosb6l, prob. short for Gk. προς βουλή
βουλευτών, 'before the assembly of councillors', fr.
προς, 'toward, to, against, before, in presence
of, dat. of βουλή, 'counsel, deliberation,
assembly', and gen. pi. of βουλευτής, 'councillor',
fr. βουλεύειν, 'to take counsel', fr. βουλή. See
pros- and boule.

## proscenium
proscenium, п., the front part of the stage. — L.,
fr. Gk. ττροσκήνιον, 'stage', fr. πρό (see 2nd
pro-) and σκηνή, 'tent, booth'. See scene.

## proscribe
proscribe, tr. v., 1) in ancient Rome, to publish

2) to outlaw. — L. prdscribere, 'to publish in
writing, confiscate, outlaw, proscribe', fr. 1st
pro- and scribere, 'to write*. See scribe and cp.

Derivative: proscrib-er, n.

## proscription
proscription, n. — ME. proscripcioun, fr. L.
proscription gen. -dnis, fr. prdscriptus, pp. of
prdscribere. See preceding word and -ion.

## prescriptive
prescriptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr- L.
prdscriptus, pp. of prdscribere. See proscribe.
Derivatives: proscriptive-ly, adv., proscriptive-
ness, n.

## prose
prose, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) prose, fr. L·. prosa
ordtid, prosa, 'straight speech, prose', fem. of
prdsus, a collateral form of prdrsus,
'straightforward, straight, direct', contraction of prdver-
sus, pp. of prdvertere, 'to turn forward', fr. 1st
pro- and vertere, pp. versus, 'to turn*. See version
and cp. retrorse, which is the antonym of prose.
Derivatives: prose, intr. and tr. v., pros-er, п.,
pros-y, adj., pros-i-ly, adv., pros-i-ness, n.

## prosect
prosect, tr. v., to dissect for demonstration or
instruction. — Back formation from next word.

## prosector
prosector, п., one who makes dissections for
demonstration or instruction. — Late L.
prosector, 'anatomist*, fr. L. prdsectust pp. of prd-
secdre, 'to cut off', fr. 1st pro- and secure, 'to
cut'. See section, and agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: prosector-ial, adj., prosector-skip,
n.

## prosecute
prosecute, tr. and intr. v. — ME. prosecuten, fr. L.

## prdsecutus
prdsecutus, pp. of prosequi, 'to follow after,
pursue', fr. 1st pro- and sequi, 'to follow'. See
sequel and cp. pursue, which is a doublet of
prosecute.

## prosecution
prosecution, n. — MF., fr. Late L. prdsecutidnem,
ace. of prdsecutid, 'a following after*, fr. L.

## prosecutus
prosecutus, pp. of prosequi. See prec. word and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:622 COLUMN:2 -->

## prosecutor
prosecutor, n. — Late L., fr. L· prosecutus, pp. of
prosequi. See prosecute and agential suff. -or.

## proselyte
proselyte, п., a convert. — ME. proselite, fr. OF.
proselite (F'. proselyte), fr. Late h.proselytus, fr.
Gk. προσήλυτος, 'a convert to Judaism', lit.
One who has arrived', fr. προς (see pros-) and
έλυθ-, 'to come' (whence also έλεύσομοα, *Ι
shall come', ήλυθου, Ί came', έλεόθειν, 'to
bring', prop, 'to come with'), which is of
uncertain etymology.
Derivatives: proselyte, tr. and intr. v., proselyt-
er, п., proselyt-ic-al, adj., proselyt-ism, п.,
proselyt-ist, п., proselyt-ist-ic, adj., proselyt-ize,
v.
prosenchyma» п., tissue of elongated'cells (hot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. προσεγχεΐν, 'to pour in besides',
fr. προς, 'toward, to', έν-, 'in*, and χύμα, 'that
which is poured out', which is rel. to χυμός,
'juice'. See pros-, 2nd en- and chyme, and cp.
enchymatous.
Derivative: prosenckymat-ous, adj.

## Proserpina
Proserpina, п., Persephone. — L., altered, through
the medium of the Etruscans, fr. Gk.
Περσεφόνη (see Persephone); influenced in form also
through a folk-etymological connection with
prdserpere, 'to creep forth' (as if she were the
goddess who caused plants to germinate). See
Varro, De lingua Latina, 5, 68.

## Proserpinaca
Proserpinaca, п., a genus of plants, the mermaid-
weed (bot.) — L. proserpinaca (herba), 'the plant
Polygonum*, prop, 'the plant dedicated to
Proserpina'. See prec. word.

## prosify
prosify, tr. v. — Formed fr. prose and -fy.
Derivative: prosifi-er, n.

## prosit
prosit, interj., may it be profitable (to you). — L.
prosit, 3rd pers. sing. pres. subjunctive of prdd-
esse, 'to do good, be profitable', fr. 1st pro- and
esse, 'to be' (see esse, is). The -d- in prddesse is
prob. due to the influence of forms like red-ed,
Ί go back', red-imd, Ί buy back', etc.

## proso-
proso-, combining form meaning 'forward,
onward'. — Fr. Gk. πρόσω, which is prob. rel.
to προς, 'toward, to; hard by, near'. See pros-,

## prosodemfc
prosodemfc, adj., passing from one person to
another (said of diseases). — Coined fr. proso- and
the abbreviation of epidemic.

## prosodtacal
prosodtacal, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
Late L. prosddiacus, fr. Gk. προσωδιακός, fr.
προσωδία. See next word,

## prosody
prosody, п., the science of versification. — L.
prosddia, fr. Gk. προσωδία, *a song sung with
accompaniment', lit. 'a singing in addition to
(another song)*, fr. προς (see pros-) and ωδή,
'song*. See ode.
Derivatives: prosod-ic, prosod-ic-al, adjs., pros-
od-ic-al-ly, adv., prosod-ist, n.

## prosopopoeia
prosopopoeia, п., personification. — L., fr. Gk.
προσωποποι/ta, 'the putting of speeches into the
mouths of others', fr. πρόσωπον, 'face,
countenance, person*, and ποιεϊν, 'to make'. The first
element lit. means 'that which is toward the
eyes', fr. προς (see pros-) and ώψ, gen. ώπός,
'eye, face'; see -opia. For the second element see
poet,

## prospect
prospect, n. — ME. prospecte, fr. L. prospectus,
'lookout, prospect', fr. prospectus, pp. of pro-
spicere, 'to look forward*, fr. 1st pro- and spe-
cere, spicere, 'to look at'. See species and cp.
aspect and words there referred to.

## prospect
prospect, intr. and tr. v. — h.prdspectare, freq. of
prdspicere; partly derived directly fr. prospect, n.
Derivatives: prospective (q.v.), prospector (q.v.)

## prospective
prospective, adj. — Late L. prdspectivus,
'pertaining to a prospect' (whence also F'. prospectif,
fem. prospective), fr. ^prospectus. See prospect,
п., and -ive.
Derivatives: prospective-ly, adv., prospective-
ness, n.

## prospector
prospector, n. — L., fr. prospectus, pp. of
prdspicere. See prospect, п., and agential suff. -or.

## prospectus
prospectus, n. — L. prospectus. See prospect, n.

## prosper
prosper, intr. and tr. v. — ME. prosperen, fr. MF._
( — F.) prosperer, fr. L. prosperare, 'to render
happy', fr. prosperus or prosper, 'favorable,
fortunate, happy*. See prosperous,

## prosperity
prosperity, n. — ME. prosperite, fr. OF. prospe-

## rite (F. prosperite)
rite (F. prosperite), fr. L, prosperitdtem, ace. of

## prosperitds
prosperitds, 'desirable condition, prosperity', fr.

prosperus or prosper. See next word and -ity.
prosperous, adj. — ME., fr. MF. prospereux, fr.
L. prosperus or prosper, 'agreeable to one's
wishes, favorable, fortunate, happy*, prob.
formed fr. prospere, for OL- pro spere, corresponding
to L. pro spe~, 'according to expectation', fr. pro,
'for' (see 1st pro-), and abl. ofspes, 'hope*, which
is cogn. with OSlav. spejg, speti, 'to be
successful', spechu, 'endeavor, aspiration', Lit. speju,
speti, 'to have time, to be quick enough', OE.
spedan, 4o be successful, make successful', sped,
'success, prosperity', spdwan, 'to prosper', fr.·
l.-E. base *spe(i)-, *spe-, *to draw, stretch,
extend, swell; to be successful', whence also L.
spatium, 'space'. See space, speed and cp.
despair, desperate, Esperanto. For the ending of
prosperous see suff. -ous.
Derivatives: prosperous-ly, adv., prosperous-
ness, n.

## prostat-
prostat-, form of prostato- before a vowel.

## prostate
prostate, п., a gland situated at the base of the
bladder in the male (anat.) — Medical L.
prostata, fr. Gk. προστάτης, 'leader, ruler,
guardian', lit. 'one standing before', fr. προΐστάναι, 'to
stand before', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-), and ίστάναι,,
'to stand' (see state); so called as the organ
standing before the bladder.
Derivatives: prostat-ic, adj., prostat-ism, n.

## prostatectomy
prostatectomy, п., excision of the prostate {med.)
— Compounded of prostat- and -ectomy.

## prostatitis
prostatitis, п., inflammation of the prostate {med.)
— Medical L. See prostate and -His.

## prostato-
prostato-, before a vowel prostat-, combining
form denoting the prostate. — Gk. προστατο-,
προστατ-, fr. προστάτης. See prostate.

## prosthesis
prosthesis, п., 1) addition of a letter or a syllable
to a word; 2) addition of an artificial limb to the
body (surg.) — L., fr. Gk. πρόσθεσις, 'an
addition', fr. προστιθέναι, 'to put to, add to', fr.
προς (see pros-) and τίθέναι, 'to put, place'.

prostylos, 'having columns in front*, fr. Gk.

Protargol, п., an antiseptic silver protein of a

protero-, before a vo^vel proter-, combining form

## protest
protest, tr. and intr. v. — ME. protesten, fr. MF.
(= F.) protester, fr. L. protestari, 'to declare in

public, to bear witness to', fr. 1st pro- and
testdrl, 'to be a witness', fr. testis, 'witness'. See

## Protestant
Protestant, n. and adj., a member of

Identical with the preceding word. The name

τεύς, lit. 'first', fr. πρώτος, 'first'. See proto-.

## prothalamium

Derivative: prot(h)onotari-al, adj.

proto-, before a vowel prot-, combining form

πρώτος, 'first*, prob. contraction of *πρόατος,

Protococcus, п., a genus of green algae (bot.) —

τέμνει,ν, 'to cut offin front', fr. πρό (see 2nd pro-)

protoplasm, n. (biol.) — G. Protoplasma, lit.

πλάσμα, gen. πλάσματος, 'anything molded"1,

gelatinous fluid found in living tissue. Next year
this term was taken over by the German
botanist Hugo von Mohl (1805-72) to denote the
material within tissues generally.
Derivatives: protoplasm-al, protoplasmat-ic,
protoplasm-ic, adjs.

## protoplast

Late L. protoplasms, fr. Gk· πρωτόπλαστος,

proverbial-ly, adv.

provide, tr. and intr. v. — ME. providen, fr. L.

providere, 'to see beforehand, to act with

provid-er, п., provid-ing, conj. (prop. pres.part.

providence, n. — ME., fr. OF..( = F.)providence,

provident, adj. — ME,, fr. L. providens, gen. -entis,

provocative, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (— F.)
provocate/(fern, provocative), fr. Late L. provoedtivus,
'called forth', fr. L. provoedtus, pp. of provocdre.
See next word and -ative.
Derivatives '.provocative, п.,provocative-ly, adv.,
provocative-ness, n.

## provoke
provoke, tr. v. — ME. provofcen, fr. OF. (= F.)
provoquer, fr. L. provocdre, 'to call forth,
challenge, appeal, provoke', fr. 1st pro- and vocdre,
'to call'. See voice and cp. convoke, invoke.
Derivatives: provofc-ee, п., provok-er, п.,

provok-ing, adj., provok-ing-ly, adv., provok-
ing-ness, n.

provost, п., a prefect. — ME. provost, fr. OE.
prafost,profost, fr. OF. provost, fr. Late L.
propositus [whence also OProvenc. probost and
OHG. probost (G. Propst)], which stands for L.

## praepositus
praepositus, *a presiding official' (whence OF.

## prevost
prevost, F.prevdt), prop. pp. of praeponere, 'to
put before*. See praepostor and pp. preposltor,
priest.
Derivatives: provost, intr. v.,provost-ry, п.,
provost-ship, n.

## prow
prow, п., the forepart of a ship. — ME., fr. OF.

## proe (F. proue)
proe (F. proue), fr. OProvenc. proa, fr. Genoese

prua, dissimilated fr. L. prora, fr. Gk. πρφρα
(for *πρώ5αι.ρα), rel. to πρωί, 'early in the

'before'. Cp. OI. purvah, 'former, first'. OSlav.

pruvu, 'first' and see 2nd pro-. Cp. also prore,

Derivative: prow-ed, adj.

## prow
prow, adj., valiant, brave {archaic). — ME., fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:624 COLUMN:3 -->
OF. prou, preu (F. preux), objective case of
proz, pros, 'valiant, brave', fr. Late L. prodis,
'useful, advantageous' (whence also OProvenc.
pros, 'valiant, brave'), fr. Late L. prode (whence
It. prode, pro, 'valiant, brave'), back formation
fr. L. prdd-esse, 'to be useful', fr. pro, 'before'.
See 1st pro- and cp. pride, proud, prude, improve.
Cp. also preux chevalier.

## prowess
prowess, п., bravery. — ME. prowess, proues, fr.
OF. proesce (F. prouesse), 'bravery', fr. OF.
prou, 'gallant, valiant'. See prow, adj., and -ess.
Derivative: prowess-ed, adj.

## prowl
prowl, intr. v., to move about stealthily; tr. v.,
to traverse stealthily. — ME. prollen, 'to go
about searching', of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: prowl, п., prowl-er, п., prowl-ing,
adj., prowl-ing-ly, adv.

## proximal
proximal, adj., proximate. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. proximus, 'nearest, next', superl.
of prope. See propinquity.

## proximate
proximate, adj., nearest or next. — VL. proxi-
mdtus, pp. of proximare, 'to draw near, ap-
adj. pro ach, fr. L. proximus. See prec. word
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: proximate-ly, adv.

## proximity
proximity, п., immediate nearness. — MF. { —
F.) proximite, 'nearness, proximity', fr. h.proxi-
mitdtem, ace of proximitds, of s.m., fr.
proximus. See proximal and -ity.

## proximo
proximo, adv., in the next month. — L. proximo,
abl. sing, of proximus. See proximal.

## proxy
proxy, п., 1) the action of a deputy; 2) a deputy.
— ME. prokesie, contraction of procuracie, fr.
ML. procuratia. See procuracy and cp.
procurator, proctor.
Derivatives: proxy, tr. and intr. v., and adj.

## prude
prude, п., a woman who affects modesty. — F.f

discreet, modest woman', which stands for preu de
femme, fern, equivalent of prud'homme, 'a brave
man'. See prow, adj., and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also prud'homme, preux chevalier.
Derivatives: prude-ly, adv., prudery (q.v.),
prud-ish, adj., prud-ish-ly, adv., prud-ish-ness, n.

## prudence
prudence, n. — ME., fr. OF. (— F.) prudence, fr.
L. prudentia, 'foreseeing, knowledge, prudence,
discretion', fr. prudens, gen. -entis. See prudent
and -ce and cp. providence, which is a doublet
of prudence.

## Prudence
Prudence, fern. PN. — From prec. word.

## prudent
prudent, adj., cautious in conduct; discreet;
sensible. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) prudent, fr. L.
prudentem, ace of prudens, 'foreseeing; skilled,
experienced', contraction of providens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of providere, 'to foresee'. See
provident, which is a doublet of prudent.
Derivatives: prudent-ly, adv.,prudent-ness, n.

## prudential
prudential, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. prudentia. See prudence.
Derivatives: prudentials, n. pi., prudential-ism,
п., prudential-ist, п., prudential-it>, n.

## prudery
prudery, n. — F. pruderie, fr. prude. See prude and
-ery.

## prud'homme
prud'homme, п., 1) formerly, a wise or discreet
man; 2) now, a member of the conseif des prud"-
hommes, i.e. conciliation board. — F., fr. OF.
produme, prodome, preudhome, *a valiant, brave
or discreet man', fr. prou, preu, 'valiant, brave,
discreet', de (fr. L. de), 'from, away from', and
ome, home (F. homme), 'man' (fr. L. hominem,
ace. of homo. See prow, adj., de-, and human.

## pruinose
pruinose, adj., covered with a white powder or
bloom ibot.) — L. pruinosus, 'frosty, rimy', fr.
pruina, 'hoarfrost', for *pruswina, *pruwina, fr.
I.-E. base *preus-, *prus-, which unites the
opposite meanings 'to freeze', and 'to burn*. See
freeze and cp. frost. Cp. also prurient.

## pruinons
pruinons, adj., pruinose. — L. pruinosus. See prec.
word.

## prune
prune, п., plum. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)prune, fr.
ML. ргй/ш, fem. sing. fr. L. pruna, neut. pi. of
L. prCmum, 'plum' (prunus, 'plum tree*), fr. Gk.
προΰμνον,'plum'(προύμνγ;,'plum tree') ;borrow-
ed from a language of Asia Minor. The
disappearance of Gk. m in L. prunum (for *prum-
num) is due to dissimilation. E. plum is a Latin
loan word. Cp. prunella, 'a textile'.

## prune
prune, tr. v., to trim (vines). —Earlierproine, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:625 COLUMN:1 -->
OF. proigner, prooingier, 'to trim (vines)' (= F.
provigner), fr. OF. provain (F. provin), 'layer of
a vine', fr. propaginem, ace. of propago, 'layer
