Derivatives: prim-able, adj., prun-abfe-ness, п.,
prun-abt-y, adv., prun-er, п., prun-ing, n". and
adj.

## prune
prune, tr. v., to trim the feathers, to preen
{archaic). — ME. proinen, preinen, fr. OF. poroin-
dre, fr. pref. por, fr. VL. por, 'foreward, forth*,
which is rel. to L.pro, 'before, for' (see 1st pro-),
and oindre, 'to annoinf, fr. L. ungere. See
unguent and cp. preen, 'to trim*. For the
contraction of por- into pr-*cp. proffer.

## Prunella
Prunella, п., a genus of plants, the self-heal (bot.)
— ModL., fr. earlier BritneUa, fr. G. Braune,
'quinsy, croup*, fr. MHG. briune, 'the state of
being brown', fr. MHG. brun, 'brown' (from
the brownish-red color of the mucous
membranes); see brown. The plants of this genus
were called Prunella, because they were
supposed to heal quinsy or croup. Cp. former E.
prunella, 'quinsy'.

## prunella
prunella, prunello, п., a stout textile, formerly
used for clergymen's and barristers' gowns. —
F. prunelle, prop, 'sloe colored', fr. prunelle,
'sloe', dimin. of prune, 'plum'. See prune, 'plum*.

## prunelle
prunelle, п., a kind of yellow plum. — F., dimin.
of prune. See prune, 'plum'.

## Prunus
Prunus, п., a genus of trees of the almond family
(bot.) — L·. prunus, 'plum tree'. See prune,'plum'.

## prurience
prurience, pruriency, n. — Formed from next
word with sufT. -ce, resp. -cy.

## prurient
prurient, adj., itching; lascivious, lewd. — L.
prurtens, gen. -ends, pres. part, of prurlre, 'to
itch, burn', which is rel. to pruina, 'hoarfrost'.
See pruinose and cp. prurigo. For the ending see
suff. -ent.
Derivative: prurient-ly, adv.

## pruriginous
pruriginous, adj., suffering from prurigo. — Late
L. pruriginosus, 'having the itch, scabby', fr. L.
prurigo, gen. -iginis. See next word and -ous.

## prurigo
prurigo, п., a chronic inflammatory skin disease
characterized by itching papules {med.) — L.,
'itching, the itch', fr. prurlre. See prurient.

## pruritus
pruritus, п., itching of the skin without visible
eruption. — L., 'itching, the itch', fr. prurit-
{um), pp. stem of prtlrire. See prurient.

## Prussia
Prussia, n. — ModL. Prussia, prob. formed fr.
Slav. Po-Rusi, '(the land) near the Rusi ( =
Russians)'. For the pref. see post- and cp. Pome-
rania.
Derivatives:Prussi-an, adj. andn.,Prussi-an-ism,
п., Prussi-an-ize, tr. v., Prussi-an-iz-ation, п.,
Prussi-an-iz-er, n.
Prussian blue. — Transl. of F. bleu de Prusse; so
called because it was discovered in Berlin, the
capital of Prussia (by Diesbach in 1704).

## prussiate
prussiate, п., a salt of prussic acid (chem.) —
Formed with chem. suff. -ate fr. ModL.
Prussia. See Prussia.
prussic acid. — Adaptation of F. acide prussique,
fr. acide, 'acid', and prussique, 'Prussian', fr.
{bleu de) Prusse, 'Prussian blue'. See Prussian
blue and adj. suff. -ic.

## pry
pry, intr. v., to search, spy. — ME. prien, pryen,
of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pry-ing, adj., pry-ing-ly, adv., pry-
ing-ness, n.

## pry
pry, п., a lever. — Back formation fr. prize, 'a
lever", mistaken for a plural (as if the spelling
were pry-s).
Derivative: pry, tr. v., to raise, break open,
lever.

## prytaneum
prytaneum, п., a public building in an ancient
Greek city, containing the sacred hearth of the
city (Greek antiq.) — L., fr. Gk. πρυτανεΐον,
'the magistrate's hall', fr. πρύτανις, 'magistrate,
prince, ruler'. See next word.

## prytany
prytany, п., presidency of the senate in Athens
(Greek antiq.) — Gk. πρυτανεία, 'presidency',
fr. πρύτανης, 'prince, lord, president, a member
of one of the ten sections into which the Council
of Elders (= the Senate) in Athens was divided',
prob. a loan word from a language of Asia
Minor. Cp. Lycian e-priti, 'satrap', Etruscan
purine, e-prft-ne, 'chief, president', and L. Frutis,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:625 COLUMN:2 -->
Etruscan name of Venus (= Aphrodite), whose
worship was brought into Italy by the
Etruscans. For the ending of prytany see sufT. -y
(representing Gk. -είά!.

## psalm
psalm, n. — ME. psalm, salm, fr. OE. psealm,
sealm, fr. Eccles. L. psalmus, fr. Gk. ψαλμός, 'a
plucking, twitching, of the harp' (in Eccles. Gk.
'song, psalm'), fr. ψάλλει,ν, 'to pluck, twitch the
harp, to play on a stringed instrument', whence
also ψάλμα, 'tune played on a stringed
instrument', ψάλτης, 'harper', ψαλτήριον, 'stringed
instrument, psaltery, harp', ψαλμωδία,
'singing to the harp'; rel. to ψηλαφαν, 'to feel
or grope about' (compounded of *ψαλα, 'a
twitching', and άφαν, 'to touch') and cogn. with
L. palpare, 'to touch softly, stroke*, palpitare,
'to move quickly', palpebra, 'eyelid'. See feel
and cp. psalmody, psalter, psaltery, and the first
element in Pselaphidae. Cp. also palpable.
Derivatives: psalm-ic, adj., psalm-y, adj.

## psalmist
psalmist, п., a composer of psalms. — Eccles. L.
psalmista, fr. Eccles. Gk. ψαλμι,στής, of s.m.,
fr. Eccles. Gk. ψαλμός. See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: psalmist-ry, n.

## psalmodize
psalmodize, intr. v., to practice psalmody. —
Eccles. L. psalmodizdre, fr. psalmodia. See next
word and -ize.

## psalmody
psalmody, п., ]) the singing of psalms; 2) psalms
collectively. — ME. psalmodie, fr. Eccles. L.
psalmodia, fr. Late Gk. ψαλμωδία, 'singing to
the harp', fr. ψαλμός, 'psalm', and ώδή, 'song'.
See psalm, ode and -y (representing Gk. -ία}.
Derivatives: psalmodi-al, psalmod-ic, psalmod-
ic-al, adjs., psalmod-ist, п., psalmodize (q.v.)

## Psalter
Psalter, п., the Book of Psalms. — ME. psalter,
Salter, fr. OE. psaltere, saltere, fr. Eccles. L.
psalterium, 'the songs of David, the Psalms', fr.
L., 'stringed instrument, psaltery', fr. Gk.
ψαλτήριον, 'stringed instrument, psaltery, harp',
fr. ψάλλειν, 'to pluck, twtich the harp.' See
psalm and cp. psaltery. Cp. also santir.
Derivatives: psalter-ian, adj., psalter-ist, n.

## psalterium
psalterium, п., the third stomach of ruminants
(zool.) — Eccles. L.psalterium (see prec. word);
so called because of its resemblance to the folds
of a book.

## psaltery
psaltery, п., an ancient stringed instrument. —
OF. psalterie, fr. L. psalterium. See Psalter and
-y (representing L. -ium).

## psammite
psammite, п., sandstone (petrogr.) — F., fr. Gk.
ψάμμος, 'sand', which is rel. to ψάμαθος,
άμαθος, 'sand', and cogn. with L. sabulumt 'sand'.
See sabulum and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: psammit-ic, adj.

## psammo-
psammo-, combining form meaning sand. — Gk.
ψαμμο-, fr. ψάμμος, 'sand'. See prec. word.

## psammoma
psammoma, п., a tumor of the cerebral meninges.
(med.) — Medical L., coined by the German
pathologist Rudolf Virchow (1821-1902) fr. Gk.
ψάμμος, 'sand' (see prec. word) and suff. -oma;
so called because it contains calcareous,
sandlike matter.

## Psaronius
Psaronius, п., a genus of fossil ferns (palaeontol.)
— ModL. Psaronius, short for Psaronius lapis,
lit. 'starling stone' (loan translation of G.
Staarstein), fr. Gk. ψάρ, gen. ψαρός, 'starling',
which is cogn. with Goth, sparwa, OE. spearwa,
'sparrow*. See sparrow,

## Pselaphidae
Pselaphidae, n. pi., a family of beetles (zool.) —
ModL. Pselaphidae, fr. Pselaphus, the type
genus, fr. Gk. ψηλαφαν, 'to grope about',
compounded of *ψαλα, 'to twitch', and άφαν, 'to
touch'. For the first element see psalm, for the
second see apsis, for the ending see suff. -idae.

## psellism
psellism, п., stammering. — ModL·. psellismus, fr.
ΰ^.ψελλισμός, fr. ψελλίζει,ν, 'to stammer', fr.
ψελλός, 'faltering in speech', which is prob. of
imitative origin. For the ending see suff. -ism.

## psephism
psephism, п., a decree of the popular assembly in
Athens. — L. psephisma, fr. Gk. ψηφίζειν, fr.
ψήφισμα, 'to cast one's vote with a pebble, to
count, reckon', fr. ψήφος (Dor. ψαφος), 'small
stone, pebble (used in counting or voting)*,
which is rel. to ψάμμος (for *ψάφμος), 'sand'.
See psammite and the suff. -ize and -ma and cp.
next word.

## psephite
psephite, п., fragmental rock consisting of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:625 COLUMN:3 -->
pebbles. — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk.
ψήφος. See prec. word.
Derivative: psephit-ic, adj.

## pseud-
pseud-, form of pseudo- before a vowel.

## psendaxis
psendaxis, п., a sympodium. — ModL., lit. 'a
false axis', fr. pseud- and axis.

## pseudepigrapha
pseudepigrapha, n. pi., writings falsely ascribed
to the Bible. — Gk. ψευδεπίγραφα, neut. pi. of
ψευδεπίγραφος, 'with false superscription'. See
pseudo- and epigraphy.

## pseudepigraphal
pseudepigraphal, psendepigraphic, pseudepi
graphical, pseudepigraphous, adj., of the nature of
pseudepigrapha; spurious. — Gk.
ψευδεπίγραφος, 'with false superscription'. See prec. word
and -al, resp. -ic, -ical, -ous.

## pseudepigraphy
pseudepigraphy, п., the ascription of false
authorship to books. — See pseudepigrapha and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## pseudo-
pseudo-, before a vowel pseud-, combining form
meaning 'false, feigned, erroneous'. — Gk.
ψευδό-,ψευδ-, fr. ψευδός, 'He, falsehood*, fr. ψεύ-
δει,ν, 'to cheat by lies' (whence also ψευδής, 'lying,
false*), which is prob. re] to ψυδρός, 'lying,
false', ψύ&ος, 'a lie', and possibly cogn. with
Arm. sut, 'false, lying'.

## pseudobulbar
pseudobulbar, adj., in pseudobulbar paralysis, a
condition simulating true bulbar paralysis
(med.) — A hybrid coined fr. pseudo-, L. bulbus,
'bulb' (see bulb), and adj. suff. -ar.

## pseudocarp
pseudocarp, п., a false fruit. — Compounded of
pseudo- and Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.
Derivative: pseudocarp-ous, adj.

## pseudoclassic
pseudoclassic, adj., pretending to be classic. —
Compounded of pseudo- and classic.
Derivatives: pseudoclassic, п., pseudoclassic-alt
adj., pseudoclassic-ism, n.

## pseudograph
pseudograph, п., a writing falsely ascribed to
somebody. — Late L. pseudographus, 'having a
false superscription*, fr. Late Gk. ψευδογράφος,
'writer of falsehoods', fr. Gk. ψευδό- (see pseudo-)
and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
-graph.

## pseudomorph
pseudomorph, п., an irregular form. — Lit. 'a
false form', compounded of pseudo- and Gk.
μορφή, 'form, shape'. See morpho-.
Derivatives: pseudomorph-ic,
adj.,pseudomorphism, п., pseudomorph-ous, adj.

## pseudonym
pseudonym, also spelled pseudonyme, п., a
fictitious name. — Fr. pseudonyme, fr. Gk. ψευδώνυ-
μον, neut. of ψευδώνυμος, 'under a false name',
which is compounded of ψευδό- (see pseudo-)
and ονυμα, dialectal form of δνομα, 'name'.
See name and cp. onomato-.
Derivatives: pseudonym-al, pseudonym-ic, adjs.,
pseudonym-it у, п., pseudonym-ous, adj., pseu-
donym-ous-ly, adv., pseuchnym-ous-ness, n.

## pseudopod
pseudopod, n. — The same as pseudopodium.

## pseudopodium
pseudopodium, п., temporary extension of the
protplasm of a cell serving for locomotion. —
ModL., compounded of pseudo- and ModL.
-podium., fr. Gk. -πόδιον, fr. πόδιον, dimin. of
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See podinm.
Derivatives: pseudopod-aly pseudopod-ial, adjs.

## pseudoscope
pseudoscope, п., an optical instrument which
makes convex objects appear concave and vice
versa. — Compounded of pseudo- and Gk.
-σκόπιον, fr. σκοπέtv, 'to look at, examine*. See
-scope.

## pshaw
pshaw, interj. — Imitative.

## Psidium
Psidium, п., a genus of trees of the myrtle family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ψίδιον, a collateral
form of σίδιον, 'pomegranate-peeP, fr. σίδη,
'pomegranate', which is prob. a loan word from
a language of Asia Minor.

## psil-
psil-, form of psilo- before a vowel.

## psilanthropy
psilanthropy, п., the teaching that Jesus was a
mere man. — Formed fr. Gk. ψΐλάνθρωπος,
'merely human', fr. ψΙλός, 'naked, bare, mere',
and άνθρωπος, 'man'. See next word, anthropo-
and -y (representing Gk. -ία).
Derivatives: psilanthrop-ic, ad'}.,psilanthrop-ism,
п., psilanthrop-ist, n.

## psilo-
psilo-, before a vowel psil-, combining form
meaning 'mere, bare'. — Gk. ψιλό-, ψϊλ-, fr.
ψιλός, 'naked, bare, mere*, rel. to ψάω, ψην, 'to
rub, smoothe; to rub away, crumble away',
ψίω, ψΐειν, 'to feed', and cogn. with 01. ba-
bhasti andpsati, 'chews, consumes, devours'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:626 COLUMN:1 -->
sand and cp. psilosis, epsilon, upsilon. Cp. also
psora,

## psilomelane
psilomelane, п., a black hydrous manganese oxide
(mineral.) — Compounded of psilo- and Gk.
μελαν-, stem of μέλας, gen. μέλανος, 'black'.
See melanism,

## psilosis
psilosis,. п., loss of hair owing to disease (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. ψΐλωσις, 'a stripping bare
of hair', fr. ψϊλοϋν, 'to strip bare of hair4, fr.
ψιλός. See psilo- and -osis.

## psilotic
psilotic, adj.» pertaining to psilosis. — Gk. ψϊλω-
τικός, 'making hairless', fr. ψϊλωτός, verbal
adj. of ψϊλοϋν. See prec. word and -ic.

## Psittacidae
Psittacidae, n. pi., a family of parrots (ornithol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. psitta-
cus, 'parrot', fr. ΰ^ψιττακός, which is a foreign
word.

## psittacine
psittacine, adj., pertaining to the parrot family.
— L. psittacinus, fr. psirtacus. See prec. word
and -ine (representing L.-inus).

## psittacosis
psittacosis, п., an infectious disease of parrots
(med.) — Medical L., formed fr. Gk. ψιττακός,
'parrot' (see Fsittacidae), with suif. -osis.

## psoas
psoas, п., either of two muscles of the loin (anat.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. ψόα (also ψοία, ψύα),
'a hip muscle'. Gk. ψόας, the gen. of the
feminine noun ψόα, was mistaken by the French
anatomist Jean Riolan (1577-1657) for thenom.
of a (nonextant) masculine noun. It was he who
introduced this erroneous form into anatomy.

## psoitis
psoitis, п., inflammation of the psoas muscle(s)
(med.) — Medical L., formed from prec. word
with suff. -itis.

## psora
psora, п., itch, scabies (med.) — L., fr. Gk. ψώρα,
'itch, mange, scab*, from the stem of ψάω, ψήν,
Чо rub*, whence also ψιλός, 'naked, bare, mere'.
See psilo-.

## Psoralea
Psoralea, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ψωραλέος, 'scabby',
fr. ψώρα (see psora); so called in allusion to the
glands or dots.

## psoriasis
psoriasis, п., a non-contagious inflammatory skin
disease (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. Gk.
ψώρα (see psora) with suff. -iasis.

## psoriatic
psoriatic, adj., pertaining to, or affected by,
psoriasis. — See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## psoric
psoric, adj., pertaining to psora (med.) — L. pso~
ricus, fr. Gk. ψωρικός, fr. ψώρα. See psora and
-ic.

## psych-
psych-, form of psycho- before a vowel.

## psychasthenia
psychasthenia, п., a neurotic state characterized
by lack of energy and by phobias (med.) —
Medical L., lit. 'weakness of the soul', fr. Gk.
ψυχή, 'soul'and ασθένεια, 'weakness, debility'.
See psyche and asthenia.

## psyche
psyche, п., 1) the human soul; 2) the mind. — L.
psyche, fr. Gk. ψυχή, 'breath, life, spirit, soul,
mind', which derives fr. ψΰχειν, 'to breathe,
blow; to make cold', whence also ψϋχος, 'cold';
from the stem of* ψύειν, 'to breathe, blow', which
is cogn. with OI. bhas-, of s.m. Cp. psychrometer,
psykter, metempsychosis, panpsychism. For the
sense development of Gk. ψυχή, ср. L. spfritus,
'breath, breath of life, soul, mind, spirit', which
derives fr. spirare, 'to breathe', and Heb. пё-
phesh,'soul, life,person', lit.'that which breathes',
which comes from the stem n-ph-sh, 'to breathe'.

## Psyche
Psyche, п., in Greek mythology, a maiden
beloved by Eros; personification of the soul. —
Gk. ψυχή, fr. ψυχή, 'soul'. See prec. word.

## psychedelic
psychedelic, also psychedelic, adj., 1) pertaining
to a mental state of pleasurable calm; 2)
pertaining to any drug producing such calm. —
Compounded of psyche, resp. psycho-, Gk.
δήλος, 'visible, clear' (see adelo-), and adj.
suff. -ic.

## psychiater
psychiater, п., an expert in mental disease. —
Compounded of Gk. ψυχή, 'soul', and Εατήρ,
'healer', which is rel. to Εατρός, 'healer,
physician'. See psyche and -i a trie.

## psychiatry
psychiatry, n,, the treatment and cure of mental
disease. — Medical L. psychiatria, lit. *a healing
of the soul', fr. Gk. ψυχή, 'soul', and ίατρεία, 'a
healing.' See psyche and -iatry.
Derivatives: psychiatr-ic, psychiatr-ic-al, adjs.,
psychiatr-ic-al-lyt aav.,psychiatr-ist,n.,psychiatr-
ize, tr. v.

## psychic
psychic, adj. — Gk. ψυχικός, Of life, of the soul,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:626 COLUMN:2 -->
spiritual', fr. ψυχή. See psyche and adj. suff.
-ic.
Derivatives: psychic, n-,psychic-af, adj.,psychic-
al-ly, adv., psych-ics, n.

## psychism
psychism, п., psychical research. — Formed fr.
ψυχή, 'soul' (see psyche), with suff. -ism.

## psychist
psychist, п., one who engages in the study of
psychical phenomena. — See prec. word and -ist.

## psycho-
psycho-, before a vowel psych-, combining form
meaning 'mind, spirit, consciousness'. — Gk.
ψΰχο-, ψϋχ-, fr. ψυχή. See psyche.

## psychoanalysis
psychoanalysis, п., a system of psychotherapy
introduced by Freud and Jung. — ModL.,
compounded of psych- and analysis.

## psychoanalyst
psychoanalyst, n. — See prec. word and -ist.

## psychoanalytic
psychoanalytic, psychoanalytical, adj. — See prec.
word and -ic, resp. also -al.

## psychoanalyze
psychoanalyze, tr. v. — See psychoanalysis and
-ize.

## psychodeile
psychodeile, adj. — See psychedelic.

## psychogenesis
psychogenesis, п., the origin of the mind and its
development. — ModL., compounded of
psycho- and genesis.

## psychogenetic
psychogenetic, also psychogenetical, adj.,
pertaining to psychogenesis. —- See prec. word and
-ic, resp. also -al.
Derivatives: psychogenetical-iy, adv., psycho-
genet-ics, n.

## psychogenic
psychogenic, adj., having mental origin. —
Compounded of psycho- and -genie.

## psychology
psychology, n. — ModL. psychologia, prob.
coined by Melanchthon (and first used by him as
title of a prelection), fr. Gk. ψυχή, 'soul' (see
psyche), and-λογία, fr.-λόγος, One who speaks
(in a certain manner); one who deals (with a
certain topic)' (see -logy). In its modern sense
the word psychology is treaceable to C. Wolff's
Psychologia empirica (1732).
Derivatives: psycholog-ic-al, adj., psycholog-ic-
al-ly, adv., psycholog-ism, п., psycholog-ist, п.,
psycholog-ize, intr. v.

## psychometer
psychometer, п., 1) one who practices divination
through psychometry; 2) a measuring
instrument used in psychometry. — Back formation
fr. psychometry.

## psychometrics
psychometrics, п., measurement of the duration
in time of mental phenomena. — Compounded
of psycho-, Gk. μετρικός, 'metrical' (see
metrical), and pi. suff. -s.

## psychometry
psychometry, п., 1) divination of the qualities of
an object, or'of persons that have been in
contact with it, through physical contact with, or
proximity to, that object; 2) psychometrics. —
Compounded of psycho- and Gk. -μετρία,
'measuring of. See -metry.
Derivatives: psychometr-ic, psychometr-ic-al,
adjs., psychometr-ic-al-ly, adv., psychometr-ist,
n.

## psychomotor
psychomotor, adj., pertaining to physical
movements induced by mental processes. —
Compounded of psycho- and motor,

## psychopath
psychopath, п., one suffering from mental disease.
— Compounded of psycho- and Gk. -παθής,
'suffering'. See -path.
Derivatives: psychopath-ic, adj., psychopaih-isi,
п., psycho-pathology, п., psychopatholog-ist, п.,
psyckopath-y, n.

## psychophysics
psychophysics, п., that branch of science which
deals with the relations between physiological
and psychological phenomena. — G. Psycho-
physik, coined by Gustav Theodor Fechner
(1801-87) in his Elemente der Psychophysik
(i860). See psycho- and physics.
Derivatives:psychophysic-al, adj.,psychophysic-
ist, n.

## psycho physio logy
psycho physio logy, n. — Compounded of psycho-
and physiology,

## psychosis
psychosis, п., 1) mental disease; 2) any mental
process. — ModL., fr. Gk. ψΰχωσις, 'a giving
of life, animation*, fr. ψΰχοϋν, 'to give life to', fr.
ψυχή, 'life, soul'. See psyche and -osis.

## psychosomatic
psychosomatic, adj., pertaining to the relation
between mind and body. — Compounded of
psycho- and somatic.
Derivative: psychosomat-ics, n.

## psychotherapeutics
psychotherapeutics, psychotherapy, п., the
treatment of disease by hypnotism, suggestion, or
other psychological methods. — Compounded

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:626 COLUMN:3 -->
of psycho- and therapeutics, resp. therapy.

## psychotic
psychotic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized by,
psychosis. — Formed fr. psychosis. For the
ending see suff. -otic.
Derivative: psychotic, п., a psychotic person.

## psychrometer
psychrometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the moisture in the atmosphere. — Compounded
of Gk. ψυχρός, *cold', and μέτρον, 'measure'.
The first element derives fr. ψϋχος, 'cold (п.);
cold weather'; see psyche. For the second
element see meter, 'poetical rhythm',

## psykter
psykter, п., a vessel for cooling wine (Greek an-
tiq.) — Gk- ψϋκτήρ, fr. ψΰχειν, Чо breathe,
blow; to make cold'. See prec. word.

## Psylla
Psylla, п., a genus of plant lice (zoo/.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. ψύλλα, 'flea'. See Pulex.

## psyllid
psyllid, п., any insect of the family Psyllidae. —
See next word.

## Psyllidae
Psyllidae, п., a family of plant lice (bot.) —
ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-idae.

## Psyllium
Psyllium, п., the fleawort (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. ψύλλα, 'flea'. See Psylla and 1st -ium.

## Ptah
Ptah, п., the chief god of ancient Memphis. —
Egypt. Ptah.

## pturmic
pturmic, adj., sternutative. -— Gk. πταρμικός,
'causing to sneeze', fr. πταρμός, 'the act of
sneezing', from the stem of πταίρειν, πτάρειν,
also πτάρνυσθαι, 'to sneeze', which is cogn.
with L. sternuere, of s.m. See sternutation and
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: ptarmic, n., a sternutatory, ptarmic-
al, adj.

## Ptarmica
Ptarmica, п., another name for Achillea (bot.) —
ModL., prop, 'sneezewort', fr. Gk. πταρμικός.
See prec. word.

## pturmigan
pturmigan, п., a bird of the grouse family. —
Gael, tarmachan.

## Ptelea
Ptelea, п., the hop tree (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
τττελέα, 'the elm', of uncertain origin; possibly
cogn. with L. tilia, 'the linden tree' (see Tilia).

## pteno-
pteno-, combining form meaning 'flying, winged',
as in Ptenoglossa. — Gk. πτηνό-, fr. πτηνός,
'flying', rel. to πτήναι, aorist inf. of πέτεσθαι,
'to fly'; fr. l.-E. base *pt(a)-, zero degree of base
*pet-, 'to fly, to fall upon', whence also πτερόν,
'wing'. See ptero- and cp. ptilo-.

## Ptenoglossa
Ptenoglossa, п., a division of gastropods (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of pteno- and Gk.
γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## pter-
pter-, form of ptero- before a vowel.

## pteridine
pteridine, п., a yellow crystalline base, CSHJN4 —
G. Pteridint coined fr. pter-, -ide and chem.
suff. -ine; so called because it occurs in the
pigments of the wings of butterflies.

## pteridology
pteridology, п., the study of ferns (bot.) —
Compounded of Gk. πτερίς, gen. πτερίδος, 'fern',
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See Pteris and -logy.
Derivatives: pteridolog-ic-al, adj.,pteridolog-ist,
n.

## Pteridophyta
Pteridophyta, n. pi., a division of fiowerless
plants including the ferns, mosses and
horsetails (bot.) — ModL-, compounded of Gk.
πτερίς, gen. πτερίδος, 'male fern', and φυτόν,
'plant'. See Pteris and phyto-.

## pterldophyte
pterldophyte, п., one of the Pteridophyta. — See
prec. word.
Derivatives: pteridophyt-ic, pteridophyt-ous,
adjs.

## pterin
pterin, п., a compound containing the pteridine
ring system. -— G. Pterin, coined fr. pter- and
suff. -in; so called because it occurs in the
pigments of the wings of butterflies.

## Pteris
Pteris, п., a genus of ferns (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. πτερίς, 'male fern', which is rel. to πτερόν,
'wing'. See ptero-,

## ptero-
ptero-, before a vowel pter-, combining form
meaning 'feather, wing', as in pterodactyl. —■
Gk. πτερό-, πτερ-, fr. πτερόν, 'feather, wing',
fr. *pt-, zero degree of l.-E. base *pet-, 'to fly, to
fall upon', whence Gk. πέτεσ&αι, 'to fly'. See
feather and cp. Pteris, pterygium. Cp. also

## pteno-
pteno-, ptilo-, ptomaine, symptom. Cp. also the
second element in malabathrum.

## pterodactyl
pterodactyl, п., name of an extinct flying reptile.
— Compounded of ptero- and Gk. δάκτυλος,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:627 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PTEROGRAPHY | 6QQ -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:627 COLUMN:1 -->
'finger'. See dactyl,

## pterography
pterography, п., description of (birds') feathers.
— Compounded of ptero- and Gk. -γραφίά, fr.
γράφει,ν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: pterograph-ic, pterograph-ic-al,
adjs.

## pteropod
pteropod, п., one of a group of mollusks with
wing lobes on the feet {zool.) — Gk. πτερόπους,
gen. πτερόποδος, 'wingfooted*, compounded of
πτερόν, 'wing', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'.
See ptero- and -pod.
Derivative: pteropod-ous, adj.

## Pteropus
Pteropus, п., a genus of fruit bats. — ModL., fr.
Gk. πτερόπους, 'wingfooted'. See prec. word.

## pterosaur
pterosaur, п., name of an extinct flying reptile;
the pterodactyl. — Compounded of ptero- and
Gk. σαΰρος, 'lizard'. See saurian.

## Pterospora
Pterospora, п., a genus of plants, the pine drops
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of ptero- and Gk.
σπορά, 'a sowing, seed'. See spore.

## -pterous
-pterous, combining form meaning'having (a
specified number or form of) wings', as in dipterous.
— Compounded of ptero- and -ous.

## pteryg-
pteryg-, form of pterygo- before a vowel,

## pterygium
pterygium, п., a triangular mass of conjunctiva
growing on the inner side of the eyeball (med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. πτερόγιον, *a little wing,
flap, fold', dimin. of πτέρυξ, gen. πτέρυγος,
which is rel. to πτερόν, 'wing'. See ptero-,

## pterygo-
pterygo-, before a vowel pteryg-, combining
form meaning'wing'. — Gk-πτερυγο-, πτερυγ-,
fr. πτέρυξ, gen. πτέρυγος, 'wing', rel. to πτερόν,
'wing'. See ptero- and cp. prec. word.

## pterygoid
pterygoid, adj., winglike. — Formed fr. pterygo-
and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'.
See -oid.

## ptil-
ptil-, form of ptilo- before a vowel.

## Ptilimnium
Ptilimnium, п., a genus of plants, the mock
bishop's weed (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
πτίλον, 'soft feather, down', and λίμνη, 'marsh'.
See ptilo- and limno-.

## ptilo-
ptilo-, before a vowel ptil-, combining form
meaning 'down, feather'. — Gk. πτΛο-, πτιλ-, fr.
πτίλον, 'soft feather, down', fr. *pt-, zero degree
of I.-E. base *pet-, 'to fly, to fall upon', whence
also πτερόν, 'feather, wing', See feather and cp.
pteno-, ptero-.

## ptisan
ptisan, п., barley water. — ME. tisane, fr. OF.
(F. tisane, ptisane), fr. L. tisana, fr. Gk.
πτισάνη, 'peeled barley, barley gruel', fr. πτίσ-
aet.v, 'to crush, grind', which is cogn. with L.
pinsere, 'to beat, pound', pistillum, 'pestle'. See
pestle and cp. tisane. The disappearance of Gk.
π in L. tisana (for *ptisana) is due to the
phonetic law according to which the first of two
explosive sounds at the beginning of a word must
needs disappear. Cp. L. tunica, which stands for
*ctunica (see tunic).

## Ptolemaic
Ptolemaic, adj.,pertainingtoPtolemy,the
astronomer and geographer, or to the Ptolemies, the
kings of Egypt. — Fr. Gk. Πτολεμάΐκός, fr.
Πτολεμαίος. See Ptolemy and adj. suff. -ic

## Ptolemaist
Ptolemaist, п., a believer in the system of
Ptolemy, the astronomer. — Formed with suff. -1st
fr. Gk. Πτολεμαίος. See Ptolemy.

## Ptolemy
Ptolemy, п., masc. PN. — F. Ptolemee, fr. L.
Ptolemaeus, fr. Gk. Πτολεμαίος, lit. 'warlike*,
fr. πτόλεμος, collateral form of πόλεμος, 'war'.
See polemic.

## ptomaine
ptomaine, п., alkaloid substance formed by the
putrefaction of animal or vegetable porteins
(biockem.) — It. ptomaina, coined by the Italian
chemist Selmi fr. Gk. πτώμα, 'corpse', fr. *pt-,
zero degree of I.-E. base *pet-, 'to fiy, to fall
upon*. See symptom and cp. the next two words.
For the sense development of Gk. πτώμα ср.
Heb. nebheldh, 'carcass, corpse', fr. ndbhel, 'it
decayed, withered', which is rel. to naphdl, 'he
fell', and L. cadaver, 'corpse', fr. cadere, 'to fair
(see cadaver).
Derivative: ptomain-ic, adj.

## ptosis
ptosis, п., a falling down of an organ, esp. the
drooping of the upper eyelid (med.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. πτώσης, 'a falling', fr. *pt-, zero
degree of I.-E. base *pet-, *to fly, to fall upon',
whence also πτώμα, 'corpse'. See symptom and
cp. prec. and next word.

## ptotic
ptotic, adj., pertaining to ptosis. — Formed with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:627 COLUMN:2 -->
suff. -ic fr. Gk. πτωτός, 'fallen', verbal adj. of
πΐπτειν, 'to fall*, which stands for *πί-πτειν,
fr. *pf-, zero degree of I.-E. base *pet-, *to fly,
to fall upon'. See symptom and cp. the prec. two
words.

## ptyal-
ptyal-, form of ptyalo- before a vowel.

## ptyaim
ptyaim, п., the amylase found in the saliva (bio-
ckem.) — Formed with suff. -in fr. Gk. πτύαλον,
'spittle', fr. πτύω, πτυειν, 'to spit', which prob.
stands for *σπιΰ!.ω or *πιΰιω, and is cogn.
with L. spud, spuere, 'to spit', Goth, speiwan,
OE. spfwan, 'to spit, vomit'. See spew and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the second
element in hemoptysis,

## ptyalism
ptyalism, п., salivation. — Gk. πτυαλισμός,
'salivation', fr. πτυαλιζειν, 'to spit milch', fr.
πτύαλον, 'spittle'. See prec. word and -ism.

## ptyalo-
ptyalo-, before a1 vowel ptyal-, combining form
meaning 'spittle'. — Gk. πτυαλο-, πτυαλ-, ft.
πτύαλον. See ptyalin.

## pub
pub, n. — Shortened fr. public house.

## puberal
puberal, adj., relating to puberty. — Late L. рй-
berdlis, 'pertaining to puberty', fr. L. puber,
'adult'. See puberty and adj. suff. -al.

## pubertal
pubertal, adj., puberal. — See prec. word. The -t-
isprob. due to the influence of the noun, puberty.

## puberty
puberty, п., the condition of being capable of
procreation. — ME. puberte, fr. L. pubertast
gen. pubertdtis, 'the age of maturity, puberty'—
possibly through the medium of MF. (= F.)
puberte—fr. puber or pubis, gen. puberis,
'grown up, adult*, which is rel. to pubes, gen.
pubis, 'hair that appears on the body at the age
of puberty; the private parts', and topuer, 'boy'.
See pnerile and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also public,

## puberulent
puberulent, adj., covered with fine down (bot.) —
Formed with suff. -ulent fr. L. puber, 'grown up;
covered with soft down, downy'. See puberty,

## pubes
pubes, п., pubic hair (anat.) — L. pubes. See
puberty and cp. pubis,

## pubescence
pubescence, n. — F., fr. Late L·. pubescentia, fr. L.
pubescens, gen. -entis. See pubescent and -ce.

## pnbescency
pnbescency, n. — Late L. pubescentia. See prec.
word and -cy.

## pubescent
pubescent, adj. — F., ft. L. pubescentem, ace. of
pubescens, pres. part, of pubescere, 'to reach the
age of puberty', fr. pubes, gen. pubis. See pubis
and -escent and cp. pubes.

## pubic
pubic, adj., pertaining to the region of the pubes
or the pubis (anat.) — See pubes and -ic.

## pubis
pubis, п., the pubic bone (anat.) — Medical L.,
short for L- ospubis, ^pubic bone', fr. pubes, gen.

## pubis
pubis, 'the hair which appears on the body at
the age of puberty: the private parts'. See
puberty, and cp. pubes.

## public
public, adj. — ME. pubfique, fr. MF (= F.)

## public (fern
public (fern, publique), fr. L. pubficus, which is
prob. a blend of OL. poplicus, 'belonging to the
people' (contraction of *populicus, fr. populus,
'people'), and L. *pubicus, 'belonging to
adults', fr. pubes, 'the hair that appears on the
body at the age of puberty; adults, people'. See
people and puberty.
Derivatives: public, п., public-ly, adv.,
subtleness, n.

## public
public, n. — Abbreviation of public house. Cp.
pub.

## publican
publican, п., 1) in ancient Rome, a collector of
public revenues; 2) (British) an innkeeper. — F.

## publicain
publicain, fr. L. publicdnus, 'a farmer of the
Roman revenues', prop, subst. use of the adj.
publicdnus, 'pertaining to the public revenue', fr.

## publicus. See public
publicus. See public, adj., and -an.
Derivative: publican-ism, n.

## pnblication
pnblication, n. — ME. publicacioun, fr. L. publi-
cationem, ace. of publicutid, fr.publicdtus, pp. of

## publicare
publicare, 'to make known, publish', fr.publicus.
See public, adj. and -ation and cp. publish,

## publicist
publicist, п., a journalist who writes about public
affairs. — F. publiciste, a hybrid coined fr. public
(see public, adj.) and -iste (see -ist), a suff. of
Greek origin; introduced into English by Burke,

## publicity
publicity, n. — F. publicite, fr. ML. publicitdtem,
ace. of publicitds, fr. L. publicus. See public, adj.,
and -ity.

## publicize
publicize, tr. v. — See public, adj., and -ize.

## publish
publish, tr. v. — ME. publishen, fr. OF. (= F.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:627 COLUMN:3 -->
publier (fr. L. publicare), 'to publish', on analogy
of other English verbs in -ish, in which this suff.
corresponds Ίο OF. -is-, -iss-, and ult. to the
Latin inchoative suff. -isc-. See pnblication.
Derivatives: publish-able, adj., publish-er, п.,
publish-ment, n.

## pubo-
pubo-, combining form used in the sense of 'pubic
and'. — Incorrectly formed fr. L. pubes, 'hair
that appears on the body at the age of puberty'.
See pubes, puberty,

## pnecoon
pnecoon, п., any of the plants of the borage
family.— Virginianpuccoon. See poke, 'pokeweed'.

## puce
puce, п., a brownish color. — F., 'flea; fiea color*,
fr. Ь.рйНсет, асе. of pulex, 'flea'. SeePulex and
cp. puceron.

## pucelle
pucelle, п., virgin, maid (obsol., except in the
phrase La Pucelle, loan of Arc). — F., fr. OF.
pucele, frj.VL. *pullicella, 'maid' (whence also
It. pulcella, О Proven?, piussela), dimin. of L.
pulla, fern, of pullus, 'young animal'.

## pneeron
pneeron, п., a plant louse. — F'., a derivative of
puce, 'flea'. See puce,

## puchero
puchero, п., olla podrida. — Sp., 'pottage', fr. L.
pultdrius, 'vessel', prop, and esp. 'a vessel for'
pottage', fr. puis, gen. pultis, 4a thick pottage'.
See pulse, 'seeds', and cp. words there referred
to.

## puck
puck, п., a mischievous spirit, hobgoblin. — ME.
ройке, puke, fr. OE. риса, 'goblin', rel. to ON.
puki, 'imp', ult. prob. fr. Gk. Φωκάς, 'patron of
ships and navigation'. Cp. pug, 'a breed of dog'.
Derivatives: puck-ish, adj., puck-ish-ly, adv.,
puck-ish-ness, n.

## puck
puck, п., the flat disk used in playing hockey. —
Fr. Ir. рос, 'bag'. See pock,

## pucka
pucka, pukka, adj., good, genuine. — Hind, pak-
ka, 'ccoked, ripe', fr. OI. pakvdk, fr. pdcati,
'cooks', which is cogn. with L. coquere, 'to
cook'. See cook, n.

## pucker
pucker, intr. and tr. v., to contract into wrinkles.
— A frequentative formed fr. poke, 'bag'. For
the ending see freq. suff. -er.
Derivatives '.pucker, a wrinkle, bulge, pucker-er,
п., pucker-y, adj.

## pud
pud, n.( foot (a baby word). — Cp. MDu. pote,
poot, Du. poot, 'paw', and see paw and words
there referred to.

## puddening
puddening, п., a thick fender made of rope yarn.
— Formed with suff. -ing fr.pudden, a dial, form
of pudding; so called because of its softness.

## pudding
pudding, n. — ME. poding, pudding, prob. fr. F.
boudin, 'black pudding', which is prob. of
imitative origin. For the change of F. b top in English
cp. purse. The alteration of F. -in to E. -ing is
due to change of suff.; ср. Е. cony, fr. ME.
coning, fr. OF. conin.

## puddle
puddle, п., a small muddy pool. — ME. podel,
dimin. formed fr. OE. pudd, 'ditch', rel. to G.
pudeln, 'to splash in water', whence Pudel,
'poodle'. Cp. poodle.
Derivative: puddl-y, adj.

## puddle
puddle, intr. v., to dabble in a puddle; tr. v., to
make muddy. — ME. podelen, fr. podel. See
puddle, n.
Derivatives: puddl-ed, adj., puddl-er, п.,
puddling, n.

## pudency
pudency, п., modesty, bashfulness. — Late L. pu-
dentia, ft. L. pudens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of

## pudere
pudere, *to be ashamed*, which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. pudendum, pudic, impudent. Cp. also
repudiate. For the ending see suff. -ency.

## pudendum
pudendum, n. (usually in the pi. pudenda), the
external organs of generation. —L., 'that which
one should· be ashamed of, neut. of the
gerundive of pudere, 'to be ashamed'.'See prec. word.
For other gerundives or their derivatives used in
English cp. agenda and words there referred
to.
Derivative: pudend-al, adj.

## pudge
pudge, п., a short and thick person. — A var. of
podge.
Derivatives: pudg-y, adj., pudg-i-ness, n.

## pudic
pudic, adj., pudendal. — F.pudique, fr. L.pudicus,
'shamefaced, bashful', fr. pudere, 'to be a-
shamed'. See pudency.

## pudicity
pudicity, п., modesty. — MF. (= F.)pudicite, fr.
VL. *pudicitdtem, ace. of *pudicitds
(corresponding to L. pudfeitia), 'shamefacedness,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:628 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 601 | PULSE | ness, n. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:628 COLUMN:1 -->
modesty', fr. pudicus. See pudic and -ity.
риеЫо, п., an Indian village. — Sp., 'people;
village', fr. L. populus, 'people'. See people and cp.
popular, public.

## puericulture
puericulture, п., the art or science of training or
educating children. — Compounded of L.puer,
'boy', and cultura, 'cultivation". See next word
and culture.

## puerile
puerile, adj., I) childish; 2) immature. — F.
pueril, fr. L. puerilis, 'boyish', fr. puer, 'boy,
child', which is rel. to putus, 'boy', Oscan pu-
klum (ace.) 'boy', and cogn. with OI. putrah,
'son, boy', pStah, 'young animal', Avestic
puftra-, 'son, child', fr. I.-E. base *p5-, *p*u-,
*pou-, 'small, little, young'. See few and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-lie.
Derivatives: puerile-ly, adv., puerile-ness, n.

## puerility
puerility, п., 1) childishness; 2) immaturity. — F.
puerilite, fr. L. puerilitatem, ace. of puerilitas,
'childishness', fr. puerilis. See prec. word and
-ity.

## puerperal
puerperal, adj., pertaining to, or connected with,
childbirth. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
puerpera, 'a woman in labor', which stands for
*puero-para, fr. puer, 'boy, child', and parere, 'to
beget, bear'. See puerile and parent.
Derivative; puerperal-ism, n.

## puerperium
puerperium, п., confinement during and after
childbirth. — L., 'childbirth', fr. puerpera. See
prec. word.

## puff
puff, tr. and intr. v. — ME. puffen, 'to blow', fr.
OE. pyffan, 'to blow with the mouth', of
imitative origin. Cp. ME. buffen, 'to strike', It. buffo,
'blast of wind', buffetare, 'to pant, puff', and see
buff, 'a blow', buffoon. Cp. also puffin.
Derivatives: puff, п., puff-ed, adj., puff-er, п.,
puff-ery, п., puff-ily, adv., puff-ing, adj. and п.,
puff-ing-ly, adv., puff-i-ness, п., puff-y, adj.

## pnffin
pnffin, п., a sea bird. — Formed fr. puff; so called
in allusion to its blown-up appearance.

## pug
pug, п., a breed of dog; a pug nose. — The earliest
meaning was 'sprite'; prob. a var. of puck,
'mischievous spirit'.
Derivatives: pugg-ed, adj., pugg-ish, adj.

## pug
pug, tr. v., to mix clay. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pug, п., pugged clay, pugg-er, п.,
pugg-ing, n.

## pug
pug, п., the footprint of a wild beast (India). —
Hind, pag, fr. OI. padakah, 'foot', fr. pat, ace.
padam, 'foot'. See foot.
Derivative: pug, tr. v., to trace by pugs.

## pug
pug, n. (slang) — Abbreviation of pugilist.

## puggree
puggree, п., a veil worn over the hat to protect the
head from the sun. — Hind, pagri, 'turban'.

## pugh
pugh, interj. expressing contempt. — Imitative.

## pugilism
pugilism, п., boxing. — Formed with suff. -iam fr.
L. pugil, 'boxer', which is rel. to pugnus, 'fist'.
See pugnacious.

## pugilist
pugilist, п., a boxer. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: pugilist-ic, pugilist-ic-al, adjs.,
pugiiist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## pugnacious
pugnacious, adj., given to fighting. — Formed
with suff. -ious fr. L. pugnSx, gen. pugnacis,
'fond of fighting, combative', fr. pugndre, 'to
fight' (whence pugna, 'fight'), fr. pugnus, 'fist',
which is cogn. with Gk. πύξ, 'with clenched fist',
πυγμή, 'fist, boxing', πύκτης, 'boxer'. All these
words derive from I.-E. base "peug-, 'to stab'.
From a nasalized form of the same base comes
L. pungere, 'to pierce, prick'. See pungent and
cp. expugn, impugn, oppugn, repugnant,
inexpugnable. Cp. also pugilism, pugilist, puneca,
pygmy.
Derivatives: pugnacious-ly, adv., pugnaclous-
ness, n.

## pugnacity
pugnacity, n. — L. pUgnaciias, 'fondness for
fighting, combativeness', fr. pugnax, gen.
pugnacis. See prec. word and -ity.

## puisne
puisne, adj., junior; of lower rank (law) — OF.
puisne (F. puine), 'younger', lit. 'born
afterward'. See puny.

## puissance
puissance, п., power, might. — ME.puissaunce, fr.
MF. (— F.) puissance, fr. puissant. See next word
and -ce.

## puissant
puissant, adj., powerful, mighty. — ME. puis-
saunt, fr. MF. (= F.)puissant, fr. VL. 'possen-
tem, ace. of 'possens, pres. part, of L. posse, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:628 COLUMN:2 -->
be able'. Cp. h.potens; 'able, mighty, powerful',
prop. pres. part, of posse, and see potent. For the
ending see sufT. -ant.
Derivatives: puissant-ly, adv., puissant-ness, n.

## puja
puja, п., honorable reception. — OI. puja, 'honor,
esteem, worship', prob. of Dravidian origin.

## puka
puka, п., a New Zealand tree.

## pukatea
pukatea, п., a New Zealand forest tree. — Maori.

## pukateine
pukateine, also pukatein, п., an alkaloid found in
the bark of the pukatea (chem.) — Formed fr.
pukatea with chem. suff. -ine, resp. -in.

## puke
puke, intr. v., to vomit. — Prob. for "spuke, and
rel. to G. spucken, 'to spit', which is a freq. of
speien. See spew.
Derivative: puke, n.

## pukka
pukka, n. — See pucka.

## pulchritude
pulchritude, п., beauty. — ME. pulcritude, fr. L.
pulchritudo, fr. pulcher, 'beautiful', which is of
uncertain origin. It stands perh. for 'polkros,
earlier 'pelkros, dissimilated form fr. *perkros,
fr. I.-E. base *perk-, 'motley, variegated'. See
perch, 'name of a fish', and -tude.

## pulchritudinous
pulchritudinous, adj., beautiful. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. pulchritudo, gen. pulchritudinis.
See prec. word.

## pule
pule, intr. v., to whine. — Of imitative origin.

## pulegone
pulegone, п., the principal constituent of
pennyroyal oil. — ModL. pulegium in Mentha pule-
gium, 'pennyroyal', fr. L. puleium, pulegium,
'pennyroyal', which is of uncertain origin. For
the ending see suff. -one.

## Fulex
Fulex, п., the genus of fleas (zool.) — L. pulex,
gen. pulicis, 'fiea', cogn. with OI. plusih, Gk.
ψύλλα, OSlav. blucha, Lith. blusa. Arm. lu (for
*pluso·), 'flea'. Hung, boiha, 'fiea', is a Slavonic
loan word. Cp. Fsylla, pnee.

## pulicat
pulicat, pulicate, п., a bandanna (India). —
Named after Pulicat, a town on the Madras
coast.

## pulicene
pulicene, adj., pertaining to, or full of, fleas. —
Formed with suff. -ene fr. L. pulex, gen. pulicis,
'flea'. See Pulex.

## pulicid
pulicid, п., a flea of the family Pulicidae. — See
next word.

## Pulicidae
Pulicidae, n. pi., a family of fieas (zool.)— ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. L. pulex, gen. pulicis,
'fiea'. See Pulex.

## pull
pull, tr. and intr. v. — ME. pullen, fr. OE. pullian,
'to pluck, twitch', of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pull, п., pull-ed, adj., pull-er, n.

## pulldoo
pulldoo, п., the coot. — Fr. F. poule d'eau, lit.
'water hen'. See pullet and Eau de Cologne.

## pullet
pullet, n. — ME. pulett, fr. MF. (= F.) poulet,
dimin. of poule, 'fowl', fr. VL. pulla, 'hen', fem.
of pullus, 'young animal; chicken'. See foal and
-et and cp. polecat, poltroon, pony, pooi (in
gambling), poult, poulter, poultry, pucelle,
pullulate.

## pulley
pulley, n. — ME. polie, Тт. OF. polie (F. poulie),
fr. Late Gk. "πολίδιον, dimin. of Gk. πόλος,
'pivot'. Cp. It. puleggia, Sp. polea, 'pulley', and
see pole, 'extremity'.
Derivative: pulley, tr. v.

## Pullman car
Pullman car, also Puliman, п., a sleeping car on a
passenger train. — So called after its designer,
George M. Pullman (1831-97), an American
inventor.

## pullulate
pullulate, intr. v., 1) to germinate; to bud; 2) to
teem. — L. pullulatus, pp. of pullulare, 'to put
forth, sprout', fr. pullulus, dimin. of pullus,
'young animal'. See pullet and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: pullulat-ion, п., pullulat-ive, adj.,
pullulat-ive-ly, adv.

## pulmo-
pulmo-, pulmoni-, pulmon-, combining forms
meaning 'lung'. — Fr. L. pulmo, gen. -onis,
'lung'. See pulmonary.

## pulmometer
pulmometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
breathing capacity of the lungs. — A hybrid
coined fr. pulmo- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## pulmometry
pulmometry, п., determination of the breathing
capacity of the lungs. — A hybrid coined fr.
pulmo- and Gk. -μετρία, 'a measuring of. See
-metry.

## pulmonary
pulmonary, adj., pertaining to the lungs. — L.
pulmonarius, fr. pulmo, gen. -onis, 'lung', which
is cogn. with Gk. πλεύμων 'lung' (for the
collateral form πνεύμων see pneumo-), OSlav.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:628 COLUMN:3 -->
plusta, pljusta (pi.), GPruss. plauti (pi.), Lith.
plauciai (pi.), Lett, plaiisi (pi.), 'lungs', prob. also
with OI. kloman- (if dissimilated fr. 'pieman-),
'the right lung'. All these words derive from
I.-E. base "pleu-, 'to swim, float', for which see
flow and pluvial. Pulmonis, etc., orig. meant 'the
floating (parts)'. They were so called because,
when after the slaughtering of an animal, its
lungs are thrown into a vessel with water, they
(unlike the heart and the liver) remain floating
on the surface. See E. L. Liden, Armenische Stu-
dien, Goteborg, 1906, p. 115. For sense
development ср. Е. lung and lights.

## Pulmonale
Pulmonale, n. pi., an order of gastropod mollusks
(zool.) — ModL., lit. 'having lungs'. See next
word.

## pulmonale
pulmonale, adj., 1) having lungs; 2) pertaining to
the Pulmonata; п., one of the Pulmonata. —
ModL. pulmonatus, 'having lungs', fr. L. pulmo,
gen. -onis. See pulmonary and adj. suff. -ate.

## pulmonic
pulmonic, adj., pertaining to the lungs. — F. pul-
monique, fr. L. pulmo, gen. -onis. See pulmonary
and -ic.
Derivative: pulmonic, n.

## Pulmomfera
Pulmomfera, n. pi., 1) the same as Pulmonata; 2)
a group of snails (zool.) — ModL., lit. 'bearing
lungs', fr. L. pulmo, gen. -onis (see pulmo-), and
the stem oifero,ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See -fer.

## pulmonic's
pulmonic's, п., inflammation of the lungs (med.)
— A Medical L. hybrid formed fr. L. pulmo, gen.
-onis (see pulmo-), with -iris, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## pnlmotor
pnlmotor, п., trade name for an apparatus serving
for artificial respiration. — Shortened for pul-
mo-motor (see haplology).

## pulp
pulp, n. — F. pulpe, fr. L. pulpa, 'fleshy part of a
fruit, pulp, pith', which stands for "pelpa, and is
rel. to pulmentum (for *pelp-men-tom), 'any
food prepared from pulp', and to Umbr. pelm-
ner (gen.), 'of pulp'.
Derivatives: pulp, tr. and intr. v., pulp-al, adj.,
pulp-er, п., pulpi-fy, tr. v., pulpi-fi-er, п., pulp-
less, adj., pulp-y, adj., pulp-i-ness, n.

## pulpit
pulpit, n. — ME., fr. Late L. pulpitum, 'scaffold,
platform' (whence also MHG. pulpit, G. Pull,
'desk'), which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: pulpit, tr. and intr. v., pulpit-al,
adj., pulpit-arian, adj., and п., pulpit-eer, п.,
pulpit-er, n.

## pulpitis
pulpitis, п., inflammation of the pulp of a tooth
(med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L.
pulpa (see pulp) and -iris, a suff. of Greek origin.
The correct form is endodontics (q.v.)

## palpous
palpous, adj., pulpy. — L. pulposus, fr. pulpa. See
pulp and -ons.
Derivative: pulpous-ness, n.

## pulque
pulque, п., a Mexican drink made from the
fermented juice of the agave. — Sp., from a
Mexican Indian language.

## pulsate
pulsate, intr. and tr. v., to beat, throb; to vibrate.
— L. pulsatus, pp. of pulsare, 'to push, beat,
strike', freq. of pello, pellere (pp. pulsus), 'to
beat, strike'. See pulse and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: pulsat-ile, adj., pulsation (q.v.),

## pulsator (q.v.)
pulsator (q.v.), pulsat-ory, adj.

## pulsation
pulsation, n. — F. pulsation, fr. L. pulsationem,

## ace. of pulsatio
ace. of pulsatio, 'a beating or striking', ft.

## pulsatus
pulsatus, pp. of pulsare. See prec. word and -ion.

## pulsator
pulsator, п., beater; pulsating part of a machine.
— L., formed fr. pulsatus, pp. of pulsare. See
pulsate and -ator.

## pulse
pulse, п., throb; rhythmical beating of the heart
and the arteries. — ME. pous, fr. OF. pous (F.

## pouls)
pouls), fr. L. pulsus, 'beating', pulsus venarum,
'beating of the blood in the veins, pulse', fr.

## pulsus
pulsus, pp. of pellere, 'to beat, strike, knock,

## push
push, drive', which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base
'pel-, 'to shake, swing', whence also Gk. πάλ-

## Xetv
Xetv, 'to wield, brandish, swing; to quiver',
πελεμίζειν, 'to shake, cause to tremble',
πόλεμος, 'war'. See polemic and cp. words there

## referred to. Cp. also appeal
referred to. Cp. also appeal, compel, compulsion,

## dispel
dispel, expel, expulsion, impel, impulse,

## interpellate
interpellate, peal, propel, propulsion, pulsate, pursy,
'stout', push, repeal, repel, repulse, repulsion. Cp.
also Apollo.
Derivatives: pulse, п.,pulse-less, adj., pulse-less-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:629 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: PULSE | 602 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:629 COLUMN:1 -->

## pulse
pulse, intr. v., to throb. — L. pulsare, fr. pulsus.
See prec. word.

## pulse
pulse, п., seeds of leguminous plants, — ME. puis,
fr. OF. pols, pous, fr. L. puis, gen. pultis,
'pottage, porridge', fr. Gk. πόλτος, 'porridge'. See
pollen and cp. poultice, puchero.

## pul si meter
pul si meter, п., an instrument for measuring the
force or rate of pulse. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
pulsus, 'beating; pulse*, and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See pulse, 'throb', and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## pulsometer
pulsometer, п., a pump for raising water by steam
without using pistons. — A hybrid coined from
the same elements as pulsimeter (q.v.)

## pultaceous
pultaceous, adj., pulpy. — Formed with suff.
-aceous fr. L. puis, gen. puitis, 'pottage'. See
pulse, 'seeds'.

## pulton
pulton, pultun, п., a native infantry regiment in
India. — Hind, paltan, fr. E. battalion; prob.
influenced in form by E. platoon.

## pulverize
pulverize, tr. v., to reduce to dust; intr. v., to be
reduced to dust. — MF. (= F.) pulveriser, fr.
Late L. pulverizare, fr. L. pubis, gen. -eris, 'dust'.
See pollen and cp. powder.
Derivatives: pulveriz-able, adj., pulveriz-ation,
п., pulveriz-er, n.

## pulverulence
pulverulence, п., the state of being covered with
dust, — Formed from next word with suff. -ce.

## pulverulent
pulverulent, adj., covered with dust. — L. pulveru-
lentus, 'full of dust', fr. pulvis, gen. -eris. See
pulverize and -lent.
Derivative: pulverulent-ly, adv.

## pulvillus
pulvillus, п., the pad between the claws on an
insect's foot (zool.) — L., 'a little cushion',
contraction of puhinulus, dimin. of pulvinus. See
pulvinus.

## pulvinar
pulvinar, adj., resembling a pulvinus. — L. pulvi-
naris, 'pertaining to a cushion', fr. pulvinus. See
pulvinus and adj. suff. -ar.

## pulvinate
pulvinate, pulvinated, adj., cushion-shaped. — L.
pulvinatus, fr. pulvinus, 'cushion'. See next word
and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also -cd.
Derivatives: pulvinate-ly, adv., pulvinat-ion, n.

## pnivinus
pnivinus, п., the cushionlike base of a petiole (bo!.)
— L. pulvinus, 'cushion, pillow, elevation', of
uncertain origin. Cp. pulvinar, pulvinate,
pulvillus. Cp. also pillow.

## pulwar
pulwar, п., a kind of light river boat used in
Bengal (India). — Hind, palwar.

## puma
puma, п., the cougar. — Sp., fr. Quechua.

## pumice
pumice, п., porous volcanic rock used as an
abrasive. — ME. pomis, fr. OF. pomis (also ponce,
whence F. ponce), fr. Late L. pomicem, ace. of
рбтех, prop, a dialectal (prob. Oscaa) form of
L-рйтех, 'pumice stone', which is rel. to spuma,
'foam'; see foam and cp. pounce, 'a fine powder*,
spume. It.pomice, Sp.pomez, Port.pomes,
'pumice stone', also derive fr. Late L. pomicem. E.
pumice has been assimilated in form to Latin
pumicem.
Derivatives: pumice, tr. v., pumic-ed, adj.,
pumic-ег, n.

## pumiceous
pumiceous, adj., of the nature of, or resembling,
pumice. — L. pumiceus, 'of pumice stone', fr.
рйтех, gen. pumicis. See prec- word and -ous.

## pummel
pummel, n. and v. — A var. of pommel.

## pump
pump, п., a device for raising water. — ME.
pompe, pumpe, fr. MDu. pompe, fr. Sp.-Port.
bomba, 'pump', which is of imitative origin. Cp.
pompier.
Derivatives: pump, tr. and intr. v., pump-er, n.

## pump
pump, п., a kind of low shoe. — Prob. meaning
orig. 'a shoe used for pomp*, fr. LG. pump,
'pomp', fr. L. pompa; see pomp. For sense
development cp. G. Pumphose, 'knickerbocker', orig.
'trousers worn on festive occasions'.

## pumpernickel
pumpernickel, п., Westphalian dark rye bread. —
G., orig. an abusive word compounded of pum-
pern, 'to break wind' and Nickel, 'bumpkin',
prop, a shortened form of the PN. Nicolas. See
Nicholas and cp. nickel.

## pumpkin
pumpkin, n. — Fr. earlier pompion, pumpion, fr.
MF. pompon, fr. L. peponem, ace. of pepo,
'melon, piyupkin', fr. Gk. πέπων, 'melon*, prop,
'cooked by the sun, ripe\ from the stem of
πέπτειν, 'to cook' (see peptic and cook); so
called because it is not eaten until it is quite ripe.

## pun
pun, п., a play upon words. — Prob. shortened

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:629 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. It. puntiglio, 'a fine point', dimin. of L. рйпе-
tum, 'point'; see point, п., and cp. punctilio. For
sense development cp. F. pointe, 'conceit, witty
phrase, quip', and pointe d'une'eplgramme, E.
point of an epigram.
Derivatives: pun, intr. and tr. v., punn-er, п.,
pun-ter, n.

## puna
puna, п., a desert region. — Sp., fr. Quechua.

## punch
punch, п., a tool. — Shortened fr. puncheon.
Derivatives: punch, v. (q.v.), punch~yt adj.,
punch-i-ness, n.

## punch
punch, tr. v., to perforate. — Either derived fr.
punch, 'a tool', or a collateral form of pounce,
'to emboss'.
Derivatives: punch-able, adj., punch-ed, adj.,
punch-er, п., punch-ing, n.

## punch
punch, п., a short, thick-set person; anything
short and thick. — Prob. fr. the PN. Punch (q.v.)

## punch
punch, п., a beverage. — Hind, panch, fr. Ol.
panca, 'five*, which is cogn. with Gk. πέντε, L.
quinque, Goth, fimf, OE. fif (see five and cp.
Fanchatantra, panchayat); so called because
orig. the punch was composed of five
ingredients.

## punch
punch, tr. v., to strike, to thrust. — Prob. a
collateral form of pounce, 'to swoop down, to
attack', and influenced in form by the verb punish.
Derivative: punch, п., a thrust.

## Punch
Punch, п., the hero of the puppet show Punch and
Judy. — Abbreviation of Punchinello.

## puncheon
puncheon, п., a stamp or die. — ME. ponchon,
ponson, punson, 'pointed tool', fr. OF.poinchon,
ροίηςοη, ροηςοη (F. ροϊηςοη), 'awl, bodkin', fr.
L. punctidnem, ace. oTpunctio, 'apricking,
piercing', used in the concrete sense of 'a piercing or
perforating instrument*. L. punctio is formed fr.
punctus, pp. of pungere, 'to prick, pierce'. See
point, v., and cp- punch, 'a tool'. Cp. also pounce,
'claw of a hawk', pounce, 'to emboss'.

## puncheon
puncheon, п., a large cask. — ME. poncion, fr.
OF. poinchon, ροΐηςοη, ροηςοη, 'wine vessel'. It
is probable that the original meaning of the
OF. word was 'a perforated vessel', and that,
accordingly, puncheon, 'cask', and puncheon,
'die, stamp', are of the same origin.

## Punchinello
Punchinello, п., 1) the prototype of Punch; 2) a
buffoon. — Corruption of Polichinello, fr.
Neapolitan Polecenella, corresponding to literary It.
Pulcinella, dimin. ofpulcina, 'chicken', fr. h.pul-
licena, pullicina, fern, of pullicenus, pullicinus, 'a
young bird, chicken', fr. pullus, 'a young animal,
young bird'. See pullet and cp. Punch, punch, 'a
short person', Polichinelle.

## punctate
punctate, adj., dotted. — MedL.punctatus, pp. of
puncture, 'to mark by points', freq. ofh.pungere,
pp. punctus, 'to pierce'. See pungent and cp.
punctum. For the ending see adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: punctat-ed, adj.

## punctatlon
punctatlon, п., the action of making punctate. —
Formed with suff. -ion fr. MedL. punctatus, pp.
of puncture. See prec. word.

## punctilio
punctilio, п., ]) a nice point in behavior; 2) exact
observance of formalities. — Fr. It. puntiglio or
Sp. puntillo, diminutives formed fr. L. punctum,
'point'. See point, п., and cp. pun. The spelling
punctilio shows the influence of L. punctum.

## punctilious
punctilious, adj., attentive to punctilios. —
Formed fr. prec. word on analogy of It. puntiglioso,
Sp. puntilloso, F. pointilleux. For the ending see
-ous.
Derivatives: punctilious-ly, adv.,
punctiliousness, n.

## punctual
punctual, adj., 1) of, or pertaining to, a point; 2)
on time; prompt. — ML. punciudlis, fr. h.punc-
tum, 'point*. See punctum and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: punctual-ist, п., punctual-ity, п.,
punctuaj,-ly, adv., punctual-ness, n.

## punctuate
punctuate, tr. v., to mark with points; to insert
punctuation marks in; intr. v., to use
punctuation marks. — ML. punctuatus, pp. ofpunctuare,
'to mark by points', fr. L. punctus, pp. οι
pungere, 'to pierce'. See pungent and verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: punctuation (q.v.), punctuat-ive,
adj., punctuator, n.

## punctuation
punctuation, n. — ML. punctuatio, gen. -onis, fr.
punctuatus, pp. of punctuare. See prec. word and
-ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:629 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: punctuation-al, adj.

## punctule
punctule, п., a small point. — Late L. punctulum,
dimin. of L. punctum, 'point*. See punctum and
-ule.

## punctum
punctum, п., a point (anat., zool., bot.) — L.
punctum, prop. neut. pp. of pungere, 'to pierce*,
used as a noun. See pungent and cp. point, n.

## puncture
puncture, п., the act of pricking, perforation. —
L. punctura, 'a pricking', fr. punctus, pp. of
pungere. See pungent and -ure and cp. aenpnncture.
Derivatives: puncture, tr. and intr. v., punctur-
ation, п., punctur-ed, adj., punctur-er, n.

## pundit
pundit, п., a learned man. — Hind, pandit, fr. OI.
panditah, 'learned, wise; learned man', which is
of uncertain origin. Cp. pandit, Pandy.
Derivatives: pundit-ic, adj., pundit-ic-al-ly, adv.,
pundit-ry, n.

## puneca
puneca, п., name of a fish (Dormitator maculatus).
— Amer. Sp. puneca, fr. Sp. puho, 'fist', fr. L.
pugnus, 'fist*. See pugnacious.

## pungency
pungency, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## pungent
pungent, adj., sharp, piercing. — L. pungens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of pungere, 'to pierce, sting,
bite', from a nasalized form of I.-E. base *peug-,
'to stick, stab', whence L. pugnus, 'fist'. See
pugnacious and cp. poignnnt, which is a doublet
of pungent. Cp. also appoint, disappoint,
compunction, counterpane, embonpoint, expugn, ex-
punction, expunge, impugn, inexpugnable, inter-
punction, oppugn, point, n. and v., poniard, pun,
puncheon, 'a die or stamp', puncheon, 'a large
cask', punctate, punctation, punctilio, punction,
punctual, punctum, puncture, puneca, punt, 'to
gamble', punty, spontoon.
Derivative: pungent-ly, adv.

## Punic
Punic, adj., pertaining to Carthage or the
Carthaginians. — L. Punicus, also Poenicus, formed
fr. Poenus, 'a Carthaginian', fr. Gk. Φοϊνιξ,
'Phoenician', on the analogy of Gallicus, 'Gallic'
(fr. Gallus, 'a Gaul'). See Phoenicia and adj. suff.
-ic and cp. next word.
Derivative: Punic, п., the Punic language.

## puniceous
puniceous, adj., purple red. — L. puniceus, fr.
Punicus, 'Punic'. See prec. word and -eous. For
sense development see Phoenician.

## punish
punish, tr. and intr. v. — ME. punisshen, fr. MF.
(= F.) puniss-, pres. part, stem of punir, 'to
punish', fr. OF. punir, fr. L. punire, 'to punish',
fr. archaic poenire, fr. poena, 'penalty,
punishment'. See penal and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ish. For the
change of L. oe to и ср. Punicus, fr. Poenus (see
Punic), mfmire, 'to build a wall', fr. earlier moe-
nire, fr. moenia, 'wall'.
Derivatives: punish-able, adj., punish-abil-ity,
п., punish-er, п., punishment (q.v.)

## punishment
punishment, n. — ME. punisshement, fr. MF. pu-
nissement, fr. punir, fr. OF. See prec. word and
-menr.

## punition
punition, п., punishment. — ME. punicion, fr.
MF. (= F.) punition, fr. L. рйпШдпет, асе. of
punitio, 'punishment*, ft. ρ unit us, pp. of punire.
See punish and -ition.

## punitive
punitive, adj., inflicting punishment. — F. punitif
(fern, punitive), fr. ML, punltivus, fr. L. punitus,
pp. of punire. See punish and -ive.
Derivatives: punitive-ly, adv., punitive-ness, n.

## punitory
punitory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L.
punitus, pp. of punire. See punish.

## punk
punk, п., decayed wood, touchwood. — Prob. fr.
Algonquian/шпА:, ponk, 'live ashes'.

## punk
punk, п., 1) a prostitute (obsol.); 2) a young
gangster (slang). — Of uncertain origin.

## punka
punka, punkah, п., a large curtain serving to fan a
room. — Hind, pankhd, 'a fan', fr. pankh,
'feather, wing', fr. OI. paksah, paksas, 'wing,
side, half, which is possibly cogn. with Lett.
paksis, 'corner of a house', Russ. pach, 'flank'.

## punner
punner, п., a rammer. — Formed fr. й\а\рип, 'to
pound, beat', with agential suff. -er.

## punnet
punnet, п., a small round chip basket. — Of
unknown origin.

## punt
punt, п., a long, narrow, fiat-bottomed river boat.
— ME. *punt, fr. OF. punt, fr. L.ponto,pontonis,
'a kind, of Gallic barge, punt', fr. pons, gen.
pontis, 'bridge'. See pons and cp. pontoon.
Derivatives: punt, tr. v., to propel with a pole;

punter, п., punt-ist, n.

## punt
punt, п., a point in some games of chance. — F.
ponte, fr. Sp. punto, 'point; point on dice or
cards', fr. L. punctum, 'point'. See point, л.

## punt
punt, intr. v., to bet against the banker. — F.
ponter, fr. ponte. See prec. word.
Derivative: punt-er, n.

## punt
punt, tr. v., to kick (the ball dropped from the
hands) before it touches the ground; intr. v., to
punt a ball. — Of unknown origin.
Derivatives: punt, п., the act of punting a ball,
punt-er, n.

## punty
punty, п., an iron rod used for manipulating
glass. — F. pontil, a dimin. formed fr. L.
punctum, 'point'. See point, n.

## puny
puny, adj., 1) (obsol.) puisne; 2) weakly. — F.
puine, fr. MF. puisne, 'born afterward', fr. OF.
puisne, fr. puis, 'after', and ne, 'born'. OF. (= F.)
puis derives fr. L. posted, 'afterward', which is
compounded of post, 'after' (see post-) and ea,
'there' (prop. abl. of ea, 'she', fem. of is, 'he';
see idem). OF. ne (F. ne) derives fr. L. ndtus,
pp. of ndscor, ndsci, 'to be born'; see natal. Cp.
puisne, which is a doublet of puny.

## pup
pup, п., puppy. — Abbreviation of puppy.
Derivative: pup, intr. v., to bring forth young
(said of a bitch).

## pupa
pupa, п., the form of insects between the stages of
larva and imago (entomol.) — L. pupa, 'girl;
doll, puppet', fem. ofpupus, 'boy, child', rel. to
puer, 'boy, child'. See puerile and cp. pupil,
puppet, puppy.
Derivatives: pup-al, adj., pup-ate, intr. v.,
pupation, n.

## pupil
pupil, п., a child or young person in school, a
scholar; 2) {law) a minor under the care of a
guardian. — ME. pupille, fr. MF. (= F.) pupille,
masc, fr. L. pupillus, 'orphan, ward', lit. 'little
boy', dimin. of pupus. See pupa and cp. next
word.
Derivatives: pupil(iyaget п., pupil(l)-ar, adj.,
pupil(l)4ze, intr. v., pupillary (q.v.)

## pupil
pupil, п., opening in the iris of the eye. — ME.
pupille, 'pupil of the eye', fr. MF. (— F.) pupille,
fem., fr. L. papilla, prop, 'a little girl', dimin. of
pupa; see pupa and cp. preceding word. In its
anatomical sense, pupilla is a loan translation of
Gk. κόρη, 'girl; pupil of the eye'. The pupil of
the eye was so called from the little images
('puppets'), which appear in it. Cp. Plato, Alci-
biades, 1, 133a.
Derivative: pupil{l)-ate, adj..

## pupillary
pupillary, adj., pertaining to a pupil or scholar. —
L. papillaris, 'pertaining to a ward, pupillary',
fr. papillus, pupilla, 'orphan, ward'. See pupil,
'scholar', and adj. suff. -ary,

## pupillary
pupillary, adj., pertaining to the pupil of the eye.
— Fr. L. pupilla, 'pupil of the eye'. See pupil,
'opening in the iris of the eye', and adj. suff. -ary.

## pupiparous
pupiparous, adj., giving birth to a fully developed
larva (entomol) — Compounded of L. pupa (see

## pupa) and -parous
pupa) and -parous,

puppet, n. — ME. popet, fr. OF. poupette,
'puppet', dimin. ofpoupe (whence F. роирёе), fr. VL.

puppa, fr. L. pupa, 'girl; doll, puppet'. See pupa

Derivatives: puppet-eer, п., puppet-ism, п.,

puppet-ize, tr. v., puppet-ry, n.

puppy, п., ]) a young dog; 2) a conceited young

doll, puppet'. See puppet and cp. pup.

puppy-hood, п., puppy-ism, п., puppy-ish, adj.

## pur-
pur-, pref. — AF. and E. correspondent of OF.

## por-
por-,pur- (F.pour-), 'for', fr. VL.por-, fr. L. pro,
'before, for'. See 1st pro- and cp. purchase,

## purlieu
purlieu, purport, purpresture.

## Purana
Purana, п., ancient Sanskrit writings of a
legendary character. — Ol. purdnah, lit. 'ancient,

former', whence 'things of old, ancient history,

## legend'
legend', fr. purd, 'formerly, before', which is rel.

to Avestic pare, 'before', and cogn. with Gk.

## fore
fore, 'before*. See fore, adv., and cp. 1st and 2nd

## pro-
pro-,

## purblind
purblind, adj., l) {archaic) wholly blind; 2) partly

blind', a hybrid coined fr. pure (fr. F. pur, fr. L.

Derivatives: purblind-ly, adv., purblind-ness, n.

## purchase
purchase, n. — ME. purchas, porchas, fr. OF.
porchas, purchas, from the verb purchaciert por-
chacier. See purchase, v.

## purchase
purchase, tr. v. — ME. purchasen, porchacen, fr.
OF. porchacier, purchacier (F. pourchasser), 'to
pursue eagerly', fr. par-, pur- (see pur-) and
chacier, 'to hunt, chase'. See chase, v.
Derivatives: purchase, n. (q.v.), purchas-able,
adj., purchas-abil-ity, n.

## purchaser
purchaser, n. — ME. purchasour, fr. AF., fr. OF.,
porchacier, purchacier. See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.

## purdah
purdah, п., curtain guarding women from public
view in India, — Hind- and Pers.pardah, 'veil'.

## pure
pure, adj. — ME.pur,pure, fr. OF. (= F.)pur, fr.
L. purus, 'pure, clean', which is ret. to putus,
'clear, pure',/wrare,'to cleanse, clean', and cogn.
with 01. pavate, pundti, 'purifies, cleanses',
putah, 'pure', putib, 'purification', pavitar-,
'purifier', Mir. ar, 'fresh, new', OHG. fowen, 'to
sift'. See putative and cp. purblind, puree,
purgatory, purge, purify, depurate, expurgate. Cp.
also pious and words there referred to.
Derivatives: pure, adv., pure-, pref. meaning
'purely', pure-ness, n.

## puree
puree, п., mash, thick soup. — F., fr. purer, 'to
strain, pass through a sieve', fr. L. purare, 'to
purify', fr. parus. See prec. word.

## purfle
purfle, tr. v., to decorate with a border of
embroidery. — ME. purfilen, fr. OF. porfifer, pur-
filer, fr. VL. *profilare, fr. 1st pro- and L./iVum,

profile.
Derivatives: purfl~ed, adj., purfl-er, п., purfl-ing,
п., purfl-y, adj.

## purgation
purgation, п., the act of purging. — ME. purga-
cioun, fr. OF. purgacion (F. purgation), fr. L.
purgationem, ace of purgatid, 'a cleansing,
purifying', fr. pargatus, pp. oipurgdre. See purge and
-ation.

## purgative
purgative, adj., tending to purge. — ME.purgatif,
fr. MF. (= F.) purgatif (fem. purgative), fr. L.
purgdtivus, fr. purgatus, pp. of purgare. See
purge and -ive and cp. compurgation.
Derivative: purgative, n.

## purgatory
purgatory, n. — ME., fr. ML. purgatorium, prop.
neut. of the Late L. adj. pargdtorius, 'cleansing,
purging', fr. L. purgatus, pp. of purgare. See
purge and subst. suff. -ory.
Derivative: purgatori-al, adj.

## purge
purge, tr. and intr. v. — ME. purgen, fr. OF. pur-
gier, purger (F. purger), fr. L. purgare, 'to
cleanse, purify', fr. OL. purigdre, which is
compounded οι purus, 'pure', and agere, 'to set in
motion, drive, lead'. See agent, adj., and cp.
spurge, expurgate. Cp. also the second element
in litigate, navigate.
Derivatives: purge, n.,purg-er, n.,purg-ing, adj.
and n.

## purification
purification, n. — MF. ( = F.), fr. L. purificatio-
nem, ace. of purifiedtio, fr. purificatus, pp. of
purificdre. See purify and -ion.

## purificatory
purificatory, adj. — Late L. parifiedtorius,
'tending to purify', fr. L. purifiedtus, pp. ofparificare.
See next word and adj. suff. -ory.

## purify
purify, tr. v., to make pure; to cleanse. — ME.

## purifien
purifien, fr. OF. (= F.) purifier, fr. L. purificdre,
'to make pure, purify', which is compounded of

## parus
parus, 'pure', and -ficdre, fr. facere, 'to make'.
See pure and -fy.
Derivative: purifi-er, n.

## Purim
Purim, п., name of the Jewish festival occurring
on the 14th of the Jewish month Adar. — Heb.

## purim
purim, 'lots', pi. ofpur; which is identified (in the
Book of Esther 3 : 7, and 9 : 24) with haggordl,
'the lot'; pern, a loan word fr. Akkad. puru,
baru, 'stone, urn', which itself is prob. a loan
word fr. Sumeric bur.

## purine
purine, purin, п., a white crystalline compound
(chem.) — Coined by the German chemist Emil
Fischer (1852-1919) from the abbreviation of L.

## purum
purum, neut. οι purus, 'clean, pure*, ML. uricum,
'uric acid', and chem. suff. -ine, -in. See pure and
uric.

## purism
purism, п., strict adherence to purity in language.
— F. purisme, fr. pur, fr. L. purus. See pure and
-Ism.

## purist
purist, n,, a strict adherent of purity in language.
— F. puriste, fr. pur. See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: purist-ic, purist-ic-al, adjs.

## Puritan
Puritan, n. — Lit. 'a purifier', formed with suff.
-an fr. Late L. puritds. See next word.
Derivatives: puritan-ic, puritan-ic-al, adjs., pu-
ritan-ic-al-ly, adv., puritan-ic-al-ness, п.,
Puritan-ism, п., Puritan-ize, intr. and tr. v., Puritan-
iz-er, n.

## purity
purity, n. — ME. purete, fr. OF. purte, purete (F.
purete), fr. Late L. paritatem, ace. of puritds,

## purl
purl, п., a twisted thread of gold or silver used for
embroidering; inversion of stitches in knitting;
tr. and intr. v., to embroider with a thread of
gold or silver; to invert stitches in knitting. —
Fr. earlier pyrle, prob. fr. It. pirofare, 'to twirl',
fr. pirolo, 'a top'. See pirouette,

## purl
purl, intr. v., to flow with a murmuring sound;
п., a murmuring sound — Prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. Norw. purla, 'to gush out'.

## purl
purl, п., a drink of hot beer. — Perh. another
spelling of pearl, used in the sense of 'bubble'.
Cp. F. perle, 'pearled', pp. of perler, .'to pearl,
form in pearls', Sucre perle, 'boiled sugar
resembling pearls'.

## purl
purl, intr. v., to throw, spill (said of a horse); tr.
v., to cause to purl. — Another spelling of
archaic pirl, 'to spin, revolve'; prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. .purl, 'to flow with a murmuring
sound'.
Derivative: purl-er, п., a throw, spill.

## purlieu
purlieu, п., part of a forest, separated from it after
the perambulation of its boundaries (Hist, of
Law). — ME. purlewe, fr. AF. puralee,
'perambulation', fr. OF. puraler, 'to go through,
perambulate', fr. pur- (see pur-) and aler, 'to go'.
See alley. Purlieu was influenced in form by OF.
(= F.) lieu, 'place' (see lieu).

## purlin
purlin, п., a timber resting on the principal rafter
and supporting the common rafters. — Of
uncertain origin,

purloin, tr. v., to filch. — ME. purloinen, fr. AF.

purple, n. — ME. purpel, purpul, dissimilated fr.

purpl-ish, adj. and п., purpl-ish-ness, п., purpl-yr

## purport
purport, п., bearing, tenor, meaning, intention,

See port, 'to carry'.

## purport
purport, tr. v., to convey the meaning or intention

purpose, n. — ME. porpos, purpos, fr. OF'. porpos,

purpos (F. propos), fr. porposer, purposer, 'to

## purpose
purpose, intr. and tr. v. — ME. purposen, fr. OF.

porposer,purposer, 'to propose', collateral forms

pos-ive-ly, adv., purpos-ive-ness, n.

purpresture, п., appropriation of another's land

prendre, fr. L. prendere, 'take'. See prehensile

## purpura
purpura, п., a disease characterized by purple
