## purpure
purpure, п., the color purple (heraldry). — ME.,
fr. OE. purpure. See purple.

## purpureal
purpureal, adj., purple. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. purpureas, 'purple-colored, purple', fr.
purpura. See purple.

## purpuric
purpuric, purpurine, п., a crystalline compound
C14Hg06 (chem.) — Formed with chem. suff.
-in, resp. -ine, fr. L. purpura. See purple.

## purr
purr, intr. v. — Of imitative origin.
Derivatives: purr, n.,purr-er, n.

## purree
purree, п., a yellow pigment, from which Indian
yellow is obtained. — Hind, piuri, rel. to OI.
pltah, 'yellow', which is of uncertain origin.

## purse
purse, n. — ME. purs, fr. OE. purs, lit. 'made
from leather', fr. Late L. bursa, 'leatherbag', fr.
Gk. βύρσα, 'hide'. See burse and cp. words there
referred to. For the change of ρ to b ср. Е.
gossip, fr. ME. gossib (see gossip and sib).
Derivatives: purse, tr. v., purs-ed, purse-ful,
adjs., purs-er, n.

## purslane
purslane, п., name of a plant. — ME. purcelane,
purslane, fr. MF.porcelaine, pourcelaine, formed
—with change of suff.—fr. L. porcildca, a var.
of portuldca, 'purslane', which derives fr. por-
tula, 'a little door', dimin, of porta, 'gate, door'
(see port, 'gate'); so called because its seed-case
is provided with a small covering serving as a
'door' for the seeds. Cp. Porrulaca.

## pursuance
pursuance, n. — Formed fr. pursue with suff.
-ance.

## pursuant
pursuant, adj., carrying out, following; according.
— ME., fr. MF. porsuiant, pres. part, of
porsuir. See pursue and cp. pursuivant.

## pursue
pursue, tr. and intrv. v. — ME. pursuen, fr. AF.
pursuer, fr. OF. porsuir, a collateral from of
porsivre (F. poursuivre), fr. VL. prosequere, for
L. prosequi, 'to follow, pursue'. See pur- and
sue and cp. prosecute.
Derivatives: pursu-able, adj., pursu-al, п.,
pursuance (q.v.), pursuant (q.v.), pursu-er, n.

## pursuit
pursuit, n. — ME., fr. AF. purseute, fr. OF. por-
suite (F. poursuite), prop. fern. pp. of porsuir.
See pursue.

## pursuivant
pursuivant, п., 1) an officer ranking below a
herald ; 2) a follower, attendant. — ME.pursevant,
fr. OF. porsuiant, porsivant (F. poursuivant),
pres. part, of porsuir, porsivre, 'to pursue'. See
pursue and cp. pursuant.

## pursy
pursy, adj., stout, puffy. — ME. purseyf, fr. AF.
porsif (whence also earlier E. pursive), fr. OF.
polsif (F. poussif), fr. polser (F. pousser), 'to
push, to breathe with difficulty', fr. L. pulsdre,
'to push, beat, strike', freq. of pellere (pp.
pulsus), 'to beat, strike, knock, push, drive'. See
pulse, 'throb', and cp. push.
Derivative: pursi-ness, n.

## pursy
pursy, adj., pursed, wrinkled up, puckered. —
Formed with adj. suff. -y fr. purse, v. See purse.

## purtenance
purtenance, п., an appurtenance. — ME. pur-
tenaunce, lit. 'that which pertains (to
something)', alter, (prob. due to the change of suff.per-
to pur-) of MF. partenance, pertinence. See pur-
and pertinence and cp. appurtenance.

## purulence
purulence, purulency, п., quality of being
purulent. — Formed from next word with suff. -ce,
resp. -cy,

## purulent
purulent, adj., consisting of, or resembling, pus.
— L. purulentus, 'festering, mattery', fr. pus,

## gen. puris
gen. puris, 'matter, pus'. See pus and -ulent.
Derivative: purulent-ly, adv.

## purusha
purusha, п., the original man, the soul of universe
{Hinduism) — Ol. purusah, 'man', of uncertain
origin.

## purvey
purvey, tr. v., to supply (food or provisions);

## intr. v.
intr. v., to make provision, prepare. — ME.

## porveien
porveien, purveien, fr. AF. porveire, purveire, fr.

## OF. porveeir
OF. porveeir, porveoir (F. pourvoir), 'to provide',
fr. L. providere. See provide. For the pref. see

## pur-
pur-,

## purveyance
purveyance, n. — ME. porveance, purveiaunce, fr.

## OF. porveance
OF. porveance, purveance, fr. porveeir, porveoir.
See prec. word and -ance.

## purveyor
purveyor, n. — ME. purveour, fr. OF. porveort
purveor. See purvey and agential suff. -or.

## purview
purview, п., 1) the body of an act or bill; 2) scope,
range. — AF. purveu, fr. OF. porveu (F. pourvu),
'provided', pp. of OF. porveier (F. pourvoir), 'to

## provide' (see purvey
provide' (see purvey, provide). AF. purveu

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:631 COLUMN:2 -->
occurred esp. in the legal phrases purveu est, 'it is
provided', and purveu que, 'provided that',
whence the substantial use of E. purview in the
sense of 'proviso, provision',

## purwannah
purwannah, п., an order; a royal letter or grant
(Anglo-Indian). — Hind, parwdnah, fr. Pers.
parwdnak, 'order'.

## pus
pus, п., yellowish matter produced by an
infection. — L. pus, 'viscous matter, pus', rel. to
putere, 'to stink, be rotten', puter, putridus,
'foul, rotten', fr. l.-E. base *pu-, *to rot, stink',
whence also OI. puyati, 'rots, stinks', putih,
'stinking, foul', Gk. πύον, πΰον, 'discharge from
a sore; matter', πΰθειν, 'to cause to rot', Goth.
fuls, ОЕ./й/, 'foul*. See foul, adj., and cp. words
there referred to.

## Fuseyism
Fuseyism, п., another name for Oxford Tractar-
ianism, mostly used contemptuously. — Named
after one of the leaders, E. Bouverie Pusey
(1800-82). For the ending see suff. -ism.

## Puseyite
Puseyite, п., a Tractarian. — See prec. word and
subst. suff. -ite.

## push
push, tr. and intr. v. — ME. posshen, pusshen, fr.
OF. polser, poulser (F. pousser), earlier poulser,
fr. L. pulsdre, 'to push, beat, strike', freq. of
pellere (pp. pulsus), 'to beat, strike, knock,
push, drive'. See pulse, 'throb' and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also pousse-cafe, poussette,
repousse.
Derivatives: push, п.,push-able, &oj.,push-er, п.,
push-ful, adj., push-ful-ly, adv., pusk-ful-ness, п.,
push-ing, adj. and п., push-ing-ly, adv., push-
ing-ness, n.

## pusillanimity
pusillanimity, п., cowardliness; faintheartedness.
— ME. pusillanimite, fr. MF. (= F. pusillant-
mite), fr. Eccles. L. pusillanimitdtem, ace. oipu-
sillanimitdS) 'faintheartedness', fr. pusillanimis.
See next word and -ity,

## pusillanimous
pusillanimous, adj., cowardly; fainthearted. —
Eccles. L. pusillanimis, 'fainthearted*, fr. L.
pusillus, 'very small', and animus, 'mind'. The
first element is a dimin. of OL. pusus, 'boy',
which is rel to L. puer, 'boy, child'; see puerile.
For the second element see animus, for the
ending see -ous.
Derivatives: pusillanimous-ly, adv., pusillani-
mous-ness, n.

## puss
puss, п., a cat. — Imitative of the spitting of a
cat. — Cp. Du. poes, Norw. puse, Ir. and Gael.
pus, Alb.piso, Ruman.pisicd, Tamilpusie,pusei,
'cat'.

## pussy
pussy, п., a pet name for a cat. — Dimin. of puss.
For the ending see dimin suff. -y.

## pussyfoot
pussyfoot, intr. v., to move stealthily. — The
proper meaning is 'to tread stealthily like a cat'.
See pussy and foot,

## pustulant
pustulant, adj., producing pustules. — Late L.
pustulans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of pustulare.
See next word and -ant.

## pustulate
pustulate, tr. v., to form into pustules; intr. v-,
to form pustules. — Late L. pustulatus, pp. of
pustulare, 'to blister, cause blisters', fr. L. pus-
tula. See pustule and verbal suff. -ate.

## pustulate
pustulate, adj., covered with pustules. — Late L.
pustuldtus. See pustulate, v.

## pus tula t ion
pus tula t ion, n. — Late L. pustuldtid, gen. -onis, 'a
breaking out into pustules', fr. pustuldtus, pp. of
pustulare. See pustulate, v., and -ion.

## pustule
pustule, n. — ME., fr. hpustula, 'blister, pimple,
pustule', from the I.-E. imitative base *pu-t
*pku-, 'to blow, swell', whence also OI. pupphu-
sdft, 'lung', pkut-karoti, 'blows, shouts', Gk.
φΰσα, 'pair of bellows; breath, blast, wind,
bubble', φϋσαν, 'to blow', Lith. рйбш, pusti, 'to
blow, swell', Lith. pusle, Lett, puslis, 'bladder*,
Lett, pusma, 'breath', OSlav. puchati, 'to blow',
ON. fjuk, 'snowstorm'. Cp. Physalia, Physeter,
emphysema. Cp. also prepuce. For the ending
see suff. -ule.
Derivative: pustul-ar, adj.

## put
put, tr. and intr. v. — ME. puten, putten, fr. OE.

## putian
putian, a collateral form of potian, 'to push,
throw', rel. to MDu. pote, 'scion, plant', Du.

## poten
poten, 'to plant', Dan putte, 'to put', Icel. pota,
'to poke*. The original sense of all these words
was 'to push, thrust'. Cp. potter, 'to dawdle'.
Cp. also putt.
Derivatives: put, п., putt-er, n.t putt-ing, verbal

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:631 COLUMN:3 -->
n.

## putamen
putamen, п., the hard stone of certain soft-fleshed
fruits, such as peach, plum, cherry (bot.) — L.
putamen, gen. -inis, 'that which falls off in
trimming or pruning, clippings, waste; shell, peel',
fr. putdre, 'to trim, prune, lop, clean, cleanse'.
See pututive. For the ending see suff. -men.

## pntaminous
pntaminous, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
putamen, gen. -inis. See prec. word.

## putanism
putanism, п., harlotry, prostitution. — F. puta-
nisme, fr. putain, 'harlot', fr. OF. pute, prop.
fem. of the adj. put, 'dirty, bad', orig. 'rotten,
foul*, fr. L. putidus, fr. putere, 'to stink*. Cp.
OProvenc. put, 'bad', and puta,putan, 'harlot',
and see pus and -ism. Cp. also putois.

## putative
putative, adj., presumed; reputed. — ME., fr.
Late L. putdtivus, fr. L. putdtus, pp. of putdre,
'to trim, prune, lop, clean, cleanse; to think
over, consider, reckon, count', which is prob.
rel. to puteus, 'well, pit' (lit. 'a hole cut'), and to
pavire, 'to beat, ram, tread down'. Cp. compute,
count, 'to reckon*, deputy, dispute, impute,
repute. Cp. also pit, putamen, puteal, amputate.
Cp. also pave. Cp. also pure. For the ending of
putative see suff. -ive. For the sense
development of L. putdre cp. L. caedere, *to cut, lop,
cut down', whence decidere, 'to cut off; to
decide'.
Derivative: putative-ly, adv.

## puteal
puteal, п., a curb round the mouth of a well
(archit.) — L.,fr. puteus, 'a well'. See prec. word
and adj. suff. -al and cp. pit. Cp. also pozzolana.

## putid
putid, adj., rotten. — L. putidus, fr. putere, 'to
stink, be rotten'. See pus.
Derivatives: putoid-ly, adv., putid-ness, n.

## putlog
putlog, п., a horizontal piece of timber in
scaffolding. — Prob. compounded'of the verb
put and log, 'a heavy piece of wood'.
Derivative: putlog, tr. v.

## putois
putois, п., a brush used in decorating pottery. —
F. putois, 'polecat', fr. OF. put, 'stinking,
rotten', fr. L. putere (see putanism); so called
because orig. made of polecat's hair.

## Putorius
Putorius, п., a subgenus of mammals of the
musteline family including the polecats (zool.) -»-
ModL., fr. L. putor, 'a foul smell, stench', from
the stem οι putere, 'to stink'. See pus and cp.
putois, putunism.

## putrefacient
putrefacient, adj., putrefactive. — L. putrefaciens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of putrefacere. See
putrefactive and -ent.

## putrefnetion
putrefnetion, n. — ME. putrefaccion, fr. L. putre-

## factio
factio, gen. -onis, fr. putrefactus, pp. of
putrefacere. See next word and -ion.

## putrefactive
putrefactive, adj., putrefying. — MF. (= F.)
putrefactif (fern, putrefactive), fr. L. putrefactus,
pp. of putrefacere,'*to make rotten', which is
compounded of putrere, 'to be rotten', and

## facere
facere, 'to make, do'. See putrid, fact and -ive.

## putrefy
putrefy, tr. v., to make rotten; intr. v., to become
rotten. — ME. putrefien, fr. MF. (= F.) putre-

## fier
fier, fr. L. putrefacere. See prec. word and -fy.
Derivative: putrefi-er, n.

## putrescence
putrescence, also putrescency, п., state of being
putrescent. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## putrescent
putrescent, adj., becoming putrid. — L. putre-
scens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of putrescere, 'to
become rotten, to molder, decay', inchoative of
putrere, 'to be rotten'. See putrid and -escent.

## putrescible
putrescible, adj., capable of becoming putrid. —
Formed with suff. -Ible fr. L. putrescere. See
prec. word.
Derivatives: putrescible, п., putrescibil-ity, n.

## pntrescine
pntrescine, п., a crystalline ptomaine found in
putrid animal food (biochem.) — Formed with
chem. suff. -ine fr. L. putrescere. See putrescent.

## putrid
putrid, adj., rotten, decayed. — L. putridus, fr.

## putrere
putrere, 'to be rotten*, fr. puter, 'rotten*, fr.

## putere
putere, 'to be rotten', which is rel. to pus, gen.

## puris
puris, 'pus, matter*. See pus and 1st suff. -id and
cp. putanism, putid, putois, Putorius. Cp. also
olla podrida and potpourri.
Derivatives: putrid-ity, п., putrid-ly, adv., pu-
trid-ness, n.

## Putsch
Putsch, п., revolt, riot. — G., a Swiss dialect
word, lit. meaning 'thrust, shock'; of imitative
origin.

## putt
putt, п., the act of hitting the ball into the hole
(golf);p"tt, a. v., to hit(the ball)into the hole;
intr. v., to play a putt. — From the verb put.
Derivatives: putt-er, п., putt-ing, n.

## puttee
puttee, puttie, п., strip of cloth worn as a gaiter.
— Hind, pat a, 'strip of cloth, bandage', fr. 01.
pattab, of s.m.
Derivative: puttee, puttie, tr. v.

## puttl
puttl, n. pi, figures of naked Cupids. — It., pi.
of putto, 'a small boy', fr. L. piitus, 'boy', which
is rel. to puer, 'boy'. See puerile.

## putty
putty, n. — Fr. F. potee, 'potful; putty', fr. pot,
'pot'. Cp. F. potee d'etain, 'putty powder', and
see pot, 'vessel'.
Derivative: putti-er, n.

## puy
puy, п., a hill of volcanic origin. — F., fr. L.
podium, 'a height, balcony', prop, 'support', fr.
Gk. πόδιον, dimin. of πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'.
See podium.

## puzzle
puzzle, n. — Of uncertain origin; possibly aphet-
ic for opposal, in the sense of 'question,
problem'. Cp. pose, 'to puzzle'.
Derivatives: puzzle, tr. and intr. v., puzzl-ed,
adj., puzzl-ed-ly, adv., puzzl-ed-ness, п., puzzle-
dom, п., puzzle-ment, п., puzzl-er, п., puzzl-ing,
adj., puzzl-ing-ly, adv., puzzl-ing-ness, n.

## puzzolana
puzzolana, n. — See pozzolana.

## py-
py-, form of pyo- before a vowel.

## Pyanepsia
Pyanepsia, n. pi., a festival in honor of Apollo
held on the 7th of the month Pyanepsion (Greek
religion). — Gk. Πυανέψια (pi.), lit. 'the feast of
cooking beans', fr. πύανος, 'bean', which is of
uncertain origin' and βψειν, 'to boil, cook',
which is cogn. with Arm. ep'em, I cook'; so
called because at this festival a disk of pulse was
offered to Apollo.

## Pyanepsion
Pyanepsion, п., the 4th month of the Attic Greek
calendar (corresponding to
October-November). — Gk. Πυανεψιών, fr. Πυανέψια. See prec.
word.

## pycn-
pycn-, form of pycno- before a vowel.

## Pycanthemum
Pycanthemum, п., a genus of plants, the
mountain mint (йог.) — ModL., compounded of
pycn- and Gk. #νθεμον, 'flower', fr. α\ι*ος,
'flower'. See anther.

## pycnidlum
pycnidlum, п., a spore-bearing receptacle
occurring in certain fungi (boi.) — ModL., formed fr.
Gk. πυκνός (see pycno-) and suff. -idlum.
Derivative: pycnidi-al, adj.

## pycno-
pycno-, before a vowel pycn-, combining form
meaning 'close, thick, dense', as in pycnometer.
— Gk. πυκνό-, πυκν-, fr. πυκνός, 'close, solid,
thick, dense', fr. πύκα, 'thickly, solidly' (whence
πυκάζειν, 'to crowd together, condense'), which
is cogn. with Avestic pusS-, 'headband'. Alb.

## pud
pud, Ί kiss', prop. Ί embrace'; not rel. to πύξ,
'with the clenched fist'. Cp. pyknic.

## pycnometer
pycnometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
density of liquids or solids. — Compounded of
pycno- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## pycnostvle
pycnostvle, adj., having columns arranged closely
together (arch.) — L. pycnostflos, fr. Gk. πυκ-
νόστϋλος, 'close-columned', 'fr. πυκνός (see
pycno-) and στΰλος, 'column*. See style,
'gnomon'.

## pyel-
pyel-, form of pyelo- before a vowel.

## pyelitis
pyelitis, п., inflammation of the pelvis of the
kidney (med.) — Medical L., formed with suff.
-itis fr. Gk. πύελος. See next word.

## pyelo-
pyelo-, before a vowel pyel-, combining form
denoting the pelvis of the kidney. — Gk. πύελο-,
πυελ-, fr. πύελος, 'basin, trough, vat', dissimilat-
ed fr. *πλύελος, which is rel. to πλυνειν, 'to
wash, clean', fr. I.-E. base *pleu-, 'to flow,
swim', whence also πλέειν, 'to swim', L. pluvia,
'rain'. See flow and cp. pluvial.

## pyemia
pyemia, pyaemia, п., a form of blood poisoning
(med.) — Medical L., fr. F. pyoemie, which was
coined by the French physician Pierre-Adolphe
Piorry(l794-l879), ft. Gk. πύον or πϋον, 'pus',
and αϊμα, 'blood'. See pyo, hemal and 1st -ia.
Derivative: py(a)em-ic, adj.

## pyg-
pyg-, form of pygo- before a vowel.

## pygal
pygal, adj., pertaining to the region of the rump.
— Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. πϋγή,
'rump', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
pygidium.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:632 COLUMN:2 -->

## pygarg
pygarg, n. (obsol), 1) a kind of antelope, proo.
the addax; 2) the osprey.—L. pygargus, fr. Gk.
πϋγαργος, 'white rump', which is compounded
of πϋγή, 'rump' (see prec. word), and <2ργος,
'white'. See argent.

## pygidium
pygidium, п., the posterior part of the body, esp.
in insects (zool.) — ModL., formed fr. Gk.
πϋγίδιον, dimin. of πϋγή, 'rump'. See pygal and
-idium.
Derivative: pygidi-al, adj.

## pygmaean
pygmaean, pygmean, adj., Pygmy. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. pygmaeus. See next word.

## pygmy
pygmy, п., one of a fabulous race of dwarfs in
Greek mythol.; a dwarf. — L. pygmaeus, fr. Gk.
πυγμαίος, lit. 'a πυγμή tall', fr. πυγμή, 'fist;
the measure of the distance from the elbow to
the knuckles', rel. to πύξ, 'with clenched fist',
and cogn. with L. pugnus, 'fist'. See pugnacious
and cp. pugilism.
РУВ°-, before a vowel pyg-, combining form
denoting the rump. — Gk. πΰγο-, πϋγ-, fr. πϋγή,
'rump'. See pygal.

## pyic
pyic, adj., pertaining to pus. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ic fr. Gk. πύον or πΰον, 'pus'. See pyo-.

## pyjnmas
pyjnmas, n. pi. — See pajamas.

## pyknic
pyknic, adj., fat, plump. — Formed with suff.
-ic fr. Gk. πυκνός, 'close, thick, dense'. See
pycno-.

## pyle-
pyle-, before a vowel pyl-, combining form
denoting the porta! vein. — Gk. πύλη-, πυλ-, fr.
πύλη, 'gate'. See pylon.

## pylic
pylic, adj., pertaining to the portal vein. — See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## pylon
pylon, п., the gateway to a temple in ancient
Egypt. — Gk. πυλών, 'gateway to a temple or
another building', fr. πύλη, 'gate', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. pyle-, pylorus, propylaeum,
tetrapylon.

## pyloro
pyloro,- before a vowel pylor-, combining form
denoting the pylorus. — See next word.

## pylorus
pylorus, п., the lower orifice of the stomach
(anat.) — Late L., fr. Gk. πυλωρός, 'gatekeeper',
which is compounded of πύλη, 'gate', and
-ωρός, 'watcher, guardian', lit, 'seer', fr. όραν,
'to see', but influenced in form by ώρα, 'care,
heed'; see pylon and ware, 'alert'. Galen called
the lower orifice of the stomach στενότης, lit.
'narrowness', but compared it with the
gatekeeper, πυλωρός, whence its name in modern
anatomy.
Derivative: ρylor-ic, adj.

## pyo-
pyo-, before a vowel py-, combining form
meaning 'pus'. — Gk. πυο-, πυ-, fr. πύον or
πϋον. 'pus', which is rel. to πυθειν, 'to rot', and
cogn. with L. pus, 'viscous matter, pus', putere,
'to be rotten'. See pus and cp. Pythium.

## pyogenesis
pyogenesis, п., the formation of pus (med.) —
Medical L-, compounded of pyo- and Gk.
γένεσις, 'origin, source, birth, race, descent'.
See genesis.

## pyogenic
pyogenic, pyogenetic, adj. — See prec. word and
-genie, resp. -genetic.

## pyoid
pyoid, adj., resembling pus. — Gk. πυοειδής,
compounded of πύον or πΰον, 'pus' and -οειδής,
'like', fr. εϊδος, 'form, shape'. See pyo- and -oid.

## pyorrhea
pyorrhea, pyorrhoea, п., a discharge of pus (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of pyo- and -rrhea.
Derivative: ρyorrhe-al, adj.

## pyosis
pyosis, п., suppuration (paihol.) — Medical L.,
formed with suff. -osis fr. Gk. πύον or πΰον,
'pus'. See pyo-.

## pyr-
pyr-, form of pyro- before a vowel.

## Pyracantha
Pyracantha, n. pi., a genus of thorny shrubs of
the apple family (bot.)— ModL., fr. Gk.
πυράκανθοι, name of a shrub, compounded of Gk.
πΰρ, 'fire' and άκανθα, 'thorn, thorny plant'.
See pyre and acantha.

## pyralidid
pyralidid, pyralid, adj., pertaining to the family
Pyralididae. — See next word.

## Pyralididne
Pyralididne, n. pi., a family of moths (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -ideae fr. Gk.πυραλίς,
πυραλλίς, name of an insect, fr. πΰρ, 'fire' (see
pyre); so called because it was supposed to be
able to live in fire.

## pyramid
pyramid, n. — L. pjiramis, gen.' -idis, fr. Gk.
πΰραμίς, gen -ίδος, which was prob. formed
through metathesis fr. OEgyptian pimar.
Derivatives: pyramid, intr. and tr. v.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:632 COLUMN:3 -->
pyramidal, adj., pyramid-al-ly, adv., pyramid-wise, adv.

## pyran
pyran, п., an isomeric cyclic compound, C5HeO
(chem.) — Abbreviation of pyrokoman. See
pyrone.

## pyrargyrite
pyrargyrite, п., a sulfide of antimony and silver,
Ag3SbS3 (mineral.) — Compounded of Gk. πΰρ,
'fire', ίργυρος, 'silver' and subst. suff. -ite. See
pyr- and argent.

## pyre
pyre, n. — L. pyra, fr. Gk. πυρά, 'funeral pyre',
fr. πΰρ, gen. πυρός, 'fire', which is cogn. with
OE. fyr, etc., 'fire'. See fire and cp. antipyrin,
apyretic, apyrexia, empyreal, empyreuma,
pyrites, pyrosis, pyrrhic, adj., pyrrho-, pyrrole. Cp.
L. burrus, 'red', fr. Gk. πυρρός, 'fiame-colored,
yellowish red', which is assimilated fr. *πυρσός,
fr. πΰρ, 'fire'; see Bornchio, bnrrito, burro,
sbirro. (The change of Greek π to Latin b is
prob. due to Etruscan influence; cp. box, 'the
tree').

## pyrene
pyrene, п., a white hydrocarbon, С1(НИ. —
Formed with suff. -ene fr. Gk. πΰρ, 'fire'. See
pyre.

## pyrene
pyrene, п., the stone of a drupelet. — Gk. πϋρήν,
'stone of a fruit', rel. to πυρός, 'corn, wheat',
and cogn. with OE. fyrs, 'furze'. See furze and
cp. the second element in Agropyron, Diospyros,
Fagopyrum, Melampyrum.

## pyreno-
pyreno-, before a vowel pyren-, combining form
meaning 'stone of a fruit', as in pyrenoid, Pyre-
nomycetes. — Gk. πϋρηνο-, πΰρην-, fr. πϋρήν,
gen. πυρήνας. See prec. word.

## pyrenoid
pyrenoid, adj., resembling a fruit stone. —
Compounded of pyreno- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## Pyrenomycetes
Pyrenomycetes, n. pi., a class of fungi (boi.) —
ModL., compounded of pyreno- and Gk.
μύκης, gen. μύκητος, 'fungus'. See -mycetes.

## Pyrethmm
Pyrethmm, п., a genus of plants; the
chrysanthemum (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. πύρεθρον, 'the
feverfew', fr. πϋρ, 'fire'; see pyre and cp. next
word; so called because of its medicinal
qualities. For sense development cp. feverfew. Cp.
pellitory, 'pyrethrum'.

## pyretic
pyretic, adj., pertaining to fever; feverish (med.)
— Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. πυρετός,
'burning heat, fever', fr. πΰρ, 'fire'. See pyre.

## pyreto-. combining form meaning 'fever'
pyreto-. combining form meaning 'fever', as in
pyretology. — Gk. πυρετό-, fr. πυρετός. See
prec. word.

## pyretology
pyretology, п., that branch of medicine which
treats of fever. — Lit. 'the study of fever', fr.
pyreto- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner), one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: pyretolog-ist, n.

## pyretotherapy
pyretotherapy, п., the treatment of disease by the
artificial induction of fever. — See pyreto- and
therapy.

## Pyrex
Pyrex, п., a type of glass resisting to heat. — A
coined trade name.

## pyrexia
pyrexia, п., fever (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
πυρέσσειν, fut. πυρέξω, 'to be feverish', fr.
πυρετός, 'fever'. See pyreto- and 1st -ia.
Derivatives: pyrexi-al, pyrex-ic, pyrex-ic-al,
adjs.

## pyrgeometer
pyrgeometer, п., an instrument for measuring
radiation from the earth. — Coined ft. Gk. πϋρ,
'fire', γη, 'the earth' and μέτρον, 'measure'. See

## pyre
pyre, geo- and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## pyrhellometer
pyrhellometer, п., an instrument for measuring
solar radiation. — Coined fr. Gk. πΰρ, 'fire',
ήλιος, 'sun' and μέτρον, 'measure'. See pyre,

## helio- and -meter
helio- and -meter,

## pyridine
pyridine, п., a liquid obtained by distillation of

## coal tar and bone oil
coal tar and bone oil, CtH5N (chem.) — Coined
fr. Gk. πΰρ, 'fire' (see pyre), and suff. -idine.

## pyriform
pyriform, adj., pear-shaped. — ML. pyriformis,

## fr. ML. pyrum
fr. ML. pyrum, for L. pa-urn, 'pear', and L.

## forma
forma, 'form, shape'. See pear and form, n.

## pyrite
pyrite, п., a metallic iron disulfide, FeSs (mineral.)
— See next word.

## pyrites
pyrites, n,, any of various metallic sulfides. — L.,
ft. Gk. πυρΐτης, 'of fire', in πυρΐτης λίθος,
'firestone, a stone that strikes fire', fr. πΰρ, 'fire'.
See pyre and subst. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: pyrit-ic, pyrii-ic-al, adjs.

## pyritiferous
pyritiferous, adj., containing pyrites. — See prec.
word and -ferous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:633 COLUMN:1 -->

## pyro-
pyro-, before a vowel pyr-, combining form
meaning'fire'. — Gk. πύρο-, πυρ-.fr. πυρ, gen.πυρός,
'fire'. See pyre.

## pyrochemical
pyrochemical, adj., pertaining to chemical changes
caused by high temperature. — Compounded
of pyro- and chemical.
Derivative: pyrochemical-ly, adv.

## pyrogallol
pyrogallol, п., a crystalline poisonous compound,
C„H4(OH)3 (chem.) — Coined fr. pyrogallic
{acid) and suff. -ol; so called because first
prepared (by Scheie in 1786) by heating gallic acid.
See pyro- and gallic.

## pyrogenic
pyrogenic, adj., producing heat or fever. —
Compounded of pyro- and -genie.

## pyrography
pyrography, п., the process of producing a design
on wood with a hot iron. — Lit. 'writing with
fire', fr. pyro- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives : pyrograph-erb п., pyrograph-ic, adj.

## Pyrola
Pyrola, n.f a genus of plants, the wintergreen
(bot.)—ModL., a dimin. formed fr. Pyrus (q.v.)

## Pyrolaceae
Pyrolaceae, n. pi., a family of trees (bot.) —
Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## pyrolaceous
pyrolaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## pyrolatry
pyrolatry, п., fire worship. — Compounded of
pyro- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρία, fr. λατρεία,
'worship'. See -latry.

## pyroligneous
pyroligneous, adj., obtained by dry distillation
from wood. — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. πυρ,
gen. πυρός, 'fire', and L. lignum, 'wood'. See
pyre and ligneous.

## pyrology
pyrology, п., the study of heat. — Compounded
of pyro- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives:pyrolog-ic-al, ady,pyrolog-ist, n.

## pyrolusite
pyrolusite, п., manganese dioxide, Mn02
(mineral.) — G. Pyrolusit, compounded of pyro- and
Gk. λούειν, 'to wash', which is cogn. with L.
lavare, 'to wash' (see lave); so called because it
is used as glass soap. The ending -it goes back
to Gk. -ϊτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## pyrolysis
pyrolysis, п., decomposition by heat (chem.) —
Compounded of pyro- and Gk. λύσις, 'loosing,
releasing'. See -lysis.

## pyrolytic
pyrolytic, adj., pertaining to pyrolysis. —
Compounded of pyro- and Gk. -λυτ(.κός, fr. λυτικός,
'able to loose, loosing'. See -lytic and cp. prec.
word.

## pyromancy
pyromancy, п., divination by fire. — ME. piro-
mancie, fr. OF. (— F.) piromancie, fr. Late L.
pyromantia, fr. Gk. πυρομαντεία, fr. πυρ, gen.
πυρός, "fire', and μαντεία, 'divination'. See
pyro- and -mancy.

## pyromania
pyromania, п., a morbid tendency to set things on
fire. — Compounded of pyro- and Gk. μανία,
'madness, frenzy'. See mania.

## pyromaniac
pyromaniac, n. — Compounded of pyro- and
ML. maniacus. See maniac.
Derivative: pyromaniac-al, adj.

## pyrometer
pyrometer, п., an instrument for measuring high
temperatures. — Coined by the Dutch physicist
Pieter van Musschenbroek (1622-1761) fr. Gk.
πυρ, gen. πυρός, 'fire', and μέτρον, 'measure'.
See pyro- and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: pyrometr-ic-al, adj., pyrometr-y, n.

## pyrone
pyrone, п., a cyclic compound C5H402(cAem.) —
Abbreviation of pyrokoman, a word coined fr.
pyro- and Gk. κομαν, 'to let the hair grow long*,
fr. κόμη, 'hair, foliage, tail of a comet'. See
coma, 'a tuft of hairs'.

## pyrope
pyrope, n., a variety of deep, flery red garnet (mi л-
eral.) — ME. pirope, fr. OF. pirope (F. pyrope),
L. pyropus, fr. Gk. πυρωπός, lit. 'fiery eye',
compounded of πυρ, 'fire' and ώψ, gen. ώπός,
'eye'. See pyro- and -opia.

## pyrophobia
pyrophobia, п., a morbid fear of fire (med.) —
Medical L., compounded of pyro- and -phobia.

## pyrophoric
pyrophoric, pyrophorous, adj., igniting
spontaneously. — Lit. 'fire-bearing', fr. Gk. πυροφόρος,
fr. πΰρ, gen. πυρός, 'fire', and -φόρος, 'bearing'.
See pyre, -phore and -ic, resp. -ous.

## pyrophorus
pyrophorus, п., any substance that ignites
spontaneously. — ModL. See prec. word.

## pyrophotometer
pyrophotometer, п., an instrument for measuring

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:633 COLUMN:2 -->
very high temperatures. — Compounded of
pyro- and photometer.

## pyrosis
pyrosis, п., heartburn (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. πύρωσις, 'a burning', fr. πυροΰν, 'to burn',
fr. πΰρ, 'fire*. See pyre and -osis.

## pyrostat
pyrostat, п., a thermostat, esp. one for high
temperatures. — Coined fr. pyro- and -stat, on
analogy of thermostat (q.v.)

## pyrotechnic
pyrotechnic, pyrotechnica], adj., pertaining to
fireworks. — Compounded of pyro- and Gk.
τεχνικός, 'made by art', fr. τέχνη, 'art'. See tech-
nic, resp. also adj. suff. -al.

## pyrotechnics
pyrotechnics, п., the art of making fireworks. —
See prec. word and -ics.

## pyrotechny
pyrotechny, п., pyrotechnics. — See prec. word
and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## pyrotfc
pyrotfc, adj., caustic. — Gk. πυρωτικός,
'pertaining to burning', fr. πυροΰν, 'to burn', fr.
πΰρ, 'fire'. See pyre and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: pyrotic, n.

## pyrotoxin
pyrotoxin, п., a toxin causing fever (med.) —
Coined fr. pyro- and toxin.

## pyroxene
pyroxene, п., a mineral composed especially of
calcium and magnesium (mineral.) — F.
pyroxene, coined by the French mineralogist Abbe
Rene Just Haiiy (1745-1822) in 1796 fr. Gk. πΰρ,
'fire', and ξένος, 'stranger' (see pyro- and xeno-);
he so called it from the erroneous notion that
the mineral does not occur in igneous rocks.

## pyroxenite
pyroxenite, п., an igneous rock containing
pyroxene, but without olivine (petrogr.) — Formed
fr. prec. word with subst. suff. -ite.

## pyroxylin
pyroxylin, also pyroxyline, п., a cellulose nitrate
mixture (chem.) — F. pyroxyline, coined by the
French chemist Theophile-Jules Pelouze (1807-
67) in 1836 fr. pyro-, Gk. ξύλον, 'wood' (see
xylo-), and chem. suff. -ine.

## pyrrh-
pyrrh-, form of pyrrho- before a vowel.

## pyrrhic
pyrrhic, п., an old Greek war dance. — L. pyr-
rhicha, fr. Gk. πυρρίχη (scil. ορχησις), name of
an old Greek war dance, so called after Πύρ-
ριχος, the inventor of this dance. The name
Πύρριχος lit. means 'reddish', fr. πυρρός,
'flame-colored'; see pyrrho- and -ic.

## pyrrhic
pyrrhic, adj., pertaining to the pyrrhic dance. —
L. pyrrhichius, fr. Gk. πυρρίχιος, fr. πυρρίχη.
See prec. word.

## pyrrhic
pyrrhic, п., a foot of two short syllables (prosody)
— Fr. L. pyrrhichius (pes), fr. Gk. πυρρίχιος
(πους), 'pyrrhic measure or foot', prop, 'the
measure of the pyrrhic dance'. See prec. word.
Derivative: pyrrhic, adj., pertaining to the
pyrrhic foot.

## Pyrrhic
Pyrrhic, adj., pertaining to Pyrrhus, king of Epi-
rus. — Fr. L. Pyrrhicus, fr. Gk. Πυρρικός, fr.
Πυρρός, 'Pyrrhus'.— Pyrrhic victory is a
victory gained at a ruinous cost; so called in
allusion to the victory of Pyrrhus over the Romans
at Heraclea (279 B.C.E.)

## pyrrho-
pyrrho-, before a vowel pyrrh-, combining form
meaning 'red'. — Gk. πυρρό-, fr. πυρρός (for
*πυρσός), 'reddish, red', lit. 'fiame-colored', fr.
πΰρ, 'fire'. See pyre and cp. pyrrhic, adj. Cp.
also burro, sbirro.

## Pyrrhonic
Pyrrhonic, adj., pertaining to Pyrrhonism. — L.
Pyrrhdneus, fr. Pyrrho, fr. Gk. Πύρρων, a
philosopher of Elis. See next word. For the
ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## Pyrrhonism
Pyrrhonism, п., the sceptical system of
philosophy founded by Pyrrho of Elis (about 360-
275 B.C.E.) See prec. word and -ism.

## Pyrrhonist
Pyrrhonist, п., an adherent of Pyrrhonism. — See
prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: Pyrrhonist-ic, adj.

## pyrrhotite
pyrrhotite, also pyrrbotine, п., a magnetic iron
sulfide, FeS (chem.) — G. Pyrrhotin, formed
with suff. -in, '-ine' (see chem. suff. -ine), fr. Gk.
πυρρότης, 'redness', fr. πυρρός,'reddish, red';
see pyrrho-. Pyrrhotite was forftied with change
of suff. (see subst. suff. -ite) fr. pyrrhotine.

## pyrrole
pyrrole, pyrrol, п., a colorless, weakly basic
liquid, C4HeN (chem.) — G. Pyrrol, coined fr.
Gk. πυρρός, 'reddish, red* and L. oleum, 'oil'.
See pyrrho- and oil.

## Pyrula
Pyrula, п., a genus of marine mollusks (zool.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:633 COLUMN:3 -->
ModL., fr. ML. pyrum, for h.pirum, 'pear' (see
pear); so called from the pear-shaped shell.

## Pyrularia
Pyrularia, п., a genus of plants, the oil nut (bot.)
— ModL., a dimin. formed fr. Pyrus. Cp. prec.
word.

## Pyrus
Pyrus, n. (bot.) — ML. pyrus, for L. pirus, 'pear-
tree', which is rel. to pirum, 'pear'. See pear and
cp. prec. word.

## pyruvic acid
pyruvic acid, an organic acid, CH3COCOH
(chem.) — Pyruvic is a hybrid coined fr. Gk.
πΰρ, 'fire', and L. uvat 'grape'. See pyre, uva
and adj. suff. -ic.

## Pythagorean
Pythagorean, adj. pertaining to Pythagoras of
Samos, Greek philosopher of the 6th century
B.C.E., or to his philosophy. — Formed with
suff. -an fr. L. Pythagoreus, fr. Gk.
Πυθαγόρειος, fr. Πυθαγόρας, 'Pythagoras'.
Derivatives: Pythagorean, п., an adherent of
Pythagoras or of his philosophy, Pythagorean-
ism, n.

## Pythagorism
Pythagorism, n. — The same as Pythagoreanism.
Sec prec. word and -ism.

## Pythia
Pythia, п., the priestess of Apollo at Delphi
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Πυθία (scil. ίέ-
ρει,α), 'the priestess of Pythian Apollo at Delphi',
fem. of Πύθιος, prop, 'the Delphian', epithet
of Apollo, fr. Πΰθώ or Πΰθών, the older name
of Delphi and its environs. Cp. Pythian.

## Pythiad
Pythiad, п., the time between two celebrations of
the Pythian games in ancient Greece (= 4 years).
— Gk. Πΰθιάς, gen. Πΰθιάδος, fr. τά Πυθία
(scil. ίερά), 'the Pythian games*, neut. pi. of
Πύθιος, 'Delphian'. See prec. word, and -ad.
For the suff. cp. Olympiad.

## Pythian
Pythian, adj., 1) pertaining to Delphi or to the
oracle and priestess of Apollo at Delphi; 2)
pertaining to the Panhellenic games held at Delphi
every four years. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L.
Pythius, fr. Gk. Πύθιος, 'Delphian'. SeePythia.
Derivative: Pythian, п., 1) Apollo; 2) Pythia.

## Pythium
Pythium, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL,, fr.
Gk. πυθειν, *to rot', which is rel. to πύον, πΰον,
'pus'. See pyo- and 1st -ium.

## pythogenic
pythogenic, pythogenetic, adj., generated by
decomposition. — Compounded of Gk. πυθ-ειν,
*to rot' (see prec. word), and -genie, resp.
-genetic.

## pathogenesis
pathogenesis, п., generation by decomposition. —
See prec. word and genesis.

## Python
Python, п., 1) the huge serpent slain near Delphi
by Apollo (Greek mythol); 2) (not cap.), any
large serpent; 3) (cap.) a genus of snakes (zool.)
— L. Pftho, the serpent slain by Apollo, fr. Gk.
Πυθων, of s.m., anameprob. rel. to the place
name Πΰθώ. See Pythia and cp. next word.

## python
python, п., a familiar spirit. — Late L. pythot
'familiar spirit', fr. Late Gk. πίθων, of s.m., fr,
Gk. Πυθων, 'a prophet inspired by Apollo'.
This name is prob. identical derivatively with
Πυθων, name of the serpent slain by Apollo.
See prec. word.

## pythoness
pythoness, п., ]) the priestess of Apollo at Delphi
(Greek mythol.) 2) a woman supposed to have
the power of divination. — ME. Pkitonessef fr.
pkitonise (F. pythonisse), 'sorceress', fr. ML.
phitonissa, fr. Late L. pythonissa, fem. of pythot
'familiar spirit'. See prec. word and 1st -ess.

## pyuria
pyuria, п., discharge of pus with the urine (med.)
— Medical L., compounded of py- and Gk.
-ουρία, fr. οδρον, 'urine'. See -uria.

## pyx
pyx, п., receptacle for coins. — L. pyxis, fr. Gk.
πυξίς, 'box of box wood', πύξος, 'the box tree,
box wood'. See box, the tree, and box, 'a
receptacle', and cp. pyxidium, pyxis.
■Derivative: pyx, tr. v.

## Pyxidanthera
Pyxidanthera, п., a genus of plants (bot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. πυξίς, gen. πυξί-
δος, 'box of box wood', and ανθηρός, 'flowery*,
fr. άνθος, 'flower'. See pyx and anther.

## pyxidium
pyxidium, п., a capsule. — ModL., fr. Gk. πυξί-
διον, dimin. of πυξίς, 'box'. See pyx and -idium.

## pyxie
pyxie, п., also pixie, pixy, name of a shrub. —
— From Pyxidanthera barbulata, the botanical
name of this shrub (see Pyxidanthera).

## pyxis
pyxis, п., asmallbox. — L.,fr. Gk. πυξίς. See pyx.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:634 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:634 COLUMN:1 -->

## qoph
qoph, п., name of the 19th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — See koph.

## qua
qua, conj., as, in the capacity of. — L. qua, abl.
fem. of the relative qui, 'who'. See which, who
and cp. quaquaversal.

## quack
quack, intr. v., to utter a sound like a duck; п.,
the sound made by a duck. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. MDu. quacken,Du.kwaken, G. quaken,
OSlav. kvakaii, L. coaxdre, 'to croak', Gk. κο-
άξ, 'the croaking of frogs', Hitt. akuwakuwash,
'frog', which all are imitative. Cp. also
quacksalver.

## quack
quack, n. — Abbreviation of quacksalver.
Derivatives: quack, intr. v. and adj., quack-ery,
п., quack-isht adj., quack-ish-fy, adv., quack-y,
adj.

## quacksalver
quacksalver, п., a fraudulent pretender to
medical skill. — Obsol. Du. quacksalver (now kwak-
zalver), fr. MDu. quacsalver, lit. 'one who
quacks orpatters about his salves' in trying to sell
them, fr. MDu. quacken, quaken (Du. kwaken),
'to quack like a duck' (see quack, v.), and MDu.
salven (Du. zalven), 'to rub with ointment',
which is rel. to salve, 'to apply a salve to' (q.v.)
Cp. G. Quacksalber, Dan. kvaksalver, Swed.
kvacksalvare, 'quacksalver', which are of the
same origin.

## quad
quad, п., quadrat {print.) — Abbreviation of
quadrat.
Derivative: quad, tr. v.

## quad
quad, п., quadrangle, campus. — Abbreviation
of quadrangle,

## quad
quad, adj., quadruple. — Abbreviation of
quadruple.

## Quadi
Quadi, n. pi., name of a German tribe. — L.
Quadi, lit. 'the Speakers'; ср. ОЕ. cwedan, 'to
speak, say' (see quoth).

## quadr-
quadr-, combining form. — See quadri-.

## quadrable
quadrable, adj., capable of being squared. — See
quadrate, v., and -able,

## quadragenarian
quadragenarian, ]) adj., forty years old; 2) п., а
quadragenarian person. — Formed with suff.
-an fr. L. quadr agendri us, 'forty years old', fr.
quadrdgeni, 'forty each', fr. quadrdgintd (for
*quatrd-gintd), 'forty', which is formed fr. quat-
tuor, 'four', with -gintd, a suff. denoting tens.
This suff. is cogn. with Gk. -κοντά in
τριάκοντα, 'thirty', τεσσαρα-κοντα, 'forty', etc. See
four and cp. quadri-. For the etymology of the
Gk. suff. -κοντά, L. suff. -gintd, see penteconta-.
Cp. quarantine, cuarenta.

## Quadragesima
Quadragesima, п., ]) the forty days of Lent; 2)
the first Sunday in Lent {Eccles.) — ML. qua-
drdgesima (scil. dies), 'the fortieth day', fem. of
L. quadr agesimus, 'fortieth*, fr. quadrdgintd.
See quadragenarian.
Derivative: Ouadtagesim-al. adi.

## quadrangle
quadrangle, п., ])aplane figure having four angles
and four sides; 2) a quadrangular building. —
ME., fr. MF. ( = F.), fr. Late L. quadrangulum,
prop. neut. of the L. adj. quadrangulus, 'having
four corners', fr. quadri-, used in compounds in
the sense of quattuor, 'four' (see quadri-), and
angulus, 'angle, corner'. See angle, 'corner'.
Derivative: quadr angl-ed, adj.

## quadrangular
quadrangular, adj., having four angles and four
sides. — Late L. quadr anguldris, 'having four
corners', fr. quadrangulum. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ar.
Derivatives: quadr angular-ly, adv., quadrangu-
lar-ness, n.

## quadrant
quadrant, п., the fourth part of a circle (geom.) —
ME., fr. L. quadrans, gen. -amis, 'a fourth part*,
prop. pres. part, of quadrare, 'to square'. See
quadrate, adj., and -ant and cp. quadri-.

## quadrantal
quadrantal, adj., containing the fourth part of a
measure. — L. quadrantalis, fr. quadrans.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.

## quadrat
quadrat, п., a small piece of type metal (prim). —
See next word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:634 COLUMN:2 -->

## quadrate
quadrate, adj., squared; rectangular. — L. qua-
drdtus, 'squared, square', pp. of quadrdre, *to
square; to put in order, complete', fr. quadrus,
'square'. See quadri- and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: quadrate, n. (q.v.), quadrat-ic, qua-
drat-ic-al, adjs., quadrat-ic-al-iy, adv.

## quadrate
quadrate, п., a square. — L. quadrdtum, 'a square,
quadrate', prop. neut. of quadratus, pp. of qua-
drure. See quadrate, adj.

## quadrate
quadrate, tr. v., to make square; intr. v., to
square (with). — L. quadrants, pp. o£ quadrare.
See quadrate, adj.

## quadrature
quadrature, п., the act of squaring. — L. quadrd-
tura, 'a squaring, quadrature', fr. quadratus, pp.
of quadrare. See prec. word and -ure.

## quadratus
quadratus, п., name of several square-shaped
muscles (anal.) — L. quadratus, 'squared*, pp.
of quadrare. See quadrate, adj.

## quadrennial
quadrennial, adj., 1) occurring once every four
years; 2) lasting four years. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. quadriennium, 'a period of
four years', fr. quadriennis, Of four years',
which is compounded of quadri- and annus,
'year'; see annual. For the change of Latin a (in
annus) to ^(in quadri-ennium) see accent and cp.
words there referred to.

## quadri-
quadri-, quadr-, combining form with the sense
'having four, consisting of four'. — L., rel. to
quattuor, 'four', fr. I.-E. *qwetwor-, *qwetur,
whence also Goth, fidwor, OE. feower, 'four'.
See four and cp. quadrnnt, quadrate, quadrille,
'a square dance', quadroon, quarantine, quarrel,
arrow, bolt', quarry, 'a place for excavating
stones', quart, quatrain, quire of paper, squad,
squadron, square and the second element in
trocar.

## quadric
quadric, adj., of the second degree. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ic fr. L. quadra, 'a square', which
is rel. to quattuor, 'four'. See quadri-.
Derivative: quadric, n.

## quadri centennial
quadri centennial, п., the four hundredth
anniversary of an event; adj., pertaining to a quadri-
centennial. — Compounded of quadri- and
centennial.

## quadriceps
quadriceps, п., the large extensor muscle of the
leg (anat.) — Compounded of quadri- and L.
-ceps, fr. caput, 'head' (see capital, adj., and cp.
biceps, triceps); so called because it is divided
into four parts.

## quadrifid
quadrifid, adj., divided into four parts. — L. qua-
drifidus, lit. 'four-cleft', fr. quadri- and fid-,
stem of findere (perf. fidt), 'to cleave, split'. See
fissile.

## quadriga
quadriga, п., a four-horsed chariot. — L.
quadriga, contraction of *quadrijugae, fem. pi. of *qua-
drijugus, 'pertaining to a team of four',
compounded of quadri-and the stem of jungere, 'to
join'. See join.

## quadrigeminal
quadrigeminal, adj., fourfold. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. quadr igeminus, 'fourfold', fr.
quadri- and geminus, 'twin, double'. See Gemini.

## quadrilateral
quadrilateral, adj., four-sided. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. quadrilaterus, which is
compounded of quadri- and latus, gen. lateris, 'side'.
See lateral.
Derivatives: quadrilateral, п., quadrilateraf-fy,
adv., quadriiateral-nessy n.

## quadrilingual
quadrilingual, adj., of four languages; knowing
four languages. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
quadri- and L. lingua, 'tongue'. See lingual.

## quadriliteral
quadriliteral, adj., consisting of four letters. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. quadri- and L.
littera, litera, 'letter'. See letter, literal.

## quadrille
quadrille, п., game of cards played by four
persons. — F., fr. Sp. cuartillo, fr. cuarto, 'fourth',
fr. L. qudrtus, of s.m. (see 1st quart); assimilated
in form to next word.

## quadrille
quadrille, п., a square dance. —'Sp. cuadrifla, fr.
cuadro, 'square', fr. L. quadrus, 'square', which
is rel. to quattuor, 'four'. See quadri-:

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:634 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: quadrille, intr. v.

## quadrillion
quadrillion, п., 1) in the United States and France,
the fifth power of a thousand (i.e. 1 followed by
15 zeros); 2) in Great Britain and Germany, the
fourth power of a million (i.e. 1 followed by 24
zeros). — F., formed fr. quadri- on analogy of
million (q.v.) Cp. billion and words there
referred to.

## quadrinomial
quadrinomial, adj., consisting of four terms (alg.)
— Formed fr. quadri- with suff. -nomial on
analogy of binomial (q.v.)

## quadripara
quadripara, п., a woman who has borne four
children (med.) — Medical L., fr. quadri- and
L. pario, parere, 'to bring forth'. See parent.

## quadripartite
quadripartite, adj., consisting of four parts. — L.
quadripartitus, pp. of quadr ipar tire, 'to divide
into four parts', fr. quadri- and partire, 'to
divide into parts', fr. pars, gen. partis, 'part'. See
part, n.

## quadriplegia
quadriplegia, п., paralysis affecting all the four
limbs of the body (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid
coined fr. L. quadri-, 'four', and Gk. πληγή,
'stroke'; see quadri- and plague. The correct
form would be tessaraplegia (fr. Gk. τέσσαρες,
'four', and πληγή, 'stroke').
Derivative: quadriplcg-ic, adj.

## quadrireme
quadrireme, п., a galley having four banks of
oars. — L. quadriremis, compounded of quadri-
and remus, 'oar'. See bireme and cp. words
there referred to.

## quadrisyllable
quadrisyllable, adj., consisting of four syllables.
— Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. quadri- and L.
syllaba. See syllable.

## quadrisyllable
quadrisyllable, п., a word of four syllables. —
Compounded of quadri- and syllable.

## quadri valence
quadri valence, quadrivalency, п., the state of
being quadrivalent (chem.) — Formed from
next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## quadrivalent
quadrivalent, adj., having a valence of four
(chem.) — Compounded of quadri- and L. va-
Jens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of valere, 'to have
power'. See -valent.

## quadrivial
quadrivial, adj., pertaining to the quadrivium. —
ML. quadrividlis, fr. quadrivium. See next word
and adj. suff. -al.

## quadrivium
quadrivium, п., in the Middle Ages, a group of
sciences consisting of geometry, astronomy,
arithmetic and music. — ML., fr. L. quadrivium,
'place where four roads meet, crossroads',
compounded of quadri- and via, !way, road,
path'. See via and cp. trivium.
Derivative: quadrivi-al, adj.

## quadroon
quadroon, п., the child of a mulatto and a white
person. — Sp. cuarteron, prop, 'one who has a
fourth part of Negro blood', fr. cuarto, 'a fourth
part', fr. L. qudrtus, 'fourth'; assimilated to
words beginning with quadr-. See quadrate, adj.,
and quart.

## quadru-
quadru-, combining form meaning 'having four,
consisting of four'. — L., a var. form of quadri-
(q-v.)

## quadrumanous
quadrumanous, adj., having four hands. —
Compounded of quadru- and L. mantis, 'hand'. See
manual and -ous.

## quadruped
quadruped, п., an animal having four feet; adj.,
four-footed. — Compounded of quadru- and L.
pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. See foot and cp. pedal.
Derivative: quadruped-al, adj.

## quadruple
quadruple, adj., fourfold. — MF. ( = F.), fr. OF.,
fr. L. quadruplus, 'fourfold', formed fr. quadru-
with -plus, '-fold', on analogy of duplus, 'double'.
See double and cp. next word.
Derivatives: quadruple, п., quadrupl-et, n.

## quadruple
quadruple, tr. v., to multiply by four; intr. v., to
be multiplied by four. — ME. quadruplet!, fr.
MF. (= F.) quadrupler, fr. Late L. quadruplare,
'to multiply by four, make fourfold', fr. L. qua-
druplus. See quadruple, adj.

## quadruplex
quadruplex, adj., fourfold; used especially of a
telegraph system in which four messages may be

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:635 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: QUADRUPLEX | 608 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:635 COLUMN:1 -->
sent simultaneously over the wire. — L., formed
fr. quadru- with -plex, gen. -plicis, '-fold', on
analogy of duplex, gen. duplicis, 'double'. See
duplex and cp. next word.

## quadruplex
quadruplex, п., an instrument used for sending
messages in quadruplex telegraphy. — Fr.
quadruplex, adj.

## quadruplicate
quadruplicate, adj., fourfold. — L.
quadruplicate, pp. of quadruplicare, 'to make fourfold', fr.
quadruplex, gen. quadruplicis. See quadruplex,
adj.
Derivative: quadruplicate, n.

## quadruplicate
quadruplicate, tr. v., to multiply by four. — L.
quadruplicate, pp. of quadruplicare. See
quadruplicate, adj.
quadruplicating n. — Late L. quadruplicated, gen.
-onis, 'a making fourfold', fr. L. quadruplicates,
pp. of quadruplicare. See prec. word and -ion.

## quaere
quaere, v., imper., inquire; п., a query. — L,,
imper. of quaerere, 'to seek, search for; to ask,
inquire'. See query and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivative: quaere, п., a query.

## quaestor
quaestor, п., any of an order of Roman
magistrates. — L., contraction of quaesitor, 'seeker,
searcher', fr. quaesitus, pp. of quaerere. See prec.
word and agential surf, -or.

## quaestorial
quaestorial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. quaestorius, 'pertaining to a quaestor', fr.
quaestor. See prec. word.

## quaestuary
quaestuary, adj., seeking to make profit; п., one
who seeks to make profit. — Late L. quaestud-
rius, 'pertaining to money making, mercenary',
fr. L, quaestus, 'gain, acquisition', fr. quaes-, stem
of quaerere, 'to seek'. See query and adj. suff.
-ary.

## quaff
quaff, tr. and intr. v., to drink repeatedly or
copiously. — Prob. fr. MLG. quassen (whence
obsol. E. quass), 'to quaff', through a misreading
of ss as ff. In early manuscripts and prints the
letters/and s were almost equal in form.
Derivatives: quaff, п., quaff-er, п., quaff-ing-ly,
adv.

## quag
quag, intr. v., to quake (obsol.) — Prob. a var. of
quake.

## quag
quag, п., bog, marsh. — Rel. to quag, v.
Derivative: quagg-y, adj.

## qungga
qungga, п., a South African animal, allied to the
zebra. — A Hottentot name of imitative origin.

## quagmire
quagmire, п., bog, marsh. — Fr. earlier quakemire,
which is compounded of quake and mire. Cp.
quag, 'bog, marsh'.
Derivative: quagmir-y, adj.

## quahog
quahog, also quahaug, п., the N. American clam.
— Of Algonquian origin.

## quaich
quaich, quaigh, п., a shallow drinking cup. —
Gael, cuach, Olr. cuach, fr. Late L. caucus, 'a
drinking vessel'. Cp. Gk. καύκα, καυκίον, 'a
kind of drinking vessel'.

## Quai d'Orsay
Quai d'Orsay, the French Foreign Office. — F.,
lit. 'quay of (General) Orsay\ name of a quay
on the south bank of the Seine in Paris, on which
the French Foreign Office is situated.

## quail
quail, п., a migratory bird, Coturnix coturnix. —
ME. quaille, quaile, fr. OF. quaille (F. caille), fr.
ML. quaccola, which is of imitative origin. Cp.
Du. kwakkel, and OHG. wahtala, MHG. wach-
tele, G. Wachtel, OE. wihtel (for *wahtei), which
are also of imitative origin. Cp. Coturnix. (There
is no relation between the above Teut. words
and 01. vdrtikd, Gk. δρτυξ, 'quail'.)
Derivative: quail-ery, n.

## quail
quail, intr. v., to lose heart, to shrink. — Fr.
obsol. quail, 'to curdle', fr. ME. quailen, fr. OF.
coailler (F. cailler), fr. L. coaguldre. See
coagulate.

## quaint
quaint, adj. — ME. cointe, queynte, queint, 'well
known, skillful, neat, elegant', fr. OF. coint,
cointe, 'well known, skillful, neat', fr. L. cogni-
tus, 'well known', pp. of cognoscere, 'to know".
See know and cp. cognition, cognoscible. Cp. also
acquaint.
Derivatives: quaint-ly, adv., quaint-ness, n.

## quake
quake, intr, v. — ME. quaken, fr. OE. cwacian,
prob. of imitative origin. Cp. quag, quagmire.
Derivatives: quake, п., quak-er, n,, quak-ing, n.
and adj., quak-ing-ly, adv.

## Quaker
Quaker, п., the name given to a member of the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:635 COLUMN:2 -->
religious sect calling themselves the Society of
Friends, founded by George Fox in 1648-50. —
So called by Justice Bennet in 1650, who was
warned by Fox 'to quake at the word of the
Lord'. See prec. word and agential suff. -er.
Derivatives: Quaker-dom, п., Quaker-ish, adjv,
Quaker-ism, п., Quaker-ize, tr. v., Quaker-iz-
ation, п., Quaker-ly, adj. and adv.

## qualification
qualification, n. — ML. qudlificdtio, fr. qudlificd-
tus, pp. of qualificare. See qualify and -ation.

## qualiflcator
qualiflcator, n. — ML. qualificator, formed fr.
qudlificdtus, pp. of qualificare. See next word
and agential suff. -or.

## qualify
qualify, tr. and intr. v. — MF. (= F.) qualifier, fr.
ML. qualificare, 'to make of a certain quality',
which is compounded of L. qudlis, 'of what
kind', and -ficdre, ft.facere, 'to make, do'. See
qnnlity and -fy.
Derivatives: qualifi-ed, adj., qualifi-er, п.,
qualify-ing, adj., qualify-ing-ly, adv.

## qualitative
qualitative, adj. — ML- qualitative, 'relating to
quality', fr. L. qualitds, gen. -dtis. See next word
and -ative.
Derivative: qualitative-ly, adv.

## quality
quality, n. — ME. qualite, fr. OF. qualite (F.
qualite), fr. L. qudlitdtem, ace. of qualitds,
'quality', fr. qudlis, 'how consituted, of what kind',
which derives from the pronominal base *quo-,
whence also L. quisl 'who', quidl 'what', qui,
quae, quod, 'who, which, what', Goth, has, OE.
hwd, 'who'. See who and words there referred
to, and cp. the first element in kickshaw. For the
ending see surf. -ity. L. qudlitus was formed by
Cicero fr. qudlis as loan translation of Gk.
ποιότης, 'quality', which was coined by Plato
fr. ποΐος, 'of what kind'. Cp. L. quantitas, loan
translation of Gk. ποσότης (see quantity).

## qualm
qualm, п., feeling of faintness; scruple. — ME.
qualm, 'pestilence, plague', rel. to Du. kwalm,
'thick vapor', G. Qualm, 'smoke, vapor; stupor';
possibly rel. to OE. cwealm, 'death, pestilence,
plague', fr. Teut. base *kwel-an, 'to kill, destroy,
die', whence OE. cwelan, 'to die', cwellan, 'to
kill'. See quell.
Derivatives: qualm-ish, adj., qualm-ish-ly, adv.,
qualm-ish-ness, п., qualm-y, adj.

## quamash
quamash, n. — A var. spelling of camas.

## quandary
quandary, п., a state of perplexity. — Of
uncertain origin.

## qnandong
qnandong, quandang, п., a small Australian tree.
— From Australian native name.

## quant
quant, п., a pole. — ME. quante, of uncertain
origin; possibly derived fr. L. contus, fr. Gk.
κοντός, 'pole', which stands in gradational
relationship to κεντεΐν, 'to prick, goad', κέντρον,
'horse goad prickle, point'. See center and cp.
kent, 'pole'.

## quantic
quantic, п., a rational, homogeneous function of
two or more variables {math.) — Fr. L. quantus,
'how much'. See quantum and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: quantic-al, adj.

## quantification
quantification, n. — See next word and -ation.

## quantify
quantify, tr. v., to determine the quantity of. —
ML. quantificare, fr. L. quantus, 'how great'. See
quantum and -fy.
Derivatives: quantifi-able, adj., quamifi-er, n.

## quantitative
quantitative, adj., pertaining to quantity. — ML.

## quantitative
quantitative, fr. L. quantitas. See next word and
-ative.
Derivatives: quantitative-ly, adv., quantitative-

## ness
ness, n.

## quantity
quantity, n. — ME. quantite, fr. OF. quantiie (F.

## quantite)
quantite), fr. L. quantitatem, ace. of quantitas,
'greatness, amount, quantity', fr. quantus, 'how

## great
great, how much, how many'; see qnantum. L.
quantitas was formed fr. quantus as loan
translation of Gk. ποσότης, fr. πόσος, 'how great, how

## much'. Cp. L. qualitds
much'. Cp. L. qualitds, loan translation of Gk.
ποιότης (see quality).

## quantum
quantum, п., quantity; an object that has
quantity. — L-, neut. of quantus, 'how great, how

## much
much, how many', rel. to Umbr. pant a ( — L.
quanta); for *qudm-to, fr. quam, 'in what

## manner
manner, as much as', which is rel. to Oscan pan,

## Umbr. pane
Umbr. pane, 'as, as much as\ and cogn. with

## OE. hu
OE. hu, 'how', hwa, 'who'; see how, who, and cp.
the first element in quasi. The second element in
*qudm-to expresses the idea of greatness, so that

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:635 COLUMN:3 -->
E. 'how great' is the literal rendering of L.
quantus ( = *qudm-to) in accordance with the two
elements of this word. Cp. aliquant.

## quaquaversal
quaquaversal, adj., turning in all directions (said
of geological strata). — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. qudqudyersus, 'turning in whatever
direction', which is compounded of L. qudqua,
'wherever', fr. reduplication of qua, 'in what
direction', and pp. of vertere, 'to turn'. See qua
and version.
Derivative: quaquaversal-ly, adv.

## quarantine
quarantine, п., a period (orig. of forty days) of
isolation to prevent the spread of disease. — It.
quarantina, fr. quaranta, 'forty', fr. L. quadra-
ginta. See quadragenarian and cp. cuarenta. The
term goes back to It. quaranta giorni, 'forty
days'. Ships coming from the Levant and Egypt
were isolated at special ports for thirty, later
forty, days. This measure for preventing the
spread of contagious diseases was first enforced
at Ragusa in 1377. SeeK. Sudhorf,
"Epidemiological Rules from the Past", in Essays in the
History of Medicine, trans. F. H. Garrison, New
York, 1926, p. 152.
Derivatives: quarantine, tr. v., quarantin-er, n.

## quarrel
quarrel, п., dispute. — ME. quarel, quarelle, que-
rele, fr. OF. querele (F. querelle), fr. L. querela,
also querella, 'complaint', fi.queri, 'to complain',
which is prob. cogn. with Ol. ivdsati, svasiti,
'blows, breathes, sighs', OE. hwiesan, 'to
wheeze'. See wheeze and cp.querimonious,
querulous. Cp. also cyst.
Derivatives: quarrel, v. (q.v.), quarrel(l)-er, п.,
quarrel(l)-ing, adj., quarrel(l)-ing-ly, adv.,
quarrel-some, adj., quarrel-some-ly, adv., quarrel-
so me-ness, n.

## quarrel
quarrel, intr. v., to engage in a quarrel. — Partly
fr. OF. quereler (F. quereller), partly fr. prec.
word.

## quarrel
quarrel, п., 1) arrow or bolt, formerly used with a
crossbow; 2) small diamond-shaped pane of
glass. — ME., fr. OF. quarel, quarrel (F. car-
reau), fr. ML. quadrellus, dimin. of quadrus,
'square'. See quadrate, adj., and -el.

## quarry
quarry, п., anything hunted, prey. — ME. querre,
quirre, fr. OF. cuiree (F. curie), 'the spoil,
quarry*, fr. cuir, 'hide, skin', fr. L. corium. The
original meaning of quarry was 'parts of a slain-
animal placed on its hide as the hound's reward*.
See corium and cp. cortex, cuirass.

## quarry
quarry, п., quarrel. — A later var. of 3rd
quarrel.

## quarry
quarry, п., a place for excavating stones. — ME.
quarey, fr. earlier quarrere, fr. OF. quariere (F.
carriere), fr. Late L. quadrdria, fr. L. quadrdre,
'to square* (said also of stones). See quadrate, v.
Derivatives: quarry, tr. v., to excavate stones
from a quarry, quarri-ed, adj., quarri-er, п.,
quarry-ing, n.

## quart
quart, п., a measure for liquids. — ME., fr. MF.
(= F.) quarte (fem. of quart, 'fourth'), fr. L.
qudrta (pars), |the fourth part', fr. qudrtus,
'fourth*, prob. dissimilated from *qwtur-tos, fr.
quattuor (for *q"etwor), 'four'. See four, fourth,
andep. quadrille, *a game of cards'. Cp. also the
second element in tankard.

## quart
quart, п., 1) a position in fencing; 2) a sequence
offour cards of a suit. — F. quarte, subst. use of
quarte, fem. of quart, adj., 'fourth'. See prec.
word and carte.

## quartan
quartan, adj., 1) pertaining to the fourth; 2)
occurring every fourth day; п., fever recurring
every fourth day (counting both days of
consecutive occurrence). — F. (fievre) quartaine,
'fever of the fourth day', fr. L. (febris) qudrtdnaf
fem. of qudrtdnus, 'pertaining to the fourth;
occurring every fourth day', fr. qudrtus, 'fourth'.
See 1st quart and -an.

## quartation
quartation, п., process of alloying three parts of
silver with one of gold (assaying). — Formed
with surf, -ation fr. L. qudrtus, 'fourth'. See 1st
quart.

## quarter
quarter, n.— ME.,fr. OF. (= F.) quartier, 'a fourth
part, quarter; district', fr. L, qudrtdrius, 'a fourth
part, quarter', fr. qudrtus. See 1st quart and adj.
suff. -ary.
Derivatives: quarter, tr. and intr. v., quarter-age,
п., quarter-ing, n. and adj., quarter-ly, adv., adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:636 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 609 | QUERY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:636 COLUMN:1 -->
and η.

## quartern
quartern, п., a measure. — ME. quarteroun,
quartrun, fr. OF. (^ F.) quarteron, 'the quarter
(of a pound, etc.)', fr. quartier, 'a fourth part,
quarter". See prec. word.

## quartet
quartet, also quartette, п., ]) a group of four
persons ;2)esp.a group of four singers.—F. quartette,
fr. It. quartetto, dimin. of quarto, 'the fourth;
the fourth part', fr. L. quartus. See 1st quart and
-et, -ette.

## quartic
quartic, adj., of the fourth degree. — Formed
with adj. surf, -ic fr. L. quartus, 'fourth'. See
1st quart.

## quart lie
quart lie, п., the aspect of two heavenly bodies
that are 90° distant from each other {archaic). —
ML. quartilis, 'pertaining to the aspect of two
heavenly bodies that are 90° distant from each
other', fr. L. quartus, 'fourth*. See 1st quart and
-ile.

## quartile
quartile, adj., pertaining to a quartile aspect. —
See quartile, n.

## quarto
quarto, п., a size of paper. — Fr. L. in quarto, 'in
one fourth (of the original size)', abl. of quartus,
'fourth'. See 1st quart.

## quartz
quartz, п., a crystalline mineral, SiOa. — G.
Quarz, fr. kwardy, a Western Slav, dialectal
equivalent of Pol. twardy, Czech and Slovak
tvrdy, 'quartz', prop, adjectives meaning 'hard',
used as nouns, and rel. to OSlav. tvrudu, Lith.
tvirtas, 'hard', Lith. tveriu, tverti, 'to seize,
contain', and prob. cogn. with Gk. σειρά, 'cord,
rope, string'.

## quartziferous
quartziferous, adj., containing quartz. — A hybrid
coined fr. quartz and L. ferre, 'to bear, carry';
see -ferous.

## quartzite
quartzite, п., a rock composed of quartz. — A
hybrid coined fr. quartz and subst. suff. -ite.

## quash
quash, tr. v., to make void, annul. — ME. quas-
sen, fr. OF. quasser (F. casser), 'to break; to
annul, quash', fr. L. quassdre, 'to shake
violently', freq. of quatere (pp. quassus), *to shake'
(whence -cutere in concutere, 'to shake
violently', discutere, 'to shake violently, shatter, dash
to pieces', percutere, 'to pierce through'); see
concuss, discuss, percuss); prob. fr. l.-E. base
*(s)qut-, 'to shake', whence also Lith. kuteti, 'to
shake up', kutrus, 'quick, swift, nimble', OS.
skuddian, 'to move violently', OHG. scutten,
scuten, scutilon, G. schutteln, 'to shake', OE.
sciidan, 'to hasten'. Cp. squash. Cp. also cascara,
casco, cassation, rescue, sagrada, sconcheon, and
the second element in fracas, fricasee. Cp. also
shudder.

## qnash
qnash, tr. v., to suppress. — ME. quashen, fr. OF.
quasser (F. casser). See prec. word.

## quasi
quasi, adv., as if. — L. quasi, fr. *quam-si,
compounded of quam, 'as, as much as', and si, 'if.
For the first element see quantum, for the second
see nisi.

## quasi-
quasi-, combining form meaning 'as if, as it were'.
— Fr. L. quasi. See prec. word.

## Quassia
Quassia, п., a tropical plant. — Named after
Graman Quassi, a Surinam Negro, who was the
first to discover the medicinal properties of this
plant (in 1730).

## quassin
quassin, also quassiin, п., a white crystalline,
bitter compound CiaH30O6 {chem.) — Formed
from prec. word with suff. -in.

## quater-
quater-, combining form meaning 'four times'. —
L., rel. to quattuor, 'four'. Cp. Avestic ca&rush,
Ol. catuh, 'four times', and see quadri-.

## quatercentenary
quatercentenary, п., a four hundredth
anniversary. — Compounded of quater- and centenary.

## quaternary
quaternary, adj., consisting of four elements. —
L. quaternarius, 'consisting of four each,
containing four', fr. quaterni, 'four together, four
each'. See qunter- and adj. surT. -ary and cp.
casern, quire, 'sheets of paper'.
Derivative: quaternary, n.

## quaternate
quaternate, adj., arranged in sets of four. —
Formed with adj. surT. -ate fr. L. quaterni. See
prec. word.

## quaternion
quaternion, п., a set of four things. — ME. qua-
ternioun, fr. Late L. quaternid, gen. -onis, fr. L.
quaterni. See quaternary and cp. carillon.
Derivatives: quaternion-ic, adj.

## quaternary
quaternary, п., a group of four persons regarded
as one. — Late L. quaternitds, fr. L. quaterni.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:636 COLUMN:2 -->
See quaternary and -ity and cp. trinity.

## quatorzain
quatorzain, п., a poem of fourteen lines. — MF.
(= F.) quatorzaine, 'a group of fourteen', fr.
OF., 'a period of fourteen days', fr. quatorzet
'fourteen', fr. L. quattuordecim, 'fourteen', fr.
quattuor, 'four', and decern, 'ten'. See four and
ten and cp. quadri- and deci-,

## qnatrain
qnatrain, п., a four-lines stanza. — F., fr. quatre,
'four', fr. L. quattuor. See quadri- and cp.
sextain.

## quatrefoil
quatrefoil, п., a flower with four leaves. — ME.
quaterfoil, fr. OF. quatrefoil, 'four leaves', fr.
quatre, 'four', and foil, 'leaf, fr. L. folium. See
qundrl- and folio and cp. foil, 'space in the
tracery of a window'.

## quattrocento
quattrocento, п., the 15th cent., an important
period in Italian art and literature. — It., lit.
'four hundred', short for mil quattro cento, 'one
thousand four hundred*, as referring to the
period beginning with 1400. It. quattro derives
fr. L. quattuor, cento fr. L. centum. See quadri-
and cent and cp. cinquecento, trecento.
Derivatives: quattrocent-ism, п., quattrocent-
ist, n.

## quaver
quaver, intr. and tr. v. — ME. quaveren, freq. of
quaven, which is prob. of imitative origin. Cp.
LG. quappig, 'puffy, swelled', Du. kwabbig,
'flabby', G. quabbeln, 'to wobble, shake, quake',
which all are imitative. Cp. also quiver, v.,
squab.
Derivatives: quaver, п., quaver-ег, п.,
quavering, verbal п., quaver-ing-ly, adv., quaver-yt adj.

## quay
quay, n. — ME. kai, kei, fr. OF. chai (F. quai),
fr. Gaul, caio, 'circumvallation', which is rel. to
W, cae, 'fence, hedge', Co. кё, 'hedge', fr. l.-E.
base *quagh-, 'to encompass, enclose', whence
also L. caulae, 'hole, enclosure', ON. hagi, hage,
'pasture', OE. haga, 'hedge*. See hedge and cp.
haw, 'enclosure'. The spelling quay is due to the
influence of F. quai.
Derivatives: quay, tr. v., quayage (q.v.)

## quayage
quayage, п., charge for use of a quay. — F.
quayage, formed fr. quai with suff. -age. See prec.
word.

## quean
quean, п., a woman (in a derogatory sense).—
ME. queue, queti, fr. OE. cwene, 'woman, female
serf, prostitute', rel. to OS., OHG. quena, ON.
kona, Goth, qino, 'woman, wife', OE. cwen,
'wife, woman, queen*, fr. l.-E. *gwena·, *gwund,
'woman', whence also Ol. janih, 'wife', gna,
gand, 'wife of a god, goddess*, Avestic jainish,
'wife', Toch. A Sam, В sno, 'wife*, Arm. kin (pi.
kanaik'), 'woman*, Gk. γυνή, Boeot. βάνα,
'woman, wife', OSlav. zena, OPruss. genna,
genno, Olr. ben (for *gwena), 'woman'. Cp.
queen. Cp. also gyneco-, zenana, and the first
element in banshee.

## qneasy
qneasy, adj., causing nausea; fastidious;
overscrupulous. — Fr. ME. coisy, of uncertain
origin; perh. connected with OF. coissier, *to hurt',
or with ON. kveisa, 'whitlow, boil*.
Derivatives: queasi-ly, adv., queas-i-ness, n.

## quebracho
quebracho, п., any of several American trees,
distinguished by their very hard timber. — Sp.,
lit. 'breaking the axe', compounded of quebrar,
'to break', and hacha, 'axe'. The first element is
dissimilated fr. L. crepitare, 'to crack, rattle';
see crepitate. The second element is a loan word
fr. Teut. *happya (cp. OHG. happa, *axe'),
whence also F. hachey 'axe'; see hatchet.

## queen
queen, П. — ME. quen, quene, 'queen', fr. OE.
cwen, 'wife, woman, queen', rel. to Goth, qens,
OS. quan, 'wife', and to OE. cwene, 'woman'.
See quean.
Derivatives: queen, intr. and tr. v., queen-domy
п., queen-hood, п., queen-less, adj., queen-like^
adj., queen-ly, adj., queen-li-ness, n.

## queer
queer, adj. — Prob. fr. G. quer, 'cross, transverse,
oblique; across, athwart', fr. MHG. twerch,
dwerch, fr. OHG. twerh, dwerah (in the Middle
German of the 14th cent., orig. tw- became qu-);
rel. to OE. pweorh, 'cross, perverse'; fr. I.-E.
base *twereq-, 'to turn, twist, wind'. See thwart
and cp. torque. For sense development cp. G.
Querkopf, 'queer, wrong-headed fellow'.
Derivatives: queer, n. and tr. v., queer-ish, adj.,
queer-ly, adv., queer-ness, n.

## quelch
quelch, intr. v. — A blend of quench and squelch.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:636 COLUMN:3 -->

## quell
quell, tr. v., to put down, subdue; calm; quiet. —
ME. quellen, 'to kill, strike', fr. OE. cwellan,
causative of cwelan, 'to die\ rel. to OS. quellian,
'to torture, kill', ON. kvelja, Swed. kvdlja, 'to
torment, torture', MDu. quelen, Du. kwellen, 'to
vex, tease, torment', OHG. quellan, MHG.
queln, 'to suffer pain', G. quale η, 'to torment,
torture', and to OE. cwalu, 'killing, violent
death, destruction*, cwealm, 'killing, murder,
death*, ON. kvol, Dan., Swed. kval, 'torment,
torture', MDu. quale, Du. kwaal, 'complaint,
disease', OHG. quala, MHG. quale, kale, G.
Quai, 'pain, torment*. These Teut. words are
cogn. with Arm. kelem, Ί torture*, OSlav. ϊαΐϊ,
'pain', OPruss. golis, 'death', Lith. galas, 'end',
gela, 'agony', gelti, 'to prick, sting'. Cp. klil,
qualm.
Derivatives: queller (q.v.), quell-able, adj.

## queller
queller, п., one that quells. — ME., fr. OE. cwel-
lere, 'killer', fr. cwellan. See prec. word and
agential suff. -er.

## quench
quench, tr. v., to extinguish. — ME. quenchen, fr.
OE. cwencan, indcwencan,
'toextinguish*,causative of cwincan, 'to be extinguished, disappear',
rel. to OFris. kwinka, of s.m. Cp. qnelch.
Derivatives: quench, п., quench-аЫе, adj.,
quench-er, п., quench-less, adj., quench-less-ly,
adv., quench-less-ness, n.

## quenelie
quenelie, п., a ball of minced chicken. — F.,
borrowed fr. G. Knodel, 'dumpling', fr. MHG.
knddel, dimin. of knode, 'knot', which is related
to E. knot. See knot, 'bow, tie*.

## Quentin
Quentin, also Quintin, п., masc. PN. — F. Quen-
tin, fr. L. Qurn(c)tidnus, Quin(c)tinus, fr. quintus,
'the fifth'. See quint and -in.

## quercetin
quercetin, п., a yellow crystalline compound,
C15H10O7 + H20 {chem.) — Formed with suff.
-in fr. L. quercetum, Oak forest', fr. quercus,
'oak'. See Quercus and cp. quercitron. For the
suff. -etum cp. L. arboretum, 'a place grown with
trees', fr. arbor, 'tree' (see arboretum).

## quercine
quercine, adj., pertaining to oaks. — Late L.
quercinus, fr. L. quercus, 'oak'. See Quercus and
-ine (representing L. -inus).

## quercttrin
quercttrin, п., a yellow, crystalline glucoside,
C2iH3o°n + 2H2° (chem.) — Formed from
next word.

## quercitron
quercitron, п., the black oak. — Contraction of
querci-citron (see haplology), which is
compounded of L. quercus, Oak' (see Quercus), and
citron.

## Quercus
Quercus, п., a genus of trees, the oak (bot.) — L.,
'the oak', for *perqwu-s; cogn. with ON. fura,
OE. furh, 'fir'. See fir and cp. words there
referred to. In L. quercus the original p- has been
assimilated to the к of the following syllable;
cp. Gk. πέντε and L. quinque, 'five', Gk. πέσσω
and L. coquo, Ί cook' (see quinque and cook).

## querido
querido, fern, querida, adj. and п., dear, darling.
— Sp., pp. of querer, 'to wish, desire, love,
cherish', fr. L. quaerere, 'to seek, search for; to
ask, inquire'. See query and cp. words there
referred to.

## querimonious
querimonious, adj., querulous. — ML. querimo-
niosus, fr. L. querimonia, 'complaint', fr. queri,
'to complain'; see quarrel, 'dispute'. For the L.
suff. -monia see -mony and cp. words there
referred to, for the ending see suff. -ons.
Derivatives: querimonious-ly, adv., querimo-
nious-ness, n.

## querist
querist, п., one who inquires. — Formed fr.
query with suff. -ist.

## quern
quern, п., a primitive hand mill. — ME. querne,
fr. OE. cweornt rel. to ON. kvern, Dan. kvxrn,
Swed. qvarn, OFris. quern, Du. kweern, OHG.
quirn, chwtrna, Goth, qairnus (in asiluqairnus),
and cogn. with Ol. grdvd, 'stone to crush the
soma', Arm. erkan, 'millstone', Lith. girna,
'millstone', girnos (pi.), 'hand mill', Lett.
dzirnas (pi.), OPruss. girnoywis (pi.), of s.m.,
OSlav. zrunuvi (pL), 'mill', Olr. brdo, bro, W.
breuan, OCo. brou, 'hand mill*.

## querulous
querulous, adj., fretful. — ML. querulosus, fr. L.
querulus, 'complaining', fr. queri, 'to complain'.
See quarrel, 'dispute', and -ous.
Derivatives: querulous-ly, adv., querulous-ness,
n.

## query
query, n. — Anglicized fr. L. quaere, imper. of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:637 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: QUEST | 610 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:637 COLUMN:1 -->
quaerere, 'to seek, ask', which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. quaere. Cp. also acquire, acquisition,
conquer, conquest, disquisition, exquisite,
inquest, inquire, inquisition, inquisitive, perquisite,
prerequisite, quaestor, querido, quest, question,
request, require, requisite, requisition.
Derivatives: querist, n. (q.v.), query, tr. andintr.
v., query-ing-ly, adv.

## quest
quest, n. — ME. questet fr. OF. queste (F. quite),
prop, 'the act of seeking', VL. quaesita, for L.
quaesita, fem. pp. of quaerere, 'to seek, ask',
used as a noun.

## quest
quest, intr. and tr. v. — ME. questen, fr. MF.
quester, fr. OF. queste. See quest, n.
Derivative: quesi-er, n.

## question
question, n. — ME. questioun, fr. OF. ( = F.)
question, fr. L. quaestionem, ace. oi quaestid>
'inquiry, question', fr. quaerere (pp. quaesxtus), 'to
seek, ask'. See qnery and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending see suff. -ion.

## question
question, tr. and intr. v. — MF. (= F.) question-
ner, fr. question. See question, n.
Derivatives: question-able, adj.,
question-ability, η., question-able-ness, n., question-abl-у, adv.,
questionary (q.v.), question-er, п., question-ing-
ly, adv., question-less, adj. and adv.

## questionary
questionary, adj., ])havingthe form of a question;
2) asking questions. — Late L. quaestionarius,
fr. L. quaestio. See question, п., and adj. suff. -ary.

## questionary
questionary, п., a questionnaire. — Either fr. ML.
quaestionarium, questidnarium (prop. neut. of
the Late L. adj. quaestiotiarius, used as a noun,
see questionary, adj.), or fr. F. questionnaire (see
next word).

## questionnaire
questionnaire, п., a list of formal questions. — F.,
'list, set of questions, questionnaire', fr.
question. See question, п., and 2nd subst. suff. -ary,

## quetzal
quetzal, п., 1) name of a bird of brilliant plumage
in Central America; 2) the monetary unit of
Guatemala. — Amer. Sp., fr. Nahuatl quetzalli,
lit. 'tail feather'.

## queue
queue, п., I) {her.) the tail of a beast; 2) plait of
hair worn hanging down behind; pigtail; 3) a
line of persons waiting for their turn. — MF.
(= F.), fr. OF. соё, fr. L. coda, secondary form
of cauda, 'tail1. See caudal and cp. cue, 'tail'.
Derivative: queue, intr. v.

## quibble
quibble, п., a petty evasion. — Dimin, of obsol.
quib, fr. L. quibus, dat. or abl. pi. of qui, 'who,
which', used frequently in legal documents. See
who, what and cp. quid, 'essence', quiddity.
Derivatives: quibble, intr. v., quibbl-er, n.

## quick
quick, adj., 1) living, alive (archaic); 2) rapid,
swift; 3) prompt; done promptly; 4) alert. —
ME. quik, quike, 'alive, lively*, fr. OE. cwicu,
'living, alive', rel. to OS., OFris. quik, ON.
kvikr, 'living, alive*, Du. kwi(e)k, 'lively, bright,
sprightly', OHG. quec, chec, cheh, MHG. queck,
kec, 'lively', G. keck, 'bold', fr. Teut. *qwiqwa-,
'living, alive', fr. I.-E. *gwrgwos, fr. base *gwei-,
'to live', whence Goth. *qius, gen. qiwis, 'alive',
OI. jivah, 'alive', jfvati, Avestic jvaiti, 'lives',
OPers.y/w-, 'living', Gk. βίος (prob. for *pif ος,
fr, l.-E. *gwiwos), 'life, the course of life', ζην
(fr. I.-E. *gwie-), 'to live', ζωή, 'life', L. vivus,
(for *gwiwos), 'living', vivo, vtvere (for *gwiwo),
'to live', vita (for *gwiwita), 'life*, OSIav. £ivg,
fiti, 'to live', ziyu, 'alive', zivotu, 'life*, Lith.
gfvas, 'living, alive', gyvata '(eternal) life', Olr.
biu, beo, W., Co. byw, Bret, beo, 'alive', Olr.
beothu, bethu (for *biwotut·), 'life', biad, 'means
of life', Olr. bith, W. byd, 'world', Toch. Α ςοΐ,
В caul, 'life', A iosi, В saisse, 'people' (lit. 'the
living ones'), Ъдауат, 'he lives', Arm. keam(for
*gwiya), Ί live'. Hitt. huish- is not cognate. Cp.
quitch. Cp. also bio-, hygiene, jiva, vital and words
there referred to. Cp. also zodiac, zoetic, zoo-
and the second element in usquebaugh, whisky.
Derivatives: quick, adv. and п., quick-en, tr. and
intr. v., quick-ly, adv., quick-ness, n.

## quick
quick, tr. and intr. v. — ME. quiken, fr. OE.
cwician, fr. cwicu, 'living, alive'. See quick, adj.

## quicksilver
quicksilver, n. — ME. quiksilver, fr. OE. cwicseol-

## for
for, lit. 'quick (i.e. living) silver', loan
translation of L. argentum vivum, 'mercury', whence
also MDu. quicsilver (Du. kwikzilver), OHG.
quecsilbar (MHG., G. quecksilber) and It. ar-
gento vivo, F. vif-argent. See quick and silver.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:637 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: quicksilver, tr. v., quicksilver-itig,
п., quicksilver-у, adj.

## quid
quid, п., for chewing. — ME. guide, 'cud', fr. OE.
cwidu. See cud.
Derivative; quid, tr. and intr. v., quidd-er, n.

## quid
quid, п., essence, quiddity. — L., 'what,
something, anything', neut. oiquis, 'who', cogn. with
OE. hwd, 'who', hwxt, 'what'. See who, what,
and cp. quibble, quiddity, quiddle, quip.

## quid
quid, п., pound sterling, sovereign (Brit. Slang).
— Of uncertain origin; possibly fr. L. quid,
'what, something, anything'. See quid, 'essence'.

## quiddity
quiddity, п., 1) the essence of a thing; 2) quibble.
— ML. quidditds, lit. 'whatness', formed fr. L.
quid, 'what', on analogy of qualitas, 'quality'.
See quid, 'essence', and -ity and cp. qniddle.

## quiddle
quiddle, intr. v., to trifle. — Prob. formed fr.
quid, 'essence, quiddity', on analogy of verbs
like piddle, twiddle, etc.
Derivative: quiddl-er, n.

## quid pro quo
quid pro quo, something for something. — Latin.
See quid, 'essence, quiddity', and pro-,

## quiesce
quiesce, intr. v., to become quiet. — L. quiiscere,
'to rest, repose', an inchoative verb formed.fr.
quies, gen. quietis, 'rest'. See quiet, n. and -esce
and cp. acquiesce,

## quiescence
quiescence, quiescency, n. — Late L. quiescentia,
fr. L. quiescens, gen. -entis. See next word and
-ce, resp. -cy.

## quiescent
quiescent, adj., quiet, still. — L. quiescens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of quiiscere, 'to rest, repose'.
See quiesce and -ent.
Derivative: quiescent-ly, adv.

## quiet
quiet, n. — ME., fr. L. quies, gen. quietis, 'rest,
repose, quiet', fr. I.-E. base *qweye~, *qwi(y)e-,
'to rest, repose, be comfortable', whence also
the second element in L. tranquillus (for *trans-
quilnos), 'quiet, still', and Goth, fveila, OE.
kwil, 'space of time'. See while and cp. acquiesce,
acquit, coy, quiet, adj., quietus, quite, quittance,
acquiesce, acquit, requiem, tranquil,

## quiet
quiet, adj. — Fr. L. quietus, 'calm, at rest', fr.
quies, gen. quietis, 'rest'. See quiet, n.
Derivatives: quiet-en, tr. and intr. v., quiet-ly,
adv., quiet-ness, n.

## quiet
quiet, tr. v., to cause to be quiet; intr. v., to
become quiet. — L. quiitare, 'to quiet, calm', fr.
L. quies, gen. quietis. See quiet, n.
Derivative: quiet-ive, adj.

## quietism
quietism, п., a religious movement based on
mysticism, founded by Molinos (1640-97), a
Spanish priest, in Rome. — It. quietismo, lit.
'passiveness', fr. quieto, 'calm, at rest', fr. L.
quietus. See quiet, adj., and -ism.

## quietist
quietist, п., an adherent of quietism. — See prec.
word and -ist.
Derivative: quietist-ic, adj.

## quietude
quietude, п., quietness. — MF. (= F.) quietude,
fr. Late L. quietude, 'quietude', fr. L. quietus.
See quiet, adj., and -ude.

## quietus
quietus, п., final acquittance; death. — Fr. ML.
phrase quietus est, 'he is quit', fr. L. quietus. See
quiet, adj.

## quill
quill, п., the hollow stem of a feather. — ME.
quilt rel. to LG. quiele, MHG. kil, G. Kiel; of
unknown origin.
Derivatives: quill, tr. v., to fold into rolls
resembling a quill, quill-ed, adj., quill-er, п.,
quilling, n.

## quillet
quillet, п., a quibble (archaic). —Prob. a
corruption of L. quidlibet, 'what you please', fr. quid,
'what' (see quid, 'essence') and libet, 'it pleases'.
See libidinous and cp. quodlibet.

## quilt
quilt, п., padded or lined bed covering. — ME.
quilte, fr. OF. coilte, cuilte, 'quilt, mattress', fr.
L. culcita, 'a sack filled with feathers, wool, etc.,
mattress, bolster*, which is perh. cogn. with Ol.
kurcah, 'bunch, tuft of grass'. Cp. counterpane,
coutil, cushion, quoit.
Derivatives: quilt, tr. v., quilt-ed, adj., quilt-er,
п., quilt-ing, n.

## quin-
quin-, form of quino- before a vowel.

## quinary
quinary, adj., arranged in fives. — L. qulnarius,
'consisting of five, containing five', fr. quint, 'five
each', which is rel. to quinque, 'five'. See quinque-
and adj. suff. -ary.

## quinate
