quinate, adj., composed of five leaflets (hot.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. quint, 'five

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:637 COLUMN:3 -->
each'. See prec. word.

## qninate
qninate, п., quinic acid (chem.) — Formed with
chem. suff. -ate fr. Sp. quina. See quinine.

## quince
quince, n. — ME. quynce, pi. of quyne, quine, fr.
OF. cooin, coin (F. coing), fr. VL. codoneum, fr.
L. cotdneum (scil. malum), a collateral form of
cydonium (malum), fr. Gk. κυδώνιον μαλον
(lit. 'apple of Cydonia'), popular transformation
of κυδόμαλον, 'quince'. This latter word was
interpreted as a compound κυδό-μαλον and its
first element associated with ΚυδωνΕ α, a town on
the north coast of Crete, as if κυδόμαλον
meant 'apple of Cydonia*. In reality, however,
κυδόμαλον is a loan word from an ancient
language of Asia Minor and was brought from
Greece to Italy through the medium of the
Etruscans. Cp. Κυτώνιον, a town in Lydia, lit.
'Quince Town', It. cotogno, OProvenc. codonh,
Catal. codony, OHG. quitina (MHG. quiten, G.
Quitte), 'quince', which are all borrowed ult. fr.
Gk. κυδόμαλον. Ср. Cotoneaster, Cydonia, and
the second element in melocoton.

## quincentenary
quincentenary, adj., pertaining to five hundred
years; п., a five-hundredth anniversary. —
Irregular formation fr. L. quinque, 'five' (see
quinque-) and centenary, 'a period of a hundred
years'. Cp. qningentenary.

## quincuncial
quincuncial, adj., of the form of a quincunx. — L.
quincuncidlis, fr. quincunx, gen. quincuncis. See
next word, and adj. suff. -al.

## quincunx
quincunx, п., an arrangement of five objects so
that one is at each corner of a square and one in
the middle. — L. quincunx, gen. qutnquncis, 'five
twelfths', abbreviation of *quinqu(e)-uncis, 'five
twelfths', fr. quinque, 'five', and uncia, 'ounce'.
See quinque-, ounce, 'a weight', and cp. uncia.

## quinetum
quinetum, п., a mixture of alkaloids from the bark
of red cinchona (pharm.) — Coined by the
Dutch scientist Dr. De Vrij fr. quin- and L.
-etum, a suff. denoting a group of plants, as in
arboretum, *a place grown with trees' (see
arboretum).

## quin gen tenary
quin gen tenary, adj. and п., quincentenary. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ary fr. L. quingenti, 'five
hundred', on analogy of centen-ary, 'a period of
a hundred years'. See quinque- and cp.
quincentenary.

## quinic
quinic, adj., pertaining to quinine. — Formed
from quinine with adj. suff. -ic.

## qninicine
qninicine, п., a poisonous alkaloid, C20Ha4N2O3
(chem.) — F., coined by the French chemist and
bacteriologist Louis Pasteur (1822-95) in 1853
fr. quinic (in quinic acid) and chem. suff. -ine.

## quinidine
quinidine, quinidin, п., a crystalline alkaloid,
C20H24N2O2 (chem.)y— A derivative of quinine.

## quinine
quinine, n. — Sp. quina, short for quinquina,
'cinchona bark', fr. Quechua quinquina, of s.m. For
the ending see chem. suff. -ine.
Derivatives: quin-ism, п., quinin-ize, tr. v.

## quino-
quino-, before a vowel quin-, combining form
denoting: 1) cinchona bark; 2) quinic acid; 3)
quinoline; 4) quinone. — Fr. Sp. quina, 'cinchona
bark'. See quinine.

## quinoline
quinoline, п., an oily nitrogenous base, C„H,N
(chem.) — F. quinoliine, coined by the French
chemist Charles-Frederic Gerhardt (1816-56) fr.
quin-, -ol(fr. L. oleum, 'oil'), and chem. suff. -ine.

## quinone
quinone, п., either of two isomeric compounds,
CeH4Oa (chem.) — Formed from the first
syllable of quinic (acid) and suff. -one.
Derivatives: quinon-ize, tr. v., quinon-iz-ation, n.

## quinonoid
quinonoid, adj., resembling quinone. —
Compounded of prec. word and Gk. -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## quinqu-
quinqu-, form of quinque- before a vowel.

## quinquagenarian
quinquagenarian, adj., fifty years old; п., a
quinquagenarian person. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. quinquagenarius, 'fifty years old'. See next
word.

## quinquagenary
quinquagenary, adj., fifty years old. — L.
quinquagenarius, 'fifty years old', fr. quinquageni,
'fifty each', fr. qulnquaginta, 'fifty', which is
formed fr. quinque, 'five', with -gintd, a suff.
denoting tens. This suff. is cogn. with Gk. -κοντά
ϊητρια-κοντα, 'thirty', τεσσαρά-κοντα, 'forty',
etc. See five. For the etymology of Gk. suff.
-κοντά, L. suff. -ginta, see penteconta-. For the
ending of quinquagenary see adj. suff. -ary.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:638 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 611 | QUOTE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:638 COLUMN:1 -->

## Quinquagesima
Quinquagesima, n.t the Sunday before Lent (Ec-
cles.) — ML. quinquagesima (scil. dies), 'the
fiftieth day', fem. of L. quinquugesimus, 'fiftieth',
fr. quinqudgintd, 'fifty'. See quinquagenary.

## quinquangnlar
quinquangnlar, adj., having five angles, —
Compounded of quinque- and angular.

## quinque-
quinque-, before a vowel quinqu-, combining form
meaning 'five". — L., fr. quinque, fr. I.-E.
*penqwe, with assimilation of the initial p- to the
following -q-. See five and cp. penta-. Cp. also
cinq(ue), keno.

## quinquennial
quinquennial, adj., 1) occurring once every five
years; 2) lasting five years. — Formed fr. L.
quinquennalis, 'that takes place every fifth year'
(but influenced in form by biennial), fr. quin-
quennis, 'of five years'. See quinque- and annual.
For the change of Latin a~ (in annus) to ё (in
quinq-ennis) see accent and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivative: quinquennial-ly, adv.

## quinquennium
quinquennium, п., a period of five years. — L.
quinquennium, fr. quinquennis, 'of five years'. See
prec. word.

## quinquereme
quinquereme, п., a galley having five banks of
oars. — L. quinqueremis, fr. quinque, 'five', and
remus, 'oar'. See quinque- and bireme and cp.
words there referred to.

## quinquevalence
quinquevalence, quinquevalency, п., state of being
quinquevalent (спет.) — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## quinquevalent
quinquevalent, adj., having a valence of five
(chem.) — Compounded of quinque- and L.
valens, gen. -ends, pres. part, of valere, 'to have
power' (see -valent); prop, loan translation of G.
Junfwertig, which is compounded offiinf, 'five',
and Wert, 'value'. Cp. pentavalent.

## quinquina
quinquina, п., cinchona. — Sp., fr. Quechua
quinquina. See quinine.

## quinsy
quinsy, n. — ME. quinesie, quinsie, fr. MF. qui-
nancie (F. esquinancie), fr. ML. cynanche, fr. Gk.
κυνάγχη, 'sore throat*, lit. 'dog quinsy', fr.
κύων, gen. κυνός, 'dog', and &γχε(.ν, 'to squeeze
(esp. the throat), throttle, strangle', which is
cogn. with L. angere, 'to press together, throttle,
torment'. See hound and anger and cp. cynanche,
squinancy.

## quint
quint, n. — F. quinte, 'quint' (fem. of quint, 'fifth'),
fr. L. quinta (pars), 'a fifth (part)', fem, of
quintus, 'fifth*, which is rel. to quinque, 'five'. See
five, fifth and cp. quinque-, Quentin.

## quintain
quintain, n. (hist.), 1) an object used for tilting;
2) the sport of tilting pursued at a quintain. —
OF. quintaine, fr. ML. quintana, fr. L. quintana
(via), 'a street in a camp which intersected the
tents of two legions in such a manner as to
separate the fifth maniple from the sixth and the
fifth turma from the sixth', from quintdnus, 'the
fifth in order', fr. quintus, 'fifth'. See quint and
cp. quintan.

## quintal
quintal, п., a weight. — F., fr. ML. quintdle, fr.
Arab, qintar. See kantar and cp. kilderkin.

## quintan
quintan, adj., occurring every fifth day; п., fever
recurring every fifth day (counting both days of
consecutive occurrence). — L·. quintdnus, 'fifth in
order', fr. quintus, "fifth'. See quint and cp.
quintain.

## quinte
quinte, п., a thrust or parry, fifth in order
(fencing) — F. See quint.

## quintessence
quintessence, п., pure essence. — F., fr. ML.
quinta essentia, 'the fifth (i.e. the finest) essence
or element', loan translation of Gk. πεμπτή
ουσία. See quint and essence.

## quintessential
quintessential, adj. — Formed fr. prec. word with
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: quintessential-ity, п., quintessential-
ly, adv.

## quintet
quintet, also quintette, n. — F. quintette, fr. It.
quintetto, dimin. of quinto, 'fifth', fr. L. quintus.
See quint and -ef, -ette.

## quintillion
quintillion, п., 1) in the United States and France,
the cube of a million (i.e. 1 followed by 18
zeros); in Great Britain and Germany, the fifth
power of a million (i.e. 1 followed by 30 zeros).
— F., formed fr. L. quintus, 'fifth' (see quint), on
analogy of million (q.v.) Cp. billion and words
there referred to.

## quintuple
quintuple, adj., fivefold. — MF. (= F.), fr. Late
L. quintuplex, 'fivefold*, compounded of quintus,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:638 COLUMN:2 -->
'fifth', and -plex, gen. -pficis, '-fold', which is
related to the stem of plicare, 'to fold'. See ply,
'to bend', and cp. next word.
Derivatives: quintuple, n. and tr. and intr. v.,
quintupl-et, n.

## quintuplicate
quintuplicate, adj. and n. — Formed fr. quintuple
on analogy of duplicate.
Derivative: quintuplicat-ion, n.

## quip
quip, п., a jest, sarcastic remark. — Fr. earlier
quippy, fr. L. quippe, 'forsooth, indeed' (used in
an ironical sense), which stands for *quidpe, fr.
quid, 'what' (see quid, 'essence'), and the
emphatic particle -pe. Cp. Lith. kai-p, 'as', whose
two elements are cognate with L. quid, resp. -pe.
Derivatives: quip, tr. v., quipp-er, п., quipp-ish,
adj., quipp-ish-ness, n.

## quipu
quipu, п., a method used by the ancient Peruvians
to record facts by means of colored cords.— Fr.
Quechua quipu, 'knot'.

## quire
quire, п., 24 (sometimes 25) sheets of paper. —
ME. quaer, quair, orig. 'four sheets o*f paper', fr.
OF. quaier, quaer, caier, caer (F. cahier), fr. VL.
quaternum, 'four sheets (of paper)' (whence also
It. quaderno, Sp. cuaderno), fr. L. quaterni, 'four
together, four each', fr. quaiiuor, 'four'. See
quaternary and cp. cahier.
Derivative: quire, tr. v.

## quire
quire, n. — A var. spelling of choir.

## Quirinal
Quirinal, п., 1) one of the seven hills of Rome; 2)
the Italian civil government. — L. mons Quiri-
ndlis, fr. Quirinus. See Quirinus.

## Quirinus
Quirinus, п., an ancient god of war (Roman
mythol.) — L. Quirinus, rel. to Quirites. See
Quirites.

## Quirites
Quirites, n. pi., the citizens of the Roman nation.
— L. Quirites, 'Roman citizens' (orig. 'the
inhabitants of the Sabine town Cures), pi. oiQuiris
= Curis, a name which possibly derives from the
contraction of *co-wiriom, 'the whole of
citizens', fr. со-, 'together', and vir, gen. viri, 'man'.
See со- and virile and cp. Quirinal, Quirinus. Cp.
also cry.

## quirk
quirk, п., a sudden turn. — Of unknown origin.
Derivatives: quirk, tr. and intr. v., quirk-y, adj.

## quirt
quirt, п., a riding whip with a short handle and a
braided leather lash. — Mexican Sp. cuarta,
'rope', rel. to Sp. cuerda, 'rope', fr. L. corda, fr.
Gk. χορδή. See chord.
Derivative: quirt, tr. v.

## quisling
quisling, п., a traitor. — Named after Vidkun
Quisling, the notorious Norwegian traitor in
World War II.
Derivative: quisling-ism, n.

## qnit
qnit, tr. and intr. v. — ME. quiten, fr. OF. quiter,
fr. ML. quitare, quittare, 'to set free*, fr. quitus,
quittus, 'at rest, free from work, free', fr. L,
quietus, 'at rest'. See quiet, adj., and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also acquit.
Derivative: quitt-er, n.

## quit
quit, adj. — ME. quit, quite, fr. OF. quite, quitte,
fr. ML. quitus, quittus. See prec. word..

## quitch
quitch, п., also quitch grass. — ME. *quicche, fr.
OE. cwice, rel. to Dan. kvikker, Norw. kvika,
MDu. queke, Du. kweek, G. Quecke, fr. Teut.
*qwiqwa-, 'living' (see quick, adj.); so called in
allusion to the vitality of this plant. Cp. couch
grass.

## quite
quite, adv. — ME., fr. the adj. quite, 'free'. See
quit, adj.

## quits
quits, adj. — ME., fr. ML. quitus, quittus. See
quit, adj.

## quittance
quittance, п., release. — ME. quitance, fr. OF.
quitance (F. quittance), fr. quiter. See quit, v.,
and -ance.

## quittor
quittor, п., an inflammatory disease of the feet of
horses, asses and mules (veter.) — ME. quiture,
fr. OF. coiture, cuiture, 'a cooking, burning', fr.
L. coctura, fr. coctus, pp. of coquere, 'to cook'.
See cook.

## quiver
quiver, intr. v., to tremble; tr. v., to cause to
quiver. — A var. of quaver (q.v.)
Derivatives: quiver, п., quiver-ing, adj.

## quiver
quiver, п., a case for holding arrows. — ME., fr.
AF. quiveir, fr. OF. quivre (also cuivre, cuevre),
which is prob. of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. kochar,
kochdri, OE. cocur, cocer, 'quiver*, and see
cocker, 'quiver*.

## qui vive
qui vive, a sentinel's challenge corresponding to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:638 COLUMN:3 -->
E. 'Who goes there?' — F., lit. "(long) live
who ?" fr. qui, 'who' ( fr. L. qui)aa.a pres. subj.
of vivre, 'to live' (fr. L. vivere). See who and
vital.

## quixotic
quixotic, also quixotical, adj., like Don Quixote;
extravagantly chivalrous. — Fr. Sp. Don
Quixote, name of the hero of Cervantes' famous
satirical romance, fr. quixote (new spelling:
quijote), 'thigh', fr. L. coxa (see coxa, cuisse).
For the ending see suff. -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: quixotic-al-ly, adv.

## quixotism
quixotism, п., extravagant chivalry. — See prec.
word and -ism.

## quixotry
quixotry, п., quixotism. — See quixotic and -ry.

## quiz
quiz, п., 1) an odd-looking person (rare); 2) a
practical joke; 3) a questioning. — Of uncertain
origin. According to Crowther's Encyclopaedia
of Phrases and Origins, p. 110, this word owes
its existence to a wager laid down in 1780 by
Daley, the manager of a Dublin theater, who
bet that he would introduce a new word into
the English language. The new word was written
on the walls of most houses in Dublin.
Everywhere in the streets people tried to find out the
meaning of the mysterious word never heard
before. The word was quiz.
Derivatives: quiz, tr. and intr. v., quizz-ee, п.,
quizz-er, п., quizz-ic-al, adj., quizz-ic-al-ly, adv.,
quizz-ic-al-ity, п., quizz-ic-al-ness, n.

## quoad
quoad, prep., so far as. — L., compounded of
quo-ad, fr. quo, 'whither*, and ad, 'toward, to'.
The first element is prop, the abl. ofquis, 'who",
qui, 'who, which'; see who. For the second
element see ad-,

## quod
quod, 'which', in L. phrases, as e.g. quod vide
(abbreviated q.v.), 'which see', quod erat
demonstrandum (Q.E.D.), 'which was to be
demonstrated". — L., neut. of qui, 'who, which'; cogn.
with OE, hwa, 'who'. See who.

## quod
quod, п., prison (Brit. Slang). — A var. of quad,
abbreviation of quadrangle, hence lit. 'a four-
angled court enclosed by buildings or a fence'.
Derivative; quod, tr. v., to put in prison.

## quodlibet
quodlibet, п., a nicety, subtlety. — L., 'what you
please*, compounded of quod, 'what', and libet,
'it pleases'. See quod, 'which', and libidinous,
and cp. quillet.
Derivatives: quodlibet-arian, n., quodlibet-ic,
quodlibet-ic-af, adjs., quodlibet-tc-al-ly, adv.

## quoif
quoif, n. — A var. of coif.

## quoin
quoin, п., wedge. — A var. of coin.
Derivatives: quoin, tr. v., quoin-ing, n.

## quoit
quoit, п., an iron disk; quoits (pi., but construed
as a sing.), a ring for throwing at a peg. — ME.
coite, fr. OF. coite, which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: quoit, tr. and intr. v., quoit-er, n.

## quondam
quondam, adj., former. — L., 'formerly', for
*quom-dam, fr. quom, cum, 'when, as', prop,
ancient ace. of qui, 'who, which' (see who), and the
emphatic suff. -dam, which appears also in qui-
dam, 'somebody', and is rel. to the suff. -de and
the prep, de, 'of, from' (see de-).

## quorum
quorum, п., the minimum number of members
necessary for the transaction of business at an
assembly. — L. quorum, 'of whom', gen. pi. of
qui, 'who', which is cogn. with OE. hwa, 'who*
(see who); so called from the first word of the
commission issued to certain justices in
England: quorum aliquem vestrum ... unum (duos,
tres, etc.) esse volumus ('of whom we wish one,
two, three, etc., of you to be').

## quota
quota, п., proportional share. — ML., short for
L. quota pars, 'how great a part', fem. of quotus,
'which in order or number', fr. quot, 'how
many', which is short for *quoti and is cogn.
with OI. kali, Hitt. kuwatta, 'how many?', Gk.
πόσος. Lesbian πόσσος, Ion. κόσος (for *potyos),
'which (of a given number) ?', all from the
pronominal base *kwo-, whence also who (q.v.)
Cp. quotation, quote, quotient, the first
element in quotidian and the second element in
aliquot.

## quotation
quotation, n. — ML. quotdtio, gen. -onis, fr.
quotatus, pp. of quotare. See next word and
-ation.
Derivatives: quotation-al, adj., quotation-al-ly,
adv., quotation-ist, n.

## quote
quote, tr. and intr. v. — ML. quotare, 'to mark

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:639 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: QUOTH | 612 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:639 COLUMN:1 -->
off the number of chapters', fr. L. quotus. See
quota.
Derivatives: quot-able, adj., quot-abil-ity, п.,
quot-able-ness, п., quot-abl-y, adv., quotation
(q.v.), quot-ative, adj., quot-ative-ly, adv., quote,
п., quotation, quotation mark,

## quoth
quoth, tr. v., said· — ME., past of quethen, 'to
speak, say', fr. OE. cwedan, 'to speak, say', rel.
to OS. quethan, ON. kveda, OFris. quetha, OHG.
quedan, Goth, qifran. Cp. bequeath, bequest.
Quoth was influenced in form by quote,

## quotha
quotha, interj. (archaic). — ME. quoth ha, 'said

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:639 COLUMN:2 -->
he", fr. quoth and ha, the unstressed form of ME.
he, 'he*. See he.

## quotidian
quotidian, adj., occurring every day, daily. —
ME., fr. OF. cotidian (F. quotidien), fr. L. quoti-
dianus, 'daily', fr. quoti-, fr. quotus, 'which in
order or number', and dies, 'day'. See quota and
dies поп.
Derivatives: quotidian, п., quotidian-ly, adv.,
quotidian-ness, n.

## quotient
quotient, п., the number of times one quantity is

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:639 COLUMN:3 -->
contained in another. — L. quotiens, quoties,
'how often, how many times', fr. quot, 'how
many' (see quota). The adv. quotiens was treated
as if it were an adj. or noun of the 3rd
declension (i.e. with a genitive *quotientis).

## quo warrnnto
quo warrnnto, п., a writ commanding a person to
show 'by what warrant', he is holding an office.
— ML., 'by what warrant1, fr. abl. of L. qui,
'which1 (see who), and abl. of Latinized E.
warrant.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:640 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:640 COLUMN:1 -->
raad, п., legislative body in the former Orange
Free State. — Du. raad, 'advice, counsel;
council', fr. MDu. rzt, raed, rel. to OE. reed, OS. rdd,
ON. гад, OFris. red, OHG., MHG. rdt, G. Rat,
'advice, councir, OE. rskdan, 'to advise, counsel,
discuss, deliberate, guess, interpret, read'. See
read and cp. the second element in V о Iks rand.

## rabban
rabban, п., distinguishing title given to patriarchs
and the presidents of the Sanhedrin since the
time of Gamaliel the Elder, who was the first to
bear this title. — Aram, rabban, lit. Our teacher*,
fr. rabh, 'master, teacher', which is rel. to
Mishnaic Heb. rabh, of s.m. See rabbi.

## rabbet
rabbet, п., a groove cut out of the edge of
anything {carpentry).— ME. rabet, fr. OF. ( = F.)
rabat, 'a beating back', back formation fr. ra-
battre, 'to beat back'. See rebate, v.
Derivative: rabbet, tr. v.

## rabbi
rabbi, n. — Late L., fr. Gk. £αββί, fr. Mishnaic
Heb. rabbi, 'my master', title of respect, formed
with -f, pronom. suff. of the 1st person in the
singular, fr. rabh, 'chief, master, teacher', which
derives fr. Heb. rabh, 'much, many, great', from
stem r-b-b, 'to be great or numerous', whence
also robh, 'multitude, abundance, greatness',
r bkdbha , 'multitude, ten thousand, myriad',
ribbo, 'ten thousand, myriad', Heb. rabh is rel.
to Aram.-Syr. rabh, 'great; chief, master,
teacher', Akkad. rab, 'chief, captain', Arab, rabba,
'was great or dense', rabb, 'master', Ethiop.
rabdba, 'it spread'. Cp. rabban, the second word
in Ahabah Rabba and the first element in
Jeroboam, Rnbmag and Rabshakeh.

## rabbin
rabbin, п., rabbi. — F. rabbin or ML. rabbinus,
fr. Late L. rabbi. See rabbi.

## rabbinate
rabbinate, п., the office of a rabbi. — Formed fr.
rabbin with subst. suff. -ate.

## rabbinic
rabbinic, rabbinical, adj. — F. rabbinique, fr.
rabbin, 'rabbi'. See rabbin and -ic, resp. also -aj.
Derivative: rabbinic-al-ly, adv.

## rabbinism
rabbinism, п., the whole of the teaching of the
rabbis. — Formed fr. rabbin with suff. -ism. Cp.
F. rabbinisme.

## rabbinist
rabbinist, or rabbinite, п., a Jew adhering to the
oral laws laid down in the Talmud and to the
traditions of the rabbis, in opposition to the
Karaites. — Formed fr. rabbin with suff. -ist,
resp. subst. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: rabbinist-ic, rabbinist-ic-al, adjs.

## rabbit
rabbit, n. — ME. rabet, 'young of the cony', of
uncertain origin. It derives perh. fr. OF. (= F.)
rabot, 'carpenter's plane', prob. orig. 'rabbit'
(cp. F. rabouillere, 'rabbit's hole'), whence 'the
animal resembling a plane, rabbit'. It is also
possible that ME. rabet comes fr. MDu. robbe,
'rabbit', whence also Walloon robete, 'rabbit'.
MDu. robbe prob. derives fr. Rob, dimin. of
Robert. For sense development cp. robin, which
derives fr. Robin, another dimin. of Robert.
Derivatives: rabbit, intr. and tr. v., rabbit-y, adj.

## rabble
rabble, п., mob. — ME. rabel,*a pack of animals'.
The word prob. denoted originally 'a noisy
crowd of animals' and is related to rabble, 'to
gabble'.
Derivative: rabble, tr. v., to mob.

## rabble
rabble, tr. and intr. v., to gabble (obsol. or dial.)
— ME. rablen, prob. of imitative origin. Cp.
MDu. rabbelen, LG. rabbeln, 'to chatter'.
Derivative: rabble-ment, n.

## rabble
rabble, п., an iron bar for stirring molten metal
in puddling. — F. ruble, fr. OF. roable, fr. L. ru-
tabulum, 'an instrument for raking, a fire
shovel', fr. mere, 'to rake up', which is cogn. with
Lith. raju, rami, 'to pluck out, weed out', raveti,
'to weed', OSlav. ryo, Ί dig', rylu, rylo, 'spade',

## rovuy 'ditch'
rovuy 'ditch', Avestic rao(i)Sya-, 'to break up
(the ground)', G. roden, reuten, 'to root out',
Mir. ruam, 'spade'. L. mere in the sense 'to rake
up', is distinct fr. mere, *to hasten, run'. See
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, p. 453.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:640 COLUMN:2 -->
R
Derivatives: rabble, tr. v., rabbl-er, n.

## Rabelaisian
Rabelaisian, adj., resembling Rabelais or his style.
— Formed from the name of Francois Rabelais
(1494-1553) with suff. -ian.
Derivative: Rabelaisian, п., Rabelaisian-ism, n.

## Rabia
Rabia, n,, name of the third and fourth months in
the Moslem year. — Arab, rabl·, prop, 'spring
month', fr. rabl·, 'spring', from the base of the
verb raba'O, 'he abode, dwelled', which is rel. to
Aram. rebha\ Heb. rabha\ 'he lay down, lay',
Mishnaic Heb. r■ bhVa' , 'rainfall', Arab, rabada,
'he lay down on the breast, stretched himself
out', Heb. rdbkatz, 'he stretched himself out,
lay down', Akkad. rabdsu, *to lie down, dwell',
tarbasu, 'court yard' (whence Aram, tarbitza,
'garden near the house; hall, school hall').

## rabid
rabid, adj., violent, raging. — L. rabidusy 'raging,
furious, enraged', fr. rabid, rabere, 'to be mad,
to rave* (whence also rabies, 'rage'), which
together with OI. rabhas-, 'violence, impetuosity',
rabkasaft, 'violent, impetuous', prob. derives fr.
*rabh-, a secondary form of I.-E. base *labh-,
'to take, seize'; see lemma and adj. suff. -id and
cp. rabies, rage. See Walde-Hofmann, LEW.,
II, p.413s.v.rabies,andErnout-Meillet,DELL.,
p. 562 s.v. rabio.
Derivatives: rabid-ity, п., rabid-ly, adv., rabid-
ness, n.

## rabies
rabies, п., hydrophobia (med. and vet.) — L., fr.
rabere. See prec. word.

## Rabmag
Rabmag, п., title of a Babylonian official
mentioned in Jer. 39: 3. — Heb. rabk-mdgh, fr.
Akkad. rab mugi, title of an official. For Akkad.
rab see rabbi and cp. the first element in next
word. Akkad. mugi is of uncertain origin. It is
not connected with OPers. magush, 'magician'.

## Rabshakeh
Rabshakeh, п., title of the Assyrian dignitary who
treated with Hezekiah, king of Judah (see II
Kings, ch. 18 and Is., ch. 36). — Heb. rabh-
shaqe, fr. Akkad. rab-shaqu, which according to
Eberhard Schrader denotes 'the chief officer' or
'captain', fr. rab, 'chief, and shaqu, pi. shaqe,
'high' (see his Die Keilinschriften und das Alte
Testament, 2nd edition, p. 319). According to
Heinrich Zimmern the meaning of rab-shaqu is
'chief cupbearer', fr. rab, 'chief, and shaqu, pi.
shaqe, 'cupbearer' (see ZDMG., 53, pp. 116 ff.)
For Akkad. rab see rabbi and cp. the first
element in prec. word. Akkad. shaqu, 'high', is of
unknown etymology. Akkad. shaqu, 'cupbearer',
derives fr. shaqu, 'to give to drink', which is rel.
to Heb. hishqa', Aram.-Syr. ashqt, Arab, saqa,
Ethiop. saqa, 'he gave to drink', Heb. mashqeh,
'butler, cupbearer; drink', shoqeth, 'watering
trough', Aram, mashqe, mashqeya, 'drink'; cp.
sakia.

## raca
raca, п., a term of reproach. —· Fr. Aram, reqa,
emphatic state of req, 'empty; light, frivolous',
which is rel. to Heb. req, of s.m.

## raccoon
raccoon, also racoon, п., a carnivorous mammal.
— Algonquian (Powhatan dial.) arahkun, fr.
arahkunem, 'he scratches with his hands'; so
called in allusion to the raccoon's habit of
leaving scratches on the bark of the tree he climbs.
Cp. coon.

## race
race, п., running. — ME. ras, rase, fr. ON. ras,
'running, race", rel. to OE. rxs, 'running, rush',
rsesan, 'to rush headlong', MDu. rasen, 'to rave,
rage', MHG. rasen, G. rasen, OE. rasettan, of
s.m., and prob. cognate with Gk. έρωή (for
*έρωσά), 'quick, motion, rush, force', έρωεΐν
(for *έρωσεΐν), 'to rush, rush forth', L. rorarii,
'lightarmed troops', lit. 'runners'.
Derivatives: race, intr. and tr. v., rac-er, п.,
racking, verbal n. and adj.

## race
race, п., root, esp. ginger root. — OF. rati, rats,
fr. L. rddicem, ace. οι radix, 'root'. See radix.

## race
race, tr. and intr. v., to scratch. — A var. of raze.
The orig. meaning of the v. race was 'to erase'.

## race
race, п., family, tribe. — MF. ( — F.), fr. earlier

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:640 COLUMN:3 -->
rasse, fr. It. razza, which together with Sp. rata,
Port, raza, prob. derives fr. Arab, ra's, 'head,
beginning, origin', which is rel. to Heb. rush, of
s.m. See Bereshith and cp. rais, reis, resh.
Derivatives: rac-ial, adj., rac-ial-ism, п., rac-ial-
ist, п., rac-ial-ist-ic, adj., rac-ial-ly, adv., rac-y,
adj., rac-i-ly, adv., rac-i-ness, п., rac-ism, п.,
rac-ist, n.

## raceme
raceme, п., a type of flower cluster {bot.) — L.
racemus, 'the stalk of a cluster of grapes'; which,
likeGk. ρί ξ, gen. ραγός, 'berry', was borrowed
from a Mediterranean language. Cp. the second
element in acrorhagus, Haloragidaceae. Cp. also
raisin.
Derivative: racem-ed, adj.

## racemic
racemic, adj., ]) pertaining to racemes; 2)
pertaining to optically inactive compounds {chem.)
— Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. L. racemus. See
prec. word.

## racemism
racemism, п., the state of being racemic {chem.)
— Formed with suff. -ism fr. L. racemus. See
raceme.

## racemose
racemose, adj., growing in the form of a raceme
(bot.) — L. racemosus, 'clustering', fr. racemus.
See raceme and adj. suff. -ose.

## racemous
racemous, adj., racemose. — L. racemosus. See
prec. word and -ous.
Derivative: racemous-ly, adv.

## Rachel
Rachel, 1) fern. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the younger
daughter of Laban and wife of Jacob. — Late
L., fr. Gk. 'Ραχήλ, fr. Heb. Rdhel, lit. 'ewe'; rel.
to Arab, rahil, Aram, rahla, Akkad. lahru (a
metathesized form), 'ewe'.

## rachio-
rachio-, also rhachio-, before a vowel rachi-, also
rhachi-, combining form meaning 'spinal';
'spinal and'. — Gk. ραχι-. £αχιο-, fr. ράχις,
'spine'. See next word.

## rachis
rachis, also rhachis, п., 1) the spine {anat.); 2) the
shaft of a feather (zool); 3) prolongation of the
stalk in compound leaves {bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. ραχις, 'spine', which is rel. to ραχός
(£αχος), 'thorn hedge', and cogn. with Lith.
rdzas, 'a dry scion, stubble, scrub, prong of a
fork', raiis, 'stubble', Olr. /race, 'needle'. Cp.
rickets.
Derivative: rachit-ic, adj.

## rachitis
rachitis, also rhachitis, п., inflammation of the
rachis; rickets (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
ραχΐτις (scil. νόσος), lit. 'rachitic disease', fr.
ράχι,ς. See prec. word and -itis.

## rack
rack, п., instrument of torture, etc. — ME. racke
and recke, 'framework', prob. fr. MDu. recke,
of s.m.? lit. 'something stretched out', fr. recken
(Du. rekken), 'to stretch out', which is rel. to OE.
reccan, OS. rekkian, ON. rekja, Swed. racka,
OFris. reza, OHG. recchen, MHG., G. recken,
Goth, uf-rakjan, 'to stretch out', and cogn. with
Gk. όρέγειν, 'to reach, stretch out', L, regere, 'to
stretch, extend; to rule', porrigere, 'to stretch
out'. See regent, adj., and words there referred
to and cp. esp. rake, 'a tool'.

## rack
rack, tr. v., to torture. — MDu. recken, 'to stretch
out'. See prec. word.

## rack
rack, п., wreckage. — A var. spelling of wrack.

## rack
rack, tr. v., to pour off (wine) from the lees. —
ME. rakken, fr. OProven?. arracar, fr. raca,
'skins of grapes left after wine pressing'.

## rack
rack, intr. v., to move with the particular gait
called rack (said of a horse). — A var. of rock,
'to move to and fro'.
Derivative; rack, п., a particular gait of a horse.

## rack
rack, п., clouds driven before the wind. — Of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. reka, 'to drive', rek,
'wreckage'. See wrack, wreck.
Derivative: rack, intr. v., to fiy (said of driven
clouds).

## rack
rack, п., arrack. — Shortened fr. arrack. The
beginning of the Arabic word 'araq was mistaken
for the Arabic article al-, ar-, and consequently
dropped.

## racket
racket, also racquet, п., a bat for playing tennis,
badminton, etc. — MF. (= F.) raquette, orig.
rachette, with the sense 'palm of the hand', fr.
Arab, raha , in vulgar pronunciation rdhet, 'the
palm of the hand'. Sense development was
influenced by F. jeu de раите, 'tennis', lit. 'play
with the palm of the hand'.

## racket
racket, п., ]) noise, disturbance; uproar; 2)
dishonest business. — ProB. of imitative origin.
Cp. Gael, racaid, 'noise'.
Derivatives: racket, incr. and tr. v., racketeer,
п., racket-eer-ing, п., racket-y, adj.

## raconteur
raconteur, п., a narrator, storyteller. — F., fr. ra-
conter, 'to tell, narrate', fr. re- (see re-) and OF.
aconter, fr. a, 'to' (fr. L. ad, see ad-), and comer,
'to tell*. See recount and -or, suff. denoting an
agent.

## racoon
racoon, n. — See raccoon.

## racquet
racquet, n. — See racket,'a bat for playing tennis'.

## radar
radar, п., an electronic instrument for the
location of objects by radio waves. — A word
coined from the initials of the phrase radio detecting
and ranging.

## raddle
raddle, п., red ocher. — A var. of ruddle.
Derivative: raddle, tr. v., to color with red ocher.

## radeau
radeau, п., raft, float. — F., fr. OF. radel, fr. VL.
*ratellus, dimin. of L. ratis, 'raft, float'. See
rood and cp. Ratitae.

## radial
radial, adj., of, or like, a ray or radius. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. radius. See radius.
Derivatives: radial, п., radial-ity, п., radial-ize,
tr. v., radial-iz-ationt п., radial-ly, adv.

## radian
radian, п., 1) arc of a circle, equal in length.to the
radius; 2) the angle subtending this arc. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. radius. See radius.

## radiance
radiance, less frequently radiancy, n. — Formed
from next word with suff. -ce, Tesp. -cy.

## radiant
radiant, adj. — ME., fr. L. radians, gen. -amis,
pres. part, of radiare. See next word and -ant.
Derivatives: radiant, п., radiant-ly, adv.

## radiate
radiate, intr. v., to emit rays; to be radiant; tr. v.,
to emit in rays. — L. radiatus, 'furnished with
rays', pp. of radiare, 'to furnish with beams,
make beaming, irradiate', fr. radius, 'ray'. See
radius and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: radiat-ed, radiat-ing, radiat-ive,
adjs.

## radiate
radiate, adj., having rays. — L. radiatus, pp. of
radiare. See radiate, v.
Derivatives: radiate-ly, adv., radiate-ness, n.

## radiation
radiation, adj. — L. radiatio, gen. -onis, 'a shining,
radiation*, fr. radiatus, pp. of radiare. See
radiate, v., and -ion.
Derivative: radiation-al, adj.

## radiator
radiator, п., an apparatus for radiating heat. —
Formed with agential suff. -or fr. L. radiatus,
pp. of radiare. See radiate, v.

## radical
radical, adj. — Lit. 'having roots', fr. Late L.
radicalis, fr. L. radix, gen. -Icis, 'root'. See
radix and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: radical, п., radical-ism, п.,
radically, п., radical-ize, tr. and intr. v., radical-iz-
ation, п., radical-ly, adv., radical-ness, n.

## radicand
radicand, п., the number under a radical sign
{math.) — L. radlcandus, gerundive of radicare
or radicarl·, 'to take root', fr. radix, gen. -icis,
'root'. See radix. For the use of Latin gerundives
or their derivatives in English cp. agenda and
words there referred to.

## radicant
radicant, adj., bringing forth roots (bot.) — L.
radicdns, gen. -antis, pres. part, of radicare or
radicari. See prec. word and -ant

## radicate
radicate, tr. v., 1) to cause to take root, plant
firmly; 2) to establish firmly. —L. radicatus, pp.
of radicare or radicari. See radicand and verbal
suff. -ate.

## radicel
radicel, п., a rootlet. — Formed fr. ModL. radi-
cella (whence also F. radicelle), dimin. of L.
radix, gen. -ids, 'root'. See radix and cp. next
word.

## radicle
radicle, п., a minute root {bot. and anat.) — L.
radicula, dimin. of radix, gen. -icis, 'root*. See
radix and -ule and cp. prec. word.

## radicular
radicular, adj., pertaining to roots. — Formed
with suff>-ar fr. L. radicula. See prec. word.

## radiculitis
radiculitis, п., inflammation of the spinal nerve
roots (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr.
L. radicula, 'little root'. See radicle and -itis.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:641 COLUMN:2 -->

## radio
radio, п., wireless telegraphy. — Abbreviation of
radio-telegraphy.
Derivative: radio, tr. and intr. v.

## radio-
radio-, combining form meaning 1) ray or
raylike ; 2) radial; radially; {anat.) radial and; 3) by
means of radiant energy (med.); 4) radioactive;
5) by radio. — Fr. L. radius. See radius,

## radioactive
radioactive, adj., exhibiting, or pertaining to,
radioactivity. — F. radio-actif (fern,
radioactive), coined by Pierre and Marie Curie. See
next word and active,

## radioactivity
radioactivity, п., the property of giving off radiant
energy in the form of particles. — F. radio-
activite, coined by the French physicists and
chemists Pierre Curie (1859-1906) and his wife
Marie (1867-1934) in 1898 fr. radio- and F.
activite. See activity,

## radiograph
radiograph, п., ]) an instrument for measuring
radiant energy; 2) an X-ray picture. —
Compounded of radio- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γρά-
φειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: radiograph-er, п., radiograph-ic,
radiograph-ic-al, adjs., radiograph-ic-al-ly, adv.,
radiograph-y, n.

## Radiolaria
Radiolaria, n. pi., an order of microscopic marine
animals (zool) — ModL., fr. Late L. radiolus, 'a
little ray', dimin. of L. radius. See radius, dimin.
suff. -ole and suff. -aria.
Derivative: radiolari-an, adj. and n.

## radiology
radiology, п., that part of physics which deals with
radioactivity and radioactive substances. —
Compounded of radio- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, One who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: radiolog-ic(-al), adj., radiolog-ist, n.

## radiometer
radiometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
effect of radiant energy. — Compounded of
radio- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## radiometry
radiometry, п., measurement of the effect of
radiant energy. Compounded of radio- and Gk.
μετρία, 'measuring of. See -metry.

## radiophone
radiophone, п., an instrument for the production
of sound by means of radiant energy. —
Compounded of radio- and Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice'.
See phone, 'speech sound',

## radioscopy
radioscopy, п., examination of opaque objects by
means of X-rays or other rays. — Compounded
of radio- and Gk. -σκοπίά, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look
at, examine'. See -scopy.

## radiotelegram
radiotelegram, п., a wireless telegram. —
Compounded of radio- and telegram,

## radiotelegraphy
radiotelegraphy, п., wireless telegraphy. —
Compounded of radio- and telegraphy.

## radiotelephone
radiotelephone, п., wireless telephone. —
Compounded of radio- and telephone,

## radiotelephony
radiotelephony, п., wireless telephony. —
Compounded of radio- and telephony.

## radiotherapy
radiotherapy, п., treatment of disease by means of
X-rays and other rays. — Compounded of
radio- and therapy,

## radish
radish, n. — F. radis, fr. It. radice, prop, 'root*,
fr. L. radxcem, ace. of radix, 'root'. See radix
and cp. words there referred to.

## radium
radium, п., a radioactive metallic element. —
ModL., fr. L. radius, 'ray*; so called because of
its power of emitting energy in the form of rays.
See radius,

## radius
radius, п., 1) a straight line from the center of the
circle to its circumference; 2) the exterior bone
of the forearm. — L. radius, 'stake, staff, rod,
spoke of a wheel, shuttle, beam, ray; the exterior
bone of the forearm'; of uncertain origin. It is
perh. rel. to radix, 'root*. See radix and cp. ray,
'beam', radiant, irradiate. Cp. also rayon. In its
anatomical sense, the word radius was first used
by Aulus Cornelius Celsus, Roman writer of the
1st cent.

## radix
radix, п., root. — L. radix (for *h>rddix), 'root',
rel. to ramus (for *wradmos), 'branch, bough,
twig', and cogn. with Gk. ρίζα, Lesbian βρίσδα
(for *Fp%a.), 'root', Gk. ράδαμνος (for *FpaS-
αμνος), 'branch', Goth, waurts, OE. wyrt, W.
gwridd (for *wradi\ Olr. fren (for *wridno or
*wridnd), 'root*. Cp. deracinate, eradicate, race,
'root', radical, radicel, radicle, radish, radius,
ramage, ramose, rhizo-, the first element in
rami form, rampion, and the second element in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:641 COLUMN:3 -->
licorice. Cp. also root, wort, a plant, and the first
element in orchard.

## radon
radon, п., name of the heaviest gaseous element
(chem.) — Coined fr. radium, with 1st suff. -on
on analogy of argon, neon, etc.; so called because
gained from radium.

## radula
radula, п., ribbon of a mollusk. — L. radula, 'a
scraper', fr. rddere, pp. rasus, 'to scrape'. See rase.
Derivatives: radul-ar, radul-ate, adjs.

## raff
raff, п., rabble. — ME. raf, fr. OF. raffe, fr.
raffer, 'to sweep together*. See raffle, 'lottery',
and cp. riffraff.
Derivative: raff-ish, adj., worthless,
disreputable.

## raffia
raffia, п., the fiber of the Raphia pedunculata, a
Madagascar tree. — Malagasy rafia.

## raffinose
raffinose, п., a sugar, C18H3aOie (chem.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ose fr. F. raffiner, 'to refine',
fr. re- (see re-) and affiner, 'to make fine*, which
is formed fr. OF. a, 'to' (fr. L. ad), and OF. fin
(fr. VL. *ftnus), 'fine'. See ad- and fine, 'delicate'.

## raffle
raffle, п., lottery. — ME. rafle, fr. MF. (— F.)
rafie, 'a game of dice (whence rafter, 'to sweep
up the stakes; to sweep off'), fr. MDu. raffel, 'a
game of dice', which is rel. to Early Modern Du.
ravelen, 'to entangle* (Modern Du. rafelen, 'to
unravel, ravel out, fray out'), and prob. also to
MHG., G. raffen, 'to snatch away, sweep off',
OHG. raspon (for * raf son), 'to scrape together,
snatch up in haste', fr. Teut. base *hrap-, 'to
pluck out, snatch off'. OF. raffer, 'to sweep
together', and It. arraffare, 'to snatch', are also
Teut. loan words. See rasp, 'to rub', and cp.
raff, ravel.

## raffie
raffie, п., refuse. — Lit. 'a taking away', hence
etymologically identical with raffie, 'lottery'.
Rafflestа, п., a genus of Malaysian plants (bot.)
— ModL., named after Sir Thomas S. Raffles,
founder of Singapore (1781-1826). For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Rafflesiaceae
Rafflesiaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL. Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## rafflesiaceous
rafflesiaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## raft
raft, n. — ME. rafte, orig. 'rafter', fr. ON. raptr.
See rafter.
Derivatives: raft, tr. and intr. v., raft-age, п.,
raft-er, п., a raftsman.

## rafter
rafter, п., one of the sloping timbers of a roof. —
ME., fr. OE. rsefter, rel. to ON. raptr, MLG.
rafter, rachter, 'rafter'. Cp. raft.
Derivative: rafter-ed, adj.

## rag
rag, п., tatter of cloth. — ME. ragge, fr. OE. ragg
(in the adj. raggig, 'raggy'), fr. ON. rogg, 'tuft,
shagginess'. See rug.
Derivatives: ragg-ed, adj., ragg-ed-ly, adv.,
ragg-ed-ness, п., ragg-y, adj.

## rag
rag, п., a kind of hard limestone. — Of uncertain
origin.

## rag
rag, tr. v., to tease. — Of uncertain origin. Cp.
bullyrag.
Derivatives: rag, п., 'joke', ragg-er, n., ragging, n.

## ragamuffin
ragamuffin, п., a stupid person. — Fr. Ragamof-
fyn, name of a demon in old mystery plays,
which is prob. a compound of rag, 'tatter', and
moffyn, a word of uncertain origin and meaning.

## rage
rage, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) rage, fr. VL. rabia,
fr. L. rabies, 'rage, madness', fr. rabere, 'to be
mad, to rave'. See rabid and cp. rabies.
Derivatives: rage, intr. v., rag-er, п., rag-ing-ly,
adv.

## raggee
raggee, raggy, п., a South Indian cereal grass. —
Hind, ragl, fr. OI. ragin, 'red'; so called in
allusion to the color of the grain. OI. ragin is rel. to
rajyati, 'is colored, becomes red*, fr. I.-E. base
*reg-, 'to color1, whence also Gk. ρέζειν (aorist
^έξαι), 'to color", ρήγος, 'colored rug'.

## raglan
raglan, п., a kind of overcoat. — Named after the
British general Lord Raglan (1788-1855).

## ragman
ragman, п., the name given to a collection of acts
in which the Scottish nobles swore allegiance to
Edward I in 1296. — Of uncertain origin. Cp.
rigmarole.

## ragont
ragont, п., a highly seasoned stew of meat and
vegetables. — F. ragout, back formation fr. ra-
gouter, 'to revive one's appetite', fr. re- (see re-),
a, 'to' (fr. L. ad, see ad-), and gouter, fr. L.
gustdre, 'to taste'. See gust, 'relish', and cp. gusto.

## raguly
raguly, adj., notched — said especially of a cross

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:642 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 615 | RAMP -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:642 COLUMN:1 -->
(her.) — Prob. rel. to rag, 'tatter*.
Rahab, п., name of a monster in the Bible (Ps.
89:1 l,Job9:13,26 :\2).—Heb.rahabh, lit.
'storming, against, impetuous', fr. rahabh, 'he stormed
against, was impetuous*, which is те1. to Arab.
rahiba, 'he feared, was alarmed', Aram, r hebh,
'he was arrogant', Syr. rehibk, 'he was
impetuous', Akkad. rd'abu, 'to storm at (angrily)'.

## raid
raid, n. — Scot., fr. OE. rdd, 'riding, journey,
raid*, hence prop, a var. of road (q.v.);
introduced by Walter Scott. For sense development
cp. Inroad.
Derivatives: raid, tr. and intr. v., raid-er, n.

## rail
rail, п., garment chiefly used in the compound
night rail. — ME. reil, fr. OE. hrxgl, hreegel,
'garment, dress, armor', rel. to OFris. hreil,
OHG. hregil, 'garment', OE. hreol, 'reel', and
cogn. with Gk. κρέκειν, 'to weave', κρόκη,
'woof, thread', κροκίς, 'a nap of woolen cloth'.
Cp. reel, 'a revolvable instrument', and the first
element in crocidolite.

## rail
rail, п., bar (whence railroad, railway). — ME.
raile, fr. MF. reille, 'bar, rail', fr. OF. reille, fr.
L. regula, 'a straight piece of wood, ruler; rule',
fr. regere, 'to keep straight, lead straight, rule'.
See regent and cp. rule. Cp. also derail,
monorail,

## rail
rail, intr. v., to furnish with rails. — ME. railen,
fr. raile. See prec. word.

## rail
rail, intr. v., to speak reproachfully, scold. —
ME. railen, fr. MF. (= F.) railler, 'to jeer at', fr.
OProven?. ralhar, 'to joke, jest', fr. VL. *ragu-
lare, 'to bray' (whence It. ragghiare, 4o bray'),
fr. Late L. ragere, 'to neigh', which is prob. of
imitative origin. Originally OProven?. ralhar
denoted different kinds of cries, and only gradually
developed the meanings 'to babble, prattle; to
joke, jest'. Cp. rally, 'to banter', which is a
doublet of rail. Cp. also raillery.
Derivatives: rail-er, п., rail-ing, adj. and n.
ail, п., bird of the family Rallidae. — ME. rale,
raile, fr. MF. raale (F. rale), rel. to F. raler, 'to
rattle'; prob. of imitative origin. Cp. Rallus. Cp.
also rale, rattle,

## raillery
raillery, п., banter. — F. raillerie, fr. railler. See
rail, 'to speak reproachfully', and -ery.

## raiment
raiment, n. — ME. rayment, aphetic for array-
ment, 'clothing', lit. 'an arraying', fr. arraien.
See array and -ment.
Derivative: raiment, tr. v.

## rain
rain, n. — ME. reyn, fr. OE. regn, rel. to OS.
regan, ΟΝ., Swed. regn, OFris. rein, MDu.
reghen, reen, Du. regen, OHG. regan, MHG., G.
regen, Goth, rign, 'rain*, ON. raki, 'dampness',
rakr, 'damp', and cogn. with Lith. rokti, 'to
drizzle', roke, 'drizzling rain', L. rigare, 'to wet,
moisten', Alb. fje&, 'to flow'. Cp. irrigate.
Derivatives: rain, v. (q.v.), rain-y, adj., rain-less,
adj.

## rain
rain, intr. and tr. v. — ME. reynen, fr. OE. reg·
nian, fr. regn, 'rain*, rel. to ON. rigna, Swed.
regno, Dan. regne, OHG. reganon, MHG. regen,
regenen, G. regnen, Goth, rignjan. See rain, n.
Derivative: rain-er, n.

## rainbow
rainbow, n. — ME. reinbowe, fr. OE. regnboga,
rel. to ON. regnbogi, Swed. regnbage, OFris.
reinboga, MDu. reghenboghe, Du. regenboog,
OHG. reganbogo, MHG. regenboge, G. Regen-
bogen. See rain, п., and bow, 'anything bent*.

## rainette green
rainette green, a greenish yellow color. — Lit. Of
the color of the tree frog', fr. F. rainette, 'tree
frog', fr. OF. raine, 'frog', fr. L. rana. See rairine
and cp. words there referred to.

## rais
rais, reis, п., chief. — Arab, ra*ts, 'chief, fr. ra's,
'head'. See race, 'family, tribe'.

## raise
raise, tr. v. — ME. reisen, raisen, fr. ON. reisa,
which is rel. to OE. reran (for *ratz-jan), 'to
rear'; see rear, 'to raise'. OE. rzran is the
causative of risan, 'to rise'; see rise.
Derivatives: rais-ed, adj., rais-ing, n.

## raisin
raisin, п., dried sweet grape. — ME., fr. OF.
raizin, raisim (F. raisin), 'grape', fr. VL. *raci-
mus, corresponding to L. racemus, 'cluster of
grapes'. See raceme,

## raisonne
raisonne, adj., arranged logically. — F.,
'reasoned', pp. of raisonner, 'to reason', fr. raison. See

## reason
reason, n.

## raj
raj, п., rule, reign. — Hind, raj, 'rule, reign*, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:642 COLUMN:2 -->
Ol. rdjya-, fr. rdjati, 'he rules', which is rel. to
rajan-, 'king*. See next word and cp. the second
element in swaraj.

## rajah
rajah, п., an Indian king. — Hind, raja, fr. Ol.
rajan-, 'king'. See prec. word and cp. ranee, the
first element in next word, and the second
element in maharaja.

## Rajput
Rajput, п., a member of a ruling caste in northern
India. — Hind, rdjput, fr. 01. rdjaputrah, 'king's
son, prince*, which is compounded of rajan-,
'king', and putrah, 'son, boy4. For the first
element see rajah. The second element is rel. to
Avestic and OPers. pw&ra-, 'son, child', and
cogn. with L. puer, 'boy, child*; see puerile and
cp. words there referred to.

## rake
rake, п., a tool. — ME. rake, fr. OE. raca, rel. to
ON. reka, 'spade, shovel', Swed. raka, 'rake',
OHG. rehho, MHG. reche, G. Rechen, 'rake',
and to ON. raka, MLG. raken, 'to sweep away',
Goth, rikan, 'to heap up, collect', and prob.
cogn. with Gk. όρέγειν, 'to reach, stretch out*,
L. regere, 'to stretch, extend, make straight; to
rule', pern, also with L. rogus, 'funeral pile'. See
regent, adj., and cp. rack, 'instrument of torture*.
Cp. also reckon,

## rake
rake, tr. and intr. v., to use a rake, to scrape. —
ME. raken, fr. rake, G., ON. raka, 'to scrape',
MLG. raken, OHG. rehhan, Goth, rikan, 'to
scrape together', and see rake, 'a tool'.
Derivatives: rak-er, п., rak-ing, verbal п., and
adj.

## rake
rake, intr. v., to project, incline forward. — Rel.
to dial. Swed. raka, 'to reach', OE. hrxgan, 'to
jut out', MDu. raghen, MHG., G. ragen, of
s.m., and cogn. with Gk. κρόσσαι (for *qroqyd-),
'battlement, copings of parapets', Czech and
Russ. krokva, 'spar, rafter'. Cp. crosso-.
Derivatives: rake, п., inclination, rak-ish, adj.,
rak-ish-ly, adv., rak-ish-ness, n.
гаке, п., a debauchee. — Abbreviation of ME.
rakel, 'rash". See next word.
Derivatives: rak-ish, adj., rak-ish-ly, adv., rak-
ish-ness, n.

## rakehell
rakehell, п., a debauchee. — Popular
refashioning of ME. rakel, 'rash, impetuous*, which is
prob. related to OE. racian, 'to go forward'. Cp.
prec. word.
Derivative: rakehell-y, adj.

## rakshasa
rakshasa, п., goblins or evil spirits (Hindu my thol.)
— Ol. raksas-, 'goblin, evil spirit', lit. 'damage,
causer of damage', rel. to Avestic rashah-,
'damage', rashayeiti, 'damages', fr. l.-E. base
*rekp(h)-, 4o pull, tug, drag, pester', whence
also Gk. έρέχθειν, 'to rend, break, shatter',
Έρεχθεύς, a fabled king of Athens, lit. 'shaker'.
Cp. Erechtheus.

## rale
rale, п., rattling sound in the throat. — F., fr.
raler, 'to rattle', of imitative origin. Cp. rail, the
bird, Rallus.

## railentando
railentando, adj., slackening; gradually slower
(musical direction). — It., pres. part, of railen·
tare, 'to slow down' (cp. F. ralentir), fr. ra-,
contraction of L. re- and ad- (see re- and -ad)
and lento, 'slack, slow', fr. L. lentus. See relent.

## Rallidae
Rallidae, n. pi., the family of rails and other grui-
form birds (ornithol.) — ModL., formed fr.
Rallus with suff. -idae.

## Rallinae
Rallinae, n. pi., subfamily of the Rallidae
(ornithol.) — Formed fr. Rallus with suff. -inae.

## ralline
ralline, adj., pertaining to the Rallidae. See prec.
word and -ine (representing L. -inus).

## Rallus
Rallus, п., the genus of rails (zool.) — ModL., fr.
F. rale, 'rail*, fr. raler, 'to rattle', which is of
imitative origin. G. Raile, of s.m., is a French
loan word. See rail, 'the bird'.
Derivatives: ralli-form, rall-ine, adjs.

## rally
rally, tr. v., to gather, collect; intr. v., to come
together. — F. rallier, 'to assemble, rally', fr.
OF. ralier, of s.m., which is formed fr. re- (see
re-) and alier (F. allier), 'to join'. See ally, v.
Derivatives: rally, п., ralli-er, n.

## raily
raily, tr. v., to banter. — F. railler, 'to rail at',
hence a doublet of rail, 'to speak reproachfully'
(q.v.) Cp. raillery.
Derivative: railli-er, n.

## Ralph
Ralph, masc. PN. — Shortened fr. Radulf, fr. ON.
Radulfr (rel. to OE. Rxdwulf); compounded of
rad, 'counsel*, and ulfr, 'wolf*. See rede and wolf.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:642 COLUMN:3 -->

## ralstonite
ralstonite, п., a fluoride of aluminum, sodium and
magnesium (mineral.) — Named after J. Grier.
Ralston of Norristown in Pennsylvania. For the
ending see subst. suff -ite.

## ram
ram, n. — ME. ramme, fr. OE. ramm, ram, rel. to
MLG., MDu., Du. and OHG. ram, 'ram', and
prob. also to ON. ramr, 'strong'; prob. cogn.
with OSlav. гатёпй, 'impetuous, violent,
strong'.
Derivatives: ram, tr. v., ramm-er, п., ramm-ish,
adj.

## Rama
Rama, п., the sixth, seventh, or eight incarnation
of Vishnu (Hindu mythol.) — Ol. Rdmah, lit.
'lovely', from the stem of ramate, 'stands still,
rests, is pleased, is amused'; cogn. with Gk.
ήρεμα, 'gently, quietly, softly', ήρεμεΐν, 'to be
still, keep quiet', Lith. rimti, 'to become quiet,
calm down', remti, 'to stay, support', Olr. fo-
rimim, Ί set, place'.

## -rama
-rama, suff. meaning 'sight, view'. — Back
formation fr. panorama, which stands for pan-orama
and lit. means 'all-sight'. Accordingly, the suff.
should really be -orama. However, through a
misdivision of panorama into pano-rama, the
surT. -rama was formed. Cp. e.g. cinerama.

## Ramadan
Ramadan, п., the ninth month of the Moslem
year. — Arab, ramaddn, prop, 'the hot month*,
fr. ramida, 'was hot', which is rel. to Mishnaic
Heb. remetz, 'hot ashes, embers'.

## ramal
ramal, adj., 1) pertaining to a branch (hot.); 2)
pertaining to a ramus (anat. and zool.) —
Formed with adj. surT. -al fr. L. ramus, 'branch'. See
ramus.

## ramage
ramage, п., the whole of the branches of a tree.
— F., fr. L. ramus, 'branch'. See ramose and
-age.

## ramble
ramble, intr. v. — Prob. a var. of ME. romblen,
freq. of ME. romen, 'to roam'. See roam. The
-b- is intrusive. Cp. grumble.
Derivatives: ramble, п., rambl-er, п., rambl-ing,
adj., rambl-ing-ly, adv.

## rambunctious
rambunctious, adj., boisterous (colloq.) — Fr.
earlier rumbustious, for robustious.

## rambutan
rambutan, п., fruit of a Malayan tree, Nephelium
lappaceum. — Malay rambutan, fr. rambut,
'hair'.

## ramekin
ramekin, also ramequin, п., a preparation of
cheese with bread crumbs, eggs, etc., baked in a
small dish. — F. ramequin, fr. MLG. ramken,
dimin. of ram, 'cream', which is rel. to OE.
ream, of s.m. See ream, 'cream'. Fort he ending
see suff. -kin.

## ramentum
ramentum, п., 1) something scraped off; 2) a thin
scale formed on the surface of leaves (pot.) — L.
ramentum, 'what is shaved or scraped off*, for
*rdd-mentom, fr. rddere, 'to shave, scrape'; see
rase and -ment. Cp. caementum, 'stone cut from
the quarry', for orig. *caid-(s)mentom, fr. cae-
dere, 'to cut' (see cement).

## ramie
ramie, п., 1) a plant of the nettle family (Boehme-
ria nivea); a fiber of this plant. — Malay rami,
name of the plant.

## ramification
ramification, n. — ModL. rdmificdtio, formed
(prob. through the medium of F. ramification)
fr. ML. rdmificdtus, pp. of ramificdre. See ramify
and -ation.

## ramiform
ramiform, adj., branchlike. — Compounded of
L. ramus, 'branch* andforma, 'form, shape'. See
ramose and form, n.

## ramify
ramify, tr. v., to divide into branches; intr. v., to
form branches. — MF. (= F.) ramifier, fr. ML.
ramificdre, 'to form branches', fr. L. ramus,
'branch, bough, twig', and -ficare, ϊτ./acere, 'to
make, do'. See ramose and -fy.
Derivative: ramifi-ed, adj.

## ramillie
ramillie, ramillies, п., a kind of plaited wig. —
Short for Ramillies wig; named in
commemoration of Marlborough's victory over the French
at Ramillies (in 1706).

## ramose
ramose, adj., branching (hot.) — L. ramosus, fr.
ramus, 'branch', which stands for *rddmos, and
is related to radix, 'root'. See radix and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see adj.
suff. -ose.
Derivatives: ramose-ly, adv., ramos-ity, n.

## ramp
ramp, intr. and tr. v., 1) to climb; 2) to stand on
the hind legs (her.) — ME. rampen, fr. OF.
ramper, 'to climb' (whence F. ramper, 'to creep,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:643 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: RAMP | 616 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:643 COLUMN:1 -->
crawl'), fr. Frankish *rampon, 'to contract
oneself convulsively', which stands in gradational
relationship to OHG. rimpfan, 'to wrinkle,
shrivel', OE. krimpan, 'to fold, wrinkle'; see
rumple and cp. rim pie, Cp. also rampage, ram·
pant.
Derivatives: ramp, п., ramp~ing, n.

## ramp
ramp, п., a slope. — F. rampe, back formation fr.
ramper, *to creep, clamber'. See ramp, 'to climb',

## rampage
rampage, п., a riot. — Formed fr. ramp, 'to
climb', with surf. -age.
Derivatives: rampage, intr. v., rampage-ous,
adj., rampage-ous-ly, adv., rampage-ous-ness, n.

## rampancy
rampancy, п., the condition of being rampant. —
Formed from next word with sufT. -cy.

## rampant
rampant, adj., standing on the hind legs (her.) —
ME. rampaunt, fr. MF. (= F.) rampant, pres.
part, of ramper, 'to creep, crawl'. See ramp, 'to
climb', and -ant.
Derivative: rampant-ly, adv.

## rampart
rampart, n. — MF. rempart, rampart (F. rem-
part), fr. remparer, ramparer, 'to fortify', formed
fr. re-, 'again' (see re-), and emparer, 'to fortify'
(whence F. s'emparer, 'to take hold of), fr.
OProvenc. antparar, amparar, fr. VL. *ante-
parare, prop, 'to make preparations
beforehand', formed fr. ante- and L. pardre, 'to
prepare' (see pare). The t- in F. rempart is excrescent
and prob. due to the influence of earlier F.
boulevart (now boulevard).
Derivative: rampart, tr. v.

## rampion
rampion, п., a kind of campanula (bellfiower). —
Altered fr. ML. rapuncium, rapuntium (whence
MF., F. raiponce, It. raponzo, raponzolo, Sp.
raponchigo), fr. VL. *radice puntia, prop, 'root
of valerian'- For the first element see radix. The
second element is a VL. derivative of L. phu ( =
Gk. φοΰ), ace. phun, *a kind of valerian'.

## rampire
rampire, n. — An archaic form of rampart.
Derivative: rampire, tr. v.

## ramrod
ramrod, n. — Lit. 'a rod used for ramming', fr.
ram, v. (see ram) and rod.

## ramshackle
ramshackle, adj., worn out. — Back formation fr.
ramshackled, fr. ranshackled, fr. earlier ran-
sackled, pp. of ransackle, freq. of ransack (q.v.)
Derivatives: ramshackle, п., ramshackle-ness,
п., ramshackl-y, adj.

## ramson
ramson, п., the broad-leaved garlic. — ME.
ramsyn, fr. OE. hramsan, pi. of hramsa, 'broad-
leaved garlic', rel. to MLG. ramese, G. Rams,
Dan., Swed., Norw. rams, 'ramson', and cogn.
with Gk. κρόμμυον, κρόμυον, also κρέμυον (in
Hesychius), Onion', Lith. kermuse, 'wild garlic',
Russ. ceremsa, 'ramson', Mir. crem, crim, W.
craf, 'garlic'. Cp. buckrams, 'ramson'.

## ramulose
ramulose, adj., having many branchlets. — L. rd-
mulosus, fr. ramulus. See ramulus and adj. sufT.
-ose and cp. next word.

## ramulous
ramulous, adj., ramulose. — L. rdmulosus. See
prec. word and -ous.

## ramulus
ramulus, п., a small branch (bot. and anat.) — L.
ramulus, dimin. of ramus. See ramose,

## ramus
ramus, п., a branch (anat.) — L. ramus. See
ramose,

## ran
ran, п., a hank of twine. — Of unknown origin.

## ran
ran, pret. of run. — ME., fr. OE. ran, pret. of
rinnan, 'to flow', or fr. ON. ran, pret. of renna,
'to run'. See run.

## ranarium
ranarium, п., a place for raising frogs. — ModL.
fr. L. rana, 'frog'. See ranunculus and -arinm.

## ranee
ranee, п., a variety of Belgian marble. — F., of
unknown origin.

## rnnch
rnnch, п., a large farm with its buildings and
employees. — Mexican Sp. rancho, 'a small farm',
fr. Sp. rancko, 'mess, messroom', fr. OHG.
firing, 'circle, ring*. See ring, n.
Derivatives: ranch, intr. v., ranch-er, n.

## rancid
rancid, adj., stale. — L. rancidus, 'foul-smelling',
fr. rancere, 'to stink, rank', which is of
uncertain etymology. Cp. next word. For the ending
see adj. sufT. -id (representing L. -idus).
Derivatives: rancid-it у, п., rancid-ly, adv.,
rancid-ness, n.

## rancor
rancor, rancour, п., bitter resentment, spite. —
ME. rancour, fr. OF. rancour, fr. L. rancorem,
ace of rancor, 'a stinking smell, rankness,
rancidity', fr. rancere. See prec. word and -or.
Derivatives: rancor-ous, adj., rancor-ous-ly,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:643 COLUMN:2 -->
adv., rancor-ous-ness, n.

## rand
rand, п., border, edge. — ME., fr. OE. rand
'edge, margin, rim, boss of shield, shield', rel.
to ON. rond, 'rim, shield', OHG. rant, 'boss
of a shield', MHG. rant, 'rim of a shield, rim',
Dan., Swed., Du., G. rand, 'border, edge', ON.
rimi, 'ridge, hill, height', OE. rima, 'border,
bank, coast', and cogn. with Olr. rinde,
'wooden vessel'. Cp. rim and the first element in
Randal.

## Randal
Randal, masc. PN. — Shortened from OE. Rand-
wulf (a compound of rand, 'shield', and wulf,
'wolf') or from its ON. equivalent Randulfr (fr.
rand, 'shield', and ulfr, 'wolf'). See rand and
wolf.

## randan
randan, п., a kind of rowing boat for three
persons. — Of unknown origin.

## randan
randan, п., a drinking bout, spree (slang) —
Perh. a var. of random.

## randem
randem, adv., with three horses harnassed one in
front of the other; п., a carriage so harnassed
and driven. — Prob. a blend of tandem and
random.

## random
random, n. — ME. randoun, randon, random, fr.
OF. random, 'force, violence, impetuosity', de
randon, a randon, 'impetuously' (whence F. ran-
donnee, 'circuit of game; etre en randonnee, 'to
be out for a long run'), fr. OF. randir, 'to run
impetuously', fr. *rant, fr. Frankish *rant, 'a
running', which is rel. to OHG. rennen, 'to run',
OE. rinnan, 'to flow, run'; see E. run, v. — See
Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 506 s.v.
randonnee.

## randy
randy, adj., boisterous, riotous (Scot.) — Formed
with adj. SufT. -y fr. obsol. rand, a var. of rant
(Q-v.)

## ranee
ranee, rani, п., the wife of a rajah; a Hindu
queen. — Hind, rani, fr. OI. rajni, fern, ofrajan,
'king'. See rajah and cp. the second element in
maharanee. Cp. also regina, reina.

## rang
rang, pret. of ring. — ME. rang, formed on
analogy of sang, pret. of sing. See ring, 'to sound'.

## range
range, tr. and intr. v., to place in rank. —ME.
rangen, fr. MF. (= F.) ranger, fr. OF. ranger, fr.
earlier rengier, rangier, 'to place in rank or
ranks', fr. ranc (F. rang), fr. earlier renc, 'row,
line, rank*, fr. Frankish *hring, 'circle, ring'.
See ring, 'circle', and cp. rank, 'row, line'. Cp.
also arrange, derange.
Derivatives: rang-er, п., rang-y, adj., rang-i-ness,
n.

## range
range, п., row; distance. — ME., fr. MF. range,
fr. OF. range, a var. of renge, 'row, rank', back
formation fr. rangier, 'to place in rank'. See
range, v.

## rani-
rani-, combining form meaning 'frog'. — Fr. L.
rana, 'frog'. See ranine.

## rani
rani, n. — See ranee.

## ranine
ranine, adj., 1) pertaining to the frogs (zool.); 2)
pertaining to the region under the tip of the
tongue (anat.) — ML. raninus, 'pertaining to
the frogs', formed (on analogy of caninus,
'pertaining to the dogs', vulpinus, 'pertaining to the
foxes', etc.), fr. L. rana, 'frog', lit. 'croaker,
crier', which stands for *racsna, and is rel. to
raccdre, 'to roar'; of imitative origin. Cp. OHG.
ruohhon, 'to roar', which is also imitative. Cp.
also rainette green, Ranunculus, ranula, For the
ending see -ine (representing L. -ina).

## rank
rank, п., row, line. — MF. ranc (F. rang), 'row,
line, rank'. See range, v., and cp. harangne,
ranch, ranz des vaches.
Derivatives: rank, tr. and intr. v.
rank» adj., I) vigorous; 2) strong in smell. — ME.,
fr. OF. ranc, 'strong, brave', which is rel. to
Dan. rank, 'right, upright', Swed. rank, MLG.
ranc, Du., G. rank, 'slender', ON. rakkr (for
*rankr), 'straight, erect', orig. 'stretched out',
ΟΙ. ζή]άύ, 'stretches himself, Lith. raiytis, 'to
stretch oneself. All these words are derivatives
of a nasalized enlargement of I.-E. *reg-, 'to
stretch, straighten; straight, right". See regent,
adj., and cp. words there referred to. Rank was
prob. influenced in sense by F. ranee, 'rancid,
rank' (see rancid).
Derivatives: rank-ish, adj., rank-fy, adv.,
rankness, n.

## rankle
rankle, intr. v., to fester. — ME. rancfen, fr. MF.

rancler, fr. OF. rancler, earlier raoncler, dra-
oncler, 'to suppurate, run', fr. rancle, earlier ra-
oncle, drancle, draoncle, 'abscess', lit. 'a little

draco, gen. draconis. See dragon.
Derivative: rankle, n.

## ransack
ransack, tr. v., to search thoroughly; to pillage.
— ME. ransaken, fr. ON. rannsaka, 'to
ransack', lit. 'to search a house', compounded of
rann (for *rasn), 'house', and -saka, which is
rel. to soekja, 'to seek'. The first element is rel.
to Goth, razn, OE. xrn, ren, 'house'. See rest,
'repose', and cp. words there referred to. For
the second element see seek. Cp. ramshackle.
Derivative: ransack-er, n.

## ransom
ransom, n. — ME. raunsoun, ransoun, fr. OF.
ranson (F. rancon), fr. L. redemptidnem, ace. of
redemptio, 'a buying back, ransoming,
redemption'. See redemption, which is a doublet of
ransom.

## ransom
ransom, tr. v., — ME. raunsounen, ransounen,
OF. ransonner, fr. ranson. See ransom, n.
Derivatives: ransom-er, п., ransom-less, adj.

## rant
rant, intr. v., to speak in a bombastic way. —
Fr. earlier (now obsol.) ModDu. ranten, 'to
dote'. Cp. randy.
Derivatives: rant, п., rant-er, n.

## ranula
ranula, п., a swelling under the tongue (med.) —
L., 'a little frog', dimin. of rana, 'frog'. See
ranine and -ule and cp. Ranunculus.
Derivative: ranul-ar, adj.

## Ranunculaceae
Ranunculaceae, n. pi., the crowfoot family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Ranunculus with sufT.
-aceae.

## ranunculaceous
ranunculaceous, adj. — See prec. word and

## Ranunculus
Ranunculus, п., a genus of plants, the crowfoot

(prob. identical with the crowfoot), dimin.
formed fr. rana, 'frog'. See ranine and cp.
ranula.

## ranz des vaches
ranz des vaches, a melody sung by Swiss herdsmen.
— F., lit. 'line of the cows', fr. dial. F. ranz,
'row, line, rank', des, contraction of de les, 'of
the', and vaches, pi. of vacne, 'cow'. Dial. F.
ranz is rel. to F. rang, 'line, rank'; see rank,
'row'. F. de 'of, from', derives fr. L. de, 'from,
away from', les, 'the' (pi.), is traceable to L.
illds (masc), illds (fern.), ace. of Ule, resp. ilia,
'that'; see de- and ille. F. vache comes fr. L.
vacca, 'cow'; see vaccine.

## rap
rap, п., a blow. — ME. rappe, prob. of imitative
origin; cp. Dan. rap, of s.m., Swed. rapp,
'stroke'.

## rap
rap, tr. and intr. v., to strike. — ME. rappen,
prob. of imitative origin; rel. to prec. word.
Derivative: rapp-er, n.

## rap
rap, tr. v., to seize, snatch. — Back formation fr.
rapt.

## rap
rap, п., a skein of yarn of about 120 yards. — Of
unknown origin.

## rap
rap, п., a counterfeit coin of the worth of a
halfpenny. — G. Rappen, 'centime', orig, name of
an old Alsatian coin with an eagle's head,
derisively referred to as a raven, Rappen being a
dialectal var. of G. Rabe, 'raven'. See raven.

## rapacious
rapacious, adj., 1) given to plunder; 2) greedy. —
L. rapdx, gen. -dcis, 'grasping, rapacious*,
from the stem oirapere, 'to seize'. See rapid and
-acious.
Derivatives: rapacious-ly, adv., rapacious·ness,
n.

## rapacity
rapacity, п., rapaciousness. — MF. (= F.)
rapacity, fr. L. rapdeitatem, ace. of rapacitus, fr.

## rapdx
rapdx, gen. -acis. See prec. word and -ity.

## rape
rape, η., a plant allied to the turnip. — ME., fr.,
L. rdpum, also rdpa, 'rape, turnip', cogn. with
Gk. ράπυς, ρ'άφυς, 'rape', £άφανος, 'cabbage;
radish', ραφανΐς, 'radish', OSfav. repa, Lith.
rope, MDu. roeve, OHG. ruoba, ruoppa, MHG.

## ruobe
ruobe, ruebe, G. Rube, and OHG. rdba, MHG.
rabe, 'rape, turnip*. Cp. raphania, Raphanus. Cp.
also the second element in kohlrabi.

## rape
rape, tr. v., to seize and carry off by force. — ME.

## rapen
rapen, 'to seize', fr. OF. raper, fr. L. rapere. See
rapid and cp. words there referred to.

## rape
rape, п., the act of seizing; violation. — ME. rape,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:644 COLUMN:1 -->

Derivatives: rap-ert п., rap-ist, n.

## rape
rape, п., one of the six divisions of Sussex. —
First mentioned in Domesday. Book; perh. fr.
rape, an obsol. var. of rope, used in the sense of
'measure'. For sense development cp. Heb.
fyebhef, 'rope; measure'.

## rape
rape, п., refuse of grapes. — F. rape, fr. ML.
raspa, fr. WTeut. *raspdn, 'to scrape; to sweep
off'. See rasp, v., and cp. words there referred to.

## Raphael
Raphael, 1) masc. PN. 2) an archangel
mentioned in the Apocrypha. — Late L., fr. Gk.
'Ραφαήλ, fr. Heb. Repha,el, lit. 'God has healed'. Heb.
rdphd, 'he healed' (whencer phu'a , 'medicine,
remedy*, marpi, 'healing, cure'), the first
element of this compound word, is rel. to Syr.
r phd, 'he healed', Arab, rafcfa, 'he darned,
mended, repaired', Ethiop. rafaa, 'he stitched
together, mended'. For the second element in
Raphael see El.

## Raphalesque
Raphalesque, Raffaelesque, adj., in the style of
the painter Raphael. — Formed fr. the name of
Raffaelh Sanzio (1483-1520) with suff. -esque.

## raphania
raphania, п., a disease causing convulsive

Linnaeus (1707-78) fr. Gk. £αφαυΐς, 'radish'. See

## Raphanus
Raphanus, п., a genus of plants of the cabbage

which is rel. to £άπυς, 'rape'. See rape, the plant.

## raphe
raphe, п., a seam, suture (anat. and bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. £«φή, 'seam, suture (of the
skull)', fr. έάπτειν, 'to sew together, stitch',
which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *wer-p-,
*wre-p-, 'to turn, twist, sew, spin*. See vervain
and cp. the first element in Raphiolepis and in

## Raphia
Raphia, п., a genus of palms {bot.) — ModL.; see

## Raphiolepis
Raphiolepis, п., a genus of plants of the apple
family {bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
(5αφίς, 'needle', and λεπίς, 'scale, flake'. The
first element is rel. to £αφή, 'seam'; see raphe.
For the second element see leper.

## rapid
rapid, adj. — F. rapide, fr. L. rapidus, 'tearing
away, seizing, swift, rapid', fr. rapere, 'to seize
and carry off, to snatch away, to seize, plunder,
ravish', which is cogn. with Gk. έρέπτεσθαι, 'to
pluck off, feed on', Alb. rjep, Ί strip, rob',
Lith. raples, 'tongs', ap-repiu, Ί take, seize', fr.
I.-E. base *rep-, 'to snatch, seize'. Beside *rep-
stands prob. *srep-, *srp- in Gk. άρπάζειν, 'to
snatch, seize', άρτταξ, 'rapacious', αρπάγη,
'hook; rake', ^ρπη, 'sickle', άρπυιαι, 'harpies',

Derivatives: rapid, п., rapidity (q.v.), rapid-ly,
adv., rapid-ness, n.

## rapidity
rapidity, n. — F. rapidite, fr. L. rapiditdtem, ace.

## rapier

and carry off'. See rapid and cp. words there

## rapparee
rapparee, п., an Irish pikeman. — lr. rdpaire, 'a

## rappee
rappee, п., a strong kind of snuff. — Fr. F.

## rapport
rapport, п., relation. — F., back formation fr.

rapporter, 'to bring back, refer to', re-, 'again'

rapprochement, п., establishment of cordial
relations. — F., 'a bringing near*, fr. rapprocher, 'to

## bring near'
bring near', fr. re-, 'again' (see re-), and ap-

rapscallion, п., a rascal. — Later form of obsol.

rascallion, a derivative of rascal.
rapt, part, adj., carried away. — ME., fr. L.
raptus, pp. of rapere, *to seize'. See rnpid and

## raptor

## Raptores
Raptores, n. pi., an order of birds (ornitkol.) —
ModL. Raptores, fr. L. raptores, pi. of raptor.

raptorial, adj., 1) adapted for seizing prey;2)

гага avis, a rare bird. — L., fr. rdra, fern, of rdrus,

## rare
rare, adj., thin. — F., fr. L. rams, 'thin, loose,

viralah, 'distant, tight, rare', OSlav. oriti, 'to

έρημος, 'solitary, isolated', Ol. drdhah, 'part,
side, half, Lith. ardfti, 'to cleave, separate',

Derivatives: rare, adv., rare-ly, adv., rare-ness,n.

## rare
rare, adj., underdone. — ME. rere (whence also

hreran, 'to move, stir, shake', OFris. hrera, OS.
hrorian, ON. hrotra, Swed. rora, Dan. rere, Du.

## narefactive

Derivatives: rarefi-able, adj., rarefi-er, n.

## rarity
rarity, n. — L. rdritds, 'looseness of texture;

'man*, Gk. όέρσην, α"ρρην, 'male', fr. I.-E. base

moisten', whence also L. ros, gen. roris, 'dew*. See

## rascal

Derivatives: rascaf-dom, п., rascal-ism, п.,
rascal-it у, п., rascal-ly, adj. and adv.

## rasceta
rasceta, n. pi-, the transverse creases on the

rase, tr. v., to rub, scrape out, erase. — ME.

also abrade, abrase, abrasion, arrastro, erase,
race, 'to scratch', radula, ramentum, rascal, rash,
'eruption', rasher, 'a rockfish', rasorial, rasure,
razee, razor. Cp. also tabula rasa.

## rash
rash, adj., overhasty. — ME. rasch, prob. fr.
MLG. rasch or MDu. rase (Du. ras), 'quick,
swift', which are rel. to OHG. rase, 'quick,
strong, active, vigorous*, MHG., G. rasch,
'quick, fast', ON. roskr, 'vigorous, brave', and
cogn. with Olr. rethim, Ί run'.
Derivatives: rash, adv., rash-ly, adv., rash-ness,
n.

## rash
rash, п., eruption. — OF. rasche, rache, 'scurf,
rel. to OProvenc. rascar, Sp. rascar, 'to scrape,

## Rasores
Rasores, n. pi., an order of birds (ornithol.) —
ModL. Rasores, fr. L. rasores, pi. of rdsor,

## rasorial
rasorial, adj., 1) scratching the ground for food
(said of birds); 2) belonging to the Rasores. —
Formed from prec. word with suff. -ial.

## rasp
rasp, tr. and intr. v., to rub. — ME. raspen, fr.
OF. *rasper (F. raper), 'to rasp, grate*, which is
ofWTeut.origin;cp.OHG.rai/iow(for*ra/ji?/i),
'to scrape together, snatch up in haste', which is
rel. to OHG. hrespan, 'to pluck, pull', OFris.
hrespa, OE. gehrespan, 'to tear', and to MHG.,
G. raffen, 'to sweep off'. See raffle, 'lottery', and

OProvenc., Sp. raspar, 'to scrape, scratch',
which also are Teut. loan words. Cp. also

Derivatives: rasp, n. (q.v.), rasp-ed, adj.,rasp-er,

## rasp
rasp, п., file for smoothing or grating. — ME.

Derivatives: rasp-ish, rasp-y, adjs.

## rasp
rasp, n. — Dialectal abbreviation of raspberry.

## raspatory
raspatory, п., a surgical instrument for rasping
bones. — Medical L. raspatorius, fr. raspare,
'to rasp*, a word of WTeut. origin. See rasp, 'to
rub*, and subst. suff. -ory,

## raspberry
raspberry, n. — Fr. rasp, dialectal equivalent of

wine, fr. OF. vin raspe (whence F. rape), prop.

means 'rasping berry, rough berry'. For sense

'scratching or rasping berry'.

## rasse

## rasure
rasure, п., the act of scraping. — MF., F., fr. L.

## rat
rat, n. — ME. rat, ratte, fr. OE. rzt, rel. to OS.

OHG. ratta, rata, MHG., G. ratte, ON. rottu-
(iu surnames), Dan. rotte, Swed. ratta, Norw.

rata, п., a New Zealand tree. — Maori.

## ratafia
ratafia, п., liqueur flavored with kernels of

Creole F., possibly a "corruption of the Latin

people drinking one another's health. The word
tafia (q.v.) is prob. an abbreviation of ratafia.
See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 598. L. rata is
the fem. pp. of reor, reri, 'to reckon, believe,

## ratal

## ratan
ratan, n. — The same as rnttan.

## ratany
ratany, n. — The same as rhatany.

Derivative: rataplan, tr. and intr. v.

## rat-a-tat
rat-a-tat, n. — See rat-tat.

## ratch

## ratch

## rate
rate, tr. v-, to scold. — ME. raten, prob. fr. OF.

## rate
