## ribald
ribald, п., an irreverent person; adj., irreverent
(esp. in language), — ME. ribald, ribaud,
'worthless creature', fr. OF. ribauld, ribaud (F. ribaud),
'ribald', fr. riber, 'to be wanton*, which is
borrowed fr. OHG. riban, 'to be wanton', lit. 'to
rub'. See euripus.
Derivatives: ribald, adj., ribaldry (q.v.)

## ribaldry
ribaldry, п., a ribald language. — ME. ribaldrie,
ribaudrie, fr. OF. ribaulderie, fr. ribauld. See
prec. word and -ry.

## riband
riband, п., a ribbon {archaic). — Older spelling
of ribbon, with excrescent -d.
Derivative: riband-ed, adj. (cp, ribboned).

## ribband
ribband, n. (naut.) — Compounded of rib and
band, n.
Derivative: ribband, tr. v.

## ribbon
ribbon, also riband, n. — ME. riban(d), fr. OF.
riban, var. of ruban (F. ruban), fr. MDu. ringh-
band, 'necklace'. The first element of this
compound is rel. to E. ring, п., the second to E.
band, 'a tie'.
Derivatives: ribbon-ed, adj., ribbon-y, adj.

## Ribes
Ribes, п., a genus of shrubs, the currant. — ML.,
fr. Arab, ribas, 'sorrel', fr. Pers. revas.

## riboflavin
riboflavin, п., a factor of the vitamin. В complex
C17H20OeN1. — Coined fr. ribose and flavin.

## ribose
ribose, п., a pentose sugar. — Formed with subst.
sufT. -ose fr. G. Ribon(saure), a tetrahydroxy
acid, whose first element is an alteration of E.
arabinose, fr. L. Arabicus, 'Arabic, Arabian';
see Arabic (Saure, the second element in Ribon-
saure, means 'acid'.)

## Ribston
Ribston, п., a kind of sweet apple. — Short for
Ribston pippin; so called after Ribston Hall in
Yorkshire.

## Ricardian
Ricardian, adj., pertaining to the economic
theories of David Ricardo (1772-1823). — For the
ending see sufT. -ian.
Derivative: Ricardian, п., adherent of the
theories of David Ricardo.

## rice
rice, n. — ME. rys, ris, fr. OF. ris (F. riz), fr. It.
riso, fr. VL. *oryzum, fr. L. oryza, fr. Gk.
δρυζα, fr. OPers. brizi, fr. Afghan vriie, ult. fr.
OI. vrikih, 'rice'. Cp. Oryza, risotto and the
second element in bahuvrihi.
Derivative: rice-y, adj.

## rich
rich, adj. — ME. riche, a blend of OE. rice,
•powerful, strong, noble, rich', and OF. (= F.)
riche, riche, 'rich*; this latter is borrowed fr.
Frankish *riki, 'powerful'. OE. rice and Frankish
*riki are rel. to OS. riki, ON. rikr, OHG. rinhi,
'ruler; powerful,rich', Swed. rik, Dan. rig, 'rich',
OFris. rike, Du. rijk, MHG. rich, riche,
'powerful, rich', G. reich, 'rich', Goth, reiks, 'ruler;
powerful, rich'. These words derive fr. Teut.
*rik-, 'ruler', which is borrowed fr. Celtic *rig-
(cp. Olr. ri, gen. rig), 'king', a cognate of OI.
raj-, rdjan-, L. rex, gen. regis, 'king'.
Accordingly OE. rice, etc., orig. meant 'kingly, royal' [cp.
L. regius (see Regius)]. From this sense
developed that of'powerful', and finally that of'rich'.
See regent, adj., and rex and cp. Reich, the first
element in Richard, Reichstag, Rigsdag,
Riksdag, rix-dollar, and the second element in Alaric,
Aubrey, bishopric, Emery, Eric, Frederic, Frede-
rica, Geoffrey, Harriet, Henry, Roderick, Theo-
doric, Ulrica.
Derivatives: riches (q.v.), rich-ling, п., rich-lyf
adv., rich-ness, n.

## Richard
Richard, masc. PN. — ME. Rycharde, fr. OF. (=
F.) Richard, fr. OHG. Ricohard, which is
compounded of Teut. *rik~, 'ruler*, and *Aar<JH,'hard'.
See rich and hard and cp. dick, dickens, hick.

## richellite
richellite, п., a hydrous iron fluophosphate
(mineral.) — Named after Richelle, near Visa, in
Belgium. For the ending see subst. sufT. -Ite.

## riches
riches, n. pi. — Orig. the word was a sing: ME.
nchesse, fr. OF. richece (F. richesse), fr. riche,
'rich'. See rich. For the F. sufT. -esse see 2nd sufT.
-ess. For a similar exceptional development of
F. -esse into E. -es (inst. of into -ess) cp. laches.

## richterite
richterite, п., a variety of amphibole (mineral.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:665 COLUMN:2 -->
G. Richterit, named after the German
mineralogist Theodor Richter. The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -ΐτης. See subst. surf. -Ite.

## Ricinus
Ricinus, п., a genus of plants (family Euphorbia-
ceae). — L., 'the castor-oil plant', which is of
uncertain origin.

## rick
rick, п., pile, stack. — ME. reke, fr. OE. hreac,
rel. to ON. kraukr, Du. rook, 'heap', and
possibly to ON.hryggr, OE. hrycg, 'back, ridge'.
See ridge and cp. ruck, 'crowd, herd'.
Derivatives: rick, tr. v., to heap up in ricks,
rick-er, n.

## rick
rick, tr. v., to sprain; п., a sprain. — A var.
spelling of wrick.

## rickardite
rickardite, п., a copper telluride (mineral.) —
Named after the American mining engineer
Thomas Arthur Rickard (1864-1953). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## rickets
rickets, n. — Fr. rachitis; influenced in form by
rick or wrick, 'to twist, sprain'.

## rickety
rickety, adj. — Prob. fr. prec. word with adj. sufT.
-У-
Derivative: ricketi-ness, n.

## Rickettsia
Rickettsia, п., a genus of bacilluslike parasites
(bacteriol.) — ModL., named by da Rocha Lima
in honor of the American pathologist Howard
Taylor Ricketts (1871-1910). For the ending see
1st suff. -ia.

## rickle
rickle, п., a small heap or pile. — Formed fr.
rick, 'pile', with dimin. suff. -le.
Derivative: rickle, tr. v.

## rickrack
rickrack, п., serpentine braid of silk, cotton or
wool. — Antiphonic reduplication of rack, *to
stretch'.

## ricksha(w)
ricksha(w), n. — Abbreviation of jinricksha (q.v.)

## ricochet
ricochet, п., the rebounding of an object. — F.,
of uncertain origin.
Derivative: ricochet, intr. v.

## rictal
rictal, adj., pertaining to a rictus. — See next
word and adj. suff. -a],

## rictus
rictus, п., opening of the mouth, gape. — L.
rictus, pp. of ringi, 'to open wide the mouth'. See
ringent.

## rid
rid, tr. v. — ME. ruden, ryden, fr. ON. rydja, 'to
clear, empty, rid', which is rel. to OHG., MHG.
riuten, G. reuten, 'to clear land', OHG. riuti,
'cleared land', and to OFris. rothia, MLG. ro-
den, MHG. roten, G. roden, 'to clear', and prob.
cogn. with Avestic rao(i)6ya, 'to cultivate';
prob. fr. I.-E. *reudh-, 'to clear land*,
enlargement of base *reu-, 'to dig up', whence also L.
ruere, 'to dig up'. (L ruere in this sense is not
rel. to ruere, 'to fall down' (see ruin).
Derivative: ridd-ance, n.

## ridable
ridable, adj. — Formed fr. ride with suff. -able.
Derivatives: ridable-ness, п., ridabl-y, adv.

## riddel
riddel, also ridel, п., a church curtain. — ME.
ridel, riddel, fr. OF. ridel (F. rideau), 'curtain', fr.
rider, 'to wrinkle*, a loan word fr. OHG. ridan,
'to turn, twist'. For sense development cp. OHG
reid, 'crisp, frizzy'.

## ridden
ridden, pp. of ride. — ME. riden, fr. OE. (ge)riden,
pp. of ridan. See ride,

## riddle
riddle, п., enigma, puzzle. — ME. redels, rideles,
fr. OE. rxdels, rxdelse, formed with the subst.
suff. -els fr. OE. rxdan, 'to advise, counsel,
deliberate, guess, interpret, read'. The s in ME.
redels was mistaken for the suff. of the plural
and accordingly dropped. Cp; OS. rddisli, MDu.

## raedsel
raedsel, Du. raadsel, MHG. rdtsel, G. Ratsel,
*riddle', and see read.
Derivatives: riddle, tr. and intr. v., rldd-ler, п.,

## riddl-ing
riddl-ing, adj., riddl-ing-ly, adv.

## riddle
riddle, п., sieve. — ME. riddel, ridel, fr. OE.

## hriddel
hriddel, formed with dissimilation fr. earlier
hridder, 'a coarse sieve', which is rel. to OS.

## hrida
hrida, OHG. ritera, MHG. riter, G. Reiter, fr.
Teut. base *hri-, 'to srft', whence also ON.

## hreinn
hreinn, OHG. hreini, Goth, hrains, 'clean, pure'.
The corresponding I.-E. base is *(s)q(e)ri(i)-,

## whence L. cribrum
whence L. cribrum, 'sieve, riddle', Olr. crlathar,

## OW. cruitr
OW. cruitr, OCo. croider, MBret. croezr, 'sieve',
Gk. κρϊνειν, *to separate, distinguish, decide',

## L. cernere
L. cernere, 'to distinguish', certus, 'certain*. See

## certain and cp. cribriform
certain and cp. cribriform,

## riddle
riddle, tr. and intr. v., to sift. — ME. riddlen,

## ridlen
ridlen, fr. riddel, ridel. See riddle, 'sieve'.
Derivatives: riddl-er, п., riddl-ing, adj., riddl-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:665 COLUMN:3 -->
ings, n. pi.

## ride
ride, intr. and tr. v. — ME. riden, fr. OE. ridan,
rel. to OS. ridan, ON. rida, OFris. rida, MDu.
riden, Du. rijden, OHG. ritan, MHG. riten, G.
reiten. The original meaning of these words was
'to move, .go, travel'. They are cognate with
Gaul.-L. raeda, 'a travelling carriage', Olr. ria-
daim, Ί ride, travel', riad, 'a riding, traveling'.
Cp. ready, road. Cp. also the second element in
palfrey.
Derivatives: ride, п., ridable (q.v.), rider (q.v.),
rid-ing, n.

## rider
rider, n. — ME., fr. OE. ridere, fr. ridan, 'to ride'.
See prec. word and agential suff. -er.

## ridge
ridge, n. — ME. rigge, 'back, ridge', fr. OE. hrycg,
rel. to ON. hryggr, Dan. ryg, Swed. rygg, OFris.
hregg, OS. hruggi, Du. rug, OHG. hrukki, later
rucki, MHG. rucke, rilcke, G. Riicken, 'the
back', possibly also to ON. kraukr, OE. hreac,
'heap* (seerick, 'pile'); perh. cogn. with L. crux,
'cross'. See cross and cp. rick, ruck, 'a crowd',
and the first element in rucksack. Cp. also rung.
Derivatives: ridge, п., ridg-ing, п., ridg-ing-ly,
adv., ridg-y, adj.

## ridicule
ridicule, n. — F., adj. and п., fr. L. ridiculus, 'that
which excites laughter, ridiculous', ridiculum,
'jest', prop. neut. adj. used as a noun, fr. ridere,
'to laugh'. See risible.
Derivatives: ridicule, tr. v., ridicul-er, п.,
ridiculous (q.v.)

## ridiculous
ridiculous, adj. — Fr. L. ridiculosus, 'laughable',
fr. ridiculus. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: ridiculous-ly, adv., ridiculous-ness,
n.

## riding
riding, п., the act of one who rides. — Formed
fr. ride, with -ing, suff. forming verbal nouns.

## riding
riding, п., one of the three administrative districts
of Yorkshire. — ME. [th)riding, fr. OE. -priding,
'a third part*, fr. ON. pridjungr, 'a third part',
fr. pridi, 'third'. See third and 3rd -ing. The
initial p (in OE. -priding) was absorbed by the
final δ in the word nord frequently preceding it,
thus North thriding became North riding.

## ridotto
ridotto, п., entertainment. — It., orig. 'a with-,
drawing-room', prop. pp. of ridurre, 'to lead
back', in the reflexive sense 'to withdraw,
retreat', fr. L. reducere. See reduce and cp.
redoubt, п., and reduit.

## riebeckite
riebeckite, п., a mineral of the amphibole group.
— G. Riebeckit, named after the German
mineralogist Emil Riebeck. The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -ϊτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## riever
riever, n. — See reaver.

## rifacimento
rifacimento, п., recasting of a literary or musical
work. — It., lit. 'remaking', fr. rifac-, pres. stem
of rifare, 'to remake', fr. VL. *refacere
(corresponding to L. reficere), fr. re- and facere, 'to
make, do'. See fact and -ment and cp. refection.

## rife
rife, adj., prevalent, abundant. — ME. rif, rive,
fr. OE. ryfe, 'abundant, frequent', rel. to ON.
rifr, MDu. rijf, MLG. rive, 'abundant,
generous'.
Derivatives: rife-ly, adv., rife-ness, n.

## riffle
riffle, п., 1) a shoal; 2) a way of shuffling cards. —
Rel. to ripple.
Derivative: riffle, tr. and intr. v.

## riffle
riffle, п., a groove. — Cp. G. riefeln, 'to groove',
and see rifle, 'to make grooves in'.

## riffler
riffler, п., a small file with curved ends. — F.
rifloir, formed fr. rifler, 'to file', with suff. -oir (fr.
L. -orium). See 2nd rifle and subst. suff. -ory.

## riffraff
riffraff, п., rabble. — ME. riff and raff, fr. OF. rif
et raf, rifle et rafle, 'one and all', later used in the
sense of 'rabble'. See rifle, 'to plunder', and
raffle, 'lottery'.

## rifle
rifle, tr. v., to plunder. — ME. riflen, fr. OF.
rifler, 'to ransack, plunder; to plane (whence F.
rifler, 'to plane, file, scrape'), fr. OHG. riffilon,
'to tear by rubbing', which is rel. to ON. rifa, 'to
tear, break*. See rive and cp. rifle, 'to make
grooves in'. Cp. also the first element in riffraff.

## rifle
rifle, tr. v., to make grooves in (a gun barrel) —
F. rifler, 'to plane, file, scrape'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: rifle, n. (q.v.), rifl-ed, adj., rifl-er,
п., rifl-ery, п., rifl-ing, n.

## rifle
rifle, п., a portable firearm. — Fr. prec. word in
the sense of rifled (i.e. grooved) musket.

## rift
rift, п., an opening; a cleft. — ME., of Scand.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:666 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 639 | RIPARIAN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:666 COLUMN:1 -->
origin. Ср. Dan. andNorw. rift, 'a breach', ON.
ript, 'the breach of a contract', ripa, 'to break a
contract', and see rive.
Derivatives: rift, tr. v., to split, rift-er, п., rift-
less, adj., rift-y, adj.
rig, tr. v., to fit (a ship, mast, etc.) with sails. —
ME. riggen, of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. rigga, 'to
wrap round', Swed. and Norw. rigga, 'to rig'.
Derivatives: rig, n. (q.v.), rigg-er, п., rigg-ing, n.
rig, п., the distinctive arrangement of the sails,
masts, etc., on a ship. — Cp. Swed. and Norw.
rigg and see prec. word.
rig, tr. v., to manipulate fraudulently; п., a
fraudulent scheme; trick. — Of uncertain
etymology. Cp. the second element in thimblerig.
Riga balsam, balsam obtained from the Swiss
pine. — Named after Riga, capital of Latvia.
rigadoon, п., a dance. — F. rigaudon, rigodon;
according to J. J. Rousseau in Dictionnaire de
musique named after Rigaud, the inventor of
this dance. According to Mistral, Rigaud was a
renowned dancing master at Marseilles.
Rigel, п., a star in the left foot of the constellation
Orion. — Arab, rijl, 'foot'. See Regulus, name
of a star.

## rigescence
rigescence, n. — Formed from next word with
surf, -ce.

## rlgescent
rlgescent, adj., becoming stiff. — L. rigescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of rigescere^ 'to become
stiff', inchoative formed fr. rigere, 'to be stiff'.
See rigid and -escent.

## right
right, adj. — ME. rikt, right, fr. OE. riht, 'right,
straight, erect1, rel. to OS., OHG., MHG. rekt,
G. recht, ON. rear, Goth, raihts, and cogn. with
Gk. όρεκτός, 'stretched out, upright' (prop.
verbal adj. of όρέγει,ν, 'to reach, stretch out,
extend'), L. rectus, 'straight, right' (prop. pp. of
regere, 'to keep straight, lead, conduct, direct'),
Olr. recht, 'law', W. rhaith, Bret, reiz, 'just,
righteous, wise', fr. I.-E. base *reg-, 'to stretch,
straighten; straight, right; to lead, direct, rule'.
See regent, adj., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: right, n.,right-ly, adv., right-ness, n.

## right
right, n. — ME. riht, right, fr. OE. riht. See right,
adj.
Derivatives: rigkt-ful, adj., right-ful-ly, adv.,
right-ful-ness, п., right-less, adj., right-less-ness,
n.

## right
right, tr. and intr. v. — ME. rihten, rigkten, fr.
OE. rihtan, fr. riht, adj. — Cp. OS. rihtian, ON.
retta, 'to straighten, make right', OHG., MHG.
rihten, G. richten, of s.m., Goth, garaihtjan, 'to
guide', and see right, adj.
Derivative: right-able, adj.

## right
right, adv. — ME. riht, right, fr. OE. rihte, fr.
riht. See right, adj.

## righteous
righteous, adj. — Fr. earlier rightwise, fr. ME.
rigktwise, fr. OE. rihtwis, fr. riht, 'right', and
wis, 'wise, learned* (see right, adj., and wise,
adj.); refashioned with surf, -ous· on analogy of
duteous, piteous, etc.
Derivatives: righteous-ly, adv., righteous-ness, n.

## rightward
rightward, adj. — Compounded of right and
-ward, adj. suff.

## rightward
rightward, rightwards, adv. — Compounded of
right and adv. suff. -ward, resp. -wards,

## rigid
rigid, adj., stiff; strict. — L. rigidus, 'hard, stiff,
rough, severe1, fr. rigere, 'to be stiff', which is
rel. to rigor, 'stiffness', and cogn. with Gk. £ΐγος
(for *σρΤγος), 'frost, cold'. See frigid and cp.
rigescent, rigor and the first element in rhigo-
lene.
Derivatives: rigidity (q.v.), rigid-ly, adv., rigid-
ness, n.

## rigidity
rigidity, n. — L. rigiditds, 'stiffness', fr. rigidus.
See prec. word and -ity,

## rigmarole
rigmarole, п., confused, incoherent talk. —
Earlier ragman-roll, 'document with a long list of
names'. See ragman,

## rigol
rigol, п., ring; gutter, groove. — F. rigole, 'small
ditch, channel, gutter', fr. OF. regol, the blend
of MDu. regel, 'row, straight line', and richel,
'gutter', which are both borrowed fr. L. regula,
'a straight piece of wood, rule'. See rule,

## rigolet
rigolet, п., a small stream. — Amer. F., dimin. of
F. rigole. See prec. word and -et.

## rigor
rigor, rigour, п., stiffness; strictness. — ME.
rigour, fr. MF. (= F.) rigueur, fr. L. rigorem, ace.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:666 COLUMN:2 -->
of rigor, 'stiffness, hardness', which is rel. to
rigere, 'to be stiff'. See rigid and -or, -our.
Derivatives: rigo{u)r-ism, п., rigo(u)r-ist, п.,
rigo(u)r-ist-ic, adj., rigorous (q.v.)

## rigorous
rigorous, adj. — ME., fr. ML. rigordsus, fr. L.
rigor. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: rigorous-ly, adv., rigorous-ness, n.

## Rigsdag
Rigsdag, п., the Danish Parliament. — Dan., lit.
'day of the kingdom', fr. rige, 'kingdom', and
dag, 'day'. For the first element see Reich, for
the second see day (q.v.) Cp. Reichstag, Riksdag.

## Rig-Veda
Rig-Veda, п., the oldest collection of hymns in
Vedic literature. — Ol. Rgvedab, compounded
of fk, 'praise, hymn', and \edah, 'knowledge,
sacred book*. The first element is rel. to Ol.
fkvah, 'praising', arcati, 'shines, greets, praises',
and cogn. with Hitt. arkuwar, 'prayer,* Toch.
AB ydrk-, 'to honor*. For the second element
see Veda.

## Riksdag
Riksdag, п., the Swedish Parliament. — Swed.,
lit. 'day of the kingdom', fr. rike, 'kingdom',
and dag, 'day'. For the first element see Reich,
for the second see day. Cp. Reichstag, Rigsdag.

## rile
rile, tr. v., to make muddy. — A var. of roil.

## rilievo
rilievo, п., relief. — It., fr. L. relevare, 'to raise'.
See relief, 'raised work', and relieve and cp.
basso-rilievo, cavo-relievo.

## rill
rill, п., a small brook, rivulet. — LG. rille or Du.
ril, 'a small brook or channel', rel. to Fris. rill,
'narrow passage', fr. Teut. *ridele, a diminutive.
Cp. OE. rid, 'stream, rivulet', MLG. ride,
'watercourse', which derive fr. l.-E. base *rei-, 'to
move, flow, run', whence also L. rivus (for *rei-
wos), 'brook, stream1. See rival, G. Rille, Dan.
rille, 'furrow', derive fr. LG. rille.
Derivatives: rill, intr. v., to flow as a rill, rill-et,
п., a small rill.

## rillettes
rillettes, rilletts, n. pi., potted meat. — F. rillettes,
rel. to rillons, 'greaves of pork', fr, rille, 'piece of
pork*, a dialectal var. of OF. reille, 'small plank,
lath', itself a popular collateral form of regie,
'rule, plank'. See rule and dimin. suff. -ette.

## rim
rim, п., edge, border. — ME. rime, rim, fr. OE.
rima, 'border, bank, coast', rel. to ON. rime,
rimi, 'a raised strip of land, ridge', and to rand.
Derivatives: rim, tr. v., rim-less, adj., rimm-ed,
adj., rimm-er, n.

## rim
rim, п., peritoneum (obsol.) — ME. rente, rim,
fr. OE. reoma, 'membrane, ligament', rel. to
MLG. reme, OS., OHG. Homo, MHG. rieme,
G. Riemen, 'strap'.

## rima
rima, п., cleft, fissure (biol.) — L. rima, 'crack,
cleft, fissure', prob. standing for *rei-ma or *ri-
то, and cogn. with Lett, riewa, 'slit, slash',
Lith. rievd, 'cleft, rock', raivi, 'a strip', prob.
also with OE. raw, r%w, 'row'. See row, 'line',
and cp. rimose.
Derivatives: rim-al, adj., rimose (q.v.), rim-ous,
adj.

## rime
rime, n. — See rhyme, n.

## rime
rime, v. — See rhyme, v.

## rime
rime, п., hoarfrost. — ME. rim, fr. OE. hrim,
'hoarfrost', rel. to ON. hrim, Du. rijm and to
OS. hrlpo; MDu. ripe, Du. rijp> OHG. hriffo,
later rifo, MHG. rife, G. Reif, and prob. cogn.
with Lett, kreims, 'cream', kriet, 'to skim the
cream off'. F.frimas, 'hoarfrost', is a Teut. loan
word; cp. Frimaire.
Derivative: rim-y, adj.

## rimose or rimous
rimose or rimous, adj., full of fissures. — L. rimo-
sus, fr. rima. See rima and adj. suff. -ose, resp.
-ous.
Derivatives: rimose-ly, adv., rimos-ity, n.

## rumple
rumple, п., wrinkle. — Prob. fr. MLG.-MDu.
(— Du.) rimpel, 'wrinkle*, which is rel. to MHG.
rimpfen, 'to wrinkle*, OE. gehrumpen (pp.),
'wrinkled'. See rumple.
Derivative: rimple, tr. and intr. v.

## rimula
rimula, п., a small fissure (anat.) — Medical L.
rlmula, dimin. of L. rima. See rima and -ule.

## rind
rind, п., 1) the bark of a tree; 2) the peel of a
fruit; 3) the crust of bread. — ME. rinde, fr.
OE. rind, rinde, 'bark, crust', rel. to OS. rinda,
MLG. rinde, MDu. rinde, rende, OHG. rinda,
rinta, MHG. rinde, rinte, G. Rinde, and to OE.
rendan, 'to rend'. See rend, 'to tear'.
Derivative: rind, tr. v., to remove the rind.

## rinderpest
rinderpest, п., cattle plague (veter.) — G., fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:666 COLUMN:3 -->
Rinder, pi. of Rind (fr. MHG. rim, fr. OHG.
hrind, rind), 'ox', and Pest, 'pestilence'. For the
first element see rother, runt and cp. reindeer,
for the second see pest.

## rinforzando
rinforzando, adj., strengthening, reinforcing
(musical direction). — It., fr. rinforzare, 'to
strengthen, reinforce', fr. re- and inforzare, fr. in- (fr. L.
in; see in-, 'in') and forza, 'force', fr. VL.fortia,
prop. neut. pi. of L. fortis, 'strong', but
mistaken for a fern. sing. noun. See fort and cp.
force, n. Cp. also sforzando.

## ring
ring, п., circle. — ME. ring, fr. OE. firing, rel. to
ON. hringr, OS., OFris. kring, Dan., Swed., Du.
ring, OHG. firing, later ring, MHG. rinc,
ringes, G. Ring, and cogn. with OSIav. krqgu,
'circle', kroglu, 'round', and with Umbr. cringa-
tro, 'shoulder band'. Cp. ranch, rang, rank, 'a
row', rink, rung. Cp. also harangue and the first
element in ribbon.
Derivatives: ring, tr. and intr. v., to encircle,
ring-ed, adj., ring-er, п., ring-ing, n.s ring-less,
adj., ring-let, п., ring-let-ed, ring-let-y, adjs.

## ring
ring, intr. v., to sound; tr. v., to cause to sound.
— ME. ringen, fr. OE. hringan, rel. to ON.
hringja, Swed. ringa, MDu., Du. ringen; of
imitative origin.
Derivatives: ring, п., a sound produced by
metal, ring-er, п., ring-ing, n.

## ringent
ringent, adj., opened wide. — L. ringens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of ringi, 'to open wide the
mouth', which prob. stands for *rengi and is
cogn. with OSIav. regnqti, 'to open, gape, yawn',
rqgi, 'disgrace, scorn, disdain'. Cp. rictus. For
the ending see suff. -ent.

## rink
rink, п., a part of a bowling green, curling pond,
etc. — Prob. fr. OF. renc, 'row, rank', whence
F. rang and E. rank; ult. connected with ring,
'circle'.
Derivatives: rink, intr. v., rink-er, n.

## rink it e
rink it e, п., a silicate of cerium, etc. (mineral.) —
Named after the Dane Hinrich J. Rink,
inspector in Greenland. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## rinneite
rinneite, п., a chloride of iron, potassium and
sodium (mineral.) — G. Rinneit, named after
the German mineralogist Professor Fritz Rinne.
The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## rinse
rinse, tr. v. — ME. rincen, fr. OF. relncier, rain-
cier (F. rincer), prob. dissimilated fr. recincier,
fr. VL. *recentiare, 'to make fresh, to wash,
cleanse with water', fr. Late L. recentare, 'to
make fresh', fr. L. recins, gen. recentis, 'new,
fresh'. See recent.
Derivatives: rinse, п., rins-ings, n. pi.

## rio
rio, п., a river. — Sp. rlo, fr. L. rivus, 'brook,
stream', for *rei-wos, lit. 'that which flows', fr.
l.-E. base *rei-, 'to flow'. See rival and cp. ria
and the first element in rialto.

## riot
riot, n. — ME. riote, riot, fr. OF. riote (F. riotte),
fr. rioter, rihoter, 'to make a disturbance', which
is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: riot, v. (q.v.), riot-ist, п., riot-ist-ic,
adj., riot-ous, adj., riot-ous-ly, adv., riot-ous-
ness, п., riot-ry, n.

## riot
riot, intr. v. — ME. rioten, fr. riote, riot. See riot, n.
Derivatives: riot-er, п., riot-ing, adj., riot-ing-ly,
adv.

## riotous
riotous, adj. — ME., fr. OF. rioteus, fr. riote,
'riot'. See riot, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: riotous-ly, adv., riotous-ness, n.

## rip
rip, tr. and intr. v., to tear off, divide. — Of
Scand. or LG. origin. Cp. Fris. rippe, 'to tear
off1, MLG. reppen, Flemish rippen, Swed. reppa,
Dan. rippe, 'to tear, rip'; possibly of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: rip, п., a tear, a rent, ripp-аЫе, adj.,
ripp-er, п., ripp-ing, adj., ripp-ing-ly, adv.,
ripping- ness, n.

## rip
rip, п., a worthless person. -^ Prob. a var. of
rep, abbreviation of reprobate.

## rlparinn
rlparinn, adj., pertaining to the bank of a river. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. riparius, 'that which
frequents riverbanks', fr. ripa, 'riverbank,
seashore', which is prob. cogn. with Gk. έρείττειν,
'to tear down', έρίττνη, 'a broken cliff or crag',
ON. rtfa, 'to tear, break', MHG. rif, 'river-
bank'. See rive, river, and cp. Ripuarian. For the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:667 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: RIPARIOUS | 64Q -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:667 COLUMN:1 -->
ending see suff. -ian.

## riparious
riparious, adj., growing along the banks of
rivers. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. riparius.
See prec. word.

## ripe
ripe, adj. — ME., fr. OE. ripe, rel. to OS. ripi,
MDu. ripe, Du. rijp, OHG. rifi, MHG. rife, G.
reif. These words are verbal adjs. formed from
OE. ripan, 'to reap', resp. its correspondences
in the other Teut. languages. See reap.
Derivatives: ripe, v. (q.v.), ripe-ly, adv., rip-en,
intr. and tr. v., rip-en-er, п., ripeness (q.v.),
ripen-ing, adj., ripen-ing-ly, adv.

## ripe
ripe, tr. and intr. v., to ripen. — ME. ripen, fr.
OE. ripian, fr. ripe, 'ripe'. See ripe, adj.

## ripeness
ripeness, n. — ME. ripenes, fr. OE. ripnes, fr. ripe,
'ripe*. See ripe, adj., and -ness.

## riposte
riposte, п., 1) a quick thrust after parrying a
lunge (fencing); 2) a sharp retort. — F. riposte,
dissimilated fr. It. risposta, prop. fern. pp. of
rispondere, 'to reply', fr. L. respondere, of s.m.
See respond.

## ripple
ripple, tr. v., to cleanse (flax or hemp) by
removing the seeds. — ME. rippelen, ripfen, rel. to
Du. repelen, G. riffeln, 'to ripple', and to OE.
repan, ripan, 'to reap'. See reap.

## ripple
ripple, п., flax comb. — Prob. fr. prec. word; rel.
to MLG., Du. repel, G. Riffel, 'flax comb'.

## ripple
ripple, intr. v., to move in small waves; tr. v., to
cause to ripple. — ME. ripelen, 'to scratch*. Cp.
riffie, rumple.
Derivatives: ripple, п., slight motion of the
waves; wavelet, rippl-et, п., a small ripple.

## Ripuarian
Ripuarian, adj., pertaining to the Franks settled
on both sides of the Rhine near Cologne. —
Lit. 'living on the banks of a river', fr. ML. ri-
puarius, the same as L. riparius. See riparian.
For sense development cp. Lithuanian.

## rise
rise, intr. v. — ME. risen, fr. OE. risan, rel. to OS.
risan, ON. risa, Goth, ur-reisan, 'to rise', OHG.
risan, 'to rise, flow', G. reisen, 'to travel' (the
original meaning was 'to rise for a journey').
These words possibly derive fr. I.-E. base *rei-,
'to move, flow, run', whence L. rivus, 'brook,
stream'. See rival and cp. arise, raise, rear.
Derivatives: rise, п., ris-ert п., ris-ing, adj. and
n.

## risen
risen, pp. οι rise. — ME. risen, fr. OE. (ge)risen,
pp. of risan. See rise.

## risible
risible, adj. — F., fr. Late L. risibilis, 'able to
laugh', fr. L. risus, pp. of ridere, 'to laugh',
which is prob. cogn. with OI. vridyati, vrtdyate,
'is ashamed'. For sense development cp. OI.
vismayate, 'is astonished, confounded,
perplexed', fr. smayate, 'smiles, blushes'. Cp. arride,
deride, derision, riant, ridiculous, risorius, risus.
Derivatives: risible-ness, п., risibl-y, adv.

## risk
risk, n. — F. risque, fr. It. risco (now preferably
risckio), back formation from risicare (now
preferably rischiare), 'to risk', fr. VL. *risicare,
which is prob. a derivative of Gk. ρίζα, 'root'
(see rhizo-), used also in the sense of'cliff, crag'.
Accordingly VL. *risicdre orig. meant 'to
navigate among cliffs'. OProvenc. rezegue, Sp.
riesgo and G. Risiko, 'risk', are Italian loan
words. Some authorities derive It. risco fr.
Arab, rizq, 'subsistence*. It is difficult, however,
to explain how this meaning developed into
that of 'danger, risk'. Cp. risque.
Derivatives: risk-ful, adj., risk-ful-ness, п., risk-
y, adj., risk-i-ly, adv., risk-i-ness, п., risk-less,
adj.

## risk
risk, tr. and intr. v. — F. risquer, fr. It. rischiare.
See risk, n.
Derivative: risk-er, n.

## risorius
risorius, п., name of a muscle of the cheek (anat.)
— Medical L. (musculus) risorius, '(the muscle)
that causes laughter', coined by the Italian
anatomist Giovanni Domenico Santorini (1681-
1736), fr. L. risus, pp. of ridere, 'to laugh*. See
risible.

## risotto
risotto, п., rice cooked in broth with meat and
cheese. — It., fr. riso, 'rice'. See rice,

## risque
risque, adj., risky; tending toward impropriety.
— F., pp. of risquer, 'to risk*. See risk, v.

## risus
risus, п., laughter. — L. risus, gen. -us, fr. risus,
pp. οΐ ridere, 'to laugh'. See risible,

## rissole
rissole, п., minced-meat fritter. — F., fr. OF.
roissole (occurring in the XIII cent.), fr. VL.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:667 COLUMN:2 -->
*russeola, dimin. formed fr. L. russeus,
'reddish', fr. russus, 'red' (see russet and dimin. suff.
-ole); so called from its color.

## ritardando
ritardando, adj., retarding (musical direction). —
It., fr. ritardare, 'to make slow', fr. L. retardare,
'to keep back, hinder, delay'. See retard.

## rite
rite, п., a ceremonial act. — ME., fr. L. ritus,
'religious custom, usage, ceremony', cogn. with
Gk. άρί&μός, 'number', OHG., OE. rim,
'number', Olr. rim, 'number*, do-rimu, Ί
number, count, enumerate'. All these words are
derivatives of I.-E. base *rl·, 'to count,
number*, which is prob. an enlargement of base
*ar-, 'to join', whence Goth, arms, OE. earm,
arm, etc., 'the upper limb'. See arm, 'the upper
limb', and cp. ritual. Cp. also arithmetic, rhyme.

## rittingerite
rittingerite, п., a compound of arsenic, selenium
and silver (mineral.) — Named after the
Austrian mining official Peter Rittinger. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## ritual
ritual, adj. — L. ritudlis, fr. ritus, *rite\ See rite
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: ritual, п., ritual-ism, п., ritual-ist,
п., ritual-ist-ic, adj., rituaf-ist-ic-al-ly, adv., rit-
ual-ity, п., ritual-ly, adv.

## ritzy
ritzy, adj., too smart (slang). — Prop, 'imitating
the Ritz hotel in London'. The hotel was so
called because it was founded by Cesar Ritz,
a Swiss restaurateur (1815-1918). For the ending
see suff. -y.

## rivage
rivage, п., shore, bank. — F., fr. OF. rive, 'bank',
fr. L. ripa. See river and -age.

## rival
rival, n. and adj. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. rivalis,
'pertaining to a brook; one who uses the same
brook; neighbor; competitor, rival', fr. r.ivus,
'brook, stream'. In English, rival first meant
'partner, colleague'. Cp. the words of Bernardo
in Hamlet 1: "If you do meet Horatio and Mar-
cellus, The rivals of my watch". — L. rivus
stands for *rei-wos and lit. means 'that which
flows or runs', fr. I.-E. base *rei-, 'to move,
flow, run', whence also OI. rindti, rinvati,
'causes to flow', ritih, 'stream, course',
OSlav, reka, 'river', suroj, 'confluence', roj,
'swarm of bees', rinqtl, rijati, 'to flow, run', Mir.
rian, 'river, way', Olr. riathor, 'a torrent', OW.
reatir, 'waterfall', W. rhid, 'seed*, Gaul. Renos
(whence L. Rhenus), 'Rhine', lit. 'that which
•flows', OE. rid, 'stream, rivulet". See orient, п.,
and cp. Rhenish, ria, rill, rio, rivose, rivulet. Cp.
also rise.
Derivatives: rival, tr. and intr. v., rival-ism, п.,
rival-ry, п., rival-skip, n.

## rive
rive, tr. v., to tear, rend. — ME. riven, fr. ON.
rifa, 'to tear, break', which is rel. to MHG. rif,
'riverbank, seashore', and prob. cogn. with Gk.
Ιρείπζιν, 'to tear down', έρίπνη, 'a broken cliff
or crag', L. ripa, 'riverbank, seashore*. Cp.
rifle, 'to plunder', rifle, 'to make grooves in',
rift, rivel. Cp. also riparian, river.

## rivel
rivel, intr. and tr. v., to wrinkle. — ME. rivelen,
back formation fr. OE. rifelede, 'wrinkled','
which is rel. to OE. gerifod, 'wrinkled', ON.
rifa, 'to tear, break'. See prec. word.

## riven
riven, adj., prop. pp. of rive. — ME., fr. ON.
rifinn, pp. of rifa, 'to tear, break*. See rive.

## river
river, n. — ME. rivere, fr. OF. rivere, riviere,
'land lying along a river; river' (whence F.
riviere, 'river'), fr. Late L. ripdria (scil. terra),
*land lying along a riverbank', fern, of riparius,
'of a riverbank', fr. ripa, 'riverbank, seashore'.
See riparian and cp. rive. Cp. also rivage,
riverain, riviere, arriba, arrive, derive.
Derivatives: river-ed, adj., river-ine, adj., river-
let, п., river-y, adj.

## riverain
riverain, adj., pertaining to the bank(s) of a river.
— F., fr. MF. riveran, fr. rivere, riviere (F.
riviere), 'river, stream', and suff. -ain, fr. L.
-anus. See prec. word and" -an.
Derivative: riverain, п., one dwelling on the
bank of a river.

## rivet
rivet, n. — ME. ryvette, fr. OF. (= F.) river, 'to
clench*, which is prob. borrowed fr. MDu.
wriven (Du. wrijven), 'to start, put in motion,
agitate'. F. river in the above sense has nothing
to do with river, 'to land* (which comes fr. L.
ripa, 'riverbank, seashore'; cp. arrive,
derive).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:667 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: rivet, tr. v., rivet-er, п., rivet-ing, n.

## riviere
riviere, п., a necklace of diamonds. — F., lit.
'stream'. See river,

## rivose
rivose, adj., having sinuate and irregular furrows
(entomol.) — L. rivdsus, 'full of streams', fr.
rivus, 'brook, stream'. See rival and adj. suff.
-ose.

## rivnlet
rivnlet, п., a small stream. — It. rivoletto, dimin.
of rivolo, itself dimin. of rivo, 'brook, stream',
fr. L. rivus. See prec. word and the suffixes -ule
and -et.

## rix-dollar
rix-dollar, п., name of silver coins formerly
current in Holland, Scandinavia and Germany. —
Obsol. Du. rijcksdaler (now rijksdaalder), lit.
'dollar of the realm', fr. rijck (resp. rijk),
'kingdom, realm*, and daler (resp. daalder). Cp. Dan.
rigsdaler, Swed. riksdaler, G. Reichstaler, and
see Reich and dollar.

## rlyal
rlyal, also rial, п., 1) a coin of Saudi Arabia; 2)
a coin of Iraq. — Arab, riydl, fr. Sp. real. See
real, monetary unit.

## rizzar
rizzar, tr. v., to dry in the sun (Scot.) — MF. res-
sorer, 'to dry again', fr. re- (see re-) and sorer,
'to make red, to dry\
Derivative: rizzar, п., drying in the sun.

## roach
roach, п., a freshwater fish of the carp family
(Leuciscus rutilus). — ME. roche, fr. MF., fr.
OF. roche, which is of uncertain origin.

## roach
roach, п., curved cut in the foot of a square sail.
— Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: roach, tr. v., to cut with a roach.

## roach
roach, n. — Short for cockroach,

## road
road, n. — ME. rode, 'riding, journey', fr. OE.
rad, of s.m., fr. riden, 'to ride'. Accordingly road
orig. meant 'a way for riding'. See ride.
Derivatives: road, tr. v., road-ing, п., road-less,
adj., road-less-ness, п., roadster, n.

## roam
roam, intr. v. — ME. romen, of uncertain origin.
Cp. ramble.
Derivatives: roam, п., roam-er, п., roam-ing,
adj., roam-ing-ly, adv.

## roan
roan, adj., bay, chestnut-colored (said of horses,
etc.) — MF. (~ F.) rouan, fr. Sp. roano, fr.
OSp. raudano, fr. VL. *rdviddnus, fr. L. rdvidus,
'grayish', fr. rdvus, 'gray', which is cogn. with
ON. grar, OE. grxg, 'gray'. See gray.
Derivative: roan, п., a roan horse.

## roan
roan, п., leather made of sheepskin. — Prob. fr.
Roan, the ME. spelling of Rouen, a city of
France.

## roar
roar, intr. and tr. v. — ME. roren, raren, fr. OE.
rarian, rel. to MDu. reeren, 'to roar*, OHG.
гёгёп, MHG. reren, 'to bleat', G. rohren, 'to
troat', from the I.-E. imitative base *гё-, *rd-,
'to cry, roar', whence also OI. rdyati, 'barks',
Lith. riju, reti, 'to scold, chide', Lett, reju, riet,
'to bark', OSlav. revo, rjevg, Ί roar', L. raucus
(for *rawicos), 'hoarse*. 'See raucous and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: roar, п., roar-er, п., roar-ing, adj.
and п., roar-ing-ly, adv.

## roast
roast, tr. and intr. v. — ME. rosten, fr. OF. rostir
(F. rotir), fr. Frankish *hraustjan, which is rel.
to OHG. rosten (MHG. rcesten, G. rosten), 'to
roast', fr. OHG. rost (MHG. rost, G. Rost),
'gridiron, grate', and to MDu. (= Du.) roos-
ten, 'to roast', fr. MDu. roost, 'gridiron, grate*.
Cp. roster.
Derivatives: roast-able, adj.,/oast-ing-ly, adv.

## roast
roast, ri. — ME. rost, fr. MF. rost (F. rot), fr. OF.
rost, fr. rostir, 'to roast'; partly directly fr. roast,
v.

## rob
rob, tr. and intr. v. — ME. robben, fr. OF. rober
(whence F. dirober, 'to steal*), fr. OF. robe,
'booty; booty of garments; gown, dress, robe',
fr. WTeut. *rauba, 'booty'. Cp. OHG. roub,
'spoil, plunder', roubdn, 'to rob*, and see reave.
Cp. also rone.

## Rob
Rob, masc. PN. — Dimin. of Robert (q.v.)

## robalo
robalo, п., any of the fishes of the family Centro-
pomidae. — Sp. robalo, orig. pronounced robalo
(as today in Galicia, Portugal and America),
metathesized fr. *lobarro (Catal. Uobarro), fr.
lobo, 'wolf (used metaphorically in the sense of
a'wolflike fish'),fr.L./tfptfi,'wolf. See lupine, adj.

## roband
roband, also raband, robbin, n. (naut.) — Du.
raband, compounded of ra, 'sailyard', and band,
'band'. The first element is rel. to ON. ra, Dan.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:668 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 641 | ROLE | 'to roll' (corresponding to It. rotare, 'to turn | role, also role, n. — F. rule, 'part played by an -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:668 COLUMN:1 -->
raa, Swed. ra, Du. ra, MHG., G. rake, 'sail-
yard', and possibly also to MHG., G. ragen,
etc., 'to jut out'; see rake, 'to project'. For the
second element see band, 'tie'.

## robber
robber, n. — ME. robbere, fr. OF. robere, fr.
rober, 'to rob'. See rob and agential suff. -er.

## robbery
robbery, n. — ME. robberie, fr. OF. roberie, ft.
rober. See prec. word and -ery.

## robe
robe, n. — ME., fr. OF. robe, 'booty; booty of
garments; gown, dress, robe' (whence F., 'gown,
dress, robe"); see rob. Cp. OProvenc. rauba,
'booty; gown, robe', It. roba, 'things, goods;
stuff; cloth', Sp. гора, 'clothes, clothing, dress,
garments, robe, gown', which are also
borrowed fr. WTeut. 'rauba.
Derivatives: robe, tr. v., rob-er, п., rob-ing, h.

## robe-de-chambre
robe-de-chambre, a dressing gown. — F., lit. 'a
chamber gown'. See robe, de- and chamber.

## Robert
Robert, masc. PN. — F., fr. OHG. Hruodperkt,
Hrodperht, lit. 'bright with glory', fr. hruod-,
ruod- (in compounds), 'fame, glory', and beraht,
'bright'. For the first element see rummer, for
the second see bright. Cp. Rob, robbln, dobbin,
hob, 'fairy'. Cp. also the first element in
Roderick, Roger, Roland, Rudolph. Cp. also Rupert.

## robin
robin, п., name of several birds. — Short for
robin redbreast, orig. written Robin Redbreast,
from the PN. Robin, a dimin. of Robert.

## Robinia
Robinia, п., a genus of plants, the locust tree
(bot.) — ModL., named after the French
botanist Jean Robin (1550-1629) and his son
Vespasian (1579-1662), who first cultivated the
locust tree in Europe. For the ending see 1st
suff. -ia.

## roble
roble, п., any of several trees of the oak family. —
Sp., dissimilated ft. robre, fr. L. robur, gen. ro-
boris, 'oak'. See robust.

## roborant
roborant, adj., strengthening. — L. roborans,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of roborare, 'to
strengthen, invigorate', fr. robur, gen. roboris, 'strength'.
See robust and -ant.
Derivative: roborant, п., a strengthening drug, a
tonic.

## robot
robot, п., an automaton; a mechanical man. —
Fr. Czech robotnik, 'slave', fr. robota,
'compulsory service', fr. rob, 'slave', rel. to OSlav.
rabu, robu, 'slave', rabota, 'servitude, slavery',
and cogn. with Goth, arbaips, 'hardship, toil,
work', OHG. arabeit, MHG. arebeit, arbeit,
'labor, soil, distress', G. Arbeit, 'work, labor',
ON. erfidi, OE. earfod(e), 'hardship, suffering,
labor, work'. See orphan. The word robot
became popular through the play R.U.R.
(Possum's £/niversal /robots), written by Karel
Capek (1st edition 1920, English translation
1923).
Derivatives: robot-ism, п., robot-ize, tr. v.,
robot-iz-ation, n.

## roburite
roburite, n., a flameless explosive. — Formed with
subst. suff. -ite fr. L. robur, 'strength' (see
robust); so called because of the high power of
this explosive.

## robust
robust, adj., strong and healthy. — L. robustus,
'of oakwood, oaken, hard, firm, strong, robust',
lit. 'as strong as an oak', fr. robur, older rebus,
'a very hard kind of oak; oak (in general);
hardness, strength, power'. L. robur orig.
meant 'the red or dark colored tree'; it is rel. to'
L. ruber, 'red', robigo, 'rust'. See red and cp.
roble, roborant, corroborate and the first
element in rumbustious. Cp. also rubric.
Derivatives: robust-fid, adj., robust-ful-ly, adv.,
robust-fut-ly, adv., robust-ful-ness, п., robust-ic,
adj., robust-ic-ity, п., robustious (q.v.)

## robustious
robustious, adj., 1) robust, strong; 2) boisterous,
noisy (obsol.) — See robust and -ious and cp.
rambunctious.
Derivatives: robustious-ly, adv., robustious-ness,
n.

## roc
roc, п., a large, fabulous bird. — Fr. Arab, ruhh,
rohh, 'a large, fabulous bird', which is of Pers.
origin.

## rocambole
rocambole, п., a kind of leek used like garlic. —
F., fr. G. Rockenbolle, 'rocambole', lit. 'rye
bulb', fr. Rocken, a secondary form of Roggen,
'rye' and Bolle, 'bulb'. See rye and bowl, 'a
hollow vessel'.

## Roccella
Roccella, п., a genus of lichens (bot.) — ModL.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:668 COLUMN:2 -->
a blend of It. rocca, 'rock' (see rock, 'stone'),
and orcella, 'archil' (see archil).

## rochet
rochet, п., a white ecclesiastical vestment.— ME.,
ft. MF. (= F.) rochet, fr. OF., ft. Frankish
'rok-, which is rel. to OHG. roc, roch, 'coat'.
See frock and -et. It. rocchetto, Sp., Port, ro-
quete, 'rochet', are also Teut. loan words.
Derivative: rochet-ed, adj.

## rochet
rochet, п., the red gurnard. — ME. rochet, roget,
fr. MF. (= F.) rouget, fr. OF., fr. rouge, 'red',
ft. L. rubeus, 'reddish', which is rel. to ruber,
'red'. See red and -et and cp. rubric.

## rock
rock, п., stone. — ME. rokke, fr. ONF. roque,
corresponding to OF. (= F.·) roche, fr. VL.
*rocca, a word of Celtic origin. (Cp. Bret.
rock.) See Hermann Paul, Grundrifl der ger-
manischen Philologie, 2nd edition, Strassburg,
I, 929. Cp. It. rocca, Sp. roca, 'rock, stone'. Cp.
also rococo.
Derivatives: госк-ery, п., rock-y, adj.

## rock
rock, tr. v., to move to and fro; intr. v., to sway
to and fto. — ME. rocken, fr. OE. roccian, rel.
to ON. rykkja, 'to pull, tear, move', Dan.
rykke, Swed. rycka, 'to pull, pluck', Dan. rokke,
'to move', MLG., MDu. rucken, Du. rukken,
OHG. rucchan, rucken, MHG. rucken, rucken,
G. rucken, 'to move jerkily', ON. rykkr, MLG.
ruck, Du. ruk, MHG. rue, G. Ruck, 'a jerk'. Cp.
rack, 'to move with a particular gait'.
Derivatives: rock, п., the act of rocking, rock-er,
п., rock-y, adj., rock-i-ly, adv., rock-i-ness, n.

## rock
rock, п., distaff (hist.) — ME. rok, rel. to ON.
rokkr, Dan. rok, Swed. rock, MLG. rocken,
MDu. rocken, rocke, Du. rokken, OHG. rocko,
ro(c)cho, MHG. rocke, G. Rocken, 'distaff'; fr.
I.-E. base *rug-, 'to spin'. See frock and cp.
rochet, 'white ecclesiastical vestment*. Cp. also
next word.

## rocket
rocket, п., firework. — It. rocchetta, dimin. of
rocca, 'distaff', which is a Teut. loan word [cp.
OHG. rocko, ro(c)cho, 'distaff', and see prec.
word]; so called from its resemblance to a
distaff. For the ending see suff. -et. Cp. ratchet.
Derivatives: rocket, intr. and tr. v., rocket-er, n.

## rocket
rocket, п., any plant of the genus Hesperis. —
F. roquette, fr. It. rochetta, an earlier var. of
rucchetta, dimin. of ruca, fr. L. ё-гйса, 'cole-
wort', which is of uncertain origin.

## rococo
rococo, п., a style of architecture. — Lit. 'rock
work', fr. F. rocaiUe, 'rock work, grotto work'
(see rock, 'stone'); so called in allusion to the
use of shells and scrolls in this kind of
architecture.
Derivative: rococo, adj.

## rod
rod, n. — ME., fr. OE. rodd, rel. to ON. rudda,
'club', of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: rod-less, adj., rodlet (q.v.)

## rode
rode, past tense of ride. — ME. rood, fr. OE. rad,
past tense of ridan. See ride.

## rodent
rodent, adj., gnawing. — L. rodens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of rodere, 'to gnaw, eat away,
corrode', which stands in gradational relationship
to radere, 'to scrape', and is cogn. with 01. rada-
ti, 'scrapes, gnaws', radanah, 'tooth'. See rase
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
rostrum and corrode, corrosion, corrosive, erode,
erosion, erosive. Cp. also root, 'to dig'. For the
ending of rodent see suff. -ent.
Derivatives: rodent, п., rodent-ial, adj., rodent-
ial-ly, adv.

## rodeo
rodeo, п., rounding up of cattle. — Sp., fr. rodear,
'to go round, surround', ft. rueda, 'wheel', fr.
L. rota, of s.m. See rota.

## Roderick
Roderick, also Roderic, masc. PN. — OHG. Hro-
derich, Ruodrich (G. Roderick), lit. 'ruling in
fame', ft. hruod-, ruod- (in compounds), 'fame,
glory', and Teut. *r!kja-, 'rule'. For the first
element see rummer, for the second see Reich.
F. Rodrigue, It. and Sp. Rodrigo and Russ.
Rurik are German loan words.

## rodlet
rodlet, п., a small rod. — A hybrid coined fr. rod
and dimin. suff. -let.

## rodomontade
rodomontade, п., vain boasting like that of Rodo-
monte in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso. — MF.
(= F.), fr. It. rodomontata, fr. Rodomonte, PN. in
Orlando Furioso. The name lit. means 'one who
rolls (away) the mountain', fr. dial. It. rodare,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:668 COLUMN:3 -->
round', ft. rota, 'wheel'), and It. monte (fr. L.
montem, ace. of mSns, 'mountain'). See rota,
mount, 'mountain', and -ade.
Derivatives: rodomontade, intr. v., rodomontad-
ist, n:

## roe
roe, п., small deer. — ME. roo, fr. OE. rd(h), rel.
to ON. ra, Dan. raa, Swed. ra, OS., Du. ree,
OS., OHG. reh(o), MHG. rich, G. Reh, 'roe', ft.
I.-E. base *rei-, *roi-, 'streaky, spotted', whence
also Lith. raT-mas, rai-bas, Lett, raibs, Russ.
ribyj, 'variegated, spotted', OPruss. roaban,
'striped', Olr. riabhach, 'variegated, spotted',
OI. risyah, 'antelope'.

## roe
roe, п., eggs of fishes, spawn. — Obsol. roan, ft.
ME. rowne, fr. ON. hrogn [Dan., Norw. rogn
(whence F. rogue)], which is rel. to OHG. rogo,
rogan, rogin, MHG. roge(n), G. Rogen, fr. Teut.
base *hrusan, corresponding to I.-E. *qreq-,
*qrq-, 'spawn', whence Lith. kurkle, kurkulat
(pi.), Lett. kutkuVi, Russ. krjak, 'spawn of frogs'.
Derivative: ro-ed, adj.

## roebiingite
roebiingite, п., a lead calcium silicate (mineral.)
— Named after Washington Augustus Roebling
(1806-69), of Trenton, New Jersey. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## roentgeno-
roentgeno-, rontgeno-, combining form meaning
'Roentgen rays', as in roentgeno-gram,
roentgenography, roentgeno-logy, roentgeno-therapy.
See Roentgen ray.

## Roentgen ray
Roentgen ray, Rontgen ray. — So called after its
discoverer, the German physicist Wilhelm Kon-
rad Rontgen (1845-1923).

## rogation
rogation, п., supplication. — Late ME. rogacioun,
fr. L. rogatio, gen. -onis, 'inquiry, request", fr.
rogatus, pp. of rogare, 'to ask, beg, entreat',
prop, 'to have a desire for', in vowel
gradational relationship to regere, 'to guide, lead, direct,
rule'. See regent, adj., and -atlon and cp.
abrogate, arrogant, arrogate, corvee, derogate,
interrogate, prerogative, prorogue, subrogate,
surrogate.
Derivative: rogation-al, adj.

## rogatory
rogatory, adj., seeking information. — F. roga-
toire, fr. ML. rogatorius, 'supplicating', fr. L.
rogatus, pp. of rogare, 'to ask'. See rogation and
adj. suff. -ory.

## Roger
Roger, masc. PN. — OF. Rogier, ft. OHG. Hrot-
ger, Hrodger, lit. 'famous with the spear', fr.
hruod-, ruod- (in compounds), 'fame, glory', and
ger, 'spear'. For the first element see rummer,
for the second see gar. Cp. Hodge.

## rogersite
rogersite, п., a decomposition product of
samarskite (mineral.) — Named after the
American geologist William Barton Rogers (1804-
82). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## rogersite
rogersite, п., a hydrous ferric sulfate (mineral.)
— Named after the American mineralogist
Austin Flint Rogers (1877-1957) For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## rogue
rogue, п., 1) formerly, a vagabond; 2) a rascal. —
F„ rogue, prob. of Celtic origin. Cp. Bret, rog,
'haughty'.
Derivatives: rogue, v., rogu-ery, п., rogu-ish,.
adj., rogu-ish-ly, adv., rogu-ish-ness, n.

## roil
roil, tr. v., to stir up (a liquid); to disturb. — F.
rouiller, 'to make rusty, to rust', fr. rouille,
'rust', fr. OF. ruile, rouille, fr. VL. 'rdbicula,
formed—with change of suff.—fr. L. robigo,
'rust'. Cp. the OF. collateral forms ruit, rouil (fr.
VL. *robtculus), OProvenQ. rovilh, roilh (fr. VL.
*r6biculus), rovilha, rollha (ft. VL. *robicula),
and Sp. robin, of s.m. (fr. L. robiginem, ace. of
robigo). See rubiginous and cp. rile.

## roister
roister, intr. v., to swagger. — Fr. OF. ruistre,
rustre (F. rustre), 'boor', fr. ruiste, 'boorish,
gross, uncouth', fr. L. rusticus, 'countryman,
rustic, peasant', fr. rus, gen. ruris, 'country'.
See rural and cp. rustic.
Derivatives: roister, п., roister-er, п., roister-ing,
adj., roister-ing-ly, adv., roister-ous, adj., roister-
ous-ly, adv.

## rokelay
rokelay, n. — Corruption of roquelaure.

## Roland
Roland, masc. PN. — F., ft. OHG. Hruodland,
Hrodland, which is compounded of hruod-,
ruod- (in compounds), 'fame, glory', and land,
'land'. For the first element see rummer, for the
second see land. Cp. Orlando.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:669 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ROLF | 642 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:669 COLUMN:1 -->
actor*, prop, 'roll containing the actor's part',
fr. OF. role, 'roll', fr. Late L. rotulus, dimin.
formed fr. L. rota, 'wheel'. See roll, n. and
v.

## Rolf
Rolf, masc. PN. — ON. Hrolfr, rel. to OHG.
Hrodulf lit. 'wolf of fame'; see Rudolph. The
name Rolf was introduced into England by the
Normans.

## roll
roll, intr. and tr. v. — ME. rolfen, rolen, fr. OF.
roller, roler, rouler (F. router), fr. VL. *rotuldre,
fr. L. rotula, 'a little wheel', dimin. of rota,
'wheel'. See rota and cp. roll, n. Cp. also role,
control, enroll, roulade, rouleau, roulette, enroll,
roly-poly.
Derivatives: roll, n. (q.v.), roll-able, adj., roll-er,
п., roll-ing, adj., roll-ing-ly, adv.

## roll
roll, п., a scroll.'— Partly fr. ME. rolle, fr. OF.
rote (F. role), fr. ML. roiulus, 'a roll of paper',
prop, a collateral form of L. rotula, 'a little
wheel', partly from the verb roil (q.v.) OPro-
venc. role, rotle, 'roll, roller', Sp. rolde, 'circle,
group of people', are also borrowed fr. ML.
rotulus. It. ruolo and Sp. rol, 'list, roll', are
French loan words.

## rollic
rollic, intr. v., to be gay, be careless. — Prob. a
blend of roll and frolic.
Derivatives: rollic, п., gaiety; a frolic, rollick-er,
п., rollick-ing, adj., rollick-ing-ly, adv., rollick-
ing-ness, п., rollick-some, adj., rollick-some-
ness, n.

## roly-poly
roly-poly, п., pudding made of jam rolled up with
fruit, etc. — Reduplication of roll.
Derivative: roly-poly, adj., resembling a roly-
poly, pudgy.

## rom
rom, п., a male gypsy. — Gypsy rom, 'man,
husband; gypsy man', fr. 01. dombah, domah, 'a
man of a low cast of musicians', prob. of
imitative origin and lit. meaning 'he who utters or
produces the sound dom. See M. Mayrhofer, A
Concise Etymological Sanskrit Dictionary, I,
p. 464, s.v. dombah. Cp. rum, Romany.

## Romaic
Romaic, adj., pertaining to the language of
Modern Greece. — ModGk. *Ρωμαΐκός,
'pertaining to Modern Greece or the the Modern Greek
language, Modern Greek', fr. Gk. 'Ρωμαϊκός,
'Roman; of the Eastern Roman Empire*, fr.
'Ρώμη, 'Rome', fr. L. Roma. See Rome and adj.
suff. -lc and cp. next word.

## romaika
romaika, п., Greek national dance. — ModGk,
£ωμαΐκή, prop. fem. of'Ρωμαϊκός, 'Modern
Greek'. See prec. word.

## romaine
romaine, Ъ., also romaine lettuce, a variety of
lettuce. — F. romaine, short for laitue romaine,
lit. 'Roman lettuce', fem. of romain, 'Roman'
(see Roman); so called in allusion to the city
of Avignon, whence it was imported by Bureau
de la Riviere, chamberlain of Charles V and VI,
about the end of the 14th cent., i.e. the time
when Avignon was a papal seat.

## Roman
Roman, adj., of Rome. — Fr. L. Romdnus, 'of
Rome, Roman', fr. Roma, 'Rome'. See Rome
and -an and cp. Romaic, romaika, romaine,
Romance, romance, Romansh, romantic.
Derivatives: Roman, п., Roman-esque, n. and
adj., Roman~ish, adj., Roman-ism, п., Roman-ist,
п., Roman-ist-ic, adj., Roman-ity, п., Roman-ize,
tr. and intr. v., Roman-iz-ation, п., Roman-iz-er,
n.
Roman balance — It is taken for granted that
Roman balance means 'balance of Rome' or
'balance resembling the balance used in Rome'.
According to my opinion, such an explanation
of Roman balance is based on error. In reality,
Roman in Roman balance derives fr. F. romaine,
'steelyard', fr. Sp. romana, fr. Arab. rummanah,
'steelyard', fr. rummdn, 'pomegranate'. Arab.
rumman is borrowed fr. Aram, rummana,
'pomegranate', which is rel. to Heb. rimmSn, of
s.m. The steelyard was called in Arabic
rummana1, because the counterpoise used with
Arabic balances usually had the shape of a
pomegranate (Arab, rumman). Accordingly, Roman
in the sense of balance, had nothing to do orig.
with the adjective Roman, 'of Rome'; later,
however, folk etymology identified F. romaine,
'steelyard', with F. romaine, fem. of romain, 'Roman',
fr. L. Romdnus (see Roman).

## Romance
Romance, adj., designating, or pertaining to, the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:669 COLUMN:2 -->
languages developed from Vulgar Latin. — OF.
romanz, fr. Late L. Romanice, 'in Vulgar Latin',
adv. of L. Romdnicus, 'Roman'. See Romanic
and cp. next word.

## romnnce
romnnce, п., a tale of chivalry. — ME. romaunce,
romance, fr. OF. romanz (whence MF. romant,
'romance*, F. roman, 'novel'), orig. meaning
'something written in a Romance tongue', fr.
Late L. Romanice. See prec. word and cp. ro-
maunt.
Derivatives: romance, intr. v., romance-al-ist,
п., romance-an, adj., romanc-er, п., romanc-ic-al,
adj., romanc-ing, adj., romanc-ist, n.

## Romanes
Romanes, п., the Romany or Gypsy language. —
Fr. Gypsy romano, 'Gypsy'. See Romany.

## Romanic
Romanic, adj., 1) pertaining to Rome or the
Roman people; 2) Romance. — L. Romdnicus,
fr. Romdnus, 'Roman'. See Roman.
Derivative: Romanic, п., Romance.

## Romano-
Romano-, combining form meaning 'of Rome' or
'of the Roman Empire'. — L. Romano·, fr.
Romdnus, 'Roman*.

## Romansh
Romansh, Rom an sen, adj., Rhaeto-Romanic. —
Grisons Rumansch, Romansch, Romonsch, fr.
Late L. Romanice, 'in Vulgar Latin'. See
Romance and cp. Rhaeto-Romance.

## romantic
romantic, adj. — Lit. 'pertaining to a romance',
fr. F. romantique, fr. MF. romant (whence F.
roman, 'novel'), back formation fr. Late L.
Romanice, 'in Vulgar Latin'. See romance and
-ic.
Derivatives: romantic, п., romantic-al, adj., ro-
mantic-al-ly, adv. ,romantic-al-ness,n.,
romanticism, п., romantic-ist, п., romantic-ist-ic, adj.,
romantic-ity, п., romantic-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
romant-ism, п., romant-ist, п., romantic-ly, adv.,
romantic-ness, n.

## Romany
Romany, п., 1) a Gypsy; the Gypsy language. —
Gypsy romano, 'Gypsy', fr. rom, 'man,
husband'. See rom.
Derivative: Romany, adj.

## romaunt
romaunt, п., a romance. — MF. romant. See
romance.

## Rome
Rome, п., capital of Italy. — F., fr. L. Roma,
'Rome', for *Ruma, a name of Etruscan origin.
Cp. Rumon, former name of the river Tiber.
Derivatives: Rom-ish, adj., Rom-ish-ly, adv.,
Rom-ish-ness, n.

## romeite
romeite, also romeine, п., antimonate of calcium
{mineral.) — F. romeine, named after the French
mineralogist and crystallographer Jean-Baptis-
te-Louis Rome de I'lsle (1736-90). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite, resp. -ine.

## romerillo
romerillo, п., any of several American aromatic
plants. — Sp., dimin. of romero, 'rosemary', fr.
L. rds maris, 'rosemary'. See rosemary.

## Romeward
Romeward, adj., tending toward Rome or Roman
Catholicism. — Formed fr. Rome with adj.
suff. -ward.

## Romeward
Romeward, Romewards, adv., with a tendency
toward Rome or Roman Catholicism. —
Formed fr. Rome with adv. suff. -ward, resp. -wards.

## Romic
Romic, п., name of a phonetic system. — So
called by Henry Sweet (1845-1912), the deviser
of this system. The name denotes the system
that is based on the Roman alphabet.

## romp
romp, intr. v., to play noisily. — Prob. a var. of
ramp.
Derivatives: romp, п., romp-y, adj.

## rondeau
rondeau, п., a metrical form consisting often or
thirteen lines, with only two rhymes {pros.) —
F., fr. earlier rondel. See next word and cp.
rondo.

## rondel
rondel, п., a metrical form consisting of fourteen
Knes, with only two rhymes {pros.) — Earlier F.
(cp. prec. word), prop, dimin. of rond, 'round'.
See round, adj., and cp. roundel, nmdle.

## rondo
rondo, п., a musical composition with a principal
subject, which is repeated at least twice after the
introduction of several episodes. — It., fr.
rondeau. See rondeau.

## rondure
rondure, п., circular form; roundness. — F., fr.
rond, 'round'. See round and -ure.

## ronquil
ronquil, п., a fish of the family Bathymasteridae.
— Fr. Sp. ronquillo, prop, dimin. of ronco,
'hoarse', which is rel. to roncar, 'to snore', fr.
Late L. rhonchare, fr. Gk. ρόγχος,'a snoring'.
. See rhonchus.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:669 COLUMN:3 -->

## rood
rood, n. — ME. rod, rood, fr. OE. rod, 'rod, pole;
measure of land; cross*, rel. to OS. roda, 'stake,
pile, cross', Dan. rode, Swed. rod, OFris., MLG.
rode, MDu. roede, Du. roede, roe, 'rod', OHG.
ruota, MHG. ruote, G. Rule, 'rod', and cogn.
with L. ratis, 'raft', retae, 'trees standing on the
bank of a stream*, OSlav.rafi'ite,rarcw'ife, 'spear
staff', Lith. rekles, 'scaffolding'. Cp. radeau,
Ratitae.

## roof
roof, n. — ME. rof, roof, fr. OE. hrof 'roof,
ceiling; top", rel. to OFris. hrof 'roof, MDu. roof
rouf 'cover, roof, Du. roef 'deckhouse', MLG.
rof 'penthouse', ON. hrof 'boat shed*, and prob.
cogn. with Mir. его, 'stable, hovel', Bret, crou,
'stable', W. craw, 'pig sty'.
Derivative: roof-less, adj.

## roof
roof, tr. v. — ME. rofen, fr. rof. See roof, n.
Derivatives: roof-age, п., roof-ed, adj., roof-ing,
n.

## rook
rook, п., a black bird belonging to the crow
family. — ME. rok, fr. OE. hroc, rel. to ON. hrokr,
MDu. roec, Du. roek, 'rook', OHG. hruoh,
'crow', of imitative origin. See raven, n.
Derivatives: rook, tr. v., to cheat, rook-ery, п.,
rook-ish, adj., rook-ling, п., rook-y, adj.

## rook
rook, п., castle (at chess). — ME. rok, fr. OF. roc.
See roc.

## room
room, n. — ME. roum, rum, fr. OE. rum, 'space*,
rel. to ΟΝ., OS., OHG., MHG., Goth, rum,
G. Raum, Dan., Swed. rum, 'space', Du. ruim,
'hold (of a ship), nave'. These nouns are
substantivations of the Teut. adj. *ruma-
appearing in OE., MHG. rum, OHG. rumi, ON.
rumr, Dan., Swed. rum, Du. ruim, Goth, rums,
'roomy, spacious"; fr. l.-E. base *rew-, 'wide,
open', whence Toch. AB ru-, 'to open', Avestic
ravah-, 'space*, L. rus, 'open country', Olr. rdi,
roe, 'plain field'. Cp. ream, 'to enlarge a hole',
rummage. Cp. also rural, rustic.
Derivatives: room, tr. v., room-ed, adj.,
roomful, adj., room-y, adj., room-i-ly, adv., room-i-
ness, n.

## roost
roost, п., a perch for fowls. — ME. rooste, fr. OE.
hrdst, 'wooden framework of a roof, perch', rel.
to OS. hrdsi, MDu., Du. roest,'roost, framework
of a roof, ON. hrot, Goth, hrot, 'roof*. Cp.
next word.
Derivative: roost, intr. v.

## rooster
rooster, п., cock. — Lit. 'the roosting animal';
formed from prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## root
root, п., the lowest part of a plant. — ME. rot,
root, fr. OE. rot, fr. ON. rot, rel. to OE. wyrt,
Goth, waurts, 'root*, and cogn. with L. radix,
'root*. See radix and words there referred to and
cp. esp. wort, 'a plant'.
Derivatives: root-ery, п., root-less, adj.,
rootling, п., root-let, п., root-y, adj., root-i-ness, n.

## root
root, tr. v., to furnish with roots; intr. v., to take
root. — ME. roten, fr. rot. See root, n.
Derivatives: root-age, п., root-ed, adj., root-ed-
ly, adv., root-ed-ness, n.

## root
root, intr. v., to dig with the snout. — Formed,
under the influence of root, п., fr. earlier wroot,
fr. ME. wrooten, fr. OE. wrotan, fr. итог, 'snout',
which is rel. to LG. wrote, 'snout', MHG. rue^el,
G. Russel, of s.m., ON. rota, Swed. rota, 'to dig
out, roof, MLG. wroten, MDu., Du. wroeten,
OHG. гиоззеп, of s.m. These words are cogn.
with L. rodere, 'to gnaw'. See rodent and cp.
rout, 'to root'.

## rope
rope, n. — ME. гор, горе, fr. OE. rap, rel. to ON.
reip, MDu., Du. reep, 'rope*, Goth, raip in
skauda-raip, 'shoelace*, OHG., MHG., G. reif,
'ring, hoop*. Finn, raippa, 'hoop, rope', is aTeut.
loan word. Cp. the second element in stirrup.
Cp. also rape/one of the six divisions of Sussex'.
Derivatives: rope, tr. and intr. v., rop-ery, п.,
rop-ing, п., rop-ish, adj., rop-ish-ness, п., rop-y,
adj., rop-i-ness, n.

## Roquefort cheese
Roquefort cheese, Roquefort, n. — Named after
Roquefort, a village in France.

## roquelaure
roquelaure, п., a kind of cloak. — F., named after
the Duke of Roquelaure (died in 1738). Cp.
rokelay.

## roquet
roquet, tr. and intr. v., to hit another's ball with
one's own (at croquet). — An arbitrary
alteration of croqnet.

## roric
roric, adj., pertaining to dew. — Formed with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:670 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 643 | ROTCHE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:670 COLUMN:1 -->
suff. -ic fr. L. ros, gen. roris, 'dew', which is cogn.
with Lith. rasa, OSlav. rosa, 'dew', OI. rasah,
'sap, juice, fluid, essence', rasa, 'moisture', Rasa,
name of a mythic river (= Avestic Ranhd),
arsati, 'flows', rsabhah, 'bull, steer', Avestic and
OPers. arshan, 'man', Hitt. arszi, 'flows', Gk.
5ίρσην, #ρρην, 'male, masculine', prob. also 'Pa,
Scythian name of the Volga, fr. I.-E. base *ras-,
*eras-, *eres-, *ers-, 'to flow, wet, moisten'. Cp.
rasa, romerillo, rosemary, rosolio, rouse, 'to
pickle'. Cp. also the first element in rhubarb and
the second element in Ahasuerus and in Xerxes.

## rorqual
rorqual, п., any whale of the genus of large whales,
the Balaenoptera. — F., fr. Norw. royrhval, fr.
ON. reydarhvafr, fr. reydr, 'rorqual' (fr. raudr,
'red'), and hvalr, 'whale'. See red and whale.

## Rosa
Rosa, 1) fern. PN.; 2) a genus of plants, the rose
(boi.) — L. rosa, 'rose'. See rose.

## Rosabel
Rosabel, fem. PN. — Lit. 'beautiful rose',
compounded of L. rosa, 'rose', and belfa, fem. of
bellus, 'pretty, beautiful'. See rose and benuty
and cp. christabel.
rosace» п., a roselike ornament; rose window. —
F., fr. L. rosdceus, 'of roses'. See rosaceous.

## Rosaceae
Rosaceae, n. pi., the rose family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Rosa with sufF. -aceae.

## rosacean
rosacean, adj., rosaceous. — See next word and
-on.

## rosaceous
rosaceous, adj. — L. rosdceus, 'of roses', fr. rosa.
See rose and -aceous and cp. rosace.

## rosaniline
rosaniline, п., a crystalline compound obtained
from aniline, CaoH21ONs (chem.) —
Compounded of rose and aniline.

## rosarian
rosarian, п., a rose grower. — Formed with suff.
-an fr. L. rosarium, 'rose garden'. See rosary.

## rosarium
rosarium, п., rose garden. — L. See next word
and -arium,

## rosary
rosary, п., rose garden; string of beads used for
counting series of prayers. — ME. rosarie, fr. L.
rosarium, 'rose garden', in ML. also used in the
sense of 'garland; string of beads; series of
prayers', fr. L. rosa. See rose and subst. suff.
-ary.

## roscherite
roscherite, п., a hydrous basic phosphate of
aluminum, manganese, calcium and iron (mineral.)
— G. Roscherit, named after the German
mineral collector Walter Roscher. The ending -it
goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst. sufF. -ite.

## Roscian
Roscian, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, Ros-
cius. — See next word and -ian.

## Rosrfus
Rosrfus, п., an actor. — From Roscius, the
celebrated Roman actor (died in 62 B.C.E.)

## roscoelite
roscoelite, п., a vanadium mica (mineral.) —
Named after the English chemist Sir Henry
Enfield Roscoe (1833-1915). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## rose
rose, n. — ME., fr. OE., fr. L. rosa, fr. Gk. poSov,
'rose', for *fpoSov,fr.01ran.*MTc/a- (whence also
Aram, wardd, Arm. vard). Olran. *wrda-
became gul in ModPers. in the sense of the
phonetic law, according to which initial w becomes g
and -rd is changed to /. Turkish gul, 'rose', is a
Persian loan word. Olran. *wrda-, 'rose',
represents I.-E. *wrdho-, 'thorn, bramble', whence
also OE. word, 'bramble', Norw. or, 61 (for
*ord), 'currant, bush'. Cp. rhodo-. Cp. also the
first element in julep and the second element in
bedegnar.
Derivatives: rose-ate, adj., rose-ate-ly, adv., ros-
ery, п., ros-y, adj., ros-i-ly, adv., ros-i-ness,
n.

## rosella
rosella, п., an Australian parakeet. — Altered fr.
Rose-killer, fr. Rose Hill, name of the governor's
residence at Parramatta in New South Wales.

## rosemary
rosemary, n. — ME-, fr. earlier rosmarine, fr. L.
ros marinus (whence also F. romarin),
'rosemary', lit. 'dew of the sea', fr. ros, 'dew', and
marinus, 'pertaining to the sea*, fr. mare, gen.
maris, 'sea'. See roric and marine, adj. The loss
of the -n~ in English is due to a confusion of L.
marinus with E. Mary. Cp. romerillo.

## roseo-
roseo-, combining form meaning 'rose-colored';
used specifically in chemistry to denote salts of
a reddish color. — Fr. L. roseus, 'rosy, roselike',
fr. rosa. See rose,

## roseola
roseola, п., 1) any rose-colored rash; 2) German
measles. — Medical L., fr. F. rosiole, which was
formed fr. rose, 'rose', on analogy of rougeole,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:670 COLUMN:2 -->
'measles', which is a derivative of rouge, 'red'.
See rose.
Derivatives: roseol-ar, roseol-ate, roseol-ous,
adjs.

## rosette
rosette, п., a rose-shaped ornament. — F., dimin.
of rose, 'rose'. See rose and -ette.
Derivative: rosett-ed, adj.

## Rosh Hashanah
Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. — Heb.
rosk hashshanah lit. 'head of the year', fr. rosh,
'head of, and kask-skdndh, 'the year'. For the
first word see Bereshith and cp. words there
referred to. Heb. skdndh, 'year', is rel. to Aram.-
Syr. shena, shattd, Ugar. shut, Arab. sanah,
Akkad. shattu, 'year'. These words are prob.
connected with Heb. shdndh, Aram.-Syr. sk6ndt
'he changed', Akkad. skanu, 'to change', and
prop, mean 'change, period of changing
seasons'. Cp. J. Barth in ZDMG., vol. XL1 (1887),
pp. 612, 621, 636.

## Rosh Hodesh
Rosh Hodesh, also Rosh Chodesh, the beginning
of the month in the Jewish calendar. — Heb.
rosh hodesh, lit. 'the head of the month', fr. rosh,
'head', and hodesh, 'new moon, month'. For the
etymology of Heb. rosh see Bereshith and cp.
words there referred to. Heb. hodesh derives fr.
stem k-d-sk, 'to be new', whence also hiddesh, 'he
renewed', kdddsk, 'new'; rel- to Aram.-Syr.
haddeth, 'he renewed*, Arab, badatha, 'it
happened, occurred', hadutha, 'was new, was young',
hdddatha, 'he told, related', Akkad. edeshu, 'to
be new', Aram.-Syr. hddath, Arab. hadtth,
Ethiop. kadas, Akkad. eshshu, 'new', Punic
hadasht in Qart-badasht, 'Carthage', lit.
'Newtown'. Cp. Hadith.

## Rosicrucian
Rosicrucian, adj., pertaining to a secret society
allegedly founded in Germany by Christian Ro-
senkreuz (in 1484). — The name arose from the
Latinization of Rosenkreuz, lit. 'rosy cross'. See
rose, crux and -ian.
Derivatives: Rosicrucian, п., Rosierucian-ism, n.

## rosieresite
rosieresite, п., a hydrous aluminum phosphate
{mineral.) — Named after the Rosieres copper
mine near Carmaux in France. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## rosin
rosin, п., resin. — A var. of resin.
Derivatives: rosin, tr. v., rosin-y, adj.

## Rosinante
Rosinante, п., 1) Don Quixote's horse; whence 2)
a broken-down horse; jade, nag. — Sp. Roci-
nante, compounded of rocin, 'worn-out horse,
hack, jade', and antes, 'before'; so called in
allusion to the circumstance that Don Quixote's
charger was formerly a wretched hack. — Sp.
rocin derives fr. OProvenc. rocin, which,
together with OF. roncin, 'draft horse, hack', is of
uncertain origin. Sp. antes, 'before', comes fr.
L. ante; see ante-. Cp. rouncy.

## rosolic acid
rosolic acid, a dye of the triphenyl-methane series.
— Translation of G. Rosolsaure, which was
coined by the German chemist Friedlieb
Ferdinand Runge (1795-1867) fr. rosa, 'rosy' (see
rose), (Karb)ol(see carbol) and Sdure, 'acid'. For
the ending in rosolic see adj. suff. -ic.

## rosolio
rosolio, п., a sweet cordial made from raisins. —
It., fr. L. ros solis, 'sundew', fr. ros, 'dew' and
gen. of sol, 'sun'. See roric and Sol,

## rostellum
rostellum, п., a small beak-shaped process (bot.
and zool.) — L., 'a small beak', dimin. of
rostrum. See rostrum.

## roster
roster, п., a list of persons or groups. — Du.
rooster, 'gridiron, grate; list', fr. MDu.,
'gridiron, grate', fr. roosten, 'to roast*; so called from
the parallel lines dividing the list. See roast.
Derivative: roster, tr. v.

## rostral
rostral, adj., pertaining to a rostrum. — Late L.
rostralis, fr. L. rostrum. See rostrum and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: rostral, п., rostral-ly, adv.

## rostrate
rostrate, adj., having a rostrum. — L. rostratus,
'beaked', fr. rostrum. See rostrum and adj. suff.
-ate.
Derivative: roslrat-ed, adj.

## rostriferous
rostriferous, adj., having a rostrum. — See
rostrum and -ferous.

## rostriform
rostriform, adj., having the form of a rostrum. —
See rostrum and form, n.

## rostro-
rostro-, combining form used in the sense of
rostral and. — Fr. L. rostrum. See next word.

## rostrum
rostrum, n. — L. rostrum, 'beak, snout, muzzle;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:670 COLUMN:3 -->
the end of a ship's prow; the orator's pulpit,
platform*, which stands for *rod-trom, lit. 'an
instrument for gnawing', formed from the stem
of rod-ere, 'to gnaw' (see rodent), and -tro-m, a
suffix denoting an instrument. Cp. L. ara-trum,
'a plow', lit. 'an instrument for plowing' (fr.
ardre, 'to plow'), claus-trum (for *claud-trom),
'lock, bar*, lit. 'that by which anything is shut
up' (fr. claudere, 'to shut'). Cp. claustral. L.
rostrum came to denote 'orator's platform' from
the circumstance that the orators' platform in
the Roman Forum was adorned with the beaks
of the ships of the Antiate fleet captured by
Maenius in 338.

## rosulate
rosulate, adj., having the leaves arranged in the
form of rosettes (bot.) — Formed with adj. suff.
-ate fr. Late L. rosula, 'a little rose', dimin. of L.
rosa. See rose.

## rot
rot, intr. and tr. v. — ME. rotien, roten, fr. OE.
rotian, 'to decay, suppurate', rel. to OS. roton,
ON. rotna, OFris. rotia, MDu. roten, Du. rotten,
'to rot*, OHG. гоззёп, MHG. rce^en, 'to rot',
Swed. rota, Norw. reyta, Du. reten, MHG.
rcetzen, 'to cause to rot', G. rofien (also
inexactly rosten), 'to steep flax'. Cp. rot, п., rotten.
Cp. also ret.
Derivatives: rotten (q.v.), rott-er, n.

## rot
rot, п., process of rotting. — ME. rot, prob. of
Scand. origin. Cp. Icel. rot, Swed. rota, Dan.
rede, 'decay, putrefaction*, which are rel. to the
OE. verb rotian, 'to decay'. See rot, v.

## rota
rota, n. — L., 'wheel', cogn. with 01. rathah, 'car,
chariot3, Avestic ra&o, of s.m., Lith. rutas,
*wheel', ritu, Ί roll', ritulai, 'wheelbarrow', Lett.
ritens, ritulis, 'carriage wheel*, OHG.rad, MHG.
rat, G. Rad, Du. rad, OFris. reth, OS. rath, Olr.
roth, W. rhod, of s.m., Gaul, petorritum, 'four-
wheeled carriage' (for the first element of this
compound see four), Olr. rethim, Ί run'. Cp.
roll, v. and n. Cp. also redondilla,rodeo, rondeau,
rondel, rondo, rondure, Rotala, rotate, rotula,
rotund, roue, rouelle, roulette, rounce, round, adj.,
rowel, runlet, 'a small cask', rut, 'carriage', ar-
rondissement, tondo, the first element in Ra-
thayatra, rodomontade and rut, 'carriage*, and
the second element in barouche and control. Cp.
also rye grass.

## Rotala
Rotala, п., a genus of plants of the loosestrife
family (bot.) — ML., dimin. formed fr. rota,
'wheel' (see rota); so called in allusion to the
whorled leaves.

## rotang
rotang, n. — A var. of rattan.

## Rotarian
Rotarian, adj., pertaining to the Rotary Club. —
Formed from the name of the club (see Rotary
Club) with suff. -an.
Derivatives: Rotarian, п., Rotarian-ism, п.,
rotarian-ize, tr. v.

## rotary
rotary, adj., turning like a wheel. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ary fr. L. rota, 'wheel'. See rota.
Rotary Club. — So called because the members
of the first Rotary Club (founded by Paul P.
Harris in Chicago in 1905) used to meet in
rotation.

## rotate
rotate, intr. v., to turn about its axis; tr. v., to
cause to rotate. — L. rotatus, pp. of rotare, 'to
go round in a circle', fr. rota, 'wheel'. See rota
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: rotat-able, adj., rotation (q.v.),
rotat-ive, adj., rotat-ive-ly, adv., rotator (q.v.)

## rotute
rotute, adj., wheel-shaped (bot.) — L. rotatus, pp.
of rotare. See rotate, v.

## rotation
rotation, n. — L. rotatio, gen. -dnis, 'a turning
about in a circle', fr. rotatus, pp. of rotare. See

## rotate
rotate, v., and -ion.
Derivative: rotation-al, adj.

## rotator
rotator, п., that which causes rotation. — L., fr.

## rotatus
rotatus, pp. of rotare. See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.

## rotatory
rotatory, adj., that which pertains to rotation. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. rotatus, pp. of

## rotare. See rotate
rotare. See rotate, v.

## rotche
rotche, rotch, п., the dovekie (Alle alle). — Fr.

## earlier rotge
earlier rotge, fr. LG. (cp. Fris. rotgoes, pi. rot-

## gies
gies, Du. rotgans, 'brant goose'), ult. fr. Scand.
(cp, ON. hrodgas, Norw. rotgaas, Dan. rad-

## gaas
gaas, 'brant goose'). The first element of these
compound words is of imitative origin; the

second element is rel. to goose. Cp. rat goose, rood
