goose, rott goose, rout, which are dial. E. names
of the brant goose.

## rote
rote, п., routine. — ME., 'practice, custom,
routine', fr. OF. rote (F. route), 'road, way, path',
fr. VL. (via) rupta, lit. 'a broken way', fem. pp.
of rumpere, 'to break*. See route and cp. rut,
'routine*. For sense development cp. F. routine,
'practice, routine', fr. route, 'way' (see routine).

## rote
rote, п., a medieval stringed instrument. — OF.
rote, of Celtic origin. See crowd, 'a musical
instrument'. OF. rote in this sense is not related to
OF. rote, 'way'. Cp. prec. word.

## rote
rote, п., the roaring of the surf. —- Related to ON.
rauta, 'to roar'; prob. of imitative origin.

## rother
rother, п., cattle (dial. E.) — OE. hrider, kryder,
'ox, cow', pi. 'cattle*. See runt and cp. the first
element in rinderpest.

## Rotifer a
Rotifer a, n. pi., a class of microscopic freshwater
organisms (zool.) — Compounded of L. rota,
'wheel', and ferre, 'to bear, carry'. See rota and
-ferous.

## rotiform
rotiform, adj., wheel-shaped. — Compounded of
L. rota, 'wheel', and forma, 'form, shape'. See
rota and form, n.

## rotisserie
rotisserie, п., cookshop. — F. rotisserie, fr. pres.
part, stem of rotir, 'to roast'. See roast and
-ery.
rot], п., a weight used in North Africa. — Arab.
rati, rel. to ratala, 'he poised', rattala, 'he
weighed*.

## rotogravure
rotogravure, n. — A hybrid coined fr. L. rota,
'wheel*, and F. gravure, 'engraving', which is of
Teut. origin. See rota and gravure.

## rotor
rotor, п., a rotating part of a machine. —
Shortened from rotator.

## rotten
rotten, adj. — ME. roten, fr. ON. rotinn, 'rotten',
fr. rotna, 'to decay*. Cp. Swed. rutten, Dan. rud-
den, 'rotten', and see rot, v.
Derivatives: rotten-ly, adv., rotten-ness, n.

## Rotten Row
Rotten Row, thoroughfare for use of riders in
Hyde Park, London. — Probably corruption of
F. route du roi, 'the king's highway'. See route
and royal.

## rotula
rotula, п., the kneepan (anat. and astron.).— L.
rotula, 'a little wheel', dimin. of rota; see rota
and -ule. Cp. Provenc., Catal., Port, rodella,
'kneepan', Sp. rodilla, 'knee', which derive fr.
VL. rotella, fr. L. rotula.

## rotund
rotund, adj., round, rounded. — L. rotundUs,
'round', fr. rota, 'wheel'. See round, adj., and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also next word and
orotund.
Derivatives: rotund-ly, adv., rotund-ness, n.

## rotunda
rotunda, п., a circular building. — Refashioned
after the Latin form from earlier rotonda, fr. It.
rotonda, prop. fem. of the adj. rotondo used as a
noun, fr. L. rotundus, 'round'. See prec. word.
F. rotondeis a loan word fr. It. rotonda. See prec.
word.

## rotimdate
rotimdate, adj., rounded. — L. rotundatus, pp. of
rotund&re, 'to make round', fr. rotundus. See
rotund and adj. suff. -ate.

## rotundi-
rotundi-, combining form meaning 'round'. — Fr.
L. rotundus, 'round'. See rotund.

## rotundity
rotundity, п., roundness. — L. rotunditas,
'roundness', fr. rotundus. See rotund and -Ity.

## rotundo-
rotundo-, combining form meaning 'roundly'. —
Fr. L. rotundus, 'round'. See rotund.

## roture
roture, п., the state of being a roturier. — MF.
(= F.), fr. L. ruptura, 'a breaking', in VL. also
'broken land', formed fr. ruptus, pp. of rumpere,
'to break'. See rupture and cp. roto.

## roturier
roturier, п., a plebeian. — MF. (= F.), fr. roture.
See prec. word and -ier.

## rouble
rouble, n. — See ruble.

## roucou
roucou, п., dye obtained from a W. Indian tree.
— F., fr. Tupi urucu
гопё, п., a debauchee. — F., 'rake, profligate',

## prop. pp. of rouer
prop. pp. of rouer, 'to break upon the wheel', fr.

## roue
roue, 'wheel*, fr. L. rota, of s.m. See rota.

## roueile
roueile, п., a disk-shaped amulet. — F., dimin. of

## roue
roue, 'wheel*. See prec. word and -elle. Cp. also

## roulette
roulette, rowel.

## rouge
rouge, п., a reddish powder. — F. rouge, 'red', fr.
MF., fr. OF., fr. L. rubeus, 'reddish', fr. ruber,
'red'. See rubric.
Derivative: rouge, intr. and tr. v.

## rouge
rouge, п., a scrimmage (a term in Eton football).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:671 COLUMN:2 -->
— Of unknown origin.

## rough
rough, adj. — ME. rouh, rough, ruw, rugh, fr. OE.
ruh, 'rough, untrimmed, uncultivated', rel. to
MDu. ru, ruuch, ru, Du. ruig, OHG. ruh, ruker,
MHG. ruck, ruker, G. rauh, rauch, fr. l.-E. base
*ruq-, *rug-, whence also Lith. raukas, 'wrinkle',
runku, rukti, 'to shrink*, raukiu, raukti, 'to
wrinkle*, 01. ruksah, 'rough', L. ruga, 'wrinkle'.
Cp. ruga. Cp. also ruff, the fish, ruffian, rug.
Derivatives: rough, п., tr. v., and adv.,
roughage, п., rough material, rough-en, tr. and intr. v.,
rough-en-er, п., rough-er, п., rough-ish, adj.,
rough-ish-ly, adv., rough-ish-ness, п., rough-ly,
adv., rough-ness, n.

## roulade
roulade, п., a run of notes; a flourish (mus.) —
F., lit. 'the act of rolling', fr. rouler, 'to roll'. See
roll, v., and -ade.

## ronleau
ronleau, п., roll. — F., dimin. of role, 'roll'. See
role.

## roulette
roulette, п., a gambling game. — F., dimin. of
roueile, 'a small wheel', itself a dimin. of roue,
'wheel'. See rota and -ette and cp. roueile, rowel.
Derivative: roulette, tr. v.

## Roumellote
Roumellote, Rumellote, п., a native of Rumelia.
— Formed fr. ModGk. 'Ρυμελιότης, fr. 'Ρυ-
μελία, 'Rumelia'. For the ending see suff. -ote.

## rounce
rounce, п., handle of the winch regulating the
carriage of a handpress. — Du. rons, ronds, fr.
rond, 'round', fr. MF., fr. OF. room. See round,
adj.

## rouncy
rouncy, п., a riding horse (archaic). — OF. roncin,
ronci, 'draft horse, hack', which, together with
OProvenc. rocin, of s.m., is of uncertain origin.
Cp. Rosinante. F. roussin, 'cob, plowhorse', is a
blend of OF. roncin and F. roux, 'red, reddish
brown'.

## round
round, adj., circular. — ME. round, fr. MF. (=F.)
rond, fr. OF. reont (var. room), fr. VL. *retondus,
dissimilated fr. L. rotundus, 'round', lit. 'wheel-
shaped', fr. rota, 'wheel'. See rota and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: round, п., tr. and intr. v., adv., prep.,
round-ed, adj., round-ed-ly, adv., round-ed-ness,
п., round-er, п., round-ing, п., round-ish, adj.,
round-ly, adv., round-ness, n.

## round
round, tr. and intr. v., to whisper. — ME. rounen,
fr. OE. runian, 'to whisper*, fr. run, 'mystery,
secret', rel. to OS. runon, OHG. гйпёп, MHG.
runen, G. raunen, 'to whisper', ON. reyna, 'to
converse confidentially'; see rune and cp. alraun.
The d in round is excrescent. Cp. bound, 'ready',
and words there referred to.

## roundel
roundel, п., 1) a small circle; 2) a var. of rondel.
— ME., fr. OF. rondel(¥. rondel, rondeau), dimin.
formed from the adj. rond, 'round*. See round,
adj., and cp. next word and rondel, rundie.

## roundelay
roundelay, п., a song with refrain. — Altered fr.
MF. rondelet, fr. OF., a double diminutive (see
rondel and -et); influenced in form by lay, 'song*.
round table. — Loan translation of OF. (= F.)
table ronde.

## roup
roup, tr. v., to sell by auction. — MDu. (= Du.)
roepen, rel. to OE. kropan, 'to cry out, shout,
call', OS. hropan, OFris. hropa, OHG. hruoffan,
hruofan, ruoffan, ruofan, MHG. ruofen, ruefen,
G. rufen, Goth, hropjan, of s.m., ON. hropa, 'to
slander, calumniate', and possibly cogn. with
OSlav. skrobotu, 'noise', Lith. skrebu, skrebeti,
'to rustle', Gk. κρέμβαλα (pi.), 'castanets', L.
crepare, 'to rattle, crack'. See crepitate and cp.
crembalum. Cp. also unbernfen.

## roup
roup, п., auction. — Fr. roep, v. Cp. Du. roep,
'call', ON. hrop, Goth, hrops, OHG. hruoff,
hruof ruoff, ruof MHG. ruof, G. Ru/, of s.m.,
ON. hrop, 'slander, calumniation'.

## roup
roup, п., a disease of poultry. — Prob. of
imitative origin.
Derivative: roup-y, adj.

## rouse
rouse, п., 1) bumper of liquor; 2) carousal. —
Aphetic for carouse, prob. owing to a
misunderstanding of the phrase to drink carouse as to
drink a rouse.

## rouse
rouse, tr. v., to awake, stir up; intr. v., to awaken.
— ME. rousen, orig. a term of hunting; of
uncertain etymology. Cp. arouse, ronst, roustabout.
Cp. also row, 'noise*.
Derivatives: rouse, п., the act of rousing;
reveille, rous-er, п., rous-ing, adj., rous-ing-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:671 COLUMN:3 -->
rouse, tr. v., to pickle in salt. — Aphetic for
earlier arrouse, fr. OF. arrouser (F. arroser), 'to
sprinkle, spray*, fr. Late L. adrordre, 'to bedew*,
fr. ad- and L. rorare, 'to dew*, fr. ros, gen. roris,
'dew'. See roric.
Rous sea nan, adj., pertaining to the French
philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-78). — For
the ending see suff. -an.
Rousseauesque, adj., resembling the style or
theories of Rousseau. — See prec. word and -esque.
Rousseauism, п., the philosophy of Rousseau,
esp. his views on education and religion. — See
Rousseauan and -ism.
Rousseauist, п., an adherent of Rousseauism. —
See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: Rousseauist-ic, adj.

## roussette
roussette, п., 1) a bat (Pteropus vulgaris); 2) a
shark of the genus Scylliorhinus. — F., fr. MF.,
a dimin. formed fr. roux, fem. rousse, 'red,
reddish brown'. See russet.

## Roussillon
Roussillon, п., a kind of red wine made in Rous-
sillon. — Fr. Roussillon, name of an old
province of Southern France.

## roust
roust, tr. v., to rouse, stir (colloq.) — Fr. rouse.
Cp. next word.

## roustabout
roustabout, п., 1) a wharf laborer; 2) a deck hand.
— Compounded of roust and about. Cp. dial E.
rouse-about, 'a violent, boisterous person'.
Derivatives: roustabout, adj. and intr. v.

## rout
rout, п., mob, rabble. — fr. MF. route, 'host,
troop, crowd', fr. OF. rote, fr. VL. rupta, 'a
dispersed group', lit. 'a broken group', prop. fem.
pp. of L. rumpere, 'to break', used as a noun.
See route and cp. routier.

## rout
rout, tr. v., to put to flight. — Fr. prec. word. The
orig. meaning of the verb rout was 'to break the
ranks of a troop'.

## rout
rout, intr. and tr. v., to root; to furrow. — A var.
of root, 'to dig with the snout'.
Derivatives: rout-er, n. and tr. v.

## route
route, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) route, 'road, way,
path', fr. VL. rupta (via), fem. pp. of rumpere,
'to break'. See rnpture and cp. rote, 'routine',
rout, 'mob', routier, routine, rutter. Cp. also
reave.
Derivative: route, tr. v.

## routier
routier, п., brigand. — F., 'mercenary', prop, 'a
wandering robber', fr. OF. route, 'bande, troop'.
See rout, 'mob', and -ier.

## routine
routine, n. — F., fr. MF. route, 'road, way,
path*. See route and subst. suff. -ine.
Derivatives: routine, adj., routine~ly, adv.,
routin-ism, п., routin-ist, п., routin-ize, tr. v.,

## roux
roux, п., mixture of melted butter and flour used

reddish brown', fr. L. russus. See russet,

## rove
rove, intr. v., to practice robbery (obsol.) — Back

## rove
rove, 1) intr. v., to shoot at random; 2) intr. v.,

robber', and ON. rafa, rapa, 'to wander'. The
orig. meaning of rove was 'to wander about
robbing',

## rove

In gradational relationship to reeve, 'to pass
through a hole'.
Derivatives: rov-er, п., rov-ing, П. and adj., rov-
ing-ly, adv., rov-ing-ness, n.

## rove
rove, п., twisted roll of wool. — Fr. rove, 'to draw
through a small opening*.
Derivative: rove, tr. v., to twist rolls of wool.

## rover
rover, п., sea robber, pirate. — ME., fr. MDu.

## rover
rover, fr. MDu. (~ Du.) rover, fr. MDu. ( =

roof, 'spoil, plunder', which is rel. to OE. riaf

## rover
rover, п., 1) a mark selected at random (a term of

## roven
roven, 'to shoot at random; to wander'. See rove,

## row
row, п., line, rank. — ME. rawe, rowe, fr. OE.

raw, rxw, 'row, succession', rel. to MDu. rie,

Du. rij, 'row', OHG. rlhan, MHG. rihen, 'to

thread', OHG. riga, MHG. rihe, 'line', G. Reihe.

## row
row, tr. v., to propel with oars; intr. v., to propel

I.-E. base *ere-, 'to row; oar', whence also OI.
aritrah, 'oar*, Gk. έρέσσείΛΐ, έρέττειν, 'to row',
έρέτης, 'rower', έρετμόγ, 'oar', τριήρης, 'a
trireme', L. remus, 'oar*, Lith. iriii, irti, 'to row',

Derivatives: row, п., the act of rowing, row-er,

## row
row, п., noise, disturbance. — Prob. back
formation fr. rouse, n. (see rouse, 'to awake'),
mistaken for a plural. For a similar loss of the letter
s cp. pea and words there referred to. Cp.

Derivative: row, tr. v., to scold; intr. v., to

## rowan
rowan, п., 1) the mountain-ash; 2) the berries of
the mountain-ash. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. ON.

## rowdy
rowdy, п., a rough, quarrelsome person. — Prob.
a derivative of row, 'noise, uproar'.
Derivatives: rowdy\ adj., rowdi-ly, adv., rowdi-
ness, п., rowdy-ish, adj., rowdy-ism, n.

## rowel

Derivative: rowel, tr. v.

## rowlandite
rowlandite, п., an yttrium silicate (mineral.) —
Named after the American physicist Henry

## rowlock

Roxana, п., fem. PN. — L. Rdxane, fr. Gk.

## rub
rub, tr. and intr. v. — ME. rubben, rel. to Dan.

## rubbe
rubbe, 'to rub, scrub', Norw. rubba, of s.m.,

## rubben
rubben, 'rough'; of uncertain origin. Cp. rubbish,

## rub-a-dub
rub-a-dub, п., sound of a beaten drum. —
Imitative.

## rubber
rubber, п., cautchouc. — Short for India rubber

## rubber
rubber, п., a term used at whist and bridge. — Of

rubbish-ing-ly, adv., rubbish-lyy adv., rubbish-ry,

rubble, п., broken pieces of stone. — ME. robyl,

## rubefacient
rubefacient, adj., causing redness. — L. rubefa-

Derivative: rubefacient, n.

## rubefaction
rubefaction, п., the act of causing redness. — See

## rubella
rubella, п., a contagious disease with an eruption

Medical L., fr. L. rubellus, 'reddish', dimin. of ruber,

rubellite, п., a red tourmaline. — Formed with

rubeola, п., 1) measles; 2) rubella. — Medical L.,

## rubeosis
rubeosis, п., reddening of the iris {med.) — A

## Rubiaceae
Rubiaceae, n. pi., the madder family {bot.) —

## rubiaceons
rubiaceons, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## rubicund
rubicund, adj., reddish, ruddy. — F. rubicond, fr.

## rubicundity
rubicundity, n. — ML. rubicunditas, fr. L.

## rubidium

## rubify
rubify, tr. v., to redden {rare). — ME. rubifyen,

freq. of L. rubefacere, 'to make red*, fr. rubere,

## rubiginous

## rubigo
rubigo, п., a parasitic fungus. — L. rubigo, 'rust'.

## ruble
ruble, rouble, п., the unit of the monetary system
of the U.S.S.R. — F. rouble, fr. Russ. rubl\ fr.

time when metallic currency was introduced in
Russia (i.e. in the 14th cent.), it became
customary there to pay in bars of silver, the
corresponding equivalent being simply cut off.

## rubor
rubor, п., redness. — L., rel. to ruber, 'red'. See

## rubric
rubric, п., 1) a heading, entry, etc., usually written
or printed in red; 2) a liturgical direction, orig.
written or printed in red. — ME. rubrike,
'red ocher, heading of a book or its part written
in red', fr. MF. (= F.) rubrique, fr. L. rubrlca,
'red earth; title of law written in red', hence'law,
instruction', fr. ruber, 'red', which is rel. to
rubere, 'to be red', rufus, 'red, reddish', and derives
fr. l.-E. base *rudhro-, 'red*. See red and cp.
rufous. For the ending see suff. -ic.
Derivatives: rubric-al, adj., rubric-al-ly, adv.,
rubricate (q.v.), rubric-ian, п., rubric-ism, п.,
rubric-ist, n.

## rubricate

## rubricate

## rubrication

See rubricate, v., and -ion.

## Rubus

of uncertain etymology. It is perh. cogn. with
Goth, raupjan, OHG., MHG. roufen, G. raufen,
'to pluck out'; see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., 11,
445-446 s.v. rubus.

## ruby
ruby, п., a deep-red gem. — ME., fr. OF. rubi
(F. rubis), fr. ML. rubinus, fr. L. rubeus, 'red',

## rucervine

## ruche

Derivatives: ruch-ed, adj., ruch-ing, n.

## ruck
ruck, п., band, crowd. — ME. ruke, of Scand.

Derivatives: ruck, tr. v., ruck-ег, n.

## ruck
ruck, п., crease, wrinkle. — ON. hrukka, 'wrinkle',

MHG., G. runzel). Cp. frounce, wrinkle.
Derivative: ruck, tr. and intr. v., to wrinkle.

## ruckle
ruckle, п., wrinkle. — Formed fr. ruck, 'wrinkle',

Derivative: ruckle, tr. and intr. v., to wrinkle.

## rucksack

## rud

## Rudbeckia
Rudbeckia, п., a genus of plants of the aster

## rudd
rudd, п., a red-finned fish, the redeye. — Lit. 'red

## rudder
rudder, n. — ME. rother, fr. OE. roder, 'a paddle',

Du. roer, OHG. ruodar, MHG. ruoder, G.
Ruder, 'oar', formed fr. the Teut. stem *ro-, 'to

Derivatives: rudder, tr. v., rudder-less, adj.

## ruddle
ruddle, п., a variety of red ocher. — Formed fr.

## ruddock
ruddock, п., the robin. — ME. ruddok, fr. OE.

## ruddy
ruddy, adj. — ME. rudi, fr. OE. rudig, fr. rudu,

Derivatives: ruddy, tr. and intr. v., rudd-i-ly,

## rude
rude, adj. — ME. rude, fr. OF. (= F.) rude, fr. L.

ignorant', of uncertain origin; not cogn. with raudus,

Derivatives: rude-ly, adv., rude-ness, п., rud-ish,

## Riidesheimer
Riidesheimer, п., a kind of white wine. — Prop,

Germany.

## rudiment
rudiment, п., element. — L. rudtmentum, 'first
attempt, beginning', fr. rudis, 'unwrought'. See

adj., rudiment-ari-ly, adv., rudiment-ari-ness, п.,

rudiment-ation, n.

Rudolph, Rudolf, masc. PN. — Borrowed fr. G.

Rudolf, fr. OHG. Hrodulf lit. 'wolf of fame', fr.

and see ruga and -elle.

## Ruellia
Ruellia, п., a genus of plants of the family Acan-
thaceae (bot.) — ModL., named after the French
botanist Jean de la Ruelle (1474-1537). For the
ending see 1st surf. -ia.

## rnfescence
rnfescence, п., reddishness. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce.

## rufescent
rufescent, adj., reddish. — L. rufescens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of rufescere, 'to become
reddish*, an inchoative verb formed fr. rufus, 'red'.
See rufous and -escent.

## ruff
ruff, п., a kind of large collar, stiffly starched,
worn in the 17th cent. — Back formation fr.
ruffle, 'frill*. See ruffle, 'to wrinkle'.
Derivative: ruff-ed, adj.

## ruff
ruff, п., trump (at whist). — MF. raffle, ronfle,
corruption of triomphe. See triumph and cp.
trump, 'a winning card'.
Derivative: rUff, intr. and tr. v., to trump.

## ruff
ruff, п., a perchlike freshwater fish (Acerina cer-
nua). — ME. ruffe, ruf, prob. rel. to rough,

## ruffian
ruffian, п., and adj. — MF. (= F.) rufian, 'a
pimp', fr. OProvenc. rufian, rofian, fr. It. ruffia-
no, which is prob. of Teut. origin and rel. to
rough.
Derivatives: ruffian-ish, adj., rujfian-ism, п.,
rufflan-ize, tr. v., rufflan-ly, adv.

## ruffle
ruffle, tr*v., 1) to wrinkle; to draw into folds; 2)
to disturb, upset; intr. v., to be ruffled. — ME.
ruffelen, 'to wrinkle'. Cp. LG. ruffelen, 'to
wrinkle, curl'. Cp. also ruff, 'large collar'.
Derivatives: ruffle, п., that which is ruffled, a
frill, ruffl-ed, adj., ruffl-er, п., ruffl-ing, п., ruffl-
y, adj., ruffl-i-ness, n.

## ruffle
ruffle, intr. v., to swagger. — ME. ruffelen, 'to
swagger', prob. identical in origin with the prec.
word.
Derivative: ruffl-er, n.

## rufl-
rufl-, combining form meaning "red*. — Fr. L.
rufus. See next word.

## rufous
rufous, adj., reddish. — L. rufus, 'red, reddish,
red-haired*, an Osco-Umbrian word rel. to L.
ruber, 'red*. See rubric and cp. Rufus, Griffith.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.

## Rufus
Rufus, masc. PN. — Lit. 'red-haired', fr. L. rufus.
See prec. word.

## rug
rug, n. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. Swed. rugg,
'rough hair', ON. rogg, 'tuft, shagginess'; rel. to
E. rag and rough and to the next word.
Derivative: rugg-ing, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:673 COLUMN:2 -->

## ruga
ruga, п., wrinkle, fold. — L. ruga, cogn. with Lith.
raukas, 'wrinkle', runkii, ritkti, 'to shrink*, rau-
kiU, гайки, 'to wrinkle', OI. ruksah, 'rough',
OHG., OE. ruh, 'rough'. See rough and cp.
rugate, rugose, corrugate, arroyo. Cp. also ruelle.
Cp. also prec. word.

## rugate
rugate, adj., having folds. — L. rugdtus, pp. of
rugare, 'to crease, wrinkle', fr. ruga. See ruga
and adj. suff. -ate.

## Rugby
Rugby, п., also Rugby football. — So called from
the system of football first played at Rugby
School in Warwickshire.
rugged» adj. — Formed fr. rug with 1st suff. -ed.
Derivatives: rugged-ly, adv., rugged-ness, n.

## rugger
rugger, п., Rugby football (slang). — Altered fr.
Rugby (q.v.)

## rugose
rugose, adj., creased, wrinkled. — L. rugosus,
'wrinkled', fr. ruga. See ruga and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: rugose-ly, adv.

## rugosity
rugosity, п., 1) state of being rugose; 2) a wrinkle.
— Late L. rugositds, fr. L. rugosus. See prec.
word and -ity.

## rugous
rugous, adj., creased, wrinkled. — L. rugosus,
'wrinkled'. See rugose. For the ending see suff.
•ous.

## ruin
ruin, n. — ME. ruine, fr. MF. (= F.) ruine, fr:L.
ruina, 'fall, downfall, disaster, catastrophe,
ruin', fr. ruere, 'to fall violently', which is of
uncertain origin. L. congruere, 'to come together',
and ingruere, 'to rush or break into', are not
related to ruere (see congruent).

## ruin
ruin, tr. and intr. v. — MF. ( = F.) ruiner, fr. ML.
ruinare, fr. L. ruina. See ruin, n.
Derivatives: ruin-able, adj., ruinate, v. (q.v.),
ruin-ed, adj., ruin-er, п., ruinous (q.v.)

## ruinate
ruinate, tr. v., to ruin (arcfiaic). — ML. ruinatus,
pp. of ruinare, 'to demolish, destroy', fr. L.
ruina. See ruin, п., and verbal suff. -ate.

## ruination
ruination, n. — Formed with suff. -ion fr. ML.
ruinatus, pp. of ruinare. See prec. word.

## ruinous
ruinous, adj., causing ruin; decayed. — ME.
ruinose, fr. Late L. rutnosus, 'tumbling down,
going to ruin', fr. L. ruina. See ruin, п., and
-ous.
Derivatives: ruinous-ly, adv., ruinous-ness, n.

## rule
rule, n. — ME. reule, riule, fr. OF. reule, riule, fr.
L. regula, *a straight piece of wood, ruler, rule1,
which is rel. to regere, 'to keep straight, lead,
direct, rule'. See regent, adj., and cp. rail, 'bar',
regula, rillettes. In Modern French the OF.
forms reule, riule were replaced by regie, fr. OF.
regie, a learned word derived directly fr. Latin
regula.
Derivatives: rule-dom, п., rule-less, adj.

## ruie
ruie, tr. and intr. v. — ME. reulen, rulen, fr. OF.
reuler, riuler, fr. L. regulare, 'to direct, regulate',
fr. regula. See rule, п., and cp. regnlate.
Derivatives: rul-er, п., rul-er-ship, п., rul-ing,
adj. and п., rul-ing'ly, adv.

## rum
rum, п., spirit, alcoholic liquor. — Shortened fr.
rnmbuUion.
Derivatives: rumm~y, adj., 1) pertaining to rum;
drunk; п., a drunkard.

## rum
rum, adj., queer. — Orig. a cant word meaning
'good, fine', prob. a corruption of Gypsy rom,
'man, husband; gypsy man*. See rom and cp.
the first element in rumbustious.
Derivatives: rum-ly, adv., rum-ness, п., rumm-y,
adj., rumm-i-ly, adv., rumm-i-ness, n.

## Rumanian
Rumanian, also Romanian, Roumanian, adj. and
n. — Formed fr. ModL. Romania, Rumania,
'Rumania', fr. Rumanian Roman, now spelled
Romtn, fr. L. Rdmanus, 'Roman'. See Roman
and -Ian.

## rumba
rumba, п., name of a dance. — Sp., of uncertain
origin.

## rumble
rumble, intr. v., to make a low, heavy noise; tr. v.,
to cause to make such a noise. — ME. romblen,
rumblen, of imitative origin. Cp. Du. rommelen,
G. rummeln, 'to rumble', ON. rymja, 'to roar,
grumble', rymr, 'a roaring, grumbling', and see
rumor.
Derivatives: rumble, п., rumbl-er, п., rumbl-ing,
adj. and п., rumbl-ing-ly, adv.

## rumble
rumble, п., a low heavy noise. — ME. rumbel, fr.
rumblen. See rumble, v.
Derivative: rumbl-y, adj.

## rumbullion
rumbullion, п., rum (obsol.) — Prob. of imitative

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:673 COLUMN:3 -->
origin. Cp. rum, 'spirit'.

## rumbustious
rumbustious, adj., boisterous. — Prob. a blend of
rum, 'queer', and robustious (see robust).
Derivative: rumbustious-ness, n.

## rumen
rumen, п., the first stomach of ruminants. —
ModL., fr. L. rumen, 'throat, gullet', of
uncertain origin; possibly cogn. with OI. romanthah,
'chewing the cud, rumination'. Lith. raumud,
'flesh of the muscle', is not cogn. with rumen,
but with ruber, 'red*. Cp. ruminant.

## Rumex
Rumex, п., a genus of plants, the dock, the sorrel
{bot.) — ModL., fr. L. rumex, 'sorrel', of
uncertain origin.

## ruminant
ruminant, adj. and n. — L. rumindns, gen. -antis,
pres, part, of rumindri. See next word and -ant.

## ruminate
ruminate, intr. v., to chew the cud; to meditate;
tr. v., to chew over again; to muse on. — L. ru-
minatus, pp. of rumindri, 'to chew the cud', fr.
rumen, gen. -inis, 'throat, gullet*. See rumen
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: ruminat-ing, adj., ruminat-ing-ly,
adv., ruminat-ive, adj., ruminat-ive-ly, adv.

## rumination
rumination, n. — L. rumination 'a chewing the
cud', fr. ruminatus, pp. of rumindri. See prec.
word and -ion.

## ruminator
ruminator, п., a person who ruminates. — L.
rumindtor, 'one that chews again', fr. ruminatus,
pp. of rumindri. See ruminate and agential suff.
-or.

## rumkin
rumkin, п., a kind of drinking vessel. — Prob. fr.
Du. roomerken, dimin. of roemer. See rummer
and -kin.

## rummage
rummage, п., 1) a thorough search; 2)
miscellaneous articles. — Aphetic fr. MF. arrumage (F.
arrimage), 'stowing of goods in the hold of a
ship', fr. arrumer (F. arrimer) 'to stow goods in
the hold of a ship; to stow the cargo', a hybrid
coined fr. a (fr. L. ad, 'to, toward') and -rumer;
which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG., OE. rum,
'room, space', and see room. For the ending see
suff. -age. OProvenc. arumar, Sp. arrumar, 'to
stow the cargo,* are also Teut. loan words.
Derivatives: rummage, intr. v., to search
thoroughly, rummag-er, n.

## rummer
rummer, п., a large drinking glass. — Du. roemer,
fr. roemen, 'to boast', fr. roem, 'praise, glory',
fr. MDu. roem, which is rel. to OS. hrom, OHG.
hruom, ruom, MHG. ruom, G. Ruhm, 'praise,
glory', and further to OHG. hruod-, ruod- (in
compounds), ON. hrodr, OE. hrod, hrad, 'fame,
glory'. All these words are traceable to Teut.
*hro-, which corresponds to the I.-E. imitative
base *qar-, *qard-, 'to cry, shout, call', whence
OI. karuh, 'singer, poet', Dor. Gk. κάρΰξ, Gk.
κήρυξ, 'herald', καρκαίρειν, 'to resound'. See
cadnceus and cp. kerygma. Cp. also the first
element in Robert and in words there referred to.
G. Romer and F. rumer, 'rummer', are Dutch
loan words. Du. roemer orig. denoted a cup
with which the toast of a person is proposed for
the sake of praising him.

## rumor
rumor, rumour, n. — ME. rumour, fr. OF.
rumour, rumeur (F. rumeur), fr. L. гйтдгет, асе.
of rumor, 'common talk, report, hearsay', from
the I.-E. imitative base *гё-, тга-, *ru-, whence
also OI. ruyati,- 'barks', rauti, ruvati, ravati,
'roars', Gk. ώ-ρυεσ&αι, 'to howl, roar', OE.
ryn, 'a roaring', L. raucus (for *rawicos), fr.
ravus. 'hoarse'. See rancous and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: rumo(u)r, tr. v., rumo(u)r-ed, п.,
rumo(u)r-ous, adj.

## rump
rump, n. — ME. rumpe, of Scand. origin. Cp.
Dan. rumpe, Swed. rumpa, 'rump', which are
related to MLG. rump, 'trunk, body', Du. romp,
MHG. rumph, G. Rumpf, of s.m.
Derivatives: rumpy, п., rump-less, adj.

## rumple
rumple, tr. v., to wrinkle. — MDu. rompelen, rel.
to Du. rimpelen, 'to wrinkle', OE. hrympel,
'wrinkle*, OHG. hrimpfan, rimpfan, MHG.
rimpfen, G. rumpfen, of s.m., and cogn.
with Gk. κράμβος, 'dry, shriveled', κράμβη,
'cabbage', κρομβοϋν (assimilated fr. *κραμ-
βοϋν), 'to roast', Lith. krembtys, 'mushroom,
fungus', fr. I.-E. base *qremb-, a nasalized
enlargement of base *q(e)reb~, 'to curve, contract,
shrink'. Cp. rimple, ramp, 'to climb'. Cp. also
corf, Crambe, crambo and the first element in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:674 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 647 | RUT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:674 COLUMN:1 -->
Carphophis and in cromlech. Cp. also harp.

## rumple
rumple, п., wrinkle. — MDu. rompel, whence
rompelen, 'to wrinkle'. See rumple, v.

## rumpus
rumpus, п., uproar. — Of uncertain origin.

## run
run, intr. v. — ME. runnen, ronnen, pp. dfrinnen,
rennen, partly fr. ON. rinna, partly fr. OE. rin-
nan, 'to flow, run', which are rel. to OE. irnan,
iernan, iornan, 'to flow, run', Swed. rinna, Dan.
rinde, MDu. runnen, OS., OHG., Goth. rinnan,
MHG., G. rinnen, 'to flow, run'. ON. renna, OE.
gerennan, 'to cause to run*, Goth, ur-ranjan, 'to
cause to rise', OS. rennian, MDu., OHG.,
MHG. rennen, Swed. ranna. Dan. rende, 'to
cause to run', are causative forms of the
respective primitive verbs. All these words derive fr.
I.-E. base *er-, *or-, 'to set in motion, stir up,
raise', whence also OI. arnah, 'undulating,
surging (waves)', L. orirl, 'to rise1. See orient, п., and
cp. rise. Cp. also random, rennet, 'membrane of
calf's stomach*, rhine, 'ditch', rill, runlet,
'runnel', runnel, ember days.

## run
run, п., the act of running. — ME. rune, fr.
runnen, 4o run'. Cp. OE. ryne, 'running, flowing,
course, watercourse, cycle, bed of a river\ Goth.
runs, OFris. rene, 'running, course', ON. run,
'running, course', runa, 'row, rank, series', and
see run, v. Cp. also rhine.

## runagate
runagate, п., a vagabond. — Folk-etymological
alteration of ME. renegate (see renegade), taken
for the compound of run and agate, 'away', lit.
'on the road', fr. a- — on, and gate, 'road, lane'.

## runcinate
runcinate, adj., saw-toothed. — L. runcindtus, pp.
of runcinare, 'to plane off', fr. runcina, 'a plane',
a blend of Gk. £υκάνη, 'a plane', and L. run-
care, 'to weed out, clear of weeds', which are
prob. cogn. with each other and with Gk.
όρύσσω (for *όρύχιω), Ί dig', OI. luncati,
'plucks, pulls', Lett, rufcet, 'to dig', Olr. ruckt,
'hog, pig', lit. 'the rooting animal'. Cp. Oryx.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## rundale
rundale, п., a system of division of lands in
Ireland. — Compounded of run and dale,
Northern form of dole, 'small portion'.

## rundie
rundie, п., rung of a ladder. — ME. rundel, a var.
of roundel. See roundel.

## rune
rune, п., ]) any of the letters of the ancient Teut.
alphabet; 2) mystery; magic. —ME. roun, fr.
OE. run, 'mystery, secret; counsel, discussion;
whisper; runic character*, rel. to ON. run, *a
secret, magic sign, runic character', OHG.
runa, MHG. rune, 'a secret, a secret
conversation, whisper", G. Rune, 'rune, runic letter',
Goth, runa, 'a secret, a secret conversation', and
to OE. runian, ON. reyna, 'to whisper'. Cp. al-
raun and round, 'to whisper'.
Derivatives: run-ic, adj., run-ic-al-ly, adv.

## rung
rung, п., a round of a ladder. — ME. rung, rang,
fr. OE. hrung, 'staff, pole\ rel. to MLG., MHG.
runge, 'stake, stud, stave', MDu. rongke, ronge,
Du. rong, 'rung', G. Runge, 'stake, stud stave*,
Goth, hrugga, 'staff'; of uncertain origin;
possibly meaning orig. 'round staff', and rel. to OE.
hring, etc., 'ring'. See ring, n.

## runlet
runlet, п., a small cask {archaic). — OF. rondelet,
double dimin. formed fr. rond, 'round*, fr. L.
rotundus. See round, adj., and -let.

## runlet
runlet, п., runnel, rill. — Formed fr. run, п.,
with dimin. suff. -let. Cp. runnel.

## runnel
runnel, п., rivulet. — ME. rinel, runel, fr- OE.
rynel, lit. 'little runner', formed from the base of
OE. rinnan, 'to flow, run', with dimin. suff. -el.
See rim and -el.

## runt
runt, n. 1) a small ox or cow; 2) a stunted animal
or person. — Rel. to OS. hrith, OFris. hritker,
MDu., Du. rund, OHG. hrind, rind, MHG.
rint, G. Rind, OE. krlder, kryder, *ox, cow*. See
rother.

## rupa
rupa, п., form, shape {Hinduism). — OI. rupah,
'appearance, color, form, shape, likeness,
image, picture, beauty', perhaps related to OI. var-
pas, 'figure, dexterity*, and cogn. with Avestic
var p-, 'to mark', Lith. verpiu, vefpti, 'to spin'.
See vervnin and cp. next word. Cp. also rupee,
arupa.

## rupee
rupee, п., an Indian coin. — Hind, rupiyah, fr.
OI. rupyah, 'silver', orig. 'something provided
with a picture* a coin', fr. rupah, 'shape,
likeness, image*. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:674 COLUMN:2 -->

## Rupert
Rupert, masc PN. — Prob. a blend of G. Ru-
precht and Robert (q.v.)

## rupestrian
rupestrian, adj., consisting of rock. — Formed fr.
L. rupes, 'rock', which is rel. to rumpere, 'to
break, burst, tear, rend'. See rupture and -ian.
For the relationship between L. rupes and
rumpere cp. L. saxum, 'rock, stone', which is rel. to
secure, 'to cut', OE. clif, 'cliff', which is rel. to
OE. cleofan, 'to split, cleave', ON. sker, 'an
isolated rock in the sea', which is rel. to ON. skera,
'to cut, shear', and Gk. λέπάς 'a bare rock,
crag', which is prob. rel. to λέπειν, 'to strip off,
peel' (see saxatiie, cliff, skerry and lapidary, adj.)

## rupia
rupia, п., a skin disease occuring esp. in tertiary
syphilis (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. ρύπος,
'dirt, filth'. See rbyparography and 1st -ia.
Derivative: rupi-al, adj.

## Rnppia
Rnppia, п., a genus of plants, the ditch grass
(bot.) — ModL., named after the German
botanist Heinrich Bernhard Ruppius (1689-1719).

## rnpture
rnpture, n. — ME. ruptur, fr. MF. (= F.) rupture,
fr. L. rupiura, 'a fracture, breach', fr. ruptus, pp.
of rumpere, 'to break, burst, tear, rend', which
is cogn. with OE. reafian, 'to seize, rob,
plunder', reofan, 'to tear, break', ON. rjufa, 'to
break'. See reave and -ure and cp. abrupt,
bankrupt, corrupt, corruption, disrupt, disruption,
erupt, eruption, interrupt, interruption, irrnpt,
irruption, rote, 'routine', roture, rout, 'rabble',
rout, 'to put to flight', route, routier, routine,
rupestrinn, rutter.
Derivatives: rupture, tr. and intr. v., ruptur-ed,
adj.

## rural
rural, adj., of the country. — ME., fr. L. ruralis,
'pertaining to the country', fr. rus, gen. ruris,
'the country', which is cogn. with OSlav. ravinu,
'level', Olr. roi4 roe, 'plain field', OE. rum, etc.,
'space'. See room and cp. roister, Ruritanian,
rustic. For the ending see adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: rural-ism, п., rural-ist4 п., rural-ite,
п., rural-ity, п., rural-ize, tr. v., rural-iz-ation,
п., rurql-ly, adv.

## ruridecanal
ruridecanal, adj., pertaining to a rural dean. —
Compounded of L. rus, gen. ruris, 'the country',
and decanus, 'dean'. See rural and decanal.

## Ruritanian
Ruritanian, adj., Utopian. — Formed with suff.
-nn fr. Ruritania, an imaginary kingdom in The
Prisoner of Zenda, by Anthony Hope (1863-
1933). The name Rurifania was formed fr. L.
rus, gen. ruris, 'country' (see rural), on analogy
of Aquitania.

## Rusa
Rusa, п., the genus of the East Indian deer (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Malay rusa, 'deer'. Cp. rusine.

## ruse
ruse, п., trick, wile. — MF. (= F.), 'trick, wile',
back formation fr. ruser, 'to use trickery', fr.
reuser, 'to get out of the way, to cause to
retreat', fr. VL. refusare, freq. of L. refundere (pp.
refusus), 'to pour back; to fling back, refuse,
reject'. See refnse and cp. refund. Cp. also rush,
'to run forward'.

## rush
rush, п., name of various aquatic plants {bot.) —
ME. risk, rush, Тт. OE. rise, rysc, rel. to MLG.
rusch, risch, MHG. rusch, rusche, 'rush', and
possibly cogn. with Lith. rizgis, 'basket, wicker-
work', rezgu, regsti, 4o bind, lace, cord', L.
restis, for *rezgtis, 'rope, cord', OI. rajjuh, 'rope,
cord'. Cp. restiform.
Derivatives: rush, tr. v., to strew with rushes,
to work with rushes; intr. v., to gather rushes,
rush-like, adj., rush-y, п., rush-i-ness, n.

## rush
rush, intr. and tr. v., to run forward. — ME.
russhen, fr. OF. reuser, 'to get out of the way,
to cause to retreat'. See ruse, п., and cp. rustle,
'to act energetically'.
Derivatives: rush, п., rush-ing, adj., rush-ing-ly,
adv., rush-ing-ness, n.

## rusine
rusine, adj., resembling the deer of the genus
Rusa. — Formed fr. Rusa with adj. suff. -ine.
Cp. rucervine.

## rusk
rusk, п., light, soft bread or biscuit. — Sp. rosea,
'roll, twist of bread', rel. to Port, rosea; of
uncertain, perhaps pre-Latin, origin.
Derivative: rusk, tr. v.

## rusma
rusma, п., a depilatory. — It. and F., a
corruption of Turk, khorozma, inexact transliteration
of Gk. χρίσμα, 'unguent', lit. 'anything
smeared on*, fr. xpfeLv, 'to smear, anoint'. See
chrism and cp. cream.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:674 COLUMN:3 -->

## Russ
Russ, n. — F. Russe, fr. Russ. Rus, 'Russia;
Russian'.
Derivative: Russ, adj.

## Russel
Russel, п., also Russel cord, a kind of cotton-and-
wool fabric. — Prob. so called after the maker's
name.

## russet
russet, adj., reddish. — ME., fr. OF. rosset, rous-
set, dimin. of ros, rous (F. roux), fr. L. russus,
'red*, which stands for *rudh-tos or *rudh-sos
and is rel. to ruber, 'red, reddish'. Cp. OSlav.
rusu, 'fair', Lith. rauscas, 'reddish', rusvas,
'reddish brown', OHG. rosamo, 'rust', and see
rubric and -et. Cp. also rissole, roux, roussette,
rust, Rnssula.
Derivatives: russet, п., and tr. and intr. v., rus-
set-ing, п., russet-ish, adj.

## Russia
Russia, n. — ML., fr. Russi, 'the Russians', fr.
Russ. Rus. See Russ.
Derivatives: Russian, n. and adj., Russian-ism,
п., Russian-ist, п., Russian-iz-ation, n.

## Russia leather
Russia leather, also russia, n. — Named after
Russia, where it was first made.

## Russification
Russification, n. — See next word and -ation.

## Russify
Russify, tr. v., to make Russian. — Formed fr.
Russ with suff. -fy.

## Russo-
Russo-, combining form denoting Russia or the
Russians. — Fr. ML. Russi, 'the Russians', fr.
Russ. Rus. See Russ.

## russud
russud, п., grain, forage, etc., provided by local
officers (India). — Hind, rasad, lit. 'income*, fr.
Pers. rasad, 'going into, entering', rel. to OPers.
rasatiy, 'comes', which is formed from the pres.
stem of the verb ar-, 'to move', fr. I.-E. base *er-,
*or-, 'to set in motion', whence also h.oriri, 'to
rise'. See orient, п., and cp. words there referred
to.

## Russula
Russula, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) -^ ModL., fr.
Late L. russula, fem. of russulus, a dimin.
formed fr. L. russus, 'red*. See russet and -ule.

## rust
rust, n. — ME., fr. OE. rust, rel. to OS., Swed..
OHG., MHG., G. rost, MDu. ro(e)st, Du.
roest, Dan., Norw. rust, fr. Teut. *rusta-,
corresponding to I.-E. *reudh-s-to-t *rudh-s-to-,
enlargement of base *reudho-, *rudho-, 'red'.
Cp. Lith. rustas, 'brownish', rudeti, 'to rust',
Lett, rusa, 'rust', ruste, 'brown color', OSlav.
ruzda (for *rudya), 'rust', and see red, Cp. also
russet.
Derivatives: rust, intr. and tr. v., rusty (q.v.)»
rust-less, adj.

## rustic
rustic, adj., 1) rural; 2) simple. — ME. rustyk, fr.
MF. (= F.) rusiique, fr. L. rusticus, 'pertaining
to the country', fr. rus, gen. ruris, 'country'. See
rural and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: rustic, п., rustic-al, adj., rustic-al-
ness, п., rustic-ism, п., rustic~ize, tr. v., rustic-ly,
adv.

## rusticate
rusticate, tr. v., to send into the country; intr. v.,
to live in the country. — L. rusticatus, pp. of
rusticari, 4o live in the country', fr. rusticus.
See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## rnstication
rnstication, n. — L. rusticatid, gen. -onis, 'a living
in the country, country life', fr. rusticatus, pp.
of rusticari. See prec. word and -ion.

## rusticity
rusticity, п., rustic character. — MF. (= F.)
rusticite, fr. L. rusticitatem, ace. of rusticitas,
'country life', fr. rusticus. See rustic and -ity.

## rustie
rustie, intr. v., to emit a succession of soft, rapid
sounds; tr. v., to cause to rustle. — ME. rou-
schen, rouschelen, rustelen, rustlen, of imitative
origin. Cp. MLG. ruschen, MDu. ruusscen, Du.
ruisen, MHG. ruschen, riuschen, G. rauschen,
'to rustle', OE. hryscan, 'to creak'.
Derivatives: rustle, п., rustl-er, п., rustl-ing,
adj., rustl-ing-ly, adv., rustl-ing-ness, n.

## rustle
rustle, intr. v., to act energetically; tr. v., to get by
rustling. — A blend of the verbs rush and hustle.
Derivatives: rustle, п., rustl-er, n.

## rusty
rusty, adj. — ME., fr. OE. rustig, fr. rust. See rust
and -y (representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: rusti-ly, adv., rusti-ness, n.

## rut
rut, п., track; habit, routine. — Prob. fr. MF.
(= F.) route, 'way', fr. VL. rupta (via), lit. 'a
broken way*. See route and cp. rote, 'routine'.
Derivative: rutt-y, adj.

## rut
rut, п., sexual excitement of animals, esp. of
deer. — ME. rutte, fr. OF. ruit, rut (F. rut), fr.
L. rugltus, 'a roar', fr. pp. stem of rugire, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:675 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: RUT | 648 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:675 COLUMN:1 -->
roar', fr. an enlarged form of the I.-E. imitative
base *reu-, *ru-, 'to shout, roar', whence also
rumor, 'common talk, report, hearsay'. See
rumor.

## rut
rut, п., a native carriage drawn by a pony or oxen
(India). — Hind, rath, 'a chariot', fr. OI.
rdthah. See rota and cp. the first element in
Rathayatra.

## Rnta
Rnta, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — L. ruta, 'rue'.
See rue, 'a bitter herb'..

## Rutaceae
Rutaceae, n. pl„ the rue family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Rnta with suff. -aceae.

## rutaceous
rutaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## ruth
ruth, п., pity (arch.) — ME. rewthe, ruthe, fr. rew-
en, ruen, 'to pity'. See rue, 'to regret', and subst.
suff..-th.

## Rnth
Rnth, 1) fem. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the ancestress
of David. — Heb. Ruth, prob. contraction of
r uth, 'companion, friend, fellow woman',
which is rel. to rea', re'eh, 'friend, companion,
fellow'.

## Ruthenian
Ruthenian, adj. and n. — Formed fr. ML. Ruthe-
ni, 'the Little Russians', a derivative of Russi, pi.
of Russus. See Russo- and -ian.

## ruthenium
ruthenium, п., name of a* rare metallic element
(chemistry). — ModL-, a name given to this
element by the Russian chemist Karl Klauss in
1845. However, the name ruthenium is of earlier

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:675 COLUMN:2 -->
origin. It was coined by Osann in 1828 to name
with it a new metal discovered by him, but it
was Klauss who confirmed that this metal
really contained the new element. See W. E.
Flood, The Dictionary of Chemical Names,
New York, 1963, p. 19.
Derivatives: ruthen-ate, ruthen-ic, ruthen-ious,
ruthen-ous, adjs.

## ruthful
ruthful, adj. — ME. rewtheful, rutkeful,
compounded of rewthe, ruthe, 'pity', and -ful, '-ful'.
See ruth and -ful.
Derivatives: ruthfui-iy, adv., ruthfui-ness, n.

## ruthless
ruthless, adj. — ME. rewtheles, rutheles,
compounded οι rewthe, ruthe, 'pity', and -les, '-less'.
See ruth and -less.
Derivatives: rutkless-ly, adv., ruthiess-ness, n.

## rutUant
rutUant, adj., shining with a reddish light. —
L. rutilans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of rutilare, fr.
rutilus. See next word and -ant.

## rutile
rutile, п., an adamantine mineral consisting of
titanium dioxide (TiOs). — F. rutile or G. Rutil,
fr. L. rutilus, 'red; shining, glittering', which is
rel. to ruber, 'red'. See red and cp. rubric.

## rutter
rutter, п., horseman, cavalry soldier. —
Borrowed fr. MDu. rutter (whence Du. ruiter), a var. of
ruter, ruyter, fr. OF. routier, derivative of route,
'band, troop', prop. fem. of pp. rout, 'broken',
used as a noun, fr. rompre, 'to break'. G. Reuter,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:675 COLUMN:3 -->
Dan. rytter and Swed. ryttare, 'rider, horseman',
are borrowed fr. Du. ruiter. F. route, 'way, path',
is of the same origin as OF. route, 'band, troop'.
See route andrcp. rout, 'rabble'.

## -ry
-ry, noun suff. — A shortened form of -ery.

## rye
rye, п., a cereal plant. — ME., fr. OE. ryge, rel.
to OS. roggo, ON. rugr, Dan. rug, Swed. rag,
OFris. rogga, MDu. rogghe, Du. rogge, rog,
OHG. rocko, MHG. rqcke, G. Roggen, and
cogn. with OSlav. ruii, (Russ. rozh'), 'rye',
Lith. rugps, 'grain of rye', pi. rugiat, 'rye'. Cp.
the first element in rocambole.
rye grass. — From earlier ray grass, fr. ME. ray,
'd arnel', fr. Du. raai (also raaigras), which is rel.
to OS. rado, OHG. rato, G. Raden, lit.
'wheellike flower". Cp. Du. rad, OS. rath, OHG. rad,
MHG. rat, rad, G. Rad, 'wheel', and see
rotn. See Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p. 577 s.v.
Rade.

## ryepeck
ryepeck, гуреск, п., an iron-shod pole for
mooring. — Of unknown origin.

## Rynchospora
Rynchospora, п., a genus of plants, the beak rush
(bot.) — ModL„ compounded of Gk. ρύγχος,
'snout, beak', and σπορά, 'seed'. See rhyncho-
and spore.

## ryot
ryot, п., an Indian peasant. — Hind, raiyat, fr.
Arab. ra'!yah, 'flock, herd subjects', fr. ra'a, 'he
fed, pastured'. See rayah.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:676 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:676 COLUMN:1 -->

## -s
-s, suff. serving to form adverbs. — ME. -es, ft.
OE. -es, suff. of the masc. and neut. gen. sing.
Cp. always, anights, besides, betimes, needs,
unawares and the suffixes -wards, -ways.

## -'s
-'s, suff. used to form the possessive of nouns. —
ME. -es, fr. OE. -es. See prec. suff.

## sabadilia
sabadilia, п., a plant of the family Melanthaceae.
— Sp. cebadiila, dimin. of cebada, 'barley', ft.
L. cibdta, fem. pp. of cibdre, 'to give food to
animals, to feed', fr. cibus, 'food', which is of
uncertain etymology.

## Sabaean
Sabaean, adj., pertaining to Saba in S. Arabia.
— L. Sabaeus, ft. Gk. Σαβαΐος, 'inhabitant
of Saba', fr. Σάβα, ft. Arab. Saba' = Heb.
Sh bka\ For the ending see suff. -an.
Derivatives: Sabaean, п., Sabaean-ism, n.

## Sabaisin
Sabaisin, п., star worship. — Formed fr. Heb.
tzdbhd', 'host', in the sense of tz bhd hashshama-
yim, 'host of heaven, stars'. See Sabaoth and -ism.

## Sabaist
Sabaist, п., star worshiper. — See prec. word and
-ist.

## Sabaoth
Sabaoth, n. pi., armies, hosts, used chiefly in the
phrase the Lord of Sabaoth. — Late L., fr. Late
Gk. Σαβαώ*, fr. Heb. tzsbhdoth, plural of
tzdbhd', 'host, army', from the v. tzdbd, 'he waged
war; he served', which is rel. to Akkad. sabu,
'soldier' (in the pi. also 'men'), Ethiop. daba,
'he waged war', and prob. also to Arab, ddbaa',
*he lay in wait' (some scholars compare Arab.
sdbaa, 'he went forth', whence 'he gathered
together against', and S. Fraenkel, Die ara-
maischen Fremdworter im Arabischen, Leyden,
1886, p. 232, compares Arab, sabt, 'young man',
which are nearer in meaning then ddbaa'). Cp.
Sabaism. Cp. also Maccabees.

## Sabbatarian
Sabbatarian, adj., 1) pertaining to the Sabbath;
2) pertaining to the Sabbatarians or their
doctrine; п., one who keeps the seventh day of the
week as holy. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L.
sabbatdrius, fr. sabbatum, 'the seventh day of
the Jewish week'. See next word and -arian.
Derivative: Sabbatarian-ism, n.

## Sabbath
Sabbath, n. — L. sabbatum (partly through the
medium of F. sabbat) (whence also It. sabato,
OProvenc-, Catal. dis-sapte, Sp., Port, sdbado,
Serbo-Croatian suborn, Czech and Slovak sobo-
ta, Russ. subbata, etc.), fr. Gk. σάββατον, fr.
Heb. shabbdth, 'Sabbath' (whence also Aram.
shabb td, Arab, sabt, Ethiop. sanbat), prop, 'day
of rest', fr. shdbbdth, 'he rested', which is rel.
to Arab, sabata, 'he cut off, interrupted, ceased,
rested', and to Akkad. shabdtu, which prob.
means 'to cease, be completed'. Cp. Gk. "σάμβοί-
tov, a vulgar var. of σάββατον, whence VL.
sambatum (whence Ru. sSmbdtd, OSlav. sobota.
Hung, szombat, 'Saturday, Sabbath') and sam-
batl dies, the day of Sabbath' [whence OF.
sambe-di, F. samedi, 'Saturday' and—prob.
through the medium of the Gothic—the first
element in OHG. sambas-tac (MHG. samey
tac, G. Sams-tag), 'Saturday'].

## Snbbathia
Snbbathia, п., a genus of plants of the gentian
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the Italian
botanist L. Sabbati. For the ending see suff. -in.

## Sabbatic
Sabbatic, Sabbatical, adj.— L. sabbaticus, fr. Gk.
σαββατικός, 'pertaining to the Sabbath', fr.
σάββατον. See Sabbath and -Ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: Sabbatical-ly, adv.

## Sabbatize
Sabbatize, tr. v., to keep as a Jewish Sabbath. —
Late L. sabbatizdre, fr. Gk. σαββατίζειν, fr.
σάββατον. See Sabbath and -ize.

## saber
saber, sabre, п., a one-edged sword. — F. sabre,
fr. G. Subel, later Siibel, fr. Pol. szabla, ult. fr.
Hung, szablya, 'saber', lit. 'a tool to cut with',
fr. szabni, 'to cut'. Cp. sabreur and the first
element in sabretache.

## Sabian
Sabian, п., a member of a religious sect
mentioned in three passages of the Koran (2:40, 5:73,
22:17). — Formed with suff. -an fr. Arab, sdbi',
'Sabian', which prob. means lit. 'baptizer', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:676 COLUMN:2 -->
is borrowed fr. Aram. tzebha', 'he dipped, dyed'
(with the change of the ayin to hamza), which
is rel. to Heb. tzdbhd', 'he dyed', Arab, sdbahga,
Ethiop. sabdha, 'he dipped, dyed', Akkad. sibu,
'to dye'.
Derivatives: Sabian, adj., Sabian-ism, n.

## sabicu
sabicu, п., a timber tree; its wood. — Cuban Sp.
sabicii.

## Snbine
Snbine, adj., pertaining to a people in ancient
Italy; п., a member of the Sabine people. — L.
Sablnus. This name possibly means lit. 'of its
own kind', and is cogn. with Goth, sibja, OHG.
sippa, 'blood-relationship» peace, alliance', OE.
sibb, 'relationship, peace'; see Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., II, 457 s.v. Sabini. See sib and -ine
(representing L. -inus) and cp. Samnite. Cp.
also savin.

## sable
sable, п., a small animal, Mustella zibellina. —
ME., fr. MF. sable (F. zibeline), ft. OF., fr. ML.
sabelum, ft. MLG. sabel, ft. MHG. zobel, a loan
word fr. Russ. sabol', which itself is borrowed
from an East-Asiatic language. Cp. zibeline.

## sable
sable, adj., black (her.) — F. sable, prop, 'of the
color of the sable'. See prec. word.

## sabot
sabot, п., a wooden shoe. — F., blend of bot, a
dialectal var. of botte, 'boot', and savate, 'old
shoe'. See boot and snvate.

## sabotage
sabotage, п., willful destruction of machinery,
etc. — F., fr. saboter, 'to do willful damage (to
machinery and the like), fr. sabot (see prec.
word); the verb was formerly used in the sense
'to throw wooden shoes into the machinery for
the sake of damaging it'. For the ending see
suff. -age.
Derivative: sabotage, tr. v., to destroy by
sabotage; intr. v., to practice sabotage.

## sabre
sabre, n. — A var. of saber.

## sabretache
sabretache, п., a square leather case hung from
the sword belt. — F., fr. G. Sabeltasche, lit.
'saber-pocket', fr. Sdbel, 'saber', and Tasche,
'pocket'. For the first element see saber. The
second element derives fr. VL. "tasca; see tusk.

## sabreur
sabreur, п., a dashing cavalry officer. — F., lit. 'a
swordsman', ft. sabre, 'sword'. See saber and
agential suff. -or.

## sabulose
sabulose, adj., sandy. — L. sabulosus. See
sabulous and adj. suff. -ose.

## sabulosity
sabulosity, п., sandiness. — See prec. word and
-ity.

## sabulous
sabulous, adj., sandy. — L. sabulosus, 'sandy', fr.
sabulum, 'sand', which stands for *psaflom and
is cogn. with Gk. ψάμμος (for *ψάφμος),
'sand', ON. sandr, OE. sand, 'sand'. See sand
and cp. next word. For the ending see suff.
-ous.

## saburra
saburra, п., sandlike deposit in the stomach
(med.) — Medical L., fr. L. saburra, 'sand',
which is rel. to sabulum. See prec. word.
Derivative: saburr-al, adj.

## sac
sac, п., a baglike part in plants or animals (bot.
and zool.) — F., fr. L. saccus, 'sack'. See sack,
'bag', and cp. sachet.

## sac
sac, п., cause of dispute. — OE. sacu, 'dispute,
jurisdiction'. — See sake, 'purpose'.

## sacaton
sacaton, п., a coarse perennial grass. — Amer.
Sp. zacaton, augment, of zacate, 'grass, hay',
which is of Nahuatl origin. Cp. zacaton.

## saccade
saccade, п., jerk with a bridle. — F., fr. saquer,
'to jerk along', fr. Sp. sacar, 'to draw out', which
prob. derives fr. VL. *saccdre. See sack, 'pillage',
and -nde and cp. the first element in sackbut.

## saccate
saccate, adj., formed into a sac; having a sac. —
ModL. saccdtus, fr. L. saccus, 'sack, bag'. See
sack, 'a bag', and adj. suff. -ate.

## sacchar-
sacchar-, sacchari-, saccharo-, combining forms
meaning 'sugar'. — Fr. L. saccharon, fr. Gk.
σάκχαρον, 'sugar', ft. Pali sakkhard, ft. OI. sdr-
kard, 'gravel, grit, sugar'. See sugar and cp.
words there referred to.

## saccbariferous
saccbariferous, adj., containing sugar. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:676 COLUMN:3 -->
Compounded of sacchari- and -ferous.

## saccharify
saccharify, tr. v., to convert into sugar. —
Compounded of sacchari- and -fy.

## saccharimeter
saccharimeter, saccharometer, п., an instrument
for measuring the amount of sugar in a
solution. — Compounded of sacchari-, resp.
saccharo-, and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## saccharin
saccharin, saccharine, п., a white crystalline
compound, C7H503NS (chem.) — Coined by Fahl-
berg and List in 1879 ft. ML. saccharum (fr. L.
saccharon); see sacchar- and -in.

## saccharine
saccharine, adj., of the nature of sugar. — See
sacchari- and adj. suff. -ine.

## saccharo-
saccharo-, combining form. — See sacchar-.

## Saccharomyces
Saccharomyces, n. pi., a genus of fungi, the
yeasts (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'sugar fungi' (see
saccharo- and -myces), prop, a loan translation
of G. Zuckerpilz, a name given to yeast by
Theodor Schwann (1810-82). See С. С. Mettler,
History of Medicine, Philadelphia - Toronto,
1947, p. 261.

## saccharose
saccharose, п., сапе or beet sugar. — Formed fr.
Gk. σάκχαρον, 'sugar'(see sacchar-), and subst.
suff. -ose.

## sacciform
sacciform, adj., sack-shaped. — Compounded of
L. saccus, 'sack, bag' and forma, 'form, shape'.
See sack, 'bag', and form, n.

## saccule
saccule, п., a little bag. — L. sacculus, 'a little
sack or bag', dimin. of saccus. See sack, 'bag',
and -ule.

## sacerdotal
sacerdotal, adj., pertaining to the priesthood or
to priests. — ME., fr. MF., fr. L. sacerdotdlis,
'pertaining to priests, priestly', fr. sacerdds, gen.
-otis, 'priest', which stands for *sakro-dho-t-s,
lit. 'he who is made holy', fr. sacer, 'holy', and
I.-E. base *dhe-, 'to put, place; to make,
appoint'. See sacred and do. For the ending see
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: sacerdotal-ism, n.,sacerdotal-ist, п.,
sacerdotal-ist-ic, adj., sacerdotal-ly, adv.

## sachem
sachem, п., supreme chief. — Of Algonquian
origin; cp. Narraganset sachimau. Cp. sagamore.

## sachet
sachet, п., a small bag filled with aromatic
powder. — F., dimin. of sac. Seesac,'abag]ikepart',
and -et.

## sack
sack, п., a large bag. — ME., ft. OE. sacc, ft. L.
saccus, fr. Gk. σάκκος, fr. Heb. saq, 'sackcloth,
sack, bag'. Cp. sac, 'a baglike part', saccule,
sack, 'pillage', sacque, satchel, cul-de-sac, Dudel-
sack.
Derivatives: sack, to put in a sack, sack-ing\
sackcloth.

## sack
sack, п., pillage, plunder. — F. sac, 'pillage,
plunder', fr. It. sacco, of s.m., prob. ft. VL.
'saccdre, 'to plunder', orig. 'to put plundered
things into a sack', ft. L. saccus, 'sack'. See
sack, 'bag'.

## sack
sack, п., strong wine. — Formerly spelled seek,
fr. F. (vin) sec, 'dry wine', fr. L. siccus, 'dry'.
See siccative and cp. sec, secco.

## sackbut
sackbut, п., 1) a medieval wind instrument,
forerunner of the trombone; 2) a stringed
instrument resembling the guitar, in Dan 3:5 used
wrongly to translate Aram, sabb kkd. — MF.
(= F.) saquebute, fr. OF. saqueboute,
compounded of saquer, 'to pull, draw out', and
bouter, 'to thrust'. See saccade and butt, 'to
strike'.

## sackless
sackless, adj., innocent; harmless (archaic or
dial.) — ME. sakles, fr. OE. sacleas, ft. sacu,
'dispute', and -leas, '-less'. See sac, 'dispute', and
-less.

## sacque
sacque, п., sack dress. — Identical with sack,
'bag; dress', but spelled as if it were a French
word.

## sacr-
sacr-, form of sacro- before a vowel.

## sacral
sacral, adj., pertaining to religious rites. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. sacer, fem. sacra,
neut. sacrum, 'holy, sacred'. See sacred.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:677 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SACRAL | 650 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:677 COLUMN:1 -->

## sacral
sacral, adj., pertaining to the sacrum. — Medical
L. sacralis. See sacrum and adj. suff. -a).

## sacrament
sacrament, n. — ME. sacrement, sacrament, fr.
OF. sacrement, sacrament (F. sacrement), fr. L.
sacramentum, 'oath, solemn obligation*, fr. sa-
crare, 'to set apart as sacred, consecrate', fr.
sacer, fern, sacra, neut. sacrum, 'holy, sacred'.
See sacred and -ment.
Derivatives: sacrament-al, adj. and п., sacra-
ment-al-ism, п., sacrament-al-ist-ic, adj., sacra-
ment-al-ity, п., sacrament-al-ly, adv.,
sacramental-ness, n.

## Sacrumentarian
Sacrumentarian, п., one who regards the
sacraments merely as symbols; adj., pertaining to the
Sacramentarians. — Formed fr. ML. sacra-
mentarius, 'pertaining to a sacrament', fr. L.
sacramentum. See prec. word and -arian.
Derivative: Sacramentarian-ism, n.

## sacrarium
sacrarium, п., shrine, sanctuary. — L. sacrarium,
lit. 'a place for the keeping of holy things', fr.
sacrare/toconsecrate'. See sacrament and -arium.

## sacred
sacred, adj. — ME. sacred, prop. pp. of sacren,
*to consecrate, dedicate', fr. F. sacrer, fr. L.
sacrdre, 'to set apart as sacred, consecrate', fr.
sacer, fem. sacra, neut. sacrum, 'dedicated to a
divinity, holy, sacred', which is rel. to sanctre,
*to render sacred', sanctus, 'sacred, holy' (prop,
pp. of sancire), and cogn. with Hitt. skakldisji,
shaklish, 'law, rite'. ON. sdttr, 'agreement', is
not cognate with these words. Cp. consecrate,
desecrate, execrate, obsecrate, sacerdotal,
sacrament, sacrifice, sacrilege, sacristan, sacristy,
sacrosanct, sacrum, saint, sanctify, sanction,
sanctity, sanctum, sanctus, Santolina, santon,
santonica, sexton. Cp. also the second word in
cascara sagrada.
Derivatives: sacred-ly, adv., sacred-ness, n.

## sacrifice
sacrifice, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) sacrifice, fir.
L. sacrifictum, fr. sacer, fem. sacra, neut.
sacrum, 'holy, sacred', and -ficium, fr. -ficere,
unstressed form of facere, 'to make, do'. See
sacred and fact.
Derivatives: sacrifice, tr. and intr. v.,sacrific-er>
n.

## sacrificial
sacrificial, adj. — Formed with adj. surf, -al fr. L.
sacrificium, 'sacrifice'. See prec. word.
Derivative: sacrificial-ly, adv.

## sacrilege
sacrilege, п., profanation of anything sacred. —
ME., fr. OF. sacileger (F. sacrilege), fr. L. sa-
crilegium, 'the robbing of a temple, the stealing
of sacred things', fr. sacrilegus, 'temple robber,
stealer of sacred things', which is compounded
of sacer, fem. sacra, neut. sacrum, 'holy, sacred',
and -legus, from the stem of legere, 'to gather,
pick up, carry off, steal'. See sacred and lecture.
Derivatives: sacrileg-ious, adj., sacrileg-ious-ly,
adv., sacrileg-ious-ness, п., sacrileg-ist, n,

## sncring
sncring, п., consecration. — ME., verbal noun of
sacren, 'to consecrate'. See sacred and -ing, suff.
forming verbal nouns.

## sacrist
sacrist, п., a keeper of the sacred vessels;
sacristan. — ME., fr. Eccles. L. sacrista, fr. L. sacer,
fem. sacra, neut. sacrum, 'holy, sacred'. See
sacred and -ist

## sacristan
sacristan, n. — ME., fr. Eccles. L. sacristdnus, fr.
sacrista. See prec. word and -an and cp. sexton,
which is a doublet of sacristan.

## sacristy
sacristy, п., an apartment in a church where-the
sacred vessels, vestments, etc., are kept; vestry.
— Eccles. L. sacristia, fr. Late L. sacrista. See
sacrist and -y (representing F. -ie).
sacro·, before a vowel sacr-, combining form
meaning 'holy, sacred'. — From the stem of L.
sacer, fem. sacra, neut. sacrum, 'holy, sacred'.
See sacred.

## sacro-
sacro-, before a vowel sacr-, combining form
denoting 1) the sacrum; 2) sacral and. — See sn-
crum.

## sacrosanct
sacrosanct, adj., very sacred. — L. sacrdsanctus,
'consecrated with religious ceremonies, doubly
sacred', compounded of sacer, 'holy, sacred',
and sanctus, of s.m. See sacro-, 'holy', and
sanctus, saint.

## sacrum
sacrum, п., bone at the lower end of the spine
(attat.) — ModL., fr. os sacrum, 'the sacred
bone*, from mistranslation of the term
occurring in Galen: Ιερών όστοΰν, 'the strong bone',
into 'the sacred bone'. For the difference

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:677 COLUMN:2 -->
between Gk. Εερός, 'strong', and ίερός, 'sacred',
see Boisacq, DELG., p. 368.

## sad
sad, adj. — ME. sad, 'sated, full, satisfied, tired',
fr. OE. ssed, 'sated, satisfied', rel. to OS. sad,
ON. sadr,MDu. sat, sad,T>M.zad,OHG.,UWG.
sat(t), G. satt, Goth, saps, 'satiated', fr. I.-E.
base *sa-, *s -, 'satisfied, sated*, whence also L.
satis, 'enough, sufficient', satur, 'satiated',
OSIav. sytu,Lhh. sotus, of s.m., Lith. satis,
'satiation*, Olr. saith, 'satiety', saithech, 'satiated*,
Gk. άΕδτ;ν (for *saden), of s.m., όέεται (for
*saetai), 'satiates himself, #ατος (for *n-se-
tos), 'insatiable', OI. ά-sin-van, 'insatiable',
Toch. B. soy-, AB sl·, 'to be satiated*. Cp. as-
sal, assets, badro-, sate, satiate, satis, satisfy,
saturate, soil, 'to feed', and the first element in
Adephaga.
Derivatives: sadd-en, tr. and intr. v., sadd-en-
ing, adj., sadd-en-ing-lyt adv., sadd-ish, adj.,
sad-ly, adv., sad-ness, n.

## saddik
saddik, n. — See tzaddik.

## saddle
saddle, n. — ME. sadel, fr. OE. sadol, rel. to ON.
sodull, Dan., Swed., OFris., MDu. sadel, Du.
zadel, OHG. satal, satul, MHG. satel, G. Sattel,
'saddle', OS. *sadul (whence saduleri, 'saddler').
These words orig. meant 'a place to sit upon',
and derive fr. I.-E. base *sed-, 'to sit', whence
also L. sedere. Cp. L. sella (for *sed-la), 'seat,
chair', OSlav. sedlo, 'saddle', and see sedentary.
Cp. also sell, 'seat, throne'.

## saddie
saddie, tr. v. — ME. sadelen, sadlen, fr. OE. sade-
lian, fr. sadol. See saddle, n.
Derivatives: saddl-er, п., saddl-ery, n.

## Sadducean
Sadducean, adj., pertaining to the Sadducees. —
Formed fr. Late L. Sadducaei (see next word)
with suff. -an.

## Sadducee
Sadducee, п., a member of a Jewish sect during
the two centuries preceding and the century
following the beginning of the Common Era
(Jewish history). — Late L. Sadducaei (pi.), fr.
Gk. Σαδδουκαϊοι, fr. Heb. tzedhoqtm, pi. of
tz&doqt, lit, 'a disciple of Tzddhoq(= Zadok), the
highpriest (see 1 Kings 1:34, 2:35, I Chron.
29:22, II Chron. 31:10, Ezek. 40:46, 44:15,
48:11). The spelling with dd is due to the
circumstance that the LXL transliterates Tzddoq
inexactly by Σαδδούκ.

## sad he
sad he, п., name of the 19th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — See tzadbe.

## sadhu
sadhu, п., a Hindu holy man. — OI. sadhuh,
'straight, right, skilled, excellent; a holy man',
rel. to sddhati, 'reaches his goal*, sldhyati,
'reaches his goal, succeeds', sddhita- (pp.),
'perfect', fr. I.-E. base *saidh-, *sadh-, *sidh-,
'straight, right; to go ahead, reach one's goal',
whence alsoGk-ίθύ;, 'going straight, straight,
direct', ΐ&ΰς, 'impulse, purpose', ι&ύνει,ν, 'to
make straight, guide in a straight line, guide',
and perh. also Arm. a] (for *sadhyo-l), 'right*.
Cp. Siddha. Cp. also soucar.

## sadism
sadism, п., a form of sexual perversion in which
one finds pleasure in hurting one's partner; the
opposite of masochism. — F. sadisme, coined fr.
the name of Marquis de Sade (1740-1814), who
first described this perversion in his novels. For
the ending see suff. -ism.

## snfari
snfari, п., a hunting expedition. — Arab, safari,
'referring to a journey', fr. safar, 'journey,
traveling*, fr. safara, 'he started, traveled, went on
a journey'.

## safe
safe, adj. — ME. sauf, saf, fr. OF. sal/, sauf
(F. sauf), fr. L. salvus, 'saved, preserved, safe,
well, sound', which is rel. to salus, 'sound
condition, welfare, well-being, health, safety', salu-
bris, 'health-giving, healthful', solidus, soldus>
'firm, compact1. OL. sollus, 'whole, entire', and
cognate with OI. sdrvah, 'uninjured, intact,
whole, entire', Avestic Jiaurva-, 'uninjured,
intact', Toch. A salu, B. solme, 'whole, entire',
Arm. oij, 'healthful, entire', Gk. δλος (for
*6λ^ος), 'whole', Alb. gate, 'strong, fat,
vigorous'. Cp. sage, name of a plant, salutary,
salutation, salute, salvage, salvation, salve, 'hail',
Salvia, salvo, save, silly, soldo, solemn, solicit,
solid, solidus, son. Cp. also nolo- and the second
element in catholic.
Derivatives: safe, п., safe-ly, adv., safe-ness, n.

## snfe-conduct
snfe-conduct, n. — Anglicized fr. F. sauf-conduit,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:677 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. L. salvus conductus. See safe and conduct.
Derivative: safe-conduct, tr. v.

## safeguard
safeguard, n. — Late ME. saufgarde, fr. MF. (=
F.) sauvegarde, 'safekeeping, safeguard', fr. OF.
salve sauve (F. sauve), fem. otsalf, sauf(F. sauf),
'safe* and garde, 'a keeping'. See safe and guard
and cp. sagger.
Derivatives: safeguard, tr. v., safeguard-er, n.

## safety
safety, n. — ME. sauvete, saufte, fr. MF. (= F.)
sauvete, fr. OF. salvete, sauvete, fr. ML. salvita-
tem, ace. of salvitas, 'safety', fr. L. salvus. See
safe and -ty.

## saffian
saffian, п., a kind of leather made of goatskins or
sheepskins. — Russ. safyan, fr. Turk, sakhtiyan,
fr. Pers. sakhtiydn, 'goat's leather',

## saffiower
saffiower, n. — Either fr. Du. sajfioer, or directly
from OF. saflor, fr. earlier It. saffxore, which is
prob. a hybrid compounded of Arab. safrd\
fem. oiasfar, 'yellow', and It. fiore, 'flower'. See
flower.

## saffron
saffron, п., a species of crocus. — ME. saffran,
fr. OF. (= F.) safran, fr. ML. safranum, fr.
Arab, za^faran, whence also It. zafferano, Sp.
azafran.
Derivatives: saffron, tr. v., to color with saffron,
saffron-y, adj.

## safranine
safranine, п., a synthetic orange-red dyestuff
(chem.) — F., formed with chem. suff. -ine fr.
safran', 'saffron'. See prec. word.

## safrole
safrole, also safrol, п., a poisonous oil, C10H10Oa
(chem.) — A hybrid coined fr. F. safran (see
saffron) and -ol, a suff. derived fr. L. oleum, 'oil',

## sag
sag, intr. v. — Late ME. saggen, prob. of Scand.
origin. Cp. Dan. sakke, Swed. sacka, dial.
Norw. sakka, 'to sink, subside', Du. zakken,
of s.m. These verbs are denasalized derivatives
of the Teut. base *sinkwan, 'to sink' (see sink),
and have a frequentative meaning.
Derivatives: sag, п., sagg-ing, n.

## saga
saga, n. — ΟΝ., 'a saying, story', rel. to OE.
sagu, 'a saying', OFris. sege, OHG. saga,
MHG., G. sage, 'saying, report, tale*, and to
OE. secgan, OHG. sagen, 'to say'. See say, v.,
and cp. saw, 'a saying', which is a doublet of
saga.

## sagacious
sagacious, adj., I) keen in perception; 2) shrewd.
— L. sagax, gen. sagacis, 'of keen perception,
sagacious', fr. sagfre, 'to perceive quickly or
keenly', fr. I.-E. base *sag-, *seg-, 'to track
down, trace, seek', whence also ON. scekja, OE.
secan, 'to seek'. See seek and words there
referred to and cp. esp. presage. For the ending see
suff. -acious. For the formation of L. sagax fr.
sagire cp. saldx, 'lustful*, fr. saltre, 'to leap' (see
salacious).
Derivatives: sagacious-ly, &dv.,sagacious-ness, n.

## sagacity
sagacity, п., keen perception. — MF. (— F.),
sagacite, fr. L. sagdeitdtem, ace. of sagacitas,
'keenness of perception', fr. sagax, gen. sagacis.
See prec. word and -ity.

## sagamore
sagamore, п., chief of a tribe. — Of Algonquian
origin. Cp. sachem.

## sage
sage, adj., wise. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) sage, fr.
VL. *sapius (to be inferred fr. L. nesapius,
'unwise, foolish', occurring in Petronius 50, 5), fr.
sapere, 'to have taste; to be wise'. See sapient
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: sage, п., sage-ly, adj., sage-ness, n.

## snge
snge, п., a plant (Salvia officinalis). — ME. sauge,
sage, fr. MF. (= F.) sauge, fr. L. salvia, fr.
salvus, 'safe, whole*. Salvia lit. means 'the
saving plant'. See safe and cp. Salvia.

## sagger
sagger, saggar, п., 1) a protective box of fire clay
in which finer ceramic articles are enclosed
while baking; 2) the clay of which it is made. —
Prob. a contraction of safegnard.
Derivative: sagger, saggar, tr. v., to bake in a
sagger.

## Sagina
Sagina, п., a genus of plants, the pearl wort (bot.)
— ModL., fr. L. sagina, 'fat, nutrition', which is
of uncertain origin.

## Sagitta
Sagitta, п., a small northern constellation (as-
tron.) — L., 'arrow', prob. a Mediterranean
loan word. Cp. settee, *a kind of Mediterranean
vessel'.

## sagittal
sagittal, adj., arrow-shaped. — ModL. sagittdlis,
fr. L. sagitta. See prec. word and adj. suff. -aL

## Sagittaria
Sagittaria, п., a genus of plants, the arrowhead

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:678 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 651 | SALIFY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:678 COLUMN:1 -->
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. Sagittarius, 'pertaining
to an arrow', fr. sagitta (see Sagitta and adj.
surf, -ary); so called in allusion to the shape of
the leaves.

## Sngittarius
Sngittarius, п., a southern constellation; the
ninth sign of the zodiac; 'the Archer' (astron.)
— L. Sagittarius, 'archer', prop, the adj.
Sagittarius, 'pertaining to arrows', used as a noun.
See prec. word.

## sago
sago, п., starch prepared from the pith of certain
palms. — Fr. Malay saga, prob. through the
medium of Dutch. Cp. It. sagu, Sp. saga, Port.
sagu, F. sagou.

## sagum
sagum, п., mantle worn by the ancient Roman
soldiers. — L., a word of Gaulish origin; prob.
rel. to Lith. sagts, 'travelling dress of Lithuanian
women', Lett, sagsa, 'cover for women', segene,
'a large cloth', segt, 'to cover', OPruss. saxtis,
'rind, husk'. Late Gk. σάγος, 'cloth for pack-
saddles', is a Latin loan word. Cp. say, 'a cloth
resembling serge'.

## Sahara
Sahara, п., the great desert of North Africa. —
Fr. Arab, sahra', 'desert', prop. fem. of the adj.
dsharu, 'yellowish red', used as a noun; rel. to
Heb. tzdhor, 'white'.
Derivatives: Sahar-an, Sahar-ian, Sahar-ic, adjs.

## sahib
sahib, п., a title used in India. — Hind, sahib, fr.
Arab, sahib, 'companion, lord, master', fem.
sahibj1, prop. part, oisahiba, 'he accompanied'.

## said
said, pret. and pp. of say. — ME. seid, fr. OE.
saegde, sxde, resp. OE. gesxgd, gesxd. See say, v.

## said
said, adj., before-mentioned. — Prop. pp. of say.
See prec. word.

## snid
snid, n. — A var. of sayyid.

## saiga
saiga, п., an antelope (Saiga tatarica). — Russ.,
of Tatar origin.

## sail
sail, n. — ME. seyl, seil, fr. OE. segel, segl, rel. to
OS., Swed, segel, ON. segl, Dan., OFris., MDu.
seil, Du. zeil, OHG. segal, MHG. segel, sigel,
G. Segel. These words orig. meant 'a piece of
cloth cut off', and derive from the I.-E. base
*seq-, 'to cut'. See section and cp. words there
referred to. Ir. seoland W. hwyl, 'sail', are Teut.
loan words.

## sail
sail, intr. and tr. v. — ME. seilen, sailen, fr. OE.
segelian, seglian, 'to sail', fr. segel, segl, 'sail',
Cp. ON. sigla, MLG., MHG. segelen, G. segeln,
'to sail', and see sail, n.
Derivatives: sail-ed, adj., sail-er, п., a sailing
vessel, sail-ing, adj. and п., sail-or, п., sail-or-
like, adj., sail-or-ly, adv.

## sain
sain, tr. v., 1) to make the sign oflhe cross on or
over; 2) to bless. — ME. seinen, sainen, fr. OE.
segnan, fr. L. signdre, 'to sign, mark', fr. signum,
'sign'. Cp. ON. signa, OS. segnon, OHG. sega-
пбп, MHG. segenen, 'to make the sign of the
cross, to bless', Du. zegenen, G. segnen, 'to
bless', and see sign, n. and v.

## sainfoin
sainfoin, п., a leguminous plant used for fodder.
— F., fr. MF., which is compounded of sain,
'wholesome, healthy' (see sane), and foin, 'hay*,
fr. L. finum, lit. 'produce, yield', fr. base *f£-,
'to produce, yield' (see fenugreek). The first
element was often confused with saint, 'holy*. Cp.
the former collateral spelling saint-foin,
whence G. Heiligheu, 'sainfoin', lit. 'holy hay'.

## saint
saint, n. — ME., fr. OF. saint, seint (F. saint), fr.
L. sanctus, 'holy, sacred', prop. pp. of sanclre,
'to appoint as sacred'. See sncred and cp. sanctus.
Derivatives: saint, tr. v. and adj., saint-ed, adj.,
saint-dom, п., saint-hood, п., saint-isk, adj.,
saint-like, adj., saint-ly, adj., saint-li-ness, п.,
saint-ship, n.

## Saint Bernard
Saint Bernard, a breed of mastiff dogs, n. — So
called because it was used by the monks of the
Hospice to rescue travellers at the Great
Si. Bernard Pass in Switzerland.

## Saint Elmo's fire
Saint Elmo's fire, an electric light sometimes
seen in stormy weather; called also corposant.
Named after Si. Elmo, the patron saint of
sailors.

## St. Emilion
St. Emilion, п., a kind of red wine. — Named
after St. Emilion, near Libourne in France.

## sake
sake, п., purpose. — ME. sake, 'strife, lawsuit',
fr. OE. sacu, 'quarrel, strife, jurisdiction in
lawsuits', rel. to ON. sok, 'charge, lawsuit,
effect, cause', Swed. sak, Dan. sag, 'thing,
matter, affair, cause', OFris. seke, 'strife,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:678 COLUMN:2 -->
dispute, thing, matter', MDu. sake, 'lawsuit,
matter', Du. zaak, 'thing, matter, affair, cause*,
OHG. sahha, 'strife, lawsuit', MHG-, G. sache,
'thing, matter, affair, cause', Goth, sakjo,
'strife, quarrel', QE. sacan, ON. saka, 'to
quarrel, accuse', Goth, sakan, 'to quarrel', fr. I.-E.
base *sag-, *s g-, 'to track down, trace, seek',
whence also OE. secan, Goth, sdkjan, 'to seek'.
See seek and cp. sac, 'cause of dispute', soc,
socage, soke, soken. Cp. also forsake,

## sake
sake, п., national alcoholic drink of the Japanese.
— Jap.

## saker
saker, п., a large falcon used in hawking (Falco
sacer). — ME. sagre, fr. MF. (= F.) sacre, fr.
Arab, saqr, whence also Sp. and Port, sacre. It.
sagro.

## sakeret
sakeret, п., the male of the saker. — Formed
from prec. word with the dimin. suff. -et.

## sakia
sakia, sakieh, п., a water wheel used in the Orient.
— Subst. use of Arab. saqiyab, fem. of saqi,
part, of saqd, 'he gave to drink; he watered,
irrigated', which is rel. to Ethiop. saqa, Heb.
hishqa , Aram.-Syr. ashqi, 'he gave to drink',
watered, irrigated', Akkad. shaqu, 'to give to
drink'. Cp. Rabshakeh.

## Sakrn
Sakrn, п., a name of Indra (Hindu mythol.) — OI.
iakrah, 'mighty', rel. to sdkah, 'strength, help',
saka-, 'strong, helpful', saknoti, 'is able, helps',
Avestic sacaiti, 'understands, knows well'.

## sal
sal, п., the chemical name for salt, — L. sal, gen.
sdlis, 'salt'. See salt.

## sal
sal, also saul, п., an Eastern timber tree. — Hind.
sal, fr. OI. sdlah.

## salaam
salaam, salam, п., —Arab, salam, 'peace;
saluting, salutation', from the base of salima, 'he
was safe', whence also silm, salam, 'safety,
security, peace', salima, 'he was safe'; rel. to Ethiop.
salam, 'peace, welfare*, Heb. shalam, 'he was in-*
tact, was at peace, was in good health', shalam,
'completeness, welfare, peace'. See Shalom and
cp. Islam, Moslem, Musulman, selamlik.
Derivative: salaam, salam, intr. and tr. v.

## salable
salable, adj. — Formed fr. sale with suff. -able.
Derivatives: salabil-ity, п., salable-ness, п.,
salabl-y, adv.

## salacious
salacious, adj., lustful. — L. saldx, gen. -dcis,
'lustful', lit. 'fond of leaping", fr. satire, 'to
leap'. See salient and -acious. For the formation
of L. salax, from satire cp. sagdx, Of quick
perception', fr. sagire, 'to perceive keenly' (see
sagacious).
Derivatives: salacious-ly, adv., salacious-ness, n.

## salacity
salacity, п., lustfulness. — L. saldcitds, fr. salax,
gen. -acis. See prec. word and -ity.

## salad
salad, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) salade, fr.
OProvenc. salada, lit. 'salad (dish)', fem. pp.
used as a noun, fr. salar, .'to salt', fr. sal, 'salt'.
See salt and cp. words there referred to.

## salade
salade, п., helmet. — A var. of sallet.

## salam
salam, n. — See salaam.

## salamander
salamander, n. — ME. salamandre, fr. MF. (= F.)
salamandre, fr. L. salamandra, fr. Gk.
σαλαμάνδρα, which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: salamandr-ian, salamandr-ine, adjs.

## salamandroid
salamandroid, adj., resembling salamanders. —
Compounded of Gk. σαλαμάνδρα and -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See prec. word
and -oid.

## salami
salami, also salame, п., a highly seasoned, orig.
Italian, sausage, — It. salami, fr. L. sal, gen.
sdlis, 'salt'. See salt, n.

## sal ammoniac
sal ammoniac, ammonium chloride. — See 1st
sal and ammoninc and cp. salmiac.

## salariat
salariat, п., the class of those who receive
salaries.—Formed fr.salary on an&\ogyoiproletariat.

## salaried
salaried, adj. — Prop. pp. of the verb salary (q.v.)

## salary
salary, n. — ME. salarie, fr. L. saldrium, lit. 'salt-
money', i.e. 'money paid to soldiers for their
allowance of salt'. Saldrium is prop, the neut. of
the adjective saldrius, 'pertaining to salt', fr.
sal, gen. sails, 'salt'. See salt and subst. suff.
-ary and cp. salad, sausage.

## salary
salary, tr. v. — Fr. prec. word. Cp. F. salarier.

## salat
salat, п., the ritual prayer of the Mohammedans.
— Arab. salab, 'prayer', fr. Aram. tzelotha,
emphatic form of tze!o, 'prayer', fr. tzela', 'he
bowed' (whence Pa'el tzalle), 'he prayed', orig.
'he bowed in prayer', and rel. to Ethiop. saldwa,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:678 COLUMN:3 -->
'he bowed', salaya, 'he prayed', Akkad. sullu,
'to entreat', rel. also to Arab, sdlan, 'middle of
the back'. Cp. S. Fraenkel, De Vocabulis in an-
tiquis Arabum carminibus et in Corano pere-
grinis, Leiden, 1880, p. 21, Wensinck,
Encyclopaedia of Islam, art. Salat.

## sale
sale, n. — ME., fr. OE. sala, fr. ON. sala, which
is rel. to OHG. sala, Swed. salu, Dan. salg. See
sell, v., and cp. the second element in handsel.

## salep
salep, п., the dried tubers of various kinds of
orchid, used as food. — F., fr. Sp., fr. Arab.
sahlab, in vulgar pronunciation sahleb,
corrupted fr. thd'lab in busd ath-tha'lab, 'the fox's
testicles', the Arabic name of the tubers of the
Orchis mascula. Cp. saloop. For sense
development cp. Orchis.

## saleratus
saleratus, п., bicarbonate of soda. — Fr. L. sal
aerdtus, 'aerated salt'. See salt and nerate.

## salesclerk
salesclerk, n. — Compounded of the Saxon
genitive of sale and clerk.

## salesgirl
salesgirl, n. — Compounded of the Saxon
genitive of sale and girl.

## saleslady
saleslady, n. — Compounded of the Saxon
genitive of sale and lady.

## salesman
salesman, n. — Compounded of the Saxon
genitive of sale and man.
Derivative: salesman-skip, n.

## saleswoman
saleswoman, n. — Compounded of the Saxon
genitive of sale and woman.

## Salian
Salian, adj., pertaining to the Salii, priests
dedicated to the service of Mars. — The literal mean-
of L. Salii is 'dancers', from satire, 'to leap,
dance'. See salient.
Derivative: Salian, п., a Salian priest.

## Salian
Salian, adj., pertaining to the tribe of Franks who
lived near the Zuyder Zee; п., a Salian Frank.
— Formed fr. Late L. Salii, 'Salian Franks', lit.
'those living near the river Sala' (now called
Ijssel). For the ending see suff. -an.

## Salic
Salic, adj., pertaining to the Salian Franks, used
esp. in the term Salic law. — MF. (= F.) sa-
lique, fr. ML. Salicus, fr. Late L. Salii. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ic.

## salic
salic, adj., pertaining to one of two groups of
minerals (petrogr.) — Coined by the Austrian
geologist Eduard Suess (1831-1914) fr. silica,
a/iunina and adj. suff. -1c.

## Salicaceae
Salicaceae, n. pi., the willow family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. L. salix, gen. salicis, 'willow'
(see Salix), with suff. -aceae.

## salicaceous
salicaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## salicin
salicin, п., a bitter crystalline substance, С1гН1807
(chem.) — F. salicine, coined fr. L. salix, gen.
salicis, 'willow', and chem. suff. -ine (see Snlix
and -in); so called because it is obtained from
willow bark.

## Salicornia
Salicornia, п., a genus of plants, the glasswort or
samphire (bot.) — ModL., prob. of Arabic
origin. Cp. F. salicor, salicome, 'saltwort'.

## salicyl
salicyl, п., the radical of salicylic acid (chem.) —
See salicin and -yl.
Derivatives: salicylate (q.v.), salicyl-ic, adj.,
salicyl-ism, n.

## salicylate
salicylate, п., salt of salicylic acid. — Formed fr.
salicyl with subst. suff. -ate.

## salience
salience, saliency, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## salient
salient, adj., 1) projecting; 2) conspicuous. — L.
saliens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of satire, 'to leap,
spring', which is cogn. with Gk. άλλεσ*αι, of
s.m., άλμα, 'a leap, spring', Toch. A sal-, 'to
jump', Mir. saltraim, Ί trample', and prob.
also with OI. ucckalati (for *ud-salati), 'rises
quickly'. Cp. Altica, assault, consilient,
desultory, dissilient, exile, exult, halma, insult,
resilient, result, salacious, Salian, 'pertaining to the
Salii', sally, saltant, saltareilo, saltation, salti-
grade, salrunbanco, saltire, saltus, saute,
somersault, subsultory, transilient, tressllate. For the
ending see suff. -ent.
Derivatives: salient, п., sallent-ly, adv.

## saliferous
saliferous, adj., salt-bearing. — Compounded of
L. sal, gen. sdlis, 'salt' and L. ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See salt and -ferous.

## salification
salification, n. — See salify and -ation.

## salify
salify, tr. v., to make salty. — F. salifier, formed
ft. L. sdl, gen. sdlis, 'salt' (see salt), and suff.
-fier (see -fy).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:679 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SALINA | 6S2 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:679 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: salifi-able, adj.

## salina
salina, п., pool, pond, — Sp., fr. L. sdlinae,
'saltworks*. — See next word.

## saline
saline, adj., salty, — F., fr. L. "salinus, fr. sal,
gen. satis, 'salt'. See salt and -ine (representing
L. -inus) and cp. L. salinum, 'saltcellar', salinae,
'saltworks'. Cp. also salina.
Derivative: saline, n.

## salinity
salinity, п., saltness. — Formed fr. saline with
suff. -Ity.

## salbiometer
salbiometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
degree of the salinity of a solution. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. *salinus, 'salty', and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See saline and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.
sail^e, п., a variety of pyroxene {mineral.) —
Named after Sola, a town in Sweden. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## saliva
saliva, n. the fluid secreted in the mouth. — L.
saliva, 'spittle', of uncertainorigin; possibly rel.
to salix, .'willow', prop, 'the tree with grayish
leaves', and cogn. with Gael, sal, 'moist filth,
earwax'. See sallow, n. and adj.

## salivary
salivary, adj., pertaining to saliva. — L. salivdrius,
