fr. saliva. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ary.

## salivate
salivate, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. L. salivdtus,
pp. of salivare, 'to spit, salivate', fr. saliva. See
saliva and verbal suff. -ate.

## salivation
salivation, n. — F., fr. L. salivdtionem, ace. of
salivatio, fr. salivdtus, pp. of salivare. See salivn
and -ation.

## Salix
Salix, п., a genus of trees and shrubs, the willow
(hot.) — L. salix, 'willow'. See saliow, n.

## salleeman
salleeman, п., also sallyman, 1) a Morocco pirate;
2) a velella (zoo/.) — Lit. Sallee man, i.e. *a man
from Sallee', a town in Morocco, formerly the
home of pirates.

## salie
salie, п., a large room. — F., fr. Frankish *sal,
which is rel. to OHG. sal (see salon); influenced
in form by F. halle, 'hall'.

## sallenders
sallenders, n. pi., an eruption on the hock of a
horse. — F. solandre, of unknown origin.

## sallet
sallet, п., a kind of helmet. — ME., fr. MF.
sallade (F. salade), fr. It. celata, fr. L. caelata
(scil. cassis), 'an engraved helmet', fern. pp. of
caeldre, 'to carve, engrave', fr. caelum, 'chisel',
for *caed-lom, fr. caedere, 'to cut'. See cement.

## saliow
saliow, adj., yellowish. — ME. salow, fr. OE.
salu, salo, 'dark-colored', rel. to OE. sol, 'dark,
dirty', OHG. salo, 'dirty gray', ON. solr, 'dirty
yellow', MHG. sal (gen. salwes), 'dirt', OE.
sealh, etc., 'sallow' (п.), and cogn. with L. salix,
'willow' (see sallow, п.), Gael, sal, 'moist filth,
earwax', W. halawg, 'stained', OSlav. slavojo&je,
'grayish blue color', Russ. solovoj, 'isabelline,
cream-colored'. Cp. sailow, 'willow', saliva,
Salix.
Derivatives: sallow-isk, adj., sallow-ly, adv.,
sallow-ness, n.

## sallow
sallow, п., a species of willow. — ME. salewe,
salwe, fr. OE. sealh, rel. to ON. selja, Frankish
salha, OHG. salaha, sal ha, MHG. salhe, OHG.
salewida, MHG. salewide, G. Salweide (lit.
'sallow-withy'), Dan. selje, Norw. selja, Swed.
salg. Cognates outside Teut. are L. salix,
'willow', Mir. sail (gen. sallech), W. helygen, Bret.
kalegen, 'willow'. (F. saule, 'willow', is a
Frankish loan word.) AH these words prop, denote
'the tree with grayish leaves'. See sallow, adj.
Derivative: sallow-y, adj.

## sally
sally, n. — MF. (= F.) saillie, prop, fern of sailli,
pp. of saillir, 'to gush out, spout out', earlier 'to
leap, dance', fr. L. satire, 'to leap'. See salient
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: sally, intr. v.

## Saliy Limn
Saliy Limn, a kind of light teacake. — Probably
from the name of a girl who sold the cakes at
Bath about the beginning of the 19th cent.

## salmagundi
salmagundi, п., hotchpotch. — F. salmigondis, fr.
salmigondin, a word coined by the French
satirist Francois Rabelais (1490 7-1553).

## salmi
salmi, п., ragout of roasted game. — F. salmis,
salmi, shortened fr. salmigondis. See prec. word.

## salmiac
salmiac, n. (chem.) — Short for sal ammoniac.

## salmon
salmon, n. — ME. saumoun, fr. MF. saumon,
samon (F. saumon), fr. L. salmonem, ace. of
salmd, which is of uncertain origin. The
explanation of salmd as 'the leaping fish', fr. satire,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:679 COLUMN:2 -->
'to leap, jump', is folk etymology. Cp. samlet.

## Salmonella
Salmonella, п., a genus of bacteria. — ModL.,
named after the American veterinarian Daniel
Elmer Salmon (1850-1914). For the ending see
suff. -ella.

## salmonsite
salmonsite, п., a hydrous manganese iron
phosphate (mineral.) — Named after the American
mineralogist Frank A. Salmons. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## Salome
Salome, fern. PN. — Late L., fr. Gk. Σαλώμη,
which is rel. to Σαλωμών, 'Solomon'. See
Solomon.

## salon
salon, n. — F., 'reception room', fr. It. salone,
augment, of sola, 'hall', which is of Teut. origin;
cp. OHG-, MHG. sal, G. Saal, Du. zaal, OS.
seli, ON. salr, OE. sele, sxl, salor, 'hair, Goth.
salja, 'to stay at an inn', salipwos (pi.), 'inn',
OHG. selida, MHG. selde, OS. selitha, OE.
sxlp, 'dwelling'. These Teut. words are cogn.
with OSlav. selo, 'courtyard, village', selitva,
'dwelling', Lith. sola, 'village'. Cp. salle,
saloon and the second element in kursalon.

## saloon
saloon, n. — F. salon. See prec. word. For the
ending see suff. -oon.

## saloop
saloop, п., a hot drink made from powdered
salep. — A var. of salep.

## Salopian
Salopian, adj., pertaining to Shropshire. —
Formed with suff. -ian fr. Salop, which is shortened
fr. Slopesberrie, AF. corruption of OE. Scrob-
besbyrig, 'Shrewsbury'.
Derivative: Salopian, n.

## Salpa
Salpa, п., a genus of tunicates (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. L. salpa, 'a kind of stockfish', fr. Gk. σάλπη,
which is of uncertain origin.

## Salpiglossis
Salpiglossis, п., a genus of plants of the potato
family (йог.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
σάλπιγξ, 'trumpet', and γλώσσα, 'tongue'.
See salpingo- and gloss, 'explanation'.

## salpingo-
salpingo-, before a vowel salping-, combining
form meaning 'trumpet'. — Gk. σαλπιγγο-,
σαλπιγγ-, fr. σάλπιγξ, gen. σάλταγγος,
'trumpet', prob. a Mediterranean word. For the siuT.
-ιγξ ср. φόρμιγξ, 'lyre', σϋριγξ, 'pipe' (see
syrinx).

## salse
salse, п., a mud volcano. — F. salse, fr. It. salsa,
fr. L. salsa, fem. of salsus, 'salted' (see sauce, n.);
so called because it ejects salted water.

## salsify
salsify, п., a biennial plant. — F. salsifis, fr. It.
sassefrica, fr. earlier sassifrica, fr. Olt. salsifica,
a word of uncertain origin.

## Salsola
Salsola, п., a genus of plants, the saltwort (бог.)
— ModL., fr. It. salsola, dimin. of salso, 'salty',
fr. L. salsus (see salse); so called in allusion to
the saline habitat of most species.

## salsolaceous
salsolaceous, adj. — Formed fr. prec. word with
sufT. -aceous.

## salt
salt, n. — ME., fr. OE. sealt, rel. to OS., ΟΝ.,
Dan., Swed., OFris., Goth, salt, MDu. sout, D.
гоиг, OHG., MHG., G. salz, fr. I.-E. base
*sal-d-, which appears also in L. sallere (for
'saldere), 'to salt', Olr. saillim (for *sa!dim), Ί
salt', and in Lith. saldiis, OSlav. sladuku,
'sweet' (with the following stages of sense
development: 1) salted; 2) spicy, savory; 3) sweet).
Base *sal-d- is a -[/-enlargement of base *sal-
seen in Toch. B. sdlyi, A sale, Arm. ai,Ck. όίλς,
gen. αλός (masc), 'salt', (fem.) 'sea', L. sal, gen.
salis, 'salt; sea', OSlav. soli, 'salt', slanu (for
*so!nu), 'salted', Lett, sals, OPruss. sal, Olr.
salann, earlier W. halwyn, W. halen, OCo. ha-
loin, 'salt'. Cp. halieutic and words there
referred to. Cp. also sal, salad, salami, salary, salera-
tus, saliferous, salify, saline, saise, saltcellar,
sauce, sancer, saucisse, sancisson, sausage, silt,
sonse, 'salt pickle'.
Derivatives: salt, v. (q.v.), salt, adj., saltern
(<j.v.), salt-ing, п., salt-ish, adj., salt-less, п.,
salt-y, adj., salt-i-ness, п., salt-ness, п., saltpeter
(q-v.)

## salt
salt, tr. v. — ME. salten, fr. OE. sealtan, fr.
sealt, 'salt'; rel. to ON. salta, Goth, saltan,
OHG. salzan, MliG., G. salzen. See salt, n.
Derivatives: salt-ed, adj., salt-er, п., salt-ery, п.,
salt-ing, adj. and n.

## saltant
saltant, adj., leaping (said of animals, in
heraldry). — L. saltans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of
saltdre, 'to leap, jump, dance', freq. οι satire, 'to
leap*. See sailent and -ant and cp. sally, snute.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:679 COLUMN:3 -->

## saltareilo
saltareilo, п., a lively Italian dance. — It., fr.
saltare, 'to leap, jump', fr. L. saltdre. See prec.
word and cp. saltimbanco.

## saltation
saltation, n. — L. saltdtio, 'a leaping, jumping',
fr. saltdtus, pp. of saltdre. See saltant and -ation.

## saltatorial
saltatorial, adj., saltatory. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. saltdtorius. See next word.

## saltatory
saltatory, adj., 1) pertaining to dancing; 2)
proceeding by abrupt movements. — L. saltdtorius,
'pertaining to leaping or dancing', fr. salt-(um),
pp. stem of saltdre, 'to leap, jump, dance'. See
saltant and -ntory and cp. saltire.

## saltcellar
saltcellar, n. — ME. salte-seler, fr. salte, 'salt',
and seler, saler, 'saltcellar'. For the first element
see salt, n. The second derives fr. OF. salier,
'salt box', fr. L. solarium, fr. sdl, gen. salis, 'salt',
and cp. salary. Accordingly the word saltcellar
is tautological since it contains the word for salt
twice.

## Salter
Salter, п., a manufacturer of, or dealer in, salt. —
ME., fr. OE. sealtere, formed fr. OE. sealt, 'salt',
with suff. -ere. See salt and agential suff. -er.

## saltern
saltern, п., a saltworks. — OE. sealtxrn, fr. sealt,
'salt', and xrn, 'place, chamber, house'. For the
first element see salt. For the second element see
bam and cp. rest, 'repose', the first element in
ransack, and the second element in bam.

## saltier
saltier, n. — A var. of saltire.

## saMgrnde
saMgrnde, adj., having feet for leaping. —
Formed fr. L. salt us. pp. of satire, 'to leap', and the
stem of gradi, 'to walk'. See salient and grade.

## saltimbanco
saltimbanco, п., a mountebank. — It., lit. 'one
who leaps upon a bench', formed from the
phrase salta in banco], 'leap upon a bench!' See
saltareilo, in, and banc, banco. For sense
development cp. mountebank.

## saltire
saltire, snltter,n., an ordinary on'a shield
consisting of a bend dexter and a bend sinister
crossing each other (her.) — ME. sawtire, fr. MF.
saultoir, sautoir (F. sautoir), 'stirrup', fr. ML.
saltdtorium, 'stirrup', prop. neut. of L.
saltdtorius, 'pertaining to leaping', used as a noun. See
saltatory.
Derivative: saltire-wise, adv.

## saltpeter
saltpeter, saltpetre, n. — ME. salpetre, fr.· OF.
salpetre (F. salpetre), fr. ML. sdl petrae, lit.
'salt of the rock', fr. L. sal, 'salt' and petra,
'rock, stone'. See salt and petro-.

## saltus
saltus, п., a leap, a break in continuity. — ModL.,
fr. L., 'spring, leap', fr. saltus, pp. of satire, 'to
leap, jump'. See salient.

## salubrious
salubrious, adj., healthful, healthy. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. L. salubris, 'promoting health,
healthful, healthy', fr. salu-, the stem of salus,
'welfare, health'. See salnte, n.
Derivatives: salubrious-ly, adv., salubrious-ness,
n.

## salubrity
salubrity, п., healthfulness, healthiness. — L. salu·
britds, fr. salubris. See prec. word and -ity.

## Saluki
Saluki, п., a hunting dog of Arabia and Persia. —
Arab. Saluqiy, 'from Salaq', name of an ancient
city in southern Arabia.

## salutary
salutary, adj. — Either fr. F. salutaire or directly
fr. L. salutdris, 'healthful', fr. salus, gen. satutis,
'welfare, health'. See salute, v., and adj. suff.
-ary.

## salutntion
salutntion, n. — ME. salutacioun, fr. OF. saluta-
cion (F. salutation), fr. L. salutdtidnem, ace,
of salutdtid, fr. salutdtus, pp. of salutare, 'to
greet'. See snlute, v., and -ation.
Derivative: salutation-al, adj.

## salutatory
salutatory, adj. — L. salutdtorius, fr. salutdtus, fr.
pp. οι salutare, 'to greet'. See salute, v., and adj.
suff. -ory.

## salute
salute, tr. and intr. v. — ME. saluten, fr. L.
salutare, 'to greet', fr. salus, gen. salutis, 'welfare,
health, safety, a wish for somebody's welfare, a
greeting', which is rel. to salvus, 'safe'. See safe
and cp. words there referred to.

## salute
salute, n. — ME. salut, fr. OF. (= F.) salut, fr.
L. saldtem, ace. of salus. See salute, v.

## salvable
salvable, adj. — VL. *salvdbilis, fr. Late L.
solvere, 'to save', fr. salvus, 'safe'. See safe and cp.
salve, 'hail'.
Derivatives: salvabil-ity, п., salvable-ness, п.,
salvabl-y, adv.

## salvage
salvage, n. — F. salvage (now sauvetage), fr. MF.
salvage, fr. salver (F. sauver), 'to save', fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:680 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 653 | SAMSKARA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:680 COLUMN:1 -->
salvdre, 'to save', fr. salvus, 'safe'. See safe and
-age.
Derivatives: salvage, tr. v., salvag-er, n.

## salvarsan
salvarsan, п., a compound of arsenic used as a
remedy against syphilis. — Coined by its
inventor Paul Ehrlich (1854-1915) in 1910 fr. L.
salvdre, 'to save' (fr. salvus, 'safe'), and G. Arsen,
'arsenic'. See safe and arsenic.

## salvatella
salvatella, п., a vein of the back of the hand
(anat.) — ModL., formed fr. L. salvSre, 'to
save', fr. salvus, 'safe', see safe and -ella. The
noun salvatella was formed in imitation of usay·
Urn, the Arabic name of this vein, prop, a dimin.
of salam, 'peace, safety'. The name usdylim was
given to this vein because letting blood from it
was regarded as conducive to health. See
Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum, Leyden,
1653, p. 1207 (quoted by Dr. Joseph Hyrtl, Das
Arabische und Hebraische in der Anatomie,
p. 211).

## salvation
salvation, n. — ME. salvacioun, fr. OF.
salvation, fr. Late L. salvatidnem, ace. of salvdtio,
fr. L. salvatus, pp. of salvdre, 'to save', fr. salvus,
'safe'. See safe and -ation.
Derivatives: salvation-al, adj., salvation-ism, п.,
salvation-ist, n.

## salve
salve, п., ointment for wounds. — ME. sal/, salve,
fr. OE. seal/; rel. to OS. salba, MDu. salve, Du.
zal/, OHG. salba, MHG., G. salbe, 'ointment',
fr. I.-E. base *selp-, 'fat, oil', whence also Gk.
έλπος, 'fat, oil', Alb. gdipe, 'butter', Toch. A
salyp, B. salype, 'fat, oil, butter', OI. sarpsl-,
'melted butter'. Cp. olpe.

## salve
salve, tr. v., to apply a salve to. — ME. salven, fr.
OE. sealfian, 'to anoint', fr. seal/, 'ointment';
rel. to OS. saltan, MDu. salven, Du. zalven,
OHG. salbon, MHG., G. salben, Goth, salbon,
'to anoint'. See salve, n.
Derivative: salv-er, п., one who salves.

## salve
salve, tr. v., to salvage, save. — Back formation
fr. salvage.
salve, interj., hail! — L. salve, 'hail!', the usual
form of Roman greeting, prop. voc. of salvus,
'safe', but regarded as the imper. of solvere, 'to
be well', fr. salvus. See safe and cp. salvo, 'a
volley'.

## salver
salver, п., a tray. — F. salve, fr. Sp. salva, 'the
tasting of food before serving, salver', fr. salvor,
'to save, to taste food (in order to find out
whether it is poisoned)', fr. L. salvare, 'to save',
fr. salvus, 'safe'. See safe and cp. words there
referred to. E. salver (fr. F. salve) was formed on
analogy of the synonyms platter, trencher.

## Salvia
Salvia, п., a genus of plants, the sage (hot.) — L.
salvia, 'sage'. See sage, the plant.

## Salvinia
Salvinia, п., a genus of plants (hot.) — ModL.,
named after Antonio Maria Salvini (1633-1729),
professor of botany in Florence.

## Salvmiaceae
Salvmiaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.) —
ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## salvlniaceous
salvlniaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceons.

## salvo
salvo, п., a saving clause; reservation. — Short
for ML. salvd jure, 'right being reserved'; neut.
abl. of L. salvus, 'safe'. See safe and cp. next
word.

## salvo
salvo, п., discharge of guns. — Earlier salva, it.
It. salva, 'salute, volley', fr. L. salve , 'hail!'. See
salve, 'hail'.

## sal volatile
sal volatile, volatile salt ModL. See sal, 'salt',
and volatile.

## salvor
salvor, п., one who helps to salvage a vessel. —
See salve, 'to salvage', and agential suff. -or.

## Sam
Sam, masc. PN. — Short for Samuel.

## samadh
samadh, п., a tomb built over the grave of a holy
man (India). — Hind, samadk, 'intense
meditation', fr. OI. samSdki-, 'intense meditation',
lit. 'a putting or joining together', which is
formed fr. sdm-, 'together', the particle a-,
'toward', and dhd; stem of dadhsti, 'puts, places'.
OI. sum- is cogn. with Gk. δμα, 'together with',
Goth, soma, 'the same', samana, 'together', OE.
same (in same swa, 'similarly', swd same swa,
'just as'). See same. OI. particle й- is rel. to
Avestic a-, and cogn. with Gk. έ- (e.g. in έ-θέ-
λειν, 'to will'), ή-(e.g. ίηή-βαιός, 'little, small'),
ό- (e.g. in ό-κέλλειν, 'to run a ship aground');
cp. the first element in agama and in ananda.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:680 COLUMN:2 -->
For the etymology of OI. dddhdti see do. Cp.
next word.

## samadhi
samadhi, п., intense esoteric meditation through
the practice of yoga. — OI. samadhi-, 'intense
meditation'. See prec. word,

## samara
samara, п., the dry fruit of certain trees. — L.
samara, samera, 'the seed of the elm', a Gaulish
word lit. meaning 'summer seed', fr. Gaul.
*samos, 'summer*. Cp. Samolus.

## Samaritan
Samaritan, n. and adj. — Late L. Samaritdnus,
'inhabitant of Samaria', fr. Samaria, fr. Gk.
Σαμάρεια, 'Samaria', fr. Aram. Sham rayin,
ult. fr. Heb.· Skomeron, named by its founder
Omri after Shemer, the owner'of the hill, upon
which Samaria was built. See I Kings, 16:24
and cp. Kittel's commentary on that verse. For
the ending see suff. -an.
Derivative: Samaritan-ism, n.

## samarium
samarium, п., a rare metallic element. — ModL.,
coined by its discoverer, the French chemist
Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran (1838-1912)
in 1879 fr. samarskite. For the ending see chem.
suff. -ium.

## samarskite
samarskite, п., (mineral.) — Named after Col.
von Samarski, a Russian mine official. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## samba
samba, п., a Brazilian dance of African origin. —
Port., a word of African origin.
Derivative: samba, intr. v., to dance the samba.

## sambal
sambal, also sambel, п., a curry sauce. — Fr. Jav.
Malay sambal, sambil, through the medium of
Dutch. See. J. F. Bense, Dictionary of the Low-
Dutch Element in the English Vocabulary, p.
341.

## sambo
sambo, п., 1) an Indian and Negro half-breed; 2)
a Negro (slang). — Sp. zambo, 'bow-legged;
mulatto, Negro', prob. fr. L. scambus, 'bow-
legged', fr. Gk. σκαμβός, which is cogn.
with Olr. camm, W. cam, 'crooked'. See Skeat,
Notes on English Etymology, p. 256.

## Sainbocus
Sainbocus, п., a genus of plants, the elder (bot.)
— L. sambucus, 'the elder tree', of uncertain
origin.

## sambuke
sambuke, п., a triangular stringed instrument. —
L. sambuca, fr. Gk σαμβύκη, fr. Aram. sabbs-
kha. See NSIdeke In GOttingische Gelehrte An-
zeigen, 1884, p. 1022.

## same
same, adj., pron. and adv. — ME., fr. ON. samr,
'the same', rel. to OE. same, adv. (in same swa,
'similarly', swd same swa, 'just as'), OS. sama,
samo, OHG. sama, adj. and adv., Goth, sama,
adj., OHG. -samant, MHG. sament, samt,
'together', G. samt, 'together with', Goth.
samana, 'together', OE. samnian, OS. samnon,
ON. samna, OFris. samnia, MLG., MDu.
samenen, OHG. samandn, MLG., MHG. sa-
melen, G. sammeln, Du. zamelen, 'to collect',
lit. 'to bring together', OE. tdsamne, OS. te-

## samne
samne, OFris. tosamene, Du. tezamen, OHG. zi-

## samane
samane, MHG. zesamene, G. zusammen,
'together', fr. I.-E. base *sem-, *sm-, 'one,
together', whence also OI. samdh, 'even, level,

## similar
similar, equal, the same, identical', Avestic

## hama
hama, 'similar, the same', OI. samam, 'together',

## sa-kft
sa-kft, Avestic ha-kerel, 'at once, once', OI. sd-
dam, Avestic ha-δα, 'always', OI. sa-, Avestic

## ha-
ha-, OI. sdm-, Avestic ham, 'with', Toch. A

## soma
soma, B. somo, 'the same, similar', B. se-me, A

## sas
sas, 'one', Gk. δμα, 'together with, at the same

## time with'
time with', δμός, 'one and the same', δμοιος
(Old Att. δμοΐος), 'like, resembling', δμοϋ,
'together', ομαλός, 'even', εις (for *έμ-ς, I.-E.
*sem-s), neut. έν (for *έμ, I.-E. *sem-), fern.
μία (for *σμ-ία, I.-E. *sm-iy\ 'one', L. semel,
'once', similis (assimilated fr. *semi!is), 'like',

## semper
semper, 'always', OSlav. samu, 'himself, OSlav.

## sq
sq, 'with', sa,-sedu, 'neighbor' (lit. 'he who sits,

## i.e. dwells
i.e. dwells, together with somebody'), Lith. sq,

## sa
sa, OPruss. sen, 'with', Olr. som, 'himself,

## samail
samail, 'likeness', samlith, 'at once', W. ha/al,
'like', and the first element in Gk. S-παξ, 'once',
ά-πλόος, ά-πλοϋς, 'simple', ί-τερος, 'the

## other'
other', έ-κατόν, *a hundred*. Cp. acolyte, adelpho-,

## Aglaia
Aglaia, amnion, amoeba, anacoluthon,

## anomalous
anomalous, assemble, assimilate, Atalanta, dissemble,

## dissimilate
dissimilate, dissimulate, ensemble, hamn-, haplo-,

## hecatomb
hecatomb, hendeca-, hendiadys, heno-, henotic,

## hetero-
hetero-, homalo-, homeo-, Homer, homily,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:680 COLUMN:3 -->
homo-, hyphen, resemble, Samoyed, samsara,
samskara, Sanskrit^ seem, semblance, semble,
semper-, Sempervivum, sempiternal, sengreen,
similar, simple, simulncrum, simulnte, simnltane-
ous, single, singular, some and the pref. in
Skupshtina, Sobranje, soviet, sputnik.
Derivatives: same-ly, adj., same-li-ness, п.,
same-ness, n.

## samekh
samekh, sainech, п., name of the 15th letter of the
Hebrew alphabet. — Heb. samekh, 'support,
fulcrum', fr. sdmdkh, 'he leant, supported'; so
called in allusion to the ancient Hebrew form
of this letter.

## Samian
Samian, adj., pertaining to Samos. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. Samius, fr. Gk. Σάμιος, fr.
Σάμος, 'Samos', name of an island in the
Aegean sea, fr. Old @k. σάμος, 'a height'.
Derivative: Samian, п., an inhabitant of Samos.

## samisen
samisen, п., a Japanese three-stringed instrument.
— Jap., fr. Chin, san-hsien, 'three strings',

## samite
samite, п., a heavy silk material. — ME. samit,
fr. OF. (= F.) samit, fr. ML. samitum, exami-
turn, fr. Gk. έξάμιτον, prop. neut. of the adj.
έξάμιτος, 'woven with six threads', which is
compounded of it, 'six', and μίτος, 'thread'.
See nexa- and mitosis and cp. dimity,

## samlet
samlet, п., a young salmon, a parr. — Formed fr.
sam, contraction of salmon, with dimin. suff.
-let

## Sammy
Sammy, п., a soldier of the United States (slang).
— Fr. Sammy, dimin. of Sam, fr. Uncle Sam,
personification of the U.S.

## Samnite
Samnite, п., a member of the ancient people
inhabiting Samnium in Italy. — L. Samnltes (pi.),
'the Samnites', fr. Samnium; which prob. stands
for *Sabniom and is rel. to Sabinus, 'Sabine'.
See.Sabine and subst. suff. -Ite.

## Samoan
Samoan, adj., pertaining to Samoa; п., an
inhabitant of Samoa. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
Samoa, name of a group of islands in Polynesia.
Derivative: Samoan, п., an inhabitant of Samoa.

## Samolus
Samolus, п., a genus of plants, the brookweed
(bot.) — L. samolus, 'brookweed', prop. *a
summer plant', fr. Gaul. *samos, 'summer', whence
also L. samauca, name of a fish. Cp. samara.

## samovar
samovar, п., a Russian tea urn. — Fr. Tatar sana-
bar, 'tea urn', altered by folk etymology into
Russ. samovar, 'self-boiler', fr. samo, 'self, and
varif, 'to boil'.

## Samoyed
Samoyed, Samoyede, n. and adj., name of a
Siberian people. — Russ. Samoyed, lit. 'self-
eaters', used in the sense of cannibals, a name
given them by the Russians (the native name of
the people is Nenets). For the first element in
Samoyed see same. The second element is cogn.
with Gk. έδειν, L. edere, Goth, itan, OE. etart,
'to eat'; see eat.

## sampan
sampan, п., a light Chinese boat. — Fr. Chin, san
pan, 'three boards'.

## samphire
samphire, п., 1) the plant Crithmum maritimum;
2) the glasswort. — Fr. earlier sampere, sampire,
fr. F. (herbe de) Saint Pierre, 'St. Peter's herb'.
The actual French names of the plant are perce-
pierre, passe-pierre, christe-marine.

## sample
sample, n. — ME. sample, aphetic for asaumple,
fr. OF. essample, fr. L. exemplum. See example
and cp. ensample.
Derivatives: sample, tr. and intr. v., sampl-er, п.,
sampl-ing, n.

## sampler
sampler, п., needlework. — ME., fr. OF. essem-

## plaire (F. exemplaire)
plaire (F. exemplaire), fr. exemple. See exemplar
and cp. prec. word.
Sampson. — A var. of Samson.

## samsara
samsara, п., transmigration of souls (Hinduism).
— OI. samsarah, lit. 'a passing through', formed
fr. jam-, 'together', and surah, 'course'. For the
first element see same and cp. words there
referred to. The second element is rel. to sdrati,
'runs, flows', sardb, 'flowing', strd, 'river', and
cogn. with Gk. ορός' (for *σορός), L. serum,
'watery fluid, whey'. See serum and cp. words
there referred to.

## samskara
samskara, п., ceremonial purification (Hinduism).
— OI. samskdrab, 'preparation, sacrament,
consecration', lit. 'a making together', formed
fr. sam-, 'together', and kdra-, 'making,
maker'. For the first element see samsara. The
second element is rel. to krnSti, kariti, 'makes'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:681 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SAMSHU | 654 | -ary. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:681 COLUMN:1 -->
See Sanskrit and cp. words there referred to.

## samshu
samshu, п., an alcoholic liquor made in China
from rice. — Chin, san-skao, lit· 'thrice
distilled', fr. san, 'three', and shao, 'fire'.

## Samson
Samson, Sampson, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible a
judge distinguished for his enormous strength.
— Late L., fr. Gk. Σαμψών, fr. Heb. ShimshSn,
a name derived fr. tkemesh, 'sun'. Cp. Aram.
shimsha, Syr. shemsha, Arab, shams (dissimi-
lated fr. *shamsh), Akkad. shamshu, Ugar.
sk-p-sh, 'sun'.

## samsonite
samsonite, п., a silver manganese sulfantimonite
(mineral.) — Named after the Samson mine in
St. Andreasberg, Harz. For the ending see subst.
surf. -ite.

## samson post
samson post, a strong pillar in a ship. — Named
after Samson, in allusion to the verse: "Samson
took hold of the two middle pillars upon which
the house rested" etc. (Judges 16:29).

## Samuel
Samuel, masc. PN.; a celebrated judge and
prophet (Bible). — Late L., fr. Gk- Σαμουήλ, fr. Heb.
SkemHJel, lit. 'name of God\ fr. shem, 'name*,
and El, 'God'. The first element is rel. to Aram.
shim, sh ma> also skum, Ugar. sh-m, Arab, sim,
sum, ism, Ethiop. sem, Akkad. shumu, 'name'.
For the second element see El.

## samurai
samurai, n. (sing, and pi.), 1) a member of the
military retainers of the daimios (new extinct);
2) gentry; 3) an army officer. — Jap., 'guard*.

## san
san, п., name of the ancient Greek letter *^. —
Fr. Heb. shin, name of the latter sh, for shen,
'tooth1. See sin, shin.

## sanable
sanable, adj., curable (rare). — L. sdndbilis,
'curable', fr. sandre, 'to cure', fr. sdnus. See sane and
able.
Derivatives: sanabil-ity, п., sanable-ness, n.

## sanative
sanative, adj., curative. — ML. sdndtivus,
'tending to cure', fr. L. sunatus, pp. of sandre. See
prec. word and -ative.

## sanatorium
sanatorium, n. — ModL. sanatorium, prop. neut.
of the L. adj. sdndtorius, used as a noun. See
next word.

## sanatory
sanatory, adj., curative, tending to heal. — L.
sanaiorius, fr. sdndtus, pp. of sandre, 'to cure,
make healthy', fr. sdnus. See sane and adj. suff.
-ory.

## sanbenito
sanbenito, п., a penitential garment. — Sp. sam-
benito, fr. San Benito, 'Saint Benedict'; so
called because of its resemblance to the
Benedictine scapular.

## sanctification
sanctification, n. — Late L. sdnctificdtio, gen.
-onis, fr. sdnctificdtus, pp. of sanctificare. See
sanctify and -ation.

## sanctified
sanctified, adj. — Prop. pp. of sanctify. For the
ending see 1st suff. -ed.
Derivative: sanctified-ly, adv.

## sanctify
sanctify, tr. v. — ME. seintifien, fr. OF. sainte-
fier (F. sanctifier), fr. Late L. sanctificare, 'to
make holy', fr. L. sanctus, 'holy*, and -ficdre, fr.
facere, 'to make, do'; see saint and -fy. E.
sanctify was influenced in form by Late L.
sanctificare.

## sanctimony
sanctimony, п., hypocritical devoutness. — MF.
sanctimonie, fr. L. sdnctimonia, 'sacredness,
sanctity, piety*, fr. sanctus, 'holy, sacred'. See
saint. For the ending see suff. -mony and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: sanctimonious-ly, adv., sanctimo-
nious-ness, n.

## sanction
sanction, n. — L. sdnctio, gen. -onis, 'the
decreeing of something as sacred, decree, sanction'
(prob. through the medium of F. sanction),
fr. sanctus, pp. of sancire. See saint and -ion.
Derivatives: sanction, tr. v., sanction-ary, adj.,
sanction-er, n.

## sanctitude
sanctitude, п., saintliness (rate). — ME. sanctitud,
fr. L. sdnctitudO fr. sanctus, 'holy, sacred'. See
saint and -tude.

## sanctity
sanctity, п., sacredness. — ME. sauncite, fr. MF.
saintete, sainctete (F. saintete), fr. L. sanctita-
tem, ace. of sdnctitds, 'holiness, sacredness', fr.
sanctus, 'holy, sacred*. See saint and -ity.

## sanctuary
sanctuary, n. — ME. sanctuarie, fr. MF. sainc-
tuarie, saintuarie (F. sanctuaire), fr. L. sdnctud-
rium, 'a holy place, shrine', fr. sanctus, 'holy,
sacred'. See snint and subst. suff. -ary and cp.
sentry, which is a doublet of sanctuary.

## sanctum
sanctum, п., a private study; a place of retreat. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:681 COLUMN:2 -->
Lit. 'a holy place*, fr. L. sanctum, neut. of
sanctus, 'holy, sacred*. See saint.

## Snnctus
Snnctus, п., the hymn beginning with the word
Sanctus. — L. sanctus, 'holy*, the rendering of
Heb. qadhosh (in Is. 6:3). See saint.

## sand
sand, n. — ME. sond, sand, fr. OE., rel. to OS. sand,
ON. sandr, Dan., Swed. jaW, OFris.jowi/, MDu.
sant, 'sand', Du. zand, OHG., MHG. sant, G.
Sand, and cogn. with Gk. ψάμμος, ψάμαθος,
άμα&ος, 'sand', L. sabulum (for *psafiom),
'sand', Dor. ψα©ος. Att. ψήφος, 'small, stone,
pebble', and prob. also with Gk. ψώ, ψήν, 'to
rub, rub away; to crumble away'. See psilo-
and cp. ammo, psammite, psephism, sabulous,
saburra and the second element in palimpsest.
Derivatives: sand, tr. v., sand-ing, n.

## sandal
sandal, n. — L. sandaiium, fr. Gk. σανδάλι,ον,
dimin. of σάνδαλον, a word from Asia Minor
(whence also Pers. sandal), orig. meaning 'shoe
of the Lydian god SandaV. See Kretschmer,
Indogermanische Forschungen, 45, 270 (1927).

## sandalwood
sandalwood, n. — ML. sandalum (whence also
OF. sandal), fr. Arab, sandal, fr. OI. candanah,
'sandalwood' (lit. 'wood for burning incense'),
which is rel. to candrah, 'shining, glowing', and
cogn. with Gk. κάνδαρας, 'glowing, coal', L.
candere, 'to shine, glow, be white'. See candid
and cp. sanders and santal. Cp. also next word.

## sandarac
sandarac, п., 1) the sandarac tree; 2) resin
obtained from this tree; 3) realgar. — L. sanda-
raca, fr. Gk. σανδαράκη, which is of Oriental
origin. Cp. Ol. candra-rdga-, 'having the
brightness of the moon'. The first element of this
compound means 'shining, bright'; see sandalwood.

## sandblind
sandblind, adj., purblind. — ME., prob. fr. OE.
*sdm~blind, 'half blind', fr. sdm-, 'half (see
semi-), and blind, adj. The alteration of the first
element to sand is due to folk etymology.
Derivative: sandblind-ness, n.

## sanderling
sanderling, п., a wading bird (Crocethia alba). —
Formed fr. sand with the dimin. suff. -ling.

## sanders
sanders, saunders, п., sandalwood (archaic). —
OF. sandre, a var. of sandal. See sandalwood.

## sandla
sandla, п., a watermelon. — Sp., fr. Arab, (bat-
tthah) sindiyah, lit. '(the melon coming) from
Sind (India)'. See India.

## sandiver
sandiver, п., glass gall. — ME. saundiver, popular
alteration of F. suin (now spelled suint) de verre,
'sandiver', lit. 'sweating of glass". F. suin is a
derivative of suer, 'to sweat, perspire', fr. L.
suddre; see sudation. F. de, 'of, from', comes
fr. L. de, 'from, away from'; see de-, F. verre
derives fr. L. vitrum, 'glass'; see vitreo-.

## sandix
sandix, п., minion; bright red color. — L. sandix,
sandyx, fr. Gk. σάνδϋξ, 'minion, a women's
garment dyed with this color', a Semitic loan
word. Cp. Akkad. samtu, sandu, 'a red stone*.

## sandwich
sandwich, n. — Named after John Montagu,
Fourth Earl of Sandwich (1718-92), who once
spent 24 hours at the gaming table, using only
this kind of food. — The title of the Earl of
Sandwich comes fr. OE. Sandwic, lit. 'Sand
Village'. (OE. wic is a loan word fr. L. view,
'village, hamlet', for which see-vicinage.)
Derivative: sandwich, tr. v.

## sandy
sandy, adj., consisting of or abounding in sand.
— ME., fr. OE. sandig, fr. sand. See sand and -y
(representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: sand-i-ness, п., sand-y^isk, adj.

## Sandy
Sandy, п., nickname for a Scotsman. — From
Sandy, Scott, abbreviation of Alexander. Cp.
Sawney.

## sane
sane, adj. — L. sdnus, 'sound, whole, healthy',
rel. to Umbr. sanes (— L. sdnis, abl. pi.); of
uncertain etymology. Cp. sanative, sanatorium,
sanicle, snnitary, and the second element in
tutsan and in vesania.
Derivatives: sane-ly, advu sane-ness, n.

## sanforize
sanforize, tr. v., to preshrink (a cotton or linen
fabric) permanently. — Named after the
American Sanford Lockwood Cluett (born in 1874),
inventor of this process. For the ending see suff.
-ize.

## sang
sang, past tense of sing. — ME., fr. OE. sang.
See sing.

## sangar
sangar, п., breastwork, rifle pit for a few men. —
Hind, sangar, fr. Pers. sanga, sang, 'stone'.

## sangaree
sangaree, п., a West Indian drink. — Sp. sangrla,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:681 COLUMN:3 -->
'bleeding', fr. sangre, 'blood', fr. VL. sanguem
(L. sanguinem), ace. of L. sanguis, 'blood' (see
sanguine); so called because made of red wine.
Cp. sangrado.

## sang-de-boeuf
sang-de-boeuf, п., deep red color found in old
Chinese porcelain. — F. sang-de-bceuf, lit.
'bullock's blood'. F. sang, 'blood', derives fr. VL.
sanguem. See prec. word. F. de, 'of, from',
comes fr. L. de, 'from, away from'; see de-. F.
botuf, 'ox, bullock', comes fr. L. bovem, ace. of
bos; see bovine.

## sang-froid
sang-froid, п., presence of mind, composure. —
F., fr. MF., lit. 'cold blood*. For the first
element see sanguine and cp. prec. word. F. froid,
'cold', derives fr. L. frigidus; see frigid. The
word sang-froid was introduced into English by
Lord Chesterfield (1694-1773).

## sangrado
sangrado, п., an ignorant physician. — After
Doctor Sangrado, a character in Le Sage's Gil
Bias. The name is connected with Sp. sangrador,
'bloodletter', fr. sangrar, 'to let blood', fr.
sangre, 'blood'. See sangaree.

## sangrail
sangrail, sangreal, п., the holy grail. —
Refashioned fr. OF. saint graal, 'the holy grail', after
L. sanctus, 'holy*. See saint and grail.

## sangni-
sangni-, combining form meaning blood. — L.
sangui-, fr. sanguis, 'blood'. See sanguine.

## sanguification
sanguification, п., the conversion of food into
blood. — Compounded of sangui- and fication.

## Sanguinaria
Sanguinaria, п., a genus of plants, the bloodroot
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. sanguinaria herba,'la herb
that stanches blood', fr. sanguis, gen. sanguinis,
'blood' (see sanguine); so calfed from the color
of the juice.

## sanguinary
sanguinary, adj., bloody. — L. sanguindrius,
'pertaining to blood', fr. sanguis, gen. sanguinis,
'blood'. See sangnine and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: sanguinari-ly, adv., sanguinari-ness,
n.

## sanguine
sanguine, adj., of the color of blood; ruddy. —
ME. sanguin, fr. MF. (= F.) sanguin, fem.
sanguine, fr. L. sanguineus, 'of blood, blood-red,
bloodthirsty', fr. sanguis, gen. sanguinis, 'blood',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. consanguine,
consanguinity, ensanguine, exsanguinate,
sangaree, sangrado, sanguineous, and the first element
in sang-de-boenf and in sang-froid.

## sanguineous
sanguineous, 1) sanguine; 2) resembling blood. —
L. sanguineus. See sanguine and cp.
consanguineous. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.

## Sangnisorbn
Sangnisorbn, п., a genus of plants, the burnet
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of L. sanguis,
'blood' (see sanguine), and sorbere, 'to suck' (see
absorb); so called from the styptic qualities of
most plants of this genus.

## Sanhedrin
Sanhedrin, п., 1) the Supreme Jewish court (=
Sanhedhrin Gedholah) in the time of the Second
Temple, consisting of 71 ordained scholars; 2)
one of the lesser courts with 23 ordained
members called Sanhedhrin Qetannab, lit. 'the small
Sanhedrin'. — Mishnaic Heb. sanhedrin, fr. Gk.
συνέδριον, 'council*, lit. *a sitting together' (cp.
L. consessus, 'a sitting together; an assembly1),
fr. σύν, 'with, together with', and eSpfic, 'a seat*,
which stands for *sedrd and is cogn. with L.
sedere, 'to sit'. See syn- and sedentary, and cp.
synedrion. The form Sanhedrim is erroneous. It
arose from a misconception of the ending -in in
Misname Heb. sanhedhrin as the pi. suff., for
which -im, the more exact form of this suff., was
substituted. In reality, however, the suff. -in in
sanhedhrin stands for Greek -tov in the word
συνέδριον.

## sanicle
sanicle, п., any plant of the genus Sanicula. —
ME., fr. MF. (= F). sanick, fr. ML. sanicula,
lit. 'the healing plant', fr. L. sdnus, 'healthy'. See
sane and -cle.

## Sanicula
Sanicula, п., a genus of plants, the sanicle (hot.)
— ML. sanicula. See prec. word.

## sanify
sanify, tr. v., to make healthy. — Formed fr. L.
sdnus (see sane) with suff. -fy.

## sanitarium
sanitarium, п., a health station. — ModL.
sanitarium, lit. 'a place dedicated to health*. See
sanitary.

## sanitary
sanitary, adj., pertaining to health. — F. sanitaire,
fr. L. sdnitds, 'health'. See sanity and adj. suff.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:682 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 6SS | SARCASM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:682 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: sanitari-an, adj., sanitari-ly, adv.,
sanitari-ness, n.

## sanitate
sanitate, tr. v. — Back formation fr. sanitation.

## sanitation
sanitation, n. — Irregularly formed fr. sanity with
guff, -ation.

## sanity
sanity, n. — ME. sanite, fr. MF. (= F.) sanite, fr.
L. sanitdtem, ace. of sdnitds, 'health', fr. sanus,
'healthy'. See sane and -ity.

## sanjak
sanjak, п., formerly, subdivision of a vilayet in
Turkey. — Turk, sanjak, lit. 'flag'.

## sank
sank, past tense of sink. — ME. sank, fr. OE.
sane, past tense of sincan. See sink, v.

## Sanoussi
Sanoussi, n. — See Senussi.

## sans
sans, prep., without {arckaic). — F., fr. OF. sens,
a blend of L. sine, 'without' (see sine, 'without'),
and L. absentia, 'in the absence of (abl. of
absentia, 'absence'; see absence). Cp. senza.

## Sanscrit
Sanscrit, n. and adj. — See Sanskrit.

## sans-culotte
sans-culotte, п., a republican of the poorer
classes in the French Revolution. — F., lit. 'without
breeches'. For the first element see sans. F. си-
lot te is a diminutive form derived fr. cul, 'bot-·
torn, backside', fr. L. cuius; see culotte. The
name sans-culotte prop, denotes those who—in
contradistinction to the upper classes that wore
culottes—chose pantalons (long trousers) for
their distinctive costume.
Derivatives: sans-culott-ic, sans-culott-ish, adjs.

## sans-culottism
sans-culottism, h., the principles of sans-culottes.
— F. sans-cullottisme, fr. sans-culotte. See prec.
word and -ism.

## Sanskrit
Sanskrit, Sanscrit, n. and adj. — OI. samskrta-,
'prepared, refined, made or put together',
compounded of sum-, 'together', and kpa-, 'made'.
The first element is cogn. with Gk. #μα,
'together with', όμός, 'one and the same*, Goth.
sama, 'the same', samana, 'together', OE. same
(in same swd, 'similarly1, swa same swd, 'just
as1); see same and cp. samadh, samadhi. The
second element is rel. to krndti, karSti, 'makes',
Avestic kar-, 'to make', к г naoiti, 'makes', fr.
l.-E. base *qwer-, 'to make, form'. See corpus
and cp. Chamar, Karma, carcoon and the second
element in abkari, brinjarry, Prakrit, prakriti,
samskara, sircar.

## Santa Claus
Santa Claus, — American alteration of dial. Du.
Sante Klaus, 'Saint Nicholas'.

## santal
santal, п., sandalwood. — F. santal, fr. Gk.
σάνταλον, fr. OI. candanah. See sandalwood.

## Santal aceae
Santal aceae, n. pi., the sandalwood family (bot.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. ML. san-
talum, 'sandalwood'. See sandalwood.

## santalaceous
santalaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## santulin
santulin, п., a crystalline compound containing a
red coloring matter, C15H140. (chem.) — F. san-
taline, fr. santal. See santal and -in.

## santir
santir, п., a kind of dulcimer. — Arab, santir, fr.
Gk. ψαλτήρΐ,ον, 'stringed instrument, psaltery,
harp', whence also Aram. pesanterin, pesanterin,
'a (triangular) stringed instrument'. See Psalter.

## Santolina
Santolina, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. herba santonica. See
santonica and -ina (representing L. -ina).

## santon
santon, п., a saint in Mohammedan countries. —
Sp. santon, augment, formed fr. santo, fr. L.
sdnctus, 'holy'. See saint.

## santonica
santonica, п., the European wormwood. — Mod-
L., fr. L. herba santonica, 'the herb of the San-
toni\ a people of Aquitania. Cp. Santolina, san-
touin.

## santonin
santonin, п., a colorless bitter substance obtained
from santonica {chem.) — F. santonine, fr. L.
(herba) santonica. See santonica. F. santonine
(for santonique) was influenced in form by bar-
botine, which is also a vermifuge. See Bloch-
Wartburg, DELF., p. 544.

## Sanussi
Sanussi, n. — See Senussi.

## sap
sap, п., juice. — ME., fr. OE. step, rel. to MLG.,
MDu., Du. sap, OHG. saf, MHG. saf, soft, G.
Saft, 'juice', and cogn. with OI. sabar-, 'sap,
milk, nectar', fr. I.-E. base *sab-, a collateral
form of *sap-, 'to taste, perceive', whence Arm.
ham (for *sdpno-), 'juice; taste', L. sapa, 'new
wine boiled thick', sapere, 'to have taste or
flavor; to be wise, to know'. See sapient.
Derivatives: sap-less, adj., sap-ling, п., sapp-y,
adj., sap-ness, n.

## sap
sap, п., a trench. — MF. (= F.) sape, 'sapping,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:682 COLUMN:2 -->
undermining', back formation fr. saper, 'to sap,
undermine*. See sap, 'to undermine'.

## sap
sap, tr. and intr. v., to undermine. — MF. (— F.)
saper, fr. sape, 'mattock', fr. ML. sappa (whence
also It. zappa, Sp. zapa, 'spade', and the verbs
zappare, resp. zapar, 'to undermine'); of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: sapp-er, n.

## sapajou
sapajou, п., a small S. American monkey. — F.,
a Tupi loan word.

## sapanwood
sapanwood, п., a red dyewood obtained from the
tree Caesalpinia sapan. — Malay sapang.

## saphenous
saphenous, adj., designating two veins in the leg
(anat.) — ME., fr. ML. saphena, 'a vein in the
leg, saphena', fr. Arab, safin, in VArab.
pronunciation safen. For the ending see suff. -ous.

## sapid
sapid, adj., having taste, savory. — L. sapidus,
'savory, tasty', fr. sapere, 'to taste'. See sapient
and cp. insipid.
Derivatives: sapid-ity, п., sapid-ness, n.

## sapience
sapience, п., wisdom. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
sapience, fr. L. sapientia, 'wisdom', fr. sapiens, gen.
-entis. See next word. For the ending see suff.
-ce.

## sapient
sapient, adj., wise (rare). — ME., fr. OF., fr. L.
sapientem, ace. of sapiens, 'wise', pres. part, of
sapid, sapere, 'to have taste or flavor; to be wise,
to know', whence sapor, 'taste', sapidus, 'savory,
tasty', fr. I.-E. base *sap-, 'to taste, perceive',
whence also Arm. ham (for *sapno~), 'taste', OS.
an-sebbian, 'to perceive, remark', OHG. ant-
seffen, intseffen, 'to perceive, comprehend', OE.
sefa, 'mind, understanding, insight', and OS.
sebo, ON. sefi, of s.m., L. sapa, 'new wine boiled
thick'. See sap, 'juice', and cp. sage, adj., savant,
savor, savoir-faire, savoir-vivre. For the ending
see suff. -ent.
Derivative: sapient-ly, adv.

## sapiential
sapiential, adj., having or expounding wisdom.
— ME. sapiencial, fr. Late L. sapientidlis,
'pertaining to wisdom', fr. L. sapientia. See sapience
and adj. sufT. -al.
Derivative: sapiential-ly, adv.

## sapin
sapin, п., a kind of fir tree. — ME., fr. OF. ( =
F.), 'fir tree', which, together with OProvenc.
sap, of s.m., derives fr. L. sappinus (also sapinus),
'a kind of fir tree', a word of Gaulish origin. Cp.
W. syb-wydd, 'pine'.

## Sapindaceae
Sapindaceae, n. pi., the soapberry family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Sapindus with suff. -aceae.

## sapindaceons
sapindaceons, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Sapindus
Sapindus, п., a genus of plants, the soapberry
(bot.) — ModL., contraction of L. sapo indicus,
'Indian soap', fr. sapo, gen. -onis, 'soap', and
Indicus, 'Indian', fr. India. See saponaceous and
India.

## sapodilla
sapodilla, п., an evergreen tree, Achras zapota. —
Sp. sapotilla, zapotilla, dimin. of sapota, zapota.
See Sapota.

## saponaceous
saponaceous, adj., soapy. — Formed with suff.
-aceous fr. L. sapo, gen. sdponis, 'soap', which is
a Teut. loan word. See soap.
Derivative: saponaceous-ness, n.

## Saponarin
Saponarin, п., a genus of plants of the pink
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. ML. sdponarius,
'pertaining to soap', fr. L. sapo, gen. sdponis, 'soap'
(see saponaceous and -aria); so called because
the juice forms a lather with water.

## saponification
saponification, п., chemical conversion of fats
into soap. — F., fr. saponifier, 'to saponify'.
See next word and -ation.

## saponify
saponify, tr. and intr. v. — F. saponifier, 'to
saponify', fr. L. sapo, gen. sdponis, 'soap', and
-ficdre, fr. facere, 'to make, do'. See soap and
suff. -fy.
Derivatives: saponifi-able, adj., saponifi-er, n.

## sapor
sapor, п., taste, savor (rare). — L. sapor, rel. to
sapere, 'to taste'. See sapient and cp. savor.

## Sapota
Sapota, п., a genus of trees (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Sp. sapote, zapote, fr. Nahuatl tzapotl, name of
the tree.

## Sapotaceae
Sapotaceae, n. pi., the sapodilla family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Sapota with suff. -aceae.

## sapotaceous
sapotaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Sapphic
Sapphic, adj., ]) pertaining to Sappho; 2)
pertaining to any of the metrical forms used by
Sappho. — L. Sapphicus, fr. Gk. Σαπφικός, 'of
Sappho', fr. Σαπφώ, 'Sappho', name of a Greek

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:682 COLUMN:3 -->
lyric poetess of Lesbos (cca 600 B.C.E.). For tne
ending see adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: Sapphic, п., a Sapphic verse.

## sapphire
sapphire, n. — ME. safir, saphir, fr. OF. safir (F.
saphir), fr. L. sapphirus, fr. Gk. σάπφεψος, fr.
Heb. sapptr, 'sapphire; lapis lazuli', which some
scholars derive fr. OI. sani-priyam, 'sapphire',
lit. 'dear to the planet Saturn', fr. Sani, 'Saturn',
and priydh, 'dear'. See free. Cp. zaffer.

## snpphirine
snpphirine, adj., of sapphire; sapphire-like. — L.
sapphirinus, fr. Gk. σαπφείρινος, fr. σάπ-
φειρος, 'lapis lazuli'. See prec. word. For the
ending see adj. surf, -ine (representing Gk. -ϊνος).
Derivative: sapphirine, n.

## sapr-
sapr-, form of sapro- before a vowel.

## sapremia
sapremia, sapraemia, п., a diseased condition in
which putrefying matter is present in the blood
(med.) — Medical L., coined by Matthews
Duncan in 1880 fr. Gk. σαπρός, 'rotten, putrid', and
αίμα, 'blood'. See sapro-, hemal and 1st -ia.

## sapro-
sapro-, before a vowel sapr-, combining form
meaning 'putrid'. — Gk. σαπρο-, σαπρ-, fr.
σαπρός, 'rotten, putrid', rel. to σήπειν, 'to rot*.
See sepsis.

## saprogenic
saprogenic, saprogenous, adj., producing
putrefaction. — Compounded of sapro- and -genie,
resp. -genous.

## saprolite
saprolite, п., disintegrated rock (petrogr.) —
Compounded of sapro- and Gk. λίθος, 'stone'.
See -lite.
Derivative: saprolit-ic, adj.

## saprophagous
saprophagous, adj., feeding on decaying matter.
— Compounded of sapro- and Gk. -φάγος,
from the stem of φαγεΤν, 'to eat'. See -phagous.

## saprophyte
saprophyte, п., an organism that lives on
decaying matter. — Compounded of sapro- and
Gk. -φυτον, fr. φυτόν, 'a plant'. See -phyte.
Derivatives: saprophyt-ic, adj. and п., saprophyt-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## sapsago
sapsago, п., a kind of hard Swiss cheese. —
Corruption of G. Schabzieger, which is
compounded of schaben, 'to scrape', and Zieger, fr. Late
OHG. ziger, 'whey'. The first element is rel. to
E. shave (q.v.) Late OHG- ziger is prob.
traceable to Gaul. *dwi-gro-s, 'warmed twice', fr.
I.-E. *dwi-, 'twice' (see di-, 'twice'), and a
derivative of I.-E. *gwher-, 'to warm* (see warm). See
Hubschmied in Vox Romanica, 1935, I, 7 ff.,
quoted in Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p. 885 s.v.
Zieger.

## saraband
saraband, п., a slow Spanish dance. — F. sara-
bande, fr. Sp; zarabanda, borrowed fr. Persian
serbend, 'a kind of dance', through the medium
of Arabic.

## Saracen
Saracen, п., 1) an Arab; 2) a Moslem. — ML.
Saraceni (pi.), fr. Late Gk. Σαρακηνοί (pi.), fr.
Arab, sharqiyin, pi. ace. of sharqty, 'Eastern', fr.
sharq, 'east', fr. shdraqa, 'he cleft, dissected; rose
(said of the sun)'. Cp. sarcenet, sarsen,
sirocco.
Derivative: Saracen-ic, adj.

## Sarah
Sarah, also Sara, 1) fern. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the
wife of Abraham and the mother of Isaac. —
Lit. 'princess', fr. Heb. sdrdh, fern, of sar,
'prince', fr. sarar, 'he ruled', which is rel. to
Akkad. sharru, 'king', sharratu, 'queen'.

## sarangousty
sarangousty, п., stucco made waterproof. — Pers.
sarangushti, 'paste for painting the tips of the
fingers', fr. sar, 'head, extremity, tip', and an-
gusht, 'finger*. Pers. sar is cogn. with Gk. κάρα,
'head*, L. cerebrum, 'brain'; see cerebrum and
cp. serang, seraskier, sircar. Pers. angusht is rel.
to Avestic angushta-, 'toe, finger', OI. angusthah,
'big toe, thumb', and cogn. with Gk. άγκών,
'elbow', αγκύλος, 'crooked, curved', L. angulus,
'angle, corner'; see angle, 'corner'.
Saratoga trunk a large traveling trunk. — Named
after Saratoga Springs, a summer resort near
New York.

## sarbacane
sarbacane, п., a blowgun. — F., changed under
the influence of canne, 'cane, reed', fr. sarbatane
(still used in 1798 by the French Academy), fr.
Sp. cerbatana, zarbatana, fr. VArab. zarbatana*1,
fr. Arab. zabatdnah, ult. fr. Malay sumpitan, of
s.m., fr. sumpit, 'narrow'. Cp. sumpit.

## sarc-
sarc-, form of sarco- before a vowel.

## sarcasm
sarcasm, п., a taunting remark; an ironical jibe.
— F. sarcasme, fr. L. sarcasmos, fr. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:683 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SARCASTIC | 656 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:683 COLUMN:1 -->
σαρκασμός, 'jest, taunt, mockery', fr. σαρ-
κάζειν, 'to tear flesh like dogs; to bite the lips in
rage; to speak bitterly, sneer', fr. σαρξ, gen.
σαρκός, 'flesh'. See sarco-.

## sarcastic
sarcastic, adj. — Gk. σαρκαστικός, fr. σαρ-
κάζειν. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: sarcastic-ness, п., sarcastic-αΐ, adj.,
sarcastic-al-ly, adv., sarcastic-ai-ness, n.

## sarcenet
sarcenet, sarsenet, п., a fine silk material. — Late
ME. sarsenet, fr. AF. sarzinet, dimin. of ME.
sarzin, 'Saracen'. See Saracen.

## Sarcina
Sarcina, п., a genus of bacteria (bacteriology). —
ModL., fr. L. sarcina, 'bundle', fr. sarcire (pp.
sartus), 'to patch, mend, repair'. See sartorial.

## sarco-
sarco-, before a vowel sarc-, combining form
meaning 'flesh', as in sarcocarp, sarcology. —
Gk. σαρκο-, σαρκ-, fr. σαρξ, gen. σαρκός,
'fiesh', which is perh. cogn. with Avestic
bwar s-, 'to cut'. Cp. anasarcn, syssarcosis,
coenosarc, endosarc.

## sarcocarp
sarcocarp, п., the fleshy part of a fruit. —
Compounded of sarco- and Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See
carpel.

## sarcode
sarcode, п., animal protoplasm. — Gk. σαρκώδες,
'fleshy substance', subst. use of the neut. of
σοίρκώϊης, 'fleshlike', which is compounded of
σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'flesh', and -ώδης, 'like'.
See sarco- and -ode, 'like'.

## Sarcodina
Sarcodina, n. pi., a class of Protozoa (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. σαρκώδης, 'fieshlike'. See prec.
word.

## sarcology
sarcology, п., the anatomy of the soft parts of the
body. — Compounded of sarco- and -logy.

## sarcoma
sarcoma, п., tumor, malignant growth. —
Medical L., fr. Gk. σάρκοιμα, 'fleshy substance', fr.
σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'fiesh'. See sarco- and -oma.

## sarcophagus
sarcophagus, n.', stone coffin. — L., fr. Gk.
σαρκοφάγος, п., 'coffin', fr. σαρκοφάγος, adj.,
'eating fiesh', fr. σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'flesh', and
φαγεΐν, 'ίο eat*. See sarco- and -phagous. In
ancient Greece coffins were made of a kind of
limestone that consumed the flesh of the body
enclosed. L. sarcophagus was shortened into VL.
*sarcus, whence OF. sarcou (F. cercueif), 'coffin',
OHG. sarc, saruh (MHG. sarc and sarch, G.
Sarg), of s.m., MDu. sarc, sere (Du. zerk),
'tombstone'.

## sarcosine
sarcosine, п., a crystalline amino acid (спет.) —
G. Sarkosin, coined by the German chemist,
Baron von Justus Liebig (1803-73) in 1847 fr.
Gk. σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'flesh', and suff. -in. See
sarco- and chem. suff. -ine.

## sarcous
sarcous, п., pertaining to fiesh or muscle. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. σαρξ, gen.
σαρκός, 'flesh*. See sarco-.

## sard
sard, п., a variety of quartz. — F. sarde, fr. L.
sarda, fr. Gk. σάρδιον, prob. meaning lit. 'Sar-
dian stone',"fr. Σάρδεις, 'Sardis', the capital of
ancient Lydia. Cp. sardine, 'a precious stone',
sardius.

## sardine
sardine, п., a small fish. — F., fr. L. sardina, sarda,
'pilchard', fr. Gk. σαρδΐνη (also σαρδϊνος), of
s.m.; of uncertain origin. The usual explanation
of Gk. σαρδΐνη, as 'the fish from the island of
Σαρδώ (Sardinia)' is far from convincing. It is
hardly probable that the Greeks would have
obtained fish from so far as Sardinia at a time
relatively so early as that of Aristotle, from
whom Athenaios quotes a passage in which the
fish σαρδΐνας is mentioned.

## sardine
sardine, п., a precious stone. — Late L. lapis sar-
dinus, fr. Gk. σαρδϊνος λί&ος, lit. 'Sardian
stone'. See sard.

## Sardinian
Sardinian, adj., pertaining to the island of
Sardinia. — L. Sardinidnus, fr. Sardinia, fr. Gk.
Σαρδώ. For the ending see suff. -an.
Derivative: Sardinian, п., an inhabitant of
Sardinia.

## sardius
sardius, п., 1) a sard; 2) one of the twelve precious
stones in the breastplate of the Jewish high
priest. — Late L. sardius, short for L. lapis
sardius, 'Sardian stone', fr. Gk. σάρδιος λί*ος.
See sard.

## sardonic
sardonic, adj., bitter, cynical. — F. sardonique,
formed with change of suff. fr. L. Sardonius in
Sardonius risus, loan translation of Gk.
Σαρδόνιος γέλως,.ΐϋ. 'laughter caused by the plant
sardonia', which distorts the face of him that

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:683 COLUMN:2 -->
eats of it. Sardonia is another name for the plant
apium risus (lit. 'apium that causes laughter'),
and lit. means 'plant of Sardinia', fr. Gk.
Σαρδώ, 'Sardinia'. Cp. Sardinian.
Derivatives: sardonic-al-ly, adv., sardonic-ism, n.

## sardonyx
sardonyx, п., a variety of onyx. — L., fr. Gk.
σαρϊόνυξ, which prob. means lit. 'onyx of
Sardis', fr. Σάρδεις, 'Sardis', and δνυξ, 'fingernail,
claw, onyx'. See sard and onyx.

## sargasso
sargasso, п., also sargasso weed, a seaweed. —
Port, sargafo, fr. sargo, 'grape'.

## Sargassum
Sargassum, п., a genus of seaweeds (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Port, sargaco. See prec. word.

## sargo
sargo, п., a kind of seafish, the sea bream. — Sp.,
fr. L. sargus, fr. Gk. σάργος.

## sari
sari, п., principal garment of woman's dress in
India. — Hind, sari, fr. OI. sati.

## sark
sark, п., a shirt (Scot, or archaic). — ME. serk,
fr. OE. sere, rel, to ON. serkr; cp. Lith. "safkas,
Russ. sorotka, Finn, sarkki, 'shirt'. Cp.
baresark, berserker.

## Sarmatia
Sarmatia, n. — L., 'the country of the Sarma-
tians', fr. Sarmatae, 'the Sarmatians', fr. Gk.
Σαρμάται, a compound from an Asiatic
language, lit. meaning 'tribe of the steppe' (fr.
sara, 'steppe, desert', and mat, 'tribe, race'). For
the second element of this compound cp. the
Latin Asiatic tribe names ending in -matae, as
e.g. Aga-matae, Yaxa-matae. See Pavel Joseph
Safari k, Slawische Altertiimer, I 367.
Derivatives: Sarmati-an, adj. and n.

## sarment
sarment, n. — See sarmentum.

## sarmentose
sarmentose, adj., producing prostrate branches
(bot.) — L. sarmentosus, 'full of twigs or
branches', fr. sarmentum. See sarmentum and
adj. suff. -ose.

## sarmentous
sarmentous, adj., sarmentose. — See prec. word
and -ous.

## sarmentum
sarmentum, also sarment, п., a slender branch,
runner (bot.) — L. sarmentum, 'twigs,
brushwood', which stands for *sarp-mentum, fr. sar-
pere, 'to cut off, lop, trim', fr. 1-Е. base *srep-,
*Ξζρ-, 'to seize, rob', whence also Gk. £ρπη,
'sickle', άρπάζειν, 'to snatch, seize', αρπάγη,
'hook, rake'. Sec harpy and -ment and cp. assart.

## sarong
sarong, п., the chief garment of Malay men and
women. — Malay sarong.

## saros
saros, п., the number 3600; 3600 years. — Gk.
σάρος, σαρός, fr. Akkad. shorn.

## Sarothra
Sarothra, п., a genus of plants of the St.-John's
wort family (bot.)— ModL., fr. Gk. σάρωτρον,
'broom', fr. σαροϋν, 'to sweep clean', fr. σάρον,
'broom', which is rel. to σαίρειν, 'to sweep,
clean', and prob. also to σύρειν, 'to draw, draw
along'.

## Snrpcdon
Snrpcdon, п., a son of Zeus and Europa (Greek
mythol.) — L. Sarpedon, fr. Gk. Σαρπηδών,
which is of uncertain origin.

## sarpler
sarpler, п., a bale of wool. — ME., fr. OF. sarpil-
liere (F. serpilliire), 'packing cloth', which
derives perh. fr. VL. *scirpicularia, 'material made
from a rushlike tissue', fr. L. scirpiculus, 'made
of rushes' (whence the noun scirpiculus, 'a basket
made of rushes'), fr. scirpus, 'rush, bulrush'; see
Scirpus. Cp. OProvenc. sarpeliera, serpeliera,
Catal. sarpillera, Sp. harpillera, arpillera,
'packing cloth', which all derive fr. VL. *scirpicularia.

## Sarracenia
Sarracenia, п., a genus of plants, the pitcher plant
(йог.) — ModL., named after Michel Sar-
rasin de l'Etang (1659-1734), a physician of
Quebec in the 18th century. For the ending see
1st suff. -ia.

## Sarraceniaceae
Sarraceniaceae, n. pl„ the pitcher-plant family
(bot.) — Formed fr. Sarracenia with suff. -aceae.

## sarraceulaceous
sarraceulaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## sarrazin
sarrazin, п., buckwheat. — F. (ble) sarrasin, lit.
'Saracen wheat'. See Saracen.

## snrsaparilla
snrsaparilla, п., any of various tropical American
plants of the genus Smilax. — Sp. zarzaparrilla,
a hybrid coined fr. Sp. zarza, 'bramble' (fr.
Arab, sharas, 'a thorny plant'), and parrilla,
dimin. of parra, 'vine', which is of uncertain
origin.

## sarsen
sarsen, п., also sarsen stone, a large boulder of
sandstone. — Prop. Sarsen stone, i.e. Saracen
stone, fr. Saracen, used in the sense of 'pagan,
heathen'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:683 COLUMN:3 -->

## sarsenet
sarsenet, n. — See sarcenet.

## sartorinl
sartorinl, adj., pertaining to a tailor. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. ModL. sartorius,
'pertaining to a tailor', fr: L. sartor, 'patcher, tailor', fr.
sartus, pp. αϊ sarcire, 'to patch, mend', which is
prob. cogn. with Hitt. sharmink-, 'to indemnify,
compensate', Gk. ίρκος, 'enclosure, hedge,
fence', orig. 'a hurdle of wickerwork', όρκος,
Oath', lit. 'a limitation, binding, obligation'. Cp.
exorcize, Sarcina.

## sartorite
sartorite, п., a crystalline compound of lead,
arsenic and sulfur(/m'nera/.)—Named after Sar-
torius von Waltershausen. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## sartorius
sartorius, п., the long leg muscle (anat.) —
Medical L. sartorius, short for musculus sartorius,
prop, 'the muscle used in crossing the legs to
bring them into the position needed to sit like a
tailor'. See sartorial.

## Sarum
Sarum, п., the ecclesiastical name of Salisbury.
— ML. The name prob. arose from a
misunderstanding of Sar., abbreviation of Sarisburia,
'Salisbury'. The change of ML. Sarisburia to E.
Salisbury is due to the dissimilation of the first
r to I.

## sash
sash, п., an ornamental scarf or band. — Dis-
similated fr. Arab, shush.

## sash
sash, п., framework. — Alteration of F. chassis,
'framework', incorrectly pronounced sashes and
mistaken for a plural. See chassis. For similar
back formations cp. pea and words there
referred to.

## sashay
sashay, intr. v., a term in dancing. — Corruption
of F. chassez, imper. pi. of chasser, 'to chase,
hunt', fr. OF. chacier, fr. VL. *captidre. See
chase, catch.

## sasin
sasin, п., the Indian antelope. — Nepalese.

## saskatoon
saskatoon, п., a small tree, Amelanchier alnifolia.
— Aphetic for Cree misuskwatomin, which is
compounded of misaskwat, name of the tree,
and min, 'berry'.

## sassaby
sassaby, п., a large S. African antelope. —
Sechuana tsessebe.

## sassafras
sassafras, п., a small laurel-like tree of N.
America. — Sp. sasafras, ft. saxafrax, fr. saxi/raga,
ft. L. saxifraga. See saxifrage.

## Sassenach
Sassenach, п., a Saxon; an Englishman. — Ir. sa-
sanach, 'Saxon'. See Snxon.

## sassolite
sassolite, п., native boric acid (mineral.) — Named
after Sasso in Italy. For the ending see
combining form -lite.

## sassy
sassy, п., a W. African tree. — W. African; said
to derive from E. sancy.

## sat
sat, past tense and pp. of sit. — ME. sat, fr. OE.
sset, resp. ME. seten, fr. OE. geseten. See sit.

## satable
satable, adj., capable of being sated. — Formed
fr. sate with suff. -able.

## Sntan
Sntan, n. — Heb. Satan, 'adversary', fr. Sdfan, 'he
acted as an adversary of, showed enmity to; he
charged, accused', which is rel. to Aram. setan,
of s.m. Aram.-Syr. safana, Arab, shaytdn,
'adversary, Satan', are loan words from Heb. satin.
Cp. Gk. Σάταν, Σατανάς, Late L. Satan, Sa-
tanas which are transliterations of Heb. sdfdn.
Cp. also Sbaitan.
Derivatives: Satan-ism, п., Satan-ist, n.

## Satanic
Satanic, adj. — Late Gk. Σατανικός, fr. Gk.
Σάταν. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: satanic-al, adj., satanic-al-ly, adv.

## Satanology
Satanology, п., the study of Satan. — Coined fr.
Satan and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## satara
satara, п., a woolen breadcloth. — Named after
Satara, a town in India.

## satchel
satchel, п., a small bag. — ME. sachel, fr. OF.
sachel, fr. L. saccellus, dimin. of saccus, 'sack,
bag'. See sack, 'bag', and -el.
Derivative: satchel-ed, adj.

## sate
sate, tr. v., to satisfy, surfeit. — Prob. a blend of
obsol. E. sade, fr. OE. sadian, 'to satiate', and
L. sat, satis, 'enough'. See sad and cp. satiate,
satis.

## sate
sate, archaic past tense and past participle of ιιί.
— See sat and sit.

## sateen
sateen, п., a glossy cotton cloth resembling satin.
— Alteration of satin, on the analogy of
velveteen; the ending -een is a phonetic variant of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:684 COLUMN:1 -->
-lne.

## satellite
satellite, п., ]) a follower or attendant of a
superior; 2) a body that revolves round a planet.
— MF. (= F.), fr. L. sateilitem, ace. of satelles,
'an attendant', which is of Etruscan origin. The
word satellite was introduced into science by the
German astronomer JohannKeplerO 571-1630).
Derivative: sateltit-ic, adj.

## satellold
satellold, adj., resembling a satellite. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. satelles and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See prec. word and -old.

## sati
sati, n. — A var. of suttee.

## sntiable
sntiable, adj. — See satiate, v., and -able.
Derivatives: satiabil-ity, п., satiable-ness, п.,
satiabl-y, adv.

## satiate
satiate, adj., satiated. — L. satiatus, pp. of satidre,
'to fill, satisfy', fr. satis, 'enough'. See satis and
adj. sufT. -ate and cp. sate, 'to satisfy'.

## satiate
satiate, tr. v. — L. satiatus, pp. of satiare. See
prec. word.
Derivative: satiat-ion, n.

## satiety
satiety, n. — MF. (= F.) satieti, fr. L. satietdtem,
ace. of satietds, 'sufficiency, abundance', fr.
satis, 'enough'. See satiate, adj., and -ity.

## satin
satin, n. — F., fr. Arab, aflas zaytunt, 'tissue
brought from Zaitun, Arabic name of the
Medieval Chinese shipping port Tzu-t*ing (later
called Ckuanckow, now Tsinkiang), in the province
Fukien. F. satin was prob. influenced in form by
It. setino, a word of identical origin, but
assimilated to seta, 'silk'. Cp. sateen.
Derivatives: satin, tr. v., to make satiny, satin-
ity, п., satin-ize, tr. v., satin-y, adj.

## satinet
satinet, satinette, п., a kind of satin. — F., dimin.
of satin..See satin and -et, -ette.

## satire
satire, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. satura (also satira),
for satura lanx, 'a dish filled with various kinds
of fruits; mixture, medley; satire' (first applied
in this last sense to a collection of various poems
by Ennius); not related to satur, 'full of food',
satis, 'enough'.
Derivatives: satiric (q.v.), sarir-ist, п., satirize
(q.v.)

## satiric
satiric, adj. — MF. (= F.) satirique, fr. L. satiri-
cus, fr. satira. See satire and adj. suff, -ic.
Derivatives: satiric-al, adj.» satiric-al-ly, adv.,
satiric-al-ness, n.

## satirize
satirize, tr. v., to attack with satire. — F. satiriser,
fr. satire. See satire and -ize.
Derivative: satiriz-able, adj.

## satis
satis, adv., enough, sufficient. — L., rel. to satur,
'satiated', and cogn. with Gpth. saps, 'satiated',
OE. ssed, 'satisfied'. See sad and cp. words there
referred to.

## satisfaction
satisfaction, n. — ME. satisfaccioun, fr. MF. (=^
F.) satisfaction, fr. L. satisfactionem, ace. of sa-
tisfactio, 'a satisfying security, bail*, fr. satis-
/actus, pp. of satisfacere. See satisfy.

## satisfactory
satisfactory, adj. — Late L. satisfactorius, fr. L.
satisfactus, pp. of satisfacere. See next word and
adj. suff. -ory.
Derivatives: satisfactori-ly, adv., satisfactori-
ness, n.

## satisfy
satisfy, tr. and intr. v. — ME. satisfien, fr. MF.
satisfier (F. satisfaire), fr. L. satisfacere, 'to make
amends, make reparation, satisfy, give
satisfaction', orig. written in two separate words satis
facere, fr. satis, 'enough', and facere, 'to make,
do'. See satis and -fy.
Derivatives: satisfi-able, adj., satisfi-ed, adj.,
satisfi-ed-ly, adv., satisfi-ed-ness, П., satisfy-ing,
adj., satisf у~ing-ly, adv., satisfy-ing-ness, n.

## satrap
satrap, п., 1) governor in a province in ancient
Persia; 2) a despotic ruler. — ME., fr. L. satra-

## pes
pes, fr. Gk. έξατράπης, σατράπης, fr. OPers.
xsha&rapavan-, 'ruler of the province',
compounded of xshadra-, 'province', and a
derivative of pd(y)-, 'to guard, protect', which is rel. to
Ql\pati, 'guards, protects'. The first element is
rel. to OPers. xshaya-, 'king', xshayad-iya-,
'power', and cogn. with Gk. κτασθ-αι, 'to
possess', fr. I.-E. base *qpe(i)-, *qpei-, 'to possess,
rule'; see shah and cp. check, 'sudden stop'. For
the second element see food and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivative: satrap-al, adj.

## satrapy
satrapy, n. — F. satraple, fr. L. satrapia, fr. Gk.
σατραπεία, 'satrapy', fr. σατράπης. See prec.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:684 COLUMN:2 -->
word and -y (representing Gk. -ta).

## Satsuma
Satsuma, п., Satsuma Ware, a kind of Japanese
pottery. — Named after the province Satsuma
in the island of Kiusiu, Japan.

## sattva
sattva, п., truth {Hindu philos.) — Ol. sattvah,
'truth', lit. 'being', rel. to OI. satyab, 'true,
right', and cogn. with Gk. έτος (for *se-tos),
'true', Goth, sunjis, OE. sod, 'true'. See sooth
and cp. snttee.

## saturable
saturable, adj. — Formed from the verb saturate
with suff. -able.

## saturant
saturant, adj., saturating. — L. saturdns, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of saturdre. See next word and
-ant.
Derivative: saturant, n.

## saturate
saturate, tr. v., to soak completely. — L. satura-
tus, pp. of saturdre, 'to fill, saturate', fr. satur,
'full', which is rel. to satis, 'enough'. See satis
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: saturat-ed, adj.

## saturate
saturate, adj., saturated. — L. saturdtus, pp. of
saturdre* See saturate, v.

## saturation
saturation, n. — Late L. saturdtid, gen. -onis, *a
filling, saturating*, fr. L. saturdtus, pp. οι
saturdre. See saturate, v., and -ion.

## Saturday
Saturday, n. — ME. Saterdai, fr. OE. Sataern{es)-
dxg, Sieterdaeg, coined fr. L. Sdturnidies,
'Saturday', lit. 'Saturn's day', through the substitution
of OE. dsegy 'day', for L. dies. Cp. Du. zaterdag,
'Saturday', and see Saturn and day. L. Sdturni
dies is a loan translation of Gk. Κρόνου ημέρα,
'the day of Cronus'.

## Satureia
Satureia, п., a genus of plants, the savory {bot.)
•— L. satureia, 'the savory', a foreign word.

## Saturn
Saturn, п., 1) the god of agriculture in Roman
mythology; identified later with the Greek
Κρόνος; 2) name of a planet; 3) (in alchemy)
lead. — L. Sdturnus, a word of Etruscan origin.
The usual derivation of Sdturnus, as 'the god of
sowing', fr. L. serere, pp. satus, 'to sow', is
erroneous; it is due to folk etymology.
Derivatives: Saturn-al, Saturn-ian, Saturn-ic,
adjs., saturnine (q.v.), saturnism (q.v.)

## Saturnalia
Saturnalia, n. pi., the yearly festival of Saturn in
Roman religion. — L. Saturnalia, prop, subst.
use of the pi. of Saturndle, neut. of the adjective
Sdturndlis, 'belonging to Saturn', fr. Sdturnus.
See prec. Vord.
Derivative: Saturnali-an, adj.

## saturnine
saturnine, adj., gloomy. — ME., fr. MF. (— F.)
saturnin, fr. L. Sdturnus (see Saturn), lit.
meaning 'under the influence of the planet Saturn'
(according to astrologers, this planet has a
gloomy influence on mortals). For the ending
see adj, suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).
Derivative: saturnine-Iy, adv.

## saturnism
saturnism, п., chronic lead poisoning. — See
Saturn and -ism.

## satyr
satyr, п., a woodland deity, part man and part
goat. — ME., fr. L. satyrus, fr. Gk. σάτυρος,
prob. an Illyr. loan word lit. meaning 'sower',
fr. I.-E. *setor, whence L. sator, 'sower', fr. base
*se-, *to sow'. See sow, v., and cp. semen,
season. For the ending of σάτυρος, ср. Illyr.
Δει-ττάτυρος, corresponding to L. Dies-piter
(see Jupiter).

## satyriasis
satyriasis, п., morbid sexual desire in males. —
Medical L., formed fr. Gk. σάτυρος (see prec.
word) with suff. -iasis.

## satyric
satyric, adj. — L. satyricus, fr. Gk. σατυρικός,
fr. σάτυρ. See satyr and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: satyric-al, adj.

## sauce
sauce, n. — ME., fr. OF. sauce, sause, sausse (F.
sauce), fr. L. salsa (whence also It., Sp. salsa,
'sauce'), fern, of salsus (for *sald-tos), 'salted',
prop. fern. pp. used as a noun, fr. OL. sallere
(for sald-ere), 'to salt', fr. sal, gen. salts, 'salt'.
See salt and cp. sal, salse, sausage.
Derivatives: sauc-y, adj., sauc-i-ly, adv., sauc-i-
ness, n.

## sauce
sauce, tr. v. — ME. saucen, fr. sauce. See snnce,
n.

## saucer
saucer, п., a small shallow dish. — ME., fr. OF.
saussier, saussiere (F. sauciere), 'a dish for
holding sauces', fr. sauce, sausse. See sauce, п., and
subst. suff. -er.
Derivative: saucer-ful, adj.

## saucisse
saucisse, п., saucisson. — F., fr. OF., fr. VL. sal-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:684 COLUMN:3 -->
sicia, 'sausage', subst. use of the fern, of salsicius.
See sausage and cp. n*xt..word.

## saqcisson
saqcisson, п., a tube of canvas filled with
gunpowder. — F., fr. It. sahiccione, augment, otsal-
siccia, 'sausage'. See prec. word.

## sauerkraut
sauerkraut, п., pickled cabbage. — G. Sauerkraut,
lit. 'sour cabbage', fr. sauer, 'sour', and Kraut,
'cabbage*; cp. Alsatian G. surkrut, 'sauerkraut'.
See sour and bryo- and cp. choucroute.

## saul
saul, n. — See sal, the tree.

## Saul
Saul, I) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the first king
of Israel. — L. Saul, name of the 1st king of
Israel, fr. Heb. Shd'al, lit. 'asked for', passive
part, atskd'al, 'he asked for, he asked, inquired',
whence ske*elah, 'request, thing asked for',
mish"alah, 'request', rel. to Aram. ske,elt Syr.
she4, Arab, sa'ala, Ethiop. sa'ala, 'he asked',
Akkad. ska'dlu, 'to ask'.

## Saumur
Saumur, п., a white wine. — Named after Sau-
mur in the department Maine-et-Loire, France.

## sauna
sauna, п., Finnish steam bath. — Finn., lit.
'bathroom*.

## sannders
sannders, n. — A var. of sanders.

## saunter
saunter, intr. v., to stroll. — Prob. fr. F. s'aven-
turer, 'to hazard oneself, venture, take risks', fr.
se, 'oneself (fr. L. se; see sni), and aventurer, 'to
hazard, venture, risk', fr. aventuret 'venture,
risk', fr. VL. *adventura, 'a happening', fr. L.
adventurus, 'that which is going to happen'. See
adventure.
Derivatives: saunter-er, п., saunter-ing, adj., and
verbal п., saunter-ing-ly, adv.

## saur-
saur-, form of sauro- before a vowel.

## saurel
saurel, п., a fish of the genus Trachurus. — F., fr.
OProvenc. saurel, lit. 'a lizardlike fish', fr. Gk.
σαϋρος, 'lizard*. See sauro- and cp. jurel.

## Sauria
Sauria, п., a suborder of reptiles. — ModL., fr.
σαΰρος, 'lizard'. See sauro-.
Derivatives: sauri-an, adj. and n.

## sauro-
sauro-, before a vowel saur-, combining form
meaning 'lizard*. — Gk. σαυρο-, σαυρ-, fr.
σαΰρος, 'lizard', prob. rel. to σαΰλος, 'twisting,
wavering'. Cp. saurel.

## sauropod
sauropod, adj., pertaining to the Sauropoda. —
See next word.

## Sauropoda
Sauropoda, n. pi., a suborder of dinosaurs (pale-
ontol.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. σαϋρος,
'lizard', and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See sauro-
and -poda.

## Saururus
Saururus, п., a genus of plants, the lizard's tail
{bot.) — ModL., lit. 'lizard's tail', fr. sauro- and
Gk. ούρα, 'tail' (see uro-, 'tail-'); so called from

## -saurus
-saurus, combining form used to denote genera of
lizards, as in Ichthyosaurus (paleontol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. σαϋρος, 'lizard*. See sauro-.

## saury
saury, п., a lizardlike fish (Scombresox saurus).
— ModL. saurus, fr. Gk. σαΰρος, 'lizard*. See
sanro-.

## sausage
sausage, n. — ME. sausige, fr. ONF. saussiche,
corresponding to F. saucisse, fr. VL. salsicitt,
'sausage', subst. use of salsicius, 'seasoned with
salt', fr. L. salsus, 'salted'. See sance, п., and cp.
saucisse, saucisson.

## saussnrite
saussnrite, п., a variety of zoisite {mineral.) —
Named after the Swiss naturalist Horace
Benedict de Saussure (1740-99). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## saute
saute, adj., fried quickly. — F., pp. of sauter, 'to
leap, jump*, fr. L. saltdre. See saltant.
Derivatives: saute, n. and tr. v.

## Sauterne
Sauterne, also, not capitalized, sauterne, п., a kind
of sweet, white wine from the district Sauternes
in Gironde, France.

## sauve-qui-peut
sauve-qui-peut, п., a hasty flight. — F., lit. 'save
(himself) who can'.

## savable
savable, adj. — Formed fr. save, v., with suff.
-able.

## savage
savage, adj. — From earlier salvage (Spenser), fr.

cp. siwash.
Derivatives: savage, n. and tr. v., savage-dom,
п., savage-ly, adv., savage~ness> п., savag-ery> п.,

## savannah
savannah, savanna, п., a treeless plain. — Sp. za·

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:685 COLUMN:1 -->
vana (now spelled sabana), fr. Taino zavana.

savant, п., a learned man. — F., orig. pres. part.
οΐ savoir, 'to know\ fr. VL. *sapere, fr. L.

## savate
savate, п., boxing with feet or fists. — F., 'old

pata, zapato, 'shoe', whence zapatain,

## save

neur), 'save (our) honor', fr. L. salvo honore, lit.

## saveloy

Popular alteration of F. cervelas, fr. It. cervel-

## savin

## savior
savior, saviour, n. — ME. saviour, fr. OF. sal-
veour, sauveour (F. sauveur), fr. Late L. salva-
torem, ace. oisalvator, fr. salvatus, pp. of salvdre
'to save'. See save, v., and agential suff. -or,

## savoir-faire
savoir-faire, п., tact. — F., lit. 'knowledge how
to do'. F. savoir, 'to know', derives fr. VL. *sa·
pere, which corresponds to L. sapere, 4o taste,
savor, of; to know'; see sapient. F. /aire, 'to
make, do', comes fr. L. facere; see fact,

## savolr-vivre

F., lit. 'knowledge how to live*. For the first
