## savor
savor, savour, n. — ME. savor, savour, fr. OF.
savor, savour, fr. L. saporem, ace. of sapor, 'taste,
flavor', fr. sapere, 'to taste*. See sapient and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: savo(u)r, v. (q.v.), savo(u)r-y, adj.
(q.v.), savo(u)r-less, adj.

## savor
savor, savour, intr. and tr. v. — ME. savowren, fr.
OF. (= F.) savourer, fr. L. sapordre, 'to savor',
fr. sapor. See savor, n.
Derivatives: savo(u)r-ed, adj., savo(u)r-er, n.

## savorous
savorous, adj. — ME., fr. MF. saveros, saverous
(F. savoureux), fr. L.· saporosus, 'of good taste
or flavor1, fr. sapor. See savor and -ous.

## savory
savory, savoury, adj., tasty; fragrant. — ME.
savory, fr. OF. savoure (F. savoure), pp. of
savourer. See savor, v., and adj. suff. -y
(representing OF. -e (F. -if).
Derivatives: sav(o)ri-ly, adv., sav(o)ri-ness, n.

## savory
savory, п., an aromatic mint. — ME. savercy, fr.
MF. savoree, fr. OF. savereie, a blend of L.
satureia, 'savory', and MF. savourie, fem. of
savoure (F. savoureux); 'tasty, savory'; see savory,
adj. Cp. F. sarriette, 'the plant savory', dimin.
of OF. sarrie, fr. L. satureia. See Satureia.

## savoy
savoy, п., a kind of cabbage. — Short for Savoy
cabbage, translation of F. chou de Savoie, called
after the French province of this name. See
Savoyard.

## Savoyard
Savoyard, п., inhabitant of Savoie. — F., formed
fr. Savoie, former name of a province of the
kingdom of Sardinia, since 1800 part of France.
For the ending see suff. -ard.

## savvy
savvy, savvey, intr. v., to know (siang). —
Corruption of Sp. sabe in sabe Usted, 'do you know ?*
fr. saber, 'to know', fr. VL. *sapere, which
corresponds to L. sapere, 'to taste, discern, know';
cp. also Port., OProvenc. saber, It. sapere, F.
savoir, 'to know*, which all derive fr. VL. *sapere.
See sapient and cp. words there referred to.

## saw
saw, п., a saying, maxim. — ME. sawe, fr. OE.
sagu, 'a saying, report', rel. to ON. saga, OHG.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:685 COLUMN:2 -->
saga, MHG., G. sage, 'saying, report, tale', and
to OE. secgan, 'to say'. See say and cp. saga,
which is a doublet of saw.

## saw
saw, past tense of see. — ME. sauh, fr. OE. sseh,
fr. OE. sion (for *sekwan), 'to see'. See see, v.

## saw
saw, п., a cutting tool. — ME. sawe, fr. OE. sagu,
sage, rel. to ON. sog, Norw. sag, Swed. sag,
Dan. sav, MDu. saghe, Du. zaag, OHG. saga,
sega, MHG. sege, G. Sage, fr. I.-E. base *seq-,
'to cut', whence also L. secure, 'to cut', securis,
'ax, hatchet1. See section and cp. sax, Saxon, Cp.
also seesaw.
Derivatives: saw, tr. and intr. v., saw-ing, n. and
adj., saw-er, п., sawyer (q.v.)

## sawder
sawder, п., flattery; only used in the phrase soft
sawder (colloq.) — A var. of solder.

## Sawney
Sawney, п., a Scotsman. — Corruption of Sandy
(q.v.)

## sawyer
sawyer, n. — Formed fr. saw,'a cutting tool', with
suff. -yer. Cp. bowyer, lawyer.

## sax
sax, п., a single-edged sword or dagger. — ME.
sexe, fr. OE. seax, 'knife, short sword, dagger*,
ON. sax, OHG. sahs, of s.m., and cogn. with
L. saxum, 'rock'. OE. seax, etc., orig. meant
'made of stone', and, indeed, knives were orig.
made of stone. See saxatile.

## saxatile
saxatile, adj., living on rocks (bot. and zool.) —
L. saxdtilis, 'living on rocks', fr. saxum, 'rock',
which stands in gradational relationship to
secure, 'to cut1, and is cogn. with OE. seax, ON.
sax, OHG. sahs, 'knife, short sword, dagger'.
See section and cp. Saxicoia. saxifrage; cp. also
sax, Saxon, For the relationship between L.
saxum and secure cp. L. rupes, 'rock', which is
rel. to rumpere, 'to break, burst, tear, rend',
(see rupestrian and cp. words there referred to.)

## saxhorn
saxhorn, п., a brass wind instrument. — Named
after its inventor, the Belgian musical
instrument maker Antoine Joseph, called Adolphe
Sax (1814-94). — See horn and cp. saxophone.

## Saxicoia
Saxicoia, n. pi., a genus of passerine birds (or-
nithol.) — ModL., lit. 'inhabiting rocks', fr. L
saxum, 'rock' and the stem of colere, 'to
inhabit'. See saxatile and colony.

## saxicoline
saxicoline, adj., inhabiting rocks. — See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ine.

## saxicolous
saxicolous, adj., growing on rocks {bot.) — See
Saxicoia and -ous.

## Saxifraga
Saxifraga, п., a genus of plants, the saxifrage
(bot.) — ModL. See saxifrage.

## Saxifragaceae
Saxifragaceae, n. pi., the saxifrage family (bot.)
— ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## saxifragaceous
saxifragaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-nceous.

## saxifrage
saxifrage, п., any plant of the genus Saxifraga. —
ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. saxifraga (scil.
herba), lit. 'a rock-breaking herb', fem. of saxi-
fragus, 'rock-breaking', compounded of saxum,
gen saxt, 'rock' and the stem of Jrangere, 'to
break' (see saxatile and fraction); so called
because it grows among rocks. Cp. sassafras.

## Saxon
Saxon, n. and adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) Saxon,
fr. Late L. Saxonem, ace. of Saxo (pi. Saxones),
which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OE. Seaxe, Seaxan,
'Saxons', OHG. Sahsun, 'Saxons' (G. Sachse,
'Saxon'), which prob. derive fr. OE. seax, resp.
OHG. sahs, 'knife, short sword, dagger', and
orig. meant 'those armed with knives'. See sax
and section and cp. Sassenach.
Derivatives: Saxon-ian, n. and adj., Saxon-ic,
Saxon-ic-al, adjs., Saxon-ic-al-ly, adv., Saxon-
ish, adj. and п., Saxon-ism, п., Saxon-ist, n.

## saxony
saxony, п., woolen yarn produced in Saxony and
cloth made from this. — Late L. Saxonia, fr.
Saxdnes, 'the Saxons*. See Saxon.

## saxophone
saxophone, п., a single-reed keyed wind
instrument. — Named after its inventor, the Belgian
musical instrument maker Antoine Joseph,
called Adolphe Sax (1814-94). See -phone and
cp. saxhorn.

## say
say, tr. and intr. v., to utter, express in words. —
ME. seggen, seyen, sayen, fr. OE. secgan, 'to
say, tell', rel. to OS. seggian, ΟΝ., Norw. segja,
Dan. sige, Swed. saga, OFris. sedsa, MDu.
segghen, Du. zeggen, OHG. sagen, MHG., G.
sagen, 'to say*, fr. I.-E. base *seqVf-, 'to say',
whence also Toch. saks-, 'to say', Hitt. shakiya-,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:685 COLUMN:3 -->
'to declare', Gk. έννεπε (for *ensekwe), *teU!,
say!', άσπετος (for *askwetos), 'unspeakable,
unutterable', θ-εσπέσιος (for *theskwesios),
'divine', lit. 'divinely uttered* (for the first
element of this word see theo-), L. inquam (for
*insquam), Ί say', inseque, insece, 'relate!,
declare!', Lith. sakfti, 'to say*, OSlav. soeiti, 'to
vindicate, show', W. hepp, 'he said*, Olr. Insce,
'speech*, Cp. saga, saw, 'a saying'. Cp. also the
second element in Thespesia, Thespian. — Base
*seqw-t 'to say', is orig. identical with base
*seqw-, 'to see1, this latter having gradually
developed the meanings 'to show, point out,
remark, say'. See see, v., and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: say, п., say-er, п., say-ing, П.

## say
say, п., a fine cloth resembling serge. — ME., fr,
OF. (= F.) sale, fr. L. saga, pi. of sagum, *a
mantle worn by the ancient Roman soldiers',
the pi. saga having been mistaken in VL. for a
fem. sing. noun. See saguin.

## saynete
saynete, п., tidbit; a short play. — F., 'playlet,
sketch*, fr. Sp. sainete, 'any delicate bit; a one-
act farce', derived fr. sain, 'grease', fr. VL.
*sagimen, fr. L. sagnindre, 'to fatten', fr. sagina,
'a fattening, feeding; stuffing', which is of
uncertain origin.

## sayyid
sayyid, sayid, said, п., a Moslem title of honor,
applied to the descendants of Husain,
Mohammed's grandson. — Arab, sayyid, 'lord,
chief, prob. lit. 'speaker, spokesman', and rel.
to Heb. sodh, 'confidential talk, council,
counsel*, Aram, s wddha, suwadha 'friendly,
confidential speech'. Cp. sidi.

## sbirro
sbirro, п., an Italian policeman. — It., fr. Late L.
birrus, 'red', fr. Gk. πυρρός (for *πυρσΓός),
'red', lit. 'fire-colored', fr. πΰρ, 'fire'. See fire
and cp. pyre. For the change of Greek π to b in
Latin—which is prob. due to Etruscan influence
—cp. box, the tree, burro, carbasus.

## scab
scab, n. — ME., of Scand. origin. Cp. Dan. skab,
Swed. skabb, which are rel. to OE. sceabb,
'scab', sceafan, 'to scrape, shave', and cogn.
with L. scabere, 'to scratch, scrape', scabies,
'roughness; itch, mange'. See scabies.
Derivatives: scab, intr. v., scabb-ed, adj., scabb-
ed-ness, п., scabb-y, adj., scabb-i-ly, adv., scabb-
i-ness, n.

## scabbard
scabbard, п., sheath for the blade of a sword,
etc. — ME. scaubert, fr. AF. escaubert,
compounded of OHG. scar, 'blade, sword', and
-berc, 'protection', fr. bergan, *to protect*. For
the first element see shear and cp. share,
'portion, part', for the second see bury and cp. the
second element in hauberk.

## scabble
scabble, tr. v., to rough down, dress (timber). —
Fr. earlier scapple, fr. ME. scaplen, fr. OF. es·
chapler, 'to cut, rough down, dress (timber)*, fr.
es-, fr. L. ex (see 1 st ex-) and chapler, 'to cut', fr.
Late L. capulare, 'to cut off, cleave, split', fr.
I.-E. base *(s)qap-, 'to cut', whence also L. сард,
gen. -dnls, 'capon'. See capon-and cp. scapho-,
scapular, scopelism.
Derivatives: scabbl-er, п., scabbl-ing, n.

## scabies
scabies, п., the itch (med.) — L. scabies,
'roughness, scurf, itch, mange', from scabere, 'to
scratch, scrape', which is cogn. with Goth, sea-
ban, OE. sceafan, 'to scrape, shave', fr. I.-E.
base *skab-, 'to work with a stone scraper, to
scrape, scratch', whence also OSlav. skobli,
'scraper', Lith. skabus, 'sharp*, skabit, skabeti,
'to cut', skobti, 'to hollow out', Lett, skabrs,
'splintery, sharp', skabs, 'sour'. See shape and
cp. shave. Cp. also scab, scobs, skep.

## Scabiosa
Scabiosa, п., a genus of plants of the teasel family
(bot.) — ModL. See scabious, n.

## scabious
scabious, adj., scabby. — L. scabiosus, 'rough,
scurfy, scabby', fr. scabies. See scabies and -ous.

## scabious
scabious, η., any of the plants of the Scabiosa. —
Fr. ML. scabiosa (scil. herba), lit. '(plant) for
the itch', fem. of L. scabiosus (see scabious, adj.);
so called in allusion to its alleged healing
properties.

## scabrous
scabrous, adj., scabby, scurfy. — L. scabrosus,
'rough, scabrous', fr. scaber, fem. scabra, neut.
scabrum, 'rough', fr. scabere, 'to scratch,
scrape*. See scabies and -ous.
Derivatives: scabrous-ly, adv., scabrous-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:686 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 6S9 | SCAPE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:686 COLUMN:1 -->

## scad
scad, п., 1) the saurel; 2) the horse mackerel. —
Prob. a var. of shad.

## scaffold
scaffold, n. — ME., fr. OF. eschafaud (F. echa-
faud), enlarged with pref. es- (F. έ-) fr. OF.
(— F.) chafaud, 'scaffold', which derives fr. VL.
catafalicum; see catafalque. The addition of the
pref. es- is due to the analogy of OF. eschace,
'wooden leg; stilt' (whence F. echasse, 'stilt').
Derivatives: scaffold, tr. v., scaffold-age, п.,
scaffold-er, п., scaffold-ing, n.

## scaglia
scaglia, п., Italian reddish limestone. — It.,
'scale, shell, chip, fragment, thin piece of
marble', fr. WTeut. *skalja (whence also F.,
ecaille, 'scale offish, oyster shell, tortoise shell*)
which corresponds to Goth, skalja, 'tile', OHG.
scala, 'shell, scale of fish'. See scale of fish.

## scagliola
scagliola, п., ornamental plaster work. — It.
scagliuola, dimin. οι scaglia. Seeprec. word.

## scalable
scalable, adj. — Formed fr. scale, v., with suff.
-able.

## scalar
scalar, adj., resembling a ladder. — L. scalaris,
'of, or belonging to, a ladder', fr. scala. See
scale, 'measure', and adj. suff. -ar.
Derivative: scalar, n.

## scalariform
scalariform, п., having the shape of a ladder. —
Compounded of L. scalaris, 'pertaining to a
scale', and forma, 'form, shape'. See prec. word
and form, n.

## scalawag
scalawag, scallawag, п., undersized cattle. —
Prob. a corruption of Scalloway in Shetland; so
called in allusion to the Shetland ponies.

## scald
scald, tr. v., to burn or injure with hot liquid. —
ME. scalden, fr. ONF. escalder, corresp. to OF.
eschalder (F. echauder), 'to scald', fr. Late L.
excalddre, fr. 1st ex- and calidus, caldus, 'warm'.
See caldron and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also scaldino.

## scald
scald, п., a scabby spot. — A later spelling of
scalled, pp. of scall.

## scald
scald, п., a Scandinavian poet. — See skald.
Derivative: scald-ic, adj.

## scaldino
scaldino, п., a small earthenware brazier. — It.,
fr. scaldare, 'to make warm', fr. Late L. excal-
ddre. See scald, 'to injure with hot liquid'.

## scale
scale, п., a weighing instrument. — ME. scale, fr.
ON. skal, 'shell, dish, scale of a balance*
(whence Dan. and Swed. skal, 'scale of a
balance', Dan. skaal, Swed. skal, 'drinking cup,
bowl'), which is rel. to OE. scalu, OS. skala,
OHG. scala, MHG. schale, G. Sckale, 'drinking
cup, bowl; shell, scale of a balance', MLG.
schale, MDu. scale, Du. schaal, 'drinking cup,
bowl, scale of a balance'; fr. Teut. *ske~lo-,
which—according to Paulus Diaconus—orig.
denoted 'a drinking cup made from a skull';
fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'to cut, cleave, split" (so
called in allusion to the skull as separated from
the other bones of the head). See Kluge-Mitzka,
EWDS., p. 633 s.v. Schale. See shelf, 'slab of
wood', and cp. words there referred to.Cp. also
scale of fish and skull. Cp. also seal], scaliop,
scalp, school of fishes, shale, shell, shellac, shield,
shoal, 'crowd', skill. Cp. also Scylla.
Derivatives: scale, tr. v., to weigh in scales;
intr. v., to be weighed.

## scale
scale, п., membraneous outgrowth of the skin of
fish, etc. — ME. scale, fr. OF. escale, 'cup,
scale, shell pod, husk' (whence F. ecale, 'shell,
hull, husk'), fr. Frankish skala, which is rel. to
OHG. scala, MHG. schal, G. Sckale, OE. scea-
lu, 'shell, husk', Goth, skalja, 'tile', orig,
'anything scalelike, shingles', and cogn. with OSlav.
skolika, 'mussel, shell', Russ. skala, 'rind,
bark'; fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'to cut, cleave,
split'. See scale, 'weighing instrument', and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also scaglia.
Derivatives: scale, tr. v., to clear of scales,
scale-less, adj., scal-er, п., scal-ing, п., scal-y,
adj., scal-i-ness, n.

## scale
scale, п., measure. — ME., 'ladder, staircase', fr.
L. scalae (pi.) (either directly or through the
medium of It. scala), 'ladder, staircase', fr.
*scand-sla, a derivative of scandere, 'to climb'.
See scan and cp. escalade, escalator.
Derivatives: scale, tr. v., to climb up by a ladder,
scal-er, п., scal-ing, n.

## scalene
scalene, adj., having unequal sides (geom.) —
Late L. scalenus, fr. Gk. σκαληνός, 'limping,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:686 COLUMN:2 -->
halting, uneven', which is rel. to σκέλος, 'leg'
(lit. 'bending'), σκόλιος, 'crooked, bent', σκώ-
ληξ, 'worm', fr. I.-E. base *{s)qel-, 'crooked,
curved, bent, perverted'. See colon, 'punctuation
mark', and cp. scelerat, scolex, scolion, scoliosis
and the second element in isoceles, triskelion.
Derivatives: scalene, п., scalen-ous, adj.

## scalenus
scalenus, п., name of each of the muscles situated
on either side of the neck (anat.)— Medical L., fr
Gk. σκαληνός, 'uneven; triangle having unequal
sides'; see prec. word. — In its anatomical
sense the word scalenus was first used by the
French anatomist Jean Riolan (Secundus)
(1577-1657), who gave this name to the whole of
these muscles, because they have the shape of a
scalene triangle. See Joseph Hyrtl, Onomatolo-
gia Anatomica, pp. 462-463.

## scall
scall, п., scurf, esp. of the scalp. — ME., fr. ON.
skalli, 'a bald head', whence also Swed. skallig,
'bald'; rel. to scale of balance and scale of fish.
Cp. scald, 'scabby'.

## scallion
scallion, п., shallot. — ME. scalyon, fr. ONF. es·
calogne, fr. L. Ascalonia (caepa), '(onion) of As-
calon'. See shallot.

## scallop
scallop, п., a bivalve mollusk (genus Pecten).—
ME. scalop, fr. OF. escalope, 'shell*, rel. to
escale, 'cup, scale offish, shell, husk'. See scale
of fish and cp. scaglia, escalop.
Derivatives: scallop, tr. v., scallop-er, п.,
scallop-ing, n. and adj.

## scalp
scalp, п., the skin of the top of the head, usually
covered with its hair. — ME., of Scand. origin.
Cp. ON. skulpr, 'sheath', dial. Dan. skalp,
'shell', and MDu. schelpe, Du. schelp, of s.m.;
rel. to scale, 'weighing instrument', scale offish.
Derivatives: scalp, tr. v., scalp-er, п., scalp-ing,
adj., scalp-less, n.

## scalpel
scalpel, п., a small surgical knife. — L. scalpellum,
dimin. of scalprum, 'knife, chisel', fr. scalpere,
'to cut, carve, scrape', which is rel. to sculpere,
'to carve'. See sheif, 'horizontal slab', and cp.
words there referred to.

## scalper
scalper, Α., a surgical instrument. — L. scalprum,
'knife'. See prec. word and cp. scauper.

## scamiilus
scamiilus, n. (arckit.) — L., 'little bench', dimin.
of scamnum, 'bench'. See shamble, n.

## scammony
scammony, п., a gum resin. — ME. scamonie, fr.
L. scammonia or scammonium, fr. Gk. σκαμ-
μωνίά or σκαμ,μώνιον.

## scamp
scamp, п., rogue, rascal. — Prob. back formation
fr. scamper.
Derivatives: scamp-ish, scamp-y, adjs.

## scamp
scamp, tr. v., to do (something) in a hasty,
careless way. — Prob. a blend of scant and skimp.

## scamper
scamper, intr. v., to run quickly. — Prob. fr.
obsol. Du. schampen, 'to run away, flee', fr.
ONF. escamper, corresponding to OF. escham-
per, 'to run away, fiee', lit. 'to leave the field',
fr. VL. *excampdre, fr. 1st ex- and L. campus,
'field'. See camp and cp. scamp, 'rogue'. For
sense development cp. decamp. The suff. -er in
scamper is frequentative.
Derivatives: scamper, п., scamper-er, n.

## scan
scan, tr. v., 1) to analyze (verse) as to its metrical
structure; 2) to examine carefully; intr. v., to
verse. — L. scandere, 'to climb, mount, scan'
(whence ascendere, 'to climb up, mount', di-
scendere, 'to come down, descend'), fr. I.-E.
base *skand-, 'to spring, leap', whence also 01.
skandati, 'hastens, leaps, jumps', Gk. σκάνδαλον
(whence L. scandalum), 'stumbling block
offense', Mir. sescaind, 'he sprang, jumped',
scendim, Ί spring, jump', sceinm, 'a bound,
jump', W. cy-chwynnu, 'to jump up, start up'.
The omission of the -din E. scan (for scan-d) is
prob. due to its having been confused with the
suff. -ed. For a similar omission of the final -d
cp. lawn, 'stretch of grass'. Cp. ascend,
condescend, descend, descent, escalade, escalator, scale,
'measure', scandal, scandent, scansion,
scantling, slander, transcend.
Derivatives: scann-able, adj., scann-er, п., scann-
ing-ly, adv.

## scandal
scandal, n. — F. scandale, fr. Late L. scandalum,
'cause of offense or stumbling', fr. Gk.
σκάνδαλον, 'stumbling block offense'. See scan and cp.
slander, which is a doublet of scandal. Cp. also
esclandre.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:686 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: scandal, tr.v., scandalize (q.v.),
scandalous (q.v.)

## scandalize
scandalize, tr. v. — F. scandaliser, fr. Late L.
scandalizdre, fr. Gk. σκανδαλίζειν, 'to cause
offense to', fr. σκάνδαλον. See scandal and -ize.
Derivatives: scandaliz-ation, п., scandaliz-er, n.

## scandalous
scandalous, adj. — F. scandaleux (fem. scanda-
leuse), fr. scandal. See scandal and -ous.
Derivatives: scandalous-ly, adv.,
scandalousness, n.

## scandaroon
scandaroon, п., a carrier pigeon. — Fr. Scander-
oon or Iskanderun, a town in Syria named after
Alexander the Great. Accordingly, the original
meaning of scandaroon was 'a pigeon from
Scanderoon or Iskanderun'. (A regular pigeon-
post service was established between this town
and Aleppo in Syria).

## scandent
scandent, adj., climbing (said esp. of a plant). —
L. scandens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of scandere,
'to climb*. See scan and -ent.

## scandia
scandia, п., the oxide of scandium, Scs03 (chem.)
— ModL., coined by its discoverer, the Swedish
physicist Lara Fredrik Nilson (1840-99) in 1879
fr. ML. Scandia, 'Scandinavia' (fr. L. Scandia,
name of an island in Northern Europe). See
Scandian, Scandinavia and cp. scandium.
Derivative: scandic, adj.

## Scandian
Scandian, adj. and п., Scandinavian. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. Scandia, a collateral form of
Scandinavia. See next word.

## Scandinavia
Scandinavia, n. — L. Sca{n)dinavia, name of an
island in Northern Europe (prob. Zealand or
Schonen), in ML. 'Scandinavia', from a Teut.
form of ON. Skaney, name of a district in
Southern Sweden, a compound word whose
second element is identical with ON. ey, 'island'.
Cp. OE. eg, ig, leg, 'island', the ending -ey in
Jerjsey and in other names of islands, OHG.
auwia, ouwa, 'island, damp meadow', and the
first element in G. Ei-land, 'island', and see
island. Cp. Scandian, scandium.
Derivatives: Scandinavi-an, adj. and n.

## scandium
scandium, п., name of a metallic element
belonging to the rare earth group {chem.) — ModL.,
coined by its discoverer Nilson in 1879. See
scandia. Both scandia and scandium were
discovered by Nilson in the same year, but the
discovery of the former preceded that of the
latter (see J. N. Friend, Man and the Chemical
Elements, London, 1951, p. 172).

## Scandix
Scandix, п., a genus of plants, the Venus' comb
(pot.) — ModL., fr. L. scandix, 'chervil', fr. Gk.
σκάνδιξ.

## scansion
scansion, п., act or mode of scanning. — L. scan-
sio, gen. -onis, 'a climbing; scanning', fr. scdns-
(um)t pp. stem of scandere, 'to climb'. See scan
and -ion.
Derivative: scansion-ist, n.

## scansorial
scansorial, adj., adapted for climbing (said of
birds). — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. scdn-
sorius, fr. scdns-(um), pp. stem of scandere, *to
climb'. See scan.

## scant
scant, adj. — Late ME., fr. ON. skammt, skamt,
neut. of skammr, 'short', which is rel. to ON.
skemma, OHG. skemmin, 'to shorten'; cp.
scamp, 'to do in a hasty way', skimp. For a
similar use of the ON. neut. suff. -t cp. want.
Derivatives: scant, tr. v., scant-ly, adj., scant-
ness, п., scant-i-ly, adv., scant-i-ness, n.

## scantling
scantling, п., 1) a small quantity; 2) a small
timber; 3) small timbers collectively. —
Corruption of OF. escantillon (F. echantillon), 'sample,
pattern', fr. earlier eschandillon, a dimin. whose
primitive form occurs in OProvenc. escandil,
'measure of capacity', fr. L. scandere, 'to climb*,
used in the sense 'to measure the scale of
something'. Cp. ML. scandilia, 'rungs of a ladder',
scandalium, 'measure of capacity', and see scan.
See Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p. 200 s.v.
echantillon.

## scape
scape, п., shaft, stem. — L. scapus, 'stalk, shaft',
which is cogn. with Gk. σκαπος, 'staff', σκηττ-
τρον, 'staff, scepter', σκήπτειν, 'to prop,
support'. See shaft, 'stem, stock*, and cp. words
there referred to.

## scape
scape, п., scenery. — Back formation fr.
landscape (as if it were a compound of land and
scape); used to form new compounds; seascape,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:687 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SCAPE | 660 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:687 COLUMN:1 -->
cloudscape, etc.

## scape
scape, п., an escape; tr. and intr. v., to escape. —
Aphetic form of escape.

## scapegoat
scapegoat, n. — For escape goat (see prec. word),
hence lit. meaning 'a goat allowed to escape
(into the wilderness)', coined by Tyndale to
render Heb. 'dzdzel in Lev. 16:8, 10 and 26.
This rendering is traceable to Luther (der ledig'e
Bock), Sebastian Miinster (caper abiturus),
Jerome (caper emissarius), Symmachus [τράγος
απερχόμενος (16:8), resp. τράγος άφιέμενος
(16:10)], and is based on a false derivation of
Heb. '.azdzel from 'ez-ozel, 'a departing goat'.
See scape, 'escape'.

## scapegrace
scapegrace, n. — For escape grace, used in the
sense of 'one who has escaped grace'.
scapho», before a vowel scaph-, combining form
meaning 'boat-shaped', as in scapkocepkalic. —
Gk. σκάφο-, σκαφ-, fr. σκάφη, 'boat', prob.
meaning lit. 'dug out', and derived from the
stem of σκάπτειν, 'to dig out'. See capon and
cp. scyphus and the second element in
bathyscaphe.

## scaphocephalic
scaphocephalic, scaphocephalous, adj., having a
boat-shaped head (anal.) — See scapho- and
cephalic, resp. -cephalous.'

## scaphoid
scaphoid, adj., boat-shaped (said of bones). —
Compounded of scaph- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: scaphoid, n.

## scapula
scapula, п., shoulder blade (anat. and zool.) —
Late L., 'shoulder blade, shoulder', sing, of L.
scapulae, 'shoulder blades, shoulders', which is
of uncertain origin. It possibly meant orig.
'shovel', and is cogn. with Gk. σκάφειν, 'to dig
out'; see scapho-. The change of meaning from
'shovel' to 'shoulder blades, shoulders', may be
due either to the resemblance of these bones to
shovels or to the use made of them by primitive
man for digging and shoveling. See Walde-
Hofmann. LEW., II, pp. 489-90 s.v. scapulae,
and Emout-Meillet, DELL., p. 600 s.v. scapulae.

## scapular
scapular, adj., pertaining to the shoulder blade or
shoulder. — Late L. scapuldris, fr. scapula. See
prec. word and adj. sun", -ar.
Derivative: scapular, n.

## scapular
scapular, scapulary, п., a short cloak worn by
monks (Eccles.) — ME. scapulare, fr. ML. sea-
puldre, lit. 'anything worn over the shoulders',
fr. L. scapulae, 'shoulders'. See scapula and -ar,
resp. -ary.

## scapulo-
scapulo-, combining form denoting the shoulder
blade. — L. scapulo-, fr. scapulae, 'shoulder
blades, shoulders'. See scapula.

## scapus
scapus, п., 1) the shaft of a feather; 2) the basic
foot of a polyp (zool.) — L. 'shaft, stem'. See
scape, 'shaft'.

## scar
scar, п., mark left upon the skin after the healing
of a wound. — ME. escare, scar, fr. OF. escare
(F. escarre, eschare), fr. Late L. eschara, fr. Gk.
έσχάρϊ, 'hearth, brazier, scar', esp. 'scarcaused
by burning', which is of uncertain etymology;
influenced in form by obsol. E. scar, 'cleft'. Cp.
eschar.
Derivatives: scar, tr. and intr. v., scarr-ed, adj.,
scarr-ing, п., scarr-y, adj.

## scar
scar, п., rock. «- ME., fr. ON. sker, 'reef, cliff'.
See skerry and cp. scaur.

## scarab
scarab, п., a beetle, esp. the black dung beetle
held sacred by the ancient Egyptians. — F.
scarabde, fr. L. scarubaeus, fr. Gk. κάραβος,
'horned beetle; crayfish', a word of foreign
(prob. Maced.) origin, as proved by the non-
Greek suff. -bos (the Greek equivalent would
have been -φος, fr. I.-E. *bho-). See Cnrabidae
and cp. caravel, caracole, Caridea.

## scarabaetd
scarabaetd, п., any beetle belonging to the family
Scarabaeidae — See next word.

## Scarabaeidae
Scarabaeidae, n. pi., a family of beetles (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. L. scarabaeus. See scarab and
-idae.

## scarahaeold
scarahaeold, adj., resembling a scarab. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. scarabaeus, 'scarab', and Gk.
suff. -οει,δής, 'like', fr. εϊϊος, 'form, shape'. See
scarab and -old.

## Scaramouch
Scaramouch, п., 1) a stock character in the old
Italian comedy; 2) (not cap.) a boastful
poltroon. — F. Scaramouche, fr. It. Scaramuccia, a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:687 COLUMN:2 -->
stock character in Italian farces, lit. 'the
skirmisher'. See skirmish, n.

## scarce
scarce, adj. — ME. scars, fr. ONF. escars,
corresponding to OF. eschars, F. ichars, 'scanty,
scarce', fr. VL. *escarpsus, for L. excerptus,
'picked out, selected, rare', pp. of excerpere, 'to
pick out, select'. See excerpt.
Derivatives: scarce-ly, adv., scarce-ness, n.

## scarcement
scarcement, п., an offset in the wall
(architecture). — Prob. formed from the obsol. verb
scarce, 'to make less', fr. scarce, adj. See scarce
and -inent.

## scarcity
scarcity, n. — ME. scarsete, fr. ONF. escarcete,
fr. escars. See scarce and -ity.

## scare
scare, tr. v., to frighten. — ME. skerren, 'to
frighten', fr. ON. skirra, which is rel. to ON.
skjarr, 'timid'; of uncertain origin. Cp. the
second element in harum-scarum.
Derivative: scar-ed, adj., scar-er, n.

## scare
scare, п., fright. — ME. skerre, fr. skerren, 'to
frighten'. See scare, v.
Derivatives: scare-ful, scar-y, adjs.

## scarf
scarf, п., band of silk or other material. — ONF.
escarpe (F. echarpe), fr. OF. escherpe, 'pilgrim's
scrip', fr. Late L. scirpa, fr. L. scirpea, 'basket
made of rushes', fern, of scirpeus, 'made of
rushes', fr. scirpus, 'rush'. See Scirpus and cp.
sarpier and scrip, 'bag'. G. Scharpe, 'scarf, is
borrowed fr. F. echarpe.

## scarf
scarf, п., scarf joint. — ME. skarf, of Scand.
origin. Cp. ON. skarfr, Swed. skarf, Norw. skarv,
'piece added to a board or garment', which are
rel. to OE. scearfian, 'to scrape', sceorfan, 'to
gnaw, bite', fr. I.-E. base *sqer(e)p-, whence
also OSIav. iripu, 'crock, fragment, potsherd',
Lett, skirpta, 'crack, fissure'. I.-E. *sqer(e)p- is
a -p-enlargement of base *sqer-, 'to cut'. See
carnal and cp. carpel and words there referred
to.

## scarification
scarification, n. — See scarify and -ation.

## scarificator
scarificator, n. — See scarify and -ator.

## scarify
scarify, tr. v., to make a number of superficial
punctures in the skin (surg.) — MF. (= F.)
scarifier, fr. L. scarificdre, a collateral form of
scarifdre, 'to scratch open', fr. Gk. σκαριφκσ*αι,
ft. σκάρΐφος, 'a stile for drawing outlines, a
sketch', which is cogn. with L. scribere, 'to
write'. See scribe. For the ending οι scarify see
-fy. The Latin form scarificdre shows the
influence of sacrificdre, 'to sacrify'. For the ending
of scarify see suff. -fy.
Derivative: scarifi-er, n.

## scarious
scarious, adj., dry, shriveled. — F. scarieux
(fem. scarieuse), fr. ML. scariosus, fr. L. scoria,
*a thorny shrub'. For the ending see suff. -ous.

## scarlatina
scarlatina, п., scarlet fever (med.) — Medical L.,
Latinized fr. scarlet by the English physician
Thomas Sydenham (1624-89).

## scarlet
scarlet, n. — ME. scarlat, scarlet, fr. OF. escar-
late (F. icarlate); fr. ML. scarlatum (whence
also It. scarlatto); from Pers. saqirldt, itself
borrowed fr. Arab, siqillit, 'tissue adorned with
seals', which is a loan word fr. L. sigillatus,
'sealed', pp. of sigilldre, 'to seal', fr. sigillum (for
*signoiom), 'seal', dimin. of signum, 'sign'. See
sign and cp. suclat, clclatoun.
Derivatives: scarlet, adj., scarlet-y, adj,

## scaroid
scaroid, adj., pertaining to the Scaridae; п., а
scaroid fish. — See Scarus and -oid.

## scarp
scarp, п., a steep slope; an escarpment. — It.
Scarpa, whence also OF. escarpe. See escarp, п.,
and cp. counterscarp.

## scarp
scarp, tr. v., to cut in a steep slope. — Fr. prec.
word. Cp. escarp, v.

## Scarus
Scarus, п., the genus of parrot fishes (ichthyol.)
— L. scarus, name of a fish fr. Gk. σκάρος, 'the
parrot fish', lit. 'the leaping one'; rel. to σκα£-
ρειν, 'to leap, skip, bound', σκιρταν (freq. of
σκαίρειν), 'to leap, bound', άσκαρίς, 'worm in
the intestines', σκαρίζειν," Att. άσκαρίζείν, 'to
jump', fr. I.-E. base *sqer-, 'to leap, jump,
bound', whence also Lith. skerps, 'locust', lit.
'the leaping one' (cp. F. sauterelle, 'locust', fr.
sauter, 'to leap, jump'), OSIav. skortt, 'quick',
skoro, 'quickly, soon', OE. secge-scere, 'locust',
OHG. sceron, 'to be frolicsome', MLG. scheren,
'to run away quickly', G. sick scheren, 'to go
away'. Cp. scherzo. Cp. also Ascaridae and the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:687 COLUMN:3 -->
first element in Scirtopoda. Cp. also cardinal,
adj., and words there referred to.

## scat
scat, п., tax, tribute. — ON. skaltr, rel. to OE.
sceatt, 'property, money, tribute', OS. scat,
'piece of money, money, possession', Dan. skat,
Swed. skatt, 'treasure', MDu. scat, Du. schat,
'treasure', OHG. skaz, 'piece of money, money',
G. Schatz, 'treasure', Goth, skatts, 'piece of
money, money', fr. Teut. *skatta, which orig.
meant 'cattle' (cp. OSIav. skotu, 'cattle', which is
a Teut. loan word). Teut. "skatta ult. derives
fr. I.-E. base *sqet-, 'to gush, spring, bubble,
yield, result', whence also Lith. skastu, skasti,
'to leap, jump', archaic L. scatere, L. scatere, 'to
gush, spring, bubble', Gk. σκαταμίζειν (in
Hesychius), 'to leap, jump'. For sense
development cp. result, fr. F. resulter, fr. L. resultare,
'to spring back'. See Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p.
638 s.v. Schatz. Cp. scatula, scaturient.

## scat
scat, п., a blow, sound of explosion. — Of
imitative origin.

## scathe
scathe, п., injury, damage (archaic or dial.) —
ME. skathe, fr. ON. skadi, rel. to Dan. skade,
Swed. skada, OE. sceadu, OFris. skatha, OS.
skatho, MDu. scade, Du. schade, OHG. scado,
MHG. schade, G. Schade(n), Goth, skapis,
'injury, damage'. The only cognate outside
Teut. is Gk. ά-σκη&ής, 'unharmed, unscathed'.
Cp. next word.
Derivatives: scathe-ful, adj., scathe-less, adj.

## scathe
scathe, tr. v., to injure, damage (archaic or dial.)
— ME. skathen, fr. ON. skada, which is rel. to
OE. sceadian, OS. skathon, OFris. skethia, MDu.
scaden, Du. schaden, OHG. skadon, skaden,
MHG., G. schaden, Goth, skapjan, 'to injure,
damage', and to ON. skadi, 'injury, damage'.
See scathe, n.
Derivatives: scath-tng, adj., scath-ing-iy, adv.

## scatology
scatology, п., the study of fossilized excrement;
obscene literature. — Compounded of Gk.
σκώρ, gen. σκατάς, 'dung', and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. The first
element is rel. to σκωρία, 'dross of metal, slag';
see scoria and cp. skatol. For the second
element see -logy.
Derivatives: scatolog-ic, scatolog-ic-al, adjs.

## scatophagous
scatophagous, adj., dung-eating (said of certain
insects). — See prec. word and -phagous.

## scatter
scatter, tr. and intr. v. — ME. scateren, schateren.
See shatter.
Derivatives: scatter, п., scatter-ed, adj., scatter-
ed-ly, adv., scatter-ed-ness, п., scatter-er, п.,
scatter-ing, n. and adj., scatter-ing-ly, adv.,
scatter-y, adj.

## scatula
scatula, п., box used to dispense medicine
(pharm.) — ML., lit. 'box', esp. 'money box',
of Teut. origin. Cp. Goth, skatts, 'piece of
money, money*, OE. sceatt, 'property, money,
tribute', and see scat, 'tax, tribute'.

## scaturient
scaturient, adj., gushing forth. — L. scaturiens,
gen. -ends, pres. part, of scaturire, 'to stream,
gush forth', fr. scatere, 'to gush, spring'. See
scat, 'tax, tribute', and -ent and cp. prec. word.

## scauper
scauper, п., a kind, of engraving tool. — A var.
of scalper.

## scaur
scaur, п., reef, cliff. — A var. of scar.

## scavage
scavage, п., a toll formerly levied on foreign
merchants on goods offered for sale (Old Engl,
law) — ME. skawage, fr. AF. scawage, ff. dial.
OF. escauwage, 'inspection', fr. escauwer, 'to
inspect', which is of Teut. origin; cp. OHG.
scouwdn, OE. sceawian, 'to look at*, and see
show and -age. Cp. scavenger.
Derivatives: scavage, tr. and intr. v., scavag-er,
п., scavag-ery, n.

## scavenge
scavenge, tr. v., to clean (streets, alleys, etc.)
from filth; intr. v., to act as a street cleans. —
Back formation fr. scavenger.
Derivative: scavenge, n.

## scavenger
scavenger, n., one who cleans the
streets.—Formed with intrusive η fr. ME. scavager, hence
etymologically identical with scavager (see
scavage and agential suff. -er). Originally the
scavenger was an officer who had to supervise
street cleaning. For the intrusive η ср.
messenger, passenger, porringer.
Derivatives: scavenger, intr. v., scavenger-y, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:688 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 661 | SCHNITZEL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:688 COLUMN:1 -->

## scavenger's daughter
scavenger's daughter, an instrument of torture. —
Corrupted fr. Skevington's daughter; so called
from its inventor Leonard Skevington, a
lieutenant of the Tower under Henry VIII.

## scazon
scazon, п., 1) a choliambic verse; 2) an iambic
verse ending with a spondee (prosody). — L., fr.
Gk. σκάζων, prop, 'limping (verse)', pres. part,
of σκάζειν (for *sqng,ein), to limp', which is
cogn. with OI. khdnjati, 'limps', ON. hinka, 'to
limp', OHG. kinkan, MHG., G. hinken, 'to
limp'. Cp. shank.

## scelerat
scelerat, п., a villain (archaic). -~ F. scelerat, fr.
L. scehrdtus, pp. of scelerdre, 'to pollute, defile,
desecrate', fr. scelus, gen. sceleris, 'evil deed,
crime, sin', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'to bend,
curve; crooked, bent, curved, perverted'. See.
colon, 'punctuation mark', and cp. words there
referred to.

## scenario
scenario, п., outline of the plot of a play. — It.,
ft. Late L. scendrius, 'of stage scenes', fr. L.
scaena, scena. See scene.
Derivative: scenar-ist, n.

## scene
scene, n. — MF. scene (F. scene), fr. L. scaena,
scena, 'stage, scene', fr. Gk. σκηνή, 'tent, booth,
stage', which is rel. to σκιί, 'shade', fr. I.-E.
base *skd(i), *sk i-, *ski-, 'to shine, flicker,
glimmer', whence also OI. chdya, 'brilliance,
luster; shadow', Toch. B. skiyo. Alb. he,
'shadow', Goth, skeinan, ОЁ. scinan, 'to shine'. See
shine and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
proscenium, mise-en-scene.

## scenery
scenery, n. — Fr. earlier scenary, fr. L. scendrius,
'pertaining to the stage', fr. scaena, scena. See
scene and -ery and cp. scenario.

## scenic
scenic, adj. — F. scenique, fr. L. scaenuus, sceni-
cus, fr. Gk. σκηνικός, fr. σκηνή. See scene and
-ic.
Derivatives: scenic-al, adj., scenic-al-ly, adv.

## scenograph
scenograph, п., a perspective picture. — Back
formation fr. scintigraphy.
Derivative: scenograph-er, n.

## scenographic
scenographic, adj./pertaining to scenography. —
F. scenograpkique, fr. Gk. σκηνογραφικός,
'pertaining to scene-painting', fr. σκηνογραφία.
See next word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: scenographic-al-ly, adv.

## scenography
scenography, п., painting in perspective. — F.
scinographie, fr. L. scaenographia, fr. Gk.
σκηνογραφία, 'scene-painting', which is
compounded of σκηνή, 'stage, scene', and -γραφιά,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See scene and -graphy.

## scent
scent, tr. and intr. v. — ME. semen, fr. OF. (=
F.) sentir, 'to feel, to smell', fr. L. senttre, 'to
feel'. See sense. The с in the present English
spelling shows the influence of the spelling of
the word science. For a similar insertion of the
letter с ср. scythe.
Derivatives: scent, п., scent-ed, adj., scent-er, п.,
scent-ful, adj., scent-less, adj.

## scepter
scepter, sceptre, n. — ME. sceptre, septre, fr. OF.
(= F.) sceptre, fr. L. sceptrum, fr. Gk. σκήπ-
τρον, 'a royal staff, scepter', fr. σκήπτειν, 'to
prop, support', σκήπτεσ&αι, 'to lean upon',
which is cogn. with OE. sceaft, See shaft, 'stem,
stock', and cp. words there referred to.

## sceptic
sceptic, adj. and n. — See skeptic.

## schanz
schanz, п., breastwork of stones. — S. Aft. Du.,
fr. Du. schans, rel. to G. Schanze, fr. It. scanso,
'warding off, defense', which is rel. to scan-
sare, 'to go out of the way', fr. VL. "ex-
campsdre, fr. 1st ex- and L. campsdre, 'to
turn around a place, to sail by', which
derives fr. Gk. κάμψαι, aorist of κάμπτειν, 'to
bend'. Gk. κάμπτειν is cogn. with L. campus,
'field', orig. 'a bending'. See camp and words
there referred to and cp. sconce, 'cover', which
is a doublet of schanz.

## schapska
schapska, п., Polish cavalry helmet. — Pol.
czapka, rel. to Czech tapka, Russ. shapka, fr.
G. Schappe, fr. F. chape, 'cope, cover, cap'.
See cape, 'cloak', chape.

## schatchen
schatchen, п., a marriage broker. — Yiddish, fr.
ModHeb. shaddekhdn, fr. Mishnaic Heb. shid-
dekh, 'he negotiated or arranged a marriage',

## lit. 'he quieted
lit. 'he quieted, appeased, pacified', rel. to Aram.

## shsdakh
shsdakh, 'he was appeased, quiet', shaddekh, 'he

## appeased
appeased, quieted'.

## Schecbinah
Schecbinah, n. — See Shekinah.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:688 COLUMN:2 -->

## Schedius
Schedius, п., a genus of very small flies (entomol.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. σχέδιος, 'off-hand, at
random, hasty', fr. σχεδόν, 'near, hard by', prop,
'that which one has at hand', formed from the
stem of έχειν, 'to have' (fut. 2ξω and σχήσω),
and the adverbial suff. -δόν. See scheme.

## schedule
schedule, n. — L. schedula, 'a small leaf of paper',
dimin. of scheda, scida, 'a strip of papyrus bark,
a leaf of paper', fr. Gk. σχίδη, 'splintei of
wood', from the stem of σχίζειν, 'to cleave,
split'. See shed, v., and cp. schism. For the
ending see suff. -ule. Fr. ML. cedula, a simplified
form of L. schedula, derive It. cedola, Sp. cedula,
F. cedule, 'schedule'. Cp. cedula.
Derivatives: schedule, tr. v., schedul-ar, adj.,
schedul-ize, tr. and intr. v.
.scheellte, п., calcium tungstate CaW04 (mineral.)
— Named after its discoverer, the Swedish
chemist Karl Wilhelm Scheele (1742-86). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## schefferite
schefferite, п., a brown manganese pyroxene
(mineral.) — Named after.its discoverer the
Swedish chemist Η. Τ. Scheffer (1710-59). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## schema
schema, п., scheme. — See scheme,

## schematic
schematic, adj. — ModL. schematics, fr. L.
schema, gen. schemaxis. See scheme and -ic.
Derivative: schematic-al-ly, adv.

## schematism
schematism, n. -— ModL. schematisms, fr. Gk.
σχηματισμός, 'configuration; bearing,
attitude', fr. σχηματίζειν, 'to form, shape,
fashion', fr. σχήμα, gen. σχήματος. See next word.

## scheme
scheme, n. — L. schema, 'shape, figure, form,
figure of speech', fr. Gk. σχήμα, gen. σχήματος,
'form, shape, figure, the nature of a thing',
formed fr. σχη-, stem of ε'χειν, 'to have, hold,
possess' (aorist έσχον, fut. έξω and σχήσω),
fr. I.-E. base *segh-, 'to hold, hold in one's
power, have', whence also OI. sdhate, 'he
masters', sdhah, 'power, victory', Avestic hazah, of
s.m., Goth, sigis, OHG. sigu, sigo, MHG. sic,
sige, G. Sieg, MDu. seghe, Du. zege, OFris. si,
ON. sigr, Swed. seger, Dan. seier, OE. sige,
'victory'. Cp. hectic and words there referred to.
Cp. also ischo-, Schedius, school, 'place of
learning', sketch, and the second element in
cachexy, epoch, eunuch, pleonexia, Stylochus.
Cp. also the first element in Sigismund.
Derivatives: scheme, tr. and intr. v., schem-er,
п., schem-ing, adj. and п., schem-ing-ly, adv.,
schem-isi, n.

## scherzando
scherzando, adv. and adj., in a playful manner
(mus.) —-It., gerund of scherzare, 'to play,
sport', fr. scherzo, 'jest, sport'. See next word.

## scherzo
scherzo, п., a playful movement in a sonata or
symphony (mus.) — It., fr. G. Scherz, 'jest,
sport', fr. Late MHG. scherz, of s.m., which is
rel. to MHG. scherzen, 'to jump with joy; to

## jest' (whence G. scherzen
jest' (whence G. scherzen, 'to jest'), and to
MHG. scharz, schurz, 'jump', ON. skart,
'boastful attitude', fr. a -[/-enlargement of I.-E. base
*(s)qer-, 'to leap, jump, bound', whence Gk.
σκαίρειν, 'to leap, skip, bound'. See Scarus and
cp. cardinal, adj. Cp. also scorn.

## Scheuchzeria
Scheuchzeria, п., a genus of plants (bot.) —
ModL., named after the Swiss botanists Johann
Scheuchzer (died in 1738) and his brother Johann
Jakob Scheuchzer (1672-1733). For the ending
see 1 st suff -ia.

## Scheuchzeriaceae
Scheuchzeriaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## scheuchzeriaceous
scheuchzeriaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Schiedam
Schiedam, п., Holland gin. — Prop, gin made at
Schiedam, a town in Holland.

## schiller
schiller, п., a bronzelike luster.—G., fr. schillern,
'to change colors', fr. MHG. schillen, a
collateral form of schilhen (G. schielen), 'to blink,
wink, squint', which is rel. to OHG. scelah,
MHG. schel, G. scheel, 'squint-eyed', fr. I.-E.
base "sqel-, 'crooked, curved', whence also Gk.
σκαληνός, 'limping, halting, uneven'. See
scalene and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: schiller-ize, tr. v., schiller-iz-ation,
n.

## schindylesis
schindylesis, п., a form of articulation in which
one bone is received into a fissure of .another

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:688 COLUMN:3 -->
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. 'Gk. σχινδώλησις, 'a
cleaving into small pieces', fr. *σχινδύλειν, 'to
cleave', fr. σχίζειν, 'to .split, cleave', which is
cogn. with L. scindere, 'to cleave'. See schism
and cp. words there referred to.

## schindyletic
schindyletic, adj. — See prec. word and -ic.

## schipperke
schipperke, п., a kind of small dog bred in
Holland. — Du., dimin. of schipper, prop,
'little skipper' (see skipper); so called because
used as a watchdog on barges.

## schism
schism, n. — Late ME. scisme, fr. MF. scisme
(F. schisme), fr. OF. cisme, scisme, fr. Late L.
schisma, fr. Gk. σχίσμα, 'a split, rent, cleft',
from the stem of σχίζειν, 'to split, rend,
cleave'. See shed, v., and words there referred
to and cp. esp. schedule.

## schismatic
schismatic, adj. — ME. scismatike, fr. MF. scis-
matique (F. schismatique), fr. Late L. schisma-
ticus, fr. Gk. σχισματικός, fr. σχίσμα, gen.
σχίσματος. See prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: schismatic, п., schismatic-al, adj.,
schismatic-al-ly, adv.

## schismatism
schismatism, n. — See prec. word and -ism.

## schismatize
schismatize, intr. v. — F. schismatiser, fr. Late L.
schisma. See schism and suff. -ize.

## schist
schist, п., a crystalline rock with a foliated
structure. — F. schiste, lit. 'that which easily splits',
fr. L. schistus, fr. Gk. σχιστός (scil. λί*ος), 'a
fissile stone', verbal adj. of σχίζειν, 'to split'.
See schism and -ist.

## schistose
schistose, adj., pertaining to schist; resembling
schist. — See prec. word and adj. suff. -ose.

## schistous
schistous, adj., schistose. — See prec. word and
-ous.

## schiz-
schiz-, form of schizo- before a vowel.

## Schizaen
Schizaen, п., a genus of plants,· the curly grass
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Gk. σχίζειν, 'to
split' (see schism); so called in allusion to the
many-cleft fronds.

## Schizaeaceae
Schizaeaceae, n. pi., the curly grass family (bot.)
— ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## schizaeaceous
schizaeaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Schlzanthus
Schlzanthus, п., a genus of plants, the fringe-
flower (bot.) — ModL., compounded of schiz-
and Gk. ίίν*ος, 'flower'. See anther.

## schizo-
schizo-, before a vowel schiz-, combining form
meaning 'division'. — Gk. σχιζο-, σχιζ-, fr.
σχίζειν, 'to split'. See schism.

## schisocarp
schisocarp, п., fruit that splits into several single-
seeded carpels (bot.) — Compounded of schizo-
and Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.
Derivatives: schizocarp-ic, adj., schizocarp-ous,
adj.

## schizogenesis
schizogenesis, п., reproduction by fission (bot.) —
Compounded of schizo- and genesis.

## schizoid
schizoid, adj., resembling schizophrenia (med.) —
Compounded of schizo, abbreviation of
schizophrenia, and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See schizophrenia and -oid.

## schizomycete
schizomycete, п., one of the Schizomycetes, a
bacterium. — See next word.

## Schizomycetes
Schizomycetes, n. pi., the bacteria (bot.) —
ModL., lit. 'fission-fungi', coined by the Swiss
botanist Karl Wilhelm von Naegeli (1817-91)
fr. schizo- and Gk. μύκητες, pi. of μύκης,
'fungus'. See -mycetes.

## schizophrenia
schizophrenia, п., a form of mental disorder. —
Medical L., lit. 'a splitting of the mind', a word
coined by the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler
(1857-1939) fr. schizo- and Gk. φρήν, gen.
φρενός, 'mind'. See schizo- and phrenic. For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.
Derivative: schizophren-ic, adj.

## schnapper
schnapper, п., a sea fish of Australia and New
Zealand. — Alteration of snapper after G.
Schnapper.

## schnapps
schnapps, п., a kind of Holland gin. — G.
Schnaps, lit. 'a mouthful, a gulp', fr. schnappen,
'to snap'. See* snap and cp. prec. word.

## schnauzer
schnauzer, п., a breed of terrier. — G. Schnauzer,
lit. 'snarler, growler', fr. schnauzen, 'to snarl,
growl', fr. Schnauze, 'snout, muzzle', which is
rel. to ME. snute, snoute, 'snout'. See snont and
agential suff. -er.

## schnitzel
schnitzel, п., a veal cutlet. — G. Schnitzel, lit. 'a
slice', fr. schnitzen, 'to carve, cut', freq. ofschnei-
den, 'to cut'. See snead.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:689 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SCHNORRER | 662 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:689 COLUMN:1 -->

## schnorrer
schnorrer, п., a Jewish beggar. — Yiddish, ft.
scknorren, 'to go begging', prop. 'to go begging
while playing a musical instrument', fr. schnur-
ren, 'to hum, whir', fr. MHG. snurren, of s.m.,
which is rel. to Du. snorren, of s.m.; of
imitative origin.

## scholar
scholar, n. — ME. scoler, fr. OF. escoler, escoiier
(F. ecolier), fr. Late L. scholdris, 'pertaining to a
school', fr. L. sckola, 'school'. See school, 'place
of learning', and -ar.
Derivatives: scholar-like, adj., scholar-ly, adj.
and adv., scholar-ship, n.

## scholastic
scholastic, adj. — L. scholaslicus, 'pertaining to a
school', fr. Gk. σχολαστικός, 'having leisure;
devoting one's leisure to learning, learned' (first
used in this sense by Theophrastus), fr. σχολή.
See school, 'place of learning', and adj. surf. -ic.
Derivatives: scholastic, п., scholastic-al, adj.,
scholastic-al-ly, adv., scholastic-ism, п., scholas-
tic-ly, adv.

## scholiast
scholiast, п., a writer of scholia. — ML. scholias-
ta, fr. Gk. σχολιαστής, fr. σχολιάζειν, 'to
write scholia', fr. σχόλιον. See next word and
-ast.

## scholium
scholium, п., an explanatory note. — ML., fr.
Gk. σχόλιον, 'note, comment, scholium', fr.
σχολή. See next word.

## school
school, п., a place of learning. — ME. scale, fr.
OE. seal, fr. L. schola, fr. Gk. σχολή, 'leisure,
spare time; leisure devoted to learning; place of
learning, school', formed fr. σχη-, the stem
of έχειν, 'to have, hold, possess' (whence aprist
ίσχον, fut. έξω and σχήσω), fr. I.-E.. base
*segk-, 'to hold, hold in one's power, to have',
whence also σχήμα, 'form, shape'. See scheme
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also the
second element in realschule.
Derivatives: school, tr. v., school-able, adj.,
sckool-ing, п., school-ing-ly, adv.

## school
school, п., a crowd of fish, shoal. — Fr. Du.
school. See shoal, 'a crowd'.

## schooner
schooner, п., a kind of sailing vessel. — Formed
with agential suff. -er fr. dial. E. scoon, 'to skim
along'; the orig. spelling of the word was
scooner. Scoon is a Scot, word and related to E.
shunt (q.v.) — For the history of the word
schooner see Walter W. Skeat, Etymological
Dictionary of the English Language, p. 540.
Du.. sckoener, G. Schoner, are English loan
words.

## schorl
schorl, п., black tourmaline. — G. Sckdrl, 01
unknown origin.

## schorlomite
schorlomite, п., an iron calcium titanate and
silicate {mineral.) — Compounded of schorl and
Gk. άμός, 'one and the same' (see homo-); so
called because it resembles schorl.

## schottische
schottische, п., 1) a round dance resembling
polka; 2) music for this dance. — Fr. G. schot-
tische(r) Tanz, 'Scottish dance'. See Scot,
Scottish.

## schuit
schuit, also schuyt, п., a Dutch vessel. — Du.
schuit. See scout, 'vessel'.

## schwa
schwa, also shwa, п., a half vowel (pronounced
like e in agent); indicated in Hebrew by the sign:
— Heb. shewd, prob. borrowed fr. Syr. slfway-
ya, lit. 'equal', name of the accent mark:, which
corresponds to the Heb. zaqeph. See ZDMG.,
1895 (vol. 49), p. 18, note 3. Syr. shlwayya
derives fr. Aram.-Syr. skewa, 'he was like or equal',
which is rel. to Heb. shawa, 'he was even, smooth
or like', Arab, sawwd, 'he made even or fiat'.
The name shfwayya was given to the accent
mark: in allusion to its form. — In this
dictionary schwa is transliterated by l.

## Schwalbea
Schwalbea, п., a genus of plants, the chaff-seed
(pot.) — ModL., named after the Dutch botanist
Christian Georg Schwalbe, who wrote on
botany in 1715.

## sci-
sci-, form of scio- before a vowel.

## Sciaenidae
Sciaenidae, n. pi., a family of fishes, comprising
the kingfishes, drumfishes, etc. (ichthyol.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. sciaena, 'a
kind of fish', prob. 'the grayling', fr. Gk.
σκίαινα, of s.m., fr. σκιά, 'shade, shadow'.
See skiap-aphy. For sense development cp. Cy-
noscion, umber, 'the grayling', and umbrette.

## sciagram
sciagram, sciagraph, sciagraphy, n.'s. — See
skiagram, skiagraph, skiagraphy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:689 COLUMN:2 -->

## sciamachy
sciamachy, п., fighting with shadows; sham
fighting. — Gk. σκιαμαχία, 'fighting in the shade;
fighting with shadows; a sham fight', fr. σκιά,
'shade, shadow', and μάχη, 'battle'. See
skiagraphy and -machia.

## sciametry
sciametry, n. — See skiametry.

## Sciara
Sciara, п., a genus of fungus gnats (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. σκιαρός, 'dark-colored', fr.
σκιά, 'shade'. See skiagraphy.

## sciascope
sciascope, sclascopy, n.'s — See skiascope,
skiascopy.

## scintic
scintic, adj., pertaining to the hip or hipjoint. —
MF. (= F.) sciatique, fr. ML. sciaticas, fr. L.
isckiadicus, fr. Gk. ίσχ'.αδικός, fr. ίσχιάς, gen.
-άδος, 'lumbago', fr. ΐσχίον, 'the hipjoint'. See
ischium.

## sciatica
sciatica, п., neuralgia of the sciatic nerve (med.)
— Medical L., fern, of sciaticas (see prec. word),
used as a noun.

## science
science, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) science, fr. L.
scientia, 'knowledge, science', fr. sciens, gen.
scientis, pres. part, of scire, 'to know', which
prob. meant orig. 'to separate one thing from
another, to distinguish', and is rel. to scindere,
'to cut, split, cleave', and cogn. with Gk.
σχίζειν, 'to split, rend, cleave', Goth, skaidan,
OE. sciadan, 'to divide, separate'. See shed, v.,
and cp. adscititious, conscience, conscient,
conscientious, conscious, nescient, nice, omniscience,
omniscient, plebiscite, prescience, prescient,
scienter, scientific, sciolism.

## scienter
scienter, adv., knowingly; п., knowledge [law). —
L., 'knowingly', formed fr. sciens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of scire, 'to know', with the adverbial
suff. -ter. See prec. word.

## sciential
sciential, adj., pertaining to knowledge. — L.
scientialis, fr. scientia. See science and adj. suff.
-a).

## scientific
scientific, adj. — Late L. scientificus, 'pertaining
to science' (prop, loan translation of Gk.
επιστημονικός, 'pertaining to knowledge', fr.
επιστήμη, 'knowledge'), fr. L. scientia. See science
and -flc.
Derivatives: scientific-al, adj., scientif-ic-al-ly,
adv., scienttfic-al-ness, n.

## scientism
scientism, п., methods of science. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. scientia, 'knowledge, science', and
-ism, a suff. of Greek origin. See science.

## scientist
scientist, n. — A hybrid coined by the English
philosopher William Whewell (1794-1866) from
L. scientia (see science) and Gk. suff. -ιστής.
(see -ist).
Derivatives: scientist-ic, adj., scientist-ic-al-ly,
adv.

## scilicet
scilicet, adv., that is to say, to wit, namely. — L.,
abbreviation of scire licet, 'it is permitted to
know', hence 'it is evident'. See science and
license and cp. videlicet and illicit.

## Scilla
Scilla, п., a genus of plants, the squill. — L., 'the
squill', fr. Gk. σκίλλα. See squill.

## scimitar
scimitar, п., a curved Oriental sword. — It. sci-
mitarra (whence also F. cimeterre), fr. Pers.
shimshir, 'scimitar, saber*.

## Scincidae
Scincidae, n. pi., a family of reptiles, the skinks
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L.
scincus, 'a kind of lizard'. See skink, n.

## scincoid
scincoid, adj., pertaining to the skinks. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. scincus (see prec. word) and
-Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
-oid.

## scintilla
scintilla, п., a spark (only used in a figurative
sense); particle, trace. — L., 'spark, a bright
point', prob. fr. 'skint-, fr. I.-E. base *ski-, 'to
shine', whence also Goth, skeinan, OE. scinan,
'to shine'. See shine and cp. stencil, tinsel.

## scintillant
scintillant, adj., sparkling. — L. scintillttns, gen.
■amis, pres. part, of scintilldre. See next word
and -ant.
Derivative: scintillant-ly, adv.

## scintillate
scintillate, intr. and tr. v., to sparkle. — L. scin-
tillat-(um), pp. stem of scintilldre, 'to emit
sparks, sparkle', fr. scintilla. See scintilla and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: scintillat-ing, adj., scintillat-ing-ly,
adv.

## scintillation
scintillation, п., a sparkling. — L. scintillatio, gen.
-onis, 'a sparkling', fr. scintillat-(um), pp. stem
of scintilldre. See prec. word and -ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:689 COLUMN:3 -->

## scio-
scio-, before a vowel sci-, combining form
meaning 'shadow', as in sciomancy. — Gk. σκιο-,
σκι-, fr. σκιά, 'shade, shadow'. See
skiagraphy.

## sciolism
sciolism, п., a show of knowledge. — Coined fr.
L. sciolus, 'a smatterer', and suff. -ism. L. sciolus
is a dimin. of scius, 'knowing', fr. scire, 'to know'.
See science and dimin. suff. -ole.

## sciolist
sciolist, п., a pretender to knowledge. — Coined
fr. L. sciolus and suff. -ist. See prec. word.
Derivative: sciolisi-ic, adj.

## sciomachy
sciomachy, n. — See sciamachy and scio-.

## sciomancy
sciomancy, п., divination by means of consulting
the shades of the dead. — ModL. sciomantia,
compounded of Gk. σκιά, 'shade, shadow',
and μαντεία, Oracle, divination'. See scio- and
-mancy.

## scion
scion, n. — ME., fr. OF. cion, sion (F. scion),
formed with dimin. suff. -on fr. Franklsh *kith,
'scion', which is rel. to OHG. kidi, 'scion', fr.
Teut. base *ki-, 'to burst forth', whence also
OHG. chlmo, MHG. kime, G. Keim, 'seed,
germ', OE. cinan, OS., OHG. kinan, Goth.
keinan, 'to burst', Goth, us-kijans (pp.), 'come
forth' (said of seeds).

## scioptic
scioptic, adj., pertaining to sight. —
Compounded of scio- and Gk. οπτικός, 'pertaining to
sight'. See optic.

## scioptric
scioptric, adj. — The same as scioptic. The form
scioptric was formed on analogy of dioptric.

## scire facias
scire facias, п., a judicial writ. — L., 'make (him)
know'. For the first word see science. Facias is
the 2nd person of the subj. pres. of facere, 'to
make, do'. See fact.

## Scirophoria
Scirophoria, n. pi., an Athenian festival
celebrated on the 12th of the month Scirophorion
(Greek antiquities). — Gk. τά Σκιροφόρια,
compounded of σκίρον, 'the parasol (worn by
the priestesses of Athena, the priest of Poseidon
and the priest of Helios during the festive
procession)', and stem of φέρειν, 'to bear, carry'. The
first element is a derivative of σκιά, 'shade,
shadow'; see skiagraphy. For the second
element see bear, 'to carry'.

## Scirophorion
Scirophorion, п., name of the 12th month of the
Attic Greek calendar (corresponding to the
second half of June and the first half of July). —
Gk. Σκιροφοριών, fr. Σκιροφόρια. See prec.
word.

## Scirpus
Scirpus, п., a genus of plants, the bulrush (bot.)
— L. scirpus, 'rush', of uncertain origin. Cp.
sarpler, scarf, 'a band', scrip, 'a small bag'.

## scirrho-
scirrho-, before a vowel sclrrh-, combining form
meaning scirrhus. — See scirrhus.

## scirrhoid
scirrhoid, adj., resembling a scirrhus. —
Compounded of scirrh- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## scirrhous
scirrhous, adj., 1) pertaining to a scirrhus; 2)
resembling a scirrhus. — See next word and -ous.

## scirrhus
scirrhus, п., a hardened organ, esp. a hardened
gland (med.) — Medical L., fr. L. scirros, 'a
hard swelling, a tumor', fr. Gk. σκίρρος, of
s.m., fr. the adj. σκιρρός, also σκιρός, 'hard',
which is of unknown origin.

## Scirtopoda
Scirtopoda, n. pi., an order of rotifers (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. σκιρταν, 'to
spring, leap, bound', and πους, gen. ποδός,
'foot'. Gk. σκιρταν is freq. of σκαίρειν, 'to leap,
skip, bound', which is rel. to σκάρος, 'the
parrot fish', lit. 'the leaping fish'. See Scams. For
the second element see -poda.

## scissel
scissel, п., clippings of metal. — F. cisailles,
'cuttings, clippings (of metal)', fr. VL. *cisalia(= L.
caesalia), fr. caesus, pp. of caedere, 'to cut'. See
scissors.

## scissile
scissile, adj., that can be cut or split. — F-, fr. L.
scissilis, 'easily split or cleft', fr. scissus, pp. of
scindere, 'to cut, split, cleave', which is cogn.
with OI. chindtti, 'splits, cuts off', Gk. σχίζειν,
'to split, rend, cleave', Goth, skaidan, OE. scea-
dan, 'to separate'. See shed, v., and cp. scission,
exscind, jjrescind. For the ending see suff. -He.

## scission
scission, п., the act of cutting or splitting. — F.,
fr. Late L. scissidnem, ace. oiscissio, 'a cleaving,
dividing', fr. L. seisms, pp. of scindere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## scissors
scissors, n. pi. — ME. cysoures, sisours, fr. OF.
cisoires, 'shears', fr. Late L. cisoria, fr. L. caesus

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:690 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 663 | SCORDATO -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:690 COLUMN:1 -->
(in compounds -cisus), pp. of caedere (in
compounds -cidere), 'to cut'; see caesura and cp.
scissel. The spelling scissors is due to a
confusion of this word with Late L. scissor, 'one who
cleaves, a carver', fr. L. scissus, pp. of scfadere,
4o cut, split, cleave' (see scissile).
Derivatives: scissor, tr. v.,scissor-er, п.,
scissoring, n.

## scissure
scissure, п., a cleft, fissure. — F., fr. L. scissura,
fr. scissus, pp. of scindere, "to cut, split, cleave'.
See scissile and -ure.

## Sciuridae
Sciuridae, n. pi., the family of squirrels (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. sciurus,
'squirrel'. See squirrel.

## stiurine
stiurine, adj., pertaining to the family Sciuridae
(the squirrels). — Formed with adj. suff. -ine fr.
L. sciurus, 'squirrel'- See squirrel.
Derivative: sciurine, п., a squirrel.

## sciuroid
sciuroid, adj., squirrel-like. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. sciurus, 'squirrel', and Gk. -αειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See squirrel and -oid.

## sclaff
sclaff, tr. v. and п., a term of golf. — Scot., of
imitative origin.

## scler-
scler-, form of sclero- before a vowel.

## sclera
sclera, п., name of the external membrane
covering the white of the eyeball (anat.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. σκληρχ(μην[.γξ), 'the hard
(membrane)', fern, of σκληρός, 'hard'. See sclero- and
cp. sclerotic.

## Scleranthus
Scleranthus, п., a genus of plants, the knawel
(hot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. σκληρός,
'hard', and άνθος, 'flower' (see sclero- and
anther); so called in allusion to the hardened
calyx tube.

## sclerenchyma
sclerenchyma, n. (boi. and zool.) — Compounded
of Gk. σκληρός, 'hard', and έγχυμα,'infusion*.
See enchymatous.

## Scleria
Scleria, п., a genus of plants, the nut rush (bot.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. σκληρία, 'hardness*, fr.
σκληρός, 'hard* (see sclero-); so called in
allusion to the indurated •fruit.

## scleriasis
scleriasis, п., a morbid hardening (med.) —
Medical L., formed fr. Gk. σκληρός, 'hard', on
analogy of elephantiasis, psor-iasis. See sclero- and
-iasis,

## scleritis
scleritis, п., inflammation of the sclera {med.) —
Medical L., formed fr. sclera with suff. -itis.

## sclero-
sclero-, before a vowel scler-, combining form
meaning 'hard*. — Gk. σκληρό-, σκληρ-, fr.
σκληρός, 'hard', rel. to σκέλλειν, 'to dry up,
parch', and cogn. with ME. shalowe, 'faint,
feeble'. See shailow.

## scleroderma
scleroderma, п., hardening of the skin {med.) —
Medical L., compounded of sclero- and Gk.
8έρμα, 'skin*. Cp. Gk. σκληρόδερμος, 'with
hard skin', and see -derm.

## sclerodermatous
sclerodermatous, adj., having a hard skin. —
Compounded of sclero- and Gk. δέρμα, gen.
δέρματος, 'skin'. See prec. word and -ous.

## sclerodermic
sclerodermic, adj., sclerodermatous. — See prec.
word and adj. suif. -ic.

## scleroid
scleroid, adj., hard. — Gk. σκληροειδής, 'of hard
nature', fr. σκληρός, 'hard', and -οειδής, 'like*,
fr. εϊδος, 'form, shape'. See sclera- and -oid.

## scleroma
scleroma, п., induration of the tissues {med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. σκλήρωμα, 'induration', fr.
σκληροϋν, *to harden', fr. σκληρός, 'hard'. See
sclero- and -oma.

## sclerometer
sclerometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
hardness of materials. — Compounded of
sclero- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm'.

## sclerosis
sclerosis, п., morbid hardening of the tissues
{med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. σκλήρωσις, *a
hardening', fr. σκληροϋν, *to harden', fr.
σκληρός, 'hard*. See sclero- and -osis.

## sclerotic
sclerotic, adj., 1) pertaining to, or characterized
by, sclerosis; 2) pertaining to the sclera. —
Medical L. scleroticus, 'hard', fr. Gk. σκληροϋν, 'to
harden*, fr. σκληρός, 'hard*. See sclero- and
-otic.

## sclerotic
sclerotic, п., the sclera. — Medical L. sclerotica,
fem. of scleroticus (see prec. word) used as a
noun.

## sclerotitis
sclerotitis, п., inflammation of the sclerotic coat
of the eye {med.) — Medical L. See prec. word
and -itis.

## sclerotium
sclerotium, п., a' compact mass of mycelium

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:690 COLUMN:2 -->
found in certain fungi {bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
σκληρός, 'hard'. See sclero-,

## sclerous
sclerous, adj., hard. — Gk. σκληρός, 'hard'. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## scobs
scobs, п., filings, scrapings, sawdust. — L.,
collateral form of scobis, which stands in grada-
tional'relationship to L. scabere, 'to scrape',
scabies, 'roughness, scurf. See scabies.

## scoff
scoff, n. — ME. skof, prob. of Scand. origin. Cp.
ON. skaup, skop, 'scoff, jest, taunt', MDan.
skof, skuf, of s.m., Dan. skuffe, 'to mock,
deceive'. These words meant orig. 'a push, a
shove', resp. 'to push, shove', and are related to
shove.

## scoff
scoff, intr. v. — ME. scoffen, fr. scof. See scoff, n.
Derivatives: scoff-er, п., scoff-ing, adj. and п.,
scoff-ing-ly, adv.

## scold
scold, п., one who scolds; esp. a scolding woman.
— ME. scald, scold, prob. fr. ON. skald, 'poet;
satirist, lampooner'. See skald.

## scold
scold, intr. v., to rail; tr. v., to rate. — ME. seal·
den, scolden, fr. scald, scold. See scold, n.
Derivatives: scold-er, п., scold-ing, adj. and п.,
scold-ing-lyt adv.

## scolecite
scolecite, п., a calcium aluminum silicate
{mineral.) — G. Skolezit, formed fr. Gk. σκώληξ,
gen. σκώληκος, 'worm', with suff. -it. See next
word. The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης;
see subst. suff. -ite.

## scolex
scolex, п., the embryo stage of a tape worm {zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. σκώληξ, 'worm', which is
rel. to σκωλύπτεσθαι, 'to twist and turn',
σκόλιος, 'crooked, bent', σκέλος, 'leg', σκα-
ληνός, 'limping, halting, uneven'. See scalene
and cp. scowl.

## scolio-
scolio-, combining form denoting curvature in
general and scoliosis in particular. — Gk.
σκόλιο-, fr. σκόλιος, 'crooked, bent'. See prec.
word.

## scolion
scolion, п., a kind of song sung to the lyre {Greek
antiq.) — Gk. σκόλιου, also spelled, less
correctly, σκολιόν (shortened fr. σκολιόν μέλος),
lit. 'song which went round crookedly at
banquets', neut. of σκόλιος, 'crooked*. See scolex.

## scoliosis
scoliosis, п., a lateral curvature of the spine {med.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. σκολίωσις,
'crookedness, obliquity', fr. σκόλιος. See scolio- and
-osis.

## scoliotic
scoliotic, adj., pertaining to, or afflicted with,
scoliosis {med.) — See prec. word and -otic,

## scollop
scollop, n. and v. — A var. of scallop.

## scolopaceous
scolopaceous, adj., resembling a woodcock or a
snipe. — See next word and -ous.

## Scolopax
Scolopax, п., a genus of birds, the woodcock
{omithol.) — LateL.,fr. Gk. σκολόπαξ,
'woodcock, snipe', which derives from σκόλοψ,
'pointed stake'; so called in allusion to its long
pointed beak. See shelf, 'horizontal slab'.

## Scolopendra
Scolopendra, п., a genus of chilopods {zool) —
L. scolopendra, *a kind of multipede', fr. Gk.
σκολόπενδρα, of s.m., which is uncertain origin.

## Scolopendrid
Scolopendrid, п., one of the family Scolopendri-
dae. — See next word.

## Scolopendridae
Scolopendridae, n. pi., a family of chilopods
{zool.) — ModL., formed fr. Scolopendra with
suff. -idae.

## Scolymus
Scolymus, п., a genus of plants of the chicory
family {bot.) — L. scolymos, 'a kind of thistle,
cardoon*, fr. Gk. σκόλυμος, of s.m., which is
of uncertain origin.

## Scomber
Scomber, п., a genus of fishes including the
mackerel {ichthyol.) — L. scomber, 'mackerel',
fr. Gk. σκόμβρος, of s.m., which is of uncertain
origin.

## scombroid
scombroid, adj., resembling the mackerel. —
Compounded of Gk. σκόμβρος, 'mackerel',
and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
prec. word and -oid.

## scon
scon, n. — See scone.

## sconce
sconce, п., a metal bracket for holding candles.
— ME. The original meaning was 'a screened

## lantern'. ME. sconce is aphetic for OF. esconse
lantern'. ME. sconce is aphetic for OF. esconse,
'hiding place, lantern', derived—with change
of suff.—fr. VL. absconsa, fem. of absconsus,

## which corresponds to L. absconditus
which corresponds to L. absconditus, pp. of ab-

## scondere
scondere, 'to hide'. See abscond and cp.
recondite.

## sconce
sconce, п., cover, fort. — Du. schanst 'bulwark'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:690 COLUMN:3 -->
See schanz, which is a doublet of sconce, and cp.
ensconce.
Derivative: sconce, tr. v.

## sconcheon
sconcheon, n. — See scuncheon.

## scone
scone, scon, п., a thin flat cake. — Prob.
shortened fr. MDu. schoonbrot, 'fine bread'. See
sheen, 'beautiful'.

## scoop
scoop, n. — According to the difference in
meaning, partly fr. MLG. sckdpe, 'ladle' (cp. MDu.
schope, schoepe, Du. schoep), partly fr. MDu.
schoppe (whence Du. schop), 'shovel', which is
rel. (ρ OS. skufta, OE. sceofl, of s.m. See shove,
shovel and cp. scupper, 'a cut through a ship's
side'. Cp. also chopin.
Derivatives: scoop, tr. v., scoop-er, п., scoop-ing,
verbal n.

## scoot
scoot, intr. v., to go quickly. — Prob. of Scand.
origin. Cp- Swed. skjuta, 'to shoot', and see
shoot.
Derivatives: scoot, п., scoot-er, n.

## scop
scop, п., a bard, minstrel. — OE. scop, sceop,
prob. related to scoff. For sense development cp.
scold.

## scopa
scopa, п., tuft of hairs on the legs of a bee used
for carrying pollen; pollen brush. — L., 'a
broom', in gradational relationship to scapus,
'shaft*. See shaft, 'stem, stock*, and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also scopuia.
Derivative: scop-atet adj.

## scope
scope, n. — It. scopo, 'mark, target, thing aimed
at, aim, goal, object', fr. Gk. σκοπός, 'mark to
shoot at, watcher, examiner, spy, scout', in
gradational relationship to σκέπτεσ&αι, *to look
about, look carefully at*. See species and cp.
spy. Cp. also the second element in bishop,

## -scope
-scope, combining form used to denote an
instrument for examining with the eye, as in hygro-
scope, microscope. — ModL. -scopium, fr. Gk.
-σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine,
survey', fr. σκοπός, 'watcher, examiner'. See prec.
word,

## scopelism
scopelism, п., the piling of stones in a field (an-
thropol.) — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk.
σκόπελος, 'high rock, peak', which stands in
gradational relationship to σκάπτειν, "to dig',
σκαπάνη, 'spade, hoe'. See capon and cp. words
there referred to.

## scopulamine
scopulamine,scopo[amm,n.,anaIkaloidC17Hs,10JN
{chem.) — G. Scopolamine compounded of
ModL. Scopolia, a genus of plants (named after
the Italian naturalist G. A. Scopoli (1723-88)
and amine; so called because this alkaloid
occurs especially in the rhizomes of the genus
Scopolia.

## scopuia
scopuia, п., a brushlike tuft of hairs {zool.) — L.
scopulae, 'broom twig', dimin. oiscopa, 'broom'.
See scopn and -ule.
Derivative: scopul-ate, adj.

## -scopy
-scopy, combining form denoting the use of
instruments named by words ending in -scope. —
Gk. -σκοπία, fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine,
survey', fr. σκοπός, 'watcher, examiner, spy,
scout*. See scope and -y (representing Gk. -ία)

## and cp. -scope
and cp. -scope,

## scorbute
scorbute, п., scurvy {obsol.) — MF. (= F.) scor-

## but
but, fr. ML. scorbutus (whence also It. scorbuto,
Sp. and Port, escorbuto), prob. through the
medium of Du. scheurbuik or G. Scharbock. See

## scurvy
scurvy, n.

## scorbutic
scorbutic, adj., pertaining to, or having, scurvy.
— ML. scorbuticus (whence also F. scorbutique)t
fr. scorbutus. See scorbute and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: scorbutic^ п., scorbutic-al, adj., scor-

## butic-al-ly
butic-al-ly, adv., bcorbutic-ism, n.

## scorch
scorch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. scorchen, fr. OF.

## escorckiert escorcher (F. Scorcher)
escorckiert escorcher (F. Scorcher), 'to strip off

## the skin
the skin, to flay*, fr. VL. excorticare, 'to fiay'
(whence also It. scorticare), fr. 1st ex- and L.

## cortex
cortex, gen. corticis, 'cork*. ME. scorchen was
influenced in sense by a confusion with ME.

## scorklen
scorklen, 'to scorch', fr. ON. skorpnat 'to dry up,
shrivel*.
Derivatives: scorch, п., scorch-ed, adj.,

## scorcher
scorcher, п., scorch-ing, adj. and п., scorch-ing-ly, adv.,

## scorch-ing-ness
scorch-ing-ness, n.

## scordato
scordato, п., out of tune {mus.) — It., short for

## discordato
discordato, pp. of discordare, *to make

## discordant'
discordant', fr. L. discorddre. See discord, v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:691 -->
