<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:691 COLUMN:1 -->

## score
score, η. — ME. scor, fr. ON. skor, 'notch, tally;
twenty', lit. 'a cut'; in gradational relationship
to OE. sceran, 'to cut'. See shear and cp. words
there referred to.

## score
score, tr. and intr. v. — ME. scoren, ON. skora,
fr. skor. See score, n.
Derivatives: scor-ed, adj., scor-er, п., scor-ing,
n.

## scoria
scoria, п., refuse, dross. — L., fr. Gk. σκωρία,
'dross of metal, slag', fr. σκώρ, gen. σκατός,
'dung', which is cogn. with Hitt. shakar, gen.
shaknash, 'dirt', ON. skarn, OE. scearn, 'dung',
and prob. also with L. -cerda in mus-cerda,
'mouse dung', su-cerda, 'the dung of swine'
(influenced in form by merda, 'dung'). Cp. Escorial
and the first element in scatology.

## scoriaceous
scoriaceous, adj., of the nature of scoria, -r- See
prec. word and -aceous.

## scorification
scorification, n. — See next word and -arion.

## scorify
scorify, tr. v., to reduce to dross. — See scoria
and -fy.
Derivative: scorifi-ert n.

## scorn
scorn, n. — ME. scarn, scorn, fr. OF. escarne, var.
of escharne, 'derision, scorn', which is of Teut.
origin. Cp. OHG. skernon, 'to mock, deride',
skern, 'mockery', MHG. sckerzen, 'to jump
with joy; to jest' (see scherzo); influenced in
form by OF. escorne (F. ёсогпё), 'affront,
disgrace', back formation fr. escorner (F. ecorner),
'to disgrace', lit. 'to break off one's horns', fr.
Late L. excornare (whence also It. scornare), fr.
1st ex- and L. cornu, 'horn' (see horn).
Derivatives: scorn, v. (q.v.), scorn-ful, adj.,
scorn-ful-ly, adv., scorn-ful-ness, п., scorn-y, adj.

## scorn
scorn, tr. v. — ME. seamen, scornen, fr. OF. es-
carnir, var. of escharnir, 'to deride, scorn', fr.
escarne, var. of escharne. See scorn, n.
Derivatives: scorn-ed, adj., scorn-er, n.

## scorodite
scorodite, п., a hydrous ferric arsenate (mineral.)
— G. Skorodit, formed with suff. -it fr. Gk.
σκόροδον, 'garlic', which is cogn. with Alb.
hurde (for I.-E. *sqerd-), 'garlic'; so called in
allusion to its odor under the blowpipe. G. -it
goes back to Gk. -ίτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## scorpaenid
scorpaenid, п., a fish of the family Scorpaenidae.
— See next word.

## Scorpaenidae
Scorpaenidae, n. pi., a family of spiny-finned
fishes (ichtkyol.) — ModL., formed with suff.
-idae fr. L. scorpaena, a loan word fr. Gk.
σκόρπαινα, 'a kind of fish', lit. 'scorpion fish',
fr. σκορπιός, 'scorpion*. See scorpion and cp.
sculpin.

## Scorpio
Scorpio, п., 1) a zodiacal constellation; 2) the
eighth sign of the zodiac. — L. Scorpio,
'scorpion'. See scorpion.

## scorpioid
scorpioid, adj., resembling a scorpion or its tail.
— Gk. σκορπιοειδής, compounded of σκορπιός,
'scorpion', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape*. See scorpion and -old.

## scorpion
scorpion, n. — ME. scorpioun, fr. OF. (= F.)
scorpion, fr. L. scorpidnem, ace. of Scorpio, a
collateral form of scorpius, fr. Gk. σκορπιός, which
is prob. ult. connected with Heb. "aqrabh,
'scorpion'. See Albert Schott, Indogermanisch-
semitische Studien, p. 77.

## scortation
scortation, п., fornication. — Formed with suff.
-ation fr. L. scortari, 'to associate with harlots',
fr. scortum, 'harlot', prop, 'skin', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)qer-, 'to cut'. See cortex.

## Scorzonera
Scorzonera, п., a genus of plants of the chicory
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. It. scorzonera, lit.
'viper's plant', fr. scorzone, 'viper', fr. L. cur-
tionem, ace. of curtio, 'viper', which is prob. rel.
to curvus, 'curved, bent, crooked'; see curve.
The initial s- in It. scorzonera, is prob. due to
the influence of scorto, 'short'.

## scot
scot, п., contribution, tax. — ME., prob. fr. ON.
skot, which is rel. to OE. sceot, 'shot, reckoning,
contribution', fr. sciotan, 'to shoot, contribute',
and to Du. schot, G. Schofi, 'tax, contribution'.
OF. escot (whence F. ecot), 'share', is a Teut.
loan word. See shoot and shot, 'share,
contribution', which is a doublet of scot.

## Scot
Scot, n. — ME. Scottes (pi.), fr. OE. Scottas
(pi.), fr. Late L. Scoti, Scotti, 'the Irish', fr. Olr.
Scuits (sing. Scot), 'the Irish'. Cp. Scotch, Scot-
Псе.

## scotch
scotch, tr. v., to cut, make an incision. — ME.'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:691 COLUMN:2 -->
scocchen, fr. AF. escocher, fr. OF. (= F.) cache,
'a notch, nick, nock of an arrow' (rel. to It.
cocca, of s.m., OProvenc. encocar, 'to make an
incision'), fr. VL. *cocca, fr. L. coccum, 'grain
of the kermes, excrescence of a plant', fr. Gk.
κόκκος, of s.m. See coccus and cp. the second
element in hopscotch.
Derivative: scotch, a cut, incision, line.

## scotch
scotch, п., a block. — Of unknown origin.
Derivative: scotch, tr. v., to block.

## Scotch
Scotch, adj. and n. — Contraction of Scottish.

## scoter
scoter, п., a sea duck of the genera Oidemia and
Melanitta. —^Prob. rel. to ON. skoti, *a shooter',
skjota, 'to shoot out'; so called from its swift
movements (cp. darter, a name denoting the
snakebird). See shoot and cp. scout, the
guillemot.

## scotia
scotia, п., a concave molding at the base of a
column. — L., fr. Gk. σκοτία, 'darkness; a
sunken molding' (so called from the shadow
cast by its surface), fr. σκότος; 'darkness'. See
scotu-,

## Scotice
Scotice, adv., in the Scottish language. — ML.
Scotice, adv. of Scoticus, 'Scottish'. For the L.
adverbial suff. -ice cp. romance.

## Scotism
Scotism, п., the scholastic philosophy of Duns
Scotus. — Formed from the name of the
Scottish philosopher Duns Scotus (died in 1308) with
suff. -ism.

## Scotist
Scotist, п., an adherent of Scotism. — See prec.
word and -ist.

## scoto-
scoto-, combining form meaning 'darkness'. —
Gk. σκοτο-, fr. σκότος, 'darkness', which is
cognate with Goth, skadus, OE. sceadu, 'shade'.
See shade and cp. scotia.

## scotodinia
scotodinia, п., dizziness accompanied by
headache and dimness of sight (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of Gk. σκότος, 'darkness' (see
scoto-), and δϊνος, 'whirling, rotation, vertigo'.
See dinus.

## scotograph
scotograph, п., an instrument for writing in the
dark or for the use of the blind. — Compounded
of scoto- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graph.

## scotoma
scotoma, п., a blind or dark spot (med.) — Late
L., fr. Gk. σκότωμα, 'dimness of vision,
dizziness', fr. σκότος, 'darkness'. See scoto- and
-oma.

## Scots
Scots, adj. and n. — Fr. earlier Scottis, Northern
ME. vac of Scottish.

## Scottice
Scottice, adv., in the Scottish language. — A var.
spelling of Scotice.

## Scotticism
Scotticism, п., a Scottish idiom or expression. —
Formed with suff. -ism fr. Late L. Scoticus,
Scotticus, 'Scottish, Scotch'. See Scot, Scots.

## Scotticize
Scotticize, tr. and intr. v. — Formed with suff.
-ize fr. Late L. Scoticus, Scotticus. See prec.
word.

## Scottish
Scottish, adj. and n. — ME. Scottisc, fr. Late OE.
Scottisc, formed fr. OE. Scottas (pi.) 'Scots',
with suff. -isc. See Scot and adj. suff. -ish and
cp. Scots.

## scoundrel
scoundrel, п., a rascal. — Of uncertain origin.
Perh. fr. AF. escoundre, corresponding to OF.
escondre, 'to hide; to hide oneself, fr. VL. *ex-
condere, fr. L. ex (see 1st ex-) and condere, 'to
hide'. See abscond andep. words there referred to.
Derivatives: scoundrel-ism, п., scoundrel-ly, adv.

## scour
scour, tr. v., to pass over quickly; intr. v. to run
quickly. — ME. scouren, prob. a blend of ON.
(= Swed.) skura, 'to rush' (see shower), and OF.
escorre, 'to run out', fr. L. excurrere (see
excursion). Cp. scurry.
Derivative: scour, a., a rush.

## scour
scour, tr. and intr. v., to clean by rubbing. — ME.
scouren, fr. MDu. schuren, 'to polish, clean', fr.
OF. escurer (F. ecurer), fr. L. excurare, 'to take
good care of (whence also Sp. and OProvenc.
escurar), ft. Ist ex- and curare, 'to take care of,
fr. cura, 'care'. See cure, n.
Derivatives: scour, п., a scouring, cleansing,
scour-age, п., scour-ed, adj., scour-er, п.,
scouring, n.

## scourge
scourge, n. — ME. scorge, scourge, fr. AF. escor-
ge, fr. OF. escorgier, 'to whip' (whence .OF.
escorgiee, . F. escourgee, ecourgee, 'whip,
scourge'), fr. VL. *ex-corrigiata, 'whip', fr. L.
ex- (see 1st ex-) and corrigia, 'shoestring, strap',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:691 COLUMN:3 -->
which is cogn. with Olr. cuimrech, 'fetter'. Both
L. corrigia and Olr. cuimrech are compound
words. For the first element of these words see
com-. The second element derives fr. I.-E. base
*reig-, "rig-, 'to bind', whence also W. rhwym,
'fetter', perh. also MHG. ric, gen. rickes, 'band,
fetter', ricken, 'to tie up'.

## scourge
scourge, tr. v. — ME. scorgen, scourgen, fr. scorge,
scourge. See scourge, n.

## scouse
scouse, п., a sailor's dish. — Short for lobscouse.

## scout
scout, п., spy, watchman. — ME. scoute, fr. OF.
escoute, 'listener, scout, spy', fr. escolter, escou-
ter (F. ecouter), 'to listen', fr. VL. ascultare, the
beginning of this word having been mistaken for
the pref. ad-, a- (see ad-), and changed into ex-,
e- (see 1st ex-), ult. fr. L. auscultare, 'to hear
with attention, listen to'. See auscultation.
Derivative: scout, intr. v. (q.v.)

## scout
scout, intr. v., to act as a scout. — ME. scouten,
fr. scoute, 'scout'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: scout-er, п., scout-ing, n. and adj.,
scout-ing-ly, adv.

## scout
scout, tr. v., to treat as absurd, to reject. — Of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. skuta, 'a taunt'.

## scout
scout, п., the guillemot, the puffin. — Prob. a var.
of scoter,

## scout
scout, п., a Dutch vessel. — MDu. schute (Du.
schuit). Cp. sennit,

## scow
scow, п., a large, fiat-bottomed lighter. — Du.
schouw, fr. MDu. scouwe, related to MDu.
scolde, scoelde, scoude, of s.m., and to OS.
scaldan, 'to push a boat from the shore',

## scowl
scowl, intr. v., to frown. — ME. scoulen, sculen,
of Scand. origin; cp. Dan. skule, 'to scowl',
which is prob. rel. to OE. sceolh, 'wry, oblique',
sceoleagede, 'squint-eyed', OHG. scelah,
'curved' (whence MHG. schelch, G. scheel, 'squint-
eyed'), fr. I.-E. base *sqel-, 'crooked,- curved,
bent'. See scalene and cp. skulk. Cp. also
schiller.
Derivatives: scowl, п., scowl-er, п., scowl-ing,
adj., scowl-ing-ly, adv.

## scrabble
scrabble, intr. v., to scrawl. — Du. schrabbelen,
'to scratch', freq. of schrabben, 'to scrape'. See
scrape and verbal suff. -le and cp. scramble.
Derivatives: scrabble, п., scrabbl-er, n.

## scrag
scrag, п., I) a lean person or animal; 2) anything
thin. — Prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. Norw.
skragg, 'a lean person', skraggen, 'lean, scraggy',
Dan. skrog, 'a carcass', Icel. skroggsligr, 'lean,
scraggy', and E. shrink.
Derivatives: scragg-y, adj., scragg-i-ly, adv.,
scragg-i-ness, n.

## scramble
scramble, intr. and tr. v. — A nasalized form of
scrabble.
Derivatives: scramble, п., scrambl-er, п.,
scrambl-ing, adj., scrambl-ing-ly, adv., scrambl-
y, adj.

## scran
scran, п., broken victuals. — Of uncertain origin.
Cp. ON. skran, 'rubbish'.

## scrannel
scrannel, п., thin, weak. — Of Scand. origin. Cp.
Norw. skran, 'lean, thin'. Cp. also scrawny,

## scrap
scrap, п., a small piece, fragment, of anything. —
ON. skrap, 'scrapings', fr. skrapa, 'to scrape'.
See scrape.
Derivatives: scrap, tr. v., scrapp-age, п., scrapp-
y, adj., scrapp-i-ly, adv., scrapp-i-ness, n.

## scrap
scrap, п., a fight; intr. v., to fight {slang). — Fr.
scrape.
Derivative: scrapp-er, n.

## scrapable
scrapable, adj. — Formed from next word with
suff. -able,

## scrape
scrape, tr. and intr. v. — ME. scrapien, scrapen,
ft. ON. skrapa, 'to scratch out'; rel. to OE.
scrapian, screpan, 'to scrape', Du. schrapen,
schrabben, G. schrappen, of s.m., and cogn. with
Lett, skrabt, 'to scrape, scratch', Lith. skrebiti,
'to rustle', Russ. skrebu, skresf, 'to scrape',
skrob'ota, 'scurvy', lit. 'scrape, scratch'. Cp.
scrap, scrabble. Cp. also scurvy, п.. sgraffito,

## scratch
scratch, tr. and intr. v. — A blend of obsol. E.
scrat (fr. ME. scratte, 'scratch'), and ME. crac-
chen, 'to scratch', which are rel. to Swed. kratta,
MDu. cratsen, Du. krassen, OHG. krazzon,
MHG., G. kratzen, 'to scratch', ON. krota, 'to
engrave', Norw. krota, 'to cut out'. Alb. getuan,
kruan, Ί scrape, grate', gctuse, krus(f), 'scraper',
are prob. cogn. with the above words. F. gratter,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:692 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 665 | SCRUPLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:692 COLUMN:1 -->
OProvenc. gratar, It. grattare, 'to scrape', are
borrowed fr. Teutonic. See the verb cratch and
cp. grate, 'to scrape, rub'.
Derivatives: scratch, n. and adj., scratch-er, п.,
scratch-y, adj., scratch-i-ly, adv., scratch-i-ness,
n.

## scrawl
scrawl, intr. and tr. v., to write carelessly; to
scribble. — Of uncertain origin. Perh. a blend
of scribble and crawl.
Derivatives: scrawl, п., scrawl-er, п., scrawl-y,
adj., scrawl-i-ness, n.

## scrawny
scrawny, adj., thin. — Of Scand. origin. Cp.
Norw. skran, 'lean, thin', and see scrannel.
Derivative: scrawn-i-ness, n.

## scray
scray, п., the common tern. — W. yscraen, 'tern'.

## screak
screak, intr. v., and n. — ON. skrskja, rel. to OS.
skrikan, 'to screech', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qrei-. See
scream and cp. screech.

## scream
scream, intr. and tr. v. — ME. scremen, fr. ON.
skrsema, 'to terrify, scare', rel. to Swed. scrana,
'to scream', OS., OHG. scrian, MHG. schrien,
G. schreien, 'to cry', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qrel-,
whence also ON. hreimr, 'scream, cry', hrina, 'to
squeak, squeal', L. crimen, 'complaint, crime',
orig. 'cry of distress'; see crime and cp. screak,
screech. Base *(s)qrei- is an enlargement of the
imitative base *qer-; see raven.
Derivatives: scream, п., scream-er, п.,
screaming, adj. and п., scream-ing-ly, adv., scream-y,
adj., scream-i-ness, n.

## scree
scree, п., a pebble; a stone. — Back formation fr.
scree(th)es (cp. the pronunciation of clothes), fr.
ON. skrida, 'landslide', fr. skrida, 'to glide,
slide', which is rel. to OE. scridan, 'to move
smoothly, move around, glide', OS. skridan,
Du. sckrijden, OHG. scritan, MHG. sckriten, G.
schreiten, 'to stride', and prob. cogn. with Lith.
skriesti, 'to turn, twist', skrytis, 'felly of a
wheel', OPruss. scritayle, of s.m., Lett, skritulis,
'wheel'.

## screech
screech, intr. and tr. v. — Fr. earlier scritch,
which derives from the I.-E. imitative base
*(s)qrei-. See scream and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also shriek, which is a doublet of
screech.
Derivatives: screech, п., screech-er, п.,
screeching, adj. and п., screech-ing-ly, adv., screech-y,
adj., screech-i-ly, adv., screech-i-ness, n.

## screed
screed, п., orig. a strip torn off; whence 1) a long
list; 2) a long tiresome discourse, spoken or
written. — ME. screde, fr. OE. screade, 'shred';
Scot, and North E. var. of shred (q.v.)

## screed
screed, tr. v., to repeat glibly; intr. v., to make a
sound as of tearing into shreds. — Orig. 'to tear',
fr. OE. screadian, Fr. screade. See screed, n.

## screen
screen, n. — ME. scren, fr. OF. escren, escran (F.
ecran), fr. MDu. (= Du.) scherm, 'screen',
which is rel. to OHG. skirm, skerm, 'protection'.
See skirmish.
Derivatives: screen, tr. and intr. v., screen-able,
adj., screen-age, п., screen-ed, adj., screen-er, п.,
screen-ing, n. and adj., screen-ings, n. pi.

## screw
screw, n. — Fr. earlier scrue, fr. OF. escroue (F.
ecrou), 'female screw', fr. L. scroba, a collateral
form of scrdfa, 'sow', used metaphorically to
denote the female screw. Cp. It. scrofula, 'female
screw'. For sense development cp. Port, porca,
Span, puerca, 'female screw', fr. L. porca, 'sow'.
Du. schroef, MHG. schrube (whence G. Schrau-
be), 'screw', are French loan words. For the
etymology of L. scrofa see scrofula.
Derivatives: screw, tr. and intr. v., screw-ed,
adj., screw-er, п., screw-ing, n. and adj., screw-
less, adj., screwy, adj.

## scribal
scribal, adj. — Formed fr. scribe with adj. suff.
-a).

## scribble
scribble, tr. and intr. v., to write carelessly. —
ME. scriblen, fr. ML. scribillare, 'to write very
often, write hastily', freq. of L. scribere, 'to
write'. See scribe.
Derivatives: scrtbbl-age, п., scribble, п.,
scribbled, adj., scribble-ment, п., scribbl-ing, adj.,
scribbling-ly, adv.

## scribble
scribble, tr. v., to card roughly. — Prob. of Scand.
origin; cp. Swed. skrubbla, 'to card wool', freq.
of skrubba, 'to scrub'. See scrub and freq. suff.
-le.
Derivatives: scribbl-er, п., scribbl-ing-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:692 COLUMN:2 -->

## scribe
scribe, n. — ME., fr. L. scriba, 'a .public writer,
clerk, scribe', fr. scribere, pp. scrlptus, 'to write',
fr. I.-E. base 'sqeribh-, 'to scratch', whence also
Umbr. screhto, 'written' (= L. scriptum), Gk.
σκαρϊφασ*αι, 'to scratch', σκάρΐφος, 'a stile for
drawing outlines, a sketch'. OE. scrifan, 'to
allot, assign, impose, to shrive', scrift, 'legal
penalty, penance; confessor', ON. skript, 'penance,
confession', OHG. scriban (whence MHG.
schriben, G. schreiben), ODu. scrivan (whence
Du. schrijven), OFris. skriva, OS. scriban, 'to
write', are Latin loan words. For the sense
development of L. scribere, 'to write', from a base
meaning 'to tear, scratch', ср. Е. write. Cp.
adscript, nscribe, ascription, circumscribe,
circumscription, conscribe, conscript, conscription,
describe, description, escritoire, imperscriptible,
inscribe, inscription, interscription, manuscript,
postscript, prescribe, prescription, proscribe,
proscription, rescript, scarify, scribble, 'to write
carelessly', script, scriptorium, scripture, scrive,
scrivener, shrift, shrive, Shrovetide, subscribe,
subscription, superscribe, superscription,
transcribe, transcription.
Derivatives: scribe, tr. v., scrib-er, п., scrib-ing,
n.

## scrim
scrim, п., a cloth used in upholstery, etc. — Of
unknown origin.

## scrimmage
scrimmage, n. — A var. of skirmish (through the
intermediary form scrimmish). Cp. scrummage.
Derivative: scrimmag-er, n.

## scrimp
scrimp, tr. v., to make too small; intr. v., to be
sparing. — Cp. Dan. skrumpe, Swed. skrympa,
MDu. scrompelen, Du. schrompelen, G. schrum-
pfen, 'to shrink', and see shrink.
Derivatives: scrimp-ed, adj., scrimp-y, adj.

## scrinium
scrinium, п., a case for books in medieval
libraries. — L. scrinium, 'a case for keeping
books'. See shrine.

## scrip
scrip, п., a small bag. — ME. scrippe, rel. to ON.
skreppa, 'scrip', fr. Merovingian L. scrippa,
'scrip', metathesized fr. L. scirpea, 'basket made
of rushes', subst. use of the fem. of the adj. scir-
peus, 'made of rushes', fr. scirpus, 'rush'. See
Scirpus and cp. words there referred to.

## scrip
scrip, п., a writing, a provisional certificate. —
Short for subscription.
Derivative: scrip-ee, n.

## script
script, n. — Late ME., fr. OF. escript (also
escrit, whence F. e'crit), fr.L. scriptum, 'something
written', neut. pp. of scribere, 'to write'. See
scribe and cp. words there referred to.

## scriptorium
scriptorium, п., a writing room esp. that of a
monastery. — Late L., prop. neut. of L. scriptorius,
'pertaining to writing', fr. scrlptus, pp. of
scribere. See scribe and subst. suff. -ory and cp.
escritoire, which is a doublet of scriptorium.

## scripture
scripture, n. — ME., fr. L. scriptura, fr. scriptus,
pp. of scribere, 'to write'. See scribe and -lire.
Derivatives: scriptur-al, adj., Scriptur-al-ism, п.,
Scriptur-al-ist, п., scriptur-al-ly, adv., Scriptur-
ist, n.

## scrive
scrive, tr. and intr. v., to write. — ME. scriven, fr.
OF. escrivre (whence OF. escrire, F. ecrire), fr.
L. scribere, 'to write'. See scribe.

## scrivello
scrivello, п., an elephant's tusk. — Port, escrevel-
ho.

## scrivener
scrivener, n. — ME. scriveiner, fr. earlier scrivein,
fr. OF. escrivain (F. icrivain), fr. Late L. scri-
bdnus, fr. L. scribere, 'to write'. See scribe and
agential suff. -er.

## scrobe
scrobe, п., a groove (zoo!.) — L. scrobis, 'ditch,
trench', which is cogn. with Lett, skrabt, 'to
hollow out, scrape', skrabinat, 'to gnaw at', ON.
skarpr, OE. scearp, 'sharp'. See sharp and cp.
next word.

## scrobiculate
scrobiculate, adj., marked by depressions {hot.
and zool.) — Formed with suff. -ate fr. L. scro-
biculus, dimin. of scrobis. See prec. word.

## scrod
scrod, п., a young codfish. — Prob. of Dutch
origin. Cp. MDu. schrode, *a piece cut off', which
is rel. to OE. screade, 'shred'. See shred.

## scrofula
scrofula, п., tuberculosis, esp. of the lymphatic
glands. — ML., fr. L. scrofulae (pi.) 'swelling of

## the glands'
the glands', lit. 'little pigs', dimin. of scrofa, 'a

## breeding sow'
breeding sow', which is perh. a loan word from
Gk. γρομφάς, explained by Hesychius as δς
παλαιά ('old pig"). For sense development cp. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:692 COLUMN:3 -->
χοιράς, 'scrofula', which is rel. to χοίρος, 'pig',
and Alb. itltq, 'swollen glands.', which is rel. to
0/, 'pig'· For the change of Gk. γρομφάς to L.
scrofa cp. L. scruta, 'broken fragments, trash,
rubbish', fr. Gk. γρυτη (see scrutator). Cp.
Scrophularin. Cp. also screw. For the ending of
L. scrofulae see suff. -ule.
Derivatives: scroful-ism, п., scroful-ous, adj.,
scroful-ous-ly, adv., scroful-ous-ness, n.

## scraggy
scraggy, adj., stunted. — A var. of scraggy.

## scroll
scroll, n. — Fr. earlier scrowle, fr. OF. escroele,
'piece, shred', dimin. of escroe, 'shred' (whence
F. ecrou, 'entry into the prison roll'), fr. Frank-
ish 'skroda, 'shred', which is rel. to MDu.
schroode, 'shred', OHG. scrot, 'a cut', MHG.
schrot, 'a cutting, a wound', G. Schrot, 'log,
block, small shot'. See shred and cp. escrow. The
spelling of scroll is due to an association of this
word with the noun roll.
Derivatives: scroll, intr. and tr. v., scroll-ed, adj.,
scroll-ery, n.

## scroop
scroop, intr. v., to creak, grate; п., a grating
sound. — Of imitative origin.

## Scrophularia
Scrophularia, п., a genus of plants, the figwort
(bot.) — ModL., fr. ML. scrofula (see scrofula);
so called because it is a reputed remedy for
scrofula.

## Scrophulariaceae
Scrophulariaceae, n. pi., the figwort family (pot.)
— ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## scrophulariaceous
scrophulariaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## scrotal
scrotal, adj., pertaining to the scrotum. —
Formed fr. scrotum with adj. suff. -al.

## scrotitis
scrotitis, п., inflammation of the scrotum (med.)
— A Medical L. hybrid formed fr. L. scrotum
and Gk. suff. -ΐτις. See scrotum and -itis.

## scrotocelc
scrotocelc, п., hernia of the scrotum (med.) — A
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. scrotum and Gk.
κήλη, 'a swelling, tumor'. See scrotum and -cele.

## scrotum
scrotum, п., the bag of skin that contains the
testicles (anat.) — L. scrotum, rel. to scrautum,
'quiver from arrows', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qreu-t-,
a dental enlargement of *(s)qreu-, 'to cut or
break to pieces'. See shred, п., and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivative: scrot-al, adj.

## scrounge
scrounge, tr. and intr. v., to pilfer (slang). — Cp.
dial. E. scrunge, 'to squeeze'; of uncertain
origin.
Derivative: scroung-er, n.

## scrub
scrub, п., a stunted tree. — Dial. Dan. skrub,
'brushwood'. See shrub, 'a woody plant'.

## scrub
scrub, adj., stunted. — Fr. prec. word.
Derivatives: scrubb-y, adj., scrubb-i-ness, n.

## scrub
scrub, tr. and intr. v., to clean by rubbing. —
MDu. schrubben (Du. schrobben); cp. Dan.
skrubbe, Swed. skrubba. Scrub orig. meant 'to
clean by rubbing with a scrub'. See prec. word.
For sense development cp. broom and brush.
Derivatives: scrub, п., scrubb-er, n.

## scruff
scruff, n.,' the nape. — Fr. earlier scuft, scuff, fr.
ON. skopt, 'hair on the head', which is rel. to
Goth, skuft, MHG. schopf, of s.m., G. Schopf,
'tuft', and possibly cogn. with Czech and Russ.
iup, iub, 'tnft', Serb, iupa, 'tnft, hair'. It. ciuffo,
'tuft, tassel', is a Teut. loan word.' Cp. scut,
sheaf.

## scrummage
scrummage, п., usually abbreviated into scrum
(Rugby football). — A var. of scrimmage.
Derivatives: scrummage, tr. and intr. v.,
scrummag-er, n.

## scrumptious
scrumptious, adj., fine, delicious. — Invented
word prob. influenced by sumptuons.
Derivatives: scrumptious-ly, adv., scrumptious-
ness, n.

## scrunch
scrunch, v. and n. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
crunch.

## scruple
scruple, п., 1) an apothecary's weight equal to
twenty grains; 2) doubt or hesitation arising
from the difficulty of deciding what is right or
expedient. — F. scruple, fr. L. scrupulus, 'small,

## sharp stone
sharp stone, weight, one twenty-fourth of the

## ounce
ounce, scruple; difficulty, anxiety', dimin. of

## scrupus
scrupus, 'a sharp piece of stone; anxiety,

## solicitude
solicitude, uneasiness'? which prob. derives fr. I.-E.
"sqreu-p-, -^-enlargement of *sqreu-, 'to cut ot
break to pieces'. See shred and cp. scrupulous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:693 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SCRUPULOSITY | 666 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:693 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: scruple, intr. and tr. v., scrupl-er, n.

## scrupulosity
scrupulosity, n. — F. scrupulosite, fr. L. scrupuld-
sitdtem, ace. of scrupulositds, 'over-nicety', fr.
scrupuldsus. See next word and -ity.

## scrupulous
scrupulous, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) scrupu-
leux (fem. scrupuleuse), fr. L. scrupuldsus, 'full
of sharp stones; very nice, exact*, fr. scrupulus.
See scruple and -one.
Derivatives: scrupulous-ly, adv. ,scrupulous-ness,
n.

## scrutuble
scrutuble, adj. — Formed with suff. -able fr. L.
scrutdri. See scrutator.
Derivative: scrutabil-ity, n.

## scrutate
scrutate, tr. v., to investigate. — L. scrutdtus, pp.
of scrutdri. See next word and verbal suff. -ate.

## scrutator
scrutator, п., one who investigates. — L.
scrutator, 'scrutinize^ examiner, investigator', fr.
scrutatus, pp. of scrutdri. See next word and
agential suff. -or.

## scrutiny
scrutiny, п., close examination. — L. scrutinium,
'search, investigation, scrutiny', fr. scrutdri, 'to
search, examine, investigate', fr. scruta (gen.
-drum), 'broken stuff, trash, frippery', fr. I.-E.
*(s)qreu-t-, a dental enlargement of base
*(s)qreu-, *to cut or break to pieces'. See shred
and cp. scrututor.
Derivatives: scrutin-eer, п., scrutin-ize, tr. v.,
scrutin-iz-ation, п., scrutin-iz-er, п., scrutin-ous,
adj.

## scry
scry, tr. v., to descry. — Aphetic for descry.
Derivatives: scry-er, п., scry-ing, n.

## scuba
scuba, n. — Formed from the initials of the words
.self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.

## scud
scud, intr. v., to move quickly. — Of Scand.
origin. Cp. Norw. skudda, *to shove, push', and
E. scuttle, 'to hurry'.
Derivative: scud, п., the act of scudding; clouds
driven quickly by the wind.

## scudo
scudo, п., an old Italian silver coin. — It., lit. *a
shield', fr. L. scutum. See scutum.

## scuff
scuff, tr. and intr. v., to shuffle, — Of Scand.
origin. Cp. Swed. skuffa, 'to shove, push', and see
shove. Cp. also next word.

## scuffle
scuffle, intr. and tr. v. — Freq. of prec. word. See
verbal suff. -le. Cp. shuffle.
Derivatives: scuffle, п., scuffl-er, n.

## scull
scull, п., oar. — ME., of unknown origin.
Derivatives: scull, tr. and intr. v., scull-er, n.

## scullery
scullery, п., a room for cleansing dishes. — ME.,
fr. OF. escuelerie, fr. escuelier, 'keeper of the
dishes', fr. escuele (F. icuelle), 'dish*, fr. L.
scutella, 'salver, waiter', dimin. of scutula, 'a
small tray or dish', which itself is a dimin. of
scutra, 'a flat tray, dish'. Cp. It. scodella,
OProvenc. escodellat Sp. escodilla, which all
derive fr. L. scutella, and see scuttle, 'receptacle',
and -ery.

## scullion
scullion, п., 1) a servant who does menial services
in the kitchen; 2) a low person. — ME. sculion,
fr. OF. escovillon, escouillon (F. ecouvillori),
'swab, dishclout', dimin. of escouve (whence the
F. dimin. ecouvette\ *a broom', fr. L. scopa,
'broom', which stands in gradational
relationship to sedpus, 'shaft, stem'; see shaft, 'stem,
stock1, and cp. scape, 'shaft'.

## sculp
sculp, tr. v., to carve, sculpture. — Back
formation fr. sculpture,

## sculpin
sculpin, п., any of a group of spiny, usuajly
scaleless seafishes. — Prob. a corruption of F.
scorpene or It. scorpina, fr. L. scorpaena, 'the
sea scorpion'. See Scorpaenidae.

## sculpsit
sculpsit, n. — L., 'he carved', 3rd pers. sing. perf.
indie, of sculpere. See next word.

## sculptor
sculptor, n. — L., 'one who cuts or carves', fr.
sculptus, pp. of sculpere, 'to carve', which is rel.
to scalpere, 'to cut, carve; scrape'. See scalpel
and agential suff. -or.

## sculptress
sculptress, п., a female sculptor. — See prec.
word and 1st -ess.

## sculpture
sculpture, n. — ME., fr. L. sculptura, 'a carving',
fr. sculptus, pp. of sculpere. See sculptor and
-ure.
Derivatives: sculpture, tr. and intr. v.,
sculpturesque (q.v.)

## sculpturesque
sculpturesque, adj. — See sculpture and -esque.
Derivatives: sculpturesque-ly, adv., sculptur-
esque-ness, n.

## scum
scum, n. — MDu. schum(e) (Du. schuim), rel. to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:693 COLUMN:2 -->
ON. skum, Dan., Swed., Norw. skum, OHG.
scum, MHG. schum, schoum, G. Schaum, 'foam,
froth*; perh. fr. I.-E. base *sqeu-, 'to cover'.
See sky and cp. next word. Cp. also skim and
the second element in meerschaum. Cp. also
scutum, scuttle.
Derivatives: scum, tr. and intr. v., scumm-er, п.,
$cumm-ing, verbal п., scumm-y, adj.

## scumble
scumble, tr. v., to add a thin opaque coat of
color {paint.) — Formed fr. scum with freq.
suff. -le.
Derivatives: scumble, п., scumbl-ing, n.

## scuncheon
scuncheon, sconcheon, п., jamb of doors or
windows, cornerstone (archit.) — ME. sconcheon,
sconchon, fr. MF. escoinson (F. ecoinfon, ecoin-
son), formed fr. es· (fr. L. ex) and coin, 'corner',
fr. L. cuneus. See ist ex- and coin and cp.
sqninch. Cp. also esconson, which is a doublet of
scuncheon.

## scup
scup, п., an edible fish {Stenotomus chrysops). —
Shortened fr. Algonquian mishcup, lit. 'the big-
scaled (fish)'.

## scupper
scupper, п., a cut through a ship's side to let the
water flow overboard. — Shortened fr. earlier
scupper-hole; rel. to Du. schop, 'shovel', and to
scoop (q.v.)

## scupper
scupper, tr. v., to massacre in a surprise attack
(slang). — Of uncertain origin.

## scurf
scurf, n. — ME., fr. ON. *skurfr, inferred fr.
skurf(ottr), 'scurfy'; fr. Teut. base seen in OE.
sceorfan, 'to gnaw at, bite'; rel. to ON. skarpr,
OE. scearp, 'sharp' (see sharp). Cp. Dan. skurv,
Swed. skorv, MDu. scorf(t), Du. schurft, OHG.
scorf, MLG., MHG., G. schorf, 'scurf. Cp.
also scurvy, adj.
Derivatives: scurf-y, adj., scurf-i-ness, n.

## scurrile
scurrile, adj., scurrilous {archaic). — L. scurrilis,
'like a buffoon', fr. scurra, 'buffoon', an
Etruscan loan word; not cogn. with Gk. σκαίρειν, 'to
skip, dance, bound'.
Derivatives: scurrility, n. (q.v.), scurril-ous, adj.,
scurril-ous-ly, adv.

## scurrility
scurrility, n. — L. scurrtlitas, 'buffoonery', fr.
scurrilis. See prec. word and -ity.

## scurry
scurry, intr. v., to hurry. — A blend of scour, 'to
run quickly', and hurry.
Derivative: scurry, n.

## scurvy
scurvy, n. — Like Du. scheurbuik and G. Schar-
bock, 'scurvy' derived fr. ML. scorbutus (whence
also It. scorbuto, Sp., Port, escorbuto), fr. Russ.
skrobota, 'scrape, scratch'; see Kluge-Mitzka,
EWDS., p. 712 s.v. Skorbut. Russ. skrobota is
rel. to Russ. skrebu, skrest', 'to scrape', and
cogn. with E. scrape (q.v.) The noun scurvy was
influenced in form by the adj. scurvy.

## scurvy
scurvy, adj., mean, low, contemptible. — Formed
fr. scurf with adj. suff. -y. The original meaning
was 'scurfy'. Cp. scurvy, n.
Derivatives: scurvi-ly, adv., scurvi-ness, n.

## scut
scut, п., the short tail of an animal, esp. of a hare
or rabbit. — Prob. fr. ON. skopt, 'hair of the
head, fox's brush'. See scruff.

## scutage
scutage, п., money paid by a knight in lieu of
military service {feudal la w). — ML. scutdgium,
lit. 'shield money', fr. L. scutum, 'shield'. See
scutum and -age.

## scutal
scutal, adj., pertaining to a scutum (bot. and
zool.) — Formed fr. scutum with adj. suff.
-al.

## scutate
scutate, adj., shieldlike {bot. and zool.) — L.
scutatus, 'armed with a shield', fr. scutum. See
scutnm and adj. suff. -ate.

## scutch
scutch, tr. v., to separate the fibers of flax from
the woody parts. — Obsol. F. escoucher (F.
ecoucher)y 'to scutch', fr. MF., fr. VL. *exca-
ticdre, 'to skin, flay', fr. L. ex, 'out of (see 1st
-ex-), and cutis, 'skin'. See hide, 'skin', and cp.
cutis, cuticle.

## scutcheon
scutcheon, п., escutcheon. — Aphetic for
escutcheon.

## scutcher
scutcher, п., a swingle. — Formed fr. scutch with
subst. suff. -er.

## scute
scute, п., a scutum (zool.) — L. scutum, 'shield'.
See scutum.

## Scutellaria
Scutellaria, п., a genus of plants, the skullcap
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. scutella, 'a dish', dimin.
of scutum (see scutum and -aria); so called in
allusion to the appendage of the calyx.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:693 COLUMN:3 -->

## scutellate
scutellate, adj., covered with scutella {bot. and
zool.) — Formed from next word with adj. suff.
-ate.

## scuteilum
scuteilum, п., a small scale or plate (bot. and zool.)
— ModL., 'a little shield', dimin. of L. scutum.
See scutum.

## scutiform
scutiform, adj., shield-shaped. — Compounded
of L. scutum, 'shield', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See scutum and form, n.

## scutter
scutter, intr. v., to run in haste; п., a hasty
running. — Altered fr. scuttle.

## scuttle
scuttle, п., a metal receptacle. — ME. scutel, fr.
OE. scutel, 'dish, bowl', fr. L. scutella, 'salver,
waiter', dimin. of scutula, 'a small tray or dish',
which itself is a dimin. of scutra, 'a flat tray,
dish'. The orig. meaning was prob. 'a leather
vessel', fr. scutum, 'shield', orig. 'a leather
shield*. See scutum and cp. scullery, skillet.

## scuttle
scuttle, п., an opening with a lid or cover to it; a
hatchway in the deck of a ship. — ME. skottell,
fr. MF. escoutilles (F. ecoutille), fr. Sp. escotilla,
'hatchway', fr. escote, 'sloping of a jacket,
tucker in a garment'. For sense development cp.
Sp. escotar, 'to cut out a hole (esp. in a
garment)', escotadura, 'sloping of a jacket; a trap
door'. Sp. escote is a loan word fr. Goth.
skauts, 'seam, hem of a garment'. See sheet,
'piece of cloth'.
Derivative: scuttle, tr. v., to cut holes in the
bottom or sides of a ship.

## scuttle
scuttle, intr. v., to hurry; to run away. — A var.
of scuddle, freq. of scud (q.v.)

## scutum
scutum, п., a shield. — L. scutum, 'shield', prob.
for *sqeutom, and lit. meaning 'a covering
shield', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeu-t-, 'to cover',
whence also Gk. κύτος, 'skin, cover*, σκΰτος,
'leather', OE. hyd, 'skin'. See hide, 'skin*, and
cp. cutis, cuticle. Cp. also ecn, equerry,
escutcheon, esquire, scudo, scum, scutch, Scutellaria,
scuteilum, scutiform, scuttle, 'receptacle'. Cp.
also sky.

## scybalum
scybalum, п., constipated fecal mass in the bowels
(med.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σκύβαλον, 'dung,
excrement', which is of uncertain origin.
According to Suidas it is an alteration of κυσίβαλόν
τι 6ν, i.e. το τοΤς κυσΐ βαλλόμενον, 'that
which is cast before the dogs'. See hound, 'dog',
and ballistic.

## Scylla
Scylla, п., a seamonster dwelling on a rock in the
strait of Messina (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Σκύλλα, which is of uncertain origin. It is
possibly rel. to σκύλλειν, 'to tear', and lit. means
'the tearing one'. Gk. σκύλλειν prob. stands in
gradational relationship to σκάλλείν, 'to stir up,
hoe', which derives fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, 'to
cut, cleave, split'. See scale, 'a weighing
instrument'.

## scyphi-
scyphi-, scypho-, combining form meaning 'cup'.
— Gk. σκυφι-, σκυφο-, fr. σκύφος, 'cup1.* See
next word.

## scyphus
scyphus, п., a kind of deep cup (Greek Antiq.) —
L., 'cup', fr. Gk. σκύφος, which prob. stands in
gradational relationship to σκάπτειν, 'to hollow
out1. See scapho-.
Derivative: scyph-ose, adj.

## scythe
scythe, п., a mowing implement.— ME. sithe, fr.
OE. sigde, side, rel. to MLG. segede, sigde,
MDu. sichte (Du zicht), OHG. segensa, seginsa,
MHG. segense, seinse, sense, G. Sense, fr. I.-E.
base *seq-, 'to cut'. See section and cp. saw, 'a
cutting instrument'.
Derivative: scythe, tr. v.

## Scythian
Scythian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Scythia, fr. Gk. ΣκυίΚα, 'the country of the
Scythians', fr. Σκύθης, 'a Scythian'.

## se-
se-,pref.— L. se-, a collateral form of sed-, 'aside,
apart', rel. to the prep, sed, se, 'without', and
to the conjunction sed, 'but', fr. I.-E. reflexive
base *swe-, *se-, whence also OSlav. sve-ne,
sve-ηϊ, 'without'. See secret, sedition, sedalous,
select, separate, severus, solve. See also ebriety,
sober, idio-, See also zenith. For an enlarged
form of the above base see sine and prep.
sunder.

## sea
sea, n. — ME. see, fr. OE. sse, 'sea, lake', rel. to
OS. seo, 'sea; lake', OFris. se, 'sea', MDu. see,
Du. zee, 'sea', OHG. seo, se, MHG. se, G. See,
'sea; lake', ON. sxr, sjdr, 'sea', Dan. se, Swed.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:694 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 667 | SECRETIN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:694 COLUMN:1 -->
sjo, Norw. sj0, 'sea; lake', Goth, saiws, 'lake'.
Cp. son].
Derivative: sea, adj.

## sea kale
sea kale, п., a European plant. — Compounded
of sea and kale.

## seal
seal, п., a marine, fish-eating mammal. — ME.
sele, fr. OE. seolk, rel. to ON. selr, Dan. ssel,
Swed. sjol, MLG. set, OHG. selah.
Derivatives: seal, intr. v., to hunt seals, seal-er,
п., seal-ery, п., seal-ing, n.

## seal
seal, п., imprint, impression. — ME. seel, sele, fr.
OF. seel (F. sceau), fr. VL. *sigellum (whence,
also It. suggello, OProvenc. sael, Sp. and Port.
sello), dissimilated fr. L. sigillum, 'a little mark,
small figure, seal', dimin. of signum, 'sign'. Cp.
OFris. sigel, MDu seghel (Du. zegel), 'seal',
MHG. sigel (G. Siegel), Dan. «у/, Swed. Jfciff,
of s.m., which all are borrowed fr. L. sigillum.
See sign and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: seal-less, adj.

## seal
seal, tr. v., to affix a seal to. — ME. selen, fr. OF.
seeler (F. sceller), fr. seel, 'seal'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: seal-ed, adj., seal-ing, n.

## Sealyham terrier
Sealyham terrier, a breed of terriers. — So
called after Sealy Ham, a place in
Pembrokeshire (Wales).

## seam
seam, п., suture. — ME. sem, seem, fr. OE. seam,
rel. to ON. saumr, OHG., MHG. soum, G.
Saum, and cogn. with OI. sy&man-, 'ite, band',
Gk. ύμήν, 'membrane', and OPruss. schumeno,
'shoemaker's thread', fr. I.-E. base *syu-, *siw-,
'to sew'. See sew and cp. suture, hymen.
Derivatives: seam, tr. v., seam-ing, п., seam-less,
adj.

## seam
seam, п., an old measure of weight. — ME. sem,
seem, fr. OE. seam, 'burden, load', fr. VL. sau-
ma, 'packsaddle' (whence also F. som'me, 'pack-
saddle'), fr. L. sagma, fr. Gk. σάγμα, which is
rel. to σάττει-ν (for *σάκ^ν), 'to pack, stuff'.
Cp. summer, 'a large beam', sumptor.

## seamster
seamster, also sempster, п., a person, esp. a
man, employed in sewing. — ME. semester,
semster, fr. OE. slamestre, formed fr. seam
(see seam) with fern, agential suff. -estre (see
-ster).

## seamstress
seamstress, sempstress, п., a woman employed-in
sewing. — Formed from prec. word with 1st
suff. -ess.

## seaplane
seaplane, n. — Formed fr. sea and plane (the
abbreviation of airplane). Cp. hydroplane.

## sear
sear, п., the catch in the lock of a gun. — MF.
(= F.) serre, 'a grasp, grip', back formation fr.
serrer, 'to press, lock up', fr. VL. "serrdre, fr.
Late L. serdre, 'to bar, bolt', fr. sera, 'a bar (for
fastening a door)* which is rel. to serere, 'to
join, fasten'. VL. "serrdre (for L. serdre) was
prob. influenced by ferrum, 'iron'. Cp. It. ser-
rare, Sp. cerrar, which also derive fr. VL. "ser-
rare. See series and words there referred to and
cp. serry. Cp. also seraglio.

## sear
sear, also sere, adj., dried up; withered. — ME.,
fr. OE. sear, rel. to MLG. sor, MDu. soar, 'dry',
OHG. sarin, 'to become dry', fr. I.-E. base
*saus-, *sus-, 'dry', whence also OI. sosah,
'making dry', suskah, 'dry', sasyati, 'withers',
Avestic hushka-, 'dry', Gk. οώος (for *sauso-s),
'dry', L. sudus (for *susodos), 'dry, cloudless',
Alb. &αή (for "sausnio-), Ί become dry', Lith.
sausas, OSlav. suchu, 'dry'. Cp. auantic, austere,
sorrel, adj.

## sear
sear, tr. v., to dry up; to wither; intr. v., to
become dry; to wither. — ME. seren, fr. OE.
searian, fr. sear. See sear, adj.

## search
search, tr. and intr. v. — ME. serchen, fr. OF.
cerchier, fr. L. circdre, 'to go round', fr. circum,
'around'. F. chercher (fr. OF. cerchier) is due to
assimilation. See circum- and cp. circa, circle,
circus. Cp. also research.
Derivatives: search, п., search-able, adj.,
search-er, п., search-ing, adj., search-ing-ly, adv.,
search-ing-ness, n.

## season
season, n. — ME. sesoun, fr. OF. seson, seison,
saison (F. saison), fr. L. sationem, ace. of satio,
'a sowing', in VL., 'sowing time, sowing season',
fr. satus, pp. of serere, 'to sow, plant', fr. I.-E.
base *se-, whence also semen, 'seed'. See sow, v.,
and cp. .semen. Cp. also seed. In F. saison and
OProvenc iazon, the original meaning 'sowing

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:694 COLUMN:2 -->
season', was changed into 'season' in general.
The stages of sense development were: 'sowing
season; the most important season; season'.
Derivatives: season, tr. and intr. v., season-able,
adj., season-able-ness, п., season-abl-y, adv.,
season-al, adj., season-al-ly, adv., season-al-ity,
ii., season-ed, adj., season-er, п., season-ing, п.,
season-less, adj.

## seat
seat, n. — ME. sete, fr. ON. sasti, whence also
Swed. sate, Dan. ssede; rel. to OHG. sdze, MDu.
gesaete, 'seat', OHG. gisa^i, MHG. gesse^e,
'seat; siege; situation; buttocks', G. Gesafi,
'buttocks', fr. Teut. base *set-, corresponding to
I.-E. *sed-, 'to sit'. See sit.
Derivatives: seat, tr. v., seat-ed, adj., seat-er, п.,
seat-ing, п., seat-less, adj.

## seaward
seaward, adj. and n. — Compounded of sea and
•ward.

## seaward
seaward, seawards, adv. — Compounded of sea
and -ward, resp. -wards.

## sebaceous
sebaceous, adj. — L. sebdeeus, fr. sebum, 'tallow,
suet, grease', which is prob. rel. to L. sdpd,
'soap'. See soap, and cp. suet. For the ending
see suff. -aceous.

## Sebastian
Sebastian, п., masc. PN. — L. Sebastidnus, fr.
Gk. Σεβαστιανός, lit. 'inhabitant of Σεβάστεια,
Sebastia (a town in Pontus)', or 'inhabitant of
Σεβαστή, Sebaste (a name given to the city of
Samaria by Herod the Great, who rebuilt it).
The name of both these places derives fr.
Σεβαστός (lit. 'venerable, august'), epithet of
Augustus Caesar, the first Roman emperor, fr.
σέβεσ&αι, 'to venerate'. (Σεβαστός is prop,
the Greek translation of L. Augustus. See
August).

## sebesten
sebesten, sebestan, п., an Indian tree, Cordia
myxa. — ME., fr. Arab, sibistdn, fr. Pers. sipis-
tdn, fr. sapista, 'smelling badly'.

## sebi-
sebi-, combining form meaning 'tallow, suet'. —
Fr. L. sebum, gen. sebi. See sebaceous.

## sebila
sebila, п., a small wooden bowl. — F. sebile, fr.
Arab, zabil (in vulgar pronunciation zebtf),
'date basket'.

## seborrhea
seborrhea, seborrhoea, п., discharge of sebaceous
matter (med.) — A Medical L, hybrid coined fr.
L. sebum, 'tallow, suet, grease', and Gk. ρ°ίά,
'flow, flux', fr. ρεΐν, 'to flow'. See sebaceous and
rheo-.
Derivatives: seborrhe-al, seborrhoe-al,
seborrheic, seborrhoe-ic adjs.

## sebundy
sebundy, п., irregular native soldiery maintained
by the British in India. — Hind, sibandl, fr.
Pers. sihbandl, lit. 'paid every three months', fr.
si (written sih), 'three', and band, 'band, binding,
agreement'. The first element is rel. to Avestic
&П-, 'three', OPers.0ri"fi>>a, 'third', ΟΙ. tri(neut.),
'three'; see three. The second element is rel. to
OI. bandhdh, 'a tying, fastening; band,
bandage'; see bad, 'a tie'.

## sec
sec, adj., dry (said of wine). — F., 'dry', ft. L.
siccus, 'dry'. See siccative.

## sec
sec, n. — Short for secant.

## secant
secant, adj. and n. — L. secdns, gen. -amis, pres.
part, of secdre, 'to cut'; see section and -ant.
The name secant was first used by the Danish
mathematician Thomas Fincke in his Geome-
tria Rotundi (in 1583).

## secateur
secateur, п., pruning shears. — F. secateur,
learned formation from the stem of L. secdre, 'to
cut', on analogy of the numerous nouns ending
in -ateur (fr. L. -dtor). See section.
.secchio. п., a liquid measure used in Northern
Italy. — It., lit. 'pail, bucket', rel. to secchia, fr.
VL. *sicla, fr. L. situla, 'bucket, urn'; see situla.
Cp. OProvenc., Port selha, F. settle, 'pail,
bucket', which derive fr. L. situla, and F. seau,
'pail, bucket', which comes fr. VL. 'sitellus,
corresponding to L. sitella, dimin. of situla. G.
Seidel, 'mug, pint', is a Romance loan word (see
seidel).

## secco
secco, adj., dry. — Fr. L. siccus. See siccative and
words there referred to.

## secco
secco, п., painting on dry plaster. — Short for
secco painting. See prec. word.

## secede
secede, intr. v., to withdraw from an alliance,
organization, etc. — L. secedere, 'to go away,
withdraw, separate', fr. se- and cidere, 'to go'.
See cede.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:694 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: seced-er, n.

## secern
secern, tr. and intr. v., to separate, distinguish,
discern. — L. secernere, 'to set apart, separate,
distinguish', fr. se- and cernere, 'to separate,
distinguish'. See certuin and cp. secret, secrete.
Cp. also concern, decern, discern.
Derivatives: secernent (q.v.), secern-ment, n.

## secernent
secernent, adj., secreting. — L. secernens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of secernere. See prec. word
and -ent.

## secession
secession, п., the act of seceding. — L. secessio,
gen. -onis, 'withdrawal, separation', fr. secess-
(um), pp. stem of secedere. See secede and -ion.
Derivatives: secesston-al, adj., secession-ism, п.,
secession-ist, n.

## seek
seek, adj., dry, barren, unprofitable. — F. sec,
'dry', fr. L. siccus. See siccative and cp. sack,
'strong wine', sec, secco.

## Seckei
Seckei, п., a variety of sweet pear. — Named
after a farmer in Pennsylvania, who introduced
it.

## seclude
seclude, tr. v. — L. secludere, 'to shut off, shut
up', fr. se- and -cludere (used only in
compounds), fr. claudere, 'to shut, close'. See close,
adj. For the change of Latin au (in claudere) to
й (in se-cludere) see accuse and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: seclud-ed, adj., seclud-ed-ly, adv.,
seclud-ed-ness, n.

## seclusion
seclusion, n. — ML. seclusid, gen. -onis, fr. L.
seclusus, pp. of secludere. See seclude and -ion.
Derivative: seclusion-ist, n.

## seclusive
seclusive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
seciusus, pp. of secludere. See seclude.
Derivatives: seclusive-ly, adv., seclusive-ness, n.

## second
second, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) second, fr. L.
secundus, for *seq-undus, 'the second', prop,
'the following', from the stem of sequi, 'to
follow'. See sequel and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also secund, secundine, secundum.
Derivatives: second, n. and adv., second, v.
(q-v.)

## second
second, п., the sixtieth part of a minute. — F.
seconde, fr. ML. minuta secunda, shortened fr.
L. pars minuta secunda, lit. 'the second small
part (of an hour)', in contradistinction to pars
minuta prima, 'the first small part', i.e. 'minute'.
See second, adj., and cp. minute, 'the sixtieth
part of an hour'.

## second
second, tr. v., to further; to support. — F.
seconder, fr. L. secundare, 'to favor, further,
second', fr. secundus. See second, adj.
Derivative: second-er, n.

## secondary
secondary, adj. — ME. secundarie, secondarie, fr.
L. secundarius, 'pertaining to the second class,
inferior', fr. secundus. See second, adj., and adj.
suff. -ary.
Derivatives: secondary, п., secondari-ly, adv.,
secondari-ness, n.

## seconde
seconde, п., the parrying position in fencing. —
F., short for position seconde, prop, 'the second
position', fem. οι second. See second.

## secondo
secondo, п., the second part in a concerted piece,
the second singer in a duet for pianoforte (mus.)
— It., fr. L. secundus. See second, adj.

## secrecy
secrecy, n. — Formed fr. secret with suff. -cy.

## secret
secret, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) secret, fr. L.
secretus, 'separated, set apart, secret', pp. of
secernere. See secern, secrete.
Derivatives: secret, п., secretary (q.v.),
secretive, adj., secret-ive-ly, adv., secret-ive-ness, п.,
secret-ly, adv., secret-ness, n.

## secretaire
secretaire, п., a writing desk. — F. secretaire, fr.
ML. secritBrius. See secretary,

## secretariat
secretariat, secretariate, n. — F. secretariat, fr.
ML. secretariate, fr. secretSrius. See prec. word.

## secretary
secretary, n. — ML. secretdrius, 'one entrusted
with secrets', fr. L. secretus. See secret and
subst. suff. -ary.
Derivative: secretari-al, adj.

## secrete
secrete, tr. v. — L. secretus, pp. of secernere, 'to
set apart, separate, distinguish'. See secern.
Derivatives: secretion (q.v.), secret-ory, adj.

## secretin
secretin, п., a substance secreted by the intestines.
— Coined by the English physiologists Sir
William Maddock Bayliss (1866-1924) and
Ernest Henry Starling (1866-1927) fr. L.
secretus, pp. of secernere (see secrete) and suff. -in.

## secretion
secretion, η. — F. secretion, fr. L. secretidnem,
ace. of secretio, 'a setting apart, separating*, fr.
sicretus, pp. of secernere. See prec. word and
-ion.
Derivatives: secretion-al, secrelion-ary, adjs.

## sect
sect, п., a group holding similar views; a party.
— F. secte, fr. L. secta, *a trodden way, path; a
following; a school of thought', prop. fem. pp.
of sequi, 'to follow' (see sequel and set,
'number') ; early confused in sense with secta, fem,
pp. of secure, 'to cut' (see next word).
Derivatives: sect-arian, adj. and п.,
sectarianism, п., sect-arian-ize, tr. v., sect-ary, n.

## sect
sect, п., a section. — L. seems, pp. of secdre, 'to
cut'. See section.

## sectile
sectile, adj., capable of being cut. — F., fr. L.
sectilis, 'cut, cleft; that which may be cut', fr.
septus, pp. οι secure. See section and -ile.

## section
section, n. — ME. secte, fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
sectidnem, ace. of sectio, *a cutting, a cutting
off', fr. sectus, pp. of secure, 'to cut*, rel. to
securis, *axe\ fr. I.-E. base *seq-, 'to cut',
whence also OSlav. sikg, sesti, 'to cut', seeivo,
'ax, hatchet', Lith. isekti, 'to engrave, carve',
Alb. sate, *mattock\ OE. sigde, side, 'scythe',
OS. segasna, OHG. segansa, of s.m., OE. secg,
'sword', ON. sax, OE. seax, 'knife, short sword,
dagger1, Olr. doescim (for ·do-ess-secim), tes-
cim, Ί cut*, L. saxum, 'rock, stone'. Cp.
bisect, dissect, insect, intersect, saxatile, scissor,
secant, secateur, sector, securiform, segment,
sicarian, sickle, sigillate, sign, transect, trisect,
venesection, vivisection. Cp. also sail, saw, 'a
cutting too]', sax, Saxon, scythe, sedge, seesaw.
Derivatives: section, tr. v., section-al, adj., sec-
tion-al-ism, п., section-al-ize, tr. v., section-al-
iz-ation, п., section-ize, tr. v.

## sector
sector, п., a mathematical instrument, etc. — L.,
'one who cuts', fr. sectus, pp*. of secure. See
section and agential suff. -or.

## sector
sector, п., part of a circle between two radii. —
Late L., fr. L., 'one who cuts' (see prec. word);
loan translation of Gk. τομεύς, 'sector (of a
circle)', from the stem, of τέμνειν, 'to cut*.
Derivative: sector, tr. v., sector-al, adj.,
sectorial, adj. and n.

## secular
secular, adj., worldly. — ME. seculer, seculere, fr.
OF. seculer (F. seculier), fr. Late L. saecularis,
'pertaining to a generation or age*, fr. L. saecu-
lum, saeclum, 'period of a man's life, generation,
period of a hundred years', which, together with
W. hoedl, 'lifetime', OBret. hoetl, MBret.
hoazl, of s.m., prob. stands for *s i-tlom, lit.
'seed', fr. I.-E. base *se{i)-, 'to sow'; see sow, v.,
and -ar, and cp. siecle. For sense cp. Goth.
mana-sefrs, 'mankind, world*, lit. 'seed of men'.
Derivatives: secular, п., secular-ism, п.,
secularist, п., secular-ist-ic, adj., secularity (q.v.),
secularize (q.v.)

## secularity
secularity, n. — Late ME. seculerte, fr. ML. sae-
culdritds, fr. Late L. saecularis. See prec. word
and -ity.

## secularization
secularization, n. — F. secularisation, fr. sicula-
riser. See next word and -ion.

## secularize
secularize, tr. v., to make secular. — F.
secularises fr. MF., fr. Late L. saecularis. See secular
and -ize.

## secund
secund, adj., growing on one side only {bot.) —
L. secundus, 'the second'. See second, adj.
Derivative: secund-ly, adv.

## secimdine
secimdine, п., the afterbirth (med.) — Late L.
secundinae (pi.), fr. L. secundae, 'the afterbirth',
shortened fr. secundae membrdnae, 'the second
membranes', fr. secundus, 'the second'. See
second, adj.

## secundum
secundum, prep., according to. — L., 'according
to', fr. secundus, 'the second*. See second, adj.

## securable
securable, adj. — Formed fr. the verb secure (see
next word) with suff. -able.

## secure
secure, adj., safe. — L. securus, 'free from care',
fr. se- and cura, 'care'. See cure, 'care', and cp.
sure and sicker, which are doublets of secure.
Derivatives: secure, tr. v., secure-ly, п., secure-
ness, n.

## securiform
securiform, adj., hatchet-shaped. —
Compounded of L. securis, 'ax, hatchet', ana forma, 'form,
shape*. Securis is rel. to secure, 'to cut', and
cogn. with OSlav. sekyra, 'ax'; see section. For

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:695 COLUMN:2 -->
the second element see form, n.

## Securigera
Securigera, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'axe-bearers', fr. L. securis,
'axe, hatchet', and the stem of L. gerere, 'to
bear, carry'. See prec. word and gerent.

## security
security, n. — Late ME. securite, fr. L. securitds,
'freedom from care, safety', fr. securus. See
secure and -ity and cp. surety, which is a doublet
of security.

## sedan
sedan, п., sedan chair. — Of uncertain origin;
usually derived from the town of Sedan, in
France, where it was allegedly first made.

## sedate
sedate, adj., calm, quiet. — L. sedatus,
'composed, moderate, quiet, tranquil', pp. of sedare, *to
calm, allay, assuage, appease', causative of
sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: sedate-ly, adv., sedate-ness, n.

## sedative
sedative, adj., tending to calm or soothe. — F.
sidatif (fem. sedative), fr. ML. sedativus,
'calming, allaying', fr. L. sedatus, pp. of sedare. See
sedate and -ive.
Derivative: sedative, п., a sedative drug.

## sedentary
sedentary, adj., characterized by sitting; not
migratory (said of birds). — F. sedentaire, fr. L.
sedentdrius, 'pertaining to sitting, sedentary*, fr.
sedens, gen. -entis, pres. part, οι sedere, 'to sit*,
fr. I.-E. base *sed-, 'to sit', whence also ΟΙ. ά-
sadat, 'sat down', sidati, 'sits', Avestic had-, 'to
sit down', Gk. £ζεσ&αι (for *sezestkai), 'to sit',
SSpct (for *sedra), 'seat*, Olr. suide, 'seat,
sitting*, W. sedd, 'seat', Mir. sudim, suidim, Ί sit
down', OSlav. sezdq, sedeti, 'to sit*, Lith. sedmi,
sesti, and sedziu, sedeti, 'to sit', OSlav. sedg,
sesti, Lith. sedu, sesti, 'to sit down', OPruss.
sidons, 'sitting', OSlav. sadu, 'plant', Russ. sad,
'garden*, OSlav. saditi, Lith. sod[ti, 'to plant',
Goth, sitan, OE. sittan, *to sit'. See sit and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also anode, assess,
assiduous, assiento, assize, bienseance, cathedral,
cathode, cess, 'tax', chair, chaise, cosset,
dihedral, dissident, edaphic, eisteddfod, ersatz, he-
dral, hostage, Insessores, insidious, Limosella,
nest, nidus, obsess, piezo-, polyhedron, possess,
preside, president, Reseda, reside, resident,
residue, Sanhedrin, sedate, sederunt, sedilia,
sediment, see, п., sejant, sell, 'seat', sessile, session,
sewer, 'servant', siege, sizar, size, subsellium,
subsidy, supersede, surcease, synizesis,
tetrahedron. I.-E. base *sed-, 'to sit', is identical with
base *sed-, 'to go'. See cede.
Derivatives: sedentary, п., sedentari-ly, adv.,
sedentari-ness, n.

## Seder
Seder, п., the home service on the two first nights
of Passover, contained in the Haggadah {Jewish
Religion). — Heb. sedher, 'order, arrangement',
rel. to tdhercP, 'row, rank (of soldiers)',
Mishnaic Heb. sddhar, Aram, s dkar^he
arranged, ordered', Aram, sidkrd, Syr. sedhra,
'arrangement, order', Akkad. saddru, 'to arrange',
sidru, sidirtu, 'row, battle line'. Cp. Sedra, siddur.

## sederunt
sederunt, п., session, sitting. — L. sederunt, 'they
sat', 3rd person pi. past tense of sedere, 'to sit'.
See sedentary.

## sedge
sedge, n. — ME, segge, fr. OE. secg, rel. to LG.
segge (whence G. Segge), and to OE. secg,
'sword', and cogn. with Olr. seisg, 'rush', W.
kesg, 'reed, rush'; fr. I.-E. base *seq-¥ 'to cut*
(see section). OE. secg orig. meant 'the cutting
plant*.
Derivative, sedg-y, adj.

## sedilia
sedilia, n. pi., seats in the chancel of a church. —
L. sedilia, 'seats, stools', pi. of sedile, a
derivative of sedere. See sedentary.

## sediment
sediment, п., anything that settles. — F. sediment,
fr. L. sedimentum, *a settling down, subsidence',
from the stem of sedere. See sedentary and
-ment.
Derivatives: sediment-ary, adj. and п., sediment-
ari-ly, adv., sediment-ation, п., sediment-ous,
adj.

## sedition
sedition, п., revolt, rebellion. — ME., fr. OF.
sedicion (F. sedition), fr. L. seditidnem, ace. of
seditio, 'insurrectionary separation, mutiny',
lit. 'a going apart*, fr. sed-, 'beside, apart' (see
se-) and itid, gen. -onis, 'a going*, fr. /г-(нт),

## pp. stem of ire
pp. stem of ire, 'to go'. See itinerate and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-ion.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:695 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: sedition-ary, adj., sedition-ist, n.

## seditious
seditious, adj., inciting to revolt. — ME., fr. MF.
(= F.) siditieux, fr. L. seditidsus, 'turbulent,
mutinous', fr. seditio. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: seditious-ly, adv., seditious-ness, n.

## Sedra
Sedra, Sidra, п., the weekly section of the
Pentateuch read in the synagogue {Jewish Religion).
— Aram, sidhra, 'order', rel. to Syr. sedhra,
Heb. sedher, of s.m. See Seder and cp. siddur.

## seduce
seduce, tr. v. — L. seducere, 'to lead aside,
separate', in Late L., 'to lead astray, seduce',
fr. se- and ducere, 'to lead'. See dnke and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: seduc-ee, п., seduce-ment, п.,
seducer, п., seduc-ing, adj., seduc-ing-ly, adv.

## seduction
seduction, n. — F. seduction, fr. L. seductidnem,
ace. of seductid, 'a leading aside*, fr. seductus,
pp. of seducere. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: seduction-ist, n.

## sednctive
sednctive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
seductus, pp. of seducere. See seduce.
Derivatives: seductive-ly, adv., seductive-ness,
n.

## sedulity
sedulity, п., quality of being sedulous. — L.
sedulitds, 'assiduity, application', fr. sedulus.
See next word and -ity.

## sedulous
sedulous, adj., diligent, assiduous. — L. sedulus,
'busy, zealous, assiduous', fr. the adv. sechild,
'busily, zealously, assiduously', formed fr.
se(d) dolo, 'without malice*, fr. sed, se~, 'without*
(see se-), and dolus, 'guile, deceipt, deception',
which is cogn. with Gk. δόλος, of s.m. See dole,
'guile', and cp. subdolous. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: sedulous-ly, adv., sedulous-ness, n.

## Sedum
Sedum, п., a genus of plants, the stonecrop (bot.)
— L. sedum, 'the houseleek', a foreign word of
uncertain origin.

## see
see, tr. and intr. v., to perceive with the eyes. —
ME. seen, sen, fr. OE. seon, rel. to OS., OHG.
sekan, MHG., G. sehen, OFris. sia, MDu. sien,
Du. zien, ON. sja, Norw. sjaa, Dan., Swed. se,
Goth, saihan, and prob. cogn. with Hitt. sakwa-,
'eye'; fr. Teut. base *sefiw-, corresponding to
l.-E. base *seqw-, 'to see', which is etymologi-
cally identical with *seqw- in the sense *щ point
out, to say'. See say, v., and cp. seem, sight
Derivatives: see-ing, п., adj., and conj. see-ing-ly,
adv., see-ing-ness, п., seer (q.v.)

## see
see, п., the seat of a bishop. — ME. se, fr. OF.
sied, sed, se, fr. L. sedem, ace. of sedes, 'seat*,
which is rel. to sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary.

## seed
seed, n. — ME. seed, sed, fr. OE. sied, rel. to ON.
sad, OS. sdd, OFris. sed, MDu. saet, Du. zaad,
OHG., MHG. sat, G. Saat, and to the second
element of Goth, manna-seps, 'mankind', lit.
'seed of men', fr. I.-E. base *se-, 'to sow'. See
sow, v. and cp. semen. Cp. also the second
element in colza.
Derivatives: seed, tr. and intr. v., seed-ed, adj.,
seed-er, п., seed-ful, adj., seed-kin, п., seed-less,
adj., seed-ling, п., seed-y, adj., seed-i-ly, adv.

## seek
seek, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sechen, seken, fr. OE.
secan, rel. to OS. sdkian, ON. sakja, OFris.
seka, MDu. soeken, Du. zoeken, OHG. suohhan,
suohhen, MHG. suochen, suechen, G. suchen,
Goth, sokjan, fr. I.-E. base *sdg-, *s g-, 'to
track down, trace, seek*, whence also Gk.
ήγέομαι (Dor. αγέομαΟ, Ί lead* (orig. prob.
Ί track down the way'), L. sagire, 'to perceive
quickly or keenly', sdgus, 'presaging, predicting,
prophetic', sdgdx, 'sagacious', Olr. saigim, Ί
seek', and prob. also Hitt. shak-, 'to know', sha-
kaish, 'mark, sign'. Cp. beseech, sake, 'purpose',
forsake, ransack, 'to plunder', seize, hame-
sucken. Cp. also sagacious, presage. Cp. also
exegesis and words there referred to.
Derivatives: seeker (q.v.), seek-ing, n.
"seeker, n. — ME. secher, seker, fr. sechen, seken,
'to seek*. See seek and agential suff. -er.

## seel
seel, tr. v., to close the eyes (of a hawk). — ME.
silen, fr. OF. ciller, siller (F. Ciller), fr. cil,
'eyelid1, fr. L. cilium. See cilia.

## seely
seely, adj., blessed; weak, wretched {obsol.) —
ME. sely, fr. OE. gesplig; a doublet of silly.

## seem
seem, intr. v. — ME. semen, 'to seem, to befit'
(for the latter sense cp. seemiy), fr. ON. sama
(fem. scemr), 'fitting, becoming', which is rel. to

## seemly
seemly, adj. — ME. semlich, fr. ON. scemiligr, fr.
samr, 'becoming'. See seem and adj. suff. -ly.
Derivatives: seemli-ly, adv., seemli-ness, n.

## seen
seen, pp. of see. — ME. sein, sen, seien, fr. OE.
gesegen, gesewen, pp. ofseon, 'to see'. See see, v.

## seep
seep, intr. v., to ooze. — Fr. earlier sipe, fr.
ME. sipen, fr. OE. sipian, which is rel. to MHG.
slfen, Du. sljpelen, 'to ooze'.
Derivatives: seep, п., seep-age, п., seep-y, adj.

## seer
seer, п., one who sees; a prophet. — ME., fr.
seen, sen, 'to see'. See see, v., and agential suff.
-cr and cp. the second element in sightseer.
Derivative: seer-ess, n.

## seer
seer, п., a weight of India. — See ser.

## seerband
seerband, п., turban. — Hind, sirband, 'turban',
lit. 'headband', fr. OI. siras, 'head, summit',
and bandhab, 'a tying, fastening; band,
bandage'. For the first element see cerebrum and cp.
the first element in seerpaw. For the second
element see band, 'tie',

## seerpaw
seerpaw, п., a complete suit presented by the
sovereign (Anglo-Indian). — Hind, sar-d-pd, fr.
Pers. sar-d-pd, lit. 'from head to foot'. Pers. sar,
'head', is rel. to OI. Siras-, 'head, summit'; see
cerebrum and cp. the first element in seerband.
Pers. pa, 'foot', is rel. to OI. pat, ace. pddam,
'foot'; seefoot and cp. the first element in pajama.

## seersucker
seersucker, п., a kind of cotton fabric. — Hind.
Sirsakar, fr. Pers. shtr-o-shdkdr, lit. 'milk and
sugar'. Pers. shir is rel. to OI. ksiram, Ossetic
dhshir, 'milk'. Pers. shakur is rel. to Pali sak-
kkard, OI. sarkara, 'gravel, grit, sugar'. See sugar.

## seesaw
seesaw, п., antiphonic reduplication of saw,
'cutting tool'.
Derivatives: seesaw, tr. and intr. v., adj. and adv.

## seethe
seethe, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sethen, fr. OE. sio-
dan, rel. to ON. sjoda, Dan. syde; Swed. sjuda,
Norw. sjoa, OFris. siatha, Du. zieden, OHG.
siodan, MHG-, G. sieden, 'to seethe', Goth.
saups, 'sacrificial animal, victim', fr. I.-E. base
*sew-, 'to seethe, boil', whence also Avestic
hdvayeiti, 'stews'. Cp. sod, 'turf', sodden, suds,
sutler.
Derivatives: seethe, п., seeth-ing, adj., seeth-ing-
ly, adv.

## segar
segar, n. — An obsolete variant of cigar,

## segnol
segnol, п., name of the Heb.-Aram. vowel sign .
— Aram, s ghol, lit. 'cluster of grapes'; so
called from its form.

## segholate
segholate, adj. and n. (Heb. gram.) — ModL.

because the segholates always have a seghol in
the second syllable. See prec. word and adj. suff.
-ate.

## segment
segment, п., one of the parts into which a body is
divided; division, section. — L. segmentum, 'a
cutting; a piece cut off', for *' sec-mentum, fr.
sec-, stem of secdre, 'to cut'. See section and
-ment.
Derivatives: segment, tr. v., segment-al, adj., seg-
ment-al-ly, adv., segment-ary, adj.,
segmentation, п., segment-ed, adj.

## segregate
segregate, tr. and intr. v. — L. segregatus, pp. of

## segregdre
segregdre, 'to set apart, to separate from the
flock', fr. se- and grex, gen. gregis, 'flock'. See
gregarious and verbal suff. -ate and cp.
aggregate.
Derivatives: segregat-ive, adj., segregat-or, n.

## segregate
segregate, adj., segregated. — L. segregatus, pp. .
of segregdre. See segregate, v.

## segregation
segregation, n. — Late L. segregatid, gen. -onis,
fr. L. segregatus, pp. of segregdre, See segregate,
v., and -Ion.
Derivatives: segregation-al, adj., segregation-ist,
n.

## segnidilla
segnidilla, п., a Spanish dance and tune. — Sp.,
dimin. of seguida, 'the act of following,
succession', fr. seguir, 'to follow', formed—with
change of conjugation—fr. VL. sequere
(corresponding to L. sequl), 'to follow', whence also
Prov. segre, F. suiyre, and—with change of
conjugation—It. seguire, Port, seguir. See

## sequel
sequel,

## seicento
seicento, п., the 17th century (used with reference

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:696 COLUMN:2 -->
to Italian art). — It.,vlit. 'six hundred', short for
mil seicento, 'one thousand and six hundred'.
Seicerito is compounded of sei, 'six', fr. L. sex,

## seiche
seiche, п., the oscillation of water above and
below the level of lakes and landlocked seas. —
Swiss F., of uncertain origin.

## seidel
seidel, п., an old liquid measure. — G., fr. MHG.
side!, a Romance loan word ult. derived fr. L.
situla, 'bucket, urn'. See situla and cp. secchio.

## Seidlitz powder
Seidlitz powder, an aperient. — Named after a
spring in Seidlitz, Czechoslovakia.

## seigneur
seigneur, п., a feudal lord. — MF. (= F.) See
seignior.

## seigneurial
seigneurial, adj., pertaining to a seigneur. — F-,
fr. MF., fr. seigneur. See prec. word and -ial.

## seignior
seignior, also seigneur, п., feudal lord. — MF.
seignor, seigneur (F. seigneur), fr. OF. seignor,
fr. L. seniorem, ace. of senior, 'older'. See
senior and cp. sefiar-, senhor, signore, sir, sire.
Derivatives: seignior-al, adj., seignior-al-ty, n.

## seigniorage
seigniorage, also seignenrage, п., dominion. —
ME. seigneurage, fr. MF. seignorage, seigneu-
rage (F. seigneuriage), fr. OF., fr. VL. *senidra-
ticum, fr. L. senior. See prec. word and -age.

## seigniory
seigniory, also selgnory, п., dominion of a
seignior. — ME., fr. MF. seignorie, seigneurle (F.
seigneurie), fr. OF. seignorie, fr. seignor. See
seignior and -y (representing OF. and F. -ie).

## seignoral
seignoral, also seignorial, adj., pertaining to a
seignior. — Formed fr. seignior with suff. -al,
resp. -ial.

## seine
seine, п., a large fishing net.— ME., fr. OE. segne,
fr. L. sagena, it. Gk. σαγήνη, 'a fishing net',
which is of uncertain origin. F. seine, of s.m.,
also derives fr. L. sagena.
Derivative: seine, tr. and intr. v.

## seise
seise, v. — The same as seize.

## seisin
seisin, n. — The same as seizin.

## seismal
seismal, adj., seismic. — See seismo- and adj.
suff. -al and cp. coseismal.

## seismic
seismic, adj., pertaining to arj earthquake. — See
seismo- and adj. suff. -ic and cp. coseismic.
Derivatives: seismic-al, adj., seismic-al-ly, adv.,
seismic-ity, n.

## seismo-
seismo-, combining form meaning 'connected
with an earthquake, of an earthquake'. — Gk.
■σεισμό-, fr. σεισμός, 'earthquake', fr. σείειν,
'to shake, move to and fro', which stands for
*tweisein, fr. I.-E. base 'tweis-, 'to shake; move
violently', whence also OI. tvesati, 'is violently
shaken', tvesdh, 'vehement, impetuous; shining,
brilliant', Lith. tvisketi, 'to 'flame'. Cp. siriasis,
Sirius, sistrum.

## seismogram
seismogram, п., the record of an earthquake
made by a seismograph. — Compounded of
seismo- and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written,
a letter'. See -gram.

## seismograph
seismograph, п., an instrument for measuring the
motions of an earthquake. — Compounded of
seismo- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to
write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: setsmograph-er, п., seismograph-ic,
seismograph-ic-al, adjs., seismograph-y, n.

## seismology
seismology, п., the study of earthquakes. —
Compounded of seismo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: seismolog-ic-al, adj., seismolog-ist,
n.

## seismometer
seismometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
intensity and motions of an earthquake. —
Compounded of seismo- and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: seismometr-ic, seismometr-ic-al,
adjs., seismometr-y, n.

## seismoscope
seismoscope, п., an instrument for indicating the
occurrence of earthquakes. — Compounded of
seismo- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεϊν, *to look
at, examine'. See -scope.

## seizable
seizable, adj. — Formed fr. seize with suff. -able.

## seize
seize, tr. and intr. v. — ME. saysen, seysen, 'to
take possession of, to grasp', fr. OF. miiir,
seisir (F. saisir), fr. Frankish-Latin sacire, which
is prob. a blend of Frankish *sakjan, 'to lay
claim to', and *satjan, 'to set'; see Dauzat,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:696 COLUMN:3 -->
DELF., p. 646 s.v.,saisir. Frankish *sakjan is
rel. to Goth, sdkjafl, OE. secan, 'to seek'; see
seek and cp. sake, 'purpose'. Frankish *satjan is
rel. to Goth, satjan, OE. settan, 'to set'; see set,
v. Cp. seizin.
Derivatives: seiz-er, п., seiz-ing, п., seizure (q.v.)

## seizin
seizin, seisin, п., freehold possession of land (law).
— ME. seisine, seisin. The orig. meaning was
'possession', fr. OF. (= F.) saisie, fr. saisir, 'to
seize, take possession of. See seize and cp.
disseizin.

## seizure
seizure, n. — Formed fr. seize with suff. -ure. Cp.
pleasure, fr. please.

## sejant
sejant, adj., sitting; said of a lion or another
beast (heraldry). — AF. seiant, corresponding
to F. seant, 'sitting', pres. part, of seoir, 'to sit',
fr. L. sedere. See sedentary and -ant.

## Sejm
Sejm, also Seym, п., assembly, diet, specif, the
Constituent Assembly of the Polish Republic.
— Pol. sejm, 'assembly', rel. to OCzech snem,
Czech snem, for *syn-i,mu, lit. 'a taking together',
fr. pref. syn-, 'together', and *imu, .'a taking'; fr.
Pol. jql, resp. Czech jeti, 'to take'; rel. to OSlav.
imq, jeti, 'to take' (orig. *img, cp. vuz-imo, Ί
take away'), imami, imejo, imiti, 'to have', Lith.
imu, imti, Lett, jemu, jemt, 'to take'; fr. I.-E.
base *em-, 'to take', whence also L. emere, 'to
take, buy'. See exempt, v., and cp. words there
referred to.

## sekos
sekos, п., the sacred enclosure of a temple. — Gk.
σηκός, 'shrine, enclosure'; of unknown origin.

## Selachii
Selachii, n. pi., an order of elasmobranch fishes
(ichthyol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σέλαχος, 'any
cartilaginous fish; a shark', which prob. derives
fr. σέλας, 'light, brightness, flame' (see seleno-),
and is so called from the phosphorescent light
these fishes are used to emit.

## seladang
seladang, п., gaur, wild ox of Malaysia. —
Borrowed fr. Malay through the medium of. the
Dutch.

## Seladon
Seladon, п., PN. used to denote a sentimental
lover. — F. Celadon, name of a character in the
romance of l'Astree, written by Нопогё d'Urfe
(in 1610).

## seladon green
seladon green, 'bright green'; so called because
Seladon used to wear bright green clothes.

## Selaginella
Selaginella, п., a genus of mosslike plants (bot.)
— ModL., dimin. of L. seldgo, gen. -inis, name
of a plant. See Selago and -eila.

## Selaginellaceae
Selaginellaceae, n. pi., a family of mosslike plants
(йог.) — ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## selaginellaceous
selaginellaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Selago
Selago, п., a genus of plants of the figwort
family (bot.) — L. seldgo, 'a plant resembling the
savin tree', of uncertain origin.

## selah
selah, п., technical term of music in the Psalms
arid the Book of Habakkuk, chapter 3,
indicating a pause. — Heb. silah, prob. a musical
direction to raise the voice fr. Heb. base s-l-1, 'to
raise, lift', whence also m silld , 'highway'.

## selamlik
selamlik, п., the men's quarters in a Turkish
house. — Turk, selamliq, a hybrid coined fr.
Arab, saldm, 'peace', and the Turkish suff. -Ilk.
See sniaam.

## seldom
seldom, adv. — ME. selden, seldom, fr. OE. sel-
dun, seldan, seldon, formed fr. *seld, 'rare', with
the adverbial suff. -um, originally the suff. used
to form the dative of theplural (cp. whilom); rel.
to ON. sjdldan, Dan. sjelden, Swed. saltan (for
saldan), OFris., MLG. selden, Du. zelden, OHG.
seltan, MHG-, G. selten, and to the first element
in OS., OE. seld-llc, Goth, silda-leiks,
'wonderful', prop, 'of a rare form' (for the second
element of these words see -like).

## select
select, adj. — L. selectus, pp. of seligere, 'to
separate by culling out, pick out, choose', fr. se-
and legere, 'to gather, collect'. See lecture.
Derivatives: select-ed, adj., select-ed-ly, adv.,
selection (q.v.), select-ive, adj., select-ive-ly, adv.,
select-ive-ness, п., select-iv-ity, n,, select-ly, adj.,
select-ness, п., select-or, n.

## select
select, tr. v. — Back formation fr. select, adj.

## selection
selection, n. — L. selectio, gen. -onis, fr. selectus,
pp. of seligere. See select, adj., and -ion.
Derivatives: selection-ism, п., selection-ist, n.

## selen
selen, form of seleno- before a vowel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:697 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SELENE | 670 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:697 COLUMN:1 -->

## Selene
Selene, п., the goddess of the moon {Creek
mythol.) — Gk. Σελήνη, fr. σελήνη, 'moon'. See
seleno-.

## seleniferous
seleniferous, adj., containing selenium (chem.) —
See seleuium and -ferous.

## selenite
selenite, п., a variety of gypsum. — L. selenites,
fr. Gk. σεληνΐτης, short for σεληνιτης λί&ος,
lit. 'moon stone', fr. σελήνη, 'moon* (see seleno-
and subst. suff. -ite); so called because it was
supposed to wax and wane with the moon.
Derivative: selenir-ic, adj.

## selenium
selenium, п., name of a nonmetallic element
(chem.) — ModL., coined by its discoverer, the
Swedish chemist Jons Jakob Berzelius (1779-
1848), fr. Gk. σελήνη, 'moon'; so called by him
because of its resemblance to tellurium, the
element called after the earth. See seleno- and 2nd
-ium.
Derivatives: selen-ate, п., selen-ic, adj., selen-
ide, п., selen-ious, adj.

## seleno-
seleno-, before a vowel selen-, combining form
denoting the moon. — Gk. σεληνο-, σελην-, fr.
σελήνη, 'moon', rel. to σέλας, 'light, brightness,
fiame', fr. •σ/'ελ-, fr. I.-E. base *swel-, 'to burn',
esp. 'to burn without flame, burn slowly', whence
also OI. svargah, 'heaven', Lith. svilri, Lett, svelt,
'to singe', OE. sv/elan, OFris. swela, 'to be burnt
up', OE. swol, 'heat', MLG. swelen (whence G.
schwelen), 'to burn without flame, smolder',
OHG. swilizdn, 'to singe, roast', Gk. έλη, εϊλη
(for *Ffa&a, *ίέλα), 'the sun's heat'. See
sweal, swelter and cp. Selene, selenium, Selachii,
Svarga, and the second element in paraselene.
Cp. also Sol.

## selenocentric
selenocentric, adj., relating to the center of the
moon or to the moon as a center. —
Compounded of seleno- and centric.

## selenograph
selenograph, п., a chart of the surface of the moon
or of a part of it. — Compounded of seleno- and
Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See-graph.
Derivatives: selenograpk-y, п., selenograph-ic,
adj.

## selenology
selenology, п., astronomy of the moon. — Lit.
'study of the moon'; compounded of seleno- and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: selenolog-ist, n.

## selenosis
selenosis, п., poisoning of livestock, caused by the
ingestion of plants containing selenium. —
ModL., formed fr. selen(ium) with suif. -osis.

## selenotropic
selenotropic, adj., turning toward the moon (said
of plants). — Compounded of seleno- and
-tropic.

## selenotropism
selenotropism, п., tendency to turn toward the
moon (boi.) — Compounded of seleno-, Gk.
τροπή, 'a turning', and suff. -ism. See trope,
tropism, and cp. hellotropism.

## Seleucid
Seleucid, also Seleucian, adj., pertaining to the
Seleucidae. — See next word and the suffixes
-id, resp. -ian.

## Seleucidae
Seleucidae, n. pi., a dynasty which ruled over
Asia Minor, Syria and Persia (312-64 B.C.E.) —
Named after its founder Seleucus Nicator.

## self
self, n. — ME., fr. OE. self, seolf, syl/, rel. to OS.
self, ON. sjdlfr, Swed. sjalv, Dan. selv, OFris.
self, MDu. self, selve, zehe, Du. zelf, OHG. selb,
MHG. selp, G. se!b(er),se!bst, Goth, silba; prob.
fr. I.-E. base "se-lo-, 'itself, which is
compounded of reflexive pronominal base *se-, 'himself,
herself, itself (see sib and cp. sni), and
pronominal base *lo-. Cp. the first element in selvage,
selvedge.
Derivatives: selfish (q.v.), self-less, adj., self-
less-ly, adv., self-less-ness, n.

## seir-
seir-, pref. — ME., fr. OE. self-,.sylf-, fr. self,
syjf See prec. word.

## -seir
-seir, suif. — See self.

## seir-couscious
seir-couscious, adj. — Coined by the English poet
Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772-1834).
Derivatives: self-conscious-ly, adv., self-con-
scious-ness, n. (first used by Locke).

## self-control
self-control, n. — Coined by the English moral
philosopher Anthony Ashley Cooper
Shaftesbury (1671-1713).

## self-determination
self-determination, n. — Coined by President
Thomas Woodrow Wilson (1856-1924).

## self-help
self-help, n. — Coined by the Scottish essayist

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:697 COLUMN:2 -->
and historian Thomas Carlyle (1795-1881).

## selfish
selfish, adj. — Coined by the Presbyterians about
1640 from self and adj. suff. -ish.
Derivatives: selfish-ly, adv., selfish-ness, n.

## self-regarding
self-regarding, adj. — Fr. self and pres. part, of
regard, v.; first used by the English reformer
Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832).

## selihoth
selihoth, n. pi., penitential prayers recited on fast
days and the days preceding Rosh Hashanah
and during the Days of Penitence {Jewish
Religion). — Heb. * lihoth, prop, 'prayers for
forgiveness', pi. of s likd , lit. 'forgiveness', fr.
sdldk, 'he forgave'.

## Selina
Selina, fern. PN. — According to Charlotte Mary
Onge, History of Christian names, 1884, fr. F.
Celine, fr. L. Caelina, lit. 'heavenly', fr. caelum,
'heaven'. See celestial.

## Seljuk
Seljuk, п., a member of a Turkish dynasty, which
ruled from the 11th to the I3th centuries.
— Named after Seljuk (Turkish Seljuq), the
founder of the dynasty.
Derivatives: Seljuk, Seljuk-ian, adjs.

## sell
sell, tr. and intr. v., to give in exchange for
something. — ME. sellen, sillen, fr. OE: sellan, sillan,
syllan, 'to give, deliver, sell', rel. to ON. selja,
'to hand over, deliver, sell', Dan. sxlge, Swed,
salja, 'to sell', OFris. sella, OHG. sellen, 'to giye,
hand over, sell', Goth, satjan, 'to offer a
sacrifice', and to ΟΝ., OHG. sala, 'a handing over,
delivery, sale' (see sale); fr. I.-E. base *sel-, 'to
take'. The above Teut. verbs are causatives and
orig. meant 'to cause to take'; the modern sense
of the verb sell( = 'to give in exchange for
something') is of much later origin. From I.-E. base
*sel- derive also Gk. έλεϊν, 'to take', Olr. selb,
W. helw, 'possession', L. consilium, 'counsel,
deliberation', orig. 'a gathering together'. See
consult and cp. Hellen.
Derivatives: sell-er, п., sell-ing, n.

## sell
sell, п., 1) a seat, throne (obsol.); 2) a saddle
(archaic). — ME. selle, fr. MF. (= F.) selle, fr.
L. sella, which stands for *sed-la, fr. sedere, 'to
sit'. See, settle, п., and cp. saddle.

## sellenders
sellenders, n. — A var. of sallenders.

## Seltzer water
Seltzer water, also seltzer, aerated mineral water.
— Contraction of G. Selterser (Wasser),
'(water) of Sellers', a village near Wiesbaden,
Germany.

## selvage
selvage, selvedge, п., edge of web or cloth so
finished as to prevent raveling. — ME. selvage,
lit. 'its own edge', formed fr. self and edge on
analogy of, and influenced in form by, MFlem.
selvegge, selvage (fr. selv-, '-self, and egge,
'edge'). Cp. LG. sulfegge, Du. zelfkant (kant
meaning 'border') and MHG. selbende (whence
G. Salband), lit. 'self-end, self-edge'.
Derivatives: selvage, tr. v., selvag-ee, n.

## semanteme
semanteme, п., a word or part of a word which
expresses the idea inherent in the word,
distinguished from morpheme, i.e. that part of a word
which contains the affixes and suffixes. — F.
semanteme, coined fr. Gk. σήμα, 'sign', on
analogy of phoneme, which derives fr. Gk.
φώνημα, 'sound'. See semantics and cp. hy-
