pheme, morpheme, solideme.

## semantic
semantic, adj., 1) pertaining to meaning; 2)
pertaining to semantics. — Gk. σημαντικός,
'significant, meaning'. See next word.

## semantics
semantics, п., the science of the meanings of
words. — F. semantique, coined by Michel
Breal, author of Essai de semantique (1897) fr.
Gk. σημαντικός, 'significant, meaning', fr.
σημαίνειν, 'to signify', fri σήμα, 'sign', which
is cogn. with OI. dhth, dhydnah, 'thought',
dhyati, dhyayati, 'thinks'. See dhyana and cp.
semeio-, asemia, and the second element in
teloserne, diseme, triseme, tetraseme. For the
ending see suff. -ics.

## semaphore
semaphore, п., an apparatus for'signaling. — F.
semaphore, lit. 'a bearer of signals',
compounded of Gk. σήμα, 'sign', and -φόρος, 'carrying'.
See prec. word and -phore.
Derivatives: semaphore, tr. and intr. v., sema-
phor-ic, semaphor-ic-al, adjs., semaphor-ic-al-ly,
adv., semaphor-ist, n.

## semasiology
semasiology, п., semantics. — G. Semasiologie,

## lit. 'the study of meaning'
lit. 'the study of meaning', coined by Christian
Karl Reisig [1792(?)-1829] fr. Gk. σημασία,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:697 COLUMN:3 -->
'significance, meaning' (fr. σήμα, 'sign'), and
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See semantics and -logy.

## sematic
sematic, adj., serving as a sign or warning. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. σήμα, gen.
σήματος, 'sign'. See semantics.

## semblable
semblable, adj., resembling. — F., fr. sembler, 'to
seem, resemble'. See semble and -able.

## semblance
semblance, п., likeness; outward appearance. —
ME. semblaunce, fr. OF. semblance,
'resemblance' (in F. this word occursonlyinderivatives
and compounds), fr. OF. (= F.) semblant, pres.
part, of sembler, 'to resemble', fr. L. simuldre,
'to make like, represent'. See semble and -ance
and cp. vraisemblance.

## semble
semble, intr. v., it seems (legal term). — F., 3rd p.
sing. pres. ind. of sembler, 'to seem, resemble',
fr. L. simuldre, 'to make like, represent'. See
simulate and cp. resemble.

## seme
seme, adj., sown, powdered. — F., 'sown', pp. of
semer, fr. L. seminare, 'to sow', fr. semen, gen.
seminis, 'seed'. See semen.

## semeio-
semeio-, combining form meaning 'sign,
symptom'. — GJc. σημείο-, fr. σημεΐον, 'sign', fr.
σήμα, 'sign'. See semantics.

## semeiology
semeiology, п., 1) the art of using signs, sign
language ; 2) the study of the symptoms of a disease,
symptomatology. — Compounded of semeio-
and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in
a certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: semetolog-ic-al,ad}., semeiolog-ist,n.

## semeiotic
semeiotic, adj., 1) pertaining to signs; 2)
pertaining to symptoms. — Coined by the American
logician and psychologist Charles Santiago
Sanders Peirce (1839-1914) fr. Gk. σημειωτική
(scil. τέχνη), 'the doctrine of signs', fem. of
σημειωτικό;, 'pertaining to signs', fr. σημεΐον,
'sign'. See semeio- and adj. suff. -ic.

## semeiotics
semeiotics, п., symptomatology. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## Semele
Semele, п., the daughter of Cadmus and the
mother of Dionysus (Greek mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. Σεμέλη, a Thraco-Phrygian earth goddess,
fr. Phrygian Ζεμελω, 'mother of the earth'. See
Franz Altheim, Geschichte der lateinischen
Sprache, p. 132. Phryg. Ζεμελω is prob. cogn.
with OSlav. zemlja, 'earth', L. humus, 'earth,
ground, soil'. See humus.

## semen
semen, n. — L. semen, 'seed', cogn. with OSlav.
seme, OPruss. semen, 'seed', Lith. semens (pi.),
'seed of flax', OS., OHG. sumo, 'seed', MHG.
same, G. Same, of s.m.; fr. I.-E. base *se(i)-, 'to
sow'. Cp. L. serere, 'to sow', which derives fr.
*si-so, reduplication of the original base *se-.
See sow, v., and cp. seme, seminal, seminary,
semination, disseminate, inseminate. Cp. also
season. For the ending of semen see suff. -men.

## semester
semester, п., a period of six months. — G.
Semester, fr. F. semestre, fr. L. seme(n)stris (for
*sex-mens-tris), 'of six months, half-yearly', fr.
sex, 'six', and mensis, 'month'. Cp. L. menstruus,
'pertaining to a month, monthly', interme(n)-
stris, 'between two months', and see six and
moon. Cp. also menses, trimester.

## semi-
semi-, combining form meaning 'half. — ME.,
fr. L. semi-, 'half, which is cogn. with OI. sdml,
'half, ά-samih, 'not a half, complete', Gk. ήμι-,
'half-', ήμισυς (for *ήμι-τυς), 'half, OE. sum-,
OHG. sami-, 'half (cp. e.g. OE. sdm-cwicu,
OHG. sdmi-quek, 'half-alive'). Cp. hemi- and
the first element in sesqui-, sesterce. Cp. also the
first element in sandblind.

## semi-annual
semi-annual, adj., half-yearly. — Compounded of
semi- and annual.

## semibreve
semibreve, п., a note equivalent to half the length
of a breve (music). — Compounded of semi- and
breve.

## semicha
semicha, also semichah, n. — See semikah.

## semicircle
semicircle, п., a half circle. — Compounded of
semi- and circie.

## semicolon
semicolon, п., a punctuation mark (;). — A
hybrid coined fr. L. semi-, 'half, and Gk. κώλον,
'limb, part'. See semi- and colon, 'punctuation
mark'.

## semikah
semikah, also spelled semika, semichah, semicha,
п., rabbinical ordination. — Mishnaic Heb.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:698 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 671 | SENSATION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:698 COLUMN:1 -->
s mikha , 'laying on (of hands)', verbal n. of
samakh, 'he laid' (fr. Biblical Heb. samdkh, of
s.m.), used elliptically for samakh eth ydddw, 'he
laid his hands' (see Num. 27 : 25), an act
symbolizing the transference of authority. Yleb.
samakh is rel. lo Aram.-Syr. samakh, 'he stayed,
sustained, supported', Ethiop. samaka, of s.m.,
Arab, simak, 'support', samk, 'roof.

## semimembranosus
semimembranosus, п., name of a muscle (anat.) —
Medical L. semimembranosus (scil. musculus),
erroneously formed fr. L. semi-, 'half, and
membrana, 'fine skin, membrane'; see semi- and
membrane. The exact form should have been
semimembrdneus or simimembrdceus. See Joseph
HyrtI, Onomatologia anatomica, p. 474.

## semimonthly
semimonthly, adj., occurring twice in a month;
п., anything occurring twice in a month, specif.
a magazine published twice in a month. — A
hybrid compounded of semi-, 'half* (see semi-),
and E. monthly.

## seminal
seminal, adj., pertaining to seed or semen. — L.
simindlis, fr. semen, gen. seminis, 'seed'. See
semen and adj. sufT. -al.
Derivatives: seminal-ly, adv.

## seminar
seminar, п., a group of students at a university
engaged in research problems under the
direction of a professor. — G. Seminar, fr. L. simi-
ndrium. See seminary.

## seminary
seminary, n. — L. semindrium, 'seed plot, nursery
garden, seminary', prop. neut. of the adj. semi-
narius, 'pertaining to seed', fr. semen, gen. si-
minis, 'seed'. See semen and subst. sufT. -ary.
Derivatives: seminar-ian, п., seminar-ist, n.,.
seminar-ist-ic, adj.

## semination
semination, п., the act of sowing. — L. semindtio,
gen. •onis, fr. simindtus, pp. of simindre, 'to
sow', fr. semen, gen. seminis, 'seed'. See semen
and -ation and cp. seme, inseminate.

## seminiferous
seminiferous, adj., 1) bearing seed; 2) bearing
semen. — Compounded of L. semen, gen. si-
minis, 'seed*, and the stem of L. ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See semen and -ferons.

## semio-
semio-, combining form. — The same as semeio-.

## semiotic
semiotic, adj., 1) semeiotic; 2) pertaining to
semiotics. — See semeiotic.

## semiotics
semiotics, п., the study of signs and symbols, with
special regard to their function in language. —
See prec. word and -ics.

## semiparasitic
semiparasitic, adj., partly parasitic. — A hybrid
coined fr· semi-, a Latin combining form, and
parnsitic, a word of Greek origin.

## Semi-Pel a gi a nism
Semi-Pel a gi a nism, п., a doctrine of the 5th cent.,
which held the middle ground between the
freewill doctrine of Pelagius and the predestination
doctrine of Augustine. See semi- and -ism.

## semiquaver
semiquaver, п., an English term for a sixteenth
note (music). — Lit. 'the half of a quaver', a
hybrid coined fr. L. semi-, 'half (see semi-), and
E. quaver. Cp. de mi semiquaver.

## Semite
Semite, n. — ModL. Semita, fr. Late L. Sim, fr.
Gk. Σήμ, fr. Heb. Shim, the name of one of
Noah's sons (see Gen. 10: 21-30). For the
ending see subst. sufT. -ite. The term Semite was first
used by the German historian August Schl6zer
in 1781 in Eichhorn's Repertorium, VIII, p. 161.
Derivatives: Semit-ic, adj., Semit-ism, п., Semit-
ist, п., Semit-ize, tr. v.

## semitendinosus
semitendinosus, п., name of a muscle of the thigh
{anat.) — Medical L. semitendinosus (short for
musculus semitendinosus), coined by the English
anatomist William Cowper (1666-1709), fr. L.
semi-, 'half, and tendo, gen. tendinis, 'tendon'.
See semi- and tendinous.

## semitone
semitone, п., a halftone (music). — Compounded
of semi- and tone.

## semiweekly
semiweekly, adj., occurring twice a week; п., а
periodical published twice a week. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. semi-, 'half (see semi-), and E.
weekly.

## semolina
semolina, п., meal consisting of the hard kernels
of wheat. — It, dimin. of semola, 'bran', fr. L.
simila, 'the finest wheat flour', which, together
with Gk. σεμίδαλις, is a loan word from a
Semitic language. See simnel,

## semper-
semper-, combining form meaning 'always, ever'.
— L. semper-, fr. semper, 'always, ever', which
is formed fr. *sem-, 'one, together', and suff.
-per. Base *sem- appears also in L. semel, 'once\

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:698 COLUMN:2 -->
similis (assimilated fr. *semilis), 'like'; see same
and cp. sengreen. Suff. -per (which appears also
in parum-per, 'a little while', paulis-per, 'for a
little while') is rel. to parum, 'too little, not
enough', parvus, 'small, little'; see parvi-. Cp.
sempre.-

## Sempervivum
Sempervivum, п., a genus of plants, the housleek
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of L. semper,
'always', and vivum, neut. of vivus, 'living'. See
semper- and vivacious.

## sempiternal
sempiternal, adj., everlasting, eternal. — Late
ME., fr. Late L. sempiternus, 'everlasting,
perpetual, continual', fr. L. semper, 'always', and
aeternus, 'everlasting'. For the first element see
semper-, for the second see eternal.

## semplice
semplice, adj., simple {musical direction). — It.,
fr. L. simplicem, ace. of simplex, 'simple'. See
simple.

## sempre
sempre, adv., throughout (musical direction). —
It., fr. L. semper, 'always'. See semper-.

## sempster
sempster, п., seamster. — A var. of seamster.

## sempstress
sempstress, п., seamstress. — A var. of seamstress.

## sennincia
sennincia, п., a half-ounce {Roman antiq.) — L.,
formed fr. semi- and uncia. See uncia.

## sen
sen, п., a Japanese coin, one hundredth part of a
yen. — Jap., fr. Chin, ch'ien, 'coin'.

## senaite
senaite, п., a tit ana te of iron, manganese and lead
{mineral.) — Named after the ]9th cent.
Brazilian mineralogist Joachim da Costa Sena. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## sen arms
sen arms, п., a verse consisting of six iambic feet
{Latin pros.) — L. sendrius, 'consisting of six
each; a verse consisting of six feet*. See next
word.
senary» adj., pertaining to six; consisting of six.
— L. sendrius, 'consisting of six each', fr. sen!
(for *sex-nt), 'six each*, fr. sex, 'six'. See six and
adj. suff. -ary.

## senate
senate, n. — ME. senat, fr. OF. senat (F. sepat),
fr. L. sendtus, 'senate', lit. 'the council of the
elders', fr. senex, gen. senis, 'old'. See senile and
subst. suflT. -ate.

## senator
senator, n. — ME. senatour, fr. OF. senatour (F.
senateur), fr. L. sendtorem, ace. of senator, Jr.
senex, gen. senis, 'old'. See senile and agential
suff. -or and cp. prec. word.

## senatorial
senatorial, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. sendtorius, 'pertaining to a senator', fr.
senator, gen. -oris. See prec. word.
Derivative: senatorial-ly, adv.

## senatus
senatus, п., the Roman Senate. — L. sendtus. See
senate.

## send
send, tr. and intr. v. — ME. senden, fr. OE. sen-
dan, rel. to OS. sendian, ΟΝ., OFris. senda, Dan.
sende, Swed. sdnda, MLG., MDu. senden, Du.
zenden, OHG. semen, sendan, MHG., G. senden,
Goth, sandjan. These verbs orig. meant 'to cause
to go*. They are causative forms of Teut. *sinpan,
'to go, find out', whence OE. sid (for *sind),
OS. silk, OHG. sind, MHG. sint, 'way, journey',
ON. sinn, Goth, sinps, 'going, walk; time', OE.
gesid, OS. gisltk, OHG. gisindi, MHG. gesindet
'traveling companion', G. Gesinde, 'followers,
servants, domestics', Goth, gasinpa, gasinpja,
'traveling companion'. Cognates outside
Teutonic are Arm. nt'ac, 'way', Lith. siuneiu, Lett.
sutu, Ί send*, Olr. set (for *sent), 'way', W. hynt,
of s.m. — L. sentire, 'to feel', is also cognate.
See seuse and cp. godsend. Cp. also the second
element in withershins.
Derivatives: send, п., send-able, adj., send-ee, п.,
send-er, п., send-ing, n.

## semlal
semlal, п., a thin silk fabric used in the Middle
Ages. — OF. cendal, fr. Late L. cendalum, fr.
Gk. σινδών, 'fine cloth from India', lit. 'Indian',
fr. 01. Sindhuh, 'the river Indus; the country of
the river Indus'. See India and cp. sindon.

## Senecio
Senecio, п., a genus of plants, the groundsel (bot.)
— L. senecio, fr. senex, 'old man* (see senate);
prob. so called in allusion to the white hairs of
the pappus.

## senega
senega, seneca, п., a drug made from the root of
the senega root. — Named after the Seneca
Indians of North America.

## senescence
senescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## senescent
senescent, adj., growing old. — L. senescins, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of seniscere, 'to grow old', an

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:698 COLUMN:3 -->
inchoative verb formed fr. senire, 'to be old', fr.
senex, gen. senis, 'old'. See senile and -escent.

## seneschal
seneschal, п., a steward; a majordomo. — ME.,
fr. OF. seneschal (F. sinechal), fr. Frankish
*sini-skalk, 'senior servant', a compound whose
first element is related, to Goth, sineigs, Old',
sinista, 'elder, senior', and cognate with L. senex,
'old'; see senile. The second element is related
to OHG. scale, OE. scealc, 'servant'; see
marshal. Cp. It. siniscalco, OProvenc. senescal,
senescalc, which are also Teut. loan words (the
former through the medium of ML. siniscalcus
(in Lex Alaman. 79, 3, 4).
Derivatives: seneschal, tr. v., seneschal-sy,
seneschal-ty, n.

## sengreen
sengreen, п., the common houseleek. — ME. sin-
grene, fr. OE. singrine, 'green vegetables; the
houseleek4 (cp. OHG. singruoni, MHG. sin-
gruene, G. Singrun, MDu. sindergroen, Du. zene-
groen), from the adj. singrine, 'evergreen*,
which is compounded of OE. sin-, sine-,
'everlasting, enduring, great', and grine, 'green'. The
first element is rel. to OS., OHG., Goth, sin·,
ON. si-, of s.m., and cogn. with L. semper,
'always, ever*. See semper-. Cp. OHG., MHG.
sin(t)-vluot, G. Sintflut, 'the great flood', and
the secondary G. form Siindflut (as if the word
meant 'the flood caused by the sin of mankind'),
which arose from a confusion of OHG. sin· with
G. Sunde, 'sin' (see sin). For the second element
in sengreen see green.

## senhor
senhor, п., a Portuguese title corresponding to
English Mr. or Sir. — Port., fr. L. seniorem, ace.
of senior, Older", compar. of senex, 'old'. See
senior and cp. senor, sign or.

## senhora
senhora, п., a Portuguese title corresponding to
English Mrs. or Madam. — Fem. of prec. word.
Cp. scfiora, slgnora.

## senhorita
senhorita, п., a Portuguese title corresponding to
English Miss. — Dimin. of prec. word. Cp.
seftoritu, signorina.

## senile
senile, adj. — L. senilis, 'pertaining to old people,
senile', formed with suff. -ile fr. senex, gen. senis,
'old', which is cogn. with OI. sanah, 'old',
Avestic hana-, Old', Arm. kin, 'old', Gk. 2νος,
(for *senos), 'old', Lith. sinas, 'old', senis, 'an old
man', Goth, sineigs, 'old', sinista, 'elder, senior',
Olr. sen, OW., Co. kin, 'old'. Cp. senate, senior
and the first element in seneschal.
Derivatives: senile-ly, adv., senil-ism, п.,
senility, n.

## senior
senior, adj. — L., 'older', compar. of senex, gen.
senis, 'old'. See senile and cp. seigneur, seignior,
senhor, senor, sieur, signor, sir, sire, messire,
monseignenr, monsieur, monsignor. Cp. also
surly.
Derivatives: senior, п., senior-ity, n.

## senna
senna, п., I) any plant of the genus Cassia; 2) the
dried leaves of some of these plants, used as a
laxative. — ML. senna, sena, fr. Arab, sand', in
vulgar pronunciation sena\

## sennet
sennet, п., a trumpet call. — MF. sinet, senet,
segnet, dimin. of seing (F. signe), 'sign', fr. OF.
See sign, п., and -et and cp. signet.

## sennight
sennight, se'nnight, a week (archaic). —
Contraction of seven and night. For a similar
contraction cp. fortnight.

## seunit
seunit, п., braided cordage of rope yearn (naut.)
— Contraction of seven and knit. For a similar
contraction of seven see prec. word.

## senor
senor, п., a Spanish title corresponding to English
Mr. or Sir. — Sp., fr. L. seniorem, ace. of senior,
'older', compar. of senex, gen. senis, 'od\ See
senior and cp. senhor, signor.
senor а, п., a Spanish title corresponding to
English Mrs. or Madam. — Fem. of prec. word. Cp.
senhora, signora.

## sefiorita
sefiorita, п., a Spanish title corresponding to
English Miss. — Dimin. of prec. word. Cp.
senhorita, signorina.

## Senoussi
Senoussi, n. — See Senussi.

## sensate
sensate, adj., endowed with sensation. — Late L.
sinsdtus, 'gifted with sense, intelligent', fr. L.
sinsus. See sense and adj. suff. -ate.

## sensate
sensate, tr. v., to perceive by a sense or the senses.
— Back formation fr. sensation.

## sensation
sensation, n. — ML. sinsdtio, gen. -onis, fr. Late
L. sinsdtus; see sensate, adj., and -ion. ML. sen-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:699 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SENSE | 672 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:699 COLUMN:1 -->
satio is prop, loan translation of Gk. αίσθησης.
Derivatives: sensation-al, adj., and п.,
sensational-ism, п., sensation-al-ist, п., sensation-al-ist-ict
adj., sensation-ary, adj., sensation-ism, п.,
sensation-is t, п., sensation-ist-ic, adj.

## sense
sense, n. — MF. (= F.) sens, fr. OF., fir. L.
sensus, 'perception, feeling, sense*, fr. sensus, pp. of
sentire, 'to perceive by the senses, feel, think, be
of opinion', which is cogn. with OHG. sinnan
(for *sinpjan), 'to go, travel, strive after, have
in mind, perceive' (whence prob. OHG., MHG.
sin, G. Sinn, 'sense, mind*), OE. sid (for *sind),
'way, journey', fr. I.-E. base *sent-, 'to go'
[whence also Olr. set (for sent), 'way']. In L. sen-
tire the orig. meaning was prob. 'to go in a
certain direction, to find out', whence developed
the meaning 'to feel'. See send and cp. assent,
consensus, consent, dissension, dissent, insensate,
resent, scent, sensible, sentence, sentient,
sentiment, sentinel.
Derivatives: sense, tr. v., sens-ed, adj.,
senseless, adj., sense-less-ly, adv., sense-less-ness, п.,
sensible (q.v.), sensitive (q.v.), sensual (q.v.),
sensuous (q.v.)

## sensi-
sensi-, combining form denoting sensation. — L.
sensi-, fr. sensus. See sense.

## sensibility
sensibility, n. — ME. sensibilite, fr. MF. (= F.)
sensibilite, fr. LateL. sinsibilitdtem, ace. afsensi-
bilitds, fr. sensibilis. See sensible and -ity.

## sensible
sensible, adj. — Late ME., fr. MF. (= F.)
sensible, fr. Late L. sensibilis, 'that which can be
perceived by the senses; capable of perceiving*,
fr. L. sensus, pp. of sentire, 'to perceive*. See
sense and -ible.
Derivatives: sensible-ness, п., sensibl-y, adv.

## sensitive
sensitive, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) sensitif"(fern.
sensitive), fr. ML. sensitivus, 'pertaining to
sensation', irregularly formed fr. L. sensus, pp. of
sentire, 'to perceive'. See sense and -ive.
Derivatives: sensitive, п., sensitive-ly, adv., sen-
sitive-ness, п., sensitiv-ity, n.

## sensitize
sensitize, tr. v., to render sensitive. — Irregularly
formed fr. sensitive) and surf. -ize.
Derivatives: sensitiz-ation, п., sensitiz-er, n.

## sensitometer
sensitometer, п., instrument for measuring the
sensitivity to light of photographic films, etc. —
A hybrid coined from the stem of sensitize and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.
Derivative: sensitometr-y, n.

## sensorial
sensorial, adj., sensory. — Formed fr. sensory
with adj. surf. -al.

## sensorium
sensorium, п., the nervous system, including the
organs of sense. — Late L. sensorium, 'the seat
or organ of the senses, the brain', fr. L. sensus,
pp. of sentire, 'to perceive by the senses, to feel'.
See sense and subst. suff. -ory.

## sensory
sensory, adj., pertaining to the senses, to
sensation, orto the sensorium.—Formed with adj. suff.
-ury fr. L. sensus, 'perception, sense'. See sense.

## sensual
sensual, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. sensualis, fr. L.
sensus, 'perception, sense'. See sense and adj.
suff. -al.
Derivatives: sensual-ism, п., sensual-ist, п.,
sensual-ist-ic, adj., sensuality (q.v.), sensualize
(q.v.), sensual-ly, adv.

## sensuality
sensuality, n. — ME. sensualite, fr. OF. sensualite
(F. sensualite"), fr. Late L. sensudlitdtem, ace. of
sinsudlitds, fr. sensualis. See prec. word and -ity.

## sensualize
sensualize, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. Late
L. sensualis. See sensual.
Derivative: sensualiz-ation, n.

## sensuous
sensuous, adj., pertaining to, or affected by, the
senses. — Coined by Milton fr. L. sensus,
'feeling, sense' (see sense), through the addition of
suff. -ous.
Derivatives: sensuous-ly, adv., sensuous-ness, n.

## sent
sent, past and pp. of send. — ME. sende, fr. OE.
sende, resp. ME. sente, fr. OE. gesend(ed), fr.

## sentence
sentence, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) sentence, ΐτ.
L. sententia, 'way of thinking, opinion,
sentiment', fr. *sentientia (the loss of the first i is due
to dissimilation), fr. sentiens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of sentire, 'to feel, be of opinion'. See
sense and cp. sentience.
Derivatives: sentence, tr. v., sentential (q.v.),
sententiary (q.v.), sententiosity (q.v.), sententious

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:699 COLUMN:2 -->
(q.v.)

## sentential
sentential, adj., pertaining to a sentence. — L.
sententialis, 'in the form of a sentence', fr.
sententia. S.ee prec. word and -ial.

## sententiary
sententiary, п., an aphorist. — ML. sententidrius,
fr. L. sententia. See sentence and subst. suff. -ary.

## sententiosity
sententiosity, n. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. L.
sententidsus. See next word.

## sententious
sententious, adj., ]) pithy; 2) using aphorisms. —
L. sententidsus, 'full of meaning, pithy,
sententious', fr. sententia. See sentence, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: sententious-ly, adv., sententious-
ness, n.

## sentience
sentience, п., ]) capacity for feeling; 2)
consciousness. — Formed from next word with suff. -ce.

## sentient
sentient, adj., 1) capable of feeling; 2) conscious.
— L. sentiens, gen. -entis> pres. part, of sentire,
pp. sensus, 'to perceive by the senses, to feel'.
See sense and -ent and cp. dissentient.

## sentiment
sentiment, n. — F., fr. Late L. sentimentum, fr. L.
sentire, 'to perceive by the senses, to feel'. See
sense and -ment.

## sentimental
sentimental, adj. — Coined by the English
clergyman and novelist Laurence Sterne (1713-68) in
1767 (in the title of his Sentimental Journey) fr.
prec. word and adj. suff. -al. F. sentimental is an
English loan word.
Derivatives: sentimental-ism, п., sentimental-ist,
п., sentimentality, п., sentimental-ize, tr. v.,
sentimental-ly, adv.

## sentinel
sentinel, п., guard. — F. sentinelle, fr. It. senti-
nella, a derivative οι sentire, 'to hear, perceive',
fr. L. sentire, 'to perceive by the senses, to feel'.
See sense.
Derivative: sentinel, v.

## sentry
sentry, п., soldier placed on guard. — Shortened
for sentery, sentuarie, obsolete collateral forms
of sanctuary (q.v.) Sentry orig. meant 'a place
of safety*. Cp. obsolete E. sentry, in the sense of
'sanctuary'.

## Senussi
Senussi, Senoussi, also Sannssi, Sanoussi, п., а
Moslem sect in North Africa. — Named after
its founder Sidi Muhammad ibn Ali ibn as-
Sanussi (died in 1859).

## senza
senza, prep., without. — It., aphetic from L.
absentia, 'in the absence of, abl. οι absentia,
'absence'. See absence and cp. sans and sine,
'without':

## sepal
sepal, п., any of the leaves of the calyx (bot.) —
F. sepal, fr. ModL. sepalum, which was coined
by H. J. de Necker in 1790 fr. L. separdtus,
'separate', and petalum, 'petal'. See separate and
petal.
Derivative: sepal{l)-ed, adj.

## -sepalous
-sepalous, combining form meaning 'having a
specified number of sepals'. — Formed fr. prec.
word with suff. -ous.

## separable
separable, adj. — ME. separable, fr. L. separdbilis,
fr. separdre. See separate, v., and -able.
Derivatives: separabil-ity, п., separable-ness, п.,
separabl-y, adv.

## separate
separate, tr. and intr. v. — L. separatus, pp. of
separdre, 'to put apart, separate', fr. se- ana pa-
rare, 'to prepare, arrange'. See pare and verbal
suff. -ate and cp. sever, which is a doublet of
separate. Cp. also sepal.
Derivatives: separation (q.v.), separat-ism, п.,
separat-ist, п., separat-ist-ic, adj., separative
(q.v.), separator (q.v.), separat-ory, adj.

## separate
separate, adj. — L. separdtus, pp. of separdre. See
separate, v., and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: separate-ly, adv., separate-ness, п.,
separatism (q.v.), separatist (q.v.)

## separation
separation, n. — ME. separacion, fr. MF. (— F.)
separation, fr. L. separationem, 'a sundering,
separation', fr. separdtus, pp. of separdre. See
separate, v., and -ion.
Derivatives: separation-ism, n.,'separation-ist, n.

## separative
separative, adj. — Late L. sipardtivus, fr. L.

## separatus
separatus, pp. of separdre. See separate, v., and
-ive.
Derivatives: separative-ly, adv., separative-ness,
n.

## separator
separator, n. — Late L. separator, 'he that
separates, separator', fr. L. separdtus, pp. οι se-

## pardre. See separate
pardre. See separate, v., and agential suff. -or.

## Sephardlc
Sephardlc, adj., pertaining to the Sephardim. —
See next word and adj. suff. -ic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:699 COLUMN:3 -->
Sephardim, n. pi., descendants of the Jews who
lived in Spain and Portugal. — Inexact
rendering of ModHeb.-S phdraddtm, 'Spaniards; Jews
of Spain', pi. of tfphdraddi, fr. Heb. Sephdradk,
mentioned in Obadiah, v. 20, and prob.
meaning 'Asia Minor' or a country in it (perhaps
Lydia or Phrygia), but identified by the
Jonathan Targum with Spain.

## Sepher Torah
Sepher Torah, the scroll of the Law (Jewisk
religion). — Heb. sepher tordh, 'book of the law', fr.
sepher, 'book', and torah, 'direction, instruction,
teaching, law'. Heb. sepher is prob. an ancient
loan word fr. Akkad. skipru, 'letter*, prop.
'something sent', fr. skapdru, 'to send', esp. 'to
send a letter', hence 'to write a letter' (for sense
development cp. Gk. επιστολή, 'letter', lit.
'something sent, message*, fr. έπιστέλλειν, 'to
send to'; see epistle). The Hebrew verbs sdphar,
'he counted', sipper, 'he recounted, related', are
denominated fr. sepher. Cp. next word and
Sopherim. For the etymology of Heb. tordh see
Torah.

## sephirah
sephirah, sephira, п., pi. sephiroth, any of the ten
potencies or agencies of the divine
manifestation (a term of the Cabala). — Heb. sephirah, 'a
counting', prop, verbal n. of sdphar, 'he
counted' (see prec. word); influenced in meaning by
Gk. σφαίρα, 'sphere'.

## sepia
sepia, п., 1) (cap.) a genus of sea mollusks
comprising the cuttlefishes; 2) any mollusks of the
genus Sepia; 3) the ink of the cuttlefish; 4)
pigment prepared from the ink of the cuttlefish.
— L. sepia, fr. Gk. σηπία, 'cuttlefish', which is
rel. to σήπει-ν, 'to make rotten*, σήψ, 'a
venomous kind of lizard', σήψις, 'putrefaction'. See
sepsis and cp. seps. F. seche, 'sepia', is a loan
word fr. L. sepia.
Derivatives: sepia, sep-ic, adjs.

## sepiollte
sepiollte, п., meerschaum. — Compounded of
sepia and Gk. λί&ος, 'stone'. See -lite,

## sepoy
sepoy, п., a native Indian soldier. — Port, sipai,
sipaia, fr. Hind, and Pers. sipdhi, 'soldier', fr.
sipdh, 'army'. See spahi.

## seps
seps, п., a lizard of the genus Ckalcides. — L.
seps, fr. Gk. σήψ, 'a venomous kind of lizard,
from the stem of σήπειν, 'to make rotten'. See
next word and cp. sepia.

## sepsis
sepsis, п., putrefaction. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
σηψις, 'putrefaction', from the stem of σήπειν,
'to make rotten', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. sapro-, sepia, seps, septic.

## sept
sept, п., a tribe or clan, esp. and Irish clan. — A
blend of sect and L. saeptum, septum, 'hedge'.
See septum.
Derivative: septal (q.v.)

## sept-
sept-, form of septi- before a vowel.

## septal
septal, adj., pertaining to a septum. — See
septum and adj. suff. -al.

## septal
septal, adj., pertaining to an Irish sept. —
Formed fr. sept with adj. suff. -al.

## septan
septan, adj., occurring every seventh day; п.,
fever recurring every seventh day (counting both
days of consecutive occurrence). — ModL.,
formed fr. L. septem, 'seven' (see septem-), on
analogy of quartan, quintan. For the ending see
suff. -an.

## septangle
septangle, п., a heptagon (geom.) —
Compounded of sept- and angle.

## septangular
septangular, adj., having seven angles. —
Compounded of sept- and angular.

## septarium
septarium, п., a rock nodule. — ModL., fr. L.
saeptum, septum, 'enclosure'. See septum and
-arlum.

## septate
septate, adj., divided by a septum. — ModL.
saeptdtus, septatus, fr. L. saeptum, septum,
'enclosure'. See septum and adj. suff. -ate,

## septem-
septem-, combining form meaning 'seven'. — L.
septem-, fr. septem, 'seven'. See seven and cp.
hepta·.

## September
September, п., the ninth month of the year. — L.
September (mensis), lit. 'the seventh month (of the
Roman year)', fr. septem, 'seven'; see septem-.
The Roman year began with March (cp.
October, November, December).

## Septembrist
Septembrist, п., one who took part in the
September Massacres of royalists in Paris, 1792. —
F. Septembriste, fr. Septembre, fr. L. September.
See prec. woTd and -ist.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:700 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 673 | SERAPIS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:700 COLUMN:1 -->

## septemparrite
septemparrite, adj., divided into seven parts. —
Compounded of septem- and partite.

## septemvir
septemvir, п., one of seven men associated in some
office or authority (Roman hist.) — L. septem-
viri (pi.), compounded of septem- and viri, pi. of
vir, 'man'. See virile.

## septenarius
septenarius, п., a verse of seven feet {prosody). —
L-je^/ewar/tfj/consisting of seven'. See nextword.

## septenary
septenary, adj., consisting of seven. — L.
septenarius, 'consisting of seven', fr. septeni, 'seven
each', fr. septem, 'seven'. See septem- and adj.
suff. -ary.
Derivative: septenary, the number seven; a
group of seven.

## septennary
septennary, adj., septennial. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ary fr. L. septennium. See septennium.

## septennate
septennate, п., a period of seven years. — F.
septetmat, formed fr. L. septennis, 'of seven
years' (see next word), on analogy of decanat,
'deanery', and other nouns ending in -at, fr. L.
■dtus (see subst. suff. -ate).

## septennial
septennial, adj., 1) lasting seven years; 2)
occurring every seven years. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. septennium, 'period of seven years'.
See next word.
Derivative: septennial-ly, adv.

## septennium
septennium, п., a period of seven years. — L., fr.
septennis, 'of seven years', formed fr. septem,
'seven', and -ennis, fr. annus, 'year'. See septem-
and annual. For the change of Latin a (in annus)
to ё (in sept-ennium) see accent and cp. words
there referred to.

## Septentrion
Septentrion, п., the constellation of the Great
Bear (astron.) — ME. septemtrioun, fr. L. sep-
tenlriones (pi.), 'the seven stars near the North
Pole, the Great Bear; the northern regions',
prop, 'the seven plow oxen', fr. L. septem,
'seven', and trio, gen. tridnis, 'plow ox', from the
stem of terere (perf. trivi, pp. tritus), 'to rub'.
See seven and thriw and cp. terebra, trite.
Derivatives: Septentrion, adj., pertaining to the
north, septentrional (q.v.)

## septentrional
septentrional, adj., pertaining to the north,
northern. — L. septentriondlis, fr. septentridnes. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: septentrion-al-ly, adv.

## septet
septet, septette, п., a composition for seven
persons, voices or instruments (mus.) — Formed fr.
sept- with suff. -et, -ette, on analogy of duet,
tercet, quartet, etc.

## septi-
septi-, sept-, combining form meaning 'seven', as
in septilateral. — L. septi-, sept-, fr. septem,
'seven'. See septem-.

## septi-
septi-, also septo- before a vowel sept-, combining
form meaning 'septum', as in septifragai. — Fr.
L. septum. See septum.

## septi-
septi-, before a vowel sept-, combining form
meaning 'decomposed', as in septicemia. — Fr.
Gk. σηπτός, 'rotten, putrid'. See septic.

## septic
septic, adj., causing putrition. — L. septicus, fr.
Gk. σηπτικός, 'putrefactive, septic', fr. σηπτός,
'rotten, putrid', verbal adj. of σήπειν, 'to make
rotten'. See sepsis and adj. suff* -ic and cp.
aseptic, antiseptic.
Derivatives: septic, п., a substance that causes
sepsis, septic-al, adj., septic-al-ly, adv., septic·
ity, n.

## septicemia
septicemia, septicaemia, п., septic condition of the
blood; blood poisoning (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. F. septicoemi (now spelled septicemie),
which was coined by the French physician
Pierre-Adolphe Piorry (1794-1879), in 1837 fr.
Gk. σηπτικός, 'putrefactive', and αίμα, 'blood'.
See septic and hemal.

## septifragai
septifragai, adj., breaking away from the
partitions, applied to a form of dehiscence (bot.) —
Compounded of L. saeptum, septum, 'enclosure,
partition', and the stem offrangere, 'to break'.
See septum and fraction.

## septilateral
septilateral, adj., seven-sided. — Compounded of
septi-, 'seven-', and lateral.

## septillion
septillion, п., 1) in the United States and France,
a thousand raised to the eighth power (i.e. 1
followed by 24 zeros); 2) in Great Britain and
Germany, a million raised to the seventh power
(i.e. 1 followed by 42 zeros). — F. septillion,
formed fr. L. septem, 'seven' (see septem-), on
analogy of million (q.v.) Cp. billion and words

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:700 COLUMN:2 -->
there referred to.

## septimal
septimal, adj., pertaining to the number seven. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. Septimus,
'seventh'. See next word.

## septlme
septlme, п., the seventh position in fencing. — F.,
fr. L. septima, fem. of Septimus, 'seventh', fr.
septem, 'seven'. See seven.

## septo-
septo-, combining form. — See 2nd septi-.

## septuagenarian
septuagenarian, adj. and п., septuagenary. — See
next word and -an.

## septuagenary
septuagenary, adj., seventy years old; pertaining
to a person seventy years old; п., a person 70
years old, or between the years 70 and 80. — L.
septudgendrius, 'consisting of seventy', fr. sep-
tudgeni, 'seventy each', which is rel. to
septudgintd, 'seventy'. See Septuagint and adj. suff.
-ary.

## Septuagesima
Septuagesima, п., the third Sunday before Lent.
— L. septudgfsima (dies), 'seventieth (day)',
fem. of septudgesimus, fr. septudgintd, 'seventy'.
See next word.

## Septuagint
Septuagint, п., the oldest Greek translation of
the Bible; the translation was so called because
according to tradition it was made by 70 (more
exactly 72) Jewish scholars. — L. septudgintd,
'seventy', formed, on the analogy of octodgintd,
a var. of octogintd, 'eighty', fr. septem, 'seven',
with -gintd, a suff. denoting tens. This suff. is
cogn. with Gk. -κοντά in τριάκοντα, 'thirty',
τεσσαρακοντα, 'forty', etc. See seven. For the
etymology of Gk. suff. -κοντά, L. suff. -gintd,
see penteconta-.

## septum
septum, partition. — L. saeptum, septum, pp. of
saeplre, sipire, 'to fence in, enclose', fr. saepes,
sepes, gen. -itis, 'hedge, fence, enclosure', which
is cogn. with Gk. αίμός, (ior*saipmo-), 'thicket',
αίμασία, 'bushes; wall of dry stones'. Cp.
septate, dissepiment, transept.

## septuple
septuple, adj. — F., 'sevenfold', fr. L. septuplus,
formed from the stem of sept-em, 'seven' (see
septem-), with suff. -plus, '-fold', on analogy of
duplus, 'double'. See double and cp. words there
referred to.

## sepulcher
sepulcher, sepalchre, п., grave; tomb. — ME.
sepulcre, fr. OF. sepulcre (F, sepulcre), fr. L.
sepulcrum (less correctly sepulchrum), 'grave,
tomb', for *sepel-tlom, from the stem of sepelire
(pp. sepultus), 'to bury', which prob. meant orig.
'to honor, worship', and is cogn. with 01. sa-
parydti, 'honors', and prob. also with Ol. sdpati,
'applies himself to, caresses, fondles', Gk. ϊπειν,
'to be about, 1>usy oneself with'. Cp. hoplite. For
sense development cp. the E. phrase 'to do the
funeral honors to a person'.
Derivatives: sepulcher, sepulchre, tr. v.,
sepulchral (q.v.), sepulchr-ous, adj.

## sepulchral
sepulchral, adj. — L. sepulcralis, fr. L. sepulcrum.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: sepulchral-ly, adv.

## sepulture
sepulture, п., burial. — ME., fr. OF., fr. L.
sepultura, 'burial1, fr. sepultus, pp. of sepellre,
'to bury'. See sepulcher and -ure.
Derivatives: sepulture, tr. v., sepultw-al, adj.

## sequacious
sequacious, adj., following. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. sequdx, gen. -acis, 'following after,
sequacious', fr. sequor, sequi, 'to follow'. See
next word and -ious.
Derivatives: sequacious-ly, adv., sequacious-
ness, n.

## sequel
sequel, n. — ME. sequele, sequel, fr. MF. (= F.)
sequelle, fr. L. sequela, 'consequence, sequel',
lit. 'that which follows', from the stem of sequor,
sequi, 'to follow', which is cogn. with OI. sdcate,
sascati, 'accompanies, follows', Avestic hadaiti,
of s.m., Toch. A sdk-, 'to follow', Gk. έπεσ*αι,
'to follow', Lith. seku, sekti, 'to follow', Olr.
sechim, sechur, Ί follow', and prob. rel. to L.
socius, 'fellow, companion, associate'. Cp. con-
sectary, consecutive, consequence, ensue, execute,
exequatur, exeqnies, extrinsic, intrinsic,
obsequies, obsequious, persecute, prosecute, pursue,
second, sect, seguidilla, sequence, seqnester,
subsequent, sue, suit, suite, suivez.

## sequela
sequela, п., 1) consequence; 2) morbid condition
as the result of a disease (med.) — L. sequela,
'that which follows, consequence'. See prec.
word.

## sequence
sequence, п., succession; series. — ME., fr. Late

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:700 COLUMN:3 -->
L. sequentia, fr. L. sequins, gen. -entis. See next
word and -ce.

## sequent
sequent, adj., following. — L. sequins, gen. -entis,
part, of sequi, 'to follow'. See sequel and -ent.
Derivatives: sequent, п., sequent-ial, adj., se-
quent-ial-ly, adv.

## sequester
sequester, tr. and intr. v., 1) to separate; 2) to
seize, confiscate. — Late ME. sequestren, fr.
MF. (= F.) sequestrer, fr. Late L. sequestrdre,
'to give up for safe keeping', fr. sequester, 'a
depository, trustee', prop, 'that which follows,
is at hand', prob. from 'sequos, whence also L.
secus, 'otherwise', prop, 'following', from the
stem of sequor, sequi, 'to follow'. See sequel.
Derivatives: sequester, п., sequester-ed, adj.,
sequestr-able, adj., sequestr-al, adj., sequestrate
(q.v.)

## sequestrate
sequestrate, tr. v. — Late L. sequestrdtus, pp. of
sequestrdre. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## sequestration
sequestration, n. — Late L. sequestrdtio, gen.
-onis, 'a depositing', fr. sequestrdtus, pp. of
sequestrdre. See sequester and -ion.

## seqnestrator
seqnestrator, n. — Late L. sequestrator, fr.
sequestrdtus, pp. of sequestrdre. See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.

## sequestrum
sequestrum, п., a piece of dead bone, separated
from the healthy bone (med.) — Medical L., lit.
'anything separated', neut. of L. sequester, used
as a noun. See sequester,

## sequin
sequin, п., 1) an Italian gold coin; 2) an
ornamental disk or spangle. — F., fr. It. zecchino, 'coin',
dimin. formed fr. zecca, 'a mint', fr. Arab.
sikkah, 'a die for stamping'. Cp. sicca,

## sequin
sequin, п., ornament on women's dresses. —
Named in 1802 after the French chemist Sequin,
inventor of the shining artificial flowers.

## Sequoia
Sequoia, п., a genus of trees of the pine family
(bot.) — Named after Sequoyah, prop. Sikwayi,
a Cherokee Indian, inventor of the Cherokee
syllabary (died 1843).

## ser
ser, also seer, п., a weight of India'varying in size
in different parts of the country. — Hind, ser, fr.
01. setak.

## sirac
sirac, п., a pinnacle of ice on a glacier. — Swiss
F. serac, 'a kind of cheese', derived fr. L. serum,
'whey' (see serum); so called from its shape.

## seraglio
seraglio, п., 1) harem; 2) (capit.) name of the old
palace of the sultan in Constantinople. — It.
serraglio, lit. 'enclosure', later also used in the
sense of 'palace' (prob. under the influence of
Turk, serai, 'palace'), fr. ML. serrdculum, 'bar
(of a door), bolt', fr. VL. 'serrdre, 'to bar, bolt',
fr. Late L. serdre, of s.m., ft. L. sera, 'a bar (for
fastening a door)'. See sear, 'catch in the lock
of a gun'. The suff. -aglio in It. serraglio
represents L. -dculum, used to form place names. Cp.
e.g. L. cend-culum, 'dining room1.

## serai
serai, п., a place for the accommodation of
travelers in the East. — Turk, serai, 'palace', fr.
Pers. sardi, 'mansion, inn', fr. OPers. srdda,
'residence', from base prd-, 'to protect', whence
also Avestic brdyeihti, 'they protect'. See
caravanserai,

## serang
serang, п., boatswain of a ship in the East Indies.
— Pers. sarhang, 'commander', compounded of
sar, 'head, chief, and hang, 'power'. Pers. sar is
cogn. with 01. slras-, 'head, summit', Gk. καρά,
'head', L. cerebrum, 'the brain'. See cerebrum
and cp. the first element in sarangousty, seerpaw,
seraskier, sircar,

## serape
serape, п., a shawl. — Mexican Sp. sarape.

## seraph
seraph, n. — Back formation fr. Heb. s rdphtm,
pi. of sdrdph, lit. 'the burning one', from the
verb Sdrdph, 'he burned', which is rel. to Akkad.

## shardpu
shardpu, 'to burn'. Cp. OEgypt. srf, 'to be hot'.
Derivatives: seraph-ic, seraph-ic-al, adj., seraph-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## seraphim
seraphim, n. pi., seraphs. — Heb. serdph!m. See

## seraph
seraph,

## seraphine
seraphine, п., an obsolete reed instrument. —
Formed fr. seraph with suff. -ine.

## Serapias
Serapias, п., a genus of orchids (bot.) — L., fr.
Gk. σεραπιάς, 'an OTchid', prop. *a plant
dedicated to Serapis', fr. Σέραπις. See Serapis.

## Serapis
Serapis, п., a famous god of the lower world
(Egyptian, Greek and Roman mythol.) — L., fr.
Gk. Σέραπις, fr. earlier Gk. Σάραπις, fr.

## Egypt. User-hapi
Egypt. User-hapi, lit. 'Osiris-Apis'. See Osiris

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:701 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SERASKIER | 674 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:701 COLUMN:1 -->
and Apis and cp. prec. word.

## seraskier
seraskier, п., Turkish commander in chief. —
Turk, ser asker, lit. 'head of the army', fr. Pers.
sar, 'head'» and Arab, askar, 'army'. For the
first element see cerebrum and cp. serang and
words there referred to. For the second element
see lascar.

## Serb
Serb, п., 1) a native of Serbia; 2) Serb language.
— Fr. Serb Srb.
. Derivatives: Serb-ian, adj. and n.

## Serbonian
Serbonian, adj., pertaining to, or designating,
Lake Serbonis in Egypt (now dry). — Gk.
Σερβωνίς ή λίμνη. For the ending see sufT.
-ian.

## sere
sere, adj., dried up; withered. — See sear, adj.

## sere
sere, п., the catch in the lock of a gun. — A var.
of sear, n.

## serein
serein, п., a fine, misty rain. — F., fr. OF. seirein,
fr. seir (F. soir), 'evening', fr. L. serum, 'late
time', prop. neut. of the adj. serus, 'late', used
as a noun. See serotlne and cp. soiree.

## Serena
Serena, fern. PN.— Fr. L. serena, fem. of serenus,
'clear, fair, bright, joyous'. See serene.

## serenade
serenade, n. — F. serenade, fr. It. serenata, lit.
'calm sky', fr. sereno, 'serene, calm', fr. L.
serenus. See serene and -ade. It. serenata was
influenced in meaning by the noun sera, 'evening'
(fr. L. sera, fem. of serus, 'late'), whence arose
the sense 'music played at night'. See serotine
and cp. serein.
Derivatives: serenade, tr. and intr. v., serenad-er,
n.

## serenata
serenata, п., serenade. — It., whence F. serenade.
See serenade.

## serendipity
serendipity, п., the gift of .finding interesting
things by chance. — Coined by the English
author Horace Walpole (17] 7-97) in a letter to
Mann in January 1754 from the title of his tale
The Three Princes ofSerendip, who were
endowed with the same faculty. Serendipor Serendib is
the former name of Ceylon. For the ending see
suff. -ity.

## serene
serene, adj., clear, bright; calm. — L. serenus,
'clear, fair, cloudless, serene', of uncertain
origin. It possibly stands for *kseresnos and is
cogn. with Gk. ξηρός, 'dry', OI. ksarah,
'burning, corroding', ksdyati, 'burns', OHG. sera-
wen, 'to become dry'. Cp. elixir, xerasia, xero-.
Derivatives: serene, n. and tr. v., serene-ly-, adv.,
serene-ness, п., serenity (q.v.)

## serenity
serenity, n. — MF. (= F.) serinite, fr. OF. sere-
nite, fr. L. serenitdtem, ace. of serenitas,
'clearness, serenity1, fr. serenus'See serene and -ity.

## serf
serf, n. — F.f fr. L. servum, ace. of servus, 'slave*.
See serve.
Derivatives: serf-age, п., serf-dom, serf-hood, n.

## serge
serge, n. — ME. sarge. fr. MF. sarge, serge (F.
serge), fr. OF., fr. VL. *sarica, fr. L. serica, fem.
used as a noun fr. the adj. sericus, 'of silk', fr.
Gk. σηρικός, lit. 'the Seric fabric', fr. Σηρικός,
'pertaining to the Σηρες'. See Seric. Cp. OProv-
enc., Sp. sarga, 'serge', and Rum. sarica,
'frieze', which also derive fr. VL. *sarica, and
It. sargia, 'serge', which is a French loan word.

## sergeant
sergeant, serjeant, n. — ME., fr. OF. sergent,
serjant (F. sergent), fr. L. servientem, ace. of
serviens, pres. part, of servire, 'to serve'. See
serve and -ant and cp. servant, which is a
doublet of sergeant.
Derivatives: sergean-cy, serjean-cy, п., ser-
geanty, serjeanty (q.v.)

## sergeanty
sergeanty, serjeanty, п., a tenure of land on
condition of rendering some specified personal
service to the king (Eng. feudal law). — ME.
sergeantie, fr. OF. sergentie, serjantie, fr.
sergent, serjant. See prec. word and -y
(representing OF. -ie).

## Sergius
Sergius, masc. PN. — L., of Etruscan origin.

## serial
serial, adj., arranged in a series. — Formed fr.
series with adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: serial, п., serial-ity, п., serial-ize,
tr. v., serial-ly, adv.

## seriate
seriate, adj., arranged in a series. — ML. seriatus,
pp. of seridre, 'to arrange in a series', fr. L.
series. See series and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: seriate-ly, adv., seriat-ion, n.

## seriatim
seriatim, adv., serially. — ML. seriatim, fr. L.
series. See series. For the suff. -atim see gradatim.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:701 COLUMN:2 -->

## Seric
Seric, adj., Chinese. — L. Sericus, fr. Gk.
Σηρικός, 'pertaining to the Σηρες', a people of
Eastern Asia, identified with the Chinese. Cp. serge,
sericeous, silk. For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## sericate
sericate, adj., sericeous. — See next word and
adj. suff. -ate.

## sericeous
sericeous, adj., silky. — Late L. sericeus, fr. L.
sericum, 'silk' (prop, subst. use of the neut. of
the adj. sericus, 'silken'), fr. Gk. σηρικόν, 'silk',
lit. 'the Seric fabric', neut. of σηρικός, 'silken*,
fr. Σηρικός, 'pertaining to the Σηρες*. See
Seric and -ous.

## sericite
sericite, п., a species of silky muscovite (mineral.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. L. sericus,
'silken', lit. 'of the Seres*. See prec. word.

## Sericocarpus
Sericocarpus, п., a genus of plants, the white-
topped aster (bot.) — ModL., lit. 'silky fruit'.
See sericeous and carpel.

## sericulture
sericulture, п., production of silk by breeding
silkworms. — Shortened fr. F. sericiculture, fr.
L. siricum, 'silk', and cultura, 'culture'. See
sericeous and culture.
Derivatives: sericultur-al, adj., sericultur-ist, n.

## seriema
seriema, п., the name of two large, long-legged
birds (Cariq/na cristata and Chunga burmeisteri),
— ModL., fr. Tupi seriema, which lit. means
'crested*. Cp. Cariamae.

## series
series, n. — L. series, 'a row, succession,
sequence, series', rel. to serere, 'to put in arow, join
together, connect, combine', sermo, 'talk,
discourse, speech', and in gradational relationship
to sors, 'lot'; cogn. with OI. sarat-, 'thread', Gk.
εΐρειν, 'to fasten together in rows, to insert',
έρμα, 'band, noose, earring', δρμος, 'necklace',
όρμα&ός, 'row, chain', Goth, sarwa (pi.),
'armor, arms', OE. searo (gen. searwes), OHG.
saro (gen. sarawes), of s.m., ON. sorve,
'necklace of stringed pearls', Olr. sernaid, 'he joins
together', sreth, W. ystret, 'row'. Cp. assert,
assort, consort, desert, 'to leave', desert, 'waste',
dissert, exert, exsert, insert, resort, sear, 'the
catch in the lock of a gun', sermon, Sertularia,
sorcerer, sort, the first element in sortilege and
the second element in Laertes.

## serif
serif, n. — See ceriph.

## serin
serin, п., a yellow finch (Sermus hortulanus). —
F., prob. fr. L. siren, fr. Gk. σειρήν, 'siren',
used also to denote a species of bird. See siren.

## serinette
serinette, п., a musical instrument used in
training songbirds, esp. serins. — F., formed fr.
serin with suff. -ette.

## seringa
seringa, п., a Brazilian rubber tree. — Port. See
syringa.

## serio-
serio-, combining form meaning 'serious and'. —
L.jerio-, fr. serius. See serious.

## seriocomic
seriocomic, adj., serious and comic at the same
time. — Compounded of serio- and comic.
Derivatives: seriocomic, n, seriocomic-al, adj ,
seriocomic-al-ly, adv.

## seriosity
seriosity, n. — ML. seriositas, fr. Late L. seriOsus.
See next word and -ity.

## serious
serious, adj. — F. sirieux (fem. serieuse), fr. Late
L. seriosus, fr. L. serius, 'grave, earnest, serious',
which is cogn. with Lith. sveriu, sverti, 'to weigh,
lift', svarus, 'heavy', svaras, 'pound, balance',
OE. swxre, swier, swdr, 'heavy', OS. swdr, ON.
svarr, MDu. swdre, Du. zwaar, OHG. swar{i),
sward, MHG. swxre, swdre, G. schwer, 'heavy1,
Goth, swers, 'honored, esteemed', lit. 'weighty'.
Cp. also Gk. Ερμα, 'ballast', which prob. stands
for *swerma and prop, means 'center of
gravity*.
Derivatives: serious-ly, adv., serious-ness, n.

## serjeant
serjeant, serjeanty. — See sergeant, sergeanty.

## sermon
sermon, n. — ME., fr. OF. (— F.) sermon, fr. L.
sermonem, ace. of sermo, *a speaking, talking,
conversation, diction', lit. 'that which is put
together in a certain order', Tr. sero, serere, *to
join or bind together, combine, compose'. For
the sense development of sermo, fr. serere cp.
the term orationes serere, 'to compose speeches'.
For the etymology of serere see series. The
meaning of F. and E. sermon ('discourse delivered
from the pulpit of a church'), is due to the
elliptical use of L. sermo in the sense of sermo reli-
giosus, 'a religious discourse*. Cp. It. strmone,
Sp. sermon, which are of the same origin and
meaning as OF. sermon.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:701 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: sermon, tr. and intr. \.,sermon-er,
п., sermonet, sermonette (qq. v.), sermonettino
(q.v.), sermon-ic, sermon-ic-al, adjs., sermon-
ic-al-ly, adv., sermon-ics, n. pi., sermon-ize,
intr. and tr. v., sermon-iz-er, n.

## sermonet
sermonet, sermonette, п., a short sermon. — Form- ·
ed fr. sermon with dimin. suff. -et, resp. -ette.

## sermonettino
sermonettino, п., a very little sermon. — It., a
double dimin. formed fr. sermonetto, 'a little
sermon', fr. sermone, 'sermon'. See sermon and
cp. sermonet, sermonette.

## sero-
sero-, combining form meaning 'in connection
with serum*. — Fr. L. serum, 'whey'. See serum.

## serology
serology, п., the study of serums. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. serum, 'whey', and Gk. -λογία,
fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain
manner) ; one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See
serum and -logy. The correct form is orrhology,
in which both elements are of Greek origin.
Derivative: serolog-ic-al, adj.

## seroon
seroon, п., a bale for fruit, etc., covered in an
animal's hide. — Sp. seron, 'hamper, crate', rel.
to Port, seira, of s.m.; of uncertain origin.

## serosity
serosity, п., the state of being serous. — F. sero-
site, fr. MF., fr. sereux, 'serous'. See serous and
-ity.

## serotherapy
serotherapy, п., the treatment of disease by
injecting serum into the veins. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. serum, 'whey*, and Gk. θεραπεία, 'service,
attendance'. See serum and therapy. The correct
form is orrhotherapy, in which both elements are
of Greek origin.

## serotine
serotine, adj., late. — F. serotine, fr. L. serotinus,
'that which comes, happens, late, or in the
evening', fr. serus, 'late', which is rel. to L. setius,
'later', and cogn. with Olr. sir, 'long, for a long
time, everlasting', W., Co., Bret, hir, 'long*, OI.
sdyam, 'in the evening', Goth, seipus, 'late', OE.
sid, 'late', siddan, 'since, later'. All these words
are derivatives of I.-E. base *se(i)·, 'to be slow,
come late'. See since and adj. suff. -ine and cp.
serotine, п., and serein, soiree. Cp. also the
second element in menhir.

## serotine
serotine, п., a small bat, Vespertilio serotinus. —
F. serotine, fr. L. serotinus, 'that which comes
late or in the evening'. See serotine, adj.

## serotinous
serotinous, adj., appearing later in the season
than is usual. — L. serotinus. See serotine, adj.
For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -Hi, see -ous.

## serous
serous, adj., pertaining to, or producing, serum.
— F. sereux, fem. sereuse, fr. L. serum, 'whey'.
See serum and -ous and cp. serosity.

## serow
serow, п., any of the antelopes of the genus
Naemorhedus. — East Indian native name.

## Serpens
Serpens, п., a constellation adjoining Ophiuchus
{astron.) — L. serpens, 'serpent'. See next word.

## serpent
serpent, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) serpent, fr. L.
serpentem, ace. of serpens, 'serpent, snake',
prop. pres. part, of serpere, 'to creep', hence lit.
meaning 'a creeping thing'. L. serpere is cogn.
with OI. sarpati, 'creeps', sarpah, 'serpent', Gk.
δρπειν, 'to creep', έρπετόν, 'serpent', Alb.
gdrpsr, 'serpent*. Cp. herpes, serpigo, Serpula.
For the ending see suff. -ent. L. serpere is prob.
not rel. to repere, 'to creep' (see reptile).
Derivatives: serpent-ile, adj., serpent-ize, tr. and
intr. v., serpent-ly, adv.

## serpenti-
serpenti-, combining form meaning 'serpent'. —
L. serpenti-, stem of serpens, gen. serpentis,
'serpent, snake'. See serpent.

## Serpentid
Serpentid, n. {astron.) — Formed fr. Serpens
with suff. -id.

## serpentiform
serpentiform, adj., resembling a serpent. —
Compounded of serpenti- and L. forma, 'form,
shape'. See form, n.

## serpentine
serpentine, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) serpentin
(fem. serpentine), 'like a serpent', fr. Late L.
serpentinus, fr. L. serpens, gen. -entis. See
serpent and adj. suff. -ine.
Derivatives: serpentine, n. and intr. v., serpen-
tin-ic, adj., serpentin-ize, tr. v., serpentin-iz-
ation, п., serpentin-ous, adj.

## serpentry
serpentry, п., 1) serpents collectively; 2) a place
where serpents are kept. — Coined, by the
English poet John Keats (1795-1821) fr. serpent
and suff. -ry.

## serpierite
serpierite, п., a basic sulfate of copper and zinc
(mineral.) — Named after the Italian engineer

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:702 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 675 | SETTEE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:702 COLUMN:1 -->
J. В. Serpieri, explorer of the mines at Laurium,
Greece. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## serpiginous
serpiginous, adj., of the nature of serpigo. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Medical \. serpigo,
gen. -inis. See next word.
Derivative: serpiginous-ly, adv.

## serpigo
serpigo, п., ringworm; herpes (med.) — Medical
L. serpigo, 'a creeping skin disease', fr. L. ser-
pere, 'to creep', whence also serpens, 'serpent,
snake'. See serpent.

## Serpula
Serpula, п., a genus of marine worms (zool.) —
L. serpula, 'a little snake', fr. serpere, 'to creep'.
See serpent and -ule.

## serra
serra, п., a sawlike organ (zool.) — L., 'a saw', of
uncertain origin. Cp. sierra. Cp. also сего.

## serradelia
serradelia, п., a kind of clover. — Port, serradela,
a dimin. noun formed fr. serrado, 'serrated', fr.
L. serratus. See serrate.

## Serranidae
Serranidae, n. pi., a family of fishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., fr. Serranus, name of the type, fr. L.
serra, 'saw'. See serra and -idae.

## serranoid
serranoid, adj., pertaining to the Serranidae. —
A hybrid coined fr. ModL. Serranus and Gk.
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
piec. word and -oid.

## serrate
serrate, adj., notched, resembling the teeth of a
saw. — L. serratus, 'sawlike', fr. serra. See
serra and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: serrat-ed, adj., serrat-ion, n.

## Serricornia
Serricornia, n. pi., a class of beetles with serrated
antennae (zool.) — ModL., lit. 'having sawlike
horns', fr. L. serra, 'saw', and сотпй, 'horn'. See
serra and horn and cp. corn, 'a horny
induration'. For the ending see 2nd suff. -ia.

## serriferous
serriferous, adj., having serrated edges (hot. and
zool.) — Compounded of L. serra, 'saw', and
the stem oiferre, 'to bear, carry'. See serra and
-ferous.

## serriform
serriform, adj., sawlike. — Compounded of L.
serra, 'saw', and forma, 'form, shape'. See serra
and form, n.

## serrulate
serrulate, adj., finely toothed. — Fr. L. serrula, *a
little saw', dimin. of serra, 'saw'. See serra, -ule
and adj. suff. -ate.

## serry
serry, intr. and tr. v., to press closely together. —
F. serre, pp. otserrer, 'to press together', fr. VL.
'serrdre, 'to bar, bolt', fr. Late L. serare, fr. L.
sera, 'a bar (for fastening a door)'. See sear, 'the
catch in the lock of a gun'.
Derivatives:serri-ed-ly, adv.,serri-ed-ness, n.

## Sertularia
Sertularia, п., a genus of branching hydroids
(zool.) — ModL., fr. L. sertula (pi.), dimin. of
serta, 'wreathes of flowers, garlands', which is
prop. pi. neut. pp. of serere, 'to join together'.
See series and cp. words there referred to.

## Sertullarian
Sertullarian, adj., pertaining to the genus Ser-
tullaria. — See prec. word and -an,

## serum
serum, n. — L., 'watery fluid; whey', cogn. with
Gk. οράς (for 'σορός), 'whey', OI. sarah,
'flowing', sarit, 'brook, river', Gk. ορμή,
'assault, attack, onset, impulse', όρμαν, 'to urge,
stimulate', Lett, sirt, 'to make a raid', fr. I.-E.
base *ser-, *sor-, 'to run, flow'. Cp. hormone,
orrho-, serac and the second element in Apsaras,
samsara. I.-E. base *ser-, *sor-, 'to flow, run',
is rel. to base *srew-, of s.m; see rheo-.

## servable
servable, adj. — Formed fr. serve with suff. -able.

## serval
serval, п., an African wild cat (Felix servaf). —
F., introduced by Buffon fr. Port, lobo cerval,
'lynx', which is formed—with change of suff.—
fr. L. lupus cervdrius (whence also F. hup cer-
vier), 'lynx', lit. 'wolf that hunts the stag',· fr.
lupus, 'wolf, and cervdrius, 'pertaining to a
stag', fr. cervus, 'stag'. See cervine.
Derivative: serval-ine, adj.

## servant
servant, n. — ME,, fr. OF. (= F.) servant, pres.
part, ot servir, 'to serve', fr. L. servire, fr. servus,
'slave'. See serve and -ant and cp. sergeant, which
is a doublet of servant.
Derivative: servant-ry, n.

## serve
serve, tr. and intr. v. — ME. serven, fr. OF. (= F.)
servir, fr. L. servire, 'to be a slave, to serve', fr.
servus, 'slave', which is an Etruscan loan word
(see E. Benveniste in Revue des Etudes Latines,
Paris, 10, 429 ff.); cp. the name of Servius Tul-
lius, who was of Etruscan origin. L. servus is not
related to ser'vare, 'to save, preserve'. Cp. serf,
servant, servient, servile, sirvente, concierge,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:702 COLUMN:2 -->
deserve, dessert, subserve, subservient.
Derivatives: serve, п., serv-er, п., serv-ing, n.

## service
service, п., act of serving. — ME. servise, service,
fr. OF. servise, service (F. service), fr. L. servi-
tium, 'state of a slave', fr. servus, 'slave'. See
serve and -ice.
Derivatives: service, tr. v., serviceable (q.v.)

## serviceable
serviceable, adj., ready to serve. — ME. servisable,
fr. MF., fr. OF., fr. servise, service. See service
and -able.
Derivatives: serviceability, п., serviceable-ness,
п., serviceabl-y, adv.
service trie. — ME. serves, pi. meaning 'service
berries', mistaken for a singular, fr. OE. syrfe,
'service tree', fr. VL. *sorbea, fr. L. sorbus,
'service tree'. See sorb,

## servient
servient, adj., subordinate. — L. serviens, gen.
■entis, pres. part, of servire, 'to serve'. See serve
and -ient.
Derivative: servient-ial, adj.

## serviette
serviette, п., a table napkin. — F., fr. servir, 'to
serve'. See serve and -ette.

## servlie
servlie, adj. — ME., fr. L. servilis, 'belonging to
a slave; slavish, servile', fr. servus, 'slave'. See
serve and -He.
Derivatives: servile-ly, adv., servile-ness, п.,
servil-ism, п., servil-ity, n.

## servitor
servitor, п., servant. — ME. servitour, fr. OF.
servitour (F. servtteur), Тт. Late L. servitdrem,
ace. of servitor, 'servant', fr. L. servire, 'to
serve'. See serve and agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: servitor-ial, adj., servitor-ship, n.

## servitude
servitude, п., bondage. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
servitude, fr. L. servitudo, 'slavery', fr. servus,
'slave'. See serve and -hide,

## sesame
sesame, п., 1) an East Indian plant, whose seeds
yield an oil and are used as food; 2) its seeds. —
F. sesame, fr. L. sesamum, fr. Gk. σήσαμον,
'seed or fruit of the sesame plant', σησάμη,
'sesame plant', fr. Dor. σάσαμον, which is a
Semitic loan word. Cp. Aram. shumshema, 'sesame',
Arab*, simsim, Akkad. shamashskamu, of s.m.
Through the medium of the Phoenicians this
Semitic word was borrowed by the Greeks very
early. It is found in 15th cent. Mycenaean
Greek. See Michael Ventris and John Chad-
wick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek
(Cambridge University Press), Index, s.v. Semitic
Loanwords. Cp. the words chiton, chrysalis,
cumin.

## sesamoid
sesamoid, adj. and n. — Lit. 'shaped like a
sesame seed', fr. Gk. σησαμοειδής, 'like sesame
or sesame seed', which is compounded ofσήσα-
μον, 'sesame', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See prec. word and suff. -oid.
Derivative: sesamoid-al, adj.

## Sesban
Sesban, n. — The same as Sesbania.

## Sesbania
Sesbania, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(hot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, saysaban, fr. Pers.
sisabttn. For the ending see 1 st suff. -ia.

## Sesia
Sesia, п., a genus of moths (zool.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. σης, 'moth', which is of Semitic origin.
Cp. Heb. sds, Aram, sdsd, Arab, sits, susa ,
Ethiop. ddde. Akkad. sdsu, 'moth'. For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## sesqul-
sesqul-, combining form meaning 'one half more'.
— L., contraction of *slm(i)sque, 'and a half
(more)', fr. semi-, 'half (see semi-), and -que,
'and', which is cogn. with OI., Avestic ca,
OPers. cd, Gk. τε, Phryg. κε, Goth -h, Bulg. fe,
Olr. -ch, 'and',

## sesquicentennial
sesquicentennial, adj., pertaining to a century
and a half; п., the one hundred and fiftieth
anniversary. — Compounded of sesqni- and

## centennial
centennial,

## sesquipedalian
sesquipedalian, adj., a foot and a half long. —
Formed with suff. -ian fr. L. sesquipeddlis,
which is compounded of sesqni- and peddlis,
'pertaining to the foot'. See pedal, adj.

## sessile
sessile, adj., attached directly to the main stem
(hot.) — L. sessilis, 'pertaining to sitting, for

## sitting'
sitting', fr. sess-(um), pp. stem otsedere, 'to sit'.
See sedentary and -ile.
Derivative: sessil-ity, n.

## session
session, n. — ME., fr. OF., fr. L. sessionem, ace.

## of sessio
of sessio, 'a sitting; a session', fr. sess-(um),

## pp. stem of sedere
pp. stem of sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary and
-ion. F. session has been reborrowed fr. English.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:702 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: session-al, adj.

## sesterce
sesterce, п., an ancient Roman coin. — L.
sestertius, short for sestertius nummus, contraction
of semis-tertius, lit. 'half the third', i.e. 'two and
a half. See semi- and tertian.

## sestertium
sestertium, п., one thousand sesterces. — Fr. L.
(duo milia) sestertium ('two thousand) sesterces',
where sestertium is the contracted gen. pi. of
sestertius, 'sesterce'. The 5μίτ". -um in sestertium
was mistaken for the nom. sing. suff. of neuter
nouns pertaining to the second declension. See
sesterce.

## sestet
sestet, п., 1) a sextet; 2) the last six lines of a
sonnet. — It. sestetto, fr. sesto, 'sixth', fr. L.
sextus, 'sixth'. See sixth and cp. sextet.

## sestina
sestina, п., a verse form consisting of six stanzas,
invented by Arnaut Daniel, a Provencal
troubadour of the 12th cent. — It., fr. sesto, 'sixth'. See
prec. word.

## Sesuvium
Sesuvium, п., a genus of plants, the sea purslane
(bot.) — ModL., of unknown origin.

## Set
Set, also Seth, п., an Egyptian god of evil. — Gk.
Σή», fr. Egypt. Setesh.

## set
set, tr. and intr. v. — ME. setten, fr. OE. settan,
'to cause to sit, set, plant, build, found', rel. to
OS. settian, ON. setja, Dan. ssette, Swed. sdtta,
OFris. sella, MDu. setten, Du. zetten, OHG.
sezzen, MHG., G. setzen, Goth, satjan; ft.
Teut. *sat-, causative of *set-, 'to sit', whence
OE. sittan, OS. sittian, etc. See sit, sedentary.
Derivatives: set, п., the act of setting, setter
(q.v.), sett-ing, n.

## set
set, п., a'number of group of persons or things.
— ME. sette, sett, set, fr. OF. sette, 'sequence',
a var. of secte, fr. L. secta, 'a following; sect',
fern. pp. of sequi, 'to follow'. See sequel and
words there referred to and cp. sect.

## set
set, adj., fixed. — ME. sett, prop. pp. of setten,
'to set'. See set, v.

## seta
seta, п., pi. setae, a bristlelike part or organ (bot.
and zool.) — L. saeta (less correctly seta), 'stiff
hair, bristle', which is prob. cogn. with OI.
seluh, 'band, fetter, bridge', Avestic haetu-,
'dam, dike', OSlav. siti, 'cord, rope', Lith. sitas,
sietas, 'a fine sieve (esp. of horsehair)', OE. soda,
OHG. seid, seito, 'noose, snare', OHG. saita,
MHG. seite, G. Saite, 'string, chord'. These
words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *sdi-, 'to bind',
whence also OI. sydti, sindti, 'binds', OSlav. silo,
'rope', Lett, sienu, siet, 'to bind', OHG., MHG.,
G. seil, 'rope', ON. seimr, 'chord'. Cp. seton, se-
tula, and the second element in Catasetum,
Equisetum, Trisetum.

## setaceous
setaceous, adj., bristly. — ModL. setdceus, fr. L.
saeta, seta. See prec. word and -aceous.

## Setnria
Setnria, п., a genus of plants, the bristly foxtail
grass (bot.) — ModL., ft. L. seta, 'bristle'. See
seta, adj. suff. -ary and 1st -ia.

## Seth
Seth, masc. PN.; in the Bible the third son of
Adam. — Lit. 'set, appointed', ft. Heb. shith, 'to
put, set', which is rel. to Syr. shiyyutha,
'quality, appearance'.

## Seth
Seth, n. — See Set.

## setiferous
setiferous, adj., bearing bristles. — Compounded
of L. saeta, seta, 'bristle', and the stem oiferre,
'to bear, carry'. See seta and -ferous.

## setiform
setiform, adj., having the form of a bristle. —
Compounded of L. saeta, seta, 'bristle', and

## forma
forma, 'form, shape'. See seta and form, n.

## setigerous
setigerous, adj., the same as setiferous. — L.
saetiger, setiger, 'having bristles, bristly',
compounded οι saeta, seta, 'bristle', and the stem of
gerere, 'to bear'. See seta and -gerous.

## seton
seton, п., twist of horsehairs or thread of silk or
linen to keep a wound open (surg.) — F. seton,
fr. It. setone, augment, of seta, 'silk', fr. VL.
seta, 'silk', fr. L. saeta, seta. See seta.

## setose
setose, adj., bristly, setaceous. — L. saetosus, se-
tosus, 'full of bristles, bristly', fr. saeta, seta. See
seta and adj. suff. -ose.

## setous
setous, adj., setose. — See prec. word and -ous.

## sett
sett, п., 1) name of various tools; 2) sett for
paving. — A var. of set, п., 'the act of setting',
fr. set, v.

## settee
settee, п., a kind of long seat with back and arms.
— Formed with dimin. suff. -ее fr. set, 'the act
of setting'. See set, v.

## settee
settee, п., a kind of sharp-prowed Mediterranean

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:703 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SETTER | 676 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:703 COLUMN:1 -->
vessel. — F. scetie, setie, fr. It. saettia, fr. saetta,
'arrow', fr. L. sagitta, of s.m. See sagittal.

## setter
setter, п., one who sets. — ME., fr. setten, 'to
set'. See set, v., and agential surf. -er.

## settle
settle, п., a bench with a high back. — ME. setel,
setil, fr. OE. sell, 'a seat', rel. to MLG., MDu.
setel, Du. zetel, OHG. se$$al, MHG. se^el, G.
Sessel, Goth, sitls, fr. I.-E. base *sedld-, whence
also Laconic Gk. έλλα (for *sedld), 'seat', L.
sella (for *sedld), 'seat, chair', OSlav. sedlo,
"saddle', Arm. eti, 'place', teli, of s.m., OE.
sadol, 'saddle'. I.-E. *sedld- is an enlargement
of base *sed-, 'to sit'. See sit, sedentary and cp.
saddle and sell, 'seat'.

## settle
settle, tr. and intr. v. — ME. setlen, settlen, fr.
OE. "setlan, fr. setl, 'a seat', rel. to OHG. gisi-
dalen, MHG. sidelen, G. siedeln, 'to settle,
colonize'; see settle, n. In the sense 'to settle a
quarrel', E. settle seems to have been confused
with ME. sahtlen, 'to reconcile', which derives
fr. OE. saht, 'reconciliation', fr. ON. ssett, satt,
'reconciliation'.
Derivatives: settl-ed, adj., settl-ed-ly, adv., settl-
ed-ness, п., settlement (q.v.), settl-er, n.

## settlement
settlement, n. — Formed fr. E. settle, v., with
suff. -ment,

## setuia
setuia, п., a small bristle. — Late L. saetula, se-
tula, dimin. of L. saeta, seta, 'bristle'. See seta
and -ule.

## setwall
setwall, п., valerian.-— ME. setevale, cetevale, fr.
OF. citoual, citouar, fr. ML. zedodria, ult. fr.
Pers. zedwar. See zedoary.

## seven
seven, adj. — ME. seven, sevene, fr. OE. seofon,
rel. to OS. sebun, ON. sjau, Swed. sju, Dan. syvt
OFris. si(u)gun [on analogy of the g in ni(u)gun],
MDu. seven, Du. zeven, OHG. sibun, MHG.
siben, G. sieben, Goth, sibun, and cogn. with OI.
sapta, Avestic hapta, Toch. A spat, B. sukt, suk
(with к for p, on analogy of the к of the
following numeral okt, 'eight'), Hitt. skipta, Arm.
evt'n, Gk. επτά, L. septem, Alb. state (prob.
assimilated to gaSte, 'six'), OSlav. sedmi (for
*sebdmi), Lith. septyni, Olr. secktn, W. saith,
'seven*. Cp. hebdomad, hepta-, septem-,
September.
Derivatives: seven, п., seven-fold, adj. and adv.,
seven-fold-ed, adj.

## seventeen
seventeen, n. — ME. seventene, fr. OE. seofon-
tyne. See seven and -teen.

## seventeenth
seventeenth, adj. — ME. sevententhe; see prec.
word and numeral sufT. -th. The OE. form is
seofon-teoda.

## seventh
seventh,.adj. — ME. seventke; see seven and

ON. sjaundi, OS. sivondo, Dan. syvende, Swed.
sjunde, OHG. sibunto, MHG. sibende, G sie-
bente, siebte. Cp. also septfmal, septime.

## seventieth

## seventy
seventy, adj. — ME., fr. OE. seofontig. See seven
and numeral suff. -ty.
Derivatives: seventy, п., seventieth (q.v.)

## sever
sever, tr. and intr. v. — ME. severen, fr. OF.

cent., 'to wean'), fr. VL. seperdre, fr. L. separdre,

enc. sebrar, 'to separate1, also derive fr. VL. se-
perdre. See separate, v., and cp. several,
severance, dissever, disseverance.
Derivative: sever-able, adj.

## several
several, adj. — ME., fr. AF., fr. ML. separdlis, fr.
L. separ, 'separate, different', back formation
fr. separare. See separate, v., and adj. suff. -al
and cp. sever.
Derivatives: several, п., several-ly, adv.

## severalty
severalty, п., ]) the condition of being several; 2)
property held by individual right; 3) the
condition of property so held. — ME. severalte, fr.

## AF. severalte
AF. severalte, severaute, See prec. word and
subst. suff. -ty.

## severance
severance, n. — ME. severaunce, fr. OF. se-

## vrance
vrance, fr. sevrer. See sever and -ance.

## severe
severe, adj. — MF., fr. L. severus, 'serious, grave,

strict, austere', prob. fr. *se (se) vero, 'without
kindness'. The first element is identical with the

prep, se, 'without'; see se- and cp. words there

έρανος (for * f έρανος), 'a meal to which

## severity
severity, n. — MF. ( — F.) severite, fr. L. severi-

## Seville orange
Seville orange, also Seville, n. — Named from the
city of Seville in Spain.

## Sevres
Sevres, п., porcelain made at Sevres in France.

## sew
sew, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sewen, sowen, fr. OE.

sye, Swed. sy, OHG. siuwan, Goth, siujan, 'to

Gk. ύμήν, 'thin skin, membrane', (κασ)σύειν,

L. suere, 'to sew, sew together', OSlav. sijg, siti,
'to sew', Silo, 'an awl', sivu, 'seam', Lett, siuviu,
siuti, 'to sew', siulas, 'thread', siuvikis, 'tailor',
OPruss. schuwikis, 'shoemaker', schumeno,
'shoemaker's thread', Russ.-Church Slav. sivci,
'tailor, shoemaker', Russ. svec, 'tailor', Czech
svec, 'shoemaker', Hitt. shumanza, 'rope'. Cp.
seam. Cp. also hymen, sutra, suture, subulate,
accouter.
Derivatives: sew-er, п., sew-ing, n.

## sewage
sewage, n. — Short for sewerage. See sewer,

## seweliel
seweliel, п., a burrowing rodent, the mountain
beaver. — Fr. Chinook shewallal, 'blanket made
of two seweliel skins', but mistaken for the
name of the animal itself.

## sewen
sewen, sewin, п., the bull trout. — Of uncertain
origin.

## sewer
sewer, п., one who sews. — Formed fr. sew with
agential suff. -er.

## sewer
sewer, п., head servant at meals (hist.) — ME.,
aphetic for AF. asseour, fr. OF. (— F.) asseoir,
'to seat, set', fr. L. assidere, 'to sit beside, aid,
assist, attend upon', fr. ad- and sedere, 'to sit'.
See assiduous,

## sewer
sewer, п., conduit. — ME., fr. AF. sewere,
aphetic for MF. esseveur, fr. essever, 'to drain', fr.
es-, fr. L. ex, 'out of, and OF. ever, 'to water,
drench', fr. VL. aqudre, fr. L. aqua, 'water'. See
1st ex- and aquatic and cp. ewer.
Derivatives: sewer, tr. v., sewer-age, п.,
sewered, adj.

## sex
sex, n. — ME., fr. L. sexus. The word orig.
meant 'division' and is rel. to secure, 'to cut'.
See section.
Derivatives: sex, adj. and tr. v., sex-ed, adj.,
sex-less, adj., sex-less-ness, n.

## sex-
sex-, sexi-, combining form meaning 'six'. — L.
sex-, fr. sex, 'six'. See six and cp. words there
referred to.

## sexagenarian
sexagenarian, adj. and п., sexagenary. — See
sexagenary and -an.

## sexagenary
sexagenary, adj., sixty years old; pertaining to a
person sixty years old; п., a person sixty years
old, or between the years 60 and 70. — L.
sexdgendrius, fr. sexdgeni, 'sixty each', fr. sexd-

## ginta
ginta, 'sixty', which is formed fr. sex, 'six' (see
six), with suff. -gintd, denoting tens. For the

## etymology of this suff.
etymology of this suff., which is cogn. with Gk.
-κοντά in τριάκοντα, 'thirty', τεσσαρακοντα,
'forty', etc. see penteconta-. For the ending of
sexagenary see suff. -ary.

## Sexagesima
Sexagesima, п., the second Sunday before Lent.
— L. sexagesima (dies), 'sixtieth (day)', fem. of

## sexdgesimus
sexdgesimus, fr. sexdgintd, 'sixty*. See prec.
word.

## sexagesimal
sexagesimal, adj., pertaining to the number sixty.
— ML. sexdgesimdlis, fr. L. sexdgesimus,.'the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:703 COLUMN:3 -->
sixtieth'. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
sexangle, п., a hexagon. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
sex, 'six' (see"sex-), and E. angle.
sexangular, adj., having six angles. —
Compounded of sex- and angular.
Derivative: sexangular-ly, adv.
sexcentenary, adj., pertaining to six hundred
years; п., a six-hundredth anniversary. —
Compounded of sex- and centenary,
sexeunial, adj., ]) lasting six years; 2) occurring
every six years. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr.
L. sexennium, 'a period of six years'. See next
word and cp. biennial,

## sexennium
sexennium, п., a period of six years. — L., fr.
sexennis, 'lasting six years', formed fr. sex, 'six',
and -ennis, fr. annus, 'year'. See sex- and annual.
For the change of Latin a (in annus) to ё (in
sex-ennis, sex-ёптит) see accent. Cp. biennial.

## sexi-
sexi-, combining form meaning 'six'. — See sex-,

## sexidigitate
sexidigitate, adj., having six fingers or toes (zool.)
— Compounded of sexi- and digitate.

## sexisyllabic
sexisyllabic, adj., having six syllables. —
Compounded of sexi- and syllabic.

## sexisyllable
sexisyllable, п., a word of six syllables. —
Compounded of sexi- and syllable.

## sexivalent. adj.
sexivalent. adj., having a valence of six (chem.) —
Compounded of L. sex, 'six', and valens, gen.
valentis, pres. part, of valere, *to have power'.
See sexi- and -valent and cp. bexavalent.

## sexpartite
sexpartite, adj., divided into six parts. — Coined
fr. L. sex, 'six' (see sex-), and E. partite.

## sext
sext,n., one of the canonical hours. — Eccles. L.

## sextain
sextain, п., a stanza of six lines (pros.) — Formed

See prec. word and cp. sestina.

## sextan
sextan, adj., occurring every sixth day; п., fever
recurring every sixth day (counting both days of
consecutive occurrence). — Formed with suff.
-an fr. L. sextus, 'sixth'. See sixth and cp.
quartan, quintan, septan.

## Sextans
Sextans, п., an equatorial constellation south.of
Leo (astron.) — See next word,

## sextant
sextant, п., ]) the sixth part of a circle; 2) an
instrument for determining latitude. — L.
sextans, gen. -amis, 'the sixth part', fr. sextus, 'the
sixth'. See sixth and -ant.

## sextet
sextet, sextette, п., a composition for six voices
or instruments (mus.) — Formed fr. L. sextus,
'the sixth', on analogy of tercet, quartet, quintet.
See sixth and cp. sestet.

## sextile
sextile, adj., at a distance of sixty degrees; п., the
aspect of the celestial bodies which are at the
distance of sixty degrees from each other. — L.
sextilis, 'the sixth', fr. sextus. See sixth and -lie.

## sextillion
sextillion, п., 1) in the United States and France,
a thousand raised to the seventh power (i.e. 1
followed by 21 zeros); 2) in Great Britain and
Germany, a million raised to the sixth power
(i.e. 1 followed by 36 zeros). — F., formed fr.
L. sextus, 'the sixth' (see sixth), on analogy of
million (q.v.) Cp. billion and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: sextillion-th, adj. and n.

## sexto
sexto, п., the size of a book in which the sheets
are folded into six leaves. — L. sexto, abl. of
sextus, 'the sixth'. See sixth.

## sextodecimo
sextodecimo, п., a sheet folded into sixteen leaves.
— L. sextodecimo, abl. of sextusdecimus, 'the
sixteenth', which is compounded of sextus, 'the
sixth', and decimus, 'the tenth'. See sixth and
decimal and cp. sixteenmo.

## sexton
sexton, п., a church custodian. — ME. sekesteyn,
fr. OF. secrestein (F. sacristatn), fr. ML. sacris·
tabus. See sacristan, which is a doublet of sexton.

## sextry
sextry, п., 1) sacristy; 2) the residence of a
sacristan (history). — Formed fr. sexton on analogy
of vestry.

## sextuple
sextuple, adj., sixfold. — Formed fr. L. sextust
'the sixth' (see sext), on analogy of quadruple
(q.v.)
Derivative: sextuple, tr. v., to multiply by six.

## Sextus
Sextus, masc. PN. — L., prop, meaning 'the
sixth', and orig. denoting a sixth child, fr. sextus,
'the sixth1. See sixth and cp. sext. Cp. also
sistine.

## sexual
sexual, adj. — Late L. sexualis, 'relating to sex',

sexual-ly, adv.

## seybertite
seybertite, п., aluminum manganese and calcium
silicate {mineral.) — Named after the American

## Seym
Seym, n. — A var. of Sejm.

## Seymeria
Seymeria, п., a genus of plants (bor.) — ModL.,

mer (1745-1800). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## sforzando

## sfumato

## sgraffito
sgraffito, also sgrafflato, п., a kind of plastering.

## shantnez
shantnez, п., cloth woven of wool and linen

Shaban, п., the eighth month of the
Mohammedan year. — Arab, sha'ban, which prob. means

## shabash
shabash, interj., well done. — Pers. sha-bash, for

## shabby
shabby, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -y fr. now

Derivatives: shabbi-ly, adv., shabbi-ness, n.

## shabrack
shabrack, п., a saddlecloth. — G. Schabracke, fr.

## Shabuoth
Shabuoth, n. pi., the Feast of Weeks, celebrated

'seven'. Cp. Aram, sh bka' (masc), shabtia,
Ugar. skb* (masc), skb*t (fem.), Arab, sab1
(masc), sab'ah (fem.), Ethiop. sab'H (masc),

## shack
shack, п., hut, shanty. — Prob. back formation

derives fr. dial. E. shackle, 'to shake', fr. dial. E.

(q.v.)

## shack
shack, п., fallen acorns or mast, refuse fish, etc.
— A dial. var. of shake.

## shackle

## shad
shad, п., a fish of the herring family, — ME.,

## shade
shade, n. — ME., fr. OE. sceadu, scead, 'shadow,

ness, n.

## shadoof
shadoof, п., a device for raising water. — Arab.

shadow, n. — ME. shadwe, fr. OE. sceaduwe,

## shadow
shadow, tr. v. — ME. schadewan, fr. OE. scead-

Derivatives: shadow-ed, adj., shadow-er, n.

## shaft
shaft, п., stem, stock, pole, bar. — ME., fr. OE.
