scaft, MGH., G. schaft, Du. schacht. The
original meaning of these words was 'stem or branch
stripped of its bark', fr. I.-E. base *sqSp-,
'scraped, scratched, cut with a sharp tool',
whence also Gk. σκήπτρον, 'staff, scepter', Dor.
Gk. σκαπτον, σκδπος, of s.m., L. scapus, 'shaft,
stem', Alb. Skop, 'staff, scepter'. Cp. scape,
'shaft', scapus, scepter, scopa, scullion, escoha.
Derivatives: shaft-ed, adj., shaft-er, п.,
shafting, n.

## shaft
shaft, п., a cylindrical excavation in a mine. -—
From LG. schacht, 'shaft', which is rel. to Du.
schacht, 'shaft', and to shaft, 'stem, pole'.

## shag
shag, п., 1) rough matted hair or wool; 2)

Derivatives: shagg-y, adj., shagg-i-ly, adv.,

## shagreen

Derivative: shagreen, adj.

## shah
shah, п., the title of the king of Persia. — Pers.

## Shaharlth
Shaharlth, п., the daily morning prayer (Jewish
liturgy). — Mishnaic Heb. shaharlth, 'morning
time', fr. Biblical Heb. shdhar, 'dawn', which is
rel. to Aram, shahura, Arab, sahar, Akkad.

## shahzada
shahzada, shahzadah, п., son of a king; title of
the heir apparent. — Pers. shah-zadah,
compounded pf shah, 'king' (see shah), and zddan,

rel. to Avestic zdra-, 'born', and cogn. with L.
gignere (for gi-gn-ere), 'to beget, bear, bring
forth, produce'. For the first element see shah,
for the second see genus and cp. the second
element in mirza.

## shaitan
shaitan, п., an evil spirit; the devil. — Arab.
shaytan, a loan word fr. Heb. satan. See Satan,

## shake
shake, tr. and intr. v. — ME. schaken, shaken, fr.
OE. scacan, 'to shake, to move quickly, fiee,
depart', rel. to ON. and Swed. skaka, Dan.
skage, 'to shift, turn, veer', fr. I.-E. base *skag-
'to move quickly', whence also 01. khajati,

its various senses.
Derivatives: shake, п., shak-able, adj., shaker
(q.v.), shak-ing, adj., and п., shak-ing-ly, adv.

## shaker
shaker, n. — ME. schakare, fr. schaken. See prec.

## shako
shako, п., cylindrical soldier's hat, with a plume.
— F-, fr. Hung, csako, lit. 'peaked (hat)', fr. G.
Zacke, 'sharp point, edge, peak'. See tack,

## shale
shale, п., scale of fish, etc. — ME. schale, schal,
fr. OE. scalu, scealu, 'shell, dish, husk, scale of
balance'. See scale, 'weighing instrument', and

also next word.
Derivatives: shale, v., shal-ed, adj.

## shale
shale, п., a fissile rock formation (petrogr.) — G.
Schale, 'shell, scale, husk'. See prec. word.

## shall
shall, auxil. v. — ME. schal, shal, fr. OE. sceal,
past used as pres.; rel. to OS. sculan, ON. skola,

## skula
skula, Dan. skulle, Swed. skola, Norw. skula,
MDu. sullen, Du. zullen, OHG. solan, MHG.

## suln
suln, soln, G. sollen, Goth, skulan, 'to o.we, be

## under obligation'
under obligation', OS. sculd, OE. scyld, 'guilt',

OHG. sculd, scult, MHG. schulde, schult, G.
Schuld, 'guilt; debt'. Cognates outside Teutonic
are: Lith. skola, 'debt', skeleti, 'to owe', skilti,

and—without the initial s—Lith. kaltas,

## shailoon
shailoon, п., a light woolen fabric. — F. chalon,
fr. CAa/onj-sur-Marne, town in France, where
the fabric was first made,

## shallop
shallop, п., a kind of light boat. — F. chaloupe,
fr. Du. sloep. See sloop,

## shallot
shallot, п., a kind of onion, Allium Ascalonicum.
— Aphetic fr. MF. eschaloite (F. echalotte),
itself formed with change of suff. fr. OF. escha-
logne, fr. VL. *scalonia, shortened fr. L. Asca-
lonia (caepa), 'onion of Ascalori, fr. Ascalo, gen.
-onis, 'Askelon', name of a town in Palestine,
fr. Heb. Ashq Ion. Cp. It. scalogno, Sp. escalona,
OProvenc. calonha, 'shallot', and E. scallion,
eschalot,

## shallow
shallow, adj. — ME. schalowe, rel. to OE. sceald,
'shallow', Swed. skall, 'thin; stale, insipid',
which is rel. to MLG., MHG., G. schal, 'stale,

dry', whence also Gk. σκέλλειν, 'to dry',
σκληρός, 'hard', Lett, kals, 'thin', kalst, 'to
become dry'. See sclero- and cp. shoal, adj.
Derivatives: shallow, n. and intr. and tr. v.,
shallow-ish, adj., shallow-ly, adv., shallow-ness,
n.

## shaloin
shaloin, п., the usual Jewish form of greeting. —
Heb. shalSm, 'peace', prop, 'completeness,
soundness, welfare', from the stem of shdlam,
'he was intact, was complete, was in good
health', whence also shdlem, 'complete, sound',
shelem, 'peace offering'; rel. to Aram, sh lam,
sh lama, 'welfare, peace', Arab, salima, 'he was
safe*, aslama, 'he surrendered, submitted', sa-
lam, Ethiop. saldm, 'welfare, peace', Akkad.
shalamu, 'to be complete, be safe', shalamu,

## sham
sham, n. — A northern var. of shame; the

## shama
shama, п., an Indian song bird. — Hind, samd,
fr. OI. sydmah, 'black, dark-colored'.

## shaman
shaman, п., priest of the Ural-Altaic peoples. —
Tungus soman, 'priest, medicine man'.
Derivatives: shaman-ic, adj., shaman-ism, п.,
shaman-ist, п., shaman-ist-ic, adj.

## Shamash
Shamash, п., the chief sun god of Assyria and
Babylon. — Akkad. shamash, shamshu, 'sun;
the god of the sun', rel. to Heb. shemesh, 'sun',
Krum.shimsha, Syr. shemshd,Ugai. sh-p-sh,Arab.
shams (dissimilated fr. *shamsh), of s.m.; prob.
from the Semitic base s-m-s-m, 'to be swift' (said
of the quivering sunrays). Aram, shumshdna,
Arab, sumsum, Aram, shumsh mdnd (whence
through syncope shumshdna, whence through

## metathesis shushmdna)
metathesis shushmdna), *ant', are of the same
base. See Fleischer, Beitrage zu Jacob Levy's
W6rterbuch iiber die Targumim, II, pp. 577f.

Cp. Samson,

skabhnati, skabhndti, 'fastens, supports', skam-

shamefaced, adj. — Folk-etymological alteration

shamefast, adj., shamefaced. — ME., fr. OE.

## shampoo
shampoo, tr. v. — Hind, champo, imper. of

Derivatives: shampoo, п., shampoo-er, n.

## shamrock
shamrock, п., a trifoliate plant, the national

shandrydan, п., an old-fashioned chaise. — Of

shandygaff, п., mixture of beer and ginger beer.

## shanghai
shanghai, tr. v., to drug a man into

## shank
shank, n. — ME. schanke, shanke, fr. OE. scanca,

G. schenkel, 'shank, leg', and to Du. schonk, 'a

kharijati, 'limps', Gk. σκάζειν (for *sqngyein),
'to limp', ON. skakkr, 'lame, crooked', ON.
hinka, OHG. hinkan, MHG., G. hinken, 'to
limp'. Cp. scazon, skate (for gliding over ice),
skink, 'to serve'. Cp. also the second element in
nuncheon.
Derivatives: shank, tr. and intr. v., shank-ed,
adj.

## shantung
shantung, п., a coarse silk. — Named after the
Chinese province Shan-Tung.

## shanty
shanty, п., hut. — Can. F. chantier, 'workshop',

gelding; a rafter', fr. Gk. κανθήλιος, 'a pack
ass'. See chantier.
Derivative: shanty, intr. v.

## shanty
shanty, п., sailor's song. — Corruption of chantey
(q.v.)

## shapable
shapable, shapeable, adj. — Formed fr. shape, v.,

## shape
shape, tr. v. — ME. shapen, fr. earlier form
schapen, fr. schap, 'shape', fr. OE. -sceap in ge-
sceap, 'something created or shaped', fr. OE.
sceppan, scieppan, scyppan, 'to create, form,
shape, do'; rel. to ON. skapa, Dan. skabe,
OFris. skeppa, OHG. scaffan, MHG., G. schaf-
fen, of s.m., Goth, ga-skapjan, 'to create', fr.
I.-E. base *skab-, 'to work with a stone scraper,
to scrape, scratch; a scraping, scratching',
whence also L. scabere, 'to scratch, scrape'; see
scab, scabies. This orig. meaning of base "skab-,
which arose in the Stone Age, was widened later
in the Teut. languages into 'creative activity' in
general. The primary meaning 'to scrape'
remained in *skap-, a collateral form of base
"skab-. See shave and cp. skep, suff. -ship and
suff. -scape in landscape.
Derivatives: shap-ed, adj., shap-er, п., shap-ing,
п., shap-ing-ly, adv.

## shape
shape, n. — ME. schap, shap. See shape, v.

## -shapen
-shapen, combining form meaning 'of a specified

shape'. — Fr. shapen, the old strong pp. of

## shard
shard, sherd, п., a fragment. — ME. sherd, shard,

## share
share, п., portion, part. — ME. schare, share, fr.

skara, MHG., G. schar, 'troop, band', prop, 'a

Derivatives: share, tr. and intr. v., shar-er, n.

## share
share, п., plowshare. — ME. schare, share, fr.

## Shariah
Shariah, п., the law of islam {Mohammedan relig.)
— Arab. sharl'ah, 'the revealed law of Islam',-fr.

## shark
shark, п., a large, voracious marine fish. — Prob.

## shark

## Sharon
Sharon, п., name of the fertile coastal plain

G. scharf, 'sharp', lit. 'cutting', cogn. with Lett.

## shastra

Shavian, adj. — In the style or manner of George

of cloth', which is rel. to ON. skaut, 'seam, hem
of a garment', Goth, skauts, of s.m. MDu. scoot,
Du. school, 'bosom, lap', OHG. scoso, sco^a,
MHG. scho~3, G. Schofi, of s.m., and prob. also
to OE. sceotany 'to shoot'. See shoot and cp.
sheet, 'rope'. Cp. also scuttle, 'hatchway'.
Derivatives: sheet, tr. v., sheet-ed, adj., sheet-er,
.п., sheet-ing, n.

## sheet
sheet, п., rope fastened to a sail. — ME. shete,
fr. OE. sceata, 'lap, bosom, piece of cloth; foot
of a sail', rel. to sceat, 'lap, bosom, piece of
cloth*, ON. skaut, 'rope fastened to a sail', Du.
schooty G. Schote, of s.m.; see sheet, 'piece of
cloth'. It. scotta, Sp. escota, F. escote (now
ecoute), of s.m., are Teut. loan words.
Derivative: sheet, tr. v.

## Sheffield plate
Sheffield plate, plate of copper between two sheets
of silver. — Named after Sheffield, Yorkshire,
where it was first made.

## shehitah
shehitah, also shehita, shechitah, schechita, п., the
ritual slaughtering of animals or poultry for. use
of food (Jewish Religion). — Heb. shshitdb,
'slaughtering', verbal n. of shdhat, 'he
slaughtered', which is rel. to Aram, sh hat, Arab, sahata,
'he slaughtered', Akkad. shakhdtu, 'to flay'. Cp.
shohet.

## sheik
sheik, sheikh, п., the head of an Arab, family,
tribe or clan. — Arab, shaykh, 'an old man,
elder, chief, from the base of shakha, 'he grew
old*.

## Sheila
Sheila, fern. PN. — Irish equivalent of Celia,
abbreviation of Cecilia. See Celia, Cecilia,

## shekel
shekel, п., an old Jewish unit of weight and
money. — Heb. sheqel, lit. 'weight*, from the stem
of shuqaU 'he weighed, weighed out a price,
paid', whence also mishqal, 'weight'; rel. to
Aram, t qal, 'he weighed', Bibl.-Aram. t qel,
Aram, tiqld, 'shekel', Arab, thaqula, 'was heavy',
thaql, 'load', Ethiop. saqala, 'he hung up,
weighed', Akkad. shaqalu, 'to weigh, to pay', shiqlu,
'shekel'. Cp. slglos, miskal.

## Shekinah
Shekinah, Schecninah, п., the Divine Presence. —
Mishnaic Heb. shekhina , 'dwelling place (of
God)', from the base of shdkhdn, 'he dwelled,
abode*, which is rel. to Aram.-Syr. sh khen,
Arab, sakuna, 'he dwelled', Akkad. shakdnu, 'to
lay, set, deposit' (whence mashkdnu, 'dwelling
place; place; deposit'). All these verbs are prop.
Shaph'el (= causative) forms of the Sem. base
k-w-n, 'to stand firm, to be', and orig. meant 'he
caused to stand, caused to be established'.

## sheldrake
sheldrake, n. — For sheld-drake, lit. 'shield
colored drake'; so called in .allusion to the variegated
markingson the bird,which remind one thepaint-
ings on a shield. See shield and drake. For sense
development cp. G. schildern, 'to paint, depict*,
fr. Schild, 'shield*.

## shelf
shelf, п., a slab of wood, etc., fixed horizontally
lo a wall; a ledge. — ME. schelfe, shelfe, fr. OE.

## scylfe
scylfe, 'plank, bench, shelf, rel. to MLG. schelf,

## ON. skjolf 'bench'
ON. skjolf 'bench', and cogn. with L. scalpere,
'to cut, carve, scrape*, sculpere, 'to carve', Gk.
σκάλοψ, 'mole* (lit- 'the digger*), σκόλοψ,
'pale, stake', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel(e)-p, a -p-en-
largement of base *(s)qel-, 'to cut, cleave, split*.

## See shell and cp. scalpel
See shell and cp. scalpel, Scolopax, sculptor,

## sculpture. Cp. also scale
sculpture. Cp. also scale, 'weighing instrument',
and words there referred to. Cp.—without initial
л—ΟΙ. kfptah, 'arranged', kalpate, 'is arranged',

## kalpayati
kalpayati, 'arranges, allots', Avestic hu-kerepta-,
'well-formed', Goth, halbs, OE. healf 'half,

## prop
prop, 'cut off, divided*. See half and cp. colter.
Derivatives: shelf tr. v., to put on a shelf, shelf-

## ful
ful, shelf-y, adjs.

## shell
shell, n. — ME. schelle, shelle, fr. OE. sciell, rel.

## to Goth
to Goth, skalja, 'tile*, orig. 'anything scalelike,

## shingles'
shingles', OE. scealu, 'shell, husk', and cogn.

## with OSlav. skolika
with OSlav. skolika, 'shell*, Russ. skala, 'bark,
rind'; fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel-, *to cut, cleave, split*.
'See scale, 'weighing instrument', and cp. words

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:706 COLUMN:3 -->
there referred to. See also shelf.
Derivatives: shell, tr. and intr. v., shell-ed, adj.,
shell-ing, п., shell-y, adj.

## shellac
shellac, n. and tr. v. — A compound of shell and
lac, 'a red resinous substance'; loan translation
of F. laque en ecailles, lit. 'lac in plates'.

## shelta
shelta, п., secret slang of Irish tinkers. — Of
unknown origin.

## shelter
shelter, n. — ME. scheldtrome, sheldtrume, shel-
trome, sheltroun, fr. OE. scildtruma, lit. 'a troop
with shields', fr. scild, 'shield', and truma, 'troop,
band, legion', which is rel. to getrum, 'troop,
multitude', trum, 'firm, strong'. See shield and
trim.
Derivatives: skelter, tr. and intr. v., shelter-ed,
adj., shelter-er, п., shelter-y, adj.

## shelty
shelty, sheltie, п., a Shetland pony. — Fr. Shelly,
abbreviation of Sheltand, which is a metathesis
of Shetland.

## shelve
shelve, tr. v., to place on a shelf; to put away as
on a shelf. — Formed fr. shelves, pi. of shelf.
Derivatives: shelv-er, п., shelv-ing, п., shelv-y,
adj.

## shelve
shelve, intr. v., to slope. — Prob. fr. shelf, 'ledge',
so that the orig. meaning of shelve would have
been 'to form a shelf or ledge'.

## Shi-ma
Shi-ma, п., one of the most important parts of the
Jewish daily liturgy, consisting of the three
sections: Deut. 6:4-9, 11: 3-21, Num. 15: 37-41.
— Heb. shema\ lit. 'hear', imper. of Heb. shdma\
'he heard*, whence shema*, 'sound', shema',
'hearing', sh mud, sh mutaht 'report'; rel. to
Aram.-Syr. sh ma\ Ugar. shm', Arab, sami'a,
Ethiop. samSia, 'he heard', Akkad. shemu, 'to
hear'. The prayer is called Shema from the first
word of Deut. 6 : 4, the verse containing Israel's
confession of faith. Cp. Ishmael, Simeon,
smouse, Tashmitum.

## Shi-mini Atzereth
Shi-mini Atzereth, also spelled Shi-mini Atzeret,
the concludine feast of Sukkotht prop, the
eighth day of this festival, observed on the 22nd
day of Tishre. — Heb. sh mint ''atzereth (so
called after Num. 29: 35), fr. sh mini, 'the eighth
(scil. day)', fr. shemdnah, 'eight* (see tomin), and
"atzereth, 'festive assembly', which derives from
the verb dtzar, 'he restrained, kept back,
stopped', and prob. means lit. 'stoppage (of work)',
in reference to the abstention from hard work
prescribed for this day; see Num. 29 : 35. Heb.
'dtzar is rel. to Mishnaic Heb. ldtzar, 'hepressed,
squeezed', and to Aram. (Targum) and Syr.
'atzar, 'he squeezed, pressed out, crushed', Arab.
asara, Ethiop. 'asara, 'hepressed', Akkad. eseru,
'to retain, restrain'.

## Shemite
Shemite, n. — The same as Semite.
Derivative: Shemit-ic, adj. (= Semitic).

## shemittah
shemittah, п., the sabbatical year, i.e. every
seventh year, in which fields and vineyards must
not be tilled (Jewish Religion). — Heb. skemiffdh,
'remission, release' (short for sh nath hash-
sh mitta , 'the year of release'), fr. skamat, 'he
let loose, let drop, let fall; he let (the land) rest',
which is rel. to Aram. skemat, 'he let loose,
loosened, detached; he unsheathed, drew (said
esp. of a sword)', Syr. shemat, 'he drew (a
sword)*, Arab, samata, 'he hung up
(something)', sammata, 'he released (a debtor)*,
Akkad. shamdtu, 'to declare null and void'.

## shenanigan
shenanigan, п., foolery. — Perh. fr. Ir. sionnach,
'fox'.

## stiend
stiend, tr. v., to put to shame. — ME. shenden,
fr. OE. scendan, fr. scand, 'shame, disgrace',
formed with Teut. suff. -pa {= I.-E. -ta) fr.
scamu, sceamu, 'shame' (with the change of
-m- to -n- before the following dental sound).
Cp. OFris. skande, MDu. scande, Du. schande,
OHG. scanta, MHG., G- schande, Goth, skanda,
'shame, disgrace', OHG. scentan, MHG. schen-
ten, G. schanden, 'to put to shame', and see
shame, n.

## Sheol
Sheol, п., the grave, hell. — Heb. sheol, 'the
netherworld', of unknown etymology.

## shepherd
shepherd, n. — ME. schephirde, schepherde,
sheephirde, sheepherde, fr. OE. sceaphyrde,
which is compounded of sceap, 'sheep*, and
hyrde, 'herdsman*. See sheep and herd,
'herdsman'.
Derivatives: shepherd, tr. v., shepherd-ess, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:707 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SHEPHERDIA | 680 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:707 COLUMN:1 -->

## Shepherdia
Shepherdia, п., a genus of plants (hot.) — ModL.,
named after John Shepherd, curator of the
Botanic Garden in Liverpool (1764-1836). For the
ending see 1st suff. -in.

## Sherardia
Sherardia, п., a genus of plants, the field madder
(йог.) — ModL-, named after the English
botanist William Sherard (1659-1728). For the
ending see suff. -ia.

## Sheraton
Sheraton, adj. — Made in the style of the
cabinetmaker Thomas Sheraton (1751-1806).

## sherbet
sherbet, п., a drink made of diluted fruit juice
and sugar. — Turk., Pers. sherbet, fr. Arab.
sharbtr, 'one drink', fr. sharab, 'drink, beverage',
fr. shariba, 'he drank', which is rel. to Mishnaic
Heb. idraph, 'he absorbed, sipped, sucked'. Cp.
sirup, shrub, 'a drink', sorbet and the second
word in loll shraub.

## sherd
sherd, п., a fragment. — A var. of shard.

## shereef
shereef, sherif, п., I) a descendant of Mohammed
through his daughter Fatima; 2) the governor
of Mecca. — Arab, shartf (in vulgar
pronunciation sherif), 'noble', fr. sharafa, 'he was exalted,
was noble'. Cp. ashrafl, tashrif, xerafmi.
Derivative: shereef-ian, sherif-ian, adj.

## sheriff
sheriff, n. — ME. shereve, fr. OE. scir-gergfa,
'president of a shire', which is compounded of
scir, 'shire', and gergfa, 'officer, governor'. See
shire and reeve, 'official'.
Derivatives: sheriff-ess, п., sheriff-dom, п.,
sheriff-ry, n.

## sherry
sherry, n. — Back formation fr. earlier sherries
(which was mistaken for a plural), fr. Xeres
(pronounced sheris), now spelled Jerez (de la Fron-
tera), a town near Cadiz, Spain, fr. L. (oppidum)
Caesaris, '(the town) of Caesar'. Hence sherry
prop, means 'wine of Jerez'. For similar back
formations cp. pea and words there referred to.

## shew
shew, v. — A var. spelling of show'.

## shewbread
shewbread, n. (Jewish Religion). — Coined by
Tyndale on analogy of G. Schaubrot, which
itself was coined by Luther as a loan translation
of Heb. lihem (hap-)pdntm, lit. 'the bread of the
Divine presence', fr. Uhem, 'bread', and pdntm,
'face; presence'. See Ex. 25 : 30.

## Shiah
Shiah, п., 1) a Mohammedan sect whose
adherents regard Ali as the lawful successor of
Mohammed; 2) an adherent of this sect, a Shiite.
— Arab. shi'ah, 'company, faction, party',
shortened fr. sht'at Ali, 'the party of Ali'. Arab.
skt'd1, is rel. to Talmudic Heb. sVah, Aram.
si'utha, 'company, society, party'.

## shihah
shihah, shivah, п., the seven days of mourning
(Jewish Religion). — Heb. shibh'ah, 'seven', short
for sh\bh'dth ylmg ha'ebhel, 'the seven days of
mourning'. See Shabuoth and cp. words there
referred to.

## shibboleth
shibboleth, п., 1) test word used by Jephthah to
distinguish the Gileadites from the Ephraimites,
who could not pronounce the sound sh (see
Judges 12: 6); 2) a test word, a catchword; 3)
a custom or usage distinguishing members of
one group from those of another. — Heb.
shibboleth, 'ear of corn; flowing stream; current
(of a river)', dissimilated fr. "shubbdleth. Cp.
Arab. sdbalah, sunbulah, Aram. shebhalta, Syr.
shebbelta, Akkad. shubbaltu, 'ear of corn'.

## shield
shield, n. — ME. sheld, shild, fr. OE. scield, sceld,
'a shield', rel. to ON. skjoldr, Dan. skjold, Swed.
skold, OS. skild, MDu. scilt, scild, Du. schild,
OHG. scilt, MHG. schilt, G. Schild, Goth.
skildus, of s.m. The original meaning of these
words prob. was 'a split piece of wood', fr. I.-E.
base *(s)qel-, 'to cut, cleave, split', whence also
Lith. skilit, Ί split, cleave', skiltis, 'a slice'. See
shell, and cp. shilling and the first element in
shelter. Cp. also slit and words there referred to.
Derivatives: shield, v. (q.v.), shield-less, adj.,
shield-less-ly, adv., shield-less-ness, n.

## shield
shield, tr. v. — ME. shelden, shilden, fr. OE.
scieldan,scildan, fr. scield, 'a shield'. See shield, n.
Derivatives: shield-ed, adj., shield-er, п.,
shielding, n.

## shieling
shieling, n. — See shenling.

## shier
shier, shyer, п., a horse inclined to shying. —
Formed fr. shy, v., with agential suff. -er.

## shier
shier, adj. — Comparative of shy.

## shift
shift, tr. and intr. y. — ME. schiften, shijten, 'to
^divide, change, remove', fr. OE. sciftap, scyftan.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:707 COLUMN:2 -->
'to divide'; rel. to ON. skipta, 'to divide, change,
separate', Dan. skifte, Swed. skifta, of s.m.,
OFris. skifta, 'to decide, determine, test', Du.
schiften, 'to divide, turn', MHG., G. schichten,
'to classify', Schicht, 'shift', and to sheave, 'the
grooved wheel of a pulley', shive, 'slice', shiver,
'splinter'.
Derivatives: shift, п., shift-er, п., shift-ing, adj.
and п., shift-ing-ly, adv., shift-ing-ness, п., shift-
У, adj.

## Shiism
Shiism, п., the doctrine of the Shiites. — See next
word and -ism.

## Shiite
Shiite, п., one belonging to that Mohammedan
sect which regards Ali as the lawful successor of
Mohammed. — Formed fr. Shiah with subst.
suff. -ite.

## shikar
shikar, п., hunting, sport. — Pers. shikar.
Derivative: shikar, tr. v,

## shikari
shikari, shikaree, п., hunter, a hunting guide. —
Pers. shikari, fr. shikar. See prec, word.

## shillelagh
shillelagh, п., a cudgel, esp. of oak or blackthorn.
— Prop, 'cudgel from the wood of Shillelagh', a
barony in the county Wicklow, famous for its
oaks.

## shilllbeer
shilllbeer, п., 1) an omnibus; 2) a hearse with seats
for the mourners. — Named after the English
coach builder George Shillibeer (1797-1866).

## shilling
shilling, n. — ME. schilling, skilling, fr. OE.
scilling, rel. to OS., Dan., Swed., OFris., OHG.
skilling, ON. skillingr, MDu. scillinc, scellinc,
Du. schelling, MHG. schillinc, G. Schilling,
Goth, skilliggs, fr. Teut. "skilling, prob.
assimilated fr. 'skildling, and rel. to Goth, skildus, OE.
scield, sceld, etc., 'shield' (see shield, n.); formed
with -ing, a suff. used in the Teut. languages to
form nouns denoting coins (cp. farthing, penny).

## shilly-shally
shilly-shally, n. and intr. v. — From former shill
I — shall I, from the old subjunctive shill Π
and the indicative shall /?

## shim
shim, п., a slip of wood. — Of unknown origin.
Derivatives: shim, tr. v., to fill with a shim,
shimm-er, n.

## shimmer
shimmer, n. — ME. schimeren, fr. OE. scimrian,
'to glitter', freq. of scimian, 'to shine', fr. sclma,
'light, brightness'; rel. to Swed. skimra, Du.
schemeren, 'to glitter', G. schimmern, of s.m.,
and to OS. skimo, OHG. scimo, MHG. schlme,
'light, brightness', Goth, skeima, 'lantern'. All
these words derive fr. I.-E. base *skt-, 'to shine'.
See shine, v., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: shimmer, Q., shimmer-y, adj.

## shimmy
shimmy, п., chemise. — Popular alteration of
chemise, which was mistaken for a plural. For a
similar misunderstanding of a singular noun cp.
pea and words there referred to.

## shin
shin, п., the fore part of the leg. — ME. shine, fr.
OE. scinu, rel. to Du. scheen, scheenbeen, OHG.
scina, MHG. schine, schinebein, G. Schienbein,
'shin, shinbone', G. Schiene, 'iron band, rail',
OE. scia, 'shin', and cogn. with Lett. Sk'iene,
'breastbone of birds, iron band, rail'. These
words are derivatives of I.-E. *sqgi-, *sqhgi-, 'to
cut, split, separate', whence also OI. chydti,
'cuts off', Gk. σχαν, σχάζειν, 'to split, slit'. See
shed, v., and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also chine, 'backbone of animals'. It. schiena,
'backbone', and F. echine, of s.m., are Teut.
loan words.
Derivative: shin, tr. and intr. v., to climb (a pole
or rope), prop, 'to use the shins for climbing'.

## shin
shin, п., name of the 21st letter of the Heb.
alphabet. — Heb. shin, for shin, 'tooth' (which
derives from the stem of shanan, 'sharpened',
and is rel. to Aram, shinna, Syr. shennd, Arab.
sinn, Ethiop. senn, Akkad. shinnu, 'tooth'); so
called in allusion to the ancient Hebrew form of
this letter. Cp. san, 'name of letter'.

## shine
shine, intr. and tr. v. — ME. schinen, shinen, fr.
OE. scinan, rel. to OS., OHG. skinan, ΟΝ.,
OFris. skina, Dan. skinne, Swed. skina, Du.
schijnen, MHG. schinen, G. scheinen, Goth.
skeinan, 'to shine, appear'; formed with -w-for-
mative element of the present tense, from I.-E.
base *skl-, *sku(i)-, *skii-, 'to shine, flicker,
glimmer', whence also OSlav. sinqti, 'to flash
up, shine', OI. chaya, Gk. σκιά, 'shade'. See
scene and cp. sheer, 'bright', shimmer, Gegen-
schein. Cp. also chaya, Sciaenidae, sciara,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:707 COLUMN:3 -->
scintilla, scio-, Scirophorian. skiagraphy,
Derivative: shine, n.

## shingle
shingle, п., rounded stones found on the seashore.
— Cp. Norw. singl, singling, of s.m.; of imitative
origin.

## shingle
shingle, п., a piece of split wood. — ME. scincle,
scingle, schingle, fr. L. scindula [whence also
OHG. scindula (MHG., G. schindel)], a
collateral form of scandula, 'roofing shingle', fr. sctn-
dere, 'to cleave, split', which is cogn. with Gk.
σκεδαννύναι, 'to scatter, spread, abroad', σχί-
ζειν, 'to cleave, split', Goth, skaidan, OE. scga-
dan, scddan, 'to divide, separate'. See shed, v.,
and cp. schedule, schism. It. scandola, F. echan-
dole, OSlav. skodelu, 'shingle', also derive fr. L.
scandula.
Derivatives: shingl-ed, adj., shingl-er, п., shingl-
У, adj.

## shingles
shingles, п., an inflammatory disease of the skin.
— ML. cingulus, loan translation of Gk. ζώνη,
'belt, girdle; shingles', fr. L. cingulum, 'girdle',
fr. cingere, 'to gird'; see cincture. The disease is
so called from the rings of vesicles on the skin,
which is one of its symptoms.

## shinny
shinny, also shindy, shinty, п., a primitive form of
hockey. — Cp. Gael, sinteag, 'a bound, jump'.
Derivative: shinny, intr. v., to play, shinny.

## Shinto
Shinto, п., Japanese religion. — Jap. Shinto, fr.
Chin, shin too, 'the path of the gods'.
Derivatives: Shinto-ism, п., Shinto-ist, n.

## ship
ship, n. — ME. schip, ship, fr. OE. scip, rel. to
ΟΝ., OS., Goth, skip, Dan. skib, Swed. skepp,
MDu. scip, Du. schip, OHG. ski/, MHG. schif,
G. Schiff. The orig. meaning prob. was 'a tree
cut out', from base *sqeib-, whence also Lith.
Ski'bit, 'to cut, hew'. Base *sqeib- is a
^-enlargement of I.-E. base *sqei-, 'to cut'. See shed, v.,
and cp. words there referred to. — It. schifo, F.
esquif, 'skiff', and F. e'quiper, 'to equip', are Teut.
loan words. Cp. equip, schipperke, skiff, skipper.
Derivative: shipper (q.v.)

## ship
ship, tr. and intr. v. — ME. schippen, shippen, fr.
schip, ship, 'ship'. See ship, n.
Derivatives: ship-ment, a., shipp-ing, n.

## -ship
-ship, suff. — ME. -schipe, fr. OE. scipe, rel. to
OS. -scepi, -scipi, -scap, ON. -skapr, Swed. -skap
Dan. -skab, OFris. -skip, MDu, -scap, Du.
-schap, OHG. -scaf, -scaft, MHG., G. -schaft,
and to OE. gesceape, 'shape'. See shape and cp.
-scape in landscape.

## shipper
shipper, n. — ME. schiper, shiper, fr. OE. scipere,
formed fr. scip, 'ship', with suff. -ere. See ship
and agential suff. -er.

## shire
shire, n. — ME. shir, shire, fr. OE. scir, Office,
administration; district, county, province', rel.
to OHG. scira, 'business'. Cp. the first element
in sheriff.
Derivative: shire, tr. and intr. v.

## shirk
shirk, п., a parasite. — A var. of shark, 'swindler'.

## shirk
shirk, tr. v., to avoid, evade; intr. v., to evade a
duty. — Fr. shirk, 'a parasite'.
Derivative: shirk, п., one who shirks, shirk-er,
п., of s.m.
shin·, tr. v., to gather (cloth) on parallel threads;
п., a gathering by threads. — Of unknown
origin.

## shirt
shirt, n. — ME. schirte, shirte, sherte, fr. OE.
scyrte, 'skirt, tunic', rel. to ON. skyrta, Dan.
skjorte, Swed. skjorta, 'shirt, kirtle', MDu'.
scorte, Du. schort, 'apron', MHG. schurz, G.
Schurz, Schiirze, 'apron' (whence schiirzen, 'to
tuck up'). The original meaning of these nouns
was 'a short garment', fr. OE. scort, 'short', resp.
its equivalents in the other Teut. languages. See
short and cp. skirt, which is a doublet of shirt.

## shirty
shirty, adj., irritable. — Formed fr. the phrase 'to
have one's shirt out'. See shirt and adj. suff. -y
. (representing ME. -i, -y, -ie).

## shittah
shittah, п., shittah tree, the tree of whose wood
the Ark and the altars, tables, and bars of the
Tabernacle were made (Acacia nilotica). — Heb.
shittah (pi. shittim), for 'shintd, prob. fr. Egypt.
sh-n-s-t (Late Egypt, shonte), whence also
Akkad. samtu, Arab, sant, 'acacia'.

## Shiva
Shiva, n. — See Siva.

shivah, n. — See shihah,

Shivaism, Shivaist, n.'s. — See Sivaism, Sivaist.

shivaree, п., charivari. — Popular alteration of

## shive
shive, п., a slice. — Rel. to sheave (q.v.)

## shiver
shiver, intr. v., to tremble. — ME. chiveren,

## shiver
shiver, п., splinter. — ME. scifre, shivere, shiver,

## shoal
shoal, adj., shallow; whence п., a shallow place.

Derivatives: shoal, intr. v., shoal-y, adj., shoal-i-
ness, n.

## shoal
shoal, п., a crowd, a large number. — ME.

Derivative: shoal, intr. v., to crowd, throng.

## shochet
shochet, n. — See shohct.

## shock
shock, tr. and intr. v., to collide. — ME. schok-
ken, fr. MF. (= F.) choquer, fr. Du. schokken,

Derivatives: shock-able, adj., shock-er, п.,
shock-ing, adj., shock-ing-ly, adv., shock-ing-
ness, n.

## shock
shock, п., collision. — MF. (= F.) choc, fr.
choquer. See prec. word.

## shock
shock, п., group of sheaves. — ME. schokke,

Schock, 'heap, sixty pieces', and—without

Derivative: shock, tr. v.

## shock
shock, adj., shaggy; п., a shaggy mass of hair. —
Prob. a var. of shng.

## shod
shod, adj., wearing shoes. — For shoe-d; pp. of

## shoddy
shoddy, п., a kind of fibrous material. — Of
unknown origin.
Derivatives: shoddy, adj. and tr. v.

## shoe
shoe, n. — ME. sho, shoo, fr. OE. scoh, rel. to
ON. skdr, Dan., Swed. sko, OFris. skoch, OS.
skok, MDu. scoe, scoen, Du. schoen, OHG.
scuoh, MHG. schuoch, G. Sckuk, Goth. skBhs;

Derivatives: shoe, v. (q.v.), shoe-less, adj.

## shoe
shoe, tr. v. — ME. shoen, shooen, fr. OE. scdgan,

Derivatives: shoe-ing, п., sho-ег, n.

## shofar
shofar, n. — See shophar.

## shogun
shogun, п., title of the military governors of Japan
until 1868. — Jap. shogun, lit. 'leader of an
army', fr. Chin chiang-chun, 'leader of an
army'.

## shogunate
shogunate, п., office of the shogun. — A hybrid
coined fr. shogun and 3rd -ate, a suff. of Latin
origin.

## shohet
shohet, п., also shochet, п., a person officially
authorized as slaughterer of animals and
poultry for use of food (Jewish Religion). — Heb.
shohet, prop, active part, of shahat, 'he
slaughtered'. See shehitah.

## shone
shone, past tense and pp. of the v. shine. — ME.
schoon, shoon, fr. OE. scan, past tense of sclnan,
'to shine'. Cp. the OE. pp. (ge)scinen [whence
ME. schine(n)]. See shine.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:708 COLUMN:2 -->

## shoo
shoo, interj. — Of imitative origin.
Derivative: shoo, tr. and intr. v.

## shook
shook, п., a set of staves. — Prob. related to
shock, 'a group of sheaves'.

## shook
shook, past tense of shake. — ME. schook, shook,
fr. OE. scoc, past tense of sceacan. See shake.

## shoot
shoot, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sheten, shoten, fr.
OE. sceotan, rel. to OS. skiotan, ON. skjota,
Swed. skjuta, Dan. skyde, OFris. skiata, MDu.
scieten; Du. schieten, OHG. skiotan, MHG.
schie^eh, G. schiefien, fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeud-, 'to
throw, shoot; to run, haste', whence also OI.
skundate, 'hastens, makes haste', OSlav. is-
kydati, 'to throw out', Lith. skudrits, 'quick,
nimble'. Cp. scoot, scot, 'contribution', scoter,
scuttle, sheet, shot, shut, shuttle, 1st skeet, skit,
skite, skitter, skittish, and the second element
in wainscot.
Derivatives: shoot, п., shoot-able, adj., shoot-er,
п., shoot-ing, п.,

## shop
shop, n. — ME. schoppe, shoppe, fr. OE. sceop-
pa, 'stall, booth', rel. to OE. scypen, scipen,
'shed for cattle', OHG. scop/, 'a building without
walls, a porch', G. Schuppen, 'a shed', and prob.
also to OS. skoj, OE. sceaf, 'sheaf. See sheaf.
Derivatives: shop, intr. and tr. v., shopp-er,
п., shopp-ing, п., shopp-y, adj.

## shophar
shophar, also spelled shofar, п., the ram's horn
blown on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
[Jewish Religion). — Heb. shophar, 'ram's horn',
rel. to Arab, sawafiru, 'ram's horns', Akkad.
shapparu, 'wild goat'.

## shore
shore, п., edge of land. — ME. shor, shore, prop,
'land cut off', fr. OE. scoren, pp. of sceran,
scieran, 'to cut, shear'. See shear and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: shore, tr. v., to set on shore,
shoreless, adj.

## shore
shore, п., large beam, prop. — ME. schore, rel.
to MDu. schooren, 'to prop', Du. schoor, 'a
prop', ON. skorda, of s.m., and prob. also to
OE. sceran, scieran, 'to cut, shear'. See shear
and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: shore, tr. v., to prop, shor-ing, n.

## shore
shore, past tense of shear. — ME. schar, shar, fr.
OE. scser, past tense of sceran, scieran, 'to cut,
shear'. See shear.

## shoreward
shoreward, adj. — Compounded of shore, 'edge
of land', and adj. suif. -ward.

## shoreward
shoreward, shorewards, adv. — Compounded of
shore and adv. surf, -ward, resp. -wards.

## shorn
shorn, pp. of shear. — ME. schoren, fr. OE. scoren,
pp. of sceran, scieran, 'to cut, shear'. See shear.

## short
short, adj. — ME. schort, short, fr. OE. sceort,

of, skort, skortr, 'shortness', OHG. scurz,
'short', from a dental enlargement of I.-E. base

cordus, 'late born', originally meaning 'stunted
(in one's growth)', OSlav. kratuku, Russ. korot-
kij, 'short', Lith. skurstu, skufsti, 'to be stunted
(in one's growth)', skardlis, 'steep', Olr. cert,
'small', Mir. corr, 'stunted, dwarfish'. See shear
and cp. shirt, skirt. Cp. also curt and the first
element in curtail. Cp. also kirtle.
Derivatives: short, adv. and п., short-en, tr:
and intr. v., short-en-er, п., short-en-ing, п.,
short-ish, adj., short-ly, adv., short-ness, n.

## shot
shot, п., contribution. — A doublet of scot,
'contribution' (q.v.)

## shot
shot, п., act of shooting, missile, bullet. — ME.

gescot, gesceot, 'missile', from the base of
sceotan, 'to shoot'; rel. to OE. scyte, 'a shooting',

MDu. scote, Du. schot, 'shot', OHG. scoi,
'missile', scuj, MHG. schus, G. Schufi, 'a shot'.
See shoot.
Derivative: shott-ed, adj., loaded with shot.

## shot
shot, past tense and pp. of shoot. — See next
word.

## shot
shot, adj., woven with the warp and weft of
different colors. — ME. shoten, shot, fr. OE.
gescoten. See next word.

## shorten
shorten, adj., having shot its spawn and
accordingly of inferior value. — ME. shotyn, fr.
shoten, shotyn, pp. of sheten, shoten, fr. OE. scb~otan

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:708 COLUMN:3 -->
(pp. gescoten), 'to shoot'.* See shoot.

## should
should, past tense of the «uxir. v. shall. — ME.
scholde, sholde, fr. OE! scolde, sceolde, past

## shoulder
shoulder, n. — ME. shuldre, shulder, fr. OE.

schulderie), MDu. scouder, Du. schouder, OHG.
scultra, sculterra, MHG. schulder, schulter, G.
Schulter; of uncertain origin.
Derivative: shoulder, tr. and intr. v.

## shout
shout, intr. and tr. v. — ME. shouten, of

Derivatives: shout, п., shout-er, п., shout-ing, n.

shove, tr. and intr. v. — ME. shouven, shoven, fr.

Derivatives: shove, п., shov-er, n.

shovel, n. — ME. shovele, fr. OE. sceofol,

scuvala, scufia, MHG. schuvel, G. Schau/el, fr.

Derivatives: shovel, tr. and intr. v., shovel{l)-er,

## show
show, archaic spelling shew, tr. and intr. v. —
ME. schewen, schowen, shewen, showen, fr. OE.
sceawian, 'to look, see, behold' (in modern
English the sense is causative: 'to cause to be
seen'); rel. to OS. skauwon, 'to look at', OFris.
skdwia, Du. schouwen, OHG. scouwon, MHG.
schouweh, G. schauen, 'to look at', OE. sciene,
scene, scyne, OS., OHG. skoni, MDu. scone,
Du. schoon, Goth, skaunjai (nom. pi.),
'beautiful', orig. 'conspicuous', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qeu-,
*(s)qiu-, 'to look at, observe, perceive', whence
also OI. kavlh, 'wise, sage; seer, poet', a-kuvate,
'intends', Arm. quqanem, Ί show', Gk. κοέω
(for *xofeo>), *I mark, perceive, hear', κΰδος
(for qudos), 'glory, fame' (lit. 'that which is
heard of), the second element in *υο-σκόος,
(for **υο-σκόΓος), 'sacrificing priest', L.
cavere, 'to beware', OSlav. iujo, £uti, 'to feel,
perceive, hear', iudo, gen. -ese (for *qeudos),
'wonder', lit. ('that which is heard of), Czech
(z)koumati, 'to perceive, be aware of. See hear
and cp. scavage, scavenger, sheen. Cp. also

## shower

## shower
shower, п., a short fall of rain. — ME. schour,
shour, showre, fr. OE. scur, rel. to ON. skur,
OS., OHG. scur, MHG. schur, G. Schauer,
Goth, skura in skura v/indis, 'storm of wind',
and cogn. with Arm. curt (for *skur-do-), 'cold,
shower', L. caurus, 'northwest wind', OSlav.

'raging, stormy', Maury's, 'north wind', £iaure,
'north'. Cp. Caurus.
Derivatives: shower, tr. and intr. v., shower-y,
adj., shower-i-ness, n.

OE. scranc, past tense of scrincan. See shrink.

shrapnel, n. — Named after its inventor, Gen.

shred, n. — ME. shrede, fr. OE. screade, scread,

MLG. schrot, schrat, 'piece cut off', OHG.
scrot, 'a cutting, piece cut off, MHG. schrot,
'stroke, blow, wound, piece cut off, G. Schrot,

hrjopa, 'to peel off, pare', fr. I.-E. base
*{s)qreu-t-, whence also L. scrutari, 'to search,
examine, investigate', orig. 'to cut in, scratch',
scrautum, 'quiver for arrows', scrotum,
'scrotum', Lith. skraudus, 'brittle'. Base *(s)qreu-t- is
a dental enlargement of base *(s)qreu-, 'to cut

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:709 COLUMN:1 -->
or break to pieces', which itself derives from
base *(s)qer-, 'to cut, separate'. See shear and

scrotum, scruple, scrutiny,
Derivatives: shred, v. (q.v.), shredd-y, adj.

## shred
shred, tr. and intr. v. — ME. schreden, shreden,

## shrew
shrew, п., a small mouselike animal. — OE.

## shrew
shrew, п., a scolding woman. — ME. schrewe,

## shrew
shrew, tr. v., 1) to curse (pbsol.); 2) to beshrew. —

shrewd, adj. — ME. skrewede; see shrew, п., and

## shrewish
shrewish, adj. — Formed ft. shrew, п., with adj.

Derivatives: shrewish-ly, adv., shrewish-ness, n.

## shri
shri, n. — See sri.

## shriek
shriek, intr. and tr. v. — ME. schriken, shriken,
Cp. ON. skrxkja, 'to screech', and see screak.
Derivatives: shriek, п., shriek-er, п., shriek-y,

## shrieval
shrieval, adj., pertaining to a sheriff. — Formed

## shrievalty
shrievalty, п., the office of a sheriff. — Formed fr.

shrift, n. — ME. schrifl, shrift, fr. OE. scrift,

## shrill
shrill, adj. — ME. schril, shril, fr. schrillen, shril-

shrill, intr. and tr. v. — ME. schrillen, shrillen,

shrimp, п., a small edible shellfish. — ME.

writhe, dry up, shrink', MLG. schrimpen, MHG.

shrimp-ish, adj., shrimp-ish-ness, п., shrimp-y,
adj.

## shrine
shrine, n. — ME. schrin, shrin, fr. OE. serin, 'the

ceptable', and derives fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, -to
bend, turn, twist', whence also L. curvus, 'curved,
crooked'. See curve, п., and cp. scrinium.

## shrine
shrine, tr. v., to enshrine. — ME. shrinen, fr.

## shrink
shrink, intr. and tr. v. — ME. schrinken, shrinken,

prob. to Dan. skrumpe, Swed. skrympa, 'to

scrompelen, Du. schrompelen, G. schrumpfen,
'to shrink', and to OE. scrimman, 'to bend,
writhe, dry up, shrink'. See shrimp and cp.
scrng.
Derivatives: shrink-age, п., shrink-ing, п.,
shrink-ing-ly, adv.

## shrive
shrive, tr. v. — ME. schriven, shriven, fr. OE.
'scrifan, 'to impose penance; to decree; to
shrive', fr. L. scribere, 'to write', whence also
OS. scriban, ODu. scrivan, Du. schrijven, 'to
write', OHG. scriban, MHG. schriben, G.
schreiben, of s.m., ON. skript, 'penance,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:709 COLUMN:2 -->
confession'. See scribe and cp. shrift, Shrovetide.

## shrivel
shrivel, intr. and tr. v. — Cp. dial. Swed. skryvla,
'to wrinkle'.
Derivative: shrivel, n.

## shroff
shroff, п., name of a money changer in the Far
East. — Hind. sarrSf fr. Arab, sarrdf, 'money
changer', fr. sarrafa, 'he changed money',
second conjugation of sarafa, 'he turned'.

## shroud
shroud, n. — ME. schrud, skrud, shroud, fr. OE.
scrud, 'dress, garment', rel. to ON. skrud, 'the
shrouds of a ship, ornament, furniture of a
church', Dan., Swed. skrud, 'dress, attire', and

scread, 'shred, paring'. See shred, n.
Derivatives: shroud, tr. v., shroud-ed, adj.,
shroud-ing, п., shroud-less, adj., shroud-y, adj.

## Shrovetide
Shrovetide, п., the time for confession before

tense shrove), and of tide.

## Shrove Tuesday
Shrove Tuesday, n. — See Shrovetide; so called
from the custom of confessing sins before Ash
Wednesday.

## shrub
shrub, п., a low woody plant. — ME. schrubbe,
schrub, shrub, fr. OE. scrybb, 'underwood', rel.
to dial. Dan. skrub, 'brushwood', Norw. skrubba,
'a dwarf cornel tree'. Cp. scrub, 'a stunted tree'.
Derivatives: shrubb-ery, п., shrubb-y, adj.,
shrubb-i-ness, n.

## shrub
shrub, п., a drink. — Arab, shurb, 'a drink',
formed from the base of shariba, 'he drank'. See
sherbet.

## shrug
shrug, tr. and intr. v. — ME. schruggen, of
uncertain origin. Cp. Dan. skrugge, 'to stoop,
crouch'.
Derivative: shrug, n.

## shrunk
shrunk, pp. of shrink. — ME. shrunke, shrunken,
fr. OE. gescruncen, pp. of scrincan. See shrink.

## shrunken
shrunken, adj. — Old pp. of shrink. See prec.
word.

## shruti
shruti, n. — See sruti.

## shuck
shuck, п., husk, shell. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivative: shuck, tr. v.

## shudder
shudder, intr. v. — ME. schuderen, shoderen,
shoddren, rel. to LG. schuddern, G. schaudern,
'to shudder'. These verbs are frequentatives
formed with suff. -er fr. Teut. base *skud-, 'to
shake', whence also OS. skuddian, 'to move
violently', MDu., Du. schudden, 'to shake',
OHG. scutten, scuten, scutilon, MHG. schutelen,
G. schutteln, 'to shake', G. schutten, 'to pour,
shed'. Teut. base *skud- corresponds to
I.-E. base *(s)qut-, 'to shake', whence L.
quatere, 'to shake'. See quash, 'to make void'.
Derivatives: shudder, п., shudder-ing-ly, adv.,
shudder-y, adj.

## shuffle
shuffle, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. shove with
freq. suff. -le. Cp. scuffle, which is a doublet of
shuffle.
Derivatives: shuffle, п., shuffl-er, п., shuffl-ing,
adj., shuffl-ingly, adv.

## Shulhan Aruk
Shulhan Aruk, code of Jewish law by Rabbi
Joseph Karo (1488-1755). — Heb. shulhan
'arukh, lit. Table Set', fr. shulhan, 'table', and
'drukh, passive part, of 'drdkh, 'he arranged, set
in order'.

## shun
shun, tr. v., to avoid. — ME. schunien, shunien,
fr. OE. scunian, 'to avoid, fear, abhor'; of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: shun-less, adj., shunn-er, n.
'shun (mil.) — Abbreviation of attention.

## shunt
shunt, tr. v., to divert; intr. v., to be diverted. —
ME. schunten, shunten, of uncertain origin;
perh. rel. to shun.
Derivatives: shunt, п., shunt-er, п., shunt-ing, n.

## shut
shut, tr. and intr. v. — ME. schitten, schutten,
shutten, fr. OE. scyttan, 'to shut'; prob. rel. to
snoot. For sense development cp. the phrase 'to
shoot a bolt'. Cp next word. Cp. also the second
element in wainscot.
Derivatives: shutt-er, п., shutt-er, tr. v., shutt-er-
less, adj., shutt-ing, n.

## shuttle
shuttle, Q. — ME. schytel, fr. OE. scytel, 'missile,
dart', a gradational variant formed from the
stem of scgotan, 'to shoot'; so called from its
being 'shot' across the threads in weaving. See
shoot and dimin. suff. -le and cp. prec. word.
Cp. also skittle, which is a doublet of shuttle.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:709 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivative: shuttle, tr. and intr. v.

## shwa
shwa, n. — A var. of schwa.

## shy
shy, adj., timid; bashful. — ME. schey, shey,
'shy', fr. OE. scioh, 'timid', rel. to MLG.
schu(we), Du. schuw, 'shy', MHG. schiech, G.
scheu, of s.m., OHG. sciuhen, MHG. schiuhen,
'to shy at, to fear', G. scheuchen, 'to scare
away'. The only non-Teutonic cognate is
OSIav. Siuti, 'to hunt, incite'. It. schivare, 'to
avoid', is a Teut. loan word. Cp. eschew.
Derivatives: shy, intr. v., shy-er, п., shy-ly, adv.,
shy-ness, n.

## shy
shy, tr. and intr. v., to fling, throw. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivative: shy, п., a throw.

## Shylock
Shylock, п., a merciless creditor. — From a
character of Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice.

## shyster
shyster, п., an unscrupulous lawyer. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivative; shyster, intr. v., to act as a shyster.

## si
si, п., the seventh note in solmization (mus.)

## si
si, adv., yes. — It., Sp. and Port., fr. L. sic, 'so'.
See sic.

## slal-
slal-, form of sialo- before a vowel.

## sialid
sialid, adj., pertaining to the family Sialidae. —
See next word.

## Sialidae
Sialidae, n. pi., a family of insects (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk, σιαλίς, gen. σιαλίδος, name of a
bird; of.unknown origin. For.the ending see
suff. -idae.

## sialo-
sialo-, before a vowel slal-, combining form
meaning 'saliva'. — Gk. σιαλο-, σιαλ-, fr.
σίαλον, 'saliva', of uncertain origin.

## sialoid
sialoid, adj., resembling saliva. — Compounded
of sial- and Gk. -οειήδς, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -old.

## siamang
siamang, п., a species of large black ape. —
Malay sidmang, fr. among, 'black'.

## Siamese
Siamese, adj., pertaining to Siam; п., a native of
Siam, the language of Siam.

## Siamese twins'
Siamese twins', — So called from the Siamese
twins Eng and Chang (1811-74). — They were
united at the waist by a band of flesh.

## sib
sib, n. and adj. — ME., fr. OE. sibb, rel. to OS.
sibbia, OFris., MDu. sibbe, OHG. sippa, MHG.,
G. sippe, Goth, sibja, 'kin, kindred', and cogn.
with Russ. sob, 'character, individuality', OSIav.
o-sob-a, 'person', sobistvo, 'character,
individuality', OPruss. subs, 'self. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base *s(w)e-bh-, 'of the same
kind', which is a -AA-enlargement of the
reflexive pron. base *se-, 'self. See sui and, cp.
gossip. Cp. also Sabine, Samnite.

## Siberian
Siberian, adj. and n. — Formed fr. Siberia with
suff. -an. The name Siberia derives fr. Sibir, an
ancient Tatar fortress at the confluence of the
rivers Tobol and Irtysh.
Siberian dog. — A breed of dogs, esp. used for
drawing sledges.

## siberite
siberite, п., a variety of tourmaline (mineral.) —
Named 'after Siberia. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## sibilance
sibilance, sibilancy, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy,

## sibilant
sibilant, adj., having, or making, a hissing
sound. — Ls sibildns, gen. -antis, pres. part, of
sibilare, 'to hiss, whistle', fr. sibilus, 'hissing,
whistling', which is of imitative origin. Cp. the
imitative words: Gk. σίζειν, 'to hiss', Lett, sikt,
'to hiss', OSIav. svistati, 'to hiss, whistle'. Cp.
also chiilo, siffle, persiflage.
Derivative: sibilant-ly, adv.

## sibilate
sibilate, tr. and intr. v., to hiss; to pronounce
with a hissing sound. — L. sibilatus, pp. of
sibilare. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: sibilat-ion, n.

## sibyl
sibyl, п., prophetess. — L. Sibylla, fr. Gk.
Σίβυλλα, name of several prophetesses; of
uncertain origin.

## Sibylline
Sibylline, adj., pertaining to a sibyl or the sibyls.
— L. Sibyllinus, fr. Sibylla. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## sic
sic, adv., thus. — L. sic, 'so, thus', contracted
from the older form sice, for si-ce, which is
compounded of si, 'if, orig. meaning 'so', and
-ce, an emphatic particle. L. si, orig. sei, is rel.
to Oscan sval, suae, Umbrian sve. It., Sp. and
Port, si, 'yes', F. si, 'so' (in answer to a neg.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:710 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 683 | SIGNAL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:710 COLUMN:1 -->
question) 'yes', derive fr. L. sic. Cp. nisi, quasi.
For the etymology of the L. suff. -ce see he. Cp.
the first element in cy-pres.

## sicarian
sicarian, п., an assassin. — Formed with suff. -an
fr. L. sicarius, 'an assassin, murderer', fr. sica, 'a
curved dagger', which is rel. to sicilis, 'a sickle'
(prop, 'a cutting instrument') and to seed,
secure, 'to cut'. See section and cp. sickie. For the
ending see suff. -ian.

## sicarius
sicarius, п., sicarian. — L. sicarius. See prec.
word,

## sicca
sicca, п., 1) a die; 2) a newly coined rupee. —
Hind, sikkd, fr. Arab. sikkah, 'a die for
stamping'. Cp. sequin,

## siccative
siccative, adj. — Late L. sicedtivus, 'drying,
siccative', fr. L. sicedtus, pp. of siccdre, 'to dry', fr.
siccus, 'dry', which is cogn. with Avestic hiku-,
'dry', Gk ισχνός, 'dry, withered', Lith. seklus,
'shallow', Lett, sekls, of s.m., Lith. senku, sekti,
'to fall' (said of the water level), nu-sekti,
'become dry', Lett, siku, sikt, 'to dry up', Mir.
sesc, 'dry', and with OI. sincati, 'makes dry'. Cp.
desiccate, exsiccate, hortus siccus, sack, 'strong
wine', sec, secco. Cp. also phthisis. For the
ending see suff. -ative.

## sice
sice, also slse, п., the number six on dice. —
For OF. sis (whence F. six), fr. L. sex. See
six.

## sice
sice, п., groom. — VArab. sayis, fr. Arab, sa'is,
'groom'.

## Sicel
Sicel, п., one of the Siculi; adj., pertaining to the
Siculi. — Fr. Gk. Σικελοί (pi.) (whence Siculi,
an ancient people on the Tiber, whence part of
them emigrated to the island named after them
Σικελία, whence L. Sicilia ( — Sicily).

## Siceiiot
Siceiiot, п., one of the-ancient Greeks settled in
Sicily; adj., pertaining to the Siceliots. —
Formed fr. Gk. Σικελοί and the suff. -ώτης. See
prec. word and -ote.

## Sicilian
Sicilian, n. and adj. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Sicilia. See Sice],

## sick
sick, adj. — ME. sik, sek, fr. OE. se~oc, rel. to ON.
sjukr, Swed. sjuk, Dan. syg, OS. siok, OFris.
sidk, MDu. siec, Du. ziek, OHG. sioh, MHG.,
G. siech, Goth, siuks, 'sick, ill', siukan, 'to be
ill'. Nils Lid [in Norsk Tidskr. f. Sprogvidensk.
7, 170 (1934)] connects these words woth OE.
sugan, ON. suga, etc., 'to suck'. (According to
Teut. belief diseases were caused by the sucking
of demons.) See suck and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: sick-en, intr. and tr. v., sick-en-er,
п., sick-en-ing, adj., sick-en-ing-ly, adv., sick-ish,
adj. sick-ish-ly, adv., sick-lsh-ness, п., sick-ly,
adv., sick-li-ness, п., slck-ness, n.

## sick
sick, tr. v., to seek. — A var. of seek,

## sicker
sicker, adj., safe (now only Scot.) — ME. siker,
fr. OE. sicor, which—together with OS. sikor,
OFris. sikur, MDu. seker (Du. zeker), OHG.
sichur, sichor, MHG., G. sicker—derives fr.
VL. *sicurus (whence also It. sicuro),
corresponding to L. securus, 'free from care' (whence
OF. seur, F. sur and Sp. seguro, 'sure, safe').
See secure,

## sickle
sickle, n. — ME. sikel, fr. OE. sicol, which^-
together with MDu. sickele (Du. sikket), OHG.
sihhila (MHG., G. sichely—derives fr. VL.
"sicila corresponding to L. secula, 'sickle'
(whence It. segolo, 'hatchet'), fr. I.-E. base *seq-,
'to cut'. See section and cp. scythe.

## Siculian
Siculian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -ian fr.
L. Siculi (pi.) See Sicel.

## Sicyos
Sicyos, п., a genus of plants, the one-seeded bur
cucumber (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σίκυος,
'cucumber', which according to Paul de Lagarde
(in Armenische Studien. § 1975, and in Mit-
teilungen, 1,234 and II, 356)is borrowed fr. Heb.
*qishshu'd (pi. qishshu'tm), 'cucumber'. See
Heinrich Lewy, Die semitischen Fremdworter
im Griechischen, Berlin, 1895, p. 30. For the
equivalents of Heb. qishshu'tm in the other Sem.
languages see Gesenius-Buhl, Η WAT, p. 731.
Cp. cucumber.

## Sida
Sida, п., a genus of plants of the mallow family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σ(δη, 'pomegranate; a
water plant'; which is prob. a loan word from
Asia Minor.

## Siddha
Siddha, п., one who has attained perfection and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:710 COLUMN:2 -->
bliss (Hinduism). — OI. siddhah, 'accomplished,
achieved, successful, possessing supernatural
power, sorcerer, saint', rel. to sldhyati, 'reaches
his goal, succeeds', sadhuh, 'right, skilled,
excellent ; a holy man'. See sadbu.

## siddur
siddur, п., the Jewish prayer book. — Mishnaic
Heb. siddur, 'arrangement, order', ft. sidder, 'he
arranged, ordered', Pi'el (= intensive form) of
sddhdr, which is rel. to Biblical Heb. sedher,
'order'; see Seder and cp. Sedra. Siddur in the
sense 'prayer book', is an abbreviation of siddur
tepkil!ab, 'arrangement of prayer'. Cp. the term
sedher tepki!ldtli, lit. 'order of prayers', used as a
synonym of siddur.

## side
side, n. — ME., fr. OE. side, rel. to OS. sida, ON.
sida, Dan. side, Swed. sida, MDu. side, Du.
zij(de), OHG. sita, MHG. site, G. Seite, and to
OE. sid, 'long, broad, spacious', ON. sidr,
'long, hanging down', OHG. sito (adv.), 'loose',
and cogn. with Lith. sietuva, 'deep place in a
river', Mir. sith, 'long'.
Derivatives: side, adj. and tr. and intr. v.,
sided, adj., sid-er, п., sid-ing, n.

## sideling
sideling, adv., sidelong. — Formed fr. side with
adverbial suff. -ling. Cp. sidelong and sidle.

## sidelong
sidelong, adv. — Compounded of side and -long.

## sider-
sider-, form of 1st sidero- before a vowel.

## sideral
sideral, adj., pertaining to the stars (rare). — L.
siderdlis, fr. sidus, gen. sideris. See sidereal.

## sideration
sideration, п., blast, blight; use of green manure.
— h.siderdtid, gen. -6nis, 'constellation; disease
caused by a constellation, blast of plants', fr.
sidus, gen. sideris. See next word and -ation and
cp. apoplexy.

## sidereal
sidereal, adj., pertaining to the stars. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. sidereus, fr. sidus, gen.
sideris,Lstar', esp. 'a groupof stars', whichis cogn.
with Lith. svidits, 'shining, bright', svidu, sviditi,
'to shine', Lett, sv/idu, swist, 'to dawn', and prob.
also with ON. svida, OHG. swidan, 'to burn'.
Cp. consider, desire.

## siderlte
siderlte, п., native ferrous carbonate, FeCOs
(mineral.)—L. siderttis (masc.) orsideritisffetn,),
'loadstone', fr. Gk. σιδηρίτης (masc.) or σιδη-
ρίτις (fem.) (scil. λί*ος), 'stone of iron', fr.
σίδηρος, 'iron', which is of uncertain origin.
Cp. the first element in siderolite and the second
element in Metrosideros.
Derivative; siderit-ic, adj.

## sidero-
sidero-, before a vowel sider-, combining form
meaning 'iron*. — Gk. σίδηρο-, σιδηρ-, fr.
σίδηρος, 'iron'. See siderite.

## sidero-
sidero-, combining form meaning 'star'. — L.
sidero-, fr. sidus, gen. sideris, 'star'. See
sidereal.

## siderolite
siderolite, п., an ironstone meteorite. — Lit. 'iron
stone', fr. 1st sidero- and Gk. λί*ος, 'stone'.
See siderite and -lite.

## sideroscope
sideroscope, п., an instrument for detecting the
presence of iron. — Compounded of 1st sidero-
and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at,
examine'. See -scope.

## siderosis
siderosis, п., 1) deposit of iron in a tissue of фе
body, esp. in the lungs; 2) inhalation of iron
dust (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. Gk.
σίδηρος, 'iron'. See 1st sidero- and -osis.

## sideward
sideward, adj. — Compounded of side and adj.
suff. -ward.

## sideward
sideward, sidewards, adv. — Compounded of
side and adv. suff. -ward, resp. -wards.

## sideways
sideways, adv. — Compounded of side and adv.
suff. -ways.
Derivative: sideways, adj.

## sldhe
sldhe, n. — See shee.

## sidle
sidle, v., to move sideways. — Back formation fr.
the obsol. adv. sidling, a var. of sideling (q.v.)
Derivatives: sidle, п., sidl-er, п., sidl-ing, п.,
sidl-ing-ly, adv.

## Sidonian
Sidonian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
L. Siddnius, fr. Gk. Σιδώνιος (also Σιδόνιος),
fr. Σιδών, 'Sidon', an ancient Phoen. city, fr.
Phoen. (= Heb.) Tzidhon, lit. 'fishing-place',
ft. tzud, 'to hunt, capture'. Cp. sadhe.

## siecle
siecle, п., century, age. — F., fr. L. saeculum,
'period of a man's life, generation, period of a
hundred years'. See secular.

## siege
siege, n. — ME. sege, 'seat, siege', fr. OF. sege,
siege (F. siege), fr. VL. 'sedicum, 'seat', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:710 COLUMN:3 -->
*sedicdre, 'to sit', fr. L. sedere, 'to sit'. See
sedentary and cp. see, n. Cp. also besiege.
Derivatives: siege, tr. v., sieg-er, n.

## sienna
sienna, п., an earthy pigment of brownish color.
— Fr. It. terra di Siena, 'earth of Sienna', in
Northern Italy. Cp. umber.

## sierra
sierra, п., a range of hills, jagged, sawlike ridges.
— Sp., lit. 'saw', ft. L. serra. See serra.

## siesta
siesta, п., midday nap. — Sp., fr. L. sexta (hard),
'the sixth hour (i.e. after the sunrise), noon',
fem. of sextus, 'sixth'. See sixth and cp. sext.

## sieve
sieve, n. — ME. sive, seve, fr. OE. si/e, rel. to
MDu. seve, Du. zee/, OHG. sib, MHG. sip,
G. Sieb, 'sieve'; Of uncertain origin. Cp. sift.
Derivative: sieve, tr. v., to sift.

## sifaka
sifaka, п., any of the lemurs of the genus Pro-
pithecus. — A Malagasy word.

## siffle
siffle, tr. v., to whistle; п.,a sibilant rale (med.)—
F. siffler, fr. VL. *sifildre, ft. L. sibildre, 'to hiss'.
See sibilant and cp. zuflfolo.

## sift
sift, tr. and intr. v. — ME. siften, fr. OE. si/tan,
fr. sife, 'sieve', rel. to Du. ziften, MLG. sickten,
G. sichten, 'to sift'. See sieve.
Derivatives: sift-ed, adj., sift-er, п., sift-ing, n.

## sigh
sigh, intr. and tr. v. — Back formation ft. ME.
sih-te, sigk-te, pp. of siken, sighen, 'to sigh', fr.
OE. stcan, which is prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives; sigh, п., sigh-ing, adj., sigh-ing-ly,
adv., sigh-ing-ness, n.

## sight
sight, n. — ME. sith, sikt, sight, fr. OE. sihp,
gesihp, gesiehp, rel. to Dan. sigte, Swed. sigt,
MDu. sicht, gesichte, gesickt, Du. zicht, gezicht,
OHG., MHG. siht, gesiht, G.Sicht, Gesicht; fr.
Teut. base *sehw-, 'to see'. See see, v.
Derivatives: sight, tr. and intr. v.", sight-ed, adj.,
sight-ег, п., sight-ing, п., sight-less, adj., sigkt-
less-ly, adv., sight-less-ness, п., sight-ly, adj.,
sight-li-ness, n.

## sigil
sigil, п., seal. — L. sigillum, 'littie figure, sign,
mark', dimin. οι signum, 'sign'. See sign and cp,
seal, 'stamp'.

## siguTate
siguTate, adj., decorated with marks. — L. sigilld-
tus, pp. of siglllare, 'to mark with a sign or seal',
fr. sigillum. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.

## sigillate
sigillate, tr. v., to seal. — L. sigilldtus, pp. of
sigillare. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## Sigismund
Sigismund, masc. PN. — G., a compound lit.
meaning 'protection through victory'. The first
element is rel. to OHG. sigu, MHG. sic, sige,
G. Sieg, MDu. segke, Du. zege, ON. sigr,
Swed. seger, Dan. seier, OE. sige, gesig,
Goth, sigis, 'victory', and cogn. with OI. saha-,
'victory', sahate, 'overcomes, masters', Gk. 2χειυ
(fr. I.-E. base *segh-), 'to have, hold'. See
scheme and cp. words there referred to. The
second element is iel. to OHG. munt, OE., ON.
mund, 'hand, protection', and cogn. with L.
manus, 'hand'; see manual, adj., and cp. the
second element in Edmund, Osmond, Raymond.

## siglos
siglos, п., silver coin unit in ancient Persia. —
Gk. σίγλος, σίκλος, fr. Heb. sheqel, an old
Jewish unit of weight and money, lit. 'weight'.
See shekel.

## sigma
sigma, п., name of the 18th letter of the Greek
alphabet. — Gk. σίγμα, metathesis of Heb.
sdmekk (prob. through the medium of an
Aramaic form *simkha). See samekh.
Derivatives: sigm-ate, adj. and tr. v., sigm-at-ic,
adj., sigm-oid (q.v.)

## sigmoid
sigmoid, adj., shaped like a sigma. — Gk.
σιγμοειδής, 'having the shape of sigma', compounded
of σίγμα and suff. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος,
'form, shape'. See sigma and -oid.
Derivatives: sigmoid-al, adj., sigmoid-al-ly, adv.

## sign
sign, n. — ME. signe, fr. OF. (= F.) signe, fr. L.
signum, 'mark, token, sign', which is prob. rel. to
secure, 'to cut'. See section and cp. assign,
consign, countersign, design, designate, ensign,
insignia, resign, sain, seal, 'imprint', sennet, signal,
signature, signet, significance, signify, and the
second word in al segno and in da] segno. See
also the first element in scarlet and the second
element in tocsin.

## sign
sign, tr. and intr. v. — ME. signen, fr. MF. ( —
F.) signer, fr. OF. seignier, fr. L. signdre, 'to set
a mark upon, mark, sign', ft. signum. See sign, n.
Dttivatives:sign-able,adj.,signal(ci.v.),sign-er,n.

## signal
signal, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) signal, fr. Late

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:711 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SIGNAL | 684 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:711 COLUMN:1 -->
L. signale, 'a signal', prop. neut. of the
adjective signdlis, 'pertaining to a sign', fr. L. signum.
See sign, п., and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: signal, tr. and intr. v., signal, adj.
(q.v.), signal-ist, п., signal-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
signal(I)-er, n.

## signal
signal, adj. — Formed fr. F. signale, pp. of si-
gnaler, 'to signal', fr. signal. See signal, n. For the
loss of the French pp. suff. -έ in English cp.
costive, defile, 'a narrow valley', trove.

## signalment
signalment, n. — F. signalement, fr. signaler, 'to
signal', fr. signal. See signal, п., and -ment

## signatory
signatory, adj. — L. signatorius, 'pertaining to
sealing', fr. signdtus, pp. of signdre. See sign, v.,
and adj. suff. -ory.

## signature
signature, n. — F., fr. ML. signdtura, fr. L.
signdtus, pp. of signdre. See sign, v., and -ure.
Derivatives: signature, tr. v., signatur-al, adj.

## signet
signet, n. — ME., fr. MF. ( = F.) signet, dimin.
ofsigne. See sign and -et and cp. sennet, wjiich is
a doublet of signet.
Derivative: signet, tr. v.

## significance
significance, also significancy, n. — ME. signifi-
caunce, fr. L. significantia, fr. significdns, gen.
■amis. See next word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## significant
significant, adj. — L. significdns, gen. -amis, pres.
part, of significdre. See signify and -ant.
Derivatives: significant, п., significant-ly, adv.,
significant-ness, n.

## signification
signification, n. — ME. significacioun, fr. OF. ( —
F.) signification, fr. L. significdtionem, ace. of
signifiedtid, 'a pointing out, denoting,
indication', fr. signifiedtus, pp. of significdre. See
signify and -ation.

## significative
significative, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) signifi-
catif (fem. significative), fr. L. signifiedttvus,
'denoting, signifying', fr. signifiedtus, pp. of
significdre. See signify and -ive.

## signify
signify, tr. and intr. v. — ME. signifien, fr. OF.
(= F.) signifier, fr. L. significdre, 'to show by
signs, publish, notify, signify', which is
compounded of signum, 'sign', and -ficdre, tr.facere,
'to make, do'. See sign, п., and -fy.
Derivative: signifi-er, n.

## signor
signor, п., an Italian title corresponding to
English Mr. — It., shorter form of sigaore (q.v.)

## signora
signora, п., an Italian title corresponding to
English Mrs. — Fem. of signor, signore. Cp.
senora, senhora.

## signore
signore, п., an Italian title corresponding to
English Sir. — It., fr. L. seniorem, ace. οι senior,
'older', compar. of senex, 'old'. See senior and
cp. mousignor, seflor, senhor.

## signorina
signorina, п., Italian title corresponding to
English Miss. — It., dimin. of signora.

## Sikh
Sikh, п., member of a Hindu religious
community founded by Guru Nanak about the end of
the 16th cent. — Hind., lit. 'disciple', fr. 01.
siksati, 'studies, learns', desiderative of saknoti,
'is able, is competent'.

## sikhara
sikhara, sikara, п., a pyramidal tower {India). —
OI. itkharah, 'pointed; summit', rel. toSikhd-,
'point', uekharah, 'top, summit', and prob. also
to 01. sdnah, 'whetstone', Utah, 'sharpened', si-
sd-ti, 'sharpens', and cogn. with Gk. κώνος,
'pine cone'. See cone.

## Sikhism
Sikhism, п., the tenets of the Sikhs. — Formed fr.
Sikh with suff. -Ism.

## silage
silage, п., fodder packed in a silo. — Aphetic for
ensilage. See silo and -age.
Derivative: silage, tr. v.

## Silas
Silas, masc. PN. — Late L., fr. Gk. Σίλας,
contraction of Σιλουανός, which is the
transliteration of L. Silvdnus, a name lit. meaning 'living
in, or presiding over, woods', fr. silva, 'wood,
forest'. See silvan.

## silence
silence, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. silentium,
fr. silens, gen. -entis. See sileut and -ce.
Derivatives: silence, tr. v., silenc-er, n.

## Silene
Silene, п., a genus of plants of the pink family
(bot.) — ModL., coined by Linnaeus fr. L.
Silenus. See Silenus.

## silent
silent, adj. — L. silens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
silere, 'to be silent', which, together with Goth.
ana-silan, 'to calm or settle down' (said of a
wind), derives fr. I.-E. base *se(i)-, 'to leave,
leave off", whence also L. sinere, 'to set down;
to leave, let'. See site and cp. words there

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:711 COLUMN:2 -->
referred to. For the ending see suff. -ent.
Derivatives: silent, п., silent-ly, adv.

## silential
silential, adj. — Formed with suff. -al fr. L.
silentium. See silence.
■ silehtiary, n. — Late L. silentidrius, 'a servant
watching for the domestic silence', fr. L.
silentium. See silence and adj. suff. -ary.

## silentious
silentious, adj. — L. silentiosus (whence also F.
silencieux), fr. silentium. See silence and -ous.

## Silenus
Silenus, п., a leader of the satyrs and companion
of Bacchus (Greek mythol.) — L. Silenus, fr.
Gk. Σειληνός, which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly means lit. 'inflated with wine' and
derives fr. Thracian ζίλαι, 'wine', which is
connected with Gk. χάλις, 'neat wine', and lit. means
'swollen with wine'. See Albert Carnoy, Dic-
tionnaire etyrriologique de la mythologie greco-
romaine, Louvain, p. 184 s.v. Silenos.

## silesia
silesia, п., a cloth used for lining. — Orig. the
word meant 'linen made in Silesia (a province
in Prussia)'.

## silex
silex, п., silica. — L. silex, 'flint, pebblestone'.
See silica.

## silhouette
silhouette, п., outline; profile. — F., named
satirically after Etienne de Silhouette, French
finance minister (1709-67), who was ridiculed
by the nobility for his undue economies.
Derivatives: silhouette, tr. v., silhouett-ish, n.

## silic-
silic-, form of silico- before a vowel.

## silica
silica, п., hard silicon dioxide, SiOa (chem.) —
ModL., fr. L. silex, gen. -icis, 'flint,
pebblestone', which is of uncertain origin.

## silicate
silicate, п., a salt of silicic acid (chem.) — See
prec. word arid chem. suff. -ate.
Derivative: silicat-ed, adj.

## siliceous
siliceous, silicious, adj., pertaining to, or
containing, silica. — See silica and -ous.

## silicic
silicic, adj., derived from, or pertaining to, silica.
— See silica and adj. suff. -к.

## siliciferous
siliciferous, adj., containing silica. — See silica
and -ferous.

## silicify
silicify, tr. v., to convert into silica; intr. v., to be
converted into silica. — See silica and -fy.

## silico-
silico-, before a vowel silic-, combining form
indicating the presence of silicon. — See silicon.

## silicle
silicle, п., a small and short silique. — L. silicula,
'a little husk or pod', dimin. of siliqua. See
silique and dimin. suff. -le.

## silicon
silicon, п., name of a nonmetallic element (chem.)
— Coined fr. L. silex, gen. silicis, 'flint', on the
analogy of carbon. See silica.

## silicosis
silicosis, п., disease caused by the inhalation of
silica or quartz (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid
coined fr. silica and -osis, a suff. of Gk. origin.

## siliculose
siliculose, siliculous, adj., containing silicles. —
ML. sillculdsus, fr. L. silicula. See silicle and adj.
suff. -ose, resp.,-ous.

## siliqua
siliqua, п., 1) the same as silique; 2) a very small
weight; 3) a small coin. — L. siliqua. See next
word.

## silique
silique, п., pod or fruit characteristic of the
mustard family (bot.) — F., ft. L. siliqua, 'pod,
husk; a very small weight; a very small coin',
which is of uncertain etymology.

## silk
silk, n. — ME. selk, silk, fr. OE. sioloc, seolc; cp.
ON. si7fci. These words prob. derive fro'm a
Baltic or Slavonic language (cp. OSlav. ielku, Lith.
Silkai, OPruss. silkas, 'silk'), and ult. from an
East-Asiatic language (cp. Mongolian sirkek,
'silk'), and prop, mean 'the Chinese fabric'. It is
of the same origin as. Gk. Σηρες, a people of
Eastern Asia, identified with the Chinese,
whence L. Seres, of s.m., sericum, 'silk', lit. 'the
Seric fabric'. See Serlc and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: silk, adj. and v., silken, adj. (q.v.),
silk-er, п., silk-y, adj., silk-i-ness, n.

## silken
silken, adj. — ME., fr. OE. jeolcen, fr. seolc. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -en.

## sill
sill, n. — ME. sille, sylle, fr. OE. syll, 'base,
support', rel. to ON. svill, syll, Swed. syll, Norw.
svill, Dan. syld, 'the framework of a building,
sill', MLG. sal, OHG. swelll, MHG. swelle,
G. Schwelle, 'sill', and cogn. with Gk. σελίς,
σέλμα, 'beam'. Ср. the second element in
groundsel, 'sill'.

## sillabub
sillabub, п., a mixture of cream or milk with wine
and sugar. — Fr. earlier sillibouk, lit. 'a happy

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:711 COLUMN:3 -->
belly' (cp. dial, merribouk, lit. 'a merry belly').
The first element in sillibouk is identical with
silly in its. orig. sense (= 'happy, fortunate').
For the second element see buck, 'the body of a
wagon',

## suladar
suladar, п., a soldier of irregular cavalry, who
provides his own weapons and horse (Anglo-
Indian). —'Pers. sildhddr, lit. 'armor-bearer', fr.
Arab, sildh, 'weapon', and Pers. ddr, 'possessing,
holding'. The first element is rel. to Heb. shdlah,
'weapon', Ugar. sh-l-h, of s.m., and prob. also
to Heb. shdlah, 'he sent', Akkad. shalu, 'to send,
hurl, shoot (an arrow)'; cp. sirdar, which is a
doublet of silladar. For the second element see
amnildar and cp. words there referred to.

## siller
siller, n. — A Scot. var. of silver.

## SDlery
SDlery, п., a champagne. — Named after Sillery,
a village near Reims in France.

## silly
silly, adj. — ME. sely, seely, seilye, 'happy,
blessed, innocent', fr. OE. sSHg, ges&tig, 'happy,
fortunate', formed with suff. -ig (= E. -y), fr. sxl,
'time, season, occasion, fortune, happiness',
which is rel. to ON. ssell, 'happy', ssela,
'happiness', Goth, sels, 'good, kindhearted', selei,
'goodness, kindness', Dan., Swed. salig, 'happy,
blessed, blissful', OS. salig, MDu. sdlich, Du.
zalig, OHG. sdlig, MHG. sslec, sselic, G. selig,
of s.m. The most important phases of the sense
development of the adj. silly (fr. OE. sislig) are:
happy, innocent, simple, foolish. The above Teut.
words derive fr. I.-E. base *sel-, 'happy', whence
also—with vowel gradation—Gk. ιλαρός, 'gay,
cheerful, gay', ΐλάσκομαι, Ί appease,
propitiate, reconcile to myself, L. soldri, 'to comfort',
salvus, 'whole, safe'. Cp. console, disconsolate,
hilarious, salvage, salvation, solace. Cp. also
seely and the first element in sillabub.
Derivatives: silly, п., silli-ly, sill-i-ness, n.

## silo
silo, п., an airtight structure for storing grain. —
Sp., fr. L. sirus, ft. Gk. σΐρός, 'pit for storing
grain', which is of uncertain origin. Cp. eusjle,
ensilage.
Derivative: silo, tr. v.

## Silphium
Silphium, п., a genus of plants, the rosin-weed
(bot.) — L., name of an umbelliferous "plant,
from Gk. σίλφιον, which is prob. of African
origin. L. sirpe, name of a plant, is from the
same source.

## silt
silt, n. — ME. sylt, of Scand. origin; cp. Norw.
and Dan. sylt, 'salt marsh', which are rel. to
OHG. sulza (for *sult-ja), 'salt water', MHG.
sulz(e), G. Sulze, 'brine, brawn', and to E. salt.
Derivatives: silt, tr. and intr. v., silt-ing, п., silt-
age, п., silt-ation, п., silt-y, adj.

## silundum
silundum, п., a silicon carbide. — Coined fr.
ii/icon and carbonuu/um.

## Silurian
Silurian, adj., pertaining to the Silures, an ancient
British people in Wales. — Formed fr. L. Silures
with suff. -ian.

## Silurian
Silurian, adj., pertaining to the geological period
that preceded the Devonian. — Prop,
'pertaining to the rocks of Wales, once inhabited by the
Silures' (see prec. word). The name Silurian was
given to this period by the geologist Sir Roderick
Impey Murchison (1792-1871), because the
rocks characteristic of this period are especially
frequent in Wales.
Derivative: Silurian, n.

## silvan
silvan, sylvan, adj., 1) living in the woods; 2)
wooded. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. silva,
'wood, forest', which is of uncertain origin. The
spelling sylvan (with у for i) is due to the
influence of Gk. ΰλη, 'forest', from which silva
was supposed to derive. Cp. savage, Silns,
Silvester, Silvia.
Derivatives: silvan, sylvan, п., silvan-ity, п.,
silvan-ry, n.

## silver
silver, n. — ME. silver, fr. OE. seolfor, siolo/r,
silofr, rel. to OS. silubar, ON. silfr, Dan. seiv,
Swed. silver, MDu. silver, Du. zilver, OHG.
sillabar, silabar, MHG., G. silber, Goth, siiubr.
Cp. OSlav. sirebro, OPruss. siraplis, Lith. sidd-
bras, 'silver'. All these words are prob.
borrowed ult. fr. Akkad. sarpu. 'silver', lit. 'refined
silver', which is rel. to sardpu, 'to refine, smelt',
sarrapu, 'goldsmith', Heb. tzdrdph, 'he refined,
smelted', tzoreph, 'goldsmith, silversmith',
Aram.-Syr. tz raph, 'he refined, smelted', Arab.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:712 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 685 | SINCIPUT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:712 COLUMN:1 -->
far/, 'pure (wine)'.
Derivatives: silver, tr. v. and adj., silver-ed, adj.,
silver-er, п., silvern (q.v.), silver-y, adj., silver-i-
ness, n.

## sllverize
sllverize, tr. v., to cover with silver. — A hybrid
coined fr. silver and -ize, a suff. of Greek origin.

## silvern
silvern, adj. — ME. silveren, fr. OE. seolfren,
silfren, fr. seolfor, siolofr, silofr, 'silver1. See
silver.

## Silvester
Silvester, masc. PN. — Lit. 'woody; silvan, rural',
fr. L. Silvester, fr. silva, 'wood, forest'. See
silvan,

## Silvia
Silvia, fem. PN. — Lit. 'belonging to, or living
in, a wood', fr. L. Silvia, fem. of silvius, fr. silva,
'wood, forest*. See silvan,

## silviculture
silviculture, п., forestry. — Formed fr. L. silva,
'wood, forest', and cuilura, 'cultivating,
culture'. See silvan and cnlture.
Derivatives: silvicultur-al, adj., silvicultur-ist, n.

## Silybum
Silybum, п., a genus of plants, the milk thistle
(bot.) — L. silybum, name of an edible thistle,
fr. Gk. σίλυβον, which is of uncertain origin.

## simar
simar, п., a loose robe. — F. simarre, fr. It. zi-
marra, dissimilated fr. Sp. zamarra, fr. Arab.
sammur, 'weasel'. Cp. chimere, zimarrn.

## Simarouba
Simarouba, п., a genus of plants, the quassia
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Galibi simaruba.

## Simaroubaceae
Simaroubaceae, n. pi., the quassia family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## simaroubaceous
simaroubaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## Simeon
Simeon, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the second son
of Jacob and Leah; a tribe of Israel. — Late L.,
fr. Gk. Συμεών, fr. Heb. Skim'on, lit. 'hearing',
fr. shdma\ 'he heard'. See Shema and cp. Simon.
Cp. also Ishmael.

## simhah
simhah, also spelled simcha, п., a joyful occasion,
as in a birth, bar mitzvah or wedding. — Heb.
simhd , 'joy, gladness, merriment, mirth', fr.
sdmah, 'he was glad, rejoiced', which is possibly
rel. to Arab, shdmaha, 'was high, was proud'.
For sense development ср. Е. elated, which
unites the following meanings: 'in high spirits;
proud; joyful' (see elated).

## Simhath Torah
Simhath Torah, also spelled Simhat Torah, Sim-
chas Torah, the last day of Sukkoth, observed
on the 23rd of Tishre in celebration of the
conclusion о f the reading of the Torah in the annual
cycle (Jewish Religion). — Heb. simhath Torah,
lit. 'rejoicing over the Torah', fr. simhath, constr.
state of simhah, and Тага1'. See prec. word and
Torah.

## simian
simian, adj., pertaining to the monkeys and apes.
— Formed with suff. -an fr. L. simia, 'ape', fr.
simus, 'flat-nosed, snub-nosed', fr. Gk. σιμός,
of s.m., which is of uncertain origin.

## similar
similar, adj. and n. — F. similairefrft. L. similis,
'like', assimilated fr. 'semilis, fr*. OL. semol,
semul (L. simul), 'together' (the classical L. form
simul was influenced by similis), which is rel. to
L. semel, 'once', and to the first element in
semper, 'always'. See same an4 words there referred
to and cp. esp. assemble, assimilate, dissemble,
dissimilar, dissimilate, ensemble, resemble,
semblance, semble, simulacrum, simulate,
simultaneous, and the second element in verisimilar.
Derivatives: similar-ly, adv., similar-ity, n.

## simile
simile, п., a figure of speech in which a thing is
compared to another. — L. simile, neut. of
similis, 'like'. See similar.

## similitude
similitude, п., likeness. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr.
L. similitudinem, ace. of similitudo, 'likeness,
resemblance', fr. similis. See similar and -rude
and cp. verisimilitude.

## similize
similize, tr. and intr. v. — A hybrid formed fr. L.
similis, 'like- (see similar), with suff. -ize.

## simmer
simmer, intr. v., to be just below the boiling point;
tr. v., to keep just below the boiling point. — A
later var. of simper, of s.m.—which is now dial.
English—fr. ME. simperen, which is prob. of
imitative origin.
Derivative: simmer, n.

## simnel
simnel, п., a sweet cake. — ME. simenel, fr. OF.
simenel, 'fine wheat flour', fr. VL. 'siminellus,
dissimilated fr. "similellus, masc. dimin. of si-
mila [whence also OHG. semala, simila, 'the
finest wheat flour' (MHG. seme!, of s.m., G.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:712 COLUMN:2 -->
Semmel, 'roll')], which, together with Gk. σε-
μίδαλις, is a Sem. loan word; cp. Akkad.
samldu, Aram.-Syr. simidha, 'finest flour'. Cp.
semolina, cymling..

## Simon
Simon, masc. PN. — L fr. Gk. Σίμων, fr. Heb.
Shim'on, but influenced in form by the Greek
PN. Σίμων, lit. 'snub-nosed' (fr. σιμός, of
s.m.), whence the Talmudic name Simon. See
Simeon.

## Simon Pure
Simon Pure, the right, genuine person. — Name
of a Quaker in Susanna Centlivre's play A Bold
Stroke for a Wife (1717). In part of the play
Simon Pure is impersonated by another
character (Colonel Feignwell) and the real Simon
Pure is dealt with as an impostor and is believed
only after he has proved his identity.

## simoniac
simoniac, п., one who practises simony; adj.,
pertaining to simony. — ML. simdniacus, fr. simo-
nia. See simony.
Derivatives: simoniac-al, adj., simoniac-al-ly,
adv.

## simony
simony, п., the buying or selling of sacred things.
— F. simonie, fr. ML. simonia, fr. Simon Magus,
who was rebuked by Peter when he offered him
money for the gift of the Holy Ghost. — See
Simon.
Derivatives: simoniac (q.v.), Simoni-an, n. and
adj., simon-ist, n.

## simoom
simoom, п., a hot dry desert wind. — Arab.
samum, 'a sultry wind', lit. 'poisonous', fr.
samma, 'he poisoned', fr. sam, 'poison', a loan
word fr. Aram, samma, 'drug, poison', which is
rel. to Bibl. Heb. sam, 'spice', Mishnaic Heb.
sam, 'drug, poison', and prob. also to Arab.
shamma, 'smelled', mashmum, 'any fragrant
plant'.

## simper
simper, intr. v., to smile affectedly. — Prob. of
Scand. origin. Cp. Swed., Norw. and dial. Dan.
semper, 'affected'.
Derivatives: simper, п., simper-er, п., simper-
ing-ly, adv.

## simpie
simpie, adj. ^- ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. simplus,
'simple', var. of simplex, of s.m., fr. I.-E. base
*sem-, 'one, together' (whence also semel, 'once')
and *plac-, '-fold'. For the first element see same
and cp. similar. For the second element see ply,
v., and cp. double and words there referred to.
Derivatives: simple, п., simple-ness, п., simpl-y,
adv., simplification (q.v.), simplify (q.v.)

## simpleton
simpleton, п., a fool. — Formed fr. simple with
suff. -ton. (Cp. singleton, fr. single).

## simpUci
simpUci,ter, adv., simply; wholly. — L., 'simply,
plainly, directly', adv. of the adj. simplex, gen.
simplicis. See simple.

## simplicity
simplicity, n. — ME. simplicite, fr. OF. simpltcite
(F. simplicite), fr. L. simplicitdtem, ace. of sim-
plicitas, fr. simplex, gen. simplicis. See simple
and -ity.

## simplification
simplification, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. simplifier. See
next word and -ation.

## simplify
simplify, tr. v. — F. simplifier, fr. MF., fr. ML.
simplificare. See simple and -fy.
Derivative: simplifi-er, n.

## simulacrum
simulacrum, п., 1) an image; 2) semblance; 3) a
sham. — L., 'likeness, image, form,
representation, portrait', dissimilated—because of the
preceding /—fr. *simulaclom, fr. simuldre, 'to
make like'. See simniate.

## simulant
simulant, adj. — L. simuldns, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of simulare. See next word and -ant.

## simulate
simulate, tr. v., to feign. — L. simulatus, pp. of
simulare, 'to make like, imitate', fr. simul, 'at the
same time, together'. See similar and cp. words
there referred to. For the ending see verbal suff.
-ate.
Derivatives: simulat-ive, adj., simulat-ive-ly,
adv., simulat-or, п., simulat-ory, adj.

## simulation
simulation, n. — ME. simulacion, fr. OF. (= F.)
simulation, fr. L. simuldtionem, ace. of simula-
tio, gen.-on/j, 'a false show, feigning, pretense',
fr. simulatus, pp. of simulare. See prec. word and
•ion.

## simultaneity
simultaneity, n. — See next word and -ity.

## simultaneous
simultaneous, adj. — Late L. simultdneus, fr. L.
simul, 'at the same time'. The t in simul-t-dneus
is prob. due to the influence of mdmentdneus,
