instantttneus (in which, however, the r is
organic). See similar and -aneous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:712 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: simultaneous-ly, adv., simultaneous-
ness, n.

## simurg
simurg, п., a gigantic Bird in Persian mythology,
prob. identical with the roc. — Pers. simurgh,
rel. to Avestic sqend mereyo, 'eagle', OI. syendh,
'eagle', Arm. ςίη, 'kite'.

## sin
sin, п., transgression. — ME. sinne, fr. OE. synn,
syn, 'wrong-doing, injury, hostility; sin', rel. to
OS. sundia, MDu. sonde (Du. zonde), OHG.
sunt(e)a (MHG., G. sunde). These words seem
to be early loan words fr. L. sons, gen. sontis,
'guilty, criminal', which is prob. pres. part, of
sum, esse, 'to be', and stands in gradational
relationship to -sens, gen. -sentis in compound
verbs (as praesens, from praeesse, 'to preside',
see present). Accordingly the orig. meaning of
sons would have been 'that which is' whence
arose the meaning 'that which is really true' and
'he whose guilt has been doubtless established.'
See Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p. 765 s.v. Sunde,
and Walde-Hofmann, II, p. 500, s.v. sons. For
other cognates of L. sons see sooth. See also
esse and cp. absent, present.
Derivatives: sin, v. (q.v.), sin-ful, adj., sin-ful-ly,
adv., sin-ful-ness, п., sin-less, adj., sin-less-ly,
adv., sin-less-ness, n.

## sin
sin, intr. and tr. v. — ME. singen, sinnen, fr. OE.
syngian, 'to sin', fr. synn, 'sin'. See prec. word.
Derivative: sinn-er, n.

## sin
sin, п., name of a Hebrew letter. — Heb. iin, var.
of shin, lit. 'tooth'. See shin, name of letter.

## Sinaitic
Sinaitic, adj., pertaining to Mount Sinai. —
ModL. Sinaiticus, fr. the name of Mount Sinai,
fr. Heb. Sinay. For the ending see suff. -itic.

## Sinanthropus
Sinanthropus, п., a sub-human species, the Peking
man. — Lit. 'the Chinese man', fr. Ptolemaic
Gk. ΣίνΜ, 'China', and Gk. ίν*ρωπος, 'man'.
See Sino- and anthropo-.

## sinapine
sinapine, п., an alkaloid, CleH25OeN (chem.) —
G. Sinapin, formed with suff. -in (see chem. suff.
-ine) fr. L. sinapis, sinapi, 'mustard' (see
sinapism); so called because this alkaloid is found
in the seeds of the black mustard.

## sinapism
sinapism, п., a mustard plaster. — L. sindpismus,
fr. Gk. σιναπισμάς, fr. σιναπίζειν, 'to treat
with a mustard plaster', fr. σίνάπι, 'mustard',
which is rel. to ναπυ, an earlier word of s.m.,
both being of Egyptian origin. L. napus, 'turnip',
which is a Greek loan word, was borrowed into
English in the form of тер. Ср. the second
element in parsnip and in turnip. Cp. also thio-
sinamine. For the ending see suff. -ism.

## since
since, adv. — ME. sins, sinnes, a contraction of
sithens, formed with the adverbial gen. ending
-es, -s (cp. besides) from sithen (often shortened
into sin), fr. OE. siddan, 'after that, since, later',
which stands for sid dan, for sid don, 'after that'.
OE. sid is rel. to OS. nfA.'after that, since', OHG.
sid, MHG. sit, G. seit, 'since', Goth, seipus,
'late'. These words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*se(i)-, 'to leave, leave off, be slow, come late',
whence also OI. sdyam, 'in the evening', L. serus,
'late'. See serotine and cp. site, sith. The second
element in OE. siddan (for sid don, see above),
is the instrumental case of bset. See demonstr.
pron. that.
Derivatives: since, adj. and conj.

## siacere
siacere, adj. — MF. (= F.) sincere, fr. L. sincirus,
'clean, pure, whole, genuine, sincere', which is
of uncertain origin. It possibly stands for sine
*сёгй in the sense of sine carte, 'without decay'.
For the first element see sine, 'without'. The
second element is cogn. with Gk. Κήρ, 'the goddess
of death; doom, destruction', κηραίνειν, 'to
harm, destroy', ακήρατος, 'unhurt', L. caries,
'decay, rottenness'. See caries and cp. cerauno-.
Derivatives: sincere-ly, adv., sincere-ness, п.,
sincerity (q.v.)

## sincerity
sincerity, n. — MF. (— F.) sincerite, fr. OF. sin-
cerite, fr. L. sinceritatem, ace. of sinceritds,
'purity, soundness, wholeness', fr. sincerus. See
prec. word and -ity.

## sincipital
sincipital, adj., pertaining to the sinciput. —
Formed with adj. suff. -a] fr. L. sinciput, gen.
sincipitis, 'half a head'. See next word.

## sinciput
sinciput, п., the forepart of the head. — L., 'half
a head, one of the smoked cheeks of a pig',
contraction of *sim(i)-caput, 'half a head', fr. semi-,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:713 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SINDON | 686 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:713 COLUMN:1 -->
'half, and caput, 'head'. See semi- and capita],
adj., and cp. occiput.
Derivative: sincipit-al, adj.

## sindon
sindon, п., a fine fabric of linen. — L„ fr. Gk.
σινδών, 'linen', lit. 'Indian stuff'. See sendal.

## sine
sine, n. (trigon,) — L. sinus, 'the fold of a garment;
bosom; curve, gulf, in Late L., 'sine'; cogn.
with Alb. gi-ri (for *gin-ri), 'bosom, womb'. As
a mathematical term, L. sinus was first used by
Gherardo of Cremona in his translation from
the Arabic (about the year 1150) to render Arab.
jayb, 'chord of an arc; sine' (fr. 01. jiva-,
'bowstring'), which he confused with Arab, jayb,
'fold of garment'. Cp. cosine.

## sine
sine, prep., without (in Latin phrases). — L. sine,
'without', is an enlarged form of L. sed, se,
'without' and is cogn. with OI. sanituh,
'without, outside', sanutar, 'far away', Gk. &τερ (for
*sn-ter)\ 'without', Goth, sundro, 'alone,
separate', OHG. suntar, MHG. sunder, 'aside, apart',
OE. sundor, 'apart, asunder', MHG. sundern, G.
sondern, 'but*. See sunder, and cp. se- and the
first element in sincere and in sinecnre. Cp. also
sans.

## sinecure
sinecure, п., 1) benefice without a cure of souls;
2) an office with emolument, but with no duties.
— Fr. L. sine curd, 'without a cure', a term used
in Eccles. L. in the term beneficium sine curd, 'a
benefice without (the duty of) curing (the souls)'.
See sine, adv., and cure, 'care'.
Derivatives: sinecur-ism, п., sinecur-istrn.

## sine die
sine die, without a date fixed. — L. sine die, lit.
'without a day', fr. sine, 'without', and die, abl.
of dies, 'day'. See sine, prep., and dies поп.

## sine prole
sine prole, without issue (law). — L., 'without
offspring', fr. sine, 'without', and prole, abl. of
proles, 'offspring, descendant'. See sine, prep.,
and proletarian.
sine qua поп, п., an indispensable condition. —
L., short for conditio sine qua поп, lit. 'a
condition without which not', fr. sine, 'without', qua,
fern. abl. of the relative pron. qui, quae, quod,
'which' (see quod), and поп, 'not'. See поп.

## sinew
sinew, n. — ME. senewe, sinewe, fr. OE. seonu,
sinu, rel. to OS. sinewa, ON. sin, sina, Norw. sin,
Swed. sena, Dan. sene, OFris. sine, MDu. se-
nuwe, senewe, Du. zenuw, OHG. senawa, MHG.
senewe, senne, G. Sehne, fr. I.-E. base *sai-,
*sei-, *si-, 'to bind', whence also Ol. sndvah,
'sinew', Avestic sndvar , of s.m., Ir. sin, 'chain',
Lett, pa-sainis, 'cord, string'. Cp. setn.

## sinfonia
sinfonia, п., a symphony. — It., fr. L. symphonia.
See symphony.

## sing
sing, intr. and tr. v. — ME. singen, fr. OE. singan,
rel. to OS. singan, OFris. sionga, siunga, MDu.
singhen, Du. zingen, OHG. singan, MHG-, G.
singen, ON. syngva, Dan. synge, Swed. sjunga,
Goth, siggwan, and cogn. with Gk. όμφή (for
*songhwa), 'voice, oracle'. Cp. song and the
second element [n meistersinger, minnesinger.
Derivatives: sing, п., sing-able, adj., sing-er, п.,
sing-ing, n. and adj., sing-ing-ly, adv.

## singe
singe, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sengen, fr. OE.
sengan, 'to singe, scorch', rel. to OFris. of-
sendza, MDu. singhen, senghen, Du. zengen,
OHG. Ы-sengan, MHG., G. sengen, 'to singe',
MHG. senge, 'dryness', sine, 'the act of singeing',
and prob. cogn. with OSlav. pri-sqeiti, 'to dry';
not related to sing, as most lexicographers would
have it.
Derivatives: singe, п., singe-ing, adj., singe-ing-
ly, adv.

## Singh
Singh, п., title of the Sikhs after their initiation
ceremony. — Hind, singh, fr. OI. simhah, 'lion'.
Cp. next word.

## Singhalese
Singhalese, also Sinhalese, adj., pertaining to
Ceylon; п., a native of Ceylon. — Formed with
suff. -ese fr. OI. Simhala-, lit. 'of lions', fr.
simhah, 'lion*. Cp. prec. word.

## single
single, adj. — ME., fr. OF. sengle, fr. L. singulus
(in classical L. used only in pi. singull), 'one to
each, separate, single', for I.-E. "sem-go-lo-, fr.
base *sem-, 'one, together', and formative

## elements go- and lo-
elements go- and lo-, which occur also in Goth.
ain-ak-l-s, 'single'. See simple and cp. singular.
Derivatives: single, n. and tr. v., single-ness, п.,(

## single-et
single-et, п., singleton (q.v.), singl-y, adv.

## singlet
singlet, п., a man's undershirt (British). —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:713 COLUMN:2 -->
Formed fr. single with suff. -et,

## singleton
singleton, п., at whist, a single card of a suit in a
hand. — Formed fr. single on analogy of
simpleton. Cp. lushington.

## singletree
singletree, n. — Corruption of swingletree, whose
first element was mistaken for the adjective
single.

## singsong
singsong, п., adj. and tr. and intr. v. — Formed
fr. sing and song:

## Singspiel
Singspiel, п., a lyrical drama, in which dialogue
and song alternate. — G., lit. 'a singing play',
fr. singen, 'to sing', and Spiel, 'play'. See sing
and spiel.

## singnlar
singnlar, adj. — ME. singuler, fr. OF. singuler
(F. singulier), fr. L. singuldris, 'alone, single,
solitary, singular', fr. singull, 'one to each,
separate, single'; see single, adj., and -ar. E. singular
was refashioned after L. singuldris.
Derivatives: singular, п., singular-ly, adv.,
singular-ism, п., singular-ist, п., singularity (q.v.)
singular-ize, tr. v., singulari-iz-dtion, n.

## singularity
singularity, n. — ME. singularite, fr. OF. singu-
larite (F. singularite*), fr. L. singuldritdtem, ace.
of singularitas, *a being alone', fr. singuldris. See
prec. word and -ity.

## Sinic
Sinic, adj., Chinese. — ML. Sinicus, 'Chinese',
fr. Sina, 'China', fr. Late L. Sinae (pi.), 'the
Chinese'. See Slno- and -ic.

## Sinicism
Sinicism, п., Chinese custom or usage. — Formed
from prec. word with suff. -ism.

## sinigrui
sinigrui,n.,acrystallineglucoside(C10HIeKNO,S,)
(chem.) — Formed with suff. -fn from the
abbreviation of L. sina pis nigra, 'black mustard'.
See sinapism, Negro and -in.

## sinister
sinister, adj., of evil omen; evil. — ME. sinistre,
fr. L. sinister, 'left, on the left side'; 'favorable'
(according to the ancient Roman custom);
'unfavorable' (according to the later Greek
conception); prob. cognate with OI. saniydn, 'more
profitable, more advantageous', sanoti, 'wins,
acquires', Avestic hanaiti, of s.m., Gk. #νϋμι,
άνύω, Ί accomplish'. These words are
traceable to I.-E. base *sen-, 'to reach one's aim'.
Accordingly the word sinister represents a
euphemism. For the very reason that the left side
was regarded as the side connected with evil, it
was deliberately called the 'good' side. Cp. OI.
vdriyan, 'better', and Avestic vairya-, 'desirable',
with Avestic yairyastara-, 'to the left', Gk.
άριστος, 'best', with αριστερός, 'left, on the
left side', ευώνυμος, 'left, on the left side', lit.
'of a good name', and OHG. wini, 'friend', with
winstar, 'to the left'. For the suff. (originally a
compar. suff.) cp. L. dexter, 'right, on the right
side' (see dexter).
Derivatives: sinister-ly, adv., sinistr-al, adj.,
sinistr-al-ly, adv., sinistro-, combining form,
sinishorse (q.v.), sinistr-ous, adj.

## sinistrorse
sinistrorse, adj., twining from right to left (hot.)
— L. sinistrdrsus, 'toward the left side, to the
left', contraction of sinistroversus, lit. 'turned
toward the left', fr. sinister, 'left', and versus, pp.
of vertere, 'to turn'. See prec. word and version
and cp. dextrorse.

## sink
sink, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sinken, fr. OE. sincan
(only used in an intransitive sense), rel. to OS.
sinkan, ON. sokkva, Norw. sokka, Dan. synke,
Swed. sjunka, MDu. sinken, Du. zinken, OHG.
sinkan, MHG., G. sinken, Goth, sigqan, prob.
fr. I.-E. base *sengw-, 'to fall, sink', whence also
Arm. ankanim, Ί fall, yield', Gk. έάφ*η (for
·έσάφ*η), 'he sank'. Cp. sag.
Derivatives: sink, п., sink-age, п., sink-er, п.,
sink-ing, п., sink-y, adj.

## Sine-
Sine-, combining form meaning 'Chinese;
Chinese and'. — Fr. Late L. Sinae (pi.), 'the
Chinese', fr. Ptolemaic Gk. Σίναι, of s.m., which
derives ult. fr. Chin. Hs'in or Ch'in, name of the
First Dynasty of China, which reigned 255-206
B.C.E. The name Hs'in or CA'iw lit. means 'man'.
Cp. China.

## Sinologist
Sinologist, п., student of sinology. — Formed fr.
Sinology with suff. -ist.

## Sinologue
Sinologue, п., sinologist. — See next word.

## Sinology
Sinology, п., the study of the Chinese language,
history, etc. — Compounded of Sino- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks in a certain
manner; one who deals (with a certain topic)'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:713 COLUMN:3 -->
See -logy.

## Sinon
Sinon, п., a"perfidious person. — L. Sinon, who
by a false tale induced the Trojans to drag the
wooden horse into their city, as described by the
Roman poet Vergil (70-19 B.C.E.) in his Aeneid
(2, 57-194).

## sinopite
sinopite, п., a red earthy silicate (mineral.) — G.
Sinopit, fr. L. Sinopis. See next word. The G.
ending -it goes back to Gk. -ϊτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## sinople
sinople, п., a kind of red quartz (mineral.) — F.,
prop, 'earth of Sinopis', fr. L. Sinopis (scil.
terra), fr. Gk. Σινωπίς, 'the country Sinopis',
fr. Σινώ7τη, 'Sinope', a seaport in Asia
Minor.

## sinter
sinter, п., a deposit of silica or calcium carbonate
formed from mineral waters. — G., fr. OHG.
sintar, 'dross'. See cinder.
Derivatives: sinter, intr. and tr. v., sinter-er, n.

## sinuate
sinuate, adj., winding. — L. sinudtus, pp. of sinua-
re, 'to wind, bend, curve'. See sine, п., and adj.
suff. -ate and cp. insinuate.

## sinuosity
sinuosity, n. — ML. sinuositds, fr. L. sinudsus.
See next word and -ity.

## sinuous
sinuous, adj., winding. — L. sinudsus, 'full of
bendings and windings-', fr. sinus, *a bend, curve,
fold'. See sine, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: sinuous-ly, adv., sinuous-ness, n.

## sinus
sinus, п., 1) a cavity (anat. and zool.); 2) a pus-
filled cavity (med.) 3) a depression between two
consecutive lobes of a leaf (bot.) — L-, 'the fold
of a garment; bosom; curve; gulf. See sine, n.

## sinusitis
sinusitis, п., inflammation of a sinus (med.) — A
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. sinus and -itis, a
suff. of Greek origin.

## Siouan
Siouan, adj., pertaining to the language of the
Sioux. — Formed fr. Sioux with suff. -an.

## Sioux
Sioux, п., an important group of N. American
Indian tribes. — F., aphetic for Nadowessioux,
fr. Ojibway Nadowessi, lit. 'little snakes', fr.
Nadowe, 'Iroquois', lit. 'big snake'. This name
was given them by their neighbors, whereas the
Sioux themselves called themselves Dakota.,
which means 'allies'.

## sip
sip, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sippen, rel. to OE.
sypian, sipian, 'to sip, absorb', MDu. sippen, 'to
sip'; in gradational relationship to OE. supan,
'to absorb, drink'. See sup, 'to sip', and cp.
sippet, sop.
Derivative: sip, п., sipp-er, n.

## siphon
siphon, п., a bent pipe for drawing off liquids. —
F., fr. L. sipkd,.gsn. -onis, fr. Gk. σΐφων, 'pipe,
tube', which is of uncertain etymology. Cp. the
second element in Erysiphe.
Derivatives: siphon, tr. and intr. v., siphonet
(q.v.)

## siphonet
siphonet, п., the honey tube of certain insects
(zool.) — Formed from prec. word with the
dimin. suff. -et.

## siphono-
siphono-, before a vowel siphon-, combining form
meaning 'siphon, tube'. — Gk. σίφωνο-,
σΐφων-, fr. σΐφων. See siphon.

## Siphonophora
Siphonophora, n. pi., an order of marine
organisms (zool.) — ModL., compounded of siphono-
and Gk. -φόρα, neut. pi. of -φόρος, 'bearing,
carrying'. See -phore.

## siphonostele
siphonostele, п., the tubelike stem of ferns and
certain other plants. — Compounded of si-
phono- and Gk. στήλη, 'a block of stone'. See
stele.

## siphuncle
siphuncle, п., a small tube passing through the
partitions in the shell of some cephalopods
(zool.) — Lit. 'a small tube', fr. L. siphunculus, a
diminutive formed fr. siphd. See siphon and -cle.

## sippet
sippet, п., a small piece of toasted or fried bread.
— Dimin. of the noun sip. See sip and -et.

## slpylite
slpylite, п., a niobate of erbium, cerium and other
rare earth metals (mineral.) — Named after
Sipylus, one of the children of Niobe, in allusion
to the name niobium. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## sir
sir, n. — Reduced form of sire, orig. used only in
unstressed position.
Derivative: s/'r,· tr. v.

## sircar
sircar, п., i) master, lord; 2) government. —
Hind, and Pers. sarkttr, 'chief, fr. Pers. sar,
'head', and -kdr, 'worker'. Pers. sar is rel. to OI.
siras-, 'head, summit', and cogn. with Gk. κάρα,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:714 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 687 | SIXTY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:714 COLUMN:1 -->
'head', L. cerebrum, 'the brain'; see cerebrum
and cp. sprang and words there referred to. Pers.
tear, 'worker', is rel. to OPers. kar-, Avestic kar-,
'to make', к г naoiti, 'makes', 01. krnoti, karSti,
'makes', fr. I.-E. base *qwer-, 'to make, form';
see corpus and cp. the second element in Prakrit,
Sanskrit, abkari.

## sirdar
sirdar, п., military commander in India,
Afghanistan and Pakistan. — Hind, sirdar, fr. Pers.,
contraction of silab-dar. See silladar.

## sire
sire, n. — ME., fr. OF. sire, fr. *seior, vulgar
form of L. senior\ 'older', compar. of senex. See
senior and cp. sir. Cp. also seignior, senhor,
scfior, sieur, signore.
Derivative: sire, tr. v.

## siren
siren, n. — ME., fr. OF. sereine (F. sirene), fr.
Late L. sirina, fr. L. Siren, fr. Gk. Σειρήν, prob.
meaning lit. 'the Binder', fr. σειρά, 'cord, rope*,
which is prob. cogn. with Lith. tveriu, tverti, 'to
seize', fr. I.-E. base *iwer-, 'to seize, hold'; see
paries. See Hofmann, EWG., p. 308 s. w.
σειρά and Σειρήν, and Albert Carnoy, Dic-
tionnaire etymologique de la mythologie greco-
romaine, p. 183 s.v. Seirines.
Derivatives: siren, adj. and tr. v., siren-ic, siren-
ic-al, adjs., siren-ic-al-ly, adv.

## Sirenia
Sirenia, n. pi., an order of marine mammals
(zool.) — ModL., fr. L. Siren, 'siren'. See prec.
word and 2nd -ia.

## sirenian
sirenian, adj., pertaining to the order Sirenia. —
See prec. word and -an.
Derivatives: sirenian, п., a sirenian mammal.

## sirgang
sirgang, п., an East Indian crested bird (Cissa
chinensis). — Of uncertain origin.

## Sirian
Sirian, adj., pertaining to the star Sirius. — See
Sirius and -an.

## siriasis
siriasis, п., sunstroke (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
σειρίασις, fr. σείριος, 'hot, scorching', fr.
σείειν, 'to move to and fro'. See seismo-.

## siris
siris, п., the tree Acacia lebbek. — Hind, siris, fr.
Ol. iirisah.

## Sirius
Sirius, п., the Dog Star. — L., fr. Gk. Σείριος,
lit. 'hot, scorching'. See siriasis.

## sirloin
sirloin, п., the loin of beef, or a part of it. — A
var. spelling of surloin, lit. *the upper part of the
loin', fr. OF. surlogne, surlonge (F. surlonge),
from sur, 'above', and logne, longe (F. longe),
'loin'. See sur- and loin.
Derivative: sirloin-y, adj.

## sirocco
sirocco, п., a hot wind blowing from the Lybian
deserts. — It. sirocco, scirocco, dissimilated fr.
VArab. shoruq, 'the east wind', fr. Arab, sharqt,
'eastern; east wind', fr. sharaqa, 'he cleft,
dissected; rose' (said of the sun). Cp. Saracen,
sarcenet, sarsen.

## sirrah
sirrah, п., a term of address used to men or boys,
expressing anger or contempt (obsol.) — Alter,
of sir.

## sirup
sirup, syrup, n. — ME. sirop, sirup, fr. OF. (= F.)
sirop, fr. ML. sirupus, syrupus, fr. Arab, shardb,
'drink, beverage', from the stem of shariba, 'he
drank', whence also Sp. jarabe, jarope, and
OProvenp. eissarop. It. sciroppo is also borrowed
fr. ML. sirupus. See sherbet and cp. shrub, 'a
drink', sorbet, and the second word in loil
shraub.
Derivative: sirup-y, syrup-y, adj.

## sirvente
sirvente, п., a kind of medieval Provencal song.
— F., fr. Proven?. sirventes(c), 'a kind of song',
prop, 'a song referring to service', fr. sirven,
'serving', pres. part, of servir, fr. L. servire, 'to
serve'. See serve.

## sis
sis, п., a girl (colloq.) — Abbreviation of sister.
Cp. sissy.

## -sis
-sis, sufT in nouns of Greek origin denoting
action, process, state, condition. — Gk. -σις,
identical in meaning with L. -entia (whence E. -ence)
and with E. -ing. Cp. -asis, -esis, -osis.

## sisal grass
sisal grass, sisal hemp. — Named after Sisal, a
seaport in Yucatan.

## siscowet
siscowet, п., a fat variety of the namaycush. —
Can. F. ciscovet, ciscoette, of Algonquian
origin. Cp. cisco.

## siskin
siskin, п., a species of finch. — MDu. sijskijn,
(Du. sijsje), dimin. of sijs, rel. to MHG. zise,
Dan. sise, MLG. czitze, ult. fr. Czech biz, which
together with Pol. czyi, Russ. cii, is of imitative
origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:714 COLUMN:2 -->

## siss
siss, intr. v., to hiss. — Of imitative origin. — Cp.
G. zischen, 'to hiss', and E. sizzle.

## sissoo
sissoo, п., an East Indian tree. — Hind. sisu.

## sissy
sissy, п., 1) an effeminate man or boy; 2) a girl;
adj., effeminate. — Formed fr. sis with dimin.
suff. -y. Cp. prissy.
Derivative: sissy-ish, adj.

## sister
sister, n. — ME. sister, of Scand. origin; cp. ON.
systir, Swed. sister, Dan. sester, which are rel.
to OE. sweostor, swustor, OS. swestar, OFris.
swester, suster, MDu. suster, Du. zuster, OHG.,
MHG. swester, G. Schwester, Goth, swistar,
from I.-E. base *swesor, whence also OI. svasar-,
Avestic xvarjhar-, Toch. A sar, В ser, Arm. k'oir,
L. soror, OSlav. sestra, OPruss. swestro, Lith.
sesuo, Olr. siur, W. chwaer, OCo. huir, 'sister',
Gk. Εωρ (in the vocative έορ). I.-E. *swesor is
compounded of the reflexive base *swe~, 'his,
one's own' (see sui) and -sor, 'woman', fr. I.-E.
*ser-, 'woman', which appears also in the OL
fem. forms tisrah (dissimil. fr. *tri-sor), 'three',
and catasrab, 'four'. Accordingly sister orig.
meant 'the woman belonging to one's own
kindred'. Cp. cousin, cozen, sorority.
Derivatives: sister, tr. v., sister-hood, п., sister'
ly, adj., sister-li-ness, n.

## sistine
sistine, adj., pertaining to any of the popes Sixtus.
— It. Sistino, fr. Sisto, fr. the Latin PN. Sextus,
lit. 'the sixth'. See Sextus and adj. suff. -ine.

## sistrum
sistrum, п., rattle used in ancient Egypt in the
worship of Isis. — L. sistrum, fr. Gk. σεΐστρον,
formed fr. σείειν, 'to shake', with -τρον, a suff.
used to form names of instruments. See seisme-
and cp. words there referred to.

## Sisymbrium
Sisymbrium, п., a genus of plants, the hedge
mustard (bot.) — L.f a fragrant herb, fr. Gk.
σισύμβριον, 'bergamot mint', which is of
uncertain origin.

## Sisyphean
Sisyphean, adj., resembling the labors of
Sisyphus. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Sisypheius,
fr. Gk. Σϊσύφειος, fr. Σίσυφος. See next word.

## Sisyphus
Sisyphus, п., a crafty king of ancient Corinth,
condemned in the netherworld to roll forever
up a hill a rock, which constantly rolled down
again. — L., fr. Gk. Σίσυφος, a name of
uncertain origin. Its connection with σοφός, 'wise,
crafty' (see sophist), is based on folk etymology.

## Sisyrinchium
Sisyrinchium, п., a genus of plants, the blue-eyed
grass {bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σισυρίγχιον, a
kind of plant, which is of uncertain origin.

## sit
sit, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sitten, fr. OE. sittan,
rel. to OS. sittian, ON. sitja, Swed. sitta, Dan.
sidde, OFris. sitta, MDu. sitten, Du. zitten,
OHG. sizzan, MHG., G. sitzen, Goth, sitan, fr.
Teut. base *set-, corresponding to I.-E. base
*sed-, 'to sit', whence OI. sidati, 'he sits', Gk.
£ζεσ&αι (for *sedyestkai), 'to sit', 2δρα (for
*sedra), 'seat', L. sedere, 'to sit', sides, 'seat'. See
sedentary and cp. words there referred to. Cp.
also saddle, seat, set, v., settle, n. and v., soot
and the second element in Alsace and in cosset.
Derivatives: sit. п.. sitt-er. п.. sitt-ing, adj.

## site
site, n. — ME., fr. L. situs, 'situation, position',
fr. situs, pp. ofsinere, 'to set down; to leave, let',
which derives fr. I.-E. base *si(i)-, 'to leave,
leave off, be slow, come late', whence also L.
silire, 'to be silent', sirus, *late\ OE. sid, 'after',
siddan, 'after that, since'. Cp. situate, adj., situs.
Cp. also depose, desinence, position, post, prest,
adj., presto, serotine, silent, since.
Derivative: sit-ed, adj.

## sith
sith, adv. and conj., since {obsolete). — ME. sith,
fr. OE. siddan. See since.

## sito-
sito-, combining form meaning 'food'. — Gk.
σίτο-, fr. σίτος, 'wheat, corn, meal', of
uncertain origin. Cp. syssitia.

## sitology
sitology, п., study of food. — Compounded of
sito- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## sitophobia
sitophobia, п., morbid aversion to food. —
Coined fr. sito- and Gk. -φοβία, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See
-phobia,

## sitosterol
sitosterol, п., a crystalline sterol found in some
plants (спет.) — Coined fr. sito- and the last
two syllables of cholesterol.

## sitotoxism
sitotoxism, п., food poisoning. — Coined fr. sito-,
Gk. τοξικού, 'poison' (see toxic), and suff. -ism.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:714 COLUMN:3 -->

## situate
situate, adj. — Late L. situatus, pp. of situare, 'to
place', fr. situs, pp. oisinere, *to set down, leave,
let'. See site and adj. suff. -ate.

## situate
situate, tr. v. — Late L. situatus, pp. of situare.
See situate, adj.
Derivatives: situat-ed, adv., situation (q.v.)

## situation
situation, n. — MF. (— F.), fr. ML. situatidnem,
ace. of situatio, fr. Late L. situatus, pp. οι situare.
See situate, adj., and -ion.

## situla
situla, п., bucket, pail, urn {Roman antiquities).
— L., cogn. with Lith. sietas, 'sieve', Mir.
sithlad, 'the act of sifting'. Cp. secchio, seidel.

## situs
situs, п., situation. — L. See site.

## sitz bath
sitz bath, hip bath. — A hybrid coined fr. G. Sitz·
bad, lit. 'bath in a sitting position', by
substituting E. bath for Bad, its German equivalent.
G. Sitz, 'a sitting; seat', derives fr. MHG. siz,
fr. OHG. siz, fr. OHG. sizzan, 'to sit*. See sit
and cp. next word.

## sitzkrieg
sitzkrieg, п., static warfare. — G. Sitzkrieg, lit.
'sitting war', fr. Sitz, 'a sitting; seat*, and Krieg,
'war'. For the first element see prec. word, for
the second see kriegspiel.

## Siiim
Siiim, п., a genus of plants, the water parsnip
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σίον, a kind of marsh
plant.

## Sivn
Sivn, Shivn, п., one of the three supreme gods of
Brahminism. — Hind. Shiva, fr. Ol. Sivah, lit.
'propitious, gracious', which is cogn. with L.
civis, 'citizen'. See civil.

## Sivaism
Sivaism, Shivaism, п., worship of Siva. —
Formed fr. Siva, Shiva, with suff. -ism.

## Sivaist
Sivaist, Sbivaist, п., a worshiper of Siva. —
Formed fr. Siva, Shiva, with suff. -ist.
Derivative; Sivaist-ic, Shivaist-ic, adj.

## siwash
siwash, п., an Indian of the northern Pacific coast
of North America. — Chinook, corruption of
"F. sauvage, 'savage'. See savage.
Derivative: siwash, intr. v., to live, esp. to camp
like an Indian.

## six
six, adj. and n. — ME. sex, six, fr. OE. seox, siex,
six, rel. to OS. seks, ON. sex, Dan. seks, Swed.
sex, OFris. sex, MDu. sesse, ses, Du. zes, OHG.,
MHG. sehs, G. sechs, Goth, saihs, 'six', and
cogn. with OI. sas (assimilated fr. sas), Avestic
xshvash, Toch. A sdk, В skas, Arm. vec, Gk.
Ц (dial. Gk. Щ), Alb. gate, L. sex, OSlav.
sesti, Lith. sesi, Olr. si, W. chwech, 'six', OPruss.
uschts, 'sixth'. Cp. hexa-, sex-. Cp. also samite,
senary, sestet, sestine, sextant, Sextus, sice on
dice, siesta.
Derivatives: six, п., six-fold, adj.

## sixain
sixain, п., a stanza of six lines (pros.) — F., fr.
six, 'six', fr. L. sex. See six and cp. sextain.

## sixpence
sixpence, n. — Compounded of six anopence, pi.
of penny.

## sixte
sixte, п., the sixth parry in fencing. — F., fr. OF.,
a var. spelling of siste, 'sixth', fr. L. sextus,
'sixth'. See sixth and cp. tierce, quart, n.

## sixteen
sixteen, adj. — ME., sixtene, fr. OE. sixtyne, six-
tine, fr. six, 'six', and -tyne, -tine, '-Jeen'; rel. to
ON. sextan, Du. zestien, OHG. seh(s)zen,
MHG. sehzehen, G. sechzehn. See six and -teen.
Derivatives: sixteen, п., sixteen-er, n.

## sixteenmo
sixteenmo, п., a book composed of sheets of
sixteen leaves. — From the English reading of L6-
mo, the symbol for L. sexto decimo. See
sextodecimo.

## sixteenth
sixteenth, adj. — Formed with numeral suff. -th
fr. sixteen on analogy of fourth, etc. The OE.
form is sixteoda.
Derivative: sixteenth, n.

## sixth
sixth, adj. — ME. sixte, fr. OE. sixta, rel. to
Goth, saihsta, OHG. sehsto, Du. zesde, MHG.
sehste, G. sechste. Cp. OI. sasthah, Avestic
xshtva-, Toch. A shkasht, В shkaste, Gk. 2κτος,
L. sextus, OSlav. sestu, Lith. sestas, OPruss.
uschts, Olr. sessed, W. chweched, 'sixth'. See
six. For the ending of six-th, which is due to the
analogy of fourth, see numeral suff. -th.
Derivatives: sixth, п., sixth-ly, adv.

## sixtieth
sixtieth, adj. — Formed with numeral suff. -th fr.
sixty, on analogy of fourth, etc. The OE. form is
sixteogoda.
Derivative: sixtieth, n.

## sixty
sixty, adj. — ME., fr. OE. sixtig, rel. to OHG.
seh(s)zug, MHG. sehzig, G. sechzig. See six and
-ty, a suff. denoting tens.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:715 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SIZABLE | 688 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:715 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: sixty, n.

## sizable
sizable, adj., of large size. — Formed fr. size, v.
(see 1st size) with suff. -able.
Derivatives: sizable-ness, п., sizabl-y, adv.

## sizar
sizar, п., a student in the universities Cambridge
and Dublin, who was granted certain
allowances. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. size in the
sense of'ration'.
Derivative: sizar-ship, n.

## size
size, п., 1) quantity, bulk; 2) ration, allowance
(obsol.) — Aphetic for assize in its original sense
'that which is assessed'. Cp. size, 'glue'.
Derivatives: size, tr. and intr. v., siz-ed, adj.,
siz-er, п., siz-ing, n.

## size
size, п., a kind of glue. — It. sisa, assisa, 'painter's
glue, size', prop. fem. pp. of assidere, 'to make
to sit, to settle', fr. L. assidere, 'to sit by', hence
ult. derivatively identical with size, 'bulk'.
Derivatives: size, tr. v., to cover with size, siz-y,
adj.

## sizzle
sizzle, intr. v., to make a hissing sound; п., а
hissing sound. — Of imitative origin. Cp. siss.
Derivatives: sizzl-ing, adj., sizzl-ing-ly, adv.

## sjambok
sjambok, п., a heavy whip. — S. Afr. Du., fr.
Malay chamboq, ult. fr. Pers. chabuq, 'a whip'.
Cp. cbabouk.
Derivative: sjambok, tr. v.

## -sk
-sk, reflexive suff. in words of Danish origin. —
Contracted fr. ON. sik, reflexive pron.
corresponding to Goth, sik, OHG. sih, MHG., G.
sich, 'himself, herself, itself, fr. I.-E. base *se-,
whence also L. si, 'himself, herself, itself; see
sui. The suff. -sk appears e.g. in bask, lit. 'to
bathe oneself, busk, 'to prepare' (intr.)

## skald
skald, п., one of the ancient Scandinavian poets.
— ME., fr. ON. skald, which is of uncertain
origin. Cp. scald, п., 'poet', scold.

## skat
skat, п., a card game. — G. Skat, fr. It. scarto,
'rejection of a card', back formation fr. scartare,
'to reject a card', fr. s- (fr. L. ex) and -cartare,
fr. Late L. carta, 'a leaf of paper'. See 1st ex-
and card, 'piece of pasteboard', and cp. ecarte.

## skate
skate, п., frame fastened to the boot for sliding on
ice. — Back formation fr. skates (whose final s
was mistaken for the pi. ending), fr. Du. schaats-
en, 'skates', fr. OF. eschace (F. echasse), 'stilt',
fr. Frank, 'skatja, which is rel. to Fris. skatja,
'stilt', LG. shake, 'leg', and to MLG. schenke,
OE. scanca, 'leg' (see shank); skate prop, means
'lengthened leg'. For similar back formations
cp. pea and words there referred to.
Derivatives: skate, intr. v., skat-er, п., skat-ing,
n.

## skate
skate, п., an edible fish of the genus Raja. — ON.
skata; of uncertain origin.

## skatol
skatol, skatole, п., a crystalline compound,
C,H,N, found in the feces and urine (chem.) —
Coined from the stem of Gk. σκωρ, gen.
σκατάς, 'dung'; see scatology and 1st -ole and
cp. scoria. The use of the suff. -o! is rather
striking since skatol is neither an oil nor an
alcohol.

## skean
skean, п., a dagger, dirk. — Gael, sgian, 'knife'.

## skean
skean, n. — A var. of skein.

## skean dhu
skean dhu, a small dirk worn by Scottish
Highlanders. — Lit. 'black knife', fr. Gael, sgian,
'knife' (see skean, 'dagger'), and dubh, 'black'.

## skedaddle
skedaddle, intr. v., to run away; п., a running
away (colloq. and slang). — Of unknown
origin.

## skeet
skeet, п., a form of trapshooting. — Prob. derived
fr. ON. skjota, 'to shoot'. See shoot.

## skeet
skeet, п., a scoop used for wetting the saiis of a
yacht. — Of uncertain origin.

## skeg
skeg, п., part of the keel of a boat. — Du. scheg,
schegge, fr. Dan. skjeg. Cp. ON. skaga, 'to jut
out, project'.

## skein
skein, п., a quantity of yarn, wool, etc., doubled
and knotted. — ME. skayne, skeyne, fr. OF.
escagne (F. ecagne), which is of uncertain origin.
Derivative: skein, tr. v.

## skeletal
skeletal, adj., pertaining to the skeleton. — See
skeleton and adj. suff. -al.

## skeleto-
skeleto-, combining form denoting the skeleton.
— See skeleton.

## skeletology
skeletology, п., the study of the skeleton. —
Compounded of skeleto- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:715 COLUMN:2 -->
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## skeleton
skeleton, n. — ModL., fr. Gk. σκελετόν,
'mummy, skeleton', a loan word fr. Syr. sheladdd,
'skeleton', fr. Akkad. shalamdu, shalamtu, prop,
meaning 'the whole (corpse)', fr. shaldmu, 'to be
complete', which is rel. to Heb. shdlam, 'was
complete'; see shalom. See W. Muss-Arnolt in
Transactions of the American Philological
Association, Vol. XXIII, p. 148. The explanation
of Gk. σκελετόν, 'mummy, skeleton', as used
elliptically for σκελετόν σώμα, supposed to
mean 'dried up body' (as if σκελετόν, were the
neut. verbal adj. of σκέλλειν, 'to dry up') is folk
etymology. Cp. endoskeleton, exoskeleton.
Derivatives: skeleton-ic, adj., skeleton-ize, tr. v.,
skeleton-iz-ation, п., skeleton-iz-er, п., skeleton-
У, adj.

## skelluin
skelluin, п., rogue, rascal {archaic or dial.) — Du.
schelm, borrowed fr. G. Schelm, 'rogue, rascal',
fr. MHG. schalme, schelme, schelm, 'carrion,
corpse', later 'rogue', fr. OHG. scalmo, scelmo,
'carrion, corpse*, which is perh. rel. to OE. hold,
'corpse', ON. hold, 'fiesh', and cogn. with Olr.
colainn, 'body, corpse', W. celain, 'corpse'.

## skelp
skelp, tr. and intr. v., to slap; п., a slap. — Of
imitative origin.

## skelp
skelp, п., a flat of iron. — Prob. a derivative of
prec. word. Accordingly the orig. meaning
would have been 'beaten (metal)'.
Derivatives: skelp, tr. v., to turn into skelp,
skelp-er, n.

## skene
skene, n. — A var. of skean.

## skep
skep, п., 1) a kind of basket; 2) a beehive.'— ME.
skeppe, 'skep, skepful', fr. OE. sceppe, 'skepfuP,
fr. ON. skeppa, 'basket, bushel', which is rel. to
OS. skepil, MDu. scepel, Du. schepel, OHG.
sceffil, MHG., G. scheffel, 'bushel', and to OS.
skap, MDu. scap, OHG. scaf, MHG. schaf, G.
Schaff, 'cask, barrel'; fr. I.-E. base *skab-, 'to
work with a stone scraper, to scrape, scratch'.
See shape, п., and cp. skipple.

## skeptic
skeptic, sceptic, adj. — F. sceptique, fr. L. scepti-
cus, fr. Gk. σκεπτικός, 'inquiring, thoughtful,
doubting', which is rel. to σκέπτεσθαι, 'to look
carefully, consider', σκέψις, 'inquiry, doubt',
and—with vowel gradation—to σκοπεϊν, 'to
look at, examine', σκοπός, 'watcher, mark to
shoot at'. See scope and words there referred to.
For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: skeptic, n. (q.v.), skeptic-al,
sceptical, adj., skeptic-al-ly, sceptic-al-ly, adv., skeptic-
al-ness, seeptic-al-ness, п., skeptic-ism,
scepticism, n.

## skeptic
skeptic, sceptic, n. — F. sceptique, fr. L. scepticus.
See prec. word.

## skerry
skerry, п., an isolated rock in the sea. — ON.
sker, rel. to skera, 'to cut, shear'; see shear and
cp. scar, 'reef, cliff. For the relationship
between ON. sker and skera cp. L. rapes, 'rock',
which is rel. to L. rumpere, 'to break, burst, tear,
rend' (see rupestrian and cp. words there referred
to).

## sketch
sketch, n. — Du. schets, fr. It. schizzo (whence
also G. Skizze and F. esquisse) fr. L. schedium,
'an extemporaneous poem', fr. Gk. σχ^έϊιος,
'temporary, extemporaneous', which is related
to σχήμα, .'form, shape, appearance, bearing',
σχεΐν, aor. inf. of ϊχειν, 'to have'. See scheme
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also esquisse.
Derivatives: sketch, tr. and intr. v., sketch-er, п.,
sketch-ing, п., sketch-y, adj., sketch-i-ly, adv.,
sketch-i-ness, n.

## skew
skew, intr. v., to take an oblique direction; tr. v.,
to make oblique. — ME. skewen, fr. ONF.
eskiuwer, escuer, corresponding to OF. eschuer,
eschiver. See eschew.
Derivatives: skew, adj. and п., skew-ed, adj.,
skew-ly, adv., skew-ness, n.

## skewbald
skewbald, adj., marked with spots of white and
some other color — Compounded of the adj.
skew (see prec. word) and bald in its old sense
'white'. Cp. piebald.

## skewer
skewer, п., a pin to fasten meat. — Fr. dial. E.
skiver, 'skewer', which is rel. to Swed. skifer, 'a
slate', and to E. shiver, 'splinter'.
Derivative: skewer, tr. v.

## ski
ski, n. — Norw., fr. ON. skid, 'wooden billet,
snowshoe', which is rel. to OE. scid, 'stick of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:715 COLUMN:3 -->
wood' (whence obsol. E. shide), OHG. skit,
MHG. schit, G. Scheit, 'log', and to OE. scea-
dan, scadanf 'to divide, separate'. See shed, v.,
and cp. skid.
Derivatives: ski, intr. v., ski-er, n.

## skiagram
skiagram, sciagram, п., skiagraph. — See
skiagraphy and -gram.

## skiagraph
skiagraph, sciagraph, п., X-rays photograph. —
See next word and -graph.

## skiagraphy
skiagraphy, sciagraphy, п., photography by X-
rays, radiography. — F. sciagraphie, fr. L. scid-
graphia, fr. Gk. σκιαγραφία, 'a drawing in light
and shade', fr. σκιά, 'shade', and -γραφιά, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. The first element is rel. to
Gk. σκηνή, 'tent, booth, stage', and cogn. with
01. chdya, 'shade', OSlav. sent (for *sksi-ni-s),
'shade', Goth, skeinan, OE. scinan, 'to shine'.
See scene and cp. ascian, amphiscian, antiscians,
Cynosciom. For the second element see -graphy.
Derivatives: sktagraph-ic, sciagraph-ic, adj.,
skiagraph-ic-al, sciagraph-ic-al, adj., skiagraph-
ic-al-ly, skiagraph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## skiametry
skiametry, sciametry, п., study of radiography.
— Lit. 'measurement of shadows', fr. Gk.
σκιά, 'shade, shadow', and -μετρία, fr.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See prec. word and -merry.

## skiascope
skiascope, sciascope, п., an instrument for
measuring the refractive power of the eye. —
Compounded of Gk. σκιά, 'shade, shadow', and
-σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεϊν, 'to look at, examine'.
See skiagraphy and -scope.

## skiascopy
skiascopy, sciascopy, п., examination of the
refractive power of the eye by the skiascope. —
See prec. word and -scopy.

## skid
skid, п., a plank or bar used as a support. — Of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. skid, 'a wooden billet',
and see ski.
Derivatives: skid, intr. and tr. v., skidd-ed, adj.,
skidd-er, п., skidd-ing, n. and adj.

## skiff
skiff, п., a small boat. — F. esquif, fr. It. schifo,
'little boat', fr. OHG. ski/, 'ship'. See ship, which
is a doublet of skiff.
Derivative: skiff, intr. and tr. v.

## skill
skill, n. — ME. skile, skil, fr. ON. skit, 'skill,
discrimination, reason', which is rel. to skilja,
'to separate, distinguish, discriminate', MLG.
schillen, 'to differ', Scheie, 'difference', and to. Ε
shell (q.v.)
Derivatives: skil(l)-ful, adj., skil[f)-ful-ly, adv.,,
skii{J)-ful-ness, п., skil-less, adj.
skil], intr. v., to have understanding; to make a
difference (archaic). — ME. skilen, fr. ON.
skilja. See skill, n.
Derivatives: skill-ed, adj.

## skillet
skillet, п., a frying pan. — ME. skelet, fr. OF.
escuelete, dimin. of escuele (F. icuelle), fr. L.
scutella, 'salver, waiter', dimin. formed fr. L.
scutra, 'a flat tray, dish'. See scuttle, 'a metal
receptacle', and -et.

## skilly
skilly, п., oatmeal broth. — Shortened fr. earlier
skilligalee, a word of uncertain origin-

## skim
skim, tr. and intr. v. — ME. skimmen, prob. fr.
OF. escumer (F. ecumer), fr. escume (F. ёсите),
fr. OHG. scum (MHG. schum, schoum, G.
Schaum); rel. to MDu. schum(e), whence E.
scum (q.v.) For the change of и to / cp. brisk (fr.
F. brusque) and ribbon (fr. F. ruban).
Derivatives: skim, п., skimm-ing, п., skimm-ing-
ly, adv.

## skimmer
skimmer, п., 1) a person or thing that skims; 2) a
utensil used for skimming liquids; 3) any of
various marine birds (genus Rhynchops) — ME.
skemour, skemere, fr. OF. escumoir, 'utensil for
skimming', fr. escumer, 'to skim' (see skim);
partly formed directly from the verb skim with
suff. -er.

## skimmer
skimmer, intr. v., to shimmer. — A var. of
shimmer.

## skimp
skimp, tr. and intr. v., to scrimp. — Prob. a blend
of scamp and scrimp.
Derivatives: skimp-y, adj., skimp-t-ly, adv.
skin.n. — ME. skynn, fr. ON. skinn; rel. to OHG.

## scinten
scinten, MHG., G. schinden, 'to flay, skin', and

## prob. cogn. with Bret
prob. cogn. with Bret, scant, 'scale of fish', Ir.

## scdinim
scdinim, Ί tear, I burst'.
Derivatives: skin, tr. and intr. v., skinn-ed, adj.,

## skinn-er
skinn-er, п., skinn-ery, п., skinn-y, adj.

## skink
skink, п., a kind of lizard. — L. scincus, fr. Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:716 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 689 | SLATE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:716 COLUMN:1 -->
σκίγκος, 'a kind of lizard', which is of uncertain
origin.

## skink
skink, tr. and intr. v., to serve {archaic). — ME.
skinken, fr. MDu. schinken, scfienken, rel. to
OE. scencan, 'to give to drink', OHG. skenken,
MHG., G. schenken, 'to give*. The original
meaning of these verbs was 'to hold in a
slanting position'. See shank and cp. nuncheon.

## skip
skip, intr. and tr. v., to leap. — ME. skippen,
prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. skopa, 'to run',
MSwed. skuppa, dial. Swed. skopa, 'to skip,
leap'.
Derivatives: skip, п., skipper (q.v.), skipp-ing, n.

## skip
skip, п., captain of a team or side. — Shortened
fr. skipper, 'captain of a ship'.

## skip
skip, п., bucket, basket. — A var. of skep.Cp.
ski ρ pet.

## skipper
skipper, п., one who skips. — Formed fr. skip, v.,
with agential surf, -er. Cp. schipperke.

## skipper
skipper, п., captain of a small ship. — ME.
skypper, fr. MDu. (= Du.) schipper, fr. schip,
'ship'. See ship and agential suff. -er.

## skippet

## skirmish
skirmish, n. — ME. skyrmissh, prob. a blend of
1) ME. scarmuch, skarmish, fr. MF. escar(a\-
moche, escar(a)muchet prob. fr. It. scaramuccia,

2) ME. skirmysshen, fr. MF. eskermiss-, escre-
ntiss-, pres. part, stem of eskermir, escremir
(whence F. escrimer), 'to fight with the sword,
fence4, which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG.
skirmen (MHG., G. schirmen), 'to defend,
protect*, which derives fr. OHG. skirm, skerm,
'protection, shield' (whence MHG. schirm, scherm,
of s.m., G. Schirm, 'shelter, protection; screen,
umbrella'). This noun orig. denoted the hide
that covered the shield. It is cogn. with OI.
carman-, Avestic tar man-, 'skin, hide', L. со-
rium, of s.m. It. schermire, OProvenc. escremir,
escrimir, Sp., Port, esgrimir, 'to fence', are also
Teut. loan words. See corium and cp. Seara-
mouch, scrimmage. Cp. also screen.

## skirmish
skirmish, intr. v. — ME. skyrmysshen, prob. a

cia. See skirmish, n.
Derivative: skirmish-er, n.

## skirr
skirr, intr. v., to move quickly. — Of uncertain

## skit

skua, п., a dark-brown gull, a jaeger. — ON.

## skull

## Skupshtina
Skupshtina, п., the parliament of Yugoslavia. —
Serb., lit. 'assembly', fr. skupiti, 'to gather,
meet*, which derives fr. pref. so-, s-, 'with,
together with', and OSlav. кирй, 'heap'. Pref. so-,
s- comes fr. OSlav. su, 'with, together with'
(whence also ORuss. su, Russ. so, s, Bulg. su, s,
Czech se, s, Slovak so, st Pol. ze, z, etc.), which
is rel. to OPruss. san- (pref.), sen (prep.), 'with',
Lith. son-, sa-, Lett, sua-, *with*, OSlav., ORuss.
samu, Bulg. sam, Czech and Slovak sum, etc.,
*(him)self, and cogn. with OI. sam-, 'with',
Gk. όμός, 'one and same', όμοΰ, 'together', OI.
samah, 'even, the same', L. similis, 'like*, Goth.
satna, 'the same', samana, 'together*; see same
and cp. the pref. Sobranje, soviet, sputnik. For
the etymology of OSlav. кирй, 'heap', see henp.

## sky
sky, n. — ME. skie, 'cloud, sky*, fr. ON. sky,
which is ref. to OE. sceo, OS. scio, 'cloud', OE.
scua, scuwa, OHG. scuwo, ON. skuggi,
'shadow', Goth, skuggwa, 'mirror', fr. I.-E. base
*sqeu-, *(s)qewa~, 4o cover', whence also OHG.
scura, later лсшга (whenceMHG. schiur,schiure,
G. Scheuer), 'barn', OI. skunati, skunoti, skauti,
'covers', Arm. ciw, 'roof, Gk. σκύνια,
'eyebrows', σκύλον, σκύλος, 'animal's skin, hide',
L. scutum, 'shield', bb-scurus, 'dark', and perh.
also Goth, skohs, OE. scoh, 'shoe'. Cp. hide,
'skin*, hide, 'to conceal', house, huso, scum, shoe,
shower, skim. Cp. also cutis, equerry, escutcheon,
obscure, scutch, scuttle, 'receptacle', scutum. Cp.
also scum. For the derivatives of base *{s)que-
dh; an enlargement of base *(s)qeu-, 'to cover,
hide*, see custody and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: sky, v., sky-ey, adj., sky-less, adj.

## skyscraper

## skyward

## slab

(q.v.)

sluggish, languid'. See languid and cp. lack,

## Slav
Slav, n. and adj. — G. Slave, fr. ML. Sclavus,
Slavus, fr. MGk. Σκλάβος. See slave.
Derivatives: Slav-ian, Slav-ic, Sfav-isk, adjs.,

ize, tr. v., Slav-iz-ation, n.

## slave
slave, n. — ME. sclave, fr. OF. (— F.) esclave, fr.
ML. Sclavus, Slavus, fr. MGk. Σκλάβος,
σκλάβος, 'slave', prop, 'a slave of Slav descent*,
back formation fr. MGk. Σκλαβηνός,
'pertaining to the Slavs', from the η. οί Σκλαβηνοί
(pi.), 'the Slavs', which was formed—with
inserted κ—fr. OSlav. Sloveninu, 'Slav'. This
sense development arose in the consequence of
the wars waged by Otto the Great and his
successors against the Slavs, a great number of
whom they took captive and sold into slavery.
For sense development cp. OE. wealh, 'slave,
serf', prop, 'foreigner, Briton, Welshman'.
OSlav. Sloveninu is a derivative of OSlav. slovo,
'word', fr. l.-E. base *kleu-, 'to hear', whence
also OI. iravas-, 'praise, glory', Avestic sravah-,
'word', Gk. κλέος, 'fame', L. cluere, 'to hear*,
OE. hlu-d, 'loud'. Sec loud and cp. esclavage,
Slav, Slovak, Slovene. Accordingly the name
Slav lit. means 'speaker*. For sense
development cp. Church Slavic Nemici, 'Germans',
which is rel. to пётй, 'dumb'.
Derivatives: slave, intr. v., slaver, n. (q.v.),
slavery, п., slav-ish, adj., slav-ish-ly, adv., slav-ish-
ness, n.

sleeve, n. — ME. sieve, sleeve, fr. OE. slef slief
slyf rel. to OHG., MHG. sloufen, 'to put on or

MLG. sliipen, Du. sluipen, OFris. slepa, OHG.
sliofan, MHG. sliefen, G. schliefen, Goth, sliu-
pan, 'to slip, glide'. (Cp. G. Schleife, 'bow, loop,

formation fr. MHG. sloufen.) All these words
derive fr. l.-E. base *sleub-, *to slip, slide',
