slutt-ish-ness, n.

## sly
sly, adj. — ME. sleigh, slegh, sleh, fr. ON. slxgr,
'crafty, cunning'; rel. to LG. slu (whence Du.
sluw, Dan. slu, Norw. slu, slug, Swed. slug, G.
schlau), 'cunning, sly'. These words prob. meant
orig. 'able to strike', and are rel. to OE. slean,
Goth, slahan, 'to strike'; see slay, v., and cp.
sleight. For sense development cp. MHG. ver-
slahen, 'to hide, cheat' (orig. 'to put aside by
striking', fr. slaken, 'to strike'), whence G. ver-
schlagen, 'cunning, sly', and schlagfertig, 'ready-
witted', lit. 'ready {fertig) to strike (schlagen)\
Derivatives: sly-ish, adj., sli-ly, sly-ly, adv.,
slyness, n.

## slype
slype, п., a covered passage way between the
transept and chapterhouse {arch.) — Of
uncertain origin.

## smack
smack, п., taste, flavor. — ME. smak, fr. OE.
smsec, 'taste, flavor', related to OFris. smaka,
Du. smaak, OHG., MHG. smac, G. Geschmack,
and cogn. with Lith. smaguriai, 'dainties',
smaguris, 'forefinger, index', prop, 'the nibbling
(finger)'.

## smack
smack, inir. v., to have a smack of, to taste of. —
ME. smaken, fr. smak, 'taste*. See prec. word.

## smack
smack, п., a sharp sound. — Of imitative origin.
Cp. Swed. smak, 'slap', Dan. smsek, 'smack,
rap', and Lith. smagiu, smogiau, smdgti, *to
strike, knock down, whip', which all are
imitative.

## smack
smack, adv., suddenly. — Lit. 'with a smack,
sharply'. See prec. word.

## smack
smack, tr. v., to part (the lips) noisily; to slap;
intr. v., to make a sharp noise. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. Du smakken, 'to fling down', Dan.
smsekke, 'slam', and see smack, 'a sharp sound'.
See also smack, 'a sailing vessel'.
Derivatives: smack-er, п., smack-ing, n. and
adj., smack-ing-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:719 COLUMN:2 -->

## smack
smack, п., a single-masted sailing vessel. — Du.
smak, fr. MDu. smakke (whence also LG.
smak, smakke, G. Schmacke, Dan. smakke,
Swed. smack, F. semaque, Sp. zumaca, It. se~
macca), fr. MDu. and MLG. smacken, 'to
slap' (the vessel was so called from the noise
made by its sails). See smack, 'to slap'.
Derivatives: smack-ful, adj., smack-ing, adj.

## small
small, adj. — ME. smal, fr. OE. smxl, 'narrow,
slender; small', rel. to OS., Dan., Swed., MDu.,
Du., OHG., MHG. smal, G. schmal, 'narrow',
Goth, smalista, 'smallest', ON. smali, 'small
cattle, sheep', and cogn. with Gk. μήλον,
'sheep, goat' (prop, 'small cattle'), Arm. mal,
'sheep, ram', Olr., OCo., W. mil, 'a small
animal', OSlav. malu, 'small', and prob. also with
L. malus, 'bad' (prop, 'insignificant, of inferior
value'). Cp. mal- and words there referred to.
Derivatives: small, п., small-ish, adj., smalf-
ness, n.

## small age
small age, п., wild celery. — ME. smalege, fr.
earlier smalache, which is compounded of smal,
'small', and F. ache, 'parsley', fr. L. apium. See
small and ache, 'parsley'.

## smallpox
smallpox, n. — Fr. earlier small pokkes, 'small
pox'; so called in contradistinction to the 'great
pox', i.e. syphilis. See small and pox. For sense
development cp. F. petite verole, 'smallpox'.

## smalt
smalt, n. — MF. (— F.), fr. smalto, which is of
Teut. origin. Cp. OHG., MHG. smalz, G.
Schmalz, 'melted fat', OHG. smelzan, MHG.
smelzen, G. schmelzen), 'to melt', and see smelt.
Cp. also enamel.
Derivative: smalt-er, n.

## smaragd
smaragd, п., an emerald. — ME1, smaragde, fr.
OF. smaragde, fr. L. smaragdus, fr. Gk. σμάρα-
■γδος. See emerald.

## smaragdite
smaragdite, п., a green variety of amphibole. —
F., formed with subst. sufl*. -ite fr. Gk. σμάρα-
γδος, 'emerald'. See prec. word.

## smart
smart, intr. v. — ME. smerten, fr. OE. smeortan,
rel. to MDu. smerten, smarten, Du. smarten,
OHG. smerzan, MHG. smerzen, G. schmerzen,
'to pain*, orig. to bite', rel. to LG. murten, 'to
fall to pieces, to decay', and cogn. with Gk.
σμερδνός, σμερδαλέος, 'terrible, fearful', lit.
'rubbing, crushing', OI. mardayati, 'grinds,
rubs, crushes', mardati, mrdnati, 'presses, rubs',
Arm. mart, 'combat, fight'. L. mordere, 'to
bite', Lett, merdet, 'to waste, emaciate; to starve
(tr.); fr. I.-E. base *(s)mer-d-, a -ίί-enlargement
of base *(s)mer-, 'to rub, pound, consume, wear
away, exhaust, worry; to be consumed', whence
Gk. μαραίνει, 'to waste away'. Cp. smart, n.
and adj. Cp. also almuerzo, amaranth, ambrosia,
amrita, mar, marasmus, marble, marcid,
marmoreal, ' morbid, morceau, mordant, mordent,
morsel, mortal, mortar, murder, murrain, pre-
morse, remorse, smorzando.
Derivatives: smart, adj. (q.v.), smart, adv.,
smart-ing, adj., smart-ing-ly, adv., smart-en, tr.
v., smart-y, adj.

## smart
smart, n. — ME. smert, fr. OE. smeart, rel. to
MDu. smerte, smarte, Du. smart, OHG. smerzo,
MHG. smerze, G. Schmerz, 'pain', and to OE.
smeortan, 'to smart, pain'. See smart, v.

## smart
smart, adj. — ME. smerte, 'painful', fr. OE.
smeart. See smart, n.
Derivatives: smart-ly, adv., smart-ness, n.

## smash
smash, tr. and intr. v. and n. — A blend of
smack and mash.
Derivatives: smash, adv. (colloq.), smash-age,
п., smash-er, n. smash-ery, п., smash-ing, adj.,
smash-ing-ly, adv.

## smarter
smarter, intr. v., to talk with a superficial
knowledge. — ME. smateren, 'to make a noise', of
imitative origin. Cp. Swed. smattra, 'to crackle'.
Derivatives: smatter-er, п., smatter-ing, n. and
adj., smatter-ing-ly, adv., smatter-y, adj.

## smear
smear, n. — ME. smere, fr. OE. smeoru, smeru,
'fat, grease', rel. to OS., OHG. smero, ON.
smjor, smor, Dan. smer, Swed. smor, MDu.
smere, Du. smeer, MHG. smer, G. Schmer,
'grease, fat', Goth, smairpr, 'fatness', fr. I.-E.
*smeru-, 'grease', whence also Gk. μύρον,
'unguent, balsam', μυρ£ζειν, σμυρίζειν, 'to rub with
ointment' (but not σμύρι,ς, 'emery', see emery),
Toch. B. smare, 'smooth', Olr. smi(u)r,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:719 COLUMN:3 -->
'marrow', W. mer, of s.m., and perh. also Lith.
smarsas, 'fat'. Cp. Myristica, Amyris, and the
first element in myrobalan, Myroxylon. Cp. also
medulla.
Derivatives: smear, v. (q.v.), smear-y, adj.,
smear-less, adj., smear-i-ness, n.

## smear
smear, tr. v. — ME. smeren, fr. OE. smervan,
smiervan, rel. to ON. smyrva, smyrja, Dan.
smere, Swed. smorja, Du. smeren, OHG. smir-
wen, MHG. smir(we)n, G. schmieren, 'to smear',
and to OE. smeoru, smeru, 'fat, grease'. See
smear, n.
Derivatives: smear-ed, adj., smear-er, n.

## smectic
smectic, adj., purifying. — L. smecticus,
'cleansing', fr. Gk. σμηκτικός, fr. σμηκτός, verbal
adj. of σμήχειν, 'to cleanse*. See smegma and
-ic.

## smectite
smectite, п., a claylike mineral. — Gk. σμηκτίς,
'fuller's earth', fr. σμήχεω, 'to cleanse'. See
prec. word and subst. suff. -ite.

## smee
smee, n. — A var. of smew,

## smegma
smegma, п., soapy matter secreted from the
glands. — L., fr. Gk. σμηγμα, 'soap', fr.
σμήχει,ν, 'to wipe off, wipe, clean, cleanse', fr.
σμάειν, Att. σμήν, 'to rub, wipe', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)mei-, 'to rub', whence also Czech smetana,
'cream', MDu., MHG. smant, of s.m., and
E. smite (q.v.) For the ending see suff. -ma.

## smell
smell, tr. and intr. v. — ME. smellen, smullen,
not found in OE., rel. to LG. smelen, Du.
smeulen, 'to smolder', and to E. smolder (q.v.)
Deriva tives: smell-able, adj., smell-ed, adj.,
smell-er, п., smell-ing, n.

## smell
smell, n. — ME. smel, smul, fr. smellen, smullen.
See smell, v.
Derivatives: smell-ful, adj., smell-y, adj.

## smelt
smelt, tr. and intr. v., to melt. — Prob. fr. MDu.
(= Du.) smelten, which is rel. to OHG. smelzan,
MHG. smelzen, G. schmelzen, Dan. smelte,
Swed. smalta, Norw. smelta, 'to melt', and to
OE. melta, 'to melt*. See melt and cp. smalt.
Derivatives: smelt-er, п., smelt-ery, n.

## smelt
smelt, п., a small edible fish. — ME., fr. OE., rel.
to Du., Dan. smelt, "smelt', Norw. smelta.
'whiting', and to E. smelt, 'to melt'; the fish was
called after its soft fiesh. See prec. word and cp.
smolt.

## smew
smew, п., seaduck. — Rel. to the first element in
Du. smient, Fris. sment, 'smew'. The second
element in these words is rel. to ON. ond, OE.
aened, OHG. anut, 'duck', and cogn. with L.
anas, of s.m. (see Anas).

## Smilacaceae
Smilacaceae, n. pi., a family of plants (pot.) —
ModL., formed fr. L. smflax, smilacis,
'bindweed'. See smilax and -aceae.

## smilacaceous
smilacaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## Smilacina
Smilacina, п., a genus of plants, the false
Solomon's seal (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. smilax, gen.
smilacis. See next word.

## smilax
smilax, п., 1) (cap.) a genus of plants, the green
brier (bot.); 2) a twining vine of East Africa.
— L. smilax, 'bindweed', fr. Gk. σμΐλαξ, which
is rel. to μΐλαξ, of s.m.

## smile
smile, intr. and tr. v. — ME. smilen, rel. to OE.
smerian, 'to laugh at', Dan. smile, Swed.,
Norw. smila, LG. smilen, OHG. smieron, MHG.
smielen, smieren, 'to smile',fr. I.-E. base *(s)mei-,
*(s)mi-, *to smile, to be astonished*, whence also
L- mints (for *smei-ros), 'wonderful'. See
miracle and cp. smirk.
Derivatives: smile, п., smile-ful, adj.,
smile-fulness, п., smil-er, п., smil-ing, adj., smil-ing-ly,
adv., smil-ing-ness, n.

## smirch
smirch, tr. v., to soil. — A blend of smear and OF.
esmorcher, esmorcer, 'to torment', orig. 'to bite;
to'cause to bite'. OF. esmorcer is compounded
of pref. es- (fr. L. ex) and L. morsus, pp. of
mordere, 'to bite*. See 1st ex- and morsel and cp. F.
amercer, 'to bait', fr. VL. *admordere, which
corresponds to L. admordere, 'to bite at', fr.
ad- and mordere.
Derivative: smirch, n.

## smirk
smirk, intr. v., to smile affectedly. — ME. smir-
ken, fr. OE. smearcian, smercian; formed fr.
I.-E. base *(s)mei-, *(s)mi-, 'to smile' (see
smile), with imensive suff. -k. The same suff.
appears in the verbs lurk, stalk, talk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:720 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 693 | SNATH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:720 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: smirk, n.

## smite
smite, tr. and intr. v. — ME. smiten, fr. OE.
smitan, 'to daub, smear*, rel. to Swed., Norw.,
smita, Dan. smide, 'to smear, fling', OFris.
smita, MLG., MDu. smiten, 'to cast, fling', Du.
smijten, 'to throw, fling', OHG. smitan, *to rub,
strike', MHG. smiten, 'to smear, cast, fling',
G. schmeifien, 'to cast, fling', Goth. Ы-
smeitan, ga-smeitan, 'to spread, smear', fr.
*smeid-, -(/-enlargement of I.-E. base *sme\i)-,
'to smear, rub'. The unenlarged base *(s)mei-
appears in Gk. σμάω, σμην, 'to anoint, smear,
rub, wipe, cleanse', σμήμα, 'unguent', σμήχειν,
'to clear off, soap, purge*, L. macula for *(s)met-
la, 'spot, mark'; cp. macula, mackle, mail,.
'armor', smectic, smectite, smegma. Cp. also
mission. The original meaning of base *(s)me(i)-t
prob. was 'to throw', orig. 'to throw (mud) at
the wall', whence developed the secondary
meaning 'to besmear, rub'.
Derivatives: smite, п., smit-er, n.

## smith
smith, n. — ME., fr. OE. smidt rel. to OS. smith,
ON. smidr, Dan., Swed. smed, OFris. smith,
OHG. smid, MHG. smit, G. Schmied, Goth.
-smipa in aiza-smipa, 'coppersmith', and to
OHG. smida, 'metal*, smeidar, 'worker in
metal*, fr. I.-E. base *smei-, *smi-, 'to carve, cut',
whence also Gk. σμίλη, 'knife, graving tool,
chisel', σαινύη, *a two-pronged hoe or
mattock'.

## smith
smith, tr. v. — ME. smithen, fr. OE. smidian, fr.
smid. See smith, n.
Derivatives: smith-er, п., smith-ery, п., smithy
(q.v.)

## smithereens
smithereens, n. pi., fragments. — Ir. smidirin,
dimin. of smiodar, 'fragment', which is of
uncertain origin. For the ending cp. colleen.

## smithite
smithite, п., a silver sulfantimonite (mineral.) —
Named after the English scientist C.F. Herbert
Smith (died in 1953). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## smithsonite
smithsonite, п., a zinc carbonate (mineral.) —
Named after James Smithson (1765-1829),
founder of the Smithsonian Institute at
Washington, D.C. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## smithy
smithy, n. — ME., fr. ON. smidja, fr. smidr,
'smith'; rel. to OE. smidde, OHG. smitta,
MHG. smitte, G. Schmiede. See smith, n. and
subst. suff. -y.

## smitten
smitten, pp. of smite. — ME. smiten, fr. OE. ge~
smiten, pp. of smitan. See smite,

## smock
smock, п., a loose overgarment. — ME. smok, fr.
OE smoc(c), rel. to ON. smokkr, OHG. smoccho,
'smock', and to OE. smugan, 'to creep into',
ON. smiuga, 'to creep through a narrow
opening', Du. smuigen, MHG. smiegen, G. schmie-
gen, 'to cling to, press close, nestle' (whence
the intensive verbs MHG. smucken, resp. G.
schmucken, 'to adorn*), fr. I.-E. base *smeugh-,
'to press', whence also OSlav. smykati se, 'to
creep', Lett, smaugs, 'slender, slim, svelte*. Cp.
smug, smuggle.
Derivatives: smock, tr. and intr. v., smock-ing,
n.

## smog
smog, n. (U.S.A.) — A blend formed—after
Lewis Carrol's example—from smoke and fog.

## smoke
smoke, n. — ME., fr. OE. smoca, 'to smoke*, rel.
to MLG., MDu. smooc, Du. smook, 'smoke',
MHG. smouch, G. Schmauch, and to OE. smeo-
can, 'to smoke', fr. I.-E. base *smeug(h)-,
*smeuqh-, 'to smoke; smoke', whence also Arm.
mux (gen. mxoy), 'smoke', Gk. σμΰχειν, 'to
burn with a smoldering fiame', Lith. smaugiu,
smaugti, 'to choke' (with smoke), Olr. much,
W. mwg, 'smoke*.
Derivatives: smoke-less, adj., smoke-less-ly,
adv., smoke-less-ness, п., smok-y, adj., smok-i-
ly, adv., smok-i-ness, n.

## smoke
smoke, intr. and tr. v. — ME. smoken, fr. OE.
smocian, fr. smoca, 'smoke', Cp. OE. smeocan,
smiecan, 'to smoke*, MLG., MDu. smoken, Du.
smoken, G. schmauchen, of s.m., and see smoke,
n.
Derivatives: smok-er, п., smok-ing, adj. and n.

## smolder
smolder, smonlder, intr. v., to burn without flame.
— ME. smolderen, prob. dissimilated fr. smorth-
eren. See smother, v.
Derivative: smolder, smoulder, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:720 COLUMN:2 -->

## smolt
smolt, п., a salmon in its second year. — Prob. in
gradational relationship to smelt, name of a
fish.

## smooth
smooth, adj. — ME. smothe, fr. OE. smod, in
gradational relationship to smede, whence
ME. smethe (whencedial, smeeth), 'smooth'; of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: smooth, tr. and intr. v., n. and
adv., smooth-en, tr. and intr. v., smooth-er, п.,
smooth-ish, adj., smooth-ly, adv., smooth-ness, n.

## smorzando
smorzando, adj., becoming slower (musical
direction). — It., lit. 'becoming reduced in intensity',
gerund of smorzare, 'to reduce in. intensity, to
dull (a sound)', fr. pref. s- (fr. L. ex, 'out of,
from'), and morte, 'death' (fr. L. mortem, ace.
of mors). — See 1st ex- and mortal.

## smote
smote, past tense of smite. — ME. smoot, fr. OE.
smdt, past tense of smitan. See smite.

## smother
smother, п., thick, suffocating smoke, dust, etc.
— ME., fr. earlier smorther, fr. OE. smorian, 'to
choke, suffocate', rel. to LG. smoren, of s.m.
(whence G. schmoren, 'to stew'). Cp. smolder.
Derivatives: smother-y, adj., smother-i-ness, n.

## smother
smother, tr. and intr. v., to suffocate. — ME.
smotheren, fr. earlier smortheren, fr. smorther.
See prec. word.
Derivatives: smother-ation, п., smother-er, п.,
smother-ing, adj., smother-ing-ly, adv.

## smoulder
smoulder, n. — A var. of smolder.

## smouse
smouse, smonch, п., a Jew (slang.) — Du. smous,
fr. G. Schmus, 'talk', fr. G. Slang schmuofi, fr.
Yiddish schmuofi, fr. Heb. shemu'oth, pi. of
sh mvta , 'report, news', fr. shama\ 'he heard'.
See Shema.

## smriti
smriti, п., inspiration, tradition; the second class
of the shastras (Hindu law). — OI. sm[tik, 'that
which is remembered', rel. to smarati,
'remembers', Avestic maraiti, of s.m., fr. I.-E. base
*(s)mer-, 'to care for, remember, be anxious
about', whence also Gk. μέριμνα, 'care,
thought', L. memor, 'mindful, remembering',
Goth, maurnan, OE. murnan, 'to be anxious
for*. See memory and cp. words there referred
to.

## smudge
smudge, n. and tr. and intr. v. — ME. smogen,
"to smear'; a later var. of smutch; related to
smut (q.v.)
Derivatives: smudge, tr. and intr. v., smudg-ed,
adj., smudg-ed-ly, adv., smudg-er, n.

## smug
smug, adj. — LG. smuk, 'neat, smart, trim', fr.
MLG., fr. smucken, 'to adorn', which is rel. to
MHG. smucken, of s.m. See smock and cp. next
word.
Derivatives: smug, п., smugg-ery, п., smugg-ish,
adj., smugg-ish-ness, п., smug-ly, adv.,
smugness, n.

## smuggle
smuggle, tr. and intr. v. — LG. smuggeln, rel. to
Dan. smugle, Norw. smugla, Swed. smuggla,
Norw. smokla, Du. smokkelen, 'to smuggle',
and to OE. smugan, 'to creep'. See smock
and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: smuggl-er, п., smuggl-ing, n.

## smut
smut, п., 1) soot; 2) smudge. — LG. smutt, rel.
to MHG. smuz, 'grease, dirt*, G. Schmutz,
'dirt', MHG. smutzen, G. schmutzen, 'to make
dirty', ME. smoten, bi-smoteren, of s.m, See
mother, 'dregs', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: smut, tr. and intr. v., smutt-er, п.,
smutt-y, adj., smutt-i-ly, adv., smutt-i-ness, n.

## smutch
smutch, n. and tr. v. — See smudge.
Derivative: smutch-y, adj.

## snack
snack, intr. v., 1) to snatch something with the
teeth {dial); 2) to lunch; tr. v., to seize by
snatching (chiefly Scot.) — ME. snaken, fr.
MDu. snacken, 'to seize, snatch'. See snatch and
cp. snack.

## snack
snack, п., 1) a share; 2) a light meal. — ME.
snake, fr. snaken. See snack, v.

## snaffle
snaffle, п., a kind of bridle bit. — Prob. fr. Du.
snavel, 'beak; horse's muzzle', which is rel. to
OFris. snavel, 'mouth', OHG. snabul, MHG.
snavel, G. Schnabel, 'beak; face', MLG., MDu.
nebbe, 'beak', OE. nebb. ON. nef, 'beak, nose',
Du. sneb, 'beak*, ON. snipa, 'snipe', fr. I.-E.
base *snab-, 'beak; to snatch with the beak, to
snap', whence also Lith. snupas, 'beak, bill*. Cp.
neb and words there referred to.
Derivative: snaffle, tr. v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:720 COLUMN:3 -->

## snafu
snafu, (Mil. Slang) adj., in confusion; п.,
confusion ; tr. v., to throw into confusion. — Formed,
from the initials of the words situation normal
flll/ouled ир.

## snag
snag, п., a sharp projection. — Of Scand. origin;
cp. dial. Norw. snag, 'a projecting point;
stump, spike', ON. snagi, 'clothes peg1.
Derivatives: snag, tr. v., saagg-ed, adj., snagg-
er, п., snagg-y, adj.

## snail
snail, n. — ME., fr. OE. snxgel, snegel, snxgl,
rel. to OS. snegil, ON. snigill, MHG. snegel,
dial. G. Schnegel, OHG. snecko, MHG.
snecke, G. Schnecke, 'snail', ON. snakr, snokr,
OE. snaca, 'snake', fr. I.-E. base *sneg-, *sneq-,
'to creep', whence also OHG. snahhan, 'to creep',
Olr. snaighim, *i creep', Lith. snake, 'snail'.
Cp. snake, sneak, snorkel.
Derivatives: snail, v., snail-ery, п., snail-ish,
adj., snail-ish-ly, adv., snail-like, adj., snail-y,
adj.

## snake
snake, n. — ME., fr. OE. snaca, rel. to ON.
snakr, snokr, 'snake', Swed. snok, MLG. snake
(whence G. Schnake), 'ring snake'; lit. 'the
creeping animal', fr. I.-E. base *sneg-, *sneq-, 'to
creep'. See snail and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: snake, tr. and intr. v., snak-ery, п.,
snak-ing, adj. and п., snak-ish, snak-y, adjs.

## snap
snap, tr. and intr. v. — Du. snappen, fr. MDu.,
rel. to MHG. snappen, G. schnappen, fr. I.-E.
base *snab-, 'beak; to snatch with the beak, to
snap', whence also OFris., MDu. snavel, 'beak,
bill". See snaffle and cp. scimapper, schnapps.
Derivatives: snap, п., adj. and adv. snapp-er, п.,
snapp-'mg, adj., snapp-ish, adj., snapp-ish-ly,
adv., snapp-ish-ness, п., snapp-y, adj., snapp-i-ly,
adv., snapp-i-ness, n.

## snaphance
snaphance, п., I) an armed marauder (obsol.); 2)
a kind of flintlock. — Fr. Du. snaphaan,
'musket, firelock', lit. 'a snapping cock*. See snap
and hen.

## snapper
snapper, п., 1) a person or animal that snaps; 2)
any of a group of seafish. — Formed fr. the
verb snap with agential suff. -er. Cp. schnapper.

## snare
snare, n. — ME., fr. OE. sneare, fr. ON. snara,
'snare, noose, halter', rel. to MDu. snare, Du.
snaar, OHG., MHG. snare, and in gradational
relationship to MDu., Du. snoer, OHG., MHG.
snuor, G. Schnur, 'noose, cord'. All these words
are derivatives of I.-E. base *(s)ner-, 'to turn,
twist, bind together', whence also OHG. narwa,
MHG, narwe, G. Narbe, 'a scar*, orig.
'contraction of the skin over a wound', Lith. nuras,
'loop', nerti, 'to thread (a needle)', nar-νά, 'cell
of the queen bee', Lett, nars, nare, 'ferrule'. Cp.
the related base *(s)ner-q-, whence Gk. νάρκη,
'cramp, numbness', Arm. nergew, 'fine, thin,
tender, slim', prop, 'twisted up, shriveled up'
Cp. snarl, ensnare. Cp. also narcotic, narrow.
Derivatives: snare, tr. v., snar-er, п., snare-less,
adj., snar-ing-ly, adv.

## snark
snark, n.', an imaginary creature. — Coined (as a
blend of snake and shark) by Lewis Carrol (pen
name for Charles L. Dodgson) in The Hunting
of the Snark.

## snarl
snarl, intr. and tr.'v., to growl. — Freq. of earlier
snar, which is related to MDu., MHG. snarren,
G. schnarren, 'to rattle', ME. sneren, 'to scorn',
MHG. snurren, G. schnurren, 'to hum, buzz',
from the I.-E. imitative base *sner-, *snur-. Cp.
sneer, snore, snort.
Derivatives: snarl, п., snarl-er, п., snarl-ing, adj.,
snarl-ing-ly, adv., snarl-ish, adj., snarl-y, adj.

## snarl
snarl,-п., tangle. — Formed fr. snare with dimin.
suff. -le.
Derivatives: snarl, tr. and intr. v., snarl-y, adj.

## snatch
snatch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. snacchen, snecchen,
rel. to MDu. snacken, Du. snakken, 'to seize,
snatch; to gasp'. Cp. snack, sneck.
Derivatives: snatch, п., snatch-ing, adj., snatch-
ing-ly, adv., snatch-y, adj., snatch-i-ly, adv.

## snath
snath, also snathe, п., scythe, shaft. — ME.
snede, fr. OE. snxd, 'morsel', lit. 'something
cut off", from the stem of snidan, 'to cut', which
is rel. to OS. snithan, ON. snida, OFris. snftha,
MDu. sniden, Du. snijden, OHG. snidan, MHG.
sniden, G. schnp.iden, Goth, sneipan, 'to cut', fr.
I.-E. base *sneit-, 'to cut', whence also Czech
snet, 'bough, branch*, Ir. sneid, 'small', lit. 'cut

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:721 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SNEAK | 694 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:721 COLUMN:1 -->
short'. Ср. schnitzel, snick and snee and the
second element in specktioncer.

## sneak
sneak, intr.. and tr. v. — Related to OE. snican,
ME. sniken, 'to creep, crawl', and to E. snail,
snake.
Derivatives: sneak, п., sneak-er, п., sneak-ing,
adj., sneak-ing-ly, adv., sneak-ing-ness, п.,

## sneak-ish
sneak-ish, adj., sheak-ish-ly, adv., sneak-ish·
ness, п., sneak-y, adj.

## sneck
sneck, п., latch or catch of a door or window
{chiefly Scot, and dial. English). — ME. snekke,
snekk, rel. to snecchen, snacchen, 'to snatch'.
See snatch and cp. snack.
Derivatives: sneck, tr. and intr. v., .sneck-er, n.

## sneer
sneer, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sneren, 'to scorn',
rel. to Dan. snserre, 'to grin like a dog', MDu,,
MHG. snarren, 'to rattle'. See snarl and cp.
words there referred to.
Derivatives: sneer, п., sneer-er, n,.sneer-ful, adj.,
sneer-ful-ness, п., sneer-ing, adj., sneer-ing-ly,
adv., sneer-y, adj.

## sneeze
sneeze, intr. v. — ME. snesen, assimilated fr. ME.

## fnesen
fnesen, fr. OE. fneosan, which is rel. to MDu.

## fniesen
fniesen, Du. fniezen, 'to sneeze', ON. fnysa, 'to
snort', and to ON. hnjdsa, Swed. nysa, 'to
sneeze', MDu. niesen, Du. niezen, OHG. niosan,
MHG., G. niesen, 'to sneeze'; of imitative
origin.These words are not cognate with Gk. πνεΐν
'to breathe', which, however, is also of
imitative origin.
Derivatives: sneeze, п., sneez-er, p., sneez-ing,
п., sneez-y, adj.

## snell
snell, п., a short line of gut. — Of uncertain origin.

## snell
snell, adj., quick, nimble {dial.) — ME. snel, snell,
fr. OE. snel, snell, 'brave, quick, active, strong',
rel. to OS. snel, snell, 'fresh, vigorous', MDu.
snel, snell, Du. snel, 'lively, quick', OHG.,
MHG. snel, snell, 'brave, quick, strong', G.
schnell, 'quick', ON. snjaltr, 'bold, able, valiant'.
It. snello, 'quick', is a Teut. loan word.

## snick
snick, tr. v., to cut. — Prob. back formation fr,
snick and snee.
Derivative: snick, a small cut.

## snick and snee
snick and snee, also snicker snee, intr. v., to fight
with knives. — For stick ami snee (the st-of
stick having been assimilated to the sn- of snee),
fr. Du. steken en snijden, 'to stab and cut'. See
stick and snath.

## snicker
snicker, intr. v., to laugh in a partly suppressed
manner; to giggle; п., a half-suppressed laugh;
a giggle. — Of imitative origin. Cp. snigger.

## snide
snide, adj., spurious; mean; base; п., a snide
person or thing. — Of uncertain origin.

## Snider
Snider, п., a kind of rifle. — Named after its
inventor, the American Jacob Snider (died in
1866).

## sniff
sniff, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative- origin. Cp.
snuff, snuffie, snivel.
Derivatives: Sniff, п., sniff-er, п., sniff-ing, adj.,
sniff-ing-ly, adv., sniff-ish, adj., sniff-ish-ness, n.
sniffing valve. — The first word is pres. part, of
snift, a dialectal form of sniff.

## snigger
snigger, intr. v. and n. — A var. of snicker.
Derivatives: snigger-er, п., snigger-ing, adj.,
shigger-ing-ly, adv.

## sniggle
sniggle, intr. v., to fish for eels. — Formed fr.
dial, snig (fr. ME. snygge), 'eeP, with verbal
suff. -le.

## snip
snip, tr. and intr. v. — Derived from, or rel. to,
Du. snippen, 'to snap', which is of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: snip, п., 1) a small piece nipped
off; 2) a tailor {archaic), snipp-ing,· n.

## snipe
snipe, n. — ME., fr. ON. -snipa (in myri-snipa,
lit. 'moor snipe'), which is rel. to OS. sneppa,
MDu. snippe, Du. snip, OHG. snepfa, MHG.
snepfe, G. Schnepfe, 'snipe', and to OFris.,
MDu. snavel, OHG. snabul, 'beak'. The bird is
called after its long beak. See snaffle.
Derivatives: snipe, intr. and tr. v., snip-er, п.,
snip-ish, adj.

## snippet
snippet, п., a small fragment. — Formed fr. the
noun snip (see snip) with the dimin. suff. -et.
•Derivative: snippet-y, adj.

## snitch
snitch, п., 1) the nose; 2) an informer. — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: snitch, intr. and tr. v., snitch-er, n.

## snite
snite, tr. v., to blow the nose; intr. v., to blow

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:721 COLUMN:2 -->
(the nose) {Scot, and dial.)—ME. sniten, fr. OE.
snytan, rel. to ON. snyta, Swed. snyta, Dan.
snyde, MDu. snuten, Du. snuiten, OHG. snuzen,
MHG. sniuzen, G. schneuzen, 'to blow one's
nose', and to E. snot, snoot, snout (qq.v.)

## snivel
snivel, intr. v., to run at the nose. — ME. sne-
velen, snivelen, fr. OE. *snyflan (whence snyflung,
'running of the nose'), fr. snofl, 'mucus of the
nose'; of imitative origin. Cp. sniff, snuff,
snuffle.
Derivatives: snivel, п., snivel-ed, adj., snivel-er,
п., snivel-ing-, п., snivel-y, adj.

## snob
snob, n. — Of uncertain origin. The original
meaning of this word was 'cobbler's
apprentice*. Ernest Weekley in his Etymological
Dictionary of Modern English, 1369 s.v. snob
compares snip, 'a tailor', and suggests that snob is
rel. to the verb snub in its primary sense 'to cut
short'.
Derivatives: snobb-ery, п., snobb-ish, adj.,
snobb-ish-ly, adv., snobb-ish-ness, п., snobb-ism,
n.

## snood
snood, п., band, fillet. — OE. snod, rel. to Swed.
snod{d), 'string, cord', and cogn. with Lett.
sndte, 'a linen cover', Olr. snathe, 'thread', fr.
I.-E. base *{s)ne-, 'to spin, sew with a needle'.
See needle and cp. words there referred to.

## snook
snook, п., name of various sea fishes. — Du.
snoek, 'pike, snook', fr. MDu. snoec, 'pike'.

## snook
snook, intr. v., to smell, sniff {Scot.) — Of
imitative origin. Cp. MHG. snouken, *to smell, sniff',
whence the German verb schnokern, 'to snuffie*.
Derivative: snook, n.
snooker pool. — Of uncertain origin.

## snoop
snoop, intr. v., to pry; tr. v., to pry into. — Du.
snoepen, 'to eat something on the sly, to eat
sweets', of imitative origin.
Derivatives: snoop-er, п., snoop-y, adj.

## snoot
snoot, п., face, grimace. — ME. snute, rel. to
MLG. snute, 'snout', and to E. snout (q.v.)
Derivatives: snoot, tr. and intr. v., snoot-y, adj.

## snooze
snooze, intr. v., to doze; п., a short sleep {colloq.)
— Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: snooz-er, п., snooz-y, adj.

## snore
snore, intr. and tr. v. — ME. snoren, rel. to
MLG., MDu., MHG. snarren, G. schnarren, 'to
rattle*, Du. snorren, MHG. snurren, G. schnur-
ren, 'to hum, buzz, drone', from the I.-E.
imitative base *sner-, *snur-. Cp. sneer. Cp. also
Du. snorken, MHG. snarchen, G. schnarchen,
Swed. snarka, dial. Norw. snerka, 'to snore',
Lett, snirgudt, *to sob, to spit like a goose',
Lith. snargtys, Lett, snurgalas, 'mucus' (prop,
'that which rattles'), which are g- enlargements
of the imitative base above mentioned. Cp.
next word. For other enlargements of the same
base see snarl, snort.
Derivatives: snore, п., snor-er, п., snor-ing, adj.,
snor-ing-ly, adv.

## snorkel
snorkel, п., a device for submarines. — G.
Schnorchel, 'air intake, snort, snorkel', fr. dial.
G., 'snout1, fr. schnorchen, 'to snore', a
collateral form of G. schnarchen, 'to snore'. See snore.

## snort
snort, intr. and tr. v. — ME. snorten, fr. LG.
snorten, which is rel. to ME. snoren, 'to snore'.
See snore.
Derivatives: snort, п., snort-er, п., snort-ing,
adj., snort-ing-ly, adv., snort-y, adj.

## snot
snot, п., mucus from the nose {vulg.) — ME., fr.
OE. gesnot, rel. to OFris. snotta, MLG., MDu.
snotte, MDu., Du. snot, MLG. snute, and to
next word.
Derivatives: snot, tr. and intr. v., snott-er,n.,
snott-y, adj.

## snout
snout, n. — ME. snute, snoute, rel. to MLG.
snute, Du. snuit, G. Schnauze, Norw. snut, Dan.
snude, 'snout', ON. snyta, OE. snytan, OHG.
snuzen, 4o blow the nose', prop, 'to drip
mucus', fr. I.-E. base *sneu-, 'to flow', whence also
Mir. snuad, 'river', Gk. νέειν (fut. νεύσομαι),
'to swim'. Base *sneu-, is rel. to base *sndu-, 'to
flow', seen in OI. sndti, 'bathes', L. ndre, 'to
swim'. See natation, and cp. snite, snoot, snot,
schnauzer.
Derivatives: snout, tr. and intr. v., snout-ed, adj.,
snout-er,n., snout-ish, adj., snout-y, adj.

## snow
snow, n. — ME. snaw, snow, fr. OE. snow, which
is rel. to OS., OHG. sneo, OFris., MLG., MHG.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:721 COLUMN:3 -->
sue, MDu. snee, Du. sneeuw, G. Schnee, ON.
snjor, snjdr, snser, Dan. sne, Swed. sno, Goth.
snaiws, 'snow', OE., OHG. sniwan, MDu. snu-
wen, snouwen, Du. sneeuwen, MHG. snien^G.
schneien, 'to snow', fr. I.-E. base *snoigwhos,
'snow', resp. *sneigw-, 'to snow', whence also
Lith. sniegas, Lett, sniegs, OPruss. snaygis,
OSlav. snegu, Gk. νίφα, 'snow*, Homeric Gk
νιφετός, 'falling snow, snowstorm*, άγάν-νιφος
'much snowed on*, L. nix, gen. nivis, Olr
snechti (pi.), Mir. snechta, W. nyf, 'snow'
Olr. snige, 'dcop, rain', Avestic snaeiaiti,
Gk. νείφει, νίφει, L. nivit, Lith. sniega (inf.
sniegti), Olr. snigid, 'it snows', W. nyfio, 'to
snow', and, with presential n: L. ninguit, Lith.
sninga (inf. snigti), 'it snows'. Cp. neve, nival,
Niv6se, nivosity.
Derivatives: snow, intr. and tr. v., snow-y, adj.,
snow-i-ly, adv., snow-i-ness, n.

## snow
snow, п., a kind of vessel {naut.) — Du. snauw,
fr. LG. snau, 'beak'. Accordingly snow prop,
means 'a beak-shaped vessel*. See snaffic and
words there referred to. F., It. and Port, senau
and Dan., Swed. snau are Dutch loan words.

## snub
snub, tr. v., ]) to check; 2) to treat with scorn. —
ME. snubben, fr. ON. snubba, 'to chide, rebuke*,
rel. to Dan. snubbe, Swed. snubba, of s.m. The
primary sense of these words was 'to nip off,
cut short'. Cp. snob.
Derivatives: snub, n. and adj., snubb-er, п.,
snubb-ish, adj., snubb-ish-ly, adv., snubb-ish-
ness, п., snubb-y, adj., snubb-i-ness, n.

## snuff
snuff, tr. and intr. v., to sniff. — MDu. snoffen,
snuffen (Du. snuffen), rel. to Late MHG.
snupfe, G. Schnupfen, 'cold in the head'; of
imitative origin. Cp. sniff, snivel, snuffle.
Derivatives: snuff, п., a sniff, snuff-ing, adj.,
snuff-ing-ly, adv., snuff-y, adj.

## snnff
snnff, п., wick of candle. — Fr. snuff, 'a sniff'. See
prec. word.
Derivatives: snuff, tr. v., to nip off the snuff
of a candle, snuff-er, п., snuff-ing, n.

## snuff
snuff, п., powdered tobacco. — Du. snuf, snuif,
shortened fr. snuftabak, snuiftabak, lit. 'tobacco
for sniffing'. See snuff, 'to sniff'.
Derivatives: snuff, intr. v., to inhale powdered
tobacco, snuff-er, п., snuff-y, adj., snuff-i-ness, n.

## snuffie
snuffie, intr. and tr. v. — Freq. of snuff, 'to sniff'.
Cp. G. schnuffeln and see snivel. For the ending
see freq. suff. -le.
Derivatives: snuffle, п., snujfle-er, n.

## snug
snug, adj., ]) cozy; 2) neat, trim. — Of Scand.
origin; cp. Swed. snygg, 'neat, tidy', dial. Dan.
snog, of s.m., ON. snoggr, 'smooth-haired'. Cp.
snuggle.
Derivatives: snug, п., and intr. and tr. v.,
snuggery, п., snug-ly, adv., snug-ness, n.

## snuggle
snuggle, intr. and tr. v., to cuddle; to nestle. —
Freq. of the verb snug. See snug and freq. suff.
-le.
Derivative: snuggle, n.

## so
so, adv., pron., and conj. — ME. so, sa, swa, fr.
OE. swa, 'so*, rel. to OS., MDu., OHG., MHG.
so, ON. sva, so, Dan. saa, Swed. sa, Norw. so,
OFris. sa, so, Du. zo, G. so, 'so', Goth, swa, 'so',
swe, 'as*, and cogn. with Gk. ώς (for *oft&c),
'as*,OL. sudd, 'so', Oscan. sval,suae, 'if, Umbr.
sue, 'if. All these words are derivatives of the
I.-E. reflexive pronominal base *swe-, *se-,
whence also L. se, 'himself, herself, itself, suus,
'his*. See sui and words there referred to and
cp. especially such. Cp. also the second element
in also and in yes.

## so
so, п., the fifth note (== G.) in the scale of С
major {mus.) — The same as sol.

## soak
soak, tr. and intr. v. — ME. soken, fr. OE. socian,
in gradational relationship to OE. sucan, 'to
suck*. See suck and cp. soggy, sowens.
Derivatives: soak, п., soak-age, п., soak-er, п.,
soqk-ing, adj., soak-ing-ly, adv., soak-y, adj.

## soap
soap, n. — ME. sope, fr. OE. sdpe, which is rel. to
MLG.sepe, Du. zeep, OHG.seiffa,seifa, MHG.,
G. seife, 'soap', OHG. seifar, 'foam', and prob.
also to OE. sdp, 'resin'; fr. I.-E. base *se{i)b-,
'tallow, resin*, whence also L. sebum, 'tallow,
suet, grease', and prob. also Toch. A sepal,
'ointment*, sep-, sip-, 'to anoint'. L. sdpo, 'soap*,
is a Teut. loan word. Cp. saponaceous, sehace-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:722 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 695 | SOIL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:722 COLUMN:1 -->
ous.
Derivatives: soap, tr. v., soap-er, п., soap-ery, п.,
soap-у, adj.

## soar
soar, intr. v. — ME. soren, fr. F. essorer, 'to fly
up', fr. VL. *exaurdre, 'to expose to the air1,
which was formed fr. 1st ex- and L. aura, 'air'.
See aura.
Derivatives: soar, п., soar-er, n.

## soave
soave, adv., sweetly, gently (musicaldirection). —
It., 'sweet, gentle', fr. L. sudvis. See suave,

## sob
sob, intr. andtr.v.—ME. sobben,pxob.xe\.toOE.
siofian, seofian, 'to lament', and to OHG. sufan,
MHG. sufen, 'to sip; to draw breath'; see sup.
Fr. OHG. sufan derives OHG., MHG. suft,
'sigh', whence MHG. siuften, 'to sigh', siufzen
(for *siuftesen), G. seufzen, of s.m.
Derivatives: sob, п., sobb-ert п., sobb-ing, adj.,
sobb-ing-ly, adv., sob-ful, adj.

## sober
sober, adj., not drunk. — ME. sobre, fr. OF. and
F. sobre, fr. L. sobrius, lit. 'not drunk', fr. *so(d),
a var. of se(d), 'without', and ebrius, 'drunk'.
See se- and ebriery.
Derivatives: sober, tr. and intr. v., sober-er, п.,
sober-ing, adj., sober-ing-ly, adv.
soboles. п., a shoot; a sucker (bot.) — L. soboles,
more correctly suboles, 'a sprout, shoot, twig',
fr. sub- and the stem of *olire, 'to grow*, which
is rel. to alere, 'to nourish*. See aliment.

## Sobranje
Sobranje, п., the national assembly of Bulgaria.
— Bulg-, 'assembly', lit. 'a bringing together',
formed fr. pref. so-, s-, 'with, together with', and
OSlav. berg, birati (for earlier *birti), 'to bring,
bear, take', fr. I.-E. base *bher-, *to bear, carry'.
See bear, 'to carry'. For the pref. see Skupbstina.

## sobriety
sobriety, п., the state of being sober. — ME.
sobrietie, fr. OF. sobriete (F, sobrjete), fr. L.
sdbrietdtem, ace. of sobrietds, fr. sobrius. See
sober and -ty,

## sobriquet
sobriquet, п., nickname. — F., fr. MF. soubriquet,
with the original meaning 'chuck under the
chin'. The first element of this compound word
comes fr. L. sub, 'under' (see sub-). The second
element is of uncertain origin.

## soc
soc, п., jurisdiction (legal kist.) — ME. soc, sok,
fr. OE. soc, a var. of socn, 'jurisdiction,
prosecution4, which stands in gradational relationship
to OE. sacan, *to quarrel', and to Goth, sokan,
OE. secan, 'to seek'. See seek and cp. sake,
'purpose'. Cp. also soke, soken.

## socage
socage, also soccage, п., a form of tenure (legal
hist.) — ML. socagium, socedgium, fr. soca,
'jurisdiction', which is borrowed fr. OE. soc.
See prec. word and -age.

## soccer
soccer, also socker, п., a kind of football game.
— Formed with agential suff. -er from the
abbreviation of association in the phrase
association football.

## sociability
sociability, n. — ME. sociabilite, fr. L. socidbilis.
See next word and -fry.

## sociable
sociable, adj. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. socidbilis,
'easily united, sociable', fr. socidre, 'to
accompany', fr. socius, 'companion'. See social and
-able.
Derivatives: sociable, п., sociable-ness, п.,
spciabl-y, adv.

## social
social, adj. — L. socidlis (whence also F. social),
'pertaining to companionship, companionable,
social', fr. socius (for *soq¥Vios), 'companion',
which is cogn. with OE. secg, ON. seggr,
'companion', and prob. also with 01. sakhd,
'companion, friend', and prob. rel. to L. sequi, 'to
follow'. See seqnel and cp. sociable, society,
associate, consociate, disassociate, dissociate.
For the ending see adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: social, п., socialist (q.v.), sociality
n. (q.v.), social-ize, tr. v., social-iz-ation, п.,
social-ly, adv.

## socialism
socialism, n. — Formed fr. social with suff. -ism.
The name was first applied (about 1830) to the
teachings of Robert Owen. Cp. F. socialisme,
which appears first about the same time and orig.
denoted the teachings of Saint-Simon. Pierre
Leroux (1797-1871), idealistic social reformer
and Saint-Simonian publicist, expressly claims
to be the originator of the word socialisme.

## socialist
socialist, n. — Formed fr. social with suff. -ist.
The name arose about the same time as
socialism and orig. denoted the adherents of Robert

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:722 COLUMN:2 -->
Owen. Cp. F. socialiste, which appears first
about the same time and was first used of the
adherents of Saint-Simon. Cp. also socialistus,
a word used—in quite a different sense—by the
Dutch jurist Grotius (1583-1645), and socialista,
a word applied in the XVIII. cent, to the pupils
and followers of Grotius. See Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 565.
Derivatives: socialist, adj., socialist-ic, adj., so-
cialist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## socialite

## sociality

## society
society, n. — MF. ( = F.) societe, fr. OF. societe,

association, alliance*, fr. socius, 'companion'.

## Socinian

nism; п., an adherent of Socin or Socinianism.

## Socinianism
Socinianism, п., the doctrines taught by Socinus.
— Formed from Socinus, the Latinized name of
the Italian theologians Fausto Sozzini (1539-
1604) and his uncle Lelio Sozzini (1526-62),
who taught anti-Trinitarian doctrines. For the
ending see the suffixes -an and -ism.

## Socinianist

## socio-

## sociology
sociology, n. — F. sociologie, a hybrid coined by

(1798-1857) fr. L. socius, 'companion', and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See social and -logy.
Derivatives: sociolog-ic, adj., sociolog-ic-al, adj.,
sociolog-ic-al-ly, adv., sociol-og-ist, n.

## sock

sockdolager, n. (American Slang). — Corruption

which are cogn. with L. sus, Gk. ΰς, σΰς,

sollicitus. See solicit. For E. -ous, as equivalent to

L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: solicitous-ly, adv.^ solicitous-ness,n.

## solicitude
solicitude, п., uneasiness of mind, anxiety. —

## ME.
ME., fr. MF. (= F.) solliciti/de, fr. L. sollicitu-

## dinem
dinem, ace. of sollicitudo, fr. sollicitus. See solicit
and -ude.

## solid
solid, adj. — ME., fr. L. solidus, 'firm, compact,

## solid'
solid', which is rel. to sollus, 'whole, entire', sal-

## vus
vus, 'safe'. See safe and cp. sol, 'a former French

## coin'
coin', Soldanella, solder, soldier, soldo, Solidago,

## solidary
solidary, solideme, solidus, sou, consolidate.
Derivatives: solid, n. and adv., solid-ly, adv.,

## Solidago
Solidago, п., a genus of plants, the golden rod
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. L. solidare, 'to
strengthen, make sound', fr. solidus (see solid);
so called from its medicinal qualities.

## solidarism
solidarism, п., solidarity. — F. solidarisme, fr. so-
lidaire, 'solidary'. See solidary and -ism.

## solidarist
solidarist, n. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: solidarist-ic, adj.

## solidarity
solidarity, n. — F. solidarite, fr. solidaire, 'solid,
solidary'. See next word and -ity.

## solidary
solidary, adj. — F. solidaire, fr. L. in solidum, 'for
the whole', fr. in (see in-) and solidum, 'the whole
sum', subst. use of the neut. of solidus, 'solid'.
See solid and adj. suff. -ary.

## solideme
solideme, п., a solid compound word. — Coined
fr. soild and (phon)eme (qq.v.) Cp. hypheme.

## solidification
solidification, п., the act of solidifying; the state
of being solidified. — See next word and -ation.

## solidify
solidify, tr. and intr. v. — F. solidifier, formed fr.
solide with sufT. -fier. See solid and -fy.
Derivatives: solidifi-able, adj., solidifi-er, n.

## solidity
solidity, n. — MF. (= F.) solidite, fr. L. solidita-
tem, ace. oisoliditas, fr. solidus. See solid and -ity.

## sol id ungulate
sol id ungulate, adj., solid-hoofed (zool.) —
Compounded of solid and ungulate.

## solidus
solidus, п., name of a Roman gold coin {Roman
Antiq.) — L., prop, the adj. solidus, 'firm, strong,
solid', used as a noun. See solid and cp. words
there referred to.

## solifldian
solifldian, п., one who holds that faith alone is
sufficient to make one worthy of salvation. —
Formed with suff. -ian fr. L. solus, 'alone', and
fides, 'faith'. See sole, 'alone', and fidelity.

## soliloquy
soliloquy, п., talking to oneself. — Late L. sdli-
loquium, coined by Augustine on analogy of Gk.
μονολογία (ср. monologue), fr. L. solus, 'alone',
and loqui, 'to speak'. See sole, 'alone', and
loquacious.
Derivatives: soliloqu-ize, intr. v., soliloqu-iz-ery
п., soliloqu-iz-ing, adj., soliloqu-iz-ing-ly, adv.

## sollped
sollped, п., a solidungulate animal (zool.) —
ModL. sdlipis, gen. -pedis, a blend of L. solidi-
pes, 'solidhoofed*, and solus, 'alone'. See solid
and pedal and cp. solidungulate.

## solipsism
solipsism, п., the doctrine that the self is the only
existing thing (metapkysics). — Coined fr. L.
solus, 'alone', ipse, 'himself, self, and suff. -ism.
See sole, 'alone', and ipseity.

## solitaire
solitaire, п., 1) a single diamond or another
precious stone; 2) a game played by a single person.
— F., fr. L. solitdrius. See next word.

## solitary
solitary, adj., 1) alone; 2) single; 3) lonely. —
ME., fr. L. solitdrius, 'alone, lonely, solitary*
(whence also F. solitaire), fr. solitas, 'loneliness',
fr. solus. See sole, 'alone', and adj. suff. -ary and
cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: solitary, п., solitari-ly, adv.,
solitariness, n.

## soiltude
soiltude, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. OF., fr. L.
sdlitudinem, ace. of sdlitudo, 'loneliness', fr.
solus. See sole, 'alone', and -rude.

## solivagant
solivagant, adj., wandering about alone. —
Formed with suff. -ant fr. L. sdlivagus, which is
compounded of solus, 'alone', and vagus,
'wandering'. See sole, 'alone', and vagary.

## solleret
solleret, п., a steel shoe with flexible plates. — F.
soleret, solleret, fr. OF., dimin. of soler, soller,
'shoe', fr. Late L. subtelaris (scil. calceus), 'shoe
covering the hollow of the foot', fr. subtel, 'the
hollow of the foot', which is compounded of
sub- and L. talus, 'ankle bone'. See talus, 'ankle*.
F. Soulier, 'shoe', developed fr. OF. soler with
change of suff.

## solmlzation
solmlzation, п., sol-fa system (music). — Formed
from the syllables sol, mi, and suff. -ization. See
gamut and cp. sol-fa.

## solo
solo, п., piece sung or played by a single person.
— It., lit. 'alone', fr. L. solus. See sole, 'alone*.
Derivatives: solo, adj. and intr. v., soloist (q.v.)

## soloist
soloist, п., singer or player of a solo. — A hybrid
coined fr. solo with -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## Solomon
Solomon, masc. PN.; name of David's son, king
of Judah and Israel, the wisest of all men. Hence
the name Solomon is often used to denote a very
wise man. — Gk. Σολομών, also Σαλωμών, fr.
Heb. Sh lomd , which is rel. to shalom, 'peace*.
See shalom and cp. Salome. The Arabic PN.s

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:724 COLUMN:2 -->
Soliman, Suleiman derive fr. Heb. Sk lomoh.

## Solon
Solon, п., a wise Athenian statesman and
lawgiver. His name is sometimes used
metaphorically to denote a wise man. — Gk. Σόλων.

## Solpuglda
Solpuglda, п., an order of spiders (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -ida fr. L. sollpugay
solpuga, alt. ofsalpuga, 'a kind of venomous ant
or spider', which is of uncertain origin. The
forms solipuga, solpuga are due to a
folk-etymological association of the word with sol, 'sun'.

## solstice
solstice, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. solsti-
tium (for *sol-statiom), lit. 'the standing still of
the sun', compounded of sol, 'the sun', and the
stem of stare, 'to stand'. See Sol and state, п.,
and cp. interstice.

## solstitial
solstitial, adj., pertaining to, or occurring at, the
time of a solstice. — L. solstitialis, fr. solstitium.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: solstitial-ly, adv.

## solubilize
solubilize, tr. v., to render soluble. — A hybrid
formed fr. Late L. solubilis (see soluble) with
-Ize, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivative: solubiliz-ation, n.

## soinble
soinble, adj. — OF. (= F.), fr. Late L. solubilis,
'that may be loosened, dissolvable*, formed fr.
L. solu-, stem οι solvere (pp. solutus), 'to loosen,
untie, dissolve'. See solve and -ble and cp. sol·
vnble.
Derivatives: solubil-ity, п., soluble-ness, п.,
solubl-y, adv.

## solum
solum, п., the soil. — L. solum, 'the ground*. See
sole of the foot.

## solution
solution, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. OF., fr.'L.
solutionem, ace. of solutid, 'a loosening,
dissolution', fr. solutus, pp. of solvere. See solve and
-ion.
Derivatives: solution-al, adj., solution-er, n.

## Solutrean
Solutrean, Solutrian, adj., pertaining to the geo-'
logical period preceded by the Aurignacian and
Magdalenian. — Named after Solutre in the
department Seine-et-Loire, France. For the
ending see surf, -an, resp. -ian.

## solvable
solvable, adj. — Formed fr. the verb solve with
suff. -able.
Derivatives: solvabil-ity, п., solvable-ness, n.

## solve
solve, tr. v. — ME. solven, fr. L. solvere, 'to
loosen, untie, dissolve', for *se-luere,
compounded of se-, a collateral form of se- (see
se-) and luere, 'to loose', which is rel. to lues,
'plague, pestilence', lit. 'that which dissolves'.
See lose and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
absolute, absolve, assoil, consolute, dissolute,
dissolve, resolute, resolve.

## solvency
solvency, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## solvent
solvent, adj. and n. — L. solvins, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of solvere. See solve and -ent.
Derivative: solvent-ly, adv.

## soma
soma, п., 1) an East Indian plant (Sarcostemma
acidum); 2) a beverage said to .be prepared from
this plant and playing an important part in the
Vedic ritual. — Ol. somah, 'soma' (name of the
sap of this plant and of the plant itself), rel.
to Ol. sunoti, 'squeezes', fr. l.-E. base *seu-,
'sap, juice; to squeeze, press; to rain, flow',
whence also Ol. surah, 'intoxicating drink', Gk.
ϋειν (for *suwein), 'to rain', υετός (for
*suwetos), 'rain'. See hyeto- and cp. sura,
'fermented sap of palms*.

## soma
soma, п., the body of an organism. — Gk. σώμα,
'body', prob. standing for *two-mn, and lit.
meaning 'something thickset', and rel. to σάος
(for *σά/ος), Att. σώος, σώς, 'safe, sound,
whole', for orig. *twewos, prop, 'of a full or
thickset body', and cogn. with L. tdmentum (for
*tow mentom), 'stuffing for cushion', fr. I.-E.
base *tu-, 'to swell', whence also L. tumere, 'to
swell', tumidus, 'swollen'. See tumid and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also somite. Cp. also
Soter and words there referred to.

## somat-
somat-, form of soma to- before a vowel.

## somatic
somatic, adj., pertaining to the body. — Gk.
σωματικός, fr. σώμα, gen. σώματος, 'body'
See soma, 'body', and 1st -atic.
Derivative: somatic-al-ly, adv.

## somato-
somato-, before a vowel somat-, combining form
meaning 'body'. — Gk. σωματο-, σωματ-, fr.
σώμα, gen. σώματος, 'body'. See soma, 'body'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:724 COLUMN:3 -->

## somatogenetic
somatogenetic, somatogenic, adj., originating in
the body. — Compounded of somato- and
genetic, resp. genie.

## somatology
somatology, n., study of the body. —
Compounded of somato- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: somatolog-ic, somatolog-ic-al, adj.,
somatolog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## somber
somber, sombre, adj., dark. — F. sombre, possibly
fr. Late L. subumbrare, 'to put in shade* (whence
also Sp. sombra, 'shade', sombrio, 'shady') fr.
sub- and L. umbra, 'shadow, shade*. See umbra
and cp. next word.
Derivatives: somber-ly, sombre-ly, adv., somber-
ness, sombre-ness, п., sombr-ous, adj.

## sombrero
sombrero, п., a broad-brimmed felt hat. — Sp., fr.
sombra, 'shade'. See prec. word.

## some
some, adj. — ME. som, fr. OE. sum, rel. to OS.,
OFris., OHG. sum, ON. sumr, Goth, sums, and
cogn. with Ol. samah, 'some one4, Gk. άμός
(for *samos), 'some one', άμη (for *same),
'somehow', άμό&εν, Ion. άμόθεν, 'from some
place', οΰδ-^μός, 'no one', ούδ-αμώς. 'by no
means'. See same, adj., and cp. words there
referred to. See also 1st -some.
Derivative: some, pron.

## -some
-some, suff. denoting likeness or tendency, as in
gladsome. — ME. -som, fr. OE. -sum, rel. to ON.
-samr, OFris. -sum, Du. -zaam, OHG., MHG.,
G. -sam, Goth, -same and to E. some (q.v.)

## -some
-some, combining form denoting the body, as in
chromosome, plasmosome. — Fr. Gk. σώμα,
'body'. See soma, 'body'.

## somersault
somersault, п., heels-over-head turn of the body.
— MF. sombresault, alteration of soubresault
(whence F. soubresaut), borrowed fr. OProveng.
sobresaut or Sp. sobresalto, which lit. mean 'a
leap above', and derive fr. L. supra, 'above, on
the top', and saltus, 'a leapl. See supra- and
salient and cp. saltation. The word somersault
was influenced in form by an association with
E. summer, 'beam'; cp. the var. spelling
summersault.
Derivative: somersault, intr. v.

## somite
somite, п., one of the serial segments of the body
of an animal. — Formed fr. Gk. σώμα, "body'.
See soma, 'body', and subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: somit-ic, adj.

## sommaite
sommaite, п., a plutonic rock (petrogr.) — Named
after Monte Somma, Vesuvius, Italy, where it is
found. For the ending see subst. surf. -ite.

## somnambnlant
somnambnlant, adj., walking in one's sleep. —
Formed fr. L. somnus, 'sleep', and ambulans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of ambulare, 'to walk'.
See next word and -ant.

## somnambulate
somnambulate, intr. v., to walk in one's sleep. —
Formed fr. L. somnus, 'sleep', and ambuldt-(um),
pp. stem of ambulare, 'to walk*. See somnolent
and ambnlance.
Derivatives: somnambulat-ion, п., somnambulat-
or, n.

## somnambnlism
somnambnlism, п., sleepwalking. — See
somnambulate and -ism.

## somnambulist
somnambulist, п., a sleepwalker. — See prec.
word and -ist.
Derivative: somnambulist-ic, adj.

## somni-
somni-, combining form meaning 'sleep'. — L.,
fr. somnus, 'sleep'. See somnolent.

## somnifacient
somnifacient, adj., inducing sleep. —
Compounded of somni- and L.faciens, gen. -entis, pres. part,
of facer-e, 'to make, do'. See fact and -ent.

## somniferons
somniferons, adj., sleep-producing. — Com-
pounded of somni- and -ferous.

## somniloquence
somniloquence, п., somniloquy. — Compounded
of somni- and L. loquentia, 'a talking*, fr. lo-
quens, gen. loquentis, pres. part, of loqui, 'to
speak*. See loquacious and cp. next word.

## somniloquy
somniloquy, n., talking in one's sleep. — See prec.
word. For the ending of the second element cp.
soliloquy.

## somnolence
somnolence, somnolency, п., sleepiness. —
Formed from next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## somnolent
somnolent, adj., sleepy. — F., fr. L. somnolentus,
'sleepy, drowsy', formed with suff. -lentus, fr.
somnus, 'sleep', which stands for *swepnos or
*swopnos and is cogn. with 01. svapnah, 'sleep',
Avestic xvqfna-, Arm. klun (gen. k"noy), Toch.

nos), 'sleep*, Lith. sapnas, Lett, sapnis (for *sop-
nos), OSlav. sunu (for *supnos), Olr. suan, W.
hun, Bret, hurt (for *sopnos), Alb. ^ume (for
*supnos), 'sleep', OE. swefnt ON. svefn, *a
dream'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*swep-, *sup-, *to sleep'. Cp. hypno-, insomnia,
sopor.
Derivative: somnolent-ly, adv.

## son
son, n. — ME. sune, sone, fr. OE. sunu, rel. to
OS., OFris. sunu, ON. sonr, Dan. son, Swed. son,
MDu. sone, Du. zoon, OHG. sunu, sun, MHG.
sun, G. Sohn, Goth, sunus, 'son*, and cogn. with
OI. suntik, Avestic hunush, OSlav. synu, Lith.
sunus, 'son', and—without w-formative
element—with Toch. В soya, Ase, Gk. υιός, 'son',
Arm. ustr, 'son' (influenced in form by dustr,
'daughter'), OI. sutah, 'son', sate, suyate, savati,
'begets, procreates', Olr. suth (for su-tu), 'fetus'.
All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *seu-, *su-,
'to bear, bring forth; birth'.

## sonance
sonance, sonancy, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy. Cp. assonance,
consonance, dissonance, resonance.

## sonant
sonant, adj. and n. — L. sondns, gen. -amis, pres.
part, of sonare, 'to sound', which stands for
*swenare and is rel. to sonus (for *swonos),
'sound', fr. base *swen·, 'to sound'. See sound,
'noise', and cp. assonant, consonant, dissonant,
resonant, resound, sonata, sonnet, sound, 'noise',
and the second element in unison. For the ending
see suff. -ant.
Derivatives: sonant, n.( sonant-al, adj., sonant-
ic, adj.

## sonar
sonar, п.,a device for the detection of submarines,
mines or other objects under water. — Formed
from the first letters of the words sound
navigation ranging.

## sonata
sonata, п., an instrumental composition {mus.) —
It., lit. 'anything sounded', fr. sonare, 'to sound*,
fr. L. sonare. See prec. word.

## sonatina
sonatina, n. (mus.) — It., prop, a short sonata,
dimin. of sonata.

## Sonchus
Sonchus, п., a genus of plants, the sow thistle
(bot.) — L., 'the sow thistle', fr. Gk. σόγχος.

## song
song, n. — ME. sang, song, fr. OE. sang, song,
rel. to ON. sdngr, Norw. song, Swed. sang, OS.,
Dan., OFris., OHG., G. sang, MDu., MHG.
sane, Du. zang, Goth, saggws; in gradational
relationship to sing (q.v.)

## songster
songster, n. — ME., 'singer', fr. OE. sangestre,
'woman singer', formed fr. sang, 'song1, with
suff. -estre. See -ster.

## songstress
songstress, n. — Formed fr. song, with double
fern, suff., viz. E. -ster (q.v.) and F. -esse, which
corresponds to Gk.-L. -issa. See 1st -ess and cp.
prec. word. Cp. also sempstress,

## sonic
sonic, adj., 1) pertaining to sound; 2) pertaining
to the speed of sound in the air. — Formed fr.
L. sonus, 'sound' (see sonant), with suff. -ic. Cp.
the second element in supersonic, ultrasonic.
Derivative: sonic-al-ly, adv.

## soniferous
soniferous, adj., producing or conveying sound.
— Compounded of L. sonus, 'sound*, and ferre,
'to bear, carry'. See sonant and -ferous.

## sonnet
sonnet, п., a poem of fourteen lines with rhymes
arranged according to a fixed pattern. — F., fr.

## It. sonetto
It. sonetto, fr. OProvenc. sonet, 'a kind of song',

## prop
prop, dimin. of son, 'sound, song', fr. L. sonus,
*sound' (cp. OF. sonet, dimin. of son, 'song').
See sonant and -et.
Derivatives: sonnet, intr. and tr. v., sonnet-ize,
intr. and tr. v.

## sonneteer
sonneteer, п., a writer of sonnets. — It. sonettiere,

## fr. sonetto. See sonnet and -ier
fr. sonetto. See sonnet and -ier, resp. -eer.
Derivative: sonneteer, intr. and tr. v.

## sonny
sonny, п., familiar address to a boy. — Formed
fr. son with dimin. suff. -y.

## sonometer
sonometer, п., an instrument for measuring
sounds. —A hybrid coined fr. L. sonus, 'sound',
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See sonant and

## meter
meter, 'poetical rhythm*,

## sonorescence
sonorescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## sonorescent
sonorescent, adj., capable of emitting sound
under the influence of radiation. — Coined fr. L.

## sonorus
sonorus, 'resounding' (see sonorous), and suff.
-escent.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:725 COLUMN:2 -->

## sonority
sonority, n. —■ Late L. sonoritas, 'fullness of
sound', fr. L. sonorus. See next word and -ity.

## sonorous
sonorous, adj. — L. sonorus, 'resounding', fr. so-
nor, 'sound ,noise\ fr. sonare, 'to sound'; see so·
nant. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see-oos.
Derivatives: sonorous-ly, adv., sonorous-ness, n.

## sonsy
sonsy, sousie, adj., lucky; good-natured (Scot.) —
Fr. dial, some, sons, 'prosperity', a word of
Celtic origin. Cp. Gaelic and Ir. sonas, 'luck,
fortune'.

## soon
soon, adv. — ME. sone, soone, fr. OE. sona,
'immediately', rel. to OFris. son, OS. san, sana,
sano, OHG. san, sano, Goth, suns, 'soon'. Cp.
the second element in eftsoons.

## soorky
soorky, п., pounded brick mixed with lime to
form a mortar {India). — Pers. surkhi, 'redness',
fr. surkh, 'red', fr. MPers. sukhr, which is rel. to
Avestic suxra-, OI. sukrah, 'bright',

## soot
soot, n. — ME. sot, soot, fr. OE. sot, rel. to ON.
sot, ODu. soet, lit. 'that which settles', fr. Teut.
base *set-, 'to sit, set', corresponding to I.-E-
*sed-, 'to sit', whence OSlav. sazda, Lith. suod-
ziai (pi.), Olr. suide, W. huddyl, Bret, huzel,
'soot'. See sedentary. For sense development cp.
sediment.
Derivatives: soot, tr. v., soot-y, adj., soot-i-ly,
adv., soot-i-ness, n.

## sooth
sooth, n. — ME. soth, sooth, fr. OE. sod, 'true;
truth', rel. to ON. sannr, 'true', OS. soth, OHG.
sand, 'true', Goth, sunja, 'truth'. These words
orig. meant 'that which is', and derive from the
Teut. participial base *sanp-, which corresponds
to I.-E. *essont-, fr. *es-, 'to be'. See esse and
cp. etymon, sattva, snttee. Cp. also sin,
'transgression'. Cp. also absent, present.

## soothe
soothe, tr. v. — ME. sothen, fr. OE. sddian, 'to
show the truth of*, fr. sod, 'true'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: sooth-er, п., sooth-ing, adj., sooth-
ing-ly, adv.

## soothfast
soothfast, adj. and adv., truthful (archaic). —
ME. sothfast, soothfast, fr. OE. sodfzst,
'truthful, righteous'. See sooth and fast, 'firm*,

## soothsay
soothsay, intr. v. — Back formation fr. soothsayer,

## soothsayer
soothsayer, n. — ME. sothseyer, lit. 'a speaker of
truth', fr. soth, 'truth', and seyer, sayer, 'sayer'.
See sooth, say, v., and agential suff. -er,

## sop
sop, п., bread or other food dipped in liquid. —
ME. sop, soppe, fr. OE. sopp, rel. to OE. supan,
'to sip, sup, drink', Du. zuipen, G. saufen, 'to
drink'. See sup, 'to sip, drink', and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivative: sop, tr. and intr. v., to dip (bread),
etc. into liquid, sopp-er, п., sopp-ing, adj. and n.

## soph
soph, n.—Abbrevi ation of sophist tr or sophomore.

## Sopherim
Sopherim, n. pi., 1) the Hebrew scribes, orig.
copyists and interpreters of the Bible; in a special
sense; 2) a body of teachers who interpreted the
Law in the last centuries of the second
Commonwealth. — Heb. soph rim, 'scribes', pi. of sopker,

## lit. 'bookman'
lit. 'bookman', denominated fr. sepher, 'book'.
See Sepher Torah.

## Sophia
Sophia, fem. PN. — Fr. Gk. σοφία, 'wisdom', fr.
σοφός, 'wise'. See next word.

## sophism
sophism, n. — ME. sopkime, fr. OF. soffime, so-

phime, sophisme (F. sophisme), fr. L. sophisma,
fr. Gk. σόφισμα, from the stem of σοφίζειν, 'to

make wise, instruct', σοφίζεσ&αι, 'to become
wise; to devise, cleverly, play subtle tricks', fr.
σοφός, 'clever, skilled, prudent, cunning,

learned, wise', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.

## Sophia
Sophia, sophist, sophisticate, the first element in
sophomore and the second element in panso-

## phism
phism, philosophy. For the ending of σόφισμα see

## sophist
sophist, п., I) (often capitalized) in ancient Greece,

## one of a group of public teachers of rhetoric
one of a group of public teachers of rhetoric,

## philosophy
philosophy, etc.; 2) a learned person; 3) a
fallacious reasoner. — F. sopkiste, fr. L. sopkista,
fr. Gk. σοφιστής, 'a clever, skillful, wise man;

## one who gave lessons (in grammar
one who gave lessons (in grammar, rhetoric,
etc.) for money; a quibbler*, from the stem of
σοφίζειν. See prec. word and -ist and cp. gymno-
sophist.

## sophister
sophister, п., student in his second or third year
in Oxford and Cambridge Universities. — ME.,

## fr. OF. sopkistre
fr. OF. sopkistre, fr. L. sopkista. See prec. word.

## sophistic
sophistic, sophistical, adj. — L. sophisticus, fr. Gk.
σοφιστικός, 'pertaining to a sophist', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:725 COLUMN:3 -->
σοφιστής. See sophist and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivatives: sophistical-ly, adv., sophistical-
ness, n.

## sophisticate
sophisticate, tr. v., ]) to render sophistical; 2) to
falsify; 3) to make artificial or worldly-wise;
intr. v., to practice sophistication; п., a
sophisticated person. — ML. sophisticate, pp. of so-
phisticdre, 'to sophisticate'. See prec. word and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: sophisticat-ed, adj., sophistication
(q.v.), sopkisticat-or, n.

## sophistication
sophistication, n. — ME. sophisticacioun, fr. ML.
sophisticatid, gen. -onis, fr. sopkisticatus, pp. of

## sophistry
sophistry, п., clever but unsound reasoning. —
ME. sophistrie, fr. OF. sophisterie, sophistrie (F.
sophisterie), fr. sopkiste. See sophist and -ry.

## sophomore
sophomore, п., a second year student at an
American university. — Alteration of obsolete so-
phumer, formed fr. sophume, an old var. of
sophism, fr. Gk. σόφισμα, 'cunning contrivance,
device, invention', fr. σοφός, 'clever, skilful,
wise'; see sophism. The change of sophumer to
sophomore was due to a popular misconception
of the former word as a compound of σοφός,
'clever', and μωρός, 'foolish, dull'.
Derivatives: sophomor-ic(-ai), adj., sophomor-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## Sophora
Sophora, п., a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, su/ara1, 'yellow
plants', which is rel. to asfaru, fem. safrd\
'yellow'. See saffron.

## Sophronia
Sophronia, fem. PN. — Gk. Σωφρονία, fr.
σώφρων, gen. σώφρονος, 'discreet, prudent',
prop, 'of sound mind', compounded of σώς,
'safe, sound, whole', and φρήν, 'midriff; heart,
mind'. For the first element see Soter, for the
second see phrenetic and cp. Phronima.

## -sophy
-sophy, combining form meaning 'knowledge'. —
ME. -sophie, fr. OF. ( = F.), fr. L. -sophia, fr.
Gk. -σοφία, fr. σοφία, 'skill, wisdom,
knowledge*, fr. σοφός, "clever, skilled*. See sophism.

## sopor
sopor, п., lethargic sleep. — L. sopor, *deep sleep',
from a causative form of I.-E. base *swep-,
*sup-, 'to sleep', whence also OI. svdpayati,
Mulls to sleep'. See somnolent.

## soporiferous
soporiferous, adj., causing sleep. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. soporifer, 'sleep-bringing', fr.
sopor, 'deep sleep', and ferre, 'to bear, carry'.
See prec. word and -ferous.
Derivatives: soporiferous-ly, adv., soporiferous-
ness, n.

## soporific
soporific, adj., causing sleep. — Formed fr. L. so-
por, 'deep sleep', and -ficus, fr. -ficere, unstressed
form offacere, 'to make, do'. Sc-esopor and -fie.
Derivatives: soporific, п., soporific-al, adj.,
soporific-al-ly, adv.

## soprano
soprano, п., the highest female voice (mus.) — It.,
a var. of sovrano, 'highest; supreme, sovereign',
fr. Late L. superdnus, fr. L. supra, 'above'. See
super- and cp. sovereign.

## sora
sora, п., a North American rail, Porzana Carolina
(prnithol.) — A native Indian name.

## sorb
sorb, п., the service tree. — F. sorbe, 'the fruit of
the service tree', fr. L. sorbum, of s.m., fr. sor-
bus, 'the service tree', which prob. stands for
*sor-dhos, and lit. denotes 'the tree with the red-
colored berries', and is cogn. with Lith. saf-tas
'foxy in color', Lett, sorts, 'red-faced'. Cp.
service tree.

## Sorb
Sorb, п., one of the ancestors of the Slavonic
tribe called the Wends. — G. Sorbe, of Slavonic
origin. Cp. Serb.

## sorb
sorb, tr. v., to take up by adsorption or
absorption {physical ckem.) — L. sorbere, 'to suck in,
swallow up'. See absorb.

## Sorbaria
Sorbaria, п., a genus of plants of the rose family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. sorbus, 'the service tree'.
See Sorbus and -aria.

## sorbefacient
sorbefacient, adj., causing absorption. —
Compounded of L. sorbere, 'to suck in, swallow up',
and faciens, gen. -entis, pres. part, offacere, 'to
make, do'. For the first element see absorb, for
the second see -facient, for the ending see suff.
-ent. Cp. absorbefacient.
Derivative: sorbefacient, n.

## sorbet
sorbet, п., sherbet. — F., fr. It. sorbetto, fr. Turk.-
Pers. sherbet (see sherbet); influenced in form by

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:726 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 699 | SOUFFLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:726 COLUMN:1 -->
It. sorbire, 'to sip'.

## Serbian
Serbian, adj., pertaining to the Sorbs; п., a Sorb.
— Formed fr. Sorb with suff. -ian.

## sorbite
sorbite, п., a constituent of carbon steel
(metallurgy). — Named after the English geologist and
metallographist Henry Clifton Sorby (1826-
1908). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## sorbitol
sorbitol, also sorbite, п., an alcohol, CeHJ4Os
(ckem.) — See sorb, subst. suff. -ite and suff. -ol.

## Sorbonist
Sorbonist, п., a doctor of the Sorbonne. — F.
Sorboniste, fr. MF., formed with suff. -iste (see
-ist) fr. Sorbonne, a celebrated institution of
learning in Paris; so called from its founder
Robert de Sorbon, chaplain and confessor of Louis
IX. Robert de Sorbon himself is named after
Sorbon, a place in the Ardennes, where he was
born in 1201.

## Sorbus
Sorbus, п., a genus of trees, the service tree, the
mountain ash (bot.) — L. sorbus, 'service tree'.
See sorb,

## sorcerer
sorcerer, n. — MF. (= F.) sorcier, fr. OF., fr.
VL. *sortidrius, 'a caster of lots', fr. *sortiari, 'to
cast lots', corresponding to L. sortirt, fr. sors,
gen. sortis, Mot'. See sort, n. For the repetition
of the suff. -er see poulterer and cp. words there
referred to.

## sorceress
sorceress, n. — ME. sorceresse, fr. AF. sorceresse,
formed fr. sorcer-er with suff. -esse. See prec.
word and 1st -ess.

## sorcery
sorcery, n. — ME. sorcerie, fr. OF. sorcerie, fr.
sorcier. See sorcerer and suff. -y (representing
OF. -ie). Cp. F. sorcellerie, which arose through
dissimilation fr. *sorcererie.

## sordamente
sordamente, adv. (to be played) in a muffled
manner {musical direction). — It., formed fr.
sordo, 'deaf, dull-sounding*, fr. L. surdus, 'deaf;
dull', with adv. suff. -mente, fr. L. mente, abl. of
mens, 'mind, reason, thought'. See surd and
mental, 'pertaining to the mind'.

## sordavalite
sordavalite, п., a dark-brown glassy substance
(petrogr.) — Named after Sordavala in Finland.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## sordellina
sordellina, п., a kind of small bagpipe. — It., fr.
sordo, 'deaf; dull-sounding', fr. L. surdus, 'deaf;
dull'. See surd and cp. sordine.

## sordes
sordes, п., filth, foul matter. — L. sordes, 'dirt,
filth'. See next word.

## sordid
sordid, adj., ]) filthy; 2) ignoble. — F. sordide,
fr. L. sordidus, 'dirty, foul, filthy, squalid', fr.
sordes, 'dirt, filth', whence also sordere, 'to be
dirty, filthy'; fr. I.-E. base *sword-, 'dark, black,
dirty', whence also Goth, swarts, OE. sweart,
'black'. See swart and cp. prec. word-
Derivatives: sordid-ly, adv., sordid-ness, n.

## sordine
sordine, п., a device used to produce a muffled

F. sourdine, fr. It. sordino, sordino, formed with

## sordino
sordino, п., a mute (mus.) — It. See prec. word.

## sore
sore, adj. — ME. sar, sor, fr. OE. sdr, 'painful,

With Olr. saeth, 'pain, sickness', L. saevus,

Hofmann, LEW., II, p. 262 s.v. saevus and
Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., pp. 698-699 s.v. sekr.
Cp. sorry.
Derivatives: sore, adv. (q.v.), sore-ly, adv.,
soreness, η.

## sore
sore, п., boil, ulcer, etc. — ME. sar, sor, fr. OE.

## sore

## sorel
sorel, n. — See sorrel.

## Sorex
Sorex, п., the genus of shrews (zool.) — L. sorex,

## soricine

## sorites

## sororate
sororate, n.t marriage with a wife's sister. —
Coined by Sir James George Frazer (1854-1941) on

## sororicide
sororicide, п., one who kills his sister. — L. soro-

## sororicide

## sorority

tas, 'sisterhood', fr. L. soror, gen. sororis, 'sister'.

## sorosis
sorosis, п., a compound pulpy fruit, as that of the

## sorption
sorption, п., the act of sorbing (physical ckem.) —

## sorrel
sorrel, adj., reddish brown (said esp. of horses);

## sorrel
sorrel, п., a plant, Rumex acetosa (bot.) — ME.

## sorrow
sorrow, n. — ME. sorewe, sorwe, fr. OE. sorg (in

raga, sorga, MHG-, G. sorge, Goth, saurga, and
prob. cogn. with Ol. surksati, 'cares for, is

OSlav. sraga, 'sickness', Lith. sergu, sifgti, 'to be

Derivatives: sorrow, v. (q.v.), sorrow-er, п.,

## sorrow-ful
sorrow-ful, adj., sorrow-ful-ly, adv.,
sorrow-fulness, n.

## sorrow
sorrow, intr. v. — ME. sorowen, sorwent fr. OE.

## sorgian
sorgian, 'to grieve, be anxious*, fr. sorg. See
sorrow, n.
Derivatives: sorrowing, adj., sorrow-ing-ly, adv.

## sorry
sorry, adj. — ME. sary, sory, fr. OE. sarig, fr. sar,
'pain, grief; see sore, n. and adj., and -y
(representing OE. -ig). The spelling sorry (with two

Derivatives: sorri-ly, adv., sorri-li-ness, n.

## sort
sort, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) sorte, fr. OF.,

## which prob. derives fr. ML. sortem
which prob. derives fr. ML. sortem, ace. of sors,
'sort, kind', fr. Late L., 'way, manner', fr. L.,
'fate, lot, condition, state* (whence also OF.,
MF., F. sort, 'lot, fate'), which stands in grada-

## tional relationship to serere
tional relationship to serere, 'to join, connect';
lots were called sortis because they used to be

## strung or threaded. Cp. It. sorte
strung or threaded. Cp. It. sorte, Sp. suerte,

Derivative: sort-al, adj.

## sort
sort, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sorten, fr. sort. See
sort, n.
Derivatives: sort-able, adj., sort-abl-y, adv.,
sort-edt adj., sort-ег, n.

## sortes
sortes, n. pi., the lots. — L. sortes, pi. of sors. See

## sortie
sortie, п., attack of the besieged upon the

Derivative: sortie, intr. v.

## sortilege
sortilege, п., divination by casting lots. — ME.,
fr. OF. sortilege (F. sortilege), fr. ML. sortile-
gium, fr. L. sortilegus, 'one who divines by lots',
which is compounded of sors, gen. sortis, 'fate,
lot', and the stem of legere, 'to pick up, select,
read'. See sort, п., and lecture.
Derivatives; sortileg-ic, adj., sortileg-er, n.

## sorus
sorus, п., a cluster of spore cases in ferns (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. σωρός, 'a heap', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. soredium, sorites, sorosis and

## sostennto
sostennto, adv., sustained, prolonged (mus.) —
It., pp. of sostenere, 'to sustain, maintain', fr. L.
sustinere. See sustain.

## sot
sot, п., a fool; a habitual drunkard. — ME. sott,

Derivatives: sot, tr. v., to befool, sott-isk, adj.,
sott-ish-ly, adv., sott-isk-ness, n.

## Soter
Soter, п., 1) an epithet of Zeus (Greek mythol.) —
Gk. σωτήρ. 'savior, deliverer', rel. to σφζειν,
*to save% σάος, Att. σώος, σώς, 'safe, sound,
whole'. See soma, 'body', and cp. Sophronia,
sozin and the second element in creosote.

## Sothic
Sothic, adj., pertaining to, or named after, So-
this. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. Σώ&ΐς,
the Egyptian name of Sirius, the Dog Star.

## sotnia
sotnia, п., a squadron of Cossack cavalry. —
Russ. sotnya, 'a hundred', fr. sto, 'a hundred",
which is rel. to OSlav. suto, and cogn. with
Lith. Simtas, Lett, simts, Ol. satdm, Gk. έ-κα-
τόν, L. centum, OE. hund, etc., of s.m. See

## sotto voce
sotto voce, in an undertone (mus.) — It., lit.
