tal. sotz, OSp. soto, OPort. sotto. L. subtus
comes fr. sub, 'under'; see sub, prep., and cp.
soutune. Voce derives fr. L. vocem, ace. of vox,
'voice'; see voice.

## sou
sou, п., a small French coin. — F., fr. L. solidus,
a gold coin of the Latin Empire, from the adj.
solidus, 'firm, solid*. See solidus.

## soubise
soubise, п., a sauce. — F., named after Charles de
Rohan (1715-87), Prince de Soubise, fr. Soubise,
a village near Rochefort in France, which was
an ancient seigneury of the Rohan family.

## sonbrette
sonbrette, п., an intriguing maidservant in
comedy. — F., fr. Proven?, soubreto, 'affected,
conceited', fem. of soubret, fr. soubra, 'to leave
apart', orig. meaning *to exceed*, fr. OProvenc.
sobrar, fr. L. superare, 'to rise above, overcome,
be left over', fr. super, 'over, above, beyond'.
See super- and cp. words there referred to.

## soubriquet
soubriquet, n. — See sobriquet.

## soucar
soucar, п., a Hindu banker. — Hind, sahukar, 'a
great merchant, banker', fr. 01. sadhuh,
'straight'. See sadhu.

## souchong
souchong, п., a kind of fine black Chinese tea. —
Chin, hsiao chung, 'small or fine kind*.

## souffie
souffie, п., soft sound heard through the
stethoscope (med.) — F., lit. 'puff, breath', back
formation fr. souffier, 'to blow', fr. L. sufflare, fr. sub-
апй flare, 'to blow'. See flntus and cp. soffione.

## souffie
souffie, п., a light—sweet or savory—dish. — F.,
pp. of soujfler, 'to blow*, used as a noun. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:727 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SOUGH | 700 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:727 COLUMN:1 -->
prec. word.

## sough
sough, intr. v., to make a moaning or murmuring
sound. — ME. swoghen, swoughen, fr. OE.
swogan, 'to sound, make a noise', which is re],
to OE. swegan, of s.m., OS. swugan, 'to rustle',
Goth, gaswogjan, 'to sigh', and cogn. with Lith.
svageti, 'to sound', and possibly also with OI.
vagnuk, 'sound'. L. vdgire, 'to cry, roar, sound',
Gk. ήχεΐν, 'to resound', ήχή, ήχώ, ήχος,
'sound; echo'. See echo and cp. vagitus.

## sough
sough, п., a moaning or murmuring sound. —
ME. swogk, swough, fr. swoghen, swoughen. See
sough, v.

## sought
sought, past tense and pp. of seek. — ME. soukt,
fr. OE. sohte, resp. gesdht, past tense, resp. pp.,
of secan. See seek.

## soul
soul, n. — ME. saule, soule, fr. OE. sdwol, rel. to
OS. seola, siala, ON. sola, OFris. sele, MDu.
stele, Du. ziel, OHG. seula, slla, MHG. sele, G.
Seele, Goth, saiwala. These words prob. derive
fr. OTeut, "saiwalo, 'that which is related to a
lake or sea', fr. *saiwa-z, 'lake, sea'; see sea.
According to ancient Teutonic conceptions
lakes used to serve as dwelling places of the
souls after death. See Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS.,
p. 697 s.v. Seele.
Derivatives: soul-ed, adj., soul-ful, adj., soul-ful-
ly, adv., soul-ful-ness, п., soul-less, adj., soul-
less-ly, adv., soul-less-ness, n.

## sound
sound, п., noise. — ME. soun, fr. OF. ( = F.) son,
fr. L. sonus, 'sound', which stands for *swonos,
and is rel. to sonare (for *swendre), 'to sound',
fr. I.-E. base *swen-, 'to sound', whence also
OI. svdnatl, 'it sounds', svanas-, 'noise', svanah,
'sound, tone', svanah, 'rustling', Olr. senim, 'the
playing of an instrument', OE. geswin, 'music,
song', swinsian, 'to sing', ON. svanr, OE. swan,
'swan', prop, 'the singing bird'. See sonant and
cp. swan. The d in sound is excrescent. Cp.
bound, 'ready', and words there referred to.

## sound
sound, intr. and tr. v., to make a sound. — ME.
sonen, fr. OF. soner (F. sonner), fr. L. sonare, 'to
sound'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: sound-er, п., sound-ing, adj., sound-
ing-ly, adv., sound-ing-ness, n.

## sound
sound, adj., healthy. — ME. sound, sund, fr. OE.
gesund, rel. to OS. gisund, OFris. sund, Du. ge-
zond, OHG. gisunt, MHG. gesunt, G. gesund,
'healthy', OE., OS. swid, 'strong', ON. svinnr,
'intelligent, wise*, Goth, swings, MLG. geswin-
de, MHG. geswinde, 'strong', G. geschwind,
'fast, quick'. Cp. the second element in Milicent.
Derivatives: sound, adv., sound-ly, adv.,
soundness, n.

## sound
sound, п., a narrow channel. — ME. sound, sund,
fr. ON. or OE. sund, 'act of swimming; place of
swimming, the sea; a stretch of water which one
can swim across', for *swum-d, which stands in
gradational relationship to swim (q.v.)

## sound
sound, tr. and intr. v., to measure the depth of
water. — ME. sounden, sonden, fr. OF. ( = F.)
sender, 'to sound', which prob. derives fr. Late
L. subunddre, 'to submerge', fr. sub- and L. undo,
'wave'; see undate. It is also possible that F.
sonder, is of Teut. origin; cp. OE. and ON.
sund, 'a stretch of water which one can swim
across', OE. sundline, 'sounding line', sundrap,
'a sounding rope', and see prec. word.
Derivatives: sound, п., an instrument used to
sound a cavity of the body, sound-able, adj.,
sound-er, п., sound-ing, п., sound-less, adj.,
unfathomable (rare).

## soundless
soundless, adj. — Formed fr. sound, 'that which
is heard", with suff. -less; first used by
Shakespeare,
Derivatives: soundless-ly, adv., soundless-ness,
n.

## sonp
sonp, n. — F. soupe, fr. OF., which is of Teut.
origin. See sup, 'to sip', and words there referred
to.
Derivatives: soup-er, п., soup-y, adj.

## soupcon
soupcon, п., suspicion. — F., 'suspicion', fr. MF.
sospecon, fr. OF., fr. VL. suspectidnem, ace. of
suspectio, corresponding to L. suspicio. See
suspicion.

## sour
sour, adj. — ME. soure, fr. OE. sur, rel. to ON.
surr, Dan., Swed., Norw. sur, MDu. suur, Du.
zuur, OHG., MHG. sur, G. sauer, and cogn.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:727 COLUMN:2 -->
with OSlav. syru, 'moist, raw', Lith. suras,
'salty', suris, 'cheese'. F. sur, 'sour, tart' (whence
the diminutive noun surelle, 'sorrel'), is a Teut.
loan word. Cp. sorrel, the plant, surette.
Derivatives: sour, n. and adv., sour-ed, adj.,
sour-ed-ness, п., sour-ing, п., sour-ish, adj., sour-
ish-ly, adv., sour-ish-ness, п., sour-ly, adv.,
sourness, n.

## source
source, n. — ME. sours, fr. OF. sorse, surse,
sorce (later source), fem. of sors, pp. of sordre,
'to rise', used as a noun, fr. L. surgere, 'to rise'.
See surge and cp 3rd souse, resource.

## sourdine
sourdine, n. — F. See sordine.

## souse
souse, п., salt pickle. — ME. souse, fr. OF. souz,
souce, which—together with OProvenc. solz,
It. soldo, of s.m.—is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG.
sulza (for *sult-Ja), 'brine' and see salt. Cp. also
silt.

## souse
souse, tr. v., 1) to pickle; 2) to soak, drench; intr.
v., to be or become soaked. — ME. sousen, fr.
OF. souz, souce. See prec. word.

## souse
souse, п., the act of swooping down (said of a
hawk). — MF. sors, pp. of sordre, 'to rise, to
spring'. See source.
Derivative: souse, intr. v., to swoop down.

## soutache
soutache, п., braid. — F., fr. Hung, sujtas,
'trimming, galloon', prop, 'blow, strike', fr.
sujt-ani, 'to strike'.

## sontane
sontane, п., a cassock worn by Roman Catholic
priests. — F., fr. earlier sottane, fr. It. sottana,
'petticoat', lit. 'undergarment', which derives fr.
sotio, 'under', fr. L subtus, 'below', fr. sub,
'under'. See sub-. F. soutane (for sottane) owes
its form to the influence of F. sous, 'under'.

## souteneur
souteneur, pimp; bully. — F., 'supporter,
protector; bully', fr. soutenir, 'to sustain', fr. VL.
'sustenire, corresponding to L. sustlnere. See
sustain and cp. sostenuto.

## sonth
sonth, adv. — ME. suth, south, fr. OE. sud,
'southward, in the south', formed—with
compensatory lengthening of the vowel—fr. Old
Teut. *sunp-, whence also OS., OFris. suth,
'southward, in the south', MDu. sum, of s.m.
(whence MHG. suth, 'south wind', earlier New
High German Sud, 'south'; G. Sud, 'south',
goes back to a dial. Du. pronunciation with tf.
Cp. the now more usual G. form Suden, 'south',
which is also of Dutch origin, and the Modern
Du. forms zuid, zuiden, 'south'). Cp. Old
Teut. 'sunpan, 'from the south' (whence OE.
sudan, OHG. sundan), and Old Teut. *sunp{r)a,
'southward' (whence OS. suthar, ON. sudr,
OHG. sundar). These words are possibly rel. to
E. sun. Accordingly south would prop, mean 'the
region of the sun'. For sense development cp.
east. Others connect south, etc., with Teut.
*suinpa-, 'strong; healthy; right' (see sound,
'healthy'). In the sense of this derivation south
would prop, denote the region to the right of
him who faces east (as at the time of prayer).
For sense development cp. Heb. ydmin, Arab.
yamtn, 'the right hand; the south'; cp. also
north and the examples given there.
Derivatives: south, adj., п., and intr. v.,
southerly, adj., southern (q.v.), south-ing, n.

## southern
southern, adj. — ME. southren, fr. OE. suderne,
fr. sud. See south and -em.
Derivatives: southern-er, п., southern-ize tr. v.

## southron
southron, п., inhabitant of the southern part of a
country; an Englishman (archaic). — ME., ap
ter. of southren (under the influence of Brit-on
and other names ending in -on). See prec. word.

## southward
southward, adj. and n. — Compounded of south
and adj. suff. -ward.

## southward
southward, southwards, adv. — Compounded of
south and adv. suff. -ward, -wards.

## sonvenir
sonvenir, п., a memento, keepsake. — F., from
fr. OF., from the verb souvenir,'4o remember',
fr. L. subvenire, 'to come up, come to one's
mind', which is formed fr. sub- and venire, 'to
come'. See come and cp. subvene, subvention.

## sovereign
sovereign, adj. and n. — ME., fr. OF. soverain,
sovrain (F. souverain), fr. ML. superdnus
'chief, principal' (whence also Sp. soberano, It.
soprano), fr. L. super, 'above'. See super- and cp
sopraao. The spelling of E. sovereign (with g) is
due to the influence of-reign, with which the
word sovereign was associated by folk

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:727 COLUMN:3 -->
etymology-
Derivatives: sovereign-ly, adv., sovereign-ness,
п., sovereignty (q.v.)

## sovereignty
sovereignty, n. — ME. soverainte, sovereinte, fr.
OF. soverainete, fr. soverain. See prec. word and
-ty·

## soviet
soviet, n. — Russ. sovet, lit. 'council', formed fr.
pref. so-, 'with, together with', and -vet, which
occurs only in compounds as ot-vet, 'answer,
pri-vet, 'greeting', and is related to OPruss.
vaitiat, 'to speak'. For the pref. see Skupshtina.
Derivatives: soviet, adj., soviet-dom, п., soviet-
ic, adj., soviet-ism, a., soviet-ist, п., soviet-ize,
tr. v., soviet-iz-ation, n.

## sovran
sovran, п., sovereign. — Milton's spelling of
sovereign (as if it derived from It. sovrano).

## sow
sow, п., female pig. — ME. suwe, sowe, fr. OE.
sugu, su, rel. to OS., OHG., MHG. su, G. Sau,
Du. zeug, ON. syr, Dan., Swed. so, and cogn.
with OI. sukardh, 'wild boar, swine', Avestic hit,
'wild boar', Toch. В suwo, 'swine', Gk. ΰς, συς,
'swine', ΰινος, 'swinish', Alb. #/,L. sus, 'swine',
L. sulnus, 'pertaining to swine', OSlav. svinija,
'swine', Lett, suvens, sivens, 'young pig', W.
hucc, Ir. suig, 'swine', Olr. socc, 'snout;
plowshare'. All these words derive from the I.-E.
imitative base *su-, *suw-, which is proved by
the OI. equivalent su-karah, lit. 'maker (= ut-
terer) of the sound su'. Cp. hog, hyena, socket,
soil, 'to make dirty', suilline, sully, Sus, swine,
and the first element in sybotic, syphilis, Hyos-
cyamus, Hystrix.

## sow
sow, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sawen, sowe/ι, fr. OE.
sdwan, rel. to ON. sa, Dan. saa, Swed. sA, OS.
sdian, MDu. sayen, Du. zaaien, OHG. sdwen,
sdjen, MHG. sxjen, G. saen, Goth, saian, fr. I.-E.
base *se(i)-, 'to sow', whence also L. serd, past
tense sevi, pp. satum, 'to sow', OSlav. sejo,
sejati, Lith. seju, seti, 'to sow'. Cp. semen. Cp.
also season, secular, seed and the second element
in colza.
Derivatives: sow-er, п., sow-ing, n.

## sowar
sowar, п., a native cavalry soldier; a mounted
orderly {India). — Pers. sawdr, 'horseman,
rider', fr. MPers. asbdr, fr. OPers. asabdra-,
"horseman', which is compounded of asa-,
'horse', and -bdra, 'carried by'. The first
element is rel. to Avestic aspa-, OI. dsvah, 'horse';
see equine. The second element is rel. to Avestic
baraiti, 'carries; rides', OI. bharati, 'bears'; see
bear, 'to carry'.

## sowens
sowens, n. pi., porridge made from the bran or
husks of oats. — Gael, sughan, name of the
liquid used to make sowens, fr. sugh, 'juice',
which is cogn. with OE. socian, 'to soak', sucan,
'to suck'. See soak, suck.

## sown
sown, pp. of sow. — ME. sowe(n), fr. OE. ge-
sawen, pp. of sdwan. See sow, v.

## soy
soy, п., 1) a Chinese or Japanese sauce for fish
made from soybean; 2) soybeans. — Jap. shoyii,
fr. Chin, chiang-yu, lit. 'soybean oil'.

## soybean
soybean, soya-bean, n. — See prec. word.

## sozin
sozin, п., protein defending the animal body
against bacteria and their toxic products
(biochem.) — Coined fr. Gk. σωζειν, 'to save'.
See Soter and -in.

## spa
spa, п., a mineral spring. — Fr. Spa, a town in
Belgium having mineral springs.
Derivative: spa, intr. v.

## space
space, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) espace, fr. L.
spatium, 'space, room, extent', which prob.
derives fr. I.-E. base *spe(i)-, *sps-, 'to draw,
stretch, span, spread, extend, swell, be
successful', whence also OI. sphayate, 'increases',
sphitdh, 'extended, wide', Gk. σπδν, 'to draw,
to tear away', σπάθη, 'a flat wooden
instrument, a broad fiat sword', L. spes, 'hope', OSlav.
spejo, speti, 'to be successful', spechu, 'endeavor,
aspiration', Lith. speju, speti, 'to have leisure,
be quick enough', OSlav. sporu, 'abundant', OS.
sped, 'success', Du. spoed, 'haste, speed', OHG.,
MHG. spuot, 'success', OS. spddian, 'to cause
to succeed', MDu., Du. spoeden, OHG. spuoten,
'to hasten', G. sich sputen, 'to make haste', OE.
spdwan, OHG. spuo(e)n, 'to prosper, succeed',
and possibly Goth, spediza, 'later', spedumists,
'latest', OHG. spdti, MHG. spate, G. spat,
'late'. Cp. expatiate. Cp. also despair, desperate,

epaulet, epaullere, espadon, espalier, Esperanto,
prosperous, spade, 'a tool for digging', spade on

spathe, spathic, spatula, spay, speck, 'fat meat',
specktioneer, speed, spick, 'fat meat', sphacelate,
sphendone, spheno-, sphygmus, spin, spissated,
spondyl, spontaneous, spoon.
Derivatives: space, tr. v., space-less, adj.,
spacer, п., spac-ing, n.

## spacious
spacious, adj. — ME., either fr. MF. (— F.)
spacieux, fr. OF. spacios, or directly fr. L. spa-
tiosus, 'roomy, ample', fr. spatium. See space
and -ous.
Derivatives: spacious-ly, adv., spacious-ness, П.

## spadassin
spadassin, п., a swordsman, bravo. — F., fr. It.
spadaccino, 'swordsman', fr. spaday *sword\ fr.
L. spatha, fr. Gk. σπάθη. See next word.

## spade
spade, п., a tool for digging. — ME., fr. OE.
spadu, rel. to OS. spado, OFris. spada, Dan.,
Swed., MDu., Du. spade, 'spade', MHG. spat(e),
G. Spaten, and cogn. with Gk. σπάθη, 'a flat
wooden instrument; a broad, two-edged sword'
(whence L. spada, *a broad wooden instrument,
a broad, two-edged sword'). These words are
formed—with t/A-formative element—fr. I.-E.
base *spe(i)-, *sp -, 'to draw, stretch, span,
spread, extend', whence also L. spatium, 'space,
room, extent'. See space and cp. spadassin,
spade on cards» spadilla, spadix, spado, spathe.
Cp. also epaalet and words there referred to.
Derivatives: spade, tr. v., to dig with a spade,
spade-ful, adj.

## spade
spade, п., black heart-shaped figure representing
a spade (cards). — Sp. espada, fr. L. spatha, *a
flat instrument; a broad sword' (whence also It.
spada, F. ёрёе, 'sword'), fr. Gk. σπάθη. See
spade, 'a tool for digging'.

## spade
spade, п., a castrated animal. — Fr. L. spado. See
spado.

## spadger
spadger, п., sparrow (slang). — Altered fr.
sparrow.

## spadiceous
spadiceous, adj., of the nature of a spadix. —
Formed with suff. -eous fr. L. spadix, gen. spd-
dicis. See spadix.

## spadicose
spadicose, adj., spadiceous. — Seeprec. word and
adj. suff. -ose.

## spadille
spadille, п., асе of spades (omber and quadrille).
— Sp. espadilla, dimin. of espada, 'sword', fr. L.
spatha. See spade (on cards).

## spadix
spadix, п., spike of flowers -with a fleshy axis,
surrounded by a spathe (bot.) — L. spadix, 'a
broken palm branch with its fruit', fr. Gk.
σπαδϊξ, which is rel. to σπάδων, 'eunuch',
σπαδίζειν, 'to strip off', σπαν, *to draw, to tear
away'. See spade, 'a tool for digging'.

## spado
spado, п., a castrated person. — L. spado, fr. Gk. .
σπάδων, 'eunuch', which is rel. to σπαν, Чо
draw, to tear away'. See prec. word.

## spaghetti
spaghetti, n. pi., an Italian paste made in solid
cords. — It., pi. of spaghetto, dimin. of spago,
'cord, thread*, which is of uncertain origin.

## spahi
spahi, spahee, п., formerly a Turkish, later an
Algerian cavalryman. — F. spahi, fr. Turk.
sipahi, fr. Pers. sipahi, 'warrior, soldier*, which
is rel. to Avestic spada-, Pahlavi spah, 'army'.
Cp. sepoy.

## spake
spake, archaic past tense of speak. — ME. spake,
fr. earlier spak, fr. OE. spaec, fr. earlier sprite,
past tense of sprecan. See speak.

## Spalax
Spalax,,n., a genus of rodents (zool.) — Gk. σπά-
λαξ, 'mole*, lit. 'the digging animal'. See spoil, n.

## spnil
spnil, п., chip. — ME. spalle, prob. a var. of
spalde, fr. spalden, 'to chip, split' (whence also
obsol. E. spald), rel. to MLG. spalden, spolden,
MDu. spalden, spouden, spouwen, Du. spouwen,
OHG. spaltan, MHG., G. spalten, 'to split',
ON. spjald, speld, 'board, tablet', Goth, spilda,
'table, board', fr. I.-E. base *(s)p(h)el-, 'to
cleave, split', whence also L. spolium, 'skin
stripped from an animal; arms taken from an
enemy; prey, booty'. See spoil, п., and cp. spill.
Cp. also spelt, split.

## spall
spall, tr. v., to chip, split; intr. v., to break up. —
ME. spalden. See spall, n.

## spalpeen
spalpeen, п., a rascal (Irish). — Ir. spailpin,
'rascal', prop, 'conceited', fr. spailp, 'braggart,
conceited', which is rel. to spailp, 'to strut'.

## span
span, n. — ME. spanne, fr. OE. spann, 'stretch,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:728 COLUMN:2 -->
span', rel. to ON. spdnn, Swed. spann, Dan.
spand, MDu. spanne, Du. spanne, span, OHG.
spanna, MHG. spanne, spange, G. Spanne,
'span', and to the Ё. verb span (q.v.)
Derivative: span-less, adj.

## span
span, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spannen, fr. OE.
spannan, 'to clasp, fasten, stretch, span', rel. to
ON. spenna, Dan. spxnde, Norw., OFris.
spanna, MDu., Du. spannen, OHG. spannan,
MHG., G, spannen, 'stretch, span'; prob.
formed—with л-formative element—fr. I.-E.
base *spe(i)-, *spe-, 'to draw, span, stretch,
extend, swell', whence L. spatium, 'space, room,
extent'. See space and cp. spin, spontaneous; cp.
also spancel, spang, spangle, inspan. In some
senses the verb span derives directly from the
noun span (q.v.)
Derivative: spann-er, n.

## span-
span-, form of spano- before a vowel.

## spandrel
spandrel, п., the space between the curve of an
arch and the mold enclosing it (archit.) — ME.
spaundrell, dimin. formed fr. AF. espaundre, fr.
OF. espandre (F. epandre), 'to spread out,
extend', fr. L. expandere. See expand.

## spanemia
spanemia, spanaemia, п., anemia (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. σπανός, 'scarce', and αίμα,
'blood'. See spano- and -emia.

## spangolite
spangolite, п., a basic sulfate of aluminum and
copper (mineral.) — Named after Norman
Spang of Etna-, Alleghany County,
Pennsylvania. For the ending see combining form -lite.

## Spaniard
Spaniard, n. — ME. Spaignard, fr. OF. Espaig-
nard, fr. Espaigne, 'Spain'. See Spanish and -ard,

## spaniel
spaniel, п., any of several breeds of dogs of
Spanish origin. — ME. spainel, 'Spanish; spaniel', fr.
ME. espaignol (F. epagneul), lit. 'a Spanish
dog', fr. Sp. espanol, 'Spanish', fr. VL. Hispd-
niolus, fr. L. Hispania, 'Spain'. See Spanish.

## Spanish
Spanish, adj. — ME. Spainish, fr. Spain, fr. OF.
Espaigne (F. Espagne), fr. L. Hispania, which is
prob. of Iberian origin. The pref. /- in
(Hispania represents the Iberian def. article. Cp.
Hellenistic Gk. Σπανία and Late L. Spania,
'Spain'. For the ending see adj. suff. -ish. Cp.
the two prec. words.

## spank
spank, intr. v., to move swiftly. — Back
formation fr. spanking.

## spank
spank, tr. and intr. v., to strike; п., a slap. — Of
imitative origin.

## spanking
spanking, adj., fine, strong. — Of Scand. origin.
Cp. Dan. spanke, 'to strut'.

## span-new
span-new, adj., quite new. — ME. spannewe, fr.
ON. spannyr, spanyr, which is compounded of
spann, 'chip, shaving', and nyr, 'new'. The first
element is rel. to MDu. spsen, Du. spaan, OHG.,
MHG. span, G. Span, OE. spon, 'chip, shaving';
see spoon and cp. words there referred to. For
the second element see new. For sense
development cp. spick and span.

## spano-
spano-, before a vowel span-, combining form
meaning 'scarce*-(med.) — Gk. σπανό-, σπαν-,
fr. σπανός, 'rare, scarce, uncommon'; of
uncertain origin.

## spar
spar, п., mast, yard. — ME. sparre, 'spar, beam,
rafter', rel. to ON. sparri, Dan., Swed. sparre,
OS., OHG. sparro, MDu., MHG. sparre, Du.
spar, G. Sparren, 'spar, rafter', Du. sperren, 'to
bar, block up', G. sperren, 'to close, shut, bar'
(the orig. meaning was 'to furnish with spars*;
whence 'to close with spars'). See spear.
Derivative: spar, tr. v., to furnish with spars..

## spar
spar, п., a nonmetallic lustrous mineral. — LG.
spar, 'gypsum', fr. MLG., rel. to OE. spxr- in
spxr-stdn, 'gypsum', and to spxren, Of gypsum';
cp. fluorspar. The modern use of spar is due to
a confusion with G. Spat, 'spar'; see spathic
and cp. feldspar.
Derivative: sparr-y, adj.

## spar
spar, intr. v., to fight with the fists. — MF. es-
parer (F. eparer), 'to fight with the fists', fr. It.
sparare, fr. pref. s- (fr. L. ex, 'out of, from') and
parare, 'to ward off'. See 1st ex- and parry.
Derivatives: spar, п., the act of sparring,
sparring, n.

## spar
spar, п., a member of the Women's Reserve of
the U.S. Coast Guard formed November 23,
1942. — Formed from the initials of the motto
of the Coast Guard: Semper Paratus — Always

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:728 COLUMN:3 -->
.fleady ('always ready is the translation of L.
semper pardtus).

## sparable
sparable, п., a small headless nail. — Corruption
of sparrow-bill; so called from its shape.

## spare
spare, adj. — ME., fr. OE. spxr, 'sparing, frugal',
rel. to ON. span, OHG. spar, 'spare', and to
OE. sparian, 'to spare', and cogn. with OSlav.
sporu, 'abundant, long lasting', Russ. sptfryj,
Czech spory, 'abundant, copious', Czech spofiti,
'to spare, save', OI spharafa, 'extensive', sphirdh,
'fat', Arm. p"artiam, 'abundant'. All these
words are derivatives of I.-E. base* spe(i)-,*sp -,
'to draw, stretch, span, spread, extend*. See
space and cp. spare, v.
Derivatives: spare, п., spare-ly, adv., spare-ness,
n.

## spare
spare, tr. and intr. v., to show mercy to, to spare.
— ME. sparen, fr. OE. sparian, rel. to OS. spa-
ron, ΟΝ., S wed. spara, Dan., Norw. spare, OFris.
sparia, MDu., Du. sparen, OHG. sparon, sparen,
MHG. spam, G. sparen, and to OE. spxr,
'sparing, frugal1. See spare, adj., and cp. epergne.
Derivatives: spar-er, п., spar-ing, adj.,
sparingly, adv.

## spamib
spamib, п., a piece of pork consisting of ribs
with a little meat adhering to them. — MLG.
ribbesper, compounded of ribbe, 'rib', and sper,
'spit'; see rib and spear. Ribbesper orig. meant *a
spit thrust through with pieces of ribs'. Earlier
Dan. ribbenspaer and G. Rippespeer are also
borrowed from MLG.

## sparger
sparger, п., I) a sprinkler; 2) a vessel for
sprinkling. — Fr. obsol. sparge, fr. OF. espargier, fr.
L. spargere, 'to scatter, sprinkle'. See sparse
and agential suff. -er and cp. Spergula.

## Sparidae
Sparidae, n. pi., a family of marine fishes, the
sea bream (ichthyol.) — ModL., formed with
suff. -idae fr. L. sparus, 'gilthead', fr. Gk.
σπάρος. See Sparus and cp. sparoid.

## spark
spark, п., a glowing particle. — ME. sparke, sper-
ke, fr. OE. spearca, rel. to MLG. sparke, 'spark*,
sparken, 'to sparkle*, MDu. spranke, 'spark',
spranken, 'to sparkle', fr. I.-E. base *sper(e)g-,
*spher(e)g-, 'to strew, sprinkle', whence also L.
spargeref 'to scatter, sprinkle'. See sparse and cp.
sparger. Cp. also spree, spry.
Derivatives: spark, v. (q.v.), spark-ish, adj.,
spark-ishly, adv., spark-ish-ness, п., spark-less,
adj.,spark-like, adj.,spark-y,adj.,spark-i-ness,n.

## spark
spark, intr. v. — ME. sparken, fr. OE. spearcian,
fr. spearca, 'spark'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: spark-er, п., spark-itig, n.

## spark
spark, п., a gallant, a beau, a loverl — Prob. fr.
ON. sparkr, 'lively', and rel. to spark, 'a glowing
particle'.

## sparkle
sparkle, intr. v., to emit sparks. — ME. sparklen,
freq. of sparken. See spark, v. and п., and freq.
suff. -le.
Derivatives: sparkl-er, п., sparkl-ing, adj.,
sparkl-ing-ly, adv., sparkf-ing-ness, n.

## sparkle
sparkle, п., a little spark. — Formed fr. the noun
spark with dimin. suff. -le.

## sparklet
sparklet, п., a little spark. — Formed fr. the noun
spark with dimin. suff. -let.

## sparoid
sparoid, adj., pertaining to the Sparidae; п., one
of the Sparidae, a sea bream. — Compounded
of Gk. σπάρος, 'gilthead', and -οειδής, 'like', fr.
εϊδος, 'form, shape'. See Sparus and -old.

## sparrow
sparrow, П. — ME. sparwe, sparewe, sparowe, fr.
OE. spearwa, rel. to ON. sporr, OHG. sparo,
MHG. spar (gen. sparwes), G. Sper-ling, Goth.
sparwa, and cogn. with Co. frau, Bret, frao,
'crow', OPruss. spurglis, 'sparrow', Gk. σπέρ-
γουλος, σποργίλος, 'a small field bird', ψαρ,
gen. ψαρός, 'starling* (formed with metathesis
of sp- into ps-), and perh. also with L. parra (for
*psarra ?), *a bird of ill omen'. For a similar
simplification of initial ps to pep. Gk. ψηλαφαν,
'to grope*, with its Latin cognate palpare, 'to
touch, stroke'. Cp. Psaronius, spavin.

## sparrowgrass
sparrowgrass, п., asparagus (colloq.) — Formed
by folk etymology from asparagus.

## sparse
sparse, adj. — L. sparsus, pp. of spargere, 'to
scatter, sprinkle*, fr. I.-E. base *sper(e)g-,
*spher(e)g-, Чо strew, sprinkle; to sprout, swell,
burst', whenc ealso OI. sphurjati, 'it crackles',
Avestic fra-spareya-, *branch, twig', Gk. σφα-
ραγεΤν, Чо crackle', σπαραγμός, 'a tearing,

## sparsile
sparsile, adj., scattered (astron.) — Late L. spar-
silis, fr. L. sparsus, pp. of spargere. See prec.
word and -ile,

## sparsity
sparsity, п., sparseness. — Formed with suff. -ity
fr. L. sparsus, pp. of spargere. See sparse.

## Spartacist
Spartacist, п., an adherent of the extreme
socialist party founded by Karl Liebknecht in 1918.
— Named after Spartacus, leader in the
Gladiatorial War (73-71 B.C.E.) For the ending see
suff. -ist.

## Spartan
Spartan, adj. and n. — L. Spartanus, 'of Sparta',
fr. Sparta, fr. Gk. Σπάρτη, name of the capital
of Laconia.
Derivatives: Spartan-ic, adj., Spartan-ic-al-ly,
adv. Spartan-ism, П., Spartan-ize, tr. and intr.
v., Spartan-ly, adv.

## sparteine
sparteine, spartein, n., a colorless liquid, C15HMNa
(ckem.) — Formed fr. Spartium with suff. -in (e).

## sparterie
sparterie, п., fabric made of esparto grass. — Sp.
esparterie, fr. esparto. See esparto and -ery.

## Spartina
Spartina, п., a genus of plants, the cord or marsh
grass (bot.)— ModL., fr. Gk. σπαρτίνη, 'rope,
cord', fr. σπάρτον, 'rope, cable; Spanish
broom; esparto'. See esparto and cp. next word.

## Spartium
Spartium, п., a genus of plants, the Spanish
broom {bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σπαρτίον, 'a
small cord; Spanish broom', dimin. of σπάρτον,
'rope, cable; Spanish broom; esparto'. See
esparto and cp. prec. word.

## spartle
spartle, intr. v., to kick about (Scot.) — Du. spar-
teien, Чо flounder', fr. MDu. spartelen, sperte-
len, which is of uncertain, possibly imitative,
origin.

## Sparus
Sparus, п., a genus of fishes of the sea bream
family (ickthyol.) — L. sparus, 'gilthead', fr.
Gk. σπάρος, prop, 'a spearshaped fish', and
derivatively identical with L. sparus, 'a hunting
spear", which is prob. cogn. with ON. spjor, OE.
spere, 'spear'. See spear and cp. Sparidae, spar-
oid.

## spasm
spasm, п., involuntary muscular contraction. —
ME. spasme, fr. MF. spasme, fr. L. spasmus, fr.
Gk. σπασμός, 'spasm, convulsion', fr. σπαν,
'to draw, tear, tear out', fr. I.-E. base *spe(i)-,
*spe-, 'to draw, span, stretch, extend'. See
space and cp. spasmatic, perispomenon. Cp. also
stadium.
Derivative: spasm-ic, adj.

## spasmodic
spasmodic, adj., characteristic of spasms,
convulsive. — ML. spasmodicus, formed with adj. suff
-icus (see -ic) fr. Gk. σπασμώδης, 'of the
nature of a spasm', fr. σπασμός, 'spasm', and
-ώδης, 'like*. See spasm and -ode, 'like'.
Derivatives: spasmodic-al, adj., spasmodic-al-ly,
adv., spasmodic-al-ness, n.

## spasmophilia
spasmophilia, п., a disease characterized by a
tendency to spasms (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of Gk. σπασμός, 'spasm, convulsion',
and φιλία, Move, friendship', fr. φίλεΐν, Чо
love'. See spasm, -phi] and 1st -ia.
Derivative: spasmopkil-ic, adj.

## spastic
spastic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized by,
spasm. — L. spasticus, fr. Gk. σπαστικός,
'drawing in', fr. σπαν, Чо draw'. See spasm and
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: spastic-al-ly, adv., spastic-ity, n.
spastic paralysis {med.) — A term coined by the
Irish physician William Stokes (1804-78).

## spat
spat, п., spawn of oyster; intr. v., to spawn (said
of oyster). — Prob. a blend of spit, Чо eject',
and spatter.

## spat
spat, п., a short gaiter. — Abbreviation of
spatterdashes.

## spat
spat, п., a sharp sound, a blow. — Of imitative
origin.

## spat
spat, п., something that splashes. —Du. spat, rel.
to spatten, Чо splash, spatter'; of imitative origin.

## spat
spat, past tense of spit. — ME. spatte, fr. OE.
spxtte, past tense of spsetan. See spit, Чо eject'.

## Spatangina
Spatangina, п., a suborder of sea urchine (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Late L. spatangius, *a kind of sea
urchin', fr. Gk. σπατάγγης, of s.m., which is of
unknown origin.

## spatchcock
spatchcock, п., fowl killed and cooked
immediately. — Prob. an alteration ofspitchcock.
Derivative: spatchcock, tr. v.

## spate
spate, п., flood, esp. flood of a river. — ME., of
uncertain origin; possibly derived fr. OF. es-
poit, 'flood', fr. Du. spuiten, Чо flow, spout',
which is rel. to spout.

## spathaceous
spathaceous, adj., having a spathe; resembling a

## spathe
spathe, п., a sheathing bract (bot.) — F., fr. L.

tree', fr. Gk. σπάθη; formed—with -dh-forma-
tive element—fr. I.-E. base *sp€(i)-, *spe-, Чо
draw, stretch, spread, extend'. See spade, 'a

## spathic
spathic, adj., resembling spar. — F. spathique, fr.

which is formed—with -/-formative element—
fr. I.-E. base *spe(i)-, *spe-, 'to draw, stretch,
spread, extend; a flat piece of wood'. Dan.,
Swed. spat, Du. spaat, It. spatto, Sp. espato,

space and cp. the second element in feldspar,
feldspathic. Cp. also prec. word. For the ending
see adj. suff. -Ic.

## spathiform
spathiform, adj., resembling spar. — A hybrid
coined fr. G. Spat(h) and L. forma, 'form,
shape'. See prec. word and form, n.

## spathose
spathose, adj., spathaceous. — See spathe and
adj. suff. -ose.

## spathose
spathose, adj., spathic. — A hybrid coined fr. G.
Spat(h) (see spathic) and -ose, an adj. suff. of
Latin origin.

## spathous
spathous, adj., of the nature of spathe. — See
spathose, 'of the nature of spathe', and -ons.

## spatial
spatial, adj., pertaining to space. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. L. spatium, 'space'. See spnce.
Derivatives: spatial-ity, п., spatial-ly, adv., spa-
tial-ize, tr. v., spatial-iz-ation, n.

## spatter
spatter, tr. and intr. v. — Prob. of imitative
origin. Cp. Du. spatten, 'to splash, spatter'.
Derivatives: spatter, п., spatter-ing, adj., spat-
ter-ing-ly, adv.

## spatterdashes
spatterdashes, n. pi., a long gaiter. —
Compounded of spatter and dash. Cp. spat, 'short gaiter'.

## spatula
spatula, п., an instrument resembling a knife. —
L., lit. 'a broad piece', dimin. of spat(h)a, 'a

spathe and -ule.
Derivatives: spatul-ar, spatul-ate, adjs.

## spatule
spatule, п., spatula. — F., fr. L. spatula* See prec.
word.

## spatuliform
spatuliform, adj. — See spatula and form, n.

## spavin
spavin, п., disease of the hock joint of the horse.
— ME. spaveyne, fr. OF. esparvin (F. eparvin),
prob. fr. Frankish *sparwun, ace. of *sparo, fr.
Teut. *sparwo, *sparrow', which is rel. to OHG.

so called from the jerky motion of a spavined
horse resembling the hopping of a sparrow.
Cp. It. spavenio, Sp. esparavan, Port. esparavSo,
'spavin*, and see sparrow.
Derivative: spavin-ed, adj.

## spawn
spawn, tr. v., to produce or deposit (eggs or
spawn); intr. v,, to produce or deposit spawn.
— ME. spawnert, for *spaunden, fr. AF. espaun-
dre, corresponding to OF. espandre (F. epan-
dre), 'to spread, scatter, shed*, fr. L. expanderet
Чо spread out'. See expand and cp. spandrel,
Derivatives: spawn, п., spawn-er, n.

## spay
spay, tr. v., to remove the ovaries of a female
animal. — ME. spayen, fr. AF. espeerf Чо cut with
a sword', fr. espee (F. ёрёе), *a sword', fr. L.
spatha, fr. Gk. σπά&η. See spathe and cp. spado.
Derivative: spay-ing, n.

speak, intr. and tr. v. — ME. speken, fr. OE. spe-
can, fr. earlier sprecan, rel. to OS. sprecan,
OFris. spreka, MDu. spreken (var. speken), Du.

to-), 'eloquent'. All these words derive fr. base

meant 'to make a noise, shout, cry, crackle*, fr.

spear, n. — ME. spere, fr. OE. spere, rel to OS.

Derivatives: spear, tr. and intr. v., spear-y, adj.

## special
special, adj. — ME., fr. OF. especial (F. special),

## speciality
speciality, n. — ME. specialite, fr. MF. (= F.)

## specialty
specialty, n. — ME. specialte, fr. MF. especialti,
a var. of specialite. See prec. word.

## specie
specie, п., coin (in contradistinction to paper
money). — Fr. L. specie (more exactly in specie),

specifiable, adj. — Formed fr. specify with suff.

specific, adj. — ML. specificus, fr. L. species. See

Derivatives: specific, п., specific-al, adj., sped-
flc-al-ity, п., specific-al-ly, adv., specific-al-ness,

specification, n. — ML. specificatio, gen. -onis

specify, tr. v. — ME. specifien, fr. OF. specifier

Derivative: specifi-er, n.

## specimen
specimen, n. — L., 'indication, mark, example,

## speck
speck, п., a small spot. — ME. spekke, fr. OE.
specca, rel. to earlier Du. speckel, Du. spikkel,

## speckle
speckle, п., a small spot. — Formed fr. speck, 'a

Derivatives: speckf-ed, speckf-ed-y, adjs.

specktioneer, specksioneer, п., chief harpooner in

## specs
specs, n. pi. — Abbreviation of spectacles.

spectacularism, n. — A hybrid formed fr.

## spectator
spectator, n. — L. spectator, 'looker on, beholder,

at, behold', freq. of specere. See species and

Derivatives: spectator-ial, spectator-y, adjs.,

## spectatress
spectatress, n. — See prec. word and 1st -ess.

## specter
specter, spectre, n. — F. spectre, fr. L. spectrum,

## spectral
spectral, adj. — Formed fr. seeptrum with adj.

-γράφος, fr. γράφει,ν, 'to write'. See spectro-

## spectroheliogram
spectroheliogram, п., a photograph of the sun. —
Se next word and heliogram.

## spectroheliograph
spectroheliograph, п., an instrument for
photographing the sun. — A hybrid word coined fr.
L. spectrum, 'appearance, image*, Gk. ήλιος,
'sun', and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See spectro- and heliograph.

## spectroiogy
spectroiogy, п., the study of spectrum analysis. —
A hybrid coined fr. L. spectrum, 'appearance,

al-ly, adv.

## spectrometer
spectrometer, п., an instrument for measuring

п.,

## spectrophone

πίον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine*. See

## specular

Derivative: specufar-ly, adv.

## Specularia
Specularia, п., a genus of plants, the Venus's

Veneris, ('Venus's looking-glass'), the ML.
name of the campanula. See speculum and -ia.

## specuiate

speculate, pp. of speculari, 'to watch, observe,
examine', fr. specula, 'lookout, watchtower', fr.
specere, 'to see, look at'. See speculum and
verbal suff. -ate and cp. prec. word.

## speculation
speculation, n. — ME., fr. Late L. speculdtio, gen.
-onis, fr. L. speculdtus, pp. of speculari. See prec.
word and -ion.

## speculative
speculative, adj. — ME. speculatif, fr. MF. ( =
F.)speculatif(fem. speculative), fr. Late L.
speculative (fern, speculdtiva), fr. L. speculate, pp.
of speculari. See speculate and -ive.
Derivatives: speculative, п., speculative-ly, adv.,
speculative-ness, n.

## speculator
speculator, n. — L. speculator, 'looker out, spy,
explorer', fr. speculdtus, pp. of speculari. See
speculate and agential suff. -or.
speculator^, adj. — L. speculdtorius, fr.
speculdtus, pp. of speculari See speculate and adj. suff.
-ory.

## speculum
speculum, п., mirror. — L., fr. specere, 'to see,
look at'; see species and cp. speculate. Cp. also
spiegeleisen. For sense development cp. looking-
glass.

## sped
sped, past tense and pp. of the verb speed. — ME.
spedde, fr. OE. spedde, past tense and pp. of
spedan. See speed, v.

## speech
speech, n. — ME. speche, fr. OE. spsec, fr. earlier
sprxc, rel. to OS. spraka, OFris. spreke, MDu.
sprake, Du. spraak, OHG. sprahha, MHG.
sprache, G. Sprache, 'speech*, and to OE.
sprecan, *to speak'. See speak.
Derivatives: speech, п., speech-er, п., speech-ful,
adj., speech-ful-ness, п., speech-ing, п.,
speechless, adj., speech-less-ly, adv., speech-less-ness, n.

## speechification
speechification, n. — Formed from next word.
For the ending see suff. -fication.

## speechify
speechify, intr. v., to make speeches (used
humorously or contemptuously). — A hybrid coined
fr. speech and suff. -fy.
Derivatives: speechifi-er, п., speechify-ing, n.

## speed
speed, n. — ME. spede, fr. OE. sped, 'success,
prosperity', rel. to OS. sped, 'success', Du. spoed,
'haste, speed', OHG., MHG. spuot, 'success',
OS. spodian, *to cause to succeed*, MDu., Du.
spoeden, OHG. spuoten, 'to hasten', G. sich spu-
ten, 'to make haste', OE. spdwan, OHG.
spuo(e)n, 'to prosper, succeed', fr. I.-E. base
*spe(i)-, *sp -, 'to stretch, extend', whence also
L. spatium, 'space, room, extent'. See space and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: speed, v. (q.v.), speedy (q.v.)

## speed
speed, intr. and tr. v. — ME. speden, fr. OE.
spedan, 'to succeed; to make successful', fr.
sped, 'success, prosperity*. See speed, n.
Derivatives: speed-er, п., speed-ing, adj.

## speedily
speedily, adv. — ME. spedily, fr. spedy. See
speedy and adv. suff. -ly.

## speedometer
speedometer, п., an instrument for measuring
speed. — A hybrid coined fr. E. speed, п., and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure1; see meter, 'poetical
rhythm*. The correct form is tachometer (q.v.),
in which both elements are of Greek origin,

## speedy
speedy, adj. — ME. spedy, fr. spede. See speed,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:730 COLUMN:3 -->
and adj. suff. -y.
Derivative: speedi-ness, n.
speer, intr. and tr. v., to inquire (Scot.) — ME.
speren, spiren, fr. OE. spyrian, 'to inquire', prop,
'to follow the track of. See spur,
speiss, п., a mixture of arsenides (metal.) — G.
Speise, 'food; speiss', fr. MHG. spise, fr. OHG.
spisa, fr. ML. spisa, spensa, 'provisions', fr. L.
expensa, 'disbursement', prop. neut. pi. pp. of
expendere, 'to weigh out money, pay down'.
See expense,
spelaean, spelean, adj., pertaining to a cave. —
Formed with suff. -an fr. L. spilaeum, speleum,
'cavern, cave', fr. Gk. σπήλαιον, which is rel. to
Homeric Gk. σπέος, σπεΐος, of s.m. Cp. spe-
luncar.
spelaeology, speleology, п., the study of caves. —
Compounded of Gk. σπήλοαον, 'cavern, cave*,
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)*. See prec. word and -logy,
spclican, n. — A var. of spillikin,
spell, п., charm. — ME., 'speech, talk, tale', fr.
OE., 'narrative, story, saying, discourse,
message', rel. to OS. spell, ON. spjall, 'report,
discourse, tale', OHG., MHG. spel, Goth, spill, of
s.m., OE. spellian, ON. spjalla, OHG. spellon,
Goth, spillon, 'to talk, tell', OE. bispell, 'parable,
proverb, example, story', MHG. bispel, of s.m.,
G. Beispiel, 'example'; and possibly cogn. with
Lett, pelt, 'to blame, slander', Gk. απειλή (for
*άπελνια), 'threat', in the pi. also 'boasts,
bragging words', Arm. afaspel, 'legal tale,
proverb, riddle'. All these words supposedly derive
fr. I.-E. base *(s)pel-, 'to speak with emphasis'.
Cp. spell, 'to name the letters of a word', and
the second element in gospel.
Derivative: spell, tr. v., to charm.

## speli
speli, tr. and intr. v., to name the letters of a word.
— ME. spellen, fr. OF. espel{l)er (¥. epeler), fr.
Frankish *spellon, 'to tell', which is rel. to OHG.
spellon, of s.m. See spell, 'charm',

## spell
spell, tr. v., to take the place of (another) at work;
intr. v., to rest from work for a short time. —
ME. spelen, 'to act for another, represent', fr.
OE. spelian, of uncertain origin; perh. rel. to
OE. spilian, 'to play'. See spiel.
Derivative: spell, п., turn of work.

## spelt
spelt, n. — ME., fr. OE., fr. Late L. spelta, which
is a Teut. loan word. Cp. OHG. spelta, spelza
(MHG. spelte, spelze, G. Spelt), 'spelt', which is
related to G. Spelze, 'glume, chaff', and to OHG
spaltan, 'to cleave, split*, fr. I.-E. base *(s)p(h)el-,
'to cleave, split', whence also L. spolium, 'skin
stripped from an animal; arms taken from an
enemy; prey, booty'. See spoil, п., and cp. spall,
spill,

## spelter
spelter, п., zinc. — Prob. a blend of LG. spialter
or Du. spiauter, 'pewter', and It. peltro, 'pewter*.
See pewter.
Derivative: spelter, tr. v.

## speltoid
speltoid, п., a kind of wheat. — A hybrid coined
fr. Late L. spelta, 'spelt', and Gk. -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape*. See spelt and -oid.

## speluncar
speluncar, adj., of the nature of a cave. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. spelunca, 'cave, cavern,
den', fr. Gk. σπήλυγγα, 'ace. of σπηλυγξ,
'cave', fr. σπήλοαον, 'cavern*. See spelaean. For
the derivation of the Latin word from a Greek
accusative cp. Numidia and words there referred to.

## speluncean
speluncean, adj. — See prec. word and -ean.

## spence
spence, п., larder, pantry (arch.) — Aphetic for
OF. despense (F. dipense), 'expense', fr. despen·
ser, dispenser, 'to distribute'. See dispense and
cp. spend,

## spencer
spencer, п., a trysail. — Of unknown origin.

## spencer
spencer, п., a short overcoat. — Named after
George John, the second Earl Spencer (1758-
1834).

## Spencerian
Spencerian, adj., pertaining to Herbert Spencer
or his philosophy. — Formed with suff. -ian
from the name of Herbert Spencer (1820-1903).

## Spencerianism
Spencerianism, Spencerism, п., the doctrine of
Herbert Spencer. — See prec. word and -ism.

## spend
spend, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spenden, fr. OE.
-spendan (as in aspendan), 'to spend*, fr. L.

## expendere
expendere, 'to weigh out money, pay down', or fr.
OF. despendre, fr. L. dispendere, 'to weigh out'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:731 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SPENSERIAN | 704 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:731 COLUMN:1 -->
See expend, resp. dispense, and cp. spence and
the second element in forspent.
Derivatives: spend-able, adj., spend-er, n.

## Spenserian
Spenserian, adj., pertaining to Edmund Spenser
or his style. — Formed with sufT. -ian from the
name of Edmund Spenser (\ 552-99).

## spent
spent, past tense and pp. of spend.

## Spergnln
Spergnln, п., a genus of plants, the spurry (boi.)
— ModL., 'the sand spurry', fr. L. spargere, 'to
scatter'(see sparger, sparse); so called with
reference to the seeds. Cp. spurry. For the ending
see surT. -ule.

## sperm
sperm, п., semen. — OF. esperme (F. sperme)t fr.
Late L. sperma, fr. Gk. σπέρμα, 'seed, germ,
sperm', fr. σπείρειν, 'to sow, scatter', which is
rel. to σπορά, 'a sowing', fr. I.-E. base *sp(h)er-,
'to sow, scatter', whence also MDu. (— Du.)
sproeien, 'to sprinkle, pour, spray', G. spruhen,
'to sparkle, drizzle'. See spray, 'jet of water', and
cp. spore, sporadic. Cp. also sprout, v. Base
*sp(h)er-, 'to sow, scatter*, is prob. identical
with base *sp(h)er~, 'to move convulsively'. See
spurn and cp. words there referred to. For the
ending -μα in Gk. σπέρμα see surf. -ma.

## sperm
sperm, n. — Abbreviation of spermaceti.

## sperm-
sperm-, form of spermo- before a vowel.

## spermaceti
spermaceti, п., white substance obtained from the
oil of the sperm whale. — ML. sperma ceti,
'sperm of the whale', fr. Late L. sperma, 'semen,
sperm', and L. ceti, gen. of cents, 'whale'. See
prec. word and cetucean.

## spermary
spermary, п., sperm gland. — Formed with subst.
suff. -ary fr. Gk. σπέρμα. See sperm,
'semen'.

## spermat-
spermat-, form of spermato- before a vowel·

## sperinatheca
sperinatheca, п., a receptacle in the oviduct of
female insects to receive the spermatozoa (zool.)
— ModL., formed fr. Gk. σπέρμα, 'seed, germ,
sperm', and θήκη, 'receptacle'. See sperm,
'semen', and theca.
Derivative: spermathec-al, adj.

## spermatic
spermatic, adj., pertaining to sperm. — Formed
with adj. stiff, -ic fr. Gk. σπέρμα, gen.
σπέρματος. See sperm, 'semen*.

## spermatium
spermatium, п., ]) a non-motile gamete in the red
algae; 2) a sporule in some lichens and fungi
{hot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σπερμάτιον, dimin. of
σπέρμα, gen. σπέρματος. See sperm, 'semen'.

## spermato-
spermato-, before a vowel sperm at-, combining
form meaning 'sperm', as in spermatoblast. —
Gk. σπερματο-, σπερματ-, fr. σπέρμα, gen.
σπέρματος. See sperm, 'semen'.

## spermatoblast
spermatoblast, п., a cell from which a
spermatozoon develops. — Formed fr. spermato- and Gk.
βλαστός, 'bud, sprout, shoot'. See blasto-.

## spermatogenesis
spermatogenesis, п., the development of
spermatozoa. — ModL., compounded of spermato- and
genesis.

## spermatogenous
spermatogenous, adj., producing sperm. —
Compounded of spermato- and -genous.

## spermatoid
spermatoid, adj., resembling sperm. —
Compounded of spermato- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like*,
fr. εϊδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## spermatophorc
spermatophorc, п., a capsule containing
spermatozoa. — Compounded of spermato- and Gk.
-φόρος, 'bearing'. See -phore.
.Derivative: spermatophor-al, adj.

## Spermatophyta
Spermatophyta, п., pi., the phylum of the most
highly developed plants (bot.) — Lit. 'seed
plants', fr. Gk. σπέρμα, gen. σπέρματος, 'seed',
and φυτά, pi. of φυτόν, 'plant'. See spermato-
and -phyte.

## spermatorrhea
spermatorrhea, spermatorrhoea, п., involuntary
flow of sperm (med.) — Medical L.,
compounded of spermato- and Gk. -ρροία, from the stem
of petv, 'to flow'. See rheo-.

## spermatozoal
spermatozoal, adj., pertaining to a spermatozoon.
— See spermatozoon and adj. suff. -al.

## spermatozoan
spermatozoan, adj., spermatozoal. — See next
word and -an.

## spermatozoon
spermatozoon, п., a male sexual cell serving to
fertilize the egg (zool.) — ModL., compounded
of spermato- and Gk. ζώον, 'animal'. See zoo-.

## spermine
spermine, also spcrmin, п., a crystalline basic
compound C10H36N4 (biochem.) — See sperm
and chem. suff. -ine, -in.

## spermism
spermism, п., the old theory that the
spermatozoon contains the germ of the future animal. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:731 COLUMN:2 -->
See sperm and -ism.

## spermist
spermist, п., an adherent of the theory of
spermism. — See prec. word and -ist.

## spermo-
spermo-, before a vowel sperm-, combining form
meaning 'sperm*. — See sperm.

## spermology
spermology, п., the study of seeds in botany. —
Compounded of spermo- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy,

## spermophile
spermophile, п., a burrowing rodent of the genus
Citellus. — Lit. 'seed lover', fr. Gk. σπέρμα,
'seed*, and φίλος, 'friend'. See sperm and-phile.

## sperrylite
sperrylite, п., a platinum arsenide {mineral.) —
Named after the chemist Francis L. Sperry of
Sudbury, Ontario, Canada. For the ending see
combining form -lite,

## spew
spew, intr. and tr. v. — ME. spewen, fr. OE.
spiwan (strong v.), speowan, (weak v.), 'to spit',
rel. to OS. spiwan, ON. spyja, Dan., Swed. spy,
OFris. spi(w)a, MDu. spieny spijen, spuwen,
spouwen, Du. spuwen, OHG. spl(w)an, MHG.
spi(w)en, G. speien, Goth, speiwan, 'to spit', and
cogn. with Gk. πτόειν, 'to spit', πτύαλον,
'spittle', L. spuere, 'to spit', Lith. spiauju,
spiauti, OSIav. pljujq, pljivati, of s.m. All these
words derive fr. the I.-E. imitative base *spyu-t
*spyeu-, 01. stkivati, 'he spits', Arm. t'k'anem,
Ί spit', are also of imitative origin, but not
related to the words mentioned. See spit, 'to eject*,
and cp. puke. Cp. also conspue, cuspidor, ptyatin,
sputum.
Derivatives: spew, п., spew-er, п., spew-ing, n.

## sphacelate
sphacelate, intr. v., to become gangrenous. —
Medical L. sphacelat(us), pp. of sphacelate, 'to
mortify', fr. sphacelus, 'gangrene*. See sphacelus
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: spkacelat-ion, n.

## sphacelous
sphacelous, adj., gangrenous. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. Gk. σφάκελος, 'gangrene'. See next
word.

## sphacelus
sphacelus, п., gangrene (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. σφάκελος, 'convulsive movement,
gangrene', which possibly derives fr. *sp(k)ek-, -k-
enlargement of I.-E. base *spe(i)-, *sp&-, 'to
draw, stretch, spread, extend'; see Hofmann,
EWG., p. 345, s.v. σφάκελος, See space and cp.
sphygmus.

## sphaer-
sphaer-, form of sphaero- before a vowel.

## Sphaeralcea
Sphaeralcea, п., a genus of plants of the mallow
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
σφαΤρα, 'sphere* (see sphere), and L. alcea,
'mallow', fr. Gk. άλκαία, 'vervain mallow*, which
is of uncertain origin.
sphaero», before a vowel sphaer-, combining form
meaning 'sphere, spherical'. — Gk. σφαιρο-,
σφαιρ-, fr. σφαΤρα. See sphere.

## Sphagnum
Sphagnum, п., a genus of mosses (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. σφάγνος, 'a kind of fragrant moss*,
which is of uncertain origin.

## sphalerite
sphalerite, п., an ore of zinc, ZnS (mineral.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. σφαλερός,
'slippery; uncertain; deceitful* (the mineral was
called 'deceitful', because the miners mistook it
for lead ore), fr. σφάλλει, 'to cause tb fall,
overthrow', orig. prob. meaning 'to put an obstacle
before somebody', and rel. to σφαλός, 'block
of wood', σφέλας, 'block of wood, log*,
ά-σφαλής, 'firm, fast; sure, certain*, lit.
'unshakable', σφαλάσσειν (Hesychius), 'to cut'.
These words derive fr. I.-E. base *(s)p(k)el-, 'to
cleave, split', whence also L. spolium, 'skin
stripped from an animal; arms taken from an'
enemy; prey, booty'; see Hofmann, EWG,. p.
345 s.v. σφάλλω. See spoil, п., and cp. words
there referred to.

## sphen-
sphen-, form of spheno- before a vowel,

## sphendone
sphendone, п., a headband worn by women in
Greece (Greek antiq.) — Gk. σφενδόνη, 'sling,

## anything resembling a sling
anything resembling a sling, headband', rel. to
σφόνδυλος, σπόνδυλος, 'vertebra*, σφαδάζειν,
'to move convulsively', fr. base *sp(h)ed-,
*sp(h)end-, enlargement of base *spi(l)-, spe-, 'to

## draw
draw, stretch, spread, extend'. See space and
words there referred to and cp. spondyl. Cp. also

## L. /undo
L. /undo, 'sling, casting net, purse', and see

## Fronde
Fronde,

## sphene
sphene, п., titanite (mineral.) — F. sphene, fr. Gk.
σφήν, 'wedge'; so called from the usual shape

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:731 COLUMN:3 -->
of its crystals. See spheno-.

## spheno-
spheno-, before a vowel sphen-, a combining form
meaning 'wedge'. — Gk. σφηνο-, σφην-, fr.
σψήν> ёеп- σφη^ός, 'wedge*, which stands for
*σφάν (ср. σφάνιον = *σφήνιον, abbreviation
of σφηνόπους, 'with wedge-shaped legs); prob.
cogn. with ON. spann, sponn, 'splinter', OHG.
span, of s.m., OE. spon, 'chip of wood*. See
spoon.

## sphenoccipital
sphenoccipital, adj., of the sphenoid and occipital
bones (anat.) — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. σφήν,
gen. σφηνός, 'wedge', and L. occipitalis,
'pertaining to the back of the head'. Seespheno-and
occiput.

## sphenocephalic
sphenocephalic, sphenocephalous, adj., having a
wedge-shaped head (cranial.) — Compounded
of Gk. σφήν, gen. σφηνός, 'wedge', and κεφαλή,
'head'. See spheno- and cephalic, resp. -cephal-
ous.

## sphenocephaly
sphenocephaly, п., wedge shape of the head
(craniol) — See prec. word and -y (representing
Gk. -ία).

## sphenogram
sphenogram, п., a cuneiform character. —
Compounded of Gk. σφήν, gen. σφηνός, 'wedge*,
and γράμμα, 'letter, character', lit. 'that which
is written'. See spheno- and -gram.

## sphenographic
sphenographic, adj., pertaining to, or written jn,
cuneiform characters. — Compounded of Gk.
σφήν, gen. σφηνός, 'wedge', and γραφικός,
'pertaining to writing', fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See
graphic.

## splenography
splenography, п., cuneiform writing. — See prec.
word and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## sphenoid
sphenoid, adj., wedge-shaped. — Gk. σφηνοειδής,
compounded of σφήν, gen. σφηνός, 'wedge',
and -οειδής, 'like*, fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
spheno- and -oid.
Derivative: sphenoid-al, adj.

## sphenoid
sphenoid, п., the sphenoid bone (anat.) — Fr. L.
os sphenoideum, 'wedge-shaped bone',
translation of Gk. όστοϋν σφηνοειδές, a name coined
by Galen from the adjective σφηνοειδής,
'wedge-shaped'. See prec. word.

## spheral
spheral, adj., pertaining to a sphere. — L. sphae-
rdlis, fr. sphaera. See next word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: spheral-ity, n.

## sphere
sphere, n. — ME. spere, fr. OF. espere (F. sphere),
fr. Gk. σφαΤρα, 'ball, globe, sphere', which is of
uncertain origin. It possibly meant orig. 'that
which rebounds', and is rel. to σπαίρειν, 'to
move convulsively', from I.-E. base *sp(h)er·, 'to
move convulsively, to jerk', whence also 01.
spkurati, 'kicks, tramples', OE. spurnan, 'to kick
with the foot, spurn'; see Hofmann, EWG., pp.
344-345 s.v. σφαΤρα, and Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., II, p. 512 s.v. sperno. See spurn and cp.
the second element in atmosphere, chromosphere
hemisphere, hydrosphere, stratosphere.
Derivatives: sphere, tr. v., spheric (p..v.), spher-
У> adj.

## spheric
spheric, adj., spherical. — See next word.
Derivatives: spherical (q.v.), spheric-ity, n.

## spherical
spherical, adj., 1) shaped like a sphere; 2)
pertaining to a sphere or spheres. — Formed with
adj. suff. -al fr. Late L. sphaericus, fr. Gk.
σφαιρικός, fr. σφαίρα. See sphere and adj. suff.
-ic.
Derivatives: spherical-ly, adv., sphericat-ness,n.

## spherics
spherics, п., spherical geometry and trigonometry.
— See spheric and -ics.

## spharo-
spharo-, combining form. — See sphaero-.

## spheroid
spheroid, п., a body resembling, but not identical
with, a sphere. — Late L. spkaeroeides, fr. Gk.
σφαιήοειδής, 'spherical', which is compounded
of σφαίρα, 'ball, sphere', and -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See sphere and -oid.
Derivatives: spkeroid-al, adj., spheroid-al-ly,
adv., spheroid-ic, spheroid-ic~al, adjs., spheroid-
ic-ity, n.

## spherometer
spherometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
curvature of a spherical surface. — F. sphero-
metre. See sphere- and -meter.

## spherule
spherule, п., a minute sphere. — Late L. sphae-
rula, dimin. of L. sphaera, fr. Gk. σφα,ϊρα. See
sphere and -uie.
Derivatives: spherul-ar, spherul-ate, adjs.

## spherulite
spherulite, п., a spherical group of minute crystals
found in glassy rocks (petrogr.) — See prec.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:732 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 70S | SPINEL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:732 COLUMN:1 -->
word and subst. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: spherulit-ic, adj., spherulit-ize, tr. v.

## sphincter
sphincter, п., a muscular ring surrounding an
opening of the body (anat.) — Late L., fr. Gk.
σφιγκτήρ, 'that which binds tight, lace, band;
muscle closing an aperture', fr. σφίγγειν, Чо
bind tightly, press together', which is of
uncertain origin; cp. Sphinx. In its anatomical sense,
σφιγκτήρ was first used by Galen. See Joseph
Hyrtl, Onomatologia anatomica, p. 484.
Derivatives: sphincter-al, sphincter-ate, sphinc-
ter-ial, sphincter-ic, adjs.

## Sphinx
Sphinx, п., 1) any Egyptian statue or figure having
the body of a lion and the head of a man, ram.
or hawk; specif., cap., the huge statue near the
pyramids of Gizeh in Egypt, with a man's head
and a lion's body; 2) in Greek mythology, a
winged monster with a woman's head and lion's
body; specif., the Sphinx of Thebes, who
strangled those unable to solve a riddle propounded
by her; Oedipus succeeded in solving the riddle
and the Sphinx killed herself. — L. sphinx, fr.
Gk. σφίγξ, 'sphinx; rapacious person', lit.
meaning 'she that binds', or 'she that strangles',
fr. σφίγγειν, Чо draw tight, bind tightly'. See
sphincter and cp. criosphinx.

## sphragide
sphragide, п., Lemnian earth. — L. sphragis, gen.
-idis, fr. Gk. σφραγές, gen. -ίδος, 'a seal'; so
called because sold in sealed packets. See next
word and -ide.

## sphragistic
sphragistic, adj., pertaining to a seal. — Gk.
σφραγιστικός, fr. σφραγιστός, 'sealed', verbal
adj. of σφραγίζειν,'to close with aseal, to seal',
fr. σφραγίς, 'seal', which is of uncertain origin.
For the ending see suff. -istic.

## sphragistics
sphragistics, п., the science of seals. — See prec.
word and -ics.

## sphygmic
sphygmic, adj., pertaining to the pulse. — Gk.
σφυγμικός, fr. σφυγμός. See sphyginus and adj.
suff. -ic.

## sphygmo-
sphygmo-, combining form meaning pulse. — Gk.
σφυγμό-, fr. σφυγμός. See sphygmus.

## sphygmogram
sphygmogram, п., record of the pulse made by a
sphygmograph. — Compounded of sphygino-
and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is written'. See
-gram.

## sphygmograph
sphygmograph, п., an instrument for recording
the pulse. — Compounded of sphygmo- and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: sphygmograph-ic, adj., sphygmo-
graph-y, n.

## sphygmoid
sphygmoid, adj., pulselike. — Compounded of
sphygmo- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. εϊδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## sphygmology
sphygmology, п., the study of the pulse. —
Compounded of sphygmo- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic'). See -logy.

## sphygmomanometer
sphygmomanometer, п., an instrument for
measuring blood pressure in the arteries. —
Compounded of sphygmo- and manometer.

## sphygmometer
sphygmometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the strength of the pulse beat. — Compounded
of sphygmo- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## sphyguiophone
sphyguiophone, п., an instrument for rendering
the pulse beat audible. — Compounded of
sphygmo- and Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice'. See
phone; 'speech sound'.

## sphygmoscope
sphygmoscope, п., an instrument for examining
the pulse beat. — Compounded of sphygmo-
and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at,
examine'. See -scope.

## sphygmus
sphygmus, п., the pulse (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. σφυγμός, 'pulsation', fr. σφύζειν, (for
*σφύγ-ιειν), 'to beat, pulsate', whence also
όί-σφυκτος, 'pulseless'; possibly derived fr.
*sphuk-, a gradational var. of *sph k-, 'to move
convulsively', whence σφάκελος, 'convulsive
movement, gangrene'; see sphacelus and cp.
sphygmo-, asphyxia. See Hofmann, EWG,, p.
347 s.v. σφύζω.

## Sphyraena
Sphyraena, п., a genus of pikelike fishes (icktkyol.)
— ModL., fr. L. sphyraena, 'a kind of seafish',
fr. Gk. σφύραινα, 'hammer fish*, fr. σφϋρα,
'hammer*, which is rel. to σφυρόν, 'ankle*,
σπαίρειν, 'to move convulsively*, from I.-E.
base *(s)p(h)er-, 'to move convulsively'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:732 COLUMN:2 -->
spurn and cp. words there referred to.

## Sphyraenidae
Sphyraenidae, n. pi., a family of fishes {icktkyol.)
—ModL.,formed fromprec. word with suff.-idae.

## spica
spica, п., a spike {bot.) — L. spica, 'ear of corn*.
See spike and cp. spicate.

## s pic ate
s pic ate, spicated, adj., 1) forming a spike; 2)
arranged in spikes. — L. spicatus, pp. of spicare,
'to furnish with ears or spikes', fr. spica. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also -ed.

## spiccato
spiccato, adj., detached (musical direction) — It.,
pp. of spiccare, 'to detach, cut off', formed with
change of pref. fr. impiccare, 'to hang', which is
of uncertain etymology.

## spice
spice, n. — ME., fr. OF. espice (F. epice), fr. Late
L. species^ 'spice', fr. L. species, 'kind, sort'. See
species.
Derivatives: spice, tr. v., spic-ed, adj., spic-er, п.,
spic-y, adj., spic-i-ly, adv., spic-i-ness, n.

## spicery
spicery, n. — ME. spicerie, fr. OF. espicerie (F.
epicerie), fr. espice. See spice and -ery.

## spick
spick, п., fat meat (obsol.) — ME. spyk, fr. OE.
spic. See speck, 'fat meat'.

## spick-and-span
spick-and-span, adj. — Short for spick-and-span-
new, lit. 4iail-and-chip-new', fr. spick, a var. of
spike, 'nail', and span-new.

## spicular
spicular, adj., spiculate. — Formed with suff. -ar
fr. L. spiculum. See spicule.

## spiculate
spiculate, adj., 1) having the shape of spicules; 2)
covered with spicules. — Formed with adj. suff.
-ate fr. L. spiculum. See spicule.

## spicule
spicule, п., any small pointed object. — F., fr. L.
spiculum. See next word.

## spiculum
spiculum, п., any small, sharply pointed organ
(zool.) — L. spiculum, 'a small, sharp point, dart,
arrow', dimin. of spicum, a collateral form of
spica. See spica and -ule.

## spider
spider, n. — ME. spyder, fr. earlier spithre, fr. OE.
spidra, fr. Teut. *spen-pro- (whence also Dan.
spinder), lit. 'spinner', formed fr. OE. spinnan
with agential suff. -er. Cp. MLG., MDu., MHG.,
G. spinne, Du. spin, 'spider', and see spin.
Derivatives: spider-ly, adj., spider-y, adj.

## spiderling
spiderling, п., a young spider. — Formed fr.
spider with dimin. suff. -ling.

## spiegeleisen
spiegeleisen, п., a variety of cast iron. — G., lit.
'mirror iron', fr. Spiegel, 'mirror*, and Eisen,
'iron'. The first element derives fr. OHG. spia-
gal, fr. ML. speglum, fr. L. speculum; see
speculum. For the second element see iron.

## spiel
spiel, п., speech; intr. v., to talk. — G. Spiel,
'play, performance', spielen, 'to play', fr. OHG.
spil, resp. spilon, rel. to OFris. spil, spelt MDu.,
Du. spelf 'play', OE. spilian, OS. spilon, ON.
spila, OFris. spilia, MDu., Du. spelen, 'to play'.
Cp. the second element in bonspiel, glockenspiel,
krlegspiel, Singspiel. Cp. also spell, 'to take the
place of (another) at work*,

## spifflicate
spifflicate, spiflicate, tr. v., to confound (slang).
— Of uncertain origin.

## spiflfy
spiflfy, adj., smartly dressed (slang). — Prob. of
imitative origin.
Derivatives: spiff-i~ly, adv., spiff-i-ness, n.

## Splgelia
Splgelia, п., a genus of plants, the pinkroot (bot.)
— ModL., named after the Flemish botanist
Adrian van den Spieghel, Lat. Spigelius (1558-
1625).

## spigot
spigot, п., a small plug or peg. — ME., prob. fr.
OProvenc. *espigoty dimin. of espiga, 'ear of
corn', fr. L. spica, of s.m. See spica, spike.

## spike
spike, n. — ME., rel. to ON. spikry 'spike, nail',
Swed., Norw. spik, 'nail', MDu. spicher, Du.
spijfyer, 'nail', OE. spaca, OHG. speihha, 'spoke',
fr. l.-E. base *{s)pei-, *(s)pi~t 'something
pointed', whence also L. spica, 'ear of corn', spina,
'thorn, prickle, backbone', pinna, *pin;
battlement along the top of a wall', Toch. A spin-ae
(dat.), 'peg', Gk. σπιλάς, σπίλος, 'rock, cliff",
Lett, spile, 'a wooden fork', Lith. speigliaX (pi.),
'thorns', spitna, 'tongue of a buckle', OE. spitu,
'a spit'. Cp. pinna, spica, spiculum, spigot, spine.
Cp. also spile, spire, 'a tapering roof, spit, 'a

## pointed bar of iron'
pointed bar of iron', spitz, spoke, and the first
element in spick-and-span.
Derivatives: spike, tr. v., spik-ed, adj., spik-er,
п., spik-y, adj., spik-i-ly, adv., spik-i-neis, n.

## spikelet
spikelet, n. — Formed fr. spike with dimin. suff.
-let.

## spikenard
spikenard, n. — ME., fr. ML. spica nardi, 'spike

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:732 COLUMN:3 -->
of nard'. See spike and nard.

## Spilanthes
Spilanthes, п., a genus of plants of the thistle
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
σπίλος, 'stain', which is of uncertain origin, and of
άν&ος, 'flower'. See anther.

## spile
spile, п., a small plug; a vent peg. — MLG.,
'splinter', rel. to Du. spijl, 'bar, skewer', MHG.
spille, 'peg*, ON. spila, G. Speller, 'skewer*, fr.
I.-E. base *(s)pe(i)-> *(s)pi-, 'something
pointed*. See spike.
Derivatives: spile, tr. v., spil-ing, n.

## spill
spill, tr. v., to cause to run out; intr. v., to flow.
— ME. spillen, fr. OE. spilian, Чо destroy, kill',
rel. to OHG. spildan, 'to spill*, OS. spildian, ON.
spilia, 'to destroy', and to MDu. spillen, 'to
waste', MDu. spalden, OHG. spaltan, 'to split'.
See spail, 'chip'.
Derivatives: spill-er, п., spilth (q.v.)

## spill
spill, п., splinter. — Prob. a blend of spile and
MDu. spille, 'stalk, spindle'. See spindle and cp.
spillikin.
spiller» Ц.., a fishing line. — Ir. spilear.

## spillikin
spillikin, also spellican, п., a strip of wood or bone
used in the game of jackstraws; in the pi., the
game of jackstraws. — ME. spelleken, fr. MDu.
spilleken, dimin. of spille, 'peg, pin', which is
prob. rel. to OE. speld, 'splinter of wood'. See
spill» 'splinter', and -kin.

## spilth
spilth, п., 1) the act of spilling; 2) something
spilled. — Formed fr. spill, v., with subst. suff.
-th.

## spin
spin, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spinnen, fr. OE.
spinnan, rel. to ΟΝ., Swed., OFris. spinna, Dan.
spinde, Du. spinnen, OHG. spinnan, MHG., G.
spinnen, Goth, spinnan, and cogn. with OSlav.
pinq, 4 span', Arm. henum, Ί weave', Gk.
πάτος (for *pntos), 'garment', lit. 'that which is
spun', σπινδεΐρα (Hesychius), 'plow', Lith. pinu,
*I plait, braid', spandau, Ί span', OSlav. pqto,
'fetter*, MW. cy-ffiniden, 'spider*. All these
words are derivatives of I.-E. *spen-, 'to draw,
stretch, span, spin*, an -«-enlargement of I.-E.
base *spi(i)-t *sp -, 'to draw, stretch, span,
spread, extend1; see Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p.
728 s.v. spinnen. See space and words there
referred to and cp. esp. span, v. Cp. als'o spider,
spindle, spinster.
Derivatives: spin, п., spinn~er, п., spinn-ery, n.

## spin-
spin-, form of spino- before a vowel.

## spinaceous
spinaceous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling,
spinach. — See next word and -aceous.

## spinach
spinach, n. — MF. espinache, espinage (whence
—with change of suff.—MF. espinarde, espi-
nard, F. epinard), fr. ML. spinachia, spinachium,
which—prob. through the medium of Sp. espi-
naca and Andalusian Arab, isbinakh—derives
fr. Arab, isbanakh, earlier isfanakh, isfdnakh, fr.
Pers. aspanakh, 'spinach'. Fr. ML. spinachia,
spinachium derive also It. spinace and—with
change of suff.—OProvenc. espinarc and MHG.
spinat (G. Spinat).

## spinal
spinal, adj. — Late L. spinalis, 'spinal', fr. L.
spina. See spine and adj. suff. -al.

## spindle
spindle, n. — ME. spindel, fr. OE. spinel, prop,
'an instrument for spinning', fr. spinnan, 'to
spin'; rel. to OS. spinnila, OFris. spindel, OS.,
OHG. spinnila, MHG. spinnel, G. Spindel. See
spin and instrumental suff. -le. For the -d-,
which is epenthetic, cp. kindred.
Derivatives: spindle, intr. v., spindl-ed, adj.,
spindl-er, п., spindl-ing, adj. and п., spindl-y,
adj., spindl-i-ness, n.

## spindrift
spindrift, n. — A var. of spoondrift.

## spine
spine, n. — ME., 'thorn, backbone', fr. OF. espine
(F. epine), fr. L. spina, 'thorn, spine, prickle,
backbone*, which is cogn. with Toch. A spin-ae
(dat.), 'peg';fr. I.-E. base *(s)pi~, *(s)pei-,
'something pointed', whence also L. spica, 'ear of
corn', ON. spikr, 'spike, nail*. See spike and
words there referred to and cp. spinel, 'a
mineral', spinney. Cp. also the second element in
porcupine. Cp. also fin.
Derivatives: spin-edt adj., spine-less, adj., spine·
less-ly, adv., spine-less-ness, п., spin-y, adj., spin-
i-nesst n.

## spinel
spinel, п., a crystalline mineral. — F. spinelle, fr.
It. spinella, dimin. οι spina, fr. L. spina, 'thorn,
spine'. See spine.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:733 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SPINEL | 706 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:733 COLUMN:1 -->

## spinel
spinel, п., yarn used for making tape. — G.
Spinal.

## spinet
spinet, п., a primitive harpsichord. — Named
after its inventor Giovanni Spinetti of Venice
(cca 1500).

## spini-
spini-, combining form meaning: 1) 'thorn'; 2)
'backbone'. — Fr. L. spina. See spine.

## spiniferous
spiniferous, adj., producing spines. —
Compounded of spini- and -ferous.

## Spinifex
Spinifex, п., a genus of Australian plants (bot.) —
ModL. Spinifex, compounded of L. spina,
'thorn', and -fex, gen. -ficis, 'making', fr.facere,
'to make, do'. See spini- and fact. The second
element in Spinifex was formed on analogy of
L. an if ex, 'craftsman' (see artifice), and other
Latin nouns ending in -fex.

## spiniform
spiniform, adj., having the shape of a spine. —
Compounded of spini- and L. forma, 'form,
shape'. See form, n.

## spink
spink, п., the chaffinch. — ME. spynke, of Scand.
origin; cp. Swed. spink, 'sparrow', dial Norw.
spikke, 'a kind of small bird'. Cp. also Gk.
σπίγγος, 'chaffinch', σπίζα (for *spig-ya), of
s.m., σπίζειν (for *spig-yein), 'to chirp, pipe'.
All these words are of imitative origin. Cp.
finch.

## spinnaker
spinnaker, п., a large triangular sail {naut.) —
Formed fr. spinx, misreading of Sphinx, the
name of a yacht that carried the sail.

## spinneret
spinneret, п., silk spinning organ of the silkworm.
— Diminutive formed from the noun spinner.
See spin, agential suff. -er and -et.

## sphiney
sphiney, п., copse, thicket. — MF. espinaye (F.
epinaie), fr. VL. *spin€ta, fr. L. spinetum, 'thorn
hedge, thicket*, fr. spina, 'thorn, spine'. See
spine. For the Latin surf, -etum cp. arboretum,
pinetum.

## spino-
spino-, before a vowel spin-, combining form used
in the sense of: ]) 'thorn, spine'; 2) 'the spinal
cord'. — Fr. L. spina. See spine.

## spinose
spinose, adj., spiny, prickly. — L. spindsus, 'full
of thorns, thorny', fr. spina, 'thorn, spine'. See
spine and adj. surf, -ose.
Derivatives: spinose-ly, adv., spinose-ness, n.

## spinosity
spinosity, n. — Late L. spinositds, 'thorniness', fr.
L. spindsus. See prec. word and -ity.

## spinoso-
spinoso-, combining form meaning 'spinose'. —
L. spinoso-, fr. spindsus. See spinose.

## spinous
spinous, adj., 1) having spines; 2) difficult to
handle. — L. spindsus, 'thorny'. See spinose and
-ous.
Derivative: spinous-ness, n.

## Spinozism
Spinozism, п., the philosophy of Spinoza. —
Formed with sufT. -ism fr. the name of Baruch
( = Benedict) de Spinoza (1632-77).

## Spinozist
Spinozist, п., an adherent of the philosophy of
Spinoza. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivative: Spinozist-ic, adj.

## spinster
spinster, п., 1) a woman who spins; 2) an
unmarried woman. — ME. spinnester, 'a woman who
spins', fr. spinnen, 'to spin'. See spin and -ster.
Derivatives: spinster-hood, п., spinsterial (q.v.),
spinster-ish, adj., spinster-ish-ly, adv., spinster-
ly, adv. and adj.

## spinsterial
spinsterial, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. spinster
and -ial, a suff. of Latin origin.

## spinthariscope
spinthariscope, п., an instrument for examining
the scintillation caused by the impact of the
alpha rays against a screen. — Coined fr. Gk.
σπιν&αρίς, 'spark', and -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν,
'to look at, examine*. The first element is rel. to
σπινθήρ, 'spark', and cogn. with Lith. spindiiu,
spindeti, 'to shine', Lett, spuo-drs, 'brilliant'. For
the second element see -scope.

## spinule
spinule, п., a small spine. — L. spinula, 'a little
thorn', dimin. of spina. See spine and -ule.
Derivatives: spinul-ate, spinul-ated, adjs., spinul-
ation, n.

## spinuliferous
spinuliferous, adj., bearing spinules. —
Compounded of L, spinula (see prec. word) and
-ferous.

## spinuliform
spinuliform, adj., having the form of spinules. —
Compounded of L. spinula, 'a little thorn', and
forma, 'form, shape*. See spinule and form, n.

## spinulose
spinulose, adj. — ModL. spinulosus, 'covered with
spinules', fr. L. spinula. See spinule and adj. suff.
-ose.
Derivative: spinulose-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:733 COLUMN:2 -->

## spiracle
spiracle, п., breathing hole, air hole. — ME.
spirakle, fr. L. spiraculum, 'breathing hole', fr.
spirare, 'to breathe'. See spirit and -de.

## spiracular
spiracular, adj., pertaining to a spiracle. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. spiraculum. See prec.
word.

## spiraculate
spiraculate, adj., bearing spiracles. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. spiraculum. See spiracle.

## Spiraea
Spiraea, п., a genus of plants of the rose family
(pot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σπείραία, 'Spiraea ul-
maria', fr. σπειραν, 'to twist', fr. σπεϊρα, 'coil,
twist' (see spire, 'coil'); so called in allusion to
the twisting pods. Cp. aspirin.

## spiral
spiral, adj. — ML. spiralis, fr. L. spira, 'coil'. See
spire, 'coil', and adj. suff. -aj.
Derivatives: spiral, п., and tr. and intr. v., spiral-
ity, п., spiral-ize, tr. v., spiral-ization, п.,
spirally, adv.

## spirant
spirant, n. and adj. (phon.) — Fr. L. spirdns, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of spirare, 'to breathe, blow'.
See spirit and -ant.

## spirated
spirated, adj., spirally twisted. — Formed fr. L.
spira, 'coil' (see 2nd spire), with the suffixes -ate
and -ed.

## spire
spire, п., 1) stalk of aplant, blade of grass; 2) the
top of a tapering object; summit; 3) a tapering
roof or tower. — ME. spir, spire, fr. OE. spir, 'a
tapering stalk of grass', rel. to ON. spira, 'a
stalk, a slender tree', MLG. spir, 'a small point
or top' (whence G. Spier, 'a thin stalk, blade of
grass'), and to E. spit, 'pointed bar' (q.v.). The
original meaning of spire was 'stalk of grass,
sprout'.
Derivatives: spire, intr. and tr. v., to taper,
spired, spir-y, adjs.

## spire
spire, п., spiral, coil. — F., fr. L. spira, fr. Gk.
σπείρα, 'coil, twist', whence σπείραμα, Ion.
σπείρημα, 'coil, twist*, σπείραία, 'Spiraea ul-
maria' (see Spiraea). Cp.—with vowel
gradation—Gk. σπάρτον, 'rope, cable; Spanish
broom; esparto', σπυρίς, ace. σπυρίδα, 'woven
basket* (whence L. sporta, sportula, of s.m.),
Lith. spartas, 'bond'. Cp. spiral, spireme, Cp.
also esparto, Spartina, Spartium, sportuia.
Derivative: spir-y, adj.

## spireme
spireme, spirem, п., that stage in the division of a
cell, when the chromatin has a threadlike form.
— Ion. Gk. σπείρημα, 'coil, twist'. See spire,
'spiral'.

## spiriferous
spiriferous, adj., having a spire (zool.) —
Compounded of L. spira, 'a coil', and ferre, *to bear,
carry'. See 2nd spire and -ferous.

## sptrillosis
sptrillosis, п., a disease caused by bacteria of the
genus Spirillum (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid
coined fr. Spirillum and -osis, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## Spirillnm
Spirillnm, п., a genus of bacteria of spirally
twisted shape (bacterial.) — Medical L., formed with
L. dimin. suff. -ilium, fr. spira, 'coil, twist'. See
2nd spire.

## spirit
spirit, n. — ME., fr. OF. espirit, esprit, spirit (F.
esprit), fr. L. spiritus, 'breathing, breath, breath
of life, soul, mind, spirit, courage*, fr. spirare, *to
breathe', which prob. derives from the I.-E.
imitative base *$peis-, 'to blow', whence also
OSlav. pislo, piskati, 'to pipe, play on the flute',
and possibly also OI. picchora, 'pipe, flute'. Cp.
sprite, which is a doublet of spirit. Cp. also
aspire, conspire, esprit, expire, inspire, perspire,
respire, spirant, sprightly, suspire, transpire.
Derivatives: spirit, tr. v., spirit-ed, adj.,
spiritism, п., spirit-ist, п., spirit-ist-ic, adj.

## spiritless
spiritless, adj. — Formed fr. spirit with suff. -less;
first used by Shakespeare.
Derivatives: spiritless-ly, adv., spiritless-ness, n.

## spiritual
spiritual, adj. ME. spirituel, spiritual, fr. OF. (=
F.) spirituel, or directly fr. L. spiritudlis, fr.
spiritus, 'of breathing, of the spirit*. See spirit and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: spiritual, п., spiritual-ism, п.,
spiritual-ist, п., spiritual-ist-ic, adj., spiritual-ist-
ic-al-ly, adv., spirituality (q.v.), spiritual-ize, tr.
v., spiritual-iz-ation, п., spiritual-ly, adv.,
spiritual-ness, n.

## spirituality
spirituality, n. — ME. spiritualite, fr. MF. ( — F.)
spiritualite', fr. Late L. spiritualitatem, ace. oispi-
ritudlitas, fr. L. spiritudlis. See prec. word and
-ity and cp. next word, which is a doublet of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:733 COLUMN:3 -->
spirituality.

## spiritualty
spiritualty, п., the clergy. — ME. spiritualte, fr.
MF. spiritualte, fr. ML. spiritualitatem, ace. of
spiritualitds. See prec. word.

## spirituel
spirituel, fern, spirituelle, adj., delicate, witty. —
F., fr. L. spiritudlis. See spiritual.

## spirituous
spirituous, adj., pertaining to, or containing,
alcohol. — MF. (= F.) spiritueux (fern, spiritu-
euse), fr. VL. *spirituosus, fr. L. spiritus. See spirit
and -ous.
Derivatives: spirituous-ly, adv., spirituous-ness,
n.

## spiritus
spiritus, п., breathing, aspiration {grammatical
term). — L. spiritus, 'breathing, breath'. See
spirit.

## spirivalve
spirivalve, п., having a spiral shell. —
Compounded of L. spira, 'coil, twist', and valva, 'valve'.
See spire, 'spiral', and valve.

## spiro-
spiro-, combining form meaning 'spiral, whorled'.
— Fr. L. spira, 'a coil, twist*. See spire, 'spiral'.

## spiro-
spiro-, combining form meaning 'breathing,
respiration'. — Fr. L. spirare, 'to breathe'. See
spirit.

## Spirochaeta
Spirochaeta, п., a genus of bacteria characterized
by a spiral form (bacterial.) — ModL., coined
fr. spiro-, 'spiral*, and Gk. χαίτη, 'long flowing
hair, mane'. See chaeto-.

## spirochete
spirochete, also spirochaete, п., any of the bacteria
constituting the genus Spirochaeta. — See prec.
word.

## Spirodela
Spirodela, п., a genus of plants of the duckweed
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
σπείρα, 'coil, twist' (see spire, 'spiral'), and
δήλος, 'visible, clear'. See 2nd spire and adelo-.

## spirograph
spirograph, п., an instrument for recording
movements made in respiration. — Compounded of
spiro-, 'respiration*, and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## spirometer
spirometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
capacity of the lungs. — Compounded of spiro-,
'respiration', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: spirometr-ic, spirometr-ic-al, adjs.,
spirometr-y, n.

## spirt
spirt, v. and n. — The same as spurt.

## spissated
spissated, adj., thickened. — Formed with suff
-ed fr. L. spissdtus, pp. of spissdre, 'to thicken',
fr. spissus, 'thick, crowded, compact, dense',
which stands for *spid-tos, or *spid-sos and is
cogn. with Gk. σπίδιος, 'extended', Lith. spis-
tas, 'crowded', Lett, spiedu, spiezu, spiest, 'to
press'. All these words are traceable to I.-E. base
*spe(i)-, *sp -, 'to draw, stretch, span, spread,
extend'. See space and cp. words there referred
to. For the ending of L. spissdtus see adj. suff.
-ate. Cp. also inspissate.

## spit
spit, n.t a long, pointed bar for roasting meat. —
ME. spite, spyte, fr. OE. spitu, rel. to MDu. spit,
spet, Du. spit, O&n.^pid, Swed. spett, OHG.,
MHG. spi3, G. Spiefi, 'spir, OHG. spizzi,
MHG. spitz(e), G. spitz, 'pointed*. (OF. espois,
Sp. espeto, 'spit', are Teut. loan words.) The
above words derive from I.-E. base *(s)pei-,
*(s)pi-t 'something pointed', whence also L. spi-
ca, 'ear of corn', ON. spikr, 'spike, nail'. See
spike and cp. next word. Cp. also spitz.
Derivative: spit, tr. v., to pierce with a spit,
spitted, adj., spitt-er, n.

## spit
spit, п., the depth of earth equal to the length of a
spade blade. — Du., fr. MDu., rel. to MDu. ( =
Du.) spitten, 'to dig, spade', and prob. also to
MDu. spit, spet, OE. spitu, 'spit'. See spit, 'a
pointed bar'.

## spit
spit, tr. v., to eject; intr. v., to eject saliva from
the mouth. — ME. spitten, fr. OE. spittan, rel.
to OE. spxtan, and to ON. spyta, Dan. spytte,
Swed. spotta, Du. spuiten, MHG. spiuzen, G.
bpeuzen, spiitzen, fr. the I.-E. imitative base
*spyu-, *spyeu-, 'to spit*. See spew and cp.
spittle, spittoon, spout.
Derivatives: spit, п., saliva, spitt-ing, n. and adj.

## spital
spital, п., hospital (obsol.) — Aphetic for hospital
(q.v.) Cp. G. Spital.

## spitchcock
spitchcock, п., an eel split and cooked. — Prob.
an alteration of spit-cooked, i.e. 'cooked with a
spit*. Cp. G. Spiefibraten, 'meat roasted on a
spit'. See spit, 'pointed bar', and cook and cp.
spatchcock.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:734 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 707 | SPONDYLITIS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:734 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: spitchcock, tr. v.

## spite
spite, n. — Aphetic for despite.
Derivatives: spite, tr. v., spite-fuf, adj.,
spite-fully, adv., spite-ful-ness, n.

## spittle
spittle, n. — ME. spetif, fr. OE. spsetl, spdtl, fir.
spxtan, 'to spit'. See spit, v.

## spittoon
spittoon, n. — Formed fr. spit, v., with suff. -oon.

## spitz
spitz, п., also spitzdog, a breed of small
Pomeranian dog— G. Spitzhund, fr. spitz, 'pointed', and
Hundt 'dog'; so called because of its tapering
muzzle. For the etymology of G. spitz see spit,
'pointed bar'. For sense development cp. Icel.
snati, 'trackhound', which is rel. to Norw. snat,
'point', ON. snata, 'spear'.

## Splachnum
Splachnum, п., a genus of mosses (hot.) — ModL.,
erroneously coined by Linnaeus for Splanchnum
fr. Gk. σπλάγχνον, 'any of the inward parts;
moss'. See splanchnic.

## splanchn-
splanchn-, form of splanchno- before a vowel.

## splanchnic
