splanchnic, adj., pertaining to the viscera. — Fr.
Gk. σπλάγχνον, mostly used in the pi.
σπλάγχνα, 'the inward parts, entrails', which is rel.
to σπλήν (orig. *σπλήγχ), 'spleen*. See spleen
and adj. suff. -ic and cp. next word.

## splanchno-
splanchno-, before a vowel splanchn-, combining
form denoting the viscera. — Gk. σπλάγχνο-,
σπλαγχν-, fr. σπλάγχνον. See prec. word.

## splanchnology
splanchnology, п., the study of the viscera. —
Compounded of splanchno- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, One who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: splanchnolog-ic-al, adj., splanchnol-
og-ist, n.

## splanchnoskeleton
splanchnoskeleton, п., skeleton of the viscera
(anat.) — Compounded of splanchno- and
skeleton. The term splanchnoskeleton was introd uced
into science by the English anatomist Sir
Richard Owen (1804-92). Cp. endoskeleton, exo-
skeleton.
Derivative: splanchnoskelet-al, adj. w

## splanchnotomy
splanchnotomy, п., dissection of the viscera. —
Compounded of splanchno- and Gk. -τομία, 'a
cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.
Derivative: splanchnotom-ic-al, adj.

## splash
splash, tr. and intr. v. — Alteration of plash (q.v.)
Derivatives: splash, n. and adv., splash-er, п.,
splash-ing, п., splash-y, adj.
splatter» intr. and tr. v. — Prob. a blend of splash
and spatter.

## splay
splay, tr. v., to spread out; п., spread; adj., spread
out. — ME. splayen, aphetic for displayen. See
display. For a similar aphesis cp. sport, stain,
stress.

## spleen
spleen, n. — Fr. OF. esplen or directly fr. L. splen,
fr. Gk. σπλήν, which stands for *σπληγχ and is
rel. to σπλάγχνα, 'the inward parts' (see
splanchnic), and cogn. with OI. plihan-, Avestic sp rezan
(for *sp(gh-en), Arm. p"aica\n, L. lien, OSlav.
slezena (perh. for *selgh~ena), Lith. bluSnis,
bluzne, OPruss. blusne (the Baltic forms are
prob. dissimilated fr. *blun%nis, fr. l.-E. *blngh~),
Olr. selg, MBret./t»j'A (for *spelghd-), 'spleen'.
Cp. Asplenium, lienal, lienculus.
Derivatives: spleen, tr. and intr. v., spleen-ful,
adj.

## splen-
splen-, form of spleno- before a vowel.

## splenalgia
splenalgia, п., pain in the spleen. — Medical L.,
formed fr. splen- and .Gk. -αλγία, fr. άλγος,
'pain'. See -algia.
Derivative: splenalg-ic, adj.

## splendent
splendent, adj., 1) shining; 2) illustrious. — L.
splendens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of splendere, 'to
shine'. See splendid and -ent.

## splendid
splendid, adj., I) brilliant; 2) magnificent,
sumptuous. — L. splendidus, 'bright, brilliant,
magnificent', fr. splendere, 'to shine, gleam, glisten',
which is prob. cogn. with Lith. splendziu, Ί
shine', Mir. lainn (for *pl ndis), 'bright', fr.
l.-E. base *{s)plend-, 'bright, brightness'. For
the ending see 1st suff. -id.
Derivatives: splendid-ly, adv., splendid-ness, n.

## splendiferous
splendiferous, adj. — Formed fr. L. splendor,
'brilliance', on analogy of auriferous, vociferous,
and other words ending in -iferous. See prec.
word and -ferous.
Derivatives: splendiferous-ly, adv., splendiferous-
ness, n.

## splendor
splendor, splendour, n. — Fr. AF. esplendour.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:734 COLUMN:2 -->
splendour, or directly fr. L. splendor, gen. -oris,
'brilliance', fr. splendere, 'to shine'. See splendid
and -or, -our.
Derivatives: splendo(u)r, tr. and intr. v., splen-
dor-ouSy splendr-ous, adj.

## splenectomy
splenectomy, п., surgical removal of the spleen.
— Compounded of splen- and Gk. -εκτομία, *a
cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, *a cutting out*. See
-ectomy.

## splenetic
splenetic, adj., 1) pertaining to the spleen; 2) ill-
tempered, irritable (the spleen is regarded as the
seat of the emotions). — Late L. spleneticus,
'affected with spleen', fr. L. splen, fr. Gk. σπλήν,
'spleen*. See spleen and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: splenetic, п., splenetic-al, adj.,
splenetic-al-ly, adv.

## splenial
splenial, adj., pertaining to the splenius. —
Formed fr. splenius with adj. suff. -al.

## splenic
splenic, adj., pertaining to the spleen. — L. spleni-
cus, fr. Gk. σπληνικός, fr. σπλήν, 'spleen'. See
spleen and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: splenic, п., a remedy for the spleen.

## splenitic
splenitic, adj., pertaining to splenitis. — Formed
from next word with adj. suff. -ic.

## splenitis
splenitis, п., inflammation of the spleen {med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. σπληνΐτ^ς (fem.),
'pertaining to the spleen', fr. σπλήν, 'spleen'. See spleen
and -itis.

## splenius
splenius, п., a large muscle on either side of the
back of the neck {anat.) — Medical L. splenius,
fr. h.splenium, 'plaster, patch', fr. Gk. σπλήνιον,
'bandage', orig, 'bandage for the spleen', fr.
σπλήν, 'spleen'. See spleen.

## spleno-
spleno-, before a vowel splen-, combining form
meaning the 'spleen', or 'splenic and'. — Gk.
σπληνο-, σπλην-, fr. σπλήν, 'spleen'. See
spleen,

## splenoid
splenoid, adj., resembling the spleen. —
Compounded of splen- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape*. See -oid.

## splenology
splenology, п., the study of the spleen. —
Compounded of spleno- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one
who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: splenolog-ic-al, adj.

## spleuchan
spleuchan, п., tobacco pouch. — Gael, spliuchan.

## splice
splice, tr. v. — MDu. splissen (Du. splitsen), 'to
splice", rel. to MDu. spliten, Du. splijten, 'to
split'. See split and cp. splint, splinter.
Derivatives: splice, п., splic-er, п., splic-ing, n.

## spline
spline, п., a long strip of wood. — Prob. rel. to
splint, splinter.

## splint
splint, п., a thin piece split off. — MDu. splinte
(Du. splint), rel. to Dan. splint, 'splinter', Norw.,
Swed. splint, 'wooden peg, wedge*. These words
represent a blend of the two Teut. bases *split-
and * flint. See split and flint and cp. splinter.
Derivatives: splint, tr. v., splint-y, adj.

## splinter
splinter, п., a chip, fragment. — Of. MDu.
origin. Cp. Du. splint, splinter, 'splinter'. Cp. also
G. Splitter, of s.m., and see splint.
Derivatives: splinter, tr. and intr. \.,.splinter-y
adj.

## split
split, tr. and intr. v. — MDu. (= Du.) splitten,
rel. to Dan., Fris. spline, and to OFris. spltta,
MLG., MDu. spliten, Du. splijten, MHG.
spliten, G. spleifien, 'to split*, and prob. also to
MLG. spalden, OHG- spaltan, 'to split'. See
spall and cp. slice.
Derivative: split, п., splitt-er, п., splitt-ing, n.
and adj.

## splodge
splodge, n. — A var. of splotch,

## splotch
splotch, п., blot; stain. — Prob. a blend of spot
and splash.
Derivatives: splotch, tr. v., splotch-y, adj.,
splotch-i-ly, adv., splotch-i-ness, n.

## splurge
splurge, п., a showy display; intr. v., to make a
showy display {colloq.) — Prob. of imitative
origin,

## splutter
splutter, intr. and tr. v. — Prob. a blend of
splash and sputter.
Derivatives: splutter, п., splutter-er, n.

## spode
spode, п., a fine sort of porcelain. — Named after
its first maker Josiah Spode (1754-1827), a
potter in Stoke-on-Trent, England.

## spodiosite
spodiosite, п., calcium fluophosphate {mineral.)
— Formed with subst. suff. -itefr. Gk. σπόδιος,
*ash-colored', fr. σποδός, 'ashes' (see spodo-);

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:734 COLUMN:3 -->
so called from its color.

## spodo-
spodo-, combining form meaning 'ashes', as in
spodomancy. — Gk. σποδό-, fr. σποδός, 'ashes',
which is of uncertain origin.

## spodomancy
spodomancy, п., divination by means of ashes. —
Compounded of spodo- and Gk. μαντεία,
'divination*. See -mancy.

## spodumene
spodumene, п., a lithium-aluminum silicate
{mineral.) — F. spodumene, a name coined by
the French mineralogist, Abbe'Reno-Just Hauy
(1743-1822) in 1800 fr. Gk. σποδούμενος, pass,
pres. part, of σποδοΰν, 'to burn to ashes', fr.
σποδός, 'ashes' (see spodo-); so called from its
color. For the passive part. suff. -meno- see
alumnus and cp. words there referred to.

## spoil
spoil, п., booty. — ME. spoile, fr. MF. espoille, fr.
L. spolia, pi. of spolium, 'skin stripped from an
animal; arms taken from an enemy; prey, booty'
(but mistaken for a fern. sing, noun), whence spo-
liare/to strip;to rob, plunder, pillage, spoil'.The
orig. meaning of spolium was 'something
stripped off'; it derives fr. l.-E. base *{s)p{h)el-, 'to
cleave, split', whence also Gk. άσπαλον (Hesy-
chius), 'skin,'hide', σπολάς, 'flayed skin', σπά-
λαξ, άσπάλαξ, 'mole', lit. 'the digging animal*,
άσπάλα&ος, 'a spinous shrub', lit. 'that which
ίββΓβ',ψάλις, 'scissors', Lith. spaliai{p\.))ishives of
flax', OSlav. ra-splatiti, 'to cleave, split', MLG.
spalden, OHG. spaltan, 'to split', OI. sphatayati,
'splits', phalati, 'bursts', phalah, 'plowshare',
prop, 'that which tears the soil', OSlav. plevo,
pleti, 'to weed', plevelu, 'weed'. Cp. spoil, v.,
despoil, spoliation. Cp. also Spalax, spall, spelt,
sphalerite, spill, 'to flow', spool.

## spoil
spoil, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spoilen, fr. OF. es-
poillier, fr. L. spoliare, 'to strip; to rub, plunder,
pillage, spoil'. See spoil, n.
Derivatives: spoil-age, п., spoil-er, п., spoil-ing,
n.

## spoke
spoke, п., radius of a wheel; rung of a ladder. —
ME. spake, spoke, fr. OE. spaca, rel. to OS.
speca, OFris. spake, spike, Du. spaak, OHG.
speicha, MHG., G. speiche, 'spoke', fr. I.-E.
base *{s)pei-, *{s)pi-, 'something pointed',
whence also L. spica, 'ear of corn*, ON. spikr,
'spike, nail'. See spike and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: spoke, tr. v., spoke-less, adj.,
spoke-wise, adv., spok-yy adj.

## spoke
spoke, past tense of speak. — Back formation fr.
spoken.

## spoken
spoken, pp. of speak. — ME. spoke{n), formed fr.
speken, 'to speak' (see speak), on the analogy of
ME. broke(n), pp. of breken, 'to break' (see
break).

## spoliation
spoliation, п., robbery, plunder. — L. spoliation
gen. -onis, 'a robbing, plundering, pillaging', fr.
spolidtus, pp. oispoliare. See spoil, v., and-ation.

## spoliator
spoliator, п., robber, plunderer. — L. spoliator,
'pillager, plunderer, spoiler', fr. spolidtus, pp. of
spoliare. See spoil, v., and -ator.

## spoliatory
spoliatory, adj., of the nature of spoliation. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. spolidtus, pp.
of spoliare. See spoil, v.

## spondaic
spondaic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized by,
spondees. — F. spondalque, fr. L. spondaicus, a
less correct var. of spondiacus, fr. Gk. σπονδει,-
ακός, 'used at libations; pertaining to a
spondee', fr. σπονδεΐος (scil. πους). See spondee and
-ic.

## spondaize
spondaize, tr. v., to make spondaic. — Formed
fr. spondee with suff. -ize.

## spondee
spondee, п., a metrical foot consisting of two
long syllables. — F, spondee, fr. L. spondeus, fr.
Gk. σπονδεΤος, (scil. πους), name of the
metrical foot consisting of two long syllables, lit.
'the meter used in verses recited when libations
were offered', from σπονδή, 'drink offering,
libation'. See sponsion.
Derivative: sponde-an, adj.

## spondulics
spondulics, п., money {slang). — Of uncertain
origin.

## spondyl
spondyl, spondyle, п., a vertebra. — F. spondyle,

## fr. L. spondylus
fr. L. spondylus, fr. Gk. σπόνδυλος, σφόνδυλος,
'vertebra*, which stands in vowel gradation to
σφενδόνη, 'sling'. See sphendone.

## spondyl-
spondyl-, form of spondylo- before a vowel.

## spondylitis
spondylitis, п., inflammation of the vertebrae

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:735 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SPONOYLO- | 708 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:735 COLUMN:1 -->
(med.) — Medical L., formed with suff. -itis fr.
Gk. σπόνδυλος, 'vertebra'. See spondyl.

## spondylo-
spondylo-, before a vowel spondyl-, combining
form meaning 'vertebra'. — Gk σπόνδυλο-, fr.
σπόνδυλος, 'vertebra'. See spondyl.

## sponge
sponge, n. — ME., fr. OF. esponge (F. e'ponge),
fr. L. spongia, fr. Gk. σπογγία, 'sponge' (rel.
to σπόγγος, Att. σφόγγος, of s.m.), which—
together with Arm. sung, sunk, 'sponge, cork
tree, pumice stone'—is borrowed from an
unknown source. L. fungus, 'mushroom, fungus*,
is a loan word fr. Att. σφόγγος. See fungus and
cp. spunk.
Derivatives: sponge-ful, sponge-less, spong-y,
adjs., spong-i-ness, n.

## sponge
sponge, intr. and tr. v. — ME. spongen, fr. sponge.
See sponge, n.
Derivatives: spong-ed, adj., spong-er, п.,
sponging, n. and adj.

## spongelet
spongelet, п., spongiole. — Formed fr. sponge,
п., with dimin. suff. -let.

## spongiform
spongiform, adj., resembling a sponge. —
Compounded of L. spongia, 'sponge', and forma,
'form, shape'. See sponge, п., and form, n.

## spongiole
spongiole, n. — F., fr. L. spongioid, 'rose gall,
small roots', dimin. of spongia, 'sponge'. See
sponge, п., and 2nd -ole.

## spongo-
spongo-, combining form meaning 'sponge'. —■
Gk. σπόγγο-, fr. σπόγγος, 'sponge'. See
sponge, n.

## spongoid
spongoid, adj., of the nature of a sponge. —
Compounded of spongo- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like*, fr.
εϊδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid,

## spongology
spongology, п., study of sponges. —
Compounded of spongo- and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: spongolog-ist, n.

## sponsal
sponsal, adj., pertaining to marriage; spousal. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. sponsus, pp. of
spondere. See next word.

## sponsion
sponsion, п., 1) the act of becoming surety; 2) a
formal pledge, esp. one made on behalf of
another person. — L. sponsio, gen. -onis,
'engagement', fr. sponsus, pp. of spondere, 'to engage
oneself, promise' (whence despondere, 4o
promise, pledge', respondere, 'to answer'); cogn. with
Gk. σπένδειν, 'to pour out a libation; to
promise', σπονδή, 'libation; treaty', Hitt. shipan-
tahhi, Ί pour out a libation, I sacrifice', ishpan-
tuzzi, 'offering a libation'. Cp. despond,
espouse, respond, response, riposte, spondee,
sponsor, spouse.

## spouson
spouson, п., a curved projection from a ship's
side. — Perhaps a popular alteration of
expansion.
Derivative: sponson, tr. v.

## sponsor
sponsor, n. — L. sponsor, 'surety', fr. sponsus, pp.
of spondere, 'to warrant'. See sponsion and
agential suff. -or.
Derivatives: sponsori-al, adj. and п.,
sponsorship, n.

## spontaneity
spontaneity, n. — See next word and -ity.

## spontaneous
spontaneous, adj. — Late L. spontaneus, 'of one's
free will', fr. sponte, 'of one's free will,
voluntarily', abl. of *spons, 'free will', which is of
uncertain origin. It is possibly cogn. with OE.
spanan, 'to instigate, persuade, allure', gespan,
'persuasion, allurement', OHG. spanan, 'to
entice, deceive', gispanst, 'enticement*, MHG. ge-
spenste, 'enticement, ghost', G. Gespenst,
'ghost', abspenstig, 'disaffected', and with OE.
spannan, 'to clasp, fasten, stretch, span', OHG.
spannen, 'to stretch, strain, span'. See span, v.,
and -eons. The word spontaneous was first used
by the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes
(1588-1679) in 1656.
Derivatives: spontaneous-ly, adv., spontaneous-
ness, n.

## spontoon
spontoon, п., a kind of halberd carried by
infantry officers in the 18th cent. — F. esponton,
sponton, fr. It. spuntone, which is formed fr.
pref. s- (fr. L. ex-, 'out of, from'), and punto,
'point', fr. L. punctum. See 1st ex- and point, n.

## spoof
spoof, п., a hoax, joke (slang). — Coined by the
English comedian Arthur Roberts (1852-1933).
Derivatives: spoof, tr. v., spoof-er, п., spoof-ish,
adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:735 COLUMN:2 -->

## spook
spook, n. — Du., rel. to G. Spuk, 'ghost,
apparition', Swed. spok, 'scarecrow', Norw. spjok,
'ghost, specter', Dan. speg, 'joke', and possibly
cogn. with Lett, spigana, 'dragon, witch', spi-
ganis, 'will o* the wisp', Lith. spingu, spingeti,
'to shine', OPruss. spanksti, 'spark*.
Derivatives: spook-ish, spook-y, adjs.

## spool
spool, п., a reel for winding thread, yarn, etc.,
upon. — MDu. spoele (Du. spoel), rel. to Dan.,
Norw., Swed. spole, OHG. spuola, MHG. spu-
ole, G. Spule, fr. I.-E. base *sp(n)el-, 'to cleave,
split'. See spoil, n.
Derivatives: spool, tr. v., spool-er, n.

## spoon
spoon, п., implement for conveying food or drink
to the mouth. —■ ME. spone, spoon, fr. OE. spon,
'chip of wood*, rel. to ON. spdnn, sponn, 'chip,
splinter', Dan spaan, Norw. spon, Swed. span,
'a wooden spoon', MDu. spaen, Du. spaan,
OHG., MHG. span, G. Span, 'chip, splinter',
and prob. cogn. with Gk. σφήν, 'wedge'. These
words are prob. formed—with -га-formative
element—fr- I.-E. base *spe~(i)-, *spe-, "to draw,
stretch, span, spread, extend; a flat piece of
wood'. See space and cp. spheno-. Cp. also
span-new, spick and span. The modern sense
of spoon developed from the primitive meaning
of 'chip of wood' through the intermediate
phase 'chip of wood used for conveying liquid
to the mouth*.
Derivatives: spoon, tr. v., spoon-ful, adj.,
spoonlike, adj.

## spoon
spoon, п., a simpleton; a foolish lover. —
Figurative use of prec. word.
Derivatives: spoon, intr. v., to make love (slang),
spoon-y, adj., spoon-i-ly, adv., spoon-i-ness, n.

## spoonerism
spoonerism, п., involuntary transposition of
initial sounds. — Named after Rev. William A.
Spooner (1844-1930), warden of New College,
Oxford. — For the ending see suff. -ism.

## spoor
spoor, п., track, trace. — MDu. spor, spoor (Du.
spoor), rel. to OE-, ΟΝ., OHG., MHG. spor, G.
Spur, 'track, footprint, trace'. See spur.
Derivatives: spoor, tr. and intr. v., spoor-er, n.

## spor-
spor-, form of sporo- before a vowel.

## sporadic
sporadic, sporadical, adj., 1) scattered; 2)
occasional. — ML. sporadicus, fr. Gk. σποραδικός,
'scattered', fr. σποράς, gen. σποράδος,
'scattered', which is rel. to σπορά, σπόρος, 'a
sowing; seed'. See spore.
Derivatives: sporadical-ly, adv., sporadical-ness,
n.

## sporange
sporange, п., sporangium. — See sporangium.

## sporangium
sporangium, п., acasecontainingspores.—ModL.,
fr. Gk. σπόρος, 'a sowing', and άγγεϊον, dimin.
of άγγος, 'vessel, receptacle'. For the first
element see spore, for the second see angio- and cp.
synangium.

## sporation
sporation, п., production of spores- — A hybrid
formed fr. Gk. σπορά, 'a sowing' (see next
word), with -ation, a suff. of Latin origin.

## spore
spore, п., the reproductive body in fiowerless
plants corresponding to the seeds of flowering
plants. — ModL. spora, fr. Gk. σπορά, 'a
sowing, seed', which is rel. to σπόρος, 'a sowing,
seed', and stands in gradational relationship to
σπείρειν, 'to sow, scatter*. See sperm· and cp.
sporadic, the first element in sporangium and
the second element in Diaspora.
Derivative: spore, intr. v.

## sporo-
sporo-, before a vowel spor-, combining form
meaning 'spore'. — Gk. σπόρο-, σπορ-, fr.
σπορά, 'a sowing, seed'. See prec. word.

## Sporobolus
Sporobolus, п., a genus of plants, the rush grass
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of sporo- and
the stem of Gk. βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See ballistic.

## sporocyst
sporocyst, п., a cyst which contains sphores. —
Compounded of sporo- and Gk. κύστις,
'bladder, bag'. See cyst.
Derivative: sporocyst-ic, adj.

## sporogenesis
sporogenesis, п., reproduction by means of spores
{biol.) — ModL., compounded of sporo- and
genesis.

## spurogenous
spurogenous, adj., reproducing spores. —
Compounded of sporo- and -genous.

## sporogonium
sporogonium, п., a stalk with capsule producing
spores. — ModL., compounded of sporo- and
suff. -gonium, which is rel. to suff. 'gonia. See
-gony.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:735 COLUMN:3 -->

## sporogony
sporogony, п., formation of spores. — See prec.
word,

## sporophore
sporophore, п., a spore-bearing stalk or branch.
— Compounded of sporo- and Gk. -φόρος,
'bearing'. See -phore.
Derivative: sporophor-ic, adj.

## sporophyll
sporophyll, п., a leaf producing spores on
sporangia (bot.) — Compounded of sporo- and Gk.
φύλλον, 'leaf. See phyllo- and cp. cataphyll,
hypsophyll.

## -sporous
-sporous, adj., combining form meaning 'having
spores'. — Formed fr. Gk. σπορά, 'seed' (see
spore), with suff. -ous.

## Sporozoa
Sporozoa, n. pi., a class of parasitic Protozoa
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of sporo- and
Gk. ζωα, pi. of ζωον, 'animal'. See -zoa.

## sporran
sporran, п., a leather pouch with the fur left on.
— Gael, spor an.

## sport
sport, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sporten, aphetic for
disporten. See disport, v. For a similar aphesis
cp. splay, stain, stress.
Derivatives: sport-ing, adj., sport-ing-ly, adv.

## sport
sport, n. — ME., aphetic for disport. See disport,
n.
Derivatives: sport-ive, adj., sport-ive-ly, adv.,
sport-ive-ness, п., sport-less, adj., sport-y, adj.

## sportula
sportula, п., gift, present. — L., lit. 'small basket',
dimin. of sporta, 'plaited basket, basket', a
word borrowed fr. Gk. σπυρίδα, ace. of σπυρίς,
'woven basket', which is rel. to σπάρτον, 'rope,
cable; Spanish broom; esparto', σπεΤρα, 'coil,
twist*. See 2nd spire and cp. esparto. The
change of δ (in Gk. σπυρίδα) to t (in L. sporta)
is due to Etruscan influence; cp. catamite. For
the ending see suff. -ule. For the derivation of
the Latin word from a Greek accusative cp.
Numidia and words there referred to.

## sporular
sporular, adj., pertaining to a sporule. See
next word and adj. suff. -ar.

## sporule
sporule, п., a small spore {biol.) — ModL. spo-
rula, formed fr. spora with the dimin. suff. -ula.
See spore and -ule,

## spot
spot, n. — ME. spotte, spot, rel. to MDu. spot,
spotte, 'stain, blot', ON. spotti, 'small piece',
Norw. spot, 'spot, small piece of land'.
Derivatives: spot-less, adj., spot-less-ly, adv.,
spot-less-ness, п., spott-y, adj., spott-i-ness, n.

## spot
spot, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spotten, fr. spotte,
spot. See spot, n.
Derivatives: spott-ed, adj., spott-ed-ness, n.

## spousal
spousal, adj., pertaining to marriage. — See next
word.

## spousal
spousal, п., marriage. — Aphetic for espousal.

## spouse
spouse, п., husband or wife — OF. espous,
espouse (F. ёроих, fem. ipouse), fr. L. sponsus,
fern, sponsa, 'betrothed', pp. of spondere, 'to
engage oneself promise'. See sponsion and cp.
espouse.
Derivative: spouse-less, adj.

## spout
spout, intr. and tr. v. — ME. spouten, rel. to-
MDu. spoiten, Du. spuiten, 'to flow, spout',
Swed. sputa, 'to spout', and to E. spit, v. (q.v.)
Cp. spate.
Derivatives: spout, n. (q.v.), spout-er, n.

## spout
spout, n. — ME. spoute, rel. to MDu. spoite, Du.
spuit, 'spout', and to ME. spouten, 'to spout*.
See spout, v.
Derivatives: spout-less, п., spout-y, adj.

## sprag
sprag, п., a piece of wood used to prevent a
vehicle from rolling backward. — Prob. rel. to OE.
sprxc, 'shoot', and to E. spray, *a small branch*.
Derivatives: sprag, tr. v., spragg-er, n.

## sprain
sprain, tr. v. — MF. espraindre, espreindre (F.
epreindre), 'to press out*, fr. OF., fr. L. expri-
mere, of s.m., fr. 1st ex- and premere, 'to press'.
See press, v.
Derivative: sprain, n.

## spraints
spraints, n. pi., otter's dung. — MF. espraintes,
espreintes (F. epreintes), prop. fem. p]. espraint,
espreint, pp. of espraindre, espreindre. See prec.
word.

## sprang
sprang, past tense of spring. — ME., fr. OE.
See spring.

## sprat
sprat, п., a small European herring (Clupea sprat-
tus) — ME. sprot, sprotte, fr. OE. sprott, rel. to
Du. sprot, 'sprat', and prob. to E. sprout.
Derivative: spratt-er, n.

## sprawl
sprawl, intr. v., to stretch out the limbs in a care-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:736 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 709 | SPUTTER -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:736 COLUMN:1 -->
less manner. — ME. sprewlen, sprawlen, fr. OE.
spreawlian, 'to move convulsively', rel. to Norw.
sprala, Dan. sprxlle, sprxlde, 'to fling one's
arms and legs about'; of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: sprawl, п., sprawl-er, п., sprawl-ingt
adj. and п., sprawl-ing-ly, adv.

## spray
spray, п., a small branch. — ME., rel. to Dan,
sprag, OE. sprsec, 'shoot, twig', fr. I.-E. base
*sper(e)g-, *spker(e)g-, 'to strew, sprinkle; to
sprout, burst, swell', whence also L. spargere,
'to scatter'. See sparse and words there referred
to and cp. esp. sprag, sprig.
Derivative: spraye-y, adj.

## spray
spray, п., jet of water. — LG. sprei, 'spray,
drizzle', rel. to MDu. spraeien, 'to sprinkle, pour,
spray', MHG. sprxjen, sprxwen, 'to spray, fly'.
G. spruken, 'to sparkle, drizzle*, OHG., MHG.
spriu, G. Spreu, 'chaff' (lit 'that which fiies
about'), fr. I.-E. base *sp(k)er-, 'to sow, scatter*,
whence also Gk. σπείρειν, 'to sow, scatter*. See
sperm and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: spray, intr. and tr. v., spray-er, п.,
spraye-y, adj.

## spread
spread, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spreden, fr. OE.
sprxdan, rel. to Dan. sprede, OSwed. spreda,
MDu. spreiden, spreden, Du. spreiden, OHG.,
MHG., G. spreiten, 'to spread'. Outside
Teutonic cp. OLith. sprainas (for *spraidnas),
'staring', lit. 'opening wide one's eyes', Lett, spriezu,
Ί span, measure'.
Derivatives: spread, п., spread-er, п., spread-ing,
adj., spread-ing-ly, adv., spread-ing-ness, n.

## spree
spree, п., ]) a frolic; 2) a drinking bout. — Of
uncertain origin;; possibly rel. to Ir. spre, Gael.
spraig, 'spark', which seem to be loan words fr.
ON. sprakr. See spark and cp. spry.
Derivative: spree, intr. v.

## sprig
sprig, п., a small twig. — ME. sprigge, rel. to OE.
sprsec, 'a shoot', and to E. spray, 'a small
branch*.
Derivatives: sprig, tr. v., sprigg-ed, adj., sprigg-
ert n., sprigg-y, adj-.

## sprightly
sprightly, adj., lively. — Formed with suff. -ly fr.
spright, erroneous spelling of sprite.
Derivative: sprightli-ness, n.

## spring
spring, intr. and tr. v. — ME, springen, fr. OE.
springan, rel. to ΟΝ., OFris., Swed. springa,
Dan. springe, MDu. springhen, Du. springen,
OS., OHG. springan, MHG., G. springen, fr.
I.-E. base *sprengk-, a nasalized variant of base
*spergh-, 'to move quickly', whence OI. sp(ka-
yati, 'desires eagerly', ΰ^'σπέρχεσ&αι, 'to
hurry*. Base *spergh- itself seems to be an enlarged
form of the primitive base *sper-, *spker-, 'to
move convulsively; to scatter', whence OI.
spkurati, 'kicks with the foot', Gk. σπαίρειν, 'to
move convulsively'. See spurn and cp. springe.
Cp. also the first element in springbok and the
second element in klipspringer.
Derivatives: spring, n. (q.v.), spring-er, п.,
spring-ing, adj. and п., spring-ing-ty, adv.,
spring-y, adj., spring-i-ly, adv., spring-i-ness, п.,
spring-less, adj., spring-like, adv.

## spring
spring, п., 1) a leap; 2) source of water; source,
origin; 3) the season in which plants'spring up
and grow. — ME., fr. OE. spring, 'springing;
source of water', fr. springan. Cp. MHG. sprinc,
'leap, jump, Source of water, fountain', OHG.
sprung, MHG. sprunc, 'source of water', G.
Sprung, Du. sprang, 'leap, jump', and see spring,
v.

## springal
springal, sprlngald, п., a young man {archaic). —
Formed fr. the verb spring with -aid, a French
suff. derived fr. OHG. -waldo, -walto, fr. waltan,
*to govern'. See wield and cp. the suffix in
herald.

## springbok
springbok, п., a South African gazelle. — S. Afr.
Du., lit. 'springing buck', fr. Du. springen, 'to
spring' (fr. MDu. springhen), and bok, 'buck*
(fr. MDu. boc); so called from its habit of
springing high into the air when frightened. See
spring, v., and buck.

## springe
springe, п., a snare. — ME. sprenge, springe, rel.
to OE. springan, 'to spring1. See spring, v.
Derivative: springe, tr. v, to catch in a snare;
intr. v., to set springes.

## springlet
springlet, п., a small spring of water. — Formed
fr. the noun spring, п., with the dimin. suff. -let.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:736 COLUMN:2 -->

## sprinkle
sprinkle, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sprenkelen,
sprenklen, rel. to MDu. sprenkel, 'a small spot,
speckle' (whence Du. sprenkelen, 'to sprinkle'),
MLG. and MHG. sprenkel, sprinkei, 'a small
spot, speckle' (whence G. Sprenkel, of s.m.),
prob. derived fr. *spreng-, nasalization of I.-E.
base *sper(e)g-, *spner(e)g-, 'to strew, sprinkle',
whence Swed. spriickel, MHG. spreckel, 'small
spot', Dan. spraglet, 'spotted, speckled', and L.
spargere, 'to scatter, sprinkle'. See sparse and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: sprinkle, п., sprinkl-er, п.,
sprinkling, n.

## sprint
sprint, intr. v., to run fast. — ME. sprenten, of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. spretta, 'to start, startle',
Swed. spritta, 'to start, startle'.
Derivatives: sprint, n.f sprint-er, n.

## sprit
sprit, п., a spar that extends diagonally from the
mast (naut.) — ME. sprei, sprit, fr. OE. spreot,
'pole', rel. to LG. spriet (whence G. Spriet) and
to OE., OS. sprutan, etc., 'to sprout'; see sprout,
v. The orig.meaningof jprjV was 'shoot, branch'.
Cp. bowsprit.

## sprit
sprit, п., a rushlike plant. — From prec. word in
the meaning of'shoot, branch'.

## sprite
sprite, п., elf, fairy. — ME. sprit, fr. OF. (= F.)
esprit, fr. L. spiritus; a doublet of spirit (q.v.)

## sprocket
sprocket, п., projection on the rim of a wheel. —
Of uncertain origin.

## sprout
sprout, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sprulen, sprouten,
fr. OE. sprutan, rel. to OS. sprutan, OFris. spruta,
MDu. spruten, Du. spruiten, OHG. sprio^an,
MHG. sprie^en, G. spriefien, 'to sprout', and to
OE. sprot, sprota, ME. sprote, ON. sproti, OHG.
spro330, MHG. sprote, spro$, G. Sprofi,
'sprout', G. Sprosse, 'sprout; rung', MLG.
sprote, MDu. sporte, Du. sport, 'rung'. Cp.
sprat, sprint, sprit, spruit, spurt, 'to gush out'.
Derivatives: sprout, n. (q.v.), sprout-ed, adj.,
sprout-er, п., sprout-ing, п., sprout-ling, n.

## sprout
sprout, n. — Fr. sprout, v.

## spruce
spruce, п., a coniferous tree. — Shortened fr.
spruce fir, fr. ME. Spruce, 'Prussia', alteration
of Pruce, fr. ML. Prussia (see Prussia); hence
spruce fir orig. meant 'Prussian fir'.

## spruce
spruce, adj., neat, dapper. — Fr. ME. Spruce,
'Prussia'. See spruce, n.
Derivative: spruce (up), tr. v., to make spruce.

## sprue
sprue, п., a tropical disease. — Du. spruw,
sprouw, fr. MDu. sprouwe, 'thrush' (the disease);
of uncertain origin.

## sprue
sprue, п., a hole through which metal is poured
into a mold. — Of unknown origin.
Derivative: spru-er, n.

## spruit
spruit, п., 1) a sprout; 2) a channel of rain (5.
Africa). — S. Afr. Du., fr. MDu. sprute, fr.
spruten, 'to sprout'. See sprout, v.

## sprung
sprung, pp. of spring.— ME. sprungen, sprongen,
fr. OE. gesprungen, pp. of springan. See spring,
v.

## spry
spry, adj., nimble. — Prob. of Scand. origin. Cp.
dial. Swed. sprygg, ON. spraekr, 'sprightly,
'lively', prop, 'sparkling'. See spark and cp. spree.
Derivatives: spry-ly, adv., spry-ness, n.

## spnd
spnd, п., a small spade. — ME. spudde, rel. to
Dan. spyd, ON. spjot, 'spear', OS. spiot, OHG.
spios, MHG. spie^, G. Spiefi, 'spear, lance'.
Derivatives: spud, tr. v., spudd-y, adj.

## spue
spue, intr. and tr. v., to spue. — A dial. var. of
spew.

## spume
spume, п., foam, froth. — ME., fr. L. spuma,
'foam* (prob. through the medium of MF.
espume), which is rel. to Ъ.рйтех, 'pumice', and
cogn. with OE. /am, OHG. veim, 'foam'. See
fonm and cp. pumice.
Derivatives: spumescent (q.v.), spum-y, adj.,
spum-i-ness, п., spumous (q.v.)

## spumescence
spumescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## spumescent
spumescent, adj., foaming, frothing. — L. spu-
mescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of spumescere,
'to grow frothy', formed fr. spuma, 'spume',
with the inchoative suff. -escere. See spume and
-escent.

## spumose
spumose, adj., spumous. — L. spumosus. See next
word.

## spumons
spumons, adj., pertaining to, or covered with,
foam; foamy. — L. spumosus, 'full of foam', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:736 COLUMN:3 -->
spuma. See spume and -ous.

## spun
spun, pp. of spin. — ME. sponnen, fr. OE. ge~
spunnen, pp. of spinnan. See spin,

## spunk
spunk, п., touchwood; spirit, courage. — Gael.
spong, or Ir. sponc, 'tinder, sponge', fr. L. spon-
gia. See sponge.
Derivative: spunk-y, adj.

## spur
spur, n. — ME. spure, spore, fr. OE. spura, spora,
rel. to ON. sport, MDu. spore, Du. spoor, OHG.
sporo, MHG. spor, G. Sporn, 'spur', OE. spor,
'track, footprint, trace*, ON. spor, MDu. spore,
spor, spoor, Du. spoor, OHG. spor, MHG. spor,
spur, G. Spur, of s.m., OE. spyrian, ME. spuryen,
spuren, 'to follow the track of, track down,
investigate', ON. spyria, OFris. spera, MLG.
sporen, MDu. sporen, Du. speuren, OHG. spu-
rian, spur(r)en, MHG. spur(e)n, of s.m., G.
spuren, 'to follow the track of, track down,
investigate; to feel', Dan. sperge, Swed. sporje, 'to
ask*, and to OE. spurnan, 'to kick with the foot*;
see spurn and cp. speer, spoor. It. sp(e)rone, F.
eperon, Sp. espuela, Port, espora, 'spur', are
Teut. loan words.
Derivatives: spur, tr. and intr. v., spurr-ed, adj.,
spurr-er, п., spurr-i-er, п., spurr-y, adj.

## spurge
spurge, п., any of a group of plants having an
acrid milky juice. — ME., fr. OF. espurge (F.
epurge), back formation fr. espurgier, espurger
(F. epurger), fr. L. expurgare, 'to cleanse,
purge'. See expurgate,

## spurious
spurious, adj., not genuine. — L. spurius, prob.
fr. Etruscan spural, 'public'; accordingly spurius
lit. means 'a public child', i.e. 'a child that has
no father*. See Sigwart, Glotta, VII, pp. 139
foil. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivatives: spurious-ly, adv., spurious-ness, n.

## spurn
spurn, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spurnen, fr. OE.
spurnan, 'to kick with the foot, drive away', rel.
to OS., OHG. spurnan, OFris. spurna, ON.
sporna, 'to kick', spyrian, 'to track down,
investigate' (see spur), fr. I.-E. base *sp(k)er-, 'to
move convulsively, to jerk', whence also OI.
spkurati, 'kicks, tramples, jerks, tosses', sphu-
rah, 'trembling, quivering', Avestic sparaiti,
'tramples', Gk. σπαίρειν, 'to move convulsively',
σφύρα, 'hammer', σφυρόν, 'ankle', L. spernere,
'to reject, spurn', Lith. spiriu, spirti, Lett, sperti,
'to kick', OSlav. pero, pirati, 'to tread', Lith.
spafnas, 'wing', Mir. seir (for *speret-s), 'heel',
W. ffer, fern, 'heel', and possibly also Gk.
σφαϊρα, 'ball, globe, sphere'. Cp. Sphyraena,
sphere. Cp. also sperm, spore. Cp. also spring.
Derivative: spurn-er, n.

## spurrite
spurrite, п., a calcium silicate and carbonate
(mineral.) — Named after the American
geologist Josiah Edward Spurr (1870-1950). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## spurry
spurry, also spurrey, п., any of the plants of the
genus Spergula. — Du. spurrie, fr. MF. spurrie,
which prob. derives fr, ML. spergula, 'spurry'.
See Spergula.

## spurt
spurt, v., to gush out. — ME. sprutten, *to sprout',
fr. OE. spryttan, which is rel. to MHG. sprutzen,
G. spritzen, 'to squirt', and to OS., OE. sprutan,
'to sprout'. (The orig. meaning οΐ-spurt was 'to

## sprout'.) See sprout
sprout'.) See sprout, v., and cp. spirt, which is a
var. οι spurt. Cp. also sprit.
Derivatives: spurt-er, п., spurt-ive, adj.

## spurt
spurt, п., a sudden effort. — Of uncertain origin.

## It is perh. orig. identical with spurt
It is perh. orig. identical with spurt, 'a sudden
gushing forth'; see prec. word.

## sputnik
sputnik, п., an artificial satellite of the earth,
launched by Soviet Russia (the first sputnik was

## launched on October 4
launched on October 4, 1957, the second on

## November 2
November 2, 1957). — Russ., lit. 'traveling

## companion'
companion', short for sputnik zemlyi, 'traveling
companion of the earth'. Russ. sputnik is

## compounded of pref. s-
compounded of pref. s-, 'with', put\ 'way, path,

## journey'
journey', and agential suff. -nik. For Russ. pref.
s- see skupshtina. Russ. put' comes fr. OSlav.

## poti
poti, 'way' (whence also Czech pout, Slovak
put\ Pol. pqc, etc., 'pilgrimage'), which is a
derivative of I.-E. base *pent-, 'to go, pass*; see

## find. For the suff. -nik see nudnik
find. For the suff. -nik see nudnik,

## sputter
sputter, intr. and tr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
Du. sputteren. Cp. also splutter.
Derivatives: sputter, п., sputter-er, п., sputter-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:737 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SPUTUM | 710 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:737 COLUMN:1 -->
ing, adj., sputter-ing-ly,adv., sputter-y, adj.

## sputum
sputum, п., saliva, spit, esp. together with mucus.
— L. sputum, 'spittle', prop. neut. pp. of spuere,
'to spit', used as a noun. See spew and cp.
conspue.

## spy
spy, tr. and intr. v. — ME. spien, espien, fr. OF.
espier (F. e'pier), fr. Frankish *spehon, which is
rel. to OHG. spehon, MHG. spehen, 'to examine
closely', G. spahen, 'to spy', MLG. spien, MDu.
spien, 'to spy', ON. spa, v., 'to prophesy', spa,
п., 'prophesy'» OHG. speho, 'spy', spdhi, -ida,
'wisdom', OHG., OS. spdhi, 'wise, prudent', fr.
I.-E. base *spefc~, *to look at, examine, spy',
whence also L. specere, 'to see, look at', species,
'a seeing, sight, look, appearance, shape, form,
kind, quality, aspect'. See species and cp· words
there referred to. It. spiare, Sp. espiar, 'to spy',
are also Teut. loan words.

## spy
spy, n. — ME. spie, fr. OF. espie (whence F. epie),
fr. espier, 'to spy'. Cp. It. spia, 'spy', fr. It. spi-
are, 'to spy', Sp. espia, 'spy', fr. Sp. espiar, 'to
spy'. Cp. also F. espion, 'spy', which is a loan
word fr. It. espione, augment, of spia, and see
spy, v. Cp. also espy.

## squab
squab, п., a short, stout person; adj., short and
.stout. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. dial. Swed.
skvabb, 'anything loose or fat', skvabba, 'a fat
woman', skvabbig, 'flabby'. These words are rel.
to Swed. kvabba, 'to quiver' (see quaver), and to
OS. quappa, MLG. quappe, quabbe (whence
Pan. kvabbe, Swed. kvabba, G. Quappe), Du.
kwab, 'eelpout', and cogn. with OPruss, gawa-
bo, 'toad', OSlav. zaba, 'frog'.
Derivatives: squab, tr. v., squabb-y, adj.

## squabble
squabble, intr. and tr. v. and л. — Prob. of Scand.
origin. Cp. dial. Swed. skvabbel, 'dispute',
skvappa, 'to chide', which are of imitative origin.
Derivatives: squabbl-er, п., squabbl-ing, adj.,
squabbl-ing-ly, adv., squabbl-y, adj.

## squacco
squacco, п., a small, crested heron. — Dial. It., of
imitative origin.

## squad
squad, п., a small group. — Earlier F. esquade
(F. escouade), fr. It. squadra and Sp. escuadra,
'squad', prop, 'square', fr. Late L. *exquadrdre>
'to form into a square'. It. squadra and Sp.
escuadra orig. meant 'troops formed into a
square'. See square and cp. squadron.
Derivative: squad, tr. v.

## squadron
squadron, n. — It. squadrone, formed fr. squadra,
'square', with the augment, suff. -one. See
squad and -oon and cp. escadrille.

## squall
squall, п., a kind of game. — Cp. obsol. skayles,
kayles, 'skittles', rel. to OHG. kegil, 'stake, pile',
MHG., G. kegel, 'skittles', Du. keg, 'wedge',
dial. Swed. kage, kagge, 'trunk of a tree*. See
keg.

## squalid
squalid, adj., foul, filthy; sordid. — L. squdlidus,
'rough, filthy', fr. squalere, 'to be filthy', fr,
squalus, 'foul, filthy', which stands for *sqy/d-
los and is rel. to squa-ma, 'scale'; not cogn. with
Gk. πηλός, 'clay*, and nor with OSlav. kalu,
'dirt'. Cp. squama.
Derivatives: squalid-ity, п., squalid-ly, adv.,
squalid-ness, n.

## squall
squall, intr. v., to squeal. — Of Scand. origin. Cp.
ON. skvala, 'to squeal*, which is prob. of
imitative origin. Cp. also squeal.
Derivatives: squall, п., squall-y, adv.

## Squalodon
Squalodon, п., a genus of fossil toothed whales
(paleontol.) — ModL., a hybrid coined fr. L.
squalus, 'a large fish', and Gk. οδών, gen.
οδόντος, 'tooth'. See Squalus and odonto-.

## squaloid
squaloid, adj., resembling a shark. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. squalus, 'a large fish', and Gk.
-οειδής, 'like', fr. εϊδος, 'form,· shape'. See
Squalus and -oid.

## squalor
squalor, n. — L. squalor, 'filth', fr. squalere, 'to
be filthy'. See squalid and -or.

## Squalus
Squalus, п., a genus of fishes of the family of
sharks (ichtfiyol.) — L.r *a large kind of sea
fish', cogn. with ON. hualr, OE. kwsel, 'whale'.
See whale.

## squam-
squam-, form of squamo- before a vowel.

## squama
squama, п., scale. — L. squama, rel. to squalus,
'foul, filthy'. See squalid and cp. desquamate, es-
quamate.

## squami-
squami-, combining form meaning 'scale'. — Fr.
L. squama. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:737 COLUMN:2 -->

## squamiferous
squamiferous, adj., bearing scales. —
Compounded of squami- and -ferous,

## squamiform
squamiform, adj., having the form of a scale.—
Compounded of squami- and form, n.

## squamo-
squamo-, before a vowel squam-, combining form
meaning 'scale'. — Fr. L. squama. See squama.

## squamoid
squamoid, adj., having the form of a scale. —
A hybrid coined fr. L. squama, 'scale', and Gk.
-οείδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape*. See
squamo- and -oid.

## squamose
squamose, adj., squamous. — L. squdmosus. See
squamous and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: squamose-ly, aav.,squamose-ness, n,

## squamous
squamous, adj., resembling, or covered with,
scales. — L. squdmosus, 'scaly', fr. squama,
'scale'. See squama and -ous and cp. next word.
Derivatives: squamous-ly, adv., squamous-ness,
n.

## squamule
squamule, п., a small scale. — L. squamula, 'a
small scale', dimin. of squama, 'scale'. See
squama and -ule.

## squander
squander, tr. v. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: squander-er, п., squander-ing-lyf
adv.

## square
square, n. — ME., fr. OF. esquarre, esquerre (F.
equerre), fr. VL. *exquadra, back formation fr.
*exquadrdre, 'to form into a square', fr. 1st ex-
and L. quadra, 'a square', fem. of the adj. qua-
drus, 'square', used as a noun. Cp. It. squadra,
Sp. escuadra, which are of the same origin. See
quadri- and cp. squad, squadron, escadrille.
Derivatives: square, adj., tr. and intr. v., adv.,
square-ly, adv., square-ness, п., squar-ish, adj.

## squarrose
squarrose, adj., with rough projections (hot. and
zool.) — Late L. squarrosus, 'scurfy, scabby',
prob. cogn. with OSlav. skvruna, 'dirt, filth*,
skvara, 'filth', Russ. skverna, 'dirt, filth', skver-
no, 'ugly'. For the ending see adj. suff. -ose.

## squarrous
squarrous, adj., squarrose. — Late L. squarrosus.
See prec. word and -ous.

## squarson
squarson, п., formerly a clergyman who was also
a landowner. — A blend of squire and parson.

## squash
squash, tr. and intr. v., to crush, squeeze. — MF.
esquasser, fr. OF., fr. VL. *exquassare, fr. 1st
ex- and quassdre, freq. of quatere (pp. quassus),
'to shake', See quash, *to make void'.
Derivatives: squash, п., squash-er, п., squash-y,
adj., squash-i-ly, adv., squash-i-ness, n.

## squash
squash, п., the fruit of various trailing plants of
the genus Cucurbita. — Algonquian. Cp. Narra-
ganset askutasquash, 'squash*, lit. 'eaten green',
fr. askut, 'green, raw', and asquash, 'eaten*.

## squat
squat, intr. v., to crouch or cower; tr. v., to cause
to squat. — ME. squatten, fr. OE. esquaier,
formed fr. es- (fr. L. ex, 'out of, from', see 1st ex-)
and quatir, 'to press down, flatten', which
derives fr. VL. *coactire, fr. L. codctus, pp. of
cogere, 'to drive together, compel'. See cogent
and cp. coact.
Derivatives: squat, п., and adj., squat-ly, adv.,
squat-ness, п., squatt-ish, adj., squatt-y, adj.,
squatt-i-ly, adv., squatt-i-ness, n.

## squaw
squaw, п., an American Indian woman. — A word
denoting 'woman', in the Algonquian dialects;
cp. e.g. Narraganset squaws, 'woman'.

## squawk
squawk, intr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp. squeak.
Derivatives: squawk, п., squawk-er, п.,
squawking, adj., squawk-ing-ly, adv., squawk-y, adj.

## squeak
squeak, intr. v. — ME. squeken, of imitative
origin. Cp. Swed. sqvdka, 'to croak', G. quieken,
'to squeak'. Cp. also squawk.
Derivatives: squeak, п., squeak-er, п.,
squeaker у, п., squeak-ing, adj., squeak-ing-ly, adv.,
squeak-y, adj.

## squeal
squeal, intr. and tr. v. — ME. squelen, prob. of
imitative origin. Cp. Swed. sqvala and E. squall.
Derivatives: squeal, п., squeal-er, n.

## squeamish
squeamish, adj., 1) prudish; 2) excessively
fastidious. — Formed—with change of suff. -ous to
-ish—fr. ME. esquaymous, fr. AF. escoymous,
which is of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: squeamish-ly, adv., squeamish-
ness, n.

## squeegee
squeegee, п., a wooden instrument with a rubber
blade. — Formed with suff. -ее fr. squeege, a
popular form of squeeze.
Derivative: squeegee, tr. v., to treat with a
squeegee.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:737 COLUMN:3 -->

## squeezable
squeezable, adj. — Formed fr. squeeze with suff.
-able.
Derivatives: squeezabil-ity, п., squeezable-ness,
п., squeezabl-y, adv.

## squeeze
squeeze, tr. and intr. v. — A hybrid coined fr. s-
(which corresponds to F. es- fr. L. ex, Out of,
from*, see 1st ex-), and OE. cwesan, cwisan,
cwysan, 'to bruise, squeeze', which is prob. of
imitative origin. Cp. MDu. quetsen, Du. kwetsen,
'to injure, wound'. G. quetschen, 'to squeeze'.
Derivatives: squeeze, п., squeez-er, п.,
squeezing, adj., squeez-ing-ly, adv., squeez-y, adj.

## squelch
squelch, tr. v., to crush down; intr. v., to produce
a splashing sound, as by treading heavily in
water; п., the act of squelching. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. qnelch.
Derivatives: squelch-er, п., squelch-ing, adj.,
squelch-ing-ly, adv., squelch-ing-ness, п., squelch-
У, adj.

## squib
squib, п., I) firework burning with a hissing noise;
2) a lampoon. — ME. squippen, 'to move
quickly', prob. fr. ON. svipa, 'to swoop, dart', which
is rel. to OHG. sweifan, MHG. sweifen, 'to
swing', and to E. swoop, sweep, swift.
Derivatives: squib, tr. and intr. v., squibb-er, п.,
squibb-ish, adj.

## squid
squid, п., a ten-armed marine mollusk. — Fr.
squit, a dial. var. of squirt; so called from its
squirting out a black substance.
Derivative: squid, intr. v., to fish with squid.

## squiffy
squiffy, adj., intoxicated (slang). — Of uncertain
origin.

## squilgee
squilgee, n. and tr. v. — A var. of squeegee.

## squill
squill, п., sea onion. — ME., fr. L. squilla, scilla,
'sea onion, squill', fr. Gk. σκίλλα, which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. Scilla.

## Squilla
Squilla, п., a genus of crustaceans. — L. squilla.
See prec, word.

## squinancy
squinancy, п., quinsy wort. — ME., fr. ML.
squinancia, a blend of Gk. συνάγχη and
κυνάγχη, both names of diseases of the throat. Cp. F.
esquinancie and see the English variants cynan-
che and quinsy.

## squinch
squinch, п., a small arch serving as an interior
corner support. — A var. of scuncheon.

## squint
squint, adj. — Aphetic for asquint, from the ME.
adv. asquint. Cp. Du. schuin, 'slanting, sloping',
schuinte, 'slant, slope', Dan. paa skens, 'aslant',
and E. askance.
Derivatives', squint, intr. v. and adj., squint-ing,
adj., squint-ing-ly, adv.

## squire
squire, n. — Aphetic for esqnire.
Derivatives: squire, tr. v., squire-hood, п., squire-
let, п., squire-ship, n.

## squirearchal
squirearchal, adj., pertaining to a squirearchy. —
Formed from next word with adj. suff. -al.

## squirearchy
squirearchy, п., landed gentry. — A hybrid
coined fr. squire and Gk. -αρχία, 'rule'. See -archy.

## squireen
squireen, п., a petty squire in Ireland. — A hybrid
coined fr. squire and the Irish dimin. suff. -in
(see -een).

## squirm
squirm, intr. v., to wriggle. — Prob. of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: squirm, п., squirm-er, п.,
squirming, adj., squirm-ing-ly, adv., squirm-y, adj.

## squirrel
squirrel, n. — ME. squirel, squerel, fr. OF. es-
quireul, escurel (F. ecureuil), fr. VL. *scuriolus,
dimin. of *scurius, fr. L. sciurus, fr. Gk.
σκίουρος, lit. 'that which makes a shade with its
tail', fr. <ma, 'shade', and ούρα, 'tail'. For
the first element see skiagraphy, for the second
see uro-, 'tail'. Cp. Sciuridae.

## squirt
squirt, intr. v.,"to gush; tr. v., to cause to gush. —
Cp. ME. swirten, squirten, which, together with
LG. swirtjen, is prob. of imitative origin. Cp.
squid.
Derivatives: squirt, п., squirt-ing, adj., squirt-
ing-ly, adv.

## sraddha
sraddha, п., ceremony of offering of balls of rice
to the ancestors (Hinduism). — OI. srdddhah, fr.
sraddha, 'faith', which is rel. to srad-dadhdti,
'trusts, believes*, and cogn. with L. credere, 'to
believe'. See creed,

## sri
sri, also shri, adj., fortunate, prosperous (said
esp. of divinities, kings and heroes). — OI. srifr,
'beauty, splendor, well-being, dignity,
happiness', rel. to Avestic sri, 'beauty*, OI. irfrdh,
Avestic srira-, 'beautiful', and cogn. with Gk.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:738 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 711 | STALL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:738 COLUMN:1 -->
κρείων, κρέων, 'lord, master'.

## sruti
sruti, also shruti, п., revealed literature, esp.
applied to parts of the Vedas and the Upanishads
(Hinduism). — OI. srutih, 'the act of hearing;
what is heard', rel. to OI. srutdh, 'what has been
heard', and cogn. with Gk. κλέος, 'fame, news',
κλυτός, 'heard, loud, famous', L. in-clutus,
'famous', OS., OE. hlud, 'loud'. See loud and cp.
words there referred to.

## stab
stab, tr. and intr. v. — Prob. a var. of dial, stob,
'to pierce, stab', fr. stob, 'stake, nail', which
itself is a var. of stub.
Derivatives: slab, stabb-er, п., stabb-ing, adj.,
stabb-ing-ly, adv.

## stabile
stabile, adj., stable; stationary. — L. stabilis. See
stable, adj.

## stability
stability, n. — ME. stabilite, fr. MF. (= F.) sta-
bilite, fr. L. stabilitdtem, ace. of stabilitds, fr.
stabilis. See stable, adj., and -ity.

## stabilize
stabilize, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. L.
stabilis, 'stable'. See stable, adj.
Derivatives: stabiliz-ation, п., stabiliz-er, n.

## stable
stable, adj., firm. — ME., fr. OF. stable, estable
(F. stable), fr. L. stabilis, 'firm, steady, constant',
from the stem of stare, 'to stand'. See state and
-able and cp. establish. Cp. also the second
element in thermostable.
Derivatives: srable-ness, п., stabl-y, adj.

## stable
stable, п., a building for horses or cattle. — ME.,
fr. OF. estable (F. etable), fr. L. stabulum, 'stable,
stall, lair, hut', which stands for *st -dhlo-m and
lit. means 'a place for standing', from the stem
of stare, 'to stand'. See state and cp. the second
element in constable.
Derivatives: stable, tr. v., to put into a stable,
intr. v., to be kept in a stable, stabl-ing, п., the
act of putting into a stable; accommodation (for
horses, etc.) in a stable or stables.

## stabllsh
stabllsh, tr. v. (archaic). — Aphetic for establish.

## staccato
staccato, adj. and adv., disconnected (musical
direction). — It., pp. of staccare, aphetic form of
distaccare, 'to detach, disconnect', which is rel.
to OF. destachier (F. detacher), 'to detach'. See
detacb.

## Stachys
Stachys, п., a genus of plants, the hedge nettle
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. stachys, 'horsemint', fr.
Gk. στάχυς (for *stnghu-), 'spike', which is
cogn. with ON. stinga, OE. stingan, 'to thrust,
sting'. See sting, v., and cp. the second element
in Agastache, Eustace.

## stack
stack, n. — ME. stak, fr. ON. stakkr, 'stack',
which is rel. to Dan. stak, Swed. stack, 'heap,
stack', and cogn. with OSlav. stogu, 'heap', Lith.
st&kas, 'pillar'. See stake.
Derivatives: stack, tr. v., stack-er, п., stack-ful,
adj., stack-less, adj.

## stacte
stacte, п., one of the eleven spices used by the
ancient Hebrews used to make incense. — L.
stacte, 'oil of myrrh', fr. Gk. ατακτή, prop,
fem. of στακτός, 'oozing out in drops', verbal
adj. of στάζειν, 'to let drop, distil; to drop,
drip', which is prob. cogn. with L. stagnum,
'pond'. See stagnate and cp. epistaxis.

## stactometer
stactometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
drops of a liquid. — Compounded of Gk.
στακτός, 'oozing out in drops', and μίτρον,
'measure'. See prec. word and meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## staddle
staddle, п., support. — ME. stathel, fr. OE. sta-
ool, 'foundation, support', rel. to ON. stodull,
'milking place', OFris. stathul, 'foundation',
OHG. stadal, MHO., G. stadel, 'barn'. The
literal meaning of these words is 'standing place,
stand'; they derive fr. I.-E. base *std-, 'to stand',
whence also Goth., OE. standan, 'to stand'. See
stand and cp. the first element in stalwart. For
sense development cp. the cognate L. stabulum,
'stable, stall', from the stem οι stare, 'to stand'
(see stable, n.)

## stallholder
stallholder, also stadtholder, п., governor of a
province. — Du. stadhouder, lit. 'holding the
place', fr. stad, 'place', and houder, 'holder';
influenced in form by E. holder (stadtholder shows
also the influence of G. Stadt, 'town'). See stead,
hold, v., and agential suff. -er. Du. stadhouder—
like MLG. stedeholder, Dan. stadholder, Swed.
stathallare and G. Statthalter, of s.m.—are
prop, loan translations of L. locum tenens (see

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:738 COLUMN:2 -->
locum tenens).

## stadholderate
stadholderate, stadtholderate, п., office of a
stadholder. — A hybrid coined fr. prec. word and
-ate, a subst. suff. of Latin origin.

## stadium
stadium, п., 1) a Greek measure of length; 2) a
racecourse. — L-, fr. Gk. στάδιον, 'racecourse,
stadium\ which is a blend of σπάδιον,
'racecourse', and στάδιον, neut. of στάδιος, 'fix,
firm'. Σπάδιον is a derivative of σπαν, 'to draw,
tear' (see spasm). Στάδιος derives fr. I.-E. base
*std-, 'to stand'; see state.

## staff
staff, n. — ME. staf, fr. OE. stxf, 'stick, staff', rel.
to OS. staf, ON. stafr, Dan. stay, Swed. staf,
OFris. «re/; MLG., MDu., Du. staf, OHG. stab,
MHG. slap, G. Stab, Goth, "staf-s (in dat. pi.
stabim), 'element', and cogn. with OLith. stdbas,
'idol', Lith. stebas, 'staff, pillar', Lett, stabs,
OSlav. stoboru, 'pillar', OPruss. stabis, 'stone',
OI. stabhndti, stabhnuti, 'supports'. All these
words derive fr. I.-E. base *steb(h)-, 'to cause to
stand, place, support; to step'. See step and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also stave and the
second element in distaff, Gustavus, palstave.
Derivatives: staff, tr. v., staff-ed, adj.

## staffage
staffage, п., accessories. — G., fr. staffieren, 'to
dress up, trim, garnish', fr. MLG. stofferen, staf-
feren, fr. MDu. stofferen, fr. OF. estofer (F. itof-
fer), fr. OHG. stopfon (MHG., G. stopfen), 'to
stuff, fill'. OF. estofe (F. etoffe), 'stuff, material',
is prob. a back formation fr. estofer (F. etoffer).
See stuff and -age.

## stag
stag, n. — ME., fr. OE. stagga, 'stag', orig. 'a
male animal', rel. to ON. steggi, 'a male bird, a
male cat", dial. E. stag, 'gander'. These words
derive fr. *stegh-, a denasalized form of I.-E.
base *stengh-, 'to sting'. The original meaning
of stag prob. was 'provided with a male organ'.
See sting, v.

## stage
stage, п., platform. — ME., fr. OF. estage (F.
etage), lit. 'place to stand upon', fr. VL. *stati-
cum, a derivative of L. std, stare, 'to stand'. See
state, n.
Derivatives: stage, tr. v., stag-er, п.,stag-ing, п.,
stag-y, adj., stag-i-ness, n.

## staggard
staggard, п., stag of the fourth year. — Formed
fr. stag with suff. -ard.

## stagger
stagger, intr. and tr. v. — ME. stakkeren, fr. ON.
stakra, 'to push, to cause to reel', fr. staka, 'to
push'; prob. rel. to Swed. stake, 'stake', and to
E. stake (q.v.)
Derivatives: stagger, п., stagger-er, п.,
staggering, adj., stagger-ing-ly, adv.

## Stagirite
Stagirite, п., a native of Stagira, esp. Aristotle. —
L. Stagirites, fr. Gk. Σταγειρΐτης, fr. Στά-
γειρα, 'Stagira', a town in Macedonia. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: Stagirit-ic, adj.

## stagnancy
stagnancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## stagnant
stagnant, adj. — L. stdgndns, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of stagndre. See next word and -ant.
Derivatives: stagnant-ly, adv., stagnant-ness, n.

## stagnate
stagnate, intr. v., to cease to flow. — L. stdgndtus,
pp. of stagndre, 'to cause to stand, make
stagnant', fr. stagnum, 'pool', which is prob. cogn.
with Gk. σταγών, 'drop', στάζειν (for *στάγ-
Ι,ειν), 'to let drop, distil; to drop, drip'. Cp.
stacte. For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: stagnat-ton, n.

## stagnicolous
stagnicolous, adj., living in stagnant water. —
Compounded of L. stagnum, 'pool', and the
stem of colere, 'to till (the soil), dwell, inhabit'.
See stagnate, colony and -ons.

## staid
staid, adj., 1) settled; 2) sedate. — Identical with
stayed, pp. of stay.
Derivatives: staid-ly, adv., staid-ness, n.

## stain
stain, tr. and intr. v. — ME. steinen, aphetic for
disteinen, fr. OF. disteindre (F. diteindre), 'to
take the color out of, fr. VL. "distingere, fr. dis-
and L. tingere, 'to dye'. See distain, which is a
doublet of stain. For a similar aphesis cp. splay,
sport, stress.
Derivatives: stain, п., stain-able, adj., stain-ed,
adj., stain-er, п., stain-less, adj., stain-less-ly,
adv., stain-less-ness, n.

## stair
stair, n.—ME. steyer, steir, fr. OE. stseger, fr. *stag-
ir, fr. Teut. base 'staig-, *sttg-, corresponding
to I.-E. *stigh-. See sty, 'to ascend'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:738 COLUMN:3 -->

## staith
staith, п., a wharf. — ME. stathe, a blend of OE.
stsed, 'bank, shore', and ON. stop, 'landing
place'. Both these words are rel. to OS. stath,
OFris. sted, OHG. stad, stado, MHG. stade, G.
Staden, Gestade, Goth, stapa (dat.), 'bank,
shore'. These words derive fr. I.-E. base *sta-,
'to stand', and orig. meant 'a place for
standing'. See state and cp. stead.

## stake
stake, n. — ME., fr. OE. staca, rel. to ON. stiaki,
Swed. stake, Dan. stage, Du. staak, and cogn.
with Lett, stega, stigs, 'rod, pole, perch', Russ.
stofar', of s.m., and possibly also with L. tig-
num, 'building material, log, beam'. Cp. stack,
stagger, stockade, estacade. Cp. also contigna-
tion.
Derivatives: stake, tr. v., stak-er, n.

## stakhanovism
stakhanovism, п., an efficiency system in which
workers increase their piecework production
and are rewarded with bonuses and special
privileges. — Named after Aleksei Grigorievich
Stakhanov, a Soviet coalminer who, in 1935,
introduced an efficiency system to attain a higher
production rate. For the ending see suff. -ism.

## Stakhanovite
Stakhanovite, п., a worker who excelled under
the system of stakhanovism. — See prec. word'
and subst. suff. -ite.

## stalactic
stalactic, stalactical, adj. — Formed with suff.
-ic, resp. -ical, fr. Gk. σταλακτός, 'dropping,
dripping'. See stalactite.

## stalactiform
stalactiform, adj. — A haplological var. of stalac-
titiform.

## stalactite
stalactite, п., an icicle-shaped formation hanging
from the roof of a cave. — ModL. stalactites, fr.
Gk. σταλακτός, 'dropping, dripping', verbal
adj. of σταλάσσειν, 'to let drop; to drop, drip'.
See stale, 'to urinate', and cp. stulagmite. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivatives: stalactit-ed, stalactit-ic, stalactit-ic-
al, adjs.,stalactit-ic-al-ly, adv., stalactit-ious, adj.

## stalactitiform
stalactitiform, adj. — See stalactite and form, n.

## stalagmite
stalagmite, п., a cone-shaped deposit on the floor
of a cave. — ModL. stalagmites, fr. Gk.
σταλαγμός, 'a dropping, dripping', fr. σταλάσσειν.
See stalactite.
Derivatives: stalagmit-ic, slalagmit-ic-al, adjs.,
stalagmit-ic-al-ly, adv.

## stale
stale, adj., not fresh, stagnant. — ME. stale, prop,
'that which has stood long'; rel. to stall (q.v.)
Derivatives: stale, tr. v., to make stale, stale-ly,
adv., stale-ness, n.

## stale
stale, п., decoy (archaic). — ME., 'bird used as a
decoy', fr. AF. estate, fr. OF. estaler (F. etaler),
'to spread out', fr. Frankish *stall, 'place for
standing', which is rel. to OHG. stall, 'stall,
stable'. See stall.

## stale
stale, intr. v., to urinate (said of horses and
cattle). — ME. stolen, fr. OF. estaler, a word of
OFrankish origin; cp. Du., G. stallen, Dan.
stalle, stalde, Swed., Norw. stalla, 'to urinate',
fr. I.-E. base *(s)tel-, *(s)tal-, 'to drop, urinate',
whence also Gk. σταλαΥ, σταλάσσειν, 'to let
drop; to drop, drip', τέλμα, 'standing water,
pond, marsh', Lith. teliiit, teliti, 'to urinate'.
Cp. stalactite, stalagmite, telmato-.
Derivative: stale, п., urine of horses or cattle.

## stalk
stalk, п., a stem. — ME. stalke, dimin. of ME.
stale, fr. OE. stela, 'a stalk'; prob. fr. I.-E.
base *st(h)el-, 'to place'. See stall and cp. words
there referred to.

## stalk
stalk, intr. v., to walk furtively. — ME. stalken,
fr. OE. bestealcian, which is formed with -к, а
suff. of iterative force, fr. OE. stelan, 'to steal';
see steal. For this force of the suff. -k cp. hark,
fr. hear, and talk, fr. tell.

## stalklet
stalklet, n.—Diminutive formed fr. stalk, п.,with
suff. -let.

## stall
stall, n. — ME. stall, fr. OE. steall, stall, 'stable',
rel. to ON. stallr, 'pedestal for idols, altar',
Swed. stall, Dan. staid, OFris., Du. stal, OHG.
stall, stal, 'stand, place, stable, stall*, MHG.

## stall
stall, stal, G. Stall, 'stable', and to OHG.,
MHG-, G. stellen, 'to place', G. Stelle, 'place',
fr. I.-E. base *st(h)el-, 'to cause to stand, to

## place
place, to stand', whence also OI. sthalati, 'stands

## firm'
firm', sthuna (for *sthulna), 'column', Arm. ste-

## lem
lem, Ί place', Gk. στέλλειν, 'to set in order,

## arrange
arrange, equip; to send', στελεα, στελεόν, Att.
στελεός, 'the hole for the handle of an ax',,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:739 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: STALLION | 712 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:739 COLUMN:1 -->
στέλεχος, 'the stump', στήλη, Dor. στάλα,
'post, monument', στόλος, equipment,
expedition, army**, στολή, 'adjustment, equipment,
garment*, OL. stlocus, L. locus, 'place' (lit.
'where something is placed"), stolidus, 'slow,
dull' (prop, 'standing still*), stultus, 'foolish',
OPruss. stallft, 'to stand', Lett, stalls, 'stately*.
С p. forestall, install. Cp. also npostie, diastaltic,
diastole, epistle, Gestalt, local, locus, pedestal,
peristalsis, peristaltic, stale, 'not fresh', stale,
'decoy', stalk, п., stallion, stalwart, stele, still, adj.,
stilllon, stilt, stole, 'a long garment', stolid,
stolon, stall, stultify, systaltic, systole. Base
*st(h)el- is an enlargement of base *st(h)d-, 'to
stand'. See state.
Derivatives: stall, tr. and intr. v., stall-age, n.

## stallion
stallion, п., a male horse. — ME. stalun, fr. OF.
estalon (F. etalon), 'stall', fr. VL. *stallonem,
ace. of *stallo, lit. 'a horse kept in the stall', fr.
Frankish *stall. See stall.

## stalwart
stalwart, adj , ]) sturdy, robust; 2) resolute. —
ME. stalworth, fr. OE. stselwyrde, staelwierde,
'serviceable' (said of ships), contraction of sta-
dolwierde, lit. 'worthy in foundation, of a firm
foundation', fr. stadol, 'foundation'» and wyrde,
wierde, 'worthy'. See staddle and worth, n.
Derivatives: stalwart, п., stalwart-ly, adv., stal-
wart-ness, n.

## stambouline
stambouline, п., the long coat formerly worn by
Turkish officials. — From Stamboul (Istanbul),
the Turkish name of Constantinople. The name
Stamboul-Istanbul itself is a corruption of Gk.
(ει)ς τάν (=■ ~ήν) πόλιν, 'into the city*. For
the ending see suff. -ine.

## stamen
stamen, п., the pollen-bearing organ of a flower.
— L. stamen, 'warp in the upright loom, thread,
fiber', cogn. with Gk. στήμων, 'warp', fr. l.-E.
base *st(h)d-, 'to stand', whence also OI. stha-
nian, 'place for standing, station', Toch. A
sktdm, 'tree', Goth, stoma, 'base, material', Lith.
stomuo, stuomud, 'stature', lr. tamum, 'stem of a
tree'. See state and cp. stamin, stamina. Cp. also
etamine, stem, п., Stemona, tammy, 'woolen
fabric*.
Derivative: stamen-ed, adj.

## stamin
stamin, п., coarse muslin. — ME., fr. OF. esta-
mine (F. etamine), fr. VL. *stdminea, a noun
formed fr. the fem. of the adj. stdmineus,
'consisting of threads', fr. stamen, gen. stdminis
(whence It. stame, OProvenc. estam and Sp.
estambre, 'stamen'). See prec. word.

## stamin-
stamin-, form of stamini- before a vowel.

## stamina
stamina, п., vigor. — Prop, pi., fr. L. stamina, pi.
of stamen. See stamen.

## staminal
staminal, adj., pertaining to stamens. — Formed
with adj. sufT. -al from L. stamen, gen. stdminis.
See stamen.

## staminate
staminate, adj., having stamens. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ate fr. L. stamen, gen. stdminis. See
stamen.

## stamincal
stamincal, adj., pertaining to stamens. — Formed
with adj. stiff, -al fr. L.sramineus, an adjective
derived fr. stamen, gen. stdminis. See stamen and
cp. stamina!.

## stammeous
stammeous, adj., pertaining to stamens. — See
prec. word and -eous.

## stamini-
stamini-, before a vowel stamin-, combining form
denoting the stamen. — L. stamini-, stamin-, fr.
stamen, gen. stdminis. See stamen.

## staminiferous
staminiferous, adj., producing stamens. — Com·
pounded of stamini- and -ferous.

## staminodium
staminodium, п., an abortive stamen (hot.) —
ModL., formed fr. stamini- and ModL. -odium,
a suiF. denoting 'likeness', fr. Gk. -ώ8ης, 'like*.
See -ode, 'like'.

## stammel
stammel, п., linsey-woolsey. — F. estamel,
formed—with change of suffix—fr. OF. estamine.
See stamin.

## stammer
stammer, intr. and tr. v. — ME. stameren, fr. OE.
stamerian, fr. stamer, stamur, stamor,
'stammering', rel. to OE. stamm, ON. stamr, stammr,
OHG. stam, stomal, Goth, stamms,
'stammering*, ON. stama, OS. stamaron, LG. stamern,
MDu. stameren, Du. stamelen, OHG. stamma-
Ιδη, stamalon, MHG. stamelen, stammelen, G,
stammeln, 'to stammer*, OS., OFris., OHG.,
MHG. stum, G. stumm, 'dumb', fr. I.-E. base
*stem-, 'to stem, hold back*, whence also stem.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:739 COLUMN:2 -->
'to check'. OE. stamerian, etc., orig. meant 'to
be held back in speaking*. Cp. stum, stumble.
Derivatives: stammer, п., stammer-er,
stammering, n. and adj., stammer-ing, n. and adj.,
stammer-ing-ly, adv.

## stamnos
stamnos, п., a kind of wine vessel (Greek antiq.)
— Gk. στάμνος, prop, 'that which stands', from
the stem of ϊστημ-t, Ί put, place', which is cogn.
with L. store, 'to stand*. See state and cp. stem,n.

## stamp
stamp, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stampen, rel. to ON.
stappa (for *stampa), Dan. stampe, Swed.,
Norw. stappa, stampa, MLG., MDu., Du.
stampen, OHG. stampfon, stapfon, MHG., G. stam-
pfen, 'to stamp with the foot, beat, pound', and
to OE. stempan, 'to pound (in a mortar)', OS.
stamp, OHG. stamp/, G. Stampfe, 'pestle', fr.
I.-E. base *stemb(h)-, 'to tread firmly, to stamp*,
whence also Gk. στέμβειν, *to crush with the
feet, handle roughly, misuse*. This base is a
nasalized enlargement of base *steb(h)-, 'to tread,
step'. See step and words there referred to and
cp. esp. stampede. Cp. also tamp, contemn. It.
stampare, 'to stamp, impress', stampa, 'stamp,
impression', Sp. estampar, 'to stamp, print',
estampa, 'print, stamp', F. estamper, 'to stamp,
impress', estampe, 'stamp, print', Provenc,
estampir, 'to rustle, rush*, are Teut. loan words.

## stampede
stampede, п., ]) a sudden running away of
frightened horses, cattle, etc.; 2) any sudden
impulsive movement of a large number of people. —
Mexican Sp. estampida, 'stampede', fr. Sp.
estampida, 'impetuous movement, rush', fr.
Proven?, estampida, fr. estampir, 'to rustle, rush',
which is of Teut. origin. See stamp, v.

## stance
stance, п., manner of standing, posture. — MF.
estance, fr. OF., fr. VL. *stantia, 'place, abode',
lit. 'a standing', fr. L. stdns, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of stare, 'to stand*. See state, п., and cp.
stanchion, stanza.

## stanch
stanch, staunch, tr. v., to stop the flow of (blood);
intr. v., to cease to flow. — ME. stanchen,
stauncfien, fr. OF. estanchier (F. etancher), 'to
check the flow of a liquid, to stanch blood',
prob. fr. VL. *stanticdre, a derivative of L. stare,
'to stand'. See state and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also stank, n.
Derivatives: sta(u)nch, adj. (q.v.), sta(u)nch-er,
n.

## stanch
stanch, adj. — See staunch.

## stanchion
stanchion, п., an upright post. — ME. stanchon,
fr. OF. estanchon (F. έίαηςοη), fr. OF. estance,
estanche, 'the act of standing' (whence F. etance,
'roughly-squared timber for a stanchion'), fr.
VL. *stantia, 'place*, lit. 'a standing', fr. L. stdns,
gen. stands, pres. part, of stare, 'to stand'. See
state and cp^ stance, stanza.
Derivative: stanchion, tr. v.

## stand
stand, intr. and tr. v. — ME. standen, fr. OE.
standan, rel. to ON. standa, OS., Goth, standan,
OHG. stantan, and to Dan. staa, Swed. stu, Du.
staan, OHG., MHG. start, sten, G. stehen, 'to
stand', and cogn. with OI. tisthati, 'stands*, Gk.
ϊστημί, Ί cause to stand, set, place', ίίστηκα,
Ί stand', L. stare, 'to stand', fr. I.-E. base
*st(h)d-, 'to stand*. See state, п., and words there
referred to and cp. esp. staddle, stadholder,
stalth, stay, 'to prop1, stead, stound, Stundist.
Derivatives: stand, п., stand-er, п., stand-ing,
adj. and n.

## standard
standard, n. — ME., fr. OF. estendard, estandard
(F. etendard), a hybrid formed with the Teut.
surT. -ard fr. OF. estendre (F. itendre), 'to stretch
out', fr. L. extendere; see extend. Some senses
of the noun standard are due to the erroneous
association of this word with the verb stand.
Derivatives: standard, adj., standardize (q.v.)

## standardize
standardize, tr. v. — A double hybrid formed fr.
standard with -ize, a sufT. of Creek origin.
Derivatives: standardiz-ation, п., standardiz-er,
n.

## standish
standish, п., inkstand {archaic). — Compounded
of stand and dish.

## standpoint
standpoint, n. — Loan translation of G. Stand-

## punkt
punkt, which is compounded of Stand, 'a
standing, stand', and Punkt, 'point'. See stand and
point.

## stanhope
stanhope, п., a kind of light, single-seated, open
carriage. — Named after the English clergyman

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:739 COLUMN:3 -->
Fitzroy Stanhope (1787-1864).

## stank
stank, п., pool; tank. — ME., fr. OF. estanc (F.
^tang), back formation fr. estanchier (F.
etancher), 'to check the flow of a liquid'. See stanch.
OF. estanc is erroneously derived by most
lexicographers fr. L. stdgnum, 'pool'.

## stank
stank, past tense of stink. — ME., fr. OE. stanc,
past tense of stincan. See stink.

## stannary
stannary, п., a tin mine. — ML. stanndria, fr. L.
stagnum, stannum, 'tin'; prob. of Celtic origin.
Cp. Gael., Ir. stdn, Co., Bret, sten, W.ystaen,
'tin'. It. stagno, F. etain, Sp. estano, 'tin', are
Latin loan words. Cp. the second element in
costean. For the ending see suif. -ary.
Derivative: stannary, adj.

## stannate
stannate, п., salt of stannic acid (ckem.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ate fr. L. stannum, 'tin'. See
prec. word.

## stannic
stannic, adj., of tin. — Formed with adj. suif. -ic
fr. L. stannum, 'tin'. See stannary.

## stanniferous
stanniferous, adj., containing tin. —
Compounded of L. stannum, gen. stanni, 'tin* (see stannary),
and -ferous.

## stnnnite
stnnnite, п., a mineral compound containing tin,
copper, iron, and sulfur. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. stannum, 'tin', and Gk. suff. -ΐτης. See
stannary and subst. suff. -ite.

## stannous
stannous, adj., containing tin. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. stannum, 'tin'. See stannary.

## stanza
stanza, п., a group of rhymed verse lines. — It.,
'habitation, room', fr. VL. *stantia, 'place,
abode', lit. 'a standing'; see stance. For sense
development cp. Arab, bayt, which unites the
meanings 'house, room; verse'.
Derivatives: stanza-ed, adj., stanza-ic, adj.

## stapes
stapes, п., the stirrup bone in the middle ear
(anat.) — ML. stapes, 'stirrup', prob. formed
from the base of L. stare, 'to stand', and pes,
pedis, 'foot'. See state and pedal.

## staphyl-
staphyl-, form of staphylo- before a vowel.

## Staphylea
Staphylea, п., a genus of plants, the bladder nut
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σταφυλή, 'bunch of
grapes'. See staphylo-.

## Staphyleaceae
Staphyleaceae, n. pi., the bladder nut family (bot.)
— ModL., formed from prec. word with sufF.
-aceae.

## staphyleaceous
staphyleaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## staphylo-
staphylo-, before a vowel staphyl-^ combining
form denoting the uvula (anat.) — Gk. σταφυλο-,
σταφυλ-, fr. σταφυλή, 'a bunch of grapes',
which is prob. rel. to σταφίς, 'raisin*, and stands
in gradational relationship to στέμφυλα (pi.),
'mass of pressed grapes', ά-στεμερής,
'unshakable', στέμβειν, 'to crush with· the feet, shake
about, agitate, handle roughly'. See step and cp.
Staphylea. Cp. also next word.

## Staphylococcus
Staphylococcus, п., a genus of bacteria of the
family Coccaceae (bacterial.) — ModL., coined by
the surgeon and bacteriologist Alexander Og-
ston (1844-1929) in ]882 fr. staphylo- and Gk.
κόκκος, 'kernel, berry*. See coccus.

## staphyloma
staphyloma, п., the bulging of the cornea (med.)
— Late L., fr. Gk. σταφύλωμα, gen. στα-
φυλώματος, 'defect in the eye inside the cornea',
fr. σταφυλή, 'bunch of grapes'. See staphylo-
and -oraa.
Derivatives: staphylomat-ic, staphylomat-ous,
adjs.

## staple
staple, п., a U-shaped bar, wire. — ME. stapel, fr.
OE. stapol, 'post, pillar; flight of steps', rel. to
OS. stapal, stapel, 'candle, small tub', OFris.
stapul, stapel, 'stem or visible part of a tooth;
block for executions*, MLG., MDu., Du. stapel,
'stake, pile, market, emporium', OHG. staffal,
stafful, MHG. staffel, stapfel, G. Staffel, 'rung
of a ladder' (G. Stapel, 'stocks', is borrowed fr.
MLG. stapel), and in gradational relationship
to ON. stopull, 'post, tower', Du. stoep, '(flight
of) steps*, OHG. stuofa, stuoffa, 'step, degree*.
See step, v., and words there referred to and cp.
esp. next word and etape.
Derivatives: staple, tr. v., to fasten with a staple,
stapl-ing, n.

## staple
staple, п., principal commodity of a country,
district, etc. — ME. stapel, fr. OF. estaple, 'market,
staple' (whence F. etape, 'halting place, stage of
journey'), fr. MDu. stapel, 'stake, pile, market,
emporium'. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:740 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 713 | STATOR | staart, OHG., MHG., G. sterz, fr. I.-E. base | sterling, stet, stool, stound, stow, 'to pack', stud -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:740 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: staple, adj., staple, tr. v., to grade,
classify, stapl-er, п., stapl-ing, n.
star, n. — ME. sterre, fr. OE. sieorra, rel. to OS.
sterro, ON. stjarna, Swed. stjerna, Dan. stierne,
OFris. stera, MLG. sterne, MDu. sterre, Du.
ster, OHG. sterro, sterna, stern, MHG. sterre,
sterne, stern, G. Stern, Goth, stairno, and cogn.
with 01. star-, 'star', nom. pi. tdrah, 'stars',
ihstr. pi. stfbhih, 'by means of stars', Toch. A
sre-n (pi.), 'stars', Hitt. shittar, Gk. αστήρ,
ίστρον, L. Stella (for 'ster-ld), OCo., Bret.
sterenn, W. seren, 'star'. All these words prob.
go back to an l.-E. primary form *astero, which
is of uncertain origin. It possibly derives from
the name of the evening star called after the Sem.
goddess Astarte, i.e. Ishtar, 'Asktdreth (see
Aphrodite). See Zimmern in E. Schrader, Die
Keilinschriften und das Alte Testament, 3rd ed.,
p. 425 and Jensen in Wiener Zeitschrift fur die
Kunde des Morgenlandes 6, 70. Cp. aster,
asterisk, Astraea, astral, astrology, astronomy,
constellation, disaster, Esther, stellar.
Derivatives: star, tr. and intr. v., star-less, adj.,
star-like, adj., starr-ed, adj., starr-y, adj., starr-
i-ness, n.

## starboard
starboard, п., the right side of a ship. — ME.
sterbord, fr. OE. steorbord, lit. 'steer board', rel.
to ON. stjdrnbordi, LG. sturbord, Du. stuur-
boord, G. Steuerbord; F. tribord, It. tribordo,
'starboard', are Teut. loan words. See steer, 'to
direct', and board,

## starch
starch, n. — ME. sterche, starche, back
formation fr. sterchen, 'to starch', fr. OE. stercan, 'to
stiffen', fr. stearc, 'stiff'. Cp. G. Starke, 'strength;
starch', and see stark.
Derivatives: starch, adj. and tr. v., starch-ed,

steal, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stelen, fr. OE. stelan,

to OS. stehli, ON-, MLG. stal, Dan. staal, Swed.

stal, MDu. stael, Du. staal, OHG. stahal, MHG.
