winter). All these words are prob. traceable ult. to
I.-E. base *sta-, 'to stand'. See state.
Derivatives: steel, adj. and tr. v., steel-y, adj.,
steel-i-ness, n.

## steelyard
steelyard, n., a kind of balance. — From the
Steelyard, factory of the Hanse towns in London,
erroneous translation of MLG. stalhof, 'sample
yeard*, fr. stal, 'sample*, which was confused
with MLG. stal, 'steel' (see steel). For the
second element see yard,

## steen
steen, n. — A var. spelling of stean.

## steenbok
steenbok, п., a small African antelope. — Du., fr.
steen, 'stone', and bok, 'buck'. See stone and
buck and cp. steinbok.

## steenkirk
steenkirk, п., a kind of lace cravat. — Named
from the battle of Steenkirk, in Belgium (1692).

## steep
steep, adj., precipitous. — ME. stepe, 'steep', fr.
OE. steap, 'lofty, tall'; in gradational
relationship to stoop and stoup (qq.v.) Cp. steep, 'to
soak', steeple.
Derivatives: steep, п., steep-en, tr. and intr. v.,
steep-ly, adv., steep-ness, п., sieep-y, adj. (poet.)

## steep
steep, tr. v., to soak. — ME. stepen, prob. fr. ON.
steypa, 'to pour out, prop, 'to make to stoop',
causative of stupa, 'to stoop'. Cp. Swed. stopa,
Dan. stebe, 'to steep (corn)', and see E. stoop.
Derivatives: steep, п., act or state of steeping,
steep-er, n.

## steeple
steeple, п., church tower, usually surmounted
with a spire. — ME. stepel, fr. OE. stepel, stypel,
'a lofty tower*, fr. steap, 'steep'. See steep, adj.
Derivative: steepl-ed, adj.

## steeplechase
steeplechase, п., horse race over a course with
obstacles. — Compounded of steeple and chase.
The orig. meaning was 'a race with a steeple as
goal'.
Derivatives: steeplechase, intr. v.,
steeplechaser, п., steeplechas-ing, n.

## steeple jack
steeple jack, п., one who climbs steeples,
chimneys, etc., for making repairs. — Prop. 'Jack
(used in the sense of 'fellow, man'), working on
steeples'.
Derivatives: steeple jack, intr. v.

## steer
steer, tr. and intr. v., to direct. — ME. steeren,

## steren
steren, fr. OE. stieran, 'to steer, guide', rel. to

## ON. styra
ON. styra, Dan. styre, Swed. styra, OFris.

## stiora
stiora, Du. sturen, OHG., MHG. stiuren, G.

## steuern
steuern, 'to steer', Goth, stiurjan, 'to establish,

## assert'
assert', OE. steor- (in compounds), ON. styri,

## OFris. stiure
OFris. stiure, Du. stuur, OHG. stiura, MHG.

## stiure
stiure, G. Steuer, 'rudder, helm', prob. rel. also

## to ON. staurr
to ON. staurr, 'pale, stake, pole', and cogn.
with Gk. σταυρός, of s.m., OI. sthavarah, 'thick,

## solid'
solid', sthavirafa, 'broad, thick', sturab, 'strong',

## Arm. stvar
Arm. stvar, 'thick', L. -staurdre in in-staurare,
'to renew, repair, restore', re-staurare, 'to

## repair
repair, restore'. All these words prob. derive fr.
I.-E. *st(h)iu-ro-, *st(h)du-ro-, *st(h)euro-,
*st(h)uro-, 'strong, stiff', enlargements of base
*st(h)du-, *st(h)Q-, 'stiff, upright; post, pillar*,
whence Gk. στυειν, 'to make stiff, erect, place,

## set'
set', στύλος, 'wooden pole, style for writing;

## see Walde-Hofmann
see Walde-Hofmann, LEW., I, 705-706 s.v.

## instaurdre and KIuge-Mitzka EWDS.
instaurdre and KIuge-Mitzka EWDS., pp. 747-
748. Cp. the first element in starboard. Cp. also

## stauro-
stauro-, instauration, restaurant, restauration,

## store
store, story of a house. Cp. also stua, stoic, style,
'gnomon', stud, 'nail, peg', stuff. Base *st(h)du-,
*st(h)ii-, stands in gradational relationship to
base *st(h)a-, 'to stand'. See state.
Derivatives: steer-able, adj., steer-age, п., steer-

## er
er, п., steer-ing, n.

## steer
steer, п., a young ox. — ME., fr. OE. steor, rel.

## to OS. stior
to OS. stior, ON. stjorr, frjorr, Swed, (/«/-.Dan.

## tyr
tyr, MDu., Du., MHG., G. stier, Goth, stiur,
'Ьи1Г, and cogn. with Gk. ταύρος, L. taurus,
'bull, bullock, steer', OSlav. turu, 'bull, steer',

## Lith. tauras
Lith. tauras, 'aurochs', OPruss. tauris, 'bison'.
All these words are prob. borrowed—directly
or indirectly—from the Sem. languages. Cp.

## Aram
Aram, tor, Heb. shor, 'bull, bullock, ox', and
see Taurus. Many an attempt has been made to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:742 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 715 | STERADIAN -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:742 COLUMN:1 -->
trace Gk. ταΰρος, etc., to an I.-E. source (cp.
e.g. the 'etymology', that connects these words
with Ol. sthurah, 'thick', and explains Gk.
ταΰρος, Goth. stiur, etc., as 'the thick animal').

## steeve
steeve, п., the angle made by a bowsprit from the
horizontal. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: steeve, tr. and intr. v., to form or
be formed at an angle with the horizon, steev-
ing, n.

## steeve
steeve, tr. v., to stow. — ME. Steven, fr. MF. ( =
F.) estiver, fr. L. stipare, 'to compress' (whence
also It. stivare, Sp. estibar, Port, estivar, 'to
compress, stow'), fr. I.-E. base *stei-, *sti-, 'to
stiffen, be compressed'. See stone and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also the first element in
stevedore.
Derivative: steeve, п., spar used in stowing
cargo.

## steg-
steg-, form of stego- before a vowel.

## stegano-
stegano-, combining form meaning 'covered', as
in steganography. — Gk. στεγανό-, fr.
στεγανός, 'covered', fr. στέγειν, 'to cover'. See stego-.

## steganography
steganography, п., the same as cryptography. —
Formed fr. stegano- and Gk. -γραφιά, fr. γρά-
φειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.

## stego-
stego-, before a vowel steg-, combining form
denoting covering, roof, or house. — Gk. στεγο-,
στεγ-, fr. στέγη or στέγος, 'roof, room, house',
fr. στέγειν, 'to cover', which is cogn. with OI.
sthagati, sthagayati, 'hides, covers', L. tegerei
'to cover'. See tegnment and cp. stegano-.

## Stegumyia
Stegumyia, п., a former genus of mosquitoes
(zool.) — ModL., compounded of stego- and
Gk. μυΐα, 'fiy', which is cogn. with L. musca,
'fly'. See muscle and cp. myo-.

## Stegosaurus
Stegosaurus, п., a genus of dinosaurs (paleontol.)
— ModL., compounded of stego- and Gk.
σαυρος, 'lizard'. See sauro-.

## Steinberger
Steinberger, п., a fine kind of White Rhenish
wine. — G., short for Steinberger Wein, i.e.
'wine produced at Steinberg', near Wiesbaden,
Germany.

## stelnbok
stelnbok, п., a steenbok. — G. Steinbock, fr.
Stein, 'stone', and Bock, 'buck'. See stone and
buck and cp. steenbok.

## Steironema
Steironema, n., a genus of plants of the primrose
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
στείρος, 'sterile*, and νήμα, 'thread'; so called
with reference to the staminodia. The first
element is cogn. with Ol. starih, 'barren cow', L.
sterilis, 'unfruitful*: see sterile. The second
element derives fr. νέειν, 'to spin'; see nemato-.

## stelar
stelar, adj., pertaining to a stele. — See stele and
adj. sufT. -ar.

## stele
stele, п., an inscribed stone slab. — Gk. στήλη,
'a block of stone, gravestone', rel. to στέλλε lv,
'to set in order, arrange, equip', στολή,
'adjustment, equipment, clothing', fr. I.-E. base
*st(h)el-, an enlargement of base *st(h)a-, 'to
stand'. See stull and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also epistle.

## Stella
Stella, fern. PN. — L. stella, 'star'. See next
word and cp. Est el la.

## stellar
stellar, adj., pertaining to stars. — L. stellaris, fr.
stella (for *ster-la), 'star', which is cogn. with
Gk. αστήρ, όίστρον, 'star', Goth, stairno, OE.
steorra, 'star'. See star and cp. prec. word and
Estella, estoile.

## stellate
stellate, adj., star-shaped. — L. stellatus, pp. of
stellare, 'to set with stars', fr. stella, 'star'. See
prec word and adj. suff. -ate and cp.
constellate.
Derivative: stellate-ly, adv.

## stelliferous
stelliferous, adj., abounding with stars. —
Compounded of L. stella, 'star' (see stellar), and
-ferous.

## stelliform
stelliform, adj., star-shaped. — Compounded of
L. stella, 'star', and forma, 'form, shape'. See
stellar and form, n.

## stellular
stellular, adj., star-shaped. — Formed with suff.
-ar fr. L. stellula, dimin. of stella, 'star*. See
stellar and -ule.

## stellulate
stellulate, adj., star-shaped. — See prec. word
and adj. suff. -ate.

## stem
stem, n. — ME., fr. OE. stxfn, stefn, stemn,
'stem of a tree, stem of a ship', rel. to OS.
stamn, ON. stafn, 'stem of a ship', Dan stamme,
Swed. stam, 'trunk of a tree', OHG., MHG.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:742 COLUMN:2 -->
stam, G. Stamm, of s.m., and cogn. with OI.
sthdman, 'place for standing, station', Gk.
στήμων, 'warp', L. stamen, 'warp, thread,
fiber'. See stamen and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: stem, tr. v., to remove the stems;
to provide with stems; intr. v., to derive,
stemmed, adj., stemm-er, п., stem-less, adj.

## stem
stem, tr. v., to check, hold back. — ME. stem-,
men, fr. ON. stemma, which is rel. to Dan.,
Norw. stemme, Swed. stamma, OS. stemmian,
MDu., MHG. stemen, G. stemmen, 'stop, resist
oppose', fr. I.-E. base *stem-, 'to strike against
something', whence also Lith. stumiu, Lett.
stumju, Ί thrust, push', and stammer, stumb,
stumble.
Derivative: stem, п., a check, holding back.

## stemlet
stemlet, п., a small stem. — Formed fr. stem, п.,
with the dimin. suff. -let.

## stemma
stemma, п., pedigree. — L., 'garland; pedigree',
fr. Gk. στέμμα, 'garland, wreath', from the
stem of στέφειν, 'to surround, encircle, wreathe,
crown', fr. I.-E. base *stegwh-, 'to encircle,
crown', whence also Pers. tu], 'crown'. Cp. ste-
pbano- and the second element iu Agrostemma.
Cp. also taj. For the ending see suff. -ma.

## Stemona
Stemona, п., a genus of plants {bot.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. στήμων, 'warp'. See stamen.

## stemple
stemple, stempel, п., cross timber. — G. Stempel,
'stamp, die, prop', fr. LG. stempel, lit. 'an
instrument for stamping', formed from the stem
of MLG. stampen, 'to stamp' (see stamp), with
-el, a suff. used to form names of tools.

## stemson
stemson, п., a supporting timber bolted to the
stem and keelson of a ship near the bow. —
Coined fr. stem, п., and the second syllable in
(keel)son. Cp. sternson.

## sten-
sten-, form of steno- before a vowel.

## stench
stench, n. — ME., fr. OE. stenc, 'smell, odor', rel.
to OE. stincan, 'to smell'. See stink.

## stencil
stencil, tr. v., to paint by means of a perforated
plate. — ME. stansilen, stensilen, fr. OF. esten-
celer, 'to spangle', fr. estencelle, 'spark' (F. etin-
celle), fr. VL. *stincilla, formed with metathesis
fr. L. scintilla, of s.m. See scintilla and cp. tinsel.
Derivatives: stencil, п., stencil-er, stencill-er, n.

## steno-
steno-, before a vowel sten-, combining form
meaning 'narrow'. — Gk. στενό-, στεν-, fr.
στενός, 'narrow', rel. to στείνειν, 'to make
narrow', στεΐνος, 'a narrow space'; of
uncertain origin.

## stenograph
stenograph, п., script in shorthand. —
Compounded of steno- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γρά-
φειν, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: stenograph-er, п., stenograph-ic,
adj., stenograph-ic-al-ly, adv.,

## stenography
stenography, п., shorthand. — Lit. 'narrow
writing', compounded of steno· and Gk. -γραφία,
fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.

## stenopaic
stenopaic, stenopeic, stenopaeic, adj., having a
narrow opening, esp. applied to spectacles. —
Coined by the Dutch ophthalmologist Frans
Cornells Donders (1818-89) in 1854 fr. Gk.
στενός, *narrow' (see steno-), and όπαΐος,
'provided with a hole', fr. οπή, 'opening, hole', fr.
I.-E. base *okw-, 'eye, to see'. See optic.

## stenosis
stenosis, п., the narrowing of the opening of a
passage in the body (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. στένωσις, 'a narrowing, straitening', fr.
στενός. See steno- and -osis.

## stenotype
stenotype, п., letter or group of letters used in
shorthand to denote words or sentences. —
Compounded of steno- and type.

## Stentor
Stentor, п., 1) the Greek herald in the Trojan war
(Greek mythol.); hence, 2) a person with a
powerful voice. — L. Stentor, fr. Gk. Στέντωρ. The
name lit. means 'groaner; roarer', and derives
fr. στένειν, 'to groan, roar', from the I.-E.
imitative base *(s)ten-, 'to groan, roar, thunder',
whence also OI. stanati, staniti, tanyati, 'it
thunders', L. tonare, 'to thunder', MLG., MDu.,
Du., MHG. stenen, G. stohnen, OE. stenan, 'to
groan', OE. stunian, 'to resound', ON. stynia,
'to groan', OHG. donar, OE. punor, 'thunder'.
See thunder and cp. words there referred to.

## stentorian
stentorian, adj., very loud. — Formed with suff.
-ian fr. L. Stentoreus, fr. Gk. Στεντόρειος,
'having a voice like Stentor', fr. Στέντωρ, gen.
Στέντορος. See prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:742 COLUMN:3 -->

## step
step, n. — ME. steppe, step, fr. OE. staepe, stepe,
which is rel. to OFris., MDu., Du. stop, OHG.
stapfo, staffo, MHG., G. stapfe, 'footstep', and
to OS. stopo, OE. stopel, 'footmark', Du. stoep,
'(flight of) steps', OHG. stuofa, stuoffa, MHG.
stuofe, 'footstep', G. Stufe, 'step, degree', fr.
I.-E. base *steb(k)-, 'to tread, step'. From
*stemb(k)-, a nasalized form of the same base,
derive OI. stambhate, 'becomes stiff', Gk. στέμ-
βειν, 'to crush with the feet, handle roughly,
misuse', ά-στεμφής, 'unshakable, steadfast*,
OE. stempan, 'to pound (in a mortar)', OHG.
stampfon, *to stamp with the foot, beat, pound'.
Cp. estafette, etape, staff, stamp, stampede,
staple, 'bar, wire', staple, 'commodity*, stemple,
stoep, stump. Cp. also Staphylea, staphylo-.

## step
step, intr. and tr. v. — ME. steppen, fr. OE. stxp-
pan, steppan, 'to step, go, proceed', rel. to
OFris. stapa, steppa, MDu, stappen, steppen,
Du. stappen, OHG. stapfdn, MHG., G. stapfen,
'to step', and to OE. staepe, stepe, 'step'. See
step, n.
Derivatives: stepp-ed, adj., stepp-er, п.,
stepping, п., step-wise, adv.

## step-
step-, combining form denoting relation through
remarriage. — ME. step-, fr. OE. steop-, rel. to
OFris. stiap-, ON. stjup- (cp. ON. stjupr,
'stepson'), Swed. styv-, MLG. stef-, Du. stief-,
OHG. stiof-, MHG., G. stief-, 'step-', ON.
stjupr, 'stepson4, OE. astiepan, bestiepan, 'to
deprive*, OHG. arstiufen, bistiuf'en, 'to deprive of
parents or of children'. For sense development
cp. L. privignus, 'stepson', which is rel. to privus,
'deprived' (see deprive).

## stephan-
stephan-, form of stephano- before a vowel.

## Stephana
Stephana, fem. PN. — ModL., fern, of L. Ste-
phanus. See Stephen.

## stephane
stephane, п., a kind of hairdress (Greek antiq.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. στεφάνη, 'that which encircles;
diadem', fr. στέφειν, 'to encircle, crown,
wreathe'. See stemma and cp. stephano- and
words there referred to.

## stephanion
stephanion, п., the point where the sutura coro-
nalis crosses the temporal ridge (craniol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. στεφάνιον, dimin. of στέφανος,
'crown', 'that which encircles, crown, wreath*,
which is rel. to στεφάνη, 'that which encircles;
diadem', used also as a medical term to denote
the sutura coronalis. For this use of στεφάνη
see Aretaeus Medicus, ed. K. Hude, Corpus
Medicorum Graecorum, II, Χρονιών νόσων
θ-εραπευτικόν, Ι, 2. See prec. word.

## stephanite
stephanite, п., a black mineral. — G. Stephanit,
named after Archduke Stephan, mining director
of Austria (died in 1867). The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -ϊτης; seesubst. suff. -ite.

## stephano-
stephano-, before a vowel stephan-, combining
form denoting crown. — Gk. στέφανο-, fr.
στέφανος, 'that which encircles;crown; wreath',
fr. στέφειν, 'to encircle; to crown; to wreathe',
See stemma and cp. Stephana, stephane,
stephanion, Stephanos, Stephanotis, Stephen and the
second element in Dasystephana.

## Stephanos
Stephanos, п., a kind of headdress (Gk. antiq.) —
Gk. στέφανος, 'crown'. See stephano-.

## Stephanotis
Stephanotis, п., a genus of plants of the milkweed
family (bot,) — ModL., fr. Gk. στεφανωτίς
(fem.), 'fit for a crown', fr. στεφανοϋν, *to
crown', fr. στέφανος, 'crown'. See stephano-.

## Stephen
Stephen, masc. PN. — L. Stephanus, fr. Gk.
Στέφανος, lit. 'crown'. See stephano- and cp.
Stephana.

## stepney
stepney, stepony, п., summer drink made of
raisins, lemon juice and sugar. — Theword orig.
meant 'beverage of Stepney (an old district of
London)'.

## steppe
steppe, п., one of the vast plains of southeastern
Europe and of Asia without forests.—Russ.jtep*.

## -ster
-ster, suff. denoting trade, occupation; often
used in a depreciatory sense. — ME. -estere,
-stere, -ster, fr. OE. -estre, -istre; in OE.
restricted, to feminine nouns (cp. baxter, spinster)
although, according to its origin, the suff. is of
common gender. Cp. the L. equivalent -aster in
poetaster, 'a would-be poet', etc., and see -aster.

## steradian
steradian, п., the unit of measure for solid angles
(math.) — A hybrid coined fr. Gk. στερεός,
'solid', and L. radius, 'staff, rod, spoke of a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:743 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: STERCORACEOUS | 716 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:743 COLUMN:1 -->
wheel, ray'. See stereo- and radius.

## stercoraceous
stercoraceous, adj., pertaining to dung. —
Formed with suff. -aceous fr. L. stercus, gen. -cor is,
'dung', which is.prob. cogn. with Gk. στεργά-
νος, (Hesych.), 'dung, excrement', τάργανον,
'sour wine', τρύξ, gen. τρυγός, 'dregs', W.
trwnc, 'urine, dregs', W. troeth, 'urine, lye',
Lith. trisiu, tristi, 'to dung*, tersiit, tefSti, 'to
soil, dirty', ON. prekkr, 'mud, dung, excrement',
OFris. threkk, MHG. dree, G. Dreck, of s.m.,
L. troia (for *trogya), 'sow', lit. 'the dirty one'.

## stercoral
stercoral, adj., stercoraceous. — See prec. word
and adj. suff. -al.

## Sterculia
Sterculia, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. L. Sterculius, 'the deity that presides over
manuring', fr. stercus, 'dung, manure' (see
stercoraceous); so called from the fetid odor of this
genus.

## Sterculiaceae
Sterculiaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the
chocolate family {bot.) — ModL., formed from
prec. word with suff. -aceae.

## stere
stere, п., a cubic meter. — F. stere, fr. Gk
στερεός, 'solid'. See stereo-.

## stere-
stere-, form of stereo- before a vowel.
stereo» n. — Abbreviation of stereotype.

## stereo-
stereo-, before a vowel stere-, combining form
meaning 'solid, firm'. — Gk. στέρεο-, fr.
στερεός, 'firm, hard, solid, stiff', fr. I.-E. base
*ster-, 'stiff, rigid*. See stare and cp. sterile. Cp.
also the second element in cholesterol.

## stereohate
stereohate, п., a solid substructure without
columns. — Compounded of stereo- and Gk.
βάτης, 'that which steps or treads', which is rel.
to βάσις, 'a stepping, that on which one steps'.
See base, п., and cp. stylobate.
Derivative: stereobat-ic, adj.

## stereochemistry
stereochemistry, п., that branch of chemistry
which treats of the arrangement of molecules
and atoms in space. — Compounded of stereo-
and chemistry.

## stereochromy
stereochromy, п., the process of painting with
colors mixed with waterglass. — Compounded
of stereo- and Gk. χρώμα, 'color'. See chrome
and subst. suff. -y (representing Gk. -ία).
Derivatives: stereochrom-ic, adj., stereochrom-
Ic-al'ly, adv.

## stereognosis
stereognosis, п., the ability to recognize an object
by touch. — ModL., compounded of stereo-
and gnosis.

## stereognostic
stereognostic, adj., pertaining to stereognosis. —
See prec. word and gnostic.

## stereogram
stereogram, п., a picture giving the impression of
solidity. — Compounded of stereo- and Gk.
γράμμα, 'something written*. See -gram.

## stereograph
stereograph, п., a photograph representing
objects with an impression of solidity. —
Compounded of stereo- and Gk. -γράφος, fr. χρά-
φειυ, 'to write'. See -graph.
Derivatives: stereograph, tr. and intr. v., stereo-
graph-er, п., stereograph-ic, stereograph-ic-al,
adjs., stereograph-ic-al-ly, adv., stereograph-y, n.

## stereome
stereome, п., the supporting tissues of plants (bot.)
— Gk. στερέωμα, 'a solid body', fr. στερεός,
'firm, solid'. See stereo- and -oma.

## stereometer
stereometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
volume of a body. — Compounded of stereo-
and Gk· μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm*.

## stereometry
stereometry, п., the art of measuring the volume;
that branch of geometry which deals with
solids. — ModL. stereome tria, fr. Gk. στερεομε-
τρία, 'measurement of solids', which is
compounded of στερεός, 'solid', and -μετρία, 'a
measuring of. See stereo- and -merry.
Derivatives: stereometr-ic, stereometr-ic-al,aa}S.,
stereometr-ic-af-ly, adv.

## stereopticon
stereopticon, п., a double magic lantern
producing dissolving views. — Compounded of
stere-and Gk. ότττικόν, neut. of οπτικός,
'pertaining to sight'. See optic.

## stereoscope
stereoscope, п., an instrument blending into one
image two pictures of an object, so as to give the
impression of solidity. — Coined by the English
physicist Sir Charles Whetstone (1802-75) fr.
stereo- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look
at, examine*. See -scope.
Derivatives: stereoscop-ic, stereoscop-ic-al, adjs.,
stereoscop-ic-ally, adv., stereoscop-y, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:743 COLUMN:2 -->

## stereotype
stereotype, n. {print.) — Compounded of stereo-
and -type.
Derivatives: stereotype, tr. v., stereotyp-er, п.,
stereotyp-ist, п., stereotyp-y, n.

## stereotypography
stereotypography, п., the art of printing from
stereotypes. — Compounded of stereotype and
-graphy.

## steric
steric, adj., spatial. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic
fr. Gk. στερεός, 'solid'. See stereo-.

## sterigina
sterigina, п., stalk, filament {bot.) — ModL.
sterigma, fr. Gk. στήριγμα, 'a support*, from
the stem of στηρίζειν, 'to prop, support', prop,
'to make firm', which is rel. to στερεός, 'firm,
solid; stiff; hard*. See stereo- and -ma.

## sterile
sterile, adj., 1) barren; 2) free from living germs.
— L. sterilis, 'barren, unfruitful', cogn. with OI.
starih, 'abarren cow', Gk. στερεός, 'firm, solid;
stiff; hard', στείρα, 'a barren woman, a barren
cow', στέρκρος, 'firm, hard, sterile', Arm. sterj,
'unfruitful, sterile', Alb. Stjere, 'lamb, young
cow', OSlav. sterica, *a barren cow', Goth.
stafro (fem.), 'barren', MLG. sterke (whence G.
Sterke), 'heifer', ON. stirtla, 'a barren cow'; fr.
I.-E. base *ster-, 'barren, sterile', orig. identical
with base *ster-, 'stiff, rigid'. See sture and cp.
words there referred to. For the ending see suff.
-He.

## sterility
sterility, n. — ME. sterylite, fr. MF. (— F.) steri-
lite, fr. L. sterilitdtem, ace. of sterilitds, fr.
sterilis. See prec. word and -ity.

## sterilize
sterilize, tr. v. — Formed with suff. -ize fr. L.
sterilis. See sterile.
Derivatives: steriliz-ation, п., steriliz-er, n.

## sterlet
sterlet, п., a kind of small sturgeon. — F., fr.
Russ. sterlyad\ which is of Teut. origin. Cp.
Russ. osetr, 'sturgeon', and see sturgeon.

## sterling
sterling, n.— ME-, 'a silver penny*, prob. fr. OF.
esterlin, estrelin, fr. WFrankish *ester(e)ling, a
hybrid coined fr. OF. estedre, ester, 'stater', and
the Teut. suff. -Ung. OF. estedre derives fr. VL.
istater, fr. L. stater, fr. Gk. στατήρ; see stuter.
See KJuge-Mitzka, EWDS., p. 747 s.v. Sterling.
Sterling is not related to ME. sterre, 'star' (as
suggested by most lexicographers).
Derivative: sterling, adj.

## stern
stern, adj., austere, severe. — ME. stierne, stirne,
sterne, fr. OE. stierne, styrne, rel. to MHG.
sterre, G. starr, 'stiff', storrig, storrisch,
'obstinate', Goth, andstaarran, 'to be stiff', ON. stara,
OE. starian, 'to look or gaze upon'. See stare
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: stern-ly, adv., stern-ness, n.

## stern
stern, п., the back part of a ship. — ME., prob.
fr. ON. stjorn, 'a steering', which is rel. to ON.
styra, 'to steer'. See steer, v.
Derivative: stern-ed, adj.

## sternal
sternal, adj., pertaining to the sternum. —
Medical L. sterndlis, fr. L. sternum. See sternum and
adj. suff. -nl.

## sterno-
sterno-, combining form meaning 'sternal and*.
See sternum.

## sternson
sternson, п., sternpost bolted to the keelson. —
Coined fr. the noun stern and the second
syllable in keelson. Cp. stemson.

## sternum
sternum, п., breastbone (anat.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
στέρνον, 'breast, breastbone*, prop. 'flat»and
broad part of the chest', and rel. to στορνύναι,
'to spread out', στρώμα, 'bedclothes, mattress',
lit. 'that which is spread out', fr. I.-E. base
*ster-, *stor-, *str-, 'to spread out, extend,
strew', whence also OI. strnati, strnoti, starati,
'strews, scatters', L. sternere (pp. stratus), 'to
strew, stretch out, spread out'. See stratum and
cp. words there referred to.

## sternutation
sternutation, п., sneeze, sneezing. — L. sternutd-
tio, gen. -onis, 'act of sneezing', fr. sternutdt-
{um)t pp. stem of sternutare, freq. of sternuere,
'to sneeze*, cogn. with Gk. πταίρειν, πτάρειν,
'to sneeze', Arm. p*rngam, p'rncem, of s.m.,
Olr. sreod, 'act of sneezing', sren(n)im, "I snore*,
W. ystrewi, 'to sneeze*, trew, 'act of sneezing';
fr. I.-E. imitative base *pster{eu)-. Cp.
stertorous. Cp. also arnica, ptarmic, Ftarmica. For the
ending see suff. -ation.
Derivatives: sternutat-ive, adj., sternutat-or, п.,
sternutat-ory, adj.

## sternward
sternward, adj. and adv. — Compounded of
stern, п., and suff. -ward.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:743 COLUMN:3 -->

## sternwards
sternwards, adv. — Compounded of stern, п.,
and suff. -wards.

## steroid
steroid, п., any of a group of compounds
including the sterols, bile acids and sex hormones. —
Coined fr. ster(ol) and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## sterol
sterol, п., any of a group of solid alcohols {bio*
chem.) — Back formation fr. cholesterol.

## stertor
stertor, п., heavy snoring (med.) — Medical L.,
fr. L. stertere, 'to snore'. See stertorous and -or.

## stertorious
stertorious, adj., stertorous. — See next word.
Derivatives: stertorious-ly, adv., stertorious-ness,
n.

## stertorous
stertorous, adj., characterized by snoring. —
Formed with the suffixes -or and -ous fr. L. ster-
tere, 'to snore', which is prob. rel. to L.
sternuere, 'to sneeze'. See sternutation.
Derivatives: stertorous-ly, adv., stertorous-ness,
n.

## stet
stet, intr. v., direction to printer to disregard
correction made in the texts, whence stet, tr. v., to
cancel a correction. — Fr. L. stet, 'let it stand',
3rd sing. pres. subj. οι stare, 'to stand'. See state.

## stetho-
stetho-, combining form meaning 'breast, chest',
as in stethoscope. — Gk. στη&ο-, fr. στήθος,
'breast', prob. cogn. with OI. stanah, 'teat,
nipple', Avestic fshtdna-, Arm. stin, of s.m.

## stethometer
stethometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
expansion of the chest during breathing. —
Compounded of stetho- and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure*. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: stethometr-ic, adj., stethometr-y, n.

## stethoscope
stethoscope, п., an instrument for examining the
sounds produced in the body. — F. stethoscope,
lit. 'instrument for examining the breast', coined
by the French physician Rene-Theophile-Hya-
cinthe Laennec (1781-1826) in 1819 fr. Gk.
στηθ-ος, 'breast', and -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν,
'to look at, examine'. See stetho- and -scope.
Derivatives: stethoscope, tr. v., stethoscop-ic,
stethoscop-ic-al, adjs., stethoscop-ic-al-ly, adv.,
stethoscop-y, п., stethoscop-ist, n.

## stevedore
stevedore, п., one employed at loading and
unloading ships. — Sp. estibador, fr. estibar, 'to
pack', fr. L. stipdre, 'to crowd together, corn-

suff. -dor represents L. -tor; see -tor.

## Stevia
Stevia, п., a genus of shrubs {bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Spanish botanist Pedro Jaime
Esteve (died in 1566). For the ending see 1st
suff. -ia.

## stew
stew, tr. and intr. v., to cook slowly. — ME.
stuen, stuwen, 'to bathe', fr. OF. estuver, 'to
bathe in warm water' (whence F. etuver, 'to
heat, stove, stew'), fr. VL. *extufdre (whence
also It. stufare), fr. 1st ex- and *tSfdre, 'to heat',
which is cogn. with Gk. τύφος, 'mist, vapor*,
h./Qmus, 'smoke'. See typhus and cp. stove. Cp.
also next word.
Derivatives: stew, п., dish cooked by stewing,
stew-able, adj., stew-ed, adj., stew-y, adj.

## stew
stew, п., a brothel. — ME. stuwe, stue, fr. OF.
estuve (F. etuve), 'sweating room in baths;
drying room', back formation fr. estuver, 'to
bathe in warm water'; see prec. word. For sense
development it should be considered that
public baths used to be the meeting places of
women of ill-fame.

## stew
stew, п., a fishpond. — ME. stewe, fr. OF. estui,
'prison; case, depository' (whence F. etui, 'case,
box*), back formation fr. OF. estuier, 'to shut
in, hold, keep', which, together with OProvenc.
estojar, estujar, of s.m., prob. derives fr. VL.
*studidre, 'to direct one's attention to something,
to study', fr. L. studium. See study, n.

## steward
steward, n. — ME., fr. OE. stigweard, stiweard,
lit. 'sty ward', compounded of OE. stig, 'sty,
hall, house', and weard, 'warden, guard'. See
sty and ward, 'one who guards'.
Derivatives: steward, tr. and intr. v.,
stewardess, п., steward-ly, adj. and adv.

## Stewartia
Stewartia, п., a genus of plants of the tea family
{bot.) — ModL., named after John Stuart—also
written Stewart—(1713-92), Marquis of Bute.
For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## sthenia
sthenia, п., vigor (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
σ&ένος, 'strength'. See next word and 1st -ia
and cp. asthenia, neurasthenia, disthene.

## sthenic
sthenic, adj., morbidly active, vigorous. —

## stibial
stibial, adj., pertaining to antimony. — Formed

stibialism, п., poisoning by antimony. — See

## stiblne
stiblne, stibin, п., a colorless, poisonous gas,
SbHj (chem.) — Formed from next word with

## stibium
stibium, п., antimony. — L. stibium, 'powdered

antimony', ft. Egypt, stm, Demotic sum. Cp.
antimony,

## stibnite
stibnite, п., native trisulfide of antimony, Sb2S3

## stichic
stichic, adj., made up of lines. — Gk. στιχικός,

ometry.
Derivative: stickic-al-ly, adv.

## sticho-
sticho-, combining form meaning 'row, line'. —
Gk. στίχο-, fr. στίχος, 'row, line, rank; verse'.

## stichometry
stichometry, n. — Late Gk. στιχομετρία, lit.

line, rank; verse', and -μετρία, 'a measuring
of. See sticho- and -inetry.

## stichomythy
stichomythy, stichomythia, п., verse dialogue, as
in ancient Greek plays. — Gk. στιχομϋίΗα,
'conversation in alternate lines', fr. στίχος,
'row, line, rank; verse', and μϋ*ος, 'word'. See
sticho-, myth and -y, resp. -ia.

## -stichous
-stichous, combining form meaning 'having (a
specified number of) rows'. — Fr. Gk. στίχος,
'row, line, rank; verse'. See sticho- and -ous.

## stick
stick, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stikien (weak v.), 4o
prick; to be infixed', and steken (strong v.), 'to

guere, 'to distinguish', Gk. στίζειν (for *στί-
γ^ειν), 'to prick, puncture', στικτός (prop,

Cp. stick, п., and the first element in

etiquette, extinguish, instigate, instinct, steak,

stick, n. — ME. sticke, fr. OE. sticca, rel. to ON.

G. Stecken, 'stick, staff', and to OE. stician, 'to

stab, prick, pierce'; in many meanings directiy

stickle, intr. v., to contend. — ME. stightlen, 'to

arrange', freq. of stighten, fr. OE. stihtan, 'to

dispose, arrange, govern', rel. to MDu. (= Du.)

stichten, OHG., МЙС, G. sti/ten, 'to found,

establish'. The orig, meaning of the verb stickle

stickleback, п., a small fish of the family Gastero-

called stickleback in allusion to the prickles on

## stiff
stiff, adj. — ME. stif, ft. OE. stif, rel. to ON.
stffr, Du. stijf, OHG., MHG. stif, G. steif, 'stiff',
and cogn. with L. stipes, 'log, stock, trunk of a

στίφος, 'a close, compact body', στιφρός, 'close,

## stiffen
stiffen, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stiffnen, formed fr.

## stifle
stifle, tr. andintr. v.—Alter. oSME.stuflen,stufflen,

stove, stew'; see stew, 'to cook slowly').

ly, adv.

## stifle
stifle, п., the joint above the hock of a horse or
dog. — Of uncertain origin.

## stigma
stigma, п., mark; reproach. — L., fr. Gk. στίγμα,
'puncture, brand', from the stem of στίζειν (for
•στίγ^ειν), 'to prick, point, mark'. See stick, v.,
and cp. astigmatism. Cp. also the second
element in Pachystima. For the ending see suff.
-ma.

## stigmatic
stigmatic, adj., marked with a stigma or with
stigmata. — ML. stigmaticus, fr. L. stigma, gen,
-atis. See prec. word and 1st -atic.
Derivatives; stigmatic, п., stigmatic-al, adj.,
stigmatic-al-ly, adv., stigmatic-al-ness, a.

## stigmatiferous
stigmatiferous, adj., bearing stigmas. —
Compounded of L. stigma, gen. -atis (see stigma),

## stigmatism
stigmatism, п., property of a lens or of the cornea

## stigmatist
stigmatist, п., one marked with a stigma or with

ματίζειν, fr. στίγμα, gen. -ατός. See stigma

Derivative: stigmatiz-ation, n.

stigmatose, adj., stigmatic. — Formed with adj.

stigma,

## stiibene
stiibene, п., a crystalline hydrocarbon СЦН12
{chem.) — F. stiibene, coined by the French
chemist Auguste Laurent (1807-53) in 1843 fr.
Gk. στίλβειν, 'to glitter', and suff. -ine, '-ene'.
See stilbite and -ene.

## stilbestrol
stilbestrol, п., a synthetic sex hormone. CI1HMOa
(biochem.) — Coined fr. stiibene, estrus and suff.
-ol.

## stilbite
stilbite, п., a mineral of the zeolite family,
Na2CaAI2 Si,0M.6H20. — A word coined by the
French mineralogist Abbe Rene-Just Haliy
(1743-1822)in 1796ft. Gk. στίλβειν, 'to glitter';
so called by him because of its luster. Gk.
στίλβειν is rel. to στιλπνός, 'glittering', and

## prob. cogn. with Olr. sell
prob. cogn. with Olr. sell, 'eye', sellaim, Ί

## regard
regard, consider'. For the ending see subst. suff.

## stile
stile, п., steps. — ME., ft. OE. stigel, 'device for

climbing ladder', rel. to OHG. stigila, of s.m.,
ft. Teut. base *stig-, to climb'. See sty, 'to

## stile
stile, п., an upright piece in the frame of a door.
— Du. stijl, 'doorpost', fr. MDu., prob. fr. L,
stilus, 'pike, pale'. See 2nd style.

## stlietto
stlietto, п., a small-dagger. — It., dimin. of stilo,

## still
still, adj. — ME. stille, fr. OE. stille, 'at rest,
silent', rel. to OFris., MLG., MDu. stille, Du.
stil, OS., OHG. stilli, MHG. stille, G. still, fr.
I.-E. base *st(h)el-, 'to place'. Still prop, means

See stall and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: still, п., adv. (q.v.), still, v. (q.v.),
still-ness, п., still-y, adj. and adv.

## still
still, tr. and intr. v., to calm. — ME. stillen, fr.
OE. stillan, ft. stille, 'at rest', rel. to OS. stillian,
ΟΝ., Swed., Norw. stilla, Dan. stille, Du.,
OHG., MHG., G. stillen. See still, adj.

## still
still, tr. and intr. v., to distill (obsol.) — ME.
stillen, aphetic for distillen, fr. OF. (= F.) dis-
tiller, fr. L. distillSre, later distillare, 'to drip,

and stillare, 'to drop, trickle', fr. stilla, 'drop',
which prob. stands for *stir(a)la, dimin. of

thicken, compress, stiffen; stone'. See stone and

Derivative: still, п., an apparatus for distilling.

## stUIiform
stUIiform, adj., having the form of a drop. —

## stilling

*st(h)el-, 'to place'. See stall and cp. still, adj.

Stillingia, п., a genus of plants of the family

(1720-71). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## stilt
stilt, n. — ME. stilte, rel. to Dan. stylte, Swed.
stylta, Norw. stilta, MDu. stelte, Du. stelt,
OHG. stelza, MHG., G. stelze, fr. Teut. base

and cp. stout.
Derivatives: stilt, tr. and intr. v., stilt-ed, adj.,
stilt-er, п., stilt-y, adj., stilt-i-ness, n.

## Stilton
Stilton, п., a kind of cheese. — Short for Stilton
cheese4, so called ft. Stilton, in Huntingdonshire,
where it was first made.

## stimulant
stimulant, adj. — L. stimulans, gen. -antis, pres.

## part
part, of stimulate. See next word' and -ant.
Derivative: stimulant, n.

stimulate, tr. v., to rouse to action. — L. stimu-
latus, pp. of stimulare, 'to prick with a goad,

## stimulate'
stimulate', fr. stimulus. See stimulus and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: stimulat-ing, adj., stimulat-ing-ly,

## adv.
adv., stimulat-ive, adj., stimulator (q.v.), stimu-
lose (q.v.)

## stimulation
stimulation, n. — L. stimulatio, gen. -onis, fr.

## stimulants
stimulants, pp. of stimulare. See stimulate and
-ion.

## stimulator
stimulator, n. — L. stimulator, fr. stimulatus, pp. of
stimulare. See stimulate and agential suff. -or.

## stimulose
stimulose, adj., having a sting. — Late L. stimulo-

## sus
sus, 'full of incentives', fr. L. stimulus. See next
word and adj. suff. -ose.

## stimulus
stimulus, п., that which stimulates, incentive. —

L., 'goad, sting, spur, incentive', formed fr.
*sti-mos, fr. I.-E. base *stei-, *sti-, 'pointed',

whence also L. stilus, 'pointed instrument',

Avestic staera-, taira- 'summit', Afghan, terq,
'sharp, pointed'; see style, 'pointed instrument'.
For the derivatives of *steig-, an enlarged form
of base *stei- see stick, v., and cp. words there
referred to.

## stimy
stimy, n. — See stymie,

## sting
sting, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stingen, fr. OE. stin-

## gan
gan, rel. to ON. stinga and stanga, OHG.,

MHG. stungen, 'to prick', Goth. us-stagg\,
'prick out', OS. stanga, ON. siong, Dan. stang,

Swed. stang, Norw. stong, staang, MLG. stange,

MDu. stanghe, Du. stang, OHG. stanga, MHG.,

G. stange, 'pole,, perch', OS., OHG. stengil,

MLG., MHG., G. Stengel, 'stalk, stem' (prop.

Derivatives: sting, п., sting-er, п., sting-ing, aUj.,
sting-ing-ly, adv., sting-ing-ness, п., sting-ness>

## stingaree
stingaree, п., a sting ray. — Altered fr. sting ray.

## stinge
stinge, intr. v., to act stingily. — Back formation
fr. stingy.

## stingo
stingo, п., stong beer (slang). — Formed fr.

## sting
sting, v.

## stingy
stingy, adj., miserly. — Prop, 'stinging4.; formed
fr. sting, v., with suff. -y. For the softening of
the hard g cp. dingy.
Derivatives: sting-i-ly, adv., sting-i-ness, n.

## stink
stink, intr. and tr. v. — ME. stinken, fr. OE.
stincan, 'to emit (good or bad) odor\ rel. to OS.
stincan, OHG. stinkan, MHG. stinken, of s.m.,
G., Du. stinken, 'to stink', and perh. cogn. with
Gk. ταγγός, 'rancid'. Cp. stench.
Derivatives: stink, п., stink-ard, п., stink-er, п.,
stink-ing, adj., stink-ing-ly, adv.

## stint
stint, tr. v., to limit, restrain; intr. v., to be
sparing or frugal. — ME. stinten, 4o cease,
stint*, fr. OE. styntan, 'to blunt, stupefy', from
an OTeut. adj. represented by OE. stunt, 'dull*,
ON. stuttr (assimilated from orig. *stuntr),
'short, scant', and MHG. stunz, 'blunt, short';
rel. to OS. stotan, ON. stauta, Du. stolen, OHG.
std^an, Goth, stautan, 'to push, thrust', OHG.
erstutzen, 'to chase away', G- stutzen, 'to cut
short, curtail; to stop short, hesitate', Du. stui-
ten, 'to stop, check, arrest, stem', fr. I.-E. base
*(s)teud-, 'to beat, strike, push, thrust', whence
01. tundate, tudati, 'he thrusts', tustah, 'dust',
lit. 'that which is pounded*, L. tudes, gen. -itis,
'hammer', tundere (perf. tutudi), 'to beat, strike',
Arm. t'ndal, t'ndel, 'to be shaken, tremble', Alb.
stun, Ί push, thrust'. Cp. stoat, stoss, stunt,
stutter. Cp. also contund, contuse, obtund, obtuse,
pertuse, pierce, retund, refuse, toil, 'to work
hard', tund, tussal, tussicular, Tussilago, Tynda-
reus. Cp. also study.
Derivatives: stint, п., stint-ed, adj., stint-ed-ly,
adv. stint-ed-ness, п., stint-ing, adj., stint-ing-ly,
adv., stint-less, adj.

## Stipa
Stipa, п., a genus of plants, the feather grass
(hot.) — ModL., fr. L. stipa, stupa, stuppa, 'the
coarse part of flax, tow, hards', fr. Gk. στύππη.
See stupe.

## stipate
stipate, adj., compressed (hot.) — L. stipatus, pp.
of stipare, 'to press together, compress', which
is rel. to stipes, 'log, stock, trunk of a tree', fr.
I.-E. base *steip-, 'compact, stiff". See stiff and
adj. suff. -ate and cp. stipe, stipulate, stipule,
constipate, obstipation.

## stipe
stipe, п., stalk (bot.) — F., fr. L. stipes, 'log,
stock, trunk of a tree'. See prec. word.

## stipei
stipei, п., a small stipule (bot.) — F. stipefle,
dimin. of stipule, fr. L. stipula. See stipule.
Derivatives: stipell-ate, adj., having stipels.

## stipend
stipend, п., salary. — ME. stipende, fr. L. stipen-
dium, 'tax, pay, gift', shortened fr. *stipi-pen-
dium (see haplology), fr. stips, gen. stipis,
'payment, donation', and the stem of pendere, 'to
pay'. The first element is rel. to L. stipulari, 'to
demand a formal promise, stipulate', and to
stipes, 'log, stock, trunk of a tree'; see stipulate,
v. For the second element see pension, pendant.

## stipendiary
stipendiary, adj. — L. stipendiarius, 'pertaining
to payment, receiving pay*, fr. stipendium. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivative: stipendiary, n.

## stipes
stipes, п., stipe. — L. See stipe.
'stipiform, adj. — Compounded of L. stipes, 'log,
stock, trunk of a tree', and forma, 'form, shape'.
See stipe and form, n.

## stipitate
stipitate, adj., having a stipe. — Formed with
adj. suif. -ate fr. L. stipes, gen. -itis, 'stalk, stem'.
See stipe.

## stipple
stipple, tr. v., to paint with dots. — Du. stip-

## pefen
pefen, 'to make points', fr. stippel, 'point, dot*,
dimin. of stip, 'point*, which prob. derives fr.
I.-E. base *stei-, *sti-, 'pointed'. See stimulus
and cp. style, 'pointed instrument'.
Derivatives: stipple, п., stippl-ing, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:745 COLUMN:2 -->

## stipulaceous
stipulaceous, adj., stipular. — Formed with suff.
•aceous fr. L. stipula. See stipule.

## stipular
stipular, adj., pertaining to a stipule. — See
stipule and adj. suff. -ar and cp. prec. word.

## stipulate
stipulate, intr. v., to make an arrangement; tr. v.,
to require as a condition. — L. stipulatus, pp. of
stipulari, 'to demand a formal promise,
bargain, stipulate', rel. to stipula, 'stalk, stem,
straw'; see stipule and verbal suff. -ate. Stipulari
orig. meant 'to break a straw'. In ancient Rome
the breaking of a straw by the parties was a
symbolic act proving that they had come to an
agreement.

## stipulate
stipulate, adj., having a stipule {bot.) — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. stipula. See stipule and
cp. exstipulate.

## stipulation
stipulation, п., agreement. — L. stipuldtio, gen.
-onist fr. stipulatus, pp. of stipulari. See stipulate,
v., and -ion.

## stipulation
stipulation, п., arrangement of stipules. —
Formed with suff. -ation fr. L. stipula. See stipule.

## stipulator
stipulator, п., one who stipulates. — L. stipulator,
formed fr. stipulatus, pp. of stipulari. See
stipulate, v., and agential suff. -or.

## stipule
stipule, п., one of the two small, leaflike
appendages at the base of the petiole of a leaf. — L.
stipula, 'stalk, stem; stubble', rel. to stipes, 'log,
stock, trunk of a tree', stipare, 'to press together,
compress*. See stipe and -ule and cp. the first
element in stipend. Cp. also etiolate.
Derivative: stipul-ed, adj.

## stipuliform
stipuliform, adj., having the form of a stipule. —
See stipule and -form.

## stir
stir, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stirien, styrien, fr. OE.
styrian, 'to set in motion, agitate', rel. to MDu.
stoeren, stooren, storen, Du. storen, 'to disturb',
OHG. storan, storren, MHG. stceren, 'to
scatter, destroy', G. storen, 'to disturb', MHG.
sturn, 'to move, disturb', ON. styrr,
'disturbance', and prob. also to E. storm.
Derivatives: stir, п., stirr-er, п., stirr-ing, adj.,
stirr-ing-ly, adv., stir-less, adj.

## stirpiculture
stirpiculture, п., the breeding of special races of
animals. — Compounded of L. stirps, gen.
stirpis, 'stock, stem', and cultura, 'a cultivating,
culture'. See next word and culture.

## stirps
stirps, п., a common ancestor. — L., 'stem,
stock', cogn. with Lith. stirpti, 'to grow up, rise'.
Cp. extirpate.

## stirrup
stirrup, n. — ME. stirop, stirep, fr. OE. stigrap,
'stirrup', rel. to ON. stigreip, OHG. stegareif,
MHG., G. stegreif. These compound words
orig. meant 'a ring for mounting a horse'. For
the first element cp. OE. stigan, 'to climb', stigel,
'stile', and see sty, 'to ascend'. For the second
element see rope.
Derivatives: stirrup, tr. v., stirrup-less, adj.

## stitch
stitch, n. — ME. stiche, fr. OE. slice, 'puncture,
stab, stitch, stitching', rel. to OE. stician, 'to
prick'. See stick, v., and cp. etiquette, ticket.

## stitch
stitch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stichen, fr. stiche.
See stitch, n.
Derivatives: stitch-er, п., stitch-ing, n.

## stithy
stithy, adj., smithy (arcnaic) — ME., fr. ON.
stedi, 'anvil', which is rel. to ON. stadr, 'place'.
See stead.

## stiver
stiver, п., a small coin, a trifle. — Du. stuiver,
name of a coin.

## stoa
stoa, п., a portico. — Gk. στοά, 'colonnade,
porch, corridor', for*aT6)f-i.a, collective noun
formed fr. *στω5-ό-ς, 'a column', fr. I.-E. base
*stndu-, *sthau-, *stnu-, 'upright; a post, pillar'.
See steer, 'to direct', and cp. stauro-.

## stoat
stoat, n. — ME. stot, 'male animal; stoat;
bullock', rel. to ON. stutr, 'bull', Swed. stut, 'bull*,
Dan. stud, Ox', Goth, stautan, 'to push, thrust'.
See stint and cp. stoss.

## stoccado
stoccado, п., a thrust with a rapier. — It. stoccato,
fr. stocco, 'rapier', which is of Teut. origin; see
stock and -ade and cp. bastinado, bravado. The
word stoccado was influenced in form by the
numerous words of Spanish and Portuguese
origin ending in -ado.

## stochastic
stochastic, adj., conjectural. — Gk. στοχαστικός,
fr. στοχάζεσ&αι, 'to aim at, guess, conjecture',
fr. στόχος, 'aim, target, mark', from base
*stegfi-t 'to point, prick, sting'. Cp. the nasalized
var. *stengh-, whence the English verb sting

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:745 COLUMN:3 -->
(q.v.) For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## stock
stock, n. — ME. stok, fr. OE. stocc, 'trunk, log,
stock', rel. to ON. stokkr, 'block of wood, trunk
of a tree', Dan. stok, Swed. stock, OS., OFris.
stok, MDu. stoc, 'tree trunk, stump', Du. stok,
'stick, cane*, OHG., MHG. stoc, 'tree trunk,
stick', G. Stock, 'stick, cane', and to OE. stycce,
OS. stukki, ON. stykki, Swed. stycke, MDu.
stuc(ke), Du. stuk, OHG. stucci, MHG. stucke,
G. Stuck, 'piece', OE. stocu, ON. stuka, OHG.
stuhha, 'sleeve', and cogn. with Lith. stugti, 'to
be prominent', stungis, 'knife handle', OI. tujati,
tunjati, 'he pushes'. OF. estoc, 'stem, trunk*, It.
stocco, 'dagger; rapier', are Teut. loan words.
Cp. chock, stoccado, stoker, stook, stucco, and
the second element in alpenstock, linstock,
maulstick.
Derivatives: stock, tr. and intr. v., adj., stock-
less, adj., stock-er, п., stock-y, adj., stock-i-ly,
adv., stock-i-ness, n.

## stockade
stockade, п., a barrier of stakes. — F. estacade,
'line of piles; pier on piles, stockade' (earlier
also estocade owing to a confusion with F. esto-
cade, 'a thrust'), fr. Sp. estacada, a derivative of
estaca, 'stake, pile, post', which is of Teut.
origin. See stuke and -ade and cp. estacade.
Derivative: stockade, tr. v.

## stockfish
stockfish, n. — MDu. stokvisch (Du. stokvis), fr.
stok, 'stick, stock', and visch (Du. vis), 'fish'.
See stock and fish. For sense development cp. Sp.
bacalao, 'codfish', fr. L. baculum, 'stick, staff*
(see baculao).

## stockinet
stockinet, п., an elastic machine-knitted fabric
used for making stockings, undergarments,
etc. — Formed fr. stocking with dimin. suff.
-et.

## stocking
stocking, n. — Formed fr. stock with -ing, a suff.
expressing relationship.
Derivatives: stocking-ed, adj., stocking-less, adj.

## stodge
stodge, tr. v., to stuff full; to satiate; intr. v., to
be stuck in the mud. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: stodg-er, п., stodg-y, adj., stodg-i-
ly, adv., stodg-i-ness, n.

## stoep
stoep, п., a raised platform at the front, and
sometimes round the sides, of a horse; veranda. —
S. Afr. Du., fr. Du. stoep, 'threshold; (flight of)
steps', rel. to OHG. stuofa, stuoffa, MHG.
stuofe, G. Stufe, 'step, degree', and to OE.
stxpe, stepe, 'step, degree'. See step, n. and v.

## stogie
stogie, stogy, п., a kind of long cigar. — Named
after Conestoga, a town of Pennsylvania.

## stogy
stogy, п., a rough boot. — Prop, 'boot of Cone-
stoga'. See prec. word.

## Stoic
Stoic, п., 1) a member of a school of philosophy
founded by Zeno about 300 B.C.E.; 2) (not cap.),
a person indifferent to pleasure or pain. — L.
Stoicus, fr. Gk. Στωϊκός, 'Stoic', lit. 'man of
the Porch', fr. *στωα, for στοά, 'colonnade,
porch, corridor', so called fr. the Στοά Ποικίλη
('the Painted Porch'), in the market place of
Athens, where Zeno and his followers taught.
See stoa and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: stoic-al, adj., stoic-al-ly, adv., stoic-
al-ness, п., stoic-ism, n.

## Stoic
Stoic, also Stoical, adj., 1) pertaining to, or
resembling, the Stoics or their teachings; 2) (not
cap.) indifferent to pleasure or pain. — L.
Stoicus. See Stoic, n.
Derivative: stoic-al-ly, adv.

## stoichiometry
stoichiometry, also stoechiometry, stoicheiometry,
п., the art of determining the atomic and
molecular weights of the elements (chem.) — G. Sto-
chiometrie, lit. 'measurement of elements',
coined by the German chemist Jeremias Benjamin
Richter (1762-1807) in his "Anfangsgrunde der
StOchiometrie oder MeBkunst chemischer Ele-
mente" (1792) fr. Gk. στοιχεΐον, 'element', and
-μετρία, 'a measuring of. The first element is a
derivative of στοίχος, 'row, line, rank', which
is rel. to στίχος, 'row, line, rank; verse', στεί-
χειν, 'to go; to march in order'; see stichic. For
the second element see -metry.
Derivatives: stoichiometr-ic, stoichiometr-ic-al,
adjs.

## stoke
stoke, tr. v., to poke (a fire); intr. v., to poke a
fire. — Back formation fr. stoker.

## stoker
stoker, п., one who tends a fire. — Du., fr. stoken,
'to poke a fire', fr. stok, 'stick'. See stock and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:746 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 719 | STOUP -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:746 COLUMN:1 -->
agential suff. -er.

## stole
stole, п., a long garment. — L. stola, fr. Gk.
στολή, 'equipment, garment', which stands in
gradational relationship to στέλλειν, 'to set in
order; to arrange; to equip; to send'. See stall
and cp. stele, apostle.
Derivative: stol-ed, adj.

## stole
stole, п., a stolon {rare). — See stolon.

## stolen
stolen, pp. of steal. — ME. stolen, fr. OE. ge-
stolen, pp. of stelan. See steal.

## stolid
stolid, adj., dull. — L. stolidus, 'dull, obtuse,
stolid', prop, 'immovable', rel. to stultus,
'foolish', fr. I.-E. base *st(h)el-, 'to cause to stand,
to place'. See stall and cp. stultify. Cp. also still,
adj., stolon.

## stolidity
stolidity, п., dullness. — L. stoliditas, 'dullness,
obtuseness*, fr. stolidus. See prec. word and -ity.

## stolon
stolon, п., a shoot, sucker. — L. stolo, gen. -onis,
cogn. with Arm. stein, 'trunk (of a tree); branch',
Gk. στέλεχος, 'trunk, stem, log', στελεί, 'haft,
shaft', στήλη, 'block of stone', Lett, stulms,
'trunk (of a tree), arm, leg', fr. I.-E. base *st(h)el-,
'to cause to stand, to place'. See stall and cp.
stolid.

## stolonate
stolonate, adj., having a stolon. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ate fr. L. stolo, gen. -onis. See prec.
word.

## stoloniferous
stoloniferous, adj., producing stolons. — See
stolon and -ferous.

## stoma
stoma, п., a minute mouthlike orifice. — Gk.
στόμα, gen. στόματος, 'mouth', whence
στόμαχος, 'throat, gullet, stomach'. See stomach.

## stomacace
stomacace, п., canker of the mouth (med.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. στομακάκη, 'scurvy of the
gums', lit. 'disease of the mouth', fr. στόμα,
'mouth', andxifao], 'wickedness, vice', which is
rel. to κακός, 'bad, evil'. See prec. word and
caco-.

## stomach
stomach, n. — ME. stomak, fr. OF. ( = F.) esto-
mac, fr. L. stomachus, 'gullet, esophagus,
stomach, liking, taste', fr. Gk. στόμαχος, 'throat,
gullet, esophagus, stomach', fr. στόμα, 'mouth',
which is cogn. with Avestic staman-, 'mouth (of
a dog)', Hitt. shtamar, 'mouth', MBret. staffn,
'mouth; jawbone', Co. stefenic, 'palate'. Cp.
stoma.
Derivatives; stomach, tr. v., stomachal (q.v.),
stomach-ed, adj., stomach-er, п., stomach-ful,
adj., stomachic (q.v.), stomach-less, adj.,
stomach-y, adj.

## stomachal
stomachal, adj., pertaining to the stomach. — See
prec. word and adj. suff. -al.

## stomachic
stomachic, stomachical, adj., 1) pertaining to the
stomach; 2) digestive. — L. stomachicus, fr. Gk.
στομαχικός, 'pertaining to the stomach', fr.
στόμαχος. See stomach and adj. suff. -ic, resp.
also -al.

## stomat-
stomat-, form of stomato- before a vowel.

## stomatitis
stomatitis, п., inflammation of the mucous
membrane of the mouth (med.) — Medical L.,
formed with suff. -itis fr. Gk. στόμα, gen. στόματος,
'mouth'. See stoma.

## stomato-
stomato-, before a vowel stomat-, combining form
meaning 'mouth', as in stomatology. — Gk.
στοματο-, στοματ-, fr. στόμα, gen.
στόματος, 'mouth'. See stoma.

## stomatology
stomatology, п., the study of the diseases of the
mouth. — Compounded of stomato- and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who speaks (in a certain
manner); one who deals (with a certain topic).'.
Derivatives: stomatolog-ic, stomatolog-ic-al,
adjs., stomatolog-ist, n.

## stomatopod
stomatopod, п., any of the Stomatopoda. — See
next word.

## Stomatopoda
Stomatopoda, n. pi., an order of crustaceans
(zoo!.) — ModL., formed fr. stomato- and Gk.
πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See foot.

## stomatous
stomatous, adj., having a stoma or stomata. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. στόμα, gen.
στόματος, 'month'. See stoma.

## -stomatous
-stomatous, combining form. — The same as
-stomous. Cp. prec. word.

## stomodeum
stomodeum, stomodaeum, п., the oral part of the
alimentary canal (zool.) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. στόμα, 'mouth', and όδαϊος, 'that
which is on the way', fr. οδός, 'way'. For the
first element see stoma, for the second see odo-
graph.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:746 COLUMN:2 -->

## -stome
-stome, combining form denoting the mouth, as
in cyclostome. — ModL. -stoma, fr. Gk. στόμα,
'mouth'. See stoma.

## Stomoisia
Stomoisia, п., a genus of plants of the bladder-
wort family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
Gk. στόμα, 'mouth', and οϊσος, 'withy'. For the
first element see stoma. Gk. οίσος stands for
*foϊτFoς and is rel. to είτέα, which prob.
stands for * 5ειτέα; fr. I.-E. base *wei-, 'to bend,
twist'. See withy and cp. Itea.

## -stomous
-stomous, combining form meaning 'having a
mouth' (zool. and bot.) — Gk. -στομος, 'having a
mouth, mouthed', fr. στόμα, 'mouth'. See stoma.

## stone
stone, n. — ME. stan, ston, stoon, fr. OE. start,
rel. to ON. steinn, Dan. steen, Swed. sten,
OFris., OS. sten, Du. steen, OHG., MHG., G.
stein, Goth, stains, fr. I.-E. base *stai-, *stei-,
*stl, 'to thicken, compress, stiffen; stone',
whence also 01. styayate, 'curdles, becomes
hard', part, styanah, 'curdled', Avestic std-,
stay-, 'heap', Gk. στέαρ, gen. στέατ,ος, 'fat,
tallow', στία, στΐον, 'pebble', στίλη, 'drop', L.
stiria, stilla, 'drop', OSlav. stina, 'wall'. Cp.
stean, steato-, the first element in steenbok,
steinbok, and the second element in Athelstan,
felstone. Cp. also distil, instil. Cp. also stiff.
Derivatives: stone, v. (q.v.), stone, adj., stone-
less, adj., stony (q.v.)

## stone
stone, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stanen, stonen, fr.
stan, ston, 'stone'. See stone, n.
Derivatives: ston-ed, adj., ston-er, n.

## stony
stony, adj. — ME. stany, stony, stoony, fr. OE.
stanig, fr. stan, 'stone'. See stone, п., and adj.
suff. -y (representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: ston-i-ly, adv., ston-i-ness, n.

## stood
stood, past tense and pp. of stand. — ME., fr. OE.
stod, past tense of standan. See stand.

## stooge
stooge, п., 1) an actor who assists a comedian;
2) a person acting as a foil to another (colloq.)
— Of unknown origin.
Derivative: stooge, intr. v., to be a stooge.

## stook
stook, п., a shock of corn (chiefly Brit.) — ME.
stouke, rel. to MLG. stake, 'tree stump, heap,
sleeve', OE. stocu, ON. stuka, OHG. stuhha,
MHG. stuche, G. Stauche, 'sleeve', and to OE.
stocc, 'trunk, log, stock'. See stock.
Derivative: stook, tr. v.

## stool
stool, n. — ME. stol, stool, fr. OE. stol, 'a seat',
rel. to OS., OFris. stol, ON. stall, Du. stoel,
OHG., MHG. stuol, G. Stuhl, 'seat', Goth.
stols, 'a high seat, throne'. These words are
formed with -to (a suff. denoting place) fr. I.-E.
base *sta-, 'to stand', whence also OSlav. stolu,
'stool', Lith. pa-stotas, 'stand'. See state and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the second
element in fauteull.
Derivative: stool, intr. v.

## stool pigeon
stool pigeon, 1) a decoy pigeon; 2) a person used
as a decoy; informer, spy. — Lit. 'a pigeon
fastened to a stool'. The word was originally used
of wild pigeons fastened by hunters to a stool
and used as a decoy.

## stoop
stoop, intr. and tr. v., to bend forward toward the
ground. — ME. stupen, fr. OE. stupian, rel. to
ON. stupa, 'to stick up, stand upright', MDu.
stupen, 'to bow, bend', and in gradational
relationship to steep, adj. and v.
Derivatives: stoop, п., stoop-er, п., stoop-ing,
adj., stoop-ing-ly, adv.

## stoop
stoop, п., porch, platform. — A var. spelling of
stoep.

## stop
stop, tr. and intr. v. — ME. stoppen, fr. ΟΈ,./ογ-
stoppian, 'to stop up, close', rel. to MLG. (=
Du.) stoppen, OHG. stop/δη (MHG., G. stop-

## fen). These words derive fr. ML. stuppare
fen). These words derive fr. ML. stuppare, 'to
stop with tow' (whence also It. stoppare,
OProvenc. estopar, F. itouper, 'to stop with
tow'), fr. L. stuppa, stupa, 'the coarse part of
flax, tow', fr. Gk. στύππη, of s.m., which is
cogn. with 01. stupdh, 'tuft of hair'. The Teut.
words mentioned were influenced in meaning by
L. stuplre, 'to be stunned, be stupefied'. Cp.
stopple, estop, estoppel.
Derivatives: stop, п., stopp-able, adj., stopp-age,
п., stopp-er, п., and tr. v., stopp-ing, adj. and n.

## stopple
stopple, п., stopper. — ME. stoppel, fr. stoppen,
'to stop'. See stop and -le.
Derivative: stopple, tr. v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:746 COLUMN:3 -->

## storax
storax, п., resin. — Late L. storax, fr. Gk.
στύραξ, 'a kind of resin', fr. Heb. tzori, 'resin of
the lentisk and of the terebinth'. Cp. styrax.

## store
store, tr. and intr. v. — ME. storen, fr. OF. eslo-
rer, 'to establish, give birth to, restore', formed
—with change of pref.—fr. L. in-staurare, 'to
renew, repair, restore'. Cp- restaurant, restore,
instauration.
Derivatives: stor-able, adj., stor-age, n.

## store
store, n. — ME. star, fr. OF. estor, 'provision',
back formation fr. estorer. See store, v.

## storey
storey, n. — See story, of a house.

## storiated
storiated, adj., adorned with historical scenes. —
Aphetic for historiated.

## storiation
storiation, п., decoration with historical scenes.
— See prec. word and -ation.

## storied
storied, adj., 1) celebrated; 2) adorned with
historical scenes. — Formed fr. story, 'history',
with sufT. -ed.

## storied
storied, storeyed, adj., having (a certain number
of) stories (said of a building). — Formed fr.
story, storey, with 3rd suff. -ed.

## storiette
storiette, п., a short tale. — Formed fr. story,
'history', with suff. -ette.

## storiology
storiology, п., the study of folk tales. — A hybrid
coined fr. story, 'history', and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: storiolog-ic-al, adj., storiolog-ist, n.

## stork
stork, n. — ME., fr. OE. store, rel. to ON. storkr,
Dan., Swed. stork, MDu. store, OHG. storah,
MHG., G.storch, 'stork', and to OE. stearc,
'rigid, strong', OHG. gi-storchanen, 'to become stiff'
(see stark), the bird having been named from its
stiff posture. OSlav. struku, Russ. sterch, Lith.
starkus, 'stork', are Teut. loan words.

## stork's bill
stork's bill, any plant of the genus Pelargonium.
— Named after its shape. Cp. G. Storchschnabel
and F. bee de cicogne, 'stork's bill'. Cp. also Gk.
γεράνιον, 'crane's bill', fr. γερανός, 'crane', and
E. crane's bill, which is a loan translation of Gk.
γεράνιον (see geranium).

## storm
storm, n. — ME., fr. OE. storm, rel. to OS.,
MLG., MDu., Du. storm, ON. stormr, OHG.,
MHG., G. Sturm. These words, in which the m
has the force of a suff., are prob. rel. to stir (q.v.)
OF. estour, 'onset, tumult', It. stormo, of s.m.,
are Teut. loan words. Cp. stour and the second
element in Iandsturm.
Derivatives: storm, tr. and intr. v., storm-er, п.,
storm-less, adj., storm-y, adj., storm-i-ly, adv.,
storm-i-ness, n.

## storting
storting, storthing, п., the Norwegian parliament.
— Norw., lit. 'the great meeting', formed fr.
ON. storr, 'great', and ping, 'meeting'. For the
first element see stour, 'strong', for the second
see thing, 'assembly'.

## story
story, п., history, narrative. — ME. storie, fr. OF.
estorie, estoire, fr. L. historia. See history.

## story
story, п., a horizontal section of a building. —
Prob. fr. Anglo-L. (h)istoria, 'story of a
building', which was prob. used orig. in the sense of,
'part of a building marked by painted
windows', fr. L. historia, 'history'; hence of the same
origin as story in the sense of 'history'. Cp. ML.
historiare, 'to narrate, depict; to carve, paint',
whence E. 'storied4 windows. Cp. also
historiated.

## stoss
stoss, adj., facing the direction from which a
glacier moves.—G.5rojS,4hrust', fr. ζΐοββη,'ίο push,
thrust', MHG. stolen, fr. OHG. st6$an, rel. to
OS. stStan, ON. stauta, MDu. stoten, Du.
stolen, Goth, stautan, ON. steyta, OFris. steta, 'to
push, thrust', and to OE. styntan, 'to blunt,
stupefy'. See stint and cp. words there referred
to.

## stound
stound, п., time, moment (archaic and dial.) —
ME. stund, stond, stound, fr. OE. stand, 'point
of time, time, hour', rel. to OS. stunda, ON.
stund, OFris. stunde, MDu. stonde, stont, OHG.
stunt(a), MHG. stunde, of s.m., Du. stond, 'time,
moment^ hour', G.mStunde, 'hour'; prob. fr.
Teut. base *standan, 'to stand'; see stand.
Accordingly stound orig. meant 'a point of
standing (in the course of time)'. Cp. Stundist.

## stoup
stoup, also stoop, п., drinking vessel; pail. —
ME. stowp, of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. staup,
which is rel. to MLG. stop, Du. stoop, OHG.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:747 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: STOUR | 720 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:747 COLUMN:1 -->
MHG. stouf, G. Stauf, and stands in
gradation a] relationship to steep, adj., and v., and to
stoop, 'to bend'.

## stour
stour, п., tumult (archaic). — ME. stoure, sture,
fr. OF. estour, 'onset, tumult', a Teut. loan
word. Cp. OHG. sturm, OE. storm, 'storm', and
see storm.

## stour
stour, adj., strong, hard. — ME. star, star, fr. OE.
star, rel. to LG. stur, fr. l.-E. base *ster-, 'strong,
firm, stiff, rigid'. See stare and cp. words there
referred to. Cp. also the first element in storting.

## stout
stout, adj. — ME. stoute, stowte, fr. OF. estolt,
estout, 'bold, fierce, proud', of Teut. origin. Cp.
OFris. stulr, 'proud', MLG. srolt, 'stately,
portly, proud', MHG., G. stolz, 'proud, haughty,
arrogant, stately'. These Teut. words prob. stand
in gradational relationship to OHG. stelza, ME.
stilte, etc., 'stilt' (see stilt). See Kluge-Mitzka,
EWDS., p. 753 s.v. stolz.

## stoyaine
stoyaine, stovain, п., a crystalline compound used
as a local anaesthetic. — Coined in 1904 fr.
stove, п., translation of the French word four-
neau (prop, 'furnace') in the name of the French
chemist Ernest-Francois-Auguste Fourneau
(1872-1949), the discoverer of this compound.
The ending -aine shows the influence of cocaine.

## stove
stove, n. — ME. stove, 'heated room, bathroom',
fr. OE. stofa, rel. to ON. stofa, Norw. stova,
Dan. stue, Swed. stuga, 'room', MDu. stove,
OHG. stuba, MHG. stube, 'a heatable room,
bathroom', Du. stoof, 'foot warmer, foot stove',
G. Stube, 'room'. All these words are Romance
loan words. Cp. It. stufa, F. etuve, 'sweating
room (of baths)', which derive fr. It. stu/are,
resp. F. etuver,'to dry, heat, stove', fr. VL. *ex-
tufdre, fr. 1st ex- and VL. *tufus, fr. Gk. τΰφος,
'mist, vapor' (see Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p.
760 s.v. Stube), which is a derivative of I.-E. base
'dhubh-, 'to fill with smoke, to cloud, darken; to
be dull, dumb or deaf. See deaf and words there
referred to and cp. stew, 'to cook slowly'.
OSlav. istuba, izba, Lith. stuba, Hung, szoba,
Finn, tupa, 'room', are directly or indirectly
borrowed fr. Teutonic; cp. isba.
Derivatives; stove, tr. v., srov-er, n.

## stove
stove, past tense and pp. of stave.

## stover
stover, п., provision; fodder (obsol.) — See
estovers.

## stow
stow, tr. v., to pack. — ME. stowen, 'to place', fr.
stowe, 'place', fr. OE. stow, 'place', which is rel.
to OFris. sto, 'place', MLG., MDu., Du. stou-
wen, 'to stow', OHG., MHG. stouwen, 'to stop,
check; to command; to complain, scold,
accuse', G. stauen, 'to stow', Goth, stojan, 'to
judge', and cogn. with OSlav. stavljg, siaviti, 'to
place', stavu, 'structure', Lith. stoviu, stoveti, 'to
stand', Lett, stavu, stdveju, stavet, of s.m. AH
these words derive fr. I.-E. *st(h)du-, *st(h)u-,
'stiff, upright', which is an enlargement of base
*st(h)d-, 'to stand'. See state and cp. bestow. Cp.
also stud, 'peg'. Cp. also steer, 'to direct'.
Derivatives: stowage, п., stow-er, п., stow-ing,
n.

## strabism
strabism, п., strabismus. — See strabismus.

## strabismal
strabismal, strabismic, strabismical, adj.,
pertaining to strabismus. — See next word and adj.
suff. -al, resp. -ic, -ical.

## strabismus
strabismus, п., squint. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
στραβισμός, fr. στραβίζειν, 'to squint', fr.
στραβός, 'crooked, squinting', which stands in
gradational relationship to στρεβλός, 'crooked,
twisted', στραβός, 'a whirling round',
στρόβιλος, 'anything that whirls round; a top;
fircone, pine cone; whirlwind', στρόβιλος,
'spinning, whirling', fr. I.-E. *streb-, a parallel form of
base 'strebh-, 'to turn'. See strophe and -ism.
Derivatives: strabism-al, strabism-ic, strabism-
ic-al, adjs.

## strabo-
strabo-, combining form meaning 'squinting,
strabismus'. — Gk. στραβό-, fr. στραβός,
'squinting'. Seeprec. word.

## strabotomy
strabotomy, п., a surgical operation to cure
squint. — Compounded of strabo- and Gk.
-τομία, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See
-tomy.

## Strad
Strad, n. — Abbreviation of Stradivarius.

## straddle
straddle, intr. v., to stand, sit or walk with the
legs wide apart; tr. v., to have one leg on either

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:747 COLUMN:2 -->
side of. — Formed from the verb stride with
freq. suff. -le.
Derivatives: straddle, п., straddl-er, п.,
straddling, adj., straddl-ing-ly, adv.

## stradiot
stradiot, п., a mercenary»cavalryman from Greece
or Albania serving in Italy in the Middle Ages.
— It. stradiotto, fr. Gk. στρατιώτης, 'soldier',
fr. στρατιά, 'army, company, band', fr.
στρατός, 'army'. See strategy and cp. Stratiotes.

## Stradivarius
Stradivarius, n. — A violin made by Antonio
Stradivarius of Cremona (1644-1737) or his sons.
Cp. Amati, Guarneri.

## strafe
strafe, tr. v., to bombard heavily; to punish. —
Fr. strafe in the German phrase Gott strafe
England, 'God punish England', used in World War
I.
Derivative: strafe, n.

## straggle
straggle, intr. v., to wander from one's course; to
stray, rove. — ME. straglen, prob. a freq.
formed fr. ME. straken, 'to wander',which stands in
gradational relationship to OE. streccan, 'to
stretch'. See stretch and freq. suff. -Ie and cp.
straight, strake.
Derivatives: straggl-er, п., straggl-ing, adj.,
straggl-ing-ly, adv., straggl-y, adj.

## straight
straight, adj. — ME. streght, streiht, straight, pp.
of strecchen, 'to stretch'. Accordingly straight
prop, means 'that which is stretched'. See
stretch.
Derivatives: straight, n. and adv., straight-en, tr.
and intr. v., straight-en-er, п., straight-ly, adv.,
straight-ness, n.

## strain
strain, tr. and intr. v., to stretch. — ME. streynen,
streinen, strainen, 'to strain, stretch', fr. OF.
estraign-, estreign-, pTes. part, stem of estraindre,
estreindre (F. etreindre), *to strain', fr. L. strin-
gere, 'to draw tight'. See stringent and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: strain, п., tautness, tension, strain-
able, adj., strain-ed, adj., strain-er, п.,
straining, adj., strain-ing-ly, adv.

## strain
strain, п., breed, ancestry, generation. — ME.
strene, stren, streen, fr. OE. streon, strion, 'gain,
procreation, progeny', which is rel. to OE.
streonan, strienan, strynan, 'to get, gain, beget',
OHG. striunan, 'to get, gain'.

## strait
strait, adj., narrow (archaic). — ME. streit, strait,
fr. OF. estreit (F. etroit), fr. L. strictus, pp. of
stringere, 'to draw tightly'. See strain, 'to stretch',
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: strait, п., strait-en, v., strait-ly,
adv., strait-ness, n.

## strake
strake, п., a streak. — ME., prop, 'something
stretched', rel. to strecchen, 'to stretch';
influenced in form by a confusion with streak, to
which it is not related. See stretch and cp. straggle.

## stramazon
stramazon, п., a cut with the edge of a sword
(fencing). — F. estramacon fr. It. stramazzone,
fr. stramazzare, 'to reverse with force', which is
formed fr. augmentative pref. stra- (fr. L. extra-),
and the noun mazza, 'sledgehammer'. See extra
and mace, 'weapon'.

## stramineous
stramineous, adj., 1) like straw; 2) of the color of
straw (archaic). — L. stramineus, 'made of straw,
like straw', fr. strdmen, gen. -minis, 'straw,
litter', lit. 'that which is spread out'; cogn. with
01. stariman-, 'spreading out, extension', strtah,
stlrndh, 'spread out', Gk. στορνύναι, στορεν-
νύναι, στρωννύναι, 'to spread out', στρώμα,
'bedclothes, mattress', lit. 'anything spread out',
fr. I.-E. base *stor-, *ster-, *str-, 'to spread out'.
See stratum. For the ending see suff. -eons.

## stramonium
stramonium, п., the thorn apple (Datura) and the
poisonous drug obtained from it. — ModL., of
uncertain origin.

## strand
strand, п., beach of the sea, bank of a river. —
ME., fr. OE. strand, rel. to Dan., Swed. strand,
'beach, shore, strand', ON. strond, 'border,
edge, shore', MLG. strant (whence Late MHG.
strant, G. Strand), Du. strand, 'beach'. These
words prob. meant orig. 'extended tract of land',
and derive fr. I.-E. base *ster-, *stor-, *str-t 'to
spread out'. See stratum and cp. words there
referred to.
Derivatives: strand, tr. and intr. v., strand-age,
п., strand-er, п., strand-ing, verbal n. and adj.

## strand
strand, п., fiber or thread of yam. — ME. strond,
prob. fr. OF. estran, which is of Teut. origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:747 COLUMN:3 -->
Cp. MDu. strene, OHG. streno, MHG. strene,
G. Strdhne,-'skein, strand'; of uncertain origin.
Derivative: strand, tr. v., to make a rope by
uniting threads,

## strange
strange, adj. — ME., fr. OF. estrange (F. έ-
trange), 'strange, foreign', fr. L. extrdneus,
'strange, foreign', fr. extra, 'outside'. See extra
and cp. estrange, extraneous.
Derivatives: strange-ly, adv., strange-ness, n.

## stranger
stranger, n. — ME., fr. MF. estrangier (F. etran-
ger), 'foreign; foreigner', fr. estrange, 'strange,
foreign', fr. OF. See prec. word.

## strangle
strangle, tr. v., to choke. — ME. stranglen, fr.
MF. estrangier (F. etrangler), fr. OF., fr. L.
stranguldre, 'to strangle, choke'. See next word.
Derivatives: strangle, n.,strangl-er, п., strangles,
п., an infectious disease of horses,

## strangnlate
strangnlate, tr. v., to strangle. — L. stranguldtus,
pp. of stranguldre, 'to strangle, choke', fr. Gk.
στραγγαλοϋν, of s.m., which is rel. to στραγ-
γάλη, 'halter'. See stringent and cp. strangle.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## strangulation
strangulation, n. — L. stranguldtio, gen. -onis, fr.
stranguldtus, pp. of stranguldre. Seeprec. word
and -ion.

## strangurious
strangurious, adj., pertaining to strangury. — See
next word and -ous.

## strangury
strangury, п., painful urination (med.) — L.
stranguria, fr. Gk. στραγγουρίά, 'strangury', which
is compounded of στράγξ, gen. στραγγός, *a
drop', and ουρον, 'urine'. For the first element
see strangulate, for the second see urine.

## strap
strap, n. — A doublet of strop, fr. ME. strope, fr.
OE. stropp, fr. L. stroppus, struppus, 'strap,
thong, fillet', fr. Gk. στροφός, 'twisted band or
cord', which is rel. to στροφή, 'a turning,
twisting', στρέφειν, 'to turn'. F. estrope, etrope,
'strop', and Du. strop, 'halter', are also
borrowed fr. L. stroppus. See strophe and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: strap, tr. v., strapp-ed, adj.,
strapper, п., strapp-ing, adj. and n.

## strappado
strappado, п., a form of torture in which the
victim was attached (usually by his wrists) to along
rope, raised into the air and suddenly dropped
almost to the ground. — Formed—according to
my opinion, prob. under the influence of the
synonym bastinado—fr. It. strappata, 'a sharp
tug, pull, snatch, wrench', fr. strappare, 'to pull',
which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. stroufen, 'to
fiay', OE. -strypan in bestrypan, 'to plunder',
and see strip, v. The first a in It. strappare, is due
to the influence of stracciare, 'to tear asunder'.
[In Johnson's Dictionary (1662) strappado is
confused in meaning with bastinado, which
corroborates the supposition that the ending -ado
in strappado was formed on the analogy of
bastin-ado.]

## strass
strass, п., a brilliant lead glass used to make
artificial gems. — F. strass, stras, named after Stras,
the inventor of the process.

## strass
strass, п., refuse of silk in skein making. — F.
strasse, fr. It. straccio, back formation fr.
stracciare, 'to tear asunder', fr. VL. *distractiare, fr.
L. distractus, pp. of distrahere, 'to pull apart'.
See distract,

## stratagem
stratagem, п., artifice, trick. — F. stratageme, fr.

## earlier strattegeme
earlier strattegeme, fr. L. strategema, 'artifice,

## stratagem'
stratagem', fr. Gk. στρατήγημα, 'the act of a
general, piece of generalship, stratagem', fr.
στρατηγεΐν, 'to be a general, to command', fr.
στρατηγός. See strategy. For the ending of Gk.
στρατήγημα see suff. -ma.
Derivatives: stratagem-ic-al, adj., stratagem-ic-

## al-ly
al-ly, adv.

## strata)
strata), adj., pertaining to strata. — Formed with

## adj. suff. -al fr. L. stratum. See stratum
adj. suff. -al fr. L. stratum. See stratum,

## strategic
strategic, strategical, adj. — F. strategique, fr. Gk.
στρατηγικός, 'of, or pertaining to, a general',
fr. στρατηγός. See strategy and adj. suff. -ic,
resp. also -al.
Derivatives: strategic-al-ly, adv., strateg-ics, n,

## strategus
strategus, also strutegos, п., the leader of an army,
general. — L. strategus, fr. Gk. στρατηγός. See
next word.

## strategy
strategy, n. — F. stratigie, fr. Gk. στρατηγία,
'office of a general', fr. στρατηγός, 'strategus,

## general'
general', lit. 'leader of the army', compounded

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:748 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 721 | STRICK -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:748 COLUMN:1 -->
of στρατός, 'army', and the stem οίΊΚγε^ν, *to
lead'. For the first element see stratum and cp.
stradiot, for the second see agent, adj.

## strath
strath, a., a wide river valley. — Gael, sratk,
'valley', fr. Olr. sratk, of s.m., fr. L. strata (via),
'paved way', fem. pp. of sternere, 'to spread out'.
See street,

## strathspey
strathspey, п., a Scottish dance and the music for
it. — Named after Strathspey, a district in
Eastern Scotland.

## strati-
strati-, combining form meaning 'stratum*. — L.
strati-, fr. stratum. See stratum,

## straticulate
straticulate, adj., arranged in thin layers. —
Formed fr. strati-, -cule and adj. suff. -ate.

## stratification
stratification, n. — ML. stratificdtio, gen. -onis,
formed fr. stratificatus, pp. of stratificare. See
stratify and -ation.

## stratiform
stratiform, adj., having the form of a stratum. —
Comp'ounded of strati- and L. forma, 'form,
shape'. See form, n.

## stratify
stratify, tr. v., to form in strata. — F. stratifier,
fr. ML. stratificare, 'to form strata'. See strati-
and -fy.
Derivatives: stratifi-ed, adj., stratifi-er, n.

## stratigraphy
stratigraphy, п., description of the arrangement
of strata. — A hybrid coined fr. L. stratum, 'a
covering', Gk. -γραφία, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'.
See -graphy.
Derivatives: stratigraph-ic, stratigraph-ic-al,
adjs., stratigraph-ic-al-ly, adv., stratigraph-ist, n.

## Stratiomyiidae
Stratiomyiidae, n. pi., the family of soldier fiies
(zool.) — ModL., formed with surT. -idae fr. Gk.
στρατιώτης, 'soldier', and μυϊα, 'fiy'. See
strategy and myo-,

## Stratiotes
Stratiotes, п., a genus of plants of the family
Hydrocharitaceae (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
στρατιώτης, 'soldier, yarrow, milfoil'. See
strategy and cp. stradiot.

strato-, combining form meaning 'army'. — Fr.

## straw

strawberry, n. — ME., fr. OE. streawberige,

## stray
stray, intr. v., to wander, go astray. — ME. strai-
en, fr. MF. estraier, v., 'to go astray', fr. OF., fr.

estraier, 'wandering stray, lost', fr. VL. *strdtd-
rius, lit. 'abandoned on the road', fr. Late L.
strata (via). See stray, v., and cp- estray.
Derivative: stray, adj., straying.

strica, 'mark, stroke of the pen*, OHG., MHG.,
G. strich, Goth, striks, 'stroke, line', and to OE.
strican, 'to rub, move'. See strike.
Derivatives: streak, tr. v., streak-y, adj., streak·

## stream
stream, n. — ME. strem, streme, fr. OE. stream,
'flowing, current; running water, river', rel. to
OS. strom, ON. straumr, Dan. strem, Swed.
strom, Norw. straum, OFris. strum, Du. stroom,
OHG., MHG. stroum, strom, G. Strom,
'current, river', fr. l.-E. base *sreu-, 'tofiow\ whence
also OI. srdvati, 'flows', srotah, 'stream',
Arm. aroganem, Ί moisten, wet', Gk. ρέειν (for
*σρέΓειν), 'to flow', ρόος (for *σρόΓος),
'stream', Lett, strauma, 'stream, river', Pol.
strumien, 'brook', Lith. sraveti, 'to trickle, ooze*,
OSlav. struja, 'river1, o-strovu, 'island', lit. 'that
which is surrounded by a river', Olr. sruaim, Ir.
sruth (gen. srotha), Co. streth, 'river'. Cp. the
river name Στρόμων, lit. 'River'. Cp. rheo-,
rheumatic, rheumatism, rhythm, the first element
in rhyolite and the second element in Calirrhoe,
catarrh, hemorrhoids, diarrhea, pyorrhea,
seborrhea. Cp. also strudel and the second element
in maelstrom. Base *sreu- is an enlargement of
base *ser-, whence Gk. άρμη (for *σορμή ), 'on-
set', ορός (for *σορός), 'whey', L. serum,
'whey'. See hormone and serum.
Derivatives: stream, v., stream-er, п.,
streaming, n. and adj., stream-ing-ly, adv., stream-y,
adj., stream-i-ness, n.

## streamlet
streamlet, п., a small stream. — Formed fr.
stream with dimin. suff. -let.

## street
street, n. — ME. strete, 'paved way', fr. OE.
street, fr. Late L. strata (via), 'paved way', fem.
pp. of sternere, 'to spread out, pave'. Cp. Pro-
venc. estrada, 'street', Olr. srath, 'valley', which
are of the same origin. For the etymology of L.
sternere see stratum. Cp. estrade, strath, stray,
'to wander', Al Sirat.
Derivative: street-age, n.

## stremma
stremma, п., a Greek measure of land. — ModGk.
στρέμμα, fr. Gk. στρέμμα, 'that which is
twisted', from the stem of στρέφειν, 'to turn, twist'.
See strophe and cp. words there referred to. For
the ending see suff. -ma.

## strength
strength, n. — ME. strengthen fr. OE. strengpu,
which is rel. to OHG. strengida, 'strength', and
stands in gradational relationship to strong. For
the ending see subst. suff. -th.
Derivatives:strength-en, tr. andintr.v.,5/r£wg*A-

en-ing, ao'j.,strength-en-ing-ly, adv., strengthiess,

strong', στρηνος, 'arrogance, eager desire', and

with OE. stierne, 'hard, severe, keen'. These

there referred to. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L.

## Strephon
Strephon, п., a lover, swain. — Fr. Strephon, the
shepherd lover in Sir Philip Sydney's Arcadia.

Streptococcus, п., a genus of bacteria of the
