## streptomycin
streptomycin, п., an antibiotic drug first isolated
by the American microbiologist Selman
Abraham Wdksman (born in 1888) in 1944. —
Coined fr. strepto-, Gk. μύκης, 'fungus' (see myco-),
and suff. -in.

## Streptoneura
Streptoneura, n. pi., a subclass of mollusks (zool.)
— ModL., lit. '(animals) with twisted nerves',
compounded of strepto- and Gk. νεϋρον, 'nerve'.
See neuro-.

## stress
stress, tr. v. — ME. stressen, fr. MF. estrecier, fr.
OF., fr. VL. *strictiare, freq. formed fr. strictus,
pp. of stringere, 'to draw tight'; see stringent. In
some meanings the verb stress is aphetic for
distress, in some it derives directly fr. stress, n.
Cp. strain, 'to stretch'.
Derivative: stress-er, n.

## stress
stress, n. — ME. stresse, aphetic for distresse. See
distress. See also stress, v. For a similar aphesis
cp. splay, sport, stain.
Derivatives: stress-ful, adj., stress-ful-ly, adv.,
stress-less, adj., stress-Iess-ness, n.

## stretch
stretch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. strecchen, fr. OE.
streccan, rel. to Dan. straekke, Swed. strdcka,
OFris. strekka, OHG. strecchan, MLG., MDu.,
OHG., MHG., G. strecken, Du. strekken, 'to
stretch', prop, 'to make straight'. Cp. MHG.
strac, G. strack, 'straight' and E. straight,
straggle, stroke.
Derivatives: stretch, п., stretch-er, п., stretch-y,
adj., stretch-i-ness, n.

## stretto
stretto, п., part of a fugue in which the answer
crowds upon the subject (music). — It., from
the adj. stretto, 'drawn tightly', fr. L. strictus,
pp. of stringere. See stringent and cp. strict.

## strew
strew, tr. v. — ME. strewen, strowen, fr. OE.
streowian, streawian, strewian, 'to scatter', rel.
to OS. stroian, ON. stra, Dan. stre, Swed. stro,
MDu.-struwen, strouwen, strooyen, Du. strooien,
OHG. strewen, MHG. strouwen, G. streuen,
Goth, straujan, fr. l.-E. base *ster-, *stor, *str-,
'to spread out, extend, strew', whence also OI.
strnati, strnSti, starati, 'strews, scatters', Gk.
στορνύναι, στορεννύναι,, στρωννύναι, 'to
spread out', στρώμα, 'bedclothes, mattress',
prop, 'anything spread out', L. sternere (pp.
stratus), 'to spread out, stretch out', struere, 'to
put together, construct'. See stratum and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also strand, 'shore',
strath, straw, stray.
Derivatives: strew, п., strew-er, n.

## stria
stria, п., a narrow stripe, groove. — L., 'furrow,
channel', cogn. with Du. striem, OHG. strimo,
MHG. strieme, streime, G. Strieme, 'stripe,
streak', and prob. rel. to L. striga, 'stroke, stripe,
furrow', strigilis, 'scraper', stringere, 'to draw
tight'.See stringent andcp. words there referred to-

## striate
striate, adj., striped, variegated. — L. stridtus, pp.
of stridre, 'to groove, fiute', fr. stria. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: striate-ly, adv.

## striate
striate, tr. v., to mark with striae. — L. stridtus,
pp. of stridre. See striate, adj.
Derivatives: striat-ed, adj., striat-ion, n.

## striature
striature, п., striatum. — L. stridtura, fr. stridtus,
pp. οι stridre. See striate, adj., and -иге.

## strict
strict, adj. — L. strtctus, 'drawn tightly', pp. of

## stricture
stricture, п., criticism. — L. strictura,

## stride
stride, n. — ME., fr. OE. stride, rel. to MLG.
strede, 'stride', Dan., Swed. strid, Du. strijd,
OHG., MHG. strit, G. Streit, 'fight, contention,
combat', and to ON. stridr, 'strong, hard,
stubborn, severe'. These words prob. meant orig.
'stubbornness, opposition, resistance' (cp. the
meaning of ON. stridr), and derive fr. I.-E. base
*ster-, 'strong, firm, stiff, rigid', whence also OE.
starian, 'to look fixedly at'. See stare.

## stride
stride, intr. and tr. v. — ME. striden, fr. OE.
stridan, 'to stride, step', rel. to MLG. striden, 'to
straddle*, OS. stridian, ON. strida, Dan. stride,
Swed.srri'i&,'tofight',Du.Jin/i/en,OHG. stritan,
MHG. striten, G. streiten, 'to fight, struggle,
contend', and to OE. stride, 'stride*. See stride,
n.
Derivatives: strid-er, п., strid-ing-ly, adv.

## stridence
stridence, stridency, n. — Formed from next word
with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## strident
strident, adj., harsh-sounding. — L. stridens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of stridere, 'to make a shrill or
creaking sound, whizz, buzz', from the imitative
base *strid-; cp. stridulate. Cp. the collateral
base *(s)trig-, whence Gk. τρίζειν, 'to utter a
shrill cry', στρίγξ, στρίξ, στλίξ, Owl', lit. 'the
screeching bird'. Cp. Strix, trismus and the
second element in Aniphitrite.
Derivative: strident-ly, adv.

## stridhana
stridhana, п., property belonging to a woman
{Hindu law). — OI. stri-dhana-, 'woman's
property', fr. sin, 'woman', and dhanam, 'booty,
possession, property'. The first element prob. derives
from the I.-E. reflexive base *s(w)edh-, 'made
one's own'. See sui. For the second element see
dhan.

## stridulate
stridulate, intr. v., to produce a creaking noise. —
Formed with verbal suff. -ate fr. L. stridulus,
'creaking', fr. stridere. See strident and -ule.
Derivatives: stridulat-ion, п., stridulat-or, n.

## stridulent
stridulent, adj., creaking. — Formed with suff.
-ent fr. L. stridulus, 'creaking'. See strident.

## stridulous
stridulous, adj., making a creaking sound. — L.
stridulus, 'creaking', fr. stridere. See strident. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: stridulous-ly, adv., stridulous-ness,
n.

## strife
strife, n. — ME. strif, fr. OF. estrif, estrit,
'contention, strife, effort', which is of Teut. origin.
Cp. OHG. strit, 'fight, combat, quarrel', stritan,
'to fight, combat, contend', and see stride (q.v.)
Cp. also strive.

## striga
striga, п., bristle, hairlike scale {bet.) — L. striga,
'stroke, stripe, furrow'; rel. to strigilis, 'scraper',
stringere, 'to draw tight', stria, 'furrow,
channel'. See stria and cp. strigil.

## strigil
strigil, п., an instrument for scraping the skin. —
L. strigilis, 'scraper', reL to striga, 'stroke, stripe,
furrow'. See prec. word.
Derivative: strigill-ation, n.

## strigose
strigose, adj., covered with bristles (hot.) —
ModL. strigosus, fr. L. striga. See strign and adj.
suff. -ose.

## strigous
strigous, adj., strigose. — ModL. strigosus. See
prec. word and -ous.

## strike
strike, tr. and intr. v. — ME. striken, 'to strike,
stroke, rub', fro OE. strican, 'to move, stroke,
Tub', rel. to ON. strykva, 'to stroke', OFris.
strika, MDu. streken, Du. strijken, 'to smooth,
stroke, rub', OHG. strihhan, MHG. stricken,
G. streicken, of s.m., MHG., G. streich, Goth.
striks, 'stroke*, and cogn. with L. striga, 'stroke,
stripe, furrow', strigilis, 'scraper', stria, 'furrow,
channel', stringere, 'to draw tight'. See stringent
and cp. streak, strickie, stroke.
Derivatives: strike, п., strik-er, п., strik-ing, adj.
and п., strik-ing-ly, adv., strik-ing-ness, n.

## string
string, n. — ME. streng, string, fr. OE. streng,
'string of a bow or harp, cord, rope, sinew', rel.
to ON. strengr, Dan. streng, Swed. Strang, MDu.
strenge, stringe, Du. streng, OHG. Strang,
MHG. strange, stranc, G. Strang, 'rope, cord',
and cogn. with L. stringere, 'to draw tight'. See
stringent.
Derivatives: string, tr. v., string-ed, adj.,
stringer, п., string-y, adj., string-i-ness, п., string-less,
adj.

## stringency
stringency, n. — Formed fr. stringent with suff.
-cy.

## stringendo
stringendo, adv. and adj., increasing the tempo
(musical direction). — It., fr. L., abl. of the
gerund of stringere, 'to draw tight'. See next word.

## stringent
stringent, adj. — L. stringens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, οι stringere, 'to draw tight, to draw, bind
or press together; to draw from the sheath; to
check, restraint'. According to Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., II, pp. 604-605, in L. stringere, two,
originallydistinct, verbs seem to have merged: 1)
one cogn. with L. striga, 'stroke, stripe, furrow',
strigilis, 'scraper', stria, 'furrow, channel', Gk.
στρίγξ, gen. στριγγός, 'row, line', OE. stri-
can, 'to rub, move', Goth, striks, G. Streich, 'a
stroke', OSlav. strigo, stristi, 'to shear', OPruss.
strigli, 'thistle'; see strike and cp. stria, strign,
strigil, strike; 2) the other verb derives fr. earlier
*strengere and is cogn. with Gk. στράγξ, gen.
στραγγός, 'a drop', lit. 'that which is squeezed
out', στραγγός,'twisted, crooked'; flowing drop
by drop', στραγγάλη, 'halter', στραγγαλίζει,
στραγγαλοϋν, 'to twist, strangle', στρογγυλός,
'twisted, round', Mir. srens'im,'Ipull,draw,drag',
Ir. sreangaim, *I tear, drag', sreang, 'string, rope',
Lett, stringt, 'to become tight', OE. streng, ON.
strengr, 'string of a bow or harp, rope, sinew',
OE. Strang, ON. strangr, 'strong, severe'. Cp.
astringe, astringent, constrain, v., constrict,
distrain, distress, district, estrangelo, obstriction,
prestige, restrain, restrict, strain, v., strait,
strand, 'fiber', strangle, strangulate, stress, stret-
to, strict, stricture, string, strong, strungyle. For
the ending of stringent see suff. -ent.
Derivatives: stringent-ly, adv., stringent-ness, n.

## strip

to tear off; intr. v., to take off all clothing —
ME. stripen, strepen, fr. OE. -strypan in bestry-

## pan
pan, 'to plunder', rel. to MDu. (= Du.) stropen,
'to strip off; to ramble aboutplundering', OHG.
stroufen, MHG. streifen, stroufen, 'to strip off,
plunder', G. streifen, 'strip off, touch upon; to
ramble, roam, rove'.

## strip
strip, п., a narrow piece. — Derived fr. strip, v.;
influenced in meaning by stripe.
Derivative: stripling (q.v.)

## stripe
stripe, n. — ME., prob. fr. MDu. stripe (Du.
streep), 'stripe, streak', which is rel. to LG.
stripe, Dan. stribe, MHG. strife, G. Streifen,
'stripe', MLG., MDu. stripen, MHG., G.

## streifen

*streibd-), 'stripe'.
Derivatives: stripe, tr. v., strip-ed, adj., strip-y,
adj., strip-i-ness, n.

## stripling
stripling, п., a youth. — Formed fr. strip, п.,
with dimin suff. -ling.

## strive
strive, intr. v. — ME. striven, fr. OF. estriver, 'to
contend, strive*, fr. estrif, 'contention, strife,
effort'. See strife.
Derivative: striv-er, n.

## Strix
Strix, п., a genus of owls (ornitkol.) — L. strix,
fr. Gk. στρίξ, στρίγξ, 'an owl', lit. 'a
screeching bird', from the imitative base *strig-, a
collateral form of base *strid-, whence L.
stridere, 'to make a shrill sound, whiz, buzz'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:749 COLUMN:3 -->
See strident.

## strobic
strobic, adj., resembling a top. — Formed with
adj. suff -ic fr. Gk. στρόβος, 'a twisting round1.
See strobile.

## strobila
strobila, п., 1) a stage in the life of a jellyfish; 2)
a segmented tapeworm. — ModL., fr. Gk.
στροβίλη, 'a plug of lint twisted into an oval
shape like a pine cone', fr. στρόβιλος, 'pine
cone*. See strobile.

## strubilaceous
strubilaceous, adj., resembling a cone; producing
strobiles, — A hybrid word formed fr. Gk.
στροβίλη, 'pine cone' (see prec. word), and
-aceous, a suff. of Latin origin.

## strobilation
strobilation, п., reproduction by division (as in
tapeworms, etc.) — A hybrid coined fr. strobila
and -ation, a suff. of Latin origin.

## strobile
strobile, п., pine cone. — Late L. strobilus, fr. Gk.
στρόβιλος, 'anything twisted; whirlwind; pine
cone', fr. στρόβος, 'a twisting or whirling
round', which stands in gradational
relationship to στρεβλός, 'twisted', στραβός,
'squinting', στρέφειν, 'to turn'. See strophe.

## stroboscope
stroboscope, п., an instrument for studying
periodic motion. — Compounded of Gk. στρό-
βος, 'a twisting or whirling round', and -σκό-
mov, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See
prec. word and -scope.

## strode
strode, past tense of stride. — ME. strod, fr. OE.
strad, past tense of stridan. See stride.

## stroke
stroke, tr. v. — ME. straken, stroken, fr. OE.
stracian, 'to stroke', in gradational relationship
to OE. strican, 'to move, stroke, rub'. See strike.
Derivatives: strok-er, п., strok-ing, adj., strok-
ing-ly, adv.

## stroke
stroke, n. — ME. strak, strake, strok, stroke,
rel. to MLG. strek, MHG., G. streich, Goth.
striks, 'stroke', and to OE. strdcian. See stroke,
v.

## stroll
stroll, intr. v., ]) to walk idly; 2) to rove. — Fr.
earlier G. strollen, 'to stroll about', which is rel.
to G. strolchen, Swiss. G strolen, 'to stroll
about', Strolch, 'a tramp, vagabond'.
Derivatives: stroll, п., stroll-erf n.

## stroma
stroma, п., the supporting framework of an organ
(anat.) — L. stroma, 'bedcovering, coverlet', fr.
Gk. στρώμα, which is cogn. with OI. stari-man-9
'spreading out, extension', L. stramen, 'straw',
lit. 'that which is spread out'; see stratum and
cp. stramineous.
Derivative: stromat-ic, adj.

## stromeyerite
stromeyerite, п., a silver copper sulfide {mineral.)
— Named after the German chemist Friedrich
Stromeyer (1776-1835). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## strong
strong, adj. and adv. — ME., fr. OE. strong,
'strong, rigorous, severe', rel. to ON. strangr,
Dan. streng, Swed. strung, of s.m., Du streng,
'strict, rigorous', OHG. Strang, strangi, 'strong,
bold, hard', MHG. strenge, G. streng, 'strict,
rigorous', and cogn. with L. stringere, 'to
draw tight'. See stringent. Cp. also string.
Derivative: strong-ly, adv.

## strongyle
strongyle, п., any of an order of roundworms
{zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. στρογγυλός, 'twisted,
round', which stands in gradational relationship
to στραγγός, 'twisted, crooked; flowing drop
by drop', στράγξ, gen. στραγγός, *a drop', lit.
'that which is squeezed', στραγγαλίζειν,
στραγγαλοϋν, 'to twist, strange', and is cogn. with L.
stringere, 'to draw tight*. See stringent and
words there referred to and cp. esp. estrangelo.

## strongylosis
strongylosis, п., a disease due to roundworms in
the intestines (med.) — Medical L., formed fr.
strongyle with suff. -osis.

## strontia
strontia, п., strontium monoxide (chem.) —
ModL. See strontium.

## strontian
strontian, п., 1) strontianite; 2) strontia; 3)
strontium. See strontium and -ian.

## strontianite
strontianite, п., native strontium carbonate SrCOs
(mineral.) — See next word and subst. suff. -ite.

## strontium
strontium, п., name of a light metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., coined by the English
chemist Sir Humphry Davy (1778-1829) fr.
Strontian in Argyllshire, Scotland, where it was
first found in 1787 (by Cruikshank).
Derivatives: stront-ic, stront-it-ic, adjs.

## strop
strop, n. — ME. strop, fr. OE. stropp. See strap.
Derivative: strop, tr. v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:750 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 723 | STUMP -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:750 COLUMN:1 -->
strophanti™, п., a bitter, poisonous crystalline
glucoside. — Formed from next word with stiff.
-in.

## Strophantus
Strophantus, п., a genus of tropical plants (hot.)
— ModL-, coined by the Swiss botanist Augus-
tin Pyrame de Candolle (1778-1821), fr. Gk.
στροφή, 'a turning', and άνθος, 'flower'. See
next word and anther.

## strophe
strophe, n. — Gk. στροφή, lit. 'a turning,
twisting', rel. to στροφός, 'cord', στροφεύς, 'one of
the vertebrae', στροφάλιγζ, 'whirl, whirlpool',
στρέφειν, 'to turn, twist', στρέμμα, 'that which
is twisted, a sprain', fr. I.-E. base *strebh-, 'to
turn, twist'. Cp. the related base *streb~, whence
Gk. στρεβλός, 'twisted", στροφός, 'squinting'.
Cp. stremma, strepto-, and the second element
in anastrophe, antistrophe, apostrophe,
catastrophe, epistrophe, monostrophe, boustrophe-
don, Ommastrephes. Cp. also strabismus,
strobile. Cp. also strap.
Derivatives: stroph-ic, stropk-ic-a/, adjs., stroph-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## Stroud
Stroud, п., a coarse woolen blanket. — Named
after Stroud, in Gloucestershire.

## strove
strove, past tense of strive. — Formed fr. strive
on analogy of drove, past tense of drive.

## strow
strow, tr. v. — ME. strowen, fr. OE. streawian;
an archaic var. of strew.

## struck
struck, past tense and pp. of strike. — Formed fr.
strike, prob. on analogy of stuck.

## structure
structure, n. — ME., fr. L. structura, 'a fitting
together, adjustment, construction', fr. structus,
pp. of struere, 'to pile up, join together, build,
fabricate, make' (whence struts, 'heap'), which
is cogn. with Goth, straujan, OE. streowian,
streawian, strewian, 'to strew'. See strew and
-lire and cp. construct, construction, construe,
destroy, destruction, industry, instruct,
instruction, instrument, obstruct, obstruction,
obstruent.
Derivatives: structure, tr. v., structur-al, adj.,
structur-al-ly, adv., structur-ed, adj.,
structureless, adj., structure-less-ness, п., structure-ly,
adv., structurist (q.v.)

## structurist
structurist, п., a builder. — A hybrid formed fr.
L. structura (see prec. word) with -ist, a suff. of
Greek origin.

## strudel
strudel, п., a kind of pastry. — G. Strudel, lit.
'eddy, whirlpool', in gradational relationship to
OHG. stredan, 'to bubble, boil, whirl, eddy',
and cogn. with Gk. £ά*ος (for *srodhos), 'roar
of waves', fr. I.-E. *sr-et-, enlargement of base
*ser-, 'to flow'. See stream and cp. words there
referred to.

## struggle
struggle, intr. v. — ME. struglen, of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: struggle, п., struggl-er, п.,
struggling, adj., struggl-ing-ly, adv.

## Struldbrug
Struldbrug, п., people who never die, but after
the age of eighty become senile and entirely
useless. — Coined by Jonathan Swift (1667-
1745) in his Gulliver's Travels (1726).
Derivatives: Struldbrug-ian, adj., Struldbrug-
tsm, n.

## strum
strum, intr. and tr. v., to thrum. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. thrum and drum.
Derivative: strum, n.

## struma
struma, п., I) scrofula; 2) goiter; small swelling
of an organ (bot.)'— L. struma, 'a scrofulous
tumor', of uncertain etymology.

## strumatlc
strumatlc, adj., scrofulous. — Formed from prec.
word with 2nd suff. -atic.

## Strumella
Strumella, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL.,
dimin. formed fr. L. struma, 'a swelling'. See
struma and -elln.

## strumose
strumose, adj., strumous. — L. strumdsus, fr.
struma, 'a swelling, tumor'. See struma and adj.
suff. -ose.

## strumous
strumous, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
struma. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. struma.
See struma and cp. prec. word.

## strumpet
strumpet, п., a prostitute. — ME. strompet,
strumpet, of uncertain origin.

## strung
strung, past tense and pp. of the verb string. —
See string.

## strut
strut, intr. v., to walk pompously. — ME. strou-
ten, 'to swell out, strut', fr. OE. strutian, 'to
stand stiffly, be rigid', rel. to Dan. strutte,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:750 COLUMN:2 -->
strude, Swed. strutta, MHG., G. strotzen, 'to be
puffed up, be swelled', LG. strutt, 'rigid', MHG.
striuzen, 'to contend, resist'. ME. strout, MHG.
strU3, G. Straufl, 'fight'. All these words are
traceable to I.-E. base *ster-, 'strong, firm, stiff,
rigid', whence also OE. starian, 'to look fixedly
at'. See stare and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: strut, п., the act of strutting,
strutt-er, п., strutt-ing, n. and adj., strutt-ing-ly,
adv.

## strut
strut, п., a prop, stay. — Rel. to LG. strutt,
'rigid', and, accordingly, to prec. word.

## Struthio
Struthio, п., a genus of birds, the ostrich (zool.)
— L. struthio, 'ostrich', fr. Gk. στρουθίων,
'ostrich', fr. στρουθός, Att. στροΰ&ος, 'bird;
ostrich; sparrow', which prob. stands for "στρου-
σ*ός and derives fr. I.-E. "trzdos, 'thrush'. See
thrush, the bird, and cp. Turdus. Cp. also the
second element in ostrich.

## struvite
struvite, п., a hydrous ammonium magnesium
phosphate (mineral.) — Named after the
German-Russian astronomer Friedrich Georg Wil-
helm von Struve (1793-1864). For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## strychnia
strychnia, п., strychnine (archaic). — See
strychnine and 1st -ia.

## strychnic
strychnic, adj., pertaining to strychnine. — See
next word and adj. suff. -ic.

## strychnine
strychnine, strychnin, n. (chem.) — F., formed fr.
L. strychnos, 'nightshade', fr. Gk. στρύχνος, of
s.m., which is of uncertain origin; so called
because it was first found in the plant Strychnos
Ignatii (in 1818).
Derivatives: strychnine, tr. v., strychnin-ism, п.,
strychnin-ize, tr. v., strychnin-iz-ation, n.

## stub
stub, п., a stump. — ME. stubbe, stubb, fr. OE.
stubb, stybb, rel. to ON. stubbi, 'stub', stufr,
'stump', and cogn. with Gk. στύπος, 'stump,
stick', Lett, stupe, stups, 'a used broom', fr.
I.-E. base *(s)tup-, 'to strike, cut, hew', whence
also Gk. τύπτειν, 'to beat, strike, τύπος, 'blow'.
See type and cp, stub. Cp. also stubborn.
Derivatives: stub, tr. v., stubb-ed, adj., stubb-er,
п., stubb-ly, adv., stubb-y, adj., stubb-i-ness, n.

## stubble
stubble, n. — ME. stuble, stubbel, fr. OF. estuble
(F. eteule), fr. Late L. stupula, assimilated fr.
L. stipula, 'stalk, stem, straw, stubble', whence
also MDu. stoppele (Du. stoppel), OHG. stup-

## fala (MHG. stupfel
fala (MHG. stupfel, G. Stoppel). It. stoppia,
Proven?, estobla also derive fr. Late L. stupula.
See stipule and cp. etiolate.
Derivatives: stubble, tr. v., stubbl-ed, stubbl-y,
adjs.

## stubborn
stubborn, adj. — ME. stibourne, stoburn, fr. OE.
stubb, stybb; see stub. For sense development cp.
G. storrig, 'stubborn', fr. Storren, 'stump of a
tree, stub'.
Derivatives: stubborn-ly, adv., stubborn-ness, n.

## stucco
stucco, п., a kind of fine plaster used as a coating
for walls. — It., fr. OHG. stucchi, 'crust,
coating, piece' (whence MHG. smcke, G. Stuck,
'piece'); rel. to OS. stukki, ON. stykki, OE.
stycce, 'piece', and to E. stock (q.v.)
Derivatives: stucco, tr. v., stucco-er, n.

## stuck
stuck, past tense and pp. of stick. — Formed
prob. on the analogy of stung, past tense and
pp. of sting. See stick, v.

## stud
stud, п., a collection of horses. — ME. stod,·
stode, fr. OE. stod, 'stud, herd of horses', rel. to
ON. stod, MLG. stod, OHG., MHG. stuot,
'herd of horses', G. Stute, 'mare', and cogn.
with OSlav. stado, 'herd', Lith. stodas, 'a drove
of horses'. These words derive fr. I.-E. "stadho-,
an enlargement of base *sta-, 'to stand', and
orig. meant 'a standing place for horses'. See
state and cp. steed.

## stud
stud, п., peg, nail. — ME. stode, stude, fr. OE.
studu, 'post, buttress', rel. to ON. stod, 'staff,
stick, prop, stay', Swed. stod, 'prop, post', OE.
stow, 'place', MLG., Du. stutten, 'to prop, prop
up, support', OHG. stuzzen (in untarstuzzeri),
MHG. stutzen (in understiitzen), G. stutzen, 'to
prop, stay', and cogn. with Lett, stute, 'a rod, a
broom worn to the stump', Gk. στϋλος, 'pillar'.
All these words are derivatives of I.-E. base
*st(h)du-, *st(h)u-, 'stiff, upright; post, pillar'.
See stow and cp. next word.
Derivatives: stud, tr. v., to supply with studs,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:750 COLUMN:3 -->
studd-er, п., studd-ing, n.

## studdle
studdle, п., a prop. — ME. stodul, 'sleyofaloom',
fr. OE. stadia, 'a loom', rel. to ON. studill,
'stud, prop, stay', OHG. stuodal, MHG. stuodel,
'post', and to OE. studu, 'post, buttress". See
prec. word and instrumental suff. -le.

## student
student, n. — L. studens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
studere, 'to apply oneself to'. See study and -ent.

## studerite
studerite, п., a variety of tetrahedrite (mineral.)
— Named after the Swiss geologist B. Studer
(1794-1887). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## studio
studio, п., artists's workroom. — It., lit. 'study',
fr. L. studium. See study, n.

## studious
studious, adj., fond of, or given to, study. — ME.,
fr. L. studiosus, 'devoted to study, assiduous,
zealous', fr. studium. See study, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: studious-ly, adv., studious-ness, n.

## study
study, n. — ME. studie, fr. OF. estudie (F. etude),
fr. L. iWt/f'Hm,-'application, eagerness, zeal,
assiduity, study', which is rel. to studere, 'to apply
oneself to, to study'. Studere prob. meant orig.
'to strike at something', whence 'to aim at
something', and is rel. to tundere, 'to beat,
strike". See stint and words there referred to and
cp. etude. Cp. also stew, 'fishpond'.

## study
study, tr. and intr. v. — ME. studien, fr. OF. es-
tudier (F. itudier), fr. estudie. See study, n.
Derivatives: studi-ed, adj., studi-ed-ly, adv.

## stuff
stuff, n. — ME. stuffe, stoffe, fr. OF. estoffe (F.
etoffe), 'stuff, material'. The word and its
equivalents in the other Romance languages prob.
meant orig. 'silk', i.e. 'stuff that contracts', and
ult. derive ft. Gk. στόφειν, 'to contract, draw
together', fr. I.-E. base *stu-bh-, an enlargement
of base *jr(A)a«-, *st(h)u-, 'to condense; stiff,
upright'; seesteer,'to direct'.TheGreekoriginof OF.
estoffe and its equivalents is substantiated by the
fact that silk culture (originating in China) was
introduced into Byzantium by Justinian as early
as in 552; see Kluge-Mitzka, EWDS., p. 752.
The derivation of OF. estoffe, etc., fr. L. stuppa,
'tow', occurring in most etymological
dictionaries, must be rejected.
Derivatives: stuff, adj., stuff-ing, п., stuff-y, adj.,
stuff-i-ly, adv., stuff-i-ness, n.

## stuff
stuff, tr. and intr. v. — Late ME., fr. OF. estoffer
(F. etoffer), 'to use material in making
(something), to stuff", which is rel. to, and prob. derives
from estoffe, 'stuff material'. See stuff, n.
Derivative: stuff-ing, n.

## stuggy
stuggy, adj., short; stodgy (dial. E.) — Prob. a
blend of stocky and stodgy.

## Stuka
Stuka, п., a German dive bomber in World War
II. — G. Stnrztaimpfflugzeug, compounded of
Sturz, 'fall', Kampf, 'battle', and Flugzeug,
'aircraft'.

## stuU
stuU, п., a large piece (obsol. or dial.) — Rel. to
OHG. stollo, MHG. stolle, 'prop, support', G.
Stollen (masc), Stolle (fem.), 'prop, support;
loaf-shaped cake', ft. I.-E. base *st(h)el-, 'to
cause to stand, to place'. See stuii and cp. words
there referred to.

## stultification
stultification, n. — See staltify and -ation.

## stultify
stultify, tr. v., to make foolish. — Late L. stulti-
ficdre, formed fr. L. stultus, 'foolish', and -ficare,
fr. facere, 'to make, do'. The first element is rel.
to L. stolidus, 'slow, dull, obtuse'; see stolid.
For the second element see -fy.

## stum
stum, п., unfermented grape juice. — Du. stom,
fr. stom, 'dumb, silent', which is rel. to G.
stumm, of s.m.; see next word. For sense
development cp. F. vin muet, 'stum', lit. 'dumb
wine'.

## stumble
stumble, intr. and tr. v. — ME. stomblen, stomlen,
stomelen, stumblen, rel. to ON. stumra, dial. Dan.
stumle, dial. Swed. stomla, MDu. stommelen,
'to stumble', to OS., OFris., OHG., MHG.
stum, G. stumm, Du. stom, 'dumb, silent', and to
OE. stamer, 'stammering', stamerian, 'to
stammer'. See stammer and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: stumble, п., stumbl-er, п.,
stumbling, adj., stumbl-ingly, adv., stumbl-y, adj.

## stumbling block
stumbling block, n. — First used-by Tyndale.

## stumer
stumer, п., a forged check (slang). — Of
unknown origin.

## stump
stump, п., the lower end of a tree. — ME. stompe,

## stumpe
stumpe, rel. to ON. stumpr, Dan., Swed. stump,
MLG. stump, Flemish stump, stomp, Du. stomp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:751 COLUMN:1 -->
OHG., MHO., dial. G. stump/, G. Stump,
'stump', Du. stomp, 'blunt, dull', OHG., MHG.
s/iiiwp/.'mutilated', G. j/Hmp/'blunt, dulI'.OHG.
stumbal, MHG. stumbel, 'mutilated', OHG.
stumbal, MHG. stumbel, stummel, G. Stummel,
'a piece cut off', OHG. stumbildn, MHG.
stumbeln, verstumbein, G. verstummeln, 'to

Derivatives: stump, tr. and intr. v., and adj.,
stump-er, п., stump-ish, adj., stump-y, adj.

## stump
stump, п., roll, or cylinder, of paper. — Flemish
stump, stomp (possibly through the medium of
F. estompe); see F. J. Bense, Dictionary of the
Low-Dutch Element in the English Vocabulary,
p. 484. See stump, 'the lower end of the tree'.
Derivative: stump, tr. v.

## stun
stun, tr. v. — ME. stonen, stunen, 'to stun,
astonish', fr. OF. estoner, 'to stun, astonish; to
resound' (whence F. etonner, 'to stun, astonish,
amaze'), fr. VL. *extondre, formed with change
of sun", fr. L. attonare, 'to stun, astonish', fr.
ad- and tonare, 'to thunder'. See 1st ex- and
thunder and cp. astonish.
Derivatives: stun, п., stunn-er, п., stunn-ing, adj.,
stunn-ing-ly, adv.

## Stundism
Stundism, п., the doctrine of the Stundists. —
Russ. shtundism, a hybrid coined fr. shtunda
(see next word) and -ism, a suff. of Greek origin.

## Stundist
Stundist, п., member of a Russian Evangelical
sect. — Russ. shtundist, a hybrid coined fr.
shtunda, 'Stundism', fr. G. Stunde, 'hour, lesson',
and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin; so called from
their Bible lessons. For the etymology of G.
Stunde see stound.

## stung
stung, past tense and pp. of sting. — ME. stungen,
fr. OE. gestungen, pp. of stingan. See sting,
v.

## stunk
stunk, past tense and pp. of stink. — ME. stunken,
fr. OE. gestuncen, pp. of stincan. See stink.

## stunt
stunt, adj., stunted (chiefly dial.) — ME., fr. OE.
stunt, 'dull, foolish', in gradational relationship
to stint (q.v.); influenced in meaning by the
related ON. stuttr (assimilated from orig.
*stuntr), 'short, stunted'.
Derivatives: stunt, tr. v., to check the normal
growth of, stunt-ed, adj., stunt-ed-ly, adv.,
stunt-ed-ness, п., stunt-y, adj., 'short*.

## stunt
stunt, п., a showy performance (slang). — Of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: stunt, intr. v., stunt-y, adj., showy.

## stupa
stupa, п., a domelike mound or tower. — 01.
stupah, 'tuft of hair; top of the head; tope'. See
next word and cp. tope, 'stupa'.

## stupe
stupe, rl., compress. — L. stupa, 'tow', fr. Gk.
στοππη, which is cogn. with OI. stupah, 'tuft of
hair; top of the head', stupah, 'tuft of hair',
stuM, of s.m. Cp. prec. word. Cp. also Stipa.
Cp. also stop.
Derivative: stupe, tr. v.

## stupefacient
stupefacient, adj., stupefying. — L. stupefaciens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of stupe/acere. See stupefy
and -ent.

## stupefaction
stupefaction, п., the act of stupefying. — See
stupefy and -faction.

## stupefactive
stupefactive, adj., stupefying. — Formed with
suff. -ive fr. L. stupefactus, pp. of stupefacere.
See stupefy.

## stupefy
stupefy, tr. v., 1) to stun; 2) to astonish. — F.
stupefier, fr. L. stupefacere, 'to stupefy, benumb',
which is compounded of stupere, 'to be
stunned, be stupefied', and facere, 'to make, do'.
See stupid and -fy.
Derivatives: stupefi-ed, adj., stupefi-ed-ness, п.,
stupefi-er, n.

## stupendous
stupendous, adj., amazing. — L. stupendus,
'amazing', gerundive of stupere, 'to be stunned, be
stupefied'; see stupid. For E. -ous, as equivalent
to L. -us, see -ous.

## stupeous
stupeous, adj., having long hairs or scales. — L.
stupeus, 'of tow', fr. stupa, 'tow'. See stupe and
cp. stupose. For the ending cp. piec. word.

## stupid
stupid, adj. — MF. (= F.) stupide, fr. L. stupidus,
'amazing, dull, stupid', fr. stupere, 'to be
stunned, be stupefied', which is rel. to stuprum,
'dishonor, disgrace'; fr. I.-E. base *(s)tup-, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:751 COLUMN:2 -->
strike, cut, hew', whence also Gk. τύτττειν, 'to
beat, strike', τύπος, 'blow'. See type and cp.
stupendous, stupefy, stupor, stuprum, styptic. Cp.
also stub.
Derivatives: stupid, n. (colloq.), stupid-ly, adv.,
stupid-ness, n.

## stupidity
stupidity, n. — MF. (= F.) stupidite, fr. L. stupi-
ditatem, ace. of stupiditas, 'dullness, stupidity',
fr. stupidus. See prec. word and -ity.

## stupor
stupor, п., torpor, lethargy. — ME., fr. L.,
'numbness, dullness', fr. stupere. See stupid and -or.
Derivative: stupor-ous, adj.

## stupose
stupose, adj., having towlike filaments. — ML.
stuposus, fr. L. stupa, 'tow'. See stupe and adj.
suff. -ose and cp. stupeous.

## stuprum
stuprum, п., illicit sexual intercourse (law). — L.,
'dishonor, disgrace'. The orig. meaning was
'stupefaction', stuprum being rel. to L. stupere,
'to be stunned, be stupefied'. See stupid and
cp. the second element in masturbate.

## sturdy
sturdy, adj., firm, resolute. — ME. stourdi,
'stubborn, sturdy', fr. OF. estourdi (F. etourdi),
'astounded, thoughtless', pp. of estourdir (F.
etourdir), 'to stun, daze, make thoughtless', fr.
VL. *exturdire, 'to be stunned like a thrush
drunk with grapes', fr. 1st ex- and L. turdus,
'thrush'. Cp. It. stordire, earlier Sp. estordir
(whence, with change of pref., Sp. atordir), 'to
stun, daze, stupefy', which also derive fr. VL.
*extordlre. See Turdus and words there referred
to. For sense development cp. It. tordo, 'thrush;
silly', Gk. κωφότερος κίχλης, 'more foolish
than a thrush'.
Derivatives: sturdi-ly, adv., sturdi-ness, n.

## sturdy
sturdy, п., gid (a disease of sheep). — MF. es-
tourdie, 'giddiness', fr. OF., prop. fem. pp. of
estourdir, 'to stun', used as a noun. See sturdy,
adj.

## sturgeon
sturgeon, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) esturgeon, fr.
Frankish 'sturjo, which is rel. to OS., OHG.
sturio, MHG. store, sture, G. Stor, MDu. store,
store, Du. steur, OE. styria, ON. styrja. These
Teut. words are cognate with OPruss. esketres,
Lith. ersketras, Russ. osetr, 'sturgeon'. Cp. ML.
sturio. It. storione, OProvenc. esturjon, Sp. es-
turion, 'sturgeon', which also are Teut. loan
words. Cp. also sterlet.

## sturine
sturine, sturin, п., a protamine from the sperm of
sturgeons (biochem.) — Coined with chem.
suff. -ine, -in, from the stem of ML. sturio,
'sturgeon'. See prec. word.

## Sturm imd Drang
Sturm imd Drang, name of the period of German
literary romanticism in the late 18th cent. —
G., lit. 'storm and stress', so called from the
title of a romantic drama written by the German
poet Friedrich Maximilian von Klinger (1752-
1831), who gave it this name in 1776 at the
suggestion of Christoph Kaufmann. For the
etymology of the words Sturm, und and Drang see
storm, and, throng.

## stumoid
stumoid, adj., like the starlings. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. sturnus, 'starling', and Gk. -οειδής,
'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See Sturnus
and -oid,

## Sturnus
Sturnus, п., a genus of birds, the starling (orni-
thol.) — L. sturnus, 'starling', cogn.· with Gk.
ίστραλος (Hesychius), OE. stssr, ON. stari,
'starling', OPruss. starnite, 'gull'. See starling
and cp. tern.

## stuss
stuss, п., a gambling game. — Colloquial G.
Stufi, 'nonsense', fr. Yiddish shtuss, fr. Mish-
naic Heb. sh tuth, 'folly, nonsense', which is rel.
to shotih, 'fool'. See sot.

## shit
shit, intr. and tr. v., to stutter (obsol.) — See
next word.

## stutter
stutter, intr. and tr. v. — Freq. of stut, fr. Late
ME. stutten, fr. Teut. base *stut-, which stands
in gradational relationship to *staut-, whence
OS. stdtan, OHG. Stefan, Goth, stautan, 'to
push, thrust'. See stint and cp. stoat, stoss.
Derivatives: stutter, п., stutter-er, п., stutter-ing,
n. and adj. stutter-ing-ly, adv.

## sty
sty, intr. v., to go up, ascend (obsol.) — ME. styen,
fr. OE. stigan, rel. to ΟΝ., OFris. stiga, MDu.
stlghen, OS., OHG. stigan, MHG. stigen, G.
steigen, Goth, steigan, OE. stlg, ON. stigr,
OHG. stlg, MHG. site, G. Steig, 'path', fr.
Teut. base *stig-, which corresponds to I.-E.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:751 COLUMN:3 -->
'stfgh-, 'to stride, step, walk, climb', whence OI.
stighnoti, 'mounts, rises, steps', Gk. στείχειν,
'to go; to march in order', στίχος, 'row, line,
rank; verse', στοίχος, 'row, line, rank'. Alb.
stek, 'passage, way', OSlav. stignqti, 'to
overtake', stidza, 'path', stigna, 'place*, Lith. staiga,
'suddenly', staig-us, 'hasty', staigytis, 'to hasten,
hurry" (intr.), Lett, steigtis, of s.m., si/gO,'path',
Olr. tlagaim, Ί walk', techt, 'arrival', W. taith,
'going, walk, way'. Cp. next word. Cp. also
stair, stile, 'steps', stirrup. Cp. also acrostic and
words there referred to.

## sty
sty, п., enclosure for swine. — ME. slie, fr. OE.
sti, var. stlg, rel. to ON. -sti, 'stall', stta, 'sty,
kennel', OHG. stiga, MHG. stige, 'pen for
small cattle', and perh. also to OE. stigan, 'to
ascend'. See prec. word and cp. the first element
in steward.
Derivative: sty, tr. v., to enclose in a sty.

## sty
sty, stye, п., swelling on the eyelid. — Back
formation from earlier styany (mistaken for the
contraction of sty on eye), fr. OE. stigend, 'sty
in the eye', from the stem of stigan, 'to ascend,
rise'. See sty, 'to ascend'.

## Stygian
Stygian, adj., pertaining to the Styx or the nether
world. — L. Stygius, fr. Gk. Στύγιος, 'Stygian',
fr. Στύζ, gen. Στυγός, 'Styx (a river of the
nether world)'. See Styx and -ian.

## styl-
styl-, form of stylo- before a vowel.

## style
style, п., 1) gnomon; 2) part of the pistil bearing
the stigma (bot.) — Gk. στϋλος, 'pillar, column',
rel. to στυειν, 'to make stiff, erect; to place,
set', fr. I.-E. base *st(h)au-, *st(h)u-, 'stiff,
upright ; post, pillar'. See steer, 'to direct', and cp.
words there referred to.

## style
style, п., pointed instrument for writing,
whence: way of writing or speaking, etc. —
ME. stile, fr. OF. style, stile (F. style), fr. L.
stilus, 'pointed instrument, spike, pale', which
stands for *stoi-lo, *sti-lo-, 'something sharp,
pointed', and is rel. to L. sti-mulus, 'point, goad',
Insti-gare, 'to goad, prick'. See stimulus and cp.
2nd stile and stiletto. Cp. also the second
element in cyclostyle. The spelling style (with у for
orig. /) is due to a confusion of this word with
Gk. στϋλος, 'pillar' (see style, 'gnomon').
Derivatives: style, tr. and intr. v., styl-er, п.,
styl-ing, п., styl-ish, adj., styl-ish-ly, adv., styl-
ish-ness, п., stylist, n. (q.v.), stylize (q.v.)

## stylet
stylet, п., a small pointed instrument. — F.
stylet, fr. MF. stilet, fr. It. stiletto, dimin. of
stilo, 'a pointed instrument'. See stiletto.

## Stylidium
Stylidium, п., a genus of plants. — ModL.,
formed fr. Gk. στΰλος, 'pillar', and dimin.
suff. -idium. See style, 'pillar'.

## styliform
styliform, adj., having the form of a style. —
Formed fr. style, 'pointed instrument', and L.
forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## stylist
stylist, n. — Formed with suff. -ist fr. L. stilus, *a
pointed instrument'. See style, 'pointed
instrument'.
Derivatives: stylist-ic, adj., stylist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## stylite
stylite, п., an ascetic living on the top of a pillar.
— Eccles. Gk. στϋλϊτης, formed fr. στϋλος,
'pillar', with suff. -ιτης. See style, 'gnomon',
and subst. suff. -ite.

## stylize
stylize, tr. v. — Formed on analogy of G. stili-
sieren, fr. L. stilus, 'pointed instrument', and
suff. -ize. See style, 'pointed instrument'.

## stylo
stylo, n. — Abbreviation of stylograph,

## stylo-
stylo-, before a vowel styl-, combining form mean-
ing'pillar', as in stylobate.—Gk. στΰλο-, στυλ-,
fr. στϋλος, 'pillar'. See style, 'gnomon'.

## stylo-
stylo-, before a vowel styl-, combining form
meaning 'sharp, pointed', as in stylograph. — Fr. L.
stylus, incorrect spelling for stilus, 'a pointed
instrument'. See style, 'pointed instrument'.

## stylobate
stylobate, п., a base for two or more columns. —
Late L. stylobatis, fr. Gk. στυλοβάτης, 'base
of a column', which is compounded of στΰλος,
'pillar, column', and -βάτης, from the stem of
βαίνειν, 'to go'. See style, 'gnomon', and base,
n.

## Stylochus
Stylochus, п., a genus of worms (zoo!.) — ModL.,
lit. 'bearing a style', fr. 1st stylo- and Gk. δχός
'holding', from the stem of 6χεΐν, 'to bear,
carry', which stands in gradational relationship
to ίχειν, 'to have, hold'. See hectic and cp.

epoch.

## stylograph
stylograph, п., a kind of fountain pen. —
Compounded of 1st stylo- and Gk. -γράφος, fr.
γράφειν, *to write'· See -graph.
Derivatives: stylograph-ic, stylograph-ic-al, adjs.,
styhgraph-ic-al-ly, adv., stylograph-y, n.

## styloid
styloid, adj., styliform; pertaining to certain
pointed processes of bones (anat.) — Medical L.
styloideus, fr. Gk. στϋλοειδής, 'resembling a
pillar', coined by Galen fr. στΰλος, *pillar', and
-οειδής, 'like*, fr. είδος, 'form, shape'; see
style, 'gnomon', and -oid and cp. Joseph HyrtI,
Onomatologia Anatomicat p. 499.

## Stylops
Stylops, п., a genus of insects (zool.) — ModL., a
hybrid coined fr. L. stilus, 'something pointed*,
and Gk. ώψ, gen. ώπος, 'eye*, from l.-E. base
*5qw-, 'eye'. See -ops.

## Stylosanthes
Stylosanthes, п., a genus of plants of the pea
family (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
στϋλος, 'pillar*, and όίνθ-ος, 'flower'. See styfe,
'gnomon', and anther,

## stylus
stylus, п., an instrument for writing. — L. stilus,
inexactly spelled stylus. See style, 'pointed
instrument*.

## stymie
stymie, stimy, п., position of a player's ball
between the opponent's ball and the hole {golf) —
The orig. meaning was 'inability to see clearly'.
Cp. earlier E. styme, 'flicker, glimmer* (in not to
see a styme), which is of uncertain origin;
applied figuratively to a random shot.

## Styphelia
Styphelia, п., a genus of plants of the epacris
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. στυφελός,
'rough'; so called in allusion to the rough
hairs of the corolla tube. Gk. στυφελός derives
fr. στυφειν, 'to contract, be astringent',
whence also στύψης, 'contraction'. See next
word and 1st -ia.

## styptic
styptic, adj., checking bleeding, astringent. — L.
stypticus, fr. Gk. στυπτικός, from the stem of
στυφειν, 'to contract, be astringent', fr. I.-E.
base *stu-bh-, 'to strike, cut, hew'. Cp. the
related base *(s)tup-, whence Gk. τύτττειν, 'to
strike'. See type and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: styptic, п., styptic-alt adj., styptic-
itу, П.

## Styracaceae
Styracaceae, n. pi., a family of plants, the storax
family. — ModL., formed fr. Styrax with suff.
-aceae.

## styracaceous
styracaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Styrax
Styrax, п., a genus of trees yielding a fragrant
resin (bot.) — L. styrax, storax, fr. Gk. στύραξ,
'styrax', fr. Heb. tz6ri% 'resin of the lentisk and
of the terebinth'. The Greek form of the word is
due to the influence of Gk. στύραξ, 'shaft of a
lance'. Cp. storax.

## styrene
styrene, п., a colorless hydrocarbon, C9H8 (ckem.)
— Formed with suff. -ene from Styrax; so
called because found in liquid storax.

## Styx
Styx, п., a river of the nether world. — L., fr. Gk.
Στύξ, gen. Στυγός, lit. 'the horrible', rel. to
στύξ, 'chill, frost; hatred, abhorrence', στυγεΐν,
'to hate, abhor' (orig. 'to shudder with cold'),
στυγνός, 'hated, abhorred', and cogn. with
Russ. istygnut% stugnut\ 'to freeze'* Cp.—with
-(/-formative element—OSlav. studu, 'cold'.

## suable
suable, adj. — Formed from the verb sue with
suff. -able.
Derivatives: suabil-ity, п., suabl-y, adv.

## Suaeda
Suaeda, п., a genus of plants, the sea blite (bot.)
-— Arab, suwayd, 'blackish', standing for usay-
wid, dimin. of aswad, 'black', fr. sdwida, 'was
black'. Cp. Sudan,

## suasion
suasion, п., persuasion. — ME. suasioun, fr. L.

## suasio
suasio, gen. -onis, fr. suasus, pp. of suadere, 'to
advise, recommend, persuade', which is rel. to

## suavis
suavis, 'sweet'. See suave and -ion and cp.

## dissunsion
dissunsion, persuasion,

## suasive
suasive, adj., persuasive. — Formed with suff.

## -ive fr. L. suasus
-ive fr. L. suasus, pp. of suadere. See prec. word.
Derivatives: suasive, п., suasive-ly, adv., sua·

## sive-ness
sive-ness, n.

## suave
suave, adj., smoothly polite, bland, gracious. —
MF. (= F.), fr. L. suavis, 'sweet, pleasant,

## agreeable'
agreeable', which stands for *swddwis, and is cogn.

## with OI. svaduh
with OI. svaduh, 'sweet*, Gk- ηδύς (Dor. αδύς),
'sweet, pleasant, agreeable', ηδονή, 'pleasure',

## OS. swoti
OS. swoti, OE. swete, 'sweet'. See sweet and cp.

Derivatives: suave-ly, adv., suave-ness, n.

## suavity
suavity, n. — ME. suavitee, fr. MF. (= F.) sua-
vite, fr. L. suavitatem, ace. of suavitas,
'sweetness', fr. suavis. See prec. word and -ity.

## sub
sub, n. (colloq.) — Short for subaltern, submarine,
subscription, substitute, etc.

## sub
sub, prep., under. — L. See sub-.

## sub-
sub-, pref. of Latin origin meaning 'under'. —
Sub- regularly becomes sue- before c, suf- before
/, sug- before g, and sup· before p. It often
becomes sum- before m and sur- before r. It is
simplified to su- before sp. Before c, ρ and t it
sometimes has the form sus- (for subs-, an
earlier form of sub-). — L. sub-, etc., fr. sub (for
*sup), 'under, below, beneath', rel. to Oscan
συπ, Umbr. su, 'under', and cogn. with ΟΙ. ύρα,
'near, under, up to, on', Gk. ύπό, 'under,
below', Goth, и/, 'under', Olr. fo, W. guo-,
Gaul, vo-, ve-, 'under', Goth. iupt ΟΝ., OE. upp,
'up, upward', Hitt. up-zi, 'rises' (said of the
sun). All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *upo-,
'from below', whence arose the meanings
'turning upward, upward; up, over, beyond*. See up
and cp. supine, sum, summary, summit, soutane
and the first element in surge and in Upanishad;
cp. also hypo-, Fr. I.-E. base *upo- developed
the comparative *uper-, *uperi-, 'over, above,
beyond', whence OI. upari. Over, above,
beyond', Gk-ύπέρ, L. super, 'over, above, beyond'.
For sense development cp. L. alius, which unites
the meanings 'high' and 'deep'. See over and cp.
super-, supra-, hyper-. Cp. also subter-, Cp. also
opal.

## subabdominal
subabdominal, adj., that which is beneath the
abdomen. — Formed fr. sub- and abdominal.

## subacid
subacid, adj., moderately acid. — L. subacidus,
'sourish'. See sub- and acid.
Derivatives: subacid-ity, n.( subacid-ly, adv.,
subactd-ness, n.

## subacute
subacute, adj., moderately acute. — Formed fr.
snb- and acute.

## subaerial
subaerial, adj., situated on the surface of the earth.
— Lit. 'under the air', used in the sense of
'under the sky'; formed fr. sub- and aerial.
Derivative: subaerial-ly, adv.

## subagency
subagency, n. — Formed fr. sub- and agency.

## subagent
subagent, n.f a person employed by an agent. —
Formed fr. sub- and agent.

## subah
subah, п., a province or division of the Mogul
Empire (India). — Hind, subah, fr. Pers. suba ,
'collection; collection of districts, province', fr.
Arab. subah, 'collection'.

## subahdar
subahdar, subadar, п., governor of a subah;
viceroy (India) — Hind., fr. Pers. subahdar, lit.
'holder of a subah', fr. subab, 'province', and
-dar, 'holder, possessor'. For the first element
see subah, for the second see aumildar and cp.
words there referred to.

## subaltern
subaltern, adj., subordinate; n. (chiefly British), a
subaltern officer. — F. subalterne, fr. Late L.
subalternus, fr. sub- and L. altemus, 'one after
the other', fr. alter, 'the other (of two)'. See
alternate.
Derivatives: subaltern-ate, adj. and п., subal-
tern-ation, П., subaltern-ity, n.

## subaquatic
subaquatic, adj., partly aquatic. — Formed fr.
sub- and aquatic.

## subaqueous
subaqueous, adj., situated, or to be used, under
water. — Formed fr. sub- and aqueous.

## subarctic
subarctic, adj., pertaining to the region
contiguous to the Arctic. — Formed fr. sub- and arctic.

## subaudition
subaudition, п., the understanding of something
not expressed in words. — Late L. subauditio,
gen. -onis, fr. subauditus, pp. of subaudire, 'to
understand a word omitted*, fr. sub- and L. au-
dire, *to hear'. See audition.

## subaural
subaural, adj., situated below the ear. — Formed
fr. sub- and aural, 'pertaining to the ear1.

## subaxiliary
subaxiliary, adj., I) situated beneath the armpit;
2) situated beneath the axil (bot.) — Formed
fr. sub- and axillary.

## subcaudal
subcaudal, adj., situated beneath the tail (zool.)
— Formed fr. sub- and caudal.

## subclavian
subclavian, adj., situated beneath the clavicle. —
Formed fr. sub- and L. cldvis, 'key'. See clavicle
and -ian.

## subconscious
subconscious, adj. — Formed fr. sub- and

Derivatives: subconscious, п., subconscious-ly,
adv., subconscious-ness, n.

## subcutaneous
subcutaneous, adj., situated, or applied, beneath
the skin. — Formed fr. sub- and cutaneous.
Derivative: su6cutaneous-ly, adv.

## subdeacon
subdeacon, n. — Formed fr. sub- and deacon, on
analogy of Late L. subdidconns.
Derivatives: subdeacon-ate, п., subdeacon-ess,
п., subdeacon-ry, n.

## subdititious
subdititious, adj., secretly substituted. — L. sub-
diticius, fr. subditus, pp. of subdere, 'to
substitute', lit. 'to place under', fr. sub- and dare, 'to
give'. See date, 'point of time'. For E. -ous, as
equivalent .to L. -us, see -ous.

## subdivide
subdivide, tr. and intr. v., to divide again. — Late
L. subdividere, fr. sub- and L. dividere, 'to
divide'. See divide,

## subdivisible
subdivisible, adj. — Formed fr. sub- and divisible,

## subdivision
subdivision, n. — Late L. subdivisio, gen. -onis, fr.
subdivisus, pp. of subdividere. See subdivide and
-ion.

## subdolous
subdolous, adj., sly, crafty. — L. subdolus, fr.
snb- and dolus, 'guile, deceipt, deception'. See
dole, 'guile', and cp. sedulous. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: subdolous-ly, adv., subdolous-ness,n.

## subdonunant
subdonunant, п., the fourth note of the scale
(mus.) — Formed fr. sub- and dominant,

## subduce
subduce, tr. v., to take away. — L. subducere, *to
draw away, withdraw, remove', lit. 'to lead or
draw from under', fr. sub- and duceref 'to lead'.
See duke and cp. subdue,

## snbduct
snbduct, tr. v., to subduce. — L. subductus, pp. of
subducere. See prec. word.

## subdue
subdue, tr. v., 1) to overcome; 2) to soften. —
ME. soduen, later subdewen, fr. OF. soduire (F.
siduire), *to seduce', fr. L. subducere, 'to draw
away, withdraw, remove' (but confused· in
sense with L. subdere, 'to subject, subdue'). See
subduce.
Derivatives: subdu-able, adj., subdu-ubl-y, adv.,
subdu-able-ness, п., subdu-al, п., subdu-ed, adj.,
subdu-ed-ly, adv., subdu-ed-ness, п., subdu-ing,
adj., subdu-ing-ly, adv.

## suber
suber, п., cork. — L. suber, *cork tree, cork',
prob. borrowed fr. Gk. σΰφαρ, 'wrinkled skin',
which is of uncertain origin.

## subereous
subereous, adj., pertaining to cork. — L. sube-
reus, 'of cork', fr. suber. See prec. word and
-eous.

## suberic
suberic, adj., pertaining to cork. — F. suberique,
formed fr. L. suber, 'cork', with suff. -ique. See
suber and adj. suff. -ic.

## suberia
suberia, suberine, п., а waxy substance contained
in cork (biockem.) — Formed with suff. -in»
-fare, fr. L. suber, 'cork'. See suber.

## su lie rose
su lie rose, adj., subereous. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ose fr. L. suber, 'cork*. See suber and cp.
snbereous.

## snbfuscous
snbfuscous, adj., dusky. — L. subfuscus, suffuscust
'dusky', fr. sub- suidfuscus, 'dusky'. See fuscous,

## subjacency
subjacency, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## subjacent
subjacent, adj., situated underneath. — L. sub-

## jacens
jacens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of subjacere, 'to
lie underneath', fr. sub- and jacere, 'to lie*. See
adjacent.
Derivative: subjacent-ly, adv.

## subject
subject, adj. — ME. suget, subget, fr. OF. suget,
subject (F. sujet), fr. L. subjectus, pp. of subicere,
less correctly subjicere, 'to subject, include,
comprise', lit. 'to throw under', fr. sub- and

jacere (pp. jactus), 'to throw'. See jet, 'to spirt
forth', and cp. words there referred to. For the
change of Latin a (in jactus) to ё (in sub-jectus)
see accent and cp. words there referred- to.
Derivative: subject, adv.

## subject
subject, п., 1) theme; 2) (gram.), the part of a
sentence about which something is said. — ME.
suget, subget, fr- OF. suget, subject, (F. sujet), fr.
L. subjectum,. 'grammatical subject*, neut. of
subjectus, pp. of subicere, used as a noun. Sub-

jectum is prop, a loan translation of G k. ύποκεί-

Derivative: subject-less, adj.

## subject
subject, п., person owing allegiance to a ruler. —
L. subjectus, pp. οι subicere. See prec. word.

## subject
subject, tr. v. — ME. subjecten, fr. MF. subjecter
(F. sujettir), fr. OF., fr. L. subjectdre, freq. of

Derivatives: subject-ed, adj., subject-ed-ly, adv.,
subject-ed-ness, n.

## subjection
subjection, n. — ME. subjeccioun, fr. MF.

ace. of subjectid, fr. subjecttts, pp. of subicere.
See subject, adj., and -ion.
Derivative: subjection-al, adj.

## subjective
subjective, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. subjectivus, 'of
the subject, subjective', fr. L- subjectum,
'subject'. See subject, 'theme*, and -ive.
Derivatives: subjective, п., subjective-ly, adv.,
subjective-ness, п., subjectiv-ism, п.,
subjectivity, n.

## subjoin
subjoin, tr. v. — MF. subjoin-, stem of subjoindre,
fr. L. subjungere, *to affix, append', fr. sub- and
jungere, 'to join*. See join and cp. subjunctive.

## subjiigable
subjiigable, adj., capable of being subjugated. —
Formed with suff. -able fr. L. subjugdre. See
next word.

## subjugate
subjugate, tr. v. — ME. subjugaten, lit. 'to bring
under a yoke', fr. L. subjugdtus, pp. of subjugdre,
'to subjugate', fr. sub- and jugum, 'yoke*. See
yoke and cp. jugate.
Derivatives: subjugat-ion, п., subjugat-or, n.

## subjunctive
subjunctive, adj. and n. — Late L. subjunciivus,
'connecting', fr. L. subjunctus, pp. οι subjungere;
see subjoin and -ive. Late L. subjunciivus is prop,
a loan translation of Gk. υποτακτικός,
'pertaining to subordination, subordinated', fr.
ύποτάσσειν, 'to place under, subordinate*.
Derivative: subjunctive-ly, adv.

## sublate
sublate, tr. v., to refuse, deny. — L. subldtus (used

lotus (used as pp. of ferre, 'to bear, carry'),
which stands for *tlatos, fr. *//-, zero degree
of I.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry', whence
L. tollere, 4o lift up, raise', tolerare, 'to bear,
support'. See tolerate and cp. collate and words
there referred to.

## snblimate
snblimate, tr. v., to refine, purify. — L. sublimatus,
pp. of sublimare, 'to lift up*, fr. sublimis. See
sublime and verbal suff. -ate.

## sublimate
sublimate, adj., sublimated. — L. sublimatus, pp.
of sublimare. See sublimate, v.

## sublimation
sublimation, n. — ME. sublimaclon, fr. MF. (=
F.) sublimation, fr. ML. sublimationem, ace. of
sublimatid, fr. L. sublimatus, pp. of sublimare.
See sublimate, v., and -ion.

## sublime
sublime, adj., ]) noble; 2) lofty. — F., fr. L.
sublimis, 'high, lofty, exalted', back formation fr.
sub limen, hence lit, meaning '(coming) up to
below the lintel', fr. sub (see sub-) and limen,
'lintel'. See lhnen.
Derivatives: sublime, п., sublime-ly, adv., sub-
lime-ness, Q.

## sublime
sublime, tr. and intr. v. — ME. sublimen, fr. MF.
(= F.)sublimer, fr. L. sublimare. See snblimate, v.

## Sublime Porte
Sublime Porte, former titie of the Ottoman
Government. — F. la Sublime Porte* lit. 'the High
Gate', loan translation of Arab. Bab "Alt, title
of the Ottoman Court in Constantinople. Cp.
Porte.

## snbliminal
snbliminal, adj., below the threshold of
consciousness (psyckol.) — Lit. 'below the threshold',
formed fr. sub-, L. limen, gen. liminis,
'threshold', and adj. suff. -a). See limen and cp.
sublime.
Derivative: subliminal-ly, adv-

## snblimity
snblimity, п., the quality of being sublime, subli-
meness. — L. sublimitas, fr. sublimis. See
sublime, adj., and -ity.

## sublunar
sublunar, sublunary, adj., 1) situated beneath the
moon; 2) pertaining to this world. — ModL.
sublunar is, fr. sub- and L, lundris, 'pertaining to
the moon'. See lunar.

## submarine
submarine, adj., living or occurring below the
surface of the sea. — Formed fr. sub- and
marine, adj.
Derivatives: submarine, п., submarin-er, n.

## submerge
submerge, tr. v., to place under water, cover with
water; intr. v., to plunge into water; to be
submerged. — L. submergere, 'to plunge under,
sink; to overwhelm*, fr. sub- and mergere, 'to
dip, immerse, plunge*. See merge and cp. words
there referred to.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:753 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: submerg-ed, adj., submerge-ment,
п., submerg-ence, п., submerg-ible, adj., sub-
merg-ibil-ity, n.

## submerse
submerse, tr. v., to submerge. — L. submersus,
pp. οΐ'submergere. See submerge.
Derivatives: submers-ed, adj., submers-ible, adj.,
submers-ibil-ity, n.

## submerse
submerse, adj., submersed. — L. submersus, pp.
of submerge, 'to plunge under, sink'. See prec.
word.

## submersion
submersion, n. — Late L. submersid, gen. -dnis,
fr. L. submersus, pp. of submergere, 'to plunge
under, sink*. See submerge and -ion.

## submission
submission, n. — ME., fr. MF., fr. L. submis-
sidnem, ace. of submissio, lit. 'a letting down*,
formed fr. submissus, pp. of submittere. In
ModF., submission is obsolete; it has been
replaced by its doublet soumission. See submit and
-ion.

## submissive
submissive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
submissus, pp. of submittere. See submit.
Derivatives: submissive-ly, adv., submissive-
ness, n.

## submit
submit, intr. v., to yield, surrender; tr. v., to
present for consideration. — ME. submitten, fr. L.
submittere, summittere, 'to furnish, provide', lit.
'to place or send down', fr. sub- and mittere, 'to
send1. See mission and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: submitt-al, п., submitt-er, n.

## suboceanic
suboceanic, adj., situated beneath the floor of the
ocean. — Formed fr. sub- and oceanic. See
ocean and adj. suff. -ic.

## subordinate
subordinate, adj. — ML. subdrdindtus, fr. sub- and
L. ordindtus, pp. of ordindre, 'to set in order,
appoint'. See ordain and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: subordinate, п., subordinate-ly,
adv., subordinate-ness, n.

## subordinate
subordinate, tr. v. — ML. subdrdindtus. See prec.
word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: subordinat-ion, п., subordinai-ion-
ism, п., subordinat-ion-ist, n. and adj., subordinat-
ive, adj.

## suborn
suborn, tr. v., to procure by bribery; to procure
(a person) to commit a crime. — MF. (= F.)
suborner, fr. L. suborndre, 'to provide, furnish;,
to instigate', fr. sub- and drndre, 'to equip'. See
ornate.
Derivative: suborn-er, n.

## subornation
subornation, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. Late L.
subdrndtidnem, ace. of suborndtid, fr. L. subdr-
natus, pp. of subdrnare. See prec. word and
•ation.

## subphrenic
subphrenic, adj., situated beneath the diaphragm.
— A hybrid coined fr- L. sub, 'under*, and Gk.
φρήν, 'diaphragm; mind'. See sub- and phrenic.

## subpleural
subpleural, adj., situated beneath the pleura. —
Formed fr. sub- and pleural.

## subpoena
subpoena, п., summons to appear in court; tr. v.,
to serve with a subpoena. — Back formation fr.
L. sub poena ('under penalty*), words
introducing the writ commanding the presence of a
person under a penalty of failure. See sub and
penal.

## subreption
subreption, п., obtaining of a favor by unlawful
representation (law) — L. subreptid, surreptid,
gen. -onis, 'a snatching away', fr. subreptus, sur-
reptus, pp. of subripere, surripere, 'to snatch
away*, fr. sub- and rapere (pp. raptus), 'to seize,
snatch'. See rapid and -ion and cp. surreptitious.
Cp. also obreption. For the change of Latin ά
(in raptus) to ё (in sub-reptus, sur-riptus) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.

## snbrogate
snbrogate, tr. v., to substitute. — L. subrogdtus,
pp. of subrogdre, 'to put in another's place,
substitute', fr. sub- and rogare, 'to ask, beg,
entreat; to offer (somebody) for election'. See
rogation and cp. surrognte.

## subrogation
subrogation, п., substitution. — ME. subrogaci-
oun, fr. MF. (= F.) subrogation, fr. ML. subro-
gdtidnem, ace. of subrogatid, fr. L. subrogdtus,
pp. of subrogdre. See prec. word and -ion and
cp. surrogation.

## subsacral
subsacral, adj., situated beneath the sacrum. —
Formed fr. sub- and sacral, 'pertaining to the
sacrum'.

## subscribe
subscribe, tr. and intr. v. — ME. subscriben, fr. L.
subscribere, 'to write below, write down, sign',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:753 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. sub- and scribere, 'to write'. See scribe.
Derivative: subscrib-er, n.

## subscript
subscript, adj. and n. — L. subscriptus, pp. of
subscribere. See subscribe and cp. script.

## snbscription
snbscription, n. — ME. subscripcioun, fr. L. sub-
scriptid, gen. -dnis, 'subscription', lit. 'anything
written below', fr. subscriptus, pp. οι subscribere.
See subscribe and -ion.

## subscriptive
subscriptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
subscriptus, pp. οι subscribere. See subscribe.
Derivative: subscriptive-ly, adv.

## subsellium
subsellium, п., a low bench. — L., 'bench, seat',

sedere, 'to sit'. See sedentary and cp. seat, settle.
Cp. also the second element in Limosella.

## subsequence
subsequence, n. — Late L. subsequentia, 'the act
of following^ succession', fr. L. subsequens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -ce.

## subsequent
subsequent, adj., following in time; later. —
ME., fr. L. subsequens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of
subsequi, 'to follow, succeed', fr. sub- and sequi,
'to follow*. See sequel and -ent.
Derivatives: subsequent, п., subsequent-ly, adv.,
subsequent-ness, n.

## subserve
subserve, tr. v., to serve in a subordinate manner;
to promote. — L. subservire, 'to serve, comply
with', fr. sub- and servire, 'to serve*. See serve.

## subservience
subservience, Subserviency, n. — Formed from
next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## subservient
subservient, adj., subordinate; serving to
promote. — L. subserviens, gen. -entis, pres. part,
of subservire. See subserve and -ent.
Derivatives: subservient, п., subservient-ly, adv.,
subrervient-ness, n.

## subside
subside, intr. v., 1) to sink; to settle; 2) to abate.
— L. subsidere, 'to settle down', fr. sub- and
sidere, 'to sit down, settle', which is rel. to
sedere, 'to sit'. Cp. 01. sidati (for *sidzati),
'sits', Gk. ϊζω (for *si-zdd), Ί seat, set*, and see
sedentary.

## subsidence
subsidence, п., the process of subsiding. — L.
subsidentia, 'a settling down, subsidence', fr.
subsidens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of subsidere.
See prec. word and -ence.

## subsidiary
subsidiary, adj. — L. subsididrius, 'belonging to a

and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: subsidiary, a., subsidiari-ly, adv.

## subsidize
subsidize, tr. v. — See next word and -ize.
Derivative: subsidiz-er, n.

## subsidy
subsidy, п., a grant of money. — ME. subsidie, fr.
L. subsidium, 'support, help; auxiliary troops,
reserve', fr. subsidere, 'to settle down; to stay,
remain', fr. sub- and sidere, 'to sit down, settle'.
See subside and -y (representing L. -ium).

## subsist
subsist, intr. v., to continue; tr. v., to support,
maintain. — L. subsistere, 'to stand still,
remain', fr. sub- and sistere, 'to cause to stand
still, to place; to stand still, stand', from the
reduplicated base of stare, 'to stand'. See assist
and cp. words there referred to.

## subsistence
subsistence, n. — ME., fr. Late L. subsistentia, fr.
L. subsistens, gen. -entis. See next word and -ce.
Late L. subsistentia is prop, a loan translation
of Gk. ύπόστασις, 'subsistence', lit. 'anything
placed under', fr. ύφίστημί, *Ι place under,
stand under*, fr. ύπό, 'under', and ϊστημι, Ί
make to stand; I stand'.

## subsistent
subsistent, adj. — L. subsistens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of subsistere. See subsist and -ent.
Derivative: subsistent, п., that which subsists,
substance.

## subspecies
subspecies, п., subdivision of a species. — ModL.
subspecies. See snb- and species.

## substance
substance, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.),fr. L.
substantia, 'that of which a thing consists', fr. sub-
stdns, gen. -antis, pres. part, of substdre, 'to
stand or be under, to be present', fr. sub- and
std, stare, 'to stand'. See state and cp.
substantive. For the ending see suff. -ce.

## substantial
substantial, adj. — ME. substancial, fr. Late L.
substantidlis, 'pertaining to the substance or
essence', fr. L. substantia. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -a), and cp. consubstantia).
Derivatives: substantialism (q.v.), substantia-
list (q.v.), substantial-ity, п., substantialize (q.v.),
substantial-ly, adv., substantial-ness, n.

## substantialism
substantialism, п., the doctrine that reality (or

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:754 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 727 | SUCCISA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:754 COLUMN:1 -->
substance) underlies all phenomena (pkihs.) —
Formed with stiff, -ism fr. Late L. substantidlis.
See prec. word.

## substantiaHst
substantiaHst, п., an adherent of substantialism.
— Formed with suff. -ist fr. Late L.
substantidlis. See substantial.

## substantialize
substantialize, tr. v., to give reality to. — Formed
with suff. -ize fr. Late L. substantidlis. See
substantial.

## substantiate
substantiate, tr. v., 1) to give substance to; 2) to
show to be true. — ModL. substantiatus, pp. of
substantidre, fr. L. substantia. See substance and
verbal suff. -ate and cp. consubstantiate.

## substantiation
substantiation, n. — ModL. substantidtio, gen.
•onis, fr. substantiatus, pp. of substantidre. See
prec. word and -ion and cp. consubstantiation.

## substantival
substantival, adj., pertaining to a substantive. —
Formed fr. substantive, п., with adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: substantival-ly, adv.

## substantive
substantive, adj., having a real existence;
independent.—ME., fr. OF. (=F.) substantif (fern.
substantive), fr. hateL·.substantivus,lse\f-e\htent,
substantive', fr. L. substantia. See substance and
-ive.

## substantive
substantive, n. — ME. substantif, fr. MF. ( = F.),
fr. Late L. substantivum, neut. of substantivus
(see prec. word); in Latin used only in the term
verbum substantivum, which is a loan
translation of Gk. ρήμα ύπαρκτικόν, to denote the
auxiliary verb esse, 4o be'. The grammatical
term substantivum (in French: substantif) was
introduced by the French to denote the noun
in contradistinction to the adjective.
Derivatives: substantive-ly, adv., substantive-
ness, n.

## substituent
substituent, п., an atom or group substituting
another. — L. substituens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of substituere. See next word and -ent.
Derivative: substituent, adj.

## substitute
substitute, n. — ME., fr. L. substitutum, neut. pp.
of substituere, 'to put instead of, replace,
substitute', fr. snb- and statuere, 'to place, put*. See
statute. For the change of Latin a (in statuere)
to ϊ (in substituere) see abigeat and cp. words
there referred to.

## substitute
substitute, tr. and intr. v. — L. substitutus, pp. of
substituere. See substitute, n.
Derivatives: substitut-ed, substitut-ive, adjs.

## substitution
substitution, n. — ME. substitucion, fr. MF. ( =
F.) substitution, fr. Late L. substitutionem, ace.
of substitutio, fr. L. substitutus, pp. of
substituere. See substitute, adj., and -ion.
Derivatives: substitution-al, adj.,
substitution-ally, adv., substitution-ary, adj.

## substratum
substratum, п., lower stratum. — ML.
substratum, п., fr. L. substratum, neut. pp. of subster-
nere, 'to spread under', fr. sub- and sternere, *to
strew, spread out'. See stratum.
Derivatives: substrat-al, substrat-ive, adjs.

## subsultory
subsultory, adj., leaping. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ory fr. L. subsult-(um), pp. stem of subsi-
lire, 'to spring upward', fr. sub- and salire, 'to
spring, jump'. See salient. For thechange of
Latin ά (in salire) to й (in sub-sultum) see
desultory and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: subsultori-ly, adv.

## subsume
subsume, tr. v. — ModL. subsumere, 'to take
under', fr. sub- and L. sumere, 'to take'. See
assume and cp. words there referred to.

## subsumption
subsumption, n. — ModL. subsumptio, gen. -onis,
fr. subsumptus, pp. of subsumere. See prec.
word and -ion and cp. sumption and words
there referred to.

## subsumptive
subsumptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr.
ModL. subsumptus, pp. of subsumere. See
subsume and -ive.

## subtend
subtend, tr. v., to extend under. — L. subtendere,
'to stretch underneath', fr. sub* and tendere, 'to
tretch'. See tend, 'to move in a certaindirection'.

## subtense
subtense, adj. — L. subtensus, pp. of subtendere.
See prec. word and cp. tense, adj.

## subter-
subter-, pref. meaning 'beneath, lower than'. —
L., fr. subter, .'below, beneath', formed fr. sub
(see sub-) with compar. suff. -ter. See -ther and
cp. inter-, preter-.

## subterfnge
subterfnge, n. — Late L. subterfugium, fr. L.
subterfugere, 'to flee secretly', fr. subter- and
fugere, 'to fiee'. See fugitive and cp. refuge.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:754 COLUMN:2 -->

## subterrane
subterrane, п., an underground room, a cave. —
L. subterrdneum, 'a subterranean place', neut.
of the adj. subterrdneus (see next word) used
as a noun.
Derivatives: subterrane-al, adj., subterranean
(q.v.)

## subterranean
subterranean, adj., underground. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. L. subterrdneus, 'underground,
subterranean', fr. sub terra, 'under the ground',
fr. sub, * under', and terra, abl. of terra, 'earth,
ground'. See sub- and terra.
Derivative: subterranean, п., subterranean-ly,
adv.

## subterrene
subterrene, п., 1) an underground dwelling; 2)
(with the), the underworld. — L. subterrenus,
'underground' (adj.), compounded of sub,
'under', and terra, 'earth, ground'. See prec.
word.

## subterrestrial
subterrestrial, adj. — Formed fr. sub- and
terrestrial.

## snbthoracic
snbthoracic, adj., situated under the thorax·. —
Formed fr. sub- and thoracic.

## subtile
subtile, adj., subtle. — ME. subtil, subtile, fr.
MF. (= F.) subtil, fr. OF. soutil, sotil, sutil, fr.
L. subtilis; influenced in spelling by L. subtilis.
See subtle.
Derivatives: subtile-ly, adv., subtile-ness, п.,
subtilize (q.v.), subtilty (q.v.)

## subtilize
subtilize, tr. and intr. v. — Formed with suff.
-ize fr. L. subtilis. See subtile.
Derivatives: subtiliz-alion, n. subtiliz-er, n.

## snbtilty
snbtilty, n. — ME. subtiltee, altered fr. sutilte
under the influence of L. subtilis. See subtlety.

## snbtle
snbtle, adj., 1) delicate; 2) evasive; 3) clever,
crafty. — ME. sutel, soutil, fr. OF. soutil, sotil,
sutil (F. subtil), fr. L. subtilis, 'fine, thin;
delicate, subtle; clear, simple', which stands for
*sub-texlis, fr. sub- and tela (for *texla), 'a web',
from the stem of texere, 'to weave'; see textile.
The spelling of F. subtil, E. subtle, is due to the
influence of L. subtilis.
Derivative: subtl-y, adv.

## subtlety
subtlety, n. — ME. sutilte, sotilte, fr. OF. soutil-
te, sutilte (F. subtilite), fr. L. subttlitatem, ace. of
subtilitas, 'fineness, simplicity', fr. subtilis;
influenced in spelling by L. subtilis. See subtle
and -ty and cp. snbtilty, which is a doublet of
subtlety.

## subtonic
subtonic, п., in music, the seventh tone of the
scale. — Coined by James Rush (see his
Philosophy of the Human Voice, 4th ed., Philadelphia,
1855, p. 82) fr. sub- and tonic.

## subtract
subtract, tr. v. — L. subtractus, pp. of subtrahere,
'to draw off, withdraw', fr. sub- and trahere, 'to
draw'. See tract and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: subtract-er, п., subtraction (q.v.),
subtract-ive, adj.

## subtraction
subtraction, n. — Late L. subtractid, gen. -dnis,
fr. L. subtractus, pp. of subtrahere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## subtrahend
subtrahend, п., number to be subtracted. — L.
subtrahendus, *to be subtracted*, gerundive of
subtrahere, *to subtract'. See subtract. For the
use of Latin gerundives or their derivatives in
English cp. agenda and words there referred to.

## subulatu
subulatu, adj., slender and pointed; awl-shaped.
— ModL. subulatus, fr. L. subula, *awl\ which
stands for *su-dhl-a and is rel. to L. suo, suere,
4to sew'. Cp. OSIav. Silo, Czech Sidlo, Pol.
szydio, *awF, OHG. siula, *awl, needle', and see
sew. For the ending see adj. suff. -ate.

## subuliform
subuliform, adj., awl-shaped. — Compounded of
L. subula, *awl' and forma, 'form, shape'. See
prec. word and form, n.

## suburb
suburb, n. — L. suburbium, 'suburb', fr. sub- and
urbs, gen. urbis, 'city'. See urban,

## suburban
suburban, adj. — L. suburbanus, 'near the city',
formed fr. sub-, urbs, gen. urbis, 'city*, and suflf.
-anus. See urban.
Derivatives: suburban'ity, п., suburban-ize, tr.
v., suburban-iz-ation, n.

## suburbicarian

See suburban.

## subvene
subvene, intr. v., to come to aid; to intervene. —

L. subvenire, 'to come to the aid of, lit. 'to

## subversion

Derivative: subversion-ary, adj.

## subversive
subversive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.

## subvert
subvert, tr. v., to overthrow, destroy. — ME.

L. subvertere, 'to turn upside down, upset,

version.
Derivative: subvert-er, п.,

subway, n. — A hybrid coined fr. sub-, a suff. of
Latin origin, and the English word way,

## sne-
sne-, pref. — Assimilated form of sub- before c.

## sucende
sucende, п., preserved fruit. — ME. socade, fr.
MF. succade, fr. It. zuccata, fr. zucco, 'gourd'.
See zucchetto and -ade and cp. sucket.

## succedaneous

something, substituted for something*, ir.succe-
dere. See succeed and -eous.

succedaneum, п., substitute. — ModL., prop.

## success

adv., success-ful-ness, п., succession (q.v.),
successor (q.v.)

## succession

cessus, pp. of succedere. See succeed and
agential suff. -or.

## succin-
succin-, form of succino- before a vowel.

which is a loan word from a N. European
language and has been assimilated in form to

## succinct
succinct, adj., concise. — L. succinctus,

Derivatives: succinct-ly, adv., succinct-ness, n.

## snecino-

meaning 1) amber; 2) succinic acid. — L.

## Succisa
Succisa, п., a genus of plants, the devil's bit
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. succisa, fem. pp. of

so called in allusion to the premorse rootstock.

## succise

off (bot.) — L. succisus, pp. of succidere, 'to cut

the change of Latin ae (in caedere) to ι (in

referred to.

succor, succour, п., help, aid. — ME. socour, fr.

## succor
succor, succour, tr. v., to help, aid. — ME. so-
couren, fr. OF. succurre (F. secourif), 'to help,
assist1, fr. L. succerrere, 'to help, assist', lit. 'to

Derivatives: succo(u)r-able, adj., succo(u)r-er,

## succory
succory, п., chicory. — Altered on analogy of Du.

## succose
succose, adj., juicy, sappy. — Formed with adj.

succotash, п., a dish of corn and beans. — Narra-

## Succoth
Succoth, n. — See Sukkoth.

## succubns
succubns, п., a lascivious spirit. — L. succuba,

and cp. also incubus,

succulence, also succulency, п., juiciness. —

succulent, adj., juicy. — L. succulentus, 'juicy', fr.

assistance'. See succor, n.
Derivative: succursal, n.

## succus
succus, п., juice. — L. succus, sucus. See

## succession
succession, п., the act of shaking. — L. succussio,

qnash, 'to make void', and -ion and cp.
concussion, percussion,

## such
such, adj. — ME. swile, swulch, swuck, suck, fr.
OE. swelc, swelce, swile, swyle, rel. to OS. sulik,
ON. sltkr, Swed. slik, Dan. slig, OFris.selik,selk,
salk, MDu. sole, selc, Du. zulk, OHG. sulik,
solik, MHG. sulick, solck, G. solck, Goth.

See so and the adj. like and cp. the second

Derivatives: suck, pron., suck-like, adj. and п.,

## suck
suck, tr. and intr. v. — ME. suken, souken, fr.
OE. sucan, rel. to OE. sugan, OS., OHG. sugan,
ON. suga, Dan. suge, Swed. suga, MDu. sughen,
Du. zuigen, MHG. sugen, G. saugen, *to suck',
and cogn. with L. sugere, 'to such', sucus,
succus, 'juice, sap*, Lett, suzu, sukt, W. sugno,
'to suck'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*seuq-, resp. *seug-, 'to suck; sap*. Cp. sick,
soak, soweus, succose, sncculent, suction, sugent,
sugglllate, sumen and the second element in
honeysuckle. I.-E. bases *seuq-, *seug-, are
enlargements of base *seu-, 'sap, juice; to squeeze,
press; to rain, flow', whence 01. sunoti,
'squeezes', Gk. ΐίειν (for *suwein), 'to rain' ύετός
(for *suwetos), 'rain*. See hyeto- and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also sup, *to sip'.

## sucker
sucker, n. — ME. sukerf souker, fr. suken,
souken, 'to suck'. See suck and agential suff. -er.

## sucket
sucket, n. — A dial. var. of succade.

## suckle
suckle, п., honeysuckle. — ME. socle, sokel,
short for honisocle. See honeysuckle.

## suckle
suckle, tr. v. — Formed fr. suck with freq. suff. -le.

suckling, п., 1) clover; 2) honeysuckle. — ME.

*subitdnus (L. subitdneus), 'sudden', fr. subitus,

sudoriferous, adj., secreting sweat. —
Compounded of L. sudor, 'sweat' (see prec. word),

sudorific, adj., causing sweat. — Compounded

- of L. sudor, 'sweat', and -ficus, fr. -ficere,

Sndra, п., the lowest Hindu caste. — OI. sudrah.

## sue

snf-, assimilated form of sub- before/.

## suffer
suffer, tr. and intr. v. ·*— ME. suffren, soffren, fr.

corresponding to L. sufferre, which is formed

rire. See bear, 'to carry*, and cp. confer and

snffete, п., chief Carthaginian magistrate. — L.

## snfflce
snfflce, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sujfisen, sufficen,

sujfic-ing-ness, n.

## sufficiency
sufficiency, n. — Late L. sujficiemia, fr. L. sujfi-
ciens, gen. -entis. See next word and -cy.

## sufficient
sufficient, adj. — L. sufftciens, gen. -entis, pres.

Derivatives: sufficient, п., sujficient-ly, adv.,
sufficient-ness, n.

## suffix
suffix, n. — L. suffixum, neut. pp. of suffigere, 'to

Derivative: suffix-al, adj.

## suffix

Derivatives: suffix-ation, п., suffix-ion, n.

## suffocate
suffocate, tr. and intr. v., to choke. — L. suffocd-

## suffocation
suffocation, n. — L. suffocatio, gen. -onis, fr.

## suffragan

## suffragan
suffragan, adj., serving as deputy of a diocesan.
— See suffragan, n.

## suffrage
suffrage, п., 1) vote; voting; 2) the right to vote.
— MF. (— F.), fr. L. suffrdgium, 'voting tablet;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:756 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 729 | SUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:756 COLUMN:1 -->
vote, assent, support', prop, 'shout of
approval', fr. sub- and fragor, 'breaking to pieces;

## snft'ragette
snft'ragette, п., a woman who advocates female

## suffumigate

## suffumigation
suffumigation, n. — Late L. suffumigdtio, gen.

## suffusion
suffusion, n. — L. suffusio, gen. -onis, fr. suffusus,

## Sufi
Sufi, п., member of a Mohammedan mystic
order. — Arab, suft, fit. 'man of wool', i.e. 'a

so called from the habit of 'putting on the holy
