## sufic
sufic, adj., pertaining to a Sufi. — Formed fr.
Sufi with adj. surf. -ic.

## Sufism
Sufism, п., mystical doctrines of the Sufis. —
Formed fr. Sufi with suff. -ism.

## sug-
sug-, assimilated form of sub- before g.

## sugar
sugar, n. — ME. suger, sugre, fr. OF. (= F.)
Sucre, fr. ML. succarum, fr. Arab, sukkar, fr.
Pers. shdkdr, fr. Pali sakkard, fr. OI. sarkard,
sarkarah, 'gravel, grit, sugar', which is cogn.
with Gk. κρόκη, κροκάλη, 'pebble', and with
the first element in κροκό-δΐλος, 'crocodile'.
Cp. It. zucchero, Sp. azucar, Port, agucar. Rum.
zdhar, OHG. zucura (whence MHG. zuker, G.
Zucker), 'sugar', which all are borrowed fr.
Arab, sukkar. (The inital a in Sp. azucar, Port.
acucar represents the Arab, article al). Cp. sac-
char-, saccharin, sucrate, sucrose. Cp. also
jaggery, the first element in crocodile, and the
second element in seersucker.
Derivatives: sugar, tr. and intr. v., sugar-less,
adj., sugar-tike, adj., sugar-y, adj., sugar-i-ness,
n.

## sugeilt
sugeilt, adj., suctorial. — L. sugens, gen. -entis,
pres. part, of sugere, 'to suck', which is rel. to
sucus, succus, 'juice, sap', and cogn. with OE.
sucan, sugan, 'to suck'. See suck and -ent.

## suggest
suggest, tr. v. — L. suggestus, pp. of suggerere,
'to lay beneath; to furnish, supply', fr. sub- and
gerere, 'to bear, carry'. See gest.
Derivatives: suggest-er, п., suggest-ible, adj.,
suggest-ibil-ity, п., suggest-ible-ness, n. suggest-
ibl-y, adv., suggest-ing, adj., suggest-ing-ly, adv.,
suggest-ive, adj., suggest-ive-ly, adv., suggest-
ive-ness, n.

## suggestion
suggestion, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. OF.,
fr. L. suggestionem, ace. of suggested, fr.
suggestus, pp. of suggerere. See snggest and -ion.

## suggllate
suggllate, tr. v., to beat black and blue. — L. sugil-
latus, suggillatus, pp. of sugilldre, suggilldre,
which is a derivative of sugere, 'to suck' (see
sugent). The orig. meaning of sugilldre,
suggilldre was 'to cause the blood to flow'. For the
ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## suggillation
suggillation, n. — L. sugilldtid, suggilldtio, gen.
-onis, fr. sugilldtus, suggillatus, pp. of sugilldre,
suggilldre. See prec. word and -ion.

## sui
sui, pron. used in Latin phrases like sui generis,
sui juris, etc. — L. sui, gen. of suus, 'his, her,
its; one's', fr. OL. sovos, of s.m., from the l.-E.
reflexive base *swe-, whence also Ol. svah,
Avestic hva-, xva-, OPers. huva, 'one's own',
Gk. ός, Dor. *ίός, Homeric έός (for *swo-s,
*sewo-s), 'his, her, its', OSIav. svojt, OPruss.
swats, 'his, her, its; one's own', OSIav. svojaku,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:756 COLUMN:2 -->
'relative, kinsman', Goth, swes, adj., one's
own'; п., 'property', OHG. swas, 'one's own,
beloved', Goth, seins (for "swei-no-s), OHG.,
MHG., OS., OE. sin, G. sein, ON. sinn, Dan.,
Swed. sin, 'his', Olr./gin, fadiin, 'himself, etc.,
Arm. in-k'n, gen. ink'ean, of s.m. From I.-E.
*se-, a collateral form of base *swe- derive
Gk. 8, 'himself, herself, itself, σ-φί(ν), 'to
them', L. se~, of s.m., OSIav. sg, Lith. si,
OPruss. sien, 'himself, etc., L. sibi, OSIav. sebe,
OPruss. sebbei, 'to himself, etc., Goth., ΟΝ.,
LG., MDu. sik, OHG. sih, MHG. sick,
'himself, etc., G. sick, 'himself, etc., 'to himself,
etc. (Du. zich is a HG. loan word). Cp. the
.first element in suicide. Cp. also aseitv, pcrseity,
desolate, Sabine, Samnite, self, sib, sister, -sk,
so, soi-disant, sole, 'alone', such, swadeshi,
swami,swaraj.Cp. also assuetude, consuetudinary,
custom, ethical, ethnic, stridhana and the second
element in gossip.

## suicidal
suicidal, adj. — See suicide, п., and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: suicidal-ly, adv.

## suicide
suicide, п., the act of killing oneself intentionally.
— Lit. 'killing of oneself, compounded of L.
sui, 'of oneself (see sni), and -cidium, 'killing',
fr. -ctdere, 'to kill'. See -cide, 'killing'.

## suicide
suicide, п., one who commits suicide. — Lit.
'killer of oneself, compounded of L. sui, 'of
oneself, and -cida, fr. -cidere. See prec. word
and -cide, 'killer'.

## suilline
suilline, adj., piglike. — Formed with suff. -ine
(representing L.-inus) fr. L. suillus, 'of swine',
fr. sus, gen. suis, 'swine', which is -cogn. with
OE. sugu, 'female pig'. See sow, n.

## suint
suint, п., natural grease of wool. — F., fr. suer,
'to sweat', fr. L. suddre. See sudation.

## snit
snit, n. — ME. siute, seute, fr. OF. siwte (read
state), later metathesized into suite (F. suite), fr.
VL. 'sequita (L. secuta), fem. pp. of sequere (L.
sequi), used as a noun. See sequel and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives; suit, tr. and intr. v., suit-able, adj.,
suit-abil-ity, n.,suit-able-ness, п., suit-abl-y, adv.,
suit-ed, adj., suit-ing, п.,

## suite
suite, п., 1) a group of attendants; retinue; 2) a
series or set, esp. of rooms or furniture. — A
French loan word. See snit.

## suitor
suitor, n. — ME. sutor, suitor, fr. AF. suitor, fr.
L. secutor, 'follower, pursuer', fr. secutus, pp.
of sequi, 'to follow'. See sue and agential suff.
-or.

## suivez
suivez, v., direction to the accompanist to follow
the soloist in tempo, etc. (mus.) — F., 'follow',
imper. pi. of suivre, 'to follow', which was
refashioned fr. suit, metathesized form of siut,
*sieut, fr. VL. *sequitus, pp. of sequere, 'to
follow'. See suit.

## sukey
sukey, п., tea kettle. — From Sukey, pet form of
Susan.

## Sukkoth
Sukkoth, Succoth, п., the Feast of Tabernacles
(Jewish Relig.) — Heb. sukkoth, pi. sukkah,
'booth, tabernacle', prop, 'covert', from sdk-
hakh, 'he covered, screened'.

## sulcate
sulcate, also sulcated, adj., marked with grooves,
(bot.) — L. sulcdtus, pp. of sulcdre, 'to furrow',
fr. sulcus, 'furrow, trench', which is cogn. with
Gk. ολκός (for *solqos), 'furrow', ίλκειν (for
'selqeiri), 'to draw', Arm. heig, 'slow, lazy', Alb.
kel'k, kek', Ί tear off", OE. sulk, 'plow', Olr.
osailcim (for *ad-solcim), Ί tear away', OSIav.
vlekg, Lith. velku, Ί draw', Toch. B. sdlk-, salk-
(perf. stem), 'to take away; to suck'. Cp. Hol-
cus. For the ending see adj. suff. -ate, resp. also
3rd -ed.

## sulcate
sulcate, tr. v., to mark with grooves. — L.
sulcdtus, pp. of sulcdre. See sulcate, adj.

## sulcated
sulcated, adj. — See sulcate, adj.

## sulcation
sulcation, п., a furrowing or grooving. — See
prec. word and -ion.

## sulcus
sulcus, п., a furrow, a groove. — L. See sulcate,
adj.

## sulf-
sulf-, sulfa- (also spelled sulph-, salpha-),
combining form meaning 'containing sulfur'. — See
sulfur.

## sulfate (also spelled sulphate)
sulfate (also spelled sulphate), п., salt of sulfuric
acid (chem.) — See sulf- and chem. suff. -ate.

## sulfatize (also spelled sulphatize). tr. v.
sulfatize (also spelled sulphatize). tr. v., to turn
into sulfate. — See sulfate and -ize.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:756 COLUMN:3 -->

## sulfide (also spelled sulphide)
sulfide (also spelled sulphide), п., a compound of
sulfur with another element or radical (chem.)
— See suif- and -ide.

## sulfite (also spelled sulphide)
sulfite (also spelled sulphide), п., asalt of sulfurous
acid (chem.) — See sulf- and subst. suff. -ite.

## snlfo- (also spelled sulpho-)
snlfo- (also spelled sulpho-), combining form
meaning 'sulfur-' or 'containing sulfur'. — F.
sulfa-, fr. sulfure. See sulfur.

## sulfone (also spelled sulphone)
sulfone (also spelled sulphone), п., any of
compounds containing the sulfonyl group (SOa). —
Coined fr. combining form sulf- and suff. -one.

## sulfonium (also spelled sulphonium)
sulfonium (also spelled sulphonium), п., the
univalent radical SH, (chem.) — ModL., coined fr.
sulfar and ammonium.

## suifonyl (also spelled sulphonyl)
suifonyl (also spelled sulphonyl), п., the bivalent
radical S02 (chem.) — Coined fr. sulfone and
suff. -yl.

## sulfur (also spelled sulphur)
sulfur (also spelled sulphur), n. — L. sulpur,
sulphur, sulfur, prob. cogn. with Toch. B. salp-, AB
salp-, 'to burn'. There is prob. no connection
between L. sulphur and Goth, swibls, OE. swefel,
'sulfur'. Cp. solfahira.
Derivatives: sulfur (sulphur), adj. and tr. v. sulf
urate (sulphur-ate), tr. v., sulfur-ation (sulphur-
ation), n, sulfur-ic (sulphur-ic), adj., sulfurize
(q.v.), sulfurous (q.v.), sulfur-y (sulphur-y), adj.

## sulfureous (also spelled sulphureous)
sulfureous (also spelled sulphureous), adj. — L.
sulpureus, sulphureus, 'pertaining to sulfur'.
See prec. word and -eous.
Derivatives: sulfureous-ly, adv., sulfureous-ness,
n.
sulfuret (also spelled sulphuret) п., a sulfide. —
ModL. sulphuretum, fr. L. sulphur. See sulfur.
Derivative: sulfuret, tr. v., to combine with
sulfur.

## sulfurize (also spelled sulphurize)
sulfurize (also spelled sulphurize), tr. v., to
combine or impregnate with sulfur or a compound
of sulfur. — F. sulfuriser, fr. L. sulfur. See'
sulfur and -ize.
Derivative: sulfuriz-ation, n.

## sulfurous (also spelled sulphurous)
sulfurous (also spelled sulphurous), adj., 1)
containing sulfur; 2) resembling burning sulfur
(chem.) — L. sulphurosus, sulfurosus, 'full of
sulfur', fr. sulphur, sulfur. See sulfur and -ous.
Derivatives: sulfurous-ly (sulphurous-ly), adv.,
sulfurous-rtess (sulpkurous-ness). n.

## sulk
sulk, intr. v., to be sulky. — Back formation fr.
sulky.

## sulky
sulky, adj., silently sullen. — Formed—with
change of suff. -en to -y—fr. OE. -solcen,
'slothful', in dsolcen, pp. of dseolcan, 'to be slothful',
which is rel. to MHG. selken, 'to drop, fall'-
and possibly cogn. with Olr. selg, 'hunt, hunt,
ing', sleg, 'spear', OI. srjdti, sdrjati, 'releases,
pours, shoots'.
Derivative: sulky, n.

## sullen
sullen, adj., morose; gloomy. — ME. solein, so-
lain, fr. OF. solain, 'lonely', fr. L. solus, 'alone'.
See sole, 'alone', and -an.
Derivatives: sullen-ly, adv., sullen-ness, n.

## sully
sully, tr. v., to stain, tarnish. — MF. (= F.)
souiller, 'to soil, dirty'. See soil, 'to dirty'.

## sulph-
sulph-, sulpha-, sulphate, etc. — Var. of sulf-,
sulfa-, sulfate, etc.

## sultan
sultan, n. — F., fr. Arab, sultan, 'sultan', fr. Aram.
shulfdnd, 'power', sometimes used in the sense
'possessor of power', from sh let, 'to have
power'. See Noldeke, Beitrage zur semitischen
Sprachwissenschaft, Strassburg, 1910, p. 39.
Aram. shllit, is rel. to Heb. shdldt, 'he ruled,
was master', Akkad. shaldtu, 'to have power',
shaltu, shitlutu, 'powerful, mighty'.
Derivatives: sultana (q.v.), sultan-ate, п., sultan-
ess, п., sultan-ship, n.

## sultana
sultana, п., a sultan's wife, mother, daughter or
sister. — It., fem. of sultano, fr. Arab, saltan,
'sultan'. See prec. word.

## sultry
sultry, adj., oppressively hot. — Formed from the
obsolete verb to suiter, a var. of swelter.
Derivatives: sultri-ly, adv., sultri-ness, n.

## sum
sum, n. — ME. summe, somme, fr. OF. summe,
somme (F. somme), fr. L. summa, 'top, summit;
chief point; amount',, prop. fem. of the adj.
summus, 'highest', used as a noun. Summus
stands for *sup-mos and is rel. to L. super,
'above', sub, "under'. See sub-, super-, and cp.
summary, summit, consunuunte. Cp. also OI.
upamab, 'the highest, uppermost', OE. ufema, of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:757 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SUM | 730 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:757 COLUMN:1 -->
s.m., Gk. ΰπατος (dissimilated fr. *ΰπαμος), of
s.m., which are all cogn. with L. summits,
'highest'. For the sense development of L. summa,
'sum', lit. 'the highest", one should bear in mind
that the Romans used to write the sum over the
addends (in contradistinction to our own habit
of putting the sum under the addends).
Derivatives: sum-less, adj., sum-less-ness, n.

## sum
sum, tr. v. — ME. summen, sommen, fr. OF.
summer, sommer (F. sommer), fr. ML. summdre, fr.
L. summa. See sum, n.
Derivative: summ-ed, adj.

## sumac
sumac, sumach, п., any of the plants of the genera
Rhus and Toxicodendron. — ME. sumac, fr.
MF. (= F.), fr. OF. sumac, fr. ML. sumach, fr.
Arab, summaq, 'the sumac tree', fr. Syr. sum-
mag, 'red'.

## sumbul
sumbul, п., the root of muskroot. — F. sumbul, fr.
Arab, siinbul, 'spikenard'.

## sumen
sumen, n.T a sow's udder; the fat of something
(fig·) — L. sumen, 'breast of women, a sow's
udder*, for *sugs-men, fr. sugo, sugere, 'to suck'.
See sugent. For the ending see suff. -men.

## Sumer
Sumer, п., an ancient district of Babylonia.

## Sumerian
Sumerian, adj., 1) pertaining to Sumer; 2)
pertaining to the inhabitants of Sumer, their
language or civilization; п., an inhabitant of Sumer.
— Formed fr. Sumer with suff. -ian.

## summary
summary, adj., brief. — ML. summdrius, an adj.
formed from the Latin noun summdrium. See
next word.
Derivatives: summari-ly, adv., summari-ness,
n.

## summary
summary, п., a brief statement, review. — L.
summarium, 'a summary, abstract', fr. summa. See
sum, п., and subst. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: summar-ist, п., summar-ize, tr. v.,
summar-iz-ation, п., summar-iz-er, n.

## summation
summation, n. — ModL. summdtio, gen. -onis, fr.
ML. summdtus, pp. of summdre, fr. L. summa.
See sum, п., and -ation.

## snmmer
snmmer, п., a season. — ME. sumer, somer, fr.
OE. sumor, rel. to OS., ΟΝ., Norw., OHG.
sumar, Dan. sommer, Swed. sommar, OFris.
sumur, MDu. somer, Du. zomer, MHG. sumer,
G. Sommer, and cogn. with OI. soma, 'season,
half-year, year', Avestic hama, 'summer', Arm.
am, 'year', amarn, 'summer', Olr. sam, samrad,
OW. ham, W. hdf, 'summer'. All these words are
traceable to I.-E. base *sem-, *sam-, 'summer;
season'. Cp. the second element in gossamer.
Derivatives: summer, intr. and tr. v., and adj.,
summer-ing, п., summer-less, adj.

## summer
summer, п., a large beam. — ME. somere, sumer,
fr. MF. (= F.) sommier, 'pack animal, beam,
rafter', fr. OF. sumer, fr. Late L. sagmdrius,
'pack animal', fr. sagma, 'packsaddle', fr. Gk.
σάγμα, of s.m., which is rel. to σάττω (for
♦σάκ^ω), Ί pack, stuff'. Cp. OHG., MHG.
soum, G. Saum, OE. seam, 'burden, load of a
beast of burden'. Cp. also seam, 'measure',
sumpter.
summer herring. — Translation of Du. zomerha-
ring, of s.m.

## summersault
summersault, n. — A var. spelling of somersault.

## snmmit
snmmit, n. — ME. somette, fr. MF. somete, fr.
OF., fern, of somet, dimin. of лот, 'summit', fr.
L. summum, prop, the neut. oisummus, 'highest',
used as a noun. See sum, п., and -et and cp.
consummate.
Derivatives: summit-al, adj., summit-less, adj.

## summon
summon, tr. v. — ME. somonen, somenen, sumnen,
fr. OF. somondre, semondre, fr. VL. summonere
(3rd conjugation), corresponding to L. summo-
пёге (2nd conjugation), 'to remind, warn',
assimilated form of submonere, fr. sub- and monere,
'to warn'; see monition and cp. words there
referred to. For a similar change of conjugation
cp. respond.
Derivatives: summon-er, п., summon-ing-fy, adv.

## snmmons
snmmons, n. — ME. somouns, fr. OF. somonce,
semonce (F. semonce), fr. earlier semottse, prop,
fern. pp. of OF. semondre, 'to remind, warn',
used as a noun. See prec. word.
Derivatives: summons, tr. v.

## sump
sump, п., marsh, mud; the lowest part of a mine
or pool. — Fr. MLG. sump, *a marsh', which is
rel. to E. swamp (q.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:757 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: sump, tr. and intr. v., sump-er, n.

## sumpitan
sumpitan, п., blowpipe for shooting arrows, used
by the savages of Borneo. — Malay sumpitan-
'blowgun', fr. sumpit, 'blowpipe', lit. 'narrow',
Cp: sarbacane.

## sumpter
sumpter, п., a pack horse. — ME., fr. OF. som.
metier,, 'driver of a pack animal', fr. VL. *sag-
matdrius, fr. Late L. sagmdrius, fr. sagma, 'pack-
saddle'. See summer, 'beam'.

## sumption
sumption, п., a major premise (logic) — ME.
sumpcion, fr. L. sumptid, gen. -onis, lit. 'a taking',
fr. sumptus, pp. of sumere, 'to take, select,
assume; to use, spend, consume', which is a
contraction of *sub-emere, fr. sub- and emere, 4o
take, buy'. See exempt, adj. and -ion and cp.
assume, assumption, consume, consumption,
presumption, resume, resumption, subsume, sub-
sumption. Cp. also the next two words.

## sumptuary
sumptuary, adj., pertaining to expense. — L.
sumptudrius, formed with suff. -arius fr.
sumptus, 'expense', fr. sumptus, pp. of sumere, 'to
take; to spend'. See prec. word and adj. suff.
-ary.

## sumptuous
sumptuous, adj., luxurious. — MF. (= F.) somp-
tueux (fern, somptueuse), fr. L. sumptuosus,
'costly', formed with suff. -osus, fr. sumptus, pp. of
sumere, 'to take; to spend'. See sumption and
-ous.
Derivatives: sumptuous-ly, adv., sumptuous-ness,
n.

## sun
sun, n. — ME. sonne, fr. OE. sunne, rel. to ΟΝ.,
OS., OHG. sunna, MDu. sonne, Du. zon, MHG.,
G. sonne, 'sun', Goth, sunno. These words are
-e«-enlargements of l.-E. base *sdu-, *su-, 'to
shine; sun', and cogn. with Avestic xvng (for
*swen-s)t 'of the sun', xvanvant, 'sunny'. For-l-
enlargements of base *sdu·, *su- see Sol. Cp.
sonth.
Derivatives: sun, tr. and intr. v., sunn-y, adj.,
sunni-ness, n.

## sunburn
sunburn, n. — Compounded of sun and burn, n.

## sunburn
sunburn, tr. and intr. v. —■ Back formation fr.
sunburnt.

## snnburned
snnburned, sunburnt, adj. — Compounded of sun
and pp. of burn.

## sundari
sundari, п., name of an East Indian tree (Heritiera
fomes) — OI. sundari, lit. 'beautiful', fem. of
sundarab, a later form corresponding to Vedic
sunarah, 'of full vitality' (cp. Avestic hunara-, of
s.m.), formed fr. I.-E. pref. *su-, 'well, good,
beautiful', and base *ner-, 'vital energy, vigor'.
I.-E. *su- appears also in Gk. 0- in ύ-γιής,
'healthy'; see hygiene. I.-E. *ner- occurs also in
OI. naryab, 'virile', Gk. ά-νήρ, 'man'; see
andro-.

## Sunday
Sunday, n. — ME. sonnedai, fr. OE. sunnandzg,
'sun's day', prop, a loan translation of L. Solis
dies, itself a loan translation of Gk. Ήλιου
ημέρα, lit. 'day of the sun'. Cp. OS. sunnun
dag, ON. sunnu{n)dagr, OFris. sunnandei, MDu.
sonnendach, Du. zondag, OHG. sunnun tag,
MHG. sun(nen)tac, G. Sonntag, and see sun and
day.

## sunder
sunder, tr. and intr. v., to separate, divide. —
ME. sundren, fr. OE. sundrian (only in the
compounds dsundrian, gesundrian, onsundrian, td-
sundrian), fr. sundor, 'asunder', which is rel. to
OS. sundar, ON. sundr, Swed. sonder, OFris.
sunder, OHG. suntar, 'aside, apart', MHG.
sunder, G. sonder, Du. zonder, 'without', Goth.
sundro, 'apart*. Cp. ON. sundra, Swed. sondra,
MLG. sunderen, Du. -zonderen, OHG. suntaron,
MHG. sundern, sundern, G. sondern (now used
only in the compounds absondern, aussondern),
'to separate', which derive from the adverbs ON.
sundor, resp. its equivalents given in the prec.
sentence. These words are cogn. with OI. sanu-
tar, 'far away*, Avestic hanar , 'without', Toch.
A snu, B. snai, sne, 'without', Gk. όί-τερ (for
*sn-ter), 'without*, L. sine, 'without', Olr. sain
(for *sani), 'different', OW. han, 'another*,
hannr, W. hanner, 'the half (lit. 'the other part').
All these words ultim. derive from I.-E. base
*seni-, 'away from, without'. Cp. sine, prep.,
sinecure, sincere. Base *seni- is an enlargement
of the reflexive base *se-. See se-.

## sunderance
sunderance, n. — A hybrid coined fr. sunder and
-ance, a suff. of Latin origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:757 COLUMN:3 -->

## sundry
sundry, adj.,various. — ME., fr.OE. syndrig/sep-
arate, several', fr. sundor, 'apart'. Cp. OHG.
suntarig, 'sundry', and see sunder and -y
(representing OE. -ig).
Derivative: sundries, n. pi.

## sung
sung, pp. of sing. — ME. sungen, fr. OE. gesungen,
pp. of singan. See sing.

## sunk
sunk, pp. of sink. — ME. sunken, fr. OE. gesun-
cen. See sink.

## sunken
sunken, pp. of sink. — ME. See prec. word.

## sunlit
sunlit, adj. — Coined by Shelley from sun and pp.
of the verb light.

## sunn
sunn, п., name of an Indian plant, India hemp. —
Hind, san, fr. OI. sanafy, 'a kind of hemp', which
derives from the same source as Gk. κάνναβις,
OHG. hanaf, OE. haenep, 'hemp'. See hemp.

## Sunna
Sunna, Sunnah, п., orthodox Mohammedan law
based on Mohammed's actions and teachings.
— Arab. sunnah, 'way, custom, course, tradition'.

## Sunni
Sunni, п., an orthodox Mohammedan. — Lit.
'adherent of the Sunnah' (i.e. 'traditionist'), fr.
Arab, sunnt, which is formed fr. sunna*1 with -i,
a suff. expressing relationship. See Sunna.

## Sunnite
Sunnite, п., Sunni. — Formed fr. Sunna with
subst. suff: -ite,

## sunnud
sunnud, п., a diploma, patent or deed of grant
(India). — Arab, sanad, fr. sanada, 'he leaned
upon*. Cp. musnud.

## sunward
sunward, adj. — Compounded of sun and adj.
suff. -ward.

## sunward
sunward, sunwards, adv. — Compounded of sun
and adv. suff. -ward, resp. -wards.

## sunwise
sunwise, adv., in the direction of the sun. —
Compounded of sun and combining form -wise.

## sup
sup, tr. and intr. v., to sip. — ME. soupen, supen,
'to sup, drink', fr. OE. supan, rel. to ON. supa,
'to sip, drink', Swed. supa, MLG. supen, Du.
zuipen, 'to drink, tipple, booze', OHG. sufan,
MHG. sufen, 'to drink, sip', G. saufen, 'to drink,
sipple, booze'. The orig. meaning of these verbs
was 'to draw in, suck in'. They derive fr. I.-E.
*sub-, which seems to be a -6-enlargement of
base *seu-, 'sap, juice; to squeeze, press; to rain,
flow', whence also—with /c-formative element—
L. sucus, succus, «sap, juice', sugere, 'to suck',
OE. sucan, sugan, 'to suck'. See suck and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also sip.
Derivative: sup, п., a mouthful.

## sup
sup, intr. v., to take supper; tr. v., to provide
with supper. — A blend of OF. soper, super,
souper (F. souper\ and ME. soupen, supen, 'to
drink'. See prec. word and cp. supper.

## sup-
sup-, assimilated form of sub- before p.

## super
super, n. (slang). — Abbreviation of
supernumerary; used especially in the sense of super-
numerary actor.

## super-
super-, pref. meaning 'above, over'. — L. super-,
fr. super, Over, above, on the top of; beyond',
rel. to suprd, of s.m., and cogn. with OI. upari,
Gk. υπέρ, Over, above, beyond', fr. I.-E. base
*uper-, *uperi-, Over, above, beyond', which is
prop, a comparative from base *upo-, 'from
below; turning upward, upward; up, over,
beyond', whence also L. sub, 'under'. See over and

sovereign, superable, superb. Cp. also pref. sur-,

flcial-ness, n.

## superlative
superlative, adj. — ME. superlatif fr. MF. ( =

F.), fr. OF., fr. L. superldtivus, 'exaggerated; in

## superman
superman, n. — A hybrid coined by G. B. Shaw

## supernal

supernatural, adj. — ML. super naturdlis, fr. L.

(= F.) superstitieux, fr. L. superstitiosus, fr. su-

perstitid, gen. -onis. See prec. word and -ous.

See supplicate and -ant.

supra-, pref. used in the sense 'above, over';

suprarenal, adj., situated above the kidneys (anat.)
— Formed fr. supra- and renal,

## supraspinatus
supraspinatus, п., name of a muscle of the back of

## supremacy
supremacy, n. — Formed from next word with

## supreme
supreme, adj., highest; greatest. — L. supremus,

## sur-
sur-, assimilated form of sub- before r.

## sur-
sur-, pref. meaning 'above, over, beyond*. —
ME., fr. OF., F. sur, 'on, upon, over, above*, fr.
L. super. See super- and cp. e.g. the first element
in surcease, surface, surround, survive.

## sura
sura, п., chapter of the Koran. — Arab. surah,

## sura
sura, п., a god; a spirit, demon. — 01. surab,
formed fr. asurah, 'a god, a good spirit', later *an
evil spirit'. This latter sense arose from a mis-
division of the word asurah into a-surafy, the a-
having been mistaken for the priv. pref. (see
priv. pref. an-, a-). The word asurah was thus
interpreted as 'non-god' and so the new word
surab was formed in the sense of 'god'. For the
etymology of asurah see asura.

## sura

palms. — Ol. surab, 'intoxicating drink', fr. I.-E.
base *seu-, 'sap, juice', whence also OI. somaft,
'soma*. See soma, an East Indian plant.

## surah

## sural

— Medical L. surdlis, fr. L. sura, 'calf of the leg',
which is prob. cogn. with Gk. ώρη, ώρη, 'calf
of the leg*. For the ending see adj. suff. -al.

## surat
surat, п., a kind of coarse cotton cloth made at
Surat, a town in Western India. — Cp. surah.

## surbase

## surcease

— Formed fr. F. sursis, pp. of surseoir, 'to

## surcharge

F.) surcharger, 'to overload, overburden,

See charge, v., and cp. supercargo.
Derivatives: surcharge, п., surcharg-er, n.

## surcingle

— Late ME. sursengle, fr. MF. surcengle,
formed fr. snr-, 'above', and cengle, 'girdle', fr. L.
cingulum, 'girdle'. See cincture and cp. cingnlum,
shingles.
Derivative: surcingle, tr. v.

## surcoat
surcoat, п., an outer coat. — ME. surcote, fr. OF.
surcote. fr. sur, 'on, upon, over, above'. See sur-,
'above', and cont.

## surculose
surculose, adj., producing suckers (bot.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ose fr. L. surculus, 'shoot,
sprout, sprig', dimin. of sums, 'twig, shoot,
sprout', which is prob. cogn. with 01. svarub,
'stake, pole', OE. swer, sweor, 'pillar', MHG.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:759 COLUMN:3 -->
swir, Swiss G. Sckwirren, 'pole'.

## surculous
surculous, adj., surculose. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. surculus. See prec. word.

## surd
surd, adj., irrational (said of numbers). — L. sur-
dus, 'deaf, dull; irrational', rel. to susurrus, *a
hum, whisper', from the I.-E. imitative base
*swer-, *sur-, *to sound'. See swarm and cp.
sordamente, sordellina, sordine, sordino, sourdine,
absurd. Cp. also susurration. In its mathematical
sense, L. surdus is a loan translation of Arab.
asdmm, 'deaf', mjadhr asdmm, 'surd root*. As a
mathematical term, Arab, asdmm itself is prob.
a loan translation of Gk. άλογος, 'speechless',
used by Euclid in the sense of
'incommensurable, irrational' (see the tenth book of his
Geometry).
Derivative: surd, п., an irrational number.

## sure
sure, adj. — ME. sur, suret fr. MF. seur, sur (F.
sur), fr; OF., fr. L. securus, 'free from care, free
from danger; careless'. See secure, adj., and cp.
assure, ensure, insure.
Derivatives: sure, adv., sure-ly, adv., sure-ness,
n.

## surette
surette, п., an American tree (Byrsonima crassi-
folia) — F. suret, fem. surette, 'sourish' (whence
surette, 'sorrel, wood, sorrel*), dimin. of sur,
'sour', a loan word fr. Frankish *sur, 'sour',
which is rel. to OE., OHG. sur, 'sour'. See sour
and -et, -ette and cp. sorrel.

## surety
surety, n. — ME. seurte, surte, fr. MF. surte (F.
surete), fr. L. sicuritdtem, ace. of securiids,
'safety, security', fr. securus. See sure and -ty and cp.
security.

## surf
surf, п., waves breaking on the shore. — Fr.
earlier suffe; of uncertain origin.
Derivative: surf-y, adj.

## surface
surface, n. — F., fr. OF., fr. earlier superface, fr.
L. superficies. See sur-, 'above', and face and cp.
superficies.

## surfeit
surfeit, n. — ME. surfait, surfet, fr. OF. sorfait
(F. surfait), prop. pp. of sorfaire (F. surfaire), 'to
increase, overdo, overcharge', used as a noun,
fr. sor, sur, 'above, beyond', and/aire, 4o make,
do'. See sur-, 'above', .and fact.

## surfeit
surfeit, intr. v. — ME. swfeten, fr. surfet. See
surfeit, n.
Derivatives: surfeit-er, n.

## surge
surge, intr. v., to rise. — MF. sourgir, fr. Catal.
sorgir or Sp. surgir, 'to cast anchor', lit. 'to rise
(at sea)', fr. L. surgere, 'to raise, erect; to rise',
contraction of *subs-regere, fr. sub- and regere,
'to direct'; see regent, adj. Cp. OF. sordre
(whence F. sourdre), 'to rise, spring, gush forth;
to result', which derives directly fr. L. surgere.
F. sourdre is now used only in the inf. and only
in an elevated style. It has been replaced by
surgir, 'to rise, surge', as a loan word fr. Sp. surgir
(see above). Cp. surge, n. Cp. also assurgent,
insurgent, insurrection, resource, resurge,
resurgent, resurrection, sortie, source,

## surge
surge, п., a large mass of moving water; wave. —
Fr. MF. sourge-, altered (owing to the influence
of L. surgere) fr. sourje-, stem of sourdre, 'to rise'.
Cp. F. surgeon, 'sucker, offshoot', altered fr. OF.
sourjon through the influence of surgere. See
surge, v.
Derivatives: surg-ing, п., surg-y, adj.

## surgent
surgent, adj., rising in waves, swelling. — L. sur-
gens, gen. -ends, 'rising*, pres. part, of surgere.
See surge, v., and -ent.

## surgeon
surgeon, n. — ME. surgien, fr. AF. surgien, suri-
gien, contracted fr. OF. cirurgien (F. chirurgien).
See chirurgeon.
Derivative: surgeon, tr. v.

## surgery
surgery, n. — ME. surgerie, fr. OF. surgerie,
contracted fr. serurgerie, cirurgerie, fr. Late L. chi-
rurgia. See chirurgery.

## surgicnl
surgicnl, adj. — See surgeon and -kal.
Derivative: surgical-ly, adv.

## surkate
surkate, adj., a burrowing mammal of South
Africa; also calledmeerkat. — F. surikate, prob.
from a native African name.

## surloin
surloin, n. — A var. of sirloin.

## surly
surly, adj., rude; churlish. — Another spelling of
earlier sirly, lit. 'sirlike*, fr. sir and adj. suff. -ly.
The orig. meaning of surly was 'haughty,
imperious*. For sense development cp. lordly and
G. herrisch, 'domineering, imperious*, fr. Herr,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:760 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 733 | SUSURRATION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:760 COLUMN:1 -->
'master, lord'.
Derivatives: surli-fy, adv., surli-ness, n.

## surmise
surmise, tr. and intr. v. — ME. surmisen, fr. MF.
surmis, surmise, masc. and fem. pp. of surmetre,
'to lay to one's charge, accuse', lit. 'to put upon',
fr. sur-, 'above', and metre (F. mettre), 'to put*,
fr. L. mittere, 'to send'. See mission.
Derivatives: surmis-ed, adj., surmis-ed-ly, adv.,
surmis-er, n.

## surmise
surmise, n. — ME., fr. MF-, 'charge, accusation',
prop. fem. pp. of the verb surmetre, used as a
noun. See surmise, v.

## surmount
surmount, tr. v. — ME. surmounten, fr. MF. ( =
F.) surmonter, fr. OF., fr. sur-, 'above', and
monter, 'to mount'. See mount, v.
Derivatives: sur mount-able, adj., surmoum-ed,
adj., surmount-er, n.

## surmullet
surmullet, п., a European fish, the red mullet. —
F. surmulet, fr. OF. sormulet, lit. 'red mullet*, fr.
OF. sor (F. saure), 'reddish brown, red'. See
sorrel, adj., and mullet,

## surnaioe
surnaioe, n. — A blend of ME. sournoun, fr. OF.
so(u)rnoun (F. surnom; see sur-, 'above', and
noun) and name.
Derivative: surname, tr. v.

## surpass
surpass, tr. v. — MF. ( = F.) surpasses 'to excel',
fr. OF., fr· sur-, 'above', and passer, 'to pass'.
See pass, v.
Derivatives: surpass-er, п., surpass-ing, adj.,
surpass-ing-ly, adv., surpass-ing-ness, n.

## surplice
surplice, п., a loose white robe. — ME. surpfis, fr.
OF. surpliz, surplis, fr. ML. superpellicium (ves-
timentum), lit. 'over fur garment'. See super- and
pelisse.
Derivatives: surplice, adj., surplic-ed, adj.

## surplus
surplus, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. OF. sor-
plus, fr. VL. *superplus, 'excess'. See super- and
plus.
Derivatives: surplus, adj., surplus-age, n.

## surprise
surprise, n. — ME., fr. MF., fr. OF. (= MF., F.)
surprise, fem. pp. of surprendre, 'to surprise', fr.
sur-, 'above', and prendre^ 'to take'. See
prehensile.

## surprise
surprise, tr. v. — MF. surprise, fr. OF., fem. pp.
οι sur prendre. See prec. word.
Derivatives: surpris-al, п., surpris-ed-ly, adv.,
surpris-er, п., surpris-ing, adj., surpris-ing-ly,
adv., surpris-ing-ness, n.

## surra
surra, surrah, п., a form of pernicious anemia in
horses, cattle and camels (veterin.) — Marathi
sura.

## surrealism
surrealism, п., name of a French movement in
literature and art. — F. surrealisme, lit.
'movement going beyond realism', fr. sur-, 'above,
beyond', and realisme, 'realism'. See realism,

## surrealist
surrealist, n. and adj. — F. surrealiste. See prec.
word and -ist.
Derivatives: surrealist-ic, adj., surrealist-ic-al-ly,
adv.

## surrebut
surrebut, intr. v., to make a surrebutter (law). —
Back formation fr. surrebutter. Cp. rebut,

## surrebutter
surrebutter, п., plaintiff's reply to defendants
rebutter (law.) — Coined fr. sur-, 'above', and
rebutter,

## surrejoin
surrejoin, intr. v., to make a surrejoinder (law). —
Back formation fr. surrejoinder. Cp. rejoin,

## surrejoinder
surrejoinder, п., plaintiff's reply to defendant's
rejoinder (law). — Coined fr. sur-, 'above', and
rejoinder,

## surrender
surrender, tr. and intr. v. — ME. surrenderen, fr.
MF. surrehdre, fr. sur-, 'above', and rendre,
'to give, give up'. See render.

## surrender
surrender, n. — ME., fr. AF.; fr. MF. surrendre,
inf. used as a noun. See surrender, v.

## surreptitious
surreptitious, adj., done in a stealthy way/— ME.
surreptitious, fr. L. surreptfcius, subreptlcius,
'stolen, furtive, clandestine, surreptitious', fr.
surreptus, subreptus, pp. of surripere, subripere,
'to creep or steal along', fr. sub- and -ripere, fr.
rapere, 'to seize, snatch'. See rapid and cp.
subreption. Cp. also obreptirious. For the change of
Latin ά (in rapere) to ё (in sub-reptus) see accent
and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: surreptitious-ly, adv., surreptitious-
ness, n.

## surrey
surrey, п., a two-seated, four-wheeled pleasure
carriage. — So called because it was first made
in Surrey, England.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:760 COLUMN:2 -->

## surrogate
surrogate, tr. v., to substitute. — L. surrogatus,
pp. of surrogdre, 'to put in another's place,
substitute', fr. snb- and rogare, 'to ask, demand, to
offer somebody for election'. See rogation and
cp. subrogate.

## surrogate
surrogate, п., a substitute. — L. surrogatus, pp. of
surrogdre. See surrogate, v.
Derivative: surrogate-skip, n.

## surrogarion
surrogarion, п., substitution. — ML. surrogdtio,
gen. -dnis, fr. L. surrogatus, pp. of surrogdre. See
surrogate, v., and -ion.

## surround
surround, tr. v. — ME. surrounden. The word orig.
meant 'to overflow', and derives fr. MF. so·
ronder, 'to overflow', fr. OF., fr. Late L. super-
unddre of s.m., fr. snper- and L. unda, 'wave'.
See undate and cp. abound. E. surround was
influenced both in form and meaning by an
erroneous association with the adjective round.
Derivatives: surround, п., surround-ed, adj., sur-
round-ed-ly, adv., surround-er, п., surround-ing,
adj. and п., surround-ings, n. pi.

## surtax
surtax, п., an extra tax. — Formed on analogy of
F. surtaxe, fr. sur-, 'above', and tax, n.
Derivative: surtax, tr. v.

## surtont
surtont, п., overcoat. — F., lit. 'an over all', fr.
sur, On, upon, over, above', and tout, 'all', fr. L.
totus. See sur-, 'above', and total. For sense
development ср. Е. overalls.

## surveillance
surveillance, п., watch kept over a person;
supervision. — F., 'supervision*, lit. 'a watching over',
fr. surveiller, 'to watch over', fr. sur-, 'above',
and veillery 'to watch*, fr. L. vigilare, 'to be
awake', fr. vigil, 'awake, wakeful'. See vigil and
•ance.

## survey
survey, tr. v. — ME. surveyen, fr. AF. surveier, fr.
MF. surveeir, surveoir, fr. OF., fr. sur-, 'above',
and veeir, veoir (F. voir), 'to see', fr. L. videre.
See vision and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: survey, п., survey-ing, п., surveyor
(q.v.)

## surveyor
surveyor, n. — AF. surveiour, fr. MF. surveor,
surveour, fr. surveeir. See prec. word and
agential suff. -or.
Derivative: surveyor-ship, n.

## survive
survive, tr. and intr. v. — ME. surviven, fr. MF.
(= F.) survivre, 'to outlive', fr. L. supervivere, fr,
super- and L. vivere, 'to live'. See vivid.
Derivatives: surviv-al, п.,surviv-or, п., surviv-or-
ship, n.

## Surya
Surya, п., the sun-god in Hindu mythology. —
01. Suryafy, fr. suryah, 'sun*, fr. l.-E. sdwel-,
*sul-, 'sun*, whence also Avestic hvar , Gk.
αέλιος, ήέλιος, ήλιος (for *sdwelios), L. sol,
'sun'-. See Sol and words there referred to and
cp. esp. Svarga.

## Sus
Sus, п., the genus of swine (zool.) — L. sus,
'swine'. See sow, п., and cp. suUline.

## sus-
sus-, form oisub; used in some Latin compounds
in which the second element begins with s, ρ or
t. — L., prop, a contraction of subs-, an earlier
form of sub-, fr. sub, 'under'. See sub-,

## Susannah
Susannah, Susanna, fem. PN. — L. Susanna, fr.
Gk. Σουσάννα, fr. Heb. shoskannah, skoskdn,
shuskan, 'lily'; cp. Akkad. sheshanu, Aram.
skuskantd (whence Arm. skushan, Arab, sausan,
VArab. susan), 'lily'. All these words derive fr.
Egypt. s(sh)shn (Coptic skdsken), 'lotus'. Cp.
Gk. σοΰσον, 'lily', which is a Semitic loan word.

## susceptibility
susceptibility, n. — ML. susceptibilitds, fr. suscep-
tibilis. See next word and -ity.

## susceptible
susceptible, adj. — ML. susceptibilis, fr. L. sus-
ceptus, pp. of suscipere, 'to take up, receive', fr.
sus- and capere (pp. captus), 'to take* (see
captive and -ible). Cp. intussusception. For the
change of Latin ά (in captus) to ё (in sus-ceptus)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: susceptible-ness, п., susceptibl-y,
adv.

## susceptive
susceptive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
susceptus, pp. of suscipere. See susceptible.
Derivatives: susceptiv-ity, п., susceptive-ness, n.

## susi
susi, п., an E. Indian fabric of silk and cotton. —
Pers.-Hind. susi.

## suslik
suslik, п., a ground squirrel of Eastern Europe
and Western Asia. — Russ., dimin. of susol,
which is rel. to Pol. susel, Czech sysel,
'marmot', from the I.-E. imitative base *sus-t 'to
rustle', whence also OSlav. sysati, Russ. sykai\

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:760 COLUMN:3 -->
Czech syceti, Pol. syczec,. 4o hiss, whistle', 01.
sus-, 'to breathe heavily'.

## suspect
suspect, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) suspect, fr.
L. suspectus, pp. of suspicere, 'to look up,
respect, regard; to mistrust, suspect', fr. sus- and
specere, 'to look'. See species and cp. spy,
suspicion. Cp. also aspect and words there referred
to.
Derivative: suspect, n.

## snspect
snspect, tr. and intr. v. — ME. suspecten, fr. MF.
(= F.) suspecterf fr. L. suspectdref 'to mistrust,
suspect', freq. of suspicere. See snspect, adj.
Derivatives: suspect-able, adj., suspect-ed, adj.,
suspect-ed-ly, adv., suspect-ed-ness, п., suspect-
er, suspect-or, n.

## suspend
suspend, tr. v. — ME. suspenden, fr. OF. (= F.)
suspendre, fr. L. suspendere, 'to hang up, check,
suspend', fr. sus- and pendere, 'to cause to hang
down; to weigh*. See pendant.
Derivatives: suspend-ed, adj., suspend-ible, adj.

## suspense
suspense, n. — Back formation fr. in suspense,
transl. of F. en suspens, fr. en, 'in', and the adj.
suspens, 'suspended', fr. L. suspensus, pp. of
suspendere.

## suspension
suspension, n. — Late L. suspensio, gen. -onis, fr.
L. suspensus, pp. of L. suspendere. See suspend
and -ion.

## suspensive
suspensive, adj. — ML. suspensivus, fr. L.
suspensus, pp. of suspendere. See suspend and -ive.
Derivatives: suspensive-ly, adv., suspensive-
ness, n.

## suspensor
suspensor, п., a suspensory (anat.) — ML.
suspensory fr. L. suspensus, pp. of suspendere. See
suspend and agential suff. -or.

## suspensory
suspensory, adj., suspended, suspensive. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ory fr. L. suspensus, pp. of
suspendere. See prec. word.

## suspensory
suspensory, п., a suspensory muscle; a suspensory
bandage. — Fr. prec. word.

## suspicion
suspicion, n. — ME. suspension, fr. AF. suspeci-
oun, corresponding to OF. sospegon, suspegon
(F. soupgon), fr. Late L. suspectidnem, ace. of
sus pec tie, 'mistrust, suspecion', fr. L. suspectus,
pp. of suspicere; see suspect, adj., and -ion, and
cp. βουρςοη which is a doublet of suspicion. The
word suspicion has been refashioned after L.
suspicio, 'suspicion'.

## suspicious
suspicious, adj. — ME. suspicious, suspicieus, fr.
MF. suspeciouSy fr. L. suspicidsus, 'exciting
suspicion', fr. suspicio, 'suspicion', which is rel.
to suspicere, 'to suspect'. See suspect, adj., and
-ous.
Derivatives: suspicious-ly, adv., suspicious-ness,
n.

## suspiration
suspiration, n. — ME., fr. L. suspirdtio, gen.
-onis, fr. suspirdtus, pp. of suspirdre. See next
word and -ation.

## suspire
suspire, intr. v. ME. suspiren, fr. L. suspirdre, 'to
draw a deep breath, to sigh', fr. sub- and spirdre,
'to breathe'. See spirit and cp. words there
referred to.

## sussexite
sussexite, п., a borate of manganese, zinc and
magnesium (mineral.) — Named after Sussex
County in New Jersey. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## sustain
sustain, tr. v. — ME. susteinen, fr. AF. sustein-,
stem of OF. sustenir, soustenir (F. soutenir), 'to
hold up', fr. VL. *sustenire, corresponding to
L. sustinere, 'to hold up, maintain', which is
formed fr. sus- and tenere, 'to hold*. See tenable
and cp. abstain and words there referred to. Cp.
also sostenuto, sonteneur.

## sustenance
sustenance, n. — ME., fr. OF. sustenance, souste-
nance (F. soutenance), fr. Late L. sustinentia,
'endurance', fr. L. sustinens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of sustinere. See prec. word and -ance.

## sustuntation
sustuntation, п., maintenance; preservation. —
OF. sustentacion (F. sustentation), fr. L. susten-
tdtionem, ace. of sustentdtid, 'maintenance', fr.
sustentdtus, pp. of sustentdre, 'to hold up,
support', freq. of sustinere (pp. sustentus). See sus-'
tain and -ation and cp. prec. word.

## susurrant
susurrant, adj., whispering. — L. susurrans, gen.
-amis, pres. part, of susurrdre. See next word.

## susurration
susurration, п., whisper, murmur. — ME., fr. L.
susurrdtio, gen. -onis, fr. susurrdt(um), pp. stem
of susurrdre, 'to hum, whisper, murmur', fr.
susurrus, 'whisper, murmur', from the redupli-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:761 COLUMN:1 -->
cation of the I.-E. imitative base *swer-, *sur-,
*surr-, 'to sound', whence 01. svarati, 'sounds,
resounds', Gk. σϋρίγξ, 'flute', υρον (for
*σύρον), 'beehive, swarm, crowd*, L. surdus,
'dull'. OSlav. svirati, 'to whistle', Lith. surma,
'pipe, shawm', G. schwirren, surren, 'to buzz*,
OE. swearm, 'swarm'. See swarm and cp. surd,
sordine, sordinella, Sorex, syrinx.

## susurrous
susurrous, adj., whispering, rustling. — Formed
with sufT. -ous fr. L. susurrus. See prec. word.

## sutler
sutler, п., a person who follows the army to sell
food to the soldiers. — MDu soeteler, 'bad
cook, camp cook' (whence Du. zoetelaar,
'sutler'), fr. soetelen, 'to cook badly', which is
rel. to Late MHG. sudelen, of s.m., and to MDu.,
MHG., G. sieden, Du. zieden, *to seethe'; see
seethe. (G. sudein in the above sense is not to be
confused with G. sudein in the sense of'to cover
with filth, to dirty', which is rel. to OE. besutian,
of s.rri., fr. I.-E. base *seu-, whence also Gk.
uet.v 'to rain*; see hyeto-). See Kluge-Mitzka,
EWDS., p. 763 s.v. sudein.
Derivatives: sutler-age, п., sutler-y, adj.

## sutra
sutra, п., a series of aphorisms {Buddhism). — OI.
satram, 'thread, string; string of rules,
collection of aphorisms', cogn. with L. suere, 'to sew',
sutura, 'seam'. See suture.

## suttee
suttee, sati, п., 1) Hindu widow who cremates
herself on the funeral pyre of her husband's
body; 2) such self-cremation. — OI. sati,
'faithful wife*, femin. of sat, 'good, wise','lit, 'being,
existing', pres. part, of asmi, Ί am'. See esse and
cp. sooth.

## sutteeism
sutteeism, п., practise of suttee. — A hybrid
coined fr. suttee and -ism, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## surural
surural, adj., pertaining to a suture. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. sutura. See suture.
Derivative: sutural-ly, adv.

## suturation
suturation, n.( suturing. — Formed with suff.
-ation fr. L. sutura. See next word.

## suture
suture, п., 1) the act of sewing; 2) seam. — F., fr.
L. sutura, 'a sewing together, seam', fr. sutus,
pp. of suere, 'to sew', which is cogn. with OI.
stvyati, 'sews', sutram, 'thread, string', Gk.
(κασ)σύειν, 'to patch', Goth, siujan, OE. seo-
wan, 'to sew*. See sew and cp. sutra. Cp. also
accouter. For the ending see suff. -ure.
Derivatives: suture, tr. v., sutur-ed, adj.

## suzerain
suzerain, п., sovereign, ruler. — F., formed on
analogy of souverain (see sovereign) from the
adverb sus, 'above', fr. VL. susum, fr. L. sursum,
'above*, which stands for *subs-vorsom, sub·
versum, lit. 'turned upward'. See sub- and
version.

## suzerainty
suzerainty, n. — F. suztrainete, fr. suzerain. See
prec. word and -ty.

## Svarga
Svarga, п., heaven (Hinduism). — OI. svdrgah.
'heaven*, rel. to svarati, 'shines', Avestic hvar· >
'sun', fr. I.-E. *sawel-, *sul-, 'sun'. See Surya.

## svelte
svelte, adj., slender; lithe. — F., fr. It. svelto,
prop. pp. of svellere, svegliere, 'to pluck, pull,
twitch', fr. s- (fr. L. ex-) and VL. *vellitus, pp.
of L. vellere, 'to pull, pluck'. See 1st ex- and
velllcate and cp. convulse.

## swab
swab, tr. v., to use a swab on; to clean with a
swab. — Back formation fr. swabber.
Derivative: swab, n.

## swabber
swabber, п., 1) a person who uses a swab; 2) a
clumsy person; 3) a swab. — Du. zwabber, fr.
zwabberen, 'to swab', which is rel. to G. schwab-
beln; prob. of imitative origin. For the ending
see agential suff. -er.

## Swabian
Swabian, adj. and n. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
ModL. Suabia, fr. G. Schwuben, fr. OHG.
Swaba, name of a German tribe; rel. to L.
Suebus, Suevus, 'pertaining to the Suevi', a
tribe in north-eastern Germany.

## swaddle
swaddle, tr. v. — ME. swatklen, 'to bind,
swaddle', fr. OE. swaedel, 'bandage*, a derivative of
swadu, 'band'. See swath and instrumental suff.
-le.
Derivative: swaddle, tr. v.

## swadeshi
swadeshi, п., Indian boycott of foreign, esp.
British goods. — OI. svadesin, 'native', fr. sva-
desa-, One's own country', compounded of
svah, 'one's own', and desi, 'pertaining to a
country', fr. desdh, 'place, region, country'. О I.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:761 COLUMN:2 -->
svah, is cogn. with L. suus, 'one's own'; see sui
and cp. the first element in swami, swaraj. OI.
deMh orig. meant 'direction', and is rel. to OI.
disati, 'shows', disd, 'direction', and cogn. with
L. dicere, 'to say, tell'; see diction.

## swag
swag, п., 1) a bundle; 2) a swaying; 3) plunder,
booty (slang). — The primary meaning was 'a
bulging bag*. Prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. Norw.
swaga, 'to sway*, and see sway.

## swag
swag, intr. and tr. v., to sway. — See sway and
cp. prec. word. Cp. also swagger.

## swage
swage, п., name of a tool. — ME., fr. MF. sou-
age (F. suage), fr. OF. soue, 'rope', fr. VL. soca,
'rope', which is prob. of Gaulish origin; cp.
Bret, sug (for *sdg), 'cord'.
Derivatives: swage, tr. v., swag-er, n.

## swagger
swagger, intr. and tr. v. — Formed fr. swag, 'to
sway', with freq. suff. -er.
Derivatives: swagger, n. and adj., swagger-ing,
adj., swagger-ing-ly, adv.

## Swahili
Swahili, n. and adj., name of a Bantu people on
the coast of South-Africa. — The name
literally means 'coast-dwellers', it is formed fr.
Arab, sawahil, pi. of sahil, 'coast', and the gen-
tilic suff. -Ϊ.

## swain
swain, п., 1) country boy; 2) lover. — ME.
swein, swain, fr. ON. sveinn, 'young man,
servant', which is rel. to OE. swan, 'swineherd,
herdsman', OS. swen, OHG. swein, of s.m. Cp.
boatswain, coxwain.

## swale
swale, п., a depression. — Orig. 'a cool place*;
fr. ON. svalr, 'cool*.

## swallet
swallet, п., underground stream (provinc.) —
Prob. derived fr. the stem of the verb swallow.

## swallow
swallow, tr. and intr. v. — ME. swelowen, swale-
wen, fr. OE. swelgan, rel. to OS. farswelgan, ON.
svelgja, Swed. svalja, 'to swallow', MDu. swel·
ghen, Du. zwelgen, 'to gulp, swallow*, OHG.
swelakan, swelgan, 'to swallow', MHG. swelhen,
swelgen, 'to swallow', G. schwelgen> 'to revel*.
Cp. swill and the second element in groundsel,
'name of a plant'.
Derivatives: swallow-able, adj., swallow-er, n.

## swallow
swallow, п., the act of swallowing; gullet. — ME.
swelowe, swalowe, fr. OE. geswelg, 'gulf, abyss*,
fr. swelgan, 'to swallow'. Cp. MHG. swalch,
'abyss', ON. svelgr, 'swallower; whirlpool", and
see swallow, v.

## swallow
swallow, п., the bird. — ME. swalowe, fr. OE.
swalwe, rel. to OS., ΟΝ., OFris., Swed. svala,
Dan. svale, MDu. zwalewe, Du. zwaluw, OHG.
swalawa, swalwa, MHG. swalwe, swalbe, G.
Schwalbe, 'swallow', and cogn. with Russ.
solowij, Czech and Slovak slavtk, Pol. slowik,
'nightingale'. All these words derive from the
I.-E. bird name *swol-wi- or *swal-wi-,

## swam
swam, п., past tense of swim. — ME., fr. OE.
swam, past tense of swimman. See swim.

## swami
swami, п., master (title given to a Brahmin). —
Hind, svdmi, fr. OI. svamin, 'master, lord', lit.
'one's own master', fr. svah, 'one's own', and
amah, 'pressure, vehemence*. OI. svah is cogn.
with L. suus, 'one's own*; see sui and cp. the
first element in swadeshi, swaraj. OI. amah is rel.
to amiti, 'presses on', which has also the
meaning 'asserts emphatically', and is prob. cogn.
with Gk. όμνύναι, 'to swear'. Cp. the second
element in synomosy.

## swamp
swamp, n. — Of. LG. origin; cp. MLG. sump,
'marsh, swamp', which is rel. to MHG., G.
sumpf, 'swamp, marsh'. The orig. meaning of
these words was 'spongy ground'. They are rel.
to OHG. swam, swamp, OE. swamm, Goth.
swamms, ON. svoppr, -sponge', and cogn. with
Gk. σομφός (for *swombhos), 'spongy*. Cp.
sump.
Derivatives: swamp, tr. v., swamp-er, п., swamp-
ish, adj., swamp-y, adj.

## swan
swan, n. — ME., fr. OE. swan, rel. to OS. swan,
ON. svanr, Dan. svane, Swed. svan, MDu.
swane, Du. zwaan, OHG., MHG. swan, G.
Schwan. Swan, prop, means 'the singing bird'.
The name derives from a gradational var. of
I.-E. base *swen-, *swon-, 'to sound', whence
sonare (for *swonare\ 'to sound'. See sonant
and cp. words there referred to.

## swank
swank, intr. v., to swagger (slang); п., swagger
(slang). — Of uncertain origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:761 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: swank-y, adj., swank-i-ly, adv.,
swank-i-ness, n.

## swan song
swan song, — Loan translation of G. Schwanen-
gesang, which is compounded of Schwan, 'swan',
and Gesang, 'song'. See swan and song.

## swap
swap, also swop, tr. and intr. v., to exchange,
trade (colloq.) — ME. swappen, 'to strike', of
imitative origin. The primary meaning of to
swap was 'to strike (the hands at the conclusion
of) a bargain'. Cp. swop.
Derivatives: swapp-er, п., swapp-ing, adj. and n.
swaraj. п., self-government. — 01. svd-rdj, 'self-
ruling', fr. sva-, 'one's own', and raj, 'rule*. The
first element is cogn. with L. suus, 'one's own';
see sui and cp. the second element in swadeshi,
swami. For the second element in swaraj see raj.

## sward
sward, п., grass-covered ground, turf. — ME., fr.
OE. sweard, sweard, 'skin, rind, rind of bacon',
rel. to OFris. swarde, 'skin of the head', MDu.
swarde, swxrde, Du. zwoord, 'rind, of bacon*,
MHG. swarte, 'hairy scalp*, G. Schwarte, 'thick,
hard skin, rind', ON. svordr, gen. svardar,
'skin, esp. of the head; walrus hide', grassvordr,
'greensward', Dan. svzer, Norw. svor, Swed.
svcl, 'rind of bacon', and prob. cogn. with Lett.
scherwe (fr. *scherdwe, fr. Old Baltic *sverdve),
'thick skin'. The sense development of E. sward
is Scand. Cp. Dan. gronsvxr, 'greensward (see
M. O'C. Walshe, A Concise German
Etymological Dictionary, p. 205 s.v. Schwarte);
Derivatives: sward, tr. and intr. v., sward-y, adj.

## sware
sware, archaic past tense of swear, — See swear.

## Swarf
Swarf, п., gritty material. — Of Scand. origin.
Cp. ON. svarf, which is rel. to sverfa, 'to file'.
Cp. OE. geswearf, gesweorf, 'filings', fr. sweor-
fan, 'to file', and see swerve.

## swarm
swarm, n. — ME. swarm, fr. OE. swearm, rel. to
OS., MLG. swarm, Swed. svarm, Dan. svxrm,
MDu. swerm, Du. zwerm, OHG. swarm, swa-
ram, MHG. swarm, G. Schwarm, 'swarm', ON.
svarmr, 'giddiness', ON. svarra, 'to swarm',
MLG. swirren (whence G. schwirren), Dan.
svirre, Swed., Norw. svirra, 'to whiz, whir', fr.
the I.-E. imitative base *swer-, *sur-, *surr-, 'to
sound', whence also OI. svarati, 'sounds, re-
sounds', Gk. ύρον (for *σύρον), 'beehive,
swarm, crowd', L. susurrus, 'whisper, murmur'.
See susurration and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: swarm, tr. and intr. v., swarm-er,
п., swarm-ing, adj. and n.

## swarm
swarm, tr. and intr. v., to climb. — Of uncertain
origin.

## swart
swart, adj., swarthy (poetic). — ME. swerte,
swarte, fr. OE. sweart, 'dark', rel. to OS.,
OFris., MLG., MDu. swart, ON. svartr, Swed.
svart, Du. zwart, OHG., MHG. swarz, G.
schwarz, Goth, swarts, 'dark-colored, black*,
orig- 'of the color of dirt', fr. I.-E. base *sword-,
'dirty, dark, black', whence also sordis, 'dirt,
filth'. See sordid and cp. swarthy.
Derivative: swart-ly, adv.

## swarthy
swarthy, adj., dark; dusky. — Formed with adj.
suff. -y fr. swarth, dial. var. of swart.
Derivatives: swarthi-ly, adv., swarthi-ness, n.

## Swartzia
Swartzia, п., a genus of trees (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Swedish botanist Olaus Swartz
(1760-1818). For the ending see 1st suff -ia.

## swash
swash, tr. and intr. v., to dash, splash. — Of
imitative origin. Cp. swish.
Derivatives: swash, swash-er, п., swash-ing, adj.

## swashbuckle
swashbuckle, intr. and tr. v. — Back formation
fr. swashbuckler.
Derivative: swashbuckl-ing, n.

## swashbuckler
swashbuckler, n. — Lit. 'one who moves his
shield noisily', compounded of swash and
buckler.
Derivatives: swashbuckler-ing, п., swashbuckler-
y, n.

## swastika
swastika, п., a symbol in the form of a Greek
cross with the ends of the arms bent at right
angles; used as the emblem of the Nazi party.
— OI. svastikah, lit. 'being fortunate*, fr.
svastih, 'welfare', a word compounded of su-,
'good, well', and dsti, 'is', which is cogn. with
Gk. εστί, L. est, 'is' (see esse); so called
because it was regarded as auspicious.

## swat
swat, tr. v., to strike, crush. — Of imitative
origin.

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 735 | SWINK -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:762 COLUMN:1 -->

## swath
swath, swathe» п., line of one cut made by a
scythe, mower, etc. — ME. swathe, fr. OE.
swxd, swadu, 'track, trace, band', rel. to OFris.
swethe, 'boundary made by a scythe', MDu.
swade, Du. zwade, MHG. swade% G. Schwad,
Sckwaden, la row of cut grass'.

## swathe
swathe, tr. v., ]) to wrap; 2) to surround, enclose.
— ME. swathen, fr. OE. swadian, fr. swadu,
'track, trace, band'. See prec. word and cp.
swadle.
Derivatives: swathe, п., swath-er, n.

## sway
sway, intr. and tr. v., to move to and fro. — ME.
swayen, fr. earlier sweyen, fr. ON. sveigja, 'to
bend, swing1. Cp. Du. zwaaien, 'to wield', and
E. swag, swagger.
Derivatives: sway, п., sway-ed, adj., sway-er, п.,
sway-ing, n. and adj., sway-ing-ly, adv., sway-
less, adj.

## sweal
sweal, intr. v., to burn (dial.) ME. swelen, fr.
OE. swaelan, 'to burn, be burnt up', rel. to
OFris. swela, 'to burn, be burnt up', MLG.
swelen, 'to smother'. See swelter.

## swear
swear, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sweren, fr. OE.
swerian, rel. to OS. swerian, ON. sverja, Swed.
svarja, svara, Dan. sverge, OFris. swera, MDu.
swaren, sweren, Du. zweren, OHG. swerien,
swerren, MHG. swern, G. schworen, Goth.
swaran, 'to swear', ON. svara, 'to answer*, fr.
I.-E. base *swer-, 'to speak, say', whence also
Oscan sverrunei (dat.), 'to the speaker', OSlav.
svara, 'quarrel', lit. 'a wordy contest', Toch. B.
serp-, AB sarp-, *to teach, instruct'; L. sermo,
'conversation*, is prob. not cognate with these
words. Cp. forswear, answer.
Derivatives: swear-er, п., swear-ing-ly, adv.

## sweat
sweat, intr. and tr. v. — ME. sweten, fr. OE.
swxtan, from the noun swat, 'sweat', which is
rel. to OS., OFris. swet, ON. sveiti, Dan. sved,
'sweat', Swed. svett, Norw. sveite, MDu. sweet,
Du. zweet, OHG., MHG. swei3, G. Schweifi, fr.
l.-E. base *sweid-, *swoid-, *swid-, 'to sweat',
whence also 01. svedah, 'sweat', svidyati, sveda-
te, 'he sweats', Avestic xvaeda-, 'sweat', Gk.
ΐδρώς (for *swidros), 'sweat, perspiration', ΐδος
(for *swidos), 'heat', Armen. k'irtn (metathesis
for *swidrn), L. sudor, Lett, swiedri (pi.), W.
chwys, Co. whys, 'sweat'. Cp. exude, hidrosis,
sudntion, suint, and the first element in sandiver.
Derivatives: sweat-ed, adj., sweater (q.v.)

## sweat
sweat, n. — ME. swet, a collateral form of swot,
fr. OE. swat, 'sweat'. See sweat, v.
Derivatives: sweaty (q.v.), sweat-less, adj.

## sweater
sweater, n. — Formed fr. sweat, v., with agential
stiff, -er.

## sweaty
sweaty, adj. — ME. swety, fr. swet. See sweat, п.,
and adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: sweat-i-ly, adv., sweat-i-ness, n.

## Swede
Swede, п., a native of Sweden. — LG., fr. MLG.
Swede. Cp. OE. Sweon, ON. Sviar, OSwed.
Sviar, Svear, 'Swedes'.

## swede
swede, п., also cap. Swede, the Swedish turnip.
— Short for Swede turnip.

## Swedenborgjan
Swedenborgjan, adj., pertaining to the teaching
of Swedenborg. — Formed with suff. -inn
from the name of the Swedish philosopher
Emanuel Swedenborg (1688-1772).
Derivative: Swedenborgian-ism, n.

## Swedish
Swedish, adj. and n. — .Formed fr. Swede with
adj. suff. -ish on analogy of G. schwedisch.

## sweeny
sweeny, п., muscular atrophy in horses. — Of
uncertain origin.

## sweep
sweep, intr. and tr. v. — ME. swepen, 'to sweep,
move quickly', rel. to OE. swapan, 'to swoop'
(see swoop), and to OS. swepan, 'to sweep (with
a broom)', ON. sveipa, 'to swoop, sweep; to
wrap', OHG. sweifan, MHG. sweifen, 'to
swing', G. schweifen, 'to roam about, rove,
ramble', MLG., MDu. sweven, Du. zweven,
OHG. sweben, MHG. sweben, G. schweben, 'to
float, hover, soar', OHG. sweibon, 'to soar', ON.
svlfa, 'to rove, ramble, turn; make a sweep',
OE. swlfan, 'to move in a course, sweep'. See
swift and cp. sqnib, swipe. Cp. swifter, swivel.
Derivatives: sweep, п., sweep-er, п., sweep-ing,
adj., sweep-ings, n. pi., sweep-ing-ly, adv.,
sweep-ing-ness, n.

## sweep
sweep, n. — ME. swepe, fr. swepen, 'to sweep'.
See sweep, v.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:762 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: sweep-y, adj.

## sweepstake(s)
sweepstake(s), n. — The word prop, means
'sweeping up (i.e. winning) the stakes'.

## sweet
sweet, adj. — ME. swete, swote, fr. OE. swete,
'sweet, pleasant', rel. to OS. swoti, ON. sxtr,
Swed. sot, Dan. sod, MDu. soete, Du. zoet,
OHG. swuo3i, $11031, MHG. sue3e, G. sufi, fr.
I.-E. base *swad-, 'sweet, pleasing to the taste',
whence also OI. svadah, 'agreeable taste, flavor',
svadati, 'makes savory', svadate, 'tastes, is
savory', svaduh, 'sweet', Gk. ηδύς (for *swddu),
'sweet', ήδεσ&οα (for * swadesthai), 'to rejoice',
άνδάνειν (for *swandanein), 'to please', L.
sudvis (for *suadvis), 'sweet', suadere, *to advise'
(lit. 'to make tasteful'), Lith. sudyti, 'to spice,
salt'. Cp. Aedes, assuage, dissuade, hedonic,
persuade, soave, suave, the first element in Hedychi-
um and the second element in algedonic.
Derivatives: sweet, п., sweet-en, tr. and intr. v.,
sweet-en-ing, п., sweet-ing, п., sweet-ish, adj.,
sweet-ish-ly, adv., sweet-ish-ness, n.', sweet-ly,
adv.

## sweetheart
sweetheart, n. — Compounded of sweet and
heart.
Derivatives: sweetheart, tr. and intr. v., sweet-
heart-ing, П.

## swell
swell, intr. and tr. v. — ME. swellen, fr. OE.
swellan, rel. to OS. swellan, ΟΝ., Norw. svella,
Swed. svalla, OFris, swella, MDu. swellen, Du.
zwellen, OHG. swellan, MHG. swellen, G.
schwellen.
Derivatives: swell, n., swell, adj. (colloq.),
swell-ing, n. and adj., swell-ish, adj. (colloq.)

## swelter
swelter, intr. v., to be faint from heat. — ME.
sweltren, swelteren, freq. of swelten, 'to die,
faint', fr. OE. sweltan, 'to die', rel. to OS. swel-
tan, ON. svelta, Goth, sviltan, 'to die', Du.
zwoel, G. schwul, 'sultry', OE. swelan, OFris.
swela, 'to be burnt up', OE. swot, 'heat', MLG.
swelen (whence G. sckwelen), 'to burn without
fiame, to smolder', OHG. swilizon, 'to singe,
roast', fr. I.-E. base *swel-, '-to burn*, esp. 'to
burn without fiame, burn slowly', whence also
Lith. svilti, Lett, svelt, 'to singe', Gk. σέλας,
'light, brightness, flame', σελήνη, 'moon',
έλη, εΓλη (for *^Αέλα, *f έλα), 'the sun's heat',
έλάνη (for * Γελανη), 'torch'. Cp. sweal, sultry.
Cp. also seleno- and words there referred to.
For the possible connection between the above
words and Gk. ήλιος, L. sol, 'sun', see Sol.
Derivatives: swelter, п., swelter-ing, adj., swel-
ter-ing-ly, adv.

## sweltry
sweltry, adj. — Formed fr. swelter with adj. suff. -y.

## swept
swept, past tense and pp. of sweep.

## Swertia
Swertia, п., a genus of plants of the gentian
family (bot.) ~ ModL., named after the Dutch
botanist Emanuel Swert (Sweert) (born in 1552).
For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## swerve
swerve, intr, andtr. v., to turn aside— ME. swer-
ven, fr. OE. sweorfan, 'to scrub, file', rel. to ON.
sverfa, 'to scour, file', OS. swebran, 'to wipe off',
OFris. swerva, 'to rove', OHG. swerban, 'to
wipe, rub', Du. zwerven, 'to rove, wander',
Goth, af-swairban, 'to wipe off', and possibly
cogn. with W. chwerfu, 'to whirl, roll*, and with
Gk. σΰρειν, to trail, drag, sweep away'. See
syrma.
Derivatives: swerve, п., swerv-er, п., swerve-less,
adj.

## Swietenia
Swietenia, п., a genus of trees of the mahogany
family (bar.) — ModL., named after the
Austrian botanist and physician Gerard van Swie-
ten (1700-72). For the ending see 1st suff. -in.

## swift
swift, adj., quick, rapid. — ME., fr. OE., prop,
pp. of swifan, 'to move in a course, sweep', rel.
to OE. swipu, ON. svipa, 'a whip', ON. sveipa,
'to swoop, sweep', OHG. sweifan, MHG.
sweifen, 'to swing', G. schweifen, 'to roam
about, rove, ramble', OE. swapan, 'to sweep,
rush'. See sweep, swoop. For the suff. -t, which
corresponds to I.-E. *-to, cp. old, cold, loud.
Derivatives: swift, n. and adv., swift-ly, adv.,
swift-ness, n.

## swift
swift, п., swift-moving bird, or insect or object.
— Fr. swift, adj.

## swifter
swifter, п., the forward shroud of a lower mast
(naut.) — Formed with agential suff. -er fr. dial.
E. swift, 'to tauten', which is prob. of Scand.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:762 COLUMN:3 -->
origin. Cp. ON. svipta, 'to sweep off, reef,
svifa, 'to turn, rove, ramble', and see sweep, v.
Cp. also swift, adj.
Derivative: swifter, tr. v., to tauten with a
swifter.

## swig
swig, tr. and intr. v., to drink; п., a drink. — Of
uncertain origin.

## swig
swig, tr. v., to tighten, hoist; intr. v., to sway
about, to rock (naut.) — Of uncertain origin.

## swill
swill, tr. and intr. v., to wash. — ME. swilen, fr.
OE. swillan, swilian, 'to wash', rel. to the verb
swallow.
Derivatives: swill, п., swill-er, n.

## swim
swim, intr. and tr. v., to move in water, float. —
ME. swimmen, fr. OE. swimman, rel. to OS.,
OHG. swimman, ON. svimma, symja, Dan.
svomme, Swed. simma, 'to swim', Du. zwemmen,
MHG. swimmen, G. schwimmen, Goth, swumfsf,
'pool'. Cp. sound, 'a narrow channel'.
Derivatives: swim, п., swimm-er, п., swimm-ing,
n. and adj., swimm-ing-ly, adv.

## swim
swim, intr. v., to be dizzy. — Identical with swim,
'to move in water, float'. For sense development
cp. G. verschwommen, 'hazy, vague, indistinct',
pp. of у er schwimmen, 'to fade away', lit. 'to
swim away'.
Derivatives: swim, п., dizziness, swimm-y, adj.

## swimmeret
swimmeret, п., appendage under the abdomen
used by crustaceans for swimming. — Lit.
'little swimmer'. See swim, 'to move in water4,
agential suff. -er, and dimin. suff. -et.

## swindle
swindle, tr. and intr. v. — Back formation fr.
swindler. For similar back formations cp. cadge,
peddle.
Derivatives: swindle, п., swindl-ing, п., swindl-
ing-ly, adv.

## swindler
swindler, п., cheat, sharper. — G. Sckwirtd/er,
'giddy person; dreamer, visionary', fr. schwin-
deln, 'to be dizzy, to scheme fantastic things', fr.
MHG. swindeln, fr. OHG. swintilon, 'to swoon;
to be dizzy', freq. of swintan (whence MHG.
swinden, G. schwinden), 'to waste away,
languish, disappear', whicn is rel. to OE. swindan,
'to waste away, languish, vanish', and possibly
cogn. with Aram, k'andem, Ί destroy', Olr. a-
sennad, 'finally'. The sense development of G.
Schwindler, which now means 'cheat, sharper,
impostor', is due to the influence of E. swindler.
Derivative: swindler-ly, adj.

## swine
swine, n. — ME. swin, fr. OE. swin, rel. to OS.,
OFris., MLG., OHG. MHG. swin, ON. svin,
Dan., Swed. svin, MDu. swijn, Du. zwijn, G.
Sckwein, Goth, swein, and cogn. with Gk.
ύς, σϋς, 'swine*, ΰινος, 'swinish', L- sus,
'swine', suinus, 'of swine', OSlav. svinu, 'of
swine', svinija, 'swine', OE. sugu, su, 'sow'. See
sow, п., and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
the second element in keelson.
Derivatives: swin-ery, п., swin-ish, adj., swin-ish-
ly, adv., swin-ish-ness, n.

## swing
swing, intr. and tr. v. — ME. swingen, fr. OE.
swingan, 'to beat, strike, whip', rel. to OS.,
OHG. swingan, OFris. swinga, MLG., MHG.
swingen, G. schwingen, 'to swing, swingle, os-
cillate', MDu. swinghen, 'to waver', Goth, af-
swaggwjan, 'to cause to swing', factitive of
*swiggwan, 'to swing', and prob. cogn. with OI.
svajate, 'embraces', Olr. seng, 'slender, slim'
(orig. 'flexible'). Cp. swinge, swingle, swink.
Derivatives: swing, п., swing-er, п., swing-ing-ly,
adv., swing-y, adj.

## swinge
swinge, tr. v., to strike (arch.) — ME. swengen, fr.
OE. swengan, 'to beat, strike1, causative of
swingan, 'to swing'. See swing.
Derivatives: swinge-ing, adj., swinge-ing-ly, adv.

## swingle
swingle, п., an instrument for beating flax. —
ME- swingel, fr. OE. swingel, swingele, 'beating;
stick to beat', fr. swingan, 'to beat, strike, whip'.
Cp. Du. zwengel, G. Schwengel, lit. 'instrument
for swinging'. See swing and instrum. suff. -le
and cp. swingletree.
Derivative: swingle, tr. v.

## swingletree
swingletree, п., a whippletree. — Compounded of
swingle and tree. Cp. singletree.

## swink
swink, intr. v., to labor, toil. — ME. swinken, fr.
swincan, a collateral form of swingan, 'to beat,
strike, whip'. See swing.

## swink
swink, п., labor, toil. — ME., fr. OE. swine, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:763 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SWIPE | 736 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:763 COLUMN:1 -->
swincan. See swink, v.
swipe» п., a sweeping blow. — Alter, of sweep, n.

## swipe
swipe, intr. and tr. v., to strike with a sweeping
motion. — Partly alter, of sweep, v., partly fr.
swipe, n.
Derivative: swip-ery n.

## swirl
swirl, intr. v., to whirl; tr. v., to cause to whirl. —
Of imitative origin. Cp. ON. sverra, 'to whirl'
(whence the freq. verb svirla), G. sckwirren, 'to
whiz, whir, buzz'.
Derivatives: swirl, п., swirl-y, adj.

## swish
swish, tr. and intr. v. — Of imitative origin. Cp.
swash.
Derivatives: swish, п., swish-er, п., swish-ing-ly,
adv.

## Swiss
Swiss, adj. — MF. (= F.) Suisse, fr. MHG.
Swizer. See Switzer.
Derivative: Swiss, n.

## switch
switch, п., a flexible rod. — MDu. swijck, 'scourge,
whip', rel. to OHG, MHG. zwec, 'wooden
peg', G. Zweck, 'aim, design' (orig. 'peg in the
target'), MHG. zwict G. Zwick, 'wooden peg'.
Derivatives: switch, tr. and intr. v., switck-ed,
adj., switch-er, п., switch-y, adj.

## Switzer
Switzer, п., a Swiss {archaic). — MHG., fr.
Switz (whence G. Schweiz), 'Switzerland'.
Switzerland was named after Sckwyz, one of its
ancient cantons. Cp. Swiss. For the ending see
suff. -er.

## swivel
swivel, n. — ME. swivell, rel. to OE. swifan, 'to
move in a course, sweep'. See sweep, v., and cp.
words there referred to.

## swollen
swollen, pp. of swell. — ME., fr. OE. geswollen,
pp. of swellan. See swell.

## swoon
swoon, intr. v. — ME. swowenen, swownen, back
formation fr. swowening, 'swooning', fr. OE.
geswogen, *in a swoon', pp. of a lost verb. Cp.
LG. swogen, 'to sigh', and sough.
Derivatives: swoon, п., swoon-ing-ly, adv.

## swoop
swoop, tr. and intr. v., to sweep down. — ME.
swopen, fr. OE. swapan, 'to sweep, rush', rel. to
ME. swepen, 'to sweep, rush', rel. to ME.
swepen, *to sweep, move quickly'. See sweep.
Derivatives: swoop, п., swoo-per, n.

## swoop
swoop, tr. and intr. v., to swap. — A var. of swap.
Derivative: swoop, n.

## sword
sword, n. — ME. swerd. fr. OE. sweord, swurd,
sword, rel. to bs„ OFris. swerd, ON. sverd,
Dan. sverd, Swed. svurd, MDu. swaert, Du.
zwaard, OHG., MHG. swertf G. Schwert, fr.
Teut. *swerda, lit. 'the cutting weapon', formed
fr. l.-E. base *swer-, 'to press, torment*, orig. 'to
cut', and Teut. suff. -da. Avestic xvara, 'wound',
OI. svar-, 'to torment', are from the same base.
For the sense developmeent of OE. sweord, etc.,
cp. OI. krpanafr 'sword', lit. 'a cutting weapon*,
fr. I.-E. base *(s)qerp-, 'to cut' (see harvest).
Derivatives: sword, v., sword-less, adj.

## swore
swore, past tense of swear. — ME. swor, fr. OE.
swor, past tense of swerian. See swear.

## sworn
sworn, pp. of swear. — ME. sworen, fr. OE.
sworen, pp. of swerian. See swear.

## swot
swot, п.,hard work, toil (slang). — Avar, of sweat
Derivative: swot, intr. v.

## swum
swum, pp. of swim. — ME. swummen, fr. OE. ge-
swummen, pp. of swimman. See swim, 'to move
in water'.

## swung
swung, past tense and pp. of swing. — ME. swang,
swong, past tense, resp. swungen, pp. oiswingen,
fr. OE. swang, past tense, resp. geswungen, pp.
of swingan. See swing.

## sy-
sy-, pref. — Gk. συ-, form of συν-, before σ
followed by a consonant and before ζ. See syn-.

## syagush
syagush, п., the caracal. — Pers.-Hind. siyah-
gosh, lit. 'black ear', fr. siyah, 'black', and gosh,
'ear'. The first element is rel. to OI. iyamah,
Avestic soma, 'black', and cogn. with L. cimex,
*a bug', lit. 'the dark-brown insect'; see cimex.
The second element derives fr. OPers. gausha-,
ModPers. gosh, 'ear', which is rel. to Avestic
gaosho-, 'ear', and to OI. ghosah, 'noise'.

## Sybarite
Sybarite, п., and adj. — L. Sybarfta, fr. Gk.
Συβαρΐτης, inhabitant of Sybaris, fr. Σύβαρις,
name of a Greek town in southern Italy (now
called Sibari). The inhabitants of Sybaris were
famous for their luxury, whence Sybarite came
to denote a luxurious person. — For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:763 COLUMN:2 -->

## Sybaritic
Sybaritic, also Sybaritical, adj. — L. Sybariticus,
fr. Gk. Συβαριτικός, fr. Συβαρΐτης. See prec.
word and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivative: Sybaritical-ly, adv.

## sybotic
sybotic, adj., pertaining to a swineherd. — Gk.
συβωτικός, compounded of συς, gen. συός,
'swine', and the stem of βόσκειν, 'to feed'. Gk.
σϋς is a collateral form of δς; see sow, 'female
pig'. For the second element see botany, for
the ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## sycamine
sycamine, п., mulberry. — L. sycaminus, fr. Gk.
σϋκάμΐνος, fr. Phoen. shiqmin, corresponding
to Heb. shiqmfm,xA. of shiqmah, 'mulberry'; cp.
Aram, skiqmd, pi. shiqmin. Cp. also next word.

## sycamore
sycamore, sycomore, п., 1) a tree of Egypt and
Asia Minor, the sycamore of the Bible; 2) a
Eurasian maple tree; 3) the plane tree. — ME.,
fr. OF. sicamor (F. sycomore), dissimulated fr.
L. sycomorus, is. Gk. σϋκόμορος. For the first
element of this compound word see prec. word.
The second element is identical with Gk. μώρος,
μόρος, 'mulberry'; see mulberry.

## syce
syce, п., an Indian groom. — Arab, sa'is (in
vulgar pronunciation sdyis), 'groom', prop,
pres. participle of the verb sasa, 'he
administered'.

## sycee
sycee, п., ingots of silver. — Chin, hsi-se, 'fine
silk'.

## sychnocarpous
sychnocarpous, adj., bearing fruit for several
seasons (bot.) — Compounded of Gk. συχνός,
'many, frequent, dense, compact', and καρπός,
'fruit1. The first element is of uncertain origin.
For the second element see carpel, for the
ending see sufT. -ous.

## Sycon
Sycon, п., a genus of sponges (zool.) — ModL.
Sycon, fr. Gk. σΰκον, 'fig', which is prob. a
loan word from a Mediterranean language. Cp.
next word and Busycon.

## syconium
syconium, п., fleshy fruit with the ovaries borne
in a hollow receptacle, as in the fig. (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. σΰκον, 'fig'. See prec. word.

## sycophancy
sycophancy, n. — h.sycopkantia, fr. Gk.
συκοφαντία, fr. συκοφάντης. See next word and -cy.

## sycophant
sycophant, п., flatterer; toady. — L. spcophanta,
fr. Gk. συκοφάντης, 'informer, denouncer', lit.
'fig shower', fr. σΰκον, 'fig', and -φάντης, from
the stem of φαίνειν, 'to show'; see sycon and
phantasm. Several attempts have been made to
explain how the expression 'fig shower' came
to denote an informer in Greek, but they all
lack probability.
Derivatives: sycophantic (q.v.), sycophant-ish,
adj., sycophant-ish-ly, adv., sycophant-ism, n.(
sycophant-ize, intr. v., sycophant-ry, n.

## sycophantic
sycophantic, adj. — Gk. συκοφαντικός, fr.
συκοφάντης. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## sycosis
sycosis, п., skin disease attacking especially the
bearded part of the face. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
σΰκωσις, 'ulcer resembling a fig', formed fr.
σΰκον, 'fig', with suff. -ωσις. See Sycon and
-osis.

## sydnone
sydnone, п., a group of compounds that contains
a five-membered ring (chem.) — Coined fr.
Sydn(ey) and suff. -one; so called because it was
discovered by Earl and Mackney) in Sydney (in
1935).

## syenite
syenite, п., a gray, igneous rock allied to granite
(petrogr.) — L. Syenites (lapis), lit. \stone)
from Syene\ coined by Pliny as loan translation
of Gk. Συην ιτης λί&ος (a term used by Diodorus
Siculus), lit. 'stone from Syene', fr. Συήνη (L.
Syene), name of a town in Upper Egypt, fr.
Egypt. Swn (Copt. Suan, Heb. Seweneh, Arab.
Aswan; now called Assuan); so called because
it was anciently quarried at Syene. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: syenit-ic, adj.

## syl-
syl-, pref. — Gk. συλ-, assimilated form of συν-
before λ. See syn-.

## syllabary
syllabary, п., a list of syllables. — ModL. sylla-
barium, formed fr. L. syllaba, 'syllable', with
suff. -drium. See syllable and subst. suff. -ary.

## syllabic
syllabic, -dj. — ModL. syllabicus, fr. Gk.
συλλαβικός, fr. συλλαβή, 'syllable'. See syllable and
adj. suff. -ic and cp. monosyllabic, dissyllabic,
trisyllabic, tetrasyllable, decasyllabic, nendecasyl-
labic, dodecasyllabic, parisyllabic, polysyllabic.
Derivatives: syllabic-al, adj., syllabic-al-ly, adv.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:763 COLUMN:3 -->
syllabic-ness, n.

## syllabicate
syllabicate, tr. v., to syllabify. — ML.
syllabicate, pp. of syllabicare/to syllabicate', fr. L.
syllaba. See syllable and verbal suff. -ate.

## syllabication
syllabication, п., syllabification. — ML.
syllabicate, gen. -onis, fr. sylfabiedtus, pp. of sylla-
bicare. See prec. word and -ion.

## syllabification
syllabification, п., the act of syllabifying. — See
next word and -ation.

## syllabify
syllabify, tr. v., to form or divide into syllables.
— Formed fr. L. syllaba, 'syllable', and suff.
-ficare. See syllable and -fy.

## syllabize
syllabize, tr. v., to syllabify. — ML. syllabizare,
fr. Gk. συλλαβίζειν, fr. συλλαβή, 'syllable*. See
next word and -ize.

## syllable
syllable, n. — ME. sillable, fr. MF. sillabe (F.
syffabe), fr. OF., fr. L. syllaba, fr. Gk. συλλαβή,
'syllable', lit. 'a holding together (scil. of letters)',
fr. συλλαμβάνειν, 'to take or put together', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and λαμβάνειν, 'to take, grasp,
seize'. See lemma and cp. words there referred
to. Cp. also monosyllable, dissyllable, trisyllable,
tetrasyllable, decasyllabic, dodecasyllable.

## syllable
syllable, tr. v., to pronounce in syllables. — Fr.
syllable, n.; first used by Milton.
Derivative: syllabl-ed, adj.

## syliabas
syliabas, п., outline, compendium, — Eccles. L.
syllabus, 'list', fr. Gk. σύλλαβος, prop, an
erroneous reading occurring in early printed
editions of Cicero's Letters to Atticus (IV, 5 and
8) for σίλλυβος, 'a strip of parchment attached
to a book and bearing the name of the author,
title slip'; cp. σίλλυβα, 'fringes'. Both these
words are prob. alterations of orig. σίττυβος,
resp. σιττυβά, σιττυβή, whose etymology is
unknown.

## syllepsis
syllepsis, п., use of a word in both a literal and
metaphorical sense (rhet.) — L., fr. Gk. σύλ-
ληψις, 'a taking together, comprehension', fr.
συλλαμβάνειν, 'to take together'. See syllable.

## sylleptic
sylleptic, adj., pertaining to a syllepsis (rhet.) —
Gk. συλληττΓΐκός, 'collective, comprehensive',
fr.συλλαμβάνειν. See prec.word and adj.suff.-ic.
Derivatives: sylleptic-al, adj., sylleptic-al-lf, adv.

## syllogism
syllogism, п., a form of reasoning (log.) — ME.
silogisme, fr. MF. silogisme (F. syllogisme), fr.
OF., fr. L. syllogismus, fr. Gk. συλλογισμός,
'computation, calculation', fr. συλλογίζεσ&αι,
'to compute, reckon', lit. 'to think or reckon
together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and λογίζεσ&αι, 'to
compute, reckon'. See logos and -ism.

## syllogistic
syllogistic, adj., pertaining to syllogisms. — L.
syllogisticus, fr. Gk. συλλογιστικός,
'inferential', fr. συλλογ£ζεσ&αι, 'to compute, reckon'.
See prec, word.
Derivatives: syllogistic, п., syllogistic-al, adj.,
syllogistic-al-ly, adv.

## syllogize
syllogize, intr. and tr. v., to infer by the use of
syllogisms. — Gk. συλλογίζεσθαι, Чо compute,
reckon'. See syllogism.
Derivatives: syllogiz-ation, п., syllogiz-er, n.

## sylph
sylph, п., an air spirit. — F. sylphe, fr. L. sylpkus,
'spirit, genius*, occurring only in some
inscriptions, but resumed by Paracelsus (1493-1541) in
the sense of 'dwarf spirit of the air'.
Derivatives: sylpk-ic, adj., sylpkid (q.v.), sylph·
ish, sylph-y, adjs.

## syl phi d
syl phi d, п., a young or small sylph. — F. sylphide,
fr. sylphe. See sylph and 4th -id.
Derivatives: sylphid, adj., sylphid-ine, adj.

## sylvan
sylvan, adj. — See silvan.

## sylvanite
sylvanite, п., mineral consisting of a gold silver
telluride. — Formed from the second element
in Transylvania, name of the country in which it
frequently occurs. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Sylvester
Sylvester, masc. PN. — See Silvester.

## sylvestral
sylvestral, adj., growing in the woods. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. silvestris, 'belonging to a
wood, wooded, woody', fr. silva, 'wood'. See
silvan.

## Sylvia
Sylvia, fem. PN. — Lit. 'inhabiting woods', fr. L.
silva, 'wood'. See silvan.

## sylvite
sylvite, sylvine, п., native potassium chloride
KC1 (mineral.) — Formed from its former
name, the ModL. sal digestivus Sylvii [prob. so
called after Franz de la Вое" Sylvius (1614-72),
professor of medicine at Leyden]. For the end-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:764 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 737 | SYNALLAGMATIC -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:764 COLUMN:1 -->
ing see subst. suff. -Ite, resp. -ine (representing
L.-inus).

## sym-
sym-, pref. — Gk. συμ-, assimilated form of
συν- before μ. See syn-.

## symbion
symbion, symbiont, п., an OTganism living in
symbiosis (Wo/.) — ModL., lit. 'living together', fr.
Gk. συμβίων, gen. συμβιοϋντος, pres. part, of
συμβιοϋν, 'to live together', fr. σύμβιος, 'living
together', fr. συν- (see syn-) and βίος, 'life'. See
bio- and cp. words there referred to.

## symbiosis
symbiosis, п., a living together (biol.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. συμβίωσις, 'a living together', fr.
συμβιοϋν. See prec. word and -osis.

## symbiotic
symbiotic, symbiotical, adj., pertaining to
symbiosis. — Gk. συμβιωτικός, fr. συμβιωτής,
'one who lives together', fr. συμβιοϋν. See
symbion and -otic.
Derivatives: symbiotical-ly, adv., symbiot-ics, n.

## symbiotism
symbiotism, п., symbiosis. — See prec. word and
-ism.

## symbol
symbol, п., I) sign, token; 2) emblem; 3)
confession of faith, creed. — Partly fr. Eccles. L.
symbolum, 'the baptismal creed' (fr. L.
symbolum), partly directly fr. L. symbolum, 'sign,
token, mark, sign of recognition', fr. Gk. σύμ-
βολον, 'token, sign, pledge, gnarantee,
symbol', prop, 'something thrown together', fr.
συμβάλλειν, 'to throw together', fr. συν- (see
syn-) and βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See ballistic and
cp. hyperbole, parable.
Derivatives: symbol, tr. v., symbolic (q.v.),
symbolism (q.v.), symbolist (q.v.), symbolize (q.v.)

## symbolic
symbolic, symbolical, adj. — L. symbolicus, fr.
Gk. συμβολικός, 'pertaining to a symbol', ft.
σύμβολον. See pjrec. word and -ic, resp. also -al.
Derivatives: symbol-ics, n. pi., symbolic-al-ly,
adv., symbolic-al-ness, n.

## symbolism
symbolism, п., i) the representation of things by
use of symbols; 2) the practice of using symbols;
3) the name of a group of French poets (see next
word). — Formed fr. symbol with suff. -ism. In
sense No. 3 derived fr. F. symbolisme, fr. sym-
bole. See next word.

## symbolist
symbolist, п., 1) one who uses symbols; 2) one
versed in the interpretation of symbols; 3) one
who regards the elements in the Eucharist as
mere symbols; 4) one of a group of writers in
France and in'Belgium who rejected realism and
naturalism and attached symbolic meaning to
objects, ideas and emotions, etc. — Formed fr.
symbol with suff. -ist.; in sense No. 4 derived fr.
F. symboliste, which was coined by the French
symbolist pbet Paul Verlaine (1844-96) in 1885
fr. symbole.
Derivatives: symbolist, symbolist-ic, symbolist-
ic-al, adjs., symbolist-ic-al-ly, adv.

## symbolization
symbolization, n. — F. symbolisation, fr. sym-
boliser. See next word and -ation.

## symbolize
symbolize, tr. and intr. v. — MF. (= F.) sym-
boliser, fr. symbole, fr. L. symbolum. See symbol
and -ize.
Derivative: symboliz-er, n.

## symbolo-
symbolo-, combining form meaning 'symbol'. See
symbol.

## symbology
symbology, п., the study of symbols. —
Contraction of symbolology, fr. Gk. σύμβολον, 'token,
symbol', and -λογίδ, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See symbulo- and -logy.
For the contraction see haplology.
Derivatives: symbolog-ic-al, adj., symbolog-ist,
n.

## symbololatry
symbololatry, п., worship of symbols. — Formed
from symbolo- and Gk. -λατρεία, -λατρίά, fr.
λατρεία, 'worship'. See -latry.

## symbolology
