symbolology, n. — See symbology.

## symmetrical
symmetrical, also symmetric, adj. — Formed fr.
symmetry with suff, -ical, resp. -ic. Cp.
asymmetrical, dissymmetrical.
Derivatives: symmetrical-ly, udv.,
symmetrically, п., symmetrical-ness, n.

## symmetrophobia
symmetrophobia, п., fear of symmetry. — ModL-,
compounded of Gk. συμμετρία, 'symmetry',
and -φοβία, fr. φόβος, 'fear'. See symmetry and
-phobia.

## symmetry
symmetry, n. — F. symmetric (now spelled syme-
trie), fr. L. symmetria, fr. Gk. συμμετρία, 'due
proportion', lit. 'a measuring together', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:764 COLUMN:2 -->
σύμμετρος, 'commensurate, of like measure', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter,
'poetical rhythm', and cp. asymmetry,
dissymmetry.
Derivatives: symmetrical (q.v.), symmetr-ist, п.,
symmetr-ize, tr. v., symmetr-iz-ation, n.

## sympalmograph
sympalmograph, п., an instrument for recording
sound vibrations. — Compounded of sym-, Gk.
παλμός, 'vibration', and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. Gk. παλμός derives from the base
of πάλλειν, 'to shake, throw', and stands in
gradational relationship to πελεμίζειν, 'to
shake', πόλεμος, 'fight, war'. See polemic. For
the etymology of γράφειν see -graph.

## sympathetic
sympathetic, adj. — ModL. sympathetica, fr. Gk.
συμπαθητικός, 'sympathetic', fr. συμπαθής,
'affected by like feelings'. See sympathy. — In
its anatomical sense {sympathetic nerve) the
word derives fr. Modern L. {nervus)
sympathies, which was coined by Winslow. See Joseph
HyrtI, Onomatologia anatomica, pp. 514-17.
Derivative: sympatketic-al-ly, adv.

## sympntnism
sympntnism, п., suggestibility. — See sympathy
and -ism.

## sympathize
sympathize, intr. v. — MF. (= F.) sympathiser,
fr. sympathie, fr. L. sympathia. See sympathy
and -ize.
Derivatives: sympathiz-er, п., sympathiz-ing,
adj., sympatkiz-ing-ly, adv.

## sympathy
sympathy, n. — L. sympathia, fr. Gk. συμπάθεια,
'fellow-feeling sympathy', fr. συμπαθής,
'affected by like feelings', fr. συμπαθεΐν, 'to be
affected by like feelings', lit. 'to suffer with', fr. σύν
(see syn-) and πά&ος, 'suffering'. See pathos and
cp. antipathy, apathy, homeopathy.

## sympetalous
sympetalous, adj., having the petals united (bot.)
Formed fr. sym- and -petalous.

## symphonic
symphonic, adj., pertaining to a symphony. — Gk.
συμφωνικός, fr. συμφωνία. See symphony and
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: symphonic-al-ly, adv.

## symphonious
symphonious, adj., characterized by harmony. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. συμφωνία. See
symphony.
Derivative: symphonious-ly, adv.

## symphonize
symphonize, v., to harmonize. — See next word
and -ize.

## symphony
symphony, n. — ME. sympkonie, fr. OF. simpho-
nie (F. sympkonie), fr. L. symphonia, fr. Gk.
συμφωνία, 'concord of sound, harmony,
agreement', fr. σύμφωνος, 'agreeing in sound', fr.
σύν (see syn·) and φωνή, 'sound'. See phone,
'speech sound', and cp. words there referred to.

## Symphoricarpos
Symphoricarpos, п., a genus of plants, the snow-
berry (bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk.
σύμφορος, 'accompanying', and καρπός,'fruit';
so called from the clustered berries. The first
element derives from the stem of συμφέρειν, 'to
bear together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and φέρειν, 'to
bear, carry'; see bear, 'to carry'. For the
etymology of καρπός see carpel.

## symphyllous
symphyllous, adj., having leaves joined together
(bot.) — Formed fr. sym- and -phyllous.

## symphyseal
symphyseal, adj., pertaining to symphysis. — See
next word and adj. suff. -al.

## symphysis
symphysis, п., union (anat. and zool.) — Medical
L., fr. Gk. σύμφυσις, 'a growing together', fr.
συμφύειν, 'to cause to grow together', fr. σύν
(see syn-) and φύειν, 'to bring forth, produce,
make to grow'. See physio-.

## Symphytum
Symphytum, п., a genus of plants, the comfrey
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σύμφυτον, 'comfrey',
lit. 'grown together', prop. neut. verbal adj. of
συμφ'ύειν. See prec. word and -phyte.

## sympiesometer
sympiesometer, sympiezometer, п., a barometer
for measuring atmospheric pressure from its
action on a liquid. — Compounded of Gk. συμ-
πίεσις, 'compression', and μέτρον, 'measure'.
The first element derives fr. συμπιέζειν, 'to
compress', fr. σύν (see syn-) and πιέζειν, 'to
compress'; see piezo-. For the second element see
meter, 'poetical rhythm'. Cp. piezometer.

## Symplegades
Symplegades, n. pi., two rocks at the entrance of
the Hellespont, which clashed together and
crushed whatever came between them (Greek
mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Συμπληγάδες (scil.
πέτοαι), 'the Clashing (Rocks)', fr. σύν (see
syn-) and the stem of πλήσσειν, 'to strike',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:764 COLUMN:3 -->
whence also πληγή, 'blow, stroke'. See plague
and words there referred to and cp. esp. Ple-
gadis.

## Symplocarpus
Symplocarpus, п., a genus of plants, the skunk
cabbage (bot.) — ModL.., shortened from *Sym-
ploco-carpus (see haplology), fr. Gk. συμπλοκή,
'connection', and καρπός, 'fruit'. The first
element is formed fr. σύν (see syn-) and πλοκή,
'the act of plaiting', which is rel. to πλέκειν, 'to
twine, twist, plait'; see ply, 'to bend'. For the
second element see carpel.

## Symplocos
Symplocos, п., a genus of plants, the sweetleaf
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. σύμπλοκος,
'connected', which is rel. to συμπλοκή, 'connection', (see
prec. word); so called in allusion to the united
stamens.

## sympodium
sympodium, п., an apparent main axis composed
of successive branches (bot.) — ModL., formed
fr. sym- and Gk. πόδιον, dimin. of πους,
gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See podium.
Derivatives: sympodi-al, adj., sympodi-al-ly,
adv.

## symposiac
symposiac, adj., pertaining to a symposium. — L.
symposiacus, fr. Gk. συμποσιακός, 'pertaining
to, or fit for, a drinking party', fr. συμπόσιον.
See symposium and -ac.

## symposiaL adj.
symposiaL adj., pertaining to a symposium. —
Formed fr. symposium with adj. suff. -al.

## symposiarch
symposiarch, п., president of a symposium. — Gk
συμποσίαρχος, compounded of συμπόσιον,
'drinkingparty', and άρχος, 'leader, chief ruler'.
See next word and -arch.

## symposium
symposium, п., 1) in ancient Greece, a drinking
party; 2) a meeting, conference for conversation
or discussion. — L., fr. Gk. συμπόσιον, 'a
drinking feast', lit. 'a drinking together', fr. σύν (see
syn-) and πόσις, 'a drinking', which is rel. to.
πίνειν, 'to drink'. See potion.

## symptom
symptom, n. — Late L. symptdma, fr. Gk.
σύμπτωμα, 'chance, occurrence', lit. *a falling
together', fr. συμπΐπτειν, 'to fall together', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and πΐπτειν, 'to fall', which
stands for *πϊ-πτειν, fr. *pt-, zero degree of
I.-E. base *pet-, 'to fly, to fall'. See feather and
cp. ptomaine, ptosis, anaptotic, aptotic,
asymptote, diptote, triptote.

## symptomatic
symptomatic, adj. — Late L. symptomatica, fr.
symptdma, gen. -atis. Cp. Gk. συμπτωματικός,
'accidental, casual', and see prec. word and 1st
-atic.
Derivatives: symptomatic-al, adj., symptomatic-
al-ly, adv.

## symptomatology
symptomatology, п., the study of symptoms. —
Medical L. symptdmatologia, compounded of
Gk. σύμπτωμα, gen. συμπτώματος, 'chance,
occurrence', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See symptom and -logy.
Derivatives: symptomatolog-ic-al, adj., symp-
tomatolog-ic-al-ly, adv.

## syn-
syn-, pref. meaning 'with, together with'. — Gk.
σύν, ξύν 'with, together with' (whence ξϋνάς,
'commun'); of uncertain origin. Cp. sy-, syl-,
sym-, sys-,

## synaeresis
synaeresis, syneresis, п., coalescence; contraction
of two vowels into one syllable. — Gk. συν-
αίρεσις, 'a grasping together, contraction', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and αϊρεσις, 'a taking for
oneself, a choice'. See heresy and cp. aphaeresis,
diaeresis.

## synagogal
synagogal, adj. — See synagogue and adj. suff.
-al.
synagogica], adj. — See synagogne and -ical.

## synagogue
synagogue, synagog, n. — ME. synagoge, fr. OF.
sinagoge (F. synagogue), fr. Late L. synagoga, fr.
Gk. συναγωγή, 'assembly, synagogue', lit. 'a
bringing together', fr. συνάγειν, 'to lead or bring
together', which is formed fr. σύν (see syn-) and
άγειν, 'to lead'. See agent, adj., and cp. ngon-
istic. Gk. συναγωγή is prop, a loan translation
of Heb. к neseih, 'assembly* (whence beth к -
neseth, 'synagogue') (lit. 'house of assembly'),
fr. kanas, 'he assembled'. Cp. Kneseth.

## synallagmatic
synallagmatic, adj., expressing reciprocal
obligations. — Gk. συναλλαγματικός, fr.
συνάλλαγμα, gen. συναλλάγματος, 'covenant,
contract', fr. σύν (see syn-) and άλλαγμα, 'a thing
taken in exchange', from the stem of άλλάσσειν,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:765 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SYNALOEPHA | 738 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:765 COLUMN:1 -->
'to exchange, barter', prop, 'to make other than
it is', fr. άλλος, 'another', which is cogn. with L.
alius, of s.m. See else and cp. alias. For the
ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## synaloepha
synaloepha, synalepha, п., contraction of two
syllables· — L. synaloepha, fr. Gk. συναλοιφή, lit.
'a smearing together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and
αλοιφή, 'anything to sme'kr with', which is rel.
to άλείφειν, 'to smear over', and to λίπος, 'fat'.
See adipose.

## synangium
synangium, п., the common bloodvessel of several
arteries (anat. and zool.) — Medical L., formed
fr. syn- and Gk. άγγεΐον, 'vessel'. See angio- and
cp. sporangium.

## synantherous
synantherous, adj., having the anthers united
(bot.) — See syn-, anther and -ous.

## synanthous
synanthous, adj., producing flowers and leaves at
the same time (bot.) — Formed fr. syn-, Gk.
άυθ-ος, 'flower' (see anther), and -ous.

## syiiaphea
syiiaphea, synapheia, п., metrical continuity in
the lines of a verse (Greek pros.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. συνάφεια, 'combination union, junction',
fr. συναφής, 'united, connected', from the stem
of συνάπτειν, 'to join together'. See next word.

## synapse
synapse, п., the junction between two nerve cells
(physiol.) — Gk. σύναψης, 'contact, point or
line of junction', rel. to συνάπτειν, *to join
together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and άπτειν, 'to touch,
fasten; to kindle'; see apsis. The word synapse
was introduced by the English physiologist Sir
Michael Foster (1836-1907) at the suggestion of
the English classical scholar Arthur Woollgar
Verral (1851-1912).

## synarthrosis
synarthrosis, п., an immovable articulation (anal.)
— Medical L., fr. Gk. συνάρ&ρωσις, 'a joining
together', fr. συναρθροϋν, 'to join together', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and άρ&ρον, 'a joint'. See arthro-
and -osis.

## Syncarida
Syncarida, п., a division of crustaceans (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. syn- and Gk. καρίς, gen.
καρίδος, 'shrimp, prawn'. See Caridea.

## syncarp
syncarp, п., a multiple fruit (bot.) — Formed fr.
syn- and Gk. καρπός, 'fruit'. See carpel.
Derivative: syncarp-ous, adj.

## synchondrosis
synchondrosis, п., articulation of bones by means
of cartilages (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
συγχόνδρωσις, 'a growing together into one
cartilage', fr. σύν (see syn-), χόνδρος, 'cartilage*
(see chondri), and suff. -osis.

## synchronic
synchronic, also synchronical, adj., belonging to,
or occurring at, the same time. — F. synchro-
nique, fr. Late L. synchronus. See synchronous
and -ic, resp. -leal.
Derivative: synchronical-ly, adv.

## synchronism
synchronism, п., state of being synchronous. —
ModL. synchronismus, fr. Gk. συγχρονισμός,
fr. συγχρονίζειν. See synchronize and -ism.

## synchronistic
synchronistic, adj., synchronous. — See prec.
word and -istic.
Derivatives: synchronistic-al, adj., synchronis-
tic-al-ly, adv.

## synchronize
synchronize, intr. v., to happen at the same time;
tr. v., to cause to happen at the same time. —
Gk. συγχρονίζειν, 'to be contemporary with',
fr. σύγχρονος. See next word and -ize.
Derivatives: synchroniz-ation, n.f synchroniz-er,
n.

## synchronous
synchronous, adj., occurring at the same time. —
Late L. synchronus, a loan word fr. Gk.
σύγχρονος, 'contemporary', fr. σύν (see syn-) and
χρόνος, 'time'. See chronic. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, Gk. -ος, see -ous.
Derivatives: synchronous-ly, adv., synchronous-
ness, n.

## synchrony
synchrony, п., synchronism. — See synchronism
and -y (representing Gk. -ία, -εία).

## Synchytrium
Synchytrium, п., a genus of algae (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. syn- and Gk. χύτριον, dimin. of
χύτρα, 'earthen pot', which is rel. to χυτός,
'poured, shed', verbal adj. of χεΐν, 'to pour'.
See chyle and cp. words there referred to.

## synclastic
synclastic, adj., curved similarly in all directions.
— Formed fr. syn-, Gk. κλαστός, 'broken',
verbal adj. of κλαν, 'to break' (see clastic), and
adj. suff. -ic.

## synclinal
synclinal, adj., inclined downward on both sides.
— Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. συγκλϊνειν,
'to incline, lean', fr. σύν (see syn-) and κλϊνειν,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:765 COLUMN:2 -->
'to slope, lie'. See clinical.

## syncline
syncline, п., a synclinal fold. — See prec word
(geol.)

## syncopate
syncopate, tr. v., 1) to shorten by syncope; 2)
(music) to change the rhythm by displacement
of the beat. — Late L. syncopatus, pp. of synco-
pare, 'to faint away, swoon; to syncopate'. See
syncope and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: syncopat-ίοη, n.

## syncope
syncope, п., 1) fainting, swooning; 2) contraction
of a word by the loss of one or more interior
letters; 3) (music) the change of rhythm by
displacement of the beat. — Late L. syncope, syn-
copa, fr. Gk. συγκοπή, *a cutting up, cutting
short; syncope', from the stem of συγκόπτειν,
'to cut up', fr. σύν (see syn-) and κόπτει-ν, 'to
cut'. See capon and cp. comma, Coptis, pericope.

## syncoptic
syncoptic, adj., syncopic. — Formed with suff. -ic
fr. Gk. συγκόπτειν, 'to cut up'. See prec. word.

## syncotyledonous
syncotyledonous, adj., having the cotyledons
united (bot.) — Formed fr. syn- and cotyledonous.

## syncretic
syncretic, adj., characterized by syncretism. —
See syncretism and -ic.

## syncretism
syncretism, п., reconciliation of different beliefs
in religion, philosophy, etc. — F. syncretisme, fr.
Gk. συγκρητισμός, 'union', fr. συγκρητίζειν',
'to combine against a common enemy', fr. σύν
(see syn-) and the stem seen also in κεραννύναι,
'to mix, blend',κρασις,'mixture'. See crater and
cp. crasis. For the ending see suff. -ism.

## syncretist
syncretist, п., one who advocates syncretism. —
See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: syncreiist-ic, syncretisti-ic-al, adjs.

## syncretize
syncretize, tr. v., to attempt to reconcile; intr. v.,
to be reconciled to practice syncretism. — Gk.
συγκρητίζειν, 'to combine against a common
enemy'. See syncretism and -ize.

## syncytium
syncytium, п., a tissue containing many nuclei
(biol.) — ModL., formed fr. syn- and Gk.
κύτος, 'a hollow vessel*. See -cyte, and 1st -ium.
syndacty], adj., having two or more digits united
(zool. and anat.) — Formed fr. syn- and Gk.
δάκτυλος, 'finger*. See dactyl.
Derivatives: syndactyl-ism, п., syndactyl-ous,
adj., syndactyl-y, n.

## synderesis
synderesis, п., synteresis. — A var. of synteresis;
cp. F. synderese. The change of Mo d is prob.
due to the Medieval Greek pronunciation of nt
as nd.

## syndesmo-
syndesmo-, combining form denoting ligaments.
— Gk. σύνδεσμος, 'that which binds together,
fastening, conjunction', fr. σύν (see syn-) and
δεσμός, 'band', which is cogn. with διά-δημα,
'a headband, fillet'. See diadem.

## syndesmosis
syndesmosis, п., articulation of parts of bones by
means of ligaments (anat.) — Formed with suff.
-osis fr. Gk. σύνδεσμος, 'that which binds
together'. See prec. word.

## syndetic
syndetic, adj., connecting.—Formed with adj. suff.
-ic fr. Gk. σύνδετος, 'bound together*, verbal
adj. of συνδεΐν, 'to bind together', whence also
σύνδεσμος, 'that which binds together'. See
prec. word and -etic.

## syndic
syndic, п., the accredited agent or manager of a
corporation, esp. of a university. — F., fr. Late
L. syndicus, fr. Gk. σύνδικος, One who helps in
a court of justice, advocate', fr. σύν (see syn-)
and δίκη, 'custom, usage; judgment, justice',
which is cogn. with L. dicere, 'to show, tell'. See
diction and words there referred to and cp. esp.
dicast.
Derivatives: syndic-al, adj., syndi-cal-ism, п.,
syndic-al-ist, adj. and п., syndic-al-ist-ic, adj.,
syndic-al-ize, tr. v.

## syndicate
syndicate, п., 1) a body of syndics or the office of
a syndic; 2) an association of bankers,
merchants, etc., to carry out some important
enterprise; 3) an association of publishers for
purchasing articles, stories, etc., and publishing
them simultaneously in a number of newspapers
or periodicals. — ML. syndicatus, prop. pp.
of syndicare, 'to examine, censure', fr. Late L.
syndicus. See syndic and subst. suff. -ate.

## syndicate
syndicate, tr. v., ]) to form into a syndicate; 2) to
sell articles, etc., for simultaneous publication.
— Partly fr. ML. syndicatus, pp. of syndicare,
partly fr. syndicate, n. (q.v.)

## syndrome
syndrome, п., a number of symptoms occurring

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:765 COLUMN:3 -->
together and characterizing a disease. —
Medical L., fr. Gk. συνδρομή, 'a running together,
concourse', from the stem of συνδραμεΐν, 'to
run together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and δραμεΐν,
'to run*. See dromedary and cp. prodrome,

## synecdoche
synecdoche, п., figure of speech in which a part is
used for a whole or vice versa (rhet.) — L., fr.
Gk. συνεκδοχή, lit. 'a receiving together or
jointly', which is rel. to συνεκδέχεσ&αι, 'to receive
together or jointly', fr. σύν (see syn-) and
έκδέχεσθ-αι, 'to receive', fr. έκ, 'out of (see ec-),
and δέχεσ&αι, 'to receive', which is cogn. with
L. decet, decere, 'to be seemly or fitting'. See
decent and cp. dogma and the second element in
pandect.

## Synedrion
Synedrion, also Synedrium, п., the Sanhedrin. —
Gk. συνέδρίον, lit. 'a sitting together'. See
Sanhedrin.

## synergetic
synergetic, adj., working together. — Gk. συν-
εργητικός fr. συνεργεΐν, 'to work together*, fr.
συνεργός, 'working together, co-operative', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and έργον, *work'. See work and
cp. ergon and words there referred to.

## synergism
synergism, п., 1) a working together,
co-operation (said esp. of drugs; 2) in theology, the
doctrine that divine grace and human will
co-operate in the work of regeneration. — Formed
with suff. -ism fr. Gk. συνεργός. See prec. word.

## synergist
synergist, п., an adherent of the doctrine of
synergism. — See prec. word and -ist.
Derivatives: synergist-ic, synergist-ic-al, adj.

## synergy
synergy, п., combined action of bodily organs. —
Gk. συνεργία, 'co-operation', fr. συνεργός. See
synergetic and -y (representing Gk. -£ct).

## synesis
synesis, п., construction according to sense
against the strict requirements of syntax
(gram.) — Gk. σύνεσις, 'comprehension,
intelligence', lit. 'a coming together', fr. συνιέναι,
'to bring together' (in the middle voice, 'to
come together'), fr. σύν (see syn-) and ίέναι, 'to
move forward, throw, send*, which stands for
*yi-ye-nai and is cogn. with h.jace're, 'to throw*.
See jet, 'to spirt forth', and cp. catheter,

## syngenesis
syngenesis, п., reproduction through the union of
two parents. — ModL., formed fr. syn- and
genesis.

## Syngnathidae
Syngnathidae, n. pi., a family of fishes comprising
the seahorses and pipefishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., formed fr. pref. syn-, Gk. γνά&ος, 'jaw*
(see gnathic), and suff. -idae.

## syngnathous
syngnathous, adj., pertaining to the family
Syngnathidae. — See Syngnathidae and -ous.

## synizesis
synizesis, п., contraction of two vowels (pros.) —
L., fr. Gk. συνίζησις, lit. *a sitting together*, fr.
συνίζειν, 'to sit together*, fr. σύν (see syn-) and
ϊζειν, 'to sit', which is rel. to Εζεσ&αι, 'to sit',
and cogn. with L. sedere, *to sit'. See sedentary
and cp. words there referred to.

## synod
synod, п., an ecclesiastical council. — ME., fr.
Late L. synodus, fr. Gk. σύνοδος, "meeting,
assembly', fr. σύν (see syn-) and οδός, 'way*. See
odograph and cp. the second element in anode,
cathode, stomodeum.

## synodal
synodal, adj., pertaining to a synod. — Late L.
synodalis, fr. synodus. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.

## synodical
synodical, also synodic, adj., pertaining to a synod.
— Late L. synodicus, fr. Gk. συνοδικός, fr.
σύνοδος. See synod and the suffixes -ic and -al.
Derivative: synodical-ly, adv.

## Synodontidae
Synodontidae, n. pi., the lizard fishes (ichthyol.)
— ModL., formed fr. syn-, the stem of Gk.
οδών, gen. οδόντος, 'tooth' (see odonto-), and
suff. -idae.

## synoecious
synoecious, adj., having male and female flowers
in the same flower head (bot.) — Formed fr. pref.
syn-, Gk. οίκος, 'house' (see economy), and suff.
-ous. Cp. dioecious.
Derivatives: synoecious-ly, adv., synoecious-
ness, n.

## synoecism
synoecism, п., the union of several towns into one
city-state (Greek antiq.) — Gk. συνοικισμός, 'a
living together', fr. συνοικίζει, 'to cause to live
together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and οίκίζειν, 'to
found (a colony), settle, colonize', fr. οΐκος,
'house'. See economy and cp. synoecious. For
the ending see suff. -ism.

## synomosy
synomosy, п., a political society bound by oath

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:766 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 739 | SYZYGY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:766 COLUMN:1 -->
{Greek antiq.) — Gk. συνωμοσία, 'a swearing
together', fr. συνομνύναι, 'to swear together', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and όμνύναι, 'to swear', which is
prob. cogn. with OI. amiti, 'presses on; asserts
emphatically*. Cp. the second element in swami.

## synonym
synonym, n. — ME. sinonyme, fr. Late L. syno-
nymum, fr. Gk. συνώνυμον, neut. of the adj.
συνώνυμος, 'synonymous', used as a noun. The
literal meaning of συνώνυμος is 'having the
same name as'; it is formed fr. σύν (see syn-)
and βνυμα, dial, form of ίίναμα, 'name'. See
and name cp. onomato-. Cp. also antonym,
homonym, anonymous.
Derivatives: synonym-ic, adj., synonymity (q.v.)

## synonymity
synonymity, п., the quality or state of being
synonymous. — Formed fr- synonymous with suff.
-ity.

## synonymize
synonymize, tr. v., to give a synonym or
synonyms (for a word); intr. v., to use synonyms. —
See synonym and -ize.

## synonymous
synonymous, adj. — ML. syndnymus, fr. Gk.
συνώνυμος. See synonym. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## synonymy
synonymy, п., ]) the study of synonyms; 2) a list
of synonyms. — Late L. synonymia, fr. Gk.
συνωνυμία, fr. συνώνυμος. See synonym and -y
(representing Gk. -to·).

## synopsis
synopsis, п., a general view, outline. — Late L.,
fr. Gk. σύνοψις, 'general view', lit. 'a seeing
together', fr. σύν (see βνη-^βηύοψις, 'sight, view'.
See -opsis,

## synoptic
synoptic, adj., pertaining to a synopsis. — ModL.
synopiicus, fr. Gk. συνοπτικός, 'taking a general
view', fr. σύνοψις. See prec. word and optic.
Derivatives: synoptic, п., synoptic-al, adj.,
synoptxc-al-ly, adv., synopt-ist, n.

## synosteology
synosteology, п., the study of the joints of the
body, arthrology. — Formed fr. syn- and
osteology.

## synosteosis
synosteosis, synostosis, п., another word for
ankylosis (anat. and physiol.) — Formed fr. syn-,
Gk. όστέον, 'bone', and suff. -osis.

## synostotic
synostotic, adj., pertaining to synostosis. — See
prec. word and -otic.

## synovia
synovia, п., an albuminous fluid secreted by
certain glands {anat.) — Medical L., coined by
Paracelsus.
Derivative: synovi-al, adj.

## synovitis
synovitis, п., inflammation of the synovial
membrane (med.) — Medical L., formed fr. prec.
word with sufT. -itis.

## syntactical
syntactical, also syntactic, adj., pertaining to
syntax. — ModL. syntacticus, fr. Gk.
συντακτικός, 'putting together in order*, fr.
συντάκτης, 'put in order, arranged', verbal adj. of
συντάσσειν. See next word. For the ending see
the suffixes -ic and -a).
Derivatives: syntactical-ly, adv., syntactic-ian,
n.

## syntax
syntax, n. — F. syntaxe, fr. Late L. syntaxis, fr.
Gk. σύνταξις, *a putting together, a putting
together of words, syntax', from the stem of
συντάσσειν, 'to put together in order', fr. σύν
(see syn-) and τάσσειν, Чо order, arrange'. See
taxis and cp. prec. word.

## synttresis
synttresis, п., innate knowledge of right and
wrong. — ML. synteresis, fr. Gk. συντήρησις,
'preservation', fr. συντηρεΐν, 'to preserve, look
after', fr. σύν (see syn-) and τηρεΐν, 'to watch
over, take care of, guard', which prob. derives
fr. I.-E. base *qwei-, *qwi-, 'to respect, consider',
whence also Gk. ποινή, 'bloodmoney, fine,
penalty, punishment'. See penal and cp. synderesis.
Cp. also the second element in Pinnotheres.

## synthesis
synthesis, п., the act of putting together;
combination. — L., fr. Gk. σύν&εσις, 'a putting together,
composition', from the stem of συντι&έναί, 'to
put together', fr. σύν (see syn-) and τι&έναι, Чо
put, place'. See thesis and cp. next word.
Derivatives: synthes-Ш, п., synthes-ize, tr. and
intr. v., synthes-iz-ation, n.

## synthetic
synthetic, adj., pertaining to, or produced by,
synthesis. — ModL. syntketicus (whence also F.
synthetique), fr. Gk. συν&ετικός, 'constructive',
fr. σύν&ετος, 'put together, constructed,
compound*, verbal adj. of συντι&έναι, Чо put
together*. See synthesis and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: synthetic, п., syntketic-al, adj.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:766 COLUMN:2 -->
syntkeiic-al-ly, adv.

## synthetist
synthetist, п., a synthesist. — Formed with suff.
-ist fr. Gk. σύνθετος, 'put together'. See prec.
word.

## synthetize
synthetize, tr. and intr. v., to synthesize. —
Formed with suff. -ize fr. Gk; σύνθετος, 'put
together'. See synthetic.

## syntonic
syntonic, adj., pertaining to, or placed in,
resonance. — See syntony and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives:syntonic-aly ad}.,syntomc-al-ly, adv.

## syntonize
syntonize, tr. v., to place in resonance with each
other. — See next word and -ize.
Derivatives: syntoniz-ation, п., syntoniz-er, n.

## syntony
syntony, resonance. — Gk. συντονία, 'agreement'
fr. σύντονος, 'in harmony', lit. 'strained tight',
fr. σύν (see syn-) and τόνος, 'pitch of voice', lit.
4hat which is stretched'. See tone and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## syphil-
syphil-, form of sypnilo- before a vowel.

## syphilis
syphilis, п., an infectious venereal disease. —
ModL., from the title of the work by Girolamo
Fracastoro, Syphilis sive de morbo Gallico ( =
Syphilis, or the French disease'), published at
Verona in 1530; so named after the hero Sypki-
lus, a shepherd whose name lit. means 'friend of
swine4, fr. Gk. σΰς (gen. συός) = υς (gen. ύός),
'swine', and φίλος, "friend'. For the first
element see sow, п., for the second see pnilo-.
Derivatives: syphil-itic, adj., syphil-ize, tr. v.,
syphiloid, adj., sypkilous (q.v.)

## sypnilo-
sypnilo-, before a vowel syphil-, combining form
for sypkilis. — See syphilis.

## syphilology
syphilology, п., the study of syphilis. —
Compounded of sypnilo and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
One who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: syphilolog-ist, n.

## syphilous
syphilous, adj., syphilitic. — A hybrid coined fr.
syphilis and -ous, a suff. of Latin origin.

## syren
syren, n. — See siren.

## Syria
Syria, п., name of a country in Asia on the
Mediterranean Sea. — L. Syria, fr. Gk. Συρία,
'Syria', fr. Σύριοι, 'the Syrians', a name orig. given
to the Assyrians (see Herodotus 7, 63), Σύριοι
being an aphetic form of Άσσύριοι,
'Assyrians', fr. Άσσυρία, 'Assyria'. See Assyria.

## Syriac
Syriac, adj. and п., (pertaining to) the Syrian
language.— L. Syriacus, 'Syrian', fr. Gk. Συριακός,
fr. Συρία. See prec. word and -ac.

## Syriacism
Syriacism, п., a Syriac idiom. — See Syriac and
-ism and cp. Syriasm.

## Syrian
Syrian, n. and adj. — ME. sirien, fr. MF. Sirien
(F. Syrien), formed with suff. -ien fr. L. Syrius,
'Syrian*, fr. Syria. See Syria and -an and cp.
sorghum.

## Syriasm
Syriasm, п., a Syriac idiom. — Formed fr. Gk.
Συρ(.άζειν, a supposed var. of Συρίζειν, 'to
speak Syriac', fr. Σύρος, 'Syrian'. See Syro-.

## syring-
syring-, form of syringo- before a vowel.

## Syringa
Syringa, п., a genus of plants: ]) the mock
orange; later applied to 2) the lilac. — ModL., fr.
Gk. σΰριγξ, gen. σΰριγγος, 'pipe, tube'; the
mock orange was so called in allusion to the use
of its hollow stems for making pipes. See next
word and cp. seringa.

## syringe
syringe, п., a narrow tube for injecting a liquid in
a stream. — ML. siringa, syringa, fr. Gk.
σΰριγξ, gen. συρίγγος, 'pipe, shepherd's pipe,
tube, whistle'. See syrinx.
Derivative: syringe, tr. v.

## syringeal
syringeal, adj., pertaining to the syrinx. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. Gk. σΰριγξ, gen. συριγ-
γος, *pipe, tube*. See syrinx.

## syringitis
syringitis, п., inflammation of the Eustachian
tube {med.) — Medical L., formed fr. syrinx
with suff. -itis.
syringo·, before a vowel syring-, combining form
meaning 'pipe, fistula; spine*. — Gk. σϋρίγγο-,
σϋριγγ-, fr. σΰριγξ, gen. συριγγος, *pipe,
tube'. See syrinx.

## syringotomy
syringotomy, п., operation on the anal fistula
{med.) — Compounded of syringo- and Gk.
-τομία, 'a cutting of, fr.τομή, *a cutting'. See
-tomy.

## syrinx
syrinx, п., anything tubular. — Gk. σΰριγξ, gen.
σΰριγγος, 'pipe, shepherd's pipe, tube, whistle',
rel. to σΰρίζειν, Чо pipe, whistle, hiss*, from the
I.-E. imitative base *swer-, *sur-, *surr-, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:766 COLUMN:3 -->
sound', whence also Ol. svarati, 'sounds, re-
sounds', L. susurrus, 'whisper'. See susurration.
For the suff. of σΰριγξ ср. φόρμιγξ, 'lyre',
σάλπι,γξ, 'trumpet* (see salpingo-).

## syrma
syrma, п., a trailing robe worn esp. by tragic
actors {Greek antiq.) — Gk. σύρμα, lit. 'that which
is trailed or dragged', fr. σόρειν, 'to trail, drag,
sweep away', which is rel. to σαίρειν, 'to sweep,
clean', συρφός, συρφετός, 'sweepings', and
possibly cogn. with Goth, af-swairban, Чо wipe off',
ON. sverfa, Чо scour, file', OE. sweorfan, Чо
scrub, file'. See swerve and cp. Syrtis and the
second element in Hedysarum. For the ending
of syrma see suff. -ma.

## Syro-
Syro-, combining form meaning 'Syrian and',
'Syriac and'. — Gk. Σύρο-, fr. Σύρος, 'Syrian'
(see Herodotus 2, 104), which is prob. a back
formation fr. Συρία, 'Syria'. See Syria.

## syrphus fly
syrphus fly, a fly of the genus Syrphus. — ModL.
Syrphus, fr. Gk. σύρφος (Hesychius), 'gnat',
which is perh. rel. to σέρφος 'a small winged
insect', prob. *a kind of gnat'.

## syrt
syrt, п., quicksand {rare). — L. syrtis, fr. Gk.
σϋρτις. See next word.

## Syrtis
Syrtis, п., the. name of two quicksands off the
northern coast of Africa, whence syrtis,
quicksand. — L., fr. Gk. Σύρτις, σύρτις, fr. σϋρειν,
'to trail, drag, sweep away'. See syrma.

## syrup
syrup, n. — A var. spelling of sirup.
Derivatives: syrup, tr. v., syrup-yt adj.

## sys-
sys-, pref. — Gk. συσ-, assimilated form of συν-
before σ (if this latter is followed by a vowel).
See syn-.

## syssarcosis
syssarcosis, п., the union of bones by means of
muscles (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. συσ-
σάρκωσις, 'a being overgrown with fiesh', fr.
συσσαρκοΰν, 'to cover over with fiesh*, fr. σύν
(see syn-) and σαρξ, gen. σαρκός, 'fiesh'. See
sarco- and -osis.

## syssitia
syssitia, п., communal meals in Sparta and the
cities of Crete (Greek antiq.) — Gk. συσσίτια,
lit. 'the act of messing together', fr. σύσσιτος,
'messmate', fr. σύν (see syn-) and σίτος, 'grain,
food'. See sito- and 1st -ia.

## systaltic
systaltic, adj., alternately contracting and
dilating. — Late L. systalticus, fr. Gk.
συσταλτικός, 'drawing together', from the stem of
συστέλλειν, 'to draw together'. See systole and
adj. suff. -ic.

## system
system, n. — Late L. systema, fr. Gk. σύστημα,
'composition', lit. 'a placing together', from the
stem of συνίστάναι, Чо place together', which is
formed fr. σύν (see syn-) and Ιστάναι, 'to place;
to stand'. See state and cp. words there referred
to.
Derivatives: systematic (q.v.), system-ις, adj.,
system-ic-al-ly, adv., system-less, adj.

## systematic
systematic, adj. — Gk. συστηματικός, from
σύστημα, gen. συστήματος. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: systematic-al, adj., systematic-al-ly,
adv.

## systematism
systematism, п., the practice of systematizing. —
Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk. σύστημα, gen.
συστήματος. See system.

## systematist
systematist, п., a systematizer. — Formed with
suff. -ist fr. Gk. σύστημα, gen. συστήματος. See
system.

## systematize
systematize, tr. v., to make into a system. —
Formed with suff. -ize from the stem of Gk.
σύστημα, gen. συστήματος. See system.
Derivatives: systematiz-ation, п., systematiz-er,
n.

## systole
systole, п., periodic contraction of the heart and
arteries, the opposite of diastole. — ModL., fr.
Gk. συστολή, 'contraction*, which is rel. to
συστέλλειν, Чо draw together*, fr. σύν (see
syn-) and στέλλειν, Чо set, place'. See stail and
cp. diastole.

## systyle
systyle, adj., with columns placed two diameters
from one another {arckit.) — L. systylost fr. Gk.
σύστΰλος, 'with columns standing close', fr.
σύν (see syn-) and στύλος, 'column'. See style,
'gnomon'.

## systylous
systylous, adj., having the styles united. — See
prec. word and -ous.

## syzygy
syzygy, п., the conjunction or opposition of a
heavenly body with the sun {astron.) — Late L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:767 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: SYZYGY 740 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:767 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: syzygi-al, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:767 COLUMN:2 -->

## syzygia
syzygia, fr. Gk. συζυγία, 'yoke, pair', fr. σύν
(see syn-) and ζυγόν, 'yoke'. See zygo-, yoke.
For the ending see -y (representing Gk. -lot).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:768 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:768 COLUMN:1 -->

## -t
-t, suff. forming past participles and participial
adjectives, as in gil-ι, slep-t, spen-t; a var. pfl st
-ed (q.v.)

## -t
-t, var. of subst. suff. -th, as in keigh-t, sleigh-t.

## taal
taal, п., the Dutch dialect spoken in S. Africa. —
Du. taal, 'speech, language', fr. MDu. tale,
which is related to E. tale (q.v.)

## tab
tab, п., 1) a small flap; 2) a tag. — Of uncertain
origin.
Derivatives: lab, tr. v., to furnish with tabs,
tabb-er, n.

## tabard
tabard, п., a short-sleeved or sleeveless coat worn
by heralds. — ME., fr. OF. tabard, tabart, which
is of unknown origin. Cp. It. tabarro, Sp. tabar-
do. Cp. taberdar.
Derivative: tabard-ed, adj.

## tabaret
tabaret, п., a fabric of satin and watered silk. —
Prob. related to tubby.

## tabasco
tabasco, п., a pepper sauce. — Trade name for a
sauce made from a species of capsicum;
suggested by Tabasco, name of a river and State in
Mexico.

## tabasheer
tabasheer, tabashir, п., a siliceous substance found
in the joints of the bamboo. — Arabo-Persian
tabashir, 'chalk, mortar'.

## tabatiere
tabatiere, п., a snuffbox. — F., fr. earlier taba-
quiere, it. tabac, 'tobacco'. See tobacco.

## tabby
tabby, п., a kind of watered silk. — F. tabis, fr.
Sp. tabi, fr. Arab, attabi, fr. at-Attdbiycl·', name
of a suburb of Bagdad, where this kind of silk
stuff was fabricated. The suburb was named
after Prince Attab, a descendant of the Om-
miads. Cp. tabinet, tobine.
Derivative: tabby, tr. v,

## tabefaction
tabefaction, п., emaciation. — Formed with suff.
-ion fr. L. tdbefactus, pp. of tubefacere. See next
word.

## tnbefy
tnbefy, tr. and intr. v., to waste away (rare) —
MF. tabefier, fr. L. tubefacere, 'to melt, dissolve',
which is compounded of L. tabes, 'a wasting
away', andfacere,'to make, do*. See tabes and-fy.

## tabeDion
tabeDion, п.; a scrivener in the Roman Empire
and in France (until 1789). — Late L. tabellio,
gen. -onis, fr. L. tabella, 'tablet; document',
dirnin. of tabula, 'tablet'. See tuble.

## taberdar
taberdar, п., foundation scholar of Queen's
College in Oxford. — Lit. 'wearer of a tabard' (see
tabard); so called from the gown formerly worn
by such a scholar.

## tabernacle
tabernacle, п., I) a temporary shelter; 2) (cap.)
the portable sanctuary carried by the Jews in the
wilderness. — F., fr. L. tabernaculum, 'tent',
dimin. of taberna, 'hut, booth'. See tavern and
-cule,
Derivative: tabernacle, tr. and intr. v.

## tabernacular
tabernacular, adj. — Formed'with suff. -ar fr. L.
tabernaculum. See prec. word.

## tabas
tabas, п., emaciation (med.) — L. tabes, 'a
melting, wasting away', fr. tdbere, 'to melt, waste
away, be consumed', fr. I.-E. *tab(h)-, a labial
enlargement of base *ta-, 'to melt'. See thaw
and cp. words there referred to.

## tabescence
tabescence, п., state of wasting away. — Formed
from next word with suff. -ce. Cp. contabescence.

## tabescent
tabescent, adj., wasting away. — L. tdbescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of tdbescere, 'to melt
gradually, waste or pine away, decay', inchoative of
tdbere. See tabes and -escent and cp. contabes-
cent.

## tabetic
tabetic, adj., pertaining to, or suffering from,
tabes. — Formed ft. L. tabes (see tabes) on the
false analogy of diabetic and other adjectives
ending in -etic. The etymologically correct form
is tabic.

## ruble
ruble, adj., tabetic. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic
fr. L. tabes, gen. tains. See tabes.

## tabid
tabid, adj., tabetic. — L. tabidus, 'wasting away',
fr. tdbere. See tabes and -id.
Derivatives: tabid-ly, adv., tabid-ness, n.

## tabinet
tabinet, п., fabric of watered silk and wool. — F.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:768 COLUMN:2 -->
τ
formed with suff. -inet, fr. tabis, 'tabby'. See
tubby.

## Tairitha
Tairitha, fern. PN. — Late L., ft. Gk. Ταβι»ά,
Ταβει*ά, fr. Aram. tabhyethd, emphatic state
of tabhya, 'gazelle', which is rel. to Heb. tzebhi,
fem. tzebhiyydh, Arab, zaby, Akkad. sabitu, of
s.m.

## tabitude
tabitude, п., emaciation. — L. tdbitudo, 'a
wasting away', fr. tdbere. See tubes and -ude.

## tablature
tablature, п., 1) an early name for musical
notation; 2) a tablelike painting; 3) a graphic
description. — ML. tabuldtura (whence also It. ta-
volatura, G. Tabulatur), fr. Late L. tabuldre, 'to
board, to floor', fr. L. tabula, 'plank, writing
tablet'. See table, adj. suff. -ate and suff. -ure.

## table
table, n. — ME.,fr. OF.( = F.),fr.L.taWa,'board,
plank, writing tablet, picture' (whence also It.
tavola, 'table'), rel. to Umbr. tafle, 'on the
board'; of uncertain origin. Cp. tabellion,
tableau, tablier, tabula, tabnla rasa, entablature,
entablement, taffrail. Cp. also the first element
in dolmen.
Derivatives: table, tr. v., tableau (q.v.), tabl-ed,
adj., table-ful, adj., tablet (q.v.), tablier (q.v.),
tabl-ing, п., tabloid (q.v.)

## tableau
tableau, п., picture. — F., 'picture, painting',
dimin. of table. F. dimin. suff. -eau derives fr. L.
-ellus; see -el.

## tabie-d'hdte
tabie-d'hdte, п., common table for guests at a
hotel. — F., lit. 'table of the host'. See table and
host, 'one who receives guests'.

## tablet
tablet, п., a small slab. — ME. tablette, tablett,
ft. OF. tablete (F. tablette), dimin. of table, fr.
L. tabula. See table and -et.
Derivatives: tablet, tr. v., tablet-ary, adj.

## tablier
tablier, п., an apron. — F., lit. 'that which
belongs to the table', fr. table, 'table'. See table and
-ier.

## tabloid
tabloid, п., a small tablet of medicine; a
trademark. — A hybrid coined fr. table and Gk.
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## taboo
taboo, tabu, adj., forbidden. — Tongan tabu, rel.
to Polynesian tapu, 'sacred'. The original
meaning prob. was 'exceedingly marked', fr. ta,
'mark', and pu, 'exceedingly'. See
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 1947, vol. 21, p. 732.
Derivatives: taboo, tabu, n. and tr. v.

## tabor
tabor, also tabour, п., a small drum resembling a
tambourine. — ME., fr. OF. tabour, 'drum;
stool', fr. Arab, tabu!, pi. of tab!, 'drum'. Cp.
tambour, taboret.

## taboret
taboret, also tabouret, п., a small tabor, tabret. —
F. tabouret, dimin. of OF. tabour, 'drum; stool'.
See prec. word.

## tabret
tabret, п., a small tabor. — A var. of prec. word.

## tabula
tabula, п., table; tablet. — L. See table.
Derivatives: tabular (q.v.), tabul-ate, adj. and
tr. v., tabul-at-ed, adj., tabul-at-ion, п.,
tabulator, п., tubul-at-ory, adj.

## tabular
tabular, adj., having the form of a table; flat. —
L. tabularis, 'of boards or planks', fr. tabula. See
prec. word. For the ending see suff. -ar.
Derivative: tabular-ty, adv.

## tabula rasa
tabula rasa, an erased or blank tablet; a clean
slate; hence the mind in its primary state, i.e.,
before impressions are recorded on it by
experience. — ML., 'an erased tablet', fr. L. tabula,
'tablet' (see table), and fem. pp. of rddere, 'to
scrape away, erase' (see rase). ML. tabula rdsa
is a loan translation of Aristotle's πινακίς
άγραφος, 'unwritten tablet' (see his De anima,
7, 22).

## tacamahac
tacamahac, п., 1) the balsam poplar; 2) gum resin
of several tropical trees. — Sp. tacamahaca (now
tacamaca), of Nahuatl origin.

## tac-au-tac
tac-au-tac, п., parry and riposte (a term of
fencing). — Fr. F. riposter du tac au tac, 'to parry
with the riposte', lit. 'to riposte from click to
click', fr. tac, 'the click of steel', a word of
imitative origin.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:768 COLUMN:3 -->

## tace
tace, intr. v., imper. 'be silent!'. — L. tace, imper.
of tacire, 'to be silent'; rel. to Umbr. tacez,
tases (= L. tacitus, pp. of tacere), Goth, pahan,
ON. pegja, 'to be silent', ON. pagna, 'to grow
dumb', OS. thagian, OHG. dagen, 'to be silent'.
Cp. tacit, taciturn, reticent.

## tacet
tacet, intr. v., musical direction that a voice or an
instrument should remain silent. — L. tacet, 3rd
sing. pres. of tacere. See prec. word.

## tache
tache, tach, п., a buckle, clasp (archaic). — ME.,
fr. OF. tache, 'a nail.jhook'. See tack, 'a small
nail', and cp. words there referred to.

## tache
tache, п., spot on the skin; freckle (obsol.) — ME.,
fr. MF. (= F.) tache, 'a spot, blemish', prob. a
blend of OF. iecAe,'distinctivemark,quality',and
estache, 'fastener, stake, post', fr. estachier, 'to
fasten'. OF. teche derives fr. Frankish *te"kan,
'sign', which is rel. to Goth, taikns, OE. tdcen,
tden, 'sign, token'; see token. OF. estachier has
been formed—with change of prefix—fr. OF.
atachier, 'to tack or fasten to'; see attach and
cp. tache, 'a buckle'. See Bloch-Wartburg,
DELF., p. 591 s.v. tache. Cp. techy.

## tacheometer
tacheometer, tacheometry. — See tachymeter,
tachymetry.

## tachina fiy
tachina fiy, fly of the genus Tachina. — ModL.
tachina, fr. Gk. ταχινάς, a secondary form of
ταχύς, 'swift'. See tachy-.

## tacho-
tacho-, combining form meaning 'speed'. — Gk.
ταχο-, fr. τάχος, 'speed'. See tachy-.

## tachometer
tachometer, п., an instrument for measuring
speed. — Compounded of tacho- and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See tachymeter.

## tachometry
tachometry, п., the art of measuring speed. —
Compounded of tacho- and Gk. -μετρία, 'a
measuring of and tachymetry.

## tachy-
tachy-, combining form meaning 'swift, quick'.
— Gk. ταχύ-, fr. ταχύς, 'swift', rel. to τάχος,
'speed'; possibly cogn. with Lith. deugti, 'to run
quickly'.

## Tachyglossus
Tachyglossus, п., the genus of the echidnas (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of tachy- and Gk.
γλώσσα, 'tongue'. See gloss, 'interpretation'.

## tachygraph
tachygraph, п., a stenographic manuscript; a
stenographer. — F. tachygraphe, fr. Gk. ταχυ-
γράφος, 'a fast writer', which is compounded
of ταχύς (see tachy-) and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See -grnph.

## tachygrapher
tachygrapher, п., a stenographer. — See prec.
word and agential suff. -er.

## tachygraphy
tachygraphy, п., shorthand, stenography. —
Compounded of tachy- and Gk. -γραφίά, ft.
γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graphy.
Derivatives: tachygraph-ic, tachygraph-ic-al,
adjs., tachygraph-ic-al-ly, adv.

## tachylyte
tachylyte, also spelled tachyilte, п., black basaltic
glass (petrogr.) — G. Tachylyt, coined by the
German mineralogist Johann August Fried.
Breithaupt (1791-1873) in 1826 fr. tachy- and
Gk. λυτός, 'soluble', verbal adj. of λύειν, 'to
dissolve' (see -lyric); so called by him because it
can be decomposed by acids. The spelling tachy-
lite is due to a confusion with the combining
form -lite.
Derivative: tachylyt-ic, adj.

## tachymeter
tachymeter, п., an instrument for surveying. —
Compounded of tachy- and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'; see meter, 'poetical rhythm'. Tachymeter
lit. means 'speedy measurer'. Cp. tacheometer,
tachometer.

## tachymetry
tachymetry, п., the use of a tachymeter. —
Compounded of tachy-and Gk. -μετρία, 'a measuring
of, fr. μέτρον, 'measure'. See prec. word and
-merry.

## tacit
tacit, adj., silent, unspoken. — L. tacitus, pp. of
tacere, *to be silent'. See tnce.
Derivatives: tacit-ly, adv., tacit-ness, n.

## taciturn
taciturn, adj., habitually silent. — F. taciturne, fr.
L. taciturnus, 'quiet, taciturn', fr. tacitus, pp. of
tacere, 'to be silent'. See tace.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:769 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TACITURNITY | 742 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:769 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: taciturn-ly, adv.

## taciturnity
taciturnity, n. — ME. taciturnite, ft. MF. (— F.)
taciturnite, fr. L. taciturnitdtem, ace. of tacitur-
nitds, 'a being silent, silence, taciturnity', fr. ta-
citurnus. See prec. word and -ity.

## tack
tack, п., a small nail. — ME. takke, fr. ONF.
toque, 'nail', which, together with its OF.
equivalent tacke, 'nail', is ofTeut. origin. Cp. MLG.
tacke, tac, Du. tak, 'bough, branch, spike,
prong'; cp. also MHG. zacke, G. Zacke, Zacken,
'sharp point, tooth, prong', which are LG. loan
words. Cp. tache, 'buckle', which is a doublet of
tack. Cp. also tackle, tag, 'appendage'. Cp. also
attach, attack, detach, staccato, shako.
Derivatives: lack, tr. and intr. v., tack-er, п.,
rack-ing, adj., tack-ing-ly, adv., tack-y, adj.,
tack-i-ness, n.

## tack
tack, п., food, provisions. — Back formation
from tackle.

## tackle
tackle, п., apparatus; equipment. — ME. take/,
fr. MLG. takel (whence also G. Takel), which is
formed with sufT. -el fr. tacke, tack, 'tack'. Cp
ME. takken, 'to fasten', and see tack, 'small
nail', and instrumental surf. -le.
Derivatives: tackle, tr. and intr. v., tackl-er,
.п..

## tact
tact, n. — F., fr. L. tactus, 'a touch; effect', fr.
tactus, pp. of tangere, 'to touch'. See tangent and
cp. contact, intiict.
Derivatives: tact-ful, adj., tact-ful-ly, adv., tact-

## ful-ness
ful-ness, п., tact-less, adj., tact-less-ly, adv., tact-
less-ness, n.

## tactic
tactic, п., the same as tactics. — See tactics.

## tactician
tactician, п., an expert in tactics. — See next word
and -ian.

## tactics
tactics, п., maneuvering of armed forces. —
ModL. tactica, fr. Gk. τακτικά, 'tactics', neut.
pi. of τακτικός, 'fit for ordering or ordering;
pertaining to tactics', used as a noun, fr.τακτός,
'ordered', verbal adj. of τάσσειν, 'to put in
order, arrange'. See taxis.
Derivatives: tactic-al, adj., tactic-al-ly, adv.

## tactile
tactile, adj., pertaining to touch; tangible. — F.,
fr. L. tactilis, 'tangible', fr. tactus, pp. of tangere,
'to touch'. See tangent and -ile.

## tactility
tactility, п., quality of being tactile; tangibility.
— Formed with surf, -ity fr. L. tactilis. See prec.
word.

## tactometer
tactometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
sharpness of the sense of touch. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. tactus, 'touch', and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. The first element derives ft. L. tactus,
pp. of tangere, 'to touch'; see tact. For the
second element see meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## tactual
tactual, adj., pertaining to the sense of touch. —
Formed with adj. surf, -al fr. L. tactus, 'touch'.
See tact and cp. contactual.
Derivative: tactual-ly, adv.

## tadpole
tadpole, n. — ME. taddepol, compounded of tade,
tadde. 'toad', and pol, polle, 'head'; see toad and
poll, 'head'. Tadpole accordingly lit. means 'toad
head'.

## taedium vitae
taedium vitae, weariness of life. — L. See tedium
and vital.

## tael
tael, п., Chinese money of account. — Portug., fr.
Malay tahil, 'weight', fr. Hind, tola, fr. OI. tula,
'balance', which is cogn. with Gk. τάλαντον,
'balance; a weight', L. tollere, 'to lift up, raise*,
tolerttre, 'to bear, support'. See tolerate and cp.
talent. For the sense development of tael cp.
Heb. shiqel, 'weight; a coin', ft. shaqal, 'he
weighed' (see shekel).

## tu'en
tu'en, pp. — Contraction of taken.

## taeni-
taeni-, taenii-, taenio-, combining form meaning
1) ribbon; 2) tapeworm.

## taenia
taenia, п., 1) headband; 2) a ribbonlike part
(anat.); 3) a tapeworm {zool.) — L. taenia,
'ribbon, band, fillet, tapeworm', fr. Gk. ταινία,
'band, ribbon, fillet', derivative of the adj.
•ταινός, which stands for 'τανιός, 'narrow', and
is rel. to τείνειν, for "τέν^ειν, 'to stretch'; see
tend, 'to move in a certain direction', and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the second
element in cryptotaenia. In its anatomical sense
('ribbonlike organ') the word was first used by
the Swiss anatomist Albrecht von Haller (1708-
77). See Joseph Hyrtl, Onomatologia anatomica,
p. 210.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:769 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: taeni-an, adj.

## taeniacide
taeniacide, п., a remedy destroying tapeworms
(med.) — Compounded of taenia and L. -cida,
'killer', fr. caedere, 'to kill'. See -cide, 'killer'.
Derivative; taeniacid-al, adj.

## taeniafuge
taeniafuge, п., a substance expelling tapeworms.
— Compounded of taenia and L. -fugus. See
-fuge.

## Taenidia
Taenidia, п., a genus of plants of the carrot family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. ταινέδιον, 'alittleband',
a dimin. formed fr. ταινία (see tuenia); so called
in allusion to the small ribs.

## tafferel
tafferel, n. — See taffrail.

## taffeta
taffeta, taffety, п., a fine smooth lustrous silk
cloth. — ME. taffeta, fr. MF. (= F.) taffetas, fr.
It. taffeta, ft. Pets, taftah, 'twisted fabric', fr.
taftan, 'to shine; to spin, twist'. See tapestry.

## tuffrail
tuffrail, also tafferel, п., the rail across the stern
of a ship. — Du. tafereel, dimin. of tafel, 'table',
which, together with OHG. zabal (MHG.
zabel), 'board, plank', OHG. tavala, tabala
(MHG. tavele, G. Tafel), 'table, board', is
borrowed ft. L. tabula, 'board, plank'; see table.
The form taffrail arose through the assimilation
of the ending of tafferel to E. rail.

## taffy
taffy, п., candy made of sugar or molasses. —'■ F.
tafia. See tafia.

## Taffy
Taffy, Welshman (colloq.) — From Teifi, Welsh
corruptionof David; acommonWelsh nickname.

## tafia
tafia, п., a kind of rum obtained from the refuse
of sugar. — Creole, prob. shortened fr. ratafia
(q.v.) Cp. taffy.

## tag
tag, п., appendage, the end of something. — ME.
tagge, prob. of Scand. origin. Cp. Swed. tagg,
'prickle, point, tooth', Norw. tagge, 'tooth',
which are proh. related to G. Zacke, Zacken,
'sharp point, tooth, prong', and to E. tack,
'small nail' (q.v.)
Derivatives: tag, tr. v., tagg-er, п., tagg-y, adj.

## tag
tag, п., a children's game. — Prob. ft. prec. word.

## tagatose
tagatose, п., a crystalline sugar (chem.) —
Formed by transposition of most of the letters of
galactose, from which it was obtained.

## Tagetes
Tagetes, п., a genus of plants of the ester family
(hot.) — ModL., a misreading of Late L. tra-
ganthes, a species of Artemisia, contracted fr.
tragacanthum, fr. Gk. τραγάκαν&α, lit. 'goat's
thorn'. See tragacanth. Tagetes has nothing to
do with the Etruscan deity Tages.

## tahona
tahona, п., a kind of arrastre. — Sp., 'a crushing
mill', fr. Arab. tdhanah, fr. tahana, 'he ground',
rel. Heb. tahan, Aram. tehan, Syr. Агел, 'he
ground', Akkad. tenu, lenu, 'to grind', Ethiop.
tehn, 'fiour'.

## tahsildar
tahsildar, п., revenue officer of a district. — Pers.-
Hind. tahsildar, a hybrid lit. meaning
'collection holder', formed fr. Arab, tahsil, 'collection',
prop, infinitive of hassala, 'he gathered,
collected, acquired', and the Persian suff. -dar, 'holder,
possessor'. For this latter see aumUdar and cp.
words there referred to.

## taiga
taiga, п., belt of coniferous forests in Siberia. —
Russ.

## tail
tail, п., the hindmost part of an animal. — ME.
tail, teil, fr. OE. tsegel, tiegl, rel. to OHG. zagal,
MHG., G. zagel, 'tail'. The orig. meaning of
these words was 'tuft of hair' (cp. Goth, tag!,
'hair', ON. tagl, 'horse's tail'); They are rel. to
Goth, tahjan, 'to drag', ON. tag, 'fiber', and
cogn. with Olr. dua!(toi *doklo-), 'lock of hair',
OI. dasah, 'fringe; wick'. Cp. the second
element in wagtail.
Derivatives: tail, tr. and intr. v., tail-ed, adj.,
tail-ing, п., tail-less, adj., tail-y, adj.

## tail
tail, п., limitation of ownership (law). — ME.
taille, fr. OF. (= F.) taille, 'a cutting', back
formation fr. taillier (F. miller), 'to cut'. See tailor
and cp. taille, tallage, entail.

## tail
tail, adj., limited (law). — ME. taille, fr. OF.
taillie (F. taille), pp. of taillier. See prec. word.

## tnilor
tnilor, n. — ME. taillour, fr. OF. tailleor, tailleur
(F. tailleur), lit. 'cutter', fr. taillier (F. tattler),
'to cut', fr. VL. *taliare, 'to split, cut' (whence
also It. tagliare, OProvenc. talhar, Sp. tajar), fr.
L. tdlea, 'rod, stick, bar', which is cogn. with
Gk. ταλις, 'a marriageable girl', τηλις,
'fenugreek', τηλε&αν, 'to bloom, flourish', OI. talah,
'wine palm', tali, name of a tree. Lith. attolas.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:769 COLUMN:3 -->
atolas, 'aftermath', OLith. taldkas, 'a young
girl', and prob. also with Etruscan dalna, name
of the goddess of youth. Cp. tail, limitation of
ownership', taille, tallage, tally, atajo, detail,
entail, intaglio, retail and the first element in
talipot.
Derivatives: tailor, tr. and intr. v., tailor-ing, п.,
tailor-ly, adj., tailor-y, n.

## tain
tain, п., a thin sheet of tin. — ME. tein, rel. to
ON. teinn, 'twig', OE. tan, Goth, tains, OHG.
zein, 'twig, rod', OS., OFris. ten, Du. teen, 'osier
switch', MLG. ten, 'a thin sheet of metal'. These
words possibly derive fr. I.-E. base *ten-, 'to
extend; thin'. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and cp. words there referred to.

## tain
tain, п., a cattle raid; epic about a cattle raid. —
Ir. tain, 'cattle, cattle raid*.

## taint
taint, tr. and intr. v. — Partly fr. F. teint, pp. of
teindre, 'to dye, paint', partly aphetic for
attaint, partly a blend of both. F. teindre derives
fr. L. tingere; see tinct, tinge.

## taint
taint, n. — Of the same origin as taint, v.
Derivatives: taint-less, adj., taint-less-ly, adv.

## taj
taj, п., cap worn by Moslem dervishes. — Arab.
taj, 'crown*, ft. Pers. tdj, of s.m. See stemma.

## take
take, tr. and intr. v. — ME. taken, fr. OE. tacan,
fr. ON. taka, rel. to MLG. tacken, MDu. taken,
Goth, tekan, 'to touch'; of uncertain etymology.
Cp. the second element in wapentake. Late OE.
tacan has replaced OE. niman, which has
survived only in the adjective nimble.
Derivatives: take, п., tak-able, adj., tak-er, п.,
tak-ing, n. and adj., tak-ing-ly, adv., tak-ing-
nes's, n.

## taken
taken, pp. of take. — ME. taken, fr. OE. getacen,
pp. of tacan. See take.

## talanoin
talanoin, п., a Buddhist monk. — Port, talapdes,
pi. of talapao, fr. Talaing tola poi, 'our lord'.

## talapoin
talapoin, п., a small West African monkey. —
Fr. prec. word. For sense development cp.
monk and monkey.

## talar
talar, п., a robe reaching down to the ankles. —
L. talaris, 'of the ankle, reaching to the ankle',
fr. talus. See talus, 'ankle', and -ar.

## talaria
talaria, n. pi., the winged sandals of Hermes and
of other deities (Greek mythol.) — L. talaria,
'winged shoes', prop. neut. pi. of the adjective
talaris, used as a noun. See prec. word.

## talayot
talayot, п., one of the megalitic towerlike
monuments on the Balearic Islands (archaeol.) — Sp.
atalaya. See atalaya.

## talbot
talbot, п., name of an extinct variety of hound.
— Prob. from the English family name Talbot.

## talc
talc, п., a soft mineral, magnesium silicate. — F.,
fr. Sp. talque, fr. Arab, tdlaq, talq, whence also
It. talco, G. Talk (this latter prob. through the
medium of French).
Derivatives: talck-y, adj., talc-like, adj.

## talcoid
talcoid, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, talc. —
A hybrid coined ft. talc and Gk. -οειδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## talcose
talcose, adj., talcoid. — A hybrid coined fr. talc
and -ose, an adj. suff. of Latin origin.

## talcous
talcous, adj., containing or resembling talc. — A
hybrid coined fr. talc and -ous, a suff. of Latin
origin. Cp. prec. word.

## tale
tale, n. — ME., fr. OE. talu, 'story, tale', rel. to OS.
tola, 'number, speech', ON. tal, tala, 'number,
story, tale', Dan., Swed. tal,'number',OFris. tale,
tele, MDu., Du. tal, 'number'. MDu. tale, Du.
taal, 'speech, language', OHG. zala, MHG. zal,
G. Zahl, 'number'. The original meaning of
these words seems to have been 'incision, notch
in the tally', whence arose the secondary
meaning of 'counting, calculation, number'. The
above words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *del-,
*dol-, 'to hew, cut', whence also OI. dalati,
'splits, bursts', daldyati, 'cleaves, splits, dalam,
'part, piece', Arm. tal, 'mark impression', Gk.
δαιδάλλειν, to work skillfully', L. doldre, 'to
chip, hew, cut out'. See dole, 'grief, and cp.
daedal. Cp. also talk, tell.

## Talegallus
Talegallus, п., a genus of Australian birds (orni-
thol.) — ModL., a hybrid coined fr. Malagasy
taleva, 'waterhen', and L. gallus, 'cock'. See
gallinaceous.

## talent
talent, n. — ME., 'sum of money; desire', fr. L.
talenta, pi. of talentum, ft. Gk. τάλαντον, *bal-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:770 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 743 | TAME -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:770 COLUMN:1 -->
ance' (in the pi., "pair of scales'); a weight; sum
of money corresponding to a talent of silver', fr.
τάλας, gen. τάλαντος, 'bearing, suffering,
enduring', fr. I.-E. base *tel, *ta!-, *tol-, 'to bear,
carry, support, endure', whence also Gk. ταλάσ-
σαι (aor.), 'to bear, suffer', Ol. tula, 'balance',
tulayaii, 'lifts up, weighs', L. tollere, 'to lift up,
raise', tolerare, 'to bear, support'. See tolerate
and cp. Atalanta, Atlas, tael, tantalus, telamon.
Cp. also thole, 'to endure'.
Derivatives: talent-ed, adj., talent-less, adj.

## taler
taler, also thaler, п., an old German silver coin.
— G. Taler, formerly spelt Thaler, abbreviation
of Joachimst(h)aler, 'coin made in Joachims-
t(h)al'. See dollar.

## tales
tales, п., ]) a person summoned to make up a
deficiency in the jury; 2) a writ summoning
such a person to serve on a jury, (law) — From
L. tales, the first word in the phrase tales de
circumstamibus, 'such of the bystanders', pi.
of talis, 'such', which is formed with suff. -/ fr.
the I.-E. pron. base "to-, Cp. Gk. τηλίκος, 'so
old', OSlav. toll, 'so', toliku, 'so much', Russ.
tollko, 'only', which are similarly formed. For
other derivatives of l.-E. base *to- see the and
words there referred to.

## talesman
talesman, п., a person summoned to make up for
a deficiency in the jury. — A hybrid coined
from prec. word and man.

## Talinum
Talinum, п., a genus of plants of the family
Portulacaceae (hot.) — ModL., of Senegalese
origin.

## talion
talion, п., retaliation. — F-, fr. L. tdlionem, ace.
of tdlio, 'retaliation in kind', which is prob.
cogn. with Olr. taile, 'pay', W. tdl,
'compensation', OBret., Co. tal, 'paid'. Cp. retalinte.
Derivative: talion-ic, adj.

## taliped
taliped, adj., clubfooted. — See next word.
Derivative: taliped, п., a clubfooted
person.

## talipes
talipes, п., clubfoot (med.) — ModL. talipes, fr.
L. talipedare, 'to be weak in the feet, to totter',
lit. Ίο walk on the ankles', fr. talus, 'ankle', and
pes, gen. pedis, 'foot'. For the first element see
talus, 'ankle', for the second see foot and cp.
pedal.

## talipot
talipot, п., a fan-leaved palm (Corypha umbra-
culifera). — Bengali talipot, 'palm leaf, fr. OI.
tali, name of a tree, and patram,pattram, 'leaf.
See tailor and feather.

## talisman
talisman, п., amulet; charm. — F. talisman, fr.
Sp. talisman, fr. VArab. tilsaman, pi. of tilsdm,
which corresponds to Classical Arabic (llasm, a
loan word fr. Late Gk. τέλεσμα, 'consecration,
mystery', fr. Gk. τέλεσμα, 'payment', fr. τελεΐν,
'to fulfil, perform; to pay; to initiate into
mysteries', fr. τέλος, 'fulfilment, end'. See tele-.
Derivatives: talisman-ic, talisman-ic-al, adjs.,
talisman-ic-al-ly, adv.

## talk
talk, intr. and tr. v. — ME. talken, prop. freq.
formed fr. OE. talian, 'to reckon, account,
enumerate', whioh is rel. to OE. talu, 'story, tale'.
Cp. EFris. talken and see tale. For the
frequentative force of the suff. -k cp. hark, freq. of hear,
and stalk, {тец.'of steal.
Derivatives: talk, п., talk-able, adj., talkative
(q.v.), talk-er, п., talkie (q.v.), tdlk-ing, n. and
adj.

## tnlkative
tnlkative, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. talk and
-ative, a suff. of Latin origin.
Derivatives: talkative-ly, adv., talkative-ness, n.

## talkie
talkie, п., a sound motion picture. — Formed fr.
talk on the analogy of movie.

## tall
tall, adj. — Prob. fr. ME. tal, 'seemly', fr. OE.
getxl, 'swift, prompt, ready', later used in the
sense of 'handsome, brave', which is rel. to
OHG. gi-zal, 'quick', Goth, un-tals, 'indocile',
and prob. also to OE. talu, 'tale', ON. tal,
'number', telja, 'to tell'. See teli and tale.
Derivatives: tall, п., tall, adv., tall-ness, n.

## taliage
taliage, п., tax paid by the tenant to his lord
(Engl. Feudal Law). — ME. taillage, talliage,
tallage, fr. OF. taillage, lit. 'that which is cut',
fr. taillier (F. tailler), 'to cut'. See tailor and
-age and cp. tail, 'limitation of ownership'.

## tallboy
tallboy, п., 1) a high chest of drawers (British); 2)
a kind of tall chimney pot. — Lit. 'high wood',
fr. F. haul bois, E. tall being the translation of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:770 COLUMN:2 -->
F. haut and E. boy a corruption of F. bois. See
tall and bush and cp. highboy, lowboy and
bautboy.

## tallith
tallith, п., prayer shawl (Jewish Religion). —
Mishnaic Heb. jalltth, 'covering, sheet, cloak;
prayer shawl', prob. fr. Biblical Heb. tillel, 'he
covered over, roofed' (a hapax Iegomenon in
the Bible, occurring Neh. 3:15), corresponding
to Heb. tzdldl, 'was covered with shade, was
overshadowed, grew dark', whence tzel,
'shadow, shade'. Cp. Aram, rldla, Ugar. zl, Arab.
Zill, Akkad. sillu and sululu, 'shadow, shade'.

## tallow
tallow, n. — ME. talgh, talow, fr. MLG. talch,
whence also Du. talk, G. Talg. MLG. talch
meant perh. orig. 'a firm, compact material',
and is rel. to Goth, tulgus, 'firm, solid', and
cogn. with Gk. έν-δελεχής, 'forbearing', L. in-
dulglre, 'to be complaisant, forbearing'. See
indulge and cp. words there referred to. For the
development of meaning cp. Gk. στέαρ, 'tallow',
which is cogn. with E. stone.
Derivatives: tallow, tr. and intr. v., and adj.,
tallow-er, п., tallow-ing, п., tallow-ish, adj.,
tallow-y, adj., tallow-i-ness, n.

## tally
tally, п., a piece of wood with notches. — AF.
tallie, corresponding to OF., F. taille, 'notch,
cut', fr. Anglo-L. tdlia, tallia, fr. L. talea, 'rod,
stick'. See tailor and cp. tail, 'limitation of
ownership'.
Derivative: tally, tr. and intr. v.

## tallyho
tallyho, п., huntsman's cry. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. OF. thialau, taho, F. talaut.
Derivative: tallyho, tr. and intr. v.

## talma
talma, п., a kind of cloak. — Named after the
famous French actor Francois-Joseph Talma
(1763-1826).

## talml gold
talml gold, a kind of gilt brass. — F. talmi,
shortened fr. Та llois-de m i-or, lit. half-gold (made by)
Tallois' (see demi- and -or, п.); so called after
Tallois of Paris, who first manufactured it.

## Talmud
Talmud, n. — Mishnaic Heb, talmudh, 'learning,
teaching, instruction', fr. Idmddh, 'he learned',
orig. 'he exercised, accustomed to', whence
malmadh, 'ox goad', talmtdh, 'scholar, disciple,
pupil', Mishnaic Heb. Idmudh, 'accustomed',
rel. to Aram, fmadh (rare), 'he learned', Syr.
lammedh, 'he accustomed', Ugar. Imd, Akkad.
lamddu, 'to learn', Ethiop. lamada, 'was
accustomed*. Cp. lamed, melammed.
Derivatives: Talmud-ic, Talmud-ic-al, adjs.,
Talmud-ist, п., Talmud-ist-ic, Talmud-ist-ic-al,
adjs.

## talon
talon, п., orig. the heel or hinder part of the foot
of certain animals; now, claw. — ME., fr. OF
(= F.), 'heel', fr. VL. *tdlonem, ace. of *talo,
'heel', fr. L. talus, 'ankle, heel'. Cp. It tallone,
Sp. tafan, and see talus, 'ankle'.
Derivative: talon-ed, adj.

## Talos
Talos, п., 1) a man of bronze made by
Hephaestus and given by Zeus to Minos, king of Crete,
to watch over the island; 2) nephew and pupil
of Daedalus (Greek mythol.) — Gk. Τάλως, of
uncertain origin; perh. orig. a personification
of the sun, which, according to Hesychius, was
called τάλως in Crete. See Albert Carnoy,
Dictionnaiie etymologique de la mythologie
greco-romaine, Louvain, p. 191 s.v. *Talos.

## talose
talose, п., a sugar, CeH12Oe (chem.) — G. Talose,
fr. Talon, which is formed through the
transposition of some of the letters of Galacton in
Galactonsaure ('galacionic acid'). See galactonic
and subst. suff. -ose,

## Talpa
Talpa, п., the genus of moles (zool.) — L. talpa,
'mole', of uncertain origin. It is possibly rel. to
L. darpus, 'a mammal', prob. 'the mole';
possibly of Gaulish origin.

## taluk
taluk, п., an estate belonging to a native in India;
a subdivision of a district in India. — Hind., fr.
Arab, ta'alluq, 'estate', lit. 'dependency',
infinitive of ta'allaqa, 'he was attached to', 5th
form of 'aliqa, 'he cleaved to, adhered to', which
is rel. to Heb. 'aluqab, Aram, 'dluqta, Akkad.
ilqitu, 'leech', lit. 'the clinging animal'.

## talakdar
talakdar, п., owner of a taluk. — Pers. ta'alluq-
dar, lit. 'holder of an estate', a hybrid coined fr.
Arab, ta'alluq, 'estate' (see prec. word), and
Persian suff. -ddr, meaning 'holder, possessor'.
For this latter see aumildar and cp. words there

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:770 COLUMN:3 -->
referred to.

## talus
talus, п., ankle, ankle bone (anat.) — L. talus,
'ankle, ankle bone, heel; die' (so called because
orig. made from the knuckle bones of
animals). L. tdlus prob. stands for *taxlos. Cp.
taxillus, *a little die', which is a dimin. of tdlus.
Cp. also talipes, talon, tassel, 'ornament'. Cp.
also solleret.

## talus
talus, п., slope; the slope of a wall. — F., fr.
Gaul.-L. talutium, 'the superficial indication of
the presence of gold under the earth', a·
derivative of Gaulish talo, 'forehead', which is rel. to
Ir. taul, Bret. tal. Provenc. tauvero, 'border of a
field', is also traceable to Gaulish talo.

## tarn
tarn, n. — Short for tam-o'-shanter.

## tamale
tamale, п., a dish made of crushed Indian corn
and meat seasoned with pepper. — Sp. tamal,
fr. Nahuatl tamalli.

## tamandua
tamandua, п., the little anteater, Tamandua tetra-
dactyla. — Port, tamandua, a loan word fr.
Tupi.

## tamanoir
tamanoir, п., the great anteater or ant bear. — F.,
a loan word from Caribbean tamanoa.

## tamanu
tamanu, п., the poon tree. — Of Tahitian origin.

## tamarnck
tamarnck, п., the N. American black larch. — Of
Algonquian origin.

## Tamaricaceae
Tamaricaceae, n. pi., the tamarisk family (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. Tamarix with suff. -aceae.

## tainaricaceous
tainaricaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## tamarin
tamarin, п., the S. American marmoset. — A
loan word from the Caribbean dialect of
Cayenne.

## tamarind
tamarind, п., 1) a tropical tree; 2) its fruit. — Sp.
tamarinda (also Port, and It.), fr. Arab, tamr
Hindi, 'Indian date', fr. tamr, 'date', and Hindi,
'Indian', which is formed fr. Hind, 'India', with
gentilic suff. -f. The first element is rel. to
Heb. tdmar, 'palm tree, date palm', Aram.
tamra, Syr. tlmarta, Ethiop. tamr, 'date', 'date
palm', and prob also to Arab, itma'drra, 'was
erect or stiff, (said of a lance). For the second
element in tamarind see Hindu, India.

## tamarisk
tamarisk, п., an evergreen shrub or small tree
with slender branches and feathery clusters of
pinkish flowers. — Late L. tamariscus, fr. L.
tamarix, 'tamarisk', prob. fr. Heb. tdmar, 'palm
tree', or Arab, tamr, 'date'. See tamarind and
cp. Tamarix.

## Tamarix
Tamarix, п., a genus of trees, the tamarisk (bot.)
— L. tamarix, 'tamarisk'. See prec. word.

## tamas
tamas, п., darkness, ignorance (Hinduism). —
OI. tamas-, 'dark-ness', rel. to tdmisrdh,
'darkness', Avestic tsmah-, 'darkness', and cogn.
with L. tenebrae (for temebrae, fr. *temesrae),
'darkness'. See tenebrae and cp. tombac,

## tamasha
tamasha, п., entertainment, show (Anglo-Ind.)
— Arab, tamdshin, 'a walking about', infinitive
of the VI conjugation of masha, 'he walked'.

## tamhouki
tamhouki, tambookie, п., a S. African shrub or
tree — S. African Dutch, fr. Tembu, name of a
Kaffir tribe in the region called Tembuland in
South Africa.

## tambonr
tambonr, п., 1) a drum; 2) a drumlike frame for
embroidering. — F., fr. OF., fr. Arab, fabul, pi.
of tabl, 'drum'; influenced in form by VArab.
tanbur (= Classical Arab, tunbur), 'lute'. Cp.
tabor.
Derivative: tambour, tr. and intr. v.

## tambourin
tambourin, п., 1) a kind of long drum; 2) a dance
accompanied by this drum. — F., ft. earlier
tabourin. See tabor and cp. prec. word.

## tambourine
tambourine, п., a small drum. — Fr. F. tambourin,
hence etymologically identical with prec. word.
Derivative: tambourine, intr. v.

## tame
tame, adj. — ME. tame, fr. OE. tarn, rel. to ON.
tamr, OS., Dan., Swed., OFris., MLG., MDu.,
Du. tarn, OHG., MHG. zam, G. zahm, 'tame'.
These adjectives prob. derive from an Old Teut.
verb attested only in OHG. ζαηιΰη, MHG.
zamen, 'to tame', fr. I.-E. base *domd-, *demd-,
*dem-, whence also 01. damayati, damaydti,
'tames', damya-, 'a young steer', prop, 'an
animal that must yet be tamed', damita, 'tamer',
damtah, 'tamed', ModPers. dam, *a tame
animal', Gk. δαμαν, 'to tame, subdue', δμητός,
'tame', δμώς, 'a slave taken in war' (lit.
'subdued'), ά-δμής, 'unsubdued; unwedded', δαμά-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:771 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TAME | 744 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:771 COLUMN:1 -->
λης, 'a young steer', L. domare, Чо tame,
subdue', Ossetic domun, 'tamer', Olr. damnaim,
Ί tie up, fasten; I tame, subdue', dam, 'ox'. All
these words are derivatives of I.-E. base *domd-,
*dema-, *dem-, 4o build*, and their orig.
meaning was 4o accustom animals to the house'.
This sense development may best be illustrated
by L. domare, 4o tame' (see above), lit, 4o
accustom the house', fr. domus, 'house'. See dome,
'a building', and cp. adamant, daunt, diamond,
doe, indomitable and the second element in
Hippodamia. Cp. also timber.
Derivatives: tame-ly, adv., tame-ness, n.

## tame
tame, tr. v. — ME. tamen, fr. tame, Чате'; rel.
to OE. temian, 4o tame', ON. temja, Dan.
taemme^wea. tamja,OFris. tema, MLG., MDu.,
Du. temmen, OHG., MHG. zemmen, G. zah-
men, Goth, gatamjan. See tame, adj.
Derivatives: tam-able, adj., tam-abil-ity, п.,
tam-able-ness, п., tame-less, adj., tam-er, n.

## Tamias
Tamias, п., the genus of ground squirrels (zool.)
— ModL., fr. Gk. ταμίας, 'one who distributes,
dispenser, steward', orig. 'one who cuts up
portions for the sake of distributing them'; in gra-
dational relationship to τέμνον, Чо cut', τόμος,
'piece cut off, section'. See tome.

## Tamil
Tamil, п., a Dravidian people and its language.
— Fr, 01. Dravida (through the intermediate
stages Dramida, Dramila, Damila). See Bishop
Caldwell, Comparative Grammar of the Dravi-
dian Languages, p. 10 f. (quoted in the
Encyclopedia Britannica, ed. 1947, vol. 21, p. 773).
Derivative: Tamil-ian, adj.

## tamis
tamis, п., a strainer made of cloth. — F. tamis, fr.
Sp. tamiz, fr. Arab, tamyxz, 'separation', verbal
n. of mazza, the second (= intensive)
conjugation of maza, 'he distinguished, separated'.

## Tammany
Tammany, п., also Tammany society. — Named
after Tammany or Tamanend, a Delaware chief,
who lived in the second half of the 17th and in
the first half of the 18th century.

## Tammanyisin
Tammanyisin, п., Tammany policy. — Formed
fr. Tammany with suff. -ism.

## Tammuz
Tammuz, п., 1) a Babylonian and Assyrian god;
2) name of the fourth Jewish month. — Heb.
Tammuz, fr. Babyl. Du'ilzu, Dilzu, contraction
of original Dumu-zi, 4he son who rises', also
interpreted as 'the faithful son'.

## tammy
tammy, п., a fine woolen fabric. — Fr. obsol.
tamin, fr. F. etamine, fr. OF. estamine, formed
—with change of suff.—fr. VL. staminea,
prop. fem. of the L. adj. stamineus, "made of
threads', fr. L. stamen, gen. staminis, 'thread;
warp'. Cp. It. stamigna, OProvenc. estamenha,
Sp. estamena, 'a kind of woolen fabric', and
see stamen.

## tammy
tammy, n. — Short for tum-o'-shanter.

## tum-o'-shanter
tum-o'-shanter, п., a kind of woolen cap. —
Named after Tarn o'Skanter, the hero of Robert
Burn's poem of this name.

## tamp
tamp, tr. v., to pound, ram. — Back formation
fr. F. etamper, Чо stamp, punch', fr. OF. es-
tamper, fr. Frankish *stampdn, which is rel. to
Du. stampen, OHG. stamp/on, Чо pound'. See
stamp, v. and cp. tampon.
Derivatives: tamp-er, п., tamp-ing, n.

## tampan
tampan, п., a poisonous S. African tick. — A
native name.

## tamper
tamper, intr. v., to interfere; to meddle. — Orig.
a var. of temper, v.

## tampion
tampion, п., a wooden plug or stopper put in the
nuzzle of a gun, when it is not in use. — A
var. of tampon. Cp. tompion.

## tampon
tampon, п., a plug of cotton inserted into a
wound, orifice, etc., to stop bleeding. — F.,
a nasalized var. of tapon, 'plug', formed with
suff. -on fr. Frankish *tappo, which is rel. to
OHG. zapfo, OE. taeppa, 'tap'. See tap, 'pipe;
cock'.
Derivative: tampon, tr. v.

## tamponade
tamponade, tamponage, tamponment, n. —
Hybrids coined fr. tampon, with the suffixes -ade,
-age, resp. -ment, which all are of Latin origin.

## tam-tam
tam-tam, п., 1) a kind of gong; 2) a tom-tom. —
F. tamtam, fr. Hind, tamtam, 'drum', which is
of imit. origin. Cp. tom-tom.

## tan
tan, п., oak bark. — F., fr. ML. tannum, which is
of Celtic origin. Cp. Bret, tann, 'oak tree'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:771 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: tan, adj., of the color of tan.

## tan
tan, tr. v., to convert (hide) into leather by
steeping in tannin; intr. v., to become tanned. — OF.
tanner, fr. ML. tannare, fr. tannum. See tan, п.,
and cp. tawny.
Derivatives: tann-able, adj., tann-ed, adj.,
tanner (q.v.), tann-ery, п., tann-ic, adj.

## tana
tana, п., a police station (India). — See thana.

## Tanacetum
Tanacetum, п., a genus of plants, the tansy (bot.)
— ModL. See tansy.

## Tanach
Tanach, п., the Holy Scriptures. — Heb. t(a)n-
(a)kk, a word formed from the initials of the
words torah, 'teaching' (used to denote the five
books of Moses), η bhVim, '(the books of the)
Prophets', kethubhim, 4he writings' (used in the
sense of 'Hagiographa').

## tanager
tanager, п., any of the small American oscine
birds constituting the family Tanagridae. —
ModL. Tanagra, name of the genus, fr. Port.
tangara, which is a Tupi loan word.

## Tanagra
Tanagra, п., made in, or coming from, Tanagra
(applied to terra-cotta figurines) — Gk.
Τανάγρα, name of a town in ancient Boeotia.

## tanagrine
tanagrine, adj., pertaining to the tanagers.—
— Formed fr. tanager with adj. suff. -ine.

## tanagroid
tanagroid, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
tanager. — A hybrid coined fr. tanager and Gk.
-οε^δής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See-oid.

## tnndem
tnndem, adv., one behind the other (said esp. of
two horses); п., a carriage drawn by horses
harnessed tandem; a team so harnessed; adj.,
consisting of two arranged tandem. — L.
tandem, 'at length' (taken humorously in the sense
of 'lengthwise one behind the other'), for *tam-
dem, compounded of tarn, which derives from
the pron. base *to- (see the and words there
referred to) and of the particle of identity -dem,
fr. I.-E. *de (see de- and cp ibidem). Cp.
tantamount.

## tandstickor
tandstickor, п., wooden match. — Swed. tand-
stickor, pi. of tandsticka, 'match', compounded
of tanda, Чо kindle', and sticka, 'splinter', See
tinder and stick, n.

## tang
tang, n,, spike, sharp point. — ME. tange, fr. ON.
tangi, 'point, tang of a knife', which is prob. rel.
to ON. tunga, 4ongue'. See tongue.
Derivatives: tang, tr. v., to furnish with a tang;
tang-у·, adj.

## tang
tang, п., seaweed. — Dan. tang, 'seaweed'. Cp.
ON. pang, 'seaweed', Swed. tang, Fris. tung, Du.
tang, G. Tang, of s.m., and E. tangle. Cp. also
the denasalized forms ME. tagle, dial. Swed.
taggla.

## tang
tang, intr. and tr. v., to sound loudly, to ring. —
Of imitative.origin. Cp. twang.
Derivative: tang, п., ringing sound.

## tariga
tariga, п., also tank a, name of various coins in
India and Turkestan. — Hind, tanga, lit.
'weight', fr. OI. tankah, 'stamped coin; a
weight', which is prob. connected with Tartar.
tanka, 'a silver coin', ModPers. tanga, Arm.
t*anka, 'a small coin'.

## tangeite
tangeite, п., a hydrous vanadate of copper and
calcium (mineral.) — Named after the Tange
gorge in Fergana, Uzbek. For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## tangelo
tangelo, п., a hybrid of the Tangerine orange and
the pomelo. — Coined from the first two
syllables of Tangerine and the last syllable of pomefo.

## tangency
tangency, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## tangent (geom.)
tangent (geom.), adj., touching; meeting at a
point without intersecting; п., a tangent line. —
L. tangens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of tangere, 'to
touch', which is prob. cogn. with Gk. τε-ταγ-
ών, 'grasping', and with OE. Paccian, 'to pat,
flap' у first used by the Danish mathematician
Thomas Fincke in his Geometria Rotundi (in
1583) and adopted by the German
mathematician Bartholomaus Pitiscus (1561 -1613) in 1595.
Cp. tact, tactile. Cp. also attain, contact,
contagion, contaminate, contiguity, contiguous,
contingent, entire, intact-, intangible, integer,
integrity, noli-me-tangere, task, tasse, taste, tax.
Derivatives: tangent-ial,&u'}.,tangent-ial-ly, adv.

## Tangerine
Tangerine, adj., pertaining to Tangier; п., an
inhabitant of Tangier. — Formed fr. F. Tanger,
'Tangier', seaport in Morocco, fr. L. Tinge or

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:771 COLUMN:3 -->
Tingi. For the ending see suff. -ine.

## tangerine
tangerine, п., a Tangerine orange. — From prec.
word.

## tanghin
tanghin, п., poison of the tree Tanghinia veneni-
fera. — F., from Malagasy tangena.

## tangible
tangible, adj. — Late L. tangibilis, that which
may be touched', fr. L. tangere. See tangent and
-ible.
Derivatives: tangible, п., tangibii-ity, п., tan-
gible-ness, п., tangibl-y, adv.

## tangle
tangle, п., seaweed. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. ON.
pongull, a derivative of pang, 'seaweed', and see
tang, 'seaweed'.

## tangle
tangle, tr. v., to hamper, ensnare; intr. v., to
become tangled. — ME. tangilen, formed with
freq. suff. -le fr. Dan. tang, 'seaweed' (see tang,
'seaweed'). The orig. meaning of the verb
tangle was Чо form a mass comparable to
seaweed*. Cp. entangle. Cp. also toggle.
Derivatives: tangle, п., mass, confusion, tangle-
some, adj., tangl-y, adj.

## tnngo
tnngo, п., a Span.-American dance. — S. Amer.
Sp.

## tangram
tangram, п., a Chinese puzzle. — Prob. formed
on analogy of words like anagram, cryptogram,
etc.

## tangun
tangun, п., a strong, little pony of Bhutan and
Tibet (Anglo-Indian). — Hind, tangan, tanghan,
prob. fr. Tibetan rtaniani, fr. rta, 'horse'.

## tanist
tanist, п., the elected heir of a Celtic chief. — Tr.
tanaiste, 'second; second in rank', fr. Olr.
tanise.
Derivatives: tanist-ic, adj., tanist-ry, п., the
system of electing a tanist during the chief's
lifetime.

## tank
tank, п., 1) reservoir; 2) an armored car {mil.) —
Hind, tankh, 'cistern, tank', which prob.
derives fr. OI. tadagam, 'pond, tank'. The Hind,
word was brought to Europe by the Portuguese
in whose tongue it coincided in form with
tanque, an aphetic var. of estanque, 'pond' (a
word derived fr. L. stdgnum, 'pool, pond'),
with which it has nothing in common. — When
the first armored cars of the British army were
made in 1915, the workers were made to believe
that they were fabricating ingredients for
benzene tanks. Thus tank obtained a new meaning,
that of an armored car.
Derivatives: tank-age, п., tank-er, n.

## tanka
tanka, п., name of various coins in India and
Turkestan. — See tanga.

## tankard
tankard, п., a large drinking vessel. — ME., fr.
OF. tanquart, 'a liquid measure', compounded
of tant quart, 'as much as a quarter', fr. L. tan-
turn, 'as much as', and quart, 'a quarter'. See,
tantamount and quart.

## tannaim
tannaim, n. pi., Jewish teachers mentioned in the
Mishnah (Jewish literature). — Talmudic Heb.
tannaim, pi. of tannd, 'teacher', specif, 'teacher
mentioned in the Mishna', fr. Aram, tanna, of
s.m., fr. t nd, 'he repeated, learned', which is rel.
to teren (dissimilated fr. *tenen), 'two', Aram.
tinyana, Syr. tenyuna, 'second'; Heb. sh nayim,
'two', sheni, 'second', mishne, 'double', shdnd ,
'he repeated1 (in Mishnaic Heb. 'he learned'),
Mishnaic Heb. mishnah, 'repetition, oral study,
oral law'. See Mishnah.

## tannate
tannate, п., salt of tannic acid. — Formed fr. tan
