with chem. suff. -ate.

## tanner
tanner, n., sixpence (slang). — Of unknown origin.

## tanner
tanner, п., one whose business is tanning. —
Formed fr. tan, v., with agential suff. -er.

## tanni-
tanni-, combining form denoting tannin.

## tanniferous
tanniferous, adj., yielding tannin. —
Compounded of the combining form tanni- and suff. -fe-
rous.

## tanhin
tanhin, п., tannic acid (chem.) — F. tanin, tannin,
fr. tan. See tan and -in.

## tanrec
tanrec, n. — A var. of tenrec.

## tansy
tansy, п., a plant of the genus Tanacetum. — ME.
tanesey, tansy, fr. OF. tanesie (F. tanaisie), fr.
VL. *tanaceta, neut. pi. mistaken for fem. sing.
fr. Late L. tanacetum (whence OProvenc. tena-
zet), which is of uncertain origin.

## tantalate
tantalate, п., salt of tantalic acid (chem.) —
Formed fr. tantalum with chem. suff. -ate.

## tantaliten.
tantaliten., a black crystalline mineral, Fe(TaOa)a.
—Formed fr. tantalum with subst. suff. -ite.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:772 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 745 | TARGE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:772 COLUMN:1 -->
tantalize, tr. v., to torment. — Lit. 'to torment
with pains similar to those of Tantalus'. See
Tantalus and -ize.
Derivatives: ranraliz-arion, п., tantaliz-er, п.,
tantaliz-ing, adj., tantaliz-ing-ly, adv., tantaliz-
ing-ness, n.

## tantalum
tantalum, п., name of a metallic element (chem.)
— ModL., coined by its discoverer, the Swedish
chemist Anders Gustaf Ekeberg (1767-1813), in
1802 fr. Tantalus, to illustrate the tantalizing
work he had until he succeeded in isolating this
element.
Derivatives: tantalate (q.v.),tantal-ic, adj., tan-
talite (q.v.)

## Tantalus
Tantalus, п., son of Zeus, condemned to stand in
water, which receded whenever he tried to
drink (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Τάνταλος,
lit. 'the Bearer or Sufferer', fr. dissimilation of
*Τάλ-ταλος, which is the reduplication of the
I.-E. base 'tel-, *tal-, 'to bear, carry, support,
endure', whence τάλαντον, 'pair of scales,
balance, a weight'. See talent.

## tantalus
tantalus, п., a stand containing decanters, open
at the sides, and yet not removable without a
key. — Fr. prec. word.

## tantamount
tantamount, adj. — Fr. the obsol. verb
tantamount, fr. AF. tant amunter, 'to amount to as
much', fr. OF. ( = F.) tant, 'so much', and
amonter, 'to amount to'. OF. tant comes fr. L.
tantus, 'so much', which stands for *tamtos and
derives fr. tarn, 'so', from the l.-E. pronominal
stem *to-. See the and cp. the first element in
tandem. Cp. also taunt. Cp. also the first
element in tankard and the second element in a·
taunt. For the second element in tantamount see
amount and cp. paramount.

## tantara
tantara, п., succession of notes on a trumpet or
horn. — Of imitative origin. Cp. taratantara.

## tantivy
tantivy, п., a hunting cry; swift galfop; adv.,
swiftly, headlong; adj., swift. — Of imitative
origin.

## tantra
tantra, п., one of a class of Sanskrit religious
books. — OI. tantram, 'thread, loom, warp; the
essential; doctrine, system', from the stem of
tanoti, 'he stretches', fr. l.-E. base *ten-, 'to
stretch, extend', whence also Gk. τείνειν, L.
tendere, 'to stretch'. See tend, 'to move in a
certain direction', and cp. the second element in
Fanchatantra. Cp. also tatty.

## tantrism
tantrism, п., doctrines contained in the tantras. —
Formed fr. tantra with suff. -ism.

## tantrist
tantrist, п., a student of tantrism. — Formed fr.
tantra with suff. -ist.

## tantrum
tantrum, п., outburst of petulance (colloq.) — Of
unknown origin.

## tany-
tany-, combining form meaning 'stretched out,
long' (zool.) — Gk. τανυ- (as in τ*νύγλωσσος,
'long-tongued', etc.), rel. to Homeric Gk. ταναός,
'stretched out, long', Gk. τανύειν, 'to stretch
out', andcogn. with OI. taniik, 'thin, tender', L.
tenuis, 'thin, slender', ON. punnr, OE. pynne,
'thin'. See thin and cp. tantra.

## Taoism
Taoism, п., a Chinese religious system founded
by Lao-tse. — Formed with suff. -ism fr. Chin.
tao, 'way, right path, reason'.

## tap
tap, п., faucet, cock. — ME. tappe, fr. OE. tseppa,
rel. to MDu. tappe, Du. tap, OHG. zapho,
MHG. zapfe, G. Zapfen, fr. Teut. *tappo-. Cp.
the Teut. loan words: F. tapon and its nasalized
var. tampont 'plug, stopper', It. zaffo, Sp. tapon,
of s.m. (see tampon). Cp. also tapadera, tapster,
tip, 'end', and the first element in tattoo,
'drumbeat'.

## tap
tap, tr. v., to supply with a tap. — ME. tappen,
fr. OE. tseppian, fr. tseppa, 'tap'; rel. to MLG.
tappen, MHG., G. zapfen, 'to tap'. See prec.
word.

## tap
tap, tr. and intr. v., to strike lightly. — ME.
tappen, fr. OF. (= F.) taper; of imitative origin.
Cp. tappet and tip, 'to touch gently'. Cp. also
dab, 'to strike lightly'.
Derivative: tap, п., a light blow, tapp-er, п.,
tapp-ing, n.

## tapa
tapa, п., cloth made from the inner bark of the
tree Papyrius papyrifera. — Of Marquesan
origin.

## tapadera
tapadera, also tapadero, п., leather cover of the
stirrup of a Mexican saddle. — Sp. tapadera,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:772 COLUMN:2 -->
'lid, cover', fr. tapar, 'to cover, stop up, plug',
fr. Teut. 'lappa-, 'plug, stopper'. See tap,
'faucet, cock'.

## tapas
tapas, п., the heat of asceticism (Hinduism). —
OI-, 'heat', rel. to tapati, 'warms, heats, burns',
tapu-, 'burning', and cogn. with L. tepere, 'to be
warm or lukewarm'. See tepid and cp. topaz.

## tape
tape, n. — ME. tappe, tape, fr. OE. tseppa, tsppe,
'tape, ribbon',' prob. back formation fr. L.
tapete, 'carpet', whose ending -re was mistaken
for a suff., and consequently dropped. See
tapestry and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: tape, tr. v.

## taper
taper, п., a small candle. — ME. tapre, taper, fr.
.OE. tapor, tapur, dissimilated fr. L. papyrus
(through the intermediate form "tapurus). Cp.
dial. It. papijo, papejo, 'wick', Sard, pavilu,
Rhaeto-Rom. pavier, pavel, of s.m. All these
words derive fr. L. papyrus (see papyrus, paper).
For the development of meaning it should be
borne in mind that the pit of papyrus was used
in Rome as wick. For a similar development of
meaning cp. OHG. charza, kerza (whence
MHG., G. kerze), 'candle', fr. L. charta, fr. Gk.
χάρτης, 'papyrus; roll made from papyrus; the
wick made from the pith of the papyrus'.
Derivatives: taper, adj., tapering, taper, intr.
and tr. v., taper-er, п., taper-ing, adj., taper-ing-
ly, adv., taper-ness, п., taper-wise, adv.

## tapestry
tapestry, n. — ME. tapistry, fr. MF. (= F.) ta-
pisserie, fr. tapis, 'carpet', fr. OF. tapiz, fr.
tapition, the MGk. pronunciation of Gk. τα-
πήτιον, dimin. of τάττης, gen. τάιτητος,
'hanging, carpet' (whence L. tapes, gen. tapetis), a
word of Iranian origin. Cp. ModPersian tdb-αδ,
inf. taftan, tab-ϊ-δαη, 'to turn, twist', fr. Iranian
'tap-, corresponding to I.-E. *tmp-, 'to stretch,
extend', whence L. templum, 'place of
observation, temple'. See temple, 'place of worship',
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also taffeta,
tape, tapetum, tapis.
Derivative: tapestry, tr. v.

## tapetum
tapetum, п., 1) part of the chorioid of the eye in
cats and some other animals (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. L. tapete, a collateral form of tapes, gen
tapetis, 'carpet'. See prec. word.

## Taphrina
Taphrina, п., a genus of parasitic fungi (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. τάφρος, 'ditch', which is rel. to
τάφος, 'burial', θάπτειν, 'to bury' (aor. έτά-
φην). See cenotaph.

## taplno-
taplno-, before a vowel tapin-, combining form
meaning 'low' (used in anthropol.) — Gk.
ταπεινό-, ταπειν-, fr. ταπεινός, 'low; humble',
orig. 'compressed', fr. I.-E. base 'tap-, 'to press,
squeeze', whence also OI. sam-tapati,
'compresses'.

## tapioca
tapioca, п., a granular substance prepared from
cassava starch. — Port-, dissimilated from Tupi
and Guarani tipioca, fr. tipi, 'dregs', and ok, 'to
squeeze out'.

## tapir
tapir, п., a tropical hoglike mammal. — Sp.,
fr. Tupi tapiira.

## tapiroid
tapiroid, adj., resembling the tapirs. — A hybrid
coined fr. tapir and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. εϊδος,
'form, shape'. See -oid.

## tapis
tapis, п., tapestry (history; now used only in the
phrase on the tapis). — MF. (= F.), fr. OF.
tapiz. See tapestry.

## tappet
tappet, п., projecting arm in a machine. —
Formed fr. tap, 'to strike lightly', with suff. -et.

## tapster
tapster, п., a person employed to tap liquors. —
ME., fr. OE. tseppestre, 'a woman employed to
tap liquors', fr. tseppa, 'tap'. See tap, 'pipe',
and -ster.

## tapu
tapu, n. — A var. of taboo.

## tar
tar, п., a viscous liquid. — ME. terre, fr. OE.
teoru, teru, rel. to ON. tjara, Dan. tjsere, Swed.
tjara, OFris. tera, MDu. tar, ter, terre, Du.
teer, G. Teer. These words orig. meant
'pertaining to a tree'. They derive fr. I.-E. 'derew(o)-,
*drew(o)-, 'tree', whence OI. ddru, 'wood', Gk.
δόρυ, 'beam, shaft of a spear, spear', δρυς, 'tree,
oak', Goth, triu, OE. treow, 'tree'. See tree and
cp. the first element in tarpaulin.
Derivatives: tar, tr. v., tarr-ed, tarr-y, adjs.

## tar
tar, п., sailor (colloq.)—Abbreviation of tarpaulin.

## tara
tara, also tara fern, п., a kind of New Zealand
brake with edible rootstock. — Maori tara,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:772 COLUMN:3 -->
'spear'.

## taradiddle
taradiddle, n. — The same as tarradiddie.

## taramellite
taramellite, п., a basic barium and iron silicate
(mineral.) — Named after the Italian
mineralogist Torquato Taramelli (died in 1922). For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## tarand
tarand, п., the reindeer (obsol.) — F., fr. L. taran-
drus, which derives—with change of suff. -dus
to -drus—fr. Gk. τάρανδος, 'reindeer', a loan
word from a language of the North.

## tarantara
tarantara, п., succession of notes on a trumpet or
horn. — Of imitative origin. Cp. taratantara.

## tarantass
tarantass, п., a large, four-wheeled carriage. —
Russ. tarantas, which is of uncertain origin.

## tarantella
tarantella, п., a lively Italian dance. — It., lit.
'dance of Taranto', formed with dimin. suff.
-eila fr. Taranto, name of a town in southern
Italy, fr. L. Tarentum, fr. Gk. Τάρας, gen.
Τάραντος. The association of tarantella with
tarantula—as if tarantella orig. denoted 'a dance
resembling the movements of one bitten by a
tarantula'—is folk etymology.

## tarantism
tarantism, п., a kind of nervous disease. —
Medical L. tarantismus, fr. It. tarantismo, formed fr.
Taranto; (see tarantella); so called because the
dance tarantella was regarded as the best
remedy for the disease. For the ending see suff. -ism.

## tarantula
tarantula, п., a large venomous spider. — ML.
tarantula, fr. It. tarantola, fr. Taranto; so called
because of this spider's frequent occurrence in
the country around Taranto. Cp. tarantella,
tarantism.
Derivatives: tarantul-ar, tarantul-ary, tarantul-
ated, adjs.

## taratantara
taratantara, п., tantara. — L., of imitative origin.
Cp. tantara.

## Taraxacum
Taraxacum, п., a genus of plants of the chicory
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. Arab, tarakhshaqun,
tarakhshaquq, fr. Pers. talkh chakdk, lit. 'bitter
herb'.

## tarboosh
tarboosh, п., a brimless felt cap worn by
Moslems. — F. tarbouch(e),'Tr. Arab, tarbush, lit.
'sweating cap', a hybrid coined fr. Turk, ter,
'sweat', and Pers. pushiddn, 'to cover'.

## tardamente
tardamente, adv., slowly (musical direction). —
It-, 'slowly', formed fr. tarda, fem. of tardo,
'slow', and adverbial suff. -mente, fr. L. mente,
abl. of mens, 'mind'. See tardo and mind and cp.
mental, 'relating to the mind'. Cp. also lenta-
mente, tostamente.

## Tardenoisean
Tardenoisean, adj., pertaining to the transitional
period between the Old Stone and the New
Stone Ages. — Named after La Fbtt-ta-Tarde-
nois, near Rheims, France. For the ending see
suff. -ean.

## Tardigrada
Tardigrada, n. pi., a division of arthropods (zool.)
— ModL., fr. L. tardigradus. See next word.

## tardigrade
tardigrade, adj. and п., moving slowly; п., a
tardigrade animal. — F., fr. L. tardigradus, 'slow-
paced', Which is compounded of tardus, 'slow',
and gradior,gradi,' to step'. See tardy and gradus.

## tardo
tardo, adj., slow; adv., slowly, (musicaldirection).
— It., 'slow, slowly', fr. L. tardus, 'slow'. See
tardy and cp. tardamente.

## tardy
tardy,adj.,late. — Fr. earliertardif,ix.OF. (=F.)
tardif, fr. VL. tardivus, fr. L. tardus, 'slow',
which is of uncertain origin. Cp. tardo,
tardamente, retard and the second element in bustard.
Derivatives: tardi-ly, adv., tardi-ness, n.

## tare
tare, п., allowance in weight. — ME., fr. MF.
(= F.) tare, fr. Sp. tara, of s.m., fr. Arab.
tarha1, 'that which is thrown away', fr. taraha,
'he threw, threw away'. Cp. mattress.
Derivative: tare, tr. v., to find the weight of the
tare.·

## tare
tare, п., 1) a kind of vetch; 2) a weed, prob. the
darnel. — ME., prob. fr. MDu. tarwe, ter we
(Du. tarwe), 'wheat', which is cogn. with Bret.
draok, dreok, W. drewg, 'darnel', OI. durvtt, 'a
kind of millet grass', Delphic Gk. δαράτϊ,
Thessal. δάρατος, 'bread'. Cp. doob. Cp. also
L. dravoca, 'a bur', which is a Gaulish loan
word (see dredge, 'a mixture of grain').

## targe
targe, п., shield, buckler. — ME., fr. OF. targe,
targue (F. targe), fr. Frankish 'targa; cp. LG.
targe, OHG. zarga, MHG., G. zarge, 'border,
edge, frame', OE. targe, targa, ON. targa,
'shield, buckler', orig. 'edge of a shield'. The

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:773 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TARGE | 746 | turms, n. — A var. of trass. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:773 COLUMN:1 -->
orig. meaning of these Teut. words was 'border
edge'. They are perh. cogn. with Gk. δράσ-
σεσθαί, 'to cluth, grasp, seize*, properly 'to
enclose', δραχμή, 'drachma', δράγμα, 'a sheaf,
lit. 'a handful'; see dram and cp. target. ML.
targ{i)a, OProvenc. targa (whence It. targa), Sp.
tarja, 'shield', are also Teut. loan words. G.
Tartscke, 'small round shield; target*, has been
re-borrowed fr. OF. targa.

## turge
turge, tr. v., to harass with questions (Scot.) —
Of uncertain origin.

## target
target, n. — ME., fr. MF. targete (F. targette), 'a
small shield, target', dimin. of targe. See targe»
'shield', and -et.
Derivatives: target, tr. v., target-eer, n.

## Targuin
Targuin, п., Aramaic translation of the Bible. —
Mishnaic Heb. targum, 'interpretation,
translation', fr. Heb. r/>gem,'heinterpreted,translated',
which is rel. to Aram, targem, Arab, tarjama, of
s.m. All these verbs are denominated fr. Akkad.
targumanu, 'interpreter' (fr. ragumu, 'to call'),
whence also Aram, turg типа, 'interpreter,
translated. Cp. meturgeman. Cp. also dragoman.
Derivatives: Targum-ic, adj., Targumist (q.v.)

## Targuinist
Targuinist, п., 1) writer of a Targum; 2) student
of the Targnms. — Formed fr. Targnm with
suff. -ist.
Derivative: Targumist-ic, adj.

## tariff
tariff, n. — Sp.-Port. tarifa, fr. Arab, ta'rtf, 'a
making known, information', verbal noun of
farrafa, 'he made known, he taught1, second
conjugation of tarafa, 'he knew'. Cp. It. tariffa.
Derivative: tariff, tr. v.

## tarlatun
tarlatun, п., a kind of thin, open muslin. — F.
tarlatane, prob. of E. Indian origin.
Tarmac» п., trademark for a kind of tarmacadam.
— Short for tarmacadam.

## tarmacadam
tarmacadam, п., pavement constructed by
spraying or pouring a tar binder over crushed stone.
— Compounded of tar and macadam.

## tarn
tarn, п., a small lake in the mountains. — ME.
terne, tarne, fr. ON. tjorn, 'a small lake". Cp. dial.
Swed. tjurn, of s.m.

## tarnish
tarnish, tr. and intr. v. — Fr. F. terniss-, stem of
the pres. part, of ternir, 'to tarnish', which is of
Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. tarni, 'hidden, dark',
tarnjan, MHG. ternen, 'to hide, darken', OE.
derne, OS. derni, OFris. dern, 'concealed, dark',
and see dark. For the ending see verbal sufT. -ish.
Derivatives: tarnish, п., tarnish-able, adj.,
tarnish-er, n.

## taro
taro, п., a tropical plant, Cofocasia eseulenta. —
Polynesian.

## taroc
taroc, п., playing card. — It. tarocchi (sing, taroc-
co), fr. Arab, taraha, 'he rejected, put aside'; see
Lokotsch, EW., No. 2024. Cp. mattress, and
tare, 'allowance in weight', which are traceable
to the same Arabic verb.

## tarot
tarot, п., the same as taroc. — F. tarots (pi. of
tarot), fr. It. tarocchi (pi. of tarocco). See prec.
word.

## tarpan
tarpan, п., wild horse of the Russian steppes. —
Of Tatar origin.

## tarpaulin
tarpaulin, п., a waterproof covering of canvas. —
A hybrid coined fr. tar, 'dark, viscid liquid', a
Teutonic word, and palling, 'covering',
derivative of pall, 'cloak, coverlet', a word of Latin
origin.

## Tarpeian rock
Tarpeian rock, rock on the Capitoline Hill in
Rome. — Fr. L. (mons) Tarpeius, '(rock) of Tar-
peia', so called after Tarpeia, a Vestal virgin who
betrayed the capitol to the Sabines, and was
buried at its foot. The name Tarpeia is prob. of
Etruscan-Tyrrhenian origin.

## tarpon
tarpon, п., a large fish of the herring family. —
Prob. of American Indian origin.

## tarr a diddle
tarr a diddle, п., lie, fib. — An invented word.

## tarragon
tarragon, п., a plant with aromatic leaves. — Sp.
taragona, fr. Arab, farkkun, 'dragon wort', fr.
Gk. δρακόν-π,ον,'adderwort', lit. 'a little
dragon' ; dimin. of δράκων, gen. δράκοντος,
'dragon'. Cp. It. targone and F. estragon, which
are of the same origin and meaning, and see
dragon.

## turragona
turragona, п., a kind of Spanish wine resembling
port. — Short for Tarragona wine, fr. Tarragona,
a province in N.-E. Spain.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:773 COLUMN:2 -->

## tarrock
tarrock, п., a young kittiwake. — From
Greenland Eskimo tdteraq.

## tarry
tarry, intr. and tr. v. — ME. tarien, 'to vex,
irrigate; to hinder, delay', fr. OE. tergan, tyrgan, 'to
vex, irritate*, rel. to Du. tergen, G. zergen, 'to
vex, irritate*, and cogn. with Russ. dergaC, 'to
pluck, drag'. ME. tarien was confused in
meaning with ME. targen, 'to delay', fr. OF. targier,
tardier, fr. VL. *tardicare, freq. of L. tardare, 'to
delay' (whence F. tarder, of s.m.); see tardy.
Derivatives: tarri-ance, п., tarri-er, п.,
tarrying, n.

## tars-
tars-, form of tarso- before a vowel.

## tarsal
tarsal, adj., pertaining to the tarsus. — Formed
fr. tarsus with adj. suff. -al.

## tarsia
tarsia, п., mosaic. — It, fr. Arab. tarsf\ 'inlaid
work', verbal noun of rassa'a, 'he laid in'. Cp.
Heb. ratza\ 'he bored, pierced', martze'a,
'boring instrument, awl', Mishnaic Heb. ratz'an,
Aram, rutz'dna, 'shoemaker'.

## tarsier
tarsier, п., arboreal lemur of the East Indies. —
F., fr. tarse, 'tarsus' (see tarsus and -ier); so
called from its long tarsus.

## Tarsipes
Tarsipes, п., a genus of Australian marsupials
(zooi) — ModL., compounded of ModL.rar-
sus, 'ankle', and L. pes, 'foot'. See tarsus and
foot, and cp. pedal.

## tarso-
tarso-, before a vowel tars-, combining form
denoting the tarsus (anat.) — See tarsus.

## tarsus
tarsus, п., the ankle {anat.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
ταρσός, 'wicker work; flat of the foot; ankle;
edge of the eyelid*, rel. to *τρασιά, Ion. ταρσιή,
'crate for drying figs', fr. I.-E. base *trs-, *ters-,
'to dry', whence alsoGk^peocoSm, 'to be or
become dry, dry up', τερσαίνεΐ-ν, 'to make dry,
to dry', L. terra (for *tersa-), 'land, ground,
soil', lit. 'the dry one'. See terra and cp. torrid.
Cp. also thirst.

## turt
turt, п., fruit pie. — ME. tarte, fr. OF. tarte, a
variant of torte, tourte (F. tourte), 4art, fruit
pie', lit. 'round cake', fr. L. torta. See tarta.

## tart
tart, adj., sour, acid. — ME., fr. OE. teart,
'severe', which is prob. rel. to teran, 'to tear'. See
tear, 'to pull apart'.
Derivatives: tart-ly, adv., tart-ness, n.

## tartan
tartan, п., a single-masted vessel. — F. tartane, fr.
It. tartana, prob. fr. Arab. tartdah, 'a small ship',
fr. tarada, 'he hunted, pursued, persecuted',
which is rel. to Heb. taradh, 'he pursued, chased,
was continuous', inTalmudic Hebrew, 'he stirred
up, troubled, wearied', Aram.-Syr. t radh, 'he
drove away', Akkad. farddu, 'to drive away'. Cp.
Sp. tarida and tartanat 'tartan*, which also
derive fr. Arab. tartdab.

## tartan
tartan, п., a kind of woolen fabric. — ME. tir-
taine, fr. OF. (= F.) tiretaine, fr. Sp. tiritana, 'a
thin silk stuff, lit. 'the rustling stuff', fr. tiritar,
'to shiver', a word of imitative origin.

## Tartan
Tartan, п., title of an Assyrian commander-in-
chief (see II Kings 18 : 17 and Is. 20 : 1) — Heb.
tartan, fr. Akkad, tardinnu, tartenu, 'the second',
fr. terdu, 'follower', fr. redu, 'to follow'; see
Ungnad, Joseph, der Tartan des Pharaoh,
ZATW., 41, pp. 204-207. For sense
development cp. L. secundus, 'the second', fr. sequi, 'to
follow' (see second, adj.)

## Tartar
Tartar, n. and adj. — ML. Tartarus, fr. Pers.
Tatar, ult. fr. Tata, name of the Mongols, who
coming from the Gobi desert invaded Russia in
the 9th cent. The first r in Tartar is due to a
confusion with L. Tartarus, 'hell'; see Tartarus.

## tartar
tartar, п., 1) potassium bitartrate, KHC4H4Oe
{chem.); 2) a hard deposit on the teeth. — ME.
tartre, tartar, fr. OF. tartre, fr. ML. tartarum,
fr. Gk. Τάρταρος (see Tartarus); so called by
Paracelsus with regard to the burning effect of
this compound.
Derivatives: tartar-eous, tartar-ic, tartar-ish,
adjs., tartar-ize, tr. y., tartar-iz-ation, п., tartar-
ous, adj.

## Tartarean
Tartarean, adj., pertaining to Tartarus. —
Formed fr. Tartarus with suff. -ean.

## Tartarus
Tartarus, п., the abyss below Hades; place of
punishment; Hades, netherworld; hell (Greek
mythol.) — L„ fr. Gk. Τάρταρος, prob. a word
of imitative origin, suggestive of something
frightful. Cp. tartar.

## tartlet
tartlet, п., a small tart. — Formed fr. tart, п.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:773 COLUMN:3 -->
with dimin. suff. -let. Cp. F. tartelette.

## tartrate
tartrate, п., salt of tartaric acid (chem.) — F.,
formed with chem. suff. -ate fr. tartre, 'tartar'.
See tartar.

## Tartuf(f)e
Tartuf(f)e, п., a hypocrite. — F., fr. the principal
character of Moliere's comedy of this name.
Tartuf(f)e derives fr. It. Tartufo, lit. 'truffle'. See
truffle.
Derivatives: tartuf(f)-ery, п., tartuf(f)-ish, adj.,
tartujXj)-ism, n.

## taseometer
taseometer, n., an instrument for measuring
structural stresses. — Coined fr. Gk. τάσις, gen.
τάσεως, 'stretching, tension', and μέτρον,
'measure'. See tasimeter.

## tashlik
tashlik, п., a propitiatory rite, observed on the
afternoon of Rosh Hashanah (New Year's Day)
near a stream of water. On this occasion several
Biblical passages, amongst them the verses Mi-
cah 7: 18-20 are recited {Jewish religion). —
Heb. tashlikh, 'thou wilt cast', imperfect of
hishlikh, *he cast". The rite is so called from the
first word of the orig. Heb. text of Micah 7:19
'Thou wilt cast (tashlikh) all their sins into the
depths of the sea'.

## Tashmitum
Tashmitum, п., a Babylonian goddess, the wife of
Nebo. — Akkad. Tashmitum, lit. 'proclaimer',
fr. tashmitum, 'a hearing', fr. shemu, 'to hear',
which is rel. to Heb. shuma\ 'he heard'. See
She ma.

## tashrif
tashrif, also tashreef, п., honor, respect {Anglo-
Indian) — Arab, tashrif, 'an honoring', verbal
noun of sliarraja, 'he ennobled, elevated,
honored', second form of sharuja, 'he was exalted, he
was noble'. See shereef and cp. words there
referred to.

## tasimeter
tasimeter, п., an electrical instrument for
measuring changes in pressure caused by changes in
temperature. — Coined fr. Gk. τάσις,
'stretching, tension", and μέτρον, 'measure'. Gk. τάσι,ς
stands for I.-E. "tntis, whence also OI. tatih,
'row, line, thread'; from *tn-, zero degree of
base *ten-, "to stretch', whence OI. tanSti,
'stretches', Gk. τείνειν, L. tendere, 'to stretch'.
See tend, 'to move in a certain direction', and
cp. ectasis and words there referred to.
Derivatives: tasimetr-ic, adj., tasimetr-y, n.

## task
task, n. — ME. taske, fr. ONF. tasque, fr. OF.
(asche (F. tache) fr. VL. *tasca, metathesized fr.
ML. taxa, which is a back formation fr. L. ta-
xare, 'to touch sharply, handle; to appraise,
estimate'. See tax and cp. tasse and the second
element in sabretache.

## tass
tass,n., a drinking cup; a smalldraft.—MF.( = F.)
tasse, 'cup*, fr. OF., fr. Arab. tassaht tass, fr.
Pers. tasht, 'cup, saucer'. Cp. OProvenc. tassa,
It. tazza4 Sp. taza, 'cup', which are of the same
origin. Cp. also tazza.

## Tass
Tass, п., the official news agency of the U.S.S.R.
— Formed from the initials of the Russian
words 7elegrafnoje Agenstvo Sovjetskeho So·
juza (= 'Soviet Telegraphic Agency').

## tasse
tasse, п., one of a series of plates forming a sort
of kilt or shirt {armor). — MF. tasse, 'pocket',
fr. MHG. (= G.) tasche, fr. OHG. tasca, which,
together with MLG. taske, OS. dasga, is
borrowed fr. VL. *tasca; see task. The phases of
the sense development of VL. * tasca prob. are:
'appraisal, estimate; amount of work imposed
by authority; recompense for such work; daily
wages; pocket into which the wages are put;
any pocket'.

## tussel
tussel, п., ornament. — ME., fr. OF. tassel
(whence F. iasseau, 'cleat, strip, bracket'), fr.
VL. *tassellus, fr. L. taxillus, 'a small die',
dimin. of talus, 'knucklebone, heel'. See talus,
'ankle'.
Derivatives: tassel, tr. v., tassel-y, adj.

## tassel
tassel, n. — A var. of tercel.

## taste
taste, tr. and intr. v. — ME. tasten, 'to feel, taste',
fr. OF. taster (F. tater), 'to feel, touch, handle',
fr. VL. *taxitare, freq. of L. taxare, 'to touch
sharply', itself freq. of tangere, 'to touch' (see
tangent). Cp. OProvenc. tastar, It. tastare, Sp.
and Port, tastar, 'to feel, taste', which are of the
same origin. To account for the sense
development 'to feel; to taste', Bloomfield (in Indoger-
manische Forschungen) suggests the hypothetic
VL. form "tastare, which should have arisen as

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:774 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 747 | TAXIS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:774 COLUMN:1 -->
a blend of L. gustare, 'to taste', and tangere, 'to
touch'.
Derivatives: tast-er, п., tast-ing, n. and adj.,
tast-ing-ly, adv.

## taste
taste, n. — ME. tast, 'touch, taste', fr. OF. tast
(F. tat), fr. taster. See taste, v.
Derivatives: taste-ful, adj., taste-fuhly, adv.,
taste-ful-ness, п., taste-less, adj., taste-less-ly,
adv., taste-less-ness, п., tast-y, adj., tast-i-ly,
adv., tast-i-ness, П.

## tat
tat, intr. v., to do tatting; tr. v., to make by
tatting. — Back formation fr. tatting.

## tat
tat, п., a coarse cloth (India). — Hind. tat.

## tat
tat, п., in the phrase tit for tat. — See tit.

## tata
tata, п., good-bye. — Of imitative origin (child's
language).

## Tatar
Tatar, n. — See Tartar.

## tatter
tatter, п., a torn piece; rag. — ME. tater, tatter,
of Scand. origin. Cp. Icel. totturr, tottur, totur,
(pi. tottrar, totrar), 'tatter, rag', Norw. totra (pi.
totror), of s.m., LG, tater, 'tatter". See tod and
cp. the first element in next word.
Derivatives: tatter, tr. and intr. v., tatter-ed,
adj., tatter-ed-ly, adv., tatter-ed-ness, п., tatter-
y, adj.

## tatterdemalion
tatterdemalion, п., a ragged person. — A
compound formed fr. tatter and a second element of
uncertain origin.

## tatting
tatting, п., a kind of handmade lace. — Of
uncertain origin.

## tattle
tattle, intr. v., ]) to talk idly; to chatter; 2) to tell
tales; tr. v., to tell (a secret). — MDu. tatelen,
tateren, 'to stammer*, of imitative origin. The
primary meaning was 'to repeat the syllable ta\
Cp. tittle-tattle.
Derivative: tattle, п., tattl-er, п., tattl-ing, adj.

## tattoo
tattoo, п., drum beat. — Du. taptoe, lit. 'closing
of the taps', fr. tap. Чар', and toe, 'to; shut' (for
sense development cp. G. zu, 'to; closed'). See
tap, 'pipe', and to.

## tattoo
tattoo, tr. v., to mark (the skin) with pigments; п.,
the act of tattooing. — Of Polynesian origin;
cp. Tahitian tatau, tatu, 'puncturation, mark
made on the skin*.
Derivatives: tattoo-age, п., tattoo-er, п.,
tattooing, n.

## tattoo
tattoo, п., a native-bred pony in India. — Hind.
tattu, prob. fr. OI. tarati, 'passes over*, fr. I.-E.
base *ter-, *to go through, pass beyond', whence
also L. terminus, 'boundary line, boundary'. See
term.

## tatty
tatty, п., mat of cuscus hung in a window or door
and kept wet to cool the air. — Hind, tatti,
which possibly derives fr. OI. tantram, 'thread,
loom, warp; the essential; doctrine'. See tantra.

## tau
tau, п., the 19th letter of the Greek alphabet. —
Gk. ταυ, fr. Heb. taw, name of the last letter
of the Hebrew alphabet, lit. 'sign, mark'. Cp.
tav.

## Taube
Taube, п., German military monoplane. — G.,
lit. 'dove'·, rel. to E. dove (q.v.)

## taught
taught, past tense and pp. of teach. — ME.
taugkt(e), fr. OE. tahte, resp. getxht, past tense,
resp. pp. of txcan. See teach.

## tannt
tannt, tr. v., to reproach, provoke. — MF. tauter,
var. of tenter (F. tenter), fr. OF. tempter, tenter,
'to tempt, put to-the test', fr. L. tempture, 'to
handle, touch, feel, put to the test, try', whence
also OProvenc. temptar, Sp. tentar, It. tentare,
'to touch, feel with the fingers; to tempt,
instigate; to attempt, try, test, prove'; see Bloch-
Wartburg, DELF., p. 600 s.v. tenter. See tempt.
Derivatives: taunt-er, п., taunt-ing, adj., taunt-
ing-ly, adv., taunting-ness, n.

## taunt
taunt, adj., very tall (naut.; said of a mast). — F.
tant, *so great, so much', fr. L. t ant us. See
tantamount, and cp. ataunt.
tains form of tauro- before a vowel.

## tauri-
tauri-, combining form meaning 'bull'. — L.
tauri-, fr. taurus, 'bull*. See Taurus.

## tauriform
tauriform, adj., having the form of a bull. —
Compounded of tauri- and -form.

## taurine
taurine, adj., pertaining to a bull. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ine fr. L. taurus. See Taurus.

## tauro-
tauro-, before a vowel taur-, combining form
meaning 'bull'. — L. tauro-, taur·, fr. taurus. See
Taurus.

## tauromachy
tauromachy, п., bullfighting. — Gk. ταυρομαχία,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:774 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. ταϋρος, 'bull', and -μαχία, fr. μάχη, 'fight,
battle'. See Taurus and -machy.

## Taurotragus
Taurotragus, п., the genus of the elands (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. tauro- and Gk. τράγος,
'goat'. See tragacanth.

## Taurus
Taurus, п., 1) a constellation, containing the
Pleiades and Hyades; 2) one of the signs of the
zodiac (astron.) — L. taurus, 'bull', cogn. with
Gk. ταύρος, OSlav. turu, 'bull', Lith. tauras,
'aurochs', OPruss. tauris, 'bison*; prob. of Sem.
origin. Cp. Aram. rora,'ox, bull, steer*, Heb. shor,
Akkad. skuru, Arab, thor, Ethiop. sor, of s.m.
Cp. also steer, 'young ox', toreador, torero, toro
and the second element in Minotaur. Cp. also
the second element in bittern.

## taut
taut, adj., drawn tightly, tense. — ME. toght,
toht, prop, weak pp. of togen, towen, 'to pull,
draw'. See tow, v.
Derivatives: tauten, v. (q.v.), taut-ly, adv., taut-
ness, n.

## tauten
tauten, tr. and intr. v. — Formed fr. taut with
verbal suff. -en.

## tauto-
tauto-, combining form meaning the same'. —
Gk. ταυτο-, contraction of το αυτό, 'the same'.
To, the neut. def. article derives from the I.-E.
pronominal base * to-; see the, art. For αυτό see
auto-,

## tautochrone
tautochrone, п., curve down which a body moving
from any point under the force of gravity will
always reach the lowest point in the same time.
Lit. 'of the same time*. See tauto- and chronic.

## tuutochronism
tuutochronism, п., property of a tautochrone. —
See prec. word and -ism.

## tautochronous
tautochronous, adj., having the property of a
tautochrone. — See tantochroue and -ous.

## tautog
tautog, п., an edible marine fish of the Atlantic
coast of N. America. — Narraganset tautaaog.

## tautology
tautology, п., repetition of the same idea in other
words. — Late L. tautologia, fr. Gk.
ταυτολογία, lit. 'the saying of the same thing',
compounded of ταυτο- (see tauto-) and -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, One who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)*. See -logy.
Derivatives: tautolog-ic, tautolog-ic-al, adjs.,
tautolog-ist, п., tautolog-ize, intr. v.

## tautomerism
tautomerism, п., the phenomenon, shown by
certain compounds, of reacting as if each possessed
two or more structures (chem.) — Compounded
of tauto-, Gk. μέρος, 'part*, and suff. -ism. See
mero-, 'part', and cp. merism.

## tautoineter
tautoineter, п., an instrument to measure taut-
ness. — A hybrid coined fr. E. taut and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## tantophony
tantophony, п., repetition of the same sound. —
Gk. ταυτοφωνία, compounded of ταυτο-
(see tauto-), φωνή, 'sound, voice', and suff. -y
(representing Gk. -ία). See phone, 'speech
sound'.
Derivatives: tautophon-ic, tautopkon-ic-al, adjs.

## tnv
tnv, also taw, п., name of the 22nd letter of the
Hebrew alphabet. — Heb. taw, 'sign, sign mark'
(see Ezek. 9:3). Cp. tau.

## tavern
tavern, n. — ME. taverne, fr. OF. (— F.) taverne,
fr. L. taberna, 'hut, booth, tavern', which is of
uncertain origin; it is perh. dissimilated fr. *tra-
berna, a derivative of trabs (gen. trabis), 'beam,
timber'. See trabea and cp. tabernacle, contu-
bernium. For the suff. see cavern.

## taverner
taverner, п., ]) the keeper of a tavern; 2) (obsol.)
a frequenter of taverns. — ME. tavernere, fr.
OF. (= F.) tavernier, fr. L. taberndrius, fr.
taberna. See prec. word and agential suff. -er.

## tavernous
tavernous, adj., tavernlike. — Formed fr. tavern
on the analogy of cavernous; see -ous.

## tavistockite
tavistockite, п., a basic calcium aluminum
phosphate (mineral.) — Named after Tavistock in
Devonshire, England. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## taw
taw, tr. v., 1) to prepare (skins); 2) to make
(skins) into leather. — ME. tawen, fr. OE.
tawian, 'to prepare, dress (leather)', rel. to
OFris. tawa, OS. toian, MDu. tauwen, touwen,
Du. touwen, OHG. zouwen, 'to prepare', OHG.
zawen, 'to succeed', Goth, taujan, 'to make,
prepare', OE. tol, 'tool'. See tool and cp. tew, 'to
prepare', tow, 'fiber of hemp'. Cp. also taws and
the second element in heriot.
Derivatives: taw-er, п., taw-ery, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:774 COLUMN:3 -->

## taw
taw, п., 1) game of marbles; 2) a line from which
the players shoot in this game. — Of uncertain
origin.

## tawdry
tawdry, adj., showy, gaudy. — Short for tawdry
laces, which is a corruption of St. Audrey's laces,
i.e. laces sold at St. Audrey's Fair, which was
neld annually at Ely in England on October
17th; hence tawdry orig. meant 'resembling the
showy laces sold at St. Audrey's Fair'. For the
origin of the name Audrey see Audrey.
Derivatives: tawdri-ly, adv., tawdri-ness, n.

## tawny
tawny, adj., tan colored. — ME. tauni, tawny, fr.
OF. lane, tanne (F. tanne), pp. of taner, tanner,
'to tan'. See tan, v.
Derivatives: tawny, п., tawni-ness, n.

## taws
taws, tawse, п., a whip for chastising children
(Scot.) — Prob. rel. to taw, 'to prepare skins',
which formerly had also the meaning 'to whip,
flog, lash".

## tax
tax, tr. v. — ME. taxen, fr. MF. (= F.) taxer, L.
taxare, 'to touch sharply, handle; to appraise,
estimate, compute; to censure'; in ML. also 'to
impose a tax', freq. of tangere, 'to touch'. See
tangent and cp. task, tasse, taste.
Derivatives: tax, п., tax-able, adj., tax-ability,
п., tax-able-ness, п., tax-abl-y, adv., taxation
(q.v.), tax-ative, adj., tax-ative-ly, adv., tax-er,
п., tax-ing, adj., tax-ing-ly, adv., tax-less, adj.

## tax-
tax-, form of taxi- before a vowel.

## Taxaceae
Taxaceae, n. pi., the pine family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Taxus with suff. -aceae.

## taxation
taxation, n. — ME. taxacioun, fr. MF. (— F.)
taxation, fr. L. taxationem, ace. of taxatio, *a
rating, valuing, appraisal', fr. taxdtus, pp. of
taxare. See tax and -ation.
Derivative: taxation-al, adj.

## taxi
taxi, n. — Abbreviation of taximeter or taxicab.
Derivative: taxi, intr. v.

## taxi-
taxi-, before a vowel tax-, combining form
meaning 'arrangement'. —Gk. ταξί-, fr. τάξις,
'arrangement*. See taxis.

## taxi arch
taxi arch, п., commander of a taxis (Ancient Greek
Hist.) — Gk. ταξίαρχος, compounded of
τάξις, 'a body of soldiers', and άρχος, 'leader,
chief, ruler'. See taxis and arch-,

## taxicab
taxicab, n. — Abbreviation of taximeter cab (see
taximeter).
Derivative: taxicab, intr. v.

## Taxidea
Taxidea, п., a genus of animals, the American
badger (zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idea
fr. ML. taxus, 'badger*, a word of Teut. origin.
Cp. MDu., Du. das, OHG., MHG. dahs, G.
Dachs, and the second element in Dan. and
Norw. svin-toks, of s.m. These words prob.
derive fr. I.-E. base *tekth-, 'to build, carpenter,
weave', whence also OI. tak$an, 'carpenter', Gk.
τέκτωυ, of s.m., τέ^νη, 'art, skill', L. texere,
'to weave, construct', accordingly, MDu. das,
etc., prob. mean lit. 'the builder'. See text and
words there referred to and cp. the first element
in dachshund and the second element in ratel.

## taxidermist
taxidermist, п., a person who prepares, stuffs and
mounts the skins of animals. — See taxidermy
and -ist.

## taxidermy
taxidermy, п., the art of preparing, stuffing and
mounting the skins of animals. — Compounded
of taxi-, Gk. δέρμα, 'skin*, and suff. -y
(representing Gk. -ία). See derma and cp. the second
element in pachyderm.
Derivatives: taxiderm-al, adj., taxiderm-ic, adj.,
taxidermist (q.v.)

## taximeter
taximeter, п., an automatic instrument installed
in taxi cabs showing the fare due. — F. taximetre,
fr. taxe, 'rate, charge, tax, duty', back
formation fr. taxer, and -metre. See tax and meter,
'poetical rhythm*. The original name given to
this instrument was taxametre. This name was
changed into the correct form taximetre by
Theodor Reinach in a letter sent by him to the
Temps in 1906.

## taxine
taxine, adj., pertaining to the yew. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ine fr. L. taxus, 'yew'. See Taxus.

## taxine
taxine, taxin,n., a poisonous alkaloid C37H51NO10
(chem.) — Formed with chem. suff. -ine, resp.
-in, fr. L. taxus, 'yew'. See Taxus.

## taxis
taxis, п., 1) a division of the ancient Greek army;
2) the replacing of a displaced part (surgery); 3)
involuntary movement of a cell in relation to an

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:775 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TAXITE | 748 | tea. -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:775 COLUMN:1 -->
external stimulus (biol.) — ModL., fr. Gk.
τάξις, 'arrangement, order position; a body of
soldiers', from the stem of τάσσειν, Att.
τάττειν, *to arrange, array, post, place,
appoint' (whence also ταγή. Order of battle',
ταγός, 'commander, chief, τάγμα, 'order,
rank'), which is prob. cognate with Lith. pa-
togiis, 'convenient, comfortable, decent', Lett.
pa-tags, of s.m., Lith. su-togti, 'to agree with'.
Cp. tactics and next word. Cp. also ataxy, hypo-
taxis, parataxis, syntax.

## taxite
taxite, п., a kind of lava formed from fragments
of different colors (petrogr.) — Formed with
subst. surf, -ite fr. Gk. τάξις, 'arrangement,
order'. See prec. word.

## Taxodium
Taxodium, п., a genus of plants, the bald cypress
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of Gk. τάξος,
'yew' (fr. L. taxus), and -ώδης, 'like'. SeeTaxus
and the suffixes -ode, 'like', and -ium.

## taxonomy
taxonomy, п., science of classification, founded
by the Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus (Karl
von Linne) (1707-78). — F. taxonomie,
irregularly formed fr. Gk. τάξις, 'arrangement, order',
and -νομίοί, fr. νόμος, 'law'; see taxis and
-nomy. The regular form would be taxionomy.
Cp. Gk. φυσιολογία and see physio logy.
Derivatives: taxonom-ic, taxonom-ic-al, adjs.,
taxonom-ist, n.

## Taxus
Taxus, п., a genus of plants, the yew (bot.) — L.,
'yew', a Scythian loan word. Gk. τόξον, 'bow',
is of the same origin (see toxic). For sense
development cp. ON. yr, which unites the meanings
'yew' and 'bow'. See Hehn, Kulturpflanzen und
Haustiere, 8th edition, p. 621.

## taylorite
taylorite, п., a potassium ammonium sulfate
{mineral.) — Named after the American
mineralogist William J. Taylor (1833-64). For the
ending see subst. surf. -ite.

## tazza
tazza, п., a shallow, ornamental bowl. — It.,
'cup', of the same origin as F. tasse. See tass.

## tea
tea, n. — F. the (the orig. pronunciation of E. tea
was td), fr. Malay, teh, fr. dial. S. Chin, te, which
corresponds" to Chin. chai. Cp. Thea, theine.

## teach
teach, tr. v. — ME. tecken, fr. OE. txcan, 'to
show, teach', rel. to OE. tdcen, tdcn, 'sign,
token', and to tion (for *tih-an), 'to accuse', of-
teon, 'to deny', OHG. zihan, MHG. ziken, G.
zeiken, 'to accuse', OHG. zeigon, MHG., G.
zeigen, 'to show', Goth, ga-teikan, 'to announce',
fr. I.-E. base *deik-, *dih-, 'to show', whence
also Ol. disati, 'shows', Gk. δεικνύναι, 'to show',
L. dicere, 'to say', dicdre, 'to dedicate,
consecrate'. See diction and cp. teen, toe, token.
Derivatives: teach-able, adj., teach-abil-ity, п.,
teack-able-ness, п., teach-er, п., teach-ing, adj.,
feack-ing-ly> adv.

## Teague
Teague, п., a nickname for an Irishman. — From
the Irish PN. Tadhg.

## teak
teak, п., an East Indian tree {Tectona gradis). —
Port, teca, fr. Malayalam tekka, fr. OI. sakah
(whence also Arab. saj). G. Tiekbaum is an
English loan word.

## teal
teal, п., any of certain fresh water ducks of the
genera Nettion and Querquedula. — ME. tele,
rel. to MDu. teling, Du. taling.

## teallite
teallite, п., a lead sulfostannate (mineral.) —
Named after the English geologist J. J. Harris
Teall. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## team
team, п., 1) animals harnessed to the same vehicle
or plow; 2) a number of persons associated in
the same action. — ME. teme, fr. OE. team,
'progeny, race, family, team, animals harnessed
in a row', rel. to ON. taumr, Norw. taum, Swed.
torn, Dan. temme, OFris. tdm, Du. toom, OHG.,
MHG. zoum, G. Zaum, 'bridle', lit. 'that which
draws, pulls', fr. I.-E. base *deuk-, 'to draw,
pull', whence also Gk. δαιδύσσεσθαι (Hesy-
chius), 'to drag', L. ducere, 'to draw, lead'. See
duke and cp. tow, 'to draw*, tug, 'to pull, drag4.
Cp. also teem, 'to bring forth'.
Derivatives: team, tr. v., team-ing, п., team-lessy
adj., teamster, п., team-wise, adv.

## teapoy
teapoy, п., tea table. — Hind, tipai, 'a three-legged
table', fr. tin (fr. OL tri), 'three', and pdi (fr. OI.

## padah)
padah), 'foot*. See three and foot and cp. char-
poy and pajama. The spelling teapoy is due to
folk etymology which connected this word with

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:775 COLUMN:2 -->

## fear
fear, п., drop of liquid from the eye. — ME. teret
ter, tear, fr. OE. tear, contraction of teagor, rel.
to ΟΝ., OFris. tar, OHG. zak(li)ar, MHG. za-
kert G. Zahre, Goth, tagr, 'tear', fr. I.-E. *dakru-
*tear\ whence also Gk. δάκρυ, δάκρυον,
δάκρϋμα (whence OL. dacruma, L. lacruma, la-
crima), Olr. der, W. deigr, Co. dagr, OBret. dacr;
cp.—without the initial dental sound—OI.
asm, Avestic asru, Toch. A dkar, Lith. aSara,
Lett, asara. Cp. also Arm. artasuk* (pi.; the sing,
is artausr), with change of dr- to rt-. See
lachrymal and cp. train oil.
Derivatives: tear-ful, adj., tear-ful-ly, adv., tear-
ful-ness, п., tear-less, adj., tear-less-ly, adv., tear-
less-ness, п., tear-y, adj.

## tear
tear, tr. and intr. v., to pull apart, rend. — ME.
teren, fr. OE. teran, rel. to OS. terian, 'to
consume', far-terian, 'to destroy', MLG., MDu.,
Du. teren, 'to consume', OHG. zeran,fir-zeran,
'to destroy; to consume (whence MHG. zern,
ver-zern, G. zehren, ver-zehren, 'to consume'))
OHG., MHG., G. zerren, 'to tear*, Goth, dis-
tairan, ga-tairan, 'to tear, destroy; to tear to
pieces', fr. I.-E. *dere-, *der-, Ίο rend, divide;
to fiay', whence also OI. drnati, 'cleaves, bursts',
Gk. δέρειν, *to flay', δέρμα, 'skin', δορά, 'skin'
δάρσις, 'tearing, flaying, separation', OSlav.
dero, dirati, *to tear, flay', Lith. dirii, dirti, 'to
flay', Arm. terem, Ί flay', W., Co. Bret, darn,
'piece*. Cp. also Toch. tsar, 'a hand', prop, 'that
which tugs or tears'. Cp. derma and words there
referred to. Cp. also darn, dartars, Derris, drab,
'a kind of cloth', drape, tart, 'sour', tetter, trap,
'clothes'.
Derivatives: tear, п., rent, division, tear-ery п.,
tear-ing, adj.

## tease
tease, tr. v., 1) to card or comb (wool, flax, etc.);
2) to worry, vex. — ME. tesen, teesan, fr. OE.
txsan, 'to pluck, pull apart; to tease (wool)', rel.
to Dan. txse, MDu. tesen, Du. tezen, OHG,
zeisan and to E. touse (q.v.) Cp. next word.
Derivatives: tease, п., teas-er, п., teas-ing, adj.,
teas-ing-ly, adv., teas-y, adj.

## teasel
teasel, also teazel, teazle, п., a plant of the genus
Dipsacus; esp. Dipsacusfullonum, i.e. the fuller's
teasel. — ME. tesel, fr. OE. tsesel, rel. to txsan,
'to pluck; to tease'. See prec. word,
Derivatives: teasel, tr. v., teasel-er, teazl-er, n.

## teat
teat, n. — ME. tete, fr. OE. tete, fr. OF. tete (F.
tette), which, together with It. tetta, OProvenc.
and Sp. teta, is of Teut. origin. Cp. OE. tit, LG.
title, Du. tit, MHG-, G. zitze, Swed. tiss. The
Teut. words themselves are of imitative origin.
Cp. tit, 'a teat'.
Derivatives: teat-ed, adj., teat-like, adj.

## teazel
teazel, teazle, n. — Var. of teasel.

## Tibet
Tibet, Tebeth, п., name of the tenth Jewish
month. — Heb. tebheth, fr. Akkad. tebetu, which
is of uncertain origin. It means perh. lit. 'month
of sinking in, muddy month', and derives fr.
tebu, 'to sink in', which is rel. to Heb. tabha\
Aram. febha\ 'he sank', Mishnaic Heb. tdbha'
and Aram. tebha, also 'he sealed, stamped,
coined' (whence Arab, taba'a, of s.m.),' Ethiop.
tame'a, 'he dipped'.

## technetium
technetium, п., a radioactive metallic element
(ckem.) — ModL., coined by the It.-Amer.
physicist Emilio Gino Segre (1905- ), fr.
Gk. τεχνητός, 'artificial', verbal adj. of τεχ-
νασ&αι, 'to make by art', fr. τέχνη, 'art, skill'.
See techuic. For the ending see chem. suff. -ium.

## technic
technic, adj. — Gk. τεχνικός, 'pertaining to art,
made by art', fr. τέχνη (for *teks-na-) 'art, skill',
rel. to τέκτων, 'carpenter', and cogn. with OI.
taksan, 'carpenter', L. texere, 'to weave'. See
text and words there referred to and cp. esp.
Tectona, tectonic and the second element in
architect. Cp. also prec. word. For the ending see
adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: technic-al, adj., technic-al-ism, п.,
technic-al-ity, п., technic-al-ly, adv., technic-ian,
п., technic-ism, п., technic-ist, n.

## technicon
technicon, п., a device for exercising the hands of
a pianist. — Gk. τεχνικόν, neut. of τεχνικός,
'pertaining to art'. See prec. word.

## technique
technique, п., method or skill in performance. —
F., fr. the Greek adjective τεχνικός, 'pertaining
to art', used as a noun. See technic.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:775 COLUMN:3 -->

## techno-
techno-, combining form meaning 'art, skill'. —
Gk. τεχνο-, fr. τέχνη. See technic.

## technocracy
technocracy, п., government of society by
technicians. — Compounded of techno- and Gk.
-κρατία,'rule of, fr. κράτος, 'strength, power,
rule'. See -cracy.

## technocrat
technocrat, п., an adherent of technocracy. —
Compounded of techno- and -crat.
Derivative: tecfinocrat-ic, adj.

## technology
technology, п., the study of industrial arts. —
Compounded of techno- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: technolog-ic, technolog-ic-al, adjs.,
technolog-ist, n.

## techy
techy, also spelled tetchy, adj., fretful. — Formed
with adj. suff. -y fr. ME. tecche, tache, 'habit;
bad habit, caprice', fr. OF. teche, 'distinctive
mark, quality (good or bad)', whence also OF.
entechie, 'marked (either in good or bad sense)'
(whence F. entiche, 'infatuated'). See tache,
'spot', and cp. touchy.
Derivatives: tetchi-ly, adv., tetchi-ness, n.

## tecno-
tecno-, combining form meaning 'child'. — Gk.
τέκνο-, fr. τέκνον, 'child', which is rel. to
τίκτειν, 'to bear, bring forth, produce', and
cogn. with OI. takman-, 'descendant, child', ON.
pegn, 'thane, freeman*, OE. pegn, 'thane, man,
servant, attendant, soldier'. See thane and cp.
the first element in teknonymy. Cp. also toco-,
anatocism.

## Tecoma
Tecoma, п., a genus of shrubs and trees, the
trumpet flower (bot.) — ModL., abridged from
Nauhatl tecoma-xochitl, fr. tecoma, 'pot tree',
and xochitl, 'flower'.

## Tectibranchia
Tectibranchia, n. pi., a suborder of gastropods
(zool.) — A ModL. hybrid lit. meaning 'with
protected gills', fr. L. tectus, pp. of tegere, 'to
cover', and Gk. βράγχιον, 'gill'. See tegument
and branchia.

## tecto-
tecto-, combining form meaning 'carpenter,
builder'. — Gk. τεκτο-, fr. τέκτων, 'carpenter,
builder'. See tectonic.

## tecto-
tecto-, combining form meaning 'roof. — L.
tecto·, fr. tectum, 'roof', prop. neut. pp. of tegeret
'to cover', used as a noun. See tegument.

## tectology
tectology, п., a sub-division of morphology which
regards the organism as composed of morphons
of different order (biol.) — Compounded of the
combining form tecto- (fr. Gk. τεκτο-) and Gk.
-λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See -logy.
Derivative: tectolog-ic-al, adj.

## Tectona
Tectona, п., a genus of trees of the verbena
family (bot.) — ModL., of uncertain origin; perh·.
derived fr. Gk. τεκτονία, 'carpentry', fr.
τέκτων , gen. τέχτονος, 'carpenter'. See next
word."

## tectonic
tectonic, adj., pertaining to building. — Late L.
tictonicus, fr. Gk. τεκτονικός, fr. τέκτων,
'carpenter', which is rel. to τέχνη, 'art, skill'.
See technic.
Derivatives: tecton-ics, п., tectonic-al-ly, adv.

## tectorial
tectorial, adj., pertaining to covering, forming a
cover (anat.) — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
tectdrius, 'forming a cover', fr. tectus, pp. of te·
gere, 'to cover'. See tecto-, 'roof, and adj. suff.
-ory.

## tectrices
tectrices, n. pi., the tail coverts of a bird (ornithol.)
— L. tectrices, pi. of tectrix, 'that which covers',
fr. tectus, pp. of tegere, 'to cover'. See tegument.

## ted
ted, tr. v., to spread new-mown grass. — Prob. of
Scand. origin. Cp. ON. tedja (pp. taddr), 'to
spread manure', tad, 'manure', which are rel. to
OHG., MHG. zetten, 'to scatter*, G. verzetteln,
'to scatter, disperse in vain, squander', Du. tas,
'heap, stack' (whence F. tas, 'heap', tasser, 'to
compress, squeeze*, entasser, 'to heap up, pile'),
Goth, ungatass, 'undisciplined, disorderly'.
These Teut. words are prob. derivatives of I.-E.
base *det-, 'to divide, distribute, spread', whence
also Gk. δατεΐσθα^, 'to divide', δάσμα, 'share,
portion', δασμός, 'division of spoil', Toch. A
tat-k, 'to divide'. Base 4d?t- is a -r-enlargement
of base *da-, 'to divide', whence OE. tld, 'time',
tima, 'time, date'. See tide and cp. time.

## tedder
tedder, п., a machine for spreading hay. — Form-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:776 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 749 | TELEOLOGISM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:776 COLUMN:1 -->
ed from prec. word with agential suff. -er.

## teddy bear
teddy bear, toy bear. — Fr. Teddy, dimin. of
Theodore; named after Theodore Roosevelt.

## tedious
tedious, adj., tiresome; wearisome. — ME, ft. OF.
tedieus, fr. L. taediosus, 'wearisome, tedious',
fr. taedium. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: tedious-ly, adv., tedious-ness, n.

## tedium
tedium, п., tediousness. — L. taedium, 'weariness,
irksomeness', fr. taedere, 'to disgust, weary',
which is possibly cogn. with OSIav. tezo, teiiti,
'to be dull, be listless', Lith. tingiu, tingeti, of
s.m., tingus, 'lazy, dull'. Cp. the second element
in fastidious.

## tee
tee, п., 1) the letter T; 2) anything shaped like a
tee. — From the name of the letter T.

## tee
tee, п., an umbrella-shaped ornament on the top
of a pagoda. — Fr. Burmese h'ti,
'umbrella".

## tee
tee, п., the mark aimed at in games (quoits,
curling, etc.) — Prob. from the letter Τ used as a
sign to mark the place.
Derivative; tee, tr. v., to place on a tee; intr. v.,
to play ball from a tee.

## teem
teem, intr. v., to be prolific, abound, swarm. —
ME. lemen, fr. OE. teman, tleman, 'to breed', fr.
team, 'progeny, race, family'. See team.
Derivatives: teem-er, п., teem-ing, adj., teem-
ing-ly, adv., teem-ing-ness, n.

## teem
teem, tr. v., to pour out. — ME. temen, fr. ON.
tama, 'to pour out, empty', fr. tomr, 'empty'.
Cp. Dan. t0tnme, Swed. tomma, 'to empty', and
E. toom.

## teen
teen, п., sorrow, grief [archaic), — ME. геле, fr.
OE. teona, 'injustice, injury, grief, rel. to OE.
teon (for *tih-an), 'to accuse', tacen, tacn, 'sign,
token', txcan, 'to show, teach'. See teach and
cp. words there referred to.

## -teen
-teen, termination of cardinal numbers from 13
to 19 inclusive. — ME. -геле, fr. OE. -гуле, -геле,
rel. to OS. -tein, Du. -г/ел, OHG. -zehan,
MHG. -zehen, G. -zehn, Goth, -taihun, and
cogn. with L. -decim (whence It. -dici, Sp. -ce,
Port., Proven?, and F. -ze). See ten.
Derivative: teens, n. pi., age between twelve
and twenty years.

## teeny
teeny, adj. — A var. of tiny.

## teepee
teepee, n. — A var. of tepee.

## teeter
teeter, v., to seesaw; to vacillate. — Fr. earlier
titer, fr. ME. titeren, 'to totter', fr. ON. titra,
'to tremble', which is rel. to OHG. zittaron,
MHG. zittern, zitern, G. zittern, 'to tremble';
prob. fr. reduplication of base *dra-, 'to move
quickly, to run', whence OI. drati, 'runs', Gk.
άπο-διδράσκειν, 'to run away' (with
reduplication of base δρα-). See dromedary.

## teeth
teeth, п., pi. of tooth. — OE. tip, pi. of top. See
tooth.

## teethe
teethe, intr. v. — OE. 'tedan, fr. top, 'tooth'. See
tooth.
Derivative: teeth-ing, a.

## teetotal
teetotal, adj., of, or pledged to, total abstinence
from intoxicating drinks. — Formed fr'. total
with reduplication of the initial г for the sake of
emphasis.
Derivatives: teetotal, intr. v., teetotal(J)-er, п.,
teetotal-ism, п., teetotal-ist, n.

## teetotum
teetotum, п., a kind of four-sided toy top. — Fr.
earlier T-totum, formed from the letter T, which
stands for L. totum, 'all', and is marked on one
side of the toy, and totum, name of the toy, fr.
L. totum, neut. of totus, 'all' (see total); so called
because the side marked with а г wins all the
stakes. Cp. F. toton, which is of the same origin
and meaning.

## tefillin
tefillin, n. — See tephillin.

## teg
teg, п., a sheep in its second year. — Of unknown
origin.

## tegula
tegula, п., a tile. — L. tegula, rel. to tegere, 'to
cover'. See tegument and cp. tile.

## tegular
tegular, adj., pertaining to, or shaped like, a tile.
— Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. tegula. See
prec. word.
Derivative: tegular-ly, adv.

## tegulated
tegulated, adj., formed from scales overlapping
like tiles. — Formed with suff. -ate and -ed fr. L.
tegula. See tegula.

## tegument
tegument, п., covering of animal body or organ.
— L. tegumentum, 'a covering', fr. tegere, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:776 COLUMN:2 -->
cover', fr. I.-E. base *(s)teg-, 'to cover', whence
also ON. рак, 'roof, OE. psec, 'roof, thatch'.
See thatch and cp. words there referred to. For
the ending see suff. -ment.
Derivatives: tegument-al, tegument-ary, adjs.

## tehee
tehee, interj., n. and intr. v. — Of imitative origin.

## Tehillim
Tehillim, n. pi., the Hebrew name of the Psalms.
— Heb. t'killlm, pi. of tehillab, 'praise', fr. hillel,
'he praised'. See hallel and cp. Hillel.

## Teian
Teian, adj., 1) pertaining to the city of Teos; 2)
Anacreontic. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L.
Teius, 'pertaining to Teos', fr. Teos, fr. Gk.
Τέως, name of a town in Asia Minor, where
Anacreon was born.

## tell
tell, п., linden, lime tree. — Dial. F., fr. OF. teille,
teil, fr. L. tilia, 'linden, lime tree'. F. tilleul, of
s.m., derives fr. VL. "tiliolus, dimin. of *tilius,
which corresponds to L. tilia; see Tilia. Mir.
teile, 'linden', is borrowed—prob. through the
medium of English—ft. OF. ге;7/е, геЯ.

## teind
teind, п., tithe (Scot.) — ME. tende, 'tenth'. Cp.
ON. tiund, 'tenth', and see tenth, tithe.

## teinoscope
teinoscope, п., an optical instrument in which
prisms are so arranged as to show objects in
increased or diminished dimensions. —
Compounded of the stem of Gk. τείνειν, 'to stretch',
and -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'.
The first element is cogn. with OI. tanoti,
'stretches', L. tendere, 'to stretch, extend'; see
tend, 'to move in a certain direction'. For the
second element see -scope.

## tekiah
tekiah, п., one of the sounds of the shophar
(Jewish Religion). — Heb. teqi'ah, 'blowing (of
the shophar)', fr. taqa\ 'he thrust, struck; he
blew (the shophar or trumpet)', which is rel. to
Aram. tlqa\ 'he blew (the shophar or trumpet)',
Ethiop. taqe'a, 'he blew (the trumpet)'. The
emphatic г in Ethiop. is due to the assimilation of г
to the following q.

## teknonymy
teknonymy, п., the custom of certain savage races
of naming the parent from the child. —
Compounded of Gk. τέκνον, 'child', and δνυμα,
dialectal form of ΰνομα, 'name'. See tecno- and
name and cp. onomato-. For the ending see suff.
-y (representing Gk. -ία).

## tel-
tel-, form of tele- before a vowel.

## teia
teia, п., web-like membrane, tissue (anat.) — L.
tela, 'a web', for 'texla-, from the stem of texere,
'to weave'. See text and cp. telary.

## telamon
telamon, п., a male figure used as a column to
support an entablature (archit.) — L-, fr. Gk.
τελαμών, 'broad strap for bearing something',
fr. I.-E. base *ге/-, *tal-, *tol-, 'to bear, carry,
support, endure', whence also Gk. τάλαντον,
'pair of scales, balance, a weight'. See taient.

## Telamon
Telamon, п., brother of Peleus and father of Ajax,
an Argonaut (Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk.
Τελαμών, lit. 'the Bearer'. See prec. word.

## Telanthera
Telanthera, п., a genus of plants of the amaranth
family (hot.) — ModL., lit. 'with perfect flowers',
fr. L. τέλεος, 'perfect, entire', and άν&ηρός,
'flowery'. See teleo- and anther.

## telary
telary, adj., pertaining to a web. — L. telaris, fr.
tela, 'a web'. See tela and adj. suff. -ary.

## telautogram
telautogram, п., message transmitted by a
telautograph. — Compounded of tel-, auto- and -gram.
Cp. autogram.

## telautograph
telautograph, п., an instrument reproducing
writing at a distance. — Compounded of tel-,
auto- and -graph.
Derivatives: telautograph-ic, adj., telautograph-
У, n.

## tele-
tele-, before a vowel tel-, combining form
meaning 'far, far off'. — Gk. τηλε-, τη?.-, ft τήλε,
'far off, at a distance', rel. to Aeol. Gk. πήλυι,
of s.m., Gk. τηλόίΗ, of s.m., τηλό*ε(ν), 'from
afar', τέλος, 'end, completion, perfection',
τέλεος, 'entire, perfect, complete', πάλαι, 'long
ago', παλαιός, 'ancient', and cogn. with OI.
caramah, 'the last', W., Co., Bret, pell, 'far off',
W. pellaf, 'utmost'. All these words are
derivatives of I.-E. base *qwel~, 'to turn, to move
about', whence also κύκλος, 'wheel'. See colony,
cycle, wheel and cp. teleo-, telo-, paleo-. Cp. also
telesterion, telic, telium, telson, talisman,
Anatolia, autotelic, entulechy, entelodont, philately,
Triteleia.

## tele-
tele-, combining form meaning 'television', as in

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:776 COLUMN:3 -->
tele-studio. — Short for television.

## teledu
teledu, п., the stinking badger, Mydaus meliceps
(zoo!.) — Of Javanese origin.

## telega
telega, п., a kind of four-wheeled wagon. — Russ.
telega, fr. ORuss.7eZe|-a, fr. OSIav. telega, which
is of uncertain origin. Perh. it goes back to Old
Teleutic tayarak, 'circle, ring', or to Turko-
Tatar (Lebed dial.) tagalak, 'to roll'. See M.
Vasmer, Russisches etymologisches Worter-
buch, Heidelberg, 1950-58, II, pp. 89-90 s.v.
telega.

## telegnosis
telegnosis, п., another word for clairvoyance. —
ModL., [it. 'knowledge of what happens afar',
fr. tele- and Gk. γνώσις, 'knowledge'. See
gnosis.

## Telegonus
Telegonus, п., the son of Odysseus and Circe
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Τηλέγονος, lit.
'born afar', fr. τηλε-, 'far off, at a distance',
and the stem of γίγνεσθαι, 'to be born' (see
tele- and genus and cp. next word); so called in
contradistinction to his half brother Telemachus,
who was born in Ithaca.

## telegony
telegony, п., the supposed influence of a sire to the
offspring subsequently born to a later sire by the
same female. — Lit. 'procreation from afar', fr.
tele- and Gk. γόνος, 'procreation'. See prec.
word.
Derivative: telegon-ic, adj.

## telegram
telegram, n. — Coined by the American E. P.
Smith in Rochester in 1852 fr. Gk. τηλε, 'far
off, at a distance', and γράμμα, gen.
γράμματος, 'that which is written, letter'. See tele-
and -gram. Telegram is an erroneous formation.
The exact form should have been telegrapheme
(cp. τηλεγράφημα, the modern Greek word for
telegram).
Derivative: telegrammat-ic, adj.

## telegraph
telegraph, n. — F. teligraphe, lit. 'that which
writes at a distance', coined by the French
diplomatist Comte Andre-Francois MiotdeMeli to
(1762-1841) fr. τήλε, 'far off, at a distance', and
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write', to denote the
signaling device invented by the Chappe
brothers in 1792; see tele- and -graph. (The original
name given to this device by its inventors was
tachygraphe, lit. 'that which writes fast'.)
Derivatives: telegraph, intr. and tr. v.,
telegrapher, п., telegraphese (q.v.), telegraph-ic, telegraph-
ic-al, adjs., telegraph-ic-al-ly, adv., telegraph-ist,
п., telegraph-y, n.

## telegraphese
telegraphese, п., style used in telegrams. — A
hybrid word coined fr. telegraph and suff. -ese.

## telekinesis
telekinesis, n. (^psychical research) — ModL., lit.
'locomotion at a distance', compounded of tele-
and Gk. κΐνησις, 'movement, motion'. See
kinesis.

## telekinetic
telekinetic, adj. — See prec. word and -etic.

## Telemachus
Telemachus, п., son of Odysseus and Penelope
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Τηλέμαχος, lit.
'fighting from afar', fr. τήλε, 'far off, at a
distance', and the stem of μάχεσ&αι., 'to fight'.
See tele and -machy.

## Telemark
Telemark, п., a form of turn in skiing. — Named
after the town Telemark in Norway.

## telemeter
telemeter, п., an instrument for measuring
distances.— Compounded of tele- and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## telemetry
telemetry, п., the art of measuring distances with
a telemeter. — Compounded of tele- and Gk.
-μετρία, 'measuring of. See -metry.
Derivative: telemetr-ic, adj.

## telengyscope
telengyscope, п., an instrument serving both as a
telescope and a microscope (optics). — Coined
fr. tel-, Gk. εγγύς, 'near', and -σκόπιον, fr.
σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See eng)scope.

## teleo-
teleo-, combining form meaning 'perfect,
complete'. — Gk. τελεο-, fr. τέλεος, 'entire, perfect,
complete', fr. τέλος, gen. τέλεος, 'end,
achievement', which is rel. to τηλε, 'far off, at a
distance'. See tele- and cp. telium.

## Teleodesmacea
Teleodesmacea, n. pi., a class of bivalves (zool.)
— ModL., compounded of teleo- and Gk.
δέσμα, 'bond; headband', which is rel. to
δέσμη, 'a bundle', δεσμός, 'bond, chain'. See
desmo- and cp. the first element in Desmanthus
and in Desmodium.

## teleologism
teleologism, п., belief in final causes. — See
teleology and -ism.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:777 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TELEOLOGIST | 750 | Arm. i'al·, 'region', faiar, 'earthen, earthen | OHG. dinstar, 'dark', finstar (with dissimilation -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:777 COLUMN:1 -->

## Ideologist
Ideologist, п., a believer in teleology. — See next
word and -ist.

## teleology
teleology, п., I) the study of final causes; 2) the
philosophical study of design in nature. —
ModL. teleologia, coioed by the German
philosopher Baron Christian von Wolff or Wolf
(1679-1754) in his Logica (1728), fr. Gk. τέλος,
gen. τέλεος, "end', and -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See teleo- and -logy.
Derivatives: iefeolog-ic, tefeohg-ic-al, adjs.

## Teleosaurus
Teleosaurus, п., a genus of fossil crocodiles of the
Jurassic period (paleontol.) — ModL.,
compounded of teleo- and Gk. σαΰρος, 'lizard*. See
sauro-.

## teleost
teleost, teleostean, adj., pertaining to the order of
Teleostei. — See next word and -ean.

## Teleostei
Teleostei, n. pi, the order of fishes with bony
skeletons (ichtliyol.) — ModL., compounded of
teleo- and Gk. όστέον, 'bone'. See osteo-.

## Teleost omi
Teleost omi, n. pi., an order of fishes (ichthyol.) —
ModL., compounded of teleo- and Gk. στόμα,
'mouth". See stoma.

## telepathy
telepathy, п., communication between minds
otherwise than through thenormal sensory
channels. — Lit. 'feeling from afar', coined by the
English writer Frederic William Henry Myers
(1843-1901) in 1882 fr. tele- and Gk. -πάθει*,
'feeling'. See -pathy.
Derivatives: telepathy intr. and tr. v., and п.,
iefepath-ic, adj., telepath-isf, п., telepath-izef tr.
and intr. v.

## telephone
telephone, n. — F. telephone, compounded of Gk.
τηλε, 'far off', and φωνή, 'voice', hence lit.
meaning 'voice from afar'. The name telephone
was coined in 1834 by the French scientist Su-
dre to denote an acoustic apparel. The word was
adopted by Alexander Graham Bell (1847-1922)
in 1876 for the real telephone invented by the
latter. See tele- and -phone.
Derivatives: telephone, intr. and tr. v., telephon-
er, п., telephon-ic, telephon-ic-al, adjs., telepkon-
ic-al-ly, adv., telephon-ist, п., telephony (q.v.)

## telephony
telephony, n. — See tele- and -phony. Cp. ModGk.
τηλεφωνία, of s.m.

## telephote
telephote, п., an electrical apparatus for
reproducing pictures at a distance. — Coined fr. Gk.
τηλε, Таг off', and φως, gen. φωτός, 'light',
hence lit. meaning 'light from afar'. See tele-
and phosphorus, and cp. photo-.

## telephoto
telephoto, adj., telephotographic. — Short for
telephotograph ic.
telephotography п., a photograph made by means
of a telephote lens. — See tele- and photograph
and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: telephotograph-ic, adj.

## telephotography
telephotography, п., the art of photographing
distant objects with a telephoto lens. — Coined fr.
tele- and photography.

## teleprinter
teleprinter, п., a teletypewriter. — A hybrid
coined fr. tele- and printer.

## teleran
teleran, п., television radar navigation. — An
invented word formed fr. the first two syllables,
resp. the first syllable and the initial, of the
words fe/evision radar navigation.

## telergy
telergy, п., the force causing telepathy. — Coined
fr. tele- and Gk. 2ργον, 'work'. See work and
cp. ergon. For the ending see suff. -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## telescope
telescope, п., an optical instrument for enlarging
the image of distant objects. — ModL. tele-
scopium, coined by Prince Cesi, president of the
Academia dei Lincei in Rome, from tele- and
Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at,
examine'. See -scope.
Derivatives: telescop-ic, adj., telescop-ic~al-lyt
adv., telescop-ist, п., telescop-y, n.

## telescreen
telescreen, п., the screen of a television receiving
set. —■ A hybrid coined fr. tele- and screen.

## teleseme
teleseme, п., a system of transmitting signals by
means of electricity. — Coined fr. tele- and Gk.
σήμα, 'sign*. See semantics.

## telespectroscope
telespectroscope, п., an instrument combining a
telescope with a spectroscope. — Coined fr.
tele- and spectroscope.

## telesterion
telesterion, п., a place for initiation ceremonies
in ancient Greece. — Gk. τελεστήριον, fr. τε-
λεΐν, 'to fulfill, accomplish, perform, finish', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:777 COLUMN:2 -->
τέλος, 'end', which is rel. to τηλε, 'far off, at a
distance'. See tele-.

## telesthesia
telesthesia, telaesthesia, п., perception of objects
at a distance (psychol.) — ModL, compounded
of tele- and Gk. αΕσθ-ησις, 'sensation,
perception'. See esthesia. For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## telesthetic
telesthetic, telaesthetic, adj., pertaining to
telesthesia. — See prec. word and esthetic.

## telethermometer
telethermometer, п., a thermometer that records
its readings to a distance. — Compounded of
tele- and thermometer.

## telethon
telethon, п., an extended television show. — A
blend of television and marathon.

## teletypewriter
teletypewriter, п., a form of telegraph in which
the receiver prints messages like a typewriter.
— Compounded of tele- and typewriter.

## televise
televise, tr. v., to transmit by television. — Back
formation fr. television.

## television
television, n. — Lit. 'seeing at a distance', a
hybrid coined by Hugo Gernsback in 1911 fr. Gk.
τηλε, 'far off, at a distance4, and L. visio, gen.
-onis, 'the act of seeing, sight". See tele- and
vision.

## televox
televox, п., a kind of robot. — A hybrid coined
fr. Gk. τηλε, 'far off, at a distance', and L. vox,
'voice'. See tele- and voice and cp. vox.

## Telford pavement
Telford pavement, also telford, п., pavement
made according to the system of the Scotch
engineer Thomas Telford (1757-1834).
Derivative: telford-ize, tr. v.

## telial
telial, adj., pertaining to telium. — Formed fr.
telium with adj. suff. -al.

## telic
telic, adj., indicating purpose, teleological; the
opposite of ecbatic {grammar). — Gk. τελ&κός,
'final', fr. τέλος, 'end'. See tele- and -ic.
Derivatives: telic-al, adj., telic-al-ly, adv.

## teliostage
teliostage, п., the last stage in the life cycle of a
rust fungus (bot.) — See next word and siage.

## telium
telium, п., the spore fruit of the teliostage of a
rust fungus (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τέλειος,
τέλεος, 'entire, complete'. See teleo-.

## tell
tell, tr. and intr. v. — ME. tellen, fr. OE. tellan,
'to reckon, calculate, consider, account', rel. to
OS. tellian, ON. telja, OFris. tella, 'to count,
tell', MDu., Du. tellen, 'to count, reckon',
OHG. zellen, MHG. zeln, 'to count, tell', OS.
talon, 'to count, reckon', Dan. tale, 'to speak',
tselle, 'to count, tell', OHG. zalon, MHG. zaln,
G. zdhlen, 'to count, reckon', and to ON. tal,
'number, story, tale', OE. talu, 'story, tale'. See
tale and cp. words there referred to. For the
sense development of tell, 'to count; to narrate',
cp. F. confer, 'to count', raconter, 'to recount',
It. contare, Sp. contar, 'to count, to recount,
narrate', G. zdhlen, 'to count', erzahlen, 'to
recount, narrate', E. recount and re-count, Gk.
άρι&μεϊν, 'to count, count out, pay', Heb.
saphar, 'he counted', sipper, 'he told, recounted,
narrated', Mishnaic Heb. hirtzah, 'he counted,
recounted, discoursed', Aram, artzi, 'he
counted, enumerated'.
Derivatives: tell-able, adj., tell-er, п., tell-er-
ship, п., tell-ing, adj., tell-ing-ly, adv.

## tell
tell, п., mound, hill. — Arab, tall (in VArab.
pronunciation tell), rel. to Heb. til, 'mount,
hill, heap', tdlul, 'lofty' (said of a mountain),
Aram, tilla, Syr. tella, 'mound, hill', Akkad.
tillu, 'mound, hill; woman's breast'.

## Tellina
Tellina, п., a genus of mollusks (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. Gk. τελλίνη, 'a small shellfish', which is of
uncertain origin.

## tellur-
tellur-, form of telluro- before a vowel.

## tellural
tellural, adj., pertaining to the earth. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. tellus, gen. telluris,
'earth'. See tellarlan, adj.

## tellurate
tellurate, п., salt of telluric acid (chem.) —
Formed with subst. suff. -ate fr. L. tellus, gen. telluris,
'earth'. See tellurian, adj.

## telluret
telluret, п., a compound of tellurium. — See
tellurium and -et.
Derivative: telluret{t)-ed, adj., containing
tellurium.

## tellurian
tellurian, adj., pertaining to the earth. — Formed
with suff. -ian fr. L. tellus, gen. -uris, 'earth', fr.
I.-E. base *tela-, *tla-, 'something flat*, whence
also Ol. talam, 'surface, plane, sole of the foot*,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:777 COLUMN:3 -->
vessel', Gk. τηλία, 'backgammon board',
OSlav. tllo, 'ground', Lith. tMis, Lett, tilandi,
'bottom boards of a boat, OPruss. talus, 'floor
(of a room)', OE. pel, of s.m., OHG. dili
(whence G. Diele), 'board, plank', Olr. talam,
'earth'. Cp. deal, 'plank', thill. Cp. also the
second element in meditullium.

## tellurian
tellurian, n. — See tellurion.

## telluric
telluric, adj., pertaining to the earth. —- Formed
with adj. suff. -ic fr. L. tellus, gen. telluris,
'earth'. See prec. word.

## telluric
telluric, adj., pertaining to tellurium. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ic fr. tellurium (q.v.)

## telluride
telluride, п., the same as telluret. — Formed with
suff. -ide fr. tellurium (q.v.)

## tellurion
tellurion, also tellurian, п., an apparatus
illustrating the rotation of the earth. — ModL.
tellurion, fr. L. tellus, gen. -uris, 'earth'. See
tellurian, adj.

## tellurinm
tellurinm, n. {chem.) — ModL., coined by the
German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth
(1743-1817) in 1798 fr. L. tellus, gen. telluris,
'earth', to denote this element as the opposite
of the one called by him uranium (q.v.) See
tellurian, adj. For the ending see chem. suff. -ium.

## telluro-
telluro-, also teiluri-, before a vowel tellur-, com·
bining form meaning: 1) earth; 2) tellurium. —
Fr. L. tellus, gen. telluris, 'earth'. See tellurian,
adj., and tellurium.

## tellurous
tellurous, adj., containing tellurium. — Formed
with suff. -ous fr. teilurium (q.v.)

## Tellus
Tellus, п., the goddess of the earth {Roman
mythol.) — L. Tellus, personification of tellus,
'earth*. See tellurian, adj.

## telmato-
telmato-, before a vowel telmat-, combining form
meaning 'stagnant water'. — Gk. τελματο-,
τελματ-, fr. τέλμα, gen. τέλματος, 'standing
water, pond, marsh', which is rel. to τελμίς,
'mud, slime', from L-E, base *(s)tel-t 'to let
drop, to drip', whence also Gk. σταλαν, στα-
λάσσειν, 'to let drop; to drop, drip'. See stale,
'to urinate', and cp. stalactite.

## telo-
telo-, combining form meaning *end'. — Gk.
τελο-, fr. τέλος, 'end*,· which is rel. to τηλε,
'far off, at a distance'. See tele-.

## telo-
telo-, combining form meaning'far, at a distance'.
— Gk. τηλο-, fr. τηλε, 'far off, at a distance'.
See tele-.

## Telopea
Telopea, n., a genus of Australian plants (bot.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. τηλωττός, 'seen from afar' (fr.
τηλε, 'far off, at a distance'), and ώψ, gen.
ώπός, 'eye'. See tele- and -opia.

## telotype
telotype, п., a printing telegraphic instrument. —
Compounded of telo- (fr. Gk. τηλε) and type.

## telpher
telpher, п., a car driven electrically. —
Contraction of telephote, lit. 'that which carries afar', fr.
Gk. τηλε, 'far off, at a distance*, and -φόρος,
'carrying'. See tele- and -phore.
Derivatives: telpher, tr. v., telpher-age, n.

## telson
telson, п., the last section of the abdomen of a
crustacean {zool·) — ModL., fr. Gk. τέλσον,
'limit', which is rel. to τέλος, 'end'. See tele-.

## Telugn
Telugn, п., name of a Dravidian people and its
language. — Native name.

## temblor
temblor, п., an earthquake. — Sp., fr. L. tremor,
*a shaking, quivering'. See tremor.

## temenos
temenos, п., the sacred area surrounding the
temple (Greek antiq.) — Gk. τέμενος, 'sacred
precinct', lit. 'a place cut off, section', from the
stem of τέμνειν, 'to cut'. See tome and cp.
words there referred to.

## temerarious
temerarious, adj., rash, reckless. — L. temerdrius,
'rash*. See next word. For E. -ous, as equivalent
to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: temerarious-ly, adv., temerarious-
ness, n.

## temerity
temerity, п., rashness. — ME. temeryte, fr. L.
temeritds, 'rashness', fr. temere, 'rashly, at
random', prop, 'in the dark', fr. I.-E. base
*temes-, 'dark', whence also L. tenebrae (for
*temebrae, fr. *temesrae), 'darkness', OI. ta-
mas-, 'darkness', tamsrah, 'dark', tamrah, 'dark-
red, coppery', Avestic temah, 'darkness', Toch.
В tamdsse, 'dark, gloomy', Lith. tamsa,
'darkness', tamsus, 'dark', Lett, timsa, tumsa,
'darkness', tumst, 'it is getting dark*, OSlav. tima,
'darkness*, timinu, 'dark', MLG. deemster,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:778 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 751 | TENANT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:778 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. orig. *pimstar), of s.m., Olr. temel,
'darkness*, Mir. teim, temen, 'dark, gray', MBret.
teffal, 'dark'. Cp. tenebrae, temulent, timid. Cp.
also tombac and the first element in malabath-
rum. For the ending see suff. -ity.

## temno-
temno-, combining form meaning 'to cut'. — Gk.
τεμνο-, fr. τέμνει/ν, 'to cut', rel. to τομός,
'cutting', τόμος, 'portion, section', lit. 'a piece cut
off', τέμενος, 'sacred precinct', lit. 'a place cut
off'. See tome and cp. temenos, tmesis.

## Tempean
Tempean, adj., pertaining to, or esembling, the
valley of Tempe. — Formed with suff. -an fr.
Gk. Τέμπη, 'Tempe*, name of a valley in
Thessaly (Greece).

## temper
temper, tr. and intr. v. — ME. temprien, tempren,
fr. OE. temprian, 'to moderate, regulate, mingle',
and OF. temprer (F. temperer), which both
derive fr. L. temperare, 'to mix in due proportion,
combine properly, moderate, regulate', fr.
tempus, gen. tempdris, 'time'; see temporal,
'pertaining to time'. E. tempp· was influenced by
OF.-MF. temperer (F. temperer), which also
derives fr. L. temper are. Cp. also OF. temprer;
tremper (F. tremper), 'to mix with water, soak,
steep, dip, temper (steel)', which is of the same
origin. Cp. tamper, temperament, temperance,
temperate, temperature, attemper, at temperate,
distemper.
Derivatives: temper, п., temper-able, adj.,
temper-ed, adj., temper-er, п., temper-ish, adj.,
temper-y, adj.

## tempera
tempera, п., distemper {painting). — It., back
formation fr. temperare, 'to temper', fr. L.
temperare. See temper.

## temperament
temperament, n. — ME., fr. L. temperamentum;
'a mixing in due proportion; disposition', fr.
temperare. See temper and -ment.
Derivatives: temperament-al, adj., temperament-
al-ly, adv., temperament-ed, adj.

## temperance
temperance, n. — ME., (fr. L. temperantia,
'moderation, temperance', fr. temperdns, gen. -an-
tis, pres. part, of temperare. See temper and
-ance.

## temperate
temperate, adj. — ME. temperat, fr. L. temperd-
tusy 'properly arranged; temperate, moderate',
pp. of temperare. See temper and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: temperate-ly, adv., temperate-ness,
n.

## temperative
temperative, adj. — Late L. temperdtivus, fr. L.
temperatus. See prec. word and -ive.

## temperature
temperature, n. — L. temperdtura, 'due measure,
proportion, composition, temper,
temperament', fr. temperatus, pp. of temperare. See
temperate and -ure. In its physical sense, L.
temperdtura was first used by the Italian
physicist and astronomer Galileo Galilei (1564-1642).

## tempest
tempest, п., a violent storm. — ME., fr. OF.
tempeste (F. tempete), fr. VL. *tempesta, fr. L.
tempestas, 'time (good or bad) weather, storm,
tempest', fr. tempus, 'time"; see temporal,
'pertaining to time'. Cp. It. tempestay which is of
the same origin as OF. tempeste. Sp. tempestad,
however, derives fr. Classical L. tempestdtem,
ace. of tempestas.

## tempestuous
tempestuous, adj. — Late L. tempestuosus,
whence also OF. tempestueus (F. tempetueux),
fr. L. tempestas. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: tempestuously, adv., tempestuous-
ness, n.

## Templar
Templar, п., a member of the religious military
order of the Knights of the Temple (or Knights
Templars) founded by the Crusaders at
Jerusalem in 1119. — ME. templere, templer, fr.
OF. (= F.) templier, fr. ML. templdrius, formed
with suff. -drius, fr. L. templum, 'sanctuary,
temple*. See temple, 'place of worship', and -ar.
— This military order was so called because
King Baldwin II of Jerusalem granted it
quarters in his palace built near the site of the Temple
of Solomon.

## template
template, templet, п., model, pattern. — F. tem-
plety temp/ette, prop, dimin. of temple, fr. L.
templum, 'place of observation, temple; small
timber, purlin'. See temple, 'place of worship',
and -et.

## temple
temple, п., place of worship. — ME., fr. OE.
tempi, tempel, (F. temple), fr. L. templum, 'an
open place marked out by the augur for the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:778 COLUMN:2 -->
observation of the sky, consecrated place,
sanctuary, temple' (partly through the medium of F.
temple). Templum orig. meant 'an extended
place'. It is a derivative of I.-E. base *temp-, 'to
stretch, strain, extend', whence also Lith. tern-
piu, tempti, 'to stretch by drawing', timpa,
'sinew, tendon', OSlav. tetiva, of s.m., OSlav. tqpu,
'blunt, thick', Arm. tLamb, 'saddle*, prop.
'padded saddle', ON. framb, 'swollen, pregnant,
thick', Cp. next word. Cp. also antenna,
contemplate, Templar, temporal (in both senses),
tempus. Cp. also tapestry and words there
referred to. I.-E. *temp- is a -p-enlargement of
base *ten-, 'to stretch'; see tend, 'to move in a
certain direction'. This etymology is to be
preferred to the one which derives L. templum,
from I.-E. base *tem-, 'to cut' (whence Gk.
τέμνειυ, 'to cut', see temenos).
Derivative: templ-ed, adj.

## temple
temple, п., side of the head. — ME., fr. OF.
temple (F. tempe), fr. VL. *tempula, *templa,
neut. pi. taken as fern, sing., corresponding to
L. tempora, pi. of tempus, 'temple of the head',
prop, 'the thin part' (i.e. that part of the head
where the skin seems to be the thinnest), fr.
I.-E. base *temp-, 'to stretch, extend'; see prec.
word. Accordingly L. tempus, 'temple of the
head', and tempus, 'time', are derivatively
identical. See temporary, 'pertaining to time', and
cp. temporary, 'pertaining to the temples'. For
the sense development of tempus, 'temple of the
head', cp. OE. pun-wang, pun-wenge, OS.
thinn-ongi, ON. punn-vangi, OHG. dunn-wengi,
