'temple of the head', lit. 'thin cheek', MLG.
dunninge, 'temple of the head', fr. dunni, 'thin1
(see thin).

## temple
temple, п., a device for keeping the web taut. —
F. See template, templet.

## templet
templet, n. — See template.

## tempo
tempo, п., degree of speed (mus.) — It., 'time', fr.
L. tempus, 'time'. See next word.

## temporal
temporal, adj., pertaining to time. — L.
temporalis, 'pertaining to time, temporary*, fr. tempus,
gen. temporis, 'time', prop, 'span of time', fr.
I.-E. base *temp-, 'to stretch, strain, extend',
whence also L. templum, 'an open place marked
for the observation of the sky, consecrated
place, sanctuary, temple'. See temple, 'place of
worship', and cp. contemporaneous,
contemporary, contretemps, extemporaneous, extempore,
tempest, tempo, temporize, tense, n. For the
sense development of L. tempus, 'time', from
a base meaning 'to extend*, cp. OI. tanoti,
'stretches, extends; lasts', and Goth, peihs (for
*terjkos), 'time', which both derive fr. I.-E. base
*ten-, 'to stretch, extend'.
Derivative: temporal-ly, adv.

## temporal
temporal, adj., pertaining to, or lying near, the
temples (anat.) — Late L. temporalis, fr. L.
tempus, gen. temporis, 'the temple of the head'.
See temple, 'side of the head'.

## temporality
temporality, п., temporal possessions, —r Late L.
tempordlitds, fr. L. temporalis, 'temporal,
temporary'. See temporal, 'pertaining to time', and
-ity.

## temporally
temporally, п., the same as temporality. — See
prec. word and -ty.

## temporary
temporary, adj., lasting only for a time. — L.
tempordrius, 'pertaining to time; lasting only for
a time', fr. tempus, gen. temporis, 'time'. See
temporal, 'pertaining to time'.
Derivatives: temporari-ly, adv., temporari-ness,
n.

## temporize
temporize, intr. v. — F. temporiser, fr. ML. tem-
porisdre, fr. L. tempus, gen. temporis. See
temporal, 'pertaining to time', and -ize.
Derivatives: temporiz-ation, п., temporiz-er, п.,
temporiz-ing, п., temporiz-ing-ly, adv.

## temporo-
temporo-, combining form denoting the temples
(anat.) — Fr. L. tempora, pi. of tempus, gen.
temporis, 'temple of the head'. See temporal,
'pertaining to the temples'.

## tempt
tempt, tr. v. — ME. tempten, tenten, fr. OF. (— F.)
tenter, fr. L. temptdre, or tentdre, 'to handle,
touch, feel, prove, put to the test, try". L. temp-
tare is prob. freq. of *tempere, fr. I.-E. *temp-,
enlargement of base *ten-, 'to stretch, extend'.
L. tentdre is freq. formed fr. base *ten-. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:778 COLUMN:3 -->
tend, 'to move in a certain direction', and cp.
taunt, 'to reproach', tent, 'lint inserted in a
wound'. Cp. also attempt, attentat, tentacle,
tentative.
Derivatives: temptation (q.v.), tempt-er, п.,
tempt-ing, adj., tempt-ing-ly, adv., tempt-ress, n.

## temptution
temptution, n. — ME. temptacioun, fr. OF.
temptation, tentation (F. tentation), fr. L. temptatid-
nem, ace. of temptatia, fr. tempidtus, pp. of
temptdre. See tempt and -ation.
Derivative: temptation-al, adj.

## tempus
tempus, п., time, used esp. as a'term of music and
prosody. — L- tempus, gen, temporis, 'time,
period of time'. See temporal, 'pertaining to
time*, and cp. tense, 'time'.

## temulence
temulence, temulency, п., drunkenness (rare). —
Late L. temulentia, fr. temulentus. See next
word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## temulent
temulent, adj., drunken {rare). — Late L-
temulentus, 'drunken', rel. to L. temetum,
'intoxicating drink, mead, wine', which is prob. cogn.
with OI. tdmyati, 'is stunned, stupefied, grows
weary', OSlav. tomiti, 'to worry, torment', Olr.
tdm, 'death*, fr. I.-E. base * femes-, 'dark,
clouded* (both in the literal and figurative sense),
whence also OI. tamas-, 'darkness', tamsrah,
'dark', L. tenebrae (for *temebrae, fr. *temes~
rae), 'darkness*, temere, 'rashly, at random',
prop, 'in the dark'. See temerity and cp.
abstemious.

## ten
ten, numeral adj. — ME. tene, ten, fr. OE. tfen,
ten, rel. to OS. tehan, ON. tin, Dan. ti, Swed.
tio, OFris. tidn, ODu. ten, Du. Hen, OHG.
zehan, MHG. zehen, zen, G. zehn, Goth, taihun,
fr. I.-E. base 4dekm, *dekmt(i), whence also OI.
da&a, Avestic dasa, Toch. A sdk, В как, Arm.
tasn, Gk. δέκα, L. decern, OSlav. deseti, Lith.
desimt, Lett, desimt, desmit, OPruss. dessimpts,
Olr., Ir. deich, Co., Bret, dek, W. deg, Alb.
djetu, 'ten', Umbrian desen-duf, 'twelve', lit. 'ten-
two'. Cp. tenth, tithe and the suffixes -teen and
2nd -ty. Cp. also dean, dec a-, decade, decanal,
decern-, December, decemvir, deci-, decimal,
decussate, dicker, dime, and the first element in
Dashahara. Cp. also penteconta-.
Derivatives: ten, п., ten-fold, adj.

## ten-
ten-, form of teno- before a vowel.

## tenable
tenable, adj. — F., fr. OF., fr. tenir, 'to hold', fr.
VL. *tentre, fr. L. tenere, 'to hold, grasp, have,
keep' (cp. Provenc. tenir, tener. It. tenere, Sp.
tener, which derive fr. VL. *tenire, resp. L.
tenere). L. tenere is rel. to tendere, 'to stretch,
extend'. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and cp. abstain, abstention, abstinence,
appertain, appurtenance, contain, content, continent,
continue, countenance, detain, detention, detinue,
entertain, impertinent, lieutenant, maintain,
malcontent, obtain, pertain, pertinacious, pertinent,
reins, retain, retentiou, retentive, retinaculum,
retinue, sustain, sustentation, tenace, tenacious,
tenacity, tenaculum, tenaille, tenant, tenement,
tenet, tennis, tenor, 'course', tenue, tenure,
tenuto.
Derivatives: tenabil-ity, п., tenable--ness, п.,
tenabl-y, adv.

## tenace
tenace, п., a term of whist. — F. tenace, from the
adjective tenace, 'tenacious', fr. L. tendx, gen.
t'endcis. See next word.

## tenacious
tenacious, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
tendx, gen. tendcis, 'holding fast, tenacious', fr.
tenere, 'to hold'. See tenable.
Derivatives: tenacious-ly, adv., tenacious-ness, n.

## tenacity
tenacity, n. — L. tendcitds, fr. tendx, gen. tendcis,
'holding fast, tenacious'. See prec. word and
-ity.

## tenaculum
tenaculum, п., a pointed instrument used by
surgeons. — L., 'an instrument for holding, a
holder', fr. tendx, gen. -dcis. See tenacious and
-cule and cp. next word.

## tenaille
tenaille, also tenaiLn., outwork in the main ditch
between two bastions (fort.) — F. tenaille,
'tongs, pincers, tenaille', lit. 'that which holds',
fr. L. tendcula, pi. of the neut. n. tenaculum (see
prec. word), in VL. mistaken for a fern. sing.
noun.

## tenancy
tenancy, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## tenant
tenant, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), prop. pres.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:779 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TENCH | 752 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:779 COLUMN:1 -->
part, of tenere, 'to hold'. See tenable and -aut
and cp. locum tenens, lieutenant.
Derivatives: tenant, tr. v., tenant-able, adj.,
tenant-less, adj., tenant-like, adj., tenant-ry, n.

## tench
tench, a., a freshwater fish, Tinea vulgaris. — ME.,
fr. OF. tenche(¥. tanche), fr. VL. tinea* which
is of Gaulish origin.

## tend
tend, intr. v., to move in a certain direction. —
ME. tenden, fr. MF. (= F.) tendre, 'to stretch,
hold out', fr. L. tendere, 'to stretch, extend,
direct one's course, aim, strive*, fr. I.-E. *tend-,
-(/-enlargement of base *ten-, 'to stretch,
extend', whence OI. tanSti, 'stretches, extends',
tanah, 'thread', tantib, 'thread, string, cord',
tanuh, fem. tanvf, 'thin, tender', lit. 'stretched
out, extended', tannik, 'thin, tender', tantram,
'thread, loom, warp; the essential; doctrine,
system', Gk. τείυειν, for *τένιείν, 'to stretch',
Homeric Gk. ταναός, 'stretched out, long', Gk.
τανύεί.ν, 'to stretch', τένων, 'sinew, tendon',
τόνος, 'rope, cord, brace* (lit. 'that which can
be stretched'), also 'tone, note', ταινία, 'band,
ribbon', τάσις (for *tntis), 'stretching,
straining', L. tenuis, 'thin', OSlav. teneto, tonotu,
'rope', впйкй, 'thin', dial. Lith. tenvas, 'slender',
Lett, tiews, 'slender', Olr. tan, 'time', tan(a)e,
'thin', tet, 'side', Lith. tinklas, 'net', Goth, pan-
jan, OHG., MHG. denen, OE. Swed. tanja, OE,
penian, 'to extend', OHG. dunni, OE. pynne.
'thin', L. templum, 'an open place marked out
for observation, temple*, prop, 'an extended
place'. Cp. antenna, atelectasis, atonic, attend,
attendant, attention, attenuate, barytone,
catatonic, contend, contention, detend, detente,
detonate, distend, distention, ectasis, entasia,
entasis, epitasis, extend, extensive, extent, exten-
tion, extenuate, hypotenuse, intend, intendant,
intention, intonate, intone, monotonous, ostensible,
ostentation, oxytone, Panchatantra, peritoneum,
portend, portent, pretend, pretense, pretone,
protasis, standard, storting, snbtend, superintend,
syntony, taenia, tain, 'a thin sheet', tantra, tany-,
tasimeter, rutty, teinoscope, temple, "place of
worship', temple, 'side of head', temporal (in
both senses), tempt and words there referred to,
tempus, tendance, tendency, tender, 'offer',
tendon, tenesmus, tennis, teno-, tenositis, tenoto-,
tenotomy, tense, 'stretched', tense, 'time', tensi-,
tensile, tensimeter, tension, tenson, tent, tenter,
'frame for stretching cloth', lentigo, tentorium,
tenuis, tenuity, tenuous, tetanus, thin, thing,
tienda, tone, tono-, tune, tussore. Cp. also ten-
nble and words there referred to.

## tend
tend, tr. v., to guard, watch over. — Aphetic for
attend.

## tendance
tendance, n. — Aphetic for attendance.

## tendency
tendency, n. — ML. tendentia, fr. L. tendens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of tendere. See tend, 'to move
in a certain direction', and -ency, and cp. next
word.

## tendentious
tendentious, also tendencious, adj., having a
definite purpose. — Coined, on analogy of G.
tendenzios (fr. Tendenz, 'tendency'), fr. ML.
tendentia. See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: tendentious-ly (tendencious-ly), adv.,
tendentious-ness (tendencious-ness), n.

## tender
tender, п., one who tends. — Formed fr. tend
with ^agential suff. ter.

## tender
tender, tr. and intr. v., to offer. — MF. tendre, 'to
stretch, hold out; to offer' (whence F. tendre,
'to stretch*), fr. L. tendere.
Derivative: tender, п., offer, tender-er, n.

## tender
tender, adj., soft, easily broken. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) tendre, 'soft, delicate, tender', fr. L. tene-
rum, ace. of tener, 'soft, delicate, tender*, which
is prob. rel. to Sabine tereno-, 'soft, delicate',
and cogn. with Ol. tarunah, 'young, tender',
Avestic tauruna-, 'young', Gk. τέρην, 'tender,
delicate*, Arm. tlarm, 'young, fresh, green',
Goth, pariks, 'not fulled', prop, 'fresh' (see S.
Feist, Vergleichendes Worterbuch der gotischen
Sprache, 3rd edition, Leiden, 1936 ff., p. 490).
It. tenero, Proven?, tenre, tendre, Sp. tiernot
Port, tenro, 'tender', also derive fr. L. tenerum.
Derivatives: tender-ize, tr. v., tender-ling, п.,
tender-ly, adv., tender-ness, n.

## tendinous
tendinous, adj., related to, or resembling, a
tendon. — Formed with surf, -ous fr. ML. tendo.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:779 COLUMN:2 -->
gen. tendinis, 'sinew, tendon'. See next word.

## tendon
tendon, п., sinew (anat.) — ML. tendo, gen.
tendinis, formed fr. L. tendo, tendere, 'to stretch,
extend', on analogy of Gk. τένων, 'sinew,
tendon*, which derives from the stem of τείνειν
(for *τένιειν), 'to stretch'. See tend, 'to move in
a certain direction'. The anatomical term tendo
Achillis ('Achilles' tendon*) was first used by the
German surgeon Heister. The original name
was chorda Achillis ('Achilles' sinew') and was
coined by the Dutch anatomist Philip Verheyen
in 1693, when he dissected his own amputated
leg. He so called it with reference to the myth of
Achilles whose heel was the only vunerable spot
of his body. Cp. teno-, tenonto-.

## tendril
tendril, п., slender, spirally coiling organ of
climbing plants. — Shortened fr. F. tendrillon, di-
min. of tendron, 'a tender shoot', fr. tendre,
'soft, delicate, tender'. See tender, 'soft'.
Derivative: tendrill-ar, adj.

## tenebrae
tenebrae, n. pi., the matins and lauds for the last
three days of the Holy Week {Roman Catholic
Religion). — L., 'darkness'. See next word.

## tenebrous
tenebrous, adj., dark. — ME., fr. OF. tenebrus (F.
tenebreux), fr. L. tenebrosus, 'dark', fr. tenebrae,
'darkness', which stands for *temebrae, fr.
*temesrae, and is rel. to L. temere, 'rashly, at
random', prop, 'in the dark'. See temerity and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: tenebrous-ly, adv., tenebrous-ness,
n.

## tenement
tenement, n. — ME., fr. OF. (F. tenement), lit. 'a
holding', fr. ML. tenimentum, fr. L. tenure, 'to
hold'. See tenable and -ment.
Derivatives: tenement-al, tenement-ary, adjs.,
tenement-er, n.

## teneral
teneral, adj., said of a state of the imago of an
insect (entomol.) — Lit. 'soft, tender'; formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. tener. See tender, 'soft'.

## tenesmus
tenesmus, п., a straining, esp. a vain straining to
evacuate, (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. τενε-
σμός, 'a vain desire to evacuate', lit. 'stretch,
strain', fr. τείνειν (for *τένί.ειν), 'to stretch,
strain*, which is cogn. with L. tendere, of s.m.
See tend, 'to move in a certain direction'.
Derivative: tenesm-ic, adj.

## tenet
tenet, п., principle. — Prop, 'a thing held (to be
true)', fr. L. tenet, 'he holds', 3rd pers. sing.
indie, pres. fr. tenere. See tenable.

## tengerite
tengerite, п., a mineral supposed to be an yttrium
carbonate (mineral.) — Named after the
Swedish chemist C. Tenger, who analyzed it. For
the ending see subst. suff. -He.

## tennantite
tennantite, п., a sulfarsenite of copper (mineral.)
— Named after the English chemist Smithson
Tennant (]761-]8]5). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## tenner
tenner, п., a ten pound or ten dollar note (slang).
— Formed fr. ten with 2nd suff. -er.

## tennis
tennis, n. — ME. teneis, fr. AF. tenetz, fr. OF.
(= F.) tenez, 'hold!', pi. imper. of tenir, 'to
hold'; see tenable. The game was so called from
the word used by the server when throwing the
ball.

## teno-
teno-, before a vowel ten-, combining form
denoting the tendon (anat.) — Gk. τενο-, τεν-, fr.
τένων, 'sinew, tendon'; see tendon and cp.
tenonto-,

## tenon
tenon, п., a projection inserted to make a joint.
— ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. tenir, 'to hold'.
See tenable.
Derivatives: tenon, tr. v., tenon-er, n.

## tenonto-
tenonto-, before a vowel tenont-, combining form
denoting the tendon (anat.) — Gk. τενοντο-,
τενοντ-, fr. τένων, gen. τένοντος, 'sinew,
tendon'. See teno-.

## tenor
tenor, п., course; bearing. — ME. tenour, tenor,
fr. OF. tenour (F. teneur), fr. L. tenorem, ace. of
tenor, 'course, career, tenor', lit. 'a holding*,
from the stem of tenere, 'to hold'. See tenable.

## tenor
tenor, п., high male voice (music). — It. tenore, fr.
L. tenorem, ace. of tenor, 'course', lit. 'a holding'
(see prec. word); so called because of its
dominant character in singing. Cp. tenorino,
countertenor.
Derivatives: tenor, adj., tenor, intr. v., tenor-ist,
n.

## tenorino
tenorino, adj., falsetto (music). — Dimin. of tenor,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:779 COLUMN:3 -->
'high male voice'.

## tenorite
tenorite, п., a native cupric oxide (mineral.) —
Named after G. Tenore, president of Naples
Academy. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## tenoroon
tenoroon, п., a musical instrument. — It. tenoro-
ne, augment, of tenore. See tenor, 'high male
voice', and -oon.

## tenosltis
tenosltis, п., inflammation of a tendon (med.) —
Medical L., formed fr. Gk. τένων, 'tendon*.
See teno- and -itis.

## tenotomy
tenotomy, п., cutting or dividing of a tendon
(med.) — Compounded of teno- and Gk.
-τομΕα, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See
tome,

## tenrec
tenrec, tanrec, п., an insectivorous mammal
(Tenrec ecaudatus). — Malagasy tandraka.

## tense
tense, adj., stretched, strained. — L. tensus, pp.
of tendere, 'to stretch'. See tend, 'to move in a
certain direction'.
Derivatives: tense, tr. and intr. v., tense-ly, adv.,
tense-ness, n.

## tense
tense, п., time as a grammatical term. — ME.
tens, tense, 'time, tense', fr. MF. tens (F. temps),
fr. OF., fr. L. tempus, 'time* (whence also It.
tempo, Provenc. temps, Sp. tiempo, Port, tempo).
See tempus.

## tenslbility
tenslbility, n. — Late L. tensibilitas, fr. tensibilis.
See next word and -ity.

## tensible
tensible, adj., capable of being stretched; tensile.
— Late L. tensibilis, 'that which may be
stretched', fr. L. tensus, pp. οι tendere. See tense, adj.,
and -ible.
Derivatives: tensible-ness, п., tensibl-y, adv.

## tensile
tensile, adj., ]) capable of being stretched; tensile.
— ModL. tensilis, fr. L. tensus, pp. of tendere.
See tense, adj., and -He.

## tensimeter
tensimeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
tension of gases. — A hybrid coined fr. L. ten-
sio, 'tension', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure*. See
tension and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## tension
tension, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. tensionem, ace.
of tensio, 'a stretching, tension', fr. tensus, pp.
of tendere. See tense, adj., and cp. extension.
Derivatives: tension, tr. v., tension-al, n.

## tensive
tensive, adj. — F. tensif(Tem. tensive), fr. MF., fr.
L. tensus, pp. of tendere. See prec. word and
-ive.

## tenson
tenson, tenzon, п., contest in stanzas between
troubadours. (Provenf. lit.) — F. tenson (fr.
MF., fr. OProvenc, tenson), resp. It. tenzone, fr.
*VL. tentionem, ace. oi*tenti5, 'strife, quarrel',
fr. L. tentus, pp. of tendere, 'to stretch', which
in VL. had also the meaning of 'to exert
oneself, to strive'. Cp. Sp. tenzon, Port, tengao, and
see tend, 'to move in a certain direction*. Cp. also
contention, intention.

## tensor
tensor, п., a muscle that stretches a part (anat.) —
Medical L. tensor, fr. L. tensus, pp. of tendere,
'to stretch'. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and agential suff. -or.

## tent
tent, п., shelter. — ME. tente, tent, fr. OF. (= F.)
tente, lit. 'something stretched out', fr. L. tenia,
fem. of tentus, pp. of tendere, 'to stretch'; L.
tentus is equivalent to OI. tatah, Gk. τατός,
'stretched*. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction', and cp. It., OProvenc. tenda, Sp. tienda,
which are refashioned from the present tense of
L. tendere (see tienda). For the sense
development of OF. tente, etc., cp. L. tentorium, 'tent',
fr. tentus, pp. of tendere, 'to stretch'.
Derivatives: tent, tr. v., to cover with a tent,
tent-ed, adj., tenter (q.v.)

## tent
tent, п., lint inserted in a wound to keep it open.
— ME. tente, tent, fr. MF. (= F.) tente, fr. OF.,
back formation fr. tenter, 'to put to test, try'.
See tempt.
Derivative: tent, tr. v., to keep a wound open by
inserting a plug into it.

## tent
tent, п., attention (now Scot, and dial. English).
— Aphetic for attent.

## tent
tent, tr. v., to attend to (now Scot, and dial.
English). — Prob. short for take tent. See
prec. word.

## tent
tent, п., a sweet Spanish wine. — Sp. Unto, 'red
(wine)', lit. 'dyed, tinged', fr. L. tinctus, pp. of
tingere, 'to soak in color, dye'; See tinge and cp.
taint, tint, tincture,

## tentacle
tentacle, п., a slender, flexible organ for feeling.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:780 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 753 | TEREPHAH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:780 COLUMN:1 -->
— Lit. 'feeler', fr. ModL. tentdculum, ft. L. ten-
tare, 'to try'. See tempt and -cle.
Derivative: tentacl-ed, adj.

## tentacular
tentacular, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ar
ft. ModL. tentdculum. See prec. word.

## tentaculate
tentaculate, adj., furnished with tentacles. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. ModL.
tentdculum. See tentacle.
Derivative: tentaculat-ed, adj.

## tentaculi-
tentaculi-, combining form fr. ModL. tentdculum.
— See tentacle.

## tentacuium
tentacuium, п., a tentacle (zool.) — ModL. See *
.tentacle.

## tentative
tentative, adj. — ML. tantdtivus, formed with
suff. -ive ft. L. tentdtus, pp.' of tentdre, 'to try'.
See tempt and -ative.
Derivatives: tentative, п., tentative-ly, adv., ten-
tative-ness, n.

## tenter
tenter, п., one who lives in a tent. — Formed fr.
tent, 'shelter', with agential suff. -er.

## tenter
tenter, п., one who is in charge of something. —
Formed fr. tent, 'to attend to", with agential
suff. -er.

## tenter
tenter, п., framework for stretching cloth so that
it may dry evenly. — ME. tenture, tentoure, ft.
F. tenture, 'stretching, spreading', a blend of
tente, 'tent', and OF. tendeure, which is a
derivative of tente. See tent, 'shelter*, and -ure and
cp. tenterhook.
Derivatives: tenter, to stretch on tenters, tenter-
er, n.

## tenterhook
tenterhook, п., one of the hooks that hold cloth
stretched on a tenter. — Lit. 'hook for
stretching'. See tenter, 'framework for stretching',
and hook.

## tenth
tenth, numeral adj. — ME. tenthe, teonthe,
formed fr. ten on analogy αϊ fourth etc. See ten and
numeral suff. -th and cp. OE. teoda, 'tenth', and
E. tithe.
Derivatives: tenth, n. and v., tenth-ly, adv.

## Tenthredinidae
Tenthredinidae, n. pi., a family of Hymenoptera,
the sawflies (entomol.) — ModL., formed with
suff. -idae fr. Gk. τεν*ρηδών, 'a kind of wasp',
which is a blend of τευ&ρήνη and πεμφρηδών,
'a kind of wasp'. Gk. τεν*ρήνη is rel. to ϋ>ρώ-
ναζ, 'drone', *ρήνος, 'dirge'; from the I.-E.
imitative base *dhren-, 'to hum, buzz, murmur',
whence also Goth, drunjus, 'sound', OE. dran,
'drone', see drone and cp. threnetic, Anthrenus.
Gk. πεμφρηδών is prob. also of imitative
origin.

## tentigo
tentigo, п., priapism. — L. tentigo, lit. 'tension',
fr. tentus, pp. of tendere, 'to stretch'. See tend,
'to move in a certain direction'.

## tentorial
tentorial, adj., pertaining to the tentorium (anat.)
— Medical L. tentoridlis, fr. L. tentorium. See
next word and adj. suff. -a].

## tentorium
tentorium, п., partition between the cerebrum
and cerebellum (anat.) — Medical L. tentorium,
ft. L., 'tent', fr. tendere, 'to stretch' (see tend, 'to
move in a certain direction', and cp. tent,
'shelter'); so called from its shape.

## tenue
tenue, п., bearing, behavior, deportment. — F.,
prop. fem. pp. of tenir, 'to hold', used as a
noun. See tenable.

## tenul-
tenul-, combining form meaning 'thin, slender'.
— L., ft. tenuis. See next word.

## tenuis
tenuis, п., a term denoting any of the three
sounds expressed by the letters p, t, k. — L.,
'thin, slender, fine', prop, loan translation of Gk.
ψιλός, 'bare'.(i.e. 'unaspirated'), used by
Aristotle to denote any of the sounds rendered by
the letters v., τ, π. — L. tenuis is cogn. with OI.
tanuh, 'thin', lit. 'stretched out', Homeric Gk.
ταναός, 'stretched out, long', Gk. τείνειν, 'to
stretch out'. See thin and cp. tenuity, tenuous,
extenuate.

## tenuity
tenuity, п., thinness. — L. tenuitds, 'thinness,
slenderness, fineness', fr. tenuis. See prec. word
and -ity.

## tenuous
tenuous, adj., thin. — Formed with suff. -ons ft.
L. tenuis. See prec. word.
Derivatives: tenuous-ly, adv., tenuous-ness, n.

## tenure
tenure, п., a holding of something. — ME., fr.
OF. teneure, tenure, fr. tenir, 'to hold', fr. VL.
*tenire, fr. L. tenere, 'to hold'. See tenable and
-ure and cp. tenue.
Derivatives: tenuri-al, adj., tenuri-al-ly, adv.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:780 COLUMN:2 -->

## tenuto
tenuto, adj., sustained to its value (musical
direction). — It., 'held', pp. of tenere, 'to hold', fr. L.
tenere. See tenable.

## tenzon
tenzon, n. — See tenson.

## teocalli
teocalli, п., place of worship of the ancient
inhabitants of Mexico. — Sp., compounded of
Nahuatl teotl, 'god', and colli, 'house'.

## tepee
tepee, п., an American Indian tent or wigwam. —
Dakota tipi.

## tepefy
tepefy, tr. v., to make tepid; intr. v., to become
tepid. — L. tepefacere, 'to make tepid', formed
from the stem of tepere, 'to be warm or
lukewarm', and facere, 'to make, do'. See tepid and
-fy.

## tephillin
tephillin, also spelled tefillin, n. pi., the
phylacteries containing the four passages Ex. 13: ]-]0;
Ex. 13: 11-16; Deut. 6: 4-9, and Deut. II: 13-20,
which are tied on the left arm and on the head
and are worn during the morning prayer on
week days (Jewish Religion). — Mishnaic Heb.
tephilltn, pi. of tephillih, 'prayer; phylactery', fr.
Bibl. Heb. tephillah, 'prayer', from the stem of
the verb pillel, 'he prayed', which is of uncertain
origin. It is perh. rel. to Heb. ndphal, 'he fell,
prostrated himself, and orig. meant 'he
prostrated himself in prayer' (see Ahrens, ZDMG.,
64, 163), or is orig. identical with Heb. pillel, 'he
judged', and lit. means 'he invoked as a judge'
(see Goldziher, Abhandlungen zur arabischen
Philologie, I, p. 36).

## tephrite
tephrite, п., an ash-colored igneous rock (petrogr.)
— Formed with suff. -ite ft. Gk. τέφρδί, 'ashes',
which stands for *dhegwh-rd-, fr. I.-E. base
*dhegwh-, *dhogwh-, 'to burn'. See fever and cp.
day.

## tephro-
tephro-, combining form meaning 'ash-gray'. —
Gk. τεφρό-, fr. τέφρα, 'ashes'. See prec. word.

## Tephrosia
Tephrosia, п., a genus of plants, the hoary pea
(bat.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τεφρός, 'ash-colored',
fr. τέφρα. See tephrite.

## tepid
tepid, adj., moderately warm, lukewarm. — L.
tepidus, fr. tepere, 'to be warm or lukewarm',
which is cogn. with OI. tapati, 'makes warm,
heats, burns', tapu-, 'burning', tapah, 'heat',
Avestic tafnush, 'fever', Toch. B. tsap-, 'to make
lukewarm', an-tdpce, 'fire, conflagration' (an- in
antdpce is a prefix of intensity), OSlav. topiti, 'to
warm', tepla, 'warm', teplostt, 'heat; warmth',
Olr. tene, gen. tened (for *tepnet-), ten, 'fire', te
(for "tepent-), 'hot', W. tes, 'heat', Alb. Gheg
/to/, Tosk /toh (for *ve-tip-sk-), 'to deprive of
heat' (see N. Jokl in Indogermanische Forschun-
gen, 37, 103). Cp. tapas, topaz and the second
element in Beltane and in pardao. For the ending
of tepid see 1st suff. -id.
Derivatives: tepid-ity, п., tepid-ly, adv., tepid-
ness, n.

## tepidarium
tepidarium, п., intermediate room in the Roman
bath, situated between the caldarium and frigi-
darium. — L., 'a moderately warm room', prop,
neut. of the adjective tepiddrius, 'pertaining to a
lukewarm bath', used as a noun. Tepidarius
derives fr. tepidus, 'warm, lukewarm'. See tepid
and -arium.

## tequila
tequila, п., a Mexican brandy. — Named after
Tequila, a town in Mexico.

## ter-
ter-, combining form meaning 'three times'. —
L. ter-, ft. ter, 'three times', which derives ft.
"tris (cp. Gk. τρίς, 'three times'), through the
medium of *ters. Cp. L. tertius, 'third', which
stands for I.-E. *tritios, whence also Gk. τρίτος,
Goth, pridja, OE. pridda, 'third'. See three and
cp. third, thrice. Cp. also tri-, trias, triad, trine,
trinity, trio,

## terai
terai, п., a kind of felt hat. — Short for Terai hat,
ft. Terai (Hind. Tardi), a swampy belt in
Northern India.

## teraphun
teraphun, n. pi., household idols (see Gen. 31:19
and 30). — Heb. terdphim, of uncertain origin.
According to Neubauer in Zeitschrift fur Assy-
riologie, 2, 95 and others, rel. to Heb. rephd'im,
'shades, ghosts'.

## teras
teras, п., monster, monstrous formation (med.)
— Gk. τέρας, 'marvel, monster'. See terato-.

## terato-
terato-, before a vowel terat-, combining form
meaning 'marvel, monster'. — Gk. τερατο-,
τερατ-, ft. τέρας, gen. τέρατος, 'marvel,

## monster'
monster', prob. cogn. with Lith. keras, 'charm',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:780 COLUMN:3 -->
keriii, kereti, 'to bewitch', OSlav. caru, cara,
'charm', and possibly also—with initial s—with
OI. d-scaryah, 'wonderful, extraordinary', ON.
skars, 'monster', skyrse, 'bad omen, phantom'.
These words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *qwer-,
'to make, form', in specific sense: 'to bewitch,
charm'. See corpus and cp. peloria.

## teratoid
teratoid, adj., resembling a monster, abnormal,
pathological. — Compounded of terato- and
-oid. Cp. Gk. τερατώδης, 'prodigious,
monstrous', fr. τέρας, gen. τέρατος, 'marvel,
monster', and -ώδης, 'like' (see terato- and -ode,
'like').

## teratology
teratology, п., the study of montrosities or
abnormal formations in man, animals, or plants. —
Compounded of terato- and -logy. Cp. Gk.
τερατολογία, 'the telling of marvels', ft. τερα-
τολόγος, 'a teller of marvels'.
Derivative: teratolog-ist, n.

## terbium
terbium, п., a rare metallic element. — A name
coined by the discoverer of the element, the
Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander (1797-
1858), from the Swedish town name Ytterby and
chem. suff. -ium. Cp. erbium, ytterbium, yttrium.

## terce
terce, n. — A var. of tierce.

## tercel
tercel, п., a male falcon. — ME., fr. OF. terguel
(F. tiercelet), ft. VL. *tertiolus, a derivative of
tertius, 'third'; so called because the male is one
third smaller than the female.

## tercentenary
tercentenary, adj., pertaining to a period of three
hundred years; п., the three hundredth
anniversary or its celebration. —■ Compounded of ter-
and centenary.
Derivatives: tercentenari-al, adj., tercentenari-
an, adj. and n.

## tercet
tercet, п., three successive lines rhyming together,
triplet. — F. tercet, ft. It. terzetto, dimin. of ter-
zo, 'third', ft. L. tertius, 'third'. See tertian and
-et.

## Terebeila
Terebeila, п., a genus of marine worms (helmin-
thol.) — ModL., dimin. of terebra, 'borer'. See
terebra and -ella.

## terebellid
terebellid, adj. and n. — See next word.

## Terebellidae
Terebellidae, n. pi., a family of marine worms
(helminthol.) — ModL., formed fr. Terebeiia
with suff. -idae.

## terebene
terebene, п., a disinfecting liquid made from oil
of turpentine (chem.) — Coined fr. terebinth
and suff. -ene.

## terebic
terebic, adj., pertaining to a white organic acid,
CjHjuOj (chem.) — Coined ft. terebinth and adj.
suff. -ic.

## terebinth
terebinth, п., a tree of the sumac family yielding
turpentine. — L. terebinthus (whence also F. te-
rebinthe), fr. Gk. τερέβιν*ος, which is prob. a
Creto-Minoic loan word. Cp. turpentine.
Derivatives: terebinth-ic, adj.

## terebinthina
terebinthina, п., turpentine. — ModL.,prop. fem.
of L. terebinthinus, 'of the terebinth', used as a
noun. See next word.
Derivative: terebinthin-ate, tr. v. and adj.

## terebinthine
terebinthine, adj., 1) of the terebinth; 2) of, or
resembling, turpentine. — F. terebinthine, fr. L.
terebinthinus, 'of the terebinth', fr. Gk. τερεβίν-
θινος, fr. τερέβινθος. See terebinth and adj.
suff. -ine.

## terebra
terebra, п., 1) borer; 2) ovipositor of certain
insects (entomol.) — L. terebra, 'borer, drill, auger',
formed fr. terere, 'to rub, grind, wear away',
with instrumental suff. -bra. See throw and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also Terebeila.

## terebrate
terebrate, tr. v., to perforate. — L. terebrdtus, pp.
of terebrdre, 'to bore, pierce, perforate', fr.
terebra. See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.

## teredo
teredo, п., shipworm. — L. teredo, 'a worm that
gnaws wood', fr. Gk. τερηδών, lit. 'a boring
worm', from the base of τείρειν, 'to rub', τέρε-
τρον, 'borer'. See throw and cp. terebra.

## terek
terek, п., a sandpiper (Terekia cinerea) — Named
after the river Terek in the Caucasus.

## terephah
terephah, п., also spelled trefa, ritually unclean
food (Jewish religion). — MedHeb. t&rephah, fr.
Mishnaic Heb., 'an animal with organic defect',
ft. Bibl. Heb., lit. '(an animal) torn (by wild
beasts)', fr. tdraph, 'tore to pieces, seized, rent'
(said esp. of a wild beast), whence also terepli,
'prey', tdraph, 'plucked' (adj.); rel. to Aram.
t raph, 'he tore, seized', Arab, tara/a, 'grazed

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:781 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TEREPHTHALIC | 754 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:781 COLUMN:1 -->
off' (said of a camel), tarufa, 'was freshly
plucked'.

## terephthalic
terephthalic, adj., in terephthalic acid, a
tricarboxylic acid (ckem.) — Coined fr. tere(bene) and
phthalic; so called because it is the form of
phthalic acid derived from turpentine. Cp. the
first element in terylene.

## teres major
teres major, name of a muscle (anat.) — Medical
L. (muscufus) teres major, lit. 'the larger round
muscle', fr. L. teres, 'rounded, rounded οίΓ,
smooth*, and major, 'greater, larger'. See terete
and major.

## teres minor
teres minor, name of a muscle (anat.) — Medical
L. (musculus) teres minor, 'the smaller smooth
muscle', fr. L. teres (see prec. word) and minor,
'smaller'. See minor.

## terete
terete, adj., cylindrical and slightly tapering. —
L. teres, gen. teretis, 'rounded, rounded off,
smooth', orig. 'rubbed smooth', fr. terere, 'to
rub'. See throw and cp. terebra.

## terfa
terfa, п., an edible fungus. — F. terfez, fr. Arab.
tirfas, 'truffle'.

## tergal
tergal, adj., pertaining to the back. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. tergus, tergum, 'back',
which is of uncertain origin. It is possibly cogn.
with Gk. στέρφος, τέρφος, 'hide, skin (esp. of
the back)'.

## tergiversate
tergiversate, intr. v., to be evasive; to become a
renegade. — L. tergiversatus, pp. of tergiversari,
'to turn one's back', compounded of tergum,
'back*, and versari, passive of versdre, 'to turn
about', freq. of vertere, *to turn'. See tergal and
version.

## tergiversation
tergiversation, n. — L. tergiversdtio, gen. -onis, fr.
tergiversatus, pp. of tergiversari. See prec. word
and -ion.

## terlinguaite
terlinguaite, п., a mercuric oxychloride (mineral.)
— Named after Terlingua in Brewster County,
Texas. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## term
term, n. — ME. terme, fr, OF, terme, fr, ML.
terminus, 'expression, definition, term', fr. L.
terminus, 'boundary line, boundary, limit', which
is rel. to termen, gen. termini's, 'boundary stone',
and cogn. with OI. tarati, 'passes over, crosses
over*, tarantah, 'sea', Hitt. tarmaizzi/he bounds,
limits', Gk. τέρμα, 'boundary, end, limit', τέρ-
μων, 'boundary', τέρ&ρον, 'the end of the sail
yeard, end', Alban. S-tir, Ί cross (a river)', Goth.
palrh, OE. park, 'through', ON. prdmr, 'edge,
chip, splinter', OE. pyrel, 'aperture, hole;
perforated*. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*ter-t *tr-, 'to go through, pass beyond*. See
trans- and cp. through and words there referred
to. Cp. also terminate, conterminous, determine,
exterminate, interminable, terminology, terse,
train, 'vehicle', trance, trumeau. Cp. also tattoo,
'a pony', and the second element in avatar and
in Dhanvantari. Cp. also trout and words there
referred to.
Derivatives: term, tr. v., term-er, п., term-or, n.

## termagant
termagant, п., a scolding woman, shrew. — ME.
tervagant, PN., fr. OF. Tervagan, Tervagant,
which is rel. to It. Trivigante; of uncertain origin.

## Termes
Termes, п., the genus of the family Termitidae
(entomol.) — ModL., fr. L. tarmes, termes, gen.
-mitis, 'a worm that eats wood, woodworm', lit.
'the boring worm', cogn. with Gk. τερηδώυ,
'woodworm', fr. I.-E. base *ter-, 'to rub, bore'.
See throw and cp. termite. Cp. also terebra,
teredo.

## terminable
terminable, adj. — See terminate and -able.
Derivatives: terminabil-ity, п., terminable-ness,
п., terminabl-y, adv.

## terminal
terminal, adj. — L. terminahs, 'pertaining to
boundaries; pertaining to the end', fr. terminus.
See terminus and adj. suff. -al.

## Terminalia
Terminalia, n. pi., an ancient Roman festival held
on the 23rd of February (Roman antiq.) — L.,
lit. 'festival in honor of Terminus, 'god of the
boundaries', fr. Terminus. See Terminus.

## Terminalia
Terminalia, п., a genus of plants of the myrobalan
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. terminalis,
'pertaining to the end' (see terminal and 1st -ia and
cp. prec. word); so called from the leaves at the
end of the branches.

## terminate
terminate, tr. v., to end; intr. v., to cease. — L.
terminatus, pp. of terminare, 'to set bounds to,
bound, limit*, fr. terminus. See terminus and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:781 COLUMN:2 -->
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: termination (q.v.), terminat-ive, adj.,
terminat-ive-ly, adv., terminator (q.v.),
terminator у, adj.

## termination
termination, n. — ME., fr. L. termindtio, gen.
-onis, 'a bounding', fr. terminatus, pp. of
terminare. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: termination-al, adj.

## terminative
terminative, adj., tending to end. — ME., fr. ML.
terminativus, fr. L. terminatus, pp. of terminare.
See terminate and -ive.
Derivatives: terminative, п., terminative-ly, adv.

## terminator
terminator, п., 1) one who or that which
terminates; 2) the line dividing the illuminated and
unilluminated parts of the disk of the moon or
a planet. — L. terminator, 'he who sets bounds',
fr. terminatus, pp. of terminare. See terminate
and agential suff. -or.

## terminer
terminer, п., a determining (law.) — F. terminer,
'to end', fr. L. terminare; see terminate. For the
subst. use of the infinitive in law. terms cp.
attainder and words there referred to.

## terminism
terminism, п., the doctrine that the offer of divine
grace is limited to a certain period. — G. Termi-
nismus, coined fr. L. terminus, 'boundary, limit',
and suff. -ismus. See terminus and -ism.

## terminist
terminist, п., an adherent of terminism. —
Coined fr. L. terminus (see terminus) and suff. -ist.
Derivative: terminist-ic, adj.

## terminology
terminology, n. — G. Terminoiogie, a hybrid
coined by C. G. Schutz of Jena in 1786 fr. ML.
terminus, 'expression, term', fr. L. terminus,
'boundary, limit', and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See terminus and
-logy.
Derivatives: terminolog-ic-al, adj., terminolog-
ic-al-ly, adv.

## terminus
terminus, п., boundary. — L., 'boundary line,
boundary, limit', rel. to terme», 'boundary
stone'. See term and cp. conterminal, conter-
minus.

## Terminus
Terminus, the Roman god of boundaries. — L.
terminus, 'boundary'. See prec. word and cp.
Terminalia, 'a Roman festival'.

## termitarium
termitarium, termitury, п., a nest of termites. —
ModL. termitarium, fr. Termes. See Termes and
-arium, resp. subst. suff. -ary, and cp. next word.

## termite
termite, п., a white ant. — ModL. Termes, gen.
Termitis, 'the genus of termites', fr. L. termes,
gen. termitis, 'a worm that eats wood,
woodworm', lit. 'the boring insect'. See Termes.

## tern
tern, п., any of the birds of the subfamily Sterni-
nae. — Of Scand. origin; cp. Dan. terne, Swed.
tarna., Norw. terna, ON. perna. These words are
related to OE. stearn, 'starling', and cogn. with
L. sturnus, 'starling'. See starling and cp. Stur-
nus.

## tern
tern, п., a set of three. — L. terni, 'three each', fr.
ter, 'three times'. See ter- and cp. ternary.
Derivative: tern-ai, adj.

## ternary
ternary, adj., threefold. — ME., fr. L. terndrius,
fr. term, 'three each'. See 2nd tern and adj. suff.
-ary.

## ternate
ternate, adj., arranged in threes. — ModL. terna-
tus, fr. L. terni, 'three each'. See 2nd tern and
adj. suff. -ate.

## terne
terne, also terneplate,n., an alloy of lead and tin.
— F. terne, 'dull*, fr. MF., fr. ternir, 'to tarnish,
to dull'. See tarnish.

## ternery
ternery, п., breeding place of terns. — Formed fr.
2nd tern with suff. -ery.

## ternion
ternion, п., a set of three. — L. ternio, gen. -onis,
fr. terni, 'three each'. See 2nd tern.

## terpens
terpens, п., any of a group of hydrocarbons,
C10Hie (chem.) — Shortened fr. terpentine, the
orig. form of turpentine.

## terphenyl
terphenyl, п., a hydrocarbon whose molecule is
formed from three benzene rings. — Formed fr.
ter- and phenyl.

## terpin
terpin, п., the compound C10HW(OH)2 (chem) —
Coined by the Swedish chemist Jons Jacob Ber-
zelius (1779-1848) fr. terp- (for terpentin, the
orig. form of turpentine) and chem. suff. -in(e).
Cp. terpene.

## terpodion
terpodion, п., a keyboard instrument, invented in
1816 by Buschmann in Berlin (mus.) — ModL.,
coined from the stem of Gk. τέρπειν, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:781 COLUMN:3 -->
gladden', and ώδή, 'song'. See next word and ode.

## Terpsichore
Terpsichore, п., the Muse of the dance (Greek and
Roman mythol.) — L. Terpsichore, fr. Gk.
Τερψιχόρη, lit. 'enjoyment of dance', a name
compounded of τέφψις, 'enjoyment, gladness,
delight', and χορός, 'dance*. The first element is a
derivative of τέρπειν, 'to delight, please', fr.
I.-E. base *terp-, 'to satisfy', whence also OI.
Hpyati, trpnoti, tarpati, 'takes one's fill', Avestic
&rafda-, "satiated, satisfied', Toch. AB tsarw-, 'to
rejoice', tsarwo, 'joy', Lith. tarpstit, tafpti,
'to thrive, prosper', tarpa, 'thriving, prosperity',
Lett, tarpa, of s.m., OPruss. en-terpo, 'it is
useful', en-terpen, en-terpon, 'useful'. Cp. Euterpe.
For the second element see chorus.
Derivative: Terpsichore-an, adj., pertaining to
Terpsichore; hence, pertaiuing to dance.

## terra
terra, п., earth. — L., prob. for *tersd- and lit.
meaning 'dry land' and rel. to OL. tonus (for
*torsus), 'dry', L. torrere, 'to parch, roast', and
cogn. with Olr. tir (for *teros), 'land', fr. I.-E.
base *ters-, *trs-, *lo be dry', whence also OI.
tarsayati, 'dries up', tfsyati, 'thirsts', tistah,
'hoarse', trsiih, 'greedy, desirous', Avestic
tarshu-, 'dry, solid', Arm. fafamim, Ί wither,
dry up', erasht, metathesized fr. *trast (for l.-E.
*t£sti), 'dryness, drought', Gk.TapaeoSm, 'to be
or become dry, dry up', τερσαίνει,ν, 'to make
dry, to dry', ταρσός, 'wickerwork; flattof the
foot; ankle', τρασια, Ion. ταρσιή, 'a crate for
drying figs', Alb. ter, Ί lay out*, Goth, paiirsus,
'dry, barren', OHG. thurri, durri, MHG. durre,
durre, G. durr, Du. dor, OS. thurri, ON. purr, OE.
pyrre, 'dry', OHG. darra, MHG., G. darre, 'kiln
drying'. Cp. inter, 'to bury', mediterranean,
parterre, subterranean, tarsus, terrace, terra cotta,
terrain, terramara,terramycin, tcrrane,terrestrial,
terrier (in both senses), terrine, territory, thirst,
toast, torrid, trass, traulism, tureen and the
second element in verditer. Cp. also torsk.

## terrace
terrace, n. — MF! terrasse, terrace, 'pile of earth,
terrasse* (whence F. terrasse), fr. OProvenc. ter-
rassa, fr. VL- *terracea, a derivative of L. terra,
'earth'. See prec. word and cp. terrazzo.
Derivatives: terrace, tr. v., terrac-er, п.,
terrac-ette, п., terrac-ing, n.

## terra cotta
terra cotta, hard pottery, compounded of fine clay
and fine sand. — It., lit. 'cooked earth', fr. terra,
'earth' (fr. L. terra), and cotta, fern. pp. of cuo-
cere, 'to cook' (fr. L. coquere). For the first word
see terra, for the second see cook and cp. coc-
tion.

## terrain
terrain, п., a tract of land. — F., fr. L. terrenum.
See terrene.

## terramara
terramara, п., an earthy deposit. — Dial. It., for
terramarna, fr. It. terra, 'earth', and dial. It.
тага (for It. mama), 'marl* (see terra and marl); so
called because made of dry earth.

## terramycin
terramycin, п., an antibiotic derived from an
earth mold. — Coined fr. L. terra, 'earth', Gk.
μύκης, 'fungus*, and suff. -in. See terra and
myco-.

## terrane
terrane, п., a geological formation. — F. terrain,
fr. L. terrenum, 'land, ground' (whence also Sp.
terreno, OProvenc. terren), prop. neut. of ter-
renus, 'of earth', used as a noun. Sec terrene.

## terraneous
terraneous, adj., terrestrial. — See term and
-aneous.

## terrapin
terrapin, п., name of several species of turtles. —
Of Algonquian origin.

## terraqueous
terraqueous, adj., consisting of both land and
water. — Compounded of terra and aqueous.

## terrarium
terrarium, п., a vivarium for terrestrial animals.
— ModL., fofmed fr. L. terra, 'earth' (see terra),
with suff. -arium on the analogy of aquarium.

## terrazzo
terrazzo, п., a kind of flooring. — It., rel. to ter-
razza, 'terrace', "See terrace and cp. trass.

## terrene
terrene, adj., earthy, earthly. — L. terrenus, 'of,
or pertaining to, the earth, earthy, earthly', fr.
terra. See terra and -ene.
Derivative: terrene, n.

## terreplein
terreplein, п., platform of a rampart (fort.) — F.
terre-plein, fr. It. terrapieno, back formation fr.
terrapienare (orig. written in two words: terra
pienare), 'to fill with earth', fr. terra, 'earth*, fr.
L. terra, and pienare, 'to fill', fr. VL. *pie~ndre,
fr. L. plinus, 'full'. For the first element"see
terra, for the second see full, adj., and cp. pie-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:782 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 7SS | TESTIFY -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:782 COLUMN:1 -->
num.

## terrestrial
terrestrial, adj., earthly, earthy. — ME., formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. terrestris, 'of or
pertaining to the earth', fr. terra. See terra.
Derivatives: terrestrial, п., terrestrial~ity, n.

## tercet
tercet, п., ring of a harness pad. — ME. teret,
toret, fr. OF. toret, touret, 'small wheel', dimin.
of tour, 'circuit'. See tonr and -et.

## terrible
terrible, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. terri-
bilis, 'frightful, dreadful', fr. terreo, terrere, 'to
frighten', which stands for *terseyo and is cogn.
with OI. trasati, 'trembles', Avestic tarshta,
'feared, revered', teresaiti, 'is afraid of, Gk.
τρέειν (for *tresein), 'to tremble; to flee', Lith.
trisu, triseti, 'to tremble', OSlav. treso, Ί shake',
treso se, Ί tremble', Mir. tarrock, 'timid', fr.
I.-E. base *teres-t *tres-, 'to tremble'. Cp. deter.
Cp. also Tirshatha, Treron. For the ending see
suff. -ible. — Cp. the collateral I.-E. bases;
*trem-, whence Gk. τρέμειν, L. tremere, 'to
tremble', and *trep-, whence L. trepidus,
'restless, anxious, solicitous'. See tremble and
trepidation.
Derivatives: terrible-ness, п., terribl-y, adv.

## terricolous
terricolous, adj., living on the ground (zool. and
bot.) — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. terricola,
'inhabiting the earth', fr. terra, 'earth', and
-cola, 'inhabiting', which is rel. to colere, 'to till
(the ground); to inhabit*, incolere, 'to inhabit',
incola, 'inhabitant', coldnus, 'cultivator of the
ground*. See terra and colony and cp. the second
element in pratincole. For the ending see suff.
-ous.

## terrier
terrier, п., akind of dog. — F., prop, ckien terrier,
lit. 'earth dog', fr. ckien, 'dog' (fr. L. canis), and
ML. terrarius, 'of, or pertaining to, earth or
land', fr. L. terra, 'earth, land'. See terra and
-ier.

## terrier
terrier, п., a document stating the boundaries of
landed property. — F., fr. MF., fr. ML. (liber)
terrarius, 'book relating to land', fr. L. terra,
'earth, land'. See prec. word.

## terrific
terrific, adj. — L. terrificus, 'frightful', lit.
'causing terror*, compounded of the stem of terrere,
"to frighten', and -ficere, unstressed form οι fa-
cere, 'to make, do'. See terrible and -fie.
Derivatives: terrific-al-ly, terrific-ly, ad vs.,
terrific-ness, n.

## terrify
terrify, tr. v. — L. terrificdre, 'to frighten* (whence
also F. terrifier), fr. terrificus. See prec. word
and -fy.
Derivatives: terrify-ing, adj., terrify-ing-ly, adv.

## terrigenous
terrigenous, adj., 1) earthbom; 2) produced by the
earth. — L. terrigena, 'born of the earth', fr.
terra, 'earth', and the stem of gignere (pp. geni-
tus), 'to beget, bear, bring forth'. See terra and
genus.

## terrine
terrine, п., an earthenware dish. — F., fr. MF.,
fem. of the adj. terrin, 'pertaining to the earth,
earthen', fr. VL. *terrinus, fr. L. terrenus. See
terrene and cp. tureen.

## territorial
territorial, adj. — L. territoridlis (whence also F.
territorial)) fr. territorium, 'domain, territory'.
See territory and cp. exterritorial,
extraterritorial.
Derivatives: territorial, п., territorial-ism, п.,
territorial-ist, п., territorial-ize, tr. v., territorial-
iz-ation, п., territorial-lyy adv.

## territory
territory, n. — L. territorium, 'domain, district,
territory*, formed fr. terra, 'earth' (see terra),
with -orium, a suff. denoting place (see subst.
suff. -ory). Cp. dormitdrium, 'sleeping room' (see
dormitory).
Derivatives: territorial (q.v.), territori-an, п.,
territori-ed, adj.

## terror
terror, n. — ME. terrour, fr. MF. (= F.) terreur,
fr. L. terrorem, ace. of terror, 'great fear, alarm',
fr. terrere, 'to frighten'. See terrible and -or.

## terrorism
terrorism, n. — F. terrorisme, formed fr. L. terror
(see prec. word) with suff. -isme (see -ism).

## terrorist
terrorist, n. — F. terroriste, formed fr. L. terror
(see terror) with suff. -iste (see -ist).
Derivatives: terrorist-ic, terrorist-ic-al, adjs.

## terrorize
terrorize, tr. v. — Formed, fr. L. terror (see terror)
with suff. -ize.
Derivatives: terroriz-ation, п., terroriz-er, n.

## terry
terry, п., uncut loop in velvet. — Prob. fr. F. tire,
'drawn, pulled', pp. of tirer. See tire, 'to pull*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:782 COLUMN:2 -->

## terse
terse, adj., concise. — L. tersus, pp. of tergere,
*to rub, wipe off', which is cogn. with Gk. τρώ-
γειν, 'to gnaw', τρώγλη, 'hole', Goth, paitko,
'hole', fr. I.-E. *tro-g-, *tre-g-, enlargement of
base *ter-> *ΐζ-, 'to go through, pass beyond*.
See term and cp. absterge, abstersion, deterge,
detersion. Cp. also through, truglodyte, trout.
Derivatives: terse-ly, adv., terse-ness, n.

## terrial
terrial, adj., referring to the flight feathers of the
third row (ornithol.) — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. tertius, 'third'. See next word.
Derivative: tertial, n.

## tertian
tertian, adj., recurring every other day. — Prop.
'recurring every third day', the first and the
third day being reckoned inclusively, fr. L. ter-
tidnus, fr. tertius, 'the third'. See third and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also sesterce.

## tertian
tertian, п., tertian fever. — L. tertidna, short for
febris tertidna, 'tertiam fever'. See prec. word.

## Tertiary
Tertiary, adj., pertaining to the era preceded by
the Mesozoic (geol.) — L. tertidrius, 'containing
a third part*, fr. tertius, 'third' (see third and adj.
suff. -ary); so called because the Mesozoic was
formerly named Secondary.
Derivative: Tertiary, n.

## tertiary
tertiary, п., a member of third order in a
monastic system. — See prec. word.

## tertium quid
tertium quid, something intermediate between
two things. — L.^'a third something',
translation of Gk. τρίτον τί. See tertian and quiddity.

## teruah
teruah, п., a succession of 9 tremulous notes of
the shophar (Jewish Religion). — Heb. t гй'аь,
'shout, cry, alarm, blast of trumpet or shophar,
a succession of tremulous notes', formed from
the stem of heriai, 'he sounded a signal, he
shouted in triumph' (in Mishnaic Heb. also 'he
blew the shophar'), which is prob. rel. to Arab.
raghd, 'he shouted'.

## terylene
terylene, п., trademark for a synthetic textile fiber
based on terephthalic acid. — Coined fr. tere-
phthalic and suff. -ene.

## terza rima
terza rima, a verse in which the rhymes are
arranged according to the following formula: aba,
beb, cdc. — It., lit. 'third rhyme'. It. terza is fem.
of terzo, fr. L. tertius, 'third'. See tertian, adj.,
and rhyme.

## terzetto
terzetto, п., trio; vocal trio. — It., dimin. of terzo,
'third', fr. L. tertius. See tertian, adj.

## teschemacherite
teschemacherite, п., an acid ammonium
carbonate (mineral.) — Named after the English
chemist Frederick E. Teschemacher (died in
1863). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## tessara-
tessara-, combining form meaning 'four'. — Fr.
Gk. τέσσαρα, neut. of τέσσαρες, 'four', rel. to
Att. τέτταρες, Ion. τέσσερες, Aeol. πίσυρες,
Lesbian πέσυρες, fr. I.-E. base *qwetur-, 'four'.
See four and cp. tessera-, diatessaron, tetarto-,
tetra-, tetrad and the first element in trapezium.

## tesselia
tesselia, п., a small tessera. — L., 'a little cube',
dimin. of tessera. See tessera- and -ella.

## tessellar
tessellar, adj., composed of tesserae. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. tesselia. See prec. word.

## tessellate
tessellate, tr. v., to pave by inlaying small square
blocks in mosaic. — L. tesselldtus, pp. of tessel-
lare, 'to chequer, tessellate', fr. tesselia. See
tesselia and verbal suff. -nte.
Derivatives: tessellat-ed, adj., tessellat-ion, n.

## tessera
tessera, п., a small, square piece of stone, a die.
— Lit. 'having four sides', fr. Ion. Gk. τέσσερα,
neut. of τέσσερες, which is rel. to Gk. τέσσαρες,
'four'. See tessara-.

## tessitura
tessitura, п., range of a voice part (mus.) — It.,
'texture', fr. tessere, 'to weave', fr. L. texere. See
texture.

## test
test, п., a cupel for refining or trying metals;
examination, trial. — ME., fr. MF., fr. OF., fr.
L. testu, testum, 'vessel, earthen vessel, pot',
which is rel. to testa, 'piece of burnt clay,
potsherd, shell, scale', and prob. cogn. with Avestic
tashta-, 'cup', Lith. tlStas, 'vessel made of willow
twigs', and with L. texere, 'to weave', fr. I.-E.
base *tekth-, 'to weave'. See text and cp. testudo.
Cp. also tester, 'canopy'.
Derivatives: test, tr. v., to refine in a cupel; to
put to the test; to try, examine, testable (q.v.),
tester (q.v.), test-ing, adj., test-ing-ly, adv.

## test
test, п., the hard shell of many invertebrates (zool.)
— L. testa, 'shell'. See test, 'cupeF.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:782 COLUMN:3 -->

## testable
testable, adj., capable of being tested. — Formed
with suff. -able fr. test, 'to try'. See test, 'cupel'.

## testable
testable, adj., capable of being disposed of by
will (law.) — L. testdbilis, 'that has a right to
give testimony', fr. testdri. See testament and
-able.

## Testacea
Testacea, n. pi., an order of invertebrates covered
with shells, (zool.) — ModL., fr. L. testdceus,
'covered with a shell'. See testaceous.

## test ace an
test ace an, adj., any of the Testacea. — See prec.
word and -an.
Derivative: testacean, п., a testacean animal.

## testaceous
testaceous, adj. — L. testdceus, 'covered with a
shell', fr. testa. See test, 'shell', and -aceous.

## testacy
testacy, п., state of being testate. — Formed fr.
testate with suff. -cy.

## testament
testament, n. — ME., fr. Eccles. L. testdmentum,
'covenant, Scripture', fr. L.,'declaration of one's
will; last will, testament', fr. L. testdri, 'to be a
witness, bear witness, testify', fr. testis, 'witness',
which is formed fr. *tristo, a compound
meaning 'the third standing by*. Cp. Oscan. tristaa-
mentud(~ L. testdmento). The first element of
this compound is related to L. tres, 'three'; see
three and cp. tri-. The second element is formed
from the stem of sto, stare, 'to stand'; see state.
Testament in the sense of Bible is due to a
confusion of the two meanings of Gk. δια&ήκη: 1)
'covenant'; 2) 'last will and testament', the word
used in the Septuagint to render Heb. bsritk,
'covenant'. Cp. attest, contest, detest, intestate,
obtest, protest, protestant, testamur, testate,
testify, testimonial, testimony. For the ending
of testament see suff. -meat.
Derivatives: testament-al, adj.,testament-aryta.dj.

## testamur
testamur, п., English university certificate. — L.
testamur, 'we attest, testify', fr. testdri (see
testament) ; so called from the word testamur used
in the text of the certificate.

## testate
testate, adj., having left a valid will (law.) — ME.,
fr. L. testdtus, pp. of testdri, 'to witness, testify'.
See testament and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: testate, n.

## testator
testator, п., a person who makes a will. — L.
testator, 'one who makes a will', fr. testdtus, pp. of
testdri. See testament and agential suff. -or.

## testatrix
testatrix, п., a female testator. — L. testatrix,
fem. of testator. See prec. word and -trix.

## teste
teste, п., the witness being ... — L., abl. of testis,
'witness', used in absolute construction. For the
etymology of L. testis see testament.

## tester
tester, п., one who tests. — Formed with agential
suff. -er from test, 'to try'. See test, 'cupel*.

## tester
tester, п., canopy. — ME. tester, fr. OF. testiere,
'headpiece, helmet' (whence F. tetiere, 'infant's
cap*), fr. teste (F. tete), 'head', fr. L. testa, 'piece
of burnt clay, potsherd, shell, scale*, to which, in
Late Latin, was added the meaning 'skull', and,
in Vulgar Latin, the meaning 'head', orig. used
only in a humerous sense. Cp. OProvenc. testa,
'scale, nutshell; head', It. testa, 'head', Rum.
fasra, 'skull'. See test, 'cupel', and cp. teston,
testy, tete-a-tete. For the sense development
of L. testa in the Romance languages cp.
OE. cuppe, OHG. cnuph, kopf, 'cup', MHG.
kopf, 'drinking vessel; skull', G. Kopf, 'head'
(see cup). Cp. also OI. carah, 'kettle, pot', which
is prob. rel. to OI. karankas, 'skull', and cogn.
with Goth, fvairnei,'skull', OE. nwer, 'kettle' (see
corrie).

## tester
tester, п., name of several coins. — A var. of
teston.. Cp. tizzy.

## testicle
testicle, п., a male gland secreting the
spermatozoa, testis. — L. testiculus, dimin. of testis,
'testicle'. See testis.

## testicular
testicular, adj., pertaining to the testicles. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr. L. testiculus. See
prec. word.

## testiculate
testiculate, testiculated, adj., having testicles. —
Late L. testiculdtus, fr. L. testiculus. See testicle
and adj. suff. -ate, resp. also -ed.

## testification
testification, n. — L. testification gen. -dnis, fr.
testifiedtus, pp. of testificdri, 'to bear witness to'.
See testify and -ion

## testify
testify, intr. and tr. v. — ME. testifien, fr. OF.
testifier, fr. L. testificdri, 'to bear witness to',
formed fr. testis, 'witness', and -ficdri, fx.facere,
'to make, do'. See testament and -fy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:783 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TESTIMONIAL | 756 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:783 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: testifi-er, n.

## testimonial
testimonial, n. —«MEL., ft. Late L. testimonialis,
in litterae testimonialis, 'letters serving for
evidence', fr. L. testimonium. See testimony and
adj. suff. -al.

## testimonialize
testimonialize, intr. v., to honor with a
testimonial. — Formed fr. L. testimonium (see prec.
word) with suff. -ize.
Derivative: testimonializ-ation, n.

## testimony
testimony, n. — ME., fr. Late L. testimonium,
'testimony of the Decalogue, the Decalogue' (loan
translation of Heb. 'edutk, 'testimony, testimony
of the Decalogue'), fr. L. testimonium, 'evidence,
attestation', which was formed fr. testis,
'witness' (see testament), with suff. -monium. See
-mony and cp. words there referred to.

## testis
testis, п., testicle. — L., 'witness; testicle'. See
testament. For sense development cp. F. ti-
moins, 'testicles', pi. of temoin, 'witness', and
Gk. παραστάται, 'testicles', pi. of παραστάτης,
which literally means 'one who stands by'.

## teston
teston, п., name of several coins. — MF., fr. It.
testone, augment, formed fr. testa, 'head'. The
coin was so called because it bore the image of
the sovereign's head. Cp. tester, 'coin', and see
tester, 'canopy'· Cp. also toston.

## testosterone
testosterone, п., the male sex hormone. — Coined
fr. L. testes, pi. of testis (see testis), ster(ol) and
suff. -one.

## testudlnal
testudlnal, adj., pertaining to a tortoise. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. testudo, gen. testudinis,
'tortoise'. See testudo.

## testudinarious
testudinarious, adj., colored like a tortoise shell.
— Formed with suff. -arious fr. L. testudo, gen.
testudinis, 'tortoise'. See testudo.

## testudinate
testudinate, adj., resembling a tortoise shell. —
L. testudinatus, fr. testudot gen. testudinis,
'tortoise'. See testudo and adj. suff. -ate.

## testudineous
testudineous, adj., resembling a tortoise shell. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. testudo, gen.
testudinis, 'tortoise'. See testudo.

## testudo
testudo, п., 1) shed, movable shelter {Roman an-
tiq.); 2) {cap.) a genus of turtles, the land
tortoise (zool.) — L. testudo, 'tortoise', fr. testu,
'earthen vessel', which is rel. to testa, 'shell'. See
test, 'cupel', and -ude.

## testy
testy, adj., irritable. — ME. testif, fr. AF. testif
(fem. testive), formed—with change of suff. -u to
-if—ϊτ. OF. testu (F. tetu), 'stubborn', lit. 'heady,
headstrong', fr. OF. teste (F. tete), 'head'. See
tester, 'canopy'.
Derivatives: testi-ly, adv., testi-ness, n.

## tetanic
tetanic, adj., pertaining to, or characterized by,
tetanus. — L. tetanicus, fr. Gk. τετανικός, fr.
τέτανος. See tetanus and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: tetanic, п., a substance producing
tetanic spasms.

## tetano-
tetano-, before a vowel tetan-, combining form
denoting the tetanus. — Medical L., fr. Gk.
τέτανο-, τεταν, fr. τέτανος. See tetanus.

## tetanus
tetanus, п., infectious disease characterized by the
rigidity of voluntary muscles. — L., fr. Gk.
τέτανος, 'convulsive tension of the muscles',
which is rel. to τέτανος, 'stretched, rigid', from
a reduplicated form of the I.-E. base *ten-, *to
stretch', whence τείνείν (Κ>Γ*τένιειν), L. tendere,
'to stretch'. See tend, 'to move in a certain
direction'.
Derivatives: tetanic (q.v.), tetan-ize, tr. v., tetan-
iz-ation, n.

## tetarto-
tetarto-, before a vowel tetart-, combining form
meaning 'one fourth'. — Gk. τέταρτο-, τε-
ταρτ-, fr. τέταρτος, 'fourth; one fourth', rel.
to Att. Gk. τέτταρες, Gk. τέσσαρες, 'four'. See
tessara- and cp. terra-.

## tetchy
tetchy, adj. — See techy.

## tete-a-tete
tete-a-tete, adv., privately; adj., private; п., a
private meeting. — F., lit.'head to head*, fr. F. tete,
fr. OF. teste, 'head'. See tester, 'canopy\and -a.

## tete-beche
tete-beche, adj., reversed in relation to each other
(said of stamps). — F., alteration of beckevet,
'head to foot', prop, 'from the head of one to
the feet of another', which is compounded of
pref. bes-, 'twice', fr. L. bis, and chevet, 'head of
something', fr. L. capitium, dimin. of caput,
'head'; see bis and chevet. The change of
beckevet to tete-beche is due to the circumstance that
the exact meaning of the word beckevet was no

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:783 COLUMN:2 -->
more clear and the necessity was felt to place
the word tete, 'head', before it.

## teth
teth, п., name of the 9th letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb. teth, a word connected by Ge-
senius with Arab, tayf, 'serpent', whereas Du-
nand renders it by 'ball, clew'. Cp. theta.

## tethelin
tethelin, n.» a lipide {biochem*) — Formed with
suff. -in fr. Gk. τε&ηλώς, perf. part, of θάλ-
λειν, 'to thrive, flourish*. See Thalia, 'the
Muse of comedy'.

## tether
tether, п., a rope for fastening an animal. — ME.
tethir, tedir, prob. fr. ON. tjodr, rel. to Dan.
toir, Swed. tjuder, OFris. tiader, tieder, MDu.
tuder, Du. tuier, 'line, rope', OHG. zeotar,
MHG. zieter, 'pole of a cart'.
Derivative: tether, tr. v.

## terra-
terra-, before a vowel tetr-, combining form
meaning 'four'. — Gk. τετρα-, τετρ-, 'four-',
rel. to τέταρτος, 'fourth'. See tetarto-.

## tetr a chord
tetr a chord, п., 1) an instrument with four strings;
2) a series of four tones, with the interval of a
fourth between the first and the last {music). —
Gk. τετράχορδον (scil. όργανον), 'an
instrument with four strings', neut. of the adjective
τετράχορδος, 'four-stringed', which is
compounded of τετρα- (see tetra-) and χορδή,
'chord'. See chord.

## tetract
tetract, adj., having four rays. — Compounded
of tetr- and Gk. άκτίς, gen. άκτΐνος, 'ray'. See
actinic.

## tetrad
tetrad, п., I) the number four; a group of four
things. — Gk. τετράς, gen. τετράδος, rel. to
Att. Gk. τέτταρες, Gk. τέσσαρες, 'four'. See
tessara-, and -ad.
Derivative: tetrad-ic> adj.

## tetraJymite
tetraJymite, name of a mineral, called also
telluric bismuth. — Formed with subst. suff. -ite fr.
Gk. τετράδυμος, 'fourfold*, which is
compounded of τετρα- (see tetra-) and suff. -δυμος,
which is rel. to δύο, 'two', δίδυμος, 'twin'. See
di-, 'two, double', and didymium. The tetrady-
mite owes its name to the circumstance that its
crystals appear in groups of four.

## tetragon
tetragon, п., a quadrangle. — Late L. tetragonum,
fr. Gk. τετράγωνον, neut. of the adjective
τετράγωνος, 'with four angles', fr. τετρα- (see
tetra-) and γωνία, 'corner, angle'. See -gon.
Derivatives: tetragon-al, tetragon-ous, adjs.

## tetrugram
tetrugram, п., a word consisting of four letters. —
See next word.

## Tetragrammaton
Tetragrammaton, п., the quadriliteral name of
God in the Hebrew Bible. — Gk. τετρα-
γράμματον, 'the word of four letters', prop. neut.
of the adj. τετραγράμματος, used as a noun,
fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and γράμμα, gen.
γράμματος, 'letter'. See -gram.

## tetragynous
tetragynous, adj., having four pistils {pot.) —
Compounded of tetra- and -gynous.

## tetrahedral
tetrahedral, adj., pertaining to a tetrahedron. —
See next word and adj. suff. -al.

## tetrahedron
tetrahedron, п., a solid figure contained by four
triangular surfaces. — ModL., fr. Gk. τετρά-
εδρον, prop. neut. of the adjective τετράεδρος,
'having four sides', fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and
ίίδρα (for *sedra-), 'seat; base, side, face'. See
-hedron.

## tetrakis-
tetrakis-, combining form meaning 'four times'.
— Gk. τετράκ^ς, 'four times', formed fr. τετρα-
(see tetra-) and ακίς, 'needle, point', which is
rel. to άκή, 'point', from I.-E. base *a&-, 'sharp',
whence also ακμή, 'edge', ίίκρος, 'pointed', L.
acus, 'needle', acuere, 'to sharpen', acer, 'sharp'.
See acrid and cp. triakis- and the second
element in Thrinax.

## tetrakishexaeoron
tetrakishexaeoron, п., a polyhedron of 24
congruent isosceles-triangular faces {geom.) —
Compounded of tetrakis- and hexaedron.

## tetralogy
tetralogy, п., a series of four dramas. — Gk.
τετραλογία, compounded of τετρα- (see tetra-)
and -λογία, fr. λόγος, 'word, speech, discourse,
story, reason, account'. See logos, -logy.

## tetrameter
tetrameter, п., a verse of four metrical feet (pros.)
— Formed fr. tetra- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## tetrandrous
tetrandrous, adj., having four stamens (bot.) —
Compounded of tetra- and -androus.

## Tetraonidae
Tetraonidae, n. pi., a family of birds (ornitkoL) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. tetrad,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:783 COLUMN:3 -->
'heath cock', fr. Gk. τετράων, which, together
with τέτραξ (whence L. tetrax), name of a
bird, derives from a base of imitative origin. Cp.
OI. tittirak, tittirik, 'partridge', ModPers.
tadarv, 'pheasant', L. tetrinnire, 'to quack', tur-
tur, 'turtledove', Arm. t'rt'rafc, 'a good speaker',
OSIav. tetrevi, 'pheasant', Lith. terva, 'black
grouse', Russ. totoriV, 'to babble, chatter*. Cp.
turtle, 'turtledove*.

## tetrapla
tetrapla, п., a book containing four versions in
parallel columns. — ModL., fr. Gk. τετραπλά,
neut. pi. of τετραπλόος, τετραπλούς,
'fourfold', fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and suff. -πλόος,
-πλους, '-fold', which occurs also in άπλόος,
άπλοΰς, 'simple'. See haplo- and cp. hexapla.

## tetrapod
tetrapod, adj., having four feet. — ModL. tetra-
podus, fr. Gk. τετράπους, gen. τετράποδος,
'four-footed', fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and πους,
gen. ποδός, 'foot1. See -pod.

## tetrapody
tetrapody, п., a verse consisting of four feet {pros.)
— Gk. τετραποδία, 'a measure or length of
four feet', fr. τετράπους, gen. τετράποδος. See
prec. word -y (representing Gk. -ία).
Derivative: tetrapod-ic, adj.

## tetrapolis
tetrapolis, п., a group of four cities. — Gk. τε-
τράπολις, an adjective meaning 'of four cities',
fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and πόλις, 'city'. See
policy, 'method of government'.

## tetrapterous
tetrapterous, adj., having four wings. — Gk. τε-
τράπτερος, 'four-winged', fr. τετρα- (see tetra-)
and πτερόν, 'wing'. See ptero-. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## Tetrapturus
Tetrapturus, п., a genus of fishes (icktkyol.) —
ModL., compounded of tetra-, Gk. πτερόν,
'wing', and ούρα, 'tail'. See ptero- and uro-,
'tail-'.

## tetrapylon
tetrapylon, п., a building with four gates. — Gk.
τετράπυλον,ρΓΟρ. neut. of the adjective τετρά-
πυλος, 'having four gates', used as a noun;
compounded of τετρα-(see tetra-) and πύλη, 'gate'.
See tetra- and pylon.

## tetrarch
tetrarch, п., ruler of a part (originally a fourth
part) of a province {Classical kist.) — Late L.
tetrarcka, fr. L. tetrarckes, fr. Gk. τετράρχης,
lit. 'governor of the fourth part (of a province)',
fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and -άρχης, 'ruler'. See
-arch.
Derivative: tetrarck-ate, n.

## tetrarchic
tetrarchic, adj., pertaining to a tetrarchy or a
tetrarch. — Gk. τετραρχικός, Of a tetrarch', fr.
τετράρχης. See prec. word and -ic.

## tetrarchy
tetrarchy, п., the district or oHce of a tetrarch. —
L. tetrarchia, fr. Gk. τετραρχίά, 'the province
of a tetrarch', fr. τετράρχης. See tetrarch and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## tetraseme
tetraseme, п., a foot corresponding to the length
of four short syllables {Greek prosody). — Late
L. tetrasemus, 'of four syllables', fr. Gk. τετρά-
σημος, fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and σήμα, 'sign'.
See semantics.
Derivative: tetrasem-ic, adj.

## tetrastich
tetrastich, п., a poem consisting of four lines. —
L. tetrastichon, fr. Gk. τετράστί.χον, prop. neut.
of the adjective τετράστιχος, 'of four lines',
used as a noun; compounded of τετρα- (see
tetra-) and στίχος, 'row, line, rank; verse'. See
stichic and cp. acrostic and words there referred
to.

## tetrastyle
tetrastyle, adj., having four pillars. — L. tetra-
stylos, fr. Gk. τετράστϋλος, fr. τετρα- (see
tetra-) and στύλος, 'column'. See style, 'gnomon'.

## tetrastyle
tetrastyle, п., a building with four columns. — L.
tetrastylon, fr. Gk. τετράστΰλον, neut. of the
adjective τετράστϋλος, used as a noun. See
tetrastyle, adj.

## tetrasyliabic
tetrasyliabic, adj., having four syllables. —
Formed with suff. -ic fr. Gk. τετρασύλλαβος, 'having
four syllables', fr. τετρα- (see tetra-) and
συλλαβή, 'syllable'. See sylinble and cp. syliabic,

## tetrasyllable
tetrasyllable, п., a word of four syllables. —
Formed fr. tetra- and syllable. See prec. word.

## tetravalent
tetravalent, adj., quadrivalent (chem.) — A
hybrid coined fr. Gk. τετρα- (see tetra-) and L.
valins, gen. -erttis, pres. part, of valere, 'to be
strong, have power' (see -valent). The correct
form is quadrivalent (fr. L. quadri-, 'four', and
valens, 'having power').

## tetrolic
tetrolic, to adj., pertaining the acid CH3. С : С .

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:784 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 757 | THANE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:784 COLUMN:1 -->
СООН (скет.) — Coined fr. tetr- and -olic; so
called from the four carbon atoms.

## tetronic
tetronic, adj., pertaining to the acid, CO . СНг
CO . CHsO (chem.) — Coined fr. tetr- and
-onic; so called from the four carbon atoms.

## tetroxide
tetroxide, tetroxid, п., an oxide, each molecule of
which contains four atoms of oxygen (chem.) —
Formed fr. tetr- and oxid(e).

## tetryl
tetryl, a synonym of butyl, C4H, [chem.) —
Coined fr. tetr- and -yl; so called from the four
carbon atoms.

## tetter
tetter, п., a vesicular skin disease. — ME. teiere,
fr. OE. teter, 'ringworm (a skin disease)', rel. to
OHG. zittaroh, MHG. ziteroch, dial. G. Zit-
teroch (cp. G. Zittermal, *tetter\ for the second
element of which see mole, 'spot'); cogn. with
OI. dadruh (also darduh, dardruh), 'a kind of
skin disease', Lith. dedermne, Lett, dedere, de-
derene, 'tetter', fr. I.-E. *dedru-, reduplication
(for the sake of emphasis) of *deru-, which
appears in W. darwyden, darwden, MBret. daroue-
den. Mod Bret, dervoeden and in Gaulish L. der-
bita, 'tetter'. These bases prop, mean 'torn skin',
and are enlargements of I.-E. base *der-, 'to
tear'. See tear, 'to rend', and cp. dartars.
Derivatives: tetter, tr. and intr. v., tetter-ous,
adj., tetter-y, adj.

## tettix
tettix, п., the cicada (rare). — ModL., fr. Gk.
τέττΐξ, 'cicada', which is of imitative origin.

## Teucrian
Teucrian, adj., pertaining to Teucer or to the
Trojans. — Formed with suff. -ian, fr. L. Teucer,
fr. Gk. Τεύκρος, name of the first king of Troy.

## Teucrium
Teucrium, п., a genus of trees, the germander
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τεύκριον, 'germander',
which is of uncertain origin. It is possibly named
after Τεύκρος, 'Teucer', the first king of Troy,
who was allegedly the first to use this plant in
medicine.

## Teuton
Teuton, n., a member of the Teutonic race, esp. a
German. — L. Teutones (pi.), a word of Teut.
origin. See Dutch and cp. the first element in
Theodoric. Cp. also Goth.

## Teutonic
Teutonic, adj. — L. Teutonicus, fr. Teutones. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: Teutonic, n.

## tew
tew, tr. v., to prepare by beating; to work hard.
— A var. of taw.

## tewel
tewel, п., 1) a hole (obsol.); 2) the tuyere of a
furnace. — ME. tuel, 'funnel, chimney', fr. MF.
/не/, tuiel (F. tuyau), 'pipe, tube', fr. OF., fr.
Frankish *j>uta, of s.m. (whence also OProvenc.
tudel, of s.m.), which is rel. to Goth, put-haurn,
'trumpet', lit. 'sounding horn', MDu. tute,
MLG. tute, 'anything resembling a horn'
(whence G. Tute, 'paper bag'); of imitative
origin. Cp. tuyere.

## text
text, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) texte, fr. OF., fr.
L. textus, 'texture, structure; context', from
textus, pp. of texere, 'to weave, plait, fit together',
which is cogn. with OI. tdksati, 'he fashions,
constructs', tdksan, 'carpenter', Avestic tash-, 'to
cut, carve', tasha, 'ax, hatchet', Gk. τέκτων,
'carpenter', τέχνη (for *teks-na-), 'art', OSlav.
tesla, 'ax, hatchet', teSo, tesati, 'to hew, fell, cut
down', tesu, 'beam', Lith. taSau, talfti, 'to cut,
carve', Olr. tal (for *tokslo-), 'cooper's ax,
mason's ax', Arm. t'eklem, Ί turn, wind, twist',
OHG., MHG. dahs, G. Dachs, Du. das, 'badger'
[ML. taxus, taxd, It. tasso, F. taisson, Sp.
texon (now spelled tejon), 'badger', are Teut.
loan wo'rds], lit. 'the builder', ON. pattr, 'thread,
wick'. Cp. also Hitt. taksh-, 'to join, unite,
build', takshan, 'together'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base "tekht-, *tekh-, 'to build (of
wood), carpenter; to weave'. The original
meaning of this base prob. was 'to plait, twist'. Cp.
architect, context, dachshund, pretext, snbtie,
Taxidea, technic, tecto-, 'builder', Tectona,
tectonic, tela, teiary, tessitura, test, 'cupel', textile,
thixle, tiller, tissue, toil, 'net'.

## textile
textile, adj. — L. textilis, 'woven', fr. textus, pp.
of texere. See text and suff. -lie.
Derivative: textile, n.

## textlet
textlet, п., a little text. — Formed fr. text with
the dimin. suff. -let.

## textual
textual, adj. — ME. textuel, fr. OF. (= F.) tex-
tuel, fr. L. "textualis, fr. textus. See text and adj.
suff. -al and cp. contextual.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:784 COLUMN:2 -->

## textualism
textualism, п., strict adherence to the text. — See
prec. word and -ism.

## textualist
textualist, п., one who strictly adheres to the text.
— See prec. word and -ist.

## texture
texture, n. — L. textura, 'web, texture, fabric', fr.
textus, pp. of texere, 'to weave'. See text and
-lire and cp. tessitura, contexture, intertexture.
Derivatives: textur-al, adj., textur-al-ly, adv.

## tezkirah
tezkirah, tezkere, п., a certificate. — Arab, tddh-
kirah, prop, verbal noun of dhdkkara, 'he
recalled something to someone', the second
conjugation of dhakara, 'he remembered', which is
rel. to Heb. zakhdr, 'he remembered', zekher,
'remembrance, memorial', zikkdron,
'memorial, remembrance', Aram. Syr. dekhar, Ethiop.
zakdra, 'he remembered', Akkad. zakdru, 'to
name, speak, swear', zikru, 'name'.

## -th
-th, subst. suff. forming nouns of action, state,
quality, etc. — ME., fr. OE. -δ, rel. to ON. -p,
OHG. -ida, Goth, -ipa, and cogn. with the subst.
suffixes: OI. -tati- (cp. sarvrf-fafi-A, 'universality,
wholeness', fr. sarva-h, 'whole'), Gk. -τητ- (ср.
φιλοτητ-, stem of φιλότης, 'friendship', fr.
φίλος, 'friend'), L. -tati- (cp. tibertat-, stem of
libertas, 'freedom', fr. liber, 'free'). Cp. -ty. Cp.
also subst. suff. -t

## -th
-th, suff. forming ordinal numbers. — ME. -the,
-te, -ethe, ft. OE. -da, -ta, -оба, -еда, rel. to ON.
-di, -ti, OHG. -do, -to, Goth, -da, -ta, '-th', and
cogn. with OI. -tha-b, Gk. -τος, L. -tus. Cp.
e.g. Gk. τέταρτος, L. quar-tus, 'fourth'.

## -th
-th, ending of the 3rd pers. sing. pres. indicative.
— See -eth.

## Thaddeus
Thaddeus, masc. PN. — L. Thaddaeus, fr. Gk.
Θαδδαϊος, fr. Talmudic Heb. Tadddy, a name
prob. derived fr. Aram. tldhayya (pi.), 'breasts',
which is rel. to Heb. shadh (dual shddhdyim),
Arab, thady, 'breast'.

## thakoor
thakoor, п., lord, master (a term of respect). —
Hind, fhakur, fr. OI. thakkurah, 'chief, man of
rank; idol'; prob. of поп-Aryan origin.

## thalamo-
thalamo-, before a vowel thalam-, combining
form for thalamus (anat.) — Gk. θάλαμο-,
θαλαμ-, fr. θάλαμος. See next word.

## thalamus
thalamus, п., paTt of the brain from which a
nerve emerges (anat.) — L., fr. Gk. θάλαμος,
'inner chamber', which is rel. to θαλάμη, 'den,
lair', stands in gradational relationship to
θόλος, 'vault, vaulted building', and is cogn.
with OSlav. dolu, 'hole, ditch, valley', Goth, dal,
OE. dsel, 'valley'. See dale, 'valley', and cp.
epithalamium, ophthalmo-.
Derivative: thalam-ic, adj.

## thalass-
thalass-, form of thalasso- before a vowel.

## thalassian
thalassian, adj., pertaining to the sea. — Formed
with suff. -an fr. Gk. θαλάσσιος, 'of the sea', fr.
θάλασσα, 'sea'; cp. Macedonian δαλάγχαν
(ace), 'sea', a word glossed by Hesychius; prob.
of pre-Greek origin.
Derivative: thalassian, п., sea turtle.

## thalassic
thalassic, adj., pertaining to the sea. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ic ft. Gk. θάλασσα, 'sea'. See
prec. word.

## thalasso-
thalasso-, before a vowel thalass-, combining
form denoting the sea. — Gk. θαλασσο-, θα-
λασσ-, fr. θάλασσα. See thalassian.

## thalatto-
thalatto-, before a vowel' thalatt-, combining
form identical in meaning with the prec. word.
— Att. Gk. θαλαττο-, θαλαττ-, fr. θάλαττα,
which corresponds to Gk. θάλασσα. See
thalasso-,

## thalenite
thalenite, п., an yttrium silicate (mineral.) —
Named after the Swedish physicist T. R. Thalin
(1827-1905). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## thaler
thaler, п., an old German silver coin. — G.
Thaler, former spelling of Taler. See taler.

## Thalia
Thalia, п., the Muse of comedy (Greek mythol.)
— L. Thalia, fr. Gk. Θάλεια, lit. 'the blooming
one', rel to θαλίά, 'abundance', θάλος, 'scion,
child', θαλλός, 'young shoot, green stalk,
young branch; branch', θαλεΐν, 'to bloom',
θαλερός, 'blooming, fresh', and cogh. with
Arm. dalar, 'green, fresh; verdure', Alb. dal'
(aor. doia), Ί sprout'. Cp. thallium, thalio-,
thallus. Cp also tethelin.

## Thalia
Thalia, п., a genus of plants of the arrowroot
family (bot.) — ModL., named after Johann
Thai, a German physician of the 16th century.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:784 COLUMN:3 -->
For the ending see 1 st suff. -ia.

## Thailctrum
Thailctrum, п., a genus of plants, the meadow
rue (bot.) — L., 'meadow rue', fr. Gk. θάλικ-
τρον, of s.m.

## thall-
thall-, thalli-, thalio-, combining form for 1)
thallus; 2) thallium. — Fr. Gk. θαλλός, 'young
shoot; green branch'. See Thalia, 'the Muse of
comedy'.

## thalline
thalline, adj., pertaining to a thallus. — Formed
fr. thallus with adj. suff. -ine.

## thallium
thallium, п., name of a rare metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., fr. Gk. θαλλός, 'young
shoot, green branch'; so called in 1861 by Sir
William Crookes (1832-1919), the discoverer of
this element, from the green line in its spectrum.
See Thalia, 'the Muse of comedy'.
Derivative: thall-ic, adj.

## thalloid
thalloid, adj., resembling a thallus. —
Compounded of thallus and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid,

## Thailophyta
Thailophyta, п., a division of plants (bot.) —
ModL., compounded of Gk. θαλλός, 'young
shoot', and φυτόν, 'plant'. See thallus and
-phyte.

## thailous
thailous, adj., pertaining to thallium. — See
thallium and -ous.

## thallus
thallus, п., vegetable tissue (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Gk. θαλλός, 'young shoot'. See Thalia, 'the
Muse of comedy'.

## thalweg
thalweg, п., the line that follows the bottom of a
valley (phys. geogr.) — G. (now spelled Talweg),
lit. 'dale way'. See dale and way.

## thamn-
thamn-, form of thamno- before a vowel.

## Thamnidium
Thamnidium, п., a genus of molds (bot.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idium fr. Gk.
θάμνος, 'bush, shrub', which stands in
gradational relationship to θημών, 'heap', from the stem
of τιθέναι, 'to put, place', whence also θέμα,
'anything laid down, deposit', θέσις, 'a placing,
setting'. See theme and cp. next word, the first
element in thamnria and the second element in
Chrysothamnus.

## thamno-
thamno-, before a vowel thamn-, combining form
meaning 'shrub'. — Gk. θάμνο-, θαμν-, fr.
θάμνος, 'bush, shrub'. See prec. word.

## thamuria
thamuria, п., frequency of urination (med.) —
Medical L-, formed fr. Gk. θαμά, 'often', and
οδρον, 'urine'. The first element is rel. to
Homeric Gk. θαμέες, fem. θαμειαί (pi.),
'crowded, close-set', Gk. θαμίζειν, 'to come often',
θαμνός, 'bush, shrub". See Thamnidium. For
the second element see -uria.

## than
than, conj. — ME. thanne, than, thenne, then, fr.
OE. ponne, pon, panne, 'then, than' ('than'
represents a sense development of later date);
orig. identical with then (q.v.)

## thana
thana, also tana, п., a police station (India). —
Hind, thana, thana, fr. OI. sthana-, "a place of
standing, a post', fr. I.-E. base *st(h)a-, 'to
stand', whence also Gk. Εστημί (for *σί-στημι),
Ί cause to stand, I place', L. sto, stare, 'to
stand'. See state and cp. words there referred
to.

## thanadar
thanadar, п., the chief of a police station (India).
— Hind, thanadar, lit. 'holder of a police
station', fr. Hind, thana, 'police station', and Pers.
