Tom, masc. PN.; (not cap.) the male of certain
animals — Dimin. of Thomas. Cp. tommy.

## tomahawk
tomahawk, п., a light ax used by North American
Indians. — Of Algonquian origin; cp. Virginian
tomahak. The word literally means 'that which
is for cutting'.
Derivative: tomahawk, tr. v.

## tomalley
tomalley, п., the liver of a lobster. — Prob. of
Caribbean origin.

## toman
toman, п., a Persian gold coin. — Pers. tumdn, fr.
Turki tuman, 'ten thousand*.

## tomatidine
tomatidine, п., a substance obtained from the
tomato plant (chem.) — Formed fr. tomato
with suff. -idine.

## tomatine
tomatine, п., an antibiotic made from the tomato
plant (chem. and pharm.) — Formed fr. tomato
with chem. sufF. -ine.

## tomato
tomato, n. — Fr. earlier tomate, fr. Sp. tomate, fr.
Nahuatl tomatl, lit. 'the swelling fruit', fr. to-
mana, 'to swell'. The alteration of tomate into
tomato is prob. due to the influence of potato.

## tomb
tomb, n. — ME. toumbe, tombe, fr. OF. ( = F.)
tombe, fr. Eccles. L. tumba (whence also It.
tomba, F. tombe, Sp. tumba), fr. Gk. τύμβος,
'sepulchral mound, tomb', which is сокп. with
Mir. tomm, 'a small hill*, W. torn, 'mound;
dunghill', L. tumere, 'to swell', tumulus, 'raised
heap of earth', tumor, 'a swelling*, fr. I.-E. base
*tum-, 'to swell'. See tumid and words there
referred to and cp. esp. catacomb.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:797 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: tomb, tr. v., en-tomb, tr. v., tomb-
less, adj.

## tombac
tombac, п., an alloy of copper and zinc, — F.
tombac, fr. Port, tombac, fr. Malay tambaga,
'copper', fr. OI. tdmrakab, of s.m., fr. tdmrah,
'dark-red, coppery', which is rel. to tamas-,
'darkness'. See tamas.

## tombola
tombola, п., lottery. — It., back formation fr.
tombolare, 'to turn a somersault, tumble', rel.
to F. tomber, 'to fall', orig. 'to turn a
somersault*, Sp. tumbar, 'to turn a somersault', tumbo,
'somersault', Port, tombo, Ruman. tumba, of
s.m.; of imitative origin.

## tomboy
tomboy, п., a boisterous girl. — Compounded of
Tom and boy. Cp. next word.
Derivatives: tomboy-ish, adj., tomboy-ish-ly,
adv., tomboy-ish-ness, n.

## tomcat
tomcat, п., a male cat. — Compounded of Tom
and cat.

## tome
tome, п., each of the volumes composing a book;
any book; now, usually, a large book. — F., fr.
L. tomus, fr. Gk. τόμος, 'a cut, a piece cut off,
section, part of a book, volume', which is rel. to
τομός, 'cutting, sharp', τομή, 'a cutting,
cutting off, section', τέμνει, 'to cut', τέμενος,
'sacred enclosure', τμησις, 'a cutting', fr. I.-E.
base *tem-, tm-, 'to cut*, whence also the second
element in OL. aes-tumdre, L. aes-timare, 'to
value, appraise', OSlav. tinq (for *tmno-), tuti,
*to cleave, split*, ORruss. tinu, tjati, 'to strike,
beat*, Mir. tamnaim, Ί cut off'. Cp. acroto-
mous, aim, anatomy, Artamus, atom,
craniotomy, entomology, epitome, esteem, estimate,
Tamias, temenos, temno-, tmesis, -tome, tomium,
Tomistoma, -tomy, trichotomous. Cp. also
tonsure.

## -tome
-tome, combining form used: 1) in the sense of
'part, section'; 2) to name cutting (esp. surgical)
instruments. — Gk. -τομον, fr. τόμος, (a
cutting, a piece cut off'. See prec. word.

## tomentose
tomentose, adj., covered with matted hairs. —
ModL. tomentosus, fr. L. tomentum. See tomen-
tum and adj. suff. -ose.

## tomentous
tomentous, adj., tomentose. — Seeprec. word and
-ous.

## tomentum
tomentum, п., a covering of matted hairs (bot.) —
L. tomentum, 'stuffing for cushions', of uncertain
origin. It possibly stands for *towementom and is
rel. to tumere, 'to swell'. See tumid and cp. total,

## tomfool
tomfool, п., a foolish person. — Compounded of
Tom and fool.
Derivatives: tomfool, adj., foolish, tomfool-ery,
n.

## tomin
tomin, п., 1) a weight; 2) a silver coin in some
countries of South America. — Sp. tomin, fr.
Arab, thumn (in vulgar pronunciation thomn),
'one eiehth\ from the stem of thamanin (masc),
thamdniab (fern.), 'eight', which is rel. to Heb.
sh топе (masc), sh топа' (fem.), Aram.
temane (masc), temdrtyd (fem.), Ugar. Smn
(masc), s'mnt (fem.), Ethiop. samdni (masc-),
samdnitu (fem.), Akkad. samdne (masc), samd-
nit (fem.), 'eight'. (The masc forms are used
with fem. nouns, the fem. ones with masc
nouns.) Cp. Egypt. #mn, 'eight*.

## Tomistoma
Tomistoma, п., a genus of ga vials (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'sharp-mouthed', fr. Gk. τομός,
'cutting, sharp', and στόμα, 'mouth*. The first
element is rel. to τόμος, 'piece cut off, section';
see tome. For the second element see stoma. Cp.
next word and Tomopteris.

## tomium
tomium, п., each of the cutting edges of the bill of
a bird (zool.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τομός, 'cutting,
sharp*. See prec word.

## Tommy
Tommy, п., a British private soldier. — Short for
Tommy Atkins, fr. Thomas Atkins, model name
used in official forms for the use of private
soldiers. — Tommy is dimin. of Tom, which itself
is a dimin. of Thomas.

## Tomopteris
Tomopteris, п., a genus of annelids (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'having the fins cut', fr. Gk. τόμος,
'a cut; a piece cut off', and πτερόυ, 'wing' (used
in the sense of 'fin'). See tome and ptero- and cp.
Tomistoma, tomium.

## tomorrow
tomorrow, adv. and n. — ME. to morgen, to
morwen, fr. OE. to morgenne (fr. to, 'to', and
morgenne, dat. of morgen, 'morning, morrow'),
also (unflected) to morgen. See to, prep., and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:798 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 771 | TOPEE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:798 COLUMN:1 -->
morrow, mom, and cp. today, tonight,

## tompion
tompion, n. — A var. of tampion, tampon.

## Tompion
Tompion, п., a watch made by, or resembling,
that made by Thomas Tompion (1639-1713).

## tomtit
tomtit, п., the titmouse. — Compounded of torn
and tit, 'a small bird'. Cp. titmouse.

## tom-tom
tom-tom, n. — A var. of tam-tam.
Derivative: tom-tom, intr. and tr. v.

## -tomy
-tomy, combining form meaning 'a cutting', as in
anatomy, arteriotomy — Gk. -τομία, 'a cutting
of", fr. τομή, 'a cutting, section'. See tome and
cp. -tome.

## ton
ton, п., a large weight. — ME. tonne, tunne, fr.
OE. tunne, 'a large cask', rel. to ON. tunna,
OFris., MLG., MDu, tunne, tonne (Du. ton),
OHG. tunna (MHG. tunne, G. Tonne), 'tun,
ton', fr. ML. tunna, 'tun', which is prob. of
Gaulish origin. Cp. tonneau, tun, tunnel.

## ton
ton, п., style, fashion. — F. ton, fr. L. tonus,
'sound, tone'. See tone.

## tonal
tonal, adj. — ML. tonalis, fr. L. tonus. See tone
and adj. surf, -al

## tonality
tonality, n. — F. tonalite, fr. tonal, fr. ML.
tonalis. See prec. word and -ity

## tondo
tondo, п., a circular painting. — It., aphetic for
rotondo, 'round', fr. L. rotundus. See rotund

## tone
tone, n. — F. ton, fr. L. tonus, 'sound, tone', fr.
Gk. τόνος, 'that which is stretched, a stretching,
a straining, pitch of the voice, musical note', in
gradational relationship to τείνειν (for *τέν-
ιειν), 'to stretch, strain', fr. I.-E. base "ten-,
*ton-, 'to stretch', whence also L. tenuis, 'thin,
fine', tendere, 'to stretch, extend'. See tend, 'to
move in a certain direction', and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also ton, 'style', atonic,
barytone, detonate. Intonate, intone, monotonous,
oxytone, pretone, syntony, tritone
Derivatives: tone, v., ton-ed, adj., ton-er, п.,
tone-less, adj., tone-less-ly, adv., tone-less-ness,
п., tonic (q.v.)

## tong
tong, п., a Chinese secret society. — Chin, t'ong,
'hall'.

## tong
tong, tr. and intr. v., to seize with tongs. — Back
formation fr. tongs.

## tonga
tonga, п., a light two-wheeled carriage. — Hind.
tdngd.

## tongs
tongs, n. pi. — ME. tange, tonge, fr. OE. tang,
tange, rel. to OS. tanga, ON. tong, Dan. tang,
Swed. tang, OFris. tange, MDu. tanghe, Du.
tang, OHG. zanga, MHG., G. zange, lit. 'that
which bites' (cp. OHG. zangar, 'biting, sharp'),
fr. I.-E. base *denk-, 'to bite', whence also OI.
dasati, 'biter' (for *dnketi), 'bites', Gk. δάκνειν,
'to bite', δάξ, 'biting', δήγμα, 'a biting', Alb.
done, 'tongs'. For sense development cp. F.
mordache, 'tongs', fr. mordre, 'to bite'. Cp.
Dacus and the second element in Demodex,
Mixodectes, Tridacna

## tongue
tongue, n. — ME. tunge, tange, fr. OE. tunge, rel.
to OS., ΟΝ., Swed. tunga, Dan., OFris. tunge,
MDu. tonghe, Du. tong, OHG. zunga, MHG.,
G. zunge, Goth, tuggo, and cogu. with OL. din-
gua, Toch. A kdntu, В kantwa (both metathes-
ized fr. orig. 'tank-), 'tongue'. For the change
of OL. dingua to L. lingua see lingual. The -и- in
tongue is due to the influence of F. langue,
'tongue' (fr. L. lingua). Cp. tang, 'spike', and
the second element in biltong
Derivatives: tongue, tr. and intr. v., tongu-ed,
adj., tongue-less, adj. tongu-er, tongue-ing, п.,
tongue-y, tongu-y, adj.

## tongue-tie
tongue-tie, tr. v. — Back formation fr. tongne-
tied

## tongue-tied
tongue-tied, adj. — Compounded of tongne and
pp. of the verb tie

## tonic
tonic, adj., 1) pertaining to tones; 2) having an
invigorating effect. — F. tonique, fr. Gk.
τονικός, 'of or for stretching; of or for tones'
(whence also ModL. tonicus), lit. 'that which
stretches', fr. τόνος. See tone and adj. suff. -ic
and cp. atonic, diatonic, isotonic
Derivatives: tonic, n. (q.v.), tonic-al-ly, adv.,
tonic-ity, n.

## tonic
tonic, п., 1) anything that invigorates; specifically,
an invigorating medicine; 2) in music, the first
tone of the scale. — F. tonique, fr. Gk. τονικός.
See tonic, adj.

## tonic sol-fa
tonic sol-fa, a system of teaching music based on

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:798 COLUMN:2 -->
tonality. — See sol-fa.

## tonight
tonight, adv. and n. — ME. to niht, to night, fr.
OE. to niht. See to and night and cp. today,
tomorrow.

## tonite
tonite, п., an explosive used in blasting. — Formed
(as if fr. L. 'tonitus) fr. L. tondre, 'to thunder'.
See thunder, п., and subst. surf. -ite.

## tonitruous
tonitruous, adj., thundering. — Formed with suff.
-ous fr. L. tonitrus, 'thunder', fr. tondre. See
prec. word.

## tonjon
tonjon, also tomjon, п., a kind of sedan or
portable chair used in Ceylon. — Hind, tdm-jhdm.
tonka bean. — Fr. Negro name in Guiana.

## tonnage
tonnage, n. — Formed fr. ton, 'weight', with surf.
-age.

## tooneau
tooneau, п., rear part of a motor-car with seats
for passengers. — F., lit. 'cask', dimin. of
tonne, 'tun'. See ton, 'a weight', and cp.
tunnel.

## tono-
tono-, combining form meaning 'tension; tone'.
— Gk. τόνο-, fr. τόνος, 'a stretching'. See
tone.

## tonometer
tonometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
pitch of tones. — Compounded of tono- and
Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## tonsil
tonsil, n. — F. tonsille, fr. L. tonsillae (pi.),
'tonsils', dimin. of tales (for *tonsles), 'goiter',
which is of uncertain, possibly Gaulish, origin.
Derivatives: tonsiil-ar, tonsill-itic, adjs.,
tonsillitis (q.v.)

## tonsill-
tonsill-, form of tonsillo- before a vowel.

## tonsillectomy
tonsillectomy, п., removal of the tonsils by
surgery (med.) — A Medical Latin hybrid coined
fr. L. tonsillae (see tonsil) and Gk. -έκτομίδ, 'a
cutting out of; see -ectomy. The correct form is
amygdalectomy, fr. Gk. αμυγδαλή, 'almond',
used in the sense of 'tonsil' (see amygdala), and
-έκτομία, 'a cutting out of.

## tonsillitis
tonsillitis, п., inflammation of the tonsils {med.)
— A Medical Latin hybrid coined fr. L.
tonsillae (see tonsil) and -itis, a suff. of Greek
origin. The correct form is amygdalitis (see prec.
word).

## tonsillo-
tonsillo-, before a vowel tonsill-, combining form
meaning 'pertaining to the tonsils'. — See tonsil.

## tonsorial
tonsorial, adj., pertaining to a barber or his work.
Formed With adj. suff. -al fr. L. tonsorius,
'pertaining to shearing', fr. tonsor, gen. -oris,
'shearer, barber', fr. tonsus, pp. of tondere, 'to shear*.
See tonsure.

## tonsurate
tonsurate, п., the state of one who received the
ecclesiastical tonsure. — ML. tonsurdtus, fr. L.
tonsura, 'a shearing'. See tonsure and subst.
suff. -ate.

## tonsure
tonsure, п., 1) the act of shaving of the head; 2)
the part of the head so shaven. — L. tonsura, 'a
shearing, clipping', fr. tonsus, pp. of tondere, 'to
shear, .clip', which stands in gradational
relationship to Gk. τένδειν, 'to gnaw', Mir. ro-s-
teind, 'he cut off', temm (for *tend-men), W.,
Co. tarn (for *tnds-men), 'morsel, bit', Ir. and
W. tonn, 'skin', fr. I.-E. 'tend-, *tond-,
enlargement of base 'tern-, 'to cut', whence Gk. τέμ-
νειν, 'to cut'. See tome and cp. toison. For the
ending see suff. -ure.
Derivatives: tonsure, tr. v., tonsur-ed, adj.

## tontine
tontine, п., annuity shared by a number of
persons, so that the last survivor obtains the entire
amount. — F., fr. It. tontina, short for polizza
Tontina; named after Lorenzo Tonti, a
Neapolitan banker in Paris (died in 1695), who invented
this scheme. For the ending see 3rd suff. -ine.
Derivatives: tontine, adj., tontin-er, n.

## tonus
tonus, п., ]) tonicity; tonic spasm. — L. tonus, 'a
sound, tone'. See tone.

## tony
tony, adj., high-toned (slang). — Formed fr. tone
with adj. suff. -y.

## too
too, adv. — ME. to, too, fr. OE. to, adv.,
identical with to, prep. See to and cp. G. zu, which
also unites the meanings to and too.

## took
took, past tense of take. — ME. tok, fr. Late OE.
toe, past tense of tacan. See take.

## tool
tool, n. — ME. tol, tool, fr. OE. tol, rel. to ON.
tol (pi.), 'tools'; formed with instrumental suff.
-I from the base appearing in OE. tawian, 'to
prepare'; see tuw, 'to prepare'. For the suff. cp.
shovel (ft. shove).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:798 COLUMN:3 -->
Derivatives: tool, tr. and intr. v., tool-er, п.,
tool-ing, n.

## toom
toom, adj., empty (chiefly Scot.) — ME. torn, fr.
OE. torn, in gradational relationship to teem,
'to pour out'.

## toon
toon, п., an East Indian tree, the Indian
mahogany. — Hind, tun, fr. OI. tunnah.

## toot
toot, intr. v., to blow a horn. — Of imitative
origin; cp. Du. tuiten, toeten, G. tuten. Cp. also
tootie.
Derivative: toot, п., the sound of tooting.

## tooth
tooth, n. — ME. toth, tooth, fr. OE. top, rel. to
OS., Dan., Swed., MLG., Du. tand, ON. tonn,
OFris. toth, OHG. zand, zan, MHG. zant, zan,
G. Zahn, Goth, tunpus, 'tooth', OE. tusc (for
*tunpska-), 'tusk', and cogn. with OI. dan, gen.
datdh. Arm. atamn, Gk. οδών, gen. οδόντος, L.
dens (gen. dentis), Lith. dantls, OPruss. dantis,
Olr. dit, OCo. dans, W., Bret, dant, 'tooth'. All
these words are prob. pres. participles fr. I.-E.
base *ed-, 'to eat', and orig. meant 'that which
eats'. See eat and -ent, -ant, and cp. teethe. Cp.
also anodyne, Bidens, bldent, dancetty,
dandelion, dental, Dentaria. dentl- dentifrice, dentist,
dentition, denture, Edentata, Gymnodontes,
indent, mastodon, odonto-, -odus, redan, Synodon-
tidae, trident, tusk.
Derivatives: tooth, tr. and intr. v., tooth-ed,
adj., tooth-er, п., tooth-ful, adj., tooth-ing, п.,
tooth-less, adj., tooth-less-ly, adv., tooth-less-
ness, n.

## tootle
tootle, intr. v., to toot repeatedly. — Formed fr.
toot with freq. suff. -Ie.
Derivative: tootle, n.

## top
top, п., the highest part of anything, summit. —
ME., fr. OE., related to ON. toppr, 'tuft of hair',
OFris. top, 'tuft', ODu. topp, Du. top, 'top',
OHG., MHG. zopf, 'end, tip, tuft of hair', G.
Zopf, 'tuft of hair', Cp. tuft, toupee. Cp. also
topple.
Derivatives: top, adj. and tr. v., top-less, adj.,
topp-ed, adj., topp-er, п., topp-ing, adj., lopp-
ing-ly, adv., topp-ing-ness, n.

## top
top, п., child's toy. — ME. top, fr. OE. top, back
formation fr. OF. topet (cp. OF. topoie, F.
toupie), of s.m., fr. ODu. topp, 'head or top of
something', which is rel. to OE. top, 'summit';
see prec. word. Cp. OHG. doph, top/, 'top (for
spinning)' (whence MHG., dial. G. top/, of
s.m.), which is an OF. loan word.

## top-
top-, form of topo- before a vowel.

## toparch
toparch, п., ruler of a petty state. — Late L. to-
parcha, fr. Gk. τοπάρχης, 'governor of a
district', lit. 'ruler over a place', fr. τόπος, 'place',
and -άρχης, 'ruler'. See topo- and -arch.

## toparchy
toparchy, п., a petty state. — L. toparchia, fr. Gk.
τοπαρχία, 'district governed by a τοπάρχης'.
See prec. word and -y (representing Gk. -ία).
Derivative: toparch-ical, adj.

## topass
topass, also topas, topaz, п., an Indo-Portuguese
half-caste of Christian faith; a soldier of this
class (History of India). — Of uncertain origin.

## topaz
topaz, п., a colored crystalline gem. — ME.
topas, topace, fr. OF. (= F.) topaze, fr. L. topa-
zus, fr. Gk. τάπαζος, 'topaz', which is prob.
cognate with OI. tapas, 'heat, fire', tapati,
"warms, heats, burns', L. tepere, 'to be warm or
Iukeworm', tepidus, 'warm, lukewarm'. See
tepid and cp. tapas.

## tope
tope, п., a mound containing a Buddhist shrine,
stupa. — Hind, top, prob. fr. Prakrit or Pali
thupo, fr. OI. stupah, 'tope, stupa'. See stnpa.

## tope
tope, п., a small shark. — Of uncertain origin.

## tope
tope, intr. v., to drink alcoholic liquor to excess;
tr. v., to drink (alcoholic liquor) to excess. —
F. toper, 'to strike (the hands at the conclusion
of a bargain)', whence derived the meanings 'to
drink at the conclusion of a bargain; to drink to
excess'. For sense development cp. swap. F.
toper is borrowed fr. Sp. topar, 'to strike against',
which is of imitative origin. (Sp. tope, 'top;
butt', derives fr. topar.) The usual derivation of
Sp. topar fr. tope, 'top, butt', fr. OF. top, a
word of Teut. origin (see top, 'summit'), is
justly rejected by Bloch-Wartburg, DELF., p.
608.

## tope
tope, п., a grove (India). — Tamil toppu.

## topee
topee, q. — See topi.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:799 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TOPEEWALAH | 772 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:799 COLUMN:1 -->

## topeewalah
topeewalah, η. — See topiwallah.

## topek
topek, n. — See tupek.

## toper
toper, п., one who topes; a drunkard. — Formed
fr. tope, 'to drink to excess', with agential suff.
-er.

## toph
toph, п., a small drum (music). — Heb. toph,
'timbrel, tambourine*, rel. to Aram, tuppd, of
s.m., Arab, duff, 'drum'; of imitative origin.

## Tophet
Tophet, Topheth, п., a place in the valley of Hin-
nom, south of Jerusalem, where children were
sacrificed to Moloch (Bible). — Heb. Topheth,
prob. formed from orig. *T phdth, the vowels of
which have been assimilated to those of
unrelated topheth, 'spitting', and of bosheth, 'shame'.
TOpheth prob. meant orig. 'fireplace' (i.e. place
where children were burned), and is rel. to
Aram. tephayd, 'tripod*, Syr. tephayyd,
'cooking stove', Arab, uthjiya , 'one of three stones
supporting a kettle'.

## tophus
tophus, п., calcareous concretion round the joints,
the teeth, etc., — L., 'tufa'. See tufa.

## topi
topi, topee, п., a hat, esp. one made of sola pith
(India) — Hind. topi.

## topiary
topiary, п., the art of cutting trees into
ornamental shapes, etc. — L. topidrius, 'pertaining to
ornamental gardening', fr. topia, gen. -drum,
'landscape painting; ornamental gardening', fr. Gk.
τόπια, pi. of τόπιον, dimin. of τόπος, 'place'.
See next word and adj. surf. -ary.
Derivatives: topiari-an, adj., topiar-ist, n.

## topic
topic, п., subject. — L. topica, fr. Gk. τά τοπικά,
title of a work by Aristotle on rhetoric, lit.
meaning 'things pertaining to commonplaces', prop,
neut. pi. of τοπικός, 'of a place, in respect to a
place', fr. τόπος, 'place', fr. I.-E. base *top-, 'to
arrive somewhere, reach a place', whence also
Lith. tapti, 'to become', pri-tapti, 'to meet with',
Lett, tapt, 'to become, arrive', pa-tapt, 'to
arrive*, OE. pafian, 'to consent, permit, tolerate',
lit. 'to give room to yield'. Cp. atopic, ectopia,
Ectoplstes, isotope, Utopia.

## topiwallah
topiwallah, also topeewalah, п., 1) a European;
2) a topass (Anglo-Indian). — Hind, topi-wdla,
lit. 'a hat man', i.e. 'a man wearing a hat'. See
topi and wallah.

## topo- before a vowel top-
topo- before a vowel top-, combining form
meaning 'place*. — Gk. τόπο-, τοπ-, fr. τόπος,
'place*. See topic.

## topographer
topographer, п., one who describes a place. —
Gk. τοπογράφος, compounded of τόπος, 'place',
and -γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write1. See topic
and -grapher.

## topographic
topographic, adj., pertaining to topography. —
Gk. τοπογραφικός, fr. τοπογραφία. See next
word and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivatives: topograpkic-al, adj., topographic-
al-ly, adv.

## topography
topography, п., description of a place. — ME.
topographies fr. Late L. topographia, fr. Gk.
τοπογραφία, 'description of a place', fr.
τοπογράφος. See topographer and -y (representing
Gk.-iS).
Derivatives: topographic (q.v.), topograpk-ist, n.

## topology
topology, п., study of the topography of a place.
— Lit. 'study of a place', fr. Gk. τόπος, 'place',
and -λογία, fr. -λόγος 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See topo- and -logy.
Derivatives: topolog-ic, topolog-ic-al, adjs.

## toponym
toponym, п., name of a place. — Compounded of
τόπος, 'place', and δνυμα, dialectal form of
όνομα, 'name'. See topic, п., and name and cp.
onomato-. Cp. also antonym, homonym,
synonym.

## toponymies
toponymies, п., the study of place names. — See
prec. word and -ics.

## toponymy
toponymy, п., place names of a region;
toponymies. — See toponym and -y (representing Gk.
-la).
Derivatives: toponym-ic, toponym-ic-al, adjs.

## topple
topple, intr. and tr. v. — Formed with freq. suff.
-le, fr. top, 'to tip'. See top, 'summit'.
Derivative: toppl-er, n.

## topsy-turvy
topsy-turvy, adv. — Fr. earlier topsy-tervy, for
top-so-tervy, lit. 'top as (if) turvy', i.e. 'as if the
top were overturned'. For the first element see
top, 'summit', for the second element see so. The
third element derives fr. ME. terven, tirven, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:799 COLUMN:2 -->
wallow, roll', which is rel. to OE. tearflian, 'to
roll, overturn', LG. tarven, 'to roll up a cuff',
OHG. zerben, umbi-zerben, 'to turn round'. For
a similar alteration of the adverb so cp. upside
down.
Derivatives: topsy-turvy, adj. and tr. v., topsy-
turvy-dom, n.

## -topy
-topy, combining form meaning 'position'. —
Gk. -τοπία, fr. τόπος, 'place'. See topic, п., and
cp. topo-,

## toque
toque, п., 1) a kind of round hat; 2) the bonnet
monkey. — F., fr. Sp. toca, fr. Arab. tdqiyah,
'skull cap'. Cp. tuque.

## tor
tor, п., a high, rocky hill. — ME. torre, tor, fr.
OE. torr, 'tower, rock', fr. L. turris, 'tower'.
See tower.

## -tor
-tor, masculine agential suff. — L., cogn. with
Gk. -τωρ, -τηρ, ΟΙ. -tar; ср. the suff. in
Mentor. The corresponding fem. suff· is -trix (q.v.)
Cp. -ator.

## Torah
Torah, Тога, п., the Bible; specif, the
Pentateuch. — Heb. torah, lit. 'direction, instruction,
teaching, law', verbal noun of kora , 'he pointed
out, showed, directed, instructed, taught'
(Hiph'il of stem y-r-k); prob. rel. to Arab.
rawd, 'he handed down' (see Barth, Etymolo-
gische Studien, p. 13 f.). Aram, oraythd and
Ethiop. orit, 'Torah', are loan words fr. Heb.
tordh. Cp. Sepher Torah.

## toran
toran, torana, п., gateway to a Buddhist temple
(India). — Ol. toranam, 'arch, arched' gateway*,
of uncertain etymology. Toch. A turdm, 'arch,
gateway arch', is borrowed fr. OI.

## torbanite
torbanite, п., a kind of brown shale. — Named
after Torbane Hill in Scotland. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## torbernite
torbernite, п., uranium copper phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after the Swedish chemist Tor·
bern Bergman (1735-84). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## torch
torch, n. — ME., fr. OF. torche, rag, wisp', orig.
meaning 'anything twisted', esp. 'twist of straw
or hay* (this latter meaning of the word still
exists in Modern French), fr. VL. *torca, fr.
Late L. torque (used by Varro), corresponding
to Classical L. torques or torquis, 'twisted
collar', fr. torquere, 'to twist, wind'. See torque and
cp. words there referred to. Cp. also torchon
lace.
Derivatives: torch, tr. v., torch-er, n.

## torchon lace
torchon lace, a strong bobbin lace made of coarse
linen thread. — F., 'dishcloth, duster', formed
with dimin. suif. -on fr. torche. See torch,

## torcular
torcular, п., also torcular Η его ph Hi, tourniquet
(anat.) — L. torcular (HerophUX), lit. 'press (of
Herophilus)', fr. torcular, 'a press for making
wine or oil*, fr. torculum, of s.m., a dimin.
formed fr. torquere, 'to turn, twist', See torque
and cp. words there referred to.

## tore
tore, п., torus (archit.) — F., fr. L. torus. See
torus.

## tore
tore, past tense and dial. pp. of tear. — ME. pp.
tore(n). Cp. ME. tart fr. OE. txr, past tense of
teran, 'to tear*. See tear, v., and cp. torn.

## toreador
toreador, п., a bullfighter. — Sp., fr. torear, 'to
fight bulls', fr. toro, 'bull', fr. L. tfiurus. See
Taurus and cp. next word.

## torero
torero, п., a bullfighter on foot. — Sp.,
bullfighter', prop, the adjective torero, 'pertaining
to bulls', used as a noun, fr. toro. See prec.
word.

## toreutic
toreutic, adj., pertaining to chased work. — Gk.
τορευτικός, 'of metal work', fr. τορευτός,
'worked in relief, chased', verbal adj. of τορεύ-
etv, 'to work in relief, bore through*, fr. το-
ρεύς,'sculptor's graving tool',fr. τόρος, *chisel·*,
which stands in gradational relationship to τεί-
ρειν (for *τέρ^ειν), 'to rub\ τέρετρον, 'borer*,
τερηδών, 'a worm that "gnaws wood', prop. *a
boring worm', fr. I.-E. base *ter-, 'to rub,
pierce, turn'. See throw and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.

## torfaceous
torfaceous, adj., growing in bogs (rare). — A
hybrid coined fr. ON. torf. 'peat' (see turf), and
-aceous, a suff. of Latin origin.

## torii
torii, п., sing, and pi., gateway to a Shin to temple.
— Jap.

## Torilis
Torilis, п., a genus of plants of the carrot family

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:799 COLUMN:3 -->
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. torus, 'cushion, couch',
which prob. stands for *storus and is related to
sternere, 'to spread out*. See stratum and cp.
words therereferred to. For the dropping of an
initial s before t cp. L. locus, 'place*, from
stlocus (see locus).

## torment
torment, п., ]) orig. an instrument of torture;
torture; 2) a great pain. — ME., fr. OE. torment,
tourment (F. tourment), fr. L. tormentum, 'an
instrument with which anything is turned or
twisted; an instrument for hurling missiles; an
instrument of torture; torture, pain', which
stands for *torqu-mentom, fr. torquere, 'to
twist'. See torque and cp. words there referred to.
Cp. also tormcntiJ. For the ending see suff.
-ment,

## torment
torment, tr. v. — ME. tormenten, fr. OF. tormen-
ter, tourmenter (F. tourmenter), fr. torment,
tourment. See torment, n.
Derivatives: torment-ed, adj., torment-ed-ly,
adv., torment-ing, adj., torment-ing-ly, adv.,
tormentor (q.v.)

## tormentil
tormentil, п., name of a plant of the genus Poten-
tilla. — F. tormentille, fr. Medical L. tormentilla,
fr. L. tormentum, 'pain' (see torment, п.); so
called because it is supposed to relieve pain, esp.
toothache.

## tormentor
tormentor, n. — ME., fr. AF. tormenteour, tor-
mentour, corresponding to OF. tormenteor, fr. L.
*tormentdtorem, ace. of *tormentdtor, fr.
tormentum. See torment, п., and agential suff.
-or.

## tormentress
tormentress, n. — See prec. word and 1st -ess.

## tormina
tormina, n. pi., gripes of the bowels, colic (med.)
— L-, pi. of *tormen, for *torqu-men, fr.
torquere, *to twist'. See torque and -men.

## torn
torn, pp. of tear. — ME. toren, torn, fr. OE. ge-
toren, pp. of teran. See tear, v., and cp. tore, v.

## tornado
tornado, п., I) a violent storm; 2) whirlwind,
hurricane. — Sp. tronada, 'thunderstorm', fr. tro-
nar, 'to thunder', fr. L. tondre, 'to thunder';
influenced in form by Sp. tornado, pp. of tornar,
'to turn* (fr. L. tornare, 'to turn in a lathe, to
turn, polish, fashion'). See thunder, n.
Derivative: tornad-ic, adj-

## tornaria
tornaria, п., larva of the Balanoglossus (zaol.) —
ModL. tornuria,\ fr. L. tornare, 'to turn', fr.
tornus, 'turner's wheel', fr. Gk. τόρνος, of s.m.,
which is rel. to τορεύειν, 'to bore through'. See
toreutic.

## toro
toro, п., ]) a bull; 2) a cowflsh. — Sp., 'bull', fr.
L. taurus. See Taurns and cp. toreador, torero.

## toronja
toronja, п., the grapefruit. — Sp., fr. Arab, tiirun-
jah (in vulgar pronunciation toronja), fr. Pers.
turundj. Cp. ethrog.

## torose
torose, adj., bulging, knobbed. — L. torosus, 'full
of muscles, brawny', fr. torus, 'boss, knot, bulge,
muscle'. See torus and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: toros-ity, n.

## torous
torous, adj., torose. — See prec. word and -ous.

## torpedinous
torpedinous, adj., resembling a torpedo. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. torpedo, gen. tor-
pedinis. See next word.

## torpedo
torpedo, п., 1) a fish allied to, the rays; 2) a
destructive engine. — L. torpedo, gen. torpedinis,
'numbness; crampfish', fr. torpire, 'to be numb, to be
torpid, to be sluggish; to be stupefied', which is
cogn. with Lith. tirpstu, tifpti, 'to become rigid',
OSlav. u-trupeti, of s.m., and possibly also with
Gk. στέρφνιος (Hesychius), 'stiff, rigid', OE.
steorfan, etc., 'to die'. See starve and cp. next
word.

## torpid
torpid, adj., ]) numb; sluggish; 2) inactive; dull;
lethargic. — L. torpidus, 'benumbed, stupefied',
fr. torpire. See prec. word.
Derivatives: torpid, n. (q.v.), torpid-ity, п.,
torpid-ly, adv., torpid-ness, n.

## torpid
torpid, п., usually torpids, boat races at Oxford in
Lent term. — See torpid, adj.; so called
humorously with reference to their supposed
sluggishness.

## torpify
torpify, tr. v., to make torpid. — Formed from
the stem of L. torpere, 'to be numb', and -ficdre,
fr. L. facere, 'to make, do*. See torpedo and
-fy.

## torpor
torpor, n. — L., 'numbness, stupefaction*, from
the stem of torpere. See torpedo.

## torporiflc
torporiflc, adj., tending to produce torpor. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:800 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 773 | ΤΟΤΕΜ -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:800 COLUMN:1 -->
Formed fr. L. torpor, gen. torporis, 'numbness,
stupefaction', and -ficus, fr. -ficere, unstressed
form of facere, 'to make, do'. See torpor and -flc.

## torquate
torquate, adj., collared; ringed about the neck. —
L. torquatus, 'wearing a neck chain or collar', fr.
torques, 'a twisted neck chain'. See torque and
adj. surf. -ate.

## torqnated
torqnated, adj., wearing a twisted chain. —
Formed from prec. word with 1 st suff. -ed.

## torque
torque, п., ]) a twisted metal necklace worn by
the ancient Gauls, Britons, Germans, etc.; 2)
rotating force. — L. torques, 'twisted neck-chain
necklace', fr. torquere, 'to twist, bend', fr. I.-E.
base 'tereq-, 'to turn, twist', whence also OI.
tarkuh, 'spindle', Gk. άτρακτος, 'spindle;
arrow', Alb. tjef, Ί spin', OSlav. traku, 'band,
girdle', OPruss. tarkue, 'strap, thong', OHG.
drdhsil, 'turner', G. dreckseln, 4o turn on a
lathe', Toch. AB tsark, 'to torment'. Cp. the
collateral base *twereq-, whence OE. pveorh,
'crosswise; perverse', etc. See thwart and cp.
Atractaspis, contort, distort, extort, extricate,
intricate, nasturtium, retort, tart, torch, torcular,
torment, tormina, tornaria, torques, torsade, tor-
sel, torsion, tort, tortilla, Tortrix, Tortulaceae,
tortuous, torture, trica, trousse, trousseau, truss.

## torques
torques, п., I) torque; 2) ring round the neck of
an animal formed by hair, feather etc. (zoo!.) —
L. torques, 'neck chain'. See torque.

## torrefaction
torrefaction, n. — F. torrefaction, fr. L. torrefac-
tus, pp. of torrefacere; see next word and -ion.

## torrefy
torrefy, tr. v., to parch, scorch. — F. torrefier, fr.
L. torrefacere, which is compounded of torrere,
'to parch, roast, scorch', and facere, 'to make,
do'. See torrid and -fy.

## Torrejon formation
Torrejon formation, a Lower Eocene formation
lying between the Wasatch and the Puerco
Formation (geol.) — Lit. 'Turret formation', fr. Sp.
torrejon, 'turret', dimin. of tone, 'tower', fr. L.
turris. See tower.

## torrent
torrent, п., a rapid stream. — F., fr. L. torrentem,
ace. of torrens, gen. torrentis, 'burning, roaring,
boiling; a torrent', prop. pres. part, of torrere,
used as a noun. See torrid and -ent.
Derivatives: lorrent-ial, adj., torrent-ial-ly, adv.

## Torreya
Torreya, п., a genus of trees of the family Taxa-
ceae (bot.) — ModL., named after the American
botanist John Torrey (1796-1873).

## Torricellian
Torricellian, adj., of, pertaining to, or discovered
by, Torricelli. — Formed with suff. -an from the
name of the Italian physicist Evangelista Torri-
cW/i (1608-47).

## torrid
torrid, adj., very hot. — L. torridus, 'parched,
torrid, dried up', fr. torrere, 'to parch', which is
rel. to OL. torrus (for 'tarsus), 'dry', and to L.
terra (for 'tersd-), 'earth', lit. 'dry land'. See
terra and cp. torrent.
Derivatives: torrid-ly, adv., torrid-ity, п., torrid-
ness, n.

## torsade
torsade, п., a twisted cord, an ornament
resembling a twisted cord. — F., formed with suff.
-ade fr. tors, earlier pp. (now = tordu) of tordre,
'to twist', fr. VL. 'torcere, which corresponds
to L. torquere, 'to twist'. See torque and cp. It.
torcere, Sp. torcer, *to twist', which' also derive
fr. VL. 'torcere.

## torse
torse, п., a torso. — See torso.

## torsel
torsel, п., a piece of wood or iron supporting the
end of a beam. — MF. torsel (F. trousseau),
'bundle', dimin. of torce (F. trousse), back
formation fr. trusser, torser (F. trousser), 'to bundle
up, tuck up', which prob. derives fr. VL. 'tor-
dare, 'to twist', freq. of 'torcere (L. torquere),
'to twist, bend'. See torque and cp. torch,
torsade, truss.

## torsion
torsion, п., the act of twisting. — F., fr. Late L.
torsionem, ace. of torsio, a collateral form of
tortio, fr. L. tortus, pp. of torquere, 'to twist,
bend'. See torque and -ion and cp. contortion.
Derivatives: torsion-al, adj., torsion-al-ly, adv.,
torsion-ing, n.

## torsive
torsive, adj., twisted spirally (bot.) — Formed
with suff. -ive, fr. ML. torsus, which corresponds
to L. tortus, pp. of torquere, 'to twist, bend'.

## torsk
torsk, п., the cusk (fish), Brosmius Brosme. —
Swed. and Dan., fr. ON. porskr, whence also
MLG., MDu. dorsch (Du. dors), 'codfish'
(whence G. Dorsch, of s.m.), lit. 'dried (fish)',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:800 COLUMN:2 -->
prob. fr. I.-E. base *ters-, 't£S-, 'dry', whence
also L. terra (for 'tersd), 'earth', lit. 'dry land'.
See terra and cp. words there referred to.

## torso
torso, п., trunk. — It., fr. L. thyrsus, fr. Gk.
&ύρσος, 'a light, straight shaft'. See thyrsus.

## tort
tort, п., a wrongful act (not involving a breach of
contract). — ME., fr. MF-, 'injury' (whence F.
tort, 'injury; wrong'), fr. OF., orig. 'something
twisted', fr. VL. tortum, prop. neut. of L. tortus,
pp. of torquere, 'to twist, bend'. Cp. It. torto,
OProvenc. tort, Sp. tuerto, which are of the same
origin, and see torque. For sense development
ср. Е. wrong, which is rel. to wring.

## torta
torta, п., a large fiat heap of ore. — Sp., 'a round
cake', fr. Late L. torta, of s.m., which is of
uncertain origin. It is prob. not rel. to L. tortus, pp.
of torquere, 'to twist' (see torque). Cp. tart,
tortilla.

## torticollis
torticollis, п., twisted neck caused by contraction
of the muscles or by rheumatism; wryneck. —
Compounded of L. tortum, 'twisted, bent', neut.
pp. of torquere, and of collum, 'neck'. For the
first element see torque and cp. tort, for the
second see collar.

## tortile
tortile, adj., twisted, coiled. — L. tortiiis, 'twisted,
bent', fr. tortus, pp. οι torquere, 'to twist, bend'.
See tort and -He.
Derivative: tortil-ity, n.

## fertility
fertility, n. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. L. tortiiis,
See prec. word.

## tortilla
tortilla, п., a thin fiat cake. — Sp., 'a little cake',
dimin. of torta. See torta.

## tortious
tortious, adj., involving a tort. — ME. See tort
and -ious and cp. tortuous.
Derivative: tortious-ly, adv.

## tortoise
tortoise, п., turtle. — ME. tortuce, fr. MF. ( =
F.) tortues, pi. of tortue, fr. earlier Provenc. tor-
tuga, fr. OProvenc. tartuga, fr. It. tartaruga,
which derives fr. VL. tartaruca, lit. 'the infernal
animal', fr. L. Tartarus; see Tartarus. The
Provenc. form tortuga is due to the influence of
L. tortus, 'twisted'. Folk etymology found in the
name of the animal a reference to its twisted
legs. Cp. turtle, 'tortoise'.

## tortricid
tortricid, adj., pertaining to the Tortricidae. — See
next word.

## Tortricidae
Tortricidae, n. pi., a family of moths (zool.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. Tortrix, gen.
Tortricis. See next word.

## Tortrix
Tortrix, п., a genus of moths (zool.) — ModL.,
formed fr. tortus, 'twisted, bent', pp. of torquere.
See torque and -trix.

## Tortulaceae
Tortulaceae, n. pi., a family of mosses (bot.) —
ModL., formed with suff. -aceae fr. Late L. tor-
tula, 'a small twist or bend', dimin. of torta,
'twist, bend', which is prop. fern. pp. of L.
torquere, 'to twist, bend'. See torque.

## tortuose
tortuose, adj., tortuous. — L. tortuosus. See
tortuous.

## tortuosity
tortuosity, n. — Late L. tortudsitds, fr. L.
tortuosus. See next word and -Ity.

## tortuous
tortuous, adj., I) twisting, winding; 2) not
straightforward. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) tortueux, fr.
OF., fr. L. tortuosus, 'full of turns, tortuous', fr.
tortus, 'twisted, bent', pp. of torquere. See torque
and -ous and cp. tortuose. Cp. also tortious.
Derivatives: tortuous-lyt adv., tortuous-ness,
n.

## torture
torture, n. — F., fr. Late L. tortura, 'a twisting;
torment, torture', fr. L. tortus, pp. of torquere.
See torque and -lire.

## torture
torture, tr. and intr. v. — From torture, n.; cp. F.
torturer, fr. torture.
Derivatives: tortur-able, adj., tortur-able-ness,
п., tortur-ed, adj., tortur-ed-ly, adv., tortur-er,
п., tortur-ing, adj., tortur-ing-ly, adv., torturous
(q.v.)

## torturous
torturous, adj., involving or causing torture. —
ME., fr. MF. tortureux, fr. OF. (= F.) torture,
'torture'. See torture, п., and -ous.
Derivatives: torturous-ly, adv., torturous-ness,
n.

## torula
torula, п., 1) any of certain yeasts; 2) (cap.) a
genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. torulus, 'a
little elevation; muscle, brawn; tuft', dimin. of
torus. See torus and -ule.

## toruliform
toruliform, adj., resembling a torula. —
Compounded of ModL. torula and L. forma, 'form,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:800 COLUMN:3 -->
shape'. See prec. word and form, n.

## torus
torus, п., 1) a round convex molding (archil.); 2)
a protuberance (anat.); 3) receptacle of a flower
(bot.) — L., 'prominence; knot, bulge'; of
uncertain origin. Cp. tore, n.

## torvity
torvity, п., severity. — L. torvitds, fr. torvus,
'severe', which is prob. rel. to trux, gen. trucis,
'savage, cruel, harsh, grim'. See truculent and
-ity.

## torvous
torvous, adj., severe. — Formed with suff. -ous fr.
L. torvus. See prec. word.

## Tory
Tory, n. — Ir. toraidhe, 'robber', lit. 'pursuer',
rel. to Olr. toraht, Gael, toir, 'pursuit'. The
name was orig. used of a class of Irish outlaws
in the 16th and ]7th centuries.
Derivative: Tory-ism, n.

## Tosaphoth
Tosaphoth, n. pi., explanatory and critical glosses
on the Babylonian Talmud (Hebrew literature).
— Heb. tosaphoth, lit. 'additions', pi. of tose-
pheth, fr. hostph, 'he added', Hiph'il or causative
conjugation of yasaph. See next word.

## Tosephta
Tosephta, п., a Tannaitic work containing
teachings not occurring in the Mishnah (Hebrew
literature). — Aram, tosephta, emphatic state of
tosepheth, 'addition', from oseph, the Aph'el
(= causative) conjugation of у saph, 'he added',
which is rel. to Heb. yasaph, 'he added', South
Arab, w-s-ph, Akkad. ujsupu, 'to add'. Cp. prec.
word.

## tosh
tosh, п., rubbish, nonsense (slang). — Of
unknown origin.
Derivative: tosh-y, adj.

## tosher
tosher, п., an unattached student at a university
(University Slang). — Corruption of unattached.

## toss
toss, tr. and intr. v. — Of uncertain origin. Cp.
dial. Norw. and Swed. tossa, 'to spread, strew,
scatter'.
Derivatives: toss, п., toss-er, п., toss-ing, adj.
and п., toss-ing-ly, adv.

## tostamente
tostamente, adv., rapidly (muscial direction). —
It, formed fr. tosta, fem. of tosto, 'rapid', and
adverbial suff. -mente. It. tosto derives ft. L. tos-
tus, 'parched, roasted', which, in Vulgar Latin,
came to be used in the senses 'while it is warm;
at once'; cp. OProvenc., Cat. tost, F. tot, 'early',
and see toast. It. -mente comes fr. L. mente, abl.
of mens, 'mind'. See mind and cp. mental,
'relating to the mind'. Cp. also lentamente, tarda-
mente.

## toston
toston, п., a silver coin formerly used in various
Spanish American countries. — Sp. toston,
assimilated fr. teston, lit. '(coin) bearing a head',
fr. testa, 'head'. See teston.

## tot
tot, п., a little child. — Prob. rel. to ON. tuttr,
nickname for a dwarf, Swed. tutte, 'a little child',
and to the second element in Dan. tommel-tot,
'a little child' (the first element means 'thumb';
see thumb. For the sense development of
tommel-tot ср. Е. Tom Thumb.)

## tot
tot, п., the sum total. — Abbreviation of total.

## total
total, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. ML. totalis,
fr. L. tdtus, 'all, the whole of, entire', which is
of uncertain origin. It possibly stands for
*towetos, and orig. meant 'crammed fully', from
the base seen in tomentum (for *towementom),
'stuffing for cushions', and is rel. to tumere, 'to
swell'. See tumid and words there referred to and
cp. esp. tomentum. Cp. also factotum, surtont,
teetotul, teetotum, totipalmate, tout, tutsan, tutti,
tatti-frutti.
Derivatives: total, n. and tr. and intr. v., totality
(q.v.), total-ize, tr. and intr. v., total-iz-ation, п.,
total-iz-ator, п., total-iz-er, п., total-ly, adv.,
total-ness, n.

## totality
totality, n. — ML. totalitds, 'entirety', fr. totalis.
See prec. word and -ity.
Derivatives: totalit-arian, adj. and п.;
totalitarian-ism, n.

## totara
totara, п., a timber tree, Podocarpus totara. —
Maori.

## tote
tote, tr. v., to carry. — Of uncertain origin.

## tote
tote, п., the total number (colloq.) — Back
formation fr. total.

## totem
totem, п., among primitive peoples, an animal or
a natural object considered as the emblem of a
family or clan. — Of Algonquian origin. Cp.
Ojibway ototeman, 'his relations'.
Derivatives: totem-ic, adj., totem-ic-al-ly, adv.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:801 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TOTHER | 774 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:801 COLUMN:1 -->

## totem-ism
totem-ism, п., totem-ist, п., totem-ist-ic, adj.

## tother
tother, t'other, adj., the other. — ME. the totker,
from misdivision of tket other, that other, 'the
other'; thet or that was orig. the neut. of the def.
art. See the, art., and other,

## totf-
totf-, combining form meaning 'all, whole,
wholly'. — L. toti-, fr. totus. See total.

## totipalmate
totipalmate, adj., having all the toes connected by
a web (zool.) — Compounded of L. totus, 'all'
and palmatus, 'marked with the palm of the
hand'. See total and palmate.

## totter
totter, intr. v. — ME. toteren, totren, prob. of
imitative origin. Cp. dial. Norw. totra, dial.
Swed. tuttra, 'to quiver'. Cp. also toddle.
Derivatives: totter, п., tott-er, п., totter-ing,
adj., totter-ing-ly, adv., totter-ish, adj., totter-y,
adj.

## toty
toty, п., a low-caste laborer (India). — Tamil toti,
lit. 'a digger', ft. tondu, 'to dig'.

## toucan
toucan, п., any of a group of bright-colored birds
of S. America. — F., fr. Port, tucano, ft. Tupi
tuca (with nasal a), which is of imitative origin.

## touch
touch, tr. and intr. v. — ME. tochen, touchen, ft.
OF. tochier, tuchier, touchier (F. toucher), 'to
touch; to strike', ft. VL. *toccare, 'to knock,
strike, rap', which is of imitative origin. VL.
*toccare prop, meant 'to produce the sound
tok'. The primary sense of VL. *toccare is
preserved in OProvenc. tocar, 'to ring the bells',
Sp. tocar, 'to touch, handle; to knock, strike,
rap; to ring the bells', Ruman. toca, 'to toll the
angelus with a clapper'. Cp. toccata, toccatella,
tuck, 'to sound', tncket, tusche and the first
element in tocsin.
Derivatives: touch, n. (q.v.), touch-able, adj.,
touch-able-ness, п., touch-ed, adj., touch-ed-ness,
п., touch-ing, adj. and п., touch-ing-ly, adv.,
touch-ing-ness, n.

## touch
touch, n. — Partly fr. OF. louche (fr. touchier, 'to
touch'), partly fr. touch, v.

## touchy
touchy, adj., 1) irritable; 2) sensitive. — A blend
of techy and touch.
Derivatives: touchi-ly, adv., touchi-ness, n.

## toug
toug, п., a pike with a horse's tail. — F., fr. Turk.
tugh, lit. 'horse's tail'.

## tough
tough, adj. — ME. togh, tough, fr. OE. toh, for
Teut. *tanhi-\ rel. to MLG. te\ge), tu, MDu.
taey, Du. taai, OHG., MHG. zach, OHG. zahi,
MHG. zsehe, G. zah, OE. ge-tenge, 'near,
related; oppressive', OS. Ы-tengi, 'oppressive'.
Derivatives: tough-en, tr. and intr. v., tough-ish,
adj., tough-ly, adv., tough-ness, n.

## toupee
toupee, п., a small patch of artificial hair. — F.
toupety 'tuft of hair', ft. OF. top, of s.m., ft.
Frankish 'top, of s.m., which is rel. to OHG.,
MHG. zopf, 'end, tip, tuft of hair', and to E.
top, 'summit' (q.v.)

## tour
tour, n. — ME., fr. F., ft. OF. torn, tor (F. tour),
back formation fr. OF. torner (F. tourner), 'to
turn', fr. L. tornare, 'to turn in a lathe; to turn,
fashion', ft. tornus, 'lathe; graver's tool'. See
turn, and cp. terret, tournure, detour, entourage.
Derivatives: tour, intr. and tr. v., tour-ing, п.,
tour-ism, п., tour-ist, п., tour-ist-ic, adj., tour-ist-
ry, n.

## touraco
touraco, п., a bird of the family Musophagidae. —
F., from a W. African native name, imitative of
the bird's cry.

## tourbillion
tourbillion, п., 1) whirlwind; 2) fkework with a
spiral flight. — F. tourbillon, 'whirlwind', fr.
OF. torbeillon, ult. fr. L. turbo, gen. turbinis,
'whirlwind'. Cp. OProvenc. torbelh, torbilh, Sp.
torbelUno, Port, torveiinho, 'whirlwind', and see
turbinal.

## tourmaline
tourmaline, п., a mineral of various colors used
as a gem. — F., fr. Singhalese tdramalli, 'carne-
lian'.

## tournament
tournament, п., 1) a contest between knights; 2)
a series of knightly contests. — ME. tornement,
turnement, fr. OF. torneiement (F. tournoie-
ment), lit. *a turning round', ft. OF. torneier,
tourneier (F. tournoyef), 'to turn round', fr.
torner (F. tourner), 'to turn'. See turn, v., and
-mem and cp. tourney.
Derivative; tournament-al, adj.

## tournasin
tournasin, п., a knife to cut away the excess slip
from pottery. — F. tournasin, tournassin, fr.
tournaser, tournasser, 'to turn pottery', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:801 COLUMN:2 -->
tourner, 'to turn'. See turn, v.

## tourney
tourney, п., a tournament. — ME., fr. MF. tornei,
tournei (F. tournoi), 'tournament', lit. *a turning
round', back formation ft. torneier, tourneier.
See tournament.
Derivatives: tourney, intr. v., tourney-er, n.

## tourniquet
tourniquet, п., a device for stopping bleeding. —
F., ft. in earlier F. also 'coat of arms', formed—
under the influence of tourner, 'to turn'—fr.
OF. turniquet, *a kind of uppergarment', which
is a collateral form of turniquei, turnicie, tunicie,
ft. L. tunicula, dimin. of tunica, 'undergarment*.
See tunic.

## toumois
toumois, п., money coined in Tours, France
(Hist.) — Lit. 'of Tours', ft. L. Turonensis, prop,
'of the (city) of the Turones', an ancient people
in Gallia Lugdunensis, near the site of modern
Tours.

## tournure
tournure, п., graceful manner. — F., 'shape, form,
appearance', lit. 'turn, direction, course', fr. OF.
torneure, fr. ML. torndtura, 'a turning', fr. L.
tornare, 'to turn in a lathe; to turn, fashion'. See
turn and -ure and cp. tour.

## touse
touse, tr. and intr. v., to pull roughly, to tear
(dial.) — ME. -tousen, -tusen (used only in
compounds), rel. to Fris. tusen, OHG. zir-zuson, 'to
tug, pull, dishevel', OHG., MHG. er-zusen, G.
zausen, of s.m., MHG. zus-ach, 'bush', and prob.
cogn. with OL. dusmus (L. dumus), 'thornbush,
bramble'. Cp. next word and tease, teasel,
tussle. Cp. also dumose.
Derivative: tous-y, adj.

## tousle
tousle, tr. v., to dishevel. — Freq. of touse. For
the ending see freq. sun", -le.
Derivatives: tousle, п., tousl-y, adj.

## tout
tout, intr. v., to watch, spy on. — ME. tuten, a
var. of toten, 'to peep', fr. OE. totian, 'to
project, protrude; to peep out', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. dial. E. toot, 'to peep out'.
Derivatives: tout, a lookout, tout-er, n.

## tout
tout, п., a winning of all stakes in certain games.
— F., 'all', fr. L. totus, 'all, the whole bf, entire'.
See total and cp. passe-partout.

## tow
tow, tr..v., to draw (by a rope, etc.) — ME. towen,
fr. OE. togian, 'to pull, draw', rel. to OFris.
togia, 'to pull about', ON. toga, OHG. zogon,
'to draw, pull, drag', and to OE. teon, OS.
tiohan, OFris. tie, MDu. Hen, OHG. ziohan,
MHG., G. Ziehen, Goth, tiuhan, of s.m., ON.
toginn (pp.), 'drawn', ft. I.-E. base *douk-,
*deuk-, 'to pull, draw', whence also Gk. Soli-
δύσσεσ*αι (for *δο·ι-δύκ|.εσ*αι), 'to drag', L.
ducere, 'to draw, lead'. See duke and cp. taut,
team, teem, 'to bear*, tie, tuck, v., tug, toggle,
and the second element in heretoga, Herzog,
wanton.
Derivatives: tow, п., the act of towing, towage
(q.v.), tow-ing, n.

## tow
tow, п., горе, halter. — ON. toh- in tohline, 'tow-
line', rel. to ON- tog, taug, 'rope, cord', and to
OE. togian, 'to pull, draw'. See tow, v.

## tow
tow, п., coarse fiber of hemp. — ME., fr. OE.
(used only in compounds), 'a spinning, weaving',
rel. to ON. to, 'tuft of wool', OE. tawian, 'to
prepare, dress (leather)', MDu. tou, touw, Du.
touw, 'tow'. See taw, 'to prepare'.
Derivative: tow, tr. v.

## towage
towage, n. — A hybrid coined fr. tow, 'to draw',
and -age, a sun", of Latin origin.

## toward
toward, adj. — ME., fr. OF. td-weard, 'facing,
approaching', fr. to, 'to', and -weard, '-ward*.
See to and -ward and cp. toward, prep.
Derivatives: toward-ly, adj. and adv., toward-
ness, n.

## toward
toward, towards, adv. and prep. — ME. toward,
resp. towardes, fr. OE. td-weard, resp. td-
weardes. The -es in ME. toward-es, OE. td-
weardes is the adv. gen. suff. See toward, adj.,
and adv. suff.-s.

## towel
towel, n. — ME. towaille, fr. OF. toaile, toaille
(F. touaille), fr. WTeut. "thwahlja; cp. OS.
thwahila, MDu. dwdle, dwlle, 'towel' (Du.
dwaal, 'altar cloth'), OHG. dwahila, dwehila,
MHG. dwahele, dwele, G. Zwehle, 'towel', lit.
'cloth for washing', fr. OS. thwahan, resp. MDu.
dwaen, OHG. dwahan, MHG. dwahen, G. zwa-
gen, 'to wash'. These words are rel. to OE.
pwlan, 'to wash', pweal, 'a washing', ΟΝ. ρνά.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:801 COLUMN:3 -->
Goth, pwahan, 'to wash', ON. pvdttr, 'a
washing', and cogn. with OPruss. twaxtan, 'bathing
apron'. Cp. OProvenc., Port, toalha, Catal. to-,
valla, Sp. ίοαϊϊα, It. tovaglia, 'towel', which all
derive fr. WTeut. 'thwahlja. Cp. also doily.
Derivatives: towel, tr. v., towelette (q.v.),
towel(f)-ing, n.

## towelette
towelette, п., a small towel. — A hybrid coined
fr. towel, a word of ult. Teut. origin, and the
French suff. -ette (see -ette).

## tower
tower, n. — ME. towr, tor, tur, fr. OE. torr, fr.
OF. tor, tour (F. tour), fr. L. arris, 'tower', fr. Gk.
τύρσις, τύρρις, 'tower; walled city', whence also
Τυρσηνοί, Τυρρηνοί, 'Tyrrhenians', lit.
'builders of walled cities'. Cp. Tyrrhenian, Etruscan,
Tuscan. Cp. also OProvenc. tor, Provenc., It.,
Catal., Sp. torre, 'tower', which also derive fr.
L. turris. Cp. also tor, Torreion formation.
Derivatives: tower-less, adj., tower-y, adj.

## tower
tower, intr. and tr. v. — ME. towren, torren, fr.
towr, tor, 'tower'. See tower, n.
Derivatives: tower-ed, adj., tower-ing, adj., and
п., tower-ing-ly, adv.

## town
town, n. — ME. tun, toun, town, fr. OE. tun,
'fence, enclosure, village, town', rel. to OS., ON,.
OFris. tun, 'fence, hedge', MDu. tuun, 'fence',
Du. tuin, 'garden', OHG., MHG. zun, G. Zaun,
'fence, hedge', and cogn. with the Gaul.-L. suff.
-dunum in place names (as Augustodunum, etc.),
Olr. dun, W. din, 'fortress'. Cp. obsol. E. tine,
'to enclose'. — OSlav. tynu, 'wall', is a Celtic
loan word, which was adopted by the Slavic
languages through the medium of German. (For
•Slavic у = I.-E. й ср. OSlav. dymu with L. fu-
mus, 'smoke', OSlav. byti, 'to be', with L. futu-
rus, 'about to be, future'.) Cp. the second
element in barton, Newton. Cp. also down, 'hill',
dun, 'hill', dune.
Derivatives: town, tr. v., town-ed, adj., town-ee,
п., townify (q.v.), town-ish, adj., town-ish-ly,
adv., town-ish-ness, п., town-let, п., town-like,
adj., town-ling, п., town-ship, п., town-y, adj.,
town-i-ness, n.

## townify
townify, tr. v. — A hybrid coined fr. town (fr. OE.
tun) and -fy, a suff. of Latin origin.

## tox-
tox-, form of toxo- before a vowel.

## toxemia
toxemia, toxaemia, п., blood poisoning. —
Medical L., compounded of tox- and Gk. αίμα,
'blood'. See hema-.

## toxic
toxic, adj., pertaining to poison. — ML. toxicus,
ft. L. toxicum, 'poison', ft. Gk. τοξικόν (scil.
φάρμακον), 'arrow poison', neut. of the
adjective τοξικός, 'pertaining to a bow or arrow',
fr. τόξον, 'a bow or arrow', ft. Scythian
*taxsha-, whence also L. taxus, 'yew'. Cp. taxns,
intoxicate. For the ending see adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: toxic-ity, п., poisonous quality.

## toxic-
toxic-, form of toxico- before a vowel.

## toxicant
toxicant, adj., poisonous. — See prec. word and
-ant.
Derivative: toxicant, п., a poisonous drug.

## toxico-
toxico-, before a vowel toxic-, combining form
denoting poison. — Gk. τοξικό-, τοξικ-, fr.
τοξικόν, 'arrow poison'. See toxic,

## toxicology
toxicology, п., the study of poisons. —
Compounded of toxico-and Gk.-λογία, fr. -λόγος,
'one who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.
Derivatives: toxicolog-ic, toxicolog-ic-al, adjs.,
toxicolog-ist, n.

## toxicosis
toxicosis, п., morbid condition caused by poison
(med.) — Medical L., formed with surf, -osis fr.
Gk. τοξικόν, 'arrow poison'. See toxic.

## toxin
toxin, п., organic poison (biochem.) — Formed
with suff. -in ft. Gk. τόξου, 'bow, arrow', used
in the sense of 'poison'. See toxic and cp.
antitoxin, autotoxin.

## toxo-
toxo-, before a vowel tox-, combining form
meaning'bow'.— Gk. τόξο-, τοξ-, fr. τόξον, 'bow,
arrow'. See toxic.

## toxo-
toxo-, before a vowel tox-, combining form used
in the sense of toxica-, — See toxico-.

## toxophiL toxophile
toxophiL toxophile, adj., having affinity for a
toxin (biochem.) —Compounded of 2nd toxo-
and Gk. φίλος, 'loved; loving'. See philo-.

## toxophilite
toxophilite, п., a lover of archery. — See prec.
word and subst. suff. -ite.
Derivative: toxophilit-ic, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:802 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 775 | TRAGELAPH -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:802 COLUMN:1 -->

## Toxotes
Toxotes, п., a genus of fishes, the archerfish
(ichtkyol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τοξότης,
'bowman, an archer', fr. τόξον, 'a bow'. See toxic.

## toy
toy, n. — Of uncertain origin. It derives perh. ft.
MDu. toy (Du. tuig), 'implement, tool' (cp. esp.
Du. speeltuig, 'plaything, toy'), which is rel. to
OE. getioh, OHG., MHG. geziuc, G. Zeug,
'stuff, matter, tools', G. Spielzeug, 'plaything,
toy', ON. tygi, 'gear, outfit, equipment', Dan.
tei, 'stuff, matter, equipment', Swed. tyg, of
s.m., and prob. also to MHG. ziugen, G. zeugen,
'to beget', OE. teon, 'to draw'. See tow, 'to draw'
and cp. tug.
Derivatives: toy, v., toy-ing, adj., toy-ing-ly, adv.

## tra-
tra-, shortened form of trans- before the
consonants d-, m-, n-, I-, v-, j-,

## trabea
trabea, п., state robe worn by kings and augurs
(Roman antiq.) — L. trabea, fr. trabs, gen. trabis,
'beam'; so called because it was ornamented
with 'beams', i.e. 'horizontal stripes'. L. trabs
derives fr. I.-E. base *treb-, 'to build'. See thorp
and cp. tavern, trave.

## trabeated
trabeated, adj., built with horizontal beams or
lintels (arch.) — Formed with the adj. suffixes
-ate and -ed fr. L. trabs, gen. trabis, 'beam'. See
prec. word.

## trabeation
trabeation, п., straight construction (arch.) —
Formed with surf, -ation fr. L. trabs, gen. trabis,
'beam'. See trabea.

## trabecule
trabecule, п., a structure in thananimal or
vegetable body resembling a small beam or bar. —
L. trabecula, dimin. of trabs, 'beam'. See trabea
and -cule.
Derivatives: trabecul-ar, trabecul-ate, trabecul-
ated, adjs., trabecul-ation, n.

## trabuco
trabuco, п., 1) blunderbuss; 2) a kind of cigar. —
Sp., fr. trabucar, 'to upset, overturn', formed fr.
tra- (fr. L. trans), 'through, across', and buque,
'bulk, capacity, of a ship, hull of a ship', which
is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. bah, buhhes, OE.
bite, 'belly', and see bnck, 'the body of a wagon'.

## trace
trace, п., track, trail. — ME., fr. OF. ( = F.) trace,
back formation fr. OF. trader (F. tracer). See
next word.

## trace
trace, tr. and intr. v., to draw. — ME. tracen, fr.
OF. trader, (F. tracer), fr. VL. tractiare, fr. L.
tractus, pp. of trahere, 'to draw'. Cp. It. trac-
ciare, 'to follow the track of, Sp. trazar, 'to
trace, devise, plan out', which are of the same
origin, and see tract, 'region'. Cp. also retrace.
The sense of E. trace was influenced by track.
Derivatives: trace-able, adj., trace-abil-ity, п.,
trace-able-ness, n.

## trace
trace, п., part of harness. — ME. trays, pi., fr.
OF. trais, traits, fr. sing, trait, lit. 'a stretch,
stroke'. See trait.
Derivative [trace, tr.v., to fasten(a horse) by trace.

## trache
trache, form of tracheo- before a vowel.

## trachea
trachea, п., windpipe (anat.) — Medical L.
trachea, fr. L. trachia, fr. Gk. (αρτηρία) τραχεία,
'windpipe'. Τραχεία is the fern, of τραχύς,
'rough', which is prob. rel. to *ράσσειν, 'to
trouble, disquiet', and cogn. with ON. dregg,
'dregs'; see dreg and cp. trachoma, trachyte.
— Aristotle, like all the ancients, believed that
the arteries contained air. Therefore he
distinguished between the artery par excellence,
which he called 'the smooth artery' (αρτηρία
λεία) and the windpipe, which he named 'the
rough artery' (αρτηρία τραχεία).

## tracheal
tracheal, adj., pertaining to the trachea (anat.) —
Medical L. trachealis, fr. trachea. See prec.
word and adj. surf. -al.

## trachelo-
trachelo-, before a vowel trachel-, combining
form meaning 1) neck; 2) cervix; 3) cervical and
— Gk. τράχηλο-, τραχηλ-, fr. τράχηλος,
'neck', which prob. stands in gradational
relationship to τροχός, 'wheel', and prop, means
'the turner'; see troche. For sense development
cp. L. collum, G. Hals, 'neck', which also means
prob. lit. 'the turner', fr. I.-E. *qwel-, 'to turn'
(see collar).

## Trachelospermum
Trachelospermum, п., a genus of plants, the
climbing dogbane (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
trnchelo- and Gk. σπέρμα, 'seed'. See sperm.

## trachelotomy
trachelotomy, п., incision in the neck of the uterus
isurg.) — Compounded of trachelo- and Gk.
-τομία, 'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:802 COLUMN:2 -->
-tomy.

## tracheo-
tracheo-, before a vowel trache-, combining form
denoting the trachea. — See trachea.

## tracheocele
tracheocele, п., the goiter (med.) — Compounded
of tracheo- and Gk. κήλη, 'tumor, hernia'. See
-cele.

## tracheotomy
tracheotomy, п., incision in the trachea (surg.) —
Coined by the German surgeon Lorenz Heister
(1683-1758) in 1718 fr. tracheo- and Gk. -τομίϊ,
'a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting'. See -tomy.

## trachoma
trachoma, п., a contagious disease of the eyes
(med.) — Medical L. trachoma, fr. Gk.
τράχωμα, 'roughness', fr. τραχύς, 'rough'; see
trachea and -oma. The disease is so called
because it is characterized by the roughness of the
inner surface of the eyelids.

## trachy-
trachy-, combining form meaning 'rough'. — Gk.
τράχυ-, fr. τραχύς, 'rough'. See trachea.

## trachyte
trachyte, п., a light-colored volcanic rock (pe-
trogr.) — Formed fr. Gk. τραχύς, 'rough' (see
trachea), with subst. suff. -ite; so called because
of the roughness of its fractured surface.
Derivative: trachyt-ic, adj.

## track
track, n. — ME. trak, fr. MF. trac, 'track of
horses, trace', fr. OF-, prob. of Teut. origin; cp.
MDu. treck, Du. trek, 'a drawing', MDu.
trecken, Du. trekken, 'to draw, pull*, OHG.
trehhan, 'to draw, shove', MHG. trecken, 'to
draw'. Cp. trek, trigger.
Derivatives: track, п., track-er, п., track-less,
adj., track-less-ly, adv., track-less-ness, n.

## tract
tract, п., 1) region; 2) duration. — ME. trade,
fr. L. tractus, 'a drawing; distance, district,
region; space of time', fr. tractus, pp. of trahere,
'to pull, draw', which is perh. cogn. with 01.
dkrajati, 'sweeps over, stretches, draws', dkrdjik,
'a stretching, drawing', Lett, dragat, 'to tear',
ON. draga, OE. dragan, 'to draw', Goth, dragan,
'to carry, load', OHG. tragan, 'to carry'. See
draw and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also
abstract, abstraction, attract, attraction, attra-
hent, contract, contraction, contraheiit, detract,
detraction, distract, distraction, entreat, extract,
extraction, portray, protract, protraction,
retract, retraction, retreat, strass, 'refuse of silk',
subtract, subtraction, subtrahend, trace, 'track',
trace, 'part of harness', tractable, tractate, trail,
train, trait, tram, 'silk thread', trattoria, treat,
treatise, treaty, tret.

## tract
tract, п., treatise. — Short for tractate.

## tractability
tractability, n. — L. tractdbilittts, fr. tractabilis.
See next word and -ity.

## tractnble
tractnble, adj., 1) easily managed; 2) easily
worked. — L. tractabilis, 'manageable, yielding', fr.
tractare, 'to draw violently, drag, touch, handle,
manage', freq. of trahere (pp. tractus), 'to draw'.
See tract, 'region', and -able, and cp. treatable,
which is a doublet of tractable.
Derivatives: tractable-ness, п., tractabl-y, adv.

## tractarian
tractarian, n.,' one who writes tracts. — Formed
fr. tract, 'treatise', with suff. -arian.

## Tractarian
Tractarian, п., an adherent of Tractarianism. —
See next word.

## Tractarianism
Tractarianism, п., a movement in the Church of
England, the Oxford Movement. — So called
from the 'Tracts for the Times', in which the
teachings of this movement were first laid down.
See tractarian and -ism.

## tractate
tractate, п., a treatise. — L. tractdtus, 'a touching,
handling; management, treatment, treatise', fr.
tractdtus, pp. of tractare. See tractable and subst.
suff. -ate and cp. treatise, which is a doublet of
tractate.

## tractator
tractator, п., one who writes tracts. — L. trac-
tator, 'a handler, a treater of literary questions,
a writer of treatises', fr. tractdtus, pp. of
tractare. See tractable and agential suff. -or.

## tractile
tractile, adj., capable of being drawn. — Formed
with suff. -ile fr. L. tractus, pp. of trahere, 'to
draw'. See tract, 'region'.
Derivative: tractil-ity, n.

## traction
traction, п., the act of drawing. — ML. tractid,
gen. -dnis, fr. L. tractus, pp. of trahere, 'to draw'.
See tract, 'region', and -ion.
Derivative: traction-al, adj.

## tractive
tractive, adj., drawing, tractional. — Formed
with suff. -ive fr. L. tractus, pp. of trahere, 'to
draw'. See tract, 'region'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:802 COLUMN:3 -->

## tractor
tractor, n. — ModL-, lit. 'that which draws', fr.
tractus, pp. of trahere, 'to draw'. See tract,
'region', and agential suff. -or.

## trade
trade, n. — ME. 'path, track, course', fr. MLG.
trade, of s.m., which is rel. to OS. trada, OHG.
trata, of s.m., and to E. tread.
Derivatives: trade, tr. and intr. v., trad-er, п.,
trad-ing, n.

## Tradescaiitia
Tradescaiitia, п., a genus of plants, thespidewort
(hot.) — ModL., named after John Tradescant,
gardener to Charles the First of England. For
the ending see 1st suff. -la.

## trade wind
trade wind, — Lit. 'a wind blowing in one regular
'course', fr. trade, taken in its original sense.

## tradition
tradition, n. — ME. tradicion, fr. MF. (— F.)
tradition, fr. L. traditionem, ace. of trdditio, 'a
giving up, delivering up, surrendering', fr. tradi-
tus, pp. of tradere, 'to give up, surrender', short
for transdere, fr. trans- and -dere, fr. dare, 'to
give'; see date, 'point of time', and -ion.
Tradition is a scholarly formation and represents a
doublet of treason (q.v.) See also extradite,
traitor.
Derivatives: tradition, tr. v., tradition-al, adj.,
tradition-al-ism, п., tradition-al-ist, п., tradition-
al-ist-ic, adj., tradition-al-ly, adv., tradition-ary,
adj., tradition-ari-ly, adv.

## traditive
traditive, adj., pertaining to tradition. — Obsol.
F. traditif (fem. traditive), fr. L. trdditus, pp. of
tradere. See prec. word and -ive.

## traduce
traduce, tr. v., to defame; to slander. — L. trd-
ducere, 'to lead, bring, carry, across, transfer,
remove; to make a show of, tcvridicule, disgrace,
degrade', shortened fr. transducere, fr. trans-
and ducere, 'to lead'. See dnke and cp. trocha.
Derivatives: traduc-er, п., traduc-ing, adj.,
traduc-ing-ly, adv.

## traducian
traducian, adj., pertaining to traducianism; п., а
believer in traducianism. — Late L. traduclanus,
fr. L. trddux, gen. trdducis. 'a layer for
propagation', fr. traducere. See prec. word and -an.

## traducianism
traducianism, п., the doctrine that the soul is
Propagated along with the body. — See prec.
word and -ism.

## trnducianist
trnducianist, п., a believer in traducianism. — See
traducian and -1st.
Derivative: traducianist-ic, adj.

## traduction
traduction, п., defamation; slander. — Late L.
traductionem, ace. of traductio, 'a leading across,
removing, transferring; a bringing to public
disgrace', fr. L. trdductus, pp. of traducere. See
tradnce and -ion.

## traffic
traffic, n. — MF. trafique (F. trafic), fr. It. traf-
fico, which prob. derives ft. Arab, tafrtq,
'distribution', verbal noun offdrraqa, 'he distributed',
II (= frequentative or intensive conjugation) of
faraqa, 'he split, divided'; influenced in form by
assumed L. trdficere (for *transficere), 'to make
over* (see trans- and fact). Arab, faraqa is rel. to
Heb. paraq, 'he tore away (esp. the yoke), he
rescued', peraq, 'he tore off, Aram, ρ raq, 'he
rescued', Syr. peraq, 'he withdrew (intr.); he
redeemed, rescued', Ethiop. faraqa, 'he set free'.
Derivatives: traffic, intr. and tr. v. (= F. trafi-
quer), traffic-able, adj., traffick-er, n.

## tragacanth
tragacanth, п., gum obtained from the plant
Astragalus. — F. tragacanthe, name of the plant,
lit. 'goat's thorn', fr. Gk. τράγος, 'he-goat', and
ακαν&α, 'thorn'. See tragic and acanthus and
cp. Tagetes and the second element in Tauro-
tragns.

## tragedian
tragedian, п., writer, or actor, of tragedy. — ME.
tragedien, 'a writer of tragedy', fr. MF. (= F.)
tragddien, fr. tragedle. See tragedy and -ian.

## tragedienne
tragedienne, п., tragic actress. — F. tragedienne,
fem. of tragedien. See prec. word.

## tragedy
tragedy, n. — ME. tragedie, fr. MF. (= F.) tra-
gddie, fr. L. tragoedia, fr. ,Gk. τραγωδία,
'tragedy', fr. τραγωδός, 'tragic poet or singer', prop,
'a singer competing for a he-goat as a prize', fr.
τράγος, 'he-goat', and φδή, 'a song'. Gk.
τράγος, 'he-goat', lit. means 'a gnawer'; it is
related to τρώγειν, 'to gnaw, nibble' (aor.
έτραγον). See trout and cp. tragic,trogon and the
first element in troglodyte; cp. also dredge, 'to
sprinkle'. For the etymology of Gk. ώδή see ode.

## tragelaph
tragelaph, tragelaphus, п., a fabulous animal,
partly a goat and partly a stag (Greek mythol.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:803 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TRAGELAPHUS | 776 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:803 COLUMN:1 -->
— L. tragelaphus, fr. Gk. τραγέλαφος, lit. 'he-
goat-stag', fr. τράγος, 'he-goat', and Ελαφος,
'stag'. See tragic and eland.

## Trageiaphus
Trageiaphus, п., a genus of antelopes (zooL) — L.
tragelaphus. See prec. word.

## traghetto
traghetto, п., gondola station. — It., lit. 'a
crossing over', back formation fr. traghettare, 'to
ferry across*, fr. VL. *trdjectdre, freq. of L. trdicere
(less correctly trdjicere), (pp. trdjectus), 'to go
over*, fomied fr. tra- and jacere, *to throw*;
OProvenc. trajitar and OF. tresjeter, 'to cross
over'·, are of the same origin. See jet, 'to spirt
forth*, and cp. trajectory.

## tragic
tragic, adj. — L. tragicus, fr. Gk. τραγικός, 'of a
goat; pertaining to tragedy*, fr. τράγος. See
tragedy and -ic.
Derivatives: tragic, п., tragic-al, adj., tragic-al-
ity, п., tragic-al-ly, adv., tragic-al-ness, n.

## traglco-
traglco-, combining form meaning 'tragic'. — Gk.
τραγικό-, fr. τραγικός. See tragic.

## tragicomedy
tragicomedy, n. — MR (- F.) tragicomedie, fr.
Late L. tragicomoedia, contraction of L. tragi-
cocomoedia. See tragico- and comedy. The
contraction of L. tragicocomoedia to tragicomoedia
in Late L. is due to haplology.

## tragicomic
tragicomic, adj. — See prec. word and -ic.
Derivatives: tragicomic-al, adj., tragicomic-al-
ity, п., tragicomic-al-ly, adv.

## tragopan
tragopan, п., an Asiatic pheasant. — ModL.
tragopan, fr. Gk. τραγόπαν, name of a fabulous
bird of Ethiopia, lit. 'goat of Pan', fr. τράγος,
'he-goat', and Παν, 'the god of the woods and
fields'. See tragic and Fan.

## Tragopogon
Tragopogon, п., a genus of plants, the goats beard
ibot.) — ModL., lit. 'goat's beard', fr. Gk.
τράγος, 'he-goat', and πώγων, 'beard'. See
tragedy and Pogonia.

## tragus
tragus, п., eminence at the opening of the external
ear (anat.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τράγος, prop, 'he-
goat'; so called from the bunch of hair it
contains, which resembles a goat's beard; see tragic
and cp. antitragus. In its anatomical sense the
word occurs for the first time in the Onomasti-
con of the Greek lexicographer Julius Pollux,
who lived in the 2nd century.

## trail
trail, tr. and intr. v. — ME. traifen, fr. MF. trail-
lier, trailler, 'to tow (a boat)', fr. VL. *trdguldre,
fr. L. trdgula, 'a kind of dragnet', from the stem
of trahere, 'to pull, draw'. See tract, 'region',
and cp. train. Cp. also drail.
Derivatives: trail, п., track, trail-er, п., trail-ing,
adj., trail-ing-ly, adv.

## train
train, tr. and intr. v. — ME. trainen, fr. MF.
trainer (F. trainer), 'to drag, draw long*, fr. OF.,
fr. VL. *traginare, fr. L. trahere, 'to pull, draw'.
See tract, 'region', and cp. OProvenc. traginar,
tralnar, Sp. trajinar. It. trainare, 'to drag, trail',
which all derive fr. VL. *tragindre. Cp. entrain.
Cp. also trail.
Derivatives: train, n. (q.v.), train-age, п., train·
ed, adj., train-ing, n. and adj.

## train
train, п., procession, cortege, etc.; a series, a line
of connected railroad cars pulled or pushed by
a locomotive. — ME. trayn, fr. MF. train (F.
train), back formation fr. trainer, 'to drag, draw
along*. See train, v.

## train oil
train oil, oil made from whale blubber. — From
earlier trane, train, fr. MLG. trdn, 'tear from the
eye; train oil' (whence also Du. traan, G., Dan.,
Swed., Norw. tran, 'train oil'), which is rel. to
OS., OHG. trahan, MHG. trahen, 'drop; tear
from the eye', G. Trane, 'tear from the eye', fr.
Teut. *trahnu-. Accordingly train oil is a
pleonastic term since both train (for trane) and oi/are
used metaphorically in the sense of 'liquid'. Cp.
the collateral Teut. form *takru- appearing in
Goth, tagr, ΟΝ., OFris. tar, OE. tear, 'tear from
the eye', and see 1st tear,

## traipse
traipse, also trapes, trapse, intr. v., to ramble
about. — Prob. rel. to MDu. trappen, dial.
Norw. trappa, 'to tread, stamp', and to E.
tramp, trample.

## trait
trait, n. — MF. (= F.), 'stroke, feature', fr. L.
tractus, 'a pulling, drawing, dragging,
stretching', fr. tractus, pp. of trakere, 'to pull, draw*.
Cp. It. tratto, 'a drawing, stroke, feature', Sp.
trecho, 'space, distance', and see tract,
'region*.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:803 COLUMN:2 -->

## traitor
traitor, n. — ME. traitour, fr. OF. traitor, oblique
case, fr. L. trdditorem, ace. of trdditor, 'betrayer',
fr. traditus, pp. oitrddere, 'to deliver, surrender*,
fr. tra- and -dere, fr. dare, 'to give'. See date,
'point of time', and agential sufT. -or, OF. traitre
(F. traitre), 'traitor', comes from the VL. nom.
trdditor. Cp. It. traditore, Ruman. tradator,
OProvenc. traidor, trachor, Sp., Port, traidor,
'traitor', which all derive fr. VL. traditorem. Cp.
betray, tradition, treason.
Derivatives: traitor-ous, adj., traitor-ous-ly, adv.
traitor-ous-ness, П.

## traject
traject, tr. v. — L. trdjectus, pp. of trdicere (less
correctly trdficere), 'to throw across', fr. tra-,
and jacere (pp. jactus), 'to throw'. See jet, 'to
spirt forth', and cp. traghetto. For the change
of Latin d (in jactus) to ё (in tra-jectus) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.

## traject
traject, n. — L. trdjectus, pp. of trdicere. See prec.
word.

## trajection
trajection, n. — L. trdjectio, gen. -onis, fr.
trdjectus, pp. of trdjicere. See traject, v., and -ion.

## trajectory
trajectory, п., the path described by a projectile.
— ML. trdjectorium, fr. trdjectus, pp. of
trdjicere. See traject, v., and subst. suff. -ory.

## tralatitious
tralatitious, adj., transferred, metaphorical. —
Formed with suff. -011s fr. L. truldtfcius, traldti-
tius, collateral form of trdnslaticius, trdnsldti-
tius, 'metaphorical', lit. 'handed down,
transmitted , fr. trdnsldtus, used as pp. of trdnsferre,
'to carry over, transfer'. See translate.

## tram
tram, п., a vehicle. — LG. traam, 'beam, bar,
handle', rel. to OFris. trdme, tram, 'beam, rung
of a ladder*, Norw. tram, *wooden doorstep',
traam, 'frame', dial. Swed. tromm, trumm, 'log',
and to ON. promr, 'edge*. See thrum and cp.
tramway.

## tram
tram,п., a double,twisted silk thread. —F. trame,
'weft, woof, web', fr. L. trama, 'woof, weft',
which prob. stands for *tragh-smd, fr. trakere,
'to pull, draw'. See tract, 'region', and cp. words
there referred to.

## trammel
trammel, п., 1) a fishing net; 2) a kind of shackle
for a horse; 3) anything that hampers activity.
— ME. tramaile, fr. MF. (= F.) tremail,
'dragnet, trammel', fr. OF. tremail, fr. Late L. tremd-
culum, a word occurring in the Salic law,
compounded of tres, 'three', and macula, 'spot; mesh
of net*. See three and macula and cp. mail,
'armor'. It. tramaglio, Sp. trasmallo, Port, tremalho
are French loan words.
Derivatives: trammel, tr. v., trammel(l)-ed, adj.,
trammel(l)-er, п., trammel(l)-ing, adj., trammel(l).
ing-ly, adv.

## tramontana
tramontana, п., the north wind blowing in Italy.
— It. See next word.

## tramontane
tramontane, adj., from beyond the mountains,
foreign; п., foreigner, stranger. — F., fr. It.
tramontana (i.e. Stella), 'the star beyond the
mountains; north; north wind*, fr. L. trdnsmontdnus,
'beyond the mountains', fr. trans- and montdnus,
'of the mountains', fr. mons, montis, 'mountain'.
See mountain and cp. transmontane. Cp. also
cismontane, ultramontane.

## tramp
tramp, intr. and tr. v. — ME. trampen, rel. to
MLG. trampen, 'to stamp with one's foot,
trample', Dan. trampe, Swed., Norw. trampa, 'to
tramp, stamp, tread heavily', Goth, ana-trim-
pan, 'to press upon*; fr. "tramp-, a nasalized
form of the imitative base *trap-, whence MLG.,
Du. trappen, 'to tread', MDu. trap, trappe,
MLG. treppe, trappe, 'staircase'. See trap,
'snare', and cp. traipse, trapse, 'to ramble about'.
Derivatives: tramp,n., tramp-er, п., trample{q.v.)

## trample
trample, tr. and intr. v. — ME. tramplen, freq. of
trampen. Cp. Late MHG., G. trampleln, 'to
stamp with one's foot, to trample', freq. formed
fr. MLG. trampen, and see prec. word and freq.
suff. -le.
Derivative: trample, n.

## tramway
tramway, n. — Lit. 'a way for trams'. See tram,
'vehicle', and way.

## trance
trance, п., a half-conscious condition as in
catalepsy or hypnosis. — ME. traunce, trance, fr.
MF. transe, 'swoon; extreme fear', lit. *a
passing over', fr. OF., fr. transir, 'to pass, pass over,
pass from life*, fr. L. trdnsire, 'to go across, pass
over, die'. Cp. Sp. and Port, trance, 'the time of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:803 COLUMN:3 -->
transition from life to death'. F. trance, transe,
in its modern psychological sense, has been
reborrowed from English. See transient and cp.
transire, trounce.

## trance
trance, intr. and tr. v. — ME. transen, *to swoon*,
fr. transir. See trance, n.
Derivatives: tranc-ed, adj., tranc-ed-ly, adv.

## tranquil
tranquil, adj., peaceful, quiet. — L. tranquillus,
'quiet, calm, still', for *trans-quil-nos, 'very
quiet*, formed fr. trdns, 'through, across', used
in the sense of 'very' (cp. F. tres, 'very', fr. L.
trdns), and quies, 'rest, quiet*. See trans- and
quiet, п., and cp. while.
Derivatives: tranquil-ity (q.v.), tranquil(J)ize,
(q.v.), tranquil-ly, adv., tranquil-ness, n.

## tranquility
tranquility, tranquillity, n. — ME. tranquillite, fr.
OF. tranquillite (F. tranquillite), fr. tranquillus.
See prec. word and -ity.

## trammiUze
trammiUze, tranquillize, tr. v., to render tranquill;
intr. v., to become tranquill. — See tranquil and
-ize and cp. F. tranquilliser.
Derivatives: tranquil(i)iz-ation, п.,
tranquillizer, n.

## trails-
trails-, pref. meaning 'across, over, beyond,
through'- — L. trans, rel. to Umbr. traf, trakaft
tra and cogn. with OI. tirafy, Avestic taro, W.
tra, 'across, beyond', fr. I.-E. base *ter-, 'to go
through, cross over', whence also L. terminus,
'boundary line'; see term and words there
referred to and cp. esp. tranquil, transom, tres,
trespass, trestle, trebuchet. Formally L. trdns is
the pres. part, of *traret 'to go through* (L.
intrdre, 'however', is not formed fr. pref. in- and
*trdre, but back formation fr. intra, 'within';
see enter, 'to go within').

## transact
transact, tr. and intr. v. — L. trdnsdetus, pp. of
trdnsigere, 'to carry through, accomplish, settle',
fr. trans- and agere, 'to drive, set in motion; to
do'. See agent, adj., and cp. act. Cp. also trausi-
gent.

## transaction
transaction, n. — ME., fr. L. trdnsdetio, gen.
-onis, fr. trdnsdetus, pp. of trdnsigere. See prec.
word and -ion.
Derivatives: transaction-al, adj.,
transaction-ally, adv.

## transalpine
transalpine, adj., situated beyond the Alps (from
the point of view of Italy). — L. Transalpine
'that which is beyond the Alps', fr. trans- and
Alpinus, 'Alpine', from Alpis, 'the Alps'. See
Alpine and cp. cisalpine.

## transatlantic
transatlantic, adj., situated across the Atlantic. —
Formed fr. trans- and Atlantic. Cp.
cisatlantic.

## transcend
transcend, tr. v., to go beyond the limits of; to
surpass, excel; intr. v. {archaic) to be
transcendent; to excel. — L. trdnscendere, 'to clinb or
step over, surmount, surpass', fr. trans- and
scandere, 'td climb, ascend'. See scan and cp.
ascend, descend, condescend. For the change of
Latin d (in scandere) to ё (in trans-cinder e) see
accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: transcend-ing, adj., iranscend-ing-
ly, adv., transcend-ing-ness, n.

## transcendence
transcendence, transcendency, n. — Late L.
trdnscendentia, fr. L. trdnscendens, gen. -entis.
See next word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## transcendent
transcendent, adj. and n. — L. trdnscendens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of trdnscendere. See transcend
and -ent.

## transcendental
transcendental, adj. — ML. trdnscendentdlis, fr.
L. trdnscendens, gen. -entis. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: transcendental-ism, п., transcenden-
tal-ist, п., transcendental-ist-ic, adj., transcen-
dental-ity, п., transcendental-ly, adv.

## transcontinental
transcontinental, adj., passing across the
continent. — Formed fr. trans- and continental.

## transcribe
transcribe, tr. v., to copy. — L. trdnscribere, fr.
trans- and scribere, 'to write'. See scribe and cp.
words there referred to.

## transcript
transcript, п., a copy. — ME., fr. L. trdnscriptum,
neut. pp. of trdnscribere. See prec. word and
script.

## transcription
transcription, n. — F., fr. L. trdnscriptus, pp. of
Lrdnscrjbere. See transcribe and -ion.
Derivatives: transcription-al, adj.,
transcriptionally, adv.

## transect
transect, tr. v., to cut across. — Formed fr. trans-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:804 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 777 | TRANSPIRE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:804 COLUMN:1 -->
and L. sectus, pp. of secure, 'to cut*. See section.
Derivative: transect-ion, n.

## transeiina
transeiina, п., lattice work enclosing a shrine. —
L. transenna, prob; of Etruscan origin.

## transept
transept, п., transverse portion of a cruciform
church. — ML. trdnseptum, formed fr. trans-
arid L. septum, 'a hedge, enclosure'. See septum.
Derivatives: transept-al, adj., transept~al-ly, adv.

## transfer
transfer, tr. and intr. v. — L. trdnsferre, 'to carry
over, transport*, fr. trans- and ferre, 'to carry'.
See bear, 'to carry'.
Derivatives: transfer, п., transfer-able, adj.,
transfer-abil-ity, п., transfer-ee, п.,
transference, п.; transferent-ial, adj., transfer-or, п.,
transferr-er, n.

## transfiguration
transfiguration, п., change of appearance. — ME.,
fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. trdnsfigurdtionem, ace. of
trdnsfigurdtio, fr. trdnsfigurdtus; pp. of trans·
figurdre. See next word and -ation.

## transfigure
transfigure, tr. v., to change in shape. — ME., fr.
L. trdnsfigurdre, fr. trans- ana figurare, 'to form,
fashion'. See figure, v. and n.

## transfinite
