transfinite, adj., going beyond any finite number
{math.) — G. transfinit, fr. L. trans (see trans-)
and finit, 'finite', fr. b.finitus (see finite).
Derivative: transfinite, п., a transfinit enumber.

## transfix
transfix, tr. v., to pierce. — L. trunsfixus, pp. of
transflgere, 4o pierce through*, fr. traus- and
flgere, 'to fasten, fix'. See fix, v.

## transfixion
transfixion, n. — Late L. transfixiu, gen. -onis,
fr. L. trdnsfixus, pp. of transflgere. See prec.
word and -ion.

## transform
transform, tr. v. — ME. transformen, fr. L. trdns-
formdre, 'to change the shape of, fr. trans* and
formdre, 'to form\ See form, v. and n.
Derivatives: transformation (q.v.),
transformable, adj., transform-at-or, п., transform-er, п.,
transformism (q.v.), transformist (q.v.)

## transformation
transformation, n. — ME., fr. Eccles. L. trdnsfor-
mdtionem, ace. of trdnsformdtid, fr. L. trdnsfor-
mdtus, pp. of trdnsformdre. See prec. word and
-ation.
Derivative: transformation-al, adj.,

## transformative
transformative, adj. — ML. trdnsformdtivus, fr.
L. transformdtus, pp. οι trdnsformare. See
transform and -ative.

## transformism
transformism, п., the doctrine of the
transformation of species called also the mutability of
species. — F. transformisme, fr. transformer.
See transform and -ism.

## transformist
transformist, п., an adherent of transformism. —
F. transformiste, fr. transformer. See transform
and -ist.

## transfuse
transfuse, tr. v., to transfer by pouring. — ME.
transfusen, fr. L. trdnsfusus, pp. of transfundere,
'to pour from one vessel into another', fr.
trans- and fundere, 'to pour'. See fuse, 'to melt'.
Derivatives: transfus-er, п., transfusion (q.v.),
transfus-ive, adj.

## transfusion
transfusion, n. — L. trdnsfusio, gen. -onis, fr.
trdnsfusus, pp. of transfundere. See prec. word
and -ion.

## transgress
transgress, tr. v., to go beyond a limit; intr. v., to
violate a law, etc., to sin. — F. transgresser, fr.
L. transgressus, pp. of trdnsgredi', 'to step a-
cross', fr. trans- and gradi (pp. gressus), 'to step,
walk, go'. See grade, 'step', and cp. words there
referred to. For the change of Latin a (in gradi)
to ё (in trdns-gressus) see accent and cp. words
there referred to. For the form οι gressus, pp. of
gradi, «ее congress.

## transgression
transgression, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
trdnsgressionem, ace. of trdnsgressio, *a going
across or over, a transgression', fr. transgressus,
pp. of trdnsgredi. See transgress and -ion.
Derivative: transgression-al, adj.

## transgressive
transgressive, adj. — Late L. trdnsgressivus, 'that
which passes over', fr. L. transgressus, pp. of
trdnsgredi. See transgress and -lve.
Derivative: transgressive-ly, adv.

## transgressor
transgressor, n. — Late L. transgressor, fr. L.
transgressus, pp. of trdnsgredi. See transgress
and agential suff. -or.

## transience
transience, transiency, n. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## transient
transient, adj., transitory. — L. trdnsiens, VL.
gen. *trdnsientis (L. trdnseuntis), pres. part, of
transire, 'to go across, pass through', fr. trans-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:804 COLUMN:2 -->
and ire, 'to go'. See itinerate and -ent and cp.
trance, transire, transit.
Derivatives: transient, п., transient-ly, adv.,
transient-ness, n.

## transilience
transilience, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## transilient
transilient, adj., passing from one thing to
another. — L. trdnsiliens, gen. -ientis, pres. part, of
trdnsilire, 'to spring over', fr. trans- and salire,
'to leap, jump*. See salient and cp. resile,
resilient. For the change of Latin a (in salire, 'to
/ (in tran-sxlire) see abigeat and cp. words there
referred to.

## transire
transire, п., a customs document describing the
cargo of a ship for the sake of clearing it. — L.
transire, 'to go across'. See transient and cp.
transit.

## transistor
transistor, n.( a small electronic device that
performs many of the functions of the vacuum
tube. — Trade name coined by Bell
Laboratories in 1948 fr. transfer and resistor.

## transit
transit, п., 1) passage; 2) conveyance. — L.
trdnsitus, *a going across or over*, fr. trdnsitus,
pp. of transire. See transient.
Derivative: transit, tr. v.

## transition
transition, п., passing from one state, condition,
etc., to another; change. — L. trdnsitio, gen.
•onis, 'a going across or over', fr. trdnsitus, pp.
of transire. See transient and -Шоп.
Derivatives: transitional{q .v.), transition-ary,ad}.

## transitional
transitional, adj. — Formed fr. transition with
adj. suff. -al; first used by the English poet
Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772-1834).
Derivative: transitional-ly, adv. .

## transitive
transitive, adj. — Late L. trdnsitivus, 'passing
over; (gram.) 'transitive', lit. 'that may pass
over (to another person)*, fr. L. trdnsitus, pp. of
transire. See transient and rive.
Derivatives: transitive, п., transitive-ly, adv.,
transitive-ness, п., transitiv-ity, n.

## transitory
transitory, adj. — ME. transitorie, fr. MF. (= F.)
transitoire, fr. OF., fr. L. trdnsitorius, 'adapted
for passing through, passing, transitory*, fr.
trdnsitus, pp. of transire. See transient and adj.
suff. -ory.
Derivatives: transitori-ly, adv., transitori-ness,
n.

## translate
translate, tr. v., :— L. trdnsldtus, 'carried over*
(used as pp. of trdnsferre, 'to carry over'), fr.
trans- and latus, 'borne, carried' (used as pp. of
ferre, 'to bear, carry'), which stands for *tldtos,
fr. *r/-, zero degree of I.-E. base *tel-, *tol-, 'to
bear, carry', whence L. tollere, 'to lift up, raise',
tolerdre, 'to bear, support*. See tolerate and cp.
tralatitious.
Derivatives: translat-able, adj., translative (q.v.),
translator (q.v.)

## translation
translation, n. — ME. translacioun, fr. MF. ( =
F.) translation, fr. OF., fr. L. trdnsldtionem, ace.
of tr.dnsldtid, 'a carrying over', fr. trdnsldtus,
'carried over'. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: translation-al, adj.,
translation-ally, adv.

## translative
translative, adj. — L. trdnsldtivus, 'belonging to
a transference', fr. trdnsldtus, 'carried over'. See
translate and cp. ablative, relative.

## translator
translator, n. — ME. tran$latour, fr. MF., fr. L.
trdnsldtorem, ace. of translator, fr. trdnsldtus,
'carried over*. See translate and agential suff.
-or.
Derivatives: translator-ial, translat-ory, adjs.

## transliterate
transliterate, tr. v., to write or spell words of a
language with the corresponding characters of
another language. — Formed fr. trans-, L. lit·
tera, 'letter, character' (see letter), and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: transliterat-ion, п., transliterat-or,
n.

## translucence
translucence, translucency, n. — Formed from
next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## translucent
translucent, adj., letting light pass but not
transparent. — L. trdnslucens, gen. -ends, pres. part.
of trdnslucere, 'to shine through*, fr. trans- and
lucere, 'to shine*. See lucent.
Derivative: translucent-ly, adv.

## transmarine
transmarine, adj., on the other side of the sea;
overseas. — L. trdnsmarinus, 'coming from
beyond the sea', fr. trans- and marinus, 'pertaining

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:804 COLUMN:3 -->
to the sea*, fr. mare *sea\ See marine and cp,
ultramarine,

## transmigrant
transmigrant, п., one who transmigrates. — L.
trdnsmigrans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of trdns-
migrare. See next word and -ant and cp. migrant.

## transmigrate
transmigrate, intr. v., 1) to move from one place
to another; 2) to move into another body (said
of the soul). — L. trdnsmigrdt(tum), pp. stem of
trdnsmigrdret 'to move from one place to
another*, fr. trans- and migrare, 'to wander, migrate*.
See migrate.
Derivatives: transmigration (q.v.), transmigrat-
or, п., transmigrat-ory, adj.

## transmigration
transmigration, п., 1) the act of transmigrating;
2) specif., the passing of the soul at death into
another body. — Late L. transmigrated, gen.
-onis, 'a removal from one place to another', fr.
L. trdnsmigrat-(um), pp, stem of trdnsmigrdre.
See prec. word and -ion.

## transmissible
transmissible, adj. — Formed with suff. -ible fr.
L. trdnsmissus, pp. of trdnsmittere. See transmit.
Derivative: transmissibil-ity, n.

## transmission
transmission, n. — L. trdnsmissio, 'a sending
across', fr. trdnsmissus, pp. of trdnsmittere. See
next word and -ion.

## transmit
transmit, tr. and intr. v., 1) to send over; 2) to
cause to pass through; 3) to communicate; 4)
to hand down to. — ME. transmitten, fr. L.
trdnsmittere, 'to send across, send off*, fr. trans-
and mittere, 'to send*. See mission and cp. words
there referred to.
Derivatives: transmitt-ance, transmitt-ancy,
transmitt-er, nouns.

## transmogrification
transmogrification, n. — See next word and -fica-
tion.

## transmogrify
transmogrify, tr. v., to change completely. — Fr.
earlier transmigrafy, 'to change', which is a
blend of transmigrate and modify. See Horn,
Germanisch-Romanische Monatsschrift, IX, p.
345.

## trans montane
trans montane, adj., tramontane. — L. trdnsmon-
tdnus. See tramontane,

## transmutable
transmutable, adj. — ML. trdnsmutdbilis, fr. L.
trdnsmutdre. See transmute and -able.
Derivatives: transmutabil-ity, п., transmutable-
ness, п., transmutabl-y, adv.

## transmutation
transmutation, n. — F., fr. L. trdnsmutdtionem,
ace. of trdnsmutdtio, 'a changing', fr. transmuta-
tus, pp. of trdnsmutdre. Cp. OProvenc. trans-
mutacio, Sp. transmutacion. It. transmutazione,
and see transmute and -ation.
Derivatives: transmutation-al, adj., transmuta-
tionist (q.v.)

## transmutationist
transmutationist, п., a believer in the
transmutation of metals or of species. — See prec. word
and -ist.

## transmutative
transmutative, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr.
L. trdnsmutdtus, pp. of trdnsmutdre. See next
word.

## transmute
transmute, tr. v., to change from one form into
another. — L. trdnsmutdre, 'to change, shift*, fr.
trans- and mutdre, 'to change'. See mutable.
Derivatives: transmut-er, п., transmut-ing, adj.

## transoceanic
transoceanic, adj., across the ocean. — See trans-,
ocean and adj. suff. -ic.

## transom
transom, п., a horizontal beam, a lintel. — ME.
traunsom, prob. fr. L. trdnstrum, fr. trans,
'across, beyond*. See trans- and cp. trestle,

## transpadane
transpadane, adj., on the farther (i.e. north) side
of the river Po. — L. trdnspaddnus, fr. trans-,
and Padus, 'the river Po', a name of Celtic
origin,

## transparence
transparence, transparency, n. — ML. trdnsparen-
tia, fr. trdnspdrens, gen. -entis. See next word
and -ce, resp. -cy.

## transparent
transparent, adj., that which can be seen through.
— ME., fr. ML. trdnspdrens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of trdnspdrere, 'to be transparent', formed
fr. trans- and L. par ere, 'to appear'. See appear
and -ent.
Derivative: transparent-ly, adv.

## transpierce
transpierce, tr. v., to pierce through. — MF. (=
F.) transpercer, fr. trans- and percer, 'to pierce*.
See pierce,

## transpiration
transpiration, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. transpirer. See
next word and -ation.

## transpire
transpire, intr.v., 1) to exhale; vapor, etc.; 2) to
become known, leak out; tr. v., to exhale; to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:805 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TRANSPLANT | 778 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:805 COLUMN:1 -->
excrete. — MF. (= F.) transpirer, as if fr. L.
*transspirure, 'to breathe through or across',
fr. trans- and L. spirare, 'to breathe, blow'. See
spirant.
Derivatives: transpiration (q.v.), transpir-at-ory,
adj.

## transplant
transplant, tr. v. — ME. transplaunten, fr. Late L.
transplantare, fr. trans- and L. plantdre, 'to
plant*. See plant, v.
Derivatives: transplant-ation, п., transplant-er,
n.
transpontine;, adj., lying on the other side of a
bridge. — Formed fr. trans- and L. pons, gen.
pontis, 'bridge1. See pons and adj. suff. -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## transport
transport, tr. v, — ME. transporter fr. MF. ( =
F.) transporter, fr. L. transportare, 'to carry
across', fr. trans- and portdre, 'to carry'. See
port, 'to carry'.
Derivatives: transport^ n. (q.v.), transport-able,
adj., transport-abil-ity, п., transport-able-ness,
п., transportation (q.v.), transported^ adj., trans-
port-ed-ly, adv., transport-ed-ness, п.,
transporter, п., transport-ing, adj., transport-ing-ly, adv.,
transport-he, adj.

## transport
transport, n. — ME., fr. transporter 'to transport*.
' See transport, v.

## transportation'
transportation', n. — F., fr. L. transportdtus, pp.
of transportare. See transport, v., and -ation and
cp. L. transportation gen. -dnis, 'migration'.
Derivatives: transportation-al, adj.

## transposal
transposal, п., transposition. — See next word
and subst suff. -al.

## transpose
transpose, tr. and intr. v. — ME. transposen, fr.
MF. (= F.) transposes fr. OF., fr. L.
transponere (pp. transpositus), *to place over', which
was Gallicized after F. poser, *to put, place'.
See next word and cp. compose and words there
referred to.

## transposition
transposition, n. — F., fr. ML. trdnspositionem,
ace. of trdnspositio, fr. L. transpositus, pp. of
transponere, 'to place over', fr. trans- anaponere,
'to place'. See position and cp. prec. word.
Derivative: transposition-al, adj.

## transposetive
transposetive, adj., characterized by transposition.
— Formed with suff. -ive fr. L. transpositus, pp.
of transponere. See prec. word.

## transrhenane
transrhenane, adj., on the other (i.e. the eastern)
side of the Rhine. — L. transrhenanus, fr. trans-
and Rhenanus, 'pertaining to the Rhine', fr.
Rhenus, 'Rhine*. See Rhenish.

## transsuhstantiate
transsuhstantiate, tr. v., to change into another
substance. — ML. transsubstantiatus, pp. of
trdnssubstantidre, fr. trans- and substantidre, \o
substantiate'. See substantinte.

## traussubstuntiation
traussubstuntiation, n. — ML. trdnssubstantidtid,
gen. -onis, fr. transsubstantiatus, pp. of trans-
subtantidre. See prec. word and -ion.

## transudation
transudation, n. — ModL. trdns(s)uddtio, gen.
-onis, fr. transsudates, pp. of trdns(s)uddre.
See transmit- and -ation.

## transudatory
transudatory, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ory
fr. ModL. trdns(s)uddtus, pp. of trans(s)udare.
See next word and adj. suff. -ate and -ory.

## trausude
trausude, intr. v., to pass through the pores. —
ModL. trans(s)udare, fr. trans* and L. sudare,
'to sweat'. See sudation.

## transversal
transversal, adj., transverse. — ML. trdnsversdlis,
fr. L. transversus. See next word and adj. suff.
-al.
■ Derivatives: transversal, п., transversal-ity, п.,
transversal-ly, adv.

## transverse
transverse, adj., lying across. — L. transversus,
'lying across or athwart', fr. trims- and versus,
pp. of vertere, 'to turn'. See version and cp.
traverse.
* Derivatives: transverse-ly, adv., transverse-ness,
n.

## trap
trap, п., a snare. — ME. trappe, fr. OE. treppe,
trxppe, rel. to OFfis. treppe, MDu. trap, trappe,
MLG. trappe, treppe (whence G. Treppe),
'staircase', Frankish trappa (occurring in the Salic
Law), 'trap*; from the imitative base *trap-.
Trap prop, means 'that on which an animal
steps*. From *tramp-, a nasalized form of base
*trap- derives E. tramp (q.v.) Cp. caltrop,

## entrap
entrap, trip, wentletrap.
Derivatives: trap, tr. and intr. v., to snare,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:805 COLUMN:2 -->
trapper, п., trapp-y, adj.

## trap
trap, п., any of various dark-colored igneous
rocks (petrogr.) — Swed. trapp, rel. to trappa,
'stairs', MLG. trappe, treppe, 'staircase* (see
-prec. word); so called because the rocks
frequently occur in masses rising one above
another in the form of steps.

## trap
trap, п., clothes, baggage. — ME. trappe, prob.
fr. OF. (= F.) drap, 'cloth'. See drape and cp.
trappings.

## trap
trap, tr. v., to clothe. — ME. trappen, fr. trappe,
'clothes'. See prec. word.

## Trapa
Trapa, п., a genus of plants, the water caltrop
(bot.) — ModL., abbreviation of calcitrappa,
calcitrapa, 'caltrop', which is compounded of
L. calx, gen. calcis, 'heel', and ML. trappa,
trapa, 'trap', which is Teut. origin; ср. ОЕ.
treppe, trseppe, 'trap'. See 1st trap and cp.
caltrop.

## trapan
trapan, n. and tr. v. — A var. of trepan.

## trapes
trapes, intr. v. — See traipse.

## trapeze
trapeze, п., a suspended horizontal bar used in
gymnastics. — F. trapeze^ fr. Late L. trapezium.
See trapezium.

## trapeziform
trapeziform, adj., having the form of a trapezium.
— A hybrid coined fr. Gk. τραπεζών and L.
forma, 'form, shape'. See next word and form, n.

## trapezinm
trapezinm, п., a plane figure with four sides of
which no two are parallel. — Late L., fr. Gk.
τραπέζιον, 'a little table', dimin. of τράπεζα,
'table', which stands for *πτράπεζα, a
compound lit. meaning 'provided with four feet'.
The first element represents I.-E. *qwetr-, 'four*;
see four and cp. tessares, tetarto-. The second
element is πέζα, 'foot', which is rel. to πους,
gen. πο86ς, 'foot', and cogn. with L. pes, gen.
pedis, 'foot'; see foot and cp. -pod.

## trapezius
trapezius, п., name of a pair of large, flat,
triangular muscles, together forming a trapezium
(anat.) — Medical L. (musculus) trapezius, lit.
'muscle in the form of a trapezium'; see prec.
word. The name was introduced into anatomy
by J. Riolanus, with the incorrect spelling
trapesius. The correct spelling trapezius was
established by the English anatomist William
Cowper. See Joseph HyrtI, Onomatologia ana-
tomica, pp. 560-61.

## trapezoid
trapezoid, п., a plane figure with four sides two
of which are parallel; adj., pertaining to, or
shaped like, a trapezoid. — Gk. τραπεζοειδής,
'table-shaped; trapezium-shaped', fr. τράπεζα,
'table', and -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See trapezium and -old.
Derivatives: trapezoid, trapezoid-al, adjs.,shaped
like a trapezoid.

## trappings
trappings, n. pi., cloth for a horse. — Formed fr.
trap, 'to clothe', with subst. suff. -ing.

## Trappist
Trappist,n., a monk of a branch of the Cistercian
order. — F. Trappiste, named after the
monastery of La Trappe in Normandy. For the ending
see suff. -ist.

## trapse
trapse, intr. v. — See traipse.

## trash
trash, п., rubbish. — Of Scand. origin. Cp. ON.
tros, 'rubbish, fallen twigs used for fuel', Swed.
trasa, 'rag, tatter'.
Derivatives; trash-y, adj., trash-i-ly, adv., trash-
i-ness, n.

## trass
trass, п., volcanic earth used as a hydraulic
cement. — Du. terras, tras (whence also G. Trass),
fr. F. terrasse, fr. It. terrazzo. See terrazzo.

## trattoria
trattoria, п., an Italian eating house. — It.,
'eating house*, fr. trattore, 'innkeeper, restaurant
keeper', fr. trattare, 'to treat', fr. L. tractare
freq. of trahere (pp. tractus), 'to draw', whence,
It. trarre, 'to draw'. See tract, 'region', and cp.
treat.

## traulism
traulism, п., a stammering. — Gk. τραυλισμός,
fr. τραυλίζειν, 'to lisp', fr. τραυλός, 'lisping',
which is of uncertain origin. It possibly stands
for *τρασυλός and derives fr. I.-E. base *ters-,
*t£Sr, *to be dry', whence also L. terra (for
*tersa), 'earth', lit. 'dry land'. See terra and
-ism.

## trauma
trauma, п., a bodily injury, a wound (med.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. τραύμα = Dor. τρώμα, 'a
wound, hurt, damage', rel. to Gk. τρώσις, 'a
wounding*, from the stem of τρώειν (for *τρώ-
Γειν), τιτρώσκειν, 'to wound, damage, injure'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:805 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. I.-E. base *tereu-, *treu-, whence also τρυειν,
'to wear out, distress', τέρυς, 'worn out*. Base
*tereu-, *treu- is an enlargement of base *ter-,
'to rub; to rub by turning; to turn, twist; to
bore, pierce'. See throw and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -ma.

## traumnt-
traumnt-, form of traumato- before a vowel.

## traumatic
traumatic, adj., referring to, or caused by, a
wound {med.) — Late L. traumaticus,
'concerning the healing of a wound', fr. Gk.
τραυματικός, fr. τραύμα, gen. τραύματος. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ic.

## traumatism
traumatism, п., condition produced by a trauma.
— Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk. τραϋμα, gen.
τραύματος. See trauma,

## traumato-
traumato-, before a vowel traumata combining
form meaning 'a wound, a bodily injury*. —
Gk. τραυματο-, τραυματ-, fr. τραϋμα. See
trauma.

## traumatology
traumatology, п., the study of wounds. —
Compounded of traumato- and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, One who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See -logy.

## Trautvetterla
Trautvetterla, п., a genus of plants, the false bug-
bane (bot.) — ModL., named after the Russian
botanist Ernst Rudolf Trautvetter (1808-89).
For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## travail
travail, п., 1) labor, toil; 2) the labor of
childbirth. — ME., fr. OF., 'torment,- torture'
(whence F. travail, 'work'), fr. VL. *tripalium,
'an instrument of torture'. See travail, v.

## travail
travail, intr. v., to toil. — ME. travailen,
traveller fr. OF. traveillier, travaillier, 'to torment,
toil' (whence F. travailler, 'to work'), fr. VL.
*tripaliare, prop, 'to torture with the tripalium',
fr. *tripalium, 'an instrument of torture
consisting of three stakes* [cp. Late L. trepalium, of
s.m., occurring in a decision of the Concile
tfAuxerre (year 578)], fr. L. tripdlis, having .
three stakes', fr. tres, neut. tria, 'three', and
pdlus, 'stake', See tri- and pale, 'stake'. Cp. It.
travaglio, OProvem;. trabalh, trebalh, trebail,
Sp. trabajo, Port, trabalho, 'fatigue', which all
derive fr. VL. *tripdlium. Cp. also E. travel,

## trave
trave, п., a crossbeam. — ME., fr. MF. trave,
'beam', fr. L. trabem, ace. of trabs, 'beam*. See
trabea.

## travel
travel, intr. and tr. v. — ME. travellen, travailen;
identical with travail. 'To travel' must have
first denoted 'to have a toilsome journey*,
whence arose the meaning 'to travel', in general.
This sense development appears already in
French. According to Ё. Littre, Dictionnaire de
la langue franchise, p. 2324, one of the
meanings of French travailler was 'to travel*.
Derivatives: travel, n., travel(l)-ed, adj., travel(l)-
er, п., travel(l)-ing, adj.

## travelogne
travelogne, п., a talk on travel. — A hybrid
coined by the American traveler Burton Holmes
(1870-1958) fr. trnvel and -logae, a combining
form of Greek origin.

## traverse
traverse, tr. v., to pass through, to cross; intr. v.,
to move across. — ME. traversen, fr. OF. ( =
F.) traverser, fr. travers, 'traverse' (adj.), fr.
Late L. traversus, corresponding to L.
transversus, 'lying-across'. See transverse,

## traverse
traverse, п., 1) the act of traversing; 2) that which
traverses; 3) a crosspiece, crossbeam; 4) an
obstacle. — ME. travers, partly fr. OF. travers,
*a traversing; an obstacle', fr. Late L. traversus
(see traverse, v.); partly fr. OF. traverse, 'cross-
piece', fr. Late L. trdversa, fern, of traversus,
used as a noun (see above).

## traverse
traverse, adj. — ME. travers, fr. MF., fr. OF., fr.
L. traversus, whence also OProveng. travers, It.
traverso, Catal. traves, Sp. travesio, Port, tra-
veso. See traverse, v. and cp. traverse, n.
Derivatives: traverse, п., traverse-ly, adv.

## travertin(e)
travertin(e), п., limestone used for building in
Italy. — It. travertino, alteration of tivertino, fr.
L. (lapis) Tiburtinus, ('stone) from Tibur', a
town in ancient Latium (now Tivoli).

## travesty
travesty, п., a kind of burlesque. — Prop, an

## adjective used as a noun. fr. F. travesti
adjective used as a noun. fr. F. travesti, pp. of
travestir, 'to disguise (esp. with ludicrous effect)',
fr. It. travestire, fr. tra-, 'across, beyond' (fr. L.
trans), and vestire, 'to clothe', fr. L. vestire. See
vest.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:806 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 779 | TREMULOUS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:806 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: travesty, tr. v., to make a travesty of.

## Traviata
Traviata, La, title of an opera by Verdi. — It., lit.
'the woman led astray', pp. of traviare, 'to lead
astray', lit. 'to lead beyond the way', fr. tra-,
'across, beyond' (fr. L. trans) and via (fr. L. via),
'way'. See trans- and via.

## trawl
trawl, п., a dragnet; tr. and intr. v., to fish with a
dragnet. — Prob. a var. of trail.
Derivatives: trawl-er, п., trawl-ing, n.

## tray
tray, п., a wooden vessel. — ME. tray, trey, fr.
OE. treg,tng,re\. to triow, ltreow'; see tree.The
orig. meaning of tray was 'made of wood,
wooden'.

## treacherous
treacherous, adj. — ME. trecherous, tricherous,
fr. MF. trechereus, trichereus, fr. trechier,
trickier. See next word and -ous.
Derivatives: treacherous-ly, adv., treacherous-
ness, n.

## treachery
treachery, n. — ME. trecherie, tricherie, fr. OF.
treckerie (F. tricherie), 'deceit, trickery', fr.
trechier, trickier (F. tricher), 'to deceive, cheat,
trick'. See trick, п., and -ery.

## treacle
treacle, п., 1) orig. a remedy against poison;
hence, any remedy (obsol.); 2) molasses. — ME.
triaclet fr. MF. triacle fr. OF., fr. VL. *triacula,
fr. L. theriaca, fr. Gk. &ηριακή, 'antidote'. See
theriac.
Derivative: treacl-y, adj.

## tread
tread, intr. and tr. v. — ME. treden, fr. OE. tre-
dan, rel. to OS. tredan, OFris. treda, OHG. tre-
tan, MHG., G. treten, ON. troda, Dtfh. trxde,
Swed. trada, Norw. traa Goth, trudan, 'to
tread', OHG. trotton, of s.m., MHG. trotten, 'to
run'. Cp. F. trotter, It. trottare, OProvenc. Sp.
and Port, trotar, 'to trot', which are borrowed
fr. OHG. trotton, and see trut. Cp. also trade,
treadle.
Derivatives: tread, п., tread-er, п., tread-ing, n.

## treadle
treadle, n. — ME. tredyl, *a step (to mount by)',
fr. OE. tredel, which is formed with
instrumental suff. -el, fr. tredan, 'to tread'. See prec. word
and instrumental suff. -le.
Derivative: treadle, tr. and intr. v.

## treason
treason, n. — ME. tresun, treisun, traisoun (F.
trahison), fr. L. traditionem, ace. of trdditio, 'a
giving up, delivering up, surrender'. See
tradition and cp. OProvenc. traizon, Catal. traicio,
Sp. traicion, Port, traissdo, 'treason',-which all
derive fr. L. traditionem.
Derivatives: treason-able, adj., treason-able-
ness, п., treason-abl-y, adv.

## treasure
treasure, n. — ME. tresor, tresour, fr. OF. tresor,
tresour (F. tresor), fr. L. thesaurus, fr. Gk.
θησαυρός, 'store, treasure, treasure house', a
compound word whose'jirst element prob.
derives fr. *TJ-, stem of τί*ημι, Ί put, I place'. Cp.
OProvenc. thesaur. It. tesoro, OSpan. tresoro, Sp.
tesoro, Port, tesouro, 'treasure', which all derive
fr. L. thesaurus, and see thesaurus. For the
inserted r in OF. tresor, F. tresor, cp. F./ronde, 'sling',
fr. L. i'unda (see Fronde).

## treasurer
treasurer, n. -J- ME. tresorer, fr. AF. tresorer, fr.
OF. tresorier (F. tresorier), fr. tresor (F. tresor),
'treasure'. See prec. word and agential suff. -er.

## treasure-truve
treasure-truve, п., gold or silver plate or bullion
found hidden in the earth the owner of which
cannot be traced. — AF. tresor trove (F. tresor
trouve), lit. 'treasure found'. See treasure and
trover, troubadour.

## treasury
treasury, n. — ME. tresorie, fr. OF. tresorie (F.
tresorerie), fr. tresor (F. tresor). See treasure and
-y (representing OF. -le).

## treat
treat, tr. and intr. v. — ME. treten, fr. OF. trai-
tier, tretier (F. traiter), fr. L. tractare, 'to draw,
drag; to handle, manage; to use; to discuss',
freq. of trahere (pp. tractus), 'to pull, draw'. Cp.
OProvenc. tractor. It. trattare, Sp., Port, tratar,
which all derive fr. L. tractare, and see tract,
'region'. Cp. also trentise, treaty, entreat.
Derivatives: treat, п., treatable (q.v.), treat-ee,
п., treat-er, п., treat-ing, п., treat-ment, n.

## treatable
treatable, adj. — ME. tremble, fr. OF. (= F.)
traitable, fr. L. tractdbilis, 'manageable,
yielding'. See tractable.
Derivatives: treatable-ness, п., treatabl-y, adv.

## treatise
treatise, n. — ME. tretis, fr. AF. tretiz, fr. OF.
traiteiz, fr. traitier, tretier (F. traiter), 'to treat'.
See treat.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:806 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivative: treatts-er, n.

## treaty
treaty, n. — ME. tretee, fr. MF. (= F.) tralti (F.
traiti), fr. L. tractdtus, 'a handling, managing;
a tractate, treatise', fr. tractdtus, pp. of tractare,
'to handle'. See treat and-y (representing OF. -e,
-ее). Treaty is a doublet of tractate (q.v.) Cp.
OProvenc. tractat, It. trattato, Sp. .tratado,
which all derive fr. L. tractdtus.

## treble
treble, adj., threefold, triple. — ME., fr. OF.
treble, fr. L. triplus. See triple and cp. double.
Derivative: treble, n. (q.v.), treble, tr. v., to
make threefold; intr. v., to become threefold,

## treble
treble, п., the treble or soprano part; treble voice
(mus.) — ME., fr. OF. treble, п., prop, 'a third
part (added to the alto and the bass)'. See treble,
adj.

## trebuchet
trebuchet, п., a former military engine for hurling
stones. — ME. trebochet, fr. OF. trebuchet,
'engine for hurling stones' (whence F. trebuchet,
'bird trap, snare, assay balance') backformation
fr. trebuchier, trebucher (F. trebucher), 'to
stumble', a hybrid coined fr. the pref. tres-, 'over', fr.
L. trans- (see trans-) and OF. buc, 'body, trunk',
fr. Frankish buk, 'belly', which is rel. to ON.
bukr, OE. buc, etc., 'belly'. Cp. OProvenc., Sp.,
Port, trabucar, 'to stumble', which are of the
same origin as OF. trebuchier; It. t'raboccare, of
s.m., was influenced in form by an erroneous
association of this word with It. bocca, 'mouth'.
See back, 'the body of a wagon', and cp. the
second element in sillabub and in trabuco. The
suff. -et in OF. trebuchet as well as in its
equivalents of s.m. (OProvenc. trabuquet, Sp. trabu-
quete) has diminutive force (see -et).

## trecentist
trecentist, п., a writer or artist of the trecento. —
A hybrid coined fr. It. trecento (see next word)
and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## trecento
trecento, п., the I4th cent., an important period
in Italian literature and art. — It., lit. 'three
hundred', short for mil trecento, 'one thousand
three hundred', as referring to the period
beginning with 1300. Tre derives fr. L. tres, 'three',
cento, fr. L. centum, 'a hundred'. See three and
hundred and cp. quattrocento, cinquecento.

## trecbometer
trecbometer, п., an instrument for range finding.
— Compounded of the stem of Gk. τρέχειν,
'to run', and μέτρον, 'measure'. Gk. τρέχειν
stands in gradational relationship to τροχός, 'a
wheel', lit. 'that which runs round'. See troche
and cp. words there referred to. For the second
element see meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## tree
tree, n. — ME. tre, tree, fr. OE. treow, 'tree,
wood', rel. to OS. trio, treo, ΟΝ., OFris. tre,
Goth, triu, of s.m., fr. I.-E. base *derow(o)-,
*drew(o)-, 'tree, wood, oak', whence also OI.
dru-, 'wood', ddru, 'wood, piece of wood, spear',
drumah, 'tree', Avestic dduru, dru-, 'wood',
Toch. or, 'wood', Hitt. taru, 'tree, wood', Arm.
tram (for I.-E. 'drura-mo), 'firm', Gk. δρυς,
'tree, oak', δόρυ, 'stem, tree, beam, shaft of a
spear, spear', Homeric δρυμά (neut. pi.), post-
Homeric δρυμός, 'oakwood, wood', Alb. dru,
'wood, tree, pole', druSk, 'oak', L. larix (for
-s), 'larch', durus, 'hard' (dissimilated fr.
dru-ros, for *dreu-ros, and orig. meaning 'as hard
as wood'), OSlav. efriTvo, 'tree', druva (pi.),'wood',
Russ. dromu, 'thicket, primeval forest', Lith.
derva, 'resinous wood', Olr. daw, Mir. dair, dour,
W. derwen, 'oak', Olr. dron, 'firm'. Cp. tar, 'a
viscous liquid', tray, trig, trim, true. Cp. also den-
dro-, dhoni, dinghy, doliy, 'an offering', druid,
dryad, dure, larch, the first element in drupe and
the second element in deodar, germander,
hamadryad.
Derivative: tree, tr. and intr. v.

## treenail
treenail, trenail, п., a wooden pin. —
Compounded of tree and nail,

## trefa
trefa, п., ritually unclean food. — Inexact
pronunciation of Heb. terephah. See terephah.

## trefle
trefle, п., anything resembling a trefoil. — F.
trifle, 'trefoil', fr. VL. *trifolum, refashioned fr.
L. trifolium, after Gk. τρίφυλλον. Ср. It. trifo-

## glio
glio, Rum. trifoiu, OProvenc. trefolh, Sp. trifolio,
'trefoil' (fr. L. trifolium), Sp. trebol. Port, trem,
of s.m. (fr. VL. *trifolum), and see next word.

## trefoil
trefoil, п., clover. — ME-, fr. MF. trefueil, tre-

## feuil
feuil, fr. OProvenc. trefolh. See trifolium and cp.
prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:806 COLUMN:3 -->

## treillage
treillage, п., lattice work. — F., fr. MF., fr. treille,
'vine trellis', fr. L. trichila, 'bower, arbor'
(whence also OProvenc. trelha), which seems to
be an alteration of triclinium. See triclinium.

## trek
trek, п., a journey by ox wagon. — S. Afr. Du.,
fr. MDu. treck (Du. trek), 'pull, haul', fr. tree-
ken. See trek, v.

## trek
trek, intr. v., to travel by ox wagon (S. Afr. Du.)
— S. Afr. Du., fr. MDu. trecken (Du. trekken),
'to draw, pull, tug'. See track.
Derivative: trekk-er, n.

## trellis
trellis, п., lattice. — ME. trelis, fr. MF. treliz,
'sackcloth' (later used in the sense of
'latticework, trellis'), fr. OF., prop, an adjective
meaning 'triple-twilled', fr. VL. *trilicius, fr. L. trillx,
gen. triltcis, fr. tri- and Itcium, 'thrum', which is
rel. to obllquus, 'slanting, sidelong'; see oblique.
F. treillis, 'lattice work, trellis', is a blend of OF.
treliz and F. treille, 'vine trellis' (see treillage).
Derivatives: trellis, tr. v., trellis-ed, adj.

## Trema
Trema, п., a genus of plants of the elm family
(bot.) — ModL./Tr. Gk. τρήμα, 'hole*, fr. I.-E.
Ίζ-, zero degree of base *ter-, 'to rub, rub by
turning, turn, twist', to bore, pierce'. See throw
and cp. words there referred to. Cp. also the
first element in Trematoda and the second
element in helicotrema.

## Tremandra
Tremandra, п., a genus of Australian plants (bot.)
— A ModL. hybrid coined fr. L. tremere, 'to
tremble', and Gk. άνήρ, gen. άνδρας, 'man'
(here used in the sense of 'anther'); so called
with reference to the tremulous anthers. For the
first element see tremble, for the second see
andro-.

## Tremandraceae
Tremandraceae, n. pi., a family of Australian
plants (bot.) — Formed from prec. word with
suff. -aceae.

## tremandraceous
tremandraceous, adj. — See prec. word and -ace-
ous.

## Trematoda
Trematoda, n. pi., a class of flatworms (zool.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. τρηματώδης, 'having holes',
which is compounded of τρήμα, gen. τρήματος,
'hole', and -ώδης, 'like'. See Trema and -ode,
'like'.

## tremble
tremble, intr. v. — F. trembler, fr. VL. tremuldre,
(whence also It. tremolare; Sp. temblar), fr. L.
tremulus, 'quivering, trembling, tremulous', fr.
tremere, 'to shiver, quiver, tremble', fr. I.-E.
base "terem-, *trem-, 'to tremble', whence also
Gk. τρέμειν, 'to shiver, tremble', τρόμος, *a
trembling', Lith. trimii, trlmti, Lett, tremju,
tremt, 'to chase away', OSIav. tresg, tresli, 'to
shake', Alb. Gheg trem, Tosk tremp, Ί frighten,
terrify', Goth, pramstei, 'grasshopper', Toch. A
tram-, 'to tremble', B. trem, tremem, 'a
trembling', and prob. also Gk. ταρμύσσειν, 'to
frighten, terrify'. Cp. tremendous, rrcmolant,
tremolo, Tremandra, Tremeila, tremulous,
tromometer. Cp. also terrible and words there
referred to. Base 'trem- is collateral with base
*tre-p-, for which see trepidation.
Derivatives: trembl-er, п., trembl-ing, n. and
adj., trembl-ing-ly, adv.

## Tremeila
Tremeila, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. tremere, 'to tremble'. See tremble and -ella.

## tremendous
tremendous, adj.— L. tremendus, 'causing
shivering, fearful', lit. 'that ought to be feared',
gerundive of tremere, 'to shiver, tremble'. See
tremble. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous. For the use of Latin gerundives and their
derivatives in English cp. agenda and words
there referred to.
Derivatives: tremendous-ly, adv., tremendous-
ness, n.

## tremolant
tremolant, adj., having a tremolo note (said of
musical instruments). — It. tremolante, pres.
part, of tremolare, 'to tremble', fr. VL.
tremuldre. See tremble and -ant.

## tremolite
tremolite, п., a mineral of the amphibole group.
— F. tremolite, named after the Tremola valley
in Switzerland. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## tremolo
tremolo, п., tremulous effect (music). — It., fr. L.
tremulus. See tremulous.

## tremor
tremor, п., a quivering, trembling. — L. from
the stem of tremere. See tremble and cp. temblor.

## tremulous
tremulous, adj. — L. tremulus, 'shaking,
quivering', fr. tremere; see tremble. For E. -ous, as

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:807 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TRENCH | 780 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:807 COLUMN:1 -->
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: tremuhus-ly, adv., tremulous-ness,
n.

## trench
trench, tr. and intr. v., to cut. — MF. trenchier
(F. trancher) 'to cut', fr. L. truncdre, 'to cut off
(whence also It. troncare). See truncate and cp.
trinket. In some senses the verb trench derives
fr. trench, n.

## trench
trench, п., a ditch. — ME. trencke, fr. MF.,
trencke (F. tranche), fr. trenchier. See trench, v.,
and cp. entrench,

## trenchant
trenchant, adj., ]) cutting, sharp; 2) vigorous. —
ME. trenckaunt, fr. MF. trenchant, pres. part, of
trenchier. See trench, v., and -ant.
Derivative: trenchant-lyt adv.

## trencher
trencher, п., one who trenches. — Formed fr.
trench, v., with agential suff. -er.

## trencher
trencher, п., a platter; food on a platter. — ME.,
fr. MF. trencheoir (whence F. tranchoir), fr.
trenchier. See trench, v-

## trend
trend, intr. v. — ME. trenden, 'to roll*, fr. OE.
trendan, rel. to OE. trendel, tryndel, 'circle,
ring, wheel', MHG., G. trendel, 'ball, top',
MHG.,G. trendeln/ta roll*, OE. trinde, 'around
lump', OFris. trind, trund, MLG. trunt, 'round'.
Cp. trendle, trindie, trundie.
Derivative: tren^,n.

## trendle
trendle, п., a circle, a ring; a wheel (obsol.) —
ME. trindel, fr. OE. trendel, tryndel, which is rel.
to MLG. trended trindel, 'ball, circle', MHG.
trendeln, 'to turn, rotate', trended 'top*, and to
OE. trendan, 'to roll*. See trend and cp. trindie,
trundie.

## trental
trental, п., a series of 30 masses for the dead. —
ML. trentale, fr. VL. *trenta (whence also It.
trenta, F. trente, 'thirty'), fr. L. trigintd, 'thirty*.
which is formed fr. tres, tria, 'three', with
-ginta, a suff. denoting tens. This suff. is cogn.
with Gk. -κοντά in τριά-κοντα, 'thirty', τεσ-
σαρά-κοντα, 'forty', etc. See three and pente-
conta- and cp. trigintal.

## trepan
trepan, п., a saw for perforating the skull (surg.)
— ME. trepane, fr. ML. trepanum (whence also
F. trepan), fr. Gk. τρΰπανον, 'borer*, fr. τρϋπαν,
'to bore*, fr. τρόπη, 'hole', which is cogn. with
OSlav. truplu, 'hollow', Lith. trupu, trup'eti, 'to
crumble to pieces', trupiis, 'crumbly', fr. l.-E.
*treu-p-, enlargement of base *tereu-, *treu-,
*ter-, 'to rub, bore'. See throw and cp. trephine,
Trypetidae and the first element in Trypanosoma.

## trepan
trepan, tr. v., to perforate with a trepan (surg.) —
F. trepaner, fr. trepan. See prec. word.

## trepang
trepang, п., sea cucumber. — Malay tripang.

## trephine
trephine, п., an improved form of the trepan. —
Coined by the English surgeon John Woodall
(cca. 1556-1643) fr. L. tres fines, 'three ends'
(see three and finis); so called by him with
reference to its shape. The spelling trephine
(instead of (refine) shows the influence of trepan.
Derivatives: trephine, intr. and tr.v., trephin-er, n.

## trepid
trepid, adj., trembling. — L. trepidus. See next
word and cp. intrepid.

## trepidation
trepidation, п., alarm. — L. trepiddtio, gen. -onis,
'state of alarm, agitation, consternation', fr.
trepidat-(um), pp. stem of trepidare, 'to bustle
about anxiously', fr. trepidus, 'agitated, alarmed,
restless, anxious, solicitous' (see trepid), which
stands for *trepodos, and is cogn. with OI. t%pra$s,
trpalah, 'hasty', Gk. τραπεΐν, 'to tread (grapes)',
OPruss. trapt, 'to tread', Lith. trepseti, 'to stamp
with one's feet', OSlav. trepetati,4o tremble'. All
these words derive fr. l.-E. *tre-p-, 'to shake,
tremble*. See tremble and -ation.

## Treponema
Treponema, п., a genus of spirochetes (bacteriol.)
— ModL., compounded of Gk. τρέπειν, 'to
turn', and νήμα, 'thread*. The first element
stands in gradational relationship to τρόπος, *a
turn'; see trope. For the second element see
nemato-.

## Treron
Treron, п., a genus of fruit pigeons (ornithol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. τρήρων, 'timid, shy; dove,
pigeon', prop, 'the timid bird', fr. τρέειν, 'to
fear, dread, fiee away', which stands for *τρέσειν
and is cogn. with Ol. trasati, 'trembles', trastah,
'trembling', Avestic teresaiti, 'fears, is afraid of,
L. terreo (for *terseyo), *I frighten'. See terrible
and cp. words there Teferred to.

## tres
tres, adv., very, used in musical directions. — F.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:807 COLUMN:2 -->
fr. OF. tres, fr. L. trans, 'beyond'. Cp. Olt. and
It. tra- in compounds like trafreddo (= F. tres
froid), 'very cold', and see trans-, Cp. also the
first element in trespass.

## -tresia
-tresia, combining form meaning 'perforation*
{surg.) — ModL. -tresia, fr. Gk. τρησ^ς,
'perforation*, which is rel. to τρήμα, 'hole'. See
Trema.

## tresillo
tresillo, п., a Spanish card game, ombre. — Sp.,
prop, 'a game played by three', fr. tres, 'three*,
fr. L. tres. See three.

## trespass
trespass, intr. v., I) to transgress, sin; 2) to go
unlawfully on the landof an other; 3) to encroach
upon. — ME. trespassen, fr. OF. trespasser,
'to go across or beyond' (F. trepasser, 'to die*),
fr. ML. trdnspassdre, 'to pass beyond' (whence
also Sp. traspasar, It. trapassare), fr. L. trans
(whence OF. tres), 'across', and passdre, 'to
pass*. See trans- and pass, v.

## trespass
trespass, n. — ME. trespas, fr. OF. trespas, 'a
going across or beyond, trespass' (F. trepas,
'death'), fr. trespasser. See trespass, v.
Derivatives: trespasser (q.v.), trespass-ory, adj.

## trespasser
trespasser, n. — ME. trespassour, fr. MF. tres-
passeor, fr. trespasser, 'to go across or beyond',
trespass*, fr. OF. See trespass, v., and agential
suff. -er.

## tress
tress, п., orig. a braid of hair; now a lock of hair.
— ME. tresse, fr. F. tresse, fr. OF. trece, tresse,
which is of unknown origin.
Derivatives: tress, tr. v., tress-ed, adj., tressure
(q.v.), tress,-y, adj.

## tressilate
tressilate, intr. v., to quake, tremble. — Formed
with verbal suff. -ate fr. F. tressaillir, 'to quake,
tremble', lit, *to give a start', fr. tres-, 'beyond'
(see tres), and saillir, 'to gush out, spurt out',
used in its orig. sense 'to leap, jump', fr. L.
salire. See salient.
Derivative: tressilat-ion, n.

## tressure
tressure, п., a bearing around the edge of a coat
of arms {her.) — ME. tressour, fr. treceor, OF.
tresseur, fr. trece, tresse. See tress and -ure.

## trestle
trestle, п., 1) a supporting frame; 2) a supporting
framework. — ME. trestel, fr. MF. trestel (F.
triteau), fr. OF., fr. VL. *trd(n)stellum, fr. Late
L. trd(n)stillum, dimin. of trd(n)strum,
'crossbeam'. See transom.

## tret
tret, п., allowance on goods for waste. — MF.
(= F.) trait, 'arrow, dart; turn of the scale', lit.
'a drawing, a stroke*, fr. OF. trait, pp. of traire,
*to pull, draw', fr. L. trahere. See tract, 'region',
and cp. trait, which is prop, a doublet of tret.
In ModF. traire means 'to milk', lit. 'to draw
(scil. milk)'.

## trews
trews, n. pi., trousers made of tartan (Scot.) —
Fr. trouse, which was mistaken for a plural. For
similar back formations from a singular
mistaken for a plural cp. pea and words there
referred to.
trey, п., three, at cards or dice. — ME. treye,
treis, fr. OF. trei (nom.), treis (oblique case,
whence F. trois, for both cases), fr. L. tres. See
three.

## tri-
tri-, combining form meaning 'three, thrice,
threefold'. — L. tri- or Gk. τρι-, rel. to L. tres,
neut. tria, resp. to Gk. τρεΤς, neut. τρΐα. See
three and cp. ter-.

## triable
triable, adj. — Formed from the verb try with
suff. -able.

## triacid
triacid, adj., an acid having three.hydoroxyl
radicals (chem.) — Compounded of tri- and acid.

## triad
triad, п., a group of three persons or things. —
L. trias, gen. -adis, fr. Gk. τριάς, gen. -άδος,
'the number three, a triad', formed fr. τρεις,
neut. τρία, 'three'. See tri- and cp. Trias.
Derivatives: triad-ic, triad-ic-al, adjs., triad-ism,
п., triad-ist, n.

## triage
triage, п., the act of sorting or selecting. — F., fr.
trier, 'to choose, sort, select*. See try and -age.

## triakis-
triakis-, combining form meaning 'three times'.
— Fr. Gk. τριάκις, 'three times', formed fr.
τρι- (see tri-) and ακίς, 'needle, point', which is
rel. to άκή, 'point', fr. I.-E. base *ak-, 'sharp',
whence also ακμή, 'edge', άκρος, 'pointed', L.
acus, 'needle', acuere, 'to sharpen', deer, 'sharp*.
See acrid and cp. tetrakis- and the second
element in Thrinax.

## triakisoctahedron
triakisoctahedron, п., a polyhedron of 24

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:807 COLUMN:3 -->
congruent triangular faces (geom.) — ModL.,
compounded of triakis- and octahedron,

## trial
trial, n. — AF., formed with subst. suff. -al fr.
AF. (= F.) trier, 'to choose, sort, select'. See try.

## trialogne
trialogne, п., a colloquy between three persons.
— Erroneously formed fr. tri- on the analogy of
dialogue, in which di- was mistaken for di-, pref.
meaning 'two'.

## triangle
triangle, n. — ME., fr. L. triangulum, prop. neut.
of the adj. triangulus, 'having three corners or
angles'. See tri- and angle, 'corner'.

## triangular
triangular, adj. — L. triangularis, 'pertaining to
a triangle, triangular', fr. triangulum; see prec.
word and adj. suff. -ar and cp. angnlar. The
form triangularis occurs in Classical L. only once
(in Martial, cap. 6, 579), the regular form of the
adjective being triangulus.
Derivatives: triangular-it у, п., triangular-ly, adv.

## triangulate
triangulate, tr. v. and adj. — ML. trianguldtus, fr.
L. triangulum, 'triangle*. See triangle and verbal,
resp. adj. suff. -ate and cp. angulate.

## triangulation
triangulation, n. — ML. trianguldtio, gen. -onis,
fr. trianguldtus. See prec. word and -ion,

## tri arch
tri arch, п., the ruler of one of three divisions of a
country. — Formed fr. tri- and -arch on analogy
of tetrarch.

## triarchy
triarchy, п., government by three persons. — Gk.
τριαρχία, fr. τρι- (see tri-) and -αρχία, fr.
άρχος, 'leader, chief, ruler'. See -archy and cp.
diarchy, tetrarchy, heptarchy,

## trlarii
trlarii, n. pi., Roman soldiers of the third rank
(Roman antiq.) — L. tridrii, formed fr. tres,
neut. tria, 'three* with sufl. -drii (sing, -drius).
See tri- and 1st -ary.

## Trias
Trias, п., the period preceding the Jurassic (geol.)
— G. Trias, fr. τριάς, 'the number three' (see
triad); so called by the Germans from their
threefold division of this period.

## Triassic
Triassic, adj., pertaining to the Trias. — Coined
by the German geologist Friedrich August von
Alberti (1795-1878) in 1841 fr. Trias and suff.
-ic.
Derivative: Triassic, n.

## tribalism
tribalism, п., tribal organization. — See tribe,
adj. suff. -al, and suff. -ism.

## tribasic
tribasic, adj., having three hydrogen atoms in the
molecule (chem.) — Formed fr. tri- and basic,

## tribe
tribe, n. — ME. tribu, fr. OE. tribu, fr. L. tribus,
'tribe', prob. meaning orig. 'the third part of
the Roman people', rel. to Umbr. trifu, fr.
Italic *tribku-, 'a third', which is compounded of
4tri-, 'three' (see tri-), and l.-E. *bku-, *bkeu-, 'to
be', whence also h.futHrus, 'about to be, future',
OE. beon, 'to be'; OBret. treb, 'subdivision of
the people', and Ir. treb, 'tribe', are prob. Latin
loan words. See be, future, and cp. tribunal,
tribune, tribute.
Derivatives: trib-al, adj., tribalism (q.v.), trib-al-
ly, adv., tribe-less, adj.

## tribo-
tribo-, combining form meaning 'pertaining to
friction'. — Gk. τρΐβο-, fr. τρΐβειν, 'to rub',
fr. base *terf-, *tri-, 'to rub', which appears also
in L. tri-νί, perfect of tererex 'to rub',
enlargement of base *ter-, *tr-, 'to rub. turn, twist*,
whence Gk. τείρειν (for *τέρ&ειν), 'to rub', L.
terere, 'to rub, pierce', OE. prdwan, 'to twist,
revolve'. See throw and cp. tribulation, trite,
triturate, detriment, diatribe, Tripsacum, tripsis.

## Tribolium
Tribolium, п., a genus of beetles (entomol.) —
ModL., fr. Gk. τρίβολος, 'three-pointed*, fr.
τρι- (see tri-) and the stem of βολή,- βόλος, 'a
throw', which stand in gradational relationship
to βάλλειν, 'to throw'. See ballistic and cp.
Tribulns.

## tribometer
tribometer, п., an instrument for measuring
friction. — Compounded of tribo- and Gk. μέτρον,
/measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## Tribonema
Tribonema, п., a genus of algae (bot.) — ModL.,
compounded of Gk. τρίβος, 'track, path,
rubbing', and νήμα, 'thread'. The first element is
rel. to τρΐβειν, 'to rub*; see tribo-. For the
second element see nemato-.

## tribrach
tribrach, п., a foot of three short syllables
(prosody). — Gk. τρίβραχυς, 'consisting of three
shorts*, fr. rpt- (see tri-) and βραχύς, 'short*.
See brachy-.
Derivative: tribrach-ic, adj.

## trihromo-
trihromo-, before a vowel tribrom-, combining

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:808 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 781 | TRIENTAL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:808 COLUMN:1 -->
form denoting the presence of three bromine
atoms in a molecule (ckem.) — Coined fr. tri-
and bromo-.
tribual, adj., tribal. — Formed with adj. suif. -al
fr. L. tribus, 'tribe.' See tribe.
Derivative: tribual-ly, adv.

## tribulation
tribulation, п., distress, affliction. — ME. tribu-
lacioun, fr. OF. tribulation (F. tribulation), fr.
Late L. tribulatidnem, ace of tribulatio,
'affliction', fr. L. tribulatus, pp. of tribuldre, 'to press',
in Late L. 'to afflict', fr. L. tribulum, 'a threshing
sledge', which is cogn. with Gk. τρίβειν, 'to
rub'. See tribo- and -ation and words there
referred to.

## Tribulus
Tribulus, п., a genus of plants of the bean-caper
family (bot.) — L., 'caltrop', fr. Gk. τρίβολος,
of s.m., lit. 'anything three-pointed'. See Tri-
bolhim.

## tribunal
tribunal, п., ]) court of justice; 2) place of
judgment.. — L. tribunal (tribundle), 'a raised
platform where the magistrates sat; judgment seat',
orig. 'the seat of the tribunes', prop, subst. use
of the neut. of the adj. tribundlis, 'belonging to*
the tribunes', fr. tribunus. See tribune in both
senses and adj. suff. -a],

## tribunate
tribunate, п., office of a tribune. — F. tribunal, fr.
L. tribundtus, fr. tribunus. See tribune, 'an officer',
and subst. suif. -ate.

## tribune
tribune, п., an officer (Roman hist.) — ME., fr. L.
tribunus (whence also F. tribun), orig. 'chief of a
tribe', formed fr. tribus, 'tribe', with -пй-s (for
I.-E. *no-), a suff. denoting ownership or
relation. See tribe and cp. next word. For the suff.
cp. dominus.

## tribune
tribune, п., a raised platform. — F. tribune, fr. It.
tribuna, fr. L. tribunal. See tribunal.

## tribunicial
tribunicial, less correctly tribunMal, adj.,
pertaining to a tribune. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. tribunicius (in Late L. spelled tribuni-
tius), fr. tribunus. See tribune, 'an officer'.

## tributary
tributary, adj., 1) paying tribute; 2) contributory;
п., 1) one paying tribute; 2) a stream flowing
into another. — ME. tributane, fr. L. tributartus,
'paying tribute', formed with suff. -drius fr. tri-
butum. See tribute and adj. suff. -ary.

## tribute
tribute, n. — ME. tribut, fr. L. tributum, 'stated
payment, contribution', prop, subst. use of the
neut. pp. of tribuere, 'to assign, allot, bestow,
give, grant', denominated fr. tribus, 'tribe', used
in the sense of 'division, part', orig. 'division
into three'. See tribe and cp. prec. word. Cp.
also attribute, contribute, distribute, retribution.

## rrica
rrica, п., in lichens, an apothecium with a
spherical surface (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. tricae, 'trifles,
stuff, perplexities, wiles, tricks', prob. orig.
meaning 'twisted ways', and derived fr. I.-E.
base *treik-, 'to turn, twist', which is rel. to base
*tereq-, whence torquere, 'to turn, twist'. See
torque and cp. extricate, intricate, inextricable.

## tricar
tricar, п., a motor car with three wheels. —
Formed fr. tri- and car.

## trice
trice, tr. v., to pull, to haul up. — ME. tricen,
trisen, fr. MDu. trisen, treisen (Du. trijsen), 'to
hoist', fr. trTse, 'windlass, pulley' (Du. trijs, 'race,
rope'). Cp. MLG. trlssen, 'to hoist', fr. MLG.
trisse, 'pulley, rope'.

## trice
trice, п., an instant. — Lit. 'one pull', fr. prec.
word.

## triceps
triceps, п., the great extensor muscle (anat.) — L.,
'having three heads', formed fr. tri- and caput,
'head'; see capital, adj., and cp. biceps, qnadri-
ceps. For the change of Latin й (in caput) to I
in tri-ceps see accent and cp. words there
referred to.

## Triceratops
Triceratops, п., a genus of dinosaurs (paleontol.)
\— ModL., compounded of Gk. τρικέρδϊτος,
'three-horned', and ώψ, 'eye, face, countedance'.
The first element is formed fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
κέρας, gen. κέρατος, 'horn'; see cerato-. For
the second element see -ops.

## tricerion
tricerion, п., a three-branched candlestick used
by the bishop of the Eastern Church in blessing.
— Eccles. L., fr. Eccles. Gk. τρικήριον, which
is compounded of τρι- (see tri-) and κηρός,
'wax'. See cere.

## trich-
trich-, form of tricho- before a vowel.

## trichiasis
trichiasis, п., a condition consisting in the
turning inward of the eyelashes and causing

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:808 COLUMN:2 -->
irritation (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. τριχίασις,
which is formed fr. *ρίξ, gen. τριχάς, 'hair*,
with suff. -ίασις. See tricho- and -iasis.

## trichina
trichina, п., a parasitic worm. — ModL., fr. Gk.
τρίχινος, 'hairy', fr. *ρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair'.
See tricho- and cp. prec. word.

## trichinosis
trichinosis, п., a diseased condition caused by
trichinae (med.) — Medical L., coined by Bern-
hard Rupprecht (1815-77) in 1866 fr. trichina
and suff. -osts.

## tricho-
tricho-, before a vowel trich-, combining form
meaning 'hair'. — Gk. τριχο-, τριχ-, stem of
*ρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair'. Cp. the second
element in Ir. gairb-driuch, 'brush', and seePeder-
sen, Vergleichende Grammatik der keltischen
Sprachen, I, p. J 00.

## Trichodesmium
Trichodesmium, п., a genus of algae (bot.) —
ModL., compounded of tricho- and Gk.
δεσμός, 'band'. See desmo- and 1st -ium.

## Tricholoma
Tricholoma, п., a. -genus of agarics (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Gk. *ρίξ, gen. τριχάς, 'hair',
, and λώμα, 'border'. See tricho- and loma.

## trichoma
trichoma, trichome, п., any outgrowth from the
epidermis. — Gk. τρίχωμα, 'growth of hair',
formed fr. &ρίξ, gen. τριχός, 'hair', with suff.
-ωμα. See tricho- and -oina.

## Trichomanes
Trichomanes, п., a genus of plants, the filmy fern
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L., a kind of fern, fr. Gk.
τριχομανές, which is compounded of *ρίξ, gen.
τριχάς, 'hair' and the stem of μαίνεσ*αι, 'to
rave'. See tricho- and mania.

## Trichophyton
Trichophyton, п., a genus of fungi (bot.)— ModL.,
compounded of tricho- and Gk. φυτόν, 'plant'.
See phyto-.

## trichord
trichord, adj., a three-stringed musical
instrument. — Gk. τρίχορδος, 'three-stringed',
compounded of τρι- (see tri-) and χορδή, 'chord,
string'. See chord.

## trichosis
trichosis, n^, disease of the hair (med.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -osis fr. Gk. *ρίξ, gen. τριχός,
'hair'. See tricho-.

## Trichosporum
Trichosporum, п., a genus of plants, the blush-
wort (bot.) — ModL., compounded of tricho-
and Gk. σπορά, 'seed' (see spore); so called in
allusion to the hairy seeds.

## Trichostema
Trichostema, п., a genus of plants, the blue curls
(bot.) — ModL., compounded of tricho- and Gk-
στήμα, 'stamen', which is cogn. with L. stamen,
'warp in the upright loom'. See stamen.

## trichotomous
trichotomous, adj., divided into three parts. —
Compounded of Gk. τρίχα, 'threefold', and
-τόμος, 'cut, divided' (cp. Gk. τριχοτομεϊν, 'to
trisect'). Gk. τρίχα is formed fr. τρεις, neut.
τρία, 'three', with suff. -χα; ср. δίχα, 'twofold',
which stands for δί-χα (fr. δι-, 'twice, double'),
and see tri-, three, Gk. -τόμος is rel. to τόμος,
'a cut, a piece cut off, section', 'cutting'; see
tome. For E. -ous, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, see
suff. -ous.

## trichotomy
trichotomy, п., division into three parts. — See
prec. word and -y (representing Gk. -ίά)1

## -trichous
-trichous, combining form meaning '-haired'. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. *ρίξ, gen. τριχάς,
'hair'. See tricho-.

## trichomatic
trichomatic, adj., three-colored. — Compounded
of tri- and chromatic.

## Trichuris
Trichuris, п., a genus of intestinal roundworms
(zool.) — ModL., formed fr. Gk. *ρίξ, gen.
τριχός, 'hair' and ούρα, 'tail'. See tricho- and
uro-, 'tail-'.

## trick
trick, n. — ME. trik, fr. Picard trique (F. triche),
rel. to trikier, 'to cheat', which corresponds to
OF. trechier, F. tricher, of s.m.; of uncertain
origin. G. Trick is an English loan word. Cp.
next word.
Derivatives: trick, tr. and intr. v., trick-ery, п.,
trick-ing, verbal п., trick-ing-ly, adv., trick-ish,
adj., trick-ish-ly, adv., trick-ish-ness, п., trick-
-y, adj., trick-i~ly, adv., trick-i-ness, n.

## trickle
trickle, intr. and tr. v. — ME. triklen, prob. aphet-
ic for striklen, freq. of striken, 'to strike,
proceed, flow', fr. OE. strican, 'to go, proceed'; see
strike and freq. surf. -le. The loss of the initial s-
is prob. due to the -s in tears (pi. of the noun
tear), which frequently precedes this verb.
Derivatives: trickle, п., trickl-ing, adj., trick-
ling-ly, adv., trickl-y, adj.

## trickster
trickster, n. — Formed fr. trick with suff. -ster.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:808 COLUMN:3 -->

## tricksy
tricksy, adj. — Formed fr. tricks, pi. of trick,
with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: tricksi-ly, adv., tricksi-ness, n.

## Tricladida
Tricladida, n. pi., an order of worms (zool.) —
ModL., lit. 'having three branches', fr. tri-, Gk.
κλάδος, 'branch' (see clado-), and suff. -ida; so
called from the thrtefold division of their
intestines.

## triclinic
triclinic, adj., having three axes interesecting at
oblique angles (crystallogr.) — Compounded of
tri- and Gk. κλίνειν, 'to bend'. See clinical.

## triclinium
triclinium, п., a couch extending round three sides
of a table for reclining on at meals; a room
containing such a couch; a dining room. — L.
triclinium, formed on the analogy of Latin words
like bi-sellium, 'a seat for two persons', fr. Gk.
τρικλίνιον, dimin. of τρίκλινος (scil. οίκος),
'a dining room with three couches', from the
adj. τρίκλινος, 'with three couches', which is
formed fr. τρι- (see tri-) and κλίνη, 'couch,
bed'. See clinical and cp. prec. word. Cp. also
treillage.

## tricolor
tricolor, tricolour, п., a national flag composed of
three colors. — F. tricolore, fr. earlier drapeau
tricolore, 'a flag of three colors', fr. Late L.
tricolor, 'three-colored', fr. tri- and L. color, 'color'.
See color, n.

## tricolored
tricolored, adj., having three colors. -— See prec.
word and -ed.

## tricot
tricot, п., I) a knitted fabric; 2) a kind of woolen
cloth. — F. tricot, 'knitting; (knitted) jersey',
back formation fr. tricoter, 'to knit', which is of
uncertain origin.

## tricrotism
tricrotism, п., arterial pulse with a triple beat
(physiol.) — Compounded of tri- and Gk. κρο-
τεϊν, 'to cause to rattle; to knock, beat, strike,
clap', fr. κρότος, 'the sound of rattling,
knocking, beating or clapping', whence also κρότα-
λον, 'rattle'. See Crotaius and -ism.

## tricuspid
tricuspid, adj., having three cusps or points. — L.
tricuspis, gen. -idis, 'having three points', fr. tri-
and cuspis, 'point'. See cusp and cp. bicuspid.
Derivatives: tricuspid, п., tricuspid-al, tricuspid-
ate, adjs.

## tricycle
tricycle, n. — Compounded of tri- and cycle.
Derivatives: tricycle, intr. v., tricycl-ist, n.

## Tricyrtis
Tricyrtis, п., a genus of plants of the family Me-
lanthaceae (bot.) — ModL., compounded of
tri- and Gk. κυρτός, 'bulging, swelling, convex',
which is cogn. with L. cortina, 'a round vessel',
curvus, 'bent, curved', fr. I.-E. base *(s)qer-, 'to
turn, twist'. See curve and cp. cyrto-.

## Tridacna
Tridacna, п., a genus of marine bivalves (zool.) —
L., pi-, 'a kind of oysters', fr. Gk. τρίδακνος,
'eaten at three bites', fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
δάκνειν, 'to bite'. See tongs and cp. words there
referred to.

## tridactyl
tridactyl, adj., having three fingers or toes. — Gk.
τριδάκτυλος, fr. τρι- (see tri-) and δάκτυλος,
'finger'. See dactyl.

## trident
trident, п., a three-pronged spear. — L. tridins,
gen. -entis, fr. tri- and dens, gen. dentis, 'tooth'.
See denti-.

## tridentate
tridentate, adj., having three prongs or points. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. tridens, see prec.
word.

## Tridentine
Tridentine, adj., pertaining to Trent, or the
Council of Trent (1545-63). — ML. Tridentinus, fr.
Tridentum, 'Trent'.

## tridymite
tridymite, п., a mineral consisting, like quartz, of
silica, but differing from it in form. — G. Tri-
dymit, fr. Gk. τρίδυμος, 'threefold', which was
formed fr. τρι- (see tri-) on analogy of δίδυμος,
'twin'. See deoymium. G. -it goes back to Gk.
-ϊτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## tried
tried, adj. — Prop. pp. of try.

## triennial
triennial, adj., occurring every three years. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. triennium, 'space
of three years', fr. tri- and annus, 'year'. See
annual and cp. words there referred to. For the
change of Latin ά (in annus) to e (in tri-ennium)
see accent and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: triennial, п., triennial-ity, n.

## triens
triens, п., name of a gold and a bronze coin in
ancient Rome. — L. triens, prop, 'the third part
(of an as)', fr. tres, neut. tria, 'three'. See three.

## triental
triental, adj., pertaining to a third part. — L. trien-
tdlis, 'that which contains the third part of a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:809 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TRIENTALIS | 782 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:809 COLUMN:1 -->
foot', fr. triens, gen. -entis, 'the third part of
anything; the third part of a foot'. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -al and cp. next word.

## Tricntalis
Tricntalis, п., a genus of plants, the chickweed
wintergreen (bot.) — ModL., fr^L. trientdlis (see
prec. word); so called in allusion to the height
of the plant.

## trier
trier, n. — Formed from the verb try with
agential suff. -er.

## trierarch
trierarch, п., commander of a trireme. — L. trie-
rarchus, fr. Gk. τριήραρχος, which is
compounded of τριήρης (scil. ναϋς), 'a trireme',
and άρχος, 'chief, leader'. Gk. τριήρης (whence
F. triere, 'trireme') lit. means 'having three banks
of oars', fr. τρι- (see tri-) and I.-E. *ere-, 'to
row', whence also Gk. έρέτης, 'rower', έρέσ-
σειν, Att. έρέττειν, 'to row', υπηρέτης,
'rower of a lower rank, servant, attendant', OI.
aritrah, 'rudder', aritdr-, 'rower', L. remits (for
*re-smos), 'rudder'. See blreme and cp. words
there referred to. For the etymology of Gk.
άρχος see -arch.

## trierarchy
trierarchy, п., office of a trierarch. — Gk.
τριηραρχία, fr. τριήραρχος. See prec. word and -y
(representing Gk. -ία).

## trieteric
trieteric, adj., recurring every third year
(reckoning inclusively); i.e. recurring every two years.
— L. trietericus, fr. Gk. τριετηρικός, fr. τριε-
τηρίς (scil. εορτή), 'the triennial festival', fr.
τριετής, 'of three years', formed fr. τρι- (see
tri-) and ίτος, 'year', which stands for */έτος
and is cogn. with L. vetus, 'old'. See veteran and
cp. etesian. For the ending see adj. surf. -ic.

## trifarions
trifarions, adj., threefold; arranged in three rows
(bot.) — L. trifdrius, 'of three ways, threefold,
triple', fr. trifdriam, 'in three places', prob. orig.
meaning 'that which can be expressed in three
ways', compounded of tri- and fas in the sense
of'utterance, expression, manifestation', which
is rel. to furl, 'to speak, say'. See fame, and cp.
fasti, fate. Cp. also bifarious and words there
referred to. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## trifid
trifid, adj., divided into three lobes. — L. trifidus,
'cleft in three parts', compounded of tri- and fid-,
stem of findere, 'to split, cleave'. See fissile and
cp. words there referred to.

## trifle
trifle, n. — ME. trifle, irufle, fr. OF. trufe, trufle,
'mockery, trickery', which is prob. identical
derivatively with truffle.

## trifle
trifle, intr. and tr. v. — ME. trifelen, trufien, fr.
OF. trufer, trufler, 'to mock, rail', fr. trufe,
trufle. See trifle, n.
Derivatives: trifl-er, п., trifl-ing, adj., trifl-ing-ly,
adv., trifl-ing-ness, n.

## trifoliate
trifoliate, adj., having three leaves (bot.) —
Formed fr. tri- and foilate. Cp. next word.

## Trifoilum
Trifoilum, п., a genus of plants, the clover (hot.)
— L. trifolium, 'trefoil', lit. 'three-leaved (plant)',
formed on analogy of Gk. τρίφυλλον, 'trefoil',
fr. tri- and folium, 'leaf. See folio and cp. trefoil,

## triforium
triforium, п., a gallery between the vaulting and
the roof of the aisle of a church. — ML., fr. tri-
and L. foris, 'door', which is cogn. with Goth.
daiir, 'gate', OE. dor, 'door' (see door); so called
because it often has three openings to each bay.

## triform
triform, adj., having a triple character. — L. tri-
formis, 'having three forms', formed fr. tri- and
forma, 'form, shape'. See form, n.

## triformity
triformity, n. — ML. triformitas, formed with
suff. -ity fr. L. triformis. See prec. word.

## trifurcate
trifurcate, adj., having three branches; intr. v., to
branch out into three. — Formed with suff. -ate
fr. L. trifurcus, 'having three forks or points', fr.
tri- and furca, 'fork'. See fork.
Derivatives: trifurcat-ed, adj., trifur cat-ion, n.

## trig
trig, adj., smart, trim. — ME., fr. ON. tryggr,
'firm, trusty, true'. See true,

## trig
trig, tr. v., to stop (wheels, etc.), to check. —
Prob. orig. meaning 'to make firm or solid', and
rel. to ON. tryggja, 'to- make Arm', fr. tryggr.
See prec. word.
Derivative: trig, п., a wedge or block used to
stop a wheel, etc.

## trigamist
trigamist, n. — Formed fr. trigamy with suff. -ist.

## trigamous
trigamous, adj. — Late L. trigamus, fr. Gk.
τρίγαμος, 'thrice married'. See next word. For
E. -obi, as equivalent to Gk. -ος, L. -us, see -ous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:809 COLUMN:2 -->

## trigamy
trigamy, п., triple marriage. — Late L. trigamia,
fr. Eccles Gk. τριγαμία, fr. Gk. τρίγαμος,
'thrice married', fr. tri- and γάμος, 'marriage'.
See gamo- and -y (representing Gk. -ία).

## trigeminous
trigeminous, adj., born three together; one of
three born at one birth. — L. trigeminus, 'three
born at one birth', fr. tri- and geminus, 'twin'.
See Gemini. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## trigger
trigger, n. — Orig. tricker, altered fr. Du. trekker,
fr. trekken, 'to pull'. See trek and agential suff. -er.
Derivatives: trigger, tr. and intr. v., trigger-ed,
adj., trigger-less, adj.

## trigmtal
trigmtal, п., a trental. — ML. trlgintale, fr. L. irf-
gintd, 'thirty'. See trental.

## Triglochin
Triglochin, п., a genus of plants, the arrow grass
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'three-pointed',
compounded of tri- and Gk. γλωχις, γλωχίν, 'point',
which is rel. to γλώχες (pi. of *γλώξ), 'beards
of corn', and cogn. with OSlav. glogii, 'thorn'
(see gloss, 'interpretation', and cp, next word).
The genus was so called in allusion to the three
points of the ripe fruit.

## triglot
triglot, adj., containing or speaking three
languages. — Formed fr. tri- and Gk. γλώττα, Att.
form of γλώσσα,'tongue; language'. See gloss,
'interpretation', and cp. diglot, polyglot. Cp. also
prec. word.

## triglyph
triglyph, п., an ornament in the frieze of the
Doric order. — L. triglyphus, fr. Gk. τρίγλυφος,
lit. 'thrice-carved', fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
γλύφειν, 'to carve'. See glyph and cp. diglyph.
Derivatives: triglyph-ic, triglyph-ic-αΐ, adjs.

## trigo
trigo, п., wheat. — Sp., fr. L. triticum, 'wheat'.
See Triticum.

## trigon
trigon, п., a triangle. — L. trigonum, 'triangle',
fr. Gk. τρίγωνον, 'triangle', prop. neut. of
τρίγωνος, 'three-cornered, triangular', which is
compounded of τρι- (see tri-) and γωνία,
'corner, angle'. See -gon.
Derivatives: trigonal (q.v.), trigon-ous, adj.
trigon-; form of trigono-, before a vowel.

## trigonal
trigonal, adj. — L. trigonalis, 'triangular', fr.
trigonum. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.

## trigone
trigone, п., 1) a triangle; 2) the triangular area at
the base of the urinary bladder (anat.) — F., fr.
Gk. τρίγωνον, 'triangle'. See trigon.

## trigonitis
trigonitis, п., inflammation of the trigone (med.)
— Medical L., formed fr. Gk. τρίγωνον,
'triangle' (see prec. word), with suff. -itis.

## trigono-
trigono-, before a vowel trigon-, combining form
meaning 'triangular'. — Gk. τρίγωνο-, τρι-
γων-, fr. τρίγωνος, 'triangular'. See trigon.

## trigonometry
trigonometry, п., that branch of mathematics
which deals with the relations between the sides
and angles of triangles. — ModL. trigonometria,
lit. 'measurement of triangles', compounded of
Gk. τρίγωνον, 'triangle', and -μετρία, 'a
measuring of (see trigon and -metry); first used by
the mathematician Barthelemi Pitiscus (1561-
1613) in 1595.
Derivatives: trigonometric, trigonometr-ic-al,
adjs.

## trigonous
trigonous, adj., having three angles; triangular.
— L. trigonus, fr. Gk. τρίγωνος, 'triangular'.
See trigon,

## trigraph
trigraph, п., three letters used to express a single
sound. — Compounded of tri- and Gk.
-γράφος, fr. γράφειν, 'to write'. See -graph.

## trilateral
trilateral, adj., having three sides. —
Compounded fr. tri- and lateral.

## trilby
trilby, п., a soft felt hat. — Named after Trilby,
the title and heroine of a novel by the English
artist and novelist George du Maurier (1834-
96), first published in 1894.

## trilemma
trilemma, п., choice between three things. —
Formed on analogy of Gk. δίλημμα, 'dilemma',
fr. tri- and Gk. λήμμα, 'something received,
something taken for granted; assumption,
premise'. See lemma and cp. dilemma.

## trilinear
trilinear, adj., pertaining to, or enclosed by, three
lines. — Compounded of tri- and linear.

## trilingual
trilingual, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L.
trilinguis, 'having three tongues; speaking three
languages', fr. tri- and L. lingua, 'language'. See
lingual.

## Trilisa
Trilisa, п., a genus of plants of the thistle family
{bot.) — ModL., an anagram of Liatris.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:809 COLUMN:3 -->

## triliteral
triliteral, adj., consisting of three consonants. —
Compounded of tri- and literal.

## triliteralism
triliteralism, п., linguistic law according to which
a root consists of three consonants (Semitic
pkilol.) — Formed fr. prec. word with suff. -ism.

## trilith
trilith, trilithon, п., a prehistoric monument
consisting of two large stones (megaliths)
supporting a third stone as a lintel. — Compounded of
tri- and Gk. λί&ος, 'stone'. See Iitho-.

## trill
trill, intr. and tr. v., to vibrate, shake. — It. tril-
lore (whence also F. triiler) of imitative origin
and meaning lit. 'to say trill'.

## trill
trill, п., vibration, shake. — It. trillo, fr. trillare.
See trill, n.

## Trillium
Trillium, п., a genus of plants, the wake-robin
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. tri-, 'three, threefold' (see
tri-); so called because the leaves are divided
into three parts.

## trillion
trillion, п., 1) in the United States and France, a
million raised to the second power (i.e. 1
followed by 12 zeros); 2) in Great Britain and
Germany, a million raised to the third power
(i.e. I followed by 18 zeros). — F., formed fr.
tri- on analogy of million (q.v.) Cp. biillon and
words there referred to.
Derivatives: trillion-th, adj. and n.

## trilobate
trilobate, adj., having three lobes. —
Compounded of tri- and lobate.
Derivative: trilobat-ed, adj.

## Trilobita
Trilobita, n. pi., a division of arthropods (pa-
leontol.) — ModL. See prec. word.

## triloblte
triloblte, п., any of a group of'extinct marine
arachnids (paleontol.) — ModL. TrilobXtes, name
of a division of the Arthropoda, fr. Gk. τρί-
λοβος, 'having three lobes', fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
λοβός, 'lobe'. See lobe and subst. suff. -ite.

## trilogy
trilogy, n. — Gk. τριλογία, fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
-λογία, fr. λόγος, 'word, speech, discourse,
account'. See -logy.
Derivatives: trilog-ic, trilog-ic-al, adjs., trilog-
ist, n.

## trim
trim, tr. and intr. v. — ME. trimen, fr. OE.
trymian, trymman, 'to make firm, strengthen, set
in order, array, prepare', fr. trum, 'firm, strong',
which is cogn. with OI. drumah, 'tree', Homeric
Gk. δρΰμά (п. pi.), post-Homeric δρυμός (with
G after δρυς), 'copse, thicket', Russ. dromu,
'thicket, primeval forest', Gk. δρυς, 'tree, oak',
δόρυ, 'beam, spear', OE. treow, 'tree'. See tree
and words there referred to and cp. betrim and
the second element in shelter-
Derivatives: trim, n. and adj., trim-ly, adv.,
trim-ness, п., trimm-er, п., trimm-ing, n.

## trimester
trimester, п., a period of three months. — F. tri-
mestre, fr. L. trime(n)stris, 'of three months',
which is compounded of tri- and mensis,
'month'. Cp. L. menstruus, 'pertaining to a
month, monthly', interme(n)stris, 'between two
months', and see moon. Cp. also menses,
semester.
Derivatives: trimestr-al, trimestr-ial, adjs.

## trimeter
trimeter, adj., consisting of three metrical feet; п.,
a verse of three metrical feet (pros.) — L. trime-
trus, fr. Gk. τρίμετρος, fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.
Derivatives: trimetr-ic, trimetr-ic-al, adjs.

## trindle
trindle, п., a round object; a wheel (now dial.) —
ME. trindel, fr. OE. tryndel, trendel; a collateral
form of trendle (q.v.)

## trine
trine, adj., threefold. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) trln
(fem. trine), fr. OF., fr. L. trinus, 'threefold,
triple', from the pi. trim, 'three each', fr. *tris-ni
(OL. s generally disappeared before following m
and n; cp. OL. cosmis, L. cdmis, 'courteous,
affable', and L. primus, fr. *prls-mos, 'first'). See tri-.
Derivatives: trine, п., trin-al, adj., trin-al-ity, n.

## tringie
tringie, п., 1) a curtain rod; 2) a narrow, square
molding. — F., alteration of MF. tingle (which
still occurs in Diderot's Encyclopedic), fr. MDu.
(= Du.) tingel, tengel, lit. 'wedge, piece of
wood, lath'.

## Trinitarian
Trinitarian, adj. and n. — ModL. Trinitdrius, fr.
L. trinitas. See trinity and -arian.

## trinitrotoluene
trinitrotoluene, п., a high explosive, abbreviated
into TNT (eke m.) — Coined fr. tri-, nitni- and
toluene.

## trinity
trinity, n. — ME. trinite, fr. OF. trinite (F. trini-
ti), fr. L. trinitdtem, ace. of trinitds, fr. trinus,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:810 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 783 | TRITELEIA -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:810 COLUMN:1 -->
'threefold'. See trine and -ity. Cp. It. trinita, Sp.
trinidad, which also derive fr. L. trinitdtem.

## trinket
trinket, п., 1) a small ornament; 2) a trifle. —
ME. trenket, 'a small, ornamental knife', fr.
ONF. trenquet (F. trancket), fr. trancker, 'to
cut'. See trench, v.
Derivatives: trinket-ry, п., trinket-y, adj.

## trinomial
trinomial, adj., consisting of three terms (algebra).
— Formed fr. tri- and stiff, -nomial, on analogy
of binomial (q.v.)
Derivatives: trinomial, п., trinomial-ity, п., tri-
nomial-ly, adv.

## trinomlnal
trinomlnal, adj., having three names. — Formed
fr. tri- and nominal.

## trio
trio, n. — It., formed fr. L. tres, neut. tria, 'three'
(see three), on analogy of It. duo, archaic form
of due, 'two' (see duo).

## triolet
triolet, п., a poem of eight lines with the rhyme
scheme abaaabab. — F., dimin. formed fr. It.
trio. See prec. word and -et.

## trior
trior, n. — A var. of trier.

## triose
triose, п., a simple sugar in which the molecule
contains three carbon atoms and three oxygen
atoms (chem.) — Coined fr. tri- and subst. suff.
-ose.

## Triasteum
Triasteum, п., a genus of plants, the feverwort
(bot.) — ModL., abbreviation of Triosteospe-
rum, which is compounded of tri-, Gk. δστέ-
ov, όστοϋν, 'bone' (see osteo-), and σπέρμα,
'seed' (see sperm); so called in allusion to the
three bony nutlets of the fruit.

## trip
trip, intr. and tr. v. — ME. trippen, trepen, fr. OF.
triper, tripper, neper, 'to dance', which is of
Teut. origin. Cp. Fris. trip(pel)je, LG. trippen,
trippeln, MDu. trepelen, Du. trippelen, G. trip-

## peln
peln, 'to trip', and OE. treppan, 'to tread'. These
words stand in gradational relationship to MDu.
trappan, 'to tread under one's foot'. See trap,
'snare', and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: trip, п., tripp-er, п., tripp-ing, adj.
and п., tripp-ing-ly, adv., tripp-ing-ness, n.

## tripara
tripara, п., a woman who has borne three children
(med.) — Medical L., fr. tri- and L. parid, pa-
rire, 'to bring forth, beget, bear'. See parent.

## tripartite
tripartite, adj., divided into three parts. — ME.,
fr. L. tripartitus, fr. tri- and partitas, pp. of par-
tiri, 'to share, part, divide'. See partite and cp.
unipartite.

## tripartition
tripartition, п., division into three parts.—
Formed fr. tri- and partition. Cp. prec. word.

## tripe
tripe, п., part of the stomach of a ruminant. —
F., fr. It. trippa, or Sp. tripa, ult. prob. fr. Arab.
tharb (VArab. pronunciation therb), 'fold of a
piece of cloth'.

## tripedal
tripedal, adj., having three feet. — L. tripeddlis,
fr. tri- and peddlis, 'of a foot', fr. pes, gen. pedis,
'foot'. See pedal.

## triphane
triphane, п., spodumene (mineral.) — F., fr. Gk.
τριφανής, 'appearing threefold', fr. τρι- (see
tri-) and -φανής, from the stem of φαίνεσ&αι,
'to appear', passive of φαίνειν, 'to show'. See
phantasm.

## Triphasia
Triphasia, п., a genus of plants of the family Ru-
taceae (bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τριφάσιος,
'threefold, triple'; so called from the triple
division of corolla, calyx and leaves. Gk. τριφάσιος
stands pern, for *τρι- φάτ(θς and lit. means
'struck three times' (cp. in Hesychius δίφατον,
'double*, for *δι-φάτιος, fr. δίφατος, 'double'),
and is formed fr. τρι- (see tri-) and φατός,
'struck', pp. of *είνειν, 'to strike', which stands
for *gti"in-yein, fr. I.-E. *gwhen-, 'to strike, kill',
whence also OI. hanti, 'he strikes', L. de-fendere,
'to ward off, keep away, defend'. See defend and
cp. words there referred to.

## triphibian
triphibian, adj., triphibious. — See next word and
-ian.

## triphibious
triphibious, adj., suitable for war on land, at sea
and in the air. — Lit. 'living a triple life (i.e. in
three elements); coined by Sir Winston
Churchill (1874-1965) on analogy of amphibious, mis-
divided into am-phibious. Since amphibious is
formed fr. Gk. άμφί-βιος, 'living a double life'
(see amphibious), the correct form would be tri-
bious.

## triphthong
triphthong, п., three vowel sounds pronounced in
one syllable. — Formed fr. tri- and Gk. φδόγ-
γος, 'sound, voice, vowel', on analogy of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:810 COLUMN:2 -->
diphthong (q.v.)

## tripl-
tripl-, form of triplo- before a vowel.

## triplane
triplane, п., an airplane with three supporting
planes. — Formed fr. tri- and plane, 'airplane'.

## Triplaris
Triplaris, п., a genus of plants of the buckwheat
family (bot.) —<t ModL., fr. L. triplaris,
'threefold', fr. trip/us. See triple and -ary (representing
L. -oris).

## triple
triple, adj., threefold. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr.
L. triplus, 'threefold, triple', formedfr.ii-й, neut.
tria, 'three', on analogy of duplus, 'double',
which derives fr. duo, 'two'. See three and double
and cp. treble. Cp. also triplet, triplex.
Derivatives: triple, п., tripl-et, n.

## triple
triple, tr. and intr. v., or become three times as
great; to make threefold; to multiply by three.
— ME. triplen, fr. Late L. triplare, fr. L. triplus.
See triple, adj.

## triplex
triplex, adj., triple. — L., 'threefold, triple', cogn.
with Gk. τρίπλαξ, of s.m.; compounded of L.
tri- (resp. Gk. τρι-) and suff. -plex (resp.
-πλαξ), '-fold'. See tri- and duplex.
Derivative: triplex, n.

## triplicate
triplicate, adj. — ME., fr. L. triplicdtus, pp. of
triplicdre, 'to treble, triple', fr. triplex, gen. -icis.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: triplicate, n.

## triplicate
triplicate, tr. v. — L. triplicdtus, pp. of triplicdre.
See prec. word.

## triplication
triplication, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. Late
L. triplicationem, ace. of triplicdtio, Тт. L.
triplicdtus, pp. of triplicdre. See triplicate, adj., and
-ion.

## triplicity
triplicity, n. — ME. triplicite, fr. ML. triplicita-
tem, ace. of triplicitas, fr. L. triplex, gen. tripli-
cis. See triplex and -ity and cp. duplicity.

## triplo-
triplo-, before a vowel tripl-, combining form
meaning 'triple'. — See triple.

## tripod
tripod, п., a three-legged stool, table, etc. — L.
tripus, gen. -podis, fr. Gk. τρίπους, gen.
τρίποδος, 'tripod', lit. 'anything having three feet',
fr. τρι- (see tri-) and πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'.
See -pod and cp. tripos. Cp. also trivet.

## tripoli
tripoli, п., a friable siliceous deposit, the rotten
stone. — Named after the town Tripoli in North
Africa.

## tripos
tripos, п., honors examination at Cambridge
University in England. — Prob. a 'back formation'
