of the nominative fr. the Latin genitive tripodos,
on analogy of Latin nouns endings in -os. The
correct form is tripus (see tripod). The
examination was so called from the three-legged stool on
which formerly a B.A. sat conducting a
humorous discussion with candidates for degrees.

## Tripsacum
Tripsacum, п., a genus of plants, the gama grass
(bot.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τρΐψις, 'a rubbing,
friction, resistance to touch' (see next word);
prob. so called in allusion to the polished
appearance of the spike.

## tripsis
tripsis, п., trituration (med.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. τρΐψις, 'a rubbing, friction', fr. τρίβειν,
'to rub', which is cogn. with L. tri-n, perfect of
terere, 'to rub'. See tribo- and cp. prec. word.

## triptote
triptote, п., a noun having only three cases (gram.)
— Late L. triptdta, pi., fr. Gk. τρίπτωτα, pi. of
τρίπτωτον, which is prop, the neut. of the
adjective τρίπτωτος, 'having only three cases', fr.
τρι- (see tri-) and πτωτός, 'fallen', verbal adj.
of πϊπτειν, which stands for πΐ-πτειν, fr. *pt-,
zero degree of I.-E. base 'pet-, 'to fiy, to fall'.
See feather and cp. symptom and words there
referred to.

## triptych
triptych, п., picture or carving on three panels
side by side. — Gk. τρίπτυχος, 'threefold,
consisting of three layers or plates', fr. τρι- (see
tri-) and *πτύξ, gen. πτυχός, 'fold, layer', which
is rel. to πτύσσειν, 'to fold'. Cp. diptych, poly-
ptych.

## triquetra
triquetra, п., an ornament having three angles. —
L. triquetra, fern, of triquetrus, 'having three
corners', fr. tri- and *q"adros, 'sharp', which is
cogn. with ON. hvatr, OE. hwset, 'sharp', hwet-
tan, 'to sharpen'; see whet.
Derivative: triquetr-ic (q.v.)

## triquetric
triquetric, adj., triquetrous. — See prec. word and
adj. suff. -ic.

## triquetrous
triquetrous, adj., having three angles; triangular.
— L. triquetrus. See triquetra. For E. -ous, as

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:810 COLUMN:3 -->
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## trireme
trireme, п., a galley having three banks of oars.
— L. triremis, formed fr. tri- and remus, 'oar'.
See blreme and cp. words there referred to.

## tris-
tris-, combining form meaning three times. —
Gk. τρισ-, fr. τρίς, 'three times'. See tri-.

## Trisaglon
Trisaglon, п., a Greek eccles. hymn. — Gk.
τρισάγιον, prop. neut. of τρισάγιος, 'three
times holy', fr. τρισ (see tris-) and άγιος, 'holy'.
See hagio-.

## trisect
trisect, tr. v., to cut or divide into three'parts. —
L. trisectus, pp. of trisecare, 'to cut into three',
fr. tri- and secure, 'to cut'. See section and cp.
bisect, dissect, intersect.
Derivatives: trisect-ed, adj., trisect-ion, п.,
trisect-or, n.

## triseme
triseme, п., a syllable of three times (pros.) — Late
L. trisemus, fr. Gk. τρίσημος, fr. τρι- (see tri-)
and σήμα 'sign'. See semantics,

## trisemic
trisemic, adj., having the length of three times
(pros.) — See prec. word and adj. suff. -Ic.

## Trisetum
Trisetum, п., a genus of plants (bot.) — ModL.,
fr. tri- and L. saera, 'bristle'. See seta and cp.
words there referred to.

## triskelion
triskelion, п., a figure consisting of three branches
radiating from a center. — Formed fr. Gk.
τρίσκελής, 'three-legged', fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
σκέλος, 'leg'. See isosceles,

## trismus
trismus, п., lockjaw (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
τρισμός, 'a squeaking, creaking; a grinding,
rasping', from the imitative base *(s)trig-,
whence also στρίζειν (for "strig-yein), 'to
squeak, creak', στρίγξ, στρίξ, στλίξ, 'owl,' lit.
'the screeching bird'. See Strix and cp. the
second element in Amphitrite.

## Tristania
Tristania, п., a genus of shrubs and trees (bot.) —
Named after the French botanist Jules Tristan
(1776-1861). For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## triste
triste, adj., sad, sorrowful. — ME. trist, triste, fr.
MF. (= F.) triste, fr. L. tristis, which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. next word and Tristram,

## tristeza
tristeza, п., an infectious disease of grafted citrus
trees. — Port., lit. 'sadness, sorrow', fr. L. tristi-
tia, fr. tristis. See prec. word.

## tristich
tristich, п., a stanza of three lines. — Formed fr.
tri- and Gk. στίχος, 'row, line, rank; verse', on
analogy of distich (q.v.) Cp. Gk. τριστιχία, 'a
union of three verses'.

## tristichous
tristichous, adj., arranged in three rows. — Gk.
τρίστιχος, 'in three rows', fr. τρι- (see tri-) and
στίχος, 'row'. See prec. word. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to Gk. -ος, see -ous.

## Tristram
Tristram, masc. PN.; esp. name of a medieval
legendary hero. — A blend of W. Drystan, which
is rel. to drust, drest, 'tumult', and of F- triste,
'sad', fr. L. tristis. See triste.

## trisyllabic
trisyllabic, adj., having three syllables. — F. tri-
syllabique, formed with suff. -ique fr. L. trisyl-
labus, fr. Gk. τρισύλλαβος, fr. τρι- (see tri-)
and συλλαβή, 'syllable'. See syllable and cp.
syllabic.
Derivatives: trisyllabic-al, adj., trisyllabic-al-ly,
adv.

## trisyllable
trisyllable, п., a word of three syllables. —-
Formed fr. tri- and syliabie. See prec. word.

## trit-
trit-, form of trito- before a vowel.

## tritagonist
tritagonist, п., character taking the third part in
the Greek drama. — Gk. τριταγωνιστής,
compounded of τρίτος, 'third', and αγωνιστής,
'combatant; actor'. See trito- and agonist and
cp. words there referred to.

## tritaph
tritaph, п., a tomb containing three small
chambers (Greek archaeol.) — Formed fr. tri- and Gk.
τάφος, 'tomb, grave, funeral', which is rel. to
τάφρος, 'ditch, trench', &άπτειν, 'to bury'
(passive aor. έτάφην). See cenotaph,

## trite
trite, adj., hackneyed. — L. tritus, pp. οι terere
(perf. tri-vt), 'to rub, thresh, grind; to wear

## away'
away', fr. I.-E. base *ter-, 'to rub, rub by

## turning
turning, turn, twist; to pierce'. See throw, and words

## there referred to and cp. esp. Triticuin
there referred to and cp. esp. Triticuin, tritarate,

## attrition
attrition, attritus, contrite, contrition,

## detriment and the second element in lithotrity
detriment and the second element in lithotrity, Sep-
tentrion.
Derivatives: trite-ly, adv., trtte-ness, n.

## Triteleia
Triteleia, п., a genus of plants of the lily family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. tri- and'Gk. τέλειος, 'com-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:811 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TRITHEISM | 784 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:811 COLUMN:1 -->
plete, accomplished, perfect', fr. τέλος, gen.
τέλεος, 'end, result' (see tele-); so called in
allusion to its trimerous flowers.

## tritheism
tritheism, п., belief in the existence of three
distinct gods. — Formed fr. tri- and 1st theism.

## tritheist
tritheist, п., believer in tritheism. — See prec.
word and -ist.

## Trithrinax
Trithrinax, п., a genus of fan palms (бог.) —
ModL., fr. tri- and Gk. θρΐναξ, 'trident, three-
pronged fork' (see Thrinax); so called from the
form of the leaves.

## Triticuin
Triticuin, п., a genus of cereal grasses, the wheat
(bot.) — L., trtticum, 'wheat', lit. 'grain for
threshing', from tritus, pp. of terere 'to rub,
thresh, grind'. See trite and cp. trigo. For sense
development cp. L. grdnum, 'grain', which is
cogn. with OI. jirnah, 'ground to powder'.

## trito-
trito-, before a vowel trit-, combining form
meaning 'third'. — Gk. τρίτο-, τριτ-, fr. τρίτος,
'third'. See third and three and cp. tierce.

## Triton
Triton, п., a minor sea-god, son of Poseidon and
Amphitrite (Greek mythol.) — L. Triton, fr. Gk.
Τρίτων, which is cogn. with Olr. triath, gen.
trethan (for OCeltic "triaton-), 'sea'.

## Triton
Triton, п., 1) a genus of snails (zool.); 2) (not cap.)
any of several aquatic salamanders. — Fr. prec.
word.

## tritone
tritone, п., an interval consisting of three tones
(mus.) — Gk. τρίτονος, 'of three tones', fr. τρι-
(see tri-) and τόνος, 'pitch of the voice, musical
note'. See tone.

## triturabie
triturabie, adj. — See next word and -able.

## triturate
triturate, tr. v., to rub, grind. — L. trituratus, pp.
of triturare, 'to grind to powder', freq. of terere,
pp. tritus, 'to rub, thresh, grind'. See trite and
verbal suff. -ate.

## trituration
trituration, n. — Late L. trituratid, gen. -onis, fr.
L. trituratus, pp. of triturare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## triumph
triumph, n. — ME. triumphe, fr. MF. triumphe
(F. triomphe), fr. OF., fr. L. triumphus, 'solemn
entrance of a general into Rome after an
important victory', fr. triumphe, an exclamation used
in the processions of the Arval brothers, fr. Gk.
θρίαμβος, 'procession in honor of Bacchus',
introduced into Rome through the medium of the
Etruscans. Like ίαμβος (see iamb) and
διθύραμβος (see dithyramb), θρίαμβος is a loan
word of pre-Hellenic origin. Cp. trump, 'a
winning card'. For the change of Greek ά (in
θρίαμβος) to и (in L. triumphus) cp. aplustre and
words there referred to.

## triumph
triumph, intr. v. — L. triumphare, fr. triumphus.
See triumph, n.
Derivatives: triumph-er, п., triumph-ing, adj.,
triumph-ing-ly, adv.

## triumphal
triumphal, adj. — ME., fr. L. triumpkdlis, fr.
triumphus. See triumph, п., and adj. suff. -al.

## triumphancy
triumphancy, also triuraphance, n. — Formed
from next word with suff. -cy, resp. -ce.

## triumphant
triumphant, adj. — L. triumpkdns, gen. -amis,
pres. part, oftriumphare. Seetriumph,v.,and -ant.
Derivative: triumphant-ly, adv.

## triumvir
triumvir, п., one of three men in the same office
or of the same authority. — L., back formation
fr. pi. gen. trium virorum, trium virum ,'(one) of
the three men'. See tri- and virile and cp.
duumvir, decemvir.

## triumviral
triumviral, adj. — L. triumvirdlis, 'pertaining to
the triumvirs', fr. triumvir. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -a).

## triumvirate
triumvirate, п., the office or dignity of a triumvir.
— L. trtumvirdtus, fr. triumvir. See triumvir and
subst. suff. -ate.

## triune
triune, adj., three in one. — Compounded of tri-
and L. unus, 'one'. See one.

## trlunity
trlunity, n. — Formed fr. prec. word with suff.
-ity.

## trivalent
trivalent, adj., having a valency of three (chem.)
— Formed fr. tri- and L. valens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of valere, 'to have power'. See -valent.

## trivet
trivet, п., a three-legged iron stand. — Late ME.
trevet, fr. OE. trefet, fr. L. tripedem, ace. of
tripes, 'having three feet', fr. tri- and pes, gen.
pedis, 'foot'. See pedal and cp. tripod.

## trivial
trivial, adj., trifling. — F-, fr. L. trivialis, prop,
'that which belongs to the crossroads', hence
also meaning 'that which may be found

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:811 COLUMN:2 -->
everywhere, commonplace, vulgar', fr. trivium, 'a
place where three roads meet'. See trivium and
adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: trivial-ism, п., trivial-ity, п.,
trivialize, tr. v., trivial-ly, adv., trivial-ness, n.

## trivium
trivium, п., the three liberal arts in medieval
schools. — ML., fr. L. trivium, *a place where
three roads meet, crossroad, public square', fr.
tri- and via, 'way'. See via and cp. prec. word.
Cp. also quadrivium.

## -trix
-trix, femin. agential suff. corresponding to the
masc. suff. -tor. — L., standing for 'tr-i-x. The
first element represents the zero degree of suff.
-tor (q.v.) The second element is an enlargement
of the I.-E. suff. *-f-, Cp. e.g. L. dator, 'giver',
fern, datrlx, corresponding to OI. da-tar, resp.
dd-tr-i.

## trocar
trocar, п., a surgical instrument. — F. trocart, tro-
quart, fr. trois quarts, lit. 'three quarters',
corrupted fr. orig. trois carres, lit. 'three edges' (cp.
lame a trois carres, 'a three edged sword'), fr. L.
tres (see three) and quadra, 'square' (see
quadrate and square); so called from its triangular
point.

## troch-
troch-, form of trocho- before a vowel.

## trocha
trocha, п., a line of fortifications (Sp. Amer.) —
Sp., 'a narrow crossroad', fr. L. trdducta, fem.
pp. of trdducere, 'to lead across'. See traduce.

## trochaic
trochaic, adj., pertaining to a trochee (pros.) — L.
trockalcus, fr. Gk. τροχαϊκός, fr. τροχαίος. See
trochee and adj. suff. -ic.
Derivative: trochaic, n.

## trochanter
trochanter, п., a rough process on the upper
extremity of the femur (anat.) — Medical L., fr.
Gk. τροχαντήρ, 'either of two processes at the
upper part of the thighbone', coined by Galen
fr. τροχαν, 'to be round', fr. τροχός, 'wheel'. See
troche.
Derivative: trochanter-ic, adj.

## trochantin
trochantin, п., 1) (obsol.) the lesser trochanter
(anat.); 2) the proximal segment of the
trochanter of an insect's leg (entomol.) — Coined
by the French anatomist Francois Chaussier
(1746-1828) fr. trochanter. See Joseph Hyrtl,
Onomatologia anatomica, p. 567.

## troche
troche, п., a small, circular tablet of drugs
(pharm.) — Gk. τροχός, 'anything round, a
wheel", lit. 'that which runs', fr. τρέχειν, 'to run',
whence also τρόχος, 'a running, course'; fr. I.-E.
base *dhregh, 'to run', whence also Olr. drock
(fr. Celtic *drogon), 'wheel', Lett, drast, Lith.
pa-droSti, 'to run fast'. Arm. durgn (gen. drgan),
'potter's wheel' (for "dhrdgh- or "dhorgh-). Cp.
trechometer, trochanter, trochantin, trochee, tro-
chlius, trochlea, trocho-, trochoid, truck,
'vehicle*. Ср..also trachelo-.

## trochee
trochee, п., a metrical foot consisting of two
syllables, the first long and the second short (pros.)
— L. trockaeus, fr. Gk. τροχαίος (scil. πους),
'tripping, running (foot)', which is rel. to
τρόχος, 'a running, course'. See prec. word.

## trochilics
trochilics, п., the science of rotary motion. —
Formed with suff. -ics fr. Gk. τροχιλία, 'system
of pulleys, roller of a windlass', fr. τροχός,
'wheel'. See troche.

## trochilus
trochilus, п., the crocodile bird; (cap.) a genus of
hummingbirds (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. L., a
small bird, perh. 'the golden-crested wren', fr.
Gk. 'crocodile bird; wren", lit. 'a runner', fr.
τρέχειν, 'to run'. See troche and cp. words there
referred to.

## trochlea
trochlea, п., a pulleylike cartilage in a joint (anat.)
— L., 'a case containing one or several pulleys,
a block', fr. Gk. τροχιλία. See trochilics and cp.
truckie, n.
Derivatives: trochle-ar, trochle-ary, trochle-ate,
adjs.

## trocho-
trocho-, before a vowel troch-, combining form
meaning 'wheel'. — Gk. τροχό-, τροχ-, fr.
τροχός, 'wheel'. See troche.

## trochoid
trochoid, adj., wheel-shaped. — Compounded of
troch- and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form,
shape'. See -old.
Derivative: trochoid, n.

## trochometer
trochometer, п., the same as trechometer. —
Compounded of trocho- and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'.
See meter, 'poetical rhythm', and cp.
trechometer.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:811 COLUMN:3 -->

## troco
troco, п., an obsolete English game. — Prob. alt.
of It. trucco, 'trucks'. See trucks,

## trod
trod, past tense of tread. — ME. troden, past
tense pi., altered fr. treden, past tense pi. of tre-
den, 'to tread'. See tread and next word.

## trodden
trodden, pp. of tread. — ME. troden, altered fr.
treden, pp. of treden, 'to tread' (see tread), under
the influence of such pp.s as ME. (= E.) stolen
(fr. stelen, 'to steal'), etc.

## troglodyte
troglodyte, п., cave dweller. — L. troglodytae, pi.,
fr. Gk. τρωγλοδύτης, 'one who creeps into
holes', which is compounded of τρώγλη, *a
hole', prop, 'a hole formed by gnawing' (fr.
τρώγειν, 'to gnaw'), and δύειν, 'to enter'. For
the first element see trout and cp. tragedy. For
the second element see adytum.
Derivative: troglodyt-ic, adj.

## Troglodytes
Troglodytes, п., a genus of wrens (ornithol.) —
ModL. See prec. word,

## trogon
trogon, п., any of a family of brilliantly plumed
birds (the Trogonidae) — ModL., lit. 'the
gnawer', fr. Gk. τρώγων, pres. part, of τρώγειν, 'to
gnaw'. See troglodyte,

## troika
troika, п., carriage drawn by three horses
abreast. — Russ. troika, formed with dimin. suff.
-ka fr. troe, 'three, threefold', a collateral form
of tri. See three.

## Trojan
Trojan, adj. and n. — ME., fr. L. Trojdnus, fr.
Trdia, Troja, 'Troy', fr. TrOs (fr. Gk. Τρως),
name of a king of Phrygia, the mythical founder
of Troy. For the ending see suff. -an.

## troll
troll, tr. and intr. v., to roll; to fish by trailing. —
ME. trollen, 'to roll', fr. MF. trailer, 'to roam,
wander' (whence F. troler, 'to drag about,
wander'), fr. OHG. trollen, 'to run with short
steps' (whence MHG. trollen, of s.m., G. trollen,
'to toddle along, trudge'), which is rel. to MHG.
trolle, *a ghostly monster; an awkward fellow'.
MHG. trollen orig. meant, to move about like
a monster'. See next word and cp. trolley,
Trollius, trollop, trull.
Derivatives: troll-er, п., troll-ing, n.

## troll
troll, п., a supernatural being (Scand. mythol.) —
ΟΝ., 'monster' (whence Swed. and Norw. troll,
Dan. trold, 'troll'), which is rel. to MHG. trolle.
See prec. word.

## trolley
trolley, trolly, n. — Prob. derived fr. troll, 'to
roll', and lit. meaning 'that which rolls'.

## Trollius
Trollius, п., a genus of plants, the globeflower
(bot.) — ModL., fr. G. Trollblume, 'globeflower',
fr. MHG. trolle, 'ghostly monster; awkward
fellow', rel. to ON. troll, 'monster'. See troll,
'monster'.

## trollop
trollop, п., a slatternly woman. — Fr. troll, 'to
roll' (q.v.) For sense development cp. F. rou-
leuse, fr. router, 'to roll'.

## trombone
trombone, п., a powerful brass wind instrument
(music). — It., formed fr. tromba, 'trumpet',
with the augment, suff. -one. See trump,
'trumpet', and -oon and cp. next word.

## trommel
trommel, п., a sieve for screening rock, ore, etc.
G. Trommel, 'drum', fr. MHG. trumel, fr.
trume, trumme, which is of imitative origin. Cp.
drum and words there referred to.

## tromometer
tromometer, п., an instrument for measuring
earth tremors. — Compounded of Gk. τρόμος,
'trembling', and μέτρον, 'measure'. The first
element is rel. to τρέμειν, 'to shiver, tremble',
and cogn. with L. tremere, of s.m; see tremble.
For the second element see meter, 'poetical
rhythm".

## trompe
trompe, п., an apparatus for carrying air to the
furnace. — F., 'trumpet, horn, blast engine,
proboscis'. See trump, 'trumpet', and cp. words
there referred to.

## -tron
-tron, suff. used in electricity and chemistry. —
Coined from the ending -tron in electron. Cp.

## dynatron
dynatron, kenotron, magnetron, etc.

## trona
trona, п., sodium carbonate (mineral.) — Swed.,

## fr. Arab
fr. Arab, iron, fcphetic for natrun, whence
natron (q.v.)

## trone
trone, п., I) a weighing machine; 2) a market
place. — OF., 'balance', fr. L. trutina, fr. Gk.
τρϋτάνη, 'tongue of the balance, balance', orig.
'the hole in which the tongue of the balance
moves about', which stands for *tru-tt nd and is
rel. to τρόειν, 'to rub, wear out', τρϋμα, 'hole',
τείρειν (for *τέριειν), 'to rub, wear away', fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:812 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 78S | TROWEL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:812 COLUMN:1 -->
l.-E. base *ter-, 'to rub, to rub by turning, to
turn, to twist; to pierce'. See throw and cp.
words there referred to.

## troop
troop, n. — MF. (= F.) troupe, fr. OF. trope, fr.
Late L. troppus, 'herd', fr. Frankish *prop,
metathesis of *porp, 'crowd, gathering, village',
which is rel. to OE. porp, prop; see thorp. Sp.
tropa, 'troops, soldiers', is a French loan word.
Cp. troupe.
Derivatives: troop, intr. and tr. v., troop-er, n.

## troostite
troostite, п., a solid solution of carbon in iron
{mineral.) — Named after the French chemist
Louise-Joseph Troost (1835-1911). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## troostite
troostite, п., a variety of willemite (mineral.) —
Named after the American geologist Gerard
Troost(ai&d in 1850). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Tropaeolum
Tropaeolum, п., a genus of S. American climbing
plants ,(bot.) — ModL., coined by Carolus
Linnaeus (1707-78) fr. Gk. τρόπαιον, 'trophy'
(see trophy and dimin. suff. -ole); so called
by him because the shield-shaped leaves and
helmetlike flowers are suggestive of ancient
trophies.

## trope
trope, n. — F., fr. L. tropus, fr. Gk. τρόπος, 'turn,
direction*, which is rel. to τροπή, 'turn,
turning', τρόπις, 'a ship's keel', lit. 'turner', τρέπειν,
*to turn', fr. I.-E. base *trep-, 'to turn', whence
also Ol. trapate, 'is ashamed, confused', prop,
'turns away in shame', trapa, 'shame, confusion*,
Hitt. trep-, 'he works', prop, 'he turns to and
fro, is active and busy', L. trepit, 'he turns'. Cp.
trophy, Tropaeolum, tropic, apotrupaion, Atro-
pos, atropine, entropy, heliotrope, Monotropa,
Notropis, Oxytropis. Cp. also turpitude,

## -trope
-trope, combining form meaning 'that which
turns*. — Gk. -τρόπος, fr. τρόπος, τροπή,
'turn, turning'. See prec. word.

## troph-
troph-, form of tropho- before a vowel.

## trophaliaxis
trophaliaxis,n., exchange of food (biol.)—ModL.,
compounded of troph- and Gk. άλλαξα,
'exchange', which derives fr. άλλάσσειν, Att. άλ-
λάττειν (fut. αλλάξω), 'to alter, change', fr.
άλλος, 'another', which is cogn. with L. alius,
'another'. See else and cp. alio-, alias. Cp. also
the first element in allactite, and the second
element in catallactic, parallactic,

## trophic
trophic, adj., pertaining to nutrition. — F. tro-
pkique, fr. Gk. τροφικός, 'nursing, tending', fr.
τροφή, 'food, nourishment', which stands in
gradational relationship to τρέφειν, 'to make
solid, thicken, congeal, curdle; to nourish' (lit.
'to make thick'), fr. l.-E. base *dhrebh-, 'to
make firm, curdle'. See draff and cp. atrophy,
dystrophy, hypertrophy, Jatropha, Kmitrophy.
Cp. also thrombo-. For the ending see adi. suff.
-ic.
Derivative: tropkic-al-ly, adv.

## trupho-
trupho-, before a vowel troph-, combining form
meaning 'food, nourishment, nutrition'. — Gk.
τροφό-, τροφ-, fr. τροφή, 'food, nourishment'.
See prec. word,

## trophy
trophy, п., something taken from an enemy and
preserved as a memorial of victory. — F. tro-
phee, fr. Late L. trophxum, fr. L. tropaeum, fr.
Gk. τρόπαιον, 'trophy', lit. 'a monument of the
enemy's defeat\ neut. of τρόπαιος, 'connected
with turning; connected with defeat', fr. τροπή,
'a turning; a turning about of the enemy; a
routing pf the enemy'. See trope and cp.
Tropaeolum.
Derivative: trophy\ tr. v.

## -trophy
-trophy, combining form meaning 'nourishment*.
— Gk. -τροφία, fr. τροφή, 'food, nourishment*.
See trophic,

## tropic
tropic, п., 1) either of two celestial circles parallel
to the equator, the Tropic of Cancer (23° 27'
north) and the Tropic of Capricorn (23° 27'
south); 2) either of two terrestrial circles
corresponding to the former and marking the hot
zone of the earth. — ME. tropik, fr. Late L.
tropicus, fr. Gk. τροπικός, 'pertaining to a turn'
(scil. of the sun at the solstices) [whence
τροπικός (scil. κύκλος), 'the tropic circle, the
solstice'], fr. τροπή, 'turn, turning'. See trope
and -ic.
Derivative: tropic, adj., tropical.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:812 COLUMN:2 -->

## tropic
tropic, adj., pertaining to the crystalline acid
C9H10O8 (ckem.) — Formed fr. (a)rroj>(ine)
with adj. suff. -ic. Cp. tropine.

## -tropic
-tropic, combining form meaning 'turning,
changing', as in geotropic, heliotropic. —
Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. -τρόπος, 'turning',
fr. τρόπος, 'a turning'. See trope.

## tropical
tropical, adj., pertaining to the tropics. — Formed
fr. tropic, п., with adj. suff. -a]. Cp. Neotropical.
Derivative: tropical-ly, adv.
tropica], adj., figurative, metaphorical. — L.
tropicus, fr. Gk. τροπικός, 'pertaining to a turn;
figurative', fr. τροπή, 'turn, turning*. See trope
and ~ical.

## tropine
tropine, п., a poisonous crystalline base C8Hl5NO
(chem.) — Aphetic for atropine.

## tropism
tropism, п., a turning in response to a stimulus.
— Formed with suff. -ism fr. Gk. τροπή, 'a
turning'. Tropism is prop, a back formation
from words like keliotropism, geotropism, the
second element of these words having been
taken in an absolute sense.

## tropist
tropist, п., one who deals in tropes. — Formed
fr. trope with suff. -ist.

## tropological
tropological, also tropologic, adj., 1)
characterized by tropes; 2) pertaining to tropology. —
Late L. tropologicus, fr. Late ΰ^τροπολογικός,
fr. τροπολογία. See next word and -ic, resp.
also -a).
Derivative: tropological-ly, adv.

## tropology
tropology, п., the use of tropes; figurative speech.
— Late L. tropologia, fr. Late Gk. τροπολογία,
which is compounded of Gk. τρόπος, 'a turning,
direction, trope', and -λογία, fr. λόγος, 'word,
speech, discourse'. See trope and logos.
Derivative: tropolog-ic-al, adj.

## tropopause
tropopause, п., the transition zone between the
troposphere and the stratosphere. — F.
tropopause, coined by the French meteorologist Leon-
Philippe Teisserenc de Bort (1855-1913), fr. Gk.
τρόπος, 'a turning', and παΰσις, 'a stopping,
ceasing'. See trope and pause.

## troposphere
troposphere, п., the layer of the atmosphere
below the stratosphere (meteorol.) — F.
troposphere, lit. 'sphere of change*, coined by
Teisserenc de Bort (see prec. word) fr. Gk. τρόπος,
'a turning', and σφαίρα, 'ball, globe, sphere'.
See sphere.

## troppo
troppo, adv., too much (musical direction). — It:,
fr. F. trap, 'too much', fr. Frankish *tkrop, 'a
heap, mass' (whence also OProvenc. trop),
which is rel. to OE. porp, prop, 'village'. See
thorp and cp. de trup.

## -tropy
-tropy, combining form meaning 'a turning'. —
Gk. -τροπή, -τροπία, 'a turning of, fr.
τρόπος, 'a turning'. See trope.

## trot
trot, intr. and tr. v. — ME. trotten, fr. MF- troter
(F. trotter), fr. OF., fr. OHG. trotton, 'to tread',
which is rel. to OE. tredan. See tread and cp.
trottoir.
Derivatives: trot, n. (q.v.), trott-er, n.

## trot
trot, n. — ME., fr. MF., fr. troter. See trot, v.

## troth
troth, п., 1) faith; 2) truth. — ME. trouth, fr. OE.
treowd', a doublet of truth (q.v.) Cp. betroth.

## troth
troth, tr. v., 1) to pledge; 2) to betroth. — ME.
trouthen, fr. trouth. See troth, n.

## trottotr
trottotr, п., sidewalk. — F., fr. trotter, 'to trot;
to walk'. See trot, v.

## trouhadour
trouhadour, п., one of a class of poets who wrote
on chivalric love and first appeared in Provence
and flourished from the 11th to the 13th.cent. —
F., fr. MF., fr. OProvenc. trobador, fr. trobar,
'to compose poetry; to invent; to find*, fr. VL.
*t'ropare, 'to make tropes, sing*, whence also
F. trouver, 'to find'; cp. Catal. trobador, Sp.
trovador, It. trovatore. See trover and cp.
treasure trove, trouvaille, truuvere, contrive, retrieve.

## trouble
trouble, intr. and tr. v. — ME. trublen, troublen,
fr. OF. turbler, trubler, troubler (F. troubler),
metathesized fr. VL. *turbuldre, 'to disturb,
agitate' (whence also Rum. turbura, 'to trouble,
disturb'), fr. *turbulus, 'troubled, disordered,
turbulent', which is a blend of L. turbidus and
turbulentus. See turbid and turbulent.
Derivatives: trouble, n. (q.v.), troubl-ed, adj.,
troubl-ed-ly, adv., troubl-er, п., troubl-ing, adj.,
troubl-ing-ly, adv., trouble-some, adj., trouble-
some-ly, adv., troublous (q.v.), troubl-y, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:812 COLUMN:3 -->

## trouble
trouble, n. — ME., fr. OF. tourble, trubte, trouble
(F. trouble), fr. trubler, trobler (= F. troubler).
See prec. word.

## troublous
troublous, adj. — ME. troubelous, fr. OF. trou-
bleus, fr. trouble. See trouble, п., and -ous.

## trough
trough, n. — ME. trogh, trough, fr. OE. troh, trog,
rel. to ΟΝ., OS., MDu., OHG., MHG., G. trog,
Dan., Norw., trug, Swed. trag, Du. troch,
MHG. troc, 'trough', and to OHG. truha,
MHG., G. truhe, 'trunk, chest*. These words
derive fr. I.-E. *dru-fco-, a -/c-enlargement of
I.-E. base *derew{o)-, *drew{o)-, 'tree', and orig.
meant 'a wooden vessel'. See tree.
Derivatives: trough-ing, п., trough-y, adj.

## trounce
trounce, tr. v., to beat; to thrash. — The orig.
meaning of this word was 'to frighten, terrify'.
It derives fr. ME. traunce, 'fear of death*, fr.
OF. transe, 'fear, trance', fr. transir^to pass, to
pass from life', fr. L. transire, 4o pass over'. See
trance.
Derivative: trounc-er, n.

## troupe
troupe, п., a company of performers. — F. troupe,
fr. Frankish *Prop, metathesis of porp, 'herd*.
See troop, thorp.
Derivatives: troupe, intr. v., troup-er, п., trou-
pial (q.v.)

## troupial
troupial, п., any bird of the American family Ic-
teridae (orioles, larks, blackbirds, grackles). —
Coined by the American ornithologist Robert
Ridgway (1850-1929) fr. F. troupe, 'flock, troup',
in allusion to the circumstance that the birds
belonging to this family usually fly in large
flocks. For the ending see suff. -ial.

## trouse
trouse, п., trws; trousers (obsol.) — See trousers
and cp. trews.

## trousered
trousered, adj. — Formed fr. trousers with 1st
suff. -ed.

## trousering
trousering, n. — Formed fr. trousers with 3rd
suff. -ing.

## trousers
trousers, n. pi. — Formed on analogy of drawers
fr. trouse, fr. Gael, triubhas, which is prob. a
loan word fr. OF. trebus, fr. Late L. tubraci (pi.),
a word of uncertain origin. Cp. trews.

## trousse
trousse, п., a case for holding a surgeon's small
implements. — F. See truss and cp. next word.

## trousseau
trousseau, п., a bride's outfit. — F., 'bundle,
bride's outfit', dimin. of trousse. See prec. word.

## trout
trout, п., a freshwater fish. — ME. troute, fr. OE.
trukt, fr. Late L. tructa, fr. Gk. τρώκτης, 'a
gnawer, nibbler, a fish with sharp teeth', from
the stem of τρώγείν, Чо gnaw', which is rel. to
τρώξ, 'weevil', lit. 'gnawer', and stands in
gradational relationship to τράγος, 'he-goat', lit.
'gnawer', fr. I.-E. base *tro-g-, *tr -g-, 'to gnaw',
whence also Toch. AB trask, 'to gnaw*, Arm.
t"urc, gen. t'rcoy, 'jaw'. Cp. tragedy, troglodyte,
trogon, Trutta. Cp. also dredge, 'to sprinkle*. —
l.-E. base *tro-g-, *tr -g- is an enlargement of
base *ter-, *tr-, 'to go through, pass beyond*.
See term and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: trout-er, п., trout-y, adj.

## trouvaille
trouvaille, п., a lucky find, windfall. — F., fr.
trouver, 'to find'. See trover and subst. suff. -al.

## trouvere
trouvere, п., one of a class of medieval poets of
Northern France. — F., fr. OF. trovere, nom.
of the noun whose oblique case is troveor, fr.
trover, *to compose poetry; to invent, find'
(whence F. trouver, 'to find'). OF. troveor is the
exact equivalent of OProvenc. trobador. See
troubadour.

## trove
trove, adj., found. — See treasure-trove.

## trover
trover, п., acquisition of property (law). — Lit. *a
finding', fr. OF. trover (F. trouver), 'to find',
orig. 'to compose poetry; to invent*, fr. VL.
*tropare, 'to make tropes, sing', fr. L. tropus,
'trope, song*. Cp. OProvenc. trobar, Sp. and
Port, trovar. It. trovare, 'to find', which also

## trow

## trowel
trowel, п., a tool used for spreading mortar.

plaster, etc. — ME. true/, fr. F. truelle, fr. Late

## troy

truck, п., barter. — F. troc, back formation fr.

## truck
truck, п., i) a wheel; 2) a vehicle. — L. trochus,

## truckle

truckle» inir. v., to cringe, to submit to. — Fr.

ing-ly, adv.

## trucks
trucks, n. pi., a table game resembling billiards.

## truculence

ageness, cruelty', fr. truculentus. See next word

## truculent
truculent, adj., fierce, cruel; rude. — L.

trucis, 'wild, fierce', which is prob. cognate with

Derivatives: truculent-ly, adv., truculent-ness, n.

## trudellite
trudellite, п., a hydrous basic aluminum chloride

For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## trudge
trudge, п., a long walk. — Of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: trudge, intr. v., trudg-er, n.

## true
true, adj. — ME. trewe, fr. OE. treowe, trtewe,
'faithful, trusty', which is rel. to OS., OFris.
triuwi, ON. tryggr, Dan. tryg, Swed. trygg, tro,
Norw. tru, MDu. (gke)truwe, (gke)trouwe, Du.
(ge)trouw, OHG. gitriuwi, MHG. getriuwe,
triuwe, G. treu, Goth, triggws, 'faithful, trusty', fr.
I.-E. base *dru-, 'strong, faithful', whence also
Gk. δροός (Hesychius), 'strong', Lith. drutas,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:813 COLUMN:2 -->
'firm', W. drtid, Olr. dron, 'strong', W. derw,
'true', Olr. derb, 'sure', OPruss. druwis, 'faith',
and possibly also OI. dhruvab, 'firm, fix, lasting,
certain'. Base *dru- orig. meant 'as firm as a
tree', and is rel. to base *derew(o)-, *drew(o),

Derivatives: true, adv. and tr. v., tru-ly, adv.

trueness, n. — ME. trewenesse, fr. OE. ireownes,

## trump

blow a trumpet', and cp. trumpery.
trumpery» п., deceit. — ME. tromper у, fr. MF.

## trunk

## try
try, tr. and intr. v. — M.E. trien, 'to select', fr.

tryma, п., a drupaceous nut (bot.) — ModL., fr.

## trypsin
trypsin, п., an enzyme formed in the pancreatic
juice (biochem.) — G. Trypsin, coined by the
German physiologist Wilhelm Friedrich Kixhne
(1837-1900) in 1874, prob. fr. Gk. τρυειν, 'to
rub down, wear out', with the ending -psin, on
analogy of pepsin, and so called by him because
it was obtained (by Danilewsky in 1862) through
rubbing down the pancreas with glycerin. Gk.
τρΰειυ is rel. to τέρυς, 'weak', lit. 'rubbed off',
and to τείρειν (for ·τέρ-ιειν), 'to rub'; see
throw. It is also possible that—in spite of the
Gk. ι—the word Trypsin goes back to Gk.
τρΐψις, 'a rubbing', fr. τρΐβειν, 'to rub', which
is rel. to τείρειν, 'to rub' (see above).

tuber, п., 1) a short thickened underground stem;

swelling, hump, protuberance', fr. I.-E. *tu-bk-,

Tuberculariaceae, n. pi., a family of fungi (bot.)

## tuberosity
tuberosity, n. — MF. (— F.) tuberosite, fr. L.
tuberosus. See prec. word and -ity.

## tuberous
tuberous, adj., 1) having tubers (bot.); 2) knobby.
— F. tubereux (fem. tubereuse), fr. L. tuberosus,
'full of protuberances', fr. tuber. See tuber and
-ous.
Derivatives: tuberous-ly, adv., tuberous-ness, n.

## tubular
tubular, adj., having the form of a tube. —
Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. tubulus. See tubule.

## tabulation
tabulation, п., the act of making a tube or
hollowing into a tube. — L. tubulatio, gen. -onis,

## fr. L. tubulatus
fr. L. tubulatus, pp. of tubuldre. See next word
and -ation.

## tubule
tubule, п., a small tube. — F., fr. L. tubulus,
dimin. οι tubus. See tube and -ule.

## hihuli-
hihuli-, combining form meaning; ]) tubule; 2)
tubular. — Fr. L. tubulus. See next word.

## tubulous
tubulous, adj., 1) resembling a tube; 2) containing
tubes. — ModL. tubulosus, fr. L. tubulus. See
tubule and -ous.

## tuck
tuck, tr. and intr. v., to draw up in folds. — ME.

## tuken
tuken, tucken, 'to pull, tuck', fr. OE. tucia/t, 'to

## ill-treat
ill-treat, afflict', lit. 'to tug'; rel. to MLG., MDu.

## tucken
tucken, 'to tug*, OHG. zucchen, zucken, MHG.,

## G. zucken
G. zucken, 'to pull, jerk'. See tug.
Derivatives: tuck, п., tuck-er, n. and tr. v.,

## tucking
tucking, adj.

## tuck
tuck, п., to sound (said of a drum). — ME. tuk-

## ken
ken, fr. ONF. toquer, 'to strike, beat', prop, a

## Northern form of toucher
Northern form of toucher, *to touch; to strike'.
See touch and cp. words there referred to.
Derivative: tuck, п., the sound of a drum.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:814 COLUMN:3 -->

## tucket
tucket, п., a flourish of trumpets. — Formed from
prec. word with suff. -et.

## tucu tucu
tucu tucu, п., a burrowing rodent of S. America.
— Sp. tucutucu, fr. Guarani tucutucu, imitative
of its cry.

## -tiide
-tiide, suff. corresponding in meaning to E. -ness.
— F., fr. L. -tudo, gen. -tudinis, forming nouns
from adjectives and pp.s. It is prop, a compound
of the suff. -tu-s (e.g. ac-tus, 'the act of driving')
and -do- (as in cupi-do, 'desire'), which both serve
to form abstract nouns from verbs.

## Tuesday
Tuesday, n. — ME. Tiwesdai, Twisdai, Tuesdai,
fr. OE. Tiwesdxg ('day of Tiw"). Tiw is an
ancient Teutonic war god, identified with the
Roman Mars. The name Tiw is etymologically
connected with Gk. Ζευς, gen. Διός, the first
element in L. Dies-piter, Ju(p)-piter and with L. deus,
'god'. ON. Tyrsdagr, Tysdagr (Dan. Tirsdag),
OFris. ties-dei, OHG. Ziostag (MHG. Ziestac),
lit. 'the day of Tyr\resp. 'the day of Ziu\ are the
exact equivalents of OE. Tiwesdxg. These words
are prop, a loan translation of L. Martrs dies,
'the day of Mars, Tuesday' (whence It. martedi.
Rum. marfi. Proven?, di martz, Sp. martes),
itself a loan translation of Gk. "Αρεως ήμερα, 'the
day of Ares'. For the first element see deity and
cp. Zeus, Jupiter, for the second see day.

## tufa
tufa, п., a porous rock. — It. tufo, fr. L. to/us,
tophus, 'volcanic rock', which is an Osco-
Umbrian loan word. Cp. tophus and tuff.

## tufa ceo us
tufa ceo us, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, tufa.
— Formed from prec. word with suff. -aceous.

## tuff
tuff, п., tufa. — F. tuf, fr. It. tufo. See tufa,

## tuft
tuft, n. — ME. tuft, prob. formed with excrescent
-/ fr. OF. tufe, toffe (F. touffe), 'tuft of hair', which
is of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. zopf, 'end, tip, tuft
of hair', ON. toppr, 'tuft of hair", and see top,
'the highest part of anything'. Cp. also toff.
Derivatives: tuft, tr. and intr. v., tuft-ed, adj.,
tuft-er, п., tuft-y, adj.

## tag
tag, tr. and intr. v. — ME. tuggen, an intensive
verb formed fr. OE. tion and corresponding to
OHG. zucchen, zucken, 'to pull, jerk' [whence
MHG., zucken, of s.m., MHG., G. zucken, 'to
draw quickly' (a sword, etc.)], intensive form of
ziohan (MHG., G. Ziehen), 'to draw, pull'. See
tow, *to draw', and cp. toggle.
Derivatives: tug, п., tugg-er, п., tugg-ery, п.,
tugg-ing, adj., tugg-ing-ly, adv.

## tuUle
tuUle, п., in medieval armor, plate of steel
covering the thigh. — OF. (= F.) tuile, metathesis
of tiule, fr. L. tegula. See tile.

## tuism
tuism, п., use of the second person. — Formed
fr. L. tu, 'thou' (see thou), with suff. -ism, on
analogy of egoism.

## tuition
tuition, п., 1) instruction; 2) payment for
instruction. — ME. tuicioun, fr. OF. tuicion, fr. L. tui-
tionem, ace. of tuitio, la looking after, defense,
guardianship*, fr. tuitus, pp. of tueor, tueri, 'to
look at, regard, consider; to preserve, guard,
defend'. See tutor and cp. intuition. Cp. also
thews.
Derivatives: tuition-al, tuition-ary, adjs.

## tularemia
tularemia, tularaemia, п., a disease characterized
by intermittent fever and caused by the
Bacterium tularense (med.) — Medical L., coined by
Edward Francis of the United States Public
Health Service in 1919 fr. Tulare county in
California, and Gk. αίμα, 'blood*; so called by him
because the squirrels affected by this disease and
used for experiment had been collected in Tulare
county. For the second element see hemal.

## tule
tule, п., bulrush. — Sp., a Nahuatl loan word.

## tulip
tulip, n. — F. tulipe, earlier tulipan (cp. It. tulipa-
no and Sp. tulipan), fr. Turk, tiilbend, 'white
tulip', lit. 'turban (plant)', (see turban); so called
in allusion to its resemblance to a turban. The
element an was first dropped in obsol. Du. tuli-
pa, Du. tulp, owing to a confusion with the suff.
-an.
Derivative: tulip-y, adj.

## tulle
tulle, п., a thin silk, rayon or nylon net. — Fr.
Tulle, name of the chief town of the department
Correze in France.

## tulwar
tulwar, п., a curved saber used in N. India. —
Hind, talvur, fr. OI. taravdrih, 'a one-edged
sword', which is of uncertain etymology.

## tumble
tumble, intr. and tr. v. — ME. tumble», freq. of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:815 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TUMBLER | 788 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:815 COLUMN:1 -->
tumben, fr. OE. tumbian, 'to tumble, dance,
jump', rel. to MLG. tummelen, 'to turn, dance,
jump', Du. tuimelen, 'to tumble', OHG.
tiimon, *tSmalon, MHG. tumen, tumefn, G. tau-
meln, 'to turn, reel*. These words derive fr. Teut.
base *du-, which prob. corresponds to I.-E. base
*dheu-, 'to fly about like dust, be scattered'»
whence OI. dhunoti, Gk. &εϊον [for *&Ha-
(sjtov], 'brimstone'. See thio- and freq. suff.
-le and cp. tumbrel.
Derivatives: tumbler (q.v.), tumbl-ing, adj.,
tutnbl-y, adj.

## tumbler
tumbler, п., ]) one who tumbles; one who
performs tumbling tricks, an acrobat; 2) a large
drinking glass (so called because orig. it had a
rounded or pointed bottom and could not be
set down until emptied). — ME., fr. tumbfen.
See tumble and agential suff. -er.

## tumbrel
tumbrel, tumbril, п., 1) formerly, an instrument
of torture; 2) a farmer's cart; 3) any of the carts
used to convey victims to the guillotine during
the French Revolution; 4) a two-wheeled
military cart. — ME. tomberel, tombrel, fr. OF.
tumbrel, tumberel(¥. tombereau), a blend of OF.
tumeriau, 'tumbrel', and tomber, 4o fall,
tumble'. OF. tumeriau derives fr. turner, 'to skip,
gambol, romp*, fr. Frankish *tumon, which is
rel. to OHG·. tilmdn, 'to turn, reel'; see tumble.
F. tomber, together with Rum. tumba, Sp.
lumbar, It. lombotare, 'to tumble', is prob. of
imitative origin.

## tumefacient
tumefacient, adj., causing swelling. — L. tume-
faciens, gen. -entts, pres. part, of tumefacere. See
tumefy and -indent.

## tumefaction
tumefaction, п., swelling. — MF. (= F.)
tumefaction, fr. L. tumefactus, pp. of tumefacere. See
next word and -ion.

## tumefy
tumefy, tr. v., to cause to swell; intr. v., to swell.
— F. tumefter, fr. L. tumefacere, 'to cause to
swell*, fr. tumere, 'to swell', and -ficare, fr. fa-
cere, 4o make, do'. See tumid and -fy.

## tumescent
tumescent, adj., slightly swollen. — L. tumescens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of tumescere, 'to begin to
swell', formed from the stem of tumere, 'to
swell', with the inchoative sufT. -escere. See next
word and -escent.

## tumid
tumid, adj. — L. tumidus, 'swollen', formed with
suff. -idus (see -id) fr. tumere, 'to swell', which
is rel. to tumor, 'swelling, protuberance*,
tumulus, 'a raised heap of earth, a mound', and cogn.
with Ol. tutumah, 'fruitful, strong*, tumrafi,
'turgid, fat', Avestic tuma, 'fat', OE. puma, 'thumb',
pymel, 'thimble', fr. I.-E. *tumo-, enlargement
of base *tu-, *to swell', whence also Gk. τύλος,
τύλη, 'a swelling, rising', OSIav. tyjo, tyti, 'to
become fat*, tuku, 'fat', Lith. taukaT, 'fat', tau-
kas, 'pieces of fat', tunku, tukti, Lett, tukt, 'to
become fat', OE. peon, pioh, 'thigh', and the first
element in OSIav. tysesta, tysqsta, Goth, pusun-
di, OE. Pusend, 'thousand'. Cp. tumefy, tumor,
tumult, tumulus, intumesce. Cp. also obturate,
Satyr, soma, body', tomb, tomentum, total,
tuber, turion, tylarus, tyloma, tylosis, Typha,
tyro-, and the second element in catacomb. Cp.
also thigh, thimble, thole, п., thumb and the first
element in thousand.

## tumor
tumor, tumour, n. — L. tumor, 'swelling,
protuberance', fr. tumere. See prec. word and -or.

## tumorous
tumorous, adj., pertaining to a tumor. — L.
tumorosus, fr. tumor. See prec. word and
-ous.

## tumular
tumular, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
tumulus. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. tumulus.
See next word.

## tumult
tumult, n. — ME. tumulte, fr. MF. (= F.) tu-
multe, fr. OF., fr. L. tumultus, 'an uproar,
disturbance', which is rel. to tumere, 'to swell*. See
tumid.
Derivatives: tumult, intr. v., tumult-er, п.,
tumultuary (q.v.), tumultuous (q.v.)

## tumultuary
tumultuary, n. — L. tumultuarius, fr. tumultus.
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: tumultuari-ly, adv., tumult uari-ness,
n.

## tumultuate
tumultuate, intr. v., to raise a tumult; tr. v., to
make tumultuous. — L. tumultuor, tumultuari,
'to raise a tumult', fr. tumultus. See tumult and
verbal suff. -ate.-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:815 COLUMN:2 -->

## tumnltuation
tumnltuation, п., the act of raising a tumult. —
L. tumultudtio, gen. -onis, fr. tumultudtus, pp. of
tumultuari. See prec. word and -ion.

## tumultuous
tumultuous, adj. — L. tumultuosus, 'full of bustle,
full of confusion, turbulent', formed with suff.
-dsus, fr. tumultus. See tumult and -ous.
Derivatives: tumultuous-ly, adv., tumultuous-
ness, n.

## tumulus
tumulus, п., mound, esp. a sepulchral mound. —
L., rel. to tumere, 'to swell*. See tumid.

## tun
tun, п., a large cask. — ME. tonne, tunne, fr. OE.
tunne, 'a large cask*. See ton and cp. tunnel.
Derivative: tun, tr. v., tunn-er, п., tunn-ery, n.

## tuna
tuna, п., the great tunny. — American Sp.
equivalent to tunny.

## tund
tund, tr. and intr. v., to pound, beat (obsof.) — L.
tundere, 'to beat, strike, thump', rel. to tudes,
gen. -ditis, 'hammer', and cogn. with OI. tun-
date, tudati, 'he thrusts', which is cogn. with
Goth, stautan, ON. stauta, 'to push, thrust'. See
stint and cp. words there referred to.

## tundra
tundra, п., plain in Northern Russia. — Russ., fr.
Lapp tun-tur, lit. 'a marshy plain*. See Ernest
Weekley, A Concise Etymological Dictionary of
Modern English, p. 450.

## tune
tune, п., ]) melody; 2) harmony. — ME., fr. AF.
tun, corresponding to F. ton, 'tone*. See tone.
Derivatives: tune, tr. and intr. v., tun-able, adj.,
tun-abfe-ness, п., tun-abl-y, adv., tune~ful, adj.,
tune-ful-ly, adv., tune-ful-ness, п., tune-less, adj.,
tune-less-ly, adv., tune-less-ness, n.

## tungstate
tungstate, п., a salt of tungstic acid {chem.) —
Formed from next word with chem. suff. -ate.

## tungsten
tungsten, п., a rare metallic element (ckem.) —
Coined by its discoverer, the Swedish chemist
Karl Wilhelm Scheele (1742-86), in 1780 fr.
Swed. tung, 'heavy*, and sten, 'stone' (see stone).
Derivatives: tungsten-ic, adj., tungstenite (q.v.),
tungst-ic, adj., tungstite (q.v.)

## tangsteniferous
tangsteniferous, adj., containing tungsten. — A
hybrid coined fr. prec. word and -ferous, a suff.
of Latin origin.

## tungstenite
tungstenite, п., tungsten sulfide, WS„ {mineral.)
— A hybrid coined fr. tungsten and subst. suff.
-ite (fr. Gk. -ΐτης).

## tungstite
tungstite, п., tungsten trioxide, WO, {mineral.) —
See prec. word.

## tungsto-
tungsto-, combining form meaning tungsten. —
See tungsten.

## tunic
tunic, п., 1) a shirtlike garment worn by men and
women in ancient Greece and Rome; 2) a
blouselike garment; 3) a military coat; 4) a tunicle.
— ME. tunice, tunece, fr. F. tunique, (or
directly) fr. L. tunica, which stands for *ctunica and
was borrowed, prob. through the medium of the
Phoenicians, fr. Aram, kittuna, fr. Heb. kutto-
neth, 'tunic', whence also Gk. χιτών). See chiton
and cp. tourniquet. For the disappearance of the
initial к ср. ptisan.

## Tunicata
Tunicata, n. pi., a group of marine animals with
thick outer covering (zool.) — ModL., prop,
neut. pi. of L. tunicatus. See next word.

## tunicate
tunicate, adj., covered with a tunic. — L.
tunicatus, pp. of tunicate, 'to clothe with a tunic', fr.
tunica. See tunic and adj. suff. -ate.

## tunicle
tunicle, n. — L. tunicula, dimin. of iunica. See
tunic and -de.

## tunnel
tunnel, n. — ME. tonel, fr. OF. tonel (= F. ton-
neau), 'cask, tun', dimin. of tonne, 'tun', which
derives fr. ML. tunna, tonna, of s.m. See ton
and cp. tonneau.
Derivatives: tunnel, tr. and intr. v., tunnel{l)-er,
п., tunnel(l)-ing, n.

## tunny
tunny, п., any of several large sea fishes of the
order of the mackerels. — From early tonn, fr.
MF. (= F.) thon, fr. OProvenc. ton, fr. L. thun-
nus (whence also It. tonno), fr. Gk. θ-ύννος,
'tunny', fr. Heb. tannin, 'sea monster*. Gk."
θ-ύννος was influenced in form by ΰ-ύννειν, 'to
shake*.

## top
top, п., a ram. — ME. tuppe, of uncertain origin.

## tupek
tupek, п., an Eskimo summerhouse. — Eskimo
tupek, 'tent'.

## Turanian
Turanian, adj., pertaining to a group of Asiatic
peoples or their languages. — Formed with suff.
-ian fr. Pers. Тйгйп, name of the region
northeast of Persia.

## turban
turban, n. — F. turban, earlier turbant, tulban,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:815 COLUMN:3 -->
tolliban, fr. Turk, tulbend, fr. Pers. dulb&nd,
'turban'. Cp. tulip.
Derivative: turban-ed, adj.

## turbary
turbary, п., the right to dig peat. — Late L. tur-
baria, 'place where peat is dug', fr. turba, 'turf,
peat'. See turf.

## TurbeUaria
TurbeUaria, п., a class of flatworms (helmintfiol.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -aria fr. L. turbel-
lae (pi.), 'bustle, stir', dimin. of turba, 'crowd'
(see turbid and -ella); so called from the little
currents caused in the water by their cilia).

## turbid
turbid, adj. — L. turbidus, 'confused, disordered,
muddy*, fr. turbare, 'to confuse, bewilder', fr.
turba, 'uproar, confusion, crowd*, whence also
turbo, gen. turbinis, *that which spins; violent
motion, a spinning top, whirl, whirlwind,
hurricane'; very prob. not cogn. with, but
borrowed from, Gk. τύρβη, 'confusion, tumult,
disorder', which prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *twer-,
*tur-, 'to turn, whirl*. Cp. trouble, trowel, Tur-
bellaria, turbine, turbit, turbo, turbulent, disturb,
perturb, imperturable. Cp. also turma. For the
ending see 1st suff. -id.
Derivatives: turbid-ity, п., twcbid-ly, adv., turbid-
ness, n.

## turbinal
turbinal, adj., spiral. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. turbo, gen. turbinis, 'that which spins'. See
prec. word and cp. tourbillion.

## turbinate
turbinate, adj., resembling a top or a cone. — L,
turbinatus, 'shaped like a top', fr. turbo, gen.
turbinis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: turbinate, intr. and tr. v.,
turbinated, adj., turbinat-ion, n.

## turbine
turbine, п., a water wheel serving as a motor. —
F., fr. L. turbinem, ace. of turbo, 'that which
spins'. See turbinal.

## turbit
turbit, п., a kind of pigeon. — Prob. fr. L. turbo,
gen. turbinis, 'that which spins'. See turbinal.

## Turbo
Turbo, п., a genus of snails (zool.) — L. turbo,
gen. turbinis, 'that which spins'. See turbinal.

## turbojet
turbojet, п., a jet engine in which air is expanded
through a gas turbine which drives the
compressor (aeronautics). — Formed fr. turbine and
jet, n. (see jet, v.)

## turbot
turbot, п., a large flatfish. — ME., fr. OF. tour-
bout (F. turbot), fr. OSwed. tornbut, lit. 'thorn
but'. See thorn arid but, 'flatfish*.

## turbulence
turbulence, n. — Late L. turbulentia, "trouble,
disquiet', fr. L. turbulent us. See turbulent and -ce.

## turbulency
turbulency, п., turbulence (archaic). — See prec.
word and -cy.

## turbulent
turbulent, adj., ]) disorderly; 2) disturbed;
tumultous. — F., fr. L. turbulentus, 'agitated,
confused, disturbed, troubled', fr. turba, 'uproar,
confusion*. See turbid.
Derivatives: turbulent-ly, adv., turbulent-ness, n.

## turco-
turco-, also turko-, combining form meaning ])
Turkic; 2) Turkish and. — Fr. ML. Turcus, resp.
fr. Turk.

## Turdidae
Turdidae, n. pi., the family of thrushes. — ModL.,
formed fr. Turdus with suff. -idae.

## turdiform
turdiform, adj., having the form of a thrush. —
See Turdus and -form.

## turdine
turdine, adj., pertaining to a family of singing
birds, the thrushes and bluebirds. — Formed fr.
Turdus with adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -fnus).

## turdoid
turdoid, adj., thrushlike. — A hybrid coined fr.
L. turdus, 'thrush*, and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
εΐδος, 'form, shape'. See Turdus and -oid.

## Tardus
Tardus, п., name of a genus of thrushes (zool.) —
L., 'thrush', prob. standing for mturzdos and
cogn. with ON. prostr, OE. prysce, 'thrush'. See
thrush, the bird.

## tureen
tureen, п., a large dish for soup. — Fr. earlier
terrene, fr. MF. (= F.) terrine. See terrine.

## turf
turf, n. — ME., fr. OE., rel. to ΟΝ., Swed. torf,
Dan. terv, OFris. turf, OHG. zurba, LG. torf
(whence G. Torf). OI. darbhah, 'tuft of grass',
seems to be the only cogn. outside Teut. F.
tourbe, 'turf*, is a Teut. loan word. Cp. turbary.
Derivatives: turf, tr. and intr. v., turf-en, adj.,
turf-y, adj., turf-i-ness, n.

## turgescence
turgescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## turgescent
turgescent, adj., becoming turgid. — L. turges-
cens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of turgescere, 'to
begin to swell, swell up', inchoative of turgere.
See next word and -escent.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:816 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 789 | TWADDLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:816 COLUMN:1 -->

## turgid
turgid, adj., swollen, inflated. — L. turgidus, fr.
turgere, 'to swell', which is of uncertain origin.
For the ending see 1st suff. -id.
Derivatives: turgid-ity, п., turgid-ly, adv., turgid-
ness, n.

## turion
turion, п., a scaly shoot growing from a
subterranean bud (bot.) — L. turio, gen. -onis, 'a shoot,
sprout, tendril", which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly stands for 'tu-rio and derives from the
stem οι tumere, 'to swell'. See tumid and cp.
obturate.

## Turk
Turk, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) Turc, fr. ML.
Turcus, fr. MGk. Τούρκος, ft. Turkish-Pers.
Turk. Cp. tnrkey, turquoise.
Derivatives: Turki, Turk-ic (qq.v.), Turk-ic-ize,
tr. v., Turki-fy, tr. v., Turk-ish, adj. and п.,
Turk-ish-ly, adv., Turk-isk-ness, n.

## Turkey
Turkey, n. — F. Turquie, fr. ML. Turchia, fr.
Turcus, 'Turk'. See prec. word.

## turkey
turkey, n. — The name was applied orig. to the
guinea fowl, imported from Africa through
traders who dealt chiefly with the Near East (arid
for this reason were called 'Turkey-merchants');
hence the birds sold by these merchants came
to the known as turkeys. See prec. word.

## Turki
Turki, adj., pertaining to the Southern Turkic,
including Turkish. — Pers. Turki, fr. Turk. See
Turk.
Derivative: Turki, п., the Turki languages.

## Turkic
Turkic, adj., designating, or pertaining to, a
subfamily of Altaic languages divided into
Southern (= Turki), Eastern, Central and Western
branches. — Formed fr. Turk with suff. -ic.
Derivative: Turkic, п., the Turkic subfamily of
languages.
turko-. See tnrco-.

## Turkoman
Turkoman, n. — ML. Turcomannus, fr. Pers.
Turkman, lit. 'Turklike', fr. Turk, 'Turk', and
-man, 'like'.

## turma
turma, п., troop, squadron of horse {Roman
aniiq.) — L., of uncertain origin. It is possibly
rel. to turba, crowd' (see turbid).

## turmeric
turmeric, п., an aromatic plant of the ginger
family (Curcuma. longa). — Fr. earlier tormarith, tar-
maret, fr. F. terre merite, 'saffron', fr. ML. terra
merita ( — deserved earth'), a folk-etymological
corruption of Arab, kurkum, 'curcuma*. See
Curcuma.

## turmoil
turmoil, п., tumult. — Perh. a folk-etymological
alteration (after E. turn and moil) of OF. tre-
mouille, tremuie (whence F. tremie), 'mill
hopper', fr. L. trimodia, a collateral form of trimo-
dium, 'a vessel containing three modii', fr. tri-
and modius, name of a measure, which is rel. to
modus, 'measure'. See mode. Cp. It. tramoggia,
ΟΡΓΟνβης. tremueia, Catal. tremuja, Port, tra-
monha, 'mill hopper', which all derive fr. L.
trimodia.
Derivatives: turmoil, tr. and intr. v., turmoil-er,a.

## turn
turn, tr. and intr. v. — ME. turnen, tournen,
partly fr. OE. tyrnan, turnian, partly fr. OF. torner,
turner (F. tourner) which both derive fr. L. tor-
nare, 'to turn in a lathe; to turn, fashion', fr.
tornus, 'lathe; graver's tool', fr. Gk. τόρνος,
'turner's wheel, graver's tool, a tool for drawing
a circle', which is rel. to τορεύς, 'graver's tool',
τορεύειν, 'to bore through; to work in relief,
fr. I.-E. base *ter-, 'to rub, rub by turning, turn,
twist; to pierce'. See throw and cp. toreutic. Cp.
also attorn, attorney, contour, contourne, detour,
return, tour, tourmasin, tournament, tourney,
tourniquet, tournnre, turnip, turnpike, turnsole.
Derivatives: turn, ■&'. (q.v.), turn-able, adj.,
turner, п., turn-ery, п., turn-ing, n.

## turn
turn, n. — ME., fr. OF. torn, later tour (F. tour),
back formation fr. torner, turner (F. tourner).
See turn, v.

## Turnlcidae
Turnlcidae, n. pi., the family of button quails
(ornitkol.) — ModL., formed fr. Turnix with
suff. -idae.

## turnip
turnip, n. — Prob. a contraction of turn-nip and
derived fr. ME. turnen, *to turn', and пере,
'turnip' and so called in allusion to the round
shape of the root. See turn, v., and navew.
Derivatives: turnip, tr. v., turnip-y, adj.

## Turnix
Turnix, п., a genus of birds, the button quail
(ornithol.) — ModL., aphetic for L. coturnix, 'a
quail', which is dissimilated fr. earlier cocturnix.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:816 COLUMN:2 -->
quocturnix, from base *qwok-, imitative of the
quail's cry. Cp. Coturnix. For a similar imitative
base cp. quail, the bird.

## turnpike
turnpike, n. — Compounded of turn, v., and pike,
'shaft'. Turnpike orig. denoted a revolving frame
provided with pikes.
Derivative: turnpike, tr. v.

## turnsole
turnsole, п., sunflower. — ME. turnesole, fr. MF.
(= F.) tournesol, fr. It. tornasole or Sp. tornasol,
lit. 'that which turns to the sun', fr. tornare
(resp. tornar), 'to turn', and sole (resp. sol), 'sun'.
See turn, v., and Sol. For sense development cp.
girasol and heliotrope.

## turpentine
turpentine, п., 1) oleoresin exuding from the
terebinth; 2) oleoresin derived from various
coniferous trees. — ME. terebentyne, terbentyne, fr.
OF. turbentine, terebentine (F. terebenthine), fr.
ML. terebintina (resina), 'terebinthine resin', fr.
L. terebinthus, fr. Gk. τερέβιν&ος, 'the
turpentine tree'. See terebinth.

## turpeth
turpeth, п., the root of an Asiatic plant (Ipomoea
turpethum), used as a purgative. — MF. turbit
(F. turbith), fr. Arab, turbad, in VArab.
pronunciation turbid, fr. Pers. tirbid, 'a purge'.

## turpitude
turpitude, п., depravity, infamy. — MF. (= F.),
fr. L. turpimdinem, ace. of turpitudo, 'ugliness,
foulness', fr. turpis, 'ugly, unsightly, unseemly;
disgraceful, shameful, infamous, foul', which is
of uncertain origin. It possibly meant orig.
'twisted', and is rel. to trepit, 'he turns', and
cogn. with Gk. τρέπειν, 'to turn', τρόπος,
τροπή, 'a turn'. See trope and cp. words there
referred to. For the ending see suff. -tude.

## turps
turps, n. — Colloquial abbrev. of turpentine.

## turquoise
turquoise, п., 1) a greenish-blue mineral; 2) the
turquoise color. — ME. turkeis, fr. MF. tur-
quoyse (F. turquoise), fem. oiturquoys (turquois),
'Turkish', taken as a noun, fr. turc, 'Turk,
Turkish' ; so called because first brought to Europe
from the Sinai peninsula, which at that time
belonged to Turkey. See Turkey.

## turret
turret, п., a small tower. — ME. turet, toret, fr.
MF. torete, turete (F. tourette), dimin. of OF.
tor, tur, fr. L. turris, 'tower'. See tower, п., and
-et.
Derivative: turret-ed, adj.

## turriculated
turriculated, adj., resembling a small turret or
turrets. — Formed with the adj. suffixes -ntu
and -ed fr. L. turricula, 'little tower', dimin. of
turris, 'tower'. See tower and -cule and cp. prec.
word.

## turriilte
turriilte, п., a fossil cephalopod with long turret-
like shells. — ModL. turriiites, a hybrid coined
fr. L. turris, 'tower', and Gk. λί*ος, 'stone'. See
tower and -lite.

## Turritella
Turritella, п., a genus of gastropods with long
turretlike shells (zool.) — L., dimin. of turris,
'tower'. See tower and -ella.

## tursio
tursio, п., the bottle-nosed dolphin (zool.) —
ModL., fr. L. tursio, 'dolphin, porpoise', fr. Gk.
θυρσίων, -of s.m., which is possibly related to
*ύρσος, 'a straight shaft'. See thyrsus.

## turtle
turtle, п., turtledove [archaic). — ME., fr. OE.
turtle, formed fr. L. turtur (with dissimilation of
the second r into /), which is of imitative origin.
Cp. Tetraonidae.

## turtle
turtle, п., tortoise. — Sailor's alteration of F. tor-
tue, 'tortoise', after turtledove. See tortoise.
Derivative: turtle, intr. v.

## Tuscan
Tuscan, adj. and n. — L. Tuscanus, 'Tuscan,
Etruscan', fr. Tuscus, which stands for *Truscus,
an aphetic form of Etruscus. See Etruscan and
dp. tower.

## tush
tush, interj. expressing contempt. — Of imitative
origin.
Derivatives: tush, intr. v., tush-ery, n.

## tush
tush, п., tusk; a canine tooth of a horse. — ME.
tusch, tosch, fr. OE. tusc. See next word.

## tusk
tusk, n. — ME. tusch, tosch, fr. OE. tusc, which
stands for *tunpskS- and is rel. to ON. tonn,
Goth, tunpus, 'tooth'. See tooth.
Derivatives: tusk, tr. and intr. v., tusk-ed, adj.,
tusk-y, adj.

## russah
russah, n. — A var. of tussore.

## tussal
tussal, adj., pertaining to cough (med.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. tussis, 'cough', which
is of uncertain origin. It is perh. rel. to tundere,
'to beat, strike, thump'. See tund and cp. tus-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:816 COLUMN:3 -->
sicular, Tussilago.

## tussar
tussar, tusser. — Variants of tussore,

## tussicular
tussicular, adj., characterized by a slight cough
(med.) — Late L. tussicularis, fr. tussicula,
dimin. of L. tussis, 'cough'. See tussal and the
suffixes -cule and -ar.

## Tussilago
Tussilago, n., a genus of plants, the coltsfoot (bot.)
— L. tussilago, 'coltsfoot', fr. tussis, 'a cough";
(see tussal); prop, loan translation of Gk.
βήχιον, 'coltsfoot', from the stem of βήξ, gen.
βηχός, 'a cough'; the plant was so called in
allusion to its reputed medicinal qualities.

## tussive
tussive, adj., connected with a cough. — Formed
with suff. -ive fr. L. tussis, 'cough'. See tussa].

## tussle
tussle, intr. v., to fight, scuffle. — Freq. of ME.
-tusen (used only in compounds). See touse (q.v.)
and cp. tousle.
Derivative: tussle, n.

## tussock
tussock, п., tuft of grass, etc. — Related to touse
and to dial. Swed. tuss, 'wisp of hay". For the
ending see suff. -ock.
Derivatives: tussock-ed, adj., tussock-er, п.,
tussock-y, adj.

## tussore
tussore, tussar, tusser, tussah, п., coarse fiber
produced by thesilk worm Antheraeapaphia.—Hind.
tasar, fr. 01. tdsaram, 'shuttle', which is rel. to
tamsayati, 'draws to and fro', and is cogn. with
Goth, at-binsan, 'to attract', OHG. dinsan, 'to
draw', Lith. ifsi/, 'to draw asunder, stretch'. All
these words derive fr. I.-E. base *ten-, 'to stretch,
extend'. See tend, 'to move in a certain direction'.
Cp. trasarah, which is a blend of tdsaram and
trasati, 'trembles, quivers'.

## tut
tut, interj. expressing contempt. — Imitative.

## tutelage
tutelage, п., guardianship. — Formed with suff.
-age fr. L. tutela, 'charge, guardianship', fr.
tutus. See tutor.

## tutelar
tutelar, tutelary, adj. — Formed with suff. -ar,
resp. -ary, fr. L. tutela. See prec. word.

## tutor
tutor, n. — ME. tutour, fr. OF. tutour (F. tuteur),
fr. L. tutdrem, ace. of tutor, 'defender, guardian',
ft. tutus, syncopated form of tuitus, pp. of tuerl,
'to guard, protect', which is of uncertain origin.
It is possibly cogn. with Goth, fiiup, 'that which
is good', ON. pydr, 'mild, friendly', Oir. tuath,
'left, northern', i.e. 'good, favorable'. The
primary meaning of tuerl seems to have been 'to
show friendliness to somebody". Cp. tuition,
tutelage, intuition.
Derivatives: tutor, tr. and intr. v., tutor-age, п.,
tutor-er, п., tutor-ess, п., tutor-ial, adj., tutor-ial-
ly, adv., tutor-ly, adv.

## tutoyer
tutoyer, tr. v., to thee and thou. — F-, formed
with suff. -er (for L. -are), fr. F. tu, 'thou' (fr. L.
tu), and toi, 'thou; thee' (used emphatically)
(fr. L. tf, ace. of tu). See thou and cp. the English
term 'to thee and thou'.

## tutsan
tutsan, п., St. John's wort (Hypericum androsae-
mum). — F. toute saine, for plante toute saine,
lit. 'an entirely wholesome plant', fem. of tout,
'all; entire', and of sain, 'healthy, wholesome'.
See total and sane.

## tutti
tutti, п., 1) all players; 2) all musical instruments.
— It., pi. of tutto, 'all', fr. L. totus. See total,

## tutti-frutti
tutti-frutti, sweetmeat made of different kinds of
fruits. — It., lit. 'all fruits', pi. of tutto, 'all' (fr.
L. totus), and frutto, 'fruit' (fr. L. friictus). See
total and fruit.

## tutty
tutty, п., crude oxide of zinc. — ME. tutie, fr.
MF. (= F.) tutie, fr. Port, tutia, ft. Arab.
tutiya', fr. Pers. tutiya'.

## hium
hium, pron., thine. — L·, neut. sing, of the
possessive pron. of the 2nd person, fr. tu, 'thou'.
See thou.

## tu-whit
tu-whit, tu-whoo, interj. imitating the owl's cry.
Derivative: tu-whit, tu-whoo, intr. v.

## tuxedo
tuxedo, п., a man's evening dress for semiformal
occasions. — Fr. Tuxedo Park, around Tuxedo
Lake, near New York. The word is a corruption
of p'tuksit, the name of the wolf in a N.
American Lndian dialect, which lit. means 'he has a
round foot'.

## tuyere
tuyere, п., pipe for pumping air into a furnace. —
F., 'pipe', rel. to tuyau, 'pipe, tube'. See tewel.

## Twaddeil
Twaddeil, п., a hydrometer used for measuring
densities greater than that of water. — Named
after its inventor.

## twaddle
twaddle, tr. and intr. v., to talk in a silly way; п.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:817 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: TWAIN | 790 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:817 COLUMN:1 -->
a silly talk. — Of imitative origin. Cp. tattle,
t wattle.
Derivative: twaddl-er, n.

## twain
twain, adj. and п., two (archaic) or poetic. — ME.
tweien, twein, fr. OE. twegen, masc, 'two'. See
two.

## twang
twang, intr. and tr. v. and n. — Of imitative
origin. Cp. tang, 'to ring'.

## twangle
twangle, intr. and tr. v., to twang (rare); п., а
twang (rare). — Formed fr. twang with freq.
suff. -le.
Derivative: twangl-er, n.

## twattle
twattle, intr. and tr. v., to twaddle; п., a twaddle.
— Of imitative origin. Cp. tattle, twaddie.

## twayblade
twayblade, п., an orchidaceous plant
characterized by two broad leaves. — Lit. 'two blades',
compounded of archaic tway, 'two' (see twain),
and blade.

## tweak
tweak, tr. v., to twitch. — ME. twikken, fr. OE.
twiccian. Cp. twitch, which is a palatalized var.
of tweak.
Derivatives: tweak-er, п., tweak-y, adj.

## tweed
tweed, п., a twilled fabric. — Alteration of Scot.
tweel — E. twill under the influence of Tweedy
name of a Scottish river flowing through the
region where this cloth is manufactured.
Derivatives: tweed-ed, tweed-y, adjs., tweed-i-
ness, n.

## tweedle
tweedle, intr. v., to sing; to whistle; tr. v., to play
(a musical instrument; п., a tweedling sound. —
Of imitative origin. Cp. twiddle and next word.

## tweedledum and tweedledee
tweedledum and tweedledee, designation- of two
persons or things that are almost exactly alike
and differ only in name. — Coined from tweedle
by the English poet John Byrom (1692-1763) (in
his satire On the Feud Between Handel and Bo-
noncini).
'tween, prep. — Abbreviation of between.

## tweet
tweet, interj. and п., a chirping sound; intr. v.,
to utter a tweet. — Imitative. Cp. twitter.

## tweeze
tweeze, п., a case of surgical instruments (obsol.)
— For twees, an aphetic form of etwees, pi. of
etwee, fr. F. etui, 'case, box, sheath'. See etui.

## tweeze
tweeze, tr. v., to pluck with or as with tweezers
(colloq.) — Back formation from next word.

## tweezers
tweezers, n. pi., small pincers used for grasping
small objects. — Alteration of tweeze, п., after
scissors.

## twelfth
twelfth, adj. and n. — ME. twelft/ie, fr. earlier
twelfte, fr. OE. twelfta, fr. twelj (see twelve); cp.
ON. tolfti, Swed. tolfte, Dan., Norw. tolvte,
OFris. twelefta, twilifta, Du. twaalfde, OHG.
zwelifto, zwelefto, MHG. zwelfte, G- zwolfte,
'twelfth'.

## twelve
twelve, adj. and n. — ME. twelf twelve, fr. OE.
twelf, rel. to OS. twelif, ON. tolf Swed. tolf,
Dan., Norw. tolv, OFris. twelef, twelif, MDu.
twalef, Du. twaalf, OHG. zwelif, MHO. zwelif
zwelef, zwelf, G. zwolf, Goth, twalif. These
words are compounds meaning lit. 'two left after
(ten)', 'two added (to ten)'. For the first element
see two. The second element is cogn. with L. lin-
quere, Gk. λείπειν, 'to leave behind"; see loan,
relinqnish and cp. eleven. Outside Teutonic cp.
Lith. dvy-lika, 'twelve', which is the exact
equivalent of the above Teut. words, not only in
meaning but also in derivation.

## twelvemo
twelvemo, п., the same as duodecimo. — A hybrid
arising from the misreading of the abbreviation
(12 mo (= duodecimo) for twelvemo'See twelve
and cp. duodecimo and words there referred to.

## twentieth
twentieth, adj. and n. — ME. twentithe, formed
fr. twenty on analogy offourth, fr. four, etc.; see
numeral suff. -th. Cp. OE. twentigoda,
'twentieth'.

## twenty
twenty, adj. and n. — ME. twenti, fr.«OE. twentig,
.twentig, contraction of *twegentig, rel. to OS.
twentig, OFris. twintich, Du. twintig, OHG.
zweinzug, MHG. zweinzec, zwenzic, G. zwanzig.
All these words are compounds lit. meaning
'two tens'. Cp. Goth, twai.tigjus, 'two tens', i.e.
'twenty', and see twain, two and -ty, suff.
denoting multiples of ten.

## twi-
twi-, pref. meaning two. — ME., fr. OE. twi-,
'two, double', rel. to OS., OFris. twi-, ON. tvl·,
tve-, MLG. twe-, Du. twee-, OHG., MHG. zwi-,
G. zwie-, and cogn. with OI. dvi-, Gk. St- (for
*SFl-), OL. dvi- (whence L. bi-), Liih. dvi-. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:817 COLUMN:2 -->
bi-, di-, 'two', and cp. two, twice, twig, twill,
twin, twine, twist and the first element in
zwieback.

## twibill
twibill, п., a mattock. — Orig. 'battle ax with two
blades', compounded of twi- and bill, 'ax'.

## twice
twice, adv. — ME. twies, formed fr. OE. twigea,
twiga, twiwa, 'twice', with -es, gen, suff. used
adverbially; rel. to OE. twi-, *two, double'. See
twi- and adv. suff. -s.
Derivative: twic-er, n.

## twiddle
twiddle, tr. and intr. v., to twirl idly. — Prob. of
imitative origin. Cp. ON. tvidla, 'to stir, mix
up', and E. tweedle.
Derivatives: twiddle, п., twiddl-er, п., twiddl-ing,
twiddl-y, adj.

## twig
twig, tr. and intr. v., to· understand (slang). —
Gael, tifig or Ir. tuigim, twuigim, Ί
understand*.

## twig
twig, п., a slender branch. — ME. twigge, fr. OE.,
rel. to MLG. twich, MDu. twijch, Du. twijg,
OHG. zmg, MHG. zwic, G. Zweig, 'branch,
twig". These words are rel. to two and orig.
meant 'bifurcation'. Cp. OI. dvikah. 'consisting
of two", fr. dva, 'two'.
Derivatives: twigg-ed, twigg-en, twigg-y, adjs.

## twilight
twilight, n. — ME., fr. MFlem. twilicht, a var. of
twe(e)-licht, corresponding to MLG. twilicht
(see F. J. Bense, Dictionary of the Low-Dutch
Element in the English Vocabulary, p. 516). —
See twi- and light.
Derivative: twilight-y, adj.

## twill
twill, п., a cloth woven in parallel diagonal lines.
— ME. twylle, twyll, fr. OE. twili, rel. to OE.
twilic, 'woven double', OHG. zwilih, MHG.
zwilich, G. Zwillich, 'of two threads', and prop,
loan translation of L. bilix, 'of two threads', fr.
bi- and licium, 'thread4, which is of uncertain
origin. See twi- and cp. tweed and drill.
Derivatives: tweill, tr. v., twill-ed, adj.

## twin
twin, adj. and n. — ME., fr. OE. twinn, rel. to
ON. tvinnr, tvennr, 'double, twin', ODan. tvin-
ling,OSweo.tvinlinger,MLG.twelink, MDu. twe~-
linc, Du. tweeling, 'twin', OHG. zwinal, 'double',
zwiniling, MHG. zwinelinc, zwillinc, G. Zwilling,
'twin', and cogn. with L. bini, 'two each', Lith.
dvytiu, 'twins'. See twain, two and cp. next word.
Derivatives: twin, intr. and tr. v., twinn-ed, adj.,
twinn-er, п., twinn-ing, n.

## twine
twine, п., a strong thread consisting of twisted
strands. — ME. twin, fr. OE. twin, 'linen', orig.
'a double or twisted thread', rel. to Du. twijn,
dial. Swed. tvinne, LG. twern, Ou.tweern, MHG.,
G. zwirn, "twine, thread', ON. tvinnr, tvennr,
'double". Cp. h.binus, 'double', which stands for
+duisnos and see prec. word.

## twine
twine, tr. v., to twist together; intr. v., to become
twisted together. — ME. twynen, fr. twin, 'a
double thread', rel. to ΟΝ., Swed. tvinna, Dan.
tvinde, Du. tweernen, OHG. zwirnen, MHG., G.
zwirnen, 'to thread'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: twin-er, п., twin-ing-ly, adv.

## twinge
twinge, tr. v., to cause to have a sudden pain;
intr. v., to have a sudden pain. — ME. twengen,
fr. OE. twengan, 'to press, pinch', rel. to ME.
twingen, "to afflict', OS. thwingan, OFris. thwin-
ga, ON. pvi/tga, Dan. tvinge, Du. dwingen,
OHG. thwingan, later dwingan, MHG. dwingen,
later twingen, G. zwingen, 'to compel, force',
and to OE. pwang, 'thong' (see thong); prob.
cogn. with OI. tvanakti, 'pulls together'.
Derivative: twinge, n.

## twinkle
twinkle, intr. v., to sparkle, glitter. — ME. twink-
len, freq. of twinken, 'to blink, wink\ which is
rel. to MHG. zwinken, G. zwinkern, of s.m.;
prob. of imitative origin.
Derivatives: twinkle, п., twinkl-er, п., twinkl-ing,
n. and adj., twinkl-ing-ly, adv., twinkl-y, adj.

## twirl
twirl, tr. and intr. v., to spin; to whirl around. —
Prob. a blend of twist and,whirl.
Derivatives: twirl, п., twirl-er, п., twirl-y, adj.

## twist
twist, tr. and intr. v. — ME. twisten, fr. OE.
-twist, 'a rope', lit. 'something made of two
strands', occurring in the compound mxst-twist,
'a rope for staying a mast', rel. to OE. twist,
'branch', and to ON. tvistra, 'to divide,
separate', tvistr, 'discordant', OFris., MLG., MDu.,
Du. twist, 'quarrel, discord', MHG., G. zwist,
of s.m. All these words derive fr. Teut. *twis-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:817 COLUMN:3 -->
(whence also Goth, twis-, 'in two, asunder'),
corresponding to I.-E. *dwis-, whence Gk. δις
(for *δΡίς), OL. dvis (whence L. bis), 'twice',
and OI. dvih, 'twice', dvesti, 'he hates'. See twi-
and cp. twig. See also bis.
Derivatives: twist, п., twist-ed-ly, adv., twist-er,
п., twist-ing, adj., twist-ing-ly, adv., twist-y, adj.,
twist-i-ly, adv., twist-i-ness, n.

## twit
twit, tr. v., to taunt, reproach. — Aphetic for
ME. atwiten, fr. OE. xtwitan, 'to reproach,
blame', formed fr. set, 'at' (see at), and witan, 'to
reproach, blame', which is rel. to OE. wite,
'punishment, torture', OS. witi, ON. vhi, OHG.
w*33', 'punishment', OS. witan, OHG. wi^an, 'to
punish', Du. verwijten, OHG. firwf^an, MHG.
verwi^en, G. verweisen, 'to reproach, reprove',
of s.m., Goth, fraweitan, Ίο avenge'. The orig.
meaning of these verbs was 'to observe'. They
are derivatives of I. -E. base * wid-, 'to see, know',
whence also Gk. *5ιδειν, ίδεΐν, L. videre, *to
see'; see wit and cp. idea, vision. For the sense
development of OE. setwltan, etc., cp. h.animad-
vertere, 'to give heed to, observe; to chastise,
censure, punish4.
Derivatives: twit, п., twitt-ing-ly, adv., twitt-y,
adj.

## twitch
twitch, tr. v., to pull with a jerk; intr. v., to move
with a jerk. — ME. twicchen. rel. to OE.
twiccian, 'to'pluck (fruit), twitch', LG. twicken, Du.
twikken, OHG. gizwickan, MHG., G. zwicken,
'to pinch, tweak'. E. twitch is a palatalized var.
of tweak (q.v.)
Derivatives: twitch, п., twitch-er, п., twitch-y,
adj., twitch-i-ly, adv., twitch-i-ness, n.

## twitter
twitter, intr. v. — ME. twiteren, of imitative
origin. Cp. OHG. zwizziron, MHG. zwitzern, G.
zwitschern, Dan. kvidre, Swed. kvittra, Du.
kwetteren, which all are imitative Cp. tweet.
Derivatives: twitter, п., twitter-er, п., twitter-ing,
adj., twitter-ing-ly, adv.
'twixt, prep. — Aphetic for betwixt.

## two
two, adj. and n. — ME. two, earlier twa (fern, and
neut.), twei, earlier tweien, twein (masc; whence
E. twain), fr. OE. i,wa (fem. and neut.), twegen
(masc), tu (neut.), rel. to OS. twene (masc),
twa, two (fem.), twe (neut.), ON. tveir (masc),
tvxr (fem.), tvau (neut.), OFris. twene (masc),
twa (fem. and neut.), Du. twee, OHG., MHG.
zwene (masc), zwo, zwa (fem.), zwei (neut.), G.
zwei, Goth, twai (masc), twos (fem.), twa (neut.),
fr. I.-E. base *duwo-, *duwou-, *dwo(u)-, 'two',
whence also OI. dvau, dva (masc), dvi (fem. and
neut.), Avestic dva, Toch. wu (masc), we (fem.),
B. wi (for *dwu, resp. *dwe, *dwi), 'two', the
first element in Hitt. ta-yugash, ta-ugash, 'two
years old', tan, 'again', the second elemend in
Arm. er-ku, 'two', Gk. δύο, Ion. δύω, Alb. du,
L. duo (masc. and neut.), duae (fem.), OSlav.
duva (masc), duve (neut.), Lith. du (masc),
dvi (fem.), Lett, divi (masc. and fem.), OPruss.
dwai (ace masc), Olr. dau, da (masc), di(fem.),
W. dou (masc), dwy (fem.), 'two'. Cp. twain,
twelve, twenty, twi-, twice, twig, twill, twin,
twine, twist, tub, the first element in twayblade
and the second element in between, betwixt. Cp.
also bi-, bis-, deuce, di-, 'two', dis-, double,
doubt, dozen, dual, dubious, duel, duet, duplex,
dvaita, dvandva, dyad, the first element in
balance, barouche, bevue, biscuit, doab, dopatta,
dubash, and the second element in combine,
rebel, revel, sapsago, tete-beche.

## -ty
-ty, suff. forming abstract nouns. — ME. -te,
-tee, fr. OF. -te (¥. -te), fr. L. -tatem, ace of
•tas, which is prop, a fusion of the suffixes -ta
(appearing in words like juven-ta, 'youth', vt-ta,
for *vivi-ta, 'life') and -ti. L. suff. -tas (gen.
-talis) is cogn. with Gk. -της (gen. -τητος), ΟΙ.
-tati-. Cp. e.g. L. liber-tas, 'freedom', fr. liber,
'free', Gk. φ-.λότης, 'friendship', fr. φίλος,
'friend', OI. sarva-tati-h, 'wholeness', fr. sarvah,
'whole, entire'. Cp. also -ity.

## -ty
-ty, suff. used to denote multiples often; twen-ty,
thir-ty, etc. — ME. -ti, fr. OE. -tig, rel. to OS.,
Du. -tig, ON. -tigr, OFris. -tich, OHG. -zig,
-zug, MHG. -zic, G. -zig, '-ty', and to Goth.
tigus, 'decade', a collateral form of taihun, 'ten'.
See ten and cp. twenty.

## tych-
tych-, form of tycho- before a vowel.

## Tyche
Tyche, п., Greek goddess of fortune {Creek
ntytkol.) — Gk. Τύχη, fr. τύχη, 'fortune, fate,
providence, chance', which is rel. to τεύχειν,
Ίο make ready, construct, fashion*, τυγχάνειν,
'to happen to be at a place4, and cogn. with
Goth., OE. dugan, 'to be of use'. See doughty
and cp. dow, 'to be able'. Cp. also next word
and the second element in Pentateuch» Hexa-
teuch, Heptateuch, Octateuch.

## tychism
tychism, п., a theory that regards chance as an
objective reality. — Coined by the U.S. logician,
mathematician and physician, Charles Sanders
Peirce (1839-1914), fr. Gk. τύχη, 'fortune,
chance*. See prec. word and -ism.

## tychite
tychite, п., a rare mineral. — Coined fr. Gk.
TUX*b 'fortune, chance' (see Tyche) and subst.
suff. -lie; so called because it was discovered by
chance.

## tycho-
tycho-, before a vowel tych-, combining form
meaning *fortune, chance'. — Gk. τυ/ο , τυχ-,
fr. τύχη. See Tyche.

## tycoon
tycoon, п., a wealthy and powerful businessman
(colloq.)— Jap. taikun, 'great lord', fr. Chin. tat
'great', and kiun, 'ruler, prince, lord".

## tying
tying, n. — Formed fr. tie, v., with -ing, suflf.
forming verbal nouns.

## tyke
tyke, tike, п., 1) a dog, cur; 2) a boor (now
chiefly dial.) — ME. tyke, fr. ON. tik, 'bitch',
rel. to MLG. tike, of s.m.

## tylarus
tylarus, п., pad on the under surface of the toes
of birds (ornithol.) — ModL., fr. Gk. τύλη, 'a
swelling, cushion', which is rel. to τύλος, 'a
'lump, knot; any swelling', fr. I.-E. base *tu-,
'to swell', whence also L. tumidus, 'swollen'. See
tumid and cp. tyloma, Tylopoda, tylosis,

## tyle
tyle, tyler, n. — Archaic spelling of tile, tiler,

## tyloma
tyloma, п., a callus (med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
τϋλωμα, fr. τύλος, 'callus; any swelling'. See
tylarus and-oma and cp. the second element in
Entyloma.

## Tylopoda
Tylopoda, n. pi., a division of mammals of the
camel family (zool.) — ModL., lit. 'having
callous feet', fr. Gk. τύλος, 'callus; any
swelling', and πους, gen. ττοδός, 'foot". See tylarus
and -poda.

## tylosis
tylosis, п., 1) growth of one cell into another
(bot.); 2) thickening or hardening of tissue
(med.) — ModL., formed with surf, -osis fr. Gk.
τύλος, 'lump, knot; any swelling*. See tylarus.

## tymp
tymp, п., the top of the opening of the hearth of
a blast furnace. — Shortened fr. tympan.

## tympan
tympan, п., ]) a drum or a drumlike instrument
(archaic); 2) a thin sheet of paper, parchment,
etc., placed between the platen and the sheet to
be printed. — ME., fr. OE. timpano, fr. L.

## tympanum
tympanum, 'kettledrum, timbrel, panel of a door',
fr. Gk. τύμπανον. See tympanum,

## tympan-
tympan-, form of tympano- before a vowel.

## tympanist
tympanist, п., one who beats a drum. — L.

## tympanism
tympanism, fr. Gk. τυμπανιστής, fr. τυμπανίζειν,
'to beat the drum', fr. τύμπανον. See tympan
and -ist.

## tympanites
tympanites, п., distention of the abdomen caused
by the accumulation of gas in the intestines
(med.) — ME., fr. Late L. tympanites, fr. Gk.
τυμπανΐτης, 'a kind of dropsy in which the

## belly is stretched like a drum'
belly is stretched like a drum', fr. τύμπανον,
'kettledrum*. See tympanum and subst. suff. -ite.

## tympanitic
tympanitic, adj., pertaining to, or affected with,
tympanites. — Late L. tympamticus, fr.
tympanites. See prec. word and adj. sufT. -ic.

## tympanitis
tympanitis, п., inflammation of the membrane of
the middle ear (med.) — Medical L., formed fr.
tympanum with suff. -itis.

## tympano-
tympano-, before a vowel tympan-, combining
form meaning 'pertaining to the tympanum'. —
Fr. Medical L. tympanum. See next word.

## tympanum
tympanum, п., the drum of the ear ianat.) —

## Medical L.
Medical L., introduced into anatomy by Ga-

## briele Fallopio (see Fallopian) fr. L. tympanum
briele Fallopio (see Fallopian) fr. L. tympanum,
'kettledrum', fr. Gk. τύμπανον, fr. τυμπ-, a

## nasalized form of stem tutt-
nasalized form of stem tutt-, which appears in
τύπος, 'blow, impression', τύπτειν, 'to beat,

## strike'. See type and cp. tympan
strike'. See type and cp. tympan, timpano,
timbre, timbrel.
Derivatives: tympan-aU tympan-ic, adjs., tym-

## pan-ic-ity
pan-ic-ity, п., tympan-ism, n.

## tympanum
tympanum, п., a flat triangular space (archit.) —
