## un-
un-, privative pref., as in unknown. — ME., Гг.
OE., rel. to OS., OFris., OHG., MHG., G. un-,
Goth, un-, ON. й-, б-, Dan. и-, Swed. б-,
Du. on-, and cogn. with OI., Avestic, OPers.
a-, an-, Toch. an-, en-, em-, Arm. an-, Gk. ά-,
before a vowel aw-, Oscan and Umbr. an-, L.
in-, Olr. an-, in-, ё-, W., Bret., Co. an-, Cp. the
pref. in OE. uncufa ON. йкйдг, Goth, unkunps,
01. ajnatah. Arm. ancanaul\ Gk. άγνωτος, L.
ignotus (for *in-gnotos), Olr. ingnad, 'unknown*
(see uncouth). These prefixes derive fir. l.-E. *n-,
to which base *ne, *no, not4, stands in vowel
gradation. See no and cp. the priv. prefixes an-
and in-.

## un-
un-, pref. expressing reversal, deprivation or
removal, as in undo, unfasten. — ME. un-, fr.
OE. on-, un-, rel. to OS. ant-, ON. and-, Du.
ont-, OHG. ant-, int-, MHG., G. ant-, ent-,
Goth, and-, "against*, Goth. prep, and, 'along',
and cognate with OI. anti, 'opposite', Gk. άντα,
#ντην, "opposite', αντί, 'over against, opposite,
before", L. ante, 'before', fr. l.-E. base *anta-,
*anti-, *o\er against, opposite'. See ante-, anti-.
For the fuller OE. form see answer.

## unable
unable, adj. — ME. See priv. pref. un- and able.
Cp. inability.
Derivatives: unabfe-ness, п., unabl-y, adv.

## unanimity
unanimity, n. — ME. unanimite, fr. MF. (= F.)
unanimite, fr. L. unanimitdtem, ace. of unani-
mitds, fr. ununimus, Of one mind'. See next word
and -ity.

## unanimous
unanimous, adj., of one mind. — L. unanimiis, 'of
one mind', compounded of umis, 'one', and
animus, 'mind*. See one and animus. For E. -ous,
as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: unanimous-ly, adv., unanimous-
ness, n.

## unapt
unapt, adj. — Formed fr. priv. pref. un- and apt.
Cp. inapt, inept.

## unattached
unattached, adj. — Formed fr. priv. pref. un- and
attached. Cp. tosher, which is a corruption of
unattached.

## unbelief
unbelief, n. — Formed fr. priv. pref. un- and
belief. Cp. OE. ungeliafa.

## unberufen
unberufen, interj., used in the sense of 'Heaven
forbid'. — G., lit. 'uncalled*; formed fr. pref.
un-, and berufen, pp. of berufen, 'to call', fr.
pref. be- and rufen, 'to call'. See priv. pref. un-,
pref. be- and roup, 'to sell by auction'.

## Uncaria
Uncaria, n. pi., a genus of plants of the madder
family (bat.) — ModL., fr. L. uncus, 'hook'. See
uncus and -aria.

## uncia
uncia, n. — L., 'the twelfth part of anything, the
twelfth part of a pound, an ounce; the twelfth
part of a foot, an inch', fr. *oinicia, *oincia,
'unity', and rel. to OL. oinos, L. ftnus, One'. See
one and cp. unity. Cp. also ounce, oka, inch,
uncial and the second element in semuncia.

## uriciferous
uriciferous, adj., bearing a hook (?ooL) —
Compounded of L. uncus, 'hook', and ferre, 'to bear,
carry1. See uncus and -ferous.

## unciform
unciform, adj.,' hook-shaped. — Compounded of
L. uncus, 'hook', and forma, 'form, shape". See
uncus and form, n.

## uncinal
uncinal, adj., hooklike. — Formed with adj. sufT.
-al fr. L. uncinus, 'hook, barb'. See uncinus.

## uncinate
uncinate, adj., hooked, hook-shaped. — L.
uncinates, fr. uncinus, 'hook, barb'. See next word
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivative: uncinat-ed, adj.

## uncinus
uncinus, п., a hooklike process. — L. uncinus,
'hook, barb', fr. uncus. See uncus.

## uncle
uncle, n. — ME. fr. OF. uncle, oncle (F. oncle),
fr. VL. aunculus (whence also Rum. unckiu), fr.
L. avunculus, 'uncle on the mother's side', dimin.
of avus, 'grandfather*, which is cogn. with Arm.
hav, 'grandfather', Lith. avynas, 'maternal uncle',
OPruss. awis, 'uncle', OSlav. uji, 'uncle', the
first element in OE. earn, OFris. em, Du. oom,
OHG., MHG. dkeim, 'maternal uncle', G.
Okeim, Ohm, 'uncle*, ON. afi, 'grandfather', ai,
'great-grandfather', Goth, awo, 'grandmother',
Olr. aue, haue, Mir. δα, ua, 'grandson', later
'nephew', W. ewythr, 'uncle'. Cp. avuncular,
atavism, avltal, ayah, 'a Hindu nurse', erne.
Derivative: uncle, tr. v.

## -uncle
-uncle, dimin. suff. — L. -unculus, enlargement of
suff. -cuius. See -cuius, -cule.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:822 COLUMN:2 -->

## Uncle Sam
Uncle Sam, the government or the people of the
United States (colloq.) — Extension of the
initials U.S. after Samuel Wilson (1776-1854). of
Troy (New York), popularly called "Uncle
Sam", who was a meat inspector during the war
of 1812 and stamped the barrels of meat he
packed with the initials U.S.-E.A., which stood
for C/nited States — Elbert Anderson (name of
the contractor). In a humorous way the letters
U.S. were 'explained' as the initials of Uncle
Sam. Cp. Sammy.

## unco
unco, adj., adv., and n. — Scot. var. of uncouth.

## uncouth
uncouth, adj., 1) uncommon; 2) strange;
awkward.—ME., fr. OE. ипейр, 'unknown, strange',
fr. priv. pref. un- (q.v.), and cup, 'known',
prop. pp. of cunnan, 'to know*. See can, 'to be
able', and cunning and cp. unco and the first
element in Cuthbert.
Derivatives: uncouth-ly, adv., uncouth-ness, n.

## unction
unction, п., 1) the act of anointing; 2) an unguent;
3) fervor. — ME. unctioun, fr. L. unctio, gen.
-onis, 'anointing', fr. unctus, pp. of unguere, 'to
anoint'. Seeungnent.

## unctuous
unctuous, adj., 1) oily; 2) full of unction; suave.
— ML. unctuosus, fr. L. unctus, pp. οι unguere,
'to anoint'. See unguent and -ous.
Derivatives: unctuous-ly, adv., unctuous-ness, n.

## uncus
uncus, п., hook {anat. and zool.) — L., fr. Gk.
ΰγκος, which stands in gradational relationship
to Gk. #γκος, *a bend, hollow*, a valley', άγκών,
'bend of the arm, elbow', αγκύλος, 'crooked,
curved', άγκυρα, 'anchor', OE. angel,
'fishhook*. See angle, 'fishhook', angle, 'corner',
and cp. Uncaria, unciferous, unciform, uncinate,
uncinus, aduncous, Redunca.

## undate
undate, adj., wavy. — L. undatus, fr. unda, 'wave',
which is cogn. with 01. undati, unatti, 'it springs,
gushes, moistens', udan-, udakam, 'water', Gk.
ΰδωρ, Goth, wato, OE. wxter, 'water'. See
water and adj. suff. -ate and cp. hydra, hydro-,
Cp. also abound, abundance, inundate,
inundation, redound, redundant, sound, 'to measure',
superabound, superabundance, nndine, undose,
undulate, undulous, oncograph.

## undecagon
undecagon, п., a figure having eleven angles and
eleven sides (geom.) — A hybrid coined fr. L.
undecim, 'eleven', and Gk. γωνία, 'angle*. The
first element is compounded of L. unus, 'one*,
and decern, 'ten'; see one and ten and cp. next
word. For the second element see -gon. The
correct form is hendecagon (q.v.), in which both
elements are of Greek origin.

## undecennial
undecennial, adj., occurring every eleventh year.
— Formed fr. L. undecim, 'eleven' (see prec.
word), with suff. -ennial, on analogy of decennial
(q.v.)

## under
under, .prep. — ME., fr. OE. under, rel. to OFris.
under, OS., Goth, undar, ON. undir, Dan.,
Swed., OFris. under, Du. onder, OHG. untar,
unter, MHG. under, unter, G. unter, fr. l.-E.
*ndher, 'under', whence also OI. adhah, 'below',
adharah, 'lower', Avestic adara-, 'lower', Toch.
Α άϋό, 'under', Arm. nd, 'under', L. inferus,
iower', infra, 'below' and perh. Gk. ά&ερίζειν,
'to make light of (for sense development cp. OI.
adharlna-, 'despised, made light of, fr. adhah,
'below'). Cp. inferior, infernal, infra. — Cp. also
l.-E. *nter, 'between, among', whence OE.
under, OHG. untar, Goth, undar, 'among', OI.
antar, 'among, between', L. inter, 'between,
among*, Gk. άντερα, 'intestines'. See inter,
prep., and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: under, adv. and adj.

## under-
under-, pref. — From prec. word.

## undercroft
undercroft, п., a crypt. — Compounded of under
and obsol. croft, 'vault', which is borrowed fr.
VL. crupta, fr. L. crypta, fr. Gk. κρυπτή, 'crypt,
vault'; see crypt.

## undergradnate
undergradnate, adj. and n. — A hybrid coined fr.
under and graduate, a word of Latin origin.

## undercurrent
undercurrent, n. — A hybric coined fr. under and
current, a word of Latin origin.

## underestimate
underestimate, tr. v. — Loan translation of F.
sous-evaluer, a word coined by the French poet
and critic Pierre-Charles Baudelaire (1821-67)
fr. F. sous, 'under', and evaluer, 'to estimate'.
Derivative: underestimat-ion, n.

## underlay
underlay, tr. v. — ME. underleggen, underleyen,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:822 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. OE. underlecgan, fr. under- and lecgan, 'to
lay'. See lay, 'to place'.
Derivatives: underlay, п., underlay-er, n.

## underlie
underlie, tr. v. — ME. underliggen, underlien, fr.
OE. underlicgan, fr. under and licgan, 'to lie'. See
lie, 'to recline'.
Derivatives: underlie, п., underli-er, n.

## underneath
underneath, adv. and prep. — ME. undemethe, fr.
OE. underneopan. See under and nether and cp.
beneath.

## understand
understand, tr. and intr. v. — ME. undersianden,
fr. OE. understandan, lit. 'to stand under', fr.
under- (see under) and standan, 'to stand'. Cp.
OFris. understonda and see under and stand. For
sense development cp. OE. forstandan, 'to
understand', lit. 'to stand before', MDu. verstaen,
Du. verstaan, MHG. version, versten, G. ver-
stehen, 'to understand', lit. *to stand through',
Gk. έπίσταμα!,, *I understand', lit. Ί stand
upon'.
Derivatives: under stand-able, adj., understand-
able-ness, п., understand-abl-y, adv., understand-
er, п., understand-ing, n. and adj., understand-
ing-ly, adv., understand-ing-ness, n.

## undertake
undertake, tr. and intr. v. — ME. undertaken; see
under and take. ME. undertaken is prop, a loan
translation of OE. underniman, 'to undertake'
(formed fr. under- and niman, 'to take*), which
is rel. to OS. undarniman, Du. ondernemen,
OHG. untarneman, MHG. undernemen, G. un-
ternehmen. Cp. F. entreprendre, 'to undertake',
fr. entre, 'between, among', and prendre, 'to
take'.
Derivatives: undertak-er, п., underiak-ing, n.
and adj., undertak-ing-ly, adv.

## underwrite
underwrite, tr. and intr. v. — Loan translation of
L. subscrtbere, fr. sub, 'under', and scriberet 'to
write'. See under and write.
Derivatives: underwrit-er, п., underurit-ing, n.

## undies
undies, n. pi., women's underwear (colloq.) —
Formed from the abbreviation of underwear
with -ies, pi. of dimin. suff. -y.

## undine
undine, п., a female water sprite. — G., fr. F. on-
dine, introduced by the French poet Pierre de
Ronsard (1524-85) fr. ModL. undina, a word
coined by Paracelsus fr. L. unda, 'wave'. See
undate and -ine (representing L. -ina). For sense
development cp.gnome, sprite, salamander, sylph.

## undo
undo, tr. v. — ME. undon, fr. OE. undon, ondon,
fr. un-,pref. expressing reversal, and don, 'to do'.
See do, v.
Derivatives: undo-er, п., undo-ing, n.

## undone
undone, unfastened, pp. of undo. — ME. undon%
pp. of undon, 'to undo*. See prec. word.

## undone
undone, adj., not done. — ME. undon, fr. priv.
pref. un- and don, 'done', pp. of don, 'to do'. See
do, v.

## undose
undose, adj., undulate. — L. undosus, 'wavy', fr.
unda, 'wave'. See undate and adj. suff. -ose.

## undress
undress, tr. v., to take clothes off; intr. v., to take
one's clothes off. — Formed fr. un-, pref.
expressing reversal, and the verb dress.
Derivative: undress-ed, adj.

## undress
undress, п., ordinary dress, as distinguished from
full dress. — Formed fr. priv. pref. un- and the
noun dress. See dress.

## undulant
undulant, adj., 1) undulating; 2) wavelike. —
Formed as if fr. L. *undulans, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of *undulare, back formation fr. undulatus,
which was regarded as a pp. See undulate, adj.

## undulate
undulate, adj., wavy. — L. undulatus, 'wavy,
undulated', fr. *undula, dimin. of unda, 'wave'. See
undate, -ule and adj. suff. -ate.

## undulate
undulate, intr. v., to move in waves. — L.
undulatus. See undulate, adj.
Derivatives: undulat-ed, adj., undulat-ing, adj.,
undulat-ing-ly, adv., undulat-ion, п., undu/at-ory,
adj.

## uneven
uneven, adj. — ME., fr. OE. unefen, unefn. See
priv. pref. un- and even.
Derivatives: uneven-ly, adv., uneven-ness, n.

## unfair
unfair, adj. — ME., fr. OE. unfxger, 'unlovely'.
See priv. pref. un- and fair, adj.
Derivatives: unfair-ly, adv., unfair-ness, n.

## unfold
unfold, tr. v. — ME. unfolden, fr. OE. unfealdan.
See un-, pref. expressing reversal, and fold.

## ungainly
ungainly, adj. — ME. ungeinliche, adv., fr. ungein,
'inconvenient', fr. priv. pref.-un- and ON. gegn,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:823 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: UNGUAL | 796 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:823 COLUMN:1 -->
'ready, convenient'. See gamly.

## ungual
ungual, adj., pertaining to a nail or claw. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. unguis, 'nail, hoof
claw', which is cogn. with Gk. ΐίνυξ, ON. nagl,
OE. naegel, 'nail*. See nail and ср. опух. Ср. also
unguiculate, ungniforra, Unguiata, ungulate.

## nnguent
nnguent, п., an ointment. — L. unguentum,
'ointment', fr. unguen, 'ointment', from the stem of
unguere (pp. unctus), 'to anoint', which is rel. to
Umbr. umen, 'ointment', and cogn. with OI.
andkti, 'anoints, smears', Arm. aucanem, Ί
anoint', OPruss. anctan, 'butter', OHG. ancho,
MHG., G. anke, 'butter', Olr. imb, OCo. ame-
nen, Bret, amann, W. ymenyn, 'butter*. Cp.
unction, unctuons. Cp. also anoint, axunge, ointment,
prune, 'to preen'.

## unguiculate
unguiculate, adj., having nails or claws (zool) —
ModL. unguiculatus, fr. L. unguiculus,
'fingernail', dimin. of unguis, 'nail'. See ungnal, -cule
and adj. suff. -ate.
Derivatives: unguiculate, п., unguiculat-ed, adj.

## imguiform
imguiform, adj., having the shape of a nail. —
Formed fr. L. unguis, 'nail*, and forma, 'form,
shape'. See ungual and form, n.

## Ungulatn
Ungulatn, n. pi., the hoofed mammals {zool.) —
ModL., neut. pi. of Late L. ungulatus. See next
word and cp. the second element in Notungulate.

## ungulate
ungulate, adj., hoofed; pertaining to the
Unguiata. — Late L. unguldtus, 'hoofed', fr. L. ungula,
'hoof, claw, talon', dimin. in form (but not in
meaning) of unguis, 'nail'. See ungnal, -ule and
adj. suff. -ate.

## unholy
unholy, adj. — ME., fr. OE. unhuiig. See priv.
pref. un- and holy-.
Derivatives: unholi-ly, adv., unholi-ness, n.

## uni-
uni-, combining form meaning 'having one only;
single. — L. Qni-, fr. Qnus, One'. See one and cp.
words there referred to. Cp. also the last element
in coadunate.

## uni
uni, adj., plainly woven. — F. uni, lit. 'united',
pp. of unir, 'to join, unite', fr. L. unire, of s.m.,
fr. unus, One'. See uni-.

## Uniat
Uniat, Uniate, п., pertaining to any of such
Eastern Christian Churches as acknowledge the
supremacy of the Pope. — Russ. uniyat, fr. unia,
'unity, union', fr. L. unus, One'. See uni-,

## uniaxial
uniaxial, adj., having one axis. — Compounded
of uni- and axial.

## unible
unible, adj., that may be united. — Formed with
suff. -ible fr. L. unire, 'to unite'. See unite.

## unicorn
unicorn, n. — ME. unicorne, fr. MF. (= F.) ufti-
corne, fr. L. unicornis, 'one-horned', used in the
Vulgate) for Gk. μονόκερως of the LXX text;
cp. G. Einhorn, W. ungorn, Bret, uncorn, OSlav.
ino-rogu. See uni- and horn, and cp. corn, 'a
horny induration'.

## uniform
uniform, adj. — MF. (= F.) uniforme, fr. L. uni-

## formis
formis, 'having one form', fr. L. unus, 'one', and

## forma
forma, 'form, shape'. See uni- and form, n.
Derivatives: uniform, tr. v., uniform-ly, adv.,
uniform-ness, n.

## uniform
uniform, n. — F. uniforme, 'a uniform dress1, fr.
uniforme, adj. See prec. word.

## uniformity
uniformity, n. — ME. uniformite, fr. MF. ( — F.)
uniformite, fr. Late L. uniformitatem, ace. of
Qniformitas, fr. L. uniformis. See uniform, adj.,
and -ity.

## unify
unify, tr. v. — Fr. ML. unificare, 'to unite, unify'
(either directly or through the medium of F.

## unifier)
unifier), which is compounded of L. Qnus, 'one', and
-ficdre, iv.facere, 'to make, do'. See uni- and -fy.
Derivatives: unifi-able, adj., unifi-er, n.

## unilateral
unilateral, adj., one-sided. — Coined by the
English reformer Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832)
fr. ModL. Qnilaterdlis, fr. L. йпит, neut. οι unus,
One', and latus, gen. lateris, 'side'. See uni- and
lateral.
Derivatives: unilateral-ism, п., unilateral-ist, п.,
unilateral-ity, п., unilateral-ly, adv.

## uniliteral
uniliteral, adj., consisting of one letter only. —
Compounded of uni- and literal.

## Unio
Unio, п., a genus of mussels [zool.) — ModL., fr.
L. ΰηΐδ, 'pearl', prob. meaning lit. 'that which is
unique', and rel. to unus, 'one', unio, 'unity,
union'; see union. For sense development cp. F.
solitaire, 'solitaire (diamond)', lit. 'solitary,
single' (see solitary). ·

## Uniola
Uniola, п., a genus of plants, the spike-grass. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:823 COLUMN:2 -->
Late L., name of a plant, prop, dimin. of L.
unio, 'union'. See union and dimin. suff. -ole.

## union
union,n. — ME., fr. MF. (— F.), fr. Late L. unio-
nem, ace. of unio, 'unity, union*, fr. L. unus,
'one'. See uni-.

## unionism
unionism, п., the principle of union. — See union
and -ism.

## unionist
unionist, п., an adherent of unionism. — See
union and -ist.

## uniparous
uniparous, adj., producing but one at a birth. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. unus, 'one', and
parere, 'to bring forth, beget, bear'. See uni- and
-parous.

## unipartite
unipartite, adj., not divided into parts. — Lit.
'consisting of one part only', fr. L. unus, 'one',
and pars, gen partis, 'part'. See uni-, part, п.,
and adj. suff. -ite and cp. tripartite.

## unique
unique, adj. — F. unique, fr. L. unicus, 'one only,
single', fr. unus, 'one'. See uni-.
Derivatives: unique, п., unique-ly, adv.,
uniqueness, n.

## unireme
unireme, п., a galley having but one bank of oars.
— Formed on analogy of bireme, etc., fr. L.
unus, 'one', and remus, 'oar'. See uni- and bireme.

## unison
unison, п., concert, harmony. — MF. (= F.) unis-
son, fr. ML. unisonus, 'having only one sound',
compounded of L. unus, One', and sonus,
'sound'. See uni- and sound, 'noise'.

## unit
unit, n. — Shortened fr. unity.

## Unitarian
Unitarian, п., one who rejects the doctrine of the
Trinity. — ModL. unitarius. See next word and
-ian.
Derivative: Unitarian, adj.

## unitury
unitury, adj., pertaining to a unit. — Formed fr.
unity with adj. suff. -ary.

## unite
unite, tr. and intr. v. — ME. uniten, fr. L. unitus,
pp. of unire, 'to make one, join, unite', fr. unus,
One*. See uni-.
Derivatives: unit-ed, adj., unit-ed-ly, adv., unit-
ed-ness, п., unit-er, п., unit-ing, adj., unit-ing-ly,
adv.

## unitive
unitive, adj., tending to unite. — Late L. unitivus,
fr. L. unitus. See unite and -ive.

## unity
unity, n. — ME. unite, fr. OF. unite (F. unite), fr.
L. unitatem, ace. of unites, 'unity', fr. unus, One*.
See one and cp. unit.

## univalence
univalence, univalency, n. (chem.) — Formed fr.
next word with suff. -ce, resp. -cy.

## univalent
univalent, adj., having a valency of one {chem.) —
Formed fr. tri- and L. valens, gen. -entis, pres.
part, of vaiere, *to have power'. See valiant and
cp. -valent.

## universal
universal, adj. — ME. universel, universal, fr. MF.
universal, universel (F. universel), fr. OF., fr. L.
Universalis, 'belonging to all, universal', fr. Qni-
versus. See universe and adj. suff. -al, L.
universalis was prob. coined by the Roman rhetorician
Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (cca. 35-cca. 95
C.E.) to translate Gk. κα&ολικός (see catholic).
Derivatives: universal, п., universal-ism, п.,
universal-ist, п., universal-ity, п., universal-ize,
tr. v., universal-ly, adv., universal-ness, n.

## universe
universe, n. — L. univcrsum, 'the whole world, the
universe', prop. neut. sing, of the adjective Qni-
versus, 'whole, general, universal', lit. '«turned
into one', fr. unus, 'one', and versus, pp. of ver-
tere, 'to turn'; see version and cp. words there
referred to. L. universum is prop, the loan
translation of Gk. τ6 δλον, 'the universe', subst. use
of the neut. of δλος, 'whole*.

## university
university, n. — ME. universite, fr. OF. universite
(F. universite), fr. ML. universitatem, ace. of
universitds, 'university', fr. Late L. universitas,
*a number of persons associated into one body',
fr. L., 'the whole, the whole world, a number of
persons associated into one body', fr. universus,
'whole, general, universal*. See prec. word and
-ity.

## universology
universology, п., study of the universe. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. universum, 'the universe', and
Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a
certain manner); one who deals (with a certain
topic)'. See universe and -logy.
Derivatives: universolog-ic-al, adj., universolog~
ist, n.

## univocal
univocal, adj., having one meaning only. —
Formed with adj. suff, -al fr. Late L. univocus, which
is compounded of L. unus, One', and vox, gen.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:823 COLUMN:3 -->
vocis, 'voice, sound'. See uni- and vocai.

## unkempt
unkempt, adj., not combed; untidy. — Formed
fr. priv. pref. un- and ME. kempt, pp. of kemben,
fr. OE. cemban, 'to comb', which stands in gra-
dational relationship to OE. camb, 'comb'. See
comb.

## unless
unless, conj. — Fr. earlier onlesse, onlesse that,
i.e. On less that'. Cp. F. a moins que, 'unless',
lit. On less that*, and see on and less.

## unmeet
unmeet, adj., not meet; unsuitable. — ME. un-
mete, fr. OE. unmxte, 'not meet1. See priv. pref.
un- and meet, adj.
Derivatives: unmeet-ly, adv., unmeet-ness, n.

## unruly
unruly, adj., hard to restrain, disorderly. — ME.
unreuly, fr. priv. pref. un- and reuly, ruly,
'amenable to rule', fr. reule, 'rule'. See rule, п., and
adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: unruli-ly, adv., unruli-ness, n.

## untie
untie, tr. and intr. v. — ME. untyen, fr. OE. un-
tlegan. See un-, pref. expressing reversal, and
tie.

## until
until, prep, and conj. — ME., prob. fr. unto (with
the substitution of til, 'till', for to). Cp. Dan.
indtil and Swed. infill and see unto and till.

## unto
unto, prep. — ME., contraction of *und to. The
first word means 'up to, until', and is rel. to OE.
op, OS., ΟΝ., OFris., Goth, und, OHG. unzi,
'up to, until', and to OE. end, 'end'; see end. For
the etymology of the second word see to. Cp.
prec. word.

## unwieldy
unwieldy, adj., 1) not easy to handle; 2) awkward.
— Formed from priv. pref. un- and obsolete
wieldy, 'easy to wield', from wield and adj. suff.
-y.
Derivatives: unwield-ly, adv., unwieldi-ness, n.

## up
up, adv. — ME., fr. OE. upp, up, 'up', uppe, 'on
high, up', rel. to OS. uppa, upp, OFris. up, ΟΝ.,
Swed. upp, Dan., Du. op, OHG., MHG. ы/, G.
auf, Goth, iup, 'up, upward', uf, 'under'. The
original meaning of these words was 'from
below'. They derive fr. l.-E. base *upo-, 'from
below; turning upward, upward; up, over,
beyond', whence also ΟΙ. ύρα, 'near, under, up to,
on', Gk. υπό, 'under, below', L. sub (for *suj>-),
'under'; see sub-. Fr. I.-E. base *upo- developed
the comparative *uper-, *uperl-, Over, above,
beyond', whence Ol. upari, Gk. υπέρ, L. supert
Over, above, beyond'. See over and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also upon, upper, uppish,
above, open, eaves, evil and the first element in
orlop. Cp. also hypsi-, the first element in ooftish
and the second element in daniwassal.
Derivatives: up, prep., adj., up, v. (q.v.)

## up
up, intr. v., to rise. — Fr. the adverb up. Cp. OE.
uppian, 'to rise', fr. upp, 'up', and OE. yppan, 'to
bring up, disclose', which stands in gradational
relationship to upp, *up'.

## up-
up-, pref. — From the adverb up.

## Upanishad
Upanishad, п., a class of treatises in Sanskrit
literature. — OL upanisad, lit. 'a sitting down
beside', fr. ύρα, 'near to', and ni-sad, 'a sitting
down'. For the first element see up, adv. OI. ni,
'down, downward', is rel. to Avestic ni, of s.m.,
and cogn. with OSlav. nizu, 'down', OE. nider,
'downward, down, below', and with 1$. ηϊ- in
nidus, 'nest'; see nest.

## upas
upas, п., 1) the Javanese tree Antiaris toxicaria;
2) its sap or poison. — Fr. Malay upas,
'vegetable poison', in pohn upas, lit. 'poison tree', fr.
pohn, 'poison', and upas, 'tree'. The word came
into English through the medium of the Dutch.

## upbraid
upbraid, tr. v., to chide. — ME. upbreiden, 'to
reproach, censure', fr. OE. upbregdan, fr. upp, up,
'up', and bregdan, 'to braid, twist, throw,
brandish'. See np, adv., and braid. For sense
development cp. ON. bregda, 'to braid, brandish,
upbraid', Dan. bebreide, 'to reproach, upbraid'.
Derivatives: upbraid-er, п., upbraid-ing, n. and
adj., upbraid-ing-ly, adv.

## uphoister
uphoister, tr. v. — Back formation fr. upholsterer.
Derivative: upholster-y, n.

## upholsterer
upholsterer, n. — For earlier upholdster,
secondary form of upholder, with the original sense of
One who holds up', goods for sale; see up, adv.,
hold, v., and -ster. For the redundant suff. -er in
upholsterer, cp. caterer, fruiterer, poulterer,
sorcerer.

## uphroe
uphroe, n. — See euphroe.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:824 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 797 | URINE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:824 COLUMN:1 -->
upon, prep. — ME. upon, which is a compound of
up and on. See up, adv., and on.
upper, adj. — Comparative of the adj. up. See up,
adv., and compar. suff. -er.
Derivative: upper, n.
uppish, adj. — Formed from the adj. up (see up,
adv.) with adj. suff. -ish.
Derivatives: uppisk-ly, adv., uppish-ness, n.
uproar, п., tumult. — Du. oproer, 'tumult, riot',
fr. MDu., lit. 'a stirring up', fr. op, 'up' (see up,
adv.), and riper, 'confusion', which is rel. to ON.
hrara, 'to stir up', OE. hreran, 'to move, stir,
shake'. Cp. G. Aufruhr, 'tumult', which is the
exact etymological equivalent of Du. oproer,
and see rare, 'underdone'. E. uproar was
influenced in spelling by· the verb roar.
Derivatives: uproar-tous, adj., uproar-ious-ly,
adv., uproar'ious-ness, n.

## upside down
upside down, adv. — Alteration of ME. up so
down. Cp. topsy-turvy.

## upsilon
upsilon, п., the twentieth letter of the Greek
alphabet (υ, Τ). — Gk. δ ψΐλάν, lit. 'a mere or
bare y', so called in contradistinction to the
diphthongs οι, ει, which.are pronounced in
Medieval and Modern Greek exactly like υ (= ;').
See hyoid and psilo- and cp. epsilon.

## upward
upward, adv. — ME., fr. OE. upweard. Cp. MLG.
upwart, MDu. opwaert, Du. opwaart, MHG. Bf-
wert, and see up and -ward.

## upwards
upwards, adv. — Formed from prec. word with
adv. gen. suff. -es, -s. See -wards.

## ur-
ur-, form of uro- before a vowel.

## uracho-
uracho-, combining form used in the sense of
'urachal and'. — See next word.

## urnchus
urnchus, п., a fibrous cord connecting the apex
of the bladder with the umbilicus (ana/.) —
Medical L., fr. Gk. οΰραχός, 'urinary canal of a
fetus', fr. οδρον, 'urine', and base of χεΐν, 'to
pour'. See urine and chyle.
Derivative: urach-al, adj.

## uraemia
uraemia, n. — See uremia.

## uraeus
uraeus, п., the sacred cobra as represented on the
headdress of the rulers of ancient Egypt. —
ModL., fr. Gk. ουραίος, fr. Egypt, uro, 'asp;
king'.

## Ural-Altaic
Ural-Altaic, adj., pertaining to a great group of
people and languages in Eastern Europe and
Central Asia. — Prop, 'relating to the peoples
living between the Urals and the Altaic
Mountains'.

## uralite
uralite, п., a variety of amphibole (mineral.) —
G. Uraltt, named after the Ural mountains
where it was first found. The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst. suff. -itu.

## uran
uran, п., a monitor lizard. — F. ouran, a var. of
varan, fr. Algerian Arab, liran, altered fr. Arab.
waral, 'monitor lizard'. See varan.

## uran-
uran-, form of urano- before a vowel.

## Urania
Urania, п., name of the Muse of astronomy
(Greek mythol.) — L., fr. Gk. Οΰραν'5, fem. of
ουράνιος, 'heavenly', fr. ουρανός. See urano-.
Derivative: Urani-an, adj.

## uranium
uranium, п., name of a metallic, radioactive
element (chem.) — ModL., coined by its discoverer,
the German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth
(1743-1817) in 1789 from the name of the planet
Uranus, which was discovered by Herschel in
1781. See Uranus and cp. titanium.
Derivatives: uran-ic, adj., uran-ite, n. (mineral.),
uran-it-ic, adj.

## urano-
urano-, before a vowel uran-, combining form for
uranium. — See next word.

## Uranus
Uranus, п., 1) the god of Heaven, husband of
Gaia, the Earth (Greek mythol.); 2) name of a
planet. — L., fr. Gk. Ουρανός, fr. ουρανός,
'heaven, sky', which prob. stands for *(F)opaa-
νός, hence is possibly cogn. with 01. varsam,
'rain', varsati, 'rains'. See varsha.

## uranyl
uranyl, п., the bivalent radical UOa (chem.) —
Coined fr. uran- and -yl.

## urazine
urazine, urazin, п., a crystalline compound,
CjHjN.Oj— G. Urazin, formed fr. Urin, 'urine',
fr. L. urina (see urine) and hyirazln.

## urban
urban, adj., pertaining to a city. — L. urbanus,
'pertaining to the city, cultivated, refined,
elegant', fr. urbs, gen. urbis, 'a city', esp. the city of
Rome', which is of uncertain origin. It is
possibly a loan word fr. Sumerian uru, 'city'

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:824 COLUMN:2 -->
(brought to Rome prob. through the medium of
the Etruscans). Cp. Basque uri, 'city', which
seems to be of the same origin. Cp. urbane and
suburb.
Derivatives: urban-ist, п., urban-ist-ic, adj.,
urban-ize, tr. v., urban-iz-ation, n.

## Urban
Urban, masc. PN. — Fr. L. urbanus, 'of the town
or city; refined, polished, courteous'. See prec.
word.

## urbane
urbane, adj., polished; suave. — L. urbanus; see
urhan. For a similar differentiation in form and
meaning of orig. one and the same word, cp.
german and germane, human and humane.
Derivative: urbane-ly, adv.

## urbanism
urbanism, n. — F. urbanisme, fr. L. urbanus. See
urban and -Ism.

## urbanity
urbanity, n. — MF. (= F.) urbanite, ft. L. urbd-
nitds, gen. -Otis, 'city life; refinement or elegance
in speech', fr. urbanus. See urban and nrbane.
For the ending see suff. -ity.

## urceolate
urceolate, adj., shaped like a pitcher. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. urceolus, dimin. of ur-
ceus, 'pitcher', which is of uncertain origin. It
meant perh. orig. 'an earthen vessel', and is
borrowed—togerthe with Gk. δρχη (Aeol. Βρχη),
'an earthen vessel for salted fish',—fromaSem.
language. Cp. Aram, arqa (Jer. 10: 11), 'the
earth', which is rel. to Aram.-Syr. ar'a, 'earth',
Heb. eretz, Arab, ard, Akkad. ersitu, 'earth'.
Cp. also Arakiel, name of the Angel of the earth
in the Book of Enoch, 8: 3. OSIav. vrBdl,
'pitcher', derives fr. Goth, 'aBrkeis (in gen. pi.
aurkje), 'pitcher', which itself is a loan word fr.
L. urceus. Cp. um. For the ending of L. urceolus
see dimin. suff. -Ые.

## urchin
urchin, п., 1) a hedgehog; 2) a sea urchin; 3) a
small boy, esp. a roguish one. — ME. urchon,
irchon, fr. OF. herickon, irechon, iregon, hereon
(F. herisson), formed with dimin. suff. -on ft. L.
iricius, an enlarged form of er, fr. orig. 'her,
'hedgehog', lit. 'the pricky creature', fr. I.-E.
base *gher-, 'to bristle', whence also Gk. χήρ,
gen. χηρός, 'hedgehog', Alb. def, 'wild boar,
hog', and its dimin. derk, dirk, 'young pig, sow',
Arm. jar, 'mane of the horse', Olr. garb, W.
garw, 'rough'. For derivatives of enlarged forms
of base *gker- see horror and cp. words there
referred to.

## Urdn
Urdn, п., Hindustani. — Hind, urdu, fr. Pers.
Urdu, 'camp', which is cogn. with Turk, ordu,
'horde' (see horde); used in the sense of zabdn-
i-urdu, '(language of) the camp'.

## -ure
-ure, noun suff. denoting an act or its result. —
ME., fr. OF. (= F.) -ure, fr. L. -ига,
enlargement of subst. suff. -us, which derives fr. -us, suff.
of the past participle.

## urea
urea, п., crystalline compound found in the urine
of animals (biochem.) — ModL., fr. F. игёе, а
word.coined by the French chemist Antoine-
Francois de Fourcroy (1755-1809) from the base
of the word urine (q.v.)
Derivative: ure-al, adj.

## urense
urense, п., an enzyme occurring in soybeans
(biochem.) — Coined fr. urea and suff. -ase.

## uredo
uredo, п., a kind of rust (bot.) — L. uredo, 'a
blast, blight; a burning itch', fr. Brere, 'to burn'.
See combust.

## uremin
uremin, uraemia, п., a morbid condition of the
blood (med.) — Medical L-, compounded of
ουρον, 'urine', and αίμα, 'blood'. See urine,
heinal and 1st -la.
Perivative: urem-ic, uraem-ic, adj.

## ureter
ureter, п., the duct conveying urine from the
kidneys to the bladder (anat.) — Medical L., fr. Gk.
ούρητήρ, usually in the pi. ουρητήρες, fr.
ούρεϊν, 'to pass urine', fr. ούρον. See urine.
Derivatives: ureter-al, urerer-ic, adjs.

## ureteritis
ureteritis, п., inflammation of the ureter (med.) —
Medical L., formed from prec. word with suff.
-itis.

## uretero-
uretero-, before a vowel ureter-, combining form
denoting the ureter. — Fr. Gk. ούρητήρ. See
ureter.

## urethan
urethan, urethane, п., ethyl carbamate (chem.) —
F. urethane, coined by the French chemist Jean-
Baptiste-Andre Dumas (1800-84) from the
abbreviation of the words urea and ether and suff.
-an, -ane.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:824 COLUMN:3 -->

## urethra
urethra, п., the canal through which the urine is
discharged from the bladder (anat.) — Medical
L. urethra, fr. Gk. ούρή&ρα, a word coined by
Hippocrates fr. ούρεϊν, 'to pass urine", fr. οδρον.
See urine and cp. ureter.
Derivatives: urethr-al, adj., urethr-ism, n.

## urethritis
urethritis, п., inflammation "of the urethra' (med.)
— Medical L., formed fr. Gk. ούρή*ρδ (see
prec. word) with suff. -itis.

## urethro-
urethro-, before a vowel urethr-, combining form
denoting the urethra. — ΰ^οΰρη*ρο-, ούρη*ρ-,
fr. ούρή&ρα. See urethra.

## urethroscope
urethroscope, п., an instrument for the
examination of the interior of the urethra (med.) —
Compounded of urethro- and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr.
σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See. -scope.

## uretic
uretic, adj., pertaining to urine; urinary. — Late
L. ureticus, fr. Gk. ουρητικός, 'of, or relating
to, urine', fr. ούρεϊν, 'to pass urine'. See urine
and adj. suff. -ic.

## urge
urge, tr. v. — L. urgere, 'to press, drive, urge',
cogn. with Goth, wrikan, ''to persecute', OE.
wrecan, 'to drive, expel; to avenge'. See wreak.
Derivatives: urge, п., urgent (q.v.), urg-er, n.

## nrgence
nrgence, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. Late L. urgentia.
See next word and -ce.

## urgency
urgency, n. — Late L. urgentia, fr. L. urgens, gen.
-entis. See next word and -cy.

## urgent
urgent, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.) urgent, fr. L.
urgentem, ace. of urgens, pres. part, of urgere.
See urge and -ent.
Derivatives: urgent-ly, adv., urgent-ness, n.

## -uria
-uria, combining form meaning 'relating to urine'
(med.) — Medical L., fr. Gk. -ουρία, fr. οδρον.
See urine and 1st -ia.

## Uriah
Uriah, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, a Hittite,
husband of Bathsheba. — Prob. of foreign,
possibly Horite, origin, but folk-etymol. identified
with the Heb. name Uriyya*, which lit. means
'Same of the Lord', or 'my light is the Lord'.
For the first element of this name see Urim and
cp. Uriel, for the second see Eljiah and cp. words
there referred to.

## uric
uric, adj., pertaining to urine. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ic fr. Gk. οδρον. See urine.

## Uriel
Uriel, masc. PN. — Heb. UrVel, lit. 'flame of
God' or 'my light is God'. See next word and
El.

## Urim
Urim, n. pi., one of the two objects attached to
the breastplate of the high priest (Bible). — Heb.
urim, of uncertain origin. It is perh. identical
with the pi. of Br, 'fire, flame', fr. or, v., 'it
became light' (whence also or, п., 'light'), which is
rel. to Aram, ur, 'to give light, shine', Akkad.
urru, 'light, day', Arab, dwwara, 'he kindled',
uwdr, 'heat, glow'. Cp. Uriah, prec. word and
the second element in Melchior. Cp. also the
Septuagint which renders urim by δήλωσις,
'manifestation' (fr. δηλοϋν, 'to make visible'),
and Symmachus, who translates it with the
word φωτισμοί, pi. of φωτισμός,
'illumination' (fr. φως, gen. φωτός, 'light'). Cp. Thum-
mim.

## urin-
urin-, form of urino- before a vowel.

## urinal
urinal, n. — ME. urynale, fr. OF. (— F.) urinal,
ft. Late L. Brinal, ft. L. adj. Brindlis, 'relating to
urine', fr. Brina. See urine and adj. suff. -al.

## urinary
urinary, adj. — Medical L. Brinarius,
corresponding in sense to L. Brindlis, 'relating to urine', fr.
urina. See urine and adj. suff. -ary.

## urinate
urinate, intr. v. — ML. Brindtus, pp. of urindre,
'to pass urine', fr. L. Brina, 'urine'. (L. Brlndri
means 'to plunge into water'.) See urine and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: urinat-ion, п., urtnat-ive, adj.

## urine
urine, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), ft. OF., ft. L.
urina, which is cogn. with 01. var, vari, 'water',
Avestic var, 'rain', Toch. A war, 'water', Lith.
jBres, Lett. jBra, 'sea', esp. 'the Baltic', OPruss.
wurs, 'pond', OE. wxr, ON. ver, 'sea', ON. ur,
'drizzling rain'.- AH these words derive fr. I.-E.
base *wer-, 'water, rain, wet'; cp. urea, ureter,
urethra, uretic, and the first element in aurochs.
Fr. \.-fc.*wer-s·. an-j-enlargernent of base * wer-,
derive Gk. ούρέω (for *worseyo), ούρεϊν, 'to
pass urine* (whence, with back* formation,
οδρον, 'urine'). For further derivatives of base
*wer-s- see varsha.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:825 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: URINO- | 798 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:825 COLUMN:1 -->

## urino-
urino-, before a vowel urin-, combining form
meaning 'urine'. — Fr. L. urina. See prec. word.

## urn
urn, n. — ME. urne, fr. L. urna, 'water pot, urn',
which stands for *urcnd and is rel. to urceus,
'pitcher'. See urceolate.
Derivatives: urn, tr. v., urn-ful, adj.

## uro-
uro-, before a vowel ur-, combining form
meaning 'urine1, as in urology (med.) — Gk. ούρο-,
ούρ-, fr. οΰρον, 'urine'. See urine.

## uro-
uro-, before a vowel ur-, 'tail-, tail-like', as in uro-
pod (zool.) — Gk. ούρο-, ούρ-, fr. ούρα, 'tail',
which stands for *όρσ.ρα and is rel. to δρρος
(for I.-E. *orsos), 'tail, rump, base of the spine',
and cogn. with OS., ΟΝ., OHG., MHG. ars,
'buttock'. See arse and cp. the second element
in coenurus, colure, cynosure, dasynre, squirrel.

## Urocoptis
Urocoptis, п., a genus of landsnail (zool.) —
ModL., compounded of uro-, 'tail', and Gk.
κόπτει, 'to cut, strike', which is rel. to κοπΕς,
'a knife', κόμμα, 'something cut'. See comma
and cp. Coptis.

## Uropeltidae
Uropeltidae, n. pi., a family of burrowing snakes
(zool.) — ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr.
uro-, 'tail-', and Gk. πέλτη, 'a small shield' (see
pelta); so called in allusion to the tail which ends
in a shield.

## uropod
uropod, п., any of the abdominal appendages of
an arthropod (zool.) — Componded of uro-,
'tail-', and Gk. πους, gen. ποδός, 'foot'. See
-pod.

## -urous
-urous, combining form meaning '-tailed'. —
Formed with suff. -ous fr. Gk. ούρα, 'tail'. See
uro-, 'tail-'.

## Ursa
Ursa, п., name of either of two constellations
(also called the Great Bear, resp. the Little Bear).
— L. ursa, 'she bear', fem. of ursus, 'bear'. See
Ursus and cp. words there referred to.

## Ursidae
Ursidae, n. pi., a family of large carnivores (zool.)
— ModL., formed with suff. -idae fr. L. ursus,
'bear'. See Ursus,

## ursine
ursine, adj., pertaining to a bear. — L. ursinus, fr.
ursus, 'bear'. See Ursus and -ine (representing L.
•Inus).

## urson
urson, п., the Canada porcupine. — F. ourson,
dimin. of ours, 'bear', fr. L. ursus. See Ursus.

## Ursula
Ursula, fem. PN. — Fr. L. ursulay dimin. of ursa,
'she-bear'. See Ursa and -ule.

## Ursus
Ursus, п., a genus of large carnivores, the
European brown bear and its allies (zool.) — L. ursus,
'bear', which stands for *urcsos and is cogn.
with Gk. άρκτος (also <2ρκος), 'bear'. See
arctic and cp. Ursa, ursine, urson, Ursula, Orson.

## Urtica
Urtica, п., a genus of plants, the nettle (hot.) —
L. urtica, 'nettle', lit. 'the plant that causes
burning', fr. urere, 'to burn'. See cumbast.

## Urticaceae
Urticaceae, n. pi., the nettle family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. Urtica with suff. -aceae.

## urticaceous
urticaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## urticaria
urticaria, п., nettle rash (med.) — Medical L.,
formed fr. L. urtica, 'nettle'. See Urtica.

## urticate
urticate, tr. v., to sting like a nettle. — ML.
urticatus, pp. stem of urticdre, fr. L. urtica, 'nettle'.
See Urtica and verbal surT. -ate.

## urtication
urtication, n. — ML. urticaria, gen. -onis, fr.
urticatus, pp. of urticdre. See prec. word and
-ion.

## urubu
urubu, п., the black vulture. — Port, and Sp.
urubu, A Tupi loan word.

## nrus
nrus, п., the aurochs. — L. urns, a Teut. loan
word. Ср. ОЕ., OHG. ur, 'bison*, and see
aurochs.

## us
us, objective case of we. — ME. ous, us, fr. OE.
us, re], to OS., OFris. us, ΟΝ., Swed. oss, Dan.
os, MDu., Du. ons, OHG., MHG., G. uns, Goth.
uns, fr. I.-E. base *ns-, for *nes, *nds, 'we';
cogn. with 01. nas, 'us', Avestic na, 'us', Toch.
A nas, Hitt. nash, 'us', Hitt. anzask, 'we', Alb.
na, 'us', Gk. dual νώ, νώι, 'we two', Lesbian
άμμε, Dor. αμέ (ίοΓ*άσμε; whence Ion. and Att.
ήμεΐς), Avestic ahma (for I.-E. *nsme), 'we*, L.
nos, 'we, us", OSlav. ny, 'us', nasu, 'our', OPruss.
nouson, 'our', Alb. ne, 'we', Olr. m, W., Co.,
Bret, ni, ny, 'we, us'. The rough spirit in Att.
ήμεΐς is due to the influence of ύμεΤς, 'ye,
you'. Cp. our, nostrum.

## usable
usable, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. OF. ( =
F.) user. See use, v., and -able.
Derivative: usable-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:825 COLUMN:2 -->

## usage
usage, п., the time allowed for the payment of a
bill, as established by custom. — ME., fr. OF.
(= F.) usage, fr. us, 'usage', fr. L. usus. See use,
п., and -age.

## usance
usance, n. — ME. usaunce, fr. OF. (= F.) usance,
fr. user, 'to use'. See use, v., and -ance.

## use
use, n. — ME. Hi, use, fr. OF. (= F.) us, fr. L.
usus, 'usage, custom, use', fr. usus, pp. of uti, 'to
use', fr. OL. oitier, which is rel. to Oscan uittiuf,
'use'; of uncertain origin. Cp. usage, usance,
usual, usufruct, usurp, usury, utensil, utility,
utilize, abuse, misuse, peruse.
Derivatives: use-ful, adj., use-ful-ly, adv.,
usefulness, п., use-less, adj., use-less-ly, adv., use-
less-ness, n.

## use
use, tr. v. — ME. usen, fr. OF. (= F.) user, fr.
VL. *usdre (whence also It. usare, Provenc.,
Cat., Sp., Port, usar), freq. of L- uti (pp. usus),
'to use'. See use, n.
Derivatives: us-ed, adj., us-ed-ly, adv., us-ed-
ness. п., user (q.v.)

## user
user, п., one who uses. — ME. See use, v., and
agential surT. -er.

## user
user, п., right of use (law.) — OF. (= F.) infin.
user, 'to use'. See use, v. For the subst. use of
the infinitive in law terms cp. attainder and words
there referred to.

## ushabti
ushabti, п., a small figure representing a servant,
deposited in an ancient Egyptian tomb. —
Egypt, ushebti, 'lit. answerer*.

## usher
usher, n. — ME. ussker, fr. MF. ussier, uissier (F.
huissier), fr. OF., fr. VL. ustidrius, 'doorkeeper',
fr. L. ostidrius, of s.m., fr. ostium, 'door,
entrance'. See ostiary.
Derivatives: usher, tr. v., usher-er, n.

## usine
usine, п., works, factory. — F., fr. North Eastern
F. wisine, altered fr. Picard ouchine, ult. fr. L.
officina, 'workshop, manufactury'. See officinal.

## Usnea
Usnea, п., a genus of lichens (bot.) — ModL., fr.
Arab, ushna , 'moss', which is of Persian origin.

## Usneaceae
Usneaceae, n. pi., a family of lichens (bot.) —
ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.
-aceae.

## usquebaugh
usquebaugh, п., whiskey (archaic). — Ir. and Gael.
uiscebeathadh, 'whiskey', lit. 'water of life', fr.
Olr. uisce, 'water', and bethad, gen. of bethu,
'life'. Olr. uisce stands for *wud-ko- and is cogn.
with OI. udan-, Gk. ΰδωρ, Ε. water (q.v.) The
second element comes fr. Olr. bethu, 'life', is
cogn. with Gk. βίος, L. vita, 'life', and with E.
quick (q.v.) Cp. whiskey, which is a doublet of
usquebaugh. For sense development cp. It. ac-
quavite, F. eau-de-vie, 'brandy', which are
translations of L. aqua vitae, 'water of life", a name
given to alcohol by the alchemists who thought
they had found in alcohol the elixir of life.

## ussinglte
ussinglte, п., a sodium aluminum silicate
(mineral.) — Dan. ussingit, named after the Danish
mineralogist Niels V. Ussing (died in 19] I). The
ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## Ustilago
Ustilago, п., a genus of fungi (bot.) — ModL.
ustildgo, 'smut', fr. Late L. ustilago, 'a kind of
thistle*, lit. 'the burning or itching plant', rel. to
ustuldre, 'to burn a little, to scorch'; see nstuiate.
In ModL. ustildgo is used to denote 'smut', in
allusion to the sootlike appearance of the plants
of this genus.

## ustion
ustion, п., a burning. — L. ustio, gen. -onis, fr.
ustus, pp. of urere, 'to burn'. See combust and
-ion.

## ustulate
ustulate, adj., burned, scorched. — L. ustulatus,
pp. of ustuldre, 'to burn a little, scorch', fr. ustus,
pp. of urere, *to burn'. See combust and adj. suff.
-ate and cp. Ustilago.

## ustulation
ustulation, п., a burning, scorching. — ML. ustu-
lat'w, gen. -onis, fr. L. ustulatus, pp. of ustuldre.
See prec. word and -ion.

## usual
usual, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. usudlis (whence
also OF., F. usuel), fr. L. usus, 'use'. See use, п.,
and adj. suff. -a).
Derivatives: usual-ly, adv., usual-ness, n.

## usucapion
usucapion, п., acquisition by uninterrupted
possession for a certain period of time (Roman law).
— L. usucapio, gen. -onis, 'acquisition by long
use', fr. usucapere, 'to acquire by long use',
which is compounded of usu, 'by use' (abl. of
usus), and capere, 'to take, .receive'. See use,.п.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:825 COLUMN:3 -->
captive, and -ion.

## usucaption
usucaption, п., the same as usucapion. — ML. usu-
captio, gen. -onis, refashioned fr. L. usucapio on
analogy of captio (see prec. word and caption).

## usufruct
usufruct, п., the right to the use and profits of the
property of another without damaging it (law).*
— Late L. usus fructus, frequently spelled as one
word ususfructus (whence also F. usufruit) (in
the abl. usufructu, resp. usufructu), short for usus
etfructus, 'use and fruit; use and enjoyment', fr.
usus, 'use', et, 'and', and fructus, 'fruit'. See use,
п., and fruit.
Derivative: usufruct, tr. v.

## usufructuary
usufructuary, п., one having the usufruct of
property (law). — Late L. usufructudrius, fr. usufruc-
tus. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ary.

## usurer
usurer, n. — ME., fr. OF. (— F.) usurier, fr. ML.
usiirdrius, 'usurer', fr. the Latin adjective usurd-
rius, 'pertaining to interest', fr. usura. See usury
and agential suff. -er.

## usurious
usurious, adj., 1) practicing usury; 2) pertaining
to usury. — Formed fr. usury with suff. -ous, on
analogy of adjectives in which the suff. -ous
corresponds to OF. -ous (F. -eux).
Derivatives: usurious-ly, adv., usurious-ness, n.

## usurp
usurp, tr. v., to seize without right; intr. v., to
practice usurpation. — ME. usurpen, fr. MF.
(= F.) usurper, fr. L. usurpdre, 'to get possession
of, to acquire', in Late L., 'to assume
unlawfully, to usurp', formed as if fr. an adjective
*usu-rapos, fr. usus, 'use', and rapere, 'to seize'.
See use, п., and rapid.
Derivatives: usurp-er, п., usurp-ing-ly, adv.

## nsurpation
nsurpation, n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. usur-
pdtionem, ace. of usiirpdtio, 'making use of,
taking possession of, fr. usurpdtus, pp. of
usurpdre. See prec. word and -ion.

## usury
usury, n. — ME. usurie, userie, fr. ML. usuria, fr.
L. usura, 'use, enjoyment, interest, usury*
(whence also Sp. and It. usura), fr. usus, 'use'.
See nse, п., and the suffixes -lire and -y
(representing L. -ia).

## ut
ut, п., the first tone or key-note in the scale of
Guido d'Arezzo (music). — See gamut.

## utahite
utahite, п., a hydrous basic iron sulfate (mineral.)
— Named after Utah, a state in the western
U.S.A. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## utas
utas, п., the octave (= eight days) of a feast (ec~
cles.) — AF. utaves, fr. OF. huitieve, oitauve, fr.
L. octdva (dies), 'eighth day*, fem. of octdvus,
'eighth'. See octave.

## utensil
utensil, n. — ME. utensele, utensil, fr. MF. uten-
sile, fr. L. utensilia, 'utensils', prop, subst. use
of the neut. pi. of the adj. utensilis, 'fit for use',
fr. uti, pp. usus, 'to use'; F. ustensile was
influenced in form by user, 'to use'. See use, v., and
n.

## uterine
uterine, adj., 1) pertaining to the womb; 2) born
of the same mother, but by a different father. —
L. uterinus, 'pertaining to the womb; born of
the same mother', fr. uterus, 'womb'. See uterus
and adj. suff. -ine (representing L. -inus).

## utero-
utero-, before a vowel uter-, combining form
denoting the uterus. — Fr. L. uterus, 'womb'. See
next word.

## uterus
uterus, п., the womb. — L., 'womb1, cogn. with
OI. uddram, 'belly', Maced. δδερος, 'belly,
womb', Gk. ΰστρος (Hesychius), ύστέρ α,
'womb', Lith. vedaras, 'stomach', OPruss. we-
ders, 'belly', OSlav. vedro, 'bucket'. Cp. hysteria.

## utilitarian
utilitarian, adj. — Coined by Jeremy Bentham
(1748-1832) fr. utility and suff. -arian. See next
word.

## utilitarianism
utilitarianism, п., the doctrine by Jeremy Bentham
that the end of all action should be the greatest
happiness of the greatest number iphifos.) —
Formed from prec. word with suff. -ism.

## utility
utility, n. — ME. utilite, fr. MF. (== F.) utilite>
fr. OF. utilite, fr. L. utilitdtem, ace. of utilitds,
fr. utilis, 'useful', fr. uti, 'to use'. See use, -ile and
-ity and cp. inutile.

## utilize
utilize, tr. v., to use. — F. utifiser, formed fr. L.
utilis, 'useful', with suff. -iser. See prec. word
and -ize.
Derivatives: utiliz-able, adj., utiliz-er, n.

## utmost
utmost, adj. — ME. utmest, utemest, fr. OE. ut-
m-est, ute-m-est, a double superb fr. ut, ute, 'out'.
See out and -most and cp. uttermost.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:826 -->
