<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:826 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: utmost, n.

## Utopia
Utopia, n. — ModL., lit. 'nowhere', coined by
Sir Thomas More (1779-1852) Гг. Gk. ού, 'not',
and τόπος, 'place'. See topic, п., and 1st -ia.
Derivatives: Utopi-an, adj. and п., utopi-an-ism,
п., utopi-an-ist, п., utopi-an-izet tr. v., mop-ism,
п., utop-ist-ic, adj.

## utricle
utricle, п., a little sac (zool. and bot.) — L. utricu-
lus, 'a little bag' (whence also F. utricute), dim in.
of uter, 'leather sack or bag', which prob. stands
for *udris and is cogn. with Gk. υδρία, 'water
bottle', ΰδωρ, 'water'. See water and -cle, and
cp. hydro-. Cp. also next word and Utricularia.

## utricular
utricular, adj., pertaining to a utricle. — Formed
with suff. -ar fr. L. utriculus, 'a little bag'. See
prec. word.

## Utricularia
Utricularia, п., a genus of plants, the bladder-
wort (bot.) — ModL., formed fr. L. utriculus.
See utricle and -aria.
utter» adj. — ME. uter, utter, fr. OE. uttra,
uter(r)a, Outer', rel. to OS., ON. шаг, OFris.
uttra, utera, MDu. utere, Du. utter-, OHG. u^ar,
MHG. щег, G. aufier, 'outer', compar. adjectives
formed fr. OE. ut, ute (ME. out, oute), etc.,
'out*. See out and compar. suff. -er andcp. outer,
utmost, uttermost. Cp. also next word.
Derivatives: utter-ly, adv., utter-ness, n.

## utter
utter, tr. v. — ME. uttren, fr. utter, *outside', adv.,
fr. OE. utor, adv., compar. of ut, Out'. See out
and compar. suff. -er and cp. prec. word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:826 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: utter-able, adj., utter-able-ness, п.,
utter-er, п., utter-ing, n.

## utterance
utterance, п., the act of uttering, speech. -—
Formed from the verb utter with suff. -алее.

## utterance
utterance,!!.,extremity.— ME. utteraunce, fr. MF.
(= F.) outrance, fr. OF., fr. outre, 'beyond', fr.
L. ultra; see outrance; influenced in form by an
association with the adjective utter.

## nttermost
nttermost, adj. — Formed fr. utter, adj., and
-most. See utmost.

## uvn
uvn, п., a grape, a grapelike fruit {bot.) — L. uva,
prob. fr. I.-E. *oiwa-, * iwa-, *fwa-, 'berry,
grape', whence also Gk. 6α, #η, οίη, "service
tree', δον, 'service berry', and OE. eow, iw,
'yew'. See yew and cp. pyruvic acid. Cp. also
ovea, uvula.

## uvaulte
uvaulte, п., a hydrous uranium vanadate
(mineral.) — Coined fr. «ranium, vanadium and subst.
suff. -ire.

## uvarovite
uvarovite, п., a calcium-chromium garnet
(mineral.) — Named after Count Sergei S. Uvarov
(1786-1855), president of St. Petersburg
Academy. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## uvea
uvea, п., the posterior colored surface of the iris
(anat.) — Medical L., fr. L. uva, 'a grape' (see
uva); prop, a loan translation of Gk. £αγο-
ειδής χιτών, lit. 'the covering resembling berries
or grapes' (fr. ράξ, gen. ραγός, 'grape'), a name
given by Galen to the choroid membrane and
the iris. See Joseph Hyrtl, Onomatologia Ana-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:826 COLUMN:3 -->
tomica, pp. 588-91.

## uveitis
uveitis, п., inflammation of the uvea (med.) — A
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. uvea and -itis, a
suff. of Greek origin.

## uvula
uvula, п., the fleshy lobe in the center of the
posterior part of the soft Dalate (anat.) — ML.
uvula prop, dimin. of L. uva, 'grape' (see uva and
-ule); coined by the anatomist J. Vesling (1598-
1649) in imitation of Gk. κίονίς, 'uvula', lit. 'a
small pillar', fr. κίων, gen. κίονος, 'pillar;
uvula'. See Joseph Hyrtl, Onomafologia ana-
tomica, p. 592.
Derivatives: uvul-ar, adj. and п., uvul-ar-ly, adv.

## Uvularia
Uvularia, п., a genus of plants, the bellwort (bot.)
— ModL., formed fr. ML. uvula, see uvuln and
-aria; so called in allusion to the drooping
flowers.

## uvulitis
uvulitis, п., inflammation of the uvula (med.) — A
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. uvula and -itis, a
suff. of Greek origin.

## uxorial
uxorial, adj., 1) uxorious; 2) characteristic of a
wife. — Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. uxdrius.
See next word.

## uxorions
uxorions, adj., excessively fond of, or submissive
to, one's wife. — L. uxdrius, 'pertaining to a
wife; excessively fond of a wife', fr. uxor, gen.
uxoris, 'wife'; which is of uncertain origin. For
E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: uxorlous-ly, adv., uxorious-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:827 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:827 COLUMN:1 -->

## vacancy
vacancy, η. — Late L. vacantia, fr. L. vacdns, gen.
vacantis. See next word and -cy.

## vacant
vacant, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. vacan-
tem, ace. of vacdns, pres. part, of vacdre, 'to be
empty, be unoccupied, be free, be at leisure',
which is rel. to vacuus, 'empty, void', and prob.
also to L. vastus, 'empty, waste, desert*. See
vain and cp. vacation, vacuous, vacuum, evacuate,
void. Cp. also waste, adj. For the ending see sufF.
-ant.

## vacate
vacate, tr. and intr. v. — L. vacatus, pp. οι vacdre,
'to be empty'. See prec. word and verbal suff.
-ate.

## vacation
vacation, n. — Late ME., fr. F. vacation, fr. L.
vacationer», ace. of vacatio, 'a being free from a
duty, freedom, exemption', fr. vacatus, pp. of
vacdre. See prec. word and -ion.
Derivatives: vacation, intr. v., vacation-er, п.,
vacationist (q.v.)

## vacationist
vacationist, n. — A hybrid formed fr. L. vacatio
(see prec. word) with -ist, a sufT. of Greek origin.

## Vaccaria
Vaccaria, п., a genus of plants of the pink
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. L. vacca, 'cow' (see
vaccine and -aria); so called because of its use
for fodder.

## vaccinate
vaccinate, tr. v., to inoculate with vaccine. —
Formed fr. vaccine, п., with verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: vaccination (q.v.), vaccinat-or, п.,
vaccinat-ory, adj.

## vaccination
vaccination, n. — Coined by Edward Jenner, a
Gloucestershire doctor, fr. ModL. vaccinia. See
vaccinia and -ation.

## vaccine
vaccine, adj., pertaining to a cow; pertaining to
vaccination. — L. vaccinus, 'of, or pertaining
to, a cow\ fr. vacca, 'cow', which is cogn. with
OI. vasd, 'cow'. Cp. next word. Cp. also
Vaccaria and buckaroo.

## vaccine
vaccine, п., the virus of cowpox. — Fr. L. vaccina,
'pertaining to a cow', fem. of the adjective
vaccinas, used as a noun. See vaccine, adj.
Derivative: vaccin-ic, adj.

## vaccinia
vaccinia, п., cowpox. — ModL., formed from
prec. word with 1st suff. -ia.
Derivative: vaccini-al, adj.

## Vaccinium
Vaccinium, п., a genus of plants, the blueberry
(bot.) — L. vaccinium, 'blueberry, whortleberry',
prob. a loan word fr. Gk. ΰάκίν&ος, fr. earlier
*5άκινθος, 'wild hyacinth, bluebell'; the Latin
word was influenced in form by vacca, 'cow'.
According to A. Meillet in Memoires de la so-
ciete de linguistique, 15, 162 both Gk. υάκινθος
and L. vaccinium derive from the same source.
See hyacinth and 1st -lum.

## vaccinotherapy
vaccinotherapy, п., treatment by vaccines. — A
hybrid coined fr. vaccine, a word of Latin origin,
and Gk. θεραπεία, 'service; medical
attendance'. See -therapy.

## vacillant
vacillant, adj., vacillating. — L. vacilldns, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of vacillare. See next word and
•ant.

## vacillate
vacillate, intr. v., 1) to waver, fluctuate; 2) to be
irresolute. — L. vacilldt-(um), pp. stem of
vacidare, 'to sway, waver, vacillate', which prob.
derives fr. l.-E. base *waq-, 'to be curved',
whence prob. also L. convexus, 'vaulted, arched';
see convex and cp. the first element in wang-
tooth. For the ending see verbal suff. -ate. Base
*waq- is an enlargement of base *wa-, 'to turn,
twist'; see various.
Derivatives: vacillat-ing, adj., vacillat-ing-ly,
adv., vacillation (q.v.), vaciflat-or, п., vacillat-
ory, adj.

## vacillation
vacillation, n. — L. vacillatio, gen. -onis, fr.
vacilldt-(um), pp. stem of vacillare. See prec.
word and -ion.

## vacuity
vacuity, п., emptiness. — L. vacuitds, fr. vacuus,
'empty'. See vacons and -ity.

## vacuole
vacuole, п., a small cavity or vesicle. — F., fr.
Medical L. vatuola, 'small cavity", a dimin.
formed incorrectly from the adjective vacuus,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:827 COLUMN:2 -->
ν
'empty'. See vacuum and dimin. suff. -ole.
Derivatives: vacuol-ar, vacuoi-ated, adjs., vacu-
ol-ation, n.

## vacuons
vacuons, adj., ]) empty; 2) lacking intelligence. —
L. vacuus, 'empty, void, free, at leisure*. See
vacant. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us, see
-ous.
Derivatives: vacuous-ly, adv., vacuous-ness, n.

## vacuum
vacuum, п., a space devoid of matter. — L., neut.
of vacuus, 'empty', used as a noun (see vacuous).
Vacuum is prop, a loan translation of Gk.
κενόν, lit. 'that which is empty'.
Derivative: vacuum, adj.

## vade mecum
vade mecum, a manual. — L., 'go with me'. Vade
is imper. of vadere, 4o go', which is rel. to va-
dum, 'a shallow, shoal, ford', and cogn. with
ON. vada, OE. wadan, 'to wade*. See wade and
cp. vadose. Cp. also evade, evasion, invade,
invasion, pervade, pervasion, vamoose. L. mecum,
'with me', is formed fr. me, 'me', and cum,
'with'. See me and cum,

## vadimonium
vadimonium, п., pledge, security (law). — L., fr.
vas, gen. vadis, 'bale, security', which is cogn.
with Goth, wadi, OE. wedd, 'pledge'. See wed
and cp. vas, 'pledge', and next word. Cp. also
wage. For the ending of L. -monium see -mony.

## vadium
vadium, п., pledge (law). — ML., fr. L. vas, gen.
vadis, 'bail, security'. See prec. word.

## vadose
vadose, adj., pertaining to water found in the
earth above the level of permanent ground
water (geol.) — L. vadosus, 'shallow', fr. vadum.
See vade mecum and adj. suff. -ose.

## vag-
vag-, form of vago- before a vowel.

## vagabond
vagabond, adj. — ME. vagabound, fr. MF. (= F.)
vagabond, fr. L. vagdbundus, 'wandering', formed
with gerundive suff. -bundus fr. vagari. See
vagary. Derivatives: vagabond, n. and intr. v.,
vagabondage (q.v,), vagabondism (q.v.)

## vagabondage
vagabondage, n. —. F., from the verb vagabonder,
'to roam about like a vagabond', fr. vagabond.
See prec. word and -age.

## vagabondism
vagabondism, п., vagabondage. — See vagabond
and -ism.

## vagal
vagal, adj., pertaining to the vagus (anat.) -^
Formed fr. vagus with adj. suff. -al.

## vagarious
vagarious, adj., characterized by vagaries. —
Formed from next word with suff. -ous.
Derivative: vagarious-ly, adv.

## vagary
vagary, п., 1) orig. (now obsol.), a wandering; an
excursion; 2) a whimsical idea; a caprice. — Fr.
L. vagari, 'to wander, ramble, roam about', fr.
vagus, 'wandering', which is of uncertain origin.
It is perh. a derivative of I.-E. base *wag-, 'to
bend', whence also Lith. vagiu, vdgti, 'to steal',
vagis, 'thief. Fr. *wa-n-g-, a nasal var. of this
base, come OI. vangati, 'goes, limps', Lith. vin-
gus, 'crooked, curved', vingis, 'bow; bend,
curvature*, vengiu, vengti, 'to avoid', Alb. vank, vangu,
'felloe*, ON. vakka (for *vanka), OHG. wankon,
MHG., G. wanken, 'to stagger, totter'. Base
*wag- is a collateral form of base *waq-, for
whose derivatives see vacillate and convex. Cp.
vagrant, vague, divagate, divagation,
extravagance, sollvagant. Cp. also wankle, wench, wince,
winch, wink, wonky, lapwing. Cp. also rave, 'to
speak as in delirium', and reverie, Forthe ending
of vagary see subst. suff. -ary.

## vag in-
vag in-, form of vagino- before a vowel.

## vagina
vagina, п., in female mammals, the canal leading
from the vulva to the uterus (anat.) — L. vagina,
'sheath, scabbard; vagina', cogn. with Lith.
voiiu, votti, 'to cover with a hoUow thing'. Cp.
evaginate. Cp. also vanilla.
Derivatives: vagin-al, adj., vagin-ate, vagin-at-
ed, adjs.

## vaginectomy
vaginectomy, п., removal of the vagina. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. vagina (see prec. word) and
Gk. -εκτομία, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a
cutting out*. See -ectomy.

## vaginitis
vaginitis, п., inflammation of the vagina (med.) —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:827 COLUMN:3 -->
A Medical Latin hybrid coined fr. L. vagina (see
vagina) and -tis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## vagino-
vagino-, before a vowel vagin-, combining form
denoting the vagina. — See vagina.

## vagitus
vagitus, п., the cry of the new-born child. — L.
vagitus, 'a cry', fr. vagire, 'to cry', which is cogn.
with OI. vagnuh, 'sound', Gk. ήχεΐν, 'to
resound', ήχή, 'noise', ήχώ, 'sound, echo'. See
echo and cp. sough.

## vago-
vago-, before a vowel vag-, combining form
denoting connection with the vagus. — See vagns.

## vagrancy
vagrancy, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -cy.

## vagrant
vagrant, adj. and n. — ME. vagraunt, prob. a
blend of MF. wolcrant, waucrant, fr. OF., pres.
part, of walcrer, 'to walk, wander about', with
F. vagant, pres. part, of vaguer, fr. L. vagari, 'to
wander, roam about'. OF. walcrer is a Teut.
loan word; see walk. For the etymology of L.
vagari see vagary.
Derivatives: vagrant-ly, adv., vagrant-ness, n.

## vagrom
vagrom, adj., Dogberry's corruption of vagrant
in Shakespeare's Muck Ado about Nothing.

## vague
vague, adj., 1) indefinite, 2) indistinct. — MF.
(= F.), 'wandering', fr. L. vagus, whence vagari,
'to wander, roam about'. See vagary and cp. the
second element in solivagant.
Derivatives: vague, n. and v., vague-ly, adv.,
vague-ness, n.

## vagus
vagus, п., the pneumogastric nerve (anat.) —
Medical L. (nervus) vagus, lit. 'the wandering
nerve'. See prec. word.

## vail
vail, п., gratuity. — Aphetic for avail.

## vail
vail, tr. and intr. v., to lower, take off. — Aphetic
for obsol. ovale, fr. F. avaler, 'to lower, let
down; to swallow', fr. ά val, 'to the valley,
downhill', fr. L. ad vallem, 'to the valley'. See
ad- and vale, 'valley', and cp. vendaval. Cp. also
avale.

## vain
vain, adj. — ME. vaine, vain, vayn, veyn, fr. OF.
vain, vein (F. vain), fr. L. vdnus, 'empty, void,
vain' (whence also It., Sp. vano, Provenc. va,
Port, vdo), which is cogn. with OI. unah,
'insufficient wanting', Avestic una-, 'wanting', Arm.
unain, 'empty', Gk. εΰνις (for*^fcvLq),
'bereaved of, fr. I.-E. base *(e)wd-n-, 'to be empty, to
lack'. Cp. vanish, vanity, vaunt, evanesce,
evanish, Cp. also wan, want, wanton. Cp. also vacant.
Derivatives: vain-ly, adv., vain-ness, n.

## vair
vair, п., fur (her.) — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) voir, fr.
L. varius, 'varied, variegated, particolored*. See
various and cp. the second element in miniver.

## Vaisya
Vaisya, п., the third of the great Hindu castes,
comprising agriculturists and merchants. — OI.
vaisyah, 'settler, peasant', rel. to vesah, 'house*,
visah, 'neighbor', and cogn. with Gk. οίκος,
dial. *5οΐκος, 'house', L. vicus, 'village'. See
vicinage.

## valvode
valvode, п., the title of local or provincial rulers
in certain Slavic countries of southeastern
Europe, formerly used esp. in Transylvania and in
Moldavia. — ML. vaivoda, fr. earlier Hung.
vajvoda (later contracted into vajda), fr. Serb
vojvoda, lit. 'leader of an army', fr. OSlav. voji
(pi.), 'warriors', and -voda, 'leader', from the
stem of voditi, 'to lead'. The first element is
cogn. with OI. veti, 'pursues*, Lith. vejii, vyti, 'to
hunt, pursue', vainoti, 'to revile*, L. vendri, 'to
hunt, chase'; see venery, 'hunting'. The second
element is rel. to Czech voditi, etc., and to
OSlav. vesti, Russ. vest\ Czech vesti, etc., 'to
lead', Lith. vedu, vesti, and vadau, vadyti, Lett.
vedu, vest, and vadu, vadit, 'to lead', Ir.fedim, Ί
lead, bring', Avestic vadayeiti, 'leads'. Cp.
voivode.

## vajra
vajra, п., the thunderbolt in Hindu mythol. — OI.
vajrab, 'lndra's thunderbolt', rel. to vajafr, 'force,
swiftness, race, prize', vajayati, 'drives on', and
cogn. with Goth, wakan, 'to be awake', OE.
wacian, 'to be awake^, to watch*. See wake, v.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:828 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 801 | VALVULITIS -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:828 COLUMN:1 -->
and ср. words there referred to.

## vakeel
vakeel, vakil, п., minister, ambassador, deputy»
attorney (Anglo-Ind.) — Hind, vakil, fr. Arab.
waktl, from the base of wakala, 'he
recommended, entrusted' (whence wakkala, 'he delegated,
deputed'); rel. to Heb. yakhSl, Aram. yekhil> 'he
was able, had power, prevailed*, Ethiopian tawa-
kala, 'it went over into somebody else's power*,
and also to Aram. kehel, 'was able'. These
words prob. mean lit. 'to hold, contain', and are
rel. to Heb. kal, 'it comprehended, held,
contained'.

## valance
valance, п., piece of drapery. — ME. valaunce,
vallance, prob. fr. Valence in SW. France, where
this material was made. Cp. Valencia and
Valenciennes lace.

## vale
vale, п., valley. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) val,
'valley', fr. L. valles, later vatlis (for *wal-nis),
which, together with vallum (for *wal-nom),
'wall', prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *wal-, *wel-,
'to turn, bend, twist, roll'. See volute and cp.
vail, 'to lower', valley, vailum, vaudeville, venda-
val, avale, Convallaria. Cp. also 2nd helo-.

## vale
vale, interj. and п., farewell. — L. vale, sing,
imper. of valere, 'to be strong, be well'. See
valiant and cp. the first element in next word and
the second element in carnival.

## valediction
valediction, п., farewell. — Fr. L. valedict-{um),
pp. stem of valedtcere, 'to say farewell', which is
compounded of valere, 'to be strong, be well',
and dicere, pp. dictus, 'to say, tell*. See valiant
and diction and cp. prec. word.

## valedictory
valedictory, adj., saying farewell. — Formed
with adj. sufT. -ory fr. L. valedict-(um), pp. stem
of valedicere. See prec. word.
Derivatives: valedictory, п., valedict-ori-ly, adv.

## valence
valence, valency, п., combining power of an
element or radical (cfiem.) — Late L. valentia,
'strength, vigor, power, capacity', fr. valens,
gen. -entis, pres. part, of valere. See -valent and
-ce, resp. -cy and cp. ambivalence, univalence,
bivalence, tri-, quadri-, tetravalence.

## Valencia
Valencia, п., a kind of cloth. — Named after
Valencia, a town in Spain. Cp. valance.

## Valenciennes lace
Valenciennes lace, Valenciennes, п., a kind of
bobbin lace. — Named after Valenciennes, a
town in Northern France.

## valency
valency, п., valence. — See valence.

## -valent
-valent, combining form meaning 'having a
valence of...* (cfiem.) — Fr. L. valens, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of valere, 'to be strong, have
power'. See valiant and cp. monovalent,
univalent, bivalent, divalent, trivalent, quadrivalent,
tetravalent, quinquivalent, pentavalent, hexa-
valent, octavalent.

## Valentine
Valentine, masc. PN. — L. Valentlnus, fr. Valens,
gen. Valentis, lit. 'strong', pres. part, of valere,
'to be strong, be weir. See valiant and cp. next
word.

## valentine
valentine, п., ]) sweetheart chosen on Valentine's
day; sweetheart; 2) a letter or gift sent to a
sweetheart on Valentine's day. — ME., fr. L.
Valentinus, name of a saint whose feast day
(Valentine's day), fell on February 14th. For
the etymology of the name see -valent, valiant,
for the ending see sufT. -ine (representing L.
-Inus).

## valentinite
valentinite, п., a native oxide of antimony, SbaOs
{mineral.) — G. Valentinit, named by the
Austrian mineralogist Wilhelm Karl von Haidinger
(1795-4871) in 1845 after Basil Valentine, a 15th
cent. monk. The ending -it goes back to Gk.
-ΐτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## Valeria
Valeria, fem. PN. — L., fem. of Valerius, name
of a Roman gens, from valere, 'to be strong, be
weir. See valiant and cp. next word.

## valerian
valerian, п., i) any of the plants of the genus
Valeriana {bot.); 2) a drug consisting of the roots of
some of these plants. — ME. valeriane, fr. ML.
Valeriana, prob. fem. of Valerianus, 'of Valeria',
fr. L. Valeria, name of a province in Pannonia,
place of origin of this plant. See prec. word and
-an.
Derivatives: valerian-ic, valer-ic, adjs.

## Valeriana
Valeriana, п., a genus of plants, the valerian
{bot.) — See prec. word.

## Valerianaceae
Valerianaceae, n. pi., the valerian family {bot.)
— ModL., formed from prec. word with suff.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:828 COLUMN:2 -->
-aceae.

## valerianaceous
valerianaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Valerianella
Valerianella, п., a genus of plants, the corn salad
(bot.) — ModL., formed fr. Valeriana with
dimin. suff. -ella.

## valet
valet, n. — OF. (= F.) fr. earlier vaslet. See var-
let, which is a doublet of valet, and cp. vassal.

## valetudinarian
valetudinarian, п., a sickly person; adj., sickly. —
See next word and -an.
Derivative:' valetudinarian-ism, n.

## valetudinary
valetudinary, adj., sickly; п., a valetudinarian. —·
L. valetudinarius, 'sickly, infirm', formed with
suff. -arius fr. valetudo, gen. -udinis, 'state of
health, good health, ill health', fr. valere, 'to be
strong, be well'. See valiant and the suffixes -ude
and -ary.

## valgus
valgus, adj., having the legs bent outward, bow-
legged {med.) — L.,prob. cogn. with Ol. valgati,
'he jumps with joy', valgd, 'bridle, rein', OE.
wealcan, 'to roll, whirl, wring*, OHG. walkan,
'to strike, beat'. See walk.

## Valhalla
Valhalla, п., the hall in which Odin receives the
souls of heroes slain in battle (Scand. mythol.)
— ON. valholl, 'the hall of the slain',
compounded of valr, 'the slain', and holl, *a royal
hall*. The first element is rel. to OE. wa7,
'slaughter, field of battle, bodies of those who
were slain in battle', wol, 'pestilence', OHG.,
MHG. wal, 'battlefield; slaughter', OHG. wuol,
'slaughter', and cogn. with Olr.fuil, 'blood', W.
gweli, 'wound', Toch. A wul, 'to die', Lith.
velis, 'ghosts of the dead'. The second element
is rel. to OE. heall, 'hall'; see hall. Cp. the first
element in Valkyrie.

## vali
vali, п., the governor of a Turkish vilayet. —
Turk- vali, fr. Arab. waif. See vilayet.

## valiance
valiance, valiancy, n. — ME. valiaunce, fr. MF.
(= F.) vaillance, fr. vaillant, 'valiant'. See next
word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## valiant
valiant, adj. — ME. valiaunt, fr. MF. vailant,
vaillant (F. vaillant), fr. OF., prop. pres. part, of
valoir, 'to be worth, be good for', fr. L. valere,
'to be strong, be well, be worth' (whence also It.
valere, OProvenc., Sp., Port, valer, Catal. val-
dre); fr. I.-E. base *wal-, 'to be strong', whence
also W. gallu, 'to be able', OU.flaitk, 'rule,
dominion', OW. gualart, ModW. gwaladr,
'sovereign, lord', gwlad, 'native land, home', OSlav.
vlatu, 'giant', Toch. A wal, В walo, 'prince,
king'. Cp. vale, 'farewell', valediction, valence,
valentine, Valeria, valerian, Valeriana,
Valerianella, valetudinary, valid, validity, value, avail,
convalesce, convalescent, countervail, devaluate,
equivalent, invalid, invalidate, prevail, revales-
cent. Cp. also base *wal-dh-, whence Lith.
valdau, valdyti, 'to rule', veldu, vetdeti, 'to
possess, rule', OSlav. vlado, vlasti, 'to rule', OPruss.
weldisnan (ace), 'heritage', waldnikans (ace. pi.),
'kings', Goth, waldan, OE. wealdan, 'to govern'.
See wield and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: valiant-ly, adv., valiant-ness, n.

## valid
valid, adj. — MF. (= F.) valide, fr. L. validus,
'strong, able, healthy', fr. valere, 'to be strong,
be well'. See valiant.
Derivatives: validate (q.v.), validity (q.v.),
valid-ly, adv., valid-ness, n.

## validate
validate, tr. v., to make valid. — ML. validdtus,
pp. of validdre, 'to make valid', fr. L. validus.
See prec. word and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: validat-ion, n.

## validity
validity, n. — MF. (=^ F.) validite, fr. L. validita-
tem, ace. of validitas, 'strength', fr. validus. See
•valid and -ity.

## valise
valise, п., a suitcase; a soldier's kitbag. — F., fr.
it. valigia, 'saddlebag', which is of uncertain
origin. It is pern, a loan word fr. Arab. walihah,
'bag of corn, skep, large bag'.

## Valkyrie
Valkyrie, Valkyria, Valkyr, п., one of the twelve
war goddesses in Scand. mythology, who hover
over the fields of battle choosing those who are
to be slain. — ON. valkyrja, lit. 'chooser of the
slain', fr. valr, 'the slain', and -kyrja, 'chooser',
which is rel. to ON. kjosa, OE. ceosan, 'to
•choose'. For the first element see Valhalla, for
the second see choose.

## vallation
vallation, п., a rampart. — Late L. vallatio, gen.
-onis, fr. L. vallatus, pp. of vaffdre, 'to surround
with a rampart', fr. vallum. See vallum and -ation.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:828 COLUMN:3 -->

## vallecula
vallecula, п., a groove, channel (anat. and bot.) —
Late L. vallecula, 'д little valley*, dimin. of L.
valles. See vale, 'valley', and -cula.

## valley
valley, n. — OF. valee, vallee (F. vallee), fr. val,
'valley', fr. L·.'valles, later vallis. See vale,
'valley'. Cp. It., Sp., Port, valle, Prov. val, 'valley',
which are of the s'ame origin as OF. val.

## Vallisneria
Vallisneria, п., a genus of plants, the tape grass
and the eel grass {bot.) — ModL., named after
the Italian botanist Antonio VaWsneri (1661-
1730). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Vallisneriaceae
Vallisneriaceae, n. pi., a family of aquatic plants
(bot.) — ModL., formed from prec. word with
suff. -aceae.

## vallisneriaceous
vallisneriaceous, adj. — See prec. word and
-aceous.

## vallonia
vallonia, n. — See valonia.

## Vallota
Vallota, п., a genus of African bulbous plants
{bot.) — ModL., named after the French
physician and botanist Pierre Vallot (1594-1671).

## vallum
vallum, п., a rampart. — L., 'a palisaded wall or
rampart; wall, rampart', for *wal-nom, rel. to
vallus (for *wal-nos), 'stake', and to valles,
'valley'. See vale, 'valley', and cp. circumvallate,
contravallation, interval. Cp. also wall,

## valonia
valonia, also vallonia, п., the acorn cups of the
valonia oak. — It. vallonia, fr. MGK. βαλα^ία
(r. valania), 'evergreen oak, ilex', fr. βαλάνι. (r.
valani), 'acorn*, fr. Gk. βάλανος, of s.m. See
balano-.

## valor
valor, valour, п., bravery. — ME. valour, fr. OF.
valor, valour (F. valeur), fr. L. valorem, ace. of
valor, 'worth, value, courage', from the stem of
valere, 'to be strong, be well, be worth'. See
valiant,

## valorization
valorization, n. — Port, ναΐοηζαςαο, fr. valorizare,
fr. valor, fr. L. valorem, ace. of valor. See prec.
word and -ization.

## valorize
valorize, tr. v. — Back formation fr. valorization,

## valorous
valorous, adj. — MF. (— F.) valeureux, fr. ML.
valorosus, fr. L. valor. See valor and -ous.
Derivatives: valorous-ly, adv., valorous-ness, n.

## valse
valse, п., a waltz. — F., a loan word fr. G. Waher.
See waltz.
Derivative: valse, intr. v.

## valuable
valuable, adj. — Formed fr. value, v. (see value),
and sufT. -able.
Derivatives: valuable, п., valuable-ness, п.,
valuabl-y, adv.

## valnation
valnation, n. — MF. (= F.), fr. valuer, fr. value,
п., fr. OF. See value and -ation.
Derivatives: valuation-al, adj., valuat-or, n.

## value
value, n. — ME., fr. OF., prop. fem. pp. of valoir,
'to be worth', used as a noun, fr. L. valere, 'to
be strong, be well, be worth'. See valiant and cp.
valuta, evaluate.
Derivatives: value, tr. v., value-less, adj., value·
less-ness, n.

## valuta
valuta, п., the value of a currency. — It., prop
fem. pp. of valere, 'to be worth', fr. L. valere.
See valiant,

## valval
valval, valvar, adj., valvular (biol.) — See valvulae
and adj. suff. -al, resp. -or.

## valvate
valvate, adj., having valves. — ModL. valvatus,
fr. L., 'having leaves or folds', fr. valva. See
valve and adj. suff. -ate.

## valve
valve, n. — L. valva, 'leaf, fold or valve of a door',
which stand in gradational relationship to L.
volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and cp. bivalve.
Derivatives: valv-ed, adj., valve-less, adj.

## valvulae
valvulae, n. pi., little valves {anat.) — Medical L.,
coined by the anatomist Benedict fr. L. valvolae,
dimin. of vulvae, 'leaves, folds or valves of a
door'. See prec. word and dimin. suff -ole.
Derivatives: valvul-ar, valvul-ate, adjs.
valvulae conniventes Kerkringii {anat.) —
Medical L., lit. 'the closing valves of (= discovered
by) Kerkring'; fr. valvulae (q.v.) and nom. pi.
of connlvens, pres. part, of connivere, 'to close
the eyes', see connive. The discovery of these
valves was erroneously ascribed to Theodor
Kerkring (1640-93), becausee the same valves
were already known to the anatomist Gabriel
Fallopio (see Fallbpian). See Joseph Hyrtl,
Onomatologia anatomica, p. 599.

## valvule
valvule, п., a little valve. — F. See valvulae.

## valvulitis
valvulitis, п., inflammation of the valves of the
heart (med.) — A Medical Latin hybrid coined

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:829 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VAMBRACE | 802 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:829 COLUMN:1 -->
fr. valvulae and -itis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## Yambrace
Yambrace, п., a piece of armor for the protection
of the forearm. — ME., fr. AF. vant-bras, aphet-
ic for F. avant-bras, lit. 'forearm*, fr. avant,
'for', and bras, 'arm'. See avaunt and brace, 'a
prop*, and cp. vnmp, 'front part of a boot', and
the first element in vamplate.

## vamoose
vamoose, also vamose, intr. v., to decamp (slang).
— Fr. Sp. vamos, 'let us go', fr. L. vadere, 'to
go'. See vade mecum.

## vamp
vamp, п., the front part of a boot or shoe, upper.
— ME. vampe, vaumpe, fr. OF. avampie (F.
avant-pied) 'forepart of the foot', fr. avant,
'before', and pie, pied, 'foot'. For the first
element see avaunt and cp. the first element in
Yambrace. F. pied derives fr. L. pedem, ace. of
pes, 'foot*. See foot and cp. pedal.
Derivative: vamp, v., to repair, patch together.

## vamp
vamp, п., an adventuress (slang). — Shortened
fr. vampire.

## vampire
vampire, п., in folklore, a reanimated corpse
sucking the blood of sleeping persons. — F., fr.
G. Vampir, which is of Slavic origin. Cp. Serb.
vampir, Bulg. vapir, vepir, Ukrainian uper, upyr.
The Slavic words themselves are prob. borrowed
fr. Turk, uber, 'witch'.
Derivative: vampir-ism, n.
vampire bat. — So called because of its
bloodsucking habit (whence also its popular name
'bloodsucking bat'. The name Vampyrus (Ves-
pertilio vampyrus) was applied to this bat by the
French naturalist Georges-Louis Leelerc, Count
deBuffon (1707-88).

## vampiate
vampiate, п., an iron plate for the protection of
the hand. — Lit. 'fore plate', compounded of
AF. vant, aphetic form of avant, 'before',- and
plat, 'plate'. See avaunt and plate and cp. vamp,
'front part of a boot', and the first element in
vambrace.

## Vampyrus
Vampyrus, п., a genus of bats (zool.) — ModL.,
introduced by BufTon. See vampire bat.

## van
van, п., a vehicle. — Shortened form of caravan
(q.v.)

## van
van, п., a winnowing fan. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)
van, fr. L. vannus, 'winnowing fan', which is of
uncertain origin. It is possibly rel. to L. ventus,
'wind'. See wind, 'air in motion', and cp. fan, 'an
instrument for winnowing'.
Derivatives: van, tr. v., vann-ел, n.

## van
van, n. — Shortened form of vanguard (q.v.)

## vanadate
vanadate, п., a salt of vanadic acid (chem.) — See
vanadium and chem. suff. -ate.

## vanadic
vanadic, adj., pertaining to, or containing, triva-
lent or pentavalent vanadium (chem.) — See
vanadium and adj. suff. -ic,

## vanadinite
vanadinite, п., a mineral consisting of lead
vanadate and lead chloride. — See vanadium, suff.
-in and subst. suff. -ite,

## vanadious
vanadious, adj., van ad о us. — See vanadous.

## vanadium
vanadium, п., name of a rare metallic element
(chem.) — ModL., coined by the Swedish
chemists Baron Jons Jakob Berzelius (1779-
1848) and Nils Gabriel Sefstrum (1787-1854) in
1830 from ON. Vanadis, one of the names of the
goddess Freya. For the ending see chem. suff.
-ium.

## vanadons
vanadons, adj., pertaining to, or containing,
divalent or trivalent vanadium (chem.) — See
vanadium and -ous.

## Vandal
Vandal, n. — L. Vandalus, pi. Vandalf, a name of
Teut. origin (cp. OE. Wendil, pi. Wendlas),
prob. meaning lit. 'wanderers', and rel. to G.
wandeln, *to wander'. See wander.

## vandal
vandal, adj. — Fr. prec. word; used in the sense
of 'acting, barbarously destroying, like a
Vandal'.
Derivatives: Vandal-ic, adj. and п., vandal-ish,
adj., vandal-ism, n.

## Vandyke
Vandyke, adj., of Vandyke; resembling a picture
by Vandyke. — E. spelling of the name of
Anthony Van Dyck, the Flemish painter (1599-
1641).

## Vandyke
Vandyke, п., a picture by Vandyke; a Vandyke
collar; a deeply indented border as seen on
Vandyke collars. — Fr. Vandyke, adj.

## vandyke
vandyke, tr. v., to mark with Vandykes. — Fr.
Vandyke, n.

## vane
vane, n. — ME., fr. OE.fana, 'flag', which is rel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:829 COLUMN:2 -->
to Goth, fana, 'piece of cloth', OS., OHG. fano,
of s.m., G. Fahne, 'flag, standard', and cogn.
with Gk. πηνος 'the thread on the shuttle,
woof, in the pi. 'web', πήνη (Hesychius),
'web', L. pannus, piece of cloth'. See pane.
Derivative: van-ed, adj.

## Vanessa
Vanessa, п., a genus of butterflies (entomol.) —
ModL., of uncertain origin.

## vang
vang, п., either of two ropes extending from the
end of a gaff to the deck (naut.) — Du. vang, 'a
catch', fr. vangen, 'to seize, catch, capture',
which is rel. to G. fangen, of s.m. See fang, n.
and v.

## vanguard
vanguard, n. — ME. avaunt garde, vantgard, fr.
MF. (= F.) avant-garde, fr. avant, 'before' and
garde, 'guard'. See avaunt and guard.

## vanilla
vanilla, n. — Fr. earlier Sp. vanynilla (now vai-
nilla), dimin. of vayna (now vaina), 'sheath, pod*,
fr. L. vagina (see vagina); so called from the
shape of the fruit.

## vanish
vanish, intr. v., to disappear- — ME. vanissken,
fr. OF. esvaniss-, pres. part, stem of esvanir,
evanir (F. evanouir), fr. VL. *exvanire, for L.
evanescere, 'to fade, vanish away*, which is
formed fr. ё-, 'out of (see e-), and vdnescere, 'to
fade, vanish', lit. 'to become empty', an
inchoative verb formed from the adjective vanus,
'empty, vain'. Cp. It. svanire, OProvenc. esva-
noir, esvanezir, ModProvenc avanir, Port, es-
vair, esvaecer, 'to vanish', and see vain and
verbal suff. -ish. Cp. also evanesce, evanish.
Derivatives: vanish, п., vanish-er, п., vanish-ing,
adj., vanish-ing-ly, adv.

## vanity
vanity, n. — ME. vanite, fr. OF. vanite (F. vanite),
fr. L. vanitdtem, ace. of vdnitds, 'emptiness,
worthlessness*, fr. vanus. See vain and -lty.

## vanqnish
vanqnish, tr. and intr. v. — ME. venquishen, ven-
fcisen, fr. AF. venquiss-, pres. part, stem of ven~
quir, corresponding to OF. vainquir,
refashioned (after the Latin) fr. veintre, veincre (F. vain-
cre), fr. L. vincere, 4o conquer'. See vincible and
verbal suff. -ish.
Derivatives: vanquish, п., vanquish-able, adj.,
vanquish-er, n.

## vantage
vantage, n. — ME., fr. AF., aphetic for OF. ( =
F.) avantage. See advantage.

## vanward
vanward, adv., placed in the van or front. —
Compounded of van, 'the front part', and -ward.

## vapid
vapid, adj., tasteless. — L. vapidus, 'that which
has lost its vapor, flavorless, insipid', rel. to
vappa, 'stale wine', prob. also to vapor, 'steam,
vapor'. See vapor and cp. fade.
Derivatives: vapid-ity, п., vapid-ly, adv.

## vapor
vapor, vapour, n. — ME. vapour, fr. AF. vapour,
fr. OF. vapeur (F. vapeur), fr. L. vapOrem, ace.
of vapor, 'steam, vapor', which is of uncertain
origin. It is possibly cogn. with Gk. καπνός
(for *κΓαπνός), 'smoke, vapor', Lith. kvapas,
'vapor, smoke', kvepiu, kvepti, 'to breathe,
exhale fragrance', and rel. to L. cupere, 'to desire'.
See Cupid and cp. evnporate, vapid.
Derivatives: vapo(u)r, intr. v., vapo(u)r-er, п.,
vapo(u)r-ing, adj. and п., vapor-ize, tr. and intr.
v., vapor-iz-ation, п., vapor-iz-er, n.

## vaporous
vaporous, adj. — L. vapordsus, fr. vapor. See
vapor and -ous.
Derivatives: vapo(u)rous-ly, adv., vapo(u)rous-
ness, n.

## vapulate
vapulate, tr. v., to flog. — Fr. L. vdpuldt-(um),
pp. stem of vapulare, 'to be flogged' (prop, 'to
cry out for pain'), which is cogn. with Goth.
wopjan, 'to shout, cry out, weep., ON. op, 'shout,
lamentation', OE. wepan, 'to weep*. See weep
and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: vapulat-ion, п., vapulat-ory, adj.

## vaquero
vaquero, п., a drover. — Sp., 'cowherd', fr. vaca,
'cow', fr. L. vacca. See vaccine and cp. buckaroo.

## varan
varan, п., a monitor lizard. — F., fr. ModL.
varanus, fr. Arab, wdran, altered fr. waral,
'monitor lizard'.. Cp. uran.

## Varangian
Varangian, п., one of the Northmen who founded
a dynasty in Russia. — Formed with suff. -ian

## fr. ML. Varangus
fr. ML. Varangus, fr. MGk. βάραγγος, a name
borrowed—through Slav.—from ON. Vseringi,
'a Scandinavian', prop, 'a confederate', fr. var-
(pl. vdrar), 'pledge; faith', which is rel. to OE.
wxr, agreement, treaty; promise, pledge; faith,

## fidelity
fidelity, friendship', OHG. wara, 'faithfulness,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:829 COLUMN:3 -->
grace'. See very.
Derivative: Varangian, adj.

## varec
varec, п., seaweed. — F. varec. varech, 'wreck,
wreckage, derelict', fr. AF. warec, fr. OE. wrxc.
See wreck,

## variability
variability, n. — Formed with suff. -ity fr. L.
variabilis. See variable,

## variable
variable, adj. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) fr. L.
variabilis, 'changeable', fr. variare, 'to change'. See
vary and -able.
Derivatives: variable, п., variabil-ity, п., vari-
abfe-ness, п., variabl-y, adv.

## variance
variance, n. — ME. variaunce, fr. OF., fr. L.
variantia, 'difference, diversity, variety', fr.
varians, gen. -antis. See next word and -ce.

## variant
variant, adj. and n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L.
variantem, ace. of varians, pres. part, of variare.
See vary and -ant.

## variate
variate, tr. and intr. v., to vary (obsol.); п., а
variable. — L. varidtus, pp. of variare, 'to
change'. See vary and verbal suff. -ate.

## variation
variation, n. — L. varidtionem, ace. of variatio,
'difference, variation*, fr. varidtus, pp. of vari-
are. See vary and -ation.
Derivative: variation-al, adj.

## varicella
varicella, п., chicken pox (med.) — A Medical L.
dimin., irregularly formed fr. variola, itself a
dimin. formed fr. L. varius, 'changing, varying'.
See various.
Derivative: varicell-ar, adj.

## varicocele
varicocele, п., a varicose condition of the veins
of the spermatic cord of the scrotum (med.) —
A medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. varix, gen.
-icis, 'a dilated vein', and Gk. κήλη, 'tumor'.
See varix and -cele.

## varicolored
varicolored, varicoloured, adj., having various
colors. — Compounded of L. varius (see
various), color (see color) and 1 st suff. -ed.

## varicose
varicose, adj., having dilated veins. — L. varico-
sus, 'full of dilated veins, varicose', fr. varix,
gen. -ids, 'a dilated vein'. See varix and adj.
suff. -ose.
Derivative: varicos-ity, n.

## varicosis
varicosis, п., formation of varicose veins;
varicosity (med.) — A Medical L. hybrid coined fr.
L. varix, gen. -icis (see varix), and -osis, a suff.
of Greek origin.

## varicula
varicula, п., varicosity of the veins of the
conjunctiva. — L., formed fr. varix, gen. -icis (see
varix), with dimin. suff. -ula (see -ule).

## varied
varied, adj. — Prop. pp. of vary.
Derivative: varied-ly, adv.

## variegate
variegate, tr. v., 1) to mark with different colors;
2) to diversify. — L. variegdtus, pp. of variegdre,
'to make of various colors', compounded of
varius, 'changing, varying, various', and the
stem of agere, 'to set in motion, drive, lead; to
do, act*. For the first element see varions, for the
second see agent, adj., and cp. the second
element in castigate and in words there referred to.
Derivatives: variegat-ed, adj., variegat-ion, n.

## variety
variety, n. — MF. (= F.) variete, fr. L. varieta-
tem, ace. of varietas, 'diversity, variety', fr.
varius. See various and -ity.

## variform
variform, adj., having various forms. —
Compounded of L. varius (see various) and forma
(see form, n.)

## variola
variola, п., smallpox (med.) — Medical L., a
dimin. formed fr. L. varius, 'changing, various'.
See various and dimin. suff. -ole and cp. varicella.
Derivatives: variol-ar, adj., variolous (q.v.)

## variolite
variolite, п., a kind of diorite embedded with
spherules (petrogr.) — A hybrid coined fr.
variola and suff. -ite (representing Gk. -ιτης); so
called from its smallpoxlike appearance.

## varioloid
varioloid, adj., resembling smallpox. — A hybrid
coined fr. variola and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.

## variolous
variolous, adj., pertaining to, or having,
smallpox. — Medical L.variolosus, fr. variola. See
variola and adj. suff. -ose.

## variometer
variometer, п., an instrument for the comparison
of magnetic forces (electr.) — A hybrid coined
fr. L. varius, 'changing, various', and Gk.
μέτρον, 'measure'. See various and meter,
'poetical rhythm*.

## variorum edition
variorum edition, edition of a text with notes of
various commentators. — Short for L. editio

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:830 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 803 | VAUXITE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:830 COLUMN:1 -->
cum notis variorum, 'edition with notes of
various (persons)'. Variorum is gen. pi. of varius.
See various.

## various
various, adj. — L. varius, 'different, changing,
varying, various', prob. rel. to varus, 'bent,
knock-kneed', and derived fr. I.-E. base *wa-,
'to bend, turn, twist'. For enlargements of this
base see vacillate and convex. Cp. van*, varicella,
variola, divaricate, prevaricate. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.

## variscite
variscite, п., a hydrous aluminum phosphate
(mineral.) — G. Variscit, named after Variscia,
Latin name of the Vogtland in Germany, fr.
Varisciov Varistt, variants of Naristi, name of a
Teutonic tribe. The ending -it goes back to Gk.
-ϊτης; see subst. suif. -ite.

## varix
varix, п., a varicose vein (med.) — L., 'dilated
vein, varix', prob. rel. to varus, 'blotch, pimple*,
which is cogn. with Lith. viras, 'measles of
swine'. Cp. varicose, varicosis, varicula.

## varlet
varlet, п., ]) an attendant (obsoi); 2) a knight's
page (hist.); 3) a rascal. — ME., fr. OF., 'groom,
young man', fr. earlier vaslet (whence F. valet),
fr. VL. *vassellittus, a word of Celtic origin. See
vassal and -et and cp. vaiet.
Derivatives: varlet-ess, п., varlet-ry, n.

## varment
varment, varming, п., vermin. — Dial, variants of
vermin.

## varna
varna, п., caste, more exactly, a group of castes.
— 01. varnah, 'covering, color', fr. vrnoti,
'covers, holds back', fr. I.-E. base *wer-s 'to enclose,
cover'. See weir and cp. words there referred to.
For the sense development of Ol. varnah,
'covering; color*, cp. L. color, 'color', fr. I.-E. base
*kel-, 'to hide, conceal, cover* (see color^.

## varnish
varnish, n. — ME. vernisck, fr. OF. (= F.) vernis
(fr. ML. vernix, veronix, fr. Gk. *βερονίκη
(whence also MGk. βερνίκι), fr. the Lybian
town Βερενίκη, Berenice (now Bengasi),
where varnish was first used. The town was
named after Βερενίκη (Berenike) II, queen of
Egypt. The name Βερενίκη itself is the
Macedonian var. of Gk. Φερενίκη, which lit. means
'carrying off victory*, fr. φέρειν, 'to bring,
carry*, and νΐκη, 'victory'. See bear, 'to carry',
and Nike and cp. Berenice, Veronica. Cp. also
vernis Martin and vernix caseosa.
Derivative: varnish-y, adj.

## varnish
varnish, tr. v. — ME. vernysshen, fr. OF. verni-
cier, vernicer (F. vernir, vernisser), fr. vernis,
'varnish'. See vnnrish, n.
Derivatives: varnish-ed, adj., varnisk-er, п.,
varnish-ing, adj. and n.

## varsha
varsha, п., the rainy season; monsoon (India). —
OI. varsam, 'rain', rel. to varsati, 'it rains',
v(sah, 'bull, steer', vrsan-, 'male, man, stallion*,
vrsa-bhah, 'bull, steer', vrsnih, 'male, ram', and
cogn. with Gk. 2ρση. (for *5έρση), 'dew*, Mir.

## frass
frass, fr. earlier fross, 'shower of rain', L. verres,
'boar', Lith. vefSis, 'calf, Lett. versisy 'ox*. All
these words derive fr. I.-E. base *wer-s-, 'to
wet, morsten, sprinkle*, whence also Gk. ούρέω
(for *worseyo), ούρεΤν, 'to pass urine'. See
urine and cp. Uranus
•Varsity, Varsity, n. — Colloquial abbreviation
of university.

## YarsoYienite
YarsoYienite, п., a kind of Polish dance. — F.,
short for danse varsovienne, lit. 'Warsaw dance',
fem. of varsovien, 'of, or pertaining to, Warsaw*,
fr. Varsovie, 'Warsaw'.

## Varuna
Varuna, п., the supreme deity, king of gods and
men in Hindu mythology. — OI. Varunah, 'the
god of the evening sky', prob. not cogn. with
Gk. Ουρανός, 'god of the sky' (see Uranus).

## varus
varus, п., clubfoot (med.) — L. varus, 'bent,
apart, crooked', fr. I.-E. base *wa-, 'to bend,
turn, twist', whence prob. also varius, 'different,
changing, varying*. See various and cp. words
there referred to.

## varve
varve, п., annual deposit of silt (geol.) —
Swed. varv, 'turn; layer', rel to ON. hverfa, OE.
hwerfan, 'to turn round'. See wharf.
Derivative: varv-ed, adj.

## vary
vary, intr. and tr. v. — ME. varien, fr. OF. ( =
F.) varier, fr. L. variare, 'to change, vary', fr.
varius. See various.

## vas
vas, п., a vessel; a duct (anat.) — L. vas, gen.
vasts, Vessel'. See vase and cp. vessel.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:830 COLUMN:2 -->

## vas
vas, п., pledge, security (law). — L. vas, gen.
vadis, 'vail, security', cogn. with Goth. wadi.
OE. wedd, 'pledge'. See wed and cp. vadipionium,
vadium,

## vasal
vasal, adj., pertaining to a vas (anat.) — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. vas, "vessel'. See vas,
'vessel'.

## Vascons
Vascons, Vascones, n. pi., the Basques. — L. Vas-
cones, orig. 'Foresters'. See Basque and cp.
Gascon,

## vascular
vascular, adj., pertaining to vessels or ducts (biol.
and anat.) — Medical L. vascularis, fr. L. vds-
culum. See next word and -ar.
Derivatives: vascular-ity, п., vascularize (q.v.)

## vasculum
vasculum, п., a small vessel; an ascidium; a
small box. — L. vasculum, 'a small vessel',
dimin. of vas. See next word and -culum.

## vase
vase, п., a vessel, esp. for flowers. — F., fr. L.
vas, gen. vasis, 'vessel', rel. to Umbr. vasor (pi.),
'vessels'. Cp. vas, 'vessel', vascular, vessel and
vextravasate.

## vaseline
vaseline, п., a petroleum jelly; petrolatum. —
Coined by Robert A. Chesebrough in 1877 fr.
vas- (short for G. Wasser, 'water'), -el(fr. Gk.
έλ-αιον, 'oil') and chem. suff. -Ine.
Derivative: vaseline, tr. v., to apply vaseline to.

## vaso-
vaso-, or vasi-, comb, form meaning 'pertaining
to the vascular system*. — L. vas, 'vessel'. See
vas, 'vessel'.

## vasodilator
vasodilator, adj., dilating the blood vessels (pky·
siol.) — Compounded of vaso- and dilator.

## vassal
vassal, п., 1) in the Middle Ages, a feudal tenant,
who pledges fealty to a superior lord; 2) a
subject; a slave. — ME., fr. OF., fr. ML. vassallus,
deriv. of vassus, 'servant', which is of Celt,
origin. Cp. W. gwas, 'youth, servant', Bret, gewaz,
'servant, vassal, man', Ir. foss, 'servant'. Cp.
also It., Port, vassallo, Sp. vasallo, which are
borrowed fr. ML. vassallus. Cp. also vavasor
and the second element in Gervais.
Derivatives: vassal-ic, adj., vassal-ity, п., vassal-
ry, n.

## vassalage
vassalage, n. — ME., fr. OF. (F. vasselage),
formed fr. vassal with suff. -age.

## vast
vast, adj., huge, immense. — F. vaste, fr. L.
vastus, 'huge, immense, shapeless', which stands
for *wazdhos and is cogn. with Olr. fot, fut,
'length'. L. vastus in the above sense is prob. not
identical with vastus, 'empty, waste, desert'. For
this latter see waste. See Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., II, p. 737.
Derivatives: vast, п., vastitude (q.v.), vastity
(q.v.), vast-ly, adv., vast-ness, п., vast-y, adj.,
vast-i-ly, adv., vast-i-ness, n.

## vnstitude
vnstitude, п., vastness; immensity. —L. vastitudo,
'vastness', fr. L. vastus. See prec. word and -tude.

## vastity
vastity, п., vastness (rare). — F. vastite, fr. L.
vastitdtem, ace. of vastitas, 'vastness', fr. vastus.
See vast and -ity.

## vastus
vastus, п., name of two divisions of the

## quadriceps muscle
quadriceps muscle, the vastus externus and the vastus
internus (anat.) — Medical L., prop, musculus
vastus externus, resp. internus, 'the great

## external (resp. internal) muscle'
external (resp. internal) muscle', coined by John

## Riolan (1577-1657)
Riolan (1577-1657), professor of anatomy at

Paris, fr. L. vastus, 'huge, immense'. See vast

## and external
and external, resp. Internal,

## vat
vat, п., a large vessel for holding liquids. — A

## var. of orig. fat
var. of orig. fat, 'vessel', fr. ME. fat, fr. OE.

faet. The word prop, means 'container', and is

rel. to OS., ON. fat, OFris. fet, MDu., Du. vat,

OFris. fatia, MDu., Du. vatten, OHG. fa^on,
MHG. va^en, G. fassen, 'to seize, take hold

## of
of, and prob. cogn. with Lith. puodas, 'pot'.
Cp. fettle.
Derivative: vat, tr. v.

## vates
vates, п., a Celtic divinely inspired poet. — L.

## vates
vates, 'sooth-sayer, prophet, seer*, cogn. with

## Olr. faith
Olr. faith, 'poet', W. gwawd, 'poem', Goth.

## wops
wops, 'possessed, mad', OE. wod, 'mad,

## frenzied'
frenzied', wop, 'sound, melody, song', Du. woede,
'rage', OHG. wuot, 'mad; madness', MHG., G.

## wut
wut, 'rage, fury', ON. odr, 'spirit, mind, passion,

## song
song, poetry', and possibly also with OI. api-

## vatati
vatati, 'understands', api-vatayati, 'stimulates

spiritually, causes to understand'. Cp. vnticinate.

## Cp. also Edda
Cp. also Edda, Odin, Woden, wood, adj., and the

first element in Wednesday. For the sense
development of L. vates and its cognates cp. Gk.
μάντις, 'seer, prophet', which is rel. to μαίνε-
σ&αι, 'to be mad' (see mantis).

## vatic
vatic, vatical, adj., prophetic. — Formed with
adj. suff. -ic, resp. -ical, fr. L. vates. See prec.
word.

## Vatican
Vatican, п., the Pope's palace in Rome. — L.
Vdticdnus (scil. mons), 'the hill of Vatican', one
of the hills of Rome, an Etruscan loan word; so
called because the palace of the Pope was built
on the Vatican hill in Rome; not related to
vates, 'soothsayer, seer' (see prec. word).

## Vaticanism
Vaticanism, п., the doctrine of papal supremacy
and infallibility. — Formed fr. L. Vdticdnus (see
prec. word) with suff. -ism.

## vaticlnal
vaticlnal, adj., pertaining to prophecy. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al fr. L. vdticinus. See next word.

## vaticinate
vaticinate, tr. and intr. v., to prophesy. — L.
vaticindtus, pp. of vdticindri, 'to foretell,
prophesy', fr. vdticinus, 'prophetic', compounded of
vates, 'seer, prophet' (see vates), and formative
element -cinus, which is prob- rel. to L. condri,
'to try, endeavor', and cogn. with Gk. έγκονεΤν,
'to be active', διάκονος, 'servant'. See deacon
and cp. the second element in ratiocinate.

## vaticination
vaticination, п., prophesying, prophesy. — L.
vaticinatio, gen. -dnis, fr. vaticindtus, pp. of
vdticindri. See prec. word and -ion.

## vaccinator
vaccinator, п., seer, prophet. — L. vdticindtor, fr.
vaticindtus, pp. of vaticinuri. See vaticinate and
agential suif. -or.

## vau
vau, also waw, п., the sixth letter of the Hebrew
alphabet. — Heb. wdw, *hook, pin, peg'; so
called in allusion to the ancient form of this
letter.

## vaucheria
vaucheria, п., a genus of algae (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Swiss botanist Jean-Pierre
Etienne Voucher (1763-1841). For the ending
see 1st suff. -ia.

## vaudeville
vaudeville, п., a theatrical entertainment
consisting of several acts. — F., alteration of vaidevire,
fr. Vaude Vire, 'Valley of the Vire' (in
Normandy) ; the songs of this district were highly praised
in the 15th cent. — Vau is an early form of val,
'valley'. See vale, 'valley'.
Derivatives: vaudevilli-an, adj. and п., vaude-
villist (q.v.)

## vaudevillist
vaudevillist, п., a vaudeville writer or actor. — F.
vaudevilliste, a hybrid coined fr. vaudeville and
suif. -iste (representing Gk. -ιστής). See -ist.

## vault
vault, п., an arched roof. — ME. voute, vowte, fr.
MF. vaulte, volte, vaute, voute (F. voute), fr.
OF., fr. VL. *volvita, fem. of the pp. of VL.
*volvitus (for L. volutus), pp. of L. volvere, 'to
roll'. Cp. OProvenc. and Sp. vuelta, 'turn', and
see volute. The / in E. vault is due to a later,
'etymological', insertion (cp. fault).
Derivative: vault-y, adj.

## vault
vault, tr. v., to cover with a vault. — ME. vouten,
fr. MF. vaulter, volter, fr. voute, volte. See vault,
'roof
Derivatives: vault-ed, adj., vault-ing, n.

## vanlt
vanlt, intr. and tr. v., to leap*. — ME. vauten,
vouten, fr. MF. vaulter, volter, vouter, 'to leap,
gambol', prop, 'to turn', fr. OF., fr. Olt. voltare,
'to turn', fr. volta, 'a turn', fr. VL. *volvita. See
vault,'arched roof, and cp.volt,'a turning
movement', volta, and the second element in demivolt.
Derivatives: vault-er, п., vault-ing, adj. and n.

## vault
vault, п., a leap. — MF. (= F.) volte, fr. It. volta,
'a turn'. See vault, 'to leap'.

## vaunt
vaunt, intr. and tr. v. — ME. vaunten, fr. MF.
(= F.) vanter, 'to praise, speak highly of, se
vanter, 'to boast, brag', fr. OF', fr. Late L.
vdnitdre, prop, 'to be vain', fr. L. vdnus. See
vain and cp. flaunt.
Derivatives: vaunt, п., vaunt-er, п., vaunt-ing-ly,
adv., vaunt-y, adj., vaunt-i-ness, n.

## vavasor
vavasor, vavasour, п., a vassal. — ME. vavasour,
fr. OF. vavassor, vavassour (F. vavasseur), fr.
Merovingian L. vassus vassorum, 'vassal of
vassals'. See vassal.

## vauquelinite
vauquelinite, п., a lead copper phosphate and
chromate (mineral.) — Named after the French
chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin (1763-1829).
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## vauxite
vauxite, п., a hydrous iron aluminum phosphate

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:831 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VAYU | B04 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:831 COLUMN:1 -->
{mineral.) — Named after the American
naturalist George Vaux (1863-1927). For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Vayn
Vayn, п., the god of wind in Hindu mythology.
— OI. vdyun, 'wind*, rel. to vdti, vayati, 'it
blows*, and cogn. with L. ventus, 'wind', Goth.
waian, 'to blow', Lith. ve'yas, 'wind*, OSlav.
vejati, 'to blow*. See wind, п., and cp. words
there referred to.

## Veadar
Veadar, п., name of the thirteenth, intercalary,
month of the Jewish year. — Heb. va-Adhar,
lit. 'and Adar'. i.e. 'second Adar', formed fr.
/-, va-, 'and', and Adhar, name of the twelfth
month. The exact transliteration is not Veadar
but Vaadar. See Adar.

## veal
veal, n. — ME. vel, veel, fr. MF., veel, veau (F.
veau), fr. OF., fr. L. vitellus, dimin. of vitulus,
'calf, which is rel. to Umbr. vitluf, (pi. ace),
'calves', and cogn. with Ol. vatsah, 'calf. The
orig. meaning of these words was 'yearling', fr.
I.-E. base *wet, 'year', whence also Gk. έτος,
(dial. * f έτος), 'year', Εταλον, Dor. Ετελον,
'yearling', Goth, wiprus, OE. weder, 'wether',
L. vetus, 'old*. See wether and cp. etesian,
Italian, vellum, veteran, veterinary, vitellus, vitular.

## vectis
vectis, п., an instrument used as a lever to
facilitate delivery (obstetrics). — L. vectis 'pole, bar,
lever', from the stem of vehere (pp. vectus), 'to
carry, convey'. See next word.

## vector
vector, п., a quantity having magnitude and
direction {math.) — L., 'carrier, bearer, conveyer',
fr. vectus, pp. of vehere, 'to convey'. See weigh
and cp. vehicle. Cp. also the first element in
wnlleyed.
Derivatives: vector-ial, adj., vector-ial-ly, adv.

## Veda
Veda, п., one of the ancient sacred books of the
Hindus. — 01. vedah, 'knowledge, sacred book*,
rel. to veda, *I know', vidyd, 'knowledge', vin-
dami, 'I.find', Avestic vaeda, *1 know', fr. l.-E.
base *weid-, + woid-, *wid-, 'to see; to know*,
whence also L. videre (pp. visas), 'to see'. See
vision and cp. words there referred to.

## Vedanta
Vedanta, п., a system of Hindu pantheistic
philosophy. — Ol. Vidantah, prop, 'the end of
knowledge', compounded of vedah,
'knowledge', and antak/ena\ For the first element see
prec. word. The second element is cogn. with L.
ante, 'in front of, Goth, andeis, OE. ende, 'end';
see end.

## Veddah
Veddah, п., one of the original inhabitants of
Ceylon. — Singhalese, lit. 'hunter'.

## vedette
vedette, п., a mounted sentinel placed in advance
of an outpost. — F., fr. It. vedetta assimilated—■
under the influence of vedere, 'to see'—fr. velet-
ta, fr. Sp. vela, 'watch, wake', fr. velar, 'to
watch', fr. L. vigildre, 'to be awake, keep watch,
be watchful', fr. vigil, 'awake, wakeful'. See
vigil.

## Vedic
Vedic, adj., pertaining to the Vedas. — Formed
fr. Veda with adj. suff. -ic.

## veep
veep, п., vice-president. — Coined from the
letter names V and Ρ (fr. VP, abbreviation of
vice-president).

## veer
veer, tr. v., to let or pay out (a cable). — ME.
veren, fr. MDu. (= Du.) vieren, 'to let out,
slacken' (whence also G.fieren, Oan.fire, Swed.
fira), which is rel. to OHG. fiaren, 'to give
direction to', fr. Teut. *fe~r-, 'slope, slant; side',
whence also OHG. fiara, Goth./era, 'side', OE.
δ-fer, 'edge, margin; bank (of a river), shore (of
the sea)', MLG. over, Du. oever, MHG. uover,
G. Ufer, 'bank, shore'. These words are prob.
cogn. witn Lesbian Gk. άπερρος, Dor. άπειρος,
Ion. ήπειρος, 'mainland, continent'.

## veer
veer, intr. and tr. v., to change direction. — F.
virer, 'to turn round, change direction', fr. VL.
*virdre, fr. L. vibrdre, 'to shake' (whence also
It. virare, Sp. virar); the disappearance of the b
in\L·.* virdre and its derivatives is due to
dissimilation (see W. von Wartburg, Revue de
Dialectologie Romane, 3, 467). See vibrate and
cp. environ; cp. also wear, 4o turn (a ship)
about'. The derivation fr. L. viriae, a suggested
by Diez, has been justly rejected by Meyer-
Liibke in his REW., No. 9300.
Derivatives: veer, п., veer-able, adj., veer-ing-ly,
adv.

## vega
vega, п., an open plain (Sp. American). — Sp., a

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:831 COLUMN:2 -->
word of Basque origin.

## Vega
Vega, п., the brightest star in the constellation
Lyra. — ML. Vega, fr. Arab, (an-nasr) al-waqV,
'the falling (vulture)*, fr. al-, 'the', and the part
of waqa'a, *he fell', which is cogn. with Heb.
ydqd\ 'it was dislocated'.

## vega site
vega site, п., a hydrous lead ferric sulfate (mineral.)
— Named after Las Vegas in Nevada. For the
ending see subst. sufT. -ite.

## vegetable
vegetable, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. vegetdbilis,
'enlivening', fr. vegetare, 'to enliven, animate',
fr. L. vegetus, 'vigorous, active', fr. vegere, 'to
be live, active, to quicken', which is rel. to vigil,
'awake, wakeful', vigor, 'liveliness, activity',
and cogn. with OE. wacian, 'to be awake, to
watch'. See wake, v., and cp. vigil, vigor. Cp.
also vajra. For the ending see suff. -able.
Derivatives: vegetable, п., vegetabl-y, adv.

## vegetal
vegetal, adj., pertaining to vegetables; pertaining
to vegetation. — MF. vegetal, fr. ML. vegetdlis,
fr. Late L. vegetare. See prec. word and adj. sufT.
-al.

## vegetarian
vegetarian, n. and adj. — Irregularly formed fr.
vegetable. For the ending see suff. -arian.
Derivative: vegetarian-ism, n.

## vegetate
vegetate, intr. v., 1) to grow as plants do; 2) to
lead a merely passive physical life. — Late L.
vegetatus, pp. of vegetare, 'to enliven, animate'.
See vegetable and verbal suff. -ate.

## vegetation
vegetation, n. — Late L. vegetdtio, gen. -onis, fr.
vegetatus, pp. of vegetare. See prec. word and
-ion.

## vegetative
vegetative, adj., growing, as plants. — ME. vege-
tatif, fr. ML. vegetdttvus, fr. Late L. vegetdtus,
pp. of vegetare. See vegetute and -ive.
Derivatives: vegetative-ly, adv., vegetative-ness,
n.

## vehemence
vehemence, also vehemency, n. — MF. (= F.)
vehemence, fr. L. vehementia, fr. vehemens, gen.
-ends. See next word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## vehement
vehement, adj., impectuous; violent. — MF.
(= F.) vehement, fr. L. vehementem, ace. of
vehemens, 'eager, violent, furious, vehement', lit.
'rushing', fr. vehere, 'to carry, convey'. See next
word.
Derivative: vehement-ly, adv.

## vehicle
vehicle, n. — F. vehicule, fr. L. vehiculum,
'carriage, conveyance', lit. 'means of transport',
formed with instrumental suff. -culum fr. vehere,
'to carry, convey', fr. I.-E. base + wegh-, 'to
move', whence also OE. wegan, 'to carry, move,
weigh'. See weigh and cp. betony, convention,
convective, evection, vectis, vector, vehement,
velites, velocity, vetturino, vex, vexation, voe,
vogue. Cp. also via. Cp. also the first element
in ochlocracy. For the ending see suff. -de.

## vehicular
vehicular, adj., pertaining to vehicles. — Late L.
vehicularis, fr. L. vehiculum. See prec. word and
-ar.

## vehingericht
vehingericht, п., in medieval Germany, a kind of
secret tribunal. — G. Femgericht, compounded
of Vekme, Feme, 'secret tribunal', which is rel.
to MHG. veime, MDu. vime, veem, Du. veem,
of s.m., and Gericht, 'judgment, court of
justice', which derives fr. MHG. gerihte fr. OHG.
girikti, fr. rihten, 'to judge', which is rel. to
OHG., MHG. reht, 'right'. See right, adj.

## vehmlc
vehmlc, adj., pertaining to the vehmgericht. —
See prec. word and adj. suff. -ic.

## veil
veil, n. — ME. veile, fr. OF. veile (F. voile), fr. L.
vela, pi. of velum, 'sail; piece of cloth; awning,
curtain, veil', but in VL. mistaken for a fem.
sing. noun. L. velum prob. stands for *wexlom
(cp. vexillum, 'banner, flag', the dimin. of velum),
fr, I.-E. base *weg-, 'to weave', whence also OE.
weoce, weoc, 'wick'. See wick and cp. wax, n.
Cp. also vel amen, velar, vellc, velum, voile,
reveal, revelation.
Derivatives: veil, v., (q.v.), veil-less, adj.

## veil
veil, tr. v. — ME. veilen, fr. MF. veiier (F. voiler),
fr. OF., fr. L. veldre, 'to cover, veil', fr. L. velum.
See veil, n.
Derivatives: veil-ed, adj., veil-ed-ly, adv., veil·
ed-ness, п., veil-er, п., veil-ing, п., veil-y, adj.

## vein
vein, n. — ME. veine, fr. OF. ( — F.) veine, fr. L.
vena, 'blood vessel, watercourse, vein; natural
inclination', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
venation, vennel, venose, venule and the first

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:831 COLUMN:3 -->
element in venesection.
Derivatives: vein, tr. v., vein-ed, adj., vein-er, п.,
vein-ing, n-., vein-y, adj., vein-i-ness, n.

## velamen
velamen, п., a membrane (anat.) — L. vildmen,
'a covering', fr. veldre, 'to veil, cover'. See veil,
v. and п., and -men.

## velar
velar, adj., pertaining to, or connected with, the
velum. — L. vildris, fr. velum. See velum and -ar.

## velarium
velarium, п., awning over the auditorium of an
amphitheater (Roman antiq.) — L. velarium, 'a
covering', fr. velum. See veil, п., and -arium.

## veld
veld, veldt, п., grass country in S. Africa. — S.
Afr. Du., fr. Du. veld, 'field', which is rel. to E.
field (q.v.)

## veldtschoen
veldtschoen, also veldschoen, п., shoe made of un-
tanned hide. — S. Afr. Du. veldschoen, which is
a blend of velschoen (fr. Du. vel, 'skin', see fell,
'hide', and schoen, 'shoe', see shoe) and Du.
veld. See prec. word.

## velic
velic, adj., pertaining to a sail. — Formed with
adj. suff. -Ic fr. L. velum, 'sail'. See veil, n.

## velites
velites, n. pi., light-armed soldiers (Roman antiq.)
— Pi. of L. veles, gen. vilitis, which is prob. rel.
to veloX, 'swift'. See velocity.

## velleity
velleity, п., imperfect volition. — ML. velleitds,
fr. L. velle, 'to will, wish'. See voluntury and -ity.

## vellicate
vellicate, tr. and intr. v., to twitch. — L. vellicd-
tus, pp. of vellicare, freq. of vellere, 'to pluck,
pull, twitch', which is of uncertain origin. It
possibly stands for *wefsere and derives fr. I.-E.
base *wel-, 'to break, tear, pluck', whence also
L. volnus, vulnus, 'wound*, Gk. είλωτες (for
*έ^έλ-ωτες), 'helots', άλ£σκεσ&αι (for *Γαλ-
ίσκε&αι), *to betaken prisoner', Goth, wilwan,
'to rob', wulwa, *robbery, rape', Arm. goeanam,
'to steal', Toch. B. lyafc, AB lyak, 'thief, and
possibly also L. lana, Gk. λήνος, OSlav. vluna,
Goth, wulla, OE. wull, etc., 'wool*. See wool
and cp. avulsion, convulse, convulsion, evulsion,
Helot, lasio-, revulsion, svelte, velours, velure,
velvet, villus, vulnerable, vulsellum, vulture. For
the ending see verbal suff. -ate.

## vellication
vellication, п., a spasmodic twitching. — L.
vellicatio, gen. -onis, fr. vellicdtus, pp. of
vellicare. See prec. word and -ion.

## vellum
vellum, п., a fine kind of calf skin parchment. —
ME. velim, assimilated fr. OF. velin (F. velin), fr.
OF vel, 'calf. See veal. For the change of η to m
cp. venom.

## velocipede
velocipede, п., any of early kinds of bicycles or
tricyles. — F. velocipede, compounded of L.
velox, gen. -oris, 'swift', and pes, gen. pedis,
'foot'. See next word and foot and cp. pedal.
Derivatives: velociped-al, velociped-ic, adjs.

## velocity
velocity, п., swiftness; speed. — MF. (— F.) νέΐο-
cite, fr. L. vildcitatem, ace. of velocitds,
'swiftness*, fr. velox, gen. -oris, 'swift', which is of
uncertain origin. It possibly stands for * weg-slo-s
and lit. means 'moving along quickly, rushing*,
and is rel. to vehere, *to carry, convey'. See
vehicle and -ity and cp. velites.

## velours
velours, п., a velvetlike material. — F., alteration
of OF. velous, fr. OProven?. velos, of s.m., fr. L.
villosus, shaggy', taken as a noun, from villus,
'shaggy hair'. See villus and cp. velure. Cp. also
flue, 'fluff'.

## velum
velum, п., the soft palate (anat.); a membranous
covering in fungi, in the jelly fish, etc. (bot, and
zool.) — L. velum, *sail; piece of cloth; awning,
curtain, veil*. See veil.

## velure
velure, n. — A var. of velours (q.v.)

## velvet
velvet, n. — ME. veluet, velwet, fr. VL. velluetum,
fr. *vlllutust 'shaggy', fr. L. villus, 'shaggy hair*.
See villus and cp. velours, velure.
Derivatives: velvet, velvet-ed, adjs., velveteen
(q.v.), velvet-y, adj.

## velveteen
velveteen, п., imitation velvet. — Formed fr.
velvet with sufT. -een (~ a var. of-ine).

## venada
venada, п., the pudu. — Fem. of Sp. venado,
'deer', fr. L. vendtus, 'game', fr. vendtus, pp. of
vindrt, 'to hunt, chase'. See venery, 'hunting'.

## venal
venal, adj., that can be corrupted; mercenary;
corrupt. — L. vendlis, 'that which can be
bought'^Jr.. venum or venus, 'sale', which is cogn.
with Ol. vasndh, 'purchase money', vasnam,
'reward', vasnayati, 'he bargains, haggles', Arm.
gin (for *wesnom), 'purchase money', Gk. ώνή,
ώνος, 'price paid (for a thing), purchase', Les-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:832 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 8Q5 | VENTRAL -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:832 COLUMN:1 -->
bian tfwa (for *wosnd), 'purchase', Gk. ώνεΐ-
аВ-ол, 'to buy*, Hitt. ushshaniya-, 'to sell', and
—without the suff. -no—wash·, 'to buy'. Cp.
vend, vendee, vent, 'market', vent a, and the
second element in opsonin,

## venality
venality, n. — F. venalite, fr. Late L. vendlitdtem,
ace. of venalitds, fr. vindlis, 'that which can be
bought'. See prec. word and -ity.

## venatic
venatic, adj., pertaining to hunting. — L. vendti-
cus, fr. venatus, pp. of venari, 'to hunt'. See vene-
ry, 'hunting', and 2nd -atic.

## venation
venation, п., the stystem of veins in the wind of
an insect or in a leaf. — Formed with suff.
-ation fr. L. vena, 'vein'. See vein.
Derivative: venation-al, adj.

## vend
vend, tr. v. — F. vendr<°, fr. L. vendere, 'to sell'*
shortened fr. venunddre, fr. venum dare, lit. 'to
give (i.e. offer) for sale', fr. venum or venus,
'sale*, and dare, 'to give'. See venal and date,
'point of time'.
Derivatives: vend, п., vendee (q.v.), vend-er,n.,
vend-ing, n. and adj., vendor (q.v.)

## vendace
vendace, п., a whitefish (Coregonus vandesius). —
ModL. vandesius, fr. MF. (= F.) vandoise,
'dace*, fr. Gaulish *vindesia, 'whitefish', fr.
Celtic vindo-, 'white'; see winter and cp. Wend. For
sense development cp. F. able, ablette, 'the
bleak*, fr. L. albus, 'white', and E. whitefish.

## vendaval
vendaval, п., a strong wind blowing from the sea
in Mexico. — Sp., fr. F. ventd'aval, * westerly
wind*, fr. vent, 'wind' and aval, 'downward part,
downward direction'. The first element derives
fr. L. ventus, 'wind*. F. aval stands for a val, 'to
the valley'. See wind, п., and a vale.

## Vendean
Vendean, adj., of Vendee. — F. Vendeen, fr. La
Vendee, name of a department in Western
France. For the ending see suff. -an.
Derivative: Vendean, n.

## vendee
vendee, п., the purchaser (law). — Lit. 'a person
to whom anything is sold*; formed from the
verb vend with suff. -ее.

## Vendemiaire
Vendemiaire, п., the first month (lasting fr. Sept.
2nd to Oct. 1st) of the French revolutionary
calendar. — F., lit '(month) of vintage*, coined
by Fabre d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. L. vindemia,
'vintage'. See vintage-

## vendetta
vendetta, п., a blood feud in the pursuit of
avenging the slaying of a near relative. — It.,
'revenge', fp. L. vindicta, 'vengeance, revenge', fr.
vindex, gen. vindicis, 'vindicator'. See vindictive,

## vendible
vendible, adj., that which can be sold, salable. —
ME., fr. L. vendibilis, fr. vendere, *to sell'. See
vend and -ible.
Derivatives: vendibil-ity, п., vendible-ness, п.,
vendibl-y, adv.

## vendition
vendition, п., the act of selling. — L. venditio,
gen. -onis, 'a selling, sale', fr. venditus, pp. of
vendere. See vend and -ition.

## vendor
vendor, n. — AF. vendour, vendor, fr. OF. (— F.)
vendeur, fr. L. venditorem, ace. of venditor,
'seller', fr. venditus, pp. of vendere. Cp. the noun
vender and see vend and agential suff. -or.

## veneer
veneer, tr. v., to overlay (wood) with a thin sheet
of fine wood. — Fr. earlier fineer., fr. G. fur-
nieren, fr. F. fournir, 'to furnish', fr. OHG.

## frumjan
frumjan, 'to provide'. The word was borrowed
from and re-borrowed by one and the same
language at two different periods. See furnish.
Derivatives: veneer, п., veneer-er, п., veneer-ing,
n.

## venenate
venenate, tr. v.} to poison {rare). — L. venenatus,
pp. of venendre, 'to poison', fr. venerium,
'poison'. See venom and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: venenat-ion, n.

## venerability
venerability, n. — ML. venerdbilitds, fr. L. vene-
rdbilis. See next word and -ity.

## venerable
venerable, adj. — ME., fr. L. venerdbilis, fr.
venerdri, 'to venerate*. See next word and -able.
Derivatives: venerable-ness, п., venerabl-y, adv.

## venerate
venerate, tr. v., to revere. — L. veneratus, pp. of
venerdri, 'to reverence, worship, venerate*, fr.
venus, gen. veneris, 'love, sexual desire,
loveliness, attractiveness, beauty, charm*, whence
Venus, gen. Veneris, 'the goddess of love*; cogn.
with Ol. vanas-, 'desire', vdnati, vanoti, vdnckati,
'desires, loves; wins, is victorious', Avestic va-
naiti, 'he wishes; is victorious', OE. wynn, *joy',
wunian, 'to dwell', wenian, 'to accustom, train;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:832 COLUMN:2 -->
to wean', wpscan, 'to wish'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base *wen-, 'to strive after, wish,
desire; to be satisfied; to be wont'. See wish and
verbal suff. -ate and cp. venery (in both senses),
venial, venom, Venus.
Derivatives: veneration-al, adj., venerat-ive, adj.,
venerat-ive-ly, adv., venerat-ive-ness, п.,
venerator (q.v.)

## veneration
veneration, n. — ME. veneracion, fr. veneratio,
gen. -onis, fr. veneratus, pp. of venerdri. See
prec. word and -ion.
Derivative: veneration-al, adj.

## venerator
venerator, n. — L. venerator, fr. veneratus, pp. of
venerdri. See venerate and agential suff. -or.

## venereal
venereal, adj., 1) pertaining to sexual love or
intercourse; 2) infected with a venereal disease;
3) curing venereal diseases. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. venereus, 'pertaining to love or
sexual desire', fr. venus, gen. veneris. See
venerate.

## venereology
venereology, п., the study of venereal diseases. —
A hybrid coined fr. L. venus, gen. veneris, 'love,
sexual desire', and Gk. -λογία, fr.- λόγος, 'one
who speaks (in a certain manner); one who
deals (with a certain topic)'. See venerate and
-logy.
Derivative: venereolog-ist, n.

## venery
venery,. п., hunting (archaic). — ME. venerie, fr.
OF. venerie (F. venerie), 'to hunt', fr. L. venari,
'to hunt, pursue', which prob. derives fr. I.-E.
base *wen-, 'to strive after'. See venerate and -y
(representing OF. -ie) and cp. next word, veha-
da, venatic, venision. OL veti, 'follows after',
Westic vayeiti, 'hunts', vitar-, 'pursuer', vydna-,
One pursued', vdti-, 'persecution', Lith. veju,
vyti, 'to hunt, pursue', OSlav. voji, 'warrior*,
vojina, 'war', Gk. Ιεμαι (for *Γύεμαι), Ί
aspire to, tend to, make haste, long for', OE. wdp,
'hunting', ON. veidr, 'chase, hunting, fishing',
OHG. weida, MHG., G. weide, 'pasture,
grazing, food; pasture land', are prob. derivatives
of a denasalized var. of the above base. Cp. the
first element in voivode.

## venery
venery, п., sexual love, (archaic). — From the
stem of L. venus, gen. veneris, 'love, sexual
desire'. See venerate and cp. Venus. Cp. also
prec. word.

## venesect
venesect, tr. v., to phlebotomize (med.) — Back
formation from next word.

## venesection
venesection, п., phlebotomy (med.) — Medical L.
venae sectio, 'cutting of a vein*, fr. L. venae, gen.
of vena, 'vein', and sectio, gen. -onis, 'a cutting*.
See vein and section.

## Venetian
Venetian, adj. and n. — ML. Venetidnus, Тт.
Venetia, 'Venice', fr. Veneti (Gk. Ούένετοι,
'Ενετοί or Ενετοί), an ancient people of Illy-
rian origin. For the ending see suff. -ian.

## vengeance
vengeance, n. — ME., fr. OF. (— F.) fr. venger,
'to avenge', fr. L. vindicdre, of s.m. See vindicate
and -ance and cp. avenge, revenge.

## vengeful
vengeful, adj. — Formed on analogy of
revengeful from the obsol. verb venge (fr. OF. venger),
with suff.-ful. See prec. word.
Derivatives: vengeful-ly, п., vengeful-ness, n.

## venial
venial, adj., pardonable. — ME., fr. OF., fr. L.
venialis, 'pardonable; gracious, kind', fr. venia,
'forgiveness, pardon; graceness, kindness', rel.
to venus, gen. veneris, 'love', venerdri, 'to
reverence, worship'. See venerate.
Derivatives: venial-ity, п., venial-ly, adv., venial-
ness, n.

## venin
venin, п., a toxic substance in snake venom (bio-
chem.) — F. venin, 'poison', fr. L. venenum. See
venom.

## venison
venison, п., the flesh of a deer. — ME. veneson,
veneison, venison, fr. OF. veneson, veneison (F.
venaison), fr. L. vendtionem, ace. of vendtio,
'hunting, chase', fr. venatus, pp. of venari, 'to
hunt'. See venery, 'hunting'.

## Venite
Venite, п., name of the 95th psalm. — L. venite,
'come', imper. 2nd person pi. fr. venire, 'to
come'. See come and cp. venue, 'meeting place*.
The psalm is so called from its first word Lekhu,
lcome', rendered in the Vulgate by the word
'Venite'.

## vennel
vennel, п., an alley (Scot, and Ir.) — F. venelle,
'alley', dimin. of veine, 'vein', fr. L. vena. See
vein.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:832 COLUMN:3 -->

## venom
venom, п., 1) poisonous matter secreted by some
animals (as snakes,· spiders, etc.); 2) spite,
malice. — ME. venym, venim, venon, fr. OF. venim
(F. venin), fr. VL. *venimen, which was formed
fr. L. venenum, 'a drug, potion*, through the
substitution of suff. -imen for -enum. L. venenum
orig. meant 'love potion'. It derives fr. venus,
'love, sexual desire'; see Venus, venerate and cp.
venin, envenom. Cp. Rum. venin, It. veleno,
OProvenc. veren, Catal. veri, Sp. and Port.
veneno, 'venom', which derive fr. VL. *veni-
me(n), resp. fr. L. venenum.

## venomous
venomous, adj., poisonous. — ME. venimous, fr.
OF. venimeux, which is formed fr. venim, with
suff. -eux. See venom and -ous. Cp. F. veneneux,
'venomous', which derives fr. L. venenosus,
'venomous', fr. venenum, 'venom*.

## venose
venose, adj., pertaining to a vein; veiny. — L.
venosus, 'full of veins', fr. vena. See vein, п., and
adj. suff. -ose and cp. venous.
Derivative: venos-ity, h.

## venous
venous, adj., pertaining to a vein; veiny. — L.
venosus. See venose and -ous.
Derivatives: venous-ly, adv., venous-ness, n.

## vent
vent, п.. a slit, opening in a coat. — ME. vente, a
var. of fente, fent, fr. MF. (= ¥.) fente, 'cleft,
slit*, fr. fendre, *to cleave, split', fr. L. findere
(pp. fissus); see fissile. The spelling of ME.
vente is due to a confusion with F. vent, 'wind'.
See next word.
Derivative: vent, tr. v., to let out at a vent'.

## vent
vent, п., 1) outlet for air, gas or liquid; 2)
expression. — Partly fr. F. vent, 'wind', fr. L.
ventus; partly fr. F. event, 'a breaking forth', fr.
eventer, 'to break forth', which is formed fr. pref.
έ- (= OF. es-, L. ex-), and vent, 'wind'. See
wind, 'air', and cp. ventilate.
Derivative: vent, tr. v., to let out, vent-age, п.,
vent-less, adj.

## vent
vent, п., 1) the act of selling; 2) market for sale.
— MF. (= F.) vewte,'sale', fr. VL. vendita, 'sale',
prop. fern. pp. of L. vendere, 'to sell', used as a
noun. Cp. It. vendita, Sp. venta, which also
derive fr. VL. vendita, and see vend. Cp. also next
word.

## venta
venta, п., inn. — Sp., 'sale, market; inn', fr. VL.
vendita, 'sale'. See prec. word,

## ventall
ventall, п., the lower movable part of a helmet
(hist.) — ME., fr. MF. ventaille (F. ventail), fr.
OF., fr. vent, 'wind*. See wind, 'air*, and cp.
a ventail.

## venter
venter, п., the abdominal cavity in insects. — L.
venter, 'belly, womb', for *wend-tri-, rel. to
venstca, vesica, 'bladder', and cogn. with OL
vastih, 'bladder', vanisthuh, 'rectum', OHG.
wanast, MHG., G. wanst, 'paunch, belly1. Cp.
ventricle, eventration, vesicle and the first
element in ventriloquism,

## venter
venter, п., one who vents. — Formed from vent,
v., with agential suff. -er.

## venter
venter, п., innkeeper. — Sp. ventero, fr. venta,
'inn'. See venta.

## ventiduct
ventiduct, п., a pipe for the passage of air in
ventilation (archit.) — Compounded of L. ventus,
'wind', and ductus, 'conduit', fr. ducere, pp.
ductus, *to lead'. See wind, 'air', and duct and cp.
next word.

## ventilate
ventilate, tr. v. — L. ventildtus, pp. of >v$ntildre,
'to branidsh in the air, fan, set in motion,

## agitate'
agitate', fr. ventus, 'wind'. See wind, 'air', and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: ventilation (q.v.), ventilat-ive, adj.,

## ventilat-or
ventilat-or, n.

## ventilation
ventilation, n. — L. ventildtio, gen. -onis, fr.

## ventildtus
ventildtus, pp. of ventilare. See prec. word and
-ation.

## Vent6se
Vent6se, п., the sixth month of the French
revolutionary calendar (lasting fr. February 19th to
March 20th). — A word coined by Fabre

## d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. F. ventose
d'Eglantine in 1793 fr. F. ventose, lit. 'the windy
(month)', fr. L. ventosus, 'full of wind, windy',

## fr. ventus
fr. ventus, 'wind'. Cp. F. venteux, 'windy' (fr. L.

## ventosus)
ventosus), and see wind, 'air', and adj. suff. -ose.

## ventosity
ventosity, n. — ME! ventosite, de. MF. (= F.)

## ventosite
ventosite, fr. Late L. ventositdtem, ace. of ven-

## tdsitds
tdsitds, fr. L. ventosus. See prec. word and -ity.

## ventral
ventral, adj., pertaining to the belly. — F., fr. L.

## ventrdlis
ventrdlis, fr. venter, 'belly*. See venter, 'abdom-
