inal cavily'.
Derivative: ventral-ly, adv.

## ventri-
ventri-, or ventro-, before a vowel ventr-, combining
form meaning ]) ventral; 2) ventral and. — L.
ventri-, ventro-, ventr-, fr. venter, 'belly'. See
venter, 'abdominal cavity'.

## ventricle
ventricle, п., cavity in an organ of the body. —
Fr. F. ventricule, or directly fr. L. ventriculus,
'stomach, ventricle", dimin. of venter, 'belly'.
See venter, 'abdominal cavity', and -cle and cp.
ventriculus.

## ventricose
ventricose, adj., bellied. — ModL. ventricosus, fr.
L. venter, 'belly'. See venter, 'abdominal cavity',
and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: ventricos-ity, n.

## ventricular
ventricular, adj. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. L.
ventriculus. See ventricle.

## Ventriculites
Ventriculites, п., a genus of fossil (paleontol.) —
A ModL. hybrid coined fr. ventriculus and suff.
-ite (representing Gk. -ίτης).

## ventriculogram
ventriculogram, n^ an χ ray photograph of the
ventricles of the brain. — A hybrid coined fr. L.
ventriculus and Gk. γράμμα, 'that which is
written'. See next word and -gram.

## ventriculus
ventriculus, п., one of the cavities in the brain
{anat. and zool.) — L., 'ventricle'. See ventricle.

## ventriloquial
ventriloquial, adj., pertaining to ventriloquism.
— Formed with suff. -ial fr. Late L. ventrilo-
quus, 'one who speaks from his belly', fr. venter,
'belly', and loqul, 'to speak', so called from the
belief that the voice comes from the
ventriloquist's stomach. See venter, 'abdominal cavity',
and loquacious.
Derivative: ventriloquial-ly, adv.

## ventriloqnism
ventriloqnism, п., the art of speaking so that the
voice seems to come from some source other
than the person speaking. — Formed fr. Late
F. ventriloquus (see prec. word) with suff. -ism.

## ventriloqnist
ventriloqnist, n. — Formed fr. Late L.
ventriloquus (see ventriloquial) with suff. -ist.

## ventriloquize
ventriloquize, intr. and tr. v. — Formed fr. Late
L. ventriloquus (see ventriloquial) with suff. -ize.

## ventriloquy
ventriloquy, п., ventriloquism. — F. ventriloquie,
fr. ML. ventriloquium, fr. Late L. ventriloquus,
'one who speaks from the belly*. See
ventriloquial and -y (representing F. -ie).

## ventripotent
ventripotent, adj., having a big belly. —
Compounded of L. venter, 'belly', and potens, gen.
-entis, 'powerful'. See venter, 'abdominal
cavity', and potent.

## ventro-
ventro-, combining form. See ventri-.

## venture
venture, n. — Aphetic form of ME. aventure. See
adventure and cp. venne, 'arrival'.
Derivative: venturey tr. and intr. v.

## venturesome
venturesome, adj. — A hybrid coined fr. venture,
a word of L. origin, and suff. -some (fr. OE.
-sum).
Derivatives: venturesome-ly, adv., venture-some-
ness, n.

## venue
venue, п., ]) arrival (obsol.); 2) meeting place. —
MF. (= F.), 'a coming*, fr. OF., prop. pp. of
venir, 'to come', used as a noun, fr. L. venio,
which prob. stands for *gwmid, and is cogn.
with Goth, qiman, OE. cuman, 'to come'. See
come and cp. base, n. Cp. also advene, ndvent,
adventitious, adventure, avenue, circumvene,
circumvent, contravene, convene, convenient,
convent, convention, covenant, event, eventaal,
intervene, intervention, invent, invention, nuncio,
parvenu, prevenance, prevent, provenance, reve-
nant, revenue, souvenir, subvene, subvention,
Venlte, venture.

## venue
venue, п., the neighborhood of a cause of action
or of a crime; place of trial (law). —
Lit..'neighborhood', fr. ML. vicinetum, fr. L. vlclnus,
'neighboring, near*, fr. vlcus, .'district'; see
vicinage. Venue in this sense was influenced in
form by venue, 'arrival'.

## venule
venule, п., a small vein. — L. vinula, formed fr.
vena with dimin. suff. -ula. See vein and -ule.

## Venns
Venns, n. — L. Venus, gen. Veneris, 'the goddess
of love', fr. venus, 'love, sexual desire, loveliness,
attractiveness, beauty, charm*, whence venerdri,
'to reverence, worship, venerate'. See venerate.

## vera
vera, п., name of a tree, Bulnesia arborea. — Am.
Sp., fr. Sp. vera, 'border', which derives fr. L.
6ra, 'border* (through the intermediate form
*uera; cp. Sp. hueso, 'bone' (fr. L. ossum). L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:833 COLUMN:2 -->
era (for *dsa) is a collective noun formed fr. os,
gen. -oris, 'mouth, opening, entrance'. See oral.

## veracious
veracious, adj., truthful, true. — Formed with
suff. -ous fr. L. verax, gen. veracis, 'truthful,
speaking truly', fr. virus. See veryl
Derivatives: veracious-ly, adj., veracious-ness, n.

## veracity
veracity, п., truthfulness, truth. — F. viraciti, fr.
ML. viracitatem, ace. oiveracitas, 'truthfulness',
fr. L. verax, gen. -dcis. See prec. word and -ity.

## veranda
veranda, verandah, n. — Port, varanda, 'balcony',
introduced into English from India. Port,
varanda itself is of uncertain origin. F. veranda
was borrowed from English..
Derivative: veranda(h)-ed, adj.

## verano
verano, п., the dry season in tropical America. —
Sp., fr. L. vir, 'spring*. See vernal.

## verascope
verascope, п., a small stereoscopic camera. — A
hybrid coined fr. L. virus, 'true', and Gk. -σκό-
πιον, fr. σκοπεΐν, 'to look at, examine'. See
very and -scope. The correct form would be
alethoscope (fr. Gk. αληθής, 'true' and -σκό-
πιου).

## veratral
veratral, п., the radical C9Hl0O4 (chem.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. veratrum, 'hellebore'.
See veratrine.

## veratric
veratric, adj., pertaining to a white crystalline
acid.— Formed with adj. suff. -ic fr. L. veratrum,
'hellebore' (see veratrine); so called because it is
easily obtained by the decomposition of
veratrine.

## veratridine
veratridine, also veratridin, п., an amorphous
alkaloid obtained from sabadilla seeds,
C3eH5:1OnN (chem.) — Coined fr. L. veratrum,
'hellebore' (see next word), and the chem.
suffixes -ide and -ine (resp. -in).

## veratrine
veratrine, п., also veratrin, veratrina, veratria, a
poisonous mixture of alkaloids obtained from
sabadilla seeds, used in medicine in the
treatment of rheumatism, neuralgia, etc. — F.
veratrine, fr. ModL. veratrina, fr. L. veratrum,
'hellebore', fr. verare, 'to tell the truth', fr. virus,
'true'; so called because of the sternutatory
effect of its levigated rots (with reference to the
popular belief that ascribes to sneezing the
power of confirming the truth). For the formation of
the word veratrum cp. aratrum, 'plow', from
arare, 'to plow*. See very.

## Veratrum
Veratrum, п., a genus of plants, the false
hellebore (hot.) — See prec. word.

## verb
verb, n. — ME. verbe, fr. MF. (^ F.), fr. OF., fr.
L. verbum, 'word, verb*, which derives fr. I.-E.
base *werdk-, whence also Goth, waurd, OE.
word, 'word'. See word and cp. also veracious,
veracity, veratrine, verbatim, verbiage, verbose,
proverb. For the change of I.-E. dh to b in Latin,
cp. L. ruber and E. red, L. barba and E. beard.
In its grammatical pense, L. verbum is a loan
translation of Gk. £ήμα, 'that which is said,
word; verb'.

## verbal
verbal, adj. — Late L. verbalis, fr. L. verbum,
'word*. See verb and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: verbal-ism, п., verbal-ist, п.,
verbalize, tr. and intr. v., verbal-iz-ation, п., verbal-iz-
er, п., verbal-ly, adv., verb-y, adj.

## Verbascum
Verbascum, п., a genus of plants, the mullein
(bot.) — L. verbascum, 'mullein', prob. of Ligu-
rian origin. Cp. barhasco.

## verbatim
verbatim, adv., word for word; adj., following
word for word. — ML. verbatim, 'word for
word, literally', fr. L. verbum, 'word'. See verb.
For the suif. -atim see gradatim and cp. words
there referred to.

## Verbena
Verbena, п., a genus of plants, the vervain (bot.)
— L. See vervain,

## Verbenaceae
Verbenaceae, n. pi., the vervain family (bot.) —
ModL., formed fr. prec. word with Suff. -nceae.

## verbenaceous
verbenaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## Verbesina
Verbesina, п., a genus of herbs, the crownbeard
(bot.) — ModL., arbitrarily formed fr. Verbena.

## verbiage
verbiage, п., verbosity. — F., formed with suff.
-age fr. MF. verbier, 'to chatter', fr. L. verbum,
'word*. See verb.

## verbose
verbose, adj., using too many words, wordy. —
L. verbosust 'full of words, verbose', fr. verbum.
See verb and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivatives: verbose-ly, adv., verbose-ness, n.

## verbosity
verbosity, п., wordiness. — MF. (= F.) verbositi,
fr. Late L. verbositatem, ace. of verbositas, fr. L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:833 COLUMN:3 -->
verbosus. See prec. word and -ity.

## verdancy
verdancy, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## verdant
verdant, adj-. — A blend of L. viridans, pres. part.
of viridare, 'to become green', and F. verdoyant,
pres. part, of verdoyer, 'to become green', fr.
vert, 'green'. Cp. It. verdeggiare, Proven?, verde-
jar, Sp. verdear and see viridity and -ant. Cp.
also verdure, vert, 'the green growth in a forest'.

## verdantique
verdantique,^., a variety of serpentine marble. —
It. verde antico, lit. 'ancient green'. The first
word derives fr. L. viridem, ace. of viridis,
'green', the second fr. antiquus, 'old'. See
viridity and antique.

## verderer
verderer, п., an official of the royal forests, who
has the charge of the green growth {Hist.) —
AF. verderer, fr. OF. verdier, fr. vert, 'green*, fr.
L. viridis. See viridity and cp. words there
referred to.

## verdict
verdict, п., decision, judgment. — ME. verdit, fr.
AF. verdit, corresponding to OF. voirdit, fr. L.
vire dictum, 'truly said' (whence ML. viredic-
/wm,'verdict'). See very and diction and cp.
veridical.

## verdigris
verdigris, п., a green or greenish-blue poisonous
pigment. — ME. verdegrece, fr. OF. vert de
Grece, vert de Grice, lit. 'green of Greece*. F.
vert-de-gris is a blend of OF. vert de Grice and
F- g™t *gray'. For the etymology of OF. (= F.)
vert see vert, 'green growth*. OF. (= F.) de, 'of,
from', derives fr. L. di, 'from, away from'; see
de-. For the origin of OF. Grice (F. Grece), fr.
L. Graecia, see Grecian, Greek.
Derivatives: verdigris-ed, verdigris-y, adjs.

## verditer
verditer, п., either of two pigments of green, resp.
blue color. — F. vert de terre, lit. 'green of
earth'. For the first two words see prec. word. F.
terre, 'earth', derives fr. L. terra. See terra.

## verdure
verdure, п., 1) greenness; 2) freshness. — ME., fr.
MF. (= F.) fr. OF. verd (F. vert), 'green', fr.'
L. viridis. See viridity and -ure.
Derivatives: verdur-ed, verdure-less, adjs.,
verdurous (q.v.)

## verdurous
verdurous, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr.
verdure on analogy of adjectives in which- ous
corresponds to OF.-eus (—F. eux). See tremendous.
Derivative: verdurous-ness, n.

## verecund
verecund, adj., bashful, shy. — L. vericundus,
formed with suif. -cundus, fr. verirl, 'to observe
with awe, revere, respect, fear'. See revere. For
the suff. cp. fecund and words there referred
to.
Derivatives: verecund-ity, п., verecund-ness, n.

## verein
verein, п., association, organization. — G. Veretn,
fr. pref. ver- (see for) and ein, 'one'. See one and
cp. the second element in zollverein.

## VeretiUum
VeretiUum, п., a genus of club-shaped sea pens
(zool.) — ModL., formed with dimin. suff.
-ilium fr. L. veritrum, 'the private parts*, which
is rel. to veriri, 'to revere, fear'. See revere and
cp. prec. word.

## verge
verge, п., ]) staff or office; 2) limit, margin, edge.
— ME., fr. MF. (= F.) verge, 'rod', fr. OF., fr.
L. virga, 'twig, rod, wand' (whence also It.,
Proven?., Sp., Port, verga, Rum. varga); see
virgate and cp. whisk. The sense 'limit, margin,
edge', developed from the meaning 'staff of
office', through the medium of the term within
the verge used in the sense 'within the sphere of
authority of the Royal Steward'.
Derivative: verge, intr. v., to be on the verge; tr.
v., to edge.

## verge
verge, intr. v., to bend, incline. — L. vergeret 'to
bend, incline, turn', prob. cogn. with 01. vrnak-
ti, varjati, 'he turns, twists', fr. I.-E. base *we-
reg-, *werg-. See wrench and cp. converge,
diverge.

## verger
verger, п., an officer of the church. — ME., lit.
'one bearing a verge', formed fr. MF. verge,
'staff' (see verge, п.), with agential suff. -er. Cp.
ML. virgarius in the same sense.

## veridical
veridical, adj., truthful. — Formed with adj. suff.
-al fr. L. veridicus, 'truthtelling, veracious', fr.
virus, 'true', and the stem of ulcere, 'to say,
speak'. See very and diction.
Derivatives: veridical-it у, п., veridical-ly, adv.,
veridical-ness, n.

## verifiable
verifiable, adj. — Formed fr. verify with suff.

-able.
Derivatives: verifiabil-ity, п., verifiable-ness, п.,
verifiabl-y, adv.

## verification
verification, n. — MF. (= F.) verification, fr. ML.
verificdtionem, ace. of verification fr. verifiedtus,
pp. of virificdre. See next word and -ation.

## verify
verify, tr. v., ]) to prove to be true; 2) to test the
correctness of.— ME. verifien, fr. MF. (= F.)
verifier, fr. ML. verificdre, fr. L. virus, 'true',
and -ficdre, fr. facere, 'to make, do*. See very
and -fy.

## verily
verily, adv. — ME. verraily, fr. verray, 'very'. See
very and adv. suff. -ly.

## verine
verine, verin, п., a base formed from veratric acid
(chem.) — Abbreviation of veratrine.

## verisimilar
verisimilar, adj., likely, — Formed with suff. -ar
fr. L. verisimilis, which is compounded of veri,
gen. of virum, 'the truth*, subst. use of the neut.
of virus, 'true', and similis, 'similar'. See very and
similar.
Derivative: verisimilar-ly, adv.

## verisimilitude
verisimilitude, п., likelihood. — L. verisimilitude,
fr. verisimilis. See prec. word and -hide and cp.
similitude,

## verism
verism, п., the theory that art and literature
should represent the rigid truth. — It. verismo,
formed fr. vera (fr. L. virus), 'true', and suff.
-ismo (fr. L. -ismus). See very and -ism.

## verist
verist, п., an adherent of verism. — It. verista,
formed fr. vero (see prec. word) with suff. -ista
(fr. L. -ista; see -ist).

## veritable
veritable, adj. — MF. (= F.) veritable, fr. OF.
veritable, fr. verite. See next word and -able.
Derivatives: veritabil-ity, п., veritable-ness, п.,
veritabl-y, adv.

## verity
verity, n. — ME. verite, fr. MF. (= F.) verife, fr.
OF. verite, 'truth, truthfulness, verity', fr. L.
veritdtem, ace. of Veritas, of s.m., fr. virus. See
very and -ity.

## verjuice
verjuice, n. — ME. verjus, verjuis, fr. OF. vert jus,
verjus, lit. 'green juice', fr. vert, 'green', and jus,
'juice'. See vert, 'green growth', and juice,

## vermeil
vermeil, п., ]) vermilion (poetic); 2) gilded silver,
bronze or copper. — MF. (= F.) vermeil, fr.
OF., fr. L. vermiculus, 'a little worm', whence
also It. vermiglio and Sp. bermejo. Port, ver-
melho, 'vermilion'. L. vermiculus is dimin. of
vermis. See next word and cp. vermicule.
Derivative: vermeil, adj.

## Vermes
Vermes, п., a division of animals comprising the
worms (zool.) — L. vermes, pi. of vermis, 'worm',
which stands for *wormis, *wrmis, and is cogn.
with Goth, waurms, 'serpent, worm'. See worm
and cp. vermeil, Vermetus, vermicelli, vermilion,
vermin,

## vermetid
vermetid, adj., pertaining to the Vermetidae; п., а
mollusk of the Vermetidae. — From next word.

## Vermetidae
Vermetidae, n. pi., a family of marine mollusks
{zool.) — ModL., formed fr. Vermetus with suff.
-idae.

## Vermetus
Vermetus, п., a genus of marine mollusks (zool.)
— ModL., fr. L. vermis, 'worm'. See prec. word.

## vermi-
vermi-, combining form meaning 'worm*. — L.
vermi-, fr. vermis. See Vermes,

## vermian
vermian, adj., wormlike; pertaining to the
Vermes. — Formed with suff. -ian fr. L. vermis,
'worm'. See Vermes.

## vermicelli
vermicelli, п., a paste of wheat flour made into
wormlike threads. — It., pi. of vermicello, 'little

## worm'
worm', fr. VL. *vermicellust dimin. of L.

## vermiculus
vermiculus, itself dimin. of vermis, 'worm'. See
Vermes.
Derivative: vermicelli, adj.

## vermicide
vermicide, п., a substance killing worms. —

## Compounded of vermi- and L. -cfda
Compounded of vermi- and L. -cfda, 'killer', fr. cae-

## dere
dere, 'to kill'. See -cide, 'killer*.
Derivative: vermicid-al, adj.

## vermicular
vermicular, adj., vermiform. — Late L. vermicu-

## laris
laris, fr. L. vermiculus, 'a little worm*. See ver-
micule and adj. suff. -ar.
Derivative: vermicular-ly, adv.

## vermiculate
vermiculate, tr. v., to infest with worms; intr. v.,
to be infested with worms. — L. vermiculatus,
'inlaid so as to resemble the tracks of worms',

## prop. pp. of vermiculdri
prop. pp. of vermiculdri, 'to be full of worms,

## be wormeaten'
be wormeaten', fr. vermiculus. See vermicule and
verbal suff. -ate.
Derivative: vermi culat-ed, adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:834 COLUMN:2 -->

## vermiculation
vermiculation, n. — L. vermiculatio, gen. -onis, 'a
being wormeaten', from vermiculdtus, pp. of
vermiculari, 'to be full of worms'. See prec. word
and -ion.

## vermicule
vermicule, п., a little worm. — L. vermiculus,
dimin. of vermis, 'worm'. See Vermes and -cule
and cp. vermicelli,

## vermiculite
vermiculite, п., any of several micaceous
minerals. — Formed fr. L. vermiculus (see vermicule)
with combining form -lite,

## vermiform
vermiform, adj., having the shape of a worm. —
Compounded of vermi- and L. forma, 'form,
shape'. See form, n.

## vermifuge
vermifuge, adj., tending to expel forms. —
Compounded of vermi- and -fuge.
Derivative: vermifuge, п., a drug that expels
worms.

## vermilion
vermilion, п., a bright scarlet pigment. — ME.
vermilioun, fr. OF. vermeiflon, vermilion (F.
vermilion), fr. vermeil, fr. L. vermiculus, 'a little
worm', used in the sense of 'cochineal insect'.
{Vermiculus is used in this latter specific, sense
in the Vulgate, Ex. 35:25 to translate Heb.
tdltfath shunt) See vermicule and cp. vermeil,

## vermin
vermin, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) vermine, a
collective noun formed fr. VL. *vermineus,
'pertaining to worms', fr. L. vermis. Cp. OProvenc.
vermena, 'worms', and see Vermes. Cp. also
varment,

## verminate
verminate, intr. v., to be infested with worms. —
L. vermindtus, pp. oivermindre, 'to have worms',
fr. vermis, 'worm'. See Vermes and verbal suff.
-ate.

## vermination
vermination, n. — L. vermindtio, gen. -onis, 'the
worms (a disease of animals); a crawling, itching
pain', from vermindtus, pp. of vermindre. See
prec. word and -ion.

## verminosis
verminosis, п., infestation with worms (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. vermis, 'worm'
(see Vermes) and -osis, a suff. of Greek origin.
The correct form would be helminthosis (fr. Gk.
2λμις, gen. 2λμινί>ος, 'worm').

## verminous
verminous, adj., 1) consisting of vermin; 2)
resembling vermin; 3) infested with vermin. — L.
verminosus, 'full of worms' (whence also It. ver-
minoso, OProvenc. vermenos, Sp. vermenoso), fr.
L. vermis. See Vermes and -ous.
Derivatives: verminous-ly, adv., verminous-ness,
n.

## vermouth
vermouth, п., a white wine flavored with aromatic
herbs. — F. vermout, fr. Gk. Wermut, which is
rel. to wormwood (q.v.)-

## vernacular
vernacular, adj., native to a country; п., one's
mother tongue. — Formed with adj. suff. -ar fr. L.
vernaculus, 'born in one's house' (said of slaves),
'native', fr. verna, 'a slave born in his master's
house', a word of Etruscan origin.
Derivatives: vernacular-ism, п., vernacular-ize,
tr. v., vernacular-iz-ation, n.

## vernal
vernal, adj., of, or pertaining to, spring. — L. ver-
ndlis, 'pertaining to spring', fr. vernus, of s.m.,
fr. ver, 'spring', which is cogn. with ON. vdr,
'spring', Gk. Sap, Ion. ήρ, Dor. ίήρ (fr. orig.
*Ha<xp), OI. vasantah, ModPers. bahdr, Arm.
gar-un, OSlav. vesna, 'spring*, Lith. vasara,
'summer'. Cp. verano, vernant, vernation, Eran-
themum, Eranthis, Eryngium. L. ver, etc.,
possibly derive fr. I.-E. base *wes-, *awes-, 'to
shine', whence also L. aurora, 'dawn'. See
aurora and east. For the ending of vernal see
adj. suff. -al.

## vernant
vernant, adj., vernal, springlike. — L. verndns,
gen. -amis, pres. part, of vernare, 'to appear like
spring, flourish, spring, bloom; to grow young,
renew itself, fr. vernus, 'pertaining to spring'.
See prec. word and -ant.

## vernation
vernation, п., the arrangement of leaves in the
bud (bot.) — ModL. verndtio, gen. -onis,
introduced in the above sense by the Swedish
botanist Carolus Linnaeus (1707-78). Cp. L. vernatio,
*a snake's sloughing of skin in spring', fr.
vernare, 'to appear like spring*. See -ation and cp.
prec. word,

## vernier
vernier, п., a short scale made to slide along
a graduated instrument and used to measure
fractional parts of divisions. — Named after
the inventor P. Vernier, a French mathematician
(1580-1637).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:834 COLUMN:3 -->

## verm's Martin
verm's Martin, a fine varnish used in the
decoration of furniture, etc., under Louis XV. — F.,
lit. 'Martin varnish', so called after a famous
family of French cabinetmakers during the reign
of Louis XV. For the etymol. of vernis see
varnish.

## vernix caseosa
vernix caseosa, the fatty substance covering the
skin of new-born children {med.) — ModL., lit.
'cheesy varnish'. Vernix derives fr. MGk.
βερνίκι, 'varnish'; see varnish. Caseosa, the fem.
of caseosus, 'cheesy', derives fr. edseus, 'cheese';
see cheese.

## Vernonia
Vernonia, п., a genus of plants, the iron weed
(bot.) — ModL., named after the English
botanist William Vernon (died in 1711). For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Veronal
Veronal, n,, trademark for barbital. — G.
Veronal, coined by its inventor Emil Fischer (1852-
1919) from the name of the Italian town Verona;
so called by him because he happened to be near
Verona when giving a name to this hypnotic.
For the ending see adj. suff. -al.

## Veronica
Veronica, п., a genus of plants, the speedwell
{bot.) — ModL., prob. named after St.
Veronica, a name derived fr. Gk. Βερενίκη. See
Berenice and cp. vernix caseosa.

## verriculate
verriculate, adj., having verricules. — Formed
with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. verriculum. See next
word.

## verricule
verricule, п., a tuft of hairs (entomol.) — L.
verriculum, 'dragnet', fr. verrere, pp. versus, 'to
sweep'. See war and -cule and cp. averruncate.

## verruca
verruca, п., a swart. — L. verruca, 'excrescence,
swelling, wart', which stands for *versucd and
is cogn. with OE. wearr, 'callosity, wart', wearte,
'wart'. See wart and cp. verrnga, verrugas.

## verrucose
verrucose, adj., warty. — L. verrucosus, fr.
verruca. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: verrucose-ness, n.

## verrncosis
verrncosis, п., citrus scab {plant pathol.) — A
ModL. hybrid coined fr. L. verruca, 'wart' (see
verruca), and -osis, a suff. of Greek origin.

## verrucous
verrucous, adj., 1) pertaining to a wart; 2)
characterized by warts. — Formed fr. L. verruca
(see verruca) with suff. -ous. Cp. verrucose.
verruga п., a wart (med.) — Sp., fr. L. verruca.
See verruca.

## verrugas
verrugas, п., verruga peruana, i.e. Peruvian wart
(med.) — Sp., 'warts', pi. of verruga. See prec.
word.

## versant
versant, п., the general slope of a country. — F.,
prop. pres. part, of verser, 'to pour, overturn,
upset', fr. L. versdre, 'to turn about often or
with force', freq. of vertere (pp. versus), 'to turn'.
See version and -ant.

## versant
versant, adj., concerned; conversant. — L. ver-
sans, gen. -antis, pres. part, of versdre. See prec.
word.

## versatile
versatile, adj., turning with ease from one thing
to another. — Lit. 'one who can turn round
easily', fr. L. versdtilis, 'that which turns round,
revolving, movable', fr. versatus, pp. of versdre,
'to turn about often or with force'- See versant,
п., and -ile.
Derivatives: versatil-ity, n. (cp.'F. versatilite),
versatile-ly, adv., versatile-ness, n.

## verse
verse, n. — ME. fers, vers, partly fr. OE. fers,
partly fr. OF. vers, both derived fr. L. versus,
'furrow, line, line of poetry, verse', fr. versus, pp.
of vertere, 'to turn'. See version.
Derivative: verse, tr. v., to express in verse; intr.
v., to make verses.

## versed
versed, adj., practiced. — Formed with 1st suff.
-ed fr. L. versatus (whence also F. verse), pp. of
versdri, 'to busy oneself with, be engaged in, be
employed in', passive of versdre. See versant, n.

## versed
versed, adj., turned; versed sine, reversed sine
(math.) — Formed with 1 st suff. -ed fr. L. versus,
'turned', pp. of vertere. See version,

## verset
verset, п., a short prelude (music). — ME., fr.
OF. (= F.), dimin. of veri,'line of poetry, verse'.
See verse and -et.

## versicle
versicle, п., a little verse. — L. versiculus, dimin.
of versus. See verse and -icle.

## versicolor
versicolor, versicolour, adj., changing in color. —
L. versicolor, compounded of versus, pp. of
vertere, 'to turn', and color, 'color'. See version and
color.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:835 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VERSIFICATION | 808 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:835 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivative: versicolo(u)r-ed, adj.

## versification
versification, n. — L. versificdtio, gen. -onis, fr.
versificatus, pp. of versificare. See next word and
-ation.

## versify
versify, tr. v., to turn into verse; intr. v., to
compose verses. — ME. versifien, fr. OF. (= F.)
versifier, fr. L. versificare, 'to make verses', which
is compounded of versus, 'verse', and -ficare, fr.
facere, 4o make, do'. See verse and -fy.
Derivatives: versifi-er, п., versify-ing, n.

## version
version, п., ]) translation; 2) account. — MF.
( — F.)j fr. Late L. versionem, ace. of versio, 'a
turning*, fr. L. versus,pp. of vertere, 'to turn', fr.
I.-E. *wert-, 'to turn, twist', whence also 01.
vartate, vartti, 'turns round, rolls' (intr.), var-
tulafy, 'round', vgttah, 'rolled, twisted, round',
vrttik, 'the act of rolling', Avestic varet-, 'to
turn' (intr.), OSIav. vruteti, 'to turn, roll', vratiti,
of s.m., vreteno, Russ. vreteno, 'spindle, distaff',
OSIav. vreme, 'time*, vrusti, "condition,
situation', vrusta, 'stadium', Gk. ρατάνη, 'stirrer,
ladle', Lith. verciu, vefsti, 'to turn', vartyti, 'to
turn to and fro', virstu, vifsti, 'to fall over',
Mir. fersaid, 'club', W. gwerthyd, 'spindle,
distaff', Olr. frith, 'against', Toch. В wrattsai, of
s.m., Goth, walrpan, OHG. werdan, MHG., G.
werden, OE. weordan, 'to become*. For the sense
development o/ these Teut. words ср. Е. to turn
in the sense of to become (e.g. 'to turn cold').
See -ward, weird, worth, 'to become', and cp.
adverse, adversity, advert, advertise, animadvert,
anniversary, a rovescio, averse, aversion, avert,
controverse, controversy, controvert, conversant,
conversation, converse, convert, dextrorse, divers,
divert, diverticulum, eversion, evert, extrorse,
extroversion, extrovert, inadvertent, introrse,
introversion, introvert, inverse, inversion, invert,
malversation, obverse, оbversion, obvert, perverse,
perversion, pervert, quaquaversal, retrorse,
retroversion, retrovert, reverse, revert, sinistrorse,
subversion, subversive, subvert, suzerain,
tergiversate, transverse, traverse, nniverse,
university, verse, verso, verst, versus, vertebra, vertex,
vertical, vertigo, vervel, vice versa, vortex,
vortical, vorticlsm, vertiginous. For the ending
of version see suff. -ion. I.-E. *wert- is a
-/-enlargement of I.-E. base *wer-, 'to turn, twist'.
For other enlargements of base *wer- see verge,
'to bend', vervain, wrench, wring, wrinkle, wrong.

## verso
verso, п., the reverse of a page. — Short for L.
folio verso, 'having turned the page', abl.
absolute construction in which verso is the abl. of
versus, pp. of vertere, 'to turn'. See prec. word.

## verst
verst, п., a Russian measure of length. — F. ver-
ste and G. werst, fr. Russ. versta, which is rel.
to OSIav. vrusta, 'stadium', and to OSIav.
vruteti, Russ. verte'f/to turn', and cogn. with L.
vertere, 'to turn*. See version.

## versus
versus, adv., against. — L., lit. 'turned toward,
opposed', prop. pp. of vertere, 'to turn', cogn.
with Goth, -wairps, 'having a certain direction*,
OE. -weard, '-ward(s)', Olr. frith, 'against',
Toch. В wrattsai, of s.m. See version and cp.
-ward.

## vert
vert, п., the green growth of the forest; the color
green. — ME. veert, fr. OF. verd, vert (F. vert),
4green', fr. L. viridis, 'green*, whence also Rum.,
It., Sp., Port, verde, Proven?., Catal. vert,
'green'. See viridity and cp. verdant.

## vert
vert, intr. v., to change one's faith; п., a convert
(colloq.) — Short for convert or pervert.

## vertebr-
vertebr-, form of vertebro- before a vowel.

## vertebra
vertebra, п., any bone of the spinal column. —
L., lit. 'something to turn on', formed fr. vertere,
'to turn', with -bra, a suff. denoting an
instrument. See version. For the suff. cp. terebra, pal-
pebra.

## vertebral
vertebral, adj. — ModL. vertebrdlis, fr. L.
vertebra. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: vertebr-al, adj.

## Vertebrata
Vertebrata, n. pi., a division of animals
containing all those that have a spinal column (zool.) —
ModL. (short for ammalia vertebrata), neut. of
of L. vertebrdtus, 'jointed, articulated', fr.
vertebra; see vertebra and adj. suff. -ate. The term
goes back to the French word vertebre, coined
by the French naturalist Jean-Baptiste-Pierre-
Antoine de Monet *de Lamarck (1744-1809) fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:835 COLUMN:2 -->
L. vertebrdtus- He uses the terms les animaux
vertebras (lit. 'animals with vertebrae') and les
animaux sans vertebres (lit. 'animals without
vertebrae'). Cp. In vertebrata.

## vertebrate
vertebrate, adj., having a backbone; pertaining to
the Vertebrata. — L. vertebrdtus. See prec. word.

## vertebration
vertebration, п., formation into vertebrae. —
Formed fr. vertebra with suff. -ation.

## vertebro-
vertebro-, before a vowel vertehr-, combining
form meaning 'vertebra'. — See vertebra.

## vertex
vertex, п., the highest point, summit. — L., 'top,
crown, summit, pole, whirl; whirlpool, eddy',
lit. 'that which turns', fr. vertere, 'to turn'. See
version and cp. vortex.

## vertical
vertical, adj., perpendicular to the plane of the
horizon. — F., fr. ML. verticalis, fr. L. vertex,
gen. verticis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: vertical, tr. v., vertical-ity, п.,
vertical-ly, adv., vertical-ness, n.

## verticil
verticil, п., a circle of leaves; a whorl (bot.) — L.
verticillus, 'the whorl of a spindle', dimin. of
vertex. See vertex.

## verticillate
verticillate, adj., arranged in whorls {bot.) —
Formed with adj. suff. -ate fr. L. verticillus. See
prec. word.
Derivative: verticillat-ed, adj.

## verticity
verticity, п., the tendency to turn toward a
magnetic pole. — ModL. verticitas, fr. L. vertex,
gen. verticis. See vertex and -ity.

## vertiginous
vertiginous, adj., dizzy, giddy. — L. xertiginosus
(whence also F. vertigineux), fr. vertigo, gen.
-ginis. See next word and -ous and cp.
vertiginous.
Derivative: vertiginous-ly, adv.

## vertigo
vertigo, п., dizziness, giddiness (med.) — L.
vertigo, fr. vertere, 'to turn'. See version.

## vertu
vertu, n. — The same as virtu.

## Vertumnus
Vertumnus, п., an Etruscan god {Roman mythol.)
— L. Vertumnus, fr. earlier Vortumnus, of
Etruscan origin. The derivation of this name fr.
L. vertere is folk etymology.

## verumontanum
verumontanum, п., an elevation at the point
where the seminal ducts enter the prostatic
portion of the urethra (anat.) — Medical L.,
compounded of L. verii, 'a spit', and montanum, neut.
of montanus, 'mountainous'. The first element
is rel. to Umbr. berva, 'spits' (pi.), and cogn.
with Olr. bir, W., Co. ber, 'spit'. Vera meant
perh. orig. 'branch', and is cogn. also with Gk.
βρύειν, 'to swell'; see bryo- and cp. words there
referred to. See Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II, p.
766 s.v. veru. For the second element in
verumontanum see mountain.

## vervain
vervain, п., any plant of the genus Verbena. —
ME. verveyne, fr. MF. (= F.) verveine, fr. OF.,
fr. L. verbena, usually pi. verbenae, 'leaves and
branches of laurel, sacred boughs', which stands
for *verbes-na, fr. I.-E. base *wer-b-, 'to turn,
twist, bend', whence also L. verbera (pi.), 'rods,
lashes, strokes', Lith. vifbas, 'twig, branch,
scion, rod', Lett, virbs, virbens, 'a little stick',
OSIav. vruba, 'willow*, Gk. άάβδος, 'rod, twig,
stick', ράμνος (for *(5άβνος), 'a pricky shrub;
the buckthorn*. Base *wremb-, the nasalized
form of base *wer-b-, appears in Gk. ρέμβειν,
Чо turn round all about', ρόμβος, 'a ^pinning
top, wheel, rhomb'. From the rel. base *wer-p-,
*wre-p-, 'to turn, twist, sew, spin*, prob. derive
Gk. ράπτω (for *wrp-yo), *I sew together',
ραφή, 'seam', ραφίς, 'needle', ραπίς, 'rod',
Lith. verpiii, verpti, 'to spin',1 varpste, 'spool,
spindle'. Cp. Verbena. Cp. also reverberate,
rhabdo-, Rhamnns, Rhapis, rhombus, rupa, and
the first element in Raphiolepis, rhapsody. Cp.
also warp. I.-E. bases *wer-b-, *wer-p, *wre-p-,
are enlargements of base *wer-, 'to turn, twist,
bend*. See version and cp. worm,

## verve
verve, п., vigor; enthusiasm. — F., fr. MF.,
'whim', fr. OF., 'proverb'; fr. VL. *verva,
assimilated fr. L. verba, pi. of verbum, 'word', used
in the sense of 'word of caprice'; see verb. The
word verve was introduced into English by
Dryden.

## vervel
vervel, п., a ring attached to a falcon's leg. — MF.
(— F.) vervefle, fr. VL. *vertibella, dimin.
formed fr. L. vertere, 'to turn'. See version and -elln
and cp. vertebra.

## vervet
vervet, п., an African monkey, Cercopithecus py-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:835 COLUMN:3 -->
gerythrus. — F., short for vertgrivet, lit. *a green
grivet', i.e. 'the monkey surpassing the grivet in
greenness'. See vert, 'green growth', and grivet.

## very
very, adj. — ME. verai, veray, verray, fr. OF.
verai, vrai (F. vrai), fr. VL. *verdcus (whence
also OProven^. verai), corresponding to L. ve-
rax, gen. verdcis, 'truthful', a derivative of L.
virus, 'true', which is cogn. with OE. wxr, OS.,
ODu., OHG., MHG. war, Du. waar, G. wahr,
'true', OE. wxr, *agreement, treaty; promise,
pledge; faith, fidelity, friendship*, W. gwyr,
Olr. fir, 'true', OSIav. vera, 'faith', and prob.
also with the second element in L. se-verus,
'severe'. See severe and cp. aver, veracious, vera-
trine, verdict, verify, verisimilar, verity, vraisem-
blable, vralsemblance. Cp. also warlock, warrant.
Derivative: very, adv.

## vesanla
vesanla, п., insanity {med.) — L- vesdnia,
'madness', fr. visdnus, "mad', lit. 'unhealthy', formed
from the inserjarable neeative or Deiorative
particle ve- and the adjective sanus, 'healthy'. L. ve-
prob. stands for *awe- and is rel. to the L. pref.
au~, 'away from', 01. avah, 'down, downward',
and Avestic ava, 'down'; see avatar and cp. the
first element in vesper. For the second element
in L. vesanus see sane.
Derivative: vesan-ic, adj.

## vesica
vesica, п., a bladder. — L. vensica, vesica,
'bladder; blister', cogn. with venter, 'belly, womb'.
See venter, 'abdominal cavity*.

## vesical
vesical, adj., pertaining to a bladder. — Medical
L. vesicalis, fr. L. vesica. See prec. word and adj.
suff. -al.

## vesicant
vesicant, adj., causing blister {med.) — Formed
with suff. -ant fr. L. vesica, 'blister'. See vesica.
Derivative: vesicant, п., a blistering substance.

## vesicate
vesicate, tr. and intr. v., to blister. — Formed
with verbal suff. -ate fr. L. vesica. See vesica.
Derivatives: vesicat-ion, п., vesicat-ory, adj. and
n.

## vesicle
vesicle, п., a small cavity. — Either fr. MF.
( = F.) vesicule, or directly fr. L. vesicula. See
vesicula and -cle.

## vesico-
vesico-, combining form meaning 'vesica'. — See
vesica.

## vesicotomy
vesicotomy, п., the surgical cutting of the vesica
{surg.) — A hybrid coined fr. vesica and Gk.
-τομία,' a cutting of, fr. τομή, 'a cutting*. See
-tomy.

## vesicula
vesicula, п., a vesicle {anat.) — L, vesicula, 'a
small blister', dimin. of vesica. See vesica and
-cula and cp. vesicle.

## vesicular
vesicular, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
vesicle; having vesicles. — ML. vesicularis, fr.
L. vesicula. See prec. word and adj. suff. -ar.
Derivative: vesicular-ly, adv.

## vesiculate
vesiculate, adj., vesicular. — See vesicula and adj.
suff. -ate.

## vesiculectomy
vesiculectomy, п., the removal of a vesicle {surg.)
— A hybrid coined fr. vesicula and Gk. -εκ-
τομία, 'a cutting out of, fr. έκτομή, 'a cutting
out'. See -ectomy.

## vesper
vesper, п.,evening; {cap.) the evening star. — ME.
fr. L. vesper, 'evening, evening star', whence the
adj. vesperus, 'pertaining to the evening', whence
vespera (scil. kora), 'evening*, lit. 'evening time
or hour', which is cogn. with Gk. έσπερος (for
*Γέσπερος), εσπέρα (for *fεσπέρα),
'evening', OSIav. veieru, Lith. vdkaras,W. ucher, Co.
gurth-ucher, Olx.fescor, Arm. gisher, of s.m. All
these words prob. derive fr. I.-E. *we-spero,
resp. *we-qero, in which the first element means
'down', and is cogn. with OI. flvrf£,'down,
downward* (see vesania). Accordingly pref. *we- in L.
vesper, Gk. *Ρέ-σπερος, etc., prob. denote the
setting (i.e. 'the going down') of the sun. See
west and cp. Vespertilio, vespertine, Hesperian,
pi pist rel.
vespera], adj., pertaining to the evening {rare). —
Late L. vesperalis, fr. L. vesper, 'vening'. See
prec. word and adj. suff. -al.

## vesperal
vesperal, also vespera le. п., a book containing the
office for vespers. — F. vesperal, fr. the Late L.
vesperalis. See vesperal, adj.

## vespers
vespers, n. pi., the sixth canonical hour. — Early
F. vespres (F. vepres), fr. OF., fr. ML. vesperae,
fr. L. vesperae, 'evenings', pi. of vespera,
evening', which is a collateral form of vesper, 'eve-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:836 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 809 | VIBRANT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:836 COLUMN:1 -->
ning'. See prec. word.

## Vespertilio
Vespertilio, п., a genus of bats (zool.) — L.
vespertilio, 'a bat', fr. *vespertilis, 'of the evening', fr.
vesper, 'evening'. See vesper and cp. pipistrel.

## vespertilionid
vespertilionid, adj., pertaining to the family Ves-
pertilionidae {zool) — See next word.

## VespertUionidae
VespertUionidae, n. pi., a large family of bats
{zool.) — ModL., formed fr. Vespertilio with
suff. -idae.

## vespertine
vespertine, adj., 1) pertaining to, or occurring in,
the evening; 2) appearing in the evening (said of
animals). — L. vespertinus, 'of, or pertaining to,
the evening', fr. vesper; see vesper and -ine
(representing L. -inus). The -t- in vesper-t-inus is due
to the analogy of mdtut-inus, 'of the morning',
in which the / belongs to the stem.

## vespiary
vespiary, п., a wasps' nest. — Formed on analogy
of apiary fr. L. vespa, 'wasp', which prob. was
metathesized fr. *vepsa, fr. I.-E. *wobh-sd, fr.
base *webh-, *wobk-, 'to weave', whence also
Gk. ΰφος, *web', ύφαίνειν, ΟΕ. wefan, ON.
vefa, 'to weave', OE. wsesp, wzeps, 'wasp'. See
weave and -ary and cp. wasp. Cp. also next
word.

## Vespidae
Vespidae, n. pi., a family of wasps, containing the
social wasps and the hornets (zool.) — ModL.,
formed with suff. -idae fr. L. vespa, 'wasp'. See
prec. word.

## vespiform
vespiform, adj., resembling a wasp. —
Compounded of L. vespis, 'wasp', and forma, 'form,
shape'. See vespiary and form, n.

## vespine
vespine, adj., pertaining to wasps. — Formed
with suff. -ine (representing L. -inus) fr. L. vespa,
'wasp'. See vespiary.

## vespoid
vespoid, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, wasps.
— A hybrid coined fr. L. vespa, 'wasp', and Gk.
-οειδής, 'like', fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See
vespiary and -oid.

## vessel
vessel, n. — ME., fr. OF. vaissel, vessel (F. vais-
seau)\ 'vessel, vase, ship', fr. Late L. vdscellum,
dimin. of L. vasculum, itself a dimin. of vds,
Vessel, dish'; see vase and cp. vascular. F. vais-
selle and Sp. vajilla, 'plates and dishes', derive
fr. Late L. vascella, pi. of vdscellum, which was
taken for a fern. sing, with collective sense.

## vest
vest, n. — F. veste, Тт. It. vesta, veste, fr. L. ves-
tis, 'covering for the body, clothes' (whence
vestire, 'to clothe'), fr. I.-E. base *wes-, 'to
clothe*, whence also Ol. vaste, 'he puts on,
dresses', vas-trah, vds-ana-m, 'garment*, vas-
man-, 'a covering'. Gk. έσ&ής (for *Γεσθής),
'clothing', έννύναι (for *fewi!>vai), 'to clothe',
εΐμα (Aeol. 5έμμα, Cretan 5ήμα),
'garment', Goth, wasjan, 'to clothe', wasti, *a
garment', OE. wsestling, 'sheet, blanket', werian, 'to
wear (clothes)', Arm. z-genum, Ί gut on clothes,
dress', zgest, 'garment', Alb. veS, Ί clothe',
viSem, Ί put on clothes, dress', Toch. В wastsi,
wdtsi, A. wsdl, 'clothing*, Hitt. washshusk (pi.),
'garments', washanzi, 'they put on, dress'. See
wear, 'to be clothed', and cp. devest, divest,
invest, revest, revet, travesty, vestment, vestry,
vesture. Cp. also Anemia, himation. — I.-E. base
*wes- is an enlargement of base *ew-, 'to put,
place*, whence L. ind-uere, 'to put on', ex-uere,
'to pull or strip off'. See exuviae and cp. words
there referred to.

## vest
vest, tr. and intr. v. — ME. vesten, fr. MF. vestir
(F. virir), fr. OF., fr. L. vestire, 'to clothe', fr.
vestis, 'a garment'. See vest, n.
Derivatives: vest-ed, adj., vest-ing, n.

## Vesta
Vesta, п., the goddess of the hearth in Roman
mythology. — L., of uncertain origin; possibly
cogn. with Gk. εστία (for *fεστία),'the hearth
of the house' (whence έστιαν, 'to receive at one's
hearth'), Ol. vasati, 'stays, dwells', Toch. A
washt, В ost, 'house', washamo, 'companion,
fellow', Goth, wisan, OE., OHG. wesan, 'to be',
and, together with these words, derived fr. I.-E.
base * wes-,lto dwell, stay'; see Walde-Hofmann,
LEW., II, p. 773 s.v. Vesta. See was and cp. the
first element in wassail. Cp. also Hestia, asteism,
bustee.

## vestal
vestal, adj., belonging, or dedicated, to Vesta
(Roman mytkol.) — L. Vestdlis, 'of Vesta,
dedicated to Vesta', fr. Vesta. See prec. word and
adj. suff. -al.

## vestal
vestal, п., vestal virgin. — L. Vestdlis, short for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:836 COLUMN:2 -->
virgo Vestdlis, lit. 'virgin of Vesta'. See prec.
word.

## vestiary
vestiary, п., vestry. — ME. vestiarie, fr. OF. ves-
tiarie, vestiat're (F. vestiaire), fr. L. vestidrium,
'a wardrobe*. See vestry,

## vestibular
vestibular, adj. — Formed with suff. -ar fr. L. ves-
tibulum (see next word).

## vestibule
vestibule, п., a small antechamber. — L. vestibu-
lum (whence also It- vestibulo, F. vestibule),
'entrance hall, fore court*; of uncertain origin.

## vestige
vestige, п., trace mark. — F., fr. L. vestigium,
'footprint, step, track, trace', which is of
uncertain origin. Cp. Investigate.
Derivatives: vestigi-alt adj., vestigi-al-ly, adv.

## vestlture
vestlture, п., 1) investiture; 2) clothes, clothing.
— ML. vestitura, fr. L. vestltus, pp. of vestire.
See vesture.

## vestment
vestment, п., garment. — ME. vestement, fr. OF.
vestement (F. vetement), fr. L. vestimentum,
'clothing*, fr. vestire, 'to clothe*, fr. vestis,
'garment*. See vest, п., and -mcnt.
Derivatives: vestment-al, vestment-ed, adjs.

## vestral
vestral, adj., pertaining to a vestry. — Formed
from next word with adj. suff. -al.

## vestry
vestry, п., a room in a church for vestments. —
ME. vestrye, fr. MF. vestiairiet vestiaire (F.
vestiaire), fr. OF., fr. L. vestidrium, 'a wardrobe',
prop, subst. use of the neut. of the adjective
vestidrius, 'pertaining to clothes', fr. vestis,
'garment*. See vest, п., and cp. vestiary.

## vesture
vesture, п., clothing. — ME., fr. MF. vesteure,
vesture (F. veture), fr. OF., fr. Late L. vestitura,
'clothing', fr. L. vestitus, pp. of vestire. See vest,
n. and v., and -ure and cp. vestiture.
Derivatives: vestur-ed, adj., vestur-er, n.

## vesuvian
vesuvian, п., a kind of match or fusee. —
Tradename formed from the adjective Vesuvian,
'pertaining to Mount Vesuvius', fr. L. Vesuvius,
name of the volcano on the Bay of Naples.

## veszelyite
veszelyite, п., a hydrous copper zinc phospho-
arsenate (mineral.) — G. Veszelyit, named after
the Hungarian mining engineer A. Veszelyi. The
ending -it goes back to Gk. -ίτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## vet
vet, n. (colloq.) — Abbreviation of veterinary
(surgeon).

## vet
vet, tr. v., to submit (an animal) to veterinary
examination; intr. v., to practice as a
veterinarian. — From prec. word.

## vetch
vetch, п., name of a plant. — ME. fecche, vecche,
fr. OF. veche, var. of vece (F. vesce), fr. L. vicia
(whence also It. veccia), which is prob. rel. to L.
vincire, 'to bind', and cogn. with Lett, vikne,
'tendril', vikt, 'to become flexible'. These words
prob. derive fr. I.-E. *weiq-, enlargement of
base *wei-, 'to bend, twist', whence L. viere, 'to
bend, twist', vitis, 'vine', OE. wide, 'withe',
widig, 'willow, willow twig'. See withy and cp.
Vicia. Cp. also vinculum and the second element
in periwinkie, the plant. —OS. wikka, Du. wikke,
wik, OHG. wicka, wiccha (MHG., G. wicke),
'vetch', are loan words fr. L. vicia).
Derivative: vetch-y, adj.

## veteran
veteran, adj. — L. veterdnus, 'old, veteran1, fr.
vetus, gen. veteris, 'old', which is traceable to
the noun *wetos, 'year', and orig. meant 'of
(many) years', fr. I.-E. base *wet-, 'year', whence
also Gk. Ετος (dial. 5έτος), 'year', Ol. vatsa-,
vatsard-, 'year', Hitt. witish, 'year', wittassa-,
'yearly', Alb. vjet, 'year', OSlav. vetuchu, 'old',
Lith. vituSas, 'old, aged', Ol. vatsah, L. vitulus,
'calf, lit. 'yearling', Goth, wiprus, OE. weder,
'wether'. See wether and cp. veal. Cp. also
veterinary, inveterate. For the ending see suff. -an.
For the change of the noun *wetos, 'year', to the
adj. vetus, 'old', cp. augur.

## veteran
veteran, n. — F. veteran, fr. L. veterdnus. See
veteran, adj.

## veterinarian
veterinarian, adj. and n. — Formed from next
word with suff. -ian.

## veterinary
veterinary, adj. — L. veterinarius, 'pertaining to
beasts of burden or draft', fr. veterfnus,
'pertaining to carrying burdens', esp. veterina (scil.
bestia), *a draft animal', fr. vetus, 'old', orig.
'one year old'. Veterina bestia prop, means 'an
animal one year old', hence strong enough to
draw burdens. See veteran and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: veterinary, п., veterinarian (q.v.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:836 COLUMN:3 -->

## vetiver
vetiver, п., an East Indian grass, called also cus-
cus. — F. vetiver, fr. Tamil vettiveru, which is
compounded of vettu, "digging', and ver, 'root'.

## veto
veto, п., 1) prohibition; 2) the power or right to
reject or prohibit. — L. veto, Ί forbid', inf. ve-
tdre, of uncertain origin.
Derivative: veto, tr. v.

## vetturino
vetturino, п., driver of a four-wheeled carriage in
Italy. — It., fr. vettura, 'carriage', fr. VL. vec-
tura, 'carriage', fr. L. vectus, pp. of vehere, 'to
draw, carry'. See vehicle.

## vex
vex, tr. v., to annoy, irritate; to harass. — ME.
vexen, fr. MF. (= F.) vexer, fr. L. vexare, 'to
agitate, vex', fr. vexus, a collateral form of
vectus, pp. of vehere, 'to draw, carry'. See vehicle.
Derivatives: vex-er, п., vex-ing-ly, adv., vex-ing-
ness, n.

## vexation
vexation, n. — ME. vexacioun, fr. Μ F. (= F.)s fr.
L. vexdtionem, ace. of vexdtio, 'agitation', fr.
vexus. See prec. word and -ation.

## vexatious
vexatious, adj., causing vexation. — See prec.
word and -ous.
Derivatives: vexatious-ly, adv., vexatious-ness,
n.

## vexillary
vexillary, п., a standard-bearer. — L. vexilldrius,
'standard-bearer, ensign', fr. vexiffum. See vexil-
lum and subst. suff. -ary.

## vexillary
vexillary, adj., pertaining to a military standard.
— Formed with adj. suff. -ary fr. L. vexillum.
See next word.

## vexillum
vexillum, п., a military standard. — L. vexillum,
'a military ensign or standard', dimin. of velum,
'sail, cloth'. See veil.

## via
via, п., way. — L., 'way, road, path', rel. to
Oscan via, Umbr. via, 'way'; of uncertain
origin; usually connected with vehere, 'to carry,
convey' (see vehicle). See e.g. Ernout-Meillet,
DELF., p. 731 s.v. uia. According to Walde-
Hofmann, LEW., II, p. 779 s.v. via, the form of
the word via itself shows that it cannot be related
to vehere\ if it were, its form should have been
veia. Cp. viaduct, viatic, viaticum, voyage,
convey, convoy, devinte, devions, envoy, evi table, foy,
impervious, obviate, obvious, pervious, previous,
quadrivium, Traviata, trivial, trivium.

## via
via, adv., by way of. — L. via, abl. of via, 'way'.
See via, n.

## viability
viability, n. — F. viabilite, fr. viable. See next
word and -ity.

## viable
viable, adj., capable of living.— F., fr. MF.,
formed with suff. -able fr. vie, 'life', fr. L. vita. See
vital.
Derivatives: viable-ness, п., viabl-y, adv.

## viaduct
viaduct, n. — Formed fr. L. via, 'way', and
ductus, 'a leading', on analogy of aqueduct, fr. L.
aquaeductus. See via, п., and duct. F. viaduc is a
loan word fr. E. viaduct, but was influenced in
form by F. aqueduc.

## vial
vial, п., a phial. — ME. viole, var. offiole, fr. OF.
fiole. See phial.

## viameter
viameter, п., an instrument for measuring
distances on roads. — A hybrid coined fr. L. via,
'way', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See via, п.,
and meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## viand
viand, п., article of food. — ME. viaunde, fr. MF.
viande, 'food' (whence F. viande, 'meat'), fr. OF.,
dissimilated fr. VL. *vivanda, gerundive of vi-
vere, 'to live', used as a fem. sing. noun. Cp. It.
vivanda, Sp. vianda, 'food' (both derived fr. VL.
*vivanda), and see vital. Cp. also vivandiere.

## viatic
viatic, adj., pertaining to a road. — L. vidticus,
'pertaining to a road', fr. via. See via, п., and -ic.

## viaticum
viaticum, п., provisions for a journey. — L.
viaticum, neut. of the adj. vidticus, used as a noun.
See prec. word.

## vibex
vibex, п., a subcutaneous extravasation of blood
(med.) — L. vibex, 'the mark of a blow', prob.
cogn. with Lett, wibele, 'wale, weal'.

## vlbracular
vlbracular, adj., pertaining to vibracula·. —
Formed from next word with adj. suff. -ar.

## vibraculnm
vibraculnm, п., a spinelike organ of certain bryo-
zosltis(zooL)— ModL., formed with suff. -culum
from the stem of L. vibrdre, 4o vibrate'. See
vibrate.

## vibrancy
vibrancy, n. — Formed from next word with suff.
-cy.

## vibrant
vibrant, adj., vibrating. — L. vibrdns, gen. -antis,
pres. part, of vibrdre. See vibrnte and -ant.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:837 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VIBRAPHONE | 810 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:837 COLUMN:1 -->

## vibraphone
vibraphone, п., a musical instrument resembling
the marimba. — A hybrid coined fr. L. vibrdre,
'to vibrate', and Gk. φωνή, 'sound'. See
vibrate and phone, 'speech sound4.

## vibrate
vibrate, intr. v., to move to and fro; to oscillate;
tr. v., to move to and fro. — L. vibrdtus, pp. of
vibrdre, 'to move rapidly to and fro, shake,
brandish, agitate, vibrate*, fr. I.-E. base *weib-,
'to move to and fro, to swing', whence also Lith.
wyburiu, w^burti, *to wag (the tail)', Lett, viebt,
'to turn, spin*, Dan. vippe, MLG., MDu., Du.
wippen, 'to swing' (G. wippen, 'to move up and
down, to rock', is of LG. origin), OHG. wifan,
MHG. wifen, G. weifen, 'to swing, wind, reel',
OHG. wipf, 'swing, impetus', OHG. wipfil,
MHG., G. wipfel, 'top of a tree', lit. 'the
swaying part (of a tree)'. Cp. the collateral base
*weip-, whence 01. vepate, vepati, 'is agitated,
trembles', ON. veifa, 'to wave, vibrate (whence
veif, 'something flapping'), OE. wdfian, 'to wave,
brandish', OHG. weibon, 'to move to and fro,
shake', zi-weibjan, 'to scatter'. Cp. waif, waive,
whip, v., wife, wimple, wipe, wisp, gimp, gnipure.
For the ending see verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: vibrat-ile, adj., vibrat-il-iiy, п.,
vibration (q.v.), vibrat-ive, adj., vibrato (q.v.),
vibrat-or, п., vibrat-ory, adj.

## vibration
vibration, n. — L. vibrdtio, gen. -onis, fr. vibrdtus,
pp. of vibrdre. See prec- word and -ion.
Derivatives: vibration-al, adj., vibration-less, adj.

## vibrato
vibrato, п., a tremulous effect produced by the
variation of emphasis on a tone (mus.) — It.,
pp. ofvibrare, fr. L. vibrdre. See vibrate.

## Vibrio
Vibrio, п., a genus of bacteria of the family Spi-
rillaceae; {not cap.) a bacterium of this genus
{bacterial) — ModL., coined by the Danish
naturalist Otto Friderich Muller (1730-84) fr. L.
vibrdre. See vibrate.

## vibrioid
vibrioid, adj., resembling a vibrio. — A hybrid
coined from prec. word and Gk. -οείδής, 'like',
fr. είδος, 'form, shape'. See -oid.
Derivative: vibrioid, п., a vibrioid body.

## vibrissa
vibrissa, п., stiff hair in the nostril (anat.) — L.
vibrissae (pi.), back formation fr. vibrissdre, 'to
shake (the voice), to trill', which is formed with
suff. -issdre {= Gk. -Εσσει,ν), fr. vibrdre. See
vibrate.
Derivative: vibriss-al, adj.

## vibro-
vibro-, combining form denoting vibration. — Fr.
L. vibrdre. See vibrate.

## vibrogrnph
vibrogrnph, п., an instrument for recording
vibrations. — A hybrid coined fr. L. vibrdre, 'to
shake, vibrate', and Gk. -γράφος, fr. γράφειν,
'to write'. See vibrate and -graph.

## vibroscope
vibroscope, п., instrument for examining
vibrations. — A hybrid coined fr. L. vibrdre, *to
vibrate', and Gk. -σκόπιον, fr. σκοπεΤν, 'to look
at, examine'. See vibro- and -scope.
Derivative: vibroscop-ic, adj.

## Viburnum
Viburnum, п., a genus of plants, the arrowwood
(bot.) — L. viburnum, 'the wayfaring tree', prob.
an Etruscan loan word. Cp. Viorna, liana. Cp.
also laburnum.

## vicar
vicar, n. — ME. vtcair, vicar, fr. L. vicdrius,
'deputy, substitute', prop, subst. use of the adj.
vicdrius. See vicarious.
Derivatives: vicar-age, n.( vicar-ate, п.,
vicarial, adj., vicar-ian, п., vicariate (q.v.)

## vicariate
vicariate, n.', office or jurisdiction of a vicar. —
ML. vicariaius (whence also MF.f F. vicariat),
fr. L. vicdrius. See vicar and subst. suff. -ate.
Derivative: vicariate, intr. v.

## vicarious
vicarious, adj., done by another person;
substituted. — L. vicdrius, 'substituted', fr. vicis (gen.;
pi. nom. vices), 'change, alternation', which is
cogn. with OI. vistf, 'changing, changeable',
OE. wlcan, 'to give way, yield', OS. wikan, ON.
vikja, vikva, ykva, Swed. vika, OFris. wika, Du.
wijken, OHG. wfkkan, MHG. wichen, G. wei-
chen, of s.m., OHG. wehsal, MHG. wehsel, G.
wechsel, 'change', and perh. also with οΐγνύναι
(for *ό-5ε&γ-νύνοα), 'to' open' (prop, 'to cause
to yield'). Cp. vice, 'instead of, vicissitude. Cp.
also viking, weak, week, wicked, wicker, wicket,
witch, 'tree with pliant branches'. For E. -ous, as
equivalent to L. -us, see -ous.
Derivatives: vicarious-ly, adv., vicarious-ness, n.

## vice
vice, п., a moral fault. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.)

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:837 COLUMN:2 -->
vice, fr. L. vitium, 'faul, defect, blemish, crime,
vice' (whence also Proves, vetz, OSpan. vezo,
'custom'. It. vezzo, 'usage, entertainment'),
which prob. stands for *wi-ti-om, a derivative of
I.-E. base *wi-, 'two, in two, asunder', whence
•also OI. vi-, 'asunder', Toch. A we, В wi, 'two'.
Goth, wit, 'we two', the first element in L. νϊ-
ginti, 'twenty', prop, 'two decades', and in OSIav.
vu-toru, 'the second'. See wide and with and cp.
vicennial. Cp. also vicious, vitiate, vitiligo, vi-
tiosity.

## vice
vice, п., a vise. — See vise, 'tool, device'.

## vice
vice, prep., instead of. — L., abl. οι vicis, 'change»
alternation'. See vicarious.

## vice
vice, n. — Short for vice-admiral, vice-chancellor,
etc. — See prec. word.

## vice-
vice-, pref. in titles of office, denoting a substitute
or subordinate. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
vice. See vice, 'instead of.

## vicegerent
vicegerent, n. — ML. vicegerens, gen. -entis. See
vice- and gerent.

## vicenary
vicenary, adj., pertaining to, or consisting of,
twenty. — L. vicendrius, 'pertaining to the
number twenty', fr. viceni, 'twenty each', formed on
analogy of den/, 'ten each', fr. viginti, 'twenty',
which is cogn. with OI. vimsatib, Avestic visaiti,
Gk. είκοσι, Dor. *Лхать, Arm. k'san, Toch.
A wiki, В ikam, Oix.fiche, OW. uceint, 'twenty'.
These words derive fF. I.-E. *wi-komt-, *wf-
kmt-y and lit. mean 'two tens'. For the first
element in *wi-komt-, *wi-kmt- see with and cp.
words there referred to, for the second see pen-
tecontu- and cp. ten and hundred. Cp. vicennial,
vigesimal, viginti-, vintem, eicosi', pachisi. For
the ending in vicenary see adj. suff. -ary.

## vicennial
vicennial, adj., recurring every twenty years. —
Formed with adj. suff. -al fr. L. vicennium, 'a
period of twenty years', which is compounded
of viceni, 'twenty each', and annus, 'year'. For
the first element see prec. word, for the second
see annual. For the change of Latin a (in annus),
to e in vi-cennium see biennial. Cp. vigesimal,
viginti-, vintem, eicosi-, pachisi.

## vicereine
vicereine, п., the wife of a viceroy. — F. vice-reine,
compounded of vice- and reine, 'queen', fr. L.
regina. See regina and cp. next word.

## viceroy
viceroy, п., a person ruling a country as the
representative of a sovereign. — MF. (= F.) vice-
roi, compounded of vice- and roi, 'king', which
derives fr. L. regem, ace. of rex, 'king'. See rex
and cp. prec. word.
Derivatives: viceroy-al, adj., viceroy-ai-ty, n.

## vice versa
vice versa, conversely. — L. vice versa ablative
absolute construction, lit. 'the place being
changed', fr. vice, abl. of vicis, 'change,
alternation, order', and sing. fern. abl. of versus, pp. of
vertere, 'to turn'. See vice, adv., and version.

## Vichy water
Vichy water, colloq. also vichy. — Water from the
springs of Vicky, France.

## Vicia
Vicia, п., a genus of plants, the vetch (bot.) — L.
vicia, 'vetch'. See vetch.

## vicilin
vicilin, п., a substance found in the broad bean,
pea, etc. (biockem.) — Formed from prec. word
with suff. -in.

## vicinage
vicinage, n. — ME. vesinage, fr. OF. visenage, vi-
cenage, voisenage (F. voisinage), fr. VL. *veci-
nus, dissimilated form of L. vicinus, 'near,
neighboring', fr. vicus, 'district, village, hamlet',
which stands for *woikos, and is cogn. with OI.
vesdft, 'house', vit, 'dwelling, house, settlement',
vispatifr, 'master of the house', Avestic vis,
'house, village, clan', vispaiti-, 'chief of the
clan', Gk. οίκος, dial. Gk. f οίκος, Gk. οίκία,
Cretan and Locrian Gk. f οικία, 'house',
OSlav. vtsi, 'village', Alb. vise, 'places', amvise,
'housewife', Goth, weiks, 'village', Lith. vieSpats,
'master of the house', OPruss. waispattin,
'mistress of the house'. Cp. diocese, economy,
ecumenic, parish, vaisya, 2nd venue, vicinity, villa,
village, wick, 'village'. For the ending see suff.
-age.

## vicinal
vicinal, adj., neighboring. — L. vicinalis,
'neighboring', fr. vtcinus, 'neighbor', fr. the adj. vici-
nus, 'neighboring*. See prec. word and adj. suff.
-al.

## vicinity
vicinity, n. — L. vicinitas, 'neighborhood*, fr. vi-
cinus, 'neighboring'. See vicinage and -ity.

## vicious
vicious, adj. — ME., fr. MF. vicieus (F. vicieux),

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:837 COLUMN:3 -->
fr. OF., fr. L. vitiosus, 'full of faults, faulty', fr.
vitium. See vice, 'moral fault', and -ous.
Derivatives: vicious-ly, adv., vicious-ness, n.

## vicissitade
vicissitade, п., change. — F., fr. L. vicissitudo,
'change, interchange, alternation', fr. vtcissimt
'alternately', fr. vicis, 'change, alternation'. See
vicarious and -tude.

## viclssitudinary
viclssitudinary, adj. — Formed with adj. suff. -ary
fr. L. vicissitudo, gen. -tudinis. See prec. word.

## vicissitudinous
vicissitudinous, adj. — See prec. word and -ons.

## victim
victim, n. — L. victima, 'beast of sacrifice, victim*
(whence also It. vittima, Sp. victima, Port, viti-
ma), prop, 'a consecrated animal', cogn. with
Goth, weihs, 'holy', OS., OHG. wik, MHG.
wick, early G. weick, 'holy', OS. wik, ON. ve,
'temple', OE. wik, wig, 'idol*, Goth, wikan,
OHG., MHG. wiken, G. weihen, OS. wihian,
ON. vigja, 'to consecrate', MHG. wike(n)nacht-
(en), G. Weihnachten, 'Christmas', OI. vinakti,
vivekti, 'separates, sifts'. Cp. witch, 'sorceress'.
Derivatives: victim-ize, tr. v., victim-iz-able, adj.,
victim-iz-ation, п., victim-iz-er, n.

## victor
victor, n. — ME., fr. L., fr. victus, pp. of vincere,
*to vanquish'. See vincible and agential suff. -or.

## Victoria
Victoria, fem. PN. — Lit. 'victory', fr. L. victoria.
See victory.
Derivative: Victori-an, adj.

## Victoria cross
Victoria cross, decoration founded by queen
Victoria in 1856.

## victorine1
victorine1, п., fur tippet worn by women: — Prob.
from the French PN. Victorine.

## victorious
victorious, adj. — L. victoriosus, fr. victoria,
'victory'. See victory and -ous.
Derivatives: victorious-ly, adv., victorious-ness,
a.

## victress
victress, n. — Formed fr. victor with 1st suff. -ess.

## victory
victory, n. — ME., fr. OF. victorie (F. victoire),
fr. L. victoria, 'victory', fr. victor. See victor and
-y (representing L. -ia).

## Victroln
Victroln, п., trade name of a phonograph. —:
Formed fr. Victor Talking Machine Co.

## victual
victual, п., usually in the pi., food. — ME. vitaile,
vitaille, fr. MF. vitaille (F. victuailles), fr. OF.
fr. L. vlctudlia, 'provisions' (whence also It. vet-
tovaglia. Proven?. vit{o)alha, Sp. vitualla. Port.
vitualha), neut. pi. of victudlis, 'pertaining to
nourishment', used as a noun, fr. vtctus,
'nourishment', fr. vict-{um), pp. stem of vivere, 'to
live'; see vital and subst. suff. -al, F. victuailles
andE. victual were refashioned after L. victudlia.
Derivatives: victual, tr. v., to supply with
victuals, victual-age, п., victual-, er п.,
victualling, n.

## vicuna
vicuna, п., 1) a ruminant animal of Peru; 2) fabric
made from its wool. — Sp., fr. Quechua vicunna.
Cp. F. vigogne, fr. earlier vicugne, fr. Sp. vicuna.

## vidame
vidame, п., a French feudal title. — F., fr. ML.
vice-dominus, lit. 'deputy of the lord'. See vice-
and dominate and cp. viscount.

## viddni
viddni, п., either of the two confessions of sin,
forming part of the liturgy of the Day of
Atonement. — Heb. widduy, 'confession', back
formation fr. hithwaddah, 'he confessed', reflexive
conjugation of the base y-d-h, 'to praise, thank,
confess', whence also Heb. kodka , 'he thanked',
todhab, 'thanksgiving, sacrifice of thanksgiving',
Mishnaic Heb. kodka*a , 'thanksgiving', rel. to
Aram, ddhi, 'he praised, thanked, confessed',
Arab, istaudd, 'he confessed'. Cp. Judah.

## vide
vide, v., see. — L. vide, imper. of videre, pp. vxsus,
'to see'. See vision and cp. vide.

## videlicet
videlicet, adv., namely to wit. — L. videlicet,
contraction of videre licet, 'it is clear or evident, it is
easy to see', lit. 'it is permitted to see*. See vision
and license and cp. scilicet.

## Vidian
Vidian, adj., pertaining to, or named after, the
Italian anatomist Guido Guidi (1500-1569). —
Fr. Vidus, Latinized form of the Italian name
Guidi. For the ending see suff. -an.

## vidimus
vidimus, п., inspection of documents. — L.
vidimus, 'we have seen', fr. videre, 'to see'. See vision
and cp. vide.

## vidual
vidual, adj., pertaining to a widow or widows. —
Late L. vidudlis, fr. L. vidua, 'widow', fem. of
viduus, 'widower'. Hal. vedovo, Rum. vdduv, F.
veuf, Cat. and Sp. viudo, Port, viiivo, 'widower',
and It. vedova, Rum. vaduva, OF. vedve (F.
veuve), OProveng. vezoa, Sp. viuda. Port, viiiva,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:838 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 811 | VINDICABLE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:838 COLUMN:1 -->
'widow', derive fr. L. viduus, resp. vidua. See
widow and adj. suff. -al.

## vidnate
vidnate, п., widowhood. — Late L. viduatus, fr.
L. viduatus, 'widowed', pp. of vidudre, 'to
deprive of anything, to bereave of a husband or a
wife', fr. viduus, resp. vidua. See prec. word and
subst. suff. -ate.

## vidya
vidya, п., knowledge. — OI. vidya, 'knowledge',
rel. to veda, Ί know', vedafi, 'knowledge; sacred
book', and cogn. with Gk. oiSa, Ί know',
εϊδον, Ί saw', L. videre, pp. visus, *to see'. See
vision and cp. avidya, Veda.

## vie
vie, intr. v. — ME. vien, shortened fr. envien, fr.
OF. envier, 'to challenge, invite*, a word used in
card-playing, fr. L. inviiare, 'to invite, entertain,
challenge'; see invite and cp. envy. For sense
development cp. Sp. envidar, It. inviiare, 'to
invite', both used also in the sense 'to invite to
open the game'; cp. also the French phrase a
Venvi, 'emulously vying with each other1, in
which envi is a noun derived fr. OF. envier.
Derivative: vi-er, n.

## Viennese
Viennese, adj. and n. — Formed fr. Vienna, name
of the capital of Austria, with suff. -ese,

## view
view, n. — ME. vewe, fr. MF. veue (F. vue), fr.
OF., prop. fem. pp. of veoir (F. voir), 4o see',
used as a noun, fr, L. videre. See vision and cp.
esp. interview, purview, review.
Derivatives: view, tr. v., view-able, adj., \iew-er,
п., view-less, adj., view-y, adj.

## vigesimal
vigesimal, adj., twentieth. — Formed with adj.
suff. -al fr. L. vfgesimus, a var. form oi*vfcesimus,
'twentieth', fr. vicenr, 'twenty each'. See
vicennial.

## vigla
vigla, п., a mark on a hydrographic chart
indicating the nearness of a place dangerous to»nav-
igation. — Sp. vigia, 'a watch, look out', fr.
Port, vigia t of s.m., back formation fr. vigiart 'to
watch', fr. L. vigilare, fr. vigil. See next word.

## vigil
vigil, n. — ME. vigile, fr. OF. (= F.) vigile, fr.
earlier vigilie, fr. L. vigilia, 'wakefulness', fr.
vigil, 'awake, wakeful', assimilated fr. *vegilis,h.
vegere, 'to be lively, active'. (The verb vigere, a
collateral form of vegere, owes its i to the
influence of L. vigil.) F. veille, 'watch', is a doublet
of vigile. See wake, v., and cp. vegetable. Cp.
also vigor, reveille, surveillance, vedette,
invigilate.

## vigilance
vigilance, п., alertness; watchfulness. — MF. ( =
F.), fr. L. vigilantia, 'wakefulness', fr. vigilans,
gen. -antis. See next word and -ce.

## vigilant
vigilant, adj., alert; watchful. — ME., either fr.
MF. (= F.) vigilant, or directly fr. L. vigilans,
gen. -antis, pres. part, of vigilare, 'to watch, be
wakeful', fr. vigil, 'wakeful*. See vigil and -ant,-
Derivatives: vigilant-ly, adv., vigilant-ness, n.

## viginti-
viginti-, combining form meaning 'twenty'. — L.
viginti-, fr. viginti, 'twenty*. See vicenary.

## Vigna
Vigna, п., a genus ofplantsof the pea family (bot.)
— ModL., named after the Italian botanist
Dominico Vigna (died in 1647).

## vignette
vignette, п., a small ornamental design. — F.,
dimin. of vigne, 'vine', orig. an ornament
representing a little vine, with leaves, tendrils and
grapes. See vine and -ette. The word vignette was
introduced into English by the English man of
letters Horace Walpole (1717-97).
Derivatives: vignette, tr. v., vignett-er, п.,
vignettist (q.v.)

## vignettist
vignettist, п., a maker of vignettes. — A hybrid
coined fr. vignette and -ist, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## vigor
vigor, vigour, п., active strength; energy; vitality.
— ME., fr. OF. vigor (F. vigueur), fr. L. vigdrem,
ace. of vigor, 'liveliness, activity', rel. to vigere,
'to be lively, active'. See vigil and cp. invigorate,
ravigote.

## vigoroso
vigoroso, adv., with vigor (musical direction). —
It., fr. ML. vigorosus. See next word.

## vigorous
vigorous, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (F. vigoureux), fr.
OF., fr. ML. vigorosus, fr. L. vigor. See vigor and
-ons.
Derivatives: vigorous-ly, adv., vigorous-ness, n.

## vihara
vihara, п., ]) in ancient India, Buddha's pleasure
ground; a Buddhistic or Jain monastery or
temple; 2) in Ceylon, a Buddhistic temple. — OI.
viAaroA, lit.'enjoyment, pleasure, place of
recreation', compounded of pref. νϊ·, 'asunder, away

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:838 COLUMN:2 -->
from; very, through', and the verb harati,
'brings, carries, takes away, robs'. OI. vi- derives
fr. I.-E. base *wi-, 'asunder'; see with and cp.
vice, 'a moral fault', and the first element jn vi-
mana. OI. harati is a derivative of I.-E. base
*gner-, *to seize, take', whence also Gk. χείρ,
'hand'; see chiro- and cp. the second element in
Dashahara.

## vihuela
vihuela, п., guitar. — Sp., rel. to viola, of s.m. See
viol.

## viking
viking, п., one of the Scandinavian pirates who
ravaged the coasts of Western Europe in the 8th,
9th and 10th centuries. — ON. vifcingr, fr. vik,
'bay', lit. 'one who frequents bay*'; so called in
allusion to the preference given by pirates to
nook-shotten coasts. ON. vik is rel. to OE. wic,
MLG. wtk, MHG. wick, 'bay', ON. -vik in af-
vi7c,*roundabout way,aremoteplace', vikja, vikva,
ykva, OE. wican, OS. wikan, 'to give way, yield',
ON. veikr, 'weak', OE. wac, 'weak'. See weak
and cp. wicket. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ing.

## vilayet
vilayet, п., one of the chief provinces of Turkey.
— Turk, vilayet, fr. Arab, wilaya , 'province', fr.
wali, 'governor*, partic. of waliya, 'he reigned,
governed'. Cp. blatti, Blighty, mullah, vali, wali.

## vile
vile, adj., mean, worthless. — ME. vil, vile, fr.
OF. (= F.) ι·ι7, 'vile, base, mean', fr. L. vllis,
'cheap, worthless, of little value* which is of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: vile-ly, adv., vile-ness, n.

## vilification
vilification, n. — ML. vilificatio, gen. -onis, fr.
Late L. vilificatus, pp. oTvilificare. See next word
and -ion.

## vilify
vilify, tr. v., to revile; to defame. — Late L. vili-
ficdre, 'to esteem of little value', lit. *to make of
little value', fr. L. vtlis 'of little value', and -fi-
care, fr. h.facere, 'to make, do'. See vile and -fy.
Derivative: vitifi-er, n.

## vilipend
vilipend, tr. v., to disparage, belittle. — ME. viti-
penden, fr. MF. (= F.) vilipender, fr. L. vilipen-
dere, 'to hold in light esteem*, a word occurring
only in a passage of Plautus, where it seems to
be due to the mistake of a copyist and to stand
for nili( = nihili)pendere, 'to slight, disregard',
fr. nil, contraction of nihil, 'nothing', and
pendere, 'to weigh, value, esteem'. See nihil and
pendant.

## villa
villa, n. — It., fr. L. villa, 'country house, villa,
farm", which stands for *vic-sla, and is rel. to
vicus, 'village, hamlet', whence vicinus, 'near,
neighboring'. See vicinage and cp. villnge, villain,
vlllancico, villanella, villanelle.

## villadom
villadom, п., the world of villas. — A hybrid
coined fr. villa and surf. -dom.

## village
village, n. — ME., fr. OF. (- F.), fr. L. villa-
ticus, 'pertaining to a villa or country house',
used as a noun, fr. villa, 'country house, villa*,
in Late L. 'village'. See villa and -nge and cp.
villatic.
Derivatives: village-ous, adj., villag-er, п.,
villager у, п., villag-y, village-y, adj.

## villain
villain, n. — ME. vilain, vilein, fr. MF. (— F.)
vilaint fr. OF., fr. Late L. villdnus, 'inhabitant of
a farm', fr. L. villa; see vilia and 1st -ane. The
most important phases of the sense
development of this word may be summed up as
follows: 'inhabitant of a farm; peasant; churl,_
boor; clown; miser; knave, scoundrel'. Today
both F. vilain and E. villain are used only in a
pejorative sense.

## villainous
villainous, adj. — MF. vileneus, fr. vilain, vilein.
See prec. word and -ous.
Derivatives: villainous-ly, adv., villainous-ness,
n.

## villniny
villniny, n. — ME., fr. OF. vilanie, vileinie(F. vi-
lenie), fr. vilain. See villain and -y (representing
OE. ie).

## villancico
villancico, п., a Spanish song; a cantata. — Sp.,
lit. 'a rustic (song)', fr. villano, 'rustic', fr. Late
L. villdnus. See villain.

## villanella
villanella, п., an old Italian rustic dance. — It.,
fem. dimin. of villano, 'rustic'. See prec. word.

## villnnelle
villnnelle, п., a kind of French poem. — F., fr.
prec. word.

## villatic
villatic, adj., pertaining to a villa or village. — L.
villdticus, fr. villa. See village and -atic,

## villeggiatura
villeggiatura, п., stay in the country. — It., lit.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:838 COLUMN:3 -->
'stay at a villa', fr. villeggiare, 'to go into the
country', fr. villa. See villa and -ture.

## villein
villein, п., a serf, a peasant. — A spelling var. of
villain.
Derivative: villein-age, n.

## villi form
villi form, adj., resembling villi. — Compounded
of villus, and L. forma, 'form, shape'. See form,
n.

## villosity
villosity, n. — Formed fr. L. viflosus (see next
word) with suff. -ity.

## villous
villous, adj., covered with villi; shaggy. — L. v/7-
losus, 'hairy, shaggy', fr. villus. See next word
and -ous.
Derivative: villous-ly, adv.

## villus
villus, п., a hairlike vascular process (anat.) —
L., 'shaggy hair, tuft of hair', a collateral form
of vellus, 'fleece*. See vellicate.

## vim
vim, п., vigor, energy. — L., ace. of vis, 'force'.
See vis.

## vimana
vimana, п., tower of a temple (Indian archit.) —
OI. vimanah, 'celestial chariot of the gods; car;
imperial palace; tower', lit. 'something
measured out', fr. pref. v/-, 'asunder, away from;
very, through' and matt, 'measures', OI. vi-
derives fr. I.-E. base *wi-, 'asunder'; see with and
cp. vice, 'a moral fault', and the first element in
vihara. OI. mati, 'measures', derives fr. I.-E. base
*me-, 'to measure'. See meditate and cp. matra
and the second element in firman.

## vimen
vimen, п., a slender shoot of branch. — L. vimen,
'twig, switch, osier, willow', from the stem of
viere, 'to bend, twist'. See viti- and cp. viminal,
vimineous.

## viminal
viminal, adj., pertaining to a shoot or osier. — L.
viminalis, fr. vimen, gen. viminis. See prec. word
and adj. suff. -al. Cp. Viminalis (collis), name of
one of the seven hills of Rome, lit. 'the hill of
willows', so called from the willow copse that
stood there.

## vimjneons
vimjneons, adj., viminal. — L. vimineus,
'pertaining to, or made of osiers', fr. vimen, gen. viminis.
See vimen. For E. -ous, as equivalent to L. -us,
see -ous.

## vina
vina, п., a musical instrument in ancient India. —
OI. vinah.

## vinaceous
vinaceous, adj., pertaining to the vine. — L. vina-
ceus, fr. vinum, 'wine'. See vine and -aceous.

## vinaigrette
vinaigrette, п., a bottle for holding aromatic
vinegar, etc. — F., dimin. of vinaigre, 'vinegar'.
See vinegar and -ette.

## Vinca
Vinca, п., a genus of plants, the periwinkle (bot.)
— ModL., shortened fr. L. vincapervinca,
'periwinkle', lit. 'the plant that winds', fr. vincire, 'to
bind', and pervincire, 'to bind, twine', fr. per-
and vincire. See periwinkle, the plant.

## Vincent
Vincent, п., masc. PN. — F., shortened fr. L. Vin-
centius, derivative of vincens, gen. vincentis,
'conquering', pres. part, of vincere, 'to conquer*. See
vincible and -ent and cp. Victor.

## Vincetoxicum
Vincetoxicum, п., a genus of plants, the angle-pod
(bot.) — ModL., lit. 'that which conquers
poison', fr. L. vincere, 'to conquer*, and toxicum,
'poison' (see vincible and toxic); so called in
allusion to its alleged medicinal properties.

## vincible
vincible, adj., conquerable. — L. vincibilis, 'that
which can be easily gained', fr. vincere, 'to
conquer', from a nasalized form of I.-E. base *wic-
(cp. the perf. tense vici, Ί have conquered'),
whence Goth, weihan, OHG., OE. wigan, 'to
fight', ON. vlg, OE. wig, 'fight', Goth, waihjo,
'struggle, combat', ON. veigr, 'force', Lith. ap-
veikiu, ap-veikti, 'to subdue', vieka, 'strength,
force', vikru-s, 'lively, agile', OSlav. veku,
'strength, power; age', Olr. fichim, Ί fight',
Mir. flch, 'struggle'. For the ending see suff.
-ible. Cp. convince, convict, evince, evict,
invincible, vanqnish, victor, victory, Vincent, wight,
'brave'.
Derivatives: vincibil-ity, п., vincible-ness, п.,
vincibl-y, adv.

## vinculum
vinculum, п., bond, tie. — L., 'that with which
anything is bound, fetter', fr. vincire, 'to bind',
which is prob. rel. to vicia, 'vetch'. See vetch and
-culum and cp. the second element in
cervical.

## vindicable
vindicable, adj. — Late L. vindicabilis, fr. L. vin·
dicare. See next word and -able.
Derivatives: vindicabil-ity, η., vindicable-ness.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:839 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VINDICATE | 812 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:839 COLUMN:1 -->
П., vindicabl-y, adv.

## vindicate
vindicate, tr. v. — L. vindicates, pp. of vindicare,
*to demand, lay, claim to, assume, avenge*, from
vindicta, 'vindication, protection, defence*, back
formation fr. vim dictam, ace. of vis dicta, lit.
'announced force', i.e. 'announcement of force4.
L. vindex, 'defender, vindicator', is back
formation fr. vindicare. See vis, diction, and verbal
suff. -ate and cp. avenge, revenge, vendetta,
vengeance, vengeful, vindictive.

## vindication
vindication, n. — L. vindication gen. -dnis, *a
laying of claim', fr. vindicates, pp. of vindicare. See
prec. word and -ion.

## vindicative
vindicative, adj. — ML. vindicativus, fr. L.
vindicates, pp. of L. vindicare. See vindicate and -ive.
Derivatives: vindicative-ly, adv., vindicative·-
ness, n.

## vindicator
vindicator, n. — Late L. vindicator, fr. L.
vindicates, pp. of vindicare. See vindicate and agential
suff., -or.

## vindicatory
vindicatory, adj. — See vindicate and adj. suff.
-ory.
Derivative: vindicator i-ly, adv.

## vindictive
vindictive, adj. — Formed with suff. -ive fr. L.
vindicta, 'vindication'. See vindicate.
Derivatives: vindictive-ly, adv., vindictive-ness,
n.

## vine
vine, n. — ME., fr. OF. (F. vigne), fr. L. vinea,
'vineyard' (whence also It. vigna, Rum. vie,
Proven?, vinha, Catal. vinya, Sp. viHa, Port.
vinha, 'vine'), prop. fem. of vineus, 'pertaining
to wine', used as a noun, fr. vinum, "wine'
(whence It., Sp. vino, Rum. vin, Provenc., Catal.
vi, F. vin, Port, vinho, Goth, wein, О HG.
(MHG.), OFris., OS., OE. win (G. Wein),
OSlav. vino (Russ. vino), Olr. fin, W., Bret.
gwin, 'wine' and prob. also Etruscan vinu, of
s.m. Cp. οϊνη (for *5οίνη) 'the vine', οίνος
(dial. Γοΐνος), 'wine', Alb. vine, Arm. gini,
Georgian γ vino, 'wine*. Cp. also Heb. yayin
(prob. for *wayin), Ugar. yn, *wine', Ethiop.
wayn, 'grape, wine', Akkad. inu, 'wine'. (Cp.
also Basque ayen, aiken, 'vine', which was prob.
borrowed from the Semites through
Carthaginian mediation.) The ult. origin of these words is
unknown. Some scholars trace them to the
Semites, others seek their origin in the Aegean,
still others in Asia Minor, Caucasia or in
Armenia. Cp. wine. Cp. also Vendemiaire, vignette,
vinegar,'vineyard, vinous, vintage, vintner. Cp.
also oeno-, Oenanthe, Oenius, oenomel, Oenone.
Derivative: vin-y, adj.

## vinegar
vinegar, n. — ME. vinegre, fr. OF. (= F.) vi-
naigre, compounded of vin aigre, 'sour wine'.
See vine and eager and cp. vinegaroon and agrito.
Derivative: vinegar-y, adj.

## vinegaroon
vinegaroon, п., a whip scorpion of Mexico (Mas-
tigoproctes giganteus). — Fr. Sp. vinagre,
'vinegar* (see prec. word); so called from the odor
it emits when frightened.

## vinery
vinery, n. — Formed fr. vine with surT. -ry.

## vineyard
vineyard, n. — Compounded of vine and yard,
'enclosure'. Cp. OE. wlngeard, ME. winyard,
OS. wingardo, ON. vinfcardr, Du. wijngaard,
OHG. wingart(o), MHG. wingarte, G. Weingar-
ten, Goth, weinagards.

## vini-
vini-, combining form meaning 'wine'. L. vini- fr.
vinum, 'wine'. See vine.

## vinic
vinic, adj., pertaining to wine. — Formed with
adj. surT. -ic fr. L. vinum, 'wine'. See vine.

## vialcufture
vialcufture, п., the cultivation of the vine. —
Compounded of vini- and culture.
Derivatives: vinicultur-al, adj., vinicultur-ist, n.

## villiferous
villiferous, adj., producing wine. — Compounded
of vini- and -ferous.

## viniflcation
viniflcation, п., wine making. — Compounded of
vini- and -fication.

## vino-
vino-, combining form meaning 'wine'. — L.
vino-, fr. vinum, 'wine*. See vine.

## vinology
vinology, п., the study of vines. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. vinum, 'wine', and Gk. -λογία, fr.
-λόγος, 'one who speaks (in a certain manner);
one who deals (with a certain topic)'. See vine
and -logy. The correct form is oenology, fr. Gk.
οϊνη, 'vine', and -λογία.

## vlnometer
vlnometer, п., an instrument for measuring the
strength of wine. — A hybrid coined fr. L. vf-
mim, 'wine', and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'; see

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:839 COLUMN:2 -->
vine and meter, 'poetical rhythm'. The correct
form is oenometer (q.v.)

## vinosity
vinosity, п., the character of a wine. — Late L.
vinositas, 'the flavor of wine', fr. L. vinosus. See
next word and -ity.

## vinous
vinous, adj., 1) pertaining to wine; 2) addicted to
wine. — L. vinosus, 'full of wine; drunk with
wine', fr. vinum. See vine and -ous.
Derivatives: vinous-ly, adv., vinous-ness, n.

## vintage
vintage, n. — ME. vendage, vindage, fr. MF. ven-
denge (F. vendange), fr. OF., fr. L. vindemia
(whence also It. vendemmia, Sp. vendimia,
Provenc. vendemia. Port, vindima), which stands
for *vino-demia and is compounded of vinum,
'wine', and the stem oidemere, 4o take off'. For
the first element see vine. L. demere is formed fr.
de, 'from, away from', and emere, 'to take'. See
de- and exempt. E. vintage was influenced in
form by vinter, vintry.
Derivatives: vintage, tr. v., vintag-er, п., vintag-
ing, n.

## vintem
vintem, п., a small Portuguese silver coin of 20
reis. — Port, vintem, fr. vinte, 'twenty', fr. L. W-
ginti. See vicenary.

## vintner
vintner, п., a wine merchant. — ME. vintener, fr.
earlier vineter, fr. OF. vinetier, fr. ML. vinetarius
(corresponding in sense to L.. vinarius), 'wine
dealer, vintner' (whence also It. vinattiere,
