Provenc. vinatier, Sp. vinatero), fr. L. vinetum,
'vineyard', fr. vinum, 'wine'. See vine and
agential suff. -er.

## vintry
vintry, п., a place where wine is sold or stored. —
ME. viniterie, fr. viniter, Vintner'. See prec.
word and subst. suff. -y.

## vinum
vinum, n. {pharm.) — L. vinum, 'wine'. See vine.

## vinyl
vinyl, п., the univalent radical CH2CH (ckem.) —
Coined fr. L. vinum, 'wine' (see prec. word), and
suff. -yl.

## viol
viol, п., a musical instrument. — MF. (= F.)
viole, fr. OF., fr. OProvenc. viola, viula, which,
together with It. viola, of s.m., was prob.
borrowed (possibly through the medium of OHG.
fidula), fr. ML. vitula, name of a stringed
instrument, which is possibly a back formation fr. L.
vitulari, 'to exult, be joyful'. See fiddle and cp.
next word, violin, violoncello.
Derivative: viol, intr. v.

## viola
viola, п., the tenor violin, larger than the violin
and smaller than the violoncello. — It. See prec.
word.

## Viola
Viola, п., fem. PN. — Fr. L. viola, *the violet'. See
violet.

## Viola
Viola, п., a genus of plants of the family Viola-
ceae {pot.) — L. viola, 'the violet'. See prec.
word.

## violable
violable, adj. — L. violdbilis. See violate and
-able.
Derivatives: violabil-ity, п., violable-ness, п.,
violabl-y, adv.

## Vioiaceae
Vioiaceae, n. pi., the violet family {pot.) —
ModL., formed from Viola with suff. -aceae.

## violaceous
violaceous, adj. — See prec. word and -aceous.

## vioia da gamba
vioia da gamba, the bass viol (mus.) — It., lit. 'a
viola for the leg' (i.e. a viola held between the
knees). For It. viola see viol. It. da, 'from', is a
contraction of L. de, 'from, away from', and a,
'away from, from'; see de- and a-, *away from'.
For It. gamba see gamba.

## violate
violate, tr. v. — ME. violaten, fr. L. violates, pp.
of violare, 'to treat with violence, violate, injure,
dishonor', which is prob. rel. to vis, 'strength,
force*. See vis and verbal suff. -ate and cp.
violent.
Derivatives: violation (q.v.), violat-ive, adj.,
violator (q.v.)

## violation
violation, n. — ME. violacion, fr. L. violdtio, gen.
-onis, fr. violates, pp. of violare. See prec. word
and -ion.
Derivative: violation-al, adj.

## violator
violator, n. — L. violator, fr. violates, pp. of
violare. See violate and agential suff. -or.

## violence
violence, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.), fr. L. violen-
tia, fr. violentus. See next word and suff. -ce.

## violent
violent, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
violentus, 'forcible, vehement, violent', which is rel. to
violare, 'to treat with violence'. See violate.
Derivatives: violent-iy, adv., violent-ness, n.

## vlolescent
vlolescent, adj., tending to a violet color. —

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:839 COLUMN:3 -->
Formed fr. viola with suff. -escent.

## violet
violet, n. — ME., fr. MF. violete (F. violette), fr.
OF., dimin. of viole, fr. L. viola, which is prob.
a Mediterranean loan word; cp. Viola. Cp. also
iolite. For the ending see suff. -et.
Derivatives: violet, adj., violet-y, adj.

## violin
violin, n. — It. violino} dimin. formed fr. viola.
See viol and cp. violoncello.

## violinist
violinist, n. — A hybrid coined fr. violin and -ist,
a suff. of Greek origin.

## violoncellist
violoncellist, n. — A hybrid coined fr. violoncello
and -ist, a suff. of Greek origin.

## violoncello
violoncello, п., a bass violin. — It., dimin. of vio-
lone. See next word and cp. cello.

## violone
violone, п., -a large viola (mus.) — It., formed fr.
viola with augment, suff. -one. See -oon.

## viomycin
viomycin, п., an antibiotic used against
tuberculosis. — A hybrid coined fr. violet and Gk.
μϋκης, 'fungus4 (see myco-), and suff. -in; so
called in allusion to the color of the soil mold.

## Viorna
Viorna, п., a genus of plants of the crowfoot
family (bot.) — ModL., fr. F. viorne, 'the wayfaring
tree', fr. L. viburnum. See Viburnum.

## viper
viper, n. — MF. vipere (F. vipere), fr. L. vipera,
contraction of *vivi-pera, 'that which brings
forth living young*, fr. vivere, 'to live', and the
stem of -perere, fr. parere, 'to bring forth'. See
vital and parent and cp. viviparous, weever,
wivern.
Derivatives: viperine (q.v.), viper-ish, adj.,
viperous (q.v.), viper-y, adj.

## viperiform
viperiform, adj., resembling a viper. —
Compounded of L. vipera and forma, 'form, shape'.
See prec. word and form, n.

## viperine
viperine, adj., pertaining to a viper or vipers;
venomous. — L. viperinus, 'pertaining to, or
resembling, a viper*, fr. vipera. See viper and -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## viperous
viperous, adj., pertaining to vipers; venomous.—
Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. vipera. See viper.
Derivatives: viperous-ly, adv., viperous-ness, n.

## virago
virago, п., 1) a strong, manlike woman (archaic);
2) a quarrelsome woman. — L. virago, 'a
manlike heroic maiden; a female warrior', fr. vir,
'man'. See virile.

## vlrelay
vlrelay, п., an old French verse form with a
refrain and with only two rhymes throughout the
verse. — ME. vyrelaye, fr. OF. virelai, altered
(prob. under the influence of lai, 'a kind of song,
lay*), fr. OF. vireli, 'a refrain', prob. orig. the
refrain of a song or poem, and of imitative
origin.

## virescence
virescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## virescent
virescent, adj., becoming green; greenish. — L.
virescens, gen. -entis, pres. part, of virescere, 'to
grow green', inchoative of virere, 'to be green*.
See viridity and -escent and cp. viridescent.

## virgate
virgate, adj., rod-shaped (bot.) — L. virgatus,
'made of twigs', fr. virga, 'twig, switch, rod*,
which is of uncertain origin. It stands peril, for
^wiz-ga (see rhotacism), fr. I.-E. base *weis-, 'to
turn, twist*, whence also OE. weoxian, 'to wipe'.
See whisk and adj. suff. -ate and cp. verge, 'rod',
virgin, virgnle.

## virgate
virgate, п., an old English land measure. — ML.
virgate, virgate terrae, fr. L. virga, 'twig, switch,
rod*. See virgate, adj. For sense development cp.
Heb. qdneh, 'reed', used also in the sense of
'measuring rod; measure* (see e.g. Ezek. 40: 3
and 5) and E. rod in the sense of 'measure of
length*; cp. also canon, 'rule'.

## Virgilia
Virgilia, n,, a genus of plants of the pea family
(bot.) — ModL., named after the Roman poet
Publius Vergilius (less correctly: Virgilius) Maro
(70-19 B.C.E.) Cp. Virginia, fem. PN. For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## virgin
virgin, n. — ME. virgine, fr. OF. virgine, virge (F.
vierge), fr. L. virginem (whence also It. vergine,
Provenc. vergene, verge, Catal. verge, Sp. virgen,
Port, virgem), ace. of virgo, 'virgin', which is
prob. rel. to virga, 'a young shoot, twig'; see
virgate, adj., and cp. virgo. For sense
development cp. Gk. ταλις, 'a marriageable girl', which
is cogn. with L. talea, 'rod, stick, bar'.
Derivatives: virgin, adj., virginal (q.v.)

## virginal
virginal, adj., pertaining to a virgin; maidenly. —
ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. Li vaginalis, 'pertaining

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:840 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 813 | VISION -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:840 COLUMN:1 -->
to a virgin, maidenly, virginal', fr. virgo, gen.
virginis. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al.
Derivative: virginal-ly, adv.

## virginal
virginal, п., a kind of spinet. — Orig. 'an
instrument played by girls', fr. virginal, adj.
Derivative: virginal-ist, n.

## Virginia
Virginia, fern. PN. — L. Virginia, fem. of Virgi-
nius, fr. earlier Verginius, a name prob. rel. to
Vergilius. Cp. Virgilia.

## Virginia
Virginia, п., one of the states of the United States.
— Named after the Virgin Queen Elizabeth. Cp.
Ytrgimum.
Derivatives: Virgini-an, adj. and n.

## virginity
virginity, n. — ME. virginite, fr. OF. virginite (F.
virginite)t fr. L. virginitatem, ace. of virginitas,
fr. virgo, gen. virginis. See virgin and -ity.

## virginium
virginium, п., an element of the alkali-metal fanv
ily {chem.) — ModL., coined fr. Virginia
(U.S.A.), name of the native state of the
physicist Fred Allison (1882- ), discoverer of this
element. See Virginia, 'name of state , and chem.
suff. -ium.

## Virgo
Virgo, п., the Virgin {astron.) — L. virgo. See
virgin.

## Virgnlaria
Virgnlaria, п., a genus of sea pens (zool.) —
ModL., formed fr. L. virgula, 'small rod4 (see
virgule), with surf, -arin; so called from the
rodlike rachys.
Derivatives: virgulari-an, adj. and n.

## virgulate
virgulate, adj., rod-shaped. — Formed with adj.
suff. -ate fr. L. virgula. See next word.

## virgule
virgule, п., a comma. — F., fr. L. virgula, 'a little
twig, a small rod; a critical mark', dimin. of
virga, 'rod'. See virgate, adj., and -ule.

## viri-
viri-, combining form meaning 'man, husband'.
— L. viri-, fr. vir. See virile.

## virial
virial, п., half the product of the stress due to the
attraction or repulsion between two particles
multiplied by the distance between them
(physics). — Coined by the German mathematical
physicist Rudolf Julius Emmanuel Clausius
(1822-88) from the stem of L. vires, pi. of vis,
'strength'. See vis, and -ial.

## viridescence
viridescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## viri descent
viri descent, adj., greenish. — L. viridescins, gen.
-entis, pres. part, of viridescere, 'to grow green*,
an inchoative verb formed fr. viridis. See next
word and -escent and cp. virescent.

## viridity
viridity, п., greenness. — ME. viridite, fr. MF.
(= F.) viridite, fr. L. viriditatem, ace. of v/ridr-
tas, fr. viridis, 'green', fr. virere, 'to be green, to
flourish', which is of uncertain origin. Cp.
verdant, verdantiqne, verderer, verdigris, verdure,
verditer, verjuice, vert, 'the color green', vires-
cent, farthingale.

## virile
virile, adj., manly; masculine. — F. viril, fr. L.
virilis, 'pertaining to a man, masculine, manly,
vigorous, spirited', which is rel. to Umbr. viro,
veiro, 'the men* (ace), and cogn. with OI. virah,
Avestic vira-, Toch. wir, Lith. vyras, Lett, vTrs,
OPruss. wurs, Goth, wair, OHG., OS. wer, ON.
verr, OE. wer, Olr. fer, W. gwr, 'man'. These
words prob. meant orig. 'the strong one', and
derive fr. I.-E. base *wi-ro-, enlargement of base
*wei-, 'to be strong', whence L. vis, 'strength,
force, vigor'. See vis and -ile and cp. duumvir,
triumvir, septemvir, decemvir, centum vir, cry,
curia, evirate, Fergus, Quirites, virtue, werewolf,
world.

## virilescence
virilescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## virilescent
virilescent, adj., tending to acquire characters of
the male. — Formed fr. L. virilis (see virile) with
suff. -escent.

## virility
virility, п., the age of manhood; masculinity. —
F. virilite, fr. L. virilitdtem, ace. of virilitds, 'the
age of manhood', fr. virilis. See virile and -ity.

## virology
virology, п., that branch of science which deals
with viruses. — A hybrid coined fr. L. virus (see
virus) and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, One who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic)'. See -logy. The correct
word is toxicology, in which both elements are
of Greek origin,

## virose
virose, adj., poisonous. — L. vlrosus, 'poisonous',
fr. virus. See virus and adj. suff. -ose.

## virosis
virosis, п., disease caused by a virus (med.) — A

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:840 COLUMN:2 -->
Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. virus, 'poison*
(see virus), and -osis, a suff. of Greek origin. The
correct form would be toxicosis (fr. Gk. το-
ξικόν, 'poison'.

## virous
virous, adj., virose. — L. vlrosus. See prec. word
and -ous.

## virtu
virtu, п., love of art. — It. virtu, 'virtue,
excellence', fr. L. viriutem, ace. of virtus. See
virtue.

## virtual
virtual, adj., being in effect but not in actual fact.
— ME., fr. ML. virtualis, fr. L. virtus. See virtue
and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: virtual-ly, adv., virtual-ity, n.

## virtne
virtne, n. — ME. vertu, virtu, fr. OF. (= F.) vertu,
fr. L. virtutem, ace. of virtus, 'virtue', lit.
'manliness, manhood', fr. vir. See virile.

## virtuosity
virtuosity, n. — Formed fr. virtuoso with suff.
-ity-

## virtuoso
virtuoso, п., a person skilled in one of the fine arts,
esp. in music. — It., fr. Late L. virtuosus. See
next word.

## virtuous
virtuous, adj. — ME. vertuous, virtuous, fr. MF.
vertueus, virtueus (F. vertueux), fr. OF., fr. Late
L. virtuosus, fr. L. virtus. See virtue and -ous.
Derivatives: virtuous-ly, adv., virtuous-ness, n.

## virulence
virulence, virulency, n. — Late L. virulentia, fr. L.
virulentus. See next word and -ce, resp. -cy.

## virulent
virulent, adj., poisonous, deadly; malignant. —
ME., fr. L. virulentus, 'poisonous', fr. virus. See
next word.
Derivatives: virulent-ly, adv., virulent-ness, n.

## virns
virns, п., 1) venom; esp. of a snake; 2) an
infective agent; 3) a harmful influence. — L. virus,
'poison', for *vlsos (see rkotacism), fr. I.-E. base
*weis-, 'to melt away, rot', whence also OI.
visam, 'poison', visah, 'poisonous', vesati, 'melts
away', Avestic vish-, visha-, 'poison', vaeshah-,
'mold', Gk. ιός (for *.ί4σός), 'poison', Olr.
ft, 'poison', W. gwy, 'fluid, water', gwyar,
'blood', possibly also L. viescere, 'to fade,
wither', Lith. vystu, Ί wither', ON. visna, OE.
wisnian, weosnian, 'to whither'. See wizen and cp.
Viscum. Cp. also bikh. Cp. also ooze, n.

## vis
vis, п., force. — L. vis, 'strength, force, vigor', fr.
I.-E. base *wei-t 'to be strong', whence also OI.
vayah, 'vital force', Gk. *(f)iq>i, 'strongly,
violently', Έφιος, 'strong*, prob. also L. violdre,
'to treat with violence'. Vis is prob. rel. to L. vir,
'man'. See virile and cp. vim, violate, virial, ultra
vires.

## vis
vis, viss, п., a weight used in S. India and in
Burma. — Tamil visai, 'division', from the base
of OI. vikitak, 'divided, distributed*.

## visn
visn, n. — L. visa, fem. pp. of videre, 'to see'. See
vision and cp. vise.

## visage
visage, п., face, countenance. — ME., fr. OF. (=
F.), fr. OF. vis, 'face', fr. L. visus, 'faculty of
seeing, sight, vision', fr. visus, pp. οι videre, 'to see'.
See vision and -age and cp. prec. word,
vis-avis, envisage.
Derivatives: visage, tr. v., visag-ed, adj.

## visard
visard, п., visor. — See visor.

## visarga
visarga, п., in Old Indian, ]) a final breath sound,
as h in damah', 2) the sign representing this sound
— OI. visargah, lit. 'discharge', fr. vf, 'asunder'
(see with), and sdrgah, 'action of letting go, or
pouring out', fr. szjati, 'he lets go, pours out',
which is rel. to Avestic kerezaiti, of s.m.

## vis-a-vis
vis-a-vis, adv. — F., 'face to face', fr. OF. vis,
'face*. See visage and a.

## viscacha
viscacha, п., a S. American burrowing rodent. —
Sp. vizcacha, fr. Quechua uiscacha.

## Viscaria
Viscaria, п., a genus of plants of the pink family
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. viscum, 'mistletoe,
birdlime' (see viscum and -aria); so called in allusion
to its viscous stem. For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## viscera
viscera, n. pi., the inner organs of the body. — L.
viscera, pi. of vlscus, of uncertain origin;
possibly a derivative of I.-E. base *wei·, 'to bend,
twist', whence also L. viere, 'to bend, twist*; see
Walde-Hofmann, LEW., II., p. 802 s.v. viscus.
See viti-,
viscera], adj. — ML. vlscerdlis, fr. L. viscera, pi.
of viscus. See prec. word and adj. suff. -al,

## viscerate
viscerate, tr. v., to eviscerate. — Formed with
verbal suff. -ate fr. L. viscera. See viscera and
cp. eviscerate.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:840 COLUMN:3 -->

## visceri-
visceri-, viscera-, combining form denoting the
viscera. — See viscera.
viscid, adj., sticky. — Late L. viscidus, fr. L.
viscum, 'mistletoe, birdlime'. See viscum and 1st
-id.
Derivatives: viscid-ity, п., viscid-ly, adv., viscid·
ness, n.

## vlscin
vlscin, п., a sticky substance occurring in the
berries of the mistletoe (chem.) — Formed with
suff. -in fr. L. viscum, 'mistletoe*. See
Viscum.

## viscose
viscose, adj., viscous. — Late L. viscosus, 'full of
birdlime, sticky, viscous*, fr. L. viscum. See
viscum and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: viscose, п., a kind of cellulose used
in making rayon.

## viscosity
viscosity, п., stickiness. — ME. viscosite, fr. MF.
(= F.) viscosite, fr. ML. viscositdtem, ace. of
viscositds, fr. L. viscosus. See prec. word and
-ity.

## viscount
viscount, n. — ME. viscounte, fr. MF. viscomte,
vicomte (F. vicomte), fr. OF., fr. ML. vicecomes,
compounded of L. vice, 'instead of, and comes,
'a companion'. See vice, prep., and count, 'title
of nobility* and cp. vidame.

## viscountcy
viscountcy, n. — Formed from prec. word with
suff. -cy.

## viscountess
viscountess, n. — Formed fr. viscount with 1st
suff. -ess. Cp. F. vicomtesse.

## viscous
viscous, adj., sticky. — Late L. viscosus. See
viscose and -ous.
Derivatives: viscous-ly, adv., viscous-ness, n.

## Viscum
Viscum, η., a genus of plants of the mistletoe
family (bot.) — L. viscum, 'mistletoe; birdlime'
(whence Late L. viscidus, 'bitter, sharp, sticky'),
cogn. with Gk. ίξός (for *Γ4ξός), 'mistletoe;
birdlime', OSlav. visnja, 'cherry' (whence Lith.
vySne, OPruss. wisnaytos, of s.m.), OHG. wfksi-
la, MHG. wiksel, G. Weichsel, 'morello cherry',
and the river name Goth., OHG. Wihsila
(whence G. Weichsel, OPruss. Wizla, Pol. Visla).
These words prob. derive fr. I.-E. base *weis-,
'to melt away', and are cogn. with L. virus,
'poison'. (F. gui, 'mistletoe', derives fr. L.
viscum.) See virus and cp. viscid, viscous and the
first element in Ixodidae and in weichsel wood,

## vise
vise, vice, п., a tool, device. — ME. vice, vis, fr.
OF. (= F.) vis, 'screw*, fr. L. vltis, 'vine, tendril',
fr. the base of viere, 'to bend, twist'. See viti-.
Derivative: vise, vice, tr. v.

## vise
vise, п., a visa. — F., pp. of viser, 'to inspect', fr.
VL. *visdre, freq. of L. videre (pp. visus), 'to see'.
See vision and cp. visa.
Derivative: vise, tr. v.

## Vishnu
Vishnu, п., one of the Hindu Trimurti, the other
two being Brahma and Siva (Hindu mythof.) —
OI. Visnuh, lit. 'the active one', from stem vis-,
'to be active, perform, work', which is of
uncertain etymology. Cp. the first element in next
word.

## Vishvakarma
Vishvakarma, п., one of the supreme deities in
Hindu mythology. — OI. Visvakarman, lit. 'all-
doer'. For the first element of this compound
see prec. word. OI. karman, 'action, work, deed*,
is rel. to krnSti, karoti, 'he makes'; see karma.

## visibility
visibility, n. — Late L. visibilitds, fr. L. visibilis.
See next word and -ity.

## visible
visible, adj. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
visibilis, fr. visus, pp. of videre, 'to see'. See vision and
-ible.
Derivatives: visible-ness, п., visibl-y, adv.

## Visigoth
Visigoth, п., one of the West Goths. — Late L.
Visigothl (pi.), a Teut. loan word whose first
element is prob. reh to OHG. westan, 'from the
west', etc.; see west. For the second element see
Goth. Accordingly Late L. Visigothl lit. means
'the Western Goths'; cp. Ostrogoth. The usual
explanation of the name as 'the good Goths'—
based on the alleged kinship of Late L. Visl,
'Visigoths', with OI. vasuh, 'good'—is erroneous
See S. Sigmund Feist, Vergleichendes Wbrter-
buch der gothischen Sprache, Leiden, 1939, p.
568 s.v. Wisi, and p. 298 s.v. iusiza.
Derivatives: Visigoth-ic, adj. and n.

## vision
vision, n. — ME. visioun, fr. OF. (= F.) vision,

## fr. L. visionem
fr. L. visionem, ace. of vlsio, 'the act of seeing,

## sight'
sight', fr. visus, pp. of videre, 'to see', which is

## rel. to Umbr. virseto
rel. to Umbr. virseto, 'seen', and cogn. with OI.

veda, Ί know', vedafr, 'knowledge', vindati,
'finds', Gk. οίδα (for *fotSa), Ί know', εϊδον
(for *eftSov), Ί saw', ίδεϊν (for *FcSeiv), 'to
see', ιδέα (prob. for *fιδέα), 'look, semblance;
kind, nature, class, species', είδος (for *FtX-
δος), 'form, shape', lit. 'that which is seen',
εί'δωλον, 'image, phantom', ΐστωρ, Boeot.
fiortop (for *Π8τωρ), 'knowing, learned',
ιστορία, 'learning' by inquiry, knowledge
obtained by inquiry, account of one's inquiries;
narration, historical narrative; history'. Arm.
gitem, Ί know', gtanem, Ί find*, OSlav. videti,
'to see', vedeti, 'to know*, Goth., OE. witan, 'to

'face', OPruss. waidima, 'we know', Olr, fiss,

knows'. All these words are derivatives of I.-E.

wit, v., and cp. advice, advise, belvedere, bevue,
clairvoyant, device, devise, envisage, envy,
evidence, evident, improvise, Interview, invidious,
invisible, jurisprudence, preview, previse,
providence, provident, provision, proviso, provisor,
prudence, prudent, review, revise, revision,
supervise, supervision, supervisor, survey, vide,
videlicet, vidimus, view, visa, visage, vis-a-vis,

For derivatives of Greek origin see Idea and

Derivatives: vision, tr. v., vision-al, adj., vision-
al-ly, adv., vision-ary, adj. and п., vision-ari-ly,
adv., vision-ari-ness, n.

## visit
visit, tr. and intr. v. — ME. visiten, fr. OF..( =
F.) visiter, fr. L. visitare, 'to see frequently, to go
to see*, freq. of visere, 'to look at often or
attentively', itself a freq. of videre (pp. visas), 'to
see'· See prec. word.
Derivatives: visit, п., visit-able, adj., visitant
(q.v.), visit-ative, adj., visitatorial(q.v.), visit-ing,
adj., visitor (q.v.)

## visitant
visitant, adj. and n. — L. visitdns, gen. -antis, pres.
part, of visitare. See visit, v., and -ant.

## visitation
visitation, n. — ME. visitacioun, fr. MF. (— F.)
visitation, fr. OF., fr. L. visitationem, ace. of vf-
sitdtio, fr. visitdtus, pp. of visitare. See visit, v.,
and -ation.
Derivative: visitation-al, adj.

## visitatorial
visitatorial, adj. — Formed with suff. -ia) fr. Late
L. visitdtor, 'visitor', from L. vtsitatus, pp. of
visitare. See visit.

## visitor
visitor, n. — ME. visitour, fr. MF. visiteor, visi-
teur (F. visiteur), fr. OF., fr. visiter, fr. L.
visitare. See visit and agential suff. -or.

## visor
visor, vizor, п., mask; front part of the helmet. —
ME. viser, fr. AF. visere, viser, fr. OF. visiere
(F. visiere), fr- OF. vis, 'face'. See visage.

## viss
viss, п., a weight. — See vis, 'a weight'.

## vista
vista, п., view. — It., 'sight, view', fem. of visto,
a collateral form of veduto, pp. of vedere, 'to
see', used as a noun, fr. L. videre; see vision. The
word vista was introduced into English by the
diarist John Evelyn (1620-1706).

## visual
visual, adj. — ME., fr. Late L. visudlis, fr. L.
visus, 'sight', fr. visus, pp. of videre, 'to see'. See
vision and adj. suff. -al.
Derivatives: visual-ity, п., visual-ize, tr. and intr.
v., visual-iz-ation, п., visual-iz-er; п., visual-ly,
adv.

## visuo-
visuo-, combining form meaning 'vision'. — Fr.
L. visus, 'sight'. See prec. word.

## Vitaceae
Vitaceae, n. pi., the vine family (bot.) — ModL.,
formed fr. Vitis with suff. -aceae.

## vituceous
vituceous, adj. — See prec. word,and -aceous.

## vital
vital, adj., 1) pertaining to life; 2) living; 3)
essential to life; essential; 4) fatal, deadly. —
ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L. vitalis, 'pertaining
to life', fr. vita, 'life, livelihood', which stands
for *gwiwita is rel. to L. vivus (for *gwiwos),
'living', vivo (for *gwiwo), Ί live', and cogn. with
Gk. βίος (for *gwiwos), 'life', βιοτή, βιοτεία
(for *gwiwot-), 'way of life, livelihood', Lith.
gyvata, '(eternal) life', fr. I.-E. base *gwei-, 'to
live'. See qnick, andLcp. bio- and words there
referred to. Cp. also viable, viand, victual, vitamin,
viva, vivacity, vivarium, viva voce, vivandlere,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:841 COLUMN:2 -->
vivarium, vive, Vivian, vivid, vivify, vivisection,
aquavitae, convivial, revive, revivi scent, savoir
vivre, Sempervivum.
Derivatives: vital-ism, п., vital-ist, п., vitality
(q.v.), vital-ly, adv., vital-ness, п., vital-ize, tr.
v., vital-iz-ation, п., vital-iz-er, n.

## vitality
vitality, п., vital force. — L. vitdlitds, fr. vitdlis,
'pertaining to life'. See prec. word and -ity.

## vitals
vitals, n. pi., the vital organs. — Formed fr. vital,
adj., taken as a noun.

## vitamin
vitamin, also vitamine, n. (biochem.) — G.
Vitamin, coined by the Polish biochemist Casimir
Funk (1884- ), the discoverer of vitamins, in
1913 fr. L. vita, 'life', and G. Amin; so called by
him because it was orig. supposed to be an
amine. See vital and amine and cp. avitamino-
sis.

## vitaphone
vitaphone, п., a machine used to reproduce speech
simultaneously with moving pictures. — Lit.
'life sound', a hybrid coined fr. L. vita, 'life' and
Gk. φωνή, 'sound, voice*. See vital and phone,
'speech sound'.

## vitellarium
vitellarium, п., that part of the ovary in certain
fiatworms which produces yolk-filled cells. —
ModL., formed fr. vi tell us with suff. -arium.
Derivative: vitellari-an, adj.

## vitelligenons
vitelligenons, adj., yolk-producing. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. vitellus, 'yolk of an egg', and the
Gk. suff. -γενής, 'born of, used in the modern
sense 'produced by'. See vitellus and -genous.

## vitellin
vitellin, n., protein in the yolk of an egg {biochem.)
— Formed fr. vitellus with suff. -in.

## vitelline
vitelline, adj., pertaining to the yolk of an egg. —
Formed fr. vitellus (q.v.) with chem. suff. -ine.

## viteilo-
viteilo-, combining form for vitellus. — See next
word.

## vitellus
vitellus, п., the yolk of an egg. — L., lit. *a little
calf, formed with the dimin. suff. -elius fr. vi-
tulus, 'calf; see vitular. The word vitellus was
first used in the sense 'yolk of an egg*, by Aulus
Cornelius Celsus, Roman physician and writer
of the early 1st cent.

## Vitex
Vitex, п., a genus of plants of the verbena family
(bot.) — L. vitex, 'the chaste tree', rel. to viere,
'to bend, twist', vitis, 'vine'. See viti-,

## viti-
viti-, combining form meaning 'vine', as in
viticulture. — L. viti-, fr. vitis, 'vine, grapevine', rel.
to viere, 'to bend, twist", vimen, 'twig, switch,
osier', fr. I.-E. base *wei-, 'to bend, twist',
whence also Gk. ίτέα (prob. for *ί«τέδ),
'willow', OE. wide, 'withe', widig, 'willow,
willow twig'. See withy and cp. vimen.

## vitiate
vitiate, tr. v., to render faulty or impure; to
corrupt; to pervert. — L. vitidtus, pp. of vitiare, 4o-
make faulty, mar, corrupt, vitiate', fr. vitium,
'fault, defect, blemish, crime, vice'. See vice,
'moral fault', and verbal suff. -ate.
Derivatives: vitiat-ed, adj., vitiation (q.v.),
vitiator (q.v.)

## vitiation
vitiation, n. — L. vitiatio, gen. -onis, fr. vitidtus,
pp. of vitiare. See prec. word and -ion.

## vitiator
vitiator, n. — L. vitiator, fr. vitidtus, pp. οι vitiare.
See vitiate and agential suff. -or.

## viticulture
viticulture, п., cultivation of the vine. —
Compounded of viti- and culture.
Derivatives: viticultur-al, adj., viticuttur-ist, n.

## vitfilgo
vitfilgo, п., a name of a skin disease (med.) — L.
vitiligo, 'a kind of tetter*, coined by Aulus
Cornelius Celsus, Roman physician and writer of
the early 1st cent., fr. vitium, 'fault, blemish,
taint*. See vice, 'moral fault'.

## vitiosity
vitiosity, п., viciousness. — L. vitidsitas, 'faulti-
ness, corruption', fr. vitiosus. See vicious and
-ity.

## Vitis
Vitis, п., a genus of plants, the grape (bot.) — L.
vitis, 'vine, grapevine'. See viti-.

## vitrage
vitrage, п., a curtain designed for windows. — F.,
'glazing, glasswork, glass partition', fr. vitrey
'glass*, fr. L. vitrum. See vitreo- and -age.

## vitreo-
vitreo-, combining form used in the sense of
vitreous. — Fr. L. vitreus, 'of glass*, fr. vitrum,
'glass', which is identical with vitrum, 'woad'.
The glass was called vitrum because of its bluish
woadlike color. See woad and cp. vitrescent,
Vitrina, vitriol and the last element in sandiver.

## vitreous
vitreous, adj., resembling glass. — L. vitreus, fr.
vitrum, 'glass'. See vitreo- and -ous.
Derivatives: vitreous-ly, adv., vitreous-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:841 COLUMN:3 -->

## vitrescence
vitrescence, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -ce.

## vitrescent
vitrescent, adj., tending to become glass. —
Formed fr. L.' vitrum, 'glass'. See vitreo- and -escent.

## vitrescible
vitrescible, adj., capable of becoming glass. —
See prec. word and -ible.

## vitric
vitric, adj., glasslike. — Formed with adj. suff. -ic
fr. vitrum, 'glass'. See vitreo-.

## vitrics
vitrics, п., the art of making glassware. — See
prec. word and -lcs.

## vitrifaction
vitrifaction, п., vitrification. — Compounded of
L. vitrum (see vitreo-) and -faction.

## verifiable
verifiable, adj. — Formed fr. vitrify with suff.
-able.
Derivative: vitrifiabil-ity, n.

## vitrification
vitrification, n. — Compounded of L. vitrum,
'glass' (see vitreo-), and -fication.

## vi triform
vi triform, adj., glasslike. — Compounded of L.
vitrum, 'glass*, and forma, 'form, shape'. See
vitreo- and form, n.

## vitrify
vitrify, tr. v., to convert into glass; intr. v., to be
converted into glass. — F. vitrifier, fr. MF.,
formed fr. L. vitrum, 'glass' and -ficare, fr. fa-
cere, 'to make, do'. See vitreo- and -fy.

## Vitrina
Vitrina, п., a genus of landsnails (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. L. vitrum, 'glass* (see vitreo-); so called in
allusion to the translucent spiral shell.

## vitriol
vitriol, n. — ME. vitriofe, fr. MF. (= F.) vitriol,
fr. Of., fr. ML. vitriolum, prop, subst. use of
the neut of the adj. *vitriolus, which
corresponds to L. vitreolus, 'of glass', dimin. of w-
treus, 'of glass, glassy', fr. vitrum, 'glass' (see
vitreo-); so called in allusion to the glassy lustre
of this sulfate.
Derivatives: vitriol, tr. v., vitriol-ate, tr. v., vi-
triol-ation, п., vitriolic (q.v.), vitriolize (q.v.)

## vitriolic
vitriolic, adj. — F. vitriolique, fr. vitriol. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ic.

## vitriolize
vitriolize, tr. v. — A hybrid coined fr. vitriol and
-ize, a suff. of Greek origin.
Derivatives: vitrioliz-ation, п., vitrioliz-er, n.

## Vitruvian
Vitruvian, adj., pertaining to Marcus Vitruvius
Polio, a Roman architect in the age of
Augustus. — Formed, from the name of Vitruvius
with suff. -an.

## vitta
vitta, п., tube for oil in certain umbelliferous
plants (bot.) — L. vittay 'a band, ribbon, fillet',
prob. for *vita, fr. I.-E. base *wei-, 'to bend,
twist', whence also L. viere, 'to bend, twist',
vitis, 'vine'. See viti- and cp. the next two
words.

## Vittadinia
Vittadinia, п., a genus of herbs (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Italian botanist C. Vittadini
(1800-65). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## Vittaria
Vittaria, п., a genus of ferns, the ribbon ferns
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. vitta. See vitta and -aria,

## vittate
vittate, adj., having vittae (bot.) — L. vittdtus,
'bound with a fillet or ribbon', fr. vitta. See
vitta and adj. suff. -ate.

## vitular
vitular, vitulary, adj., pertaining to a calf or
calves. — Formed with suff. -ar, resp. -nry, fr.
L. vitulus, 'calf. See veal and cp. vitellus.

## vituline
vituline, adj., pertaining to a calf or to veal. — L.
vitulinus fr. vitulus, 'calf. See veal and -ine
(representing L. -inus) and cp. prec. word.

## vi tu per able
vi tu per able, adj. — See next word and -able.

## vituperate
vituperate, tr. v., to berate, revile. — L. vituperd-
tus, pp. stem of vituperdre, *to censure, blame,
disparage', which is compounded of vitium,
'defect, blemish', and *-paros, fr. pardre, 'to
prepare'. See vice, 'moral fault', pare and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivative: vituperat-ory, adj.

## vituperation
vituperation,'n. — ME., fr. MF. (= F.), fr. L.
vituperdtionem, ace. of vituperdtio, 'censuring,
blaming', fr. vituperdtus, pp. of vituperdre. See
prec. word and -ation.

## vituperative
vituperative, adj. — Late L. vituperdtivus, fr. L.
vituperdtus, pp. of vituperdre. See vituperate and
-ive.
Derivative: vituperative-ly, adv.

## vituperator
vituperator, n. — L. vituperdtor, fr. vituperdtus,
pp. of vituperdre. See vituperate and agential
suff. -or.

## viuva
viuva, п., a rockfish (Acutomentum ovale). —
Port., lit. 'widow', fr. L. vidua, 'widow'. See
widow and cp. vidual. Cp. also widow bird.

## viva
viva, interj. and n. — It., 'long live ...', lit. 'let

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:842 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 815 | VOLAR -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:842 COLUMN:1 -->
him live', imper. of vivere, 'to live', fr. L. vivere.
See vivid.

## vivace
vivace, adj., vivacious {musical direction). — It.
See next word.

## vivacious
vivacious, adj., lively. — Formed with suff. -011s
fr. L. νϊνάχ, gen. vivdcis, 'lively, vigorous', fr.
vivere, 'to live'. See vivid.
Derivatives: vivacious-ly, adv., vivacious-ness,
n.

## vivacity
vivacity, п., liveliness. — L. vivaciids, fr. νϊνάχ,
gen. vicdcis. See prec. word and -ity.

## Ylvandiere
Ylvandiere, п., a woman who formerly
accompanied a French army and sold wine and
provisions. — F., fem. of vivandier, 'sutler, canteen
purveyor', fr. VL. *vivanda, fr. L. vivenda, neut.
pi. of the gerundive of vivere, 'to live', used as a
fem. sing. noun. See vivid and cp. viand.

## vivarium
vivarium, n. — L. vivarium, 'an enclosure in
which animals are kept alive', prop. neut. of the
adj. vivdrius, 'pertaining to living creatures',
used as a noun, fr. vivere, 'to live'. See vivid and
-arium.

## viva voce
viva voce, adv., by word of mouth. — L. viva
voce, 'with the living voice', abl. of viva vox.
Viva is the fem. of vivus, 'living', from the stem
of vivere, 'to live'. See vivid and voice.
Derivatives: viva voce, adj. and n.

## vive
vive, v. — F., 'let him live, long live...' 3 pers.
pres. subj. of vivre,'to live', fr. L. vivere. See vivid.

## Viverra
Viverra, п., the typical genus of civets (zool.) —
L. viverra, 'ferret', cogn. with ModPers. var-
varah, 'squirrel', Lith. vovere, vever'is, vaiveris,
Leth. vavere, OPruss. weware, 'male of various
animals', OSlav. veverica, W. gwywer, Bret.
gwiber, 'squirrel', and with the second element
in OHG. eihhurno, eihhorno, MHG. eichSrn, G.
Eichhorn, MDu. eencoren, Du. eekhoorn, MLG.
ekhorn, ekeren, ON. ikorni, Norw. eikorne,
OSwed. ekorne. Swed, ekorre, Dan. egern, OE.
dcweorna, dcwern [(the first element of these
Teut. words is rel. to E. oak (q.v.), the second
was assimilated to OHG., etc. (see horn)]. All
these words prob. derive fr. l.-E. base *wer-, 'to
bend'; the squirrel was so called from the bent
shape of the tail. For other derivatives of base
*wer- see version and cp. worm.

## vives
vives, п., disease of the submaxillary glands in
young horses (veterin.) — F., fr. ML. vivae, fr.
Arab. adh-dhi'bah (whence also Sp. adibas), lit.
'the she-wolf, fr. adh, assimilated form of the
art. a!,anddhi'bah, fem. of dhi'b, 'wolf, which is
rel. to Heb. z6e~bh, Akkad. zibu, Aram, debha,
'wolf, Ethiop. ze'eb, 'hyena'. F. avives, 'vives',
has been refashioned fr. original vives after
Arab. adh-dhi'bah. Cp. avives.

## vivi-
vivi-, combining form meaning 'living; alive'. —
L. vivi- fr. vivus, 'living, alive'. See vivid.

## Vivian
Vivian, masc. PN. — L. Vividnus (whence also F.
Vivien), lit. 'living, alive'. See vivid.

## Vivinn
Vivinn, Vivien, fem. PN. — Generally regarded
as borrowed fr. F. Vivienne, fem. of Vivien (see
prec. word), but prob. a misreading of the
Celtic name Slinian.

## vivianite
vivianite, п., a hydrous ferrous phosphate
(mineral.) — G. Vivianit, named after the English
mineralogist J. G. Vivian, who discovered it.
The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see
subst. suff. -ite.

## vivid
vivid, adj., 1) lively; 2) bright; 3) intense. — L.
vividus, 'full of life, animated', fr. vivus, 'living,
alive', which is rel. to vivo, vivere, 'to live', vita,
'life'. See vital and cp. words there referred to.
For the ending see 1st suff. -Id.
Derivatives: vivid-ly, adv., vivid-ness, n.

## vlviflcate
vlviflcate, tr*v., to revive, vivify. — Late L. vlvifi-
catus, pp. of vivificare, 'to make alive'. See
vivify and verbal suff. -ate.

## viviflcarion
viviflcarion, n. — Fr. Late L. vivificdtus, pp. of
vivificare. See prec. word and -ion.

## vivify
vivify, tr. v., I) to give life to; 2) to make vivid. —
F. vivifier, fr. Late L. vivificare, 'to make alive,
restore to life', which is compounded of L. vivus,
'living, alive', and -ficdre, fr. facere, 'to make,
do'. See vivid and -fy.

## viviparity
viviparity, п., the state of being viviparous. —
Formed fr. L. viviparus (see next word) with
suff. -ity.

## viviparous
viviparous, adj., producing living young. — L.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:842 COLUMN:2 -->
viviparus, 'bringing forth its young alive",
compounded of vivus, 'living, alive', and parere, 'to
bring forth'. See vivid and -parous.
Derivatives: viviparous-ly, adv., viviparous-ness,
n.

## Viviparus
Viviparus, п., a genus of snails (zool.) — ModL.,
fr. L. viviparus; see prec. word. The genus is so
called because the young are born alive.

## vivisect
vivisect, tr. v., to dissect alive; intr. v., to practice
vivisection. — Compounded of L. vivus, 'living,
alive', and secrus, pp. of secure, 'to cut'. See
vivid and section.
Derivatives: vivisect-ible, adj., vivisect-or, n.

## vivisection
vivisection, п., the dissection of a living animal.
— Compounded of L. vivus (see prec. word) and
sectio, gen. -onis, *a cutting'. See section.
Derivatives: vivisection-al, adj., vivisecrion-al-ly,
adv., vivisection-ist, n.

## vixen
vixen, п., a she-fox. — Dial. ME. fixen, fr. ME.
fyxen, fr. OH.fyxen, 'fox'; see fox and fem. suff.
-en.
Derivatives: vixen-ish, adj., vixen-isn-ly, adv.,
vixen-ish-ness, n.

## vizier
vizier, more correctly vizir, n. — Turk, vezir,
'counsellor', fr. Arab, wazir (in vulgar
pronunciation weztr), fr. Avestic vicira, "arbitrator,
judge'. In Arabic waztr superseded katib (lit.
'writer') in the meaning of 'secretary of state'.
The 'Arabic' word was 're-borrowed' by the
Persians under the Ommiads; see The
Encyclopedia of Islam, IV, 1229. Cp. alquacil.

## vizierate
vizierate, vizirate, п., the office or dignity of a
vizier. — A hybrid coined from prec. word and
subst. suff. -ate (representing L. -Stus).

## Vlach
Vlach, n. and adj. — See Walach.

## vocable
vocable, п., a word; a term. — MF. (= F.), fr.
L. vocabulum, 'designation, name', lit. 'that by
which anything is called', fr. vocdre, 'to call',
fr. vox, gen. vocis, 'voice'. See voice and -able.

## vocable
vocable, adj., capable of utterance. — Formed
with suff. -able fr. L. vocare, 'to call'. See
vocable, n.
Derivative: vocabl-y, adv.

## vocabulary
vocabulary, п., I) a list of words; 2) all the words
of a language; 3) all the words used by a person,
class or people. — ML. vocabularium, 'list of
words', fr. L. vocabulum. See prec. word and
subst. suff. -ary.
Derivatives: vocabular-ian, adj. and n.

## vocal
vocal, adj. — ME., fr. L. vocalis, 'uttering a
voice, sounding sonorous', fr. vox, gen. vocis,
'voice'. See voice and adj. suff. -al andcp.
equivocal, umvocal.
Derivatives: vocal, п., vocal-ism, п., vocal-ist,
п., vocal-ity, п., vocaf-ize, tr. v., vocal-iz-ation,
п., vocal-iz-er, п., vocal-ly, adv., vocal-ness, n.

## vocation
vocation, n. — ME. vocacioun, fr. L. vocationem,
ace. of vocdtio, fr. vocatus, 'called', pp. of
vocare, 'to call', fr. νδχ, gen. vocis, 'voice'. See
voice and -ntion.
Derivatives: vocation-al, adj., vocation-al-ly,
adv.

## vocative
vocative, adj., of, or relating to, the vocative
case (gram.) — ME. vocatif, lit. 'calling', fr. L.
vocativus, fr. vocatus, pp. of vocare, 'to call,
summon'; see vocal and -ative.

## vocative
vocative, n. (gram.) — L. (casus) vocativus, 'the
case of summoning'. See vocative, adj.

## vociferance
vociferance, n. — Formed from next word with
suff. -се.

## vociferant
vociferant, adj. — L. vociferans, gen. -amis, pres.
part, of vociferdre. See next word and -ant.

## vocifernte
vocifernte, intr. v., to shout loudly, tr. v., to utter
with a loud voice. — L. vdciferdtus, pp. of vdci-
ferdrl, 'to cry out, to shout', compounded of
vox, gen. vocis, 'voice', and ferre, 'to bear,
carry'. See voice and bear, 'to carry', and verbal
suff. -ate.
Derivatives: vociferat-ion, п., vociferat-or, Q.

## vociferous
vociferous, adj., shouting loudly; clamorous. —
Compounded of L. vox, gen. vocis, 'voice', and
the stem of ferre, 'to carry'. See voice and -fcrous.
Derivatives: vociferous-ly, adv., vociferous-ness,
n.

## vodka
vodka, n. — Russ., dimin. of voda, 'water', which
is cogn. with Gk. δδωρ, Goth, wato, OE.
wseter. See water.

## voe
voe, п., an inlet, creek in the Orkney and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:842 COLUMN:3 -->
Shetland Islands. — ON. vagr, 'sea'. See vogne.

## vogesite
vogesite, п., a variety of pyrope (mineral.) — G.
Vogesit, named after Vogesen, the German
name of the Vosges mountains. The ending -/f
goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## vogue
vogue, п., 1) popular favor; 2) popular usage;
fashion. — MF. (= F.), 'swaying motion,
rowing, vogue, fashion', back formation fr. voguer,
'to sway, move along', fr. It. vogare or OProv-
enc. vogar, of s.m., which are prob. of Teut.
origin. Cp. OS., OHG. wag, MHG. wac, 'water
in motion, wave, billow' [HG. wage (whence G.
Woge), 'wave, billow', is a loan word fr. MLG.
wage], OFris. wig, wei, ON. vagr, 'water in
motion, wave, billow, sea', Goth, wigs,
'tempest' (in the pi. 'waves, billows'). All these Teut.
words orig. meant 'water in motion', and
derive fr. Teut. base * weg-, corresponding to I.-E.
base *wegh-, 'to move', whence also OE. wegan,
'to carry, move'. See weigh and cp. prec. word
and the first element in wainscot. Cp. F. vague,
'wave', which derives fr. ON. vagr.
Derivatives: vogue, adj., vogu-ish, vogue-ish, adj.

## voice
voice, n. — ME. vols, voice, fr. OF. voiz, vois
(F. voix), fr. L. vdeem (whence also It. voce,
Provenc. votz, Sp., Port, voz), ace. of νδχ,
'voice, sound, tone, call', rel. to vocare, 'to call',
fr. I.-E. base *weqv>-, *woqv>-, 'voice; to speak',
whence also 01. vacas-, 'sound, word', Avestic
vacah-, of s.m., OI. vakti, vivakti, 'says, speaks*.
Toch. A wak, В wek, 'voice', Gk. ίπος, Cypr.
ίέπος, 'word, song, narrative', βψ (for *г"6ф),
'voice', 6σσα (for Τόκμχ), 'voice, tale', έν-οπή,
'crying, shouting, voice', OPruss. wackis,
'shouting, noise', wackttwei, 'to call', OHG. gi-
wahan(en), MHG. ge-wahenen, G. er-wdhnen, 'to
mention'. Cp. vox, vocal, vocation, vocative,
vociferate, vowel, advocate, advowee, advowson,
avocation, avouch, avoue, avow, convicium, con-
vocate, convoke, equivocal, eqnivoque, evocation,
evoke, invocation, invoke, Irrevocable,
provocation, provoke, revocation, revoke, semivocal, tele-
vox, imivocal, viva voce. Cp. also epic, epopee,
epos and the second element in Calliope.
Derivative: voice, tr. v., voic-ed, adj., voice-ful,
adj., voice-ful-ness, п., voice-less, adj., voice-
less-ly, adv., voice-less-ness, n.

## void
void, adj., empty. — ME. void, voide, fr. OF. voit,
voide, dial forms of vuit, vuide, 'empty', fr. VL.
*vocit-(um), for *vacit-(um), for L. vacat(um),
pp. stem of vacdre, 'to be empty'. See vacant and
cp. avoid, devoid.
Derivatives: void, п., п., void, v. (q.v.), void-able,
adj., void-able-ness, a., void-ed, adj., void-er, n.

## void
void, tr. v., to make empty. — ME. voiden, fr.
OF. voidier, dial, form of vuidier (F. vider), 'to
make empty', fr. OF., fr. VL. *vocitare, of s.m.,
for *vacitdret fr. *vacit(um). See void, adj.
Derivatives: void-able, adj., void-able-ness, п.,
void-ed, adj., void-er, n.

## voile
voile, п., a thin material used for women's
dresses. — F. voile, 'veil', fr. L. velum. See veil.

## voivode
voivode, п., vaivode. — Russ. voevoda, orig.
meaning 'leader of the army', fr. OSlav. vojl,
'warriors', and -voda, 'leader'. See vaivode.

## volagc
volagc, adj., fickle, flighty. — ME., fr. MF. (■= F-),
fr. L. voldticus, 'fleeting, flighty', fr. voldt-(um),
pp. stem of voldre, 'to fly'. See next word and
-age.

## volant
volant, adj., flying. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. volan-
tern, ace. of voldns, pres. part, of voldre, 'to fly',
which is of uncertain origin, It is possibly cogn.
with OI. garut, 'wing', garutmdn, 'winged; bird',
garudab, name of a mythical bird. Cp. volage,
volatile, vol-au-vent, vole (in card playing),
volet, volitant, volitation, volley, volplane, volu-
crine. For the ending see suff. -ant.

## Volapuk
Volapuk, п., an artificial language invented by
Johann Martin Schleyer (1831-1912) in 1879. —
Lit. 'world's speech', fr. vol, 'world', and рйк,
'speech'. Vol was coined fr. E. world, рйк, fr.
E. speech.

## volar
volar, adj., pertaining to the palm of the hand or
to the sole of the foot (anat.) — Formed with adj.
suff. -ar fr. L. vola, 'palm of the hand, sole of
the foot', which is prob. a derivative of I.-E.
base *wel-, 'to turn, twist, roll', whence L. vol-
vere, 'to roll'. See volute.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:843 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VOLATILE | 816 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:843 COLUMN:1 -->

## volatile
volatile, adj., flying (rare); 2) quickly
evaporating; 3) easily changing, fickle. — F., fr. L.
voUtilis, 'flying, fleeting, transitory', which was

## formed with suff. -His fr. voldt(-um)
formed with suff. -His fr. voldt(-um), pp. stem
of volare. See volant and -ile.
Derivatives: volatile-ness, a., volatil-ity, n„
volatil-ize, tr. and intr. v., volatil-iz-ation, n.

## vol-an-vent
vol-an-vent, п., a kind of pie. — F., lit. 'flying in
the wind'. See volant and wind, 'air'.

## volborthite
volborthite, п., a hydrous vanadate of copper,
barium and calcium (mineral.) — F., named in
1837 after the Russian scientist Alexander von
Volborth (1800-1876), its discoverer. For the
ending see subst. surf. -ite.

## volcanic
volcanic, adj. — F. volcanique, Тт. It. vulcanico,
fr. vuicano. See volcano and adj. suff. -ic.

## volcanicity
volcanicity, n. — F. volcanicire, fr. volcanique.
See prec. word and -ity.

## volcanism
volcanism, п., volcanic action; volcanic
phenomena. — F. volcanisme, fr. volcan. See volcano
and -ism.

## volcanist
volcanist, п., a student of volcanic phenomena.
— F. volcaniste, fr. volcan. See volcano and -1st.

## volcanize
volcanize, tr. v., to subject to volcanic heat. — F.
volcaniser, fr. volcan. See volcano and -ize.
Derivatives: volcaniz-ation, п., volcaniz-er, n.

## volcano
volcano, n. — It. vuicano, volcano, fr. L. Vulcdnus,
name of the god of fire. Cp. F. volcan, Sp.
volcan, 'volcano', und see Vulcnn.

## voicanology
voicanology, п., the study of volcanoes. — A
hybrid coined fr. volcano, a word of Latin
origin, and Gk. -λογία, fr. -λόγος, 'one who
speaks (in a certain manner); one who deals
(with a certain topic'). See -logy.
Derivatives: volcanolog-ical, adj., volcanolog-
ist, n.

## vole
vole, п., the winning of all the tricks in a deal in a
card game. — F. vole, back formation fr. voter,
'to fly', fr. L. volare. See volant,

## vole
vole, п., a rodent of the genus Nicrotus. — Short
for vole mouse, lit. 'field mouse'. E. vole, 'field',
is of Scand. origin. Cp. ON. vollr, Norw. vole,
'field, meadow', which are rel. to OE. weald,
wald, 'forest, woodland'. See wold,

## volet
volet, п., one of the wings of a triptych (paint.) —
F., fr. voter, 'to fly'. See volant and -et.

## voiitant
voiitant, adj., flying (zool.) — L. volitdns, gen.
-antis, pres. part, of volitdre, 'to fiy', freq. of
volare. See volant,

## volltution
volltution, п., the act of flying. — L. volitdtid,
gen. -dnis, Ст. volitdt(-um), pp. stem of volitdre.
See prec. word and -ation.
Derivative: volitation-al, adj.

## volition
volition, п., the act of willing. — ML. volitid, gen.
-onis, fr. L. void, velle, 'to wish, will'. See
voluntary and -ition and cp. noiltion.
Derivatives: volition-al, adj., volition-al-ly, adv.,
volition-ary, adj., volition-less, adj.

## volitive
volitive, adj., pertaining to the will. — See prec.
word and -ive.

## Volkslied
Volkslied, п., folk song. — G., compounded of
Volk, 'people, folk', and Lied, 'song'. See folk
and lied.

## Volksraad
Volksraad, п., legislative body in the former
Orange Free State. — Du., lit. 'counsel of the
people', fr. volk, 'people', and raad, 'counsel'.
See folk and raad.

## volley
volley, п., a flight of missiles. — MF. (= F.)
volee, 'flight; volley', prop. fem. pp. of voter,
'to fly', used as a noun. See volant.
Derivatives: volley, tr. and intr. v., volley-er, rt.,
volley-ing, adj., volley-ing-ly, adv.

## volplane
volplane, intr. v., to glide toward the earth in an
airplane. — F. volplane, fr. vol, 'flight', and pp.
of planer, 'to float, glide', fr. plane, '(air)plane\
See volant and plane, 'airplane'.

## volt
volt, п., a turning movement of a horse (manege).
— F. volte, fr. It. volta. See volta.

## volt
volt, п., the unit of electromotive force. —
Named after the Italian physicist, the Count
Alessandro Volta (1745-1827).
Derivative: volt-age, n.

## volta
volta, п., pi. volte, 'times'; una volta, 'once' due
volte, 'twice' (mus.) — It. volta, 'a turn; a turn
in time', fr. L. 'volvita, fr. volvere, 'to roll'. See
vanlt, 'to leap', and cp. volte-face, volti, archivolt.

## voltaic
voltaic, adj., designating electricity produced by
chemical action. — Lit. 'pertaining to Volta'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:843 COLUMN:2 -->
See volt, 'unit of electromotive force', and adj.
suff. -ic.

## Voltairian
Voltairian, adj., pertaining to the French writer
and philosopher Voltaire (1696-1778); п., an
adherent of the doctrines of Voltaire.—For the
ending see surf. -ian.
Derivative: Voltairian-ism, n.

## voltameter
voltameter, п., an instrument for measuring
electricity by electrolysis. — Coined from the name
of Volta (see volt, 'unit of electromotive force')
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, 'poetical
rhythm'.

## volte-face
volte-face, п., a turning round; a reversal of
opinion. — F., 'a turning round', fr. It. volta faccia,
lit. 'a turning of the face', fr. volta, imper. of
voltare, 'to turn', and faccia, 'face'. See volt, *a
turning movement', and face.
Derivative: volte-face, intr. v.

## volti
volti, v., turn; turn over (musical direction). —
It., pres. subj. of voltare, 'to turn'. See volt, 'a
turning movement'.

## voltmeter
voltmeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
difference of potentials in volts (elect.) —
Coined fr. volt, 'unit of electromotive force',
and Gk. μέτρον, 'measure'. See meter, poetical
rhythm'.

## voltzite
voltzite, п., a zinc oxysulfide (mineral.) — Named
after the French mining engineer Philippe L.
Voltz (1785-1840). For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## volubility
volubility, n. — Either fr. F. volubilite or directly
fr. L. volubilitds, fr. volubilis. See next word and
-ity.

## voluble
voluble, adj., glib. — MF. (= F.), fr. L. volubilis,
'rolling, whirling, fluent (of speech), voluble',
fr. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute.
Derivatives: voluble-ness, п., volubl-y, adv.

## volucrine
volucrine, adj., pertaining to birds. — Formed
with suff. -ine (representing L. -inus) fr. L. volu-
cris (scil. avis), 'a bird', fem. of volucer, 'flying,
winged', which derives from the stem of volare,
'to fly'. See volant.

## volume
volume, n. — ME. volum, volume, fr. MF. (= F.)
volume, fr. OF-, fr. L. volumen, 'a roll; a book
rolled up', fr. volvere, pp. volutus, 'to roll'. See
volute.
Derivatives: volume, intr. and tr. v., volum-ed,
adj.

## volumenometer
volumenometer, п., an instrument for measuring
the volume of a solid body. — A hybrid coined
fr. L. volumen (see prec. word) and Gk. μέτρον,
'measure'. See meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## volumeter
volumeter, п., an instrument for measuring the
volume of liquids and gases. — Contraction
of volume-meter (see haplology). See volume and
meter, 'poetical rhythm'.

## volumetric
volumetric, volumetrical, adj., pertaining to the
measurement of volume. — Contraction of
volume-metric. See volume and metric and cp.
prec. word.

## volumlnal
volumlnal, adj., pertaining to volume. — Formed
with adj. suff. -al from L. volumen, gen. volumi-
nis, 'volume'. See volume.

## voluminous
voluminous, adj., bulky. — Late L. voluminosus,
fr. L. volumen, gen. voluminis, 'volume'. See
volume and -ous.
Derivatives: voluminos-ity, п., voluminous-ly,
adv., voluminous-ness, n.

## voluntarism
voluntarism, п., the theory that the will is the
basic principle. — G. Voluntarismus, irregularly
formed by the German national economist and
sociologist Ferdinand Tonnies (1855-1936) (in
his work Zur Entwicklungsgeschichte Spinozas)
in 1883 fr. L. voluntdrius, 'of one's free will', and
suff. -ismus. See next word and -ism.

## voluntary
voluntary, adj., 1) done by one's own free choice;
2) controlled by the will. — ME., fr. L.
voluntdrius, 'of one's free will, voluntary', fr. voluntas,
'will', from the stem of void, yelle, 'to will, wish',
fr. I.-E. base · wel-, 'to will, wish, hope, choose',
whence also Goth, wiljan, OE. willan, 'to will'.
See will, v., and cp. volition, volunteer,
benevolent, malevolent, nolens-volens, voluptuous.
Derivatives: voluntary, п., voluntari-ly, adv.,
voluntari-ness, n.

## voluntative
voluntative, adj., voluntary. — ML. voluntdtivus,
fr. L. voluntas, gen. -dtis. See voluntary and -ative.

## volunteer
volunteer, п., one who offers himself of his own

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:843 COLUMN:3 -->
free will, as for military service. — F. votontaire,
fr. L. voluntdrius. See prec. word and -eer.
Derivatives: volunteer, adj. and tr. v., volunteer-
ly, adv.

## voluptuary
voluptuary, п., a voluptuous person. — L. volup-
tudrius, fr. voluptds. See next word and subst.
suff. -ary.

## voluptuous
voluptuous, adj., sensuous. — ME., fr. L. volup-
tudsus, 'full of pleasure', fr. voluptds, 'pleasure',
fr. volup(e), neut. of 'volupis, 'pleasant', which
is prob. cogn. with Homeric Gk. £λπειν, 'to
cause to hope', Gk. έλπεσ&αι, 'to hope', έλπίς,
'hope', έλπωρή, 'hope', fr. I.-E. *wel-p-, an
enlargement of base *wel-, 'to will, wish',
whence L. void, velle, 'to wish, will'. See
voluntary and -ous.
Derivatives: voluptuous-ly, adv., voluptous-ness,
n.

## volnte
volnte, п., a spiral scroll forming the chief
features in Ionic and Corinthian capitals,— F., fr.
It. valuta, fr. L. valuta, 'spiral scroll, volute',
prop, subst. use of the fem. pp. of volvere, 'to
roll, roll along, turn about', which is cogn. with
Gk. είλεϊν (for'ίελνεΐν), 'to roll, turn, twist',
είλύειν (for *ίελνύειν or *έΓελύειν), 'to roll
round, enfold, enwrap', έλύειν, 'to roll',
έλίσσειν, Att. έλίττειν, Ion. εϊλίσσειν, (for
♦ίελίκιειν), 'to wind, roll', ίλιξ (for *ίέλιξ),
'coil, spiral', Arm. gelum, 4 turn, twist', glem,
Ί roll', 01. vrnoti, urnoti, 'covers, wraps',
varutram, 'wrapper', vdlate, *turns', Toch.
wdl, 'he covered', walui, 'worms', В lykwar,
A likwdr, 'times', В wai-walau, 'giddiness',
OSlav. valiti, 'to roll', vluna, 'wave', vlajati,
'to be driven about the waves', Lith. veliu,
velti, 'to full', vilnis, 'wave', aovalits, 'round',
OSlav. olu (for *ob-vlu~), 'round'. Alb. ναΐ'ε 'the
