OE. wealwian, 'to roll round', wylm, 'billow',
wiella, 'fountain, spring', weoloc, wiluc, 'triton,
trumpet shell', Olr. fulumain, 'rolling', fillim, Ί
bend, bow', W. olwyn, 'wheel'. All these words
derive fr. I.-E. base *wel-, *wal-, resp. its
enlarged forms *nelu-, *welw-, 'to bend, turn,
twist, roll'. Cp. alytarch, avale, circumvolution,
circumvolve, convolntion, convolve, Convolvulus,
devolution, elytron, epulis, evolute, evolution,
evolve, Helen, Helenus, Helicon, heilx, Helle,
heiminth, ileus, intervolve, involucre, involute,
involution, involve, lore, 'space between eyes and
beak of birds', obvolute, parulis, revolt,
revolution, revolve, ularrophia, ulitis, Ulotrichl, vail, 'to
lower', vale, 'valley', valgus, valley, vallum,
valve, vault, 'roof, vault, 'to leap', volar, volt, 'a
turning movement', volta, volte-face, volti,
voussoir, vulva, wale, walk, wall, wallow, weal,
'mark on flesh', weld, 'to unite', well of water,
welter, whelk, 'snail', willow and the first
element in vaudeville.
Derivatives: volut-ed, adj., volut-ion, n.

## volutoid
volutoid, adj., resembling a volute. — A hybrid
coined fr. L. valuta and Gk. -οειδής, 'like', fr.
είδος, 'form, shape'. See volute and -oid.

## volva
volva, п., the membranous sac of certain fungi
(bot.) — ModL., fr. L. volvere, 'to roll'. See
volute.

## volvelle
volvelle, п., an old device serving to ascertain the
time of the rising and setting of the sun and
moon. — ML. volvella, formed with dimin.
suff. -elia fr. L. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute.

## Volvox
Volvox, п., a genus of flagellates (bot.) — ModL.,
from the stem of L. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute.

## vomer
vomer, п., a bone between the nostrils (anat.) —
L. vdmis, later form vomer, 'plowshare', prob.
standing for orig. *wogwhsmis and cogn. with
OPruss. wagnis, OHG. waganso, ON. vangsni,
'plowshare', and with ON. veggr, OE. wecg,
,'wedge'. See wedge.

## vomica
vomica, п., a cavity in the lungs (med.) — L.,
'abscess', formed from the stem of vomere, 'to
vomit'. See next word.

## vomit
vomit, n. — ME. vomet, vomit, fr. MF. vomite,
vomit, fr. L. vomitus, 'vomiting', ft. vomit-(um),
pp. stem of vomere, 'to vomit', which stands for
*wemere, fr. I.-E. base *wem-, 'to spit, vomit',
whence also Gk. έμεΤν, 'to vomit', ε*μετος,
έμεσις, 'vomiting', εμετικός, 'provoking
sickness', 01. vdmati, 'he vomits', Avestic vam-, 'to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:844 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 817 | VULSELLUM -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:844 COLUMN:1 -->
spit', Lith. vemiu, vemti, 'to vomit', ON. vxma,
'seasickness', vama, 'nausea'. Cp. emetic, Emys
and mix vomica. Cp. also wamble.

## vomit
vomit, intr. and tr. v. — ME. vomiten, fr. L.
vomitdre, freq. of vomere, 'to vomit'. See vomit,
n.
Derivatives: vomit-ing, п., vomitory (q.v.)

## vomition
vomition, п., vomiting. — L. vomitio, gen. -dm'j,
fr. vomit-(um), pp. stem of vomere. See vomit, n.
and -ion.

## vomitive
vomitive, adj., pertaining to, or causing,
vomiting. — ML. vomitivus, fr. L. vomii-(um), pp.
stem of vomere. See vomit, п., and -ive,
vomitory* adj. — L. vomitorius, 'causing
vomiting', from vomit-(um), pp. stem of vomere. See
vomit, v., and adj. s'uff. -ory.

## vomiturition
vomiturition, п., an abortive attempt to vomit
(med.) — Medical L. vomiturttio, gen. -onis,
formed fr. vomit-(um), pp. stem'of vomere, 'to
vomit' (see vomit, n. and v.), on analogy of
Latin nouns like esuritid, 'a hungering', lit. 'a
desire to eat', etc. Cp. abiturient, esurient,
parturition. For the ending see suff. -Шоп.

## voodoo
voodoo, п., witchcraft, sorcery. — Creole F.
voudou, fr. Dahomey vodu. Cp. hoodoo.
Derivatives: voodoo, tr. v., to bewitch.

## voodooism
voodooism, п., belief in voodoo. — A hybrid
coined fr. voodoo with -ism, a suff. of Greek
origin.

## voodooist
voodooist, п., a believer in voodoo. — A hybrid
coined fr. voodoo with -ist, a suff. of Greek
origin.
Derivative: voodooist-ic, adj.

## voracious
voracious, adj. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L.
vorax, gen. vordcis, 'hungry, greedy', fr. vordre,
4o swallow greedily, swallow up, devour*, from
I.-E. base *gwer-, *gwor-, 'to swallow, devour',
whence also 01. girati, gilati, g^naf/yheswallows',
garah, 'drink', Avestic gar-, 'to gulp', Gk. βορά,
'food', βρώμα, 'food', βιβρώσκειν, 'to eat',
βάρα&ρον, 'gulf, pit', Lith. geriii, gerti, 'to
drink', OSlav. iirq, ireti, 'to swallow', OSlav.
grulo, 'gullet', Lith. girtas, 'drunk', Arm. ker,
kur, 'food', keri, Ί ate', kokord, 'throat*, Alb.
ngrans, 'eaten'. Cp. vorago, -vorous, devour. Cp.
also Abroma, barathrum, broma, Bromns, Bro—
simum, and the second element in Cryptodira
and in heilebore. Cp. also gullet and words there
referred to. For base *gwrogk-, enlargement of
base *gwer-, 'to swallow, devour', see bronchus,
branchia, crnw. Cp. also gurgitation and words
there referred to.
Derivatives: voracious-ly, adv., voracious-ness,
n.

## voracity
voracity, n. — MF. (= F.) voracite, fr. L. vordci-
tdtem, ace, of voracitas, from vorax, gen.
vordcis. See prec. word and -ity.

## vorago
vorago, п., a gulf. — L. vorago, 'gulf, abyss,
whirlpool, chasm', fr. vordre, 'to devour'. See
voracious.

## -vorous
-vorous, combining form meaning 'eating (such
and such food)', as in apivorous, carnivorous,
omnivorous. — Fr. L. -vorus, from the stem of
vordre, 'to devour', whence also vorax, 'hungry,
greedy'. See voracious.

## vortex
vortex, п., whirlpool; whirling motion. — L.
vortex, a var. of vertex, 'whirl, whirlpool, top,
peak, summit', fr. vertere (also vortere), 'to
turn". See version and cp. vertex, which is
derivatively identical with vortex.

## Vortical
Vortical, adj., resembling a vortex. — Formed
with atij. suff. -al fr. L. vortex, gen. vorticis (see
prec. word); derivatively identical with vertical
(q.v.)
Derivative: vorticaMy, adv.

## vorticism
vorticism, п., a furturist artistic movement,
resembling cubism, but using vortices instead of
cubus. — Irregularly formed fr. L. vortex (see
vortex) with suff. -ism.

## vorticlst
vorticlst, п., an adherent of vorticism. —
Irregularly formed fr. L. vortex (see vortex) with
suff. -ist. Cp. prec. word.

## vorticose
vorticose, adj., having a vortex or vortices. — L,
vorticosus, fr. vortex, gen, vorticis. See vortex
and adj. suff. -ose.
Derivative: vorticose-ly, adv.

## vortiginous
vortiginous, adj., whirling. — See vortex and
vertiginous.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:844 COLUMN:2 -->
rotal, adj., votive. — Formed with adj. suff. -al
fr. L. votum. See vote,
votaress, п., a female votary. — Formed from
next word with 1st suff. -ess.
votary, п., one devoted or consecrated by a vow;
adj., consecrated by a vow. — Formed with
suff. -ary fr. L. votum. See next word.
vote, n. — ME., fr. L. votum (for *vovetom), *a
vow', prop. neut. pp. of vovere, 'to vow', used
as a noun; rel. to Umbr. vufru, 'pertaining to a
Vow', and cogn. with OL vdghat-, 'one who
offers a sacrifice*, Avestic aog da, 'he said', Arm.
gog, 'say ' Gk. ευχή, 'vow, wish', εΰχομαι, Ί
pray', perh. also with OE. wogian, 'to woo'.
Cp. vow, avow, devote, devout. Cp. also Euchite,
euchology. Cp. also woo.
Derivatives: vote, intr. and tr. v., vot-er, п.,
vote-less, adi., vot-ing, п., votive (q.v.)

## votive
votive, adj., dedicated or given in fulfillment of a
vow. — L. votivus, .'pertaining to a vow, given
in the consequence of a vow', fr. votum. See
prec. word and -ive.
Derivatives: votive-ly, adv., votive-ness, n.

## vouch
vouch, tr. v., to guarantee; intr. v., to give a
guarantee (for.). — ME. vochen, vouchen, fr.
MF. vocher, vochier, voucher, 'to call, summon',
fr. L. vocdre, 'to call', fr. vox, gen. vocis, 'voice*.
See voice and cp. avouch.
Derivatives: vouch, п., vouch-able, adj., vouch-ee,
п., vouch-er, n. and tr. v.

## vouchsafe
vouchsafe, tr. v. — ME. vouchen sauf, 'to vouch
as safe'. See vouch and safe.
Derivative: vouchsafe-ment, n.

## voussoir
voussoir, п., any of the wedge-shaped stones
forming an arch. — F., fr. VL. *volsorium,
derived fr. VL. *volsus, corresponding to L. volu-
. tus, pp. of volvere, 'to roll'. See volute,

## vow
vow, n. — ME. you, vowe, vow, fr. OF. vou, vowe
(F. v<£u), fr. L. votum. See vote,

## vow
vow, tr. and intr. v. — MF. vouer, vower, fr. OF.,
fr. vou, vowe, 'vow*. See vow, n.
Derivative: vow-ed, adj.

## vowel
vowel, n. — ME. vowelle, fr. MF. vouele (F.
voyelle), fr. OF. voiel, fr. (Jittera) vocdlis, 'vocal
letter', fr. vox, gen. vocis, 'voice'. See vocal, voice.
Derivatives: vowel, tr. v., vowel-iz-ation, п.,
vowel-less, vowel-like, adjs.

## vox
vox, п., voice. — L. vox, gen. vocis, 'sound, tone,
call'. See voice,

## voyage
voyage, n. — ME. veyage, voyage, fr. OF. veiage,
voiage, (F. voyage), fr. L. viaticum, 'traveling
money, provisions for a journey', in VL. also
'journey', prop. neut. of the adj. vidticus,
'pertaining to a road or journey*, fr. via, 'way*.
OProven?. viatge, 'journey', derives fr. L.
viaticum, it. viaggio, Sp. viaje and Port, viagem, of
s.m., are borrowed fr. OProvenc. viatge. See via
and cp. viaticum. For the ending see suff. -age.

## voyage
voyage, intr. and tr. v. — F. voyager, fr. voyage.
See voyage, n.
Derivative: voyag-er, n.

## vraisemblable
vraisemblable, adj., seeming true. — F.,
'probable, likely', coined in imitation of L. verisi-
milis, 'haying the appearance of truth', fr. F.
vrai, 'true', and semblable, 'similar'. F. vrai
derives fr. OF. verai, fr. VL. *veracus, fr. L. virus,
'true'; see very, adj. F. semblable comes fr.
sembler, 'to resemble', later, 'to seem, appear',
fr. Late L. simildre, 4o be like, resemble', fr.
L. similis, 'like'; see similar and cp. verisimilar,

## vraisemblance
vraisemblance, п., the semblance of truth,
verisimilitude. — F., 'probability, likelihood', lit.
'verisimilitude'. For the first element see prec.
word, for the second see semblance.

## vrbaite
vrbaite, п., a thallium sulfosalt (mineral.) —
Named after the Czech mineralogist Karel
Vrba of Prague. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## vriddhi
vriddhi, п., change of α to d, e (fr. earlier αϊ) to di,
о (fr. earlier au) to du, ar to ar, through the
addition of an a element (OI. grammar) — 01.
vrddhi-, lit. 'growth, increase', rel. to vrddha·,
'grown up, old', vardhate, 'grows, increases',
urdhvah, "high*, fr. I.-E. base *weredh-, 'to grow, \
increase', whence also Gk. όρ&ός (for *fop&-
Ρός), 'straight, right, erect'. See ortho-,

## Vriesia
Vriesia, п., a genus of plants of the family Brome-
liaceae (бол) — Named after the Dutch

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:844 COLUMN:3 -->
botanist W. H. de Vriese (1806-62). For the ending
see Ist suff. -la.

## vrille
vrille, п., tail spin (pviation). — F., 'tendril;
gimlet, borer; tail spin', fr. earlier ville, fr. OF.
vellle, fr. L. viticula, 'a little vine; tendril',
dimin. of vitis; see viti-. The insertion of the r in
F. vrille is due to the influence of F. virer, 'to
turn, swing round'.

## vrouw
vrouw, п., a Dutch or S. African woman. — Du.
vrouw (S. Afr. Du. vrou). See frow,

## Vulcan
Vulcan, п., the god of fire in Roman mythology.
— L. Vulcdnus, Volcdnus, of Etruscan origin.
Cp. volcano.
Derivatives: Vulcanian (q.v.), Vulcan-ic, adj.,
vulcanite (q.v.), vulcanize (q.v.)

## Vnicanian
Vnicanian, adj., pertaining to Vulcan; pertaining
to metals. — Formed with suff. -an fr. L. Vul-
cdnius, fr. Vulcdnus. See prec. word.

## vulcanite
vulcanite, п., a kind of hard india rubber. —
Formed fr. Vulcan with subst. suff. -ite.

## vulcanize
vulcanize, tr. v., to treat (India rubber) with
sulfur and heat; intr. v., to undergo vulcanization.
— A hybrid coined by William Brockedon
(1789-1854), friend of the English chemist
Thomas Hancock (1786-1865) fr. Vnlcan and
-ize, a suff. of Greek origin. Cp. volcanize.
Derivatives: vulcaniz-ation, п., vulcaniz-er, n.

## vulgar
vulgar, adj. — ME., fr. L. volgdris, vulgaris,
'pertaining to the multitude, common, vulgar', fr.
valgus. See vulgus and adj. suff. -ar.
Derivatives: vulgar, п., vulgar-ian, п.,
vulgarism, п., vulgar-ity, п., vulgar-ize, tr. v.,
vulgarization, п., vulgar-iz-er, п., vulgar-ly, adv., vulgar-
ness, n.

## Vulgate
Vulgate, п., Latin translation of the Bible
prepared by the church father Jerome (about 340-
420). — ML. vulgdta (editio), lit. 'the popular,
current, edition', fern. pp. of L. volgdre, vulgdre,
'to make general, common*, fr. volgus, vulgus.
See next word and adj. suff. -ate.

## vulgns
vulgns, п., the common people. — L. volgus,
vulgus, 'the great mass, the multitude, the
people', cogn. with OI. vargah 'division, group*,
MBret. gwaVch, 'abundance', W. gwala,
'sufficiency, enough'. Cp. vulgar, Vulgate, divulge.

## vulnerable
vulnerable, adj., 1) that can be wounded; 2) open
to attack— Late L. vulnerdbilis, fr. L. vulnerdre,
4o wound', fr. volmts, vulnus, 'a wound', which
is cogn. with Gk. ουλή (for *foXvoc or *FoX-
σ«), 'wound, scar', W. gweli (for *woliyd),
'wound', from. I.-E. base *wel-, 'to tear',
whence also vellere, 'to pluck, tear'. See velli-
cate and cp. vulture. Cp. also parulis. For the
ending see suff. -able.
Derivatives: vulnerabil-xty, n., vulnerable-ness,
п., vulnerabl-y, adv.

## vulnerary
vulnerary, adj., used for healing wounds. — L.
vulnerdrius, 'pertaining to wounds, used for
wounds', fr. vulnus, gen. vulneris. See prec.
word and adj. suff. -ary.
Derivative: vulnerary, п., a remedy for healing
wounds.

## Vulpecula
Vulpecula, п., the Little Fox (astron.) — L.,
dimin. of vulpes, 'fox'. See next word and -cula.

## Vulpes
Vulpes, п., a genus of animals, the red fox (zool.)
— L. volpes, vulpes, 'fox', of uncertain
etymology. It is perh. cogn. with Gk. άλώπηξ, 'fox',
OI. lopdsah, 'jackal, fox', Arm. aiues, 'fox'.
Lith. lape, 'fox', vilpiS^s, 'wild cat'. Cp. alopecia,
Alopccurus.

## vulpicide
vulpicide, п., a person who kills a fox. —
Compounded of L. vulpes, gen. vulpts, 'fox', and L.
-cida, 'killer', fr. caedere, 'to kill'. See Vulpes and
-cide, 'killer'.

## vulpicide
vulpicide, п., the killing of a fox. — Compounded
of L. vulpes, gen. vulpis, 'a fox', and L. -ciuium,
'killing', fr. caedere, 'to kill*. See Vulpes and
-cide, 'killing'.

## vulpine
vulpine, adj., 1) pertaining to a fox; 2) foxlike. —
L. vulpinus, 'pertaining to, or resembling, a fox,
crafty', fr. vulpes, 'fox'. See Vulpes and -ine
(representing L. -inus).

## vnlpinism
vnlpinism, п., craftiness (rare). — Formed with
suff. -Ism fr. L. vulpinus. See prec. word.

## vulpinite
vulpinite, п., a variety of anhydrite (mineral.) —
Named after Vulpino in Lombardy. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## vuisellum
vuisellum, п., a forceps with serrated blades

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:845 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: VULTURE | 818 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:845 COLUMN:1 -->
{surgery). — ModL., fr. L. volsella, vulsella, 'a
kind of pincers', dimin. of *volsa, 'a tool for
tearing", which stands in gradational
relationship to vellere, 'to tear'. See vellicate and cp.
next word.

## vulture
vulture, n.— ME. vultur y fr. OF. voltour, voutour
(= F. vautour), fr. L. voltur, vultur (whence also
Ruman. vultur, It. avoltojo, Proven?, voltor, Sp.
buitre, Port, abutrt), lit. meaning 'the tearing
(bird)', and in gradational relationship to vellere,
'to tear'. See vellicate and cp. prec. word and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:845 COLUMN:2 -->
vulnerable. Cp. also wolf.

## vulturine
vulturine, adj., pertaining to, or resembling, a
vulture. — L. vulturinus, 'pertaining to a
vulture, vulturelike', fr. vuliur. See prec. word and
-ine (representing L. -fnus).

## vulturous
vulturous, adj., 1) resembling a vulture; 2)
rapacious. — Formed with suff. -ous fr. L. vultur.
See vulture.

## vulv-
vulv-, form of vulvo- before a vowel.

## vulva
vulva, n. — L. volva, vulva, 'womb, matrix', of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:845 COLUMN:3 -->
uncertain origin. It means perh. lit. 'a covering,
wrapper*, and is cogn. with 01. ulvam, ulbam,
'womb, vulva', and rel. to L. volvere, *to roll'.
See volute and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: vulv-art vulv-ate, adjs.

## vulvitis
vulvitis, п., inflammation of the vulva (med.) —
A Medical L. hybrid coined fr. L. vulva (see
prec. word) and -itte, a suff. of Greek origin.

## vulvo-
vulvo-, before a vowel vulv-, combining form
denoting the vulva. — See vulva.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:846 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:846 COLUMN:1 -->

## wabble
wabble, v. — See wobble,

## wack
wack, also whack, п., a whacky person. — Prob.
back formation fr. wacky,

## wacke
wacke, п., a rock resembling sandstone. — G.
Wacke, fr. MHG. каске, 'a large stone', fr.
OHG. wacko, 'gravel', which prob. derives fr.
OHG. wegan, 'to move' (see weigh); a miner's
word adopted as a geological term by the
German geologist Abraham Gottiob Werner
(1750-1817).

## wacky
wacky, also whacky, adj., eccentric, irrational. —
Of uncertain origin,

## wad
wad, п., a little mass of soft material. — Du.
watten (whence also G. Watte), fr. ML. wadda
(whence also F. ouate, It. ovate, ovatta), fr.
Arab, bmin, pi. bata'in, 'lining', a derivative of
batn, 'belly, interior', which is rel. to Heb.
beten, Aram, bitna, 'belly, womb, interior',
Akkad. butnu, 'interior'. — Swed. vadd, 'wad', is
an English loan word. Cp. basan.
Derivatives: wad, tr. v., wadd-er, п., wadd-ing,
п., wadd-y, adj.

## wad
wad, п., an impure earthy ore of manganese. —
Of uncertain origin.

## waddle
waddle, intr. v., to walk with a swaying motion,
as a duck; to move clumsily. — Prob. freq. of
wade.
Derivatives: waddle, п., waddl-er, п., waddl-ing,
adj., waddl-ing-ly, adv.

## waddy
waddy, п., a wooden war club of the Australian
aborigines. — An Australian native word.
Derivative: waddy, tr. v., to beat with a waddy.

## wade
wade, intr. and tr. v. — ME. waden, fr. OE.
wadan, 'to go, advance; to advance in water,
wade', re], to ON. чада, Dan. vade, Swed. vada,
OFris. wada, MLG., MDu., Du. waden, OHG.
watan, MHG., G. waten, 'to wade', and cogn.
with L. vadere, 'to go*, vadum, 'shoal, ford', vad-
Sre, 'to wade';It. guado, F. gue, 'ford', areTeut.
loan words. See vade mecum and cp. waddle.
Derivatives: wade, п., the act of wading, wad-
able, adj., wad-er, п., wad-ing, adj., wad-ing-ly,
adv.

## wadi
wadi, wndy, п., water course; oasis. — Arab.
wadi, 'valley, bed of a river, water course'
(whence also F. oued), prop, partic. of wada, 'it
flowed'.

## Wafd
Wafd, п., name of the Egypt, national party
founded in 1918 by Saad Zaghlul. — Arab.
wafd, 'deputation', fr. wafada, 'he came,
arrived'.
Derivative: Wafd-ist, n.

## wafer
wafer, n. — ME. wafre, wafer, 'a thin cake', fr.
ONF. walfre, waufre (F. gaufre), 'honeycomb;
wafer', fr. Frankish *wafel, which is rel. toMDu.
wafel, Du. wafel, 'wafer', OHG. waba, MHG.,
G. wabe, 'honeycomb', and to OE. wefan,
OHG. weban, 'to weave'. See weave and cp.
waffle, goffer, gopher, 'a rodent'.
Derivatives: wafer, tr. v., wafer-y, adj.

## waffle
waffle, п., a crisp cake cooked over the Are in a
waffle iron. — Du. wafel, fr. MDu. wafel. See
prec. word.

## waft
waft, tr. v., to carry lightly through the air or
over water. — Back formation fr. obsol. wafter,
'a convoy boat', fr. Du. wackier, 'watcher', fr.
wacht, 'watch'. See wake and cp. watch.
Derivatives: waft, п., tr. and intr. v., waft-age,
п., waft-er, п., waft-y, adj.

## wag
wag, tr. v., to cause to move quickly back and
forth; intr. v., to move quickly back and forth.
— ME. waggen, from the stem of OE. wagian,
'to move, to wag', and to ON. vaga, 'to wag,
waddle', vagga, 'cradle', Swed. vagga, Dan.
vugge, of s.m., Swed. vagga, Dan. vugge, 'to
rock a cradle', MHG. wacken, 'to totter, shake',
Norw. vagga, OE. wecgan, OHG. weggen,
Goth, wagjan, 'to wag', OE. wegan, etc., 'to
move'. See weigh and words there referred to
and cp. esp. waggle, wagon, wain and the first

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:846 COLUMN:2 -->
element in waileyed.
Derivatives: wag, п., the act of wagging, wagg-
er, п., wagg-ing, adj., wagg-y, adj.

## wag
wag, п., a roguish fellow (used playfully). —
Short for wag-halter, 'rascal', lit. 'a person
swinging in a halter', i.e. 'hanged'. See wag,
v.
Derivatives: wagg-ery, п., wagg-ish, adj., wagg-
ish-ly, adv., wagg-ish-ness, n.

## wage
wage, n. — ME. wage, fr. ONF. wage
(corresponding to OF. and F. gage), fr. Frankish* wadi,
which is rel. to Goth, wadi, OE. wedd, 'pledge'.
Cp. It. gaggio, Sp. and Port, gage, which
are French loan words, and see wed. Cp. also
vadium, vas, gage, 'pledge'.
Derivatives: wage-less, adj.

## wage
wage, tr. and intr. v. — ME. wagen, fr. ONF. wa-
gier, corresponding to OF. gagier (F. gager), fr.
ONF. wage, n. See wage, n.
Derivative: wag-ed, adj.

## wager
wager, n. — ME. wageoure, wager, fr. ONF. wa-
geure (corresponding to OF. and F. gageure), fr.
wagier (OF. gagier). See wage, v.
Derivatives: wager, tr. and intr. v., wager-er, п.,
wager-ing, adj.

## waggle
waggle, intr. and tr. v. — Freq. of wag. Cp. MLG.
MDu., Du. waggelen, dial. Norw. and Swed.
vagla, 'to waggle', OHG. wagon, 'to move,
shake' (whence the intensive MHG. wacken, of
s.m., and the freq. MHG., G. wackeln, 'to totter,
shake'. Cp. also wiggle.
Derivatives: waggle, п., waggl-ing, adj., waggl-
ing-ly, adv.

## wagon
wagon, also waggon, n. — Du. wagen. See wain.
Derivatives: wag(g)on, tr. and intr. v., wag(g)on-
er, п., wag[g)onette (q.v.)

## wagonette
wagonette, wnggonette, n. — A hybrid coined fr.
wagon and surf, -ette,

## wngtail
wngtail, n. — Compounded of wag and tail; so
called from the wagging motion of its tail.

## WahabI
WahabI, Wahabee, п., a follower of the
Mohammedan reformer Abdu'l Wahhab (died in 1790).
— Arab, wahhabt, formed from the PN. Wahhab
with the gentilic suff. -i, which is rel, to Heb. -i,
a suff. of the same force.

## Wahlenbergia
Wahlenbergia, п., a genus of plants of the bluebell
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the
Swedish botanist GSran Wahlenberg (1780-1851).
For the ending see 1 st suff. -la.

## waif
waif, п., i) anything found by chance; 2) a stray
person or animal, esp. a homeless child. — ME.
wetf, waif, fr.ONF. waif, corresponding to OF.
golf, 'something lost and not claimed' (cp. ML.
waivium, 'thing thrown away by a thief in flight')
prob. of Scand. origin; cp. ON. veif, 'something
flapping about', ix.veifa, *to wave', and see waive.
Derivative: waif, tr. v.

## wall
wall, tr. and intr. v. — ME. weilen, wailen, fr. ON.
vsela, vala, 'to lament', fr. vx, 'woe*. See woe.
Derivatives: wail, п., wail-er, п., wail-ful, adj.;
wail-ing, n. and adj., wail-ing-ly, adv.

## wain
wain, п., a wagon. — ME. wain, fr. OE. wsegen,
wsegn, wsen, rel. to OS., OHG. wagan, ΟΝ.,
Swed. vagn, Dan. vogn, OFris. vein, MLG.,
MDu., Du., MHG., G. wagen, and cogn. with
OI. vahanam, 'vessel, ship', Gk. δχος (for
*ίόχος), OSIav. vozu, 'carriage', Lith. vaiis, 'a
small sledge', Olr. fin (for weghno-), 'carriage,
cart', W. gwain, of s.m. All these words are
derivatives of I.-E. base "wegh-, 'to move, carry'.
See weigh and cp. wagon, which is a doublet of
wain. Cp. also the first element in next word.

## wainscot
wainscot, п., modern panels lining the walls of
rooms. — ME. waynescote, fr. MLG. wagen-
schot, which is prob. compounded of wagen,
'wagon', and sckot, 'shot, crossbar, partition'.
See prec. word and shut.
Derivatives: wainscot, tr. v., wainscot{t)-ing, n.

## waist
waist, n. — ME. wast, 'waist', lit. 'growth' (the
waist being regarded as the part where the body

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:846 COLUMN:3 -->
is best developed), rel. to OE. wxstm, ON. voxtr,
Swed. vdxt, OHG. wahst, 'growth, increase',
Goth, wahstus, 'stature', lit. 'grow.th', and to
OE. weaksan, weaxan, 'to grow'. See wax, 'to
grow'.
Derivative: waist-ed, adj.

## wait
wait, intr. and tr. v. — ME. waiten, 'to watch', fr.
ONF. waitier, corresponding to OF. guaitier,
gaitier, 'to watch' (whence F. guetter, 'to watch,
lie in wait for'), fr. Frankish *wahton, which is
rel. to OS., OHG. wahta, Du. wacht, MHG.
wahte, G. Wacht, 'watch', and to OHG. wah-
hen, wahhon, OE. wacian, 'to be awake'. See
wake, v., watch, and cp. wait, 'singer'.
Derivatives: wait, п., the act of waiting,
waiting, n. and adj., wait-ing-ly, adv.

## wait
wait, п., one of a band of persons singing
Christmas carols. — ME. wait, 'watchman', fr. ONF.
waite, corresponding to OF. guaite, gaite, 'a
watching; watchman' (whence F. guet, 'a
watching'), which is either a back formation fr. OF.
guaiter, gaitier, or a loan word fr. Frankish
•wahta, 'a watching', which is rel. to OHG.
wahta. See wait, v.

## waiter
waiter, n. — ME. wattere, fr. waiten, 'to watch,
wait'. See wait, v., and agential suff. -er.

## waive
waive, tr. v., to give up, to forgo. — ME. weiven,
waiven, fr. AF. weywer, corresponding to OF.
gaiver, guesver, guever, 'to give up, abandon', fr.
gaif, 'abandoned', which is of Scand. origin. Cp.
ON. veifa, 'to wave, vibrate', which derives fr.
I.-E. base *weip-, 'to move to and fro', and see
waif. Cp. also the collateral base *weib-, whence
L. vibrare, 'to shake, vibrate', and see vibrate.

## waiver
waiver, п., the act of waiving (law). — AF.
weyver, prop, an infln.; see waive. For the subst.
use of the irrfin. in legal terminology cp.
attainder and words there referred to.

## wake
wake, intr. v., to be awake; tr. v., to rouse from
sleep. — A blend of ME. waken, fr. OE. wacan,
'to wake', and ME. wakien, fr. OE. wacian, a
var. of wseccan, 'to be awake, watch'; rel. to OS.
wakon, ΟΝ., Swed. vaka, Dan. vaage, OFris.
waka, Du. waken,OHG. wahhen, wahkon,MHG.,
G. wachen, 'to be awake', Goth. wakan,'to watch',
OE. weccan, 'to waken' (tr.), OS. wekkian, ON.
vekja, Swed. vdcka, 'to waken', Du. wecken,
'to preserve', OHG. wecchan, later wecken,
MHG., G. wecken, Goth, us-wakjan, 'to waken'
(tr.), OE. wacor, 'watchful', ON. vakr, 'lively,
awake', Dan. vakker, 'vigorous, fine, brave',
Swed. vacker, 'beautiful', MLG. wacker, 'awake
lively', Du. wakker, 'awake', OHG. wahhar,
MHG. wacker, 'awake, watchful', G. wacker,
'valiant, honest'. These words are cogn. with
OI. vajah, 'force, swiftness, race, prize', vdjdyati,
'drives on', vdjrab, 'Indra's thunderbolt', Toch.
A wac, 'combat, battle', L. vegere, vigire, 'to be
live, be active, quicken', vigil, 'awake, wakeful',
vigor, 'liveliness, activity'. Cp. awake, awaken,
waft, wait, watch, bivouac. Cp. also surveillance,
vajra, vedette, vegetable, vegetate, vigil, vigor.

## wake
wake, п., watching, vigil, watch over a dead
person. — ME., fr. waken, wakien, 'to wake*. Cp.
OE. -wacu (only in nihtwacu, 'night watch'), ON.
vaka, LG. wake, and see wake, v., Du. waak,
'watch, vigil', OHG. wacha, MHG., G. wache,
'watch; guard*.
Derivatives: wake, tr. v., to hold a wake over,
wake-fid, adj., wake-ful-ly, adv., wake-ful-ness,
n.

## wake
wake, п., the track left by a moving ship. — ON.
vok, 'a hole in the ice', rel. to Swed. vak, Dan.
vaage, of s.m., and to ON. vokr, 'moist, damp',
and cogn. with OI. uksati, 'sprinkles', Gk.
υγρός, 'moist', L. uvidus, 'wet', итог,
'moisture'. See humor and cp. words there referred to.

## wnken
wnken, intf. v., to be awakened; tr. v., to arouse.
— Orig. an intr. v., fr. ME. waknen, wakenen,
fr. OE. wsecnan, wxcnian, 'to rise, be born'.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:847 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: WALACH | 820 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:847 COLUMN:1 -->
formed with suff. -n fr. wacan, 'to arise*; cp. ON.
vakna, Goth, ga-waknan, 'to become awake',
and see wake, 'to be awake'. Cp. also awaken.

## Walach
Walach, also Wallach, n. — G. Wallache, fr.
OSlav. Vlachu, fr. OHG. Walk, 'one speaking
a Romance, i.e. foreign, language'. See Welsh.
Derivatives: Walach-ian, Wallach-ian, adj. and
n.

## Waldenses
Waldenses, n. pi., a Christian sect named after its
founder Peter Waldo of Lyons.

## Waldensian
Waldensian, adj. and n. — Formed from prec.
word with suff. -ian.

## waldhorn
waldhorn, п., a hunting horn. — G., lit. 'forest
horn', fr. Wald, 'forest', and Horn, 'horn'. The
first element is rel. to OE. wald, 'forest'; see
wold. The second element is rel. to ,OE. horn,
'horn'; see horn.

## Waldsteinia
Waldsteinia, п., a genus of plants of the rose
family (bot.) — ModL., named after the Austrian
botanist Count Franz Adam Waldstein-War-
tenberg(]759-1873). For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## wale
wale, п., a mark made on the skin by a whip; a
weal. — ME. wale, fr. OE. walu, 'ridge; mark
on fiesh', rel. to LG. wale, 'weal', OFris. walu,
'rod', ON. voir, 'a round piece of wood', Goth.
walus, 'a staff, stick', the second element in wyrt-
walu, wyrt-wala, Du. wortel, OHG. wurzala,
MHC, G. wurzel, 'root', lit. 'plant stick', Fris.,
LG. walen, 'to roll', ON. valr, 'round', and cogn.
with L. vallus (for *wal-nos), 'stake', Lith. valus,
'round'. All these words derive fr. I.-E. base
*wal-, *wel-, 'to turn, bend, twist, roll'. See
volute and cp. weal, 'mark on fiesh', and the
second element in gnnwale. Cp. also vallum, wnil.

## Walhalla
Walhalla, n. — See Valhalla.

## walk
walk, intr. v., to move about on foot, go; tr. v.,
to go through or over. — ME. walken and
walkien, 'to walk' (prob. meaning orig. 'to roll
along'), fr. OE. wealcan, 'to roll, toss' (tr. and
intr.), resp. wealcian, 'to roll up, muffle up'
(intr.), rel. to ON. valka, 'to drag about', Dan.
valke, Swed. valka, 'to full', MDu. walken, 'to
knead, press, full', Du. walken, 'to work or felt
(a hat)', OHG. walchan, 'to knead' (whence
MHG. walken, 'to knead, full', G. walken, 'to
full'), fr. I.-E. *walg-, whence also OI. valgati,
'he jumps with joy', valga, 'bridle, rein', and
prob. also L. valgus, 'bowlegged'; cp. valgus.
OF. gauchier and It. gualcare, 'to full', are Teut.
loan words. I.-E. *walg- is an enlarged form of
base * wal-, 'to turn, bend, twist, roll'. See volute
and cp. gauche. Cp. also wale.
Derivatives: walk, п., walk-able, adj., walk-er,
п., walk-ing, adj. and n.

## walk
walk, tr. v., to full (Brit.) — ME. walken, fr.
MDu-, 'to knead, press, full'. See walk, 'to go'.

## walkie-talkie
walkie-talkie, п., also walky-talky, a portable
receiving and transmitting radio set.

## Walkyrie
Walkyrie, n. — See Valkyrie.

## wall
wall, n. — ME., fr. OE. weall, rel. to OS., MLG-,
LG., MDu., Du. wal, MHG. wall, wal, G. Wall,
'rampart', fr. L. vallum (for *wal-nom), 'a wall
or rampart with palisades; wall, rampart'. See
vallum, and cp. interval.
Derivatives: wall, tr. and intr. v., wall-ed, adj.,
wall-ing, adj. and n.

## walln
walln, wallah, п., a person employed in a certain
business; fellow, man (Anglo-Indian). — Hind.
-walu, an agential suff. with the force of L. -Srius
(see -ary and -er), generally used in the sense of
'possessor, owner, man'. Cp. the second element
in boxwallah and in topiwallah.

## wallaby
wallaby, п., a kind of small kangaroo. — Native
Australian.

## Wallach
Wallach, n. — See Walach.

## wallaroo
wallaroo, п., a kind of large kangaroo. — Native
Australian.

## wallet
wallet, п., a bag. — ME. walet, prob. metathesis
of ME. watel, 'basket, bag'. See wattle.

## waileye
waileye, п., eye with a whitish cornea. — Back
formation fr. walleyed.

## walleyed
walleyed, adj. — ME. wawil-eghed, fr. ON. vagi-
eygr, 'walleyed', lit. 'having a beam in the eye',
fr. vagi, 'roost, beam; beam in the eye' (name of
a disease), and eigr, 'eyed, having eyes', fr. auga,
'eye'. ON. vagi is rel. to ON. vaga, 'to wag,
waddle', vog, 'lever', vega, 'to move, carry', and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:847 COLUMN:2 -->
cogn. with Gk. δχλεύς (for 'ίοχλεύς), 'lever',
όχλεϊν (for *Γ"οχλεΐν), 'to move', L. vectis,
'lever, handspike', vehere, 'to carry, convey', fr.
I.-E. base *wegh-, 'to move, carry'; see weigh
and cp. vectis. For the etymology of ON. auga,
'eye', see eye.

## Wallichia
Wallichia, п., a genus of palms (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the Danish botanist Nathaniel
Wallich (1768-1854). For the ending see 1st suff.
-ia.

## wailoon
wailoon, n. and adj. — MF. Wallon, lit. 'foreigner'
of Teut. origin. Cp. OHG. walk, 'foreigner', and
see Welsh.

## wallop
wallop, intr. v., 1) to move heavily; 2) to gallop;
tr. v., to beat, thrash. — ME. walopen, fr. ONF.
waloper, corresponding to OF. (= F.) galoper.
See gallop.
Derivatives: wallop, п., wallop-er, п.,
walloping, adj. and n.

## wallop
wallop, intr. v., to boil quickly and noisily (Scot.
and dial.) — Prob. of imitative origin. Cp. the
second element in pot-walioper.

## waliow
waliow, intr. v. — ME. walwen, 'to turn, roll', fr.
OE. walwian, wealwian, rel. to Goth, af-walwjan,
'to roll', waltjan, 'to roll, wallow', and cogn. with
L. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and cp. waltz.
Derivatives: wallow, п., wallow-er, п.,
wallowing, n.

## walnut
walnut, n. — ME. walnote, walnot, fr. OE.
wealkhnutu, lit. 'Celtic (or foreign) nut', fr.
wealk, 'Celtic, foreign', and hnut, 'nut'; rel. to
ON. valhnot, Dan. valned, Swed. valnot, MLG.
walnut, MDu. walnote, Du. walnoot. (G. Wal-
nufi is a LG. loan word); see Welsh and nut.
Cp. the Late Latin name of the walnut: nux
Gallica, lit. 'Gaulish nut', rendered in MHG. by
walhisch пиз, 'Welsh nut'.

## Walpurgis Night
Walpurgis Night, witches' festival on the Brocken
on the eve of May 1. — G. Walpurgisnacht, lit.
'the night of Walpurgis', so named after St.
Walpurgis (also called St. Walbwga, Walpurga),
an English missionary, who died at Heidenheim
about 780.

## walpurgUe
walpurgUe, п., a hydrous bismuth uranium
arsenate (mineral.) — Named after Walpurgis vein
in Freiberg, Saxony. For the ending see subst.
suff. -ite.

## walrus
walrus, n. — Du., fr. Swed. vallross, fr. ON.
hrossvalr (cp. OE. horshwxl), lit. 'horse whale',
fr. hross, 'horse', and hvalr, 'whale'. Cp. Dan.,
Norw. hvalros and see whale and horse.

## Walter
Walter, masc. PN. — ONF. Waltier,
corresponding to OF. Gualtier, Gautier (F. Gautier), of G.
origin. Cp. OHG. Waltkari, Walthere, lit. 'ruler
of the army', which is compounded of OHG.
waltan (whence MHG., G. walteri), 'to rule', and
OHG. Jiari, heri (whence MHG. her, G. Heer),
'host, army'. See wield and harry and cp.
Harold, herald.

## waltz
waltz, п., a dance performed to music in triple
time. — G. Walzer, fr. walzen, 'to roll, revolve,
turn one's feet in dancing', fr. MHG., fr. OHG.
walzan, 'to roll', which is rel. to ON. velta, of
s.m.; fr. I.-E. base *wel-, 'to turn, bend, twist,
roll'. See volute and cp. valse. Cp. also wnliow,
welter.
Derivatives: waltz, intr. and tr. v., waltz-er, n.

## wamble
wamble, intr. v., 1) to feel nausea (obsol.); 2) to
turn about; 3) to move unsteadily; to stagger.
— ME. wamlen, rel. to Dan. vamle, 'to feel
nausea', ON. vama, 'qualm, seasickness', fr.
I.-E. base *wem-, 'to vomit', whence also L. vo-
rnere, 'to vomit'. See vomit.
Derivatives: wamble, п., wambl-ing, adj., wambl-
ing-ly, adv.

## wampee
wampee, п., an Asiatic tree, Clausena vampi. —
Chinese hwang pi, lit. 'yellow skin'.

## wampum
wampum, п., beads made of shells, worn by N.
Amer. Indians as money or as an ornament. —
Lit. 'white string of money', fr. Algonquian
wampompeag, which is compounded of wampi,
wab, 'white', ompe, 'string', and pi! suff. -ag. Cp.
peag.

## wan
wan, adj., pale. — ME., 'faint, pale', fr. OE.
wann, wan, 'livid, dark', perh. rel. to OE. wan,
'wanting, deficient', and to E. wane, want.
Derivatives: wan, п., wann-ess, wan, intr. and tr.
v., wan-ly, adv., wann-ess, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:847 COLUMN:3 -->

## wand
wand, п., a slender rod. — ME. wond, fr. ON.
vondr, 'rod', which is rel. to Goth, wandus, 'rod',
-waddjus, 'wall', OS., Du. wand, OHG., MHG.
want, G. Wand, 'wall', orig. 'wickerwork for
making walls', fr. Teut. base "wend-, 'to turn,
twist, bend', whence also OE. windan, 'to wind'.
See wind, 'to turn'. For the sense development
of OS., wand, etc., 'wall', cp. F. batir, 'to build',
fr. Frankish 'bastjan, 'to bind with bast', which
is rel. to E. bast (q.v.)

## wander
wander, intr. and tr. v. — ME. wandren, wanderen,
fr. OE. wandrian, 'to wander', which is rel. to
OFris. wondria, MLG-, MDu. wanderen, MHG-,
G. wandern, 'to wander', OS. wandlon, OFris.
wantelia, MLG., MDu., Du. wandelen, OHG.
wantalon, MHG. wandelen, G. wandeln, 'to walk,
wander', and to OE. wendan, 'to turn', windan,
'to wind'. See wend and wind, 'to turn', and cp.
prec. word. Cp. also Vandal, Andalusian.
Derivatives: wander-er, п., wander-ing, n. and
adj., wander-ing-ly, adv., wander-ing-ness, n.

## wanderoo
wanderoo, п., a large monkey of Ceylon. —
Singhalese vanduru, fr. OI. vdnarah, 'monkey'
(whence also Hind, bandar), lit. 'forest-dweller',
fr. vanar, 'in the wood, in the forest', locative of
vanah, tree, forest, wood', which is rel. to
Avestic vand-, ModPers. bun, 'tree'.

## wane
wane, intr. v., to decrease (said esp. of the moon).
— ME. wanien, wanen, fr. OE. wanian, 'to
diminish, decline, fade, wane', rel. to OS.
wanon, ON. vana, OFris. wania, OHG. wanon,
'to wane'. These verbs derive from an Old Teut.
adj. appearing in OE. wan, ON. vanr, OS.,
OFris., OHG., MHG. wan, Goth, wans,
'wanting, deficient', Goth, wan, 'lack', G. Wahnsinn,
'madness', lit. 'lack of understanding', and cogn.
with L. vanus, 'empty, vain'. See vain and cp.
wan, want, wanton.
Derivatives: wane, n. (q.v.), wan-ed, adj., wane-
y, wan-y, adj.

## wane
wane, п., the act of waning. — ME., fr. wanen, 'to
wane'. See wane, v.
Derivative: wane-less, adj.

## wangle
wangle, tr. and intr. v., to obtain something by
trickery. — Prob. rel. to wankle (q.v.)
Derivatives: wangle, п., wangl-er, n.

## wangtooth
wangtooth, п., a molar tooth (obsol. exc. dial.) —
The first element of this compound derives fr.
OE. wang, wange, 'cheek', which is rel. to OS.,
OHG. wang, wanga, ON. vangi, Dan. vange,
MDu. wangke, MHG., G. wange, 'cheek', fr.
I.-E. base *wa-n-q-, a nasalized var. of base
*waq-, 'to be curved'; It. guancia, 'cheek', is a
Teut. loan word. See vacillate. For the second
element see tooth.

## wanion
wanion, п., a plague (a word used in imprecations
(arckaic). — Fr. ME. waniand, 'the waning
moon' (regarded as unluck), prop, north, pres.
part, of wanien, fr. OE. wanian, 'to wane'. See
wane, v.

## wankle
wankle, wankly, adj., unsteady, fickle (now dial.
English) — ME. wankel, fr. OE. wancol, rel. to
Du. wankel, OHG. wanchal, 'fickle' (whence
MHG. wankel, of s.m., wankelmuot, G. Wankel-
mut, 'fickleness, inconstancy', G. wankelmiitig,
'fickle, inconstant'), ON. vakka, OHG. wankon,
MHG., G. wanken, 'to stagger, totter'. See
wink and cp. wonky,

## want
want, n. — ME., fr. ON. vant, neut. of vanr,
'wanting, deficient', which is rel. to OE. wanian,
'to diminish'. See wane, v., and cp. words there
referred to. For a similar use of the ON. neuter
suff. -t cp. scant. In later English the verb want
is derived directly from the verb want.
Derivative: want-less, adj.

## want
want, tr. and intr. v. — ME. wanten, fr. ON.
vanta, 'to want', fr. vanr, 'wanting'. See want,
v.
Derivatives: want-ing, adj., want-ing-ly, adv.,
want-ing-ness, n.

## wanton
wanton, adj. — ME. wantowen, wantoun, wanton,

## formed fr. ME. priv. pref. wan-
formed fr. ME. priv. pref. wan-, 'wanting,
lacking, deficient, without', and pp. towen, fr. OE.
togen, pp. of tion, 'to draw, pull; to educate'.
The first element is rel. to OE. wan, 'wanting,
deficient'; see wane, v. For the second element
see tow, 'to draw'. Hence wanton lit. means 'ill-
bred'. For sense development cp. G. ungezogen.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:848 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 821 | WART -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:848 COLUMN:1 -->
'ill-bred, rude, naughty' (ft. priv. pref. tin- and
gezogen, pp. of Ziehen, 'to draw', which is rel.
to OE. teon, 'to draw').
Derivatives: wanton, n. and intr. v., wanton-ly,
adv., wanton-ness, n.

## wap
wap, tr. and intr. v., to strike (now dial.) — ME.
wappen, prob. of imitative origin. Cp. whop.
Derivative: wap, n.

## wapentake
wapentake, п., name of a division in the counties
Yorkshire, Lincolnshire, Leicestershire,
Northamptonshire, Nottinghamshire and a part of
Derbyshire, corresponding to a hundred in other
counties. — ME., fr. Late OE. wxpengetsec, fr.
ON. vapnatak, lit. 'touching of weapons', fr.
vapna, gen. pi. of vapn, 'weapon', and taka, 'to
touch' (see weapon and take); so called from the
custom of shaking lances in token of consent..
Cp. Tacitus, Germania XI.

## wapiti
wapiti, п., a North American elk, Cervus
canadensis. — Of Algonquian origin.

## war
war, ri. — ME., fr. Late OE. werre, fr. ONF.
werre (OF., F. guerre), fr. OHG. werra,
'confusion, strife, quarrel' [whence OHG. werran, fir-
werran (MHG. werren, verwerren, G. verwir-
ren)], 'to confuse, perplex', which is rel. to ON.
vorr, 'stroke of the oar'; prob. fr. I.-E. base
*wers-, 'to sweep, drag', whence also L. ver-
rere, 'to sweep, trail, draggle', OSlav. vruchg,
vriSti, 'to thrash', vrachu, 'thrashing', Hitt.
warshiya-, 'to plow' (or 'to reap'). See verricule
and cp. gnerrilla. Cp. also worse.
Derivatives: war, warr-er, n.

## waratah
waratah, п., an Australian shrub. — Native
Australian.

## warble
warble, tr. and intr. v., to sing with trills. — ME.
werblen, werbelen, fr. ONF. werbler (= OF.
guerbler), of Teut. origin. Cp. Du. wervelen, G.
wirbein, 'to whirl, roll, warble', Du. wervel,
'vertebra', OHG. wirbil, 'whirlwind', MHG.
wirbel, 'crown of the head, top, summit', G.
Wirbel, 'whirl; whirlpool; whirlwind; crown
of the head; tuning peg; vertebra', ON. hvirfill,
'circle, ring, crown of the head, top, summit'.
See whir] and cp. wharf.
Derivatives: warble, п., the act of warbling,
warbl-er, п., warbl-ing, n.

## warble
warble, п., a small hard tumor on horses or cattle.
— Of uncertain origin.

## warble fly
warble fly, a fly of the family Oestridae. — So called
because its larvae cause warbles. See prec. word.

## ward
ward, tr. v., to fend off, protect. — ME. wardien,
fr. OE. weardian, 'to keep, guard', rel. to OS.
warden, 'to guard, keep', ON. varda, Swed.
varda, 'to guard', OFris. wardia, MDu. waerden,
'to take care of, OHG. wartin, 'to guard, look
out for, expect', MHG., G. warten, 'to wait,
wait on, nurse, tend'. Cp. ONF. warder, F,
guarder, 'to keep, preserve, watch over', It. guar-
dare, Sp. and Port, guardar, of s.m., which all
are Teut. loan words. Cp, also next word,
award, guard, regard, reward, warden and the
first element in wardrobe. The above mentioned
Teut. words derive ft. l.-E. base *wer-, 'to guard,
keep safe, protect', whence also OE. warian, 'to
guard, watch over'. See ware, 'alert', and cp.
words there referred to.

## ward
ward, п., one who guards (obsol.) — ME., fr. OE.
weard, masc. 'a watchman, sentry, guardian',
rel. to OS. ward, ON. vordr, OHG. wart
(almost only in compounds), MHG., G. wart,
Goth, -wards (only in compounds), 'watchman,
keeper", and to OE. weard, fem. 'keeping watch,
guarding, protection'. See ward, 'the act of
guarding', and cp. the second element in
Edward, lord,

## ward
ward, п., the act of guarding. — ME., fr. OE.
weard, fem. 'a keeping watch, guarding,
protection', rel. to OS. warda, 'watch', ON. vardi,
varda, 'watchtbwer', MDu. waerde, 'watch-
tower', Dan. varde, Swed. vard, 'care, nursing',
OHG. warta, MHG., G. wane, 'a watching,
watchtower'. F. garde, Sp. guarda, 'custody,
guard', are Teut. loan words. See ward, v. and
cp. gnard. Cp. also prec. word.

## -ward
-ward, adj. and adv. suff. indicating direction. —
ME. -werd, -ward, fr. OE. -weard, rel. to
OS., OFris. -ward, ON. -verdr, and cogn.
with Olr. frith, 'against', Toch. В wrattsai.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:848 COLUMN:2 -->
'against', fr. I.-E. base "wer-, 'to turn, twist',
whence also L. vertere, pp. versus, 'to turn'. See
version and cp. versus. Cp. also toward. The -s
in ОЁ. -weardes, OHG. -wertes, etc., is the sufT.
of the adverbial gen. See adv. suff. -s.

## warden
warden, п., keeper, watchman. — ME. wardein,
fr. ONF. wardein, fr. warder, 'to ward, keep',
which is of Teut. origin. Cp. OS. warden, OE.
weardian, 'to guard, keep', and see ward, v.
ONF. wardein, corresponds to AF. gardein,
OF., F. gardien. Cp. G. Wardein, 'assayer;
judge', which is also a loan word fr. ONF.
wardein. Cp. also guardian, which is a doublet
of warden.

## warden
warden, wardon, п., a variety of pear. — ME.
wardon, fr. ONF. warder, 'to keep'; see ward, v.
ME. wardon orig. meant 'that which may be
kept (for a long time)'.

## wardite
wardite, п., a hydrous aluminum phosphate
(mineral.) — Named after the American
mineralogist Henry A. Ward (1834-1906). For the
ending see subst. suff. -he.

## wardrobe
wardrobe, n. — ME. warderobe, fr. ONF. warde-
robe, fr. warder, 'to guard', and robe, 'robe'. Cp.
OF. (= F.) garderobe and see ward, v., and
robe.

## -wards
-wards, adv. suff. — ME., fr. OE. -weardes, gen.
sing. neut. of the adj. suff. -weard. See -ward.
Cp. OS., MLG. -wardes, Du. -waarts, OHG.,
MHG. -wertes, G. -warts, Goth, -wairps, and
see -ward and adv. sufl". -s.

## ware
ware, п., goods. — ME., fr. QE. waru, 'goods,
ware', rel. to Late ON. and Swed. vara, Dan.
vare, OFris. were, MDu. were, ware, Du. waar,
MHG., G. ware, 'goods'. OE. waru, 'goods,
ware', etc. are prob. rel. to OE. waru,
'protection, custody', and to OE. wser, 'aware,
cautious', MHG. ware, 'attention' (see ware, 'alert').
Accordingly the noun ware would have meant
orig. 'that which is kept in custody'.

## ware
ware, adj., alert, cautious (archaic). — ME. war,
fr. OE. wser, 'aware, cautious', rel. to ON. varr,
'attentive', Dan., Swed. var, 'aware', Goth, wars,
'cautious', OS. giwar, MDu. ghewdre, OHG.
giwar, MHG. gewar, G. gewahr, 'aware', OE.
warian, OS. waron, ON. vara, OFris. waria,
OHG. biwaron, 'to guard', G. wahren, 'to
preserve', fr. I.-E. base *wer-, 'to be or become
aware of; to guard, keep safe, protect', whence
also L. vereri, 'to observe with awe, revere,
respect, fear', Gk. οδρος (prob. for Τόρνος),
'watchman' 6pav (for *fop5v), 'to see', ώρα
(for Τώρα), 'саге, concern', Homeric Gk. επί
ϋρονται, 'they watch over', Hitt. werite-, 'to be
afraid'. See ward, v., and cp. aware, beware,
garage, regard, reward, warden, warn. Cp. also
Arehinis, ephor, pylorus, revere, verecund, Vere-
tillum. Cp. also the second element in cosmora-
mn and in words there referred to.

## ware
ware, v., to take heed of, beware. — ME. waren,
fr. OE. warian, 'to guard against', which is rel.
to wser, 'aware'. See ware, 'alert', and cp.
beware.

## war game
war game, п., kriegspiel. — Loan translation of
G. Kriegspiel, which is a compound of Krieg,
'war', and Spiel, 'game'. Cp. kriegspiel.

## warison
warison, п., protection, help, reward. — ME.,
'reward', fr. ONF., 'protection, provision', fr.
warir, 'to protect', corresponding to OF. gari-
son, resp. garir. See garrison.

## warlock
warlock, п., wizard, magician. — ME. warloghe,
'deceiver, traitor', fr. OE. wSrloga, 'belier,
traitor', which is compounded of wser, 'agreement,
treaty; faith', and logo-, 'liar'. The first element
is cogn. with L. verus, 'true'; see very, adj. The
second element derives from the stem oigelogen,
pp. of leogan, 'to lie', see lie, 'to tell an untruth'.
Derivative: warlock, n.

## warm
warm, adj. — ME., fr. OE. wearm, rel. to OS.,
OFris., MLG., MDu., Du., OHG., MHG., G.
warm, ON. varmr, Dan., Swed., Norw. varm,
Goth, wormian, 'to warm', fr. I.-E. base *gwher-,
'warm', whence also 01. gharmdh, 'heat',
Arm. jerm, 'warm', Gk. θερμός (for *gwhermos),
'warm', L. formus, 'warm', fornus, fornax,
'oven', Alb. zjarm, 'heat', OSlav. goriti, goriti,
Lett, gariu, gareti, 'to burn', OSlav. varu, 'heat',
variti, 'to cook, boil' (tr.), virja, vreti, 'to seethe,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:848 COLUMN:3 -->
boil' (intr.), Lith. verdu, virti, 'to seethe' (tr.),
versme, 'source', Lett, wersme, garme, OPruss.
gorme, 'heat', OPruss. goro, 'hearth', OSlav.
goriku, 'bitter' (lit. 'burning'), Olr. fogeir,
'heated', Mir. gorim, guirim, Ί warm, heat', Ir. gor,
'heat, hatching", Olr. goirt, 'bitter' (lit.
'burning'), Toch. A carme, 'warm', Hitt. war-, 'to
burn'. Cp. forceps, Fornax, fornicata, furnace.
Cp. also therm and words there referred to.
Derivatives: warm, tr. v., and п., warm-ed, adj.,
warm-ed-ly, adv., warm-er, п., warm-ing, n.

## warmth
warmth, n. — ME. wermth, rel. to MLG. wermede,
Du. warmte, MHG. wermede, 'warmth'. See
warm and subst. suff. -tb.

## warn
warn, tr. v..— ME. warnien, warnen, fr. OE.
warnian, warenian, 'to warn, admonish', rel. to
MDu. waernen, 'to provide, warn', ON. varna,
'to admonish', OHG. warnon, 'to take heed',
MHG., G. warnen, 'to warn', and to OE. wser,
'aware, cautious'. See ware, 'alert', and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also garnish.
Derivatives: warn-er, п., warn-ing, n. and adj.,
warn-ing-ly, adv.

## warp
warp, n. — ME., fr. OE. wearp, rel. to MLG.
warp, OHG., MHG. war/, 'warp', ON. varp,
'cast of a net', Dan. varp, 'warp', and to OE.
weorpan, 'to throw'; see warp, v. In some senses
the noun warp derives directly from the verb
warp.

## warp
warp, tr. v., to bend, twist; to distort; intr. v., to
become bent or twisted. — ME. warpen, fr. OE.
weorpan, 'to throw', rel. to OS. werpan, ON. ver-
pa, 'to throw', Dan. vxrpe, Swed. varpa, 'to lay
eggs', OFris. werpa, MLG., Du. werpen, OHG.
werpan,werfan,MHG.,G.werfen,Goth.wairpan,
'to throw', and cogn. with Lith. verpiii, verpti,
4o spin', varpste, 'spool, distaff'. See vervain and
cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: warp-ed, adj., warp-er, п., warp-ing,
n. and adj.

## warrant
warrant, n. — ME. warant, warrant, fr. ONF.
warant (corresponding to OF. guarant, garant,
F. garant), 'a warrant', fr. OHG. werento,
'guarantor', prop. pres. part, of wergn, giwergn,
'to guarantee' (whence MHG. wern, gewern, G.
gewdhren, 'to grant', fr. I.-E. base *wer-, 'to be
kind, show kindness', whence also ON. vxrr,
'kind, friendly, pleasing', OHG. miti-wari,
'gentle, mild', and prob. also the second element
in L. sevgrus, 'severe'. See severe and cp. warren,
guarantee, quo warranto. ONF. warant and OF.
garant were influenced in form by ONF. warir,
resp. OF. garir, 'to defend' (see garret).

## warrant
warrant, tr. v. — ME. waranten, ft: ONF. waran-
tir (corresponding to OF. guarantir, garantir, F.
garantir), ft. warant. See warrant, n.
Derivatives: warrant-able, adj., warrant-ee, п.,
warrant-er, п., warrant-or, п., warranty (q.v.)

## warranty
warranty, n. — ME., fr. ONF. warantie
corresponding to OF. guarantee, garantie (F. garantie).
See warrant, v., and -y (representing F. -ie), and
cp.'gnaranty, which is a doublet of warranty.

## warren
warren, п., 1) a piece of land enclosed for keeping
game (obsol. except hist.); 2) a piece of land
preserved for the breeding of rabbits. — ME.
warenne, fr. ONF. warenne (F. garenne), which
prob. derives fr. OHG. wergn, 'to guarantee',
but was influenced in form by ONF. warir, 'to
defend'. See warrant, n.
Derivative: warren-er, n.

## warrener
warrener, п., a keeper of a warren. — ME. waren-
ner, ft. ONF. warennier, ft. warenne. See prec.
word and agential suff. -er.

## warrlgal
warrlgal, п., the dingo. — Native Australian.

## warrior
warrior, n. — ME. werreour, werriour, fr. ONF.
werreieor (corresponding to OF. guerreor), fr.
werreier, 'to make war', fr. werre
(corresponding to OF., F. guerre), 'war'. See war and 2nd
-ior.

## wart
wart, n. — ME., fr. OE. wearte, rel. to OS. warta,
ON. varta, Swed. varta, Dan. vorten, OFris.
warte, Du. wraf, OHG. warza, MHG., G. warze,
'wart', and to OE. wearr, 'callosity', and cogn.
with OI. varsman-, 'height, point', vdrsisthah,
'the highest', L. verruca (for *versucd)
'excrescence, swelling, wart', OSlav. vruchu,
'summit', Lith. virius, 'the upper; summit', Olr./err,
'better', orig. 'higher'. Cp. verruca.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:849 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: WARWICKITE | 822 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:849 COLUMN:1 -->
Derivatives: wart-ed, wart-y, adjs.

## warwickite
warwickite, п., a titanate and borate of iron and
magnesium (mineral.) — Named after Warwick,
New York. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## wary
wary, adj., cautious, watchful. — Formed fr.
ware, adj., with adj. suff. -y.
Derivatives: wari-ly, adv., wari-ness, n.

## was
was,v. — ME., fr.OE. wees, 1st and 3rd pers. sing, of
wesan, 'to be', rel. to OS. wesan, ON. vesa, vera,
OFris. wesa, MDu. wesen, Du. wezen, OHG.
wesan, 'to be', MHG. wesen, 'to be' (whence G.
Wesen, 'being; essence'), Goth, wisan, 'to be',
Goth, weists, OHG. wist, ON. vist, 'essence', fr.
I.-E. base *wes-, 'to dwell, stay', whence also 01.
\asati, 'he dwells, stays', Toch. A washt, В ost,
'house', washamo, 'companion, fellow', and
prob. also Gk.εστία (for*5εστία), 'thehearth
of the house', and L. Vesta, name of the goddess
of the hearth'. Cp. Hestia, Vesta and the first
element in wassail.

## wash
wash, tr. and intr. v. — ME. waschen, wasshen,
fr, OE. wascan, wsescan, which is rel. to OS.,
OHG. wascan, ΟΝ., Swed. vaska, Dan. vaske,
MDu. wasscen, Du. wassen, MHG., G. waschen;
prob. fr. Teut. *wat-sko, fr. base *wat-, 'water*;
see water. Accordingly *he above Teut. words
orig* meant 'to rinse in -ater\ For sense
development cp. OF. waschier, guashier, 'to mix, to
row', gacher, 'to mix mortar' (fr. Frankish
*waskan, 'to wash'), which must have had the
original meaning 'to stir up in water'.
Derivatives: wash, п., wash-able, adj., wash-er,
п., wash-ing, п., wash-y, adj., wash-i-ly, adv.,
wash-i-ness, n.

## Washingtoma
Washingtoma, п., a genus of palms of California
(bot.) — ModL., named after George
Washington (1732-99). For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## wnsp
wnsp, n. — ME. waspe, fr. OE. wsefs, waeps, waesp,
rel. to OS. waspa, MDu. wespe, Du. wesp, OHG.
wafsa, wefsa, MHG. wefse, webse, wespe,
G. Wespe, Dan. hveps, and cogn. with 01.
urnavabhih, 'spider', lit. 'wool-spinner', Avestic
vawazaka-, 'scorpion' (prop, 'a spiderlike
animal'), L. vespa, OSlav. vosa, Lith. vapsa,
'gadfly', OPruss. wobse, Russ. osa, 'wasp', OBret.
guoni, Co. guhien, 'wasp', Olr. foich, 'drone'.
All these words are derivatives of I.-E, base
*webh-, *wobh-, 'to weave'; see weave and cp.
words there referred to. The wasp is called *the
weaver', in allusion to the weblike form of its
nest.
Derivatives: wasp-en, wasp-ish, adjs., wasp-ish-
ly, adv., wasp-ish-ness, п., wasp-ling, п., wasp-y,
adj.

## wassail
wassail, п., 1) a drinking bout; 2) a toast. — ME.
weseil, wassail, 'be whole, be healthy', fr. ON.
ves heill, 'be hail, be healthy', fr. ves, imper. of
vesa, 'to be', and heill, 'whole, healthy,
prosperous*. Cp. the OE. greeting formula wespu hul%
'be thou healthy', and see was and hail, 'to greet'.
Derivatives: wassail, intr. and tr. v., wassail-er
n.

## wassailer
wassailer, n. — Coined by Milton fr. wassail, v.
(see prec. word), and agential suff. -er.

## wastage
wastage, n. — A hybrid coined from the verb
waste and -age, a suff. of ult. Latin origin.

## waste
waste, adj. — ME. wast, waste, fr. ONF. wast
(corresponding to OF. guast), fr. L. vastus,
'empty, waste, desert' (whence also It. guasto,
Provenc. gast, Port, gasto and MHG. waste, of
s.m.), but influenced in form by OE. weste,
'waste', and its other Teut. correspondences:
OS. wosti, Du. woest, OHG. wuosti (MHG.
wueste, G. wust), of s.m. OE. weste, etc., are
cogn. with L. vastus, and prob. also with L.
vdnus, 'empty, void, vain'. See vain· and cp.
devastate.

## waste
waste, tr. and intr. v. — ME. wasten, fr. ONF.
waster, which corresponds to OF. guaster, gater,
*to waste' (whence F. gater, 'to spoil', fr. L.
vdstare, 'to make empty, desolate, lay waste', fr.
vastus (see prec. word), but influenced in form
by pre-Teut. *wdstu, 'waste'. Cp. wastrel. Cp.
also OProvenc. g(u)astar, It. guastare, 'to lay
waste; to spoil*, Sp. gastar, 'to waste, consume',
which also derive fr. L. vastdre.
Derivatives: wast-er, п., wast-ing, n. and adj.,
wast-ing-ly, adv., wast-ing-ness, n.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:849 COLUMN:2 -->

## waste
waste, п., desert. — ME., fr. ONF. wast, п., fr.
wast, adj. See waste, adj.
Derivatives: waste-ful, adj., waste-ful-ly, adv.,
waste-ful-ness, п., waste-less, adj.

## wastrel
wastrel, п., 1) a spendthrift; 2) a
good-for-nothing. — Formed from the verb waste with the
depreciatory suff. -rel. Cp. mongrel, scoundrel.
Derivative: wastrel, adj.

## watch
watch, intr. and tr. v. — ME. waccken, fr. OE,
wxccan, rel. to OE. wacian, 'to be awake, to
watch'. See wake, v., and cp. next word.
Derivatives: watck-er, п., watch-ing, adj. and п.,
watch-ing-ly, adv.

## watch
watch, n. — ME. wacche, fr. OE. wsecce, 'vigil,
watch', fr. wseccan. See watch, v.
Derivatives: watch-ful, &d'}.,.watch-ful-ly, adv.,
watch-ful-ness, п., watch-less, adj., watch-less-
ness, n.

## water
water, n. — ME. water, fr. OE. wseter, rel. to OS.
watar, OFris. wetir, weter, wetter, LG., Du.
water, OHG. wa^^ar, MHG. wa^er, G. Wasser^
ON. vatn, Swed. vatten, Dan. vand, Goth, wato,
'water', OE. wxt, 'wet', fr. I.-E. base *wxd-,
*wod-, *ud-, 'water', whence also Hitt. watar,
gen. wetenash, 'water', Ol. udnafy, udan-, uda-
kam, 'water', anudra h, 'waterless', utsah, 'source',
undati, unatti, 'it sprinkles, moistens', Gk.
ΰδωρ, 'water', υδρία, 'waterpot, pitcher',
άνυδρος, 'waterless', OSlav., Russ., etc., voda,
'water', Lith. vandud, 'water', Lett, udens,
OPruss. wundan, unds, 'water', Arm. get (for
*wedo-), 'river', Alb. ujs, 'water', L. undo, 'wave',
uter, 'leather bag', Umbr. utur, 'water', Olr.
usee, uisce, 'water'. Cp. wash, wet, otter and the
second element in kirschwasser. Cp. also
anhydrous, dropsy, Ephydra, hydru, hydria, hydro-,
hydropsy, klepsydra, Lutra, imdate, undulate,
usquebaugh, utricle, Utricularia, vodka, whisky.
Derivatives: water, v. (q.v.), water-y, adj., water-
i-ness, n.

## water
water, tr. and intr. v. — ME. wateren, fr. OE.
wxterian, fr. wseter, 'water'. See water, n.
Derivatives: water-ed, adj., water-ing, n. and
adj., water-ing-ly, adv.

## waturshed
waturshed, n. — Loan translation of G. Wasser-
scheide.

## Watsonia
Watsonia, п., a genus of plants of the iris family
(bot.) — ModL., named after the English
botanist Sir William Watson (1715-87). For the
ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## watt
watt, п., unit of the electrical power. — Named
after the Scottish inventor James Watt (1736-
1819).

## Wattenu
Wattenu, adj., pertaining to, or made in the style
of, the French painter Jean-Antoine Watteau
(1684-1721).

## wattle
wattle, п., a fleshy part hanging from the throat
or chin of some birds and reptiles. — ME. watel,
'hurdle; basket, bag', fr. OE. watol, watel; of
uncertain origin. Cp. wallet.
Derivatives: wattle, tr. v., wattl-ed, adj., wattl-
ing, n.

## wattless
wattless, adj., without electric power. — Lit.
'without watts', formed fr. watt and suff. -less.

## wave
wave, intr. and tr. v. — ME. waven, fr. OE.
wafian, 'to wave, brandish', rel. to ON. vafra,
vafla, 'to hover about', vafa, 4o swing, waver',
fr. I.-E. base *webh-, 'to move to and fro; to
weave'. See weave and cp. waver. Cp. also
wnbble, wobble.
Derivatives: wave, n. (q.v.), wav-ed, adj.,

## wavelet

wainscot and in walleyed and the second element
in earwig, polliwog. Cp. also voe, vogue. Cp. also
vehicle and words there referred to.
Derivatives: weigh, п., weigh-able, adj., weigk-
age, п., weigh-ed, adj., weigh-ing, п., weight (q.v.)

## weight
weight, n. — ME. weght, wight, fr. OE. wlht,
which is rel. to ON. vsett, Dan. vegt, Swed.
vifct, OFris. wicht, MDu., Du. wicht, gewicht,
MHG. gewikt, G. Gewicht and to OE. wegan,
'to move, carry, weigh'. See prec. word.
Derivatives: weight, tr. v., weight-ed, adj.,
weigkt-ing, п., weight-y, adj., weight-i-ly, adv.,
weight-i-ness, п., weight-less, adj.

## weinbergerite
weinbergerite, п., a complex silicate of iron,
calcium, etc. (mineral.) — Named after the
Austrian mineralogist J. Weinberger. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## weinschenklte
weinschenklte, п., a hydrous phosphate of rare
earths (mineral.)· — G. WeinschenU.it, named
after the German mineralogist Ernst Η. Ο. Κ.
Weinschenk (1865-1921). The ending -it goes
back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst. suff. -ite.

## weir
weir, n. — ME. wer, fr. OE. wer, 'weir, dam', rel.
to ON. ver, OFris., MLG., MDu. were, Du.
weer, OHG. wart, weri, MHG. were, wer, G.
Wehr, 'defense, protection', OE. and OS. we-
rian, ON. verja, Swed. varja, OFris. wera,
OHG. werian, weren, MHG. wern, G. wehren,
Goth, warjan, 'to defend, protect', fr. I.-E. base
*wer-, 'to enclose, cover', whence also OI.
vrnoti, varati, 'holds back', apa-vrnoti,
'uncovers, opens', api-vrnoti, 'closes, covers', L. ape-
rire (for *ap-werire, 'to uncover, open', operlre
(for *op-werire), 'to cover, close', Lith. at-veriu,
at-verti, Lett, at-vert, *to open', Lith. uz-veriu,
uz-verti, 'to close, shut', OSlav. ot-voriti, 'to
open', za-vreti, 'to close, shut', vrata (pi.), 'gate,
door', Lith. vaftai (pi.), 'gate', OPruss. warto
(pi.), 'house door', Toch. B. warto, warto,
'garden' (lit. 'that which is covered or fenced',
for sense development cp. garden), OI. vartram,
'inner dike', varu-tham, 'protection', varu-tar-,
'protector', Avestic vere&ra-, 'weir', Alb. να&ε
(for *wor-td-), 'enclosure, fence, fold', Olr. fe-
ronn, 'field*, prop, 'enclosed land', Gk. Ερυσ&αι
(for Τέρυσ&αί), 'to guard, rescue'. Cp. garret,
garrison, the first element in wehrmacht and the
second element in landwehr. Cp. also aperient,
aperitif, aperitive, apert, aperture, apricate,
cover, covert, louver, operculum, overt, varna.
Derivative: weir, tr. v.

## weird
weird, п., fate, destiny (archaic). — ME. werd,
wirde, wyrde, fr. OE. wyrd, 'fate', rel. to OS.
wurd, OHG. wurt, 'fate*, ON. urdr, 'fate, one of
the three Norns', OE. weordan, OS. werthan,
ON. verda, Swed. varda, OFris. wertha, OHG.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:851 COLUMN:2 -->
werdan, MHG., G. werden, Goth, wafrpan, 'to
become'. The orig. meaning of these verbs was
'to turn'. They derive fr. I.-E. *wert-, a -r-en-
largement of base *wer-, 'to turn, twist*. See
version and words there referred to and cp. esp.
worth, 'to become'. For the sense development
of OE. weordan, OS. werthan, etc., 'to become',
from a base meaning 'to turn', ср. Е. to turn in
the sense of to become.
Derivatives: weird, adj. (q.v.), weird-ful, adj.,
weird-less, adj.

## weird
weird, adj., uncanny. — Fr. weird, n. The original
meaning was 'pertaining to fate'. The sense
'uncanny' arose from a misunderstanding of the
real meaning of the adjective weird in the term
the weird sisters (= the Fate Sisters), applied to
the Norns.
Derivatives: weird-ly, adv., weird-ness, n.

## Weismannism
Weismannism, п., the theory of the German
biologist August Weissmann (1834-1914), who
regards the germ plasm as the basis of heredity.
For the ending see suff. -ism.

## wc is bach ite
wc is bach ite, п., a variety of anglesite (mineral.) —
G. Weisbachit, named after the German
mineralogist Julius A. Weisbach (1833-1901). The
ending -it goes back to Gk. -ΐτης; see subst.
suff. -ite.

## weissite
weissite, п., a copper telluride (mineral.) —
Named after Dr. Louis Weiss, owner of the
mine in Colorado, where it was found. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## weka
weka, п., any of several large flightless birds of
the rail family of New Zealand. — Maori,
imitative of the bird's cry.

## Welch
Welch, adj. and n. — A var. of Welsh.

## welch
welch, v. — A var. of welsh.

## welcome
welcome, adj. — ME. welcome, fr. earlier ivrV-
cume, fr. OE. wilcuma, 'a welcome guest', lit.
'one who comes in accordance with another's
will', compounded of the pref. will-, fr. OE
willa, 'will pleasure', and cuma, 'guest', fr.
cuman, 'to come'; see wiil, n. and v., and come.
ME. welcome was influenced in form by the adv.
well. Cp. ON. velkominn, Late OHG. wille-
chomen, MHG. willekomen, G. willkommen.

## welcome
welcome, tr. v. — ME. welcomen, fr. earlier wil-
cumen, fr. OE. wilchumian, fr. wilcuma. See
welcome, adj.
Derivatives: welcome, п., welcom-er, п., welcom-
er, п., welcom-'mg, adj., welcom-ing-ly, adv.

## weld
weld, п., ]) the dyer's rocket; 2) a yellow dye
obtained from it. — ME. welde, wolde, rel. to
MLG. wolde and MDu. woude (Du. wouw), fr.
Teut. *walda. These words are possibly cogn.
with L. latum (for *vlutum), 'weld'. Cp. the
Teut. loan words Olt. guada, Sp. gualdo, gualda,
F. gaude, 'weld', and G. Waut Dan., Swed. vau,
'weld', which are borrowed fr. Du. wouw. Cp.
luteous.

## weld
weld, intr. v., to undergo junction by welding;
tr. v., to unite. — Back formation fr. welled*
pp. of well, 'to boil, rise, well', earlier also
meaning 'to weld'. See well, 'to spring*.
Derivatives: weld, п., 'welding', weld-able,
adj., weld-er, п., weld-ing, n.

## welfare
welfare, n. — ME. welfare, fr. welfare», 'to fare
well', fr. OE. welfaran. See well, adv., and fare,
'to get on', and cp. farewell. Cp. also G. Wohl-

## fart
fart, 'welfare', fr. wohl, 'well', and fahren, 'to
go', which are rel. to well, resp. to fare.
Derivative: welfare, adj.

## welk
welk, intr. v., to fade; tr. v., to cause to fade
(obsol. except dial.) — ME. welken, prob. fr.
MDu. (ч= Du.) welken, which is rel. to OHG.
ir-welken, MHG., G. welken, 'to fade, decay',
OHG. welk, 'moist, withered*, MDu., MHG.
welc, G. welk, 'withered', fr. I.-E. base *welg-,
'wet', whence also Lett, velgs, 'moisture,
dampness', Lith. vilgyti, 'to moisten', OPruss. welgen,
'cold (in the head)', OSlav. vlaga, 'moisture',
Czech and Slovak vlhky, 'damp'. Cp. next word
and wilt, 'to fade, droop'.

## welkin
welkin, п., sky (poetic). — ME. wolkne, welkne,
fr. OE. wolcen, 'cloud', rel. to OS. wolkan,
OFris. welken, MDu. wolke, Du. wo Ik, OHG.
wolka, wolkan, MHG. wolken, G. Wolke,
'cloud'; fr. I.-E. base *welg-, 'whet'. See prec.
word.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:851 COLUMN:3 -->
well, п., a spring. — ME. welle, fr. OE. wella,
wiella, rel. to ON. vella, 'boiling heat", Du. wel,
'spring, well, fountain*, OHG. wella, MHG., G.
welle, 'wave', from I.-E. base *wel-, 'to turn,
roll', whence also OI. urmih, Alb. val'e (fr. I.-E.
*wl-nd), 'wave', OSlav. vluna, Lith. vilnis, 'wave',
L. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also next word. Cp. also
weld, 'to unite', and the second element in pot·
waller.

## well
well, intr. v., to spring, rise. — ME, wellen, 'to
boil', fr. OE. wyllan, wiellan, rel. to OE.'weallan,
OS. wallan, ΟΝ., Norw. vella, Swed. valla,
OFris. walla, OHG. wallan, MHG., G. wallen,
Goth, wulan, 'to bubble, boil', and to OE. wella,
wiella, 'wave*. See prec. word.
Derivative: well-ing, n.

## well
well, adv. — ME. welt fr. OE. wel, rel.' to OS.
wela, wala, wola, ON. vel, val, Swed., Dan. vel,
Swed. val, OFris, wel, wol, Du. wel, OHG. wela,
wala, wola, MHG. wol, G. wohl, Goth, waila,
'well'. The orig, meaning of these words was
'according to one's will'. They are traceable to
I.-E. *wel-, 'to will, wish*, whence also OI. prati
varam, 'at will*, variyan, 'better, best',
lit.'preferable', Alb. vale, 'well', OSlav. vole, 'well*, W.
gwell, 'better', L. void, velle, 'to wish, will',
Goth, wiljan, OE. willan, of s.m. See will, п., and
v., and cp. weal, 'prosperity', wealth.
Derivatives: well, adj. and n.

## wellaway
wellaway, interj., an exclamation expressing
sorrow (archaic). — ME. welaway, alteration of
wei la wei, fr. OE. weilawei, lit. 'woe, Ιο, woe',
alteration (after ON. vei, 'woe') of OE. wdlawd,
fr. wd, 'woe*, Id, Ίο', and wa, 'woe'. ME.
welaway was influenced in form by wel, 'well', and
away.

## Wellington
Wellington, п., also Wellington boot, a kind of
long boot. — Named after the 1st Duke of
Wellington. For sense development cp. bluchers.

## well-regulated
well-regulated, adj. — Compounded of well, adv.,
and pp. of regnlate; first used by Shaftesbury.

## wellsite
wellsite, п., a silicate of aluminum, calcium,
barium and potassium {mineral·) — Named after
the American chemist Horace L. Wells (1855-
1924). For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## Welsh
Welsh, adj. — ME. walisch, welisch, fr. OE.
wazlisc, welisc, 'foreign' fr. walh, wealh, 'a
foreigner' (i.e. not of Saxon origin), hence 'a Celt',
esp. 'a Briton, a Welshman', rel. to OHG.
Walah, Walh, 'a Latin', MHG. welhisch, 'one
speaking Latin (later: a Romance language)',
G. welsch, 'foreign', Du. Waals, 'Walloon',
and to ON. Valskr, 'Gaulish, French'.- These
words derive from the name of a Celtic tribe,
whence also L. Volcae, name of a Celtic people
in Gallia Narbonensis, mentioned by Caesar.
Cp. Walach, Walloon and the first element in
walnut.
Derivative: Welsh, n.

## welsh
welsh, tr. and intr. v., to abscond. — Of
uncertain origin:

## welt
welt, п., a strip. — ME. welte, prob. fr. ME.
welten, 'to roll', fr ON. velta, 'to roll'. See
welter and cp. welterweight.
Derivatives: welt, tr. v., to furnish with a welt,
to strike, blow, welt-ed, adj.

## welter
welter, intr. v., to wallow. — ME. weltren, fr.
MLG. welteren, 'to roll', which is rel. to OE.
wieltan, ON. velta, Swed. valta, Dan. velte, Swed.
valtra, valta, OHG. walzan, MHG. welzen, 'to
turn, revolve', G. walzen, 'to roll*, sich walzen,
'to welter', Goth, waltjan, 'to roll', fr. I.-E. base
*wel-, 'to bend, turn, twist, roll', whence also
L. volvere, 'to roll'. See volute and cp. wallow,
waltz.
Derivative: welter, п., act of weltering.

## welterweight
welterweight, п., 1) a weight of 28 pounds
imposed upon a horse in a race as a handicap;
hence, a heavy weight; 2) a boxer or wrestler
who weighs between 136 and 147 pounds. —
Prob. formed fr. welt, 'to strike' (see welt, 'a
strip'), with agential suff. -er.

## wen
wen, п., a sebaceous cyst. — ME. wenn, fr. OE.
wenn, rel to MLG. wene, t)u. wen, dial. G.
Wenne; of uncertain origin.

## wen
wen, п., one of the runes (p) adopted into the OE.
alphabet with the value of ModE. w.
