## whit
whit, interj., n. and intr. v. — Imitative of the
chirp of a bird or a dull sound.

## white
white, adj. — ME. whit, white, fr. OE. kwit, rel.
to OS., OFris. hwit, ON. hvitr, Dan. hvid, Swed.
vit, Norw. kvit, Du. wit, OHG- hwi$, wij, MHG.
wis, G· weifi, 'white', Goth, heits, from I.-E.
*kweid·, a var. of base *kweit-, 'to shine;
gleaming; white', whence OI. avetah, 'white', OSlav.
sviteti, 'to shine', svetu, 'light', Lith. sviesti, 'to
shine', svaityti, 'to brighten'. Cp. wheat, the first
element in wheatear, Whitsunday and the second
element in edelweiss.
Derivatives: white, п., white-ly, adv., whiten
(q.v.), white-ness, п., whit-ing, п., the act of
making white, whit-ish, adj., whit-y, adj.

## whiten
whiten, tr. and intr. v. — ME. whitenen, fr. whit,
'white'. See prec. word and verbal suff. -en.
Derivative: whiten-ing, n.

## whither
whither, adv. — ME. whider, fr. OE. hwider, rel.
to Goth, fvadre, 'whither'; formed from the
I.-E. pron. base *qwo-7 with the compar. suff.
-ther (q.v.). See who and cp. hither, thither.

## whitlow
whitlow, п., an inflammation on a finger or toe;
felon. — ME. whitfiawe, whitfiowe, prob. folk-
etymol. alteration of dial, whickflaw, lit. 'a crack
at a sensitive part', fr. whick, 'sensitive part'
(corresponding to the E. noun quick), and the
noun βαwe. See quick, adj., and flaw, 'defect'.

## whitneyite
whitneyite, п., a copper arsenide (mineral.) —
Named after the American geologist Josiah
Dwight Whitney (1819-96). For the ending see
subst. suff. -ite.

## Whitsun
Whitsun, n. — ME. Whitson, back formation fr.
Whitsonday. See next word.

## Whitsunday
Whitsunday, п., the seventh Sunday after Easter.
— ME. Whitsonday, fr. OE. hwita sunnandseg,
lit. 'white Sunday' (see white and Sunday); prob.
so called from the white garments worn by the
candidates for baptism.

## Whitsuntide
Whitsuntide, n. — Short for Whitsunday tide. See
prec. word and -tide.

## whittle
whittle, п., a large knife. — ME. whittel, fr.
earlier thwitel, 'whittle', fr. OE. pwitan, 'to cut, cut
off', rel. to ON. pveitr, 'piece of land', lit. 'land
cut off', from the stem of pveita, 'to hew*. See
thwoite and cp. doit.
Derivatives: whittle, tr. v., to cut with a knife;
to reduce, whittl-er, п., whittling, n.

## whiz(z)
whiz(z), intr. and tr. v. andn.—Ofimitative origin.
Derivatives: whizz-er, п., whizz-ing, adj., whizz-
ing-ly, adv.

## whiz-bang
whiz-bang, whizz-bang, п., a whiz. — Prop, a
whizzing sound followed by a bang. See whiz
and bang.

## who
who, pron. — ME. hwo, ho, who, fr. OE. hwa,
'who' (whence hwset, *what'), rel. to OS. hwe,
'who', hwat, 'what',ON. hverr, 'who,which', hvat,
'what*, Dan. hvo, 'who', hvad, 'what', Swed.
vem, 'who', vad, 'what', OFris. hwa, 'who',
hwet, 'what', Du. wie, 'who', wat, 'what', OHG.
hwer, wer, MHG., G. wer, 'who', OHG. hwas,
wa3, MHG. was, G. was, 'what', Goth, has,
fem. ho, 'who', ha, 'what'. All these words
derive, from the Teut. pron. base *hwa-, *hwe-,
corresponding to I.-E. *qwo-, *qwe-, whence also
OI. kah, fem. kd, 'who, which', Avestic ко, fem.
ka, of s.m., OI. kad, 'what', OI. kada, Avestic
kada, 'when, at what time', Toch. A kus, kuc,
'which' (neut.), Hitt. kuish, 'who', OI. kati,
Hitt. kuwatta, L. quot, 'how many', Ion. Gk.
χόσος, Gk. πόσος, 'how great, how much', L.
qui, fem. quae, neut. quod, 'who, which, what',
quam, 'as, as much as', Umbr. pui, fem. pat,
neut. pud (~ L. qui, quae, quod), 'who, which,
what*, Lith. kas, 'who*, kad, 'what', kada, 'when,
at what time', Homer. Gk. τέο, Att. τοϋ,
'whose', Gk. που, 'where?', πό&εν, 'whence?,
from what place?*, OSlav. кй-to (Russ. kto),
'who', Olr. сё, cia, W. pwy, 'who*, pa, 'what',
Ir., Gael. со, 'what'. Cp. the var. I.-E. base
*qwi-, whence OI. klh, 'who ?', kirn, 'what ?', cit,
cid, Avestic -6i{, OPers. ciy, 'even, also' (enclitic
particle), Thessal. Gk. κίς, 'who?', Gk. τίς,
'who ?', τ£, 'what ?', τι (indef. particle), L. quis,
'who?', quid, 'what?', Oscan pis, pis, 'who',
pld, 'what', Umbr. pis-ί, 'who', pif-i, 'what',
svepis, 'if any one', OSlav. ci-to (Russ. ito),
'what', Ir. cid, 'what'. Cp. how, what, when,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:854 COLUMN:2 -->
whence, where, whether, which, whither, whom,
whose, why. Cp. also aliquant, aliquot, aliunde,
katha, kick-shaw, posology, qua, qualify, quality,
quantity, quantum, quasi, quibble, quid, 'essence',
quiddity, quiddle, quillet, quoad, quod, 'which',
quodlibet, quondam, quorum, quota, quote,
ubiety, ubiquity.

## whoa
whoa, interj. — A var. of ho, interj.

## whodunit
whodunit, п., a mystery story or detective story.
— Coined by Donald Gordon from the
expression who done it.

## whole
whole, adj. — ME. hale, hole, hoi, hool, 'healthy,
whole', fr. OE. Ml, 'whole, unhurt, healthy,
well', rel. to OS. hel, ON. heill, Dan., Swed- hel,
OFris. hal, hel, MDu. hiel, heel, Du. heel, OHG.,
MHG., G. heil, Goth, hails, 'complete, alone,
whole, healthy, well, sound', OE. hul, ON. heill,
'good omen, luck', OS., OFris. hel, Du., OHG.,
MHG., G. heil, 'salvation, welfare', fr. I.-E.
base *qailo-, *quailu-, 'complete, sound, well,
happy', whence also OSlav. сёШ, 'whole,
complete', Lett, kails, 'naked, bare, bald', OPruss.
kailustikan, 'health', W. coel, Omen', and
prob. also Gk. κοΐλυ (Hesychius),
'beautiful'. Cp. hale, 'healthy', which is a doublet of
whole. Cp. also hail, 'to greet', halse, heal, health,
holy and the second element in wassail. Cp. also
kevalin and the first element in celibate. The w
in whole is intrusive; cp. whore.
Derivatives: whole, n. and adv., whole-ness, п.,
whol-ly, adv.

## wholesome
wholesome, adj. — ME. holsom, formed on
analogy of ON. heilsamr, fr. hoi, hool, 'whole', and
-som, '-some'. Cp. Du. heilzaam, G. heilsam
and see whole and 1st -some.
Derivatives: wholesome-ly, adv., wholesome-
ness, n.

## whom
whom, objective case of who. — ME. whom,
wham, fr. OE. hwam, dat. of hwa, 'who'. See
who and cp. whose.

## whoop
whoop, intr. v., to shout; п., a shout. — ME.
whopen, whoupen, variants of hopen, houpen, fr.
MF. houper, fr. OF., fr. interj. houp, 'call to dogs
or horses'. Cp. hoop, 'call to animals', which is
derivatively identical with, but represents an
earlier spelling of, whoop.
Derivatives: whoop-er, п., whoop-ing, adj.,
whoop-ing-ly, adv.

## whop
whop, tr. v., to beat, strike; intr. v., to move
quickly. — Of imitative origin. Cp. W. chwap, 'a
stroke', which is also imitative.
Derivatives: whopp-er, п., whopp-ing, n. and
adj.

## whore
whore, п., a prostitute. — ME. hore, fr. OE. here,
fr. ON. hora, 'adulteress* (whence Dan. hore,
Swed. hora, 'whore'), which is rel. to ON. horr,
'adulterer', and to MDu. hoere, Du. hoer, OHG.
hoaru, MHG. huore, G. Hure, 'whore*, Goth.
hors, 'adulterer*, from I.-E. base *qa-, 'to
desire', whence also L. cdrus, 'dear, precious'.
See charity and cp. words there referred to. The
w in whore is intrusive; cp. whole.
Derivatives: whoredom (q.v.), whor-ish, adj.,
whor-ish-ly, adv., whor-ish-ness, n.

## whoredom
whoredom, n. — ME. hordom, fr. ON. horddmr,
which was formed fr. horr, 'adulterer', with suff.
-domr. See prec. word and -dom.

## whorl
whorl, п., 1) a small flywheel on a spindle; 2)
arrangement of leaves in a circle round the stem.
— ME. whorwyl, whorlwyl, wharle, whorle, prob.
dial, variants of whirle, 'whirl'. See whirl.
Derivative: whorl-ed, adj.

## whortleberry
whortleberry, n. — A var. of hurtleberry, the first
element of which derives fr. OE. horta,
'whortleberries'. Cp. huckleberry.

## whose
whose, the genitive case of who.— ME. whasy
whos, fr. OE. hwxs, gen. of hwa, 'who'. See who
and cp. whom.

## why
why, adv. — ME., fr. OE. hwi, kwp, instrumental
case of hwa, hwaet, 'who, what'. See who.
Derivatives: why, interj. and n.

## wichtisite
wichtisite, п., a variety of sordavalite (petrogr.) —
Named after Wicktis in Finland. For the ending
see subst. suff. -ite.

## wick
wick, п., twisted thread. — ME. wicke, wike, fr.
OE. weoce, 'wick', rel. to MDu. wieke, Du. wiek,
OHG. wiohha, MHG., G. wieche, fr. I.-E. base
*weg-, 'to wesve', whence also L. velum (for

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:854 COLUMN:3 -->
*wexlom), 'sail, curtain, veil'. See veil, п., and
cp. wax, n.

## wick
wick, п., village (now found only in compounds).
— ME. wik, fr. OE. wic, 'village', fr. L. vicus,
'village, hamlet' [whence also OHG. wik,
'village' (whence G. Weichbild, 'municipal area'),
Du. wijk, 'quarter, district', OFris. wik, OS. wic,
OE. wic, 'village']. See vicinage and cp. the
second element in bailiwick.

## wicked
wicked, adj. — ME. wikked, fr. wikke, 'wicked*,
which prob. derives fr. wiken, 'to give way,
yield*, fr. OE. wican. See weak, and cp. the next
two words.
Derivatives: wicked-ly, adv., wicked-ness, n.

## wicker
wicker, п., I) apliant twig; withe; 2) wickerwork.
— ME. wiker, of Scand. origin. Cp. dial. Swed.
vikker, 'willow', prop, 'the tree with the pliant
twigs', fr. Swed. vika, 'to bend', which is rel. to
OE. wican, 'to give way, yield'. See weak and cp.
prec. word.
Derivatives: wicker, tr. v., wicker-ed, adj.

## wicket
wicket, n,, a small gate. — ME. wiket, fr. AF.
wiket, corresponding to OF. guischet (F. gui-
chet), 'wicket, wicket gate'. These dimin. nouns
were prob. formed fr. ON. vik, 'nook', fr. vikja,
'to turn, bend', which is rel. to ON. vikja, 'to
move, turn*, OE. wican, 'to give way, yield'. See
weak and cp. the prec. two words. Cp. also
Viking.

## widdershins
widdershins, adv. — See withershins.

## wide
wide, adj. — ME. wide, fr. OE. wid, rel. to OS.,
OFris. wid, ON. vidr, Dan., Swed. vid, Du. wijd,
OHG., MHG. wit, G. weit, fr. Teut. *wida-,
corresponding to I.-E. *wi-ito-, which is formed fr.
I.-E. base *wi-, 'asunder*, and the pp. stem of
I.-E. *ei-, 'to go'. For the first element see with,
for the second see itinerant.
Derivatives: wide, adv. (q.v.), wide, п., wide-ly,
adv., wid-en, v., widen-er, п., wideness (q.v.),
wid-ish, adj.

## wide
wide, adv. — ME., fr. OE. wide, fr. wid, 'wide'
(adj.) See wide, adj.

## wideness
wideness, n. — ME. widnesse, fr. OE. widnes, fr.
wid, 'wide'. See wide, adj. and -ness.

## widgeon
widgeon, п., any of various kinds of migratory
wild ducks. — Prob. from a NOF. var. of F.
vigeon, vingeon, fr. L. vipidnem, ace. of vipid, 'a
kind of small crane', a word of Balearic and
prob. imitative origin. For the transition of
Latin intervocalic ρ into -ge- in French cp. F.
pigeon, fr. h.pipionem, ace. of pipio (see pigeon).

## widow
widow, n. — ME. widewe, widwe, fr. OE. widewe,
widuwe, wuduwe, rel. to OS. widoWa, OFris.
widwe, MDu., Du. weduwe, Du. weeuw, OHG.
wituwa, witawa, MHG. witewe, witwe, G. Witwe,
Goth, widuwd, 'widow*, and cogn. with OI.
vidhub, 'lonely, solitary', OI. vidhavu, Avestic
vidavd, L. vidua (whence It. vedova, Rum.
vaduva, Provenc. vezpa, OF. vedve, F. veuve, Sp.
viuda, Port, viuva), 'widow', OSlav. vldova,
OPruss. widdewu, Olx.fedb, W. guedeu, 'widow',
W. gweddw, 'widower', 'widow', Gk. ήΐ&εος
(for *·η-Γί&εΓος), 'unmarried'. All these words
derive from I.-E. base *widh-, 'to separate',
whence also L. di-videre, 4o divide*. See divide
and cp. vidual, viuva.
Derivatives: widow, tr. v., widow-ed, adj.,
widower, п., widow-hood, п., widow-ly, adj.

## widow bird
widow bird, a whidah bird. — So called after
Port, viuva, 'widow bird*, lit. 'widow', fr. L. vi-
dua (see widow); in allusion to its long tail
feathers suggestive of widow's veil. Cp. whidah
bird. Cp. also viuva.

## width
width, n. — Formed from the adj. wide with subst.
suff. -th on analogy of bread-th, leng-th.

## wield
wield, tr. v., 1) to handle (an instrument or
weapon; 2) to exercise (power, etc.) — ME. welden,
fr. OE. wealdan, wyldan, wieldan, 'to govern,
possess, have control over', rel. to OS., Goth.
waldan, OFris. walda, 'to govern, rule', ON.
valda, 'to rule, wield; to cause', Dan. volde,
Swed. valla, 'to occasion, cause', OHG. wqltan.
MHG., G. walten, 'to govern, rule', fr. I.-E.
*wal-dh-, which is an enlargement of base
*wal-, 'to be strong, to rule', whence L. valere,
*to be well, to be strong'. The fact that the
enlarged base *Wal-dh- occurs only in Teut. and
Balto-SIavonic shows the near relationship be-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:855 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: WIFE | 828 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:855 COLUMN:1 -->
tween these two language groups. See valiant
and cp. the first element in Walter and the
second element in Arnold, Bretwalda, Gerald,
Harold, herald, Isold, Oswald, Reginald,
Reynold, sprlngal.

## wife
wife, n. — ME. wif, fr. OE. wif, 'woman; wife',
rel. to OS., OFris. wif, ON. vif, Dan., Swed. viv,
MDu., Du. wijf, OHG. wib, MHG. wip, G.
Weib, and possibly also to ON. vifadr, 'covered,
veiled', veifa, 'to wave' (as e.g. the veil does in
the wind). Accordingly ON. vif, OE. wif, etc.,
would lit. mean 'the veiled one'. For sense
development cp. L. nupta, 'a married woman, bride,
wife', prop. fem. pp. of nubere, 'to cover oneself
for the bridegroom, to marry, wed'. See vibrate
and cp. the first element in woman and the
second element in hussy.
Derivatives: wife-hood, п., wife-less, wife-like,
wife-ly, wif-ish, adjs.

## wig
wig, n. — Shortened from periwig.
Derivatives: wig, tr. v., to provide with a wig;
wigg-ed, adj., wig-less, adj.

## wig
wig, also wigg, п., bun, cake. — ME. wigge, fr.
MDu. or MLG. wigge, 'wedge, wedge-shaped
cake', rel. to MDu. wegge, OE. wecg, 'wedge'.
See wedge.

## wigan
wigan, п., a kind of stiff canvas. — Named after
Wigan, a town in Lancashire, England.

## wiggle
wiggle, intr. and tr.· v., to move, or to cause to
move, to and fro with jerky motion. — ME.
wigelen, rel. to, or borrowed from, MFlem.
wiegelen, wigelen, freq. of wiegen, 'to rock', fr.
wiege (Du. wieg), 'cradle', which is rel. to OHG.
wiga, MHG. wi(e)ge, G. Wiege, MLG. wlge,
OFris. widze, of s.m., from I.-E. base *wegh-, 'to
move'. See weigh and words there referred to
and cp. esp. waggle and the second element in
earwig, polliwog.
Derivatives: wiggle, п., wiggl-er, n.

## wight
wight, п., a person (now archaic or dial.) — ME.,
fr. OE. wiht, 'thing, creature', rel. to OS. wiht,
'thing, demon', Du. wicht, 'a little child', OHG.,
MHG. wiht, 'thing, creature, demon', G. Wicht,
'creature, little child', ON. vittr, vxttr, 'thing,
creature', Dan. vette, Swed. vatte, van, 'spirit of
the earth, gnorne', Goth, walhts, 'something',
ni-waiht, 'nothing'. Outside Teut. the only
cognate is OSIav. veSti, 'a thing'. Cp. whit. Cp. also
aught, naught, not.

## wight
wight, adj., brave [dial.) — ME., fr. ON. vigr, 'in
fighting condition', which is rel. to ON. vig,
'war, battle', and cogn. with L. vincere, 'to
vanquish'. See vincible.

## wigwam
wigwam, п., an Indian hut. — A word of Algon-
quian origin, meaning 'their house'; cp. e.g.
Ojibway wigiwam, 'their house'.

## wilco
wilco, inter]., in radio and signaling, a code word
meaning that a message has been received and
will be complied with. — Coined fr. will comply.

## wild
wild, adj. — ME. wilde, fr. OE. wilde, 'wild,
savage, untamed, uncultivated', rel. to OS. wildi,
ON. villr, Dan., Swed. vild, OFris. wilde, Du.
wild, OHG. wildi, MHG. wilde, G. wild, Goth.
wilpeis, 'wild', Dan. vildt, Du. wild, OHG. wild,
MHG. wilt, G. Wild, 'game', OE. wilder, wildor,
'game' [later misinterpreted as wild(d)eor, 'wild
deer'], and cogn. with W. gwyllt, Co. gwyls,
'untamed'. Cp. wilderness. Cp. also wold.
Derivatives: wild, n. and adv., wild-ing, п.,
wild-ish, adj., wild-ly, adv., wild-ness, n.

## wildebeest
wildebeest, п., gnu. — S. Afr. Du., lit. 'wild beest',
fr. Du. wild, 'wild', and beest, 'beast'. See wild
and beast.

## wilder
wilder, tr. v., I) to cause to lose one's way; 2) to
bewilder; intr. v., I) to lose one's way; 2) to
become bewildered. — Prob. back formation from
next word and orig. meaning 'to lead into a
wilderness'. Cp. bewilder.

## wilderness
wilderness, n. — ME., formed with 2nd suff. -ess
fr. OE. wilder, 'wild beast'; cp. Du. wildernis, G.
Wildernis, Wildnis. See wild and cp. wilder.

## wile
wile, n. — ME. wile, fr. OE. wil, 'trick', fr. ONF.
"wile (corresponding to OF. guile), prob. fr. OE.
wigle, 'divination', which is rel. to OE. wicca,
'wizard', wicce, 'witch'. See witch, 'sorceress',
and cp. guile, which is a doublet of wile.
Derivative: wile, tr. v.

## Wilhelmina
Wilhelmina, fem. PN. — G. Wilhelmine, fem.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:855 COLUMN:2 -->
form of Wilhelm, 'William'. See William and
fem. suff. -ina.

## wilkeite
wilkeite, п., a member of the apatite group
(mineral.) — Named after the mineral collector
R. M. Wilke of Palo Alto, California. For the
ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## will
will, n. — ME. will, wille, fr. OE. willa, 'will', rel.
to OS. willio, ON. vili, Dan. villie, Swed. vilja,
OFris. willa, Du. wil, OHG. willio, willo,
MHG., G. wille, Goth, wilja, 'will', and to OE.
willan, etc., 'to will'. See will, v.

## will
will, tr. and aux. v. — ME. willen, fr. OE. willan,
'to will, desire, wish', rel. to OS. willian, wellian,
ΟΝ., Swed. vilja, Dan. ville, OFris. willa, Du.
willen, OHG. wellan, wellen, MHG. wellen, wol-
len, G. wollen, Goth, wiljan, 'to will, wish,
desire', Goth, waljan, 'to choose', ON. val, OHG.
wala, 'choice', fr. I.-E. base "wel-, 'to will, wish,
hope, choose', whence also OI. rrnoti, vrnmi,
'chooses, prefers', Avestic vsrsnav-, 'to wish, will
choose', OI. varyah, 'to be chosen, eligible;
excellent', variyan, 'better', L. void, velle, 'to will,
wish, desire', OSIav. roljp, voliti, 'to will', volja,
'will', veljQ, veleti, 'to command', Lith. pa-vel-
mi, Ί will', viliuos, Ί hope', W. gwell, 'better',
Gk. (with -S-enlargement) έλδομαι (for
£λ-δ-ομαι), Ί wish, long for', έλδωρ (for
έλ-δ-ωρ), 'wish'; (with -π-enlargement) 6λ-
πομαι (for έλ-π-ομοα), Ί wish, long for', 6λπίς
(for έλ-ττ-ίς), 'hope'. Cp. welL adv.. and the
first element in welcome, William, Wilhelmine,
Gilbert. Cp. also velleity, volition, volltive,
voluntary, voluptuous. Cp. also Harpalus.
Derivatives: will-ed, adj., will-ed-ness, п.,
wilier, п., wil(l)-ful, adj., wil(t)-ful-ness, п., will-ing,
adj., will-ing-ly, adv., will-ing-ness, n.

## will
will, tr. v., to bequeath. — Fr. will, n.

## willemite
willemite, п., a zinc orthosilicate (mineral.) — G.
Willemit, named after Willem (= William) I
(1772-1843), king of the Netherlands (1815-40).
The ending -it goes back to Gk. -ίτης; see
subst. suff. -ite.

## willet
willet, п., a N. American bird. — Imitative of its
cry.

## William
William, п., masc. PN. — ONF. Willaume, Wil-
lame, corresponding to OF. (= F.) Guillaume,
of G. origin; cp. OHG. Wiilahelm, which is
compounded of willio, willo, 'will', and helma,
'helmet'. See will, п., and helmet.

## williamsite
williamsite, п., a variety of serpentine (mineral.)
— Named after the American mineral collector
L. W. Williams. For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## will-o'-the-wisp
will-o'-the-wisp, ignis fatuus. — The name lit.
means 'William of the handful of straw'. It is
formed fr. Will, dimin. of William, o' and wisp.

## willow
willow, n. — ME. wilghe, wilowe, fr. OE. welig,
wilig, OS. wilgia, rel. to MLG., MDu. wilghe,
Du. wilg, and cogn. with Gk. έλίκη (for *Fe-
λίκτ;), 'willow', ίλιξ, 'coil, spiral', from I.-E.
base *wel-, 'to roll', whence also L. volvere, 'to
roll'; see volute. OE. welig, etc., 'willow', prop
means 'the tree with pliant branches'. Ср. Е.
withy, which is cogn. with L. viere, 'to bend,
twist'.
Derivatives: willow, tr. v., willow-y, adj.

## willy-nilly
willy-nilly, adv. — Contraction of wil! I, m% I, or
will he, nill he, or will ye, nillye. See will, v., and
rail.

## wilt
wilt, v. — 2nd pers. sing, of will.

## wilt
wilt, intr. v., to fade, wither; tr. v., to cause to
fade. — Prob. alter, of wilk, a dial. var. of welk
(q.v.)

## Wilton
Wilton, п., also Wilton carpet. — Named after
Wilton, a town in Wiltshire, England.

## wily
wily, adj. — ME., fr. wil, 'wile'. See wile and -y
(representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: wili-ly, adv., wili-ness, п.-

## wimble
wimble, п., a gimlet. — ME. wimbel, fr. AF.
wimble, fr. MDu. wimmel, 'auger', which is rel. to
gimlet (q.v.)
Derivative: wimble, tr. v., to bore witha'wimble;
intr. v., to penetrate.

## wimble
wimble, adj., active [now dial.) — Of uncertain
origin.

## wimple
wimple, п., a head covering for women, worn
esp. by nuns. — ME. wimpel, fr. OE. wimpel,
rel. to OS. wimpal, OFris. wimpel, MDu., Du.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:855 COLUMN:3 -->
wimpel, OHG. wimpal, MHG., G. wimpel, ON.
vimpill. OF. guimple (whence F. guimpe, 'nun's
wimple'), is a Teut. loan word (see gimp,
guimpe). The above Teut. words are rel. to Dan.
vippe, MLG., Du; vippen, 'to swing'. See vibrate.
Derivatives: wimple, tr. and intr. v., wimpl-ed,
adj.

## win
win, tr. and intr. v. — ME. winnen, fr. OE. win-
nan, 'to strive, struggle, fight', rel. to OS. winnan,
ΟΝ., Swed. vinna, OFris. winna, Du. winnen, 'to
gain, win', Dan. vinde, 'to win', OHG. winnan,
'to strive, struggle, fight', MHG. gewinnen, 'to
gain by effort', G. gewinnen, 'to gain, win', Goth.
(ga)winnen, 'to suffer, toil', fr. I.-E. base "wen-,
'to strive after, wish, desire, be satisfied', whence
also OI. vanati, vanoti, 'he desires, loves, wins',
L. venus, 'love, sexual desire, loveliness', vene-
rari, 'to worship'. See venerate and cp. wish. Cp.
also the first element in Winfred, winsome, and
the second element in Baldwin, Edwin.
Derivatives: win, п., winn-er, п., winn-ing, adj.,
winn-ings, n. pi., winn-ing-ly, adv.

## wince
wince, intr. v., to shrink; to start back. — ME.
wenchen, winchen, wincen, fr. AF. wenchir,
* wencir, corresponding to OF. guenchir, guencir,
fr. Teut. "wankjan, 'to stagger, totter, draw
back'; cp. OHG. wankon, 'to stagger, totter',
ON. vakka (for *vanka), 'to stray, hover'. See
wink and cp. gauche.

## wincey
wincey, п., fabric of cotton and wool. — A blend
of woolsey and linsey.

## winch
winch, п., 1) a crank with a handle; 2) a type of
windlass. — ME. winche, wynch, fr. OE. wince,
*a pulley', rel. to OE. wincian, 'to nod, wink'.
See wink.

## Winchester
Winchester, п., trademark for a kind of repeating
rifle. — Named after its first manufacturer, the
American industrialist Oliver Fisher Winchester
(1810-80).

## wind
wind, п., air in motion. — ME. wind, fr. OE.
wind, rel. to OS., OFris., Du. wind, ON. vindr,
Dan., Swed. vind, OHG. wind, MHG. wint, G.
Wind, Goth, winds, and cogn. with OI. vatah,
Avestic vdta-, Toch. A want, want, В yente, Hitt.
huwantis, L, ventus, OSIav. vetru, OPruss. wetro,
Lith. vejas, 'wind', Lith. ve'tra, 'tempest', Olr.
feth, 'air', W. gwynt, Bret, gwent, 'wind'. ΑΊ1
these words are derivatives of I.-E. base * we-, 'to
blow', whence also OI. vati, vayati, Avestic
vaiti, 'blows', Goth, waian, OE. wawan, OHG.
wajan, MHG. weien, G. wehen, OSIav. vijati, 'to
blow', Gk. άημι (for *άίημι), Ί blow', άήτης
(for *άΓήττ;ς), 'wind'. Ср. weather, window,
wing, winnow, winze, wither. Cp. also van,
'winnowing fan', and fan. Cp. also Aello, atmo-,
bedeguar, nirvana, Vayu, vent, 'outlet', ventail,
ventiduct, ventilate, ventilation, Ventdse, vol-au-
vent.
Derivatives: wind, tr. v., to scent, wind-less,
wind-y, adjs., wind-i-ly, adv., wind-i-ness, n.

## wind
wind, tr. and intr. v., to turn. — ME. winden, fr.
OE. windan, 'to wind, twist', rel. to OS. windan,
ΟΝ., Swed. vinda, Dan. vinde, OFris. winda, Du.
winden, OHG. wintan, MHG., G. winden, Goth.
windan, 'to wind', fr. I.-E. base *wendh-,*wndh-,
'to turn, twist', whence also OI. vandhurab, 'a
hamper (made of wickerwork)', Gk. ά&ρας [for
*5ά(ν)θρας], 'chariot'. For the causatives of
the above mentioned verbs see wend. OF. guin-
der, It. ghindare, 'to hoist', are Teut. loan words.
Cp. wand, wander, wynd, gauntlet, 'glove', and
the first element in wentletrap and in windle-
straw. Cp. also Atragene.
Derivatives: wind, п., the act of winding,
winding, n. and adj., wind-ing-ly, adv.

## windlass
windlass, п., a device for raising weights by
winding a rope round a cylinder. — ME. windelas,
windlas, fr. Icel. vindilass, fr. ON. vindass
(whence also MDu., Du. windos), which is
compounded of ON. vinda, 'to wind', and ass,
'beam, pillar'. For the first element see wind, 'to
turn'. The second element is rel. to Goth, ans,
'beam, pillar'.
Derivative: windlass, tr. and intr. v.

## windiestraw
windiestraw, windlestrae, п., a dry stalk of grass.
— ME., fr. OE. windlestreaw, which is
compounded of windel, 'basket' (fr. windan, 'to
wind'), and streaw, 'straw'. See wind, 'to turn',

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:856 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 829 | WITENAGEMOT -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:856 COLUMN:1 -->
and straw.

## window
window, n. — ME. windoge, windowe, fr. ON.
vindauga, lit. 'windeye\ See wind, 'air in motion',
and eye.
Derivatives: window, tr. v., window-ed, adj.,
window-less, adj.

## Windsor
Windsor, п., 1) the Windsor bean; 2) a Windsor
chair; 3) Windsor soap. — Named after
Windsor, a town in Berkshire, England.

## wine
wine, n. — ME. win, fr. OE. win, fr. L. \inum,
'wine', whence also OS., OFris., OHG., MHG.
win, ΟΝ. νίη, Dan., Swed. μ/η, Du. wijn, 'wine',
G. Wein, Goth, wein, OSlav. vino, Lith. vjnas,
W. gwin, Qlr.fin. See vine.
Derivatives: wine, tr. and intr. v., wine-less, adj.,
win-er, п., win-ery, п., win-y, adj.

## winebibber
winebibber, п., a drunkard. —Loan translation
of G. Weinsaufer, which is compounded of wein,
'wine\ and Saufer, 'bibber*. See wine and bibber.

## winebibbing
winebibbing, n. — See prec. word and -ing, suff.
forming verbal nouns.

## Winfred
Winfred, masc. PN. — OE. Winfrid, 'friend of
peace', fr. wine, 'friend*, anafridu, 'peace*. The
first element is rel. to ON. vinr, OHG. wini,
'friend', OE. winnan, 'to strive, stuggle, fight';
see win. For the second element see free and cp.
words there referred to.
wing» n. — ME. wenge, winge, of Scand. origin.
Cp. ON. vxngr, Dan., Swed. vinge, 'wing',
which are rel. to Du. waaien, 'to blow; to flutter
in the wind, to fiy\ OE. wdwan, 'to blow'. See
wind, 'air in motion'.
Derivatives: wing, tr. and intr. v., wing-ed,
wingless, adjs., wing-let, n.

## wink
wink, intr. and tr. v. — ME. winken, fr, OE.
wincian, 'to nod, wink\ rel. to Du. wenken,
OHG. winkan, MHG., G. winken, and in gra-
dational relationship to OHG. wankon, *to
stagger, totter*, ON. vakka (for *vanka), 'to
stray, hover*, fr. I.-E. base *wag-, 'to bend*,
whence also L. vagari, 'to wander, roam about'.
See vagary and words there referred to and cp.
esp. wankle, wince, winch, winkle, and the
second element in lapwing.
Derivatives: wink, п., wink-er, п., wink-ing, n.
and adj., wink-ing-ly, adv.

## winkle
winkle, п., an edible mollusk, a periwinkle. —
Back formation fr. 2nd periwinkle.

## winnow
winnow, tr. v, — ME. windewen, winewen, fr. OE.
windwian, 'to winnow', rel. to ON. vinza, OHG.
winton, 'to fan, winnow', Goth, diswinpjan, 'to
throw (grain) apart', and cogn. with L. vannus,
'winnowing fan', ventus, 'wind', ventilare, 'to
fan, winnow'. See wind, 'air in motion', and
words there referred to and cp. esp. ventilate.
Derivatives: winnow, п., winnow-er, п.,
winnowing, adj., winnow-ing-ly, adv.

## winsome
winsome, adj., pleasant, charming. — ME. win-
sum, fr. OE. wynsum, 'pleasant, delightful',
which is formed fr. wynn, 'joy', and suff. -sum;
cp. OS. wunsam, OHG. wunnisam, MHG.
wan(ne)sam. The first element is rel. to OS.
wunnia, OHG. wunja, wunna, wunni, MHG.
wunne, wunne, G. Wonne, 'joy, delight', and to
OE. wyscan, 'to wish*; see wish and cp. win. For
the second element see -some.

## winter
winter, n. — ME., fr. OE. winter, rel. to OFris.,
Du. winter, OS., OHG. wintar, MHG., G.
winter, Dan., Swed. vinter, Goth, wintrus, ON. vetr,
'winter*. These words meant perh. orig. 'the
white (i.e. snowy) season', and are cogn. with
Celtic vindo-, 'white* appearing in Gaul, vindo-
(whence Vindo-bona, the Latin name of Vienna,
which was built by Celtic settlers), Olr. find, W.
gwyn, 'white'. See gwyniad and cp. Wend, Yen-
dace.
Derivatives: winter, intr. and tr. v., winter-ly,
adj., wintr-y, also winter-y, adj., wintr-i-ly, adv.,
wintr-i-ness, n.

## winze
winze, п., a small shaft (mining). — Rel. to Icel.
vinza, 'to winnow', fr. ON. vindre, 'wind'. See
wind, 'air in motion', and cp. winnow.

## wipe
wipe, tr. v. — ME. треп, fr. OE. wipian, 'to wipe',
rel. to Dan. vippe, MLG., MDu., Du. vippen,
OHG. wifan, MHG. wifen, 'to swing', fr. I.-E,
base *weib-, 'to move to and fro, to swing',
whence also L. vibrare, 'to shake'. See vibrate
and cp. wisp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:856 COLUMN:2 -->
Derivatives: wipe, п., wip-er, n.

## wire
wire, n. — ME. wyre, wir, fr. OE. wir, rel. to ON.
*virr in viravirki, 'filigree work', Swed. vira, 'to
twist', OHG. wiara, 'fine gold work', and cogn.
with Olr. fiar, W. gwyr, 'bent, crooked', fr. I.-E.
base *wei-, 'to bend, twist', whence also L. viere,
'to bend, twist*. See withy. Cp. L. viriae,
'armlet, bracelet', which is a Celtic loan word and
ult. derives fr. I.-E. base *wei-. Cp. also ferrule.
Derivatives: wire, tr. and intr. v., wir-ed, adj.,
wire-less, adj. and п., wir-er, п., wir-ring, п.,
wir-y, adj., wir-i-ly, adv., wir-i-ness, n.

## wis
wis, tr. v., to know (archaic). — Back formation
fr. ME. i-wis, 'certainly', misinterpreted as / wis
(= / wist, I wit), Ί know'. For the etymology of
ME. iwis see iwis.

## wisdom
wisdom, n. — ME., fr. OE. wisdom, formed fr.
wis, 'wise', with suff. -dom. See wise, 'prudent',
and -dom and cp. OS., OFris. wisdom, ON.
visdomr, Dan., Swed. visdom, OHG. wistuom,
'wisdom', G. Weistum, 'judicial sentence serving
as a precedent*.
wisdom tooth. — Loan translation of L. denies
sapientiae, itself loan translation of Gk. σω-
φρονιστήρες, 'wisdom teeth', fr. σωφρονεΤν,
'to be sound of mind'; so called because in
contradistinction to the other teeth,they appear
when the person is already grown up.

## wise
wise, п., manner, fashion. — ME. wise, fr. OE.
wise, 'way» manner', rel. to OS. wisa, OFris. wis,
Dan., Norw., Swed. vis, MDu. wise, Du. wijs,
wijze, OHG. wis(a)t MHG. wisie), G. We'ise,
'way, manner', ON. visa, 'strophe, verse', vis in
odru vis, 'otherwise', fr. I.-E. base *weid-, *to
see; to know*. The orig. meaning of OE. wise,
etc., was 'knowledge'. See next word and cp.
gnise, which is a doublet of wise.

## wise
wise, adj., I) knowing, learned; 2) prudent. —
ME. wis, fr. OE, wis, rel. to OS., OFris. wis, ON.
viss, Dan., Swed. vis, Du. wijs, 'wise', Du. wijze,
'a wise man', OHG. wis(i), MHG. wis(e), G.
weise, 'wise', Goth, -wets (only in compounds),
'knowing', fr. I.-E. base *weid-, 'to see; to
know'. See vision and cp. wise, adj., and wit, v.
and n. Cp. also wisdom, wiseacre and the second
element in righteous.
Derivatives: wise-ly, adv., wise-ness, n.

## wise
wise, tr. v., (chiefly Scot.), 1) to show (someone)
the way; 2) to direct. — ME. wisen, fr. OE.
wisian, rel. to OS. wisian, ON. visa, Dan. vise,.
Swed., Norw. visa, OFris. wisa, MLG., MDu.
wisen, Du. wijzen, MHG. wisen, G. weisen, 'to
show the way, direct'. These verbs lit. mean 'to
make wise*, and derive fr. OE. wis, 'wise,
knowing*, resp. its equivalents in the other Teut.
languages. See wise, adj.

## -wise
-wise, combining form. — Fr. wise, n.

## wiseacre
wiseacre, п., one who pretends to know
everything. — MDu. wijs-segger, fr. OHG. wis-sago,
'prophet', popular transformation (as if fr.
OHG. wis, 'wise*, and sago, 'sayer') of OHG.
w3($)ago* a derivative of OHG. wi^an
(corresponding to OE. witan), 'to know'. OHG.
wissagen, 'to prophesy' (whence MHG. wissa-
gen, G. weissagen) is a back formation fr. wis-
sago. Cp. OE. witega, witga, ON. vitki, 'prophet',
and OE. witig, 'knowing', and see wit, v. and n.

## wish
wish, tr. and intr. v. — ME. wisshen, fr. OE.
wyscan, 'to wish', rel. to ON- xskja, Dan. vnske,
Swed. onska, MDu. wonscen, wunscen, wenscen,
Du. wensen, OHG. wunsken, MHG., G. wun-
schen, 'to wish', ON. osk, 'wish', MDu. wonsc,
wunsc, wensc, Du. wens, OHG. wunsc, MHG.,
G. wunsch, 'wish', fr. I.-E. base *wen-, 'to
strive after, wish, desire, be satisfied1, whence
also OI. vanati, vanoti, vauchati, 'he desires,
loves', vanas-, 'desire', L. venus, 'love,
loveliness', venerari, 'to reverence, worship, venerate'.
See venerate and cp. wean, ween, win, won, wont,
adj. Cp. also gain.
Derivatives: wish, п., wish-ed, adj., wish-ed-ly,
adv., wish-fui, adj., wish-ful-ly, adv.,
wish-fulness, п., wish-ing, adj., wish-ing-ly, adv.

## wish-wash
wish-wash, п., any weak drink. — Antiphonic
reduplication of wash.

## wishy-washy
wishy-washy, adj., tasteless. — Antiphonic
reduplication of washy. See wash.

## wisp
wisp, п., a small bunch. — ME. wisp, wips, of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:856 COLUMN:3 -->
uncertain origin; perh. rel. to OE. wipian, 'to wipe'.
See wipe and cp. will-o -ihe-wisp.
Derivatives: wisp, tr. v., wisp-ish, adj., wisp-y,
adj., wisp-i-ly, adv., wisp-i-ness, n.

## wissel
wissel, п., change; retribution (Scot.) — ME.
wissel, 'exchange*, fr. MDu. (= Du.) wissel,
which is rel. to OHG. wehsal, 'change'. See
week.

## wist
wist, п., an old Sussex land measure. — ML.
wista, prob. fr. OE. wist, 'food, provision,
sustenance', which is rel. to ON. vist, OHG. wist, of
s.m.

## wist
wist, tr. v., to know (archaic). — ME. wiste, fr.
OE., past tense of witan, 'to know*. Cp. Du.
wist, past of weten, G. wusste, past of wissen,
Dan. vidste, past of vide, Swed. visste, past of
veta, 'to know', and see wit, v.

## Wistaria
Wistaria, п., 1) Wisteria; 2) (not cap.) a pale
purple. — See next word.

## Wisteria
Wisteria, п., 1) a genus of woody vines (bot.); 2)
(not cap.) any plant of this genus. — ModL.,
named by the botanist Thom,as Nuttall (1786-
1859) after Caspar Wistar (or Wister) (1761-
1818), professor of anatomy in Philadelphia.
For the ending see 1st suff. -ia.

## wistful
wistful, adj., longing, yearning. — Appar. a blend
of wishful and obsol. wistly, 'intently', which is
prob. formed from whist, interj., with adv. suff.
-ly.
Derivatives: wistful-ly, adv., wist-ful-ness, n.

## wit
wit, tr. and intr. v. — ME. witen, weten, fr. OE.
witan, 'to know', rel. to OS. witan, ΟΝ., Norw.
vita, Swed. veta, Dan. vide, OFris. wita, MDu.,
Du. weten, OHG. wi^an, MHG. wi^en, G.
wissen, Goth, witan, 'to know', from I.-E. base
*weid-, *woid-, *wid-, 'to see; to know', whence
also L. videre, 'to see'. See" vision and cp. words
there referred to. Cp. also next word and twit,
wise, adj. and п., wisdom, wiseacre, witan, wite,
'to accuse', witenagemot, witness, wizard, wot,
and gnide, guise, gny, 'rope'.
Derivatives: witt-ed, adj., witt-ing, adj., witt-
ing-ly, adv.

## wit
wit, n. — ME., fr. OE., 'understanding,
intelligence, mind', rel. to OS. wit, ON. vit, Dan. vid,
Swed. vett, OFris. wit, OHG. wizzi, MHG. witze,
'knowledge, understanding, intelligence, mind',
G. Witz, 'wit, witticism, joke', Goth, unwiti,
'ignorance', and to OE. witan, 'to know'. See
wit, v.
Derivatives: wit-less, adj., wit-less-ly, adv., wit-
less-ness, wit-ling, п., witty (q.v.)

## witan
witan, n. pi., members of the national council
(English hist.) — OE., pi. of wita, 'advisor,
councilor', lit. 'wise man', fr. witan, 'to know'. See
wit, v.

## witch
witch, п., sorceress (orig. used also in the sense of
'sorcerer') — ME. wicche (masc. and fem.), fr.
OE. wicca, 'wizard' (masc), wicce(fem.),'witch',
rel. to OE. wiccian, 'to use witchcraft', and to
MLG. .wikken, wicken, 'to use witchcraft',
wikker, wicker, 'soothsayer', OE. wigle,
'divination', and prob. also to OE. wih, 'idol'. See
victim and cp. bewitch. Cp. also wile.
Derivatives: witch, tr. v., witch-ed, adj., witch-
-ed-ly, adv., witch-ery,n., witch-ing, adj., witch-
-ing-ly, adv.

## witch
witch, п., any of various trees having pliant
branches, esp. the wych elm. — ME. wyche, fr.
OE. wice, wic, prob. rel. to OE. wican, 'to give
way, yield'. See weak.

## witchcraft
witchcraft, n. — ME. wicchecraft, fr. OE. wicce-
crseft, fr. wicca, wicce (see 1st witch) and crseft,
'craft' (see craft).

## witch elm
witch elm, witch haze], — See wych elm, wych
haze].

## wite
wite, п., punishment (obsol. except Scot, and dial.
E.) — ME., fr. OE. wite, 'punishment, torture',
rel. to ON. viti, OHG. wfji, 'punishment, fine',
and to OE. witan, 'to reproach, blame'. See
wite, v.

## wite
wite, tr. v., to accuse; to blame (obsol. except
Scot, and dial. English). — ME. witen, fr. OE.
witan, 'to reproach, blame', rel. to Du. wijten,
'to blame', OHG. wizan, MHG. wl^en, G. ver-
weisen, zurecht-weisen, 'to reprove, reproach',
and to OE. witan, 'to know'; see wit, v.

## witenagemot
witenagemot, п., national assembly of the Anglo-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:857 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: WITH | 830 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:857 COLUMN:1 -->
Saxons {English Hist.) — OE. witena gemot, lit.
'meeting of the wise men', fr. witena, gen. pi. of
wita, 'a wise man', and gemut, 'meeting'. See
witan and moot, 'meeting', and cp. folkmote,
gemot, hallmoot.

## with
with, prep. — ME. with, 'against; with', fr. OE.
wid, Opposite, near; against; with', OS. with,
ON. via, of s.m.; rel. to OE. wider, 'against',
which, together with OS. witkar, 'against', ON.
vidr, 'against, with, toward, at', MDu., Du.
weder, Du. weer, 'again*, Goth. wij>ra, 'against,
opposite', derives fr. I.-E. *wi-t(e)ro-, lit.
'more apart', formed with compar. suff. -ter
(see -ther), fr. I.-E. base *wi-, 'against; apart,
asunder; two', whence also OI. vi, Avestic vi-
'asunder', OI. vitaram, 'farther, further',
Avestic vitar m, 'sideward', OSlav. vutoru (for
*vUorU), 'other, second'; Gk. ίδιος, 'one's own',
and Εσος, 'equal', are not cognate. Cp. withers
■and the first element in withershins. Cp. also
wide. Cp. also vice, 'moral fault', and the first
element in vicennial and in gnerdon, Yihara,
vimaoa, visarga. With has superseded to OE.
preposition mid, 'with', which has survived only
as a ModE. pref. (see midwife). The orig. sense
of with ('against') has survived in compounds
(cp. e.g. withdraw, withhold, withstand).

## withal
withal, adv. and prep. — ME. withall, withal,
compounded of with, 'with', and all, al, 'all'. See
with and all.

## withamite
withamite, п., a variety of epidote (mineral.) —
Named after Dr. Henry Witham of Glencoe,
Scotland. For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## withdraw
withdraw, tr. v. — Compounded of with, 'against',
and draw.

## withdrawal
withdrawal, n. — A hybrid coined fr. withdraw
and -al, a suff. of Latin origin.

## withe
withe, п., a flexible slender twig esp. of a willow.
— ME. withe, wythe, wythth, fr. OE. widde. See
withy.

## wither
wither, intr. v., to dry up, shrivel, fade; tr. v., to
cause to dry up, shrivel or fade. — ME. wideren,
widren, variants of wederen, 'to weather', fr.
weder, 'weather*; cp. G. verwlttern, 'to become
weather-beaten', fr. Witter, 'weather'. See
weather.

## witherite
witherite, п., a native barium carbonate (mineral.)
— Named after the English physician Dr.
William Withering (1741-99), its discoverer. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## withernam
withernam, n. (Early English Law), distress
against distress; a taking by way of reprisal. —
ME-, lit. 'a taking against, reprisal', fr. OE.
wider, 'against', and nam, 'a seizure', fr. niman,
'to take'. For the first element see with, for the
second see nimble.

## withers
withers, п., that part of the back of a horse or
another animal which is lying between the shoulder
blades. — ME. pref. wither-, 'against', fr. OE.
wider-, fr. wider, 'against'; see with and cp. the
first element in next word. Withers lit. means
'the resisting part'. Cp. G. Widerrist, 'withers',
fr. -wider, 'against', and Rist, 'wrist'.

## withershins
withershins, also widdershins, adv., in a direction
contrary to the apparent course of the sun. —
The earlier form is widdershins, which derives fr.
MLG. weddersinnes, fr. MHG. widersinnes, lit.
'against the way', i.e. 'in an opposite direction',
fr. widersinnen, 'to go against', fr. widet, 'against',
and sinnen, 'to travel, go', fr. OHG. sinnan, of
s.m., which is rel. to OHG. sind, 'way, journey';
see with and send. The alteration of widdershins
to withershins is due to the influence of the
obsol. E. pref. wither-, fr. OE. wider, 'against'.

## withhold
withhold, tr. v. — ME. withkolden, compounded
of with, 'against', and holden, 'to ho^d'. See with
and hold, v.

## within
within, adv. — ME. withinne, withinnen, fr. OE.
widinnan, 'inside of, lit. 'against the inside',
compounded of wid, 'against', and innan, 'in'.
See with and in.
Derivatives: within, п., prep, and adv.

## without
without, adv. — ME. wlthoute, withouten, fr. OE.
widutan, 'outside of, without', lit. 'against the
outside', fr. wid, 'against', and Utan, 'out'. See
with and out.
Derivatives: without, п., prep, and conj.

## withstand
withstand, tr. and intr. v. — ME. witkstanden, fr.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:857 COLUMN:2 -->
OE. widstandan, 'to resist', compounded of wid,
'against', and standan, 'to stand'. Cp. ON. vid-
standa, OFris. withstonda and see with and
stand.

## withy
withy, n. — ME. withi, fr. OE. widig, 'willow,
willow twig', rel. to OE. widde, 'withe', ON.
vidir, 'willow', Swed. vide, Dan. vidje, 'willow',
OHG. wida, MHG. wide, G. Weide, 'willow',
and cogn. with Avestic vaeiti-, 'osier', Gk. ίτέά
(prob. for *ίειτέά), 'willow', Ιτυς, Aeol.
Γίτύς, 'the edge or rim of anything round',
οίσύη, οϊσυον (for 'Γοιτίύη, "Fotrfuov), 'a
kind of willow', οΐσος (for "ίοΐτΐος), 'withy',
L. vttis, 'vine', vitex, 'the chaste tree', Lett.
vitols, 'willow*, Lith. vytis, 'willow twig', iilvitis,
'gray willow', OPruss. w'itwan, Pol. witwa, W.
gwden, 'willow', OSlav. viti, 'something twisted',
OSlav. vetvi, Russ. vttvina, 'branch, bough'. AH
these words derive fr. I.-E. base *wei-, 'to bend,
twist', whence also OI. vayati, 'weaves', L. viere,
'to bend, twist', L. vimen, 'twig, switch, osier',
Lith. veju, vyti, 'to turn, twist'. Cp. withe. Cp.
also gnlge, wire and the second element in
periwinkle, the plant. Cp. also vetch, Vicia, vimen,
Vinca, vinculum, viscera, vise, 'a tool', vitta,
vrille, inion, ino-, iris, Itea and the second
element in Stomoisla.

## witness
witness, n. — ME. witnesse, fr. OE. gewitness,
witness, 'knowledge, testimony', fr. wit, n. See
wit, п., and -ness.
Derivatives: witness, v., witness-er, n.

## witney
witney, п., heavy woolen material used for
blankets. — So called fr. Witney, a town in
Oxfordshire, England, where it was first manufactured.

## wittichenite
wittichenite, п., a copper bismuth sulfide
(mineral.) — Named after Wittichen in Baden. For
the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## witticism
witticism, п., a witty remark. — A hybrid formed
fr. witty with -ism, a suff. of Greek origin;
coined by the English poet John Dryden (1631-1700)
on analogy of criticism.

## wittol
wittol, п., a husband condoning his wife's
infidelity (archaic). — A var. of witwall, woodwall, fr.
ME. wodewale, 'the green woodpecker', rel. to
MDu. wedewal, MHG. witewal, G. Wittewal,
Wiedewall, 'the green woodpecker'. The first
element of these words is rel. to wood, the second
is prob. of imitative origin. For sense
development cp. cuckold, which is rel. to cuckoo.

## witty
witty, adj. — ME. witi, fr. OE. wittig, witig, fr.
wit. See wit, п., and -y (representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: witti-ly, adv., witti-ness, n.

## wive
wive, intr. v., to marry a woman; tr. v., to take
for a wife. — ME. wiven, fr. OE. wifian, 'to
marry', fr. wif, 'woman, wife'. See wife. Cp.
MDu. wiven and see wife.

## wivern
wivern, wyvem, п., a two-legged, winged dragon
(her.) — ME. quivere, wivere, 'serpent', fr. OF.
wivre (F. guivre), fr. L. vipera, 'viper'; influenced
in form by OHG. wipera, which also derives fr.
L. vipera; see viper, and cp. weever. For the
excrescent я ср. bittern.

## wizard
wizard, п., a magician. — ME. wisard, formed
with suff. -ard fr. wis, 'wise'. See wise, adj.
Derivatives: wizard, adj., wizard-ly, adj.,
wizardry, n.

## wizen
wizen, intr. and tr. v., to shrivel. — ME. wisenen,
fr. OE. wisnian, weosnian, 'to wither', rel. to ON.
visna, 'to wither', OHG. wesanen, 'to dry up',
OHG. fir-wesan, MHG., G. ver-wesen, 'to
decay, rot'. These words possibly derive from a
Teut. base "wis-, which corresponds to I.-E.
*weis-, 'to melt away, rot', whence L. viiscere,
'to fade, wither', virus (for "visos), 'poison'. See
virus.
Derivative: wizen-ed, adj.

## wo
wo, interj. — Archaic var. of woe.

## woad
woad, n. — ME. wod, fr. OE. wad, rel. to Dan.
vaid, OFris. wed, MDu. wide, weet, Du. wede,
OHG., MHG. welt, G. Waid, 'woad', and prob.
cogn. with Gk. ίσάτις (for *5ίτσάτις), 'woad',
and perh. also with L. vitrum, 'woad; glass'; see
vltreo- and cp. Isatis, vitriol. ML. waisdo and
OF. guesde (whence F. guide) and It. guado are
Teut. loan words.
Derivative: woad, tr. y.

## wobble
wobble, wnbble, intr. v., to move unsteadily. —
Rel. to LG. wabbeln, 'to wobble', MHG. wabe-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:857 COLUMN:3 -->
ten, 'to waver', and to ON. vafla and vafra, 'to
hover about', OE. wxfre, 'wavering, restless'.
See waver.
Derivatives: wobble, п., wobbl-er, п., wobbl-ing,
п., wobbl-y, adj., wobbl-i-ness, n.

## Woden
Woden, Wodan, п., Anglo-Saxon god,
corresponding to the Scandinavian god Odin. — OE.
Woden, rel. to OS. Wodan, ON. Odinn, OHG.
Wuotan and to OE. wod, 'mad, frenzied', wop,
'sound, melody, song', OHG. wuot, 'mad;
madness' (whence MHG., G. wut, 'rage, fury'),
Goth, wops, 'possessed, mad', ON. odr, 'spirit,
mind, passion, song, poetry'. These Teut. words
are cogn. with L. votes, 'soothsayer, prophet,
seer'. See vates and cp. Edda, Odin, Wednesday,
wood, adj.

## wodge
wodge, п., a bulky object. — Prob. alt. of wedge.

## woe
woe, also wo, n. — ME. wa, wo, fr. OE. wu, 'evil,
suffering; woe', rel. to OS., OFris., OHG.,
MHG. we, G. weh, MDu., Du. wee, ON. vei,
vse, Goth, wai, from the I.-E. imitative base
*wai-, 'voe', whence also OI. uve, Avestic vayor,
Gk. οά, L. vae, Lith., Lett, wai, Mir. file, W.
gwae, 'woe', Arm. ray, 'woe; misfortune'. Cp.
wail and the first element in wellaway.
Derivatives: woe-ful, adj., woe-fui-ly, adv., woe-
ful-ness, n.

## woebegone
woebegone, adj. — ME. wo begon, lit. 'beset with
woe', fr. wo, 'woe' (see prec. word), and begon,
pp. of begon, 'to surround, beset'. See begone.

## woke
woke, past tense of wake. — ME. wok, wook, fr.
OE. woe, past tense of wacan. See wake, v.

## woken
woken, pp. of wake (rare). — Formed on analogy
of spoken, on the basis of the following ratio:
speak (formerly pronounced spake): spoken =
wake: woken.

## void
void, п., a tract of elevated, open country. —
ME. wald, wold, fr. OE. weald, wald, 'forest', rel.
to OS., OFris. wald, MDu. wold, Du. woud,
OHG. wald, MHG. wait, G. Wald, 'forest',
Swed. vail, 'pasture', ON. vollr, 'soil, field,
meadow'. The fact that OS. and OHG. wald
denote not only 'forest', but also 'wilderness',
supports the view that the above words stand in
gradational relationship to wild (q.v.) Cp. weald,
Tynwald, waldhorn. Cp. also vole, 'a rodent'.

## wolf
wolf, n. — ME., fr. OE. wulf, rel. to OS. wulf,
ON. ulfr, Swed. ulf, OFris., Du., OHG., MHG.,
G. wolf, Goth, wulfs, fr. I.-E. *wlqwos-, 'wolf,
whence also OI. vfkas, Avestic vehrka-, Alb. ul'k,
OSlav. vluku, Lith. vilkas, Lett, vllks, OPruss.
wilkis, 'wolf, and prob. also Gk. λύκος, L.
lupus, of s.m. I.-E. *w\qwos- possibly derives fr.
base "wel-, 'to tear', and prop, denotes 'the
tearing animal'. See vellicate and cp. vulture.
Cp. also wolfram, wolverine and the second
element in werewolf, Adolph, Bardolph, Ralph,
Randal. Cp. also lupine, adj. and п., and lyceum.
Derivatives: wolf, tr. v., to devour greedily;
intr. v., to hunt for wolves, wolf-ed, adj., wolf-er,
п., wolf-ish, adj., wolf-ish-ly, adv., wolf-ish-ness
n.

## Wolffia
Wolffia, п., a genus of aquatic plants (hot.) —
ModL., named after the German physician and
botanist Johann F. Wolff (1778-1806). For the
ending see 2nd suff. -in.

## wolfram
wolfram, п., 1) tungsten; 2) wolframite. — G.,
lit. 'wolfs soot', fr. MHG. wolf (see wolf) and
ram, 'dirt, soot' (whence G. Rahm, of s.m.); so
called in sign of contempt because it was
regarded of lesser value than tin and caused a
considerable loss of tin during the smelting
process in the furnace. — For sense
development cp. cobalt and nickel.

## wolframate
wolframate, п., tungstate (ckem.) — Formed
from prec. word with chem. suff. -ate.

## wolframite
wolframite, п., iron manganese tungstate
(FeMn)W04 (mineral.) — G. Wolframit, formed
fr. Wolfram (see prec. word) with suff. -it, which
goes back to Gk. -ίτης (see subst. suff. -ite).

## wolframium
wolframium, п., the same as tungsten (chem.) —
ModL, fr. wolfram. For the ending see chem.
suff. -ium.

## wolisbergite
wolisbergite, п., chalcostibite (mineral.) —
Named after Wolfsberg in the Harz Mountains.
For the ending see subst. suff. -ite.

## wollastonite
wollastonite, п., a mineral consisting of a silicate
of calcium (mineral.) — Named after the Eng-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:858 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 831 | WORSE -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:858 COLUMN:1 -->
lish chemist and physicist William Hyde Wollas-
ton (t 766-1828). For the ending see subst. suff.
-ite.

## wolverine
wolverine, wolverene, п., a carnivorous mammal
(Gulo luscus). — Irregularly formed fr. wolf (pi.
wolves); so called in allusion to its wolfish
qualities.

## woman
woman, n. — ME. wimman, wumman, woman, fr.
ОЕ- wifman, wimman, lit. 'woman-man, wife-
man', compounded of wif, 'woman, wife', and
man, 'human being, man'. (In OE. man was
used of both sexes); cp. Du. vrouwmens, 'wife',
lit. 'woman-man'.) See wife and таи.
Derivatives: woman, tr. and intr. v.,
womanhood^ п., woman-isk, adj., woman-isk-ly, adv.,
woman-ish-ness, п., woman-ize, tr. and intr. v.,
woman-less, adj., woman-like, adj., woman-ly,
adj., woman-li-ness, n.

## womb
womb, n. — ME. wambe, wombe, fr. OE. wamb,
womb, 'belly, womb', rel. to ON. vomb, Norw.
vomb, Dan. vom, Swed. vamm, OFris. wambe,
wamme, MDu. wamme, Du. warn, OHG. wam-
ba, MHG. wambe, wamme, 'belly', G. Wammey
'belly, paunch*, Goth, wamba, 'belly, womb',
and to OE. umbor, 'child*. Cp. gambeson.
Derivative: womb, tr. v., to enclose as in a womb. '

## wombat
wombat, п., a marsupial mammal of Australia. —
From the native Australian name womback,
wombar.

## won
won, intr. and tr. v., to dwell (archaic). — ME.
wunien, wunen, wonen, fr. OE. wunian, 'to dwell,
remain; to be accustomed to'. See wont, adj.

## won
won, past tense and pp. of win. — ME. wunnen,
wonnen, fr. OE. gewunnen, pp. of winnan. See
win.

## wonder
wonder, n. — ME. wunder, wonder, fr. ОБ.
wundor, 'wonder, miracle', rel. to OS. wundar,
MDu., Du. wonder, OHG. wuntar, MHG., G.
wander, ON. undr, Dan., Swed. under, 'wonder';
of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: wonder, v. (q.v.), wonder-ment, п.,
wondrous (q.v.)

## wonder
wonder, intr. and tr. v. — ME. wundrien, fr. OE.
wundrian, 'to wonder', fr. wundor. See wonder, n.
Derivatives: wonder-er, п., wonder-ing, adj. and
п., wonder-ing-ly, adv.

## wondrous
wondrous, adj. — ME. wonders, 'wondrous', fr.
gen. of wonder, 'wonder' (see wonder, п., and
adv. sufT. -s); assimilated in form to the
adjectives ending in -ous.
Derivatives: wondrous-ly, adv., wondrous-ness,
n.

## wonky
wonky, adj., tottery, unsteady {British Slang) —
Formed with adj. sufT. -y from the base
appearing in OE. wancol, 'wavering'. See wankle.

## wont
wont, adj., accustomed. — ME. waned, woned,
wont, pp. of wunen, wonen, fr. OE. wunian, 'to
dwell, remain, be used to', rel. to OS. wunon,
wonon, OFris. wonia, wunia, of s.m., MDu., Du.
wonen, 'to dwell*, OHG. wonen, MHG. wonen,
'to dwell, remain; to be used to', G. wohnen,
'to dwell1, ON. una, 'to dwell; to be content',
Goth. *wunan in un-wunands, 'troubled*, lit.
'not content'. Th.e original meaning of these
verbs was 'to be content; to rejoice'. They are
rel. to OE. wynn, 'joy', fr. l.-E. base *wen-, 'to
strive after, wish, desire; to be satisfied, to be
wont'. See wish and cp. wean, ween, win, won,
'to dwell'.
Derivatives: wont, tr. and intr. v. and п.,
wonted, adj.

## woo
woo, tr. v., to court. — ME. wowen, fr. OE. wd-
gian, of uncertain origin.
Derivatives: wooer (q.v.), woo-ing, adj., woo*
ing-ly, adv.

## wood
wood, п., 1) forest; 2) timber. — ME. wode, fr.
OE.. wudu, fr. earlier widu, 'wood', which is rel.
to ON. vidr, 'tree, wood', Dan., Swed. ved,
OHG. witu, MHG. wite, 'wood', prob. fr. I.-E.
base *widhu-, 'tree, wood', whence also W.
gwydd, Gael, fiodh, 'wood', Olr. fid, 'tree', Ir.
fiodh, 'wood, timber'. Cp. OS. widohoppa, MDu.
wedenoppe, OHG. witukoffa, wituhopfa, MHG.
witehopfe, G. Wiedehopf, 'hoopoe', which prob.
mean lit. 'woodhopper'.
Derivatives: wood, tr. and intr. v., wood-ed,
wood-en, adjs., wood-ing, п., wood-less, wood-y,
adjs.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:858 COLUMN:2 -->

## wood
wood, adj., mad {archaic or dial.) — ME. wod, fr.
OE. wdd, 'mad, frenzied'. See Woden and words
there referred to.

## woodchnck
woodchnck, п., any of various marmots. — Prob.
altered fr. Cree otcheh, or Ojibwa otchig, 'fisher,
marten'. Folk etymology explained this word as
a compound of wood and chuck.

## woodruff
woodruff, п., a European herb (Asperula odorata)
— ME. woderofe, woderove, fr. OE. wudurofe,
which is compounded of wudu (see wood, n.)
and a second element of unknown origin.

## Woodsia
Woodsia, п., a genus of ferns (bot.) — ModL.,
named after the English botanist Joseph Woods
(1776-1864). For the ending see lst*uff. -ia.

## Woodwardla
Woodwardla, п., a genus of plants, the chain fern
{bot.) — ModL., named after the English
botanist Thomas J. Woodward (1745-1820). For
the ending see 1st suff. -Ia.

## wooer
wooer, n. — ME. wowere, fr. OE. wogere, fr.
wogan, 'to woo*. See woo and agential sufT. -er.

## woof
woof, п., 1) weft; 2) texture; fabric. — ME. oof,
fr. OE. dwef formed fr. pref. δ-, and wef, 'web*,
fr. wefan,lto weave'; see a-, 'on', and weave.The
initial win woof is due to the influence of weave.
Derivative: woof у, adj.

## wool
wool, n. — ME. wulle, wolle, fr. OE. wull, rel. to
ΟΝ., Swed. ull, OFris. wolle, ulle, MLG., MDu.
wolle, wulle, Du. wol, OHG. wolla, MHG., G.
wolle, Goth, wulla, fr. I.-E. *w\nd, 'wool',
whence also OI. urna, Avestic var nd. Arm.
geimn, OSlav. vlurta, Russ. volna, Lith. vilna,
'hair of wool', pi. vllnos, 'woof, Lett, vilna,
'wool', OPruss. wilna, *coat', L. Idna, Gk.
ληνός, Dor. λανος (for *5ληνος, resp. *f>.av-
ος), 'wool', Mir. olann (for *wl nd), 'wool', W.
gwldn, 'wool' (whence gwlanen, 'flannel'). I.-E.
"wfnd possibly derives fr. base *wel-, 'to tear,
pluck', and lit. means 'that which is
plucked or shorn off', whence L. vellere, 'to pluck,
twitch', vellus, 'wool shorn off, fleece'. See velli-
cate and cp. delaine, flannel, lanate, Innigerous,
lanolin, lanose, lanugo, 1 ami gin ous, lasio-,
velours, velure, velvet, villus.
Derivatives: wool, tr. v., wool(l)en (q.v.), wool(l)-
y, adj., wool(J)-i-ness, n.

## woolen
woolen, wooilen, adj. — ME. wollen, fr. OE.
wullen, fr. wull, 'wool*; cp. OE. wyllen, 'of wool,
woolen'. See wool and -en.

## woolsey
woolsey, п., linsey-woolsey. — Fr. linsey-woolsey.

## woorali
woorali, woorara, п., curare. — Variants of curare.

## wootz
wootz, п., a kind of steel made in India. —
Misprint for wook, inexact rendering of Canarese
ukku, 'steel*.

## woozy
woozy, adj., befuddled; dizzy. — Prob. alter, of
oozy. See ooze and adj. suff. -y.

## wop
wop, п., an Italian (used in a derogatory sense).
— It. (Neapolitan dial.) guappo, fr. Sp. guapo,
'stout,, courageous, bold; a bully, dandy',
formed—prob. through the medium of OF.
gape, 'insipid; idle'—fr. L. vappa, *wine that
has lost its flavor; a worthless fellow, a good-
for-nothing', which is rel. to vapidus, 'flavorless,
insipid'. See vapid.

## wop
wop, v. — A var. of whop.

## word
word, n. — ME. word, fr. OE. word, rel. to OS.,
OFris. word, Du. woord, OHG., MHG. G.
wort, ON. ord, Dan., Swed. ord, Goth, waurd,
fr. I.-E. *werdh-, whence also OPruss. wirds,
'word', Lith. vafdas, 'name', Mlr.fordat, 'they
say', L. verbum, 'word'. (For the change of
I.-E. dh to b in Latin cp. L. ruber and E. red, L.
barba and E. beard.) I.-E. *werdh- is an
enlarged form of base *wer-, *were-, *were-, 'to
speak', whence Gk. εϊρω (for *Γέριω), Ί say,
speak*, εϊρων (for *^έριων), 'dissembler', lit.
'sayer' (i.e. one who speaks in-order to hide his
thoughts), ειρωνεία, 'irony', ρήτωρ, Aeol.
5ρήτωρ, 'public speaker, orator; rhetor', £ημα
(for *5ρήμα), 'word', OI. vratam,
'commandment, order', Avestic urvdta-, of s.m., OSlav.
rota (for *vrota), 'oath*, vraei, 'physician,
magician', Hitt. weriya-, 'to call', and prob. also
Hitt. huwart-, 'to curse'. Cp. hermeneutic, irony,

## rhetor
rhetor, verb, verve.
Derivatives: word, tr. v., word-able, adj., word-
-abl-y, adv., word-age, п., word-ed, adj., word-er,
п., word-ing, п., word-less, adj., wordy (q.v.)

## wordy
wordy, adj. — ME., fr. OE. wordig, fr. word. See

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:858 COLUMN:3 -->
word and -y (representing OE. -ig).

## work
work, n. — ME. werk, work, fr. OE. were, wore,
weorc, 'work, act, action', rel. to OS. OFris.,
Du. werk, ON. verk, Dan. vxrk, Swed. verk,
MDu. ware, weorc, were, OHG. werah, were,
MHG. werch, were, G. Werk, Goth, gawaurki,
'work*, fr. I.-E. base *werg-, 'work, to work',
whence also Avestic var za, 'work, activity',
ν r zyeiti, 'he works, does', Toch. A wark,
'wicker work', Arm. gore, 'work', Gk. Εργον
(dial. 5έργον), 'work', Ερδω (prob. for *fep-
γ^ω), Ί do, sacrifice', ρέζω (prob. for*fρέv-
to>), Ί do*, δ'ργανον (for *f όργανον), 'an
instrument', бруьос (for *f όργια), 'secret rites'.
Cp. work, v., wright and the second element in
bulwark. Cp. also ergon and words there referred
to.
Derivative: work-less, adj.

## work
work, intr. and tr. v. — ME. werken, worken, fr.
OE. wyrcan, wircan, rel. to OS. werkon, wirkian,
ON. verka, yrka, Dan. virke, Swed. yrka, OFris.
werka, werkia, wirka, MDu. warken, wirken,
weerken, werken, Du. werken, OHG. wurchen,
wirchen, MHG. wiirken, wirken, G. wirken,
Goth, waurkjan, 'to work*, and to OE. weorc,
'work*. See work, п., and cp. wrought.
Derivatives: work-able, adj., work-abil-ity, п.,
work-able-ness, п., work-abl-y, adv., work-er, п.,
work-ing, adj. and n.

## world
world, n. — ME. weoreld, weorld, fr. OE. weo-
ruld, woruld, 'world, age', related to OS. werold,
ON. verbid, Swed. verld, Dan. verden, OFris.
world, wrald, Du. wereld, OHG. weralt, worolt,
MHG. werelt, werlt, welt, G. Welt. The first
element of these compound words is rel. to OE.
wer, etc., 'man'; see virile. The second element
is rel. to ON. old, 'mankind', aldr, 'age', OE.
ieldu, Goth, aids, 'age', and to OE. aid, 'old'; see
old. Accordingly OE. weoruld, etc., lit. mean 'the
age of man'.
Derivatives: world-ish, adj., world-ling, п.,
world-ly, adj.

## worm
worm, n. — ME. werm, worm, wurm, fr. OE.
wyrm, wurm, 'serpent, dragon, worm*, rel. to
OS., OHG., MHG., G. wurm, OFris., Du.
worm, ON. ormr, Dan., Swed. orm, Goth.
waarms, 'serpent, worm', and cogn. with Gk.
ρόμος (Arcadius), £όμοξ (Hesychius). (for
•δρόμος, resp. *5ρόμοξ), 'woodworm', L.
vermis (for *wormis, *wrmis), 'worm', ORuss.
vermie (coll.) 'insects', OPruss. vormyan, urmi-
nan, 'red', lit. 'of the color of a worm', Lith.
vafmas, 'insect, gnat'. AH these words derive fr.
I.-E. base *wer-, 'to bend, turn, twist'. Cp.
Vermes and words there referred to. For
derivatives of *werg- and *wergn-, enlargements of
base *wer' see verge, 'to bend*, worry.
Derivatives: worm, v., worm-er, п., worm-lesst
adj., worm-y, adj.-, worm-i-ness, n.

## wormwood
wormwood, n. — ME. wermod, fr. OE. wermod,
rel. to OS. wermoda, MLG. wermot, wermode,
Du. wermoet, OHG. werimuota, wermuota,
wormuota, MHG. wermuote, wormuot, G.
Wermut. Cp. vermuth.

## worn
worn, pp. of wear, 'to carry on the body*. — ME.
worn, woren, fr. OE. geworen. See wear.

## worry
worry, tr. and intr. v. — ME. worien, fr. OE.
wyrgan, 'to choke, strangle', rel. to MDu. wor-
ghen, wurghen, Du. worgen, wurgen, OHG.
wurgen, MHG., G. wurgen, MHG. erwergen,
'to strangle', OS. wurgil, ON. virgill, 'rope*, fr.
I.-E. *wergh-, whence Gk. δρχατος (for* ^όρχα-
τος), 'a piece of land enclosed', έρχαταν (for
*^ερχαταν), 'to hedge in*, Lith. verziu, veHti,
'to bind tightly, compress*. For derivatives of
I.-E. *werg- see worm. For nasalized derivatives
of *werg- and *wergk- see wrangle, wVench,
wring, wrinkle.
Derivatives: worry, п., worri-able, adj., worri-ed,
adj., worri-ed-ly, adv., worri-ed-ness, п.,
worrier, п., worry-ing, adj., worry-ing-ly, adv.

## worse
worse, adj. — ME. werse, wurse, worse, fr. OE.
wyrsa, wiersa, rel. to OS. wirs, wirsa, ON. verri,
Dan. vserre, Swed. varre, OFris. wirra, werra,
OHG. wirslro, Goth, wairsiza, 'worse*. These
words are comparatives of a lost positive, which
was perh. rel. to OHG. werra, 'strife', fir-
werran, 'to confuse, perplex*. See war and cp.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:859 -->

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:859 COLUMN:1 -->
worst.
Derivatives: worse, adv. (q.v.), worse, п.,
worsen, tr. and intr. v.

## worse
worse, n. — ME., fir. OE. wyrse, subst. use of the
adj. wyrse, neut. of wyrsa. See worse, adj.

## worse
worse, adv. — ME. werse, wurse, worse, fr. OE.
wyrs, wiers, rel. to ON. verr, OHG. wirs, Goth.
wairs and to OE. wyrsa, 'worse' (adj.). See
worse, adj.

## worship
worship, n. — ME. wurikscipe, worschipe, fr. OE.
weordscipe, *dignity, honor', compounded of
weord, 'worthy', and scipe, 'shape, condition';
hence worship lit. means 'the condition of being
worthy'. See worth, adj., and -ship.
Derivatives: worships tr. and intr. v., worship-
able, adj., worship(p)-er, п., worship-ful, adj.,
worshipful-ly, adv., worshipful-ness, n.

## worst
worst, adj. — ME. werst, wurst, worst, fr. OE.
wyrrestat wyrsta,wiersta, contraction of wyrsesta,
superl. corresponding to the compar. wyrsa,
wiersa, 'worse*. Cp. OS. wirsisia, ON. verstr,
Dan. vserst, Swed. varst, OFris. wersta, OHG.
wirsisto, 'worst', and see worse, adj.
Derivatives: worst, adv. (q.v.), worst, n. and tr. v.

## worst
worst, adv. — ME. werst, worst, fr. OE. wyrst,
wierst, superl. corresponding to the compar.
wyrs, wiers. See worst, adj., and cp. worse, adv.

## worsted
worsted, п., a kirid of twisted woolen yarn. —
Named after Worsted (now spelled Worstead),
a town in Norfolk, England.

## wort
wort, п., a plant. — ME. wurt, wort, fr. OE. wyrt,
•plant, herb, root*, rel. to OS. wurt, ΟΝ., Dan.
urt, Swed. ort, OHG. wurz, 'plant, herb', MHG.
wurz, 'plant, herb, root', G. Wurz, Goth, waurts,
ON. rdt, *root\ and cogn. with Gk. ρίζα, Lesb.
βρ£σδα, 'root', £άδαμνος, 'branch*, L. radix,
'root'. See radix and cp. rhizo-. Cp. also root
and the second element in mangelwiirzel.

## wort
wort, п., infusion of malt before fermentation. —
ME. wurte, fr. OE. wyrt, rel. to OS. wurtia, ON.
vlrtr, Du. wort, OHG. wirz, MHG., G. wurze,
G. Bierwurze, 'wort', and to OE. wyrt, 'root,
plant, herb'. See prec word.

## worth
worth, adj. — ME. wurthe, fr. OE. weord,
word, 'worthy', rel. to OS., OFris. werth, ON.
verdr, Dan. vakrd, Swed. vard, Du. waard, OHG.
werd, MHG., G. wert, Goth, wafrps, 'worth,
worthy', and to OE. wierde, of s.m., and prob.
cogn. with Avestic avar ta-, 'a valuable object',
W. gwerth, 'price'. OSIav. vredu, OPruss. werts
and Lith. ve7tas, 'worth', areTeut. loan words.
Cp. worth, п., worthy, the first element in
worship and the second element in stalwart.

## worth
worth, п., value. — ME. wroth, fr. OE. weord,
wurd, wyrd, 'worth, price, redemption, ransom',
rel. to OS. werth, ON. verd, OFris. werd, wert,
Du. waarde, OHG. werd, MHG., G. wert,
'worth, value*, Goth, wairp, 'price, value'.
These words are prop, subs tan ti ν a lions of the
adjectives: OE. weord, resp. its equivalents, in
the other Teut. languages. See worth, adj.
Derivatives: worth-less, adj., worth-less-lyt adv.,
worth-less-ness, n.

## worth
worth, intr. v., to come to be, become {archaic),
— ME. worthen, fr. OE. weordan, 'to become',
rel. to OS., ODu. werthan, ON. verda, OFris.
wertha, OHG. werdan, MHG.,G. werden, Goth.
wairpan, 'to become'. The orig. meaning of
these words was 'to turn' (ср. Е. to turn in the
sense *to become*). They derive fr. I.-E. base
mwert-, 4o turn, twist', whence also L. vertere, 'to
turn'. See version and cp. words there referred to.

## worthy
worthy, adj. — ME. worthi, wurthi, fr. worth, n.
See worth, п., and -y (representing OE. -ig).
Derivatives: worthy, п., worth-i-ly, adv.,
worthiness, n.

## wot
wot, v., 1 know; he knows (archaic). — ME. wot,
1st and 3rd person sing. pres. of witen, 'to
know*. See wit, v.

## would
would, v., past tense of will. — ME. wolde, wulde,
fr, OE. wolde, past tense of willan. See will, v.
wound* n. — ME. wunde, wound, fr. OE. wund,
rel. to OS. wunda, ON. und, Du. wond, wonde,
OFris. wunde, OHG. wunta, MHG., G. wunde,
'wound', OE., OS. wund, OHG., MHG. wunt,
G. wund, Goth, wunds, 'wounded'. The ult.
origin of these words is uncertain. Cp. zounds.
Derivatives: wound-yx adj., wound-i-ly, adv.,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:859 COLUMN:2 -->
wound-less, adj.

## wound
wound, tr. v. — ME. wunden, wounden, fr. OE.
wundian, fr. wund, 'wound'. See wound, n.
Derivatives: wound-ed, adj. and п., wound-ed-ly,
adv.

## woimdless
woimdless, adj. — Coined by the English poet
Edmund Spenser (cca. 1552-99) fr. wound, п.,
and surf. -less.

## wourali
wourali, n. — See woorali.

## woven
woven, pp. — ME. woven, wooven, formed fr.
weave on the analogy of stolen (fr. steal).

## wow
wow, п., a great success (U.S. Slang). — Of
imitative origin.

## wrack
wrack, also rack, п., ruin, destruction {archaic).
— ME., fr. OE. wrsec, 'misery, punishment', rel.
to wrecan, 'to drive, push, expel*. See wreak and
cp. next word.

## wrack
wrack, п., 1) a wrecked ship; 2) seaweed, marine
vegetation cast up on the shore. — ME. wrak,
'a wrecked ship', fr. OE. wrsec, 'misery,
punishment', lit. 'something cast ashore'. Cp- Du.
wrak, 'a wreck'. E. wrack is prop, a var. of wreck
(q.v.) Cp. varec.
Derivative: wrack, tr. v., wrack-er, n.

## wraith
wraith, п., specter, apparition. — Of uncertain,
possibly Celtic, origin. Cp. Gael, and Ir. arrach,
'specter, apparition*.

## wrangle
wrangle, intr. v., to dispute angrily; tr. v., to argne
dispute. — ME. wranglen, rel. to LG. wrangen,
'to struggle', wrangeln, 'to wrangle*, and in
gradational relationship to wring (q.v.) For the
ending see freq. surf, -le.
Derivatives: wrangle, п., wrangl-er, п.,
wrangler-ship, n.

## wrap
wrap, tr. and intr. v. — ME. wrappen, of
uncertain origin.
Derivatives: wrap, п., wrapp-age, п., wrapp-er,
n. and tr. v., wrapp-ing.

## wrasse
wrasse, п., a European seafish. — Co. wrach,
gwrach, gwragh, rel. to W. gwrachen, 'wrasse*.

## wrath
wrath, n. — ME. wrathe, wraththe, fr. OE. wrxp-
po, wrxppu, *anger\ fr. wrap, 'angry*, orig.
'crooked, twisted', rel. to OHG. reid, 'twisted',
ON. reidr, 'angry', ON. rida, OE, wridan, 'to
twist, writhe'. See writhe and cp. wroth. Cp. also
wreath.
Derivatives: wrath, adj., wrath-ful, adj., wrath-
ful-ly, adv., wrath-ful-ness, п., wrath-y, adj.,
wrath-i-ly, adv.

## wreak
wreak, tr. v., to inflict. — ME. wreken, fir. OE.
wrecan, 'to drive, push, expel, avenge', rel. to
OS. wrekan, ON. reka, 'to drive, push, compel,
pursue, throw*, OFris. wreka, MLG., MDu.,
Du. wreken, of s.m., OHG. rehhan (fir. earlier
* wrehhan), MHG. rechen, G. rachen, 'to avenge*,
Goth, wrikan, 'to persecute*, fr. I.-E. base
*wreg-, *wrg-, 'to drive, push', whence also L.
urgere, 'to press, drive, urge*, and prob. also
Gk. εϊργειν(ίθΓ*έ^έργειν), 'to constrain'. Cp.
wreck, wretch, urge. Cp. the collateral I.-E. base
*werg-, whence Lith. vafgas, 'distress', vafgti,
'to suffer distress', OPruss. wargan, 'distress',
Lith. vergas, Lett, vergs, slave', OSIav. vragu,
*enemy*.
Derivatives: wreak-ful, wreak-less, adjs.

## wreath
wreath, п., a garland. — ME. wrethe, f/. OE.
wrxp, 'band, bandage1, rel. to wridan, 'to twist,
writhe'. See writhe and cp. wreathe. Cp. also
wrath, wroth.
Derivative: wreath-у, adj.

## wreathe
wreathe, tr. and intr. v. — Partly fr. ME. wrethen,
a var. of writhen, pp. of writhen, 'to twist,
writhe' (see writhe); partly back formation fr.
wreath.
Derivatives: wreath-ed, adj., wreath-er, п.,
wreath-ing, n.

## wrenthen
wrenthen, adj. — ME. wrethen, a var. of writhen,
pp. of writhen. See prec. word.

## wreck
wreck, п., 1) something cast όπ the land by the
sea (esp. after a shipwreck); 2) destruction of a
ship, shipwreck; 3) destruction, ruirf. — ME.
wrek, fr. AF. wrec, wrech, which is of Scand.
origin. The original meaning is 'that which is
driven'; cp. ON. reka (for * wreka), 'to drive',
rek (for *wrek), 'wreckage', Icel. rek, reki,
'anything driven ashore'; rel. to OE. wrsec,
'exile, misery', wrecan, 'to drive, expel'. F.
varech, 'wrack, seaweed', is an English loan

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:859 COLUMN:3 -->
word (see varec). See wreak and cp. wrack. Cp.
also rack, 'wreckage*, rack, 'clouds driven
before the wind', wretch.
Derivatives: wreck, tr. and intr. v., wreck-age,
п., wreck-ed, adj. wreck-er, п., wreck-ing, n. and
adj.

## wren
wren, п., a small singing bird. — ME. wrenne, fr.
OE. wrsenna, wrenna, rel. to Icel. rindill, OHG.
wrendo, wrendilo, 'wren*.
Derivative: wren-let, п., a little wren.

## wrench
wrench, п., a sharp twist. — ME. wrench, 'guile,
deceit', fr. OE. wrenc, 'a twisting; artifice, trick*,
rel. to MHG. ranc, 'a sudden twisting*, G.
Rank, 'intrigue, trick', OHG. renken, MHG., G.
renken, 'to twist, wrench*, MLG. wrank, 'to
wring', OE. wrincle, 'wrinkle', wringan, 'to
twist'; fr. I.-E. *wreng-, whence also 01. vrnakti,
'turns, twists', Lith. rengtis, 'to grow crooked,
to writhe*, rangfti, 'to crook, curve*. I.-E.
*wreng- is a nasalized form of *werg-, 'to bend,
turn, twist'. See worry and cp. verge, 'to bend',
wrangle, wring, wrinkle, wrong. I.-E. *werg- is
an enlargement of base *wer-, 'to bend, turn,
twist'. See version,

## wrench
wrench, intr. and tr. v. — ME. wrenchen, fr. OE.
wrencan, 'to twist, turn, be deceitful', rel, to
wrenc, 'a twisting; artifice, trick'. See wrench, n.
Derivatives: wrench-ed, adj., wrench-er, n.

## wrest
wrest, tr. v. — ME. wresten, wrasten, fr. OE.
wrxstan, 'to turn, twist, wrest', rel. to ON.
reista, 'to bend, twist', Dan. vriste, of s.m., fr.
I.-E. base *wrei-, 'to turn, twist'. See writhe and
cp. next word.
Derivatives: wrest, п., wrest-er, п., wrest-ing, п.,
wrest-ing-ly, adv.

## wrestie
wrestie, intr. and tr. v. — ME. wrestlen, wrastlen,
fr. OE. wrxstlian, freq. of wrxstan. See prec.
word and freq. suff. -le. Cp. MLG., MDu., Du.
worstelen, 'to wrestle'.
Derivatives: wrestle, п., wrestl-er, п., wrestl-ing,
n.

## wretch
wretch, п., a miserable person. — ME. wrecche,
fr. OE. wraecca, wrecca, 'stranger, exile, wretch',
rel. to OS. wrekkio, *a banished person, exile',
OHG. reckeo, recko, of s.m., MHG., G. recke,
'renowned warrior, hero*, fr. Teut. base *wrak-
jan, a derivative of base * wrehhan, whence also
OS. wrekan, 'to requite, punish', OE. wrecan,
'to drive, push, expel, avenge'. See wreak and
cp. garcon.

## wretched
wretched, adj., ]) deeply afflicted; 2) very
miserable. — ME. wrecched, fr. wrecche, 'wretch*.
See prec. word and 1st -ed.
Derivatives: wretched-ly, adv., wretched-ness, n.

## wretchiess
wretchiess, adj., reckless (obsol.) — Erroneous
spelling of reckless, the initial w being due to a
confusion with wretch.
Derivatives: wretchless-ly, adv., wretchless-ness,
n.

## wriggle
wriggle, intr. and tr. v., to move to and fro by
twisting. — ME. wrigglen, fr. MLG. wriggeln,
"to wriggle, which is rel. to Du. wriggelen, of
s.m., dial Norw. vrigla, rigla, 'to totter', and
to OE. wrigian, 'to turn, incline, go forward*.
See wry.
Derivatives: wriggle, п., wriggl-er, п., wriggl-
ing-ly, adv., wriggl-y, adj.

## wright
wright, п., one who works in wood (now chiefly
in compounds). — ME. wrighte, wright, fr. OE.
wyrhta, wryhta, 'worker, maker5, fr. wyrcan, 'to

## wring
wring, tr. v., to twist, squeeze. — ME. wringen,
fr. OE. wringen, 'to wring, press out', rel. to
OS. wringan, OFris. wringa, MDu. wringhen,
Du. wringen, 'to wring*, OHG. ringan (fr. earlier
mwringan), *to move to and fro, to twist; to
strain, struggle, wrestle' (whence G. ringen, 'to
wrestle'). These words derive fr. Teut. *wreng-,
nasalization of I.-E. *werg-, 'to bend, turn,
twist'. See worry and cp. words there referred to.
Derivatives: wring, п., wring-er, n.

## wrinkle
wrinkle, п., a small ridge on a surface. — ME,
wrinkel, fr. OE. wrincle, a dimin. formed fr.
wrencan, 'to twist, turn'. See wrench and cp.
wring. Cp. also frounce and ruck, 'crease'.
Derivatives: wrinkle, tr. and intr. v., to form
wrinkles, wrinkl-ed, adj., wrinkl-y, adj.

## wrist
wrist, n. — ME. wrist, wirst, fr. OE. wrist, rel. to

ON. rist, Swed. vrist, 'instep', OFris. wrist,
wirst, MLG., MDu. wrist, MHG. rist(e), G.
Rist, 'back of the hand; instep'; prop, meaning
'the turning joint', and rel. to OE. wrxstan, 'to
